en: The *Kāśikā-vivaraṇa-pañjikā*, also known by the alternative title *Nyāsa*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who was a disciple of the illustrious Bodhisattva.
The Kāśikā Commentary: An Exposition on the Four Ancillary Subjects.
Victorious forever are those virtuous ones by whom [perfection] has been attained in every way.
It is a great collection of virtues and a cleansing of faults.
Just as this *Kāśikā* was composed by taking its essence from other [works], so too is this *Pañjikā* being made for it according to my ability. (2)

Regarding the verse beginning with "ṭhvṛtau" and so forth: now, for what purpose is this verse presented at the commencement of the *Kāśikā*? It is for the sake of avoiding prolixity (*agaurava*) in that work and for the sake of demonstrating its weightiness (*gaurava*). For if this were not present here, [the same would apply] previously in other [treatises].

If the *vṛtti*s had been composed first, those who suspect the fault of tautology—that this [work] was composed afterwards—would feel a lack of respect for it, rather than respect. But since this is the case, that fault does not arise; for by this [work], that specific excellence of hers is declared.

It is the cause for the correct derivation of all words without exception; when it exists, there is no ground for the fault of redundancy, nor does it cause a lack of respect, but rather reverence arises.
Furthermore, that fault of redundancy—when it is absent, there is no lack of respect; what [then]...?

In that case? Due to the aforementioned distinction, there is indeed greater weight [to the former]. And in that regard, the *vṛtti* is a commentary on the sūtras composed by Pāṇini, written by Cūlli, Bhaṭṭi, Nallūr, and others; the *bhāṣya* is [a commentary] on those composed by Kātyāyana.
This is an exposition of sentences composed by Patañjali. The word "tathā" (likewise) is used in the sense of conjunction;

that is to say, it refers to the roots, nouns, suffixes, and so forth. Alternatively, it signifies similarity: just as in the *Vṛtti* and other works a compendium of the essence of the scattered system is being made, so too [is this work].
"In the *dhātupārāyaṇa*, *nāmapārāyaṇa*, and so forth" means as follows:
*dhātavaḥ* are the verbal roots beginning with *bhū*; *nāmāni* are the nominal stems (*prātipadika*). They reach the further limit, the ultimate conclusion, of these.

The word *pārāyaṇa* is connected to each of those two treatises—namely, the *dhātupārāyaṇa* and the *nāmapārāyaṇa*. The term "those which have these at their beginning" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. By the word "beginning," the inclusion of the *śikṣā* and other such works is intended.

"Of that which is scattered" means of that which is dispersed or extended. "Of the *tantra*" means of the grammatical treatise (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*); for that is like a *tantra* (loom/warp), as it consists of threads (*tanta*) spread out in length.
They are called "systems" (*tantra*). Just as that [loom] is the supporter of many transverse threads, so too is this [grammar] the supporter of many objects to be characterized;
this is its similarity to a system. Alternatively, it is a "system" (*tantra*) because by means of it words are woven (*tantryante*) and explained (*vyutpādyante*).

Regarding the etymology (*vyākaraṇa*): since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *tan* (DhP 1978), which means "to support a family," is used here in the sense of "derivation. Alternatively, *tantra* means "established doctrine" (*siddhānta*), as Amarasimha states: "The word *tantra* is used for the primary [subject] and for established doctrine" (3.3.185).

Regarding the term "Sārasaṃgrahaḥ": this word *sāra* is neuter in gender when it signifies that which does not deviate from what is right (*nyāyādanapeta*). Accordingly, he will state among the *ardharca* group [of words] that "the word *sāra* is masculine in the sense of excellence (*utkarṣa*), and neuter when it signifies that which does not deviate from what is right" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.31).

Thus: it is called a *saṃgraha* because by means of it the *lakṣya* (the subject to be defined) and the *lakṣaṇa* (the definition) are correctly (*samyak*) or entirely (*samasta*) grasped (*gṛhyate*). The suffix *ap* is applied in the sense of an instrument according to Pāṇini 3.3.58, *grahavṛdṛniścigamaśca*. It is both an essence (*sāra*) and a compendium (*saṃgraha*), hence it is the *Sārasaṃgraha*. Furthermore, this very work is a specific type of commentary (*vṛtti*) known as the *Kāśikā*.

Here, by the word "essence" (sāra), freedom from defects is indicated. For it is not possible for a scripture that possesses defects to be free from deviation from logic (nyāya), since such a scripture would be understood [as being flawed] by means of logic. This is the summary.

It is also made known by a word that possesses excellence; for otherwise, it would not be possible to correctly encompass all the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the defined (*lakṣya*) by means of this [word].
What, then, are the excellences (*guṇa*) in this context? They are: the quality of having desirable additions (*iṣṭopasaṃkhyānavattva*), and the quality of being a pure enumeration (*śuddhagaṇatva*).

It possesses the quality of having the meaning of the sūtras explained and made manifest, as well as the quality of establishing grammatical forms through etymological analysis. And so he will state at the end of the treatise:
"The pure collection [of sūtras], which includes desired supplementary additions, has its hidden meanings of the sūtras fully revealed."
"This work, named the *Kāśikā*, is an exposition [of the rules] whose forms have been fully analyzed.

Alternatively, this word "compendium" (*saṃgraha*) is derived in the sense of an action (*bhāvasādhana*): it is a "gathering" (*saṃgrahaṇa*), a "compilation" (*saṃkṣepa*), meaning the collecting together and establishing in one place the system of grammar that was scattered across various treatises.

To this extent, the word *sāra* (essence) signifies the principal [matter]. That extent of textual composition by which the fullness of the etymological derivation of the words is achieved is the *sāra*. A compendium (*saṃgraha*) of that essence is a *sārasaṃgraha*; its composition is for the purpose of easy comprehension. For when [the material] is established in one place...
It is easy to grasp that which is concentrated, but difficult to grasp that which is scattered. The grasping of the essence is for the purpose of discarding the peripheral trappings;
for that [essence] is what is beneficial to it.
The subordinate is that which is not primary; the other, however, is the principal because it is that which is assisted by the former.
"Now" (*atha*), and so forth: the word *atha* signifies "commencement" (*adhikāra*); commencement means introduction, [in this case] the instruction on words (*śabdānuśāsana*).

The word *atha* (now/then) indicates this meaning: "the treatise is being introduced. For if only "instruction on words" (*śabdānuśāsanam*) were stated, a doubt might arise: "Is the instruction on words being commenced, or is it being recited?"

Is it heard? When the word *atha* is employed, however, this meaning—that [the subject] is being introduced by way of excluding other topics—is determined. "Instruction" (*anuśāsanam*) means that by means of this, words are instructed, refined, and etymologically explained. It is the instruction of words.

*Śabdānuśāsanam*. On this point, some raise an objection: "By the rule *ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.66), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is applied here; consequently, by the rule *karmaṇi ca* (Pāṇini 2.2.14), there ought to be a prohibition of compounding."

This is incorrect; for where there is the possibility of both [the cow and the milker], it is said that "the milking is done by one untrained and not a cowherd. Thus, the milking of cows that are difficult to milk by one who is untrained and not a cowherd is indeed a matter of wonder here.
The word "extraordinary" (*āścarya*) is intended for the purpose of instruction; thus, by implication, the inclusion of both [the teacher and the student] is established, as it cannot be otherwise.
However, in the expression "instruction in words" (*śabdānuśāsana*),...

This is the instruction regarding words, not regarding meanings— since this much alone was intended to be expressed— it is possible to convey this even without mentioning the teacher by way of his agency.
Since it is possible [to understand the agent otherwise], the mention of the teacher (*ācārya*) is superfluous.

Therefore, there is no mention here of either the agent or the object that would be obtained through their inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*). Consequently, even the "attainment of both" does not exist at all. And since this is not the case...
In that case, the genitive is not applied by the rule *ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.66); rather, by which [rule] then? By the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65).
And from that, [the word] *iṣma-pra-*...
The compound will be formed like *vraścana*. Or rather, this genitive case is simply one characterized as "residual" (*śeṣa*); thus, this is not a point for objection.

Furthermore, since this is called "Grammar" (*vyākaraṇa*) for the purpose of explaining the connection [of words], and its name is "Instruction in Words" (*śabdānuśāsana*), it is by that very [definition]...
Since the purpose has already been indicated, it need not be explicitly stated. For when words are being taught, one's engagement occurs with respect to that [purpose];
and whatever one engages in for the sake of something, that becomes the purpose of that [engagement]. This is what is meant:
"The instruction of words is its purpose. And this is the direct purpose, while the protection of the Vedas and so forth are the indirect purposes.
The purposes are to be understood from the commentary. As for the relationship, it is characterized by the state of being the goal and the means:
the relationship between the goal, which is the instruction of words, and the means, which is grammar—that is the purpose.
Thus it is included.

[The question is: "Of which words? But how can there be a reference by means of the word *kim* to those words that have become subordinate (*guṇībhūta*) within the grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*)?

Is there not a subsequent reflective cognition (*pratyavamarśa*)? This is not a fault; for it is observed that even when a subordinate element is included within a principal one, it can be mentally separated and referred to by means of the word "whose" (*kiṃ*), as in: "This is the king's man; whose [man]?"
Regarding the word "of the King" (*rājñaḥ*): what, then, is the intention of the questioner here? He thinks as follows:

in the expression "instruction in words" (*śabdānuśāsana*), the word *śabda* is a general term. And a general term, when devoid of context and the like, does not [necessarily] refer to a specific [instance].

[One] is capable of using [them], and since there are many other sounds as well, such as the roar of the ocean and so forth, does it not follow that their derivation should also be undertaken? However, here grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is the subject at hand, and it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the Vedas; and an auxiliary is something that provides assistance. And thus—

That [grammar] becomes beneficial to the Veda if by it alone the Vedic words are refined, and the worldly words are made subservient to that [Veda]. The subservience of the worldly words to the Veda, however, consists in their expressing its meaning; therefore, within the scope of this instruction of words, only those [words] distinguished [as Vedic] are treated here.
Words are intended to be derived [by grammar], but not even the roar of the ocean and the like.

Thinking that if such sounds were also derived, grammar would lose its status as an auxiliary to the Vedas (*vedāṅga*), he says, "of worldly [words]," and so forth. "Worldly" (*laukika*) means those known in the world (*loke viditā*).
In this context, while the term *vidita* ("known") continues to apply, the suffix *ṭhañ* is added by the rule *lokasarvalokāṭṭhañ* (Pāṇini 5.1.44).

Alternatively, *laukika* means "pertaining to the world" (*loke bhavā laukikāḥ*), where the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied according to the group beginning with *adhyātma* (Vārttika 456). The same applies to *vaidika*. [The distinction is that] those of the Veda [are superior] to those of the world.
The separate mention [of Vasiṣṭha] is for the purpose of manifesting his preeminence. For example: "The Brāhmaṇas have arrived;

Vasiṣṭha has also arrived. Here, although Vasiṣṭha’s arrival is already established by virtue of his being a Brāhmaṇa, he is mentioned separately for the purpose of manifesting his preeminence. And this manifestation of preeminence is...
This is for the sake of the Vaidikas’ effort to eliminate corruption;
for it is observed that when their [words] are corrupted in a sacrificial rite, there is a great transgression—as in the case of "helayo helayaḥ.
Or else, those who...

The words of common speech are the causes for worldly conduct; since their status as worldly is well-established by that very fact, Vedic words are mentioned separately. Among those, the worldly ones have no fixed sequence of phonemes, such as *gauḥ*, *aśvaḥ*, *puruṣaḥ*, *hastī*, and so forth.
The Vedic [mantras], however, possess a fixed sequence, such as "ṭhśanno devīrabhiṣṭaye" (Ṛgveda 10.9.4) and others.
For in this grammatical exposition, the recitation of each individual word (*pratipadapāṭha*) must be accepted. Of that [recitation] as well, there are three types:

[The distinction arises] through the difference between the teaching of words, the teaching of non-words, and the teaching of both; and because words are infinite, that [teaching] is impossible in every respect.
For it is heard thus: "Bṛha..."
"Śaunaka taught the complete recitation (*pārāyaṇa*) of the hymns arranged according to the *pratipad* method to Indra for a thousand divine years,
yet he did not reach the end. Thus, even with such a speaker, such a student, and such a duration of study, there was no reaching of the end.

How could there be such instruction for him now, when his progeny is short-lived? And thinking that there is no other means [to achieve this], he says: "How? and so forth. How is there instruction? Not by anyone.

The meaning is that grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is the instruction (*anuśāsana*) of words by way of their various forms. Alternatively, here the word *anuśāsana* functions as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*). Instruction (*anuśāsti*) is *anuśāsana*; it is refinement (*saṃskāra*), insofar as no refinement of words is possible in any other way.
To demonstrate another means by which one may comprehend vast masses of linguistic expression with only slight effort, he says:
"by the conceptualization of the division into base (*prakṛti*) and so forth," and so on.
That which is produced prior to the suffix (*pratyaya*) is the base (*prakṛti*); those things of which the base is the first are "base and so forth" (*prakṛtyādayaḥ*).
The word "etcetera" (ādi) is for the purpose of including [grammatical] suffixes and so forth.

Their "distinction" (vibhāga) is their non-confused nature. The "conceptualization" (kalpanā) of that is the mental construction by means of a conceptualizing intellect (parikalpikayā buddhyā). The "instruction of words" (anuśāsana) is by means of that conceptualization.

Or, it is the instruction of grammar (*vyākaraṇānuśiṣṭi*). Here, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of cause (*hetau*); for without that [grammar], there is no instruction of grammar, nor can the instruction of words be performed without it. By the phrase "by way of conceptualization" (*parikalpanayā*), this...

He establishes this: the division into *prakṛti*, suffixes, and so forth is merely conceptual (*kalpanāmātra*); the ultimate reality (*paramārthavastu*) is the aggregate (*samudāya*) itself, in which the division into *prakṛti*, suffixes, and so forth has subsided, as that which denotes some meaning.

Regarding the phrase "by a definition possessing both generality and particularity," this instrumental case ending (*tṛtīyā*) expresses the instrument (*karaṇa*). Generality (*sāmānya*) and particularity (*viśeṣa*) together are "generality-and-particularity" (*sāmānyaviśeṣau*);
that definition in which these two reside is a "definition possessing generality and particularity" (*sāmānyaviśeṣavat lakṣaṇam*).

In that regard, a rule characterized by generality (*sāmānyavat*) is like [the rule] *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1). For in that case, the specific conditions are "after a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) and "without a prefix" (*anupasarge*). There, by means of a rule possessing generality, the division into base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*) is established through conceptual construction (*parikalpanā*), as in *kumbhakāraḥ* ("pot-maker") and *kāṇḍalāvaḥ* ("reed-cutter").

One encounters a great flood of such sounds as "śaralāva" and so forth; however, there are specific [names] such as "pārṣṇitraḥ," "godaḥ," and "kambaladaḥ. It should be understood that the same applies elsewhere as well.
The Section on Withdrawal (*Pratyāhāra-prakaraṇa*). "Now," and so forth. He thinks as follows: the instruction of words (*śabdānuśāsana*) has been undertaken; therein, those words which are taught—

The intended meaning of the question is: "Instruction is appropriate for that [phoneme] alone, and no refinement (*saṃskāra*) of any word is effected by instruction regarding these [phonemes]; therefore, this is a statement of something irrelevant. [The word] "of the phonemes" (*varṇānām*) refers to the phonemes.
The vowels beginning with *a* and so forth; the initial pronunciation of these is "instruction" (*upadeśa*). Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of *pratyāhāra*":

*pratyāhāra* refers to the traditional collection of phonemes (*akṣarasamāmnāya*) characterized by a specific sequence and specific *anubandhas*, such as *aiuṇ* (Māheśvara Sūtra 1), wherein [the phonemes] are brought together (*pratyāhriyante*).

[The term *saṃkṣepa*] is used in the sense that "the phonemes (*varṇāḥ*) are condensed within this. The purpose of the instruction of the phonemes is so that [the grammarian] may possess such [a concise means]. To whom does this belong? Since that too is not applicable to the subject at hand, the same fault remains; therefore, he says: "*Pratyāhāraḥ*..."
"By way of brevity," and so forth. Brevity (*lāghava*) is the state of being brief; that, moreover, is a small amount of effort.

For an object that is accomplished with little effort is called "brief" due to its connection with minimal exertion. By means of that brevity, [the rule] regarding the elision of *ḍha* in the treatise...

The meaning is that [the mention of *pratyāhāra*] is for the purpose of the application and accomplishment of rules such as "pūrvasya dīrgho’ṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.111). For when there is a *pratyāhāra*, the rule "ādirantyena sahetā" (Pāṇini 1.1.71) operates.
And when that [term *aṇ*] is employed, designations such as "aṇ" and so forth for the vowels beginning with *a* are established. Consequently,
wherever the inclusion of the vowels beginning with *a* is intended,
they are all indicated by that very designation, "aṇ," and so forth, even though they are many.

The formulation of the treatise is achieved with brevity. If that [the concept of a "final element"] did not exist, the application of rules such as "ṭha, etc., together with the final element" would not occur, because of the absence of a beginning and an end. For indeed, in the absence of a specific arrangement [of elements], [such a rule cannot function].
Those two would not arise,
and in the absence of their occurrence, the aforementioned designations would not exist; therefore, in whichever sūtra [the term] "a" occurs—

If it were intended that as many [elements] as *kāra* and so forth are to be included, they would have to be specified by their own forms; thus, the composition of the treatise would not proceed with brevity. Therefore, for the sake of accomplishing the subject matter at hand with minimal effort—
Therefore, there is no occasion for the aforementioned fault.
[Pāṇini 1.1.7] Now, why is it that here the substitution of *guṇa* and so forth— which is an operation concerning vowels (*ac*)— does not take place?

This is due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) according to the rule *plutapragṛhyā aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.125). Their status as *pragṛhya* is established by the provision of the *pragṛhya* designation in the rule *nipāta ekājanāṅ* (1.1.14). Their status as a *nipāta* (particle), however, results from their inclusion among the *ca-ādi* group [of particles]. Precisely because of this status as a *nipāta*, even when [the suffix] *ṭāp* has been produced [after a meaningful base],...
The hearing of a case-ending does not occur here. Since it lacks meaning, the derivation of a case-ending would be impossible;

therefore, one should understand that the designation of *prātipadika* is to be extended even to a meaningless particle (*nipāta*) by means of an additional rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*). "In this sequence" [is said].

By this sequence. But what is the reason that this very order is adopted and not another? To this it is said: here, by the mention of *aṇ*, the inclusion of all three—*a*, *i*, and *u*—is intended; however, in the case of the mention of *iṇ*, the inclusion of *a* is not intended, and in the case of the mention of *uṇ*...

Furthermore, this applies to both *akāra* and *kāra*. Since this would not be accomplished by resorting to a different sequence, this very sequence is adopted. And here, because of the supplementary rule (upasaṃkhyāna) stating that the suffix *kāra* is added after a phoneme (*varṇāt kāraḥ*, Vārttika 320), [the form *akāra* is established].

Someone might have the doubt that these [sounds] are not actually phonemes (*varṇa*), but rather other things that merely imitate their shadow—namely, certain parts of the vowels *ai*, *au*, and *r* and *l*; therefore, to refute that, he says "the phonemes" (*varṇān*). As for the suffix *-kāra*, however...

This is added as a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) to the sūtra *rogākhyāyāṃ ṇvul bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.108). The point is that, because of this, even though [the letters] *ṣa*, *ba*, *hu*, *la*, *va*, *na*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *l*, and *s* possess the nature of being phonemes (*varṇatva*), the suffix does not apply. This is because the letter *ṇ* occupies an intermediate position, falling between the preceding and following phonemes.

It is not final; therefore, it should not receive the designation *it*. Even if, somehow, it were final, nevertheless, according to the principle to be stated later, because it is subordinate (*apradhāna*), just as in that case no operation pertaining to a vowel (*ackārya*) applies to it.

Likewise, for one who might have the delusion that even the notion (*saṃjñā*) does not exist, it is said "it has gone" (*ita*) and "gone away" (*anta*). Even though the preceding and succeeding phonemes—
Although this [final letter] is of a middle status in relation to that [preceding vowel], it nevertheless possesses the quality of being final (antyatva) in relation to the preceding phonemes.

And since that [quality of being final] exists, the designation *it* must apply even to what is not primary, by virtue of the force of the instruction (*upadeśa*); otherwise, [the rule would be meaningless].

For otherwise, that instruction would be useless; rather, its purpose is so that technical designations such as *aṇ* and the like may occur by means of the rule "The first [element] together with the last [indicates the class] to which it belongs" (Pāṇini 1.1.71).

The instruction (*upadeśa*) of the indicatory letters (*anubandha*), such as *ṇ* and others, is for that purpose; the intention is that if the designation *it* were not applied, that [instruction] would not take place. Regarding the phrase "of that" (*tasya*) and so forth: the instrumental case in "by one" (*ekena*) is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārtha*), while "of that" (*tasya*) refers to the base.

Thus, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*). For the purpose of making that *ṇakāra* known as a technical term (*saṃjñin*) within the specific rule-utterances (*pradeśavākya*), it occurs in combination with only one vowel, the letter *a*.
Indeed, for the phonemes beginning with *a*, the designation (*saṃjñā*) consists only of the letter *a* joined with [the *ṇakāra*], neither alone nor otherwise.
It is accompanied by other phonemes. Therefore, for the sake of communication, it is employed together with that [other phoneme], neither alone nor even when accompanied by other phonemes.
Others, however, say: "of it" (*tasya*) is a genitive in the sense of the agent (*kartari*); and "by one" (*ekena*) is used in connection with the sense of accompaniment (*sahayoge*).
The third [interpretation]:
by this, the meaning is that the letter *ṇa*, accompanied by the initial letter, becomes the indicator (*grāhaka*) of the other letters occurring in between as well as of the initial letter itself.

Others say: because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *gṛhṇāti* here functions in the sense of "pronouncing," as in the rule *grahaṇavatā prātipadikena* (Pāṇini 1.1.72). Therefore, the meaning is this:
it occurs together with one [of the two] at the time of pronunciation. Now...
How is it determined that this [ṣīdhvam] is not included by the vowel *i* in the rule *ṭhiṇaḥ ṣīdhvam* (8.3.78)?
[It is determined] because [the *i* in 8.3.78] is formed by the coalescence (*saṃsarga*) of the *i* and *u* vowels in the rule *ṭhati śnudhātubhruvāṃ yvoḥ* (6.4.77).
Because of the specific mention [in the rule]. If this were to be included by the vowel *ī*,
then for the sake of brevity, he would have simply mentioned "ṭhiṇ" (ṭh + iṇ), having combined them as "ṭhyvoḥ."
In the formulation [of the rule], there would be three and a half morae (mātrā) in the case of the mention "iṇ," whereas in the formulation "iṇi" there are only three;

since the desired result is established by the lighter formulation, the fact that he undertakes the more laborious effort indicates that this letter ṇ is not included within the term "i. In that case, here [in the following example]...

Why does the inclusion [of the root *sādh*] not occur by means of the letter *u* in the rule *kṛvāpājimisvadisādhyaśūbhya uṇ* (Uṇādisūtra 1.86)? Because there is nothing else to be grasped other than the letter *u*, and that [letter *u*] is indicated precisely in its own form.

"Ṭha, the short *a*-vowel," and so forth. "Prayoga" refers to that which is employed, such as a verbal root and the like. When the short *a*-vowel occurs in such an employment, it is "closed" (*saṃvṛta*). It is called "closed" because of its association with the quality of being closed, just as a cloth is called "white" because of its association with the quality of whiteness.

"But the long and protracted [vowels] possess openness (*vivṛtatva*). This means they possess the quality of openness. Thus say the authors of the *Śikṣā*: "The vowels have open articulation (*vivṛtakaraṇa*); among them, *e* and *o* are more open (*vivṛtatara*), and even more so than those two..."

"From these two, *ai* and *āṬ*, as well as from *ā*, the vowel *a* [is produced]; [and] the closed (*saṃvṛta*) vowel *a*. Regarding the phrase "of those," etc.: the purpose here in this treatise is so that the technical term *savarṇa* (homogeneous) may apply to those short vowels and the rest, according to the rule "That which has the same place of articulation and effort is *savarṇa*" (Pāṇini 1.1.9).

The short vowel *a* is accepted as having the quality of being "open" (*vivṛta*). Otherwise, because the effort (*prayatna*) would be different, there would be no homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*); consequently, in forms such as *daṇḍāḍhakam*, the rule "a long vowel replaces [the preceding and following vowels] when followed by a homogeneous vowel" (*ṭhakaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*, Pāṇini 6.1.101) would not apply.

There would be no long vowel [resulting from the combination]. But surely, even though the status of being "open" (*vivṛtatva*) is asserted, the long vowel would still result for *a* and *ā* when combined with a short or prolated vowel under the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*, because the prolated vowel is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when that operation is to be performed? This is not a fault; for it is stated: "The prolated vowel is established (*siddha*) in the context of vowel-sandhis (*svarasandhi*)."

Because the *pluta* vowel is established as already accomplished within the junctions of vowels (*svarasandhi*); for otherwise, there would be the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule "the *pluta* and *pragṛhya* vowels remain unchanged before a vowel" (Pāṇini 6.1.125).

The rule would otherwise be rendered meaningless. And although it is stated here that "it is pronounced open" (*vivṛtaḥ*), nevertheless, because of the statement "for the sake of establishing their homogeneity" (*sāvarṇya-prasiddhy-artham*), it is understood to be more open (*vivṛtatara*). For [homogeneity] does not exist between that which is merely open and that which is more open.
Homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) is established either because of the difference in effort (*prayatna-bheda*), or by the force of the declaration that [the vowels] are "opened" (*vivṛta*).
Even for that which is less opened (*avivṛtatara*), there will be homogeneity with that which is more opened (*vivṛtatara*). If only this much were stated here—namely, "if *i* and *th*"—then...

Because proximity and the context of the subject matter are present, it should be understood that only the *vivṛta* [open] vowel occurring within the phonetic sequence (*akṣarasamāmnāya*) is what is being promised; not those residing in verbal roots, nominal stems, suffixes, or particles. Consequently, due to the difference in articulatory effort (*prayatna*), there would be no homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between them.

Because it is not included in the traditional list of phonemes (*akṣarasamāmnāya*), it would not possess the status of being a vowel (*actva*). And that being absent, in the word *śāmyati*, the technical rule concerning vowels (*ac-paribhāṣā*) would not apply; consequently, since the original substitute (*sthānin*)—the letter *a*—would lack the status of being a vowel, [the rule] "of the eight roots beginning with *śam*" (*śamāmaṣṭānām*)... [would not apply].

The lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by "dīrghaḥ śyani" (Pāṇini 7.3.74) would not occur. In the case of *dṛṣad*, the rule "the final syllable of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is acute" would not apply to its end; for that [rule] pertains to the properties of vowels (*aj-dharma*). In the case of *nāyaka*, this is because the vowel *a* of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is not a vowel (*anact*).

In that case, the substitution of *ā* would not occur. Furthermore, in the word *avanamati*, the initial acute accent (*ādyaudātatva*)—prescribed by the rules "Particles have the acute accent on the first syllable" (*nipātā ādyudātāḥ*, Phiṭ-sūtra 4.80) and "Preverbs [also have the acute accent on the first syllable], with the exception of *abhi*" (*upasargāścābhivarjam*, Phiṭ-sūtra 4.81)—would not apply. Moreover, if the long vowel were not present in the form of the letter *ā* used in the reference to the *anuvṛtti*, there would be no homogeneous relationship (*sāvarṇya*) for the long vowel.

There would be no inclusion [of the whole]. What is the fault in that? Regarding the rule *ṭhasya cvau* (Pāṇini 6.4.32), the substitution of *ī* would apply only here in the case of *śuklībhavati*; however, it would not apply in the case of *mālībhavati*. Furthermore, regarding the rule *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), the elision of the vowel *a* would apply only here in the cases of *vākṣiḥ* and *plākṣiḥ*, but not elsewhere.

But this would not apply in the case of *vālāki*. Therefore, the inclusion of the word "in this treatise" (*śāstra*) was made for the purpose of demonstrating that whatever is merely a vowel (*avarṇa*) in this treatise, all of that is asserted to be *vivṛta* (open). Now, even though there is homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) [between them]...

The inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*) is not established by means of the letter-form (*ākāra*) situated in a rule that involves *anuvṛtti* (carrying over), because it is not an *aṇ*. For those *a*-sounds and others that appear in a rule involving *anuvṛtti* are not *aṇ*s; rather, they are those [letters] found in the traditional alphabet (*akṣarasamāmnāya*). If it is argued that there is no fault because one relies on the theory of the universal (*jāti*), we say no; for in the theory of the universal...
This fault does not arise because the *Grahana-ka-śāstra* has been rejected. For here, in individual instances (*vyakti*), there are two factors:
similarity and difference. Among these, sometimes one or the other is intended to be predominant; when it is similarity [that is intended].
Then, because that similar portion is common to all individual instances (*vyakti*),
there occurs an inclusion of all individuals without exception, since the difference [between them] is not perceived. This is the case in the *pratyāhāra*.

Since the primary instruction consists of similar parts, it is established that all individual instances of phonemes (*avarṇa*) possess the status of being *aṇ* (atomic) when they serve as the basis for the application [of grammatical rules]. But what, then, is this?

What is the distinction between similarity (*sādṛśya*) and the universal of the *a*-sound (*avarṇajāti*)? This is the distinction: this similarity resides only in the short (*hrasva*) manifestations of the *a*-sound, not in the long (*dīrgha*) or protracted (*pluta*) ones; whereas the universal of the *a*-sound resides in the long and protracted ones as well.
That [the vowel *a*] exists [in this treatise] has already been established.
Now, how is it understood that the vowel *a* is here prescribed (*pratijñāyate*) as being "open" (*vivṛta*) in this treatise?
To this, he says: "Of that," and so forth. If the vowel *a* were not previously open...

If it were so admitted, then one would not apply the rule *ṭh-a* (Pāṇini 8.4.68) for the sake of restoring that [quality], because "restoration" (*pratyāpatti*) means the re-attainment of a state after having fallen away from one's own form; how could that be possible for something whose own form remains unaltered? Alternatively, if it were *vivṛta*...

If it is so asserted, then would its application remain exactly as it was even upon the completion of that treatise? Anticipating this objection from the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he says "of that" (*tasya*), etc. The word "object" (*artha*)...

It expresses exclusion, as in the expression "smoke for the sake of mosquitoes. The meaning is that there should be a cessation of the application of that which is concealed (*saṃvṛta*). Alternatively, the word *artha* signifies purpose; by the word "of it" (*tasya*), the concealed [meaning] is referred back.

That for which the purpose or motive is application (*prayoga*) is described as such. It is neuter because it functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). This is what is meant: [it serves] as the cause for the application of that conventional term when it has deviated from its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
A restoration will be made; since [the rule] occurs at the conclusion of the treatise, this application does not apply to that very same [case].
2. ṛlṛk.
"His apprehension occurs by means of three. How is apprehension by means of three obtained?

If it is an adjunct (*anubandha*) of the whole (*samudāya*), it is not an adjunct of the parts (*avayava*); or if it is an adjunct of the parts, then it is not an adjunct of the whole—thus, [the apprehension occurs] by means of only one.
Would there not be the fault of [the suffix] being included? This is not a fault; for the usage of the *anubandhas* is by means of a formal declaration (*pratijñā*).
But the declaration is a human act, and a person, while making the declaration, does not cease [its application] in both cases.

Because there is no contradiction. For the status of being a suffix attached to a composite whole is not contradicted by the proposition that it is attached to its individual parts; otherwise, one would not be the other. Therefore, what was stated is logical:
"the inclusion occurs by means of three. This should be applied in the same way everywhere.

In this treatise, the instruction regarding the phonemes (varṇas) is for the sake of a specific purpose. With the intention that no purpose whatsoever can be found for the instruction of the phoneme *lṛ*, he says: "The phonemes beginning with *ṭh*. That which is employed (*prayujyate*) is called "employment" (*prayoga*).

The term *dhātvādiḥ* [refers to] the beginning of a verbal root and so forth. It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those for which the object (*viṣaya*) is an occurrence (*prayoga*) that is abundant (*pracura*) and extensive (*prabhūta*), characterized by not occurring elsewhere" (*ananyatrabhāva*). Alternatively, *prayoga* means application (*prayukti*), that is, utterance (*uccāraṇa*); thus, it is the object of that [utterance].

This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). With the word *pracura*, it forms a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*). It was stated for the purpose of excluding the scope of that statement—"the purpose of their instruction is easily understood"—[which might otherwise apply]. For if this were not said, [the rule would apply] only to the *ḷ*-vowel.
If it is asked, "Why is the purpose alone being questioned?", then there would be occasion for this statement:
"The sound *ḷ* is used only in the context of the root *klṛp*. Here, the word *tu* [serves to] distinguish [it] from *a* and the other vowels.

This is for the sake of distinction. It might be argued: "Since that [element] is related to *klṛp*, the substitution of *upadhā* should be performed for the sake of those operations that apply to vowels (*ac*). To this he says: "And of *klṛp*" and so forth. If there is non-establishment (*asiddhatva*), then what follows? To this he says: "In that case, the vowel *ṛ*..."

"Thus," and so forth; "those [rules] by which the substitution of *l* is prescribed," and so forth. That by which the substitution of *l* (*latva*) is prescribed is "the prescription of the substitution of *l*" (*latvavidhāna*). The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). Alternatively, *vidhi* means "prescription" (*vidhāna*) in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*); thus, it is "the prescription of the substitution of *l*" (*latvasya vidhānam*).

This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). [The rule] "those that follow *tat* and *adaḥ*" and so forth indicates by this that the substitution of *l* for *r* is established (*siddha*) in those cases. For in the preceding [section], what follows is considered unestablished (*asiddha*), but not here.

The preceding [syllable] is protracted (*pluta*) before the following one; as in the example *ṭhklṛptaśikhaḥ* ("one whose crest is fashioned"). Here, the compound *bahuvrīhi* is analyzed as "one whose crest (*śikhā*) is fashioned (*klṛptā*). In this context, the protraction (*pluta*) is prescribed by the rule *guroranṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.86), and that [protraction] applies to the vowel (*acaḥ*).

In this way, [the rule] brings forward the original element (*sthānin*). Since the *ḷ*-vowel is not taught as an *ac*, it would not possess the status of an *ac*; therefore, that [substitution] would not occur. [End of *pa*.]

Regarding the word *praklṛptaḥ*: here, by the rules "particles have the acute accent on the first syllable" (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.80) and "prepositions also [have the acute on the first], with the exception of *abhi*" (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.81), the vowel *a* in the word *pra* becomes acute. The letter *ḷ* is likewise [acute].
By the accent of the verbal root (*dhātu*),
it is indeed acute (*udātta*). Once the accent of the *niṣṭhā* suffix has been applied, [the rule] "A word is unaccented (*anudātta*) except for one syllable" (Pāṇini 6.1.158) applies.

Subsequently, that [suffix] becomes *anudātta*. When the compound is formed by the rule "kugatiprādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.2.18), and the status of being *udātta* for the entire compound would otherwise have applied, the rule "katiranantaraḥ" (Pāṇini 6.2.49) applies;
by virtue of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member, the word *praśabda* itself remains *udātta*. Therefore, for the following *luk* [elision],...

By the rule "ṭhudātādanudātasya svaritaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.66), the circumflex accent (*svarita*) is prescribed; that would not occur if *ac* were non-existent, because it is a property of vowels (*aj-dharma*). For example: *klṛptaḥ*, *klṛptavān*.
By the rule *ṭh-aṇ-aci ca* (8.4.47), reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is prescribed for a *yar* consonant following a vowel (*ac*); that too would not occur if [the consonant] were not a *anac*.
Thus, he refutes what was stated [by others], namely: "The root *klṛp* is used only in the sense of 'standing' (*stha*)."
To demonstrate another purpose, he says "and that which... and so forth.
A power other than the capacity for uttering correct words (*sādhuśabda*) is "incapacity" (*aśakti*); that which is produced from that is "born of incapacity" (*aśaktija*).
Regarding the statement, "the correctness (*sādhutva*) of even its imitation is desired," this is due to a difference in meaning.

Because it is a different word and because it is employed by a student, like any other correct word distinct from it. Now, one might object that since the original (anukārya) is incorrect, the imitation (anukaraṇa) must also be incorrect, according to the rule "an imitation is like its prototype" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇaṃ bhavati*). This is not so; for [the status of] grammatical correctness is indeed...

In this context, the original form (*prakṛti*) is resorted to; and by the expression "as in the original," it is precisely the grammatical operation (*kārya*) based on the treatise that is extended (*atidiśyate*). Furthermore, the form of an incorrect word (*asādhuśabda*), which arises from incapacity, is not [extended].

It is neither a grammatical *prakṛti* nor is it an ungrammatical form (*apaśabda*) whose status is established by the treatise; for even grammar is not able to declare something to be an *apaśabda*, since its function is solely for the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of correct words (*sādhuśabda*). Therefore—

The imitation of a sound is indeed correct; however, even in that case, the operations pertaining to vowels (*ac-kāryāṇi*) would not apply to the *ḷ*-sound situated therein if it were not taught [as a vowel].
For example, in "kumārylṛtakaḥ," since the *ḷ*-sound possesses the status of a vowel (*actva*), when it follows [the preceding vowel],...

The substitution of *yaṇ* occurs. But surely, even if the instruction of the number [of phonemes] were not given in the rule "iko yaṇ aci" (Pāṇini 6.1.77), the purpose of instructing the phoneme *ḷ* would still be established; for if the instruction of *ḷ* did not exist, that [purpose] would indeed be appropriate.

But this is not the case; let there be no enumeration of the numbered items, for even in its absence, the determination will be made by the paribhāṣā rule "sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ" (P. 1.1.50). Then the designation *it* serves another purpose: for if it were not taught [with that designation], [the form] *gamlṛ*...

In the case of roots such as *sṛplṛ* in the sense of "going" (*dhā.pā.* 982, 983), the designation *it* would not apply by the rule *upadeśe 'janunāsikaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.2). And if that [designation] were absent, the suffix *aṅ* would not be applied by the rule *puṣādidyutādyalṛditah parasmaipadeṣu* (Pāṇini 3.1.55).

It might be argued that this is not so; for even in the absence of an explicit instruction (*upadeśa*), the designation *it* will be established because the rule for the suffix *aṅ* is prescribed after a verbal root marked with *ḷ* or *it*, and thus there is no purpose for the instruction. Therefore, the purposes are indeed those previously stated, and they are as follows:

These [rules] were stated without relying on the statement that "the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) should be declared for *ṛ* and *ḷ*. For if that [statement] were relied upon here, even though there is the teaching of the phoneme *ḷ*, [the following would occur]: *ṭh*...
By the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.69), since the *ṛ*-vowel includes [the *ḷ*-vowel] when it is being grasped by the *ṛ*-vowel, these [cases] are established simply through that inclusion.

And it was not stated as "pūrvāśca" (and the preceding ones), because its inclusion among the preceding [roots] is impossible. Now, why is this [root *kṛ*] not included by the vowel *a* in the rule "ṣidbhidādibhyo 'ṅ" (Pāṇini 3.3.104)? Regarding this, some say: "The first [vowel] [is significant] with the last [vowel]."

In the rule *sahetā* (Pāṇini 1.1.71), the term *apratyaya* ("not being a suffix") is carried over from the preceding rule *ṭhāṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ* (1.1.69). Consequently, the following meaning is established: "The initial [phoneme], together with the final [indicatory phoneme], is the designator [of its own class]."
[The rule] "it occurs, provided that there is no suffix" [is stated];
however, this [suffix] is indeed a suffix, and therefore it would not be a *grāhaka* (a term that causes another element to be included).
And in that case, even in the rule "that which ends in a *sup* or a *tiṅ* is a *pada*" (Pāṇini 1.4.14), the suffix would not be a *grāhaka*.
Therefore, it should be understood that because [the meaning] is not expressed here, there is no inclusion by means of a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated term).

For *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and compound formations are characterized by their expressive power (*abhidhāna*). Furthermore, when the suffix *aṅ* is produced after roots such as *ṣid* and *bhid* according to Pāṇini 3.3.104 (*ṣidbhidādibhyo 'ṅ*), the intended meaning is not expressed.
It occurs here [in this rule] by means of the letter *a* in "ṭhśāsa idaṅhaloḥ" (6.4.34) and "ṛdṛśo'ṅ guṇiḥ" (7.4.16).

Why is there no inclusion [of the *aṅ* substitute] by way of *pratyāhāra*? Because of the inclusion of both the *aṅ* that resembles *ciṇ* and the *aṅ* that resembles *caṅ*. For in the rule "śāsa idaṅ-haloḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.34), the phrase "bhañjeśca ciṇi" (6.4.33) is understood as a governing rule (*anuvartate*). Also, [the rule] "ṛdṛśo’ṅi guṇaḥ" (7.4.16).

In the rule *guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.84), as well as in the rule *ṇau caṅyupadhāyā hrasvaḥ* (7.4.1), the term *aṅ* is qualified by the term *caṅ* through grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*)—namely, "in the case of *caṅ*" and "in the case of *aṅ*"—for *caṅ* does not occur in place of *aṅ*. Rather, it is the *aṅ* stem that is modified by the suffix *caṅ*. Thus, by the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍukaplutinyāya*), the term *caṅ* from the preceding rule is understood here as a qualifier of *aṅ*.
Because of its extreme distinctness,
the meaning is understood there through implication alone; for words employed in reference to other objects convey their sense even without the word *iva*.
The particle *iva* conveys the sense of a formal application (*prayoga*), as in "the boy is fire" (*agnir māṇavakaḥ*) or "the Vāhīka is a cow" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*).
Therefore, the meaning is this:
*caṅ-ivāṅ* means that *aṅ* is similar to *caṅ*; and what is *aṅ* that is similar to *caṅ*? That which [replaces] *cli*.

It is prescribed in its proper place; thus, the term *aṅ* is understood as referring specifically to that which has *cli* as its substitute, and not to the pratyāhāra [of the same name]. Likewise, in the rule *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.34), when *aṅ* is qualified by the mention of *cli*, it refers to the *aṅ* that is a substitute for *cli*.

It should be understood that only the *aṅga* belonging to the *cliṣṭhānika* (the state immediately preceding the suffix) is intended to be grasped here. Why, then, in the rules "sani ca" (2.4.47), "iṅśca" (2.4.48), "parimāṇākhyāyāṃ sarvebhyaḥ" (3.3.20), and "iṅśca" (3.3.21), is [the term] used with the vowel *i*?

Is there no inclusion of the *pratyāhāra*? First, it is not included in the preceding rule, because of the prescription of *kit*-hood by the rule *ṭhiko jhal* (Pāṇini 1.2.9). For if this were a *pratyāhāra*, [the rule would apply].

If there were no absence of reaching the end of the quarters (i.e., if the suffixes did not extend that far), then because the *guṇa* substitution would not apply, the prescription of *kit*-ness would be purposeless. First, it does not occur in the preceding case; for if it were [the case], then by the very letter *ka* in *tiki*, one would form a *pratyāhāra*.

One should [not] do so; for there is no possibility of a *san* suffix following a verbal root that ends in a *ṅit* (a marker of the *ṅ* class), such that the inclusion of the *ṅ* sound in the pratyāhāra would be meaningful. Nor does it apply in subsequent cases, as that would result in redundancy. For instance, from roots ending in *i*, [the suffix] *ac* is applied by the rule *therac*.
It should be *it* [as in *it-i*]; from those ending in *u*, the suffix *ap* is applied by Pāṇini 3.3.57 (*ṛdorap*).
There are no [roots] ending in *lṛ* at all. For those ending in *ej*, [the substitution of *ā* occurs] even before the production of the suffix, by Pāṇini 6.1.45 (*ādeca upadeśe’śiti*).

According to the rule *upadeśe 'śiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.45), [the vowels] ought to be replaced by *ā*; therefore, even those [vowels] do not exist at the time of the prescription of the suffixes. Only the vowel *ṛ* remains; consequently, if the suffix *ghañ* is intended to be applied, the inclusion of the *pratyāhāra* [of the vowels] would be purposeless.
It may be so; one should simply say *uḥ*. For even in the rule *krīṅjīnāṃ ṇau* (Pāṇini 6.1.48), the roots *krīṇāti* and *jayati* are mentioned separately by the author [of the Aṣṭādhyāyī].

[If it is argued: "The inclusion [of *ai* and *au*] does not occur; their separate mention is for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyama*) so that among those ending in *i*, only those two may undergo *yat* [the substitution of *ya*]"—this is not correct; for even so, one would have performed the *pratyāhāra* (abbreviation) with the letter *k* alone, since the *ātva* (substitution of *ā*) applies to those ending in *e* and *o*.
Because it is established by the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) alone; furthermore, in the rule *ṭhiṅdhāryyoḥ śatrakṛcchriṇi* (Pāṇini 3.2.130),
it should be understood that due to its association with the verbal root *dhārayati*, the term *ṭhiṅ* refers to the verbal root and not to the technical abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*).
4. aiāṬc | Here,
by the rule "The first [letter] together with the last [of the group] is called a pratyāhāra" (Pāṇini 1.1.71),
the term *aj* refers to the vowels beginning with *a*.

The technical name (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed. And just as that [name] applies to *i*-sounds and so forth, it would likewise apply to *ṇa*-sounds and so forth when they are attached as suffixes (*anubaddha*), because those too are taught therein. Consequently, by means of that [name], in other rules such as "ṭh-ik-oh yaṇ aci" (Pāṇini 6.1.77), [the substitution would apply] to them as well.

With the intention that just as the *yaṇ* substitution occurs in nominal bases (*prātipadika*) such as *dadhyatra*, it might likewise occur in forms such as *dadhi-ṇakārīyati*, he says: "In the *ṭh*-pratyāhāra," and so forth. How is it that [the rule] does not apply in the case of the mentions of *ac*?

The word "kāryam" (an operation) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Since this technical name "ṭhacaḥ" is employed in various application rules (*pradeśavākya*), those instances of its mention are instances of the mention of vowels (*ajgrahaṇa*).
When these exist, how could the operations pertaining to vowels (*ackārya*) not apply to the letter *ṇ* and others? The meaning is that they would certainly apply.

Regarding the phrase "by usage" (*ācārāt*): *ācāra* means conduct, such as that of the teachers (*ācārya*). Therefore, on account of this indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*), [the rule] does not apply. For instance, [Pāṇini teaches]:

"The *uṇādi* suffixes are diverse" (3.3.1), "After the roots *tṛṣ*, *mṛṣ*, and *kṛś*, [the suffix *ka* is applied] according to Kāśyapa" (7.2.25), and "When a vowel follows, the augment *ṅmuṭ* is added after a short vowel ending in *ṅ*" (8.3.32).

By not applying the *yaṇ* substitution when the suffixes beginning with *ṇ*, such as *ṭā*, *ṅsi*, and *ṅs*, follow— as prescribed by the rules *nityam* (Pāṇini 8.3.32) and *ṭhṅsiṅsośca* (6.1.110)— he thereby indicates [the following].
"Even though the designation [aj-] exists, the grammatical operations do not take place"— or rather,
by this activity of the Teacher, it is indicated that "this designation *aj* simply does not apply to these [sounds]. For if it were a designation...

It might be that the Teacher would perform grammatical operations (*akārya*) upon those [terms]. Having thus established the non-existence of the technical name (*saṃjñā*) by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), he now says—"because it is not the primary element"—in order to establish it by means of logic (*nyāya*). Terms such as *aṇ* and so forth are technical names (*saṃjñā*).
The subsequent elements (anubandhas) are uttered in order to lead [the listener] toward the comprehension of that form;
consequently, because they are employed for the sake of another, they possess a subordinate status.
The others, however, are employed for their own sake, and thus they possess primacy. Therefore—
This designation applies to those [roots] themselves,
not to their suffixes; for when a primary and a non-primary element are in proximity, it is the primary element alone that enters into a relationship with the grammatical operation.
Not otherwise. Thus the author of the Bhāṣya said: "It is established because the understanding of the effect [occurs] with respect to the primary element.
If this is so, then this designation would not apply even to the letter *a*, since it too certainly possesses the status of a subordinate member (*aṅga*) when the designation is being conveyed?
Because of the force of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the phrase "and of its own form" (*svasya ca rūpasya*), there is no fault in [the rule] applying to that [element].
With these two reasons just mentioned, he says— "and elision" (*lopaśca*)— in order to demonstrate that it will not occur.

And so forth. "Balavattara" means simply "more powerful," where the suffix *tarap* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*), as in the rule "that which has fewer syllables is placed first" (Pāṇini 2.2.34). For the *anubandhas* are designated by the technical term *it*;
therefore, by the rule "there is elision of that" (Pāṇini 1.3.9), they are elided even before the designation *ac* [of vowels] could apply.

It must be so, because of its strength. How can there be the designation (*saṃjñā*) of those [sounds] which are non-existent? And if that [designation] is non-existent, how can there be the operation of *ac* (*ackārya*) in the case of the apprehension of vowels (*ajgrahaṇa*)?

What is its occurrence? However, the elision (*lopa*) takes precedence due to its being subsequent and its being obligatory; for the rule concerning elision is subsequent to the rule concerning technical names (*saṃjñā*), and thus it also possesses the quality of being subsequent.

Its permanence [is established] because it applies whether the designation has been made or not. Even when the designation has been made, the elision must occur; even when it has not been made, it must occur. However, the designation does not come into being once the elision has already taken place, for [the designation belongs to] the named entities.

Because it exists. If this were so, then just as in the case of bases ending in *aj* (such as *pati*), there would first be the elision of the indicatory letters (*anubandha*) such as *ṇ*, so too there would be the elision of the letter *c*; consequently, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) "beginning with *aj*" (*ajit*) would not be established.
[Answer: By the force of the explicit statement (*vacana-sāmarthya*), its elision will not occur prior [to the others]. Even when it has been elided...
Or rather, in that case, the vowel *a* accompanied by that which occurred previously will be the designation (*saṃjñā*). However, for those ending in *a*,
when the *ṇakāra* and other [suffixes] have been elided, it is not appropriate for them to be the designation in the case of [stems] beginning with *i*.
Because there is room for [this objection].
Here, these phonemes beginning with *a* are held to consist of multiple parts, as evidenced by the rules:
"The first half-mora of that is acute" (Pāṇini 1.2.32) and "An *ec* vowel that is not a *pragṛhya*, when not used in address from a distance... (Pāṇini 6.1.127).

This is because of the rule: "In place of the first half [of ṛ and ḷ], i and u are substituted before a vowel" (Pāṇini 8.2.107). Furthermore, certain constituent parts of some phonemes resemble other phonemes; for example, the *repha* (the sound r) in the phoneme *ṛ*, and in the phoneme *ḷ*...

The letter *la*; in *e* and *ai*, the letters *a* and *r*; in *o* and *au*, the letters *a* and *u*. In the long vowels beginning with *ā*, the short vowels beginning with *a* [are present]. Now, as for those which are the constituent parts (*avayava*) of the phonemes beginning with *ṛ*—what [is their status]?

Are [the vowels] to be understood by the mention of "color" (*varṇa*) or not? In the former case—regarding *agne iha* and *vāyo udakam*, the rule for lengthening before a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇadīrghatva*) would apply;
regarding *praṇīya* and *ālūya*, the insertion of *t* (*tuk*) based on a short vowel would apply.

Such defects as these also follow in this final position, and they are to be understood from the Bhāṣya. In the other case, however, the letter *ṛ* must be explicitly mentioned in the rules for the augment *nuṭ*, the substitution of *la*, and the change of the vowel (*vināma*). First, regarding the rule for the augment *nuṭ*: in the root "ṛdhū vṛddhau" (to increase)...

In the case of *liṭ* [perfect tense], in forms such as *anṛdhatuḥ* and *ānṛdhuḥ*, because the *ṛ*-vowel does not include the *r*-consonant when "consonant" (*hal*) is mentioned, there is an absence of being "two-consonantal" (*dvihaltva*). Consequently, the augment *nuṭ*—prescribed by the rule "therefore *nuṭ* for a two-consonantal root" (*tasmānnuḍ dvihalaḥ*, Pāṇini 7.4.71)—does not apply. This is illustrated in the rules for the substitution of *l*-sounds in forms such as *klṛptaḥ* and *klṛptavān*.

The substitution of *l* for the *r* in the root *ṛp-* [as prescribed by Pāṇini 8.2.18, *ṛkṛpo ro laḥ*] would not be established; furthermore, in the rule concerning the addition of *ṇ*, [the forms] *mātṛṇām* and *pitṛṇām* would lack the substitution of *ṇ*. Therefore, he says "among the phonemes," etc. This means: among the phonemes beginning with *ṛ*.

Regarding the phrase "parts of a phoneme" (*varṇaikadeśāḥ*): the term "parts" (*ekadeśāḥ*) is used for the purpose of making known that [the *repha* and so forth] are of the very nature of the phonemes themselves. This is what is meant: the parts that constitute the essence of the phonemes are "parts of a phoneme.
For if only the word "parts" (*ekadeśāḥ*) were stated, then someone might fall into error.
It might be argued: "These parts are indeed distinct entities.
To exclude even those parts of letters such as *u* and so forth, he says: "having forms similar to other letters."

"Having forms identical to other phonemes (*varṇāntarasamānākṛtayaḥ*). This means those parts whose form is identical to that of other phonemes; the sense is that they have a form equal to other phonemes that do not constitute constituent parts [of the word]. "In them" (*teṣu*) refers to the portions of the phonemes. "That operation" (*tatkāryam*).

Thus [it is said]. An operation involving a different phoneme (*varṇāntara-kāryam*), such as the lengthening of a vowel when followed by a homogeneous vowel (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*), does not occur. He asks: "What is the reason it does not occur? and replies:
"For they follow its shadow," and so forth. "Its shadow" means its form.

It is merely the form of the other phonemes, such as *a* and so forth, that they imitate; because they possess a form similar to those, they are not those very sounds themselves. For identity does not arise merely by imitating the form of something else. Thus, for example, the parts of a *gavaya* imitate the parts of a cow, yet [they are not the cow].
And their nature is that [of being produced by effort]. But what is the reason that they are not those very [efforts]? He says:

"separately" (*pṛthak*), and so forth. "Effort" (*prayatna*) means the exertion (*prayatana*), which is the operation of the articulatory places (*sthāna*) and the organs (*karaṇa*). That which is to be brought about (*nirvartya*) in a manner distinct from—i.e., other than—the effort that is the cause of other phonemes.

The teachers maintain that the phonemes (*varṇa*) are what are to be produced; thus, these phonemes are the constituent parts (*avayava*). If they were [independent] phonemes, they would have to be brought about by a separate effort, but this is not the case. For instance, they are produced by that very same effort which serves the purpose of the composite whole. Therefore, it is as follows: *agrahaṇaka-*...

By relying on the [other] alternative (*pakṣa*), the undesirable consequences (*prasaṅga*) regarding those defects that would arise under the alternative of actual apprehension (*grahaṇa-pakṣa*) have been refuted. But surely, the alternative of apprehension has also been established in the Bhāṣya; therefore, the defects associated with it—

Because of the avoidance [of that fault], for what reason was it abandoned? Because there would be much to be remedied; whereas in the position of non-apprehension (*agrahaṇaka*), little needs to be remedied.
Therefore, that alone...
The author of the Vṛtti has relied [on this].

If, then, they are indeed included, the inclusion of the vowel *ṛ* in the rules for the suffix *nuṭ* and so forth remains necessarily to be performed; therefore, he says: "In the rules for *nuṭ*, for substitutes beginning with a consonant (*lādeśa*), and for the change of *n* to *ṇ* (*vināma*)," and so on.

The meaning is that a remedy must be provided for whatever objection arises regarding the application of the augment *nuṭ* in the domain of the vowel *ṛ*. In that regard, concerning the rule for *nuṭ*, first:
the *ṛ*-vowel [is included] as the letter *r* by the term "consonant" (*hal*).
It is understood. Therefore, here too, the augment *nuṭ* occurs for a stem ending in two consonants—as in "ānṛdhatuḥ" and "ānṛdhuḥ.
This very point has been established by the author of the Vṛtti himself. Now, is this [augment] situated within the vowel *ṛ*?

Is the letter *repha* (the sound *r*) composed of phonemes (*varṇātmaka*)? No, he says; for it was just stated: "For they merely imitate its shadow, but they are not that [shadow] itself. Then, are those phonemes such as *ha* and so forth, which are taught in the traditional recitation of the alphabet (*akṣarasamāmnāya*), composed of phonemes?

"No," he says; for he will state later in the *Māheśvara-sūtras* (sūtra 5), "having taught these letters, beginning with *ha*, *ya*, *va*, and *ra*. Now, how is it that by the inclusion of the consonants (*hal*), which consist of the individual letters, there is also the inclusion of the *repha* (the letter *r*) situated within the *ṛ*-vowel, even though that *repha* does not consist of the *a*-vowel?

Does it occur? The intention is that it does, by virtue of the inclusion of the term *dvi-hal* (a word consisting of two consonants). For in that case, one would have to state only "tasmān nuṭ" (the augment *nuṭ* after that [consonant]).
It is not so.
And if it were stated in this way, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) even in cases such as *āṭatuḥ* and *āṭuḥ*;

for the rule "ṭhaśnoteśca" (Pāṇini 7.4.72) is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning: "if [a root] has two consonants (*dvihala*), it must be *aś* alone, and not any other. If it is argued that this [restriction] is for the purpose of excluding *aś*, [we reply: no.

This is incorrect. For if this were the sole purpose, he would have simply formulated the prohibition as "not after *naś*. Thus, since the result is established even without the mention of "having two consonants" (*dvihal*), the fact that he does include the mention of "having two consonants" serves this [other] purpose.

The purpose [of this rule] is so that it may apply to those which imitate a double-consonant (*dvihala*) and a shadow (*chāyā*); for even that which has one primary consonant and another as a member [is included], because of its similarity in form to that [double-consonant], by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

This is for the purpose that [the designation] may also apply to that which is worthy of being designated as *hal*; and how is this obtained? If the term *hal* here is a direct mention (*śruti*), it applies even to a manifestation of the letter *r* situated in place of *ṛ*, which imitates the shadow of *hal*, and not otherwise.
Therefore, by the mention of "two *hal*s" (*dvihal*)...
The *repha* situated within the vowel *ṛ* is also included; otherwise, the mention of "two consonants" (*dvihala*) would be purposeless.

It was stated there as "the *repha*" according to the common usage of others. For indeed, among those who maintain that [the term] refers to the phoneme itself, even the portion of the vowel *ṛ* is commonly known as "the *repha*. This was stated in this way on account of their similarity. For it is so.

Due to similarity, there is a designation of something as that very thing even when it is not that thing—just as one says, "The boy is fire" (*agnirmāṇavaka*). Alternatively, in the rule *ṭhādiphaḥ* (Vār.
321), the term *varṇāt* does not carry over from the preceding rule *varṇātkāraḥ* (Vār. 320).
Therefore, even from a vowelless element, the suffix *pho* occurs, either by virtue of the rule of abundance (*bahulavacana*) or because of this very principle; likewise,
it should be understood that the suffix *kāra* occurs even from a vowelless constituent that is similar in form to the letter *l*, such as the *l*-sound belonging to the phoneme *ḷ*.
Even in the rule prescribing the substitute *l*, the general term *ṛ* is employed. By this, both the pure *r* and that which resides within the vowel *ṛ* are included.
*L* likewise is a general term. Consequently, in place of the pure *r*, there occurs the pure *l*.
An injunction is prescribed:

even for the vowel *ṛ*, the vowel *lṛ* is substituted by way of partial modification (*ekadeśavikāra*). And thus, such grammatical references as "and in the case of *luṭ*, [the substitution occurs] after *klṛp*" (Pāṇini 1.3.93) become justified. This [is the case with] *kṛp*.

Regarding the rule *ro laḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.18), the author of the Vṛtti himself has explained: "In this case, the general property (*sāmānya*) 'ra' is taken as the referent" (Kāśikā on 8.2.18). This means that, setting aside the distinction based on whether something is a phoneme (*varṇa*) or not a phoneme, [the term] applies to the individual instance (*vyakti*) of the letter *repha* which consists of the general property of being a phoneme.

Since the verbal cognitions "ṭha" are identical even for those two [phonemes] which are differentiated by the distinction between being a letter and not being a letter, those two [cognitions] are taken as the basis; but not—

The manifestation of the letter *r* consists precisely of the phoneme (*varṇa*). By the phrase "by that," both [the individual instance and the universal] are grasped through the inclusion of the universal, because that universal exists in both. "The letter *l* is likewise nothing but a universal."

Thus [it is said]. The word "is taken up" (*upādīyate*) is required [as a complement]. Here too, it would have had to be explicitly stated that both the simple *l*-sound and that which resides in *ḷ* are included; however, because this is understood by following the previous [rule], it has not been stated. "Therefore, this..."

And so forth. Since both the letter *repha* (ṛ) and the letter *la* are thus included, this substitute *la* is prescribed in place of the solitary *repha*. Furthermore, because of their closest phonetic proximity (*antaratamatva*), *lṛ* is also substituted for *ṛ*.

But even if both [the *ṛ* and *lṛ* sounds] are indeed perceived, how is it obtained that the *lṛ* sound occurs in place of the *ṛ* sound? For the *repha* residing in the *ṛ* sound does not become the *ṛ* sound;
rather, what is it? It is a constituent part (*avayava*) of it. Nor does the *lakāra* residing in the *lṛ* sound become the *ṛ* sound; what then...?
What then? It is a part of that [letter].

In that case, when both [the *ṛ* and *ḷ* sounds] are perceived, the *l*-sound residing in the *ḷ*-vowel is the most similar [substitute] for the *r*-sound residing in the *ṛ*-vowel, by virtue of being a single constituent part of the phoneme.

In order to refute this objection—that [the word] "becomes" (bhavati)—it was stated, "by way of a partial modification. That "part" is the *repha*, which is a constituent element (*avayava*) of the vowel *ṛ*; its "modification" (*vikāra*) is the letter *la*, which is a constituent element of the vowel *lṛ*. Alternatively, [one may explain it as follows:]

Alternatively, the *lakāra* residing in the *ekadeśa* (single part) of the *ṛkāra*—that very [element] is the modification (*vikāra*). It is precisely that which is the modification of the single part, namely the *repha* residing in the *ṛkāra*. "Door" (*dvāra*) means the entrance, that is to say, the means.
By that [means], the entire *lṛkāra* is the substitute (*ādeśa*) in place of the entire *ṛkāra*.

It is prescribed. For if a separation between the sounds *ṛ* and *ḷ*, as well as between the *repha* and *lakāra* residing therein, were possible, then it would be possible to prescribe the *lakāra*—the constituent part of *ḷ*—as being distinct from the *repha*—the constituent part of *ṛ*. But such a separation does not exist for them.
A separate existence is possible; therefore, in the manner already described, the substitution of *ṛ* for *ḷ* is prescribed.
The introduction of the passage beginning with "and thus" (*tathā ca*) is for the purpose of strengthening the point just stated. Since...
Thus, by means of this partial substitution, the substitution of *ḷ* for *ṛ* is prescribed.

This being the case, grammatical references such as "ṭhluṭi ca klṛpaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.93) and others become logically consistent, whereas they would not otherwise. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), [the rule] "ṛdupadhāccāklṛpicṛteḥ" is included.
(3.1.110) There is the inclusion of both rules: *tāsi ca klṛpaḥ* (7.2.60).
Even regarding the rule for the substitution of *ṇa*, having stated that "it should be said: *ṛvarṇācca*" (Vārttika 946), [the author says]:

"Or rather, it is established by the fact that the reference is made through the commonality of the sound *ra*; and even when there is an intervention by a portion (*bhakti*) of an *a*-vowel, the substitution of *ṇa* occurs."

In the rule regarding the *kṣubhnādi* group, the inclusion of *nṛnamana* and *tṛpnoti* should be understood as being for the purpose of prohibiting the substitution of *ṇ*. Alternatively, it is precisely by this that it is indicated that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs even after a vowel containing *ṛ* (*ṛ-varṇa*).
This has been refuted by the author of the Vṛtti himself [in Kāśikā 8.4.1]:
"It is established because of the commonality of the phonetic form (*śruti*) of *ra*. Here, "the phonetic form" (*śruti*) refers to the sound *ra*.

The term *śruti* refers to that which is perceived as the letter *ra*. Setting aside the distinction between being a phoneme (*varṇa*) or not being a phoneme— which pertains to that [letter *ra*] alone and to that which resides within the vowel *ṛ*— it is the universal (*sāmānya*) consisting of the mere *ra* that is indicated here, and not [the specific instances].

The manifestation of the *repha* is indeed of the nature of a phoneme (*varṇa*). By this, the substitution of *ṇ* is established even in cases such as *tisṛṇām*, *catasṛṇām*, *mātṛṇām*, and *pitṛṇām*, because that same commonality of the sound *ra* exists even in the vowel *ṛ*. This might be argued:

In the syllable *ṛ*, there are three constituent phonemes; in the middle of these is the *repha*, which consists of half a mora (*ardhamātrā*), and it is indicated precisely by the commonality of the sound *ra*.

It is established. To resolve the objection that [the rule] would fail because of the intervention of that *avarṇa*-portion which follows the letter *r*, there is the following explanatory passage (*jñāpaka*): namely, that this [mention of *kṣubhna* etc. is for the purpose of prohibiting the substitution of *ṇ* in the *kṣubhnādi* group.

He recites the words *nṛnamana* and *tṛpranoti*; by this it is indicated that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs even when there is an intervention by a portion containing the letter *ṭh*. For otherwise, the recitation of those two [words] there would be purposeless.

It might be so, because of the absence of attainment (*prāpti*), and because prohibitions are preceded by attainment. Even though the specific manifestation of the sound *ra* (*repha*) consisting of the phoneme itself is being indicated, he says "Or rather" (*atha vā*) and so forth in order to show that it is established. This is because of the indication of the commonality of the sound *ra* (*raśruti-sāmānya*) introduced in the preceding rule.
By means of the subsequent example (*parayā*), it was indicated that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs even when there is an intervention; however,
the distinction here is that it occurs only when there is no intervention by a vowel (*ṛ*) as prescribed in the rule (*sūtra*).

Others, however, say that all these counter-arguments are formulated by relying on the position that [the *ṭakit* rule] applies to the apprehension of a single portion of a phoneme (*varṇaikadeśagrahaṇapakṣa*), and this is incorrect; for, according to the position relied upon in the rules for the augment *ṭh*, the augment *ṇuṭ*, the substitution of *l* (*lādeśa`), and the modification of *ṛ* (*vināma`), [the rule does not apply] to the vowel *ṛ*.

It was stated that "it must be refuted" (vā. 1); it is therefore appropriate to refute it right there. Otherwise, by the commentator (vṛttikāra), having accepted the position of non-perception and yet proceeding to offer a refutation even regarding the position of perception, he would display nothing but a lack of skill.
One's own [nature] would be made manifest.
5. *Hayavaraṭ*. Regarding its inclusion [in the alphabet], it occurs by means of the single letter *ṭ* in the rule *śaś chāe ṭi*; here, [the reference is] to *śaś chāe ṭi*.

(8.4.63) This should be understood as an illustration of the rule regarding specific injunctions (*pradeśavākya*). The intended meaning here is that in such references, the inclusion is made by means of the vowel *a*, and not by means of any other phoneme; however, this does not apply to the inclusion by the vowel *a* within this very sūtra itself.

It occurs [as follows]: because in the rule *ṭh-ḍ-k-up-v-ā-ha-num-v-ay-āve’pi* (8.4.2), as well as in *dīrghād-aṭi* (8.3.9), the presence of the letter *a* is intended for the sake of *ghaṇ*. Now, regarding *luṅ-laṅ-lṛṅkṣvaḍ-udāttaḥ* (6.4.71):

Why, then, does the inclusion [of the *ś*] not also occur here by means of the letter *a*? Because of the rule: "Before *sit*, even when there is intervention by *aṭ*" (Pāṇini 7.3.63). For in this pratyāhāra, since the letters beginning with *a* are considered different from it, there would have to be another *aṅga* [element] according to the paribhāṣā concerning the final vowel (*alo'ntyaparibhāṣā*).
Because each [element] individually lacks the designation *aṭ*, and because the substitutes (*ādeśa*) such as *ā* and so forth apply to each one individually;

thus, since they would be included by the mention of the final [element], the intervention of *aṭ* would not be possible. Now, even if they lack the designation individually, it might be assumed that the status of being a substitute applies to them collectively.

In this way, because there would be multiple *al* sounds, it would result in a replacement for the entire [stem]; and if that were so, the original substitute (*sthānin*) *s* would no longer exist. Consequently, in the case of *abhy-a-ṣuṇot*, by what could there be an intervention for which the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) would occur? Now, consider the rule: *ṭhārdhadhātukasyeḍ valādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.35).

Why is this [the letter *t*] not included here by means of the vowel *i*? Because of the explicit mention in the rule "tatra vidita iti ca" (Pāṇini 5.1.43). For if this were a pratyāhāra (abbreviated compound), then according to the rule "ādeḥ parasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.54), one of the letters beginning with *i* would have to be substituted for the initial *t*. Such being the case, [the rule would apply].
And thus, the form "viditam" is not tenable.
Now, why is there no inclusion by the vowel *i* in the rule "dīdhīvevīṭām" (Pāṇini 1.1.6)?
[As in the forms] "jayati" and "sambhavati"?

This is because of such indications as "ṭhava-harati" and so forth; for if this were a mere *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated compound), such indications would be impossible, precisely because [in that case] the substitution of *guṇa* would be prohibited.

Desiring to point out the fault that arises when the letter *r* follows the letter *y* in its formal instruction (*upadeśa*), he says: "In the case of *ṭhayaṃ*" and so forth. However, the instruction of *ṭh* [in *ṭhaj*] occurs because it is included among the semi-vowels (*vāl*).
Thus, from the rule *jīveradānuk* (Pāṇini 3.2.163), we derive *jīradānuḥ*; and from *godhāyāḥ ḍhrak* (Pāṇini 4.1.129), [we derive *gaudheraḥ*].
In the word *gaudhera*, the purpose [of including *ra*] is so that the elision of *v* and *y* prescribed by *ṭhlopo vyor vali* (Pāṇini 6.1.66) may occur,
and so that the letter *v* is not included when *ra* is mentioned; for if the *repha* (*r*) were situated before the *va*...

If it were taught [after the *ra*], then in the case of *devitvā* and *videviṣati*, the *kit* designation might optionally apply by virtue of the rule "ṭhralo vyupadhāddhalādeḥ saṃśca" (Pāṇini 1.2.26). Now, one might object: even if the *ra* is taught after the *ya*, [the fault remains].
Is it not the case that the letter *va* is indeed included by the mention of *ra*, since it is also taught among the *jaś* sounds?
This is not so; for the two are distinct because they are produced by different qualities (*guṇa*), and their difference is established.
