As it has been said: "They maintain that the phonemes are produced by distinct efforts. This is because, due to being semivowels (*antaḥstha*), one [the *y*] has a slightly contacted articulation (*īṣatspṛṣṭakaraṇa*), while the other [the *v*], being a contact consonant (*sparśa*), has a fully contacted articulation (*spṛṣṭakaraṇa*).
...because of that. And this *va* is a dental-labial (*dantoṣṭhya*).
As for that which is intended [in the Māheśvara Sūtra] as "ṭh jabagaḍadaś" (Mā. Sū. 10), it should be understood as labial (*oṣṭhya*). But [one might object]: by means of the letter *va*—
This [letter] does not follow the letter *ya*, but rather follows the letter *va*. Why then is it said that it follows the letter *ya*?
Because the word "following" (*para*) is used even when there is an intervention, as in the expression "after childhood" (*bālyāt param*).

There is no fault in [calling this] "the state of being after" (*vṛddhatva*). Here, even though the state of being after (*vṛddhabhāva*) is intervened by the letter *y*, the word *para* (after) applies.

He asks: "If it is taught as being after the letter *y*, then what follows? and answers with the words "by the inclusion of *ya* and *ra*" (*tasya yargrahaṇena*), etc., regarding this technical term *yar*.

"By means of grasping and uttering"—that is, by means of grasping and uttering this technical name (*saṃjñā*). Alternatively, it means "by means of grasping and taking up the names (*saṃjñā*), and by means of grasping and taking up the named objects (*saṃjñin*). [This occurs] "when there is grasping."
When there is grasping (*upādāna*),
by the grasping of that [the latter], there is the grasping of this [the former], because the latter also possesses that designation and because it is included within it.
It leads one to heaven (*svarga*).

In this case, because the place of articulation (*sthāna*) is the same according to the rule "ṛ, ṛ, u, ū, ra, and ṣa are cerebrals," when the letter *na* follows the letter *ra*, the *parasavarṇa* substitute—a cerebral *ṇa*—occurs; for no specific exception has been stated. But if this were so...

The rule *sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ* (in the place [of another], that which is most similar) would be sublated; for is it not the case that the letter *ṇa* is not the most similar to the letter *r*, due to the difference in their effort (*prayatna*)? This is not so; for this is the principle: "the individual phoneme (*vyakti*) is the meaning of the word."

This objection is raised by relying on the *darśana* (the view of the grammatical school). Therefore, in this case, there is no room for concern regarding sublation (*bādha*) by means of non-statement (*aparibhāṣā*), because the operation of that [rule] occurs only where both the most proximate (*antaratama*) and the least proximate (*anantaratama*) are found. It does not [apply here].

And here there exists an internal [rule] (*antaratama*), because with respect to a manifested entity (*vyakta-padārtha*), a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) applies to each individual instance (*pratilakṣyam*). Due to infinity (*ānantya*), not all defining characteristics can be explicitly stated. In that regard, this is the defining characteristic concerning this subject matter.

If [the rule] were not to apply even to the *ṇakāra* which is most proximate due to the difference in effort (*prayatnabheda*), then for whom would it be useless? Therefore, this paribhāṣā should be understood to apply when the universal (*jāti*) is the word-meaning (*padārtha*), and not when the individual substance (*dravya*). As in: "madrahṛdo bhadrahradaḥ. [This concerns] the vowels (*ac*).
Since this *repha* follows after the letter *ha*, it becomes subject to doubling (*dvirvacana*), as the rule "after *cha*,

there is doubling of *ra* and *ha*" (Pāṇini 8.4.46) follows the word *yaḥ* from the preceding rule "before a nasal, *ya* and *ra* may optionally become nasals" (Pāṇini 8.4.45). Thus, when doubling occurs, [the result is] of two [consonants].

There would be the hearing of the *repha* (the sound *r*). If it is argued that by the rule *ṭhro ri* (Pāṇini 8.3.14), there will be the elision of one of them, we say no; for when an elision is to be applied, the doubling (*dvirvacana*) is not yet established as valid. [This is because of the rule] *halo yamāṃ yami lopaḥ*.
(8.4.64) If that is so, by this [rule] there will be the elision of the single *i* sound; for when this elision is established, reduplication occurs. Even so, in one alternative, of two...

The hearing of two *repha*s would result [as a fault], for in that context, the term "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) follows from [Pāṇini 8.4.62] *ṭhjhayo ho’nyatarasyām*. Even if that [term] were not to follow, even so—
By the force of the rule prescribing reduplication, the elision will not occur; for otherwise, the prescription of reduplication would be purposeless.
In the case of *ṭhkuṇḍaṃ rathena*, by the rule *anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.58),
since no other *parasavarṇa* is possible for it, the *repha* (the sound *r*) itself would be the *parasavarṇa* of the *repha*.
This is because of the principle that "there are no homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*) for *repha*, *ūṣman*, or *ṇ*."

Nor should it be suspected that the *repha* has no homogeneous (*savarṇa*) counterpart; for that was stated with reference to other phonemes, since other phonemes possess different places of articulation (*sthāna*) and efforts (*prayatna*) as the case may be. However, among the individual instances of the *repha*, [they are homogeneous].
There is indeed homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) by virtue of mutual dependence, because they possess the same place and effort of articulation (*tulyasthānaprayatnatvāt*).
Others, however, say: "In *ṭhyayi*, the *anusvāra* should become the nasal *ṇakāra* as its homogeneous substitute (*parasavarṇa*), because of the identity of their place of articulation."
Thus they describe it; however, this is incorrect. For one does not become a *savarṇa* (homogeneous) sound merely by having a similar place of articulation. What then?
By having both a similar place of articulation and a similar effort (*prayatna*). And the effort of the letter *ra* is not similar to that of the letter *ṇa*.

Because the letter *repha* is slightly contacted (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*) and the letter *ṇakāra* is fully contacted (*spṛṣṭa*). Thus, when the opponent has raised an objection based on the view that the individual entity (*vyakti*) is the meaning of the word, [the following is said regarding] the universal (*jāti*)—

Desiring to state the resolution by relying on the meaning of the word (*padārtha*), he says: "This is not a fault," and so forth. "In the *ākṛti*" means in the *jāti* (universal). For some, the word-meaning is the universal (*jāti*); for others, it is the substance (*dravya*); but for Pāṇini, both are so, according to the requirements of the linguistic data (*lakṣya*). That [is the case] in certain instances...

Something must be resorted to as the referent. In that regard, when the universal (*jāti*) is resorted to as the word-meaning, it is the universal alone that is denoted by the word; however, because it is inseparable from them, the individuals (*vyakti*) which are its substrata are cognized, since a universal cannot be cognized without its substratum.

In this view, properties such as being the substituendum (*sthānitva*), being the substitute (*ādeśatva*), posteriority (*paratva*), and non-intervention (*avyavahitatva*)— which are useful for the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of words— are mediated through the individual (*vyakti*). Therefore...
The rule beginning with "ṭhyaro'nunāsike'nunāsiko vā" (Pāṇini 8.4.45), while being applied, operates only upon individual instances that possess the universal.

It functions [therein]; thus, through that functioning, it becomes manifested in the universal (*jāti*). Furthermore, among those individuals, there is no proximity or remoteness with respect to the universal such that it would function only in some and not in all;
for [the universal] is connected [to them all].

Because it is not distinct [from that]. Therefore, when it operates there, provided it is not sublated by another statement or by logic, it operates everywhere. And thus, having operated, it has operated upon the whole.

It occurs "once" (*sakṛt*); that is, a single time and not repeatedly, because the purpose of the grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) is fulfilled by its application just once. In this view, [the rule] *yaro 'nunāsike 'nunāsiko vā* applies.

(8.4.45) How could this definition function? Does it apply without distinction to all objects whatsoever that possess a genus, or does it apply with distinction only to some? If it were without distinction, that same fault would remain as before.

If it must be stated with a qualification, then it would follow that [the substitute] is qualified; therefore, he says: "ṭhyaro'nunāsike," etc. By this, the *sthānāntaratama-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding the most similar substitute in place of the original) [is applied].

He shows that by virtue of its proximity (*upasthāna*), it operates only toward those [objects] which are most proximate (*antaratama*) and not toward others— by means of the passage beginning with "Therefore,
by this," and so forth. Precisely because it operates only toward those most proximate, for that reason, by this definition...

Those sounds which are the nearest (*antaratama*) to *ga* and the others by virtue of both place of articulation (*sthāna*) and quality (*guṇa*), namely *ṅ* and the rest, are prescribed as nasalized (*anunāsika*).
"According to their respective [correspondents]" (*yathāsvam*).

Thus: "according to their own" means that those [sounds] which are most similar to others are prescribed for them. In the phrase "of *ga* and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes *ja* and the other [velars].
In the phrase "the *ṅ* and so forth," the word "and so forth" likewise includes the nasalized sounds such as *ñ*.

They are grasped there as being most similar both in terms of place and quality. For example, for *ga*, *ja*, *ḍa*, *da*, and *ba*, the corresponding [nasals] are *ṅ*, *ñ*, *ṇ*, *na*, and *ma* respectively.
Thus, according to the rule "the sounds *ṭha*, *ku*, *ha*, and *visarjanīya* are gutturals," the *ga* and *ṅ* sounds share the same [place of articulation].
The throat (*kaṇṭha*) is the place of articulation.

According to the rule "ṭ, th, c, u, y, ś are palatals" (*tālavya*), the letters *ja* and *ña* are palatal. According to the rule "ṛ, ṭ, u, ra, ṣ are cerebrals" (*mūrdhanya*), the letters *ṅ* and *ṇ* are... [cerebrals].
The *mūrdhan* (cerebrals) [are produced at the palate]. According to the rule "ṭh-l-tu-la-sa are dentals," the sounds *da* and *na* are dental.

According to the rule "u-p-u-padhmānīya are labials," the sounds *ba* and *ma* are labial. However, the *guṇa* (articulatory effort) for all these is the same; namely, "the articulation (*karaṇa*) of the *sparśas* (stops) is *spṛṣṭa* (complete contact)."

Thus: "The consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma* are the *sparśas* (stops). But those which are neither by place of articulation nor by quality"—this refers back to the term "most similar" (*antaratama*). This is connected with what is to be stated later by the phrase "all these are excluded."
The non-prescription of these [substitutes] is itself their exclusion, as expressed by the phrase "merely by place" or "merely by quality.
Even there, the requirement "the most similar" (antaratama) is expected.
And the connection is as before. In that case, however, there is neither similarity by place nor by quality [to determine the substitute].
The nasalized sounds (*anunāsika*) are as follows:

among *ga*, *ja*, *ḍa*, and *na*, the letters *ya*, *va*, *la*, and *na* are nasalized; there are also those that are non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*), and these are indeed the closest [substitutes] for them by virtue of their place of articulation (*sthāna*) and quality (*guṇa*). However, the mention of "nasalized" is...
In the sūtra "ṭhyaro'nunāsike" (Pāṇini 8.4.45) and others, because the *anunāsika* is prescribed as a substitute (*ādeśa*),

there is a closest correspondence based on place of articulation (*sthāna*) between the letter *ga* and *ka*, and between the letter *ya* and *ya*, respectively, since their respective places of articulation are the throat and the palate.

It does not exist; for the phonemes *ja* and *la* have the palate and the teeth as their points of articulation (*sthāna*), while *ḍa* and *ya* have, respectively, the throat and the palate as their points of articulation, and the head, teeth, and lips as their points of articulation. This is also the case with respect to their qualities (*guṇa*).

There is no immediate proximity [of phonetic similarity] here: because the *ga*-sounds and others have a complete contact (*spṛṣṭa*) mode of articulation, while the *ya*-sounds and others have a slight contact (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*) mode of articulation; for there is a statement [to this effect]: "The semi-vowels (*antasthā*) have a slight contact as their mode of articulation. The semi-vowels are *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*. They are the most proximate [substitutes] merely by virtue of their place of articulation.

The nasals (*anunāsika*). For example: among the [consonants] *ja*, *da*, *ba*, and *na*, the [nasalized] *ya*, *la*, and *va* are the nasals. Here, the letter *ya* has the same place of articulation as the letter *ja*; this is because both have the palate (*tālu*) as their place of articulation. The letter *la* has the same place of articulation as the letter *da*; this is because both have the teeth (*danta*) as their place of articulation. The letter *va* has the same place of articulation as the letter *ba*.
Because both have the lips as their place of articulation. Even though the labio-dental *va* has the teeth as an additional place of articulation, nevertheless,
since the lips are the common place for both, the similarity based on that [shared locus] certainly exists.

Regarding the similarity between the letters *u* and *o*: the place of articulation for *u* is the lips, whereas for *o* it is both the throat and the lips, according to the statement, "The letters *ṭha* and *au* have the throat and the lips as their places of articulation.
Nevertheless, the place of articulation for *ya* and *ta* is equally the lips.

The state of being the closest (āntaratamya) certainly occurs. And just as there is closeness between those two [the dental *t* and the palatal *c*] despite the difference in their place of articulation (*sthāna*), so too is it between the letters *ba* and *va*. Those that are closest by virtue of having the same quality (*guṇa*) alone are, for example, *ṅ*, *ṇ*, and *n* in relation to *j*, *b*, and *d* respectively; this is because all of them share the quality of being "contacted" (*spṛṣṭa*).

There is no internal similarity among them in terms of their place of articulation (*sthāna*); for the *ja*-group consonants have, respectively, the palate, the lips, and the roof of the mouth as their places of articulation, whereas the *ṅ-ṇ-n-m* group have the throat, the roof of the mouth, the teeth, and the nose as their places of articulation. [Regarding the phrase] "in this manner" (*ittham*) and so forth: the particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*). Since it is thus in terms of place of articulation—
Those which are the most similar by virtue of both [place and effort] are alone prescribed by this rule; all others, however, are excluded.
Therefore, the letter *ṇa* is not the most similar to the letter *ra* by place alone.

The closest relationship between the two [the letter *ṛ* and the letter *ra*] is based on place of articulation alone, because both have the same place of articulation, namely the head (*mūrdhan*). However, there is no closeness in terms of quality (*guṇa*), due to the difference in qualities such as being "contacted" (*spṛṣṭa*) and so forth.
[Furthermore,] for the letter *ṛ*, [there is a relationship] with the letters *ya* and *ra*.

"In the case of *rbhāva* existing"—this is the reason for the attainment of the *yaṇ*-substitution. "The *yaṇ*-substitution has been attained" means that there is reduplication. For that [reduplication] occurs to the *repha* because it is included within the *yaṇ*, just as it does for other *yaṇ*s. "That..."
And so forth. Regarding the reduplication [of a consonant], the status of the letter *r* as a cause (*nimitta*) is directly taught (*sākṣāt śiṣṭa*),
being explicitly prescribed (*pratyakṣa-vihita*), because the rule "after an *ac*, following *r* or *h*" (Pāṇini 8.4.46) prescribes reduplication by taking the letter *r* as the cause.

But that which is to be performed [by a rule] is inferred from its inclusion within another; for as it is stated [in the *Kātantra-pariśiṣṭa* 95]: "Between the perceptually established (*pratyakṣa*) and the inferred (*anumita*), the perceptually established is stronger. Thus, having taken the directly prescribed *ṛ* as the cause (*nimitta*), the doubling [of the following consonant] occurs.
Because of the specific injunction; for that which is to be accomplished by another [operation] is inferred through its inclusion therein.

According to the rule, "Between what is directly perceived and what is inferred, the directly perceived is stronger" (Kātantra Paribhāṣā 95), the status of being a cause (*nimittabhāva*) is directly prescribed for the letter *r*.

The secondary application (dvirvacana) is set aside; for example, in the case of "Let the Brāhmaṇas be fed; let Māṭhara and Kauṇḍinya serve the food," here, because Māṭhara and Kauṇḍinya are directly enjoined as the instruments for the act of serving, their status as Brāhmaṇas—which was merely inferred in relation to the act of eating—is superseded.

That status as a means [of accomplishment] is sublated. If this is so, there is a fault regarding *dadhi-udaka* and similar forms. For in the rule "iko yaṇ aci" (Pāṇini 6.1.77), since the vowel (*ac*) is included within the term *aj*, the status of the vowel *i* as a cause for the substitution of *yaṇ* is merely inferred; however, the substitution of *yaṇ* itself is directly taught [by the sūtra], as in the word "ikaḥ."

Because it is prescribed by taking that which begins with *sākṣāt* as the object of the action; and consequently, the status of being a cause (*nimittabhāva*) for the suffix *ika* is set aside by that which is directly taught (*sākṣācchiṣṭa*). In that case, because the individual (*vyakti*) is dependent upon the word-meaning (*padārtha*)—
This is not a fault. It has been stated that when the individual (vyakti) is the word-meaning, the definition applies to each specific instance.

This fault does not arise because the definition is indeed one and the same, which finds its application in cases such as *arkka* and *markka*. Therefore, even though [in words like] *madrahra* and so forth...

Although it does not prescribe doubling (dvirvacana), there is nonetheless no consequence of futility. By the phrase "the letter *r* is not said to be doubled," the particle *iti* indicates that the meaning just mentioned serves as the reason for the absence of doubling.

Regarding the rule *anusvārasya* and so forth: it is not only the rule *yaro 'nunāsike 'nunāsiko vā* (Pāṇini 8.4.45) that, as the most proximate (*antaratama*), prescribes [the substitution] only once;
rather, there is also the rule *anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ* (8.4.58).

58) "This also" is the meaning of the word *api*. It might be argued: "Even though [the rule] prescribes the most similar sound (*antaratama*), nevertheless, in this case, there must indeed be a homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*) with the letter *r*, because that too is the most similar. To this [it is said]:
He says: "And not," and so forth. The connection is: "And there is no homogeneous [letter] for the *repha*.
Of what kind is it that does not exist? It is "the closest relative (*antaratama*) of the *anusvāra*.
This means: the most similar to the *anusvāra*. For this reason, [the rule] does not apply to *kuṇḍam*.

In the word *rathena*, there is a substitution with a homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*). But how can it be the closest homogeneous sound (*anusvārāntaratama*) when there is no homogeneous sound for the letter *r*? It is said: for the letter *r*, the letter *r* itself is the homogeneous sound, and no other phoneme is. And that [letter *r*] is not the closest homogeneous sound for the *anusvāra*.

This is due to the difference in place of articulation and the difference in quality. For the place of articulation of the letter *r* is the palate (*mūrdhan*), whereas for the *anusvāra*, it is held that "the *anusvāra*, the *ya-mas*, and the *nāsikya*s [are nasal]," but not so for others. Even though the third and fourth letters of the classes (*varṇa*), the semivowels (*antaḥstha*), the letter *h*, and the *anusvāra* [are also nasal].

And since the *yama*s— which are the third and fourth [consonants] of each class— as well as the *nāsikya*s, possess the qualities known as external efforts (*bāhyaprayatna*), such as being produced with a closed glottis (*saṃvṛtakaṇṭha*), having *nāda* as their secondary emission (*anupradāna*), and being voiced (*ghoṣavat*),
the letter *repha* (r) is a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) sound for the *anusvāra*, because it is the most similar to it among those possessing such qualities as a closed glottis.

Nevertheless, this definition of "most similar" (*antaratama*) is not capable of prescribing a *parasavarṇa* substitution based on quality alone. Where there are *parasavarṇas* for the *anusvāra* that are most similar both in terms of place of articulation and quality— as in the case of *śaṅkitaḥ*— [the rule applies].

In this context, the term "obstructed" (*kuṇṭhita*) is used because its purpose has been fulfilled. Here, even by way of place of articulation (*sthāna*), the anusvāra—whose place of articulation is the nose—is most similar to *ṅ* and *ṇ*, since those two also have the nose as their place of articulation.

This is according to the statement: "The sounds *ṭh*, *ñ*, *ma*, *ṅ*, *ṇ*, *na*, and *ṇa* have their own respective places of articulation and also have the nose as their place of articulation. It is also so by way of quality (*guṇa*).

Because they are followed by the previously mentioned qualities of the anusvāra, according to the statement: "As are the third [letters] of the classes, so are the fifth"; for by this [rule], namely "the third and fourth of the classes," and so forth.

Those qualities of the third letters of the consonant classes, such as *ga* and so forth, which were stated by the author to be common to the *anusvāra*, are here specified for *ṅka* and so forth. One should substitute the *repha* even when it is merely similar in quality, provided it occurs more than once.

That [suffix] is applied. It is not stated that it is applied repeatedly, on the grounds that repeated application would be purposeless. Regarding "uraḥkeṇa" and so forth: [it means] one who cries out with the chest (*uraḥ kāyati*), or one who protects the chest (*uraḥ pāti*). [The roots are] *kai* in the sense of sound (DhP 916) and *pā* in the sense of protection.
By these two [roots], according to *Pāṇini* 3.2.3 (*ātaścopasarge*), the suffix *ka* is applied;

by 6.4.64 (*ātolopa iṭi ca*), the vowel *ā* is elided; then follows the formation of an *upapada* compound, the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*), and finally, by 8.2.66 (*sasajuṣo ruḥ*), the substitution of *ru*.

For that [word-final *r*], according to the rules "the *visarjanīya* occurs before a hard consonant (*kha-ra*) or at the end of a word" (Pāṇini 8.3.15) and "before *k* or *p*, [the *visarjanīya* is replaced by] *k* or *p*" (Pāṇini 8.3.37),
the *visarjanīya* or the *upadhmānīya* [are substituted] as appropriate.
The two jihvāmūlīya sounds.

6. laṇ | This letter *ṇ* is written twice—thus before [the rule] and thus after it. In this regard, a doubt arises concerning the mentions of *aṇ* (the *aṇ*-pratyāhāra) and the mentions of *aṇ* (the individual letter *a* and *ṇ*): would they apply by virtue of the former?
Or [is it] by the subsequent [letter]? Therefore, for the purpose of excluding that [possibility], he says: "The *iṇ*-grahaṇas," and so forth.

In this regard, it has been explained in the rule *ṭhaiuṇ* (Māheśvara Sūtra 1) how all *iṇ*-grahaṇas are taken with the subsequent *ṇ*. However, those *aṇ*-grahaṇas which are [taken] with the subsequent *ṇ*...
These [rules] have been established previously. What, then, are they? They are:
*ṣṭhūlopa pūrvasya dīrgho’ṇaḥ* (P. 6.3.111), *ke’ṇaḥ* (P.
7.4.13), *aṇo’pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ* (P. 8.4.57), and *uraṇ raparaḥ* (P. 1.1.51).

Regarding the mentions of *aṇ* in these sūtras: first, in that preceding sūtra, the inclusion of the word *vṛḍha* among the *dṛḍha*-group [of words] is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that "the mention of *aṇ* does not apply to what follows. For if it were to apply to what follows, the form would not be *vṛḍhaḥ*.

[If that were so,] it would follow that the inclusion of the form *vṛḍha* in the list beginning with *dṛḍha* would be untenable; for [the root] *bṛhū* "to exert" (DhP 1347), when followed by the suffix of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), [would undergo] the substitution of *at* and *gh*.

When the substitutions for *ṣṭu*, *ṭha*, *ḍha*, and elision have been performed, the form becomes *ṭhvṛḍha*. Furthermore, since the rule *acaśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.28) is brought into proximity by the explicit mention of "long" (*dīrgha*), the vowel *ac* alone must undergo lengthening.
And thus, if [the lengthening] were to apply to the subsequent [vowel], it would also apply to the vowels falling within the interval.
If lengthening were intended, one would have simply used the term *ajjhan* to avoid ambiguity. Alternatively, one might not even have used that;
for by the rule "ṭhacaśca" alone, the lengthening of all vowels would be established.

Therefore, by the force of the mention of *aṇ*, it is understood that the reference is to the preceding [rule]. Even by the rule "ke'ṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.13), since it is impossible for consonants (*hal*) to follow *k* when they are *aṇ*s, a short vowel (*hrasva*) is prescribed only for vowels (*ac*).
In that case, if the shortening of all vowels were intended, [the author] would have used [a term] for the sake of avoiding ambiguity—
One should simply include the mention of *j*. Alternatively, one need not even do that;
for the desired meaning is established by the very rule "ṭhacaśca" (Pāṇini 6.4.139), which is brought to mind by the mention of the short vowel (*hrasva*).
Furthermore, the third rule also prescribes an anusvāra for an *aṇ* at the end of a word, and [this is] not...

Since there are hal-sounds at the end of words that are not *aṇ*, the nasalization (*anunāsika*) should be prescribed for vowels alone. In that case, if the intention were to prescribe nasalization for all vowels, one would simply use the term "vowel" (*ac*) to avoid ambiguity. Or rather—

One should not do even that; for it is only vowels (*ac*) that receive the designation *pragṛhya*, not consonants (*hal*). In that case, by the maxim of "negation joined with *nañ* or *iva*," since there is a prohibition of the *pragṛhya* status, the operation will be understood to apply to only those [sounds] similar to them, namely the vowels. Therefore...

In that case as well, because of the lack of capacity [to refer to the subsequent rule], the mention of *aṇ* is understood to belong to the preceding [rule] alone. Furthermore, even in the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ* (P. 1.1.51), the citation *hotṛpraśāstṛṇām* (P. 6.4.11) indicates that "here, the mention of *aṇ* does not belong to the subsequent [rule]. For if the mention of *aṇ* belonged to the subsequent [rule], [the form *hotṛpraśāstṛṇām* would be impossible].

By the rule *ṭhNāmi* (Pāṇini 6.4.3), a long vowel followed by *ra* would be substituted; however, in that case, the form *praśāstṝṇām* would not be possible as an illustration. Furthermore, no consonants other than *repha* (*r*) are ever prescribed in any grammatical treatise as substitutes for the *ṛ*-vowel when followed by a vowel (*aṇ*). For instance:

By the rule *ṭhiko yaṇaci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77), a *ṛ* would be replaced by *ra*. However, there is no difference whether the *ṛ* in place of the vowel *ṛ*—as in *ṭhkartrartham* and so on—is prescribed as followed by *ra* (rapara) or not followed by *ra* (arephapara); for once [the substitution] has been made with *ra* following (*kṛte hi rapare*), [the result is the same].

In that case, there ought to be elision of one *r* by the rule *ṭhro ri* (Pāṇini 8.3.14). Therefore, this mention of *aṇ* would also serve only the purpose of [excluding] the subsequent *ṇ*. In that regard, if [the substitution] were to take place in the place of all vowels (*ac*),...

If the substitution of *ra* for *ṇ* were intended for those [rules] currently being prescribed, he would have used the mention of *ac* alone for the sake of avoiding ambiguity. Therefore, it is certain that this mention of *ac* is connected only with the preceding *ṇ*.
"By this [rule], 'aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ' (Pāṇini 1.1.69), there is one [instance]; and here,
in the rule 'ṝta iddhātoḥ' (7.1.100), it is not at all possible for the vowel *ṛ* to be a grāhaka of its homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*), because it is itself being taught (*bhāvyamānatvāt*).
This is not so, because of the prohibition: "An *aṇ* being taught [as a substitute] does not include its homogeneous (*savarṇa*) counterparts" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 35). For he will state there:
"And this *aṇ* is not being taught as a substitute; rather, it is for the purpose of precluding other substitutes."

"It is the very own nature that is being affirmed. Regarding the form *acīkṛtat*, [the root] *kṛt* in the sense of "uttering" (*saṃśabdane*) from the Dhātupāṭha (1653) takes the *ṇic* suffix of the curādigaṇa; then there is the *luṅ* tense, and by Pāṇini 3.1.48, *cleḥ ṇiśridruḥ*, the *cli* is replaced by *aṅ*.
By the rule *caṅ* [the suffix *caṅ* is applied]; by *ṭhurṛtaḥ*, the letter *aṅ* is replaced by *ṛ*; there is the elision of the *ṇi* suffix;
by *caṅ* (Pāṇini 6.1.11), reduplication occurs; by *urat* (7.4.66), the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* takes place; *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* applies; and by *sanvallaghuni*.
Thus, by [Pāṇini 7.4.93], there is the substitution of *i*, and by [Pāṇini 7.4.94], there is the lengthening of the short vowel.

Now, why is it that the mention of *ac* (vowels) is not simply omitted? The intention is that where [the rule] is applied, no doubt whatsoever arises. What is the reason? It is because it cannot be done in this way; therefore, he says:

"For even among the semivowels (*antaḥstha*), etc."— because of the statement that "the semivowels are divided into two types: those excluding *ra*, [namely] with nasality (*sānunāsika*) and without nasality (*niranunāsika*)," the letters *ya*, *va*, and *la* are [considered] with nasality.
Because of the statement [in the *Śikṣā*], "and so forth," the *ya*, *va*, and *la* sounds are of two types, distinguished by being nasalized (*sānunāsika*) or non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*).
In the *pratyāhāra* [formula] as well, would they be taught as the non-nasalized ones, or as the nasalized ones? If...
Are they non-nasalized? In examples such as *sayaṅyantā*, when the *anusvāra* is replaced by a homogeneous nasal (*parasavarṇa*)—

namely, a nasalized *y* and so forth— in accordance with the rule "The *anusvāra* is replaced by the *parasavarṇa* before a *yay* [consonant]" (Pāṇini 8.4.58), there is no substitution of *y* because those [nasalized consonants] are not taught within the *pratyāhāra* [of *yay*].

The doubling (*dvirvacana*) of a *yar* sound prescribed by the rule *ṭhānaci ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.47) would not occur. However, when the term *aṇ* is included [in the definition of *pratyāhāra*], it includes its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*), and thus the doubling of these sounds is also established. But even if the doubling has taken place, [the rule] *halo yamāṃ yami lopaḥ* (8.4.64) [would apply].

64) Since the elision (*lopa*) is prescribed for only one [of them], the hearing of three *yakāra*s is simply not possible. What, then, is the purpose of the rule for doubling (*dvirvacana*)? This is not so; for that elision is optional, according to *ṭhjhayo ho’nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 8.4.62).

This is because the term *anyatarasyām* (optionally) continues to apply. In that case, in the alternative where there is no elision (*lopa*), all three [sounds] are indeed heard. Now, what if they were taught as being nasalized (*sānunāsika*)?
[The rule] regarding the substitution of a homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*) for the *anusvāra* before a non-nasal consonant (*niranunāsika*) would not apply.
It may be so; because among those [sounds], there is no arrangement [of the nasal quality] in the middle.

Regarding the passage beginning with "In the case of *ha*, *kha*, etc.": the followers of Pāṇini (Pāṇinīyas) maintain that the nasalization (*anunāsikya*) is optional. Wherever they desire it, there they acknowledge the nasalization, and not elsewhere. And in the case of the letter *la*, they [acknowledge] that of the vowel *a*.
It is prescribed [for the vowels],

not for the consonants beginning with *ha*. Regarding the statement "it has the technical designation *it*," the designation *it* is established by the rule "In the grammatical instruction (*upadeśa*), a nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) is designated as *it*" (Pāṇini 1.3.2).
Because of this rule [of the treatise]. By the words "by that" (*tena*) and so forth, he demonstrates the fruit of the vow regarding the nasal (*anunāsika*).

Since the technical designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) is extended to the sounds *ṛ* and *ḷ*, the letter *ṛ* being taken up includes the letter *ḷ* as well; consequently, it is just as in the case of [the rule] *ṭhuraṇ raparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.51).
When the *aṇ* [vowel] is prescribed as the substitute for the vowel *ṛ*, it is followed by *r*; likewise, when it is the substitute for the vowel *lṛ*, it is intended that it be followed by *l*.
Therefore, the nasalized (*anunāsika*) quality is formally asserted [for these vowels]. By this, [the rule] "beginning with *ṭh* together with the final [of its class]" (Pāṇini 1.1.71) [applies].
Thus, in the rule "ṣṭhuran raparaḥ," there is the inclusion of the pratyāhāra "ṭhra," which extends from the letter *r* up to the *a* in *laṇ*.
And in that [pratyāhāra]...
The *aṇ* substitute for the vowel *ṛ* is followed by *r*, whereas that for the vowel *lṛ* is followed by *l*. Consequently, forms such as "tavalkāraḥ" become grammatically justified.

7. [The vowels] *ñ, *ma, *ṅ, *ṇ, *na, and *m: "Its inclusion occurs by means of three [vowels]. Now, why does its inclusion not also occur by means of the vowel *a* in the rule *sṛjidṛśorjhalyamakiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.58)? [It would apply] in the case of *sākṣād-draṣṭari* (Pāṇini 5.2.91).

Because of this [specific] instruction; for if this were a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated compound), then since the substitution of vowels beginning with *a* would be prescribed therein, the word *draṣṭṛ* would not be established.
In that case, here [in the rule] "bhrasjo ropaśrayo ram anyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 6.4.47)...

Why does it not become *repha*? Furthermore, if *ra* has been adopted, how is this certainty reached that it is not *am*? For the *saṃhitā* is the same in both cases; there ought to be doubt as to whether this is *ram* or *am*. [The answer is: Certainty is obtained from the commentary (*vyākhyāna*).
If that is so,

and if it is accepted that an explanatory commentary (*vyākhyāna*) is the cause for determining [the meaning], then for this very reason, in this case and everywhere else regarding matters of this kind, [the same principle applies].
What is the purpose of presenting other excessively voluminous arguments by those who compose such works, when certainty will arise regarding the point of doubt?
As for him who thinks that [the rule] "bhrasjau ropadhayo ram" [applies here]...
If it is argued that, by the rule of established optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the inclusion of the *pratyāhāra* will not occur, then he should be asked this:
"What is the purpose of this mention of *anyatarasyām*? Is the inclusion of *ram* being made optional—i.e., 'optionally *ram*'?"

Is it grasped [as such]? Or is the suffix *ram* optionally prescribed for one of the two? If it is the mention of *ram*, then this is understood to be a mention of the phoneme *r* itself, together with the indicatory letter (*anubandha*) *m*, and not as a technical abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*).
According to this established *vibhāṣā*, the augment *ram* would not occur optionally;

for the purpose of the option has already been fulfilled by the mention of *anyatarasyām*. Indeed, there is no second occurrence of the term *anyatarasyām* by which the rule itself might be made optional, whereas in the other alternative, [the desired form] is established.
This is an optional rule (*pākṣika*); however, that which they maintain— that by means of a fixed option (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*) this refers only to the letter *ra* with the indicatory letter *m*,
and not to the *pratyāhāra*— is untenable.

Because the mention of "either one" (*anyatarasyām*) serves solely for the purpose of providing an option regarding its application. Furthermore, from what source is this determination derived that this is a *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā* (a restricted option)?
If you say it is from the commentary (*vyākhyāna*), then what now?

"By relying on tradition, it will not be necessary to include this as a pratyāhāra through [the rule of] *vyākhyāna* alone; therefore, this [objection] is trivial. For it is observed that a pratyāhāra is also formed by means of the letter *ṭh* and the letter *ñ*."

If this is so, for what purpose was it stated that [the suffix] is by means of three [letters]? It is to demonstrate that in the rule "ṭhñamantāḍḍaḥ" (Daiva-Upaniṣad 5.7), the inclusion of a *pratyāhāra* is not necessarily required; for here, even though the actual forms of the letters *ñ* and *m* are employed, [the suffix *ḍa*] may also be applied from elsewhere without the inclusion of a *pratyāhāra*.
The suffix *ḍa* is indeed established after a word beginning with *ma* and ending with [a consonant], due to the application of the rule of "great scope" (*bahulādhikāra*).
Now, even so, one should have said simply "with four" (*caturbhiḥ*), because this [suffix] is also [included] by the mention of *ña* in the rule *yamirñamanteṣu*.

[Objection: Because of the observation of the application [of the rule], this is true; if this were said with reference to mere application (*grahaṇamātra*), then it would be so. But this was not stated with the intention of referring to mere application; what then? It refers to a specific application mentioned in the Sūtra.
And this is not the application mentioned in the Sūtra; what then? It is the application mentioned in the *āniṭ-kārikā*.

"Some," and so forth. Having reflected that these *pratyāhāra* formations which have just been mentioned might be formed by the very same letter *ñ* that occurs in the rule *jhabhañ* (MbhSū 8), some teachers [hold this view].

They propose the rejection of the letter *m*. Regarding that rejection, their intention is that in rules such as *pumaḥ khayyampare* (Pāṇini 8.3.6), the letter *ñ* should be substituted in place of the letter *m*. Thus...

With the words "ca sati" and so forth, he demonstrates the fault in rejecting the suffixal marker *m* (*makārānubandha*). For if the reading were "ṅño hrasvād aci ṅñuṇ nityam" (Pāṇini 7.1.32), then because the *jha* and *bha* [classes] would also be included within the *pratyāhāra* "ṅña," the *jha* and *bha* sounds would also become substitutes (*āgaminau*)— this is what [the author intends to show].

[The opponent argues: "The rule applies when [the suffix] *dyam* falls [after the root]. Since those two [roots], *jhabh* and *ubh*, do not exist as word-final (*padānta*), the [proposed] solution will not hold. When this has been stated, the following objection must be raised again: "But surely, when the suffix *kvip* is applied to the roots *labh* and *ubj*, both [the resulting forms] indeed exist as word-finals (*padānta*)."

In that case, once the *bakāra* and *jakāra* have been substituted by [the rule] "tasmin ṭhjhalāṃ jaśo'nte" (Pāṇini 8.2.39), how could those two [substitutions] occur? This is the further rebuttal! But surely there would be an inequality because of the absence of the *jhabha* [sounds] in the augment (*āgama*), and likewise...

The three [consonants] *hi*, *ṅ*, and *ṇ* are the augments (*āgaminaḥ*), whereas the augments (*āgamāḥ*) are five: *ṅ*, *ṇ*, *n*, *jha*, and *bha*; therefore, because of this discrepancy in number, there is no "correspondence according to order" (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) between them, according to Pāṇini 1.3.10.
Thus, the correspondence of numbers...

The objection may be raised that there would be a discrepancy in the number of grammatical operations (*deśa*). This is not a fault; for as many *āgamas* as there are in the Sūtra, exactly that many *āgamins* are also recited.
In this regard, without regard for the specific forms to be modified (*lakṣya*), the *āgamas* corresponding to the letters beginning with *ṅ* are applied according to their respective order.

Once the meaning of the Sūtra has been established as "they come into being," the practical application of the work will subsequently occur according to the circumstances. For those scriptures that have transmitters, it will apply to them respectively.
"Since the letters *ṭha*, *jha*, *ka*, and *bha* do not exist as substitutes for those [letters], it follows that the augments (*āgama*) will also not occur"— this further rebuttal must be stated.
Thus, by resolving numerous objections, [the position] of the one who maintains the augments—
The sense is that if the non-existence of the letter *m* were the reason for establishing the non-existence of the traditional authority (*āgama*) as the probandum,
there would be an excessive burden of proof;
therefore, the rejection of the letter *m* is improper.
8. jhabhañ | 9. ghañadhaṣ | 10. jabagaḍadaś |
11. *khaphacchaṭhathacatav*. But surely this [the *tav* group] is already included by the letter *cch*, and since *khaph* are not included therein, for what purpose are they mentioned here?

Regarding the inclusion [of these sounds], he says: "the inclusion of *ṭ*, *kh*, and *ph*," and so forth. The meaning is that these two are included for the purpose of ensuring their incorporation within the subsequent pratyāhāras as well.

In this [grammar], the other *varṇas* (phonemes) are taught once, but the letter *ha* is taught twice. One desiring to know the purpose of its double teaching asks: "Now, for what purpose? and so forth. Regarding the word "snihitvā": [the root] *ṣṇiha* [is used] in the sense of affection (*prīti*).

(dhā.pā. 1200), *ādeḥ ṣṇaḥ snaḥ*, [and] *samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle* (Pāṇini 3.4.21), [the suffix] *ktvā*, [with] *iṭ*. Regarding *alikṣat*: from the root *liha āsvādane* (dhā.pā. 1026), the conditional (*lṛṅ*), *ho ḍhaḥ* (8.2.31), and *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ* [apply].
By the rule *si* (8.2.41), there is the substitution of *k*; by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (8.3.59), there is the substitution of *ṣ*.

[The forms] *rudihi* and *svapihi* are derived from the roots *rud* and *svap* in the imperative (*loṭ*) used for injunctions and so forth. By the rule *ser hy apicca* (3.4.87), the suffix *si* is replaced by *hi*, which is also treated as having an indicatory *p* (*apit*).
Due to the roots belonging to the *adādi* class, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*. Then, by the rule *rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke* (7.2.76), [the augment *iṭ* is added].

Thus, there is the augment *iṭ*. Regarding the form *adāgdhām*: [the root] *daha* (DhP 991), meaning "to reduce to ashes," is used with the suffix *luṅ*; for this, the suffix *cli* is applied; then, by the rule *tasthasthamipām* (3.4.101), the replacement of *tas* by *tām* occurs; finally, *sic* is substituted for *cli*.
There is *vṛddhi* by [Pāṇini 7.2.3] *vadavraja*; *gh* replaces the initial of the root by [Pāṇini 8.2.32] *dāderdhātorghaḥ*; there is the elision of *sic* by [Pāṇini 8.2.26] *jhalo jhali*;
and *t* becomes *dh* by [Pāṇini 8.2.40] *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ*.

By the rule *ṭhjhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* (Pāṇini 8.4.53), the letter *gh* is replaced by *g*. In that case, if the mention [of the substitute] were not present, then because the substitution of *gh* would also be considered asiddha, the *sij* affix would follow a letter other than *jhal* (namely, *g*), and thus its elision by *ṭhjhalo jhali* (8.2.26) would not occur. Therefore, [the mention is necessary].
The instruction of what has already been taught is so that its inclusion may occur in the rules concerning *śal*, *vaḷ*, *jhal*, and *grahaṇa*;
for if these were the purposes, let there simply be the instruction by another [grammarian], since by that alone these objectives would be accomplished.
With the intention that the previous instruction need not be given, he says: "In that case, regarding *hayavaraḍ*," and so forth;
and "Regarding the mentions of *aṭ*," and so forth. If [the letter] were not taught previously, then by the mention of *aṭ*...

And because [the word] *mahat* would not be included by the inclusion of *ca*, in the case of the form *mahān* ("great"), the substitution of *ru*, the nasalization (*anunāsikatva*), the substitution of *ya*, and the elision of *ya* (*yalopa*) would not occur. [The derivation is as follows: from the word *mahat*, the suffix *su* is added;
then, by the rule *ugidacām* (Pāṇini 7.1.70), the augment *num* is inserted; and finally, by the rule *sāntamahataḥ saṃyogasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.10) [the lengthening of the penultimate vowel occurs].

The [suffix] *dīrghaḥ* applies, followed by the elision of the final consonant (*hal*) and the following vowel (*i*, etc.), as well as the final member of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*). When *mahān hi* is established, because the *hakāra* follows, it is included by the mention of *aṭ* [in the rule], and thus [the rule] *dīrghādaṭi samānapade* (Pāṇini 8.3.9) applies.
There is *rutva* (the substitution of *r* for Visarga); by the rule "ṭhāto'ṭi nityam" (Pāṇini 8.3.3), the preceding [Visarga] becomes an anusvāra.
Because it is included by the mention of *aś*, the *repha* (the letter *r*) undergoes *yatva* (the substitution of *y*) according to the rule "bho bhago agho" (Pāṇini 8.3.17), etc.

When [the letter] *ṭh* follows, there is elision of *y* by the rule "aśīti vartamāne ṭhhali sarveṣām" (8.3.22). [This applies to the rules] beginning with "haśi ca" and so forth. This is another purpose for the previous instruction; for if that were not present, in the case of "brāhmaṇo hasati," [the following would occur].
If *ha* were not included in the term *haś*, then in its absence, the substitution of *ū* for *ru* would not occur after that [word]. From the word *brāhmaṇa*, the suffix *su* is added;
by the rule "sasajuṣo ruḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.66), *ru* is substituted for *s*; then by "haśi ca" (6.1.114), the substitution of *ū* occurs; finally, by "ādguṇaḥ," the *guṇa* substitution takes place.

(6.1.87) | "From one" (*ekasmāt*), etc. The ellipsis is that "the following [sounds] are to be understood. This connects with the word *syuḥ* ("they would be") which is to be stated later. In the term *ekasmāt*, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of spatial separation (*digyoga*). [The meaning is: "following after a single phoneme (*varṇa*)."

The meaning is that [sounds] such as the letter *ṅ* would become objects of perception (*grāhya*). Alternatively, the ablative case in "from one" (*ekasmāt*) is used with the elision of a verbal suffix ending in *-lyap*, as in the expression "he looks from the palace" (*prāsādāt prekṣate*); likewise, having brought forward or grasped a single phoneme within the constituent sentences (*pradeśavākya*).
The meaning is that [the letters] beginning with *ṅ* would be the objects of apprehension (*grāhya*). Furthermore, that is a single phoneme (*varṇa*), as in the case of *ṭh eoṅ* (Māheśvara Sūtra 3),

*jh bha ñ* (Māheśvara Sūtra 8), *ai u ṇ* (Māheśvara Sūtra 1), *kh ph ch ṭh th c ṭ t v* (Māheśvara Sūtra 11), and *h y v r ṭ* (Māheśvara Sūtra 5), where [it occurs] together with [those other letters].
The inclusion of the letters beginning with *ṅ* has been explained;
that very [rule] should be understood here as well. Regarding the rule "ṣ from two," one must supply the phrase "the subsequent [letters] are to be taken. Furthermore, as for what was supplied...

The verb *syuḥ* changes its number to the singular to accord with the sense of that [rule]. The meaning is that the letter *ṣ* should be taken after two [letters], having pronounced either "two" (*dvau*) or "after two" (*parau*). The meaning should be understood in this same way in subsequent cases as well. Which, then, are the two? They are *jhabhañ* (Māṇḍūkya Sūtra 8) and *ghaḍhaghaṣ* (Māṇḍūkya Sūtra 9).
In this context, those two by which the inclusion of the letter *ṣ* was stated are precisely these:
"From only three [roots] should *ka*, *ṇa*, and *ma* occur. Furthermore, those three are: *ṛlṛk* (Māṇḍūkī Sūtra 2) and *laṇ* (Māṇḍūkī Sūtra 6).
Regarding the rule *ṭhñamaṅṇanam* (Māṇḍūkya Sūtra 7), those very same [consonants] by which the inclusion of *ka*, etc., was explained, are referred to here as well.
It is stated: "And *ca* and *ya* are to be known [as included] after the four. Those four, moreover, are: *aiāṬc* (Māṇḍūkya Sūtra 4).

In the rule *ṭh-kap-ay* (Māṇḍūkī Sūtra 12), the inclusion of the two letters *c* and *y*—namely, the *c*-sounds and the *y*-sounds—is intended; these are precisely what is meant by "from the five *ra*s" (*hraḥ pañcabhyaḥ*).
By that [rule], there are again five.
Those very [consonants] for which the inclusion of *r* was established in the rule *ṭhśaṣasar* (Māṇḍūkya Sūtra 13) are referred to here by the expression *ṭhśalau ṣaḍbhyaḥ*. Furthermore,
those six are [the consonants mentioned] in the rules *ṭjabaḍadaś* (Māṇḍūkya Sūtra 10) and *hal* (Māṇḍūkya Sūtra 14).
Those by whom the inclusion of the sounds *śa* and *la* has been stated should be understood [as follows].
Thus ends the section on *pratyāhāra*.
Now begins the first quarter (*pāda*) of the first chapter (*adhyāya*).
1. *Vṛddhir ādaic* (Pāṇini 1.1.1).

Some explain this sūtra as consisting of three words: *vṛddhiḥ*, *āt*, and *aic*. Others, however, considering that *ādaij* is a collective (*samāhāra*) dvandva compound of *ācca* and *aic*, [interpret it accordingly].

*vṛddhiḥ*, *ādaic*—this consists of two words. For if there were mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), the plural number would be required because of the multiplicity [of the elements]. But surely, even in the case of collective conjunction (*samāhāra*), [the rule] "after a *dvandva* ending in *cu*, *da*, *ṣa*, or *ha*... [applies]?

By [Pāṇini 5.4.106], the compound-ending suffix *ṭac* would apply; however, it will not occur because the rule for compound-endings is non-mandatory (*anitya*). That non-mandatory nature will be made known in the sixth [chapter]. Now, why does the substitution of *k* for *c* (known as *kutva*)—by [Pāṇini 8.2.30] "the *c* sounds become *k*"—not take place? [Because of the rule] "for *ay-*... [etc.]...

Because of the rule "smayādīni ca chandasi" (Pāṇini 1.4.20), it receives the designation *bha*. Since the word "ādi" (etcetera) denotes a class or type, this word "aiccha" should be understood as belonging to the group beginning with "ayasmaya" and so forth. Now, one might object: in that rule it is stated "in the Vedic language" (*chandasi*), and this [word] is not...

[Objection: Since there is no desire [to apply this rule], why is there the designation "bh" (the technical term for the vowel *a*)? [Response: There is no fault, because "sūtras function like chandas.

In this context, this sūtra might either be purposeless—like the mention of udātta and other accents—or it might be for the purpose of teaching correctness (*sādhvanuśāsana*), whereby the correctness of the word *vṛddhi* and of the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* is declared by this [rule].
Is it for the purpose of restricting usage—that the term *vṛddhi* must be employed only in reference to *ā*, *ai*, and *au*?
Or is it for the purpose of substitution—that the term *vṛddhi* becomes a substitute for *ā*, *ai*, and *au*, or that they become substitutes for it?

Or is it for the purpose of establishing the relationship between an augment and that which is augmented—that the term *vṛddhi* becomes an augment for *ā*, *ai*, and *au*, or that they [become augments] for it?
Regarding the word "tasya" (of that):

is it for the purpose of establishing the relationship between qualifier and qualified—that the term *vṛddhi* is the qualifier of *ādaic*, or that *ādaic* are the qualifiers of it? For here, the fact of having the same case-ending (*ekavibhaktikatva*) is observed.

Furthermore, the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) is observed between two words in the same case-ending, as for example in "a blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*). Or is it for the purpose of establishing the relationship between a name and the named (*saṃjñā-saṃjñi-sambandha*)? For that too is seen between two words in the same case-ending, as for example in "this is a jackfruit tree" (*ayaṃ panasaḥ*). Regarding these, first, as for the initial position...
This is not tenable; for the Teacher, possessing superior knowledge regarding all states of existence,
committed to the welfare of others, with a concentrated mind, having made arrangements for the protection of his disciples, and preceded by auspicious rites—

He composed the sūtras with great effort; therein, it is impossible for even a single syllable to be meaningless, let alone this entire composition of sūtras! Nor can it be understood that the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the term *vṛddhi* and of the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* is being prescribed by this [sūtra].

Because their correctness is established by another grammatical definition; for this word *vṛddhi* is taught without qualification as being derived from the root *vṛdhu* (DhP 759) with the suffix *ktin*.

By the rule *ṭhstriyāṃ ktin* (Pāṇini 3.3.94), the suffix *ktin* is applied; by the rule *ṭhjhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* (8.2.40), the substitution of *dha* occurs; and by the rule *ṭhjhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* (8.4.53)... [the substitution of *jaś* occurs].

53) Thus, the letter *d* replaces the letter *dh*. [Objection: Since the vowels *ai* and *au* (*aic*) are also taught in the *akṣarasamāmnāya*, [the rule would apply to them as well]. If it is argued that while *ai* and *au* are taught in the *akṣarasamāmnāya*, the vowel *ā* (*ākāra*) is not, [we reply:
there is no fault, because since the class (*jāti*) of the sound *a* (*avarṇa*) is taught, that [vowel *ā*] is also included.

Furthermore, even if this is an instruction regarding the individual manifestation of the vowel *a*, there is still no fault; for by the rule "A sound that is marked with *ṭ* or *u* denotes its homogeneous counterparts, provided it is not itself an affix" (Pāṇini 1.1.69), the vowel *a* is included when the [phoneme] *a* is being grasped. Moreover, this cannot be intended as a restriction on usage; for if it were for the sake of restricting usage—

In this context, in rules such as "vṛddhi occurs for sici" (7.2.1) and "vṛddhi occurs for mṛj" (7.2.114), the use of the word *vṛddhi* when followed by vowels other than *ā*, *ai*, and *au* would not be justified. For how could one possibly establish a restriction oneself and then [apply it] to that which is not followed by *ā*, *ai*, or *au*?
One should employ [the mantra]!
But another says this is not for the purpose of restricting the application, in order to demonstrate: "And it is not for the restriction of application..."

"...is commenced for this purpose. Now, one might object: "Is this not commenced solely for the sake of a rule regarding usage, namely *pra-g-dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.80), which states that those [words] designated as *gati* and *upasarga* must be employed only before the verbal root (*dhātu*)? To this objection raised by the opponent, he provides the following resolution: "ṭh..."
"That yoga [of *pra*] is rejected, or is it not? For we observe that it is undesirable [in such cases].
Indeed, when one ought to employ the form *prapacati*, no one employs *pacati pra*. Even if it were not rejected, there would still be no fault, because:

This is a restriction regarding technical designation (*sañjñā-niyama*), not a restriction regarding usage (*prayoga-niyama*); that is to say, those particles beginning with *pra* receive the designations "motion" (*gati*) and "prefix" (*upasarga*) only when they are employed before a verbal root. Even if it were intended as a restriction regarding usage, there would still be no fault, because [the usage] of common people...

A rule regarding the usage of words when they are employed for their meanings is being undertaken; however, since the word *ādic* is a common (laukika) term, what is the purpose of a statement intended to restrict its usage? In that regard, it was said: "That which is rejected..."
To say that [the word] "yoga" is [superfluous], that is incorrect; for it is not reasonable to reject something that possesses meaning.

If you argue that it is meaningless, then the suspicion of meaninglessness would apply here as well. For if one were to maintain that the author of the Sūtras composed certain sūtras even though they are meaningless—this...
There would be a definitive determination. Therefore, by one who accepts its authority, everything composed by it must be accepted as meaningful in some manner or other.
Furthermore, even the resolution offered by resorting to the position that [the names] are restricted by convention is contradicted by the actual usage. Thus it stands.

For it is clearly stated by this passage from the *Vṛtti*— namely, "those termed *gati*s and *upasarga*s must be placed before the verbal root"— that a restriction regarding usage (*prayoga-niyama*) alone is being adopted. Nor [is there any contradiction with] the *Vṛtti*.
It is not appropriate for one who is intent on providing an explanation to offer an interpretation that contradicts it.
Furthermore, as for what was stated beginning with "of worldly words," that too does not serve the purpose of restricting usage.
This is sufficient to dispel any doubt; for instance: "vibhāṣā supo bahuc purastāt" (Pāṇini 5.3.68), "avyayasarvanāmnām akac prāk ṭeḥ" (5.3.71), and "kṛñ cānuprayujyate liṭi" (3.1.40).
Thus, even in the case of non-worldly words such as *bahuj* and others, a restriction regarding their usage is observed in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*);
in that regard, one must certainly entertain the doubt: "Is this for the purpose of restricting usage, or is it for some other purpose? But enough of this digression. Therefore:
The very same solution previously stated is appropriate.
Furthermore, this cannot even be understood as being for the purpose of an injunction (ādeśa), for if the term *vṛddhi* were [applied] to *āT*, *aiC*, and so forth by this [rule],...
An injunction would have to be formulated for those specific references: namely, "ṭhyāti vāti drāti psāti" (Pāṇini 8.4.17), "rāyo hali" (7.2.85), and "nāvo dvigoḥ" (5.4.99). These...

[The substitutes] would not be applicable. Furthermore, if the vowels *ai* and *au* were designated by the term "vṛddhi," even so, grammatical references such as "in the case of vṛddhi" (Pāṇini 6.3.28) and "of a taddhita suffix caused by vṛddhi" (Pāṇini 6.3.39) would be impossible. Therefore...
This is not tenable even from the perspective of the meaning of the traditional authority (āgama);
for when the term *vṛddhi* is prescribed as an augment (*āgama*) for the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au*, the aforementioned designations for it or for them are not logically possible.

But another says: "In the prescription of a substitute (ādeśa), there must be a genitive case [ending] to express the relationship between the original element (sthānin) and the substitute; likewise, in the prescription of an augment (āgama), there must be one to express the relationship between the part and the whole. Yet, here no genitive is found. Therefore, due to the absence of the genitive, this [rule] is neither for the purpose of a substitute nor for the purpose of an augment. This, however, is incorrect.

Even without the genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*), we observe the prescription of substitutes in rules such as *ṭhhalṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), *ṭhanite* (8.4.19), *ṭhantaḥ* (8.4.20), and *ṭhubhau sābhyāsasya* (8.4.21). Furthermore, regarding the prescription of augments (*āgama*), [we see] *ṭhna yvābhyām*...

Since it is observed that [the rule] *padāntābhyāṃ pūrvau tu tābhyāmaic* (Pāṇini 7.3.3) applies even in the absence of a genitive case, this [use of the genitive] is also considered for the purpose of establishing the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).
For indeed, the relationship of qualifier and qualified occurs only when there is both possibility and deviation [of one term from the other].
It is like "blue lotus. Nor is there any possibility here for the *vṛddhi* substitutes *ā*, *ai*, and *au* [to apply] to the word *vṛddhi*, or for those [substitutes] to apply to it.

But surely, just as the word "lotus," while occurring in all instances of the meaning "lotus," is delimited from other meanings by the word "blue"—and thus, being delimited, is the qualified (*viśeṣya*)—[so too should it be here].

[Objection: But while the word "existent" is the qualified (viśeṣya), the word "blue" is the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) because it performs exclusion; likewise, between these two [words], that which is to be excluded is the qualified, and that which performs the exclusion is the qualifier—is this not so? [Response: This is not the case.

For this [distinction] is established only when both [the general term and the specific term] possess meaning, as in the case of the words "blue" and "lotus. However, the *āT* and *aic* [vowels] do not possess meaning. Let it be granted that there is indeed a distinction between these two as qualifier and qualified; yet...

Even if such a state were possible, this [objection] is not appropriate for the purpose of establishing that point; because it serves no purpose, and furthermore, because it is irrelevant to the subject at hand. For in this treatise, which is a grammatical instruction on words (*śabdānuśāsana*), whatever statement is made that does not contribute to the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of words—

All of that is useless; for, by the specific relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) established here, no grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*)—whether of the term *vṛddhi*, or of the vowels *āT* and *aiC*, or of their accentual distinction, or of their phonetic form—is accomplished. That relationship of qualifier and qualified is precisely what [is required] for them.
If you say it is a *saṃskāra* (grammatical refinement), then if this is so, what has been stated—namely, "vṛddhir ādaic" (Pāṇini 1.1.1)—is far too little.

For even the expression "nīlotpalam" (blue lotus) ought to have been mentioned, in order to establish the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) for words such as "nīla" and "utpala. Yet it was not stated.
Therefore, this is not intended to be a *saṃskāra* (grammatical refinement), and thus its being for that purpose (*tādarthya*) is not possible. [Objection:

But is it not observed that even when words have the same case-ending, there is the superimposition of a quality upon them, as in "The boy is a lion" (*siṃho māṇavakaḥ*)? Therefore, this [refinement] will be for that purpose.
Even for the sake of those other alternative positions that some have imagined,
this [objection] does not apply, because even if there were an attribution of its qualities and meditative absorption (*samādhi*),
it would be useless here as it serves no purpose for the subject at hand. Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*):

Considering that this [rule] is intended solely for the purpose of establishing the relationship between the name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*), he says: "The word *vṛddhi* [is used] as a name," and so forth. Let it be granted that, by process of elimination, it is for that purpose. But how is this obtained? [From the rule] *vṛddhi-*...

The word *śabda* is the name (*saṃjñā*), and the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* are the named (*saṃjñin*). Why does the reverse not occur—that is, that *ā*, *ai*, and *au* are the names and the word *vṛddhi* is the named? The reverse cannot occur;
for the purpose of creating a name is brevity, so that when [the name] is uttered, it [refers to the named] in the various rules (*pradeśa*).

There is brevity for him [the teacher] by virtue of [the term] being a technical designation (*saṃjñā*). And even when the word *vṛddhi* is uttered with its case-ending, there is brevity, not [brevity] in the case of *āt* and *aic*;
because of the word *vṛddhi*.

When [the vowels] are being pronounced, there are four *mātrās*; however, in the case of *ā*, *ai*, and *au*, there are five. Nor can it be imagined that there is simplicity [of expression] because each of *ā*, *ai*, and *au* individually possesses the technical designation (*saṃjñā*).
Because the formulation of a technical name (saṃjñā) in a single location is fruitless without a specific purpose; furthermore, technical names apply to those that recur,
and while the word *vṛddhi* recurs, the word *ādaiC* does not, therefore no reversal of the relationship occurs.

Regarding the phrase "the word *vṛddhi*": the inclusion of the term "word" (*śabda*) is for the purpose of excluding the meaning. For if that were absent, since the meaning is understood from the word, the meaning itself would be understood to be the technical name (*saṃjñā*). Even though the technical name was already prescribed previously, nevertheless...

The present tense is used in the expression "it is being prescribed" (*vidhīyate*) because the tradition of disciples and grand-disciples has not yet ceased. Where one intends to exclude an operation, there one employs the mention of both words,
as for example in the rule *ubhe*.

Regarding the rule *abhyastam* (6.1.5), [the term] is either a significant technical designation (*sañjñā*) based on its etymological meaning, or it refers to the definition *halo 'nantarāḥ saṃyogaḥ* (1.1.7). For in that context, the significant technical designation is established for this purpose:
so that this designation may apply to a collective group (*samudāya*).

We shall clarify this further below; however, there is no statement here of such a kind that this designation would apply to the collection as a whole. Therefore, bearing in mind that this designation applies to each individual [letter], he says:
Regarding the phrase "each one individually":
[the opponent asks]— but surely here too, for the sake of brevity, when a single-syllable technical term (*saṃjñā*) ought to be employed, why use the long term "vṛddhi"?
Is the formation of this technical term (saṃjñā) for the sake of ensuring that it applies to the entire collection [of sounds]?

This is not the case; for this technical term serves the purpose of auspiciousness (maṅgala). For this very reason, it is pronounced first. Otherwise, if it were merely a technical term [for something already existing], [it would have been placed at the end].
The effect must exist by means of its cause; for example, in rules such as *ṭhadeṅ guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.2), that which is designated as the prior member [is the cause].

The same should be indicated here as well. Since the letter *ai* and the two letters *e* and *o* joined with other qualities (*guṇa*) are not included in the pratyāhāra, some of dull intellect might have the misconception that "these are not phonemes" (*na ime varṇāḥ*).
Therefore, in order to dispel that [misconception], he says: "of the phonemes" (*varṇānām*).

And so forth. Someone might have the misconception that because of their proximity, this designation would apply only to those [words] conditioned by that [specific context]; therefore, in order to dispel that, he says: "in general."
The intention is that this follows from the logic of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
In order to clarify the meaning of the term "in general" (*sāmānyena*), he says: "Those whose names are conditioned by that," and so forth.
Those [beings] are conditioned by that.

Those which are produced by the term *vṛddhi* are [the *vṛddhi* vowels]; others than those are not so conditioned (*atadbhāvita*). The addition of the *ta*-marker (*tapara*) in the word *ād*—as in the rule *taparastatkālasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.70)—is either for the purpose of including those [sounds] that have the same duration even when distinguished by a different quality (*guṇa*), or for the purpose of excluding those with a different...
Or is it for the purpose of excluding the [temporal] times? Regarding this, the former position is first untenable;
because in this treatise, the accents such as udātta and so forth are not differentiators [of the suffixes]. Why is this so?
Because of the mention of "udātta" in the rule *luṅlaṅlṛṅkṣvaḍudātaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.71); otherwise, [the rule would be unnecessary].
One should pronounce only that which is endowed with the quality of being clearly articulated (udātta). A second [pronunciation] is also not appropriate.

For if the vowel *ā* were a grasper (*grāhaka*) of its homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*), then, since it would thereby grasp even the vowel *a* of a different duration, the designation [of "long"] for that [shorter one] should not occur.

The addition of *t* (the *tapara* marker) is justified for the purpose of excluding the apprehension of sounds belonging to different times. However, this [long vowel] is not a grasper (*grāhaka*) of its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*), because it is not a short vowel (*anaṇ*), and because it is not included in the traditional recitation of the phonemes (*akṣarasamāmnāya*). Therefore, the addition of *t* is purposeless.
Therefore, [one might ask] why it should not be done at all; to this he says: "The addition of *ṭha*," and so forth.

That which has *ec* as its meaning or purpose is described in that way. Now, one might object: if the category (*jāti*) is the referent of the word, then the protracted (*pluta*) vowel would also be included.

It occurs; since there too is the inclusion of the vowel *a* of a non-*tapara* (short) variety, if the *tapara* marker were not employed there, that [long *ā*] would also receive the designation. Therefore, for the sake of excluding that, the employment of the *tapara* marker is indeed appropriate even for the purpose of [specifying] the form *ā*. Why, then, is it said, "for the sake of *ṭha*"? Thus...
He thinks:
even if one resorts to the position that [the vowel] is produced, by the force of its long pronunciation, the individual instances of the phoneme *a* are indeed two mātrās in duration.

It is understood that [the long vowel] is dependent [on the short]; for otherwise, for the sake of brevity, one would have simply stated "ṭhaḍ. Nor can it be assumed that the pronunciation of the long vowel is for the purpose of excluding the short vowel, because even when the long vowel is pronounced, the short [vowel]—

[The rule] indeed applies [to the vowel *ā*], because there is the possibility of its being produced from a non-vowel (*avarṇa*) even in that case. Nor was the word "ā" stated for the sake of removing doubt, because it is unique to other vowels, or because there is no doubt when it is not in *saṃhitā*. But [one might object]: "Is it not the case that [by the rule] *tapa-ras-tatkāla-*..."

In the rule *sya* (Pāṇini 1.1.70), the analysis *taḥ paro yasmāt* ("that from which 'ta' follows") was adopted as a bahuvrīhi compound; however, in this particular case (*ai*), there is no *t* followed by *a*. Therefore, he asks: how does the inclusion of *t* after *a* serve the purpose of excluding the long vowels? To this, he replies: "Even *tau* [the two vowels *ai* and *au*] are *tapara*. It is not only that which has *ta* following it that is called *tapara*.
Thus, by the word "also" (*api*), he shows that even that which is "other than that" (*tadapi*) is also "having *t* as its subsequent element" (*tapara*).
This is what is meant: not only is the *bahuvrīhi* compound resorted to there, but rather, the *pañcamī-tatpuruṣa* [genitive determinative] is also [resorted to].

Since both of these are relied upon, we shall demonstrate that very point later on; for the word "yataḥ" is used here in the sense of cause, meaning "because it is so," and therefore [the subsequent] is even more remote than the other. Thus:

The meaning is that the addition of the *ta* (the long vowel marker) is for the sake of excluding the *ai* sound. By the rule beginning with "in *khaṭvaiḍaka* and so forth," he clarifies that very purpose of the *ta* marker. [For example:
*vṛkṣa* + *elakā* = *vṛkṣailakā*. For if the *ta* marker were not applied here—
In place of the three-moraic combination of *ā* and *ai*,

by the rule "vṛddhir eci" (Pāṇini 6.1.88), a *vṛddhi* vowel would result; and if that [three-moraic *ai*] were also designated as *vṛddhi*, then by virtue of proximity (*āntaratamya*), the resulting *vṛddhi* would necessarily be a three-moraic *ai* itself— as in the case of *khaṭvā odanam*.
In the case of *khaṭvaudanam*, *khaṭvā elakā*, and *khaṭvailakā*, there too,
the *a* and *e* of the four-mora (*caturmātra*) preceding and following groups should become [the single] four-mora *ava* and *ai*, respectively; that being so—

Thinking "this would be a fault," the addition of *ta* (the *tapara* marker) is made in order to prevent the designation of *vṛddhi* for the diphthongs *ai* and *au* when they consist of three or four morae (*trimātra-caturmātra*). [Examples are] *Āśvalāyanaḥ* and *Aitikāyanaḥ*.
From the words *aśvala-* and *aitika-*, the suffix *phak* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.99: *ṭhaÑ-ṇaḍādibhyaḥ phak*.
There is elision by [Pāṇini 6.4.148] *yasyeti ca*, and there is vṛddhi by [Pāṇini 7.2.118] *kiti ca* and so forth. Thus, "ĀṬpagavaḥ":
from the word *upagu*, [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.83] *prāgdīvyato 'ṇ*. "ĀṬpamanyavaḥ" is likewise.
From the word *upamanyu*, [the suffix] *añ* is applied by the rule *bidādibhyo’ñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.104) because it is not followed immediately by a seer (*ṛṣi*).

In both cases, the substitution of *guṇa* occurs by *ṭhorguṇaḥ* (6.4.146), the substitution of *av* by *avādeśaḥ* (6.1.78), and the *vṛddhi* of the first vowel among the vowels by *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ* (7.2.117). These four [rules] apply here as well.
Examples illustrating that state: Now, since the scope for those three designata (*sañjñin*) has already been shown by the first three [rules], for what purpose—
Regarding the presentation of the fourth [example], some say: due to the difference in the cause for *vṛddhi* (vowel lengthening),
in the first two examples the cause is a *kit* or *taddhita* suffix, in the third it is a *ṇit*, and in the fourth it is a *ñit*.

And this is incorrect; for instance, under the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī* (P. 1.1.3), having cited *aṭhakarot*, the example *aṭhahārṣīt* is also cited, yet there is no difference in the cause for the *vṛddhi* substitution in those cases. Likewise, regarding the rule *na dhātulopa ārdhadhātuke* (P. 1.1.4).
In this context,
after citing *loluvaḥ*, the additional examples *ṭhpopuvaḥ* and *marīmṛjaḥ* have been presented; yet there is no difference in the cause for the elision (*lopa*) in those cases.
Or rather, there exists a specific reason for the presentation of additional examples, namely the distinction between the grounds for negation;
for this is generally the case even with other general definitions, even without [further elaboration].

An additional example is found for the sake of illustrating the difference in phonetic characteristics (*nimitabheda*). Even though the vowel *au* has already been shown in the case of "aupagava," [the term] "aupamanyava" is cited because of the difference in accent (*svarabheda*).
As for the statement, "this additional example has been presented," that too is incorrect;

it should be understood for the very reason just mentioned. If there is a difference in cause or a difference in accent, an additional example should be understood to be presented in every case, such as *śālīyaḥ* and *mālīyaḥ*.

An example of that which is not produced by it [is as follows]: here, in the rule for the designation *vṛddhi*—namely, "That which has *vṛddhi* as its initial vowel is designated *vṛddha*" (Pāṇini 1.1.73)—the citation of the suffix *chha* is for the purpose of manifesting that very result which is the designation *vṛddha*. For when the designation *vṛddha* exists, [the rule] "The suffix *chha* after a *vṛddha* [stem]" (4.2.114) applies.
By this [sūtra], the suffix *cha* is prescribed in the sense of "born from" (*jāta*) and so forth.
However, examples for the vowels *ai* and *au* that do not undergo such modification have not been shown here; this is because they follow the same principle.

It is indeed understood because it is being traversed. When the operation of the technical name *vṛddhi* is shown for a vowel that does not possess that [name] by nature, the same operation applies to those two as well; thus, it is understood precisely through that medium. What, then, are the examples for those two? They are *traimayam* and *naumayam*.
In this case, when the designation *vṛddhi* applies to the vowels *ai* and *au*, the designation *vṛddha* follows as before. When that [designation] exists,
[the suffix *aṇ* is applied] by the rule *nityaṃ vṛddhaśarādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.144), as in the examples "a modification of *rāi*" (*rāyaḥ vikāraḥ*) and "a modification of *nau*" (*nāvaḥ vikāraḥ*).
Thus, the suffix *mayaṭ* occurs.

2. *adeṅ guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.2). Regarding this, it is said: "The addition of the marker *t* [to indicate length] here serves all purposes. That is to say, its purpose (*artha*) or utility (*prayojana*) applies to every instance.

That has been stated accordingly. The word *tu* ("but") indicates a distinction from what precedes it. For in that [preceding rule], it was only for the sake of the vowel *a*; here, however, it is for the sake of all vowels, including the vowel *ā* (the purpose of the letter *a*) and the vowel *eṅ*. Indeed, if the *tapara* marker (*t*) were not present...

Since the vowels *a*, *e*, and *o* are not designated as *an*, there would be a grasping (*grahaṇa*) of their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*), and this designation would apply even to those that differ in duration.
Consequently, in the case of *ṭhtaritā*, by virtue of being the most similar (*antaratama*), the *guṇa* substitute would be a long vowel for a long vowel.
Now, one might object: "But the designation *vṛddhi* will override the designation *guṇa*; therefore—"

Whence does this undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) arise?
