It is not so; for it is only under the governing rule (adhikāra) of "a single technical term" (ekasañjñā) that one technical term is superseded by another, and here there is no governing rule of a single technical term. This might be argued:
even in the absence of the governing rule of a single technical term, just as in the case of [Pāṇini 4.1.163] *jīvati tu vaṃśye yuvā*.

Is it argued that the designation *gotra* is sublated by the designation *yuvan*, just as the designation *sārvadhātuka* is sublated by the designation *ārdhadhātuka* by the rules "ṭhliṭ ca" (3.4.115) and "liṅaśiṣi" (3.4.116), and likewise the designation *guṇa* will be sublated by the designation *vṛddhi*? This is incorrect.

In the rule prescribing the technical term *yuva*, the mention of the suffix *tu* is made for the purpose of restriction; therefore, it is logical that the technical term *gotra* is sublated by the technical term *yuva*. Likewise, it is also entirely logical that the technical term *ārdhadhātuka* sublates the technical term *sārvadhātuka*, as in the case of the rule "in the Veda, both ways."

Because of the statement [Pāṇini 3.4.117]: "In the Veda, both ways. If there were a coexistence (*samāveśa*) of the technical designations *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka*, and no relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*), then the statement "In the Veda, both ways" (3.4.117) would be purposeless. But here it is not so.
There is no such basis by which the designation "guṇa" (vowel strengthening) could be sublated by the designation "vṛddhi" (vowel lengthening).
Even if it were somehow sublated, the designation "guṇa" would still apply to that which has three morae (*trimātra*). Indeed, it cannot be sublated by that [designation], because of its...

Because it does not have that as its object. Even if the designation "guṇa" were applied to a three-mora [vowel], it would follow that a three-mora vowel would also be a guṇa. For, just as in terms of duration a one-mora *a* is not the closest similar [substitute] for the sound *ṛ*, so too a three-mora [vowel] is not. Therefore...

How is this understood? That it must be by means of its short quality (*guṇa*) alone, and not by the vowel *ā* consisting of three morae (*mātrā*). Furthermore, if the designation "quality" were to apply even to vowels occurring at different times, then in the case of *khaṭvā indraḥ > khaṭvendraḥ* or *khaṭvā urvī*, [the same fault would arise].

In the case of *khaṭvorvī*, because the substituend (*sthānin*)—consisting of the preceding and following elements taken together—is of three morae (*trimātra*), the *guṇa* substitute prescribed by "ṭhādguṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.87) would also be of three morae. [For example: *khaṭvā īṣā* → *khaṭveṣā*; *khaṭvā*...

In the case of *uḍhāukhaṭvoḍhā*, because it consists of four morae (*mātrā*), it is "four-mora" (*caturmātra*). Therefore, for the sake of all cases, the use of the *tapara* marker (*t*) must be made [in the rule]. [Examples include] *ṭhtaritā* and so forth. [The root] *tṛ* [is used] in the sense of "floating" and "crossing over" (*dhā.pā.* 969); [the suffix] *ciñ*...
From the roots *ci* (DhP 1251) and *stu* (DhP 1043), the suffix *tṛc* is applied by the rule *ṇvultṛcau* (3.1.133).
Then, the augment *iṭ* is added by the rule *ārdhadhātukasyeḍ valādeḥ* (7.2.35).

The *guṇa* substitution [of *o* for *av*] occurs by the rule "sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.84); the substitution of *anaṅ* [for the final vowel and consonant of the stem] occurs by the rule "ṛduśanaspurudaṃso'nehasām" (Pāṇini 7.1.94), etc.; and the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule "sarvanāmasthāne ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.8). These three are, respectively, examples of those [vowels] that have been transformed into *e*, *o*, and *ai*.
In the examples for [the rule] *atadbhāvitasya*, they cite *paṭhanti* and *paṭhan*.

Here, because the final vowel *ā* receives the designation *guṇa*, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.97] *ato guṇe*. This word *paṭhan* ends in the present participle suffix *-śatṛ*. An example of an operation for a single [vowel] that is not *atadbhāvita* is *aham*.
Regarding "pace" and so forth: since the vowel *o* has not been transformed into that [state], its occurrence there is not demonstrated. 3. *iko guṇavṛddhī* (Pāṇini 1.1.3).

"This is a paribhāṣā (technical rule)," [he says]. It is not an adhikāra (governing heading), because it lacks the svarita accent. Nor is it a rule prescribing *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, because those two will be prescribed by other rules. "It serves to restrict the substitute" means that the restriction concerns the original element (*sthānin*).

"Restriction of the substituend (*sthānin*) means the application [of a substitute] to one specific element by excluding other possible substituends; that which has this as its purpose is described in that way. Thus, a restriction is prescribed when there would otherwise be the contingency of no restriction, even where the substituend is not explicitly mentioned."

In rules such as *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.84) and *sici vṛddhiḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (7.2.1), since an unrestricted application would otherwise result, he establishes this restriction for them: "only [the vowel] *ik*, and not any other. Therefore, that...

This should be understood as its scope, but not that place where a specific locus (*sthānin*) is explicitly mentioned, such as in "guṇa for *ṭh* sounds" (P. 6.4.146), "of the penultimate vowel" (P. 7.2.116), and so forth; for in those cases, there is no [general] lack of restriction.

There is no such thing as attainment [of the rule]. This technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) possesses a formal indicator (*liṅga*), and its indicator is the mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*; thus, it applies there. Consequently, two genitive cases arise: one is "of *ik*" (*ikaḥ*), and the other is from "there is *guṇa* for *mid*" (*miderguṇaḥ*, Pāṇini 7.3.82).
This is the second [type], beginning with "ityevamādikā.

In that case, acting according to one's will (*kāmacāra*) is accomplished as desired. A relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) is established between those two. [The rule applies to] the root *mideḥ*.

In this case, since an *ik* [vowel] cannot exist at the end [of a word], its being a qualifier of the *aṅga* (stem) is not possible; therefore, here the *aṅga* itself is qualified by the *ik*: "the *ik* which belongs to the *aṅga* of the root *mid*. Consequently, because there is no status as a substitute (*sthāni*), when the final letter (*alo’ntyasya*) is not presented, [the rule applies] wherever [that *ik* occurs].

One specific quality becomes established for the suffix *stha*: namely, that the *aṅga* (stem) can end in an *ik* vowel, as in the rule "sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.84) and others. When the *aṅga* is thus qualified, the desired result is achieved through the application of the *tadantavidhi* (the principle that a grammatical operation applies to that which ends with the specified element). Therefore, the *aṅga* is qualified by the *ik* vowel.

Regarding the phrase "of a stem ending in /i/ or /u/" (*igantasyāṅgasya*): since this is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), the rule *alo 'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52)—which prescribes that an operation applies to the final letter—is applicable. Consequently, guna and vṛddhi substitutions occur only for a stem (*aṅga*) that ends in /i/ or /u/.

"Not for the other," meaning "by its own technical name (*svasañjñayā*). Here, the intention is that which will be stated later. "Only in place of *i*"—this shows the nature of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) for the sake of which this paribhāṣā exists: namely, "he made" (*akārṣīt*).
From the root *kṛ* (meaning "to do," Dhātupāṭha 1472), in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, by the rule *cleḥ sic* (3.1.44), *sic* is substituted for *cli*.
Then, by *sici vṛddhiḥ* (7.2.1), there is vṛddhi [of the root vowel]. By *astisico 'pṛkte* (7.3.96), the augment *iṭ* is added. Thus, we have *ahārṣīt*.
Here, the specific distinction is that the root is *hṛ* (meaning "to take away," Dhātupāṭha 899). Why [is the condition] "beginning with *ik*" stated? [Consider the example: *ita*.

It should be understood that the inquiry regarding the whole is made by means of a single part. For no purpose whatsoever is encompassed by the mention of "vowel" (*i*) alone in the rule *guṇavṛddhī*; [as seen in the example] "yānam."

If the suffix *lyuṭ* were applied to the root *yā*, the *guṇa* substitution would result in the vowel *a* by virtue of being the closest [substitute]. Consequently, when the two *a*s undergo the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule according to Pāṇini 6.1.97 (*ato guṇe*), the undesirable form *yana* would result. [The correct form is] *glāyati*.

Regarding the roots *ṭhglai* and *mlai* in the sense of "the cessation of joy" (*dhā.pā.* 903–904), here the *guṇa* substitute for the diphthong *ai* would be *e*. Consequently, once the *āyādeśa* is applied, the undesired form *glayati* would result.

Regarding the form *ṭhumbhitā*: from the roots *ṭhubha* and *umbha* in the sense of "filling" (*pūraṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 1319, 1320), with the suffix *tṛc* and the augment *iṭ*, there would be the *guṇa* substitution of *o* for the consonant *k* and the labial *u*. Consequently, once the *av-ādeśa* is applied, the undesirable form *ṭhubhavitā* would result.

Now, how is this distinction—that "those being taught by their own technical names" (*svasañjñayā*)—obtained, given that there is no mention of the term *svasañjñā* in the Sūtra? To this he says: "The further mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, etc."

In this context, the mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* from the two preceding sūtras is understood by way of anuvṛtti (carrying over). While that [anuvṛtti] is already present, the reason for repeating the mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* here is this: this restrictive rule (*niyama*) applies only where *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are prescribed by their own technical names (*svasañjñā*).

[This is] so that [the rule] might apply elsewhere; however, by the force of the repeated mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, it is established that one of these two mentions of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* has the technical term (*saṃjñā*) as its primary meaning. Thus, when an operation is prescribed by means of its own technical name, there is a restriction (*niyama*). This is—
The purpose [of this rule] is thus obtained. Otherwise, if such a prior restriction were not intended here,

then— since a restricted rule would already be established by the continued application of the mention of "guṇa" and "vṛddhi" from the context— the repeated mention of "guṇa" and "vṛddhi" here would be redundant.

Such is the intended meaning. By the words "let it not be here," etc., he shows that this kind of restriction is what is to be excluded by the rule itself—namely, the example "dyauḥ. [In this case,] the vowel *au* is substituted according to Pāṇini 7.1.84 (*diva auT*).
When a substitute is prescribed in its own form (*svarūpeṇa*), it applies only to the final letter (*alo'ntyasya*) and not to the whole word (*ikaḥ*).
In the case of *panthāḥ*, by the rule *pathimadhyṛbhukṣāmāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.85), the vowel *ā* replaces only the final [phoneme], not the whole [stem]. Then,
by the rule *ito't sarvanāmasthāne* (Pāṇini 7.1.86), the vowel *i* is replaced by *a*, and *th* is replaced by *nth*.

By [Pāṇini 7.1.87], there is the substitution of *nth* for the letter *th*. Regarding the form *ṭhiyam*: by [Pāṇini 7.2.102], the substitution of *a* occurs immediately after [the final vowel] of words beginning with *tyad*, and not [after the whole word]. By [Pāṇini 7.2.109], the letter *d* is replaced by *m*. That...
In this case, however, when this *paribhāṣā* applies, the substitution of *yat* for *tyad* and so forth would certainly not occur.

[One might argue: "But surely the rule *tadoḥ saḥ sāvanantyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.106), which prescribes the substitution of *s* for *ta* and *do*, is also [an exception to this]. Indeed, the rule *anaśca* (1.2.28) is also [relevant].

The restriction regarding the locus is intended only for the prescription of its own technical name (*sañjñā*); and even for that restriction, examples such as *dyauḥ* (heaven) are what must be excluded. Likewise...

For the author of the *Vṛtti* will state there: "When a rule is prescribed by means of its own technical name (*svasañjñā*), it is a restriction (*niyama*). The term *ac* (vowel) is understood [from the previous rule]. Let this not apply here: *dyauḥ*, *panthāḥ*, *saḥ*, *dyaubhyām*, *dyaubhiḥ*" (Kāśikā 38).
Therefore, whatever must be accomplished by such a restriction is already established by that very [restriction], and thus there is no need for [this present rule].

Why, then, is there this further mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* here for the sake of such a restriction? This is true; however, in order to facilitate understanding, there might be excessive difficulty for those listeners who are of dull intellect and beginners. Therefore, [the author] intends to favor them.

The mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is repeated here in order to establish a restrictive rule (*niyama*) for the prescription of technical names (*sañjñā*) so that their meaning may be clearly understood. Thus, whatever is to be prescribed by means of something must be done by this very [rule] alone.

Is it not the case that, since [the form] has already been prescribed, no restrictive rule (*niyama*) should be formulated regarding that assignment of technical names (*saṃjñāvidhāna*)? This is not so; for if such a restriction were not in place, then in the forms *dyaubhyām* and *dyaubhiḥ*, the substitution of *u* [for the final vowel] as prescribed by Pāṇini 6.1.131 (*diva ut*) would apply.

Being prescribed by its own form alone, it would apply only in place of a vowel (*ac*), not to the final letter of a group (*alo 'ntyasya*). For it is not possible to exclude the vowel by this restrictive rule, since that [vowel] possesses the technical designation of *guṇa* or *vṛddhi*.

4. *Na dhātulopa ārdhadhātuke* (Pāṇini 1.1.4). The designation *dhātu* (verbal root) has been assigned to a word of the stated measure. When the whole of that [word] is elided (*lopa*), and *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* substitutions would otherwise apply, that [situation] occurs precisely because of the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix; so why [is this rule stated]?

Is it by way of negation? Therefore, considering that the word *dhātu* applies to a portion of a verbal root (*dhātvekadeśa*) due to the force of the rule prescribing the negation, he says: "A portion of a verbal root is [treated as] a verbal root.
Regarding the term *dhātulope*: if this were a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the elision of a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ lopaḥ*), then...

The mention of *ārdhadhātuka* may be a qualifier of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*: "When there is elision of a verbal root (*dhātu-lopa*), those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions which would otherwise occur by reason of an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix do not take place.
Alternatively, it may be a qualifier of the elision itself: "When there is elision of a verbal root occasioned by an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix..."

[If the rule states] "guṇa and vṛddhi do not occur," then in the first case, in the example *ṭhknopayati*, the prohibition would apply; therefore, a counter-argument must be made there. In the second [interpretation], however, this fault does not arise. For in *ṭhknopayati*, the elision is not caused by an ārdhadhātuka suffix; what then? [It is caused by something else.]

[The objection is: "It is caused by the suffix *val*. However, in the second alternative (*pakṣa*), it would apply in the case of *preddham*, because here there is indeed an elision (*lopa*) caused by an *ardhadhātuka* suffix. [The response is: "But surely this prohibition concerns *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* that are characterized by the vowel *i*;
and is there not a *guṇa* here that is not characterized by *i*? [The reply is: "This is not so; even here, it is indeed characterized by *i*."
For a substitute that occurs in the place of both [elements] receives the designation of the one that follows at the end.

To illustrate: in the case of *mātuḥ* and *pituḥ*, the vowel *a* (an *aṇ*) occurring in the place of both [the final *u* and the following *ṛ*] is followed by *r*. Therefore, even under the view that the term [ṛt] is a qualifier of the elision (*lopa*), [the rule applies].
Thinking that a counter-argument must indeed be made regarding the *tatpuruṣa* compound, whereas nothing needs to be countered in the case of the *bahuvrīhi*,
[he concludes] that this is a *bahuvrīhi*.

Showing this, he says "of that" (*tasya*), and so forth. By this, it is shown that "ārddhadhātuka" is a qualifier of *lopa* (elision). And thus, [the elision] occurs in an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix only if that [suffix] is its cause (*nimitta*); and therefore—

In the case of *knopayati*, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) does not occur. Regarding the passage beginning with "there," etc.: nor is the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix qualified as the cause for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*.

This has been explained. Consequently, there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) even in the case of *preddha*, for the *guṇa* substitution [of *e* for *i*] is not caused by an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. The feminine gender in the expression “*ye te*” is used in reference to the term “*guṇavṛddhī*.”

This is because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a feminine noun. Its feminine gender, however, results from the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule "In a *dvandva* and a *tatpuruṣa*, the gender is that of the final member" (Pāṇini 2.4.26). And since that extended application applies to the meaning, it applies to the meanings of *yad-* and *tad-* as well.

The feminine gender applies to the two [terms] currently under discussion. Now, since a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is the subject at hand, it would be more appropriate for this prohibition to apply to that very rule; why then does he say, "In that case, those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* which would otherwise apply do not occur"? It is because of their predominance (*prādhānya*). Therefore...
Furthermore, because it is invariably assisted [by the cause], the restriction (niyama) itself is subordinate since its purpose is for that [assistance].
Therefore, it is logical that this prohibition applies specifically to *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*.
"ṭhloluvaḥ, popuvaḥ": from the roots *lūñ* "to cut" (DhP 1483) and *pūñ* "to purify" (DhP 1482), the suffix *yaṅ* is applied by the rule *dhātorekācaḥ* (3.1.22);
then reduplication occurs by the rule *sanyaṅe* (6.1.9); and [the substitution of] *guṇa* occurs by the rule *guṇoyaṅlukoḥ* (7.4.82).
Such is the merit of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*): when the suffix *yaṅ* is followed by the *ac*-class suffix *ac*, there is elision (*luk*) according to Pāṇini 2.4.74, *ṭhyaṅe'ci ca*;
because of that elision, there is a prohibition of the *guṇa* substitution conditioned by it; and when that [prohibition] exists, [the rule] *aci śnudhātukabhruvām* (6.4.77) applies.

77) Thus, from [the rule] *uvaṅ* onwards; regarding *marīmṛjaḥ*: the root *mṛjū* (meaning "to purify," DhP 1066) takes *yaṅ* as before, followed by reduplication, *uratva* (7.4.66), *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* (7.4.60), and [the substitution of *ī*] by *rīgṛdupadhasya ca* (7.4.90).
There is the addition of *rīk*. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the rule *lolūyādibhyaḥ*, there is the inclusion of these two: *ṭhpopūya* and *marīmṛjya*.
In the case of *lūñ* [as in] *lavitā*, as long as the designation of "root" (*dhātusañjñā*) has not yet occurred, so long—prior to all other rules—[the application of this rule takes place].
By the rule "the rule of elision is stronger" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 70), the elision of the letter *ñ* occurs; subsequently, the element *lū* receives the technical designation of "root" (*dhātu*).
Consequently, because the elision of *ñ* does not constitute an elision of a root (*dhātulopa*), [the condition for the application of Pāṇini 6.4.24 is not met].
The counter-example is *ṭhreḍ*. [This is derived from] the roots *riṣ* and *ruṣ* in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsāyām*) (DhP 1232, 1230).

By the rule *anyebhyo'pi dṛśyante* (Pāṇini 3.2.75), the suffix *vic* is applied; the presence of the letters *i* and *c* is for the purpose of ensuring that the term *apṛkta* is understood in a general sense in the rule *verapṛktasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.67).

By this very [rule], there is the elision of the letter *va*, and by the rule "pugantalaghūpadhasya ca" (Pāṇini 7.3.86), there is *guṇa* substitution. By the rule "jhalāṃ jaśo'nte" (Pāṇini 8.2.39), the letter *ṣa* becomes *ḍa*. Now, one might object that both of these counter-examples are deficient in two respects, for in this case, there is indeed no elision of the verbal root (*dhātulopa*).
It does not become so, nor does it even become characterized by being an *ardhadhātuka*; this is not the case.

For when the mention of "dhātu" (root) exists, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is obtained due to the proximity of two words. And when that exists, the elision (*lopa*) is characterized by being an *ardhadhātuka*. For if the mention of "dhātu" were absent, [the rule] "na lopaḥ... [would apply].

If it were stated as "in an *ārdhadhātuka* [affix]," then there would be a prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions based on an *ārdhadhātuka* affix, as in the case of *roravīti*. [This form is derived] from the root *ru* (DhP 1034, meaning "to sound") with the *yaṅ* suffix, according to Pāṇini 2.4.73: "frequently in the Veda."

*yaṅ*-elision, *laṭ*, *tip*, *śap*. Due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision of *śap* by Pāṇini 2.4.72; and [the augment] *iṭ* is optionally applied by 7.3.94 (*yaṅe vā*). In this case, the *guṇa* substitution caused by the *sārvadhātuka* suffix is not prohibited. Now, one might object:
This [substitution] is indeed deficient in two respects: for just as the *guṇa* substitution is not triggered by an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, would the elision (*lopa*) likewise not be? This is not so;

for when the term *ārdhadhātuka* is present, since it functions as the meaning of the other member of the compound (*anyapadārtha*), the elision is not dependent upon it, and thus it is not triggered by that [suffix].

Elision (*lopa*) is obtained; and when that [elision] exists, if only this much were stated—namely, "when there is elision of a verbal root (*dhātu-lope*)"—the meaning of the sentence would be: "whatever *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* occurs, they occur when elision exists. Consequently, because the elision is not specifically qualified, the prohibition would apply to every instance of elision whatsoever.
It is understood from the rule *abhāji*. [The root] *bhañj* [is used] in the sense of "crushing" (*āmardane*;

DhP 1453). In the *luṅ* tense, there is *cli*; then, by the rule *ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (3.1.66), there is *ciṇ*; by the rule *iṇo luk* (6.4.104), there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ta*; and by the rule *bhañjeśca ciṇi* (6.4.33), [the nasal is dropped].

Thus there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*). Regarding "rāgaḥ": here too, by the rule *ghañi ca bhāvakaraṇayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.27), there is the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*). [The root] *rañj* means "to color" (Dhātupāṭha 1167); the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). Although there is a flow (*srava*) here, nevertheless, because the word *ikaḥ* is understood from the previous rule and because an *ik* vowel is impossible here, [the rule does not apply].
Therefore, the prohibition of the *vṛddhi* substitution prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.2.116] *ata upadhāyāḥ* does not apply here.
In the case of *knopayati*: the root *knūyī* means "to sound" (*dhā.pā.* 485); the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.1.26] *hetumati ca*;
and the *guṇa* substitution occurs according to [Pāṇini 7.3.36] *artihrī*. In the case of *preddham*: the root *ñiindhī* means "to shine."
[From the root] *indh* (DhP 1448), with the suffix *kta*, there is the elision of the nasal [of the root] by the rule "aniditām" (Pāṇini 6.4.24) and so forth;
then, by the rule "jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.40), the letter *t* is changed to *dh*.
Then, by the rule "jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi" (Pāṇini 8.4.53), the *dh* of the verbal root is changed to *d*. Thus, it means "that which has become ignited."
The compound is formed by *kugatiprādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18). Regarding *kṅiti ca* (1.1.5):
if this were a locative of posteriority (*parasaptamī*), the prohibition would apply only to the immediately preceding *ik*.
In cases such as *ṭhcitaḥ* and *citavāt*, [the substitution] would apply, but in cases such as *bhinno* and *bhinnavāt*, where the [augment] is separated [from the cause], it would not apply;
this is because of the rule *tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.66).

Because the inclusion of the word "nirdiṣṭa" (specified) serves the purpose of indicating immediate proximity (*ānantarya*), one might think that if this were a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*), it would have to apply everywhere, since the relationship between cause and effect exists even between things that are separated; therefore, [the author] says: "This is a locative of cause. That is, the locative case is used because of a cause.

This is a locative of reference (*nimitasaptamī*). The compound is formed by the separation of the rule *pañcamī* from *pañcamī bhayena* (Pāṇini 2.1.37). Furthermore, that locative case is to be understood according to *yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam* (Pāṇini 2.3.37). [The suffix] *kṛt* occurs here.

By means of the cause (*nimitta*), the state characterized by the occurrence of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is indicated. Now, even in this case of the locative of cause (*nimitasaptamī*), why is a prohibition obtained for that which is separated [by intervening elements]?
Because the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) beginning with "in that" (*tatra tasmin*, P. 1.1.66) does not apply there.
Because this *ik-paribhāṣā* would also apply to rules such as "ṭhkṅiti ca" (Pāṇini 1.1.5),
there would be no designation of *vṛddhi* in forms such as *śālīyaḥ* and *mālīyaḥ*. Since this *ik-paribhāṣā* [is indeed operative]...
Because it serves as a supplement to an injunction, it applies specifically to that injunction;
so too does this paribhāṣā concerning immediate sequence (*ānantarya*). Now, neither *guṇa* nor *vṛddhi* are being enjoined here;
rather, even though they have been enjoined elsewhere, they are qualified by the rule *kṅiti*. Therefore, that [paribhāṣā] does not apply here.

By the statement "the presence of a technical designation (*paribhāṣā*)," the prohibition of even that which is immediately preceding is established. [This refers to the rule: "The *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [substitutions] which have *kṅit* as their cause. Those two are so described because they have *kṅit* as their cause; furthermore, those two should be understood as being applicable when *kṅit* is present. By this, *guṇa*— [...is prohibited. (Pāṇini 1.1.5) Note: This passage is a commentary on Pāṇini’s *Paribhāṣā-sūtra* 1.1.5 (*kṅiti ca*). It explains that the term "having *kṅit* as its cause" (*kṅinnimite*) refers to those operations (*guṇa* and *vṛddhi*) that would otherwise occur when a suffix marked with *k* or *ṅ* follows. The commentary clarifies that this technical designation serves to prohibit such operations. The ellipsis indicates the continuation of the rule prohibiting the application of *guṇa*.
He shows that the mention of *kṅit* is a qualifier of *vṛddhi*. Now, one might object:

since it is the primary element as that which is being prescribed, it would be more logical for this to be a qualifier of the prohibition itself? This is not so; for where a subordinate element (*guṇa*)...

One who has undergone self-purification (ātma-saṃskāra) is capable of rendering great assistance to the primary factor (pradhāna). In that case, having experienced the purification of oneself in order to perform the greater benefit for the primary factor, one enters into a relationship with that primary factor. As it has been said:

"One who has performed the refinement of the self attains [the goal]; for he thus abides in the service of the principal. In this context, however, there is a great [distinction] of the principal [element] with respect to the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [substitutions], which have been specified by the mention of *kṅti*.
The prohibition serves as an auxiliary, since its application is established even for that which is separated [by other elements]. Regarding "bhinnaḥ":

from the root *bhid* in the sense of "cleaving" (DhP 1439), with the suffix *kta*; the substitution of *na* for the final vowel of the *niṣṭhā* suffix occurs by Pāṇini 8.2.42 (*radābhyāṃ niṣṭhātonaḥ*). Regarding "mṛṣṭaḥ": from the root *mṛj*, [the substitution of *ṣ* occurs] by Pāṇini 8.2.36 (*vraśca*).
By these and other rules, the *j* in [the word] becomes *ṣ*, and by the rule "ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.41), it becomes *ṣṭu*. However,
in cases such as *cinute*, the status of being *kṅit* is established by the rule "sārvadhātukamapit" (Pāṇini 1.2.4).

Regarding the form *cinvanti*: the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs by the rule *huśnuvoḥ sārvadhātuke* (Pāṇini 6.4.87). In these examples—namely *citaḥ*, *citavān*, *stutaḥ*, *stutavān*, *cinataḥ*, and *cinvanti*—the [substitutions] apply as appropriate.

There is a prohibition of the *guṇa* substitution characterized by *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* [affixes], as in *bhinnaḥ* and *bhinnavān*; [there is a prohibition] of the *vṛddhi* substitution characterized by a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*) in the remaining cases, such as that prescribed by *mṛjervṛddhiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.114);
and [there is a prohibition] of the *ksnu* suffix prescribed by *glājisthaśca ksnuḥ*, provided that this *ksnu* suffix is *kit*.

In the case of *sthāsnuri*, the substitution of *ī* for the root *sthā* would apply by virtue of the rule *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām aṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.66). Therefore, to avoid that result, it is asserted that the suffix *ksnu* possesses the property of being *gita*. For it is stated therein:
He will say: "This suffix is *git*, not *kit*. Therefore, the substitution of *ī* for *sthā* does not occur" (Kāśikā 2.41).
And since it is *git*, the prohibition stated by the rule *kṅiti ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5) does not apply in cases such as *bhūṣṇuḥ* and *jiṣṇuḥ*.

[The objection] arises. Therefore, to avoid this fault, he says: "The letter *ṭ* also [occurs] here," and so forth (Kārikā 241). "Becoming a *c*-sound" means having attained the state of a *c*-sound (*cartva*). This *cartva*, however, is prescribed by the rule *khari ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.55). For if the quality of being a *g-it* (indicating that the suffix *ksnu* is marked with *ṅ*) were intended, then in the word *bhūṣṇuḥ*...

Would not the prohibition stated in *ṭhśrayukaḥ kiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.11) fail to apply? This is not a fault; for even there, the letter *g*, which has become *c* by the rule of *cartva*, is what is indicated. For instance, in the rule *ṭhglājisthaśca ksnuḥ* (3.2.139), [the *g* is intended].

In the commentary (*vṛtti*) by Jayāditya, regarding the rule *ṭhṭhkṅiti ca* (1.1.5), the letter *g* is specified as having undergone the change to *c*; therefore, no *guṇa* substitution occurs. This is also the case in the rule *ṭhśrayukaḥ kiti* (7.2.11).

"The letter *ga* is specified [in the rule], by which *iṭ* does not occur after the root *bhū*" (Kāśikā 241). Regarding the rule "after a root ending in *ś*, *r*, or *u*, [there is no *iṭ*] before a *kit* suffix" (Pāṇini 7.2.11), there is also this passage in Jayāditya’s commentary: "The letter *g* is also specified here as having undergone the change to *c* (i.e., as *j*), so that [the prohibition applies] in the case of *bhūṣṇu*. This is according to Vāmana.
All of this is undesirable; for indeed, in the commentary (*vṛtti*) composed by that very same author on that very sūtra, there is this passage:
"Some here explain the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the letter *ga* through the mention of two *ka*s, so that it might be *bhūṣṇuḥ*."
Furthermore, because this is a scriptural statement (*sautra*), in the rule *śrayukaḥ kiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.11),

the substitution of *u* for *ru* was not applied— without relying on the fact that the change of *t* to *c* (*cartva*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*)— and instead, the *visarjanīya* was applied. [This is also the case in] *glājisthaśca*.

Regarding the rule *ksnuḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.139), [the author] says: "Since *sthāsnuḥ* is already established by the inclusion of the vowel *ā* (*sthā-ā*) within that rule, this [objection] amounts to nothing" (Vārttika 802). He thinks as follows: if the suffix *ksnu* were *kit*, then the substitution of *ī* for the root *sthā* would apply.
Likewise, in order to avoid that [undesired application], it is appropriate to postulate *gitva* (the property of being marked with *g*). And since *gitva* exists,
in forms such as *jiṣṇuḥ* and *bhūṣṇuḥ*, the rule *ṅiti* is applied as appropriate to exclude the augment *iṭ* and *guṇa*.
In the rule *ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5) and in the rule *śrayukaḥ kiti* (7.2.11), the letter *g* would be appropriate if it were specified as having become a *c* sound (*cartvabhūta*). But it is not.

The suffix *kṣnu* is not *kit*; what then? It is *kit* indeed. Why, then, is there this mention of the letter *ga*, which has become *ca*, for the purpose of prohibiting *iṭ* and *guṇa*? And if *kṣnu* were *kit*, the substitution of *ā* for the root *sthā* would not apply. Therefore, [the rule states] "ṭh..."
In the rule *glājisthaśca ksnuḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.139), the vowel *ā* is elided (*praśleṣa*) so that,
for the root *tiṣṭhati* ending in the suffix *ksnu*, only the vowel *ā* may occur, and whatever else might otherwise result shall not take place.

Such is the meaning. And since [the point] is established by that very [fact], the description here of the elision of the letter *ga* in the word *sthāsnu* is of no consequence. Regarding the form *kāmayate*: [it is derived] from the root *kam-* with the suffix *ṇiṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.30). Here, *ata*...

The prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule *upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116) does not apply here. In the case of *laigavāyanaḥ*, when the suffix *phak* is applied to the word *ligu* by the rule *naḍādibhyaḥ phak* (4.1.99), the prohibition of *guṇa* by the rule *orguṇaḥ* (6.4.146) does not take effect. Now, one might object:
Is this counter-example improper because of the word *ca*? This is not so;

for here the word *ca* is employed for the purpose of drawing forward [the term] "ikaḥ. There, by virtue of being drawn forward by *ca*, the term "ika" abandons its status as a meaning-word (*arthapada*) and assumes the status of a form-word (*svarūpapada*).

Otherwise, if that which is drawn forward by the word "ca" were to have only the meaning of the word *artha* as its referent, then the employment of "ca" for the purpose of drawing it forward would be redundant, since [the referent] is already the meaning of the word *artha*.

Since the continuation [of the word *ika*] is established by its very being marked with the *svarita* accent, and since that [word *ika*]— whose own form is its meaning— is present here, the following sense results: "those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* which are prescribed as 'for *ik*' (i.e., for the vowels *i*, *u*, and *ṛ*)," having uttered this word "for *ik*" (*ikaḥ*).
"The guṇa and vṛddhi substitutions that are prescribed do not occur when kiṅ is the cause. Furthermore,
in the case of "laigavāyanaḥ," the guṇa substitution is not prescribed by explicitly uttering the word "ikaḥ" [as its antecedent].

Because that paribhāṣā does not apply there; its non-application, however, is due to the direct mention of the substitute *ukāra*. For that paribhāṣā applies only where the original element (*sthānin*) is not directly mentioned.
Now, if [the rule] "ika" here refers to its own form as the meaning...
If the locus were not specified, it would not be known for which [sounds] the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* applies; however,
this is not a fault, because by implication (*sāmarthya*), this prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is understood to apply only to those [sounds] beginning with *ik*.

For indeed, the rules for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are not enjoined by uttering this word *ik* alone as referring to something else. Alternatively, although the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) concerning *ik* is a subordinate part of the injunctions, nevertheless here—

Even when the rules for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are being prescribed, the [rule] "an-ekāl-śit sarvasya" (P. 1.1.55) is brought into proximity by means of the letter *c*. Indeed, this is the very purpose of employing the letter *c*: namely, to bring this *paribhāṣā* into proximity.
Consequently, since it is present, this prohibition applies only where that [paribhāṣā] is operative.

It is understood [from the Paribhāṣā]: "Where does this [Paribhāṣā] operate? Wherever the substituendum (sthānin) is not explicitly mentioned. But here, the substituendum is explicitly mentioned; therefore, because there is no operation of the *ik-paribhāṣā*, [the rule applies].
The counter-example begins with "mṛjeḥ" and so forth. But how is that [vṛddhi] obtained even though it is not explicitly desired?
Listen to how it is obtained: in the rule "aco ñṇiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.115), there is the reference to "mṛjervṛddhiḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.114).

Thus it proceeds; the term *anyatarasyām* from [Pāṇini 7.2.101] *jarāyā jaras anyatarasyām* also carries over by the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*), and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
A separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is made for *acaḥ*: "After *mṛj*, there is optionally [the substitution of *ṛ* for *ṝ*] before an affix beginning with a vowel when it is a *saṃkrama*."

The *vṛddhi* occurs [in this case], whereas it does not occur at all elsewhere. "In this instance, there is also a prohibition of the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*). By this, he demonstrates its status as a transition (*saṃkrama*).
Others, however...

In the subsequent sūtra, after "ṭhkaṇitā śvaḥ" and "raṇitā śvaḥ," this passage ought to have occurred; however, they explain that it was written here by careless scribes who were confused by misplaced *kāku* intonations and words. Alternatively—[the text continues with] *nimitasapta-*...

It should be understood that this very result has been demonstrated here. In the case of *acinvam* and *asunuvam*, because the *laṅ* suffix possesses the marker *ṅ*, its substitute *mip* also possesses the marker *ṅ*. This is due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), since *mip* inherits the *ṅ*-marker from *laṅ*.

In that case, this *am* [augment] would also have the property of being marked with *ṅ* (ṅtva) as before; consequently, the prohibition of *guṇa* for the suffix (*vikaraṇa*) based on that [ṅ-marker] would apply. Why not?
He says [the following] to show that this is so: "I cooked" (*ṭhacinavam*), and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), examples such as "I did" (*ṭhakaravam*) are included.

Regarding the phrase "of the letter *ṭha*": even though it is a substitute for the letter *la*, it is called "the letter *ṭha*" by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), because it is indirectly preceded by the letter *la*. Even though... [the text continues].

By accepting this, the meaning is determined as follows: because of the inclusion of the marker *ś* in the rule "halaḥ śnaḥ śānajjhau" (Pāṇini 3.2.83), which prescribes the substitute *śānac*, it is not necessarily the case that the status of being a *sthānin* applies to operations concerning *anubandhas*. Therefore, [the rule] "ṅtvivacam" and so forth [is established].
If whatever operation is prescribed for a *ṅit* [suffix] were to apply to the *lakāra* when it is *ṅit*,

then since the prohibition of *guṇa* would already be established in forms such as *cinuyāt* (where the *liṅ* suffix is *ṅit*), the rule "the *hyāsuṭ* augment is udātta in the *parasmaipada*" [would be unnecessary].

Regarding the rule *ṅcci* (Pāṇini 3.4.103), one should not apply the doubling (*dvicana*) to that *yāsuṭ* which is marked with the *ṅ*-sign, yet it has been applied; from this it is understood that "the operation prescribed for what is marked with the *ṅ*-sign does not take place when [the suffix] is a *lakāra*."
6. *dīdhīvevīṭām* | (Pāṇini 1.1.6) Regarding the phrase "of *dīdhī* and *vevī*": *dīdhīṅ* [is the root] meaning "to shine" or "to play" (Dhātupāṭha 1076); *vevīṅ* [is the root] meaning "to go."

The inclusion here is of these two [roots]: *tulya* (DhP 1077). But surely, there is also the inclusion of *dīṅ* in the sense of "decay" (DhP 1134), *dhīṅ* in the sense of "disregard" (DhP 1136), *veñ* in the sense of "weaving" (DhP 1006), and *vī* in the senses of "motion," "procreation," "beauty," "throwing," and "eating" (DhP 1048)?

Why is it not understood? If the inclusion of these [roots] were intended, then for the sake of removing doubt, one should have made the grammatical formulation (*nyāsa*) as *ṭhvīvedhīdīṭām*. However, it has been formulated otherwise.

Therefore, only the two verbal roots mentioned previously are to be understood here. As for "iṭ," this refers to that which is prescribed by the rule "ārddhadhātukasyeḍ vaḷādeḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.35). Now, regarding the roots *iṭ*, *kiṭ*, and *kaṭī* in the sense of "going" (Dhātupāṭha 318, 319, 320):
Why does the inclusion of this [term] not occur? And this would indeed be logical, due to its association with *dhātu*. This is not so;
for here, although the rule "the one with fewer vowels" (*alpa-actara*) [Pāṇini 2.2.34] should have caused *iṭ* to be placed first, there is an inversion of that.

By performing this [action], it is indicated that "some other reversal (*viparyāsa*) should also be understood here. Therefore, although the mention of *dhātu* (root) would have applied by association with *dhātu*, it is understood that only its opposite, namely *āgama* (augment), is being referred to. [Thus we have] "ādīdhyana."

The suffix *lyuṭ* [is applied] as in "ṭhādīdhyakaḥ. The suffix *ṇvul* [is applied] as in "kaṇitā śvaḥ" and "raṇitā śvaḥ," in the case of the roots beginning with "aṇa raṇa kaṇa" (Dhātupāṭha 444, 445, 449).

In the section on verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*) for the meanings of words, the roots *kaṇ* and *raṇ* are recited. From these two, by the rule *luṭi syatāsī lṛluṭoḥ* (3.1.33), the suffix *tās* is applied; then, by the rule *luṭaḥ prathamasya* (2.4.85) and so forth, there is the substitution of *ḍā* for the first person singular ending *ti*;
the *ṭi*-portion is elided, and by the rule *ārdhadhātukasya* (7.2.35) and so forth, the augment *iṭ* is added.

He asks why an example of *vṛddhi* for an *iṭ* augment has not been shown, and replies: "Vṛddhi does not occur for an *iṭ*. Vṛddhi is prescribed for a stem (*aṅga*) before an affix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*, and this *iṭ* belongs to an *ārdhadhātuka* affix. Furthermore, a stem does not receive the designation *aṅga* before an *ārdhadhātuka* affix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*.
In this suffix, therefore, the *vṛddhi* substitution for *iṭ* does not occur.
7. *halo 'nantarāḥ saṃyogaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.7). *Antaram* means an interval, a gap, a space, that is, a period devoid of phonemes. Those [consonants] between which no such interval exists...

They have been described as such [in the verse beginning] "by those of a different class" (*bhinnajātīyaiḥ*), and so forth. The mention of "those of a different class" is because in common worldly experience, only things of a different class are observed to act as separators. For instance, someone...

When asked by someone, "In which [family] among the immediate neighbors, O Brahmin? he replied: "Not in the immediate neighbor; a *vṛṣala* family dwells between these two. Here, for the sake of clarity, there should be a technical designation (*sañjñā*) for a consonant (*hal*) pronounced with a slurred articulation, as in the forms *nirvāyāt* or *niryāyāt*, according to the rule *vānyasya saṃyogādeḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.68).

Thus it would be; and here, in *saṃskariṣīṣṭa*, there is the augment *iṭ* by [Pāṇini 7.2.43] *ṛtaśca saṃyogādeḥ*; and here, in *saṃskriyate*, there is *guṇa* substitution by [Pāṇini 7.4.29] *guṇo’rtisaṃyogādyoḥ*.

Thus, many other such defects have been pointed out in the Bhāṣya regarding the individual status of the consonants (*hal*) as technical designators (*sañjñin*). Although those [defects] were somehow resolved there with great effort, nevertheless, for one who seeks to understand [the system] by avoiding that [resolution]:

In the case of the *sādhya* (the thing to be proven), the fault of showing disrespect toward the husband arises, and that is indeed unavoidable. However, when the whole (*samudāya*) is the designated entity (*sañjñin*), there is not even the slightest suspicion of such a fault. Therefore, considering that this [the whole] alone is the appropriate designated entity, he says:
"The aggregate is the designator. But surely,
effort is undertaken only where one intends an effect for things that exist together, as in the rule "both [are considered] *abhyasta*" (Pāṇini 6.1.5).
[The opponent asks: "He employs the dual number [in the rule], yet no effort has been made here; how then is the designation obtained for the entire aggregate? [The author replies:
"In this case as well, an effort has indeed been made, so there is no fault. [The opponent asks: "What further effort is that? [The author replies: "The employment of a long designation."
The reason for [creating] a technical term (*sañjñā*) is stated: "For the creation of a technical term is for the sake of brevity" (Vyāḍipañjikā 135).
Since the creation of a large technical term cannot be justified without a purpose, it follows that the referent (*sañjñin*) here must be something extensive.
To indicate this, the term "great" (*mahatī*) has been employed in the word *gamya*.
As it has been said: "The intention of the masters is perceived through a gesture, a glance, or by means of a great series of aphorisms (*sūtra-prabandha*). And thus, [it is] great.
It becomes designated [as *hal*]; if the aggregate (*samudāya*) is what is designated, then each individual consonant (*hal*) is not.
Therefore, it is established that the aggregate is the designation, as in the rule "of *hal*" (*halaḥ*).

To one who might object that the designation of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) is not established for two [vowels] because of the mention of the plural number, he replies with the words "And in the case of a genus," etc. The word *ca* (and) has the sense of "because. Because the plural is used in reference to a genus, the designation of "conjunction" is thereby established for both two and many.

Examples of forms such as *agniḥ* should be understood from [the rule] "he pours out sesame seeds" (*tilān strāvapati*), and so forth. This is while the word *vā* ("optionally") is being carried over from "when *m* follows, [the sibilant] is optionally doubled" (*he mapare vā*, 8.3.26), and the word *dhuṭ* is carried over from "after *ḍ*, *dh* is inserted before *s*" (*ḍaḥ si dhuṭ*, 8.3.29).
By the rule *ṭhnaśca* (8.3.30), the augment *dhuṭ* is optionally applied;

and by the rule *khari ca* (8.4.55), the letter *t* is substituted [for *d*]. In that regard, when *dhuṭ* is not present, it is *natasatarayāḥ*; but when it is present, it is *natasatarayāḥ*. [The example is] *titauccchatram*.

Thus: by the rule "from the root *tan*, the suffix *ḍau* is added, and it is treated as having the augment *san*" (Pāṇini 6.1.160), when the suffix *ḍau* is applied, the *ṭi*-portion is elided, and reduplication is performed, the form [is established]. [The rule] "there is elision of a final conjunct" (*saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*) would apply; if—

The intention is that the designation "trā" should occur through [the substitution of] the vowel *u* for the letter *r*. Nor should one suspect the teaching of the vowel *u* to be useless when there is elision (*lopa*), because it is heard where the designation "pada" does not apply, as in the case of *titaunī* and so forth. For example, in "pacati."

The counter-example for *rūpa* is given; the counter-example for the *kārya* (the grammatical operation) is "ṭhpanasam," [showing that] there would be elision by the rule "skoḥ saṃyogādyor lopaḥ" if the designation *saṃyoga* were to apply even to *s* and *n* when they are separated by an intervening vowel.
The intended meaning is "it may be so.
Regarding the rule *mukhanāsikāvacano 'nunāsikaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.8):
by the phrase "the nose together with the mouth is *mukhanāsikā*," this term *mukhanāsikā* [is explained].

This shows that it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound and not a *dvandva*. Furthermore, the *tatpuruṣa* should be understood as belonging to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group. And if [the word] "mukham" (face) and...
And if it were a *dvandva* compound consisting of [the word] *nāsikā*, there would be singularization (*ekavadbhāva*) by the rule *prāṇitūryasenāṅgānām* (Pāṇini 2.4.2).
Consequently, by the rule *sa napuṃsakam* (Pāṇini 2.4.17), it would have to be neuter; and in that case...
The intention is that the rule "when [a case-ending] follows, the neuter nominal stem undergoes shortening" (Pāṇini 1.2.47) would result in the application of shortening.
Now, it might be argued:

If the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) by means of this [rule], then the feminine suffix *ṅīp* ought to occur after that [base] by virtue of the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15); consequently, the mention in the form "that which speaks through the mouth and nose" (*mukhanāsikāvacanaḥ*) within a *bahuvrīhi* compound formed with that [term] as its final member would be untenable? This is not so.
This word *vacana* is a derivative of the object (*karmasādhana*) due to the rule "the suffixes *kṛtya* and *lyuṭ* are used diversely" (Pāṇini 3.3.113);
thus, it refers to the phoneme (*varṇa*) that is spoken, not to the nose. For this very reason, he says: "that which is articulated by means of it."

Thus, in the phrase "it is uttered" (*uccāryate*), the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is used in the passive sense (*karman*). Having understood it thus, this compound "uttered by the mouth and nose" (*mukhanāsikāvacana*) should be known as a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), not a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*). [The commentary says: "only of the anusvāra."

For if the *anusvāra* were being uttered, the operation would belong to the nose and not to the mouth; consequently, it would apply only to that [nasal], but not to *ñ, ma, ṅ, ṇ, na*, nor even in cases such as *ṭhabhra āpaḥ* (Ṛgveda 5.48.1).
Thus, in this context, the color [of the letter] has the shape of a half-moon; because the mouth is also involved in its pronunciation,
when the operation prescribed by the rule *ṭhyaro 'nunāsike* (Pāṇini 8.4.45) is to be performed, only the anusvāra is to be understood as the subject of that rule.

The intention is that this [designation] applies [to those], but not to the letters *ṅ* and so forth. Now, one might object: "But will it not apply to them as well, according to the maxim of 'the inhabitants of the palace'? Just as when it is said, 'Let the inhabitants of the palace be brought,' those who actually reside in the palace [are understood]," and so on.
There is also the inclusion of those who reside both in the palace and on the ground;
for just as they are brought without fear, so too here, if only "nasikya-vacanaḥ" (nasal-sound) were stated, it would refer to the anusvāra which is nasalized.

There will be the inclusion of sounds such as *ṅ* that are uttered from both the mouth and the nose; consequently, it is incorrect to say that [the rule] would apply to the *anusvāra*. However, in this way:
It must be said: "Would it not also apply to the *anusvāra*? This is not so; for in this case, three views are possible:
(1) that the nasalized (*anunāsika*) phoneme is entirely produced by the nose.
"One view is that [the word] *mukhavacana* [is the name]; the third view is that 'the preceding portion of this [word] is *mukhavacana*';
in both of these two subsequent views, [the term refers to] the nose and the mouth."

He exercises such affection toward the *bhāga* that even this [latter part] appears as if it were a portion of the *nāsikāvacana*. In that regard, there is another view concerning these two subsequent observations, which is the intention of Pāṇini; and not in this [view]...
The principle of "living in a palace" applies even to a single instance.
For if the syllables beginning with *ṅ* were pronounced in their entirety through both the nose and the mouth, then [the term] "living in a palace" would apply.

If, by logical reasoning, only the phrase "articulated through the nose" (*nāsikāvacanaḥ*) were stated, there would be the inclusion of those [nasal sounds] as well. But that is not the case for the [nasal stops] alone, because they are articulated through both the nose and the mouth. Therefore, if the mention of the "mouth" (*mukha*) were absent, there would be no inclusion of them; and in its absence...

It was rightly said that "there would be no designation [of the term *anusvāra*]," for it would apply only to [the sound] itself. [And it was said] "lest it apply to *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa*"; for these letters, beginning with *ka*, are articulated solely by means of the mouth, not by the nose.
Furthermore, if the mention of the "nose" (*nāsikā*) were absent,
[the rule] would apply to those very [sounds]. And in that case, in forms such as *śaktaḥ* and *suptam*,
the elision [of the nasal] prescribed by the rule *anudātopadeśavanatitanotyādīnām anunāsikaḥ lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.37) would undesirably follow.
In the word *ṭhodanapak*, there is lengthening according to Pāṇini 6.4.15: *ṭhānunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ kṅiti*.
Now, for what purpose is this long technical name (*sañjñā*) employed? Because the nose (*nāsikā*) functions subsequently (*anu*).

In which [place], or rather—that in which one operates following after the nose (anu-paścāt-nāsikāyāḥ), or that which operates behind the nose? Since the mouth is the subject under discussion, it is understood to be that very [place]. In that regard, those two which...
In the view of those two of whom either one is accepted as Pāṇini’s [teacher], in the former case the nose functions after the mouth.

The "face" (mukha) refers to the nose. The naming [of it] according to its literal meaning (*anvarthasañjñā*) is for the purpose of indicating the acceptance of either one of the two views previously mentioned.
That indication of acceptance, however, follows the principle of "the dweller in the palace" (*prāsādavāsinyāya*), regarding those who [use] the term "face."
[They] might perceive [them as such]; therefore, for the purpose of refuting that [view]:
9. *tulyāsyaprayatnaṃ savarṇam* (1.1.9). "Those produced with the same place of articulation and effort are homogeneous (*savarṇa*)."

The word *tulya* is derived by first forming the suffix *yat* according to the rule *ṭhnauvayodharma* (Pāṇini 4.4.91) from the sense "that which is measured by a balance" (*tulayā sammitam*). Now, one might object that it is impossible for effort (*prayatna*) to be measured by a balance, and therefore the qualifying attribute is impossible [in this context]. To such an objector, he replies:

"The word 'equal' (*tulya*)," and so forth. He thinks as follows: the comparison (*tulā*) is employed merely for the sake of etymological derivation; however, the actual sense of "comparison" does not exist here, nor does it [apply].

The meaning is "equal" (*sammita*). For this word *tulya* is indeed a synonym for *sadṛśa*. To explain: when "equal" is said, it becomes a synonym for "similar," but not [in the sense] of being measured by a scale (*tulā*).
This word *āsya* also exists ending in the suffix *ṇyat*; it is derived from the root *as* (to throw).

The term *āsyam* means "mouth. It is derived from the root *as* with the suffix *ṇyat* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.113), meaning "that by which food is cast forth. This [mouth] extends from the lips up to the *kākalaka*.
The *kākalaka* is the elevated region on the neck, which is called the "throat-jewel" (*kaṇṭhamaṇi*) in common parlance.

The word *āsya* also exists as a derivative formed with a *taddhita* suffix: namely, that which occurs in the mouth (*āsye bhavam*). When the suffix *yat* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.3.55 (*śarīrāvayavācca*), the vowel *a* is elided by 6.4.148 (*yasyeti ca*), and the *y* is elided by 8.4.64 (*halo yamāṃ yami lopaḥ*), resulting in *āsyam*.
Thus [it is said].
And this [term] denotes the palate and other [articulatory organs] situated within the mouth. In that regard, if this is the apprehension of the preceding word *āsya*, [then...]

It might be argued that even the sounds *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa* would receive the designation of "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*), because they are identical in their objective effort (*prayatna*) when referring to the meaning expressed by the word *asya* ending in the suffix *ṇyat*. This [objection applies] to this word *asya* which does not end in a *taddhita* suffix.

Having observed the fault [of ambiguity] in the inclusion [of the term], he says—showing that this is the inclusion of that which ends in the suffix *taddhita*—“*āsyam* means ‘that which exists in the mouth (*āsya*)’. He asks, “What, then, is that? and replies, “The place [of articulation] such as the palate (*tālu*) and so forth.
That in which the phonemes (*varṇa*) are produced is the *sthāna*. By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*),...
This refers to the inclusion of the nose and so forth. Now, one might object: "But surely the nose, which exists outside the mouth, does not constitute the 'mouth' (āsya)? This is not so;
for it is not this nose situated outside the mouth that is intended here, but rather [the part] within it.

Because the phonemes (varṇas) are not produced [therein]. What, then, is meant? There is a membrane stretched within the mouth, like the skin of a small drum (paṇava); the lines connected to it, upon being struck by the breath, produce the phonemes—it is this which is intended here as the "nose" (nāsikā). How, then, is this known?
Is this the inclusion of the word *āsya* as ending in a *taddhita* suffix? It is so, because of the purposeful inclusion of the term *āsya*.

For if it were the inclusion of that which does not end in a *taddhita* suffix, the inclusion of *āsya* would be meaningless; for in all such cases, the meaning is already expressed by the suffix itself.
The effort [of articulation] is the same. Indeed, there is no such thing for the sake of whose exclusion the mention of "mouth" (*āsya*) would be necessary.

Now, whether the *visarjanīya* possesses a homogeneous counterpart (*savarṇa*) or not, there is both a purpose and no fault [in its inclusion]. This is because it shares the qualities of "contact" (*spṛṣṭatā*) and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), [qualities] such as slight contact (īṣatspṛṣṭatā) and so forth are included. "A quality of the phoneme" (varṇaguṇaḥ) means a property of the phonemes beginning with *a*.
"That which has an equal effort in the mouth" (tulya āsye prayatno yasya)—by this [it is defined].

He shows that the word *tulyāsyaprayatna* is a three-membered *bahuvrīhi*. A *bahuvrīhi* indeed occurs even when its members have different substrata (*vyadhikaraṇa*), provided they possess the capacity to convey the meaning; for example: *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* ("the one who has Kāla on his throat") and *urasilomā* ("the one who has hair on his chest"). Now, [consider] the *bahuvrīhi* containing a *dvandva*.
Why is it not accepted that "tulyāsyaprayatnam" means "that which has the same oral cavity (āsya) and effort (prayatna)"— i.e., those whose oral cavity and effort are equal?
It is thought as follows:

If a *bahuvrīhi* compound containing a *dvandva* were adopted [to define "place" (*sthāna*)], then the effort (*prayatna*) would not be qualified by the location such as the palate (*tālu*). Consequently, there would be no mutual designation of *savarṇa* (homogeneity) between the letter *ka* and the letter *ṅa*,
because their external efforts (*bāhya-prayatna*) are different.

The external effort (*bāhya-prayatna*) of the sound *ka* consists of the throat being opened (*vivṛta-kaṇṭhatva*), and so forth; that of the sound *ṅ* consists of the throat being closed (*saṃvṛta-kaṇṭhatva*), and so forth. Furthermore, if the technical designation "homogeneous" (*savarṇa-sañjñā*) did not exist, then in the word *śaṅkitā*, the rule "the substitute is homogeneous with the following [consonant] when *ya* follows an *anusvāra*" (Pāṇini 8.4.58) would not apply, and thus the sound *ṅ* would not occur. Now, [if one asks...]

Even though there is a difference in external effort (*bāhya-prayatna*), the internal effort called "contact" (*spṛṣṭatā*) is the same for these two; by relying on that [internal effort], the designation of being "homogeneous" (*savarṇa-sañjñā*) will occur. If this is so, then even though there is a difference between the internal efforts of openness (*vivṛtatā*) and contact (*aspṛṣṭatā*) in the case of the letters *ś* and *c*, [the designation would still apply].

If the similarity were based on the external effort (*bāhyaprayatna*)—such as the openness of the throat (*vivṛtakaṇṭhatva*)—which is common to both of these distinct efforts, then the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) would apply [to all vowels]. Consequently, the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) to be mentioned later, namely "ṭharuścyotati," would not be tenable. Now, regarding the three-fold [classification]...

But in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the effort (*prayatna*) is qualified by the place of articulation, such as the palate; therefore, setting aside the external effort, only the internal [efforts] such as contact (*spṛṣṭatā*) and so forth are grasped,
for that alone—
It is possible [for this definition] with respect to the palate and other internal locations of the mouth, but not otherwise. When internal effort (*ābhyantara-prayatna*) is taken into account,
even though there is a difference in external effort (*bāhya-prayatna*), the designation of *savarṇa* (homogeneity) still applies between the phonemes *ka* and *ṅ*.
Because the internal effort (*ābhyantara-prayatna*) is identical,
and it is precisely that which is intended here; for even though the external effort (*bāhya-prayatna*) of the letters *ca* and *śa* is indeed identical, [it is not what is meant].

The designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) would apply [to the vowel *e*]; however, because that [designation] is not included here, and because that which is included is not identical [to the vowel *e*], it is therefore proper to rely on a three-word *bahuvrīhi* compound, and not one containing a *dvandva*. If, then, it is a three-word *bahuvrīhi*—

The word *vrīhi* is taken as the subject; because it possesses a different case-ending and is subordinate, it remains unqualified by [the term] "equal" (*tulya*). Consequently, would not the designation of *savarṇa* (homogeneous) apply even to those vowels situated in different places? This is not a fault. For when a locus is presented in relation to that which is to be contained within it, [it serves as the basis for the operation].
It is understood that "it is equal to that" means it is equal precisely by virtue of being contained within that. For instance,
when it is said, "The meal of Devadatta and Yajñadatta is equal in a bronze vessel," it follows that the bronze vessel is also equal for them both.

It is understood that when two sounds have the same place and effort of articulation (*tulyāsyaprayatna*) relative to one another, they bear the technical designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) toward each other;
however, this meaning is not obtained from the explicit statement here. Consequently, whichever [sound] is relative to which...

Anticipating the objection that "that which has the same place and effort of articulation (tulyāsyaprayatna) should be designated as homogeneous (savarṇa) even with respect to something other than that [the preceding rule]," he says:
"with respect to what is of the same class" (samānajātīyaṃ prati). That is, with respect to that which is of the same class.
That which has the same place of articulation and effort is designated as *savarṇa* (homogeneous) with respect to it, and not with anything other than that;
this is understood because both the term *tulyāsyaprayatna* ("having the same place and effort") and the term *savarṇa* ("homogeneous") are relative terms.
For a word denoting a relative brings to mind its correlative by its very nature, even without the proximity of another word, as in the expression:
"One must serve one's father. It is not said [in this context] that [the action is performed] "upon oneself" (svasmin).

This is understood from the relationship [expressed by the genitive], namely, "he who is the father of whom. So it is here as well; for although it is not explicitly stated that "that which has the same place and effort of articulation as another is termed a *savarṇa* (homogeneous) with respect to that," nevertheless, it is understood through the relationship.

It is understood that a sound with the same place and effort of articulation (*tulyāsyaprayatna*) receives the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) only with respect to one of its own kind. Alternatively, the term *savarṇa* is an etymological designation meaning "having the same color" (*samāno varṇaḥ*); therefore, it receives the designation *savarṇa* only with respect to what is of the same class.

It is so; for in this way, its *varṇa* (phoneme) is homogeneous (*samāna*) only with respect to that which is designated as having the same *savarṇa* (homogeneous) status, and not with respect to a different class (*vijātīya*). [Examples such as] "four" (*catvāraḥ*) and so on. Efforts (*prayatna*) are of two kinds: internal (*ābhyantara*) and external (*bāhya*).

Among those, four internal properties have been shown; the external ones, however, are eleven. What, then, are they? "Openness (vivāra), closure (saṃvāra), breath (śvāsa), resonance (nāda), voiced (ghoṣa), voiceless (aghoṣa), weak aspiration (alpaprāṇa), strong aspiration (mahāprāṇa), acute (udātta), grave (anudātta), and circumflex (svarita). Among these:

The vital air called *prāṇa*, impelled with effort from the region of the navel, moves upward and is restrained with effort in one of the locations beginning with the chest; being thus restrained, it strikes against that location.

From that, sound is produced through the striking of the articulatory site (*sthāna*). In space (*ākāśa*), there is the perception of similarity (*sāvarṇya-śruti*), which is the acquisition of its own nature by the similar phoneme (*savarṇa*). In that regard, when sound is being produced in the phoneme, it strikes the articulatory site;
from that striking of the articulatory site, sound is produced.

The scriptural mention of "similarity" (*sāvarṇya*) in space refers to the acquisition of its own nature by a phoneme (*savarṇa*). In that context, when the places of articulation (*sthāna*), the articulators (*karaṇa*), and the efforts (*prayatna*) touch one another while a phonemic sound (*varṇadhvani*) is being produced, that is "contact" (*spraṣṭatā*).
When they touch slightly, that is "slight contact" (*īṣatspraṣṭatā*).

*Spṛṣṭatā* (contact); when they touch [the vocal organs] by being close together, that is *saṃvṛtatā* (closure); when they touch by being at a distance, that is *vivṛtatā* (opening)—these are the four internal efforts (*ābhyantara-prayatna*). Furthermore, their status as "internal" is as follows:

Because they arise at the very moment of production through the operation of the places of articulation (*sthāna*), the articulators (*karaṇa*), and the effort (*prayatna*). Among them, the *sparśas* (contact consonants) have the *spṛṣṭa* (complete contact) articulator;
the *sparśas* are those beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*, and their quality (*guṇa*) is *spaṣṭatā* (distinctness). The *karaṇa*...

*Kṛtiḥ* refers to the manner of articulation. Those whose place of articulation (*karaṇa*) is accompanied by contact (*spṛṣṭatā*) are called *spṛṣṭakaraṇāḥ*. The same should be understood for other cases as well. The semivowels (*antasthāḥ*) have slightly contacted places of articulation (*īṣatspṛṣṭakaraṇāḥ*).
The semivowels *y*, *r*, *l*, and *v* are internal (*antaḥsthā*). The articulation (*karaṇa*) for the sibilants (*ūṣman*) and the vowels (*svara*) is wide open (*vivṛta*).
All vowels are *ac*. The sibilants (*ūṣman*) are *ś*, *ṣ*, *s*, and *h*.
Now, what are the characteristics of the external efforts? When that very breath called *prāṇa*, moving upward, is struck at the head and turns back, it strikes the abdominal cavity; at that time—

When the chest is struck, because the opening of the throat is constricted, the phonetic property known as *saṃvāra* (closure) arises; when it is open, *vivāra* (opening) arises. When the throat is constricted, there is an indistinct sound called *nāda* (tone);
when it is open, there is *śvāsa* (breath). These two reside above.
Some explain *anupradāna* as "the sounding" (*śvāsanāda*).
Others, however, say that *anupradāna* is so called because it is "given" (*pradīyate*) after (*anu*), following upon the production of the phoneme (*varṇaniṣpatti*). Furthermore, others state:
*anupradānam anu-*...

"Resounding like the ringing of a bell" means that just as the ringing of a bell experiences a reverberation (*anusvana*), so it is here. In that regard, when sound is produced by the striking of the vocal organs, if a resonance (*nāda*) is added, then from the conjunction of that resonance and the sound, a "sonorous" (*ghoṣa*) quality arises; when—

When breath is added [to the effort], then due to the contact with the sound of the breath, it is voiced; when the air is great, it is a "great breath" (mahāprāṇa), and when the air is small, it is a "small breath" (alpaprāṇa). When the effort follows all the limbs and becomes intense, then of the body...
Suppression [of the breath], the narrowing of the throat,
and the harshness of the voice due to the rapid movement of the air—
these constitute what they call *udātta*. But when the effort is mild, then [the body]...
Relaxation [of the glottis], the enlargement of the throat-cavity, and the smoothness of the voice due to the slow movement of the breath—these they call *anudātta* (unaccented).
From the proximity of the *udātta* and *anudātta* tones, the *svarita* (circumflex) arises; such are the external efforts (*bāhya-prayatna*).

Furthermore, their externality [is established] after the time of the completion of the phonemes (*varṇa*), because they arise by the force of the wind (*vāyu*). Among them, the first and second of the classes (*varga*), as well as *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, the *visarjanīya*, the *jihvāmūlīya*, the *upadhmānīya*, and the two *yamas*— both first and second— are produced with an open throat and have the emission of breath (*śvāsa*) as their secondary cause (*anupradāna*).

The unvoiced [consonants] are as follows: among the *yamās*, the first are *alpa-prāṇa* (unaspirated), while all others are *mahā-prāṇa* (aspirated). Furthermore, the third and fourth letters of each *varga*, the semivowels (*antaḥstha*), the letter *ha*, the *anusvāra*, and the two *yamās* (third and fourth) have constricted glottis (*saṃvṛta-kaṇṭha*), possess nasal emission (*nādānupradāna*), and are voiced (*ghoṣavat*).
Among those being classified, the third [consonants] and the semivowels (*antaḥstha*) are of weak breath (*alpaprāṇa*); all others are of strong breath (*mahāprāṇa*).
As are the thirds, so are the fifths; for these, nasality (*ānunāsikya*) is an additional quality.
Regarding these two types of efforts— external and internal— that have been described,

it is the four internal ones previously mentioned, such as *spṛṣṭatā* (contact) and so forth, that are relied upon here for the technical designation of "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*), and not the external ones.

[The term] "opening" (*vivāra*) and so forth [are excluded], because they have been excluded by the mention of "the mouth" (*āsya*). For it is only qualities such as contact (*spṛṣṭatā*) that occur within the mouth, not opening and the like. If this is so, for what purpose is the mention of "effort" (*prayatna*)?
Let it simply be "having the same place in the mouth" (*tulyāsyam*); for by the mention of "the mouth" alone, qualities such as contact would also [be included].

Are not the articulatory efforts (*prayatna*) also obtained as the cause for the designation of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇasañjñā*), just like the places of articulation such as the palate, since they too occur in the mouth? This is true; nevertheless, both [the place and the effort] are mentioned in order to exclude the operation [of homogeneity] on a case-by-case basis. For otherwise, just as the place [of articulation] is common...

Just as [the organ] functions in the designation of a homogeneous letter (*savarṇa-sañjñā*) independently of another location, so too effort (*prayatna*) is independent of location, and location is independent of effort.
If it were dependent [on effort], then there would be the designation of "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*) even for those whose efforts are different but whose places of articulation are the same,
or for those whose places of articulation are different but whose efforts are the same. This is because [the rule] beginning with *a a* [would apply] to those...
He demonstrates which sounds, to whatever extent and of whatever kind, possess the mutual designation of *savarṇa* (homogeneous):
for all the vowels (*akāra*), as well as *ṭha*, *ku*, *ha*, and *visarjanīya*, have the same place of articulation, namely the throat (*kaṇṭha*). The same applies to the *ikāra*s.

Regarding the *ṭh* and *cuy* sounds, [it is stated] "the palatals (*tālavyāḥ*)"; thus, for the *u*-vowels, [it is stated] "the *u*, *p*, and *upadhmānīya* are labials (*oṣṭhyāḥ*)," thus, for the *ṛ*-vowels, [it is stated] "the *ṛ*, *ṭu*, *ra*, and *ṣ* are cerebrals (*mūrdhanyāḥ*)," thus, for the *lṛ*-vowels, [it is stated] "the *lṛ*, *tu*, *la*, and *sa* are dentals (*dantyāḥ*). Thus, [the respective places of articulation are] the palate, the lips, the head, and the teeth.

Regarding the *e*-vowels and *ai*-vowels, [it is said] "Ṭha-ei are produced by the throat and palate," thus they are throat-palatal (*kaṇṭhatālavya*). Regarding the *o*-vowels and *au*-vowels, [it is said] "Ṭho-o are produced by the throat and lips," thus they are throat-labial (*kaṇṭhayauṣṭhya*).

The lips are the point of articulation (*sthāna*). As for the effort (*prayatna*), it is taught that for all these *ūṣman* sounds as well as the vowels, the organ of articulation is wide open; thus, they possess openness (*vivṛtatva*). Therefore, because their place and effort are identical, the vowel *a* and the others are designated as *savarṇa* (homogeneous) with one another. In this same way...

Up to and including the letter *au*. The semivowels (*antasthā*) are of two types: nasalized (*sānunāsika*) and non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*), excluding the letter *r*. These also bear the technical designation "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*) with respect to their own kind of semivowels.
However, for the letters *r* and the sibilants (*ūṣman*), there are no homogeneous counterparts.
Thus, the intention is that those other phonemes beginning with *a*, such as *ka* and so forth, are of a different genus (*vijātīya*).

However, those of the same genus (*tulyajātīya*)—namely, the *repha* (the sound *r*) and the sibilants (*ūṣman*)—are indeed *savarṇa* (homogeneous) when they share the same place of articulation (*sthāna*) and effort (*prayatna*).
Among these, first, for the *repha*, there are phonemes other than *ṛ*, *ṭu*, *ra*, *ṣa*, and *ya*, *va*, *la*.

Furthermore, they do not belong to the same *savarṇa* class because they have different places of articulation and different efforts of articulation. To illustrate: *ṭ*, *th*, *k*, *kh*, *v*, and *visarjanīya* are gutturals (*kaṇṭhya*); *i*, *c*, *u*, *y*, *ś*, and *ṣ* are palatals (*tālavya*); *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *t*, *th*, *l*, *d*, *dh*, *s*, and *r* are dentals (*dantya*); *p*, *ph*, *m*, and *upadhmānīya* are labials (*oṣṭhya*); *e* and *ai* are gutturo-palatals; *o* and *au* [are gutturo-labials].

According to the rule "kaṇṭhyauṣṭhyau," the points of articulation (sthāna) for the vowels beginning with *a* are the throat and so forth, as appropriate. For the letter *r*, however, since "ṛ-ṭ-u-ra-ṣ are cerebral" (*mūrdhanya*), its point of articulation is the palate (*mūrdhan*).
Regarding the effort (*prayatna*) as well, among the vowels beginning with *a* that were just mentioned, the effort for those [vowels] is "open" (*vivṛta*).

The quality of being "open" (*vivṛtatva*) belongs to the organs of the sibilants (*ūṣman*) and the vowels (*svara*). As for those beginning with *ka*, which fall within the end of the classes (*varga*), they are called "contact consonants" (*sparśa*) because their production involves contact (*spṛṣṭa*); thus, they possess the quality of "contact" (*spṛṣṭatā*). The semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*) have the quality of "slight contact" (*iṣatspṛṣṭatā*), as their production involves slight contact; this applies to the letters *ra* and *la* as well. The letters *śa* and *sa* also [possess this quality].

Due to the difference in place and effort, there are no *savarṇa* (homogeneous) sounds for the letter *r*. For those two [the *i* and *ī* vowels] are respectively palatal and dental, whereas the letter *r* is retroflex; as for the effort (*prayatna*), it is...
The openness (*vivṛtatva*) of those two [the *ṛ* and *ṝ*] is also as previously stated. As for the *repha* (the sound *r*), it is exactly as described before.

Furthermore, the various *ṛ*-sounds do not share the same phonetic quality (*savarṇa*) with the *repha* due to a difference in articulatory effort (*prayatna*), and not because of a difference in place of articulation (*sthāna*); for they too are produced at the roof of the mouth (*mūrdhan*).

However, there is a difference in the effort (*prayatna*) between the vowels *ṛ* and *ṣ*. As before, there is openness (*vivṛtatva*), but for the *repha* (the sound *r*), it is that same [effort] previously mentioned. For the *ṭavarga* (the retroflex class), there is contact (*spṛṣṭatā*).
Furthermore, the sounds *y*, *v*, and *l* are not homogeneous (*savarṇa*) solely because of the difference in their places of articulation (*sthāna*), and not otherwise.

Because of the difference in effort; for even those [semivowels] possess the quality of being slightly touched (*iṣatspṛṣṭa*). However, a difference in place of articulation (*sthāna*) does exist, since *ya*, *va*, and *la* are respectively palatal, dental, and labial.
In the same way, the *visarjanīya*, *jihvāmūlīya*, *upadhmānīya*, and *anusvāra*— as well as these *yamās*, namely *kuṃ*, *khaṃ*, *guṃ*, and *ghuṃ*—
do not constitute *savarṇa* (homogeneous) sounds with the letter *r*, precisely because their places of articulation (*sthāna*) and efforts (*prayatna*) are dissimilar.
The *visarjanīya* is guttural, the *jihvāmūlīya* is produced at the root of the tongue; the *upadhmānīya* is labial, while the *anusvāra* and the *yamas* are nasal; as for the *repha*, however—
