The effort for that [visarga], which was previously described as being "cerebral" (mūrdhanya), does not exist at all for the *visarjanīya* and other such sounds. Thus, for the letter *repha*, there is no other similar (*savarṇa*) phoneme except for another *repha*. By this same principle, it should also be understood for the sibilants (*ūṣman*), such as *śa* and the rest.
It should be understood that this applies when there is an absence of homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*).
For example, in the word *vargya* and so forth: "belonging to a class" (*varga*) is *vargya*. [The suffix] *yat* is applied here because it belongs to the *dig-ādi* group (Pāṇini 4.3.54).

By the rule *ṭhyasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), the vowel *ā* is elided. A phoneme belonging to a particular class (*vargya*) is homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with another phoneme of that same class which shares the same place and effort of articulation (*tulyāsyaprayatna*) within its own class.
It occurs, just as the letter *ka* [is related] with the letter *kha*;
so it should be understood in other cases as well. Regarding the phrase "of those produced in different places" and so forth:
for all these, beginning with *ka*, are [articulated by] contact (*spṛṣṭa*).
Because they possess six qualities, they require equal effort;

yet, due to their respective places of articulation—the throat, palate, head, teeth, and lips—they have different locations. For example: *ṭhtarptā*, *tarptum*. This is from the root *tṛpa* or *tṛnpha* in the sense of "satiety" (*tṛptau*) [Dhātupāṭha 1307, 1308] with the suffix *tṛc*.

And [the rule for] *tumun* and *rūpa*: "Of those with different efforts" (*bhinnaprayatnānām*), and so forth. For the vowels beginning with *i* are all identical in their place of articulation because they are palatal;
however, they differ according to their respective efforts, such as being *vivṛta* (open), *spṛṣṭa* (contact), or *īṣatspṛṣṭa* (slight contact).

They have different efforts (*prayatna*). Although the effort for the phoneme *i* and the phoneme *ś* is indeed the same, nevertheless, because he will state their exclusion [from being homogeneous], they do not constitute *savarṇa* (homogeneous sounds).

In the word *aruścyotati*, this is the form of the root *ścyut* (meaning "to flow") in the present tense (*laṭ*). Therein, the *s* of the word *arus* situated before [the suffix] undergoes *rutva* (becoming *r*).
That becomes a *visarjanīya*. For that as well, by the rule *vā śari* (Pāṇini 8.3.36), there is an optional *s*. For that as well...

"The sound *ścu* is the phoneme *ś*. [The example] is 'ṭhhotṛkāraḥ'. But how, then, does the phoneme *ṛ* become the substitute here? For [one might ask], since the substituend is the entire complex consisting of both the phonemes *ṛ* and *lṛ*, why is that [substitute *ṛ*] the most similar (*antaratama*)? To this he says: "Of both."

And so forth. The letter *ṛ* is a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*), whereas the letter *lṛ* is dental (*dantya*). In that case, if a single long vowel were possible as the most similar substitute (*antaratama*) for both of them—being both retroflex and dental—then that most similar substitute would [be the replacement].
That [substitute] is not possible; therefore, it must be that which is the most similar (*antaratama*) to the constituent part (*avayava*).

Even in that case, if the long *ḷ* were to exist, it would also have to occur by way of alternation (*paryāyeṇa*), yet such a thing does not exist. Consequently, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*), it must be that which is the most similar to the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) as a whole.
That very [sound] becomes the letter *ṛ*.
10. *Nājjhalau* (Pāṇini 1.1.10).
He states the reason for the contingency [of the rule], namely that "even those with equal place and effort [are not homogeneous]," because a contingency must be preceded by its application.

Regarding the prohibition: in the case of "daṇḍahasta," both the vowel *a* and the consonant *ha* have the same place of articulation (*sthāna*) because both are produced in the throat (*kaṇṭha*); they also have the same effort (*prayatna*) because both involve an open articulation (*vivṛta-karaṇa*). In the case of "dadhi śītam" as well, for this very reason, there is equality of effort.

Because both [sounds] belong to the palate (*tālavya*), they share the same place of articulation (*tulyasthānatva*). He demonstrates the result of the prohibition: "the rule for lengthening by homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*) does not occur. Now, one might object: in the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.101), there is the condition *aci*; [how then can this prohibition apply?]
This is how it proceeds:
even in the absence of a prohibition there, lengthening will not occur, as in the case of *kumārī śete*;
therefore, these two examples are inappropriate. It might be argued: "By the rule *ṭh-ṇ-it savarṇasya*..."

Although there is the status of being a vowel (*actva*) because [the letter *a*] is included by its similarity (*sāvarṇya*) with both the vowels *a* and *i* according to Pāṇini 1.1.69 (*cāpratyayaḥ*), nevertheless, since it is taught among the consonants (*hal*),
it also possesses the status of being a consonant (*haltva*); thus, [there is no fault].
That they are merely *dhakāra* and *śkāra* is true; however, they are also *hal*s. This, moreover, is the intention of the author of the Vṛtti here:
that the rule "nājjhalau" (Pāṇini 1.1.10) must necessarily be formulated for another purpose.
The mention of "yasya" (of which) is for the purpose of preventing its elision (*lopābhāva*). Although this [mention] was made for the sake of something else, it would also serve this purpose.

In that case, the cumbersome process of comprehension that would otherwise result from having to establish the absence of length (*dīrghatvābhāva*) by means of the non-continuation (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule is thereby dispensed with.

Regarding the example *ṭhvaipāśaḥ*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied by the rule *tatra bhavaḥ*. In the rule *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), when the vowel *i* is prescribed, it includes the letter *śa* as well due to their homogeneous nature (*sāvarṇya*). Consequently, the elision of that [ś] would follow. Regarding *ānahuham*: this means "the modification (*vikāra*) of an anaḍuh."

In the rule *ṭhprāṇirajatādibhyo'ñ* (4.3.154), and therein in the rule *yasyeti ca* (6.4.148), the author of the commentary (*gṛhyakāra*) might include the letter *ha* as well; consequently, its elision would occur as in the previous case.

11. *īdūded dvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam* (Pāṇini 1.1.11). Is this to be understood as: "That which is a dual ending beginning with *i*, *u*, or *e* is *pragṛhya*"? Or rather: "That which ends in *i*, *u*, or *e* [and is a dual] is *pragṛhya*"?

Or is it that whatever is a dual ending (*dvivacana*) is *pragṛhya*? In that regard, according to the first position, the designation *pragṛhya* would not apply in cases such as *pacete*, for here it is not merely the phoneme *e* that is the dual ending, but rather the word-form *āte*. Regarding this first [position]...
Having observed the fault in the first position, he states the second position, beginning with:

"That which ends in *ī*, *ū*, *e*, or *o*," and so forth. Now, even in this position, forms such as *agnī* would not be established; for in this case, the dual ending consists only of *ī* and the others, and not that which ends in them?
By the rule "that which is single [is treated] like what precedes and what follows" (1.1.21), the status of being "like the final" (antavadbhāvaḥ) occurs; thus there is no fault.

In "agnī," lengthening occurs by the rule "the preceding [vowel] is homogeneous with the following in the case of the first two [cases]" (6.1.102). Here, since the designation *pragṛhya* applies, [the vowel remains short].
Because of the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *ṭhplutapragṛhyā aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.125),

the substitution of a long vowel for two homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) by the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (6.1.101) does not occur when the word *iti* follows. Similarly, in the case of *vāyu*, the substitution of a semivowel for the vowel *i* by the rule *iko yaṇaci* (6.1.77) also does not take place.
Thus is the substitution of *yaṇ*.

In the remaining examples as well, there is the substitution of *ay*. In "khaṭve," the substitution of *śī* occurs by the rule "āṬṅ āpaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.18), followed by "ād guṇaḥ" (6.1.87). In "pacete" and "yajete," [the same process applies].

The *ātmanepada* suffix is used because the root is marked with the *svarita* accent; [the suffix] *ātām* occurs, followed by the substitution of *e* for *ṭi*, and the substitution of *ī* for *ā* according to *āto ṅtiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.81).
Then, by *lopo vyor vali* (Pāṇini 6.1.66), there is the elision of the *y*.
Thus, "vṛkṣāv atra" and "plakṣāv atra" are examples of the dual number; it does not [follow that they are not dual].

[The suffix] *ī* [is applied] after that which ends in *u*, *ī*, or *e*. Because there is no preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by that [rule], the substitution indeed occurs. In the example "kumāry atra," once the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "vayasi prathame" (Pāṇini 4.1.20), the word "kumārī" ends in the vowel *ī*; however, it is not [the case that the original form is preserved].

It ends with two vowels (*dvivanacāntam*); therefore, even though the status of being a *prakṛtibhāva* (original form) does not apply, the substitution (*yaṇādeśa*) indeed occurs. Now, what is the purpose of the inclusion of the marker *t* (*taparakaraṇam*)? If it is argued that it is for the sake of excluding the protracted vowel (*pluta*), we say no; for the protracted vowel is desired [to be included]. And this is because even when the marker *t* is applied, the designation *pragṛhya* applies to the protracted vowel.

It is established that, as stated in the Bhāṣya, "the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is not established (*asiddha*); because of its non-establishment, [it is included] at that very time" (Mahābhāṣya 1.66), and so forth;
this is for the purpose of including those sounds of the same duration that differ in their secondary qualities (*guṇa*).
If this is argued, it is not so; because of the statement in the *Śikṣā*, "The qualities (*guṇas*) do not cause differentiation in the technical treatises" (*so.pa.* 80), he says:

"The inclusion of the *ta* (the *tapara* marker) is for the sake of removing ambiguity. For if the *tapara* marker were absent, there would be a substitution of *yaṇ* for both the vowel *ī* and the vowel *ū*; and consequently, there would indeed be ambiguity.
It might be asked: "Is this the inclusion of the letters *y* and *v*, or rather the inclusion of *i* and *u*? [The answer is: "It must be explained. This means that it must be interpreted.
In this regard, the following interpretation has been given: the upcoming mention of Śākalya applies here as well.

By the logic of the "lion's glance" (siṃhāvalokita), that [rule] is a settled explanatory statement (vyavasthita-vibhāṣā); therefore, there will be a prohibition regarding words such as *maṇī*, as in *maṇīva*, *dampatīva*, and *rodasīva*. Regarding *maṇīva*...

The words *dayau* and so forth end in the dual number. In that case, if they were not *pragṛhya*, the single substitution (*ekādeśa*) would indeed occur according to the rule "a long vowel replaces [a vowel] with its homogeneous counterpart" (Pāṇini 6.1.101).

12. *adaso māt* (Pāṇini 1.1.12). [The commentary explains: "The *m* which belongs to *adas*. The genitive case is used here to denote a relationship characterized by the distinction between part and whole (*avayava-avayavibhāva*).

In the case of *ṣaṣṭhī atra*, from the word *adas* followed by *jas*, the substitution of *śī* occurs [by Pāṇini 7.1.17]; then the substitution of *at* for the final vowel and following consonant [by 7.1.102];
then the single substitute *guṇa* for *a* and *i* [by 6.1.97], resulting in the form *amū*; finally, with the long *ī*, the *guṇa* substitution of *e* for *a* and *ī* occurs [by 6.1.87].

By the rule *ṭheta īdbahuvacane* (8.2.81), there is the substitution of *ī* for *e*, and by (8.2.80), the substitution of *m* for *d*. This rule is commenced for the purpose of excluding the dual number. *Amū*.

Regarding the form *āsāte*: the dual ending for the pronoun *adas* is *au*. By the rule "the substitution of *yat* for *tyad*-class [pronouns]" (*tyadādyatvam*), the initial *a* is replaced by *ya*; then, by the rule "vṛddhi in place of *eC* followed by *eC*" (*vṛddhireci*, 6.1.88), a *vṛddhi* vowel is substituted.

By the rule "for the long *au* of *adas* that does not end in *as*, *u* is substituted" (*adaso'serdādudo maḥ*, 8.2.80), in place of the long *au*, an *ū* is substituted due to similarity (*antaratamya*). Here too, the operation concerning the *ū* vowel is considered asiddha.
[The rule] was not applicable previously. Therefore, this [new rule] is commenced in order to set aside the principle that "what precedes is as if non-existent" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*, 8.2.1).
But how can the principle *pūrvatrāsiddham* be set aside by the force of this statement? This is not so; for when the operation of a *pragṛhya* vowel has already been established...
[One might argue that] the rule "an unpragṛhya ṭhaṇ becomes nasalized" (Pāṇini 8.4.57) would require this statement for its purpose; but it is not so, for there is not just a single purpose [for it].
It initiates the application of the rule. For if this were the only purpose, he would have stated it right there [in the rule for *anunāsika*]:
"The *anunāsika* occurs for a non-*pragṛhya* *ṇa*, and for *adas*. [Examples: *śamyatra*, *dāḍimyatra*.

Thus: by the rule "ṣid-gaurādibhyaś-ca" (Pāṇini 4.1.41), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied; by "yasyeti ca" (6.4.148), there is the elision of the vowel *a*. This long *ī* follows the letter *m*, but it is not related to the word *adas*. [The phrase] "amuke 'tra" is used here.

By the rule *ṭhavyayasarvanāmnām* (5.3.71), the suffix *akac* is added; by *ṭhjasaḥ śī* (7.1.17), *jas* is replaced by *śī*; by *ṭhādÂguṇaḥ* (6.1.87), *guṇa* substitution occurs; and as before, through the rules for *utva* and *matva*, the form *amuke* is derived.

When the word *ati* follows [the word ending in] *ṭha*, *eṅ*, or a word-final [vowel], there is the substitution of the single preceding form (*pūrvarūpatva*) according to Pāṇini 6.1.109: *ṭheṅḥ padāntādati*.

Regarding the statement "ṭhśe": since the hearing of the sound *śe* is indistinguishable, it would follow that the word *śe* occurring in "kāśe kuśe" is also included; therefore, with the intention of stating a distinction, he asks: "What is this?"

Regarding "śe": [this refers to] the rule *supām* etc. The intention is that the form *śe*, which results from the words *kāśa* and *kuśa* when the seventh case singular ending is applied and the *guṇa* substitution (*ādguṇaḥ*, 6.1.87) is performed, is not included here, because it occurs only incidentally (*lākṣaṇikatvāt*). [The examples are] *yuṣme* and *asme*.

The substitution of *śe* for the sixth case plural (*ṣaṣṭhībahuvacana*) occurs by the rule *supāṃ suluk...* (Pāṇini 7.1.39), while the elision [of the case-ending] follows from *śeṣe lopaḥ* (7.2.90). Alternatively, this is the substitution of *śe* for the first case plural (*prathamābahuvacana*) itself;
because this is Vedic usage (*chāndasatvāt*), the rule *yūyavayau jasi* (7.2.93) does not apply here.
The forms *tve* and *me* arise; here, the substitution of *śe* occurs for both the singular locative and the singular ablative.
By the rule *tvamāvekavacane* (Pāṇini 7.2.97), the substitutes *tvam* and *mā* replace *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. However, as for the other [forms]...
"An imitation of the worldly"—this is the sense when [the forms] such as *yuṣme* are used; that is, when they are imitations of worldly usage.
When [words] such as *yuṣme* and *asme*, which reside in Vedic sentences, are extracted according to their meaning...

In order to establish [the forms] in their own original form (*svarūpa*), the particle *iti* is supplied by the authors of the grammatical rules (*padakāra*); thus, examples such as "ṭhyuṣme" and "ṭhasme" come into being.
However, the other [usage] is worldly (*laukika*).

When "imitation" is mentioned, even in these Vedic sentences— "na yuṣme vājabandhavaḥ" (Ṛgveda 8.69.19), "tve rāyaḥ" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.2.5.2), and "me rāyaḥ" (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 4.22)— that form of the word which ends in the elided sound *yuṣme* and so forth exists in its own essential nature.
To demonstrate this, he says: *yuṣme*, *asme*, *tve*, and *me*.
If this is so, for what purpose is the citation of such passages as *na yuṣme vājabandhavaḥ* (Ṛgveda 8.69.19)? For in these Vedic sentences, there are the words *yuṣme* and so forth.
These are sounds; the purpose [of the sūtra] is to demonstrate that these are imitations of them, for otherwise it would not be known of what these are imitations.
14. *nipāta ekājanāṅ* (Pāṇini 1.1.14).
Is this term *ekāj* a *bahuvrīhi* compound or a *karmadhāraya*? If it were a *bahuvrīhi*, [then in the case of] the word *pra-*...

In that case, this [compound] would also receive the designation *pragṛhya*. Consequently, the rule-reference "from *pra* and *upa*" (Pāṇini 1.3.42) would not be tenable, nor would the counter-example *prāgnayaḥ*. Therefore, this is a *karmadhāraya* compound.

Having considered this, he says: "The word *eka* is both *accha* and *ekāc*. The three examples beginning with *ṭha apehi* are Vedic (*cchāndasa*), while the others are secular (*laukika*). In that regard, in the phrase *ṭhā evaṃ nu manyase*, the vowel *ā* [is the subject].

The particle *vā* serves to complete the sentence. However, in the phrase "ṭhā evaṃ kila tat," it has the sense of recollection (*smaraṇa*). Regarding "ṭhcakārātra": this is the perfect tense (*liṭ*) of the root *kṛ*.
By the rule "parasmaipadānām" (Pāṇini 3.4.82), *tiP* is replaced by *ṇal*, and the vowel substitution (*vṛddhi*) occurs.

The substitution of *ra* and *pa* [for *ṛ* and *ḷ*]. By the rule "when there is reduplication, provided it is not an *ac*" (1.1.59), reduplication occurs through the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). Then, the substitution of *u* [for *ṛ*] by 7.4.66, and the substitution of *c* [for *k* and *h*] by 7.4.62.
Thus, there is the substitution of *cu* (the letter *c*). This suffix *ṇal* is a single-vowel (*ekāc*) element, but it is not a particle (*nipāta*).

Regarding the word *prāgnaye*: the prefix *pra-* is a particle, but it is not a single-vowel element. Consequently, the rule *plutapragṛhyā aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.125), which prescribes the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), does not apply. [This is because of the rule] *akaḥ savarṇe*.
However, the lengthening [of the vowel] does indeed occur by virtue of [Pāṇini 6.1.101].
For here, the letter *ā* is introduced as qualified by the marker *ṅ*; it is not known where that *ṅ*-ness applies, and where...
And [it is] not [so]. Therefore, in order to demonstrate the distinction between the scopes of the suffixes *ṅtva* and *aiṅtvi*, he says:
"In the sense of 'slightly' (*īṣadarthe*)," and so forth.
Therein, in the sense of "slightly": *ā-uṣṇam* / *oṣṇam* means "slightly warm" (*īṣaduṣṇam*). In connection with an action (*kriyāyoge*)...
In the definition of the term *upasarga*, only that which is specifically qualified by the marker *ṅ* is recited:
*pra, parā, apa, sam, anu, ava, ni, dur, vi, āṅ, ni, adhi, api, ati, su, du, abhi, and a*.
"They are to be understood along with *prati*; here, the definition applies to *pary* and *upa* as well. [Thus it is said:
*ā ihi*—*ehi*; *ā atiu*—*āti*. Even in the case of limit (*maryādā*) and inclusion (*abhividhi*), only that which is specifically marked by the *ṅit* designation is recited; thus says *Āha*.

Regarding the rule "maryādābhividhyoḥ" (Pāṇini 2.1.13): *maryādā* means a boundary, a limit, or a demarcation. For example: "One should follow a departing friend as far as the edge of the water (*udakāntāt*)," where the term implies a limit. *Abhividhi* means pervasion or inclusion. For example: "As far as Ahicchatra (*ā ahicchatrāt*)."

"It rained at Ahicchatra. The meaning is: "Having taken [the umbrella] to Ahicchatra, it rained. Because of the prohibition of the *pragṛhya* designation by the rule "ṅidviśiṣṭasya ṭhanāṅ," vowel sandhi (*svarasandhi*) occurs. Now, [consider] "etamātam."
In this case, why does the substitution of *enā* not occur by the rule "the second case ending *ṭā* and *auṣ* are replaced by *ena*" (Pāṇini 2.4.35)? [The answer is:

the term "in an anvādeśa" (Pāṇini 2.4.32) is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*) there; and since there is indeed an anvādeśa here, the application [of the rule] would seem to occur? [To this, the author replies:
the Vṛttikāra himself has shown in that very section how it does not occur.

It will be stated [later] (Kārikā 162), and thus it is not mentioned here again: "ātam. The letter *t* in the syllable *āta* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation (*mukhasukhārtha*). For those, however, who read the syllable *ā* as accompanied by the nasal *ṅ*—that is, as *āṅ*—the statement "one should know *ṅti*" would be redundant; for [the rule applies] to that which is accompanied by the nasal *ṅ*.
Because the status of being marked with the *ṅ* (ṅit) is understood from the very recitation [of the rule], therefore this vowel *ā* must be recited as following immediately after the letter *t*.
[The root] *ṭh* [is used] in the sense of "speaking" (*vākya*) and "remembering" (*smaraṇa*). By the word *vākya*, the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is expressed.

This is due to the metaphorical application of the designation [of the whole] to the designated [part]. For this [particle] is employed with reference to some previously introduced sentence-meaning, as in:
"Do you think thus? The meaning is that "in this way this sentence-meaning is understood.
This particle *atha* is intended to indicate the sentence-meaning that was previously introduced.

It is employed [in this sense]. Alternatively, this is employed to alter the meaning of a sentence previously introduced, as in "Is this how you now think?"—meaning, "You did not think so before, but now you think thus.
Alternatively, by the word *vākya*, the sentence itself is meant; the meaningless [element] is a constituent part of the sentence (*vākyāvayava*).

Thus the form *eva* is employed. *Smṛti* means remembrance; in that context, whatever form exists as an indicator of remembrance becomes *ṅni*. [The phrase] "it is indeed thus" (*evam kila tat*) means "this has been understood in this way.
What is known is precisely what is remembered. Alternatively, it refers to the object of that which is to be remembered.

The form *ā* is employed first; subsequently, after the recollection [of the word] as *ṭhā*, the meaning is expressed. The sense is that for this very *ā*, there arises the thought "it is indeed thus," which means "this is the meaning. Thus, the designation *pragṛhya* certainly applies to the form *ā* in both sentences and recollections.

By the rule "ṭhplutapragṛhyā aci" (6.1.125), there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). Consequently, by that [rule], the *vṛddhi* substitution prescribed by "ṭhvṛddhireci" (6.1.88) does not occur.

16. *sambuddhau śākalyasyaitāv anārṣe* (Pāṇini 1.1.16). [The commentary says: "That which has the vocative as its cause" (*sambuddhi-nimittaḥ*). This means that for which the vocative is the cause is so described.
By this, he shows that the term *sambuddhau* is a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*). For if it were a locative of proximity (*para-saptamī*), [the rule would not apply].

In the case of *trapo*, [the substitution] would not occur, because the vocative ending (*sambuddhi*) has been elided by the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.23); this is the intended meaning. This is stated while the rule *sambuddhau ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.106) is still in force.

The *guṇa* substitution prescribed by the rule "ṭhhrasvasya guṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.108) is caused by the vocative (*sambuddhi*), because it is ordained by taking that status of being caused by the vocative as its basis. As in the example: "He says 'gavi'."

When someone, intending to say "gaur" (cow), says "ṭhgo" due to a deficiency in their vocal organs, and another person imitates that, this serves as a counter-example. [One might object: But surely [the imitation] possesses meaning because it has the same meaning as the original form to be imitated?
Since a case ending (*vibhakti*) ought to occur here when there is a nominal base (*pratipadika*), he says "here," etc.

Here, if the distinction between the original form being imitated (*anukriyamāṇa*) and the imitation itself (*anukaraṇa*) were intended to be expressed, then a case ending would occur because [the imitation] would possess meaning; however, that distinction is not intended to be expressed.

Whence could there be an occasion for that [objection]? For in this science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*), the primary cause of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of a word is not merely the existence of the object (*vastu*), but rather the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*). And that [intention] is absent here.
[The mention of] "Śākalya" is for the sake of providing an option (*vibhāṣā*). By this, the suspicion that it is for the sake of honor (*pūjārtha*) is [refuted].
He rejects [this view]. For the underlying intention is that if it were intended solely for the purpose of worship, there would be no alternative [interpretation].
>ĀṢ | (1.1.18) The purpose of the continued application of the mention of Śākalya is that "thereby three forms come into being."
[The author] demonstrates this:

for if the mention of Śākalya were not carried over here, then in that alternative where the *pragṛhya* designation for *uñ* was not prescribed by the preceding rule, the substitution of *ṭh*, *āṬ*, or *āṢ* would necessarily apply by this [present rule].
From that, there would be two forms, namely *ṭhu* and *ṭh>ÄṢ*; there would not be a third, *vitī*. However, if the reference to Śākalya were to continue [in the rule], then in whatever [case]...

In the alternative view (*pakṣe*), the designation *pragṛhya* was not applied to *uṅ* by the preceding rule; when that [designation] is absent, the substitution of *āṬ* is optionally prescribed, whereby the third form, *vitī*, is established. 19. *īdūtau ca saptamyarthe* (1.1.18).
"Upon this my body"—this Vedic statement is to be understood. Here, the words *māmakī* and *tanū* have their locative case endings elided according to *sūpāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). In that regard:
When the word *iti* is employed to establish a term's own form by delimiting it from other meanings—
as in the examples *māmakī* and *tanū*, as well as *saṭsomo gaurī*.
The citation beginning with "māmakyām" is for the purpose of demonstrating the meaning of the locative case.
The phrase "the substitute ḍā" [is applied] by the rule *supāṃ suluk* etc. (Pāṇini 7.1.39). In that context, when the word *iti* follows, [the substitution applies] to the vowel *ak*.
Lengthening (*dīrghatva*) occurs before a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇa*), as in *dhītī* and so forth.

After the words *dhīti*, *mati*, *suṣṭhu*, and *ati*, there is either lengthening by the preceding homogeneous vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghatva*) or elision (*luk*) of the third-case singular ending. This same rule applies here when followed by the word *iti*.

The substitution of a long vowel of the same class (*savarṇa-dīrghatva*) indeed occurs. By the words "dhītyā" and so forth, he demonstrates that [the word *nadyām*] functions in the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārtha*). In the examples "vāpyāmaśvaḥ" ("a horse in the pond") and "nadyāmātiḥ" ("a boat in the river"), there is a compound with the locative case (*saptamī-samāsa*) according to Pāṇini 2.1.44, "In the sense of a name (*sañjñāyām*). Now, regarding the inclusion of the term "meaning" (*arthagrahaṇa*)...
Even though [the locative case] is being applied here, why does it not occur? For the meaning of the locative (*saptamī*) is indeed present here as well.
This is not so, because of the force of the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*). When "meaning" is included, only that which is the pure, uncombined meaning of the locative is intended here.

It is apprehended. In such a compound, the sense of the locative case is not possible, because in a *vṛtti* (compound), the meanings of the constituent words (*varti-pada*) possess a distinct dual nature.

This is the solution stated regarding the *ajahatsvārthā* (non-abandoning of its own meaning) type of *vṛtti*; however, in the case of the *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning of its own meaning) type, [the following applies]:
Since a word abandons that meaning which has become subordinate in the state of the sentence,
the sense of the locative case is simply absent. Therefore, when the term "meaning" (artha) is included [in the rule],
the designation *pragṛhya* does not apply to a compound.
Now, for what purpose is the application of *tap* (the *tap-pratyāhāra*)? If it is argued that it is for the sake of excluding the *pluta* vowel, we say no; because such a case is impossible.
For there exists no form ending in *ī*, *ū*, or *ṛ* that is both a *pluta* and a meaningful (*sārtha*) entity, from which [the *pluta*] would need to be excluded.
The addition of the *tapara* (the long vowel marker) is performed.
If it is argued that this is for the purpose of including those [vowels] which are distinguished by other qualities (*guṇa*) but are simultaneous [in duration], we say no;
because in the treatise (*śāstra*), qualities do not cause differentiation. Therefore, he says: "The addition of the *tapara*," and so forth.

For if the *tapara* (the marker *t*) were not present, there would be a substitution by *yaṇ*. Consequently, a doubt would arise as to whether this [substitute] is long or short; so that such a doubt may not occur, the *tapara* is employed.

"Ṭhīdūtau saptamī," etc. Let the sūtra simply be "Ṭhīdūtau saptamī"; what is the purpose of including the word *artha*? [The answer is: "Because when [a case-ending] is elided, the rule applies by virtue of the inclusion of *artha*. Here, in the example "somo gaurī adhiśritaḥ" (Ṛgveda 9.12.3), [the ending is] elided—
The inclusion of the word "meaning" (artha) is for this very purpose: so that the designation *pragṛhya* may apply even in the case of the locative case (*saptamī*).

For here, in the absence of the locative case itself, the *pragṛhya* designation would not occur; however, by virtue of the inclusion of "meaning," it does occur because the meaning of the locative is present.

Because [the vowel] exists; for it is said, "if this [vowel] is homogeneous with the preceding one. This might be argued: here, the elision (*luk*) is not effected by the seventh case ending (*saptamī*); rather, it is effected by the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39), and so forth.

The *ī* vowel is the same as its preceding sound (*pūrvasavarṇa*). In that case, when the lengthening rule (*dīrghatva*) applies to a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇa*) following an *ak* vowel, because it possesses the status of being "as if it were the end" (*antavadbhāva*), it is indeed included by the mention of the locative case (*saptamī*); therefore, there would be no need for the explicit mention of the word "meaning" (*artha*). However, this is incorrect; for if that were the case, the substitution of *āṭ* for *ām* would [not occur].

It follows as a logical consequence (*prasajyate*). If there were *pūrvasavarṇa* [dīrgha] substitution here, then, because it is subsequent, it would subvert the *savarṇadīrgha* rule (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*) and result in the occurrence of *āṬ* by "āṬ ṇadyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.112), as well as *ām* by "ReĀrāmnadyāmnībhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.116). This is the consequence.

[The word "arthe" means] appearance, or [existence] of that which exists. Therefore, the elision (luk) should have been applied as before; consequently, in the absence of the locative case, the designation *pragṛhya* would not occur. Should the mention of "artha" (meaning/purpose) therefore be made? It need not be made; because:

Since the elision (*luk*) of the locative case (*saptamī*) must occur everywhere, there would be no locative case anywhere. To this it is said: "In that case, by the force of the specific rule (*vacana-sāmarthya*), it will occur even when that [locative] has been elided. This is not so.
Where there is lengthening due to a specific statement, it will occur there; for example: "dṛtiṃ na śuṣkaṃ sarasī śayānam" (Ṛgveda 7.103.2).
In this case, because of the supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) "after the word *saras*, the suffixes *ṭhī*, *yāṭ*, *iyāṭ*, *jīkār*,

and *āṇ* [are applied] to the following locative case" (Kāśikāvṛtti 820), or alternatively, because of the rule "transposition [of suffixes] occurs frequently" (Pāṇini 3.1.85), the long vowel *ī* is substituted for the locative ending.

When the suffix *kta* is present, the seventh case (*saptamī*) is applied; therefore, because this rule has its scope here, it would not apply in the case of "somo gaurī adhiśritaḥ" (Ṛgveda 9.12.3). [The author says: "If there were the word *sarasī*.
If the word *sarasī* exists, then even here there would be no scope for that [seventh case]. And it does exist.

The word *sarasī*. For instance, according to the rule "and *pippalyādayaḥ*" (Gaṇasūtra 47) under the heading "gaurādiṣu" (Pāṇini 4.1.41), the suffix *īkāra* is applied to the word *saras*, which falls within the *pippalyādi* group; thus, the form *sarasī* is produced.

And likewise, in the Deccan region, large lakes are called *sarasī*. The purpose of assigning the *pragṛhya* designation to the word *sarasī* is as follows: when the locative case ending (*saptamī*) derived from it is elided (*luk*), and the word *iti* is supplied, then in the form *sarasī*, there occurs no vowel sandhi (*svarasandhi*).

Such is the state of affairs; thus, the word *sarasī* certainly exists. Even in the passage, "Like a dried leather bag lying in a *sarasī*" (*Ṛgveda* 7.103.2), the word *sarasī* is employed with the locative case ending elided; and so it is.
That very point remains:

the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*) has been rejected on the grounds that [the desired forms] will result from the explicit statement [of the rule]. If that is so, then this would serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the fact that [the suffixes] end in *ī*, *ū*, or *ed*.

Regarding the rule *dvivacanam* (Pāṇini 1.1.11), four interpretations are adopted. For either the vowels beginning with *ī* are qualified by the term "dual"— meaning "that which is a dual and begins with *ī*"— or the dual is qualified by the vowels beginning with *ī*.
"Whatever word-form ends in *ī* and so on and ends in a dual suffix";
or, it means "a word-form that ends in a dual suffix and has *ī* and so on as its base," [referring to] both [the suffix and the base];
or, having first specified the dual suffix by means of *ī* and so on, [it refers to] that which subsequently ends in such a dual suffix.
The *prakṛti* (base form) is that word-form which ends in *id* and so forth— that is, it means ending in the dual number (*dvivacana*) such as *id* and so on. In that regard,
there is a fault in the third alternative (*pakṣa*).

It was stated: "In the case of *kumāryoragāram* (the house of two maidens) and *vadhvoragāram* (the house of two brides), the designation *pragṛhya* would apply here; for this [word] ends in *ī*, etc., and ends in the dual number."

Regarding the phrase "by means of the characteristic of a condition" (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*), a fault has been stated even in the fourth alternative (*pakṣa*). In the case of the expressions *aśukle vastre śukle sampadyetām* ("may two white cloths become white") and *śuklyāstāṃ vastre* ("may the two cloths be made white"), [the suffix -ya] would result [from the base *śukla*]. This is because, from the word *śukla*, after the addition of the suffix *Cvi*, the rule *napuṃsakācca* applies.

(7.1.19) Thus, when *śī* is substituted for *auṅ*, there is elision (*luk*) by [Pāṇini 2.4.82] "after a word ending in *adhi*, etc., there is elision of *āp* and *sup*. For this [word] ends in *ī* and so on, and has a dual suffix, according to the principle of "characterization by the affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). By the phrase "in the case of its being that-ending," he indicates the third and fourth positions; that is, in the position where it ends in that.

In the third and fourth [arguments], this inclusion of the word "artha" (meaning) would serve as an indicator: that in this section concerning *pragṛhya* vowels, the designation *pragṛhya* does not apply by virtue of the disappearance of an affix (*pratyayalopa*). For if it were so, the inclusion of the word "artha" would be purposeless.

This much could have been said: "And *ī* and *ū* [are *pragṛhya*] in the locative (*saptamī*). Once the elision (*luk*) of the locative suffix has occurred, by the rule of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the presence of the suffix being treated as if it were still there), the designation *pragṛhya* would apply to those *ī* and *ū* sounds which are accompanied by a locative suffix, or to those *ī* and *ū* sounds that follow a locative suffix.

Thus, there is no purpose in the inclusion of the word *artha*. From the inclusion of *artha*, it is understood that "the designation *pragṛhya* does not occur by virtue of the condition of being a suffix. Consequently, the defect mentioned regarding the two positions concerning *tadanta* (ending in that) does not arise. [Regarding the statement] "or let it be so for the preceding member (*pūrvapada*)," the term *pūrvapada* refers to the compound (*samāsa*).
It is observed that this distinction of "prior member" (*pūrvapada*) and "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) occurs only when there is a compound.

Therefore, what is being said is this: the inclusion of the word *artha* (meaning) is for the purpose of preventing the designation *pragṛhya* from applying to compounds such as *vāpyaśvaḥ* ("a horse belonging to a pond") and *nadyātīraḥ* ("the bank of a river"). And so, when that [word *artha*] is present, in the case of a compound—
The designation *pragṛhya* applies; this has already been explained previously.
20. *dādhā ghu adāp* (Pāṇini 1.1.20).

Regarding the term "dā-dhā": this is a dvandva compound formed by first applying *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) to the four roots ending in *dā*, and then applying *ekaśeṣa* to the two roots ending in *dhā*. Now, an objection is raised: according to the principle that when a rule applies both to what is indicated by a general definition (*lakṣaṇa-ukta*) and to what is explicitly stated as a specific term (*pratipada-ukta*), the rule applies only to the specifically stated one.
By the paribhāṣā "there is the inclusion [of the root], but not of that which possesses a defining characteristic" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 3),
there is no inclusion of these roots: *ḍu* in the sense of "breaking" (Dhātupāṭha 1148), *deṅ* in the sense of "protecting" (Dhātupāṭha 962), and *dheṭ* in the sense of "drinking" (Dhātupāṭha 902).
Could this be so?
It is not so; for that metarule has the following exception: "In the case of the mention of *gām-*, *āṅ-*, and *ā* [as substitutes], there is no distinction" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 124).

Thus, even though they are characterized by their specific technical definitions (*lākṣaṇikatva*), *ud* and *eṅ* are indeed included here. The inclusion of *dheṭ* is also inferred from the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Furthermore, that [mark] is the indicatory letter *ṛ* (in *ṛdṛśo’ṅ guṇaḥ*) and the *pakāra* suffix in *daip*;
for that [suffix] serves as a general prohibition of *dāp*, as seen in the rule "ṭhadāp".

The purpose [of this rule] is for inclusion. Furthermore, if this *paribhāṣā* were to apply here, the addition of the indicatory letter *p* to the root *daip* would be useless; for, by virtue of being defined by a technical rule (*lākṣaṇikatva*), its inclusion would not otherwise occur. What, then, is the point of this prohibition?

By means of inclusion? But surely even the forms *dārūpam* and *dhārūpam* from the root *dheṭ* are not possible as technical (lākṣaṇika) forms, because since [the root] with its anubandha (*dheṭ*) does not end in a vowel (*anejanta*), the substitution of *āt* is impossible? This is not a fault, because of this [rule]: "In the opinion of the Northerners, after *māṅ*..."

In the rule *vyatīhāre* (Pāṇini 3.4.19), he provides a reference to the root *meṅ*, which has an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) and has undergone the change to *ātva*; this indicates the metarule: "The status of being a root ending in a vowel (*ajanta*) is not determined by an indicatory letter" (*Śabdakaustubha* 15). But what about the root *māṅ* in the sense of "measuring" (Dhātupāṭha 1142)?

This [rule] would also be an indication for that; how then is it an indicator? This is not so. It is only the root *mīṅ* in the sense of "bestowing" (*praṇidāna*)—from Dhātupāṭha 961—that functions in the sense of exchange (*vyatīhāra*), and not the root *māṅ* in the sense of "measuring" (*māna*).

Thus [it is stated in the Dhātupāṭha, 1142]. Therefore, this mention of *meṅ* with the vowel *ā* substituted (*kṛtātva*) is for the purpose of providing an indication (*jñāpana*). In the example "praṇidadāti," since the designation *ghu* applies by the rule "nergadanadapatapadaghumāsyatihanti" (Pāṇini 8.4.17), the substitution of *ṇ* occurs here. [The form is] "praṇidātā."
Thus [it ends] in the suffix *tṛc*.
In the form "praṇidyati," there is the elision of the vowel *o* by [Pāṇini 7.3.71], "otaḥ śyani. This form, ending in *dā*, occurs in a context where a *śit* suffix does not apply.

In the case of *bhavati*, the designation *ghu* indeed applies, as in the example "dātaṃ barhiḥ" (the sacrificial grass is cut). Due to the absence of the *ghu* designation, the substitution of *dad* [for *dā*] prescribed by Pāṇini 7.4.46 (*do dad ghoḥ*) does not occur. In the case of "avadātam," here too—
The suffix *kta* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.102] *niṣṭhā*. In this case, the substitution of *t* for the final letter [of the root] by [Pāṇini 7.4.47] *aca upasargāt taḥ* does not occur.

21. *Ādyantavad ekasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.21). By the words "of that which is without a companion," etc., he demonstrates the purpose for the commencement of this rule. The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of cause (*hetu*). For [this rule serves] those operations which have been taught for the beginning and the end.
These [designations] do not succeed for one who lacks a companion; therefore, this extension (*atideśa*) is commenced.

For the words "beginning" (*ādi*) and "end" (*anta*) function in dependence upon a second companion. To illustrate: in common usage, when there is another companion and there is an absence of what precedes, one designates it as "the beginning. When...

And because there is no "end" when the preceding [element] is absent, therefore both of those do not exist in that which has no companion. In that case, grammatical operations conditioned by the beginning and the end would not occur.

If this extended application (*atideśa*) is undertaken, then because of the expression "in one" (*ekasmin*), it is understood that the suffix *vati* occurs after a word in the locative case, as in the rule "like that which has a beginning or an end" (*ādyantavat*). Thus he says: "The suffix *vati* is used in the sense of the locative. That which is like the beginning and the end is "beginning-and-end-like" (*ādyantavat*).

In this context, the suffix *vati* is applied by the rule *tatra tasyeva* (Pāṇini 5.1.116). In the example *āṬpagava*, the result designated as belonging to the initial element (*ādi-vyapadiṣṭa*) is the very fruit of this extended application (*atideśa*).

For indeed, the acute accent (*udātta*) on the initial [of the suffix] is prescribed by the rule *pratyaya-ādy-udātta* (Pāṇini 3.1.3), which states that the first syllable of a suffix is acutely accented.

Regarding the phrase "by these two" (*ābhyām*): here, the lengthening taught for the penultimate letter is indeed taught for the final letter, according to the rule *ṭhalo'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52). Thus, from *idam* + *bhyām*, the substitution of *tyadādi* [y] occurs.

By [Pāṇini 7.2.102], *ato guṇe* (6.1.97), there is substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*); by *hali lopaḥ* (7.2.113), there is elision of the form *id*; and by *supi ca* (7.3.102), there is lengthening.

22. *tarap-tamap-au ghaḥ* | (1.1.22) Regarding "kumāritarā": the suffix *tarap* is applied by the rule *dvivacana-vibhajyopapade* (5.3.57), etc. Regarding "kumāritamā": the suffix *tamap* is applied by the rule *atiśāyane* (5.3.55), etc. When these two have the designation *gha*, [the following applies].
The shortening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *satyaṃ ṭhgharūpakalpa* (Pāṇini 6.3.43), etc.
23. *bahugaṇavatuḍati saṃkhyā* (Pāṇini 1.1.23).

In this context, the words *bahu* and *gaṇa* are nominal stems (*prātipadika*), while *-vatu* and *-ḍati* are suffixes (*pratyaya*). Regarding "bahukṛtvaḥ," it is derived by the rule "kṛtvasuc is added to a numeral in the sense of counting the repetition of an action" (Pāṇini 5.4.17). Regarding "bahudhā," [it is derived by the rule "dhā is added to a numeral in the sense of manner"].
Regarding "bahukaḥ": [it is derived] from the rule *sakhyāyā vidhārthe dhā* (Pāṇini 5.3.42), and [the suffix] *kan* is applied by the rule *sakhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan* (Pāṇini 5.1.22).

Regarding the phrase "ṭhtāvatkṛtvaḥ" and so forth: from the word *tat*, when the suffix *vatup* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.39 (*yatadetebhyaḥ parimāṇe vatup*), and when the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel of the pronoun is applied according to 6.3.91 (*ā sarvanāmnaḥ*), the form *tāvat* is obtained.

It becomes [bhavati]; from the word *kim*, when the suffix *ḍati* is applied in the sense of numerical measure (*saṃkhyāparimāṇa*) and the *ṭi*-portion is elided, the form *kati* arises; from those two [words], the suffixes *kṛtvasuc* and so forth are applied in the same manner as before.
Regarding the phrase "of the words *bahu* and *gaṇa*," and so forth: this word *bahu* denotes both number and abundance;
the word *gaṇa* also denotes both number and a group (*saṅgha*). Among these, those two...
The words *vaipulya* and *saṅgha* are not included here; rather, this designation of number is prescribed for those two only when they denote numbers. Therefore, how [can they be considered] numbers?

This is a designation based on its etymological meaning: it is "number" (*saṃkhyā*) because one is numbered by means of it. Furthermore, it is not by the word *bahu* as it occurs in the sense of "vastness," nor by the word *gaṇa* as it occurs in the sense of a "group," that one is numbered. For instance, [one does not say] "much rice" (*bahurodanaḥ*).

When this is said, "extensiveness" (vaipulya) is understood; likewise, when it is said, "a great multitude of monks," the Saṅgha is meant, not a mere numerical count. Therefore, because the designation is made according to its etymological meaning, [it refers to those] by way of excluding the numbers one and two.
They state that it is a specific number, and thus only those two [the *eka* and *dvi*] are to be understood.

If this is so, for what purpose is this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) prescribed for them, given that they are already included within worldly numbers as words denoting number? Furthermore, in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), it is the worldly number that is accepted.

Otherwise, in the rule *saṃkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan* (Pāṇini 5.1.22), the prohibition *atiśadantāyāḥ* would be meaningless, because there would be no such thing as a technical (*śāstrīyā*) number ending in *atiśat*; therefore, he says: "of *bhūri* and so forth."
"For the purpose of exclusion":
there exist words of that class denoting abundance, such as *bhūri* (much) and *prabhūta* (plentiful); the purpose is so that [the suffix] may not apply to them.

The designation "number" (saṃkhyā) is prescribed for the words *bahu* and *gaṇa*. By this, he shows that this prescription of the designation is for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*). For a restriction depends upon similar classes;
therefore, by way of restriction, it applies only to *bhūri* and the others belonging to that same class.

An exclusion is made for others [by the rule] "and that which has *ardha* as its prior member" (*ardhapūrvapadaśca*). That compound which has the word *ardha* as its prior member and ends in a ordinal suffix is [governed by this rule].
The meaning is that this must be explained as having the sense: "the first member [of the compound] is also designated as a number.
He asks, "For what purpose? and says: "for the sake of the rules concerning compounds and *kan* suffixes. The explanation there is as follows:
the *ca* (and) in the rule *ḍati ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.25) is marked with the *svarita* accent here.

It is established by the principle of the "lion’s glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*); and that [particle *ca*] has the sense of an unmentioned conjunction. By this, a compound whose first member is *ardha-* and which ends in a ordinal suffix is designated as a numeral (*saṃkhyā*). For example: *ardhapañcamaśūrpaḥ*. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those of which a half is the fifth."

In the expression "bought for four and a half winnowing baskets" (*ardhapañcamaiḥ śūrpaiḥ krītam*), there is a compound (*samāsa*) according to Pāṇini 5.1.51: *taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca*. By Pāṇini 2.1.52: *saṃkhyāpūrvo dviguḥ*, it receives the technical designation of *dvigu*. [The subsequent rules apply:]...

The suffix *añ* prescribed by "śūrpādañanyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 5.1.26), or the suffix *ṭhañ*, undergoes elision (*luk*) by the rule "adhyardhapūrvadvigorlugasaṃjñāyām" (Pāṇini 5.1.28). Thus, [from *adhyardha-pañca-śūrpa*] we have *adhyardhapañcakaḥ*. [This applies when the first member is] a numeral...
The suffix *kan* is applied after a word ending in *atiśad*. (Pāṇini 5.1.22)

24. *ṣṇāntā ṣaṭ* (Pāṇini 1.1.24). [The commentary begins: "Because of the mention in the feminine gender," and so forth. The term *ṣṇāntā* is mentioned in the feminine gender, yet nothing in the feminine gender is heard here, nor is anything else under discussion.

Regarding the word "saṃkhyāyāḥ": because of that feminine gender indication, the numeral itself is qualified by the qualifier "ending in ṣ or n" (in the rule *ṣṇāntā*). Thus, [the term] "ṣaṭ" [is understood].

And it is connected with this designation [of *ṣaṭ*]. If, in the rule *ṣṇāntā ṣaṭ*, the feminine gender were not specified, then every word-form ending in *ṣ* or *n* would be designated as *ṣaṭ*. Consequently, even in cases such as *pāmānaḥ* and *vipruṣaḥ*, [the designation *ṣaṭ* would apply].
The elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule *ḍbhyo luk* (Pāṇini 7.1.22) would consequently apply. [Objection:

But surely the word *saṃkhyā* will be supplied as an *anuvṛtti*; so how can there be such an over-extension? [Reply: This is true; however, that very *anuvṛtti* is indicated here in the feminine gender.

It is clarified as follows: if the term "number" (saṃkhyā) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], then by the very force of the context, it will be understood as ending in that [ṣ or ṇ];
for there is no such thing as a number consisting of merely the letter ṣ or merely the letter ṇ. Therefore, the inclusion of the word "end" (anta) is redundant. This is not so.

The inclusion of the word "final" (anta) is for the purpose that, in the stage of instruction, whatever ends in *ṣ* or *n* should receive the designation "six" (*ṣaṭ*). If that [word "final"] were absent,
[the designation would apply to] hundreds.

If the augment *num* were applied [to *sahasra*], the designation *ṣaṭ* would apply; and here, in the case of *aṣṭānām*, once the substitution of *ā* for *aṣṭan* has been made, the designation *ṣaṭ* would not apply. Consequently, the suffix *nuṭ* [prescribed] by the rule *ṣaṭcaturbhyaśca* (Pāṇini 7.1.55) would not occur.
It occurs.
25. *ḍati ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.25): "A numeral that ends in *ḍati* receives the technical designation *ṣaṭ*. By the mention of "numeral" (*saṃkhyā*) here as well, [the same applies].

He shows that the [suffix] *saṃkhyā* follows. But for what purpose does it follow here? It is so that [the suffix] *ḍati* does not apply to *pati* in the case of *pateḥ ḍatiḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.83), as in *patayaḥ*. Now...

Even though the continuation of the designation "number" (saṃkhyā) applies here, why does [the rule] not apply in this case? For this too is indeed designated as a "number," since the designation "number" was previously prescribed for the suffix -ḍati in a general sense. This is not so; because of its association with the suffix -vat.
In that context, only the *taddhita* suffix *-ḍati-* is understood, not the *kṛt* suffix; and this [suffix in question] is a *kṛt*.
26. *Kva* and *ktavatu* are called *niṣṭhā*. (Pāṇini 1.1.26)

In the form *bhuktavān*, there is the substitution of *k* for *c* by the rule *coḥ kuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.30). There is lengthening of the vowel by the rule *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.14). Now, by which [rule] are these technical names (*saṃjñā*) assigned to the suffixes *kta* and *ktavat*?

Is it prescribed? It is by this very technical name (*saṃjñā*). He will state in the third [chapter] that "the *niṣṭhā* [is applied]" (Pāṇini 3.2.102). If this is so, then *kta* and *ktavatu* are produced by the technical name *niṣṭhā*, and the technical name *niṣṭhā* depends precisely upon those two.

There would be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*); for in the treatise, operations based on mutual dependence are not prescribed. (Vyā. 28) This is not a fault; for the designation will be understood as something prospective (*bhāvinī*), just as one says, "I am weaving a cloth of this thread. Those two [terms] refer to the past time.
"Of yours," those two for which this designation "vihita-niṣṭhā" is prescribed.
27. *sarvādīni sarvanāmāni* (1.1.27). "The words beginning with *sarva* are called pronouns (*sarvanāman*)."
"The word *sarva* is the first among those which are these 'beginning with *sarva*' (*sarvādi*).
This is a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (possessive) *bahuvrīhi* compound;
for otherwise, since the word *sarva* would function merely as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), it would not constitute a technical name (*saṃjñā*). Not so.
For that which serves as a secondary indicator (upalakṣaṇa) becomes connected with the action only insofar as it is subordinate. To illustrate:
when it is said, "Let the owner of brindled cows be brought," the bringing of the cows themselves does not occur.
This is the indicative mark (liṅga) for a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the quality is included in the cognition (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*). Such is the case here.

The mention of *sarveṣām* (Pāṇini 7.3.100) is an indication [of this]. The augment *suṭ* for the word *sarva* is an operation belonging to a pronoun (*sarvanāman*); otherwise, it would not be possible.
[Examples are] *sarvaḥ*, *sarvau*, *sarve*. Here, the example is *sarve*; for in this case—

In the context of the designation *sarvanāman*, the substitution of *śī* for *jas* must be applied according to Pāṇini 7.1.17 (*ṭh jasaḥ śī*). However, by virtue of association with those two preceding [terms], this applies to the word *sarve*.
This introduction is intended to demonstrate both the masculine gender and the presence of an audible case-ending; otherwise,
if only "sarve" were stated, one might think this was a usage of the feminine gender with its case-ending elided.
Someone might have the misconception:
"for all" (*sarvasmai*), [thinking it is derived] from *sarvanāmnaḥ smai* (Pāṇini 7.1.14);
or "from all," "in all" (*sarvasmāt*, *sarvasmin*), [thinking it is derived] from *ṅsiṅyoḥ smātsminau* (Pāṇini 7.1.14). [Thus: *sarvasmāt*.

Regarding "sarvasmin": [the forms] *smāt* and *smin* are substituted for the case endings *ṅsi* and *ṅi* respectively, according to Pāṇini 7.1.15 (*ṅsiṅyoḥ smātsminau*). Regarding *sarvakaḥ*: the suffix *akac* is added before the final vowel (*ṭi*) of indeclinables and pronouns, according to Pāṇini 5.3.71 (*avyayasarvanāmnām akac prāk ṭeḥ*).

This word *ubha* is employed only in connection with the dual number and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*— as in "ubhau" and "ubhe. Furthermore, no case-ending operation (*sarvanāma-kārya*) such as *smai* and so forth is possible for it.

This is because [the suffix *aka*] applies according to the requirements of either the singular or the plural number. The suffix *akac*, however, does not trigger the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) in this way, because there is no distinction [between the forms]. For whether *akac* or the suffix *kap* is prescribed after that [base], no difference in form occurs. Why, then, is it mentioned here?

What is the purpose of this recitation? He says: "In the word *ubha*, etc. By means of the rule *sarvanāmnaḥ tṛtīyā ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.27), he shows that the recitation here is for the sake of ensuring that both the third and sixth case endings may occur—as in *ubhābhyāṃ hetubhyām* ("by both causes") and *ubhayoḥ hetvoḥ* ("of both causes").
Regarding "ṭhḍataratama": these refer to the two rules "ṭhkiṃyatadornirdhāraṇe dvayorekasya ḍatarac" (Pāṇini 5.3.92) and "ṭhvā bahunāṃ jātiparipraśne ḍatamac" (Pāṇini 5.3.93).
The mention of the two conditions [is made] by the rule "to be stated later," namely by "prathama-carama" (Pāṇini 1.1.33) and so forth.
As for "how," etc.: when the word *sama* has the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), [the form] *āmi*...
By the rule *sarvanāmnaḥ suṭ* (Pāṇini 7.1.52), when the suffix *suṭ* is applied, it ought to be *sameṣām*;
so how does it become *sāmānām*? Furthermore, when the suffix *smin* is applied to the locative singular, it ought to be *samasmim*; so [how is it *samāyām*]?
The intention [of the objection] is: "How can the usage 'one should sacrifice on level ground' (same deśe yajet) be justified? [The reply is: "Not everywhere. This means:
not for that which functions in every sense. And this is because "all names are called *sarvanāman* (pronominal names)."

This is understood from the fact that the name is given according to its literal meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñākaraṇāt*). For that very word *sama* becomes the name for all [things] which is a synonym for the word *sarva* (all); however, in the other two usages, the word *sama* is not a synonym for *sarva*.
To illustrate: in the expression *samānām*, the word *sama* functions in the sense of "equal" (*tulya*); likewise, in *same deśe* ("in an equal place").

Thus, here too, [the term] *aviṣama* means "devoid of unevenness," such as depressions or elevations. Precisely because the name is given according to its literal meaning (*anvartha-saṃjñā*), the designation does not apply to those that have become subordinate members of a compound (*saṃjñopasarjanībhūta*). For example: "There is someone named Sarva;
give to that Sarva. [This applies even when the word has passed beyond its primary scope.]

"O Sarvamatīsarva, give to that Atisarva. For names of such a kind do not belong to everyone, because they refer to specific objects. In the rule "sarvanāmāni," [the suffix *ṅīp* is applied] after a preceding word...
The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* in the word *saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 8.4.3) does not apply here, precisely because of this specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*).

28. *vibhāṣā diksamāse bahuvrīhau* (1.1.28). Regarding the term *digupadiṣṭe*: that which is taught or stated concerning the directions (*diś*) is "taught by the directions" (*digupadiṣṭa*). Furthermore, that [is as follows]:

The compound referred to here is that which is formed by the rule *ṭhdiṅnāmānyantarāle* (Pāṇini 2.2.26). This, moreover, is obtained through the *lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā* (the maxim concerning what is taught by a general rule versus what is taught by a specific rule). The recourse to the specifically taught compound is for the sake of [expressing] "that direction which is both eastern and northern" (*yā pūrvā dik sottarā*).
In the case of *gdhasya*, [the form] *ṭhasmai pūrvotarāya dehi*—meaning "give to him who is between the east and the north"—should not occur; rather, it should be *ṭhutarapūrvasmai*.
This is because of the previously mentioned rule: "that which is between the directions of the north (*uttarasyāḥ*) and the east (*pūrvasyāḥ*)."
In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound,

according to the rule "in all types of compounds, the preceding member of a pronominal undergoes masculine substitution" (*sarvanāmno vṛtimātre pūrvapadasya puṃvadbhāvaḥ*), there is masculine substitution for the preceding member.

There is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), the singular dative case ending, the *yāṭ* augment by the rule "sarvanāmnaḥ syāḍḍhrasvaśca" (Pāṇini 7.3.114), and the *vṛddhi* strengthening by the rule "āṭaśca" (Pāṇini 6.1.90).

"What is the purpose of mentioning 'compound' (*samāsa*)?"—the intention is that since a *bahuvrīhi* never deviates from being a compound, the qualification is redundant. [The answer is: "It refers to a *bahuvrīhi* which is indeed a compound."

It should be understood that when the status of being a *bahuvrīhi* is not prescribed by way of extension (*atideśa*), that is simply a *samāsa* which is a *bahuvrīhi*. Furthermore, that is the one prescribed under the heading of *samāsa*.
As for the phrase "by way of the status of being a *bahuvrīhi*," it refers to that whose *bahuvrīhi*-hood is derived through extension.

The compound *dakṣiṇadakṣiṇasyai* is a bahuvrīhi by virtue of being treated as a bahuvrīhi. This occurs while the term "as if a bahuvrīhi" (*bahuvrīhivat*) from rule 7.1.9 is still in force, [and] by rule 8.1.10, *ābādhe ca*.

There is a doubling of the word *dakṣiṇā*. Due to the treatment as a *bahuvrīhi*, there is elision of the case-ending (*subluk*). By virtue of this *bahuvrīhi*-like treatment, the optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) regarding it being a *bahuvrīhi* does not apply.

Even the prohibition that will be stated later in the rule "not in a *bahuvrīhi*" (Pāṇini 1.1.29) does not apply here; for in that case as well, the governing topic is *samāsa* (compound). [The example is] "of the south, north, and east. In this instance, [the rule] "and in a *dvandva*" [applies].
Thus, the prohibition is indeed constant; therefore, *suṇ* does not occur in that alternative case.
If this were so, then by the rule "sarvanāmno vṛtimātre" (Pāṇini 6.3.91), the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would not apply here; however, this is not the case.

Because a single component [of a compound] cannot be a *dvandva*. Now, one might object: even without the mention of *bahuvrīhi*, the prohibition by the rule "and in a *dvandva*" (Pāṇini 1.1.31) would necessarily apply here;
therefore, the mention of *bahuvrīhi* is useless. This is not so; for that which is a *dig-dvandva* (a *dvandva* of directions) is not...
That would be its scope. However, if the term *digdvandva* were not present, this option (*vibhāṣā*) would apply only when there is a *bahuvrīhi*.
Therefore, [the mention of] *bahuvrīhi*—
Should the mention of *hi* be made? It need not be made. Why does it not apply?

Because here, by the rule "dakṣiṇottarapūrvāṇām," there is the inclusion of the compound as explicitly stated (*pratipadokta*). If that is so, then [the mention of *hi*] is for the sake of a subsequent rule.

The mention of *bahuvrīhi*: its purpose will be explained in the rule "not in a *bahuvrīhi*" (1.1.29). However, the intention of the author of the Vṛtti is this: "It must necessarily be performed for the sake of subsequent rules; since it was performed for the sake of those subsequent rules, it applies here as well."
"It will become clear in meaning.
29. *na bahuvrīhau* (1.1.29).
[This refers to] "in the designation of a pronoun" (*sarvanāmasaṃjñāyām*), and so forth. How was this previously understood?

Is it accepted that this rule applies *tadanta* (to that which ends with the specified element)? Precisely because of this prohibition; otherwise, the prohibition would be fruitless. For if the application of the *tadanta* rule were accepted, then the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) would apply even in cases such as *paramasarvasmai* and *uttamasarvasmai*. And [the sūtra] begins with "here" (*iha ca*), etc., of this...

The connection is with the phrase "the prohibition is now commenced. This refers to a case where, having analyzed [the compounds] as *tvaṃ pitā asya* and *ahaṃ pitā asya*, a bahuvrīhi compound is formed;
and when there is a desire to express meanings such as "unknown" (*ajñāta*) and so forth, if the prohibition were not in place.
In that case, the suffix *akac* would be applied by the rule "ṭhavyayasarvanāmnāmakac prāk ṭeḥ" (Pāṇini 5.3.71), and consequently, forms such as *tvakatpitṛkaḥ* and *makatpitṛkaḥ* would result.
Thus, such an undesirable form would result. Therefore, the prohibition is commenced so that *akac* does not occur;
by this, only *ka*—as prescribed by "prāgivāt kaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.3.70)—is applied. In that case, subsequently, [the rule] "pratyayottarapadayośca" (Pāṇini 7.2.98) applies.

When *yuṣmad* and *asmad* have been reduced to *tvam* and *aham* respectively, and when the compound-ending suffix *kaP* is applied by the rule "ṭhaÑ ca" (Pāṇini 5.4.153), the forms *tvatkapitṛkaḥ* and *matkapitṛkaḥ* are established. But [one might object]: [The objection follows: "But..."
Since the designation [of the term] is established according to its etymological meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), once the [literal] name has been set aside, the suffix *akac* will not occur;

for here [in this case], the state of being "all-inclusive" (*sarvārthatā*) is not possible, because it refers to a specific [limited] scope. This is not so; for while the composite [word] applies to a specific [scope], the first member [of the compound] possesses the quality of being all-inclusive.
Let it be that these two preceding examples fall within the scope of this sūtra;

however, forms such as *priyaviśvāya* and the like are not justified. For words such as *priyaviśva* and so forth are not names of all [beings], nor do they possess any [specific] status regarding the words *viśva* and others that constitute their components.

The operation of the sarvanāman (pronominal) designation does not apply here; for while the suffixes *smai* and so forth are operations dependent on the *aṅga* (stem), words such as *viśva* and others are not *aṅgas*. One might think: "In the case of *tvatkapitṛkaḥ* and *matkapitṛkaḥ* [the rule would apply]."
Thinking, "Let there not be the suffix *akac* here," this [sūtra] must indeed be commenced for that purpose;
furthermore, it will serve to clarify cases such as "priyaviśvāya" and so forth.
Now, since the term "in a bahuvrīhi" (*bahuvrīhau*) is already in force, he asks: for what purpose is the term "bahuvrīhi" mentioned again? He says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "in a *bahuvrīhi*," etc., and the example "those for whom clothing (*vastra*) is the interval (*antara*) and garments (*vasana*) are the interval": having first formed the *bahuvrīhi* compound "those for whom clothing is the interval" (*vastrāntara*), one then forms the *dvandva* compound "clothing-intervals and garment-intervals" (*vastrāntarāś ca vasanāntarāś ca*). This is how it is treated here.
Because the *dvandva* compound is currently under discussion, [the rules] "in a *dvandva*" (Pāṇini 1.1.61) and "optionally before the suffix *jas*" (Pāṇini 1.1.32) apply to the *dvandva*.
The prohibition [of the feminine suffix] based on the *vibhāṣā* rule would apply, but not the obligatory one based on the *bahuvrīhi*.
However, because of the repeated mention of *bahuvrīhi*, the obligatory prohibition applies by virtue of being based on even that which was formerly a *bahuvrīhi*. [This concerns] the word *vasana*.

Furthermore, in this context, the word *gṛha* (house) functions as a locus-based derivation (*adhikaraṇasādhana*), meaning "that which dwells in this," and thus refers to a house, not a garment; otherwise, since the words *vastrāntara* and *vasanāntara* would be synonyms, they could not form a copulative compound (*dvandva*), because of the rule prescribing the retention of one term (*ekaśeṣa*) for dissimilar words with identical meanings: "There is *ekaśeṣa* of dissimilar words that have the same meaning."

30. *Tṛtīyā-samāse* (Pāṇini 1.1.30). Now, one might object: since the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) indeed continues from the previous rule, *vibhāṣā diksamāse* (1.1.28), why is it stated here again?

But for what purpose is the mention of "compound" (samāsa) made again? To this he says: "While [the word] 'compound' is being carried over," and so forth. There certainly exists a primary instrumental compound (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*) in which...
There is identity of truth, identity of accent, and identity of case-ending.

And there is the secondary (gauṇa) [usage], wherein, because of its being for the sake of that, the word for that object is applied even to what is not that. That, moreover, is for the purpose of a compound with the third case-ending.

Regarding this statement: if the term "compound" (*samāsa*) were not mentioned there again, then according to the principle that "between the primary and the secondary, the grammatical operation applies only to the primary," the prohibition would apply only to the primary [denotation], and not to the other.
Therefore, so that the prohibition may also apply there, [the word "compound" is mentioned].
The term "compound" (samāsa) is mentioned again for the purpose of [restricting] the sense of "it might be so" (syāt). If,

then, the prohibition applies even to a sentence that has the meaning of a third-case compound, then the prohibition would apply everywhere in any sentence whatsoever that possesses the meaning of a third-case compound.
Consequently, in the cases "tvayakā kṛtam" and "mayakā kṛtam," the suffix *akac* would not occur;
for this [suffix] is indeed intended for the purpose of that compound which is formed by the rule "kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam" (Pāṇini 2.1.32).

Regarding the statement: "In that case, when the suffix *ka* is applied, the forms would be *tvatkena kṛtam* and *matkena kṛtam*"; therefore, he says: "pūrvasadṛśa" and so forth. And this is obtained by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) concerning the distinction between what is taught by a general definition and what is taught by a specific word.
Regarding the forms *tvayakā* and *mayakā*: as before, the substitutes *tvam* and *āvām* are applied, and the suffix *akac* is added after the word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*).

In some places, the reading *tvakayā* and *makayā* occurs, but that is incorrect. If the suffix *tvakac* were derived from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the forms would be *tvakayā* and *makayā*, which is not the case here.

And here, the derivation of *akac* is not desired from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), but rather from the word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). For it will be stated in the rule for the formation of *akac*: "from the nominal stem" and "from the case-suffix"—both of these [terms] recur here. In that regard, the determination is based on usage (*abhidhāna*); in some cases...
The suffix occurs before the final *ṭi* of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and in some cases, before the final *ṭi* of a fully inflected word (*subanta*).
In the examples "yuṣmakābhiḥ," "yuṣmakāsu," "asmakāsu," "yuvakayoḥ," and "āvayakayoḥ," it occurs before the final *ṭi* of the nominal stem.
In the forms *tvayakā*, *mayakā*, *tvayaki*, and *mayaki*, [the substitution of *śe* occurs] because of the rule "of that which ends in a case-suffix" (*subantasya*).
31. And in a *dvandva* compound. (Pāṇini 1.1.31)

32. *vibhāṣā jasi* (Pāṇini 1.1.32). Regarding the rule "the operation [of the substitution] of *jas*," and so forth: this is because this option (*vibhāṣā*) is of the nature of a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).

It is obtained. Alternatively, in the rule "jasi," this is a locative of support (*ādhārasaptamī*) with respect to the grammatical operation, and not a locative of posteriority (*parasaptamī*) with respect to the items beginning with *sarva*; therefore, the optionality applies only to that operation which occurs when *jas* is present—that is, the operation supported by *jas*, namely the substitution of *śī* for *jas*—and not elsewhere.
To the question "For what reason is it explained in this way?", he says: "Because *akac* does not occur.
Here, the word "hi" (because) indicates the reason.
When it is explained in this manner, *akac* does not occur in the case of "katarakatamakāḥ."

Because the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is prohibited by the preceding sūtra; for otherwise, if the technical name were optionally applied when *jas* follows, then in one alternative case *akac* would necessarily occur. And thus, because it would fall within that [technical name] and be included by its mention, the optional substitution of *śī* would result. However, when the suffix *kap* is present...
Therefore, because of this very intervention, this fault does not arise.

33. *prathama-carama-taya-alpārdha-katipaya-nemāś ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.33). [The word] *ubhaya*, ending in the suffix *tayap*, [is included here]. [The rule for the suffix *tayap* is: *saṃkhyāyā avayave tayap* (Pāṇini 5.2.42).

Although the rule "ityubhaśabdādvihitasya tayapo yadyapi 'ubhādudāto nityam'" (Pāṇini 5.2.44) prescribes the substitution of *ayac* for the suffix *tayap* after the word *ubha*, nevertheless, by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), that [suffix] is still captured by the mention of *tayap*; thus, the word *ubhaya* ends in the suffix *tayap*.

"Because it is recited in the *gaṇa* [of sarvanāman], its designation as a pronoun (*sarvanāma-sañjñā*) is compulsory. However, by this rule, even the subsequent one [the optional application] does not occur optionally. And this is obtained because it is a fixed option (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*).
As it is said: "The application of *kā* and *ca* occurs according to the requirement. Therefore, in the case of the words *ubhaya* and *nema*—

Because it belongs to the *sarvādi* group, the suffix *akac* is applied invariably; however, for words beginning with *prathama*, the suffix *kap* is applied— such is the meaning according to the application of the rule.

34. *pūrvaparāvaradakṣiṇottarāparādharāṇi vyavasthāyām asaṃjñāyām* | (1.1.34) Regarding the phrase "provided it is not a name" (*asaṃjñāyām*): this means that if *pūrva* and the others are used as names (*saṃjñā*), [the rule does not apply].
The meaning is "they come to be.
Regarding the phrase "dependent upon its own denotation" and so forth: *avadhi* means a limit or boundary;
the *niyama* of that is its necessary occurrence—the state of being a limit.

Failure of the debate. Of what nature is the restriction of the limit? For the "easterness" and so forth of objects denoted by words such as "east"—that is, their status as being east—is established only in dependence upon some specific limit, and not independently of a limit; as, for example, [the easterness] of a location to the east.

That which is "prior" exists in relation to a subsequent location; likewise, that which is "subsequent" exists in relation to a prior location. Therefore, there must necessarily be some limiting point (avadhi) in relation to what is expressed by words such as "prior."

It must be understood as follows: therein, regarding that very limit (*avadhi*), the exclusive state of being a limit (*avadhibhāva*) which depends upon the meanings of words such as "east" (*pūrva*) and so on—that restriction (*niyama*) or fixed arrangement (*vyavasthā*)—when it is implied, this technical designation applies to the words "east" and so forth when they function in reference to their own denotata; but not otherwise.

Regarding that which is to be expressed: for how could that restriction of another object serving as a limit—which is distinct from the meaning denoted by words such as *pūrva*—be itself expressible by those words like *pūrva*?
As in the example "the eastern mountains" (*pūrve parvatāḥ*), it is understood here that [the direction] is determined solely with respect to another limit.
"Ṭhpare, parāḥ"—it is understood that this follows from the very same preceding rule. "Pravīṇāḥ"—the meaning is "skilled. Here, [the suffix applies] by virtue of skill alone.

The rule that the word *dakṣiṇa* (southern) functions independently of a limit (*avadhi*) is not understood [from the previous statement]. Regarding the phrase "only when [it exists]," etc.: it is established that the word *uttara* (northern) functions there with reference to Jambūdvīpa as the limit.
Such is the established rule.
35. *svam ajñāti-dhana-ākhyāyām* (1.1.35).
"In this case as well, the designation of 'pronoun' (*sarvanāman*) would apply invariably," because it is included in the list [of pronouns] in the *gaṇapāṭha*.
The same should be understood for what follows hereafter. By the words "If not," and so forth, he explains the meaning of the term *jñātidhanākhyā*.
And where there is another word—
The word *sva*, being independent [of other terms], denotes relatives and wealth by its own form; therein, it functions toward those two as a technical designation (*saṃjñā*). [The commentary says:
"The meaning is 'one's own. But how can this be the meaning, since in the phrase 'one's own sons' (*sve putrāḥ*), it has the sense of 'relatives'?"
Is it understood that "one's own cows" (*sve gāvaḥ*) has the meaning of "wealth"? This is not so;

due to the proximity of the words "son" (*putra*) and "cow" (*go*), neither of those two [meanings] is understood. By the word *sva*, only the state of being one's own (*ātmīyatva*) is understood—as in "one's own kinsmen" (*svā jñātayaḥ*).

In both cases, the words *prabhūtāḥ* and *svāḥ* denote kinsmen and wealth respectively by their own inherent form as the word *sva*, without depending on any other term. If this is so, then the subsequent application of the word *jñātayaḥ* (kinsmen) would not be appropriate.

Because they are synonyms; for example, when the word *vṛkṣa* has been employed, the subsequent employment of the word *taru* would be contradictory—yet this is not a fault; for in the case of a synonymous term where there is either multiple meaning or ambiguity of meaning, it serves precisely to clarify that meaning.

The employment of another synonym for the purpose of clarification is not contradictory; just as, for example, when the word *varāha*—which has multiple meanings such as "cloud" and so forth—is used, the word *śūkara* is employed [to specify]. Likewise, it is the case when the word *pika*, whose meaning is ambiguous, is used.

Regarding the word *kokila*, this term itself has multiple meanings; therefore, in the absence of a subsequent application [of a governing rule], there would be doubt as to what its specific scope is when it is employed. 36. *antaram* [is used] in the senses of "separation" (*bahiryoga*) and "undergarment" (*upasaṃvyāna*). (Pāṇini 1.1.36)

Regarding the rule "in the case of connection with *barhis*": by the word *barhis*, an uncovered place is meant. Connection with that is "connection with *barhis*" (*barhiryoga*).
