And that occurs with an external object that is not covered. Regarding the rule "and in the case of *upasaṃvyāna*": that which is wrapped around or put on is *upasaṃvīyate*.
That is the *upasaṃvyāna* (undergarment). The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of the object according to Pāṇini 3.3.113: *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*.
Alternatively, it is called *saṃvyāna* because one is wrapped or covered by it, according to Pāṇini 3.3.117: *karaṇādhikaraṇayoś ca*.

The suffix *lyuṭ* [is applied]. There is an extension [of this rule] for the word *saṃvyāna* (undergarment). Because of the semantic requirement [of the context], it should be understood that this applies only when there is no connection with "outside" (*abāhya*). For example: "those outside the city. By this, he demonstrates the connection with "outside"—[it refers to] that which is called "the undergarment" (*paridhānīya*).
Thus, this example has been presented regarding "upasaṃvyāna.
An object covered by another garment is said to be "concealed" (apihita) by that other garment;
even though the expression is used without qualification, it refers to what is covered by another garment by virtue of the contextual implication (sāmarthyāt).

That alone is called the *upasaṃvyāna* (undergarment), and nothing else. Regarding the phrase "not a *prāvaraṇīya*": that by which one is covered or concealed is a *prāvaraṇīya*; that is not what is being designated here.
For if that were designated, it would follow that it is connected with the exterior.
The intention is that this example would belong to the *bahiryoga* (external connection) category.

In the phrase "a mendicant lives within," because there is no technical designation (*saṃjñā*), the substitution of *smin* for the locative case ending does not occur. Now, one might object: "But the word *jas* is understood [from a previous rule]; so why [does this not apply]?"
Since [the previous rule] was cited as a counter-example ending in the locative case, he says: "And of the *gaṇa*-sūtra," and so forth.

Regarding the statement "it should be stated that 'not for a city (*apuri*)'," because the phrase "and of the *gaṇa*-sūtra" is mentioned immediately thereafter, it is understood that this very *gaṇa*-sūtra is what must be stated. Even though...

Although the word *antara* is recited in the *Gaṇasūtra*, nevertheless, according to the principle "when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 29),
since the city situated outside the rampart (*prākāra*) is also connected with the exterior, [the suffix applies] there as well.
The designation *sarvanāman* would also apply to the word *antarā*, even when it ends in the feminine suffix *ṭāp* and is used in the present sense;
therefore, it must be stated that [the rule] does not apply to the city (*apurī*). Consequently, in the form *antarāyām*, the substitution of *syāṅ* does not occur.
Regarding the phrase "in the section concerning the option" (*vibhāṣāprakaraṇe*) and so forth: here, the meaning of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is "presentation" (or "stating").

The meaning is that within this section on *vibhāṣā*, the designation (*saṃjñā*) of "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*) must be established for words ending in the suffix *tīya*. In that regard, the following is the demonstration: in the rule *vibhāṣā jasi* (Pāṇini 1.1.32), the word *vibhāṣā*...
Thus the division of the rule (*yoga-vibhāga*) is made; therein, the rules "sarvādīni" and "dvandve" are no longer operative, and by that,
[the suffix] *tīya* [is applied].

The designation *sarvanāman* will apply [to *vibhāṣā*] by virtue of the rule "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*). And this being so, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because the desired result is achieved through the splitting of the rule (*yogavibhāga*);
nor does it follow that the rule "optionally after the second and third cases" (Pāṇini 7.3.115) would become redundant.

Because it is intended to include the elaborations (*prapañca*). Therefore, regarding the case ending *jasi*, there is a second rule (*yoga*). Here, the mention of "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*), the mention of "the group beginning with *sarva*" (*sarvādi*), and the mention of "compound" (*dvandva*) are carried over [from the previous rules].
37. *svarādinipātamavyayam* (Pāṇini 1.1.37).

Among the *svarādi* group, the words *svasti* and *asti* are recited. In that regard, what is the purpose of the recitation of *svasti*, since [its status as an indeclinable] would follow simply from the recitation of *asti* by means of the rule of extension to what ends with that (*tadantavidhi*)?
The same will also apply to the word *svasti*.

One should not raise the objection that [the suffix] would not be established because of the prohibition of the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) by the metarule "by a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) accompanied by the mention of [a suffix] *ṭ*. This is because [the designation] "indeclinable" (*avyaya*) is a major technical term (*mahatī saṃjñā*).

This is done so that the term may be understood as having a meaning consistent with its etymology (*anvarthasaṃjñā*): because it does not take on specific gender, case-role (*kāraka*), or number, it does not deviate—that is, it does not undergo variety—and thus it is called *avyaya*. Furthermore, there is a prohibition against its being treated as a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) and a rule regarding its inclusion when it occurs at the end of a compound (*tadantavidhi*).
The purpose [of the rule] is this: since the designation is made according to its literal meaning (*anvartha*), it will apply even to that which ends in such a word;
thus, the word *svasti* itself does not cease to be [a *gati*]. This is true;
however, by making the designation *anvartha*, the rule of "extension to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*) is obtained here.

This example is given for the sake of clarity: "The *taddhita* suffixes beginning with *tasil* and ending with *edhāc*. This refers to the section starting from *pañcamyāstasil* (Pāṇini 5.3.7) up to *edhācca* (5.3.46).
This extends up to the point [of the rule] "śastasī.

[The suffixes] *śas*, *tasi*, and *kṛtvasuc* are applied respectively by the rules: "bahvalpārthāc chas kārakād anyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 5.4.42), "pratiyoge pañcamyās tasiḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.44), and "saṃkhyāyaḥ... [kṛtvasuc].

Regarding the rule *kriyābhyāvṛttigaṇane kṛtvasuc* (Pāṇini 5.4.17), and *dvitricaturbhyaḥ suc* (5.4.18), as well as *āsthālau*: by the Uṇādi sūtra *iṇa āsiḥ* (Uṇādi 9.81), the suffix *āsi* is added to the root *iṇ*. An example is the word *ayāḥ*.

Regarding the rule *ṭhpratnapūrvaviśvemātthāl cchandasi* (Pāṇini 5.3.111), it is stated that *cvyarthāśca* [are also included]. In the sense of "becoming what one was not" (*abhūtatadbhāve*), the suffix *cvi* is applied after a verbal root when used with a verb meaning "to make" (*kṛ*) or "to become" (*bhū*), provided the agent is the subject of the transformation (*sampadyakartari*), according to *ṭhkṛbhyastiyoge sampadyakartari cviḥ* (5.4.50). Furthermore, the suffix *sāti* is optionally used in the same sense when there is totality (*vibhāṣā sāti kārtsnye*, 5.4.52).

"Let it be so. [Question: "Why is it that [the word] *ati* is not included among the indeclinables (*avyaya*) by the rule 'tiṅavyayadhādāmvadravyaprakarṣe' (Pāṇini 5.4.11)? [Answer: Because they will be taught as particles (*nipāta*).
[Question: Then why are they not recited among the *svarādi* group? What advantage would there be in doing so?

Regarding the mention of "particle" (nipāta) in the definition of a secondary suffix (avayaya), it is because [the term] is seen used in connection with action— as in "they see from heaven" (svaḥ paśyanti) and "they ascend to heaven" (svar ārohanti). In that case, if particles such as *ca* and so forth were recited [in the list], even though they denote existence (*satva*), [they would still be included].
The designation *avyaya* (indeclinable) would undesirably apply to present [tense] forms as well.
To show that this is an etymological designation (*anvarthasaṃjñā*)—meaning "that which does not go away"—he says: "similar. In the three [genders].

It is "similar" (*sadṛśam*)—that is, equal—in all genders, namely feminine, masculine, and neuter, because it does not adopt any specific gender and because it takes up the general category of gender. And [it applies] "in all case-endings" (*sarvāsu ca vibhaktiṣu*); it is called a "case-ending" (*vibhakti*) because it is caused by a case-ending.

Alternatively, the term *vibhakti* refers to the case-roles (*kāraka*), such as the object (*karman*) and so forth, which are of the nature of capacities (*śakti*), because by means of them the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*) is divided.
[Vacaspati-miśra] says:

"And in these [words]" refers to the singular, dual, and plural numbers. Here, because the designator is uttered with reference to the designated object, a number exceeding one is understood; for it does not deviate from [the object], since it does not require the specific application of gender, number, and so forth.

It does not undergo various diversities; therefore, it is "unchanging" (*avyaya*). Thus, the etymological consistency of the term is established. Furthermore, it has been stated that the purpose [of this designation] is the prohibition of its status as a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) and the application of rules to what ends with it (*tadanta-vidhi*). Among these, the prohibition of its status as a subordinate member is as follows:

*atyuccaiḥ*, *atyuccaisau*, *atyuccaisaḥ*. For here, the application of the meaning as previously demonstrated is not possible. However, where it is possible, there the designation of indeclinable (*avyaya*) certainly applies to that which ends in [the suffix]; as in *paramasvaḥ* and *utamasvaḥ*. For in these cases...

Because of the predominance of the word *svara*, there is an impossibility of [gender] and so forth being the qualificands; however, in the previous case, it is because of the opposite regarding the word *uccais*.
Paryāya:
38. *Taddhitaś cāsarvavibhaktiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.38).
When a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned [in a rule], there is the inclusion of that which begins with the element from which it is prescribed and ends with that suffix.
He says, "The word ending in a taddhita suffix," because it is understood that the technical designation applies to what ends in a taddhita suffix. He says, "Not from everything," and so forth.

In this context, the word *sarva* functions with reference to the entirety of its parts. The meaning is that "all" refers to those three types of words for which the technical designation *vibhakti* (case-ending) has been established, because they do not arise from anything other than those [three].

Regarding "tataḥ" and "yataḥ": from the word *yad*, which is in the ablative case (*pañcamī-samartha*), the suffix *tasil* is applied by the rule *pañcamyāstasil* (Pāṇini 5.3.7); then, by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (2.4.71), there is the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*); and [the resulting form] is designated as an inflection (*vibhakti*) by the rule *prāgdiśo vibhaktiḥ* (5.3.1).

Because they are case endings (*vibhakti*), the substitution of *tyad* and so forth (*tyadādyatva*) applies; by the rule "ato guṇe" (Pāṇini 6.1.97), there is the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpatva*). Thus: *tatra*, *yatra*. [The suffix] *tral* is applied by the rule "saptamyāstral" (Pāṇini 5.3.10). [Examples are: *tadā*, *yadā*, *sarvadā*. The suffix *dā* is applied by the rule "sarvaikānyakiṃyatadaḥ kāle dā" (Pāṇini 5.3.15). All these—beginning with *tataḥ* and so forth—are included.

These [suffixes] have the meaning of the case-ending as their primary sense. Since that meaning of the case-ending has become the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the nominative alone occurs for the meaning of the nominal stem. Even so, because there is no specific number, not all [numbers] apply; rather, it is only the singular.
Because it is the general rule (*utsarga*). And so it has been said:
"The singular number shall be used as the general rule. Of that [term], there is elision (*luk*) by the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.82). Thus, "ekaḥ" [is formed].

Thus [it is stated]. Here, there is the absence of connection with all case-endings (*asarvavibhaktikatva*), because duality is incompatible with singularity. It does not occur because it is not a *taddhita* derivative, as in the example "ĀṬpagavaḥ. In this case, because the form ending in a *taddhita* suffix is connected with all case-endings, [the rule] does not apply.
39. *kṛnmejantaḥ* | (1.1.39) As in "he eats making it sweet" (*svāduṅkāraṃ bhuṅkte*). [This is derived] from the rule *svādumi ṇamul* (3.4.26). It is understood precisely from the word *svādumi*.

By virtue of this specific rule (*nirdeśa*), the fact that the following word (*upapada*) ends in *m* is treated as an irregularity (*nipātana*). Furthermore, the inclusion of *svādu* is taken as a reference to its meaning; consequently, the suffix *ṇamul* occurs even when words such as *sampanna* function as the following word. Regarding *vakṣe*: it is derived from *vaca* in the sense of "speaking" (*paribhāṣaṇe*; DhP 1063), according to the rule *bruvo vaciḥ*.

(2.4.56) Thus, there is optionally the substitution of *brūñ*. By the rule "ṭhcoḥ kuḥ" (8.2.30), there is the substitution of *k* [for the palatals]. Regarding the phrase "the mention of 'anta'" and so forth: it is for the purpose of understanding that which is "original" (*aupadeśika*). Because a *bahuvrīhi* compound is understood in the sense of "constant connection," there is the understanding of that which is original. In the *upadeśa*...
"Bhava" refers to that which is taught [in the rules]. "Pratipatti" is knowledge; that whose purpose is this [knowledge] is "tathā" (of such a nature).

He thinks as follows: even without the mention of the word "anta" (end), since the rule "that by which a prescription is made applies to what ends with it" (Pāṇini 1.1.72) establishes the application of the rule to what ends with that [element] by virtue of its inherent capacity, the fact that the word "anta" is explicitly mentioned here serves this purpose.

The purpose is so that there may be the recognition of only that which necessarily possesses the status of ending in a vowel (*ejanta*) precisely at the stage of its original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*). Regarding the form *ādhaya*: from the root *dadhāti* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, the suffix *ki* is applied by Pāṇini 3.3.92 (*upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ*), and [the final *ā*] is elided by 6.4.34 (*āto lopa iṭi ca*).
Thus there is the elision of the vowel *ā*. In the singular of the dative case, there is *guṇa* substitution by the rule *gher ṅiti* (Pāṇini 7.3.111).

Regarding the form *cikīrṣadaḥ*: from the root *kṛ*, the suffix *san* is added; there is lengthening by the rule *aj-jhan-gamāṃ sani* (6.4.16); the suffix *u* is added by the rule *san-āśaṃsa-bhikṣa uḥ* (3.2.168); then there is the elision of the final *a*; the remainder is as follows.

As before. In the case of *kumbhakārebhyaḥ*, there is a compound formed by *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1) and *upapadam atiṅ* (2.2.19); then the substitution of *e* occurs by *bahuvacane jhalyet* (7.3.103).

Now, one might object that this is already established by the paribhāṣā concerning the distinction between what is taught in a general rule (*lakṣaṇa*) and what is taught in a specific rule (*pratipadoka*), or by the principle that [what is taught later is] "not established" (*asiddha*).

Alternatively, the designation [of "avyaya"] will not apply here at all by the rule *bahirangam antarange* (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 42). For the operations such as *guṇa* are *bahiranga* because they are prescribed in dependence upon the case-ending suffix (*vibhakti-pratyaya*), whereas the designation *avyaya* is *antaranga*, being dependent only on what is external.

This is true because there is no reliance on the sign (nimitta); however, in this way, there would be a prolixity in the comprehension of the meaning. Therefore, the mention of "extremes" (anta) was made in order to avoid that.
40. *ktvā-tosuN-kasuN-aḥ* | (1.1.40) For example:

*kṛtvā*, *hṛtvā*. The suffix *ktvā* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.4.21]: *samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle* ("when two actions have the same agent, the suffix *ktvā* is used for the earlier action"). *Hṛtvā*... [etc.]

Regarding "udetoḥ": from the root *iṇ* in the sense of "going" (DhP 1045), there is *guṇa* substitution by Pāṇini 7.3.84 (*sārvadhātuka*). Regarding "apākarttoḥ": from the root *kṛ*. Regarding "visṛpaḥ": from the roots *gamlṛ* (DhP 942) and *sṛplṛ* (DhP 983). Regarding "ātṛdaḥ": [from the root *tṛd*].
The root *tṛd* is listed as "to injure" and "to tear apart" (*dhātupāṭha* 1447).
41. *Avyayībhāvaś ca*. (Pāṇini 1.1.41) For example, in the case of *upāgni*, [the term is designated as an indeclinable] by the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti...* (Pāṇini 2.1.6), and so forth.

In the sense of proximity, there is an *avyayībhāva* compound. By the rule *avyayāt* (Pāṇini 2.4.82), the case-ending is elided. Thus, "near the fire" is *upāgni*. The term *upāgnimukha*, meaning "one whose face is near the fire," is a *bahuvrīhi* compound containing within it an *avyayībhāva*. In that context, the rule *mukhaṃ svāṅgam* (Pāṇini 6.2.167) applies.

Thus, when the rule for the acute accent on the final syllable of the final member (*uttarapadāntodātta*) would have applied, it is prohibited by *ṭhnāvyaya* (Pāṇini 6.2.168). When that is prohibited,
the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*) applies, according to the rule *bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā* (Pāṇini 6.2.1), and so forth.

Furthermore, that [word] has its acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*), because the word *upāgni* has its acute accent on the final syllable by virtue of the accentuation rule for compounds (*samāsasvara*). [The example] "one who makes milk his object" (*upapayaskāra*) is formed in this way by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1).
In the case of *ṭhupapayaḥkāmaḥ* as well, this is either a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose desire is for water" (*upapayaḥkāmo yasya*).

*Kāmaḥ* is that which is desired; here the suffix *ghañ* is applied even in the sense of the object (*karman*) by the rule *akartari ca kārake saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.19). Since the substitution of *s* [for *ṣ*] is prohibited by the rule *anavyayasya* (Vārttika 939), [the form becomes *payaskāmaḥ*]. [The rule continues with: *kupvoḥ...* [etc. *Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-rule; the full grammatical derivation would continue with the application of the *ṣatva* rule and its subsequent exceptions.*

By the rule *ka pau ca* (Pāṇini 8.3.37), either the jihvāmūlīya or the visarjanīya occurs [in place of *k* before *p*]. In this case, the articulation of the mouth and the tone (*svaropacāra*) serve as the purpose when they are being brought about, but they are not themselves what is being prescribed; rather, it is the elision (*luk*) that is being prescribed. Now, one might object:
Since there certainly exists an effect such as *akac* which is based on a case-ending (*cāp*), from where is this restriction regarding effects obtained? To this he says:
"All," and so forth; "this," namely, "a taddhita suffix that does not take all case-endings."
(1.1.38) and so forth.
Some [terms] are recited according to their very own form (*svarūpa*), while the meaning of others is [expressed] through another synonym (*paryāyāntara*).

That [usage], however, is said to be by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) based on the property of the object denoted (*abhidheyadharma*). In that regard, [there is the rule]: "The suffix *kṛt* occurs after the root *kṛ*, and [the word] ends in *sandhi* or *r*."

Thus, the meaning of the rule *kṛnmejantaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.39) is recited as follows: *ktvā*, *tosun*, *kasun*, and *avyayībhāva* [are indeclinables] by their very form; and *tasil* and so forth, which are *taddhita* suffixes ending in *edhāc* and *paryab*.
"...up to the word *anta*. And "those having the sense of *cv-*" means excluding those derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes.

This is the meaning of the rule "the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) that does not take all case-endings [is called *avyaya*]. The phrase "for the purpose of making known the non-universality of the suffix *ṭhaN*" follows because it is the subject under discussion; [and the word] "of a name (*saṃjñāyāḥ*)" [is understood].
Therefore, when an operation beginning with *a-kac* (the suffix *ka*) is to be applied, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) does not occur.
This is the case in the example *upāgnikam*, where there is an intention to express meanings such as "unknown" (*ajñāta*).

What does not occur here, and what indeed does occur? In this case, one who considers himself "near the jar" (*upakumbham*) is called *upakumbhammanyaḥ*. When the suffix *khaś* is applied by the rule *ātmamāne khaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.83), the rule *khityanavyayasya* (6.3.66) [applies].

While this [rule] continues to apply, the prohibition of *mum* by the rule "ṭharurdviṣadajantasya mum" (Pāṇini 6.3.67) does not take effect. Regarding what will be stated later under the heading "iha ca," namely that "there is no prohibition of *tosun* and *kasun* when there is a prohibition of indeclinables," its irrelevance here [is established].

He demonstrates this: in the phrase "of the sun" (*sūryasya*), the genitive case is used according to Pāṇini 2.3.65, *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* ("the [genitive] of the agent and the object when a *kṛt* suffix follows").
42. *śi* is a *sarvanāmasthāna*. (Pāṇini 1.1.42) As in the example *ṭhkuṇḍāni* and so forth: by the rule *jaśśasoḥ śiḥ* (7.1.20), *śi* is substituted [for *jas* and *śas*];
this [substitute] is a *sarvanāmasthāna*.

"Since this [term] exists, there is no occasion for the neuter. This great technical designation was indeed introduced by the ancient teachers even without a specific purpose; that its adoption is made here is due to what was established by them.

This is for the purpose of indicating that the instruction of grammar (*śabdānuśāsana*) is indeed defective; furthermore, it is for the purpose of avoiding the fault of redundancy in one's own treatise. For if that [other system] were indeed defective, then the composition of this [work] would be justified, but not otherwise.

43. *sujanapuṃsakasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.43). The term *suc* is used here as a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated designation), beginning with the word *su* and extending up to the letter *ṭ* in *āṬṭ*. In that context, there are only five [suffixes].
He states that these [suffixes] are not included within the *vacana*s (numbers): "The five *vacana*s are called *suḍ*," and so forth;

and "Except for the neuter," and so forth. By this, he shows that the word *anapuṃsaka* functions as an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). For if it were a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), this would primarily consist of a prohibition.

The statement would be: "It does not occur for the neuter. Consequently, whatever application of the designation *sarvanāmasthāna* might occur for *suṭ*, there would be a prohibition of all of it. For instance, [in the case of] *kuṇḍāni*.

In the case of the word *tiṣṭhanti*, there would be no designation (*saṃjñā*) even by the preceding rule. However, the scope for that [designation] is the substitution of *śi* for the *śas* [case-ending].
Even though there is the principle that "a rule or a prohibition applies only to what is immediately contiguous" (Vyāḍipāṭha 19).

By relying on this very point, even in the case of a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), this fault can be avoided; nevertheless, there would be the fault of excessive complexity in understanding (*pratipatti-gaurava*). For instance, because injunction and prohibition are contradictory, they cannot [be expressed] by a single sentence.

In that case, since it would be impossible to formulate [the rule] as a single sentence, a split in the statement (*vākyabheda*) must be made: "The *suṭ* augment receives the designation *sarvanāmasthāna*; and for the neuter, it does not.
Consequently, the statement of the prohibition [of the designation] would be disconnected [from the rest of the rule].
Otherwise, this prohibition might be suspected of also applying to the previously mentioned attainment (*prāpti*);
consequently, in order to avoid that [misinterpretation] and establish the intended meaning, the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) would inevitably arise. Therefore:

"For the sake of easy understanding, only a *paryudāsa* (exclusion) is resorted to; [it is said] 'there is no injunction in the neuter,' because the augment *suṭ* is mentioned in connection with the feminine and masculine; and it is 'not a prohibition,' because a *paryudāsa* has injunction as its primary function."
By this, he demonstrates that this rule has no operation regarding the neuter gender— namely, the phrase beginning with "tena" (by that).

Since there is no operation of this [rule] in the case of the neuter, whether in its prescription or its prohibition, therefore, the designation for the substitution of *śi* for *jas* certainly occurs by means of that preceding rule, because it is not prohibited.
In the case of *rājā*,

there is lengthening of the preceding vowel (*pūrvad-dīrghaḥ*), followed by the elision of the consonant and the following vowel (*hal-ṅy-ādi-lopaḥ*). In the case of *sāmanī* and *vamanī*, the substitution *āṬ* is applied according to *napuṃsakācca* (Pāṇini 7.1.19).
There is the substitution of *śī*. In that case, because the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) [of "vowel"] is absent, the lengthening does not occur.
44. *na vā iti vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 1.1.44). The word *na vā* is also a single indeclinable (*nipāta*) expressing negation, just as in the example: *na vā*.
In the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "it should be stated because the meaning has already been expressed," if that [term] were to be included here,
then after stating "optionally in a compound of directions in a bahuvrīhi" (Pāṇini 1.1.28), [the author would have said] "not in a bahuvrīhi."
In this case, however, the inclusion of the negation would be purposeless. Therefore, demonstrating that this is not a collection of particles, he says: "The word *na* is a negation."

Regarding the passage beginning with *dhaḥ*: Now, it may be objected that elsewhere in this grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), when establishing the relationship between a technical name (*saṃjñā*) and that which is named (*saṃjñin*), it is well known that only the word-form itself is intended; for example, in the rules *taraptamapau ghaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.22) and *dādhā ghvadāp*.

Thus, here too, it is appropriate to take the words *na* and *vā* themselves [as the technical terms]. To the question, "How then is the designation obtained for their meanings? he says: "The suffix *ṭhak* is a *karaṇa*," and so forth. It is called a *karaṇa* because it is made (*kriyate*).

Furthermore, because it is a *karaṇa* (instrument) of this [word], it is called *itikaraṇa*; its purpose is so that there may be a designation (*nirdeśa*) of the object (*artha*) which is the named entity (*saṃjñin*). For the word *iti* causes a reversal [of meaning]. Just as in the expression *gavityarthamāha*, when used after the word *go*, [the word *go*] refers to the actual sound of the word "cow" rather than its meaning.

The word *itaḥ*, by displacing that [word] from the status of having meaning as its referent (*arthapadārthakatva*) and establishing it in the status of having sound as its referent (*śabdapadārthakatva*),
functions in such a way that when the word *iti* is employed after the two words *na vā*,
those two [words] come to have their own forms as their referents (*svarūpapadārthaka*).

Having displaced [the word *na*] from its status as a mere particle (*nipāta*), it establishes it as having the meaning of a noun (*arthapadārthaka*). Therefore, the word *iti* is employed solely for the purpose of indicating the meaning. Thus, since the two meanings "not" (*na*) and "or" (*vā*) are understood—namely, negation (*pratiṣedha*) and option (*vikalpa*)—it is this [term *na vā*] that becomes the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for those two; it is not the word *navā* [as a single compound].

With the words "there, by means of negation," etc., he demonstrates the sequence of operation and the difference in function between negation and option (*vikalpa*). Regarding "when made equal": when brought to a state of parity.
Regarding "option proceeds": for the sake of accomplishing the effect in one of the two alternatives. But surely, is it not the word *vā* itself [that expresses this]?

It is well known in the world as having the sense of an option (*vikalpa*); when employed in specific contexts, it effects a result by way of an alternative. For instance, should an option be made regarding a matter that has already been established, or regarding one not yet established? If it were regarding what is already established, since that establishment already exists, the negation itself would constitute one of the two sides of the alternative.

It must be performed. Now, if it has not already been established? Since a prohibition is necessarily preceded by an establishment, that [prohibition] is not tenable without it; therefore, only the injunction must be performed in that case, not the prohibition. And both of these [functions] are capable of being expressed when the word *vā* (or) is employed.
In order to accomplish this, he asks: "For what purpose is this technical term (*saṃjñā*) being made? He replies: "They cause [the rules] to be optional (*vibhāṣā*) in both cases.
Since the subject under discussion is the technical term, it is understood that [the term *vibhāṣā* refers to the name]. This is as in the rule *vibhāṣā śveḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.30).
Would the operation of the word "or" (*vā*) be by way of negation, or by way of affirmation? In that regard, if it were by way of negation, such as "it does not exist," then—
What is the application? Since a prohibition is preceded by an occurrence, that very [occurrence] is its domain;

thus, this [rule] proceeds for the sake of prohibiting [the substitution of *guṇa*] only in the case of the *kit* suffixes. In that regard, by the rule "vacisvapi... (Pāṇini 6.1.15), [the substitution of *samprasāraṇa* applies] to the root *śvi*.

Because the *samprasāraṇa* has been prescribed [only] for the *kit* suffixes, it does not apply to the *pit* suffixes; for in that case, it has not been prescribed by anything at all. Furthermore, since this single sentence fulfills its purpose solely in effecting the prohibition with respect to the *kit* suffixes.

It is not tenable for there to be an engagement by way of a positive injunction (*vidhi*). If it were to proceed by way of a positive injunction, such that "it comes to be," then only where there is no prior attainment would that be the object of the injunction;
thus, the meaning of the injunction would apply optionally only to those who have already attained [the state].

It operates there [in the case of *ki*]; however, because its purpose has been fulfilled, it does not operate in the case of *kit*. But there is no fault in the formulation of the technical name (*saṃjñā*); for when that exists, the prohibition operates.
He equalizes that very *māna* which had been the subject of distinction based on whether it was caused by *samprasāraṇa* or not;
he brings about equality by making everything equally caused by *samprasāraṇa*. When that has been equalized, [the rule applies] before a *kit* suffix.

Furthermore, when an alternative (*vikalpa*) operates by way of negation (*vidhimukha*), it accomplishes the effect optionally in every instance, such that the *samprasāraṇa* occurs in one alternative. Since non-application (*aprāpti*) remains established in the other alternative, everything desired is accomplished.

Therefore, since [the condition] applies both when [the suffix] is present and when it is absent, this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed for the sake of the option (*vibhāṣā*). For example: *śuśāva*.
[This is derived from] the root *śvi* (DhP 1010) meaning "to move" or "to grow," with the *liṭ* suffix, the *ṇal* affix, and the *saṃprasāraṇa* substitution.
When [the suffix] Kta is applied, the augment vṛddhi and the substitution ādeśa take place; thus we have *śuśuvatuḥ* and *śiśviyatuḥ*.
By the rule *aci śnudhātu* (Pāṇini 6.4.77) and others, the substitutions *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* occur.
45. *Igyaṇaḥ saṃprasāraṇam* (1.1.45).

Regarding the term "bhūtaḥ": where [a grammatical element] prescribed by another rule is restated by means of a past-participle case-ending (*bhūtavibhakti*) for the sake of another operation, as in *saṃprasāraṇasya* (6.1.139).

Regarding the rule *saprasāraṇācca* (Pāṇini 6.1.108), there it says: "whether already occurred (*bhūta*) or yet to occur (*bhāvī*). This refers to cases where [a term] is mentioned for the purpose of prescribing [an operation] by means of a case-ending that is to be applied [later], as in the case of *ṣyaṅ*.

Regarding *samprasāraṇam* (Pāṇini 6.1.13) and *vasoḥ samprasāraṇam* (6.4.131), [the former] refers to what is yet to come (*bhāvī*). For in this case, there is no *iṅ* that occupies the place of *ṣyaṅ* or the place of *vasu*, for which the designation [of *samprasāraṇa*] would apply according to the rule. It is like [saying] "the cloth of the loom" (*śāṭakaṃ sūtrasya*).

"Vaya" means that *ig* occurs in place of *yaṇ*, for which the designation "samprasāraṇa" is applied when it has already occurred. For example, in "iṣṭam" and "uptam," there is *samprasāraṇa* by the rule "vacisvapiyajādīnāṃ kiti" (Pāṇini 6.1.15).
In the word *gṛhīta*,
there is also vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) according to the rule *grahijyāvayi-* (Pāṇini 6.1.16), and the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *graho 'liṭi dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.37).
With the words "Some," and so forth, he shows the opinion of those who do not rely on a future designation.
But how, then, can these two meanings of a single sūtra be obtained from a single sentence? By means of *tantra* (simultaneous application) or by repetition (*āvṛtti*). Now, [one might object]:...

And it has been stated that in the rule for assigning technical names (*saṃjñāvidhi*), the inclusion of only the word-form (*śabda*) is well-established; therefore, it is appropriate that the phoneme (*varṇa*) alone should be the named entity (*saṃjñin*). But how could this apply to the meaning (*artha*)? If you argue that it is as in the rule *ṭhna veti vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 1.1.44), we say: no, that is not correct; because in that case, there is the particle *iti*—

Because that [explanation] was employed for the purpose of indicating the meaning of the *syāt* [particle], whereas here it does not exist, [you claim it is] improper; however, even here it is indeed proper, since either the repetition of the system (*tantra*) or the logical principle (*nyāya*) has been relied upon. And of these two meanings of the sūtra...
The indication of a specific case-ending is a sign [of a technical term]. Since, in prescriptive rules such as "ṣyaḍaḥ saṃprasāraṇam" (Pāṇini 6.1.13),
he employs a mention using the case-ending currently being discussed, it is understood from that that [the rule refers to] the meaning of the sentence.
Regarding the term "saṃjñī": since [Pāṇini] employs a past-participle case ending in rules such as *samprasāraṇasya* (6.3.139), it is understood from this that—

Regarding the term "the letter *ṭh*": therefore, it is logical that even the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) can be the designated object (*saṃjñin*). What is the nature of this sentence-meaning? He says: "located in the place of the substituendum" (*sthānyadeśa*), and so forth. With the words "therein," etc., he [establishes] the distinction between the scopes of the two preceding sūtra-meanings.

He demonstrates this by stating that a phoneme (*varṇa*) cannot be the object of a rule (*vidhi*). In an injunctive statement such as "the *samprasāraṇa* [substitution] occurs for *ṣi*, *yaṅ*, and *ḍaḥ*" (Pāṇini 6.1.13), the primary meaning of the sūtra presents itself first. However, in the case of a non-injunctive [restatement],...

Since [the rule] "of the *samprasāraṇa*" (6.3.139) and so forth prescribes [the substitution], the first [interpretation] is ineffective regarding what is to be prescribed; therefore, the second [interpretation] is adopted, as in the example "aduhitarām."
In this regard, the Bhāṣya states that because [the vowel] is the substitute for a *yaṇ*, it would receive the designation *saṃprasāraṇa*; and if that were the case,
the lengthening prescribed by the rule *ṭhhalaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.2) would undesirably apply.
To dispel this objection, he says: "Because of the correspondence of number" (*saṃkhyātānudeśāt*), and so forth.
Here, there are four substituends (*sthānin*)—the *yaṇ*s—and likewise four substitutes (*ādeśa*) for the *ik*s; therefore, there must be a correspondence based on the equality of their numbers.

By the rule "The subsequent mention [is] according to the respective order" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.10), and so forth, the designation *samprasāraṇa* applies only to that *i*-vowel which occupies the place of the letter *y*. However, in this case, the *i*-vowel does not occupy the place of the letter *y*; what then?
[This refers to] the *lakāra* suffix.
How, then, could there be an occasion for that [suffix]? [The root is] *druh* "to injure" (DhP 1014); [the suffix] *laṅ*;
[and the rule] *karmavat karmaṇā*.

By the extension rule *tulyakriyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.87), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) and the augment *iṭ* apply when the object itself acts as the agent (*karmakartṛ*). Since the suffixes *yak* and *ciṇ* are prohibited for the roots *duh*, *snū*, and *nam* by the rule *na duhasnunamāṃ yakciṇau* (Pāṇini 3.1.89), the suffix *śap* is applied. Because this root belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix. Thus, the form *aduhi* is established.

The suffix *tarap* is applied by the rule *ṭhtiṅśca* (Pāṇini 5.3.56). The suffix *ām* is applied by the rule *kimetiṅvyayaghādāmvadravyaprakarṣe* (Pāṇini 5.4.11). The mention of *tarap* here is for the purpose of establishing the designation (*saṃjñā*) of "stem" (*aṅga*).
46. *Ādyantau ṭakitau* (1.1.46).

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the metarule *ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā* (1.1.49). Consequently, by virtue of that connection, this rule is also understood to be a metarule (*paribhāṣā*). If, then, [the suffix] *ādiṣṭi*...

If [the suffix] were internal (*antaḥ*), then suffixes such as *ṭha* in "ṭhcareṣṭaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.16) and *ka* in "āto ’nupasarge kaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.3) would also become initial (*ādibhūta*) with respect to the roots *sy-* and *ū-*. Furthermore, if a suffix beginning with *ṭi* were initial, [the rule] "ṭiḍḍhāṇañ... (Pāṇini 4.1.15) [would apply].

one should not suspect that the *ṅīp* suffix prescribed for a *ṭit* [word] is without scope (*niravakāśa*), for there are cases where the status of being a *ṭit* is established by the base itself (*prakṛti*).
In cases such as *nadaḍ* and *bhaṣaḍ*, that [rule] will find its scope.
Furthermore, if the suffix were *ṭit*, then forms such as *kurucara* would be established; however, if it were *kit*, it would have to be final.

In the case of *ādhyoḥ* and *vidhyoḥ*, because the suffix *ki*— prescribed by the rule *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.92)— is included within the base (*prakṛti*), it is part of the verbal root (*dhātu*).

If there were grasping by means of grasping, the accent prescribed by *ṭhudātayaṇo halpūrvāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.174) would not apply, because of the prohibition in *ṭhnoṅ dhātvoḥ* (6.1.175); therefore, he says:
"Because the mention of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhīgrahaṇa*) applies [here] by way of the 'lion's glance' (*siṃhāvalokita*) maxim. But even so—

The suffixes *gāpoṣṭak* (Pāṇini 3.2.8) and *vrīhiśālyorḍhak* (5.2.2) would otherwise apply as initial and final [suffixes]; this is not a fault, for according to the rule *purastādapavādā anantarāt vidhīn bādhante notarān* (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 9), "exceptions [occurring] earlier sublate the rules immediately following them, but not those further away," this is an exception specifically to the application by position (*sthāneyoga*).
It will exist, not as something dependent on conditions. Another says:
the first and last parts cannot exist without the whole; therefore, having implied the whole, they subsist within it.

Furthermore, in the case of a relationship between a part and a whole, when a part such as *yaL* (the *ya*, *ra*, or *la*) is prescribed at the beginning or end [of a suffix], that part must be indicated by means of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*); thus, by implication, it is understood that [the rule applies] to that which is indicated by the "genitive of the part. But this is not the case here.

The two suffixes *gāpoṣṭak* (Pāṇini 4.2.8) and *vrīhiśālyorḍhak* (Pāṇini 5.2.2) would both result in being applied at the beginning and the end [of the word], because here the bases are specified by means of a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). What then? [It is that] "substitutes for case-endings (*sup*) become case-endings (*sup*)."
The phrase "by that" refers to the genitive case used in the sense of the ablative. Regarding the form *bhīṣayate*:

from the root *ñibhī* (meaning "fear," Dhātupāṭha 1084), the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied; then, by the rule *bhiyo hetubhaye ṣuk* (Pāṇini 7.3.40), the augment *ṣuk* is added, and finally, by the rule *bhīsmyorhetubhaye* (Pāṇini 1.3.68), the verb takes the ātmanepada endings.
Thus ends the section on the ātmanepada.
47. *midaco’ntyātparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.47).
Here, if *acaḥ* (from Pāṇini 4.3.31) were a fifth-case [ablative] term, then by this [present rule], [the augment *m*] would follow after the final vowel.

There would be coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatva*) with the fifth [case ending]. Consequently, by the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.52), the augment *num* would occur here after the final vowel—as in *kuṇḍāni*; for such is indeed the case here.

In the case of a neuter noun, it would be the final vowel; however, in the form *payāṃsi*, this would not apply, as by the rule *alo'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52), it would instead apply only in place of the letter *s*.

It is not the vowels (*ac*) that are being selected here; rather, it is the *sakāra*. Therefore, showing that this is a genitive used for specification (*nirdhāraṇa*), he says "of the vowels" (*acām*) and so forth. The plural number is used in reference to the genus (*jāti*).
In the sūtra as well, the singular form *acaḥ* refers to the genus alone. If, then, this is a genitive of specification, [then...]

Since the final [letter] is not specified, [the rule would apply] without distinction, such that a *m* could follow any final [letter]; for there is no second mention of "final" (*aj*) by which the final [letter] might be specified. This is not a fault.

For in the world, the cognition of selection occurs only with respect to that which is of the same class; thus, when it is said, "Among cows, the black one is the most excellent in beauty," it is understood that a cow alone [is meant].

It is understood [as such], neither as a non-vowel (*ajā*) nor as a horse (*aśva*). Therefore, here too, among vowels, that which is determined as the final by taking the last vowel as the limit is understood to be a vowel of the same class (*samānajātīya*) alone. Consequently, it will follow immediately after the very last vowel.

This [sūtra] is commenced for the purpose of setting aside the application of the notion of "substitution" (*sthāneyogitva*) and its subsequent status. Among these, for the purpose of setting aside the application of "substitution," [the rule] *śemucādīnām* (Pāṇini 7.1.59) applies, whereby *num* occurs:
*muñcati*. [And] by *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.72), [num occurs]: *payāṃsi*.

The rule *rudhādibhyaḥ śnam* (Pāṇini 3.1.78) is intended as an exception (*apavāda*) to the principle of dependence on a subsequent condition (*pratyayaparatva*). [It states: "He obstructs" (*ruṇaddhi*). Now, one might object:

according to the metarule *purastādapavādā anantarān vidhīn bādhante notarān* (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 9), "Exceptions set aside the rules immediately preceding them, not those further away," it would be more logical for this to be an exception specifically to the application of the term *sthāne* (in place of), rather than [to the general rule of suffix-dependence].
Regarding the dependence on a suffix (*pratyayaparatva*), this is not the case; for if it were so, the designation *mit* for the augment *śnam* would be purposeless due to having no scope.
If it is argued that it is not purposeless because it serves the purpose of being heard [in pronunciation], we say no; for [the rule] "ṭhṛṇaha im" (Pāṇini 7.3.92) [would otherwise be redundant].
Because of this specific mention; for if the intention were merely to hear [the word], the mention would have been "tṛṇam ha im.

Therefore, it is appropriate that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule regarding the subsequent occurrence of an affix (*pratyayaparatva*). If this is so, then by the principle that "that which falls in the middle of something is included by the mention of that thing," [the *im* is included].
Thus,

because the element *śnam* falls within the *prakṛti* (the base), it would be included by the mention of that [base], and due to its being subsequent [to the base], it would not receive the designation of "suffix" (*pratyaya*).

And likewise, by the rule *ṭhlaśakvataddhite* (1.3.8), the *it*-designation prescribed for the letter *ś* at the beginning of an affix would not occur. This is not a fault; because it is prescribed within the governing context (*adhikāra*) of "affix" (*pratyaya*), it will receive the designation of "affix. Even though [the rule] is subsequent, and even though...

In the case of being included within the *prakṛti* (base); for example, the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*) in *bahujaka*. In the absence of [any other rule] being subsequent, the designation *pratyaya* (suffix) applies to these two—namely, *bahupaṭavaḥ* and *uccakaiḥ*—by the rule *citaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.163).

Thus, the final acute accent (antodāttatva) indeed occurs. Regarding the rule "of the root *masj*" and so forth: the term *anuṣaṅga* is a designation used by the ancient teachers for the penultimate letter *n*.

Regarding the root *ṭhṭhuam* (*majj*), meaning "to purify" (DhP 1416), [the author] will state the augment *num* by means of the rule *ṭhmasjinaśorjhali* (Pāṇini 7.1.60). And if that *num* were to follow after the final vowel, then [the rule] *ṭhskoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ* [would apply].
Thus, by the rule (8.2.29), there would be no elision of the *sakāra*, and by the rule "ṭhaniditām" (6.4.24), there would be no elision of the *nakāra*;
for they are not, respectively, initial [in their respective stems].
And because of the rule regarding the final [consonant]: therefore, the *num* augment should be inserted between the *j* and *s* that precede the final *j*.
How it is obtained as preceding the final will be explained in the seventh [chapter]. As in the example "magnaḥ" (*oditaśca*, Pāṇini 8.2.45).

The state of being a final consonant (*niṣṭhānatva*) does not apply here because that [suffix] is unestablished; therefore, by the rule *ṭhcoḥ kuḥ* (8.2.30), the *k*-substitution (*kutva*) of the letter *j* results in the letter *g*.
In the form *maṅktā*, once the *g* has been produced as before, by the rule *khari ca* (8.4.55)— [The rule *khari ca* applies.]
The *cartva* [substitution] is the letter *k*. By the rule "ṇaścāpadāntasya jhali" (Pāṇini 8.3.24), an *anusvāra* is substituted.

By the rule "anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.58), this becomes the letter *ṅ*. Furthermore, this *mit* augment should be understood as belonging to the preceding element (*pūrvabhakta*); otherwise, by the rule "vahābhre lihaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.32), [the suffix would apply to] the root *lih*.

When the suffix *khaś* is applied and the augment *mum* is added by the rule "ṭharurdviṣadajantasya" (Pāṇini 6.3.67), in the case of the form *vahaṃlih*, the anusvāra prescribed for a word-final position by the rule "mo'nusvāraḥ" (8.3.23) would not occur, because [the *m*] would no longer be at the end of a word (*apadāntatvāt*).

48. *eca igghrasvādeśe* (Pāṇini 1.1.48). This is a *paribhāṣā* (technical rule) intended to regulate the application of substitutes; it applies in rules such as *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya* (1.2.47). Here, *ec* refers to the individual phonemes that constitute the composite sounds. Among these, *ai* is [the first].

Of these two [vowels], the former part has the same phonetic form as a letter (*varṇa*), consists solely of a measure (*mātrā*), and is palatal (*tālavya*). For this very reason, it is stated: "The *ai* and *o* are produced in the throat and the palate" (Āpiśali Śikṣā 17).
The grammarians recite [the rule] as *ṭhoṭhaU*; this is because its two constituent parts are produced by the throat and the palate.
The first portion of these two, *ṭho* and *āṬ*, is exactly like that of the vowels *e* and *ai*.
However, the latter part has the same form as the vowel *u*, consists of one mora (*mātrika*), and is labial. For this very reason, [the rule is stated as] *ṭho āṬ*.
The authors of the Śikṣā recite: "The throat and the palate" (Āpiśali-Śikṣā 18); this is because their constituent parts are the throat and the palate.
In that case, since there is no short vowel among the e-series (*ec*) that is most similar to the whole [diphthong], [the rule does not apply].

That which is the most similar (*antaratama*) to its constituent part must be joined with that very part; moreover, that [most similar part] is either *a*, *i*, or *u*. In that regard, when a short vowel is prescribed for *e* and *ai*, it might sometimes be *a* and sometimes *i*; the same applies to *o* and *au*.
This is undertaken so that there might sometimes be the vowel *a* and sometimes the vowel *u*,
and so that the vowels *i* and *u* alone may occur as appropriate, while at no time should the vowel *a* ever be absent.

In this case, although there is equality among these [substitutes], nevertheless, there is no application according to numerical correspondence (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*), because this is not an injunction (*vidhāyaka*), but rather a restrictive rule (*niyāmaka*). And since a restriction presupposes a prior possibility of occurrence (*prāpti*),
those internal [substitutes] which have already been established are restricted.

The short vowels *e*, *o*, and *ai* are [the subject]; by this [sūtra], a restriction is made for them. And since *ṛ* and *ḷ* are not obtained [as substitutes] here, how can there be a correspondence according to order (*yathāsaṃkhyatva*)?
If this is so, one should simply say "iṇ" and not "ak"; that is true.

However, if it were stated in this way, a doubt might arise: "Is the pratyāhāra [of vowels] formed with the preceding *ṇ* or with the following one? Therefore, it is stated as *iK* to eliminate ambiguity. Examples are *atiri* and *atinu*, meaning a Brahmin family that has surpassed wealth (*rāya*) or has surpassed a boat (*nau*).
By the rule *ṭhatyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe dvitīyayā* (Vārttika 91), a compound is formed with *kugati* (Pāṇini 2.2.18) and so forth; and by the rule *paravalliṅgaṃ dvandvatatpuruṣayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.26),
it takes the masculine gender.

When the feminine gender would otherwise apply, in the case of *dvigu*, *prāpta*, *āpanna*, *alaṃpūrva*, and *gatisamāsa* compounds, that [original] gender alone remains. By the rule "the final vowel of a nominal stem is short in the neuter" (Pāṇini 1.2.47), there is a shortening; thus, for the vowel *e*—which is produced at the throat and palate—the substitute *i* is applied.

The vowel *i* becomes palatal (*tālavya*). For the labial (*oṣṭhya*) vowel *au*, which belongs to the throat (*kaṇṭhya*) and the lips (*oṣṭhya*), the labial *u* is substituted. Thus, we have *upagu*, meaning "near the cow" (*goḥ samīpam*). By the rule "an indeclinable [compound] beginning with a case-ending" (*avyayaṃ vibhakti* 2.1.6), etc., there is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of proximity. By the rule "of a word ending in *go* or a feminine [suffix], when it is a subordinate member" (*gostriyor upasarjanasya* 1.2.48), the shortening of the vowel occurs.
The letter *u* [is substituted] for *e* when followed by *ka*, *ṭha*, *leṣṭha*, *la*, *kāra*, *sa*, or *oṣṭha*. An example of *e* is:

"He has passed beyond this word 'he' (*he atikrāntaḥ*)," resulting in *atihi brāhmaṇakulam*. And "he has passed beyond a bed" (*atihi khaṭvām*), resulting in *atikhaṭvaḥ*. As before, when a *prādi* compound is formed, [the rule] *gotriṅ upasarjanaṃ svaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.48) applies.

By such rules as these, the short *a*-vowel alone becomes the most similar (*antaratama*). For example, in "devadatta," when the substitution of an acute accent (*udātta*) for the first syllable due to being in vocative address is to be applied, and in "devada3ta," when the substitution of prolation (*pluta*) is to be applied by the rule "guroranṛto 'ntyasya" (Pāṇini 8.2.86), [the short *a* is the closest substitute].
The suffix *iṅ* does not occur in the sense of "that which is to be done."

49. *ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā* (1.1.49). Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of restricting the application": *yoganiyama* means the restriction of connection; that which has this as its purpose or motive is [the rule].

Thus it has been stated: if this [rule] is for the purpose of restricting the application of *yoga*, then the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) used in the treatise applies only to the *sthāna-yoga* (the relationship of "in place of"), and not to any other kind of *yoga*.
This being the case, the genitive in the rule "ṭhūdupadhāyā gohaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.89) is also [restricted to the *sthāna-yoga*].

It would have to be a connection by way of position (*sthāna-yoga*), not a connection by way of the relationship between a whole and its parts (*avayava-avayavi-sambandha*). Consequently, because the genitive case in the sixth case [of the rule] *alo'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52), which denotes position, is restricted to the final [element], the substitution of *ū* would apply to the final *h* of the root *goḥ* (by the rule *gohaḥ*); and [furthermore, by the rule] *upadhāyāśca* (Pāṇini 7.1.101)...

Because [the rule] "of the penultimate vowel" (*upadhā-mātrasya*) would apply by the general statement, he says: "In this treatise, that which has an invariant connection with the genitive case," and so forth. When there is the possibility of non-restriction, a restriction is established by this [rule]. And where is there the possibility of non-restriction? Where there is doubt.

As in the rule *yathā-ṭhasterbhūḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.52). For here there arises the doubt: does [the substitution] take the place of *asti*, or rather of that which immediately precedes it? However, in the former case, because the substitute *bhū* is delimited by its specific constituent (*avayavin*)—namely, the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) as a constituent (*avayava*)—this [substitution] applies only to the constituent *ṭhali*.
It is certain;

therefore, her operation does not apply here. Regarding the phrase "only by connection with the position" (*sthāneyogaiva*): *sthāne* is a locative of cause (*naimittikasaptamī*), and *yogaḥ* means connection.

The connection [is as follows]. By this, the following is stated: namely, that the connection is indeed caused by position (*sthāna*). Making this very point clear, he says: "When the connection of position has become the cause," and so forth. That is to say, when the connection of position has attained the status of being a cause (*nimitta*).

If [the condition] exists, that [designation] is to be understood. For here the word *bhūta* functions in the sense of "having attained" (*prāpta*); as in the expression *devabhūtaḥ*, the meaning is "one who has attained the state of a god" (*devatva*). By employing the term *nimitta* (cause/condition) in the Sūtra, [Patañjali indicates] that [the designation applies] through the connection with the substituend (*sthāneyoga*).

He shows that this is a locative of occasion (*nimita-saptamī*). Furthermore, "connection" (*yoga*) here is characterized by the relationship between the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*). Why is this so? Because of that very [original element]—the *sthānin*—...

Because it is the cause. The word *sthāna* (place/position) is derived in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva-sādhana*); "staying" is *sthāna*. Furthermore, that is threefold: displacement (*apakarṣa*), cessation (*nivṛtti*), and extension (*prasaṅga*). For example, "Let the horse be tied in the place of the cow" is displacement.

The word *sthāna* has three meanings: that which is to be occupied (*āstheya*), cessation (*nivṛtti*), and occasion (*prasaṅga*). For example, in the phrase "bitter medicine [is used] in place of phlegm," it means cessation. In the phrase "one should spread *śara* grass in place of *darbha* grass," it means occasion. Of these, the first two meanings are not possible here.

Because the relationship between word and meaning is eternal, a first [usage] is not possible; because the root *as* is taught in its general form, a second [usage] is not possible. Therefore, considering that the third alone is the intended meaning, he says: "And the word *sthāna*. However, the occasion (*prasaṅga*) refers to that which serves as the cause for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
The time has come; [the rule] "in the case of *as* [meaning] 'to be' when there is occasion" applies. Regarding the action of *as*, characterized by the communication of its own meaning—of that...

The meaning is that the occasion for time (*kāla*), which serves as the cause (*nimitta*), has arrived. By the phrase "the cause of the connection in the context" (*prasaṅge sambandhasya nimitabhūta*) and so forth, he demonstrates the possibility [of the rule's application] in an example of the meaning of the *sūtra*.
Furthermore, the mention of "the root *brū*" (*bruvaḥ*) is merely illustrative; [it applies to] the root *as* (*asti*) as well.
For even in the case of [words] such as *tyad* and so on, the application of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would indeed follow, since the relation has arisen as its cause.

But what are the many meanings of the genitive, for the sake of which this [rule] is stated regarding the genitive in order to exclude other objects of relation? To this he says: "For there are many," and so forth. For in the case of a word...

There exist relations based on proximity, immediate succession, modification, part-whole, and so forth; however, these do not include relations such as "offspring" and "progenitor. Therefore, he says, "as many as are possible for a word. Now, regarding the term *sthāneyoga*: is it a non-compound (*asamāsa*) or a compound (*samāsa*)?

If it were not a compound (*asamāsa*), then, because the word *yoga* is masculine, its designation in the feminine gender would be improper, and grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "sixth" (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would not be achieved; for *yoga* would not be in the genitive case. Therefore, is it a compound?

Is it a *tatpuruṣa* compound, or rather a *bahuvrīhi*? If it is a *tatpuruṣa*, then those two previously mentioned faults would occur, as well as the undesirable consequence of the elision (*luk*) of the locative case-ending. If, on the other hand, it is a *bahuvrīhi*, even so, the occurrence of elision here remains unavoidable.
To this he says: "The sixth [case-ending] is used in the sense of 'in place of' (*sthāne-yoga*)," and so forth; the meaning has already been explained. 50. *sthāne’ntaratamaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.50).

This is a metarule intended to restrict the application of substitutes; [it means] "among those obtained in place [of an original]. By this, it is shown that this is not an injunctive statement, but rather [it serves to exclude] others from those nearest [in sound] which have been obtained through another rule.
He shows that this is for the purpose of restriction, namely, that only that which is the most similar (*antaratama*) becomes [the substitute].
For if it were a positive injunction (*vidhāyaka*), it would undesirably apply even in cases such as *dadhi madhu* (curd honey), since [substitution] occurs by virtue of proximity (*antaratamya*).
What, then, is undesirable here? [The answer is: as much as [is required] by proximity...

The two [substitutes] would apply to the words *dadhi* and *madhu*; for those two substitutes as well, there would be other two words *dadhi* and *madhu* that would serve as substitutes, and for those too, yet others— thus, there would be an infinite regress of substitutes.

Because there would be an infinite regress due to the application of further rules (*parāvidhāna*), there would consequently be no functional application (*viniyoga*) of words toward the communication of meaning, since the activity of the explanatory treatise (*anvākhyāyaka-śāstra*) would never cease. For it is only when the treatise has ceased its operation that those [words] are employed as explained, and not otherwise; thus, an undesirable consequence follows. But surely—
Since the purpose of the characteristic has been fulfilled by its single occurrence,

it will not occur again; this is not so, for that which was stated applies where an action is undertaken for a specific purpose, whereas here, on the contrary, the most proximate [element] is prescribed spontaneously.

Thus, his activity would indeed be uninterrupted. Even if this were a restrictive rule (*niyama*), if it were to restrict those [acts] already enjoined, the statement would be entirely purposeless. For it would be like saying to one who has already eaten: [“Eat!”]
If one were to say, "Do not eat," what would that do for him? Therefore,
it is only at the stage when [the action] is being reached that the purpose is accomplished through the combination of this [injunction] with other sentences.

Because this [substitute] is a part of that [original], it is called "most similar" (*sadṛśatama*). He explains the meaning of the word *antaratama* with the words "in terms of meaning" (*arthataḥ*), and so forth. From the word *vataṇḍa*, in the sense of a female offspring, [the suffix *ṅīp* is applied] by the rule *vataṇḍācca* (Pāṇini 4.1.108).

Thus, from *yañ*, there is the elision of the vowel *a* by [Pāṇini 6.4.143], *ṭhūlk striyām*. Then, the compound *vataṇḍī cāsau yuvatiśca* ("she who is both a Vataṇḍī and a young woman") is formed according to [Pāṇini 2.1.65], *poṭāyuvati-*, etc. In that context, by this [sūtra], [the word] becomes "masculine-like" (*puṃvat*).

By the rule "karmadhārayaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.42) and others, when the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is to be applied, every masculine word would be applicable; therein, by this [rule],
for the sake of the meaning "the offspring of Vataṇḍī"—
The word *vātaṇḍya* is the closest in meaning to the word *vataṇḍī*; indeed, the word *vātaṇḍya* has the sense of "the offspring of Vataṇḍa.

In [the examples] such as *pākaḥ*, the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). Regarding [the examples] such as *cakārasya*: "of the first letters of the classes... [and so forth].

Regarding the rule "alpaprāṇāḥ" (Āpiśali Śikṣā 4.3), the letters *ca* and *ka* are of weak breath (*alpaprāṇa*). Among the vargas, the first and second letters, as well as *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, *visarjanīya*, *jihvāmūlīya*, *upadhmānīya*, and the two *yamas*, are those with an open throat (*vivṛtakaṇṭha*).

"Those produced with breath and lacking voicing are unvoiced" (Āpiśali-śikṣā 4.2); thus [the two] are unvoiced. Regarding "of the letter *ja*" and so forth: "The third and fourth letters of the [five] classes (*varga*), the semivowels (*antaḥstha*), *ha*, the anusvāra, the *yamas*—both second and fourth—and the *nāsikya*s have a constricted (*saṃvṛta*) throat."

The sounds *n*, *d*, *ān*, *upadhmanīya*, and *visarga* are voiced (*ghoṣavat*) and "great-breathed" (*mahāprāṇa*); [the others] are "small-breathed" (*alpaprāṇa*). In the forms *ṭham uṣmai* and *amūbhyām*, the substitution of *yatva* for the base *adas-* occurs when followed by the dative singular suffix *bhyām*; then, by the rule *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97), there is the substitution of the single resultant form (*pararūpa*), and [the rule] *sarvanāmnaḥ*... [applies].
The substitution of *smai* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.1.4]. In the case of *bhyām*, there is lengthening by [Pāṇini 7.3.102];
thereafter, for a short vowel, a short *u* is substituted, and for a long vowel, a long *ū*.
Regarding the phrase "when *sthāna* is understood as the governing term": the word *sthāna*, being under discussion, signifies "occasion" (*prasaṅga*).
When that term is carried over [from the previous rule], the meaning obtained is: "among those [substitutes] that are to be obtained on the occasion [of the original], the most similar one occurs."
But surely, where there is multiple proximity (*āntarya*), proximity of place (*sthāna*)— such as the palate— is more powerful; therefore, it should be so.
Furthermore, the word *sthāna* (place), which denotes the locations such as the palate and so forth, is employed once again.

If this is the case, one might object: "In this context, since proximity (*sannikarṣa*) based specifically on place is what has been specially adopted, would that based on articulatory effort (*pramāṇa*) and so forth not be abandoned? This is not a fault, for the connection there is established by treating the sentence as a distinct syntactical unit (*vākyabheda*).

It is stated: "When [elements] are to be substituted in place [of others], the most similar (antaratama) substitute occurs. In the preceding sentence, the word *sthāna* signifies the occasion (*prasaṅga*) for substitution; in the subsequent one, it signifies the physical location such as the palate (*tālu*).

Thus, when there is a connection through a division of sentences, it is understood that in the first sentence there is the inclusion of the proximities (*āntarya*) produced by position (*sthāna*) and so forth; whereas in the second, there is the relative strength and weakness of those very same [proximities]. [The word] "in position" (*sthāne*).

And thus, this is a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*). By this, the following is stated: where there is more than one degree of proximity (*āntarya*), that which is the most proximate (*antaratama*) by way of its position as the cause is the one that occurs. And the mention of the superlative suffix *-tama* is the indicator (*liṅga*) for the split of the sentence; for by it, excellence in similarity is expressed.
That [excellence] is intended to be established; and that occurs when there is a multiplicity of similarities in relation to other similarities.
Since, within a single sentence, other similarities are excluded by the mention of "position," in relation to what could there be an excellence of similarity? Therefore—
From the inclusion of the term *tama*, a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) is inferred; otherwise, it would be redundant.
Regarding the word *cetā*: here, because the vowel *i* is palatal (*tālavya*), while the vowel *e* is both guttural-palatal (*kaṣṭha-tālavya*).
Proximity by place [of articulation] (*sthāna*):

for example, between *i* and *a*, because both have the same measure (*mātrika*). In the word "stotā," here too, there is proximity by place, because the phoneme *u* is labial and the phoneme *o* is velar-labial.

Proximity (*āntarya*). Regarding the *u*-vowels and the *a*-vowel, however, [proximity] is by way of measure (*pramāṇataḥ*) as before. In that case, if the mention of "place" (*sthāna*) were not repeated, then due to proximity by way of measure, the *a*-vowel might sometimes be the *guṇa* substitute, and due to proximity by way of place, the *e*-vowels might [sometimes be the substitute].

Furthermore, because of the mention of "place" (sthāna), the internal effort produced by the place of articulation is stronger; therefore, only *e* and *o* arise, and never *a*. [This is indicated by] the terms *soṣmaṇaḥ* and *soṣmāṇaḥ*.

And so forth. The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*); the meaning is that because the sibilants (*soṣman*) are the second [consonants of their respective classes], therefore the second [consonants] are applicable to the sibilant *ha*. This applies likewise to such statements as "to those possessing *nāda*, [those] possessing *nāda," and so on.

The meaning of "cause" (*hetu*) should be applied here. For the *Śikṣā* states: "The sibilants (*śādayaḥ*) are *ūṣman* sounds; [the second letters] correspond by place of articulation (*saṃsthāna*), and the fourth [letters] correspond with the letter *ha*. (Ā. Śi. 1.4).

8.10) Here, by the statement "the sibilants (ūṣman) beginning with ś," the possession of *ūṣman* (aspiration) for the letter *ha* is established; by the statement "the second [letters] of each class have the same place of articulation [as the first]," that of the second letters of the classes, such as *kha* and so forth; and by the mention of the letter *ha*...

By the phrase "the fourths," the fourth letters of each class, such as *dh* and so forth, are meant. That which has the same place of articulation (*sthāna*) is "having the same place" (*sasthāna*). In the expression "by that having the same place" (*sasthānena*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of a characteristic (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇe*). By means of the second [letter] having the same place, the sibilants (*ūṣman*) are characterized. This is what is stated.
It is said: "Just as their heat (ūṣman) exists only in its own place, so too these [consonants] are the second 'heat' (ūṣman) of the classes.
Alternatively, this third case [ending] expresses a connection with an equal object; the word "equal" (tulya) is to be supplied [as an ellipsis].
Their status as *ūṣman* (aspirates) should be understood through their similarity. In that regard, the letter *ha* has the same place of articulation (*sthāna*) as *kha*;

*śa* has the same as *ccha*; *ṣa* has the same as *ṭha*; and *sa* has the same as *tha*. There is no *ūṣman* with the same place of articulation as *pha*; therefore, its status as an *ūṣman* is characterized by its specific distinction [from the other consonants].

Because they are similar to that. By this, the meaning is that just as the letter *ha* is a sibilant (*ūṣman*), so too are those [other letters]. Regarding the phrase "possessing resonance" (*nādavataḥ*) and so forth: by the previously mentioned passage beginning with "the third and fourth of the classes," it was stated that the third letters and the letter *ha* possess resonance. Those which are sibilants (*soṣmaṇaḥ*) and possess resonance (*nādavantaḥ*).

Thus, the sibilant nature (*ūṣmatva*) of the letter *ha* is declared by the rule "the letters beginning with *ṭha* and *śa* are sibilants" (ĀŚ 1.4.8); however, the possession of resonance (*nādavatva*) for the fourth letters of the classes is declared by the rule "the fourth letters [are produced] by means of *ha*" (ĀŚ 1.4.1), while for both sets of classes, it is established by the rule "the third and fourth letters of the classes... and so forth.
By what was stated previously:

51. *uraṇ raparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.51). Here, three positions are possible: that by this [sūtra], both [the substitution of] *u* in place of *ṛ* and the property of having *r* as a subsequent element (*raparatva*) are [prescribed].

"One view is that [the substitution] is prescribed [by this rule itself]. "The second view is that, after an *aṇ* has been substituted for *u* by another rule, this [rule] merely effects the state of having *r* as a subsequent element (*raparatva*). "By another rule, [the substitution] for *u*..."

The third [view] is that the *aṇ* being prescribed is, at the very time of its prescription, combined with that other rule (*lakṣaṇāntara*) and is thus produced by this [present rule] as qualified by the substitution of *r* (raparatva). Among these, if it were the first [view]:

If this position were adopted, the acute (*udātta*) and other accents would not apply to the place of *ṛ*, because they would be sublated by this [rule]; furthermore, in the case of *kṛti*, the initial acute accent prescribed by *ñnityādinityam* (P.
6.1.197) would not occur, as in the word *prakṛtam*.

If [the accent were applied] in place of the vowel, then when the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) is applied by the rule *gatiranantaraḥ* (P. 6.2.49), the rule *anudātaṃ padamekavarjam* (P. 6.1.158) would not apply to render it unaccented (*anudātta*), nor would the rule *udātanudātasya svaritaḥ* (P.
8.4.66) apply to produce a circumflex (*svarita*) accent. This is because [the accent would have to be assigned] to the vowel.
Although [the rules for] *udātta* and so forth are prescribed, nevertheless, since they have no other scope,

only that *aṇ* which is explicitly taught (*pratipadokta*) in place of the *ṛ*-vowel would be followed by *ra*. Furthermore, there are other substitutes explicitly taught in place of the *ṛ*-vowel, such as in the rule "ṛta id dhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.100).
By such other characteristics as these, the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* would not occur in those cases;
consequently, forms such as *ṭhkirati* would not be established.
Now, if the second alternative is adopted, then when a suffix beginning with *tṛc* is prescribed after the root *tar*, the *guṇa* substitution would be enjoined.
On the basis of the measure [of the vowel], due to internal proximity, a long [vowel] would result only in a long [vowel]; and thus forms such as *ṭh-tharitā* would not be established. Furthermore—

When the *vṛddhi* [substitution] is prescribed in the case of suffixes beginning with *ṇvul*, since there is no specific proximity (*antaratamya*) for the vowel *ṛ* with respect to any particular *vṛddhi*-named vowel, all vowels designated as *vṛddhi* would apply by way of alternation (*paryāyeṇa*). Consequently, in certain instances, forms such as *ṭhnāyakaḥ* and *stāvakaḥ* [would arise].

"Even if the form were undesirable"—having thus seen the faults in the first two positions, he resorts to the third position and says: "In its proper place, *aṇ* is applied," and so forth. By this other rule, that which is being prescribed—

He shows that at the very time of the prescription (*vidhāna*), this paribhāṣā operates by acting in conjunction with it, characterized by the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ*. And this is obtained through the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of "two places" (*sthāna*) here; for by the preceding mention of "place"...
By the first [word], the meaning "in place of" (*sthāne*) from the rule *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ* is obtained; by the second, however, the word *prasajyamānaḥ* is [obtained].
For thus, when the locative form *sthāne* is understood as being carried over (*anuvartamāna*) from the present context:
By virtue of that [contextual] power, the word ending in the nominative case is established; furthermore, this word *sthāna* denotes "occasion" (*prasaṅga*).
Consequently, when the *aṇ* is qualified by the "place" (or occasion) in the sense of "the place of the *aṇ*," then the meaning arises that "the *aṇ* is precisely that which is occasioned."
Regarding the phrase "prasajyamānaḥ": it means being connected by way of a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*). Regarding the word "eva" (only):
here, restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is understood as having the result of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), since all sentences possess restriction by virtue of that very result.

How, then, does it become a locus? Indeed, it does not become a locus at all; rather, due to its connection with that [locus], there is a designation of it as a locus, just as in the case of "the sticks."

"Let him enter," [is said] because of the connection with the staff; this is the designation of men. But is it not the case that "the most similar [substitute] takes the place" (*sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ*) is obtained? This is not a fault; for by virtue of the mark of the *svarita* accent, wherever a word occurs, it denotes by implication only that meaning which is capable of undergoing that specific grammatical operation.

It stands in proximity (*sannupatiṣṭhate*). Therefore, although in the preceding sūtra the word *sthāna* denotes the place [of articulation] such as the teeth (*tālu*), etc., nevertheless here, being in proximity, it stands in the sense of "occasion" (*prasaṅga*) alone. Thus, because this is not an independent rule enjoining [the substitution] of that which is characterized by the *apṛkta* suffix *ra*, therefore, in the first case...

The defect that exists in the [first] alternative does not occur here; therefore, it is not the case that *raparatva* (the substitution of *r*) is prescribed for the *aṇ* subsequently ordained by another rule. What then? While the *aṇ* is being produced by another rule, it acquires the assistance of that [substitution] and is realized as having *r* as its final element (*rapara*). Thus, in the second alternative—

Whatever fault [might be alleged], that too does not apply here. For, according to the rule prescribing *ra* as the substitute (*raparatva*), just as the vowel *ṛ* possesses the sound *r*, so too the substitute itself possesses the sound *r*. Consequently, by virtue of similarity (*antaratamya*), for the *ṛ*-sound which possesses the sound *r*, there arises a [substitute] of the same kind.
In this way, the substitution of *ra* followed by *śruti* (the sound *ś*) occurs, and other substitutions designated as *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are excluded.

If, however, it were merely a case of *prasajya* (an occurrence without exclusion), then because [the substitute] consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it would follow that it must replace the whole [of the original]. This is not a fault; for this—
He provides the illustration "ṭhtarati"; from this it is made known that [the substitution] is not a universal replacement (sarvādeśa).
[The examples are] "kartā" and "hartā," derived from the roots "ḍukuñ karaṇe" (DhP 1473) and "hṛñ haraṇe" respectively.

From these two [roots], by the rule *ṭhṇvultṛcau* (Pāṇini 3.1.133), the suffix *tṛc* is applied; by *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ* (7.3.84), *guṇa* substitution occurs; and by *aco rahābhyām* (8.4.46), doubling takes place. Thus: *kirati*.

[The forms] *girati* and [the others] are derived as follows: from the roots *kṛ* "to scatter" (DhP 1410) and *gṛ* "to swallow" (DhP 1411), the present tense suffix (*laṭ*) is applied; by the rule *śeṣāt kartari parasmaipadam* (Pāṇini 1.3.78), the third-person singular ending *tip* is added;
because these belong to the *tudādigaṇa*, the suffix *śa* is applied; and by the rule *ṛta id dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.100), the *ṛ* is changed to *i*. [The word] *dvaimāturaḥ*...

Regarding the term *traimāturaḥ*: it means "the offspring of two mothers" or "the offspring of three mothers. By the rule *māturut saṃkhyāsaṃbhadrapūrvāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.115), the suffix *aṇ* is applied, and the letter *u* is substituted for the final syllable. Then, by the rule *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.117), *vṛddhi* is substituted for the first vowel.
