Regarding "kheya": the suffix *kyap* is applied by the rule "ī ca khanaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.111), with the substitution of the vowel *i* for the final letter, and the *guṇa* substitution by "ādguṇaḥ" (6.1.87). Regarding "saudhātaki": the suffix *iñ* is applied by the rule "sudhāturakaṅ ca" (4.1.97).
When the substitution of *ak* for *akaṅ* is being performed through that [substitution], it does not become followed by *r* (rapara), because it is not an *aṇ*.
Now, why does that which is an *aṇ* here not become followed by *r*? Because it is not a substitute (*ādeśa*). For in this case, the entire aggregate is the substitute, not its constituent part.
This is not a fault; for that which occurs in place of two things indicated by the genitive case receives the designation of either one, just as in the case of Devadatta's [son].
"The son of Devadattā is the son."
52. *alo'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52).

The mention of *al* is a qualifier of the final [element], not of the substitute (*ādeśa*); for otherwise, he would have simply said *alantyasya*. Furthermore, in this context, the substitute is understood to consist of a single phoneme (*ekāl*). For any other [substitute] that consists of multiple phonemes (*anekāl*) or is marked with *ś*, it replaces the whole (*sarvasya*).

Thus, he will state that [the substitute] is a universal replacement (*sarvādeśa*). Regarding the rule "of that which is designated by the genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhīnirdiṣṭasya*), even though the word is used in a general sense, it should be understood as referring to that which is designated by a genitive of place (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), because of the governing rule "the genitive is connected with 'place'" (*ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*, 1.1.49); otherwise...

Even when measured by a single letter (*ṭit*), those [substitutions] prescribed by a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) indicating a relationship with a constituent part (*avayava*) should apply to the final [element]. This is stated in *ṭid goṇyāḥ* (P. 1.2.50). This genitive case is taken as referring to the final phoneme—meaning "the substitution of *i* for the final phoneme. Thus, we have *pañcagoṇiḥ*.

In the expression *pañcabhir goṇībhiḥ krītaḥ* ("bought for five bags"), there is a compound (*samāsa*) by the rule *taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca* (Pāṇini 2.1.51). Then, [the suffix] *ṭhak* is applied by the rules *tena krītam* (4.4.1) and *prāgvahateṣṭhak* (5.1.37).
There is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix] by the rule *adhyardhapūrvadvigor lug asaṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 5.1.28).
If a substitute occurs for that which is designated by a genitive case ending and is the final element,
then— due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "of an *id*-ending stem" (*idaḥ*) from the rule *ido'y puṃsi* (7.2.111)— [the substitution occurs] before a consonant (*hali*).

The elision (*lopa*) being prescribed [by Pāṇini 7.2.113] would apply to that which is the final element of this form *id*. And if that were so, the form *ābhyām* would not be established; this is not the case.
There is no fault; by the paribhāṣā "ṭhnānārthake'lo'ntyavidhiranabhyāsavikāreṣu" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 62), [the substitution] will not apply.
53. *ṅcci* (Pāṇini 6.3.25):

[The example is] "hotāpotārau" (the Hotṛ and the Potṛ). This is a dvandva compound of the words *hotṛ* and *potṛ*; the substitution of *ānaṅ* occurs when the suffix *āṬ* follows, according to the rule *ṛto*.

By the rule *ṅsi-rvanāmasthānayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.110), there is guṇa substitution, and by *raparatvam*, the substitute is followed by *r*. By the rule *aptṛntṛc* (Pāṇini 6.4.11), etc., there is lengthening [of the vowel]. Thus, "mātāpitarau" [is formed]; and by the rule *pitā mātrā* (Pāṇini 1.2.70), [the singular form is "mātāpitarau"].
This is an illustration in that case where there is no *ekaśeṣa*: if the substitute for *ṅ* (the *ṅit* affix) were to replace the final portion of the whole, then [in the case of] *tātaṅ*—

Since [the substitution] occurs for this [suffix], he says "tāt" and so forth. Therein, it is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa*, as in *cinutāt* and similar forms; for here there is the application of *guṇa* conditioned by the *sārvadhātuka* suffix.
It is for the purpose of prohibiting *vṛddhi*, as in *mṛṣṭāt*.
For here, by the rule "mṛjer vṛddhiḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.114), the substitution of *vṛddhi* would otherwise apply. Thus,

since the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* serves its purpose in this way, and since the addition of the marker *ṅ* to the suffix *tātaṅ* has its own scope of application, when that [marker] is present—

Because of its priority, by the rule "anekālśitsarvasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.55), the substitute *tātaṅ* becomes a replacement for the whole [stem]. The scope of the rule "ṅcci" is, for example, "hotāpotārau" and so forth; the scope of the rule beginning with "anekāl" is where...
By the rule *ṅt-ṭhisterbhūḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.52), we have forms such as *bhavitu*.

In cases such as *jīvatāt*, where both [substitutions] would apply, the substitution *tātaṅ* occurs because it is subsequent [in the order of the rules] and because it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*).

The substitution occurs for the entire word, as in "May you live" (*jīvatād bhavān*) and "Live, you! (*jīvatāt tvam*). The form *jīvatāt* is derived by the rule "In the sense of benediction, the suffixes *liṅ* and *loṭ* [are used]" (Pāṇini 3.3.173).
By the rule "loṭ, tip, ṭeret, tuhyostātaṅ" (Pāṇini 7.1.35), *tātaṅ* is substituted [for *hi*].

54. *ādeḥ parasya* | (1.1.54) This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule concerning the final letter (*alo'ntyasya*). Nowhere in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) is an operation prescribed by explicitly uttering the word "of the subsequent" (*parasya*). Therefore, with the intention that this [rule] would otherwise be without scope, he says "And where... and so forth.

Regarding the statement "where there is a mention in the fifth case": according to the rule *tasmād ity uttarasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.67), where there is a mention in the fifth case, an operation is prescribed for what follows. For example, in the word *āsīnaḥ*: from the root *ās* in the sense of "sitting" (Dhātupāṭha 1021), with the suffix *laṭ*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs because the root is marked with an indicatory vowel *anudātta*, and the suffix *śānac* is applied.
Because it begins with the letter *a*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix. Thus we have *dvīpam*, *antarīpam*, and *samīpam*.

Having analyzed the compounds as "in which waters (*āpaḥ*) have gone twice (*dvi-gatāḥ*), have gone within (*antaḥ-gatāḥ*), or have come together (*saṃ-gatāḥ*)," they form *bahuvrīhi*s. [The rule] *ṛkpūḥ...* [is applied].
By [the rule] beginning with (Pāṇini 5.4.74), the suffix *a* is applied as a compound-final (*samāsānta*) suffix.

55. *anekālśitsarvasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.55). Although *śit* possesses multiple phonemes (*anekāl*) due to its suffixal marker *ś*, the separate mention of *śit* is for the purpose of making known the rule: "The status of having multiple phonemes is not caused by a suffixal marker" (*nānubandhakṛtamanekāltvam*; Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 14). However, that [rule]...
The purpose [of this rule] is to ensure that there is no substitution for the whole [of the original element] in rules such as "diva ut" (Pāṇini 6.1.131).

56. *sthānivadādeśo'nalvidhau* (1.1.56). *Sthāna* means occasion; its nature has been explained previously. *Atideśa* (extended application) is of many kinds—[such as] based on cause (*nimitta*), etc.

The *deśa* (locus) consists of: the extension of designation (*vyapadeśātideśa*), the extension of the science (*śāstrātideśa*), the extension of form (*rūpātideśa*), and the extension of operation (*kāryātideśa*). Among these, first of all, the cause (*nimitta*) cannot be extended, for the properties of verbal roots (*dhātu*) and so forth [cannot be transferred].

The specific individuals (vyakti) belonging to classes such as verbal roots (*dhātu*), which serve as the grounds for the application of words (*śabdapravṛttinimitta*), are capable of bringing about a substitution (*ādeśa*) of another entity; just as in the expression "one should behave toward this Kṣatriya as one would toward a Brāhmaṇa," the ground for the application of the word "Brāhmaṇa" [is not the individual, but the class].

It is possible to apply [the designation] to a *kṣatriya*; likewise, because it is impossible [in this case], neither the extension of the indicative mark (*nimitta*) nor the extension of the designation (*vyapadeśa*) is resorted to here. This is because, in the relationship between a name and the named (*saṃjñā-saṃjñi-sambandha*), there is no difference [between them]. Regarding the relationship between the name and the named:

For otherwise, the employment of the particle *hi* would be purposeless, since that [result] is established even without it. Furthermore, because it is not the primary element, it is not appropriate here to resort to the extension of designation (*vyapadeśātideśa*). For this very reason, the extension of the technical rule (*śāstrātideśa*) is also precluded.

Furthermore, even those two [the *sthānins*] are non-primary with respect to the effect, because they have become subordinate members (*aṅga*) of it. It is also improper to resort to the transfer of the form (*rūpātideśa*) of the substituends, because it would be fruitless.
For if the form of the two substituends were transferred to the substitute, the substitute itself would be rendered redundant.

In the rule *dvirvacane 'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59), even though there is an extension of the form (*rūpātideśa*), the substitute is not rendered useless, because its purpose is to ensure the correct pronunciation after the reduplication has occurred. Therefore, since resorting to another type of extension would be improper, an extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*) is adopted.
"It functions similarly to the substituend (*sthānin*)," because it performs the same operation as that [substituend], according to Pāṇini 5.1.115: *tena tulyam*.
"In those cases which have the substituend as their basis" (*sthānyāśrayeṣu*):
this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those for which the substituend is the basis. "In those cases which do not have *ala* as their basis" (*analāśrayeṣu*): *ala* is the basis.

Having formed the *bahuvrīhi* compound *eṣām*, [the term] *analāśrayāṇi* is a *nañ*-compound meaning "not having *ala* as their basis. To clarify the very point just mentioned, he says: "*ṭhsthānyalāśrayāṇi*" and so forth. *Sthānī* = *ala*.

Those whose basis is such [an *al*] are described as "those" (*tathoktāni*). By the inclusion of the word "basis" (*āśraya*), the term *alvidhi* used in the Sūtra is a compound with elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopin*), meaning "a rule whose basis is an *al*" (*alāśrayo vidhir alvidhiḥ*).
He demonstrates this: furthermore, having formed a compound by virtue of its inclusion in the *mayūravyaṃsaka*-group and so forth, a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) is then formed.
"A non-al-vidhi" means [a rule] that is not dependent on *al*. But what, then, is a rule dependent on *al*? It is one that relies solely upon a phoneme (*varṇa*).
But that which depends on a collection is based on fire; expressing the meaning of the injunctive word by means of a verbal noun (*bhāvasādhana*) in the form of "is enjoined" (*vidhīyate*).
The statement "this is the rule" (vidhiḥ) shows that it serves as the means for accomplishing the grammatical operation (karmasādhana).
The question "What is the example? is asked. The answer is "The substitutes for verbal roots and so forth are the purpose" (prayojanam).
It is called a "purpose" (prayojana) because one is employed by means of it; and since one is employed by means of an example, [the examples] are the purpose. This is the implication.
The answer is in accordance with the question.
But surely, when an *ardhadhātuka* suffix follows, there must be [the application of] both the augment (*bhāvi*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*); in that case—

To the question, "What is the purpose of this instruction here?", he says: "In the domain of an *ardhadhātuka* affix," and so forth, beginning with "having taken as one's nature" (*prakṛtya*). The compound is formed by the rule "kugatiprādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.2.18).

In the rule "In a compound not preceded by *nañ*, *lyap* replaces *ktvā*" (Pāṇini 7.1.37), we have the example "dadhikam. This is derived from "prepared with curds" (*dadhnā saṃskṛtam*), according to the rule "The suffix *ṭhak* after *dadhi*" (Pāṇini 4.2.18). Then there is the example "adyatanam."
By the rule *sāyaṃciram* (Pāṇini 4.3.23), the suffix *ṭaL* is applied, along with the augment *tuṭ*, and the substitution of *an* for the *y* and *u*.
[The forms] *akurutām* and *akurutaṃ* are derived from the root *kṛ* in the *laṅ* tense, by the rule *tasthasthamipām* (Pāṇini 3.4.101).

By these and other rules, *tasi* becomes *tām*, and *thas* becomes *tam*; because the root belongs to the *tanādi* class, the suffix *u* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.79 (*tanādikṛñbhya uḥ*), the guṇa substitution of the root vowel occurs, and by 6.4.110 (*ata ut sārvadhātuke*), the final *a* is replaced by *u*.
"The village is our own, the countryside is our own. Here, *vas* and *nas* are the substitutes for the genitive plural of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*,
according to the rule "the genitive plural [of] *yuṣmad* and *asmad* [takes] *vas* and *nas*" (Pāṇini 7.1.21).

"What is the purpose of the instrumental suffix (*ṭhvatkaraṇam*)?"—the intention is that even without it, its meaning is understood, as in [rules] such as *ṭhasaṃyogālliṭ kit* (Pāṇini 1.2.5). [The commentary continues with] "of the place" (*sthāna*) and so forth; for in this [work], it is generally...

In the Pāṇinian system, rules such as "vṛddhir ādaic" (1.1.1) are seen to serve solely the purpose of establishing the relationship between a technical name (*saṃjñā*) and that which is named (*saṃjñin*). Therefore, in the absence of the suffix -vat, it would be understood that a technical name is being prescribed for the substitute (*ādeśa*) itself. Thus, let it not be understood in this way:

The particle *vat* is used for this very purpose. But why, one might ask, is the designation (*saṃjñā*) not desired for both the original element (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*)? To this he says: "Even that which depends on its own form," and so forth. For a designation exists for the purpose of making known the designated object (*saṃjñin*); it does not itself undergo an operation, but rather the designated object is made known by it. In this regard, if...

The designation [of "substitution"] would apply to the substituendum (*sthānin*), for the operation would belong only to the substitute (*ādeśa*) as the designated entity, and not to the substituendum which has become the designation. Consequently, [the rule] "after *ṭhā*, *āṅ*,
and *yama-han*" (Pāṇini 1.3.28) [would be problematic].
The *ātmanepada* suffix shall apply after the root *vadhi*, but not after *han*. However, when the term "vat" (as in *vadrītyā*) is employed, this constitutes an extension (*atideśa*);

and by means of such an extension, the grammatical operation associated with one element is effected in another, but the operation inherent to that [original] element itself is not thereby sublated. Thus...

For when there is an extension (atideśa) such as, "One should behave toward this Kṣatriya as one does toward a Brāhmaṇa," the function associated with that non-Brāhmaṇa [i.e., the Brāhmaṇa] is projected onto the Kṣatriya; however, that which belongs to the Brāhmaṇa by virtue of its own substratum— such as eating first and so forth— is not excluded.

The word "also" (*api*) in the phrase *svāśrayam api* implies that, by virtue of the extended application (*atideśa*), [the property] may also reside in another even when [the operation] occurs in place of [the original]. Regarding the form *āhata*: it is the *luṅ* aorist of the root *han*;
*kitva* applies by the rule *hanaḥ sic* (Pāṇini 1.2.14); and [the elision of the *s*] follows from the rule *anudātopadeśa...* (Pāṇini 6.4.37).

By these and other rules, there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*). By the rule *ṭhhsvādaṅgāt* (Pāṇini 8.2.27), there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *sic*. Regarding the form *āvadhiṣṭa*: the substitute *vadh* is applied by the rule *ṭhātmanepadeṣvanyatarasyām* (3.1.54); then follows the augment *iṭ*, the elision of the final *a* by *ṭhato lopaḥ* (6.4.48), and finally the substitution of *ṣ* and *ṭh*.

"What is the purpose of including the mention of *sthā* (the substitute)? [The answer is: This word *sthānī* is a relative term (*sambandhiśabda*). In that regard, just as when it is said, "He is stout like his father" (*pitṛvat sthūlaḥ*), the word "son" is understood even without the explicit mention of "son" because it is a relative term; so it is here.

The intention is as follows: when it is stated "it is like the original" (*sthānivat*), even without the explicit mention of "substitute" (*ādeśa*), it is understood that the substitute itself is treated like the original because it is a relative term. Regarding the phrase "of the inferential," etc., [the rule] is *asterbhūḥ* ("*as-* becomes *bhū-*").
In examples such as this, both the *sthānin* (the original element) and the *ādeśa* (the substitute) are directly expressed by the word;
for instance, in *pacatu*, both the *sthānin* and the inferential *ādeśa* are present. To illustrate: in the rule *ṭheruḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.86), it is not the case that...

The substitute is not merely the phoneme *i*, but rather the word *ti*; nor is the replacement merely the phoneme *u*, but rather the word *tu*. However, for the sake of brevity, only the phonemes *i* and *u*, which are parts of those words, are uttered.

Thus, by means of a single part, the whole is prescribed as the substitute for the whole. In that regard, just as the whole possessing horns is inferred from the observation of a single part, namely the horn, so too [the whole] is inferred from a single part, such as the vowel *i* or the vowel *u*, as well as the word *ti* or the word *tu*. And in this grammatical treatise, of that which...
Furthermore, the connection with an action is perceived directly from the word itself in one case,
while in the other it is inferred from some factor such as the meaning or the context; of these two, the former possesses primacy, whereas the latter is the reverse.

It is accepted as follows: for instance, in the rule *sahayukte 'pradhāne* (Pāṇini 2.3.19), the author of the *Vṛtti*, having cited examples such as *putreṇa sahāgataḥ* ("he has come with his son"), will state: "In this case, the father's connection with the action and so forth is expressed by the word, whereas that of the son is merely implied; thus, the son is subordinate (*apradhāna*)."

And when both the primary and the non-primary are present, it is logical that the understanding of the effect should pertain to the primary alone. Thus he said: "It is established because the understanding of the effect pertains to the primary."

For if "substitute" (*ādeśa*) were not mentioned here, then only that which is designated by the word "substitute" and thus possesses primacy because it is being enjoined would undergo the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), and not the subordinate, inferred [element]. Therefore, so that even that [inferred element] may have the status of being like the original—

The mention of "syāt" and so forth is for the purpose of including the entire form. By this, even in cases such as *pacatu*, the designation of a "pada" (word) is established by the rule *suptiṅantaṃ padam* (Pāṇini 1.4.14). From what, then, is this determined?
It is determined because, through the medium of its constituent part, the word *tu* [is understood] by the rule *er-uḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.86) as a whole.
It is not prescribed that the mere vowel *i* is to be replaced by the mere vowel *u* exactly as heard [in the rule];
for in the case of *pacatu*, the grammatical operation dependent on the designation of a "word" (*pada*) is observed, and that [designation] does not occur without the word-designation,
nor does that [word-designation] occur without [the presence of] a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*).

And that [suffixal status] does not occur without the designation of a collection (samudāya). For when that exists, the status of being a *tiṅ* is obtained through the application of the rule "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), which has been established by effort; it is not otherwise. This point has already been explained.

Now, when that which is inferential (anumānika) has been apprehended, how is the apprehension of the other obtained? It is thought thus: the single rule "sthānivat" should be formulated; by this rule, the substitute (ādeśa), being the primary element because it is a relative term, is obtained.

Therefore, this second rule is an injunction for the sake of establishing the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for that which is established through inference; and here, the term "like the original" (*sthānivat*) is understood to carry over. In this way, the inclusion of both those taught by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and those taught by inference (*anumāna*) becomes logically justified.

"In the rule regarding the prescription of a place" (*ṭhanalvidhau*)—this is supplementary to both rules. "The substitutes *āṬ*, *pathin*, *mathin*, and *ṛbhukṣan*," and so forth; namely, these [rules]: *diva āṬt* (7.1.84), *pathimathyṛbhukṣāmāt* (7.1.85), and *tyadādīnāmaḥ* (7.1.102).

In the application of the rule *halṅyābbhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), when the elision of *su* is to be performed, [the preceding elements] do not behave as if they were in their original state (*sthānivat*); for that [elision] proceeds by depending solely upon a consonant (*hal*), and thus does not depend upon a vowel (*al*).

57. *acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau* || (1.1.57) For what purpose is this stated? The status of being "as if in the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) has been declared [to apply] when there is no operation concerning an *al* (phoneme); this [sūtra] is for the sake of operations concerning an *al*. [For example,] in forms such as *paṭayati*, [the substitution of *i* for *a* by P. 6.4.123 is treated as if it were the original *a*] by P. 7.2.116: *ata upadhāyāḥ*.

The *vṛddhi* [substitution] depends on an *al*; because the penultimate (*upadhā*) vowel *a* has the property of being an *al*, some say that it does not apply by the preceding rule. Others, however, hold that it is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), meaning that only when a substitution conditioned by what follows (*paranimittaka*) is to be performed regarding what precedes, does it become as if it were the original (*sthānivat*).

The phrase "ṭhaca iti sthāninirdeśaḥ" means that by the word "ṭhacaḥ," he shows that it is in the genitive case denoting a *sthāna* (the element to be replaced). Regarding the statement "parasminniti saptamīti," the intention is that this is not a locative absolute (*parasaptamī*), because the sense of "following" is already expressed by the word "para" itself. "ṭh... [The rest of the passage follows].

Regarding the phrases "in a rule concerning what precedes" (*pūrvavidhau*) and "in the domain" (*viṣaye*): because of the context, it is understood that this refers to the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). The meaning is: [a substitute] becomes like the original in the domain of a rule concerning what precedes, but not in any other [domain]. A rule concerning what precedes is a *pūrvavidhi*. [The word] *vidhi*—

And this word [vidhi] is derived as an object (karmasādhana)—it is a "rule" (vidhi) because it is enjoined (vidhīyate). Or it is derived as an abstract state (bhāvasādhana)—a "rule" (vidhi) is an enjoining (vidhāna). For when it is derived as an object, the genitive case in the word "pūrvasya" (of the preceding) is used according to the rule for the remainder (śeṣalakṣaṇā). Of the preceding...

The meaning is that [the rule applies] when an action (*kārya*) is to be performed in relation to something that is established and has attained its own existence (*labdhasattāka*). However, in the case of a derivation based on the abstract state (*bhāvasādhana*), the word "of the preceding" (*pūrvasya*) [is used] because of its connection with a *kṛt* suffix.
The genitive case here denotes the object of the indication (*lakṣaṇā*). The meaning is: "when the formulation of what precedes—which is not yet established—is to be performed.
That is to say, "in the formulation of what precedes."
Furthermore, "priority" (*pūrvatva*) here depends either on the substitute (*ādeśa*), on the vowel (*ac*), or on the cause (*nimitta*),
because these very elements— the substitute and so forth— are present in this context. Among them, the substitute is proximate due to its being marked with the *svarita* accent.
But for the other two [cases], they are included right here in this very sūtra. Now, an objection is raised: there is a fault in all three of these cases;
how, then, can "priority" (pūrvatva) be maintained in relation to the substitute (ādeśa)?
For if priority were maintained in relation to the substitute, as in the case of *paṭayati* and so forth...

The status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is not established; for in that case, the elision (*lopa*) is indeed the substitute, and with it, priority and posteriority (*pūrvaparatā*) cannot exist, because its nature is that of non-existence.
It might be argued: "There is priority and posteriority in relation to that which is the locus (*sthānin*) of the elision."
To say that this will be figurative even with respect to the instruction by way of that [suffix] is a mere pretext;
for in cases such as *bahukhadavaka*, the primary [application] occurs in relation to the preceding [element].

Because the conceptualization [of the word's meaning] as metaphorical is untenable. There is no fault, however, because one adopts the view that "the individual (vyakti) is the word-meaning. For when the individual is the word-meaning, the grammatical rule (lakṣaṇa) applies to each specific instance. In that case, if [the suffix] is used in forms such as *paṭayati* and so forth, it is due to its being metaphorical (*aupacārikatvāt*).
The status of being "as that which stands in its place" (sthānivadbhāva) would not apply to the sequence of what precedes and follows;
since this rule [of sthānivadbhāva] would have no scope [in such cases], it would be rendered useless. Therefore, this first position is indeed faulty.
In the second case, however, this fault does not arise; for in that regard,
the meaning of the sūtra is that when an operation is to be performed on what precedes a vowel, that [substitute] is treated as the original (sthānivat),
and here [the rule] "na yvābhyāṃ padāntābhyām" (Pāṇini 7.3.3) applies.

Because of the statement [in the Vārttika], the substitution of *yaṇ* must indeed occur first due to the rule *ejāgamāt*. Consequently, since *ai* and *au* do not possess "priority" (*pūrvatva*) in relation to the vowel *a*, the status of being a *sthānin* does not apply; and in the absence of that, the substitutions of *āy* and *āv* for *ai* and *au* would also not be obtained. However, in this case, the word "of *ac*" (*acaḥ*)— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical flow of the grammatical argument.]

The genitive ending was intended for the purpose of specifying the location (*deśaviśeṣaṇa*), and not the ablative ending. At that time, however, [the word] *acaḥ* becomes an ablative ending. In that case, this is the fault: here, in the word *tanvanti*, the augment *iṭ* is applied due to the substitution of *yaṇ*.

[The augment] would not be obtained, for here no operation is prescribed for the preceding [element] which remains fixed; because, due to the status of the *yaṇ* substitute as being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), the augment *iṭ* would not occur. However, in the third alternative, the *yaṇ* substitute itself is what precedes the cause; when the augment *iṭ* is applied to that which remains fixed...

Since the status of being like the original (sthānivadbhāva) is obtained when something is to be prescribed, there is no occurrence of the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the augment iṭ in the case of *tanvanti*; however, the defect that exists in the first position would also apply here [in the second],
as in *vaiyākaraṇaḥ* and *sauvaśvam*.

In this case as well, "the *y* and *v* come before the cause. Now, it might be objected that the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is prescribed when an operation is to be enjoined for what precedes the cause;
however, no operation whatsoever is here enjoined for the *y* and *v* that precede the cause, for there are no substitutions of *āy* and *āv*.

Is it the operation of *y* and *v*, or rather that of *ai* and *au*? This is not so; for whatever operation applies to *ai* and *au* necessarily applies to *y* and *v* as well, because the latter are parts (*bhakta*) of the former and constitute their constituent elements (*avayava*).

To this it is replied: the fault that was stated regarding the two initial and final positions does not indeed apply here; for *ai* and *au* are "external" (*bahiraṅga*), because they depend upon a *taddhita* suffix and depend upon a nominal stem (*aṅga*), whereas *āy* and *āv* are "internal" (*antaraṅga*), because they are independent of the *taddhita* suffix and depend only upon phonemes (*varṇa*). [The rule] *asiddhaṃ*...

Because of the rule "that which is external is [treated as] non-existent with respect to that which is internal" (Vyākaraṇa-mahābhāṣya 1.1.57), the substitutions *āy* and *āv* for *ai* and *au* will not occur.
Furthermore, the defect mentioned regarding the other alternative does not arise at all;
for in that case, since everything desired is not established when the term is derived as a passive (*karman-sādhana*), it is also accepted as being derived as an action (*bhāva-sādhana*).

Therefore, in the case of *tanvanti*, when a rule is to be applied concerning a preceding vowel (*ac*) that is itself not yet fully established—such as the substitution of *iṭ*—the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (behaving like the original element) is established.

There is no fault even if the term is derived in the passive sense (*karmasādhana*); for in this instance, it is the *yaṇ* substitute itself that precedes the vowel, and it is with respect to its application [that the rule operates].

It must indeed be understood as that which is to be performed (*kartavya*). For an augment *iṭ* is not prescribed for some preceding fixed element [other than the substitute]; rather, it is prescribed for the substitution of *yaṇ* itself.
However, if that [augment] were treated as an abstract action (*bhāva-sādhana*), then...
There is a fault; for [the augment] *iṭ* is prescribed precisely for that which precedes the substitution of *yaṇ*, as it is not yet fully established.
Therefore, even in that case, the word *vidhi* must be accepted as having the sense of an abstract action (*bhāvasādhana*).

[The example] "paṭayati": the suffix *ṇic* is applied by the rule "he does that" (*tat karoti*) or "he describes that" (*tad ācaṣṭe*), and [the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs] because of the rule "in *ṇi*, like *iṣṭhan*" (*ṇāviṣṭhavad*).

There is elision of the *ṭi* by the rule "prātipadikasya" (Vārttika 813). Now, one might object that because of the intervention [of the suffix], the status of being "preceding" (*pūrvatva*) is not possible here;
this is not a fault, for the word "preceding" (*pūrva*) applies even when there is an intervention, as in the expression "from Mathurā."

"Previously, 'pāṭaliputraṃ' [was used]. But surely, since the suffix *ṇic* arises after a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*), there—relying on the internal case-ending (*antarvatinyā vibhaktyā*)—the designation "word" (*pada*) applies; and once the substitution of *jaś* has occurred, it ought to be *paḍayati*. As for the elision of the *ṭi*...

If it is argued that *jaś*-substitution does not occur due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), we say no; for there is a prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* in the rule prescribing *jaś*-substitution. Thus, this fault does not apply. For in the rule "he describes that" (*tadācaṣṭe*), the word *tat* (that) is not construed with the second case (*dvitīyā-samartha*); how then? It is construed with the object (*karman*). From what [source] is this known?
Because it is intended to specify the meaning. This is what is meant: the suffix *ṇic* is applied after a word designated as an object (*karman*) in the sense of "he expresses that."

Therefore, because the suffix *ṇic* arises from a non-substantive compound (*asubandha*), the designation *pada* does not apply, and consequently the substitution of *jaś* (the voiced unaspirated stops) does not take effect. [The form] "avadhīt" is derived from the root *han* with the *luṅ* suffix; by the rule "hano vadha luṅ" (Pāṇini 2.4.42), the word *vadha* is substituted, which ends in the vowel *a*.

The substitution [of *as* for *asti*] is prescribed by "the elision of *at*" (6.4.48). The augment *iṭ* is applied by "the *iṭ* of the *ārdhadhātuka*" (7.2.35) and "after *as* and *sic*, before an *apṛkta* suffix" (7.3.96). The elision of *sic* occurs by "an *iṭ* is elided before an *iṭ*" (8.2.28). [The term] "characterized by a final consonant" refers to "the [strengthening of the vowel] of *vad*, *vraj*, etc. (7.2.3).

From such a sūtra as this, because the term *hal* is understood by way of anuvṛtti, the vṛddhi [substitution] prescribed by "ato halāder laghoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.7) is characterized by having a consonant at its end. Thus, we have *bahukhaṭvakaḥ*. Now, one might object: "With respect to a rule concerning accent (*svaravidhi*), [the word-final position does not apply]..."

[The opponent argues: "Since he will state the prohibition [in Pāṇini 1.1.56], 'it becomes like the original (sthānivat),' there is no possibility at all for the application of *sthānivadbhāva*; therefore, this example is incorrect.
[The author replies: This is not so; for that [prohibition] applies only to specific cases.

The prohibition states: "In the case of vowel (*svara*), long (*dīrgha*), and *y*-elision (*yalopa*), a substitute for an elided element (*lopājādeśa*) does not behave as if it were the original (*na sthānivat*). And since this is a substitute for an elided element, it is not a vowel;

therefore, the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the vowel *a* following the letter *kha* does not occur. [This is because] by the rule "in *kap*, the preceding [vowel is acute]" (Pāṇini 6.2.173), the subsequent—
The word-final udātta accent remains exactly as it is.
In the case of *praśnaḥ*, the suffix *naṅ* is applied by the rule *yajayācayatavicchapraccha-* (Pāṇini 3.3.90),
and [the substitution] does not occur when there is *tuk*.
The phrase "it becomes like the original" (sthānivadbhavati) means that when the augment *tuk* is to be applied, it does not become like the original.

For if it were so, then once the substitution of *ś* for the mere letter *ch* had been made, the *tuk* prescribed by virtue of that *sthānivadbhāva* would be heard; however, some maintain that this is incorrect.

For here, because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), the *tuk* augment itself must occur first by the rule "ṭhche ca" (Pāṇini 6.1.73). Nor does the principle "an operation concerning a vowel is stronger than one concerning a suffix" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 39) apply here, because they have different bases (*nānāśrayatva*). Where...
When, depending on a single cause, one simultaneously obtains both a vowel-substitute (*vārṇa*) and an augument (*āṅga*), then this [rule] applies:
namely, *ṭhiyāya*.
Here, depending on the vowel *ā*, there is the *yaṇ*-substitution for the preceding *ī* by the rule *ṭhiko yaṇ aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77).

[The form] *praśnī* is obtained, and by [the rule] *ṭhabhyāsasyāsavarṇe* (Pāṇini 6.4.78), the substitution *iyaṅ* also applies. In that case, because the maxim *vārṇādāṅgaṃ balīyaḥ* (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 39) takes effect, only *iyaṅ* occurs. However, in the case of *praśna*, [it is different].

The substitute *ś* takes as its locus the nasal [sound], whereas the augment *tuk* takes the letter *ch* as its locus; therefore, because they have different loci, the rule does not apply. Consequently, the augment *tuk* must necessarily occur here.
Furthermore, this must certainly be understood in this way; otherwise, [the rule] *cch-avoḥ śūḍ-anunāsike ca* would be contradicted.
In this regard, what the author of the Vṛtti will say— namely,

that "since the substitution [of *t*] by *che ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.73) is internal (*antaraṅga*), once the augment *tuk* has been applied, this substitute [of *ī*] belongs to the form with the *tuk*"— that would be contradicted.
Others, however, explain that in the rule "ccchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.19),
the letter *cccha* was taught by a certain teacher to his students as being accompanied by the *tuk* augment.

They have been explained by some as "of the pure [syllable] devoid of the *tuka*"; and both of these are authoritative. In that case, the two are qualified either by the *aṅga* or by the letters *cha* and *va*.

Regarding the term *vāṅgam*: in the first alternative (*pakṣa*), the meaning of the sentence is that the *ś* substitute applies to that which is the *aṅga* (stem) before the suffix *cha*; this is because the stem is taken as the locus (*sthānin*) together with its *tuk* augment. Since the *tuk* is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), the rule "the designation of the final letter applies when the element has no other meaning" (*nānarthake alo'ntyavidhiḥ*, Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 62) precludes the application of the rule regarding the final letter of the complex.

The substitute occurs for the entire cluster itself. When, in the rule prescribing the letter *ś*, there is the mention of *cc* with the *t* augment (*satukka*), as in the word *praśna*, then the mention of *aj* is not a counter-example at all; for in that case, there is no possibility for the *tuk* augment to apply again. However, when...

When the stem (*aṅga*) is qualified by both the letters *cch* and *v*, then the stem ending in *cch* possesses the status of the element to be replaced (*sthānitva*). In this view, it should be understood that in the rule for the suffix *śa*, only the pure letter *cch* is intended. However, due to its being an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), [the substitution of *ś* occurs first].

Once *tuK* has been applied first, the rule regarding the final letter (*alo’ntyaparibhāṣā*) subsequently presents itself; consequently, only the letter *cch* is replaced by *ś*. Once that has been done, because the cause (*nimitta*) for *tuK* no longer exists, [the *tuK* is elided].

[The term] *nivṛtiḥ* [means] "the cessation [of an operation]. For example, in the case of *sthātā*, when the substitution of *ṣ* has ceased, there is the substitution of *ṣṭu*. In this view, *praśnaḥ* serves as a counter-example for the inclusion of the vowel *a* [in the rule]. If the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) were to apply here, there would be the recurrence of the augment *tuk*; because the cause [for its application] is present, just as in the case of *praty-aṣṭhāt*.

In this context, regarding the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭu*, the meaning of the rule "it does not become like the original (sthānivat) when *tuK* follows" is as follows: that very *tuK* which had been elided due to the absence of its cause— [that same *tuK* is not treated as sthānivat].
Regarding the statement "it does not become as if it were the original (sthānivat) with respect to what follows after [the operation]," this refers precisely to the reapplication (*pratyāvṛtti*).
As for the phrase "a rule concerning what precedes" (*pūrvavidhi*): one might object that if there were a reapplication of the *tuk* augment here, then [the rule] would apply to the *naṅ*.

The suffix *ṅt* would be purposeless. For that [suffix] is applied either for the sake of *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) in the case of the root *pracch*, or for the sake of prohibiting *guṇa* (vowel reduction) in the case of the root *vicch*.
In that regard, there should be no *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization) for *pracch*, because of the rule: "And in the case of a question concerning immediate time... (*praśne cāsannakāle*).

This is due to the irregular formation (*nipātana*) [of the word *prastutya*] according to Pāṇini 3.2.117. Furthermore, if there were a recurrence of the augment *tuk* even when the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) were present, then it would also be for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa*; however, the *guṇa* substitution does not occur precisely because the penultimate vowel is not heavy (*alaghūpadhatvāt*).

"It will not occur, and therefore this [rule] would be useless"? No, it is not useless; for its purpose is to indicate that "the teaching of grammatical rules is non-eternal" (Pāṇini 1.1.56). Regarding this indication of non-eternality:
Regarding this, he will state in the *Āgamaśāsana* under the rule *snukramoranātmanepadanimite* (Pāṇini 7.2.36):

"But in the case of the root *kram*, when it belongs to the domain of the ātmanepada in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), there is a prohibition [of the augment *iṭ*] in the presence of a *kṛt* suffix, provided that the ātmanepada has not actually occurred."

It should be stated that "it must be said" and "it need not be said. Furthermore, such grammatical indications as "ucchi uñche" (DhP 215), "viccha gatau" (DhP 1424), and "sanādyantā dhātavaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.32) become logically established.
Regarding the form *ākṛṣātām*: from the root *kṛṣ* in the sense of "tearing" (*vilekhane*) [DhP 990], with the prefix *ā*, the suffix *luṅ* is applied;
then *cli* is substituted, and by the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "the *sic* suffix is optionally used after *spṛś*, *mṛś*, *kṛṣ*, *tṛp*, and *dṛp*," [the *sic* suffix is introduced].

There is the substitution of *sic* for the root *kṣi* in the [perfect] *pakṣa*; then, by the rule "anudātasya ca dupadhasyānyatarasyām" (6.1.59), the augment *am* is added; there is the *yaṇ* substitution;
and by the rule "vadavrajaḥ" (7.2.3), etc., there is *vṛddhi*.

Regarding the term *vaiyāghrapadya*: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose feet are like those of a tiger. By the rule *pādasya lopo'hastyādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.138), there is elision of the final [syllable] of *pāda*. With the form *vyāghrapād* established, the suffix *yañ* is applied because it belongs to the *gargādi* group. [Then follows: *ṭh...*

The substitution of *pad* [for *pād*] occurs by the rule *pādaḥ pat* (Pāṇini 6.4.130). Regarding the form *adīdhye*: due to its belonging to the *ad*-class, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*.
Now, why does the elision not occur here even earlier, prior to the substitution of *et* for the final vowel of the suffix? It would have occurred, if...

But if it were stated as "in the subsequent [element]," then because the status of being like the original (sthānivadbhāva) would be absent, the substitution of *e* for *ṭi* would not apply once [the elision] had been performed;

thus, the elision would be non-permanent (*anitya*). However, the substitution of *e* for *ṭi* is permanent (*nitya*) because it applies whether [the elision] has been performed or not. Therefore, that [substitution] occurs first.
In the form *gauḥ*, because the sarvanāmasthāna [suffix] is marked with the *ṇ* indicator by the rule *goto ṇit* (Pāṇini 7.1.90),

there is *vṛddhi* [substitution] according to *aco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115). Regarding the phrase "when the elision of the vocative suffix (*sambuddhi*) is to be performed," [the rule applies] by *eṅ hrasvāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.69).
By the rule *sambuddheḥ* (6.1.69). Regarding the form *bābhravyasya*:
the suffix *yañ* is applied by the rule *madhubabhvorbāhmaṇakauśikayoḥ* (4.1.106), meaning "the descendant of Babhru"; then *orguṇaḥ* (6.4.146) applies, and [the rule] *vānto*... [is applied].
By the rule *yi pratyaye* (6.1.79), there is the substitution of *vānta*; then, with the initial *vṛddhi*, the form *bābhravya* is established.
Thereafter, by the rules *vṛddhāc chaḥ* (4.2.114) and *yasyeti ca* (6.4.148), the letter *a* is elided. [In this case,] the substitution of *ava* does not apply.

"It becomes like the original element" (*sthānivad bhavati*). But even if there were no *sthānivadbhāva*, [the objection might be raised that] by the rule "an operation conditioned by a specific configuration is not the cause for the destruction of that configuration" (*sannipātalakṣaṇo vidhir animittaṃ tad-vighātasya*), the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) should not occur here at all; for instance:

Since its own acquisition has been obtained through the substitution of *ya* for *ava*, it is not able to subvert that [substitution]; this is not so, for here the "conjunction" (*saṅghāta*) is characterized by the meeting [of sounds], and not the individual consonant (*hal*);
or even if that were the case, [the objection remains].

If [the rule] has the characteristic of being a *sannipāta* (a combination), there is no fault at all; for the technical designation (*paribhāṣā*) concerning *sannipāta* is non-eternal (*anitya*). Its non-eternality, however, will be made known by the rule "there is no elision of the *su*-affix when it concerns accent" (*na lopaḥ supsvara*, 8.2.2).
Regarding the term *ṭhnaidheyaḥ*: the root *ḍudhāñ* (DhP 1092) preceded by the prefix *ni-*; by *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.92), the suffix *ki* is applied, and by *āto lopaḥ*, the *ā* is elided.
With *nidhi* established, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied according to *dvayacaś chandasi mantrēṣv iṣṭakābhiḥ saṃskriyamāṇābhiḥ* (4.4.125) and *itaś cāniñaḥ* (4.1.122).
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that *pūrvavidhiḥ* means a rule [occurring] before another? [This concludes the explanation of the formation of the word.]
Since even a genitive compound (*pañcamī-samāsa*) is desired, when a rule is to be applied based on what precedes [the substitute], the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) must apply;
for he will state under the rule *ṭh-ikaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.50): "mathita is his merchandise" (*mathitaṃ paṇyam asya*).
In the case of *māthitika*,

once the elision of *y* has been performed by the rule *yasyeti ca* (6.4.148), the substitution of *k* for *ik* occurs by virtue of the status of being "as if present" (*sthānivadbhāva*), according to the rule *ṭh-s-uk-tāntāt kaḥ* (7.3.51).
[The objection is: "Since the rule characterized by the combination [of sounds] (*sannipātalakṣaṇa*) has no cause for its own destruction, it does not occur;

for the elision of the letter *a* possesses the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). It is said: 'A substitute also behaves like the original even with respect to a preceding rule. Thus, in this way...

Since, by this rule, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (substitute-like behavior) occurs even with respect to what precedes [the original operation], it follows that *sthānivadbhāva* must necessarily apply even in cases such as "he gauḥ" and so forth; therefore, these [objections] are untenable.

Regarding the counter-examples (*pratyudāharaṇa*) such as *naiṣa doṣaḥ* ("this is not a fault"), these are improper because [the substitution] must indeed occur by virtue of the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*). This is not a fault,
because [the rule applies] when there is an operation conditioned by what precedes (*pūrvasmād vidhau*).

That which is to be performed [by the rule] is subject to the status of being "as if it were the original" (sthānivadbhāva); because that [original] does not exist [in the current state], for this very reason—and because it is non-eternal—it is considered subordinate. Thus, in the *Vṛtti*, the word "from the preceding" (*pūrvasmāt*) was not cited for this rule in order to demonstrate that very subordination. Why?

Is its impermanence established again? It is established by the mention of *seṭ* in the rule *niṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.52). That very purpose is served so that the elision of *ṇi* may occur once *iṭ* has been applied. For if the elision of *ṇi* were to take place while that [augment] had not yet been applied, [the desired form would not result].
In that case, the augment *iṭ* would not occur in the form *kārita*, because of the prohibition [by Pāṇini 7.2.10] stating "after a root consisting of one syllable.
And so he will say there: "What is the purpose of [specifying] 'with *iṭ*'? [Consider] *saṃjñāpitaḥ paśuḥ*; [and the rule] *sanīvantardha* (7.2.49)."

Thus, *iṭ* is optionally prescribed for the root *jñā*. By the rule *hyasya vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 7.2.15), there is a prohibition of *iṭ* in the case of the *niṣṭhā* suffixes. Now, however, regarding the term *ekāc*:
In that case, [the rule] follows: "In that state of completion (niṣṭhā), the augment iṭ must occur here.

The mention of *seṭ* (having the augment *iṭ*) would be redundant; it is included for the purpose of determining the timing. Once the augment *iṭ* has been applied, the elision of the *ṇi* suffix occurs.

"So that it might be so": if that *ṭi*-elision were not performed, then in the case of *kāritam*, the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "after a one-syllable root which is unaccented in its original enunciation" (Pāṇini 7.2.10) would apply, and *iṭ* would consequently arise. Furthermore, if there were a rule [of elision] after what is preceded by *r*:

The status of being a substitute (sthānivadbhāva) would always apply to what ought to be done; since the status of being a substitute applies to the elision of the *ṇi* suffix, there would be no occasion at all for the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* due to the presence of more than one vowel (*anekāctva*), and thus [the author] would not have included the mention of "seṭ" (having the augment *iṭ*). Yet it has been included. Therefore, it is understood that [the rule applies] "from what precedes."

"The status of being like the original (sthānivadbhāva) does not apply when a rule is to be applied based on what precedes. Therefore, in cases such as *gaur* and so forth, when a grammatical operation is to be performed based on what precedes, the status of being like the original does not occur.

Now, what is the purpose of including the term "vidhi" (rule), since the desired result is already established by the word "pūrvasya" (of the preceding) alone? For it could be argued that the genitive case here will be used in relation to the operation (*kārya*), meaning "when a rule (*vidhi*) concerning the preceding is to be performed. This is not so; for if [the term *vidhi*] were absent...

For if, in the inclusion of the term "rule" (vidhi), it were said "of the preceding," then in a rule concerning what precedes, the status of being like the original (sthānivadbhāva) would not apply. On the other hand, if it were said "from the preceding," then in a rule concerning the preceding [element], it would not apply.

Since the mention of "vidhi" (prescription) allows for both a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) and an ablative compound (*pañcamīsamāsa*), the rule is established in all cases. Therefore, the mention of "vidhi" must be made for the sake of these two types of compounds.

58. [The term *sthānin*] is not [denoted by the word *tad*] in rules concerning: substitution (*ādeśa*), reduplication (*dvirvacana*), the elision of *repha* (*rephalopa*), accent (*svara*), homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa*), nasalization (*anusvāra*), lengthening (*dīrgha*), and the substitution of voiced unaspirated stops (*jaś*) and voiceless unaspirated stops (*car*). (Pāṇini 1.1.58)

Here too, the word *vidhi* (injunction) is both an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*) and an object noun (*karmasādhana*), and it is connected to each [term] individually. In that regard, as appropriate, in some cases it is understood as an abstract noun, and in others as an object noun. In that context:

In the rule prescribing reduplication (*dvirvacana*), it is used as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*), for in that case it is that very [reduplication] which is to be prescribed; indeed, there is no further operation to be performed upon that which is already established. In other instances, however, it is used as an object noun (*karmasādhana*), because in those cases another operation is prescribed for the word-final element (*padānta*) and so forth, which is already established.

[The question is: "In the forms *kau staḥ* and *yau staḥ*, [the substitution of] *as* for the root *as* takes place; there is the suffix *tas*; due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of *śap*;

and when the substitution of *āv* (for *as*) and the *yaṇ* substitution are to be applied, would [the elided *śap*] be as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhavati*)? But how could it be as if it were still present?
Is it not the case that since grammar is applied solely for the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of words, a word such as *staḥ* is refined independently of other words,
with respect to the rule concerning that which precedes an unindicated vowel?
The status of being a substitute (sthānivadbhāva) must apply; however, this principle is not possible in the case of word-formation (*pada-saṃskāra*) that is independent of other words,
such as in the forms *staḥ* and so forth.
When a word is being refined, because other words such as *kā* and so forth are not present [in the derivation], what then is this royal decree—
that the instruction of words (*śabdānuśāsana*) must be undertaken solely for the sake of refining words? Or rather...

If it is argued that this is the intention of the author of the treatise (*śāstrakāra*) himself, we say no; for the author of the treatise has prescribed the middle and other persons when *yuṣmad* and so forth are the subordinate words (*upapada*), even when they are coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the verb, as stated in Pāṇini 1.4.105: "When *yuṣmad* and so forth are the subordinate words, the middle person [is used] even when [the pronoun] is present."

It has been indicated that this treatise is also concerned with the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of sentences. In this regard, when the word *staḥ* and so forth undergoes refinement after the word *kau* and so forth has already been established, the vowel *au* and others occur before the final vowel (*avacaḥ pūrva*) since they have not yet been prescribed (*anādiṣṭa*).
There would be the status of being like the original (sthānivadbhāva). Therefore, a prohibition is stated.

Now, an objection is raised: even when the status of being like the original is prohibited in cases such as *dadhy atra*, since the external substitution (*yaṇ*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the internal reduplication (*dvirvacana*) should not occur.
Why, then, did he say "it occurs because of this statement"? Nor can it be argued that "because of the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva*,
the rule *asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam* (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 42) does not apply."
Where both [the original and the substitute] reside in a single word— as in *paṭvyau*, *paṭvyaḥ*,
*śucyau*, *śucyaḥ*, and so forth— there is no such fault, because the prohibition of the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) serves a purpose in those cases.

The doubling itself is indeed *bahiraṅga*, because it depends on more factors. For [the rule] "after a vowel" (*acaḥ*), [the rule] "for *y* and *v*" (*yaṇoḥ*), and [the rule] "not before a vowel" (*anaci*)—these three [rules] depend upon it. The substitution of *yaṇ*, however, depends only upon two: "of *iK*" (*ikaḥ*) and "before a vowel" (*aci*). Regarding the word "in *vare*": but surely, since this is a compound, there ought to be elision (*luk*) of the locative case ending? That...

How is there the designation "vare"? Precisely because of this irregular formation (*nipātana*), there is no fault in the absence of *luk* elision; others, however, maintain that there is an elided *ī* vowel (*īkāra-praśleṣa*) here.

They describe it thus and establish the connection as follows: "That which is a substitute for *ajādi* (vowels) is not *sthānivadbhūta* with respect to a rule (*vidhi*) concerning *vṛddhi*, nor is it *sthānivadbhūta* with respect to a rule concerning *ī*. By this, [the form] *āmalakyāḥ phalam*...

The suffix *mayaṭ* is applied [to form *vikāra*] by the rule "the suffix *mayaṭ* is always used after words denoting 'old age' (*vṛddha*) and *śara*, etc. (Pāṇini 4.3.144); its elision is effected by the rule "there is elision (*luk*) of *mayaṭ* when it denotes the fruit" (4.3.163). Therefore...
Regarding the rule *ṭhūlope pūrvasya dīrgho 'ṇaḥ* (6.3.111), when the suffix *ṅīṣ*— which is characterized by its inclusion in the *gaurādi* group— is elided by the rule *ṭhul-taddhitaluki* (1.2.49),

the elision [of the penultimate vowel] would apply by virtue of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* according to the rule *yasyeti ca* (6.4.148). This occurs because [the elided suffix] was followed by the vowel *ī*.

The rule does not apply to that [substitute] because of the prohibition of the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*). Now, it might be argued: "It is stated that a substitute for a vowel (*ajādeśa*) which has a subsequent cause becomes 'as if the original' in a preceding operation;
however, since there is no sequence (*paurvāparya*) with respect to *luk*, for this very reason the status of being 'as if the original' does not occur."
[If you argue that] it will [occur], then the elision of the vowel *ī* (in *praśliṣya*) is useless;
for even by means of elision, there would be no sequence of prior and posterior, and thus the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) would not apply even in cases such as *paṭayati*.
It may be so. Now, if a sequence based on the substituend (*sthānin*) is possible there, it would be the same here as well.

However, those who do not accept the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *ī* [in the rule *āyaneyīnīyiyaḥ*] maintain that the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of deriving forms such as *āmalakyāḥ phalam*, *vikāraḥ*, and *āmalakam*.
They form [the word] *yāyāvara*. [The suffix] *yaṅ* is applied by the rule "dhātorekācaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.22), etc., because it goes (*yāti*) excessively (*atyartham*).
There is reduplication; the short vowel of the reduplicated syllable is applied; then, by the rule *dīrgho 'kitaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.83), a long vowel is substituted;

thereafter, the suffix *varac* is added; when the elision of the *at* suffix (*ato lopaḥ*) has been performed, the *yakāra* is elided by the rule *lopo vyor vali* (Pāṇini 6.1.66). This elision of the *at* suffix is caused by what follows, namely, when an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix follows.

Because of the rule [of deletion]. Having raised the objection: "If the deletion (*lopa*) is caused by what follows, then for what purpose is the mention of *ṭhaC* in the rule *ṭhaco yat* (Pāṇini 3.1.97), since he will later state that *ṇyat* follows a stem ending in a consonant (*hal*)," [the author] says: *ṭha...* [and so on].
This is so that the rule may apply even to those [stems] which were previously vowel-ending (*ajantabhūtapūrva*).

Otherwise, it would contradict what will be stated later regarding *ditsyam* and *dhitsyam*; for when the *lopa* of *at* has occurred due to a subsequent cause, a grammatical operation (*vidhi*) based on a stem that was previously vowel-ending cannot possibly occur, since the operation would have already taken effect.
Because there is no absence of elision (*lopābhāva*), while the absence [of the suffix] is due to the absence of the subsequent cause (*paranimitta*).

There is no contradiction because the two positions differ. For in that context, the term *ārdhadhātuka* is understood to carry over. Furthermore, there are two positions: that this [term] is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*) regarding "in an *ārdhadhātuka*," and that it is a locative of sequence (*parasaptamī*).

When there is an intention to express the general category of *ārdhadhātuka*, a sequence of priority (*paurvāparya*) is not possible in a general sense; therefore, it is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*). However, when there is an intention to express a specific individual instance of *ārdhadhātuka*, a sequence of priority is possible for that individual instance; therefore, it is a locative of posteriority (*parasaptamī*). When...
However, when the priority and posteriority of the general category (*sāmānya*) are intended by means of its individual instances (*vyakti*),
even then the locative case of the "other" (*parasaptamī*) alone applies.
In that regard, according to the first view, since the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix is the object [of the operation], the elision of the augment *at* occurs prior to its very arising.

[This occurs] when that [suffix] has arisen in other instances; however, regarding the rule *ṭhaco yat* (Pāṇini 4.3.158), the purpose of the inclusion of the term *aj* will be explained later by relying on the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). As for the elision of *at* (*ato lopaḥ*) in this context...

It was stated that [the term] *paranimittaka* refers to the other alternative (*pakṣa*). Therefore, there is no contradiction because the objects (*viṣaya*) differ. However, in the alternative where [the word] *para* is in the locative case, the mention of *aj* there should be understood as being solely for the sake of clarity.

But how is it known that the *parasaptamī* (locative of reference) interpretation is also intended there? Because of the inclusion of the phrase "and [roots] beginning with a consonant and marked with an anudātta" (*anudātetaśca halādeḥ*, Pāṇini 3.2.149). For that [inclusion] is made for this purpose: lest [the rule apply] only to those ending in a consonant (*halanta*).

Regarding the form *vijñāyī*: if it were understood in this way, then in the forms *jugupsanaḥ* and *mīmāṃsanaḥ*, the suffix *yuc* would not occur, because they would end in a vowel (*ajantatvāt*). Furthermore, if this [locative case] were intended as a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*) in the sense of "when an ārdhadhātuka follows," [the following objection applies].

Otherwise, the mention of "the beginning" (*tad-ādi*) in the rule would be meaningless; for once the elision of the vowel *a* has occurred in the domain of *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes, both *jugupsati* and *mīmāṃsati* would also be considered *halanta* (ending in a consonant).
Therefore, by virtue of the mention of "the beginning," it is understood that the interpretation based on the locative case of the subsequent element (*parasaptamī*) is also intended there.
In the view that this is a locative of reference (*viṣayasaptamī*), however, the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*) therein should be understood as being for the sake of clarity alone. [Examples:
*kaṇḍūtiḥ*—[derived] from *kaṇḍvādibhyo yak* (Pāṇini 3.1.27) and *striyāṃ ktin* (3.3.94). [Examples:
*cikīrṣakaḥ*, *jihīrṣakaḥ*—[derived] from the words *cikīrṣa* and *jihīrṣa*.

The suffix *ṇvul* [is applied] by the rule "after the roots *śiṣ* and *piṣ*. [The roots are: *śiṣlṛ* "to distinguish" (DhP 1452) and *piṣlṛ* "to crush" (DhP 1453). [The process involves] doubling, substitution of *dh* for *th*, substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭu*, and substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaś*). Then, by the rule "the substitute *hi* for *si* is not marked with *p*" (3.4.87), *hi* is substituted for *si*.

When [the suffix] *hi* is applied, there is the substitution of *dhi* by the rule "ṭhhujhalbhyo herdhiḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.101). Then, by the rule "ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ" (8.4.41), there is the substitution of *ṣṭu*, and by the rule "jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi" (8.4.53), there is the substitution of *jaś*. Now, in this case...

There is no possibility at all for the application of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original element); for it is stated that the *sthānivadbhāva* applies in a rule concerning that which precedes an *ac* (vowel) which has not been subject to grammatical operation (*anādiṣṭāt*), and the augment *ām* does not precede such an *ac*.

Why, then, is there a prohibition? This is not a fault; for the original element (*sthānin*) *na*, even though it is not subject to grammatical operation, is indeed in relation to [the preceding *ac*].

Since the status of being "prior" exists [in the substitute], the *anusvāra* which is its substitute is also understood— by virtue of the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaving like the original)— to be prior to the vowel that has not yet been prescribed as a substitute.

"ṭhśiṣanti," etc. But for what purpose is this further example introduced, since it would have been more appropriate to cite "śiṇḍhaī" and so forth, which was mentioned immediately before? He thinks as follows: if that very same [example] were cited, then in a case where there is *parasavarṇa*—
In that case, there ought to be an *anusvāra*, for it is precisely therein that it is prescribed; and consequently,
because of its necessary connection, when the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is prohibited in the rule for *parasavarṇa*, it is likewise prohibited in the rule for *anusvāra*.

The prohibition of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) has already been established; therefore, someone might have the misconception that the mention of *anusvāra* need not be made separately.
Consequently, where...
The *parasavarṇa* substitution is not possible; therefore, that very example is appropriate.
Regarding "pratidivnā": this form is derived from the root *div* with the suffix *kanin* according to [Uṇādi Sūtra] 6.51, etc. Regarding "hali ca": [this refers to] Pāṇini 8.2.78, *upadhāyāñca*.
This has been written now by contemporary scribes out of negligence;

for indeed, regarding the rule *ṭhupadhāyāñca* (8.2.78), he will state: "But in the case of *pratidīvnaḥ*, there is lengthening by [the rule] *ṭhhali ca* (8.2.77). Now, even though the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) has been prohibited...

By the rule *ṭhna bhakurchua-rām* (Pāṇini 8.2.79), there ought to be a prohibition of lengthening here; why then does he say, "It occurs by virtue of this specific statement"? Nor can it be argued that the prohibition does not apply here due to the force of the prohibition against the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*.
It cannot be so imagined; for the prohibition of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) is intended for cases such as *pipaṭhīḥ*.
For here, when the suffix *kvip* is applied to *pipaṭhiṣati*, after the elision of the final *a* and the application of *rutva* (the substitution of *r*), this *rutva* [is again subject to the rule].

Because of the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham*, the substitution of *ṣ* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*); therefore, if the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) were not prohibited, then [the substitute] would be as if it were the original (*sthānivat*) for the elision of the vowel *a*.

Because of the governing rule *bhāvāt ṛt-hvor upadhāyā dīrgha ikaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.76), lengthening is prohibited for a *bha*-stem ending in *r* or *v*. And this [stem] is not a *bha*-named stem ending in *r* or *v*, but rather...
Regarding "not ending in a nasal" (*nākarāntam*):

in the word *sagdhiḥ*, it is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) meaning "common eating" (*samānā gdhiri*). The substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* occurs by the rule *samānasya cchandasyamūrdhaprabhṛtyudarkeṣu* (Pāṇini 6.3.84). Regarding *babdhām*: [from the root] *bhas*.

[The root] *ghas* [is used] in the senses of "threatening" and "shining" (*dhā.pā.* 1100). According to the rule *abhyāse car ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.54), the *jaś*-substitution of the *bha*-sound in the reduplication results in the letter *ba*.
Thus we have the forms *cakṣatuḥ* and *jakṣuḥ*. According to the rule *liṭaḷnyatarasyām* (2.4.40), there is the substitution of *ghasl* [for *ad*]. [End of excerpt]

By the rule *kuhośca* (Pāṇini 7.4.62), the *cutva* (substitution of a palatal) of the *gh* in the reduplication becomes *jh*; as before, its *jaśtva* (substitution of a voiced unaspirated stop) becomes *j*. Regarding the statement "in the plural there is the substitute *ghasl*"—this is by the rule *luṅsanorghaslu* (Pāṇini 2.4.37). [The example] is *bahukhaṭvakaḥ*; here...
Due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), by the rule "before a short vowel at the end, [the accent falls] on the syllable preceding the final one" (6.2.174),

the *kh* sound does not receive the acute accent (*udātta*). Rather, by the rule "in the case of *kap*, [the accent falls] on the preceding [syllable]" (6.2.173), it is the vowel *a* of the word *tva* that receives it.

In the forms *ṭhkiryoḥ* and *giryoḥ*, the lengthening of the vowel *ik*—which would otherwise occur by Pāṇini 8.2.76 (*ṛt-ṣṭhvor upadhāyā dīrgha ikah*) and 8.2.77 (*hali ca*)—does not take place. This is stated with reference to the theory of derivation (*vyutpatti-pakṣa*), according to which the words *kiri-* and *giri-* are derived by the rule *kṛ-gror ic ca*. However, in the theory of non-derivation (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*), [the forms are established without such derivation].
Even if the status of being *sthānivadbhāva* were not present, the lengthening would simply not occur due to the absence of *dhātutva* (the status of being a verbal root).

For, relying on the view that words are non-etymological (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*), he will state under [Pāṇini 8.2.78] *upadhāyāṃ ca*: "The *uṇādi*-derived forms are non-etymological nominal stems (*prātipadika*)," as in the case of *kiryaḥ*.

"In cases such as *giryoh* and so forth, the long vowel does not occur. [In the case of] *vāyvoḥ*, the elision of *y* by [the rule] *lopo vyor vali* (Pāṇini 6.1.66) does not take place. 59. *dvarvacane 'ci* (1.1.59).
Previously, the extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*) was established; now, however, this [sūtra] is commenced for the purpose of the extension of form (*rūpātideśa*).
Alternatively, according to the view that [the doubling occurs] "prior to the cause" (*nimittāt pūrvam*), the rule for doubling (*dvirvacana*) is [established] by the immediately preceding sūtra.

It should be understood that this [sūtra] is commenced because a prohibition has been reached [by the previous rule]. In the rule *dvirvacane 'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59), both locative cases are in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Therein, *ac* is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and *dvirvacana* is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). And the purpose of this relationship between qualifier and qualificand is illustrated by the example *dudyūṣati*.

A counter-example will be shown. But how, then, is *aj* (a vowel) expressed by the term "reduplication" (*dvirvacana*)? Because it is the cause of reduplication. For this very reason, it is stated in the commentary (*vṛtti*): "in the case of an *ac* which is the cause of reduplication.
Indeed, [it occurs].
The designation [of the vowel] by that term occurs because it is caused by that; as in the example "Clarified butter is longevity.

And since this [term *ajādau*] is also a locative of the "other" type (*parasaptamī*), according to the rule "In a rule where an operation is prescribed, the mention of 'that' includes the beginning of that [element]" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 127), it means "in [a word] beginning with an *ac* vowel."
It should be understood as follows: because of the context, "in the subsequent" (*parasmin*) is understood to mean "in a subsequent [element] beginning with a vowel" (*ajādau*).

Alternatively, since reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is caused by a specific suffix, the mention of reduplication brings the suffix to mind; therefore, it is understood that [the rule applies] when a suffix beginning with a vowel follows. If...

In that case, since a substitute for [an element] beginning with a vowel (*ajādi*) would be treated as the original (*sthānivat*), the form *papau* would not be established; for the substitute here does not begin with a vowel, but rather consists of the vowel itself. However, there is no fault here, because the status of beginning with a vowel exists by virtue of the principle of "designation-like behavior" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). But then, this [other case] would not be established: [The text continues: ...here it is not established—

Regarding the statement "they two made" (*cakratuḥ*): is it not the case that the *yaṇ*-substitution is prescribed only when a vowel (*ac*) follows, and not when [the suffix] begins with a vowel (*aj-ādi*)?
This is not a fault; for the *yaṇ*-substitution which is prescribed here when a vowel follows also certainly occurs when [the suffix] begins with a vowel.
If, when a vowel is the cause of reduplication, the substitute is treated as the original (*sthānivat*), [then the rule applies].
Since it might be thought that [the substitution] could occur even after the doubling, at any stage whatsoever, he says:

"only when the doubling is to be performed. By the word *eva* ("only"), he shows that the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) does not exist at any time other than the time of the act of doubling. How so?
Furthermore, this is obtained because there is one mention of "doubling" (*dvirvacana*), and by that, the vowel *aj* is qualified. It is thought thus: even the second mention of "doubling"—
The intervening sūtra is carried over here;
or alternatively, by applying the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining one of two identical words) as "dvirvacanaṃ ca," the designation "dvirvacane" was made.
In this context, by the first mention of the term "dvirvacana," the meaning "when an *ac* vowel is the cause of reduplication" is obtained;

by the second, however, the meaning "only when reduplication itself is to be performed" is obtained. Here, when reduplication is to be performed, there is the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*).

It is understood that this [rule] is prescribed solely for the purpose of the operation of reduplication (*dvirvacana*). Since reduplication is prescribed for that which possesses a consonant (*sāc*), it does not apply to that which lacks a consonant (*anack*); therefore, its status as being for the purpose of the operation of reduplication is logical.
Regarding this [substitute], its purpose is for the operation of reduplication (*dvirvacana*).

As for one who, out of delusion, thinks: "If this [substitute] were for the purpose of the operation of reduplication, then in forms such as *cakratuḥ* and *cakruḥ*, once reduplication has been applied to this [root] which lacks a vowel (*anacka*), the desired form of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) would not be established"—[the author addresses] him.
He replies:
"And this is an extension of form (*rūpātideśa*). The word "and" (*ca*) is used for emphasis;
the meaning is that it is indeed an extension of form, not an extension of grammatical operation (*kāryātideśa*). But from what source is this certainty derived? Sa...
Is this [the rule] "an atideśa of form"? Because of the mention of *aj* (the vowel). For that mention has this purpose:

so that [the rule] does not apply in cases such as *jeghrīyate* and *dedhmīyate*. If this were an atideśa of the operation of reduplication rather than an atideśa of form, the mention of *aj* would be useless.

Let there be the status of being like the original (sthānivadbhāva) in this case; nevertheless, there is no difference whatsoever. For instance—even if the status of being like the original applies here, reduplication must still take place; and even if the status of being like the original does not apply, reduplication must likewise take place—because in both instances [the substitute] possesses a consonant (sāckatvāt).
And then, how is this a counter-example? How does this mention of *aj* become meaningful?
If this were a substitution of *ra*, it would be extended to the form *rarūpa*.
If the mention of *ac* (vowels) were not made when [the rule] is being recited, then even here, when there is an extension of form (*rūpātideśa*),
there would be reduplication of *dhra-* and *dhma-*, and thus an undesirable form of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) would result.
Therefore, because of the mention of *ac*, this is an extension of form.
Thus it is determined. If this is so, the suffix *vat*—which is based on difference (*bheda*)—would not apply;
for since the original element (*sthānin*) itself has merely been made to regain its own form, how could there be any difference?
There is no fault here, because the intended meaning is a difference in form by virtue of the elements being *ātideśika* (transferred), even though they are designated as such.

In order to clarify the meaning of what was stated— that "reduplication must indeed be performed"— he says, "occurring at a fixed time. By the words "when reduplication has been performed," and so forth,
he demonstrates that very state of having a fixed time.

Regarding "jaghnatuḥ": by [Pāṇini 7.3.55] *abhyāsācca*, there is the substitution of *k* for the letter *h*. Regarding "āṭiṭat": the suffix *ṇic* is added to the root *aṭ* in the sense of causation (*hetumat*); then the *luṅ* [aorist] suffix is applied, followed by *caṅ*; and by [Pāṇini 6.1.11] *caṅy*, [the *guṇa* of the first syllable is replaced by the *vṛddhi* substitute].
Since it begins with *a*, [the rule applies].

There is reduplication by [Pāṇini 6.1.2] *dvitīyasya*. The augment *āṭ* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.72] *āḍajādīnām*. [The forms] such as *ninaya* and so forth arise; when, by [Pāṇini 7.1.91] *ṇal utamo vā*, the status of being *ṇit* does not apply, then...

The suffix *guṇa* [is applied]; when there is the property of being marked with *Ṇ* (*ṇitva*), then there is *vṛddhi*. Thus: *jagle*, *magle*. From the roots *glai* "to lose joy" (DhP 904) and *mlai* "to bend the limbs" (DhP 904), the substitution of *ā* occurs by the rule *ādeśa upadeśe 'śiti* (6.1.45). This is in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*).

[The suffix] is *ātmanepada*; [the substitute] *eś* is applied by the rule *liṭas tajhayoreśirec* (Pāṇini 3.4.81). [Objection: "Why does the *ā* not become audible? [Response: When the mention of *dvirvacana* (doubling) is not made for the purpose of delimiting the time [of application], then even at a subsequent stage, the form of the original element (*sthānin*) would still persist.

Consequently, there would be the mere hearing of the vowel *ā*. However, the elision of *ā* (*āto lopaḥ*) finds its scope in forms such as *godah*. And when the vowel *ā* is heard, there would be a *vṛddhi* [substitution] with the following sound, as in *dudyauṣati* from the root *div* with the suffix *san*, according to Pāṇini 7.2.49: *sanīvantardha*.
By these and other such rules, when the augment *iṭ* is not applied to the stem, then by *ṭhiko jhal* (1.2.9) and *ṭhhalantācca* (1.2.10), there is *kitva*; from that,
by *cchÂavoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca* (6.4.19), there is *ūṭh*, and that [substitution] is caused by reduplication.

It does not occur. In that case, if *nā* were not qualified by being the cause of reduplication (*dvirvacana-nimitta*), then even for that *yaṇ*-substitute which occurs before *ūṭ*, there would be the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*.
