And thus, the reduplicated form would be heard with a final *i*-vowel. However, when the cause of reduplication is included [as a qualifier], as in "dyau"—
Thus, there is a reduplication of this [root]. In that case,

through the application of the "remainder of the consonant-initial" (*halādiśeṣa*) rule and the shortening of vowels, the form of the reduplicated syllable in *dudyūṣati* is established as ending in the vowel *u*.
60. *Adarśanaṃ lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.60). [The sūtra begins with] "adarśanam" and so forth. Now, one might object: the words "adarśana" and "anupalabdhi" are both general terms for non-perception.

The terms "non-hearing" (*aśravaṇa*) and "non-proceeding" (*anupaccāraṇa*) are words expressing a specific kind of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi-viśeṣa*). For when the words "non-hearing" and so forth are uttered, it is the non-apprehension of sound itself that is understood, not non-apprehension in general; moreover, general and specific terms do not have the same meaning. Therefore...

Why did he say "not a different thing"? He thinks as follows: even general terms function with reference to a specific instance by virtue of the context. And here, words are the subject under discussion because they are what are to be explained; therefore...

Although the words "non-seeing" (adarśana) and "non-apprehension" (anupalabdhi) are general terms, nevertheless, by the force of the context here, they refer specifically to the non-apprehension of a word (śabdānupalabdhi).
In this system, technical designations (*saṃjñā*) such as "vṛddhi" have been prescribed for words;

likewise, here too, the designation "elision" (*lopa*) would belong to the word "non-appearance" (*adarśana*) itself. Consequently, since the word "non-appearance" alone would be substituted in all instances where "elision" is prescribed, that [word] itself would become the substitute.
To address this, he says: "By these words," and so forth. How is this obtained previously?

He thinks as follows: from the rule *na veti vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 1.1.44), the particle *iti* continues [into subsequent rules] for the purpose of indicating the meaning (*arthanirdeśārtha*). For by that, a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is understood, as for example—

"For an action disciplines a substance, not that which is without substance. Even without the application of the suffix *itikaraṇa*, the designation of the very form of the word is indeed established, as in the rule "taraptamapau ghaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.1.22). Therefore—

The meaning understood from the capacity of the term *karaṇānuvṛtti*— namely, "non-observation"— is precisely what this designation refers to, not the sound itself. Furthermore, the designation "elision" (*lopa*) is made as a grand one so that it may be understood as a technical term based on its etymological meaning.

*Lopana* means *lopa*; the meaning is non-perception or non-utterance. Furthermore, this term *adarśana* (non-seeing) is not itself a form of sound whose essence is negation; rather, it refers to its object. Therefore, because the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is understood according to its literal meaning (*anvartha*), this is a name for the object itself. If, then, this belongs to the object alone...
If it were defined as "perception" (*saṃjñā*), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For every word is not observed outside of its own specific domain;

consequently, in the case of *ṭhtrapu-jatu*, the non-observation of the suffix *kvip* would be subject to the technical designation of elision (*lopa*). And this being the case, [the rule] "when a suffix is elided, [the effect of] the suffix... [would apply].

Since the *tuk* augment would apply by the rule "a short vowel takes *tuk* before a *kṛt* suffix ending in a *pit* vowel" (Pāṇini 6.1.71), he says "of that which is applicable," and so forth. Is this technical name (*saṃjñā*) for the mere non-observation [of the cause]? No.

If so, [it refers to] the non-occurrence of that very [suffix] which might have been expected from either the technical rule (*śāstra*) or from the meaning (*artha*). In this case, there is no occasion for the occurrence of *kvip* by any means; therefore, how could there be an occasion for it? How then is this distinction established?
Is this obtainable? Since there is no explicit mention here of "that which is applicable" (*prasaṅga*), nor has that been stated?

It is thought thus: the term *sthānin* ("original element") from the rule *sthānivat* is understood here as well; for *sthānin*, *prasaṅgavat*, and *prasakta* are indeed synonyms. By this, the following meaning is obtained:

This is the designation for that which is not seen despite being applicable. For example, in the form *gaudheraḥ*: by the rule *godhāyā ḍhrak* (Pāṇini 4.1.129), the suffix *ḍhrak* is applied, resulting in the replacement of the final vowel with *ey*;
then, although the elision of the *y* was applicable according to the rule *lopo vyor vali* (6.1.76), it is not seen [in this specific case]. [Similarly in] *paceraṇ*.
In this case as well, the *sīyuṭ* [augment] is [omitted] by rule;

likewise, in other instances as well, the occurrence [of such omissions] should be understood according to the requirements. In the words *jīradānuḥ* and *āstremāṇam*, there is the elision of the *v* of the preceding member. [The root is] *strivu* (meaning "to go" and "to dry up") [DhP 1.967].

1109) Regarding the form *āsremāṇam*, which ends in the suffix *manin* according to Pāṇini 5.2.58 (*sarvadhātubhyo manin*), the long vowel of the penultimate (*upadhā*) is substituted for the short vowel (*etva*) in the second case singular.

[The rule] "of the subsequent [element], beginning with the *anubandha*" refers to the *anubandha* beginning with the letter *k*; by the word "beginning" (*ādi*), [other *anubandhas* are also included].
[The augment] *sīyuṭ* [is added] after the letter *s*.
61. *pratyayasya luk-ślulupaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.61):
Just as the term "vṛddhi" is a designation for those things transformed by it as well as those not so transformed, so too...

Even names such as *luka* and so forth would apply even to that which has not been conditioned by them (*atadbhāvita*), and consequently, there would be a confusion of technical terms (*saṃjñāsaṃkara*).
For when there is a confusion of technical terms, they would become intermingled; therefore, he says: "And because multiple technical terms are prescribed."

And so forth. If these designations were to apply even to that which has not been cultivated [by meditation], then the creation of multiple designations would be purposeless; for the accomplishment of all functions would belong to that single [unconditioned] entity alone.

Therefore, because multiple designations are prescribed, that non-perception which is cultivated—that is, brought about—by whichever designation is uttered belongs to that very non-perception of the suffix and not to any other; thus, there is no confusion. If this is so, then the fault of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya) arises.
For instance: the non-perception (adarśana) qualified by the name (saṃjñā) is what is to be brought about; and since that non-perception exists, the name must be brought about.
Therefore, he says: "And in the case of rules prescribing [an operation]," and so forth.
The non-appearance (*adarśana*) of that which is prescribed is designated by technical terms such as *luk* and so forth;
thus, because the designation is understood as something yet to come (*bhāvinī*), the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) does not arise. [For example:
"he offers" (*juhoti*). By the rule "after roots beginning with *ad*, there is *luk* of *śap*" (Pāṇini 2.4.72), there is *luk* of *śap*. "He offers."
Thus:
"The *ślu* [elision] occurs after roots such as *hu*," according to Pāṇini 2.4.75. Regarding "Varaṇāḥ":
it refers to a village situated not far from Varaṇa trees. According to Pāṇini 4.1.83, the suffix *aṇ* [is applied] in the sense of "belonging to" (*prāgdīvyataḥ*). Of that—

By the rule *ṭhvaraṇādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.2.82), there is elision (*lup*). Thus we have "the Agastis" and "the Kuṇḍinas. If the mention of the suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa*) were not made, [the elision would apply to] the descendant of Agastya...
The suffix *ṛṣyaṇ* is applied [to form *āgastya*] according to Pāṇini 4.1.114: *tyāni bahūni ṛṣyandhakavṛṣṇikurubhyaḥ*.
The suffix *yañ* is applied [to form *kauṇḍinya*] because it belongs to the *gargādi* group, according to Pāṇini 4.1.105: *gargādibhyo yañ*.
When the case ending *jas* follows those two words, *āgastya* and *kauṇḍinya*:
In the case of *āgastya* and *kauṇḍinya*, by [Pāṇini 2.4.70] *agastikuṇḍinayo ragastikuṇḍinac*, elision (*luk*) is applied, and *agasti* and *kuṇḍina* are the substitutes (*ādeśa*).
Then, due to this disparity, there would be three [substitutes] for each of the two bases (*sthānin*) specified in the genitive.
The substitutes would occur by turns. In that case, when *luk* is applied, there would result the hearing of the mere case-ending alone.
Furthermore, even if [the substitute] were *al-*...

[If it were so,] what would happen to the final [element]? Even in this case, one would have *āgastyaḥ* and *kauṇḍinyaḥ*, whereas *agastayaḥ* and *kuṇḍināḥ* are what is intended. Even if there were a substitution of *kuṇḍina-* for the word *āgastya-* and a substitution of *āgasti-* for the word *kauṇḍinya-*, the undesired result would still follow.

For the form of the word *āgastya* in the nominative plural is intended to be *agastayaḥ*, while that of the word *kauṇḍinya* is *kuṇḍināḥ*. For this very reason, they are presented in the sequence *agastayaḥ* and *kuṇḍināḥ*.
Furthermore, why is it that by virtue of internal similarity (*āntaratamya*), the word *agasti* alone is the substitute for the word *āgastya*, and not *kuṇḍina*;
and why is it that the word *kuṇḍinaja* is the substitute for the word *kauṇḍinya*, and not the word *agasti*?

Even so, liberation from the undesirable consequence does not occur. For instance: although forms such as *āgastyaḥ* and *kauṇḍinyaḥ* are established in this way, nevertheless, when a suffix beginning with *aj-* that occurs after a word ending in *div-* is intended, [the rule] "from a *vṛddha* [base], *cha*" (Pāṇini 4.2.114) applies.

Otherwise, the elision (*lopa*) would not occur because the suffix is not "vṛddha" (long). However, when there is the mention of a suffix (*pratyaya-grahaṇa*), this designation (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed specifically for its non-appearance; therefore, the elision (*luk*) applies to that [suffix] alone.
Even when there is the intention to express a suffix such as *parija* and so on, by the rule "go’tre ’lug aci" (Pāṇini 4.1.89), the elision (*luk*) takes place.
When [the formation] is prohibited, the suffix *cha* also occurs after a word ending in *vṛddhi*. For example: *agastīnāṃ chātrāḥ* (the pupils of the Agastis) becomes *āgastīyāḥ*.

However, from the word *kauṇḍinya*, even though elision (*luk*) occurs, only the suffix *aṇ* applies by the rule *kaṇvādibhyo gotre* (Pāṇini 4.2.111)—thus, *kauṇḍinyānāṃ chātrāḥ* becomes *kauṇḍinyāḥ*. Therefore, in that case...
The fault of the absence of the suffix should not be raised [as an objection].

62. *pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam* (Pāṇini 1.1.62). Regarding the term *pratyayalakṣaṇam*: it means that the suffix (*pratyaya*) is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of that [operation], where the compound is formed with another word as its referent (*anyapadārtha*) in the sense of an effect (*kārya*).
[Bahuvrīhi compound. By the words "the cause for the suffix" (*pratyayanimittam*) and so forth, he states the purpose for the commencement of the rule.

Now, one might object: "But this is already established even by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original). This is not so; for it is desired that an operation conditioned by a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) should take place even when the suffix is elided, provided that the operation does not depend on the phonetic form of the suffix itself (*alāśraya*). For instance, in the case of *agnicit*: [The text continues with the example of *agnicit* and its grammatical derivation.]

Even when there is reliance on *al* [the preceding vowel], the *tuk* augment indeed occurs by the rule *ṭhṛtvasya piti kṛti tuk* (Pāṇini 6.1.71). For example, in *agnicit*: the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *ṭhagnau ceḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.91);
then, by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), there is the elision of the *i*.

Due to the rule *adāditvāc chapo luk* (Pāṇini 2.4.72), there is the elision of the *śap* suffix. By the rule *dāder dhātor ghaḥ* (8.2.32), there is the substitution of *gh*. By the rule *ekāco baśo bhaṣ* (8.2.37) and so forth, *bhaṣ* occurs, which is the letter *dh*.
By the rule *jhalāñ jaśo 'nte* (8.2.39), there is the substitution of *jaś*, whereby the *gh* becomes *g*. Of that [g],...

The letter *k* [in *vaha*] results from the substitution of *c* according to *ṭhva-avasāne* (8.4.56). [The term] *pratyayaḥ* [is understood] from the preceding rule [1.3.1], and *vartamāne* is supplied from the previous sūtra [3.2.123]. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by *āho yamahanaḥ* (1.3.28), and the elision of the penultimate vowel occurs by *gamahana* (6.4.98), etc.
The suffix *gha* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.18] *ṭhho hanteḥ* (7.3.54).

Regarding *saṃgmīya*: the ātmanepada ending is applied to the root *gam* preceded by the prefix *sam* by [Pāṇini 1.3.29] *samo gami* etc.; the substitution of *at* for the *iṭ* augment occurs by [Pāṇini 3.4.146] *iṭo't*; [the suffix is applied] extensively...

By the rule *chandasi* (Pāṇini 2.4.73), there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*. As before, there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*). [The objection that] "the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) does not occur" is refuted by the rule *anudāttopadeśa* (Pāṇini 6.4.37), etc.

In the case of *ṭhraikulam*, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). In the case of *ṭhgohitam*, it is by virtue of the rule beginning with *ṭhcaturthī* (Pāṇini 2.1.36). Here, there is indeed the elision of the affixes of the genitive and dative singular; however, this is because the substitution of *ay* and *āv* is prescribed before a vowel.

In that rule, the suffix (*varṇa*) is the basis, not the affix (*pratyaya*). Therefore, since those two are caused by the *varṇa*, and not caused by the affix, they do not occur. But is it not the case that here the elision (*lopa*) of the affix is performed? What then?

[Reply: No, this is not so; for the term *lopa* (elision) is a general designation for non-appearance (*adarśana*), whether it is produced by that [specific grammatical operation] or not produced by it. Therefore, *luk* (zero-substitution) is indeed a form of *lopa*.
63. *na lumatāṅgasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.63). Regarding the term *lumatā*: that which contains the word *lu* is *lumān*. What, then, is this?
It is the technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*) such as *luk* and so forth. This instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*), as in *he tau va*.
Or, [the term *itthambhūtalakṣaṇa*] refers to a characteristic mark of such a state. When a suffix is elided by means of the word *lumat*, the meaning is: "by that reason" or "characterized by that.
Now, how is this [word] *pratyaya* obtained? It is obtained precisely from the non-observation of a suffix.

Because of the prescription of technical names such as *lugādi* (elision, etc.). [The rule] "When a suffix is elided by the word *lup*, that which is the stem (*aṅga*)... refers back to that very same suffix.

It should be understood that by relying on the *nimita* (cause), the designation (*saṃjñā*) of a specific grammatical element is obtained. Although there is no explicit mention of a distinction— that its function is not characterized by being a condition (*pratyaya*)— nevertheless, due to proximity, it is precisely that [element] which is elided by the term *lumat*.
It is understood that an elided suffix is not a cause for the designation of an *aṅga* (base), because it is characterized by that [suffix]. For example, in the word "gargāḥ":

from the rule "yañ after Garga and others" (4.1.105), the suffix *yañ* is applied; then, by the rule "elision of *yañ* and *añ* when more than one [descendant] is meant" (2.4.64), there is elision (*luk*) in the plural.
In this case, by the rule "in secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), [the augment *ṭi* is added] after those beginning with vowels other than *a*" (7.2.117), [the augment *ṭi* would apply to the base].

There is no *vṛddhi* [vowel strengthening]. In the case of "mṛṣṭaḥ": the suffix *tas* is added to the root *mṛj*, the *śap* is elided because it belongs to the *adādi* class, *ṣatva* is applied by the rule beginning with *vraśca* (8.2.36), and *ṣṭutva* is applied; thus, by the rule "vṛddhi for *mṛj*" (7.2.114), the *vṛddhi* does not take place. In the case of "juhutaḥ": when *tas* follows, there is *ślau* (doubling) after the roots beginning with *hu*.

When [the suffix] *kṛt* is applied, the guna substitution characterized by *sārvadhātuka* does not occur. In all cases, whatever suffix is relied upon for the designation (*saṃjñā*) of an *aṅga*, that very same suffix is the cause for operations such as *vṛddhi*. And here, because no specific [suffix] is relied upon, not only that which is prescribed under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning *aṅga* [is excluded].

The grammatical operation (*kārya*) is prohibited; however, this includes even that which is prescribed outside the governing heading of "the member" (*anaṅgādhikāra*). Consequently, in the cases of *gargāḥ*, *bidāḥ*, and *uṣṭragrīvāḥ*, the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*)—even though prescribed by the rule *ṭhñnityādir nityam* (Pāṇini 6.1.197)—does not take effect because it is prescribed outside the governing heading of "the member. And here, in the case of *atrayaḥ*—

The final syllable of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is udātta by the rule *kitaḥ* (6.1.165). Thus, for *gargāḥ* and *bidāḥ*, the suffix *yañ* is applied respectively from the *garga*-class and others; then the suffix *añ* is applied by the rule *anṛṣyānantarye vidādibhyo 'ñ* (4.1.104);
and finally, there is elision (*luk*) by the rule *hyañañoś ca* (2.4.64).

"Uṣṭragrīva" [is formed as follows]: the suffix *kan*, prescribed by the rule "ṭhivaḥ pratikṛtau" (Pāṇini 5.3.96), undergoes elision (*lup*) by the rule "devapathādibhyaśca" (Pāṇini 5.3.100). "Atrayaḥ":
in the sense of "the offspring of Atri," the suffix *ḍhak* prescribed by the rule "itaścāniñaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.122) undergoes elision by the rule "atribhṛgukutsavasiṣṭha... (Pāṇini 2.4.65).

By [the rule] beginning with (2.4.65), there is elision (*luk*) when many [objects] are expressed, as in "five" (*pañca*) and "seven" (*sapta*). By [the rule] "elision after *ṣaṣ* and the following" (7.1.22), there is elision of the case endings *jas* and *śas*, as in "milk" (*payaḥ*) and "Sāman chant" (*sāma*). Here too, [the rule] "elision of *su* and *am* after a neuter [stem]" applies.

(7.3.23). Here, although the suffix has been elided by *lumat* and the designation of "stem" (*aṅga*) is based upon that [suffix], nevertheless, by the rule of "characteristic of the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the designation of "word" (*pada*)—according to Pāṇini 1.4.14, "that which ends in a *sup* or *tiṅ* is a word"—still certainly occurs; for this [designation] is not an operation belonging to the stem, but rather...

For the prior portion of a suffix-bearing complex (samudāya) is indeed the base (aṅga). And here, the designation "base" (aṅgasaṃjñā) does not depend on that very same element which has been elided by *lumat* and upon which the designation "word" (padasaṃjñā) would otherwise depend.

[The word] *padam* attains [the designation]. When this designation of *pada* exists here, in the case of *payaḥ*, the substitution of *ru* occurs by the rule "sasajuṣo ruḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.66). Furthermore, the *visarjanīya* [substitution] occurs before a *khar* [consonant] or at the end of a pause (*avasāna*), as these are operations pertaining to a *pada*. For example: *pañca*, *sapta*, *sāma*. In these cases as well, the elision of *n* [occurs]...

The elision of the *n* by the rule "tipadikāntasya" (Pāṇini 8.2.7) is an operation dependent on the designation of a word (*pada*). In the form "kāryate," the *lakāra* suffix occurs in the sense of the object after a causative (*ṇic*) stem; here, by the rule "sārvadhātuke yak" (3.1.67), the suffix *yak* is applied, and the rule "na lumatā pratyayasya" (1.1.63) does not apply.

What, then, has been elided? It is the *ṇi* by the rule "ṭhṇer aniṭi" (Pāṇini 6.4.51); for here, the mention of "elision" (*lopa*) from the preceding rule "āto lopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.64) is understood as a carry-over. Consequently, the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) conditioned by the suffix still takes place.
64. *aco'ntyādi ṭi* (Pāṇini 1.1.64).
The term "ṭhantyādi" is a bahuvrīhi compound: that form of a word which has as its beginning the final vowel (*ac*) among the vowels.

That has been stated accordingly. Now, one might object that since the word *antya* (final) here requires *acām* (of vowels), a compound with the word *ādi* (initial) cannot occur due to a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*). This is not a fault;
for the word *antya* is a relative term (*sambandhiśabda*), and relative terms possess a constant requirement for a correlative (*nityasāpekṣatva*).
Because it conveys meaning, a compound occurs even when there is a state of mutual dependence, as in the example "Devadatta’s teacher’s family" (*devadatasya gurukulam*).
Regarding the statement "the genitive is used in the sense of specification (*nirdhāraṇa*)," if this genitive were [governed] by the rule *yataśca nirdhāraṇam* (Pāṇini 2.3.41),
then since specification occurs only when there is a collection of many [entities], the singular number in the word *acaḥ* would be inappropriate.
Since there are many [vowels], one might expect the plural case-ending; therefore, he says: "The singular is used for the genus (*jāti*).
The meaning is that it is because the genus is a single entity. Regarding the phrase "the final among those vowels arranged in succession": how, then, is this specific term *ac* [distinguished]?
It is obtained, even though there is no second mention of the suffix *ac* here, nor is it the subject under discussion?

He thinks as follows: in common usage, selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) is well-known to apply only to things of the same class. For instance, in the expression "the black cow is the one among cows that has the most milk," it is understood to be a cow itself even without a second occurrence of the word "cow."

It is understood. Therefore, even though there is no second mention of the word *aja* here, it is nevertheless determined that what is being selected is specifically one of the same class, namely an *aja*. The term *antya* means "that which exists at the end"; [the suffix] *yat* is applied according to the rule for the *digādi* group.
Regarding "tadādi":

the analysis of the compound is "that which has this as its beginning. "The word *icchabdaḥ*" and so forth are examples of forms; however, the grammatical operation (*kārya*) pertains to the word *icchabda*.

When the suffix *ṇic* is applied in the sense of "he describes one who has piled the fire-altar" (*agni-citaṃ ācaṣṭe*), the elision of the *ṭi* portion occurs by the rule "in the case of *ṇā*, as in the case of *iṣṭhan*,
for a nominal stem" (*ṭhṇāviṣṭavad prātipadikasya*), resulting in the form *agniṃ cayati*.

[The forms] *ṭhātām* and *āthām*. Regarding these two, however, the operation based on the technical designation *ṭi* is as follows: by the rule *ṭita ātmanepadānāṃ ṭere* (Pāṇini 3.4.79), there is the substitution of *ṭe* [for the final vowel and following consonant of the suffix]. Examples of this operation are *pacete* and *pacethe*. Now, how is it that the letter *i* in *vahimahiṅ* [is designated as *ṭi*]?

[Objection: There is no such thing as a "final" [element] for which that designation [of "first"] could exist; thus, how can it be designated as "beginning with *a*"? [Response: This is not a fault; by virtue of the designation of a single entity as being "like the beginning and the end" (*ṭhādyantavad ekasmin*), there will be the designation of it as both "the beginning" and "the final."

65. *alo'ntyātpūrva upadhā* (Pāṇini 1.1.65). The two ablative cases in *alo'ntyāt* are in apposition. [The phrase] "in a collection of phonemes at the beginning of a verbal root" is used. But surely, there is no mention here of a "collection of phonemes," nor...
That is the subject under discussion. How, then, is this meaning obtained? From the mention of "the final" (antya):
it is only the final letter of a *samudāya* (composite) that is "final," not a solitary one.
Therefore, this meaning is obtained from the mention of "the final."

Regarding the phrase "on land alone" (*ṭhaleva*): by the use of the particle *eva*, the collection of vowels (*al-samudāya*) is excluded. Now, since there is no second mention of the term *al* here, why does this designation not apply to the collection of vowels as well?

And from common worldly usage: for in the world, when it is said of these Brahmins, "Let the one preceding the last be brought," only that single person preceding the last is brought, not the entire group. Even so, why should this designation apply here to that which is separated [by other elements]?

Does it not exist? Even when separated, the word "prior" (pūrva) certainly still applies. Precisely for this reason, based on the worldly example: for in common usage, when one says, "Bring what is prior to the last," no one brings something that is separated [by others], but rather only that which is immediately preceding. For if this were a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) only in this specific context, [it would not apply elsewhere].
It does not refer to the entire complex;

for regarding the rule *ṛtaśca saṃyogāder guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.10), he will state: "In the prescription of the guna [substitution] for a root beginning with a conjunct consonant, the mention of 'having a conjunct as a penultimate' must be made."

That [definition] is contradicted; for, while the designation "penultimate" (upadhā) applies only to this specific position, it is not possible for a "conjunction" (saṃyoga)— which by its nature consists of a collection of several consonants occurring without any intervening vowels— to possess the status of being a penultimate element.

Since the constituent of the conjunction is the penultimate element (*upadhā*), there is no contradiction in designating the whole by means of the property of its part; for indeed, a whole is designated by means of the property of its parts, as for example: [text omitted].
"This city is well-known.
Alternatively, one should understand that the mention of "penultimate" (*upadhā*) there is intended to indicate that the conjunction [of consonants] is preceded by a short vowel (*al*).
Forms such as *akāra* are examples of the word-forms; however, the grammatical operation regarding the vowel *a* depends upon its being designated as "penultimate."
In the case of *pācakaḥ* and *pāṭhakaḥ*, there is *vṛddhi* [substitution] by the rule "ṭhata upadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.116).
However, for the vowels *i* and *ṛ*, we have *bhedakaḥ*, *chedakaḥ*, *vartakaḥ*, and *varddhakaḥ*;
here, there is *guṇa* [substitution] by the rule "pugantalaghūpadhasya" (Pāṇini 7.3.86).

Regarding the word *śiṣṭaḥ*: the root *śās* is used in the sense of "instruction" (*anuśiṣṭau*; DhP 1075). It takes the suffix *niṣṭhā*. By the rule *śāsa idaṅ haloḥ* (6.4.34), the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is changed to *i*. For in that rule, the term *upadhā* is understood by virtue of its recurrence from the preceding sūtra *aniditām* (6.4.24). Furthermore, [the *s* of the root] is changed to *ṣ* by the rule *śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca* (8.3.60), and so forth.
The word "from the aggregate" (*samudāyāt*) and so forth means: from the aggregate consisting of the letter *a* and the letter *s*.

The purpose is that the preceding *ś* should not receive the designation of *upadhā* (penultimate). For if it were [to be designated as such], then *itva* (the substitution of *i*) would apply to that very [letter *ś*].
66. When that [subsequent element] is specified, [the former is understood].
(Pāṇini 1.1.66). For what purpose is this? [It is so that] in rules such as "iko yaṇ aci" (6.1.77), there may be a relationship of locus and located between the term *aci* and so forth.
It is based on proximity (*pratyāsati*), as in the expression: "A hamlet dwells in the Ganges.
Here, the Ganges possesses that proximity both with respect to what precedes it and with respect to what follows it.
Consequently, in cases such as curdled milk and water, it is not known which one among the preceding elements is the possessor of proximity.

Is it the substitution of *yaṇ*, or is it [the substitution] of what follows? Since such a doubt arises, this paribhāṣā is commenced for the purpose of providing a restrictive rule (*niyama*). If it is thus commenced as a subject of doubt, then it applies wherever there is a doubt.

Consequently, the expression "curd-water" (*dadhyudakam*) would be established; however, this [expression] "curd here" (*dadhyatra*) is not established. But surely this is established even without the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), for there is no doubt in this case. Well then, this [other case] is not established: [The text continues: ...this is not established.

"Samid-atra," "agnicit-atra. For if this technical rule (paribhāṣā) did not apply where there is no doubt—since it would not be present here due to the intervention [of other rules]—then the substitution of *yaṇ* would certainly occur even when there is an intervening element. Therefore, this rule applies even in cases where there is no doubt.

One should make such an effort as is required for a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*). This is what is being done: here, first of all, the rule "that which is designated by the locative case [is related] to the preceding" (P. 1.1.66) should be formulated; for by this much alone, the desired meaning is established. Even there, the meaning is as follows:

In order to dispel the suspicion that the word-form itself [is being referred to], the particle *iti* need not have been employed; for nowhere in the scripture is a word heard indicated by the locative case, such that one might suspect it refers to its own form. Thus, although this [result] is established by a brief rule, [the author has used] this extensive one...

He composes this aphorism (sūtra) because it is a technical definition (paribhāṣā) of great scope; that is, for the purpose of indicating [the rule]. And thus it becomes of great scope if it applies everywhere—both to cases where there is doubt and elsewhere.

This might be the case: although when it is said "that which is indicated by the locative case," the locus is indeed indicated by the locative, nevertheless, because that [locus] has the thing located within it as its primary referent, in the rule *iko yaṇ aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77), the substitution of *yaṇ* is understood to apply to that *ac* which is situated after the *ik*; and therefore, it would apply only here.

"It might be that [the rule applies] in the case of *dadhi bhunakti* ('he eats curd'), but here it would not apply in *dadhy atra*; however, under the other formulation, this fault does not exist, and therefore a great sūtra has been composed.
This is not so; for he provides the technical indication *dādhāghvadāp* (Pāṇini 1.1.20).
This indicates that the grammatical operation, such as the substitution of *yaṇ*, occurs only in the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and not in the superstratum (*ādheya*). Furthermore,
even according to the alternative formulation (*anyāsa*), because the locus is primarily characterized by what is to be received, [the operation] occurs only in the superstratum.
Since this paribhāṣā applies everywhere to operations such as the substitution of *yaṇ*, everything desired is established.
Here, by the rule "In the absence of a technical designation, a word denotes its own form" (Pāṇini 1.1.68), there is the inclusion of the word's own form itself.

It must be so; and consequently, this *paribhāṣā* would apply only where that very word "tasmin" is uttered, as in the rule "tasminnaṇi ca yaṣmākāsmākau" (Pāṇini 4.3.2). For indeed, there is scope for that *paribhāṣā* in this case.
The purpose is the cessation of the other: "Give what belongs to you to you;
give what belongs to us to us.
That is, "Give what belongs to you to you; give what belongs to us to us. [This refers to] the rule for *ika*.

However, this [principle] does not apply in cases such as "yaṇ aci" (Pāṇini 6.1.77); therefore, he says: "in that," meaning "when there is a designation of the sense of the locative case. He thinks thus: for the particle *iti* has been used here, and it...
Having set aside the status of its own form (*svarūpa*) as the referent (*padārtha*), it establishes that the word *nitya* has meaning (*artha*) as its referent;
thus, there is the apprehension of the meaning alone. Furthermore, that meaning must necessarily be expressed by some word or other.
It is to be specified because it has multiple meanings; thus, it is indicated by the word *tasmin*, which expresses a general sense.
Now, one might object that a temporal sequence between a word and its meaning is impossible, since such a sequence cannot exist with respect to the meaning itself.

"There is no fault, for it will be understood by means of the word that denotes it. To this, the following objection is raised: "The particle *iti* is employed so that there may be a grasping of the meaning (*artha*), but not a grasping of the intrinsic form (*svarūpa*) [of the word]."

And that apprehension of the word-form itself is possible by virtue of the rule *tasminnaṇi ca yuṣmākāsmākau* (Pāṇini 4.3.2); for if there were an apprehension of the word-form, it would occur precisely in that [rule].

One should have included the word "pūrva" (previous), yet it was not done; therefore, it is understood that even without the particle *iti*, there will be the grasping of the meaning itself and not of its own form—so what is the purpose of it? This is true; however, for those who are of dull intellect...
The particle *iti* is employed for the sake of easy comprehension with respect to those who are unable to grasp [the meaning] through direct application (*pratipattuṃ asamarthān*).

The mention of the word *nirdiṣṭa* (indicated) serves as a qualifier of this very sense. And here in this treatise, in sentences such as "iko yaṇ aci" (Pāṇini 6.1.77), wherever there is the sense of the locative case, [it is understood].
In that case,
since it has already been specified in every instance, the qualification "specified" (nirdiṣṭa) in the definition is useless because there is no possibility of deviation; therefore, he says:

Regarding the phrase "the mention of *nirdiṣṭa*," and so forth: that whose meaning is immediate succession (*ānantarya*)—that is, non-intervention (*avyavadhāna*)—is described as such. But how does that [word] come to have the sense of immediate succession? Because it is understood from that [context]. For this root *diś* has the action of utterance (*uccāraṇa*) as its meaning; the prefix *niḥ*— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]

The word *iha* (here) indicates uninterruptedness (*nairantarya*). In that regard, when the compound *nirantara-diṣṭaḥ* (shown without interval) is formed as a *prādi*-compound, it is clearly understood that [the object] has been uttered immediately [afterward].
But for what purpose is immediate succession (*ānantarya*) resorted to? To this he says: "In the case of *agnicit*," and so forth.

This word "prior" (*pūrva*) applies even when there is an intervention. The intention is that if immediate succession were not resorted to there, it would apply even when there is an intervention. Now, [one might object]: "In the case of *aci*..."
Thus, the locative case is understood as the "proximate" (aupaśleṣika) locus, and that which is separated is not proximate.

Therefore, what is the purpose of mentioning the term "indicated" (nirdiṣṭa) for the sake of immediate succession? This is incorrect; for if the mention of "indicated" were absent, the proximate locus itself could not be understood.
Because the word *pūrva* (preceding), even when referring to something separated [by others], effects the exclusion of only what follows it, and not of what precedes it even if separated; however,
when the term *nirdiṣṭa* (specified) is employed, it refers to the locative case (*saptamī*) which denotes immediate proximity as its locus.
Proximity (*pratyāsatti*) is adopted [as the criterion for application]. And that proximity is not set aside by the mention of "preceding" (*pūrva*);

rather, the meaning obtained is that only the exclusion of subsequent [elements] is effected. Consequently, an operation does not apply to what is separated [by an intervening element]. Furthermore, the mention of "specified" (*nirdiṣṭa*) must indeed be made for the sake of the subsequent rule.
67. *Tasmād ityuttarasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.67).

For what purpose is this [sūtra]? The [term] *tiṅ* here [in the rule] *tiṅṅtiṅaḥ* (8.1.28) is not a case-ending (*vibhakti*) denoting a grammatical relation (*kāraka*); rather, it is [the term] from *dikśabdādañcūttarapada* (2.3.29).

The term "characterized by spatial separation" (*digyogalakṣaṇā*) [is used]. The word *dik* (direction) must be supplied; in that case, should one supply the word *pūrva* (prior) and apply the *nighāta* (elision of accent) to what precedes the finite verb (*atiṅaḥ pūrvasya*), or rather [the word] *para* (subsequent)?
When the doubt arises as to whether [the operation] is to be brought forward from another rule, this technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) is commenced for the purpose of restriction.

[The word] "nirdiṣṭa" (specified) is understood to follow [from the previous rule]. Therefore, because that [term] has the sense of immediate proximity (*ānantarya*), [the operation applies] to what is not separated [by anything else].
The meaning is that it does not constitute an effect (*kārya*). Here too, the particle *iti* is employed for the purpose of indicating the meaning (*artha-nirdeśārtha*).
With the intention that, by this means, the sense of the ablative case (*pañcamy-artha*) is grasped rather than the actual form of the word (*śabda-svarūpa*), he says:
"from that" (*tasmāt*). This is the indication of the sense of the ablative case (*pañcamy-arthanirdeśaḥ*).

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: since the particle *iti* will be carried over from the preceding sūtra itself, what is the purpose of this *iti* being repeated? It is for the purpose of indicating that a portion from the preceding sūtra is carried over in this manner.
It is explained that the phrase "the mention [of the word] as indicated by the particle *iti* shall recur" follows here.
However, another says: "In this context, the particle *iti* removes the notion that the limit (*avadhi*) is dependent on the bounded object (*avadhimat*).
Consequently, it is understood as belonging to what follows the limit, not to the bounded object itself."
The particle *iti* is not intended for the purpose of excluding the grasping of the word's own form (*svarūpa*), because that own form does not exist [in this context].
As for the rule "therefore, after *śas*, *naḥ* occurs in the masculine" (Pāṇini 6.1.103), even there, it follows from the long vowel of the same quality as the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*).

"There is no doubt that the former [suffix] *śas* does not occur; therefore, the word 'iti' is used solely for the purpose of excluding the dependence of the limit (*avadhi*) upon the thing limited (*avadhimat*). To this, it is replied: if the operation were indeed of that which follows the limit, as in...

The particle *iti* is employed for the purpose that "there may not be [an object] possessing a limit" (*avadhimat*), in order to dispel the notion that the limit (*avadhi*) is dependent upon that which possesses the limit; there is no need for this, as it is established by common worldly usage alone.

Because that is established in common worldly usage: for when it is said in the world, "Let the one superior to him be fed," it is the one superior to the limit (the *avadhi*) who is fed, not the possessor of the limit (*avadhimat*). Therefore, here too, even without the particle *api*, the action will apply to the one superior to the limit, and not to the possessor of the limit.
As for what was also stated— "Therefore, in the case of [the rule] *tasmāc chaso naḥ puṃsi* (Pāṇini 6.1.103),

the *śas* [suffix] cannot occur before the long vowel resulting from the homogeneous substitution (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*)"— that too is incorrect; for this is so both from the word *aśva* and from the word *ādi*.
When *śas* follows, by the rule of long vowel substitution with the preceding sound (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*), and once the word *vṛkṣa* and others have been established as ending in *śas*,
[the form] *gacchatām* [is derived].

In the expressions *vṛkṣān upalabhate* and *gacchato vṛkṣān na upalabhate*, the suffix *śa* is indeed possible following the long vowel resulting from the homogeneity of the preceding sounds (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*).

Now, where there is a mention of both [the genitive and the locative], with respect to which one should the grammatical operation (*kārya*) take place? In that case, since the locative is without scope (*anavakāśā*), it will provide room for the other;
therefore, the operation will belong to that which is indicated by the genitive.
For example, in the rule *ṭhāne muk* (Pāṇini 7.2.82), the locative [in *ṭhāne*] is without scope, because of [the presence of] *ṭhataḥ*.

By the rule *yeyaḥ* (7.2.80), the genitive case will be substituted for the ablative case (*iti*) from the preceding rule which has its own scope; likewise, by the rule *īdāsaḥ* (7.2.83), the ablative—

In the previous rule, "myāna," the locative case (*saptamī*) has its scope. Where both [the ablative and the locative] have their scope, the ablative (*pañcamī*) will, by virtue of its higher priority, supplant the locative as a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). For example: *āmi sarvanāmnaḥ*.
In the rule *suṭ* (7.1.52), the ablative case in *ṭā-ḍasi-ṅasām asuk* (7.1.50) has its own scope;
the locative case in *āmi* is for the sake of the subsequent rule.
Therein, the ablative *āt* is interpreted as a genitive in relation to the locative *āmi*, and by that—

The augment *suṭ* is applied to the case-ending *ām* following a pronominal stem. In this context, however, although the locative case in the preceding rule *cche ca* (6.1.73) has its own scope of application, it is nonetheless superseded by the rules *dīrghāt* (6.1.75) and *padāntādvā* (6.1.76).

Because it possesses its own inherent accent (*svaritatva*) and continues from the preceding rule (*pūrvayoga*), that [seventh case ending] is without scope; therefore, it will cause the seventh case to be interpreted as a sixth case. The fifth case, however, having established the sense of sequence (*paurvaparya*), remains with its own scope.
[The rule] is set aside. Therefore, this is the meaning of the sūtra:

when a *ch* follows a long vowel (*dīrgha*), then *tug* is substituted for that very preceding long vowel. In the rule *sārvadhātuke yak* (Pāṇini 3.1.67), the locative case (*saptamī*) [in *dhātau*], even though it has no other scope, [is understood as referring to the root].

Even though the fifth case [the ablative] is available, one does not conceive of it as having the status of the sixth case [the genitive]; for otherwise, the substitutes *yaK* and so forth would belong to the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself.
Consequently, because the continued application of the rule "that which follows" (*paraśca*, Pāṇini 3.1.2) would be sublated, the *yaK* and other suffixes [would not apply].

Furthermore, the formulation of the *anubandha* (indicatory letter) would become purposeless; for if they were substitutes for verbal roots (*dhātu*), their status as "subsequent" (*para*) would not be tenable, since they indeed occur after the root.

68. *Svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasyāśabdasaṃjñā* (Pāṇini 1.1.68). [The commentary begins: "In the treatise (*śāstre*), its own form (*svam eva*)," and so forth. The mention of "treatise" (*śāstra*) is because in common usage (*loke*), only the meaning (*artha*) is what is grasped. In the word "of the word" (*śabdasya*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), according to the rule *kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā* (Pāṇini 2.3.71); thus, it is "the word."

It causes one to grasp, to understand, and to comprehend its own very form; this is the meaning. But what, then, is the difference between the word and its own form, such that there occurs this genitive case based on their distinction?

In the ultimate sense, there is no distinction whatsoever regarding the actual entity. For instance, the "own form" (svarūpa) of a word is its very nature (svabhāva). If that [form] were something other than the word, then the word would indeed lack its own nature.
It may be so; however, even in the absence of an actual difference, the genitive case occurs by relying on a difference constructed by the intellect.
For the intellect, arising through the maturation of its own seeds, comes into being while assuming a particular form.

Even though there is no actual difference in the object, it brings about a distinction, as in "the head of Rāhu" or "one's own nature. By the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "there is no external object," he shows that which is excluded.
He states an exception to what has been excessively over-applied: "The designation 'śabda'... and so forth. He asks, "For what purpose is this commenced?
and replies: "By means of the word... and so forth; that is, by the word being uttered, the meaning [is conveyed].
It is understood by virtue of its utility for the task at hand, not as the mere form of the word. For instance,
when it is said, "Let the cow be perceived," one attends to the object itself to perceive it, not to the form of the word.

In grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), however, operations such as the prescription of suffixes are not possible for a meaning, because there is no temporal sequence (*paurvāparya*) between a word and its meaning. Furthermore, there is no utility for the subject at hand by means of a suffix prescribed on account of a meaning. Therefore, [the rule] *agner ḍhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.33).
33) When this is said, the following understanding does not arise: "The referent of the word *agni* (fire) is the agent here;
its action is what is being prescribed. Consequently, those words which denote that referent would themselves be the things to be prescribed.
For example, as in the case of those who maintain that the universal (*ākṛti*) is the denotatum.
When the word "Let the cow be milked" (gaur duhyatām) enjoins the genus,

since that action is impossible in the genus itself and possible in the individual which is its substratum, and because of their constant association, comprehension occurs only with respect to that individual, not the genus; so it is here as well.

This [sūtra] is commenced for the purpose that there should be comprehension of those words which denote that [time]. The genitive case in "tadvācinām" (of those denoting that) is used in the sense of the object.
The meaning is that this is commenced so that [the rule] might not be understood as applying to those which denote that [time].

Regarding this, some say: "Since both the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and the modes (*paryāya*) would be applicable to the effect, this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is for the purpose of restriction, so that it may be understood as applying only to what is explicitly heard, and not to the modes."

Others, however, say: "A technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) possesses a *liṅga* (indicative mark), as for example, in the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī* (Pāṇini 1.1.3), where *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* serve as the *liṅga*. Or it is supplementary to another injunction; for example—"

Some maintain that this is a rule for technical terminology (*saṃjñāsūtra*), on the grounds that [according to the principle] "in case of conflict, the subsequent operation prevails" (Kātantra Paribhāṣā 67), a subsequent other rule would become subordinate to it; however, neither a gender indicator (*liṅga*) nor the status of being subordinate to another rule exists for this [sūtra]. Even though [this is so] in the commentary (*vṛtti*):

Although the word "technical name" (saṃjñā-śabda) is not explicitly uttered, nevertheless, by the author of the Vṛtti stating, "the very form itself is what is to be grasped as the word," it is effectively declared that it is indeed a technical name. This applies to words such as *agni* and others when they are distinguished from other words.
There exists both a common form, such as "soundness" (*śabdatva*), and an uncommon form, such as "the nature of the word 'fire'" (*agniśabdatva*).

In this context, the term *svam* ("its own") is employed for the purpose of excluding the common form and adopting the uncommon form, such as "the nature of the word 'fire'. For that [uncommon form] alone is its own form; the other is not.

Furthermore, with respect to another [person] as well, because there is no instruction toward cognition, it is the word's own form (*svarūpa*) that is proximate, not its meaning; for the opposite is the case, and because [the form] is not to be abandoned, and because it is eternally connected to it. For instance, words of imitation (*anukaraṇa*) abandon their meaning, but not [their own form].
The essential nature (*svarūpa*) is the unique form (*asādhāraṇaṃ rūpam*), whereas the meaning (*artha*) is common (*sādhāraṇa*), because it is conveyed by other words as well.
Thus, because it is proximate, eternally connected, and unique, the form alone belongs to the word.

It is not the meaning [that is intended by "sva"]. Therefore, since the inclusion of the form (*rūpa*) is already established by the mention of "sva" alone, the mention of "rūpa" is for the purpose of making it known that in grammar, like the form, the meaning (*artha*) is also accepted as a factor. By this—
Thus, the principle "that which is meaningful is included by the mention [of a term], but not that which is meaningless" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 1) becomes established.

Furthermore, although the word *śabdasya* ("of a word") is already established from the very context of the instruction on words (*śabdānuśāsana*), the explicit inclusion of the word *śabda* serves to indicate: wherever a designation refers to the word itself, there its own form (*svarūpa*) is understood, and not where the designation refers to the meaning (*artha*).

This is for the purpose of making [the meaning] known. Consequently, in the rule *ṭh sve puṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.40), there is no apprehension of the actual phonetic form; rather, that the reference is to the meaning is understood from the uninterrupted tradition of the teacher's instruction.
"Āgneyam": the suffix *ḍhak* is applied here in the sense of "Agni is its deity.
"Audaśvitkam": here too, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied in the sense of "prepared with buttermilk (*udaśvit*). [From] *udaśvita-*...
In the rule *anyatarasyām* (4.2.19), because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of *dadhnaṣṭhak* (4.2.18),
the substitution of *ka* for *ṭhak* occurs by the rule *isusuktāntāt kaḥ* (7.3.51).

Regarding the phrase "in the case of the inclusion of *ṭh*, *gh*, etc. and so forth: if words such as *ghu* were also technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*) that denote their own form (*svarūpa*), then in the rule *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.92), although there is the governing context of "root" (*dhātu*), the suffix *ki* would still apply after the word *ghu* itself because of the inclusion of *ghu*. However, the mention of "prefix" (*upasarga*)...

It would serve as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). For example, in the rules "ṭhañ after *nāsikā* in a name, and [the substitute] *nasa-* when not preceded by *sthūla*" (5.4.118), and "also after a prefix" (5.4.119); and in the case of *kumārīgha*, once the technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*) "gha" has indicated its own form (*svarūpa*), [the rule] "in the case of *gha*, *rūpa*, and *kalpa*" [applies].
By [the rule] beginning with (6.4.43), shortness would result when the word *gha* follows.
Now, one might object that by the force of the formulation of the technical name (*saṃjñā-vidhāna*), there is no apprehension of the actual form of the name itself.
For a name is indeed created for the purpose of making known the named object; if the word that serves as the name were itself to denote its own form,
the prescription of the name would be purposeless, but this is not the case,
because it denotes the named object by virtue of the very power of its being prescribed as a name.
And because of the force of the formulation of this technical definition (*paribhāṣā*), its own form [is understood]. Therefore, should a prohibition be made?
No, it need not be made;
by virtue of the *jñāpaka*, a technical term (*saṃjñā-śabda*) will not be a grasper of its own form. This is shown by the rule "ṣṇāntā... [P. 1.1.24].

By prescribing the technical name *ṣaṭ* for the numeral ending in the letter *ṣ* in the rule "ṣaṭ" (Pāṇini 1.4.24), he indicates that a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*) does not denote its own form; otherwise, [the rule] "ṣaḍbhyaḥ... [would have been unnecessary].
In the rule *luk* (Pāṇini 7.1.22), because the word *ṣaṭ* indicates its own form (*svarūpa*), elision (*luk*) occurs even from that; thus, for a numeral ending in the letter *ṣ*,
the form is *ṣaṭ*.
One should not form such a designation. For the word "ṣaṭ" is a number ending in the letter *ṣ*, and nothing else;
this is true. Nevertheless, for those who might experience difficulty in understanding the meaning through the medium of an explanatory indicator (*jñāpaka*), [the following applies]:

The prohibition "the term *saṃjñā*" was made in order to exclude those [terms] that are well-known; the mention of the word "term" (*śabda*) indicates that the prohibition applies only to that which is a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) within grammar, and not to others.
The phrase "of the worldly" (*laukikyā*) is for the sake of illustration.

Regarding the passage beginning with "of the specific [sounds]" (*siddhaviśeṣāṇām*), where the inclusion of the specific sounds is intended, there the letter *s* should be designated as having the technical marker *it*, as in the cases of *vṛkṣasya* and *mṛgaḥ*. Therefore, it must be stated.

Having made such a mention, this technical definition (*paribhāṣā*)— namely, "of those whose specific [forms] begin with *sita*," and so forth— should be formulated either in the first chapter or elsewhere: "That [term] whose *s* is marked with the technical designation *it* is the designator of the specific varieties of that, such as *khadira* and other specific types of trees."

This must be stated: in this same way, it should be understood in cases such as *ṭhpitparyāyavacanasya ca svādyartham* (Kātyāyana-vārttika 519) and so forth. Furthermore, this point to be established is proven by logic as well;
we shall demonstrate how it is proven in due course below.
The presentation of the text beginning with "for the sake of easy comprehension of the specific white [factors]" is intended for the purpose of easy understanding.

69. *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ* | (1.1.69) This is a technical definition (*saṃjñāsūtra*), not a governing rule (*paribhāṣā*). For the latter serves the purpose of restriction; and [in this case], there are no *aṇ* sounds or those marked with *u* that possess homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*)—

It might follow that many other [sounds] would also be included, so a restriction is made—namely, "the inclusion of a *pratyāhāra* is by means of a following *ṇ*-letter"—so that only those of the same class (*savarṇa*) are included.
By this, the intention is that even *ṛ*-vowels and others are established as including their own homogeneous sounds. And by a following [ṇ-letter]...
The inclusion of the *ṇ* [in the term *ṇakāra*] for the purpose of forming a *pratyāhāra* was explained in the rule *ṭh-i-u-ṇ*.
From the preceding sūtra, the phrase "its own form" (*ṭh-svaṃ rūpam*) is carried over here;
and by virtue of the sense, a change of case occurs.

It becomes a word ending in the sixth case (genitive). By this, he shows that even its own form is included under the term *aṇ*, and thus it becomes the grāhaka (the apprehender) of both *aṇ* and *udic*. Thus he says: "and of its own form," and so forth, beginning with "ādguṇaḥ. As in this [example]: [The text continues: ...as in this case.
Just as *guṇa* occurs in the case of *devendra*, so too does *guṇa* occur here in *khaṭvendra*. This is according to the rule *ṭhasya cvau* (Pāṇini 7.4.32),
as in the example *paṭībhavati*.
The same applies here in the case of *mālībhavati*. By the rule *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), just as the elision occurs in *dikṣiḥ*, so too does it occur in *cauḍiḥ*.
The suffix *iñ* is applied to the word *cūḍā* because it belongs to the *bāhv-ādi* group. [Regarding the statement] "vowel-quality, nasality," etc.: in the Sūtra, it is the acute (*udātta*) vowel.

When being perceived, it becomes the perceiver even of that which is distinguished by a different accent; likewise for the unaccented (*anudātta*) and the circumflex (*svarita*). Similarly, the nasalized (*sānunāsika*) is the perceiver of the non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*), and that [non-nasalized] is also the perceiver of the former.
[This is stated because] "it does not become long"—if there were no prohibition [by the rule] "not when it is a suffix" (*apratyaya*).

A suffix (*pratyaya*) would also be a grasper (*grāhaka*) of its own homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*). Consequently, even a long vowel (*dīrgha*) would [be so grasped]. Now, it might be argued that this is stating too little by saying "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*); rather, one should say "not a suffix, a substitute (*ādeśa*), nor those marked with *ṭ*, *k*, *i*, or *m*" (*apratyayādeśaṭitkinmit*). [This is because] in a suffix...
An example is provided: regarding the substitute—by *idama iś* (Pāṇini 5.3.3), [from *asmāt*] we get *itaḥ*, with *tasil* by *pañcamyāstasil* (5.3.7);
and [from *asmin*] we get *iha*, with *haḥ* by *idamo haḥ* (5.3.11). For in this case, if there were a reference to homogeneous vowels (*savarṇagrahaṇa*), [the rule would apply].

If the substitution of *yat* for *tyad* and so forth had not yet occurred when the substitution of *īś* took place, then by the principle of closest proximity (*antaratamya*), a three-moraic *īkāra* would result; however, if it has already occurred—

It would be three and a half morae (*mātrā*). If [the rule] "ṭhato guṇe" (Pāṇini 6.1.97) were applied such that the single-substitute form (*pararūpa*) had not yet occurred, it would still be three and a half morae;
but if it had already occurred, then it would be two and a half morae. Alternatively, since there is neither a three-and-a-half-mora nor a four-and-a-half-mora [vowel], it is two morae.
And it would consist of only a feminine suffix (*strīmātra*). Regarding the *ṭit* [suffix], by the rule "an *iṭ* is added to an *ardhadhātuka* beginning with a consonant" (7.2.35), we have *lavitā*;

if there were the inclusion of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇagrahaṇa*), the long vowel (*dīrgha*) would also occur. Regarding the *kit* [suffix], by the rule "the *vuk* augment is added to *bhū* in the *luṅ* and *liṭ* tenses" (6.4.88), we have *babhūva*; here, the nasalized form (*sānunāsika*) would also occur. For indeed...

The *yaṇ* [substitutes] are both nasalized (*sānunāsika*) and non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*). [For example, consider] *mit*—[as in the case of] *catur-anuḍuhorāmudāttaḥ* (P. 7.1.98) and *am sambuddhau* (P. 7.1.99); here, in *anaḍvān*, there would also be a long vowel. Should it then be stated in this way? No.

It must be stated: the particle *ca* (and) is used here, and it will serve the purpose of including prohibitions that have not been explicitly mentioned. Consequently, those [sounds] such as substitutes (*ādeśa*) for which the status of being a grasper (*grāhakatva*) is not desired do not grasp their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*).
They will come to pass.

But others say: "The term *apratyaḥ* here is not a technical designation (*saṃjñāgrahaṇa*); rather, it is a literal definition (*anvarthagrahaṇa*). That which is recognized, prescribed, or produced is a *pratyaya*. Therefore, [the term] *apratya*..."

The meaning of this is as follows: "A vowel (*aṇ*) being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇān na gṛhṇāti*). Since *ha*, *śa*, and so forth are also taught—that is, they are produced—they too are suffixes (*pratyaya*);
therefore, they do not include their homogeneous counterparts. This is the purpose of the word *ca* ("and").

The purpose [of this rule] must be stated. If it is argued that the purpose is the attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*) of the rule "its own form" (*svaṃ rūpam*), we say no; for because it has already been attracted, it would not continue to apply in subsequent rules. Nor is this purpose tenable, since its continued application is established by its very being marked with the *svarita* accent.
Now, if it is thought: "The word *svam* ending in the nominative case is the subject under discussion here, and its meaning is indicated by the genitive case;
therefore, the letter *ca* is used with effort so that it may take the genitive ending"—this too is not correct, for [the desired result] follows from the very sense of the matter.
Because the transformation of the case endings is established.

70. *taparas tatkālasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.70). He shows that *tapara* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, meaning "that after which *t* follows," and also a *pañcamī-tatpuruṣa* compound, meaning "that which is further than *t*. Furthermore, that [word ending in *t*] is in the fifth case (*pañcamī*).

It should be understood that this is a compound due to the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). But how can these two compounds be obtained when there is only one word, *ekaspara*? There is no fault here, for even a single word may be divided into two ways through repetition (*āvṛtti*). For in this context, there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the *bahuvrīhi*: namely, the rule "ato bhisa ais" (Pāṇini 7.1.9).
(7.1.9) Thus, the inclusion of *ta* (in *tapara*) is for this purpose.
For a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound is not applicable here; for what is intended here as *tapara* is the vowel *a*, not the case-ending *bhis*. And if it were a genitive *tatpuruṣa* here—
If that were so, then [the suffix] *bhis* would have to be followed by a *tapara* vowel; for in this context, a *tapara* is said to be a phoneme (*varṇa*), and this [suffix *bhis*] is not a phoneme.
What then? It is a collection thereof. However, there is evidence for a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound in the rule "vṛddhir ādaic" (Pāṇini 1.1.1), where the use of the *tapara* marker is employed.

For a *bahuvrīhi* compound is not appropriate here; if it were a *bahuvrīhi*, then the vowel *ā* would have the marker *t* (i.e., it would be *āt*), yet the addition of the marker *t* is not for the sake of the vowel *ā*, but rather for the sake of *ai* and *au*. This has been explained in that very place.

The term "of a similar vowel" (savarṇasya) continues [from the previous rule], yet a vowel cannot be similar to itself; indeed, it would apply to a collection of phonemes (varṇasamudāya). Therefore, even though no specific distinction is stated, it is understood that only a phoneme (varṇa) followed by *t* (tapara) is intended; thus he says: "A phoneme followed by *t*. The compound *tatkālasya* is a bahuvrīhi: "that which has the same duration as that."

"Time belongs to this"—this designation is improper. For instance: by the word *tat* (that), the "ta-para" (the letter *t* followed by *ra*) is referred to, and a *ta-para* is a phoneme (*varṇa*). Time, however, is held to be a specific kind of action (*kriyāviśeṣa*). Thus it has been said:
"Furthermore, others who know time understand time as the movement of the sun, planets, and constellations, which is differentiated by various divisions. (Vākyapadīya 3.9.76).
How then [could this apply] to the two words *tapara* and *kāla*, which denote specific phonetic qualities (*varṇa*) and actions (*kriyā*)?

What is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)? It is as follows: that whose time is like the time of that [action] is "tatkāla" (of that time). To demonstrate the meaning of this, he says:
"by itself," and so forth.

Although it might be argued that the application of the word *ātman* there [in Pāṇini 1.1.69] is appropriate due to its proximity to the mention of *tapara*, nevertheless, here [in Pāṇini 1.2.27], by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), it refers to the act of pronunciation known as "time" (*kāla*) which is associated with it. Why is this so? Because it is impossible for an action to be equal to a phoneme followed by *t* (*tapara*).

The designation [of a sound] by the name of another arises from association (*sāhacarya*). This is what is meant: "of that which has the same duration as the action associated with the sound followed by *t*. That is to say, the pronunciation of the sound followed by *t* is such that the pronunciation [of the other sound] is likewise.

"Of which there is an action" means: "of that which is endowed with another quality. This means: of that which is articulated as distinguished by a quality called a *dharma*—such as the acute (*udātta*) accent—and which is then connected with other qualities such as the acute and so forth.

"And of its own form" (*svasya ca rūpasya*). Since that [word *aṇ*] also recurs here, is this sūtra intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) or as an original injunction (*vidhyartha*)? If *aṇ* is understood to recur, then, since the matter would already be established by the preceding [sūtra], the commencement of this one would be for the sake of restriction (*niyama*).
"The meaning is that an *aṇ* vowel followed by *t* (tapara) is the grasper of its own duration alone,
and not of any other.
Now, since the term *aṇ* has been withdrawn, it serves the purpose of an injunction.

In that regard, according to the first position, under the view that "qualities are differentiators," the long vowel *ā*— which is followed by *t* and is devoid of nasality (*niranunāsika*)— is prescribed in the rule *ṭhviḍvanoranunāsikasyāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.41).

It would not be the grasper of that which possesses nasalization, because it lacks the quality of *aṇ*. Consequently, the substitute would be only that which is devoid of nasalization (*niranunāsika*). However, thinking that in the other alternative, even though there is a distinction between qualities, this fault does not arise, he states [the following] by resorting to the second position:

"This [rule] is for the purpose of an injunction. He asks, "How is it for the purpose of an injunction? and replies: "'The term *aṇ* does not recur,' and so on, including 'of *aṇ*s and others. It is logical that the *grahaṇaka-śāstra* (the rule of inclusion) applies only to other [sounds] with a following *t* (tapara), because their inclusion by the preceding [rule] is unestablished (*asiddha*). But as for the *aṇ*s...
Since the status of being the apprehender (*grāhakatva*) is already established by the preceding rule, how is this so? To this he says: "From this, *ais* for *bhis*, etc.
It might be argued that here too that [rule] would apply because it is without scope (*anavakāśatvāt*); to this he says: "From this..."

"Others," and so forth. In rules such as "ād guṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.87), the scope belongs to *aṇ* vowels that do not have a following *t* (*ataparāḥ*). However, the scope of this [present rule] belongs to long vowels that do not have the designation *aṇ* and which do have a following *t* (*anaṇas taparāḥ*), such as in "viḍvanoranunāsikasyāt" (Pāṇini 6.4.41). As for those *aṇ* vowels that do have a following *t*, [their scope is as previously defined].
The intention is that when both [rules] are applicable, this very *grahaṇaka-śāstra* (the rule for specific mention) operates on account of its priority. For example:
*vṛkṣaiḥ*, *plakṣaiḥ*. Here, the third-case plural ending is *bhis*. According to Pāṇini 7.1.9, *ato bhisa ais*, [the *ais* replacement applies].

Thus, there is the substitution of *ai*; then, by the rule "vṛddhir eci" (Pāṇini 6.1.88), a vṛddhi vowel is substituted [to form *apsvajaḥ* and *gojāḥ*]. Regarding the forms "apsvajaḥ" and "gojāḥ": the root *janī* (Dhātupāṭha 1149) means "to come into being"; thus, [the former] means "born in the waters," and [the latter] means "born among cows."
The rule states: "The suffix *viṭ* is applied after the verbal roots *da*, *jana*, *sana*, *kaka*, *khana*, and *krama*" (Pāṇini 3.2.67).

An example provided is *khaṭvābhiḥ*. But how can this serve as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), since by the rule "and like the end and the beginning" (Pāṇini 6.1.85), the status of being the end or the beginning must apply here, and consequently, the substitution of *ais* ought to occur?

But as for the inclusion of the long vowel *t* (taparakaraṇa), that which is to be excluded will be the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from the following vowel, as in "kīlālapābhiḥ" and "somapābhiḥ.
This is not a fault.

Regarding the rule *antādivacca* (Pāṇini 6.1.85), he will state there: "In a rule that depends on a specific phoneme (*varṇa*), the treatment as being either the end or the beginning is not desired. For instance, in the case of *khaṭvābhiḥ*, because the treatment as the end (*antavadbhāva*) does not apply, [the substitution of *ais* for *bhis* by the rule] *ato bhisa ais* [does not take place].
[The rule] "ais" (Pāṇini 7.1.9) does not apply.
Alternatively, in the word "ataḥ," a doubling of the vowel *a* has been made so that [the rule] may apply to the actually heard *at*.
71. *Ādirantyena sahetā* (Pāṇini 1.1.71).

This rule is commenced to avoid [the application of] a prescription regarding the own-form (*svarūpa*) [of a word]. This too is a technical definition (*saṃjñā-sūtra*). With respect to a thing that is not the first, a preceding thing does not possess the status of being "first" (*āditva*); and with respect to a thing that is the last...

Consequently, the "other" would possess the quality of being final. Moreover, in this case, it is not logical for the states of being "first" and "final" to be mutually dependent upon one another; for if that were so, there would be a further entity [between them].

Because there is the state of being a technical term (*saṃjñin*), a term consisting of the first [element] together with the last, along with its own accent (*svara*), would become a technical designation (*saṃjñā*). Consequently, for the purpose of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *svaṃ rūpam* (Pāṇini 1.1.68) here, the status of having a circumflex accent (*svaritatva*) would have to be assumed. Therefore, by means of the words "first" (*ādi*) and "last" (*anta*)...

Thinking that, by implication, the entity falling between the first and the last is indicated as being the *saṃjñin* (the named), he says: "of those falling between them. This plural number is used with reference to the class (*jāti*); otherwise, the word *aiṅ* would not be the designation (*saṃjñā*) for the vowel *o*.
It might be so.
But surely, by the words "beginning" and "end," specific spatial parts are denoted,
and parts [constitute] the whole, which is a collection.

Since it is a relative term (*sambandhiśabda*) meaning "belonging to *rūpa*," it is appropriate that the very same [term *rūpa*] is implied as the designatum (*saṃjñin*) by the words "beginning" (*ādi*) and "end" (*anta*). However, it should have been stated thus: "of the aggregate (*samudāya*) of those falling between them."

Thus he thinks: since [the author] provides the instruction by making the letter *y* the substitute for *yaṇ* when it follows a collection of letters—as in the rule "tasmādityuttarasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.67)—it is understood from this that the collection of letters is not the thing designated (*saṃjñin*); what then?

[The opponent argues: "Each [phoneme] is indeed a *varṇa* itself; otherwise, since the collection of *varṇas* is the designated object (*saṃjñin*), one would have made the designation by applying the *yaṇ*-substitution to the subsequent series of *varṇas*. [The proponent replies: "If you say that it was not done because it is impossible, we say no; for the substitution whose nature is a series of *varṇas* is indeed possible. Then..."

If it is argued that an operation cannot possibly apply to a collection as the designated entity, then, if an operation cannot apply to a collection from the perspective of what follows, let the individual phonemes themselves be the designated entities; in that case, the operation [applies].

It is possible [that it would apply]; why [then] by means of the whole [term]? [The answer is: so that there might not be a grasping by the [single sound] *ṭh*. But surely even that [sound *ṭh*] is at the very end of that much of a limit?
No; because that much of a limit is not intended to be expressed. For this [is merely] the letter *ṭ*.

In the rules *ṭhṭāṅsiṅsāminātsyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.12) and *dvitīyāṭaussvenaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.34), [the mention of] *ṭ* is for the purpose of qualifying the third case singular (*ṭā*), and not for the purpose of forming a pratyāhāra (abbreviated term).
Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *ādi* (beginning)? It is so that the entire group together with the final letter does not become the technical name (*saṃjñā*).

This is not so; for names and words possess the property of recurrence (*āvṛti*). It is only the initial element that recurs in the various rule-utterances (*pradeśavākya*), not the entire aggregate; therefore, even without the explicit mention of the "initial" (*ādi*), [the desired result follows].

By implication, it is understood that the designation applies only to the first [phoneme] together with the last, and not to the entire collection. If this is so, then for the purpose of clarifying precisely that meaning which has been obtained through implication, [the word] "first" (ādi)—

[The word] "grahaṇam" [is used]. Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the word "saha" (together), since the sense of "together" is understood by the instrumental case alone, as in the rule "vṛddho yūnā" (Pāṇini 1.2.65)? This is not so; for [the word "saha"] is also [necessary] in the sense of "characteristic of such a state" (itthambhūtalakṣaṇa).

The third [alternative] exists. And if that were the case, then a beginning [element] alone, characterized by the final element designated as *it*, would constitute the technical name (*saṃjñā*). Consequently, in the specific rules (*pradeśa*), the case-ending would not be applied to the aggregate [of sounds] in the forms *akaḥ*, *ikaḥ*, and *aci*, because, being devoid of meaning, they would not be nominal stems (*aprātipadikatvāt*). [This is addressed by the word] "together" (*saha*).

However, because "perception" (saṃjñā) is mentioned as co-occurring [with the word], it functions as the name for the entire collection; thus, since it possesses the status of a nominal stem (prātipadika), the case ending is obtained.

The inclusion of the letter *i*, however, is for the purpose of ensuring that the designation [of the *it*] does not apply to the letter *c* in the rule "ṭha-ṭha-ta-ta-va" (Pāṇini 1.3.7), which is not designated as an *it* by the rule "ṭaci" (Pāṇini 1.3.6). Its status as the final [element] is as previously stated, and not with respect to the entire group. If this is so, then...

The designation *it* would apply [to the final letter] by the rule "ṭh-ḷ-antyaṃ" (1.3.3); for that reason, in the rule "na vibhaktau tu-smāḥ" (1.3.4), a separation of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) must be made by adding the word "na."

72. *yenavidhistadantasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.72). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasya*. This too is a technical definition (*saṃjñāsūtra*), not a governing rule (*paribhāṣā*). For here the restrictive nature, which is the characteristic of a *paribhāṣā*, is not present. [The word] *yena*— [Note: The text provided ends abruptly with "yena". The full sūtra is *yenavidhistadantasya*: "That by which a grammatical operation is prescribed applies to that which ends with it."]

The third case ending (*karaṇe tṛtīyā*) is prescribed. Since it is performed as something previously non-existent, the word *vidhi* has *karman* as its grammatical derivation (*sādhana*); it ends in the suffix *ki*, according to the rule "upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ" (Pāṇini 3.3.92).

Regarding the expression "tadantasya": this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has that as its final member. By the word *tat*, that very same word functioning as the instrument (*karaṇa*) is referred back. This word *anaṭ* denotes a constituent part (*avayava*), and a constituent part belongs to a whole (*samudāya*). Therefore, this [suffix] belongs to that very [whole].
He says that a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is understood [by this rule]: "The name applies to the aggregate," as in *avaśyalāvyam* and *avaśyapāvyam*. [The root] *lūñ* means "to cut" (Dhātupāṭha 1484).

From the root *pūñ* meaning "to purify" (*dhā.pā.* 1483), after the vowel has been lengthened, the substitution of *āv* occurs by the rule *vānto yi pratyaye* (Pāṇini 6.1.79). A compound is formed because it belongs to the *mayūravyaṃsaka*-group;
then, the letter *m* is elided according to the rule *lumped avaśyamaḥ kṛtyeḥ* (Kāśikā 6.1.144).

Now, why is it that a technical name (*saṃjñā*) cannot apply here to a stem ending in a vowel, according to the rule "ṭheco'yavāyāvaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.78)? What would be the consequence? In forms such as *cayanaṃ* (the act of piling), *cāyakaḥ* (one who piles), *lavanaṃ* (the act of cutting), and *lāvakaḥ* (one who cuts), because [the substitutes] consist of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), the *ay*-class substitutions would have to be replacements for the whole (*sarvādeśa*). This is not a fault.

"Substitutes apply to that which is being specified" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 106); thus, they will apply only to this very [element], not to everything ending in it. Alternatively, such a domain does not exist for this rule at all; therefore, it does not operate here. For instance, in the case of the instrumental [case] in the word *yena*.

It has been stated that it is the third [factor]; and since there can be no instrument (karaṇa) without an agent (kartṛ), the agent is also implied. Furthermore, in this context, because it is a relative term, the "whole" (samudāya) is understood by means of the word "end" (anta), which denotes a part; and due to the subject under discussion, both the essential nature (svarūpa) and the agent are indicated by the three [suffixes].
[The term *dvivacanam*] is present [in the sūtra] in various ways. In some cases, it is due to explicit mention (*nirdeśāt*), as in "īdūded dvivacanam" (P.
