1.1.11); here, the dual number (*dvivacanam*) is mentioned as the agent (*kartṛ*). Thus, by means of the instruments (*karaṇa*) consisting of *ī*, *ū*, and *e*, it prescribes the designation *pragṛhya*. In other cases, it is due to context (*prakaraṇāt*), as for example...

Regarding the rule *ṭherac* (Pāṇini 3.3.56): here, because of the governing authority (*adhikāra*) of *dhātoḥ* (3.1.91), the verbal root (*dhātu*) is present by implication, and the agent (*kartṛ*) is proximate. That [agent] effects the vowel (*ac*) by means of the instrumental suffix *-ika*.
In some cases, this occurs by virtue of contextual necessity (*sāmarthya*), as in *iko jhal* (1.2.9).

Thus, here the suffix *san* is prescribed after the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone and not after anything else; therefore, by implication, the agent (*kartṛ*)—which is the verbal root—is present [as the base].
That [agent], through the letter *i*, effects the *kit*-status of *san*. Consequently, [the rule] "īdūded dvivacanam" [applies].

In such cases as (1.1.11), since both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*) are present, that [agent] constitutes the scope of this sūtra; therefore, the rule of extension to the end of the compound (*tadantavidhi*) applies there. However, in the case of *ṭheco'yavāyāvaḥ* (6.1.78), it is not so.
An agent is not present by any means whatsoever, and an instrument cannot exist without an agent; therefore,
since neither the agent nor the instrument is present, this is not the subject matter of this sūtra.

The rule of *tadanta-vidhi* (application of an operation to that which ends with a specified element) is not possible here; therefore, it must be "stated" (*vaktavya*), meaning it must be explained. In this regard, the following explanation is given: in rules such as *dvitīyā śrita-* (Pāṇini 2.1.24), the case endings (*sup*) are qualified by words such as *śrita*, and not the words *śrita* and so on by the case endings.
And by means of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*),

the rule of "extension to that which ends in it" (*tadantavidhi*) applies, but not by means of the qualified (*viśeṣya*). Since the instrumental case in the word *anena* denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*),
and an instrument is dependent and exists for the sake of another, whereas the qualified is not, therefore [the rule applies] to the qualifiers.

In the case of [rules] such as *śritādibhis tadantavidhir na bhavati* ("there is no application of the rule regarding that which ends in those beginning with *śrita*") and *naḍādibhyaḥ phak* ("the suffix *phak* after those beginning with *naḍa*"),
here too, the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) are qualified by *naḍa* and the others,
and not the nominal stem by *naḍa* and the others.

Therefore, even here, the rule of "specification by the final element" (tadantavidhi) does not apply—except in the case of the mention of *u* and *g* as markers (*ugit*) or the mention of a phoneme (*varṇa*). In the expression "by *ugit*" and "by a phoneme," the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is qualified;
and by means of a qualifier, the rule of specification by the final element certainly does apply.
"In that which [there is] a rule," and so forth. When the rule of "extension to the end" (*tadanta-vidhi*) would have applied, the rule of "extension to the beginning" (*tadādi-vidhi*) is stated.
By the phrase "in that which" (*yasmin*), he shows the extension to the beginning when a locative case (*saptamī*) is indicated. This applies wherever there is a mention of *al* (a phoneme).

When a rule is prescribed for that which is designated by the locative case (saptamī-nirdiṣṭe), it should be understood as applying to what precedes it and begins with it; the meaning is "in the beginning of that which follows *al*. If, however, the rule were to apply to what ends with that (*tadanta-vidhi*) even there, then it would apply only in this case—namely, *śriyau*—but it would not apply here: *śriyaḥ*. But if the rule applies to the beginning of that (*tadādi-vidhi*), [it applies correctly].
The term *śriyā* occurs both in the sense of "possessing" (*satī*) and in the sense of "one's own form" (*svasya ca rūpasya*). Regarding rule 73:

*vṛddhir yasyācām ādis tad vṛddham*—"That [group] of which the first vowel among the vowels is called *vṛddhi* is termed *vṛddha*. Here, the word *yasya* refers to the entire group; it means that for that very group, the first among its vowels is designated by the technical term *vṛddhi*.

A technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed for the form of the word [consisting of the letters *vṛddhi*]. And since that [form] necessarily consists of a collection [of phonemes], by implication, even the general term "that of which" (*yasya*) denotes the collection itself. The expression "that of which" (*yasya*) is stated for the purpose of indicating the bearer of the designation (*saṃjñin*). [This refers to] those whose technical designation is "vṛddhi," as indicated by the phrase "among the vowels," and so forth.
By demonstrating that the selection of a single part from a whole is intended, he shows that the genitive case in *acām* functions as a genitive of selection (*nirdhāraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*).
Here, the word *ādi* occurs in the sense of "commencement" (*upakrama*); it is called *upakrama* because it is commenced (*upakramyate*).

The meaning is "pronounced first. Because of the use of the plural number in the term *acām*, that which is preceded by a vowel (*ac*) designated as *vṛddhi* among many vowels must alone receive the designation *vṛddhi*; it does not apply to that which occurs between two [vowels].
In order to remove this objection, he says:
"Of vowels," and so forth.
If, then, this is a genitive of selection (*nirdhāraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*)—meaning "among vowels"—then, in that case, [the operation] would apply only to those of the same class.

The sense would be that this is a specification (*nirdhāraṇa*), meaning that among vowels, [the term *vṛddhi*] should apply only to those beginning with *ā*. And if that were the case, then a name such as *Āśvalāyana*, which begins with the vowel *ā*, would not be designated [by the term *vṛddha*], for [the rule] does not apply to the vowel *ā* alone.

The primary status [of the term *mukhya*] exists because of its application to the sense organs (*akṣu*); however, it may be used figuratively, as in the rule "a vowel (*uṇ*), when followed by an *it*, denotes its homogeneous sound, except when it is itself an affix" (Pāṇini 1.1.69).

Thus, by this [rule], even that which is not an *ac* performs the function of an *ac*. Nor is it proper to resort to a secondary (*gauṇa*) sense when a primary (*mukhya*) one is available, because in the case of a primary and a secondary sense, the operation is understood to apply to the primary.
This is not a fault; for, according to the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*), one may resort to the secondary status of *ac* even for the letter *ā*.
Otherwise, he would have prescribed the mention of *aṬ* alone, rather than the mention of *vṛddhi*.
[Examples are] *śālīyaḥ*, *mālīyaḥ*, and so forth. Here, since the designation *vṛddha* applies, [the suffix] *cha* is applied by Pāṇini 4.2.114: *vṛddhāccchaḥ*.
Thus it is said.

But surely, there should not be a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for the words *śālāmālā* and *kāpaṭua*, for these [words]— [...do not denote a genus, etc. (The sentence is incomplete in the source text).

Is the initial [element] that which is designated as *vṛddhi*? No; rather, it is the consonant (*hal*). This is not so; for even though a consonant exists here, it is not taken into account, because the status of being "initial" is relied upon with reference to vowels (*ac*) alone. Indeed, this is precisely the purpose of the mention of *ac*: how indeed could that [status of being initial] depend upon it?

Is it so that [the status of] being the first vowel (*āditva*) may be understood? Otherwise, [the operation] would have to be performed there [in every case]. When the mention of *ac* (vowels) is made, the meaning becomes correct: "among the vowels (*ac*), whichever one has the designation *vṛddhi* and is situated at the beginning of *ajeḥ*" [i.e., *aj-ādi*]. [This applies] to [vowels] other than those [specific] vowels.

The meaning is that for which the term "vṛddhi" (the technical name for the vowels ā, ai, and au) is pronounced first. By this, the designation [of "vṛddha"] is established even for words such as *śālā*.
In the rule "sābhāsannayanaḥ," because the designation "vṛddhi" is absent, only the suffix *aṇ* occurs, and not the suffix *ccha*.

If, however, the mention of "ādi" (beginning with) were not made, then this designation would apply even to that [vowel] among the vowels which has some sound designated as *vṛddhi*— such as the *sabhāsannayana*— in its midst. Although the word *vṛddhi* is heard here, nevertheless...

The technical rule (paribhāṣā) regarding "that which possesses the same marker" (talliṅgaka) does not apply here. This is because that rule operates where *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are prescribed for a specific substitute;
it functions there to restrict the original element (*sthānin*). And this has already been stated previously.

Furthermore, there is no prescription for *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* in this [rule]; therefore, that [term] has no operation here. Consequently, even for one whose initial element is designated as *vṛddhi* regardless of its position, that designation still applies.

It is established: "Or [the term *nāmadheya* applies] to a name," and so forth. This designation should be understood as applying to those words—such as "Devadatta" and the like—which are uttered by people for the sake of worldly transaction; it applies to those very words.
The word *nāmadheya* is used in its conventional sense (*rūḍha*), and not in the case of words such as *go* (cow) and so forth, which are based on causes such as genus (*jāti*) and the like,

and which fall within beginningless linguistic usage. But surely, because of their inclusion in the *kāśyādi* group, the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha* ought to apply by the rule *kāśyādibhyaṣ ṭhañ* (Pāṇini 4.2.116)?
That is incorrect, as it is an example of a word ending in the suffix *ccha* [forming *devadattīya*]. This is not a fault; for he who belongs to Devadatta is indeed called "Devadatta."

The word *devadatta* [in this context] is based on its function (*kriyānimittaka*); its recitation there refers to that very word in its functional sense, not to the word as a proper name (*saṃjñāśabda*). Therefore, when the designation *vṛddha* applies to the word *devadatta* as a proper name, then the suffix *cha* occurs;
otherwise, however, the suffix *aṇ* applies. This is seen in rules such as "after a word ending in a *gotra* suffix," and likewise in the rule "not after a compound."

The suffix *cha* is applied after a word ending in the patronymic suffix *aṇ* that is *vṛddha*, as well as after a compound that is not *vṛddha*. For example: *ghṛtarauḍhiḥ*. This is according to the Vārttika: "In the section concerning grammatical coordination (*samānādhikaraṇa*), there is an addition for compounds such as *śākapārthiva* and others, with the elision of the final member."
This is a compound. Similarly, for "the descendant of Uta-rūḍha" and "the descendant of Pāṇina," the suffix *iñ* is applied according to *Pāṇini* 4.1.95 (*ata iñ*).
In the list of *bāhvādi* stems, the rule *sambhūyo'mbhasaḥ salopaśca* (Gaṇasūtra 66) is recited.
The word *kāśyapa* ends in the suffix *añ*, according to the rule for the *bidādi* group. [Examples are] *jaihvakātāḥ* and *hāritakātāḥ*.
The word *kātya* ends in the suffix *yañ*, according to the *gargādi* group. A *kātya* who is fickle-tongued is a *jihvākātya*;

a *kātya* who eats green [vegetables] is a *haritakātya*. From these two, the regular suffix *aṇ* is applied by the general rule [Pāṇini 4.1.83], [the elision of which is governed by] "of that which [ends in a taddhita suffix]" (*yasyeti*).
There is elision of the letter *a* by [Pāṇini 6.4.148] *ca*; and there is elision of the letter *ya* by [Pāṇini 6.4.151] *āpatyasya ca taddhite 'nāti*.

74. *Tyadādīni ca* (1.1.74). Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the subsequent [rule]": since this [term] has a purpose in the following sūtra, one might ask why it does not also serve the purpose of this [present] rule. To this he says: "it is not connected here."
Thus, if this were also connected here, then the meaning would be:

"That [word] for which the *tyad*-class [words] constitute the initial vowel among its vowels is augmented [with *su-*, etc.]"; and consequently, it would apply only in cases such as *tvatputraḥ* and the like, but not to the *tyad*-class words when they are used alone.

Such is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: in expressions such as *tvatputraḥ* ("your son") and *matputraḥ* ("my son"), the words *tvad* and *mad* are subordinate members (*upasarjana*), and for such subordinate members, the status of being a *tyadādi* (a pronoun of the *tyad*-class) [does not apply].
[This has been] refuted; so how can this objection arise?

If the phrase "of that which begins with *a* and so forth" were connected here [to the word *sarvanāman*], then, because it is subordinate (*upasarjana*), by virtue of the rule, the designation would apply only to those beginning with *tyad* and so forth, and not [to others].

[The author] considers [the word "only" (*kevala*)] to apply to these alone. But how, then, can that which is being carried over here be disconnected? Because it is carried over as connected to its own [own] context.
[This is seen in] "That whose initial vowels among its vowels are *vṛddhi* is called *vṛddha*" (Pāṇini 1.1.73), and likewise in the case of "the pronouns beginning with *tyad*" (Pāṇini 1.1.74).
They are termed *vṛddhi*. Regarding the rule "That [word] is called *vṛddha* whose first vowel among its vowels is a *vṛddhi*" (Pāṇini 1.1.73), that is *vṛddha*.

In the rule "The *eṅ* sounds [denote] the eastern regions" (1.1.75), the mention of "the first among its vowels" (*yasyācāmādi*) is understood to carry over, while the mention of "*vṛddhi*" has ceased to apply. Thus...
The mention of *vṛddhi* is discontinued. Thus, while the word *vṛddhi* continues to be connected [to the previous rule], it cannot be connected with *tyad* and so forth. For example:
*tvādāyaniḥ*, *mādāyaniḥ*. [This is governed by] *udīcāṃ vṛddhādagotrāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.157).

Thus, by the suffix *phiñ*, and by the rule "ṭhpratyayotarapadayośca" (Pāṇini 7.2.97), the substitutes *tvā* and *mā* replace *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. The particle *ca* (and) serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; therefore, it is unnecessary to state the supplementary rule "vā nāmadheyasya" (Vārttika 15) and so forth.
75. *eṅ prācāṃ deśe* (1.1.75).

[The commentary states: "*ṭhprācāṃ deśābhidhāne*" (in the case of denoting a region of the easterners). The meaning is: when there is a designation of that region which belongs to the easterners (*prācām*).

By this, he shows that the qualification "of the Easterners" (*prācām*) is not intended as an optional alternative; rather, it is explained that the phrase "according to the opinion of the Easterners" (*prācāṃ matena*) is not meant to be emphasized. [Examples include] *aiṇīpacanīyaḥ* and so forth. From words such as *eṇīpacana*, the suffix *cha* is applied. [This is according to the rule] *āhicchatraḥ*.
In the case of "Kānyakubjaḥ," the suffix *aṇ* alone occurs after the words *Ahicchatra* and *Kānyakubja*.
In the case of "Devadattaḥ," although the rule *vāhīkagrāmebhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.2.117) prescribes the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭh* under the heading governing *vṛddha* [names],
they do not apply here because [Devadatta] belongs to the *kāśyapādi* group.

Even from the recitation [of the word], those two do not occur; for the word *devadatta* is recited there as being based on an action (*kriyānimittaka*), and this is a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) for a technical name (*saṃjñāśabda*). And this is so when [the rule] "or [it applies] to a proper name" (*vā nāmadheyasya*, Vārttika 15) is [in effect].

When the designation "vṛddha" does not apply, it should be understood as follows: in the case of *gau-matāḥ*, everything is present there, yet it is not a name for a country. For instance, the river Gomatī is in the eastern region, but [the term] is not the name of a country. Indeed, it is a river.
It is included by the term "region" (*deśa*); for in the rule *nadīdeśo’grāmāḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.7), the river is mentioned separately [from the region].
Also in *eṅ prācāṃ deśe* (4.2.103) and *udīcāṃ vṛddhādagotrāt* (4.1.157).

In such passages as these, "eastward and northward" (prāgudañcau) are heard, yet their distinction is not understood. Therefore, for the sake of that understanding, he says: "Eastward and northward," etc. [There is] a river named Śarāvatī; [the region] to the east of it...
The eastern region is established as the east, and the northern region as the north. The Śarāvatī river divides these two;

that is, it establishes them through division, for it is only when that boundary exists that their distinction is fully understood. For what purpose does it divide them? [For the sake] of the learned...

"For the sake of establishing words" means for the sake of the derivation of words among the learned grammarians. How does he analyze it? "Just as a swan [separates] milk and water. Regarding the term "milk and water":

The singular form [of the compound] is due to the rule "jātir aprāṇinām" (Pāṇini 2.4.6). In some places, the reading is "kṣīrodake"; this should be understood according to the rule "sarvo dvandvo vibhāṣayaikavad bhavati" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 91), which states that every *dvandva* compound may optionally be treated as a singular. For example:
Just as a swan establishes milk and water that have come into a state of mixture separately without confusion, so too [does it establish] the Śarāvatī flowing eastward and northward.
Because of the necessary connection between "yat" and "tat," by the mention of "sā" (she), even though it was not explicitly stated, [it is understood].

This is what is obtained: "May she who divides [the directions] protect us. However, in the well-known reading where the verse says *prāgudīcāu*, how is it that the vowel *ī* occurs there, given that it is prescribed for a stem marked with the technical term *bha* by the rule *acaḥ ṭhuda īt* (Pāṇini 6.4.139)? And how is it that [the suffix] *ṭhak* applies to stems ending in *uc* or *ac*?
It must be considered why the *num* augment does not occur [in this case] by the rule "sarvanāmasthāne 'dhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.70). On this point, they explain as follows:
"ac-pratyanvavapūrvāt sāmalomnaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.75).

In this case, the suffix *ac* is applied by means of splitting the rule (*yogavibhāga*) [Pāṇini 3.3.56]. Consequently, when *ac* follows, the designation *bha* applies and the substitution of long *ī* (ītvam) occurs; however, the augment *num* does not occur, because [the condition for *num*] is a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix other than *ac*.
Regarding the phrase "because of being separated":
however, others form the compound *prāgudīcām* as a collective (*samāhāra*).
According to them, when the suffix *ṭac* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) by the rule *dvandvāccudaṣahāntāt samāhāre* (Pāṇini 5.4.106), [the form *prāgudīcām* arises].
As before, the substitution of *ī* occurs and the elision of *num* takes place.
In some places, however, the reading is *prāg udīcaḥ*; there, the plural number is used because one intends to express plurality with respect to the location of the constituent parts.
The meaning is that they divide [the world] into eastern regions and northern regions.
This is from the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā* composed by the venerable teacher Jinendrabuddhi, a follower of the Bodhisattva school.
The first quarter of the first chapter.
Now begins the second quarter of the first chapter: 1. gāṅ-kuṭādibhyaḥ añ-ṇini-t (Pāṇini 1.2.1).
In this regard, three possible interpretations are conceivable: either the letter *ṅ* bearing the technical designation *it* is brought into being by this [rule];

or those suffixes following roots beginning with *gāṅ* and *kuṭādi* that are not marked by *ṇ* or *it* become "marked by *ṅ*" (*ṅta*), meaning, in effect, that the letter *ṅ* bearing the designation *it* becomes associated with them; for it is in this way that they become "marked by *ṅ*" (*iṅta*).

For if the marker *ṅ* is prescribed as an *anubandha* for them, it cannot be otherwise; indeed, Devadatta does not become "possessor of brindled cows" (*citragu*) without the brindled cows themselves. Alternatively, this [sūtra] establishes the technical name *ṅit*:
those affixes following the root *gāṅ* and the roots beginning with *kuṭ* that are not marked with *ṇ* or *i* are designated as *ṅit*.

They become marked with the *ṅ* [indicatory letter], so to speak. This may be an extended application (*atideśa*): the meaning is that those affixes following roots beginning with *gāṅ* and *kuṭ* which are not marked with *ṇ* or *it* become as if they were marked with *ṅ*; that is, they become as if they possessed the *ṅ* [indicatory letter]. Among these, in the first case...
In the alternative view (*pakṣe*), when the ablative case in the rule *gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ* is interpreted as a genitive by virtue of the rule *aṇṇit*—
which originally appears in the nominative— the letter *ṅ* becomes a substitute (*ādeśa*) in place of the initial *al* (phoneme), according to the statement *ādeḥ parasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.54).
In the second alternative,
however, there would be no comprehension of the *saṃjñin* (the thing named) in the rule "ṭhaniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti" (Pāṇini 6.4.24).
Because of the difference in the words [used]. For the word *ṅ* is one thing, while the word *k* is another.

Furthermore, in the rule *ṅd-agrahaṇe grahy-ādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.1.16), there would result the inclusion of these very technical names (*saṃjñin*), and not of *yaṅ* and so forth; for when there is a choice between a technical term (*kṛtrima*) and a non-technical term (*akṛtrima*), the technical term is preferred.

This is because of the statement: "The cognition of the effect [arises from the word]" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 6). Even if these defects could somehow be avoided, in the case of the first two positions, when activity is established by means of avoiding those defects, the fault of excessive complexity (*pratipatti-gaurava*) would result.
That [objection] is indeed unavoidable. However, thinking that there is no fault whatsoever in the third alternative, he relies on that very one and says: "This is an extended application (atideśa).
If this is so, the designation should have been made using the suffix -vat; otherwise, its meaning would not be understood.

This is not so; for words employed in reference to the entities of another [category] convey the sense of the suffix *vati* even without it being explicitly stated, as in "the boy is a lion" (*siṃho māṇavakaḥ*) or "the Vāhīka is an ox" (*gaurvāhīkaḥ*).

The substitution of *gāṅ* for *iṅ* is understood from the rules "after *iṅ*, [the substitute is *gā*] when followed by *liṭ*" (*iṅśca*, 2.4.48) and "for *iṅ*, *gāṅ* is substituted when *liṭ* follows" (*gāṅ liṭi*, 2.4.49).

Regarding the rule *vibhāṣā luṅ-lṛṅoh* (Pāṇini 2.4.50): this refers to that substitution of *gāṅ* which will be taught in place of *iṅ*, and not to the root *gāṅ* meaning "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 950). Now, why is the root *gāṅ* meaning "to go" not taken [as the referent]?
He says "it occurs" and so forth, beginning with "of the sound *ṅ*.

Is the purpose of this [mention] of the sound *ṅ* belonging to the substitute *iṅ* such that, in this rule (*sūtra*), only that [specific *ṅ*] should be grasped and nothing else should serve as the basis for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*)? No; [this is not the case] regarding the middle voice.

Because it is already established by the very nature of being a *sthāna* (place of articulation), therefore only the *iṅ* region is understood [by the term *sthāna*]; otherwise, the letter *ṅ* would be redundant. But surely, the letter *ṅ* might serve to include both [the *iṅ* and *ūṣman* regions] as general categories—so how could there be redundancy? This is not so; for if those two...

In that case, its purpose would be to include both as a general category only if they were identical; however, they are not identical. This is because the *ṅ* of the root *gāṅ*, which has the sense of "going," serves the purpose of [indicating] the *ātmanepada* suffixes, whereas for the other [root], the *ṅ* never fulfills such a function. Therefore, since their purposes are not the same, it is incorrect to treat them as a general category.

The word *gāṅ* is understood here. But for what purpose is it pronounced in this way? Why not simply say *gā*? It cannot be done so; for if that were the case, according to the rule "when there is a mention of a base without an *anubandha*, a base with an *anubandha* is not included" (*Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā* 53), only the root *gai* (meaning 'to sing') from the Dhātupāṭha (916–917) would be grasped.

It would be so; for the *kuṭ*-class [of roots] begins from *ṭhkuṭa kauṭilye* (DhP 1366) and extends as far as *ṭhkuṅ śabde* (DhP 1401). This is because after that point, due to the application of the marker *vṛt*, it is impossible for any further roots to belong to the *kuṭ*-class.
Regarding *adhyagīṣṭa*: since the suffix *sic* has a *ṅ*-marker, the substitution of *ī* occurs by the rule *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām hali* (Pāṇini 6.4.66).

For here, from the preceding rule *dīṅo yuḍ aci kṅiti* (6.4.65), the term *kṅti* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*), and from *īdyati* (6.4.65), the term *īt* is also carried over. Regarding *adhyagīṣata*.

The substitution of *at* [for *ā*] occurs by the rule "ṭhātmanepadeṣvanataḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.5). Now, why has no example been shown for the substitution of *gāṅ* that occurs in the *liṭ* [perfect tense]? He thinks as follows: this is indeed a case of *luṅ* [aorist], and it does not require the mention of *liṭ* here; for [the rule] "aṃsayogālliṭ" [prescribes *gāṅ*] specifically for the *liṭ*.
Because it is already established by the rule that will be stated as *kit* (1.2.5). Regarding *utkuṭitā*:
the root is *kuṭa* in the sense of "crookedness" (*kauṭilye*; DhP 1366). Regarding *utpuṭitā*:
the root is *puṭa* in the sense of "joining together" (*saṃśleṣaṇe*; DhP 1367). Now, regarding *uccukuṭiṣati*, [this is] from the root *kuṭ* with the suffix *san*.

Why does the Ātmanepada ending not occur because of the presence of the marker *ṅ*? Because of the governing rule concerning "original instruction" (*upadeśa*). For in that context, the term "original instruction" (*upadeśe*) from Pāṇini 1.3.2 is understood to carry over. And here, the status of having the marker *ṅ* is not one belonging to the original instruction; rather, it is one resulting from extended application (*atideśika*).

Regarding the rule *ṭhvyaceḥ* and so forth: the root *vyaca* in the sense of "deceit" (*vyājīkaraṇe*) is listed among the *tud*-class roots, prior to the *kuṭ*-class roots. As for the form *vicitā*, the suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied here by the rule *grahy-ādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 6.1.16).

The prefix *sam-pra* is applied. [The form] *uru-vyacāḥ* is derived by adding the suffix *asun* according to *asarvadhātubhyo 'sun* (Dhātupāṭha 9.49). The lengthening of the vowel occurs according to *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.14).
[The rule] *vija iṭ* (Pāṇini 1.2.2) applies.
"An affix beginning with *iṭ*": that which has *iṭ* as its initial element, such as *tṛc* and so forth, is thus described. Now, why is there not an inclusion of the *iṭ* of the third person singular?
Because its status as *kit* is already established by the rule "A sārvadhātuka affix that is not *pit* is *kit*" (Pāṇini 1.2.4).

This is not so; for where [the substitution] is not established by that [rule], there the mention of *iṭ* would be for the purpose of prescribing the third person singular ending *ṅ*. And where is it not established by that?
In the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix *liṅ* used in the sense of benediction (*āśis*), as in "uiddvijīṣīya. Therefore, this is correct.

There is the inclusion of the third person singular [suffix], but not of the augment; this is due to two *paribhāṣās*: "when there is the mention of something meaningful, that which is meaningless is not included" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 9), and "between a suffix and a non-suffix, only the suffix is to be understood" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 72). Even if, however, the augment *iṭ* were somehow included...

[Objection: Even so, only that [suffix] itself would obtain the designation *ṅit*, but not a suffix beginning with it. Why, then, does he say: "A suffix beginning with *iṭ* becomes *ṅit*"? [Response: He thinks as follows:
the term "beginning" (*ādi*) from [Pāṇini 1.1.73], "That whose first vowel is *vṛddhi*," is understood here by way of anuvṛtti.
If it were [the augment] by that [rule], it would be distinguished [from others]. Furthermore, the first-person singular [suffix] does not possess the property of being marked with *ṅ* (ṅtvam);
rather, it is the augment itself that has this property. Therefore, that [augment] alone is understood [to be intended].

And since there is no purpose for that [augment] alone when it is the initial element, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), the suffix beginning with *iṭ* is understood to have the property of being marked with *ṅ*.
It is understood as "udvijitā. Because of the *ṇ* [in *udvij*], the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya* (Pāṇini 7.3.86) does not apply, and thus no *guṇa* substitution occurs.
3. *vibhāṣorṇoḥ* (1.2.3).
In the form *prorṇuvitā*, since the suffix is marked with ṅ, guṇa is prohibited; consequently, by the rule *aci śnudhātu* (Pāṇini 6.4.77), the substitution of *uvaṅ* occurs.
4. *sārvadhātukam apit* (Pāṇini 1.2.4). Regarding the word *apit*: is this a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (a simple negation) or a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion)? What is the consequence here?
In the former case, for the first person singular of the imperative (*loṭ*), [the rule] "āṭ is added to the first person singular, and it is also *pit*" would apply.

When the augment *āṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.4.92] in the case of *tudāni*, the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for the vowel *ā* of the class-marker (*vikaraṇa*) and the vowel *i* of the affix *pit* is treated as the beginning of the subsequent element by virtue of [Pāṇini 6.1.85], "and that which is substituted for the end of a preceding element is treated like the beginning of the following.
Thus, because it is grasped by the term *pit*, it possesses the status of *pit*; and since it is *pit*...
Even if [the rule] were applied, there would be a prohibition of the *ṅt* designation; consequently, *guṇa* substitution for the root would result.

However, in the other alternative, in cases such as "they move" (*cyavante*) and "they float" (*plavante*), since the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for the *śabanta* [stem-final] *ā* and the *i* of the *pit* suffix is distinct from the *pit* [suffix], the *ṅt* designation would be precluded, and consequently—

Does the *guṇa* substitution not apply to the verbal root? [Objection: But because the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for [the final vowel of the root] and [the initial vowel of] *pit* is treated as the beginning of the subsequent element, it would be included by the mention of "the following" (*para*), and thus the rule would apply. [Response: It shall be exactly as you wish;
there is no fault in either case. First, there is no fault in the former view; because [the substitute] belongs to *pit* itself...
In the case of *tudāni*, there is a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) [of the augment *āṬ* and the suffix], but not [the substitution] of *pi* for *apit*. For it is thus:
by the rule *āḍuttamasya pi ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.92), the status of being *pit* is prescribed only for the final person of the imperative (*loṭ*), and not for the augment *āṬ*.
There is no fault in the other case either, because by the term *api* (in the rule *apittād ārdhadhātukam*), the sārvadhātuka suffix is qualified.
"Whatever else [is a suffix] is sārvadhātuka, except for that which has an *ap* augment. Now, the final vowel *ā* of the word *anta* is not itself the *sārvadhātuka*;
what then? It is a portion thereof. Furthermore, that which is the *sārvadhātuka* here does not undergo a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with it;
and that with which it does undergo a single-substitute is not the *sārvadhātuka*. Therefore—
Even though this single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is other than a *pit* [suffix], nevertheless it is not a *sārvadhātuka*;

so how could there be the possibility of it being called *ṅti*? Or, even if it were *ṅti*, even though it has that *ṅt*-designation, there is no possibility of the absence of *guṇa* [strengthening] because of it, since "an operation concerning a vowel (*vārṇa*) takes precedence over an operation concerning a suffix (*āṅga*)."

Because of the rule "balīyaḥ" (Pāṇini Vyākaraṇa Paribhāṣā 39), the substitutes [for the roots] fall away even before the replacement of the root; thus, in the case of *plavante*, the guṇa substitution ought to occur.
In the case of *kurutaḥ*, after the replacement of the final *n* by *u* (*ṅtv*), the guṇa of the suffix (*vikaraṇa*) does not take place because the suffix is marked with *s*.

The substitution of *u* for the vowel of this root *kṛ* occurs by the rule *ṭhata ut sārvadhātuke* (Pāṇini 6.4.130). For in that rule, the condition *kṅti* is carried over from the preceding sūtra *gamahana* (6.4.98).
5. *asaṃyogāl liṭ kit* (Pāṇini 1.2.5).

Since the *liṭ* suffix is prescribed only after a verbal root (*dhātu*) and not after anything else, the root is brought into proximity by the force of the *liṭ*; and that [root] is qualified by the mention of "not being a conjunct" (*asaṃyoga*), and by that qualification...

He states that the rule of "specification by the final letter" (tadantavidhi) applies, saying: "after a root ending in a consonant other than *ṭh*. If, however, the *kit* status of the *liṭ* suffix is prescribed only after a root that does not end in a conjunct consonant (*asaṃyogānta*), then forms such as *vavṛte* and *vavṛdhe* would not be established, because the *guṇa* substitution would have to occur due to its higher priority.
The scope for *kit* [status] is in the case of "ījatuḥ," "ījuḥ"; the scope for *guṇa* is in the case of "vartitvā," "vardhitvā.
When both would apply in cases such as "vavṛte" and "vavṛdhe," *guṇa* alone would occur by virtue of its being the subsequent rule;
however, this is not so, because the word "subsequent" (*para*) expresses what is intended (*iṣṭa*), and here *kit* status itself is what is intended.
But this [suffix] itself is supreme; therefore, it will indeed be that [suffix], and thus there is no fault.

And here, if the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "after what does not end in a *ṭh*" is resorted to, then when something other than a conjunct (*saṃyoga*) is grasped, by the maxim of the negative particle and the word *iva* (*nañ-iva-yukta-nyāya*), [the suffix applies]. (Vyāḍipañjikā 65)

There would be the apprehension of only that which is similar—since *hal* (a consonant) is similar to another *hal* that is not accompanied by anything else, the *kit* status would apply only after a stem ending in a consonant (*halanta*), and not after one ending in a vowel (*ajanta*). Consequently, forms such as *cakre* and *cakruḥ* would not be established. Therefore, this is a prohibitive negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), not an exclusionary negation (*paryudāsa*)—namely, "if [the suffix] is not..."

By the rule *saṃyogāt yajādīnāṃ kiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.15), [the substitution of samprasāraṇa] is prescribed after roots such as *yaj* when a *kit* suffix follows, not a *ṅit* suffix—as in *bibhidatuḥ* and *bibhiduḥ*. Due to the *kit* status, there is an absence of *guṇa* strengthening according to *pugantalaghūpadhasya* (7.3.86). However, in *sasraṃse* and *dadhvaṃse*, because of the absence of *kit* status, [the substitution does not apply].

The elision of the nasal [of the suffix] by the rule *ṭhaniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24) does not occur here. From the roots *stransu* and *dhvansu* in the sense of "falling down" (*adhaḥ-patane*; Dhātupāṭha 754–755), the Ātmanepada is applied because they are marked with an anudātta vowel; then, by the rule *liṭastajhayoreśirec* (Pāṇini 3.4.81), the substitute *eś* is applied for the *ta* and *jhi* endings. Thus, we have *bibheditha*.
*Sip*, *thal*, and [the suffixes] beginning with *krādiniyama* take the augment *iṭ*.
6. And [it is added] after the roots *indh* and *bhavati*.
(Pāṇini 1.2.6). Regarding the term *samīdhe*: the root *ñiindhī* means "to shine" (Dhātupāṭha 1448); as before, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) applies.
This is the elision of the root [of *eṣ*], due to its being marked with the *k*-sign, by the rule "anunāsika-lopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.24),
followed by reduplication and the lengthening of a vowel before a homogeneous vowel (6.1.101). Now, why does the suffix *ām* not occur here by the rule "ijādeśca gurumato 'nṛcchaḥ" (3.1.36)?

Because this [suffix] has the *mantra* as its domain, and because there is the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "in a *mantra*" (*mantre*) in that context; if that is so, then since a *mantra* is indeed a *chandas*, by the rule "in *chandas*, both ways" (*cchandasyubhayathā*, 3.4.117), there is the status of being a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, and consequently, by the rule "before a *sārvadhātuka* ending marked with *p*" (*sārvadhātukam apit*, 1.2.4), there is the *ṅtva* designation (i.e., the prohibition of *guṇa*). Precisely for this reason...

Since the elision of the nasal [of the root] will occur by the rule beginning with *ṅtvi* (Pāṇini 6.4.24), for what purpose is the *kit* status prescribed for the *liṭ* suffix following the root *indh*? It is for the sake of providing an indication (*jñāpana*). By this, it is indicated that this *ām* augment is non-permanent (*anitya*). For if the *ām* were permanent, then because of its intervention, [the *liṭ* suffix] would not follow immediately after *indh*.
Since it is impossible for [the root] to occur [in that form], the prescription of the *kit* suffix is not justified;
therefore, this [root] is impermanent. Consequently, the usage "samīdhe" is also justified even in the vernacular (*bhāṣā*).

In *abhūva* and *babhūvitha*, because of the *kit* designation [of the affix], the *vṛddhi* and *guṇa* substitutions do not occur respectively. By the rule *bhuvo vug luṅliṭoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.88), the augment *vuk* is applied. By the rule *bhavateraḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.73), the substitution of *ā* occurs for the reduplication. Now, one might object: even if the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* were already applied, by the *vuk*...

The suffix *vuk* must be permanent (*nitya*), even in cases where it has not yet been applied; for it applies both when [the condition] has been fulfilled and when it has not. Since *vuk* is permanent, once it has been applied, there is no possibility at all for *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* to occur, because the root *bhū* would then lack a light penultimate vowel (*alaghūpadha*) and would not end in a vowel (*anajanta*).

Is the inclusion of the term *bhavati* purposeless? This is not so; according to the rule "A grammatical operation that applies when another word-form [is present] is considered non-eternal" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 100), the *vuk* suffix is also non-eternal. Consequently, because it would be superseded by *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, the *vaṅ* replacement would not occur once those two have already taken effect. Therefore...

The inclusion of the word "bhavati" must be made. Now, even when guna and vṛddhi have been applied, since that which has undergone a partial modification is not different from the original, there is no difference in the word-form; this being so, it would be possible to omit the mention of "bhavati. Why then is it included?
For the sake of clarity:

now, regarding the form *babhūva*, how is there a prohibition of the *vṛddhi* [substitution] prescribed by *aco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115), given that *ekaḥ* is still being supplied as an anuvṛtti? [The answer is: By the rule *kṅiti ca* (1.1.5), the *vṛddhi* is characterized by having *iK* as its cause.

It is prohibited, and this [prohibition] does not apply to a *vṛddhi* characterized by *i*, because its locus has been specifically specified. Here, by the force of the prescription of *kit*-ness, the prohibition will apply even to a *vṛddhi* that is not characterized by *i*; otherwise, the prescription of *kit*-ness would be purposeless.
If it is argued that [the rule] should apply, we say no; for that [suffix *thāl*] serves the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* in the case of both *thāl* and *utamam*.

If this is so, then the mention of *ṅt* also continues [from the previous rule]; since there is no other purpose when that continues, there is thus a prohibition even of a *vṛddhi* not characterized by *ṅt*.
"It will be so. The mention [of *bhū*] in the rule for *ṭhindeḥ* is for the sake of forming a *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster)—so says the *Kāśikā*.
Because it ends in a *saṃyoga*, the [substitution of *iṭ*] is not established by the preceding rule.
[The mention of *bhū*] is for the sake of *bhavati* having the augment *pi*. It is not for the sake of *api*; because it does not end in a *saṃyoga*, it is [treated as] *apit*."
Because [the desired result] is already established by the preceding rule; here, the mention of *bhū* with the suffix *śtip* is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-lopa (the elision of *yaṅ*).
That is to say, let there not be *kit* status for the *liṭ* [affixes] following a form ending in *yaṅ*-lopa. Thus, "bobhāva" [is formed]. And so it has been said:

"Whatever is taught with the marker *ś*, with the marker *p*, with an *anubandha*, by means of a [verbal] class (*gaṇa*), or where there is the mention of a single vowel (*ekāj*)—these five do not apply in the case of *yaṅluk*. (Puṣpabhūti 94). Thus, for example, in the case of *ṭhanthigranthi* and so forth; [the roots] *śrantha* and *grantha* in the sense of "binding" (Dhātupāṭha 1512, 1513).

The meaning is that for these roots as well—*ḍambhṛ* (in the sense of deceiving, *dhā.pā.* 1290) and *ṣvaj* (in the sense of embracing, *dhā.pā.* 973)—as well as for *śranth*, *granth*, and so forth, the *liṭ* suffix is treated as having the *kit* property;
this is how the rule is to be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the particle *ca* (and) serves to include those not explicitly mentioned.

It is done so that, by that [rule], even for roots such as *śranth*, which end in a conjunct consonant, the *liṭ* suffix will have the *kit* designation; thus [we derive] forms such as *śrethatuḥ*. Due to the *kit* designation, there is the elision of the nasal according to *aniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24). Furthermore, [the rule] *tṛphalabhajatrapaśca* (Pāṇini 6.4.122) [applies].

Because the particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned, the substitution of *e* for *ai* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) apply even when [the root] is situated between multiple consonants.

Thus: *pariṣasvaje*. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs because the root is *anudāteta*. Regarding the preceding *s*, while the rule *sthādiṣvabhyāsena cābhyāsasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.64) is in effect, [the rule] *upasargāt...* [is applied].

The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule "sunoti" (Pāṇini 8.3.65). However, for the subsequent *s*, there is a prohibition of the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule "ṣadisvañjayoḥ parasya liṭi" (Pāṇini 8.3.118).
[The suffix] *ktvā* follows the roots *mṛḍ*, *mṛd*, *gudh*, *kuṣ*, *kliś*, *vad*, and *vas* [with the augment *iṭ*]. This is according to Pāṇini 1.2.7.

*ṭhmuḍa* "to delight" (Dhātupāṭha 1516), *ṭhmṛda* "to crush" (Dhātupāṭha 1515), *ṭhgudha* "to be angry" (Dhātupāṭha 1517), *ṭhkuṣa* "to extract" (Dhātupāṭha 1518), *ṭhkliśū* "to afflict" (Dhātupāṭha 1522), *ṭhvida* "in the sense of distinct speech" (Dhātupāṭha 1009), *ṭhvasa*...

Regarding the root *nivās* (DhP 1942), [the author] will state that the prohibition of the *kit* designation applies because of the rule "na ktvā seṭ. Now, one might object: "But this very rule will serve as a restrictive one (*niyamārtha*), meaning that the *ktvā* suffix with the augment *iṭ* is *kit* only after roots such as *mṛḍ* and others, and not after any others; thus, forms like *devitvā* would be established."

Regarding the passage beginning with "sevitvā" and so forth: for what purpose will he state the prohibition [of *iṭ*] by the rule "ṭhna ktvā seṭ" (Pāṇini 1.2.18)? It is for the sake of clarity; otherwise, some might imagine a reversed restriction—that the suffix *ktvā* occurs only after roots such as *mṛḍ*.

"It becomes *kid*, not anything else. Regarding the phrase "an anticipation [of a rule] (*purastādapakarṣaḥ*)," etc.: the term *apakarṣaḥ* means an exception (*apavādaḥ*). Regarding "having afflicted" (*kliśitvā*): the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *kliśaḥ ktvāniṣṭhayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.50).
Regarding "having spoken" (*uditvā*) and "having heated" (*uṣitvā*), [the substitution of *samprasāraṇa* occurs] by the rule concerning the roots *vac* and others (6.1.15).
There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*). By the rule *vasateṣṭhśāsivasidhasīnāñca* (8.3.60), there is the substitution of *ṣ*;
by *vasatikṣudhoḥ* (7.2.52), there is the augment *iṭ*.
[The rule] *rudavidamuṣagrahisvapipracchaḥ saṃśca* (1.2.8) [applies].
The roots *rudir* in the sense of shedding tears (DhP 1067), *vid* in the sense of knowing (DhP 1064),
*muṣ* in the sense of stealing (DhP 1530), *grah* in the sense of seizing (DhP 1533), *ñiṣvap* in the sense of sleeping (DhP 1068), and *pracch* in the sense of desiring to know (DhP 1413).

"Regarding *grah*, it is for the purpose of enjoining [the *k*it quality] alone"—meaning that there should be a re-enjoinment of the *k*it quality which had been prohibited by the rule "na ktvā seṭ" (Pāṇini 1.2.18). "Regarding *svapi*, it is for the purpose of enjoining [the *k*it quality] alone," and so forth. [The question is: "Is it for the sake of the *saN* affix?
Then, why is this statement not for the sake of the *ktvā* affix? To this he says: "For it is only for the sake of the *k*it quality..."

Because the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "the suffix *ktvā* [is] after roots ending in a single vowel that are unaccented in their original form" (*svapi-pracchyor hiṭ ekāca upadeśe 'nudātāt*, 7.2.10) applies, the *ktvā* suffix does not become *seṭ*; therefore, the prohibition "a *seṭ* [suffix] is not [added] after *ktvā*" (*na ktvā seṭ*, 1.2.18) does not apply. Consequently, *ktvā* is indeed *kid*. Thus, [we have] "having wept" (*ruditvā*).

The suffix *ktvā* is applied by the rule *samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle* (Pāṇini 3.4.21), resulting in *gṛhītvā*. By the rule *graho 'liṭi dīrghaḥ* (7.2.37) and the *grahyādi*-sūtra (6.1.16), there is *saṃprasāraṇa*. For *jighṛkṣati*, there is the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha* by *ho ḍhaḥ* (8.2.31), and the substitution of *ka* for *ṣa* and *ḍha* before *si* by *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si* (8.2.41).
By [Pāṇini 8.2.41], there is the substitution of *k* for *t*;
by [Pāṇini 8.2.37], *ṭhekāco baso bhaṣ*, the *g* is replaced by *gh*; and by [Pāṇini 7.2.12], *sani grahaguhośca*, there is the prohibition of the augment *iṭ*. Thus, we have *suṣupsati*.

By the rule *vacyādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 6.1.15), there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*). Thus, we have *pipṛcchiṣati*. Here too, there is vocalization by the rule *grahyādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 6.1.16); then the augment *tuk* is applied by the rule *che ca* (6.1.73), and the substitution of *ścu* occurs by the rule *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ* (8.4.40).

[The word] "having finished with *ktvā*" is excluded. Since the original (*aupadeśika*) *kitva* of the *ktvā* suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant still exists, its continued application here would be purposeless. However, the mention of *san*...

The word ending in the nominative case is understood here; its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the term *jhali* is thus established. Therefore, by virtue of this syntactic connection (*sāmarthya*), the rule is understood to apply to that which begins with such [a *jhal* sound];
hence he says: "A *san* beginning with a *jhal* is treated as *kit*."

Now, why does the rule of *tadantavidhi* (specification of that which ends with [the preceding element]) not apply here—[namely,] that the desiderative suffix (*san*) ends in a *jhal* consonant? It is thought thus:
from the rule concerning the technical term *vṛddha* (Pāṇini 1.1.73), the mention of "beginning with" (*ādi*) is carried over (*anuvartate*) here; therefore, it is the *jhal* that is qualified.
Consequently, only the rule of *tadādividhi* (specification of that which begins with [the preceding element]) is understood, and not the other.
Regarding the rule "tadantavidhi" (the application of an operation to that which ends with [a specific element]): if, however, this were a *tadantavidhi*, what would happen?

It would apply only in cases where, after the elision (*lopa*) of the final vowel (*at*), the root ends in a *jhal* consonant—such as in *cikīrṣitā* and the like; but it would not apply in cases such as *cikīrṣati*, because there the root ends in an *at* vowel.

The fact that [the substitute] does not end in a *t* sound (*adantatvam*) is due to the fact that the single substitute for both *sañ* and *śakāra* is treated as if it were the final element (*antavat*) with respect to what precedes it.
Now, why is the root *ika*, from the root *iṅ* "to remember" (DhP 1047), not understood here?
Is it so? No, because it is more logical that *jhal* itself be the *pratyāhāra*; furthermore, because the word *jigīṣu* is listed among the *gargādi* group.

For if there were a mention of "dhātu" (root), then the *san* following *jayati* would not be *kit*, and consequently the word *jigīṣu* would not be established. Furthermore, if there were a mention of "dhātu"...

For if [the word *dhātu*] were present, a *hal* (consonant) could not occur immediately after it; thus, even the rule *ṭhhalantācca* (1.2.10) would become untenable. Therefore, it is logical that the *pratyāhāra* (the set of consonants) alone is intended, and not the word *dhātu*. [The example] *cicīṣati* [is explained by] *ajjhanagamāṃ sani* (6.4.16).
The long vowel [is substituted] by the previously mentioned rule, "ṭhekācaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.10), which prohibits the augment iṭ.

Furthermore, wherever else the augments iṭ is not heard [in the grammatical tradition], its prohibition should be understood through this very same rule. However, where there is a specific exception, that must indeed be stated separately.
In *tuṣṭūṣati*, the remaining *kha* sounds [are retained] by the rule *śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.61).

In *śiśayiṣate*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *pūrvavat sanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.62). In the same way, the application of the middle voice after desiderative forms ending in *san* in subsequent cases should be understood through this very rule.

"But for what purpose [is this asked]? and so forth. Here, the intention is that which will be stated below. "Let there not be a *guṇa* substitution"—this is the reason why this is said; he states it in order to reveal the intention with which he asked the question: "In the case of roots ending in *aj*, *han*, *gam*, and *m*, before the suffix *san*," and so forth. If...

Even if lengthening (*dīrghatva*) were applied, the *guṇa* substitution would still occur; in that case, the lengthening would be rendered purposeless (*vaiyarthyam*). Therefore, lest this [lengthening] be purposeless, the lengthening will serve as an annulment (*bādhaka*) of that *guṇa*. To point out the flaw in this position, he says: "In that case, just as... and so forth.
Since, in the absence of this [rule], there would be no occasion for the lengthening to act as a sublater of the *guṇa*—

as expressed by "therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth— because this fault would otherwise attach itself when this [rule] is not commenced, [the rule is stated] in order to provide an occasion for the lengthening.
Why, then, is this [kitva] being undertaken? Even if this were undertaken, why would this fault not occur?

To this he says: "in *cicīṣati*" and so forth. Because when *kit* is present, it sublates the *guṇa* (vocalization) by that very fact. In forms such as *cicīṣati* and *tuṣṭūṣati*, the lengthening (*dīrghatva*) has its scope.

It occurs; and because of that subsequent status, the elision of the *ṇi* affix is not sublated. For when the *kit* status is present, it cannot be said that, "just as the lengthening sublates the *guṇa*, so too does it sublate the elision of the *ṇi*"; because the *guṇa* is not sublated by the lengthening—what then?
By virtue of being *kit*, the scope for lengthening (*dīrghatva*) is shown here, whereas the scope for the elision of the *ṇi* suffix (*ṇilopa*) is as follows:

*pāktiḥ* from *pācayati*, *yāṣṭiḥ* from *yājayati*, and so forth. In the case of *jñīpsati*, where both [rules] would apply, the elision of the *ṇi* suffix occurs by virtue of its higher priority, overriding the lengthening. [The root is] *jñā* in the sense of "understanding."

The suffix *ṇic* is applied because these roots are listed in the *curādi* group: *māraṇatoṣaṇaniśāmaneṣu* (DhP 811) and *micca* (DhP 1624). By the rule *artihrī* (7.3.36), the augment *puk* is added.
By the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* (6.4.92), shortening occurs. Others, however, [cite] *jñapa*...

They read [the root] as *māraṇatoṣaṇaniśāmaneṣu* (Dhātupāṭha 1624). From that, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is added; then the desiderative suffix (*san*). By the rule *sanīvantarddha* (Pāṇini 7.2.49), there is optionally the absence of the augment *iṭ*. By the rule *kaṭhāpjñapṛdhāmīt* (Pāṇini 7.4.55), the substitution of *ī* occurs. Then, by the rule *atra lopo'bhyāsasya* (Pāṇini 7.4.58), the elision of the reduplicated syllable takes place.
Thus, there is the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*). Then, by the rule *taṭhṇeraniṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.51), there is the elision of the suffix *ṇi*.

[The phrase] "the *kit*-ness of *ika*" and so forth follows. Now, for what purpose is the *kit*-ness of the subsequent *san* prescribed after [a root ending in] *ik*, and for what purpose is the split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) made as *ikaḥ* and *jhal*?
Should not this single sūtra alone be recited: "ṭhiko jhal halantācca"?

He states the purpose: "guṇo mā bhūt" (let there be no *guṇa* substitution). In forms such as *cicīṣati*, the *guṇa* prescribed by "sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.84) would otherwise apply; that [substitution] must not occur.
The suffix *kit* is prescribed for the purpose that [the root] should become long. This is not a valid purpose;

because the rule "ṭhajjhanagamāṃ sani" (Pāṇini 6.4.16) prescribes lengthening before the suffix *san* even when the guna substitution has not yet taken effect, therefore, due to the application of this lengthening, the guna will not occur. Otherwise, indeed...

The mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) would be purposeless. But surely, in the case of *cukūṣate*, the mention of "long" is meaningful; for here, by the rule *gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.1), when there is the marker *ṅ*, a *guṇa* vowel does not apply before a *s*-affix. This is not so; for a grammatical rule is not commenced merely for the sake of a single example.

He employs [this reasoning]: for if this were the intended purpose, he would simply have used the term *ṇi*. Alternatively, with regard to the mere aggregate [of letters], the paribhāṣā beginning with "that which precedes a word" (*purastādapadādāḥ*) does not exist at all.

10. *halantācca* (1.2.10). The term *ikaḥ* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. In this context, if the word *anta* were to signify a "part" (*avayava*), there would be no connection between the *ik* vowel and the *hal* consonant; for it is impossible for an *ik* vowel to be a constituent part of a *hal* consonant. For that which...
That by which something is commenced, being non-distinct in location from it, becomes its constituent part (*avayava*);
for example, the threads of a cloth. But the plow is not commenced by the handle;
therefore, this word "end" (*anta*) does not denote a constituent part, but rather it is appropriate that it denotes proximity.

Having considered this, he says: "This word *anta* means 'proximity'. But surely, since a verbal root (*dhātu*) is implied here by the force of the context, the consonants (*hal*) will possess the status of being constituents (*avayava*) with respect to that [root];
this is not so. For in that case, the word *anta* would be redundant, according to the rule: "That by which an operation is prescribed applies to what ends with it" (*yena vidhis tadantasya*).

Since the rule of "taking that which ends in [the specified element]" (*tadantavidhi*) is already obtained by this very rule (Pāṇini 1.1.72), he demonstrates that it is a *karmadhāraya* compound through the specific analysis: "it is both a *hal* (consonant) and at the end. But of what is this the end? It is the end of the *ik* (vowel) under discussion. If this is so, then [the compound] would be *asamartha* (incapable of syntactic connection) because it is dependent on something else.
If it is argued that a compound of the word *anta* with *bhavatītika* is not possible because [the latter] is dependent [on something else], this is not a fault;

for here the word *anta* is the principal member (*pradhāna*), and it will be made known in the second chapter that a compound is indeed possible even when the principal member is dependent, as in the rule: "That which is compared is compounded with *vyāghra* and so forth, provided that a common quality is not expressed" (*upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ sāmānyāprayoge*).

In this context [of rule 2.1.56], by the inclusion of the term *sāmānyāprayoga*, [the word] *igantāt* forms a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). But surely, since *ikaḥ* is established as ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*), how can there be a genitive compound? This is not a fault; for although it ends in the fifth case—

This is the subject at hand. Nevertheless, here, because there exists a relationship between that which is proximate and that which is proximate to it, [the word *ika*] undergoes a change of case-ending (vibhaktivipariṇāma) and assumes the form of a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), as in "from that which is proximate to an *ik*" (*ikaḥ samīpagatāt*).
That is to say, "from that which has an *ik* situated nearby" (*ikaḥ samīpavartinaḥ*). [As in the example] "he desires to know" (*bubhutsate*). [The root is] *budh*.

In the root *avagamana* (Dhātupāṭha 1172), the substitution of the voiced aspirate (*bhaṣ*) for the unvoiced unaspirated (*ca*) occurs according to the rule *ṭh-ekāco baśo bhaṣ* (Pāṇini 8.2.37), and so forth;
thus, wherever the substitution of *bhaṣ* occurs hereafter, it should be understood by this very rule. [The rule] *khari ca* (8.4.55) [also applies].

Thus, the substitution of *t* for the *dh* is indeed optional; as in the form *ṭhyiyakṣate*, there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* [vocalization] by virtue of the rule beginning with Pāṇini 6.1.15 (*yajivraścādibhyaḥ*).
If the word *amant* signifies "proximity," then the *s* of the suffix *san* following the root *dambh* does not possess the *kit* designation.

It is established. For instance: since that *hal* which is proximate to the *ik* is not subsequent to it, and that which is subsequent to it is not proximate to the *ik*, he says "of *dambh*" and so forth.
By the term *hal*, the class (*jāti*) of consonants is denoted, not the individual (*vyakti*). Therefore, when those very [consonants]...

There is the view that "the universal (jāti) is the individual (vyakti) when its distinctions have been abandoned"; according to that view, there is no intervention between those individuals (*vyaktis*) which are resorted to as the *hal* [consonant] class. Therefore, since the *hal*-universal itself is immediate (*samīpavartinī*), the *san* suffix prescribed after the root *dambh-* is *kit*.

This is indeed established. Even when a universal, which is a distinct entity from the individuals, is entirely present in each individual and is itself partless and one, even then there is no intervention;
for it is one individual that acts as an intervener for another individual, but not for the universal. This is because of its [the universal's] nature.

Because it is incorporeal. Therefore, even in this view, since the genus *hal* is distinct [from its individuals], the suffix *san* following that which is proximate to it—namely, the root *dambh*—becomes *kit*. Now, as for that genus *hal*, which is distinct from its individuals, with respect to what is its status as being "proximate"?

Furthermore, that which constitutes the posteriority of the suffix *san* with respect to the class (*jāti*) of the letter *n*—both of these should be understood as mediated through the individual instance (*vyakti*). In this regard, since the individual instance of the letter *n* is proximate to the vowel *i*, the class of consonants (*hal-jāti*) residing in that [instance] is also proximate to the vowel *i*; thus, the suffix *san* is posterior to the individual instance of the letter *bh*.

Furthermore, since the universal (*jāti*) is that which serves as the substratum for that [sound], the sound cannot be posterior to the universal independently of the individual (*vyakti*). Nor can the sound’s posteriority relative to the universal be established independently; both of these must be understood as mediated through the individual. In this regard, the individual *n*-sound is distinct.

"Located nearby" (*samīpagata*) means that the *san* suffix is subsequent to the universal (*jāti*) which is the substratum of the individual (*vyakti*) "bh," just as it is subsequent to the individual "bh" itself; for proximity cannot possibly belong to a universal independently of an individual, nor can it exist in relation to a universal alone.

The priority (*paratva*) belongs to the former [letter], because a universal (*jāti*) is incorporeal. If, then, both of these [priority and posteriority] are mediated by the individual (*vyakti*), then conversely, the latter would also be mediated by the individual. For instance, if the individual *bh* situated nearby does not exist, then the universal would likewise not exist.
If [the suffix] *san* does not exist after the manifestation (*vyakti*) of the letter *n*, it would likewise not exist after the genus (*jāti*);

and consequently, even though the mention of *hal* (consonants) refers to the genus, the *kit*-status of *san* following the root *dambh* would still not be established? This is not so; for although the genus is [perceived] through the medium of the individual manifestation (*vyakti*), [the grammatical operation applies].

Proximity and its opposite [distance] belong to the *san* suffix as well; for although its priority and its opposite are dependent on the genus (*jāti*) by way of the individual (*vyakti*), nevertheless, in this case, there is a single proximity of the generality of the *hal* (consonant) [to the vowel].

And since the status of being "para" (subsequent) depends upon something else, the *kitva* (the status of having *k* as an indicatory letter) will have that very thing as its basis; however, even though the reverse case exists, it is simply not taken into account, because the rule must conform to the specific forms (*lakṣya*) to be explained.
Now, one might object: is there not indeed a universal (*jāti*) called *haltva* (the property of being a consonant)? For instance, the word *hal* is a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*).

It functions solely by virtue of convention, like words such as "Ḍittha" and so on. For it cannot be maintained that there exists an undifferentiated universal called "phonemeness" (*haltva*) among phonemes such as *ha* and so on, in the same way that there exists an undifferentiated universal called "cowness" (*gotva*) in cows and so on.

Because there is an absence of a connection to that [root], what was stated is incorrect—namely, that it is established because the inclusion of *hal* in the rule for the root *dambh* refers to the genus (*jāti*). This is not so; for even those technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*) which denote a single individual object according to the view of those who maintain that the referent of a word is a genus (*jātipadārthavādin*).

Even in the case of [names] such as Devadatta, where a genus (*jāti*) is admitted due to the multiplicity of imagined forms across different states of those objects, how much more so must this be the case for conventional designations (*saṃjñāśabda*) like "ha," which have multiple phonemes as their referents? Otherwise, the established rule for the meaning of words would be over-extensive (*ativyāpin*).
Furthermore, you must first be asked this: what is the basis for the existence of the universal (*jāti*) in cows and the like, by virtue of which it is admitted there?
If you say it is because of the application of a single designation and cognition toward things that are distinct, then this [same reason] applies elsewhere as well.

They are identical. For just as those two [the universal and the particular] persist as following after [the individuals] even when cows and the like are distinct, once the convention has been established, so too do they [persist] in the case of the letter *ha* and others.
Just as those two do not exist in them prior to the convention, so too do they not exist in cows and the like [prior to it]. Therefore...
Since those two— the designation and cognition as non-different despite being applied to different individuals— which serve as the grounds for the conviction in the existence of a universal,
are present even in the case of consonants (*hal*), one must therefore admit that there is a universal called "consonant-ness" (*haltva*) there as well, and not only in cows and the like.

The existence of "gotva" and so forth is indeed absolute. Regarding the forms *dhīpsati* and *dhīpsati*: this is an illustration for those cases where, according to the rule *sanīvantardha-* (Pāṇini 7.2.49), the augment *iṭ* is absent; [in such cases], the substitution of *i* occurs by the rule *dambha icca* (Pāṇini 7.4.56).
There is also the substitution of *ī* for the vowel; here, by the rule "ṭhata upadhāyā dīrgha ikaḥ" (7.4.58), there is the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-lopa*).
By the rule "ṭhkhari ca" (8.4.55), the *cari* substitution occurs, whereby the *bh* is changed to *p*.
Since the suffix is *kit*, there is no elision of the nasal by the rule "ṭhaniditām" (6.4.24). Then, by the rule of *bhaṣ*-bhāva, the *d* is changed [to *dh*].
The letter *dh*.
11. *liṅsicāvātmanepadeṣu* (Pāṇini 1.2.11). [The commentary states:

"The *liṅ* and *sic* [suffixes] occur when the ātmanepada [terminations] follow. But how can the *liṅ* occur when the ātmanepadas follow, given that it is only the *sic* that can possibly occur when the ātmanepadas follow, and not the other?

Regarding the term *liṅ*: he thinks as follows—the word *liṅ* here refers to a portion of the *liṅ*, namely the *sīyuṭ* suffix, just as in the rule "na dhātulopa ārdhadhātuke" (Pāṇini 1.1.4), the word *dhātu* refers to a portion of a verbal root (*dhātu*). Therefore, by this method, the *kit* status belongs to the *sīyuṭ* itself.

It is prescribed. Or rather— just as in the rule *halṅyābhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), this qualification "after a long [vowel]" applies only to those two cases where the lengthening is possible,
so too here, it applies only to that *sic* after which the ātmanepada suffix can possibly follow.
This is a qualification of that very [term]. The mention of the *ātmanepada* is for the purpose of excluding the *parasmaipada*.
"Bhistīṣṭa"—here the *liṅ* [suffix] is used because of the rule "In the sense of benediction, the *liṅ* and *loṭ* [are used]" (Pāṇini 3.3.173).

The *ātmanepada* [ending] occurs because of the *svarita* accent. In the same way, in subsequent cases as well, it should be understood that the *ātmanepada* ending occurs for roots marked with *ñ* or *k* when denoting the agent, by this very rule. By the rule *suṭ tithoḥ* (3.4.107), the augment *suṭ* is applied.
There is *śnam* in the sense of the agent, and by the rule *liṅ salopo'nantyasya* (7.2.79), there is no elision of the *s*.
[The suffixes] *bhaviṣyati* and *bhavatu* [are treated as ārdhadhātuka] because of the rule *ṭhliṅaśiṣi* (Pāṇini 3.4.116), since they are designated as ārdhadhātuka;

whereas those two [other suffixes] are prescribed for the *sārvadhātuka*. Regarding *bhotsīṣṭa*, one should understand that the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) applies to the root *budh* by the rule *anudātetaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.12).
The same applies to the following cases due to the rule *anudātetaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.12).

The ātmanepada [suffix] in the sense of the agent is to be understood by this very [rule]. In *abhita*, there is the elision of *sic* by [Pāṇini 8.2.26]: *jhalo jhali*. In *abuddha*, there is the substitution of *dha* for the *ta*-sound by [Pāṇini 8.2.40]: *jhaṣastathordho’dhaḥ*.

The letter *dh* [becomes *d*] by the rule "jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi" (Pāṇini 8.4.53), whereby the preceding *dh* becomes *d*. Regarding "yakṣīṣṭa": because it is marked with the *svarita* accent, it takes the ātmanepada endings. As before, there is the substitution of *ṣ* and *k*.
Regarding "for there would be vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*)": this is according to the rule for the roots beginning with *vac* (Pāṇini 6.1.15).

"He saw" (*aṣṭākṣīt*). The augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule "there is *iṭ* for *sic* before an unaccented suffix" (7.3.96), and the *vṛddhi* substitution is applied by the rule "of a vowel following *vad*, *vraj*, or a root ending in *hal*, [before a suffix with *iṭ*]" (7.2.3). As before, the rules for *ṣatva* and *katva* apply.
12. *uśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.12).

Since the terms *liṅ* and *sic* are being carried over [from the previous rule], they bring to mind a verbal root (*dhātu*), because it is precisely from that [root] that those two suffixes are prescribed. Nor is [the vowel] qualified by the sound *ṛ*; for according to the principle "that by which a rule is prescribed applies to what ends with it," [the rule applies to the whole base ending in *u*, not to the *ṛ* alone].
Thus, by means of the vowel *ṛ*, the rule of "specification by the final letter" (*tadantavidhi*) is understood; so he says: "from a root ending in the vowel *ṛ*," and so forth.
Now, why is there not an inclusion of the root *ṛ* (meaning "to go") from the Dhātupāṭha (number 1098)?

This is the style of the Teacher: wherever he intends to include a particular verbal root, he provides its mention by means of the *śtip* affix, as in "ṛti-pipartyośca" (Pāṇini 7.4.77) and "sarti-śāsty-artibhyaśca" (Pāṇini 3.1.56); however, no such mention by means of the *śtip* affix has been made here.
Therefore, this application [of the rule] is only for the vowel *ṛ*, not for the verbal root. Regarding "ṭhakṛta":

there is the elision of *sic* by the rule "ṭhhrasvādaṅgāt" (Pāṇini 8.2.27). Regarding "variṣīṣṭa": this is a form belonging either to the root *vṛṅ* or *vṛñ*. The augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule "liṅsicorātmanepadeṣu" (Pāṇini 7.2.42).

13. Or *gamaḥ* | (1.2.13). Regarding "saṃgasīṣṭa": the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by [the rule] "samo gamṛcchi... (1.3.29) and so forth. Regarding "samagata": [this is formed by the same rule].

By the rule *hrasvāṅgāt* (8.2.27), there is the elision of the suffix *sic*. Regarding *āhata*: by the rule *hanaḥ sic* (1.2.14), [the augment *iṭ* is not applied]. By the rule *āṅe yamahanaḥ* (1.3.28), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is employed. As before.
There is the elision (*lopa*) of *sic*.

[The example is] "āhasata," where the substitution of *at* occurs by the rule "ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.5). Now, since the mention of *sic* was already established [by the previous rule], for what purpose is *sic* mentioned again? To this he says:

"The mention of *sij* is for the purpose of excluding *liṅ*. For the mention of *sij* under discussion is connected with *liṅ*; therefore, if that were to recur, one might suspect that *liṅ* would also recur. Consequently, the mention of *sij* is made in order to exclude it. But [one might object]: "In the case of *hanti* with *liṅ*..."

It should be understood as an injunction for substitution (*vadhādeśa*); and since no undesirable consequence arises there even though the *kitva* status remains, why is the mention of *sic* made for the purpose of excluding the *liṅ*?
To this he says: "In what follows," and so on. If the *liṅ* were to carry over from here, then [the rule] would apply in what follows.
The intention is that its [the suffix *sij*'] application would follow from that [rule], and consequently, by the subsequent sūtra, it too would possess the *kit* designation;
however, in this case, since the *ātmanepada* is not specified by the *sij* in the *vṛtti*, the *ātmanepada*...
Someone might have the misconception that [the rule] is restricted; therefore, in order to refute that, he says:
"The mention of the *ātmanepada*," and so forth. To the question, "Why does this not also apply here?", he says:
"But here," and so forth. [This refers to the fact that] by the rule *luṅ ci* (Pāṇini 2.4.43), the *luṅ* [suffixes] follow *han* in the *parasmaipada*.

The substitution of *vadh* is prescribed, and that is obligatory (*nitya*). Its obligatoriness follows from the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") in the subsequent rule, *ātmanepadeṣvanyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 2.4.44). Furthermore, there is no purpose for the *kit*-designation (*kitva*) when the substitution of *vadh* is obligatory.
Therefore, the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the ātmanepada here is not tenable.

Now, for what purpose is the *kit* designation prescribed for the *sic* following the root *han*, given that by the rule "the *sārvadhātuka* suffix which is not *pit*" (Pāṇini 1.2.4), the *sārvadhātuka* suffix following *sic* [is already *kit*]?
Is this [the *i*] not indeed present? In that case, the elision of the nasal is established by the rule *aniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24).
If it is argued that it is not established because the *sic* has an indicatory *i* (*it*), we say no;
for the *i*-sound of *sic* is merely for the sake of pronunciation. For instance, in the rule *cleḥ sic* (Pāṇini 3.1.44), [the *i* is similarly for pronunciation].

He will say: "The letter *i* [in *cli*] is for the sake of pronunciation. If it is argued that even so, because *cli* is marked with the *it* designation (*idit*), the *sic* suffix would also acquire the *it* designation by virtue of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, and thus [the desired result] would not be established—[we reply: no;
for the letter *a* in *cli* is for the sake of pronunciation. For instance, in the rule "cli luṅ" (Pāṇini 3.1.43),...

He will state: "The phoneme *i* is for the sake of pronunciation. If that is so, then since the status of being *ṅt* is already established by the designation *sit*, the fact that he again prescribes the *kit* status of the suffix *sic* here in the rule *hanaḥ sic* (1.2.14) serves to indicate that the rule *aniditām* (6.4.24), which applies to a stem ending in *sic*, depends upon an external *sārvadhātuka* suffix.

Thus, there is no elision of the nasal [anusvāra]; by this, forms such as *āraṃsta*, *amaṃsta*, and *āyaṃsta pādam* are established. Otherwise, if the elision of the nasal were applied, the undesirable form *āyata* would result.

15. *yamo gandhane* (Pāṇini 1.3.28). Now, since the root *yam* is recited as "to cease" (*uparame*, Dhātupāṭha 984), how can it function in the sense of "hinting" (*gandhane*)? To this he says: "because [roots] have multiple meanings. This refers to the rule *āṅo yamahanaḥ* (1.3.28).

In this context, the term *akarmaka* ("intransitive") from the rule *ṭhakarmakācca* (1.3.26) is understood by anuvṛtti. To the question, "How then can there be the *ātmanepada* ending here when the verb is transitive (*sakarmaka*)?", he says: "Even though it is transitive," and so forth. Its transitivity, however, exists here because the motion (*kramaṇa*) of the foot and so on is present. [He then says: "udāyaṃsta..."
"Foot"—the meaning is that he drew it back.
16. *vibhāṣopayamane* (Pāṇini 1.2.16).
Regarding the term *dārakarma*: the word *karman* denotes an action; thus, the meaning is "the act of taking a wife."
17. *sthāghvoricca* (Pāṇini 1.2.17).
By the word "ca" (and), it is shown that the *kit* status is added [to the suffix *sic*] by the rule stating "the *sic* also becomes *kit*.
But for what purpose is the *kit* status of *sic* prescribed? For its purpose is simply the prohibition of *guṇa*.

As for the suffix *phal*, by the very force of the prescription of the vowel *i*, there will be no *guṇa* substitution; otherwise, one would have prescribed the single vowel *e*. This is not so; for the prescription of the vowel *i* would be for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*).
Pronouncing a short vowel is more concise than pronouncing a long one. Thus: *upāsthita*.

While the mention of *stha* continues from "samapravibhyaḥ sthaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.22), the word *upa* is supplied from "upānmantrakaraṇe" (Pāṇini 1.3.25). Consequently, by the principle "a rule conditioned by a specific phonetic combination does not cause the destruction of that very combination" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 12), the substitution of *it* (the augment *i*) is unable to affect the *sic* suffix.

To prevent that, how could there be elision? This is not so; for it is not said that "itva" [the substitution of ī for i] occurs before *sic*, but rather that "the letter *i* becomes a final substitute and *sic* becomes *kit*.
Even if it were conditioned by *sic*, there would still be no fault; for its...

And because a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) is not universally obligatory; its non-obligatoriness will be made known in the seventh chapter (Kāśikā 7.1.13), as in the rule *ṭhicca* and so forth. Here, the word "cause" (*hetu*) is to be supplied [from a previous rule]. Therefore, [the rule] *ṣaṣṭhī hetuprayoge* ("the sixth case [is used] when a cause is employed") [applies].

(2.3.26) Thus, when the word *hetu* (cause/reason) is employed, the genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs [to answer the question] "of what? In the term *takāret*, *it* means "the letter *t*"; or, that which has *it*—namely, the letter *t*—is *takāret*. The state of being *takāret* is *takāretva*. In the rule *iccēti*, regarding the mention [of the vowel], of what cause is there the vowel *i*?

Why is the letter *takāra* (t) employed? The meaning is: for what purpose is the letter *ikāra* (i) followed by *tapara* (the marker *t*) employed? Alternatively, this genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) expresses a relationship with the grammatical operation (*kārya*) as a residual characteristic (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇā*). That is to say, for the sake of accomplishing which grammatical operation is the letter *ikāra* followed by *tapara* employed?
