[The rule] "let it not be long" [is stated]; for if *tapara* were not present, when *aṇ* is being grasped, it would include its homogeneous (*savarṇa*) counterparts; thus, since the long vowel *ī* would include its homogeneous sounds, the paribhāṣā "the most similar [substitute] in place" (*sthānentaratama*) would apply, resulting in a long vowel in place of the long vowel in the word *aditā*.

It occurs; lest that [shortening] should take place, the rule is made with a long *ṝ* (*taparatva*). [The rule] "ṛte'pi saḥ" [is stated]. By the word "saḥ," there is a reference back to the long vowel.
Even without this specific statement, the lengthening is established by the rule "ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām" (Pāṇini 6.4.66).

Therefore, the intention is that by the force of the statement itself, the long vowel will not occur. Furthermore, because of the rule "an *aṇ* being in the process of being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) does not include its homogeneous counterparts" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 30), the long vowel will not occur. However, this solution has not been stated here, because even by an *aṇ* being in the process of being taught, [the inclusion of homogeneous sounds] occurs in some cases.

Because of the inclusion of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa*). For instance: when the suffix *au* follows *adas*, after the substitution of *ya* for the *tyad*-group [of pronouns], and once the *vṛddhi* has been applied by the rule "vṛddhir eci" (P.
6.1.88), the letter *u* prescribed by the rule "adaso'serdādu do maḥ" (P. 8.2.80) applies to the vowel *au* because of the inclusion of homogeneous vowels.

In the place of a long vowel, only a long vowel occurs—as in *amū*. [This is stated] so that a protracted (*pluta*) vowel does not occur when there is no interval; for the present rule is commenced for the purpose of excluding what is immediate. Why is this so? Because a short vowel being substituted in the place of a dissimilar long vowel (*ākāra*) [would otherwise apply].
[The vowel] becomes [long], but not the *pluta* [vowel]. Therefore, the *tapara* designation must be made in order to exclude the *pluta*.
This too is not a purposeful requirement, because it is said: "And the *pluta* is prescribed for its specific scope. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a reason.
For the *pluta* is indeed already stated [by rule 8.2.84] to occur in specific scopes such as calling from a distance and so forth. In that case...
If the *pluta* were prescribed by this [rule], then it would have to apply everywhere— in cases such as "dūrāddhūta" and elsewhere— and consequently, even in the case of "dūrāddhūta" and so forth,

there would be the fault of stating what has already been established (*uktānuvāda-doṣa*), because that [pluta] would be produced again despite having already been produced. Therefore, this position...

In the Bhāṣya, the inclusion of *t* (i.e., the designation *tapara*) is rejected on the grounds that [if it were present], there would be the fault of restating what has already been said (*uktānuvādadoṣa*), and thus [the vowel] will remain short (*hrasva*) and not protracted (*pluta*).
Others, however, explain that the mention of *tapara* does not apply here because of the rule: "And the protracted [vowel] is prescribed for its specific scope" (*plutaśca viṣaye smṛtaḥ*).
It is not being rejected; rather, its purpose is being explained. In cases such as "dūrāt" (from afar), a *pluta* vowel is desired and intended, yet it does not occur.
By the rule of "the most similar substitute in place of [the original]" (*sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ*, Pāṇini 1.1.50), only a long vowel would take the place of a long vowel.

It is prescribed. But was it not already stated that the long vowel is established? The restatement of what is already established would be for the purpose of subverting the protracted (*pluta*) vowel. And the protracted vowel is desired in cases such as calling from a distance.
Therefore, the *tapara* (the *t* following the vowel) must be applied so that the long vowel does not subvert that [protracted vowel]. By means of that—
When these are being considered, the *pluta* vowel indeed occurs according to Pāṇini 6.1.85.
Regarding Pāṇini 1.2.18, *na ktvā seṭ*:
the *kit*-status of the suffix *ktvā* is indeed present by virtue of its position [in the *gaṇapāṭha*]; therefore, the augment *iṭ* does not apply to the suffix *ktvā*.
Since the inclusion [of the letter *k*] would cause even a suffix with the augment *iṭ* to be subject [to the rule], this prohibition is commenced:

"The suffix *ktvā*, when accompanied by the augment *iṭ*, does not become *kit*. Now, is it because the letter *k* is prohibited from receiving the designation *it* that it does not possess *kit*-status? [No, rather it is because of the absence of the function of *kit*.]

Or is it because of a prohibition? For if the intention here were to prescribe the status of not being an *kit* (akitva) due to the prohibition of the *it*-designation for the letter *k*, then the author would have composed the rule in the section on *it*-designations as "ṭh-ḷ-śa-k-vaseṭ-ktvā-taddhitayoḥ.
In that case, indeed, the double prohibition would not need to be made. Therefore...

Since the prohibition applies to that *ktvā* which is not bound by *kit*, this rule effects the non-*kit* status of the *seṭ* *ktvā* suffix; it does not, however, serve to prohibit the *it*-designation of the letter *k*.
Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the *anubandha* (indicatory letter)? Why not simply say "na tvā"? For in that case—
Is the sūtra not too brief? This is not the case;

for if the letter *k* were not pronounced, someone might understand even the [root] *dviṣ*. There is no *k*-anubandha at all for the *ktvā* suffix when it is *seṭ*, because it is pronounced without an anubandha. Therefore, so that this [misunderstanding] does not occur—

The term is pronounced with its indicatory letter (*sānubandhaka*). But why, when a rule applies to a root with the augment *iṭ* (*seṭ*), is a form without an indicatory letter (*niranubandhaka*) pronounced? Even so, only that which has *iṭ* would be included, and not that which lacks it (*aniṭ*), because [the latter] possesses an indicatory letter.

Regarding "ṭhnigṛhītiḥ": by the rule "striyāṃ ktin" (Pāṇini 3.3.94), and considering that "the prohibition [of iṭ] for grah and others must be stated" (Vārttika 831) regarding the rule "tutu-trata-tha" (Pāṇini 7.2.9), the prohibition of iṭ by the rule "tutu-trata-tha" etc. does not apply here. Regarding "upasnihitiḥ".

In the three examples— *ṣṇiha* from the root *ṣṇih* (meaning "affection," Dhātupāṭha 1200), *nikucitiḥ*, and [the forms derived from] *kuncu* and *kruncu* (meaning "crookedness" and "becoming small," Dhātupāṭha 185, 186)— there is, respectively,
the substitution of semivowels for vowels (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and the prohibition of *guṇa*. This is governed by the rule *aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.24).

Thus, the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) occurs because [the suffix] has the *k*-marker. Regarding the rule "not after a root with the augment *iṭ*" (*na seṭ*), etc.: by this much alone, namely the application of the rule "not after a root with *iṭ*," forms such as *devitvā* would be established even without the *k*-marker. But for what purpose is the mention of *ktvā*? For without it, even when there is no *k*-marker—

If it is argued that [the substitution of *i* for *u*] would apply to the past participle (*niṣṭhā*) in forms such as *nigudhitaḥ*, *nigudhitaḥ*, and *nigudhitavān*—based on the root *guh* in the sense of "covering" (DhP 1120)—this is not so;
because the rule is restricted to the past participle by [Aṣṭādhyāyī] 1.2.19: *niṣṭhā śīṅ-svidi-midi-kṣvidi-dhṛṣaḥ*.

Because of this restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), the augment *iṭ* will not occur in the case of the past participles (*niṣṭhā*): namely, that the *niṣṭhā* after roots such as *śīṅ* etc. is *seṭ* (possessing the augment *iṭ*), but it is not so for other verbal roots. However, one should not suspect a reverse restriction—that the *niṣṭhā* occurs only after *śīṅ* etc.—for a grammatical treatise does not intend to convey unintended meanings.

[If it were argued that] "there will be no [application of the] *praklṛpti* [rule]," then there would be a prohibition of the *kitva* status for the *liṭ* [affix]; consequently, in forms such as *jagmiva* and *jagmuḥ*, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) by the rule "gamahana... (Pāṇini 6.4.98) would not occur. Therefore, he says: "On account of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), [the rule does not apply] in the case of the *parokṣā* [tense]. In the *parokṣa*...

The direct mention (*śruti*) of *liṭ* prescribed by the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.115] is said to be "remote" (*parokṣa*); therefore, the prohibition of *kitva* will not apply to it. How so? By means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). What is that indicator? He says: "They know the mention of *jhal* in the rule for *san*" (referring to Pāṇini 1.2.10). This is because of the rule "after *ik*, [a suffix beginning with] *jhal*" (1.2.9).

He provides a specific qualification; from that, it is understood that this prohibition—"there is no [application of] *kit* when there is a *seṭ*"—applies to the *kit* status that is directly taught (*aupadeśika*), and not to that which is extended by rule (*ātideśika*). For the mention of *jhal* is made for the purpose of preventing *kit* status in cases such as *śiśayiṣate*. And if...

The prohibition "seṭ" would apply even to the *kitva* (the status of being *k*) that is extended by analogy; thus, the mention of "jhal" would be purposeless. Let there be *kitva* here, and the prohibition "seṭ" will apply to it. Therefore, this is a prohibition of the *kitva* that is extended by analogy.

Regarding the phrase "not for that which is extended" (*nātideśikasya*): the mention of *jhal* would be an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of this meaning, so that in the rule *sthādhvoricca* (Pāṇini 1.2.17), the substitution of *i* occurs before a *sic* beginning with *jhal*, but not before one beginning with a vowel—as in *upāsthāyiṣātām*. For in this case...

By the rule *ṭhsyasicsīyuṭtāsiṣu* (Pāṇini 6.4.62), the status of being like *ciṇ* (*ciṇvadbhāva*) applies, as does the substitution of *it*. In that case, because it is subsequent, the augment *iṭ* takes precedence over *ciṇvadbhāva*. When *ciṇvadbhāva* has occurred, the suffix *yuk* is applied by the rule *ṭhāto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ* (7.3.33). In that context, if the mention of *jhal* were absent...

Even in the case of *iḍā* and others, the substitution of *it* (the short vowel *i*) would apply in place of the letter *y*; however, this is not so. Why? Because the substitution of *it* is prescribed in conjunction with the condition of being a *kit* suffix. For the status of being a *kit* is the primary factor, while the substitution of *it* is taught as a secondary (*anvācaya*) consequence. Therefore, in the absence of the *kit* status, that substitution of *it* will not occur. Now...

Why does *kit* status not also apply here in the rule *ṭhsthādhvoricca* (1.2.17)? Because it is prohibited by the rule *na seṭ* alone. "It is equal to [the substitution of] *repha* in *sudhīvan*"; this substitution of *it* is equal to *repha*. Where?
What is the illustration? In the word *sudhīvanī*. [The derivation is as follows: that which has excellent *dhīvans* (singers) is *sudhīvā*.

When the prohibition of *ṅīp* is applied here by the rule *ṭhano bahuvrīheḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.12), then, just as the *repha* (the suffix *ra*) prescribed by the rule *vano ra ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.7) along with the application of *ṅīp* would not occur in its absence.

Just as that [property] occurs through the application of the *kit* designation, so too this [property] being prescribed by the application of *kit* will not occur in its absence. For what purpose, then, is the mention of *ktvā*? The mention of *ktvā* is for the purpose that the prohibition of *kit* designation does not apply to the *kvasu* suffix.
It must be done. For in that case, since the *kit* status is taught [by rule], its prohibition would occur by the very rule "na seṭ" (Pāṇini 1.2.18).

Consequently, in the form *jagmivān*, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) would not take place. [This is why it is said: "The *kit* status is for the sake of the *vasu* suffix, because of the extension [of the rule] beyond [the scope of] *atideśa*. No.

The word "will be" (*bhaviṣyati*) is to be supplied [as the verb]. Let it be that there is a prohibition of the *kit* status [of the affix] taught by direct rule (*aupadeśika*); even if that exists, since there is a *kit* status [of the affix] transferred by extension (*ātideśika*) according to the rule "the *liṭ* [affixes] following a root ending in *ṭh* or a consonant cluster are *kit*" (Pāṇini 1.2.5), by that [transferred *kit* status], the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) will take place.

It has already been stated that because of the mention of "jhal" and "ra," there will be no prohibition of the *kit* status [of the suffix] which is extended by rule (*ātideśika*). Therefore, the mention of *ktvā* will not be for the sake of the forms ending in *-vas*.
If this is so, then its purpose is [to provide] *nigṛhīti*; however, let there be no prohibition in the case of the suffix *ktin*.

The meaning is that the mention of the suffix *ktvā* is for the purpose of [preventing the augment] *bhū*. In the form *jagmivān*, the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule "vibhāṣā gamahanavidaviśām" (Pāṇini 7.2.68),
and the nasal *num* is applied by the rule "ugidacām" (Pāṇini 7.1.70).
By the rules *halṅyādisaṃyogāntalopau* (Pāṇini 6.1.68; 8.2.23) and *sāntamahataḥ* (6.4.10), the long vowel [is substituted].
19. *niṣṭhā śīṅsvidimidikṣvididhṛṣaḥ* (1.2.19).

The roots are: *śīṅ* "to sleep" (DhP 1032), *ñiṣvidā* "to perspire" (DhP 1188), *ñimidā* "to become moist" (DhP 1243), *ñikṣvidā* "to become moist or to release" (DhP 1244), and *ñidhṛṣā* "to be bold" (DhP 1269). [From these, the forms] *śayitavān* [and so forth are derived].

Thus [it is said]: by the rule "ṭhatvasantasya cādhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.14), there is lengthening of the vowel. In the case of "śayitaḥ," the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule "gatyarthākarmaka... (Pāṇini 3.4.72). In "prasveditaḥ" and similar forms, the word "pra" indicates the beginning of an action (*ādikarma*) according to the rule "ādikarmaṇi ktaḥ kartari ca" (Pāṇini 3.4.71).

It indicates the beginning with the word "pradharṣitaḥ. This is an example other than [the case of] *vaiyātya*; for in that case, by the rule "dhṛṣi-śasi-vaiyātye" (Pāṇini 7.2.19), there ought to be a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*.
One remembers that when the root (*prakṛti*) is mentioned, the *yaṅluk* formation is also included. Therefore, in the *yaṅluk*, [the rule] "eranekācaḥ" [applies].
By [the rule] beginning with (6.4.82), the substitution of *yaṇ* is applied.
20. *mṛṣa* is used in the sense of endurance (*titikṣā*).

(1.2.20) Endurance (*titikṣā*) indeed means patience (*kṣamā*), forbearance (*kṣānti*). If this is so, should not the term "patience" (*kṣānti*) alone have been employed? For in that way the sūtra would have been more concise. True, this is so; however, it was not done for the sake of variety.
"Ṭhapamṛṣitam" means "unexamined," since verbal roots have multiple meanings.

This multiplicity of meaning is understood from the inclusion of the term "titikṣā" (forbearance). For if that were not the case, the root *mṛṣ* would be recited only in the sense of forbearance, and [the author] would not have included it here, as there would be nothing to exclude.

21. *udupadhādbhāvadikarmaṇoranyatarasyām* | (Pāṇini 1.2.21) "That which occurs in the sense of an incipient action" (*ādikarmaṇi vartamānaḥ*). An "incipient action" (*ādikarman*) is the first moment of an action; that *kta*-suffix which is intended to be expressed as having already occurred (*bhūtatvena vivakṣate*) within that [moment] occurs in the sense of an incipient action.

"Ṭhdyotitam anena, dyautitam anena": the root *dyauta* (meaning "to shine") [DhP 7.41] takes the suffix *kta* in the neuter sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). Similarly, this applies to *ṭhmoditam anena, muditam anena*, derived from the root *muda* (meaning "joy") [DhP 1.6].

In cases such as *pradyotitaḥ*, however, by the rule *ādikarmaṇi ktaḥ kartari ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.71), the suffix *kta* is prescribed specifically for the agent (*kartṛ*) and not for the object (*karman*), because the verbal root is intransitive (*akarmaka*). Nor is it used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*), for that would lead to no distinction from the examples given for the abstract state. Thus, the *kta* here is derived in the sense of the agent.
It is called *ādikarman* because of its connection with the beginning of an action; however, this connection with the beginning of an action is mediated by the meaning [of the root].

Regarding the word "rūcitam": since the root *ruc* (in the sense of "to shine," DhP 745) is intransitive, the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the agent according to Pāṇini 3.4.72 (*gatyarthākarmaka...*), resulting in the meaning "shining."

The meaning is "a kārṣāpaṇa coin. Here, the inception of the action (*ādikarman*) is not intended. In the example "the rice has been eaten" (*prabhukta odanaḥ*), the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object according to Pāṇini 3.4.70, which states that *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khalartha* suffixes occur after roots denoting those two [actions]—namely, eating and consuming. Since this [root *bhuj*] is connected with the inception of the action, it functions in the sense of the inception of the action.
The root *guh* (meaning "to conceal") belongs to the *divādi* class (*dhā.pā.* 1120).

In the form *nigudhitam*, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the action (*bhāve*). If [the rule] applies only to roots with the *śap* conjugational marker by virtue of the *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (restricted optionality), then for what purpose is the *niṣṭhā* (past participle suffix) specified here by the mention of *seṭ*? For [in this case], it would not apply simply because the root lacks the *śap* marker.

In the case of *prabhukta*, [the rule] does not apply. For *bhuji* is not characterized by the *śap* affix (*śabvikaraṇa*), but rather by the *śnam* affix (*śnamvikaraṇa*). This is true; however, the mention of "having an augment *i*" (*seṭ*) must be carried over for the sake of the subsequent rule.
Therefore, since that [mention] is being carried over for the sake of what follows, its inclusion here also serves to facilitate easy comprehension for those of dull intellect.
The word "syāt" is used for this purpose. Here, the letter *t* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation (*mukhasukha*), not for the sake of excluding the long vowel;
for, precisely because the penultimate syllable is not heavy (*alaghūpadhatva*), there is no possibility of the occurrence of *guṇa* in those [roots] which have a long penultimate vowel.
22. *pūṅḥ ktvā ca* (Pāṇini 1.2.22). It has been stated that "it does not apply to [a root] having *iṭ*" (*na seṭ*). This follows from [the rule] *na ktvā seṭ* (1.2.18). Now, one might object:
surely there should be no *iṭ* at all after the roots *pū* and *mū* before the suffixes *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā*, because of the rule *śryukaḥ kiti*.

Because of this prohibition [in Pāṇini 1.2.11], one might object that the continued application of the mention of *seṭ* (having an indicatory *i*) is useless; to such an objector, he replies with the words "pūṅśceḍ vihitaḥ" and so forth.
To the question, "Why has an example for the *ktvā* suffix not been shown?", he says: "of the *ktvā* suffix..."

And so forth. For if the *kit* status of the suffix *ktvā* were prohibited by this rule (*yoga*), then an example for that prohibition would have been demonstrated; however, it is not prohibited by this [rule]. Why? Because it is already prohibited by the rule "na ktvā seṭ" (Pāṇini 1.2.18). Therefore...

The meaning is that no example of this has been shown. He says "And so... and so forth, in order to confirm that the suffix *ktvā* is prohibited by the rule "na ktvā seṭ" (Pāṇini 1.2.18). In the rule "pūṅśca" (Pāṇini 7.2.51), regarding those [cases] between two optional rules (*vibhāṣā*)...

Thinking that these rules are eternal (*nitya*), the followers of Bhāradvāja have stated: "The suffix *ktvā* is eternally excluded (*akittva*) when followed by *iṭ* and so forth. Here, "those beginning with *iṭ*" refers to the suffixes *iṭ*, *ktvā*, and *niṣṭhā*. If, then, the exclusion of *kit* for *ktvā* were indeed eternal in the presence of *iṭ* and so forth, then the mention of *ktvā* [in the rule] would be purposeless.
For in this context, the mention of that [suffix] with the option (*vikalpa*) is meaningful for the sake of ensuring the *akitva* (the absence of *kit* status); otherwise, it would not be so.

Having raised the objection that the permanence of the prohibition of *kit* status is already established by the rule "na ktvā seṭ" (Pāṇini 1.2.18), this was stated: "The mention of *ktvā* is for the sake of what follows."

What is the purpose of pronouncing the root with its *anubandha* as *pūṅ*? It is so that there may not be a prohibition of *kit*-tva for forms such as *popuvitaḥ*, *popuvitavān*, and *popuvitvā* derived from the *yaṅ*-luṅ form. However, the pronunciation of the root with its *anubandha* is not justified for the sake of excluding *pū*; [for *pū* is already excluded by other rules].

This is because of the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *ṭhśrayukaḥ kiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.11), and because there is an absence of the augmented forms of *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā* following the root *pūñ*.

23. *nopadhāt thaphāntād vā* (Pāṇini 1.2.23). [The word] *ṭhniṣṭhā* has ceased [to apply], because it was not carried over from the previous rule. [Examples: *grathitvā*. In the alternative where the suffix is *kit*, there is the elision of the nasal according to *aniditām* (6.4.24). [Example: *guphitvā*.

Thus [it is said]: "gupha" and "gunpha" mean "to bind" (DhP 1317, 1318); "riphitvā" [is derived from] "ripha," which means "boasting, fighting, censuring, harming, or giving" (DhP 1306). But surely, even in the absence of this option (vikalpa), [the form would be established] by [the rule] *ralo vyupadhāt* (Pāṇini 1.2.26) and so forth? [Note: This fragment appears to be a commentary discussing the derivation of the word *riphitvā* and its relationship to specific verbal roots and grammatical rules.]
There must be an option; yet, is there not even some distinction between these two options?
If that is so, then by the force of the inclusion of the term *upadha*, even an option established by another rule is sublated by this one. But surely—

The root with the vowel *ṛ* as its penultimate letter will serve as the counter-example for the rule concerning roots having *n* as their penultimate letter, namely *ṛpha* and *ṛnpha* in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsāyām*; DhP 1315, 1316), as in the form *arphitvā*. However, this is not the case;
for here we must derive three forms from these two roots: *arphitvā*, *ṛmphitvā*, and [the third].

Regarding the form *ṛphitvā*: whether the vowel *u* is present as a penultimate (*upadhā*) or not, this form is indeed established by this very rule. First, if the penultimate *u* is present, then because the root *ṛph* has a penultimate *u*, the prohibition in Pāṇini 1.2.18—"after a root ending in *ktvā* with an *iṭ* augment, [the *ṇic* suffix] is not applied"—applies, and thus *ṛphitvā* is established. However, if it does not have a penultimate *u*...

When this option applies to the root *ṛmph*, the two further forms *ṛmphitvā* and *ṛphitvā* are established. Even if the mention of the penultimate vowel (*nopadha*) were not present, all three of these forms would still be established provided this option exists. Therefore, it is rightly stated that this is a counter-example.

Having repeated [the word], since the rule "that which is the locus of an operation applies to that which ends with it" (Pāṇini 1.1.72) already establishes the application of the suffix to what ends with it (*tadantavidhi*), the inclusion of the word *anta* ("ending in") is for the purpose of indicating:

"In this section concerning the *ktvā* suffix, the application of the suffix to what ends with it does not occur without a specific effort. By means of this, in the subsequent sūtra, the verbal root *ṛ* is understood in its own form.
It is understood [as the root itself], and not as ending with that [suffix].
24. *vañci-luñcy-ṛtaś-ca* (Pāṇini 1.2.24). [The roots] *vañcu* "to deceive" (Dhātupāṭha 1703), *luñca* "to pluck away" (Dhātupāṭha 187), and *ṛt*.

Thus, these are the two verbal roots mentioned in the Sūtras, wherein the suffix *īyaṅ* is prescribed by the rule *ṛterīyaṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.29). The rule *ṛterīyaṅ* applies in the domain of *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes.
"It is optionally applied" by the rule *ādāya ārdhadhātuke vā* (3.1.31). "Having spoken" (*vacitvā*)—here there is elision of the nasal *n* by the rule *aniditām* (6.4.24).
"He should speak" (*vaktavā*)—here, in one alternative, there is the absence of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *udito vā* (7.2.56). The letter *ca* [indicates this optionality].
The inclusion of the word "vā" (or) is for the purpose of making its *svarita* accent clear.
By this, the mention of Kāśyapa in the subsequent rule is for the sake of honor (*pūjārtha*); otherwise, it would be understood as having the sense of an option (*vikalpārtha*). And thus:
Because it falls between two alternative rules (*vibhāṣā*), this rule would be considered permanent (*nitya*). 25. *tṛṣimṛṣikṛśeḥ kāśyapasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.25).
[The roots] *tṛṣ* in the sense of "thirst" (Dhātupāṭha 1228), *mṛṣ* in the sense of "endurance," and *kṛś*.

(Dhātupāṭha 1164), *kṛśa* "to make thin" (Dhātupāṭha 1227). Regarding the statement, "The mention of Kāśyapa is for the sake of honor," honor consists precisely in manifesting a unique knowledge, namely: "This knowledge concerning this subject belongs to Kāśyapa alone, and not to others. Tas... [text fragment]
By means of that worship, the worship of the scripture itself is also performed, characterized by the manifestation of its great significance.

Such indeed is the great significance of the scripture that even such seekers of liberation (mumukṣu) hold it in high esteem. For this reason, why should the mention of Kāśyapa not be for the purpose of providing an alternative?
To this he says: "For it exists as 'or' (vā) indeed."
26. *ralo vyupadhāddhalādeḥ saṃśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.26).

Since the suffix *ktvā* has its *kit*-status prohibited by *na ktvā seṭ* (1.2.18), and since the suffix *san* is also established as having no *it*-augment (*akit*) by its very nature, this rule applies to both cases by way of positive prescription (*vidhimukhena*).
In the view that [the root] *pravartate* occurs, the *kit* status applies;
thus, one says *vididyotiṣate*—as stated in the *Kāśikā* and the *Padamañjarī*.
In the form *vididyotiṣate*, there is the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the reduplication according to the rule *dyautisvāpyoḥ saṃprasāraṇam* (Pāṇini 7.4.67).

Regarding *ṭheṣiṣiṣati*: from the root *iṣu* in the sense of "desire" (*dhā.pā.* 1351), when the augment *iṭ* is applied, the second monosyllabic (*ekāc*) portion is reduplicated according to *ajāderdvitīyasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.2).
Regarding *bubhukṣate*: by the rule *halantācca* (Pāṇini 2.1.10), the suffix is invariably *kit*.

Although it would have been simpler to state "from a root having *ṭh* as an upadhā," the expression "from a root having *vy* as an upadhā" was used in order to indicate that all mentions of *iṇ* refer to the *iṇ* followed by the subsequent *ṇ*. By this,
what was stated regarding the rule "ṭhlaṇ"— namely, "all mentions of *iṇ* refer to the *iṇ* followed by the subsequent *ṇ*"— is justified.
It comes to be.
27. *Ūkālo 'j jhrasvadīrghaplutaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.27).

That vowel (*aj*) whose time (*kāla*) is *ū* is called *ūkāla*. Now, is this designation not improper? For, *ū* is a word (*śabda*), whereas time (*kāla*) is an action (*kriyā*); how then can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) here?

This is not a fault; because here, by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), the word "ṭhū" refers to the act of pronunciation associated with "ṭhū. Even so, this is incorrect; for that pronunciation associated with "ṭhū" belongs only to the vowel *ū*, and not to any other vowel. How then...

One might object: "In that case, [the suffix] ūkāraka would apply because of an action connected with another [person], for Devadatta does not become 'possessor of brindled cows' merely by virtue of brindled cows belonging to Yajñadatta.
This is not a fault; for it has been stated here that the sense of the suffix *vat* is implied. Thus, this has been explained.

It is as follows: that vowel whose duration is equal to the time of the act of pronunciation associated with the sound "ū"—that is, the act of pronouncing [the sound] "ū" itself—is called "having the duration of ū" (ūkāla). Now, one might object: "The term 'having the duration of ū' (ūkāla) is a single designatum (saṃjñī), yet there are three designations (saṃjñās); therefore, because of this discrepancy in number, the principle of corresponding assignment (saṃkhyātānudeśa) does not apply."
To one who might think thus, he replies: "The term 'ṭhū' refers to three," and so forth.

The meaning is that the designation 'ṭhū' is made by applying the single long substitute (ekādeśa) according to the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.101) for the three [sounds] of the *mātrikās*. But how is it known that this refers to three?

Is this a designation by means of phonetic conjunction (*praśleṣanirdeśa*)? No, because of the capacity of the rule to establish three distinct technical terms (*saṃjñā*). For the prescription of multiple terms for a single entity is not purposeful unless there is a distinct purpose for each. And here, in the case of assigning multiple terms to a single thing, there is no such distinct purpose. [This refers to the rule] "short, long, and protracted" (*hrasvadīrghapluta*).

If this single word were to be a technical name (saṃjñā), then, since the purpose of creating a technical name is for the sake of brevity, it would be improper to create such a long technical name. Furthermore, technical names possess the property of recurrence (āvṛti) in various rules (pradeśa), and this [word] as a whole is not a technical name.
[The phonemes] exist in their respective locations (*pradeśa*), and this aggregate (*samudāya*) does not recur in those locations;

rather, the words "short" (*hrasva*) and so forth apply to each [phoneme] individually. Therefore, considering that they are indicated by forming a *dvandva* compound, he says: "short, long, and protracted," and so on. As for the singular form of the *dvandva*, [it follows the rule] "every *dvandva*..."

This is because of the statement: "In the case of *vibhāṣā*, it becomes a singular. Now, one might object: "Since it is a *dvandva* used as a singular (*ekavadbhāva*), it ought to be neuter according to the rule *sa napuṃsakam* (Pāṇini 2.4.17); so how can there be a masculine designation? [The answer is: "Because this designation is based on the *sūtra* (i.e., it is archaic), and in Vedic usage (*chandas*) there is a transposition (*vyatyaya*) [of gender]."
The change of gender is stated by the rule *bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.1.85). Furthermore, because "the sūtras are like the Vedic meters" (*chandovatsūtrāṇi bhavanti*;
Mahābhāṣya 1.1.1), its masculine gender is not contradictory. The coalescence (*praśleṣa*) of these [vowels] occurs according to this sequence: *u*, *ū*, *ū3*.
[The author] demonstrates this. But from what [source] does this certainty arise—that "this alone is their sequence"?

He thinks as follows: because of the rule "vibhāṣā pṛṣṭaprativacane heḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.93), which prescribes a *pluta* vowel for the *hi* consisting of one *mātrā*, it is known that the *hi* consisting of one *mātrā* is not the final [element]. For if it were final, [the *pluta* would apply to it].
There would be the designation "protracted" (*pluta*). And in that case, the prescription of protraction would be purposeless;

for even a [vowel] of two morae (*mātrā*) does not become final, since the prescription of protraction for a [vowel] of two morae occurs by the rule *ṭhūm abhyādāne* (Pāṇini 8.2.87). For if it were indeed final, then...

If there were the designation *pluta* [for the vowel], then the prescription of *pluta* for a *pluta* would be purposeless. Therefore, at the end, there are not those [vowels] consisting of one mātrā and two mātrās. Nor is there one consisting of one mātrā in the middle, because of the rules "ato dīrgho yañi" (Pāṇini 7.3.101) and "supi ca" (Pāṇini 7.3.102).

Because of the force of the rule for long vowels (*dīrghavidhāna*). If there were a single-moraic (*ekamātrika*) vowel in the middle, then it would receive the designation "long" (*dīrghasaṃjñā*); in that case, the mention of a "long" vowel for a long vowel would be redundant. Therefore, [it follows that] it must be single-moraic at the beginning.
By process of elimination, [the vowel] in the middle has a duration of two mātrās, and at the end, three mātrās; thus: *ṭhu ū ū3*.
Here too, in the act of pronunciation associated with the initial *u* sound and so forth, the terms *u* and so forth are applied.
In this way, since "time" (*kāla*) is defined as the vowel (*aj*), there is the elision of the letter *y*.

But has it not been stated that this *u* being taken as a vowel (*aṇ*) includes its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*), and thus, when the long and protracted (*pluta*) *u*s are included by the short *u*, they too would receive the designation "short"? To this he says:
“The mention of time (*kāla-grahaṇa*),” and so forth. For when the mention of time is made, these designations are prescribed for those [vowels] which possess that duration.

For them, the qualifiers of having one mora (*ekamātrikatva*), two moras (*dvimātrikatva*), and three moras (*trimātrikatva*) are obtained respectively. For instance, when the duration of time is taken and the completion of the sentence is applied to each [term], there arise three *bahuvrīhi* compounds: *uḥ*...
That which has the duration of *ka* is *ukāla*; that which has the duration of *ū* is *ūkāla*;

that which has the duration of *ū3* is *ū3kāla*. Of these, respectively, vowels (*ac*) having one measure (*mātrā*), two measures, and three measures are the referents of the other members of the compound. This is because the vowel *ṛ*, which has exactly one measure, is associated with this [term].
It is of equal duration to the act of pronunciation of [the sound] *u*;
likewise, the vowel *ā* [in the word] *ṭhū* is of equal duration to the act of pronunciation associated with it;
thus.
An *ac* vowel consisting of exactly three measures (*trimātrika*) is simultaneous with the act of pronunciation associated with "ṭhū3"; and this being the case,
the designation of "short" (*hrasva*) is prescribed for an *ac* vowel whose measure is one measure (*mātrā*), even when the vowel *u* is present.

When the long and protracted [vowels] are included, that [rule] does not apply to them, for they are not measured by a single mora (*mātrā*). Therefore, in forms such as *ālūya* and *pariṇīya*, the substitution *tuṭ* does not occur on the basis of a short vowel.

Regarding *ṭhpratyakṣya* and *prarakṣya*: from the roots *takṣū* and *tvakṣū* meaning "to make thin" (*dhātupāṭha* 655, 656), and *rakṣa* meaning "to protect" (*dhātupāṭha* 658), when a compound is formed according to *kugatiprādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18), the suffix *lyap* is applied by *samāse 'nañpūrve ktvo lyap* (Pāṇini 7.1.37). In that context, following [the rule]:

Since the two *hal* sounds [in *mātṛbhyām*] that possess the designation "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) also possess the property of having an *ū* vowel as their *kal*, if the mention of *aj* were absent, the designation "short" (*hrasva*) would apply;
and consequently, the augment *tuk* would be triggered by that short vowel.

It would follow [that the rule] applies in the case of *titauccchatram*. Here, because the aggregate of the vowels *a* and *ū* possesses the duration of two mātrās due to having the quality of *ūkāla*, it would receive the designation "long" (*dīrgha*). Consequently, [the rule] *padāntādvā* (P. 6.1.76) [would apply].

Thus, the undesirable consequence (prasajyeta) would follow regarding what is conceptualized as *ac*. However, when *ac* is not included [in the definition], the designation "long" (*dīrgha-saṃjñā*) does not occur, because a collection of vowels (*ac-samudāya*) is not captured by the inclusion of *ac*. Now, even if that [designation] were present—

When the designation "long" (dīrgha) is based on the whole, this designation "short" (hrasva) will be based on its constituent part. However, the *tuṅ* [augment] would necessarily depend on that [whole]; this is not the case, because due to its posteriority, the optional application of *tuṅ* based on the "long" vowel would prevail. Furthermore, in such a context, there is no recognition of a "re-occurrence" (*punar-prasaṅga*) where—
A preceding rule, while being applied, does not sublate the cognition of a subsequent rule;

in that case, it is said: "It is established by the principle of the cognition of recurrence. But here, an obligatory (nitya) rule sublates the cognition of an optional (vikalpa) rule that follows it.

Because there is a contradiction between the permanent [application] and the optional [application], and because of the paribhāṣā rule: "When two rules apply simultaneously and there is a conflict, that which is sublated remains sublated," the option would occur by that very rule. Therefore, the mention of *aj* [is necessary].

28. *acaśca* (1.2.28). This is a governing rule (*paribhāṣā*) characterized by a gender marker, intended to restrict the application to the substituend (*sthānin*); it applies in the various rules (*pradeśa*), such as *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya* (1.2.47).

In such instances as these, [the term *prātipadika*] is brought into proximity (*upatiṣṭhate*); and upon that proximity, two genitive cases (*ṣaṣṭhī*) appear, since there is freedom of choice regarding the relationship between qualifier and qualified. In the rule "The short vowel replaces the final of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) in the neuter" (Pāṇini 1.2.47), the nominal stem being referred to by the word *ac* is thus qualified.

The rule applies to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that ends in *aj*, but the nominal stem is not qualified by *aj*. For if the nominal stem were qualified by *aj*— meaning "that which belongs to a nominal stem ending in *aj*"— then even a vowel situated in the middle would undergo shortening.

Regarding the statement "the *brāhmaṇa* family has beautiful speech" (*suvāg brāhmaṇakulam*), since it is the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that is being qualified here, this genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) expresses the relationship of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) with respect to the stem itself, and not a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*).

Consequently, by the rule "of the final vowel" (*alo 'ntyasya*), only the final vowel of the stem undergoes shortening. [This is contrasted with] the rule "the final syllable (*ṭi*) of a sentence is protracted (*pluta*) and acute (*udātta*)."
In this rule (8.2.82), the term *ṭi* which is being grasped is qualified by the vowel *ac*: "the *ṭi* which is an *ac*.

By this, even a vowel situated in the middle of a *ṭi* undergoes prolation (*pluta*). However, if the *ṭi* were qualified by the vowel *ac*—that is, "the *ṭi* ending in an *ac*"—then [prolation] would apply only here: *devadatā3*; but not in the following case.

It may be [the case of] "agnicit. By the word *ca* ("and"), *ajit* is drawn forward; its purpose will be stated right here. Examples such as *atirit* and so forth have been explained under [Pāṇini 1.1.48], *ṭheca igghrasvādeśe*. [In the term *agnicit*, the suffix *kvip* is applied] in the sense of the passive (*karmaṇi*), as in "that by which the fire-altar is built" (*cīyate*).
Regarding the letter *lakāra*, he provides the reasoning for the rule "the designation is restricted" by stating: "the term *aj* is understood [to recur].
For when the mention of *aj* is being carried over, the short vowels and other such terms that are also being carried over bring to mind only the vowels (*ac*).

They function [as qualifiers] because that [substitute] presents itself spontaneously. Consequently, while having their own forms alone as their referents, they serve as qualifiers for the vowel (*ac*) being enjoined. In this regard, the connection is made thus: "In place of *aḥ*, [there is] *aj*."

It is that which is prescribed by such technical designations as "short" (*hrasva*), "long" (*dīrgha*), and "protracted" (*pluta*). For example: *dyauḥ*, *panthāḥ*, *saḥ*. These have been explained under the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī* (Pāṇini 1.1.3).
And in these cases, according to the requirements, [the rule] *diva aut* (7.1.84) applies.

By the rules *ṭhpathimathyṛbhukṣāmāt* (7.1.85) and *ṭhtyadādīnāmaḥ* (7.2.102), the vowels *au*, *ā*, and so forth, being prescribed in their own forms (*svarūpeṇa*), are not prescribed by means of technical names such as *dīrgha* (long); therefore, they occur in place of consonants (*hal*) alone, and not of vowels (*ac*). [Thus, we have] *dyobhyām*.

In the case of *dyaubhiḥ* as well, the vowel *u* prescribed by the rule *diva u* (Pāṇini 7.1.131) is not enjoined with the technical designation of "short" (*hrasva*); therefore, it occurs in place of the consonant alone, and not of a vowel (*ac*). Now, one might object that the three examples beginning with *dyauḥ* are already covered by the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī* (Pāṇini 1.1.3).

They are established by the rule for the application of technical names (*saṃjñāvidhānaniyama*), for in that context these very counter-examples were previously presented; therefore, there is no purpose for a rule prescribing a technical name for this sake? This is true; however, he thinks as follows:
A restriction must be formulated regarding the assignment of technical names (saṃjñā) for cases such as *dyaubhyām* and *dyaubhiḥ*;

for the vowel *u* possesses neither the name "guṇa" nor the name "vṛddhi. Since this [result] is already established by the aforementioned restriction on the assignment of technical names, this [present rule] serves another purpose.

This rule for the application of technical names is being made in order to favor even those who are forgetful and do not remember the purpose of the previous rule; thus, it also serves the purpose [of establishing the names] for *dyauḥ*, *panthāḥ*, and *saḥ*.

29. *uccair udāttaḥ* (1.2.29). Terms such as *udātta* and the rest are well-known in both common usage (*loka*) and the Veda (*veda*). To one who might raise the objection, "What is the purpose of providing these technical designations? [the author replies:]...
He replies with the words "The words 'udātta' and so forth," etc. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the *anudātta* and *svarita* accents are included.
The particle "eva" (only) is to be understood as displaced in order, and should be read immediately after the phrase "is a property of the phoneme" (*varṇadharma*).

In both worldly usage and the Veda, properties such as *udātta* (high pitch) and so forth are well-known as qualities (*guṇa*) belonging specifically to the phonemes (*varṇa*), and not to the vowel (*ac*) that follows them. Therefore, here in grammar, the properties such as *udātta* are designated—that is, defined—as being qualities of whichever vowel they belong to; otherwise, [the rule would be meaningless].

The intention is that because words such as "udātta" (high-pitched) are heard in reference to specific locations (*pradeśa*), they would be understood as properties of the phoneme (*varṇa*) itself, and not as belonging to that which possesses it (*tadvān*).
The word "highly" (*uccais*) refers to excellence of audibility (*śrutiprakarṣa*); one speaks "highly" when there is excellence of audibility. *Uccaiḥ*.
Regarding the word "paṭhati" (he recites): there exists the expression "Devadatta stands high," where "high" (uccaiḥ) denotes a locus of measurement;
that is, "high" is a measure, and its locus is what is expressed here by the word "high.
Therefore, in this context, the meaning of the second occurrence of the word "high" is taken, not that of the other.

To demonstrate this, he says: "‘Loudly’ (*uccaiḥ*)". However, the meaning of the word *uccaiḥ* when employed in a sentence such as "he speaks loudly" (*uccair bhāṣate*), namely "excessiveness of hearing," is not what is intended here by the term *uccaiḥ*. If...

If it were grasped [as a mere property], then in the case of the *upāṃśu* (whispered) recitation, the designations such as "acute" (*udātta*) and so forth would not apply; because of the absence of excellence (*prakarṣa*), and since these [accents] are established through excellence, they would not be distinguished. For that very same sound which is high (*uccaiḥ*) with respect to one person is indeed low (*nīcaiḥ*) with respect to another. And thus...
The intention is that everything would be *udātta*, even that which is intended to be the most *anudātta*.

Regarding the phrase "produced by the place" (*sthānakṛta*) and so forth: let it be granted that there is a specific measure [of pitch], yet the place (*sthāna*) which serves as its substratum would become high-pitched (*uccaiḥ*). And in this case, not everything would be *udātta*.
The meaning is that what is unaccented (anudātta) is called "high" (uccaiḥ).
Regarding the term "bhāgavatsu": those which possess parts (bhāga) are "bhāgavanti.
Those parts are situated in the articulatory locations (sthāna), such as the palate and so forth, in a vertical arrangement. The location (sthāna) is "high."
It is expressed by the word; why then is "highness" (uccais) a qualifier of the named object (*saṃjñin*)?

Because it is produced in a high location. In that regard, when the location is the same, that which is produced in the upper portion is designated as *udātta*. If a vowel (*ac*) is produced in the upper portion of the location—
It is merely stated that "it becomes high-pitched" (*udātasaṃjña*); however, in this way, the same fault of instability (*anavasthita-doṣa*) remains.

For instance, the very same portion of the palate (*tālu*) and other articulatory sites that is high-pitched in small-bodied persons becomes low-pitched in large-bodied persons relative to their respective palates and other sites. Therefore, [the term] "equal" (*samāna*)—

This has been stated as a qualification of the location (*sthāna*). Because the purpose of creating a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is brevity, this [qualification] is obtained by employing a multi-syllabic name when a single-syllabic name ought to have been made. From an increase in the text comes an increase in the meaning.

"It exists. Now, one might object: from the mere fact that there is an excess of text here, it is understood only that some additional meaning intended by the Teacher is present; how, then, is this specific point—that there is equality—obtained? It is obtained from the uninterrupted lineage of oral instruction. Furthermore, as for that equality:
It should be understood that [the accent] is due to the non-difference of the speaker, and not due to the non-difference of the locations such as the palate;
otherwise, the acute accent (*udātta*) would depend solely on the palate and not on the throat and other places.
Even though the palate and so forth—which are distinct—become identical by means of the non-difference of the speaker, this [accentual distinction] is still perceived.

There is no fault. What, then, is the characteristic of this "accomplished high-pitched" (*uccabhāganiṣpanna*) [intonation]? He says: "In which," and so forth. The explanation of "extension" (*āyāma*) is "restraint" (*nigraha*). Restraint is stiffness. "Closed throat" (*saṃvṛtakaṇṭhatā*) means the closure of the opening of the throat. Precisely for this reason...

As the wind slowly exits, it dries the parts of the throat; there arises roughness and lack of moisture. Regarding the forms *te* and *ke*: from the words *ya-* and *ka-*, the substitution of *yat* for the pronouns beginning with *tyad-* occurs; then, by *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97), the single substitute of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) takes place; then *jasaḥ śī* (7.1.17) applies; and finally, by *ādguṇaḥ* (6.1.87), the guṇa substitution is effected. In this case:
The base is acute by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). The case-ending has the grave accent (*anudātta*) according to Pāṇini 6.1.158 (*ṭhanudātau suppitau*).
However, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from their combination is acute by virtue of Pāṇini 8.2.5 (*ekādeśa udātenodāttaḥ*).

30. *nīcairanudāttaḥ* (1.2.30). The explanation of *anvavasarga* is *mārdava*, meaning softness or laxity. The explanation of *mṛdutā* is *snigdhatā* (smoothness). The explanation of *urutā* is also *mahatā* (greatness).

Furthermore, because the opening of the throat is large, the air exiting quickly does not dry out the parts of the throat; therefore, the tone becomes smooth (*snigdha*). The words *tva*, *sama*, *sima*, and *nema* are listed among the *sarvādi* group as being "not high-pitched" (*anuccāni*). They are low-pitched.

"Low-pitched" (*anuccāni*) means "unaccented" (*anudātāni*). In the passage beginning with *namaste rudra*, the word *te* is unaccented because of the governing rule *anudātam sarvam apādādau* (Pāṇini 8.1.18), which states that everything [except the vocative] at the beginning of a metrical quarter is unaccented. Furthermore, the words *rudra* and so forth are also [unaccented] by virtue of the rule *āmantritasya ca* (Pāṇini 8.1.19).
By this eighth [rule], all [vowels] become *anudātta*.

31. *samāhāraḥ svaritaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.31). The words *udātta* and *anudātta* are technical designations (*saṃjñā*) for specific qualities. For technical designations, when uttered in the rules (*pradeśa*), [refer to the things they designate].

They cause the notion [of the two] to be conveyed. When those two, the udātta and the anudātta, are present here as following [the vowel], there is a cognition [of them]; therefore, the designation *svarita* is prescribed for the vowel (*ac*) whose nature consists of a combination [of the two].

Furthermore, the word *samāhāra*—derived as "the act of collecting" (*samāharaṇam*) or "that which is collected" (*samāhṛtaḥ*)—is a term established in common usage as a collective whole (*samudāya*) through its derivation denoting an abstract state (*bhāva-sādhana*). Now, no collection of vowels (*ac-samudāya*) consisting of both acute (*udātta*) and grave (*anudātta*) accents is possible; therefore, since the bearer of the designation (*saṃjñin*) cannot exist, the designation (*saṃjñā*) itself is also impossible.
To one who might raise this objection, he replies with the words "And because of its capacity," and so forth. This is what is stated:

[the rule] says that the combination of an udātta and an anudātta becomes known as svarita; however, there is no possibility of a vowel (ac) consisting of a technical (pāribhāṣika) combination of udātta and anudātta. In that case...

By implication, only those two properties—udātta and anudātta—which are well-known in both worldly usage and the Veda, are to be understood here; not the vowels (ac). But even so, the same fault remains: this designation is prescribed for vowels that are already established in the world as being udātta or anudātta by nature; for what, then, [is it prescribed]?
The acute (*udātta*) and grave (*anudātta*) tones, well-known from both worldly usage and the Vedas, are combined (*samāhriyete*) within a vowel;

and since such a combination of these two can indeed occur even in a single vowel, how could there be an impossibility regarding the designatum (*saṃjñin*)? [This is the meaning of the phrase: "they are combined within which."

By saying this, it is shown that this word *samāhāra* (collection/aggregate) functions as a locus (*adhikaraṇasādhana*) rather than as an abstract state (*bhāvasādhana*). The meaning is that [the two] are brought together (*samāhriyete*), joined together (*saṃhanyete*), or perceived in combination. Regarding the word "suspended loop" (*śikyam*): [it is derived from the root] *pūñ*.

In the rule *yaṇṇug hrasvaśca* (Daiva-Upaniṣad 16), while the word *yat* is understood from the context, the form [kanyā] is derived from the root *śraṃs* by applying the suffix *yat*, replacing the initial *ś* with *śi*, and adding the augment *kuṭ*. Because it bears the marker *t*, it is *svarita* (circumflex). [The word] *kanyā*.

Thus: according to the *Phitsūtra* 4.76, "In *tilya*, *śikya*, *martya*, *kāśmarya*, *dhānya*, *kanyā*, *rājanya*, and *manuṣya*, [the vowel] at the end is circumflex (*svarita*). Regarding "sāmānya": it means "skilled in the *sāman*. The suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *tatra sādhuḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.98). [The word] *kva* is derived from the interrogative pronoun *kim*.
The suffix *at* is applied by the rule "saptamyantāt kimo't" (Pāṇini 5.3.12), and the substitution of *kvā* occurs by the rule "kvāti" (Pāṇini 7.2.105).

32. *tasyādita udāttardhahasvam* (Pāṇini 1.2.32). *Āditaḥ* means "at the beginning" (*ādau u*); the suffix *tasi* is used here in the sense of the locative case. This very mention serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the rule stating that the suffix *tasi* occurs after words such as *ādi*. Therefore, within the section concerning *tasi*, [the suffix applies] after words such as *ādi*.
The supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) [Vārttika 634] need not be stated. Regarding the expression *arddha-hrasvam*:

the meaning is "half of a short vowel. The compound is formed by *ardhaṃ napuṃsakam* (Pāṇini 2.2.2). Consequently, according to the rule *paravalliṅgam* (Pāṇini 2.4.26) and others, the compound should take the masculine gender.
This is not the case because the word *hrasva* (short) is masculine; for the word *hrasva* is applied by taking up a specific dimension as its quality (*guṇa*),

and since it is a quality-word (*guṇavacana*)— according to the rule "the gender and number of words denoting qualities follow those of their substratum"— it [would take the gender of its substrate], just like the word *śukla* (white).

Thus, the word *hrasva* (short) is of three genders. Fearing that the designation "short" (*hrasva*) might apply only to that which consists of one *mātrā*, and not to the long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*), he says: "half-short" (*arddha-hrasvam*), and so forth. Half of a short vowel is half a *mātrā*; therefore, it becomes a half-*mātrā*.
Therefore, by the mention of "half-short" (*arddhahrasva*), the half-mora (*ardhamātrā*) is indicated. For this very reason, it was stated [in the sūtra] "of that" (*tasya*).

This is for the purpose of indicating the three types of *svarita* vowels—short, long, and protracted. And if the mention of "half-short" is an indication of the half-mora, then the mention of these three becomes meaningful.
It occurs thus, and not otherwise.

Regarding the statement "the mention of 'short' (hrasva) is non-essential" (*atantra*): "non-essential" means secondary, because it serves as a mere indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*). Just as in the expression "let the curd be protected from crows," where the crows [merely indicate the cause of potential contamination], by this [principle], this [rule] applies to all short vowels and so forth.

There is a division of the *svarita* accent. [Objection: Even so, the division of the eighth [type of] *svarita* is not established, because it is unestablished (*asiddha*). [Response: This is not so; for a subsequent rule (*paravidhi*) is unestablished with respect to a preceding rule (*pūrvavidhi*). And this is not a rule; what then? It is that which has been prescribed for it.

The purpose is to explain the division [of the rule]. Alternatively, it is established by means of a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) in the rule *na mu ne* (Pāṇini 8.2.3), as in the phrase *evaścir vā*. This first part is pronounced more clearly with an acute accent (*udātta*); being colored by that, it attains, as it were, the very form of that [accent].

The subsequent portion, like a crystal gem colored by a proximate object, cannot be designated as "anudātta" (unaccented) because it is distinct from the pure udātta due to having a different phonetic quality; nor can it be designated as "udātta."

It does not deserve [to be called so], because it is merely a coloring (uparāga). Therefore, some maintain that there is only one accent. Others, however, say: when the latter part is not colored by the preceding part—which has not produced an excellence of form—then, because it appears in its own form, it is designated as "anudātta" (unaccented).

But when, like a crystal gem with a proximate substrate, it is overwhelmed by a more intense whiteness from the preceding part and becomes colored accordingly, it attains as it were that very form; at that time,
it is designated as "having a single sound" (*ekaśruti*), being non-different, unitary, and of identical form with the sound of the preceding part.

This is because of the perception (*śruti*) of [the *svarita* accent] belonging to that [syllable]. For at that time, there is no distinction whatsoever regarding the perception of the *svarita* between the preceding and the following [syllables], since both are perceived as possessing the quality of being acute (*udātta*).
33. *Ekaśruti dūrāt saṃbuddhau* (Pāṇini 1.2.33).

"The statement 'the *ṭheka* is heard' is a sentence (*vākya*). By using the term "sentence," he excludes both the individual word (*pada*) and a portion of a word (*padaikadeśa*), because those two lack the capacity for address (*sambodhana*).
Since the sentence assumes the status of an instrument when an address is to be performed, it [is the basis for the rule].

This is its capacity. Therefore, its monotony (*ekaśruti*) is prescribed. But from what source is that statement? He says: "by which one addresses from afar. By this, the status of the sentence as an instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the vocative is shown. "From afar"— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.*

The ablative case is used [here] by the rule *dūrāntikārthebhyo dvitīyā ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.35). By the statement "addressing is *sambuddhi*" (*sambodhanaṃ sambuddhiḥ*) and so forth, he demonstrates that the mention of *sambuddhi* is based on its etymological meaning (*yathārtha-grahaṇa*), and not the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) definition of *sambuddhi*. If the technical *sambuddhi* were being referred to...

In that case, regarding the reading *brahmāṇaḥ* in the *Padamañjarī*, there would be no monotonous intonation (*ekaśruti*) for the word *brahmāṇaḥ*; this is because the technical term "vocative" (*sambuddhi*) does not apply here.
However, if one adopts the etymological sense, it does occur; for here too, there exists a "vocative" in the form of the action characterized by addressing.
The meaning is "because it exists. But why is this interpretation of the term as being literal (*anvartha*) determined?

Because of the mention of "distance" (*dūra*). When the term is interpreted literally, the vocative case is produced by the word *dūrāt*. [Note: This line does not exist in the Kāśikā. "When a distant address is to be made..."

Therefore, the term *dūra* (far) functions as an ablative (*apādāna*) in its literal sense; however, if it were taken in its technical (*pāribhāṣikī*) sense, it would be entirely irrelevant. For there is no "remoteness" inherent in the case-ending of a vocative (*āmantrita-vibhakti*). And although remoteness is not fixed, nevertheless, where speech is established by natural effort, [it does not apply].

It is heard [in the scriptures]; therefore, it should be understood here as being far [removed from ordinary speech]. Regarding the passage beginning with "of vowels" (*svarāṇām*), this line does not exist in the *Kāśikā*. The subsequent explanation is: "non-distinction" (*avibhāgaḥ*) refers to the description of the nature of monotonous intonation (*ekaśruti*), which is the concealment of differences (*bhedatirodhānam*).

The non-perception of specific accents such as the acute (*udātta*) and so forth, and the cognition of the mere phonemes such as *a* and so on, is what is meant by "monotone" (*ekaśruti*). For example: *āgaccha bho māṇavaka devadattā3*. Here, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) occurs in this very sense according to [Pāṇini 8.2.84], *dūrāddhūte ca*; and that [protracted vowel] is acute (*udātta*). [This applies to] the end of a sentence...

Because of the governing rule "ṭeḥ pluta udātaḥ" (8.2.82), the introduction of that single accent (ekaśruti) for the acute (udāta) is desired in order to exclude the protracted (pluta) vowel; he will explain how this is obtained. In the counter-example, there is indeed the threefold accent (traisvarya); in that case, the vowel "ā" [is a particle] because it is a nipāta.

The word *ādi* is acute-accented (*udātta*) by *Phiṭ-sūtra* 4.80, "ādyaudātāḥ," and *upa-* is acute-accented by *Phiṭ-sūtra* 4.81, "upasargāścābhivarjam. In the word *gaccha*, there is the *nighāta* (elision of accent) by *Pāṇini* 8.1.28, "tiṅṅatiṅaḥ. The particle *bho* is acute-accented on its first syllable by the rule "nipātā ādyaudātāḥ. [The vocative] *māṇavaka*—
The *nighāta* (anudātta accent) applies to the words *devadatta* and *śabda* by virtue of the rule *amantrite ca* (8.1.19).

34. *yajñakarmaṇyajapanyūṅkhasāmasu* (1.2.34): [This refers to] "Agni is the head of heaven" (*agnirmūrdhā divaḥ*), etc. [The roots] *ag-i* and *rag-i* have the meaning of "motion" (*gatyarthāḥ*) according to the Dhātupāṭha (146, 144).

While the rule "ni after the roots *vi*, *jyā*, and *jvari*" (Daivamukha 1.18) is in force, the suffix *ni* is applied by the rule "after the root *aṅg*, there is *ni* and elision of *na*" (Daivamukha 1.20); furthermore, the elision of *na* occurs. The word *agni* is oxytone due to the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). [The root] *murvī* (meaning "to bind") [is used with the suffix] *akanin*.

From the rule *yu-vṛṣi-takṣi-rāji-dhani-vidy-u-pratidivaḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 6.51), while the suffix *kanin* is still in force, the word *mūrdhan* is prescribed as ending in the suffix *kanin* by the rule *śvan-ukṣan-pūṣan-plīhan-kledan-snehan-mūrdhan-majjan-aryaman-viśvapsan-parijman-mātariśvan-maghavan* (Dhātupāṭha 6.55). Thus, due to this specific prescription (*nipātana*), the first syllable is udātta. The change of the letter *va* to *dha* occurs here precisely because of this prescription. From the root *divu* (meaning "to play," etc., Dhātupāṭha 1107), the suffix *ḍvin* is added. The vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Because of the power of the inclusion of the *ḍ* as an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), even though it is not part of a nominal stem (*abha*), [the suffix *ṭa* is applied].

By the rule *eḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.143), there is the elision of the *ṭi* portion. When *div* remains, by the rule *ūḍidampadādyappumraidyaubhyaḥ* (6.1.171), the case-ending (*vibhakti*) receives the acute accent on its final syllable.
Regarding the word *kakud*, it is printed [in the commentaries] that "the final syllable of a word ending in *pphiṣ* is acute."
The word *pati* is udātta on the final syllable according to the rule "A nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is udātta on the final syllable" (Phiṭ-sūtra 1.1).

The word *pati* ends in the suffix *ḍati*, as per the rule "from the root *pāti*, [the suffix] *ḍati*" (Daiva-nighaṇṭu 1.27); thus, by the accent of the suffix, it is udātta on the first syllable. Consequently, in the compound *kakutpatiḥ* (the lord of the hump), [the first member retains its original accent].

It is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), and by the rule *ṣaṭ-samāsasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.223), it has an udātta accent on the final syllable. [The root] *prath* (meaning "to become famous," Dhātupāṭha 1553) takes the suffix *ṣivan* with vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule *pratheḥ ṣivan saṃprasāraṇañ ca* (Daiva Uṇādi Sūtra 8.124).

From the word *pṛthivī*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *ṣid-gaurādibhyaś-ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.41). By the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), [the word *pṛthivī* is acute on the final syllable].
The suffix *īṣ* [denoting] a root-stem (*dhātu*) or a secondary member (*praty-aṅga*) has its first syllable udātta. The sixth case singular ending is *ṅsi*.

By the rule "ṭhāṇnadyāḥ," it becomes anudātta. There is a long vowel by *savarṇadīrgha*. The substitution of *yaṇ* occurs by the rule "iko yaṇ aci" (6.1.77). The case-ending is udātta by the rule "udātayaṇo halpūrvāt" (6.1.174).

Regarding the word *idam*: from the root *ṣṭhā* (in the sense of "standing")—as in *ṣṭhidi paramaiśvarye* (Dhātupāṭha 63)—the augment *num* is applied by the rule *ṣṭhivuklamvācamāśruvaso num dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.58).
Then, by the rule *ṣṭhindeḥ kamir nalopaś ca* (Pañcapādī Uṇādi-sūtra 596), the suffix *kamin* is added and the nasal (*n*) is elided;
thus, the word *idam*, due to the suffix *kamin*, has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). [In the nominative singular] *sau*...

By the rule *parataṣṭhido'y puṃsi* (Pāṇini 7.1.111), there is a substitution of the form *id* for *idam*. Regarding the term *apām*: from the root *āplṛ* (meaning "to pervade," Dhātupāṭha 1260), the suffix *kvip* is applied with a short vowel by the rule *āpnotehrasvaśca* (Daiva-Uṇādi-sūtra 1.127); this is the genitive plural. [The elision of the final *m* occurs] by the rule *ūḍidaṃ padam* (Pāṇini 6.1.171).

The case ending is udātta; therefore, *apām* has its final syllable as udātta. [In the word *retāṃsi*: from the root *ṛ* "to go" (DhP 1404), the suffix *asun* is added by the rule *struribhyāṃ tuṭ ca* (Daiva-Upaniṣad 9.62). There is the augment *tuṭ*. By the rule regarding *nit*-svarita, *retāṃsi* is udātta on its first syllable. [Regarding the word *jinvati*: from the root] *ji*...

From the root *ji* (DhP 5.61), the present tense suffix (*laṭ*) is applied, followed by the substitution of *śatṛ*. By the rule *vyatyayo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.1.85), there is an irregular application (*vyatyaya*) of the *śnu* suffix. By the rule *huśnuvoḥ sārvadhātuke* (6.4.87), the *yaṇ* substitution occurs.
By the rule *ugitaśca* (4.1.6), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added. Finally, by the rule *ambārthanadyorhrasvaḥ* (7.3.107), the shortening of the vowel takes place.
Thus, [the vowel] is short. By the rule "ṭheṅ hrasvāt sambuddheḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.69), there is elision of the suffix *su*.

While the context of "ye yajñakarmaṇi" (8.2.88) is still in force, by the rule "praṇavaṣṭeḥ" (8.2.89), the substitution of the syllable *oṃ* (*praṇava*) occurs. And that [substituted syllable] is protracted (*pluta*).

And it is acute (*udātta*), because of the governing rule: "The final syllable of a sentence is protracted and acute" (Pāṇini 8.2.82). They call the *praṇava* either the vowel *o* or the syllable *oṃ*.

By virtue of the prescription that the *praṇava* is acute, and because [the *praṇava*] is not considered established (*asiddha*) for the purposes of the rule concerning a vocative following a word, [it remains acute].

By the rule *ca* (Pāṇini 8.1.19), the [final syllable] does not become unaccented (*anudātta*); however, it does so for the remainder. When these accents have been obtained, the single accent (*ekaśruti*) is prescribed [for the Vedic recitation]. This is so that it may not occur during *saṃpāṭha*. *Saṃpāṭha* refers to the time of private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), such as "mām agne" and so forth.
From the root *kṣapaṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 1209), the suffix *madik* is applied according to *yuṣyasimyāṃ madik* (Daiva-Uṇādi-sūtra 6.50).
The word *asmad* is udātta on its final syllable due to the accent of the suffix. [In the formation of] the singular genitive case of *yusmad* and *asmad*, [the rule] *yuṣmadasmadbhyām*...

By the rule *ṅso 'ś* (Pāṇini 7.1.27), there is the substitution of *aś* for the genitive ending; by the rule *tavamamau ṅsi* (7.2.96), there is the substitution of *mama* for *asmad*. Due to the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), it is oxytone. By the rule *ato guṇe* (6.1.97), there is the single-substitute form (*pararūpa*). By the rule *ekādeśa udātenodātah* (8.2.5), this applies to the word *agni*.

The *nighāta* (anudātta accent) applies by the rule "ṭhāmantritasya ca" (Pāṇini 8.1.19). Regarding the word *varcas*: from the verbal root *varc* in the sense of "to shine" (Dhātupāṭha 162), the suffix *asun* is added according to "ṭhasun" (Daiva Uṇādi Sūtra 9.49). By virtue of the *nit*-accent, the word *varcas* has its first syllable udātta. Regarding the root *hveñ* in the sense of "to contend" (Dhātupāṭha 1008): [the rule] "ṭhhvaḥ saṃprasāraṇañca nyabhyupadiṣu" [applies].
By [Pāṇini 3.3.58], the suffix *ap* is applied. By [Pāṇini 2.2.19], "the subordinate word (*upapada*) which is not a finite verb," a compound is formed.

Although the rule "a *kṛt*-suffix following a motion-word (*gati*), an agentive factor (*kāraka*), or a subordinate word (*upapada*)" [Pāṇini 6.2.139] would result in the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member, while the term "final" (*antaḥ*) [from Pāṇini 6.2.143] is being carried over, [the rule] "of those ending in *thā*, *tha*, *ghañ*, *kta*, *ac*, *ap*, *itrac*, and *araṇ*" [Pāṇini 6.2.144] applies.

(6.2.144) Thus, there is the udātta accent on the final syllable; in the locative plural, by *ṭhbahuvacane jhalyet* (7.3.103), there is the substitution of *e*, and due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, the vowel *e* remains udātta. From the root *asa bhuvi* (DhP 1065), in the imperative (*loṭ*), with the suffix *tip*, by *ṭheruḥ* (3.4.86), there is the substitution of *u*.

Because [the root] begins with *a*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix. By the rule "ṭhtiṅṅtiṅḥ" (Pāṇini 8.1.28), the word *astu* is unaccented (*anudātta*). Regarding the statement "japa is a mantra of imitation": the term "japa" is an explanation of the meaning, namely that it is a "mantra of imitation. Imitation (*anukṛti*) means imitation (*anukaraṇa*). This applies everywhere.
The clear pronunciation of a mantra is what constitutes an *anukaraṇa-mantra* (imitative mantra). For this very reason, he says: "the practice of whispering" (*upāṃśuprayoga*).
This refers to recitation by one submerged in water.
In some places, the reading is *akaraṇa-mantra*; in that case, the meaning is as follows: "slight making" (*īṣatkaraṇa*) refers to the act of utterance.
"Of whom that is the mantra of non-doing"; for the negative particle *nañ* has the sense of "slight" (*īṣadartha*).

The word *eṣa* is a particle (*nipāta*). [According to] *Phiṭ-sūtra* 4.80: "Particles are udātta on their first syllable. [The root] *viś* means "to enter" (*praveśane*) [Dhātupāṭha 1424]; [the suffix] *kvan* is applied [according to] *Daiva-nirukta* 125: "After the roots *aś*, *pruṣ*, *laṭi*, *kaṇi*, *khaṭi*, and *viś*, the suffix *kvan* [is added]."

The word *viśva* is acutely accented on its first syllable by the *nitsvara* rule because it ends in the suffix *kvap*. The compound *samattriṇam* is a descriptive determinative (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) consisting of *samam* and *atriṇam*; it takes the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound. [Regarding the verb: from the root *dah* in the sense of "reducing to ashes" (DhP 991), there is the imperative (*loṭ*), second person singular (*sip*), the substitution of *hi* for *si*, and the elision of *hi* after *ataḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.105).

By the rule (Pāṇini 6.4.105), there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *hi*; and because the rule (Pāṇini 8.1.28) prescribing the suppression of accent (*nighāta*) applies, the word *daha* is unaccented (*anudātta*). Some read the word as *vahā3*, ending in a protracted vowel (*pluta*); for those who do not wish to admit such an irregularity (*sāhasa*), it is stated in the Mahābhāṣya (3.420): "In all cases, the protracted vowel should be declared to be optional."
From this statement, the *pluta* (protracted vowel) must be mentioned, and that is acute (*udātta*).

Others, however, read it with a final long *ā*; for them, the long *ā* occurs because it is Vedic (*chāndasa*). Indeed, even a short vowel becomes long by way of metrical or grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*), as in the examples "puruṣaḥ" and "nārakaḥ."
"Verses situated within specific sentences. As Jaimini has stated:
"The designation *sāman* applies to songs (*gīti*). A song is a particular kind of sound.
For what purpose is the word "action" (*karman*) included? One might simply say "in sacrifice" (*yajñe*), since [the verses] belong to the sacrificial mantras.

"Will it apply to the ritual act because its purpose is the performance of sacrifice? True, this is so; for the mention of the word "act" (*karman*) is indeed for the sake of clarity. Or rather, it is for the purpose that it may also apply to those sacrifices not commonly known, such as the *pañcayajana* and others; otherwise, if only "in sacrifice" (*yajñe*) were said, [it would refer only to] the well-known [sacrifices].
Whatever sacrifice there may be, such as the Aśvamedha and others, it should take place right there.
35. "Or the *vaṣaṭ*-call is higher.

(1.2.35) [The commentary states: "By the word *vaṣaṭ*, the word *vauṣaṭ* is indicated here," because they have the same meaning; this is the intended sense. Both of them are used to denote the giving to the gods, just as...
The word *ṭhvaṣaṭ* denotes the offering to the gods, and so too does the word *vauṣaṭ*.
Therefore, because they share the same meaning, the word *ṭhvaṣaṭ* indicates (*lakṣayati*) the word *vauṣaṭ*.

The inclusion of the term "word" (*kāraśabda*) is intended to signify that it functions as a linguistic unit (*śabdapadārthakatvena*), setting aside its status as a meaningful semantic unit (*arthapadārthakatva*).
This is for the purpose that the excellence of that [word] being employed in the act of giving may be manifested;
it is observed as having the word itself as its referent when the particle *kāra* is used, as in the case of the particle *eva*.

Others explain that the mention of *kāra* is so that the rule might apply to other cases as well; by this, in the expression *ṭhastu śrauṣaṭ*, this [suffix] becomes more highly accented (*udātatarah*). The suffix expressing excellence in *uccais-tarām* is that which is prescribed by the rule *brūhipreṣyaśrauṣaḍāvahānāmādeḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.91) in the case of the word *vauṣaṭ*.

The *pluta* [protracted vowel] should be understood as being prescribed in relation to that; for it is acute (*udātta*), because there exists a degree of excellence (*prakarṣa*) in comparison to that acute *pluta* which is prescribed by the rule "the end of the *yajyā*" (Pāṇini 8.2.90). Alternatively, this is simply another word for its own form (*svarūpaśabdāntara*) ending in a suffix denoting excellence (*prakarṣa*).

But others say: by the rule "A word is unaccented except for one [syllable]" (6.1.158), the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is acute (*udātta*), while the other is more gravely accented (*anudāttatara*). 36. *vibhāṣā chandasi* (1.2.36).
"ṭhiṣe tvā," etc. [The root] *ṭhiṣ* is used in the sense of "desire" (*icchāyām*, Dhātupāṭha 1351).

By the rule *ṭhanyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 3.2.178), the suffix *kvip* is applied. Since this [root] possesses the augment *iṭ*, the suffix *ap* is added by the supplementary rule *lugadhikārasya ṭhapratyayaḥ* (Vārttika 492); it is accented on the first syllable by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).

From the word *iṣa*, the seventh case singular ending [is applied]; by "ṭhādguṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.87), guṇa substitution occurs, and by "ekādeśa udātenodātaḥ" (8.2.5), the single substitute is acute. For the word *yuṣmad* ending in the second case, the substitute *tvām* is applied by "ṭhtvāmau dvitīyāyāḥ" (8.1.23); that [substitute] is unaccented; [and by] "anudātam... [the preceding vowel becomes unaccented].

This is because of the governing rule *sarvam apādādau* (Pāṇini 8.1.18). Regarding *agne*, the acute accent on the first syllable is due to the rule *āmantritasya ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.198). [The form *ānaya*] is derived from the root *yā* in the sense of "reaching" (*prāpaṇe*) (Dhātupāṭha 1049), preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, in the imperative (*loṭ*), second person singular (*sip*).
The substitution of *ser* [for the imperative suffix] is acute according to *āṅ ṭhupasargāścābhivarjam* (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.81).

By *ṭhtiṅṅtiṅ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28), there is the *nighāta* (elision of accent) for the word *yāhi*. In the root *vī* meaning "motion" and so forth (Dhātupāṭha 1019), the suffix *ktin* is acute by *mantrevṛṣeṣapaca* (Pāṇini 3.3.96) and following rules.

In the singular dative case (*caturthī-ekavacana*), by the rule *ṭhgher ṅiti* (Pāṇini 7.3.111), there is *guṇa*, which is replaced by *ay*. Both [the *guṇa* and the replacement] are acute (*udātta*) by virtue of being *sthānivadbhāva*; the remainder is unaccented (*anudātta*). The word *agni* is, as before, oxytone (*antodātta*) due to the accent of the suffix *nip*. In the singular accusative case (*dvitīya-ekavacana*), [before] *am*:

The quality of being prior (*pūrvatva*). [In the rule] "An *ekādeśa* [substituted for an *udātta* vowel and another vowel] is *udātta*" (Pāṇini 8.2.5), [the root] *īḍ* (in the sense of "praising") [is cited]. Because it is *anudātta*, the *ātmanepada* [suffixes] are used. By the rule "A *tiṅ* [ending] is unaccented after a *tiṅ*" (Pāṇini 8.1.28), the word *īḍe* receives the *nighāta* accent. Having analyzed *puraḥ* as "in a prior place" (*pūrvasmin deśe*).

In the rule *pūrvāparādharāvarāṇām asi puradhavaś caiṣām* (Pāṇini 5.3.39), the suffix *asi* is applied, and the word *pūrva* undergoes the substitution *pur*. The word *puraḥ*, by virtue of the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), is oxytone (*antodātta*).
Regarding the root *dhā*, when the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is applied, the substitution *hi* occurs according to the rule *dadhāter hiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.42).

When the designation *gati* is established by the rule *puro’vyayam* (Pāṇini 1.4.67), a compound is formed according to *kugatiprādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18). Although the final syllable of a compound would normally be accented (*antodātta*), the word *puraḥ* retains its original accent as the first member of the compound by the rule *gatiranantaraḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.49), and thus it is *antodātta*.
The word *śam* is a particle (*nipāta*) because it begins with the letter *a*; by the accent rule for particles, it is udātta on its first syllable. The word *asmad* is in the genitive case;

by the rule "for the plural [of *asmad*], *vas* and *nas* [are substituted] in the nominative and accusative" (Pāṇini 7.1.26), the substitution of *nas* is anudātta, because the governing topic is "anudātta. The word *divas* [is derived from the root *div*] with the suffix *ac*, as in the *pac-ādi* group. [The suffix *ac* is applied] among the *pac-ādi* [roots].
