Here, the word for the quality—the term "brindled" (*citra*)—is subordinate because it functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); the word for the possessor of the quality—the term "cow" (*go*)—is primary because it functions as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
In some cases, a meaning other than the two subordinate elements is expressed—as in *plakṣanyagrodhau* (the *plakṣa* and the *nyagrodha*).

For instance, it is not only the base and the suffix that together express the meaning of the suffix; rather, in certain instances, they also express the meaning of the base, as in the case of self-descriptive (*svārthika*) suffixes such as *śuklataraḥ* (whiter) and *śuklatamaḥ* (whitest). Likewise...
Some say that, by its very nature, the primary element in verbal forms (ākhyāta) is the meaning of the root— that "the verb has action as its primary element.
Others, however, believe that in verbal forms, it is indeed the meaning of the suffix that is the primary element.

It is spoken of in the form of a power (*śakti*), as [a suffix] is expressed by case-endings (*vibhakti*) in certain grammatical elements (*pratyaya*); however, the entity possessing that power (*śaktimat*) is not said to have attained the state of a substance (*dravya*). Therefore, when there is a connection with another action, another power manifests, as in the expression "look at the agent" (*kartāraṃ paśya*).

All such infinite varieties of the capacity to denote meanings can be taught; therefore, the comprehension of meaning arises from worldly usage alone. How, then, is this known? To this he says: "By those as well," and so forth. This is easy to understand.
57. *Kālopasarjane ca tulyam* (1.2.57).

It has been stated that "the meaning [of time] is established by other means of knowledge. Now, at the point of the question—"How, then, is this same reason applicable here as well?"—he says: "The word *tulya* (equal/similar) is for the purpose of drawing forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) the preceding reason. How?

Furthermore, does the word "tulya" (equal) serve to draw forward the reason? It is considered thus: "tulyam" is an adverbial modifier of the act of refutation (*pratyākhyāna*). This refutation is equal to the refutation mentioned immediately prior. And it is "equal" in this way if that which belongs to it...

That very same [rule] serves as the reason for this as well. Therefore, by virtue of its capacity to draw in what is similar, the preceding rule follows along as the reason. Thus, the word *tulya* (similar) serves the purpose of attracting (*anukarṣaṇa*) the preceding reason.
[This applies to the rule] beginning with "from an improper rising" (*anyāyyād utthānāt*). Rising (*utthāna*) refers to rising from bed during the last watch of the night.

What has been said is logical. "Lying down" refers to sleeping, and that too is proper during the first watch of the night. Thus, it is meant that this entire day, the last watch of the preceding night, and the first watch of the coming night constitute the time for today.
"Midnight on both sides," and so forth. This refers to the entire day and the midnight on both sides [of the day].
Others maintain that it refers to the time belonging to the present day, consisting of the remainder of the past night and the beginning of the coming night.

58. *jātyākhyāyām ekasmin bahuvacanam anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 1.2.58). By the statement "this single object is called a genus (*jāti*) and so forth," [the author] states the purpose for the commencement of the sūtra. Now, one might object: "Does number not exist in a genus? For that [number] is a property of substance (*dravya*). Even though...

The category of number (*saṃkhyā*) as included within the category of quality (*guṇa-padārtha*) established in the Vaiśeṣika system does not exist here; nevertheless, there is no fault, because in our own system, where "qualities are the differentiators," that number which consists merely of differentiation (*abhedamātra*) certainly exists. Regarding the phrase "the designation of the genus" (*jāterākhyā*): *ākhyāna* is *ākhyā*.

The term *pratyāyanam* means "in reference to a single object. This signifies that an object denoted by a genus (*jāti*) behaves as if it were plural; that is to say, [the singular form] occurs when the object is designated by a genus. By this, he demonstrates that it would not be the case that [the singular form] fails to occur after qualifiers of the genus such as *sampanna* ("abundant") and so forth.

The intention is that these [words] do not denote a genus (*jāti*). But how, then, is the plural number (*bahuvadbhāva*) obtained for that which denotes a genus? Because the term is taken in its etymological sense (*anvarthagrahaṇāt*). Here, the plural number is not understood in its technical (*pāribhāṣika*) sense; what then? It is taken in its etymological sense. [The word] *ukti*...

The word *vacana* means "expression. The expression of many is *bahuvacana*. Since the expression of many is not possible for a single object, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), the meaning "many" is understood as referring to a single object—that is, "one who speaks of many regarding a single object.
In this manner, the sense of a genus (*jāti*) comes to behave as if it were plural. Regarding the phrase "by that," etc.: since...

The plural form is prescribed for the meaning of a genus (*jāti*); therefore, the plural number is justified for qualifiers of a genus when they do not themselves denote a genus, just like words denoting a genus. For example, "Devadatta. The word "Devadatta" is an arbitrary name (*yadṛcchāśabda*). By this [word], a single...
A substance is denoted as that which is followed by multiple individuals; for a genus has multiple individuals as its substratum.

Therefore, since there is no such thing as a genus called "Devadatta-ness," the plural form does not apply here. Now, one might object: "But surely Devadatta-ness exists here with multiple substrata through the distinction of different states. This is not so; for in this way...
For otherwise, the mention of "genus" (jāti) would be purposeless, since a genus is possible in all cases.

Therefore, by the force of mentioning "genus," it is understood that only those words recognized in common usage as genus-words are intended here by the term "genus-word"; and the word "Devadatta" is not [such].
In common worldly usage, the word *jāti* is well-known [as denoting a generic class]. For example:

"A representation of Kāśyapa is 'Kāśyapa'. Here, *Kāśyapa* means "the descendant of Kāśyapa," formed with the suffix *añ* by the rule *anṛṣyānantarye vidādibhyo 'ñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.104). Then, in the sense of "like that" (*iva*), [the suffix *cha* is applied] by the rule *ive* (5.3.96).

The suffix *kan* is applied by the rule *pratikṛtau* (Pāṇini 5.3.96). The elision (*lup*) occurs by the rule *lup manuṣye* (5.3.98). This is a word denoting a genus (*jātiśabda*), according to the definition: "A *gotra* [name] together with the names of *caraṇas* [schools]" (Mahābhāṣya on Pāṇini 4.1.63), because it ends in a *gotra* suffix. But this [is not so].

It is not expressed as a genus (jāti), but rather as a representation (pratikṛti). If that is so, then when the communication of a genus is intended, there ought to be a plural form; however, the communication of a genus is not intended here—what then?

The explanation of the counter-example is as follows: "vrīhiyavau" (rice and barley). By this [rule], the plural number is prescribed for a single meaning consisting of a genus (*jāti*). However, in this case, two meanings consisting of genera are intended to be expressed.
The word *vaktavya* means "to be explained. Herein is the explanation:

The rule "anyatarasyām" is a fixed option (vyavasthitavibhāṣā). Therefore, it will not apply when used in conjunction with a numeral. Alternatively, in the expression "one grain of rice has ripened," the word "one" being employed brings forth the singularity of the generic class (jāti), and that [singularity] is in contradiction with plurality.
Therefore, because of the contradiction between oneness and plurality, the plural form shall not occur here.

59. *asmado dvayośca* (Pāṇini 1.2.59). Here too, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of plurality to the meaning. [The rule states: "The meaning of *asmad* becomes as if plural. Consequently, even a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) occurring therein takes the form of the plural number.

"We say: 'In oneness and in duality,' and so forth. [The objection: "It is appropriate that this applies when there is oneness, but how can it apply in duality? For duality is not possible for the referent of the word 'we' (asmad), since the word 'we' has the self (ātman) as its object, and the self is one. This is not a fault; for selfhood..."

When it is used metaphorically with respect to another [body], as in "this is my second self," then because the word *asmad* (we/I) applies there as well, it is possible for it to have two referents. Alternatively— according to the rule that among the pronouns beginning with *tyad*, whichever is further [in the order] remains— the word *asmad* alone remains.

It is logical that there is a twofold meaning because he has spoken for your sake as well; thus, a twofold meaning is appropriate. Now, if the word *asmad* is employed in the plural, then this refers to a single object and not a twofold object; whereas if it refers to a twofold object, it does not refer to a single object.

How is the application of this [word] determined when there is a scope for both a single meaning and two meanings? From the context (*prakaraṇa*). For example, the word *ārāt* has its application in the meanings of "far" and "near. Regarding the form *aham*: the substitution of *am* occurs by the rule *reĀ prathamayoram* (Pāṇini 7.1.28), and the substitution of *tvāhau* occurs by the rule *tvāhau sau* (Pāṇini 7.2.94).
This is the section on the substitutes for *asmad*. Regarding "we" (*vayam*): by the rule *jasi maparyantasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.91) and *yūyavayau jasi* (7.2.93), the substitute *vaya-* is applied;
then, by *śeṣe lopaḥ* (7.2.90), the remaining portion is elided, resulting in *vayam*. Regarding "us two" (*āvām*):

when the suffix *āṬ* follows, by *yuvāvau dvivacane* (7.2.92), the substitute *āv-* is applied. [And] regarding the nominative case... (*prathamāyāśca*)... *(Note: The provided fragment ends mid-rule. The full rule is Pāṇini 7.2.89: prathamāyāś ca dvivacane bhāṣāyām, which prescribes the substitution of au for āṬ in the dual of the nominative in the spoken language.)*

By [the rule] beginning with (7.2.88), the substitution of *āt* is stated; "it should be explained" means it should be interpreted. As for the interpretation, one must rely on the fact that the term *anyatarasyām*, which is being carried over [from a previous rule], has the status of a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). [This applies to the rule] *yuṣmadi gurāvekeṣām*.
Thus, this too is included by the sūtra itself, because the particle *ca* has the sense of collecting what has not been explicitly stated.
60. "And in the case of the *nakṣatra*s Phalgunī and Proṣṭhapadā" (Pāṇini 1.2.60). [The commentary states:

"The word *ca* (and) is for the purpose of drawing both [the preceding rules] forward. Now, one might object: since there are exactly two *nakṣatra*s named Phalgunī and likewise two named Proṣṭhapadā, the plural number should apply here precisely because of their duality.

It will be so; what then is the purpose of the word "ca" (and) for the sake of drawing in [the term] "dvayoḥ" (of two)? In that case, this indicates that the mention of "nakṣatra" (asterism) is intended as an illustration for "jyotis" (luminaries). By this, the following is also established: "the Pūrvaphalgunīs have risen," and "the two Pūrvaphalgunīs have risen."
If it were not made known that the mention of "nakṣatra" (lunar mansion) is intended as an illustration for "jyotis" (luminary), then this [application] would not occur here;

because the status of being a *nakṣatra* for luminaries occurs only when there is conjunction with the moon, and not at other times—at other times they are merely *jyotir* (luminaries). Furthermore, [the word] does not denote the *nakṣatras*.

In the expression "the former Phalgunīs have risen," there is the use of the word *phalgunī*; what then? It denotes the luminaries (*jyotis*) themselves. Since the quality of being a luminary (*jyotiṣṭva*) exists even in a single one, it is appropriate to employ the particle *ca* (and) in order to exclude that [single case] and to draw in the sense of "two. If...
Furthermore, the mention of "nakṣatra" would not be for the purpose of indicating "jyotis"; if that were so, where would it apply? It would apply only here—such as in the cases:
"Today is Pūrvaphalgunī," or "Today are the two Pūrvaphalgunīs. For indeed, such usage exists here.

The status of *phalgunī* as a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) is due to its conjunction with the moon. Thus it is said: "Time conjoined with a lunar mansion" (Pāṇini 4.2.3), whereby the suffix *aṇ* occurs. However, the form *śravaṇa* does not occur [in this context], because [the suffix] has been elided by the rule "elision when there is no distinction" (Pāṇini 4.2.4).

"Ṭh-phalgunyau māṇavike" means "two girls born under the two Phalgunīs. The suffix *ṭa* is applied by the supplementary rule (vārttika 451): "ṭānau after *phalgunī* and *āṣāḍhā*. Then, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by Pāṇini 4.1.15: "ṭi-ḍ-ḍha-aṇ-añ...".

61. In the Vedic language (*cchandasi*), the dual form of *punarvasū* is optionally replaced by the singular. (1.2.61) 62. And likewise for *viśākhe*. (1.2.62) 63. In a *dvandva* compound of lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), the plural ending of *tiṣya* and *punarvasū* is invariably replaced by the dual. (1.2.63)
(1.2.63) "The students are Tiṣya and Punarvasu.

By means of the words *tiṣya* and *punarvasu*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.2.3], *nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ*. Of that [suffix], there is elision (*lub*) when no distinction is intended.

(4.2.4) Thus, there is elision (*lup*). Consequently, in the cases "a young boy born under Tiṣya" (*tiṣye jātaḥ māṇavakaḥ*) and "two young boys born under Punarvasū" (*punarvasvorjātau māṇavakau*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.16] *saṃdhivelādi*, and that suffix is elided by [Pāṇini 4.3.34] *śraviṣṭhāphalgunyanurādhā*. This applies even to synonyms.

"So that it may be thus. This occurs because when there is the mention of *nakṣatra* (asterism), the meaning is understood; and it has been stated that when there is the mention of *śabda* (word), this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "one's own form" (Pāṇini 1.1.68) applies.
In the absence of that [mention of *śabda*], it also applies to synonyms, as in the example: *siddhyapunarvasū*.

The word *siddhya* is a synonym for *tiṣya*. He shows the analysis by way of its parts in the phrase "those whose [naksatras] are Tiṣya and Punarvasū. However, the collective whole should be understood as the meaning of the compound.
Now, regarding the form *tiṣyapunarvasavaḥ*: there are persons whose minds are confused by [misapprehending this as] a *bahuvrīhi*.

Thus they are spoken of; consequently, this would not even be a compound of lunar mansions (*nakṣatrasamāsa*). Therefore, to one who might object, "What is the use of including the term *dvandva* (copulative compound) for the sake of excluding that [possibility]?", he replies with the words "Tiṣya and so forth," and so on. Having perceived Tiṣya and the others otherwise due to the fault of his own description, [he says:]

These [asterisms] such as Tiṣya and the rest, being perceived by practitioners in reverse order, are expressed in this way by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound; however, they do not refer to persons. Therefore, this is indeed a compound of asterisms, as in the expression "this belongs to Tiṣya and Punarvasu. But by what rule here does the singular form (*ekavadbhāva*) occur?

If it is argued that [the term *tiṣya*] is a genus-word (*jātiśabda*) according to Pāṇini 2.4.6, "The [names of] non-living beings are genus-words," we say no; for it is a proper name (*saṃjñāśabda*), like the word *Devadatta*. This is not a genus-word, because a genus consists of many individuals, whereas Tiṣya and the others are not such. Furthermore, he will state later: "And when there is a focus on the predominance of the genus..."
"This singular treatment (*ekavadbhāva*) applies to genus-words (*jāti*) and substance-words (*dravya*), not when there is an intention to express a specific substance.

However, in this case, there is indeed an intention to express a specific substance; therefore, singular treatment is not justified by the rule "jātir aprāṇinām" (Pāṇini 2.4.6). Nor is there any other rule for singular treatment [applicable here]. In that regard:

In the case of the nakṣatras Tiṣya and Punarvasu, since they form a dvandva compound consisting of multiple items, the plural number ought to apply; thus, the mention of the plural would be redundant. To this, he says: "Every dvandva is optionally [treated as singular]," and so forth.

Since he employs the plural number here for the purpose of excluding the singular, it is understood that this paribhāṣā exists: "Every dvandva compound may optionally be singular" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 91). Therefore, the intention is that the inclusion of the plural number here is intended to exclude the singular.

64. *sarūpāṇām ekaśeṣa ekavibhaktau* (Pāṇini 1.2.64). When the *bahuvrīhi* compound *sarūpāṇām* is formed, the substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* occurs by the rule *jyotir-janapada-* (6.3.85), etc. Here, the word *rūpa* refers to "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*). [Of those] having the same form...

In the phrase "of words" (*śabdānām*), the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). By this, among their own forms (*svarūpāṇām*), that which is similar (*sarūpa*)—being of the same class—is alone retained as one, and not that which is dissimilar (*virūpa*).
For selection applies only to what is of the same class, not to what is of a different class. Alternatively—

This genitive case [in *sarūpāṇām*] has the sense of a collective (*samudāya*). And that which falls within a homogeneous collective remains homogeneous itself, not heterogeneous. Therefore, only the homogeneous form is retained. [The rule states: "*eka-vibhaktau*" (when there is one case-ending).
The word *eka* here has the meaning of "identical" (*samāna*), as in the example *ekadhana* ("of identical wealth"). Thus, it means "that which is both *eka* and a case-ending."
The compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.49] *pūrvakālaika-* and so forth. This also applies to the expression *ekaśeṣa*.

However, in this context, the word *eka* denotes a number (*saṃkhyā*), while the word *śeṣa* indicates a specific state through exclusion (*nivṛtti*), not mere existence. For this very reason, he says: "one remains."

"Others are excluded," as in "the tree and the tree are two trees" (*vṛkṣaśca vṛkṣaśca vṛkṣau*), and so forth. This *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) applies to words that lack case endings, because the case ending is not the cause [of the operation]. For this rule is not prescribed in dependence upon a subsequent case ending. Here, the phrase "in a single case ending" (*ekavibhaktau*) is an indicator for similarity of form (*sārūpya*).

This is not a specification of a formal marker (*nimitta*). When certain forms are observed following a single case-ending (*vibhakti*), the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) occurs even while that case-ending has not yet been produced.
Only after the *ekaśeṣa* has been effected does the case-ending then apply. Alternatively—

The *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) applies only to those forms that possess case-endings (*savibhaktika*). How so? For by the word "vibhakti" (case-ending), the grammatical factor (*kāraka*) is denoted, since it is that by which the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*) is divided.
Thus, what is meant is this: when there is a single, identical, and non-different grammatical factor, those [words] which have the same form...

"For those very [words] that possess a single *kāraka*, there is a single *śeṣa* (elision). If this is so, then the commentary (*vṛtti*) stating "after [the word] *para*" would not be tenable; for a *kāraka* is a power (*śakti*) inherent in the meaning, and it is not possible for words to have a sequence of priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*) by means of that [power]. And how [could it be explained] by the term "case-ending" (*vibhakti*)?

When a *kāraka* (grammatical participant) is being expressed, is the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) obtained for those [words] that possess case-endings? It is said: first, the text of the commentary (*vṛtti*) is consistent; for this word "para" signifies "desired" (*iṣṭa*). Thus, "when another case-ending follows" means "when one desired case-ending [is present]. And this is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*).

Or it is the locative case used in the sense of "when existing" (*sati-saptamī*). That is to say, when a single *kāraka* is intended as the object (*viṣaya*), the locative case is optionally employed. What, then, constitutes an intended *kāraka*? It is that which is intended to be expressed (*vivakṣita*). Therefore, because it is intended to be expressed, the *kāraka* [attains its designation] by its own cause.
The formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) is obtained for words that possess case-endings.

And this *ekaśeṣa* occurs when there is an intention to express coexistence; it happens only if one intends to denote the meaning of all [the items] simultaneously by means of a single [word], and not otherwise. But surely—

If it is argued that "the meaning of a word is the genus (*jāti*), and since the genus is one and the same, there is no possibility at all for many words [to refer to the same thing] due to that oneness of the genus—so what is the point of formulating the rule for *ekaśeṣa*?"—on this occasion of such an objection, [the author] speaks the words beginning with "pratyartham," relying upon the view that "the meaning of a word is the substance (*dravya*). Regarding "pratyartham": [The word *pratyartham* is used in the sense of] "with respect to each individual object."

Since the application and occurrence of words is based on their being established for each individual meaning, it follows that a single word cannot express multiple meanings. In this view, since the expression of meanings must be performed by each word individually, the consequence would be the necessity of using multiple words [for what is intended to be expressed by one].
As many as there are meanings, so many words would necessarily be employed; however, a single-word form (ekaśabdatā) is desired. Therefore, the rule for "retention of one" (ekaśeṣa) is commenced.
[The question] "What is the purpose of mentioning *rūpa* (form)? is asked. He thinks thus: when the mention of *rūpa* is made...
If it were said that "the meaning is to be understood by following two words," there would be heaviness in comprehension (*pratipati-gaurava*);

whereas when it is stated "of similar [words]," the meaning is understood by following a single word, resulting in lightness in comprehension (*pratipati-lāghava*). Therefore, the term "similar" (*samāna*) alone must be employed?

The inclusion of the term "form" (*rūpa*) is so that [the designation] may apply even when the referent (*artha*) is distinct. If the inclusion of "form" were not made, then, because no specific distinction would be stated, the designation would apply only where both word and referent are identical, such as in the case of *vṛkṣāḥ* and the like, but it would not apply in cases such as *akṣāḥ*, due to the difference in referents. Likewise...
The word *akṣa* occurs in the sense of a sense organ (*indriya*), a part of a chariot, and in meanings such as the *bibhītaka* fruit;

the word *pāda* also occurs in the sense of a *kārṣāpaṇa*, a quarter-verse (*ślokapāda*), a foot, a hand, and so forth; and the word *māṣa* also [occurs] in the sense of rice and other grains. [The rule is stated] "lest [the suffix] remain when two or many are left" (*dvibahvoḥ śeṣe mā bhūt*). But surely, [one might object]:...

If the intention were to express the number one by using the word *śeṣa* (remainder), then there would be no remainder for two or many [elements]; this is not so. In this context, because it is that which is being prescribed, the *śeṣa* itself is the primary factor (*pradhāna*), and a number is not intended to be expressed regarding a primary factor. For instance, [in the rule] "the object (*karman*) is that which is most desired by the agent" (*kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma*).

(1.4.49) Thus, the designation *karman* [is applied]; because that which is most desired (*īpsitatama*) is primary. When there is no intention to express number, the designation *karman* applies to both two and many. However, when it is a subordinate factor (*guṇa*), number is intended to be expressed, as for example—

Since the suffixes beginning with *sva-* (the case endings) are being prescribed by the rule *ṭhṅyāpprātipadikāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.1), they are the primary element; whereas the *ṅyāpprātipadika* (the nominal stem ending in feminine suffixes or a nominal base) is the subordinate element. Therefore, in that [subordinate] element, the number is intended to be expressed (*vivakṣyate*).

Therefore, the singular number is established for each individual member. Even in the case of a quality (*guṇa*), the number is sometimes not intended to be significant in accordance with the technical definition (*lakṣaṇa*), as in this very rule: *sarūpāṇām* ("of those that are identical in form").
Consequently, when there are two identical forms, only one remains.

[The word "śeṣa" is used] so that there should not be a substitution [of the whole]. If the mention of "śeṣa" were absent, the rule "sarūpāṇām" would be a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*); consequently, there would be a substitution. And thus, [the suffix] *kvan* [would apply] by the rule "ṭhaśūpruṣilaṭikaṇikhaṭiviśibhyaḥ kvan" (Dhātupāṭha 8.125).
Since the word *aśva* ending in the *kvan* suffix is udātta on its first syllable due to the *nit* accent,

when there is the substitution [of a single substitute] for two *aśva* words both having the udātta on the first syllable, the substitute would necessarily have the udātta on its first syllable as well, because of proximity (*āntaratamya*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "payaḥ": one word *payaḥ* ends in the nominative case and serves as the agent (*kartṛpada*), while the second ends in the accusative case and serves as the object (*karmapada*). Consequently, because they possess different case endings (*bhinnavibhaktikatva*)—that is, because they do not follow a single common case ending—the rule for *ekaśeṣa* (retention of only one of identical words) does not apply.

In the case of "ṭh brāhmaṇābhyām," the first word *brāhmaṇa* ends in the third case (*tṛtīyā*), while the second ends in the fourth case (*caturthī*). Therefore, even here, there is no identity of case endings (*samānavibhaktikatva*).
65. *Vṛddha* [is designated] by a *yuvan* [term], provided that the distinction lies solely in those characteristics.

(1.2.65) This word *vṛddha* exists as a worldly term, referring to one who is in the final stage of life; it also exists as a technical (śāstrīya) term—namely, "that whose first vowel among its vowels is subject to *vṛddhi* increase is called *vṛddha*" (Pāṇini 1.1.73); and it also exists as...

Regarding the terminology of the ancient teachers: "the offspring is [called] *vṛddha* when it has disappeared. In that case, if the worldly sense were to be taken, then by association with that term, the word *yuvan* would also refer only to the worldly distinction of age; consequently, [the rule] would apply to the *aj* and...

In such cases as "varkara" and so forth, an over-extension would occur; for a specific type of animal in its mature stage is called "aja" (goat), whereas in its youth it is called "varkara. If, on the other hand, the technical (śāstrīya) sense were adopted, then [the same form] would also apply to cases such as "aupagavaḥ" and "aupagaviḥ. Having considered this, he says:

"The word *vṛddha*," and so forth. By this, he shows that this is the inclusion of the technical term (*saṃjñā*) for "old" as formulated by the former teachers (*pūrvācārya*). How, then, is this obtained? From the traditional instruction (*upadeśa*). Or rather, he thinks as follows: although the word *yuva* is conventionally established in common usage (*loka*) as referring to the second stage of life, nevertheless...

By the force of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "but [the suffix] occurs when a descendant in the lineage is living" (Pāṇini 4.1.163), only that which denotes a descendant is taken [as the referent]. Therefore, by association with that, it is appropriate to take only the word *vṛddha* as having the sense of a descendant; however, the mention of *gotra* is not [required].

This was done for the sake of variety. By the mention of *saha* (with) in the rule "when spoken with a youth" (*yūnā saha vacane*), it is shown that this third case ending occurs in connection with a companion (*sahayoga*). Therefore, because the third case is prescribed in connection with a companion, it is understood that a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) occurs when there is an intention to express co-existence (*sahabhāva*).

By the words "samānāyām" and so forth, he shows that this [rule] refers to cases where the dissimilarity arises solely from the cause of the *vṛddha* and *yuvan* suffixes. "Ākṛti" is the basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of a word, such as being a descendant of Garga (*gārgyatva*) and so on; when that is "samānā," meaning non-different, in a case where [the forms] differ only through the *vṛddha* and *yuvan* suffixes themselves—

The meaning is that there is no other [cause] such as *prakṛti* (the base form) and so forth; rather, in that case, the difference in form arises solely due to the cause of the suffixes for the elder (*vṛddha*) and the youth (*yuvan*). [For example: "Gārgya," and so on. From the words *garga* and *vatsa*, the suffix *yañ* is applied because they belong to the *gargādi* group, resulting in *gārgyaḥ* and *vātsyaḥ*. From these two, [the suffix for] the descendant in the younger generation (*yūni apatye*)...

The suffix *phak* is applied by the rule *ṭhyañiñośca* (Pāṇini 4.1.101). Thus, Gārgya and Gārgyāyaṇa are "the two Gārgyas," and Vātsya and Vātsyāyana are "the two Vātsyas. Here, the meaning of the younger generation (*yuvan*) is understood through context and other factors. Regarding the phrase "and Garga": this word *garga* is the original base (*mūlaprakṛti*); it does not refer to the elder generation (*vṛddha*), nor...

In the case of "Gārgyavātsyāyanau" [referring to an elder and a youth], there is not only a distinction based on the causes for perceiving them as old or young, but also one based on the etymological base (*prakṛti*). The word *bhāgaviti* refers to a descendant in the lineage (*gotrāpatya*).
The word *bhāgavita* ends in the suffix *iñ*. Regarding the form *bhāgaviti*, from the word *bhāgavita*, when deriving the patronymic (*yaūnya-apatya*),

the suffix *ṭhak* is applied under the rule "vṛddhāṭ ṭhak sauvīreṣu bahulam" (Pāṇini 4.1.148), with the word "kutsane" (in the sense of contempt) being understood as a carry-over from the preceding rule "gotrastriyāḥ kutsane ṇa ca" (4.1.147).
Thus ends the section on the suffix *ṭhak*.
66. *Strī-puṃvac-ca* (1.2.66).

This rule is stated because the previous one does not suffice due to the addition of the cause for morphological difference (*vairūpya*) in the feminine meaning. By the expression "and like the masculine" (*puṃvac-ca*), this is an extended application (*atideśa*). The word "feminine" (*strī*) here refers to the inclusion of feminine suffixes (*strī-pratyaya*).

What could this mean? Is it the inclusion of the word *strī-artha-vṛtti* (functioning as the meaning "female"), or the inclusion of *artha* (meaning)? If it were the inclusion of the feminine suffix (*strī-pratyaya*), then by this [rule] only that [suffix] would be set aside—namely, that the feminine suffix becomes like the masculine (*puṃvat*)—but the setting aside of the meaning "female" (*stry-artha*) would not be effected.

In the case of "gārgyaśca gārgyāyaṇaśca" resulting in "gargāḥ," the elision [of the suffix] prescribed by "ṭhyañañośca" (Pāṇini 2.4.64)— which occurs while "ṭhastriyām" (2.4.62) is still in force— would not take place. However, in the case of "iha tu gargān paśyati," the substitution of *n* for the final letter [of the stem] as prescribed by "tasmācchaso naḥ puṃsi" (6.1.103) does not occur.

It might be argued: "In the second alternative, however, by this [rule] the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment) is applied to a word denoting a female referent, but the cessation of the feminine gender itself does not occur; even so, that same fault would remain. But if there is the inclusion of the 'referent' (*artha*), no fault arises at all; therefore, this is the inclusion of the referent of a female."
Having considered this, he says: "That which has the meaning of feminine becomes like the masculine. But how is it that the word *artha* (meaning) is understood here? It is said:

because feminine suffixes depend upon the thing denoted (*abhidheya*), whereas the meaning (*artha*) lacks such dependence [and thus] lacks primacy. A subordinate element follows the principal; [here], because of its lack of primacy, [the meaning does not govern].
However, its lack of primacy is due to its dependence on the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*).

The meaning (*artha*) lacks primacy because it is not dependent [on anything else]. When there is a conjunction of the primary and the subordinate, it is logical to grasp the primary; therefore, only the feminine meaning is taken, as in "Gārgī and Vātsī."

From the words *gārgya* and *vātsya*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.16] *ṭhyaÑ-aś-ca*; as before, there is the elision of the letters *a* and *ya*. Thus, *dākṣī*: here, as before, *ṅīp* is applied. And *dākṣāyaṇa*: [this is derived from] "the offspring of Dākṣi" by [Pāṇini 4.1.95] *yañ-iñoś-ca*.
Thus, by [Pāṇini 4.1.101], the suffix *phak* is applied.
67. *pumān striyā* (Pāṇini 1.2.67).
[The commentary states: "Only if the distinction consists in the characteristics of male and female. If this were the case, it would not apply here:
in the example "This is a bull (*gauḥ*) and this is a cow (*gauḥ*); these two cows (*gāvau*) stand," for in this instance...

Is there some distinction made on account of gender? Let it not be that [the rule] will apply by means of the sūtra "sarūpāṇām" (Pāṇini 1.2.64), etc. This is not so; for if it were by that [sūtra], the single-remainder (ekaśeṣa) would also result for the word *strī* (woman). And consequently, the feminine gender would also [result].

The gender is not subject to formal prescription because it relies upon common usage. When the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of feminine forms has been performed, there is no fault, as masculinity is intended to be expressed.
Alternatively, a grammatical split (*yogavibhāga*) is made for the rule "pumān"; by means of that, [masculinity is understood] here as well, even though it is not explicitly present.

When there is a distinction between female and male, the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of only one) applies to the male alone. And this being so, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because the desired result is established through the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). For example: *brāhmaṇī*, *kukkuṭī*, *mayūrī*. This is according to [Pāṇini 4.1.63]: "The feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after a genus term (*jāti*) that does not denote a female, provided it has a short vowel as its penultimate letter."

The suffix *ṅīṣ* [is applied]. In the example "the cock and the peahen" (*kukkuṭamayūryau*), there is not only a distinction made on the basis of gender, but rather one also made on the basis of form and sound. In the example "Indrāṇī," the suffix *ṅīṣ* and the augment *ān* are applied by the rule "indravaruṇa... (Pāṇini 4.1.49). "Prācī" is formed from "prāk."
The word *prāñcī* is derived from the root *añc-* preceded by the prefix *pra-*. By the rule *ṛtvig-ādinā kvin* (Pāṇini 3.2.59), the suffix *kvin* is applied;

by the rule *kvin-pratyayasya kuḥ* (8.2.62), the substitution of *ku* occurs [for the final consonant]. From this stem ending in *kvin*, the suffix *astāti* is added by the rule *dik-chabdebhyaḥ* (5.3.27). For that suffix, the elision (*luk*) is prescribed by the rule *añceḥ luk* (5.3.3).

Regarding "luk | ṭhprācī": from the word *prāc*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied because of the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) to the sūtra *ugitaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.6), which includes the root *añc*. Regarding "prāgityavyayam":
its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) follows from the rule *taddhitaścāsarvavibhaktiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.38).
68. *bhrātṛputrau svasṛduhitṛbhyām* | (1.2.68) 69.

*napuṃsakamanapuṃsakenaikavaccānyatarasyām* | (1.2.69) Regarding the phrase "with a neuter [word]" (*napuṃsakena*), [the examples] beginning with "what" (*kim*) are given. But surely, even without a neuter [word],...

By the rule beginning with *sahavacanena sarūpāṇām*, a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) indeed occurs. Therefore, what is the distinction here between the single remainder being prescribed by that [rule] and by this one? To this he says:
"The singular number (*ekavacana*) does not occur. If the single remainder were to occur by this [present rule], then there would be the state of singular number optionally.
It might be so; however, when *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one from among many) occurs, it does not happen. Now, for what purpose is the word *asya* stated?
If *asya* were not stated, the term *ekavat ca* would also carry over into the subsequent rule.
Consequently, in the subsequent case where *ekaśeṣa* is to be performed, the status of being treated as a singular (*ekavadbhāva*) would undesirably apply to that [retained form].

Therefore, this mention of "of this" (*asya*) is for the purpose that the singular treatment (*ekavadbhāva*) applies only to this neuter [dual], but not to that which will undergo *ekaśeṣa* later on. For if the word "of this" were not used, it would be redundant; thus, to avoid its redundancy, the rule "and as a singular" (*ekavat ca*) must also apply to what follows.

It does not follow. But surely it will not follow simply because it lacks the *asvarita* accent? If that is so, then that very lack of *asvarita* accent is being explained by this method for the sake of clarity.
The vowel *e* follows here. By means of it, one forms *himam ca himānī ca = himahimānyau*.
In the case of *araṇyam* and *araṇyānī*, as well as *araṇyāraṇyānyau*, [the suffix *ṅīp*] does not occur;
for by the rule *indravaruṇādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.49), there is the statement of the Vārttika: "The suffix *ṭāp* is applied after *himā* and *araṇya* when denoting greatness."
Greatness is another distinction.

70. *pitā mātrā* (1.2.70). [The compound] *pitarau* [is formed as follows]: by the rule *ṛto ṅ* (7.3.110), there is *guṇa* [substitution]. [In the case of] *mātāpitarau*, *ānaṅ* is substituted [for the final vowel of the first member] by the rule *ānaṅ ṛto dvandve* (6.3.25); furthermore, because she is more venerable (*abhyarhitatva*), the mother is placed first.
71. *Śvaśuraḥ śvaśvā* (Pāṇini 1.2.71). [The compound] *śvaśrūśvaśurau* is formed; the prior placement [of *śvaśura*] is as in the previous rule.
72. *tyadādīni sarvair nityam* (Pāṇini 1.2.72). [The commentary states:

"The inclusion of the word *sarvaiḥ* (by all) is for the sake of completeness (*sākalyārtham*). Without it, one might suspect that the phrase *anapuṃsakena* (except with a neuter [word]) continues [from the previous rule]; consequently, [the rule would apply] only when combined with a neuter [word].

It would not apply. Or rather, one might suspect that the phrase "if the distinction itself is characterized by that" is being carried over here; consequently, it would apply only where the distinction is produced by pronouns such as *tad* (e.g., *sa ca yaśca yāv* and so forth), but it would not apply here in the case of *sa ca devadattaśca tāv*.

Therefore, there is the inclusion of "all" [in the rule]. As for the example "sa ca Devadattaśca tau" ("He and Devadatta, those two"), this is an illustration when there is a desire to express a distinction; however, when there is a desire to express a generality, then Devadatta is also connected with the word *tat* (that), and thus it is established by the rule itself, "Of those that have the same form" (Pāṇini 1.2.64).
Regarding the phrase "that which is subsequent," it should be understood that "subsequent-ness" (paratva) is relative to the list of gaṇas.

73. *strī* [is used] for non-youthful groups of domestic animals (*grāmyapaśusaṅgheṣvataruṇeṣu*). (Pāṇini 1.2.73). Regarding the term *grāmyāṇām*: those which exist in a village (*grāme*) are "domestic" (*grāmyāḥ*). This is derived by the suffix *ya*, according to Pāṇini 4.2.94: *grāmādyakhañau*.
Now, it might be objected that a group (*saṅgha*) cannot possibly possess youthfulness, nor is there anything to be excluded by such a qualification.
Since [the members] are young, the qualification "among those who are not young" (*ataruṇeṣu*) is inappropriate;
thus he says, "The mention of 'not young,' etc. This qualification is indeed stated, but it is not possible for a *saṅgha* (group) itself to possess it;
therefore, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), the *saṅgha* of others is understood. For example: "These cows... (*gāva imāḥ*).

Thus [it is said]. The employment of the word *imāḥ* (these) is for the purpose of manifesting the feminine gender. [The example is: "These two cows. But how can this be a counter-example, since a collection (*saṅgha*) certainly occurs even with two?
This is not a fault, because it might be thought that the mention of "collection" would be redundant.

Because there is no [other] thing to be excluded [by the rule]. Regarding the phrase "among those with many hoofs" (*anekaśapheṣu*) and so forth: the meaning is that this *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) occurs among those things which possess many hoofs or claws; such is the form of the explanation to be provided.
In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is carried over here, and it...
It is understood that this is a rule of restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*); therefore, it applies only to animals with uncloven hooves and not to others.
Thus ends the first chapter of the *Kāśikāvivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who was a teacher of the Bodhisattvas.
The Second Pāda
Now, [the second section] of the first chapter.
The Third Pāda.
1. *Bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ* (1.3.1).
Those whose beginning is *bhū* are called *bhūvādayaḥ*. By this, those [roots] recited in the ten groups (*daśagaṇī*) are understood.

Regarding the passage beginning with "it becomes" (*bhavati*): since the designation *dhātu* (verbal root) applies here, the suffix *laṭ* is introduced by the rule *vartamāne laṭ* (Pāṇini 3.2.123), while the governing rule *dhātoḥ* (3.1.91) is understood to follow. By the statement, "words such as *bhū* and so forth receive the designation *dhātu*," this [designation] is established solely through the recitation of the list of roots (*gaṇapāṭha*).

This shows that the designation "root" (dhātu) is prescribed [only for specific items]. By this, it is stated that forms such as *aṇapayati* and *kaḍḍhayati* do not receive the designation "root. If this is so, then what of forms such as *yā*, *vā*, *div*, and so forth, which denote pronouns, alternatives, and heaven?

Someone might have the misconception that even those words which share the same sound as "dhātu" (root) but do not denote an action would also receive the designation "dhātu"; therefore, in order to dispel that, he says: "The word *dhātu*," and so forth. For teachers desire that a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) be made for the sake of brevity; thus, [the term used] consists of a single syllable.

The purpose of resorting to the great terminology of the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*) when a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is to be made is this: so that this designation may apply to those very same types of items to which they applied the designation "verbal root" (*dhātusaṃjñā*). And those [ancient teachers] applied it only to those things that express action (*kriyā*).

They have established the technical designation *dhātu* (verbal root). Therefore, here too, by relying on the terminology of the ancient masters (*pūrvācārya*), the designation *dhātu* is prescribed only for those that express an action (*kriyā*).
Consequently, the intention is that it does not apply to words such as *yā*, *vā*, and *div*, which, though sharing the same phonetic form as verbal roots, do not express an action.
But surely, when the bahuvrīhi compound *bhūrādir yeṣām* is formed, if there is a *saṃhitā* reading before the word *ādi*, then by the rule *ṭhiko yaṇ aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77),
the *yaṇ* substitution would apply, and the form should be *bhvādayaḥ*; however, if there is no *saṃhitā* reading, then it would be *bhū ādayaḥ*.
Thus, from where does this letter *va* come, such that when it exists there is the designation "bhū-v-ādayaḥ"?

To this he says: "of *bhū* and the others," and so forth. In the designation of the named items (*saṃjñin*) beginning with *bhū*, this letter *va* is employed for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). Auspiciousness is the purpose (*artha*) or motive.
That which possesses this [quality] is so described. That auspicious word is a discourse on Dharma (dharmaparyāya), meaning it has Dharma as its purpose.

Just as in the Veda, in the passage "We worship Tryambaka," the letter *ya* has no visible purpose; therefore, its recitation is for the sake of Dharma alone, being for an invisible purpose (adṛṣṭārtha). So it is here as well.

Regarding the letter *va*: Alternatively, in this world, the acquisition of a previously unobtained object is considered auspicious, such as the obtaining of curd and other items at dawn; likewise here too, the acquisition of the previously unobtained letter *va* is a praiseworthy auspiciousness. This refers to a praiseworthy matter.

This is an auspicious word. As it has been said: "Treatises that begin with an auspicious word, have an auspicious word in the middle, and end with an auspicious word, flourish; they become treatises of heroic men and long-lived men" (Mahābhārata 1.1.1). And here, at the beginning, is the word *vṛddhi*.
The auspicious syllable *maṅgala* is here, with the letter *va* in the middle (1.3.), and at the end the word *udaya* according to [Pāṇini 8.4.67]: *svariteto 'yam*.
[This refers to] "for the sake of *bhū* and *va*" (*bhuvo vārtham*), and so forth. Alternatively, in the mention of *bhūvādayaḥ*:

This is not the usage of the word "ādi," nor does it have the sense of "maṅgala" (auspiciousness) as the letter *va* might suggest; rather, it is the word "vādi" derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes. The meaning is "those who speak" (*vadanti*), that is, "expressers."

The suffix *iñ* is applied to the verbal root *vada* in the sense of the agent, according to the rule: "After the roots *vas*, *vap*, *yaj*, *rāj*, *vraj*, *sad*, *han*, *vāś*, *vād*, and *vāri*, [the suffix] *iñ* [is added]" (Daiva-Uṇādi-sūtra 1.53). Although in this sūtra the form *vādī* is cited as having a causative (*ṇyanta*) ending, nevertheless, by virtue of the term *bahulam* ("variously"), it is also [applied] after the non-causative (*aṇyanta*) form.
It occurs [in the rule] "those whose meaning is *bhū*. This is an adjective qualifying those roots beginning with *vad*. *Bhū* is the act of becoming (*bhavanam*);
the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) because it belongs to the class beginning with *sampad*. The meaning of the root *bhū* is general action (*kriyāsāmānyam*).

Those whose meaning is *bhū* are "those whose meaning is *bhū*" (*bhvarthāḥ*). But why are they "those whose meaning is *bhū*"? Because they express the meaning of *bhū* optionally (*bhuvo vārthaṃ vadanti*).

Thus: the particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason—because they express or denote the meaning of the verbal root *bhū*, therefore they are "those whose meaning is *bhū*" (*bhvarthāḥ*). Such expressive words as *bhū* and so forth are designated by the technical term "verbal roots" (*dhātu*). Thus, in this sūtra, those [words] are intended and remembered as the "named" (*saṃjñin*).

The meaning is "intended. Thus, it is stated that words denoting action, such as *bhū* and so forth, receive the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "root" (*dhātu*). Consequently, words like *yā*, *vā*, and *div*, which have the same phonetic form as roots but do not denote action, do not receive the designation of "root."
By virtue of the authority of the *gaṇapāṭha*, the actual recitation [of the words] is also accepted.

Consequently, it is stated that even for words such as *aṇapayati* which denote actions, the designation "root" (*dhātusaṃjñā*) does not apply. In this interpretation, the term *bhūvādayaḥ* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
It should be understood as follows: *bhū-vā-ādayaḥ* means "those beginning with *bhū* and *vā*.

Alternatively, the word *ādi* here is used after the root *vā*, meaning "to go" or "to scent" (DhP 1050). Thus, *vā-ādayaḥ* refers to those for which *vā* is the first [root]. In this context, the word *ādi* expresses the sense of "type" or "kind."

The meaning is "of such kinds. "Kind" (prakāra), however, means similarity; that [similarity], moreover, consists in having action as their essence, as he said: "those whose meaning is 'to be'. They possess the nature of "being" because they express the meaning of the root *bhū*. Words of this sort, which have such kinds [of meanings], are recorded here in the sūtra as the technical designata (*saṃjñin*). Thus, by this method...

It has been stated that only those beginning with *bhū* and expressing action (*kriyā*) receive the designation of "root" (*dhātu*). Consequently, words identical in sound to roots, such as *yā*, *vā*, *div*, and so forth, do not receive the designation of "root," for they do not express action; rather, they denote accomplished entities (*niṣpannavastu*), since their essential nature is that of something being brought into existence (*sādhyamānasvarūpa*).

Action is sometimes partless, and sometimes it consists of sequential parts whose nature as a completed entity is not yet established. However, the inclusion [of such verbs] in the *gaṇa* list is accepted just as before; therefore, for words such as *aṇapayati* and others—
Regarding the statement "the notion of a root does not occur," in this explanation as well, the rule *bhūvādayaḥ* is to be understood as a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*),
and the genitive case is to be understood as characterized by the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakasaṃbandha*).

2. *Upadeśe 'janunāsika it* (Pāṇini 1.3.2). [The word] *upadeśaḥ* means "that by which something is taught" (*upadiśyate 'neneti*). The suffix *ghañ* is applied here in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*), according to the rule *akartari ca kārake saṃjñāyām* (3.3.19). Now, it is stated that this suffix is used when there is a technical name (*saṃjñāyām*), yet is this not a technical name?

This is not so; because of the word "bahulam" (in various ways) in the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.113), it occurs even when it is not a technical name (*saṃjñā*), so there is no fault. Regarding the phrase "the statements of the Śāstra," this is its explanation: "the recitation of the Sūtras and the recitation of the Khilas. As for the recitation of the Khilas:

The list of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*) and, by the word "and" (*ca*), the list of nominal stems (*prātipadikapāṭha*). Now, how is it that the nasalization (*ānunāsikya*) occurs for *ragelage* and so forth? For their nasalization is not recited in the list [of roots].
If it occurs even for those not recited [in the list], then why does it not occur for *bhū* and the others?
He says: "The followers of Pāṇini [maintain] that nasality is based on formal agreement (pratijñā)," and so forth.
Those for whom nasality exists by virtue of a formal agreement are called *pratijñānunāsikya*.
Wherever the followers of Pāṇini formally agree (*pratijānate*) that there is nasality, even if it is not explicitly recited there, [it is understood].

It occurs [only] there, and not elsewhere. Furthermore, this proposition is not established by mere arbitrariness; rather, it must exist only where the teachers (ācāryas) record it. Just as *svaritatva* and *anudāttatva* are understood through such recording, so too is *ānunāsikya*.
If, then, nasality exists merely by virtue of being a formal postulate (*pratijñāmātrabhāvin*), for what purpose is it recited in certain instances, such as in *ḍupacaṣ pāke* (DhP 996)?
It is for the purpose of demonstrating that such a meaning is to be understood as nasalized (*anunāsika*).

In the case of *ṭhabhra āṅ apaḥ*, because of this specific instruction (*upadeśa*), the nasalization (*anunāsika*) is prescribed by the rule *āṅe 'nunāsikaś chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.126) at a later stage; therefore, the designation *it* does not apply to it. Now, one might object: "But surely, [the designation *it* does not apply] precisely by virtue of the force of the prescription of nasalization itself."

"It will exist; so what is the use of including it in the *upadeśa*? For if it were marked with the *it*-designation, then by the rule 'its elision' (Pāṇini 1.3.9), its elision would occur, and consequently, the prescription of its nasalization (*anunāsika*) would be purposeless.
This is true; however, he thinks as follows: the inclusion in the *upadeśa* is certainly necessary for the sake of subsequent rules.

It must be performed. Being performed for the sake of what follows, it will also serve to clarify the meaning here. Alternatively—this direction for a counter-example has been shown by the author of the Vṛtti. But this is the counter-example in this context:
*aṇo'pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.57); as in *dadhiṃ brāhmaṇakulam*. If [the letter *i*] were to receive this designation (*itsaṃjñā*) here...
[Otherwise], by the rule "num is added to a verbal root ending in ṭh or id" (Pāṇini 7.1.58), the augment *num* would apply. Now, it might be argued:

since the word "verbal root" (*dhātu*) is stated [in the rule], the *num* is prescribed for a verbal root; however, this is not a verbal root, but rather a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). So how could *num* apply? This is not so; for [the suffix] *kvip* is added [to a root].

The statement "it does not lose its status as a verbal root" (*dhātutvaṃ na jahati*, *Vyāḍiyapadīya* 132) implies that it retains its status as a verbal root because it ends in the suffix *kvip*. One who desires curds for himself forms *dadhīyati* according to *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8). From *dadhīyati*, the suffix *kvip* is applied to form *dadhi*; thus, "the Brāhmaṇa family [desires] curds. By the rule *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.48), the vowel *a* is elided.

In the rule "ṭhlopo vyorvali" (6.1.66), because the mention of *lopa* (elision) occurs at the beginning, the elision of the letter *y* takes place first; then, by the rule "ṭhverapṛktasya" (6.1.67), the letter *v* is elided.
By means of the principle of "indicating the presence of a suffix" (*pratyayalopalakṣaṇa*), the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs according to the rule "ṭhakṛtasārvadhātukayoḥ" (7.4.25).
The shortening [of the final vowel] occurs by the rule *ṭhhrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.47).

When the nasalization (*anunāsika*) is applied by the rule *ṭhaṇo'pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.57), the suffix *num* would follow because of the principle *ṭhkvabantā dhātutvaṃ na jahati* (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 132). Thus, the forms are *aśmā* and *bhasma*.
In the rule *ṭhāto manin* (Pāṇini 3.2.74), the letter *m* does not receive the designation *it*. For if it were so,
then by the rule *ṭhanyebhyo'pi dṛśyante* (3.2.75), which prescribes *manin* after bases ending in consonants (*hal*), the suffix would follow after the final letter of the base.
"Let it not apply to every vowel"—that is, even those belonging to words such as *daridra* and so forth.

3. *Halantyam* (Pāṇini 1.3.3). [The word] *antya* means "that which exists at the end" (*ante bhavam*). The suffix *yat* is applied because it belongs to the *dig-ādi* group. This word *anta* refers to completion, as in the expression "the forest ends here" (*etadantaṃ vanam*). It denotes that by which a composite whole is brought to its conclusion.

That which is at the end is *antaḥ*. It occurs at the conclusion (*samāpti*) of the interior; thus it is called *antya* (final). Since the word *hal* is of both genders, the term *antya* is used here in the neuter gender.

Regarding the phrase "of the beginning of a root" (*dhātvādeḥ*), etc.: by the word "beginning" (*ādi*), the sūtras, nominal stems (*prātipadika*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), augments (*āgama*), and substitutes (*ādeśa*) are included.
Regarding the inclusion [of specific letters]: therein, the letter *ñ* is found in the root *ḍukṛñ* (DhP 1472);
the letter *ṇ* is found in the sūtra *aiuṇ* (Māheśvara Sūtra 1); the letter *ṭ* is found in the prātipadika *navaṭ*;
[the form] *nadaḍ* is recited among the *pacādi* group; and [the letter *t* is found] in the suffix.

The letter *n* [is added] by the rule *guptijkidbhyaḥ san* (3.1.5); the letter *k* [is added] to the augment by the rule *trapujatunoḥ ṣuk* (4.3.138); and the letter *ñ* [is added] to the substitute by the rule *cakṣiṅḥ khyāñ* (2.4.54).

"An *agni-cit* (one who has piled the fire-altar), a *soma-sut* (one who has pressed the Soma). [This is derived] from the roots *ci* (to pile) and *su* (to press) with the suffix *kvip*, [forming] *agni-cit* and *soma-sut*, with the augment *tuk*.
But surely, in the recitation of the *pratyāhāra* "hal," the final letter *l* does not have the designation *it*?

[The definition of *it*] would apply; for there is a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). To explain: when the designation *it* is being established by the rule "the first [element] together with the last constitutes a *pratyāhāra*" (Pāṇini 1.1.71), the term *hal* occurs as a *pratyāhāra*. And upon that [establishment], the designation *it* applies to that letter *l* by the rule "the last [element] among the *hal*s is *it*" (Pāṇini 1.3.3). Thus, this mutual dependence is indeed quite evident.
Since it is stated in the treatise that "effects based on mutual dependence are not postulated" (Vyāḍipañjikā 28), he says:
"The *ha* [is used] for the sake of *hal*, etc.
That which benefits many even without a distinction of repetition—

*Tantra* (extension): for example, a well-kindled lamp benefits many students. Here, however, a specific effort is intended by the word *tantra*. By that *tantra*, it should be understood that a second mention of the term *hal* (consonant) is included or adopted here. For example, *śveto*...
The intention is that just as two sentences are uttered by a single effort when one says "dhāvati," so too here two *hal* sounds are uttered by a single effort.
In the expression "hasya l hal," the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denotes a relationship of proximity between the two. Regarding the phrase beginning with "tena" and so forth:
Since a second mention of the letter *ha* has been made according to the principle of the tantra (the "all-pervasive" rule),
the *it*-designation is applied directly to the letter *la* in the *pratyāhāra* recitation— which is the *ha* situated near the [first] *ha*— and not by means of relying on the *pratyāhāra* itself.
And this being the case, in the recitation of the *pratyāhāra* [table] at the rule *ṭhL-antyam* (Pāṇini 1.3.3), the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) does not arise.
4. *na vibhaktau tusmāḥ* (1.3.4).

In the case of *vṛkṣāt*, since the letter *t* would have the designation *it*, it would follow that it is *svarita* according to the rule *ṭitsvaritam* (Pāṇini 6.1.185). [Examples of this are] *apacatāt* and *apacatam*. Here, from the root *pac* with the suffix *laṅ*, the substitutes *ta* and *tam* are applied by the rule *tasthasthamipāṃ tāntantāmaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.101).

Regarding your point: in the rule *kimo't* (Pāṇini 5.3.12), it is understood that the letter *u* is an *anubandha* (indicatory marker) for the purpose of protecting the letter *m* from being designated as an *it*, because of the preceding rule *prāg diśo vibhaktiḥ* (5.3.1).
For if [the substitution] were obligatory, then by this very prohibition, the letter *m* would not receive the designation of *it*.
If [the suffix] were to exist [as such], the inclusion of the indicatory letter *u* (*ukārānubandha*) would be purposeless.
5. *Ādir ñiṭuḍavaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.5).
Here, by the inclusion of *ṭu*, the entire *ṭa*-class is understood through the rule *ṭu-ṇ-ud-it savarṇasya ca apratyayaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.69).

Why does the inclusion [of the letter ṭ] not occur? Because the nasality (*anunāsikatva*) of the vowel *ū* has not been formally asserted, and because of the inclusion of *ṭu* in the rule *ṭhcuṭū* (Pāṇini 1.3.7). If there were an inclusion of the *ṭ*-class (*ṭavarga*) here, then since the beginning of a suffix would already be established by this very rule, the inclusion of *ṭu* would be purposeless. [The example is] *minnaḥ*.

In *vepathuḥ*, there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rules *ṭhñītaḥ ktaḥ* (3.2.187) and *āditaśca* (7.2.16). [The suffix] *athuc* is applied by the rule *ṭvito'thuca* (3.3.89). In *paktrimam*, [the suffix] *ktri* is applied by the rule *ḍvitaḥ ktriḥ* (3.3.88). [The word means] "prepared by cooking" (*pākena nivṛtam*), and [the suffix] *mam* is added by the rule *ktrermam nityam* (4.4.20).

*map*—in *ṭhuptrimam*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule *vacyādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 6.1.15). In *paṭūayati*, there is lengthening by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* (7.4.25) following *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (3.1.8). In *kaṇḍūayati*, [the suffix] *yak* is applied by the rule *kaṇḍvādibhyo yak*.

(3.1.27) But how, then, is the designation *it* obtained here, given that in the sūtra the words *ṭu* and *aḍ* are introduced with short vowels (*hrasva*), whereas these two [words *ṭu* and *aḍ*] have long vowels (*dīrgha*)? This is not so; for although they come to have long vowels once the lengthening has been applied, nevertheless, at the time of their formal enunciation (*uddeśa*), they have short vowels, according to the rule "in the original enunciation" (1.3.2).

And this [rule] continues here as well. In that regard, because the word *paṭu* is included in the *pṛthvādi* group, the fact that the stem *paṭu-* ends in a short vowel is established by its being taught (*upadeśe*) with a short vowel. Because the word *kaṇḍū* is included in the rule *kaṇḍvādibhyo yak* (Pāṇini 3.1.27), the same applies to the stem *kaṇḍū-*. For there are two kinds [of stems]:...

The *kaṇḍvādi* group consists of both verbal roots (*dhātu*) and nominal stems (*prātipadika*). Among them, the verbal root *kaṇḍu* ends in a short vowel; however, the nominal stem *kaṇḍu* ends in a long vowel.
Alternatively, even if the term "in the original instruction" (*upadeśe*) does not carry over [from the previous rule], nevertheless, regarding the long vowel...

Even when a partial modification has occurred, because the entity remains non-different [from the original], the application [of the rule] indeed exists. In the case of *ñikārīyati*, the suffix *kyac* is applied as before. Since the word *ñikāra* is not listed anywhere [in the lexicon], the designation *it* does not apply here. If it were to apply, the form would not be correct once the elision (*lopa*) had taken place.
It would be accomplished.

6. *ṣaḥ pratyayasya* (1.3.6). [The example is] *rajakī*. Because it has the marker *ṣ*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.49]: *ṣid-gaurādibhyaś-ca*. Now, by what rule is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) effected here? If one says it is by [Pāṇini 6.4.24]: *an-iti-n-ṛtām*, that is not so; for in that case...
It is stated that [the rule applies] when there is *k* or *ṅ* followed by *t* (*kṅt*), yet here there is no such *kṅt* suffix. This is not a fault;

the assignment of the technical designation *mit* to the roots *jan*, *jṛṣ*, *knasu*, and *rañj*—as well as those ending in *m* and *n* (Gaṇasūtra on Dhātupāṭha 817)—is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that [the rule applies] even when there is no *k* or *ṅ*.

Some maintain that the elision of its nasal occurs; otherwise, since the letter *a* of the root *rañj* would not be penultimate when the causative suffix *ṇiC* is applied, the rule "ṭhata upadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.116) would not require the application of *vṛddhi*, and thus the assignment of the technical designation *mit* would be purposeless.
Regarding the rule *ṭhghañi ca bhāvakaraṇayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.27),

others maintain that because the word *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccayārtha*), there is occasionally a loss of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) of the root *rañj* even when the suffix *ktin* follows.

Regarding the form *ṣoḍaḥ*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one who has six teeth. By the rule *vayasi dantasya datṛ* (Pāṇini 5.4.141), the substitute *datṛ* is applied; the vowel *ṛ* is for the purpose of triggering operations dependent on an *ugit* suffix. Then, by the rule *ṣaṣa utvaṃ datṛdaśadhāsūtrapadādeṣṭutvaṃ ca* (Vārttika 765), the substitution of *u* for the final vowel of *ṣaṣ* occurs, and by its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group, the change of *ṣ* to *ṣṭ* takes place.

The final *ṣ* becomes *ū* by "ṣaṣo'ntyasyotvam," and there is *guṇa* substitution by "ṭhādguṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.87). By the rule "the initial [consonant] of the second member [becomes cerebral]" (*utarapadādiṣṭutavam*), the *d* is changed to *ḍ*. When the form *ṣoḍat* is established, one applies the causative suffix *ṇic* according to the Vārttika "that which does it, that which makes it known" (*tatkaroti tadācaṣṭe*) (Vārttikas 200, 201). Regarding the *ṇic* suffix, the operations are like those of the *iṣṭhan* suffix (*ṇāviṣṭhavat kāryam*).

By the rule *prātipadikasya* (Vārttika 813), there is the elision of the *ṭi* portion due to the application of the *iṣṭhavan-bhāva* [treatment as if it were the suffix iṣṭha]; thus, from *ṣoḍayati*, there is the suffix *ac* (the first of the *pacādi* group) and the elision of the causative marker *ṇi*.
Hence, *ṣaṇḍaḥ*. [The root] *ṣaṇu* [is used] in the sense of "giving" (*dāne*) (Dhātupāṭha 1464). [The suffix] *ḍa* is applied after roots ending in *ñam* (Daiva 5.7).

Due to the word "bahulam" (in various ways) in the rule *ṭhuṇādayo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.1), the substitution of *s* for *ṣ* as prescribed by *dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.64) does not occur. Alternatively, the word *ṣaṇḍa* is an unanalyzed (avyutpanna) nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

Regarding the form *ṣaḍaṅgulikaḥ*: from the word *ṣaḍaṅgulidata*, the suffix *ṭhac* is applied in the sense of compassion (*anukampā*) by the rule *bahvaco'manuṣyanāmnaṣṭhajvā* (Pāṇini 5.3.78). By the rule *ṭhājādāvūrdhvaṃ dvitīyādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.83), there is elision of *aṅgulidata*; then, by the rule *ṭhasyekaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.50), the suffix *ṭha* is replaced by *ika*.
Thus, there is the substitution of *i* (the *it-ekādeśa*). Then, by the rule *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), the letter *a* of the word *ṣaḍa* is elided.

If that [elision] were to possess the status of being "as if present" (*sthānivadbhāva*), then because of the intervention [caused by it], the designation *bha*—according to the rule *yaci bham* (Pāṇini 1.4.18)—would not apply to the word *ṣaṭ*. However, by relying on the internal case-ending (*vibhakti*), it possesses the status of a *pada*.

By the rule *ṭhjhalāṃ jaśo'nte* (Pāṇini 8.2.39), there is the substitution of a *jaś* sound; thus, the *ṣ* of *ṣaṇḍa* becomes *ḍ*. If this *ṣ* were to receive the technical designation *it*, then when the feminine gender is intended, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would apply by the rule *ṣid-gaurādibhyaś-ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.41). Although this word *ṣaṇḍa* refers to a bull, nevertheless...

Even in the case of a female cow (*strīgavī*), its existence is indeed possible through connection with the property of being neuter (*ṣaṇḍa*). Although these [terms] such as *ṣoḍa* and others are technical (*lākṣaṇika*), nevertheless, by means of the mention of the enunciation (*uddeśa*), the letter *ṣ* is specified;
thus, these serve as counter-examples (*pratyudāharaṇa*) for the rule regarding the mention of an affix (*pratyayagrahaṇa*). For here too, there is an enunciation.

The letter *ṣakāra* [is used as follows]: *ṭhaviṣaḥ*, *mahiṣaḥ*. [These are derived from] the roots *ava* "to protect" (*dhā.pā.* 600) and *maha* "to honor" (*dhā.pā.* 1867), according to the rule *avimahyaeṣṭiṣac* (*da.u.* 9.3). Now, one might object that because of the expression "the *ṭhuka*-class suffixes are diverse" (*3.3.1*), the designation of a suffix (*pratyayasaṃjñā*) does not even apply here due to the word "diversely" (*bahulam*).
Even when that [condition] exists, the designation "it" (itsaṃjñā) will not occur because of the use of the plural;
why, then, is the mention of "beginning" (ādi) continued here? He thinks thus:
the mention of "beginning," which must necessarily be continued for the sake of what follows, will also serve to clarify the meaning here.

7. *cuṭū* (Pāṇini 1.3.7). [Example: *kauñjāyanyaḥ*. From a word ending in *cphañ*, the suffix *ñya* is applied in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*) by rule 5.3.113: *vrātacphañor astriyām*. [The author] will state that *ch* is replaced by *ey*; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the designation *it*.

"Ṭhśāṇḍikyaḥ": by the rule "ṭhśaṇḍikādibhyo ñyaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.3.92), the suffix *ñya* is applied in the sense of "one whose ancestral home (*abhijana*) is Śaṇḍika," for in that context the phrase "that is his ancestral home" (*so'syābhijanaḥ*) is understood to be in force.
"Mandurajaḥ": by the rule "ṅyāpoḥ saṃjñāccchandasorbahulam" (Pāṇini 6.3.63).
Thus, there is the shortening of the vowel in the word *mandūra*. Regarding the rule "from *anna* [comes] *ānna*" (*ṭhannāṇṇaḥ- ānnaḥ*), [the form] *anna-labdhā* is derived from the suffix *ṇa*.
For in that context, following the rule "one who has obtained a collection of wealth" (*dhanagaṇaṃ labdhā*, Pāṇini 4.4.84), the word *labdhā* is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*). Now...

For what purpose is a separate rule (*pṛthag-yoga*) formulated? Why not simply formulate a single rule as "ṭh-cu-ṭu-aṣāḥ pratyayasya" [the letters ṭh, cu, ṭu, and aṣ are the substitutes for the final letter of a suffix]? To this, he says:
"The formulation of a separate rule," and so forth. By means of that [separate rule], such as "tena vittaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.2.26), etc., of this...
He demonstrates the purpose of making known the non-eternality of the rule (vidhi).
8. *laśakvataddhite* (1.3.8).

Regarding "priyaṃvadaḥ": by [the rule] *priyavaśe vadaḥ khac* (3.2.38), the suffix *khac* is applied; then, by *arurdviṣadajantasya* (6.3.67), the augment *mum* is inserted. Regarding "jiṣṇuḥ": by [the rule] *glājisthaśca ksnuḥ* (3.2.139), the suffix *ksnu* is applied.

Thus [it is said]. According to the opinion of those who desire that the suffix *kṣnu* be marked with the indicatory letter *ṅ*, this is an example of the letter *g*. However, according to the opinion of those who desire it to be marked with the indicatory letter *k*, this also becomes an example of the letter *k*.

Regarding the form *cūḍāla*: the suffix *lac* is applied in the sense of possession (*matvartha*) by the rule *prāṇisthādāto laj anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.2.96). Now, one might object that the designation *it* will not apply here due to the absence of a purpose;
if it is argued that the purpose is the acute accent (*udātta*) on the syllable preceding the suffix ending in *l*, we say no, because of the accent of the *cit* suffix.

Since the accent of the suffix would already be established as having the udātta on the final syllable by the rule of accentuation for suffixes (*pratyayasvara*), because it is an exception (*apavāda*) to all other [rules], the purpose of employing the *cit* marker is this: that the accent should be precisely the *cit-svara*, and whatever other accent might otherwise apply should not occur. This, however, is the counter-example: [The text continues with the specific grammatical analysis of the word *sāmgrahaṇī*: In the case of *sāmgrahaṇī*, the suffix *cha* (forming the feminine *ī*) is added after the word *saṃgrahaṇa*. Since *saṃgrahaṇa* is derived from the root *grah* preceded by the prefix *sam*, it is a *nitya-ṅīp*-formation according to Pāṇini 3.1.124 (*saṃgrāma-han-ḍa-bhaḥ*). Thus, the word *saṃgrahaṇa* ends in *ṅīp*. When *cha* is added, the *ṅīp* is elided by Pāṇini 6.4.148 (*yasyeti ca*). Now, since the suffix *cha* is marked with *cit*, the *cit-svara* applies, resulting in the udātta on the first syllable of *sāmgrahaṇī*. However, if one were to argue that the *citaḥ* rule (Pāṇini 6.1.163) should apply here, it is countered: no, because the *citaḥ* rule is superseded by the subsequent rule *taddhitasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.164), which assigns the udātta to the penultimate syllable of a taddhita formation. Therefore, the udātta falls on the syllable *ṇa* of *sāmgrahaṇī*. Thus, the *cit* marker in *cha* serves its purpose only when there is no other accent to intervene; in this instance, the *taddhitasya* rule prevails. Hence, this is the counter-example.

Is it not the case that the suffix *śa* is applied by the rule "lomādipāmādi" (Pāṇini 5.2.100), as in *lomaśa*, meaning "one who has body hair"? This too is not so; for here also, because there is no purpose [for the application of the suffix], the designation *it* will not occur. In that case, here is a counter-example: "from *karṇa* and *lalāṭa*, the suffix *kan* when it denotes an ornament."

By the rule (Pāṇini 4.3.65), the suffix *kan* is added in the sense of abstract action (*bhāvārtha*), resulting in *karṇikā*. If this were to be a technical name (*saṃjñā*), then by the rule "before *ṭh* and *kit*" (7.2.118), etc., there would be *vṛddhi* [vowel strengthening], and consequently, the desired form would not be established at all. If this is so, why is only this case presented as an objection and not the others? He thinks thus for this purpose: [the following].

Since the rule "ṭha-taddhite" (Pāṇini 6.4.145) is formulated here as well, it may also serve to avoid the difficulty of comprehension for those of dull intellect in cases such as *cūḍālaḥ* and *lomaśaḥ*.
9. *tasya lopaḥ* (1.3.9).

Now, for what purpose is *tasya* stated? Since the designation *it* is the subject under discussion, by virtue of the context, the elision (*lopa*) will occur only of that for which the *it*-designation has been prescribed.

He says: "The mention of *tasya*," and so forth. But what is this element designated by the term *it*, for the purpose of which the mention of *tasya* serves to exclude [the operation] from the final letter? He says: "The initial [augment] *ñ, ṭ, ṭh, ḍ, dh*. If the mention of *tasya* were not present, these augments beginning with *ñ* would also [be understood to apply] to the final letter by the rule *alo'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52).

According to this statement, there would be elision of the final [element]. However, by the mention of *tasya* (of that), the subject under discussion—the one designated as *it*—is brought to mind, and thus the elision applies to the whole, not just the final element;
otherwise, the mention of *tasya* would be purposeless. This is because of the rule: "When [a substitute] is meaningless (*anarthaka*), the operation of the final [element] does not apply."
(Vyā.pa.62) If this paribhāṣā were relied upon, then the mention of *tasya* could have been omitted. It is nevertheless included for the sake of clarity.
10. *Yathāsaṃkhyamanudeśaḥ samānām* (1.3.10).

"By the word 'number' (saṃkhyā), sequence is indicated here. Where there are multiple subjects (uddeśin) and correlates (anudeśin), since an unrestricted connection would otherwise result, this [sūtra] is commenced for the purpose of providing a restriction. This applies where both the subjects and the correlates are of multiple numbers.

In that case, there must necessarily be a distinction in number; and where there is a distinction in number, there is an invariably concomitant sequence, because it is impossible to utter those things possessing distinct numbers simultaneously. Therefore, by association, sequence is indicated by the word "number. However, the property of being an object [of cognition] resides in the word.

It has been stated that by means of the word "number" (*saṃkhyā*), sequence (*krama*) is indicated. Why was the term "according to sequence" (*yathākrama*) not used? It is for the sake of variety. In the expression "yathāsaṃkhyam," there is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) formed with the particle *yathā* in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*), according to Pāṇini 2.1.7: *yathā'sādṛśye*.

"An *anudeśa* is that which is pointed out subsequently (*anu-diśyate*). The suffix *ghañ* is applied by the rule "after [a verbal root], when not denoting an agent, provided it is a technical term (*saṃjñā*)" (Pāṇini 3.3.19).
It is called "subsequent" because the word *anu* has the sense of "after," and because the action of utterance occurs twice. "Equal enumeration" (*samasaṃkhyāna*) means...

It demonstrates equality by way of having an equal number. The reading in the root text (*Kāśikā*) is "of those recited equally" (*samaṃ paripaṭhitānām*); [another version reads] "of those recited with equal enumeration" (*samagaṇanaparipaṭhitānām*). It clarifies that very same meaning through different words: "of the *uddeśins* and the *anudeśins*."

The genitive case is used here in relation to the word "respectively" (*yathākramam*). Although the items being enumerated (*uddeśinaḥ*) are not explicitly heard in the sūtra, they are nonetheless understood because of their inherent connection and because they are subsequently grasped through the mention of the things being referred to (*anudeśa*).

Regarding the term "respectively": it is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) formed with the sense of "according to," as previously explained, and it functions here as a word ending in the third case.

This is the meaning here: by whatever order exists between the *uddēśins* (the terms mentioned first) and the *anudēśins* (the terms mentioned subsequently), the *anudēśins* are connected with the *uddēśins* according to that same order. Although the word "of the *uddēśins*" (*uddeśinām*) is presented in the genitive case, nevertheless, for the sake of the sense, there will be a transformation of the case-ending.

The word ending in the third case is [the antecedent]. By the rule "from the first, the first," and so forth, he demonstrates the connection according to the respective order.
