The word "etc. (*ādi*) is for the purpose of including "from the third, the third," "from the fourth, the fourth," and so on. In examples such as *taudeya*, [the rule] "that is his ancestral origin" (*so'syābhijanaḥ*, Pāṇini 4.3.90) applies.
In this sense, there is a secondary derivative (taddhita).

Regarding the rule beginning with "ṭhiha" and so forth: according to [Pāṇini 5.2.131], "veśoyaśaāderbhagāt," there are two bases (*prakṛti*), namely *veśa* and *yaśas*, and there are likewise two suffixes (*pratyaya*), namely *yal* and *kha*; therefore, they correspond respectively (*yathāsaṃkhyena*).
The intended meaning is that [the suffix] must be applied. Here, a certain teacher caused his students to memorize this as a single rule:

"After *veśas*, *yaśas*, and so forth, [the suffix] *bhaga* and others, *yal*, and *kha*. Others, however, consider these to be two rules: one is "after *veśas*, *yaśas*, and so forth, [the suffix] *bhaga*," and the other is "*yal* and *kha*."

Thus ends the second [section]. In that regard, for those disciples who have been led to believe that this *yoga* is indeed one and the same, this question is posed. The author of the *Vṛtti*, relying on that very same view, has stated the solution with the words "svaritena" and so forth. As for those who...
The intention is this: for those who have been led to believe that "these two are indeed [the] yogas," this question does not arise;

for if the correspondence were established by the mere separation of the *yoga*s themselves, then the formulation of the separation of the *yoga*s would be purposeless. But how, then, is the correspondence established by means of the circumflex (*svarita*) accent as an indicator?

Since there is no mention of the *svarita* accent here, he says: "The governing authority (*adhikāra*) is by means of the *svarita*," and so forth. By dividing the rule *svaritenādhikāraḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.11) into two parts—namely, *svaritena* as one rule and *adhikāraḥ* as the second—the first rule is as follows:

The word "also" (*api*) connects [the term *yathāsaṃkhyam*] with what precedes, namely "according to the order of enumeration" (*yathāsaṃkhyam*), and by virtue of that same word "also," it also connects with what follows, namely "the governing rule" (*adhikāraḥ*). If, then, the correspondence according to order occurs by means of the indicatory mark (the circumflex accent), such being the case, there would indeed be doubt. For instance:

Regarding the phrase "according to the respective order" (*yathāsaṃkhyam*), even though there is a governing rule (*adhikāra*) indicated by the circumflex accent (*svarita*), it is not known therein whether the attachment of the circumflex accent is for the purpose of a governing rule or for the purpose of indicating the respective order;
this is merely a doubt. Regarding all such doubts, it is said: "It occurs... (*bhavati*).
"The specific [meaning] is understood through explanation; for it is not the case that something is not a defining characteristic because of doubt" (Vyāyāpavārttika 75).

11. *svaritenādhikāraḥ* | (1.3.11) [The rule] "the third case ending is used in the sense of a characteristic mark of a particular state" (*hitthambhūtalakṣaṇe tṛtīyā*) [is governed by this]. This is because the governing authority (*adhikāra*) is to be indicated by the sign of the circumflex accent (*svarita*). If, in this context, the term *svarita* were taken in its technical sense...
If there were such an inclusion, then in the rule *ṭhraṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ samānapade* (8.4.1),
the status of the *ṇakāra* as a governing heading (*adhikāra*) would not be established;

for that which is defined by technical convention (*paribhāṣika*) possesses the nature of a vowel (*aj-dharma*), and since the *ṇakāra* lacks a vowel (*anackatva*), [the objection] was raised with this in mind for all [cases].

Demonstrating that this refers to the phonetic property (*varṇadharma*) called *svarita* belonging to vowels, consonants, and semivowels (*hal*), and not to the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) term, he says:

"The so-called *svarita* is a defect of pitch (*svaradoṣa*) which is a property of the phoneme (*varṇadharma*). The mention of it as a property of the phoneme, however, is for the purpose of understanding its governing scope (*adhikāra*).

This is understood here even from the coloring [of the vowel] with the *svarita* accent. "The *adhikāra* is application (*viniyoga*)," meaning the performance of an operation. "Because it is the governing topic (*adhikṛta*), it applies (*upatiṣṭhate*) to what follows. Just as a person who is appointed to a city or similar place remains present there, so too [does the *adhikāra*].

A word-form endowed with the quality of the svarita accent, as prescribed by the author of the Sūtras, applies itself in various places according to the author's rule. The expression "subsequently" (uttaratra) is intended as an illustration; in some cases, it indeed applies even to what precedes.
But where does its existence occur, and where does it not? To this he says:
"The followers of Pāṇini hold that [vowels] are *svarita* by convention (*pratijñā*). Those for whom [vowels] are *svarita* by convention are so described.
This is what is meant: wherever those teachers [declare] the state of being *svarita*, [there it exists].

They declare that its existence occurs only in those specific cases and not elsewhere. Furthermore, that declaration is not made without restriction; rather, it occurs only where the teachers have recorded it. And this rule should be understood as being comparable to the analogy of the "ornamented prose" (kalāgadya).

It is employed for the sake of an operation, but once its task is accomplished, it ceases; it does not remain inherent in the application (*prayoga*). By means of the rule "The affix" (3.1.1) and others, those governing headings (*adhikāra*) that are delimited by the *svarita* accent are illustrated; now [the examples are shown]. Atha...

For what purpose is this governing rule (*adhikāra*) established? If it is argued that it is for the sake of ensuring that the term "to him" (*tasmai*) is not required at each individual application, we say no; for example, when it is said, "Let a cow be given to Devadatta, and a blanket," the word "to Devadatta" is not repeated again, and yet—
Because Devadatta has been introduced [as the subject] and because the phrase "the blanket" is expectant of a correlate,

the connection is made with that very [subject]; and likewise, because sentences such as "in the sense of a stable state" (Pāṇini 3.3.17) and "in the sense of an abstract action" (3.3.18) are also expectant, [the connection is made] with the *ghañ* suffixes and so forth.
Since it has been introduced, its connection will be with those very [terms]; so what is the use of an adhikāra?

This is true; it applies where there is no mention of anything else, but where there is a mention of something else, it must indeed serve to exclude that which was previously under discussion. For instance:

When it is said, "Let a cow be given to Yajñadatta; a blanket to Viṣṇumitra," Devadatta, who was the subject under discussion, is excluded by the mention of others. Thus, since he is excluded by the mention of others, [the rule] *Pāṇini 3.3.44*, *abhividhau bhāva inuṇ*, is set aside by the mention of *inuṇ*.

Since the *ghañ* suffix under discussion has been withdrawn, in the rule "ṭhākrośe'vanyorgrahaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.3.45), there would be a connection with the immediately preceding *inuṇ* suffix, and not with the *ghañ* which is separated by an interval; yet, *ghañ* is desired here. But surely, by the power of observed continuity (*dṛṣṭānuvṛtti*), *ghañ* itself will continue to apply?
The connection will be with that very [suffix], and so he will say there:
"By the force of following what is seen, *ghañ* alone follows there, not the immediately preceding *inuṇ*.
This is not so; for if, by the force of following what is seen, the following were only of *aghañ*, [then it would be as you say].

In that case, under the rule *ṭhṛdorap* (Pāṇini 3.3.57), the suffix *ghañ* alone would continue to apply in the subsequent rules as well, rather than the suffix *ap*. As for what will be stated later—"by the force of observed continuity"—there, the term "force of observed continuity" refers precisely to the state of being *svarita*. What is "observed" regarding the continuity...

"Capability" (*sāmarthyam*) refers to the word-form under discussion, by forming a *bahuvrīhi* compound with "that from which" (*yasmāt*). Therefore, the meaning here is "because of its being marked with the *svarita* accent. If this were the intended meaning of the author of the Sūtra, one might ask: why was it not simply stated as "because of its being *svarita*"?

No; for the operation of words is not according to one's own whim, but rather the meaning must be examined—thus this objection is not valid. Therefore, since the mention of something else serves to exclude what has been introduced, a restrictive specification (adhikāra) must be made. And when that is made, [the intended meaning follows].
To show the means for understanding that [distinction], the rule "svaritenādhikāraḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.11) must be formulated.

12. *anudātaṅti ātmanepadam* (Pāṇini 1.3.12). Regarding this, it is stated: "In that regard, this restriction is established. Because the suffix (*pratyaya*) is that which is being prescribed (*vidhīyamāna*), it is understood that the restriction applies to the suffix and not to the verbal root (*prakṛti*). For this very reason, he says: "Those roots which have an indicatory vowel (*it*) that is *anudātta*..."
"And ṅti after those [roots]. If, however, this were a restriction on the *prakṛti* (the base), then what would happen?

No other suffix would follow bases ending in anudātta vowels or ṅ-sounds. One might argue that another suffix could indeed occur by virtue of the power of the explicit statement (*vacana*), but this objection can be raised.

To avoid [this objection]: however, if there should be the fault of overburdening the listener when the intended meaning is understood through the power of the words themselves, that indeed cannot be avoided. If, then, this is a restriction regarding comprehension, then, because verbal roots (*prakṛti*) are unrestricted, from them...
Could there also be the *parasmaipada*? It will not occur;

because of the formulation of the second restrictive rule, "The *parasmaipada* occurs after the remainder [roots] when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed" (Pāṇini 1.3.78), the *parasmaipada* occurs only after the remainder and not from any other [root]. For example, *āste* and so forth. [The root] *ās* [is used] in the sense of "sitting" (Dhātupāṭha 1021); [the root] *vas*...

Regarding the roots *ācchādane* (DhP 1023), *ṣūṅ prāṇigarbhavimocane* (DhP 031), and *śīṅ svapane* (DhP 1032): because they belong to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix. Thus, we have "he lies" (*śete*). According to the rule *śīṅḥ sārvadhātuke guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.21), there is *guṇa* substitution [of the vowel of the root].
13. *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* | (1.3.13) "Bhāva" refers to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) as consisting of action; "karman," however, is purely technical (*pāribhāṣika*).

In this regard, it is stated that [the rule] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*); this is the distinction. This [rule] also is a restriction regarding the suffixes (*pratyaya-niyama*), as was the previous one.

The *ātmanepada* occurs only when there is the sense of the action being for oneself (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*); it is not a restriction on the meaning. If it were a restriction on the meaning, then in such cases as "What gift was given by you? (*ko bhavatā dāya udattaḥ*) or "What gain was obtained by you? (*ko bhavatā lābho labdhaḥ*), the suffix *ghañ* and others would be difficult to obtain in the sense of the object (*karman*). [Example: "He sleeps" (*supyate*). [Root: *ñiṣvap* "to sleep" (DhP 1068).

By [the rule] *vacy-ādinā* (Pāṇini 6.1.15), there is *samprasāraṇa*. Thus, "it is done" (*kriyate*). By [the rule] *riṅ śayagliṅkṣu* (Pāṇini 7.4.28), there is the substitution of *riṅ*. In the case of "the field is mown by itself" (*lūyate kedāraḥ svayameva*), [this occurs] under the rule *karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.87).

Someone might have the misconception that, between the two positions—designation (*vyapadeśa*) and extension (*atideśa*)—the *parasmaipada* should apply to the object-as-agent (*karmakartṛ*) because it is subsequent;
therefore, in order to refute that, he says "in the case of the object-as-agent" (*karmakartari*), etc. This is the second...

The mention of "the agent" (*kartṛ*) is understood [from the previous rule], from the sūtra "when there is reciprocal action, [the suffixes are used] in the sense of the agent" (1.3.14). By this, the Parasmaipada suffixes occur when the agent alone—that is, the pure or absolute agent—is devoid of the status of being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*);
whereas where there is the status of being like the object, the Ātmanepada suffixes occur.

It occurs as follows: under the view that there is an extension of the operation (*kāryātideśapakṣa*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is formed by the rule itself, "That which has an action similar to that of an object through its own action" (3.1.87).
[And also] by "When there is a reciprocal action, the *ātmanepada* suffixes occur in the sense of the agent" (1.3.14).

"The word *karman* denotes action (*kriyā*). By this, he shows that what is understood here as *karman* is the worldly action consisting of activity, not the technical (Pāṇinian) definition. How is this obtained? From proximity (*pratyāsatti*).
For action is proximate to the verbal root (*dhātu*), because it applies directly (*sākṣād-vṛtti*) to it. And direct application is...

Because action (*kriyā*) is denotable by a verbal root (*dhātu*). However, in the case of the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) object consisting of a means (*sādhana*), the verbal root does not directly denote it; for that [object] is not denotable by a verbal root. Therefore, there is no immediate proximity (*pratyāsatti*) of that [object] toward the verbal root, and thus [the rule] is not applied when there is an exchange of the object as a means (*sādhana-karma*).

The ātmanepada occurs—as in *devadattasya dhānyaṃ vyatilunanti*. The root *lū* (to cut) is used here in the sense of "appropriating" (*upasaṃgraha*) during the act of cutting. The meaning is: "They appropriate by means of cutting that grain which was previously gathered by Devadatta."

Furthermore, because the act of milking (*dhānaya*) belonging to one person is performed by another, there occurs an exchange of the object of the action (*sādhanakarmavyatīhāra*). Regarding the phrase "belonging to another": it means that this action is performed by one who desires the action intended for another agent, thinking, "I shall perform this action."

It is intended here as being connected with another; otherwise, if an action produced by one were intended here as being connected with another, then the reciprocal exchange (*vyatihāra*) would not be possible, for it is not possible to produce again what has already been produced by another. [This is illustrated by the example] "they cut [the grain] reciprocally" (*vyatilunate*).

The substitution of *at* [for the final vowel] occurs by the rule *ṭhātmanepadeṣvanataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.5), and the elision of the long *ā* occurs by the rule *ṭhśnābhyastayorātaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.112). Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*)?
If it is argued that it is for the purpose of excluding the states of being (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), we say no.
The *ātmanepada* affix is applied because the action is intended for the agent (*kartṛ*)— as in "the army is encountered" (*vyatibhūyate senayā*),

"the villages are traversed" (*vyatigamyante grāmāḥ*), and "the bandits are struck down" (*vyatihanyante dasyavaḥ*). If it is argued that this rule is unnecessary because the desired result would follow by the rule "in the sense of the action or the object" (*bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*, 1.3.13) alone, [the answer is as follows:]...

No; because there is no distinction. For there is no difference whatsoever whether that [rule] applies or this one, provided the ātmanepada occurs. If it were by this [rule], then the prohibition "not after [roots] meaning motion or injury" (1.3.15) would apply; however, when the ātmanepada is prescribed by that [other rule], this [prohibition] does not occur.

If it is argued that this is a fault, we grant that it is true; let this be the distinction. Nevertheless, the mention of the agent (*kartṛ*) need not be made. For, according to the rule "A prescription or a prohibition applies to what is immediately preceding" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 19), it is the immediately following application that is prohibited, not the preceding one. Therefore...

The Ātmanepada will apply in the sense of the state (bhāva) and the object (karman). Therefore, he says: "The mention of 'the agent' (kartṛ) is for the sake of the subsequent rule. But what is this subsequent rule for which this serves a purpose? He says: "From the rest," and so forth.

15. Not after roots meaning "motion" or "injury. (Pāṇini 1.3.15) [Examples: *vyatigacchanti* ("they go against each other"). By the rule *iṣugamiyamāṃ chaḥ* (7.3.77), *gacchanti* becomes *icchanti*, and by *che ca* (6.1.73), the augment *tuk* is added. [Example: *vyatisarpanti* ("they glide against each other"). [Roots: *gamlṛ* and *sṛplṛ* mean "to go."
(dhā.pā. 982, 983), there is *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. Regarding "vyatihiṃsanti": the roots *tṛhi* and *hiṃsi* are used in the sense of injury (*hisāyām*) (dhā.pā.
1348, 1829). Regarding "vyatighnanti": the root *hana* is used in the senses of injury and motion (*hiṃsā-gatyoḥ*) (dhā.pā. 1012).
By the rule *gamahana-* (Pāṇini 6.4.98), there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*), and [the substitution of] *ha*...

The substitution of *ku* occurs by the rule *hanterṇinneṣu* (Pāṇini 7.3.54). Regarding the phrase "in the case of a prohibition," etc.: the meaning of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is "explanation" (*pratipādana*).
Here, because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is used in the sense of "explanation. And that...

Since the subject under discussion is the prohibition, it is understood that this refers to the demonstration of the prohibition of the *ātmanepada* endings for [roots] beginning with *has*. Thus, the meaning is this:

when a prohibition is to be made, the demonstration of the prohibition of the *ātmanepada* for *has* and the others must also be performed. In this regard, the following demonstration is given: the rule is split (*yogavibhāga*) by adding "not" (*na*).

Therefore, [the prohibition] will apply to *has* and the others as well. Consequently, there is a second rule: "After roots meaning motion or injury" (*gatihiṃsārthebhyaḥ*). In this case, the word "not" (*na*) is understood to carry over. But for what purpose is this [second rule]?
It is for the purpose of making known that the preceding rule does not have universal application; by means of this, [the word] "not" (*na*)...
By means of a *yogavibhāga* (division of the rule), the prohibition will apply only to *hasa* and the others, and not to others.
16. *itaretarānyo'nyopapadācca* (1.3.16).
A word uttered near [another] is an *upapada*. That [compound] which has the words *itaretara* and *anyo'nya* as its *upapada* is [governed by this rule].
Thus it has been stated. Now, for what purpose is the mention of the term *upapada*? One might say: "Let it be stated as *netaretarānyo'nyābhyām*.

It is impossible to state it thus; for if it were stated in that way, because of the reference to the ablative case (*pañcamī*), by the rule *tasmādityutarasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.67), the substitution would apply only to what follows—namely, to *itaretara*.
Regarding the phrase "they cut each other" (*vyatilunanti*), it would not apply here in the form "they cut one another's [hair]" (*vyatilunantītaretarasya*).

Therefore, it must be explained that the meaning of the rule "it should be stated that [the prohibition applies] when *paraspara* is the upapada" is that the prohibition occurs when the word *paraspara* is the upapada (governing word) of the suffix. In this regard, the following...
The commentary: the particle *ca* is used here; it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.
By this, the prohibition will also apply when there is a mutual connection with an *upapada*.
17. *ner viśaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.17).

Regarding the form *niviśate*: the root *viś* (meaning "to enter," 1424) takes the suffix *śa* because it belongs to the *tudādigaṇa*. Regarding the form *nyaviśata*: someone might have the misconception that the *ātmanepada* ending should not occur here because of the intervention of the augment *aṭ*; therefore, he says the following in order to dispel that doubt.

"Augments are included by the mention of the [root] itself"—so state the *Kāśikā* and the *Padamañjarī*. Regarding the examples "aḍāgamaḥ" and so forth, and "madhuni viśanti": here, the ātmanepada ending would apply to the root *viś* following the prefix *ni*;
why, then, does it not occur? To this he says: "of the prefix *ni*" and so forth.

In the neuter dual form of the word *madhu*, by the rule "ṭhiko'ci vibhaktau" (Pāṇini 7.1.73), the augment *num* is applied, resulting in the form *madhunī*; and its constituent part, the syllable *ni*, is devoid of meaning.

18. *parivyavebhyaḥ kriyaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.18). [The example is] *parikrīṇīte*. There is the substitution of *ī* by [the rule] *ī halyaghoḥ* (6.4.113). [The question is: "How is it that *paryādayaḥ* are understood as *upasargas*? [The answer is: The genitive case in *kriyaḥ* is a genitive of relation (*sambandha-lakṣaṇā*). It is not...

Fifth [interpretation]: "Those beginning with *pary-* which are related to an action (*kriyā*). Their relationship is mediated by meaning and is characterized as that between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*). And that [relationship] is possible only with prepositions (*upasarga*) such as *pary-*, not with others; thus, by implication, the term "preposition" (*upasarga*) is understood [in the rule]. [The word] *bahuvi-*...
"He buys. [In the compound] *bahuvayaḥ*, it is a *bahuvrīhi* [possessive compound] meaning "that in which there are many birds (*vayas*). Here, the word *vi-* refers to a bird.

19. *viparābhyāṃ jeḥ* (1.3.19). [The phrase] "due to association" (*sāhacaryāt*) refers to the reason for including the term "preposition" (*upasarga*); that is, in the rule *nerviśaḥ* (1.3.17), there is the inclusion of the preposition *ni*. This is also the case in the immediately preceding rule (1.3.18).
Only the prefixes (*upasarga*) beginning with *pari* are to be understood here.
Therefore, some maintain that by virtue of proximity within this specific context, the words *adhi* and *parā* are taken as prefixes.
Others, however, explain that proximity is merely an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*); for those [words] with which there is such proximity...
They must necessarily be proximate;
therefore, because concomitance (*sāhacarya*) is inseparable from proximity (*pratyāsatti*), proximity is obtained through it. This is what is meant:
the prefixes *vi-* and *pari-* are understood as qualifying proximity. And proximity is...

[The suffix] occurs only after the verbal root *ji* when preceded by the prefixes *vi-* and *parā-*, and not when they are absent as prefixes. For it is thus: the meaning of "conquering" (*jayati*) is qualified specifically by those two [prefixes], and not by any others.

20. *āṅe do'nāsyaviharaṇe* (1.3.20). It is only for the root *dā* that an application [of the prefix *āṅ*] is possible in the sense of opening the mouth (*āsya-viharaṇa*), and not for other roots having the form *dā*. Therefore, by means of that prohibition, it is understood that only that [root *dā*] is being referred to; hence he says:
Regarding the rule *ṭhāṅpūrvāddāñaḥ*: [the form] *ṭhādate*. As before, there is the elision of the vowel *ā*, and by the rule *ṭhkhari ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.55), there is the substitution of *c* for *t*.
It should also be stated that the prohibition applies even when the action is identical to the opening of the mouth (*āsyaviharaṇa*).
By means of this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*), he shows that its scope extends to the act of moving (*viharaṇa*). How so?

The mention of "moving" (*viharaṇa*) need not be made; here, one should simply state: "after the root *dā* [meaning 'to give'], when followed by the suffix *ṭhāṅ*, there is the substitution of *do*, provided it does not refer to the mouth (*anāsye*).
Since the application of *dā* to the mouth is impossible, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), [the rule applies] to that which is inherent in the mouth.

The application [of the rule] will be understood as occurring in the context of action (*kriyā*); the prohibition applies precisely there. Therefore, what is the purpose of including the mention of "moving about" (*viharaṇa*)? But surely, if only this much were stated—"the substitution of *da* for *ṣṭhā*, except when referring to the mouth"—then the prohibition would also apply in the case of "Devadatta takes his own mouth. This is not a fault, because [the rule] indeed refers specifically to the domain of the mouth.

The action (*kriyā*) existing therein becomes one whose locus is the mouth; indeed, moving about (*viharaṇa*) alone has the mouth as its domain, whereas grasping (*grahaṇa*) has both the mouth and the grasper as its domains.
Thus, since [the action] is established even without the mention of moving about, that which is done by including "moving about" has this purpose:

The purpose [of this rule] is as follows: some say it is so that this prohibition may apply even in cases where the action is identical to that of opening the mouth (*āsya-viharaṇa*). Furthermore, the particle *ca* is understood from the rule "ṭhitaretarānyo'nyopapadācca" (Pāṇini 1.3.16), and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.
Others maintain that by this [rule], there is also a prohibition of the action of moving (*viharaṇa*) and the like.
Regarding the rule "also after [a verb] having a limb of one's own body as its object" (*svāṅgakarmakācca*), the words "it should be stated" (*vaktavyam*) are to be supplied as the remainder.
And here, a technical definition of "limb of one's own body" (*svāṅga*) characterized by being non-fluid and possessing form is not intended; rather, what is intended is...
"His own limb, his own limb" (*svamaṅgaṃ svāṅgam*): that whose object (*karman*) is [his] own limb is "one having his own limb as the object" (*svāṅgakarmaka*).
The meaning is that it must be stated that the prohibition applies from such an action having one's own limb as its object.
Therefore, when [the verb] becomes transitive by means of a mouth belonging to another (*parasambandhinā*), then...
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) indeed occurs—as in: "ants open the mouth of the moth.
The word *vaktavya* means "that which is to be explained. In this regard, the following is the explanation:

the term *kartari* (in the sense of the agent) is understood from the previous context, and *āsya* is a relative term; thus, it is understood as follows: [the rule applies] when the mouth is the agent.

Regarding the rule "if the *ātmanepada* occurs when the agent itself is the object, then [the root] has the sense of 'eating' (*āsyam*)": the term "āṅ" is treated as a separate *yogavibhāga* (rule-segment). Its purpose is to indicate such cases as: "wait for the boy" (*āgamayasva tāvan māṇavakam*), "the jackal sniffs" (*āghrāyate śṛgālaḥ*), and "he asks leave of his teachers" (*āpṛcchate gurūn*). By this, [the rule] "of the root *ā-gam-i*, in the sense of forbearance" (*āgameḥ kṣamāyām*) [is established].
Thus, it is not necessary to add [the following] as supplementary rules (*anupasaṃkhyeya*): Vārttika 35, "iti," and Vārttika 40, "ṭhāṅ nuprisaccchayoḥ."
21. *krīḍo 'nusaṃparibhyaś ca* (Pāṇini 1.3.21). [The commentary states:

"Because of association with *sam*. Although prefixes such as *anu* and others deviate from being [exclusively] *upasargas*, the word *sam* does not so deviate; therefore, by virtue of association with it, *anu* and the others are indeed *upasargas*.
It is understood as: "he plays after the boy" (*māṇavakamanukrīḍati*). The meaning is that he plays together with the boy.

By the rule *tṛtīyārthe* (Pāṇini 1.4.85), the word *anu* receives the technical designation *karmapravacanīya*. Regarding the term *āgameḥ*: this refers to the root *gam*, preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, in its causative (*ṇyanta*) form. *Kṣamā* means indifference or forbearance.

*Kālaharaṇa* means the passing of time; that is, waiting for a specific time. In the word *āgamayasva*, the designation *mit* is applied according to the rule *janījṛṣvanasurañjo'mantāśca* (Gaṇasūtra on Dhātupāṭha 817), and because it is a *mit* root, the shortening of the vowel occurs by the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.92).

The form *loṇ* is the second person singular middle voice (*madhyamapuruṣaikavacana*). By the rule "ṭhthāsaḥ se" (Pāṇini 3.4.80), *thās* is replaced by *se*; and by "ṭhsavābhyāṃ vāmau" (Pāṇini 3.4.91), *vām* is optionally substituted [for *hi*]. Regarding the term "śikṣeḥ": the root *śaki-* followed by the desiderative suffix (*san*) is understood here. In the phrase "vidyāsu śikṣate," the meaning is that he exerts himself in order to desire to know (*jijñāsituṃ*) knowledge. [The formation is] from *śak-* with *san*, according to "sani... [and so forth].

The elision of *iṭ* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.4.54] *mīmāghurabhalabhaḥ*. Here, the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) occurs by [Pāṇini 7.4.58] *atra lopo'bhyāsasya*. The elision of the *s* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.29] *skoḥ saṃyogādyorante ca*. Once *śikṣ* is established, the present tense suffix (*laṭ*) is applied. As for [the root] *śikṣa* in the sense of "acquiring knowledge" (*vidyopādāne*), [it is a different root].
It is recited as such in the *Dhātupāṭha* (605); therefore, because it does not have an indicatory letter *ā*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is indeed established.

[The rule] "the root *nāth* is used in the sense of benediction" applies. "Habitual movement" (*gatitācchīlya*) means habituation to movement; "habituation" (*tācchīlya*) refers to having that as one's natural disposition. For example: "The horses imitate their father," "The cows imitate their mother."
Thus, the meaning is that their nature is to go [to others] as toward a father or as toward a mother. "He resembles the mother;
he resembles the father" means that he imitates the form of the mother and the form of the father. It means he is like the mother and like the father.

*Paitṛkam* means "inherited from the father"; [the suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied by *piturṛtaṣṭhañ* (Pāṇini 4.3.78), and *ka* is substituted by *isusuktāntāt kaḥ* (7.3.51). In the expression *māturanuharati*, neither the sense of a gati-particle nor habitual action (*tācchīlya*) is intended.
Regarding *kirateḥ* and so forth: the root *kṛ* (meaning "to scatter") has "scattering" (*vikṣepa*) as its sole meaning.

Joy and the like are the objects of that [action]. Here, joy is the cause of distraction (*vikṣepa*), and the making of a livelihood and a nest is its result. It is precisely with regard to these meanings that the *ātmanepada* occurs after the root *kṛ* (kirati). As in: "He scatters about" (*apaskirate*). [This is governed by] Pāṇini 6.1.142: "After *apa*, [the suffix -ṭa is added] when referring to quadrupeds and birds, in the sense of scratching."
Regarding "suṭ": [the root] *ṇu* is used in the sense of "praising" (*stutau*), belonging to the second class (*adādi*).
Here, however, it functions with the meaning of "longing" (*utkaṇṭhā*) preceded by sound. Regarding "āpṛcchate": [the root] *pracch*.
The root *jñīps* (Dhātupāṭha 1413) belongs to the Taudādika class; there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) according to Pāṇini 6.1.16.
"Touching the body with speech" is *upalambhana*; it is a specific kind of oath. For instance:

When one makes an oath, saying "I touch the body of Devadatta," the expression *devadatāya śapate* ("he swears at Devadatta") is employed. By the rule *ślāghahnuṅsthāśapām* (Pāṇini 1.4.34) and others, the designation *sampradāna* (recipient) is applied; thus, the fourth case (*caturthī*) is used for the *sampradāna*, resulting in *devadatāya*.

The meaning of "śapati" is "he reviles. Regarding the passage beginning with "samo'kūjane" (Vārttika 34), whatever meaning [the root] *śap* has up to the point of "perceiving," that is included here by the particle *ca*, which serves to aggregate what was not explicitly mentioned; for it is precisely that meaning, as conveyed by the particle *ca*, [that is intended].
This treatise has been composed for the sake of clarification.

22. *sam-ava-pra-vi-bhyaḥ sthaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.22). Regarding the form *saṃtiṣṭhate*: by the rule *pāghrā-dhā-mnā-dṛśya-arti-sarti-śada-sadāṃ-piba-jighra-dhama-pyāya-cchāya-śīya-sīdāḥ* (7.3.78), there is the substitution of *tiṣṭha*.
In the phrase *astiṃ sakāram ātiṣṭhate*, it refers to the verbal root *asti* alone, [ending] in the letter *s*.
The teacher Āpiśali maintains this position. For instance—the *gaṇa*-list does not read "ṭhas bhuvi" as Pāṇini does (*Dhātupāṭha* 1065);
rather, he reads it as "ṭhsa bhuvi. He likewise maintains that "the augment [is applied] when there is *guṇa* or *vṛddhi*. He...
He maintains the two grammatical rules regarding *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*; for this means that he acknowledges them as authoritative.
23. *prakāśanastheyākhyayośca* (1.3.23).

[The word] *stheyaḥ* is derived as "that in which they stand" (*tiṣṭhanty asmin*). By the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (3.3.113), the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of locus (*adhikaraṇe*) according to *aco yat* (3.1.97). By the rule *īdyati* (6.4.65), the *i*-substitution occurs; then the *guṇa* [is applied].

Regarding the word "dispute" (*vivāda*), it refers to a matter of doubt. Regarding the word "decider" (*nirṇetā*), it means one who ascertains, that is to say, one who has become an authoritative source of knowledge (*pramāṇabhūta*). But how does the cognition of that [authority] arise from the word *stheya*, given that the word *stheya* is also used in the sense of a state (*bhāva-sādhana*) and signifies the cessation of movement? To this he says: "of him" (*tasya*).

And so forth. The mention of the term "ākhyā" (name/designation) is for the purpose that there may be a recognition in common usage of that which has the name "stheya. Thus, the mention of "ākhyā" was made to demonstrate that its recognition occurs by means of that mention of "ākhyā. [Example: "The girl stands" (*tiṣṭhate kanyā*).

"From the students" (*chātrebhyaḥ*): since the designation *saṃpradāna* (recipient) applies here as in the previous case, the fourth case ending is used, resulting in *chātrebhyaḥ*. "The meaning is that he reveals himself": among roots that have multiple meanings, the root *sthā* is used here in the sense of revealing. "Having doubted" (*saṃśayya*).
How could one who, having achieved his purpose, still remains in doubt regarding the followers of Kaṇāda not abandon him?
For association with the unrighteous is indeed an obstacle to victory.

This portion of the verse, "the footsteps of calamities that crush," from *Kirātārjunīya* 3.14, has been cited here. Regarding the word *saṃśayya*: having become doubtful concerning the matter that is the subject of dispute, they remain among Karṇa and the others.
Among those such as Karṇa and Śakuni who are regarded as adversaries,
he remains by setting aside their respective positions, because he resorts only to the position demonstrated by them.

24. *udo'nūrdhvakarmaṇi* (Pāṇini 1.3.24). When it is stated that [the suffix *lyap* is used] after [the root *sthā*] when it does not denote an upward action (*anūrdhvakarma*), someone objects: "But surely, since the root *sthā* denotes an intransitive action (*akarmaka-kriyā*), its occurrence in the sense of an object (*karma*) is not possible."
Why, then, is it said "from that which exists in a non-upward action"? In response to that, he says:
"denoting action. To clarify the meaning of what was stated—"from that which exists in a non-upward action"—he says: "from that which denotes action and is qualified by a non-upward action."

"It should be stated that [the suffix] *ṭhuc* occurs after the root *sthā* when it means 'striving' (*īhā*). The meaning is that this form of explanation should be provided: namely, that the *ātmanepada* suffix occurs after the root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *ud*, when it signifies striving, that is, physical movement (*parispandana*). In this regard, the following...

The explanation is as follows: although the inclusion of the term "object" (*karman*) is unnecessary since the root *tiṣṭhati* is established as functioning solely with respect to action (*kriyā*), its inclusion was made for the purpose of indicating that specific action which is well-known in common worldly usage as an "object. And that [action] consists exclusively of physical motion (*parispanda*).
[This refers to] such actions as lifting and moving a jar; for one who performs these is said to be "active" (*sakriya*).
On the other hand, even while performing [actions] such as standing or sitting, which consist of a lack of displacement, one is said to be "inactive" (*niṣkriya*).
Therefore, this ātmanepada [suffix] occurs only in the sense of effort (*īhā*) due to the inclusion of the term "action" (*karman*).

[The substitution of] *ī* occurs from the present [tense] for the future. When it is stated that "the substitution of *ī* occurs in the sense of *īhā* (endeavor)," someone might have the misconception that the mention of *īhā* is an exception (*apavāda*) to upward motion (*ūrdhva-karman*). Therefore, in order to dispel that [misconception], he says: "The mention of *īhā*" and so forth. It is a qualifier.
What is intended here is clarification. This is what is meant:

regarding that which was stated, "it should be said that 'uda' [is used] in the sense of *īhā* (effort)," the mention of *īhā* there is for the purpose of clarifying that it is a qualification specifically of the upward action (*anūrdhva-karman*) included in the sūtra; for in this context, upward action consists of *īhā*.
The meaning is: for the purpose of demonstrating that which is intended to be expressed.

25. *Upāt* [is used] when a mantra is the instrument (*mantrakaraṇe*) (Pāṇini 1.3.25). Regarding the phrase "when a mantra is the instrument": that verbal root whose meaning has a mantra as its most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) is described in that way. Regarding "from *upa*" and so forth: here, the word *vaktavya* means "to be explained."

In this regard, the following is the explanation: the word "ca" (and) is carried over from the subsequent sūtra, and it serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; by virtue of that, the ātmanepada occurs after the root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *upa*, even in the sense of worshipping a deity and so forth.

Regarding the rule "ṭh vā lipsāyām" (Pāṇini 6.1.204): *lipsā* means the desire to obtain (*labdhum icchā*). This meaning—that [the suffix ṭhañ] occurs when the sense of "desire to obtain" is understood—should be known; it does not mean that the suffix is applied to the root *sthā* when it is currently denoting that [desire], for "desire to obtain" is not the primary meaning of the root *sthā*. For instance, [in the case of] a beggar...

In the expression "he approaches the Brahmin family," the verb *tiṣṭhati* signifies approaching (*upasaṃkramaṇa*). Desire (*lipsā*), however, is understood as the cause of that approach. The meaning is: "He approaches the Brahmin family because of [his] desires."

26. *Akarmakācca* (1.3.26). Regarding the term *akarmakāt*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has no object" (*na asya karma asti*). [The root] *ḍukṛñ* (in the sense of "making," DhP 1472);
[the suffix] *manin* is applied according to *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante* (Pāṇini 3.2.75).

There is *guṇa* substitution for the verbal root (*dhātu*), and the suffix *kap* is added by the rule "ṭhśeṣādvibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 5.4.154). Now, one might object: since a verbal root denotes action (*kriyā*), it is impossible for it to be intransitive (*akarmaka*); therefore, the qualification "from an intransitive [root]" is improper because there is nothing to be excluded (*vyavacchedya*). To this, he replies: "denoting an action that lacks an object."

That which is both "without an object" (*akarmikā*) and an "action" (*kriyā*) is an "intransitive action" (*akarmakakriyā*). That which expresses this is an "expression of an intransitive action" (*akarmakakriyāvacana*). By this, he demonstrates that this is a qualifier based on the meaning—that is, by association with that [meaning], it denotes the property of the expressed object belonging to the verbal root's meaning.

By way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), the verbal root (*dhātu*) is considered intransitive (*akarmaka*). And this qualifier is appropriate for the meaning (*artha*), since that [meaning] can be both transitive (*sakarmaka*) and intransitive. Regarding the phrase "as much as has been eaten" (*yāvadbhuktam*): the word *yāvat* is an indeclinable particle (*nipāta*); it forms an avyayībhāva compound with the sense of "according to" (*yathārthe*) in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*).
And this [word] ends in the seventh case; for this very reason he says: "it is present at every meal.
[The suffix] *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), according to the rule "the suffix *kta* is used in the neuter in the sense of an abstract state" (Pāṇini 3.3.114).

27. *udvibhyāṃ tapaḥ* (1.3.27). [The commentary states: "It should be stated that [the ātmanepada occurs] also after *tap* when its object is one's own limb (*svāṅga*). The meaning is that this rule must be explained as having the sense: "the ātmanepada occurs after the root *tap* when its object is a part of one's own body. In this regard, the following...

Explanation: The particle *ca* is carried over from the preceding sūtra; because it has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned, the rule will apply even when the object (*karman*) is one's own limb (*svāṅga*).
Furthermore, "one's own limb" (*svāṅga*) here is not used in its technical (paribhāṣika) sense; rather, it means simply "one's own body part" (*svam aṅgam*).
The meaning is "one's own limb. Regarding the form *niṣṭapati*, the cerebral [ṣ] is substituted [for the dental s] by the rule *niṣastapatāvanāsevane* (Pāṇini 8.3.100).
28. *āṅe yamahanaḥ* | (1.3.28) Regarding *āhate*: the nasal is elided by the rule *anudātopadeśa...* (6.4.37).
Regarding *āghnate*: the penultimate vowel is elided by the rule *gamahana...* (6.4.98), and [the *h* is changed to *gh*] by the rule *ho hanteḥ*.

By [the rule] beginning with (7.3.54), the substitution of *k* occurs. Regarding the statement, "It should be stated that [the suffix *ṇamul* is applied] after a verb whose object is one's own limb (*svāṅga*)," its meaning is the same as before;
the explanation is also exactly as before.

29. *samo gamy-ṛcchi-pracchi-svṛ-arty-ati-śru-vidi-bhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.29). Regarding *saṃsvarate*: the root *svṛ* is listed as "to sound" and "to afflict" (*svṛ śabdopatāpayoḥ*, Dhātupāṭha 932). Regarding *samaranta*:
from the root *ṛ*, [the substitution of *sam* for *sam* is applied] by the rule *sarti-śāsty-artibhyaś-ca* (3.1.56), which follows from the *puṣādi* sūtra.

Because of the continued application of the mention of the *parasmaipada* (active voice), someone might have the misconception that [the substitution] should not occur for the *āṅga* (stem) when *ātmanepada* (middle voice) endings follow; therefore, to dispel that, he says "for in that case," and so forth.
Regarding "saṃśṛṇute": from the root *śru* in the sense of "hearing" (*śravaṇe*, DhP 942), by the rule "śruvaḥ śṛ ca" (Pāṇini 3.1.74).
The suffix *śnu* is applied, and there is the substitution of *śṛ*.
[This refers to] "the inclusion of the non-substituted form of *ṛcch*"—that is, of the root *ṛcch* in the sense of "going, loss of the senses, dissolution, and becoming solid" (Dhātupāṭha 1296).
In the form *smṛcchiṣyate*, the suffix *lṛṭ* is applied, followed by the suffix *syap*. If [it were] the substituted form...

If there were such a grasping [of the root *ṛ*], this would not be established; for by the rule *prādhrādi* (Pāṇini 7.3.72), the substitution of *ṛccha* for *ṛ* is prescribed specifically for the [affix] beginning with *ś*. Now, he asks: why is there no grasping even of that which is substituted for *ṛ*? He says:
"Of that which has the designation *ṭh*, [the term] *ṭh*," and so forth.
Alternatively—if there were a reference to that which lacks the designation (*anādeśa*), the *ātmanepada* would not be established for that which has the designation (*ādeśa*); therefore, he says:
"But for the root *ṛt* [the substitution of *ṛ*] occurs as *ṛt*," and so forth. The intention is that this is by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*).
Regarding "not for the root meaning 'to obtain' (*labh*)," this refers to the root *vidlṛ* in the sense of obtaining (DhP 1432).
Now, why was it not also stated: "but not for the root meaning 'to exist' (*as*), nor for the root meaning 'to investigate' (*vicār*)"? It is thus...
He considers that, because these two roots are invariably ātmanepada, the apprehension of the meaning of the ātmanepada would not even be suspected;
therefore he says, "It should be stated: 'and after dṛśi'. This refers to the root *dṛśir* in the sense of "seeing" (Dhātupāṭha 988).

The meaning is that it must be explained that the *ātmanepada* occurs after the prefix *sam-* when this specific sense is intended. The explanation, however, is the same as before. In the form "saṃpaśyate," the substitution of *paśya-* [for *dṛś-*] occurs by Pāṇini 7.3.78.

30. *nisamupavibhyaḥ hvaḥ* | (1.3.34.30) Regarding the term *hvaḥ*, this is a reference to the root *hveñ* (meaning "to contend" and "to call out") from the Dhātupāṭha (1008), after its vowel has been changed to *ā* and the *ā* of the verbal root has been elided according to Pāṇini 6.4.140 (*āto dhātoḥ*).

Regarding the form *nihvayate*: one might object that since the reference is made to the form containing the vowel *ā* (i.e., *hvā*), the ātmanepada ending should not occur here, for a modification (*vikṛti*) does not include its original base (*prakṛti*), as they are distinct. This is not a fault; for in some cases, even a modification does indeed include its original base. How is this known? Because this [author]...

The mention of *vyeñ*—which has undergone the substitution of *ā* by the rule "ṭhna vyo liṭi" (6.1.46)—instructs that there is a prohibition against the substitution of *ā*. From this it is known that a derivative form (*vikṛti*) also includes the original base (*prakṛti*); otherwise, the base *vyeñ* would not be included by the mention of "vyaḥ."
Of what would this be a prohibition?

[It is a prohibition] of the rule "after a prefix, there is optionally the substitution of *v* for the *s* of √as and √ūh" (Pāṇini 8.3.87). The meaning is that it must be stated [as an exception]. [The roots are] √as in the sense of "throwing" (Dhātupāṭha 1209) and √ūh in the sense of "reflection" (Dhātupāṭha 648); [the form] *asyati* is derived with the suffix *śyan*.

By virtue of the specific mention [in the rule], the root belonging to the *divādi* class is intended to be included, and not the root *as* belonging to the *adādi* class— namely, the one defined as "asa bhuvi" (Dhātupāṭha 1065).

31. *āṅ* [is used] in the sense of rivalry (*spardhā*). (Pāṇini 1.3.31). Regarding the phrase "in the sense of rivalry": here, "rivalry" is intended as the domain of the verbal root's meaning (*dhātvartha*), not of the root itself. Therefore, he says: "Rivalry is competition; it is the desire to overcome another."

Having shown the nature of competition (*spardhā*), he says—"That is the object of the verbal root-meaning"—in order to show the domain of the verbal root-meaning. What, then, is this so-called meaning of the verbal root whose object is thus [defined]?
He says: "The verbal root, however, has 'making sound' as its action," and so forth. "Making sound" (*śabdana*) is *śabda*; that is the action.

That [root] is described as such; that is to say, it denotes the action of calling. Although the root *hvayati* is also listed in the sense of "contending," nevertheless, when preceded by the prefix *ā*, it does not function in that sense.
Just as the root *sthā* is listed in the sense of "cessation of motion," yet when preceded by *pra*, it functions only in the sense of "motion" and not otherwise.
[This occurs] upon the cessation of motion; for when it is said "he is established," the meaning is that he moves.

Therefore, since there is no occurrence of the root *hvayati* (to call) preceded by the prefix *ā-* in the sense of rivalry, rivalry is the object of the root's meaning. That rivalry is the object of the root's meaning should be understood as being by way of its being the cause thereof.
32. *gandhanāvakṣepaṇasevanasāhasikyapratiyatnaprakathanopayogeṣu kṛñaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.32).
[The example] "apakāraprayuktam" is a compound with the third case (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*). It means "with reference to injury" (*apakāram uddiśya*).

Whatever proceeds [in this context] should be understood as being motivated by malice. Regarding the term "of a harmful nature" (*hiṃsātmakam*): one who harms is *hiṃsaḥ*; [this is formed with] the suffix *ac* according to Pāṇini 3.1.134. That whose essence (*ātmā*) is such a harmer is described as *hiṃsātmakam*.
The meaning is "causing pain. Regarding "slander" (*sūcanam*): it is the exposing of faults.
How is it known that such an indication is a "hinting" (gandhana)? He says: "Thus indeed," and so forth.
By the words "the object" (*vastu*) and so on, he shows that the verbal root *gandhayati* functions in the sense of *ardayati* (to afflict).
By the statement "√*arda* is in the sense of injury" (*hiṃsā*), he demonstrates that *ardayati* consists of the nature of injury. And thus...

By showing that the root *gandhayati* has the same meaning as *ardayati*, which signifies "harming," it is demonstrated that the meaning expressed by the word *gandhana* is essentially of the nature of violence (*hiṃsā*). "Threatening" (*bhartsanam*) means contemptuous treatment (*tiraskaraṇam*). "Following" (*anuvṛttiḥ*) means the discernment of another's intention. "Boldness" (*sāhasikyam*) means rashness (*sāhasam*).
Regarding the word "karma": by the rule *ojaḥ saho'mbhasā vartate* (Pāṇini 4.4.27), the suffix *ṭhak* is applied, resulting in *sāhasikaḥ*.

Its action (*tasya karma*) is [denoted] by the suffix *ṣyañ*, because it belongs to the class beginning with *guṇavacana* and *brāhmaṇa* (Pāṇini 5.1.124), thus forming *sāhasikyam*. Regarding the phrase "application" (*upayoga*): it is the utilization (*viniyoga*) for the purpose of dharma and so forth.

One for whom there is a purpose (*prayojana*) regarding dharma and so forth is described as such. The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is used to include desire (*kāma*). [As in the example: "The fuel improves the water. The augment *suṭ* is applied by the rule "after the prefix *upa*, [it is added] in the sense of improvement, transformation, and ellipsis of a sentence" (Pāṇini 6.1.139). [This applies to the root] *kṛ*.
The genitive case [is used] by [the rule] "pratiyatne" (Pāṇini 2.3.53).

33. *adheḥ prahasane* (Pāṇini 1.3.33). [The example is] *tam adhitaṣṭhe*. This is the root *kṛ* with the suffix *liṭ*, and for that, the substitute *aiś* is applied. Due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* by the rule *dvirvacane 'ci* (1.1.59), there is reduplication; then, by the rule *urat* (7.4.66), the substitution of *u* occurs.

There is also the substitution of *ra* for *la* (*raparatva*), the retention of the first consonant when followed by *ṭh* or *hal* (*ṭhhalādiḥ śeṣaḥ*, 7.4.60), and the substitution of *c* or *u* for *k* or *h* (*kuhoścuḥ*, 7.4.62).

34. *veḥ śabdakarmaṇaḥ* | (1.3.34) In rules such as *kartari karmaṇi* (1.3.14), the word *karman* is sometimes observed to denote an action (*kriyā*). To ensure that it is not understood here in that same sense [of denoting an action], he says:

"The word *karman* here denotes the *kāraka* (grammatical participant). Now, why does it not denote the action (*kriyā*)? Because the root *kṛ*, preceded by the prefix *vi*, cannot function in the sense of the action of producing sound. [The phrase] "of that which has sound as its *karman*" refers to this [rule] by way of the meaning of the verbal root.

The qualification is: "sound is its object" (śabdaḥ karma asya). Thus, the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) has sound as its object. Since that meaning has sound as its object, the verbal root itself is also said to have sound as its object by way of that [meaning]. Otherwise, since a verbal root expresses an action (kriyā), how could the connection "sound is its object" be logically established?
35. *Akarmakācca* (Pāṇini 2.3.35).

[The examples] "ṭhodanasya pūrṇāḥ" ("full of rice")—as stated in the *Kāśikā* and the *Padamañjarī*—and "paripūrṇāḥ" ("completely full") [are given]. When used in connection with words having the sense of *suhita* ("satisfied"), the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is employed, according to the rule *pūraṇaguṇasuhitārtha-* (Pāṇini 2.2.11).

By this and other such prohibitions against the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), it is made known that the genitive case occurs in connection with words having the sense of *suhita* (being satisfied). Words having the sense of *suhita* mean words having the sense of satisfaction (*tṛpti*); the meaning is "full" or "satisfied."
36. *niya* [is used] in the senses of honoring, lifting up, acting as a teacher, knowing, wages, counting, and expenditure.
(1.3.36) [The commentary says:
"When honoring and the others are the qualifiers. What, then, is qualified here?

Is "leading" (*nayati*) the qualifier because it is by means of this [action] that one leads? Or rather, is "leading" itself the qualifier, on the grounds that it is distinguished—that is, set apart—from other meanings?
In that regard, "honoring," "acting as a teacher," and "wages" are included under the very same meaning as the preceding [root].

The qualifiers [are as follows]: whereas the remaining [words] have the nature of the root meaning *nī* (to lead), they function as qualifiers by means of the second [factor]. In the expression "the Cārvī leads the Lokāyata," here the meaning of *nayati* is "leading" (*prāpaṇa*), which is the qualificand;
however, the honoring of the disciples is its qualifier by way of being its fruit.

"Because of that connection, the teacher is also called 'Cārvī'. Just as when it is said, "Do not let the spears enter," the word 'spear' (kunța) applies to the men as well due to their connection with the spears, so too here the word 'Cārvī' applies to the teacher because of his connection with Cārvī. [The phrase] "having made firm" means:
The meaning is "having made them motionless. Their motionlessness, however, consists in their being directed toward no other purpose.

Regarding the phrase "being established": it refers to the correct comprehension of the categories of existence (*padārtha*) within the Lokāyata treatise. Regarding the phrase "they become honored": for them, honor consists precisely in the accomplishment of their desired objects.
The intended meaning, however, is that in the Lokāyata treatise there is a correct understanding of categories (padārtha);

[the word "uddeśa"] means "it casts up. By this, he shows that *upasañjanam* (the act of bringing near) is the meaning of the root *nī*, and not a qualifier of it. The same applies to such expressions as "it determines" (*niścinoti*).
It should be understood that [the teacher] leads knowledge and the other qualities to their respective objects as far as possible, thereby demonstrating them.

Regarding the phrase "by such [a method]," the meaning is: by whatever procedure is prescribed in the treatise (śāstra). Here too, the act of making someone a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa*) is a qualification of the object "leading" precisely by way of its result.

Regarding the phrase "he brings laborers near" (*karmakarān upanayate*): here, "wages" (*bhṛti*) is a qualifier of the act of bringing near (*samīpakaraṇa*), which constitutes the meaning of the root *nī*, by way of being its cause. Regarding the phrase "of debt, etc. (*ṛṇādeḥ*): by the word "etc.
(*ādi*), there is the inclusion of taxes (*kara*), tolls (*śulka*), fines (*daṇḍa*), and so forth. A "tax" (*kara*) is a portion to be taken from cultivators by the king.
It was devised for the sake of protection. Regarding the phrase "in regard to dharma and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes desire and the like as well.

37. *kartṛsthe cāśarīre karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 1.3.37). Regarding the rule *nayateḥ kartā*, it should be understood that the relationship is mediated by the meaning [of the word]. As for the statement *tadekadeśo 'pi śarīram*, words that apply to wholes [may also] apply to parts thereof. For words are indeed applied to collections [of parts].

The sense is that [the terms] are used even for parts [of the whole]. But how, when the primary meaning exists, is the inclusion of the secondary meaning obtained? From the use of the word "body" (śarīra). For here, although it would have been sufficient to use the word "frame" (kāya) because of its brevity, he uses the word "body" (śarīra).

This is for the purpose of designating even a single part of that body by the name "body" through the use of the term *śarīra*. In the expression "he restrains anger," the agent of the verb *nayati* (restrains) is indeed Devadatta or another person, whose nature consists of the aggregate of the intellect, the sense organs, and the body; it is precisely therein that the object, anger, resides.

In the case of [the verb] *vartate* ("he exists"), the object (*karman*) resides in the agent (*kartṛstha*) and is bodiless (*aśarīra*). Likewise, in examples such as *gaḍuṃ vinayati* ("he cures the goitre"), it should be understood that the objects—the goitre and so forth—are parts of the body and thus lack the status of residing in the agent. Furthermore, in this context, the result of the action, namely the removal of anger and the like, is intended solely for the benefit of the agent (*kartrabhiprāya*).

Since this is already established by the rule *svaritañitaḥ kartrabhiprāye* (1.3.72), this statement should be understood as a restrictive rule (*niyama*): [the ātmanepada occurs] only when the object resides in the agent and is not part of his body,
and not otherwise.
38. *vṛti-sarga-tāyaneṣu kramaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.38).
Since the rule for the *parasmaipada* endings would otherwise apply to the root *kram-* by virtue of its being included in the *śeṣa* category, the *ātmanepada* ending is here prescribed.
The meanings "encircling" (*vṛti*) and so forth are well-known in the senses of non-obstruction, enthusiasm, and expansion.

39. [The prefix *upa* is used with the verb *parā*] when it means "to pass over" (*upaparābhyām*, Pāṇini 1.3.39). In the form "saṃkramati," the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule "kramaḥ parasmaipadeṣu" (Pāṇini 7.3.76).
40. [The prefix *āṅ* is used with the verb *kram*] when it means "to rise up" (*āṅ udgamane*, Pāṇini 1.3.40).
"The young boy ascends the water-skin (*kutapa*). The meaning is that he presses against it.

Regarding the rule "it should be stated [that the ātmanepada occurs] when there is the rising of luminaries": the ātmanepada occurs only when there is the rising of luminaries, such as planets, constellations, and so forth.
The meaning is that the form *bhavati* must be explained in this sense. Here is the explanation:

the word *vā* ("or") from the rule *anupasargādvā* (Pāṇini 1.3.43) is understood here by way of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*) maxim; furthermore, that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore—
The rising of light will occur only there, and not elsewhere. If, then, the word "or" (vā) is carried over [from the previous rule], would it not be carried over for both rules?
There is no fault, as it will not be carried over according to the maxim of the frog's leap (maṇḍūkaplutinyāya).
41. *vi* in the sense of "stepping with the feet" (Pāṇini 1.3.41). As in:
"He whose joints do not give way (*vikrāmati*) strides forward. It means to split asunder; that is, it breaks into two parts.
42. [The root *kram* takes the *ātmanepada* endings] after the prefixes *pra* and *upa*, when they are semantically connected [to the action].
(1.3.42) For example: *prakramate*, *upakramate*. The meaning is "he begins. 43.
Or [it takes the *ātmanepada* endings] optionally when no prefix is present. (1.3.43)
"This is a *vibhāṣā* [optional rule] regarding what has not been previously established," because the *nivṛtti* (cessation) of the *vṛt* and other roots applies.
44. *apahvave jñaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.44).
Regarding the example "he denies a hundred" (*śatamapajānīte*), there is the substitution of *jā* for the roots *jñā* and *jan* according to *jñājanorjā* (7.3.79), and the suffix *śnā*.
As before, there is the substitution of *i* by [Pāṇini 6.4.113] *ṭhī halaghoḥ*.

45. *Akarmakācca* (Pāṇini 1.3.45). [The question] "How can this [verb] be intransitive? is raised. The intention is as follows: ghee (*sarpiḥ*) and so forth are intended to be expressed as the object (*karman*) in the sense of being that which is to be known; therefore, the meaning is that this [verb] is indeed transitive (*sakarmaka*) by virtue of that object.

"How? means "in no way whatsoever. With the words "And thus," etc., he provides the reasoning for the point that here *sarpiḥ* (clarified butter) and so forth are not intended as the object (*karman*), but rather as the instrument (*karaṇa*)—namely, "by means of *sarpiḥ*," etc. [This refers to] one who has an attachment to *sarpiḥ*, without which...

There is no desire for the act of eating itself; rather, with respect to his engagement in eating, ghee becomes the means (*upāya*). Thus, by that means, he proceeds. [Question: Why is it stated "after an intransitive verb" (*akarmakāt*)? [Answer: Here, ghee and so forth are not intended to be expressed as the object of cognition (*jñeyatvena*).

What then? By stating "as an instrument" (*karaṇatvena*), the author of the Vṛtti implies that the ātmanepada occurs after a root that possesses an instrument when that instrument is directly expressed by the word [in the sentence]. And thus, it should have been stated simply as "after one possessing an instrument" (*sakaraṇāt*); what is the purpose of including the mention of "intransitive" (*akarmaka*)? This is the sense.
To show that [the suffix *kyaṅ*] may occur even after a transitive verb when it is connected with an instrument, he says:
"He recognizes the son by his voice."
46. *saṃpratibhyāmanādhyāne* (1.3.46).

Regarding the phrase "longing remembrance" (*utkaṇṭhāsmaraṇam*), this means remembrance preceded by longing. Regarding the word "of the mother" (*mātuḥ*), the genitive case is used according to Pāṇini 2.3.52: *adhīgarthadayeśāṃ karmaṇi* ("the genitive is used for the object of verbs meaning 'to remember,' 'to grieve,' and *īś*").

47. *Vada* [is used] in the senses of speaking (*bhāsana*), conversing (*upasaṃbhāṣā*), knowing (*jñāna*), effort (*yatna*), disagreement (*vimati*), and inviting (*upamantraṇa*). (1.3.47) [The Kāśikā and Padamañjarī state:
"When *bhāsana* and so forth are the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). Here too, what exactly is being qualified?

Is "vadati" (he speaks) the qualifier because it denotes the meaning by means of this [word], or is it rather the meaning itself that is denoted? For a qualifier is so called because it distinguishes—that is, delimits—[the object] from other meanings.
In this context, *upasambhāṣā* (addressing), *upalālana* (consoling), and *upamantraṇa* (inviting) constitute the meaning of "vadati" itself through its second sense.

This is the qualifier. However, the remaining terms, such as *bhāsana* (shining) and so forth, are qualifiers by means of the first sense [of the root]. By the phrase "the shining of 'māna'," etc., he shows that the shining is a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root (*vadati*) either by way of being its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) or by way of being its cause (*hetu*). For it is thus in this case:

In the word *bhāsamāna*, the suffix *śānac* is prescribed by the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.126). By the phrase *jānāti* and so forth, he shows that knowledge is a qualifier of the act of speaking (*vadati*) through the relation of being its object (*viṣayibhāvena*). For by means of knowledge, one speaks.

He knows. Here, by whatever cognition one speaks, that [cognition] becomes the object (*viṣayībhavati*) of that very [act of speaking] through its being the cause of the meaning of the act of speaking, by means of that same object which is to be determined (*paricchedya*). By the phrase "having that as its object" (*tadviṣayam*), etc., [it is shown] where there is the manifestation of the meaning of the act of speaking.

He explains that the qualification is by way of being the cause (*hetubhāva*). For enthusiasm (*utsāha*), when it is manifested, becomes the means (*sādhana*) known as the object (*karman*) of the act of manifestation; and a means is a cause (*hetu*), because factors of action (*kāraka*) are the causes of an activity. This is shown by the passage beginning with "those who have fallen into disagreement" (*vimatipatitāḥ*).
He shows that "doubt" (*vimati*) is a qualification [of speech] by way of being the cause of the meaning of what is spoken.

When doubt exists, people speak in various ways (*vicitram*), that is, in many different manners. For if their understanding were undifferentiated, they would speak in an undifferentiated manner. Regarding the phrase "he entices" (*upacchandayati*): "O auspicious lady, serve me; this..."
The meaning is that [the scripture] impels one toward the desired object by means of such statements as "I shall give those to you."

*varatanu saṃpravadanti kukkuṭāḥ, payo vijahīhi*.

Even when a single hen crows, it is said "the hens are crowing" because of the determination of the specific class (*viśeṣaparicchedāt*).

In the word *varatanu*, the vowel of the word *tanū* is shortened by the rule *ṭhambārthanadyorhrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.63). Due to the force of the singular number of the short vowel, the guna substitution prescribed by *ṭhhrasvasya guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.108) does not take place.
It occurs among men; the word "of men" was not used [in the verse] for the sake of variety.

49. *anor akarmakāt* (Pāṇini 1.3.49). [The example is] *anu vadati*. Here, the word *anu* functions in the sense of *punar* (again). Thus, the meaning is "he speaks again. In this case, the root becomes transitive (*sakarmaka*) by virtue of the object being the *yajus* (sacrificial formula).

50. *vibhāṣā vipralāpe* (1.3.50). Regarding the phrase "consisting of *vipralāpa*": *vipralāpa* is contradictory speech characterized by mutual contradiction; that whose essence or nature (*ātmā*, *svabhāva*) is such is described as "consisting of *vipralāpa*. [The commentary states: "This is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*)."
This is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *ṭhvyaktavācāṃ samuccāraṇe* (1.3.48).
[as in] *avagirate*. By the rule *ṛta id dhātoḥ* (6.4.100), there is the substitution of *i* for the *ṛ*, and the substitution of *r* as the subsequent element (*raparatva*).
52. *samaḥ pratijñāne* (1.3.52). 53.

*udaścaraḥ sakarmakāt* (1.3.53). [Examples: "He promises to give the house" (*geham uccarati*). Here, the root *car-* has the sense of "going. [Also: "He utters the teacher's word" (*guruvacanam uccarati*).

In this context, the root *car* (to move), being transitive by virtue of its action consisting of an upward departure (*utkramaṇa*), becomes intransitive through the word of the Guru [Pāṇini] when it signifies "he goes out" (*uccarati*) as in "he emits vapor. The meaning here is "he goes upwards"; since no object is intended to be expressed, it is intransitive.
54. *sam* [is used] when joined with an instrumental case-ending.

(1.3.54) If "instrumental" (*tṛtīyā*) is understood here, then it would also apply in this instance: *ubhau lokau sañcarati imāṃ cāmuṃ ca devale* ("He wanders through both worlds, this one and that one, O Devala"). Here too, the sense of the instrumental is indeed understood: [he wanders] by means of austerity (*tapasā*) and sacred learning (*śrutena*).
Having considered that [the third case] indeed exists, he says: "The third [case].
[This means] "the third case-ending (vibhakti) is understood. If this is so, then a connection between the root (dhātu) and that [third case] is not tenable;
for the third case is not denoted by the root. To this he says: "By that," and so forth. The meaning...

That which has a door as its mouth or means is described as such. By using the third case (instrumental) sense, he shows that the connection with the root meaning is metaphorical, since the connection with the third case sense of the root is possible here even without an actual instrument (*karaṇa*).
Thus it is said: "Even though here a connection with that sense is possible. Without an instrument.

Because there is an absence of the completion of the action, even so, it does not occur. Regarding the passage beginning with "But in the third [case]," etc.: the inclusion of the phrase "joined with the third case" (tṛtīyāyukta) is indeed for this purpose—that it should apply when the word is actually joined with the third case; otherwise, one would have to say simply "with *sama*. Even if it were not stated...

The use of the instrumental case is established by its very nature; for without it, the accomplishment of the action is not possible. Therefore, wherever the instrumental is heard, that is the primary example (*mūlodāharaṇa*);
but wherever it is not heard, that is the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*).
55. *dāṇaśca sā ceccaturthyarthe* (1.3.55).

How, then, could the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) have the sense of the fourth case-ending (*caturthyarthe*)? The meaning is: "Not in any way. The intention is that there is no grammatical rule (*śāstra*) prescribing such a thing. [The author of the Vārttika says: "This very point must be stated."

The meaning is that it must be explained. Here is the explanation: when that very same recipient (*sampradāna*) is intended to be expressed as the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*), then even though the fourth case (*caturthī*) would [normally] apply, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) occurs due to the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).

This is on the grounds that [words] become grammatical factors (kārakas), but not because they possess an intrinsic nature (svabhāva). Furthermore, that intention (vivakṣā) relies upon worldly usage, not technical (prauḍhika) usage. And in the world, it occurs only in the linguistic practice of the unrefined (aśiṣṭa), and nowhere else. Thus, it is the worldly intention that is relied upon here.

The word *cet* is employed to illuminate this very meaning: "he asks for a garland from a maidservant. For when one gives a garland to a maidservant who is contrary to the Dharmaśāstras in order to desire her, that constitutes improper conduct (*aśiṣṭavyavahāra*) on his part; thus, there is indeed improper conduct here. [The root] *sam-pra-dā* is used.

Thus, by the rule *pāghrādisūtra* (Pāṇini 7.3.78), there is the substitution of *yaccha* for *dāṇ*. How then can the ātmanepada [suffix] occur? The meaning is: "not in any way. This is because, in the rule *tasmādityuttarasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.67), the mention of the term *nirdiṣṭa* serves the purpose of indicating immediate succession (*ānantarya*). He thinks as follows: "In the case of *sama*..."

"Regarding the genitive [case] in the rule *viśeṣaṇe ṣaṣṭhī*," and so forth: if *samaḥ* were a fifth case (ablative) rather than a sixth case (genitive), then because of the intervention by the word *pra*, the ātmanepada suffix would not occur; therefore, this is not a fifth case, but rather a sixth case—meaning that which is related to the qualifier *samaḥ* is the qualified [word], namely *dāṇ*.

And thus, even when separated by an intervening element, the relationship of qualifier and qualified (viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva) occurs; therefore, despite that intervention, the ātmanepada suffix is applied.
56. *Upādāmaḥ* in the sense of taking for oneself (*svakaraṇe*).

(1.3.56) To refute the objection that if the *ātmanepada* were applied merely in the sense of "taking for oneself," it would also apply to the acceptance of goods such as vegetables (*śākaṭaka*), he says: "the grasping of the hand" (*pāṇigrahaṇa*), and so forth. Thus...

He thinks: "The powers of words are indeed restricted to specific objects, because the root *yami* preceded by *upa* is exclusively used in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in this specific sense of acceptance, and not in every sense.
Therefore, only acceptance consisting of taking the hand is understood here. Thus [he says], "they marry" (*upayacchante*).
As before, there is the substitution of *cha*.
57. *jñā-śru-smṛ-dṛśāṃ sanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.57).

[This refers to] "by three rules," namely *apahnave jñaḥ* (1.3.44) and so forth. In the example *dharmaṃ jijñāsate*, the root *jñā* (meaning "to understand," Dhātupāṭha 1507) takes the suffix *san*; there is reduplication.
The shortening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) occurs by *Pāṇini* 7.4.59, and the substitution of *i* for *a* occurs by *Pāṇini* 7.4.79 (*sanyataḥ*). Thus we have *śuśrūṣate*.

Regarding *śru* in the sense of "hearing" (*dhātupāṭha* 942): the suffix *san* is marked as *kit* by *Pāṇini* 1.2.9 (*iko jhal*), the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* applies by *Pāṇini* 7.2.11 (*śrayukaḥ kiti*), and [the doubling of the consonant] applies by *Pāṇini* 6.4.16 (*ajjhanagamāṃ sani*).
Thus [the form] *dīrghaḥ* [is derived]. Regarding *susmūrṣate*: the root *smṛ* is used in the sense of "thinking" (*ādhyāne*;

DhP 807). As before, because of the *kit* designation, there is the substitution of *u* by *udoṣṭhaḷpūrvasya* (7.1.102), followed by the replacement of *u* with *r*. Regarding *didṛkṣate*: there is *kit* designation by *halantācca* (1.2.10), and consequently—
The substitution of *ṣ* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.36] *vraścādinā*, and the substitution of *k* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.41] *ṭhṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si*.

58. *nāno jñaḥ* | (1.3.58) [The word] "by the preceding" means that the *yat* [suffix] obtained by the immediately preceding rule is prohibited—on the grounds of the maxim: "A rule or a prohibition applies to what is nearest" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 19). And so it is.

And so forth. Since the *ātmanepada* ending *eyat* would apply by the immediately preceding sūtra, this [present rule] serves as its prohibition. This being the case, this prohibition applies only to transitive (*sakarmaka*) verbs;
for the immediately preceding sūtra prescribes the *ātmanepada* after transitive roots, whereas [the prohibition does not apply] to intransitive (*akarmaka*) ones.
Since the ātmanepada has already been prescribed by the rule *ṭhakarmakācca* (1.3.45), the immediately preceding rule is understood to apply to roots that have an object (*sakarmaka*);
and because this is so, the ātmanepada [for the causative] follows from the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* (1.3.62) when the root is intransitive (*akarmaka*).
It is indeed so: "desiring to know [the nature of] the herb."

59. *pratyāṅbhyāṃ śruvaḥ* (1.3.59). [The commentary states: "And this is a mention of a prefix (*upasarga*). How so? Regarding the word *śruvaḥ*, the genitive case is used in a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*). By that, the following connection is established:

The *ātmanepada* affix does not occur after a root ending in *śru* preceded by *prati* and *āṅ* when these function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) due to their connection with it; rather, because they qualify the root *śru* by means of the sense conveyed through the prefixes (*upasarga*),
the term "prefixes" (*upasarga*) is understood by implication.

In the expression "he waits upon Devadatta" (*devadattaṃ prati śuśrūṣate*), the word *prati* receives the designation of *karmapravacanīya* by the rule "in the sense of indication (*lakṣaṇa*), in the sense of 'having become such' (*ityambhūtākhyāna*), etc. (Pāṇini 1.4.90). Consequently, *prati* is connected only with Devadatta, and not with the meaning of the verbal root.

60. *śadeḥ śitaḥ* | (1.3.60) If this is explained by accepting that these two ablative cases in "after the root *śad*, when followed by a suffix marked with *ś*" (*śadeḥ śitaḥ*) are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*), such that it means "the ātmanepada occurs after that *śit* which follows *śad*," then...

Because it is based on a *sārvadhātuka* [affix], before the production of that [affix], the root remains as the remainder; therefore, in the state of *l* [the suffix], the *parasmaipada* would occur. Consequently, intending to explain that which is caused by that, he says:
"The *śit* of *śad*" (*śadiryaḥ śit*). By this, these two [words] are in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) in the rule "after *śad*, when a *śit* [follows]."

He shows that [the two forms] are in the fifth case (pañcamī). But how can *śad* become *śit*, given that the letter *ś* belonging to the *vikaraṇa* is designated as an *it*, and not the *śad* itself? To this he says:
"that which is to become *śad*" (*śadbhāvī*). This word *bhāvin* is used according to Pāṇini 3.3.3: *bhaviṣyati gamyādayaḥ*.
It has the future time as its object. "That which will have *śit*" means that which will come to possess *śit* is "that which will have *śit*.
This is what is meant: because it is caused by *śit*, the term *śit* is used metaphorically for *śadi*.
For such a designation occurs through the metaphorical application of the effect to the cause.

For example: "naḍvalodakaṃ pakādarogaḥ" (the water of a reed-thicket is a disease for the *pakva* plant), or "śito vā sambandhī" (or [the term] *śit* is related [to the root]). By this, he shows that *śitaḥ* is in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*). What is the relationship of *śit* to the root *śad*? That which is its original form (*prakṛti*). Even prior to the suffix *śit*, the status of being its original form certainly exists.
The ātmanepada occurs after the root *śad* when it has the sense of "falling. As in "śīyate," the substitution of *śī* is applied by the rule *pāghrādhmādheṭdṛśaḥ śaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.78).

61. *mriyater luṅliṅoś ca* (Pāṇini 1.3.61). [The commentary states: "This statement is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). That is to say, it is so that the *śit* [suffixes] alone may follow the root *mriyati* in the *luṅ* and *liṅ* tenses.
If this is the case, what is the purpose of including the mention of *ṅt*? For [otherwise], in other instances, the *ātmanepada* would [already apply].
