Is it not to be so? It is said: it is taught for the sake of the accent. For in the case of *mā hi mṛta*, the suffix *luṅ* is introduced;

then, by the rule "the *sārvadhātuka* [suffix] following an unaccented [root] with an indicatory letter *ṅ* or *d* is unaccented" (6.1.186), once the unaccented nature is applied, the root retains its final acute accent (*antodātatva*). [This is further governed by] "a finite verb (*tiṅ*) is unaccented after another finite verb" (8.1.28).

Thus, the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) is prohibited here by the rule *ṭhhi ca* (Pāṇini 8.1.34). The augment *aṭ* is also prohibited by the rule *ṭhna māṅyoge* (6.4.74). In the form *amṛta*, there is the elision of *sic* by the rule *ṭhhrasvādṅat* (8.2.27). In the form *mṛṣīṣṭa*, it is the *liṅ* (optative) in the sense of benediction (*āśis*), according to the rule *ṭhliṅaśiṣi*.

(3.4.116) Because it is *ārdhadhātuka*, there is an absence of the *vikaraṇa* suffix; by "ṭhsuṭ tithoḥ" (6.4.107), *suṭ* is added; by "vali" (6.1.66), there is the elision (*yalopa*) of *ya*. Regarding "mriyate": because it belongs to the *tudādigaṇa*, the suffix *śa* is applied; by "ṛṅ śayagliṅkṣu" (7.4.28), *riṅ* is substituted [for the root vowel]; and by "aci śnudhātu" (6.4.77).
By this rule (*ityādinā*), *iyan* [is substituted]; [in the form] "mariṣyati," the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule "ṛddhanoḥ sye" (Pāṇini 7.2.70).
62. *pūrvavat sanaḥ* (1.3.62). Regarding *pūrvavat*: the suffix *vati* is applied by the rule *tena tulyaṃ kriyā cedvatiḥ* (5.1.115).
Because the word *pūrva* is a relative term (*sambandhiśabda*), it requires a limit (*avadhi*). And that limit—
He says, "Because it is heard [in scripture], that which is preceded by *san* is indeed understood to exist"—namely, "the root (*dhātu*) which is preceded by *san*.

If this is so, since the inclusion [of the root] is useful only for the purpose of establishing a limit (*avadhi*), then the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would apply to a root ending in *san*; however, that is not obtained there. From what, then, would it arise?

This cannot be [the case] based on the mere verbal root (*dhātu*); for if it were so, the sequential listing of the *ātmanepada* and *parasmaipada* endings would be purposeless. If, on the other hand, it were [based on] that which ends in an affix (*pratyaya*), even then the mention of "saṅ" (the suffix) would be purposeless; rather, it should have been stated as "from the preceding affix" (*pratyayāt*).

It may be so. Therefore, having abandoned the suffix *san*, which is closely proximate [to the root], it is not proper—not logical—to postulate another suffix that has not been heard [in the rule]; thus it is understood that [the suffix] occurs from *san* itself. By the words "by which" (*yena*) and so forth, he explains the sense of the suffix *-vat*. "That very thing is the cause" (*tadeva nimittam*).

The status of having an *anudātta* vowel and the suffix *ṅt* remain causes [for doubling] even when the root is in a different state, because of the force of the statement regarding the causative (*sannanta*). For example: *ṭhasisiṣate*. Once *iṭ* has been applied, by the rule "of the second [syllable] beginning with a vowel" (*ajāder dvitīyasya*, 6.1.2), there is reduplication of the syllable *si*. Also: *nivivikṣate*.

Thus: from the root *viś* (DhP 1424) meaning "to enter," as before, there is the application of *kit*-tva, *ṣatva*, and *katva*. Regarding the form *ācikraṃsate*: because it is occasioned by the *ātmanepada* endings, the augment *iṇ* does not occur, in accordance with the rule *snukramoranātmanepadanimite* (Pāṇini 7.2.36).

Regarding the forms *ṭhśiśatsati* and *mumūrṣati*: here, the first part [of the suffix *saN*] has the status of being a cause for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), because we observe the middle endings in *śīyate* and *mriyate*.
Consequently, someone might have the misconception that the middle voice must necessarily occur [here]; therefore, [the author] addresses that...

In order to refute [this], he says: "it does not exist," and so forth. He asks, "What is the reason? and replies: "For not," and so forth. What then? "Even that which is marked by *śit* (*śidādyapi*). Here, by the word *śit*, both the state of being produced by a *śit* suffix and the relationship with a *śit* suffix are expressed. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the *luṅ* and *liṅ* [suffixes] are included; and that [is what is meant] here.
"It does not exist" (*nāsti*): for here, the preceding portion of the suffix *san* possesses neither the state of being preceded by a *śit* [augment] nor a connection with a *śit* [augment];
because in this context, a *śit*-marked suffix is absolutely impossible, nor do the *luṅ* or *liṅ* [suffixes] occur after the root *mriyate*; therefore, it is not the case here.
Since *śad* and *mriyati* possess the status of being causes for the *ātmanepada*, the *ātmanepada* ending does not occur [in their case].
But then, why does it not occur here—[as in] *anucikīrṣati* and *parācikīrṣati*? For the *ātmanepada* is prescribed for the root *kṛ* when it has meanings such as "hinting" (*gandhana*) and so forth.

Therefore, he states "of that which... and so forth, to show that even from a desiderative form (*sananta*), [the *ātmanepada*] must occur when that [desiderative sense] is not intended to be expressed;

for in the case of meanings such as "hinting" (*gandhana*) and so on, since the *parasmaipada* was prescribed by the rule "after *anu* and *parā*, from *kṛ*" (Pāṇini 1.3.79) in the preceding state of being non-desiderative.

The absence of the ātmanepada for the root *kṛ* is established; therefore, because these two [roots] lack the conditions for the ātmanepada even when followed by a desiderative suffix (*san*), the ātmanepada does not occur.
[Objection: But how is it that the ātmanepada occurs in cases such as *jugupsate* and *mīmāṃsate*, given that...

It is stated [in Pāṇini 1.3.62] that "the *sana* suffix is like the preceding," yet in the case of roots such as *gup*, the *ātmanepada* endings do not occur before the *sana* suffix. Therefore, since there is no extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule "like the preceding," one might think that the *ātmanepada* endings should not occur here; to this he says: "In this case," etc., namely, "he feels disgust" (*jugupsate*).

The suffix *san* is applied by the rule "guptijkidbhyaḥ san" (Pāṇini 3.1.5). Thus [we have] "mīmāṃsate. The suffix *san* is applied by the rule "mānbadha... (Pāṇini 3.1.6) et cetera; and because of the rule "sanyataḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.79), there is lengthening of the vowel of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) after it has undergone *it*-vocalization.
But how can there be the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) here by the rule "anudātaṅti ātmanepadam" (Pāṇini 1.3.12), given that...

The fact that the low-pitched accent (*anudāteta*) applies to the root *gup* and others as individual components (*avayava*), and not to *jugups* and others as composite wholes (*samudāya*), is the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Therefore, he says: "That which is applied to a component," and so forth. Just as a characteristic mark applied to a component such as the ear of a cow serves to distinguish the whole, so too [is it] with respect to the component *gup* and others.
The designation of the udātta accent has been applied to the entire complex [of the root] in cases such as *jugupsa* and others for the sake of distinction.
If this is so, then it would follow that it should also apply in cases such as *gopayati*, *tejayati*, and *saṅketayati*;
this is true. It might be argued: "The indicative mark (*liṅga*) was applied to a part of it..."
A suffix ending in *san* qualifies the whole (*samudāya*), for that particular member [the root] does not deviate from the whole;
however, a suffix ending in *ṇic* does deviate from it, and therefore the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) should not occur here. This objection is invalid.
Since even that which is constant may deviate— as in "gopayati" and so forth, where the action occurs even without that [suffix]—
it follows that there is no such thing as a complete aggregate (*samudāya*) that the root *gup* and others never deviate from. Therefore, because such an aggregate is impossible,
the fact that the low-pitched (*anudātta*) accent is applied to every individual part of the root *gup* and others serves as the indicator (*liṅga*) for the whole aggregate.

It will be a distinguishing feature (*viśeṣaka*). Consequently, the *ātmanepada* affix would also result after roots such as *gup* and others. If that is so, then in the rule *nigaraṇacalanārthebhyaśca* (Pāṇini 1.3.87), the word *ca* ("and") is employed for the purpose of including what has not been mentioned; by this, [the *ātmanepada* applies] to the causative forms (*ṇyantebhyaḥ*) of *gup* and the other roots.
An exception to the rules for the *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* endings will now follow.

63. *Āmpratyayavat kṛño 'nuprayogasya* (Pāṇini 1.3.63). Regarding the phrase *āmpratyayavat*: the suffix *vati* is applied here after a word in the genitive case, according to Pāṇini 5.1.116 (*tatra tasyeva*).
In the phrase *kṛño 'nuprayogasya*, both genitives are in apposition. [Example: *īkṣāñcakre*.

And so forth. [The roots] *īkṣ* "to see" (DhP 6.10), *īh* "exertion" (DhP 6.32), and *ūh* "reflection" (DhP 6.48) take the *liṭ* suffix. By the rule *ijādeḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.36) and others, and by the rule *āmaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.81), there is elision (*luk*) of the *liṭ*. Since it is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the case-ending *su* is obtained. *Suḥ*.

Because it belongs to the *svarādi* group, it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), and thus there is elision of the case-ending (*subluk*). By the rule *kṛñ ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.40), there is the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of the root *kṛ* following the perfect tense (*liṭ*). By stating that "this commencement is for the sake of [an action] not intended for the agent," it is implied that this is for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*). In that regard, within this injunctive sense, whatever...
He states "if," etc., in order to point out that fault: "he made [them] straight" (*udbajāñcakāra*).

[The root] *ubj* is used in the sense of "straightening" (*ārjava*) [Dhātupāṭha 1303]; from this, with the prefix *ut*, the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) is formed, and the augment *ām* is applied as before.
By the rule "for the parasmaipada endings" (Pāṇini 3.4.82), *tip* is replaced by *ṇal*. Thus: "he made [them] straight" (*udumbhāñcakāra*).
Thus: the resolution is given by the rule "ubha umbha pūraṇe" (Dhātupāṭha 1319, 1320), namely through the word "ubhayam" and so forth.
[The question is: "How? Since it is impossible to perform both of these with a single effort, he says:
"as before," and so forth. There is not indeed a single effort here; rather, there are two.

"One effort" refers to the rule *ṭhāmpratyayavat*; "the second" refers to the continued application of the term *pūrvavat*. Therein, by the first effort, a prescription (*vidhi*) is established; by the other, a restriction (*niyama*). That is to say: if the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs for the auxiliary verb *kṛ* following the compound, it happens only when the action is as previously described, and not otherwise.

Therefore, it is not the case that one says "he bent" (*udubjāñcakāra*) at the beginning; for the *ātmanepada* endings are not possible for roots such as *ubj*, because they belong to the *parasmaipada* class.
[The forms] "he looked" (*īkṣāmāsa*)—here *ām* is used with the auxiliary *as*; and "he looked" (*īkṣāmbabhūva*).
With the intention that in the rules "ṭhbhavetaraḥ" (7.4.73) and "ṭhkṛñca" (3.1.40), only the root *kṛ* is to be understood, he says: "How then... and so forth;
and "The term 'kṛñ' is a pratyāhāra," and so forth. In that [pratyāhāra], there is also the inclusion of the roots *as* and *bhū*.

This is the "sannideśa" (proximity). The sense is that, because of this proximity, there is also the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of those two [roots *kṛ* and *bhū*]. If this is so, then the subsequent application of *sampad* would also follow, since it too is indeed situated there, according to the rule:
"and with *sampad* in the sense of limit-inclusive" (*abhividhau sampadā ca*, 5.4.53). Even though there is such a situation...

There is no fault, because that [root] is not included in the inclusion (*pratyāhāra*). We shall explain later, in another context, how its non-inclusion occurs. Now, what is the purpose of the phrase "like the suffix *ām*"?
For if that were absent, the ātmanepada would apply only to the subsequent usage (*anuprayoga*)—as in *devadattaḥ*.

Regarding the question "Does he do?"—here too, "as before" is understood to carry over. Nevertheless, one might ask here: [if the rule were simply] "he strives, he does," and it were stated as "the suffix *ām*," would it not follow that, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) must be of *ām* itself, and not of any subsequent application in general? Therefore, there would be no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
It comes to be.
64. *propābhyāṃ yujerayajñapātreṣu* (Pāṇini 1.3.64).

Since the ātmanepada is already established for the root *yuj* (meaning "to concentrate," *dhā.pā.* 1177) because it is anudāteta, the author states [the following] with the intention that its mention here is inappropriate:

Regarding the root *yuj* in the sense of "joining" (*yoge*), as in the form *prayuṅkte*: because it belongs to the *rudh*-class, there is the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *śnasorallopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.111). By the rule *coḥ kuḥ* (8.2.30), there is the substitution of *ku* for the palatals, whereby the *ja* becomes *ga*; then, by the rule *khari ca* (8.4.55), there is the substitution of a *ca*-sound, whereby the *ga* becomes *ka*.
The anusvāra is substituted [for *n*] by the rule "ṭhnaśca" (8.3.24), and the nasal *ṅ* is substituted [for that anusvāra] by the rule "anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ" (8.4.58).

Regarding the statement "it should be stated that [the term *upasarga* applies] to those preceded or followed by a vowel (*svara*)," a vowel (*svara*) is a vowel sound (*aj*), whether it occurs at the beginning or at the end.

The meaning is that this should be explained as follows: "That [root] which has *pra* at its beginning and *upa* at its end—after that root, when preceded by those [prefixes], the *ātmanepada* occurs due to its connection with them. In this regard, the explanation is as follows:
in this sūtra, the word *pra* is intended to indicate a prefix ending in a vowel (*ajanta*), and the word *upa* is intended to indicate a prefix beginning with a vowel (*ājadya*).

The prefix *upa-* is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for vowels and so forth; therefore, the ātmanepada occurs after the root *yuji* when it is joined with any prefix ending in a vowel or beginning with a vowel, as well as with a prefix [beginning with a consonant]. Why [specify] "preceded by a prefix beginning or ending with a vowel"? [Consider:
*niryunakti*.

65. *samaḥ kṣṇuvaḥ* | (1.3.65) [The word] "from that which is transitive" (*sakarmakāt*) is understood to carry over there [from the previous rule]. Thus, it is intended that the *ātmanepada* ending occurs after the root *kṣṇu* even when it is transitive. For this very reason...

An example of a transitive verb has been presented: *saṃkṣṇute śastram* ("he sharpens the weapon"). Due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*. In *saṃkṣṇuvāte*, the substitution *uvaṅ* occurs by the rule *aci śnudhātu* (Pāṇini 6.4.77), etc. In *saṃkṣṇuvate*, the same substitution as before applies.
66. *bhujo'navane* (1.3.66).

Regarding the phrase "by the prohibition of *avana*" and so forth: *avana* means protection. By the prohibition of that [meaning], it is understood that the root *bhuj* belonging to the *raudhādika* class is intended here, and not the one belonging to the *taudādikā* class—namely, *bhujau*.

[This refers to] the root *bhuja* in the sense of "protecting" (*kauṭilye*) from the Dhātupāṭha (1417). For just as when it is said, "Let a cow with its calf be brought," only that cow which has a possible connection with a calf is brought—
that is, a cow (*godhenu*), and not a buffalo or other such animal— so too here, by the prohibition of [entering] the forest...
Only that root which has "bhuja" as its form when followed by the suffix "ana" is understood to belong to the *raudhādika* (Rudhādi) class;

therefore, it is recognized as referring to that [specific root] alone. Consequently, in forms such as *nirbhujati* and *vibhujati*, the ātmanepada ending does not occur for the *taudādika* (Tudādi) root.
67. *ṇeraṇau yatkarma ṇau cetsa kartānādhyāne* (Pāṇini 1.3.67). [Example:

"The elephant-keepers mount the elephant" (*ārohanti hastinaṃ hastipakāḥ*). This was stated for the purpose of demonstrating the object (*karman*) in the non-causative (*aṇau*). However, the following is the illustration here: "He causes himself to be mounted" (*ārohayate*).

In the case of "The elephant itself mounts" (*hastī svayamevārohati*) and "The elephant-keepers mount the elephant" (*ārohanti hastinaṃ hastipakāḥ*), the root *ruh* preceded by the prefix *ā-*—meaning "to sprout from a seed" or "to appear"—has two actions to be expressed: descending (*nyagbhavana*) and causing to descend (*nyagbhāvana*). Among these, the elephant is the agent (*kartṛ*) of the action of descending.

"Those who subdue the elephant" refers to the elephant-keepers. The meaning is that they cause the elephant, which is already submissive, to become further subdued. However, when the elephant—due to being well-trained and highly obedient—attains a state of extreme compliance toward the act of subduing by itself;
Then, that elephant is intended to be expressed as the instigator (*prayojaka*) with respect to the elephant-keepers,
while the elephant-keepers are intended to be expressed as the instigated (*prayojya*). The elephant prompts the elephant-keepers,
saying, "Mount me," and thus, when the relationship between the instigated and the instigator is intended to be expressed.

The suffix *ṇic* is applied in the sense of a causal agent (*hetu*). Likewise, in subsequent cases as well, because the object is intended to be expressed as the agent, the suffix *ṇic* is prescribed when there is a desire to express the state of being an instigator (*prayojaka*). Once that [suffix] has arisen, when the prompted agents (*prayojya*) are no longer intended to be expressed—because their own form is already known and they have fulfilled their purpose—then...
Because the relationship between the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the instigated (*prayojya*) has ceased, the root *ruh* (to rise) functions merely in the sense of becoming subordinate.

An example of this is: *ārohayate hastī svayam eva* ("The elephant makes himself mount"). For in this case, that which was the object (*karman*) in the *ṇic*-less form becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) in the *ṇic*-derived form; and it is not...
Even when the relationship between the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the one being instigated (*prayojya*) has ceased, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) does not cease,

because there is no cause for its cessation. For just as the root *pac* does not cease from denoting "cooking" even when Devadatta’s activity has ceased— as in "the rice cooks by itself"— so it is here as well.

It should be understood that even when the operations of the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the instigated (*prayojya*) have ceased, the cessation of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) does not necessarily follow.
For example, in "they cause [the elephant] to sprinkle" (*siñcanti*), etc., even here, when the elephant being sprinkled (*sicyamāna*) is the object (*karman*).

Because of being well-trained and being easily obedient, it possesses a preeminent suitability for the act of sprinkling; when, therefore, the intention is to express its status as the instigator (*prayojaka*) and that of the elephant-keepers as the prompted (*prayojya*), the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied. When that has been done, [the formation proceeds] as before.

When the prompted agents (*prayojya*) are not intended to be expressed, that which is the object (*karman*) in the causative (*ṇyant*) becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) in the causative; as in "they cause [the king] to see" (*paśyanti*), and so forth. Here too, because the king being seen attains a state of extreme favorability toward the act of seeing, he possesses the status of an instigator (*prayojaka*).

When there is a desire to express the state of being employed by servants, the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied. When that [suffix] is prescribed, if—as in the previous case—the agency of the one to be employed is not intended to be expressed, then that very king who was the object (*karman*) of the root *dṛś* in its non-causative form (*aṇyantāvasthā*) becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) in the causative form (*ṇyanta*). Furthermore, in all these examples, the action (*kriyā*) remains exactly the same as it was in the non-causative state.

That same [rule] applies even when the suffix *ṇic* is present; for although *ṇic* is present, the relationship between the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the one being instigated (*prayojya*) has been removed, and no other action arises.
Thus, we have forms such as *gaṇayati*. The root *gaṇa* (DhP 1853), meaning "to count," ends in a long vowel and belongs to the *cur-ādi* group.
It is read [in the Dhātupāṭha]. Then, by the rule "ṇic, and the elision of ṭha" (6.4.48), there is the elision of the vowel *ā*.

Since that [elided *ā*] is treated as if it were still present (*sthānivat*) when a preceding operation is to be performed, the rule "vṛddhi for the penultimate vowel after ṭha" (7.2.116) does not apply. Thus: "The cowherd counts the herd of cows" (*gaṇayati gogaṇaṃ gopālakaḥ*); "The group counts" (*gaṇayati gaṇaḥ*).

Regarding the phrase "svayameva" (himself): when he, being counted, is intended to be expressed as the prompter (*prayojaka*) by favoring the act of counting, while the cowherd (*gopālaka*) is intended as the prompted (*prayojya*), then the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied. Once that has been applied, as before, when there is no intention to express the prompted agent, that very [form] [arises].
The agent of that very action becomes the object [of the causative]. Nevertheless, because of the statement "when there is an *aṇ*," the ātmanepada ending does not occur;

for the group [of roots] was not previously an *aṇ* with respect to the object, but rather only when ending in *ṇi*. But then, in the rule "from an intransitive root having a conscious agent when there is an *aṇ*" (1.3.88), what is the purpose of the term "*aṇau*"?
Having stated, "Some offer the counter-example: 'it impels that which is intending, [and thus] it intends,'" the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*) will say;
that is incorrect, because the rule for the causative suffix *ṇic* applies to the cause, and the prohibition also, by virtue of proximity, applies to that very same [cause].

If it is argued that [the agent and the object] are logically distinct, and if that were true, then even the following counter-example would be improper: "The cowherd counts the herd of cows," and "The herd of cows counts itself.
But this is not the case, because the distinction is not intended to be expressed. For if the distinction were intended to be expressed, then...

Since the rule [P. 6.1.57] is one that prescribes an affix with the causative marker *ṇic* based on its cause (*hetumaṇṇic*), the prohibition would also apply specifically to that [causative], due to proximity, and not to the *ṇic* of the *cur*-class which is remote. Furthermore, no distinction is intended here, because the mention of "of *ṇi*" (*ṇeḥ*) refers to the general class (*jāti*). Therefore, it is a prescription for *ṇic* in general; consequently, the prohibition applies as well.

It is correct that this counter-example should apply only to the *ṇic* suffix itself; for in rules such as "after an intransitive [verb], with the suffix *aṇ*" (Pāṇini 1.3.88), the term "*aṇau*" refers exclusively to the causative *ṇic*. Therefore, since the rule applies specifically to the causative *ṇic*, it is logical that its prohibition should also pertain to that alone, just as in the case of *prāyāsate*.

In that regard, we shall demonstrate later on that very point why the inclusion of the causative *ṇic* in the sense of "causing" (*hetu*) is intended there. However, no such basis exists here by which it could be determined that the term "of *ṇi*" (*ṇeḥ*) refers exclusively to the causative *ṇic*;
for even the roots belonging to the *curādika* class are not invariably followed by the *ṇic* suffix.

Since there exist certain roots that take the causative suffix *ṇic* (as shown in the *Vibhāṣā*), for those very roots which have an object in their non-causative (*aṇyanta*) state, that same object can also function as the agent when they are in the causative (*curādi-ṇijanta*) state.
Therefore, it is the intention of the author of the Sūtra that the term *ṇeḥ* here refers to the causative suffix *ṇic* in general.
It is observed as follows:

now, in the case of *gaṇayati gogaṇaḥ svayam eva* ("the herd of cows counts itself"), why does the ātmanepada not occur here by virtue of the extension (*atideśa*) of rule 3.1.87, *karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyāḥ* ("that which has an action equal to that of the object behaves like the object")?

Because it has a state residing in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvakatva*). For here, this verb *gaṇayati* (he counts) refers to a specific cognition consisting of a delimitation based on number, which is precisely what is designated as "counting" (*saṃkhyāna*). And that specific cognition resides in the agent, because it is inherent (*samaveta*) in him, not in the object. Therefore...

The ātmanepada does not occur here because the action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvakatva*). It is desired that the ātmanepada occurs for actions residing in the object (*karmasthakriyā*) and actions whose essence resides in the object (*karmasthabhāvaka*), by means of the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule "the object behaves like the object" (*karmavat*); it does not occur for others.

Regarding the example "he causes [the reaper] to cut with a sickle" (*lunāti dātreṇa*), and so forth: although the sickle is an instrument (*karaṇa*) due to its sharpness, because it constitutes a specific operation, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is employed when one intends to express the status of the person who reaps as the instigator (*prayojaka*).

Regarding the phrase "if [the rule] were stated as 'in the case of ṇic' (ṇau cet)," and so forth: here, if it were merely stated that "whatever is the object in the case of ṇic is the agent," then—by implication—it would be understood that whatever was the object in the case of aṇic becomes the agent specifically in the case of ṇic.
Therefore, what is the purpose of the expression "if in the case of ṇic" (ṇau cet)? That being so, in the case of ṇic...

The inclusion of the word *ced* (if) is understood for the purpose of indicating an identical action—that is, if the very same action that exists in the state of being an object also occurs in the state of being an agent. This is what is meant:
if that which was the object of a particular verbal root-meaning is intended to be expressed as its agent.
Thus, the middle voice (ātmanepada) occurs in this way and not otherwise. Therefore, in the sentence "The elephant-drivers mount the elephant;
being mounted, the elephant sprinkles the frightened ones with urine," the middle voice does not apply to the root *siC* (to sprinkle), because the action is different. For instance:
"In the act of bending down (*nyagbhāvana*), [the tree] was previously intended as the object (*karman*);
however, in the act of sprinkling (*secanakriyā*), it is subsequently intended as the agent (*kartṛ*).

'The mention of *yat* is for the purpose of excluding other objects'—[this applies] if that which is the object in the non-causative form (*aṇyant*) is also the object in the causative form (*ṇyant*)."

That very same action becomes the agent, not another action; in this way the ātmanepada occurs, and not otherwise. But is this not contradictory—namely, that at one and the same time there is both the state of being an object and the state of being an agent for the very same thing? This is not contradictory; for one is a property of the entity, and the other is [another].

The property of being intended for expression (*vivakṣādharma*): when independence is intended to be expressed, [the agent] possesses the property of being intended as the agent; and when being mounted is intended, [the elephant] possesses the property of being the object (*karmatva*), because it is a property of the thing itself. In the example "He makes the men mount the platform" (*sthalam ārohayati manuṣyān*), there is also another object. It is not the case that only the elephant is the object, as in the case of "He makes the men mount. Thus, it is not so.

The ātmanepada [suffix] occurs. If this is so, then in the case of *bhītān secayati mūtreṇa* ("he sprinkles the frightened ones with urine"), the ātmanepada will not occur because of the existence of another object; for here too there is indeed another object—namely, "the frightened ones. Therefore, it need not be stated that [the rule applies] when the action is the same in the causative (*ṇic*).
If you ask why this is so, it is not the case that "the frightened ones" (*bhītān*) is the object of the root *sic* (to sprinkle); rather, it is the object of the root *ā-ruh* (to mount).

The meaning is: while causing the frightened ones to mount, he sprinkles himself with urine. This is incorrect, for in the form *ārohyamāṇaḥ*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) suffix would be improper [if it were the object of *sic*].

And the suffix *śānac* would not occur, because another action exists [as the object]. If that is not the case, then the suffix *śānac* is not prescribed here; what then? It is the suffix *cānaś*, as prescribed by the rule "tācchīlyavayovacanaśaktiṣu" (Pāṇini 3.2.129). In that context, if the mention of *ṇau* were not made for the purpose of referring to an identical action, [the rule would fail to apply].

In that case, since the very same object that is the object (*karman*) of the root *ā-ruh* when followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*) becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) of the root *siñc* when followed by the causative suffix, it would follow that the very same thing is both the object and the agent; thus, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would necessarily apply.
Therefore, the mention of "if [the action] is in the causative" (*ṇau cet*) must be made for the purpose of ensuring the identity of the action (*samānakriyārtha*).

Regarding the phrase "ṭhkarteti kim" ("What is the purpose of [mentioning] 'agent'?"): by this rule, the ātmanepada is prescribed only for the agent (*kartṛ*), because [the ātmanepada] for the state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*) is already established by the rule 1.3.13. Therefore, the intention is that the "agent" is understood through the force of the context (*sāmarthya*). The mention of the "agent" is intended so that [the ātmanepada occurs] only when that which was the object in the *ṇic*-less form is the very same thing that is the object in the *ṇic*-inflected form.
He says this to show that the *ātmanepada* ending is employed only when the agent (*kartṛ*) is intended to be expressed, and not otherwise: "The elephant-keepers mount the elephant;
the mahout causes them to mount it. In this case, the elephant is indeed the object (*karman*) of the root *āruh* (to mount) in its causative form.
That very [agent] which was intended as the agent in the causative (*ṇyanta*) is not what is intended here; rather, it is the *mahāmātra* (high official).

Therefore, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) does not occur. And this is understood from the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*), because that [mention] serves no other purpose. Now, it was indeed stated that the mention of "that" (*yat*) is for the purpose of excluding another object, and here too—

There exists another rule called *hastipaka*; therefore, since that [desired form] will not occur simply by virtue of including [the word "agent"] in the present rule, what is the purpose of this inclusion of the term "agent" (*kartṛ*) for the sake of excluding it? This is not so; for if the inclusion of the term "agent" were not made, then [it would be understood that] whatever is the object in the *aṇ* (causal) verb, if that same thing is the agent in the *ṇi*-derived (non-causal) verb, only that object which is the agent [would be designated as the subject].

And it is for the purpose of establishing this meaning— that the inclusion of the term "agent" (kartṛ) is meaningful— that [the rule] is formulated; for if the mention of the "agent" were absent, that [mention] would not even need to be made, so how could the identity of the object (samānakarmatā) be understood?
"He remembers the forest thicket"—this is stated for the purpose of demonstrating the object (*karman*) in the case of the non-causative (*aṇau*).

It is said in order to show the object (*viṣaya*) by means of the "remainder" (*śeṣatva*), which is the subject (*viṣayin*) that has the object as its domain. But surely there is no object here, because it is intended to be expressed as a remainder; for it is said [in Pāṇini 2.3.50], "In the sense of a remainder (*śeṣe*)."

While this [rule] continues to apply, this genitive case is prescribed by the rule *ṭhadhīgartha* (Pāṇini 2.3.52), etc., when the object is intended to be expressed as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*). Therefore, this must be shown as: "He remembers the thicket of trees" (*smarati vanagulmam*). Or rather—even though that [object] is intended to be expressed as a residual relation—nevertheless...

Because it is being remembered, its status as the object (*karman*) indeed exists in reality; thus [we have] "he causes to remember" (*smarayati*). [The root] *smṛ* is used in the sense of "intense reflection" (*ādhyāna*) [DhP 807]. When the forest thicket is intended to be the instigator (*prayojaka*), the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied.
Because it belongs to the *ghaṭādi* group, it receives the designation *mit*; by the rule "the short vowel for *mit*-roots" (Pāṇini 6.4.92), the shortening of the vowel occurs.

Regarding the word *ṭhenam*: since the designation "object" (*karma*) applies by the rule "roots meaning motion, cognition, or consumption" (Pāṇini 1.4.52), the substitution of *en* for *am* occurs by the rule "the second case ending [is used] after a root ending in *au*, *t*, *us*, or *ṇ*" (Pāṇini 2.4.34). Now, one might object that the inclusion of the term *yat* is intended to exclude other objects, yet here there is another object, namely *kokilaḥ*.
And since there would be another grammatical operation [the *ātmanepada* suffix] in that case, the *ātmanepada* would not occur;
so what is the purpose of including the term "not for meditation" (*anādhyāna*) to exclude it? This is not so;
this counter-example is presented because one intends to express merely the act of meditating (*ādhyāna*). However, as for the expression "him" (*enam*), [it serves a different purpose].

It should be understood that this is intended to demonstrate the meaning: "The forest thicket is the agent, not the cuckoo. Likewise, "the forest thicket causes the forest thicket to remember" means "it causes itself to remember by itself," once the causative suffix (*ṇic*) has been applied.

Since the cuckoo, as the prompted agent (*prayojya*), is intended [as the subject], once the relationship between the prompted and the prompter (*prayojyaprayojakabhāva*) has ceased, the root *smṛ* with its causative suffix (*ṇyanta*) retains its original meaning. Now, one might object: "Recollection is a property of sentient beings, yet a forest thicket is insentient; how then could it remember? This is not so.
The metaphorical attribution of consciousness to insentient things is as in the expression, "the riverbank wishes to fall.

[This is justified] because of the rule "the root *ruh* has its action residing in the agent" (*ruhaḥ kartṛsthakriyaḥ*), since its meaning—consisting of the act of becoming subservient—is inherent in the elephant-drivers. Likewise, [it is justified] by the rule "the root *dṛś* has its state residing in the agent" (*dṛśiśca kartṛsthabhāvakaḥ*), since its meaning—the act of seeing—is...
Because it is established among the agents who are the servants.

68. *bhīsmyor hetubhaye* (1.3.68). Regarding the phrase *hetubhaye*: "fear caused by a cause" is *hetubhayam*. This is a compound formed according to *pañcamī bhayena* (2.1.37). *Bhītiḥ* means fear (*bhayam*), that is, terror (*trāsaḥ*), which is the apprehension of the occurrence of something undesirable.
Regarding the statement, "And from that, fear arises": if fear arises from that cause, which is the instigator (*prayojaka*), then the *ātmanepada* occurs, and not otherwise.
If this were so, the meaning of the root *smi* would not be specified; for [the rule states] "from which fear... [arises].

The meaning [of the rule] belongs only to the root *bhī* (to fear) and not to *smṛ* (to remember); consequently, the ātmanepada ending would occur even in cases such as *rūpeṇa vismāyayati* ("he astonishes with his form"), whereas it would not occur in cases such as *muṇḍo vismāpayati* ("the shaven-headed one causes astonishment"). Therefore, he says: "The mention of *bhaya*," and so forth. For the mention of *bhaya*...

This is for the purpose of indicating the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). The intended meaning is that if the action denoted by the root proceeds from an instigator (*prayojaka*), then [the suffix *ṇic* is applied]. Consequently, even if astonishment (*vismaya*) arises from that very same cause—namely, if this matter is obtained—the sense of "being amazed" (*smayati*) is likewise specifically qualified. Astonishment (*vismaya*) means wonder (*āścarya*).

Regarding "ṭhmuṇḍaḥ": he is called *muṇḍa* because he is endowed with the quality (*guṇa*) of being shaven-headed (*muṇḍa*). Regarding "ṭhbhīṣayate": from the root *ñibhī* in the sense of fear (DhP 1084), the vowel substitution *ā* occurs optionally by the rule "vibhāṣā līyateḥ" (6.1.51), since the mention of "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) is carried over [from that rule] to the rule "bibheterhetubhaye" (6.1.56). Thus, in one alternative, there is the substitution of *ā*.
The suffix *ṣuk* is applied by the rule *ṭhbhiyo hetubhaye ṣuk* (Pāṇini 7.3.40). Regarding the form *vismāpayate*:

the root *smiṅ*—from the Dhātupāṭha, *smiṅ īṣaddhasane* (948)—is used. By the rule *nityaṃ smayateḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.57), *ātvam* (the substitution of *ā* for *i*) occurs; then, by the rule *artihrī* (Pāṇini 7.3.36) et al., the suffix *puk* is added.

"He frightens him with a key. Here, the fear arises from the instrument (*karaṇa*), not from the causal agent (*hetu-prayojaka*). Therefore, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) does not occur. Furthermore, the *ṣuk* augment does not apply here either; for that is desired only after a root ending in long *ī*, as in the rule "ṣuk is added to *bhī* when there is fear caused by a cause" (*bhiyo hetubhaye ṣuk*, Pāṇini 7.3.40). In this case, [the root is *bhī*].

Because of the instruction involving the elision (praśleṣa) of the vowel *ī*— as in "he causes wonder by means of his form" (*rūpeṇa vismāyayati*)— here the wonder arises from the instrument (*karaṇa*) itself, not from the cause (*hetu*).
69. *gṛdh* and *vañc* [take the ātmanepada] in the sense of deceiving (Pāṇini 1.3.69). 70. *lī* [takes the ātmanepada] also in the senses of honoring and making someone humble (Pāṇini 1.3.70).
[Regarding the phrase] "because there is no distinction": how, then, can there be no distinction, given that...

There is indeed a distinction between these two, namely that one is without an indicatory letter (*niranubandhaka*) while the other is with an indicatory letter (*sānubandhaka*); consequently, by the metarule "when there is the mention of a [root] without an indicatory letter, [there is no mention of] one with an indicatory letter" (*vyā.pa.* #a53), there ought not to be a mention of *liṅ* [in place of *līṅ*]. Therefore, what was said is incorrect.

Is it not the case that both [forms] are included because there is no distinction? This is not a fault, for here the suffix *lyap* occurs with its *anubandha* (indicatory letter) dropped. And when the *anubandha* is dropped, only two things remain as differentiators: the meaning and the fact of being a different word.

In this regard, first of all, the meaning of these two is one and the same, nor is there even a difference in their verbal forms. A difference in verbal form occurs through a difference in root (*prakṛti*) or a difference in suffix (*vikaraṇa*). However, in these two forms derived from the causative suffix (*ṇic*), there is neither a difference in root nor a difference in suffix, because they both take the *śap* suffix. Furthermore, even if...

Regarding the rule *vibhāṣā līyateḥ* (6.1.51), which prescribes the substitution of *ā* for the vowel, that too applies to both [roots]. And so he will say: "What is this *līyate*? It is an indication [of the form] of both *līnāti* and *līyati* by means of the adventitious suffix *yak*.
"Subordination" (*nyagbhāvam*) means being overcome. "With matted locks" (*jaṭābhiḥ*).

The third case ending is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*). For matted hair (*jaṭā*) is indeed the cause for attaining honor and the like. Thus it is said: "In this world, one who possesses matted hair is honored by people who have conceived the conviction that 'this ascetic is great'."

71. *mithyopapadāt kṛño 'bhyāse* (Pāṇini 1.3.71). Regarding the phrase *mithyopapadāt*: a word uttered near [another] is an *upapada*; that which has the word *mithyā* as its *upapada* is described as such. For example: *padaṃ mithyā kārayate* ("he causes the foot to be performed falsely").

In this case, because the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) has already indicated the sense of repetition, the doubling (*dvirvacana*) prescribed by Pāṇini 8.1.4 (*nityavīpsayoḥ*) does not occur. Regarding the term *sāpacāra*: it means "accompanied by fault" (*sadoṣa*). By this, he explains the meaning of the word *mithyā*. Regarding *svarādiduṣṭam*: this refers to the same meaning as the preceding [term].

It makes [the meaning] manifest. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of "form" (rūpa) is intended. Regarding the phrase "not repeatedly," he demonstrates the meaning of the word "repetition" (abhyāsa) by means of an example.
72. *svaritañitaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale* (Pāṇini 1.3.72).

Regarding the term *kartrabhiprāye*: [the word] *kartrabhiprāyaḥ* is derived from *kartāram abhipraiti* ("it aims at the agent") by applying *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1). If, in a general sense, wherever the fruit of the action aims at the agent, there the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs.

In that case, this would also apply here: "the cooks cook" (*pacanti pācakāḥ*) and "the sacrificers sacrifice" (*yajanti yājakāḥ*). For in these instances, the fruit of the action—the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)—is intended for the sacrificers who are the agents, and the wages for the cooks; therefore, he says: "The fruit of the action," and so forth. [This refers to] that fruit which is the primary one.

Therefore, in this context, that [which is the primary object] is understood as the action (*kriyā*). Nor is the fruit of the action, such as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth, the primary element;

consequently, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). To the question, "What then is that which is the primary element? he says: "That for the sake of which," and so forth. By this, it is meant that [the action] is not [defined merely by what it produces], but rather by that toward which this action, such as sacrifice and the like, is undertaken.
"But for the sake of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of which": it refers to heaven and the like, but not the sacrificial fee and the like.

For indeed, rites such as sacrifice are undertaken for the sake of heaven and so forth, but not for the sake of the sacrificial fee and the like. The phrase "for the sake of which" is an adverbial modifier of the action. By the word *yat*, the primary fruit of the action is indicated.
It is explained as follows: if the "purpose" (artha) were intended to mean the mere result of the undertaking of an action, then the mention of "result" (phala) would be redundant;
for there is no such case where the result of an action does not [in some way] relate to the agent.

It does not apply [to that case]; therefore, one should state: "when the intention belongs to the agent (*kartrabhiprāye*) with respect to the action (*kriyāyāḥ*). Even when this is stated, since the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) indicates that which is related to the action when the intention belongs to the agent, it follows by implication that the fruit alone is understood as belonging to the agent with respect to the action. For there is no other [result] than the fruit.

It refers to the agent who is connected with the action. Therefore, by virtue of the capacity for grasping the fruit (*phala*), the primary fruit is understood. Or else—the primary fruit is understood precisely because of its primacy.
And so it has been said: "Because the understanding of the effect resides in the primary [agent], it is established. In this interpretation...

The mention of "fruit" (phala) is for the sake of clarity, since the ātmanepada is prescribed when there is an agent. He says "And that" (*tacca*), etc., to explain that it is understood: "if the fruit belongs to that very agent who is proximate to the verbal meaning. This has already been explained. Regarding the phrase "heaven and so forth" (*svargādi*):
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), rice and other such items are also included.

With the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) and so forth, [the author] shows that the fruit consisting of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and the like is not primary. That for the sake of which an action is undertaken is the primary fruit intended here; and [that fruit] is for the sake of heaven and so forth.
An action such as a sacrifice is commenced for its own sake, not for the sake of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and so forth.
Therefore, because it is not the motivating factor, that [fee] is not primary. Consequently, even though it intends toward the agent, the ātmanepada suffix does not occur.

Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the term *abhipragrahaṇa* (the prefix *abhi-*)? It is so that [the designation "fruit"] may apply even when the fruit is remote. For the fruit of an action is of two kinds: proximate and remote. Among these, the proximate is that whose accomplishment occurs immediately after the activity has ceased; whereas the remote is that which occurs when the activities have already subsided.

That which arises after a long time due to the ripening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), depending on another cause and a temporal distance, is [the second type]. Among these, the former is primary because it is proximate, observed, and because it is non-deviant with respect to its arising;
the other is [secondary].

Furthermore, because it is remote, because it is an object of inference, and because there is the possibility of deviation, there is a deviation with respect to its arising. Even though that [the result] is primary because the activity begins for its sake, nevertheless, in comparison with a result that is not remote, its lack of primacy certainly remains. In that regard, if the prefix *abhi-* were included...

If it were not so, then [the suffix] would occur only in cases such as *lunīta* ("cut") and *punīta* ("purify"), where the fruit of the action is immediate; however, it would not occur in cases such as *yajate* ("sacrifices"), where the fruit of the action, such as heaven (*svarga*), is remote, because the grammatical operation is understood to apply to the primary element. But this is not the case when there is an apprehension of the object (*abhigrahaṇe*).

There is a fault; for the prefix *abhi* functions in the sense of "facing toward" (*abhimukhya*), while the prefix *pra* functions in the commencement of an action (*sattvārambha*). Therefore, when the completion of the result is understood to depend upon the intellect, everything is established by taking the mere commencement as being "facing toward" [the result].
But surely, if the mention of *abhi-pra* were not made, [what would happen to] the verbal roots?
Because specific auxiliary details (anubandha) are attached to sacrifices and the like, the result will indeed occur even though it is remote;
otherwise, that [injunction] would be purposeless. This is not so, because it is meaningful in cases such as malevolent magic (abhicāra), where a non-remote result is observed.
Therefore, for the purpose that [the result] might occur even when it is remote and not the primary factor, the inclusion of the word "iṭ" must indeed be made.
73. *apādvadaḥ* | (1.3.73) By the phrase "by the censure of justice" (*nyāyāpavādena*), etc., he shows the intention with which one who desires wealth censures justice.

74. *ṇicaśca* | (1.3.74) 75. *samudāṅbhyo yamo’granthe* | (1.3.75) "Udyacchati" [he exerts himself]. "Cikitsā vaidyaḥ" [the physician’s medical treatment]; [this refers to] making an effort (*udyama*) to master the science of medicine (*cikitsā-śāstra*).
The meaning is "he performs."

76. *anupasargājjñaḥ* | (1.3.76) This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one for whom there are no prepositions (*upasarga*)"; that is, [a verbal root] which has no prepositions. And this is intended for the sake of transitive roots (*sakarmaka*), because [the formation of the gerundive] is already established by the rule *akarmakācca* (1.3.45).
77. *vibhāṣopapadena pratīyamāne* (1.3.77).
Here, the five sūtras beginning with *svaritañitaḥ* (1.3.72) are understood to carry over.
[The phrase] "when the fruit of the action is intended for the agent" (*kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale*)—by what is this indicated? By the *upapada*.

It should be understood that [the rule] applies because of the *ātmanepada* ending due to the subject matter at hand. [The objection is raised: "In a case where the meaning is already indicated by an accompanying word (*upapada*), the rule would not apply," because words whose meaning has already been expressed are not employed. By this, he shows that this is an optional rule (*aprāpta-vibhāṣā*) for cases where [the suffix] was not otherwise required. Now, as for the example *svaṃ yajñaṃ yajate*:

Is it not untenable because *sva* is a subordinate word (*upapada*)? For, according to the rule "In that context, what stands in the locative case is called *upapada*" (Pāṇini 3.1.92), within the governing heading of the second section on verbal roots, whatever is specified by the locative case receives the designation *upapada*;
however, the word *sva* is not of such a kind. Thus he says: "in proximity" (*samīpe*).

Regarding the phrase "being heard" (*śrūyamāṇam*) and so forth: by this, he shows that the term *upapada* is taken in its etymological sense—as a word uttered in proximity (*upa-uccāritam padam upapadam*)—and not in its technical (*pāribhāṣika*) sense. And this is understood because the technical sense is impossible here. [Example: *svaṃ yajñam*.

By the phrase "ityādinā" (beginning with this), he cites the first sūtra among the five; by "svaṃ putram" (one's own son) and so forth, he cites the second. The phrase "thus one should cite examples for the five sūtras" implies that this applies elsewhere as well. This refers to what has been cited within the sūtras contained in the group of five.
The meaning is that this should be cited as an example elsewhere as well: *svaṃ kaṭaṃ kārayate*, *kārayati* vā;
*svaṃ vrīhiṃ saṃyacchate*, *saṃyacchati* vā; *svaṃ bhāramudyacchate*, *udyacchati* vā; *svaṃ vastramāyacchate*, *āyacchati* vā; *svaṃ gāṃ jānīte*, *jānāti* veti.
These are the examples, as appropriate, for the sūtras beginning with "ṭhṇicaśca" (Pāṇini 1.3.74).

78. *śeṣāt kartari parasmaipadam* (1.3.78). [The commentary says: "By the preceding [rule]," namely by *anudāttetaḥ* (1.3.12) and so forth. "It applies everywhere," meaning even from those not included in the remainder (*aśeṣa*). "This is stated for that purpose," meaning so that the *parasmaipada* endings apply in all cases.

Since [the application of the suffix] would otherwise follow [too broadly], this is for the purpose of excluding that; for the word *artha* signifies exclusion, as in the expression "smoke is for the sake of mosquitoes" (*maśakārtho dhūmaḥ*). Thus, it is stated that this is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*). By the words "from whichever roots" (*yebhyo dhātubhyaḥ*) and so forth, he demonstrates the status of being a remainder (*śeṣatvam*). "By which qualification... (*yena viśeṣaṇena*)...
Thus, [the rule applies] by means of the *anubandha* (indicatory letter) and so forth. "He goes" (*yāti*) and "he blows" (*vāti*) are examples for the remainder of the *anubandha*.

"He enters" (*praviśati*) and "he enters" (*āviśati*) are examples for the remainder of the prefix (*upasarga*) and also for the remainder of the meaning (*artha*). In this same way, examples such as "he does" (*karoti*) and so forth are to be understood as applying elsewhere than in cases of threatening (*gandhana*) and the like.

But is it not the case that by the rule *śeṣāt* (Pāṇini 1.3.74), which ends in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) and is in grammatical apposition with the verbal root (*dhātu*), it is the root itself that is qualified, and not its meaning? Consequently, the *parasmaipada* ending would result even for meanings other than those beginning with "hinting" (*gandhana*) and so forth. This is not so; for "hinting" and the others are indeed the meanings of the verbal base (*prakṛti*) itself.

In that case, as this [term] is withdrawn by the inclusion of the word "the rest" (*śeṣa*), it also causes those [terms] to be withdrawn— namely, "it is cooked" (*pacyate*) and "it is gone" (*gamyate*). But surely, if the *parasmaipada* were to occur here,
then the rule "in the sense of the impersonal (*bhāva*) and the passive (*karman*)" (Pāṇini 1.3.13) would be rendered purposeless, because it would have no scope of application.

This is not so; for there is indeed scope for that [rule]. What, then, is this? It is that which is "non-remaining" (*aśeṣa*)—namely, that which is expressed as "he sits," "he lies down," or "it is done. The state of having an anudātta accent and the marker *ṅ* constitute "non-remaining. In the rule *śeṣāt kartari* (Pāṇini 1.3.78), the mention of the agent (*kartṛ*) is taken in its general sense; therefore, that which...

He states the objection regarding that [rule]: "In the case of the agent of the action" (*karmakartari*), and so forth. He refutes this with the rule "When there is a reciprocal action, [the suffix *śānac* is used] in the sense of the agent" (*kartari karmavyatīhāre*, 1.3.14), and so forth, stating: "The agent who is indeed the agent.
This means: an agent who is pure, an agent who is devoid of the state of being [treated as] an agent.
79. [The suffix *ṇamul* is used after the root *kṛ* when preceded by the prefixes *anu* and *pari*.
(1.3.79) 80. [The suffix *ṇamul* is used after the root *kṣip* when preceded by the prefixes *abhi*, *prati*, and *ati*.
(1.3.80) Regarding the form "abhikṣipati": because it belongs to the *tudādigaṇa*, the suffix *śa* is applied.
81. *prādvahaḥ* | (1.3.81) 82. *paremṛṣaḥ* | (1.3.82) Regarding the form *parimṛṣyati*: because it belongs to the *divādi* class, the suffix *śyan* is applied.
83. *vyāṅparibhyo ramaḥ* | (1.3.83) 84.

*upācca* | (1.3.84) Regarding the rule "and after *upa*": the particle *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) with respect to what precedes it. [Thus, the suffix *ātmanepada* is applied] after *uparamati*.

"Devadatta! [he says]. But surely the root *ram*, preceded by the prefix *upa*, is intransitive (*akarmaka*). For when this root is preceded by *upa*, its meaning is "destruction"; as for example, from "they have ceased" (*uparatāni*), it is understood that "they have perished" (*naṣṭāni*).
Or it means "desisting," as in "he desists from his Vedic study" (*svādhyāyāduparamate*), which means "he turns away from it."
It is understood that for this meaning [of cessation], the transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) of the verb as it occurs here is not logically tenable.

Therefore, he says—"meaning 'he causes to cease'"—in order to show that it is appropriate to provide an example of a transitive verb. By this, he demonstrates the transitivity of the root *upa-ram* by showing that it functions with the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇyartha*).
For a root that is originally intransitive becomes transitive when it occurs in the sense of the causative (*ṇyartha*).

Now, how is it possible for a root ending in *aṇ* (the present participle suffix) to function in the sense of the causative? That has been explained accordingly. For such a form, its status as having an object is indeed established by means of the "impelled" (*prayojya*) agent.

Now, for what purpose is a separate rule (yoga) formulated? One might ask: "Let there be only a single rule, 'na vyāṅparyupebhyo ramaḥ'. To this, he says: "The formulation of a separate rule," and so forth. The meaning has already been explained.
85. *vibhāṣā'karmakāt* (1.3.85). Regarding the example *yāvadbhuktam*: *yāvad* forms an avyayībhāva compound according to *yāvadavadhāraṇe* (2.1.8). Regarding *bhuktam*:
the suffix *kta* is applied according to *napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ* (3.3.114). As many as...
The meaning is that one should desist from meals for their sake. Alternatively, *yāvad-bhuktam* is an avyayībhāva compound used in its literal sense with distributive repetition (*vīpsā*),
meaning one should desist from meal after meal.
86. After the roots *budh*, *yudh*, *naś*, *jan*, *iṅ*, *pru*, *ru*, and *bhrū*, [the suffix] *ṇi* [is replaced by *ka*].

(Pāṇini 1.3.86) *budha* in the sense of "understanding" (Dhātupāṭha 1172); *yudh* in the sense of "fighting" (Dhātupāṭha 1173); *ṇaś* in the sense of "disappearance" (Dhātupāṭha 1194); *janī* in the sense of "coming into being" (Dhātupāṭha 1149); *iṅ*... [iha]... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with *iṅ*. The full list of roots for this rule includes *iṅ* "to study," *pru* "to flow," *ru* "to sound," and *bhrū* "to move.")
[The roots] *adhyai* (DhP 1046), *cyai* (DhP 955)— from which *cāyūṅ*,

*jyūṅ*, *jhayūṅ*, *prūṅ*, and *plūṅ* [are derived]— and [the roots] meaning "to go," namely *du* and *dru* (DhP 944, 945), as well as *su* and *sru* (DhP 940). [The form] "janayati" [is derived from the root *jan*].
By the rule *ṭhjanījṛṣ* (Gaṇasūtra on roots, 817), the designation *mit* is applied; for those designated *mit*, there is shortening (*mitāṃ hrasvatvam*).

Thus, "he causes to study" (*adhyāpayati*). By the rule *ṭhkrīḍajīnāṃ ṇau* (Pāṇini 6.1.48), there is the substitution of *ā* [for the vowel]; as before, the augment *puk* is added. "These are the examples pertaining to this subject."

The meaning is that these [roots] have, respectively, attainment (*prāpti*), dissolution (*vilayana*), and flowing (*syandana*) as their objects; for example, *prāvayati* and so forth. In common worldly usage, "flowing" (*syandana*) is well known to mean "motion. Therefore, it should be understood that in other contexts, *syandayati* means "to cause to flow. *Prāvayati* means "to cause to reach" (*prāpayati*), and *drāvayati* means "to cause to dissolve" (*vilāpayati*).
"Srāvayati" means "he causes to flow" or "he causes to trickle.
87. *Nigaraṇacalanārthebhyaśca* (Pāṇini 1.3.87).
Regarding "nigārayati": the root is *gṛ* (meaning "swallowing," Dhātupāṭha 1410). Regarding "āśayati": the root is *aś*.

Regarding *bhojane* (DhP 1523): *bhojayati*. [The root] *bhuja* is listed as "in the sense of protecting and eating" (DhP 1046). Regarding *calati*: *cala* is listed as "in the sense of shaking" (DhP 832). Because it belongs to the *ghaṭādi* group, there is the designation *mit*; consequently, as before, there is shortening of the vowel. Regarding *copayati*: *cupa*...

In the sense of "moving slowly" (*mandāyāṃ gatau*), [the suffix *ṇic* is applied] as in "he causes to tremble" (*kampayati*). Regarding "to tremble" (*kapi calane*), this rule (*yoga*) also serves the purpose of making the verb transitive and for the purpose of having a non-conscious agent (*acetana-kartṛka*). From those that are the opposite of these...

This is because the rule is already established by *ṭhaṇāvakarmakāccitavatkartṛkāt* (Pāṇini 1.3.88). Among those examples that have been presented there, two—*cali* and *kampī*—are intransitive (*akarmaka*); for these two, this rule [the present one] is intended for cases where the agent does not possess consciousness (*acitavat-kartṛka*). For the remaining ones, however, it is intended for cases where they are transitive (*sakarmaka*).
"It should be stated" means it should be explained. Here is the explanation:

the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) from the rule *vibhāṣākarmakāt* (Pāṇini 1.3.85) is carried over by "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*), and that is understood to be a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).

Therefore, the *parasmaipada* ending occurs invariably after roots other than those beginning with *ad*, but it does not occur at all after *ad*. For example, in "ādayate devadattena" (Devadatta causes to eat), the designation of the object (*karmasaṃjñā*) does not apply under the rule "gati-buddhi... (Pāṇini 1.4.52); this is because of the prohibition stated in the Vārttika: "There is a prohibition for roots beginning with *ad*, *khād*, *nī*, and *vah*."
Because of the scriptural statement.
88. *aṇāvakarmakāccitavatkartṛkāt* (Pāṇini 1.3.88).
[The example given is] *cetayamānam*. The root *citī* in the sense of "perceiving" (*saṃjñāne*) belongs to the curādigaṇa.

This root is intransitive (*akarmaka*) and has an agent who possesses consciousness (*citavat-kartṛka*). [This rule provides] the prescription for the causative suffix *ṇic* in the sense of "causing to do."

From the rule *budhādeḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.86), the mention of the causative suffix *ṇic* is carried over here, and that is specifically the causative *ṇic* used in the sense of "instigation" (*hetumaṇṇic*), because no other *ṇic* is possible after roots such as *budh*. Since the prescription of the instigatory *ṇic* applies, it is logical that its prohibition alone should follow by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*). As it has been stated:
Thus, that which partakes of an injunction must likewise partake of a prohibition,
due to proximity. For instance, when it is said, "Let the Brāhmaṇas enter, excluding those who study other [subjects]," the exclusion applies to those of the same kind for whom entry was enjoined.
The exclusion [of the *karmakartr̥*] is understood due to proximity. The printed reading is "ārohyamāṇaḥ";

however, it should be "ārohyamāṇam," with the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) by virtue of the rule *ṇer aṇau* (Pāṇini 1.3.67). Even though here the elephant is intended to be the instigator (*prayojaka*) with respect to the elephant-keepers, [the reflexive voice applies].

Although [the elephants] have been designated as such, nevertheless, in the state of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the elephant-drivers are not intended to be expressed as the prompted agents (*prayojya*); for otherwise, that which is the object in the non-causative (*aṇ*) would not be the agent in the causative (*ṇau*). In that case, when the status of being a prompted agent is not intended—having mounted...

The root *māṇ* itself has the meaning "he causes to mount"; when another person employs that [root] which is already causing [someone] to mount, then a second *ṇic* affix is introduced in the sense of a causal agent (*hetumat*). From that form ending in *ṇic*, the *ātmanepada* ending occurs by the rule *ṇicaśca* (Pāṇini 1.3.74). Therefore, the form *ārohayate* is indeed correct.
A counter-example.

89. *na pā-damy-āṅ-yama-saṃ-pari-muha-ruci-nṛti-vada-vasaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.89). Regarding the term *pā*, by the rule "when there is a choice between a root with a *luk*-suffix and one without, the one without the *luk*-suffix is taken" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 50), only the root *pā pāne* (Dhātupāṭha 925) is understood, and not the root *pā* [rakṣaṇe].

[This refers to] the root *rakṣ* (DhP 1056, meaning "to protect"). [The roots] *damu* (DhP 1203, "to pacify"), *yam* (DhP 984, "to cease"), and *yasu* (DhP 1210, "to strive")—these two are preceded by the prefix *ā*.
[The root] *muha* (DhP 1198, "to be bewildered") is preceded by *pari*, and [the root] *ruc* (DhP 745, "to shine").

The roots *nṛt* (DhP 1116) in the sense of "moving the limbs," *vad* (DhP 1009) in the sense of "distinct speech," and *vas* (DhP 1005) in the sense of "dwelling"— the inclusion of *vas* in the sense of "covering" does not occur here for the very reason stated previously. [This refers to] "by the two preceding rules."

The meaning is "in the interval. Regarding the statement "the root *nṛt* also has the sense of 'moving'," the word "also" (*api*) implies that it also has the sense of an agent possessing consciousness. Regarding "he causes to drink" (*pāyayate*), [the suffix] *yuk* is applied by Pāṇini 7.3.37: "After the roots *śā*, *chā*, *sā*, *hvā*, *vyā*, and *vep*, [the suffix *yuk* is added]. However, in the case of the root *pā* ("to drink"), when there is a desire to express its intransitive nature...

The *parasmaipada* ending occurs. In the case of "pālayati," the augment *luk* is applied by the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "the *luk* [elision] of the root *pā-* should be stated" (Vārttika 2 on Pāṇini 7.3.37). In "damayate," as before, the shortening [of the penultimate vowel] occurs by the rule "the short [vowel] for roots ending in -i, -u, and -ṛ" (Pāṇini 6.4.92).
Regarding "āyāmayate," one might object: "But surely, since the *pi*-affix is present here, there would be shortening [by 6.4.92]."

Since it must be so, he says: "The root *yam* is used in the sense of non-servitude. For in that context, the word "not" (*na*) is understood to follow from the rule "not for *kam*, *am*, and *cam*" (Gaṇasūtra on the list of roots). Regarding "āṅ":
this is a specific mention of the vowel *ā* characterized by the marker *ṅ*, for the purpose of indicating that it is a prefix (*upasarga*).

Therefore, there is no inclusion of that *ā* which resembles a prefix (*upasarga*). [The rule] "there is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of *dheṭ* among the *pā*-roots" uses the locative case in the sense of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*).
The word *upasaṃkhyāna* means "presentation" (*pratipādana*). [This applies to] *dheṭ* as it occurs within the scope of the *pā*-roots.

The establishment of the prohibition of the *parasmaipada* [voice] must be explained. The meaning is that this prohibition of the *parasmaipada*, which concerns the roots beginning with *pā*, applies to the root *dheṭ* as well. In this regard, the following explanation is given: the word "not" (*na*) is separated by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule), and by that, it applies to *dheṭ* as well.
There will be a prohibition. If this is so, since the result is already established by the word "na" (not) alone, is the mention of "pāda" and the others useless? It is not useless;
it is for the purpose of making known that the preceding rule does not apply to all cases. [The example] "dhāpayete" [is formed from] the root "dheṭ".

In *pāne*, the substitution of *ā* [for *ai*] occurs by the rule *ādeca upadeśe’śiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.45), and the augment *puk* is added as before. Regarding *śiśum*, the accusative case is used because [the child] receives the designation of object (*karman*) by the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārthaśabdakarmākarmakāṇām aṇikartā sa ṇau* (Pāṇini 1.4.52).
90. *vā kyaṣaḥ* | (1.3.90) Regarding the example "lohitāyati": in the sense of "that which was not red becomes red," the suffix *kyaṣ* is applied by the rule *lohitādi-ḍājbhyaḥ kyaṣ* (3.1.13).
The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *ṭhakṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.25). Regarding the form *paṭapaṭāyati*:

when the suffix *ḍāc* is to be applied to the word *paṭat*, there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*) by the supplementary rule *ḍāci bahulaṃ dve* (Vārttika 888), according to the rule *avyaktānukaraṇāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.57) and so forth.

By the rule *ḍāci nityamāmreḍite* (Pāṇini 6.1.100), regarding the final *t* of the word *paṭa* and the *p* that follows it—of these two, [the question is] "how? (*katham*). The meaning is "not in any way. He states the reason why [the desired form] is not obtained:

"Up to the point where it says ‘ṭhyāvatā’ etc."—for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is restricted by rules such as *anudātaṅtiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.12), and therefore it cannot be understood [as occurring] after a suffix ending in *kyaṣ*. He refutes this with the words "In that case, then... and so on; "optionally" (*vikalpitam*) means "alternatively" (*vibhāṣitam*).

The meaning is that it is optional (*pākṣika*). Now, one might object: since the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is excluded by the active voice (*parasmaipada*), it cannot be understood here because it is not present; to this, he says "And that," etc.
When the fruit of the action is intended to belong to the agent (*kartrabhiprāya*), the middle voice would apply, but [the rule] serves as an exception to that.

The *parasmaipada* ending is prescribed by two rules beginning with "ṭhamāvakarmakāt" (Pāṇini 1.3.88). An exception (*apavāda*) to that [prescription] was established by the immediately following rule; by that exception, which removes the *parasmaipada*, the *ātmanepada* is brought into proximity. Regarding this exception...

When [the suffix] has been removed, there must necessarily be an elision (*utsarga*). Thus, the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) brought to mind by this prohibition is connected here. If, then, by this rule the *ātmanepada* alone is optionally prescribed for the agent, how is the *parasmaipada* (active voice) accounted for in the alternative case?
He says that it is obtained with the words beginning with "by that" (tena), and so forth.
91. *dyaudbhyo luṅ* (1.3.91). Now, since the root *dyauti* is singular, one might object that its mention in the plural is not justified; to this he says:
"By association with that," and so forth. Just as by association with a single person carrying an umbrella, others [who are also carrying umbrellas] are understood...

Those who accompany him are called "those with umbrellas," as in the expression "those with umbrellas are going"; likewise here too, due to association with *dyauti*, the roots *śvit* and others are also designated as "*dyauta*. But how, when there is the designation of only one, is this intended meaning accomplished? To this he says:

Regarding the phrase "because of the mention in the plural," etc., he shows that this meaning is established even without the word "ādi" (and so forth). By the expression "ending with *kṛp*" (*kṛpūparyantāḥ*), he explains that those which are recited after *kṛp* do not belong to the *dyutādi* group. And this...

Immediately following that, it is understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, the completion of the section on the formation of *vṛt*—that [the rule applies] to "vyadyautat. Because it belongs to the *puṣādi* class, there is the suffix *aṅ*. If this is so, then since *aṅ* is prescribed for those very roots, the *parasmaipada* endings will follow from them; what is the purpose of this *yoga*? This is not the case; for by virtue of the indicative mark, it is obligatory.

The *luṅ* [suffix] is understood as *parasmaipada*. Furthermore, one might suspect that the *ātmanepada* does not occur in *luṅ* except in other cases. But surely, by the power of the assignment of the anudātta accent, it will not occur elsewhere? This is not so; for the assignment of the anudātta accent is for the sake of [the rule] "and from that which has an anudātta [indicatory vowel], beginning with a consonant" (*anudātetśca halādeḥ*).
Thus, it would have the sense of *yuj* (to join). Therefore, this rule (*yoga*) must be formulated. *Aluṭhat*.
[The roots] *ṭhruṭha* and *luṭha* mean "to strike against" (*pratīghāta*). (Dhātupāṭha 747, 749).
92. *vṛdbhyaḥ syasanoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.92).

Regarding the phrase *syasanoḥ*: this is a locative case (*saptamī*) used in the sense of "when [the suffixes] *sy* and *san* are present. In forms such as *vartsyati*, since the word *asici* is being carried over from the preceding rule *se'sici* (7.2.57), meaning "when there is no *sic*," the augment *iṭ* is applied after the root *gam*.

From the rule *parasmaipadeṣu* (7.2.58), the prohibition of *iṭ* applies by the rule *na vṛdbhyaścaturbhyaḥ* (7.2.59) when in the *parasmaipada*; however, in the *ātmanepada*, the *iṭ* augment indeed occurs. Thus we have *vivṛtsati*. Because the suffix is *kit* by the rule *halantācca* (1.2.10), there is an absence of *guṇa*.

93. *luṭi ca klṛpaḥ* | (1.3.93) Regarding the phrase "the letter *ṭh* [in the sūtra] then... and so forth: the intention is that since [the suffixes] *syat* and *san* would already be established by virtue of [the root *klṛp*] belonging to the *vṛt* group, this is a rule for optional application (*vikalpa*). With the words "if this is so then" (*evaṃ tarhi*) and so forth, a specific injunction (*viśeṣavidhāna*) [is made] regarding the general injunction (*sāmānyavidhāna*).

It is understood that it constitutes an annulment (*bādhaka*). But if this *prāpti* annuls the *prāpti* of *kṛp*, would it not follow that its recitation in the list beginning with *dyaut* is rendered purposeless? This is not so, because it serves a different purpose. But [one might object]: [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical flow of the argument.]
It is intended that the *svarita* accent applies to the word *syasanoḥ*; therefore, there will be no sublation of it.

This is true; however, the author of the Sūtras used the particle *ca* for the sake of variety, not for the sake of the *svarita* accent. Regarding the form *kalptā*: while the two governing rules (*adhikāra*) continue as before, [the suffix *tṛc* is applied].

There is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *ṭhtāsi ca klṛpaḥ* (7.2.60). The substitution of *ḍā* [for *ta*] occurs by the rule *ṭhluṭaḥ prathamasya ḍāraurasaḥ* (2.4.85). The change of *ra* to *la* occurs by the rule *ṭhkṛpo ro laḥ* (8.2.18), resulting in *ciklṛpsati*. As before, due to the *kit* designation, there is an absence of *guṇa* strengthening.
Thus ends the first chapter of the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who was a teacher of the Bodhisattvas.
The Third Pāda
Now begins the first chapter.
The Fourth Pāda. 1. *Ā kaḍārādekā saṃjñā* (P. 1.4.1).
[The word] “*yā parā*” [is understood]. Where there is a conflict, [the rule] “*vipratiṣedhe param*” (P. 1.4.2) applies.

It prevails by virtue of being an exception (*parā bhavati*). As for the statement, "And that which has no scope," even a technical term (*saṃjñā*) for which there is no scope anywhere proceeds by setting aside other technical terms because it is an exception. If this is so, then for this very reason there will be no co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of technical terms; therefore—

What is the purpose of the governing rule (adhikāra) for "one technical name" (ekasaṃjñā)? This is not so; for it is only when there is a conflict that something can function as an exception (apavāda).

Conflict, however, is precisely contradiction, and such contradiction occurs only when the governing rule for "one technical name" exists, not when it does not. For instance, in cases where the governing rule for "one technical name" is absent, [there is no conflict].
There is no contradiction at all, as in the case of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for suffixes (*pratyaya*) and so forth;

rather, a conflict arises only when this governing rule (*adhikāra*) is present. And when such a conflict exists, by the statement "in case of conflict, the latter [prevails]," the subsequent rule takes effect, because it is an exception (*apavāda*) and is thus without occasion (*anavakāśa*).
Therefore, this designation (*adhikāra*) must be established.

If that is so, then in the case of the technical name *aṅ*, the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the designations *bh* and *pada* must be stated—[as in] *bābhravyaḥ* and *dhānuṣkaḥ*. [The former is derived] from the word *babhru* by [the rule] *madhubabhvrorbrāhmaṇakauśikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.106).
Thus, regarding *yañ*: because it is a *bha*-stem, there is *guṇa* substitution by Pāṇini 6.4.146 (*ṭhorguṇaḥ*); because it is an *aṅga*, there is initial *vṛddhi*;

and therein, by Pāṇini 6.1.79 (*vānto yi pratyaye*), there is the substitution of *av*. Furthermore, from the word *dhanus*, [the form] *dhanuṣka* is derived by adding *ṭhak* according to Pāṇini 4.4.57 (*tadasya praharaṇam*), and then *ka* by Pāṇini 7.3.51 (*isusuktāntāt kaḥ*).
By [Pāṇini 7.3.51], there is the substitution of *ka*; here, because it is a *pada*, there is the substitution of *ṣ* by [Pāṇini 8.3.39].

Since it is an *aṅga*, the initial *vṛddhi* need not be stated. From [Pāṇini 1.3.90], *vā* is understood to carry over; and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, in some cases...
"There will be a convergence of designations. "Elsewhere" means in both common usage and in technical treatises. First, in common usage:

the convergence of designations is observed in such cases as Indra, Śukra, and Purandara. In technical treatises as well: [the convergence of] suffixes, primary suffixes (*kṛt*), and secondary suffixes (*kṛtya*). It is the same elsewhere.

This [designation] might also apply here due to the overlapping of designations; therefore, this rule is for the purpose of restriction so that there may be only one designation. For example: *bhidi* and *cchidi*. The scope of the short designation (*laghu-saṃjñā*) is as follows. Its purpose, however, is seen in forms such as *bhetā* and *chetā*, by virtue of the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya* (Pāṇini 7.3.86).
This is an instance of the [mutual] application of both [technical names]. Regarding the term *guṇa*: "śikṣirbhikṣiḥ. This is the scope for the designation *guru*.
The purpose [of this designation] is seen in "śikṣā" and "bhikṣā," where the suffix *a* is applied by the rule *gurośca halaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.103).
However, the designation *laghu* does not apply here because there is no purpose for it. In this case, both [designations] would otherwise apply.

In the forms *atatakṣat* and *ararakṣat*, the designation *guru* (heavy) applies because of their subsequent position. [The roots are] *takṣū* and *tvakṣū* in the sense of "making thin" (DhP 6.55, 6.56), and *rakṣa* in the sense of "protecting" (DhP 6.58).
