[The derivation is as follows: the causative suffix *ṇic* is added in the sense of agency (*hetu*), followed by *luṅ* (the aorist marker), *cleścaṅ* (the substitution of *caṅ* for *cli*), the elision of *ṇi*, and finally the application of *caṅ* (Pāṇini 6.1.11).

The repetition of the word [is for this purpose]: if the designation *laghu* were to apply here, then by the rule *sanvallaghuni* (Pāṇini 7.4.93), there would be the treatment as *san* (the reduplication of the root *san*), and so forth. Since that [designation] does not exist, it does not occur; thus he says: "In the case of *sanvallaghuni*" and so on. "This rule" refers to the rule concerning the treatment as *san*. Of the subsequent...
This example has been stated. Now, that which provides no [other] occasion is being explained: "ayante yonirṛtviyaḥ.

[The word] *ṛtu* means "that which has arrived"; from this, by the rule *ṛtoraṇ* (Pāṇini 5.1.105), and then by *chandasi ghas* (5.1.106), the suffix *ghas* is applied; when the substitution of *iy* for *gha* is made, by the rule *siti ca* (1.4.16) [the preceding vowel becomes long].
Both the designation *pada* would apply and the designation *bha* [would apply] by the rule *ṭhyaci bham* (Pāṇini 1.4.18);

however, because it is without scope (*anavakāśatva*), the designation *pada* alone prevails. If the designation *bha* were to apply, then the *guṇa* substitution [of *o* for *au*] would occur by the rule *orguṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.146).

The term *bha-saṃjñā* finds its scope in examples such as *aupagava*. The inclusion of the limit "up to *kaḍāra*" (*ā kaḍārāt*) is for the sake of variety; otherwise, he would have simply said "from *ṭha* up to *dvandva*. For there is no purpose in prescribing a single technical designation (*eka-saṃjñā*) beyond *dvandva* up to *kaḍāra*.
For it is because of this that the grasping of such a limit becomes purposeful.
2. *vipratiṣedhe paraṃ kāryam* (Pāṇini 1.4.2).
"Conflict is *vipratiṣedha*," because the word *vipratiṣedha* is well-known in common usage as denoting opposition. For instance, when contradictory things are stated, speakers say:
They say: "This which is stated is contradictory"; that is understood to mean "contrary.
To show the scope of that contradiction, he says "where," and so forth. "Prasaṅgau" means two applications or two injunctions. "Anyārthau" means having different objects or scopes.
Those two for whom there is a purpose are described as such; the meaning is that they have achieved their ends in another object or domain.

Regarding the word "ekasmin" (in one): it means non-different. "Simultaneously" means at one and the same moment. The word "sa" (that) is connected with the word "vipratiṣedha" (contradiction). That contradiction is "vipratiṣiddha," which refers to the domain of contradiction.

This is the meaning. Because it is the object of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the term "conflict" is used here to indicate the object by means of the subject; for neither a contingency (*prasaṅga*) nor its substratum can constitute a conflict. [Conflict is] "a contradiction between two things of equal strength."

Thus [it is said]. The term *virodha* (contradiction) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which there is a contradiction between two things of equal strength. This explanation is made by relying on the view that the word refers to a *jāti* (universal). However, in the view that the word refers to a *dravya* (substance), this is the distinction: *anyārthau* means "those two whose purpose (*artha*)—that is, their objective (*prayojana*)—is different (*anya*), hence they are 'having different purposes'. The rest [is as before].
It is the same. Furthermore, in the rule "vipratiṣedhe," this locative case is used in the sense of "when [two rules] exist simultaneously" (satī saptamī).

This refers to cases such as "the general rule and the exception" (*utsargāpavāda*). Where there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), that is the scope of application for this *yoga* (rule). And a conflict occurs only between two rules of equal strength.

"Not between two [rules] of unequal strength. This has been explained by the author himself through the passage beginning with "for where two [rules] apply to different purposes," which demonstrates its scope. Since there is no equality of strength in cases such as general rules (*utsarga*) and exceptions (*apavāda*), that [principle of equal strength] does not apply to this *yoga*.

The scope [of the general rule] is such that it remains powerful therein; there, the general rule (*utsarga*) operates. For example: *ārdhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.35), because the suffix *iṭ* is prescribed for any *valādi* [suffix] in general. A specific rule (*viśeṣa*) is an exception (*apavāda*), as in: *neḍ vaśi* (Pāṇini 7.2.8).

Because of the rule *kṛti* (Pāṇini 7.2.8), which prohibits the augment *iṭ* when a *kṛt* suffix follows, this prohibition is prescribed specifically for those *kṛt* suffixes beginning with *vaś* that follow a consonant (*val*). That which is prescribed for a specific case is more powerful; for instance, in the injunction "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas, but buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya," the specific prescription [for Kauṇḍinya] prevails.
The gift of *takra* (buttermilk) will serve as an exception (*bādhaka*) precisely to the general rule regarding the gift of curd (*dadhi*).

Therefore, even when a *kṛt* suffix follows, the augment *iṭ* does not occur; rather, there is simply a prohibition—as in the case of the rule "after the roots *sthā*, *īś*, *bhās*, *pis*, and *kas*, the suffix *varac* [is applied]" (Pāṇini 3.2.175), resulting in the form *īśvara*.

Between two rules, one that is permanent (*nitya*) is stronger than one that is non-permanent (*anitya*). For example, the substitution of *ais* by "bhisa ais" (Pāṇini 7.1.9) [is stronger]. For that [substitution] applies whether the substitution of *et* by "bahuvacane jhalyet" (7.3.103) has been performed or not; even when it has not been performed, *ais* is applied to the suffix *bhisa* because of its reference to the state of having previously ended in the vowel *a*.
[The rule is] established on the grounds that it has been prescribed. Furthermore, a rule that applies whether [an operation] has already taken place or not is considered obligatory (*nitya*).
And so, he will say there (Pāṇini 7.1.9):
"If the substitution of *et* occurs in the case of *bhis* because it is subsequent, then where will the substitution of *ais* take place?"

Even when the substitution of *ait* has been applied, the [suffix] *nitya* would still apply by virtue of the priority of the original form (*bhautapūrvya*). This being the case, [the rule] is as follows.

Thus, that [rule] is eternal (*nitya*). However, the substitution of *ai* for *e* does not obtain; for the cause [of the rule], namely the suffix beginning with *jhal*, has been prescribed. The scope for the substitution of *ā* for *e* is in cases such as *vṛkṣeṣu*; and since that [scope] exists, it is improper to resort to the consideration of what existed previously (*bhūtapūrvagati*). Therefore, that [substitution of *ai*] is non-eternal (*anitya*). And whatever is non-eternal...

That which depends on the existence or non-existence of another is weak; by contrast, that which is constant is always strong. Therefore, in the case of *vṛkṣaiḥ*, the substitution of *ait* does not occur for the following vowel; rather, only the elision (*aisbhāva*) takes place.

Between the internal (*antaraṅga*) and the external (*bahiraṅga*), the internal is stronger; this is observed from worldly experience itself. For in the world, having risen in the morning, one first performs internal tasks such as washing the face, and only afterwards performs external tasks such as going to the king’s palace.

He begins to perform his duties. This should also be understood in the case of grammatical treatises (*śāstra*). [For example: "He whose desire is for heaven" is *dyaukāmaḥ*; his offspring is *dyaukāmiḥ*, according to the rule *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95).

Although the suffix *iñ* is prescribed after the word *dyaukāma*, nevertheless, the followers of Pāṇini maintain that "those who have performed their internal rearrangements do not undo what has already been established."

(Vyā.pa.84) It is said that even a rule already applied is set aside: in the analytical exposition (*anvākhyāna*), when the form *div-kāma-iñ* has been established, once the substitution of *u* by *div-ut* (P.
6.1.131) has taken place, the *yaṇ* substitution would then apply; however, because of its higher status, the rule *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ* (P. 7.2.117) prevails.
Does [the rule for] *vṛddhi* apply? No; because it is *antaraṅga*, the substitution of *yaṇ* is performed first, and only afterwards does the *vṛddhi* of the vowel *u* take place.

The status of *yaṇ*-substitution as *antaraṅga* is due to its dependence on the phonemes (*varṇa*), whereas *vṛddhi* is *bahiraṅga* because it depends on the external secondary suffix (*taddhita*). [This is according to the principle: "An internal operation (*āṅga*) is stronger than one based on phonemes (*vārṇa*)."
This [rule] does not apply here because of their having different bases (*vyāśrayatvāt*).

Regarding the phrase "in the case of non-application," etc.: when the position is that "the form (*ākṛti*) is the word-meaning," then, since the two rules have already served their purpose elsewhere, there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between them.

Due to mutual obstruction, non-occurrence itself results; for example— just as if here there were a single servant belonging to two [masters] of equal strength, and they both sent him simultaneously with tasks in different directions, then if he were one who desires to avoid conflict:

In that case, the operation of both [definitions] would not apply to the effect (*kārya*). However, since a definition operates upon each individual instance (*vyakti*) within a substance (*dravya*) as a category (*padārtha*), it follows that the two definitions would operate alternately because neither has fulfilled its purpose—
just as, for example, there is an alternation in the act of eating among Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and others who do not eat simultaneously at a single vessel.

It may be so. Since the purpose [of the rule] is fulfilled when the word-meaning is the genus (*jāti*), this is commenced for the sake of a prescription regarding the occurrence of doubling (*dvirvacana*): "When there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the subsequent operation takes effect.
In that case, if something is already established and the prior operation would also apply, that too indeed occurs. Regarding this, it is said:

Furthermore, it is established through the understanding of the context (*prasaṅga*). However, since the two rules would otherwise apply alternately because the individual word-meaning (*vyakti*) has not yet fulfilled its purpose, this [sūtra] is for the sake of restriction:
"In the case of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the subsequent rule alone takes effect, not the preceding one. To that end, the following is stated:
"In a conflict between two rules that apply simultaneously, that which is sublated remains sublated" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 40).
3. Feminine stems ending in *ī* and *ū* are called *nadī*. (Pāṇini 1.4.3)

Regarding the statement "ī ca ū ca yū," one might object: "Since [the rule] *dīrghāj jasi ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.105) prohibits the substitution of a single long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) for the first two cases (*prathamayoḥ*), and since the *yaṇ* substitution would then apply, the form should be *yvau*. How then can there be the designation *yū*? To this he replies: "This is a designation without case-endings (*avibhaktika*)."

Because the case-ending (*vibhakti*) has been elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39), there is no case-ending present in this [word]; thus it is called *avibhaktika*. Regarding the phrase *stryākhyau*, it means "those two which denote a female. Now, one might object: once the suffix *aṇ* is applied by *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1) and the augment *yuk* is added by *āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.33), [the form would be different].

It should have been stated as *stryākhyau* [nominative dual]; how then can it be *stryākhyau* [accusative dual]? If it is argued that this form arises when the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3), we say no; for in this case, the root *cakṣiṅ* is accompanied by a prefix (*sopasarga*). Therefore, he says:
Regarding the phrase "because of the observation of *mūlavibhuja* and others": the suffix *ka* is also desired after words such as *mūlavibhuja*.

Accordingly, he will state in the third chapter, in the section on the suffix *ka*: "An addition [to the rule] for *mūlavibhuja* and others" (*vā.* 232). By this, [the rule] "the two [stems] called feminine... applies to the word [in question].
The suffix *ka* is seen in formations such as *mūlavibhuja*.

Is this designation (*saṃjñā*) prescribed here for the words *idam* and *etad* themselves, or for those that end in them? If the first alternative were adopted, it would not apply to feminine forms ending in *kṛt* suffixes—such as "O Lakṣmī" (*he lakṣmi*) or "O Yavāgū" (*he yavāgvi*).

For in this context, it is the *samudāyas* (composite wholes) that are designated as feminine, not the vowels *ī* and *ū* themselves. Having observed this defect in the first position (*pakṣa*), he resorts to the second position and says: "ending in *ī* or *ū*" and so forth.

But surely, because of the inclusion of the word *anta* ("end") in the rule *suptiṅantaṃ padam* (Pāṇini 1.4.14), [the designation applies] elsewhere in the formulation of technical terms (*saṃjñāvidhi*)...
When a suffix is mentioned, the rule of "inclusion of that which ends with it" (tadantavidhi) is not obtained; this is not a fault.

Since the author teaches the prohibition in the rule "neyaṅvaṅsthānau" (Pāṇini 1.4.4), that indicates: "In this section, the inclusion of that which ends with [the specified element] does occur. Otherwise, the prohibition would be purposeless.
It may be so. For it is not merely the vowels *i*, *u*, and *ū* that are called feminine (*stryākhyā*) and possess the *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* substitutes;
rather, it is those [stems] which end in them. For example: *kumārī*. Here, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule "ṅīṣ in the first age" (Pāṇini 4.1.20). *Gaurī*.
Here, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule "from [stems ending in] *ṣit* roots and from *gaura*-etc. (Pāṇini 4.1.41). *Śārkaravī*. Here...

‘The suffix *ṅīn* is applied after [stems ending in] *śāra*, *cāru*, and *vādya*’ (Pāṇini 4.1.73). Regarding the word ‘*lakṣmīḥ*’: from the root ‘*lakṣa* in the sense of seeing or marking’ (Dhātupāṭha 1538), while the rule ‘the suffix *ī* after *avitṛ*, *tṛ*, and *tantri*’ (Daiva-Uṇādi 1.82) is being carried over, [the rule] ‘*muṭ* is added to *lakṣi*, and by the word *ca* (and), the vowel *ī* as well’ (Daiva-Uṇādi 1.84) applies. Regarding ‘*brahmabandhūḥ*’: [it is formed similarly].

The suffix *ūṅ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.66] *ūṅutaḥ*. The letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of specification in [Pāṇini 6.1.175] *ṅnoṅdhātvoḥ*. Regarding the form *yavāgūḥ*: from the root *yū* in the sense of "mixing" (Dhātupāṭha 1033), the suffix *āgūc* is applied by [Daiva 10.4] *suyūvacibhyo'nyujāgūjakÂnuc*.

These are examples of feminine bases (*rūpa*). However, the effect [of the rule] is seen in cases such as *ṭhambārthanadyorhrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.107). In the forms *mātre* and *duhitre*, because the designation *nadī* (feminine noun ending in long /ī/ or /ū/) does not apply, the rule *āṇ nadyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.112) [does not apply].

Thus, it does not occur [in these cases]: *grāmaṇīḥ*, *khalapūḥ*. These two function as masculine. Therefore, because the designation *nadi* is absent, the shortening [of the vowel] prescribed by "the short vowel is substituted for the final of *ambā-artha* and *nadī*" (Pāṇini 7.3.107) does not take place. [The forms] *grāmaṇīḥ* and *khalapūḥ* are derived from the roots √nī and √pū with the suffix *kvip* according to "after the roots √sad, √sū, √dviṣ, etc. (Pāṇini 3.2.61).

The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *agragrāmābhyāñca* (Kātyāyana-vārttika 5064). In the word *khalaṃ punāti*, the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 3.2.178). In the phrase *grāmaṇye striyai*, the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs by the rule *eranekāco 'saṃyogapūrvasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.82). [In the word] *khalapve*...

Regarding the word *strī*: here too, by the rule *oḥ supi* (Pāṇini 6.4.83), the feminine gender (*strītva*) is expressed by the word *strī* through its connection with another word [in a compound]; therefore, the designation *nadī* does not apply, and consequently, the substitution of *āṭ* does not occur.
However, in the case of words such as *iṣu* and *aśani*, which possess both genders, the feminine gender is inherent in the very meaning of the word itself.

The designation *nadī* (feminine stem) indeed applies [to words like] *iṣvī* and *aśanī*. If the *nadī* designation were not to apply when femininity is expressed by another word (*padāntara*), then in the case of *paṭvī striyāḥ*, since the word *paṭu* is observed to denote a male as well, the femininity here would be expressed by another word; consequently, the *nadī* designation would not apply.

This is not so; for there are two types of words. In some cases, for a word whose application is suspected to be general, another word excludes other denotable objects of that generality, as in the case of the word *go* (cow) among cows, horses, and so forth, where [the word] *gauḥ vāk* (the cow is speech) [functions]. In other cases...
It functions only in its primary sense, as in "the Vāhīka is a cow" (gaur vāhīkaḥ).

In this case, the fact that a general term such as "cow" (go) is restricted to a specific instance through its connection with another word is already included within the word itself; therefore, it is not excluded by the mention of the term "verbal expression" (ākhyā).

However, the application of the feminine gender to the word *grāmaṇī* is effected by another word and is not excluded [by its own form]. Therefore, it is set aside by the mention of the term *ākhyā* (designation). But for these two [words, *grāmaṇī* and *paṭu*], since they are conventional action-words (*kriyāśabda*), their primary application is in the masculine. As for the word *paṭu*:
There is a distinction [between the two types of *yū*]: that which brings about clarity (*pāṭava*) applies even to the primary [vowels] in another [context].
4. *neyaṅuvaṅsthānāvastrī* (Pāṇini 1.4.4):
"Those *yū* which are in the place of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are not designated as *nadī*, provided they are not [the feminine suffix] *strī*. This is stated by way of the *yū*.
This prohibition is understood to apply to [the vowels] *y* and *v* when they occur at the end of a word, and not to them alone, because there is no possibility [of their occurrence in that state].

For *y* and *v* do not exist as feminine names (*stryākhyau*) when they are isolated—as in "he *śrīḥ*" or "he *bhrūḥ*. Since the designation *nadī* (feminine noun) is absent here, the rule "a short vowel is substituted for [the final vowel] of a monosyllabic word ending in *am*, and for a *nadī* [ending]" does not apply.

Thus, by [Pāṇini 7.3.107], the short vowel does not occur. From the root *śriñ* in the sense of "service" (*sevāyām*) [Dhātupāṭha 897], the form *śrīḥ* arises when the suffix *kvip* is applied and lengthening is performed according to the Vārttika: "In the case of *kvip*, there is lengthening for *vac*, *pracch*, *śri*, *sru*, *dru*, *pru*, and *jū*, as well as the absence of *samprasāraṇa*. [The root] *bhramu* means "unsteadiness."

From the root *bhram* (DhP 1205), by applying the suffix *ḍūa* according to *bhramerḍūaḥ* (DaU 1.177), and with the elision of the *ṭi*-portion, the form *bhrū* is obtained. Since both [of these forms] undergo the substitution of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* by the rule *aci śnudhātu...* (Pāṇini 6.4.77) and so forth, they are designated as *iy-uv-sthāna*. Thus, the two vowels [ī and ū] are those that stand in the place of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*.

Regarding the word *strī*: [the root] *styai* (DhP 911) and *ṣṭyai* (DhP 910) mean "to sound" and "to congeal. By the rule *ādeca upadeśe 'śiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.45), there is the substitution of *ā*; from the root *styāyati*, the suffix *ḍraṭ* is added. By the rule *ṭeḥ* (6.4.155), the final syllable (*ṭi*) is elided. Then, by the rule *lopo vyor vali* (6.1.66), the *v* of the suffix is elided.

The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...* (Pāṇini 4.1.15). Since there is no prohibition of the designation *nadī* (feminine noun) in this case, the shortening [of the vowel] indeed takes place. Because the word *strī* has the substitution of *iyaṅ* prescribed by the rule *striyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.79), the long *ī* is in the position of *iyaṅ*.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *sthāna* (place/position)? If it is argued that it is so that a prohibition may apply to those [sounds] having the same place as *iy*, *u*, and *vaṅ*, we say no; for if this were the intended purpose, one should have simply said "of *iy*, *u*, and *vaṅ*" (*iyUvaṅeḥ*). Even so, the meaning remains the same: those two *y*s which are related to *iy*, *u*, and *vaṅ*.

The designation "nadī" does not apply to those two. And which are those two related [yū] that belong to them? They are those which have *iy* and *uv* as their substitutes (*pratyādeśa*). Even without the mention of the word "sthāna" (substitute), it will be understood that the prohibition applies to those having *iy* and *uv* as their substitutes. This, then, is the case: [The sūtra: *na yvābhyāṃ padāntābhyām ajvābhyām* (P. 1.4.3). [The commentary: Why is this stated? Because otherwise, the designation "nadī" would apply even to *yū* that occur at the end of a word (*padānta*) when followed by vowels other than *a*. For example, in *kṣīre*, *mātre*, *dhenvai*, *dhenve*, *dhenyoḥ*, and *dhenūnām*, the designation "nadī" would undesirably apply to the *yū* [i.e., *e* and *o*]. Therefore, it is stated: "not after *y* and *v* that stand at the end of a word. But what about *yū* that do not stand at the end of a word? [In that case, the designation "nadī"] applies. For example, in *kṣīrayoḥ*, *mātṛyoḥ*, *dhenvoḥ*, and *dhenūnām*. But what about *yū* that occur in the middle of a word (*padamadhyastha*)? [In that case, the designation "nadī"] applies. For example, in *kṣīrasya*, *mātuḥ*, *dhenvām*, and *dhenūnām*. But what about *yū* that occur at the beginning of a word (*padādista*)? [In that case, the designation "nadī"] applies. For example, in *yuvām*, *yuṣmān*, *yuvābhyām*, and *yuṣmabhyam*. But what about *yū* that occur in the middle of a word (*padamadhyastha*)? [In that case, the designation "nadī"] applies. For example, in *yuvām*, *yuṣmān*, *yuvābhyām*, and *yuṣmabhyam*. But what about *yū* that occur in the middle of a word (*padamadhyastha*)? [In that case, the designation "nadī"] applies. For example, in *yuvayoḥ*, *yuṣmākam*, *yuvayoḥ*, and *yuṣmāsu*. But what about *yū* that occur at the end of a word (*padāntastha*)? [In that case, the designation "nadī"] applies. For example, in *yuvām*, *yuṣmān*, *yuvābhyām*, and *yuṣmabhyam*. But what about *yū* that occur in the middle of a word (*padamadhyastha*)? [In that case, the designation "nadī"] applies. For example, in *yuvayoḥ*, *yuṣmākam*, *yuvayoḥ*, and *

The purpose of employing the term *sthāna* (place/substratum) is so that the prohibition may apply where there is the presence or actual occurrence (*abhinivṛtti*) of *iyaṅ* and *vaṅ*, but not where those two are superseded by an exception (*apavāda*). For example: *ādhyai* and *varṣābhvai*. [The root] *dhyai* is used in the sense of "thinking" (Dhātupāṭha 908).

The suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *anyebhyo’pi dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 3.2.178), and there is also vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). Indeed, the inclusion of the term *dṛśi* [in that sūtra] serves to incorporate other rules; for it has been stated that in some cases there is lengthening, and in others reduplication.

He will state [later] that "there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) for the root *dhyai*" (Vārttika 292). For that which has undergone vocalization, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs in the singular dative case by the rule "for a word with more than one vowel, the final phoneme is replaced" (6.4.82), and so forth.
The same applies to the word *varṣābhū*, by the rule "and for *varṣābhū*" (6.4.84).

5. vā''mi | (1.4.5) Even though there is similarity in their phonetic form (*saṃhitā*), the term *ām* refers to the genitive plural ending, and not to the accusative singular; for in that case, the grammatical operation (*kārya*) pertaining to the designation *nadī* does not apply. Nor...

The *ām* [ending] of the seventh case is what is intended here; for that [ending] receives the designation *nadī* subsequently, because the rule "ReĀrāmnadyāmnībhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.116) prescribes the addition of *ām*. In the example "śrīṇātra," the augment *nuṭ* is applied according to the rule "hrasvanadyāpo nuṭ" (Pāṇini 7.1.54) when the *nadī* designation applies. In this case...
The phrase "designated as feminine" (*stryākhyāt*) carries over [from the previous rule], and since this designation *nadī* is prescribed in connection with case-endings (*vibhakti*),

it is logical that the *nadī* designation applies only to a word-form designated as feminine when it is connected with a case-ending. Therefore, where only a part [of the word] is designated as feminine, the *nadī* designation does not apply— as in *atiśriyam*.
Of the Brahmins; that is, of those Brahmins whose eyebrows meet.

6. *ṅiti hrasvaśca* (1.4.6). If the term *yū* were not carried over here as a qualifier for "short" (*hrasva*), then it would apply here as well—namely, in the case of *mātre* and *duhitre*; therefore, it is carried over here.

If that which follows were to follow as having the nominative case-ending (*prathamānta*), then the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) between the two nominative forms regarding the shortening (*hrasvatva*) would not be possible. Therefore, by virtue of the sense of the context, it arises here with the genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*); hence he says: "And [the shortening applies] to *y* and *v*."

"Related to them. But which short vowel is related to those two? It is that short vowel which is homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with them; by implication, this refers to the vowels *i* and *u*, for no other short vowel can be homogeneous with *ī* and *ū*. [Examples: "kṛtyai," "kṛtaye. This is when the designation *nadī* applies.

In that case, it is as previously stated; otherwise, however, because [the word] is designated as *dhi* by the rule "the remainder is *dhi*, except for *sakhi*" (Pāṇini 1.4.7), the *guṇa* substitution applies according to "for a *ghi* stem, before a suffix beginning with a *ṅ*" (7.3.111). Here too, wherever a portion of the word-form associated with a case-ending is feminine in gender, the procedure follows the method previously described.
The designation "river" does not apply [to the following]: *atikṛtaye brāhmaṇāya* and *atiśriye*.

7. *śeṣo ghy-asakhi* (Pāṇini 1.4.7). Regarding the word *sakhyā*: because of the designation *ghi*, the substitution of *nā* [for *ā*] by the rule *āṅe nāstriyām* (7.3.120) does not occur. Furthermore, in the forms *sakhye* and *sakhyuḥ*, there is no *guṇa* substitution by the rule *gher ṅiti* (7.3.111).

In the case of *sakhyau*, the substitution of *ā* prescribed by *ṭhacca gheḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.119) does not occur; rather, the substitution of *au* prescribed by *idudbhyām* (7.3.117) and *āṬt* (7.3.118) takes place. Regarding *sakhyuḥ* as well, it has been stated that [the rule] *khyatyāt parasya* (6.1.112) applies. Here, in the case of *susakhī*—meaning "one who has a good friend"—[the same principles apply].

In the case of *susakher āgacchati*, a prohibition would apply by means of the rule for extension to what ends in such [a stem] (*tadantavidhi*); however, that does not occur because of the prohibition:

"There is no extension to what ends in [a word] when the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is accompanied by a suffix that causes elision" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 89). Here, the designation *ghi* is of two kinds: that which depends on the constituent part (*avayavāśrayā*), and...

And it is based on a collection. Among those, that which is based on the individual parts is prohibited, whereas that which is based on the collection certainly exists; for there is no prohibition of the latter.

8. *patiḥ samāsa eva* (1.4.8). [The commentary says: "When the designation *ghisamjñā* for the word *pati* has been established. The remainder [of the meaning] is: "by the immediately preceding rule itself. [In the example] *prajāpatinā*, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). If [the designation] were already established...

Since this [rule] is commenced under the heading of the notion of "option" (*ghisaṃjñā*), then—as it is said, "When something is already established, its restatement is for the purpose of restriction" (*du.si.kā.sū.vṛ*.

59)—the restriction is indeed obtained even without the particle *eva*. Therefore, he asks: "For what purpose is the particle *eva* employed? and answers with the words "The employment of the particle *eva*" and so forth. Without...

By means of the particle *eva*, even the opposite might be suspected—that the husband alone is the wife—and consequently, [the rule] would not apply in cases such as *dṛḍhamuṣṭinā*; however, when the particle *eva* is present, it does apply. For thus, the employment of the particle *eva* immediately after the word *samāsa*—
In that case, the restriction applies elsewhere; thus, it is the word *pati* alone that is restricted, not the compound.
9. *ṣaṣṭhīyuktaśchandasi vā* (Pāṇini 1.4.9).

In this context, if the intended meaning were that the word *pati*, when ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and joined [with another word], becomes *ghi* and *jña*, then the inclusion of the term *yukta* ("joined") would be purposeless.

One should say "the sixth [case]. Therefore, when there is a connection with another word ending in the sixth case, the meaning understood is "connected with that," which is why he says: "by one ending in the sixth case," and so forth. Furthermore, if the word *pati* (husband) ending in the sixth case were to receive the technical designation *ghisamjñā*, what would happen then?
The substitution [of *paśya* for *pāhi*] would occur in that very case, but it would not occur here: *kruñcānām apataye namaḥ*.

In the phrase *mayā patyā*, the word *pati* is joined with the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*). Here, the substitute *mā* occurs for the entire form ending in *map* of the pronoun *asmad* by the rule *asmado maparyantasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.91), and *tvam* and *mā* are substituted in the singular by the rule *tvamāvekavacane* (Pāṇini 7.2.97). This is according to the rule *yo 'ci* (Pāṇini 7.2.89).
The letter *ya*.

10. *hrasvaṃ laghu* | (1.4.10) In the case of *bhetā*, there is *guṇa* substitution by [Pāṇini 7.3.86]: *pugantalaghūpadhasya ca*. In *acīkarat*: *kṛñ* with *ṇic*, *luṅ* [augment], *aṭ* augment, *caṅ* for *cli*, and elision of *ṇi*; [then] *ṇau*...

The shortening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *caṅy upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.1). The statement *oḥ puyaṇjyapare* (Pāṇini 7.4.80) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that what is performed in relation to the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivat*). By the rule *caṅ* (Pāṇini 6.1.11), the word *kṛś* is reduplicated. Then, by the rule *urat* (Pāṇini 7.4.66), the substitution of *u* occurs, followed by the substitution of *r* for the semivowel (*raparatva*).

When the designation "light" (*laghu*) applies by the rule *sanvallaghuni* (Pāṇini 7.4.93), there is the substitution of *i* due to the treatment as *san*-like (*sanvadbhāva*), and then lengthening by the rule *dīrgho laghoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.94).
11. A heavy syllable (*guru*) [is defined as having a long vowel or being followed by a consonant cluster].
(Pāṇini 1.4.11) Examples: *kuṇḍā*, *huṇḍā*. [The roots] *kuḍi* (to burn) [DhP 270] and *huḍi* (to heap together) [DhP 269] [are cited].

Because of the rule stating that [a root] "behaves like its original form" (*upadeśivad-bhāva*) when the augment *num* is prescribed, the *num* occurs precisely at the stage of the original form (*upadeśāvasthā*).

Regarding the words ‘śikṣā’ and ‘bhikṣā’: the suffix *akāra* is applied [to the root] according to Pāṇini 3.3.103, ‘śikṣa vidyopādāne’ (to learn/acquire knowledge), and the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied according to 4.1.4, ‘ajādyataṣṭāp’.

12. And [the suffix] *dīrgha* [is applied]. (Pāṇini 1.4.12) Examples are: *īhāñcakre* and *uhāñcakre*. These two have been explained in the rule beginning with *āmpratyayavat* (1.3.63). However, the grammatical operation (*kārya*) in this case, when there is a heavy designation (*gurusaṃjñā*), is as follows: *ṭhijādeśca gurumato'nṛcchaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.36).
(3.1.36) Thus ends the section on the conviction regarding the self.

13. That which begins with the element for which a suffixal rule (*pratyayavidhi*) is prescribed is called an *aṅga* (stem) when that suffix follows. (Pāṇini 1.4.13) The word ‘kartā’ is the periphrastic future (*luṭ*). [Examples: ‘kariṣyati’ and ‘akariṣyat’, which are the periphrastic future (*luṭ*) and the conditional (*lṛṅ*). Here, the grammatical operation resulting from the designation *aṅga* is [the substitution of *guṇa*] by the rule ‘sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ’ (Pāṇini 7.3.84).

The augment *iṭ* is applied as appropriate by [Pāṇini 7.2.70]: "There is the augment *iṭ* after roots ending in long *ṝ* or *ṛ* before the suffix *sya*. Regarding the statement, "The word *yasmāt* is for the purpose of indicating the technical name (*saṃjñin*)," this means that the indication of the technical name is its purpose;
thus it is so described. Now, one might object: since the technical name is indicated here by the word *tadādi*, how [is it that *yasmāt* indicates it]?
Anticipating the objection that this is for the purpose of indicating the name (*saṃjñinirdeaśārtha*), he says—

“because of its connection with that and the following”— in order to show the reason why the phrase "from which" (*yasmāt*) serves to indicate the name. This is because, when the word "from which" is present, it refers to this subject under discussion.

The connection of the term "beginning with that" (*tadādi*) is as follows: that which is the beginning (*ādi*) of that after which the suffix is prescribed is called "beginning with that. For if this were not stated, with what would the pronoun *tat*—which refers back to what has been previously mentioned—be connected? This [objection] is untenable; for it is thus:

If the designation *aṅga* were to apply when a suffix follows [the element] beginning with the *pratyaya*, then in forms such as *kariṣyāvaḥ* and *kariṣyāmaḥ*, the *guṇa* substitution for the verbal root (*dhātu*) would not occur. Therefore, in order to specify the designated element (*saṃjñin*), the word "from that" (*tasmāt*) must be stated; for only when this connection is established [does the rule function correctly].

By the phrase "beginning with that" (*tadādi*), that which is intended here as the qualified designatum (*saṃjñin*) can be specified; otherwise, it could not be. In the rule *nerviśaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.17), the prescription applies to the prefix (*upasarga*), because this is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding the prefix and not regarding the suffix (*pratyaya*); for that [suffix] is prescribed by another grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇāntara*).

The rule *‘nerviśaḥ’* (Pāṇini 1.3.17) is merely illustrative; the rule *‘parivyavebhyaḥ kriyaḥ’* (1.3.18) should also be understood as included here. The intention is that the designation *aṅga* would apply to what begins with that [prefix], and consequently, the augment *aṭ* would be inserted before the prefix.

‘*strī iyatī*’—this means “she whose measure is this much. The suffix *vatup* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.40 (*kim-idambhyāṃ vo ghaḥ*), whereby *va* is replaced by *gha*. The *gha* is changed to *ya*, and there is the substitution of *iy* for *i*. Then, by Pāṇini 6.3.90 (*idam-kimoḥ īś-kī*), *idaṃ* becomes *īś*; and by Pāṇini 6.4.148 (*yasyeti ca*), the *ī* is elided. [The feminine suffix] *ṅīp* is added by Pāṇini 4.1.6 (*ugitaśca*).

(4.1.6) Thus, [the form] *iyatī* is derived by adding the suffix *ṅīp*. From the word *strī*, the nominative suffix *su* is added; its elision occurs by rule 6.1.68 (*halaṅyābhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*). When the state *strī iyatī* has been established, if the mention of the word *vidhi* were not made, then the technical designation *aṅga* would apply to the word *strī* when the suffix *iyat* follows; and consequently—

The elision of the letter *i* [of the suffix *ṅasi*] would result by the rule "yasyeti ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.148). Now, one might object: since the elision of *i* is itself unestablished due to the rule "asiddhavad atrābhāt" (Pāṇini 6.4.22), how can there be this contingency of its elision? The intention is that the status of being "unestablished" (*asiddha*) applies only within the scope of the governing heading "prāgbhādhikāra" (that which precedes the heading *bhā* in Pāṇini 6.4.22).

This is not the intended meaning; for the author of the Vṛtti will state there: "The phrase 'as if unestablished' (asiddhavat) is a governing rule (adhikāra); whatever we shall set forth from here until the end of the chapter is to be regarded as unestablished. For it is thus that [he says]: ā...

Does the prefix *āṅ* here signify inclusion (*abhividhi*), such that even within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "bhā" [the rule of] non-validity (*asiddhatva*) applies? If so, then by the mention of the word "vidhi" [in Pāṇini 6.4.22], this is made known: that the non-validity pertaining to the governing heading of "bhā" is not universal (*anityatva*).
Consequently, the statement [in the Vārttika], "The augment *vuk* and *yuṭ* should be declared as valid in place of *avaṅ* and *aṇ* respectively," need not be stated.
[The forms] *bhavati*, *vuk*—as in *babhūva*, and *yuṭ*—as in *upadidīya*.

[Objection: But if this is so, then because of the status of the elision of the vowel *i* as *sthānivadbhūta* by the rule "when a preceding operation is to be performed, that which follows an *ac* is treated as if it were present" (Pāṇini 1.1.57), the elision of the vowel *i* in the word *strī* would not even occur. [Response: This is not so; for...

Regarding the rule "that which precedes an ādeśa consisting of six or eight letters becomes as if it were the original (sthānivat) with respect to the operation [prescribed] for that preceding element," and so forth: the vowel *ī* of the word *strī*, which originally preceded the six-lettered element, subsequently becomes connected with the word *strī* after the formation of the compound *iyī*. Now, even if this were being performed...

Why does the technical designation *aṅga* not apply when the word "vidhi" (prescription) is included, given that there is indeed a prescription of a suffix after the word *strī*, and furthermore, the suffix *iyat* exists as something following it? This is not a fault; for when "vidhi" is included, [the designation applies] to that from which the suffix is prescribed.

Because of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the designation of "suffix" (*aṅga*) is prescribed for that which follows it. But here, the suffix that is prescribed after the word *strī* is not what follows [it], because it has been elided; and the suffix *iyat* which does follow it is not prescribed after that [word *strī*].

Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the word *ādi* (beginning) there? For even without it, when it is stated merely as "that from which a suffix is prescribed is a stem (*aṅga*) with respect to that suffix," then—
due to the constant correlative connection between *yat* and *tat*— that from which a suffix is prescribed would [be understood] as the stem with respect to that suffix.
The meaning "the designation *aṅga* applies from that which follows" is obtained; therefore, he says:

"that which begins with it (*tadādi*) is the base (*vaca*)," and so forth. If this term *tadādi* were not present, the status of being an *aṅga* would belong only to that specific element after which the suffix is prescribed, and not to the entire complex beginning with *saha*, and so on.
Nor does it apply to a collection that includes the suffix; for the suffix is prescribed as occurring at the beginning [of that collection].

When the term "beginning with that" (*tadādi*) is used, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is adopted in the sense: "that form of word of which the element from which the suffix is prescribed is the beginning. Therefore, [the rule applies] to the whole.
The designation *aṅga* (base) is established for the entire group beginning with *sahasya* when it is accompanied by *num*;

thus, the mention of "beginning with that" (*tadādivacana*) is for the sake of including the case-endings (*syādi*) and the augment *num*. By the inclusion of the word "beginning" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of suffixes and augments situated between the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*); this is because *num* serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for such augments.

In the case of *kariṣyāvaḥ*, since the suffix is prescribed after that [stem], when the entire complex beginning with that [stem]—including the substitute for *saha*—is designated as an *aṅga*, the lengthening occurs by the rule *ṭhato dīrgho yañi* (Pāṇini 7.3.101). Otherwise, where would it apply? [It would apply] in cases such as *vāvāvaḥ* and *vāvāmaḥ*.

In such examples as these: from the roots *aya*, *vaya*, *maya*, *paya*, *taya*, *caya*, *ṇaya* (meaning "to go," Dhātupāṭha 474–480), with the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix (*yaṅ-luk*), there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable according to Pāṇini 7.4.83 (*dīrgho 'kitaḥ*); and for the [suffixes] *vas* and *mas*, there is the elision of *y* according to Pāṇini 6.1.66 (*lopo vyor vali*)—here, without the addition of a verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*).

The lengthening of the root vowel occurs because the suffix *śap* has been elided by the rule "after roots beginning with *ṭhadi*, etc., there is the elision of *śap*" (Pāṇini 2.4.72). Its inclusion among the *adādi* (second class) verbs is due to its recitation in the lists beginning with "and *carkarīta*" (Dhātupāṭha 1081). "Carkarīta" is the technical name for the elision of *yaṅ* used by ancient grammarians. [The form] "kuṇḍāni" [is derived accordingly].

Thus: by the rule *jaśśasoḥ śiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.20), there is the substitution of *śi* for *jas* and *śas*. Then, by the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.72), the augment *num* is added. Now, if one adopts the view that this *num* is an initial element (*parādi*), then even without the lengthening prescribed by *supi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.102), the desired form is established through the designation of the stem (*aṅga-saṃjñā*) for the base accompanied by *num*.

Even when [the suffix *su*] is a part of the preceding element (*pūrvānta*), the lengthening is established by the rule "sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau" (Pāṇini 6.4.8), which follows from the governing rule "nopadhāyāḥ" (6.4.7). However, when it is not a part [of the preceding element] (*abhakta*), it is not established because it is not a portion of the base (*aṅga*).

Furthermore, this [suffix] *num* is not [applied]; such is the view of the author of the Sūtras. For that reason, he formulated the rule regarding "that which begins with it" (*tadādivacana*) even for the sake of *num*, stating: “for the sake of *śrī* (*śriyartham*), for the sake of *bhū* (*bhvyartham*)”. [The examples are: “this belongs to *śrī*” (*śriya idaṃ*) and “this belongs to *bhū*” (*bhruva idam*). Here, the compound is formed by the rule “the fourth case [is compounded] when meaning ‘for the sake of that’” (*caturthī tadarthārtha*, 2.1.36), and in this instance, there is indeed the singular of the fourth case.

Regarding the term *vidhi*: for if the mention of the suffix (*pratyaya*) were not repeated, the designation of "stem" (*aṅga-saṃjñā*) would apply to the words *śrī* and *bhrū* when followed by the word *artha*; consequently, the substitutions *iy* and *uvaṅ* would occur.
However, because the suffix is mentioned again in connection with what is indicated by the locative case, [the rule does not apply] to the words *śrī* and *bhrū* when followed by the word *artha*.
Otherwise, the designation "aṅga" (base) would apply to what follows [the base], and consequently, the substitutions *i*, *u*, and *aṅ* would occur there.

However, when the term "pratyaya" (suffix) is mentioned again in connection with what is specified in the locative case, there is no such fault. For it is understood thus: "when a suffix is prescribed after that [base]. And that which is prescribed after it—[is the locus for the application of the rule].

That suffix is elided. Even though the designation of "stem" (*aṅga*) is obtained for it by virtue of the rule regarding suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) despite its elision, the grammatical operation (*kārya*) is not obtained; this is because of the prohibition of the suffix-based designation by the rule *na lumatāṅgasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.63).
14. *suptiṅantaṃ padam* (Pāṇini 1.4.14).

Regarding the statement, "The terms *sup* and *tiṅ* are used as abbreviations (*pratyāhāra*)," it is indeed appropriate that *tiṅ* is taken as an abbreviation, since there exists no other word *tiṅ*. But how can *sub* be so?

Regarding the mention of *pratyāhāra*: since the locative plural (*saptamī-bahuvacana*) exists, why is it not included? This is not a fault; for there is a prohibition by the rule *ṭh na ṅsimbuddhyoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.8). If *sup* were understood as including the locative plural, then [the prohibition would apply] to the nominative singular (*ṅsi*) and the vocative (*buddhi*).

Since there would be no status as a *pada*, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would not even arise; thus, the prohibition [of its elision] would be meaningless. In the case of "brāhmaṇāḥ," since *padatva* exists, [the rules] "sasajuṣo ruḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.66) and "kharavasānayorvisarjanīyaḥ" (8.3.15) apply. In the case of "paṭhanti," since *padatva* exists here...
The *nighāta* (anudātta accentuation) is applied by the rule *‘tiṅṅtiṅḥ’* (Pāṇini 8.1.28).

Now, one might object that by the rule *‘yena vidhis tadantasya’* (Pāṇini 1.1.72), and by the metarule *‘caṭ-pratyayagrahaṇe yasmāt sa vihitastadādestadantasya’* (Paribhāṣā 24), [the term *caṭ* should refer to the entire word ending in the suffix *caṭ*].
Even without the mention of "the end" (anta), the designation would apply only to that which ends in such [a suffix];
so for what purpose is the mention of "the end"? To this he says: "In the case of the designation 'pada'," and so forth.

If, by the mention of "the end" here, the meaning were that in other rules prescribing designations there is no "inclusion of that which ends in" (tadantavidhi), [then the following would be the case].
If it were not so indicated, then in the rule *ṭhtaraptamapau ghaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.22), the technical designation *gha* would apply to that which ends in *tarap*,

and not to the suffix alone. Therefore, by the inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*) in this sense, it is indicated that in other rules prescribing technical designations (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), when a suffix is mentioned, the rule of "inclusion of what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*) is prohibited, as follows:

The inclusion of the term *anta* (end) is for this very purpose: by it, the designation *gha* applies only to the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap*, and not to that which ends in them. Thus, in the example *gaurībrāhmaṇitarā*, the shortening [of the vowel] of the word *gaurī* does not occur before the word *brāhmaṇitarā* ending in *tarap*, because of the rule *gharūpakalpa* (Pāṇini 6.3.43), etc.

It occurs; because that which ends in the suffix *tarap* is designated as *agha*. If the designation *agha* applied to the suffix alone, then the short vowel of the word *brāhmaṇī* would indeed occur when it follows that [suffix].
15. *naḥ kye* | (1.4.15) Regarding the example *rājīyati*: [it means] "he desires a king for himself. By the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (3.1.8), the suffix *kyac* is added;
and by the rule *kyaci ca* (7.4.33), the substitution of *i* occurs [for the final vowel of the stem]. Regarding *rājāyate*: [it means] "he acts like a king."
In the form *rājevācarati* ("he acts like a king"), the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied by the rule *ṭhkartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.11).

The lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.25). In the form *varmāyate*, the suffix *kyaṣ* is applied by the rule *lohitādiḍājbhyaḥ kyaṣ* (Pāṇini 3.1.13), meaning "it becomes armor" (*avarma bhavati*). [The suffix is applied] optionally...

The *ātmanepada* ending is applied by the rule *kyaṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.90). Here, the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) must be performed when the technical designation *pada* applies. Now, one might object: since these affixes beginning with *kyac* are prescribed after that which ends in a *sup* (nominal suffix), the designation *pada* is already established here by the rule *suptiṅantaṃ padam* (Pāṇini 1.4.14); therefore, what need is there for this?

To the question, "For what purpose is this undertaking? he says: "When something is already established, an undertaking is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). The word *siddhe* means "when [the designation] is established" (*siddhau*). According to Pāṇini 3.3.114, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) in the neuter; thus, because the subject under discussion is the technical term *pada*, it is understood that "establishment" refers specifically to the status of being a *pada*. Alternatively, the word *siddha* is used here because the root is intransitive (*akarmaka*).

The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). The meaning is that the grammatical operation pertaining to the technical designation "pada" applies when [the word] is established (*siddhe*) or completed (*niṣpanne*). Regarding the phrase "only that which ends in *n*" (*nāntam eva*): this is because of the prohibition of a restrictive rule (*niyama*). For if there were a contrary restriction, then since the designation "pada" would not apply to the nominative singular (*ṅsi*) and vocative (*ṅs*), the elision of the final *n* (*nalopa*) would not occur anyway; so what would be the purpose of its prohibition?

Regarding the form ‘vācyati’: by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8), the suffix *kyac* is added. Because there is no status as a *pada* when *kyac* is present, the substitution of *ku* for *c* (as prescribed by *coḥ kuḥ*, Pāṇini 8.2.30) does not occur.
16. *siti ca* (1.4.16). For example, *bhavadīyaḥ* and so forth. In such cases as *tatra jātaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.25), a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is applied in the sense of a derivative (*śaiṣika*).

Because [the word] is a *pada*, there is the substitution of a voiced unaspirated stop (*jaś*) by the rule *jhalāñ jaśo'nte* (8.2.39). As for *ūrṇāyuḥ*: [it is derived from *ūrṇā* with the suffix *u*].

When the suffix *yus* is applied by the rule *ūrṇāyā yus* (Pāṇini 5.2.123), the designation *pada* supersedes the designation *bha*; consequently, by the rule *ṭhyasyeti ca* (6.4.148), the elision of the long *ā* does not occur.
Thus we have *ṛtviyaḥ*. [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied according to *ṛtoraṇ* (5.1.148) in the sense "one for whom the season has arrived," [and this occurs] in the Vedic language (*chandas*).

By the rule *ghas* (Pāṇini 5.1.106), the form *ṛtviyaḥ* is derived; because it possesses the status of a *pada*, it lacks the status of a *bha*, and consequently, the *guṇa* substitution prescribed by *ṭhorguṇaḥ* (6.4.146) does not apply.
17. *svādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne* (1.4.17).
In this context, if the suffixes were intended to be taken starting from the seventh case plural up to *kap*,

then one would not have formulated the prohibition "not before a sarvanāmasthāna suffix," because there would be no possibility of its application. Since that prohibition has indeed been made, it is understood that the suffixes begin from the nominative singular up to *kap*.
Because the *svādi* group [of suffixes] is understood [here], he says: "In the case of *svādiṣu*, starting from the word *su* and from the singular number.
For example: *rājatvam*, *rājatā*. [These are derived] by the rule *tasya bhāvas tvatalau* (Pāṇini 5.1.119).
[And]: *rājataraḥ*. [This is derived] by the rule *dvivacanavibhajyopapade tarabīyasunau* (Pāṇini 5.3.57).

*tarap*: *rājatamaḥ*. The suffix *tamap* is applied by the rule *atiśāyane* (Pāṇini 5.3.55). In the forms *rājānau*, *rājānaḥ*, because there is no designation as a *pada* (word), the elision of the final *n* does not occur.
If this is the case, then [the elision] should also not occur in *rājati*, since [the suffix *ti*] is not a *sarvanāmasthāna* by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the presence of the suffix).

This is not a fault, because the designation "pada" does not [otherwise] exist [in that context]. The activity of the Teacher indicates that the designation "pada" occurs when *s* follows: for he teaches the prohibition [of doubling] in the rule *na ṅsiṃbuddhyoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.8). In this case, the word *saṃbuddhi* would be redundant, precisely because the status of being a *pada* is absent [without it].

Because *nalopa* (the elision of *n*) would not apply. Alternatively—this [term] ‘asarvanāmasthāne’ is a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion), not a *prasajyapratiṣedha* (a simple negation); therefore, the designation *pada* is prescribed for cases other than *sarvanāmasthāna*, but *sarvanāmasthāna* itself is not prohibited. Consequently, by the preceding rule (*Pāṇini 1.4.17*), when *su* follows...

The designation *pada* will apply. Alternatively, there is no fault even in the case of a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), because of the rule "a prescription or a prohibition applies to what is immediately preceding" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 12); thus, that acquisition which is immediate is prohibited, not that which is separated by an interval. Therefore, [the definition] "a word ending in a nominal suffix or a verbal suffix is a *pada*" (Pāṇini 1.4.14).
Thus, there is the elision of the vowel *i*.

The term *yaci* is a designation of phonemes (*varṇagrahaṇa*) specified in the locative case. Therefore, by the rule *yasmin vidhis tadādāv algrahaṇe* (Vārttika 14), the operation here must apply to that which begins with [the phoneme]. Consequently—

He says: "In cases beginning with *yakāra*, etc. In examples such as *gārgya*, when the designation *bha* applies, there is the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148). [The Vārttika states: "An addition must be made for *nabhas*, *aṅgas*, *roman*, and *manuṣa* when the suffix *vat* follows."

In this case, the result is that the designation *pada* supersedes the designation *bhas*. The phrase "like the sky" (*nabha iva*) is intended to demonstrate similarity of meaning; it does not, however, form a *vati* suffix after a word in the nominative case. Rather, it means "it exists similarly to the sky," according to Pāṇini 5.1.115: *tena tulyam*. [The example] is "like Aṅgiras" (*āṅgirasvat*).

It is the same as the preceding [case]. Regarding "manuṣvat": since the term *bahula* (diversely) is understood to follow in the rule *janeḥ usiḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 9.37), the suffix *usi* is applied to the root *man* (meaning "to know," Dhātupāṭha 1176). The substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (8.3.59).

When *manuṣ* is established, the suffix *vat* is applied as before, resulting in *manuṣvad*. If the designation *pada* were to apply here, then because the substitution of *ṣ* would be considered *asiddha*, the substitution of *r* would occur; consequently, the undesired form *manurvat* would result. Here, the term *upasaṃkhyāna* (supplementary rule) refers to the statement ‘*siti ca*’.

(1.4.16) Therefore, the particle *ca* is carried over [from the previous rule], and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. By means of that, the designation *bha* will apply to *nabhas*, *aṅgiras*, and *manus* when followed by the suffix *vat*.
[As in the example] *vṛṣaṇvasvaśvayoḥ*. Since the designation *pada* applies here by relying on the case-ending (*vibhakti*) contained within the compound, [the rule is established].

The designation *bha* is prescribed when [the condition] has been reached, and its prescription is obtained precisely through the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "and" (*ca*). In the example *vṛṣṇo’śvaḥ*, although the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) once the *bha*-designation applies,
nevertheless, the elision of the *n* is not dependent on being at the end of a word (*pada*), because of the rule *padāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.37).
And there is also the prohibition of negation.

19. *taso matvarthe* (Pāṇini 1.4.19). The term *taso* is a mention of the phonemes (*varṇagrahaṇa*). Since an affix denoting possession (*matvarthīya*) cannot occur after a mere phoneme, it is understood through the force of the context that this is a reference to what ends in those phonemes (*tadantavidhi*). Thus he says: "that which ends in the letter *t*" and so forth.

The phrase "in a suffix denoting possession" (*matvarthe pratyaye*) consists of two words in different grammatical cases (*vyadhikaraṇe pade*); it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsaḥ*). "The meaning of *matup*" is *matvartha*;

the meaning is: "in that suffix which occurs therein. Alternatively, the two words may be in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇe pade*); by association with the word *matup*, it refers to the meaning co-occurring with *matup*.

It is said: the suffix occurs when there is that which possesses the sense of *ṇatup*, but not when there is that in which [the quality] resides—that is, it is a suffix in the sense of possession (*matvartha*).
The inclusion of the word "sense" (*artha*) is so that the suffix *kamatup* may occur even in cases other than those [specifically mentioned]; for otherwise, [it would not].

If it were stated simply as *matau*, [the suffix] would apply only to those [words] ending in the matup suffix, and not to others. If the mention of the sense of matup (*matvartha*) were made, it would not apply to the matup suffix itself; for that suffix serves as a qualifier of the meaning (*artha*), and it is impossible for a qualifier to be connected with a grammatical operation (*kārya*). Indeed, when it is said, "Let the owner of brindled cows (*citragu*) be brought," [the operation does not apply to the word *citragu* itself].
Cows, being qualifiers, are also brought in; this is not a fault,

for even a qualifier is sometimes distinguished in a particular function, as for example, when it is said, "Let the Brāhmaṇas be brought from Devadatta’s house," if Devadatta, being a qualifier of the house, is himself a Brāhmaṇa.

In that case, it is indeed brought forward as well. In the example *udaśvitvān*, because it is a *bha* [suffix], the designation of a *pada* does not apply; thus, the substitution of *jaś* is established. Furthermore, by the rule *jhayaḥ* (8.2.10), the substitution of *vat* occurs;
by *ugidacām* (7.1.70), the augment *num* is added; and by *ṭhathvasantasya cādhātoḥ* (6.4.14), [the long vowel is applied].

The vowel is long, as in the examples *payasvī* and *yaśasvī*. By the rule *asmāyāmedhāsrajo viniḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.121), the suffix *vin* is applied; because [the stem] is treated as a nominal base (*bha*-status), the substitution of *ru* does not occur. While the rule *indranpūṣāryamṇāṃ sau* (6.4.12) is still in force, the lengthening of the vowel is effected by the subsequent rule *sau ca* (6.4.13).
20. *Ayasmayādīni chandasi* (Pāṇini 1.4.20).

If the designation *bha* were prescribed here, then the designation *pada* would not apply; if, on the other hand, the designation *pada* were prescribed, then the designation *bha* would not apply here. Thus, there would be no co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the designations *bha* and *pada*.

It would not [apply]; because the governing rule concerns a single designation (*saṃjñā*). However, this fault does not arise in the case of prescribing correctness (*sādhutva*), for therein the designation *bha* is prescribed for some items that possess the designation *pada*, while for others it is prescribed for those possessing both designations. Therefore, it is precisely for the purpose of prescribing correctness.
To show that this is logical, he says: "The words *ayasmaya* and so forth," and so on. But how is their correctness established?

To this he says: "In the section concerning the technical designations *bha* and *pada*," and so on. Although the term *bhāṣā* (speech) is present there [in the rule for *ayasmaya*] as a door, an opening, or a means, nevertheless, by this very [rule], the word *ayasmaya* [is justified].
Because the suffix *mayaṭ* is prescribed for Vedic usage as well, it functions as a *bha*-stem; consequently, the substitution of *ru* does not take place.
In the word *sa-ṛk-vatā*: since it possesses *ṛc*s, the suffix *matup* is added. Because it is a *pada*, the substitution of *ku* applies by *ṭhcoḥ kuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.30).
However, because it is a *bha*-stem, the substitution of *jaś* does not apply by *jhalāṃ jaśo'nte* (Pāṇini 8.2.39).
It does not occur [as such], because this is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class), since the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) denotes a type or category.
21. *Bahuṣu bahuvacanam* (Pāṇini 1.4.21).
"By this [sūtra], the number 'plurality' (*bahutva*) is prescribed as the denotable meaning of that [plural suffix]. By this, he shows that the purpose of this rule is prescriptive (*vidhyartha*).

In this regard, some hold the view that "the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of five factors: its own meaning (*svārtha*), substance (*dravya*), gender (*liṅga*), number (*saṃkhyā*), and object (*karman*) and so forth. Others hold the view that "the meaning of a nominal stem consists of three factors: its own meaning, substance, and gender. Among these, "its own meaning" (*svārtha*)...

The qualifiers are the word's own form (*svarūpa*), genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), and substance (*dravya*). The substance, however, is the qualified (*viśeṣya*); its [qualifiers] are, in turn, genus, quality, and substance. Among these, when a genus qualified by the word's own form is denoted—as in "cow" (*gauḥ*)—then the word's own form is the qualifier because it functions as such.

It becomes its own meaning (svārtha); however, the genus (jāti), because it is the qualifier, is not a substance. But when a quality qualified by the genus is expressed—as in "the white quality of the cloth"—then the genus, being the qualifier, becomes its own meaning; the quality, however, because it is the qualificand, is a substance.

But when a substance such as a cloth is expressed as qualified by qualities— as in "a white cloth"— then the quality, being the qualifier, becomes its own primary referent (svārtha), while the substance, such as the cloth,
remains the qualificand. Furthermore, when even one substance becomes a qualifier of another substance—

In expressions such as "bring the staffs" (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya*) or "bring the spears" (*kuntān praveśaya*), the substance such as the staff is the primary meaning (*svārtha*) when it has attained the status of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); whereas another substance, such as a person who has attained the status of the qualified (*viśeṣya*), is the substance itself [the secondary meaning]. In some cases, even a relation (*sambandha*) becomes the primary meaning—where...
A cognition based on a relation arises, such as "one with a staff" (*daṇḍin*) or "one with horns" (*viṣāṇin*).

Here, the relation between the staff and the person is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), while "one with a staff" is the substance (*dravya*). In some cases, even an action constitutes its own meaning, where a suffix arises based on an action, such as "a cook" (*pācaka*).

Regarding the term *pāṭhaka*: others maintain that here the "own meaning" (*svārtha*) consists of the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakasambandha*). Gender (*liṅga*) refers to femininity and so forth; number (*saṃkhyā*) refers to singularity and so forth; and "object" (*karman*) and the rest refer to the specific grammatical relations (*kārakaviśeṣa*) to be described later.
Among the two views previously mentioned, it is the second view that is adopted here.
The author of the Vṛtti has relied upon this [view].

Regarding the point that "action alone is the meaning of the verbal root," there is indeed no disagreement among the teachers. In that regard, when the nominal stem possesses the threefold meaning previously mentioned, and the verbal root consists of action, [the following applies].
If this sūtra were not stated, then, according to the rule "suffixes whose meaning is not specified [indicate] their own base-meaning" (*sī.vṛ.* 125),

the plural case endings such as *jas* prescribed after nominal stems would apply only to the three-fold set of meanings [gender, number, and case], and not to the specific number of plurality. The same would apply to suffixes such as *jhi* following verbal roots.

The plural number being prescribed would apply only to the action, and not to the numerical category of plurality. Therefore, by this very [rule], it is prescribed as expressing that numerical category of plurality; thus, this serves the purpose of an injunction. And just as by this grammatical rule—

The number "plurality" (*bahutva*) is prescribed as the denotation of the plural suffix; likewise, by rules such as *karmaṇi dvitīyā* (Pāṇini 2.3.2), the accusative case and so forth are prescribed for the object (*karman*) and other grammatical relations. Furthermore, by the rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.69), [the same applies] to the *l*-suffixes.
It is precisely action (*karman*) and so forth. Therefore, these *yogās* (grammatical rules) also must be understood as having the purpose of enjoining [the application of suffixes].

And for those who hold the view that the "fivefold" constitutes the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), it is the nominal stem itself that expresses all five meanings; the case-endings (*vibhakti*) merely serve to illuminate them. In that regard:
"Suffixes whose meaning is not specifically prescribed express their own [base] meaning" (Sī.

Vṛ. 125). Thus, even without this explicit statement, the plural suffixes *jas* and so forth are already established after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) when plurality is present. However, since those suffixes would otherwise apply indifferently even to other numbers such as singularity and so on, this rule serves to restrict them.
This is for the purpose of restriction.
But why has the author of the *Vṛtti* adopted the view that the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of a triplet [of gender, number, and case]?
Because it is logical. For instance, in such expressions as "see the tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ paśya*), [the meaning is not conveyed] without the case-endings (*vibhakti*).

The meanings of number, object, and so forth are understood. Although in cases such as *payaḥ payo jarayati* ("he causes milk to digest milk"), the meaning of number, object, and so on is understood even without an inflection, nevertheless, in cases such as *payasī*, *payāṃsi*, and *payasā*, [the case ending is required] for the sake of understanding number, object, and so forth.

A case ending (*vibhakti*) is necessarily required. For it cannot be said that, as in the case of *gargāḥ*, where the sense of "descendant" is understood through the plural number even without the *yañ* suffix, so too in the case of *gārgyaḥ*, the base alone expresses the sense of "descendant. Furthermore—*payaḥ payo*...

In examples such as *jarayati*, the cognition of the number, object, and other meanings arises precisely through the capacity of the specific case-ending (*vibhakti*) that has been produced. For it is from that very specific case-ending which has arisen that this specific meaning is understood, and not from anything else; thus, it is only the "triad" (the base, the suffix, and their combined meaning).
The meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is [already] connected [to the number].

If, then, the number "plurality" (*bahutva-saṃkhyā*) is prescribed as the expressed meaning of the plural suffix (*bahuvacana*), then in the Sūtra the indication of plurality must be made by means of an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*); otherwise, the number "plurality" would not [be established].

Should it be understood? It need not be so; even without a suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*), there can be a designation where the abstract state is the primary meaning, as in the expression "the whiteness of the cloth. But even so, since the state (*bhāva*) is a single entity, the plural form "in many" (*bahuṣu*) would not be appropriate. This is not a fault; [The remainder of the passage continues: ...for the word "many" refers to the plurality of substrata (*dharmin*), not to the plurality of the state itself. Just as when one says, "There is a single color in many things," the word "color" is used in the singular because the quality is one, yet the plural is used for the things themselves, so too here the plural is used for the substrata while the state remains singular. Furthermore, the term "state" (*bhāva*) is used here in its conventional sense of "existence" (*sattā*), which is indeed manifold insofar as it inheres in various entities. Thus, the plural is justified. Moreover, the word "state" (*bhāva*) is often used in the plural in grammatical literature, as in the rule *bhāve* (Pāṇini 3.3.18), where it refers to the plurality of verbal actions. Therefore, there is no inconsistency.

Because the distinction belonging to a substance which is the locus of the number "many" is superimposed upon the quality "manyness," the designation "in many" (bahuṣu) is made by means of the plural ending;
and furthermore, this is for the purpose of making it known that this word *bahu* expresses number (*saṃkhyā*) and does not express magnitude (*vaipulya*). Therefore...

Since "muchness" (*vaipulya*) is not what is expressed by the plural number, in cases such as *bahurodanaḥ* ("much rice") and *bahuḥ sūpaḥ* ("much soup," i.e., much broth), the singular number alone occurs after the word *bahu* which denotes muchness, and not the plural.

If plurality as a number were prescribed as the denotation of the plural suffix, then in the example "vṛkṣaṃ paśya" (look at the tree), the plural suffix would result; for here two numbers are present— the collective number, which is unity, and the individual number, which consists of the plurality inherent in the parts such as the fruit, root, and branches.

For this [number] as well, there certainly exists a relation characterized by inherence in a single substratum with the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). To explain: the number "plurality" (bahutva) inheres in those constituent parts; the meaning of the nominal stem, which is the aggregate (*samudāya*), also inheres in that very same [substratum]. Consequently, the plural suffix would follow from that [aggregate]. Therefore—

He says: "Karma and so forth," and so on. For karma and the others are proximate to the number "plurality" because they are denoted by a word in the same case-ending; therefore, due to that proximity, the plural ending occurs precisely for their plurality. Indeed, in the expression "look at the tree," it is the aggregate alone [that is the object] of the act of seeing.

Since that which is most desired [to be expressed] is pervaded [by the action], it alone assumes the status of the object (*karman*), and not its constituent parts; therefore, how could there be the possibility of a plural number? Regarding the phrase "in the case of the object and so forth" (*karmādiṣu*): the object and so forth are the denotates of the plural number. Their plurality is possible only when there are multiple objects and so forth; hence [the rule applies].
By implication, the meaning "in many [cases], such as the object (karman) and so forth," is established.

If, then, the number "many" is prescribed as the expressed meaning of the plural case-endings, then the case-affixes beginning with *su* would not occur after indeclinables (*avyaya*), which lack number; and consequently—
He says, "And where... and so forth, [meaning] that they would not have the designation *pada*. But one might object:
in the sūtra prescribing the suffixes beginning with *su* (*svādi*), number, object, and so forth are prescribed as the meanings of those suffixes by another treatise;
he will state that this [present work] forms a single syntactical unit with that [other treatise]. Therefore, how [can it be said that] the suffixes beginning with *su*...

What is meant by "being prescribed in a general rule"? For it is not possible for *sv*, *au*, *jas*, and so on, to be considered "prescribed in a general rule" (*sāmānyavihita*) merely through their syntactic unity with other rules of the grammar, such as "the plural number is used for many" (Pāṇini 1.4.21) or "the second case is used for the object" (Pāṇini 2.3.2). It is thus...

In that case, there is no fault, because it has been stated that [the suffixes] are "prescribed in general" since the indicator (jñāpaka) makes it known that *svādi* suffixes arise in general from indeclinables (*avyaya*). But what is that indicator?
It is the elision (*luk*) of the *sup* suffixes produced after an indeclinable, as prescribed by the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.82). This is not [the case for other suffixes].
For those [suffixes] that have not yet arisen, elision (luk) occurs.

22. *dvayekayordvivacanaikavacane* (Pāṇini 1.4.22). Regarding the term *dvyekayoḥ*: this is also a designation where the state (*bhāva*) is predominant; otherwise, because there would be plurality, the plural number would have been used. But since it is a designation where the state is predominant, it refers to duality and singularity.

"Since there are these two objects," the dual number is appropriate. With the words "this also," etc., he shows that this yoga as well has the purpose of being an injunction. Regarding the term "expression of the object":
that by which an object—that is, a denotable thing—is expressed is the "expression of the object."

Regarding the statement, "The term *kāraka* is a qualifier whose scope consists of the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) such as *apādāna* and so forth," it is said that its scope (*viṣaya*) consists of the designations beginning with *apādāna*. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the *sampradāna* and others are included.
[This is] the inclusion. Now, why does this technical name not apply to the *dhruva* and so forth that are about to be mentioned?

He thinks as follows: if these were indicated by technical names (*saṃjñā-śabda*), they would have been indicated here in the locative case; however, since this [word "kārake"] is indicated in the locative, therefore this is not the technical name for the *dhruva* and so forth. The word "in a factor of action" (*kārake*) is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*).

[Objection: The seventh case [the locative] is used for selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), but selection occurs only among many; how then can there be a designation in the singular? [Response: The singular is used with reference to the class (*sāmānya*). Alternatively, as it is said, "The sūtras are like Vedic meters" (*chandasvat sūtrāṇi bhavanti*), therefore [the rule] *vyatyayo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.1.85) applies.

Where plurality was applicable, the singular is used; among the *kārakas*, that *kāraka* which is fixed (*dhruva*) receives the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *apādāna*. This should be understood in other cases as well. This word *kāraka* exists as a derivative formed with the suffix *ṇvul*, being a synonym for the agent (*kartṛ*); it also [exists in another sense].

And the term *saṃjñā*—it is an unanalyzed synonym (*avyutpanna-paryāya*). In this context, if there were a reference to what was previously stated, then the word *kāraka* would not apply to the [factors] such as the ablative (*apādāna*), just as the word *kartṛ* is derived in the sense of an agent by the rule *ṇvultṛcau* (Pāṇini 3.1.133). Likewise...

The term "kāraka" (agent/causal factor) also [is problematic]; for while the agent (*kartṛ*) is independent (*svatantra*), the ablatives (*apādāna*) and so forth are not independent. How, then, could they receive the designation "kāraka"? For if the designation "kāraka" were absent, they would not be included among those designated as "kārakas. Now, if it is argued that they too [are kārakas] in some way...

If independence were accepted, then the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*) would necessarily apply there; consequently, in examples such as *grāmād āgacchati* ("he comes from the village") and *upādhyāyāya gāṃ dadāti* ("he gives a cow to the teacher"), the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would necessarily apply to the village and so forth.
Furthermore, there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). To explain:

The designation "agent" (kartṛ-saṃjñā) occurs subsequent to the etymological derivation (vyutpatti) of the word "kāraka"; if that were the case, the designation "agent" would have to be introduced by means of the term "kāraka," and much would thus require correction. Furthermore, such a correction would result in excessive complexity in understanding. However, in the case of a synonym for "cause" (nimitta)— [End of provided text]

There would be no fault in taking the word *kāraka* [in its primary sense]; therefore, thinking that this very [word] is what is intended to be grasped, he says: "This word *kāraka* is a synonym for 'cause' (*nimitta*). For example, in the expression "he comes from the village" (*grāmād āgacchati*), the village possesses the status of a cause with respect to the action of coming, which has the village as its fixed point (*dhruva*). If here...
If the village did not exist as a limit (avadhi), then the act of coming would not be accomplished; therefore, the village is a *kāraka*.
In the expression "the leaf of the tree falls," the tree is intended here as a relatum (*sambandhin*), and not [as a limit].

As for the point regarding "by way of being a cause" (*nimitatvena*): because of the inclusion of the term "kāraka" [in the rule], the designation *apādāna* does not apply to that which is intended as a cause but is not intended as a *kāraka*. This is not a suitable counter-example for the inclusion of the term "kāraka."

Because the designation of *apādāna* (ablative) is precluded here by the very inclusion of the term *dhruk*, for that which serves as a limit (*avadhi*) when separation (*apāya*) is to be accomplished is indeed *dhruva*.
