Thus the author of the Vṛtti will state: "That which serves as a limit when separation is to be accomplished" (Kāśikā 1.4.24). And in this case, the tree does not function as a limit.
Is it intended [as the agent]? No, rather, it is intended as a relation (*sambandha*). This is not so;
for the tree, whose status as a limit (*avadhi*) is intended, is intended precisely as a relatum (*sambandhin*).
The meaning is: "The leaf falls from the tree which is the limit and the relatum. For indeed...
The intention to express [the tree] as a related entity is incompatible with the intention to express it as a limit (*avadhi*).

Therefore, for the tree whose status as a limit is intended, only its state of being a related entity is intended, and not its status as a cause (*nimitta*) with respect to a separation (*apāya*), even though such a separation exists.
What is improper here [in the statement]:

"He asks the boy's father the way"? Since the designation *karman* (object) is prescribed for that which is "unspoken" (*akathita*) by the rule *akathitaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.51), [this occurs] under the heading *kārake* (1.4.82).
If this were not the case, it would apply to the boy as well. How so?

This word *akathita* is a synonym for *akīrtita* (unmentioned). And since no specific [object] has been introduced because no particular [object] is under discussion, when [the term] is employed, it would apply [to all].

If it were stated without qualification as "sarvatra" (everywhere), then it would apply to everything that is merely not mentioned. Consequently, if it were said "that which is akathita (unspoken)," then everything—both that which is a *kāraka* (participant in an action) and that which is not—would be understood as *akathita*, since nothing would have been specifically mentioned (*kathita*) by means of specific designations such as *apādāna* (ablative) and so forth; just as a father is not "spoken of" (*kathita*) by those specific designations.

The young student (*māṇavaka*) would also [otherwise] have the designation of "object" (*karman*). However, when the word "in relation to the agent" (*kārake*) is present, the designation applies only to the father, who is the cause for the act of questioning; it does not apply to the student. For he is not intended to be expressed as the cause with respect to the act of questioning; rather, [he is intended] in relation to the father.
If this [term] is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) for *dhruva* and so forth by virtue of being related [to them], and not a technical name (*saṃjñā*),
then in those instances such as "In the case of a *kāraka*, only when *ataḥ* and *śruta* follow, in the sense of a benediction" (Pāṇini 6.2.148), wherever...

If the word *kāraka* were used in its sense as a [general] action-factor (*kriyā*), then in that case, the *apādāna* and other factors would not be included by the mention of *kāraka*. However, there is no fault in the view that it is a technical term (*saṃjñā*), for a term, when applied, conveys the thing designated (*saṃjñin*).
Therefore, he says: "In the designations of *kārakas*," and so forth. Where the word *kāraka*...

In that case as well, by this very qualification, it is understood that "designation" (*saṃśabdanam*) refers to the linguistic usage characterized by the communication of the intended meaning; for even in other passages, the term *kāraka* is employed solely as a synonym for "cause" (*nimitta*). And that cause is precisely the [grammatical relation] beginning with the ablative (*apādāna*), and not...
For nothing other than that serves as the cause for an action (*kriyā*). Therefore, by the mention of "kāraka," there is the inclusion of the *apādāna* and the others.
Others, however, say: "By virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), the *apādāna* and so forth are understood as being associated with the qualifiers of the *kārakas*."

Since they are expressed by the term *kāraka*, they are included by the very mention of that term. Alternatively, the mention of *kāraka* itself should be accented; thus, the rule "an operation [is determined] by what is accented" (Pāṇini 1.3.11) applies. Therefore, by the mention of *kāraka*, the *apādāna* and the other [kārakas] are included.
It will be so.
24. *dhruvam apāye 'pādānam* (Pāṇini 1.4.24).
*Apāya* means separation, that is, disjunction. Since that [separation] resides in two things, by means of that—
That which departs by way of separation is "connected with departure" (apāyayukta), and likewise that from which it departs is also "connected with departure.
Therefore, since the ablative case ought to occur in both instances, he says for this very reason:
"that which is fixed when there is departure" and "when departure is to be accomplished. This is a locative of domain (viṣayasaptamī).
The meaning is that [the state] is the object of accomplishment as the goal to be attained (*sādhya*). Although the word *dhruva* in common usage denotes uniformity—
as in "his conduct is constant" (*dhruvam asya śīlam*) or "his form is constant" (*dhruvam asya rūpam*)—
nevertheless, since no purpose is served by such uniformity when the goal to be accomplished is the subject at hand, it is not used here.

Is stability (dhruvatā) applicable to the object of departure (apāya)? That very [stability] is what is presented, and that is precisely the state of being a limit (avadhibhāva). Because of its proximity to that departure, through a connection characterized by association, the word "stable" (dhruva) denotes the state of being a limit for that which is falling away; therefore, he says: "that which has become a limit. Hence...

In this context, when "separation" (apāya) is to be established, that which serves as the limit is expressed here by the word *dhruva*. By this, even in cases such as "he fell from the running horse," the designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*) for the horse and so forth is established;
for even though the horse and other such entities possess mobility in this instance, they still function as the limit of separation.

Now, how is it that the designation *apādāna* (ablative) applies here in such cases as "he feels aversion toward unrighteousness" (*adharmāj jugupsate*), "he desists from unrighteousness" (*adharmād viramati*), and "he neglects righteousness" (*dharmāt pramādyati*)? For is there not an actual departure (*apāya*) here? How so? Because a departure is preceded by the attainment of an effect (*kārya-samprāpti-pūrvaka*), and in these instances, there is no attainment of an effect.

He says: "Disgust," and so forth. The meaning is that when verbal roots having the sense of disgust and the like are employed, an addition (upasaṃkhyāna)—that is, a formal statement—must be made regarding the designation of the ablative (apādāna). In this regard, the following is the formal statement: [the rule] "the ablative" (apādānam) is extensive...

The designation is made for the purpose of indicating that "this designation has a wide scope. And thus it becomes wide-scope: if its object is something other than the named element (saṃjñin) mentioned in the sūtra, and not otherwise; therefore, [it applies] to *da*, *jugupsā*, and so forth.

"In the absence of actual separation (*apāya*), there will still be the designation of the ablative (*apādāna*). Alternatively: "There is indeed separation here; for separation does not necessarily occur only after the attainment of an effect (*kārya*), but rather it also occurs preceded by the attainment of consciousness (*citta*).
In this case...

To that extent, one feels aversion toward unrighteousness and desists from unrighteousness. Only that person who acts with foresight perceives in this way: "This so-called unrighteousness is a cause of suffering;
therefore, a conscious being ought not to perform it. He perceives thus: "From this [unrighteousness]..."
"Whatever desired object is accomplished, that very undertaking results only in suffering.
Reflecting thus, he grasps it with his intellect; having grasped it, he withdraws from it.
And so, the rule "the fixed point from which there is departure is the *apādāna*" is established. [Regarding the word] "he is negligent": [from the root] *madī*.
In the case of *hiṃs* (DhP 1208), the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *śamāmaṣṭānāṃ dīrghaḥ śyani* (Pāṇini 7.3.74).
Now, how is there the designation of ablative (*apādāna*) here—as in "he does not come from the village" (*grāmān nāgacchati*)? And why should it not be so?
Because the village is not connected with the act of departing (*apāya*). That [relation] in the presence of which a departure occurs is [the ablative].

Furthermore, the action of coming (*āgamana*) which has the point of departure as its instrument (*apādanasādhana*) is prohibited; if that action does not exist, how could there be a "departure" (*apāya*)? This is not a fault, for here, once the designation of "point of departure" (*apādāna-saṃjñā*) has been established, it is subsequently connected with the prohibition; otherwise, there would be no scope for the prohibition.
It would have been shown as follows: for in this way, the action of coming whose instrument is the *apādāna* (ablative) is intended to be negated.

In that case, if the negation were applied at the very outset, then because there would be no departure (*apāya*), the designation of *apādāna* for the village—which is unrelated to that [action]—would not be established. And consequently, that which...

The action of coming, which has the object of negation as its point of departure (apādāna), constitutes the domain of the negation; that [action] cannot be exhibited [prior to the negation]. Nor can a negation be stated here when its object has not been exhibited. Therefore, the designation of "point of departure" (apādāna) occurs first.
The sequence is as follows: "There is connection with a subsequent prohibition" (Pāṇini 2.2.36).
Regarding the rule *bhītrārthānāṃ bhayahetuḥ* (1.4.25):
*bhītiḥ* is fear (*bhī*); *trāṇam* is protection (*trā*). From the class beginning with *sampad*, the suffix *kvip* is applied. Thus, *bhī* and *trā* together form *bhītrau*.
Those whose meanings are "fear" (bhī) and "protection" (trā) are called *bhītrārtha*. Regarding the rule beginning with *“bibhetyarthānām”*:
here, by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), the words *bibheti* and *trāyati* function as representing the meanings of "fearing" and "protecting.
Those whose meaning is "fearing" are *bibhetyartha*; those whose meaning is "protecting" are *trāyatyartha*.

The meanings are "to protect. Regarding *bibheti*: the root *ñibhī* meaning "fear" (DhP 1084) belongs to the *jauhotyādi* class. Regarding *udvijate*: the root *uvijī* meaning "fear" and "trembling" (DhP 1460) belongs to the *tudādi* class and is *anudātta*. Regarding *trāyate*: the root *traiṅ* meaning "protection" (DhP 1027).
This belongs to the *bhū* class (*dhā.pā.* 965).

Regarding the example “he fears in the forest” (*araṇye bibheti*), the fear here does not arise from the forest itself; rather, it arises from thieves and the like situated therein. [Objection: But surely, in this case, the technical designation of locus (*adhikaraṇa-saṃjñā*) would prevail and supersede [the designation of object] due to its higher status?

It will be so. Furthermore—the word "dhruvam" (fixed/permanent) is understood from the previous context, as it was stated that "the fixed [object] is that which serves as the limit. Now, the forest is not intended here as the limit; so what is the purpose of including the term "cause of fear" (*bhayahetu*) for the sake of excluding that? If this is the case, then this is an elaboration (*prapañca*) of the preceding point. For indeed—
Destruction is preceded by physical contact; however, is that always the case?
No, for destruction can also be preceded by mental apprehension. Indeed, there exists here destruction preceded by mental apprehension, as in the case of [fearing] thieves.
Regarding the statement "he fears," that discerning person who is afraid perceives thus:

"If thieves were to see me, my death would be certain. Reflecting in this way, he encounters them through his intellect, and having encountered them, he turns away from them. In that context, by the very words "certainly" and so forth—

Success! Therefore, this is an elaboration (*prapañca*) of the preceding [rule]. And in an elaboration, one does not consider the relative weight (*gurulāghava*) [of the rules]. In the same way, the subsequent *yoga*s should be understood as elaborations of the preceding one;
for the examples thereof, such as "he loses after studying" (*adhyayanāt parājayate*), are already covered by the preceding [rule].
Because they are established; and how they are established has been demonstrated in the Bhāṣya itself.
Therefore, even in that case, one need not consider the relative weight or lightness [of the rules].

26. *parājer asoḍhaḥ* | (1.4.26) "It cannot be endured" (*asoḍhum na śakyate*). The meaning is "it cannot be experienced. In the example "he is defeated by study" (*adhyayanāt parājayate*), the meaning is that he is unable to overcome the study; he does not master it.

The ātmanepada ending is applied by the rule *‘viparābhyāṃ jeḥ’* (Pāṇini 1.3.19), as in the example *‘śatrūn parājayate’*, which means “he overcomes the enemies. Now, one might object: since the designation *apādāna* will not apply here because it is superseded by the designation *karman* due to its higher status [in the order of rules], that is not so.

What is the purpose of including the term *asoḍha* (not having endured) for the sake of excluding this? This is true; however, the consideration of relative weight (*gurulāghava*) is not applied to the detailed exposition (*prapañca*), and this is indeed such an exposition. For here, there is a loss (*apāya*) preceded by a mental association resulting from study. To illustrate: that very person who is lazy [acts] in this manner...
He thinks—"This study leads only to suffering"—and perceiving this with his intellect, he attains that [realization];
having attained it, he desists from it. Therefore, it is established by what has already been stated.
27. *vāraṇārthānām īpsitaḥ* (1.4.27).

Those whose meaning is "prevention" are called *vāraṇārthāḥ*. In the example, “He keeps the cows away from the barley” (*yavebhyo gā vārayati*), the word “cows” (*gāḥ*) receives the designation of *karman* (object), because it is intended as that which is most desired to be reached by the agent.

From the word *go*, by [Pāṇini 6.1.93] *ṭhāṬto'mśasoḥ*, there is the substitution of *ā* for *o*; when *r*-hood (*rutva*) has been applied, by [Pāṇini 8.3.17] *bhobhagoaghoapūrvasya*, there is the substitution of *y* (*yatva*); and by [Pāṇini 8.3.22] *hali sarveṣām*, there is the elision of *y* (*yalopa*). Regarding the form *vārayati*: the root is *vṛñ* in the sense of "covering" (Dhātupāṭha 1813).

The causative suffix *ṇic* is applied to roots beginning with *cur*, as in "he causes to turn back" (*nivartayati*). [This is derived from] the root *vṛt* in the sense of "turning" (*vartane*; DhP 758) with the causative *ṇic*. In the example "he keeps the cows away from the barley in the field" (*yavebhyo gā vārayati kṣetre*), the suffix does not apply to the field (*kṣetra*), which is not what is intended to be obtained (*anīpsita*).

Regarding the term *saṃjñā* (technical designation): there is the inclusion of the word "desired" (*īpsita*). Now, one might object: "Since the designation of 'ablative' (*apādāna*) would be sublated here by the designation of 'locus' (*adhikaraṇa*) due to its higher status in the order of rules, the field (*kṣetra*) will not receive the designation of 'ablative';
therefore, the inclusion of the word 'desired' is unnecessary. This objection should not be raised, because it has already been answered.

28. *Antardhau yenādarśanam icchati* (Pāṇini 1.4.28). The term "in the sense of disappearance" (*antardhau*) is a locative case used in the sense of a cause (*nimita-saptamī*). It is a locative according to the rule *nimitāt karmayoge* (Vārttika 138), as in the example: "He kills the tiger for its skin" (*carmaṇi dvīpinaṃ hanti*). This very [usage] is the indicator—

The locative case occurs [here] because of the rule stating that the seventh case is used when there is a connection with an action based on a cause (*nimitta*). For here, there is indeed a connection with the action of "not seeing. Regarding the word *yena*, the third case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). But is it not the case that the genitive should occur by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65)? This is not so; for [the rule applies only] when both [agent and object] are simultaneously applicable...

By the restrictive rule *karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.66), [the suffix] applies only to the object (*karman*), not to the agent (*kartṛ*). Here, however, the "object" is the self of the non-perception (*adarśana*), and because that is internal (*antaraṅga*), it alone is understood as the object.
Regarding the phrase "that *kāraka*": although the word *tat* ("that") is not explicitly mentioned in this sūtra, nevertheless, it...

This is understood from the constant connection with the word *yad* [in the rule *yasmād adhikaṃ yasya ca īśvara-vacanaṃ tatra saptamī*]. In the example "he hides from the teacher" (*upādhyāyād antardhatte*), the agent, the student, desires the non-perception of himself, who has become the object (*karman*), by means of the teacher. This is the cause for the hiding. The form *antardhatte* is the present indicative (*laṭ*) of the root *dhā*, according to Pāṇini 1.3.72: *svaritañitaḥ kartr-abhiprāye kriyāphale*.
Thus, the *ātmanepada* suffix is applied; there is *ślu*-substitution for *śap*; by the rule "kaṭhślau" (6.1.10), reduplication occurs;
by the rule "śnābhyasatyorātaḥ" (6.4.112), the long *ā* is elided; the *jaś*-change applies to the reduplicated syllable;
by the rule "dadhastathośca" (8.2.38), the *d* is changed to *dh*; and for the subsequent *dh*, the *ṭh*-rule applies before a *khar* sound.

By the rule *ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.55), the substitution of *c* occurs, and thus there is the letter *t*. Regarding the word *nilīyate*: the root *līṅ* meaning "to adhere" (*śleṣaṇe*) belongs to the fourth class (*divādi*).
Regarding the phrase "he does not wish to see the thieves": here, he who does not wish to see the thieves [is the subject].
By means of these [means], he desires the non-perception of himself, but not for the sake of invisibility;

rather, it is for the purpose of avoiding injury. The mention of "invisibility" (antarddhi) is for the sake of clarity. Since the designation of "object" (karman) takes precedence and subverts it, the designation of "ablative" (apādāna) will not apply here to the thieves.
It has been stated that this yoga is for the purpose of worldly manifestation (*prapañca*), and in worldly manifestation, one does not consider the relative weight or lightness [of the elements].
[The objection: "In the phrase 'the disciple disappears from the teacher,' let there be no disappearance of the disciple;
this is not so. [To this we reply: the word "fixed" (*dhruvam*) is understood by ellipsis, and it has been stated that the fixed is the limit (*avadhi*). It is not...

And it would cease to be delimited [by the agent]. If that were the case, then even if the word *dhruvam* were to carry over [from the previous rule], the absence of the expression *yena* would render the sūtra non-expressive;
therefore, so that this shall not occur, the word *yena* was stated.

29. *ākhyātopayoge* | (1.4.29) "The acquisition of knowledge preceded by a restriction. The "restriction" (*niyama*) is the student's engagement for the purpose of acquiring knowledge. That which has this as its precursor is described as such. [The suffix *ka* is added] by the rule *śeṣādvibhāṣā* (5.4.154).
In the expression “he hears the song of the actor,” the genitive case is used to denote a relationship;
here, there is no acquisition of knowledge preceded by formal instruction.

30. *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ* | (Pāṇini 1.4.30) Here, by association, the word *jani* refers to that which is produced (*janya*). For this very reason, he says: "of that which has the sense of being produced" (*janyarthasya*), and "of birth" (*janmanaḥ*). By this, he demonstrates the meaning of "that which is produced. To explain: the root *janī* [is used] in the sense of manifestation (*prādurbhāve*).

This is read [in the Dhātupāṭha] as *dhā* (No. 1149). "Manifestation" (*prādurbhāva*) is simply birth (*janman*). To the question, "Who, then, is its agent?", he says: "being born" (*jāyamānaḥ*). The substitution of *jā* for *jan* and *jñā* is according to Pāṇini 7.3.79.
Now, what is the purpose of including the root [itself] in the rule, given that the word *dhruvam* (the fixed point) is understood from the previous context?
It has been stated that the limit (*avadhi*) is necessarily a fixed point. Furthermore, the agent of birth (*janikartṛ*) is indeed the limit, which is simply the cause (*kāraṇa*).
In that case, even without the explicit mention of the word "material cause" (*prakṛti*), [the designation of *apādāna*] will apply to the material cause alone. This is not so;
for instance, in expressions such as "negligence arises from the son" (*putrāt pramādo jāyate*), the son and others would also receive the technical designation of *apādāna*.
The mention of "prakṛti" (material cause) is for this very purpose. For there are two kinds of causes:

the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) and the auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*). Among these, that which occupies the same location as its effect is the material cause, such as a lump of clay for a jar. That which is the auxiliary cause is...

[An effect] located in a different place [from its cause] is due to the effect; for example, the staff, the wheel, and so forth, belonging to that very [potter]. In that case, if the term "material cause" (*prakṛti*) were not mentioned, [the definition] would apply only to the material cause because of proximity, and not to others.
But when the term "material cause" is mentioned, it applies to every cause whatsoever.

31. *Bhuvaḥ prabhavaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.31). "The act of becoming is *bhūḥ*. [This is derived] with the suffix *kvip* because [the root *bhū*] belongs to the *sampadādi* group. That from which something originates is called *prabhava*; here the suffix *ap* is applied according to *ṛdorap* (3.3.57) to form the word *prabhava*, denoting the point of departure (*apādāna*). Now, one might object: [is this not illustrated by the example] "the Gaṅgā [originates] from the Himavat"?

The sense of "it originates" (*prabhavati*) is already established by the preceding [sūtra]. For the meaning here is simply that "the Gaṅgā is born from the Himavat. To the question, "For what purpose, then, is this [sūtra] commenced? he says: "It is perceived for the first time. And this meaning is to be understood through the fact that verbal roots possess multiple meanings.

But here, the sense of being produced (*janya*) is simply not possible; for the Himavat is not the cause of the Gaṅgā, since she has indeed arisen from other causes. It is merely that she is first perceived upon the Himavat.
32. That which one intends [to reach] by means of the object (*karman*) is the recipient (*sampradāna*). (Pāṇini 1.4.32) [The commentary says:

“By means of the object functioning as the instrument (*karaṇa*). But how can the object be the instrument? Because of its connection with a distinction in the action. For instance, in relation to the act of giving (*dadāti*), [the recipient] is that which is most desired to be reached.

Its status as an object (*karman*) [is established], while its status as an instrument (*karaṇa*) arises from its being the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) with respect to the action of approaching. Regarding the word "approaches" (*abhipraiti*), the meaning is "he connects with.

If one whom [the agent] approaches by means of an object is designated as the recipient (*sampradāna*), then in the case of "he leads the goat," [the person to whom he leads her would be the recipient].

Since the village, when connected with verbs of leading such as *nī* (to lead) having goats etc. as their objects, would incur the designation of *sampradāna* (recipient), he says: "Because the designation is understood to apply to other meanings," and so forth.
[The term] *sampradānam* [is used]; by that [rule], that which one intends through the object of the verb *dā* (to give) is the *sampradāna*.
It is understood. [Objection: Even so, would this not apply in cases such as "he gives a cloth to the washerman" or "he gives his back to the one who strikes him"?

[Response: This is not so; for what is called "giving" (dāna) is the relinquishing of one's own property with the desire to honor or favor another, resulting in the transfer of ownership to another. And that [is what is intended] here.

It does not exist; therefore, it will not come into being. For what purpose is the word *karmaṇā* [used]? If it were stated simply as “that which one intends [to give] is the recipient (*sampradāna*)”, then that very object (*karman*) toward which one intends would receive the designation of recipient. However, the designation of object (*karmasaṃjñā*) would then have no scope other than the object of the verb *dadāti* (‘to give’).
It might be [the case], as in "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*). What is the purpose of including the word *yam* ("whom")?

If it were stated simply as "that which one intends by means of the object is the recipient" (*karmaṇābhipraiti sampradānam*), then whatever one intends by means of the object would receive the designation of recipient (*sampradāna*). Consequently, the agent (*kartṛ*) would also receive the designation of recipient.

The scope for the designation *kartṛsaṃjñā* (the agent designation), however, would be where there is no connection with an object—such as in "he sits" (*āste*) or "he lies down" (*śete*). Now, what is the purpose of including the term *abhi* [in the rule]? If it were stated simply as "that which one reaches through an object is the *sampradāna*," there would be an expectation of a specific time, namely, only the present.

It would [be so]. Consequently, in cases such as *upādhyāyasya gāmadāt* ("he gave a cow to the teacher") and *upādhyāyāyaṃ gāṃ dāstīti* ("he intends to give a cow to the teacher"), [the rule] would not apply; however, when *abhi* is included, it does apply. The prefix *abhi* denotes "facing toward" (*ābhimukhya*), and that state exists even in the past. The prefix *pra* denotes the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*), that is, the commencement. That...

Since [the designation] is possible even when the action is not present but is yet to occur, the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is established in all cases. This does not justify the purpose of the prefix *abhi* in the rule *abhipragṛhyaṃ ca*.
Just as in the rule *karmaṇā* there is no intention to express the number one (*ekatva-saṃkhyā*), and just as in the rules *tyad* and *saḥ* [the singular is used generically].

Just as there is no intention to express [specific] gender and number, so too there will be no intention to express time. What is the reason? Because it serves as a mere illustration (*upalakṣaṇārthatvāt*). For example, when it is said, "That is a meaningful purpose (*artha*) which subverts what is meaningless (*anartha*)," then that which has already subverted it and that which will subvert it are also indeed meaningful purposes. Thus...
In that case, the inclusion of the prefix *abhi* is for the purpose that there may be an increase in meaning corresponding to an increase in the wording;
by this, the designation of *sampradāna* is established even for that which one intends through an action.
Otherwise, although an action—because it is most desired to be pervaded by both prayer and determination—is indeed [the object], [it would not receive the designation].

Even so, because of the absence of a connection with the act of giving, it would not be established. But how is it determined that this meaning—"that which one intends through an action is the recipient (sampradāna)"—is what is most desired to be propounded here? It is from the inclusion of the prefix *abhi*. For there is indeed [an intention] on the part of the Teacher here.

A certain additional meaning is intended, by the manifestation of which it is understood that another word has been employed; however, this is not a specific [new] meaning. For that [other word] is not its denoter.
Even though it may not be a denoter, nevertheless—
It is not to be objected that "the understanding of the specific [meaning] will arise through the observation of the object and through the uninterrupted instruction of the lineage of teachers";
for it has been stated: "The term 'grahaṇa' (taking/accepting) must also be supplied. "Grasping by means of action" is *kriyāgrahaṇa*. By which...

Action (*kriyā*) is mentioned; its explanation must be given. What, then, is that explanation? That has already been provided by us while describing the purpose of the rule for apprehension (*abhigrahaṇa*). But what here is the action, by which the intended object is desired to receive the designation of recipient (*sampradāna*)? It is that—

This is intended [to be explained]. Therefore, he says: “whom one intends by means of an action,” and so forth. Regarding the word *nigal̥hate*: the roots *garh* and *galh* are used in the sense of “censure” (*kutsā*) and are marked as *anudātta*. Regarding the phrase “he girds himself for battle”: the root *nah* is used in the sense of “binding” (*bandhana*) and belongs to the *divādi* class, being marked as *svarita*. That...

Here, *niścaya* (certainty) is the sense [of the suffix]; the meaning is that one makes a firm resolve regarding battle. In the example “she lies for her husband” (*patye śete*), the root *śīṅ* denotes lying down preceded by approaching; the meaning is that she lies down having approached her husband. Regarding the statement “the object receives the designation of instrument,” this refers to the case: “He worships Rudra with an animal” (*paśunā rudraṃ yajate*).

This should be understood as referring precisely to this subject matter. As for the rule "the root *yaj* is svarita," this is already established through the transposition of suffixes (*su-vyatyaya*) by virtue of the rule *vyatyayo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.1.85); therefore, it need not be explicitly stated.

33. *rucyarthānāṃ prīyamāṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.33). "Those which have the same meaning as *ruci* are called *rucyarthāḥ*. This compound is formed by the elision of the middle term (*madhyamapadalopa*), based on this very rule (*nipātana*) [of Pāṇini] and because it belongs to the class beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka*.

‘Having the same purpose’ (*samānārthāḥ*) means having a single purpose. Although the root *ric* is listed [in the Dhātupāṭha] as meaning ‘to shine’ (*dīptau*), it is used here in the sense of ‘desire’ (*abhilāṣe*), because roots have multiple meanings; for in that very context, the sense of ‘being pleased’ (*prīyamāṇa*) is possible. For he who has a desire is one who is being pleased.

But he who desires [something] satisfies it; "being pleased" (*prīyamāṇaḥ*) means "being satiated. This is the present middle participle (*śānac*) of the suffix *la* prescribed for the object after the root *prīñ* (DhP 1474) in the sense of "satisfying. By the phrase "having another as its agent," etc., he demonstrates that specific kind of desire.

He explains the meaning of the word *ruci*: another meaning [for the verb] is to be understood with reference to one who is being pleased (*prīyamāṇa*). That which has a different agent from the one being pleased is "having a different agent" (*anyakartṛka*). [Examples are: "it pleases," "it tastes good.
The roots *ruc* (DhP 7.45, meaning "to shine") and *svad* (DhP 1.18, meaning "to taste") are both *anudāteta*.
By the phrase "of that which resides in Devadatta" (*devadattasthasya*), etc., he shows that the desire has another as its agent. [The example is:

"A sweetmeat is pleasing to Devadatta on the road" (*devadatāya rocate modakaḥ pathi*). Because of the inclusion of the term "one who is being pleased" (*prīyamāṇa-graha*), the designation *sampradāna* (recipient) does not apply here to the road, which is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Now...

Why does Devadatta not receive the designation *saṃpradāna* (recipient) in the sentence "Devadatta desires a sweetmeat" (*devadato modakam abhilaṣati*)? Because of the absence of the meaning of the root *ruc*. For it has been stated [in Kāśikā 1.4.33]: "The root *ruc* refers to a desire whose agent is someone other [than the recipient]. And in this case, the desire does not have another as its agent; what then? [It has Devadatta himself as its agent.]
Devadatta, being pleased, is the agent of that desire which resides therein.

34. *ślāgh-hnuṅ-sthā-śapām jñīpsyamānaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.34). Regarding the term *jñīpsyamānaḥ*: the root *jñā* is listed among the *ghaṭādi* group [beginning with *ghaṭ*] in the sense of "killing, pleasing, and perceiving" (Dhātupāṭha 811). Therefore, it is used here in the sense of "perceiving," that is, "knowing."
[The form is derived] from the causative suffix *ṇic* added to the root *hetu*. Alternatively, the root *jñap* is listed in the *curādi* group [of roots] as "ṭhjñapa micca" (DhP 1624).

From that [root], the *curādi-ṇic* is applied; due to the *mit* designation, there is shortening of the vowel, followed by the desiderative suffix *san*, reduplication, the substitution of *ī* for the vowels *āp*, *jñap*, and *ṛdh* according to Pāṇini 7.4.55, and the elision of the reduplicated syllable according to 7.4.58.

Thus, there is the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*). The *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is used in the sense of the object (*karmani*), followed by the suffix *śānac* and the augment *yak*. Then, by the rule *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.48), the final *a* is elided. Regarding the form *ślāghate*: the root *ślāghu* (meaning "to praise" or "to boast") is marked as *anudāteta* (having an indicatory vowel with a low tone). Regarding the forms *apahnuve*, *kāśikā*, *nihnuve*, and *padamañjarī*: the root *hnuṅ* (meaning "to take away" or "to conceal") is used here.
(dhā.pā. 1082), belonging to the *adādi* class. Regarding "tiṣṭhate": by the rule "ṭhprakāśanastheyākhyayośca" (Pāṇini 1.3.23), the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings are applied.
Regarding "śapate": by the rule "pśapa ākrośe" (dhā.pā.
and "śapa upalambhane" (dhā.pā.), the *taṅ* endings are applied through the inclusion [of this root] in the enumeration.

35. *dharer uttamarṇaḥ* | (1.4.35) Regarding the term *uttamarṇaḥ*: [it is derived from] *ṛṇe uttam*, meaning "one who is superior (*uttama*) with respect to debt (*ṛṇa*). Precisely because of this irregular formation (*nipātana*), it is a compound;
for in a locative compound (*saptamī-samāsa*), the word *ṛṇa* would normally have been placed first. Now, one might object that the word *ṛṇa* does not [apply] to the creditor (*uttamarṇa*).

It must be so. [One might object: "By the rule *ṛṇamādhamarṇye* (Pāṇini 8.2.60), the form *ṛṇam* is a nipātana specifically for the state of being a debtor (*ādhamarṇya*); therefore, this [usage] is not valid. This is not the case; for in that rule, the mention of *ādhamarṇya* is intended as an illustration of a restriction regarding the time of payment. Consequently, the creditor (*uttamarṇa*) also certainly exists. As in the example: "He owes a hundred."
The root *dhṛ* (DhP 1412) means "to remain" (*avasthāne*). [In the phrase] "it remains for a hundred years" (*śataṃ dhriyate*), it means it persists in its own form;

it does not deviate from its own nature. Since another person causes it to do so, the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied by the rule *hetumati ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.26). Regarding the word "in the village" (*grāme*), this [causative action] does not belong to the village, which is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and the debtor (*anutamarṇa*).

36. *spṛher īpsitaḥ* | (Pāṇini 1.4.36) Regarding the form *spṛhayati*: because of the elision [of the *ya*] by rule 6.4.48, the substitution of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) applies by rule 1.1.57, "when a subsequent operation concerns a preceding rule," and thus the *guṇa* [vowel change] does not occur. However, when...

When the status of being the most desired (*īpsitatamatva*) of the flowers and so forth is intended to be expressed, then, by virtue of its higher priority, they receive the designation of "object" (*karman*) alone—as in: *puṣpāṇi spṛhayati* ("he desires flowers").

37. [The sixth case-affix is used] for those verbs whose meanings involve anger, malice, envy, or censure, toward that person at whom the anger is directed. (Pāṇini 1.4.37) *krudh* and *druh* are intransitive; since the sixth case-affix would have applied there, this rule is commenced. The other two (*īrṣy* and *asūy*) are transitive; since the second case-affix would have applied there, this rule is commenced. But how is it that these [verbs] have different meanings?
He states that the qualification of that [object] is appropriate in a general sense, namely, "anger toward someone who exists":
"First, anger," and so forth. This is easy to understand. Regarding the forms "kruddhyati" and "druhyati":
from the roots *krudh* (DhP 1189) meaning "to be angry" and *druh* (DhP 1197) meaning "to wish to harm," the suffixes *daivādika* and *akac* are applied.
Regarding the word *īrṣyati*: the roots *īrkṣ*, *sūrkṣ*, *īrṣya*, and *īrṣy* have the meaning of envy (*īrṣyārtha*). Regarding the word *asūyati*:
the word *asūya* ends in the suffix *yaṅ* belonging to the *kaṇḍvādigaṇa*. In the expression "he envies his wife" (*bhāryām īrṣyati*), there is indeed envy toward the wife, but...

But his anger is directed toward her; he simply cannot endure her being seen by others. Now, why does the designation *sampradāna* (recipient) not apply here in the case of "he hates him" (*asmin dveṣṭi*)?

Because the root *dviṣ* does not have anger (*krodha*) and the like as its primary meaning. For they record this [root] as signifying "displeasure" (*aprīti*); and thus it applies even to insentient objects.
It is applied as follows: "He hates what is beneficial"; it is understood that he does not take delight in it.

38. When *krudh* (to be angry) and *druh* (to bear malice) are accompanied by a prefix, that [object] is the *karman* [kāraka]. (1.4.38) 39. When *rādh* and *īkṣ* are used in the sense of divining the future, that [person] regarding whom the inquiry is made is the *karman*. (1.4.39) Regarding the word *rādhyati*: *rādh* and *sādh* [in the sense of] "accomplishment" (Dhātupāṭha 1262, 1263) belong to the *devādika* class.
"Daiva" refers to auspicious and inauspicious karma. The inclusion of the word "yasya" (of whom) is for the sake of clarity;

for instance, since the term "yaṃ prati" (with reference to whom) follows, when the connection is made as "the inquiry regarding whom," the meaning of "yasya" is indeed understood even though it is not explicitly employed.

40. *pratyāṅbhyāṃ śruvaḥ pūrvasya kartā* (1.4.40). Regarding the phrase "by another," and so forth: when one is requested or employed by someone else with the words, "Let this be done for me by another," he then makes a promise (*pratijānīte*). Therefore, [the agent] of the action preceding [the root *śru*] is other than the one who promises.

Acceptance occurs through one who employs [the means]. "Employer" (*prayoktṛ*) means the instigator. In the Sūtra, the masculine gender is used in reference to the preceding [term] by way of its meaning; however, when that meaning is examined, it is simply the action (*kriyā*). For it is only of the action that there is the term "agent" (*kartṛ*).
He says that it does not apply to any other meaning: "of the preceding action.

Since the one who is the agent of that preceding action becomes the instigator (*prayojaka*) of the person making the promise (*pratijñātṛ*), the designation "cause" (*hetu*) would otherwise apply; therefore, this rule is stated as an exception. [Example: *devadattāya gām*...
Regarding the expression "he promises" (*pratiśṛṇoti*): here, Devadatta is the agent of the preceding action of requesting (*yācana*).

For when he, having been requested by me with the words "Give me a cow," agrees by saying "I shall give," it is then that this construction is employed: *devadatāya gāṃ pratiśṛṇoti* ("He promises a cow to Devadatta").

Why specify "the agent of the preceding [rule]"? Without that, there would be the designation of *karman* (object) for that very thing which is accepted as such even in the absence of an agent—for instance, in the case of cows and so forth. Now, one might argue that because it is subsequent, the designation *karman* will override [the designation *kartṛ*].
This is not so; for this rule is commenced precisely when another designation has not yet applied. And here too:

In the case of the expression *devadattāya gām āśṛṇoti* ("he causes Devadatta to hear the cow"), the designation of cause (*hetu-saṃjñā*) would apply to Devadatta. In that context, if the rule "the agent of the preceding [action]" were not present, it would subvert the designation of cause for Devadatta; at that point, it would also subvert the designation of object (*karman-saṃjñā*). Alternatively: "Exceptions [apply] before [the rules they interrupt], [subverting] those immediately following..."
By the rule "vidhīn bādhante notarān" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 9), it would only sublate the technical designation of *karman* (object).
However, when the rule "pūrvasya kartā" is present, it sublates only the technical designation of *hetu* (agentive cause), not the designation of *karman*.
41. And [the suffix *kvip* is applied] after the root *gṛ* when preceded by *anu* and *prati*.

(1.4.41) Because of the mention of "anupratigṛṇaḥ" with the *śnā* affix, this refers to the root *gṛ* meaning "to sound" (*gṛ śabde*, DhP 1498), which is listed in the *kryādi* class, and not to the root *gṛ* meaning "to swallow" (*gṛ nigaraṇe*, DhP 1410).
Of the root belonging to the *tud* class: “The *hotṛ* recites first. By this, he shows that the *hotṛ* is the agent of the prior act of praising.
By the word “he encourages,” he explains the meaning of the two terms *agṛṇāti* and *pratigṛṇāti*. How?
Furthermore, it is known that the roots *śaṃs* (to praise) and *gṛ* (to sing) preceded by the prefixes *anu-* and *prati-* function in the sense of encouragement;

thus he says: "the *anugara* and the *pratigara*. That word by which the Hotṛ priest is first praised—that is the *anugara*. Likewise, that by which [the response] is sung back in reply—that is the *pratigara*.

The response is "kartā" (the doer) for the former [the Adhvaryu]; it is not [to be understood] as "sadasī" (in the assembly), lest there be a misconception regarding the location for the Hotṛ who is responding.
42. *Sādhakatamaṃ karaṇam* (Pāṇini 1.4.42).
Now, it may be objected that the accomplishment of an action depends upon a collection [of factors]; indeed, it does not occur if even one [factor] is absent.
Therefore, what excellence (*prakarṣa*) is there here, for the sake of which the term *sādhakatama* (the most effective means) is employed?

To one who might raise this objection, he replies with the words "in the accomplishment of action" (*kriyāsiddhau*), and so forth. "Excellently" (*prakṛṣṭam*) means extremely helpful. Alternatively, *prakarṣa* is the same as *prakṛṣṭam*; [the suffix] *-kta* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to Pāṇini 3.3.114. That which is helpful by means of excellence (*prakarṣeṇa*) is "excellently helpful" (*prakṛṣṭopakāraka*).
That which is intended as being the most effective in bringing about the accomplishment of an action is the *sādhakatama* (the most efficient instrument).

The inclusion of the term "intended" (*vivakṣita*) is for the purpose of making it known that the designation *sādhakatama* is understood only when something is intended to be expressed as the most effective factor; it is not so otherwise. For instance:

Whatever indeed at any time becomes an instrument by virtue of the speaker’s intention—such as "he pierces with a bow" (*dhanuṣā vidhyati*)—that very same thing, when there is an intention to express independence, experiences the state of being an agent—as in "the bow pierces" (*dhanur vidhyati*). Regarding the form *lunāti*: [it is derived from the root *lū*] "there is shortening for roots beginning with *pv*" (*pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ*, Pāṇini 7.3.80).
“What is the purpose of including the term *tamap* [in the rule]? [Consider the example: ‘A hamlet on the Gaṅgā.

If the inclusion of *tamap* were not made, then the designation of ‘locus’ (*adhikaraṇa*) would not apply here. For in this context, there are two kinds of loci: the secondary (*gauṇa*) and the primary (*mukhya*). Among these, the primary is that which is pervaded by the thing contained (*ādheya*), as in: ‘[Oil] in sesame seeds.’”

There is oil; here, the sesame seeds, which serve as the substratum, are pervaded by the oil, which is the superstratum. An example of a figurative [usage] where there is no pervasion is "a hamlet on the Ganges. For here, due to proximity, the status of being a substratum is attributed to the Ganges through metaphorical transfer (*upacara*), not in its primary sense, because of the absence of pervasion. In that case, when it is absent...

In the absence of the mention of *tamap*, by the rule "between the secondary (*gauṇa*) and the primary (*mukhya*), the grammatical operation applies to the primary" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 4), the designation of locus (*adhikaraṇa-saṃjñā*) would apply only to the primary, not to the other; however, because of the mention of *tamap*, it applies to that [secondary] as well.
Nevertheless, the mention of *tamap* need not be made here. How so? Even without it—

Because excellence is understood [by implication]. For just as when it is said that there is no practice of giving a maiden to one who is not handsome, and it is stated that "a maiden should be given to one who is handsome," it is understood—even without an explicit suffix of excellence—that she is to be given to one who is most handsome; so it is here as well.

Since the term "kāraka" (agent/cause) governs the context, a designation does not apply to that which is not effective; thus, when it is stated that "the instrument (*karaṇa*) is that which is effective (*sādhaka*)," even without the inclusion of the suffix *-tama*, it is understood to mean "that which is most effective (*sādhakatama*). Therefore, what is the purpose of including the suffix *-tama*? This inclusion of the suffix *-tama* is made for the sake of providing an indication (*jñāpana*). By this [inclusion], the following is indicated:

It is made known: "In this section concerning *kārakas*, except for this particular sūtra, excellence (*prakarṣa*) is not resorted to without the explicit mention of the suffix *-tamap*. Therefore, by the rule "The locus is the *adhikaraṇa*" (Pāṇini 1.4.45), even in cases such as "the hamlet is on the Gaṅgā," [the term applies] even to that which is not primary.
The designation of locus (adhikaraṇa-saṃjñā) is established for the substrata such as the Ganges.
43. *diva* and *karma* [are also included]. (1.4.43) Regarding the form *dīvyati*: the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *hali ca* (8.2.77).
44. *parikrayaṇe kasaṃpradānam anyatarasyām* (1.4.44).

*Parikrayaṇa* means the act of hiring (*parikrīti*). [The phrase] “for a fixed period” means it is not permanent. [The phrase] “by means of wages, etc.”—the word “etc. includes pledges and so forth. It is not permanent.

The phrase "only purchase" (*kraya eva*) clarifies that it is restricted to a specific time. Here, the prefix *pari-* indicates proximity. For indeed, what is called "purchase" (*kraya*) is absolute; whereas that which is for a limited time merely through wages and the like is described by the word *pari* as being "near" to absolute purchase.

45. *Ādhāra* is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). (Pāṇini 1.4.45) "That in which actions and qualities are supported is the *ādhāra*. The word *ādhāra* is derived in the sense of locus by means of [the rule] *adhyāyanyāyodyāvaṭa* (3.3.122), which prescribes the suffix *ghañ*.

The term "action" (*kriyā*) is included [in the definition] because a factor of action (*kāraka*) is dependent upon action. If it were defined as "that in which actions rest is the locus (*ādhāra*)," then the designation "locus" would undesirably apply only to the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), for it is in those two alone that actions rest. To illustrate: [actions] residing in the agent...

[If it is argued: "An action occurs, and because there is no scope [for both], the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for agent and object will not apply; thus this fault follows"—this is not a valid reply. For even if there were no scope, there would still be an alternation (*paryāya*) between the two; at one time, the designation of locus (*adhikaraṇa*) ought to apply to that [object].
[The author] demonstrates [this]: the prefix *prati* signifies "facing toward" (*abhimukhya*). As it is said: "That which is the substratum (*ādhāra*) with respect to an action.

The meaning is: that substratum which faces toward the action. And that which supports the action becomes facing toward the action. Now, the support of the action may be either direct or through mediation.
Because it supports the agent and the object, which are the substrata of the action. Here, the phrase "of the agent and the object" is stated in order to exclude the preceding [definition].
This is what is meant: because it supports the agent and the object, which serve as the substrata for the action.

That which is the substratum directed toward an action receives the designation "locus" (adhikaraṇa). Thus, by way of supporting the agent and the object—which themselves serve as the substrata for the action—that substratum which is directed toward the action receives the designation "locus"; since this [designation] is prescribed by this rule, it does not apply [in other cases].

The same fault as previously mentioned would follow. For the agent and the object do not possess the status of being the substratum of the action in this manner; rather, they are so because they directly support the action. [Objection: Even so, the agent and the object possess the primary status of being the substratum of the action, since they directly support the action.

However, the status of the mat and so forth as the locus of the agent or the object is secondary (*gauṇa*), because they support the action by way of supporting the agent or the object who themselves serve as the substrata of that action. Since the primary locus exists [in this case], the designation "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*) does not apply to the secondary one; thus, that defect remains as it was.

Is this so? It is not so; by the inclusion of the word *tamap*, it is indicated that even a secondary (*gauṇa*) substratum receives the technical designation of *adhikaraṇa* (locus). Granted that a secondary substratum receives the designation of *adhikaraṇa*, why does the same not apply to the primary (*mukhya*) agent (*kartṛ*) and object (*karman*) as well?

If it is argued that [the designation *adhikaraṇa*] does indeed apply, we say no; for it is sublated by the designations *kartṛ* (agent) and *karman* (object) because it is subsequent and because it lacks scope. For the designation *adhikaraṇa* is prior, secondary, and has scope regarding a substratum;
however, since the designations *kartṛ* and *karman* are the opposite of that, the former is unable to prevail when being sublated by them.

To illustrate the scope of these two: "He sits on a mat" (*kaṭe āste*) is an example where the action resides in the agent (*kartṛstha*), according to the former method [of classification], because the action of softening (*vikledana*) resides in the object (*karmastha*). [In contrast,] "in the pot" (*sthālyām*... [The text continues: ...is an example where the action resides in the object (*karmastha*), according to the latter method [of classification]. Thus, the distinction between the two methods is established by the difference in whether the action is understood as residing in the agent or in the object. Therefore, the rule for the locative case (*saptamī*) applies here. Furthermore, since the action of sitting (*āsana*) is inherently connected with the mat, the mat is designated as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Consequently, the locative suffix is applied to the word *kaṭa*. However, in the case of "he cooks rice in a pot" (*sthālyāmodanam pacati*), although the action of cooking (*pāka*) is connected with the pot, the pot is not designated as the locus because it lacks the status of being the substratum (*āśraya*) of that action; rather, it is designated as the instrument (*karaṇa*). Therefore, the instrumental suffix is applied to the word *sthālī*. This is the distinction between the two methods. Now, regarding the question: "Why is the action of sitting said to reside in the agent?"—it is because the action of sitting is performed by the agent himself, and it does not depend upon any external instrument. On the other hand, the action of cooking depends upon an external instrument, namely the pot, and thus resides in the object. Therefore, the action of sitting is said to reside in the agent. As for the action of cooking, since it depends upon the pot, it resides in the object. Thus, the distinction between the two methods is established based on the difference in whether the action is understood as residing in the agent or in the object. "he cooks"—this is an example of that [locus] where the action residing in the object is determined, because the action of moistening resides in the object.
Furthermore, that locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is of three kinds: *aupāśleṣika* (contact-based), *vaiṣayika* (objective), and...

And it is also pervasive (*abhivyāpaka*). Among these, in the first case—as in "he sits on a mat" (*kaṭe āste*) or "he cooks in a pot" (*sthālyāṃ pacati*)—there is indeed a contact characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) between the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), such as the mat, and that which is contained within it (*ādheya*); therefore, that [locus] is called *aupāśleṣika*. The *vaiṣayika* [locus] is, for example, "in the teacher" (*gurau*).
"There is a cowherd settlement on the Ganges. For "dwelling" (*prativasati*) implies the state of being nowhere else;

just as the eyes and other [senses] are said to have color-form and so forth as their objects because they do not exist elsewhere than in relation to color-form and so forth, so it is with disciples and others.

Because these [students and so forth] do not exist apart from the teacher and others, they are the objects [of the action]. But has it not been stated that "the locus is the adhikaraṇa" (Pāṇini 1.4.45)? And what constitutes a locus? It is that which serves as a support; such support occurs either through conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*), yet neither applies to students and the like.

Is it not improper for those [qualities] such as gravity (*gurutva*) and so forth to have [the body] as their substratum, since there is neither conjunction (*saṃyoga*) nor inherence (*samavāya*) with them?
This is not so; for that upon which the stability of something depends becomes its substratum even without conjunction or inherence, as for example—

A person is called "the king" because his existence is dependent upon the king; yet there is neither conjunction (*saṃyoga*) nor inherence (*samavāya*) between the person and the king. For instance, because he exists under the king's authority, it is commonly designated in the world that "the person has the king as his support," and likewise, the dependence of disciples and others upon their teachers and so forth is established.
"Abiding" (sthiti) is the logical basis for the state of being a support for those [qualities], such as the Guru and others. As for "pervasive" (abhivyāpaka):
it is like oil in sesame seeds or clarified butter in curd. This is because the sesame seeds and so forth, which are the substrates, abide pervading the oil and so forth, which are the superstrates.

The sesame seeds and so forth constitute the pervasive substratum (*abhivyāpakam adhikaraṇam*). Although there exists here a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) between the sesame seeds and the oil and so forth, nevertheless, because there is an absence of spatial separation (*deśavibhāga*), the conventional usage of "contact" (*saṃśleṣa*) does not apply; thus, this [pervasive substratum] is presented as distinct from the "contactual" (*aupaśleṣika*) substratum.
46. *adhi-śīṅ-sthāsām karma* (Pāṇini 1.4.46).
Regarding the example *adhyāste*: the root *ās* in the sense of "sitting" (*upaveśane*) belongs to the second class (*adādi*) and is marked with an anudātta accent.
47. *abhiniviśaśca* (Pāṇini 1.4.47).

48. *upānvadhyāṅvasaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.48). By the paribhāṣā rule regarding *lug-vikaraṇa* and *alug-vikaraṇa* (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 50), [the root] *vas* in the sense of "dwelling" (*nivāse*) [is understood].

This refers to the root *vas* belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa* (DhP 1005), and not to the root *vas* meaning "to cover" belonging to the *adādigaṇa* (DhP 1023). [The rule] begins with "of *vas*, when it does not mean 'to eat' (*aśyartha*)," etc. [An example is: "having fasted for one night" (*upoṣya rajanīmekām*).

And in the case of the expression *trirātram upavasati* ("he fasts for three nights"), the accusative case is used according to the rule *kālādhvanor atyantasaṃyoge* (Pāṇini 2.3.5). Alternatively, the accusative is used because [the time] functions as the object (*karman*) according to the Vārttika:

*kālabhāvādhvagantavyāḥ* (Mahābhāṣya 1.336). Here, the word *artha* signifies "cessation"; thus, the meaning is that it denotes the cessation of eating. Regarding the phrase *vaktavyam* ("it should be stated"): [this refers to the necessity of stating the aforementioned point].
The meaning is that it must be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows:

here too, the non-mention of "either one" (anyatarasyām) continues to apply, and that is understood to be a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*); therefore, the prohibition will apply to the root *vas* when it does not mean "to dwell."
49. *kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma* (Pāṇini 1.4.49). [The commentary explains:

"By the agent’s action. By this, the genitive case in *kartuḥ* is not dependent on the term *īpsitatama* (the most desired), as it might be by rule 2.3.67 (*ktasya ca vartamāne*), but rather it is dependent on the action (*kriyā*).
He shows that it is indeed the definition of the remainder (*śeṣa*). Now, an objection is raised: "But no action (*kriyā*) is mentioned here;

so how can the genitive case be employed with reference to it? Even though it is not explicitly mentioned, nevertheless, because an agent depends upon an action, this word "agent" (*kartṛ*) is a relative term; thus, [the genitive] expresses the relationship belonging to the agent.
There is no fault in this, for it brings about the action (*kriyā*). For there is a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*) "desired" (*īpsita*), meaning "that which is intended";

and there is also an etymological term (*kriyāśabda*) "desired" (*īpsita*), meaning "that which is sought after through action. In this context, the etymological term is taken, not the other; for the conventional term does not [apply] by means of an action.

The connection with the object to be accomplished by the agent is established. Regarding the term *īpsita*: from the root *āp* in the sense of "to pervade" (*āplṛ vyāptau*, Dhātupāṭha 1260), the desiderative suffix *san* is added; there is reduplication; then, by the rule *āpjñapyṛdhāmīt* (Pāṇini 7.4.55), the vowel *i* is substituted [for the radical *ā*];
then, by the rule *atra lopo'bhyāsasya* (Pāṇini 7.4.58), the reduplicated syllable is elided. Thus, we have *īpsa*.

When the suffix *kta* is applied to the root *sthā*, and after the augment *iṭ* has been added, the vowel *a* is elided by the rule "the elision of *ata*" (Pāṇini 6.4.48), whereby the word *īpsita* is formed. By this, two meanings are presented here: the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*) and the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*). Among these, he indicates the meaning of the root by the word "to be attained" (*āptum*), and [he indicates the meaning of the suffix] by the word "most desired" (*iṣṭatamam*).
For the sake of providing an illustration:

“of the horse” (*aśvasya*), following the rule “of the object” (*karmaṇaḥ*). Here, the horse possesses the status of an object (*karman*) because it is that which is most desired to be reached through the act of binding.
For he (the agent) desires to obtain the beans (*māṣān*) through the act of eating. As in the example: “he eats rice with milk.”

For if the suffix *tamap* were not employed, [the designation of "object"] would apply even to milk (*payas*). That too is desired by the agent to be reached through the act of eating. However, when *tamap* is employed, this over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) does not occur;
because of its predominance, it is only the rice (*odana*) that possesses the status of being most desired (*īpsitatama*). And the predominance belongs to the rice.

Because it is that which is to be refined (*saṃskārya*), whereas milk is subordinate because it is the means of refinement (*saṃskāraka*). Regarding the phrase "while *karman* continues to follow": this is from [Pāṇini 1.4.46], *adhiśīṅsthāsāṃ karma*.

Regarding the word "again" (*punar*) and so forth: the previous mention of *karman* was connected with the locus (*adhikaraṇa*); therefore, when it continues [into the present rule], [it refers back to that].
Since there would be a recurrence of that [rule], the word *karman* (object) is mentioned again for the purpose of excluding the *ādhāra* (locus).

He asks: "If, however, the *ādhāra* were to recur, what would happen? To this he says: "For it would belong to the *ādhāra* alone. The word *hi* has the sense of *yasmāt* (because). Because of this, he says: "the house (*geham*)."
And so forth. To demonstrate where [the action] does not occur when the substratum (ādhāra) persists, he says:

"He cooks rice," and so on. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), examples such as "He eats rice" are included. Now, how is the designation "object" (karman) applied in cases such as "The river erodes its bank"?

And how could it not be so? Because rivers and the like are insentient, and because desire (*īpsā*) is impossible for insentient things—this is not the case; for here, through its connection with another word, "river" (*nadī*), the absence of desire is understood even in the case of an insentient thing. Nor [is this a matter] of word-formation (*pada-saṃskāra*).

An object that is understood through its connection with another word is what is put to use; therefore, in cases such as "he drags the bank," the grammatical pervasion (vyāpti) is based merely on intention, and the object is refined. Even though, subsequently, through its connection with the river, insentience and the absence of intention are perceived, nevertheless—

And because it is external (*bahiraṅga*), it cannot set aside the operation of the internal (*antaraṅga*) technical designation. By this very principle, even where there is no actual [physical] pervasion and there is merely a desire alone, the designation "object" (*karman*) still applies, as in: "I wish to go to the village, but I am not [going]."
"I possess the power of movement.

Furthermore, that action (*karma*) is threefold: the produced (*nirvartya*), the modified (*vikārya*), and the attained (*prāpya*). Among these, that which is brought into being for the first time, for which its birth is effected—that is the produced (*nirvartya*).

For example: "He makes a mat. For a mat is produced while being non-existent [prior to its production]. As for the *vikārya* (the object of transformation), it is that which, having already attained existence, is brought to another state; [in this case], they are merely brought to the state known as ashes.
As for the *prāpya* (the object of attainment), it is that wherein no specific changes produced by the action are perceived other than through the action's pervasion (*vyāpti*).

For example: "He sees the sun. For the sun, which is being pervaded by the action of seeing, no change produced by that action is perceived; therefore, this is an object of attainment (*prāpyakarma*).
50. *Tathāyuktaṃ cānīpsitam* (Pāṇini 1.4.50).

The particle *ca* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). For this very reason, the *Vṛtti* says: "by that alone," and "the undesired" (*anīpsitam*). Even if this were a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), then [in the case of] "going to the village..."

In such cases as "he approaches the roots of trees" (*vṛkṣamūlāny upasarpati*), the designation *karman* (object) would not apply to the roots of the trees and so forth. For it is thus: if this were a simple prohibition (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), then by this rule (*yoga*) the designation *karman* would be prescribed only for that which is not intended (*anīpsita*);
yet the roots of the trees are certainly not unintended, since they were not previously disregarded.
Nor are they unintended, because they are not contrary [to the agent's desire].

Consequently, if the designation "object" (*karman*) were being prescribed for what is unintended, then since these [objects] are other than the intended, they would not be [included] under the category of the unintended. However, when there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), by this means the designation "object" is prescribed for that which is other than the intended.
Furthermore, there are instances such as those mentioned in the examples where roots of trees are not intended;

therefore, considering that the designation "object" (*karman*) would otherwise apply to them as well, he says "anything other than the intended" (*īpsitād anyat*) and so forth, in order to show that this is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). What, then, is that? He says:

‘Dveṣyam’ and so forth. ‘Dveṣyam’ means that which is disagreeable, such as poison, thieves, and the like. ‘Itarat’ means that which is not disagreeable, such as the roots of trees described above. Regarding the word ‘bhakṣayati’: the root ‘bhakṣ’ (meaning ‘to eat’) belongs to the curādigaṇa (Dhātupāṭha 1557).

51. *Akathitaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.51). [Note: In the printed *Kāśikāvṛtti*, however, the reading is *apādānādiviśeṣakathābhiḥ*; some versions read *apādānādibhir viśeṣakathābhiḥ*. This refers to the general designation of a *kāraka*: [The term *akathita* applies] when there is no specific mention by means of particular designations such as *apādāna* (ablative), etc. [This refers to the general designation of a *kāraka*.]

This is for the purpose of exclusion. For if the designation of "object" (*karman*) were to apply to anything that has not been mentioned [by a specific rule], then in the sentence *māṇavakasya pitaraṃ panthānaṃ pṛcchati* ("He asks the boy's father the way"), the boy (*māṇavaka*), though not a factor of action (*akāraka*), would also receive the designation of "object. [The term] "enumeration" (*parigaṇanam*) [is used].

This is for the purpose of delimiting the scope of the verbal roots. Therefore, the designation *karman* (object) is prescribed for that which is not otherwise mentioned (*akathita*) only when used with roots such as *duha* (to milk) [DhP 1014] and others, and not with other roots. The word *upayoga* means "that which is employed"; it is derived from the root *yuja* with the suffix *ghañ*, functioning as a *karma-sādhana* (denoting the object).

‘It is employed’ (*upayujyate*) means that it is put to use for the accomplishment of a desired purpose. ‘Milk and so forth’ (*payaḥ-prabhṛti*): by the word ‘and so forth’ (*prabhṛti*), alms-food (*bhikṣā*) and other such items are included. ‘The cause of that is the cow and so forth’ (*tasya nimittaṃ gavādi*):
here too, by the word ‘and so forth’ (*ādi*), the descendant of Puru (*paurava*) and others are included. ‘The milk being used upon that [cow]... (*tasyoparyujyamāna-payaḥ*)...’

Regarding the phrase "of that which has the milk and so forth as its cause": having formed a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) from *upayujyamāna* and *tat payaḥ prabhṛti*, one then forms a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the cause of that which has the milk and so forth being used. Regarding the term "of the cow and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of Paurava and others is intended. Now, [an objection is raised]:...

And the hand and so forth are also instrumental causes for the act of consumption (*upayoga*), because without them, the consumption of milk would be impossible. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), items such as a bronze vessel are included. [As it is said:
"For in that case, the technical designations of instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth are prescribed. By the word "and so forth," the designation of locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is included.

‘For that purpose’ (*tadartham*): the meaning is for the sake of preventing the designation of *karman* (object) for the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth; this is because the word *artha* here signifies cessation (*nivṛtti*). Regarding the phrase ‘in a rule not previously established’ (*apūrvavidhau*): the inclusion of the word *pūrva* (previous) here is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for any other rule. This is what is meant: for which [word] there is another...

The rule states that the designation "object" (karman) is not applied to that which is not explicitly mentioned [as such]. Therefore, even in cases where the designations "cause" (hetu) and "agent" (kartṛ) will be taught hereafter, this designation [of object] does not apply there either;
thus, although the milker is the cause of the utilization, he does not receive the designation "object."

Since it is also stated in the Sūtra, "it has been told," how could the past tense not be intended when the injunction (*codanā*) is not yet completed? This is because [the term] is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). By this, it is also stated that even for that which is about to be told by means of the designations of cause (*hetu*) and agent (*kartṛ*), the designation of object (*karman*) does not occur.
"By virtue of [the relationship with] the agent of the roots *brū* (to speak) and *śās* (to command). But what, then, is this "virtue"? He says: "The means (*sādhana*).

For the means is that which assists through action. And that which is an assistant becomes a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) in relation to the primary object (*pradhāna*) which is assisted. But which, then, is the means? He says: "The primary [object]."

"Karma"—what, then, is that? He says: "Dharma and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the Lord (*pati*) and others is intended. Dharma and the rest are primary, however, because the engagement of disciples and others is for their sake.
"Is connected" (*sambadhyate*) is an explanation of the meaning of the root *ṣac*. For instance: "the root *ṣac* [is used] in the sense of conjunction (*samavāya*)."

The root *dhā* is recited [in the Dhātupāṭha] as 997; and *samavāya* is indeed a connection (*sambandha*). One "associates" (*sacate*) with that quality, meaning one enters into a connection with it. And that which enters into a connection with it becomes connected with it.
The word "spoken" (*uktam*) is an explanation of "practiced" (*ācaritam*). This also applies to the phrase "by the author of the Sūtras."
Regarding the word "kavinā":
[the example is] "he milks the cow for milk" (*gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ*). The root *duh* (meaning "to fill," *prapūraṇe*) belongs to the second class (*adādikaḥ*).
By the rule *dāderdhātorghaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.32), the *d* is replaced by *gh*; by *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* (8.2.40), the *t* is replaced by *dh*; and by *jhalāṃ jaś*... [the *dh* is replaced by *j*].

The substitution of the *jaś* sound [d] occurs by the rule *jhaśi* (Pāṇini 8.4.53). Now, one might object: the designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*) is indeed prescribed here, for there is a separation (*apāya*) involved—since the root *duh* has the sense of "flowing," as in "the cow flows milk" (*goḥ kṣīraṃ kṣarati*), and thus the milker causes the cow to flow; and so that which is being caused to flow departs from it.
[Objection: The removal (*apāya*) is indeed evident; therefore, this example is not tenable. [Response: This is not so.

For even though there is removal, the cow is not intended here as the limit (*avadhi*), but rather merely as the cause (*nimitta*) with respect to the milk. [Objection: If that is the case, the cow would not possess the status of a *kāraka* (participant in an action), just as—

In the expression "the leaf of the tree falls," the [tree] does not [function as the agent]; for it is not intended to be the cause (*nimitta*) with respect to the action of falling. This is not so; for here, the status of being a limit (*avadhitva*) is certainly not intended, whereas its status as the cause with respect to the falling is indeed intended. [The example is: "the leaf of the tree."

In the case of "he falls" (*patati*), however, even the mere status of the tree as a cause (*nimitta*) with respect to the act of falling is not intended to be expressed, let alone its status as a limit (*avadhi*); thus, the cases are not the same. Regarding "he begs a cow from the Paurava":
one might object that here the technical designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*) has already been assigned, for such a designation indeed exists.
Is there not indeed a loss [of ownership] because one takes a cow from a Paurava? This is not so;

for loss does not occur merely through begging. What then? It is merely the status of being a cause with respect to the act of confinement. And in this state, it is intended to be expressed; yet this is not the case here.

The intended meaning here is that one causes the cow to stand by means of a reason; this is how the sense should be understood. However, the specific location where it is caused to stand is not what is being considered here. [As in the example: "He asks the boy the way.
The root *pracccha* is used in the sense of desiring to know (*jñīpsā*); it belongs to the *tudādi* class and undergoes *samprasāraṇa* according to the rule *grahijyā-vā-yi-ky-āpām ca*.

(6.1.16) *Samprasāraṇa*. Now, it might be argued that the designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*) has already been stated here, for there is indeed a departure (*apāya*): he receives instruction from him. This is not so; for a mere question does not constitute a departure. What then? It is when, having been questioned, he explains [the matter].

In that case, it is connected with the sense of "going away" (*apāya*). Even though there is indeed an "away-going," the young boy (*māṇavaka*) is not intended here as the limit (*avadhi*), but rather merely as the cause (*nimitta*) for the act of questioning.
As in: "He begs a cow from the Paurava. [The root] *bhikṣ* [is used] in the sense of "begging" (*yācñā*). (Dhātupāṭha 606).

[The sūtra begins with] *anudāteta*. Why are both *yāci* and *bhikṣi* mentioned, given that there is no difference in their meaning? Nor is this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) based on the word-form; rather, it is based on the meaning. For instance, another verb having the same meaning as *yāci* is also included.

One says, "He requests a hundred from Devadatta," or "He seeks a hundred from Devadatta. Therefore, even though there is a difference in words, it is not logical to treat those two as distinct. If that is so, then the verb *yācati* here functions in the sense of entreaty—as in "he entreats the angry man" or "he entreats the ill-behaved man."
For that purpose, there would need to be a separate mention [of the object], as in:

"He gathers fruits from the tree" (*vṛkṣam avacinoti phalāni*). Now, one might argue that the designation of *apādāna* (ablative) is indeed prescribed here, for in this case the meaning is "he takes the fruits away from the tree," which constitutes a separation (*apāya*). This is not so; for it is not the case here...

The tree is not intended as the limit (*avadhi*); rather, it is [intended] merely as the cause (*hetu*) for the gathering of fruits. The meaning is that one performs the gathering of fruits by means of the tree as the cause. Is the causal status of that tree that of a limit (*avadhibhūta*), or that of a locus (*adhikaraṇabhūta*)?
No such consideration was made [in the rule].

Thus, one says, "he speaks the dharma to the boy" (*māṇavakaṃ dharmaṃ brūte*) or "he instructs the boy in the dharma" (*māṇavakaṃ dharmamanuśāsti*). The root *brū* (DhP 1044) means "articulate speech," and the root *śās* (DhP 1075) means "instruction."

[The opponent says: "But has not the designation *sampradāna* (recipient) been stated here? For there is indeed the status of a recipient here, because [the person] is intended by means of the quality (*dharma*) to be given. [The author replies: This is not so;
the designation *sampradāna* is prescribed for one who is intended by the act of giving (*dadāti-karman*), and here there is no such quality."

It is the act of giving (*dadāti-karman*); for the roots *brū* (to speak) and *śās* (to instruct) do not have the sense of giving. Even if they were to have the sense of giving, the meaning would still be "he gives dharma on account of the boy" (*māṇavakena nimittena dharmaṃ dadāti*), because the boy is not intended to be expressed as the recipient (*sampradāna*); rather, he is the cause for the giving of dharma.
Because it is intended [to be expressed].

In the rule *bruviśāsiguṇena ca*, the word *ca* (and) serves to include what has not been mentioned. By this, it is desired that even in the employment of verbs such as *nī* (to lead), that which is "unspoken" (*akathita*) receives the technical designation of object (*karman*). Thus it has been said:
"The inclusion of *nī*, *vah*, *hṛ*, and likewise verbs meaning 'to go' among those that take two objects (dvikarmaka) is to be understood; this is the settled rule.
In this verse as well, the word "and" (*ca*) [indicates] that [the rule applies] even in the usage of verbs such as *ji* ("to conquer") when there is an unexpressed object (*akathita*).
This has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
What is the example? Devadatta leads the goat to the village; Devadatta carries the goat to the village; Devadatta brings the goat to the village; [he] wins a hundred from Devadatta.

"Yajñadatta punishes a hundred Gargas. Now, one might object: "Is not the designation of *karman* established for both [the cows and the village] by the very rule *'kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma'* (Pāṇini 1.4.49)?
If, then, the state of being most desired (*īpsitatamatva*) is intended for the goats and so forth, but not for the village and so forth, how [is that so]?"

What is the designation "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*)? Even so, it is established by the rule *tathāyuktam* (Pāṇini 1.4.50). However, when the status of being the most desired (*īpsitatva*) for villages and the like is intended without the addition of excellence (*prakarṣa*), then it is not established.
