Furthermore, for intransitive roots (*akarmaka-dhātu*), time (*kāla*), state (*bhāva*), distance (*adhvan*), and destinations (*gantavya-deśa*) are desired to receive the designation "object."
And so it has been said:
"Time, state of being, and the distance to be traversed are designated as objects (*karman*) for [verbs] that are otherwise intransitive;
likewise, the states (*daśā*) of intransitive verbs also receive the designation of object."
Thus it should be stated (MaBhā 1.336).

Therefore, the particle *ca* has been employed in that sense to include what was not explicitly mentioned: [the examples] "he sits for a month" (*māsam āste*) and "he sleeps for a month" (*māsaṃ svapiti*). As for the state (*bhāva*): "he sits during the milking of the cows" (*godoham āste*) and "he sleeps during the milking of the cows" (*godohaṃ svapiti*).

"A path to be traversed"—as in "he sits for a *krośa*" or "he sleeps for a *krośa*. This is a determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) consisting of the specific term "path" and the general term "to be traversed.
According to the rule "kaḍārāḥ karmadhāraye" (Pāṇini 2.2.38), the qualifier is placed first. [The same applies to] "place."
In the examples "he dwells among the Kurus" (kurūn āste) and "he sleeps among the Kurus" (kurūn svapiti), all these—beginning with time—are termed *akathita* (unexpressed);
this is because no preceding rule has yet applied to them.
52. *gatibuddhipratyavasānārthaśabdakarmākarmakāṇām aṇau yaḥ kartā sa ṇau* (Pāṇini 1.4.52).
In the case of the verb *yāpayati*, the suffix *puk* is applied by [the rule] *artihrī* (Pāṇini 7.3.36), etc.

"It should be stated" means "it should be explained. Here is that explanation: In the subsequent sūtra (1.4.53), the mention of the word *anyatarasyām* is understood to apply as a supplement (*śeṣa*) to both rules, and it is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*); therefore, [the suffix] will not occur after the roots *nī* and *vah*.

‘*Vaheḥ*’ and so forth. A *niyantṛ* is one who restrains—that is, one who establishes [the vehicle] in a specific place—namely, a charioteer (*sārathi*). That which has no such *niyantṛ* as its agent is called *aniyantṛ*; [the word refers to] that.
Regarding this, the rule “a prohibition must be stated for the roots *nī* and *vah*” (*Vārttika* 62), which was mentioned immediately prior, applies.
The meaning is that the phrase "of *vah* whose agent is the driver" (*vāheraniyantṛkartṛkasya*) must be explained as having this specific sense.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: because the option (*anyatarasyām*) mentioned in that very rule is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the designation of object (*karmasaṃjñā*) will apply to *vah* when its agent is the driver.

Regarding the phrase “ādikhādyoḥ” and so forth: here too, the meaning of the word *vaktavya* (to be stated) is exactly as before, and the explanation should also be made just as before. [The example] “devadattaḥ bhakṣyati piṇḍīm” (Devadatta will eat the ball) involves the *ṇic* suffix of the *curādi* class. [The example] “bhakṣayati piṇḍam devadattena” (He causes Devadatta to eat the ball) involves the *ṇic* suffix of the *hetu* (causal) sense.

"He eats the oxen and the grain. Here, the root *bhakṣ* has the sense of "injuring" (*hiṃsā*). According to the view that "all entities are sentient," the grain is injured; thus, by the eating of the grain, Devadatta becomes injured. For the injury of that whose grain it is is understood [to have occurred].

Regarding the phrase "of verbal actions" (*śabdakarmaṇām*): here, by the mention of "word" (*śabda*), the technical grammatical object (*pāribhāṣikaṃ karma*) is intended, and not the action (*kriyā*). For if the action were intended, the mention of "object" would be redundant; because we are within the governing heading of "factors of action" (*kāraka*), and since a factor of action necessarily depends upon an action, [the word "action"] refers here to an action consisting of sound.
If it is argued that "present tenses" (*vartamānā dhātavaḥ*) will be understood [by implication], then what is the purpose of mentioning "object" (*karma*)? If, on the other hand,

the technical definition of "object" (*pāribhāṣikaṃ karma*) is being taken, then [the rule] would not apply in cases such as *jalpati devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta talks") and *jalpayati devadattam* ("He makes Devadatta talk"), or *vilapati devadattaṃ kārṣāpaṇam* ("He makes Devadatta lament for a kārṣāpaṇa coin"), because [in these cases] there is nothing other than sound (*śabda*).
Since the technical sense of "object" (karman) is intended here, this fault does not apply;

it will be accounted for because it serves the purpose of cognition. For in this context, verbs such as *jalpati* ("he prattles") function toward the production of sound or the act of making understood. Thus, "Devadatta prattles" (*jalpati*) means he makes [others] understand by means of speech.

The same applies elsewhere as well. In the expression "he sees a kārṣāpaṇa," the verb *dṛś* (to see) functions in the sense of knowledge produced by the instrument of sight; the meaning is "he knows by means of the eye. Therefore, because its purpose is cognition (*buddhi*), the [rule] is established. Regarding the form *adhyāpayati*: the substitution of *ā* occurs according to Pāṇini 6.1.48, *krīṅjīnāṃ ṇau*. [This applies also to] *arti*, *hrī*, etc.

By [the rule] beginning with (7.3.36), the suffix *puk* is applied. But for what purpose is this sūtra, given that when a verbal root ends in *ṇi*, the prompted agent (*prayojya*)— by virtue of being most desired to be reached through the activity of the prompter (*prayojaka*), which consists of the acts of commanding or entreating— is already designated as the "object" (*karman*) by the rule *kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma* (1.4.49)?
Is the designation *karman* (object) established by this very [rule] alone? True; however, the statement is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*):

when the designation *karman* applies to that which is pervaded by the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*), it applies only to roots meaning "motion" (*gatyartha*) and so forth, and not to others.
53. *hṛkroranyatarasyām* (1.4.53).

The meanings of "going" (*gati*) and so forth have ceased [to apply]. Therefore, this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) in both cases. When *harati* refers to "going" or to "eating" (*abhyavahāra*), and when *karoti* is used with an object, then [the rule] applies because it was already established [by the previous sūtra]. When...

However, *harati* occurs in the sense of stealing and so forth, and *karoti* is transitive; thus, [the application of the rule] does not apply to you. Regarding the phrase "an addition" (*upasaṃkhyānam*), it means "an exposition. And since this is the subject at hand, the exposition here is as follows: "And that which is unmentioned" (*akathitaṃ ca*, 1.4.51).
Therefore, the particle *ca* (and) is carried over [from the previous rule], and it serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned.
By this, even for the roots *abhivad-* (to salute) and *dṛś-* (to see), the designation of "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*) will apply when the Ātmanepada is used.
Thus, in *abhivādayate*, the Ātmanepada ending occurs by the rule *ṇitaśca* (Pāṇini 1.3.74). [Likewise] in *darśayate*.
Thus [it is said]. Here too, [the rule] beginning with *ṇeraṇau* (1.3.67) applies. 54. *svatantraḥ kartā* (1.4.54).
This word *svatantra* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. That which has its own (*svam*) authority (*tantram*) is *svatantra*. It exists.

And it is a conventional word (*rūḍhi-śabda*) that resembles a compound, functioning in its primary sense; for example, in the phrase "This Devadatta here is independent," he is understood to be the principal one. In that case, if the preceding [word] were taken, it would apply only to the weaver; for it is indeed spread out...
The loom is the substrate (*tantra*), and that belongs only to the weaver. In cases such as "Devadatta cooks," [the term *svatantra*] would not apply [to Devadatta].

However, when the other [meaning] is taken, it applies everywhere. Therefore, thinking that by the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*) only that [weaver] is to be understood, he says: "The independent one (*svatantra*) is the primary agent (*pradhānabhūta*)."
If it were thus— that the primary [agent] is designated in dependence upon what is non-primary—

then this would apply only in cases where there exist other non-primary factors of action (*kāraka*), such as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and so forth, as in examples like "Devadatta cooks rice in a pot with wood and fire. But where, however...

Regarding their non-intentionality [to denote the agent] in cases such as "Devadatta sits" (*āste devadattaḥ*) or "Devadatta lies down" (*śete devadattaḥ*), he says "it is not subordinate" (*aguṇabhūtaḥ*) in response to one who might object that [the agent] would not be [denoted] there. He thinks as follows: the state of being non-subordinate is indicated by the primary [action]; thus, that in which the state of being subordinate does not exist is the agent.

Even when other factors [kārakas] are not intended to be expressed, the state of being non-subordinate (aguṇabhāva) certainly exists; thus, [the designation of the agent] occurs everywhere. Now, one might object: "The accomplishment of an action indeed depends upon a collection [of causes]; it is not accomplished even in the absence of a single one.
Therefore, what is the predominance here for which the term 'svatantra' (independent) is employed to include [the agent]? To this he says: "He who..."

Regarding the passage beginning with "in the accomplishment of an action" (*kriyāsiddhau*): although all [factors] are involved in the accomplishment of an action, nevertheless, that one whose independence (*svātantrya*) is intended to be expressed is alone called "independent" (*svatantra*), and no other.
In the sentence "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*), Devadatta, because he possesses the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*), [is the independent one].
The agent is expressed by the *lakāra* suffix.

55. "And the instigator of that is the cause" (*tatprayojako hetuśca*). [The compound *tatprayojakaḥ* is explained as] "the instigator of that (*tasya*) is the instigator of that (*tatprayojakaḥ*). Now, one might object: since the prohibition of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) by the rule "and in the sense of the agent" (*kartari ca*, Pāṇini 2.2.16) applies here, this [compound] should not occur; to this he replies:

‘The compound is formed by irregular derivation (*nipātana*). ‘The instigator (*prayojaka*)’ means one who impels, that is, an instructor, meaning an agent of activity. And the independence (*svātantrya*) of one being impelled by another in regard to his own activity is not lost; otherwise, one would have to say “he causes [someone] to act” even when that person is not acting. This is the state of being an instigator.

It is of two kinds: primary (mukhya) and secondary (itara). In the sentence "Devadatta causes the mat to be made," Devadatta's status is primary. In the sentence "He causes the alms to dwell [there]," the alms possess the status of being a motive (*prayojana*) by virtue of being the cause for dwelling; this is figurative (*upacarita*), not primary. For it is not the case that one says, "O alms, you dwell! in such a manner.

They employ [the term]. And here, in the section concerning *kāraka*s, it is indicated by the inclusion of the suffix *-tama* in the rule "The most effective [means] is the instrument" (*sādhakatamaṃ karaṇam*, 1.4.42) that excellence (*atiśaya*) is not intended to be expressed apart from that suffix. Therefore, even for that which possesses a figurative status as a motive (*prayojana*), rather than a primary one—

For that [agent] as well, the designation "cause" (hetu-saṃjñā) indeed occurs. Regarding the statement, "The particle *ca* is for the purpose of the co-occurrence of designations": if that were not present, then because of the governing rule of a single designation (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), the designation "agent" (kartṛ-saṃjñā) would not apply here. Therefore, the particle *ca* is employed for the purpose of the co-occurrence of designations.
By the words "because of being the cause" (*hetutvāt*) and so forth, he demonstrates the purpose of the two technical designations (*saṃjñā*).
For the suffix *ṇic* is prescribed by the rule "and when there is an instigator" (*hetumati ca*, Pāṇini 3.1.26) in reference to the activity of an instigator (*prayojaka*).
Its status as a cause is established only when the instigator possesses causality.

Because it is the cause, the causal agent (*prayojaka*) becomes the occasion for the suffix *ṇic*. Since the designation "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) occurs when there is expression by means of the *l*-suffix as an agent-suffix, it is expressed by the *l*-suffix as an agent-suffix precisely because of its status as an agent.

56. *Prāgrīśvarānnipātāḥ* (1.4.56). When the designation *nipāta* (particle) applies to *ca*, *vā*, *ha*, and *aha* by this rule, they receive the designation *avyaya* (indeclinable) according to *Svarādinipātamavyayam* (1.1.37). [The particles are... *Nipātāḥ*...

And there is also the property of having the first syllable acute, according to the rule *ādyaudātā bhavanti* (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.80). Now, for what purpose is the mention of *prāk*? For, by the force of the utterance of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) itself, the directional word *prāk* will be supplied as an ellipsis. Nor is this [word] *parām* [necessary].

The word *dik* exists [in the sūtra]. Therefore, one should not suspect the necessity of supplying an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). For if that were supplied, rules such as *cādayo’satve* (Pāṇini 1.4.57) would become incoherent, as they would lack a connection to the technical designation of *nipāta*. Consequently, [the word *dik* is indeed present].
The word "prior" (*prāk*) will be supplied [from the previous rule]. Why, then, is the word "prior" stated here?
He says: "The statement 'prior'... and so forth. The term "one technical designation" (*ekā saṃjñā*) is understood to carry over.

The designation "particle" (*nipāta*) has already fulfilled its purpose in the case of *ādi* (the group beginning with *ā*) or *prādi* (the group beginning with *pra*) when used in connection with a verb. In that context, if the word "prior" were not stated, [the designation would apply only to those].
Since the designation *nipāta* is sublated by the designations *upasarga* and so forth—which have no other scope—it would not coexist with them. Yet, such coexistence is desired here;
for that purpose, the word "prāk" (before) is stated. When that is present, the connection is made as follows: "as many [terms] as there are from [the beginning] up to Īśvara..."

All those previously established [words] are designated as *nipātas* (particles), and being *nipātas*, they are also designated as *upasargas* (prepositions) and so forth. Therefore, the designation of *nipāta* and *upasarga* occurs solely on account of the cause (*nimitta*). Furthermore, the cause is not sublated by that which possesses the cause; for otherwise, its [status as a cause] would be lost.

The status of being a *nimita* (cause/condition) would not even exist. However, if one supplies the word "prior" (*prāk*), the intended meaning would be: "all those [words] situated prior to the Lord (Īśvara), etc., are designated as *nipātas*"; but the meaning that "being *nipātas*, they are also designated as *upasargas* and so forth" is not what is intended.

It is obtained. However, this very meaning is already obtained from the word *prāk* (before) as it occurs in the sūtra; otherwise, that [word] would be redundant. Now, for what purpose is the word *īśvara* taken as beginning with the letter *r*—as in "before *īśvara*" (*prāgrīśvarāt*)—and not...?

If it were said simply "prior to Īśvara" (prāg-īśvarāt), one might assume that by proximity the word immediately following, namely *Īśvara*, would be understood; therefore, he says: "From *rīśvara*, the self of Īśvara became. *Rīśvara* is *Īśvara* together with the letter *r*. The compound is formed either according to the *śākapārthiva*-type or the *mayūravyaṃsaka*-type class.
When "īśvarāt" is stated [in the rule], let it not be [taken as] from the word *īśvara* [in general];

rather, let there be the inclusion of that very word *īśvara* which belongs to the rule "adhir īśvare" (Pāṇini 1.4.97). Let there not be the inclusion of the word *īśvara* that occurs in the rule "īśvare to-tuṅ-kasunau" (Pāṇini 3.4.13). For, if that were included...

Because there is a designation for many [sounds] due to this pervasion (*vyāpti*), according to the rule of logic, the inclusion of this very one would occur. Now, it might be argued: "But the letter *v* does not even exist there; so why is it said, 'lest it be from the word *viśvara*'?
He thinks as follows: when the sūtras are recited in their joined form (*saṃhitā*)—“*śaki*... [and so on].

Regarding the rule "ṇamulkamulāvīśvaretosunkasunau" (Pāṇini 3.4.12–13), the mention of the word *īśvara* therein is not the motivating factor for its inclusion. Even though there is a pervasive application (*vyāpti*) based on that [mention] when referring to the subsequent word *īśvara*, nevertheless, it will be the immediately preceding word *īśvara* that is understood, and not [the subsequent one].

Of the other [word]; how so? From an indicator (*jñāpaka*); namely, that the rule "that which ends in *ṭhak*, *kan*, or a suffix whose final vowel is long is indeclinable" (Pāṇini 1.1.39) teaches the designation of indeclinability for words ending in *m* or *aij* (diphthongs), thereby indicating that the word *īśvara* is to be understood as the immediately preceding one and not the other; for otherwise, [the rule would apply] to forms such as those ending in *ṇamul*.

Since the designation of *avyaya* (indeclinable) would be established by the very fact of being a particle (*nipāta*), the rule "that which ends in a *kṛt* suffix or in a long vowel (*ejanta*) is [an indeclinable]" (Pāṇini 1.1.39) would be purposeless. This is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*); for even after the rule "the suffixes *tosun* and *kasun* occur in the sense of 'lordship'" (3.4.13), there exists that which ends in a *kṛt* suffix.

There are also suffixes ending in *m*, such as those prescribed by rules like "kṛtyārthe tavaikenkenyatvanaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.14) and "ābhīkṣṇye ṇamul ca" (3.4.22). How, then, could the rule "kṛnmejantaḥ" (1.1.39) serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) [of the existence of indeclinables]? If that is so, then consider this: that the author [of the Aṣṭādhyāyī] teaches the term "avyayībhāva" for the avyayībhāva compound in the rule "avyayībhāvaśca" (1.1.41).

Thus, by teaching the designation "indeclinable" (*avyaya*), he indicates that the term *īśvara* which immediately precedes is what is being referred to. For otherwise, the rule *avyayībhāvaśca* (Pāṇini 1.1.41) would be purposeless;
since the designation "indeclinable" for the *avyayībhāva* compound is already established simply by virtue of its being a particle (*nipāta*).
To refute its status as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), [the author] says: "Among compounds, the *avyayībhāva*.

Since all compounds would be designated as indeclinables (*avyaya*) due to their being *nipātas*, the rule "and the *avyayībhāva*" (Pāṇini 1.1.39) would serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) regarding compounds: [only the *avyayībhāva* is an indeclinable].
Among the [types of compounds] beginning with *tatpuruṣa*, only the *avyayībhāva* receives the designation "indeclinable" (*avyaya*), and no other.

If that is so, then by the maxim of common usage (*laukikanyāya*), there will be the inclusion of the word *īśvara* alone, which is immediately preceding; for in the world, it is said: "One should follow a beloved person as far as the water's edge," and thus it is only that which is immediate [which is understood].
Having gone only as far as the edge of the water, the relatives turn back from that very point, not from beyond it.

Therefore, here too, by this same principle, the designation of "particle" (nipāta) will cease immediately after the word *īśvara*; hence he says: "and it transcends even what is worldly. Even that which is worldly...

The world acts by transgressing what is right, since even kinsmen, out of affection, go as far as a second person who is not beloved—by way of engaging in conversation—and then turn back. Thus, the word "Īśvara" (Lord) is pronounced with an extra *repha* (the letter *r*). Therefore, it is established that [the suffix] must not follow from "vīśvara."

57. *cādayo'satve* (Pāṇini 1.4.57). Regarding the term "asatve" (in the case of non-substance): is this an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) or a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*)? If it were an exclusion, then the particles beginning with *ca* would apply when they function elsewhere than in the case of substance (*satva*).

The meaning of the sūtra would be that [the words] *iti*, *īṣat*, and so forth, receive the designation of "particle" (*nipāta*). Consequently, the word *paśu* (beast), when listed among the group beginning with *ca* and denoting a substance delimited by a genus, would receive the designation of "particle. For that which denotes a substance qualified by a genus [is what is intended].

It expresses an object consisting of a collection of genus and substance; and such an object is distinct from a mere substance. If the designation "particle" (nipāta) were applied [by way of absolute negation], there would be no hearing of the form *paśu* with its case-ending. However, this fault does not arise if it is a relative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), for in that case—

Wherever there is even a trace of a substance, there must be a prohibition; and here, too, there is a trace of a substance, because the word "animal" (paśu) denotes not only the universal (jāti) of animality but also the substance that subsists in that universal.
Therefore, considering that this must be a purely non-implicative negation (prasajyapratiṣedha), he says:

"This is a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*). In what case, then, does the word *paśu*, being present, denote a non-existent entity? It is when it receives the designation of a particle (*nipāta*) within a compound in the sense of "as if seen"—for example:
*lodhaṃ nayanti paśu manyamānāḥ* ("They lead the *lodhra* tree, thinking it to be a beast"). Here, by virtue of the sense of "as if seen," [it denotes something unreal].
By the word *paśu*, deliberation (*manana*) is distinguished. This "seeing" is deliberation;

the meaning is that it is right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). Someone might have the misconception that this word *sattva* here refers to the quality of goodness (*sattva-guṇa*), therefore, in order to dispel that, he says: "And [the word] *sattva*..."

"Substance is said [to be that which is denoted by the word]. The word "and" (ca) is used for emphasis; the meaning is that it is substance alone, not existence (*sattā*). For if, in this context, the word "existence" were to denote the category of existence (*sattā*), the negation would be meaningless; indeed, among the group beginning with "and" (*cādi*), there is no word whatsoever that denotes the category of existence. Therefore, it is substance itself that is being denoted.
In that case, then, that object which is capable of being referred to by a pronoun is *dravya*. And so it has been said:
"Where a pronoun is employed to indicate a thing (*vastu*)," [that is *dravya*].

"That object which is intended to be expressed as the thing to be differentiated (bhedyatvena) is called a substance (dravya). Here, "as the thing to be differentiated" means "as the qualificand (viśeṣya). For this very reason, it is said: "That in which a quality subsists by way of being a qualifier (viśeṣaṇabhāvena) is called 'sattva' [the state of being] and is termed a substance."

The word *caṇ* is recited; its *ṇakāra* is for the sake of distinction, according to the rule "when joined with the particles *yad*, *yadi*, *hanta*, *ku*, *vid*, *ne*, *ca*, *ceṇ*, *kaccit*, *yat*, and *trā*" (Pāṇini 8.1.30), and it functions in the sense of the word *ced*.

The word *yatra* is read [in the text]. Its designation as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is already established by the rule *taddhitaś cāsarvavibhaktiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.38). However, it is designated as a particle (*nipāta*) for the purpose of the specific rule *nipātair yadyadihantakuvitneticennañpāṭpyāṭ* (Pāṇini 8.1.30). If it were not a particle, [the form] *yaṃ trāyate* would [not be possible], based on the root *traiṅ* in the sense of protecting (Dhātupāṭha 965).
Thus, in this context, there would be the inclusion of the *ka*-suffix [prescribed] by the rule *ṭhāto 'nupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3).
However, the form *nañ* is recited; the *ñ* of *nañ* is for the purpose of [triggering] the elision of the *n* by the rule *nalopo nañaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.73).

This is for the sake of specification. If it were merely stated that "there is elision of *n* in *nañ*," then [the rule] would apply even in the case of *pāmanaputra*. This is because, in that instance, the mention of "the subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) in the rule *ṭh-lopo 'nañaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.1)—if the term "subsequent member" were qualified by the word *nañ*, meaning "of a preceding member ending in *n*"—would lead to the undesired result. However, if [the qualification] is instead by means of the "preceding member" (*pūrvapada*)...

It is qualified—(see *Pāṇini 1.4.58*): the designation "preposition" (*upasarga*) was established by the rule [Pāṇini 1.4.59] which begins with "uttara-"; its qualification is a restriction, namely, the exclusion [of the term] from anything other than the group beginning with *pra*, so that the designation "preposition" does not apply elsewhere.

For if there were a single rule (*ekayoga*), then just as the designation *upasarga* would apply to the *pra*-class [prefixes], it would likewise apply to the *ca*-class [conjunctions]. Therefore, a separate rule (*pṛthagyoga*) is formulated so that the designation *upasarga* applies only to the *pra*-class and not to the *ca*-class—as in the example: *parāḥ senāḥ*.

Thus, because an army (*senā*) is a substance (*dravya*), the word *para* occurring therein is not included here. *Para* means "excellent" (*utkṛṣṭa*) or "situated in another place" (*paradeśasthita*). However, where the singular form is read—as in *parā senā*—it should be understood there as an illustration of the grammatical form (*rūpa*).
However, since the dual and plural endings would be designated as *avyaya* (indeclinables) due to their being *nipāta*s, there would be elision (*luk*) of the case-ending.

59. *Upasargāḥ kriyāyoge* (1.4.59). In the example *praṇayati*, because the word *pra-* functions as an *upasarga*, the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *upasargādasamāse 'pi ṇopadeśasya* (8.4.14).

Regarding the statement "the region is the leader (*praṇāyaka*)," because there is no connection with the action of leading (*nayana*) for the word *pra*, it does not receive the designation of a prefix (*upasarga*). Now, one might object that even here there is indeed a connection with the action of going (*gamana*), and thus it should still be designated as a prefix; however, this is not so.
Otherwise, the mention of *kriyāyoga* (connection with action) would indeed be purposeless. Why?

Because prepositions (*prādayaḥ*) never deviate from connection with action. Therefore, by the force of the mention of *kriyāyoga*, those prepositions which are connected with action toward a particular [action] receive the designations of *gati* and *upasarga* toward that [action], and not toward any other.

And here the prefix *pra* is not connected with the action of leading (*nayanakriyā*), but rather with the action of going (*gamikriyā*); therefore, it does not receive the designation of a prefix (*upasarga*) in relation to the root *nī*.
[The rule] "the addition of *marut* as a word" applies to the prescription of the true nature (*tattva*) [of the term]; this is the remainder [of the explanation], for otherwise—

By the rules "particles have the acute accent on the first syllable" (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.80) and "prepositions also [have the acute on the first], except for *abhi*" (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.81), the word *marut* would also have the acute accent on the first syllable. However, the word *marut* is intended to have the acute accent on the final syllable.
The purpose of the term "supplementary statement" (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is to provide this [rule]; namely, that the word *marut* receives the designation of a preposition (*upasarga*).
The meaning is that a formal demonstration must be made. Here is that demonstration: the rule "upasargāḥ" (P.
1.4.59) is treated as a separate *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule). And in this case, the phrase "prādayaḥ" (P. 1.4.58) is not connected [to it].
Consequently, the designation *upasarga* applies to the word *marut* when it undergoes the substitution of *tat*. For this very reason...

It should be understood that due to the splitting of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), the designation *upasarga* applies to the word *śrad* when it is prescribed as an *aṅga*, and to the word *antaḥ* when it is prescribed as an *aṅga* or where there is the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*.
This is the indicator (*liṅga*) of the splitting of the rule, namely: *prajñā-śraddhā-arcā-vṛtibhyo ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.101).
And there is the mention [in the sūtra] *tiro 'ntardhau* (1.4.71). From that, the second rule is *kriyāyoge*. And here, the term *prādayaḥ* is connected [to it]. For what purpose is this?
It is for the purpose of making known that the preceding rule does not have universal application—since it would otherwise be established by that alone—therefore, by this [second rule]:

There is no over-extension [of the rule]. Furthermore, it is for the purpose that the designation *upasarga* (prefix) should not apply to *pra* and the others when they are not in connection with an action. Regarding the word "marutaḥ": when the suffix *kta* is applied by the rule *upasargāt taḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.47), because of the mention of two *t*s, there is a replacement of the entire root *dru* [by *mṛ*]. Now, one might object:

Since the designation *upasarga* (prefix) would not apply here, the word *karu*—not ending in a vowel—should not undergo that [substitution]; therefore, he says: "By virtue of the force of the rule for the designation," and so forth.
For just as in the case of *upasarajaḥ*, by the force of the application of the marker *ḍit*, the elision of the suffix *ṭi* occurs even for what is not a *bha* stem.

Likewise, here too, the suffix *tva* will occur even after a stem that does not end in a vowel (anajantāt); otherwise, this statement would be purposeless. The underlying intention is that for the word *marut*, there is no other grammatical operation resulting from its being designated as an *upasarga*. Regarding the phrase "the addition of the word *śrac*," here too the meaning of the term *upasaṃkhyāna* is the same [as previously explained].

The derivation is also exactly that. But surely, since *śraddhā* is already established simply by its inclusion in the *bhidādi* group, why is the designation "prefix" (*upasarga*) applied to the word *śrac* for the sake of establishing it?
The thought is this: the inclusion there [in the *bhidādi* list] is not of Vedic origin (*anārṣa*).

Regarding the word *prakṛtya*: when it has the designation *gati*, there is a compound according to *kugatiprādayaḥ* (2.2.18). In the case of a compound that does not have *nañ* preceding it, *lyap* is substituted for *ktvā* according to *samāse 'nañpūrve ktvo lyap* (7.1.37).

Regarding the word *prakṛtam*: while the rule *kte ca* (Pāṇini 6.2.45) is in force, the word *pra* has its initial vowel accented by the rule *gatiranantaraḥ* (6.2.49), which assigns the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) to the first vowel. Regarding the phrase *yat prakaroti*:
although the rule *tiṅṅtiṅaḥ* (8.1.28) would have required the elision of the accent (*nighāta*) of the finite verb following the particle *pra*, [this does not apply here].

By the rule *‘nipātairyadyadi’* (Pāṇini 8.1.30), there is a prohibition [of the accentuation of the finite verb]; however, because the suffix *tip* is marked with *p*, it retains its original *anudātta* (unaccented) nature. Regarding this, the Vārttika states: *‘satiśiṣṭasvarasya balīyastvamanyatra vikaraṇasvarebhyaḥ’* (on Pāṇini 6.1.158), which establishes that an accent remaining after other operations (*satiśiṣṭasvara*) is stronger than the accent of a *vikaraṇa* (verbal suffix). Thus, the accent of the *vikaraṇa* [prevails].
The acute accent (*udātta*) does not apply to the prefix due to the rule [of the suffix]; rather, it applies to *karoti* itself by the rule "of the verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*, 6.1.162).

The remainder becomes unaccented (*anudātta*). Although the prefix *pra-* would have obtained the acute accent on its first syllable by the rule "and prefixes, except for *abhi*" (*upasargāścābhivarjam*, Phiṭ-sūtra 4.81), it is instead [treated] by the rule "a motion-word [is unaccented] before a motion-word" (*gatirgatau*, 8.1.70).

While the term *nighāta* (elision of accent) continues to apply, the rule *ṭhtiṅ codātivati* (Pāṇini 8.1.71) prescribes that when a finite verb (*tiṅ*) ending in an acute accent (*udāta*) follows, the preceding word becomes unaccented (*anudāta*). For in that context, the term *anudāta* is understood from the preceding rule *pūjanāt pūjitamanudātaṃ kāṣṭhādibhyaḥ* (8.1.67).
And these three purposes are to be understood as applying to the technical term *gati* (motion) in what follows.

Now, for what purpose is this division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) made? Why is the mention of *gati* not simply included in the preceding rule itself? To this he says: "The division of the rule is for the sake of what follows," by means of the words "in what follows" and so on.

He shows that the division of the *yoga* (sūtra) is for the sake of what follows. He asks: "If the designation *upasarga* were to apply here as well, what would happen? To this he says: "'In the case of *ūrī-kr̥tya*', etc. [He states:

"'The particle *ca* is for the purpose of the co-inclusion of the designations. Without the particle *ca*, because of the governing rule of "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), [only one designation would apply] in a single instance.

Because two distinct designations are prescribed, there would be an alternation (paryāya) and not a co-occurrence (samāveśa). By the words "praṇītam" and so forth, he demonstrates the result of the co-occurrence of designations: "The accent [is determined] by the rule 'the immediately preceding verb root'"; and in both examples, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* and the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occur by the rule "after a preverb."

Regarding the word *praṇītam*: the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule "after a prefix, even when there is no compound, for a root taught with an initial *n*" (Pāṇini 8.4.44). Regarding the word *abhiṣiktam*: the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule "after a prefix, for the root *sū*" (Pāṇini 8.3.65), and so forth.
Regarding the word *kārikā* and so forth: this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the indication of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*).
As for the other word *kārikā*, which ends in the suffix *ṇvul* and denotes the agent (*kartṛ*), its usage is as follows: "having composed a *kārikā*.
The meaning of the word *upākhyāna* is "explanation" (*pratipādana*). In that regard, this is the explanation:
In the subsequent sūtra, because the word *kārikā* has the sense of "collecting what has not been stated" (*anukta-samuccaya*), the designation *gati* applies [to the particle *ca*].
Thus, in the rule beginning with *punaścanasau*, the words *punar* and *canaḥ* are designated as *gati* when occurring in the context of Vedic (*chandas*) usage.

The meaning is that this form of the word *bhavataḥ* must be explained [in such a way]. The explanation, however, should be made by relying on the fact that the particle *ca* in the subsequent sūtra has the sense of an "unexpressed conjunction" (*anuktasamuccaya*). [Regarding the term] *punarustyūtam*:
the root is *ṣivu* (DhP 1108) in the sense of "weaving," followed by the suffix *niṣṭhā*; because it is marked with *u*, [the rule] *ṣṭhivuklamucamāṃ śiti* applies.

Because the augment *iṭ* is optional by the rule *vā* (Pāṇini 7.2.56), there is a prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* (7.2.15). By the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca* (6.4.19), the *uṭ* substitute replaces the *v* of *vah*, and then the *yaṇ* substitution takes place. [The form] *canohitam* is derived from the root *dhā* by the rule *dadhāter hiḥ* (7.4.42).

Thus, there is the substitution of *nahi*; by the rule "a preceding prefix [is unaccented] when followed by a verbal root" (*gatiranantaraḥ*, Pāṇini 6.2.49), the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) applies, resulting in the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable of the suffix *ṇa*. For the word *canaḥ* is acutely accented on its first syllable according to the rule "particles (*nipātāḥ*) have the acute accent on the first syllable" (*phiṭ-sūtra* 4.80).
61. *ūry-ādi-cvi-ḍācaś-ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.61). [The commentary states:
"Those ending in *cvi* and those ending in *ḍāc*. Now, it might be argued that by the inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*) in the definition of the technical term *pada*, it has been indicated that:
"In other rules prescribing technical terms, when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, there is no application of the rule of 'ending-in-that' (*tadantavidhi*)."

Thus [it is stated in] the *Pūrvapadavṛtti* (81). Therefore, only the suffixes *cvi* and *ḍāc* ought to be designated as *gati*; why then is it said that "those ending in *cvi* and those ending in *ḍāc* [are *gati*]"? He thinks as follows:
the term "in connection with an action" (*kriyāyoge*) from [Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.59] continues to apply, and a mere suffix does not have a connection with an action.

It is possible. Therefore, by virtue of the continued application of the connection with action (*kriyāyoga*), it is understood that the designation applies only to that which ends in such [a root]; thus, the designation indeed applies to that which ends in it. However, since no specific distinction is mentioned, it would follow that the designation applies whenever there is a connection with a mere verbal root (*dhātu*); therefore, he says:

Regarding the rule *cvyaḍācoḥ* and so forth: the suffix * cvi* is prescribed [by Pāṇini 5.4.50] when there is a transformation from one state to another (*abhūtatadbhāve*) in connection with the verbs *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as*. Furthermore, since the connection with *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* is carried over even to the rule *avyaktānukaraṇāt* (5.4.57) and others, the suffix *ḍāc* is also prescribed in that very same context. Therefore—

Since it is impossible for *cvi* to occur in conjunction with any other verbal root, the designation of *gati* is prescribed specifically in connection with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*. Therefore, by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*) with them, the same designation is also prescribed for *ūry-ādi* items only when they are used in conjunction with those very roots.
Since the meaning of *cvi* is not understood from *ūry-ādi* items, [the author] says the following in order to explain it:

‘*Urī*, *urarī*,’ and so forth. Because words beginning with *śrauṣaṭ* and ending with *svadhā* are listed among the *cādayaḥ* (the group of particles), they receive the designation of *nipāta* even when not joined with a verb. The word *āviḥ* is recited among the *sākṣāt-prabhṛtayaḥ* (the group beginning with *sākṣāt*). Therefore, by the rule *vibhāṣā kṛñi* (Pāṇini 1.4.72), [it optionally takes the *karmapravacanīya* designation when used with the root *kṛ*].
In connection with the root *kṛ*, the designation *gati* is optional. For example: *śuklīkṛtya*. Here, the substitution of *i* for *t* occurs by the rule *ṭhasya cvau* (Pāṇini 7.4.32).
For example: *paṭapaṭākṛtya*. The word *paṭapaṭā* has been derived [and explained] under the rule *vā kyaṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.90).

62. *anukaraṇaṃ cānitiparam* (1.4.62). Regarding the term *anitiparam*: here, is the word *itipara* a *tatpuruṣa* compound formed by the split (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule "after *iti*" (*ite para*), meaning "that after which *iti* follows"? Or does it mean "that from which *iti* is subsequent" (*itiḥ paro yasmāt*)?

Or is it a *bahuvrīhi* compound? In that case, if the first alternative were adopted, there would be a prohibition [of the suffix] in the expression *itikhāṭkṛtya*, whereas here it would not apply—as in *khaḍiti kṛtvā āgataḥ*—and this is undesirable. However, in the second alternative, this fault does not occur.

Therefore, relying on that very point, he says: "that after which 'iti' follows," and "he spat" (*niraṣṭhīvat*). Regarding the root *ṣṭhivu* in the sense of "spitting" (DhP 560), because of the prohibition stated in the Vārttika: "A prohibition must be stated for [the change of *ṣ* to *s*] in the case of roots beginning with *ṣ*, the root *ṣṭhivu*, and the root *ṣvaṣk*" (Vā. 671), the rule "the *ṣ* at the beginning of a root becomes *s*" (6.1.64) does not apply here.
The vowel *s* does not become long; [this is because] the rule "ṣṭhivuklamucamāṃ śiti" (Pāṇini 7.3.75) prescribes lengthening [only] before an affix marked with ŚIT.
63. Respect and disrespect [result] in the presence or absence [of excellence]. (1.4.63) "Excessive affection is respect"—[the *Kāśikā* states]: "Respect is agitation born of affection.
Agitation preceded by affection is "agitation born of affection"; it is that which is characterized by affection.
The meaning is the act of performing such deeds as rising from one's seat and offering a seat. Regarding the phrase "indifference toward contempt" (*paribhavaudāsīnyam*):

*paribhava* means disregard; *tiraskāra* means contempt. *Audāsīnyam* means indifference. It refers to the neglect of duties such as rising from one's seat and offering a seat due to such contempt. Thus, it is indifference caused by contempt.

Regarding the compound *paribhavaudāsīnyam*: it is a compound formed by the rule of *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule) stating "the third [case-ending]. Alternatively, *paribhavaudāsīnyam* means both contempt (*paribhava*) and indifference (*audāsīnya*).
Now, for what purpose are the terms "disrespect" (*anādara*) and "unreal" (*asat*) included? It might be argued that if one intends to express respect (*ādara*), one could simply say "real" (*sat*).

Now, how can the word *asat* (non-existent) receive the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) if it is beginningless? And how can there be grammatical operations such as compound formation (*samāsa*)? Since, by the rule of extension to what ends in [the specified element] (*tadantavidhi*), the word *asat* also receives the designations of particle (*nipāta*) and prefix (*gati*), the word *sat* [in the compound *asat*] receives the designation of an indeclinable because it is a particle.

Since the rule for *tadanta-vidhi* (application of a grammatical operation to that which ends with a specified element) is extended to the prescription of the designation *avyaya*, the word *asat* will also receive the designation *avyaya*.

Furthermore, in the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18), because a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) is the subject under discussion, [the designation applies] to that which ends in a *gati*.
A compound being prescribed for that which has a subanta [ending] will also apply to the word *asat*.

In the rule *gatiśca* (Pāṇini 2.2.18), the term *pūrvapada* is understood from the previous context; and in the rule *gatirgatau* (8.1.70), the term *pada* is also understood. Therefore, [the elision applies] to the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) which ends in a *gati* [particle].

When the *prakṛtisvara* (original accent) is prescribed, the operation is carried out exactly as stated; however, how could there be an understanding of disregard (*anādara*)? For if the term "disregard" (*anādara*) were not mentioned, there would be no negation of regard by the negative particle (*nañ*) in the sense of "neither existent nor non-existent. If regard is prohibited, what else could it be but disregard?

Could it be so? This which is stated is not logical; for a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) that is a *tatpuruṣa* conveys an object that is merely similar [to its counter-positive], as in the expression "bring a non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇam ānaya*). In this context, if the mention of "disrespect" (*anādara*) were not made, then that which is similar to "existent" (*sat*)—namely, "non-existent" (*asat*)—would apply only where there is the possibility of respect.

He went after having shown disrespect to his teacher. But where respect is entirely absent, there [the compound] would not occur—[as in] "he went after having shown disrespect to a servant. However, when the term *anādara* (disrespect) is understood as a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*), it is analyzed as:
"that in which respect (*ādara*) does not exist" is *anādara*. And a possessive compound occurs even in the case of absolute non-existence.

And since [the designation] occurs even in the absence of actual attachment (*prasakti*), the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is established in all cases. Therefore, the mention of "disregard" (*anādara*) must be made. And when that is done, the mention of "resemblance" (*asadṛśa*) must also necessarily be made. Otherwise, what would be specified by the mention of disregard—namely, that which exists in disregard?
The designation *gati* is prescribed! For it is not possible for the word *sat* to function in the sense of "disregard.
Even if that [function] is impossible for it, one might argue that it is possible for the word *asat*, which ends in that [suffix];
this is true—it is indeed possible—but the designation *gati* is not obtained for it.

Because there is no rule of *tadanta-vidhi* (application of a grammatical operation to that which ends with the specified element). For in the present case, there is no *tadanta-vidhi*, nor is there anything previously mentioned (*prakṛta*) here; therefore, the mention of the word *asat* is intended to convey disregard. However, just as in the rule "the word *goṣpada* [is used] in the senses of frequented, not frequented, and measure," where [it applies to] what is not frequented...

Just as the word *agoṣpada* is understood to mean "not frequented" because the word *goṣpada* (cow-track) cannot [logically] apply [in that sense], so too here, since the word *sat* cannot be used in the sense of disregard (*anādara*), the term *asat* would be understood to mean disregard; in that case, it would be possible for the word *asat*.
It is not for the purpose of making a formal inclusion; rather, the inclusion of the "non-existent" (asat) is made for the sake of clarity.

The expressions "having treated as existent" and "having treated as non-existent" employ the words *sat* and *asat* here in the sense of "beautiful" and "ugly," or alternatively, in the sense of "existent" and "non-existent."

64. *alam* [is used] in the sense of ornamentation (1.4.64). In the example "having adorned," the word *alam* here signifies sufficiency (*paryāpti*). 65. *antar* [is used] in the sense of exclusion (*aparigraha*) (1.4.65).

This word *antaḥ* occurs in the sense of "in the middle" when it functions as a locative (*adhikaraṇa*), and also in the sense of "enclosure" (*parigraha*). In this context, the designation of an indeclinable (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed for its use in the sense of enclosure. As for its inclusion in the list beginning with *svar* (Pāṇini 1.1.37), that is for the purpose of establishing the designation of an indeclinable even in the sense of enclosure. [The example] *antarhasya* means "having struck in the middle. [The particle] *vā*.
In the case of *lyap* (Pāṇini 6.4.38), there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*). The phrase "it should be stated" means that it must be explained;

however, the explanation has already been provided previously. Regarding *antardhā*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.106] *ātaścopasarge*. Regarding *antarddhiḥ*, the suffix *ki* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.92] *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ*.
The suffix *ki* is applied. In the form "antarṇayati," the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs according to Pāṇini 8.4.14: "After a prefix, even when there is no compound."

66. *kaṇemanasī śraddhāpratīghāte* (Pāṇini 1.4.66). The word *kaṇe* is an indeclinable (*nipāta*) that resembles a form ending in the locative case. Here, it is not understood as signifying an excess of desire; for in that case, the qualifier "in the obstruction of faith" (*śraddhāpratīghāte*) would be impossible.

The word *manas* as well, by virtue of its association with that [ear], is understood to function specifically in the sense of longing, as in the expressions "having struck at the ear" (*kaṇe hatvā*) and "having struck at the mind" (*mano hatvā*). Here, the word *kaṇa* refers to a minute particle of rice acting as the locus, while the word *manas* refers to the internal organ of thought (*cetas*).

67. *puro’vyayam* (Pāṇini 1.4.67). Regarding the example "puraskṛtya": in the sense of "having come from a place that is prior," the suffix *asi* is applied according to the rule *pūrvādharāvarāṇāmasi puradhavaścaiṣām* (5.3.39).
Furthermore, the word *pūrva* undergoes the substitution of *pur*. By the rule *taddhitaścāsarvavibhaktiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.38), it receives the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

This technical term is applied figuratively to the *s* that takes the place of the *visarjanīya*; this designation was formulated by the ancient teachers. Then, by the rule *namaspurasorgatyoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.40), the *s* is substituted [for the *r*].

"‘pūḥ’, ‘purau’, ‘having made [them] *puraḥ*, he went’—this is a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) for the phrase ‘having made [them] *puraḥ*’. The presentation of ‘pūḥ’ and ‘parau’ is for the purpose of demonstrating that the word *puraḥ* is not an indeclinable (*avyaya*), by virtue of its association with them. [The root] ‘*pṛ*’ is used in the senses of protecting and filling."

[The root] *dhā* (DhP 1489); by the rule *bhrājabhrāsa-* (3.2.177), the suffix *kvip* is applied. It has been stated that [the substitution of] *u* occurs for [the *o* of] *ud* when preceded by a labial (*oṣṭhya*), and there is also the substitution of *ra*. Because there is an absence of the designation *gati*, the operations such as compounding (*samāsa*) do not take place here. [This is illustrated by] *namaspurasorgatyoḥ* (8.3.40).

Thus, even the substitution of *s* for the *visarjanīya* does not occur. Now, one might object: if the designation *gati* were to apply here, then once the *gati*-compound is formed, the case-ending (*sup*) would have to be elided, and consequently the form *puraḥ* would not result; and if that [form] is absent, the designation itself would also cease to exist. This is not so; for although...

If the case-ending were removed, the form *puraḥ* would not exist; however, it is not the case that the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is removed, because that which has undergone a partial modification is not considered different from the original (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 16).

68. *astaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.68). Regarding the statement, "The word *astaṃ* ending in *m* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*)," its status as an indeclinable is to be understood precisely from the inclusion of the qualifier "indeclinable" itself; for if it were not an indeclinable, there would be no purpose in employing that specific qualification.

Or rather, because it belongs to the class of *cādi* (the group beginning with *ca*), as in the example: "having thrown down the section (*kāṇḍa*), he went. [The root] *asu* in the sense of "throwing" (DhP 1209);

the *niṣṭhā* suffix; the prohibition of *iṭ* as before. The letter *ca* is for the purpose of drawing forward [the rule] "an indeclinable" (1.4.57). If this is so, then because it is drawn forward by *ca*, it would apply to what follows.

Would there not be a failure of its application? There is no such fault, for the particle "ca" (and) will also carry over into the subsequent [sūtra] for the purpose of drawing that [previous term] along with it.

69. *Acccha* in the sense of "going toward" (*gatyarthavadeṣu*). [The commentary states: "The word *acccha* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) in the sense of the word *abhi*. *Abhi* signifies "facing toward" (*ābhimukhye*). [In the example] *acchā-edya*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by virtue of its belonging to the *yajādi* group, according to the rule *vacyādisūtreṇa* (Pāṇini 6.1.15).
"Accham" means that which is free from turbidity.
70. *ado'nupadeśe* (Pāṇini 1.4.70). *Upadeśa* is the statement of the meaning of what follows; and since that serves for the purpose of making [the meaning] known to another, it is said:
"Instruction is for the sake of another" (*upadeśaḥ parārthaḥ*). "Having done this" (*adaḥ kṛtvā*) means "having performed this."
71. *tiro'ntardhau* (Pāṇini 1.4.71). [The example is] "he stands having become *tiras*. This means having become non-direct, that is, having moved to the side.
72. *vibhāṣā kṛñi* (Pāṇini 1.4.72). Regarding the form *tiraskṛtya*: by the rule *tirasas tiry-onyatarasyām* (8.3.42), the *visarjanīya* is replaced by *s*.
73. *upāje’nvāje* (1.4.72).
74. *sākṣātprabhṛtīni ca* (1.4.74).

Regarding the statement, “In the case of *sākṣātprabhṛti* [words], there is the mention of the sense of *cvy-artha*,” that by which the sense of *cvi* is expressed—that is, spoken—is called *cvy-artha*.
*Tad-vyartha-vacanam* means the explanation of the sense of *cvī*. By this, the following is stated:

in this rule concerning technical designations (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), the expression "the sense of *cvī*" must be stated for the purpose of conveying the sense of *cvī* in the case of *sākṣāt* and the others. For what purpose? When [something] has not become manifest (*asākṣādbhūtam*)...

This is so that the designation "going" (gati-saṃjñā) may apply when there is direct action; however, it is not intended to apply when no direct state is produced, but rather when some other specific quality is produced in something that has already become manifest—that is, in something that has already attained the state of being perceptible. Thus...

[This applies] to words such as *mithyā* and others. When [a word] that is not false (*amithyābhūta*) is made to appear as false (*mithyābhūta*), then it should be so [treated]; otherwise, it should not be. This is the explanation:
in the rule *ūryādicviḍācaśca* (Pāṇini 1.4.61), the mention of *cv-i* is for the sake of [words ending in] *ṭhac* and *cha*.

From the rule *gatyarthavadeṣu* (1.4.69), the term *artha* ("meaning") is carried over here by the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūakapluti*). Consequently, the designation *gati* is prescribed for *sākṣāt* and the others when they occur in the sense of the suffix *cvy-artha*.

Alternatively, based on the understanding that the *vibhāṣā* (optionality) is fixed, the designation will apply to those [words] occurring precisely in the sense of *cvyanta*. And the state of being in the sense of *cvi* is possible in two ways: for words ending in *cvi* and for words not ending in *cvi*. Among these, when they end in *cvi*, then...

By the rule *ūryādicviḍācaśca* (Pāṇini 1.4.61), this [term] always receives the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "gati"; otherwise, by this same rule, the designation of "gati" would be optional. However, due to the restricted optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) of this sūtra, it applies only in the sense of the suffix *cvī*. There is also the conventional mention of its ending in the letter *m*. [Examples: *agnau*, etc.

Words such as *vaśe* and others should be regarded as particles (*nipāta*) that resemble case-endings (*vibhakti*). The words *prāduḥ* and *āviḥ* belong to the *ūry-ādi* group; the words *urasi* and *manasi* are particles resembling case-endings.
"Having placed upon the chest" (*urasikṛtya*) means "having accepted. "Having placed in the mind" (*manasikṛtya*) [means the same].
The meaning is "having ascertained."

76. *madhye pade nivacane ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.76). Regarding *madhye pade*: these are indeclinables that resemble words ending in the locative case (*saptamyanta*). Regarding *nivacane*: this is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of absence, as in *nitṛṇam* or *nivusam*. [The example is] *nivacanakṛtya*.
Thus, by virtue of the power of its utterance, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case even in a compound;
the same applies hereafter.

77. *nityaṃ haste pāṇāv upayamane* (1.4.77). [The examples are] *haste kṛtya*, *pāṇau kṛtya*. As in the previous case, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending. [The term] *dārakarma* means "the act of taking a wife."

78. *prādhvam* [is used] in the sense of "binding" (*bandhane*). (Pāṇini 1.4.78) This term "in binding" is a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*). Since the word *prādhvam* functions in the sense of "conformity" (*anukūlya*), its qualification by the word "in binding" is not logically possible; therefore, by implication, it refers to the meaning of that [binding].
Since the qualification is not understood, he says: "Conformity with that," and so forth.

That which has bondage as its cause is described in that way. Regarding the term "having made favorable" (*prādhvaṃkṛtya*): the meaning is "having rendered it favorable by means of the cause that is bondage. [The alternative form] is "having made favorable" (*prādhvaṃ kṛtvā*).
"A cart capable of traveling on a road" is understood as "having made [it] face the road.

The compound suffix *ac* is applied by the rule *upasargād adhvanaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.85). The elision of the suffix *ṭu* occurs by the rule *naḥ taddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.144). The term *pragatam adhvānam* is a *prādi*-compound (a prefix-based compound).

Since the application [of the designation *gati*] here is already established by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "the specifically mentioned [term takes precedence over the one defined by a rule]" (*lakṣamapratipadokta-paribhāṣā*),

the inclusion of the word *bandhana* is for the purpose of indicating that the term *prādhvam*, although it is defined by a grammatical rule (*lākṣaṇika*), also receives the designation *gati* when it is connected with *bandhana*. Therefore, when [it is connected] precisely with *bandhana*...

When, by virtue of the cart's capacity on the road, its orientation toward the road is intended to be expressed, then the expression "the cart has gone after having made itself ready for the road" (prādhvaṃkṛtya śakaṭaṃ gataḥ) is also established.
79. *Jīvikopaniṣadāvaupamye* | (1.4.79) [The Kāśikā states: "In the domain of comparison (*aupamye viṣaye*). Regarding "in the domain of comparison":
that by which something is compared is a *upamā*. [The suffix] *aṅ* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.3.106, *ātaścopasarge*. The state of that...]

[The suffix] *dhyañ* [is applied] in the sense of comparison (*aupamya*). Furthermore, that [comparison] is a relationship between an action and its factors (*kriyākārakasambandha*), because of the rule: "In compounds, primary derivatives (*kṛt*), and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), the expression of a relationship occurs except in cases of conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*), distinct forms (*bhinnarūpa*), and invariable relationships (*avyabhicaritasambandha*). By the use of the term "object" (*viṣaya*) in the locative case in the phrase "in the object of comparison" (*viṣaye aupamye*), it is established that this is a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*).

He demonstrates this: it is possible for the *jīvikā* and the *upaniṣad*, which serve as the points of comparison (*upamā*), to function as the objects of the respective comparisons, because without them there would be no comparison at all. [The phrase] “having made it like a livelihood” (*jīvikākṛtya*) and so forth means: having made it as if it were a livelihood; having made it as if it were a secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*). [The word] *jīvikā*...

The means of livelihood (*jīvanopāya*) is the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*), the mystery, and the cause. That which is similar to this is "livelihood-mystery" (*jīvikopaniṣad*). It is compared to the *upaniṣad* by means of the two terms "livelihood" and "mystery."
80. *te prāgdhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.80).

This is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Furthermore, this restriction may be either a restriction regarding the technical designation (*saṃjñā-niyama*)—namely, that those words beginning with *pra* are designated as "gati" or "upasarga" only when they are employed before a verbal root—or it may be a restriction regarding the sequence of utterance (*prayoga-niyama*).
[In the latter case, the meaning would be: those words beginning with *pra* are designated as "gati" or "upasarga" only when they are used prior to the verbal root.

Do they exist? Or is it a restriction regarding application—that those *pra*-prefixes, being designated as "gati" and "upasarga," must be understood as occurring before the verbal root (*dhātu*)? If the former restriction were adopted, then this would be understood as a partial statement of the rules for technical designations (*saṃjñā*): "Those *pra*-prefixes..."

[The rule] states that those termed *gati* and *upasarga* are to be employed before the verbal root (*dhātu*). Consequently, since the designations *gati* and *upasarga* have not yet been established [at the time of application], it is not logical to refer back to them as "those termed *gati* and *upasarga*. Furthermore, because the designation *nipāta* has already been established...
By this [interpretation], only the particles (nipāta) would be referred back; consequently, there would be a restriction regarding the technical designation "particle" (nipātasaṃjñā).

In the other case, however, by virtue of this restriction, this rule becomes a constituent part of the sentences defining the designations "gati" and "upasarga," and thus [the undesired consequence] does not occur at all.

There would be the undesirable consequence [of redundancy]. Furthermore, the purpose of restricting technical names (*saṃjñā-niyama*) would be the cessation of the names for those not employed in the original context, and that is improper; for even if the names exist for those not employed in the original context, nothing undesirable follows. However, for the other...

The result of the restriction is the absence of usage [of these words] before [the verb]; and that is logical, for it is not desired that those termed *gati* and *upasarga* should be used before [the verb]. Therefore, a restriction regarding usage alone is appropriate;
relying on that, he says: "Those are termed *gati* and *upasarga*. And so it is.
And so forth. The meaning is that it is exactly like, or similar to, the rule that was established. Now, one might object:

when "naiva kaścit prapaṭhati" (no one at all reads aloud) ought to be used, one instead uses "paṭhati pra"; therefore, since no undesirable result is observed, this [rule] is useless. This is not so; for although in the common language (*bhāṣā*)...
Those [words] employed after a verbal root are not observed to be designated as *gati*s or *upasarga*s;

however, they are observed in the Veda (*chandas*). In that regard, even a person of dull intellect, having observed their employment after a verbal root in the Vedic domain, [concludes] that just as they [function] in the Vedic sphere after a verbal root—

Thinking that just as [prefixes] are employed by others, they should likewise be employed in speech, there is no risk of futility because [the rule] is intended for the purpose of instructing such a person.
Now, for what purpose is the mention of *te* (they)? For, since they are already under discussion, the terms designated as "gatis" and "upasargas" [would be understood] by context alone.

He says, “The mention of *te*,” etc., because the connection [of the prefix] with prior usage is understood through that. If the mention of *te* were absent, only those [words] designated as *gati*s would be connected with prior usage, due to their immediate proximity. But since the mention of *te* is present, the *upasarga*s are also indicated; therefore, they too [are connected].

The connection [of the prefix] is established. Therefore, the mention of "dhātu" (verbal root) is for the purpose that there may also be a rule regarding the prior usage of prefixes. Now, one might object: since prefixes such as *pra* and others are designated as "gati" or "upasarga" in relation to that [root] with which they are connected in action, even without the mention of "dhātu," [the designation] would apply only to the verbal root.

The usage [of the suffix] before the verbal root will be understood; for there is no action other than that of the root—so how can it be said "before the root"? This is not so; [the rule is stated thus] so that in cases such as *pracikīrṣati* ("he wishes to do thoroughly"), the usage may also occur before the root. Here, [the suffix] *san*...

The prefix *pra* is connected with the action denoted by the desiderative suffix (*san*), so that *san* may receive the technical designations of "root" (*dhātu*) and "preverb" (*upasarga*). Consequently, if the term "root" (*dhātu*) were not mentioned [in the rule], the prefix would be placed immediately before that very suffix.
However, because the term "root" is mentioned, it is placed before the root *cikīrṣati*, and not before the suffix *san*.

81. *cchandasi pare 'pi* (Pāṇini 1.4.81). 82. *vyavahitāś ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.82). Because there is a scriptural injunction for the usage of [particles] even when separated by other words in the Veda (*cchandas*), they may also be used when separated in common speech (*bhāṣā*).

It is thus stated that there is no application [of the rule]. If this were so, then even when there is an intervention by a motion (gati), the prior application would not be obtained—as in *samāharati* and similar forms. This is not a fault; for an element of the same class does not constitute an intervention. Since the category of motion and prefixes (*upasarga*) is taken as the basis, there is no problem.

"Intervention" (*vyavadhāna*): [as in] "ā mandraiḥ" and so forth. Here, although there is intervention by the word *aṅ* and the words *mandraiḥ* etc., the verbal root *yā-* is placed before them. By saying "āyāhi," he demonstrates the connection between *ā* and *yāhi*.
83. *Karmapravacanīyāḥ*.

(Pāṇini 1.4.83) The plural number in the term "*karmapravacanīyāḥ*" is used because there will be many designata (*saṃjñin*) for this designation (*saṃjñā*) that is about to be stated. The purpose of employing such a long designation is so that it may be a descriptive (*anvartha*) name.

It should be understood thus: those who have spoken of an action (*karman*) are called *karmapravacanīya*. Since the action is past, the suffix *anīyar* is applied in the sense of the agent according to Pāṇini 3.3.113, *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. The word *karman* here denotes an action (*kriyā*). And who are those who have spoken of an action? Those who do not currently speak of the action.

Thus, by means of assigning a name according to its etymological meaning (*anvartha-saṃjñā*), those [roots] have indicated action (*kriyā*), but they do not express it; therefore, they do not denote action at present. Thus, by means of assigning a name according to its etymological meaning, those [roots] have indicated action, but not now.

It is stated that those which illuminate [an action] receive the designation *karmapravacanīya*. If they do not illuminate an action in the present tense, what then? They indicate a specific relation (*sambandhaviśeṣa*).
For example, in the expression "it rained after Śākalya’s recitation" (*śākalyasya saṃhitāmanuprāvarṣat*), [the word *anu* indicates the relation] with the action of listening (*niśamana*).

The word *anu* indicates that relationship characterized by the nature of cause and effect which has been produced between the *saṃhitā* and the *pravarṣaṇa*. Since it bears the technical designation of *karmapravacanīya*, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) occurs by virtue of the rule: "When joined with a *karmapravacanīya*, the second case is used" (Pāṇini 2.3.8).

84. *anurlakṣaṇe* | (1.4.84) Thinking that the word *lakṣaṇa* here refers to a "mark" (*cihna*), someone raises an objection, beginning with "For what purpose," etc. The other [responds] by citing [the rule]: *lakṣaṇetthambhūtākhyānabhāgavīpsāsu*.
In such rules as (Pāṇini 1.4.90), the word *lakṣaṇa* is understood to mean a "mark" or an "indicator";
however, here it refers to a "cause" (*hetu*) among the grammatical factors (*kāraka*). Therefore, with the intention that [the previous rule] does not apply there, he says in response to that:
“But the statement is for the purpose of expressing the cause,” and so forth. The word *tu* (but) serves to emphasize.

"Only for the sake of the word *hetu*. Here, the word *hetu* refers to a causal agent (*kāraka-hetu*), not to a logical indicator (*jñāpaka-hetu*); otherwise, this would not constitute a valid resolution. That which has "the meaning of *hetu*" as its object is described in that way. This is the designation of *karmapravacanīya* for the prefix *anu* when it occurs with respect to a causal agent, as follows:

The meaning is that this statement is made for the sake of [the possibility] "it might be so. But for what purpose is this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) prescribed for that which occurs in the sense of a cause? He says: "When the third case [is used] in the sense of a cause," and so forth.
For *saṃhitā* (close connection) is the cause of raining; the sacrifice performed after the *huta* offering is the cause of the pouring [of rain]; for it is thus:

Having heard (anu-niśamya) the *saṃhitā*, he rained; having heard (anu-niśamya) that the sacrifice was not being performed, he poured water. In these cases, if this designation "in the sense of cause" (*hetau*) were not stated [for the prefix *anu*], then in examples such as *śākalyasya saṃhitāmanu raprāvarṣat*, the rule for the suffix *ṭha* would not apply.

Thus, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would [otherwise] apply. Therefore, in order that the second case (*dvitīyā*) alone may prevail by overriding that [third case], this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed for *anu* when it expresses a cause (*hetu*).

85. [The suffix *kha* is used] in the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārthe*). (Pāṇini 5.4.85) As in: *nadīmanvavasitā* ("settled along the river"). Here, the sense of "together with" (*saha*) is the sense of the third case; for the third case is prescribed by the rule *sahayukte 'pradhāne* (Pāṇini 2.3.19) when there is a connection with the meaning of "together. [The word] *anvavasitā* [is derived from the root *vas* with the prefix *anu-*].
This is the form [of the word] derived from the root *ṣiñ* in the sense of "binding" (Dhātupāṭha 1477) when used with the suffix of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*).

86. *Hīne* (Pāṇini 2.3.9): “The grammarians [are] inferior to Śākaṭāyana. This means that other grammarians are inferior in comparison to Śākaṭāyana. Here, the relationship produced by way of comparison (*apekṣā*) is the basis for the case ending.

"Śākaṭāyana differs [from others]"— thus, when the sixth case (genitive) would have applied, the second case (accusative) is prescribed as an exception to it. Since the relationship residing in both [the teacher and the student] is expressed by a single case-ending, another word denoting a different related entity [is used], such as the word *vaiyākaraṇa*.
The case ending denoting a relative does not occur.
87. *Upa* [is used] also in the sense of "surpassing" (*adhika*).

(1.4.87) That which is mounted upon something else is called "surpassing. And since a surpassing thing cannot exist without that which it surpasses, this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is understood to apply when there is a relation with a surpassing object produced by the action of mounting. By the word "also" (*ca*), it is also applied in the sense of "inferior" (*hīna*).

"In the *upakhārī*, there is a *droṇa*. This means that a *droṇa* is greater than a *khārī*. The locative case is used according to Pāṇini 2.3.9 (*yasmād adhikam*), etc. Since the relationship [of comparison] is already expressed by that [locative suffix], the accusative case is not applied to the word *droṇa* according to Pāṇini 2.3.8 (*karmapravacanīyayukte dvitīyā*).
It comes to be.

88. *apa* and *pari* [are used] in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*). "By that which is connected with the subject under discussion" means by something such as the rainy season (*varṣā*) and so forth. "Of someone" means of someone such as the Trigartas and so forth. "Away from the Trigartas" (*apa trigartebhyaḥ*): [this is formed] by rule 2.3.10, *pañcamy apāṅparibhiḥ*.
The fifth [example] is: *pari pari trigartebhyaḥ*. There is reduplication by the rule *parervarjane* (Pāṇini 8.1.5).
[The next example is: *odanaṃ pariṣiñcati*. The meaning is "he sprinkles all around. *Śe*...

The augment *num* is applied by the rule *mucādīnām* (Pāṇini 7.1.59). Because the designation *karmapravacanīya* does not apply here, the designation *upasarga* (preverb) alone remains in force. Consequently, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs by the rule *upasargāt sunoti* (Pāṇini 8.3.65), and so forth.

89. *āṅ* [is used] in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*). (Pāṇini 1.4.89) Where one desires an operation upon *āṅ* in the sense of a limit or an inclusive limit (*abhividhi*), there both [meanings] are included, as for example in “*āṅ* [is used] in the sense of a limit and an inclusive limit” (2.1.13), and so forth. But here...

Only the limitative sense (*maryādā*) was intended, not the inclusive sense (*abhividhi*); therefore, someone might have the misconception that this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) should not apply in the case of the inclusive sense.
To dispel that [misconception], he says: "Because of the mention of the word (*vacana-grahaṇāt*)," and so forth. For when the word is mentioned...
The *bahuvrīhi* compound is obtained. That rule in which the word "limit" (*maryādā*) occurs is called "a statement concerning a limit. In that context, the meaning is as follows:
where there is the mention of a "limit" in a rule, the particle *āṅ* there receives the designation of *karmapravacanīya*. Furthermore, that rule is—
Regarding the rule *āṅ maryādābhividhyoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.13): since the particle *āṅ* is understood here as denoting both "limit" (*maryādā*) and "inclusion" (*abhividhi*), it applies in both cases.
But what is the distinction between "exclusion" (*varjana*) and "limit" (*maryādā*), such that [the former was not mentioned] in the previous rule?
Having stated "avoidance" (*varjana*), why does he here employ the term "limitation" (*maryādā*)? There is this distinction:
for in the case of avoidance, by means of that exclusion, a connection with something else is understood in a general sense through raining and so forth, as in:
"It has rained as far as Trigarta. For in this case, in whichever direction...

When one standing in a particular location utters this sentence, it is understood that it has rained everywhere—in that direction as well as in all other directions—with the sole exception of Trigarta.
However, when this sentence is used in the sense of a limit (maryādā)—namely, "up to..."—it is as follows: ā... [sentence continues].
When it is said, "It has rained from Pāṭaliputra," the specific distinction is that a connection with rain is understood for that region situated in the very direction associated with Pāṭaliputra.

[The rule] "mā bhūt" [is used] to prevent [the application of the rule] in the sense of "slightness" (*īṣadartha*) and in connection with a verb (*kriyāyoga*). In the case of "slightness," as in *ākaḍāraḥ*;
in connection with a verb, as in *samāharati*. In the former case, because there is no technical designation (*saṃjñā*), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) does not occur.
In the other case, by the rule "a verb [is unaccented] before a verb" (*gatir gatau*, Pāṇini 8.1.70), the *nighāta* (elision of the accent) occurs. As for that which...

The form [of the word] exists in both speech and recollection; since it possesses the property of being a *ṅ*, there is no possibility of the technical name (*saṃjñā*) applying here merely by the utterance of the sound *ṅ*.
90. *Prati*, *pari*, and *anu* [are used as prepositions] in the senses of indication (*lakṣaṇa*), description of a state (*itthambhūtākhyāna*), part (*bhāga*), and distribution (*vīpsā*).

(Pāṇini 1.4.90) Here, "indication" (*lakṣaṇa*) is intended to mean that which makes known, a cause, or a sign. That by which something is indicated or marked is a "sign" (*lakṣaṇa*). "Having attained a certain state" is "being in such a condition" (*itthambhūta*).

The narration of that is "narration of what has thus come to pass" (*itthambhūtākhyāna*). The root *bhī* (DhP 1844) is ātmanepada. From it, according to the rule *ṭhā dhṛṣādvā* (DhP 1805 onwards), there is an optional *ṇic*; when the *curādi-ṇic* is not present, then the form ending in *kta* is *bhūta*.

It is *rūpa* (form). A "portion" (*bhāga*) is that part which is being accepted. However, when the word "portion" is used for a part that is not being accepted—as in "a portion of *priyaṅgu* beans" or "a portion of the city"—that is due to its similarity to a part that is being accepted. The desire to pervade objects is "repetition" (*vīpsā*). And these...

The characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth are not what is manifested (*dyotya*) by the particles (*pratyaya*) and the rest; rather, they are their objects (*viṣayabhūta*). For this very reason, he says: "being the object. And this [is understood] by changing the gender in accordance with the rule: "the gender and number are like those of the expressed meaning" (*abhidheyavat*), thus [applying it] to the characteristics and so forth.

This [rule] is connected [to the preceding]. And this is connected with "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth, by changing the gender according to the rule: "The gender and number are like those of the thing denoted" (*abhidheyavalliṅgavacanāni bhavanti*, Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 73). If definition and so forth are not what is manifested (*dyotya*) by the suffixes (*pratyaya*) and others, then what do they manifest? They manifest a specific relation (*sambandhaviśeṣa*).

In the expression “the lightning flashes toward the tree” (*vṛkṣaṃ prati vidyotate vidyut*), the tree is the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) and the flashing lightning is the indicated (*lakṣyā*); for it is by reaching the tree that the lightning flashes. Thus, the relationship between the indicated and the indicator, produced here by the action of reaching, is expressed by the word *prati*.

"In 'Sādhur devadatto mātaraṃ prati' (Devadatta is kind toward his mother)," by means of *prati*, Devadatta’s attainment of kindness with respect to his mother is expressed. Here too, "having reached the mother,
