there is the attainment of kindness" implies that the attainment of the mother's kindness is produced precisely by the action of reaching.
The relationship characterized by the status of object and subject is expressed by the prefix *prati*.

In the phrase "that portion which [belongs] to me," and so forth, the meaning is: "let that part which falls to my share be given. Here too, there exists either a master-and-possessed relationship (*svasvāmibhāva*) produced by the act of dividing, or one produced by the act of accepting.

The connection [is as follows]: regarding the word *mām*, the substitute *mā* occurs for the word *asmad* by the rule *tvamāvekavacane* (Pāṇini 7.2.97). The substitution of *ā* occurs by the rule *dvitīyāyāñca* (Pāṇini 7.2.87). In the example *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣaṃ prati siñcati* ("he waters tree after tree"), the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is expressed solely by the reduplication. As for the word *prati*, however—

The very relationship characterized as the state of being the means and the end (sādhyasādhanabhāva), which is produced by the act of watering (sekakriyā) in relation to the tree, is what is expressed [by the accusative case]. The tree and so forth are the means (sādhana), and the watering is the end (sādhya). Furthermore, because the root *sic* is transitive, the accusative case is used here to denote the trees as the object (karman), since they are most desired to be pervaded by the watering.

This is already established by the rule *karmaṇi dvitīyā* (Pāṇini 2.3.2). Because the designation *karmapravacanīya* supersedes the designation *upasarjana*, the change of *s* to *ṣ*— as prescribed by the rule *upasargāt sunoti* (Pāṇini 8.3.65)— does not occur.
‘*Pariṣiñcati*’ means he sprinkles on all sides. Now, the objection begins with ‘*atha*’ and so forth;

the resolution begins with ‘*varjanā*’ and so forth. The justification for this lies precisely in the association with the term *apaśabda*. For in that context, because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning *karmapravacanīya*s, the term *apaśabda*—which signifies exclusion—is understood as referring only to exclusion.
The designation *karmapravacanīya* is prescribed for *pari* by the rule *tasya paryapā varjane* (Pāṇini 1.4.88).

Therefore, due to its association with that [term], the *pari* used here is understood as having the sense of exclusion (*varjana*). Consequently, when joined with this [word] as well, this fifth case (*pañcamī*) is ordained only in the domain of exclusion, not in the senses of indication (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth.

91. *abhirabhāge* (Pāṇini 1.4.91). In the example “*yad atra mām abhiṣyāt*,” there is the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *śnasorallopaḥ* (6.4.111). Since the designation *karmapravacanīya* does not apply here, the status of being a *upasarga* remains intact. Therefore—

The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule *upasargaprādurbhyāmastiryacparaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.87). Regarding the word *mām*: although the root *as-* is intransitive (*akarmaka*), even intransitive roots become transitive (*sakarmaka*) when accompanied by a prefix; thus, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is applied in the sense of the object according to *karmaṇi dvitīyā* (Pāṇini 2.3.2). Now, one might object that the word *abhi* [expresses] the connection with a portion...
Since it is merely an indicator (*dyotaka*), it has no syntactic connection with the root *ās*; how then can there be transitivity?

This is not so; for by means of its connection [to the root], the prefix *abhi-* indicates the connection with the verbal base (*bhāga*). Otherwise, if it were not connected with *asti*, even the designation "prefix" (*upasarga*) would not apply.
That being so, the designation of "upasarga" would not apply, and consequently, the substitution of *ṣ* in the form *abhiṣyāt* would also not occur.

92. *Prati* [is used] in the senses of representation (*pratinidhi*) and exchange (*pratidāna*). (Pāṇini 1.4.92) As in: “Abhimanyu is *prati* to Arjuna. Here, Arjuna is the primary (*mukhya*), while Abhimanyu is his likeness. In the sense that he imitates Arjuna, this [usage] is produced by the action of imitation (*anukaraṇa*).

The specific relation of being the original and the imitation (*anukāryānukaraṇabhāva*) is indicated by *prati*. The ablative case is used according to Pāṇini 2.3.11: *pratinidhipratidāne ca yasmāt*. Then, by Pāṇini 5.4.44: *pratiyoge pañcamyās tasiḥ*, the suffix *tasi* is applied after the ablative. As in the example: *māṣān asmai tilebhyaḥ* ("He gives beans in exchange for these sesame seeds"). [This refers to] the sesame seeds.

The repayment of debts previously given is what is meant here by "returning" (niryātana). The meaning is that one takes sesame seeds and gives back beans; the relationship produced here by the acts of giving and taking is characterized by the status of creditor and debtor.
93. *adhi* and *pari* [are used] when they are meaningless (*anarthaka*) (Pāṇini 1.4.93). Regarding the phrase "denoting no different meaning" (*anarthāntaravācinau*):
by this it is stated that they are called "meaningless" (*anarthaka*) because they do not denote a different meaning, and not because of a total absence of meaning.

[The author] demonstrates this: for if these two were meaningless because their referents do not exist, then this sūtra would be purposeless. To explain: by this [sūtra], the designation *karmapravacanīya* is prescribed for the purpose of superseding the designations *gati* and *upasarga*. It is not...

Furthermore, for the meaningless *adhi* and *pari*, there is no attainment of the designations "motion" (*gati*) or "preverb" (*upasarga*), because the designation of motion and preverb is prescribed only with respect to that [object] toward which the particles beginning with *pra* (the *prādayaḥ*) are connected with an action;
and since it is impossible for the two meaningless ones to be connected with an action, as in the example: "From where does he come after having ascended? (*kuto 'dhyāgacchati*).

The ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used here in the sense of the point of departure (*āpādāna*). It does not take the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) by virtue of the rule *karmapravacanīya* (Pāṇini 2.3.8), because of the maxim: "A case ending based on a *kāraka* relation is stronger than a case ending based on a *upapada* (governing word)" (Cāndra-vṛtti 69). The purpose for the formulation of this sūtra has already been stated. [The word] *kutaḥ* [is derived] from the interrogative pronoun *kim*.

The suffix *tasil* is applied by the rule *pañcamyās tasil* (Pāṇini 5.3.7), and the substitution of *k* occurs by the rule *ṭhku tihoḥ* (7.2.104). Because the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "karmapravacanīya" sublates the designations of "gati" and "upasarga," the elision (*nighāta*) of the accent does not occur by the rule *gatir gatau* (8.1.70). Now, it might be objected that [the word] has already been stated as *āgacchati*.

The arrival is understood as being qualified [by the prefixes], as in "he arrives over" (*adhyāgacchati*) or "he arrives around" (*paryāgacchati*). However, when combined with *adhi* and *pari*, the sense of being "above" or "on all sides" regarding the arrival is perceived;
this is another distinction. So how can these two be said to express no different meaning? This is not so.

When the prefixes *adhi* and *pari* are employed even though those two meanings are already understood from some source such as the context (*prakaraṇa*), then it should be understood that they do not express a meaning distinct [from what is already understood]. But how can the meanings be understood? This is not so; for there is indeed an employment of those two meanings.
Is it because of the rule, “There is no employment of words whose meaning has already been expressed” (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 60)? True;

however, the employment of even a word whose meaning is already understood is observed, as in the expression “two Brāhmaṇas. This is because worldly usage pays no heed to considerations of brevity or prolixity.

94. *suḥ* [is used] in the sense of praise (*pūjāyām*). (Pāṇini 1.4.94) As in: “*susiktaṃ bhavatā*” (“It has been well-sprinkled by you”). From the word *bhavat*, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). However, as before, the second case ending does not occur. [This is because] "the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is being praised. It is the highlighting of excellence (*śobhanodbhāvanam*).

Praise is itself the worship of that [person]. [The rule] "the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur when based on a prefix" applies because the designation of *karmapravacanīya* sublates the designation of *upasarga*; this is the intended meaning. In the example "suṣiktaṃ kiṃ tavātra" ("What is well-poured for you here?"), this is a reproach, not praise.

95. And [the suffix *ktvā* is used] after *ati-rati* and *atikramaṇa* (Pāṇini 1.4.95). For example: *atistutameva bhavatā* ("It has indeed been highly praised by you"). Even when the result is already accomplished, praise serves the purpose of inciting activity.
"The meaning is 'it was well done,'" thus he manifests honor.
96. *Api* [is used] in the senses of: the meaning of a word (*padārtha*), possibility (*sambhāvanā*), permission (*anvavasarga*), censure (*garhā*), and conjunction (*samuccaya*).

(1.4.96) Regarding the term *padārthe*: it indicates the meaning of another word (*anyasya padasyārthaḥ*). It does not denote its own meaning (*svārthaḥ*), nor that which is related to itself; rather, *padārtha* is the meaning of a word (*padasyārthaḥ*). This is the inclusion of the meaning of its own word (*svapadārthagrahaṇam*).
Alternatively, the mention of "the apprehension of word-meanings" would be redundant;

for the meaning of the word *api*, as well as the meaning of the phrase beginning with "that which is related to the word *api*," is simply the meaning of a word (*padārtha*) itself—so what is the purpose of mentioning "word-meaning"? Therefore:

He says— “of another word,” and so forth— because the meaning of a specific word is understood through its capacity to grasp the meaning of the constituent parts (*padārtha*). [The example] “there might even be [the suffix *ṣat*] after *sarpiḥ*” is given because the designation of *upasarga* (preverb) has been set aside by the designation of *karmapravacanīya* (governing particle).

By the rule "upasargaprādurbhyāmastiryacparaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.87), the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur. Now, why is the accusative case not applied to the word *sarpiḥ*? Because it is impossible for that [word] to be connected with the word *api*; for it is the *mātrā* (measure/portion) of *sarpiḥ* that is connected with the word *api*, not *sarpiḥ* itself.

Why, then, does it not occur from the word *mātrā*? Because of its non-usage. When it is used, however, it does not have the designation of a *karmapravacanīya* at all; for that [designation] is prescribed for a word not being used, in the sense of another word. Regarding the phrase "by expressing an additional meaning" (*adhikārthavacanena*): the additional meaning...

The sprinkling of a thousand radishes and so forth: the manifestation—that is, the disclosure—of the unimpeded power of that person's word when it comes to performing an action such as sprinkling, is "possibility" (*sambhāvanā*). For example:
"He might even sprinkle a thousand radishes," or "He might even praise the king. This [power] exists in his act of sprinkling or praising.

The meaning is that its capacity (*sāmarthya*) is not obstructed. The suffix *liṅ* is used here according to Pāṇini 3.3.154: *“When there is a possibility [of something], if ‘alam’ is used, [the suffix is applied] even when there is no connection with a verbal root. Regarding the phrase “permission for acting at will” (*kāmacārābhyanujñāna*):
“acting at will” (*kāmacāra*) means proceeding according to one’s own desire; the permission for that is “permission for acting at will.”

"‘Api siñca, api stuhi’ (Sprinkle, or praise)— the meaning is that you are permitted to do as you wish, whether you sprinkle or praise. "‘Dhig jālmam Devadattam’ (Fie on the wretch Devadatta!)"— in these three cases, beginning with *dhik*, *upari*, and so forth, the case endings for both [the accusative and the ablative] are to be applied.

The accusative case is used because of the supplementary rule (vārttika 118): "It is seen [used] after words ending in a second accusative, as well as in other instances. For example: *api siñcet palāṇḍum* ("one might even water an onion"). Here, the potential suffix (*liṅ*) is applied by the rule *arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca* (Pāṇini 3.3.69). The word *palāṇḍum* takes the accusative case in the sense of the object (*karman*).

(2.3.2) "Sprinkle as well, praise as well. Here, both the acts of praising and sprinkling are enjoined upon a single agent. This constitutes a conjunction (*samuccaya*). By the use of the particle *ca*, which signifies the well-known sense of conjunction—as in "sprinkle and praise"—it refers to that very [conjunction].
It clarifies the collection in the example.

97. *adhir īśvare* (Pāṇini 1.4.97): "This [term *adhi*] [is used] in relation to the connection between property and its owner. Here, the connection is one produced by actions such as protecting and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in that case" (*tatra*) and so on: for in every kind of connection, something is restated (*anūdyate*).

Something is being explained: that which is already established is restated (*anūdyate*), while that which is not yet established is explained—that is, it is enjoined (*vidhīyate*) or made known (*jñāpyate*). For example: "He who has earrings is Devadatta.
By restating the possession of earrings, the state of being Devadatta is enjoined through the restatement of Devadatta. And that which...

That which is enjoined is primary; the other is secondary, being a qualifier. In that context, when the owner (*svāmī*) is enjoined because he is not otherwise established, he attains a state of distinction due to his primacy. Consequently, because he is connected with the designation of a *karmapravacanīya*, the case ending [of the word denoting the object] is determined by that very distinction.

When the sixth case-affix (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would apply, it is set aside by the exception: "The seventh case-affix (*saptamī*) occurs where there is a word denoting that from which something is superior or that which has mastery over something" (Pāṇini 2.3.9). Since the relationship is already expressed by that [seventh case], the first case-affix (*prathamā*) alone occurs after the word itself, and not the seventh. However, when the status of being a master (*svāmin*) is not well-known...
When that is prescribed, then the opposite should be understood.

98. *vibhāṣā kṛñi* (Pāṇini 1.4.98). The term *adhir īśvare* ("*adhi* [is used] in the sense of lordship") is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Therefore, this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) where [the previous rule] would otherwise have applied. The verb *kṛ* preceded by *adhi* is used in the sense of "assignment" (*viniyoga*). Sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is established only for that which has been assigned. Whatever is here...
"He will appoint me. Here, *mām* is in the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) as the object of the verb. Regarding the form *adhikariṣyati*:

since the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent by the rule "In the presence of particles such as *yad*, *yadi*, etc. (Pāṇini 8.1.30) applies here, it retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*), which is acute on the first syllable (*ādyaudātatva*).

99. *laḥ parasmaipadam* | (1.4.99) Is *laḥ* in the nominative case or in the genitive? If it were in the nominative, the designation *parasmaipada* would apply to the letter *l* itself, and not to its substitutes.
[This would apply] to the *tib* and other [affixes]. Granted, for those as well, it might occur by virtue of being treated like the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*).

However, in the rule *taṅanāvātmanepadam* (1.4.100), the connection between *taṅ* and *an* with the word *laḥ* would not be tenable; for *taṅ* and *an* do not themselves become *l*-suffixes. In this context, the state of being *taṅ* and *an*...

The *lakāra* itself is designated as *taṅ* and *naḍ*; or, by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), it should be explained that only the substitutes for *l*—namely *taṅ* and *naḍ*—are referred to by the term "*ṭhla*.
Thus, if the intended meaning were established through such an interpretation, there would be an excessive burden on the understanding (*pratipatti-gaurava*).
However, this fault does not exist in the case of the genitive interpretation; therefore, relying on that, he says: "The genitive [case] in 'laḥ' and so forth.

But surely even this position is indeed faulty, for if the designation *parasmaipada* were prescribed for the substitutes of *l*, it would not apply to the *tiṅ* suffixes, because those [tiṅs] are subsequent [to the *l*-substitutes].

By the rule "tiṅstrīṇi trīṇi" (Pāṇini 1.4.101) and others, the technical designations (saṃjñā) such as *prathamapuruṣa* (third person) and so forth must apply. But what about the scope for the designation *parasmaipada*? Is there not a conflict with the scope of the suffixes *śatṛ* and *kvasu*? This is not a fault; for the author [of the Aṣṭādhyāyī] states, "vṛddhi occurs before *sic* when *parasmaipada* follows" (Pāṇini 7.2.1).

This indicates that the personal endings (tiṅ) possess the designation *parasmaipada*. For [the augment *iṭ*] is prescribed after the suffix *sic* when a *parasmaipada* follows; indeed, the suffixes *śatṛ* and *kvasu* cannot occur in the domain of *sic*.
The forms beginning with "tip-tas-jhi" are merely examples of their shapes.

100. The *ātmanepada* [is used] after the root *han* with the prefix *ni*. In the example “*katīha nighnānāḥ*” (“how many here are habitually striking?”), the suffix *cānaś* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.129 (*tācchīlyavayovacanaśaktiṣu cānaś*), following the rule for the root *han* with the prefix *ni* at 6.4.98 (*gamahana*).
By these and other rules, there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*). By the rule *hohanter ñṇinneṣu* (Pāṇini 7.3.54), there is the substitution of the guttural *k* (*kutva*).
If the suffix *cānaś* were also designated as *ātmanepada*, then the root *han*, which is *parasmaipada*, would not undergo this change.
101. *tiṅ* [denotes] three [groups], each consisting of three; [these are] the first, middle, and last.

*Tiṅ* is the nominative plural. Of what nature are the possessors of this designation (*saṃjñin*)? The meaning is that they consist of three [each] times three. The indication is made in the neuter gender with respect to the number (*vacana*).

And this [term] is repeated twice for the sake of distribution (*vīpsā*). If the three sets of three verbal suffixes are designated by the names "first person," "middle person," and "last person," then there would be six designata (*saṃjñin*) and only three designations (*saṃjñā*); thus, the rule of correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) would not apply because of the inequality. In that case—

If, because the prescription of multiple technical names for a single entity would be redundant, there were to be only one name, rather than three for each individual, then even so, since each one would be that very same [single] name, there would be a lack of fixed determination (*avyavasthā*). This is not a fault; for here, the mention of *parasmaipada* and the mention of *ātmanepada* both continue to apply.

And when those [suffixes] follow, there are two groups: one group consists of the nine *tiṅ* suffixes known as *parasmaipada*, and likewise, the second group consists of the nine [suffixes] known as *ātmanepada*. Among these, those which are in the first group...

There are three triads; and these three triads in the second group are each connected individually with this sūtra: "In the *parasmaipada* [terminations], the *tiṅ* [suffixes] are divided into three sets of three, namely the first, middle, and last; likewise in the *ātmanepada*, the *tiṅ* [suffixes] are divided into three sets of three."
"First, middle, and last"—for if this were so, there would be no contingency of the absence of a numerical designation. To demonstrate that very point, he says:
"There are eighteen suffixes for *tiṅ*. By the word "nine" and so forth, he shows two groups.

By the words beginning with "therein" (*tatra*), he establishes the connection of this sūtra with the three triplets (*trika*) in the first group; and by the words beginning with "in the ātmanepada" (*ātmanepadeṣu*), [he establishes it] with the three triplets in the second group as well.
102. Those [terms]—the singular, dual, and plural—[are applied] individually.

The plural form in the word *tāni* ("those") is for the purpose of including all the technical names (*saṃjñā*); otherwise, since there is a governing rule (*adhikāra*) regarding "one technical name" (P. 1.4.1), the technical names for person (*puruṣa*) and number (*vacana*) would apply alternatively due to the authority of the specific mention [of "one"].

And in that case, the grammatical operations such as *āṭ* prescribed by the rule "āḍajādīnām" (Pāṇini 6.4.72) and others would be only optional for the third person singular. However, this being the case, there is a co-occurrence of the technical designations (*saṃjñā-samāveśa*). For by the word "those" (*tad*), three [groups] of three are understood as having received the designation of "masculine" (*puruṣa*).

These are referred back as being designated by the terms "singular" and so forth; therefore, those very [suffixes] which have acquired the designations "first person" and so on are precisely what receive the designations "singular" and so on.
But surely, the designations "first" and so on apply to groups of three, whereas the designations "singular" and so on apply to each individual one; in that case—

"There is no contradiction at all even though there is a single designation (*saṃjñā*) for different objects of application (*viṣaya*); this is not a fault. For that [designation] exists as each individual [element], such as *puruṣa* and so on, since there is no aggregate (*samudāya*) other than the three [elements]; therefore, only the *tiP* suffixes and the like are the designata (*saṃjñin*)."

The mention of the word *tri* (three), however, is for the purpose of establishing a limit; it indicates that the designations *puruṣa* (person) apply individually to each *tiṅ* (verbal suffix) as delimited by the number three. Therefore, the designations *prathama* (first) and so forth, as well as the designations *ekavacana* (singular) and so forth, have precisely the same scope.
It is said that "those" [are the elements] for the purpose of the entry of ideation (saṃjñā).

103. *supaḥ* | (1.4.103) The term *suv* is a reference to a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated series). It begins with the word *su*, the nominative singular ending, and extends up to the letter *p* in *sup*, the locative plural ending. Now, this *pratyāhāra* is formed by the letter *p* in *kapa*.

Why is it not understood? Because it would result in the redundancy of the letter *p* in the locative plural (*saptamī-bahuvacana*). Would that [letter *p*] be for the purpose of marking an anudātta accent, or for the purpose of forming a pratyāhāra?
In that regard, it is not for the purpose of an anudātta, because an anudātta is already established by the very fact that it is a *sup* (case-ending). In that case—
If it were not even for the purpose of a pratyāhāra (abbreviated designation), then this [letter] would be entirely meaningless.

Therefore, this pratyāhāra is understood by means of that [letter] alone, and not by the letter *p* of *kap*; for in the rules concerning accents (*svaravidhi*), that [letter *p*] has already served its purpose.
104. *vibhaktiśca* (Pāṇini 1.4.104).

The particle *ca* ("and") is for the purpose of ensuring the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) such as "person" (*puruṣa*) and so on. Without it, under the governing rule of "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), there would be optionality (*paryāya*) due to the authority of the explicit statement. The purpose of *tiṅ* being designated as a "case-ending" (*vibhakti*) is [that the rule] *na*... [applies].

By the rule *vibhaktau tusmāḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.4), there is a prohibition of the technical designation *it*. However, for *sup* suffixes, there is both the *it* designation and others, such as the substitution of *tyadādi* forms and so forth.

105. When *yuṣmad* is present as a co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) word, even if it is not [immediately] situated [in the sentence], the second person [suffix] is used. (Pāṇini 1.4.105). To show that this rule is for the purpose of restriction (*niyata-artha*), he says: "Having introduced the heading ‘of *la*’" (*lasya*), and so forth. And this is the reason for its being a restrictive rule: the commencement of a rule serves to restrict it when it would otherwise be established, but not when it is not yet established. That...

Furthermore, this restriction (*niyama*) would it be a restriction on the *upapada*—meaning that when *yuṣmad* is the *upapada* of a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), only the middle person (*madhyama-puruṣa*) is used? Or would it be a restriction on the person (*puruṣa*)—meaning that only when *yuṣmad* is the *upapada* is the middle person used? In that regard, if the first restriction is adopted, [it would apply even in cases such as] "by you while acting" (*tvayā kurvatā*).

By the phrase "by one who is performing," the substitutes *śatṛ* and *śānac* do not occur for the suffixes of the second person (*yuṣmad*). Therefore, another effort must be undertaken for that purpose. In the other case, however, nothing requires such effort;
thus, relying on the second alternative, he says: "Of these, this... and so forth. And [the rule applies] even when there is an intervention.

Regarding the phrase "and even when not contiguous": [an objection is raised]—surely that word which is proximate to another is called an *upapada*, on the grounds that it is uttered near (*upa*) the other; whereas that which is separated is distant in comparison to what is not contiguous. Therefore, it ought to be separated [from its governing element].

This is not a fault; for the grasping of both "proximate" and "remote" is indeterminate, because it is relative, like the concepts of "farther" and "nearer. In that regard, if something remote is compared with what is immediate, it becomes "remote."

Nevertheless, since something becomes proximate (sannikṛṣṭa) in relation to another thing that is even more remote (viprakṛṣṭatara), it must also be [considered] separated (vyavahita) in relation to the other. If this is so, what is the purpose of mentioning the word *upapada*?
It was included for the sake of ensuring that the rule applies even when [the pronoun] has occurred previously; otherwise, [the rule would not apply] in the case of *yuṣmad*.
If only this much were stated, then by the rule "tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.66),
the second person ending would apply to the preceding [yuṣmad] only when [yuṣmad] occurs as a subsequent element, and not to the subsequent [yuṣmad] when it occurs as a preceding element.
By the inclusion of the term *upapada*, however, it applies here as well— both by the preceding rule and by the subsequent one.
An accompanying word (*upapada*) certainly occurs when it is being employed.

By explaining the term "in a coreferential [word]" (*samānādhikaraṇe*) as meaning "having the same denotation" (*samānābhidheya*), this author indicates that in the Sūtra the word *adhikaraṇa* is used in the sense of "denotation."

He demonstrates this: furthermore, regarding that which is to be expressed, since a *lakāra* (verbal suffix) arises in relation to either the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*) as the grammatical factor (*kāraka*), it is understood to refer to that very [factor] due to proximity; thus he says, "when the kāraka is the same" (*tulyakārake*), and so forth.
That whose kāraka is the same is described in that way. By the word "same" (*tulya*), the meaning of the word "identical" (*samāna*) is intended.

It has been shown [by the phrase] "even when [the substitute] is applied or not applied. By this, he explains the meaning of the term *sthānin* (the original element). The word *sthāna* signifies occasion (*prasaṅga*);
thus, a *sthānin* is that which possesses such an occasion. And what is its occasion? It is the occasion belonging to that very [element].
The meaning of which is understood, yet the word is not employed—this is what is meant:
even when *yuṣmad* is not employed, and by the force of the word "even" (*api*), also when it is employed.
Why is the mention of "coreferential" (*samānādhikaraṇa*) made? [So that the rule] does not apply in a case like "it is cooked by you" (*tvayā pacyate*), where [the pronoun] is different [in number].

This is the formal argument (adhikaraṇa). For instance: the word "by you" (tvayā) denotes the agent, because the third case-ending is prescribed for the agent; the word "is cooked" (pacyate) denotes the object, because the verbal suffix (lakāra) is prescribed for the object.

106. *Prahāse ca manyopapade manyateruttama ekavacca* (Pāṇini 1.4.106). [The commentary states: "When jest (*prahāsa*) is implied. Where, due to the absence of reality, there is mere deception, jest is understood through the revelation of the speaker's intention. "When *manya-* is the subordinate word (*upapada*)."

Thus, that which has the word *manya-* uttered as its *upapada* (governing adjunct) is described in that way. Because the middle [voice] is prescribed for the verbal root (*dhātu*), he states—"of the root"—in order to indicate that the root is understood from another place.
"And that is singular" means where there are two or many knowers.

In this case, the rule for singular formation (*ekavadbhāva*) is prescribed; elsewhere, however, the singular number is established simply because the agent (*mantṛ*) is one. Regarding the phrase "of the middle and the highest," it refers respectively to the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when they are used as co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) adjuncts (*upapada*), even if not explicitly uttered, because their meaning is present. For example:

In the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), the previous mention of *upapada* was connected with the word *yuṣmad*; one might think that it would carry over here [to the present rule] as well, but since it is impossible for it to be connected with the root *man*, the term *upapada* is mentioned again.

The mention [of the root] by means of the suffix *śyan* (as in *manute*) is for the purpose of ensuring that the inclusion of the root belonging to the *tanādi* class does not occur. Consequently, the following does not happen: "Come, you think (*manuṣe*), 'I shall go by chariot';
you will certainly not go; your father has already gone by it. For it is from the root *manoti* that this form arises.
107. *asmadyuttamaḥ* | (1.4.107) When both *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are present as co-occurring words (*upapada*), how should it be?
If the agential capacities are expected to be restricted to their respective substrates, then the verb (*ākhyāta*) [also follows suit].

It is employed separately—as in *pacasi* (you cook) and *pacāmi* (I cook). Now, if the *lakāra* suffix arises for both capacities due to the absence of contradiction, then by the rule of *vipratiṣedha* (conflict of rules), only the *uttama* (first person) remains—namely, *tvaṃ cāhaṃ ca pacāvaḥ* (you and I cook). Even though there is the rule, "among the words beginning with *tyad*, whichever is subsequent remains," [the result is] *āvām*.

For in the expression "pacāva" (let us two cook), the meaning of the second person (*yuṣmad*) must also be denoted by the word "we" (*asmad*); otherwise, the dual number would not occur, since duality is not applicable to the word "we" alone.

108. *śeṣe prathamaḥ* | (1.4.108) 109. *paraḥ sannikarṣaḥ saṃhitā* | (1.4.109) "The word *para* occurs in the sense of 'excess' (*atiśaya*)," as in the expression *paraṃ duḥkham* ("extreme suffering"). By this—

The word *para* also occurs in senses such as "direction" (*dig*) and so forth; nevertheless, he shows here that it is taken in the sense of "excess. *Sannikarṣa* means proximity (*pratyāsatti*) and also contact (*saṃśleṣa*). Showing that proximity is what is intended here, he says: "proximity is closeness" (*sannikarṣaḥ pratyāsatiḥ*).

But conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*) is not perceived, because it is impossible for it to exist among phonemes (*varṇa*). For conjunction occurs between things that exist at the same time, and simultaneity does not apply to phonemes;
this is because they are uttered in succession and perish as soon as they are uttered. Indeed, conjunction belongs to those things that are simultaneous.
[The objection] does not arise, nor does it entail the consequence that phonemes exist simultaneously;

for they are uttered sequentially, and by their very nature, what has been uttered perishes immediately. Furthermore, even if simultaneity were possible, a conjunction of phonemes could never occur. To explain: conjunction would have to result either from physical contact (*saṃyoga*)...

It might be [the cause] either through inherence (*samavāya*) or otherwise; in that regard, the former would belong only to a substance (*dravya*), but not to sound (*śabda*), because qualities (*guṇa*) are devoid of further qualities. Nor is the latter possible for sound, for one phoneme (*varṇa*) does not inhere in another phoneme, since sound inheres in space (*ākāśa*). It is not so.

Furthermore, no excellence (*atiśaya*) is possible in either conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*), because they are uniform in nature everywhere. Consequently, the qualification "the further" (*paraḥ*) would not be tenable. However, it is logical that proximity (*pratyāsatti*), being differentiated by distinctions created through relative expectation and employed according to its degree of intensity or lack thereof, is qualified by the term "the further. Thus, its [use] is appropriate.
[The status of] being a qualifier. But who is this "other" that utters the phonemes closely following [the first]?

When the speaker has ceased the operation of the palate and other [articulators] which were the producers of the preceding phoneme, and [performs] the operation of those same palate and other [articulators] which are the producers of the subsequent phoneme—
They say that the instruction regarding the operation [of conjunction] consists of a duration of half a *mātrā*. That is the separation (*vyavadhāna*) of phonemes;

that proximity (*sannikarṣa*) in which there is such a separation is "proximity characterized by a separation of half a *mātrā*. If the proximity of phonemes is a separation of half a *mātrā*, then how is it [possible] in cases such as *dadhyatra*?
Is it not the case that no time-interval between vowels is perceived, and they are apprehended as being merely joined together?

This is not so. For what purpose, then, is this [definition] undertaken, since the teachers state that *saṃhitā* is simply the closest proximity (*paraḥ sannikarṣaḥ*)? Indeed, when it is said, "Study the *saṃhitā*," [it refers to that very proximity].
Does the student study only proximity (*sannikarṣa*)? This is not so; for in common usage, the immediate succession of one word with another is designated as *saṃhitā*. Accordingly, speakers say:
"He studies the *saṃhitā*, not the individual words," or "He studies the words, not the *saṃhitā*."

And likewise, if [the term *saṃhitā* were restricted to two words], the operation of *saṃhitā* would not occur within a single word, such as in "kumāryau" and "kurmāryaḥ" according to the rule *iko yaṇ aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77). For, since this [rule] prescribes the designation *saṃhitā* for a specific proximity (*sannikarṣaviśeṣa*) of phonemes, it applies everywhere.
It comes to be.

110. *Virāma* is the term for *avasāna* (pause). (Pāṇini 1.4.110) "Cessation is *virāma*. The suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). *Virāma*, meaning the absence of the utterance of phonemes, receives the technical name *avasāna*. [Alternatively, it is derived as: "that by which one ceases [speaking]."

The word "virāmaḥ" shows the second meaning of the term *virāma*. According to the rule "kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam" (Pāṇini 3.3.13), because of the mention of "bahula" (diversity), the suffix *ghañ* is applied even when it is not a technical name (*saṃjñā*), by the rule "halaśca" (Pāṇini 3.3.121). In this view, that final phoneme by which one ceases [speaking] is designated as *avasāna* (pause).

It occurs as follows: in the former view, since there is no sequence [of sounds] in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*), this locative case in the rule *kharavasānayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.15) is understood as a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*) with respect to the pause (*avasāna*), and not as a locative of posteriority (*parasaptamī*). However, with respect to the consonant (*kha[r]*), this is indeed a locative [of posteriority].

Others, however, argue: if one concludes that sequence is impossible in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*), then the locative absolute construction (*parasaptamī*) in the rule *kharavasānayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.15) would be untenable; in that case, the locative absolute construction would likewise be untenable in rules such as *iko yaṇ aci* (6.1.77). How so? Because letters...
Because they occur sequentially and because they perish as soon as they are uttered: when one exists, the other does not;

and when the latter exists, the former does not. Now, if one were to accept the genitive case of "the other" (*parasaptamī*) by relying on a temporal sequence constructed by the intellect (*buddhiprakalpita*), then [the rule] *kharavasānayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.15) would apply.

Thinking that here too it should be understood in the same way, some maintain that the locative case in *para* (in the rule *kharavasānayor visarjanīyaḥ*) refers even to the *avasāna* (pause). Others, however, [hold that] when the final phoneme has the designation *avasāna*, [the rule applies]. "In the presence of a *khaR* or *avasāna*..."

Thus, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is understood [in Pāṇini 8.3.15]. Here, some say that the genitive denotes "position" (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) with respect to the pause (*avasāna*), as in "the *visarjanīya* replaces the *repha* at the pause. Others say that the genitive is characterized by immediate sequence (*ānantarya-lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the following consonant (*kha[r]*), as in "the *visarjanīya* [replaces the *repha*] before a hard consonant. According to that view, the genitive denoting position [is understood] from the rule *ṭhro ri* (8.3.14).

The status as a substitute (sthānitva) for the recurring letter *r* is not contradicted; thus, even though it is a single case-ending, it is divided according to its application. But surely, even in the case where [the *r*] is absent, there is no pronunciation in the preceding portion either, and in that case too, the visarga would result—as in *rathaḥ*.

Is there not, then, an utterance prior to the *repha* even here? This is not a fault; for in that case, the word "pada" which is under discussion is qualified by the *repha*—meaning "of a word ending in *repha*" (*rephāntasya padasya*). And a word does not become [so called] merely by virtue of the preceding *repha*. [Objection: But even so, this would be a designation for the meaning (*artha*) itself.

In the rule *kharavasānayorvisarjanīyaḥ* (8.3.15), the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) *tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya* (1.1.66) does not apply. For this [technical rule] applies when a word-form (*śabda*) is specified in the locative case, not when a meaning (*artha*) is specified. And because that rule does not apply here, [the substitution occurs] by means of the subsequent *repha*.

[Objection: Regarding the word *ratha* ending in the letter *repha*, the *visarjanīya* should occur for that *repha* which precedes it, even if it is separated [by other sounds]. [Response: This is not a fault; it will not occur because of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). For this very reason, in the rule "ṭhuraṇ raparaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.1.51), the author makes the mention [of the suffix] without applying the *visarjanīya* to the separated *repha*.
This indicates that the *visarjanīya* does not occur for a *repha* that is separated [by other sounds]. [Objection:
But surely, in common worldly usage, the word *avasāna* (pause) is understood only with respect to the final phoneme.

It will be so; for it is well known in the world that the term *avasāna* (pause/termination) is used with respect to the final phoneme (*varṇa*). For instance, when someone asks, "With what does he pause? speakers reply, "With the vowel *i* or with the vowel *u*.
The meaning is that he effects a pause by means of a phoneme such as *i*. Therefore, the mention of *avasāna* occurs only in specific instances (*pradeśa*).

It is not the case that the meaning [of the root] is "that which is to be done" (*kartavya*) by means of the relationship between a name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*); this is not so. For the root *syati* functions in the sense of completion—as in "the discussion is concluded" (*avasita*); it also functions in the sense of comprehension—as in "the matter is understood" (*avasita*); and it also functions in the sense of defeat—as in "the dispute between the two has been decided" (*avasita*).

Regarding the phrase "davadata": if this [sūtra] were not commenced there, then there would be doubt in the enumeration of *avasāna*—namely, whether the word *avasāna* refers to the term *abhidhāna*? However, in the rule "virāmo 'vasānam" (P.
1.4.110), one would have to include the mention of "the end"—that is, "at the end of a vowel or a consonant"? This too is not the case; for thus...

For there would indeed be doubt: does it refer to the final phoneme (*varṇa*), or to the word (*pada*), or perhaps to the sentence (*vākya*)? In that case, the mention of "phoneme" (*varṇa*) would have to be made for the sake of specifying the final phoneme. Therefore, the relationship between the name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*) must be established.

In the examples "vṛkṣaḥ" and "plakṣaḥ," [the rule] "the *visarjanīya* occurs before *kha* and *ra*" (8.3.15) applies. In "dadhiṃ madhuṃ," [the rule] "the nasalized form (*anunāsika*) occurs for an *aṇ* that is not a *pragṛhya*" (8.4.57) applies;
for here, the mention of "pause" (*avasāna*) from the preceding rule "optionally in pause" (8.4.56) is carried over.
Thus ends the first chapter of the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable Ācārya Jinendrabuddhi, who was a disciple of the Bodhisattvas.
The fourth quarter is completed, and this first chapter is finished.
The *Nyāsa*, also known by its alternative title, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, a disciple of the Bodhisattva.
The Kāśikā Commentary — Second Chapter —
First Pāda:
1. *samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ* (A 2.1.1). "This is a *paribhāṣā*" means that a *paribhāṣā* is a rule (*bhāṣā*) that operates pervasively (*paritaḥ*). Thus...

And it has been said: "A *paribhāṣā*, moreover, being located in one place, illuminates the entire treatise, just as a lamp placed on a threshold [illuminates everything]. But how is this understood—that this is a *paribhāṣā* and not an *adhikāra* (a governing heading)? From the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the mention of "the prescription of words" (*padavidhi*). For subsequently, all...

The treatment as a subsequent part of a word (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) and so forth, when being imitated, is indeed a rule concerning words (*padavidhi*). In that case, if this were a governing heading (*adhikāra*), the mention of "rule concerning words" would be redundant, because there would be nothing to exclude. However, if this is a general maxim (*paribhāṣā*), for a maxim applies everywhere in the entire treatise even if it pertains to only a single portion.

If the term "pada-vidhi" (rule concerning a word) were not included, the rule would apply even to rules concerning phonemes (*varṇa*). Therefore, the inclusion of the term "pada-vidhi," which is made for the purpose of excluding rules concerning phonemes, becomes meaningful.
Consequently, by this indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, the inclusion of the term "pada-vidhi"—this is a *paribhāṣā* (an interpretive maxim), not an *adhikāra* (a governing heading).

Thus it is determined. If this is so, then for what purpose is the mention of *sāmarthya* (semantic competency) and *yukta* (conjoined) made in rules such as *ṭhisusoḥ sāmarthye* (8.3.44) and *na cavāhāhaivayukte* (8.1.24), given that the term *padasya* (of a word) is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*) there?

In that case, since it is prescribed by reference to words (*padavidhitva*), will it not fail to apply due to a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*)? This is true; however, we shall explain the very purpose for which it is formulated right there.
This word *vidhi* indeed exists as a noun derived from the action (*bhāvasādhana*)—namely, "arrangement" (*vidhāna*) is "prescription" (*vidhi*). And it also...

Regarding the term *karmasādhana*: that which is prescribed (*vidhīyate*) is a prescription (*vidhi*). In this context, when the word *vidhi* is understood as having the sense of an abstract state (*bhāvasādhana*), the genitive case in the expression "prescription of words" (*padavidhi*) is characterized by its connection with a verbal root (*kṛd-yoga*), signifying the object (*karman*)—namely, the completion of words that have not yet been fully formed. This is because they stand in a relationship of being the objects of that prescription.

In the context of the accomplishment of action (*karmasādhana*), however, that operation which is prescribed— such as compounding (*samāsa*) and so forth— for words that are already fully established and fixed is "word-formation" (*padavidhi*). In that regard, the genitive case characterized as "the remainder" (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇā*) occurs with respect to those words, [denoting] the operation being prescribed.

Because it is introduced as being connected with the word *pada*. In that context, if the word *vidhi* were here understood as having an ontological sense (*bhāvasādhana*), then only the prescription of case-endings (*vibhakti*) would be included; the formation of compounds (*samāsa*), the treatment as if they were external members (*parāṅgavadbhāva*), the application of secondary suffixes (*taddhitavṛtti*), and so forth, would not be included, for such is not the case there.

Is there an injunction for words that do not exist? Rather, the grammatical operations such as compounding (samāsa) are enjoined only for words that are already established. However, thinking that if the word "injunction" (vidhi) were understood in its active sense, those [non-existent words] would also be included, he takes recourse to the word "injunction" (vidhi) as a passive derivative and says:
"A rule (*vidhi*) is that by which something is prescribed. [Objection: But even in this view, the prescription of case-endings (*vibhakti-vidhāna*) would not be included;

for in rules such as "the second case is used in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*, Pāṇini 2.3.2), no grammatical operation (*kārya*) is prescribed for words already established by those rules, but rather the words themselves [are prescribed].

Are they prescribed? If they were not included, that would indeed be the case; however, we shall demonstrate later that no undesirable consequence follows from their non-inclusion. Regarding the phrase "beginning with compounds" (*samāsādi*), the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) includes derivative formations (*taddhitavṛtti*) and so forth.

"Capable" (*samartha*) means "powerful" (*śakta*). The meaning is that it is fit for the accomplishment of its own function. For in common worldly usage, one is called "capable" who is able [to perform an action]. The very communication of their own meaning is the specific function of words. And all those words—both worldly and Vedic—that are under discussion here are indeed such.

They are capable of conveying their own respective meanings. Therefore, by the force of employing the qualifier "capable" (*samartha*), a certain specific distinction is resorted to. And that distinction is as follows: when a sentence is employed for the purpose of a *vṛtti* (commentary), there is a capacity to convey its meaning based on proximity (*pratyāsatti*).

He says that this [term] is understood as *tallakṣama* (characterized by that), beginning with the words "in the expression of the meaning of a compound and a sentence" (*vigrahavākyārthābhidhāne*), and so forth.

That by which something is specifically grasped or known is a *vigraha*; and a *vigraha* is a sentence. Alternatively, *vigraha* is the specific grasping; a sentence for the purpose of such grasping is a *vigrahavākya*.

This is a compound of the *madhyamapadalopa* type, following the rule for *śākapārthiva* and similar formations. "The meaning of the analytical sentence" (*vigrahavākyārtha*) refers to the sense conveyed by that sentence; that which is capable of expressing—that is, making known—that meaning should be understood as "competent" (*samartha*). For example, the compound *rājapuruṣaḥ* (king's man) is competent because it possesses the capacity to convey the meaning of the analytical sentence "the king's [man]."

The word "rājapuruṣa" (king's man) is capable of denoting that object which is the referent of the word "puruṣa," because that object is understood from it as well. Furthermore, that object is either a relation (*saṃsarga*), a distinction (*bheda*), or both distinction and relation. In this regard, [it denotes] the specific [man] who is the possessor (*svāmiviśeṣa*) of his own particular [quality].

The relation that exists by virtue of a specific owner is called "conjunction" (*saṃsarga*). The exclusion of one's own [possessions] from other owners, and the exclusion of another's owner from his own [possessions], is called "differentiation" (*bheda*).

In that regard, according to the view of the proponents of relation (*saṃsargavādinaḥ*), the meaning of a word is the relation itself, while exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is subsumed within the object. For a relation between two things—such as a master and his property—is not possible unless they are distinguished from other related entities. Thus, exclusion is necessarily included.

For the proponent of difference (*bhedavādin*), however, exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) alone is the meaning of a word, while connection (*saṃsarga*) is subsumed within the object; for there is no existence of a thing being excluded, such as ownership and the like, if it is not connected with another related entity. For the proponent of both (*ubhayavādin*), on the other hand, both [exclusion and connection] are the meaning of a word. If...

If "capable" (*samartha*) were understood as that which is able to express the meaning of a sentence through its constituent parts (*vigraha-vākya*), then capability would apply only to the domain of compounds (*samāsa*) and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*);
consequently, this paribhāṣā would not apply to the rules concerning the treatment as a subsequent member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) and the prescription of case-endings (*vibhaktividhāna*). It is not so.

For is there indeed an expression of the meaning of the syntactical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) therein? If it were not present, so be it; yet nothing undesirable would follow from its absence. To explain: the author of the *Bhāṣya* will point out that the mention of the "cause" (*nimitta*) [in Pāṇini 1.4.83] is intended to indicate the status of being like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*). And in that context, as for the cause...
The indicator certainly possesses efficacy—as in the example, "O King, [he] cuts the Madras with an axe.

Furthermore, even regarding the prescription of case endings, those which are case endings of the *kārakas* are prescribed only for those very *kārakas*, such as the object (*karman*) and so forth; thus, their connection with the action is indeed established.

Even in the case of derivative case-endings (*upapadavibhakti*), such as those governed by the rule *sahayukte 'pradhāne* (Pāṇini 2.3.19), there exists the mention of "conjunction" (*yukta*) and so forth; in those instances too, semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) certainly exists. When such a relationship is present, the case-endings are desired, but not on account of a semantic capacity characterized by the expression of a sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) as in the case of words like *vākya*.

Thus far, the word "samartha" (capable) has been shown to function in its primary sense. Now, in order to demonstrate its metaphorical function, he says "Or rather," and so forth. That which has capable words as its basis is "samarthapadāśraya"; its state [is "samarthapadāśrayatva"].

It is the state of being based on a capable word (*samarthapadāśrayatva*). For that reason, a compound (*samāsa*) and so forth is called "capable" (*samartha*). Because the basis (*āśraya*) is capable, the dependent (*āśrita*) is also designated as such by metaphorical extension (*upacāra*), due to the transfer of the property of the cause to the effect—just as, for example, "the water of the reed-thicket" is called "foot-disease. [In the rule] *samarthānām*...

By this statement, he explains the capacity characterized by designation within a sentence. For instance, in the sentence "the king’s man," the king expects the man—thinking "this is mine"—and the man also expects the king—thinking "I am his. By the phrase "of those whose meanings are conjoined," he refers to the compound (*samāsa*).

He demonstrates the semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) characterized by the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) among words. And this unification of meaning is a specific state consisting in the commonality of purpose (*sādhāraṇārthatā*) among words that were previously situated separately and possessed distinct meanings, occurring within a compound (*samāsa*). For in a sentence (*vākya*), there is no such commonality of purpose, because the meanings remain distinct.
For this very reason, in that case, a genitive case ending arises based on distinction—as in "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*).
In a compound (*vṛtti*), however, because it denotes a meaning delimited by both members, there is a commonality of meaning.
By this it is meant: for in a compound, the qualifier...

It enters into the qualificand and becomes one in meaning with it, together with the qualificand; for in a sentence, the qualifier remains distinct from the qualificand. This is so that, in the absence of [the particle *ca*], in a sentence such as "the king's cow, horse, and man," there would be no expression of a conjunction based on distinction.

The word *ca* is employed [in the rule]. However, when a compound (*samāsa*) occurs, that [separateness] ceases; this is to be understood as "one-ness of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*), as in the example: "the king's cows, horses, and men. In the examples "Behold, Devadatta, the hardship!
and "Viṣṇumitra has resorted to the teacher’s house," the word *kaṣṭa* [is connected] with the word *paśya*.

The connection [is with the word *dvitīyā*], but not with the word *śrita*; therefore, because there is no semantic compatibility (*sāmarthya*), the compound does not occur. Now, one might object: "Since words such as *śrita* are explicitly mentioned, we shall qualify the accusative case by them alone—it can indeed be designated as 'the accusative case that is related to *śrita* and the others'. [This is so] even when [the word *dvitīyā*] is absent.

However, it is understood that in that case, the second case ending is compounded with words such as *śrita* (resorted to) and so forth. Thus, even for a word that is dependent (*sāpekṣa*), a compound would indeed occur—as in *mahat kaṣṭaṃ śritaḥ* ("one who has resorted to great hardship"), for here the second case ending is caused by words such as *śrita*. Therefore, the mention of the term *samartha* (semantically connected/autonomous) must be made [in the rule]. Why? [Because otherwise] you— Please provide the remainder of the text for a complete translation.

"You will make [it] with a stick; Devadatta was broken by a stone. In this case, the breaking was performed by the stone expressed in the third case (*tṛtīyā*); therefore, since the state of being "done by that" (*tatkṛtatva*) exists, it would follow that a compound (*samāsa*) should occur.

However, it does not occur because of the inclusion of the term *samartha* ("having the same meaning"). When the term *samartha* is included, the following meaning results: [The compound occurs only when the members have the same referent.]

If the very same word ending in the third case that forms the compound were itself the one that performs the refutation (*khaṇḍana*), then a compound would be possible; however, in this instance, the refutation was not performed by that [word], and therefore no compound occurs. In other cases as well, it should be understood that there is no compound due to a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*).

2. *subāmantrite parāṅgavatsvare* (Pāṇini 2.1.2). Regarding the phrase "it is like a part (*aṅga*) of what follows": here the word *aṅga* signifies a "constituent part. Thus, "like a part of what follows" means it becomes like a single constituent part of the subsequent [word]; the meaning is that it is included by the mention of that [subsequent word]. In this way...

He states that this is understood as an extension of identity (*tādātmyātideśa*) by saying, "this is an extension of identity. Identity (*tādātmya*) means having the same nature (*tatsvabhāvatva*). He clarifies that very extension of identity with the words beginning with "the inflected word" (*subanta*): "the inflected word enters into the vocative."

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that it is included therein. In the example "kuṇḍenāṭan" (wandering with a bowl), the vowel *u* of the word *kuṇḍa* bears the accent of an address (*āmantrita-svara*). In other cases as well, the accentuation of an address accompanied by a case-ending should be understood in this way.
In the example "pīḍaḷe pīḍaḷmāna" (O you who are being oppressed, I am oppressed by your oppression), [the same applies].
The meaning is "I am being oppressed. [The root] *pīḍ* (DhP 1544) means "to press" or "to plunge"; with the causative suffix *ṇic*, the ātmanepada ending is used for the object in both cases.

In one instance, it is the first person singular of the periphrastic future (*iṭ*), and in the other, it is the present participle suffix *śānac*. [In the latter case], *yak* is added before the sārvadhātuka suffix, and there is the elision of the *ṇic* suffix.

By the rule *ṭhāsyanudātenṅidupadeśāllasārvadhātukanudātamahanviṅeḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.186), the *iṭ* augment is unaccented (*anudātta*). By the accentuation rule for suffixes (*pratyayasvara*), the suffix *yak* has its first syllable accented (*udātta*). Furthermore, by the rule *ekādeśa udātenodātaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.5), the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from the combination of these vowels is accented.

The vowel *i* in *ityā* is udātta. However, for the word *pīḍayamānā*, the portion *pīḍa*—being a vocative following a word that is not a pada—is subject to the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) by the rule *āmantritasya ca* (Pāṇini 8.1.19). In the example *gehe gārgyaḥ*, the word *geha* is antodātta because it is listed in the *uñchādi* group; the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from the combination with the locative case-ending is udātta as before.

In *gārgya*, the acute accent (*udātta*) occurs on the first syllable by virtue of the *ñ* suffix; here, there is indeed a separate accent. In the case of *devadatta kuṇḍenāṭan*, if the mention of the subsequent word (*paragrahaṇa*) were not made, then even a preceding vocative such as the word *devadatta* would be subject to the entry of the case-inflected form (*subanta*), and consequently—

From the word *devadatta*, the suffix *aṭ* following the word would undergo the grave accent (*nighāta*) by the rule "of that which follows a word and of a vocative" (Pāṇini 8.1.19). Now, one might object: if the mention of "following" (*para*) were made, then when the word *kuṇḍa* behaves as if it were a subsequent member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*), and the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) prescribed in the sixth book has been applied, [the accentuation] from the word *devadatta*...

Is it not the case that the following *aṭ* must necessarily be subject to the *nighāta* (elision of accent) because it follows a word ending in a *pāda*? This is not so; for that *nighāta* applies when the word is not at the beginning of a *pāda*, whereas here the status of being at the beginning of a *pāda* is intended.
And in that case, by the accent of the vocative (*āmantrita*), the first syllable is udātta—as in "devadatta. The same applies to "kuṇeḍanāṭan."

The suppression (*nighāta*) of the vocative does not occur here because it begins a metrical quarter (*pāda*). [As stated in the rule: "Just as a lump of clay might regain its own sound. How indeed could a collection of inflected words (*subanta-samudāya*), having become unified like a lump of clay and having attained, as it were, a single form, regain its own sound? It is for this purpose that the term *aṅga* (base) is included. For what purpose?
Furthermore, an effort is made for the sake of restoring the original form (*svarūpa*) of that which has become unified; therefore, he says "of both" (*ubhayoḥ*), and so forth.

If the mention of the "limb" (*aṅga*) were not made, then there would be one of the following: an extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*), an extension of the rule (*śāstrātideśa*), or an extension of the designation (*vyapadeśātideśa*). And such being the case...

Just as the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) of another [element] occurs in the case of a vocative form and according to the rule for initial acute accents, so too it would apply to the preceding member ending in a nominal suffix (*subanta*); consequently, both members would possess the initial acute accent.
However, when the term *aṅga* (stem) is employed, this becomes an extension of identity (*tādātmyātideśa*). Therefore—

Since a collection of *subanta* words that has become a single lump of clay (*mṛtpiṇḍībhūta*) receives the accent of acute on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) when it is a vocative (*āmantrita*), there is no possibility of both [words] receiving the acute on the first syllable simultaneously. [This is stated] so that "the operation based on its own [original form] may also take place.
In the example *āma kuṇḍenāṭan*, [this applies to] the word *aṭan*, which follows a word ending in a case-suffix (*padāt*).

When the rule *ṭhāmantritasya* (8.1.19) would otherwise require the *nighāta* accent, the word *na* is understood as being carried over from *ṭhna luṭ* (8.1.29). Since there is no single-word interval (*ekāntaratā*) [between the vocative and the verb] when the suffix *ām* is present, the accent would instead fall on the very last syllable of the inflected word (*subanta*), because the suffix *ām* does not function as a *vat* substitute; and it is not appropriate for such a form to have a single-word interval [with the verb]. This is the case when the *vat* suffix is applied.
However, since it exists, there are occasions when even its own substratum (*svāśraya*) is not a constituent part (*anaṅgatva*);

thus, the state of being separated by one syllable (*ekāntaratā*) is established, and by that, the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent is accomplished. In this regard, the division of accents is as follows:
the word *ām* has its first syllable acute (*udātta*) by virtue of being a particle (*nipāta*). The same applies to the word *kuṇḍa*.
When the status of being like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) exists, the first syllable receives the acute accent (*udātta*) by virtue of the vocative accent (*āmantritasvara*).

Likewise, when the prohibition of the *nihata* (circumflex) accent applies, this [compound] ending in *-aṭ* should also have its first syllable acutely accented according to the rule in the sixth book [of the Aṣṭādhyāyī]. For example, in "kūpe siñcan" (pouring into a well), there is no status of being like a subordinate member.

The *sakāra* becomes the beginning of a word (*padāditva*). Consequently, by the rule "sātpadādyoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.109), there would be a prohibition against its becoming a *ṣakāra*. In the case of "carman namana," here too, because the status of being like a subsequent member of a compound (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) is absent, the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*nimitin*) do not reside within the same word (*samānapadastha*).
Thus, the substitution of *ṇ* does not occur based on a common word-base (*samānapada*).

This refers to the rule stating that "when a case-inflected word (*subanta*) functions as if it were part of another word, it is treated as having the same referent (*samānādhikaraṇa*)," and so forth. But what is the reason that this [substitution] would not apply to a word with a common referent, such that this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is made?

Thus he says: "because of immediate proximity. In the rule *tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.66), since the inclusion of the word *nirdiṣṭe* (when specified) has the sense of immediate proximity (*anantarya*), [the operation] would not apply when there is an intervention; therefore, this is added as an exception. This applies in cases such as *tīkṣṇayā sūcyā sīvyan*.

In the word *sīvyann* (occurring after *tīkṣṇayā*), even though it is separated [from the preceding], the initial acute accent (*ādyaudātta*) occurs because it is treated as a subsequent member of the compound (*parāṅgavat*). In the phrase *uccair adhīyāna*, however, because the word *uccaiḥ* does not undergo treatment as a subsequent member, the initial acute accent conditioned by its being a vocative (*āmantrita*) does not occur.

In the absence of that [suffix], there is only the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*); for among the *svarādi* words, those that do not have the acute accent on the final syllable are listed. For it is said in that very same place: after teaching the items beginning with *sannatara*, *uccais*, *nīcais*, and ending with *pṛthak* separately, it is stated, "these words beginning with *sannatara* are read with the acute accent on the final syllable."

Thus it has been stated. When the status of *adhīyāna* as beginning with a *pāda* is intended, it receives the acute accent (*udātta*) on its first syllable; otherwise, it undergoes suppression (*nighāta*) by the rule "and [the vocative] of an address" (*āmantritasya ca*, Pāṇini 8.1.19).

3. *prākkaḍārāt samāsaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.3). Regarding the example *yathāvṛddham*: when the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "compound" (*samāsa*) applies here, operations such as those stated in *kṛttaddhitasamāsāś ca* (Pāṇini 1.2.46) and so forth take effect. Now, for what purpose is the word *prāk* ("before") used? For what reason [is it necessary] given that...
The word "prāk" (before) will be supplied from the very context of the fifth case-ending;

nor should it be suspected that the word "parāk" (beyond) must also be supplied because it too is a directional term, for if that were supplied, it would follow from the mention of "kaḍāra" that [the rule applies] after it.
Those which will be enumerated hereafter shall have the designation "compound" (*samāsa*);

and if that were so, one would have placed the governing rule for compounds immediately after the mention of *kaḍāra*. However, since it is placed here, by the force of its placement here, the phrase "prior to [the governing rule]" must be supplied as an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*).
Since [the desired result] will occur even so, there is no purpose for the previous statement; thus he says: "The previous statement," and so forth.

The purpose of the previous statement is so that the technical designation *samāsa* (compound) may co-occur with the subsequent designations such as *avyayībhāva* and the rest. For if that [previous statement] were not present, [the co-occurrence would not take place].
This designation [of "compound"] would be precluded by those [designations] which allow no scope;

however, for this designation of "compound," there would be scope in the case of that compound formed by the *yogavibhāga* ("splitting of the rule") of the word *saha* in Pāṇini 2.1.4— namely, in examples such as *anuprāvarṣat* and *anuvyacalat*, where the compound is formed with a finite verb (*tiṅanta*).

This is a compound (*samāsa*). Even though there is no room [for both rules to apply simultaneously], because of the authority of the explicit statement within the governing rule for "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), there would be an alternating application (*paryāyeṇa vṛttiḥ*), but not a co-occurrence (*samāveśaḥ*). However, when there is an explicit statement [of a rule] prior to the sūtra that directly introduces [the topic], a co-occurrence does take place. How so? For the connection is made in this way:
All those [compounds] situated prior to *kaḍāra* are designated as "compound" (*samāsa*);

being designated as compounds, they receive the designations of "avyayībhāva" and so forth. Therefore, the designation of "compound" is merely the cause for the designations of "avyayībhāva" and so on; it is not [the cause] for the [designated items] themselves.

The indicator (nimita) is frustrated; otherwise, it would not even possess the status of being an indicator. Therefore, its inclusion with the preceding statement cited in the Sūtra is logical. However, if that [preceding statement] were supplied by ellipsis (adhyāhṛta), then all those elements established prior to the mention of *kaḍāra* would all receive the designation of "compound" (samāsa).

The meaning "they come into being" is obtained [from this], but not the meaning "being designated as compounds (samāsa), they are designated as *avyayībhāva* and so forth. However, if that [term *samāsa*] were explicitly mentioned in the sūtra, then even that [latter meaning] would be obtained; otherwise, its explicit mention in the sūtra would be purposeless.
It may be so.

4. *saha supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4). Regarding the statement, "The inclusion of the word *saha* is for the purpose of splitting the rule (*yogavibhāga*)," one might object: "If that were not the case, the designation would apply to each [word] individually; consequently, in the case of *ṛkpādaḥ*, the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmānakṣe* [would not apply]."

In that case, the vowel *ā* would be the suffix added at the end of the compound (*samāsānta*); and here, in the example "rājāśvaḥ," there would be two accents according to the rule "of the compound" (*samāsasya*, 6.1.223). Why, then, was the word *saha* ("together") not included [in the definition of a compound] so that the designation of "compound" (*samāsa-saṃjñā*) might apply only to those elements that exist together, and not to each one individually?

How is this understood? It is thought thus: the word *saha* in the third case (*supā*) conveys the sense of accompaniment, as in the rule "an old man [is distinguished] by a young man" (*vṛddho yūnā*, Pāṇini 1.2.65). Furthermore, a long technical name (*saṃjñā*)—namely, *samāsa*—is employed so that it may be understood as a descriptive term (*anvarthasaṃjñā*). How, indeed, is it made into a descriptive term?

"Conciseness" (*samāsa*) means "compression" (*saṃkṣepa*); and compression has multiple things as its object. Therefore, even if that [compression] is absent, the technical designation *samāsa* will apply to two things that exist together. Regarding the examples "not each individually" (*na pratyekam*) and "he followed after" (*anuvyacalat*), here there is a compound with a finite verb (*tiṅanta*). In this case—

When the *nighāta* (elision of accent) has been applied by the rule "ṭhtiṅṅtiṅḥ" (Pāṇini 8.1.28), and the designation of a compound (*samāsa-saṃjñā*) is established, the property of having a final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) arises based upon that [designation].

5. *Avyayībhāvaḥ* | (2.1.5) In the case of "yathāvṛddham," since it is an *avyayībhāva*, by the rule "and an *avyayībhāva*" (2.4.18), it takes the neuter gender; then, by the rule "an *avyayībhāva* ending in a vowel [other than *a*] does not take the suffix *am*, except for the ablative" (2.4.83), this [suffix is excluded].

The rule applies. Furthermore, this is an etymological designation (*anvarthasaṃjñā*): "that which becomes an indeclinable (*avyaya*) while not being [originally] an indeclinable is an *avyayībhāva*. By stating "the predominance of the meaning of the first member," etc., he explains the purpose of the etymological designation. For in most *avyayībhāva* compounds, the first member is an indeclinable.

The subsequent word is non-indeclinable (*anyavyaya*); the compound as a whole is not [originally] indeclinable. If, by virtue of the preceding member, it acquires that property of the preceding member which is its indeclinability, then, being of a non-indeclinable nature, it becomes indeclinable. And thus, by virtue of the preceding member—
It acquires that property [of being indeclinable] if the first member is predominant, and not otherwise;
for it is logical that, by virtue of predominance, a thing should abandon its own property and undergo the acquisition of another property.
Thus, this technical name (*saṃjñā*) being etymological (*anvartha*), establishes the predominance of the meaning of the first member in the *avyayībhāva* compound.
This demonstrates that when the meaning of the first member of the compound is predominant, then an *avyayībhāva* compound occurs, and not otherwise; this is what is being stated.

6. An indeclinable (*avyaya*) [retains its original accent] when used in the senses of case-relation (*vibhakti*), proximity (*samīpa*), prosperity (*samṛddhi*), adversity (*vyṛddhi*), non-existence (*arthābhāva*), passing away (*atyaya*), "not at present" (*asamprati*), manifestation (*śabdaprādurbhāva*), sequence (*paścāt*), order (*yathānupūrvya*), simultaneity (*ayaugapadya*), similarity (*sādṛśya*), completion (*sampatti*), totality (*sākalya*), and limit (*anta*). (Pāṇini 2.1.4) For example:
*adhistri* ("concerning women"), as in the sentence *strīṣv adhikṛtya kathā pravartate*. This is governed by the rule *anabhihite* (2.3.1).

In the *Mahābhāṣya* (1.441), it is stated that "there is an exhaustive enumeration [of compoundable words] by means of nominal stems (*ṭh*), primary suffixes (*kṛt*), secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*).

Because of this enumeration, when the sense of the locative case is indicated by the word *adhi*, the seventh case ending occurs after the word *strī*. Consequently, only that which ends in *strī* is compounded; however, the word *adhi* itself remains in the nominative case.

The neuter gender is established by the rule *avyayībhāvaśca* (Pāṇini 2.4.18). The shortening of the vowel is by the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake* (Pāṇini 1.2.47). Here, the word *vibhakti* refers to a *kāraka*—so called because the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is divided (*vibhajyate*) by it. Since the locative case (*adhikaraṇa*) is intended here, he says:

Regarding the rule "an indeclinable used in the sense of the locative [is compounded]," as in the example *upakumbham*: since the word *upa* conveys the sense of proximity (*samīpa*), it introduces a distinction [from the object], whereby the genitive case arises after the word *kumbha*.
Thus, it is only that which ends in the genitive case that is compounded.

Regarding the term "samudra": when the abundance [of wealth] is predominant because it qualifies the Madras, then this compound is used; the meaning is that the prosperity exists by way of an excess of Madras. However, when the Madras themselves, being qualified by their abundance, attain the status of the primary referent, then—
By the rule *ṭhkugatiprādayaḥ* (2.2.18), this forms a *tatpuruṣa* compound: *sumadrāḥ*.
The meaning is "the Madras are prosperous.
Regarding *durgavādikam*, the meaning is that there is a loss of prosperity for the cows and so forth. Now, [one might object]:...

This is already established by the very phrase "the non-existence of objects" (*arthābhāva*); for the non-existence of objects is indeed the non-existence of things (*vastu*). What, then, is this distinction for which the loss of supernatural power (*ṛddhivigama*) is mentioned separately from the non-existence of objects? This is the distinction: for [in the case of the former], it is the non-existence of the subsequent term (*uttarapadārtha*).

The absence of a substance (*dravyābhāva*), for example: "free from flies" (*nirmakṣika*) expresses the absence of flies; however, in the case of "free from cattle and so forth" (*nirgavādika*), it does not express the absence of cows and so forth, but rather the disappearance of their prosperity (*ṛddhi*).

"Regarding the phrase 'the absence of an object' (*arthābhāva*): for what purpose is the inclusion of the word 'object' (*artha*)? It is so that a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) does not occur, as in the case of "he is not a Brāhmaṇa, [therefore he is] an abrāhmaṇa.
In this instance, the property (*dharma*) of being a Brāhmaṇa is negated, but the non-existence of the entity itself is not. Furthermore—"

Furthermore, let there be no [negation] in the case of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), such as "a cow is not a horse. In this case too, what is negated is the state of being another thing (*arthāntaratva*), and not the non-existence of the entity itself. "The cessation is the state of not having been" (*atyayo 'bhūtatvam*); "transgression" (*atikrama*) is a synonym for this very [cessation]. Transgression...

This refers to the absence of origination (*utpattyabhāva*), meaning the absence of destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*). However, the absence of an object (*arthābhāva*) is the non-existence of a thing at all times and in every location; it does not refer to the non-existence of something that has arisen later.
Thus, "passing away" (*atyaya*) is distinguished from the "absence of an object."
By the phrase "of [something] not currently being enjoyed" (*asampraty-upabhogasya*), he demonstrates the distinction based on the absence of the object.

For while the absence of an object in some cases refers to its non-existence in all three times, here, however, there is a negation specifically of that which is the present time of enjoyment; thus they differ, because this refers to the absence of the object at the present time.

Regarding the term *atitaistṛkam*: *Tisṛkā* is the name of a village. [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied according to either Pāṇini 4.3.53 (*tatra bhavaḥ*) or 4.3.74 (*tata āgataḥ*), resulting in *taisṛka*. Then, in the sense of "that which pertains to a time other than the time of enjoyment for one from Taisṛka," the form *atitaistṛkam* is derived.
