In the expression *anurūpam*, the prefix *anu* denotes suitability (*yogyatā*); the meaning is "that which bears a suitable form.
Regarding *pratyartham*: here the indeclinable *prati* expresses repetition (*vīpsā*), thus *pratyartham* means "with respect to each object" (*artham artham prati*).
Now, one might object: since this is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*), should it not be impossible for it to exist as a sentence?

This is not so; the designation *karmapravacanīya* is prescribed for the word *prati* when it has the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*), for the purpose that the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) may occur in its connection. And since its usage occurs only in a sentence and not elsewhere, even though it forms a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*), a sentence also remains possible, as in "according to one's ability" (*yathāśakti*).

Thus: "The word *yathā* [is used] when there is no overstepping of the meaning of a term. Here, "term" (*pada*) refers to a word possessing expressive power (*śakta-śabda*), and its "meaning" (*artha*) is that which is denoted by its very power (*śakti*). "No overstepping" (*anativṛti*) means not transgressing it. Thus, "he acts according to his capacity" (*yathāśakti karoti*) means he acts without overstepping what is possible. [The phrase] "in order of seniority" (*jyeṣṭhānupūrvyeṇa*) [is an example].
The meaning is "in the order of seniority.

Regarding the term *sacakram*: by the rule *avyayībhāve cākāle* (Pāṇini 6.3.81), the word *saha* undergoes the substitution *sa-* [for its initial *sa-*]. In the same way, the substitution *sa-* should also be stated for forms such as *sakikhi*.

Regarding the phrase "even when [similarity] is subordinate" (*guṇabhūte’pi*), etc.: if it were not stated that [the compound denotes] similarity (*sādṛśya*), then—since an *avyayībhāva* compound is one in which the meaning of the first member is predominant—it would only occur when similarity is the primary element by virtue of being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), as in the example "a woman who resembles Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇasya sadṛśī strī*). However, [it is required] even when similarity is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*).
But that would not be the case; rather, it comes from this statement: "sadṛśaḥ kikyā" (similar to a partridge).

By demonstrating the predominance of that which possesses similarity, the phrase "sadṛśaḥ kikyā" is stated in order to show that similarity itself is subordinate. For if the predominance of similarity were intended to be expressed, one would use the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) as in "sādṛśyam."
The designation would be appropriate as "sakikhi," with the short vowel as before.
Now, one might ask: since *sampatti* is simply prosperity (*samṛddhi*), why is it mentioned separately? To this he says:
"Prosperity is that which is appropriate," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of the Sabrahmavābhravas," it refers to what is appropriate for them.

The meaning is "the physical body" (ātmabhāva). Regarding the phrase "by stating an additional purpose": the consumption of grass is the additional purpose; by the sentence beginning with "nothing at all," he demonstrates this additional purpose. For he who consumes grass...
How can one abandon other things that are to be consumed?

Now, the word *anta* (end) occurs in the sense of completion (*parisamāpti*), and in that sense, totality (*sākalya*) is indeed present; so why is the expression "end" stated separately from "totality"? To this, he says: "End—[Kāśikā]."

Regarding the phrase "the word *anta*," and so forth: the limit (*anta*) is that completion which occurs in relation to the undertaking of a certain extent of study—namely, "this much is to be studied by me"—even though such a limit exists even when the study is incomplete; therefore, it is mentioned separately from completeness (*sākalya*).

Regarding the phrase "he has studied up to the Agni": the meaning is that he has studied as far as the *Agni* [section]. The text whose subject matter is the *Agni* is designated by the word "Agni" because it is for the sake of that [subject matter]. The *Agni* is the limit of the extent of study undertaken; it does not mean, however, that there is no study beyond that. That is so.
He says "this" and so forth to indicate that "not studied" refers merely to a lack of completeness; this is easily understood.

7. *yathā'sādṛśye* (Pāṇini 2.1.7). By this rule, [the author] explains that in the expression *yathāvṛddham*, the word *yathā* functions as distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), as in: "As Devadatta is, so is Yajñadatta"—meaning, similar to Devadatta.

The meaning is "Yajñadatta. Now, one might object: since this word *yathā* requires a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and [the word] *yajñadatta* is the object of comparison (*upameya*), a compound will not occur precisely because of a lack of syntactic independence (*asāmarthya*), according to the rule "that which is dependent is incapable [of compounding].
Therefore, what is the purpose of the prohibition [expressed by the words] "if there is no similarity" (*asādṛśye*)?

This is not so; for in this case, the word *yathā* is not the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), but rather the entire expression "just as Devadatta" (*yathā devadattaḥ*). Therefore, it is that [expression] which lacks the capacity [to function as a compound] with respect to the object of comparison (*upameya*), and not the word *yathā*.

8. *yāvad* is used in the sense of limitation (*avadhāraṇe*). (Pāṇini 2.1.8) [The commentary states: "Limitation (*pariccheda*) by this much. "By this much" (*iyatā*) means the state of being this much; that is, its measure (*parimāṇa*). Its limitation is its determination (*niścaya*). This is illustrated by examples such as "as many vessels as there are," and so forth.
He clarifies that very lack of delimitation by means of the passage beginning with "I do not ascertain," thereby demonstrating the absence of any such delimitation.

9. *sup* [is used] in the sense of "measure" (*mātrārthe*). (2.1.9) In the example *vṛkṣaṃ prati*, the word *prati* functions in the sense of a "characteristic mark" (*lakṣaṇe*), not in the sense of "measure. Now, what is the purpose of explicitly mentioning *sup* [in this rule], given that [the term *sup*] follows from the previous rule *subāmantrite* (2.1.2)?
Thinking that the term *sub* will carry over [from the previous rule], he says: "The mention of *sub*, etc.

For the mention of *sub* was previously connected with the indeclinable (*avyaya*); therefore, if that were to carry over, its [the indeclinable's] connection would also carry over. Consequently, this [mention of *sub*] is stated elsewhere for the purpose of excluding the indeclinable.
The mention of "sub" (secondary) is made.

10. *akṣa-śalākā-saṃkhyāḥ pariṇā* (Pāṇini 2.1.10). [The rule begins with] *kitava-vyavahāre* and so forth. But how is it that, even though "the practice of gamblers" (*kitava-vyavahāra*) is intended [as the scope], it is understood there? By its very nature, because the compound occurs there; for meanings are not extended [by this rule].

Because they are worldly (*laukikatvāt*). Regarding the passage beginning with "of that" (*tasya*): the connection is between "of that thrower" (*pātayituḥ*) and "his failure" (*vipātaḥ*). "Failure" (*vipātaḥ*) means defeat. Regarding "of this" (*etasya*): this refers back specifically to the dice and so forth. The singular number is used because non-difference is intended. Of this, not otherwise...

The word "fall" (pāta) is what is connected here. Regarding the phrase "otherwise" (anyathā): the intended meaning is a state of being otherwise in comparison to the manner of falling that was described in the case of victory. As for the statement, "But when the five are of one form, there is only victory," the sense is that the compound *pañcaparī* does not occur; for in the case of victory...
Since the arrangement of the dice and so forth depends on their relative positions, there must be a compound [of the results] when they are in a state other than that.
And no variation is possible among the five when they are of a single form. Therefore, victory occurs only when all five are of one form—either all face-up or all face-down. In this manner...
The justification for the rule "pareṇa catuṣpary... has been shown there. The word "pareṇa" means "in an exceeding degree.
Regarding the phrase "akṣādayas tṛtīyāntāḥ," and so forth: otherwise, this compound is intended in the *vṛtti*. In that case—
When the senses such as the eyes (*akṣa*) and so forth function otherwise [than their usual roles], they possess either the status of an agent (*kartṛ*) or an instrument (*karaṇa*);

therefore, since the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) must occur, only those words ending in that [third case] are compounded. The phrase "of what was mentioned previously" means "of the eyes and so forth. Why is this so? Because the eyes and so forth [in this context] end in the third case.

Because the dice and so forth were already mentioned previously, the singular number is used when non-difference is intended. This genitive case, used when a residual relation (*śeṣa*) is intended, denotes a connection in relation to the word "chosen" (*vṛta*);
thus, the word "chosen" must be supplied. As in the phrase "as that [is not]": as for the dice and so forth mentioned previously...
If that which was previously chosen for victory is likewise chosen now, then this compound occurs;

otherwise it does not. This compound serves to indicate a change from what was previously chosen, and since that can be effected by even a single [word], it is useless in view of the dual number and so forth; thus he says:

Regarding the rule "ṭhekatve'kṣaśalākayoḥ," the meaning is that [the suffix *ni* is applied] when *akṣa* and *śalākā* are in the singular number. Thus, this very meaning established by logic has been summarized in the verse.
Alternatively, the subsequent mention of the term "vibhāṣā" (optionally) applies here as well, according to the maxim of the lion's glance (*siṃhāvalokita-nyāya*).

[The word *pari*] is connected [to the rule]. And that is a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, it should be understood that this meaning is established solely by the explicit statement [of the rule]. [In the example] "akṣādayaḥ" (dice, etc.), what is the purpose? [It is to show: "This was not covered by the die in the same way as before in the winning throw. [In the example] "pariṇā," what is the purpose? It is so that there may not be a compound with a mere form ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*).
What is meant by "gambling transactions"? It refers to playing with two dice or many dice in a manner not previously agreed upon for the sake of winning.
11. *vibhāṣā* | (2.1.11) 12. *apaparibahirañcavaḥ pañcamyā* | (2.1.12) [Objection:
But it has not been prescribed by anyone that the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in connection with the word *bahiḥ*; how then [is this rule applicable]?

He states that there is a compound with that [word] ending in the ablative case, saying "in connection with the word *bahiḥ*," and so forth. This prescription of a compound of the word *bahiḥ* with a word ending in the fifth case (ablative) indicates that the fifth case indeed occurs in connection with the word *bahiḥ*. Now, by the force of its inclusion... *bahiḥ*...

Why is it not understood that, since the fifth case (*pañcamī*) cannot occur in connection with the word *śabda*, the compound is formed only with a nominal stem (*subanta*) that does not end in the fifth case? This cannot be so understood; for it would result in the rule for the mention of the fifth case being rendered useless. For instance, [in the rule] "ṭhapapari varjane" [Pāṇini 1.4.88].

Thus, when *apa* and *pari* have received the designation of *karmapravacanīya*, then in connection with them, by the rule "the fifth case [ending] occurs after *apa*, *āṅ*, and *pari*" (Pāṇini 2.3.10), the fifth case alone must be used, and not any other case ending.
This also applies when in connection with the word *añcu*. Furthermore, by the rule "after words other than *anya*, *arāt*,... (Pāṇini 2.3.29).
By such [rules], the compound would necessarily have to be formed with the ablative case alone; thus, the mention of the ablative (*pañcamī*) would be redundant.

But one might object: "The mention of the ablative must be for the purpose that when *pari* and *apa* function as *akarmapravacanīya*s, there should be no compound with a word ending in any case other than the ablative—such as in *parigataḥ* and *apagataḥ*?"

This is not so; because those two [words] are *para* (subsequent), they must form a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule "kugatiprādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.2.18). But is it not the case that, since this [new rule] is being introduced before that [rule] has even taken effect, it ought to be an exception (*bādhaka*) to it? This is not so; for [the word] is a *karmapravacanīya*.

As long as there is room for another [interpretation], it should be accepted here; for it will be stated that there is a prohibition of *karmapravacanīya*s in this context. Therefore, the rule for compounding the word *bahiḥ* is only with a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*), and not with any other; otherwise, the mention of the fifth case would be purposeless. Thus, it has been correctly stated—
"The fact that the ablative case occurs in connection with the word *bahiḥ* is itself the indicator (jñāpaka) of this [rule]."
13. *Āṅ* [is used] in the senses of limit (*maryādā*) and inclusion (*abhividhi*).

(2.1.13) Now, for what purpose is the mention of "limit and inclusion" (*maryādābhividhi*)? For the term "fifth case" (*pañcamī*) is understood from the previous rule, and the fifth case is prescribed specifically in connection with *āṅ* as a *karmapravacanīya*.

Regarding these two meanings alone, by the rule *ṭhāṅ maryādāvacane* (Pāṇini 1.4.89), the prefix *āṅ* receives the designation *karmapravacanīya*, and not elsewhere; therefore, even without the inclusion of the term "specification of a limit" (*maryādāvidhi*) in that [sūtra], the compound will occur only for those two meanings and not otherwise? This is true.
Nevertheless, for the sake of easy comprehension by those of dull intellect, there is the inclusion of both the limit-inclusive (*maryādā*) and the limit-exclusive (*abhividhi*) senses.

14. *lakṣaṇenābhipratī ābhimukhye* (2.1.14). [The words] *abhi* and *prati* [are compounded] with a word denoting a mark (*lakṣaṇa*) when indicating direction toward (*ābhimukhya*). Examples: *abhyagni*, *pratyagni*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: *agnim abhi*, *agniṃ prati*. Regarding the rule *karmapravacanīyayukte dvitīyā* (2.3.8), the designation *karmapravacanīya* applies to only one [of the two].

By the rule *ṭhabhirabhāge* (1.4.91); and for the other [word], by the rule *lakṣaṇetyambhūtākhyāna* (1.4.90), etc. Here, fire (*agni*) is the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*), by which the falling of the locusts (*śalabhapāta*) is indicated. Furthermore, in this context, the words *abhi* and *prati* denote facing toward (*abhimukhya*). Thus...
The meaning understood is that moths fall only toward the fire, neither from the side nor from behind; as in the expression,
"he has gone toward Srughna," [it implies] one who set out from Mathurā for Srughna but, due to a confusion of directions, [ends up elsewhere].

In the expression "he has returned to Srughna itself," Srughna is not the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). For that which one aims for when going is what constitutes the defining characteristic. But when, due to disorientation or the like, one returns to the very place from which one set out, how can that unperceived [destination] be the defining characteristic—namely, "Srughna"?

Since the designation *karman* (object) applies by the rule "and that which is not intended [by the agent], though connected in such a way" (Pāṇini 1.4.50), the second case ending occurs for the object. In the example "he went by way of the fire," the fire is indeed a *lakṣaṇa* (indicator) here because it faces [the direction of motion]; however, since the words *abhi* and *prati* are not present, [the term *lakṣaṇa*] is used in that sense.

A compound with those two words, *abhi* and *prati*, does not occur [in this sense]. For example: *abhyaṅkā gāvaḥ* ("cows marked recently") and *pratyaṅkā gāvaḥ* ("cows marked newly"). This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those cows which have a new (*abhinava*) or fresh (*pratinava*) mark (*aṅka*). Here, the word *abhi* functions in the sense of "new," and the word *prati* in the sense of "fresh. In this context, *aṅka* refers to...

The characteristic of "cows" exists, but there is no sense of "facing toward" (ābhimukhya). Now, one might argue that because it is subsequent [in the sequence of rules], it must be a *bahuvrīhi* compound, and therefore it will act as a sublater [of the *tatpuruṣa*]; so what is the use of including the term "facing toward"? It is not so; for if the term "facing toward" were not included, [the *bahuvrīhi*] would apply to all cases (*aśeṣatvāt*).

How can there be a *bahuvrīhi* compound here? Or rather, this indicates that the *bahuvrīhi* is superseded by the *avyayībhāva*. By this, the form *dvimuni vyākaraṇam* ("the two sages [Pāṇini and Kātyāyana] regarding grammar") is established; otherwise, since the *avyayībhāva* would have fulfilled its purpose in its own constituent meaning, it would not apply to *dvimuni*.
In this case, regarding the compound "vyākaraṇa," the bahuvrīhi would be sublated by the subsequent [rule] because it pertains to a different referent (anyapadārtha).

15. *anuryatsamayā* | (1.4.15) This [compound] *yatsamayā* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "that which is near to which. Now, one might object: when used in conjunction with the word *samayā*, [the rule] "in the vicinity of, all around, near to, or on the surface of" (Vārttika 119) [prescribes the indeclinable *samayā*].

Since there is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of this kind, the accusative case ought to be used; therefore, even a genitive case is not impossible, so how much less could there be a compound of it? Even if, somehow, a genitive were possible, nevertheless, because the word *samaya* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), by the rule "pūraṇaguṇa... (Pāṇini 2.2.11), [the compound would be prohibited].

Should there not be a prohibition of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*)? This is not a fault; because of the inclusion of the word "connection" (*yoga*), it is understood here that the second case ending occurs when there is a connection with the meaning of the word *samaya*. And that meaning is taken in its primary sense alone, not in a secondary sense. Furthermore, that primary meaning is "proximity. And in this case...

The word *samayā* does not have its primary meaning; rather, it has a secondary (gauṇa) meaning. It is the sun itself that is expressed by the word *samayā*; therefore, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) alone is logical as a residual indication (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇā*).
For this very reason, because it denotes a substance (*dravya*), it lacks the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*); consequently, [the rule] "pūraṇaguṇa" (Pāṇini 2.2.11) [applies].

The prohibition is not tenable [in the case of the expression] "anuryatsamayā. By this, he shows that the word *samayā* functions in the sense of the word *anu*. Now, one might ask: since the meaning of the word *samayā* is "proximity," how can the word *anu* be expressed by the word *samayā*? To this, he says: "that which expresses proximity."
By this, he explains that because the word *anu* expresses the same meaning as the word *samayā*,
it is designated by the term *samayā* through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). For indeed, by way of metaphor,
a designation is applied to that which expresses its meaning, just as one says "the poem of the abduction of Sītā" (*sītāharaṇaṃ kāvyam*).
By the word "tena" (by that), that [word] whose suffix "anu" expresses the sense of "samaya" (convention) is referred to. Now, one might object:

since that [suffix] denotes a meaning, how can there be a compound with it? Because an operation cannot apply to a meaning, the operation is understood to apply to the word expressing that meaning; and thus, for the word "tena," [the operation applies] to that which expresses its meaning.

In this context, the meaning is understood as "by means of the word. In the expression "anuvanam," there is a compound with that word "vana" which ends in the genitive case. Since it expresses the relationship between the vicinity and that which is proximate—namely, "near the forest"—the genitive case alone is appropriate.
"In *vanaṃ samayā*," the second case ending is applied to the word *vana* according to the previously mentioned supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*).

In "the lightning flashes *vṛkṣamanu*," the second case ending is used by virtue of the definition of a term denoting a mark (*kartravacanīya*). Here, the word *anu* functions as a mark (*lakṣaṇa*), not in the sense of proximity (*sāmīpya*).

16. *yasya cāyāmaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.16). Here too, because it figuratively denotes length (*āyāma*), the word *anu* itself is expressed by the term "length. For example: *anugaṅgaṃ vārāṇasī* ("Vārāṇasī extends along the Gaṅgā"). Although both the Gaṅgā and Vārāṇasī possess length, [it is the former that is so designated].

Nevertheless, because the Gaṅgā is well-known for its length, it is the Gaṅgā alone that serves as the defining characteristic here, not Vārāṇasī. For a defining characteristic must be something well-known, not something unknown.
Therefore, in this case, the compound is formed with the Gaṅgā, and not with Vārāṇasī. [The same applies] by way of the Yamunā.

"It is observed that there is length (*āyāma*) [of the Yamunā]," it should be understood that this is by means of the Yamunā itself acting as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). For a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) expressing length is compounded with another word ending in a case-suffix that serves as its defining characteristic;
and in the case of "Yamunā," the word expressing length refers to the Yamunā, not to the length of the Yamunā. It is not [the latter].
There is another dimension to this [dimension of Mathurā]; therefore, in the sense of "by means of," this third case ending [in *yamunāyāmena*] is used.

The meaning to be understood is that the dimension of Mathurā is characterized by the Yamunā—either as possessing that [length], or through the Yamunā acting as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), or having attained the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*)—by means of the Yamunā’s length.

17. *tiṣṭhadguprabhṛtīni ca* (Pāṇini 2.1.17). Since the words beginning with *tiṣṭhadgu* have already been established as correct through their inclusion in the list of gaṇas (*gaṇapāṭha*), their mention here in this section is for the purpose of assigning them the technical designation of *avyayībhāva*; it is not, however, for the purpose of forming a compound with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). Therefore...

Thus he says: "The groups themselves are treated as *nipātana*s. The very recitation of such forms is their *nipātana*. By stating, "They receive the designation of *avyayībhāva*," he indicates that only the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is being prescribed, and not that these form a compound with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*).

*tiṣṭhadgu*, *vahadgu*: the substitution of *śatṛ* for the first member of the compound is prescribed by rule. By the rule *gostriyor upasarjanasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.48), the short vowel [of the feminine suffix] is applied. That time in which cows stand is *tiṣṭhadgu*; that time in which cows carry [milk] is *vahadgu*.

The word *kālaḥ* [is the subject]. The letter *ṭh* (the *ṭ* in *ṭhakāraḥ*) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇārtha*). If that were not present, there would be a compound with the word *parama* according to the rule *sanmahatparamottamotkṛṣṭāḥ pūjyamānaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.61), as in the example *paramatiṣṭhadgu*.
However, when that [ṭ] has the sense of restriction, [the compound is formed as follows].

The rule *tiṣṭhadguprabhṛtīni* remains applicable to such cases as well. For example, in *āyatīgavam*, there is an absence of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) and the application of the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*). [That is: the time in which cows are coming in is *āyatīgavam*. Similarly, in *khaleyavam* and *khalebusam*, there is the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending.

The suffix *śānac* is irregularly applied (nipātyate) [to form] *lūyamānayava-* ("where barley is being reaped"). The same applies to *pūyamānayava-* ("where barley is being winnowed"). These are "words denoting time" (*kālaśabda*), beginning with *tiṣṭhadgu* and ending with *saṃskriyamāṇabusa*.

Regarding the expressions *samabhūmi* and *samapadāti*: when the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapada*) is predominant, such as "levelness of the ground" (*samatvaṃ bhūmeḥ*) or "levelness of the pedestrian" (*samatvaṃ padāteḥ*), it is an *avyayībhāva* compound. However, when there is an intention to express the predominance of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), such as "a level pedestrian" (*samapadātiḥ*) or "level ground" (*samabhūmiḥ*), it becomes a *tatpuruṣa* compound, specifically a *viśeṣaṇasamāsa*. Others [hold this view].
They read the word *sama* with a final *m*: "level ground" (*samambhūmi*), "equal gift" (*samampadāti*).

[Examples include] "very level" (*suṣamam*), "uneven" (*viṣamam*), "badly level" (*duḥṣamam*), and "other than level" (*aparasamam*). Regarding the word *sama*: these, beginning with *suṣama*, are compounds in which the meaning of the prior member is predominant.
In this context, a sentence such as "the excellence belongs to the year" (samasya) and so forth is to be understood.

However, when the meaning of the final member is predominant, a *prādi*-compound or a *viśeṣaṇa*-compound should be formed as appropriate. Regarding the term "āyatīsamam": the word *samā* denotes a year; thus, it forms a compound with that.

*Āyatīsama* means equal to the future. Likewise, *pāpasama* means equal to evil, and *puṇyasama* means equal to merit. Others, however, explain it as a third-case compound: "equal to the future" (*āyatyā samaṃ āyatīsamam*); and so it is in other cases as well. *Prāhṇa* means that which has advanced into the day. This too—
In these cases, the meaning of the first member is predominant. However, when the meaning of the second member is predominant, it remains a *tatpuruṣa* compound—for example:

*prāhṇekalyāṇanāmānāvetau tiṣyapunarvasū* ("these two, Tiṣya and Punarvasu, whose names are auspicious in the forenoon"). Likewise: *prathama*, *pradakṣiṇa*, *pramṛga*, *aparadakṣiṇa*, *samprati*, and *asamprati*.

By the rule *ṭhic karmavyatīhāre* (Pāṇini 5.4.127), the purpose of the suffix *ic* [added to the word *daṇḍa*] when it forms an avyayībhāva compound is the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) and its neuter gender. Thus, from "having struck stick against stick" (*daṇḍaś ca daṇḍaś ca prahṛtya*), this battle is called *daṇḍādaṇḍi*. The compound is formed by the rule *titra tenedam iti sarūpe* (Pāṇini 2.2.27).

The suffix *ic* is applied as a compound-ending by the rule *ṭhic karmavyatīhāre* (5.4.127); the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate* (6.3.137), resulting in the form *daṇḍādaṇḍi*.

18. *pāre madhye ṣaṣṭhyā vā*. (2.1.18) Now, one might object: "But isn't the *mahāvibhāṣā* already under discussion? By that alone the option will be established; so what is the purpose of including the word *vā*? To this he says: "Because of the mention of *vā*," and so forth. The meaning has already been explained. If, then...

Because of the mention of the word "vā" (or), a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) occurs optionally; as to what is accomplished by the "great option" (*mahāvibhāṣā*), he says: "By the great option," and so forth.

19. *Saṃkhyā vaṃśyena* (Pāṇini 2.1.19). Regarding the phrase *ekalakṣaṇa*: it means having a single nature (*ekasvabhāva*). A lineage (*santāna*) is a continuous series (*prabandha*). Because the members of the series (*santānin*) possess a single characteristic, the lineage itself also possesses a single characteristic. Therefore...
"Characterized by learning alone" refers to the lineage of grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇavaṃśa*) and the lineage of teachers (*upādhyāyavaṃśa*).

"By birth" refers to the Brahmin lineage (*brāhmaṇavaṃśa*) and the Kṣatriya lineage (*kṣatriyavaṃśa*). Regarding the term *vaṃśya*, it means "one belonging to that lineage"; the suffix *-ya* is applied here because it belongs to the *dig-ādi* group. "The two sages" refers to Pāṇini and Kātyāyana. "Of grammar" (*vyākaraṇasya*).

The genitive case [in "trimunivyākaraṇasya"] indicates a relationship. [The phrase] "of the grammar of the three sages" refers to the first two [sages] and the author of the Bhāṣya as the third. [The word] "by means of knowledge" means by means of that which is called grammar. [The word] "of those who possess it" refers to Pāṇini and the others. [The expression] "the intention not to express a distinction" refers to those two sages.

When one intends to express the non-difference between those two— the person and the science— in order to describe their connection with knowledge in an eminent sense, such that they are both designated as "grammar," then grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) occurs,
as in the expression: "Grammar is the two Munis."

20. *nadībhiśca* (2.1.20). By the word *ca* ("and"), the term *saṃkhyā* ("numeral") is drawn over [from the previous rule]. Because of the use of the plural number (*bahuvacana*), this refers to the meaning [of "river"], not to the specific form itself, nor to the technical name (*saṃjñā*). Therefore, [the compound is formed] with all words denoting rivers.

He states that the compound is understood [to be formed] by saying "with words denoting rivers," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "and this is desired in the sense of a collective (samāhāra)," the word *ca* (and) is used for emphasis—meaning it is intended only in the sense of a collective and not elsewhere.
If this is so, should the mention of "collective" (*samāhāra*) be made? It need not be made, because of the following:
The compound of *akṣa* and so forth occurs only in the sense of a gambling transaction (*kitavavyavahāra*).

For that very reason, this [compound] also will be a collective (*samāhāra*) compound—such as *saptagaṅgam*, meaning "seven Gaṅgās brought together. As before, there is shortening of the vowel. However, it does not occur when another word-meaning (*anyapadārtha*) is intended.
The region is called *Dvīrāvatīka*. [The suffix] *ṭhak* is applied in the sense of "consisting of five" (*pañcanavam*) and "consisting of seven Godāvarīs" (*saptagodāvaram*).
It is traditionally taught that the suffix *ac* is applied to land preceded by the names Kṛṣṇa, Udaka, and Pāṇḍu, provided that the word for the river Godāvarī follows a numeral.
By this statement, *ac* is the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*).

21. And [the suffix *cha* is applied] when it denotes another word-meaning (*anyapadārtha*) and forms a name (*saṃjñā*). (Pāṇini 2.1.21) For example: *kṛṣṇaveṇṇā*. This is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*), meaning "that which is both black and the Veṇṇā river.
*śīghragaṅgaḥ*. This is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*).

22. *tatpuruṣaḥ* | (2.1.22) Regarding the example "kaṣṭaśritaḥ": when the designation *tatpuruṣa* applies, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member [of the compound] is established by the rule "In a *tatpuruṣa*, [the word] having the sense of 'equal'... (6.2.2), and so forth. Now...

He asks: "For what purpose is this great designation (*saṃjñā*) prescribed? and replies: "And this is the designation of the former teachers. He asks: "For what purpose is its acceptance? and replies: "Its acceptance," and so forth. "Upādhi" means a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). He then asks: "What, moreover, is that specific qualifier belonging to them? and replies:
"A *tatpuruṣa* compound is one in which the meaning of the final member is predominant."

Regarding the statement "the purpose [of this rule] is for the application of compound-final suffixes" (*samāsāntāḥ prayojanam*), while the term *tatpuruṣa* is being carried over from the previous rule *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ saṃkhyāvyayādeḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.86), [the word *dvigu* is also included].

By the rules "rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac" (Pāṇini 5.4.91) and "gorataddhitaluki" (5.4.92), this suffix should apply even to a *dvigu* compound; for example, *pañcarājī*. This is a compound formed by the rule "taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca" (2.1.51), meaning "the collection of five kings."

The designation *dvigu* is applied by the rule "A compound preceded by a numeral is a *dvigu*" (Pāṇini 2.1.52). The suffix *ṭac* is added, and there is elision of the final vowel by the rule "There is elision of the *ṭi* [portion] before a *taddhita* suffix" (6.4.144). The feminine gender is indicated by the rule "A *dvigu* compound whose final member ends in the letter *ṭhakāra* is used in the feminine" (Vārttika 156), and the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "After a *dvigu* [ending in a consonant]" (4.1.21). Thus: *dvyahaḥ*.

In the case of *tryahaḥ*, there is elision of the suffix by the rule *ahnaṣṭakhoreva* (Pāṇini 6.4.145), and it takes the masculine gender by the rule *rātrahnāhāḥ puṃsi* (Pāṇini 2.4.29). In the case of *pañcagavam*, it takes the neuter gender by the rule *sa napuṃsakam* (Pāṇini 2.4.17);
thus, despite ending in the vowel *a*, it does not take the feminine gender.
This is because of the statement: "The prohibition [of the suffix] must be stated for *pātra* and so forth" (Vārttika 1.5.9).
24. *dvitīyā śritātītapatitagatyāstaprāptāpannaiḥ* (2.1.24).

Regarding the phrase "in the case of *śrita* and so forth": the meaning is that when words such as *śrita* and others are presented as the causes for forming a compound, an extension (*upasaṃkhyānam*)—that is, a formal statement—must be made to include compounds of [words] such as *gami* and *gāmi*.

The compound should also be established by these [rules]. In this regard, the following is the demonstration: the rule "after the second case" (*dvitīyā*) is divided into separate *yoga*s (rules); by this, a compound is formed even with words such as *gami* and *gāmi*. Nor is the mention of *śrita* and so forth redundant in this way.

This is for the purpose of making known that the preceding subject does not encompass all objects. The word "ādi" (and so forth) denotes a class or type. Although the goal would have been achieved by employing either the word *gami* or *gāmi*, both are employed so that it may apply to the *uṇādi* suffixes as well as others; otherwise, if...

If only the term *gami* were used, then because the word "beginning with" (*ādi*) denotes a class or type, there would be a reference only to those *uṇādi* suffixes that are of the same type as *gami*. Alternatively, if only the term *gāmi* were used, then there would be a reference only to those *uṇādi* suffixes that are of the same type as *gāmi*. Therefore, both [terms] are employed.

The inclusion [of the word *bhaviṣyati*] must be made. In the example "grāmaṃ gamī" ("one who will go to the village"), the suffix *ini* is applied by the rule "gamerini" (Daiva 6.57). And that suffix occurs in the future tense, according to the statement "bhaviṣyati gamyādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.3.3). In the case of "grāmaṃ gamī," [the suffix *ini* is applied] by the rule "āvaśyakādhamarṇyayoḥ" (Pāṇini 3.3.170).

Thus, the suffix *ṇini* is necessarily applied here. By the rule *ṭhakenorbhaviṣyadādhamarṇyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.70), the genitive case is prohibited. In the example "one who desires to eat rice" (*odanaṃ bubhukṣuḥ*), the suffix *u* is added to the root *bhuj* following its desiderative form (*san*) by the rule *sanāśaṃsabhikṣa uḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.168). [The world is] hard...

By the rule beginning with *pūraṇaguṇasuhitārthasadavyayatavyasamānādhikaraṇena* (Pāṇini 2.2.11), the genitive case is prohibited. In examples such as *kaṣṭaṃ śritaḥ*, the prohibition of the genitive is likewise by this very rule.
[Furthermore,] *svayaṃ ktena* (Pāṇini 2.1.25).
"An association with a second [word] is not possible for that," because a second referent is impossible. The word *iti* indicates a reason (*hetau*).
Since an association with a second [word] is untenable for it, therefore the mention of the second [word] is carried over for the sake of what follows, and not [for its own sake].
This is for that purpose: "the feet washed by oneself" (*svayaṃdhautau pādau*). [The root] *dhāv* [is used] in the sense of "motion" and "cleansing" (*dhā.pā.* 601).

Because this [root] is marked with an indicatory *u* (*udit*), the augment *iṭ* is optional. By the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 7.2.15), there is a prohibition of *iṭ*. Then, by the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca* (6.4.19), *ūṭh* is substituted [for the *v* of *dhau*].

There is *vṛddhi* [substitution] by the rule "ṭhetyedhatyūṭhasu" (Pāṇini 6.1.89). Regarding the term "svayaṃvilīnākhyam": the root *līṅ* is used in the sense of "adhering" (*śleṣaṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 1139). Because it is marked with the *o* indicatory letter (*odit*) according to the rule "svādaya oditaḥ" (Kāśikā 8.2.45), the substitution of *n* for *t* occurs by the rule "oditaśca" (8.2.45). In the case of the mention of a *kṛt* [suffix]...

"Even that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka* is included" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 126); thus, a compound is formed even when preceded by a *gati*. But what is the specific advantage here when this compound occurs, since this form is established even without it? To this he says: "unity of word," and so forth.

26. *khaṭvā* in the sense of reproach (*kṣepe*). (Pāṇini 2.1.26). Regarding the phrase "and that" (*sa ca*) and so forth: by the use of the particle *eva*, he excludes the possibility that the reproach constitutes the meaning of the entire sentence. This might be argued: "Even if the reproach is the meaning of the sentence, the word *khaṭvā* will still function as a sentence. To this, he says: [the following].
Regarding the phrase "For indeed not," and so forth: by means of a sentence, only the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*) is understood, but not delay (*kṣepa*).
Regarding the phrase "And the mounting of the couch," and so forth: a contrary path is a "wrong path" (*vimārga*);
setting out by that means "going. Having studied and performed the ritual bath (*snāna*), one who has been permitted by the teacher...

The bed is to be ascended; for that which is an improper ascent of the bed is a departure onto a wrong path, and not merely the act of ascending the bed itself. And here, in expressions such as "one who has ascended the bed" (*khaṭvārūḍha*), the act of ascending the bed should be understood as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for departing onto a wrong path. But what, then, is the reason for this?

He says, "It is understood," and so forth, beginning with "all indeed. Regarding the word *ārūḍha*, it is the form derived from the root *ruh* preceded by the prefix *ā*, with the suffix *kta* applied, after which the changes of *ḍha*-ness, *dha*-ness, *ṣṭu*-ness, elision of *ḍh*, and lengthening have been performed. The word *jālma* means one who acts improperly.

27. Regarding "sāmi" (Pāṇini 2.1.27), [the commentary states]: "Because it denotes a non-substance (asattva). For the power of action (karma-śakti) indeed has substance (dravya) as its substratum. Therefore, only that which denotes a substance can be connected with the accusative case-ending, not that which denotes a non-substance.

28. *Kālāḥ* | (2.1.28) [The word] *carācaraḥ* is used for the purpose of indicating non-permanent conjunction (*anatyanta-saṃyoga*). They are called *carācaraḥ* because they move (*caranti*) and wander; the meaning is that they are unstable (*anavasthita*). [This is derived by the rule: *caricalipativadīnam acyākcābhyāsasya*.
(vā. 658) Thus, from the root *car* with the suffix *ac* (pacādyac), there is reduplication of the root, the augment *ak* for the reduplicated syllable, and [the formation of *cāra*].

"Sometimes they go by day" refers to the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*); "sometimes by night" refers to the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*). By this, he clarifies that very instability of both day and night.
By those *muhūrtas*, he expresses a non-permanent conjunction (*anatyanta-saṃyoga*), as in the expression "passed three days" (*tryaharatṛtāḥ*).
In this case, the *n* of *ahan* is replaced by *r* according to Pāṇini 8.2.69, *ro'supi*. In the expression "arrived after a day" (*ahaḥ saṃkrāntāḥ*), the root *kramu* (meaning "to step") is used;
here, there is a prohibition of the *iṭ* augment that would otherwise apply to roots ending in a consonant preceded by a long vowel.

The lengthening [of the vowel] is by the rule *ṭhanunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.15). Regarding the form *māsapramitaḥ*: the root *māṅ* means "to measure" (Dhātupāṭha 1088); the suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied in the sense of the agent by the rule *ādikarmaṇi kartari ca* (3.4.71). The substitution of *it* is by the rule *dyatisyati* (7.4.40), etc. [Thus, it means] "one who has begun to measure a month."

Thus, by showing the conjunction of the moon with the first day (pratipad) as a single part of the month, he expresses the absolute connection (atyantasamyoga) of the month with it. For absolute connection is the pervasion of the entire duration of time by its own constituent; and here, the first day and the moon do not pervade the month.
Regarding the statement "there is conjunction," here there is no absolute conjunction. (Pāṇini 2.1.29) [The sūtra] "atyantasaṃyoge ca" means "and in the case of absolute conjunction.
"Kṛtsnasaṃyogaḥ" means the conjunction of the whole; it is the conjunction of the entire [object]. Of the whole...

The connection (*saṃyoga*) of time—such as a *muhūrta* and so forth—with its own related pleasure and so on is an absolute connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*). To clarify this very point, he says: "of time," and so forth; [as in the example] "pleasure for a *muhūrta*. This is based on the rule: *kālādhvanoratyantasaṃyoge* (Pāṇini 2.3.5).
Thus ends the second [type]. Here, there is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of a *muhūrta*—a portion of time—by its own related pleasure (*sukha*).
30. The third [type] is with a quality-word (*guṇavacana*) whose meaning is produced by that [time] (Pāṇini 2.1.30).

Regarding the term "tatkṛta" (produced by that): it is not compounded with the word "artha" (meaning), and it is without a case-ending (*avibhakti*). This is because the third-case ending has been elided according to *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). Furthermore, this is a qualifier in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the term "guṇavacanena" (by a word expressing a quality). For this very reason, [the question is asked] "of what kind? (*kīdṛśena*).

Being questioned, he replied: "By that which was done" (*tatkṛtena*). By using the pronoun *tat* (that) to refer back to the previously mentioned word ending in the third case, he demonstrates that it is [the quality] ending in the third case that is expressed as "by that which was done. Since it is not possible for a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*) to function as the instrument (*karaṇa*) when it ends in the third case, [the meaning is established] by implication (*sāmarthyāt*).

Since it is understood that [the word] is used in the sense of "that which is done for the sake of that," he says: "It means 'done for the sake of the meaning of that which ends in the third case. Furthermore, this should be understood as a qualification of the *guṇavacana* (quality-expressing word) by way of its meaning—that is, the meaning of the *guṇavacana* is that which is done for the sake of the meaning of the word ending in the third case. That [meaning] is also expressed in that manner. This is what has been stated.

It occurs [in the sense of] "by means of the meaning expressed by that which ends in the third case," namely, by means of the meaning of a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*). For it is indeed the meaning that is produced by that which ends in the third case, and not the word *guṇavacana* itself. A *guṇavacana* is that which has spoken of a quality (*guṇam uktavān*); here, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the agent according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.13). Now...

Or [the suffix *vati*] is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). That which expresses a quality (*guṇa*) by means of this [suffix] is called "quality-expressive" (*guṇavacana*). And that which, having first denoted a quality, subsequently denotes the substance (*dravya*) possessing that quality, is "quality-expressive.

If it were stated simply as "by means of a quality" (*guṇena*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of applying it to cases such as "dexterity by means of ghee" (*ghṛtena pāṭavam*).

Therefore, the term "word" (vacana) is included in the rule to exclude that [undesired application]. When that term is present, a compound occurs only with that which denotes a substance possessing that quality after first denoting the quality itself, but not with that which denotes the quality alone. Furthermore, words such as *pāṭava* (dexterity) and so forth do not, after first denoting a quality, subsequently...

They do not reside in the substance (*dravya*) possessing those qualities, but rather in the quality (*guṇa*) itself. Because of the inclusion of the term "word" (*vacana*), there is no compound with them; for example, *śaṅkulākhaṇḍaḥ* ("broken by a wooden wedge") and *girikāṇaḥ* ("blind from birth").
Here, the words *khaṇḍa* and *kāṇa* refer to the quality that has taken on the form of an action, namely breaking and closing [the eyes].

Having first applied [to the quality], they subsequently apply to the substance possessing that quality—either through the elision of the possessive suffix (*matup*) or by metaphorical treatment as non-different from it—and thus they become "expressive of qualities" (*guṇavacana*). Regarding the example "the meaning is grain": this word *artha* is caused by that [grain];
for instance, he was made fat by means of cows. However, the word "fat" (*vapāvat*) itself [is not used here].
Because [the word] *guṇamukta* means "one who has abandoned qualities," it is not a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*); therefore, a compound with it does not occur.

31. *pūrva-sadṛśa-sama-ūna-artha-kalaha-nipuṇa-miśra-ślakṣṇaiḥ* (2.1.31). A compound is formed with the words *sama* and *sadṛśa* when joined with these [other terms]. When they are used in conjunction with those [words], the rule *tulyārtheratulopamābhyām* (2.3.72) prescribes the third case (*tṛtīyā*).

But how is a third-case compound (*tṛtīyāsamāsa*) justified with *pūrva* and the others? For no third case ending has been prescribed by any rule in connection with them. To this he says: "Precisely for this reason," and so forth. This is easy to understand. [The Vārttika] states: "An addition should be made for *avara* among *pūrva* and the others. Regarding *pūrva* and the others...

The meaning is that when [words] are introduced as causes for forming compounds, an addition (*upasaṃkhyānam*)—that is, an explanation—must be made regarding the word *avara*. The meaning is that a third-case compound (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*) is also established by means of the word *avara*.
In this regard, the following is the explanation: the term *bahulam* ("variously") is employed in the subsequent rule.
Therefore, a compound is also formed with the word *avara*.

32. *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32). In the example *bhikṣābhir uṣitaḥ*, the third case ending is prescribed by [the rule] *hetu* (2.3.23). There is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the root *vas* by the sūtra beginning with *vaci-ādi* (6.1.15), and [the substitution of *u* for *o*] by the rule *śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca*.

By the rule (8.3.60), there is the substitution of *ṣ*; by the rule (7.2.52), there is the augment *iṭ*. [The example is: "He has reaped grain with a sickle" (*dātreṇa dhānyaṃ lūnavān*). By the rule (8.2.44), there is the substitution of *ṇ* for the final letter of the *niṣṭhā* suffix.

[The example is: "One who steals on foot" (*pādahārakaḥ*). [The analysis is: "That which is carried by means of the feet" (*pādābhyāṃ hriyate*) is *pādāhārakaḥ*. [The word] "by means of the feet" (*pādābhyām*)...

The fifth case or the fourth case [is used]. In the word *hāraka*, the suffix *ṇvul* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) according to Pāṇini 3.3.113: *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. In the expression *galecopakaḥ*, [it means] "one who is pressed upon the neck. From the root *cup* (DhP 403), meaning "to move slowly," the suffix *ṇvul* is applied as before. [This occurs] in a *tatpuruṣa* compound with a *kṛt* suffix.
The suffix *ul* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.2.127] *bahulam*.

33. *kṛtyair adhikārthavacane* (2.1.33). [The commentary states: "*stutinindāprayuktam*" (employed for praise or blame). That which is employed or set in motion by praise or blame is "employed for praise or blame. The meaning is: that which is uttered for that purpose.

Regarding the phrase "the expression of a superimposed object" (*adhyāropitārthavacana*): it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the expression (*vacana*) of an object (*artha*) that has been superimposed (*adhyāropita*), which is non-existent (*asat*) yet mentally projected (*buddhyā samāropita*). As for the rule *kartṛkaraṇayoḥ*, since the grammatical operation cannot apply to the [abstract] meaning itself, it is understood to apply to the nominal suffix (*subanta*) that denotes that meaning.

Regarding the term *kākapeyā*: from the root *pā* "to drink" (DhP 925), the suffix *yat* is applied by Pāṇini 3.1.97 (*aco yat*), and the vowel substitution *ī* occurs by 6.4.65 (*īdyati*). Here, the manifestation of the river's being full of water is a praise of the river; however, the meaning "drinkable by crows" is superimposed—meaning it is so full of water that it is [figuratively] drinkable even by crows.
"A river can be drunk even by crows standing on its bank; a well is for dogs to lick.

In the rule *ṛhalorṇyat* (Pāṇini 3.1.124), the mention of the well's proximity to water is a praise of the well. Furthermore, the quality of being "for dogs to lick" is here superimposed as a meaning—meaning that it is indeed so close to water.

"A well that is licked even by dogs; 'grass that is cut by tears'—here, the exaggeration of the excellence of Māra is a praise of the grasses. Furthermore, the meaning superimposed here is the state of being cut by tears—that is to say, the grasses are so exceedingly soft."

"Even by its steam it is possible to cut; 'the rice is to be gathered with thorns. Here too, the praise of the rice consists in manifesting its extreme clarity and manifesting its state of being thoroughly softened. Furthermore, the quality of "being gathered with thorns" is an attribute superimposed here—thus [is the meaning].

The excellence of the clarity and softness of rice-gruel is such that it can be perceived even by means of a thorn. Thus far, these are the examples regarding statements of further meaning employed for praise.
Statements of further meaning employed for censure should be understood as being exactly the same. For instance:
In the phrase "the river is drinkable by crows," the manifestation of having little water is a disparagement of the river.

However, the meaning superimposed here is precisely that which was mentioned before: the state of being "drinkable by crows. In the same way, in cases such as "lickable by dogs" and so forth, the meaning superimposed should be understood as exactly what was stated previously—that is, the river is indeed so small [in its water].
The phrase "that which can even be drunk by crows" means that the well is to be licked by dogs;

here too, the pointing out of the impurity of the water is merely a form of censure. Likewise, the statement "the rice is so meager that it is gathered up even by thorns" expresses this. But surely, because of the word *bahula* ("abundant"), there is also an additional meaning?
The compound is already established by the preceding rule; why then is this stated? He says: "of the preceding," and so forth.
Those rules are well-comprehended for which there is an elaboration (prapañca). This elaboration of the preceding [rule] is made so that it may be well-comprehended.

34. "The condiment by means of the rice," as in the expression "rice with curd" (*dadhyodana*). Now, it may be argued that the relationship between grammatical factors (*kāraka*) is produced by action (*kriyā*), and not inherently;
yet, since no action whatsoever is heard here in the *vṛtti* compound, there is an absence of semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*). This being the case—

And there would be an absence of compounding when there is semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*). If it is argued that a compound occurs even in the absence of semantic capacity by virtue of the power of the grammatical rule (*vacana-sāmarthya*), then it would also apply in cases such as "let curd be drunk" (*āsyatāṃ dadhnā*) and "let rice be eaten by Devadatta" (*odano bhujyatāṃ devadatenā*); therefore, he says: "In the formation [of the compound]," and so forth. It is not [the case].

In the absence of the act of pouring, it is not possible for there to be that which is refined and that which refines; yet here both exist. Therefore, precisely because of their existence, the action is understood as being included within the compound.
And since the relationship between the food and the condiment is mediated by that [action], the semantic competency (sāmarthya) indeed exists.

35. *bhakṣyeṇa miśrīkaraṇam* (Pāṇini 2.1.35). Regarding the term *miśrīkaraṇam*: that by which something unmixed (*amiśra*) is made mixed (*miśra*) is called *miśrīkaraṇam*. "Edible food that is distinct and solid is *bhakṣya*"—for it is in this very sense that the word *bhakṣya* is conventionally established.

36. The fourth [type of *taddhita* compound] is formed with words meaning "for the sake of that" (*tadartha*), "beneficial" (*artha*), "strength" (*bala*), "good for" (*hita*), "pleasurable" (*sukha*), and "protected" (*rakṣita*).

(Pāṇini 2.1.36) Regarding the rule beginning with "for the sake of that" (*tadarthena*): if the compound were formed merely on the basis of being "for the sake of that," then the mention of *bali* and *rakṣita* would be purposeless. To explain:
In the examples *kuberabaliḥ* and *gorakṣitam*, the sense of being for the sake of that (*tādarthya*) is understood from those very forms.

Therefore, by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the inclusion of the terms *bali* and *rakṣita*, it is understood that "a compound occurs when there is the state of being a material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) in the sense of being for the sake of that.
Now, one might object: what is the purpose of [mentioning] the dative case (*sampradāna*)?
It might be argued that there should be the designation of "recipient" (*sampradāna*) for Bali because he is the one being protected; however, this is not so.

For the designation "recipient" is intended for one who is intended by the object of the act of giving (*dadāti-karman*) or by the action itself; and here, there is no state of being intended either by the object of the act of giving or by the action. Therefore, how could there be a recipient?

Regarding the fourth [case]: by what means, then, does the fourth case occur in the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*)? He says: "Precisely for this reason," and so forth. If the fourth case did not occur in the sense of "for the sake of that," then the mention of the term *tadartha* would be purposeless.
Therefore, this very prescription of a compound with a word ending in the fourth case by means of *tadartha* [establishes its necessity].
The indicator is: "the dative case occurs in the sense of 'for the sake of that' (tādarthye).
[This refers to] the rule beginning with "arthena," etc.; the word "must be formed" (kartavyam) is the ellipsis. It is called or stated as an obligatory compound (nityasamāsa);
by this, that statement regarding obligatory compounds is to be explained. This is what is meant:
The explanation must be provided for that word *artha* by which a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*) is indicated.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is understood to carry over [from a previous rule], and it is recognized as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, with the word *artha*, there is a compulsory compound.

[The compound] will have all genders (*sarvaliṅgatā*). When the rule "the gender of a *dvandva* and a *tatpuruṣa* is that of the final member" (*paravalliṅgaṃ dvandvatatpuruṣayoḥ*, Pāṇini 2.4.26) would have applied [the gender of the final member], the possession of all genders is here prescribed.
This, however, is established because gender is based on worldly usage (*lokāśrayatvāt*). Or alternatively—

All of this is established through the continued application of the term *bahulam* ("in various cases"). In *go-hitam* and *go-sukham*, the dative case is employed by virtue of the rule *caturthī cāśiṣyāyuṣyamadrabhadrakuśalasvastyayogakṣemārthahitārtheṣu* (Pāṇini 2.3.73). However, in connection with *hita*, the dative occurs even when not expressing a blessing (*āśis*). For he will state later: "The dative is used in connection with *hita*."
"It should be stated [as follows]: (Vārttika 123).
37. *pañcamī bhayena* (Pāṇini 2.1.37).
"It should be stated that [the word *bhaya*] is used with *bhīta*, *bhīti*, and *bhī*"; for in this way, it applies to all three as well.
The meaning is that this rule, which prescribes a compound [of a word ending in the third case] with words such as *bhīta* ("afraid"), must be explained in its true sense.

To explain it himself, he says "of the preceding" (*pūrvasya*), and so forth. For just as in the rule "the agent and the instrument are frequently compounded with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix" (Pāṇini 2.1.32), there is a compounding of a word ending in the third case; [so too here].
Since the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various ways) in the rule indicates that all conditions (*upādhi*) may be set aside, a compound is formed even with words ending in other case endings—
such as *pādahārakaḥ* and *galecopakaḥ*— and likewise, compounds are formed in cases such as *vṛkabhītaḥ*.

It will be so. Therefore, this rule (*yoga*) should be understood as being for the purpose of illustrating the examples of that very previous mention of *bahulam* (variously), or for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*).
This is indicated by the words "And thus" (*tathā ca*), and so forth; because [the desired result] is achieved by that previous *bahulam* alone.

This elaboration belongs to that very [rule] itself; therefore, by virtue of the inclusion of the word "bahula" (diversely), forms such as *grāmanirgataḥ* ("one who has gone out from the village") are also established. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), examples such as *vṛkabhītaḥ* ("fearful of a wolf") and others are included.

38. *apeta*, *apoḍha*, *mukta*, *patita*, *apatrasta* [are compounded] with *alpaśas*. (2.1.38) Regarding *alpaśas*: the suffix *śas* is applied by the rule *bahvalpārthāc chas kārakād anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.4.42). It is stated that "the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is optionally compounded when it signifies 'few'. Thus, it is derived from nominal stems (*prātipadika*) signifying "few."
The meaning is that it is the fifth [case-ending] which is compounded, but not from all nominal stems (prātipadika).
39. [The words] *stoka*, *antika*, *dūra*, and those having the sense of difficulty (*kṛcchra*) [are compounded] with a word ending in a *kta* suffix. (2.1.39) For example:

*stokānmuktaḥ* ("freed from a little"), *kṛcchrānmuktaḥ* ("freed from difficulty"). [In these cases,] the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is applied by the rule "the fifth case is used for the instrument when expressing *stoka*, *alpa*, *kṛcchra*, etc. (2.3.33). Examples: *antikād āgataḥ* ("come from near"), *dūrād āgataḥ* ("come from afar").
By means of [the rule] "dūrāntikārthebhyo dvitīyā ca" (Pāṇini 2.3.35).
40. *saptamī śauṇḍṬaḥ* (2.1.40). Since the term *śauṇḍṬaḥ* is indicated in the plural, it is understood to include the first member of the list; thus he says: "with *śauṇḍa* and the others.
But by what rule is the locative case (*saptamī*) prescribed, such that a compound is formed between that [locative-ending word] and *śauṇḍa* and the others?

If it is argued that [the locative case] is prescribed by the rule "saptamyadhikaraṇe ca" (Pāṇini 2.3.36), this is incorrect. For the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is a kāraka, and as such, it depends upon an action (*kriyā*). However, in compounds such as *akṣaśauṇḍa*, no action whatsoever is heard in the formation of the word.

How, then, is the occurrence of a locus (adhikaraṇa) possible here? Nor can it be argued that the locative case will occur when joined with words such as *śauṇḍa* precisely because of this very rule; for if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) even in the case of *devadattaḥ śauṇḍaḥ*. Therefore, he says "in a compound" (*vṛttau*), and so forth. Indeed, [the condition] exists here.

The action of attachment (*prasakti-kriyā*) is indeed included within the very meaning of the compound; because it is thus understood, a verbal form for that action is not employed in the *vṛtti*. Since the locative case is prescribed for the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), which is the instrument (*sādhana*) of that action, there is no fault. Furthermore, the word *antaḥ* is read here as having the locus itself as its primary meaning. Of that—
In the case of usage, the very fact of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [substantive] is the cause for the locative case.
However, when there is predominance of the meaning of the prior member— as in *vane'ntar*, *vanāntar*, or *vasatīti*—
there occurs only an avyayībhāva compound by the rule *vibhaktyarthe yadavyayam* (Pāṇini 2.1.6), resulting in *antarvaṇam*.

The word *adhi* is recited here; when its primary sense is that of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), it forms an *avyayībhāva* compound—e.g., *adhistri*. When, however, its primary sense is that of the thing located (*ādheya*), it forms a *tatpuruṣa* compound—e.g., *brāhmaṇādhīna*, meaning "dependent on Brāhmaṇas.
The word *brāhmaṇādhi* is not used in isolation. [This is governed by] Pāṇini 5.4.7: *ṣaḍakṣāśit*.
Because, by such statements as these, the suffix *kha* is prescribed as being invariably applied in its own sense (*svārthika*) after a subsequent member of a compound.
41. [The seventh case-ending is used] with *siddha*, *śuṣka*, *pakva*, and *bandha*. (2.1.41) 42.

[The seventh case-ending is used] with *dhvāṅkṣa* when expressing censure. (2.1.42) Regarding the rule "with *dhvāṅkṣa*," it is a reference to the meaning (*arthagrahaṇa*). This is because the indication is primarily concerned with the sense. For where...

It has been established previously that in this context, because the designation is primarily concerned with the word-form (*śabda*), there is a grasping of the phonetic form itself; whereas elsewhere, there is only a grasping of the meaning (*artha*). However, the fact that the designation is primarily concerned with the meaning is understood from the uninterrupted tradition of instruction handed down by the teachers.

Either this [term] is a reference to the meaning because of the continued application of the rule for frequent usage (*bahulagrahaṇa*), or rather, since it is stated that [the compound occurs] "in the sense of censure" (*kṣepe*), and censure is indeed brought about by the meaning, it is more appropriate to take it as a reference to the meaning itself. And when there is a reference to the meaning, the compound also occurs with synonyms of *dhvāṅkṣa*; therefore he says: "by a word expressing *dhvāṅkṣa*."

And so forth. Regarding the phrase "like a crow at a sacred bathing place" (*tīrthe dhvāṅkṣa iva*): the word *iva* is employed to demonstrate that the censure of the crow is understood only when there is the state of being a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and not otherwise. However, in a compound (*samāsa*), because the meaning of the standard of comparison is already included within the compound itself, the word *iva* is not used as its purpose has been fulfilled. Just as...

For indeed, crows at a sacred bathing place (tīrtha-dhvāṅkṣa) do not remain for long; likewise, anyone else who is unstable regarding a task is called a "tīrtha-dhvāṅkṣa. As it has been said: "The meaning is 'unstable'. Instability regarding a task is precisely what constitutes procrastination (kṣepa).

43. *kṛtyair ṛṇe* (Pāṇini 2.1.43). It is intended that the compound occurs only with a word ending in the suffix *ṭhya*. But how is it obtained by means of the suffix *yat*? Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of [the word] *alpaśas*, as in the example *māsadeyam*. Here, *yat* is applied as before, and there is also the substitution of *ī* for the vowel.

For here, the seventh case (*saptamī*) should be understood as denoting the locative of proximity (*upaśleṣika-adhikaraṇa*). For when a month has passed, the day that is internal to it is proximate to that month; or [it may be understood] by the rule "when one state is characterized by another state" (*yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam*, Pāṇini 2.3.37). Indeed, by means of the state of the passing of the month—

The state of being a debt is indicated. Now, if it is said "debt" (*ṛṇa*), then this is not established: "The *sāman* is to be sung in the forenoon; the *anuvāka* is to be studied in the morning. Therefore, he says "debt," and so forth.
For a debt must necessarily be discharged.

It is accompanied by *niyoga* (necessity). Therefore, by virtue of this association (*sāhacarya*), necessity is indicated by it. And this is understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the plural designation in the word "by means of *kṛtya*s" (*kṛtyaiḥ*). How so? [From] "by means of *kṛtya*s."

The plural number here is intended to be significant; and that [plural] would result only if the act of incurring debt were to be understood as an indication of a mandatory injunction (*niyoga*) that varies according to the different bases of the action, but not otherwise,
because the suffix *yat* is singular and the compound is desired to be formed with that very same [singular] element.

44. *saṃjñāyām* (2.1.44). Regarding the phrase "an adjunct of the whole": the term "*saṃjñāyām*" (when it is a name) is not a qualifier of either the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) or the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), but rather of the entire compound as a whole.

If it is argued that the designation is understood through the aggregate, he asks: "What is established by this being so? To which he replies with the words beginning "by that" (*tena*). He provides the justification for this very point with the words beginning "for not" (*na hi*).

45. *ktenāhorātrāvayavāḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.45). [Examples include: "You will see the day-portion (*divāvṛtam*) and the night-portion (*rātrivṛtam*) here," and so forth. In these cases, there are no parts of a day or parts of a night; rather, what is meant is the entire day itself.
And because [the word] "kṛtsnā" (entire) is used with "rātriḥ" (night), a compound does not occur here.
46. Regarding this [sūtra]:

"In that context" (*tatra*)—this [word] ends in the locative case (*saptamyanta*). This is because it shares the properties of the locative case. Here, the suffix *tral* alone is expressed by the word "locative. For indeed, a thing may be designated by the name of its property through the sharing of those properties (*tāddharmyāt*). As for example:

Regarding the expression "the Vāhīka is a cow" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*), the similarity with the locative case (*saptamī*) arises because the suffix *-tral* has the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*). For just as the locative case is employed to convey a locus, so too is the suffix *-tral*. Now, why is it not understood as being the primary locative case itself?
Because the suffix *tra* cannot occur there [in the word *tatra*] itself; for its meaning is already expressed by the suffix *tra* alone.

But another says: when suffixes such as *tral* are substitutes for case-endings (*vibhakti*), then this form ending in the locative case arises precisely through the principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*). However, in the view that it is a substitute (*ādeśa*)... [the form arises] there.

It is incorrect to say that this was not adopted by the author of the Vṛtti; for here the word *anta* signifies a "part" (*avayava*). The suffix *tra* is used in the sense of the locative case, and thus it is said: "that of which the final part is [the object]."

[The example is] "ṭhavataptenakulasthitam" ("like the stay of a mongoose in hot ashes"). In this case, the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case is by the rule "tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam" (6.3.14). But what here is the censure (*kṣepa*)? It is instability in one's duties. As it is said:

Regarding the passage beginning with "This is fickleness" (*ṭhetaccāpalam*): just as mongooses do not remain for long in a heated place, so too, this expression—"the standing of a mongoose in a heated place" (*avataptenakulasthitam*)—is said with reference to another person who, having undertaken certain matters, does not persist in them for long. [The word] *udakam*...
In the verse beginning with "viśīrṇam" (shattered), there is also the censure of the fruitlessness of the undertaking. For this very reason, he says:
"That which is done fruitlessly is described in this way. [The example is] "mūtritam in the stream. The root *mūtra* (in the sense of "to urinate") belongs to the curādi class (Dhātupāṭha 1909).

48. *pātresamitādayaśca* (2.1.48). [The commentary states: *yuktārohyāviparigrahārthaḥ*. This means that the purpose (*artha*) or motive (*prayojana*) for the recitation [of this list] is the inclusion (*parigraha*) of the group beginning with *yuktārohī*. For what purpose?

Furthermore, he states that their inclusion among the *yuktārohī* group is intended so that "the acute accent (*udātta*) may fall on the first syllable of the preceding member. For, by the rule *yuktārohyādayaśca* (Pāṇini 6.2.81), the acute accent on the first syllable of the preceding member is prescribed for the *yuktārohī* group.

In that regard, if those words ending in the *kta* suffix were not recited [in the list], then they would not possess the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*). But how, then, are words such as *pātresamitāḥ* included by the mention of *yuktārohī* and so forth,
since the initial acute accent being prescribed for them applies to *pātresamitāḥ* and the others as well?

He says "it happens" with the words "for in the case of *yuktārohī* and so forth," and "in the case of the *udumbara* tree, mosquitoes, and so forth, there is a derisive comparison. He considers one who is confined right there and goes nowhere else to be particularly distinguished, thinking, "there is nothing higher than this."

Thus, one whose extent is not seen is called a "gnat in a fig tree. In this way, elsewhere too, there is disparagement based on comparison. Regarding the phrase "by practicing what is forbidden": whoever performs a prohibited act is called a "man with his mother. Regarding the phrase "due to lack of effort": he who does nothing at all...
He is designated by such words as "samarthaḥ" (capable) and "ṭhpiṇḍīśūraḥ" (a hero at the rice-ball feast).

The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇārtha*). It means that only those [compounds] such as *pātresamita* and so forth should be *yat* [ending]; let there not be any other *yat* suffix that might apply to them due to another type of compound. Therefore, in the case of *paramapātresamitāḥ*, [the rule does not apply].
By the rule "itaḥ sinmahat" (Pāṇini 2.1.61) and others, no other compound formation occurs.
49. *pūrvakāla-eka-sarva-jarat-purāṇa-nava-kevalāḥ samānādhikaraṇena* (2.1.49).
[The commentary begins: "Of that which is employed with distinct grounds for application," and so forth. The inclusion of the term "distinct grounds for application" (*bhinnapravṛttinimitta*)...

The mention of "synonym" (*paryāya*) is for the purpose of excluding [the application of the rule] to synonyms. The inclusion of the word "single" (*eka*) is for the purpose of excluding cases such as *gauraśvaḥ* ("ox and horse").

The statement "‘In the prior time’ is a specification of the meaning" is made because the specification is based on the primary meaning; the intention is that, therefore, there is no apprehension of the actual form (*svarūpa*). "For the remaining [terms], there is apprehension of their own form."

Because the indication is primarily based on the word itself—namely, "that which occurs at an earlier time [is compounded] with that which occurs at a later time. But how is this specific meaning obtained even though it is not explicitly stated? Because the word for "earlier time" is a relative term (*sambandhiśabda*);
for an "earlier time" is not possible without depending upon a "later time. Therefore...
When the inclusion of the prior time has been made, the inclusion of the subsequent time is also necessarily made.
In the expression "bathed and anointed," where one first bathes and subsequently anoints,
the word "bathed" is employed on account of the act of bathing, and the word "anointed" on account of the act of anointing.
And since the two [words] function with respect to one and the same object, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). In the case of "eka-śāṭī" (one garment),
because it is both "eka" and "śāṭī," the masculine form is applied according to the rule "puṃvat karmadhāraya" (Pāṇini 6.3.42).

50. *diksaṃkhyaṃ saṃjñāyām* | (Pāṇini 2.1.50) [The compound] beginning with *pūrveṣukāmaśamī* is a name (*saṃjñā*) of villages. It is *pūrveṣukāmaśamī* because it is both "eastern" (*pūrvā*) and "Iṣukāmaśamī. [This applies to] villages of little prosperity.

This sentence has been composed merely to demonstrate the division between the preceding and following words; for in this case, there ought not to be a [separate] sentence, since a technical name (saṃjñā) is not understood through a sentence.
51. *taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca* (Pāṇini 2.1.51).

To demonstrate that even a single locative case (*saptamī*) is divided according to its different scopes, he says: "In the scope of the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)," and so forth. If it were understood as "when the meaning of a secondary derivative is to be expressed," then...

In examples such as *pāñcanāpitir*, the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix would be difficult to obtain, because its meaning has already been expressed by the compound itself; keeping this in mind, it is stated that "in the domain of the meaning of a secondary derivative" (*taddhitārthe viṣaye*) is said in order to show that this is a locative case of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*) with respect to the meaning of the secondary derivative.

The *taddhita* suffixes are those beginning with *aṇ*; their meaning consists of "offspring" and so forth, and it is in that domain [that the rule applies]. The word "domain" (*viṣaya*) signifies exclusive occurrence, as in the expression "water is the domain of fish. For example, in the case of "Paurvaśālaḥ": [it means] one who is born in the eastern *śālā* (house/region), when that [place] serves as the domain for the meaning of the *taddhita* suffix.

First is the compound; then the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*); then the secondary suffix (*taddhita*). In the example "pūrvaśālāpriyaḥ" (one for whom the eastern hall is dear), there is first a *bahuvrīhi* of the three preceding words, based on the analysis: "he for whom the eastern hall is dear. Subsequently, when the word "priya" stands as the final member (*uttarapada*), there is a *tatpuruṣa* of the two preceding words.

When that [the suffix *a*] is present, the final accentuation of the compound occurs as in the word *śālā*. The original reading in the root-text and the *Padamañjarī* is "the word *padika* in the sense of a collective" (*samāhāre*). [The objection] "the direction [of the rule] is not possible" is raised because a collective (*samāhāra*) is indeed an aggregate (*samūha*), and such an aggregate occurs only among distinct objects existing at the same time.
The simultaneity [of objects] arises from their simultaneous apprehension by the intellect (*buddhi*), but not from the non-difference of the things themselves.

Furthermore, it is only through enumeration (*saṃkhyā*) that one expresses distinction, because enumeration denotes distinct objects, whereas the word for "direction" (*dik-śabda*) does not, since its scope is restricted to specific locations. Therefore, in the case of a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*):

Since a *dakṣiṇa* [suffix] is not possible, it is not compounded there. In the case of "pañcānāpitiḥ," the compound occurs first while the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)—namely, "the offspring of five barbers"—is the domain;
subsequently, the suffix *iñ* is applied by rule 4.1.95. In the case of "pañcakapālaḥ," [it means] "in five potsherds."
In the formation of the word *saṃskṛta*, when the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is the governing factor, the compound is formed first, and subsequently the suffix *aṇ* is added.

This suffix is then elided by the rule *dvigor lug anapatye* (Pāṇini 4.1.88). [Note: The printed reading is *pañcagavadhanam*, but it should be *pañcagavadhanaḥ*. Thus, in the case of *pañcagavadhanaḥ*—meaning "one whose wealth consists of five cows"—the three [elements] are combined first.

The *bahuvrīhi* is formed from the words [in the first stage]. Subsequently, when the word *dhana* follows as the final member (*uttarapada*), the two preceding words form a *tatpuruṣa*. When that [compound] exists, the suffix *ṭac* is applied as a compound-final augment (*samāsānta*) by the rule "ṭac after *go*, except when an *taddhita* suffix follows" (Pāṇini 5.4.92). For in that context, there is the rule "of a *tatpuruṣa* ending in *aṅguli*" (5.4.86).

Therefore, the mention of the *tatpuruṣa* compound continues [from the previous rule]. In the case of "pañcapūlī," the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the collection of five bundles" (*pañcānāṃ pūlānāṃ samāhāraḥ*). By the rule "A *dvigu* is singular" (Pāṇini 2.4.1), there is a singular form.
Furthermore, by the Vārttika (156): "A *dvigu* whose final member ends in the vowel 'a' is used in the feminine gender."

Femininity [is established] by the suffix *ṅīp* according to the rule "dvigoḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.21). Now, an objection is raised: since "samāhāra" means a collection (*samūha*), and a collection constitutes the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), the mention of "samāhāra" is redundant; for the desired result would already be established by the rule "taddhitārthe" alone. This is not so; for in the case of *pañcakumārī*, there is indeed a suffix denoting a collection.
