When the elision (*luk*) is applied by the rule "dvigor lug anapatye" (Pāṇini 4.1.21), the elision of the feminine suffix would also occur by the rule "luktaddhitaluki" (Pāṇini 1.2.49). However, when the collective compound (*samāhāra*) is understood separately, it is designated in this context as the non-occurrence of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) itself; therefore, [the feminine suffix does not appear].
This fault arises. The collection of five girls is "pañcamakumārī.

Since the technical designation *upasarjana* applies by the rule "and that which has a single case-ending, provided it is not placed first" (1.2.44), there is shortening [of the final vowel] by the rule "of a feminine stem ending in /ī/ or /ū/, when it is an *upasarjana*" (1.2.48). How so?

Furthermore, what is meant here by "having a single case-ending"? It is because of its connection with a single genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). For instance, a *samāhāra* (collection) is an aggregate; and since there must be a genitive when there is a relationship with that [aggregate], there is the genitive in "the collection of girls" (*kumārikāṇāṃ samāhāraḥ*), "see the collection of girls" (*kumārikāṇāṃ samāhāraṃ paśya*), and "by the collection" (*samāhāreṇa*).
Even though the word *samāhāra* (collection) is joined with many case-endings such as "of the maidens" (*kumārīṇām*) and so forth, the word *kumārī* is joined with only a single sixth-case ending;
thus, there is "uniformity of case-ending" (*ekavibhaktikatva*).
52. A *dvigu* compound preceded by *sakhi* [takes the suffix *ṭac*]. (Pāṇini 2.1.52).

It "becomes a suffix applied at the end of a compound" (*samāsānta*). [The suffix] *ṭac* is added, because of the extension [of the rule] from "after *rājan*, *ahan*, and *sakhi*, [the suffix] *ṭac* [is applied]" (Pāṇini 5.4.91).

53. *kutsitāni kutsanaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.53). Here, the word *kutsita* denotes a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*). Consequently, the suffix *niṣṭhā* does not signify past time. Furthermore, by the word *kutsana*, the quality that causes contempt is understood—that by which one is despised.
It is so called because one is censured by means of it. The use of the plural number is for the purpose of excluding the prescription of the word's own form (*svarūpa-vidhi*).

Consequently, it is understood that the compound occurs between a word denoting something contemptible and words expressing censure, but not between the word *kutsita* itself and a word expressing censure. Therefore, he says: "words denoting the contemptible," and so forth.

This compound should be understood as occurring when there is contempt for the cause of a word's application (*śabdapravṛttinimitta*). But how is this obtained? From proximity (*pratyāsatti*). For the cause of a word's application is proximate; therefore, it is logical that the compound occurs only when there is contempt for that [cause].
Regarding the term *vaiyākaraṇakhasūci*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "he who is a grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*) and yet a 'sky-indicator' (*khasūci*).

One who, when questioned about grammar, indicates the sky—that is, looks toward the empty space—being devoid of ready wit, is called such. For in this case, his status as a grammarian [is merely nominal].
The ground for the application of the term "grammarian" (vaiyākaraṇa) is that which is here disparaged;

that, moreover, is either the relationship with one who studies grammar or the relationship with one who knows grammar. For by means of that ground, the word "grammarian" applies to a person. The same applies elsewhere as well.

A compound should be understood to occur when there is a censure regarding the cause for the application of a word, as in "ṭhyājñikakitavaḥ" (a fraudulent sacrificer). He is a "kitava" (gambler) only in appearance; for just as a gambler engages in dice-playing while looking only at whether others possess wealth—asking "What have you got?"—but he himself [possesses nothing].

One considers [the client's] caste and so forth; likewise, a priest who, when engaged in officiating at a sacrifice, out of greed considers only the wealth of one unworthy to be sacrificed for (ayājya) and not that person's fitness for sacrifice, is called a "rogue priest" (yājñika-kitava). Therefore, it is said: "He is called one whose passion is for officiating for those unworthy to be sacrificed for."
Thus: "a Mīmāṃsaka who has become hardened. This suggests that a Mīmāṃsaka, having failed to obtain the fruit of studying Mīmāṃsā, has become an atheist (*nāstika*).
"A grammarian who is a thief. Now, a grammarian being censured for theft—

[The word *vaiyākaraṇa*] indeed becomes contemptible, and the word *vaiyākaraṇa* denotes that [contempt]. How, then, is this counter-example justified? To this he says: "For not here," and so forth. For, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), there ought to be a compound when there is contempt for the very cause of the application of the word; and that is not the case here.

The ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word "grammarian" (*vaiyākaraṇa*) is not what is being censured; for even a thief may correctly know or study grammar. Therefore, it is not the ground for the word's application that is censured here, but rather, he in whom that status of being a grammarian exists who is censured—yet the status of being a grammarian itself [is not].

That [term] is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), as in: "The grammarian is a thief," or "That which trembles is an *aśvattha* tree. Here, trembling is an indicator of the *aśvattha*. In the expression "a contemptible Brahmin" (*kutsito brāhmaṇaḥ*), the word "contemptible" (*kutsita*) denotes that which is contemptible; however, it is not...
The word "brāhmaṇa" is used here in a derogatory sense.

54. [The compound] *pāpāṇaka* is formed with words of censure (*kutsita*). It has been stated that "the words *pāpa* and *aṇaka* denote censure. If this is so, since the compound is already established by the preceding rule, one might ask: for what purpose is this stated? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of those two," and so forth.

If there were a compound with the preceding [word], then, because the word *kutsita* would be indicated by the first case, it would have to appear as the prior member; however, the words *pāpa* and *apaṇaka* would instead appear as the subsequent members. Therefore, this rule is commenced for the sake of ensuring their position as the prior member. The mention of *kutsita*...
This is for the sake of clarity; otherwise, since the word "kutsita" (despised) would carry over from the preceding rule, this [present] rule would not need to be formulated at all.

55. *Upamānāni sāmānyavacanaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.55). "That by which something is compared is the *upamāna*"—this means that the instrument by which [an object] is delimited through similarity is the *upamāna*. For example, in the expression "the *gavaya* is like a cow," the cow (*go*) is the *upamāna*; by means of it...
For the gavaya is determined through similarity; the meaning understood is, "As is the cow, so is the gavaya. A universal (sāmānya) belongs to many things;

and since here the standard of comparison (upamāna) is explicitly mentioned, and since that requires a correlate of comparison (upameya), it is common to both the standard and the correlate of comparison alone.
He says that the common property (*dharma*) is understood [from context], stating: "Of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*)," and so forth.

"This compound occurs with words denoting the object of comparison as qualified by that [property]. Thus, this compound occurs with words denoting that object of comparison which is qualified by that common property. But why [is this so]?

When it is said "by general terms," is this specific meaning obtained? It is obtained by logical necessity (*nyāya*). For instance—those which express a generality are "general terms" (*sāmānyavacana*), just as those which express a quality are "quality-expressing terms" (*guṇavacana*). And when do they become general terms? When...
Having denoted the common property (*sāmānya*), [the words] apply to the substance (*dravya*) which possesses that [property] as qualified by it.

And since that [substance] possessing the common property is the object of comparison (*upameya*)—because the word for the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is a relative term—this meaning, established by logical necessity, is shown by the author of the *Vṛtti* in the example: "Devadattā is dark like a sword-blade" (*śastrīśyāmā devadattā*).

In this case, the *śastrī* (knife) is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and Devadattā is the object of comparison (*upameya*). For that which is well-known becomes the standard of comparison, not that which is unknown. It is the *śastrī* alone that is well-known for its quality of blackness, whereas Devadattā is not. The commonality between the two—the shared attribute—is their blackness (*śyāmatva*). Having stated that blackness, [the sentence proceeds].
The word *śyāma* (dark) applies to Devadattā either through metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*) based on non-difference, or by the elision of the possessive suffix *matup*;
thus, it becomes a general term. But surely, the rule "with a word in grammatical apposition" (*samānādhikaraṇena*) continues to apply here;
and in this case, the word *śastrī* (knife/wife) functions with reference to a knife, while the word *śyāmā* functions with reference to Devadattā. Therefore—

Is it not the case that because they are in different grammatical relations (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), a compound cannot be formed? This is not so; for in all cases, since there is a distinction between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison, those words expressing them are necessarily in different grammatical relations.
Yet this [compound] is stated; therefore, even though they are in different grammatical relations, a compound is formed by the force of the explicit statement.
It will be so.
Or rather—the word *śastrī* (knife) is also used here in the sense of Devadattā;
therefore, this compound is one of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), namely: "she who is both a knife and dark-complexioned."

"Dark as a sword-blade. Now, one might object: this word "sword-blade" (śastrī) denotes a genus (*jāti*); it applies to that which possesses it by taking "sword-bladeness" (*śastrītva*) as its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). And since that "sword-bladeness" does not exist in Devadattā, how can the word apply to her? This is not a fault; for all these [words]— [The full argument continues: ...are based on a resemblance (*sādṛśya*) to the primary object denoted by the word. Just as the word "lion" (*siṃha*), though primarily denoting the genus "lion-ness," applies to Devadatta because he resembles a lion, so too the word "sword-blade" applies to Devadattā because she resembles a sword-blade in her dark complexion. Thus, there is no inconsistency.

There is also the view that "words function with respect to a substance possessing a quality by taking up that quality. In that case, the word *śastrī* (knife) will function with respect to Devadattā by taking up the quality of blackness (*śyāmatva*).
Or else, Devadattā will be denoted by the word *śastrī* because of her similarity to it (*tāddharmyāt*). For indeed, [a word can denote something] through such similarity.

That [usage] is called *tācchabdyam* (denoting the same thing), as stated previously. *Tāddharmyam* (denoting the quality thereof), on the other hand, is the state of possessing the quality of being dark (*śyāmaguṇatva*).
For example: "The rice grains are like ploughshares" (*phālā iva taṇḍulāḥ*). Indeed, the ploughshares serve as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
For it is by means of that similarity—such as length and so forth—that the rice grains are compared to them. As for the word "rice grain" (*taṇḍula*), however...

It does not denote a universal (*sāmānya*). But surely the word *taṇḍula* (rice) also denotes a universal, namely *taṇḍulatva* (rice-ness), and thus functions with respect to the substance (*dravya*) that possesses it; therefore, is it not the case that this counter-example is indeed one that denotes a universal? This is not so; for in the case of the object of comparison and the subject of comparison...
It has been stated that a common property is a universal (*sāmānya*). Now, the state of being rice (*taṇḍulatva*) does not belong to the mortars; rather, it belongs to the rice grains alone.
56. *Upamitam vyāghrādibhiḥ sāmānyāprayoge* (2.1.56). [The commentary states:

"By virtue of the sense, [the compound is formed] with words denoting the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Although the phrase "with words denoting the standard of comparison" is not explicitly mentioned in the rule itself, nevertheless, the word *upamitam* (that which is compared) necessarily depends upon both the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*māna*).
Because they are relative terms (*sambandhiśabda*), words such as "tiger" imply the state of being a standard of comparison (*upamānatva*). Therefore,
even though no specific [quality] is explicitly stated, it is understood through the force of the context that these words denoting standards of comparison form a compound [with the subject],
provided that "a word expressing the common property (*sāmānya*) is not employed."

The common attribute (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*) of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), such as bravery (*śaurya*) and so forth, is the "commonality" (*sāmānya*). If the word expressing that [commonality] is not employed, then a compound (*samāsa*) occurs; otherwise it does not. Now, since the commonality is already included within the compound, why would there be the employment of words denoting it?

[Objection: It does not exist; so what is the purpose of the negation? [Reply: This is not so. For in a compound, it is the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*)—that is, the generality (*sāmānya*)—which is included, and not its particularity (*viśeṣa*). Therefore, in the absence of the negation, there would indeed be the employment of a word expressing a specific common property; thus, the negation must be made.

It should not be formed. How so? For when a general term (*sāmānya-śabda*) is employed, that which depends upon it becomes dependent (*sāpekṣa*), and being dependent, it lacks syntactic capacity (*asamartha*); thus, due to this very lack of capacity, the compound would not occur.
In that case, this [rule] indicates: "Indeed, there is a compound even for a principal element (*pradhāna*) when it is dependent."

In this context, because the *puruṣa* (man) is the object of comparison (*upameya*), he is the primary element; however, the comparison (*upamāna*), such as the tiger (*vyāghra*) and so forth, is secondary because its purpose is for that [comparison]. What is the purpose of this indicative rule? It serves to establish forms such as "the king's man is handsome" (*rājapuruṣaḥ śobhanaḥ*). This is necessary because, otherwise, by the rule "the qualifier [is compounded] with the qualified" (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*), [such a construction would not be possible].

Thus [it is asked]: "But surely, he will state that a compound occurs between a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and a substantive (*viśeṣya*) in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*); and since there is a difference between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), there is a lack of apposition (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). Therefore, how can the application of the rule 'a qualifier with a substantive' be obtained? He thinks as follows: [the rule applies] when the object of comparison is *puruṣa* and so forth.
This compound occurs with words denoting a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), such as *vṛka* ("tiger") and so forth.

Just as the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of words denoting a standard of comparison when they function as the object of comparison (*upameya*) has been explained in the preceding rule, so it is here as well.

57. *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.57). "The qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) [is compounded] with the qualified (*viśeṣya*) in various ways. Regarding this: the root *śiṣlṛ* is listed in the printed editions as meaning "to perish" (*viśaraṇe*); however, according to the *Padamañjarī*, it is *śiṣlṛ* in the sense of "remaining" (*śeṣaṇe*), with the prefix *vi-*—that is, *śiṣlṛ* in the sense of "qualifying" (*viśeṣaṇe*). (Dhātupāṭha 1451).

From this verbal root *vi-pūrvāt* (preceded by the prefix *vi-*) with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), we derive *viśeṣaṇam*. That by which something is distinguished is a "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*). Its definition is as follows: "In the phrase 'bhadema'—that which, having operated upon an object possessing multiple modes in a general form, distinguishes it from other modes and [fixes it] upon a single mode..."
That which establishes [the distinction] is the "differentiator" (*viśeṣaṇa*). As for the statement "the differentiable is the qualified" (*bhedyam viśeṣyam*):

the object to be qualified is the "qualified" (*viśeṣya*). From that verbal root preceded by the prefix *vi-* (in the sense of "to distinguish"), the suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of the object according to Pāṇini 3.1.124 (*ṛhalorṇyat*). Its definition is this: "the differentiable."

When an object possessing multiple modes is distinguished from other modes and established within a single mode, that [object] is the "to-be-distinguished" (*bhedya*), the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Now, for what purpose are both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) employed? It is not [sufficient] for either one alone.
[Objection: It may be so, for since those two are relative terms (*sambandhiśabda*), by the mention of either one, the other is indeed understood. [Response: This is true;
however, this applies only in cases where both the preceding and the following words function individually as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*).

The mention of both [terms] is for the purpose of providing an illustration that a compound occurs, as in "blue lotus" (*nīlotpalam*). Here, the meaning of "blue" is distinguished from [other things] such as bees and is established within the lotus by means of the word "lotus"; likewise, the meaning of "lotus" [is distinguished].

Having excluded [the object] from red lotuses and so forth, it is established as "blue" by means of the sense of blueness; thus, there exists a relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) for each individual case. Where that [relation] does not exist, however, there is no compound, as in: "a tree is a *śiṃśapā*. For a tree deviates from being a *śiṃśapā*, whereas a *śiṃśapā*...

But it is not "treeness" [itself]. Therefore, because it excludes that [treeness] from other classes such as the *palāśa* and so forth, the *śiṃśapā* becomes its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), and not the qualified (*viśeṣya*).
However, the tree is the qualified; since the object "śiṃśapā" does not deviate from treeness, [the latter is not the qualifier].

That [word] becomes its qualifier. Now, why should there not be such expressions as "the *śiṃśapā* tree" or "the mango tree"? There must be a compound with a qualifier when the specific application of words such as *śiṃśapā* is not restricted to a particular instance. For it is thus:
Words such as "śiṃśapā" are denoters of the fruit, the tree, and the root; they are general terms (*sāmānya-śabda*).
Because their referents do not deviate from "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*), there is no relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-bhāva*) among them, and the word "tree" becomes the qualifier.
However, when, due to some context or meaning, the referent of "tree" and so forth [is restricted]...

If their functions have already ceased in that manner, then [the suffix] should not occur. But surely, since the word *vṛkṣa* has its function already fulfilled by the meaning "tree," its employment at that time would be untenable because its meaning has already been expressed, according to the rule: "That which has already expressed its meaning is not employed" (*Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā* 60). And therefore—
A compound would not have been applicable at all. Why, then, is the mention of "both" (ubhaya) made for the purpose of excluding that?
This is not so; for in common usage, even words whose meaning has already been expressed are seen to be employed, as in the example: "Bring two cakes."
If, then, a compound must occur wherever there is a mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified between two things,
then in such a case each member would be subordinate (*upasarjana*), because both would be qualifiers; for in this sūtra, that which is designated by the nominative case is the qualifier.

In that case, one might also say "utpalanīlam" (blue lotus), yet "nīlotpalam" (lotus-blue) is always desired? This is not a fault, because one of the two is primary and the other is secondary; for if both were primary, [the rule would apply].
Because they do not assist one another, there would be no application of two unrelated things in a single location.

Even if both are subordinate, since they depend upon a primary element, they lack mutual assistance; thus, their application in a single location would simply not occur. Therefore, in a single location...

The principal [word] is primary, while the other is secondary (*apradhāna*). That which is secondary receives the technical designation *upasarjana*, and nothing else, because the designation *upasarjana* is based on its etymological meaning: it "creates" (*sṛjati*) or "casts" (*kṣipati*) its own meaning near (*upa*) the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). And the word "blue" (*nīla*) is secondary, as is its meaning.

Because the quality (*guṇa*) is subordinate, whereas the word "lotus" (*utpala*) is primary, since its referent—the substance (*dravya*)—is primary. Therefore, it is only the word "blue" (*nīla*) that is subordinate, not the word "lotus";
thus, there is no occasion for the recurrence of the previously mentioned fault. This applies where both [words] are present.
There is a state of being subordinate by way of alternation, as in "the hunchback and the lame" (*kubjakhañja*) or "the lame and the hunchback" (*khañjakubja*).

Now, from what is the predominance of the substance (*dravya*) determined here? It is said: as in the instruction, "One should sacrifice a white goat" (*śvetaṃ chāgam ālabheta*). In this instruction...

Because even if the quality of whiteness is absent, a goat of another color may still be sacrificed; and because in the absence of a goat, a substance possessing the quality of whiteness cannot be sacrificed. For a sacrificer does not fulfill his duty by sacrificing a lump of flour merely because a goat is unavailable. Furthermore, if the quality were the primary element [rather than the substance], [the sacrifice would fail].

It might be argued that just as in the absence of a goat, a ball of flour is not accepted [as a substitute], so too in the absence of the quality of whiteness, even another goat would not be accepted. Yet, it is not the case that he is not accepted;
therefore, the substance alone is primary, not the quality. But surely, the word "lotus" (*utpala*)— [...is also applied to other things possessing those qualities...]

It is not established that this [term] is a word for a substance (*dravya*). Similarly, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the word "blue" (*nīla*), because [the quality] does not abandon its substrate-substance at all from its beginning until its destruction. Therefore, since the universal (*jāti*) is of the very nature of the substance, the word based upon it arises with the arising of the substance. [This applies to] qualities (*guṇas*).
Furthermore, while this substance exists, those things that are subject to passing away or not passing away occur and cease within it;
therefore, these are not identical in essence to the substance itself, and thus the word "substance" is not established as a term denoting them. Enough of this digression.
"Ṭhakṣaka is a serpent. Now, one might object that *takṣaka* is indeed a qualifier of the serpent;

for instance, when "serpent" is mentioned, the general category of serpents is understood, not a specific serpent. But when "Ṭhakṣaka-serpent" is mentioned, a specific serpent is determined as being excluded from those who are not Ṭhakṣaka. This is incorrect.

This is a counter-example; this is not the case. For it has been stated: "A compound occurs where one [word] exists in both [positions]. However, *takṣaka* is never the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the meaning of "serpent" (*sarpa*).
Why is it not so? Because *takṣaka* does not deviate from being a serpent (*sarpa*). But surely...

Since the word *takṣaka* has multiple meanings, is it not appropriate to use "the serpent Takṣaka" as a qualified term (*viśeṣya*) in order to exclude other types? This is not so; a proper name does not possess the same capacity for denoting meaning as an action-word (*kriyāśabda*). For an action-word denotes its meaning by following the sense of its constituent parts (*avayavārtha*).
It brings [the meaning] to mind; however, as a whole form, it is a proper name (*nāmadheya*).

Since "the conventional meaning of a whole is stronger than the conventional meaning of its parts" (*vyā.pa.* 108), when that [whole-meaning] exists, there arises no expectation whatsoever regarding the meaning of a word denoting an action (*kriyāśabda*). For example: "The red Takṣaka."
"Red" is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), but "Takṣaka" is not the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), because Takṣaka does not deviate from being red. If, then, Takṣaka is not the qualificand,
"red" would also not be a qualifier, since a qualifier depends upon a qualificand.

Nor is it possible to conceive of cloth or other objects— which are distinct entities from Takṣaka— as the qualificand (viśeṣya) such that redness could be conceived as a qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) in relation to them. For in that case, Takṣaka would likewise be dependent on a qualifier, such as "intense poison," which is an entity distinct from "red" and so forth.
Otherwise, the status of being the qualificand (viśeṣyatva) would follow [for both]. Therefore, others maintain that both are mentioned for the sake of clarity.

58. *pūrvāparaprathamacaramajaghanyasamānamadhyamadhyamavīrāśca* (2.1.58). [The commentary states: "This is an elaboration (*prapañca*) of the very same [rule]"; for it is established by that very rule. Indeed, here too there exists a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) between each of the preceding and following words individually.
59. *Śreṇyādayaḥ kṛtādibhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.59). [The Vārttika states:

"The mention of *śreṇi* and so forth is for the sake of the sense of *cvī*. This is so that there may be a compound of words denoting the state of becoming what one was not (*abhūtatadbhāva*). For when the meanings of the words *śreṇi* and so forth are not yet fully accomplished...
In this way, when they are being produced, a compound is desired. However,

when those [actions] are already completed and are expressed in another form, then— in cases where one intends to express meanings such as "rows have been made," "fined," or "honored"— a compound with the word *kṛta* is not desired.
Nor should it be doubted that the occurrence [of the suffix] in the senses of words such as *daṇḍita* (punished) is impossible;

for the root *kṛ* denotes action in general, or because verbal roots possess multiple meanings. The meaning of the statement "the mention of *śreṇi* and so forth refers to the sense of the suffix *cvi*" is as follows: the sense of the suffix *cvi* is expressed.

That by which something is made known is a statement having the sense of *cvī* (the suffix -ya). The meaning is that an explanation must be provided for that by which the state of having the sense of *cvī* is understood when [words] such as *śreṇi* are introduced as forming compounds. In this regard, the explanation is as follows:

The term *bahula* (optionally) is understood here; therefore, the compound occurs only for those meanings of *cvi* that involve the suffix *cvi*, and not for those that do not. Regarding the phrase "of those ending in *cvi*" and so forth: since the suffix *cvi* is prescribed optionally, there are two kinds of meanings of *cvi*: those ending in *cvi* and those not ending in *cvi*. Among these, those...
The compounds of those [words] beginning with *śreṇi* and ending with *ac* are formed by this [rule]. However, for those ending in the suffix *cv*,
since they receive the designation of *gati* by the rule "ṭhūryādicviḍācaśca" (Pāṇini 1.4.61),
the compound will occur by the subsequent rule "kugatiprādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.2.18).

60. *ktena nañviśiṣṭenānañ* (Pāṇini 2.1.60). This word *viśiṣṭa* exists indeed with a restrictive sense, occurring in the meaning of "superiority. For example: Devadatta and Yajñadatta are both wealthy, handsome, and discerning; however, Devadatta [is superior] to Yajñadatta.

"He is distinguished by his study of the Veda" (*svādhyāyena viśiṣṭaḥ*); it is understood that he is superior *by means of his study of the Veda alone*. Other qualities, however, remain equal. And there exists the word "only" (*eva*) used in the sense of an unrestricted superiority, as for example: "Devadatta and Yajñadatta are wealthy, handsome, and discerning; but Devadatta... [is superior].

"Yajñadatta is distinguished by his study of the Veda (svādhyāya)," from which it is understood that he is superior in his svādhyāya; other qualities, whether equal or more numerous, are not intended to be expressed here. Although these two sentences are identical in form, nevertheless, due to context and so forth—

A distinction in meaning is understood from some context, as in the case of the word *ārāt*, where there is a distinction between the meanings "far" and "near. In that regard, if the word *viśiṣṭa* were taken as occurring in the sense of "excess" without restriction,
then it would also apply to the expression *siddhaṃ ca tadabhuktaṃ ca* ("it is both accomplished and uneaten"), because here too there is a *ktānta* suffix added by the negative particle *nañ*.
Therefore, taking the word *viśiṣṭa* (qualified) as referring to that which exists with a restrictive emphasis on superiority, he says:

"that of which the qualification is by the negative particle (*nañ*) itself," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the base form and so forth" (*prakṛtyādikam*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes suffixes (*pratyaya*) and prefixes (*upasarga*). Regarding "non-negative" (*anañ*), it means that in which the negative particle (*nañ*) is absent.

"In the case of a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, that which is not negated [is expressed]. Regarding the statement, "it is both made (*kṛta*) and unmade (*akṛta*)," how can a single entity be both made and unmade? There is no fault here, because the whole is designated in such a way by means of the properties of its parts. It is "made" due to its connection with the part that has been made, and [it is "unmade"] due to its connection with the part that has not been made.

That very thing is called "unmade" (*akṛta*). Alternatively, it is "unmade" because of its incapacity for that purpose for which it was made—just as, due to his incapacity for the duties of a son, even a son is called "sonless" (*aputra*). If the compound is formed with *nañ* alone as the qualifier, while everything else, such as the base form (*prakṛti*) and so on, remains the same, then in this way:

He states that there is no compound with that which has either the augment *nuṭ* or the augment *iṭ* in addition [to the suffix], beginning with the words "the augments *nuṭ* and *iṭ*" (*nuḍiṭau*). However, since the augments *nuṭ* and *iṭ* belong to the *kta*-suffix that is qualified by the negative particle (*nañ*), they are included by the mention of that [suffix]; therefore, they do not distinguish this [compound].

The meaning is that those two are non-differentiators (*abhedaka*). Therefore, even though it exceeds [the limit of a compound], it remains qualified by the negative particle (*nañ*), and thus the compound indeed takes place. In the example "aśitānaśitena," the augment *nuṭ* is applied by the rule "tasmānnuḍaci" (Pāṇini 6.3.74). In the example "kliṣṭākliśitena," [the suffix] *ktvā* or *niṣṭhā* [is applied] after the root *kliś-* by the rule "kliśaḥ ktvāniṣṭhayoḥ."

In this view, the augment *iṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.2.50]. It would be possible to omit the mention of *anañci*. If that *nañ* were to be compounded, then being qualified by *nañ* would not be appropriate, because both [members] would be connected with *nañ*.
Therefore, precisely because of the mention of "qualified by *nañ*," the meaning is obtained that a compound which is not preceded by *nañ* is what is intended.

Thus, the mention of *anañ* (negation) is purposeless; it is included for the sake of clarity, as in the rule “*kṛtāpakṛtādīnām*” and so forth. An enumeration—that is, an exposition—must be made regarding the group beginning with *kṛtāpakṛta*. In this regard, the exposition is as follows:

The term *bahulam* (diversely) is understood to carry over here; therefore, compounds such as *kṛtāpakṛta* and others are also formed. Regarding the example *kṛtāpakṛtam*: it is "done" (*kṛtam*) because a desired portion of it has been performed, and it is "undone" (*apakṛtam*) because an undesired portion of it has been performed.

Regarding the term "bhuktavibhuktam": it is *bhukta* (eaten) because it has been consumed, and *vibhakta* because it is unseemly. Here, the prefix *vi-* conveys the sense of being unseemly, as in the word *virūpa* (ugly). Alternatively, it is *bhukta* (eaten) and *pratyāgata* (returned), thus forming the compound *gatapratyāgatam*.

That which has gone before is "anuyāta" (followed), and that which goes after is "yātānuyāta. Regarding the term "krayākrayikā": the word *kraya* denotes a large purchase, whereas the word *krayikā* denotes a small one. It is called *kraya* because of its connection with the parts of a purchase, and it is called *krayitā* because of its connection with the parts of a purchaser.

"Kraya" and "krayikā" together form "krayākrayikā"; the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *ṭhanyemām api dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 6.3.137). Similarly, "puṭa" and "puṭikā" together form "puṭāpuṭikā. "Phala" and "phalikā" together form "phalaphalikā. Likewise, "māna" and "unmānikā" together form [mānonmānikā].
"Ṭhmānonmānikā" and "in the section on coreferentiality (samānādhikaraṇādhikāre)," and so forth.
Here too, the meaning of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is "formulation" (*pratipādana*). The formulation, however, is exactly as before.

61. "The words *san*, *mahat*, *parama*, *uttama*, and *utkṛṣṭa* [form a compound] with words denoting those being honored. This is because of the statement: "[This applies] by virtue of the rule concerning words denoting honor. For the subsequent member [of the compound] possesses the status of being honored only if they are words denoting honor, and not otherwise; therefore...

Because of the inclusion of the term "being honored" (*pūjyamāna*), words expressing honor such as *sat* are understood [to be included]. For this very reason, the word *sat* does not include the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac*, for those two do not express honor.
[For example: "The excellent cow has been lifted out of the mud"; the meaning is "it has been extracted. Now, how is it that [the term applies to] "a great tree" (*mahādruma*)?

The compound is "mahodadhiḥ" (great ocean); for here no honorific sense (*pūjā*) is understood, but rather the exceeding of the measure of the second member of the compound. Even so, it will still occur by virtue of the continued application of the term "bahulam" (diversely).

62. *vandārakanāgakuñjaraiḥ pūjyamānam* | (2.1.62) Words such as *vandāraka* are generic terms (*jātiśabda*). When they function as points of comparison (*upamāna*), they express veneration (*pūjā*). In this regard, because [the group] beginning with *vyāghra* is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*), [the rule] "that which is compared is [compounded] with *vyāghra* and so forth" applies.

(2.1.56) Since this [rule] is already established by the general application, this new undertaking is for the purpose that it should apply even in such cases. By the mention of "being honored" (*pūjyamāna*), words such as *vṛndāraka* are understood as denoting those who possess honor. For otherwise, it would not be so.
The sense is that being worthy of worship is thus established.

Regarding the phrase "the serpent Suṣīma": [one might object] that the rule "the qualifier [is compounded] with the qualified" applies here, yet there is no Suṣīma other than a serpent, for this is indeed the name of a serpent. If that is so, then...
This direction for counter-examples has been shown by the author of the Vṛtti; however, the following is a counter-example here: "Devadatta is a Nāga because he is a fool."

63. *kataratama* in the sense of inquiry regarding a genus (*jātiparipraśne*). (Pāṇini 2.1.63). It is explained that [the suffixes] *katara* and *katama* are derived specifically for the purpose of inquiring about a genus. This occurs while the rule *kiṃyatadaurnirdhāraṇe* (5.3.92) is being carried over, by means of the rule *vā bahūnām* (5.3.93), and so forth. It might be argued as follows:

He asks: "For what purpose is the inclusion of the term *jātiparipraśna* (inquiry regarding a class) as a qualifier for the word *katara*? He replies: "The word *katara* also... and so forth. "It makes this very point known. If, then, the word *katama* is understood only as occurring in an inquiry regarding a class (*jātiparipraśna*), the inclusion of the term *jātiparipraśna* would be redundant, even without it...

Therefore, according to the principle stated above, the words *katara* and *katama* will be understood as functioning specifically in the sense of an inquiry regarding a genus (*jāti*). Thus, "And so forth," etc.; since the word *katama* functions even elsewhere than in an inquiry regarding a genus, and this being the case, [your question] "Which among you is Devadatta? [is answered].
Thus, the counter-example is established; otherwise, it would not be established, because that [fallacy] does not apply except in the case of an inquiry regarding a genus (jāti).

64. *kim* [is used] in the sense of censure (*kṣepa*). (Pāṇini 2.1.64). As in the example *kiṃsakhaḥ*. Here, the substitution *anaṅ* is applied by the rule *anaṅ sau* (7.1.93). Now, in cases such as *kiṃrāja*, the suffix *ṭac* is applied by the rules *rājāhaḥ-sakhibhyaṣ-ṭac* (5.4.91) and *gor-ataddhita-luki* (5.4.92).

He asks why the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) does not apply here and says: "In the case of *kimaḥ kṣepe*," etc. Here, the word "not" (*na*) is understood as a carry-over from [Pāṇini 5.4.69], *na pūjanāt*.
*poṭā*, *yuvati*, *stoka*, *katipaya*, *gṛṣṭi*, *dhenu*, *vaśā*, *vehad*, *baṣkayaṇī*, *pravaktṛ*, *śrotriya*, *adhyāpaka*, and *dhūrta* [precede] the genus (*jāti*).
(2.1.65) Since a compound would have been required by the rule beginning with "the qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇam*), this statement is for the purpose of ensuring their final position [in the compound].

For these are quality-words (*guṇaśabda*). In that case, if there were a compound with them, their prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) would necessarily follow. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *dhūrta*? Since this is a word of censure, is the compound not already established by the rule "things censured are compounded with words of censure" (*kutsitāni kutsanaiḥ*, Pāṇini 2.1.53)? To this he says:

"The inclusion of the word *dhūrta* (rogue) is for the purpose of excluding censure (*akutsārtha*). This means that a compound is understood to occur when there is censure regarding the cause for the application of a word's meaning, but not when there is censure [of the person] itself.
66. And by words of praise (2.1.66).
It is said: "Words of praise are understood as conventional terms (*rūḍhiśabda*). For words of praise are of three kinds:
first, those that express praise when used for the sake of another [object], such as *siṃha* ("lion").

Regarding the term *devadatta*: some words denoting qualities (*guṇaśabda*) become expressions of praise through the relationship between a quality and its possessor (*guṇin*), such as "the village is delightful" or "the cook is excellent.
Some are conventional words (*rūḍhiśabda*), such as *matallikā* and others; for these, praise alone is the meaning of the word. Thus, in this case...
Because of the inclusion of the word *vacana* ("word"), those conventional (*rūḍhi*) words which function specifically in the sense of praise are understood here. For example:
*goprakāṇḍam*. The meaning is "an excellent, praiseworthy ox.
The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of avoiding ambiguity; [otherwise], if only the preceding rule were concerned with words expressing praise...

If they were to be taken [as such], then there would be doubt: is each term connected individually with "poṭā" and the others, or rather with "praśaṃsā"? If it were connected with "poṭā" and the others, then a compound would also occur with their synonyms.

67. *yuvā khalatipalitavalinajaratībhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.67). [The commentary states: "With *khalati* and so forth, when they are in grammatical apposition," and so on. If this is the case, for what purpose is there the mention of *jaratībhiḥ* in the feminine gender; should it not rather have been *jaradbhiḥ*?

An explanation must be provided, for the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the word *yuvan* (masculine gender) with the word *jaratī* (feminine gender) is not tenable; thus he says:
"The mention is made in the feminine gender as *jaratībhiḥ*," and so forth. But how [is this] by means of this?

Can this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) be made known by the specific mention [of the word *jaratībhiḥ*]? If this were not the case, then the mention "by means of the words *jaratībhiḥ*" would be purposeless.
And thus, because of the governing context of coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*), this [suffix] would be connected with the coreferential word *jaratī*.

The compound is understood [as *yuva-śvaśura*]. However, there can be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between that feminine form and the word *yuvan*, which refers to a male; therefore, how can this mention be meaningful if this paribhāṣā remains in force?
For if that [paribhāṣā] exists, [the application] of the word *yuvan*...

It is logical that when there is the mention of the word *yuvati* (young woman), there is the inclusion of [the word] *jaratī* (old woman). There is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the words *yuvati* and *jaratī*, and when that exists, a compound (*samāsa*) of the two occurs. Thus, the specific mention of *jaratībhiḥ* (by old women) indicates that this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) exists.

But even so, if a compound with *jaratī* is being taught, would it not follow that [the form] *yuvajarad*—meaning "young and old"—is not obtained? This is not a fault; for in another grammatical treatise (*vṛtti*), it is read as *jaradbhiḥ*.
Since the Teacher has instructed his students in both ways, both forms are established.

68. *Kṛtyatulyākhyā ajātyā* (Pāṇini 2.1.68). [The commentary states: "And those which are synonyms of *tulya*. Now, why is it not understood that this refers to the actual word-form (*svarūpa*) itself? It is thought thus: the term *kṛtya* here is taken as referring to the meaning; therefore, by association with it, *tulya* must also refer to the meaning alone.
The inclusion [of the word "ākhyā"] is appropriate; since the operation cannot apply to the actual object (artha), it is understood that the compound occurs among those words which denote it.

Thus, the mention of "ākhyā" is for the purpose of including those with identical names. Otherwise, it would also apply in cases such as *gaur vāhīkaḥ* ("the Vāhīka is an ox"), because here the word *go* signifies similarity (*sādṛśya*). For all words indeed...

When applied to another object, words convey similarity. However, if the term "name" (*ākhyā*) were included [in the definition], then since the word *go* here does not have an identical name [with the object it denotes], there would be no compound.
In examples such as *bhojyoṣṇam*, words like *uṣṇa* are qualifiers (*guṇavacana*). In that case, if this [term "name"] were absent...

In a *yoga* where there is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*), those [words] would undergo prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*). Therefore, this [rule] is commenced for the sake of subsequent placement (*paranipāta*). Regarding the example "tulyamahān": although a compound is applicable here by the rule "sanmahat" (Pāṇini 2.1.61), nevertheless, because this [present rule] is subsequent, it applies by this very [rule].

It occurs as follows: its scope is when there is a common designation, such as "tulyaśveta" (equally white); and its scope is when there is no common designation, such as "mahāpuruṣa" (great person). In the example "bhojya odanaḥ" (rice is to be eaten), the word *odana* here denotes a genus (*jāti*).
69. *varṇo varṇena* (2.1.69).

The phrase "the qualifier [is compounded] with the qualified" (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*) from sūtra 2.1.57 is understood here. In that case, if both instances of the word *varṇa* were to be taken here as referring to their own form (*svarūpa*), there would be no relationship of qualifier and qualified.

It would not be tenable, because the meaning is non-different. For it is not possible for that very same thing to function as both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) of Devadatta. Even if one were to hold that for one [word] there is the apprehension of its own form (*svarūpa*), while for the other there is the apprehension of the object (*artha*), even so, the word *varṇa* would be a single term denoting a universal (*sāmānya*).

The second term, however, such as the word "kṛṣṇa" (black) and so forth, denotes a specific quality. Consequently, each [term] would lack the status of being either a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or a qualificand (*viśeṣya*). It has been stated previously that the purpose of including the mention of "both" was so that a compound (*samāsa*) occurs only where both [conditions] are present. Therefore, the term "artha" (meaning) must be included in both cases.

He says, "It is understood," and so forth: "denoting a specific variety of color," etc., as in "kṛṣṇasāraṅga" (black-spotted) and "lohitasāraṅga" (red-spotted). But surely the word *kṛṣṇa* (black) and the word *lohita* (red) refer to the parts, whereas the word *sāraṅga* (spotted) refers to the whole; just like the word *śabala* (variegated).

How, then, is there grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between a word such as "black" (*kṛṣṇa*), which functions with respect to a part, and a word such as "spotted" (*sāraṅga*), which functions with respect to the whole? To this he says: "by way of the parts," and so forth.
It is called "black" because of its connection with black parts, and it is called "red" because of its connection with red parts. For this very reason...

Since the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) here is secondary (*gauṇa*), the compound [rule] beginning with "the qualifier is compounded with the qualified" (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*, Pāṇini 2.1.57) does not apply; therefore, this [definition] is commenced so that the designation of a "great name" (*mahatī saṃjñā*) may be understood as being descriptive (*anvartha*). By this, that which is non-primary is the *upasarjana*. It is not [the case that the definition is unnecessary].

And here, the composite whole is not the subordinate element; rather, it is precisely the primary element. However, because the parts exist for the sake of that [whole], they possess subordination. Therefore, it is only the word denoting the part—such as the word "kṛṣṇa"—that possesses the status of a subordinate term (*upasarjana*), and not the word denoting the composite whole.
Of words such as "sāraṅga" and so forth.
70. *kumāraḥ śramaṇādibhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.70).

By the restrictive statement "the word *kumārī* (feminine) is compounded with those [words beginning with *śramaṇā*] only when it is in the feminine gender," and not when it is in the masculine gender, he shows that [the compound] does not apply to the masculine form. For [the rule] does not apply to the masculine.
The sense is that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the feminine gender is thus established. Regarding the rule "by those [words], both ways":

this means [the compound] may be feminine or masculine. But how can a compound, being stated [to occur] with masculine words, be feminine? To this he says: "when there is the mention of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)."
The meaning has already been explained.

71. [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] after a word denoting a quadruped [when it refers to] a pregnant female. (2.1.71) Regarding "quadrupeds" (*catuṣpādaḥ*): those which have four feet are "quadrupeds. By the rule "There is elision of the final part of *pāda* when preceded by words other than *hastin* and so forth" (5.4.138), the final portion is elided. Thus, [the term is] "quadruped genus" (*catuṣpājjāti*).
It must be stated that only those [words] denoting quadrupeds which express a genus (*jāti*) are compounded with *garbhiṇī*;

this is the meaning of the form of the rule that requires explanation. In this regard, the following is the explanation: the mention of "genus" (*jāti*) from the sūtra *poṭā-ādi* (Pāṇini 2.1.65) is understood here. Therefore...
Only that which is denoted by the term "four-footed" is compounded with "pregnant," and nothing else.

72. *Mayūravyaṃsakādayaś ca* (Pāṇini 2.1.72). Regarding the example "mayūravyaṃsakaḥ": it is one who is both a peacock (*mayūra*) and a deceiver (*vyaṃsaka*). Although the word *vyaṃsaka* ought to have been placed first according to the general rule, this specific recitation is for the purpose of placing it last. Thus, in this case:

[This refers to] the group beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka* and ending with *yavanamuṇḍa*. Regarding the rule *chandasi hstegṛhya* and so forth: in a compound where a negative particle (*nañ*) does not precede, the suffix *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap* (Pāṇini 7.1.37). However, in the common language (*bhāṣā*), it becomes *hastegṛhītvā* or *punardatvā*. [The rule] *ehīḍādayo'nyapadārthe* [is also applicable].
Thus: "ehīḍam" refers to that action in which one says "come, worship. Similarly, "ehiyavam" [means "come, [bring] barley"].
"Ehivāṇijā" is that action in which one says "come, merchant.
Similarly, "apehivāṇijā" and "prehivāṇijā. [Likewise, it applies to] that in which one says "ehi svāgatam" ("come, welcome").

In an action [expressed by a verb], that [suffix] is *ṭhehisvāgatā*. Likewise: *ṭhapehisvāgatā*. That action in which there is "pull out the mat" (*prauha kaṭam*) is *ṭhprohakaṭā*. Similarly, *ṭhprohakardamā* and so forth, ending with *āharavasanā*. That action in which there is "cut, O wise one" (*kṛndhi vicakṣaṇa*) is *ṭhkṛndhivicakṣaṇā*. [Also] *ṭhuddharotsṛja*.

Thus: a compound of two finite verbs (*tiṅanta*). Although this is established by the *Gaṇasūtra* "A finite verb may be compounded with another finite verb when there is continuity of action" (*ākhyātam ākhyātena kriyāsātatyai*), this statement is made for the sake of non-continuity (*asātatyārtham*). That action in which one draws out and then discards is "drawing-out-and-discarding" (*uddharotsṛjā*).
And this compound has the action as its primary element (*kriyāpradhāna*). [The example is] "flying up and falling down" (*utpatanipatā*).

*ṭhuta-m-avighamā*—thus, *uddharotsṛja* and so forth refer specifically to non-continuous action. *Uccāvacam* is an irregularly formed compound (*nipātita*). It is analyzed as *udak ca avāk ca*. And it is analyzed as *uccaiś ca nīcaiś ca*, resulting in the irregular form *uccanīcam*.
*Ācita* and *upacita*, when analyzed (*vigṛhya*), become *ṭhācopacam*. *Ācita* and *parācita* become *ṭhācaparācam*. *Niścita* and *pracita* become *ṭhniścapracam*.
*Na kiñcana* becomes *ṭhakiñcanam*. *Snatvākālakaḥ*.
The reading "pītvāsthirakaḥ" and "bhuktvāsuhitaḥ" is for the purpose of having the udātta accent on the final syllable;

furthermore, the absence of the suffix *lyap* is prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation). In the case of "proṣyapāpīyān," both the single-word status and the single tone (monotony) result from the compound. Likewise for "utpatyapākalā" and so forth. [Also] "nityarohiṇī."

"Niṣaṇṇaśyāmā," "apehiprasavā," "ihapañcamī," and "ihadvitīyā"—in these cases, there is both a single word-form (*aikapadya*) and a single accent (*ekasvarya*) within the compound. Regarding the rule: "In the sense of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*), [the particle] *jahi* is frequently used with an object, and it designates the agent," thus: *jahī*.

The second person singular ending is *loṇ*. A word ending in that is frequently compounded with an object when frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*) is implied, provided that the agent is expressed by the compound itself.
One who says "Go away, go away, you blockhead! repeatedly is called "the go-away-blockhead" (*jahijoḍa*).
In the example *jahistambam*, there is the imperative (*loṭ*) suffix; the *sip* ending is replaced by *j* according to *ṭhhanterjaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.36).
Here, the action denoted by *jahī* functions as the object (*karman*).
Regarding the rule *ākhyātam* and so forth: a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) is compounded with another finite verb when there is continuity of action (*kriyāsātatya*).

In the case of *gamyamāne* (when it is understood), where it is repeatedly said, "Eat! Drink!", there the compound *aśnītapibata* is employed. This compound has the action as its primary meaning. In the same way, compounds such as *pacatabhṛjjata* and others are to be understood. Where it is addressed, "Split the salt," that is called *bhindhilavaṇā*. Likewise...
‘Ṭhpacalavaṇā’ means ‘salted with five spices.’
Thus ends the second chapter of the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable teacher Jinendrabuddhi, who was a disciple of Bodhisattva.
First Pāda
Now, the second chapter.
The Second Pāda. 1. *pūrvāparādharottaramekadeśinaikādhikaraṇe* (2.2.1). [The commentary states:
"By implication, these denote a part (*ekadeśa*). For if the words *pūrva* and so forth— [Note: The provided source text ends abruptly here.]

If they were not words denoting a part, the status of the subsequent member as a "possessor of parts" (ekadeśin) would not be understood; for a possessor of parts exists only in relation to its parts. Therefore, it is understood that although words such as *pūrva* (eastern/first) are stated in a general sense, they are compounded by virtue of their functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) as words denoting a specific part.

In order to clarify the meaning of the statement that "the mention of a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇa*) is a qualification of the proponent (*ekadeśin*"), he says: "And one," and so forth. "One" means a substance (*dravya*) qualified by the number one. By the expression "one substance" (*ekadravya*), the word *adhikaraṇa* here refers to a substance.

He shows that [the word] "upāt" [is a locative]. But is it not the case that "ekadeśinā" ends in the third case (instrumental) and "ekādhikaraṇe" ends in the seventh case (locative)? Therefore, how can there be a relationship of qualifier and qualified through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between these two words which have different case endings?
It is appropriate; and how could it not be so? [One might object] that it is because the meanings are different. This is not the case;

for since "sūtras are like Vedic meters" (Mahābhāṣya 1.1.1), and because of the word *bahulam* in the rule "there is extensive transposition" (Pāṇini 3.1.85), the locative case here in the expression *ekādhikaraṇe* has the sense of the instrumental case.

This is not by virtue of the rule *ṭhsaptamyadhikaraṇe ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.36). Therefore, there is no difference in meaning, and thus there is no fault. [The statement] "this rule is an exception to the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*)" is made because of the expression "by one who [possesses] a part" (*ekadeśinā*); from this word, it is understood that words such as *pūrva* (eastern, etc. denote a part (*ekadeśa*).
For words denoting a related entity necessarily bring to mind their correlative.

In that context, regarding the relationship between a part and a whole, when the genitive case is produced according to the rule "the sixth [case]... (Pāṇini 2.2.8), a compound would result; therefore, this present rule is an exception to that.

In the expression "pūrvakāyaḥ" (the front part of the body), the word *kāya* (body) is a whole (*ekadeśin*) and is a single substance (*ekadravya*), because it is associated with the number one. Regarding the phrase "pūrvaṃ nābheḥ kāyasya" (that which is prior to the navel of the body): the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in "nābheḥ" is used in the sense of spatial relation (*digyoga*).
The intended meaning is: "that which is prior to the navel, belonging to the body."

Therefore, in this case, the *nābhi* (navel) is not a part-possessor (*ekadeśin*). What then? It is the limit (*avadhibhūta*); thus, the word *nābhi*, being expressive of that [limit] and ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*), does not form a compound. However, for the word *kāya* (body), which expresses the part-possessor, a compound does indeed occur, even though the word *pūrva* (prior) is dependent (*sāpekṣatve*) [on another word].

It has been indicated in the rule *upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ sāmānyāprayoge* (Pāṇini 2.1.56) that a compound occurs even for a principal term (*pradhāna*) when it is dependent, because of the predominance of the body (*kāya*). [Note:
The original reading was *pūrvaṃ chātrāṇām āmantraya*, which is the root-text and supported by the *Padamañjarī*.]

"Invite the students. Here, there is no compound because the word *chātrāṇām* refers to a single possessor (*ekadeśin*) qualified by the number plural. Now, one might object: "In this case, since it is subsequent, the prohibition of the genitive compound by the rule *na nirdhāraṇe* (Pāṇini 2.2.10) will apply; so what is the purpose of [the mention of] the locative case?"
This is the established reading. What is the purpose of including the term "single substratum" (*ekādhikaraṇa*)? This is not so;

for if the word "invite" (*āmantrayasva*) were not required, then the sentence would conclude with only the preceding words "of the students" (*chātrāṇām*), and in that case, since there would be no act of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), this would not fall within the scope of that prohibition.

Thus, even though there is no single common substratum (*ekādhikaraṇa*), a compound could still occur with that which possesses multiple numbers (*anekasaṃkhya*) as the "part-possessor" (*ekadeśin*). Now, if one were to assume a selection (*nirddhāraṇa*) by supplying some action or other— on the grounds that every sentence is completed by an action— to the earlier word *chātrāṇām* (of the students), then in the same way [one might supply an action] to *pūrvam*.

In the case of "of the body" (*kāyasya*) as well, there would be a selection (*nirddhāraṇa*), for here too there exists the act of drawing forth (*ākarṣaṇa-kriyā*) which serves as the cause for selection. And thus, this yoga being commenced with respect to the very same object as that [previous] yoga would constitute an exception (*apavāda*) to it. Furthermore, a conflict between a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*) is not logically tenable.

How then does the prohibition "not [after a word] denoting a part, when used for selection" (Pāṇini 2.2.10)— namely, "of that which is preceded by a numeral, viśva, or āvi," etc.— apply? Since he states "of *ahna-* preceded by a numeral, *viśva*, or *āvi*" (Pāṇini 6.3.110), one understands from this indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) that [the rule applies] to *ahna-* in relation to any whole (*ekadeśin*).
It becomes a compound; for otherwise, the state of being preceded by "sāya" (evening) would not be possible for the word "ahan" (day), and thus this statement would be incorrect.
2. *Ardham* is neuter. (Pāṇini 2.2.2) [The commentary states: "But when *ardha* signifies an equal division, it is a neuter word whose gender is inherent; this is the [word] being referred to here.
If this is so, should one simply have used the term "equal" (*sama*)? It cannot be done in that way.

Because the word *sama* has multiple meanings. For instance, it applies even to a place devoid of elevations and depressions—as in the injunction "one should sacrifice on level ground," which means one should sacrifice on ground free from elevations and depressions. Furthermore, it is also said to mean "equal division"; even so, [the property of] heaviness...

[Objection: Should the mention of the neuter gender (*napuṃsakagrahaṇa*) then be made? [Reply: It need not be made; for the mention of the neuter will occur simply by the fact that it is indicated by the neuter gender in the word "half" (*ardham*). [Objection: This is not so; for if the mention of the neuter were not made, the indication of the neuter would be based on the form of the word itself.

Thus it should be understood, as in the cases of "svam ajñātidhanākhyāyām" (Pāṇini 1.1.35) and "bandhuni bahuvrīhau" (Pāṇini 6.1.14); consequently, the neuter gender of the word *ardha* would not be disregarded. In this way, even when it is not neuter in gender—

It would result in a grammatical conflict. Therefore, in order to ensure that the word *ardha* retains its neuter gender, it must be stated that it is "neuter" (*napuṃsakam*). [In the example] *ardhapippalī*, the feminine gender would otherwise apply by the rule *paravalliṅgam* (Pāṇini 2.4.26). Consequently, in this case, the rule *gostriyor upasarjanasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.48) would apply.

Why does shortness (*hrasvatva*) not occur? Because [the word] is not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*). Its status as a subordinate member, however, arises from the rule *ekavibhakti ca* (Pāṇini 1.2.44). Here, the mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*) from the preceding rule *vibhāṣā chandasi* (1.2.36) is understood to carry over; and that has been explained as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).

Regarding the phrase "half of the village" (*grāmārddhaḥ*): the meaning is "one part of the village. Regarding the phrase "half of the animal belonging to Devadatta" (*ardhaṃ paśor devadattasya*): there is no compound with the word *devadatta*. This is because Devadatta is not a constituent part (*anekadeśitvāt*); for he is not a part, but rather the owner.

However, in the case of the word *paśu* used in a partial sense (*ekadeśin*), a compound is indeed formed with it. Even though the word *paśu* is dependent (*sāpekṣa*), a compound still occurs because the animal (*paśu*) is the primary element (*pradhāna*), as in: *ardhapaśur devadattasya* ("half-animal belonging to Devadatta").
3. *dvitīya-tṛtīya-caturtha-turyāṇy antarasyām* (Pāṇini 2.2.3).
Because of the inclusion of the term *antarasyām*, that [compound] also becomes a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).
Now, these words beginning with *dvitīya* end in affixes denoting ordinal numbers (*pūraṇapratyaya*); in that regard, by the rule beginning with *pūraṇa-*... [the following applies].

A prohibition of the compound ought to apply; how then can that [compound] also occur? To this he says: "pūraṇa," etc. If there were a prohibition of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) here, then the inclusion of the term "anyatarasyām" (optionally) would be purposeless, because the formation of the analytical sentence (*vākya*) is already established by the *mahāvibhāṣā* rule itself.

The word *bhāvaḥ* [is used]. "The second of alms" (*dvitīyaṃ bhikṣāyāḥ*) means the second part of the alms. "The second of the alms for the beggar" (*dvitīyaṃ bhikṣāyā bhikṣukasya*): here, a compound with the word *bhikṣuka* (beggar) does not occur. For he is not a "part-possessor" (*ekadeśin*); rather, he is the owner (*svāmī*). [This applies to] the word *turya*.
The word ending in the suffix *yat*— formed according to the rule "ṭhcaturaścchayatāvādyakṣaralopaśca" (Vārttika 571)—
is expressive of the sense of ordinal number (*pūraṇārtha*).

4. *prāptāpanne ca dvitīyayā* (Pāṇini 2.2.4). [The commentary states: "In the case of a compound with a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*), provided that [the conditions for] a second-case compound are met. This is by means of the rule *dvitīyā śrita-* (2.1.24), etc. [It further says: "Because of the prescription of the compound, that [compound] also occurs. By the word *api* ("also"), this [present rule] also applies.

In the expression *prāptajīvikaḥ*, there is the status of being a secondary member (*upasarjana*) by virtue of the rule "and that which has a single case-ending" (1.2.44). The shortening of the vowel, however, is due to the rule "of the secondary member [ending] in go or a feminine suffix" (1.2.48). And in this case, by the rule "the gender is that of the subsequent word" (2.4.26), whatever gender belongs to *jīvikā* [is applied].

Why does it not apply to the collective whole? Because of the statement: "A prohibition must be stated for *dvigu*, *prāpta*, *āpanna*, *laṃpūra*, and *ava-gati* compounds" (Vārttika 163). Therefore, whatever gender belongs to *prāpta* and *āpanna* is the gender of the collective whole. Now, when...
When the compound *prāptājīvikām* is formed by analyzing it as a *vigraha*, what is the example?

It is *prāptajīvikaḥ*. Why does the suffix *ṭāp* not appear [in the feminine]? Because the suffix *ṭāp* is eliminated through the application of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) by means of the rule-break (*yogavibhāga*) "the feminine [stem] is like the masculine" (*striyāḥ puṃvat*, Pāṇini 6.3.34).

5. *kālāḥ parimāṇinā* (Pāṇini 2.2.5). [The word] *parimāṇavacanāḥ* [is understood] by implication (*sāmarthyāt*). For it is only if the words for time (*kālaśabda*) denote a measure (*parimāṇavacana*) that the status of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) as denoting the thing measured (*parimāṇin*) is understood, and not otherwise. Therefore...

Although the term *kāla* (time) is mentioned without qualification, it is understood by implication that "words denoting time which signify measure (*parimāṇa*) are compounded. Now, one might object: time is not a measure, because it has no limit; so how can words denoting it [be said to denote a measure]?

Do they become expressions of measurement? This is not a fault; for although they are not denoters of primary measurement, they certainly are of secondary measurement. For here, since the primary nature of measurement does not belong to time—such as months and so forth—it follows by implication.

By resorting to a metaphorical designation based on the commonality of being a measure that serves as a cause for delimitation, time is intended to possess the nature of a measure. For even months and so forth indicate the movements of the sun which are related to birth and other events; therefore, they are causes of delimitation.

"The commencement of this *yoga* is for the purpose of [providing an alternative] in the domain of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). For when there is a relationship between a measure and the thing measured, the genitive case must occur after the word expressing the measure. And wherever the genitive occurs, that is the domain of the genitive compound; therefore, this *yoga* pertains to the domain of the genitive compound.
It is now commenced. In the expression *māsajātaḥ* ("born after a month"), *jātaḥ* is the object of measurement (*parimāṇī*), and *māsaḥ* is its measure (*parimāṇa*).
In the expression *dvayahajātaḥ*, *dvyahaḥ* is a compound meaning "the collection of two days. [This is formed] by Pāṇini 5.4.91: *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac*, and by 6.4.145: *ahnaṣṭakhoreva*.

There is elision of the *ṭi* [the final vowel and following consonant]. By the rule "na saṃkhyādeḥ samāhāre" (Pāṇini 5.4.89), there is a prohibition of the substitution of *ahna*. Thus, one born after two days is called *dvyahajātaḥ*. Now, what is the purpose of the plural indication in the term "kālāḥ"? If it is argued that it is for the sake of excluding a rule based on the word's own form (*svarūpavidhi*), this is not so; for indeed...

When the essential nature [of the first member] is grasped, it is understood that the subsequent member denotes the possessor of the measure (*parimāṇin*), because the word *kāla* does not denote a measure itself. Therefore, by the very fact of grasping the possessor of the measure, there will be the inclusion of words such as "month" (*māsa*) which denote specific divisions of time. If this is so, then...
This use of the plural number is intended to indicate the abundance of meaning within the composition of the Sūtras due to the great volume of material. As it has been said:
"The intentions of the Teachers [are revealed] by a gesture, by a glance, or by a great composition of Sūtras."

"are perceived. By this, it is understood that even a three-word compound (*tripada*) with a numeral as its prior member forms a *tatpuruṣa* compound with a word denoting the object measured (*parimāṇin*). Consequently, forms such as *dvyahnajātaḥ* ("born after two days") are established. This is derived by analyzing [the compound] as "two days have been born for him" (*dve ahanī jātam asya*), thus forming a three-word construction.

When that *tatpuruṣa* compound has been formed, with the word *jāta* as the final member (*uttarapada*), the two preceding members become a two-part *tatpuruṣa* by virtue of Pāṇini 2.1.51: *taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca*.
Then, by Pāṇini 5.4.88: *ahno 'hn etebhyaḥ*, the substitution of *ahna-* for *ahan-* occurs.

6. *nañ* | (2.2.6) The *ñ* in *nañ* is for the purpose of specification, so that [the rule] *nalopo nañaḥ* (6.3.73) does not apply to words such as *pāmanaputra*. [This is because of the rule: *lomādipāmādipicchādibhyaḥ śanelacaḥ*.

(5.2.100) Now, regarding the term *abrāhmaṇa*, what is the predominant element of this compound? Is it a *tatpuruṣa* compound, which has the meaning of the final member as its predominant element, as in *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man")? Or is it an *avyayībhāva* compound, which has the meaning of the initial member as its predominant element, as in *amakṣikam* ("without flies")?

The *bahuvrīhi* compound has as its primary referent a meaning other than that of its constituent members, as in the example "a country without Brāhmaṇas" (*abrāhmaṇakaḥ deśaḥ*). If this is so, then when one says, "Bring the non-Brāhmaṇa" (*abrāhmaṇam ānaya*), would it not follow that any Brāhmaṇa whatsoever could be brought? Now, if this word "Brāhmaṇa" has exclusion (*nivṛtti*) as its meaning, and that exclusion is inherent [in the word] by means of the negative particle (*nañ*), [then there is no such fault].

It is held that [the word] "dyotya" means "illuminated. And this being so, if its meaning were merely non-existence (*abhāva*), then when one says, "Bring a non-Brahmin," no one at all would be brought. This is not a fault; for every word, when employed in its own primary sense, requires an agreement regarding its usage. And thus it has been said:
"The self, having come together with the intellect, joins the mind to objects through the desire to speak.
And that knowledge is of two kinds: correct and false. The word *brāhmaṇa* applies to both of these; [it applies] when the word *brāhmaṇa* is employed preceded by correct knowledge.

There is no operation of the negative particle (*nañ*); for nothing at all is produced there by the negative particle. However, its operation certainly exists when preceded by false cognition (*mithyājñāna*). For in that case, it indicates to another the state of being produced by false cognition. And false cognition—

It is caused by a defective sense organ (*duṣṭendriya*). Since that [defect] is not possible without a similarity (*sādṛśya*), when there is a negation, the meaning of the compound arises as something similar to the other referent (*padārtha*). And so it has been said: "When joined with *nañ* (the negative particle), [the word] refers to something else that is similar; for such is the comprehension of the meaning" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 65).

Therefore, when it is said, "Bring a non-Brahmin," the cognition arises with respect to a Kṣatriya or similar person who resembles a Brahmin; thus, there is no occasion for the aforementioned defect to arise.

7. *īṣadakṛtā* | (Pāṇini 2.2.7) [The commentary states: "It should be stated that [the rule applies] with a word expressing a slight degree (*īṣadguṇavacanena*)"; the meaning is that this indeclinable *īṣat* is compounded, but not with every non-derivative (*akṛdanta*) word—this form [of the sūtra] is to be explained in this way. Now, this...

Explanation: The term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], and it is understood as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, the compound will occur only with a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*), and not with any other. In the example "īṣadgārgyaḥ," the word *gārgya* denotes a genus (*jāti*), not a quality.

But is it not said that [the suffix] *kṛt* is used [in such cases], whereby forms such as *īṣatpītaḥ* ("slightly drunk") and *īṣadunnataḥ* ("slightly raised") would not be established, because words like *pīta* are *kṛdanta* (ending in a *kṛt* suffix)? This is not a fault; for these words beginning with *pīta* should be understood as being unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*), and not as ending in a *kṛt* suffix.
8. The sixth [case].

(2.2.8) Regarding the rule *kṛdyogā ca* and so forth: it should be explained as "the sixth case characterized by connection with a *kṛt*-suffix is compounded. In this regard, the following is the explanation: namely, that this [sūtra] states *ktena ca pūjāyām*.

(2.2.12) By beginning the prohibition with the rules "and [the genitive] denoting the locus" (2.2.13), "and in the case of the object" (2.2.14), and "also in the case of the agent, [with words ending] in *tṛc* and *aka*" (2.2.15)—provided that these sūtras did not exist—it indicates this: "The genitive [case-ending] connected with a *kṛt*-suffix is compounded"; otherwise, [this would not be understood].

The undertaking of a prohibition would be purposeless, because there is no prior application [of the rule]. In the case of *idhmavraścanaḥ*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). Alternatively, by the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.113), it is used in the sense of an agent (*kartari*).
Then, by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65), the genitive case is applied to the object (*karmaṇi*), as in *palāśaśātanaḥ*.

Thus [it is said]. In the case of the causative (*ṇyanta*) root *śad*, the substitution of *t* for *d* occurs by the rule "In the case of *śad*, when not meaning 'to go', *t* is substituted" (Pāṇini 7.3.42). The suffix *lyuṭ* and the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) are applied as before. Why is this stated, given that the formation of a compound with a genitive—even one characterized by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix—is already established by the rule "with a genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhī*) alone?
To this he says: "And because [the compound] is prescribed as a specific rule," and so forth; this is easily understood. 9. *Yājakādibhiśca* (Pāṇini 2.2.9).
The word *ca* (and) serves to include those not explicitly mentioned. By that, the genitive case is compounded with words denoting qualities residing in that [person].
Thus it should not be said that "it should not be so stated," because it is already established by this very [statement].

"Abiding in that" means *tatsthāḥ*. Since there is no other subject under discussion, by the word "that" (*tat*), only the qualities (*guṇāḥ*) are referred back. Therefore, those qualities which exist within the very nature of the qualities do not [exist elsewhere].

Sometimes, when [the quality] has substance as its essence, the sixth case (genitive) is compounded with them. Although there is indeed no quality that does not reside in a substance— since every quality is dependent upon a substance—
nevertheless, certain words for qualities refer to the possessor of the quality either through the elision of the possessive suffix *matup* or by metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*).

Qualities residing in a substance cause one to understand that quality as following its substratum, as in "the cloth is white" or "the blanket is red. Others, however, define a quality as that which is distinct from its locus and does not function as a subordinate element relative to the substance, as in "the fragrance of sandalwood" or "the [color] of the monkey."

Regarding the term *rasa*: therefore, with respect to the operation of the denotative power (*abhidhāna-śakti*), the qualification "residing therein" (*tad-sthaiḥ*) is appropriate. This is what is meant: those qualities (*guṇa*) which are conveyed by their own words as not having attained the status of being subordinate (*anupasarjana-bhāva*) to the substance (*dravya*), with those [qualities] the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) is formed.

The fragrance of sandalwood is "sandalwood-fragrance" (candanasya gandhaḥ), and the taste of wood-apple is "wood-apple-taste" (kapitthasya rasaḥ). For fragrance and the other qualities are conveyed by their own words as being already distinguished from their substrates; they are never understood as following the locus or functioning as qualifiers with respect to the substance.
10. *na nirdhāraṇe* (2.2.10).

[In the example] "Among humans, the Kṣatriya is the most brave," the genitive case is applied by the rule *yataśca nirdhāraṇam* (2.3.41). [This is an exception to] the rule *pratipadavidhānā ca* etc., and is governed by *ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe* (2.3.50).

The meaning is that one must explain this form as follows: having set aside the sixth case ending prescribed by the general rule (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), that other sixth case ending which is prescribed by a specific rule (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*)—namely, the one ordained by a specific sutra (*pratipadavidhāna*)—is not compounded. In this regard, the explanation is that the word "not" (*na*) is treated as a separate *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a grammatical rule).

Therefore, the sixth case ending prescribed by a specific rule (*pratipadavidhāna*) is not compounded. If this is so, how is it that [compounds] such as *gṛhasvāmī*, *vidyādāyādaḥ*, and *pṛthvīśvaraḥ* exist? For this sixth case ending prescribed by a specific rule would otherwise be barred; thus, by means of the particle *ca*, a re-introduction (*pratiprasava*) of the sixth case is effected. Indeed, it is not [barred] for one who knows this.
The genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is prescribed by a specific rule (*pratipadavidhāna*). Therefore, the prohibition "not [in the sense] of selection" (*na nirdhāraṇe*) is enjoined.
