Furthermore, in the rule *yataśca nirdhāraṇam* (Pāṇini 2.3.41), that same genitive characterized as a "remainder" (*śeṣalakṣaṇā*) is reintroduced by means of the word "and" (*ca*); otherwise, this [genitive] would also be merely one prescribed by a specific rule.

In that case, the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) would not be possible; consequently, the prohibition "not in the sense of selection" (*na nirdhāraṇe*) would be rendered meaningless. In the example "knowledge of ghee" (*sarpiṣo jñānam*), the genitive is used for the instrument (*karaṇe*) according to Pāṇini 2.3.51: *jño 'vidarthasya*.

11. *pūraṇaguṇasuhitārthasadavyayatavyasamānādhikaraṇena* (Pāṇini 2.2.11). [The genitive case is not used] with a word ending in a ordinal number (*pūraṇa*), a quality (*guṇa*), a word meaning "satisfied" (*suhita*), a word having the sense of "existent" (*sat*), an indeclinable (*avyaya*), a word ending in *-tavya*, or a word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Example: *chātrāṇāṃ pañcamaḥ* ("the fifth among the students"). [The suffix] *ḍaṭ* is applied by the rule *tasya pūraṇe ḍaṭ* (5.3.48), and [the augment] *maṭ* is added by the rule *nāntādasaṃkhyādermaṭ* (5.3.49) [to form *pañcama-*]. This occurs in the relationship between a whole (*samudāya*) and its part (*samudāyin*).

The sixth case [ending] is used in the sense of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*). Thus, in expressions such as "the whiteness of the crane" (*valākāyāḥ śauklyam*) and "the blackness of the crow" (*kākasya kārṣṇyam*), it should be understood that the sixth case is used in the sense of the remainder with respect to the relationship between a quality and its possessor (*guṇaguṇisambandha*). In the expression "the duty of a Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇasya kartavyam*), the sixth case is used according to the rule *kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā* (Pāṇini 2.3.71). Now, how is it...?
The compound *go-viṃśati* is a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound; since a number is a quality (*guṇa*), one might object that the prohibition [of the feminine suffix] ought to apply. This is not a fault;
for when [Pāṇini] states, "Also after *niṣka*, up to *śata* and *sahasra*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.2.119), he thereby provides an indication (*jñāpaka*).

A compound occurs with a numeral. For otherwise, it would not be possible for the nominal stem *niṣka* to have "ending in a hundred or a thousand" (*śatasahasrāntatā*) without that [numeral]. [Objection: "A compound can indeed occur with *tavyat* along with its *anubandha*. [Response: No, because that [form] is not included due to the paribhāṣā regarding the absence of an *anubandha*.

Regarding the compound *brāhmaṇakartavyam*: by the rule "a *kṛt*-suffix following a verbal root, a *gati*, a *kāraka*, or an *upapada* [retains its original accent]" (Pāṇini 6.2.139), the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) becomes circumflex (*svarita*) by virtue of its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). If, however, the compound were formed even with a suffix lacking an *anubandha*, then once the original accent had been applied, it would subsequently be overridden by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).

The middle member would be udātta, and that is undesirable; therefore, the compound is prohibited with the suffixless form, but not with the one bearing the anubandha. What would happen [if it were allowed]? He thinks as follows:
even if this prohibition were made, there would still necessarily be a *viśeṣaṇasamāsa* (descriptive compound) here.

If, in this inevitable compound, it were a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), what fault would there be for which this genitive compound is prohibited? [The answer is: "There would be no fixed rule regarding the prior placement [of the members]"—as stated in the *Kāśikā* by the passage beginning with "pūrvanipātāniyamaḥ."

He states the fault: if it were a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), then since both words would be designated by the nominative case, they would both be subordinate (*upasarjana*); consequently, in some instances, even the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) would undergo prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*), which is not desired. In a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*), however, only the qualifier [is placed first].
Since it is prescribed as the first member in the rules governing compounds (*samāsaśāstra*), it undergoes prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*); thus, this undesirable consequence does not arise.

12. *ktena ca pūjāyām* (Pāṇini 2.2.12). He will state [later] that "after [roots] having the sense of *mati*, *buddhi*, and *pūjā*, [the suffix *kta* is used in the passive sense]. The word *ktam* is the remainder of the sentence. It means "this refers to that *kta*. That which is [prescribed] by the rule *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.188)— [The commentary continues: ...by this rule, [the suffix *kta* is applied]. The mention of this [suffix *kta*] here [in the present sūtra] is for the purpose of including the sense of "worship" (*pūjā*) within the category of "verbs having the sense of *mati*, *buddhi*, and *pūjā*" (*matibuddhipūjārtha*). Otherwise, since the sense of worship is not included in the group [of roots] beginning with *man* and *budh*, the suffix *kta* would not apply to the word *arcita*. Therefore, the mention of *kta* here is intended to include the sense of worship. Thus, the meaning is: "and when the sense of worship is expressed, [the sixth case ending is used] even after a word ending in *kta*. For example: *rājñām arcitaḥ* ("honored by kings"). Why is the word *pūjāyām* ("in the sense of worship") mentioned? [To show that] the sixth case ending is not used when the sense is not that of worship. For example: *odanasya pūrṇaḥ kumbhaḥ* ("a jar full of rice"). Why is the word *ca* ("and") mentioned? To indicate that the sixth case ending is used even when the sense of worship is not expressed. For example: *rājñām mataḥ* ("approved by kings"), *rājñām buddhaḥ* ("understood by kings"), *rājñām jñātaḥ* ("known by kings"). Why is the word *pūjāyām* mentioned [only once]? Because the sense of worship is not included in the group [of roots] beginning with *man* and *budh*. If it were not mentioned, the sense of worship would not be included in the category of *matibuddhipūjārtha*, and thus the suffix *kta* would not apply to the word *arcita*. The suffix *kta* has been prescribed; this [rule] applies to the inclusion of every such prescribed [suffix], not only to that which is prescribed in the sense of worship (*pūjā*). This is the intended meaning. Therefore he says:

"The mention of 'worship' (*pūjā*) is for the purpose of indication (*upalakṣaṇārtha*). For what is it an indication? It is an indication of the [section beginning with] "thought and intellect" (*mati-buddhi*).
In such rules as (3.2.188), regarding that *kta* suffix which is prescribed for meanings specified [in the sūtra],

such as those beginning with *mati*: by this, the prohibition of the sixth-case compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) applies not only to that *kta* prescribed in the sense of "reverence" (*pūjā*), but also to that which is prescribed in the senses of "thought" (*mati*) and "perception" (*buddhi*).
This was also prescribed by him [Patañjali] in the rule "rājñāṃ mataḥ" (approved by kings). The genitive case is used here by Pāṇini’s rule "ktasya ca vartamāne" (2.3.67).

What is the purpose of the word "pūjāyām" (in the sense of honor)? Consider: *chātrasya hasitam* (the laughing of the student), which is called *chātrahasitam*. Here, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*) according to Pāṇini 3.3.114, and the genitive is used as a residual relation (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇā*).

13. *Adhikaraṇavācinā ca* (Pāṇini 2.2.13). [Example: *idameṣām āsitam*. The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*), as in "that in which something is placed" (*asyate 'smin*).
By the rule *adhikaraṇavācini ca* (2.3.68), the genitive case is employed. The same applies to examples such as *pītam* and others.
Why is it stated "expressing the locus" (*adhikaraṇavācinā*)? [Consider the example: *chātrasya hasitam* (the laughing of the student), which becomes *chātrahasitam*.
This is the mention of that genitive case [prescribed] by the rule *ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi* (2.3.66).
Furthermore, this is understood from the prohibition in *kartari ca* (2.2.16); for if [it were not so],...

If this were intended to include every genitive case that occurs in relation to an object (*karman*), then the author would not have formulated the prohibition again in the rule *kartari ca* (Pāṇini 2.2.16); for [the desired result] would already be established by this very [present rule]. For in those cases where the suffixes *tṛc* and *aka* are prescribed in relation to the agent (*kartṛ*), they necessarily relate to the object (*karman*).

The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) ought to occur. Therefore, because of the repeated prohibition stated in *kartari ca* (Pāṇini 2.2.16), it is determined that the genitive prescribed here refers to that which is enjoined when both [agent and object] are eligible [for the genitive], namely the genitive in the object (*karmaṇi*).
This is the genitive [referred to] in the rule *ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.66).

In compounds such as *grahaṇādidhmavraścanaḥ* ("one who cuts fuel starting from gathering it"), *palāśaśātanaḥ* ("one who fells the *palāśa* tree"), and *ikṣubhakṣikāṃ me dhārayasi* ("you owe me the eating of sugarcane"), the prohibition of compounding does not apply.

15. *tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari* | (Pāṇini 2.2.15) In examples such as *bhavataḥ śāyikā*, the suffix *ṇvuc* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) by rule 3.3.111, *paryāyārhaṇotpattiṣu ṇvuc*. Since it means "the act of lying down" (*śayanam*), the genitive case is used for the agent (*kartṛ*) by rule 2.3.65, *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*. [The same applies] when the suffix *tṛc* is used.

In the case of a *kartṛ* (agent) [expressed by a kṛt suffix], the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) does not occur, because the agent has already been expressed by that very suffix. If so, for what purpose is the mention of the *tṛc* suffix? He says: "Therefore," and so forth. In the example "He holds a sugarcane-eater for me" (*ikṣubhakṣikāṃ me dhārayati*), the suffix *ṇyuc* is applied as before. Here, from the word *ikṣu* (sugarcane), the genitive occurs in the sense of the object (*karman*) due to its connection with a *kṛt* suffix.

The genitive case [in *kṛti*] is by virtue of the rule *kartari ṣaṣṭhī*; it applies only when there is a connection with a *kṛt* suffix. It does not apply in the context of the rule *ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.66), because of the statement in the Vārttika: "There is a prohibition regarding the suffixes *aka* and *akā*."

16. *kartari ca* (2.2.16). [The commentary states: "Because there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the suffix *it* in other cases. This refers to the agentive suffix *tṛc*. By implication (*sāmarthyāt*), this is a qualifier of the word *eka*. The reason for mentioning the term *kartṛ* here is that a qualifier is only employed when both possibility and deviation are present.

The relationship of qualifier and qualified (viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva) occurs. For the suffix *tṛc* does not deviate from the agent (*kartṛ*), since it is prescribed only for the agent; however, the suffix *ak* does deviate from the agent, as it is also prescribed in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*). Therefore, by implication (*sāmarthya*), the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) is a qualifier of the suffix *ak* alone, and not [of *tṛc*].

The *tṛca* [verse] is "apāṃ sraṣṭā. In the phrase "apāṃ sraṣṭā," the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*). In the word "apāṃ sraṣṭā," there is the substitution of *ṣ* according to Pāṇini 8.2.36 (*vraścādi*). The augment *am* is applied according to Pāṇini 6.1.58 (*sṛjidṛśorjhalyamakiti*).

"Now, as for the phrase beginning with ‘nanu ca’... The intention is that a compound must necessarily occur here because [the word *hotṛ*] is listed among the words beginning with *yājaka*. The resolution is provided by the passage beginning with “sambandhiśabdasya,” [stating] that by means of the word *hotṛ*, which is a relative term (*sambandhiśabda*), [the compound is formed].

By virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), the word *bhartṛ* is also understood there as a relative term; however, this [word under discussion] is a verbal derivative (*kriyāśabda*)—one who supports (*bibharti*) is a supporter (*bhartṛ*). In the example "the drinker of barley-meal" (*saktūnāṃ pāyakaḥ*), the suffix *yuk* is applied according to Pāṇini 7.3.33:
*āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ*. Now, for what purpose is the suffix *tṛc* used?

If you argue that the mention of the word *sānubandhakasya* (of that which has an anubandha) is for the purpose of excluding the suffix *tṛn*, this is not so; for when that [suffix] is joined [to a word], the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is prohibited by the rule "na lokāvyayaniṣṭhā" (Pāṇini 2.3.69), and so forth.
If this is the case, then this very [mention] is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that [the genitive] occurs in some instances even when joined with *tṛn*. By means of that—
Thus, the statement "Bhīṣma is the remover of the grief of the Kurus," and so forth, is established.
17. *nityaṃ krīḍājīvikayoḥ* | (2.2.17) [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] invariably after a word ending in *ṭhak*, when the word denotes either a game (*krīḍā*) or a livelihood (*jīvikā*). For example:

*uddālakapuṣpabhañjikā*. Here, while the rule *rogākhyāyāṃ ṇvul bahulam* (3.3.108) is still in force, the suffix *ṇvul* is applied by the rule *saṃjñāyām* (3.3.109), as the word refers to a name (*saṃjñā*) such as "the plucking of *uddālaka* flowers" and so forth.

The genitive case is used for the object. In the examples "dantalekhakaḥ" (one who carves teeth) and "nakhalekhakaḥ" (one who carves nails), the suffix *ṇvul* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.133 (*ṇvultṛcau*). Regarding the optional formation of a compound with the word "krīḍā" (play) as the object, the rule 2.2.8 (*ṣaṣṭhī*) provides for such a compound by means of the *mahāvibhāṣā* (the great option). Furthermore, regarding livelihood (*jīvikā*), the rule *kartari ca* [2.2.16] applies.
(2.2.16) Since this prohibition has been established, this [sūtra] is commenced. In that regard, what is the purpose of the mention of *nitya* ("obligatory")?

It is for the sake of livelihood (*jīvikā*). Otherwise, however, by the force of the commencement [of the rule], this will be obligatory. But regarding livelihood, if the mention of *nitya* were absent, [the suffix] would be optional due to the governing rule of *mahāvibhāṣā*.
The term "nitya" (invariable) was included for the purpose that there should be a compound, and also for the sake of what follows.

18. *kugatiprādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18). Regarding the statement "the word *ku* is understood as an indeclinable (*avyaya*)," its status as an indeclinable is due to its lacking gender and number, and not because it is listed among the particles (*nipāta*). For this [word *ku*] is not recited there [in the list of particles]. [The commentary continues: "It does not denote a substance."
That which exists in a substance such as earth (*pṛthivī*) and so forth is not included here. Why is this? He says:

"Because of its association with motion (*gati*) and the like. This has already been explained. Regarding the word *koṣṇam*: by the rule *īṣadarthe ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.105), there is the substitution of *kā* for *ku*.
Regarding "kavoṣṇam": the substitution of *kava* is applied by the rule *kavaṃ coṣṇe* (Pāṇini 6.3.107). Regarding "kaduṣṇam":
the substitution of *kat* is applied by the rule *koḥ kat tatpuruṣe 'ci* (Pāṇini 6.3.101). Regarding "kupuruṣaḥ," it is used in the sense of "wicked.
Regarding "duṣkṛtam," the prefix *dus-* occurs in the sense of difficulty (*kṛcchra*). [The rule applies to] that which has *i*, *u*, or *ṛ* as its penultimate phoneme.

The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule *cāpratyayasya* (8.3.41). [This rule] does not exist in the *Kāśikā*; it is seen in the *Padamañjarī*: "sustutam" (well-praised). Here, the word *su-* denotes excellence (*atiśaya*).
"atistutam" (excessively praised); here, *ati-* denotes transgression (*atikramaṇa*). "pābaddham—[Kāśikā reads] āviddham" (bound/pierced).

The prefix *āṅ* is used in connection with an action (*kriyāyoga*) or to denote a limit (*maryādā*). Regarding the rule "the group beginning with *paryā-* [is used] in the sense of being weary (*glāna*) and so forth," the group beginning with *pari* is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class). For example, "paryadhyayanaḥ" means "weary of study. Regarding the phrase "like a *vāpasī*," and so forth.

While the rule *sarvadhātubhyo'sun* (Dhātupāṭha 9.49) is being carried over, the word *vāsaḥ* is derived from the root *vas-* with the suffix *asun* according to the rule *vaserṇicca* (Dhātupāṭha 9.77);
the word *vastra*, moreover, ends in the *ṣṭran* suffix belonging to the *augādika* group. Therefore, both of these [words]—
[The word *ṭhñ*] is udātta by virtue of [Pāṇini 6.1.197] *ṭhñnatyādir nityam*.

Regarding the passage beginning with *prādiprasaṅge*: when there is an occasion (*prasaṅga*) for the application of the rules concerning prefixes (*prādi*), a prohibition must be stated regarding *karmapravacanīyas* in that context; that is to say, it must be explained. In this regard, the following...

Explanation: The designation *karmapravacanīya* applies to meanings such as *lakṣaṇa* (mark/indication) and so forth. Since those meanings are not conveyed by a compound (*samāsa*), a compound of *karmapravacanīyas* does not occur due to the absence of such usage (*anabhidhāna*). However, where those meanings are indeed conveyed, a compound certainly does occur—
"Excessive praise."

19. *upapadam atiṅ* (Pāṇini 2.2.19). [Example: *mūlakena upadaṃśam bhuṅkte*. [In the case of] *dhānāhārako vrajati*, the suffix *ṇvul* is applied by the rule *tumun-ṇvulau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām* (3.3.10). In these two rules (*upapadam atiṅ* and *kṛd-yogā ca ṣaṣṭhī*), the compound is formed by the rule *sup-supā*. *ṇa*. [End of commentary.]

The root text reads "it is connected" (*sambadhyate*), [but here it says] "it is not connected" (*nābhisambadhyate*). Now, one might object: "Is it not logical that this non-connection applies only to that rule where the mention of *atiṅ* (not being a finite verb) occurs, and not to the preceding rule? For in that [preceding] rule, the word *atiṅ* does not exist. [The author] thinks thus: [the term] "*atiṅ*"...
A *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) is performed, and it is understood to be a supplement (*śeṣabhūta*) to the preceding rule as well.

[Objection: Even so, since the term *atiṅ* is specified in the nominative case, it is logical that only the nominative form *sub* should be excluded, not the instrumental form *sup*. [Response: This is not so; because it is a general [rule].

Since the purpose is to indicate the cessation of the rule concerning *sub*-affixes, the cessation of both [the *gati* and *upasarga* designations] is logical. By the words "by that" (*tena*) and so forth, he demonstrates the utility of the indicator (*jñāpaka*). Because the term *atiṅ* was included even in the previous rule, there is a compounding of those designated as *gatis* and *upasargas* with *kṛt*-derived nouns prior to the production of *sub*-affixes.

Thus, the statement "it will be" (*bhaviṣyati*) becomes logically consistent. For in that [previous] rule, verbal roots (*dhātu*) are compounded with *kṛt*-suffixes; however, in this present rule, because of the inclusion of the term "not a finite verb" (*atiṅ*), the compounding of verbal roots with *kṛt*-suffixes—when they have a case-role (*kāraka*) or an adjunct (*upapada*)—is established prior to the production of the nominal suffix (*sub*).

For in this case, a *kāraka* (participant in an action) is compounded with words ending in *kṛt* suffixes prior to the production of case endings (*sup*). Demonstrating what is achieved when the compound exists, he says: "aśvakrītī. Here, the horse (*aśva*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*) as a *kāraka*; thus, by the rule "kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam" [Pāṇini 2.1.32], the word denoting the horse is compounded with the word ending in a *kṛt* suffix.

(2.1.32) Thus is the compound. If that were a compound at the time of the derivation of the *sup* suffixes, then, because it is *antaraṅga*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* would occur first; after that, the *sup* suffix, and subsequently the compound;
and consequently, by the rule "after a word ending in *krīta* preceded by an instrument," the suffix *ṅīṣ* would not occur. Therefore—

This is because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*). However, the scope for the suffix *ṅīṣ* is as follows: [consider] "one whose purchase (*krayaṇa*) was made with wealth" (*dhanena krītaṃ krayaṇaṃ yasyāḥ*).
Since the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is not applied after the formation of the compound—prior to the production of the case-ending—the compound itself occurs first;
thus, by virtue of ending in the vowel *ā*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is established. How so?

Furthermore, [the term] "horse" (*aśva*) and others function as *upapada*s. If it is asked, "Insofar as the designation by the locative case was made within the governing rule for the second verbal root (*dvitīyadhātva-dhikāra*), how can this be so?", there is no such fault;
for it is not the case that only that which is designated by the locative case within the governing rule for the second verbal root receives the technical name *upapada*. Rather, [it is as follows]:

Even that word which is uttered as a subordinate element (*upoccārita*) is indeed an *upapada*; this is also occasionally accepted in the grammatical treatise in such rules as "from the *sthita*, *itarētara*, *anyōnya*, and *upapada* [compounds]" (Pāṇini 1.3.16).
Therefore, even a word such as "horse" (*aśva*), because it is a word that has been uttered, is intended here as an *upapada*. This is the meaning of the word *pada*.

Furthermore, it is called an *upapada* because meaning is understood (*padyate*) through it; this is not on account of its being a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), for here a case-suffix is impossible prior to the formation of the compound, as the case-suffix has not yet been produced. If, however, any word that is uttered immediately after [the verb] were also taken here as an *upapada*, then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

It might be argued: "Even in the case of *rājaśrita*, since the compound would apply prior to the generation of the case-ending (*sup*), there would be an absence of *padatva* (wordhood) due to that [absence], and consequently, the elision of the *n* [in *śrita*] would not occur. This is not a fault, because this indicator (*jñāpaka*) does not have universal application. For by this [indicator], it is not the case that "gatis, kārakas, and upapadas are compounded with *kṛt*-derived words" applies everywhere.

It is not indicated that the compound occurs prior to the arising of the case-ending; rather, it is indicated only in certain desired instances. How is this known? From the rule "tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam" (Pāṇini 6.3.14), which prescribes the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case when a *kṛt*-derived word follows as the second member. If, then...

In all cases, the rule for compounding words with *gati*s, *kāraka*s, and *upapada*s with *kṛt*-affixes would have to occur prior to the production of case-endings (*sub*); if that were so, then the prescription of non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case when a *kṛt*-formed word follows—as in examples such as *bileśaya*—would be untenable, because the locative case would be impossible [at that stage]. Therefore...
The compound occurs only in certain instances prior to the arising of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, and not everywhere. And by adopting this view,
the formation of a compound with a word ending in *ṭāp*— as in "for she was purchased by him with wealth, dearer to him even than his own life"— becomes logically justified.
20. *Amaiva-avyayena* (Pāṇini 2.2.20). [Example:
*svāduṅkāraṃ bhuṅkte*. [The suffix] *ṇamul* [is applied] by [the rule] *svādumi* (3.4.26).
From this very [rule], because of the mention of the form ending in *m* (*svādumīti*), the upapada [of the verb] ends in the letter *m*.

It is elided. If [the rule] were merely for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*) since the compound would already be established by the preceding rule, then—given that a rule is being initiated when it is already established—it would serve as a restriction even without the use of the particle *eva*.
Therefore, he asks: "For what purpose is the particle *eva* used? and replies:

To the question, "For what purpose is the rule *ṭhak-kāraka-karaṇam*, etc., formulated again as a qualifier of that *upapada*?", he says: "*amaiva tulyavidhānam*, etc. By whichever sentence this very suffix is prescribed—and not another suffix—by that [sentence], whatever *upapada* is indicated, [it is governed by this rule].

The particle *eva* is employed for the purpose of specifying the *upapada*, so that the rule may apply only to that which has the same case-assignment (*tulyavidhāna*) as *am*. And it is understood that this compound occurs only with *am* due to proximity, and not with any other suffix. [Agra...]

In the example *bhuktvā agre bhojam*, the word *agre* is an *upapada*. Because it is prescribed by the same rule as the suffix *ktvā*—namely, by Pāṇini 2.4.24, *vibhāṣāgreprathamapūrveṣu*—it does not form a compound. The inclusion of the term *avyaya* (indefinite/indeclinable) is for the sake of clarity. It is not [required].

There exists a case where there is no distinction between a finite verb and an indeclinable; it is for the sake of excluding such cases that the mention of the term "indeclinable" (avyaya) becomes meaningful.

21. *tṛtīyā-prabhṛtīny anyatarasyām* (2.2.21). [The examples] "paryāpto bhoktum" ("sufficient to eat") and so forth are derived from the rule *śakadhṛṣajñāglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhaglāgh
The suffix *tumun* [is applied] due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of *tumun*.

22. *ktvā* ca (Pāṇini 2.2.22). As in: *ṭhalaṃ kṛtvā*, *khalu kṛtvā*. Regarding the rule *ṭhalaṃkhalyoḥ pratiṣedhayoḥ prācāṃ ktvā* (3.4.18), that [suffix] also precedes [the verb] when it follows words beginning with the third case-ending.

23. *śeṣo bahuvrīhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.23). "That which is other than what has been [previously] mentioned" means other than that which has already been designated [by another technical term]. "If no other compound designation has been stated" means where no other technical name for a compound has been prescribed. For example: *citraguḥ*.

In this case, since it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, the preceding member retains its original form" (*bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā pūrvapadam*, Pāṇini 6.2.1) applies, as in the example *unmattagaṅgam*. This is an *avyayībhāva* compound by the rule "and when used in the sense of another word [as a name]" (*anyapadārthe ca saṃjñāyām*, Pāṇini 2.1.21). For if the mention of the word *śeṣa* ("remainder") were not present here, a *bahuvrīhi* would also apply in this instance.
But surely, since the *bahuvrīhi* compound would otherwise apply, the *avyayībhāva* being initiated here must serve as its sublater;

so how can there even be the possibility of a *bahuvrīhi*? This counter-example is presented under the view that "the subsequent operation takes precedence" (*prāk kaḍārāt param kāryam*). For in that view:

If the inclusion of "the rest" (*śeṣa*) were not made [in the rule *karmadhāraye 'niṣṭhā*], then, by the authority of the statement *anyapadārthe ca saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 2.1.21), there would be an *avyayībhāva* compound. Some maintain that the *bahuvrīhi* takes precedence due to its higher status; however, this position is incorrect because it was not adopted by the author of the *Vṛtti*. Therefore...

This counter-example is presented based on the view that "the individual is the word-meaning" (*vyaktiḥ padārthaḥ*), under the alternative (*pakṣa*) that "only one technical designation [applies] from the point where a rule begins with *ṭha* or *kāra*" (*ṭhākaḍārādekā saṃjñā*). For when the individual is the word-meaning, the grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) applies to each specific instance (*pratilakṣye*). In this case, if the mention of "the remainder" (*śeṣagrahaṇa*) were not made, this rule would apply to such a domain.

Since that [cognition] has not yet accomplished its purpose, it must necessarily proceed further. Furthermore, because the governing rule concerns a single cognition, simultaneity is not possible; thus, by the authority of the scriptural statement, there is the contingency of both [cognitions], while others maintain that both would occur alternately.

When a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed from words with different grammatical subjects (*vyadhikaraṇa*), there is no expression of the intended meaning. For the meaning that is understood from the sentence "five have been eaten by him" is not conveyed by the word *pañcabhukta*.
Therefore, because it does not express [the intended meaning], a *bahuvrīhi* will not occur for words with different subjects. In cases where...

There is indeed an expression [of this]; even when there is a difference in grammatical coreference (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), the compound is indeed formed—as in *kaṇṭhekāla*. Regarding the rule "and [the word] *avyaya*," it should be connected with the statement that "it becomes a *bahuvrīhi*."

The word "and" (ca) implies that this [rule] applies to non-indeclinables as well in certain instances. This is for the purpose of providing an example where there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇya*). Nevertheless...

Because it conveys the meaning, the compound indeed occurs. Why is this so? It is due to the inherent nature of the expressive power (*śakti*) of words. And the expressive powers of words have specific bases;

they operate only in certain instances, not everywhere. [This is according to the rule: "When the first member of a compound is preceded by a locative case or a word denoting a standard of comparison, there is elision of the subsequent member. [In this case,] the locative ending is not applied.

That compound whose prior member (*pūrvapada*) is in the locative case is a "locative-prior-member" compound (*saptamīpūrvapada*). It occurs with another subsequent word (*padāntara*), and there is elision of the subsequent member (*uttarapadalopa*) of that locative-prior-member compound. Having analyzed [the phrase] as *kaṇṭhe sthitaḥ* ("situated on the throat").

The compound is formed by the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "saptamī" (Pāṇini 2.1.40). The elision of the case-ending is not applied due to the rule "tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam" (6.3.14). Thus, "kaṇṭhekālaḥ" means "one for whom Kāla resides in the throat. In this instance, because the first member ending in the locative case stands in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), the formation is indeed established.
This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; however, the elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*) is prescribed. This should be understood in other cases as well.
A compound whose first member (*pūrvapada*) is a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is compounded with another word;
for that compound whose first member is a standard of comparison, the elision of the final member is prescribed. [For example: "like a camel's face" (*uṣṭramukhamiva*).

The face of this person is like that of a camel, thus he is "camel-faced" (*uṣṭramukhaḥ*) or "donkey-faced" (*kharamukhaḥ*). Here, the camel (*uṣṭra*), as the first member of the compound, is the standard of comparison for the face.
Now, one might object: "Is it not the camel's face that is the standard of comparison for Devadatta's face, and not the camel itself?
There is no fault here, because since the camel is a part of the standard of comparison, the camel itself is also called the standard of comparison.

the suffix *ḍac* is applied as before, and the elision of the final syllable (*ṭilopa*) occurs by the rule "ṭeḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.143), which is an exception to "tirviṃśaterḍiti" (6.4.142). Regarding "āsannadaśāḥ": those who are near ten are "āsannadaśāḥ"; and these, as before, are either nine or eleven.

Regarding "adūradaśāḥ": those who are not far from ten; these, moreover, are exactly as previously mentioned. Regarding "adhikadaśāḥ": those who exceed ten; these, moreover, are eleven and so forth. Regarding "dvitrāḥ":
the analysis (*vigraha*) is "two or three. This compound occurs in the sense of "optionality" (*vārtha*). And this [optionality] is as follows:

It is doubt (*saṃśaya*), not option (*vikalpa*). If the meaning of "or" (*vā*) were taken here as option, then when there are two [sons], the plural number would not occur. Therefore, in this context, the meaning of "or" is doubt.
And when an object is doubted, the plural number is used, as in: "How many sons do you have? And it has been said:
In the Bhāṣya it is said: "When the object is not known, the plural number should be employed. How so?
Because doubt, by virtue of its reflecting upon two sides, has multiple objects as its domain.
If it did not reflect upon both sides, there would be no doubt at all. Alternatively: here, there are always only five.

They occur as such, never as two or three; thus, when "two or three" (*dvitrāḥ*) is said, it is understood that there are exactly five. This speech has five bases; therefore, the use of the plural number is appropriate. If, then, this compound is used in the sense of "or" (*vā*), [then...]

Since that meaning is the referent of another word (*anyapadārtha*), is the compound not already established by the preceding rule? It is not so established; for the preceding rule applies to the sense of possession (*matvartha*), whereas this rule does not apply to the sense of possession. Alternatively, the preceding rule establishes a compound in any case-meaning other than the nominative (*prathamā*); this present statement is for the sake of the nominative.
Regarding "ṭhtricaturāḥ": the compound ending *ac* is applied by the Vārttika "In the section on *ac*, there is an addition for *catura* preceded by *tri* and *upa*" (Vārttika 639).
Regarding "ṭhdvidaśāḥ": the analysis is *dvi-daśa*; this is a compound used in the sense of the suffix *su*.

The repetition (*āvṛtti*) which relates to ten and is indicated by the word "ten" is expressed by the word "two. Furthermore, since the meaning of the suffix *su* is the meaning of the affix itself and not the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*), it is not established by the preceding rule. Alternatively, this [suffix] occurs even in the sense of the nominative case (*prathamā*) and even in the sense of "not being so" (*amatvartha*); therefore, it is not [established] by the preceding rule.

It is established that since the compound itself is capable of conveying the meaning of the suffix *suj*, the suffix *suj* is not employed in the *vṛtti*. For example, in the expression "more than twenty cows" (*adhikā viṃśatir gavām*), the word *viṃśati* here functions solely as a number (*saṃkhyāna*); it does not [denote the objects counted].
But [it applies] to a substance that is numerable.
26. *diṅnāmānyantarāle* (Pāṇini 2.2.26).

[The example is] *dakṣiṇapūrvā* ("southeast"). This compound is also desired in the sense of the nominative case (*prathamārthe*). Furthermore, since it would not be established by the preceding rule even in the non-possessive sense (*amatvarthe*), this rule is commenced for that non-possessive sense and for the purpose of a specific prescription (*pratipadavidhānārtha*).

In the rule *vibhāṣā diksamāse* (Pāṇini 1.1.28), it is intended that only that compound of directions which is prescribed by a specific rule (*pratipadavihita*) is to be understood. And a compound of directions is prescribed by a specific rule only if this sūtra is commenced, and not otherwise. [The word] *sarvanāmnaḥ*...

"The substitution of the masculine form occurs only when there is a common substratum (*vṛtti*). This, moreover, should be understood as established by the division of rules (*yogavibhāga*) in the sūtra *striyāṃ puṃvat* (Pāṇini 6.3.34). "The mention of the word 'name' (*nāman*) is for the sake of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*)," meaning it is intended to exclude those directional terms (*dikśabda*) that are conventionally used in the world [in their feminine forms]. And [the example] *aindra*.
And regarding the words *aindrī* and *kauberī*: these two are not conventional (*rūḍhi*) terms; rather, they are etymological (*yogika*).

This [direction] belongs to Indra, thus it is *aindrī*; this [direction] belongs to Kubera, thus it is *kauberī*. The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.3.120: *tasyedam* ("this belongs to that").

27. Regarding the rule *tatra tenedamiti sarūpe* (Pāṇini 2.2.27), there is the phrase "the particle *iti* [is used] after a compound," and so forth. To demonstrate what meaning the particle *iti* conveys when intended as part of a compound, he says: "it conforms to the worldly meaning."

It follows that it means "it causes one to understand. Furthermore, showing that this worldly object consists of grasping and so forth, he says "therefore," etc. Since the particle *iti* leads one to follow the worldly meaning, for that reason, everything beginning with "grasping" is obtained.

It should be understood that by the words "reciprocity of action" (*karmavyatīhāra*), the inclusion of the term "mutually" (*paraspara*) is intended; furthermore, it should be understood that this inclusion of "mutually" is obtained precisely from the particle *iti*.
It should also be understood that, because of the particle *iti*, there is no prescription of the actual form [of the word] here. And [the word] *daṇḍaḥ*...

The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). It is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), because it is listed among the *tiṣṭhadgu* group; its designation as an indeclinable is established by the rule "and [the term] *avyayībhāva*" (Pāṇini 1.1.41).
Regarding the word *sarūpam*, [the substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-*] occurs according to the rule "for *samāna-* [there is *sa-*], except when it denotes light" (Pāṇini 6.3.85), and so forth.
The intrinsic nature.

28. *tena saha* [Pāṇini 2.2.28]: "In the sense of equal connection (*tulyayoga*)," and so forth. Equal connection (*tulyayoga*) means a common relationship (*samānasambandha*). When the word *saha* illuminates that [relationship], then it occurs in that [sense]. For example: *saputraḥ* ("with his son"). *Saha*...
The analysis (*vigraha*) should be made as "with the son" (*putreṇa*). The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is applied by the rule *sahayukte 'pradhāne* (Pāṇini 2.3.19).

The substitution of *sa-* for *saha-* occurs by the rule *vopasarjanasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.82). In this context, in the sentence "Devadatta has come with his son," Devadatta and the son possess an identical relationship through their act of coming.

It is illuminated by the word *saha*. Now, how could [the term] "sakarmaka" (transitive) and so forth apply [in such cases]? And why would it not apply? To this he says: "For here... and so on. Regarding the word "prāyikam" (general/common):
the meaning is that it does not cover every instance. But from where is its general nature obtained?
Because of the use of the particle *iti*. But surely there is another purpose for the use of *iti*; what is it?

It is so that the word *saha* may be understood as having its own form (*svarūpa*) as its referent (*padārtha*). Otherwise, this would be understood as a specification of meaning (*arthanirdeśa*). And in that case, would words such as *sākam* and *sārddham* also be subject to compounding? No, it is not so.
We reply: in this sūtra, what is obtained from the particle *iti*? Rather, it is that which is carried over (*anuvartate*) from the preceding sūtra.

29. *ca* [is used] in the sense of *dvandva*. (2.2.29) He asks: "What, then, is this so-called meaning of *ca*? and replies: "Accumulation (*samuccaya*), subsequent mention (*anvācaya*)," and so forth.
Accumulation (*samucciti*) is *samuccaya*. It refers to [the connection of] multiple means or actions with respect to a single [result].
The "multiplicity" (anekatva) of the means of action consists in their being accumulated through a differentiation of their own forms;

that is to say, it occurs only among those [means] which possess equal force and whose sequence or simultaneity is not fixed, as in the example: "Yama, the son of Vivasvat, never reaches satiety even though he leads away a cow, a horse, a man, and cattle day after day."

Conjunction by way of secondary addition (*anvācaya*) occurs where one element is primary and the other is subordinate, being added in accordance with that primary element; for example: "O boy, go for alms and bring a cow. Both mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) and collective conjunction (*samāhāra*) are merely varieties of simple conjunction (*samuccaya*). This...

For indeed, mutual dependence (*itaretarāpekṣā*) among distinct parts constitutes "mutual conjunction" (*itaretarayoga*), as in the case: "This task is to be performed by Devadatta and Yajñadatta. Both are mutually dependent with respect to that task; for if even one of them were absent, it would not be accomplished.
And since this [compound] has its parts as the primary focus, the dual number occurs because there are two [parts].
A *samāhāra* (collective compound), however, is one where the distinction between the parts is obscured and the aggregate is primary, occurring only when the parts are mutually dependent;
for example, "an umbrella and sandals" (*chatropānaham*). In this case as well, [the compound applies] with respect to some action.

The mutual dependence of the umbrella and so forth [is implied]. And because the collective whole (*saṃhati*) is predominant, the singular number is used. If, then, *samuccaya* (conjunction) and *anvācaya* (subordinate conjunction) are also meanings of the particle *ca*, then a compound would also result for those two;
therefore, he says "in that case," etc. First, regarding *samuccaya*:

Since cows and other such items are not inherently connected to one another, they are only combined when related to actions such as leading; thus, due to a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*), a compound does not occur even though that meaning exists. Furthermore, in the case of *anvācaya* (conjunction), only one element is dependent on the other, not both—as was stated previously.

In the example: bringing the cow depends upon begging for alms, but begging for alms does not depend upon bringing the cow, because the latter can be performed even without the former. If he sees a cow, he brings it as well;
if not, he simply goes about begging—thus, in this case, there is no mutual dependence.

Furthermore, a compound does not occur in the sense of *ca* ("and"). It is prescribed [only] for *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) and *samāhāra* (collective aggregate), because in those cases the semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) of all the members exists. For example: *vāktvacam*, *vāgdṛṣadam*. [This is governed by] Pāṇini 2.4.2: *dvandvāccudaṣahāntāt samāhāre* (A compound ending in *cu*, *da*, or *ṣa-ha* takes the suffix *ṭac* when it denotes a collective aggregate).

Thus, by the suffix *ṭac*, which is a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*), there is the treatment as a singular (*ekavadbhāva*) according to Pāṇini 2.4.6: "A genus (*jāti*) of non-living things [is singular]."

30. *Upasarjanaṃ pūrvam* (2.2.30). [The commentary states: "The mention of 'prior' (*pūrva*) is for the purpose of precluding usage in the reverse order. Now, one might object: surely the reversal of the order of usage is not even observed in common worldly practice; so how [can this rule apply]...?
He says "for there would be no restriction" (*aniyamo hi syāt*) because of the inclusion of the word "prior" (*pūrva*) for the purpose of excluding the application [of the rule] to what follows.
The optative (*liṅ*) is used here in the sense of possibility. He thinks as follows:
although a reversal of the order of application has not been observed, nevertheless, in the absence of a restrictive statement (*niyāmaka-vākya*), [the rule would apply indiscriminately].

Due to human error, even an inverted application might occur. Furthermore, for those who hold the view that it is the sentence itself that becomes a compound, since the sentence lacks a fixed order, its modification—the compound—would likewise lack a fixed order; thus, the composition of this *sūtra* is undertaken.
31. *rājadantādiṣu param* (Pāṇini 2.2.31). [The rule] "the subsequent member is placed first" applies here. This includes compounds such as *liptavāsitā-* up to *yuktāgāḍha-*.
Regarding those *dvandva* compounds such as *udūkhalamusala-* and others, in some cases [the order is determined] by having fewer syllables (*alpāctaratvāt*).

The rule for prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) would apply: in some cases because it ends in a vowel (*dhyanta*), in others because it begins with a vowel other than *a* (*ajādya-ntatva*); in some instances there is no fixed rule due to similarity. Furthermore, this reading "dṛṣdupala" appears to be a result of error, since the word "adṛṣat" has fewer syllables (*alpāctaratvāt*).
The initial placement [of the first member] is established in the cases of *ṭhakṣibhruvam* and *dāragavam*,
where the compound-ending suffix *ac* (Pāṇini 5.4.77–80) is applied by the rule *acaturādi-sūtra*. As for *sthūlapūlāsam*,
this appears to be a scribal error, for the same reason stated previously.

32. *dvandve ghi* (Pāṇini 2.2.32). Since the technical designation *upasarjana* was established by the rule *ṭhupasarjanam* as a term whose meaning follows its etymology (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), the status of being an *upasarjana* is prescribed for that which is subordinate. However, in a *dvandva* compound, all the constituent words are equally primary (*pradhāna*). Not...

Since there is no designation as *upasarjana* (secondary member) because nothing possesses absolute predominance, a state of unrestricted option (*aniyama*) would result; therefore, this statement is made. In this regard, where there is the possibility of several [words] being placed first, it is asked:
will there be an unrestricted option for one [word], or for all? To this he says:

"Even when there is the attainment of many [individuals], [there is the application] of one," and so forth. And this meaning is obtained by resorting to the universal (*jāti*) as the referent of the word; for if the individual were the referent of the word, the scripture would have to apply to each individual separately, and consequently, the restriction would apply to all [of them]. But in the case of the form (*ākṛti*), however—

With respect to a single object to be defined (*lakṣya*), only one definition (*lakṣaṇa*) applies at once. Consequently, when one [definition] is placed first, its purpose is fulfilled; thus, there is no fixed rule for the remaining ones.
In this way, it should be understood that in subsequent cases as well, there is a restriction for one [element], while for the remainder there is no restriction.
Regarding the term "ṭhvispaṣṭapaṭuaḥ": it is a compound formed from "vispaṣṭaḥ" and "paṭuaḥ" according to the rule governing the *mayūravyaṃsaka* group and others.

33. *ajādyadantam* | (Pāṇini 2.2.33) [The rule] "In a *dvandva*, that which ends in a vowel (*ghi*) and begins with *a* or *ā* and ends in a short *a* takes precedence by way of exception" means that, in contrast to the rule *dvandve ghi* (2.2.32), this rule *ajādyadantam* prevails by way of exception. [In the context of] *dvandva*:

The scope for the rule *ghi* is: *paṭvaśuklau*, *paṭvaguptau*. The scope for the rule *ajādyadantam* is: *uṣṭraśaśau*, *uṣṭrakharau*. In the case of *indrāgnī*, both rules would apply; therefore, by the principle of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), that which begins with a vowel (*ajādya*) and ends in *a* takes precedence.
34. *alpāctaram* | (Pāṇini 2.2.34) [This refers to the rule] beginning with *ṛtunakṣatrāṇām*. The sequence of the seasons (*ṛtu*) is determined by their appearance;
that of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) is determined by their rising. Why is there not a mention of the phonemes (*varṇa*) in the very rule *ṛtunakṣatrāṇām*?

Anticipating the fault of being asked "why was this done?", he says: "Of those with identical vowels," and so forth. A separate statement is made because even for letters that do not have identical vowels, priority in placement is desired according to their sequential order (*ānupūrvya*). And the sequence of letters is determined by their order of production (*janma*).
This is well-known in worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*). And this conventional renown is established by the Veda (*śruti*), for it is recited in the Veda:

"He created the Brāhmaṇa from his mouth, the Rājanya from his two arms, the Vaiśya from his thighs, and the Śūdra from his feet. [The rule] "after a smaller number" applies here, as does the rule regarding *dvandva* compounds.
It should be stated: "dvitrāḥ" and "tricaturāḥ" are *bahuvrīhi* compounds; "navatiśatam" is a *dvandva* compound.
35. *saptamīviśeṣaṇe bahuvrīhau* (Pāṇini 2.2.35).

[The rule] *sarvanāmasaṃkhyayoḥ* [is understood here]. This is its scope: where there is a compound with a quality-word (*guṇavacana*), that is the domain of this [rule]. However, where [the compound is] with a word denoting a substance (*dravyavācin*), [the order is determined] precisely because the pronoun (*sarvanāman*) and the numeral (*saṃkhyā*) function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*).

The rule for prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) is established by the statement "in the case of prior placement, [the word ending in] the locative [case]," and so forth. Since the word ending in the locative would otherwise be required to be placed first, it must be stated that for words such as *gaḍu* and others, the [word ending in the locative] should be mentioned as coming after [the other member]. Thus, the word ending in the locative is stated to be the subsequent member.
That by which something is explained is called *paravacana* (an explanatory statement). Herein is the explanation:
because [the word] *āhitādi* belongs to the class of *ākṛtigaṇa* (open-ended groups), words such as *gaḍuka* and *kaṇṭha* are to be understood as included therein;
therefore, [the compound] will have the locative case-ending (*saptamyanta*) following *gaḍu* and the others. [As for the question: "How is *vahegaḍuḥ* [formed]? If...

The intention is that the rule regarding the locative case applies after words such as *gaḍu* and others. Regarding the statement "the sublation of what has been established must be explained," this is the explanation: the word *vā* ("or") is carried over from the rule *vāhitāgnyādiṣu* (Pāṇini 2.2.37), and that is understood as a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (a restricted option). Therefore...
There will be an annulment of the subsequent placement that has been obtained.

36. *niṣṭhā*. (2.2.36) [Objection: But surely, in this context, "niṣṭhā" refers only to the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). The word *kṛta* is a verbal noun (*kriyāśabda*), while the word *kaṭa* denotes a substance (*dravyavacana*). In that case, just as a quality (*guṇa*) is a qualifier of a substance, so too is an action (*kriyā*). Thus...
Since the word ending in the *niṣṭhā* suffix is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), its prior placement is already established by the preceding rule [Pāṇini 2.2.36].
By means of the various analyses such as "the mat was made by him" (*kaṭekṛtam anena*), he demonstrates that the *niṣṭhā* suffix does not function as the qualifier in this analysis;
for in this analysis, only the word ending in the locative case is the qualifier, while the word ending in the *niṣṭhā* suffix is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).

The qualified (viśeṣya): for when there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), action and quality invariably experience the relationship of qualifier and qualified, but not when there is lack of coreferentiality (vaiyadhikaraṇya). To illustrate: in expressions such as "the white of the cloth" or "the flight of the crow," the quality and so forth possess the status of being the qualified, because they are that which is to be delimited; whereas the substance [is the delimiter].

But [the word *niṣṭhā*] functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), because it serves to delimit (*vyavacchedaka*). Regarding the rule "in the case of *niṣṭhā*, [the word ending in] *niṣṭhā* is placed first," and so forth: a word ending in *niṣṭhā* is stated to follow words such as *jāti* (genus), etc.; therefore, its explanation must be provided. In this regard, the explanation is as follows:
Words such as *sāraṅgajagdhī*, *māsajātā*, and *sukhajātā* fall within the category of *āhitādi* because it is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class). Consequently,

according to the rule "the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) comes after [words denoting] genus, time, pleasure, and so forth, when it follows [another word]," the form *sāraṅgajagdhī* is established.

Thus: the word *sāraṅga* denotes a genus (*jāti*). Then, while the rule *ṭhktādalpākhyāyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.51) is in effect, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *asvāṅgapūrvapadādvā* (4.1.53). [The question is raised: "How is *kṛtakaṭaḥ* [formed]? This is a question based on the fact that the word *kaṭa* denotes a genus. [The answer is: "Of that which has been obtained..."

"And non-contradiction (cābādhā) is to be explained. By this, the intention is that [the rule] will also apply in cases such as *kṛtakataḥ*. Furthermore, that non-contradiction regarding what has not been attained is to be explained just as before; likewise, it is to be explained in subsequent cases as well. Regarding "from those whose meaning is weapons" (*praharaṇārthebhyaḥ*), etc.: those whose meaning is weapons...

Thus they have been described. The meaning is that this form of the rule—stating that "the suffixes *niṣṭhā* and the locative case-ending (*saptamī*) occur after them"—must be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows:
because words such as *asyudyataḥ* (with sword raised) and *daṇḍapāṇiḥ* (staff-in-hand) are included in the *āhitāgny-ādi* group, [the suffixes] occur after them.
The two [suffixes] *niṣṭhā* and *saptamī* occur.
37. *vā''hitāgnyādiṣu* (Pāṇini 2.2.37). 38. *kaḍārāḥ karmadhāraye* (Pāṇini 2.2.38).
He states that those words beginning with *kaḍāra*, which are adjectives (*guṇa-śabda*), function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) [in a *karmadhāraya* compound].
"Of words denoting qualities," and so forth; the meaning has already been explained.
Thus ends the second chapter of the *Kāśikāvivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who was a teacher of the Bodhisattvas.
The Second Chapter:
Now begins the second chapter.
The third quarter [of the second book]. 1. *anabhihite* (Pāṇini 2.3.1).
This is a form derived from either the root *dhā* or *hi*, meaning "when not already expressed"; this is because they are identical [in this context].

Furthermore, because verbal roots have multiple meanings, there would be a doubt as to which meaning of the word *anabhihita* ("not expressed") is to be understood; therefore, in order to dispel that doubt, he says: "when [the case-relation] such as the object (*karman*) is not expressed (*anukta*)," and so forth. If, when the object and other relations are not expressed, the second case (*dvitīyā*) and the others [are employed]...
It might be stated in general that "case endings occur"; however, just as in the example *kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ* ("the mat is made"),
where the accusative case does not occur after the word *kaṭa* because the object (*karman*) has already been expressed by the suffix *-kta*,
so too [the same would apply] in *kaṭaṃ karoti* ("he makes a mat") and *bhīṣmam udāraṃ śobhanaṃ darśanīyam*.

In this case, since the accusative case produced from the word *kaṭa* expresses the object residing in *bhīṣma* and the others, the accusative would not apply to *bhīṣma* and the others. Thinking that some specific distinction must be intended here, he asks about that distinction:

"Why is it said 'when not already expressed'? The other, understanding his intention, says: "By means of verbal suffixes, kṛt-suffixes, taddhita-suffixes, and compounds," and so forth. In the word *kriyate*, the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
[The suffix] *yak* is added by Pāṇini 3.1.67 (*sārvadhātuke yak*), and [the augment] *riṅ* is applied by 7.4.28 (*riṅ śayagliṅkṣu*).

"Remote distance" (*riṅadeśaḥ*). [Examples: *śatyaḥ*, *śatikaḥ*. By the rule "After *śata*, the suffixes *ṭhan* and *yat* [occur] when it does not mean 'one hundred'" (Pāṇini 5.1.21), the suffixes *ṭhan* and *yat* are applied.

[The rule] "The plural number is used for many things," and so forth. Regarding this, it has been stated: "The [categories] beginning with *karman* (object) are also [treated as] *avyaya* (indeclinables)."

Since [number] is the expressed meaning of the case-endings (*vibhakti*), the plural number occurs when there is a plurality belonging to that [object]. By speaking thus, the author of the Vṛtti states that the second and subsequent case-endings occur when the number is based upon [grammatical relations] such as the object (*karman*). Furthermore, no specific distinction is mentioned therein.

Furthermore, there are objects and so forth that have been expressed (*abhihita*) as well as those that have not been expressed (*anabhihita*). In this regard, since no distinction is specified, just as the second case endings (*dvitīyā*) and others occur for numbers such as singularity when they reside in unexpressed objects and so forth, they would likewise occur when they reside in expressed objects and so forth. Therefore, those which are unexpressed...

The qualifier *anabhihite* ("when not already expressed") is introduced so that case-endings (*vibhakti*) may occur in respect to the oneness and other numbers residing in those [objects] which are the substrata of the action and so forth, but not elsewhere.
Thus, [the rule refers to] "the substrata of the action and so forth when they are not already expressed. Here, the action and so forth are the substrata (*āśraya*) that have not been expressed.

The term *yeṣām* is a bahuvrīhi compound. By this, he demonstrates the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) of the rule *bahuṣu bahuvacanam* (Pāṇini 1.4.21) and others with the rule *anabhihite* together with rules such as *karmaṇi dvitīyā* (Pāṇini 2.3.2)— that is, when the object (*karman*) has not been previously expressed.
"The second [rule] states that the plural number is used for many. In this way, a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) should be understood in other instances as well.
And since a single syntactical unity is not possible without a relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*), one must be subordinate and the other must be principal. In that case:

Because it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the term "unexpressed" (*anabhihita*) has a subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) in relation to the object (*karman*) and so forth; however, because the object and so forth are the qualified (*viśeṣya*), they possess primacy (*prādhānya*). Furthermore, in relation to singularity (*ekatva*) and so forth, the object and so forth have a non-primordial status because they are qualifiers, whereas singularity and so forth possess the state of being primary because they are the qualified.

Now, how does the accusative case ending arising from the word *kaṭa* denote an object (*karman*) that is associated with words such as *bhīṣma*, just as [the suffix] *-niṣṭhā* [denotes it]? If this is asked, the answer would be: "Just as in the case of the verb *kṛ* [in the sentence] *kaṭaḥ kṛto bhīṣma udāraḥ śobhanaḥ darśanīyaḥ*..."

The claim that "the *niṣṭhā* suffix arising after the word *karman* denotes even all actions such as *bhīṣma* and so forth, just as the accusative case ending arising after the word *kaṭa* [denotes the object]"—this is merely a superficial argument; for the expression *kṛtaḥ* is a designation based on the relationship between an action and its factors (*kāraka*). And the action, when it arises, [is understood] by implication.

It implies all the causal factors (kāraka-dravya). Therefore, it is logical that the suffix *kta* arising after the root *kṛ* denotes everything collectively, as long as the status of being an object (*karmatā*) extends to whatever is expressed by *karoti*. This applies even to the status of being an object residing in Bhīṣma and others.

The expression is formed by means of the *kta* suffix. However, the word *kaṭa* denotes a specific substance; therefore, the accusative case ending arising from it is capable of denoting only the action residing in that [substance], and not anything residing elsewhere.
How then can the action residing in *bhīṣma* and so forth be denoted by it? And thus, [the use of the accusative] would be meaningless.
This enumeration: since expression is possible only through verbal suffixes (tiṅ), primary derivatives (kṛt), secondary derivatives (taddhita), and compounds (samāsa),
this further presentation of examples that are possible should be understood as an *apara-parisaṃkhyānam* (an alternative enumeration), not a *parigaṇanam* (a restrictive enumeration).

2. *karmaṇi dvitīyā* (Pāṇini 2.3.2). Someone might suspect that since there is also a second case-ending among the verbal terminations (*tiṅvibhakti*), it too should be included here; therefore, to refute that, he says: "the words 'second' and so forth."

And so forth. Here, by the word *karman*, the grammatical factor (*sādhana*) as an object is intended, and not the object of an action (*kriyākarma*). For indeed, those case-meanings such as singularity and so on will be enumerated with *karman* and the rest as their qualifiers. Furthermore, duality and plurality do not exist in the object of an action.
However, [the term *ubha*] is found in the sense of the object (*sādhana-karman*); therefore, it is appropriate to take that very meaning, not the other.

Regarding the rule "ubhasarvatasoḥ" and so forth: when the words *ubha* and *sarva*, ending in the suffix *tasi*, are employed, the second case (*dvitīyā-vibhakti*) must be applied. This rule is introduced because the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), which would otherwise apply by virtue of being a "residual" (*śeṣa*) relation, is [here] superseded.

In the rule *ubha-sarvatasoḥ*, although the word *ubha* is indeed listed there, nevertheless, by virtue of its semantic fitness (*sāmarthya*), it is the word *ubhaya* that is understood; this is because of their similarity of form.
For there exists no word *ubha* ending in the suffix *tasi*. Of that [word *ubhaya*],...

Because it is the domain of the suffixes *ni*, *tyap*, the dual number, and *ṭāp*. Thus it has been stated: "The absence of the other two [suffixes] occurs elsewhere than in the case of both *ni*, *tyap*, the dual, and *ṭāp*" (Vārttika 8 and 9 on Pāṇini 1.1.27). Examples are *ubhayataḥ* and *sarvataḥ*, formed by the rule *pañcamyās tasil* (Pāṇini 5.3.7). This also applies when used in conjunction with the word *dhik*.
The accusative case is to be employed; likewise, in the three [expressions] beginning with *upari* when used in conjunction [with a noun], the accusative is to be employed.

Regarding the rule "at the end of iteratives," the meaning is "in those that have undergone reduplication. In examples such as *uparyupari grāmam*, the reduplication occurs by the rule *upary-adhy-adhasaḥ sāmīpye* (Pāṇini 8.1.7).
"Also seen elsewhere than that. The connection is: "the suffix *dvitīyā* is also seen elsewhere than what has been stated.
To the question "Where else is it seen?", he says: "from *abhitaḥ*, etc. [referring to] Pāṇini 5.4.44: *pratyabhibhyāṃ ca*.

Thus ends the section on the suffix *tasi*. The word *api* has the sense of an alternative (*vikalpa*). It is seen [to apply] even when it is not seen; by this, forms such as *hā tāta*, *hā mātaḥ*, and so forth, are established.
3. *Tṛtīyā ca hośchandasī* (Pāṇini 2.3.3). As in:

*yavāgvāgnihotraṃ juhoti*. Although this is established even by the rule *supāṃ supo bhavanti* (Vārttika 818), which prescribes the substitution of the third case for the second case in this instance;
Nevertheless, [rules such as] "one offers with milk" (*payasā juhoti*) and "one offers with clarified butter" (*ājyena juhoti*) would not be established.
For instance, due to the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the elision (*luk*) prescribed by *svamornapuṃsakāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.23) would apply to one [form],
while the substitution of *am* (*ambhāva*) prescribed by *ato'm* (Pāṇini 7.1.24) would apply to the other.

4. *Antarā* and *antareṇa* when used in conjunction with [the sense of] "between" or "without. (Pāṇini 2.3.4) It is stated: "The two words *antarā* and *antareṇa* are understood here as indeclinables (*nipāta*) because of their association.
Although this word *antarā* exists as ending in a feminine suffix, [it is taken here as an indeclinable].

Likewise, there is also [the word] ending in a non-feminine suffix (*astrīpratyaya*); however, the word *antara* ending in a non-feminine suffix is understood [here]. And that word *antarā* which ends in a non-feminine suffix is indeed a particle (*nipāta*); thus, for now, it is the particle *antarā* that is being taken. Therefore, by means of that particle—

By virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), the word *antareṇa* is also understood as referring to that very same [term]. Therefore, the second case ending does not occur in connection with either the non-indeclinable (*anipāta*) word *antareṇa* ending in the third case, or the word *antarā* ending in the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. For example: *kiṃ te bābhrāvāṇāṃ śālaṅkāyamānāñcāntareṇa* ("What do you have to do with those between the Bābhravas and the Śālaṅkāyanas?").

Regarding the word *gatena*: in the phrase "he dwells in the city between the two villages," the word *antara* here denotes a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*). The root *gam-* also denotes knowledge. The meaning is: "What use have you for this knowledge of distinctions? This rule [Pāṇini 2.3.4] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the genitive case; it supersedes the genitive that would otherwise be prescribed by the definition of the "remainder" (*śeṣa*).

Because this [term] begins when that [previous rule] has been reached, the author states "In that case," etc., in order to clarify— by means of demonstrating the meaning of the words *antarā* and *antareṇa*— that this rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the sixth [case-ending]. For the middle, being a relative term (*sambandhi-śabda*), refers to the second [element] which is not itself the middle.

It occurs in relation to a relative (*sambandhin*). In that case, when the state of being "middle" (*madhyatva*) is dependent upon something, and a distinction from that middle element is produced, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is obtained. The meaning of "without" (*vinā*) is also indeed a remainder (*śeṣa*); here too, only the sixth case is obtained, as in: *antarā tvāñca māñca kamaṇḍaluḥ* ("The water-pot is between you and me"). [This applies] to yours.

The meaning is: "In my midst there is a water-pot" (*kamaṇḍalu*). Now, why does the second case ending not occur after the word *kamaṇḍalu*? Because, even though there is a connection with *antaḥ* (in) or *antareṇa* (without), that [word] is subordinate (*aprādhānya*). For instance—the application of *kamaṇḍalu* is for its own sake (*svārthā*), whereas the application of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* is for the sake of another (*parārthā*).

Because those two function as qualifiers of the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), in that case, since the word for the water-pot exists in its own primary sense and remains established as the principal element, it does not deviate from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*); therefore, by virtue of its priority, only the nominative case occurs. However, the accusative case applies to that which is non-principal.

Since there is scope for the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, when a distinction (*vyatireka*) is produced by those two [words] together with that very word ending in the first case [the pronoun], and the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would otherwise result, the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) is prescribed. In the phrase "without human effort" (*antareṇa puruṣakāram*), the meaning is "without human exertion" (*vinā puruṣakāreṇa*).

"In the phrase 'between Takṣaśilā and Pāṭaliputra is the wall of Srughna,' the word *srughna* has its capacity exhausted by functioning as a qualifier of the wall; therefore, it does not enter into a connection with the word *antarā*."

5. *kālādhvanoratyantasaṃyoge* (Pāṇini 2.3.5). In this rule, the terms *kāla* (time) and *adhvan* (path) are taken in their sense (*arthagrahaṇa*). Therefore, he says: "from words denoting time and from words denoting path," and so forth. Examples: *māsasya dvir adhīte* ("he studies twice a month"); *krośasyaikadeśe parvataḥ* ("a mountain at one part of a *krośa*").
"In one part of a yojana there is a mountain. Here, the accusative case is not applied by the rule "kālādhvanoratyantasaṃyoge" (Pāṇini 2.3.5).

6. *apavarge tṛtīyā* | (2.3.6) Regarding the term "apavarga": this qualification is employed as the result of absolute connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*). And that [result] is possible only for the absolute connection with an action, not for anything else; thus, by implication, it is understood here.

Only absolute connection with an action (*kriyātyantasaṃyoga*) is intended here. Since every action has a completion, therefore, by the force of employing this qualification, when the attainment of the result occurs, the completion of the action is understood here as "liberation" (*apavarga*); hence he says:

Regarding the phrase "upon the attainment of the fruit" and so forth, and "in the exclusion of the agent": for when it is said, "He has studied the *anuvāka* for a month, yet he has not grasped it," completion (*apavarga*) is not understood; what then? Only the mere incapacity of the agent. And in that case, there is no designation of completion.

7. *saptamīpañcamyau kārakamadhye* (Pāṇini 2.3.7). As in: "Having eaten today, Devadatta will eat in two days" (*dvyahe bhoktā*) or "He will eat after two days" (*dvyahād bhoktā*). Now, one might object: here there is only a single agent; since the designation of being "in between" is based on a distinction of *kārakas*, how can it apply here?
Since that [distinction] exists, how can there be a temporal interval between two factors (*kāraka*) when there is no difference between the factors?

To this he says: "Of the agent and the power," and so forth. For it is not the substance (*dravya*) that is the factor, but rather the power (*śakti*); and that [power] is what differs here. For instance, in Devadatta, there are two powers.

When [the agent] is established as being one on the first day and the other having passed two days, the designation "middle" is appropriate given the distinction in the capacities of the agents. Regarding the rule "of the agent and the object" (*kartṛkarmaṇoḥ*), etc.:
the archer is the agent (*kartṛ*), and the target is the object (*karman*). Regarding the rule "of the object and the ablative" (*karmāpādānayoḥ*), [it refers to] the object.

That very [point] is the *apādāna* from which one departs further. Regarding the rule "optionally [the sixth case is used] for the object (*karman*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*)," that which is indicated here by the word "here" (*iha*) is the locus; and that same thing is also the object. As in the example "a *krośa* between those two," since the *krośa* here lacks the status of being either an *apādāna* or a locus, the seventh and fifth cases are employed.

It is not the case that [the arrow] departs from the *krośa* (the distance of a league); rather, it departs from a portion thereof. Nor is the target situated within the *krośa*; rather, it is situated in a portion thereof. Therefore, since the *krośa* would otherwise be subordinate [as a locus], the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would have been required; instead, the seventh and fifth case-endings (*saptamī* and *pañcamī*) are prescribed.

Now, why does the rule for the assignment of numerals (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) not apply here? For although there are two [categories], namely time (*kāla*) and distance (*adhvan*), there are also two [case endings], namely the seventh (*saptamī*) and the fifth (*pañcamī*); therefore, by virtue of this equality, the assignment of numerals ought to occur—[namely] the seventh case after *kāla* and the fifth case after *adhvan*. To this, he says:

Regarding the phrase "ṭhsaṃkhyātānudeśaḥ" and so forth: in the rule "ṭhsvaritenādhikāraḥ" (1.3.11), a *yogavibhāga* (separation of the rule) is made for the term "svaritena"; consequently, it also connects with what precedes it. This is so that wherever the state of being *svarita* is formally asserted, there the correspondence may occur according to numerical order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*). However, in this case...
Since the svarita accent is not present, there is no application of the rule for corresponding enumeration (saṃkhyātānudeśa).

8. The second case ending is used when joined with a *karmapravacanīya* particle. (Pāṇini 2.3.8) For example: *śākalyasya saṃhitāmanu prāvarṣat* ("It rained following the *saṃhitā* of Śākalya"). Here, the designation *karmapravacanīya* is applied by the rule *anurlakṣaṇe* (1.4.84).

9. "The locative case is used for that which is exceeded (*adhika*) and for that which expresses mastery (*īśvara*). (Pāṇini 2.3.9). For example: *upa khāryāṃ droṇaḥ* ("A *droṇa* [measure] in addition to a *khārī*"). The meaning is: "A *droṇa* exceeds a *khārī*.

By the rule *upa adhike ca* (1.4.87), the word *upa* receives the technical designation of *karmapravacanīya*. Regarding the phrase "and for that which expresses mastery": [an example is *adhi pañcāleṣu brahmadattaḥ*].

The meaning is: "and for whom there is the designation 'Lord'. For the designation "Lord" (īśvara) is possible only for a master; someone might have the misconception that the locative case should be used there [in the compound], and therefore, in order to dispel that, he says: "and for whom there is the word 'Lord'," etc. For whom...

By the phrase "this word *īśvara*," it is shown that the locative case (*saptamī*) occurs for both [the subordinate and] the master in turn. How so? For although the designation *karmapravacanīya* is prescribed for the word *adhika* by the rule *adhir īśvare* (Pāṇini 1.4.97), and *īśvara* means a master, and a master exists in relation to his own property (*sva*).

The word *adhi* is designated as a *karmapravacanīya* when it denotes the relationship between property and its owner (*svasvāmisambandha*). In that context, sometimes the owner is joined with the case-ending prescribed for a *karmapravacanīya*, and sometimes the property itself;
this has already been established previously. But how is it [expressed] for one...?

If it is said that this is the word "īśvara," then one's own [self] would also be joined with the case-ending of a *karmapravacanīya*, for there is no designation of "lord" (*īśvara*) applied to it. If that is the case, then the particle *ca* is used in the sense of including what has not been mentioned;
by means of it, the locative case is understood even in that which lacks the designation of "lord."
Thus, there is no fault.

10. *pañcamy apāparibhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.10). By the rule *apaparī varjane* (1.4.88), the technical designation *karmapravacanīya* is prescribed for the words *apa* and *pari*; and by *āṅ maryādāvacane* (1.4.89), the same is prescribed for *āṅ*.
