By this [rule], in the expression "it lightens around the tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ pari vidyotate*), the word *pari* [is used] according to the rule beginning with "lakṣaṇetthambhūtākhyāna... (Pāṇini 1.4.90).

11. And [the genitive case is used] in the sense of a substitute (*pratinidhi*) and an exchange (*pratidāna*), because [it is said]: "A substitute is similar to the original" (*mukhyasadṛśaḥ pratinidhiḥ*). That which is the "original" (*mukhya*) is whatever is established in a task, capable, well-known, or primary; that which is similar to it is the substitute (*pratinidhi*) in its absence for that task.

That which is taken up for the sake of accomplishment is a substitute (*pratinidhi*). In the example "Abhimanyu is the substitute for Arjuna" (*abhimanyurarjunataḥ prati*), Abhimanyu is the substitute for the primary [person], Arjuna; therefore, the fifth case ending occurs.
The suffix *tasi* is used after the fifth case in connection with *prati*. In the example "He gives him beans in exchange for sesame seeds" (*māṣānasmai tilebhyaḥ pratiyacchati*).

When sesame seeds were previously given, the giving back of beans (*māṣa*) in exchange for them occurs; thus, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in *tilebhyaḥ*. The meaning is: "having taken the sesame seeds, he gives beans.
Now, one might object that by the rule *pratiḥ pratinidhipratidānayoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.92), [the word *prati* should govern the accusative].

The designation *karmapravacanīya* applies only to the two meanings of "substitute" (*pratinidhi*) and "exchange" (*pratidāna*), for it is only in connection with those two that the use of *prati* is appropriate; however, [the opponent], thinking that [the word *tasya*] does not refer to those two, says: "But surely... and so forth. Regarding the phrase "from the connection of a connection": it means "it is connected."

The relation [of substitution] is the substitute (*pratinidhi*), and the relation is the counter-gift (*pratidāna*); both of these are connected with the *karmapravacanīya* "prati. The relation which exists by means of that [primary] relation is the "relation of relations" (*sambandhasambandha*).
But what is related by means of that? That of which there is the substitute and the counter-gift.

For the words "substitute" (pratinidhi) and "counter-gift" (pratidāna) are relative terms; and these two do not exist unless there is a primary object previously known and a primary object previously given. Therefore, that which has a relationship with the substitute and the counter-gift is indeed related to them by virtue of those two.
"When joined with *karmapravacanīyas*, [the two words] become [nominative]. In some places, the reading is "due to the connection of the related thing" (*sambandhisambandhāt*).
Even there, the substitute (*pratinidhi*) and the offering (*hūtidāna*) are expressed by the word "related thing" (*sambandhi*);
for both of these are connected with the *karmapravacanīya*. By that related thing, which...
The relation is a relation of the related; such is the meaning.
12. *gatyarthakarmaṇi dvitīyācaturthyau ceṣṭāyāmanadhvani* (Pāṇini 2.3.12).

If by the word *ceṣṭā* (motion/exertion) here only action in general were meant, then the inclusion of *ceṣṭā* would be purposeless; for every verbal root expresses an action. Therefore, it is a qualification [of the object].
On account of the force of the context, this word *ceṣṭā* is understood to mean "motion";
thus he says: "of motions consisting of vibration" (*parispandakriyāṇām*). Vibration (*parispanda*) is bodily activity;
those for whom that is their action are described as such.

"In the rule *ṭha adhvanaḥ*, there is the inclusion of the meaning (*arthagrahaṇa*)," because the indication is primarily concerned with the meaning and because it is indicated by the locative case (*saptamī*).
If, in this context, there were an inclusion of the word-form itself (*svarūpagrahaṇa*), one would have formulated it as *ṭhan adhvanaḥ*.
Furthermore, this should be understood as a prohibition of what has already been established (*āsthitapratiṣedha*)—as stated in the *Kāśikā*: "It is understood that by..."

A specific place, such as a village and so forth, which is to be reached, is reached by means of that specific place; in common usage, that specific place is conventionally known as a "path" (*adhvan*). And by what is that which is to be reached reached? It is reached by that path which has been traversed. Therefore, this prohibition applies only to that [path]. But when that very same [place] is reached by way of a wrong path (*utpatha*), then—
Since that path does not receive the designation of "road" (*adhvan*), the dative case indeed occurs there.

[The question] "What is the purpose of mentioning the accusative? means that since the dative is optionally prescribed for the *kāraka* "object," the accusative is obtained by default in the alternative case; therefore, it is stated.
It is for the purpose of subverting that which would otherwise obstruct [the application of the rule]. [The author says: "So that it may apply even in the domain of an exception (apavāda).

Now, what is the purpose of including the word *artha* (meaning)? One might simply say "in the case of the object of motion" (*gatikarmaṇi*), since motion is indeed the meaning [of the verb]. This is not so; for there is a motion that belongs to the agent of motion (*gamitr*) alone...

This is stated so that [the rule] may apply where there is no dependence on the proximity of another word; and it is for the purpose that only that "motion" (*gati*) which consists of the act of stepping with the feet and is the primary sense should be understood. Therefore, it does not apply here: *striyaṃ gacchati* (he goes to a woman), *ajāṃ grāmam* (he leads a goat to the village).

He leads (*nayati*). For here, the meaning of "sexual intercourse" (*gamanamithuna*) is understood from the proximity of the word "woman" (*strī*), and not from the root *gam* alone. And the meaning of *nī* is simply "bringing to" (*prāpaṇa*), which constitutes the act of giving; however, the prefix *pra-* and the suffix *-ti* are subordinate as qualifiers of that. If this is so, then [in the case of] "he causes [him] to go to the village" (*grāmaṃ gamayati*) or "for the village" (*grāmāya*)...
In the form *gamayati* (causative), because the root *gam* has become subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), the action of going is not established [as the primary object];

for here, the meaning of *gam*—such as commanding or requesting—is what follows as the primary sense. This is not a fault; for in this case, the village is not the object of the causative suffix (*ṇyanta*), but rather the object of the root *gam* itself.

13. The fourth [case ending] is used for the recipient (*sampradāna*). (Pāṇini 2.3.13) For example: *devadattāya rocate* ("It pleases Devadatta"). The designation *sampradāna* is applied here by the rule *rucyarthānāṃ prīyamāṇaḥ* (1.4.33). For example: *puṣpebhyaḥ spṛhyati* ("He longs for flowers"). Here, [the designation *sampradāna* is applied] by the rule *spṛher īpsitaḥ* (1.4.36).

By this [sūtra], the statement "there is an addition [to the rule] regarding the sense of 'for that purpose' (tādarthye)" is intended. By the word *tat*, the meaning of a word ending in the dative case is indicated. That which is for the sake of this is *tadartha*; the state of being such is *tādarthya*. In that regard, [the addition applies] to the dative case.
The meaning is that an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made to provide this explanation. In this regard, the explanation is as follows:

a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) is made for the rule "the fourth case" (*caturthī*); by means of this, the fourth case occurs in the sense of being for the sake of something (*tādarthya*). Alternatively, [it is explained] by the rule "the fourth case with words meaning 'for the sake of that,' 'beneficial,' 'strength,' 'favorable,' 'happiness,' or 'protected' (*tadarthārthabalihitasukharakṣitaiḥ*, 2.1.36)."

The statement regarding the compounding of the dative case when expressing "being for the sake of that" (tādarthya)—namely, the rule "the dative is also used in the sense of being for the sake of that"—is an indicator [of this].
This applies in the context of the rule "with roots meaning *klṛp* when [something] is being accomplished," and so forth; that is, when there is the employment of roots having the sense of *klṛp*.

When the agent (*kartṛ*) is being brought about—that is, when it is qualified by the action of being accomplished—the fourth case (*caturthī*) should be stated; the meaning is that it must be explained. This explanation, however, relies on that very same split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). The same applies in cases such as "made known by the appearance of a portent" (*utpātena jñāpyamāne*) and so forth. For example: "The barley-gruel serves for urine" (*mūtrāya kalpate yavāgūḥ*).

The meaning is that the gruel comes into being in the form of a modification of urine. When there is the occurrence of a modification, the dative case (caturthī) is to be understood. Therefore, it does not occur here: *devadattasya śālayaḥ sampadyante* ("Devadatta's rice-grains come into being"). And when non-difference (*abheda*) is intended to be expressed, then by virtue of its higher status, only the nominative (prathamā) occurs, not the dative—as in: *mūtram idam* ("this is urine").

[In the examples] "it becomes gruel" (*saṃpadyate yavāgūḥ*) and "it becomes barley-rice" (*sampadyate yavaudanaḥ*), [the word for the source] is expressed in the nominative. However, when one intends to express that the material cause (*prakṛti*) is the ablative according to the rule *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.30), then the fifth case ending alone should be used— as in "it becomes urine from the gruel" (*mūtraṃ saṃpadyate yavāgvāḥ*).

"ṭhvātāya kapilā vidyaut" (a tawny lightning flash for the wind). Here, the tawny lightning flash is an omen that serves as the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) of the wind; when the wind is made known by that [omen], the fourth case ending occurs. "ṭharocakine":
the suffix *ini* is applied according to "ata iniṭhanau" (Pāṇini 5.2.115).

14. *kriyārthopapadasya ca karmaṇi sthāninaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.14). [The commentary explains: "That for which an action intended for another action is the upapada," and so forth. But how is this meaning obtained, since a second mention of the word *kriyā* ("action") is not found in this sūtra? To this he says:

Regarding the scope of the rule *ṭhtumunṇvulau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.10), since the condition of "having a verb as a subordinate element" (*kriyārthopapada*) is possible here, it is understood that whatever possesses such a subordinate verb is itself an action. Regarding the term *sthāninaḥ*: a "place" (*sthāna*) is so called because words abide (*tiṣṭhanti*) therein.
That which possesses this [quality] is the *sthānin* (the original element). This is what is meant: that whose meaning is understood, yet for which there is no actual usage, is called the *sthānin*.
For example, in "he goes to fetch fuel" (*edhebhyo vrajati*), the verb *harati* preceded by the prefix *āṅ* is the *sthānin*, while the fuel (*edhas*) is its object.

The meaning is: "he goes to fetch fuel. Now, one might object: since there is a sense of being for that purpose (*tādarthya*) here, the dative case is already established by the rule *tādarthye* (Pāṇini 2.3.13); so what is the purpose of this statement? It is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtham*):
so that the [dative] may occur only when the underlying verb (*sthānin*) is not actually employed, and not when it is employed.

The word *bhakṣi* is the substitute for *bhuj* here, because it is understood that "enter the house and eat the morsel. In the expression *praviśa tarpaṇam* ("enter for the libation") as well, *pibati* (the root *pā*) is the substitute. However, [this does not apply] when there is a word denoting the purpose of an action (*kriyārthopapada*), because [in such cases] it is indeed a suffix ending in *tumun* or others.
[A suffix] occurs when there is a word expressing an action as a subordinate element (*kriyārthopapada*). However, this [suffix] here is the *loṭ* (imperative) ending;
and since the *loṭ* is not prescribed when a word expressing an action is the subordinate element, the root *bhakṣi* (to eat) is not here accompanied by a subordinate element expressing an action.

15. *tumarthācca bhāvavacanāt* (Pāṇini 2.3.15). [The commentary states: "Having the same meaning as *tumun*. Because it is understood from the *vṛtti*, the word "same" (*samāna*) is not explicitly used. [It means] "from that which ends in an affix denoting a state of being (*bhāvavacana*) having the sense of *tumun*. The sense of *tumun*...

That which has at its end an affix expressing an action (bhāva) is described as such. [The author] will state later, "And those expressing an action," and this is a reference to that. For only that [affix] which has the sense of *tumun* can be an affix expressing an action, and no other. In the example "He goes for the sake of cooking" (*pākāya vrajati*), although the sense of being for the sake of something else (*tādarthya*) is understood, the dative case still occurs.

It does not occur; because the sense of being for that purpose (*tādarthya*) has already been expressed by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) prescribed for that very [context], just as it does not occur in the case of *pācako vrajati* ("the cook goes"). Therefore, this [sūtra] was commenced for the sake of prescribing the dative case (*caturthī*). Alternatively—as from a word expressing an action (*bhāvavacana*) itself—just as...

It might be argued that this [rule] is for the sake of restriction so that [the error] "the cook goes" (pācako vrajati) does not occur here. [The forms] *pākaḥ*, *tyāgaḥ*, and *rāgaḥ* are formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the action (*bhāva*). But surely the mention of the word "having a verb as its object" (*kriyārthopapada*) will follow [from the previous rule], and therefore there would be a transformation of the case-ending for that purpose?
Having established this connection, [the rule] will be applied as follows: "from a word expressing an action (bhāvavacana) which has another action as its object (kriyārthopapada).

But since a word expressing an action that has another action as its object is necessarily one whose meaning is "for the sake of" (tum-artha), what is the purpose of including the term "tum-artha"? This is not so; for the inclusion of the phrase "having another action as its object" does not apply to a word expressing an action [in general].

The qualification is possible; however, it applies to the verbal root itself. Therefore, the mention of *tum-artha* (the sense of *tumun*) must indeed be made. In the example "kārako vrajati" (he goes as an agent), the suffix *ṇvul* is applied by the rule "tumun-ṇvulau" (Pāṇini 3.3.10). This [suffix] has the sense of *tumun*, but it does not express the abstract action (*bhāva*); rather, what does it express? It expresses the agent (*kartṛ*).
Therefore, it does not occur after that which ends in -t.

16. "After [words expressing] *namas*, *svasti*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *alam*, and *vaṣaṭ*, [the fourth case ending is used]. (Pāṇini 2.3.16). Regarding this, it is said: "The word *alam* is taken here in the sense of 'sufficiency' (*paryāpti*). In connection with the word *prabhavati*, which has the same meaning as the word *alam*, according to the rule "tasmai prabhavati santāpādibhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.1.101), [the fourth case is employed].

This is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the statement of the fourth case. Now, from this indicative mark, the meaning understood is that "this refers to the object (*artha*), and not to the word (*śabda*)," but it does not mean that it refers to the sense of sufficiency (*paryāpti*). And thus, there would also be the inclusion of the terms *bhūṣaṇa* (ornament) and *pratiṣedha* (prohibition).

[It might be argued: "In that case, the fourth case ending would also occur in examples such as *kanyām alaṃkaroti* ('he adorns the girl') and *alam bāle rodanena* ('enough, child, with weeping'). This is not a fault; by virtue of the semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*), there will be a selection only of the sense of 'sufficiency' (*paryāpti*). How so? In the case of *kanyām alaṃkaroti*, [the rule] *upapadavibhakteḥ*..."

Since "the case ending denoting the *kāraka* is more powerful" (Cāndra-vyākaraṇa-pañjikā 69), there must be the accusative case alone by the rule "the second [case] in the sense of the object" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.2). For the same reason, in the expression "enough with crying, child," there must likewise be the instrumental case in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), because here crying has indeed attained the status of being the instrument.
"By its connection with the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), it follows by implication that the sense of 'sufficiency' (*paryāpti*) is understood.

Furthermore, the particle *ca* serves to conjoin this very [meaning]. This means that the particle *ca* has the purpose of conjoining this rule regarding the prescription of the dative case (*caturthī*) when used in connection with words such as *namaḥ*. Because of this further injunction, the dative [is employed].

By the rule *cāśiṣyāyuṣya-* (Pāṇini 2.3.73), when a blessing (*āśis*) is intended to be expressed, even that genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) which is optionally prescribed [by 2.3.61] is set aside, and only the dative (*caturthī*) occurs. If this is so, then [one might object that] even the case-ending denoting a *kāraka* (the agentive, etc. would be set aside in examples such as *kanyām alaṅkurute*.

It would indeed be the fourth case; and consequently, as for what was stated—that by virtue of the semantic force (sāmarthya), only the sense of "pervasion" (paryāpti) will be understood—that is not tenable? This is not a fault;
because the case-ending denoting the grammatical factor (kāraka-vibhakti) is stronger, and because the restatement [of the rule] serves its purpose elsewhere.
Alternatively—the optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) that is about to be stated applies here as well by the logic of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*).
Consequently, in examples such as *kanyām alaṅkurute*, the dative case does not occur.

17. *manya-karman* [is used] optionally (*vibhāṣā*) in the sense of disregard (*anādara*), provided the object is not a living being (*aprāṇiṣu*). (Pāṇini 2.3.17) "Disregard (*anādara*) means contempt (*tiraskāra*)," because the word *anādara* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in this very sense. Contempt (*tiraskāra*) means humiliation (*paribhava*), that is to say, disrespect (*avajñāna*). For example: "I do not regard you as even a blade of grass" (*na tvā tṛṇāya manye*). [This implies] not even [as much as] a blade of grass...
The meaning is: "I consider you to be even more base. [Question: "What is the purpose of specifying the *vikaraṇa* suffix? [That is to say:
why was it not stated as "in the sense of the object of *man*" (*manikarmaṇi*)? For in that way, the rule would have been more concise. [Answer:
It is so that there may be the inclusion of the root *man* belonging to the *divādi* class, meaning "to know" (*man jñāne*, DhP 1176), and not the root *manu*.

He says "But I do not consider you a blade of grass" (*na tvāṃ tṛṇaṃ manve*) in order to show that the mention of the *vikaraṇa* suffix is for the purpose of preventing the inclusion of the root *bodhane* (DhP 1471), which belongs to the *tanādi* class.
This is just as in examples such as "I consider the stone a grindstone" (*aśmānaṃ dṛṣadaṃ manye*), where the object remains as it is established in reality.
In the statement "the own-form (*svarūpa*) is manifested," no disregard for this [rule] is perceived.
Regarding the rule *yedatadaprāṇiṣu*, it should have been stated as *tadanāvādiṣu*.
The meaning is that the mention of *anāvādi* should be made while removing the mention of *aprāṇi*. For, according to the existing formulation, it is not [correct].
The intention is that in the case of *tvā nāvaṃ manye*, the dative case would occur, but in the case of *na tvā śune manye*, the dative case would not occur.

18. *kartṛkaraṇayos tṛtīyā* (Pāṇini 2.3.18). [In the commentary on the rule for the prescription of the third case-ending, there is the reading: "An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) should be made for *prakṛti* and so forth. What, then, is the reason? It is not established [by the general rule].

Because of the absence of both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*). The intention is that their absence follows from the non-existence of any action (*kriyā*), as seen in examples such as *prakṛtyābhirūpaḥ* ("naturally handsome"). Here, by means of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), only a mere relationship is perceived, but no action whatsoever; and without that [action], there can be no agent or instrument.

[The genitive is used] by way of possibility, because those two depend upon an action. Consequently, the sixth case (genitive) would be characterized by a relationship—such as *prakṛter abhirūpaḥ* ("one who is handsome by nature"), *prāyasya yājñikaḥ* ("one who is a sacrificer by habit"), or *gotrasya gārgyaḥ* ("one who is a Gārgya by lineage").
[In examples such as] *samena dhāvati* ("he runs on level ground") or *viṣameṇa dhāvati* ("he runs on uneven ground"), although there is indeed an action here, [the genitive does not apply].

Nevertheless, in this context, the words *sama* (equal) and *viṣama* (unequal) are not intended to be expressed as instruments (*karaṇa*), but rather as objects (*karman*); consequently, the accusative case ending would be required. Even in examples such as "he buys grain for two *droṇas*," the meaning intended is that [the price] consists of two *droṇas*. [Likewise in] "he buys animals for five... [and so forth].
"He buys [them]. A herd of animals consisting of five as its measure is a "pañcaka" herd.

The meaning is that he buys the animals having formed them into groups of five. Similarly, in the expression "he buys horses for a thousand," it means having formed them into groups of a thousand; that is, having made them into thousands.
The purpose of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* (supplementation) is for the sake of demonstration. In this regard, the demonstration is as follows:

even a verb root (*kriyā*) that is merely implied serves as the cause for the grammatical factors (*kāraka*s). And here, in the expression *prakṛtyābhirūpaḥ* ("naturally handsome"), the meaning of "doing" (*karoti*) or the meaning of "being" (*bhavati*) is indeed understood.

In the expression "I am Gārgya by lineage" (*gotreṇa*), when either knowledge or becoming is understood, the lineage is perceived as an instrument (*karaṇa*). In examples such as "he runs on level ground" (*samena dhāvati*), it is understood that he runs by means of an instrument, namely, a level or uneven path. Even in the case of "by two *droṇas*" (*dvidroṇena*), the third case ending does not denote the status of an object (*karman*).

What does it indicate? It indicates the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*). For in this case, gold and the like, which serve as the price for two *droṇas* and so forth, are expressed by the word "two *droṇas*" etc. because they are intended for that purpose (*tādarthya*).
Since that [gold] also possesses the status of being an instrument, the instrumental case ending is established everywhere simply by the rule "by means of an instrument" (*karaṇe*).

19. *sahayukte 'pradhāne* (Pāṇini 2.3.19). For "conjunction with *saha*" (*sahayoga*) occurs only when there is a relation with an action, a quality, or a substance. Therefore, examples such as *putreṇa sahāgataḥ* ("he has come together with his son") are illustrations [of this rule] according to their respective relations with action and so forth.
These [examples] have been presented by the author of the Vṛtti. In all cases, the son is subordinate here; therefore, the third case ending occurs.

Now, one might object: since a connection with the action and so forth is perceived for both the father and the son, why is the son subordinate while the other possesses primacy? To this he says: "of the father here."

And so forth. Although the connection with action and so on is perceived as residing in both [the agent and the object], nevertheless, the distinction between primary and secondary is established in dependence upon the operation of the word employed—namely, that which has its connection with action and so on conveyed by the word is primary, while the other is secondary. In this case...
However, it is the father’s connection with the ritual action and so forth that is conveyed by the word, not the son’s.

Why is this? Because of the inherent nature of the word’s expressive power (*śabda-śakti*). For such is the word’s power that it is capable of making known the connection with the ritual action and so forth for the father alone, and not [for the son].

Regarding the phrase "of the son" (*putrasya*): in this way, the singular number in expressions such as "he has come" (*āgata*) is justified. Otherwise, because there would be duality [of agents], the dual number would be required—as in "the father and the son have come" (*pitāputrau āgatau*). As for the statement, "But the son, being merely implied, is subordinate," this implies that the actual meaning is the connection with the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthayoga*).

And since that [denotation] is based on a distinction, it is not possible without a connection to the son’s action and so forth; therefore, because the connection is inseparable (nāntarīyakatva), it also conveys the son’s connection to the action and so forth. This is because "the instrumental case is prescribed when used with the sense of 'together with' (saha). Why?
Is it not understood that the rule for the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is prescribed when there is a connection with the sense of "together" (*saha*)?

This is because of the inclusion of the word "connected" (*yukta*). And this is its sole purpose: so that the third case occurs in connection with the sense of "together," and nothing else—as in the example, "The teacher's cow is together with the student" (*śiṣyeṇa sahopādhyāyasya gauḥ*). In this [example],...

The genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is stated [in Pāṇini 2.3.50] for the teacher (*upādhyāya*) because of his status as the primary [referent] in the expression "the connection with a substance. In that case, if the term "non-primary" (*apradhāna*) were not included, the genitive would apply even to the teacher, who is the primary referent. [Objection: But will it not be the genitive by virtue of its higher position [in the rules]? [Response: It will not; because [the teacher] is not a subordinate element (*aśeṣatvāt*). However, when the term "non-primary" is included...
The genitive case is used here because this remainder is what remains.
20. *yenāṅgavikāraḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.20).

This word *aṅga* is well-known in the sense of a "limb" (*avayava*). If it were understood here in that very same sense, then [the rule] would apply only in this case: *akṣi kāṇam asya* ("his eye is blind"); for in this instance, the *akṣi* is indeed a limb of the body.

[A modification] is indicated by a quality (*guṇa*) that is itself a modification (*vikāra*), as in "blind in one eye" (*kāṇa*). But in this case, it would not apply—namely, in the expression "blind in the eye" (*akṣṇā kāṇaḥ*).

For here, no modification of the member (*avayava*), the eye, is perceived; rather, what is perceived is the modification of the whole (*aṅgin*), the person. Therefore, he says: "The word *aṅga* [is used] here," and so forth.

The word *aṅga* is derived as "that which has a limb" (*aṅgam asyāsti*), showing that the term *aṅga* ends with the suffix *ac* according to the rule for words beginning with *arśas*. This is because the possessor of limbs (*aṅgin*) depends upon its limbs.
That very thing in relation to which the possessor of limbs possesses the status of being the possessor of limbs is what is indicated by the word "by which" (*yena*).
He says "by which," etc., in order to demonstrate [this]. He shows the meaning obtained through the force of the context by the word "vikṛtena" (by the modified).

For a modification of the possessor of a limb is not indicated by a limb that is unmodified. "It is indicated" means "it is manifested. "One-eyed because of the eye": here, by the part that is the eye—

Since the modification of the whole, Devadatta, is perceived through the modification of a limb, the third case ending occurs [in the word *pāṇinā*]. But how can the whole be designated as such by means of a modified part? To this he says:
"By the property of the part," and so forth. For example, "this is a staff."
Just as the term "city" is applied here to the whole by means of the property of a part— namely, its being fortified—
so too here the whole is designated by means of a deformed part. But how can the word "eye" be used here, given that blindness exists even without it?

Is the quality of the aggregate not indeed perceived? This is true; for in common linguistic usage, there is no regard for such weightiness or lightness. However, one who does pay heed to it simply does not employ the word *akṣi* at all.
In the example "ṭhakṣi kāṇam asya" ("his eye is blind"), if the mention of the word *aṅga* (limb/member) were not present [in the rule], the third case ending would occur after the word *kāṇa*.
For it is observed that by means of the quality (*guṇa*) of blindness, a modification of the eye—an individual member (*avayava*)—is indicated for the whole (*samudāya*).
21. *itthambhūtalakṣaṇe* (Pāṇini 2.3.21).

By the phrase "in some manner" (*kañcit prakāram*), he explains the meaning of *ittham*. For instance, when the suffix *thamu* is prescribed by the rule *idamasthamuḥ* (5.3.24) in the sense of expressing a manner (*prakāravacana*).
"Thus" (*ittham*) means "of this form. A "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is said to be a mode (*prakāra*) that differentiates a general category (*sāmānya*).

By the word "attained" (*āpanna*), he explains the meaning of the root *bhū*. For instance, regarding the root *bhū* in the sense of "attaining," which is conjugated in the Ātmanepada (DhP 1844), and [the rule] "optionally up to *ā-dhṛṣ*" [from the *Caurādika* group].

Immediately following [the root] *dhā* (DhP 805), when the causative suffix *ṇic* is absent, the form *bhūta* arises with the *kta* suffix. Of that which has become such (*itīdṛśasya*). Regarding the word *lakṣaṇam*: it is called a *lakṣaṇa* because one is marked (*lakṣyate*) or characterized (*cihnyate*) by it;
thus, it is a mark (*cihna*). "Even you, with a water-pot... [is the example].

"He saw the student" (*chātram ādrākṣīt*): here, "humanity" (*manuṣyatva*) is the general property (*sāmānya*), and "studentship" (*chātratva*) is its specific mode (*prakāra*). For that student who has attained [that state], the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) is the secondary characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
"He [approached] the teacher with the student" (*chātreṇa upādhyāyam*): here, "humanity" is the general property, and "teachership" (*upādhyāyatva*) is...

A *prakāra* (mode); the characteristic of a teacher who has attained that [status] is the student. Regarding the rule "one identifies a wandering mendicant by his topknot": humanity is the general category (*sāmānya*), while the state of being a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) is the specific mode (*prakāra*).
The characteristic of that wandering mendicant who has attained that [status] is the topknot.

"Because the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) is included within the compound. This means that due to the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), the meaning of the indicator is not distinct from the meaning of the *bahuvrīhi*. Since the indicator is thus included as something to be expressed (*vācya*) within the *bahuvrīhi* itself, the third case ending does not occur, as its purpose has already been served. This refers to the rule "itthambhūtalakṣaṇe" (Pāṇini 2.3.21).

What? "The lightning flashes around the tree. Here, there is no indication of anything that has attained the state of flashing by means of the tree; rather, it is the flashing itself [that is indicated].
22. *saṃjño 'nyatarasyāṃ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.22).

In the example "mātrā sañjānīte" ("he recognizes [his] mother"), there is the substitution of *ja* for *jña* by *jñā-śrantho yuc* (3.3.107), the substitution of *ī* by *ī halyaghoḥ* (6.4.113), and the designation of the action as *saṃpratibhyāmanādhyāne* (1.3.46).

Thus ends the section on the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). However, in the case of *ādhyāna* (thinking of or longing for), because of the subsequent rule "after roots meaning 'to think of' (*dhī*), 'to desire' (*gṛdh*), and *day* and *īś*, [the genitive is used] for the object" (Pāṇini 2.3.52), the genitive case occurs—as in *mātuḥ sañjānāti* ("he thinks of his mother"). Furthermore, when a *kṛt*-suffix is employed, even in cases other than *ādhyāna*, because of the subsequent rule "of the agent and the object when a *kṛt*-suffix follows" (Pāṇini 2.3.65), [the genitive is used].
The sixth case ending alone occurs—namely, the suffix -tā, forming "saṃjñātā."

23. *Hetau* | (2.3.23) The cause (*hetu*) is of two kinds: scriptural (*śāstrīya*) and worldly (*laukika*). Among these, the scriptural is defined by the rule *tatprayojako hetuśca* (Pāṇini 1.4.55). The worldly cause is an object capable of being a means to achieve a result. Regarding the scriptural [cause]:

The third case ending is established by the rule *hetau ṭhakartṛkaraṇayos tṛtīyā* (Pāṇini 2.3.18). Therefore, this refers to a worldly cause; to this he says: "capable of being a means to a result," and so forth. In common usage, an object is considered a cause even if it does not actually produce the result, provided it is capable of being a means to that result.

The inclusion of the term "fit" (*yogya*) is because it is said that something is called a "cause" (*hetu*). In expressions such as "the family [is established] by wealth," although wealth and the like do not actually produce the family, they receive the designation of "cause" in common usage due to their fitness for performing that function; therefore, the third case ending is used after them. Here, however, in the expression "wood for a sacrificial post" (*yūpāya dāru*), [the wood is the material cause].
Even though it is indeed a cause, its status as a cause is not intended to be expressed here. What then?
It is the "alteration" (anyathātva) of the cause. Therefore, the fourth case ending (*caturthī*) occurs in the sense of being for that purpose (*tādarthya*).

24. When the agent is not the creditor (*ṛṇin*), the fifth case ending is used [for the instrument]. (Pāṇini 2.3.24) For example: *śatena bandhitaḥ* ("He was bound for a hundred"). This form occurs when the root *bandh* takes the causative suffix (*ṇic*) followed by the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*). It means "a debt of a hundred" because it is to be paid to the creditor (*uttamarṇa*); this is due to the [debtor] being the instigator (*prayojaka*).

Regarding the term "agent designation" (*kartṛsaṃjñā*): because the agent designation is prescribed by the word *ca* ("and") in the rule *tatprayojako hetuśca* (Pāṇini 1.4.55). Now, one might object: the worldly cause (*laukiko hetu*) was taken up in the preceding sūtra, and since it is carried over here as well, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is prescribed from that very [worldly cause] alone; yet, there is no worldly [cause] here.

[Objection: What then is the cause? [Answer: It is technical (*pāribhāṣika*). Since there is no [grammatical] attainment (*prāpti*) [of the third case], the prohibition regarding that which is not an agent (*akartari*) would be purposeless. [Response: This is not so; for in that case, since the third case is already established for a technical cause, it is the worldly cause that is being referred to. However, here the fifth case is prescribed. Not [so].

In the case of a scriptural reason, it is established by someone [through experience]; here, both types of reasons are accepted. Alternatively, even for a scriptural reason, its status as a worldly reason is not at all contradictory. For whoever employs one in binding is fit for that means of accomplishment.
It certainly exists.

25. *vibhāṣā guṇe'striyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.25). [Example: "dhanena kulam" ("the family by means of wealth"). Here, "wealth" (*dhana*) is a substance (*dravya*), not a quality (*guṇa*). For a quality is that which resides in a substance, whereas a substance itself is not [a quality]. Furthermore, in this context, the word "quality" (*guṇa*) refers to anything that is merely related [to a substance].
It is said that [the reason] has taken on the form of the object to be proven (*parārtha*); by this, even such [inferences] as "there is fire here because of smoke" become established.

Now, an objection is raised: since it is stated that [the particle *iti*] occurs "not in the feminine" (*na striyām*), would it not follow that [statements] such as "there is no jar here because of non-perception" (*nāstīha ghaṭo 'nupalabdheḥ*) are not established? This is not so; one must perform a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) as follows: "optionally when a quality (*guṇe*) [is expressed]. By this—
Wherever it is desired, the desired result is achieved through the analysis of the grammatical rules (yogavibhāga) and so forth; thus, it indeed occurs even in the feminine gender.

26. The sixth case ending [is used] when there is the employment of the word *hetu* (Pāṇini 2.3.26). Since "employment" (*prayoga*) is a property of words, it is understood that by the term *hetu*, the word *hetu* itself is intended; therefore, he says: "when there is the employment of the word *hetu*" (the *Kāśikā* reads *hetuśabdaprayoge*).

And since the word *hetu* (cause) thus includes its own form, when its synonyms— such as *nimitta*, *kāraṇa*, and so forth— are employed, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) does not occur; for what purpose, then, is this [rule] stated again, given that the sixth case after words such as *adhyayana* occurs here precisely through the intention to express the "remainder" (*śeṣa*)?

And because it stands in grammatical apposition with that [word], would it not follow that the word "reason" (*hetu*) itself [denotes the probandum]? If this is so, then it is that very same intention regarding the remainder (*śeṣa*) which is expressed by the statement in this context for the benefit of those of dull intellect.
27. *sarvanāmnas tṛtīyā ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.27). Regarding the rule:

"In the case of *nimitta*, *hetu*, and *kāraṇa*, the observation of all case-endings is generally seen," it should be understood that this is obtained because the particle *ca* (and) has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.
Regarding the purpose of this inclusion of "artha" (object), he asks why the inclusion of synonyms was made, and says:

"The inclusion of synonyms," and so forth. Without the mention of synonyms, someone might have the misconception that this is merely an inclusion of the essential nature (svarūpa); therefore, in order to dispel that [misconception]...
The inclusion of the term "synonym" (paryāya).

28. The fifth case-affix (*pañcamī*) is used for the ablative (*apādāna*). (Pāṇini 2.3.28) As in: *vṛkebhyo bibheti* ("He fears from the wolves"). [This is so] because of the rule *bhītrārthānāṃ bhayahetuḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.25), which prescribes the status of being an ablative (*apādānatva*) for the cause of fear in the case of roots meaning "to fear" or "to protect. In the example *adhyayanāt parājayate* ("He is defeated because of his studies"), [the status of being an ablative applies] by the rule *parājerasoḍhaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.26).

(1.4.26) Thus, there is the status of being an *apādāna* (ablative). By the rule "after the roots √*añj* preceded by *vi-* and *parā-*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used" (1.3.19), the middle voice is applied. Regarding the phrase "in the prescription of the fifth [case-ending]," etc.: the meaning is that an *upasaṃkhyāna*—that is, an explanatory supplement—must be made here so that the fifth case-ending may occur when there is the elision (*lopa*) of a *lyap*-affix. In this regard, this [is the statement]:...

The explanation: here, the particle *ca* is carried over from the preceding sūtra; it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. By means of that, the ablative case will apply to the object (*karman*) when there is an elision of a *lyap*-affix (i.e., after a gerund).
[This is supported by] the statement "and there is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) regarding the locus (*adhikaraṇa*)," and so forth. Here too, regarding the word *upasaṃkhyāna*—

The meaning is "explanation. As for the explanation, it should be carried out as before, by resorting to the sense of the particle *ca* as indicating an unspoken accumulation [of examples], such as in the rule "and in the case of questioning and narration," and so forth. The word *vaktavyā* means "to be explained" (*vyākhyātavyā*).
The commentary, however, should be composed by relying on that very same recurrence of the particle "ca.

Alternatively—the fifth case ending is established here simply by the rule for the ablative (*apādāna*). For instance, in the question "From where do you come? (*kuto bhavān*), it is understood that "[he] comes from somewhere"; and in the statement "From Pāṭaliputra," it is likewise understood that "[I] am coming."
Therefore, the status of the ablative (*apādānatva*) is indeed clear.

Regarding the rule *yataś cādhvakāla* and so forth: the fifth case (*pañcamī*) should be prescribed when there is a measurement of the extent of the construction of a path or time from a certain point onward. This is what is meant:

When a path (*adhvan*) or time (*kāla*) is being measured, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) should be stated or explained for that which is intended as the fixed point of reference (*avadhibhūta*). The explanation, however, should be carried out as before by relying on the recurrence of the particle *vā*. Alternatively, when a path is being measured, it is established simply by the rule [Pāṇini 1.4.29] stating "the ablative (*apādāna*)."

The fifth [case ending] is used as follows: in the expression "Sāṅkāśya is four *yojanas* from Gavīdhumata," the action of "departing" (*niḥsṛtya*) is understood; therefore, its status as an *apādāna* (ablative) is entirely appropriate. Likewise, in the expression "the month from Kārttikī to Āgrahāyaṇī," the word "by means of" (*pareṇa*) is understood; in that case, [the ablative is applied] by the subsequent rule.
The fifth case (pañcamī) will have the sense of "direction" (dig).
In rules such as *tadyuktātkāle*, the word *tat* refers back to the fifth case;
that is, when time follows what is joined with the fifth case, the seventh case (saptamī) should be stated—that is, explained—as being used there.

As for the explanation: in the phrase "the month from Kārttikī to Āgrahāyaṇī," the locative case is established by the rule *yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam* (Pāṇini 2.3.37). By means of the state (*bhāva*) of Āgrahāyaṇī, which occurs after the month following Kārttikī, that state is indicated as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

"From the first [case-ending] of the word *adhvan*," and so forth. The phrase "from that which is joined with" (*tadyuktāt*) is understood to carry over. In that context, when the non-difference (*abheda*) of Sāṅkāśya from a *yojana* (league) is intended to be expressed, then the first case-ending (*prathamā*) is used, as in: "Sāṅkāśya is four *yojanas* from Gavīṣumata. However, when difference (*bheda*) is intended to be expressed, [the rule] "and [the locative is used] by means of whose state... (*yasya ca bhāvena*) applies.

The locative case is used here by the rule *bhāvalakṣaṇam* (Pāṇini 2.3.37). For instance, in the expression "Sāṃkāśya exists when four yojanas have been traversed from Gavīdhumat," this is the meaning understood:
there, the act of traversing, which is related to the yojana, serves as the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) for the state (*bhāva*) of Sāṃkāśya.
29. *anyārāditarartedikśabdāñcūtarapadājāhiyukte* (Pāṇini 2.3.29). Regarding this, it is said:

"The word *anya* is taken here as a meaning (*arthagrahaṇa*). For the connection of one word with another occurs only through the mediation of meaning; therefore, it is understood that this is a reference to the meaning.

With the words beginning with "tena," he demonstrates the purpose of employing the term *artha*. Now, why does the ablative case (*pañcamī*) not also occur after the word *yajñadatta* in the expression "another [is] Devadatta from Yajñadatta"? It is because the ablative case produced after *devadatta* already conveys the sense of "otherness" (*anyatva*) residing in both [the source and the object].
Since that distinctness qualified by it can be conveyed by the ablative case (*pañcamī*) arising from a single [referent] alone, the ablative does not apply to the second related member.
As it is said: "The referent that is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of that which is indicated by the word 'other' (*itarat*) is what is expressed. For example:
In a certain context, two individuals are the subject—the person Devadatta and another someone.
Of these, one is first specified: "Devadatta is brave. For that person being specified, the second individual who is his relative or counterpart is expressed by the word *itara* (the other).
For example: "the other is a coward.

Regarding the phrase "the mention of 'sound' (*śabdagrahaṇa*)," and so forth: when there is the apprehension of sound, the meaning obtained is that a sound perceived in a direction is a "directional word" (*dikśabda*). By this, even that which is currently a directional word [is included], whether it refers to a location (*deśa*) or time (*kāla*).

That which exists [in relation to a direction] is also considered "defective" (*duṣṭa*) with respect to that direction; therefore, when there is a connection with such a word, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) occurs.

In that regard, the ablative is used with a word denoting a location: *pūrvo grāmāt parvataḥ* ("the mountain is to the east of the village"). It is also used with a word denoting time: *pūrvo grīṣmād vasantaḥ* ("spring is before summer"). Otherwise, it would only occur in connection with a word denoting a direction.
Thus [it is said], because in that very context the word for direction (*dik-śabda*) has its primary sense.

In the expression "to the east of the village" (*prāg grāmāt*), the suffix *kvin* is applied to the root *añc-* preceded by *pra-* according to Pāṇini 3.2.59 (*ṛtvig-ādi-sūtra*). From words ending in that [suffix] and beginning with *yad*, etc., [the suffixes] are applied after the locative, ablative, and nominative cases.

The suffix *stāti*, which is prescribed by the rule *dig-deśa-kāle* (Pāṇini 5.3.27), undergoes elision (*luk*) by the rule *ṭhañ-cer-luk* (5.3.30). Once this elision has been performed, the following examples apply: *dakṣiṇā grāmāt* (to the south of the village) and *uttarā grāmāt* (to the north of the village); likewise, *dakṣiṇāhi grāmāt* and *uttarāhi grāmāt*.
The suffixes *āj* and *āhī* are applied [to the word *dakṣiṇa*] by the rules "from *dakṣiṇa*, *āc* and *āhi*" (5.3.37) and "from *uttara*, *āc*" (5.3.38).

30. By means of an affix having the sense of *atas* (Pāṇini 2.3.30). Since affixes having the sense of *atas* occur in their own meaning (*svārtha*) after words denoting direction (*dikśabda*), that which ends in such an affix is itself a word denoting direction; therefore, this statement [prescribing] the fifth case ending applies by virtue of the preceding rule [Pāṇini 2.3.29]. For example: *puro grāmasya* ("in front of the village").

In the case of *pūrvā* and *adharā*, the suffix *asi* is applied by the rule *pūrvādharāvaṇāmasipuradhavaścaiṣām* (Pāṇini 5.3.39), and the word *pūr* undergoes the substitution of *pur*. In the case of *purastāt*, the suffix *astāti* is applied by the rule *dikśabdebhyaḥ saptamī* (Pāṇini 5.3.27), and the substitution of *pur* occurs by the rule *astāti ca* (Pāṇini 5.3.40).

Regarding "above the village" (*upari grāmasya*) and "above the village" (*upariṣṭād grāmasya*): by the rule *upary-upariṣṭāt* (Pāṇini 5.3.31), the word *ūrdhva* takes the substitute *upa*, and the suffixes *ri* and *riṣṭāt* are added. 31. *Enapā dvitīyā* (2.3.31). [When a word ending in an *enap* suffix is used, the second case ending is employed.]

"When the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is obtained by [the rule] *pūrveṇa*, this statement [is made]: 'Because *enap* has the sense of *atas*. Thus, the separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) must be performed for that purpose. A separate rule for *enap* must be formulated so that the sixth case may occur after it; otherwise, the second case would be superseded."
Then, "the second" refers to the second yoga; and here, the word "enapā" (with this) is understood to carry over.

32. *pṛthag-vinā-nānābhis tṛtīyā 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.31). "The mention of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is understood [to follow]," because it is marked as *svarita*. All these words beginning with *pṛthak* occur in the sense of "without a companion" (*asahāya*). However, their separate mention [here] is...

This is for the purpose of excluding other synonyms. Here, let there not be the third and fifth cases—as in *hirug devadattasya* ("apart from Devadatta") or *viṣvag devadattasya* ("on all sides of Devadatta"). For if the recurrence of the mention of the fifth case were absent, then, as in the case of connection with other synonyms such as *hiruk*, [the rule would not apply].
The sixth case (genitive) would occur; likewise, when used in conjunction with *pṛthak* and so forth, the sixth case might optionally occur instead of the fifth.

Therefore, the mention of the fifth case must be carried over [from the previous rule]. Since it will occur optionally by virtue of that very carry-over, what is the purpose of the mention of *anyatarasyām*? True; it was indeed made for its sake.
This is for the purpose of indicating the continuation [of the previous topic] and for the sake of what follows.

33. And in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), [the suffix *ṭhañ* is used] after the words *stoka*, *alpa*, *kṛcchra*, and *katipaya*, provided they do not denote a living being (*asattvavacanasya*). (Pāṇini 5.4.33).

Regarding the phrase "when there is merely a property" (*yadā tu dharmamātram*) and so forth: those qualities (*guṇa*) by connection with which a substance (*dravya*) receives the designation of "small" (*stoka*) and so on, are expressed by the word "property" (*dharma*). That alone...

When words such as *stoka* (a little) and the like, being expressed by verbal forms and the like, are intended to denote the instrument (*karaṇa*) rather than a substance (*dravya*), then words such as *stoka* signify non-existence (*asatva*). However, when they refer to a substance possessing those qualities based on the identity [expressed as] "this is that" (*so 'yam*), then they signify existence (*satvavat*).
[The rule] applies.

[The author says: "Let it not be so in the case of an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). Since an action (*kriyā*) is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it possesses the status of an object (*karman*). Its modifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is also an object, and that is non-substantial (*asattva*). For the action itself is...
Until then, it is not a substance (*dravya*); how then could that which qualifies it become a substance?

Even though *stoka* and the like have the same referent, they are mentioned separately for the purpose of excluding other synonyms; let it not be the case here that "he is liberated by a measure" (*mātrayā muktaḥ*).

34. *dūrāntikārthaiḥ ṣaṣṭhyantatarasyām* (2.3.34). Although [the use of] the sixth case is established here even by virtue of being a "remainder" (*śeṣa*) when the fifth case is optionally prescribed, nevertheless, this mention of the sixth case is made so that it may also apply to the rule *caturthī cāśiṣyāyuṣyamadrabhadrakuśalasukhārthahitaiḥ* (2.3.73).

By this [rule], even the dative case prescribed for the expression of benediction (*āśis*) is superseded, so that the genitive alone may occur—as in *dūraṃ hitaṃ grāmasya* (beneficial to the village from afar) and *antikaṃ hitaṃ grāmasya* (beneficial to the village from near). Now, one might ask: since the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") was already mentioned in the present context, why is *anyatarasyām* mentioned again?
To the question "For what purpose? he says: "The mention of *anyatarasyām*," and so forth.

If the mention of *anyatarasyām* were not made here, then the third case (*tṛtīyā*) would optionally apply; for that alone was heard [prescribed] in the immediately preceding rule. By making the mention of *anyatarasyām* again, [the alternative is provided].

It is understood that [the rule] is for the purpose of prescribing the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*), because there is no other purpose. For instance, this is not intended as an alternative to the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*); indeed, the alternative for the third case is already established by the previous mention of the term *anyatarasyām*. Nor is there any other case-ending [that could be intended].
What is the subject under discussion? It is the ablative case (pañcamī). Therefore, this is understood as being for the purpose of providing an option regarding the ablative case.
35. *Dūrāntikārthebhyo dvitīyā ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.35). [Note:

A sentence of this form does not exist in the Vṛtti. The word "and" (*ca*) implies that the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is also included by virtue of its recurrence from the previous rule; furthermore, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is also conjoined by means of the particle "and."
Regarding the phrase "according to their respective [forms]": it means that each [suffix] occurs in its own proper domain—that which belongs to it—and not in any other case-ending.
36. *saptamy adhikaraṇe ca*. (2.3.36) [The commentary states:

"From words meaning 'far' or 'near,' four case-endings occur. By the preceding rule (*dūrāntikārthebhyo dvitīyā ca*), there are three endings beginning with the accusative; by this [rule], the locative (*saptamī*) is added.

Regarding the rule "saptamīvidhāne ktasyenviṣayasya" and so forth: when there is a *kta*-suffix whose scope (*viṣaya*) is the particle *in*, the locative case (*saptamī*) should be prescribed for its object (*karman*). What is a *kta* whose scope is *in*? The meaning is: that which ends in such a *kta* and is used together with that very [particle *in*]. This is because the word *viṣaya* here has the sense of "not existing elsewhere" (*ananyatrabhāva*). [As in the example: *adhītī*.

Regarding the term "vyākaraṇe": it means "by him grammar has been studied. Since the word *anena* ("by him") is understood from the rule *śrāddhamanena bhuktam* (Pāṇini 5.2.85), and since the suffix *ini* is understood from the rule *pūrvādīniḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.86), the suffix *ini* is applied here by the rule *iṣṭādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 5.2.88). In this case:

Although the suffix *kta* is prescribed only with respect to the object (*karman*), nevertheless, when a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is produced, the connection [of the suffix] with the object ceases; yet, since there remains a connection between the meaning of the verbal root and grammar,
grammar itself becomes the object, and thus the second case ending is employed.

It might be so—as in the case of *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam* ("one who has previously made a mat"). Therefore, the meaning is that an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*)—that is, an explanatory statement—must be made regarding the locative case. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the agent who is "one who has studied" (*adhītī*) intends to express the grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) as the locus (*viṣaya*) of his action; therefore, it is simply [treated] as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
The seventh case is established.

Regarding the rule "sādhvasādhuprayoge" and so forth: here, the word *sādhu* is taken in the sense of non-honor (*anarcā*). For if it were used in the sense of honor (*arcā*), the locative case would already be established by the rule "sādhunipuṇābhyāmarcāyām" (Pāṇini 2.3.43). Examples include "sādhur devadatto mātari" and so on; here too, the locative case is used specifically in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

For in this case, the word "mother" (mātṛ) is applied to those actions situated in the mother, and the word "father" (pitṛ) to those actions situated in the father; and since these actions possess the status of being the object with respect to their correctness or incorrectness, the locative case is used precisely in the sense of the locus of relation (*vaiṣayika-adhikaraṇa*). As for the word *vaktavya* (to be spoken):
The word *vyākhyeya* (to be explained) functions here in the sense of "should be [so]"; the same applies in subsequent cases as well.
Regarding the phrase "and of those worthy of being *kārakas*," etc.: here the word *kāraka* has the state (*bhāva*) as its primary meaning.
Those for whom the status of a *kāraka*—that is, the status of a means (*sādhana*)—is logically appropriate with respect to an action are "those worthy of being *kārakas*" (*kārakārhāḥ*); of them...

The locative case should be stated when [the word] is worthy of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action). For example, "in the presence of the prosperous" (*ṛddheṣu*), and so forth. For those who are prosperous indeed deserve the status of being a means (*sādhana*) with respect to the act of eating; and it is precisely their status as a *kāraka* that is intended here.
Following this principle, the meaning of such expressions as "the non-*kāraka*-status of those who are worthy of being *kārakas*" is established.
It should be understood that here, too, in all cases, the locative case is established by the rule *yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam* (Pāṇini 2.3.37). For instance,
in this context,
the state of sitting and so forth associated with the poor is characterized by the action of eating and so forth associated with the wealthy.
It is observed that in the expression "one kills the tiger for its skin" (*carmaṇi dvīpinaṃ hanti*), the skin is the motive (*nimitta*) for the killing of the tiger,
and there is a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) between that [skin] and the tiger as the object (*karman*). Here too, [the same applies].

Because the particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned, the locative case (*saptamī*) is established. Now, one might object: "The particle *ca* is for the purpose of attracting the meanings of 'far' (*dūra*) and 'near' (*antika*). [We reply: It is not necessary; by means of the particle *ca* used for that attraction, the locative case is obtained precisely through the analysis of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) itself: "The locative case is used after words meaning 'far' or 'near'."
It will be so. Or else—the seventh case ending should be understood [here] because the particle *ca* in the subsequent sūtra has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.

37. *yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam* (Pāṇini 2.3.37). But what kind of action indicates another action? To this he says: "and well-known," and so forth. The word *ca* (and) has the sense of restriction; the meaning is "only that which is well-known. For that which is itself not well-known [cannot indicate].

The characteristic of the other [the locative case] is thus established. Now, how is it that in the expressions "he went when the mango trees were bearing fruit" (*phalāyamāneṣv āmreṣu gataḥ*) and "he came when they had ripened" (*pakveṣv āgataḥ*), the locative case is used, even though no verbal action (*bhāva*) is heard here? Even if it is not explicitly heard, it is nevertheless understood; the meaning is "when the fruit-bearing state had arisen."

38. And the sixth case [is used] in the sense of disregard (*anādara*). (Pāṇini 2.3.38) *Anādara* means contempt, that is to say, disrespect. In the example "rudataḥ," the suffix *śatṛ* is applied to the root *rudir* (Dhātupāṭha 1067), meaning "to shed tears."

39. [The genitive case is used] with *svāmī*, *īśvara*, *adhipati*, *dāyāda*, *sākṣin*, *pratibhū*, and *prasūta*. (2.3.39) Although *svāmī*, *īśvara*, and *adhipati* have the same meaning, they are mentioned separately for the purpose of excluding other synonyms; thus, [the genitive] should not be used here: *grāmasya rājā* ("the king of the village").
"When the sixth case ending itself is obtained" means: when the sixth case ending is obtained by way of a residual definition (śeṣalakṣaṇā).
40. And [the genitive is used] after *āyukta* and *kuśala* when [they signify] practice (*āsevā*).

(2.3.40) Since being "appointed" (*āyuktatā*) and "skillfulness" (*nipuṇatā*) pertain specifically to the making of mats and the like, the locative case alone would have been expected; this rule is stated to provide for the optional use of the genitive.
Why [is the condition] "in the sense of being habitually engaged" stated? [Consider the example: *āyukto gauḥ śakaṭe* ("the ox is yoked to the cart"). The meaning here is "slightly yoked."

41. *yataśca nirdhāraṇam* (Pāṇini 2.3.41). For what purpose, then, is this [sūtra] stated? Since the member being singled out (*nirdhāryamāṇa*) is included within the whole (*samudāya*), when the locus-ness (*adhikaraṇatva*) of that whole is intended to be expressed...

In that case, the locative case (saptamī) is indeed established, as in "the branch on the tree"; however, when there is a relationship between part and whole, then the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī) is used, as in "the branch of the tree. This is true; the statement is made for the sake of detailed exposition.
42. *pañcamī vibhakte* (Pāṇini 2.3.42).
"Vibhakta" means "division" (*vibhāga*). [The suffix] *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) in the neuter gender (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.114).
"In that which is the substratum of selection" (*yasmin nirdhāraṇāśraye*): that from which one selects is here the "substratum of selection."

Thus, since there is a division in every instance that serves as the basis for selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), it is understood—by virtue of the meaningfulness of employing the qualifier—that only where there is a division does that serve as the basis for selection; therefore, [the rule] does not apply in a case such as "Among cows, the black one is the most rich in milk. Likewise...
For when a specific portion is being singled out among cows, it is perceived as being included within the universal "cowness" (gotva);

therefore, there is no distinction [between the part and the whole]. But when it is perceived as distinct from the quality of blackness, then there is a distinction. In this case, there is no basis for the act of singling out (*nirdhāraṇāśraya*).

It is indeed a case of distinction (*vibhāga*). Here, however, in the expression "the people of Mathurā are more prosperous than those of Pāṭaliputra," the people of Mathurā are not included [in the comparison] either by way of their status as inhabitants of Mathurā or by way of their being more prosperous;
therefore, since this is a case of distinction, it constitutes the scope of this grammatical rule (*yoga*).

Others, however, say: where there is a separation of what was previously aggregated, that is the domain of the former rule (Pāṇini 2.4.1); whereas where there is the manifestation of a different quality in that which is already separate, that is the domain of this [rule].
Since in both these states there is indeed a separation (*vibhāga*), this rule as well is intended merely for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*).
For separation (*vibhāga*) is indeed falling away from a connection. And since the people of Pāṭaliputra,

when falling away from their connection with the people of Mathurā, assume the state of being the limit (*avadhi*) for that falling away from the connection, the fifth case ending is established by the rule for the ablative (*apādāna*).

43. *sādhunipuṇābhyām arcāyāṃ saptamy aprateḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.43). The reading in the Vṛtti is: "It should be stated that [the rule applies] when not accompanied by *pra* and so forth. Or rather: "It should be stated 'not after *pra* and so forth'. But what are *pra* and so forth? They are those [particles] for which [the rule] *lakṣaṇetthambhūtākhyāna...* [is prescribed].
By such rules as (Pāṇini 1.4.90), the technical designation *karmapravacanīya* is prescribed for those beginning with *prati*, *pari*, *anu*,
and so forth.
44. The third case ending is also used after the words *prasita* and *utsuka*.

This word *prasita* exists as an adjective (*guṇavacana*)—meaning "intensely attached" (*prakṛṣṭaḥ sitaḥ prasitaḥ*)—and it also exists as a verbal derivative (*kriyāśabda*) from the root *ṣiñ* "to bind" (Dhātupāṭha 1477) preceded by the prefix *pra*.

It is explained in the section on the *niṣṭhā* suffixes; there, because of its association with the word *utsuka*, which is an action-word (*kriyāśabda*), it is understood as an action-word. Therefore, he says: "one who is intent (*prasita*) is one who is attached (*prasakta*). "He who is constantly bound to that [object] is called by the word *prasita*. "Bound" (*ābaddha*) means as if bound; for he who—

Wherever one is attached, there one becomes as if bound—for example, "prasitaḥ keśaiḥ" (attached by the hair) or "prasitaḥ keśeṣu" (attached to the hair), and so forth. Since the state of being attached (*prasitatva*) and the state of longing (*utsukatva*) have the hair as their object, the locative case is already established by the rule *saptamy adhikaraṇe* (Pāṇini 2.3.36).
This statement is intended to prescribe the instrumental case optionally in certain instances.

45. *nakṣatre ca lupi* (2.3.45). Regarding the rule *nakṣatre ca lupi*, the locative case is prescribed by a transposition of cases (*subvyatyaya*) to convey the sense of the ablative. For this very reason, he says: "from the word *nakṣatra* ending in a *lup*-elision," and so forth. [Examples: *puṣyeṇa*, etc. [The rule applies] when [denoting] a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*).
In the case of *yuktaḥ kālaḥ* (4.2.3), the suffix *aṇ* prescribed [by that rule] undergoes elision by the rule *lub aviśeṣe* (4.2.4). Likewise,
in the expression *pañcāleṣu vasati*, the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by *tasya nivāsaḥ* (2.3.36) undergoes elision by the rule *janapade lup* (4.2.81).

"In *ṭhmaghāsu grahaḥ* (the planet is in Maghā)," the locative case (*saptamī*) is used here in the sense of proximity (*sāmīpye*), even though it is technically a locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Here, because the meaning of "time joined with a lunar mansion" (*nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ*, Pāṇini 4.2.3) is not intended to be expressed, the suffix *aṇ* does not occur. In "today is Puṣya," as before, there is the suffix *aṇ*, which is then elided (*lup*). The term "locus" (*adhikaraṇe*, Pāṇini 2.3.36) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], but [it is not applied here].
The intended meaning is that here the state of being a locus (adhikaraṇatva) is what is meant to be expressed.
46. The first case ending (*prathamā*) is used in the sense of the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), gender (*liṅga*), measure (*parimāṇa*), and number (*vacana*).

Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the nominal stem is existence" (*satā*): if this refers to a universal (*jāti*), then it would not apply to [proper names] such as Devadatta; if, on the other hand, "existence" (*satā*) means the state of being existent (*sato bhāvaḥ*), then it would not apply to things such as a sky-flower. Therefore, he says:

"The meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is 'being' (*sattā*). Wherever a word functions independently of other meanings, all of that is the meaning of the nominal stem. The inclusion of the term "being" (*satā*), however, is for the purpose of illustration. In the case of "highly" (*uccais*) and "lowly" (*nīcais*), the word *uccais* functions in its own sense independently of other meanings such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth. And in this case...

The purpose of [specifying] the first case is so that the optional rule for *te*, *me*, and so forth—stated in "sapūrvāyāḥ prathamāyā vibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 8.1.26)—may apply, as in: *grāma uccaiste svam* or *grāma uccaistava svam*. However, the technical designation *pada* would indeed apply even to the sixth case.

"Kumārī," "vṛkṣaḥ," and "kuṇḍam"—in these cases as well, the nominative case is established by the very fact that [gender] is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*); for gender, too, is indeed the meaning of the nominal stem. And so it will be stated under the rule *striyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.3): "But [the forms] in the feminine are established..."
Is it because [the word] qualifies the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that the feminine suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth are applied in their own sense (*svārthe*)?
This is not the case; for he will state there as well: "Or rather, let this be:
when the feminine gender is to be expressed" (*ma.bhā. 4.1.3*). Furthermore, this [suffix] relates to femininity (*strītvam*).

There would be such ambiguity; however, in the case of masculine and neuter [nouns], the gender must necessarily be expressed by the case-ending itself. For instance, if the word *taṭa* were used without a case-ending, there would be doubt as to whether it denotes masculinity or rather neuterness. In this regard, it is just as in the expression "the king’s man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*).

When there is no connection with the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), but rather a relationship of owner and owned, and that [relationship] is to be expressed, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs even in preference to the case endings; likewise, the genitive would also occur for masculine and neuter nouns.
Therefore, the mention of gender (*liṅga*) must be made.

"A *droṇa*, a *khārī*, an *āḍhaka*. But surely, in this case as well, the nominative case is established precisely because they constitute the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). For indeed, words such as *droṇa* and the like denote a measure—whether made of metal or wood—independently of any other object. True; it is established in that way.

When [words] denote only the measure (*parimāṇa*), it is well; but when they denote the measured object (*parimeya*), then it is not established. For instance, words such as *droṇa* and so forth denote the measured object, such as rice and the like, by taking up another entity—the measure, such as a *droṇa*—as their basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). But how is that so?

In that case, they exist [in the same substratum] due to the relationship of non-difference expressed as "this is that"— as in "a *droṇa* is rice measured by a *droṇa*. If this is so, since the denoted object is expressed through the form of the cause (the measure),
the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is indeed non-distinct [from the measure].

Is the nominative case already established by the rule "the meaning of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikārtha*) alone? It is not established; for when the primary meaning is present, it is not proper to resort to the secondary (figurative) meaning. But even so, the nominative will occur here simply by virtue of the mention of "gender" (*liṅga*); what then is the purpose of mentioning "measure" (*parimāṇa*)? This is not so; for in cases where that [measure]...
"There is no measure; that is the space. In this case, if there were an excess of measurement, the genitive alone would apply. Therefore, the mention of "measurement" (*parimāṇa*) must be made.
And the mention of "measurement" applies where [the word] denotes something other than the cause.

The word functions on the basis of a relation of non-difference (*abheda-sambandha*) in the form "this is that"; this should be understood as being for the purpose of indicating that [relation]. Therefore, the nominative case occurs even with unmāna and other measures which, like parimāṇa, are distinct entities [from the substance]:
*ghṛtam* (clarified butter), *palam* (a pala-weight), *dīrghaṃ kāṣṭham* (a long piece of wood), *śuklaḥ paṭaḥ* (a white cloth), *hastaḥ* (a cubit).
Thus, [measurements] such as the *muṣṭi* (fist) and the *vitasti* (span) become established. Why is this so? Because of the word *mātra*.

For here, that word is taken in the sense of pervasion (*vyāpti*), as in the examples: "he chooses a bride merely (*mātra*) [of such a kind]," or "he feeds merely (*mātra*) Brahmins. Therefore, it is understood that the mention of "measure" (*parimāṇa*) serves merely as an illustration. If [this were not the case]...
Just as in the expression "he eats only water" (*payaḥ-mātram bhuṅkte*), the word *mātra* has the sense of restriction (*niyamārtha*),
so too here it must have the sense of restriction; consequently, the nominative case would not apply to unmāna and the others,
because they are distinct from measurement (*parimāṇa*)— just as the nominative applies even to the aforementioned [qualities] such as oneness (*ekatva*) and so forth.
[The word] *syāt* [is used].

However, if the mention of "utterance" (*vacana*) were absent, the nominative case would not apply to the expressed numbers such as singularity and so forth, because of the governing rule *anabhihite* (Pāṇini 2.3.1).
But surely an exhaustive enumeration was made there? To that [it is replied]:...
Whence does this undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) arise? It is not so; for the enumeration [of examples] was rejected there.

For instance: *rūḍhaḥ karma*, *bhīṣmādayo'pi karmaṇi*, *tatra karmāṇi*, and *tatra karmaṇī*—thus the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) is established. This is because the second case is produced from the word *kaṭa*.

The general action (*sāmānyakarman*) has been mentioned, but not the specific action (*viśeṣakarman*). Since a specific action must necessarily be stated there, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) will apply to *bhīṣma* and so forth for the purpose of expressing that specific action. Alternatively—the mat alone is the object (*karman*), and because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it, the second case ending will apply even to *bhīṣma* and so forth.
There is no purpose in enumerating [all the means of expression];
as for the enumeration presented in the *Vṛtti*— namely, "by means of *dhātu*, *tiṅ*, *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and *samāsa*" (Pāṇini 2.3.1)—
that is intended to show that denotation is possible through these alone.

This should be understood as being intended to demonstrate the possibility [of such usage]. Although it is possible for numbers such as "one" and so forth to denote singularities and the like even by themselves, nevertheless, since the meaning of singularity and so on has already been expressed by those [words], the mention of "number" (vacana) implies that it is expressed by the case-ending (vibhakti) through deliberate effort.
They too have made an effort to demonstrate the possibility of such a designation, stating:

"of this particle which is meaningless," and so forth. Now, why is it that the mention of *prātipadika* (nominal stem) is not understood as being for the purpose of qualifying the meaning? For if that [mention of *prātipadika*] were absent, it would not be known—of what meaning [is it]? Thus...

Should the nominative case (prathamā) occur merely for the sake of the meaning? This is not so; for the nominative is prescribed after a nominal stem (prātipadika). In that context, if the mention of "nominal stem" were absent, it would be understood that [the nominative] occurs only for the meaning of the nominal stem itself. Therefore, the purpose of mentioning the nominal stem is exactly as stated by the author of the Vṛtti.
It is logical.

47. And [the vocative case is used] in addressing (sambodhane). Addressing is the act of making someone face one; it is included within the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadikārtha) because, according to the rule "it is added when there is an excess over that," addressing is subordinate to the action [of the verb]. Thus, it is subsumed under the meaning of the nominal stem.
It does not exist, because it is of that very nature; therefore, by that [suffix], the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) becomes augmented.
Now, how is it that here [the vocative] *he pacan* and *he pacamāna* occur? And why should they not occur?
Because the vocative has already been expressed by the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac*. These two [suffixes] also [occur] in the sense of the vocative.

The word *ca* ("and") will be explained as referring specifically to the vocative. [Objection: Let it not be by this [present rule]; it will be [covered] by the previous sūtra, since the meaning of the vocative here is included within the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) by the rule *kṛttaddhitasamāsāśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.46). [Response: The separation of the yoga (the division of the sūtra) is for the sake of what follows.

48. *sāmantritama* (Pāṇini 2.3.48). [The commentary says: "That word-form which ends in that [suffix]. Now, it has been established [in the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara*, p. 81] that "in a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, there is no extension of the rule to include what ends in that suffix (*tadantavidhi*)," as in the case of *suptiṅantaṃ padam*.

In the rule *padam* (Pāṇini 1.4.14), the inclusion of the word *anta-* [is used]; however, here in the formulation of a technical name (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), there is the mention of a suffix (*pratyaya-grahaṇa*).

How then is the technical name prescribed for that which ends in such a suffix? This is not so; although there is the mention of a suffix here in the formulation of a technical name, nevertheless, this technical name is prescribed specifically for that which ends in it. If here...

If there were the apprehension of the technical name (*saṃjñā*) for the suffix alone, then that [name] alone would be apprehended in the specific rules (*pradeśa*); and in that case, the formulation of the technical name would be purposeless. One could simply say "in the specific rules, [the word] *sambodhana*. Even so, the apprehension of the suffix alone is indeed obtained. Of that very [suffix]...
Because it is prescribed for the vocative case. Therefore, by the very fact of its being a technical name (*saṃjñā*), the name is obtained for that which ends in it.
The inclusion of the word "that" (*sā*) is so that this name may also apply to that which was prescribed for the vocative by the preceding rule—as in *he pacan* and *he pacamāna*. Otherwise...

By the previous rule itself—"In this [section], there is either an injunction or a prohibition for what is immediately preceding"—it would apply only to that [substitution] which has been prescribed; for it is with the intention that the pronominal word *sā* being mentioned here functions as a general term. Therefore, [the rule applies] to that which occurs in simple address alone.
The first [sūtra] establishes that [designation]; by means of this, the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is established everywhere.
