When the designation *āmantrita* exists, as in "he devadatta" and so forth, the acute accent (*udātta*) occurs at the beginning according to the rule "āmantritasya" (Pāṇini 6.1.198). The purpose of employing the long technical name "āmantritam" is—
For the sake of variety.

49. *ekavacanaṃ sambuddhiḥ* | (2.3.49) [The singular number is called] *sambuddhi*. As in: "he paṭo" (O cloth), "he devadatta" (O Devadatta). Here, when the designation *sambuddhi* applies, then under the governing rule "and in *sambuddhi*" (7.3.106), the substitution of *guṇa* occurs by the rule "guṇa for a short vowel" (7.3.108).

The elision of *su* occurs as appropriate by the rule "ṭeḥ hrasvāt sambuddheḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.69). Now, why was the term *sugrahaṇa* (the mention of *su*) not simply employed, given that there is no possibility of it referring to the locative plural, since the governing context is the vocative case? True; however, this is not the case, because [the term would apply to] the suffix in general.

The singular number was employed for the purpose of establishing a technical name (saṃjñā)—as in "he pacanam" and "he pacamāna"; otherwise, just as by the preceding rule a name was prescribed for that which ends in such [an affix], so too would it be here. Furthermore, no distinction is admitted here for that which lacks a name.
By the word *su*, only that which ends in it is indicated; consequently, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) would apply only to what ends in it.

Likewise, regarding the elision of *s* prescribed by "ṭheṅ hrasvāt saṃbuddheḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.69), according to the rule "ādeḥ parasya" (1.1.54), the elision would apply only to the initial [sound] of the suffix, and not to the entire suffix.
Therefore, the mention of the singular number is for the purpose that the designation [of "pratyaya"] should apply to a single suffix alone.
50. *Śeṣe ṣaṣṭhī* (Pāṇini 2.3.50). Since "object" (*karman*) and the others have been mentioned in the preceding context, "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is understood in relation to them; thus he says:
"that which is other than the object and the rest. The specific kārakas beginning with the object are distinct from that [remaining] relationship.

[The former] are the cause, while that [latter] is the fruit; and since the difference between cause and fruit is well-established, it is distinct from them. [This] distinction (*vyatireka*) is something separate from the meaning of the nominal stem (as stated in the *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī*). Distinction means excess (*ādhikya*). Or alternatively—by which...

That which is distinguished from, or made distinct from, the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is "distinction" (*vyatireka*). The distinction of the meaning of the nominal stem is "distinction of the nominal-stem-meaning" (*prātipadikārtha-vyatireka*). That is the "remainder" (*śeṣa*).
To the question "What, then, is this? he says: "The relationship between owner and owned, and so forth."

By the word "ādi" (etcetera), relations such as part and whole are included. Although a relation resides in two entities, nevertheless, because it is a single entity, it is expressed by the genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) arising from only one of the related members; consequently, the genitive does not occur for the second related member.

Even when arising from a single [word], the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs only from the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), not from the qualified (*viśeṣya*); from the qualified, however, only the nominative (*prathamā*) occurs. This is because this term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) denotes that which is a qualifier other than what is under discussion, as well as that which is for the sake of another. For thus say the learned men:

They teach that "the remainder is for the sake of another. The example of the relationship between owner and owned is "the king's man. Here, the man is primary because he is the substantive (viśeṣya); the king is secondary because he is the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa). [This applies] to the qualifier.

Because it exists for the sake of another, it has the status of a subordinate element (*śeṣa*); therefore, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs. But when both [elements] are qualifiers and require a third related entity, then the genitive occurs with respect to both, as in "the king's man's house" (*rājñaḥ puruṣasya gṛham*).

In the example "the foot of the animal" (*paśoḥ pādaḥ*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) expresses the relationship between a part and the whole. In the example "the son of the father" (*pituḥ putraḥ*), the genitive expresses the relationship between the produced and the producer. Now, what is the purpose of including the term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) [in Pāṇini’s rule], given that in rules such as "the second case is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*), there is a restriction regarding the grammatical suffix (*pratyayaniyama*) and a restriction regarding the meaning (*arthaniyama*)?

There are two positions. Regarding the position that the restriction applies to the *pratyaya* (the suffix), if the mention of "remainder" (*śeṣa*) were not made, then since the rule "the second case ending occurs only for the object" would apply, the object would be non-restricted while the second case ending would be restricted; consequently, the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would also occur there. Therefore, the mention of "remainder" must be made so that [the second case ending] occurs only in the case of the remainder and not elsewhere.

In the view that it is a restrictive rule (*arthaniyamapakṣa*)—meaning "let it not be [otherwise]"—the mention of the word *śeṣa* (remainder) could have been omitted. For the object (*karman*) is already restricted by the rule that "the second case ending occurs only for the object," whereas the second case ending itself is unrestricted. Since the second case ending would thus apply elsewhere as well, this sūtra stating "the sixth case ending" is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*).
It will be so—where both the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and another [case-ending] would apply, there only the sixth case-ending occurs;
thus it should be understood in other instances as well.

51. *jño'vidarthasya karaṇe* | (2.3.51) Although there are many roots meaning "to know" (*vid*), it is appropriate to apply this prohibition only to that *vid* for which the sense of the root *jñā* is possible, namely *vid* in the sense of "knowing" (DhP 1064).

The application of the root *jñā* is possible only in this sense; therefore, by the rule *avidarthasya*, it is understood that the prohibition applies only to the root meaning "to know. Thus he says: "of [the root] not meaning 'to know'," and so forth.
Examples are: *sarpiṣo jānīte*, *madhuno jānīte*. This refers to Pāṇini 1.3.44: *apahnave jñaḥ*.

This being the case, the *ātmanepada* ending is applied by the rule "ṭhakarmakācca" (Pāṇini 1.3.45). In the form *dhunīta*, the augment *num* is added by the rule "iko'ci vibhaktau" (Pāṇini 7.1.73). The meaning is that [the person] proceeds with clarified butter (*sarpiṣā*) as the instrument; for one to whom clarified butter is most dear, the clarified butter serves as the cause for their engagement.
Because it functions as an instrument (*karaṇa*). Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *jñā* (to know) here has the sense of "engaging" (*pravṛtti*).

In the phrase "attached to or obstructed by ghee" (*sarpiṣi raktaḥ pratihato vā*), [the author] states that attachment to and obstruction by ghee are the causes of the error of consciousness (*cit-bhrānti*). If everything were to be grasped by its own nature...

It is understood as having the nature of clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*). This being so, it would not be logical for it to have the meaning of "non-knowledge" (*asat-vid-arthatā*), because its meaning is "knowledge" (*jñāna*); therefore, he says: "False knowledge is indeed non-knowledge.
The sense is that it does not perform the function of knowledge. For [true knowledge] is the discernment of an object that is not contrary [to reality].

It is called "ignorance" (ajñāna) because it is false knowledge (mithyājñāna), and that which is false knowledge does not perform the function of knowledge; just as, for example, one is called "not a son" (aputra) because he does not perform the functions of a son.
52. *Adhīgarthadayeśāṃ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.52). Regarding the term *adhīk*: this is the inclusion of the root *ik* meaning "to remember" (Dhātupāṭha 1047) preceded by the prefix *adhi*.
The term *adhīgarthāḥ* refers to those roots having the same meaning as *adhīk*. The addition of the indicatory letter *k* (*kānubandha*) serves a specific purpose for this [root].
In this very sūtra, the term *dhātu* is used for the purpose of specification. If it were stated simply as "of those whose meaning is study," doubt would arise as to what this *dhātu* is.
By prefixing it with *adhi*, he shows that its usage occurs only when preceded by *adhi*.

Regarding the rule *karmaṇi kārake* and so forth: when that very same object (*karman*) is intended to be expressed as a "remainder" (*śeṣa*)—because it functions as a residual relation—and not as an object (*karman*), then the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs there. Regarding the example *adhyeti*: due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*. Similarly for *īṣṭe*. [The form *īṣṭe* is derived] by means of the rule concerning *vraśca* and others (Pāṇini 8.2.36).
The genitive case ending [is applied].

In the example "He remembers his mother by means of her qualities" (*mātuḥ guṇaiḥ smarati*), because of the inclusion of the term "object" (*karman*) in the rule, the genitive does not occur even when there is an intention to express the qualities as a residual relation (*śeṣa*), since they function as instruments (*karaṇa*).

53. *kṛñaḥ pratiyatne* (2.3.53). [Example: *ṭhetho dakasyopaskurute* ("He prepares the water"). The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *gandhanādi* (1.3.32), and the augment *suṭ* is added by the rule *upātpratiyatna* (6.1.139), etc.

54. *Rujārthānāṃ bhāvavacanānām ajvareḥ* (2.3.54). Some read *rujā* in the list beginning with *bhidā*; those who do not read it [there] nevertheless [include it] by the rule *cintipūjikathikumbicarccaśca* (3.3.105).

They explain the correctness of the word *rujā* either because the particle *ca* has the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccaya*), or by virtue of this very grammatical exception (*nipātana*). Those whose meaning is "sickness" (*rujā*) are called *rujārthāḥ*.
Regarding the phrase "of those expressing a state" (*bhāvavacanānām*): if [it refers to] those that denote a state (*bhāvārtha*).

If the intended meaning were "of those [roots] whose sense is 'to cause pain' (*rujārthānām*)," then this statement would be purposeless; for all roots whose sense is "to cause pain" express a state of being (*bhāva*). Therefore, the state of being expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) is not what is intended here; rather, it is that expressed by the suffix (*pratyaya*), as in the rule "in the sense of a state of being" (*bhāve*, Pāṇini 3.3.18).

The suffix *dhañ* is prescribed [here]. This word *vacana* is derived as an agent-noun (*kartṛ-sādhana*); it means "one who speaks" (*vakti*), with the suffix *lyuṭ* used in the sense of the agent according to Pāṇini 3.3.113 (*kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*). Furthermore, it is not possible for that which is the state (*bhāva*) of things whose meaning is "to cause pain" (*rujārtha*) to function as the agent (*kartṛ*) with respect to the act of speaking (*vacana-kriyā*).

By implication, it is understood that through the word *avacana*, the sense of the base (*prakṛti*) is set aside and the sense of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is intended; moreover, this [sense] is the power of the agent (*kartṛśakti*). The term *bhāvavacanānām* is a *bahuvrīhi*:

those for whom the action (*bhāva*) is the speaker (*vacana*), i.e., the agent (*kartṛ*), are "those whose speaker is the action" (*bhāvavacanāḥ*); the meaning is "those whose agent is the action" (*bhāvakartṛkāḥ*).
Having kept all this in mind, he says: "of those whose agent is the action" (*bhāvakartṛkāṇām*).

It was not stated simply as "of those whose agent is the action" for the sake of variety. In the example "it pains the thief" (*caurasya rujati*), the root *ruj* means "to break" (*bhaṅge*); it belongs to the *tudādigaṇa*. Here, the action (*bhāva*) is the pain (*roga*).

The agent [is implied]. In the phrase "he causes the thief to suffer" (*caurasyāmayati*), there is also *āmaya*. [The root] *am* meaning "disease" (*roge*) belongs to the *cur-ādi* group (Dhātupāṭha 1720).
As it is said: "He causes a living man to rejoice even beyond a hundred years. Here, *ānanda* is the state (*bhāva*).

The agent [is implied]. However, this root *ruj* does not have "injury" as its meaning; what then? It has "motion" as its meaning, as in the example: "The river breaks the banks. Here, the root *ruj* has a substance (*dravya*) as its agent, not an abstract state (*bhāva*) as its agent, because the river is a substance. This is not a valid counter-example, for the word *rujā* is a conventional term (*rūḍhi-śabda*).

[The opponent] explains it as meaning "disease"; yet here the word *ruj* does not denote disease—what then? It denotes breaking (*bhaṅga*). If that is so, then this direction for a counter-example has been shown by the author of the Vṛtti. This, however, is the counter-example here: "phlegm (*śleṣmā*) afflicts the person" (*puruṣaṃ rujati*). [This occurs] because of the disease.

The meaning is "causes to grasp. Regarding *jvarayati*: the root *jvara* (meaning "fever" or "affliction," DhP 776) takes the causal *ṇic*. Due to its inclusion in the *ghaṭādi* group, it receives the designation *mit*, and by the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* (6.4.92), the vowel is shortened. Regarding *santāpayati*: the root *tapa* (meaning "heat" or "torment," DhP 985) takes the causal *ṇic*.
In this context, the state of distress is the agent.

55. *Nātha* [is used] in the sense of benediction (*āśis*). For example: *sarpiṣo nāthate*. He for whom there is no ghee (*sarpiḥ*) thus desires it because of his need—thinking, "May ghee be mine. The reflexive voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs due to the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*): "*nātha* [is used] in the sense of benediction."
"He brings the young brahmin near" means "he requests."

56. *jāsiniprahaṇanāṭakrāthapiṣāṃ hiṃsāyām* | (2.3.56) [The rule] "not for that belonging to the *divādi* class" is stated because of the mention of "in the sense of injury" (*hiṃsāyām*). Since this [rule] does not apply there [to the *divādi* root], it follows that only the causative (*ṇyanta*) form will be understood. Therefore, what is the purpose of specifying the causative form?

Thus [it is asked]: "Who, moreover, says that this is a designation of the root *cyu*? For here, this vowel *ī* has been employed for the purpose of designating the verbal root, according to the rule: "The suffixes *ṭhik* and *śtip* are used for the designation of a verbal root" (Vārttika 319).
If this is so, how is it that the long vowel *ā* is heard in the form *jāsī*? It is said in reply: having pronounced the vowel *ā*...

A modified designation has been made; this modified designation is intended to apply only where this specific form occurs, so that it does not apply here in the case of *dasyum ajījasat*. [This is formed with] the *luṅ* [suffix], the *caṅ* substitute for *cli* by the rule *ṇi-śri-ādi* (Pāṇini 3.1.48), and the shortening of the penultimate vowel by the rule *ṇau caṅy upadhāyā hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.1).

There is reduplication by [Pāṇini 6.1.11] *ṭhcaṅ* (*dvirvacanam*); there is the treatment as *san* (*sanvadbhāvaḥ*) by [Pāṇini 7.4.93] *sanvallaghuni* etc.; there is the substitution of *i* (*itvam*) by [Pāṇini 7.4.79] *sanyataḥ*; and there is lengthening (*dīrghaḥ*) by [Pāṇini 7.4.93] *dīrgho laghoḥ*. This very purpose applies even to the roots *naṭ* and *krāth*, for which the suffix *kyaṅ* is not explicitly mentioned. Here, *mā*...

Regarding the forms *bhūtadasyumanīnaṭat* and *dasyumacikrathat*: the purpose [of the rule] is the occurrence of *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) for the root *krath*. This has been demonstrated by the author of the *Vṛtti* when he stated, "The *vṛddhi* occurs by way of *nipātana* (irregular derivation). In the *Vṛtti*, the reading is *niprahan*, whereas [another version reads] *niprahan*.

In this treatise, the basis is merely the indication of the verbal roots (*dhātu*) and the prefixes (*upasarga*); it is neither the combination of the prefix and the root, nor their specific sequential order, because those two are not intended to be significant. Consequently, there is the inclusion of the words *ni* and *pra*, whether used separately or together, and even when their sequence is reversed.

He says that this is understood from the statement: "The inclusion of [the root] *vigṛhīta* as well as *saṃghāta*. For example: *caurasya praṇihanti*. Here, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule *nergadanada-* (Pāṇini 8.4.17).
Another example is: *caurasyonnāṭayati*. Here, [the root] *naṭ* is used in the sense of "trembling" (*avaspandane*), according to the Dhātupāṭha (7.2.116).

The vṛddhi [substitution] is already established; for what purpose, then, is it said that "the vṛddhi occurs by way of nipātana"? To this he says: "For this," and so forth. "It would apply to a short vowel" refers to the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.92). The example "he grinds the thief" (*caurasya pinaṣṭi*) is given because the root *piṣlṛ* is listed as "in the sense of crushing" (Dhātupāṭha 1452).

Because it belongs to the *rudhādi* class, the suffix *śnam* is applied. In the example "he grinds the *dhānā*s," there is no violence (*hiṃsā*), because that [violence] is a property belonging only to sentient beings. Furthermore, this [rule] was commenced so that it may also apply to those actions whose agent is a non-entity, as in: "Devadatta causes the thief to disappear."

57. [The genitive case is used] after the roots *vyava-hṛ* and *paṇ* when they have the same meaning. (Pāṇini 2.3.57) For example: *śatasya vyavaharati*. This means "he employs a hundred [in trade]"—that is, he applies it to buying and selling—or "he gambles with a hundred. In the expression *śatasya paṇate*, the meaning is exactly the same.
Because the root is marked with the *anudātta* accent, the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) suffixes are applied. [The question is: "Why does the *āya* affix not occur?
The intention is that it would indeed apply by virtue of the rule *gakapūdhūpa* (Pāṇini 3.1.28). [The answer begins with: "Of that which has the sense of praise," etc.
Although there is a verbal root *paṇa* meaning "in commerce and in praise" (Dhātupāṭha 439),...

The root *paṇ* is recited with the meanings of "praising" (*stuti*) and "dealing" (*vyavahāra*); nevertheless, the suffix *āya* is desired only for the sense of praising, not for the sense of dealing. On this point, the author of the Vṛtti himself will state the reasoning. Due to its association with *paṇ* in the sense of praising, it has that very meaning [here].

One produces a wager (*paṇi*), not for the sake of legal transaction (*vyavahāra*). [In the phrase] "he transacts with a tally-stick" (*śalākāṃ vyavaharati*), the meaning is "he counts. Here, because it functions in the sense of a legal transaction, there is no identity of meaning [with the previous example]. [In the phrase] "he wagers with the Brahmins" (*brāhmaṇān paṇayati*), the meaning is "he praises. This is the meaning of the root *paṇayī*.
Because the root *vyavahṛ* has no such usage, there is a lack of semantic equivalence.
|| 58. *divas tadarthasya* || (2.3.58) [The example is] "he plays with the Brahmins" (*brāhmaṇān dīvyati*). The meaning is "he praises. The lengthening of the vowel is by [Pāṇini 8.2.77] *hali ca*.

If it were to apply only to that specific meaning, then it would have been more appropriate to include the word *div* in the preceding rule (*pūrvayoga*) itself. Therefore, for what purpose is this separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*)? To this, he says: "The separation of rules is for the sake of what follows."
59. *vibhāṣopasarge* (Pāṇini 2.3.59). [The example is: "He plays with a *śalākā*. In a different sense, such as play (*krīḍā*) and so forth, the root *div* is employed.

60. *dvitīyā brāhmaṇe* (2.3.60). Regarding *brāhmaṇe*: the word *brāhmaṇa* is a designation for the *Śatapatha*. Regarding *grāmasya*: this is a genitive of remainder (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), in relation to the word *sabhāyām*.
Regarding *tadahaḥ*: this is an illustration.

By the rule *ṭhsvamornapuṃsakāt* (7.1.23), there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *am*. While the rule *ṭhahan* (8.2.68) is being carried over, by the rule *ṭhro'supi* (8.2.69), the *n* is replaced by *r*, which then becomes a *visarjanīya*. Regarding the form *dīvyeyuḥ*: this is the potential mood (*liṅ*), with *jhi* replaced by *jus*, and [the substitution] *ato yeyaḥ* (7.2.80) applies.

Thus, there is the substitution of *iy* [for *i*]; then, by the rule "ṭhliṅ salopo'nantyasya" (Pāṇini 7.2.79), there is the elision of the *s*. One might ask: why is this statement not intended to prescribe the second case (*dvitīyā*) as obligatory for a verb with a prefix (*sopasarga*), since the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would otherwise optionally apply? To this he says: "of that which has a prefix. [This refers to] "vibhāṣopasarge" (Pāṇini 1.4.44).

By this [rule], since the second case ending will always occur in the Vedic language even by virtue of the *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (restricted option), this statement is not tenable as being intended for that purpose.

61. [The suffix *kyac* is applied] after the words *preṣya* and *bruva*, when the oblation (*havis*) is the recipient of the deity (*devatā-sampradāna*). (Pāṇini 2.3.61) Regarding the statement "of the root *iṣ* belonging to the *divādi* class":

this reference by means of the affix *śyan* to the root *iṣ* (meaning "to go," Dhātupāṭha 1127) is for the purpose of excluding other roots with the same form. It is expressed here in the second person singular of the imperative (*loṭ*).

The specification, however, is for the purpose of excluding other *lakāras*, other persons (*puruṣas*), and other numbers (*vacanas*). "In that context alone" means: only in the context of the singular number of the second person of the *loṭ* [imperative] mood. For example: "agnaye chāgasya," etc. A *chāga* is a modification (*vikāra*) of a goat (*chāga*). In that case, Agni is the deity (*devatā*).
The recipient (*sampradāna*). The sacrificial offering (*havis*) consisting of products of goats and sheep, such as the omentum (*vapā*) and so forth, is the object to be given.

[See *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī*. Now, regarding "preṣya": by the rule *ato heḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.105), there is the elision (*luk*) of *hi*. Regarding "anubrūhi": by the rule *serhyapicca* (Pāṇini 3.4.87).

There is the substitution of *hir*. Due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix. This rule applies even in the domain of the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), because the word "Vedic" (*cchandas*) is mentioned in the subsequent sūtra. Regarding the form "juhudhi": the substitution of *dhi* occurs by the rule "for *hi*, [substitute] *dhi* after roots ending in *juhoty-ādī* and after consonants" (Pāṇini 6.4.101). Regarding the phrase "agnaye gomayāni preṣya": but surely...
Cow dung is indeed a sacrificial offering (*havis*); how then can it serve as a counter-example? It is not so;

for although the inclusion of the sacrificial offering is already established by the mention of the deity as the recipient—since the term [for offering] is a relative word—the explicit mention of "sacrificial offering" once again indicates that what is intended is a sacrificial offering consisting of food to be consumed. And it is not...

The counter-example, "cow-dung is to be consumed," is appropriate. Regarding the passage beginning with "of the oblation that has been set forth" (*haviṣaḥ prasthitasya*), that oblation which is qualified by the word *prasthita* ("set forth") is what is meant by "the set forth. It must be stated that there is a prohibition of the genitive case for that [oblation]; the meaning is that this [rule] is to be explained [as an exception].

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the term *vibhāṣā* ("optionally") is carried over from the rule "vibhāṣopasarge" (Pāṇini 2.3.59), and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Consequently, [the suffix *ṣyañ*] does not apply to *prasthita* when it follows *havis*.

62. *Bahulam* (frequently) in the sense of the fourth case (*caturthī*) in the Veda (*chandas*). (2.3.62) The question "What is the purpose of including the term *bahula*? is asked by one who thinks that the rule is already established simply through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally). [The examples provided are: *kṛṣṇo rātryai* ("Kṛṣṇa for the night") and *himavato hastī* ("an elephant from the Himavat"). In these cases...

Due to the inclusion of the term *bahula* (in various cases), the dative case (*caturthī*) occurs even in the sense of the locative (*saptamī*). Regarding the statement "it should be explained" (*vaktavyā*), the meaning is "it should be expounded. In this regard, the following is the demonstration: the term *bahula* is employed here; by means of it, the dative occurs even in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in some instances, and in other instances, something else entirely—this too [is established].
The intended meaning of the frequent use of the term "reproach" (garhaṇa) is indeed exactly that.

63. And [the genitive is used] after the root *yaj* when it denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*). (Pāṇini 2.3.63) As in: "He sacrifices with ghee" (*dhṛtasya yajate*). Here, the root *yaj* refers to the worship of the gods, and in that context, ghee functions as the instrument.

64. When used in conjunction with words having the sense of *kṛtvas* (times), the locative case is employed to denote time. (Pāṇini 2.3.64) For example: *pañcakṛtvaḥ* ("five times"). [This is formed] by the rule *saṃkhyāyāḥ kriyābhyāvṛttigaṇane kṛtvasuc* (5.4.17). For example: *dvirahnaḥ* ("twice a day"). [This is formed] by the rule *dvitricaturbhyaḥ suc* (5.4.18).

"For it is understood [to be used] twice, thrice, or four times"—this is the sense, [referring to] context and so forth. Now, one might object: "Since the meaning of context and so forth is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*), and since the rule has its application fulfilled elsewhere in cases such as *pañcakṛtvaḥ* (five times), it will not apply here. If this is the case, then [the author] intends to provide this technical instruction (*jñāpaka*): [The following is the continuation of the original text: "Even when the number is expressed by a word other than a *kṛtvasuc* affix, the suffix *śas* is applied after a word ending in *dvi*, *tri*, or *catur* to denote repetition. For example: *dvirgataḥ*, *trirgataḥ*, *caturgataḥ*. The mention of *dvi*, *tri*, and *catur* is for the purpose of excluding *pañca* and so forth; otherwise, the rule would have been stated simply as "after a numeral" (*saṃkhyāyāḥ*). The mention of *gata* is for the purpose of excluding *bhukta* and so forth; otherwise, the rule would have been stated simply as "after repetition" (*vīpsāyām*). The mention of *vīpsā* is for the purpose of excluding cases like *dvirahni bhuktam* ("he ate twice in the day"). The mention of *kālādhvanoḥ* ("of time and distance") is for the purpose of excluding cases like *dvirdhāvati yojanam*. The mention of *vyāpta* is for the purpose of excluding cases like *dvirbhūtaḥ pāṭaliputram*. The mention of *bhūta* is for the purpose of excluding cases like *dvirgataḥ pāṭaliputrāt*. 65. *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65). Regarding the word *āsikā*: [it is formed] in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) by the rule *paryāyārhaṇotpattiṣu ṇvuc* (3.3.111). Regarding the word *sraṣṭā*: [it is formed] from the root *sṛj-* with the suffix *tṛc*. By the rule *sṛjidṛśorjhalyamakiti* (6.1.58), the augment *am* is applied.
The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] is applied by Pāṇini 8.2.36 (*ṭh-vraśca-ādinā*).

[The sūtra specifies "in connection with a taddhita suffix" so that it does not apply in the case of a taddhita. Now, why is the mention of *kṛt* [suffixes] not made for the purpose of ensuring that [the rule] does not apply in connection with a *tiṅ* [suffix]? Because in that case, [the rule] does not [apply].

Because the genitive case is prohibited by the rule *lokāvyayaniṣṭhā* (Pāṇini 2.3.69). In the example *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam*, the suffix *ini* is applied by the rule *sapūrvācca* (Pāṇini 5.2.87), which follows from the governing word *iniḥ* in the preceding rule *pūrvādiniḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.86). In this instance, the agent is expressed by the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) itself; therefore, [the genitive is not used].

This is indeed a syntactical construction (*vākya*); it is not a derivative formation (*prasaṅga*), for the object (*karman*) has not been expressed by that [suffix]. If the mention of the *kṛt*-suffix were absent, the genitive case would apply to the object such as "the mat" (*kaṭa*). But surely this syntactical construction is not even possible here; for in this way, the object is already expressed by the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*).
In this case, there should not be a second [case-ending], nor should there be a *taddhita* suffix, because of a lack of syntactic capacity (*asāmarthya*).

That lack of capacity, moreover, arises from the state of being dependent (*sāpekṣatva*). For instance, in the expression "the mat was made by him previously" (*kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ pūrvamanena*), the word *kṛta* depends upon the mat (*kaṭa*); but it is not so here. How could the *niṣṭhā* suffix, which is produced after a verbal root, [be dependent]?

It would denote the objecthood (*karmatā*) of the word *kaṭa*. For its capacity is only to denote objecthood in general (*karmasāmānya*), not a specific object (*karmaviśeṣa*). But then, how is the objecthood of the word *kaṭa* denoted by that [suffix] in a sentence? In that case, the denotation is appropriate, because of the word *kṛta*.

Because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). However, once a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) has been produced, coreferentiality ceases due to the formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*); thus, by what means would the status of the mat and so forth as the object (*karman*) be expressed? As for the action (*kriyā*), since it is the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), just as it becomes subordinate in a sentence and undergoes a connection with the factors of accomplishment (*sādhana*), so too [does it here].

Even in the case of a derivative formation (*vṛtti*), the status of the word *kaṭa* as an object is justified in relation to the meaning of the action expressed by the verb. Therefore, the accusative case must necessarily be employed.
Furthermore, there ought to be a sentence that possesses the same meaning as the derivative formation; however, in the case of a derivative formation, no external [object] exists.

The object such as a mat (*kaṭa*) is understood by means of which the suffix will be produced; thus, it is understood that the requirement for an object such as a mat within the sentence is purposeless. Therefore, the analysis (*vigraha*) must be made in this way: "this was done by him previously. And consequently, there is no state of being dependent (*sāpekṣatva*).

The secondary derivative (taddhita) indeed occurs [in this case], as in the rule "ṭhitarathā hi. The meaning is that if the mention of "śeṣa" (the remainder) were to continue [from the previous rule]. [Otherwise,] one would have said "kartari ca kṛti" (when a kṛt-affix follows, it denotes the agent). For even if it were stated in this way, if "śeṣa" were still to continue [as a governing term],...

Since the word "karma" is already obtained from the rule *cakārakaraṇāt* ("because of the inclusion of the particle *ca*"), what is the purpose of mentioning "karma" again? Therefore, the repetition of the mention of "karma" is for the purpose of excluding the governing scope (*adhikāra*) of the "remainder" (*śeṣa*). For by the repetition of the mention of "karma," the cessation of the preceding mention of "karma" is indicated. Upon that cessation—
Even though it is connected with that and follows from it, the mention of "remainder" (śeṣa) is set aside.
66. *ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.66). [The commentary states:
"The term *ubhayaprāptau* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. By this, it rules out the possibility of it being a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
He will state the purpose for resorting to the *bahuvrīhi* interpretation. The inclusion of the word *ubhaya* ("both") is because it is the subject under discussion.

The agent and the object are connected [to the rule]. By the statement "in which there is the possibility of both," the intention is that it refers to one and the same [suffix]. He shows the nature of the restriction "only when the object [is expressed]. However, the reverse restriction—that the [suffix] occurs only when there is the possibility of both [agent and object], and specifically when the object—is what is meant here.

It does not occur [in this case]. Lest the prescription of the genitive in the sense of the object (*karman*) by the preceding sūtra become redundant, [the present rule is stated]. As in: "The milking of cows by one who is not a cowherd is a marvel. Here, the suffix *ghañ* is added to the root *duh* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). Since both [the agent and the object] would otherwise be eligible for the genitive, the genitive occurs specifically for the object, namely, *goṣu*.

Not when the agent is *agopālaka*. Furthermore, in this context, the term *prayoga* from the rule *kṛtvo'rthaprayoge* (Pāṇini 2.3.64) does not carry over. Consequently, the genitive case occurs even when the object is merely implied, as in the rule *antardhau yenādarśanamicchati* (1.4.28).

In the case of *pāna* ("drinking"), the status of the self (*ātman*) as the object (*karman*) is understood when it is not being employed [as the agent]. This is because the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of the action itself (*bhāva*) by the rule *lyuṭ ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.115). However, this does not occur here: "It is a wonder that there is both the cooking of the rice and the appearance of the Brahmins. For in this case, the two [actions] do not occur in a single [instance of the] *kṛtya* suffix.

This is "attainment" (*prāpti*). For instance, in the expression "the cooking of the rice" (*odanasya pākaḥ*), attainment applies only to the rice as the object (*karman*), and not to the Brahmins as the agents (*kartṛ*). Indeed, the Brahmins are not intended here as the agents of the cooking;
rather, they are intended as the agents of the manifestation (*prādurbhāva*). And there is no manifestation of the Brahmins.

In this case as well, regarding the term "manifestation" (*prādurbhāva*)—which is a *kṛt* formation—the application [of the suffix] occurs only with respect to the agents (*kartṛ*), namely the Brahmins, and not with respect to the object (*karman*), namely the rice. For rice is not the object of "manifestation," since the root *bhū* is intransitive (*akarmaka*). Rather, it is the act of cooking (*pāka*) itself whose object is intended to be expressed as the rice.

Regarding the phrase "of the two [suffixes] ending in -ṭha and -ka," and so forth: this is a prohibition of the rule. The meaning is that it should be explained as having the sense that "when used with suffixes ending in -a or -ā, the restriction does not apply. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: from the rule "caturthyarthe bahulaṃ chandasi" (Pāṇini 2.3.62)...
The term "bahulam" (diversely) is understood to carry over; therefore, there will be no restriction regarding the use of the suffixes *ka* and *kā*.
As for the rule "śeṣe vibhāṣā" (optionally in the remaining cases), its meaning also relies upon the recourse to the term "bahulam."

It should be explained as follows: regarding "bhedikā," the suffix *ṇvuc* is applied as in the previous case to denote the abstract state (*bhāva*). Regarding "cikīrṣā," the suffix *a* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.3.102, *apratyayāt*.

67. *Kta* also [denotes] the present time. (2.3.67) As in: *rājñāṃ mataḥ* ("approved by the kings"). The suffix *kta* is applied here by the rule *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca* (3.2.188). In *rājñām*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denotes the agent (*kartṛ*), while the object (*karman*) is already expressed by the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). Now, why does this [rule] not apply here—?
In examples such as *śīlito devadattena* (practiced by Devadatta) and *rakṣito devadattena* (protected by Devadatta),

is the suffix *kta* prescribed only for the present tense— even in the case of roots meaning "practice" (*śīlita*), etc.— on the grounds that the particle *ca* in the rule *ṭhmatibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.188) serves to include those not explicitly mentioned?
Even if this were so, there is no fault, because the term "frequently" (*bahula*) is understood to carry over [from previous rules], and thus it will not apply here.

Alternatively—the present tense is understood from the context itself; however, the meaning of the word (*padārtha*) establishes only the state of having occurred (*bhūtatva*), not the state of being currently occurring (*vartamānatā*). As for that whose meaning...
When [the word] is used in its present sense, the genitive case indeed occurs, as in: "Hariścandra was dear to his subjects like [the moon]. [The author states:
"It is established through the understanding of the *śeṣa* (remainder). He explains the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) with the words: "And thus..."

By these and other such statements, he demonstrates that for one who undertakes a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*), even when the agency (*kartṛtva*) is not intended to be expressed, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) alone occurs, and not the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*).

68. *Adhikaraṇavācinaś-ca*. (2.3.68) [The rule states: "When used in conjunction with that, the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī vibhakti*) occurs. Wherever it is possible, if only the agent (*kartṛ*) is possible, then [the sixth case] occurs in the sense of the agent; for example: *idameṣām āsitam* ("this is the place where they sat").

In this case, because the root *as* is intransitive (*akarmaka*), only the agent (*kartṛ*) is possible, not the object (*karman*). However, where both the object and the agent are possible, it applies to both; for example: *idameṣāṃ bhuktam odanasya* ("this rice has been eaten by them"). Since the root *bhuj* is transitive (*sakarmaka*), the object, namely the rice (*odana*), certainly exists. This is governed by the rule: *ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.66).

Why does this restriction not apply? It is understood that the restriction applies precisely to the occurrence of the genitive case prescribed by *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65). According to the principle *anantarasya vidhirvā bhavati pratiṣedho vā* (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 19), "a rule or a prohibition applies to what is immediately preceding," and according to *madhye'pavādāḥ pūrvān bādhante*, "exceptions in the middle set aside [rules] that precede them."

Or [it may be interpreted as]: "They do not sublate other injunctions" (Vyāḍipāda 10). Furthermore, although it could have been stated simply as *adhikaraṇe ca*, the inclusion of the term *vāci* is for the purpose of ensuring that this is not understood as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of what is expressed by the locative case.
For if it were intended as a mere indicator, there would also be [the application of the suffix] when it functions in a different sense.
When a word derived from a root meaning "staying," "going," or "eating" is used with a *kta*-suffix, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) should be employed.
However, when the term *vāci* is included [in the rule], then when the *kta*-suffix occurs in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), the sixth case does not occur;
in that case, only the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used for the agent—as in *hāhānenāsitam* ("Hāhā sat by means of this"). It is not [the sixth case].

In this case, the suffix *kta* denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇa*); the rule is "The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the locus after roots meaning 'staying,' 'motion,' and 'eating'" (Pāṇini 3.4.76),
due to the inclusion of the word "and" (*ca*) in that sūtra.

The term *yathāprāptam* (as obtained) is used because the suffix *kta* is prescribed both in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) and in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). When, however, the *kta* suffix occurs in the sense of the agent, the genitive case is not employed there, as the agent is already expressed by that very suffix itself. In the example *iha ime āsitāḥ*, the particle *ca* serves the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*) with reference to what precedes it.

69. *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām* (2.3.69). [The commentary states: "And *kikinau* are also included. Although, because *ki* and *kin* are substitutes for *la*, they are not captured by the mention of *la* through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, nevertheless, [the rule] *liṭ ca* [applies].

(3.2.171) Thus, there must be an extension (*atideśa*) by this rule; for when there is an extension of a specific [rule], the extension of the general [rule] follows as a necessary consequence, because the specific is invariably concomitant with the general. Therefore, it is logical that the prohibition based on the general [rule] is established for the *kikin* suffixes as well.
The inclusion of these two [forms] is as follows: *pacamānaḥ* is formed with the suffix *śānac*;
because it is marked with the *svarita* accent, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is employed. *Pecānaḥ* is formed by the suffix *kānac*, according to the rule *liṭaḥ kānaj vā* (Pāṇini 3.2.106);
there is reduplication, and [the substitution of *e* for *at*] occurs by the rule *ata ekah* (Pāṇini 6.4.120).

By these [rules], the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*) are applied. In the form *pecivān*, the suffix *kvasu* is added by the rule *kvuśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.107). Once the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplication have been performed, the augment *iṭ* is added by the rule *vasvekājādghasām* (7.2.67). Then, the *num* augment is added by the rule *ugidacām* (7.1.70), and [the lengthening of the penultimate vowel] occurs by the rule *sāntamahasaḥ* (6.4.10).

By such rules, the vowel is lengthened. [The forms] *dadiḥ* and *papiḥ* are derived by applying either of the suffixes *kikin* from the rule *ādṛgamahanajanakhanaghasaḥ kikinau liṭ ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.171). Because of the extension [of properties] by the phrase *liṭ ca*, reduplication occurs. Then, by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64), the final *ā* is elided.

Thus there is the elision of the suffix *ākāra*. Regarding "cikīrṣuḥ": [the suffix] *u* is applied by Pāṇini 3.2.168 (*sanāśaṃsabhikṣa uḥ*). Regarding "alaṃkariṣṇuḥ": the suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied by Pāṇini 3.2.136 (*alaṃkṛñ*) and so forth. Regarding "āgāmukaḥ" (as found in the *Kāśikā* and the *Padamañjarī*).

The suffix *u* is applied by the rule *ṭhlaṣapatapada* (Pāṇini 3.2.154), etc. Regarding the phrase "in the prohibition of *uk*," etc., the word "is explained" (*pratipādyate*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. This explanation, however, should be carried out by relying on the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *bahulam*. [The example is] "having done" (*kṛtvā*).
The suffix *ktvā* is applied by the rule *samānakartṛkayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.21).

Regarding the phrase "in the prohibition of indeclinables" (*avyayapratiṣedhe*) and so forth, here too the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) is to be understood as before, and the explanation is likewise as before. Alternatively, [it is to be understood] in the context of the rule *avyayībhāvaśca* (Pāṇini 1.1.41).

The author of the Vṛtti has provided an explanation beginning with: "This entire section [of the sūtras] is read among the *svarādi* [group]" (Kāśikā 1.1.41). Alternatively, one may rely on the maxim: "A rule conditioned by a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is not universally obligatory" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 64). Regarding the form *udetoḥ*: it is derived from the root *iṇ* preceded by the prefix *ut*, in the sense of "indicating a state" (*bhāvalakṣaṇe*).

The suffix *tosun* is applied by the rule "stheṇkṛñvadicari" (Pāṇini 3.4.16). Regarding "visṛpaḥ," the suffix *kasun* is applied by the rule "sṛpitṛdoḥ kasun" (3.4.17). Regarding "īṣatkaraḥ," the suffix *khal* is applied by the rule "īṣad" (3.3.126), etc. Regarding "īṣatpānaḥ," the suffix *yuc* is applied by the rule "āto yuc" (3.3.128). [Regarding] "ātṛṇo... [the suffix *kan* is applied by the rule "ātṛno..."].

"From the letter *n*" means: from the *n* belonging to the suffix *tṛn*, which expresses a habitual disposition (*tācchīlika*). "Pavamānaḥ": [from the root] *pūṅ* in the sense of "purifying" (DhP 966), with the suffix *śānan* according to Pāṇini 3.2.128 (*pūṅyajoḥ śānan*).
"Naḍamaghnānaḥ": [with the suffix] *cānaś* in the sense of habitual disposition, age, or ability (Pāṇini 3.2.129).
By the rule *gamahana* (6.4.98), there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*).
By the rule *ho hanteḥ* (7.3.54), there is the substitution of *ku*-tva (i.e., *gh*). Regarding the form *adhīyan*:
by the rule *iṅ dhāryoḥ śatrakṛcchriṇi* (3.2.130), there is the substitution of the suffix *śatṛ*; then the substitution of *iyaṅ* occurs; [the word] is joined with the prefix (*upasarga*).

"Long" [refers to the vowel]. In "the agent" (*kartā*), the suffix *tṛn* is applied by the rule "after the root *ā-kvi*, the suffix *tṛn* is used in the sense of one who habitually performs that action" (*ā-kvestacchīle*, 3.2.134).

Regarding the statement "there should be an option for the use of the present participle suffix *śatṛ* after the root *dviṣ*": when the suffix *śatṛ* follows the root *dviṣ*, there should be an option regarding its usage;
this is because of the metaphorical treatment of the identity between the denoting word and the denoted object. By the word "optionally" (*vā*),...
The meaning of "or" (*vā*) has been stated. "Or" (*vā*) also implies an option (*vikalpa*). An option is that by which something is expressed or made known;
thus, it refers to a statement containing the word *vā*. The meaning is that its explanation must be provided. Here is the explanation:
the term *bahulam* (diversely) is carried over here [from a previous rule]; therefore, there is an optional prohibition of the present participle (*śatṛ*) after the root *dviṣ*.
It will be "dviṣan"; the suffix śatṛ is applied by the rule "dviṣo 'mitre" (Pāṇini 3.2.131).

70. *akenorbhaviṣyadādhamarṇyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.70). [The suffix] *ṭhak* [is applied] when the time is future; it is not [applied] in the sense of debt (*ādhamarṇya*), because that is impossible there. But [the suffix] *ṭhin* [is applied] "in the sense of future and debt," because that is possible in both cases. Now, one might object:

Should there not be an assignment of number here by way of equal enumeration (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*)? This is not so; for an assignment of number occurs by means of the *svarita* accent, and the *svarita* quality is not here formally declared for that purpose.
[For example: "The agent of the act of making a mat goes" (*kaṭaṃ kārako vrajati*). [This is established] by the rule *tumunṇvulau* (Pāṇini 3.3.10), etc.

The suffix *ṇvul* [is used], as in "one who will go to the village" (*grāmaṃ gamī*). Here, the suffix *ini* is applied to the root *gam* by the rule "gamy-ādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.3.3), and because of that statement, it refers to the future tense. In "one who gives a hundred" (*śataṃ dāyī*), the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule "āvaśyakādhamarṇyayor ṇiniḥ" (Pāṇini 3.3.170). In "one who reaps barley" (*yavānāṃ lāvakaḥ*)...

The suffix *ṇvul* is applied by the rule *ṭhṇvultṛcau* (Pāṇini 3.1.133). In the expression "one who necessarily acts" (*avaśyaṃkārī*), the suffix *ṇini* is used in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*).

In the expression "one who completes a hundred years" (*varṣaśatasya pūrakaḥ*), the root *pūrī* (meaning "to fill," *āpyāyane*) belongs to the cur-ādi group; from this root, the suffix *ṇvul* is applied according to *ṭhṇvultṛcajau* (Pāṇini 3.1.133) in the sense of future time.

The suffix *ṇvul* [is used here]. For that [suffix] occurs in all three times. [Objection: "This is the inclusion of the *aka* suffix prescribed under the heading of the future (*bhaviṣyat*). [Response: Here, "future" (*bhaviṣyat*) is marked with an accent (*svarita*). The understanding of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) is achieved by means of the *svarita* accent. Therefore...
This refers to the taking of that single [act] prescribed under the heading of "what will be," and not of everything.

71. *vā* [is used] in place of the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) when denoting the agent (*kartṛ*) of verbal derivatives (*kṛtya*). (Pāṇini 2.3.71) In the example, "The boy is to be sung (*geya*) by means of the *sāmans*," the word *geya* is derived in the sense of the agent by the rule *bhavyageya...* (Pāṇini 3.4.68). Thus, "he sings" (*gāyati*), and so he is "to be sung" (*geya*). Here, the sixth case ending is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).

It is indeed eternal. Regarding the statement "it must be stated" (*vaktavya*), the meaning is that it must be explained. In this regard, the following is the explanation: in the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhā* (Pāṇini 2.3.69), the word *na* should be treated as a separate *yogavibhāga*.
By means of that, when both [the agent and the object] are applicable, there will be no prohibition of the genitive case in the case of *kṛtya* suffixes. Therefore...

In the example "The branch is to be pulled by Devadatta to the village" (*kraṣṭavyā śākhā grāmaṃ devadateneti*), the augment *am* occurs by the rule "After the root *kṛṣ*, when followed by a suffix marked with Ṭ or which has an udātta vowel as its indicatory letter, and when the root has *ṛ* or *u* as its penultimate letter, *am* is optionally inserted" (Pāṇini 6.1.59). This is so that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) does not apply to the agent (*kartṛ*) Devadatta. Thus, when both [agent and object] are eligible for the genitive, there is a prohibition of the genitive in the case of kṛtya suffixes.

It has been stated that [the word] must be expressed. However, regarding the object (*karman*), because the branch (*śākhā*) is already denoted by the *kṛtya* suffix, the genitive case will not occur. For just as *kṛtya* suffixes apply to the primary object and not to a non-primary one, so too does the genitive. And in this case, the village (*grāma*) is not the primary object; what then?
"Is it the Śākhā? [he asked].
72. *Tulyārthair-atulopamābhyāṃ tṛtīyā’nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.72).

"With words having the sense of *tulya*" means with words having the sense of *sadṛśa* (similar). The inclusion of the term *artha* (sense) is for the purpose of including those [words] which express the sense of similarity independently of other words. Consequently, [this rule applies to] those which indicate [similarity] through the proximity of another word.

The particles *iva* and others are excluded—as in "the gavaya is like a cow" (*gaur iva gavayaḥ*) or "as a cow is, so is a gavaya. The inclusion of the word *artha* (meaning) is not for the purpose of excluding the word's own form (*svarūpa*), because the exclusion of the word's own form is already accomplished by the very use of the plural number. Here too, [the meaning is] "equal to the father."

Regarding the expression *prajñayā*, the genitive case does not occur after the word *prajñā* because *prajñā* is intended here either as the cause (*hetu*) or as the instrument (*karaṇa*). For otherwise, the third case ending would have been attracted [by the previous rule]. This is because it is mentioned in the immediately preceding sūtra. Furthermore, this very point is the purpose of the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām*.
Regarding "the purpose": that very [purpose] is drawn forward by the word *ca* (and).

73. And the fourth [case-ending] occurs with words meaning "long life" (*āyuṣya*), "prosperity" (*madra*), "auspiciousness" (*bhadra*), "well-being" (*kuśala*), "pleasure" (*sukha*), "wealth" (*artha*), and "benefit" (*hita*).

Since the inclusion of the word *artha* is already established by the very mention of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā-nirdeśāt*), the explicit mention of the word *artha* indicates that the word *artha* itself is understood as a distinct cause [for the application of the rule]. How, then, is the inclusion of the word *artha* established by the mention of the third case-ending?

Because this [term] is incomplete, the word "yoga" (connection) is supplied as an ellipsis. And since that connection is possible only with meanings and not with words, the inclusion of the term "meanings" (arthaiḥ) is established by implication.
Thus ends the second chapter of the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable Ācārya Jinenndrabuddhipāda, who was a follower of the Bodhisattvas.
The Third Pāda
Now begins the second chapter.
The Fourth Pāda.
1. *dvigurekavacanam* (Pāṇini 2.4.1).
If, in this rule, "singular" (*ekavacana*) were taken in its technical sense, then the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) would not be in the singular.

It might be argued: "The word *pañcapūlī* is beautiful," because the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) lacks the status of a *dvigu*. If the technical sense of the singular number were intended here, then one would have stated, "the singular number for a *dvigu*"; therefore, this refers to the singular number in its etymological sense.
Having in mind that the term "singular" (*ekavacana*) is not technical (*pāribhāṣika*), he says:

"The expression for one is the singular. By this, showing that the word *ekavacana* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), he demonstrates its etymological significance (*anvarthatā*). That is to say, the expression (*vacana*) which denotes one (*ekasya*) is the singular (*ekavacana*).

It is called *vacana* because it speaks (*vakti*), using the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the agent according to Pāṇini 3.3.113 (*kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*). He states "of that which has a single meaning" (*ekārthasya*) and so forth in order to clarify the meaning of "singular number" (*ekavacana*) by means of a synonym. Now, one might object that the word "singular number" ought to be in the masculine gender (*puṃlliṅga*).

How so? Because a *dvigu* compound is masculine. No; since the commonality of gender (*liṅgasāmānya*) is intended, the reference is made using the neuter gender as the common [gender], and thus there is no fault. "In this manner" refers to that very point.

The meaning is that it consists in the employment of the word *vacana* (number) in its literal sense. Furthermore, it is not possible to make a word denoting multiple objects denote a single object even by means of hundreds of explanations;
for the capacity of words to denote meanings is inherent (*svābhāvika*). And yet, this very term "number" (*vacana*) is being employed [here].
Therefore, since this extended application (atideśa) is understood through the force of the context, he says:
"The singular form (ekavadbhāva) is prescribed for the meaning of a *dvigu* compound. To clarify the meaning of this very statement, he says:
"The meaning of a *dvigu* becomes singular. If this is so, then that which is the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)...

A dual form (dvigu) would also result in the application of the *ekavadbhāva* (singular collective treatment)—as in *pañcasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtau* or *saṃskṛtāḥ*, resulting in *pañcakapālau* or *pañcakapālāḥ*—therefore he says:
"And [the singular is used] for a *samāhāra-dvigu*," etc. The word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).

The meaning is that [the term *samāsa*] refers exclusively to the *samāhāra-dvigu*. But how is it understood that it refers only to the *samāhāra-dvigu*? He thinks as follows: in the rule "and *dvandva*" (Pāṇini 2.4.2), the *dvigu* is drawn in by the word "and" (*ca*). In whatever sense the *dvandva* attains a unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), in that very same sense...

[The purpose is] so that even a *dvigu* compound may undergo singular treatment (*ekavadbhāva*). A *dvandva* becomes a single referent (*ekārthībhavati*) only when it is a collective (*samāhāra*), and not otherwise. Therefore, singular treatment occurs for a *dvigu* only in that same case [of being a collective]; hence, it is appropriate that this [rule] refers specifically to a collective *dvigu*. If, then...
This [rule] refers specifically to the *samāhāra-dvigu* [compound]; in that case, the extended application (*atideśa*) would be purposeless.
For instance: the meaning of a *dvigu* is a collective (*samāhāra*); and a collective is derived in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva-sādhana*).

"Collecting" (*samāharaṇam*) is a "collective" (*samāhāra*), which is to say, a group (*samudāya*); and that [group] is singular. Therefore, the singular number is already established by logical necessity (*nyāya-prāpta*) therein.

Is the commencement of this Sūtra fruitless? This is not so; for, according to the view that "the aggregate is non-different from its constituent parts," since the aggregate consists of multiple substances, the use of the singular number would not be established—therefore, this [Sūtra] has been commenced. And so it has been said:

In the Bhāṣya: "Because a word arises for each substratum (adhikaraṇa) and because of its grammatical coreferentiality with number, the dual and plural endings are prescribed for the *dvigu* compound, while the singular ending is prescribed [for it]. "For each substratum" means for each individual substance (*dravya*).
Regarding the arising of the word, the case-ending expresses the number inherent in the substance that constitutes the denoted object.
The motivating cause (prayojikā) arises. And the meaning of a *dvigu* compound consists of multiple substances. For instance:

"five [bundles] collected together. Because the bundles being collected are delimited by the number five, and because of their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that number, one concludes: "these are five substances. Thus it is.

The singular number for the aggregate (*samudāya*) is not established; in that case, since it is non-existent, the plural number would apply due to the multiplicity [of its parts]. Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is that the substitution of *et* is prescribed.
This sūtra [is intended] under the view that "the aggregate is something other than its constituent members."

It must indeed be rejected. And so it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Or rather, [the singular number is obtained] because the aggregate is a single entity. Or rather, there is no need for the formulation of the rule itself; for this reason: since this object called an "aggregate" (samāhāra) is a single thing, the singular number will occur there due to its oneness—this is the meaning of the sentence. As in the example "pañcapūlī" (a cluster of five bundles).

Since the feminine gender applies by the rule "A *dvigu* compound whose final member ends in the letter *ṭha* is expressed in the feminine" (*Vārttika* 156), the suffix *ṅīp* is added according to "After a *dvigu* [ending in a consonant], *ṅīp*" (Pāṇini 4.1.21). By the statement "Because the meaning is singular," etc., he demonstrates the result of the extension of the meaning (*arthātideśa*).

2. *Dvandva* [is singular] for [words denoting] parts of living beings, musical instruments, and armies. (Pāṇini 2.4.2) In this context, does the word *aṅga* (“part”) terminate in the whole collection, or does it terminate in each individual member?
If it were to terminate in the whole collection, then this would constitute a single sentence; and thus...

Furthermore, a confusion would result. For a *dvandva* compound consisting of parts of living beings, musical instruments, or army units that are mutually combined and whose members are intermingled, there would have to be a singular form (*ekavadbhāva*). However, this fault does not arise if [the sense of] completion applies to each [member] individually; for in that case, it is a *dvandva* of the parts of living beings.

The three sentences beginning with "it becomes a single unit" (*ekavad bhavati*) are thus established. Regarding its own domain, where a sentence ending in the plural is formed, by the first sentence the formation of a single unit (*ekavadbhāva*) is prescribed for that compound which consists of parts of living beings joined with other parts of living beings. By the second...

By means of the fourth [type of] sentence, there is no possibility of confusion (saṅkara) regarding musical instruments with musical instruments, nor regarding the components of an army with the components of an army; for he considers that there is no fourth sentence by which a dvandva compound with intermingled members could possess a single unified meaning.
Relying on the position that the completion of the sentence applies to each [word] individually, he says: "of the word *aṅga*," and so forth.

Similarly, in the case of "tūryāṅgānām," one expects the rule that a *dvandva* compound of parts of musical instruments becomes singular. This also applies to "senāṅgānām. Regarding "pāṇipādam": here, even if it refers to the limbs of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*),...
When [the compound] is formed by including living beings (*prāṇin*), then it is established by the rule *jātir aprāṇinām* (Pāṇini 2.4.6).
For example: *paṇava-mṛdaṅgam* ("the small drum and the clay drum") and *rathika-aśvāroham* ("the charioteers and the horsemen").
In the case of *rathika-aśvāroham*, the plurality of the referents of the compound—namely, the charioteers and the horsemen—must be shown.

Because multiplicity alone is the cause for being a constituent of an army; since there is no status as a constituent of an army in the absence of multiplicity, it should have been "rathikāśvārohau" (the charioteer and the horseman). [The opponent argues:
"In the case of 'hastyaśvādi', because of its subsequent position, it must necessarily follow the optional rule for the *paśu*-dvandva."
By the rule *vibhāṣā vṛkṣamṛga* (Pāṇini 2.4.12) and so forth, and by the phrase *itaretarayoge* and so forth,

he demonstrates the purpose of the section on *dvandva* compounds. By the statement *prāṇyaṅgādīnāṃ samāhāra eva* and so forth, he clarifies that the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) is for the sake of delimiting the scope of application.

3. *anuvāde caraṇānām* | (2.4.3) By the words "the word *caraṇa*" and so forth, he shows the scope of the sūtra. For instance, when the word *caraṇa* refers to a particular branch (*śākhā*) of study proclaimed by Kaṭha and others, then—

This is already established by the rule *jātir aprāṇinām* (Pāṇini 2.4.6). As for the phrase "when [the tree] has branches as its cause": this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has branches as its cause. Regarding the phrase "of that which is understood through another means of knowledge" (*pramāṇāntarāvagatasya*):
a "different means of knowledge" (*pramāṇāntara*) is any means of knowledge other than the word (*śabda*).

That [object], moreover, is known through perception and so forth. There is merely a verbal mention (*saṃkīrtana*) by means of a word of that which has been understood and determined by that [perception]; the word "merely" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of excluding the actual comprehension of the object.
For example: "He arose" (*udagāt*), "He stood firm" (*pratyaṣṭhāt*). These are the *luṅ* (aorist) forms of the root *iṇ* preceded by *ud*, and *sthā* preceded by *prati*.
In *atiṣṭhipat*, there is the substitution of *gā* by [Pāṇini 2.4.45], and the elision of *sic* by [Pāṇini 2.4.77].
Regarding the term *kaṭhakālāpam*: those who study what was taught by Kaṭha are called *Kaṭhāḥ*.
From the word *kaṭha*, in the sense of "taught by," [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] according to [Pāṇini 4.3.104]: "Also after Kalāpin and the pupils of Vaiśampāyana."

Thus, the suffix *ṇini* is applied; for that, by *ṭhkaṭhacarakālluk* (Pāṇini 4.3.107), there is elision (*luk*). Then, by *ṭhtadadhīte tadveda* (4.2.59), the suffix *aṇ* is applied; for that, by *ṭhproktālluk* (4.2.64), there is elision. Its being restricted to that [subject matter] is established by *ṭhcchandobrāhmaṇāni ca tadviṣayāṇi* (4.2.66). [The compound means: "one who studies what was proclaimed by Kalāpin."

*Kalāpāḥ*: The suffix *aṇ* is applied to *kalāpin* in the sense already mentioned [by the *prokta* rule]. Although the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) would have been expected by the rule *ṭhinaṇyanapatye* (Pāṇini 6.4.164), the elision of the *ṭi* portion occurs by the Vārttika: *sabrahmacāripīṭhasarpikalāpikuthumitairatilijājalilāṅgaliśilāliśikhaṣṭiśūkarasadmasuparvaṇām upasaṃkhyānam* (Vārttika 798). Thereafter, the suffix *aṇ* is added by the rule *tad adhīte tad veda* (Pāṇini 4.2.59). This *aṇ* is then elided by *proktālluk* (Pāṇini 4.2.64). As before, the dual number is formed. Thus, *kaṭhāś ca kālāpāś ca* becomes *kaṭhakālāpam*. "But when the instruction [of the text] occurs from the very beginning... [and so on].

Instruction (*upadeśa*) is the initial communication of a meaning by means of a word, through a question or an answer, when that meaning has not already been understood previously by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). When such occurs, this serves as a counter-example here: *udaguḥ*. [In this case,] *jus* replaces the suffix by [Pāṇini 3.4.110] *ātaḥ*; then, by [Pāṇini 6.1.96] *usyapadāntāt*, there is the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*). Regarding the statement "it should be stated that [the rule applies] after the roots *sthā* and *iṇ* in the aorist (*adyatanī*)," the meaning is that it must be explained [as a *vārttika*].

In this regard, the following is the explanation: from the sūtra *tulyārthairatulopamābhyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.72), the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is understood to carry over. And that is to be understood as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Consequently, the formation of a singular collective (*ekavadbhāva*) will occur for the names of Vedic schools (*caraṇas*) when used with the roots *sthā* and *iṇ* in the past tense (*adyatanī*), but not elsewhere. "Past tense" (*adyatanī*) is a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for the *luṅ* [aorist] introduced by the ancient teachers. An example is *anandiṣuḥ*.

From the root *ṣṭhivu* in the sense of "to swell" (*samṛddhau*) [Dhātupāṭha 6.7], the substitution of *jus* for *jhi* occurs by [Pāṇini 3.4.109]: *sijabhyastavidibhyaśca*. Thus, we have "udyanti. The substitution of *yaṇ* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.81]: *iko yaṇ*.

4. *adhvaryukraturanapuṃsakam* | (2.4.4) [The commentary states: "In the *Adhvaryu-veda*. By this, he shows that the word *adhvaryu* here indicates the Yajurveda. Now, as for the sacrifice (*kratu*) belonging to the specific officiant (*ṛtvij*) who is the Adhvaryu...
Why is the mention of the *adhvaryu* not understood as a qualification of the sacrifice (*kratu*) itself? Because it is impossible; for what sacrifice belongs to him?
Rather, it belongs to one whose nature is to spend wealth.
Even if he possesses agency in the sacrifice, that too is common to other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); thus, it is by means of the single *adhvaryu* [that the distinction is made].

The qualification of that [person] is improper. But surely, for the purpose of excluding a sacrifice prescribed by the Atharvaveda—which could be performed by a single Adhvaryu priest—how could there not be a qualification?
For there are no other Adhvaryus [to perform it]. This is not so; for if this much were the intended purpose, [it would have been stated as such].

In that case, he would simply have formulated the prohibition as "not by the Atharvaveda," for a direct prohibition is more concise. Or else, he would have used the term "Trayī" (the three Vedas). Furthermore, if the sacrifice were qualified by the Adhvaryu priest, then this [prohibition] would also apply to the case of the "arrows and thunderbolts."

For even the *iṣu* and *vajra* sacrifices belong to the Adhvaryu; since those two also have him as their performer, the Veda of the Adhvaryus—those who know the Yajurveda—is indicated by the term "Adhvaryu. That, moreover, is the Yajurveda. In that Adhvaryu Veda:

"The ritual for which there is an injunction is called an *adhvaryu-kratu*. By the word "injunction" (*vidhāna*), both the instruction regarding the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) and the performance consisting of the actual execution are expressed. If, then, a copulative compound (*dvandva*) of words denoting *adhvaryu-kratavaḥ* that are not neuter in gender becomes singular...

In that case, the meaning of the Sūtra would not be tenable, because the co-referential (sāmānādhikaraṇya) indication of the term *adhvaryukratu* in the Sūtra and of the rule *anapuṃsakam* [Pāṇini 2.4.17] by means of the word *dvandva*—as connected with the present context—would be impossible.
Therefore, it should have been stated as: "of those words denoting the *adhvaryu-kratu* which are not neuter. For this reason...
He says: "The compound *adhvaryukratu* is not neuter. [This is because] "this is a figurative designation (*gauṇa-nirdeśa*).

The meaning of "figurative" (*gauṇa*) is that it is non-primary (*amukhya*) or metaphorical (*aupacārika*). A *dvandva* compound consisting of parts of the *adhvaryu-kratu* is called "*adhvaryukratu*" by way of metaphor (*upacāreṇa*). That...

Thus, a *dvandva* whose constituent parts (*avayava*) are not neuter is itself non-neuter. However, the designation "non-neuter" (*anapuṃsaka*) should be understood as being used in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*) for the sake of brevity. If, on the other hand, by the term "non-neuter" the *dvandva* itself were denoted in its primary sense (*mukhya*), then this [rule] would be an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule "that [neuter *dvandva* is treated as singular] is neuter" (Pāṇini 2.4.17).
It would be understood as "arka-aśvamedham" and so forth; that is, *arka* and *aśvamedha* together form *arkāśvamedham*.
Likewise, *sāyāhna* and *atirātra* together form *sāyāhnātirātram*.
Regarding "iṣu-vajrau" and so forth, sacrifices such as the *iṣu* and *vajra*, which belong to the Adhvaryu ritual tradition (*adhvaryukratavaḥ*), are not possible [in this context], nor...
For their injunction is found in the *Adhvaryu-veda*. What then? It is in the *Sāma-veda*. [The text says:
"In the *Rājasūya* and *Vājapeya*. These two words, *rājasūya* and *vājapeya*, are also masculine; however, when they are used in the neuter gender, then this [rule applies].

The counter-example is "in Soma sacrifices" (*somayāgeṣu*). Those in which the drinking of Soma is prescribed are Soma sacrifices; it is precisely for these that the word *kratu* is used in its conventional sense (*rūḍha*). Furthermore, the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices are not Soma sacrifices. Because of the inclusion of the rule "not neuter" (*anapuṃsakam*, 2.4.4), there is no apprehension of the word's own form (*svarūpa*) here.
It occurs; for a common term denoting a sacrifice does not take the neuter gender.

5. [The name] "not remote" [is applied] on account of study (adhyayanato’viprakṛṣṭākhyānām). (2.4.5) The word *adhyayana* is derived as a noun of action (*bhāvasādhana*)—meaning "the act of studying"—or as a noun of object (*karmasādhana*)—meaning "that which is studied. [The term in the sūtra] is "on account of study" (*adhyayanataḥ*).

The suffix *tasi* is applied after a word ending in the instrumental case expressing a cause, according to the rule "An addition of *tasi* after words beginning with *sthā* and others" (Vārttika 634).
Therefore, he says: "by means of study as the cause. Regarding the term "not remote" (*aviprakṛṣṭā*):
those whose names are not remote are called "those whose names are not remote. [This refers to] the cause.
Remoteness consists in commonality and so forth. Furthermore, that cause is precisely the study of the names [of the Vedic texts] as presented in the Sūtra: "the *pada* and *krama* [recensions].
From the expressions "he studies the *pada*" and "he studies the *krama*," the suffix *vun* is applied by the rule *kramādibhyo vun* (Pāṇini 4.2.61).

"Kramakavārtikam. One who has studied a *vṛtti* is called a *vārtika*. [The suffix] *ṭhak* is applied after words ending in *kratu*, *uktha*, and so forth, as well as those ending in *sūtra* (Pāṇini 4.2.60). But how is there a lack of remoteness for one who studies the *pada-pāṭha* by means of the study of the *krama-pāṭha*? To this he says: "Recitation," and so forth.
Since the recitation of the words and their sequence is not significantly different, the *grantha* (text) is likewise similar;

therefore, it is proximate. Furthermore, because the *krama* must be studied after having mastered the individual words (*pada*), the *saṃpāṭha* (juxtaposed recitation) is also proximate to those two. And thus, by means of that study consisting of the *saṃpāṭha*, [the result follows].

The intention is that even the designation of a student as "padaka" (one who knows the *padas*) or "kramaka" (one who knows the *krama*) is closely related [to the context]. In the example "pitāputrau," the substitution of *ānaṅ* occurs by the rule "ānaṅ ṛto dvandve" (Pāṇini 6.3.25).
For in that rule, from the preceding rule "putre 'nyatarasyām" (6.3.22), the word "putra" is carried over.

The phrase "it follows" [from the previous rule] applies here as well. In this case too, the designations "father" and "son" are proximate because the cause [of the relationship] is common to both. For instance, the relationship of producer and produced (*janyajanakabhāva*) is the cause for both of them. As in the example: *yājñikavaiyākaraṇam* ("the sacrificer and the grammarian"). One who studies the sacrifice is a *yājñika*.

By [Pāṇini 4.2.60] *kratūkthādinā*, the suffix *ik* is applied: one who studies grammar is a *vaiyākaraṇaḥ*. By [Pāṇini 4.2.59] *tadadhīte tadveda*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied. Although these two designations (*ākhyā*) have as their cause the act of studying, there is no immediate proximity (*pratyāsatti*) between them; for [the result] does not arise from the study of sacrifice or the study of grammar [in the case of the other].
Nor is there proximity of action, nor even proximity of the text.

6. *Jāti* [is the name] for things that are not living beings. (Pāṇini 2.4.6) This [sūtra] also employs the term "jāti" by way of metaphorical usage (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*) to refer to a *dvandva* compound; thus, it is designated as "jāti" through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
A *dvandva* whose constituent parts denote a genus (*jāti*) is called "jāti. Furthermore, the mention of "jāti" here is intended to capture its essential nature (*svarūpa*).

It does not occur, because of the prohibition [stated] as "not for things that are not living beings" (*aprāṇinām*). In the case of *ārāśastri*, the short vowel is applied by the rule "the final vowel of a neuter nominal stem is shortened" (*hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya*).
In the case of *nandakapāñcajanyau*, this is a *dvandva* compound of two words that are proper names (*saṃjñāśabda*), and not [of common nouns].

Regarding the two terms *jāti* (genus) and *śabda* (word): by this [sūtra], he demonstrates that the rule *aprāṇinām* (of non-living beings) is a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion). He states that this results in the following meaning: "In connection with *nañ* and *iva*," and so forth. "Form, taste, smell, and touch," and so forth, are genus-classes of qualities (*guṇajāti*). "Going, contracting, and extending" are genus-classes of actions (*kriyājāti*).

Regarding the phrase "and when the genus is predominant": when there is an intention to express the genus as the primary element, then, because the genus is predominant, words denoting the genus undergo the state of being treated as a single unit (ekavadbhāva).
Regarding the phrase "not when there is an intention to express specific substances": this refers to cases where, in a particular place or similar context, specific [substances]...
When there is an intention to express specific substances, then even upon the employment of a genus-word (*jātiśabda*), the singular treatment (*ekavadbhāva*) does not occur. Why is this so?
Because by the designation "genus" (*jāti*), the primary genus is intended, not the secondary one. And this applies when the primary [genus] is [the subject].

It is obtained from the comprehension of the intended meaning (kāryasaṃpratyaya). This is what is meant: when the genus (jāti) itself is employed by depending upon a particular individual (vyaktiviśeṣa), then there is no singular treatment (ekavadbhāva); but when it is employed without depending upon a particular individual, only then does the singular treatment occur.

Regarding the phrase "jujube and emblic myrobalan fruits" (*badarāmalakāni*): here, there is a cognition of the individual instances (*vyakti*) of the jujubes and emblic myrobalans, not of the generic classes (*jāti*). For this very reason, the plural number (*bahuvacana*) is based on the individuals; otherwise, since a class is singular, there would have been only a dual number, not a plural. [This applies] to non-living things (*aprāṇinām*).

This is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). By this, the following meaning is obtained: according to the maxim of "that which is joined with *nañ* or *iva*" (*nañivayuktanyāya*), there is no singular collective expression for form, taste, touch, and so forth. In the prohibition "not having breath" (*aprāṇinām*), the plurality that is heard implies plurality even in the positive injunction; therefore—
A *dvandva* compound consisting of many bases becomes singular, but not one consisting of two bases— as in the case of *ārāśastrī*.

7. *viśiṣṭaliṅgo nadīdeśo'grāmāḥ* | (2.4.7) This word *viśiṣṭa* denotes distinction (*bheda*). Although this word *viśiṣṭa* was explained as being used in the sense of "exclusively" (*sāvadhāraṇa*) in the rule *ktena nañviśiṣṭenānañ* (Pāṇini 2.1.60), that [usage] too—

The various grammatical operations proceed precisely by means of differentiation. Therefore, even the author of the *Vṛtti* here says: "Even for those [words] of different genders—[as in the *Kāśikā*: 'there is no [application]'—and for 'villages' (*grāmāḥ*).
Because of this prohibition, he states that there is no grasping of the actual forms of these two [terms], saying: "of those denoting rivers" (*nadīvācinām*).

And so forth. If the intended meaning of the rule here were that a *dvandva* compound consisting of words denoting rivers as well as words denoting regions becomes singular (*ekavadbhāva*), then how could there be this reference in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the present subject, namely, "this *dvandva* [consisting of] river and region"?

Thus he says: "A *dvandva* compound whose constituent parts include a river is called a 'river' (*nadī*)," and so forth.
