Therefore, because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), the substitution of *gāṅ* must occur even before the substitution of *ādeśa*;

consequently, since this substitution of *aci* is caused by reduplication (*dvirvacana*), the status of being a "substitute" (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply, so how could there be the possibility of reduplication of the vowel *i*? [The purpose of] the addition of the indicatory letter (*anubandha*) in *gāṅ*...

"For the sake of specification. In the rule *gāṅ-kuṭādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.1), if it were stated simply as *gāṅ-kuṭādibhyaḥ*, there would be the inclusion of the root *kai* and *gai* "to sound" (Dhātupāṭha 916, 917).
Consequently, why would there not be an inclusion [of the substitution] in the case of *agāsīt naṭaḥ*? By what reason does it not occur?

That reason has been shown in the *Gāṅkuṭādissūtra* itself. Now, one might object: "Since the root *iṅ* will be included there by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original), what is the purpose of the letter *ṅ*? To this he says: "For not... and so forth. For in that [sūtra], there is the inclusion of the specific form *gāṅti*; and that [form] is not [included otherwise].
It is not obtained by way of having the same status (*sthānitva*); what then? By way of its function (*kārya*).
For this [rule], "A substitute is like the original" (*sthānivad ādeśaḥ*, 1.1.56), is an extension of function (*kāryātideśa*), not an extension of form (*rūpātideśa*).
50. *vibhāṣā luṅlṛṅkṣu* (2.4.50). Regarding the example *adhyaiṣṭa*: the augment *āṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 6.4.72] *āḍajādīnām*; then, by [Pāṇini 6.1.90] *āṭaśca*, there is *vṛddhi*.

51. *ṇau ca saṃścaṅoḥ* (2.4.51). Regarding the phrase "in the context of *ṇi*," and so forth: the locative case in *ṇau* is a locative of reference (*parasanamī*) with respect to *iṅ*; the locative case in *saṃścaṅoḥ* is a locative of reference with respect to *ṇi*. This is the meaning.
Regarding "adhyajīgāpayiṣati": there is the causative suffix *ṇic*. By the rule "arti-hrī-" (Pāṇini 7.3.36), the augment *puk* is added;

then the desiderative suffix *san*, the augment *iṭ*, and the substitution of *guṇa* and *āya*. Regarding "adhyāpipayiṣati": by the rule "krīṅ-jīnāṃ ṇau" (Pāṇini 6.1.48), the substitution of *ā* occurs; then *puk*; and by the rule "ajāder-dvitīyasya" (Pāṇini 6.1.2), the reduplication of the second syllable, namely "pā," [occurs].
The reduplication [is applied]. In the form *adhyajīgapat*, the suffix *caṅ* is added by [Pāṇini 3.1.48] *ṇi-śri-...*.

By [Pāṇini 7.4.1] *ṇau caṅy upadhāyā hrasvaḥ*, there is shortening of the penultimate vowel. Due to the application of *sanvadbhāva* by [Pāṇini 7.4.93] *sanvallaghuni*, the substitution of *i* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.4.79] *sany ataḥ*. Then, by [Pāṇini 7.4.94] *dīrgho laghoḥ*, the long vowel is substituted for the light syllable.
Thus, [the vowel] is long.

52. *aster bhūḥ* | (2.4.52) [The root *as* is replaced by *bhū* in the perfect tense. Regarding the example *īhāmāsa*: from the root *īh*, the suffix *ām* is applied according to *ijādeśca gurumato'nṛccchaḥ* (3.1.36). By *āmaḥ* (2.4.81), there is elision (*luk*) of the *liṭ* affix; then, by *kṛñcānuprayujyate liṭi* (3.1.40), the root *kṛ* is subsequently employed.

Thus, there is the subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) of the root *as* when followed by the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*). This is because the inclusion of *as* within the pratyāhāra [of the rule] is for the sake of its specific mention. In the rule "And *kṛñ* is employed subsequently in the *liṭ*" (Pāṇini 3.1.40), the term *kṛñ* refers to a pratyāhāra; [this applies] in cases where something not previously existing comes into being (*abhūtatadbhāve*).

By the rule *kṛbhvastiyoge sampadyakartari* (Pāṇini 5.4.50), starting from the word *kṛ* up to the letter *ñ* in *kṛño dvitīyatṛtīyaśambabījāt* (5.4.58)— that is, the *ñ* of *ā-√kṛ*— there is the inclusion of *as* as well through this mention of the pratyāhāra (*kṛn*); for this is precisely its purpose.

[The mention of] *āsa* [in the sūtra] is for the purpose that the form [of the root] should occur when it is used in conjunction with *as*. If the substitution of *bhū* were to occur even in conjunction with *as*, then the form would not occur when *āsa* is used in conjunction;
thus, the inclusion of the pratyāhāra [by mentioning *āsa*] would be meaningless. Consequently, *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* are employed in conjunction.

One should say "liṭi" (in the case of the *liṭ* suffix). In that case as well, this meaning is established: the doubt as to whether this is a reference to the *pratyāhāra* [of *liṭ*] or merely to the root *kṛ* is thereby removed;
and since the reference to the *pratyāhāra* has been made, by the force of that *pratyāhāra* reference, [the rule applies] even in the case of the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*).

The substitution of *bhū* does not occur here. By saying "And so it is said," and so forth, he confirms the very point just mentioned with the words of an authoritative person (*āptavacana*). The long vowel in *bhūḥ* is for the purpose that the short vowel be heard in the past participle (*niṣṭhā*), as in *bhūtaḥ* and *bhūtavān*.

The mention of *aster* with the marker *śtip* is intended so that it would not apply to the root *as-* (to be); this is not necessary, for by the principle of "the one without an *anubandha* [takes precedence]" (*niranubandhakaparibhāṣā*), it will not apply to *as-*. For its [the root *as-*] vowel *u* has been made an *anubandha for the purpose of specification in the rule "or when marked with *ṭh*" (*ṭhito vā*, 7.2.56).

The letter *a* in *asteḥ* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*) and is not an indicatory letter (*anubandha*). In that case, some say that the mention [of the root] with the suffix *śtip* is for the sake of variety. Others say it is because the rule regarding [roots] without indicatory letters (*niranubandhaka-paribhāṣā*) pertains only to the domain of the prescription of suffixes (*pratyaya-vidhi*).

53. *bruvo vaciḥ* (2.4.53). [The substitute *vac* is applied to the root *brū* in the sense of speaking. For example, *vaktā* ("speaker"): here, the substitution of *k* for the *c*-sounds (*coḥ kuḥ*, 8.2.30) applies. For example, *ūce* ("he spoke"): here, the *samprasāraṇa* substitution is applied by the rule *vacyādi-sūtra* (6.1.15).
54. *cakṣiṅḥ khyāñ* (Pāṇini 2.4.54). [The commentary states:

"The ātmanepada [suffixes] do not necessarily occur. For if they did, the addition of the indicatory letter *ā* would be purposeless. Therefore, [the ātmanepada occurs] when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent (*kartrabhiprāya*).
The *ātmanepada* suffix shall be used where intended, and not otherwise.
Regarding the statement "the substitute also begins with *k* or *ś*": the vowel *a* in the letters *ka* and *śa* is for the sake of pronunciation.
It must be stated that the substitute is of the form *kś* or *khyāñ*. But how is it that even though such a form is desired...
Is the substitution obtained? Yes, because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the previously mentioned term *bahulagrahaṇa* (the mention of "in various instances").

Therefore, one must provide the following explanation: due to the continued application of *bahulagrahaṇa*, there is a prohibition of the substitution in the case of *varjana* (exclusion) and in the case of the suffixes *as* and *ani*.
Regarding "saṃcakṣya": [it is formed] by Pāṇini 3.1.124, *ṛhalorṇyat*.

Regarding "nṛcakṣā": [it is formed] by the *Uṇādi* rule 9.49, *sarvadhātubhyo 'sun*, and the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by Pāṇini 6.4.14, *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ*. Regarding "vicakṣaṇaḥ": [it is formed] by the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo...* [bahulam].
The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the agent according to [Pāṇini 3.3.113] *bahulam*.

Regarding the word *bahulam* and so forth: the meaning is that this rule must be explained as having the sense that, in technical terminology (*saṃjñā*) and in Vedic usage (*chandas*), operations such as the substitution of *jagdhi* for *ad* do not occur extensively (*bahulam*). For what purpose? For the sake of food (*annādya*).

The words *annādayaḥ* (beginning with *anna*) are correct forms. The explanation for this must be made by relying on that very mention of the term *bahulam* (in various ways). Regarding the word *anna*: the substitute *jagdhi* does not occur for the root *ad*;

this is because the application of *bahulam* continues [from the previous rule] according to the maxim of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita-nyāya*). Regarding the word *vadhaka*: [the substitution of *han* for the root *vadha* occurs].

By the rule *ṭhhano vadha* (Pāṇini 2.4.42), the substitution *vadha* prescribed for the root *han* occurs even when the suffix *ṇvul* is applied. Regarding the word *gātram*: the suffix *ṣṭran* is derived from the *uṇādi* group. Furthermore, the substitution *gā* prescribed for the aorist (*luṅ*) by the rule *iṇo gā luṅ* (2.4.45) applies here as well.
[The word] *vicakṣaṇaḥ* occurs; however, the substitution of *khyāñ* for the root *cakṣiṅ* does not take place when the suffix *lyuṭ* follows.

As for the word *ajira*, it is an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) word ending in the suffix *kirac*, introduced by the *Uṇādi* rule "ajira-śiśira-śithira" (Uṇādi Sūtra 8.27). Precisely because of that irregular formation, [the rule] "ajeghañapoḥ" applies.
Thus, the substitution of *vī* [for *vi*] as prescribed by this rule does not occur. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), forms such as *praghasa* are included.
55. Or [the substitution of *vī* for *aj*] occurs before the *liṭ* suffix.

(2.4.55) 56. *Vī* is substituted for *aj* except before *ghañ* and *ap*. (2.4.56) In "pravāyakaḥ," the suffix *ṇvul* is applied. In "pravayaṇīyam," the suffix *anīyar* is applied. [This is because of the rule] "kṛtyacaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.29).
Thus, there is the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*]. Regarding the statement,

"In the prohibition concerning *ghañ* and *ap*, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) regarding *kyap* must be made," the meaning is that an addition— that is, a formal presentation— must be made regarding the prohibition of *kyap* which would otherwise apply in the case of *ghañ* and *ap*.

The genitive case in *kyapaḥ* is used because *kyap* is intended to be related to the prohibition as its cause; that is to say, it is the cause of the prohibition. In this regard, the following is the demonstration: by the rule *saṃjñāyāṃ samajanipatamanavida* (Pāṇini 3.3.99), when a name (*saṃjñā*) is to be understood, [the suffix] is applied after the root *aj*.

The designation (saṃjñā) is established as having a fixed sequence of phonemes; however, once the substitute (ādeśa) has been applied, that designation is no longer perceived. Therefore, because it is prescribed as a designation, the substitution of *vī* does not occur when the suffix *kyap* is added.
[It is said: "In the case of an *ardhadhātuka* suffix beginning with *val*, the substitution is desired optionally. How so?
Furthermore, is the augment *iṭ* obtained even when it is desired? Because the root *ej* is marked with the acute accent (*udātta*);

for that root is listed among the verbal roots (*dhātu*) as having the acute accent in the sense of "to go. If its substitution by *vī* were obligatory, then its listing with the acute accent would be purposeless; for the augment *iṭ* is not prescribed when the substitution of *vī* has already taken place.
[The suffix] *lyuṭ* is obtained; because it is unaccented (*anudātta*).
57. *vā yau* (Pāṇini 2.4.57).
The term *yau* refers to the inclusion of *lyuṭ*, since no other [suffix beginning with *y*] is possible. For example: *pravayaṇo daṇḍaḥ* ("a weaving stick").

Thus: [the word] *prājya* is formed with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), meaning "that by which one is impelled"; the substitution of *va* for *ya* is as in the preceding case.

58. *ṇyakṣatriyārṣañito yūni lugaṇiñoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.58). [The commentary states: "The suffixes beginning with *ṭhaṇ* are *gotra* suffixes," because the rule *gotrād yūny astriyām* (4.1.94) prescribes the application of a *yuvan* suffix only after a base ending in a *gotra* suffix. [And it continues: "From that [base], the *yuvan* suffix *iñ* [is applied]," according to *tasmād yūnīñ*. [And further: "From this... (*ataḥ*)...

By the rule *iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95). [It is stated: "The word *kauravya* is read in the *tikādi* group," immediately after the word *auḍulomi*. [This is because] "there, the *kṣatriya* lineage (*gotra*) is what is intended to be included," due to its association with the word *auḍulomi*, which ends in a suffix denoting a *kṣatriya* lineage. For the word *auḍulomi*...
The word [Vatsa] ends in the patronymic suffix denoting a Kṣatriya lineage, according to Pāṇini 4.1.168: "The suffix añ follows a word denoting a country when it refers to a Kṣatriya."
Regarding "ṭhṛṣyaṇ": [the suffix] is applied by the rule "ṭhṛṣyandhakavṛṣṇikurubhyaśca" (Pāṇini 4.1.114).

Regarding "ṭhkurvādibhyo ṇyaḥ": this explains the word *vāmarathya*. From that [word], the suffix *aṇ* is applied as a secondary derivative (*śaiṣika*) by the rule "kaṇvādibhyo gotre" (Pāṇini 4.2.111). But is not the word *vāmarathya*...?

It is recited among the *kurva*-group and not among the *kaṇva*-group; how then can it be said thus? Even though it is not recited [there], nevertheless, because there is a recitation stating that for Vāmarathya—as with the *kaṇva*-group and others—the rule applies "with the exception of the accent," the status of being like the *kaṇva*-group exists; therefore, it was stated in this way, and there is no fault.
Regarding the term *dākṣāyaṇaḥ*: the suffix *phak* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.101] *yañiñośca*.

Regarding the phrase *abrāhmaṇagotramātrāt*: here some have stated that "there should be an addition [to the rule] stating that when there is elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ*, the secondary suffix (*yuvan-pratyaya*) applies after a Kṣatriya gotra alone. According to them...

One does not obtain [the status] from a Vaiśya lineage; therefore, the mention of "mother" (mātṛ) is for the purpose that it may also occur from a Vaiśya lineage. For lineages exist among Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas;
therein, excluding the Brāhmaṇa lineage, [the status] arises from every other [lineage]. However, in the previous [case],...
The mention of *mātra* (matronymic) in the rule is for the purpose that [the suffix] might apply even after a *tadrāja* [patronymic] when it refers to a *kṣatriya* lineage.
For he demonstrates this by showing the addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of the suffix *ya* after a *tadrāja* following the elision (*luk*) of *ṭhañ* and *iñ*,
as in the examples of *vaiśya* lineages such as *bhāṇḍījaṅghiḥ* and so forth.

Because the Brāhmaṇa lineage is prohibited here, [the form] "Dākṣāyaṇa" does not occur. Regarding the statement "characterized by being a part of Śālva," this was said with reference to the Kṣatriya lineage.
In the case of "Bhāṇḍījaṅghiḥ," since it belongs to the Vaiśya lineage, only the suffix *iñ* applies by the rule "ata iñ" (Pāṇini 4.1.95).
It should be understood that [the rule] "it occurs" is established by the observation of Paila and others.
By stating "because Paila and others belong to the class of *ākṛtigaṇas*," he shows that these [names] are to be regarded as included therein.

59. *pailādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 2.4.59). [The commentary states: "Regarding *pīlāyā vetyaṇ*: for there, because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the suffix *aṇ* from [the rule] *śivādibhyo’ṇ* (4.1.112), other members of the *pailādi* group end in *iñ*."

In this context, the word *audañci* ends in the suffix *iñ* because it belongs to the *bāhv-ādi* group; for the word *udañc* is indeed listed among the *bāhv-ādi* stems. The pronunciation of the letter *u* is not restrictive (*atantra*), as it serves merely to indicate the verbal root. From the root *ud-añc* (meaning "to go upwards"), the suffix *kvin* is applied by the rule *ṛtvig-ādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.59). Thus, *audañciḥ* means "the descendant of *udañc*."

Due to the rule of irregular formation (*nipātana*), there is no elision of the *n* according to *ṭhaniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24), etc., nor is there elision of the vowel *a* according to *acaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.138). The word *bhauliṅgi* is derived from a part of Śālva with the suffix *iñ*.
The remaining [names], however, should be understood as ending in *iñ* by virtue of the rule *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95). Thus, *śālaṅkiḥ*.

It is recited [in the Gaṇapāṭha]; how is that so, since according to the reading "naḍādibhyaḥ phak, ṭhaśalaṅkuśalaṅkañ ca" (Gaṇasūtra 67), one would have to derive *śālaṅkāyana*? Some say that there is another base word, *śalaṅku*, and from that this suffix *iñ* is prescribed. It is precisely for this reason...
By virtue of a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*), it is understood that the suffix *iñ* is applied after the word *śalaṅku*;

furthermore, others maintain that in connection with that [suffix], there is the substitution of *śalaṅka* for the original base. Regarding the rule "after a *tadrāja* [term], the suffix *aṇ* [is elided]":

the suffix *aṇ* following a term designated as *tadrāja* causes the elision of a subsequent *yuvan* (descendant) suffix. This applies to the formation of a patronymic (*apatya*) from a base ending in two *añ* suffixes, such as *Magadha*.
Thus, by [Pāṇini 4.1.170], the suffix *phiñ* is applied; its elision (*luk*) occurs by this [rule].

60. *iñaḥ prācām* | (2.4.60) Elsewhere, the mention of "prācām" (of the easterners) is seen to have the purpose of providing an option; therefore, he says "gotraviśeṣaṇam" and so forth, so that an option might not be understood here as well.

61. Not after *taulvali* and others. (2.4.61) In the list beginning with *taulvali*, the word *antaraha* and the word *pauṣkarasādi* end in the suffix *iñ*. For indeed, the word *antaraha* and the word *puṣkarasat* are recited among the *bāhū-ādi* group.

In this case, there is a vṛddhi of both syllables because [the word] belongs to the *anu-raśatika* group; the remaining [names], however, end in the suffix *iñ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.95 (*ṭha-ita iñ*).

62. *tadrājasya bahuṣu tenaivāstriyām* (2.4.62). [The phrase] "occurring in the sense of many" means occurring in the sense of many objects. Now, why is it not explained as "when the plural number follows"? It is impossible to state it in that way.

For the word *bahu* expresses number (*saṃkhyā*), not the plural number (*bahuvacana*). If, however, the intended meaning here were "when the plural follows," then the author would not have formulated the prohibition *na striyām*; because there would be no possibility [of the suffix applying] in the feminine. Indeed, a feminine suffix produced after a *tadrāja* ending does not [apply].

There is the possibility of elision (*luk*) when a plural suffix follows [the stem *atrya*]. Furthermore, if elision were prescribed here when a plural suffix follows—as in the case of *attrayaḥ*—the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* would result.
How so? [Because] from the sense "many offspring of Atri," the suffix *ḍhak* would be applied according to *ṭhitaścāniñaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.122).
When the final udātta accent has been applied to that taddhita suffix by [Pāṇini 6.1.164–165],
and when the elision (*luk*) has occurred in the plural case ending *jas* by [Pāṇini 2.4.65],
[the rule] "anudātasya ca yatrodyatalopaḥ" (6.1.161) applies.

The case-ending would then acquire an udātta accent. Therefore, the meaning is precisely "occurring in the sense of many. Furthermore, the word "bahuṣu" (in the sense of many) is a qualifier of that which ends in a tadrāja suffix, not of the tadrāja suffix itself;
otherwise, a fault would arise in the case of a dvandva compound—such as *āṅgaśca vāṅgaśca*.

In the case of *sauhmacāṅgavāṅgasuhmāḥ*, the substitution of *huṅ* would not occur; for here the *tadrāja* suffix does not denote plurality. Rather, that which ends in the *tadrāja* suffix denotes plurality, because a *dvandva* compound expresses multiple substrates simultaneously. Therefore, this qualification applies specifically to that which ends in a *tadrāja* suffix, and not to the *tadrāja* suffix itself.

However, this passage from the *Vṛtti*— namely, "there is elision (*luk*) of a suffix designated as *tadrāja* when it occurs in the plural and is not feminine"— should be understood in this way: [it refers to] that which is designated as *tadrāja* and is related to a word ending in a *tadrāja* suffix that occurs in the plural and is not feminine.

The elision (*luk*) occurs of that suffix which bears the designation *tadrāja*. How so? This capacity is obtained only for [a compound] ending in a *tadrāja* suffix; for a suffix bearing the designation *tadrāja* cannot be related to [a compound] that does not end in a *tadrāja* suffix. Furthermore, the term "ending" (*anta*) was not even included in the rule (*sūtra*).

Since the inclusion of that which ends in a suffix is already obtained by the very paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix, nevertheless, when the elision (*luk*) of what "ends in a suffix" is stated, it is understood to apply to the suffix alone; for, according to *pratyayasya luk-ślulupah* (Pāṇini 1.1.61), the technical term *luk* is prescribed specifically for the non-appearance of a suffix. [This applies] provided that it is by that very [suffix].
Thus; the meaning is "by means of that very suffix which denotes a king. For example: *aṅgāḥ*, *vaṅgāḥ*, *suhmāḥ*.
[These mean] many descendants of Aṅga. By the rule *dvyañmagadha* (Pāṇini 4.1.170), the suffix *aṇ* is applied, and there is its elision (*luk*). For example: *lohadhvajāḥ*, *vrīhimantaḥ*.
The suffix *ñya* is applied by the rule *ṭhpūgāñÃñyo'grāmaṇīpūrvāt* (Pāṇini 5.3.112), and there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix.
Thus we have "ĀṬpagavāḥ. [In the case of] "priyavāṅgāḥ," the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *ṭhprāgdīvyato'ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.1.83).

It is a *bahuvrīhi*. In this case, plurality is not expressed by a *tadrāja* suffix; rather, it is expressed by the compound itself. Furthermore, that [compound] does not end in a *tadrāja* suffix, and therefore the elision (*luṅ*) would not apply because the *tadrāja* suffix has not been prescribed there. If that is so, then since a *dvandva* also does not end in a *tadrāja* suffix, would the elision not likewise fail to occur in that case as well?
This is not so; for even if the *dvandva* compound itself does not end in a *tadrāja* suffix, nevertheless,
each member of the *dvandva* ends in a *tadrāja* suffix and has the sense of "belonging to that" (*tad-artha*), and thus the elision (*luk*) indeed occurs there.

Nor is there a mention of the meaning "in many" (*bahuṣu*); for wherever the meaning "many" occurs, it must necessarily be accompanied by the plurality (*bahutva*) produced by that very [meaning]. What, then, is the purpose of this phrase *tenaiva*? He thinks as follows:
because it is an internal factor (*antaraṅga*), the plurality that arises at the very moment the *tadrāja* suffix is produced—[is what is intended].

If that very [base] were taken, and not one dependent on another word (*padāntarāpekṣam*), then there would be no elision (*luk*) in the case of *dvandva* compounds. However, the mention of "by that very [base]" implies that this is a second effort: namely, that the plurality of what ends in a suffix is effected by that very [suffix], as well as in all cases where it is effected even by dependence on another word.
"It occurs. If this is so, then would it not also apply here in the case of *priyavāṅgaḥ*?

This is not a fault, for the particle *eva* is used here. It establishes a restriction with reference only to those of the same class, namely, that the plurality is formed by those [stems] which undergo elision (*lopin*). And [the stem] *priyavāṅga* does not [belong to that class].
In this case, the plurality is formed by those very [names] that undergo elision (*lopin*), because here some words undergo elision while others do not.

And when such a restriction is established, even in a *dvandva* compound, where there are both words that undergo elision and those that do not, [the plural suffix] does not occur— as in "gārgya-kāśyapa-gālavānām" (of Gārgya, Kāśyapa, and Gālava).

Regarding this [rule] (8.4.67), here the elision (*lopa*) would apply to *gārgya* and *kāśyapa* by the rule "ṭhyañiñośca" (4.1.101). However, for *gālava*, because it ends in the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ*, there is no occurrence of elision (*luk*). [The form] "āṅgyaḥ" is derived with the feminine suffix *ṅīp* by the rule "ṭiḍḍhāṇañ" (4.1.15).
63. *yaskādibhyo gotre* (Pāṇini 2.4.63).

One might have the misconception that this "lineage" (*gotra*) is to be understood only in its technical sense—as defined by the rule *apatyaṃ pautraprabhṛti gotram* (4.1.162)—and not in its common, worldly sense. Therefore, [the author] addresses that [misconception]:

To refute this, he says: "And [the term] is subject to the rule for suffixes elsewhere," and so forth. It is understood that both these possibilities exist here in the treatise (*śāstra*): when the worldly *gotra* is taken, the technical (*śāstrīya*) one is included therein; however, in the case of the prescription of a suffix (*pratyaya-vidhi*), [only the technical one applies].
This is because of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that there is no inclusion of the worldly lineage (*laukikagotra*). For instance,
in the rule *gotrokṣoṣṭrorabhrarājarājanyarājaputravatsamanuṣyājād vuñ* (Pāṇini 4.2.39), having already employed the term *gotra*, the author specifically employs the term *rājanya*.

This indicates that in the formulation of suffixes (*pratyaya-vidhi*), the inclusion of worldly lineages (*laukika-gotra*) does not occur. [For example: "The students of Yāska. Here, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.120] *tasyedam*. The word *puṣkara* is also recited here; for what purpose? Since [the rule] *bahvaca iñ prācyabharateṣu* (2.4.66) [applies].

Is it thus established? It is not established; for the prohibition [stated in] *Pāṇini 2.4.67*, "not after Gopavana and so forth," would apply. For among the *gopavana* group, some read "and Taulvalya and so forth," and within the *taulvalya* group, the word *puṣkarasat* is read.

Furthermore, the fact that the *Taulvali*s and others are included in the list of *Gopavana*s and so forth indicates that this very inclusion of the word *Puṣkarasat* among the *Yaska*s and others is intended as a significant rule.

64. *yañaśca* (2.4.64). [The example is] *gārgyā*. By the rule *yañaśca* (4.1.16), the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Then, by the rule *yasyeti ca* (6.4.148), there is the elision of the vowel *a*; and by the rule *halastaddhitasya* (6.4.50), there is the elision of the consonant *y*. For in that case...

From the rule *sūryatiṣyāgastyamatsyānāṃ ya upadhāyāḥ* (6.4.149), the word *ya* is carried over; and from *allopo'naḥ* (6.4.134), the word *lopa* is carried over. Regarding *vaidyaḥ*: [it is derived] by the rule *śārṅgaravādyaño ṅīn* (4.1.73). Regarding *dvaipyāḥ* and *auṭsāḥ*.

In the sense of a secondary derivative (*śaiṣika*) such as "born in" (*jāta*), [the suffixes] *yañ* and *añ* [are applied], according to the rule beginning with "*yañaño ṭhyañādīnām*" and so forth. Since the elision (*luk*) of *yañ* and the others is prescribed when there is a plurality (*bahutva*), this statement is made because [the elision] would otherwise apply even in the case of singularity (*ekatva*) and duality (*dvitva*). Furthermore, the expression "in one or two" (*ekadvayoḥ*) is a designation in which the number is the primary meaning.

For example: "dvayekakayordvivacanaikavacane" (Pāṇini 1.4.22), which means [the dual and singular endings are used] for the states of duality and unity; the meaning of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is "presentation" (*pratipādana*).
The word "must be done" (*kartavyam*) is to be supplied. In this regard, the presentation is as follows: "vā yau" (Pāṇini 2.4.57).

Therefore, by the maxim of the frog’s leap (*maṇḍūkaplutinyāya*), the word "optionally" (*vā*) is carried over. Alternatively, the particle *ca* is used here for the purpose of including what has not been explicitly stated. By this, the elision of the genitive case occurs after *yañ* and other suffixes when one or two [members] form a *tatpuruṣa* compound. If, however, "optionally" (*vā*) is carried over, then [the elision occurs] even when there are many [members].
There might be an alternative interpretation. However, there is no fault, as it will not occur due to the understanding of the established option (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*).

Regarding the example "Āṅgakula": here, the suffix *aṇ* is applied after the word *aṅga* with the designation of *tadrāja*; and that [suffix] does not begin with *yañ*, because in this section, those beginning with *yañ* are mentioned prior to it.
Regarding "upagārgyam": this is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule "an indeclinable [preceded by] a case-ending" (2.1.6).
Regarding "paramagārgyaḥ": this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound of two words ending in the nominative case according to the rule "san, mahat, etc. (2.1.61).

65. *Atribhṛgukutsavasiṣṭhagotamāṅgirobhyaśca* (Pāṇini 2.4.65). The printed reading is *ṭhpātreyyaḥ*, but it should be *āttreyaḥ*. [The suffix] *ṅīp* is applied by [the rule] *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15).

66. *bahvaca iñaḥ prācyabharateṣu* (2.4.66). Regarding "Bharatas": those for whom Bharata was the original name-giver are the Bharatas. In examples such as "Pannāgāras" and so forth, the suffix *iñ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.95] *ata iñ*, and there is its elision (*luk*). "Bālākayas."

The suffix *iñ* is applied because [the word *hastin*] belongs to the *bāhv-ādi* group. Regarding "ṭhhāstidāsayaḥ": [the suffix] *iñ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.95], *ata iñ*. Regarding "ārjunāyanaḥ": the suffix *phak* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.101], *yañiñośca*.

67. *Na gopavanādibhyaḥ* (2.4.67). This indicates that since this is a sub-group (*antaḥgaṇa*) within the *vidādi* group, the elision (*luk*) [of the suffix] would otherwise apply. For example, in the case of *śai-gravāḥ*, the rule *orguṇaḥ* (6.4.146) applies. Now, one might object: "But aren't other names such as *harita* and others also recited here?"

To determine what those [remaining ones] are, he says: "of the remaining," and so forth. "A faulty reading" means a reading that is not of Vedic (authoritative) origin. If they are of faulty reading, then, because they do not begin with the prefix *ava*, the suffix *añ* would not apply to them; therefore, he says: "for they..."

And so forth. For since these [names] are recited in the fourth chapter among the Bidādis, immediately after Gopavana and the others, this undesirable consequence does not arise. As for their placement here after the eight [names] beginning with Gopavana, that is said to be a reading resulting from error.

68. *tikakitavādibhyo dvandve* | (2.4.68) But for what purpose is the group (*gaṇa*) indicated by the two [names] *tika* and *kitava*, rather than being indicated by one alone? This is not so; for it is appropriate that the group be indicated by the member that undergoes the grammatical operation (*kāryin*).
And here a *dvandva* compound should be formed; it is appropriate to characterize [the subject] by that very [compound].

69. *upakādibhyo 'nyatarasyām advandve* (Pāṇini 2.4.68). If [the term] "advandve" is included even when [the rule] applies to a *dvandva*, then for what purpose is it stated? He says: "The mention of *advandve*" and so forth. In this mention of *dvandva*, the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of *dvandva* is not connected here—that is, [it does not apply] to a *dvandva*.

Regarding the phrase "the section on *dvandva*": when this is connected with the negative particle *nañ*, the cessation of the section on *dvandva* is understood. Now, why is it not understood that the mention of "not a *dvandva*" (*advandva*) is for the purpose of specifying the scope—namely, that [the rule applies] when it is not a *dvandva*, or when the subject matter concerns something other than a *dvandva*? If this were the intended meaning, the mention of "not a *dvandva*" would not have been made.
For the meaning is understood even without it. How so? Here, the *tikakitava* group and others are also recited as three:
*upakalamakāḥ*, *bhraṣṭakakapiṣ�ṭalāḥ*, and *kṛṣṇājinakṛṣṇasundarāḥ*.
And for these, the mention [in the rule] necessitates only a non-dvandva (non-compounded) form, not a dvandva (compound); this is established by the preceding rule alone.

Regarding the phrase "because it is established": since those [terms] are necessarily included for the sake of excluding *dvandva* compounds, it is logical that the inclusion of the others is also for the sake of excluding *dvandva* compounds due to their association with them;
thus, the explicit mention of "excluding *dvandva*" would be entirely redundant. Therefore...

This is stated for the purpose of terminating the jurisdiction of the rule concerning *dvandva* compounds; [the meaning is] that "for these, elision (*luk*) occurs invariably by the preceding rule. Otherwise, their inclusion in the *tikakitava* group would be purposeless. However, in the case of a non-*dvandva*, there is an option by this [present rule]; it should be understood that the elision (*luk*) is what is under discussion due to its being the subject at hand.
In that context, because the suffix *phak* is prescribed after the words beginning with *naḍa* (Pāṇini 4.1.99), there is an option regarding its elision (*luk*).

After those [words] preceding the word *kapiṣṭhala*, the suffix *iñ* applies. From the words *kapiṣṭhala* and *mayūrakarṇa* onwards, up to the group beginning with *śiva* (Pāṇini 4.1.112), the suffix *aṇ* applies. This continues until before the words beginning with *khārījaṅgha*.

From the word *kaṭheraṇi*, there is the suffix *iñ*. From the word *kaṭheraṇi*, the general suffix *aṇ* [would otherwise apply]. From the words beginning with *kuṣītaka* and ending with *kṛṣṇapiṅgala*, there is the suffix *iñ* after the suffix *at*. From the word *anuloma*, there is the suffix *iñ* belonging to the *bāhv-ādi* group; for the word *loman* is indeed recited among the *bāhv-ādi* group, and that [recitation] applies the rule of inclusion of what ends in that (*tadanta-vidhi*).
He causes [it] to be employed. That whose hairs follow [the grain] is *anuloma*;
its offspring is *ānulomayaḥ*, as in *ānulomānaḥ*. For the remaining [names], the suffix *iñ* is applied after the word *ataḥ*.

70. *Āgastyagauṇḍinyayoḥ agastiguṇḍinac* (Pāṇini 2.4.70). Although the genitive case is uttered after a word ending in a suffix, nevertheless, the elision (*luk*) is understood to apply to the suffix itself, not to that which ends in it; for the term "elision" (*luk*) refers to the non-appearance of a suffix.
Considering that the designation [of "Luk"] was prescribed for the base itself and not for its end, he says:

"In the case of *āgastya* and *kauṇḍinya*, regarding the secondary suffixes (*gotrapratyaya*) [that form them]. The two genitive cases here are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*). The meaning is: "regarding those two secondary suffixes which are constituent parts of *āgastya* and *kauṇḍinya*."
Showing those two conditions in their own form, he says: "After *yañ* and after *ṭhañ*.

Although the elision (*luk*) of *yañ* is already established, it is nevertheless prescribed again so that its replacement by *kuṇḍinaja* might not be understood as an annulment (*bādha*) of it. For the word *kuṇḍinī* has its middle syllable accented (*madhyodātta*).

In the case of *kuṇḍin*, when the suffix *ini* is applied by the rule *ṭhata iniṭhanau* (Pāṇini 5.2.115), the accent of the suffix would [normally] apply. If one were to argue that "the substitute (*ādeśa*) for that [original element] should likewise be so," then by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, the word would have the middle syllable as its udātta. However, because of the marker *c* [in the suffix], the middle-udātta status does not occur. For what purpose, then, [is this]?
He says "of those two," etc., to show that this substitution is not applied only when [the suffixes] are followed by other suffixes.

If this substitution were applied only when followed by other suffixes, then the prohibition "there is no elision (*aluk*) before a vowel (*aci*) in the case of a *gotra* [patronymic]" (Pāṇini 4.1.89) would be unnecessary; for that prohibition concerns the elision (*luk*), not the substitution.

In this case, there would indeed be the substitution [of *vṛddhi*], and consequently, by the rule "from what is not *vṛddha*, [the suffix] *aṇ*," only *aṇ* would apply; thus, the undesired form *āgastāḥ* would result. Even if the substitution of *vṛddhi* were to be included under the term "*vṛddha*" due to its status as a *sthānivat* (as if it were the original), the form would still be *āgastīyāḥ*, and *āgastīyāḥ* would not be established. Nor is it the case that...

The status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) is obtained; for the designation *vṛddha* is not a rule conditioned by an *al*-substitute. Here, however, when the suffix has undergone elision (*luk*), and after the substitute has been prescribed for what remains, the elision is prohibited by the rule *gotre 'lug aci* (4.1.89), the suffix *cha* becomes established by the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ* (4.2.114). In that regard, there is a distinction.
Even if the designation "vṛddha" were present, by the rule *kaṇvādibhyo gotre* (Pāṇini 4.2.111), the suffix *aṇ* would have to apply as an exception to *cha*;
thus, there is no difference in the case of Kauṇḍinya.
71. *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.71).

Regarding the phrase *dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*: if this were a locative (*saptamī*), then the meaning would be understood as follows: "of that case-ending which is proximate to both a verbal root (*dhātu*) and a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)."

[The word] *lugbhavati* [means] "there is elision. Furthermore, proximity (*sannikṛṣṭatva*) is not possible without contact (*upaśleṣa*); therefore, this would also apply here in the case of *vṛkṣaḥ plakṣaḥ*, for even here there is contact of the case-ending with the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Thinking that this genitive is thus appropriate, he says: *supo...* [elision of the case-ending].

"Of the case-ending, there is the designation 'root' (*dhātu-saṃjñā*)," and so forth. But how can a case-ending receive both the designation 'root' and the designation 'nominal stem' (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*)? To this he says: "Included within that," and so forth.
[Objection: Even so, the case-endings would merely be parts of the roots and nominal stems, and not...

Are they termed *dhātu*s, nor are they termed *prātipadika*s? There is no fault, for words that function with respect to wholes also apply to their parts. As in the example "putrīyati": [it means] "he desires a son for himself," by which [the rules] *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8) and *kyaci ca* (7.4.36) [apply].
Thus, there is the substitution of *it*; by the rule "those ending in *san* and so forth are verbal roots" (Pāṇini 3.1.32), they receive the designation of verbal root (*dhātu*).

Since that [designation] is prescribed after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) in the case of the suffix *kyac*, it applies only to that which already possesses a case-suffix; therefore, in this instance, the case-ending is included within the verbal root. For example: *kaṣṭaśritaḥ* ("one who has resorted to hardship"). [This is analyzed as: *kaṣṭaṃ śritaḥ*.

The compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.24] *dvitīyā śrita* etc.; the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is applied by [Pāṇini 1.2.46] *kṛttaddhitasamāsāśca*. Since that [designation] applies to a compound consisting of words ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*), it occurs only for that which possesses the case-suffix (*sasupka*). Therefore, here too, the case-suffix has departed from the end of the nominal stem.

It occurs as follows: in cases such as *vṛkṣaḥ* and *plakṣaḥ*, because the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is prohibited by the rule "that which lacks an affix" (*apratyaya*), there is no designation of a nominal stem for the form including the case-ending; thus, the case-ending is not included within the nominal stem.
72. *Adiprabhṛtibhyaḥ śapaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.72).

73. *Bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 2.4.73). Regarding the form *trādhvam*: it is derived from the root *traiṅ* "to protect" (Dhātupāṭha 965), belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa*, in the imperative (*loṭ*) mood.
There is the substitution of *dhma*, the substitution of *et* for *ṭe*, and the substitution of *ām* by the rule "ṭhsavābhyām vāmau" (Pāṇini 7.1.27).

74. *yaṅe'ci ca* (2.4.74). [The commentary says: "When the suffix *ṭhac* follows. The mention of the term *pratyaya* (suffix) is for the purpose of demonstrating that *aci* here does not refer to the *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated class name) *ac*. For if the intention were to refer to the *pratyāhāra*, then [the rule would have been stated as] *aṇi*.

One should perform [the operation] by means of the letter *ṇ* alone; for the intention is that no vowels other than *a* can follow after a suffix beginning with *yaṅ*. This very mention of *ac* (vowel) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that all verbal roots fall within the *pac-ādi* group. [The example is] "loluvaḥ" [from the rule] "dhātor ekāco halādeḥ... [Pāṇini 3.1.22].

The suffix *yaṅ* is applied by the rule *kriyāsamabhihāre* (3.1.22); reduplication occurs by the rule *sanyaṅeḥ* (6.1.9); and the *guṇa* substitution is applied by the rule *guṇo yaṅlukoḥ* (7.4.82). When the form *lolūya* is established, the *pacādyac* suffix is added, the *yaṅ* is elided (*luk*), and [the prohibition of *guṇa*] is applied by the rule *na dhātulopa* (1.1.4), etc.

This is a negation of the [addition of] a suffixal *guṇa*. The substitution of *uvaṅ* occurs by the rule "ṭhaci śnudhātu" (Pāṇini 6.4.77), as in the examples "sanīsraṃsaḥ" and "danīdhvaṃsaḥ. The roots √*sraṃsu* and √*dhvaṃsu* mean "to fall down" (Dhātupāṭha 754, 755). The operations pertaining to the *yaṅ* affix apply as before; however, this does not take place because of the prohibition stated in "na lumatāṅgasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.63).

By the rule *pratyayalakṣaṇena ṭhaniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24), the elision of the nasal does not occur. By the rule *nīgvañcu* (Pāṇini 7.4.84), the augment *nīg* is added to the reduplicated syllable. Regarding the forms *lālapīti* and *vāvadīti*, the rule *dīrgho'kitaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.83) applies to the roots *lap* and *vad*.
Thus, there is lengthening of the vowel due to repetition; [the augment] *iṭ* is optionally applied by the rule "ṭhyaṅe vā" (Pāṇini 7.3.94).

75. *Ślu* is substituted for [the suffixes] beginning with *juhoty-ādi*. (Pāṇini 2.4.75) The term *śap* is understood here, not *yaṅ*; this is because it is specifically declared that *śap* alone possesses the svarita accent.
Regarding *juhoti*: by the rule *ślau* (6.1.10), reduplication occurs. Regarding *bibharti*: by the rule *uraṅ*... [etc.]

(7.4.66) there is the substitution of *i*. (7.4.60) there is the addition of *r* as a subsequent element (*raparatva*). (7.4.76) there is the substitution of *i* by [the rule] "of *bhṛñ*, etc. (*bhṛñām it*). [The form] "nenekti" is derived from the root *ṇijir* (DhP 1093) meaning "purification and nourishment.
By (7.4.75) "there is guna for the three roots beginning with *nij*" (*nijām trayāṇām guṇaḥ*), and by (6.1.10) "in the case of *ślau*" (*ślau*), there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*).

76. *Bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 2.4.76). Regarding the forms *dāti* and *dhāti*: although the reduplication (*ślau*) [of the root] would have been required by the preceding rule for the roots *dadāti* and *dadhati*, it is here prohibited *bahulam* (in many cases). There is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix. Regarding the form *vivaṣṭi*: [the root is] *vaśa* in the sense of "desire."

From the *Dhātupāṭha* (1080), since it belongs to the *adādi* class, the *śap* affix would normally be elided (*luk*), but here *ślu* is applied instead. By the rule *ślau* (6.1.10), reduplication occurs. While the rule *bhṛñām it* (7.4.76) is still in force, the substitution of *i* for the radical vowel is applied by *bahulaṃ chandasi* (7.4.78). Then, by the rule *vraścādi* (8.2.36), the substitution of *ṣ* occurs. [The resulting form is] *ṣṭuanā*.

The substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭu* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.4.41]. Regarding the term "vibhakti": the root *bhaj* in the sense of "service" (*sevā*) belongs to the *bhvādi* class; there is *ślu* replacement for *śap*, the substitution of *it* as before, and the substitution of *ku* for *cu* by [Pāṇini 8.2.30]. The reading "vivakti" occurs in some places; that [is derived from] the root *vac*.
It should be understood that this [suffix] belongs to the root *paribhāṣ* (DhP 1063), which belongs to the first class (*adādi*).

77. *gatisthāghupābhūbhyaḥ sicaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (Pāṇini 1.2.17). Regarding *agāt*: the substitution of *gā* [for *iṇ*] is by the rule *imo gā luṅi* (1.2.13). Regarding *apāt*: the root is *pā pāne* (Dhātupāṭha 925). Regarding *abhūt*: [the substitution of *bhū* for *as*] is by the rule *bhūsuvostiṅi* (6.4.88).
The negation of qualities.

Regarding the statement, "In the mention of *gā*, there is the mention of both *iṇ* and *piv*": first, it is understood from the very form *gāti* that there is a mention of the substitute *iṇ*, because of its indication by means of the *śtip* affix.

For an indication made with *śtip* is intended to signify that which is devoid of a verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*), so that there may be a mention of only that which has its suffix elided (*lug-vikaraṇa*).
It should be so; for otherwise, if the intention were to include the root *gā*, one would have simply said *gā*.

If that is the case, then by the rule "In the inclusion of *gam* and *ād* roots, there is no distinction" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 124), both will be included; what then is the purpose of the mention using the *śtip* affix? Therefore, this [mention] alone—

The mention of *śtip* indicates that this refers only to the substitute [of the root *pā*], and not to the root *gā*. Furthermore, regarding the mention of *pā*, it follows the principle that "between a root with a *luk*-suffix and one with a non-*luk*-suffix, only the one with the non-*luk*-suffix is taken" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 50). Thus, it refers specifically to the root *pibati*.
By this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), it is understood that [the form] is *aghāsīt*. [The roots] *kai* and *gai* mean "to sound" (*śabde*; DhP 916, 917).

By the rule *yamaramanamātāṃ sak ca* (7.2.73), there is the augment *sak*. Then there is the suffix *sic*, and the augment *iṭ*. By the rule *astisico 'pṛkte* (7.3.96), there is *iṭ*. [And finally, by] *iṭa īṭi* (8.2.28) [there is the elision of the preceding *iṭ*].
Thus, there is the elision of *sic*. Regarding "apāsīt": the root *pā* meaning "to protect" (DhP 1056) undergoes the same operations as before, such as the addition of *sa*.
Regarding "āgāsātām": this is the Ātmanepada for the object (*karman*). [The suffix] *ātām*—but for what purpose [is it used]?

Why is it stated as *sico luk* rather than simply *leḥ*? Does this not achieve the same purpose, such that the mention of *li* need not be made in the subsequent rule? This is not so; for if *luk* were understood here as applying to *li*, then in the case of *mā hi gātām*, the rule *thādiḥ sico 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.1.187) would apply.

Otherwise, the accentuation beginning with this [rule] would not be established, for that [accent] is udātta. Furthermore, in the case of *aguh*, the substitution of *jus* for *jhi*—as prescribed by Pāṇini 3.4.110 (*ātaḥ*) and 3.4.109 (*sijabhyastavidibhyaśca*)—would not be established. Therefore, the elision (*luk*) must be stated to apply specifically to *sic*.

78. *vibhāṣā ghrā-dheṭ-śā-chā-saḥ* | (Pāṇini 2.4.78) The roots are: *ghrā* "to smell" (Dhātupāṭha 926), *dheṭ* "to drink" (Dhātupāṭha 902), *śo* "to sharpen/thin" (Dhātupāṭha 1145), and *chā* "to cut" (Dhātupāṭha 1146).

The root *ṣo* is used in the sense of "concluding an action" (*antakarman*) [DhP 1147]. Regarding the statement "since *dheṭ* would necessarily [be subject] to the previous [rule]," this is because it bears the technical designation *ghu*. In the alternative where elision (*luk*) does not occur, the operations such as the insertion of *s* and so forth are applied as before. The mention of *dheṭ* with its *anubandha* is for the purpose of excluding the root *dhā*. If [the suffix] *kṛt* has been added after [the vowel] *ā*.
If it were so specified, then there would also be the inclusion of the root *dhā*; thus [the rule] "ṭhadhrāsātām" applies the ātmanepada when the object is the agent.

79. *tanādibhyas tathāsoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.79). [The form] *tatata* is derived as follows: the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *svaritañitaḥ* (1.3.72). The elision of the nasal [of the suffix *an*] occurs by the rule *anudātopadeśa...* (6.4.37), etc. [Thus we have] *ataniṣṭa*.
"Yayam" is the second person plural ending.

80. *mantre ghasahvaraṇaśavṛdahādṛcchṛkṛgamijanibhyo leḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.80). While the term *sicaḥ* is understood [from the previous rule], the re-mention of *liḥ* is for the purpose of excluding the operations of *sic*, such as those prescribed by *ādiḥ sico 'nyatarasyām* (6.1.187), and for the sake of subsequent rules. [Example: *aghakṣan*.

Thus: from the root *ad* in the sense of "eating" (*bhakṣaṇe*, Dhātupāṭha 1011), the *luṅ* suffix is applied; by the rule *luṅsanorghaslṛ* (Pāṇini 2.4.37), there is the substitution of *ghaslṛ*. Then, by the rule *cli luṅ* (3.1.43), the *cli* suffix is added, which is elided by this [present rule]; the *jhi* suffix is replaced by *anta*; by the rule *itaśca* (3.4.100), the initial *ik* vowel is dropped; and [finally] by the rule *saṃyogāntasya*...

(8.2.23) thus there is the elision of the letter *t*; by the rule "gamahana" (6.4.98) and others, there is the elision of the penultimate vowel; by "śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca" (8.3.60), there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*; by "jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi" (8.4.53), there is the substitution of a *jaś* sound; and by "khari ca" (8.4.55), there is the substitution of a *car* sound.

The word *hvaret* is an indication by means of an adventitious form [of the verb root]. In the form *mā hvaḥ*, there is the *luṅ* suffix; the substitution of *tiṅ* [for the verbal ending], the replacement by *ra* (*raparatvam*), the elision of the consonant by rule 6.1.68 (*halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*); and the absence of the augment *aṭ* by rule 6.4.74 (*na māṅyoge*). In the form *prāṇaṭ*, [the root is] *ṇaś* in the sense of "disappearance" (*adarśane*) [Dhātupāṭha 1194].
The operations of the *luṅ* and other tenses proceed as before. By the rule *vraścādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 8.2.36), there is the substitution of *ṣ*.

Then, by the rule *jhalāṃ jaśo'nte* (8.2.39), there is the substitution of a *jaś* sound—specifically, the *ḍa* for the *ṣ*. For that *ḍ*, by the rule *vāvasāne* (8.4.56), there is the substitution of a *car* sound—specifically, the *ṭa*. [And finally,] by the rule *upasargādasamāse'pi* (8.4.14).

[The substitution of] *ṇ* [for *n*]. In some places, the reading is *ṭh prāṇag*. In that case, while *kuḥ* is being carried over from "kvip-pratyayasya kuḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.62), the substitution of *k* [for *n*] occurs by "naśervā" (8.2.63). Regarding "āvaḥ": [from the root] *vṛñ*, there is the suffix *tip*; [then] *guṇa* [substitution], followed by *raparatva* [of the vowel *ṛ*]; [finally, the elision of the *ti* ending] by "halṅyādi" (6.1.68).
The suffix *sip* is elided. Regarding the form *dhak*: [it is derived from] the root *daha* in the sense of "reducing to ashes" (*dhā.pā.* 911).

The suffix *sip* is elided by *halṅyādinā* (Pāṇini 6.1.68). By the rule *dāderdhātorghaḥ* (8.2.32), the *h* is replaced by *gh*. Then, by the rule *ekāco baśo bhaṣ* (8.2.37), etc., [the substitution of *jhal* for *jaś* follows].

The letter *da* becomes *dha*; for *dha*, there is the substitution of the *jaś*-class (*jaśtva*), resulting in *ga*; for that, there is the substitution of the *car*-class (*cartva*), resulting in *ka*. Regarding the augment *āṭ*, there is a prohibition by the rule "In the Veda, *āṭ* is generally [not applied] even when not joined with *mā*" (Pāṇini 6.4.75). [The form] "āprāt" is derived from the root *prā* (meaning "to fill," Dhātupāṭha 1061) with the suffix *tip*.

Regarding the form *parāvark*: the suffix *tip* is added to the root *vṛj*; there is the guṇa substitution for the light penultimate vowel; then, by *halṅyādinā* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), there is elision [of the *tip*].
Due to the restriction *rātsasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.24), there is no elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*).
As before, the *j* undergoes *kutva* to become *g*, and that *g* undergoes *cartva* to become *k*. Thus: *akran*.

Thus: for the root *kṛ*, there is the substitution of *ant* for the suffix *jhi*; then the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*). Regarding "ajñata": for the suffix *jha* of the root *jan*, there is the substitution of *at* by the rule "ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.5); as before, there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*), and then the substitution of *ścu* for *st* by the rule "stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.40). In some places, it is written as "ajñan."

The reading: "In that case, [the suffix] *jhi* [is used], and from that, the *parasmaipada* should be applied; this is the usage in the Brāhmaṇa. That which was mentioned immediately after regarding the root *jan* in the Mantra is the Brāhmaṇa, a text consisting of explanations of the Mantras.
Since the elision (*luk*) of *jan* is observed in the Mantra, an example pertaining to that [Mantra] has not been presented here.
If, then, elision occurs even when there is no mantra, for what purpose is the mention of "mantra"? To this he says: "The mention of 'mantra'," and so forth.

81. *āmaḥ* | (Pāṇini 2.4.81) [The example is] *īhāñcakre*. [The root] *īh* is used in the sense of "exertion" (*ceṣṭāyām*) [Dhātupāṭha 632]. [The suffix] *liṭ* [is applied], and by the rule *ijādeśca* (3.1.36), etc., the suffix *ām* is added. Because that [suffix] ends in *m*, it is a *kṛt* ending; therefore, [the preceding element] is a *kṛdanta*.

The designation *prātipadika* [is applied]; the suffix *su* [is added]; because of its inclusion in the list beginning with *svar*, the status of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is established; by the rule "after an indeclinable, the suffixes *āp* and *sup* are elided" (Pāṇini 2.4.82), there is the elision of *su*; by the rule "and after the root *kṛ*" (Pāṇini 3.1.40), there is the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of the root *kṛ* following the perfect tense (*liṭ*); and by the rule "like that which has the suffix *ām*" (Pāṇini 1.3.63).

By [the rule] beginning with "ityādinā," the *ātmanepada* affix is applied; from that, the substitution of *eś* occurs, followed by reduplication and the operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
Then, the *anusvāra* replaces the *m* of *ām*, according to the rule "an usvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.58).
Now, why does this not occur here in *jagāma* and *śaśāma*? Because the term *ām* is understood in its meaningful form (*arthavat*), and this [term *ām*] is not present there.

And because [the suffix] would otherwise be meaningless; however, the suffix *ṭhañ* is meaningful, according to the principle that "suffixes whose meaning is not specifically stated apply in their own sense" (*pu.pa.pā.* 90). Why, then, does [the suffix] not apply here to form *āmroga*?
[Because of the rule: "Between a term defined by a general grammatical rule and one stated as a specific word-form, only the specifically stated one is to be understood."
But this [is not so], because it is based on a secondary figurative sense (lākṣaṇika).

82. *avyayād up-supaḥ* | (2.4.82) [Example: *tatra śālāyām*. From the word *tat*, the seventh case suffix *tral* is added. By the rule *prāg-diśo vibhaktiḥ* (5.3.1), it receives the technical designation *vibhakti* (case ending). Then, by the rule for *tyadādi-ātva* (substitution of *a* for the final vowel of *tyadādi* pronouns), and the addition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*: *tad + tral* → *tad + tra* (by *tyadādyatva*) → *tad + ā* (by *ṭāp*) → *tadā* (by *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*). Then, by the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ* (2.4.82), the case endings (*sup*) following the indeclinable (*avyaya*) are elided. Thus, *tadā* remains as an indeclinable. [Note: The example provided in the source text appears to be a commentary on the formation of the indeclinable *tadā* from *tat*.]

The substitution of the masculine form [of the stem] occurs by the rule *ṭhāṭasilādiṣvākṛtvasucaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.35). By the rule *taddhitaścāsarvavibhaktiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.38), the suffix *tral* is designated as an indeclinable (*avyaya*), and consequently, there is elision (*luk*) of the feminine suffix *ṭāp* produced from it. But how can the suffix *ṭāp* be produced from an indeclinable? It is produced by the rule *ajādyataṣṭāp* (Pāṇini 4.1.4).
If this is argued, [we reply: no, because the suffix *ṭāp* is prescribed for feminine nouns (*strī*), and an indeclinable (*avyaya*) lacks gender.

Therefore, since the occurrence of *ṭāp* after an indeclinable is impossible, is not the rule for the elision (*luk*) of *ṭāp* after an indeclinable redundant? It is not redundant; the term "in the feminine" (*striyām*, Pāṇini 4.1.3) refers primarily to that which possesses the quality (*guṇin*).

The suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth apply to a thing (*padārtha*) that possesses femininity (*strītva*). And in this case, within the thing expressed by the word *śālāyām* (in the hall), the indeclinable *tatra* (there) occurs as possessing femininity.
Although here femininity is the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), nevertheless, precisely because it is the meaning of the sentence, the feminine suffix [is applied].

It is illuminated [by this]: when a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) is present, the very meaning of the word becomes feminine; therefore, the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṭāp* must be stated. As in "having done" (*kṛtvā*), "having taken" (*hṛtvā*). By the rule "the suffixes *ktvā*, *tosun*, and *kasun* [are indeclinables]" (Pāṇini 1.1.40), the suffix *ktvā* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*); consequently, there is elision of the case-ending (*sup*) produced after it. By what?
If it is argued that the correct production [of the suffixes] after *puru* occurs by means of the rule *svādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.2), we say no; because in that context,
since the *svādi* suffixes are restricted by their syntactic unity with another grammatical treatise beginning with *bahuṣu bahuvacanam* (Pāṇini 1.4.21), [the suffixes would not apply].

And because indeclinables (*avyaya*) are innumerable. It might be argued: "Wherever number exists, the rules beginning with *bahuṣu bahuvacanam* (Pāṇini 1.4.21) establish the case-endings (*svādi*) and so forth; however, since indeclinables are devoid of number, the case-endings (*svādi*), which are prescribed by general rules, certainly exist for them. This is incorrect.
For, by the rule *svādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 4.1.2), since the suffixes beginning with *su* are prescribed in syntactic unity with other rules of the science such as *bahuṣu bahuvacanam* (1.4.21),
it is stated therein: "Number, object, and so forth are the meanings of the *svādi* suffixes, as ordained by another rule of the science."

Therefore, this [rule] forms a single syntactical unit (ekavākyatā) with that [preceding rule]. And if there were a single syntactical unit, how could there be a general prescription of *svādi* suffixes? For there is no other rule by which *svādi* suffixes are prescribed in a general sense. If this is so, then this very statement regarding the elision (*luk*) of the *sup* suffix produced after an indeclinable (*avyaya*) serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*).

"The case endings beginning with *su* (the nominative) occur due to the presence of an inflectional base (*pratyaya*). For it is not possible for elision (*luk*) to apply to that which has not yet arisen.
Keeping this very point in mind, it was stated: "But from indeclinables (*avyaya*), which lack number, the case endings beginning with *su*, prescribed by general rules, certainly exist."

83. *Nāvyayībhāvād ato 'matvapañcamyāḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.83). When this [prohibition] has been negated, there is indeed the hearing (i.e., the occurrence) of the ablative case. How so? Because two meanings are prescribed here, and in the prescriptive rule (*vidhāyaka-vākya*) there are exactly two [meanings]. In that regard:
The rule "ṭhnāvyayībhāvādataḥ" is one sentence that prescribes the aforementioned prohibition;

the rule "am tvapañcamyāḥ" is a second sentence that prescribes the substitution of *am*, and in that context, it requires the reference to "ataḥ" (from [an avyayībhāva] ending in *a*). For this very reason, two sentences are presented in the Vṛtti.
"‘There is no elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) following an avayavībhāva compound ending in *ṭha*’—this is one sentence;

‘but for that [compound], there is the substitution of *am*, except in the case of the fifth [case-ending]’—this is the second. In this regard, by the phrase ‘except in the case of the fifth,’ the rule is either an injunction or a prohibition of what immediately precedes” (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 19).

Only the substitution of *am* for the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is prohibited here, but not the elision (*aluk*) which was prescribed by the preceding rule. For this very reason, when there is no elision, the ablative case ending itself is heard. This is because, if there were a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*), two operations would be enjoined through a single recitation of the rule.

There would be a prohibition [of the elision] for the two operations [substitution of *am* and *su*] when not followed by the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*). This means that these two operations are to be understood as occurring with the exception of the fifth case ending. However, in the case of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), the phrase "not followed by the fifth case ending" refers to the immediately preceding substitution of *am*, and not to the non-elision (*aluk*) prescribed in another rule.

Being connected with the phrase "except for the fifth" (*tenāpañcamyāḥ*) and being prescribed in a general sense, the absence of elision (*aluk*) extends even to the fifth case; therefore, the actual hearing of the fifth case ending is indeed appropriate.
This same point is also obtained by means of the word "but" (*tu*).

But surely, grammatical factors (*kāraka*) belong to an action (*kriyā*), and it has been stated that an *avyayībhāva* compound is dominated by the meaning of the first member; since the meaning of the first member is a non-substantial entity (*asatvabhūta*), it lacks a connection with an action in the absence of such an action, and thus it cannot possess the status of an ablative (*apādāna*) or other *kārakas*. Therefore, how could [an ablative case] arise from an *avyayībhāva*?
Would there be the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) and so forth? This is not so;

for even when the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapada*) is predominant, its connection with the action is possible by depending on the subordinate meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), as in the expression "bring five bundles" (*pañcapūlīm ānaya*). In that case, although the abstract state (*bhāva*) is predominant, it is subordinate...
The connection with action depends upon a substance.

84. *Tṛtīyāsaptamyorbahulam* (2.4.84). Regarding *sumadram*: by the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti-* (2.1.6) and so forth, this is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of abundance (*samṛddhi*). Regarding *unmatagaṅgam*: [this is an *avyayībhāva*] in the sense of another word-meaning (*anyapadārtha*).
By the rule "in the sense of a name" (2.1.21), [we have] "the twenty-one Bhāradvājas. By the rule "a numeral with a word denoting lineage" (2.1.19), [we have the same].
85. *luṭaḥ prathamasya ḍāraurasaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.85).

"The substitutes *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* occur respectively for the first persons of both the *parasmaipada* and the *ātmanepada*. If this is so, then in the *parasmaipada*, [the first persons] are *tip*, *tas*, and *jhi*.
In each case, there is the designation of the first person (*prathamapuruṣa*); likewise, among the *ātmanepada* endings, there are the designations *ta*, *ātām*, and *jha*.

Since there are six substituends (*sthānin*) and only three substitutes (*ādeśa*), there is a numerical disparity; consequently, because there is no one-to-one correspondence (*anudeśa*), would it not follow that all the substitutes would apply to each [substituend] in turn? This is not so.
There is a fault; for the determination [of the replacement] would be based on immediate sequence (*ānantarya*).

And that immediate sequence is determined by the meaning: "that which has a single meaning replaces that which has a single meaning, that which has two meanings replaces that which has two meanings, and that which has many meanings replaces that which has many meanings. [In the word] *kartā*: [the suffix] *luṭ* is applied by *anadyatane luṭ* (Pāṇini 3.3.15); [then] *tip*.

Because this [suffix] has multiple phonemes (*anekāl*), the element *ḍā* is a substitute for the whole [stem]. Now, one might object: "But surely, a status of having multiple phonemes is not caused by an indicatory letter (*anubandha*)," as stated in the Vārttika (Vyā.pa. 14); and since the letter *ḍ* is an indicatory letter, how can there be a status of having multiple phonemes such that it would be a substitute for the whole? This is not a fault; for [the rule does not apply] when [the suffix] has not yet been applied...

By the rule *sarvādeśe ṭhcuṭū* (Pāṇini 1.3.7), the designation *it* is applied. In the absence of the *it*-designation, it would not be an *anubandha*; however, because it possesses multiple phonemes (*anekāl*), it becomes a substitute for the whole.
By the rule *ḍityabhasyāpi ṭeḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.143), there is elision of the final syllable (*ṭilopa*). Thus: *kartārau*, *kartāraḥ*.

Thus, by the rule *trica* (Pāṇini 7.4.51), there is the elision of the letter *s*. In this way, forms such as *adhyetu* and others belong to the root *iṅ* in the sense of "studying" (Dhātupāṭha 1046). Here, even though the substitution of *e* for the final vowel (*ṭeretvam*) would apply later, the substitutions beginning with *ḍā* (i.e., *ḍu*, *ḍa*, etc. take effect first because they are *antaraṅga* (internal/within-reach). This *antaraṅga* status [is due to their being dependent on fewer causes].

Furthermore, because those [suffixes] depend solely upon the substituendum (*sthānin*), whereas the substitution of *et* for *ṭi* is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*); for that depends not only on the substituendum but also on the verbal root (*dhātu*), since the term "of the verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) is governed [as an adhikāra] up until the end of the third chapter.

The rule *ṭhthāsaḥ se* (Pāṇini 3.4.80) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the substitution of *e* for the final *ṭi* does not apply to the substitutes *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras*. Consequently, even when these substitutes have been applied, the substitution of *e* does not occur. Thus, in the form *kartāsi*, there is the elision of the *s* by the rule *tāsastyorlopaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.50).
Thus ends the second chapter of the *Kāśikāvivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who was a disciple of the Bodhisattvas.
The fourth quarter is completed, and this second chapter is finished.
Composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who was a teacher of the Bodhisattvas;
also known by the alternative title *Nyāsa*.
The Commentary on the Kāśikā, known as the Kāśikāvivaraṇapañjikā; the Third Chapter.
First Pāda:
1. *Pratyaya* | (3.1.1) "The word *pratyaya* is introduced as a technical term (*saṃjñā*)," for the sake of brevity in the treatise. If...

If, by taking each individual technical term (*saṃjñin*)—such as the *san* suffix, the *kyac* suffix, and the *kyaṅ* suffix—one were to prescribe their designation as "suffix" (*pratyaya*) through numerous separate rules, then there would be prolixity (*gaurava*) in the treatise, because of the great number of those technical terms. For indeed, they are many. Not [only] them...

There exists such a commonality (*sāmānya*) that is undifferentiated, by resorting to which a single name may be prescribed for many, as in: "That whose first vowel among its vowels is *vṛddhi* is called *vṛddha*" (Pāṇini 1.1.73).
Now, is there not such a commonality as "existence" (*sat*), and thus the sūtra might be formulated as follows: [“That which is existent is *vṛddha*”]?

Regarding the expression "with the suffix *sap*," is the mention of the *sa-pratyāhāra* intended to include everything starting from the *s* of *san* up to the *p* of *kap*? This is not the case; for there are many other *p*s as well, such as in "the suffix *sip* is variously applied in the *leṭ*" (3.1.34) and "after the root *vad*, the suffix *kyap* is also applied before *sup*" (3.1.106).

Regarding these and other such cases: if, in that context, the letter *p* immediately following [the *k*] is taken for the purpose of the pratyāhāra by relying on proximity (*pratyāsatti*), then the pratyāhāra would be understood as consisting of *si* and *p* alone. Alternatively, if pervasion (*vyāpti*) is intended, then [the rule] "taptanaptanāthanāśca" (Pāṇini 7.1.45) [would apply].
The *tanap* suffix would indeed occur with the letter *p*. This might be argued: "One must rely on the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*) itself.

And the inclusion of the *tanap* suffix by means of the letter *p* will not be for the purpose of forming a *pratyāhāra*, but rather for the sake of *kap* itself, because of the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the rule: 'And after a monosyllabic root ending in *i*, there is the suffix *am*, as if it were a *pratyaya*' (Pāṇini 6.3.68)."

Otherwise, since the technical designation *pratyaya* (suffix) would apply even in the case of the sixth [case-ending], this [rule] would be purposeless? This is not so; for a rule serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) only when there is no other purpose, yet there is indeed a purpose for this: namely, that it should apply specifically in connection with the suffix *am*.

This [rule] would be for the purpose of restriction so that [the substitution] does not depend solely on the presence of the *pratyaya* (suffix); how then could it be redundant? Furthermore, even if the *kapa* were somehow obtainable through the *pratyāhāra* formed by the letter *pa*, there would still be an excessive burden of comprehension (*pratipatti-gaurava*). Therefore, for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*), this is established by means of an *adhikāra* (governing heading).

Thinking that it is appropriate to establish a technical name (saṃjñā), he says: "The word *pratyaya* is designated as a technical term. If this is so, then it must apply to every individual instance [of a suffix]; and since it applies there, it would connect only with the initial elements [the roots], and not with the bases (*prakṛti*) and so forth.

There is no restrictive cause [for this]. Therefore, this designation would also apply to *prakṛti*, *upapada*, *upādhi*, *vikāra*, and *āgama*. Among these: *prakṛti*—as in "san after *gup*, *tij*, and *kit*" (Pāṇini 3.1.5);
*upapada*—as in "after *rami* and *japi* when followed by *stamba* and *karṇa*" (Pāṇini 3.2.13); *upādhi*—

Regarding the rule *ṭhharaterdatināthayoḥ paśau* (Pāṇini 3.2.25): although there is no purpose for a technical name (*saṃjñā*) whose meaning is "animal," nevertheless, since such a name exists for that which expresses it, it would indeed apply to it. An example of a *vikāra* (modification) is [the suffix] by *ṭhhanasta ca* (3.1.108); an example of an *āgama* (augment) is [the suffix] by *ṭhtrapujatunoḥ ṣuk* (4.3.138).
Furthermore, if these were designated as *pratyaya*s (suffixes), they would possess the quality of being subsequent (*para*) and their initial syllable would be udātta-accented.
Although it is impossible for *gup* and the others to be subsequent to one another, or for *san* and the others to be subsequent to them simultaneously,
nevertheless, this could occur alternately— such that at times *gup* and the others would be subsequent.

They might sometimes be *san* and so forth, or else *guṇa* and so forth occurring after something else from some other source; therefore, he says: "The base and the upapada," etc. And this has been stated precisely because it is established by logical necessity. How so? First, the conditions consisting of the base (*prakṛti*) and the upapada...
Since they are indicated by means of case endings such as the fifth (ablative) for the sake of establishing another's purpose,

their verbal form ending in the fifth or other case endings is unfit to convey the relationship between a name and the named. For instance, [it would lack] coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that which ends in the first case.

A relationship between a name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*) occurs where the named— having acquired the form of the name through the intellect and having entered into a relationship of non-difference such that "this is that"— is designated together with the name,
as in "vṛddhir ādaic" (Pāṇini 1.1.1); or where [the relationship occurs] with a word ending in the genitive case.

When there is a desire to express a distinction between the name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*), the named is indicated by means of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), which generates a sense of difference from the name-word being employed as its own form, as in: "A word's own form is [meant], except for technical grammatical terms" (Pāṇini 1.1.68).
However, since *prakṛti* and the others function by employing specific case endings suitable for assisting another,

it is impossible to establish a relationship of technical name (*saṃjñā*) with them. Nor can it be argued that a name will apply to them once one supplies an elliptical case ending suitable for the relationship between a name and its bearer.

It is appropriate to assume [this]. For when there is no room for the expression [of the rule], an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) is appropriate, but not when there is such room; and here there is room, namely the existence of the term *san* and so forth. Furthermore, because the *prakṛti* (base) and other elements are subordinate, the designation is inappropriate for them. In common worldly usage, the application of an operation is understood to apply to the principal element.
It is observed as follows: when many people are walking, someone asks, "Who is this who is going?

and he replies, "The king. In that case, both the one who asks and the one who answers have their conviction directed toward the principal person, the king. Therefore, here too, [the designation applies] to the principal element, such as the *sannanta* (desiderative) base.

Its designation will arise from the cognition of its function; furthermore, its primacy is due to its being enjoined as something previously unestablished. As for the roots and so forth, since their own forms are already determined through their recitation in the *Dhātu-pāṭha* and other lists, they lack primacy because they are merely employed for the sake of deriving meanings such as the desiderative (*saN*) and others. Therefore, how could that [primacy] belong to them?

Regarding the term *saṃjñā* (name/designation): although, in the case of both a technical name (*āgama*) and a modification (*vikāra*), the designation is expressed in the nominative case because it is fit for the relationship between a name and the named, and because it possesses primacy due to being that which is to be enjoined; nevertheless, it does not constitute a *saṃjñā*.
This is because the term *pratyaya* is made a "great" designation (*mahatī saṃjñā*). Of that...

The purpose of this is so that the designation may be significant according to its meaning: "that by which one perceives objects is a *pratyaya*. And one does not perceive any object through suffixes of modification (*vikāra*) or augments (*āgama*). If, then, this designation is to be significant according to its meaning, [how do you explain] *aveḥ kaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.28) and *yāvādibhyaḥ kan* (5.4.29)?

Thus, the designation of "suffix" (pratyaya) does not apply to these and similar items, because of the absence of meaning. For meaning is of two kinds: worldly and technical (śāstrīya). Of these, the former is understood through the word itself, while the latter is understood through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka); and that [technical meaning] is absent in those cases without the suffixes.
Is it because that meaning is understood from the *prakṛti* itself? This is not a fault;

for even if their meaning is not fully grasped through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), nevertheless, "suffixes whose meaning is not explicitly stated express their own inherent meaning" (Puṇyarāja 90).

This is understood precisely from this authoritative statement (āptavacana). Therefore, since they too convey their own meaning, they are also suffixes (*pratyaya*); thus, this over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is refuted. This is established:
the designation "suffix" does not apply to *prakṛti* and the other elements. [Examples: *kartavyam*, *karaṇīyam*.

When suffixes such as *tavyat* and others receive the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "suffix" (*pratyaya*), the designation "stem" (*aṅga*) applies to that which precedes them, according to the rule *Pāṇini 1.4.13*: "That [element] from which a suffix is prescribed [is called a stem]. Now, why is it that immediately after this, bypassing the *sann* and other [affixes], only the *tavyat* and others—which are separated [from the root by intervening elements]—are cited? In that regard, even for those beginning with the acute-accented (*udātta*) [suffixes]...

Because the operation conditioned by the designation *pratyaya* (suffix) is possible [in those cases]; however, that is not possible in the case of *san* and so forth, because it is already superseded by the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*).

The word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "this is also an *adhikāra*" means that it is not merely a suffix (*pratyaya*). The expression "it stands [in force] in every connection" (*yoge yoge upatiṣṭhate*) demonstrates the distinction between a *paribhāṣā* and an *adhikāra*.

For a *paribhāṣā* (technical rule) operates throughout the entire treatise while remaining in only one location; it does not, however, appear at every individual application (*pratiyoga*). By saying "or it is a *paribhāṣā*," he shows another alternative view.
That a single part operates throughout the entire treatise is the characteristic of a *paribhāṣā*, which [is] not present in the *vṛtti*.

It has been shown; for [the distinction] is understood by way of demonstrating the governing rules (*adhikāra-dharma*).
