For if a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) were to apply itself to the actual performance [of an operation] and thereby function toward the accomplishment of the result, then there would be no difference between a governing rule and a technical rule; and thus, in this case, those two—

The separate mention [of the two] would be fruitless. This technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) possesses an indicative mark (*liṅga*), and its indicative mark is indeed the designation "affix" (*pratyaya*). The phrase "or of a root" (*dhātoḥ vā*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for a base (*prakṛti*) that expresses action; by this, even that which ends in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) is included. That too—

Because action is predominant, it can be designated as "denoting action. For designations are made according to what is predominant, as in the case of [the term] *rājadhānī* ("royal residence"). Regarding the phrase "or from a nominal stem" (*prātipadikād vā*), this is an elliptical expression for a base that does not denote action; by this, feminine suffixes in *-ī* and *-ā* are also included.

Regarding the term *taittirīyam*: the suffix *chaṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.3.102, *titirivarantukhaṇḍikokhācchaṇ*, in the sense of "taught by. From that [base ending in *chaṇ*], the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to 2.4.59, *tadadhīte tadveda*.
Then, the elision (*luk*) of that [suffix *aṇ*] occurs according to 4.2.64, *proktālluk*. Now, what is the purpose of the letter *ca* [in the rule], since it does not appear here?
Is there anything under discussion that is to be conjoined by the word "ca" (and)? To this he says:

"The word 'ca', moreover," and so forth. Since there is no other thing to be conjoined, the word "ca" is understood to have the purpose of conjoining this very [topic]; therefore, even though there is the governing rule of "bahula" (diversity), those suffixes...
Even regarding those [obligations] such as debts, posteriority is not subject to optionality.
Why, then, is this stated? [The answer is: so that it may be posterior and not prior. This is not a valid purpose; for instance, he says whatever he desires to be prior.

[This is stated] by the rule: "The suffix *akac* is added before the final vowel of indeclinables and pronouns" (Pāṇini 5.3.71). [Objection: Is it not the case that any other suffix following this [rule] will necessarily occur after [the base], even without an explicit statement? [Reply: This is not so;
for only those suffixes whose position is specifically restricted would be considered to have a fixed position.

If it were argued that another [word] here, having an indefinite location, might sometimes be "after" (para), sometimes "before" (pūrva), and sometimes "in the middle" (madhya), and therefore it must be called "after"— this need not be said;
because this ablative case (pañcamī) in the rules for verbal roots (dhātu) and nominal stems (pratipadika) is characterized by its connection with direction (digyoga).

Because there is an absence of any other cause for the ablative case, such as an *apādāna* (ablative relation), one might argue that this very [rule] will supply the word "other direction" (*paradik*). This is not so; rather, the word "eastern direction" (*pūrvadik*) would be supplied, and in that case, even in the east, there would sometimes be *sannādi* suffixes.

If you argue that the rule "tasmādityuttarasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.67) will provide the necessary restriction, this is not so; for the scope of that paribhāṣā is restricted to cases where an operation is prescribed for what follows an element indicated by the ablative case (pañcamī), whereas the suffixes *sann* and others are not indicated by the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*).
In that case as well, the operation pertaining to them is prescribed, because it is precisely they who are being brought about (*bhāvyamāna*).

But is it not the case that the operation consisting of the designation (*saṃjñā*) of "affix" is being prescribed? It is not so; for how can an operation of designation be prescribed for things that do not yet exist? Furthermore, for those [elements] for whom the very designation "affix" does not [yet apply]...

It is prescribed [by rules such as] *kaṇeṣṭhaḥ* (Daiva Up. 5.6) and *śamerḍhaḥ* (5.11), and so forth; what would be the recourse in those cases? For these are not intended to have the technical designation of "affix" (*pratyaya*), because otherwise, in words like *kaṇṭhaḥ* and *śaṇḍhaḥ*, the grammatical operations—such as the substitution of the vowel *i*—prescribed for an affix would not apply.
[It] occurs. If this is so, would not even the "subsequent-ness" (*paratva*) being stated for the suffix (*pratyaya*) fail to occur?

It will occur by virtue of the governing power (*adhikāra*) of the rule *paraśca*. For if this statement were absent, even though that *paribhāṣā* [the *vipratiṣedha-paribhāṣā*] were present, [the subsequent-ness would not apply] in the context of the governing term *bahulam* (diversely).
Because it is being prescribed, the priority [of the rule] among the uṇādi suffixes would be optional;
therefore, this must be done.
3. *ādyaudātaśca* | (3.1.3) By the phrase "when there is the possibility of a suffix with an indefinite accent," etc., he demonstrates the purpose for the commencement of this sūtra.
That which has an indefinite (*aniyata*), i.e., unsettled (*avyavasthita*) accent, is so described; and that [suffix] is...

The term *pratyaya* forms a *karmadhāraya* compound, which then enters into a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound with the word *prasaṅga*. This rule is stated for the purpose of making the initial syllable of such a suffix acute when there is the occurrence (*prasaṅga*) of a suffix whose accent is not otherwise fixed. In some places, the reading is "in the case of the occurrence of a suffix with an unfixed accent" (*aniyatasvaraprasaṅge*).

In this context, having formed an *aviśeṣa-samāsa* (non-qualificative compound) of the word *aniyata* with the word *svara*, a *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* is then formed with the word *prasaṅga*. The statement regarding the initial [syllable] being acute (*ādyudātta*) is made for the purpose of [indicating that] when there is an occurrence (*prasaṅga*) of indeterminate (*aniyata*) accents such as the acute (*udātta*), etc., [the initial syllable becomes acute]. [This applies to] "those with many vowels" (*anekāc*) and so forth; that is, those which possess many vowels (*aca*).

These [suffixes] consist of more than one syllable (*anekāc*). Since there is no fixed rule regarding the accentuation of these polysyllabic suffixes, this statement is made for the purpose of making the first syllable acute (*udātta*): so that the acute accent occurs only on the beginning, and not in the middle or at the end. For those suffixes which consist of only one syllable (*ekāc*), in their case...

Since there is no designated region (deśya), even if the mention of "beginning" (ādi) were absent, an unrestricted application to regions would not be possible; therefore, it is stated: "and in the case of polysyllabic words. For in the case of polysyllabic words, if the mention of "beginning" were absent, the accentuation would apply without restriction to the beginning, middle, or end.

It would follow that the statement regarding the initial udātta of a suffix consisting of more than one syllable is unnecessary; for there is no possibility at all of an initial anudātta or a middle or final udātta [in such cases]. To explain: when one intends a suffix to be anudātta, one applies it as such.
He attaches the *t* as an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) where he intends [the suffix] to be unaccented (*anudātta*), and says: "The *su*-suffixes and *pit* suffixes are unaccented" (Pāṇini 3.1.4);
and where he intends it to be circumflex (*svarita*), he attaches the *t* there, and says:
"A *ti*-suffix is circumflex" (Pāṇini 6.1.185); and where he intends it to have monotonous accent (*ekaśruti*), there he employs the term *ekaśruti*.
He does so, and says: "ṭhekaśruti dūrātsambuddhau" (Pāṇini 1.2.33);

and even regarding that which he desires to be udātta at the end, he adds the letter *c* as an *anubandha*, saying: "citonta udāto rita" (Kātyāyana 6.1.163); and likewise, regarding that which he desires to be udātta in the middle, he does so.

In that context, he adds the suffix *repha* as an *anubandha*, stating: "The penultimate [vowel] is acute before *rit*" (Pāṇini 6.1.217). [Objection: Will not any other suffix following this one be necessarily acute on its first syllable even without such a statement? [Response: This is not so; for it is only those [suffixes] whose accent is specifically regulated that [receive this treatment].

The suffixes would have fixed accents; however, for that suffix whose accent is not fixed, an absence of restriction regarding its accent would necessarily follow—sometimes it would be acute (udātta), sometimes another accent. Even when it is acute, it might occur at the beginning, sometimes in the middle, and sometimes at the end. Therefore...
This must be done.

4. *anudātau suppitau* (Pāṇini 3.1.4). [The commentary states: "This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule. This is because this rule is commenced even though that [preceding rule] would otherwise have applied. The term *sub* here refers to the technical abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*) for case endings, not to the locative plural ending itself; for [if it were the latter], its...

Because [the substitution] is established immediately after the elision (*anudātta*) of the *sup* suffix, for this very reason the plural number was used in the *vṛtti* in the expression "of the *sup* suffixes" (*supaḥ*). Furthermore, this mention of the *pratyāhāra* by means of the letter *p* refers only to the *sup* suffixes and not to anything else, since it serves no other purpose. As in the examples: "he cooks" (*pacati*) and "he reads" (*paṭhati*).
The example is for the *śap* [suffix], not for the *tip*; for that is already established by the rule "tāsyanudātta" (Pāṇini 6.1.186) and so forth.
5. *guptijkidbhyaḥ san* (Pāṇini 3.1.5).

"The technical designation *pratyaya* (suffix) is indeed [already] under discussion" — this is for the sake of clarity. The word *pratyaya* is introduced as a technical term; [its scope extends] "until the end of the fifth chapter" (Kāśikā 3.1.1).

Because the object to be conveyed is understood from this very statement. Now, even if the technical name *pratyaya* (suffix) were present here, the suffix *san* would certainly not be [governed] by it; for this name *pratyaya* is etymological (*anvartha*)—it is called *pratyaya* because "one understands meanings through it" (*pratiyantyanenārthān*), and one does not understand meanings through *san*.
They understand [the suffix] as having a meaning; however, because that [suffix *san*] lacks a meaning— since no meaning whatsoever is specified here for *san*— it is not correct to say,
"And since suffixes do not occur with an unspecified meaning, *san* will occur in its own sense" (*Puṣpavārttika* 90),
that *san* will occur in its own sense alone.
It cannot be so imagined; for a term like *gopana* and others, which denote one's own purpose (*svārtha*), is not perceived as being formed with the suffix *saṇ*.

If it is argued that even though it is meaningless, it will still function as a technical name (*saṃjñā*) by virtue of its being prescribed under the heading of suffixes (*pratyaya-adhikāra*), we say no; for if that were the case, [the rules] *ṭhhanasta ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.108) and *ṭhtrapujatunoḥ*... [would apply].

[If it were so,] by the rule *ṣuk* (Pāṇini 4.3.138), [the suffix] would apply even to a modification (*vikāra*) or an augment (*āgama*). This is not a fault; for there is indeed a meaning for the desiderative suffix (*san*), but what is that meaning? It is censure (*nindā*) and so forth. As it has been said: "The desiderative suffix is employed in the senses of censure, endurance, and the counteracting of disease" (Vārttika 178). Why?
Furthermore, this has been determined: are the meanings such as "disgust" (jugupsā) and so forth [the meaning] of the suffix *san*?

It is by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). For when *san* is present, as in *jugupsate* and so on, those meanings are perceived; but when *san* is absent, as in *gopayati* and so on—even though the roots *gup* and others are present—those meanings are not.
They are understood. Therefore, since [the suffix] *san* is indeed meaningful, the designation "pratyaya" (suffix) certainly applies.

In the case of *jugupsate*, because there is an absence of *ārdhadhātukatva* (the status of being an intermediate verbal suffix), *iṇ* does not occur. The absence of *ārdhadhātukatva*, however, is due to the fact that [the rule] *sano dhātoḥ* does not prescribe it. [This is governed by the rule] *kuhoścu*.

By the rule (7.4.62), there is *cutva*—the substitution of the letter *ja*. In the word "titikṣate," by the rule *coḥ kuḥ* (8.2.30), there is *kutva*—the substitution of the letter *ga*. By the rule *khari ca* (8.4.55), there is *cartva*—the substitution of the letter *ka*.

Regarding "nindākṣamā" and so forth: how, then, is the desiderative suffix (*san*) obtained when applied to *nindā* (censure) and the others? The term "vā" (optionally), which will be mentioned later, is understood as a supplement (*śeṣa*) to everything;
furthermore, that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Consequently, the desiderative suffix occurs invariably (*nityam*) in the case of *nindā* and the others, but not elsewhere.
This is the general rule; however, he will explain it otherwise for the purpose of treating a disease.

Or else—*kṣetriyāṇi* refers to weeds grown in a field for the sake of grain that must be treated [removed] and destroyed. Or else—*kṣetriyaḥ* means an adulterer; *paradārāḥ* refers to the wives of others.

"Another's field" (parakṣetra) means that [the patient] is to be treated or restrained there. It is also seen in the sense of doubt—as in "my mind hesitates" (vicikitsati me manaḥ). Although in this case doubt is understood through its connection with the prefix, it is nevertheless held to be the expressed meaning of the verbal root itself, while the prefix merely serves to indicate it.

Therefore, the mention of "remedying disease" (*vyādhipratīkāra*) is intended as a general rule (*prāyika*), for in common usage the term *cikitsati* is generally employed in the sense of remedying disease. Regarding the phrase "elsewhere": this refers to cases such as protecting (*gopana*).
The form *gopayati* is derived from the causative suffix *ṇic*. [Examples include] *tejayati* and *saṅketayati*.

The suffix *ṇic* is added after a root meaning "to cause" (*hetumaṇṇic*), as well as after roots belonging to the *curādi* group (*curādiṇij vā*). This is because these two categories are recited in both the *bhvādi* and *curādi* classes.
Now, in forms such as *jugupsate*, how is the ātmanepada ending prescribed after a desiderative (*sannanta*)? It is not [the case that it is not prescribed].
"Do we observe the *ātmanepada* [middle voice] before the suffix *san* [desiderative] in the case of *gup* and the others? To this he says:
"The addition of the *anubandha* in *gup* and the others," and so forth. This means that the *ātmanepada* should occur;

for in the case of *gup* and the others, an *anubandha* has been added for the purpose of indicating the low-pitched (*anudātta*) accent, and by the rule "that which has a low-pitched vowel as its *it* marker" (*anudātaṅtiḥ*), [the *ātmanepada* is applied].

(1.3.12) The intention is that the *ātmanepada* [middle voice] occurs [after these roots]. But one might object: "Even if the *anubandha* (indicatory letter) is attached, the *ātmanepada* should certainly not occur after them, because they are separated by the *san*-suffix. This is not so;
it will occur by virtue of the power of the attachment of the *anubandha*. Or else, the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) applied to a part [of the whole] [serves as an indicator for the whole].

Since it is stated [in the *Haima Gaṇapāṭha* 107] that "it serves as a qualifier of the aggregate," the aggregates consisting of *jugupsā* and so forth are themselves *anudāteta*; therefore, the *ātmanepada* will occur from them precisely through the intervention of their constituent parts. This being the case, whatever undesirable consequence arises here is addressed by the rule *pūrvavat sanaḥ*.

This has been presented and refuted [in the preceding discussion]. Now, for what purpose is the letter *a* taught for the suffix *san*, given that in the case of an *ardhadhātuka* suffix it must undergo elision by the rule "the elision of *ṭh*" (Pāṇini 6.4.48), and even in the case of a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, it would be subject to a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with the *śap* augment? Whether it exists or does not exist [in those cases], [it serves no purpose].

Is there no difference whatsoever in the instruction of the vowel *a*? This is not so; for here, in the form *pratīṣiṣati*, when the suffix *san* is prescribed after the root *iṇ* preceded by *pra*, if the instruction of the vowel *a* did not exist, then the doubling of the second *ekāc* (monosyllabic portion), which is ordained by the rule "of the second [element] beginning with a consonant" (*aj-āder-dvitīyasya*, 6.1.2), would not take place.

The form *sa* would not occur [in the reduplication] because the suffix *san* lacks a vowel. When there is the instruction of the vowel *a*, the second monosyllable becomes *sa*. Therefore, the instruction of the vowel *a* is for that purpose.

6. *mān-badh-dān-śān-bhyaḥ dīrghaś-cābhyāsasya* | (3.1.6) *mān* and *bandh* are anudāteta; the remaining two (*dān* and *śān*) are svariteta. Here, because of the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*), the technical rule *acaś-ca* (Pāṇini 1.2.28) is brought to bear, whereby the vowel (*ac*) qualifies the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

The lengthening being prescribed for the reduplicated syllable ending in a vowel (*ajanta*) necessarily depends upon the *halādiśeṣa* (the retention of the initial consonant); for without that, the syllable would not end in a vowel. But once that [retention] has occurred, there is nothing further to wait for, so the lengthening must take place immediately thereafter.

Furthermore, one might think that since [the substitution] occurs in place of the vowel of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), it would subvert the *it* designation of the root (*bdh*), while for the remaining [vowels] it would subvert the short vowel; consequently, an undesirable form would result. To address such a person, he says: "And there is a long vowel in place of the *ik* of the reduplicated syllable. But how [is this] so for the vowel *i*?

The long vowel is obtained because a specific rule (viśeṣavidhi) sublates a general rule (sāmānyavidhi), and the long vowel is prescribed specifically; therefore, having sublated the shortening (itvam) prescribed generally, would this [long vowel] apply only to the letter *a*? For this very reason, it is considered thus: "the long vowel [is applied] when there is no *kit*."
In this context, it should be understood that this has been made known:
"In the case of modifications of reduplication (*abhyāsa*), exceptions (*apavāda*) supersede general rules (*utsarga*).
The purpose of including the term *aki* [in the rule] is so that this does not apply here: *yaṃyamyate*, *raṃramyate*.

Thus [it is said]. And if, in the case of modifications of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), the general rules (*utsarga*) were to be set aside by the exceptions (*apavāda*), then—since the exception (*nuk*) would have been applied—the long vowel would not occur simply because the stem would no longer end in *ac*; what then would be the purpose of the rule "not when *kit* follows" (*akitaḥ*)? Yet it has been stated; therefore, from that [fact], it is made known: [the general rules] are not set aside in the case of modifications of the reduplicated syllable.

Regarding the term *bādhyabādhakabhāva* (the relationship between the sublated and the sublator): in the form *bībhatsate*, by the rule *ekāco baśo bhaṣ* (Pāṇini 8.2.37), the letter *ba* is replaced by *bha*; then, by the rule *khari ca* (8.4.55), the letter *dha* is replaced by *ta*.

Regarding the phrase "in the subsequent sūtra" (*utarasūtre*) and so forth: for here, by means of the expression "optionally" (*vāvacanena*), only the prescription (*vidhi*) of the suffix *san* is required, and not [anything else].
The rule [of "sarva-"] applies immediately after this; therefore, it is understood as a supplement (*śeṣa*) to all three preceding rules.

The inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of making it known that it is also a supplement to the rule concerning *guṇa* and so forth (3.1.5); otherwise, it would be understood as a supplement only to the immediately preceding rule.
In the case of "mānayati," it is either the causative suffix *ṇic* added with the sense of causing (hetu), or the *ṇic* of the *curādi* class, since this root is also listed in the *curādi* group.
In the case of "niśānayati" (the *Kāśikā* reads "niśānam"), the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule for roots beginning with *pac*.

7. *dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ samānakartṛkādicchāyāṃ vā* (Pāṇini 3.1.7). Since it is only when an agent is most desired to be pervaded by an action that the status of being an object (*karmabhāva*) is possible—and not otherwise—some other action must necessarily be expected here; and no such [other action] exists.

It is heard [in scripture]; and since desire is brought into proximity by virtue of being the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), it is therefore proper that it alone should be expected [as the object], according to the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*). Therefore, he says "the object of *iṣ*" (*iṣikarma*) and so forth, because the status of being an object (*karmabhāva*) is understood for that which is pervaded by that very [desire]. "The object of *iṣ*" (*iṣeḥ karma*) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

Since similarity necessarily depends upon a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), a counter-correlative must be expected; yet no counter-correlative is explicitly heard in the aphorism. In this regard, he says "by the [word] *iṣiṇā*," etc., indicating that by the previously stated logic, the status of being a counter-correlative is understood through the word *iṣiṇā* alone. *Samānaḥ* means one and the same.

The term "kartāsyeti" (that which has an agent) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; its meaning is "having a single agent. Now, one might object that the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is not applicable to the verbal root (*dhātu*), because that [objecthood] is a property of the meaning (*artha*), whereas the verbal root consists of sound (*śabda*). However, in usages such as "he desires the verbal root *karoti*" (*karoti-dhātum icchati*), the status of being an object is indeed observed for the verbal root as well.
If you ask why, we do not say that the verbal root (*dhātu*) can never function as the object (*karman*). What then?

We say that it is impossible for that [root] which is employed here as the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) that causes the arising of the desiderative (*san*), and which has a common agent (*samānakartṛka*). This is because the state of having a common agent belongs to the object that is being accomplished (*sādhyamāna*).

[The root] becomes the agent, whereas the status of being an object belongs to that which has an established nature. Furthermore, having granted for the sake of argument that the root and the agent are coreferential, a fault was stated regarding the root’s being the object; now, even that [coreferentiality] is simply not possible. For instance—the root is a word, and the agent belongs to the action, not to the word. Thus he says:
"‘The state of being an object’ (karmatva), etc. Regarding "‘mediated by the meaning’ (arthadvāraka)':

that for which the meaning is the door or the means is ‘mediated by the meaning. Because the meaning possesses the status of being an object and because they share the same agent, the verbal root denoting that [meaning] is also [called an object] through metaphorical transfer based on the property of the meaning."

It is also said that [a term] shares the same agent as the action (*karmasamānakartṛka*); for example, in the rule *dvandvaśca prāṇitūrya-* (Pāṇini 2.4.2), because the meaning [of the compound] consists of limbs of living beings, the word expressing that [meaning] is also called a limb of a living being—this is the intended sense.
In the form *cikīrṣati*, the meaning of the root *kṛ* is [so called] because it is pervaded by desire (*icchā*).
Because of their identity, the root *kṛ* has the same agent as the object of the root *iṣ*; for the very one who is the agent of *iṣ* is also the agent of that [action of *kṛ*].

Therefore, by way of that [object], the root *kṛ* also has the same agent as its object—this is the sense. Consequently, [the suffix] *san* [is applied], according to the rule "iko jhal" (Pāṇini 1.2.9).
Due to the *kit* status of the suffix, there is no *guṇa* substitution; by *ṭhajjhanagamāṃ sani* (Pāṇini 6.4.16), there is lengthening (*dīrgha*);

by *ṛta iddhātoḥ* (7.1.100), there is the substitution of *it*; by *raparatvam*, the *ra*-element follows; by *hali ca* (8.2.77), there is lengthening; and while *iṇkoḥ* (8.3.57) is being supplied as a governing rule, *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (8.3.59) applies.
Thus, there is the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣatva), reduplication (*dvirvacana*), and the operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsakārya*).

Why is the term "root" (*dhātu*) mentioned? Indeed, the mention of "root" is made for this purpose: so that [the suffix *san*] does not occur after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), as in the case of *gamanamicchati*. But surely, even if the mention of "root" were absent, *san* would still not occur after that [case-ending].
[The suffix] does not apply; for it is barred by the exception "supa ātmanaḥ kyac" (Pāṇini 3.1.8).

Therefore, with the intention that—by the principle of elimination—it will apply to the verbal root alone even without the mention of the word "dhātu," he says: "Let there be no production [of the suffix] from [a root] preceded by a prefix."

When the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), as qualified by a prefix (*upasarga*), is pervaded by the agent’s desire (*iṣiṇā*), then that very meaning, qualified by the prefix, undergoes the state of being an object (*karmatva*). Consequently, by means of that [object], the verbal root itself, together with its prefix, is designated as the "object"; thus, the designation of the object would arise from the root plus the prefix, and from that [it follows]:

In the case of *prācikīrṣat*, when reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is applied, because of the rule *sanyaṅoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.9)— which states that for a root ending in *san*, the first monosyllabic element undergoes reduplication— the reduplication would apply to the entire initial portion of the complex, namely the syllable *pra*. Furthermore, if the *laṅ* affix were to cause the designation of the stem (*aṅgasaṃjñā*) for the form including the prefix, then the augment *aṭ* would have to be inserted before that [prefix].
If, then, it is accompanied by a prefix (*sopasarga*), would there not be no derivation from a transitive root, because that [root with a prefix] is intransitive?

This is not so; for when the whole (*samudāya*) possesses the status of an object (*karman*), its parts (*avayava*) also experience the status of an object, since the whole consists of its parts. This is indeed a means of attainment (*abhyupāya*).

The status of the parts as objects [of the action] is dependent upon the status of the whole as the object; otherwise, if the parts did not themselves become objects when the whole is the object, then in the case of *mahāntaṃ putram icchati* ("he desires a great son"), the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) would not apply to the parts characterized as objects. 8.1.60. *ṭha*.

"He desires to go" (*gantum icchati*). The citation of the form ending in *lyuṭ* (*gamana*) is for the purpose of demonstrating its status as the instrument (*karaṇa*). For indeed, the counter-example concerns the non-occurrence of the suffix *san* after a verbal root (*dhātu*). Here, there is the state of having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*). To explain: the very same one who is the agent of "desiring" (*iṣ*) is also the agent of "going" (*gamana*). That...

One desires some object by means of one's own act of going, which has attained the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*). However, since the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) does not exist for the root *gam* (to go) through its meaning, [the suffix *san*] does not occur; hence [the example] "he desires Devadatta’s eating" (*devadattasya bhojanam icchati*). In the phrase "Devadatta’s," the genitive case is applied by the rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65).
Thus, the genitive case is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). For in this instance, Devadatta is the agent of eating, whereas Yajñadatta is the agent of the desire to eat;

therefore, there is no identity of agent (*samānakartṛkatva*). Regarding the phrase "he knows how to do" (*kartuṃ jānāti*), the suffix *san* does not occur here in the sense of cognition because of the specific mention of "desire" (*icchā*). [Objection: But surely, a verbal root whose object is the act of desiring (*iṣ*) [should take *san*] by the very rule for *iṣ*.

It has been stated that the suffix *san* occurs after a verb when there is a common agent with the desire (*icchā*). However, in this case, just as the desire is not the meaning of the affix, so too the root's status as the object of the desire and its having a common agent with the desirer are absent; therefore, that counter-example is incorrect due to the deficiency of three constituent factors.
This is not so; for when the mention of "desire" (icchā) is present, those two qualifiers are obtained through proximity.

But when that is absent, the status of being an object (karmatva) of the verbal root is understood with respect to any action whatsoever, and the state of having a common agent (samānakartṛkatva) is understood in relation to any counter-correlative whatsoever.
"What is the impropriety here?

[The objection is: 'By the statement of the word "vā," a sentence also occurs. The remainder [of the explanation] is: "in the subsequent sūtra. But in this case, [the formation of a sentence] is prescribed precisely by the rule "tumun in the case of verbs having the same agent" (3.3.158).

The sentence will be "kartum icchati" (he wishes to do). For if [the root] were eternal (*nityatva*), that statement regarding the suffix *san* would be purposeless. Furthermore, another purpose for the mention of the word "optionally" (*vā*) has already been stated;
the word "also" (*api*) is used there in the sense of inclusion (*samuccaya*). This is indicated by the phrase beginning with "because of the rule 'after a verbal root' (*dhātoḥ*)," and so forth.

Because the designation *ārdhadhātuka* is prescribed for an affix by the rule *ṭhārdhadhātuke śeṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.114) after the word *dhātoḥ* has been uttered— meaning it is prescribed for an affix enjoined after the term "root"— here,
since the *san* affix is enjoined after the word "root" (*dhātoḥ*) itself, the designation *ārdhadhātuka* does not apply; for indeed...
There is a specific rule for that:

"An addition [to the rule] is made in the case of apprehension. Apprehension (*āśaṅkā*) means possibility (*sambhāvanā*), and that is a property of the speaker. In the example "The riverbank wishes to fall," desire does not belong to the bank because it is insentient.

"It is not possible" means that [the result] does not obtain. This usage occurs in a context such as "I fear the bank will fall," or "The dog is about to die. As before, there is shortening due to the *kit* suffix.
It has been stated [in Pāṇini 7.1.102]: "For [a vowel] preceded by *u*, there is substitution of *o* for *ṭh*"; and there is also the substitution of *ra*. Even though this is so here...

If the living being (*jīva*) possesses consciousness, then because of its love for life, the desire of a dog to die cannot possibly arise; thus [the objection] does not apply. Furthermore, this formal argument (*prayoga*) is to be understood as referring to the sense expressed in the phrase, "I suspect the dog will die.
The word *upasaṃkhyāna* means "explanation" or "demonstration"; [it implies that] it must be formulated.
This is not to be disputed. However, the explanation is as follows: a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) must be made after the word *dhātoḥ*;
by this, the suffix *san* will apply even in cases of apprehension (*āśaṅkā*).
[The rule] begins with "after that which ends in *icchā-sana*" and so forth; that is, after that which ends in the *san* prescribed in the sense of desire (*icchā*).

The prohibition of *san* must be explained; we shall provide that explanation later. The suffix *san* is added in its own sense (*svārthe*), and the phrase "only from that which ends in *san*" is made as a qualification of the desire (*icchā*). In the form "jugupsiṣate," there is the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule "ato lopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.48).

Regarding the phrase "from a secondary derivative" (*ṭhśaiṣikāt*) and so forth: any meaning other than those beginning with *aśvapatya* and ending with *adūrabhava* is called the "remainder" (*śeṣa*). That which occurs therein is "secondary" (*śaiṣika*), as in the rule "from *adhyātma* and so forth, the suffix *ṭhañ*" (Vārttika 456). From such a secondary derivative, a subsequent suffix of the same form (*sarūpa*) is prohibited.

From *śālāyām bhavaḥ*, by the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.114), we have *śālīyaḥ*. However, from *śālīye bhavaḥ*, the suffix *cha* does not apply again. But a different form certainly occurs: from *ahicchatre bhavaḥ*, we have *āhicchatraḥ* by the rule *prāgdīvyato ’ṇ* (4.1.83); and from *āhicchatre bhavaḥ*, we have *āhicchatrīyaḥ*.
The suffix *cha* occurs after a word ending in *aṇ* that is a *vṛddha* [term] (Pāṇini 4.2.114). A suffix having the sense of the possessive suffix (*matup*) is called *matubarthīya*;
by the rule "and after words such as *gaha*" (4.2.138), the suffix *cha* is applied. A suffix that possesses the sense of the possessive suffix is called *matubarthika*;
by the rule "after a word ending in *at*, the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan*" (5.2.115), the suffix *ṭhan* is applied.

A suffix expressing the sense of *matup* (possessive) is not desired after another suffix that expresses the sense of *matup*, provided it is of the same form (*sarūpa*). For example, from "he has a staff" (*daṇḍo 'syāsti*), one forms *daṇḍikaḥ* by the suffix *ṭhan* as before; however, from this *matvarthīya* suffix (*daṇḍika*), the suffix *ṭhan* does not apply again to mean "he has a *daṇḍika*. But if the suffix is of a different form (*virūpa*), it is permitted.

It is indeed so: one who has a staff is "daṇḍī" (staff-bearer); because there are staff-bearers in this hall, it is "daṇḍavatī" (staffed) hall; thus, the suffix *matup* occurs after words ending in *in*. [The rule] "sannatān na saniṣyate" (the desiderative suffix *san* is not applied after another *san*) applies here.
The term "sarūpaḥ" (of the same form) is connected [to this]. In that regard, although there is a deviation from the formal identity (*rūpasārūpya*) of the *san* suffix...
Although [the suffix *san*] does not exist [in that context], nevertheless, by the force of the qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), one relies on the similarity of meaning (*arthasārūpya*).

By this, it is understood that [the rule applies] "after a root ending in the desiderative suffix *san*" (*icchā-sanantāt*), and because it is stated [in the Vārttika]: "First, a prohibition must be stated for [roots] ending in *san* after the desiderative suffix" (*pūrvaṃ ṭhicchā-sanantāt pratiṣedho vaktavyaḥ*). As for the *san* that occurs after roots such as *gup* in the sense of censure (*nindā*) and so forth—

That indeed occurs when there is a desire for it; and thus it has been illustrated from such a case. All of this has been illustrated precisely as it follows from the logical principle (*nyāya*). How so? For a completed base (*prakṛti*) becomes the cause for the application of an affix (*pratyaya*); and at the time of prescribing an affix that is similar (*sarūpa*) or a secondary derivative (*śaiṣika*), [the base] is not yet completed.

There is no base (prakṛti) already established as ending in such an affix at the time when an affix expressing the sense of matup is prescribed; nor is there a base already established as ending in such an affix at the time when an affix expressing the sense of desire is prescribed;
nor [is there one] from that which ends in an affix expressing desire when an affix expressing desire is being prescribed.

The base (*prakṛti*) exists as something whose being has been acquired; for it is only now that [suffixes] such as *tatra-bhavaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.53) and others are to be produced from bases that possess the same form (*sarūpa*), such as those belonging to the *śaiṣika* class.
Therefore, because they lack a base, they do not [arise] from a base of the aforementioned kind.
They come into being.
8. *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8).
Here, the word *ātman* is understood as that which, by excluding what belongs to another, expresses its opposite meaning;
it does not, however, refer to the person who is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) possessing internal activity.

It exists; if it were apprehended here [in this context], it would be ineffective. By that [ineffectiveness], desire (*icchā*) would be qualified, or else a word ending in a *su*-affix (*subanta*); in that case, since desire belongs only to the self and cannot possibly belong to another, its status as a qualifier for that [other] is untenable. As for the word ending in a *su*-affix, it too [could not be qualified] by either the desirer or by anyone else.

That which is being connected becomes connected precisely with the self [of the speaker], because both of those [the base and the suffix] are related to the self. Therefore, it is also incorrect for that [suffix] to be a qualifier of a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*); thus, only that which expresses the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of another is accepted. In this way, indeed, the exclusion of the suffix *kap* is achieved.

It can be so established, and not otherwise. Here too, because of the presence of desire (*icchā*), the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is understood for that which is pervaded by that very [desire]; thus he says: "of the object of desire" (*iṣikarmaṇaḥ*).
If desire were qualified by the mention of the self (*ātman*), then this would also apply here—as in the case of "the king's... [desire].

Regarding the phrase "one who desires a son": even when a king desires a son, the desire belongs to the seeker himself. Therefore, considering it appropriate to qualify the nominal stem (*subanta*) itself by means of self-reproach, he says: "of the seeker who is related to the self. As for this relationship to the self:

It should be understood that this pertains to the meaning of the subordinate element (*subanta*) by way of its referent. Now, how is it obtained that this [suffix] belongs specifically to the seeker (*eṣitṛ*)?
Because that which is brought into proximity by the desire is brought into proximity for the seeker. How is this so?
Because without him [the seeker], that [desire] would not exist. [The example is] *putrīyati*. [This is governed by] *kyaci ca* (Pāṇini 7.4.33).

Thus, regarding the inclusion of the term *sub*: does this inclusion here serve to exclude the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), or does it serve to exclude the verbal root (*dhātu*)? In that regard, it cannot be for the purpose of excluding the nominal stem, for [a suffix] does not [occur] after that which already ends in a *sup* [suffix].
In the production of a suffix, there is no distinction between [the case-ending] and the nominal stem (prātipadika).

Nor is it appropriate [to say that the mention of *sup*] is for the purpose of excluding verbal roots (*dhātu*), because the suffix *san* prescribed after those [roots] would constitute an exception (*bādhaka*). With this intention, he asks: "What is the purpose of mentioning *sup*? lest [the suffix be applied] from a sentence (*vākya*).

Regarding the word "bhūt": he states the purpose of including the term *su*—if the inclusion of *su* were not made, [the suffix] would apply even after a sentence; therefore, the inclusion of *su* is made to prevent that. Now, should [the suffix] not occur at all in the case of *mahāputrīyati*? It should occur when a compound (*samāsa*) has been formed.

This sentence occurs as "mahāputram icchati" (he desires a great son); however, when this sentence occurs as "mahāntaṃ putram icchati" (he desires a great son), then [the rule] should not apply. Furthermore, it should be understood that the term "sentence" (*vākya*) is used here to indicate a collection of words (*padasamudāya*). Therefore, [in the case of] "mahāntaṃ"...

From this aggregate [compound] "putram," the possibility [of the suffix] is suspected, yet this is not a sentence, because its meaning is incomplete. Furthermore, what would happen if it were so? If it were so, then the words *mahat* and *putra*, being subordinate to the meaning of the suffix, would lack the capacity characterized by "integration into a single meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*).

There would be no compound; consequently, the substitution of *ā* for *at* prescribed by the rule "ṭhānmahataḥ samānādhikaraṇajātīyayoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.46) would not apply to the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Alternatively, the word *putra*, being subordinate to the meaning of the suffix, cannot be qualified by the attribute of being honored.

If [the word] were *syāt*, there would be no compound by the rule *sanmahat* (Pāṇini 2.1.61), and in the absence of that, the substitution of *āt* would also not occur. Now, even if the mention of *sub* (a nominal ending) is made, why does this [compound] not occur here?
For is this not a *subanta* (a word ending in a nominal suffix)? This is not so; because of the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*).

When a *sup* suffix has been produced, its application occurs only from that [word] which begins with it. And here, the *sup* suffix has not been produced from the sentence; rather, it is produced from a constituent part. Therefore, there is no production [of the suffix] from the sentence. [Objection:
Why then is it not produced from the constituent part, namely the word *putra*? [Response: Because it does not convey the meaning [of the whole].

For a sentence must possess the same meaning as the nominal stem (*vṛtti*) with which it is equivalent; yet, the meaning understood here from the sentence "he desires a great son" is not conveyed by the suffix (*pratyaya*). For instance, the meaning of the sentence "he desires a great son" is as follows—

[The sealing of Vārāṇasī: For instance, when it is said "he acts like a great man" (*mahāntaṃ putrīyati*), the meaning understood—that he behaves toward someone as if toward a great son—is of a different category from the syntactic meaning of the sentence, namely, "he desires a son of the king" (*rājñaḥ putraṃ icchati*). But [one might object]: is this not a case of lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*) due to mutual dependence?

"If [the meaning] exists, it will not come to be; what is the use of grasping at a self? How is there a lack of capacity? For there is the statement: 'That which is dependent is incapable' (Cāndra-vyākaraṇa-pañjikā 27). This is not so. For when [the word] is understood as independent through the force of the context or the sense, then [the suffix] applies. And here—

"He obtains"—meaning he desires sin, he desires evil (*agham*). For here, even without the use of a third word, "of another" (*parasya*) is understood; indeed, no one desires sin for themselves. Regarding the phrase "the letter *ka*" and so forth: if the letter *ka* were not present, there would be no inclusion of this [term].
Because in the rule *ṭhnaḥ kye* (Pāṇini 1.4.15), there is the mention of that which possesses the indicatory letter *k*,

the letter *c* serves the purpose of preventing the obstruction of that [general reference]. For if the letter *c* were not present, since *kyac*, *kyaṅ*, and *kyaṣ* possess two indicatory letters (*dvi-anubandhaka*), there would be an obstruction to the general reference.

The *ca* [in the rule] does not serve the purpose of including vowels with an internal *udātta* accent, because that is already established by the rule *ṭhghātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.162). Regarding the statement "it should be stated" (*vaktavyaḥ*), the meaning is that it must be explained.

The explanation, however, should be made by relying on the fact that the term *vā* (or) which is being carried over from a previous rule functions as a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (a restricted option). By means of this—
The suffix *kyac* does not occur after words ending in *mān* or indeclinables.

Regarding the phrase "in the Veda" (*cchandasi*) and so forth: the meaning is that this rule must be explained as having the sense that *kyac* occurs even for the desire of another in the Vedic language. Furthermore, the explanation is as follows: when *kyac* has been applied, [the rule] "for *aśva*, etc., *āt*" (*aśvādyasyāt*) applies.

(7.4.37) By prescribing the *it* suffix for the word *agha* in order to prevent the application of the *it* suffix [elsewhere], he indicates this: in Vedic usage, the suffix *kyac* occurs even when there is a desire for another. For no one desires evil (*agha*) for themselves. [The example is] "aghāyavaḥ. The substitution of *ā* is by the rule of indication (*jñāpaka-sūtra*), according to Pāṇini 3.2.170: "After a word ending in *kyac*, [the suffix *u* is added] in Vedic usage."
Thus, there is the suffix *u*, the *guṇa* substitution by [Pāṇini 7.3.109] "ṭhjasi ca," and the substitution of *av*.

9. *kāmyacca* | (3.1.9) Now, since both these suffixes, *kyac* and *kāmyac*, are prescribed after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) when there is a desire for an object for oneself, why was not a single rule formulated? To this he says: "The separation of the rules" (*yogavibhāga*).

And so forth. [If] *supa ātmanaḥ kyackāmyacau* were treated as a single rule (*ekayoga*), then both suffixes would carry over (*anuvṛtti*) into the subsequent rules. Now, one might object: even if there is a division of rules (*yogavibhāga*), by virtue of immediate proximity (*ānantarya*), only *kāmyac* would carry over, not *kyac*. This is not a fault; for here, the particle *ca*...

The mention of *kyac* is made for the purpose of drawing it along [into the subsequent rule]; the purpose of drawing *kyac* along is so that its recurrence may occur in the following sūtra, since there is no application of it here. If it is asked why *kāmyac* is not also drawn along, the answer is: no, because of the force of the division of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*). Now...

Why does the letter *k* not receive the designation *it* by the rule "ṭhlaśakvataddhite" (Pāṇini 1.3.8)? To this he says: "The letter *k* [does not receive] the designation *it," and so forth. Now, one might ask: should there not simply be its elision (*lopa*)? It is not to be elided; for in this context, the instruction of a phoneme is intended either for the sake of a grammatical operation (*kārya*) or for the sake of its being heard (*śravaṇa*). [In this case,] the operation...

In this case, it does not exist. Therefore, if the purpose were merely for the sake of hearing [the form], the instruction would be useless. What, then, is the purpose? It is so that there may be a prohibition of *guṇa* in the case of "agnikāmyati.
This is not the purpose; for *guṇa* applies to the *aṅga* before both *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes.
It is said: A suffix prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*) is designated as *ārdhadhātuka*, provided it is "residual" (*śeṣa*);
however, this [suffix *-in-*, in the case of *upayaṭ*] is not prescribed after a verbal root, but rather after a word ending in a nominal suffix (*subanta*). If so, what then is the purpose?
[The purpose is that] in the case of *upayaṭkāmyati*, the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) should occur by virtue of rule 6.1.15, *vac-svapi-yaja-ādīnām*.

This is not so either; because in that case, [the suffix] *kit* would be qualified by the *yaj*-class and others—namely, "that *kit* which belongs to the *yaj*-class and so forth. And what is the *kit* belonging to the *yaj*-class and so forth? It is that which is prescribed after the *yaj*-class and others; and this [suffix] is not prescribed in such a manner. Even assuming there were a purpose [for such a qualification], he states another rebuttal:

"Because it begins with the letter *ca*. He thinks as follows: "The suffix *kyac* is applied in this way [after a word ending in a case-suffix] when one desires for oneself (*ātmanaḥ kāmyati*); thus, there is the mention of two *ca*s.
That *ca* which bears the technical designation *it* will serve to protect the technical designation *it* of the letter *ka*. Now...

What is the purpose of the second *ca*? For is it not the case that the final acute accent (*antodātta*) is already established by the rule *dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.162)? In this instance, in the form *putrakāmyiṣyīta*, the accent of the suffix *kāmyac* itself prevails by virtue of the power of its being marked with the *c*-indicator, even though it would otherwise be superseded by the accent of the *satiśiṣṭa* [the subsequent] element.
For example: *upayaj-kāmyati*. [The derivation is as follows: by the rule *vijupe chandasi* (Pāṇini 3.2.73), there is the suffix *vic*;
then, from the sense "he desires the *upayaj*," the suffix *kāmyac* is added. By the rule *vraścādibhyo vā* (8.2.36), the substitution of *ṣ* occurs;
for that [sibilant], there is the substitution of the voiced stop (*jaś*) *ḍ*; and for that too, by the rule *vāvasāne* (8.4.56), there is the substitution of the voiceless stop (*car*) *ṭ*.

10. *upamānād ācāre* (Pāṇini 3.1.10). The suffix *kyac* is understood here, but not *kāmyac*; the reason for this has been stated previously. Since the action of behaving (*ācāra*) is the meaning of the suffix, the objecthood of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is relative to that action.
As before, due to proximity [to the preceding rule].

Regarding the phrase "and from a locative" (*adhikaraṇācca*) and so forth: the meaning is that the interpretation should be understood as "the suffix *kyac* occurs after a locative when expressing an action performed in that manner" (*ācāre*). As for the interpretation itself, one should proceed as before by carrying over the inclusion of the particle *ca*.
One should act by relying on its function as a particle that includes what has not been explicitly mentioned.

11. *kartuḥ kyaṅ ca salopaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.11). This suffix *kyaṅ* is prescribed in conjunction with the elision of the suffix *sa*. Therefore, it should apply only where there is the elision of *sa*—as in *payāyate* and similar forms—but here it should not apply, as in *kākaḥ śyenāyate*.
In such passages as these, this is a single sentence, and the particle *ca* signifies conjunction (*samuccaya*). Therefore, what is being stated is this:

"the suffix *kyaṅ* and the elision of *sa* occur. And since these two are prescribed simultaneously, in the absence of the elision of *sa*, the suffix *kyaṅ* should not occur. For when these two are prescribed simultaneously—
The effect is not applicable in the absence of either one; as in the rule *sthādhvoricca* (Pāṇini 1.2.17), he says:

"anvācaśiṣṭaḥ" (prescribed as an addition), and so forth. For by this [statement], it is shown that this *ca* is not for conjunction (*samuccaya*), but rather for addition (*anvācaya*). In that case, there are two sentences: [the first is] "it belongs to the agent."

In all cases, however, where the letter *s* exists, there is also its elision (*lopa*). There, by the first rule, the suffix *kyaṅ*—being prescribed primarily without regard for the elision of *s*—also operates even in the rule prescribing the elision of *s*. As in "śyenāyate" [he acts like a hawk], according to the rule "akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.25).
"It is long.

[The commentary states: "In the rule for the elision of *s*, the option (*vā*) is also connected. Otherwise, forms such as *payasyate* would not be established. "And that [option] is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Otherwise, it would apply even to words like *ojas* and *apsaras*.

The *vibhāṣā* (optional rule) regarding the elision of the *sal* [suffix] has been stated: "In the case of *ojas*, *apsaras*, and *payas*, the elision is mandatory; however, in the case of *payas*, it is optional" (*Vārttika* 185 on Jai. Sū. 2.1.91). That [rule] is a *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā* (a restricted option), and this [text] clarifies that very point. Now, regarding the forms *haṃsāyate* and *sārasāyate*:

He asks: "Why does the elision of *sa* not occur? and answers with the words "And in the rule for the elision of *sa*" (*salopavidhau ca*), etc. If, even in the rule for the elision of *sa*, this [word] *kartuḥ* were a fifth-case (ablative) form, then—since the rule "of the final [sound]" (*alo'ntyasya*, 1.1.52) would not apply—the elision of *sa* would occur wherever it might be situated.
This would also apply here. Furthermore, in the rule prescribing the elision of *s*, this [word] "kartuḥ" is not in the ablative case;

what then? It is in the genitive. Since a change of case occurs depending on the meaning, it results in a genitive of the locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). And when the genitive of the locus is present, by the application of the rule "ṭh-lo 'ntyasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.52), [the substitution] applies only to the final [element].
There must be elision [of the penultimate vowel]. Therefore, in examples such as *haṃsāyate*, the elision does not occur.

The phrase "in the sense of behaving like" (*ācāre*) and so forth is intended as an indicator for the scope of *kyaṅ*; by this, the suffix *kvip* is prescribed as an exception to *kyaṅ*. And here, one should attach an unaccented (anudātta) *m* as an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) to words such as *avagalbha*.

The *ātmanepada* ending occurs [in the form] *avagalbhate* due to the specific grammatical instruction (*nirdeśāt*). Furthermore, the suffix *kvip* is optionally prescribed after roots such as *avalbh* and others; for instance, the root *galbh* is listed as "to be bold" (*dhārṣṭye*)—[DhP 392]—and *avagalbh* is listed as "to be bold" (*ādhṛṣṭe*)—[DhP 392]—while *klībṛ* is listed as "to be unmanly" (*apadhārṣṭye*)—[DhP 393]—or "to be intoxicated" (*made*)—[DhP 393].
The roots *ṭhūḍ* and *hoḍ*, meaning "to go," are ātmanepada (according to Dhātupāṭha 352 and 354).

In that case, when a verbal suffix (*lakāra*) is applied directly to these, forms such as *avagalbhate* will result; however, when the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied after first forming nominal stems from the past participles (*kṛta*), then [the form] *avagalbhāyate* results.
Will this be so? This is the purpose for the optional prescription of the *kvip* suffix:
so that in the case of *avagalbhāñcakre*, the augment *ām* may occur by virtue of Pāṇini 3.1.35, *kāspratyayādāmamantre*.
Otherwise, since *ām* is prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*) that either ends in a suffix or does not end in a suffix, it would not apply here [if the *kvip* were not optional].

Regarding the rule "sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ": the attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*) of *tarap* and the others must be performed for the purpose of attaching the indicatory letters (*anubandha*). And here, one expects the option "or *kvip*" in the sense of conduct (*ācāra*). Consequently, the resulting syntactical formulation is: "*kvip* occurs after all nominal stems (*prātipadika*) only in the sense of conduct. Now...

For what purpose are the markers *k* and *p* attached to the suffix *kvip*, given that the purpose of the marker *k* is to prohibit *guṇa* substitution, and no possibility of *guṇa* occurs here? This is because *kvip* is not prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*), and therefore it lacks the status of being a *sārvadhātuka* suffix.

For *guṇa* is prescribed for both *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* affixes. Furthermore, the purpose [of the marker] *p* is to render [the affix] unaccented (*anudātta*), and that is not possible for *kvip*, because it is devoid of phonemes (*anacka*) and because of the rule "ṭh-er-apṛktasya" (Pāṇini 6.1.67), which causes the elision of everything [except the single consonant]. Therefore, these two [markers, *k* and *p*], are intended to prevent the obstruction of the general designation (*sāmānyagrahaṇa*).

No; for the non-obstruction of the apprehension of the commonality is established by either one alone. Otherwise, that same purpose would require the suffix to be attached even to *vij* and *viṣṭi*; this point must be considered.

12. *bhṛśādibhyo bhuvyacverlopaśca halaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.12). Regarding the word *bhuvi*: "becoming" (*bhavana*) is *bhū*; the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) because it belongs to the *saṃpad-ādi* group. Here, by the mention of *hal*, the words *bhṛśa-* and so forth are qualified as far as possible; they are not [qualified] by the specific [suffix].
He states that this is a rule regarding the final element (tadantavidhi), beginning with "and of those ending in consonants" (halantānām ca).

Here too, as before, the elision of the consonant (hal-lopa) is taught as a secondary addition (anvācaya-śiṣṭa); therefore, even in its absence, the suffix kyaṅ occurs. In the rule for the elision of the consonant, the genitive case "from bhṛśa and so forth" (bhṛśādibhyaḥ) becomes a locative of reference (sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī).

This is due to the change of case endings by implication (*arthāt*). In that regard, since the rule "of the final [element] of *ṭha*" (Pāṇini 1.1.52) applies as a restrictive rule (*niyama*), in forms such as *bhṛśāyate*, there is no elision of a non-final consonant (*ahal-antya-halo lopaḥ*). Now, one might object:
since words such as *bhṛśa* are many, the plural form *ac-vibhyaḥ* is used in connection with them.
It must be so; therefore, as to why there is an indication by means of the singular number in the word *acveḥ*, he says:
"of *acveiḥ*" and so forth. [The term] *acveiḥ* is connected individually with both *bhṛśāt* and *śīghrāt*.
Therefore, the use of the singular number is logical.

"But for what purpose," and so forth. This is a question regarding the governing rule *ac-chaḥ*. He asks why it should not be applied, saying: "Insofar as," and so forth. By the rule beginning with *abhūtatadbhāve*, the suffix * cvi* is prescribed in connection with the verb *bhū*. Since the meaning [of the transformation] is already expressed by that very [suffix], [the suffix *cha*] does not apply after words ending in *cvi*.

Alternatively, it will be *kyaṅ*, on the basis of the rule *ṭhuktārthānām aprayogaḥ* (Vārttika 60). But would not *kyaṅ* alone apply, overriding the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*)? This is not so; for rules that have no other scope (*anavakāśa*) are subverters (*bādhaka*), whereas *kyaṅ* has its scope elsewhere. Where? In cases of those [roots] ending in *ac*.

The *bhuś* and other such suffixes occur there, because the suffix *cvi* is prescribed optionally after a word ending in a vowel (*ac*). Since the rule "after a vowel" (*ac*) continues to apply there, when both [the *bhuś* etc. and the *cvi*] would otherwise apply to words ending in *jyu*, the latter must necessarily occur due to its superior status (as a subsequent rule) in the context of the subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*). For this very reason, he says: "resembling that," and so forth.

Regarding the rule *ṭhnañivayuktamanayasadṛśādhikaraṇe tathā hyarthagatiḥ* (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 65), the prohibition *acveḥ* is intended so that words such as *abhṛśa-* and others ending in the suffix *cv-* may be understood as signifying similarity. That similarity belongs to the word ending in *cv-*, because its domain is the transformation of something into what it was not previously (*abhūtatadbhāva*).
It is the actual meaning (artha) that is relied upon, not what is produced by the word-form (*śabda*) and so forth; thus he says:
"from those whose objects consist of the transformation of what was not [into what is]," and so on.
Here, among the *bhṛśādi* group, some read words such as *manas* with prefixes; from those very forms with prefixes, [the suffix is applied].

It would become a *pratyaya*. Consequently, because the term *amanāyata*—which includes the prefix (*upasarga*)—would possess the designation of a base (*aṅga*), the augment *aṭ* would have to appear before the prefix in the form *udamanāyata*. Furthermore, in the case of *sumanāyya gataḥ*, since the prefix is incorporated within the element ending in the suffix *kvā*, it would be distinct from that [base].
If it were non-existent, there would be no compound, and consequently, [the desired form] could not be obtained? This is not so;

for just as in the case of "he wished to do" (*prakartum aicchat*), even though the object includes a prefix, the suffix is applied to the root alone—having extracted it from the prefix—by virtue of the mention of the "root" (*dhātu*).
The same will apply here as well. If it is argued that in that [previous rule] there is the mention of *dhātu* (root), [we reply:

the reason here is that the mention of *sup* (nominal suffix) continues [from the previous rule]. Words such as *sumanas* are collections ending in *sup*. Therefore, *kyaṅ* [is applied] after a collection ending in *sup*. Why is *laṅ* not [applied]?

Is this so? It is said: even in the rule for the prescription of the *laṅ* suffix, the mention of "dhātu" (root) is understood by implication (*anuvartate*). Now, while the word "lopaḥ" (elision) from [Pāṇini 3.1.11] is already being understood, what is the purpose of mentioning "lopa" again?
It is for the sake of excluding the letter *s*. For the previous mention of "lopa" was connected with the letter *s*.

Therefore, if that [preceding term] were to recur, this [subsequent one] would also have to recur; and consequently, even the infinite [term] would result in being elided. Otherwise, indeed, its recurrence would be purposeless.

13. *lohitādi-ḍājbhyaḥ kyaṣ* (Pāṇini 3.1.13). [Examples: *lohitāyate*. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *vā kyaṣaḥ* (1.3.90). [Example: *paṭapaṭāyate*. This is derived from the word *paṭat* by the rule *avyaktānukaraṇāt* (5.4.57).

Regarding the suffix *ḍāc*: by the rule "In the case of *ḍāc*, reduplication occurs diversely" (Vārttika 888), the reduplication takes place even before *ḍāc* is applied, because the term "*ḍāci*" [in the rule] is a locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*). Once *ḍāc* has been applied, there is the elision of the *ṭi* portion.

Regarding the reduplication, for the *t* which is a constituent of the syllable *at* [that results from reduplication], [the substitution of *ṭ* applies] by the rule "Necessarily when *ḍāc* follows a reduplicated form" (*nityam āmreḍite ḍāci*).

By the rule (Pāṇini 6.1.97), there is a single substitute for the subsequent form—the letter *p*. Regarding the statement "the addition of *kyaṣ* after *lohita* and words ending in *ḍāc*," and so forth:

the meaning of this prescription of *kyaṣ* by the *lohita*-sūtra is that it applies after the word *lohita* and after words ending in *ḍāc*. Now, one might object that there are other forms of words as well, such as *nīla* and others.
Since [the words] *lohita* and so forth are recited [in the list of roots], one might think that the suffix *kyaṣ* should also apply to them;

therefore, he says "among the *bhṛśādi* [roots]," and so on. Other words than *lohita* should be understood as being among the *bhṛśādi* [roots]. As for their recitation here [in the list of *lohita* etc.], that is due to negligence.

The intention is that [the word] is not an *ārṣa* (Vedic) term because it arose in a more recent time. If, then, other words are recited among the *bhṛśādi* group, the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) would be purposeless, for there is nothing else that could be included by it? To this he says: "Those which," and so forth. Those...
Since words such as *lohita* are recited in the *pramādādi* group, it should be understood that their inclusion in the *bhṛśādi* group is also intended;

however, this does not apply to words like *varman* which are not recited there. Therefore, when they are included by the mention of "etc. (*ādi*), only the suffix *kyaṣ* occurs, as in *varmāyate*. [In this formation,] the rule "there is elision of the *n* at the end of a nominal stem" (*nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*) applies.
(8.2.7) Thus there is the elision of *n*. By the rule "ṭhakṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ" (7.4.25), there is lengthening [of the vowel].

The words beginning with *nidrā* are recited here; although these denote only a state (*dharma*), they nevertheless apply to the substance (*dravya*) when the scope of the suffix *kyaṣ* is operative, due to the inherent nature of the expressive power of words.

Regarding the form "nidrāyate," the meaning is that one who is not sleepy becomes sleepy. But how can words not explicitly listed [in the *lohitādi* group] possess the status of being *lohitādi*? To this he says:
"And this is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class). How is this known? To this he says: "And thus," and so forth.

He says that the letter *k* is for the purpose of grasping the general category (*sāmānyagrahaṇa*), stating: "naḥ kye. In this regard, one might think: "The letter *k* is appended to the end of those [roots] listed among the enumerated ones that end in *n*, for the sake of the technical designation 'pada' (*padasaṃjñā*). To this he replies: "For not... and so forth. But how [is it possible] in the case of connection with *kyaṣ*?

[The question arises: "Since the rule *kṛbhvastiyoge* (Pāṇini 3.1.40) is understood [in this context], is it not the case that *ḍāc* is prescribed only when there is a connection with *karoti* and so forth, and not with *kyaṣ*? To this he says: "As if by *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *asti*," etc. This refers to the fact that *kyaṣ* occurs after those [roots] ending in *ḍāc*.

This very rule makes it known that just as the suffix *ḍāc* occurs when there is a connection with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*, so too does it occur with *kyaṣ*. Otherwise, the mention of *ḍāc* would be purposeless if *ḍāc* did not occur in connection with *kyaṣ*.
Now, one might object: when *ḍāc* occurs in connection with the root *bhū*, then [the suffix] *kyaṣ* would follow from that which ends in it (*ḍāc*).
"It will exist; so why is there pointlessness [in this rule]? This is not so; for the suffix *kyaṣ* cannot occur here, because the meaning has already been expressed by the verb *bhavati* itself.

Since the phrase "after the root *as*" (*asaḥ*) is understood to follow, *kyaṣ* is understood to apply only in cases where there is the transformation of something into that which it was not previously (*abhūtatadbhāve*).
The intended meaning is "by the logic of the *mañi*-affix. For just as in the previous rule (*pūrvasūtra*),

by virtue of the prohibition [of *kyac*] by the word *a-cveḥ*, *kyaṅ* is prescribed for the domain of "becoming that which one was not" (*abhūtatadbhāva*) according to this logic, so too is *kyaṣ* prescribed here.
14. *kaṣṭāya kramaṇe* (3.1.14).

The term *kyaṅ* is understood [from the previous rule], not *kyaṣ*, because only *kyaṅ* is marked with the svarita accent. The dative case in *kaṣṭāya* is established by the very wording of the rule itself, according to the principle "from that which is in grammatical agreement with a word ending in the fourth case."
A case-ending is obtained through semantic competency (*samarthya*); therefore, by virtue of that competency, the suffix is understood.

This word "kramaṇa" (stepping) exists in the sense of moving the foot, provided there is no lack of straightness (*anārjava*). Since the term "kramaṇa" denotes movement in general without specification, [the rule] ensures that the suffix is not understood as applying merely to the act of moving the foot.
A qualifier has been employed. *Jihmam*, *pāpam*, and *anārjavam* are synonymous.

Therefore, when [the word] is qualified by *anārjava* in this sequence, the suffix is understood to apply specifically to that movement characterized by crookedness (*anārjava*), and not to movement in general. And this is [the meaning of the rule] *dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ*.

From this and subsequent sūtras, it is understood that the term *vā* ("optionally"), which is carried over from the preceding rule, functions as a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (a restricted option). In the expression *kaṣṭāya kramaṇe*, the dative case is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*). Thus, *kaṣṭāyate* means "he practices crookedness for the sake of hardship. That is to say, he performs a crooked action directed toward hardship.

"This which has been stated is too little," because it does not encompass all the objects of application (*lakṣya*). How, then, should it be stated? He says: "satrakakṣa" (the printed reading) or "satrakaṣṭa," and so forth.
Although in this alternative analysis (*nyāsa*) there is no mention of the governing case-ending (*samarthavibhakti*), nevertheless...

Because of the governing context (*adhikāra*), a case-ending appropriate for that [meaning] must be supplied. "He intends to perform a sacrificial session" (*satrāyate*) means he desires to commit a sin (*pāpa*).
Regarding "he undergoes hardship" (*kaṣṭaṃ krāmati*): here the root *krami* refers to the movement of the feet; "hardship" (*kaṣṭam*) [is the object].

This is a word denoting an object (*karmapada*). The meaning is that he traverses a difficult and dense region. Alternatively—"difficult" (*kaṣṭam*) is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). The meaning is that the unborn one (*aja*) moves about in such a way as to be difficult.
Even in the case where it is an adverbial modifier, "difficult" ends in the accusative case. For it has been established: [text fragment].

In the sūtra "stokālpa... (Pāṇini 2.3.33), etc., it is stated that "the qualifiers of an action [function as] objects. Therefore, in this sūtra, the word *kaṣṭa* is mentioned with the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) in the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*). In the original examples (*mūlodāharaṇa*) as well, the second case, which is the appropriate case-ending (*samarthavibhakti*), must be supplied.
It is understood.

15. [The suffix *ṭhañ*] is applied after the word *karman*, when it is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*), provided that it is in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the words *romantha* and *tapas*, which are also in the ablative case. Even though there is coreferentiality with those two, the dual number [of the suffix] does not occur.

It occurs because the completion of the sentence applies to each [term] individually. Regarding the term *varticaroḥ*: *varti* means "turning" (*vartanam*); it is derived from the causative root (*ṇyanta*) with the suffix *ktin* in the feminine. But surely *ktin* should not occur here, since it is superseded by *yuc* according to Pāṇini 3.3.107: *ṇyāsaśrantho yuc*. Precisely for this reason...

There is no fault, for the suffix *ktin* will occur here by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). [The word] *caraṇam* [is derived from the root] *car* with the suffix *kvip*, because it belongs to the *sampadādi* group. [The root] *ṭhac* [is used in the sense of] moving, and so forth. That which is the chewing again, after having vomited up what was swallowed, is [the meaning].
"Movement of the jaw. Regarding this meaning, it should be explained that the suffix *kyaṅ* occurs after the word *romantha*.

This explanation, however, must be made by carrying forward the mention of the word "optionally" (*vā*) and relying on its status as a restricted option (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*). The mention of "optionally" [is required].
It must necessarily be applied so that there may be a sentence such as "he chews the cud" (*romanthaṃ vartayati*).

As in the expression "the insect chews the cud" (*kīṭo romanthaṃ vartayati*). It means that it turns over—that is, makes into a ball—the substance called *romantha*, which is either what has been vomited out (*udgīrṇa*) or what has been swallowed and then emerged through the back part of the throat (*avagīrṇa*).

The meaning is "he performs. Therefore, in this case, there is no movement of the jaw. However, in the original example [of the root], it certainly exists; for instance, in *romanthāyate*, the meaning is "having drawn back what was swallowed, he chews it again. And that chewing consists precisely of the movement of the jaw.
Others, however, explain the cognition regarding the movement of the jaw in a different way.

There exists this word *romantha*, which functions as a verbal root (*kriyāpada*), derived by forming the causative suffix *ṇic* according to the rule "the meaning of a root [is added] after a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt dhātvartha*) and so forth, and is then formed with the suffix *ghañ*. That [word]—

It occurs when there is a chewing, after drawing back, of a substance that has already been swallowed. Furthermore, this word is a denoter of a substance (*dravyavacana*) when it refers to a substance characterized by the act of rumination, whether it has been vomited or swallowed.
In this context, it is the denoter of the action (*kriyāvacana*) that is being grasped here; for even with respect to a substance, this [word]...

The present [tense] functions solely by means of action (*kriyā*); therefore, it is secondary (*gauṇa*) with respect to substance (*dravya*) and primary (*mukhya*) with respect to action. According to the principle that "when there is a choice between the secondary and the primary, the grammatical operation applies to the primary" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 4), [the suffix] occurs only from what expresses action, not from what expresses substance.

"Regarding the rule *ṭhtapasaḥ parasmaipadaṃ ca*," it requires the phrase "it should be stated" (*vaktavyam*). Since the ātmanepada would otherwise be obtained due to the indicatory letter *ṅ*, the parasmaipada must be stated—that is, explained. The explanation, however, is found under the rule *anudātaṅtiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.12) by means of the rule *napuṃsakamanapuṃsakena* (Pāṇini 1.2.69).
Based on this and other such sūtras, one should rely on the fact that the term *anyatarasyām*— which is carried over [into subsequent rules] by the logic of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*)—
is a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (an option restricted to specific cases). By means of that, [the suffix is applied] after *tapas*.

Furthermore, the *ātmanepada* does not occur after [a root] ending in *kyan*. Due to its absence, only the *parasmaipada* occurs by the rule "The *parasmaipada* is used for the agent after the remaining [roots]" (Pāṇini 1.3.78).
16. [The suffix *ṇi* is applied] after the words *bāṣpa* and *ūṣman* when meaning "emitting" (*udvamana*). (3.1.16)

Regarding the statement "it should be stated that [the suffix *kyaṅ* occurs] after the word *phena*," this must be explained as meaning that the suffix *kyaṅ* occurs after the word *phena* when it is used in the sense of vomiting. As for the explanation: one should proceed by carrying forward the letter *ca* from the rule *bhṛśādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.12) in the sense of an inclusive conjunction (*anuktasamuccaya*).
17. [The suffix *ghañ* is applied] after the words *śabda*, *vaira*, *kalaha*, *abhra*, *kaṇva*, and *megha*, when they denote the instrument (*karaṇa*).

Here, by the term "instrument," the action (*kriyā*) is meant, not the most effective means (*sādhakatama*). This is because, due to the governing rule "after an object" (*karmaṇaḥ*, Pāṇini 3.3.15), the suffix must be added to these words only when they function as objects (*karman*).

In that case, if the suffix were applied to the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*), the base and the suffix would be disconnected; furthermore, since the status of being an object (*karmatva*) depends upon an action, in the absence of an action, the status of being an object could not exist.
Therefore, having determined that the word *karaṇa* (instrument) refers exclusively to the action itself, he says: "In the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*)."

Regarding the phrase "in the sense of 'he makes'" (karoty-arthe): the expression "from *sudina* and so forth" (*sudina-ityādi*) is to be explained as having this meaning: the suffix *kyaṅ* occurs after words such as *sudina* when they function as objects (*karman*), in the sense of "he makes. As for the explanation:

Here too, one should proceed by carrying over that very particle *ca*, which serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. For this very reason, because of the particle *ca* used for the purpose of including what was not stated, there is also the inclusion of *aṭ* and the others.
By means of that, forms such as *aṭāyate* are also established.

"ṭhaṭāṭṭa," and so forth. The meaning of "grahaṇa" is "upādāna," which is "taking up" or "including. This [rule] is commenced because the suffix *ṇic* would otherwise apply by the rule "tat karoti" (Vārttika 200); yet that [application of *ṇic*] is also desired—as in the forms *śabdayati* and *vairayati*. Therefore, it should be understood that the recurrence of the particle *ca* ("and") is for this purpose as well.

18. *sukhādibhyaḥ kartṛvedanāyām* (Pāṇini 3.1.18). [The commentary states: "In the sense of 'feeling' (*vedanā*), that is, 'experience' (*anubhava*). Experience is the direct perception of an object through the senses. Now, one might object: the word *vedanā* is seen in common usage to denote mere cognition (*upalabdhi*) in general; how then is it [restricted here]?
Is a distinction obtained? We shall explain how it is obtained in the subsequent sūtra.

The agent is a factor (kāraka), and a factor exists only in relation to an action; and here, "feeling" (vedanā) is heard as the action, and no other. Therefore, the agent of that [action] alone is understood.

And he alone is understood to be the experiencer of that [pleasure and so forth]. Therefore, even though there is no specific designation, the word "agent" (kartṛ), which refers to the agent who experiences, is accepted here—this is what is meant by the phrase "if [the experience belongs] to the agent who experiences," and so on. By this inclusion of the term "agent," pleasure and the other [feelings]...

This shows that it is the agent (*kartṛ*) who is qualified, and not the feeling (*vedanā*). If the feeling were qualified by the mention of the agent—meaning that the feeling belongs to the agent—then this would also apply here:
"The beautifier feels the pleasure of Devadatta. [And] for the beautifier as well...

Feeling indeed exists as something related [to the agent], for he too is its agent. Just as the one who is being benefited experiences pleasure, so too does the benefactor. This, however, is the distinction:
