one experiences it through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), while the other does so through inference (*anumāna*); for in every respect...

If that [consciousness] were not the agent, the statement "it makes known" would be impossible, for one who is not an agent is not said to "make known. Therefore, the intention is that it is logical for the mention of the agent to be a qualification of pleasure and the other [feelings] alone. But surely, even if pleasure and the others are the qualifiers, that same fault remains.

Because pleasure and so forth are related even to the prover (*prasādhaka*) by way of a relationship characterized as the state of being produced and producer? This is not so; for in every case, pleasure and so forth are related to the agent (*kartṛ*), and this mention of the "agent" is indeed made for that reason. Therefore...

By the force of the inclusion of the term "agent" (*kartṛ*), that specific agent who is the substratum (*āśraya*) and the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of pleasure and so forth is understood. Therefore, it is recognized that the suffix occurs after words related to the agent through the relationship of substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) regarding pleasure and so forth; it does not occur after the one who brings about [the action].
Pleasure and the like do not have a material cause (samavāyikāraṇa); what then? They have an instrumental cause (nimittakāraṇa).

Those pleasures and so forth which belong to the agent—the material cause of pleasure and the rest—and which are related to him by way of the relation between substratum and superstratum, are perceived through direct perception (pratyakṣa). Therefore, that perception is of the nature of experience (anubhava).

Thus it is rightly said: "In the case of feeling (vedanā), there is the experience of an object. If, however, pleasure and so forth are qualified by the mention of the agent, and not feeling itself, then the genitive compound *kartṛvedanāyām* would not be possible due to a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*).
Since this is a scriptural statement, there is no fault in that the compound will occur even if there is a lack of semantic capacity;
or alternatively, it is simply not a compound at all, for the genitive case-ending is not heard because it has been elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39).
19. *namas-varivas-cit-raṅaḥ kyac* (3.1.19). [The commentary states:

"In the sense of a specific instrument (*karaṇa-viśeṣe*), when there is honor (*pūjā*) and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi-śabdena*), attendance (*paricaryā*) and wonder (*āścarya*) are included. By the rule beginning with *namasaḥ*, the aforementioned meaning [of the suffix] is stated immediately [after the root].

He demonstrates the division of the objects [of action]: although this meaning follows from the general term *karaṇa* (instrument), it is nevertheless obtained through the inherent nature of the expressive power [of the word], even without an explicit statement; just as, for example, the roots *pac* and others function in the sense of "softening by boiling" (*vikledana*) and so forth.

[The rule] "and after a *bahuvrīhi* [compound], when the sense of possession (*matvartha*) is intended" applies. [One says] "he pays homage to the gods" (*namasyati devān*). Now, an objection is raised: since the word *namaḥ* exists within the word *namasyati*, then by virtue of its connection with that, the dative case ought to occur according to the rule "after *namaḥ*, *svasti*, etc. (Pāṇini 2.3.16). This is not so; for there is the metarule: "When a meaningful item is mentioned [in a rule], an item lacking meaning is not included" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 1).

Because it is impossible to apply the word *namaḥ* in such a way that it possesses a [specific] meaning; or else, according to the rule "the case-ending denoting the grammatical relation (*kāraka*) is stronger than the case-ending denoting a secondary word (*upapada*)" (Cāndra-vyākaraṇa 2.1.69), the accusative alone occurs. The case-ending denoting the grammatical relation is stronger because it is independent of its connection with a secondary word.
However, the case ending derived from a secondary word (*upapada*) is weak because it depends upon another word. For example:
*namasyati* means "he performs a salutation. *Varivasyati* means "he serves. *Citrīyate* means "he causes wonder."
20. *pucchabhāṇḍacīvarāṇṇiṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.20).
[The commentary begins with] "from *puccha*" and so forth. *Udāsana* means throwing upwards; *paryāsana* means throwing all around.
When the suffix is applied in the sense of throwing upwards (*udāsana*), the prefix *ut-* is used for the sake of indicating that specific meaning.

It is employed as follows: "hutpuccchayate" (he shakes his tail). When the suffix is applied in the sense of "completely," then the word *pari* is used: "paripuccchayate. By the rule "the operation regarding the nominal stem is like that of iṣṭhan" (Vārttika 813), there is elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*) due to the application of the *iṣṭhavadbhāva* treatment. This is the act of collecting together (*samācayana*).
Accumulation; acquisition is the gaining of what has not been obtained; clothing is covering.
21. *muṇḍamiśraślakṣṇalavaṇavratavastrahalakalakṛtatūstebhyo ṇic* (Pāṇini 3.1.21).

By the rule *ṭhprātipadikāddhātvarthe bahulamiṣṭhavacca* (Dhātupāṭha-Gaṇasūtra 186), the suffix *ṇic* is established after words such as *muṇḍa*. This [present rule] is an elaboration (*prapañca*) of that very same [rule]. Although that...

The elaboration beginning with "it performs that" (*tatkaroti*) has already been stated; nevertheless, it is stated again here for the benefit of those of dull intellect. Regarding the phrase "or upon its cessation" (*tannivṛtau vā*): this refers to the cessation of eating. In the expression "he takes milk as his vow" (*payo vratayati*), the meaning is "he eats milk. In the expression "he takes the food of a *vṛṣala* as his vow" (*vṛṣalānnaṃ vratayati*), [the meaning is] he does not eat the food of a *vṛṣala*.

The meaning is "he eats. [As in the examples: "He takes hold of the ploughshare (halin), thus *halayati*; he takes hold of the dice (kalin), thus *kalayati*. Now, one might object: does this not show that here, in the case of the words *hala* and *kala*, the very same [roots] are intended? [The answer is: even in the rule (*sūtra*), only *hali* and *kali* are taken; however, the shortening of the vowel (*atva*) has been applied to those two.

[The inclusion of *halika* and *kalika*] is appropriate so that the treatment as a *san*-stem (*sanvadbhāva*), which would otherwise apply by rules such as *sanvallaghuni* (Pāṇini 7.4.93), does not occur. For in this case, the causative suffix *ṇic* is not difficult to obtain, since it is already established by the *gaṇa*-sūtra itself; this [mention of the two words] is stated merely for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*). And that...
The inclusion of *prapañca* is indeed appropriate for the inclusion of both *halika* and *kali*. However, this is the distinction:
when there is the inclusion of the two forms ending in *a*, then by the very rule of the *gaṇa-sūtra*, the suffix *ṇic* would also apply to those ending in *ī*.
Once that has been applied, by virtue of the treatment as *iṣṭhan* (*iṣṭhavadbhāva*), the elision of the *ṭi* (the *ī*) would follow; [and] of the vowel...

And by the rule *ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115), there is also the *vṛddhi* [vowel substitution]; both of these are indeed non-obligatory (*anitya*). For instance, although the elision of the *ṭi* suffix (*ṭilopa*) applies whether the *vṛddhi* has already occurred or not, it is non-obligatory because it results in the acquisition of a different form (*śabdāntaraprāpti*). To explain: once the *vṛddhi* has taken place, the *aikāra* [the long vowel *ai*]...

[The substitution] applies because the modification [of the final vowel] has not yet been performed; however, regarding the *vṛddhi* [substitution], since it would not apply once the *ṭilopa* (elision of the suffix) has occurred, it is non-permanent (*anitya*). Its non-application is due to the fact that [the stem] does not end in a vowel. Between these two non-permanent operations, the *vṛddhi* takes precedence because it is subsequent; once that has been applied, the *ṭilopa* occurs, and even then, the base (*aṅga*) does not have its initial vowel elided (*aglopi*).
If that were the case, then by applying the treatment of *saN* (the desiderative suffix) according to Pāṇini 7.4.93 (*sanvallaghuni*),
which causes the substitution of *i* for the vowel of the reduplicated syllable, and then applying the lengthening rule according to 7.4.94 (*dīrgho laghoḥ*),
the undesirable forms *acīkalat* and *ajīhalat* would result. However, in the case of the words *halika* and *kalika*...

When the forms *kṛta* and *āta* are included, although *vṛddhi* occurs because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], nevertheless, even when that [vṛddhi] has taken place, the suffix *am* is elided; thus, it becomes an *aglopy-aṅga* (a stem from which *am* is elided). Consequently, due to the application of the rule for *sanvadbhāva*, the desired forms *acakalat* and *ajahalat* are established. In that regard:

Only those two [elements] should be included whose inclusion results in the desired outcome, but not those whose inclusion leads to an undesired result; for it is not appropriate in a scientific treatise to formulate a rule that serves no purpose.
22. *dhātor ekāco halādeḥ kriyāsamabhihāre yaṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.22).

Regarding the term *ekāc*: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound and not a *tatpuruṣa*, because of the qualifying attribute *halādeḥ*. [The phrase] *kriyāsamabhihāre vartate* means "it occurs in the sense of the intensification of an action. By this—

It shows that the frequentative (kriyāsamabhihāra) serves as a qualifier of the verbal root. [The rule states: "Therefore, the suffix yaṅ occurs. Where? According to the principle that "suffixes whose meaning is not explicitly stated occur in their own sense" (Puṣpabhūṣita-pāda 90), it occurs in that very sense of the frequentative.

The primary *samabhihāra* (intensive repetition) consists in the gathering together into a single heap of things that were previously scattered across different locations, thereby attaining the state of a collective whole. However, this is not possible in the case of actions (*kriyā*) that perish as soon as they arise, because they cannot coexist simultaneously, and because a single verbal root (*dhātu*) cannot express multiple actions at once; therefore, in this context, it is used in a figurative sense.

In order to demonstrate *samabhihāra* (intensive repetition), he says: "frequency," and so forth. For both of these [frequency and accumulation] receive the designation of *samabhihāra* figuratively due to their similarity to *samabhihāra*.
Just as there is an accumulation (*samāhāra*) of substances that have been gathered together and not separated from other substances, [so too is there an accumulation of actions].
Likewise, this twofold [distinction] also applies to actions that are not separated from other actions;
thus, there is similarity. And action is of two kinds: primary and secondary.
Among these, the primary action is, for example, the softening [of grains], while the secondary action is, for example, placing [the pot] on the fire. In this regard, he who...

He who, having brought the cooking process to its conclusion at the final result and without undertaking another action, undertakes the cooking again, performs the *samabhihāra* (intensive repetition) of the primary action; *samabhihāra* is the repeated recurrence of those actions.
On the other hand, he who performs the actions beginning with placing [the pot] on the fire in their entirety, uninterrupted by other intervening actions, [performs the action in its totality].
It brings together qualities and actions; the intensification (*bhṛśārthatā*) of these is "intensive repetition" (*samabhihāra*).

Alternatively, intensification is the excellence of the result. For instance—that which, having attained the result of flaming, continues to flame or shines intensely—is said to "blaze forth" (*jājvalyate*) or "shine brightly" (*dedīpyate*).

Regarding the form *pāpacyate*: there is reduplication by the rule *sanyaṅeḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.9), and lengthening by *dīrgho'kitaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.83). In this case, there is no doubling [of the stem] according to the Vārttika *kriyāsamabhihāre dve bhavataḥ* (Vārttika 886); for the suffix *yaṅ*, which is prescribed specifically for the intensification of action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), already possesses that function inherently.

Because it possesses the capacity for that manifestation. As for the *loṭ* suffix which will be prescribed by the rule "In the case of the intensification of an action (*kriyā-samabhihāra*), let there be *loṭ*; and after *loṭ*, let there be *hi* and *sva* optionally in place of *ta* and *dhvam*" (Pāṇini 3.4.2), that *loṭ* is itself incapable of manifesting the intensification of the action and thus requires reduplication. For it [the *loṭ*]— [The sentence continues: —is not [capable of doing so on its own].

It is not prescribed for the intensification of action (*kriyā-samabhihāra*); rather, it is prescribed for the object (*karman*) and so forth, according to the rule: "The suffix *l* [is used] after transitive verbs in the sense of the object, and after intransitive verbs in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*)" (Pāṇini 3.4.69). Therefore, when that [suffix] is employed, reduplication certainly occurs—as in: "He cuts, saying 'cut! cut! (*lunīhi lunīhīty evāyaṃ lunāti*).
Regarding the form *dedīpyate*: the *guṇa* substitution is applied by the rule *guṇo yaṅlukoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.82).

Regarding the form *bhṛśaṃ prāṭati*: if the mention of the word *dhātu* ("verbal root") were not present [in the sūtra], the meaning of the rule would be that the suffix *yaṅ* occurs after a monosyllabic word beginning with a consonant (*halādi*) when it denotes the intensification of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāre*). However, because of the inclusion of *dhātu*, the intended meaning is restricted.

It might be so; and consequently, the suffix *yaṅ* would undesirably apply after the prefix *pra-* followed by the root *aṭ*. This is because the entire complex consisting of the prefix *pra-* and the root *aṭ* possesses the aforementioned qualifying characteristics. However, this undesirable consequence does not arise when the term "root" (*dhātu*) is included [in the definition]. For this [complex] is not a root; what is it then? It is a composite of a root and a prefix.
[The form] *jāgarti* [is derived thus]: due to its belonging to the *ad-ādi* class, there is the elision (*luk*) of *śap*. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "action" (*kriyā*)?
Could one not simply say "intensive repetition" (*samabhihāra*)? It cannot be so; otherwise, it would apply even in the case of the intensive repetition of a "means" (*sādhana*).
This is not the case, for this [mention of action] is a qualifier of the verbal root (*prakṛti*). And there is no intensive repetition of a means belonging to the verbal root.

The restriction is possible. Furthermore, since the term "in the sense of an instrument" (*karaṇe*, 3.1.17) continues to apply, it will qualify the repetition—namely, that the repetition must be related to an instrument.

Therefore, how could there be any occasion for the application [of the rule] to a repetition of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*)? This, then, is the purpose: [The text continues: ...this, then, is the purpose:

This is so that [the suffix] may apply when there is repetition of a mere action (*kriyāmātrasamabhihāra*); otherwise, because the understanding of the effect would pertain to the principal [action], there would be repetition only of the principal action (*pradhānakriyā*), and not of a subordinate action (*guṇakriyā*).
Regarding *sūci* and so forth: *sūca* means "malicious speech" (*paiśūnya*) [DhP 1873], and *sūtra* means "to sew" (*veṣṭana*).

Of these verbal roots— *ava-muc* (DhP 1908) in the sense of "unloosing," *mūtra* (DhP 1909) in the sense of "urination," *aṭ* (DhP 295) in the sense of "motion," *ṛ* (DhP 1098) in the sense of "motion," *aś* (DhP 1523) in the sense of "eating," and *ūrṇuñ* (DhP 1039) in the sense of "covering"— [the following applies].

Furthermore, the inclusion [of these roots] should be made in the rule (*vidhi*); and that is obtained because the preceding *ca* has the sense of an unexpressed conjunction (*anuktasamuccaya*). Why, then, is there this separate mention of these roots? He says: "For the sake of those [roots] that have multiple vowels (*anekāc*) and those beginning with a consonant other than *ha* (*ahalādi*). This means: for the sake of those that have multiple vowels and those that begin with a consonant other than *ha*.

That for which there is a purpose is described as such. There is the inclusion of the three roots beginning with *sūc*—namely *sūc*, *sūtr*, and *sīv*—along with their causative forms (*ṇijanta*), for the sake of multiple meanings;
of *ūrṇu*, however, for the sake of multiple vowels and for the sake of initial vowels and so forth; while for the remaining [roots], it is solely for the sake of initial vowels and so forth.

Regarding "sosūyate": there is the elision of the *ṇi* affix by the rule "ṇer aniṭi" (Pāṇini 6.4.51), and as before, there is *guṇa* substitution for the reduplicated syllable. Regarding "aṭāṭayate": by the rule "ajāder dvitīyasya" (Pāṇini 6.1.2), the letter *ṭa* is reduplicated;
then the "remainder is the first consonant" (*halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*) applies, followed by the lengthening of the vowel. Regarding "arāryate": [the same process applies].
By the rule *ṭhyaṅ ci* (Pāṇini 7.4.30), there is *guṇa*. There is reduplication of the second *ekāc*, namely the syllable *rya*.

However, the prohibition *na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.3) does not apply here, because of the statement in the Vārttika: "There is a prohibition for the *repha* that follows a *yakāra*. Thus, [the form] is *aśāśyate*; it is the reduplication of the second *ekāc*.
There is a doubling of the element *ṭhśya* [in the form] *prorṇunūyate*. Here too, there is a doubling of the word *nu*;

however, the *repha* (the letter *r*) is not doubled, because there is a specific prohibition to that effect: "It is not desired in cases such as *bhṛśaṃ rocate* and *bhṛśaṃ śobhate*. This is for the sake of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the phrase *vā* ("or").
The status of being a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (an option restricted by rule) is to be explained.
23. *Nityam* [is used] when *kauṭilya* (crookedness) and *gati* (motion) [are meant].

(3.1.23) [The word] "dhātoḥ" (from a verbal root) is understood from the previous rule. "In motion" (*gatau*) is an attribute of the base (*prakṛti*). The meaning is: "from a verbal root that denotes motion. He expresses this very same meaning by means of a synonym:

Regarding the rule "from a root denoting motion" (*gativacanāt dhātoḥ*): examples include *caṅkramyate* and *daṇḍramyate*. The roots *kramu* (meaning "to step," DhP 4.73), *drama*, *hamma*, and *mīmṛ* (all meaning "to go," DhP 4.66, 467, 468) take the augment *num* by the rule "the augment *num* is added after a root ending in a nasal" (*nugato'nunāsikāntasya*, Pāṇini 7.4.85). [This applies] when [the action occurs] over a shorter distance.

It performs goings and comings, accomplishing a crooked movement; thus it is said to "caṅkramyate" and "dedramyate. Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the word "nityam" (always/perpetually), since the sentence would not even arise here due to the lack of expression? For [the form] "caṅkramyate" does not [occur].
The sentence "he moves crookedly for the sake of concealment" (*vṛty-arthaṃ kuṭilaṃ krāmati*) is capable of conveying [this meaning].

For indeed, from the sentence "he moves crookedly," a doubt arises: is it a crookedness of movement, or is it a crookedness of mind? However, in the case of the derivative form *caṅkramyate* (he moves about), there is no doubt.
It is understood that the scope [of the rule] is indeed "crookedness of motion" (*gatikauṭilya*); thus he says: "The mention of 'nitya'," and so forth.

"Crookedness of motion" is the domain (*viṣaya*). That which has the restriction (*niyama*) of the *yaṅ* affix as its purpose (*artha*) or motive (*prayojana*) is described as such. By the words "because it expresses motion," and so forth, he demonstrates the purpose of the restriction.

The phrase "but not" (*na tu*) and so forth indicates what is excluded by that [rule]. Because the word *nityam* means "at all times," the suffix *yaṅ* occurs only in the sense of crookedness (*kauṭilya*), and never in the sense of the intensification of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*). Therefore, in the case of "he moves intensely" (*bhṛśaṃ krāmati*), the *yaṅ* which would have been obtained by the preceding rule [Pāṇini 3.1.22] does not apply.
[The suffix *kyaṅ*] occurs [after the following roots when contempt for the action is expressed]:
24. *lupasadacarajapajabhadahadaśagṛbhyo bhāvagarhāyām* (Pāṇini 3.1.24). [The roots are:
*luplṛ* "to cut" (Dhātupāṭha 1431), and *ṣadlṛ* "to perish, to go, to sink down."

(dhā.pā.1427), *ṭhabhra vabhra cara*—these have the meaning of "going" (dhā.pā.556, 557, 559); *ṭhjapa jalpa*—[used] in the sense of "distinct speech" (dhā.pā.397, 398); *ṭhpjabhī* [dhā.pā.} *jabha pjṛbhi*—in the sense of "bending the limbs" (dhā.pā.388, 389); *ṭhdaha*—in the sense of "reducing to ashes" (dhā.pā.991); *ṭhdanśa*...

Regarding the roots *daṃś* (to bite) [DhP 989] and *gṛ* (to swallow) [DhP 1410], the phrase "when there is censure of the root-meaning" (*dhātvarthagarhāyām*) expresses the meaning of "censure of the action" (*bhāvagarhā*). This is shown by the example "he cuts in a censurable manner" (*garhitaṃ lumpati*). Here, *garhitam* is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*); thus, "censure of the action" (*bhāvagarhā*) is intended here.
It is understood that [the action] is censurable because cutting is purposeless and because it is corrupted by faults;
in the same way, censurability should be understood in the subsequent cases as well. Regarding "cañcūryate":
the augment *nuk* is applied by the rule "caraphalośca" (Pāṇini 7.4.87), and the substitution of *u* for the following *a* is applied by the rule "utparasyātaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.88).

The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *ṭhhali ca* (8.2.77). Regarding *jañjapyate*: the augment *nuk* is applied by the rule *ṭhjapajabha* (7.4.86), followed by the substitution of *i* for the root-final *ṛ* by *ṛta iddhātoḥ* (7.1.100), the replacement of *i* by *r* (*raparatva*), and reduplication (*dvirvacana*). However, in the case of the word *giryāś*, the *repha* (the letter *r*) and the *yakāra* (the letter *y*) are eliminated by the rule *halādiśeṣa*.

There is *nivṛtti* (cessation), and as before, the suffix *guṇa* is applied; by the rule *ṭhgro yaṅ* (Pāṇini 8.2.20), there is the substitution of *la*. In the example "he recites well" (*sādhu japati*), there is no censure (*garhā*) of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*); rather, it is praise (*praśaṃsā*). In the example "the low-born man (*vṛṣala*) recites the mantra," censure of the agent (*sādhana*), namely the low-born man, is understood; for the low-born man...
Because a Śūdra lacks the qualification for the recitation of Vedic mantras.

25. *satyāpa-pāśa-rūpa-vīṇā-tūla-śloka-senā-loma-tvac-varma-varṇa-cūrṇa-curādibhyo ṇic* (Pāṇini 3.1.25). The inclusion here of words other than those beginning with *cur* is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*), since [the formation of denominative verbs] is already established by the rule: *prātipadikād dhātvarthe bahulam iṣṭhavat ca* (Vārttika 813).
Regarding the phrase "ṛgveda" and so forth: the word *vaktavya* means "to be explained. As for the explanation:

because of the rule "bahulam" (in various ways) in the sense of the root-meaning after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), which is intended to prescribe other grammatical operations, [the suffix] *ṇa* is applied to these.

The augment *apuk* occurs by virtue of its association with the suffix *ṇic*. However, it should be understood that the augment *āpuk* occurs for the word *satya* specifically because of the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in the rule "satyāpa. "Vipāśayati" means he causes the release of a noose. "Nirūpayati" means he perceives a form.

Regarding *ṭhabhiṣeṇayati*: the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule *upasargāt* (Pāṇini 8.3.65) and so forth. Regarding *tvacayati*: now, the word *tvac* ends in a consonant; therefore, when the suffix *ṇic* is added, since the status of being "like the superlative suffix" (*iṣṭhavadbhāva*) applies by the Vārttika *ṇāviṣṭhavat*, there would be the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*). In that case—

When the status of being "original" (*prakṛtibhāva*) has been applied by the rule *ṭhprakṛtyaikāc* (Pāṇini 6.4.163), the rule *ṭhata upadhāyāḥ* (7.2.116) would require a vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*). How then is it that the form must be *tvacayati*?
To this he says: "This word *tvac* ends in the letter *k*."

This is indeed another word ending in *a*, having the same meaning as the word *tvac*. For this very reason, there is the mention of the form ending in *a* (*tvaca*) in the Sūtra; once the final *a* has been elided, no *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) occurs due to the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). [The phrase] "from *cur* etc., in the sense of the root itself" refers to stealing and so forth.
"But surely, these meanings such as narrative (ākhyāna) and so forth are not included here in the Sūtra; how then are they obtained?
And if they are not obtained, how can they be indicated? To this he says: "Because it is inherent" (svābhāvikatvāt), and so on.
The denotation of meaning by words is inherent, not something resulting from explicit instruction.

That this is impossible has already been stated. Therefore, that meaning which, by its very nature, is the designator of a particular object is precisely the one appropriate to be indicated as following from the sūtra.
"According to each case" (yathāyatham) means that which belongs to each respective [object].

26. "And [the word] 'hetu' [is used]. (Pāṇini 3.1.26). Since in common usage a thing capable of being a means to an end is called a *hetu*, if that were what was intended here, then the causative suffix (*ṇic*) would also apply here—as in "he dwells for the sake of Vedic study" (*adhyayanena vasati*). Therefore...

To show that the term "cause" (*hetu*) is being used in its technical sense, he says: "The cause is the prompter of an independent [agent]. Furthermore, this is that for which the technical designation "cause" (*hetu*) is prescribed by the rule *tatprayojako hetuśca* (Pāṇini 1.4.55). But how is this understood? From the mention of the "prompted" (*hetumat*).

And because of the mention of the *curādi* group in the preceding sūtra; for here [in this sūtra], the term "instrument" (*karaṇe*) from 3.1.17 is understood, and since there is the governing context of verbal roots (*dhātu*), the suffix *ṇic* must be applied to a root in the sense of its instrument—that is, its action.
And if there were a reference to a worldly cause (*laukika-hetu*), [the word] would have been "when there is a motive" (*hetumati*).

One should not apply a qualification to the instrument (karaṇa), because there is nothing to be excluded— since every action indeed possesses a cause. Furthermore, in the preceding sūtra, one should not exclude the *cur*-class [verbs],
for even those beginning with *cur* are indeed verbal roots (*dhātu*), and their meaning is precisely characterized as action (*kriyā*).

One should make this a single rule: "And after the words *satya*, *āpa*, *pāśa*, *rūpa*, *vīṇā*, *tūla*, *śloka*, *senā*, *loman*, *tvaca*, *varman*, *varṇa*, and *cūrṇa*, the suffix *ṇic* [is applied]. For in this way, since the verbal root (*dhātu*) is the subject under discussion due to the presence of the particle *ca* ("and"), it will be understood that the suffix occurs in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). Thus, since this is established by a single rule alone—

Since he begins a separate rule and includes the mention of the *curādi* group in the preceding sūtra, it is understood that the term "cause" (*hetu*) is being taken here in its technical (paribhāṣika) sense. Regarding the phrase "connected with that" (*tadīya*), it refers to an activity consisting of an operation related to that [agent]. To the question "What, then, is this?", he says: "instigation" (*preṣaṇa*).

And so forth. *Ādeśa* is the directing of a subordinate, such as a servant, toward some purpose; it is an ordering. *Adhyeṣaṇā* is the employment of one worthy of honor, such as a teacher, preceded by respectful treatment.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the performance of actions conducive to that [purpose] is included. This—ordering and the rest—is the definition, that is, the essential nature [of authority].
That which possesses these is so described. Now, one might object that four things here possess causes:

the person to be prompted (*prayojya*), the activity of the person to be prompted such as placing [the pot] on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*) and so forth, the primary action to be accomplished by all the means such as softening (*vikleda*) and so forth, and the activity of the prompter (*prayojaka*) such as commanding (*preṣaṇa*) or requesting (*adhyeṣaṇa*).

For all four of these, there is a connection with the cause. In that regard, [the first] is because it is set in motion by that [cause], and because its intention is fulfilled. [The second] is because the cause proceeds toward a connection. [The third] is because of that which was set in motion by it.

Since the one who is prompted performs actions such as placing [the pot] on the fire by means of the instrument, and since that action is accomplished by him and he is inherent (*samavāya*) therein, the inclusion of the "prompted" (*prayojya*) is incorrect under the governing rule "in the sense of the instrument" (*karaṇe*); rather, only the others are to be included.

Since all [factors] consist of action (*kriyā*), it would be logical [to include them all]; why then is only that which has a purposeful operation (*prayojanavatkārya*) grasped? Even though all things consist of action, it is precisely the non-grasping of others that is logical. For instance, "cause" (*hetu*) is a designation for a specific type of causal factor (*kāraka*).

An agent (*kāraka*) is the cause of an action, and that becomes its cause only when it exists, whereas in its absence, the action does not occur at all. However, the operation of the one being prompted (*prayojya-vyāpāra*) does not exist only when the prompter (*prayojaka*) exists; for even in his absence, [the action may occur] simply because of the [prompter's] prior intention.

Because the operation of the prompted agent—such as the act of placing [the pot] on the fire—is possible; and even when that [operation] exists, the prompted agent does not act if he does not perceive his own purpose. Therefore, since the prompter lacks the status of a *kāraka* (participant in action) with respect to the operation of the prompted agent, he possesses no causality (*hetutva*), and thus he is not [a *kāraka*].

It possesses a cause. By this, it should be understood that even processes such as moistening are not causes for the specific primary action. Granted that it may somehow be a cause with respect to those two, nevertheless, it is not logical for those two to possess causality; because—
The suffixes *matup* and others occur when there is a desire to express abundance, censure, praise, constant connection, excellence, or association.

Because of this statement, suffixes such as *matup* are prescribed for the existence of an object qualified by abundance (*bhūman*) and so forth; however, in this case, other meanings such as abundance and the like are not possible due to their constant connection [with the word], since they are not perceived. For it is not the case that, as in the word "gomān" (possessor of cows), plurality is perceived, nor is it the case that...

And just as there is censure in the case of "kakudāvartin" (a hump-backed bull), praise in the case of "rūpavān" (handsome), and excellence in the case of "udarī kanyā" (a pot-bellied girl), so too is it in the case of the rule "hetumati. Furthermore, conjunction (*saṃsarga*) is not possible here; for conjunction is contact (*saṃyoga*), and that occurs only between two substances (*dravya*).

It is possible [for a relation to exist], as in the case of "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī*), where there is a connection between the staff and the person. However, activity (*vyāpāra*) is not a substance;

therefore, it has no connection with anything. Consequently, this possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) denotes a permanent connection (*nityayoga*), as in "trees that bear fruit" (*kṣīriṇo vṛkṣāḥ*). And it is not...

The constant connection of the operation of the person to be prompted—such as placing [the pot on the fire] and so forth, as well as the softening [of the rice] and so forth—with its cause exists; for even when that prompter has ceased, those two [operations and results] are possible.
However, even while he is present, they may not occur due to the proximity of an opposing factor, or because of impossibility. It is not [the case that the connection is non-existent].
Furthermore, a relationship is not possible when either one [of the two] is absent, because that [relationship] resides in both. Those two [the agent and the object] do not possess causality.

However, with respect to instigation (*preṣaṇa*) and so forth, there is an instigator who serves as the cause, because without him those [actions] would be impossible, and with him they become possible; therefore, he possesses the status of a *kāraka* (participant in action) in relation to them.

It arises from that; therefore, it has the designation "cause" (hetu). Even in the case of constant connection (*nityayoga*), the suffix *matup* indeed has its basis: because [the quality] exists from the moment of arising until destruction, as the activity such as impelling is inherently present in the cause. Therefore, since that [substance] alone possesses the cause, it is that which is grasped.

It is logical [to interpret] "in that which is denoted" as meaning "when the meaning is to be expressed by the suffix. By this, he demonstrates that the mention of *hetumat* (that which possesses a cause) is a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix, not a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). Consequently, those faults which arise under the view that it is a qualifier of the base-meaning [do not apply].

They have been refuted simply by not accepting that position. Furthermore, whatever objections might be raised against the view that the meaning of the suffix is qualified [by the action] have already been pointed out and resolved in the Bhāṣya itself;
they are not written here for fear of excessive prolixity.

Now, how is it that here the causative suffix (*ṇic*) occurs—as in "alms cause one to dwell" (*bhikṣā vāsayati*) or "a fire of dried cow-dung causes one to study" (*kārīṣo 'gnir adhyāpayati*)? And why should it not occur? Because [alms and fire] are insentient (*acetana*); for this [function of] commanding or entreating belongs only to one who possesses consciousness. This is not a fault; for it has been said:

Regarding this: "By the inclusion of the word 'ādi' (etcetera), there is the inclusion of the performance of actions conducive to that. By the word *tat* (that), one is connected to that which is to be employed or applied—such as clothing and so forth—in that context of wearing and so forth.
Those who are capable (*samarthāḥ*), meaning fit or suitable, such as specific satisfactions and the like; the performance (*ācaraṇam*) of those [is what is meant].

Accomplishment (*sampādana*) is the performance of that which is capable [of producing the result], and that too is indeed the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*). For alms-food, when obtained with abundant condiments, certainly produces a specific satisfaction that accords with one's taste. Likewise, even a fire of dried cow-dung (*kārīṣa-agni*) [produces heat] in windless places.
A well-kindled fire, by pacifying disturbances such as cold that are incompatible with study, bestows the capacity conducive to study;
therefore, it is appropriate for both of these [the fire and the teacher] to be considered instrumental causes.

Regarding the passage beginning with "tat karoti" (he does that): *tat* is the word for the object (*karman*). "He does this" is the indication of the meaning. The meaning is that an addition (*upasaṃkhyānam*)—that is, a formal presentation—must be made regarding the suffix *ṇic*, such that from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting an object, the suffix *ṇic* is applied in the sense of "he does that."
He asks, "For what purpose? and replies: "In order to express meanings such as 'he formulates a sūtra' (sūtrayati). Herein is the demonstration:

in the *curādi* class, the rule "after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), [the suffix *ṇic* is added] in the sense of the root-meaning" is taught as an elaboration (*prapañca*) of the rule "he does that" (*tat karoti*).
By means of this, the suffix *ṇic* is applied after nominal stems such as *sūtra* when they function as objects, in the sense of "doing."

Regarding the statement "it occurs," the sentence beginning with "from a narrative (ākhyāna) [is formed] a primary derivative suffix (kṛt)" is explained by the rule "from a narrative ending in a primary derivative suffix" and so forth. That which is narrated is a "narrative.
Whatever is narrated—be it the arrival of a king or anything else—all that is intended here by the term "narrative."

But it is not the event itself, such as the slaying of Kaṃsa, that is the "narrative" (ākhyāna). Rather, the word that denotes it is also called "narrative" by metaphorically applying the name of the denoted object to the denoting word. He says this because of the rule regarding the suffix *kṛt*;
and when a suffix is mentioned, the rule of "mentioning that which ends in it" (*tadantavidhi*) applies.

"From that which ends in a *kṛt* suffix," and so forth. "It should be stated" (*vaktavyaḥ*) means it should be explained. "That" (*tat*) is the object (*karman*). "He explains" (*ācaṣṭe*) is the meaning of the affix. "Elision of *kulluk*" (*kulluk*):
by the rule to be stated hereafter—"the elision occurs of that [suffix] by which the *kṛt*-ending expression is called"—[this is meant].

The connection [is as follows]: "There is a restoration of the original form" (*prakṛtipratyāpatti*). This means that the original base (*prakṛti*) which produced the suffix remains in its very same form, without modification of its meaning.
Regarding the phrase "and like the original base with respect to the *kāraka*": the word "and" (*ca*) is out of its regular order and should be placed immediately after "*kārakasya*."

It should be understood that the word *kārya* (effect) is to be supplied here. Thus, the meaning is this: just as the effect—such as the augment *aṭ*—occurs for a root like *han*, which is already formed (*kṛta*), so too does it occur for that same root when it is in its causative form (*ṇyantā*).
Furthermore, why is it said that "the *kāraka* also becomes like the original form (*prakṛtivat*)"? Because it is formed (*kṛtaḥ*).
Whatever the causal (*kāraka*) status of the base verb was, that same status remains even when that base is followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*).

Regarding this, the following explanation is given: in the *Cura* group of roots, the rule "from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the suffix [ṇic] is applied extensively in the sense of the verbal root's meaning, and it is treated like the desiderative suffix (*iṣṭhan*)" (Vārttika 813) is recited, as well as the rule "he does that" (*tat karoti*) and so forth.

This is an elaboration of that very point: "In many cases, it is for the purpose of prescribing what is additional; thus all this will be as stated. In the same way, the explanation should be made for subsequent cases as well. But for what purpose is the transfer (*atideśa*) of the effect described by supplying the word "effect" (*kārya*)? [It is] because [the rule] is a constituent part of the narrative (*ākhyāna*).

This is so that the grammatical operations such as the augment *aḍ* may apply to the base (*prakṛti*). Otherwise, if only an extension of the case-role (*kāraka*) were made— on the basis of the rule "the case-role is like that of the base" (*prakṛtivat kārakam bhavati*)— then, according to the maxim "when a *kṛt*-suffix is mentioned,
it includes [a word] preceded by a preverb (*gati*) or a case-role (*kāraka*)" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 126), [the suffix would apply] to words such as *kaṃsavadha*.
When the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied, the designation of "stem" (*aṅga*) and the status of being a verbal root (*nāmadhātu*) would belong to those very [words];

consequently, the augment *āṭ* and reduplication would apply to those very [words]. Furthermore, when a word is used to denote its own form as a root, it should be understood that the grammatical operation applies to a suffix attached to that [root]; thus, in the case of the word *kaṃsavadha* followed by *ṇic*, [the operation would incorrectly apply].

If the *tattva* (the state of being the root itself) were prescribed, these two [suffixes] would not occur; consequently, forms such as *kaṃsaṃ ghātayati rājānam ajīgamat* would not be established. Even in the case of the extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*), although the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is prescribed after collective expressions such as *kaṃsavadha*, nevertheless, that which belongs to the *kṛt* [suffixes]...

The *prakṛti* (base form) is [the root] beginning with *han* and so forth; just as an operation such as the augment *aṭ* occurs for that base when it is alone and not ending in a *kṛt* suffix, so too does it occur when it ends in a *kṛt* suffix once the causative (*ṇic*) has been applied. Therefore, this fault does not arise. Consequently, the grammatical operation is extended [to the derived form]. As in the example: "he causes Kaṃsa to be killed" (*kaṃsaṃ ghātayati*).

In the sense of the action of killing (*hanana*), the suffix *ap* is applied by the rule *hanaś ca vadhaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.76), and by its co-occurrence (*tatsanniyogena*), the substitute *vadha* is substituted [for *han*]. Thus, *hananam* becomes *vadhaḥ*. The compound *kaṃsasya vadhaḥ* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
From the word *rakta-kaṃsa-vadha*, the causative suffix *ṇic* is added, followed by the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ap*; there is then a restoration (*pratyāpatti*) of the original base form.

By abandoning the designation as the object of killing (*vadha*), the root *han* remains in its own form. There is a vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) by the rule "ata upadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.116), the substitution of *gha* for *ha* by "ho hanter ñṇinneṣu" (Pāṇini 7.3.54), and the substitution of *t* by "hanasta aciṇṇaloḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.32). And it is a *kāraka*.

In the case of this base [prakṛti], "kaṃsavadha," it remains exactly as it was; that is, Kaṃsa was the object (karman) and the agent (kāraka). Thus, the compound "kaṃsavadha" is formed with the genitive case of the object, characterized by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix. That Kaṃsa, by extension (atideśa), remains the very object even in the verbal action (*ākhyānakriyā*).
In the absence of such an extension [of the designation], the word *kaṃsavadha* or its referent would be the object (*karman*) of the verbal action (*ākhyānakriyā*),
because those two alone are thus pervaded [by that action].
However, since Kaṃsa has entirely relinquished his own operation within the act of narration, he does not possess the status of an object.

One should proceed accordingly. Therefore, there is an extension (atideśa) of the *kāraka* [case-role]. In the example "he causes the tribute to be bound" (*baliṃ bandhayati*), "binding" (*bandha*) is derived from the root *bandh* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). In the expression "the arrival of the king" (*rājña āgamanam*), the genitive case—which is characterized by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix—is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), and thus forms a compound. As for the remainder, such as the elision of the *kṛt* suffix and so forth, it should be understood as before, according to the appropriate application. Now...

Regarding the form *rājānam*, how is the accusative case [justified]? Since in the base form *rājāgamanam*—which ends in a *kṛt* suffix—the king was the agent (*kartṛ*), one would expect the genitive case according to the rule *prakṛtivacca kārakam* (Pāṇini 2.3.65). Alternatively, is it that the genitive is prohibited by the rule *na lokāvyaya* (Pāṇini 2.3.69)?

If that is so, does it not follow that the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) should apply? This is not a fault; because the root *gam* has the sense of "motion" according to the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārtha...* (Pāṇini 1.4.52), the king receives the technical designation of "object" (*karman*) here. Therefore, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) alone is logical.
Others, however, in order to resolve this very objection, describe the extension of the *kāraka* (the agentive factor) in a different way:

it is not understood that "like the base (*prakṛti*), like the base" means that whatever effect is desired for the base occurs only for the causative (*ṇijanta*) form; for in this case, the suffix *-vat* is not applied according to Pāṇini 5.1.116, *tatra tasyeva*.
What then? [It is formed] by the rule beginning with "tena tulyam" (Pāṇini 5.1.115). From that very [rule], it is understood:

"it behaves similarly to the *prakṛti*" is *prakṛtivat*. By the word *prakṛti* here, that which is the *prakṛti* of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), such as *kaṃsavadha* and so forth, is intended. And of that [causative base], by means of the action of narration (*ākhyāna-kriyā*)...

Because it is being pervaded, it must be performed; therefore, the meaning of the statement "the *kāraka* becomes like that of the base (*prakṛti*)" is as follows: just as the base from which the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is derived—which has become a narrative—possesses the status of an object (*karman*), so too does the *kāraka*. By this, the status of the agent (*kartṛ*) as an object is established. If this is so, then...

In the case of the expression "he knows the conjunction with Puṣya" (*puṣyayogaṃ jānāti*) or "he joins [the moon] with Puṣya" (*puṣyeṇa yojayati*), would there not also be the status of object (*karmatva*) for Puṣya? This is not so; because it is stated that "the *kāraka* is like the base form" (*prakṛtivat*), and Puṣya does not possess the status of a *kāraka*; rather, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is prescribed here due to its connection with an accompaniment (*sahayoga*).
He knows that conjunction which occurs with the moon; he joins [it] with Puṣya.

Regarding the rule "ṭhāṅlopaśca" (Pāṇini 3.4.19) and so forth: it should be stated that there is the elision of the prefix *āṅ* when it expresses a limit (*maryādā*). Because of the word "and" (*ca*) in the sūtra, the previously mentioned operations such as the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and others also apply. This refers to the rule "kālātyantasaṃyoge" (Pāṇini 3.4.26).

The pervasion of the entire duration of time is "extreme connection with time" (*kālātyantasaṃyoga*); when that is understood, [the rule] applies: "He describes the passing of the night. *Vivāsa* is the act of passing away; the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). "The passing of the night" (*rātrervivāsa*) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Subsequently, [the rule] *āṅ maryādābhividhyoḥ* applies.

(2.1.13) Thus ends the *avyayībhāva* compound. Here, the word *rātri* (night) refers to the activities associated with the night; furthermore, the root *vas* is preceded by the prefix *vi-* in the sense of "transgressing. Consequently, the meaning is this: those activities that have proceeded from the beginning of the day until the night has passed.

He explains it in its entirety: by the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule "the agent is treated like the base" (*prakṛtivacca kārakam*), when the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would otherwise be required for the agent characterized by a *kṛt* suffix, the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) occurs for the object, namely "night.
For in the act of transgressing, night is the agent; yet it possesses the status of an object (*karman*).

By the rule *pūrvavad gatyādi* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.52), [the suffix] *ṇic* is applied when "wonder" (*citrīkaraṇa*) is to be expressed; that is, when wonder is implied, the suffix *ṇic* is added. The elision of the *kṛt* suffix and so forth are as before. [Thus, *prāpayati* means] "Ujjayinī is a distant place from Māhiṣmatī."

It is a marvel that such a vast distance is traversed in so short a time. In the expression "the rising of the sun" (*sūryodgamanam*), there is a compound formed with a genitive case characterized by its connection to an agent (*kartṛ*). Here, the sun is the agent of the act of rising. In the verb "he accomplishes" (*sambhāvayate*), the meaning is "he reaches. The root *bhū* is used in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the sense of "reaching."
It is listed in the *curādi* group (*dhā.pā.* 844), and this is its form [in the present context]: *sūryam udgamayati*.

The suffix *ṇic* is added to the word *sūryodgamana*, with the elision (*luk*) of the *lyuṭ* suffix. Because of the extended application (*atideśa*) stated as "the case-role (*kāraka*) is like that of the base (*prakṛti*"), the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*), which would have applied to the agent (*kartṛ*) as before, is [prevented] by that [rule].
The second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is applied because [the word] bears the designation "object" (*karma*). The designation "object," however, is as explained previously.

Regarding the rule *nakṣatrayoge jñi*: when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) occurs in connection with a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), the suffix *ṇic* is added to that stem expressing the conjunction with a lunar mansion. The elision of the *kṛt* suffix and so forth are to be understood as before, according to the requirements of each case.
By the locative case ending in *jñī*, the meaning of the verbal root is indicated; therefore, the causative suffix *ṇic* occurs when the sense is "he knows.

The conjunction of the moon with Puṣya, which serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*), is *puṣyayoga*; from that, the suffix *ṇic* is applied, followed by the suffix *ghañ*, the elision of the *kṛt* suffix, and the restoration of the original form of the base. [The rule] "the *kāraka* remains as it was in the original" applies here.
Thus, by virtue of this extended application (*atideśa*), although Puṣya is not a factor (*kāraka*) in the act of knowing, it functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*);

hence, the third case ending is used for the instrument. However, when the intended meaning is "the conjunction of the moon with Puṣya," then it is not a subject for the extended application of *kāraka* status.
This occurs because Puṣya is not the agent; therefore, the instrumental case in "puṣyeṇa" should be understood as having the sense of "together with" (sahārtha).

27. *yak* [is added] after the class of roots beginning with *kaṇḍū*. Now, are these *kaṇḍū*-type items roots (*dhātu*) or nominal stems (*prātipadika*)? In that regard, if they were roots, then once the suffix *yak* is applied, the form *kaṇḍūy* would not be established; rather, *kaṇḍūay* would result.

But surely, the word *vā* (or) will carry over [from the previous rule], so that when the *yaṅ* suffix is absent, the form *kaṇḍūḥ* will result? This is not so; for a nominal suffix (*sub-vibhakti*) cannot possibly arise from a verbal root, since such suffixes are prescribed after nominal stems (*prātipadika*). This might be argued: [the suffix] could be added to the *yaṅ*-stem by the rule *anyebhyo 'pi*.

When the *kvip* suffix is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.178], with the elision of the vowel *a* by [6.4.48] and the elision of the letter *y* before a consonant by [6.1.66], will the form *kaṇḍūḥ* not result? This is incorrect; for the *kvip* suffix is prescribed in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), whereas by the word *kaṇḍūḥ*, only the sensation (*vedanā*) is expressed, not the agent. Nevertheless...

Since *sampad* and others belong to the class of *ākṛtigaṇa* (open-ended groups), one might derive *kaṇḍūḥ* by applying the suffix *kvip* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). Even so, forms such as *mantuḥ* and *valgūḥ* would not be established. If, however, by the recurrence of the word "or" (*vā*), the suffix *yap* optionally occurs after the words *man* and *valgu*, then [the forms are accounted for].
A case ending would not be applicable after those two; thus, *mantu* and *valgu* would remain forms lacking a case ending.

Furthermore, even if one were to apply the suffix *yak* after those two and then add *kvip*, the undesirable forms *mantūḥ* and *valgūḥ* would result. This is because once *yak* has necessarily been applied...

By the rule "ṭhakṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.25), there ought to be lengthening [of the vowel]. Now, if *kaṇḍv-ādi* were nominal stems (*prātipadika*), then the letter *y* in the suffix *yak* would be purposeless; for that [suffix] is intended to prevent the *guṇa* substitution which would otherwise apply by the rule "sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.84) due to the presence of a *kit* or *ṅit* suffix.
The prohibition [expressed by] "ca" (Pāṇini 1.1.5) is formulated for the purpose that it may take effect;
this purpose would not be applicable if those [suffixes] were *prātipadika*s, for a suffix prescribed after a *prātipadika* does not receive the designation *ardhadhātuka*. This is because...

To that [objection], he replies with the words "dvividhāḥ" (of two kinds), etc. Here, the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). Among those roots and nominal stems (*dhātu-prātipadika*), the suffix *yak* is applied to those which are roots beginning with *kaṇḍū*. The justification for this is found in the statement "because of the governing rule of 'root' (*dhātv-adhikārāt*)."

In order to confirm this very point, he says: "And thus," and so forth. Since the suffix is prescribed after verbal roots (*dhātu*) in this manner—because the context is that of verbal roots and not nominal stems (*prātipadika*)—the letter *k* is attached as an *anubandha* to the suffix *yak* for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa*. However, if [the suffix were applied] after nominal stems...

If [the element] were *yak*, since it would not be an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, there would be no possibility of *guṇa* substitution at all; therefore, the addition of the indicatory letter *k* for the purpose of prohibiting that [substitution] would be meaningless.
[The phrase] "because of the context of verbal roots (*dhātu-prakaraṇāt*), it is a verbal root" implies that it produces a suffix.
The term "dhātu" (root) from [Pāṇini 3.1.22] *dhātor ekācaḥ* continues to apply here. Therefore, only a verbal root such as *kaṇḍū* and others produces the suffix, not a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
As for the question "of what? and so forth, this attachment of the indicatory letter *k* is also for that very reason.

A verbal root (*dhātu*) produces a suffix (*pratyaya*). Otherwise, the addition of the letter *k* as an indicatory marker (*anubandha*) would be entirely meaningless according to the method previously stated. Therefore, because the suffix *yaK* is prescribed for those items beginning with *kaṇḍū* that have become roots, and because of the attachment of the indicatory marker *k*, their status as verbal roots is understood. Not [otherwise].
For [if they were] verbal roots (*dhātu*), the prescription of the suffix *yaṅ* would be untenable, nor would there be the addition of the indicatory letter *k*;
this is because there would be no purpose for it. Now, how is it determined that *kaṇḍv-ādi* items are nominal stems (*prātipadika*)?
To this he says: "And he said this," and so forth. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a reason. If these were indeed verbal roots...

Consequently, once the suffix *yaK* is applied, because the lengthening [of the vowel] would already be established by the rule *ṭhaki kṛte 'dīrghāt* (Pāṇini 7.4.25), one would not have pronounced the long vowels in *kaṇḍū-*, *hṛṇīṅ*, and *mahīṅ*; yet one does pronounce the long vowels. Therefore, it is concluded that "the verbal root (*dhātu*) is optionally [treated as such]," and thus these possess the status of verbal roots (*dhātutva*).

The meaning is "imagined" (vikalpitam). Now, one might argue that the long vowel is pronounced in the rule for the sake of ensuring that where the *yaṅ* suffix is absent—such as when suffixes like *kvip* follow roots ending in *ay*-augments—the long vowel is heard in forms such as *kaṇḍūaḥ*, *kaṇḍūatiḥ*, and *kaṇḍūatavān*. That [is not the case].

How could it be useless for that [suffix]? But how, then, do *kvip* and the others occur after verbal roots (*dhātu*), given that *yak* is only optional? And why is that so? Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "or" (*vā*). This is not correct; because this rule is compulsory (*nitya*). Its compulsion, however, is due to the fact that the mention of "or" (*vā-grahaṇa*) has been removed. Why?
Furthermore, why is its non-application not understood?

Because of the formulation of the sūtra beginning with "āyādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.31). If the word "vā" (or) were to carry over here, then because it would also carry over into the subsequent [sūtras], one would not have formulated this [rule] thinking that "āyādayaḥ" will optionally occur. And if that were not formulated, [the desired result would not follow].

The *āya* and other suffixes would also optionally apply even before *sārvadhātuka* affixes, because the mention of "optionally" (*vā*) is a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā*. Therefore, by the commencement of the rule beginning with "the *āya* and others," it is understood that the mention of "optionally" ceases; thus, the *yak* [suffix] is obligatory.

It must be so. Therefore, if these [words] were not *prātipadika*s according to their own position, the lengthening of the vowel in their utterance would be purposeless. Consequently, by the force of the lengthened vowel being uttered, they possess *prātipadika* status;
this is the definitive position. In that regard, under the view that they are verbal roots (*dhātu*), as in *kaṇḍūyate*:

In this way, [forms such as] *kaṇḍūyate*, *mantūyate*, and *valgūyate* are established; however, if the view that these are nominal stems (*prātipadika*) were not maintained, then in the absence of the suffix *yak*, forms such as *kaṇḍūḥ*, *mantuḥ*, and *valguḥ* would result. Furthermore, regarding those words ending in the vowel *a* that are listed among the *kaṇḍvādi* group, such as *magadha*, the rule "the elision of *ṭha*" (*ṭhato lopaḥ*, Pāṇini 6.4.48) applies.

There is the elision of the letter *i*: *magadhyati*, *sukhyati*, *duḥkhyati*. The words *leṭ* and *loṭ* are recited as their own forms; they are understood by their very form (*svarūpeṇa*), and not as suffixes (*pratyayatvena*), because of their association with the *kaṇḍv-ādi* group, which consists of words that are themselves forms (*svarūpaśabda*).
28. *gupū-dhūpa-vicchi-paṇi-panibhya āyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.28).

Regarding the phrase "with the meaning of praise" (*stutyarthena*), and so forth: the sequence in the [Dhātupāṭha] list is *paṇa vyavahāre stutau ca* (DhP 439) and *pana ca* (DhP 440). Among these, [the rule applies to] *pana ca*.
In this [Dhātupāṭha 440], the term "in the sense of praise" (stutau) is understood to carry over; it does not mean "for the purpose of worldly transaction.
Therefore, while *paṇi* has both the sense of transaction and the sense of praise, *pani* has only the sense of praise.
Consequently, here, due to its association with *paṇi* in the sense of praise, *pani* is also understood as having only the sense of praise.
Therefore, being engaged solely in praise, it produces conviction, but not in regard to worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).
[In the example] "of a hundred" (*śatasya*), the genitive case is used for the object according to Pāṇini 2.3.57: *vyavahṛ-paṇoḥ samarthayoḥ*.
Here, why does the ātmanepada suffix not occur in the word *paṇāyati*, given that...?

Why is *paṇi* read as unaccented (*anudātta*)? In that regard, according to the rule "that which is marked with the indicatory letter *ṅ* is *ātmanepada*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.12), just as the *ātmanepada* affixes occur after a simple root, they should likewise occur after a root ending in the suffix *ṇyat*.
To this he says: "The indicatory letter," and so forth. For that which is its indicatory letter...

In the case of *paṇati*, the purpose [of the rule] is fulfilled because it has already undergone the operations pertaining to the middle voice (*ātmanepada*); therefore, the middle voice does not occur after a root ending in the suffix *āya*, because that [form] constitutes a different verbal root (*dhātu*).

29. *ṛter īyaṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.29). The term *sautraḥ* means "belonging to a sūtra," because it is recited in a sūtra. That which exists in a sūtra is *sautra*. [The word *ṛti*] "occurs in the sense of *ghṛṇā*" (*ghṛṇāyāṃ vartate*). *Ghṛṇā* is loathing (*jugupsā*). This [word *ṛti*] occurs in that sense by its very nature. Now...

Why is it said "īy" and not simply "iy," so that when "īy" is substituted, the form *ṛtīyate* would be established? It is not established; for once the augment *iṭ* has been applied because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], the substitution of "īy" would not occur, as [the root] would no longer begin with a suffix. But surely...
Because it is *antaraṅga*, the substitution of *āya* alone will take place; its *antaraṅga* status is due to the statement:
"In the case of *āyan*, etc., there is a rule stating that they behave like the original base (*upadeśivat*) for the sake of achieving the desired accent" (Vārttika 1 on Pāṇini 7.1.2).
If this is so, then this [rule] indicates that: "The substitutions *āya*, *āna*, etc., do not [apply] to roots and suffixes..."
Thus, by applying the suffix *ḍha* to the root *śam*, forms such as *śaṇḍhaḥ* are established.

Alternatively, because of the rule stating that "in the application of vowel rules (*svaravidhi*), there is the status of being 'original' (*upadeśivadbhāva*) for the sake of establishing the accent," there is no [application of the] *antaraṅga* [rule]; consequently, due to its priority, the augment *iṭ* would occur.
Therefore, this [suffix] īyaṅ is prescribed.

30. *karmaṇi ṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.30). [The rule states: "The letter *ṇ* is for the purpose of *vṛddhi*," so that *vṛddhi* may occur according to *aca upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116). If this is so, for what purpose is it stated: "*na kampamicamām*" (Dhātupāṭha 817)?

Is it to prevent the shortening [of the vowel] by the rule "ṭhmiṭāṃ hrasvaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.92), so that the long vowel of *kāma* might not be shortened? This is not the case; for that [shortening] will not occur precisely because of the functional power (*sāmarthya*) of the designation *ṇit*. Otherwise, the application of the *ṇit* designation would be purposeless. Is it not purposeless? [No,] because of the rule "ṇer aniṭi" (Pāṇini 6.4.51).

Because it serves the purpose of grasping the general [form]. And when the affix *ṇiṅ* is absent by virtue of the rule "āyādīnām ārdhadhātuke vā" (Pāṇini 3.1.31), then the designation *mit* is prohibited so that shortening (*hrasvatva*) does not occur in the case of the causative affix *ṇic*.

31. *Āy-ādaya ārdhadhātuke vā* (Pāṇini 3.1.31). By the phrase "in the domain of the *ārdhadhātuka*," he shows that the term *ārdhadhātuka* functions as a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*). Its status as being within the domain of the *ārdhadhātuka*, however, exists when there is the intention to express it, even if it is merely present in the mind.
He says, "when there is the intention to express an *ārdhadhātuka* affix," implying that it occurs only in that case and not otherwise.
With what intention, then, is the locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*) resorted to? He thinks as follows:
under a locative of coexistence (*parasaptamī*), would there be an option between its arising or its non-arising? If it were its arising, then—

When the suffix *ktin* is prescribed after the root *gup* in the feminine, if the *āya*-pratyaya does not arise therein, then the desired form *guptiḥ* is established at will. However, when [the *āya*-pratyaya] does arise, then by the application of *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.48) and *vali lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.66), once the vowel *a* has been elided, if there is no subsequent disappearance [of the *āya* element], [the form *gopāyitṛ* is obtained].

When it is "gopāyati," then one's desire is protected and the desired goal is accomplished. But when it is "gopa," then one encounters the undesired. Whether protection exists or does not exist, if there is cessation [of the action], the desired goal is not accomplished; however, in the case of the locative of object (*viṣaya-saptamī*), it occurs upon arising.

It will arise when there is an option (*vikalpa*). Regarding the term *ārdhadhātuka*, the option applies at the very outset when there is the intention to express an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. In that regard, in the case where it does not arise, once the suffix *ktin* is prescribed for the feminine, the form *guptiḥ* is established; in the case where it does arise, [the form] is *gopāyā*. And yet—

The form *gopāti* is also undesirable, because the suffix *ktin* does not occur after a stem ending in the *āya* suffix. Nor does the undesired form *gopā* result, because the *āya* suffix is not produced [in that case]. Regarding the phrase "when there is the contingency of a compulsory suffix" (*nityapratyayaprasaṅge*), the meaning is: when the three preceding rules would have necessitated the compulsory application of the *āya* suffix and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "tadutpatau" and so forth: for those [suffixes] such as *āya* and others, the arising (*utpatti*) is optionally prescribed when an *ārdhadhātuka* affix is the domain, but not the cessation (*nivṛtti*) of those that have already arisen. For if cessation were optionally prescribed, then when an *ārdhadhātuka* affix exists as the domain, in the case of the suffix *āya*—

The intention is that if the suffix *ṭha* were prescribed by [Pāṇini 4.2.92] "nivṛte pratyayalakṣaṇena ṭha pratyayāt," and the suffix *a* were then applied, even under the condition of a locative case expressing the scope (*viṣayasaptamī*), the undesired form *gopet* would result.
Regarding the phrase "according to what is appropriate" (*yathāyatham*): whatever [suffix] is applicable from whichever [rule], that [is to be applied].
The meaning is that it arises from that [cause] at a time subsequent to the conceptualization of arising.
32. *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.32).
By means of the specific analytical statement "those whose endings (*anta*) are *san* and so forth," he demonstrates that this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
For a *bahuvrīhi* indeed occurs even when its members have different case-roles (*vyadhikaraṇa*), provided they convey the intended meaning (*gamakatva*), as for example: [the following examples].

"Kaṇṭhekālaḥ" (the one with blackness on the neck) and "urasilomā" (one with hair on the chest). By the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of all suffixes from *kyac* up to *ṇiṅ*. The term "aggregates" (*samudāyāḥ*) refers to the aggregates of base and suffix.
By this, he demonstrates that this is a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (inclusive) *bahuvrīhi* compound; otherwise, [it would refer only to] those characterized by *san* and so forth.
The designation "root" (dhātu) would be prescribed for the *prakṛtis* themselves. [As stated in] the *Kāśikā* and the *Padamañjarī*: "those whose designation is 'root' are called *dhātusaṃjñakāḥ*.
Those for whom "root" is the designation are *dhātusaṃjñakāḥ*. And here, the word "root" (*dhātu*) has its own form as its referent, not the referent consisting of the items beginning with *bhū*.

Otherwise, the terms *bhūv-ādayaḥ* (beginning with *bhū*) would be the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) for those [verbal roots] ending in *san* and so forth; and that is incorrect, for there is no purpose in establishing such a multitude of designations. Furthermore, technical designations are meant to be recurring; it is certainly not the case that all [roots] beginning with *bhū* are to be repeated.

In some treatises, it is said that the word *dhātu* does not denote that [meaning]. For here, in the rule prescribing technical names (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), there is the inclusion of suffixes such as *san* and others. And in the rule "A word ending in a *sup* or *tiṅ* is a *pada*" (Pāṇini 1.4.14), by the inclusion of the term "ending" (*anta*), this is made known: "When a suffix is mentioned, [the element] from which that [suffix] begins..."
"Whatever is prescribed [applies] to that which begins with it and ends with it" (Paribhāṣā 44).

This paribhāṣā is prohibited when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned in a rule for the assignment of technical names (*saṃjñā-vidhi*). In that case, if the word "end" (*anta*) were not mentioned, there would be no application of the rule "to that which ends with it" (*tadantavidhi*); yet this is desired. Therefore, the mention of the word "end" has been made for that purpose.

Regarding this, one who might instruct that by this mention of "the end" (*anta*), an entirely new rule concerning what ends in that is being established, is addressed as follows: "If, then, this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed for those ending in *san* and so forth,
then in the case of 'Devadattaḥ prācikīrṣat,' [the designation would apply] to Devadatta together with the prefix."

And [otherwise] the designation *saṃjñā* would result [inappropriately]. Therefore, he says: "By the very paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix," and so forth. For by this mention of *anta* (end), a previously non-existent *tadantavidhi* (rule of inclusion of that which ends in) is not being created; rather, since [the *tadantavidhi*] was prohibited by the mention of *anta* in the rule prescribing the designation *pada*, it is [reinstated] by the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix alone.

Furthermore, this is restated here: the meaning is that [the term *dhātu*], having been previously set aside, is now applied again. Consequently, the designation applies to the entire collection beginning from the very point where the suffixes *san* and others were prescribed, and not to something else preceding those words; such is the sense. Now, regarding "Roots are *bhū*, *vā*, and so forth" (Pāṇini 1.3.1):

Immediately following this, why was it not stated that "those ending in *san* and so forth are also [roots]"? For if this were the case, the mention of the term *dhātu* (root) would not need to be repeated twice. It cannot be done in this way; for if it were done thus, there would be no limitation on the scope of *san* and the other suffixes. However, when it is formulated as it is here...

It is understood that the inclusion extends up to the end of the *niṅ* [affix]. If that is so, why was it not stated as "and *bhūvādayaḥ*" immediately after "those ending in *san* and so forth are verbal roots" (Pāṇini 3.1.32)? This too is not [the case]; for if it were done in this way, [the rule] would depend on what has been previously enumerated (*anukrānta*).
The roots beginning with *bhū* would also require dependence on what has been enumerated;

consequently, the designation "root" (*dhātu*) would apply only to those enumerated [roots] such as *gup*, and not to others such as *bhū*. Alternatively, if the roots beginning with *bhū* do not require dependence on what has been enumerated, then the same would not apply to *san* and the others either; and thus—
There might be a doubt that the suffixes beginning with *san* and ending with *kṛt* (kapp) should be included; therefore, it is more logical to follow the original arrangement exactly as it stands.

33. *syatāsī lṛluṭoḥ* | (3.1.33) Here there are two forms of *lṛ*: one belonging to *lṛṭ* and the second to *lṛṅ*. Both of these are to be understood here, because it is so intended and because no distinction is specified. Consequently, these two—

And since there are three indicatory marks (*nimitta*)—namely *luṅ*, *liṭ*, and *laṅ*—while the two things to be indicated (*naimittika*) are only *syāt* and *asī*, there would be a discrepancy in number. Therefore, for one who might object that a "correspondence according to number" (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) cannot occur, he says: "The form of *lṛ*" and so forth.

By the omission of the *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) *ṭ* and *ṅ*, there is no distinction between the suffixes *ta* and *kṛtya*; thus, the form *lṛ* is common and identical for both *lṛṅ* and *lṛṭ*. Consequently, even though the causes [the suffixes] are two, [the resulting forms] are not dual; therefore, the application of number (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) is not contradicted.

This is the intended meaning. For this very reason, he says: "according to their respective order" (*yathāsaṃkhyam*). Regarding "he will do" (*kariṣyati*): the suffix *luṭ* is applied by the rule "lṛṭ śeṣe ca" (Pāṇini 3.3.13), and the augment *iṭ* is added by the rule "ṛddhanoḥ sye" (Pāṇini 7.2.70).
Regarding "he would have done" (*akariṣyat*): this is the conditional *lṛṅ*; the augment *aṭ* is added, and the vowel *i* is elided by the rule "itaśca" (Pāṇini 3.4.100).

Regarding "ṭhkartā" [he will do]: by the rule "anadyatane luṭ" (3.3.15), the suffix *luṭ* is used for the future not of today; then, by the rule "luṭaḥ prathamasya" (2.4.85) and others, the substitution of *ḍā* for *tip* occurs, and there is the elision of the *ṭi*. Regarding "iditkaraṇam" and so forth:
since it is both *it* and has the technical designation *itsaṃjñaka*, the act of making it such is "iditkaraṇam."

The meaning is that the letter *i*, which bears the technical designation *it*, is employed. Alternatively—the *tāsi* suffix that has an *idit* (an *i* marked with the *it* designation) is called *idit-tāsi*;

the employment of that [suffix] is the "employment of the *idit*," which means the employment of the *tāsi* suffix characterized by the letter *i* bearing the *it* designation. [This is] "for the purpose of preventing the elision of the nasal. However, if [this were not the case],...

In that case, by the rule *ṭhaniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24), there would be the elision of the nasal; therefore, the designation *it* is applied so that its prevention—that is, the obstruction of its occurrence—may take place. [The forms] *mantā* [are derived from] *mana jñāne* (Dhātupāṭha 1176) and *manu avabodhane* (Dhātupāṭha 1471).

Or rather: [the suffix] *ātmanepada* is applied by [Pāṇini 1.3.12] *anudātetaḥ*. Regarding the form *saṃgantā*, here too, since the root *gam* preceded by the prefix *sam-* is treated by [Pāṇini 1.3.29] *samo gami-* etc., once the *ṭilopa* has been performed in both cases, the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) would follow by resorting to the *ātmanepada* because of the *ṅ*-marker.

That [objection] is refuted by the fact that *tās* is marked with the *it*-indicator. If, then, the marking of *tās* as having an *it*-indicator is for the purpose of preventing the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*), this being the case,

then regarding what will be said in the rule "A *num* is added after a root marked with *it*" (Pāṇini 7.1.58)— namely, that "the function of the *it*-indicator applies to *tās* and *sic*..."— [that too would be problematic].
Is this not contradicted by the statement: "The vowel *i* without the nasal marker (*anunāsika*) is recited for the purpose of pronunciation [in the forms] *nāsti*"?

There is no contradiction, because they were composed by different authors. For this is the statement of Jayāditya, whereas that belongs to Vāmana. In Vāmana’s commentary (*vṛtti*), however, it is stated that the vowel *i* in the roots *tāsi* and *sic* is for the purpose of pronunciation.

The *anubandha* is not recited; therefore, no contradiction should be suspected. But with what intention did Jayāditya establish that the letter *i* in the root *tās-* serves the purpose of preventing the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika*)?
But what about Vāmana’s claim that [the rule] is for the purpose of pronunciation? Let that intention of his be heard:

the non-application (*asiddhatva*) based on the appearance [of the forms] is non-eternal (*anitya*); indeed, Jayāditya will demonstrate its non-eternality in that very same context. Of the non-application based on the appearance...

The non-validity (*asiddhatva*) of the elision of *ṭi* does not apply here; intending that this is due to its being non-eternal (*anityatva*), it was stated that the purpose [of the *ṭi*-elision] is to prevent the nasalization of the vowel *i* in *tāsi*.
Vāmana, however, considering that the non-validity of the elision does indeed apply here, stated that its purpose is merely for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). It is not so.

For, since the elision of *ṭi* would be considered *asiddha*, the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) would apply; therefore, it is incorrect to claim that the *ikāra* [in *ati*] serves to prevent that [elision]. For just as the teacher Gonardīya, relying on the presence of the *sannipātalakṣaṇaparibhāṣā*, [uses the example] "the very aged Brahmin family" (*atijaraṃ brāhmaṇakulam*).
It remains that it must be "atijarair brāhmaṇakulaiḥ" (by very old Brahmin families); however, others,

relying on the non-application of this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) due to its lack of permanence (*anityatva*), say that it must be "atijarasaṃ brāhmaṇakulam" (a very old Brahmin family) [and] "atijaraiḥ," and so too is this case.

It should be understood that the authors of the *Vṛtti* have stated this based on two purposes and relying upon the existence [of the topic] as established by the treatise (*śāstra*). Others, however, say: "The section concerning non-existence prior [to production] (*prāg-abhāva*) is unestablished. This...

It has been stated that, by relying on one view, the purpose of the letter *e* is to prevent the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika*); however, by relying on the other view—that the section concerning what is "not established" (*asiddha*) applies simultaneously with that [section]—it is said to be for the sake of pronunciation. But this cannot be understood, because the position that the section concerning what is "not established" precedes [the section on *bhāt*] has not yet been established.

Jayāditya and Vāmana do not accept this [view], because they do not rely upon it. Their non-reliance, however, is made manifest in that very commentary (*vṛtti*), and thus it should be understood from that source alone.
