Furthermore, these [substitutions] beginning with *sva-* are exceptions (*apavāda*) to all [suffixes] such as *yaṅ* and the rest, both by the maxim of "that which was not otherwise obtained" (*yenāprāpte*) and due to their being internal (*antaraṅga*).
Their status as internal (antaraṅga), however, is due to their being prescribed precisely at the stage of the *l* substitute.
34. *sibbahulaṃ leṭi* (Pāṇini 3.1.34).

[The example is] *ṭhjoṣiṣat*. From the root *juṣī* in the sense of "pleasure" or "service" (Dhātupāṭha 1288), the suffix *leṭ* is applied in the sense of the conditional (*liṅ*). The letter *i* in *sip* is for the sake of pronunciation; the letter *p* is for the sake of the accent. [Then the augment] *aṭ* is added by the rule *leṭo'ḍāṭau* (3.4.94).

Thus, after *aṭ*, by the rule "lopaḥ parasmaipadeṣu" (3.4.97), there is the elision of the *i* of the suffix; then, by "ārdhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ" (7.2.35), the augment *iṭ* is added; then the guṇa substitution for the light penultimate vowel occurs; and finally, by "ādeśapratyayayoḥ" (8.3.59), the *ṣ* substitution takes place. Thus we have "tāriṣat. [The root is] *tṛ*.

Regarding the roots *plu* (to float/swim) and *tṛ* (to cross), by the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.84) and *vyatyayo bahulam* (3.1.85), there is a transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyaya*) whereby the vowel *a* of the root is replaced by *ā*.
The remainder is as before. Regarding the form *mandiṣat*: [it is derived from] *madi*...

Regarding *pstuti*, *moda*, *mada*, *svapna*, *kānti*, and *gati*: [the root] *stu* is listed as *stuti*, *mud* as *modana*, *svap* as *svapna*, and *gai* as *giti* (according to the Dhātupāṭha 13). By the rule *ṭhthidito num dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.58), the augment *num* is added. Regarding *padāti*: [the root] *pad* is listed as *pada gatau* (Dhātupāṭha 1169).
The root *div* belongs to the first class (*divādi*) and is marked with the anudātta accent. By means of transposition (*vyatyaya*), the Parasmaipada endings are used, as is the *śap* suffix.
There is lengthening by homogeneous vowel (*savarṇadīrghatva*) together with the augment *aṭ*. Here, the elision of the *i* of *tip* does not occur;
this is because the word "optionally" (*vā*) is understood from the rule *vaito'nyatra* (Pāṇini 3.4.96) in that specific prescription. Thus we have *cyāvayāti*. [The root] *cyu*...

The roots *chāyṛ*, *jyāyṛ*, *pna*, *jhayṛ*, *pruṅ*, and *pluṅ* are listed in the Dhātupāṭha with the meaning "to go" (DhP 955, 956, 957, 958). [From these,] the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied. The addition of the marker *p* to *sip* is for the purpose of making it acute (*udātta*) by means of the accent known as *anudāttanivṛtti-svara* in forms such as *bobhūyiṣātām*.

This is for the sake of making [the *ta*] unaccented when it occurs. From the word *bobhūya*, which ends in *yaṅ*, there is the *ātmanepada* *leṭ*; then *ta*, and the substitution of *e* for *ṭi*. By "eta ai" (Pāṇini 3.4.93) and "leṭo 'ḍāṭau" (3.4.94), there is the augment *āṭ*.
Then, by the rule "anudātetaṅṅdupadeśāl lasārvadhātukamanudātam aṅgāt" (6.1.186), the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix is unaccented because the verbal root is taught with an indicatory *ṅ*.

By the rule (Pāṇini 6.1.186), the *anudātta* nature of the *sārvadhātuka* suffix is postponed in view of the accent of *sip*, despite its being an *antaraṅga* operation, due to the force of the inclusion of the marker *p*. Once that [operation] has been performed, the augment *iṭ* is added to *sip*; and that [augment] is *anudātta* by virtue of being an *āgama* (an augment). Then [the rule] "elision of *at*" (*ato lopaḥ*) applies.
By this [rule], there is the elision of the udātta vowel *a* of the *yaṅ* suffix;

its udātta quality, however, is due to the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*). Although the udātta quality would have applied by the rule "and [the vowel] of an anudātta [suffix] where there is elision of an udātta" (Pāṇini 6.1.161), the *iṭ* augment becomes anudātta because of the addition of the marker *p*.

35. *kāspratyayādāmamantre liṭi* (Pāṇini 3.1.35). By the mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*) here, there is the inclusion of affixes such as the desiderative (*san*) and others. This is according to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*): "In the case of the mention of an affix, [the term refers to] that which ends with it" (*pratyayagrahaṇe yasmāt...*), and by the rule: "That by which an operation is prescribed [denotes] what ends with it" (*yena vidhis tadantasya*).

Or rather, the rule of "extension to that which ends in such" (*tadantavidhi*) is understood here. Furthermore, because the governing topic is "roots" (*dhātu*), roots are specified by the mention of "affixes" (*pratyaya*); thus he says:
"from roots ending in affixes. The statement that "the *ām* affix occurs" is made by relying on the view that [the root] ends in a consonant (*halanta*).

It should have been stated that the suffix *ām* occurs after a stem ending in *a*; however, that was not stated, because it is understood from what will be said later—that the status of *ām* as having an indicatory letter *m* (*amitva*) results precisely from the fact that [the preceding element] ends in *a*. Furthermore, in the rule "in a mantra" (*ṭhamantra*), this is a locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*), not a locative of sequence (*parasaptamī*); therefore, there is a prohibition [of *ām*] in the case of a mantra.

This rule is understood to apply to both the *bhāṣā* (vernacular) and the *brāhmaṇa* (Vedic prose). A *brāhmaṇa* is indeed a work consisting of commentaries on the *mantras*. Now, one might object: according to the maxim of "negation with *nañ* and *iva*" (*vyā.pa.* 65), should this not apply only to the *brāhmaṇa* and not to the *bhāṣā*? This is not so; for if it were not [applicable] even to the *bhāṣā*,...

One might say, "He is a Brāhmaṇa," or "He has coughed" (*kāsāñcakre*). In the latter case, by the rule *āmaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.81), there is elision (*luk*) of the *liṭ* suffix. Since that [suffix] has been elided, the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) applies by the rule *kṛt-taddhita-samāsāś-ca* (Pāṇini 1.2.46) through the characteristic of the suffix (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*). Then the nominative suffix *su* is added; because it is read in the list beginning with *svarādi*, [it is unaccented].

Alternatively, because the particle *ca* in the rule *taddhitaścāsarvavibhaktiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.38) has the sense of an inclusive conjunction (*anuktasamuccayārtha*), the designation of indeclinable (*avyayasaṃjñā*) applies, and thus there is elision of the nominative suffix *su*. Or else,
the elision of *su* will occur here by the rule *halṅyābbhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.68).

What is the use of the designation "avyaya" (indeclinable) here? [Consider] *lolūyāñcakre*: from the word *lolūya*, which ends in *yaṅ*, the suffix *ām* is added. [Consider] *nonāva*: from the root *ṇu* in the sense of "praising" (*stutau*; DhP 1035), there is the substitution of *na* for *ṇu* by *ṇo naḥ* (6.1.65);
then *yaṅ* is added; and when we have reached the form *nonūyate*, the suffix *yaṅ* is elided by *yaṅe 'ci ca* (2.4.74).

*Luk*, *liṭ*, *tip*, and by the rule *ṭhparasmaipadānām* (Pāṇini 3.4.82), *ṇal* is substituted; there is *vṛddhi*. Here, by the principle of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (treating the suffix as present), *ām* would follow after a form ending in a suffix; however, this does not occur because of the statement *amantra* ("not in the case of a mantra").
[This refers to] the rule *kāsyanekācaḥ* and so forth. Having removed the mention of "suffix" (*pratyaya*), the mention of "having more than one vowel" (*anekāc*) is applied.

The meaning is that [the suffix] must be applied. To the question "For what purpose?", he says: "for the sake of *culumpa* and so forth. For according to the original formulation (*yathānyāsam*), after the word *ka*, which denotes Prajāpati as well as Viṣṇu, when the *kvip* suffix of habitual action (*ācārakvip*) is added, the suffix *ām* would undesirably apply even after a form ending in that; furthermore, it would not apply after roots such as *cakāsṛ* and others which end in no suffix (*apratyayānta*).

Therefore, this should be regarded as a different grammatical formulation (*nyāsa*). Others, however, maintain that because the mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*) implies "having more than one vowel" (*anekāc*), this [separate rule] need not be made;
but this is incorrect, for it is not logical that the mention of "affix" should serve as an implication for "having more than one vowel."
This is because there exist even monosyllabic roots (*dhātu*) that possess suffixes (*pratyaya*). We shall demonstrate later how this alternative interpretation (*nyāsāntara*) should be rejected.
For example: *cakāsāñcakāra*, *daridrāñcakāra*. [The root] *cakāsṛ* [is used] in the sense of "shining" (*dīptau*; DhP 1074).
The root *daridrā* is listed as "to be poor" (*durgati*) [in the Dhātupāṭha, 1073]. Regarding the form *culumpāñcakāra*:

although the root *culumpati* is not included among the enumerated verbal roots (*dhātu*), its status as a root should be understood through the authority of Kātyāyana’s statement that "the inclusion of the term 'having more than one vowel' (*anekāj*) in rules concerning the suffix *kā* is for the sake of including *culumpa* and others."

Now, one might ask why the technical designation *it* does not apply to this *am* by virtue of the rule *ṭhhalantyam* (Pāṇini 1.3.3). To this he replies: "Because of its being *amitva*," and so forth. That which has an *it* as its final element is called *it*; that which is not such is *anit*. The state of being *anit* is *amitva*. He explains how it is *amitva* with the words: "Because of its having no final vowel (*adantatvāt*)," and so forth.

For if it ended in the letter *m*, it would receive the designation *itsaṃjñā*; however, this [suffix] does not end in *m*, but rather ends in *a*. Therefore, the vowel *a* itself, being nasalized (*anunāsika*) in its original instruction (*upadeśe*), undergoes the designation *itsaṃjñā* by the rule "In its original instruction, a nasalized vowel is called *it*" (Pāṇini 1.3.2).

It prevents the designation *it* for the letter *m*. Just as in the case of *ame*, *amita*, *vama*, and *danta*, there is an absence of *guṇa* for the root *vid* due to its ending in *t*, so too, even in the absence of *guṇa*, for the root *vid* in the form *vidāñcakāra*, [the substitution] occurs only at the beginning because it ends in *ā*. Now, regarding its ending in *ā*:

In the case of *lope* by virtue of *satya-tas* (Pāṇini 6.4.48), because of the status as a *sthānivat* according to "that which follows [an elided element] is like the original when there is a rule concerning what precedes" (1.1.57), the vowel *i* does not become a *upadhā*; consequently, the *guṇa* substitution for a light *upadhā* does not occur.
However, its ending in *ad* is due to [the rule] "after *vid*, *uṣ*, *vid*, and *jāgṛ*, optionally" (3.1.38).

By this [rule], because the status of having the vowel *ā* as its final element is established through the co-occurrence (*sanniyoga*) with the suffix *ām*, he says—"And because of the prescription for *āścakāsuḥ*"—in order to demonstrate that even if one accepts the ending in *m*, it does not possess the quality of being *am*.
The connection is with the current topic, namely that "the *ām* is not *am*. This refers to the rule "after roots ending in *ā*, after *day*, and after *ās*" (Pāṇini 6.4.65). *Āsa* [is mentioned]...

[The substitution of *ām* occurs] because of the rule [Pāṇini 3.1.35]. Regarding the mention of *kāsi-* [in the rule], there is a supplementary statement (*upasaṃkhyāna*) that "the mention of *anekāc* [is for the sake of including] *culump-* and so on," and thus *cakās-* is also included. For by the inclusion of the word "and so on" (*ādi*), *cakās-* is indeed included. The purpose of designating the letter *m* as having the technical name *it* is this: [that it should be placed] after the final vowel.

Regarding the phrase "so that it may be": if *ām* were to have the status of an *am* (a case-ending), then the prescription of *ām* for the roots *cakās-* and *rā-* would be purposeless. For there is no difference whatsoever between them as to whether a *pa* occurs after the final vowel of those two roots in the *āśīrliṅ* (precative) or not; for in both cases, by the rule "ṭhakaḥ savarṇe" (Pāṇini 6.1.101), [the substitution of *āT* applies].

If it were long, that very form would remain; how then would this prescription of *ām* for the root *cakās-* be meaningful? It is meaningful only if *ām* follows immediately after [the root], and not otherwise. For there is no other purpose whatsoever; thus, due to the absence of a purpose, the designation *it* will not apply.

One should not entertain the doubt that, by virtue of the power of the rule [prescribing] the augment *āṭ*, the long-vowel substitution (*savarṇadīrgha*) will not occur here, or that the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "an augment follows after the final vowel or consonant" (P. 1.1.47) will not apply; for one who does not wish to contradict the attested forms (*lakṣya*), such an undesirable form would result. Thus, indeed, an undesirable form [would arise].

It might be so; however, it is not logical for a grammatical rule (*praklṛpti*) in the treatise to result in an unintended meaning. If, then, this [root] were indeed *adanta* (ending in /a/), the citation *āmamantra* would be untenable;
for by the rule of homogeneous lengthening (*savarṇadīrghatva*), it ought to be *āmāmantra*. To this he says: "the subsequent form" (*pararūpam*).

Regarding the phrase "as if ending in -ka": just as the single-substitute (pararūpa) [rule] applies in the case of *sarvatra lohitādikatantebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.18), so too does it apply here; thus, there is no inconsistency in the grammatical reference.

36. *ijādeśca gurumato 'nṛcchaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.36). [Note: The printed reading is *ṭhyaJ-ādeḥ*. Regarding "ijādeḥ": it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that whose beginning is *i*. Regarding "ic": this is the inclusion of the *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated term). Regarding "gurumān": this means "that which possesses a heavy (*guru*) syllable."

"Devoid of *ṛcchati*" means abandoned by *ṛcchati*; that is to say, devoid of its form. Regarding "he performed *īhā*": *īh* is [the root] "to exert oneself" (*ceṣṭāyām*, DhP 632); thus, "*ūhāñcakre*". Regarding "*ūha*":
[it is the root] "to deliberate" (*vitarke*, DhP 648).

*tatakṣa*, *rarakṣa*. [The roots] *takṣū* and *tvakṣū* mean "to make thin" (*tanūkaraṇe*; DhP 6.55, 6.56); *rakṣa* means "to protect" (*pālane*; DhP 6.58). *iyāja*, *uvāpa*. In the case of the roots *yaj* and *vap* with the suffix *ṇal* in the *uttama* (first person singular), when the option of the absence of *ṇit*-status applies according to *ṇal uttamo vā* (Pāṇini 7.1.91):

Due to the absence of *vṛddhi*, there is an absence of the status of being "heavy" (*gurumat*). Some cite *iyeṣa* and *uvoṣa* as counter-examples. [Regarding] the roots *piṣ* (DhP 3.20), *iṣ* in the sense of "desire" (DhP 4.18), and *uṣ* in the sense of "burning" (DhP 2.107):
in the *ṇal* suffix, there is the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel, followed by reduplication.

By the rule *ṭhabyāsasyāsavarṇe* (Pāṇini 6.4.78), the substitutes *iy* and *uv* are applied. Now, one might object: "Since these two [stems] also become heavy (*guru*) once the *guṇa* substitution has been made, shouldn't the augment *ām* necessarily occur? It need not occur;

for according to the maxim *sannipātalakṣaṇo vidhiranimittaṃ tadvighātasya* (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 12), a grammatical operation conditioned by a specific configuration does not cause the destruction of that very configuration upon which it depends.

The occurrence of *liṭ* is the cause for [the suffix] having a heavy syllable (*gurumatā*). And by the rule "ṭhāmo" (Pāṇini 2.4.81), this very *liṭ* is prohibited. Alternatively, in the term *gurumataḥ*, the suffix *matup* denotes constant connection; therefore, it must occur where there is a constant connection with a heavy syllable, and this is not the case for the roots *iṣ* and *uṣ*.

There is a connection with the rule regarding a heavy syllable (*gurumat*). If this is so, then in the case of *ucchī vivāse* (DhP 2.16)—as in *ucchoścakāra*—once *tuk* has been applied, the rule would not apply. This is not a fault;
for the prohibition regarding the root *ṛcchi* makes it known that [the rule] applies even to that which follows a syllable made heavy by the arrival of an augment (*āgama*).
It becomes [bhavati].
Regarding "ṛccha": from the root *ṛcch* (DhP 1296), meaning "to go, to perish, to become embodied";
by [the rule] *che ca* (6.1.73), there is the insertion of *tuk*; and by [the rule] *ṛcchatyṛtām* (7.4.11), there is *guṇa*.
There is reduplication, the *halādiśeṣa* [remains], the lengthening by *ata ādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.70),
and the insertion of *nuṭ* by *tasmānnuḍ dvihalaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.71). Now,
one might object that the rule *ṛcchatyṛtām* (Pāṇini 7.4.11) prescribes *guṇa* for the root *ṛcchati* when followed immediately by the *liṭ* [perfect] suffix.

This is an indicator (*jñāpaka*): the suffix *ām* does not occur after the root *ṛcch*. For if that [suffix] were present, it would not have indicated that [the substitution] occurs even from that which has a heavy syllable (*gurumat*) due to the cause of *āgama*. Therefore, the prohibition "not after *ṛcch*" (*anṛcche*) must be formulated.

"Of the root *ṭhūrṇoti*," and so forth. Because [the root] begins with *ij* and possesses a heavy vowel (*gurumat*), the suffix *ām* would apply; therefore, a prohibition must be stated—meaning it must be explained. The explanation, however, is as follows:
the term *anyatarasyām* (optionally), which will be mentioned later, is carried over by way of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*) maxim.

This must be understood as a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (an option restricted by specific conditions). Thus, in the form *prorṇunāva*, the reduplication of the syllable *nu* occurs according to Pāṇini 6.1.2 (*ajāder dvitīyasya*), but the *repha* (the letter *r*) is not reduplicated due to the prohibition in 6.1.3 (*na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ*).

"Or rather, *ṭhatha vā*," and so forth. [The root] *ṇu* is used in the sense of "praising" (*stutau*, Dhātupāṭha 1.35). That which behaves similarly to that is "like *ṇu*" (*nuvat*); its state is "the state of being like *ṇu*" (*nuvadbhāva*). The meaning is that it behaves in a manner similar to the root *ṇau*. But what is the purpose for which it must be expressed in such a way? To this he says:

"The purpose [of this rule] is the establishment of *yaṅ*. Now, when the *nu*-vṛddhi occurs, just as *yaṅ* applies to the root *nau*—as in *nonūyate* according to *dhātor ekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.22)—so too does it apply to the root *ūrṇu*: *prorṇonūyate*. [The mention of *ām*] is for the sake of prohibiting [the application of *yaṅ*] after *ām*.

It is required that the status of *nu* be stated [as an augment]. When that is present, just as *am* does not occur after the root *nau*—due to its inclusion in the *aniṭ* list and the absence of *guṇa*—so too it does not occur after the root *ūrṇu*:
namely, *prorṇunāva*. [This is because of the rule] "And for a monosyllabic root, [the prohibition applies] due to the prefix," [and thus] "the status of *nu* must be stated."

Thus it is connected [to the rule]. The ablative case is used according to the Vārttika 127: *karmaṇi ṭhlyablope* ("the ablative is used for the object when a word ending in *lyap* is elided"), as in *prāsādāt prekṣate* ("he looks from the palace") or *āsanāt prekṣate* ("he looks from the seat"). *Iḍupagraha* means the prohibition of the augment *iṭ*. This is what is meant: while the rule *ekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.10) is being carried over...

Regarding the augment *iṭ* that is applied by the rule "ṭhśrayukaḥ kiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.11), it must be stated that for the root *ūrṇu*, there is the substitution of *nu*. By this, just as there is a prohibition of *iṭ* for the root *nū* by the rule "ṭhśrayukaḥ kiti"— as in *nutaḥ* and *nutavān*— so too [is there a prohibition for *ūrṇu*].
Likewise, from the root *ūrṇu* as well—[we have] *prorṇutaḥ* and *prorṇutavān*.

Alternatively, this ablative case [in the rule] is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*), according to the principle: "That need not be prescribed, because the technical name itself is the authority" (Pāṇini 1.2.53). This is because the augment *iṭ* is prescribed after a monosyllabic root when it is preceded by an *upagraha* (an ātmanepada marker).

Therefore, the meaning is that for this purpose—that is, for this reason—the substitution of *nu* for the root *ūrṇu* must be stated. Now, what is the purpose of the particle *ca* in the rule "ṭhijādeśca"? It serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned;
by means of it, the need to state "kāsyanekācaḥ" (Vārttika 205) does not arise. This remains the case even under the alternative formulation.

Because forms such as *cakāsāñcakāra* are established by the inclusion of the letter *ca*. Now, if this were not stated, would it not follow that [the suffix] would also apply after a one-syllable root (*ekāc*) ending in a suffix?
If this is not desired, then one must carry forward (*anuvartayitavya*) the mention of the word "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) which will be stated later.
One must accept that this is a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).

37. *dayāyāsaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.37). [The example is] *palāyāñcakre*. In the case of the root *ayati* preceded by *parā*, there is the substitution of *l* for *y* according to the rule *upasargasyāyatau* (8.2.19).

38. *uṣavidajāgṛbhyo 'nyatarasyām* | (3.1.38) From the roots *uṣ* and *jāgṛ*, as well as from *vid*—which is *parasmaipada* and has the meaning of "knowing"—the [suffix *liṭ*] optionally takes the *parasmaipada* endings; however, this does not include the two *ātmanepada* roots *vid* having the meanings of "existence" and "investigation," nor...
Regarding the root *vid* which takes both *padas* (voices) for the sake of the suffix *lābha*,
[the author] states— “*vid* in the sense of knowing”— to show that, by association with the *jādy-ādi* group or the *ādy-ādi* group, only the *ādy-ādi* form of *vid* is intended to be included.
In the form *viveda*, because it lacks the long final vowel (*ādantatva*), the *guṇa* substitution indeed occurs, due to its connection with the suffix *ām*.
It is understood that *vid* has the property of ending in a short vowel; therefore, the absence of *guṇa* applies only there and not elsewhere. Hence he says:
"Because it is asserted that *vid* ends in a short vowel, *guṇa* does not occur before the suffix *ām*."

39. *bhī-hrī-bhṛ-hu-vām śluvac ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.39). The phrase *bhī-hrī-bhṛ-hu-vām* uses a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the sense of an ablative (*pañcamī*), according to the rule *supāṃ supo bhavanti*. The term *śluvat* means "like *ślu*" (*śluviva śluvat*). This is derived from the rule *tatra tasyeva* (Pāṇini 5.1.116).

The suffix *vati* is applied after a word ending in the seventh case (*saptamī*). This is an extension of grammatical operations (*kāryātideśa*). For this very reason, it is said: "In this [case], the operation is as in *ślu*. [This refers to] "doubling (*dvitva*) and *it*-ness. Doubling occurs by the rule *ślau* (6.1.10), and *it*-ness occurs by the rule *bhṛñām it* (7.4.76). In the absence [of these],...

Otherwise, in the case of *atideśa* (extended application), the reduplication based on *liṭ* would not occur when there is an intervention by *ām*; likewise, the substitution of *it* would also not occur, because in the rule prescribing that [substitution], the term *ślau* is understood from the preceding rule, "guṇaḥ ślau" (Pāṇini 7.4.75). Therefore, for the sake of establishing both of these, [the rule states] "as in *ślu*" (*śluvat*).
Thus ends the extension [of the rule].

40. *kṛñ* is employed after [the verbal root] when the *liṭ* suffix follows. (Pāṇini 3.1.40). Regarding the phrase "is employed after" (*anuprayujyate*): the two words *anu* and *pra* are each nominative singular forms. The word *yujyate* is a middle-voice (ātmanepada) form ending in the third person singular. Regarding the phrase "of the *ām* suffix" (*āmpratyayasya*).
The term *āmpratyaya* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that from which the suffix *ām* arises.

By using the word "afterwards" (*paścāt*), [the author] explains the meaning of the prefix *anu* and thereby rejects its prior usage. Furthermore, because all sentences have the nature of being restrictive (*sāvadhāraṇa*), the action of *kṛñ* (to do) must follow the suffix *ām* itself.

"It is employed"—this restriction is intended here; by this, its employment when there is an intervention is excluded. For when *kṛ* is employed with an intervention, it is not only the *ām* affix that is subsequently employed, but other words as well. [In the case of] *liṭ*.

By the phrase "after another suffix" (*parataḥ*), he states that there is no usage [of the auxiliary] when another suffix follows. But surely, by the rule *āmaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.81), there ought to be elision (*luk*) of the *liṭ* [perfect]; so how can *kṛñ* be employed as an auxiliary after *liṭ*? This is not a fault; for this is not the meaning here—that which [is formed] by another rule...
The meaning is that the root *kṛ* is prescribed to be employed as an auxiliary following a verb ending in the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*). Now, an objection is raised:

"Since it is stated that *kṛ* is used, the employment of *bhū* and *as* as auxiliaries—as in *pācayāmbabhūva* and *pācayāmāsa*—would not be established. To this he replies: "By means of a *pratyāhāra* [comprehensive term] for *kṛ*."

And so forth. By taking the word *kṛt* from the rule "abhūtatadbhāve kṛbhvastiyoge" (Pāṇini 5.4.50), this [word] is understood as a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated reference) by means of the letter *ñ* in the rule "kṛño dvitīyatṛtīyaśambabījāt kṛṣau" (Pāṇini 5.4.58). By that *pratyāhāra*, [the following is indicated].

The three categories—kṛt, bhv-adi, and asti—are understood here; since all three are included therein, there is no fault. Even so, the subsequent application of the root *as* is not established, because by the rule "for *as*, [substitute] *bhū*" (Pāṇini 2.4.52), it ought to be replaced by *bhū*. To this he says: "by the force of that" (*tatsāmarthyāt*). This is because of the re-introduction (*pratyāhāra*).
By the force of the inclusion of the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* [in the rule], the substitution of *bhū* for *as* does not occur.

The purpose of including these in the pratyāhāra (abbreviated designation) is so that there may be the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of *as*. If the substitution of *bhū* were to apply to the subsequent application of *as*, the inclusion in the pratyāhāra would be useless.

One might say, "The root *kṛ* is employed in conjunction with [the verbal roots] in the periphrastic future (*liṭ*). Even in that case, this doubt would be resolved: "Is this the mention of the root *kṛ*, or is it the mention of the pratyāhāra (the grammatical abbreviation)?
If, then, the mention of the pratyāhāra *kṛñ* is intended, then in this situation, regarding the term *abhividhau*:

[An objection is raised: "By the rule *sampadā ca* (Pāṇini 5.4.53), the employment of the verb *kṛ* as an auxiliary (*anuprayoga*) would follow, because [the root *kṛ*] is included within that pratyāhāra [of the suffixes *san* etc.]? [Response: This is not a fault; for the term *dhātu* ("verbal root") is carried over from the rule *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.32), and by that, the root *kṛ* is qualified—namely, the *kṛ* which is...
Regarding the term *dhātu* (root): this *dhātu* is not [defined] as "that which possesses" (*sampadana*), but rather it is a collection of a root (*dhātu*) and a prefix (*upasarga*).
Therefore, [the suffix] is not applied [to such a form]. For example, in *pācayāmbabhūva*: from the causative (*ṇyanta*) of the root *pac*, the suffix *ām* is added.

The substitution of *ay* for the suffix *ṇi* occurs by the rule *ṭhayāmantālvāyyetnviṣṇuṣu* (6.4.55). The substitution of *ā* for the vowel of the reduplication occurs by the rule *ṭhbhavateraḥ* (7.4.73). The augment *vuk* is added by the rule *ṭhbhuvo vug luṅliṭoḥ* (6.4.88).

But for what purpose is this stated, given that it is incomplete and lacks an expressed verbal action? For from this, there is only the manifestation of the time of the action (*kriyākāla*), and not the determination of the means (*sādhana*) or the number of persons (*puruṣasaṃkhyāna*). Indeed, [these cannot be known] without a word ending in a *tiṅ* suffix.
Their manifestation occurs [through them].
Therefore, since their purpose is not yet fully accomplished, the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of the roots *as* and *am* will take place;
this is so that the subsequent application of *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* may occur, but not that of *pac* and the others.

If it is argued that [the rule] "of *pac* and so forth" (Pāṇini 3.1.13) should not apply, we say no; for since *pac* and so forth denote specific actions, the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) would be untenable. Indeed, it is a word denoting a general action that is applied as a subsequent element to a form ending in *ām*, which denotes a general action.

Or [is it] that which expresses a specific [action]? In that regard, first of all, an affix ending in *ām* that expresses a general [action] cannot admit the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of a word expressing a specific [action], because such a thing is impossible. For the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* express general [actions], and no *ām* affix has been prescribed after them by anyone.

Should a word expressing a specific quality (*viśeṣavācin*) be employed as a subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) after a form ending in the suffix *ām*—which itself expresses a specific quality—is it to be one that has the same meaning (*samānārtha*), or one that has a different meaning (*bhinnārtha*)? In this regard, a word with the same meaning is certainly not employed as a subsequent application, because its meaning has already been expressed (*uktārthatvāt*). And when such a word is intended to be employed as a subsequent application after the form ending in *ām*:

The manifestation of the meaning of the entire action, time, and so forth occurs [through the root]. By implication, that very root alone should be employed as the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) where the manifestation of all [aspects] occurs. In that case, even if it has a different meaning, a preceding element that shares the same meaning as the verbal suffix (*kriyānta*) does not deserve to be used as the subsequent application; for its meaning is not manifested therein. This is the subsequent application.
[The suffix] is employed for the purpose of manifesting the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*),

and it is not possible for the means (*sādhana*) and so forth— which possess meanings entirely distinct from the meaning expressed by the verbal root— to manifest that meaning; however, they can be manifested by [the suffixes] which express a general category (*sāmānya*).

For when a specific term is in proximity, a general word is restricted to that specific sense; thus, when the general words *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* are employed as subsequent verbs (*anuprayoga*) in proximity to a form ending in *ām*, they function only with respect to the specific meaning expressed by that [form]. Therefore, it is only these—*kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*—that are to be used as subsequent verbs.

Should this [rule] not be commenced because [the result] will come about [naturally]? This is not so; for just as the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* denote action in general, so too does the root *vid*. Therefore, its subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) would also occur. Consequently, this [rule] is commenced in order to exclude that, and also to exclude separated application (*vyavahita-prayoga*).
Let it not be that [the rule] "Devadatta caused [the food] to be cooked" is excluded;
rather, the exclusion of separated usage is obtained through a specific restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). For all sentences have exclusion as their result.

This is obtained either because the particle *ca* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) as its fruit, or because it has the sense of a collective inclusion (*samuccaya*) of what has not been explicitly stated.

Furthermore, [the word] must be commenced for the purpose of excluding the contrary; however, the exclusion of the contrary is obtained from the fact that *anu* has the sense of "subsequent" (*paścāt*).

41. *vidāṅkurvantu* optionally. (Pāṇini 3.1.41) [The rule] "the suffix *ām* is prescribed after the root *vid* in the imperative (*loṭ*)" does not apply here because it is prescribed for the perfect (*liṭ*). Therefore, this is also established as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). By relying on the suffix *ām*, the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) is avoided.

And there is the absence of that [suffix]. Since the *luk*-elision prescribed by the rule *ṭhāmo* (Pāṇini 2.4.81) would not apply to the *loṭ* [mood], there is *luk* for the *loṭ*. The subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) of the root *kṛ* after a *liṭ* [verb] has been stated, but it does not apply after a *loṭ*; therefore, that too is treated as an irregularity (*nipātana*), and thus it occurs in all cases.
It is to be connected [with the previous]. Regarding "kurvantu": this is the plural form; *jhi* is replaced by *ant*; by *er uḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.86), *u* is substituted for *jhi*;

assuming the *vikaraṇa* suffix, there is *guṇa* of the root; by *ata ut sārvadhātuke* (6.4.110), *u* is substituted for the final *a*; and the *yaṇ* substitution occurs for the *vikaraṇa*. Regarding "itikaraṇaḥ" and so forth...

Since the mention of the *loṭ* endings is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), he says "not only... and so forth, in order to show what is desired [by the author]. Regarding "kurutām": by the rule *tasthas* (Pāṇini 3.4.101), *tas* is replaced by *tām*. Regarding "kuru": by the rule *serhyapicca* (Pāṇini 3.4.87).
The *hi* [suffix] is elided by the rule "ṭhutaśca pratyayāt" (Pāṇini 6.4.106), etc. Regarding "kurutam," this is the form of the suffix *tas* changed to *tam*.

42. *abhyutsādayām*, *prajanayām*, *cikayām*, *ramayāmakah*, *pāvayām*, *kriyāt*, *vidāmakran*—these forms [occur] in the Veda (*chandas*). Regarding *abhyutsādayām*: when the compound has been formed by the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18), [the suffix *am* is added].

This [word] "idam" ending in the nominative case is singular; likewise, "prajanayām" is also [singular]. The remaining forms ending in the first person suffix -ām are also nominative singulars. "Akaḥ" is the aorist (luṅ) of the root *kṛ*, ending in the third person singular. "Akran" ends in the third person plural.
Regarding "ṣadji-ni-ramīṇām": *ṣadlṛ* is [listed] in the sense of "falling apart, going, and sinking" (DhP 1427);

*janī* in the sense of "manifestation" (DhP 1449); and *ramu* in the sense of "sporting" (DhP 853). Regarding "of those ending in ṇic": this refers to those [roots] that have been converted into the causative (*hetumaṇṇic*) form. Regarding "of *pacati*": [this refers to the root *pac*].

Because it is prescribed for the *liṭ* [perfect tense], the *liṅ* [optative] would apply; therefore, it is treated as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). Regarding "of the suffix *ṭha*": this refers to the causative form of either *punāti* or *pavate*. Regarding "it is treated as an irregular formation in the *lṛṅ* [conditional] and *liṅ* [optative]": this is because, as in the previous case, the desired form would not otherwise be obtained.
Regarding "for *vid* as well, there is an absence of *guṇa*": this means that even in the case of the root *vid*, there is no strengthening by *guṇa*.

The rule *ṭhpugantalaghūpadhasya* (Pāṇini 7.3.86) would require a *guṇa* substitution; however, its absence is established here by way of a *nipātana* (irregularity). In the form *abhyutsādayām*, there is the substitution of *ay* for the preceding vowel (*ṇi*) as before. In *luṅ*, there is elision (*luk*). In the word *akaḥ*, it is the *luṅ* of the root *kṛ*, with the augment *aṭ*, the suffix *tip*, and *cli*; of this [the elision occurs] in a *mantra*.

By [the rule] *ghasahvara* (2.4.80), there is elision (*luk*); then *guṇa*; then *raparatva*; then by *halṅyābbhyaḥ* (6.1.68), there is elision of the *ti* suffix; and for the *repha*, there is the *visarjanīya*. Regarding the form *abhyudasīṣadat*:
by [the rule] *ṇiśri* (3.1.48) et cetera, there is *caṅ*; and by *ṇau caṅyupadhāyāḥ* (7.4.1) [there is shortening].
The short vowel [is substituted], then reduplication by *caṅ* (Pāṇini 6.1.11), the *halādiśeṣa* rule,

the *sanvadbhāva* by *sanvallaghuni* (7.4.93) resulting in *it*-lengthening, and finally the lengthening by *dīrgho laghoḥ* (7.4.94). This process should be understood to apply mutatis mutandis in subsequent cases as well.

Regarding the root *ṭhprajanāyām*: because of the rule *janījṛṣknasurañjo'mantāśca* (Dhātupāṭha 817), it is designated as *mit*, and thus there is shortening of the vowel. Regarding *cikayām*: here the letter *k* is also introduced by way of a nipātana; the *guṇa* and *āyādeśa* [substitutions] then apply. Regarding *acaiṣīt*: the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *astisico'pṛkte* (Pāṇini 7.3.96).

In *sici vṛddhiḥ*, [the rule applies]. In *aramayām*, [the rule] "mitāṃ hrasvaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.92) applies. In *pāvayām*, by the rule "āmaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.81), there is the elision (*luk*) of the optative suffix (*liṅ*). In *kriyāt*, the root *kṛ* takes the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of a benediction; the suffix *tip* is added, the *ikāra* is elided by "itaśca" (Pāṇini 3.4.100), *yāsuṭ* is added, and *riṅ* [is substituted for the *ikāra*].

In *śayagliṅkṣu* (Pāṇini 7.4.28), there is the substitution of *riṅ*; in *sko saṃyogādyor ante ca* (8.2.29), there is the elision of *s*. Regarding *pāvyāt*: the *liṅ* suffix is applied as before; because of the rule *liṅaśiṣi* (3.4.116), it is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka*, and thus there is no *śap* affix; furthermore, by *ṇer aniṭi* (6.4.51), [the *ṇi* is elided].

There is elision of the *ṇi* suffix. Regarding "vidām": this is the *luṅ* [aorist] of the root *vid*, with the *ām* augment, the absence of *guṇa*, and the elision of the *luṅ* suffix. Regarding "akran": this is the *luṅ* of the root *kṛ*, with the *cli* suffix, the replacement of *jhi* by *an*, the elision of the *ikāra* by Pāṇini 3.4.100 (*itaśca*), the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*), and for the *cli* suffix, the substitution of *ghas* in a mantra.

(2.4.80) [the suffix] *luk* [is applied]; [then] *aṭ* [is added], and the substitution of *yaṇ* [occurs]. [The form] "avediṣuḥ" [is derived as follows]: *iṭ* is added after *sic*, and by [Pāṇini 3.4.109], *jus* replaces *jhi*. "The particle *iti* is for the purpose of showing the actual usage. Other forms of this kind should also be understood as occurring in the Veda (*chandas*).
This is the meaning.

43. *cli luṅ* (3.1.43). [The statement] "the letter *ṭh* is for the sake of pronunciation" means that its purpose is merely pronunciation and there is no other purpose whatsoever. By this, he shows that the grammatical operation (*saṃjñākārya*) of being designated as an *it* does not apply. [The letter] *c*... [is for the sake of... *cakāraḥ*.

[The suffix] *svarārthaḥ* [is used] so that there may be the final acute accent (*antodātatva*) by [Pāṇini 6.1.163] *citaḥ*. Now, why is the letter *e* in [Pāṇini 2.4.80] *mantre ghasahvaraṇaśavavṛdahādṛckṛgamijanibhyo leḥ* not intended for the general inclusion [of all roots], and why is the letter *ca* not intended to prevent its exclusion?

How is this understood? It is thought as follows: there is no suffix after *man*, *tra*, *ghas*, and so on, for which this vowel *i* could serve the purpose of denoting a general category (*sāmānyagrahaṇa*). And since that purpose of denoting a general category does not exist, the purpose of the particle *ca*—namely, to prevent the exclusion (*avighāta*) of those [suffixes]—is also untenable. This is the case in the rule *āmaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.81).

In that case, why do the vowels *i* and *ca* not serve the purpose of preventing the inclusion of the general term? For in that context, in the rule *mantre ghasa-* (Pāṇini 2.4.80), the word *liṭaḥ* (from 3.4.78) is understood to carry over; and in the absence of *i* and *ca*, there would be the principle: "When a term without an *anubandha* is mentioned, it does not include one with an *anubandha*."

[Objection: In that case, there would be the elision (*luk*) of that [suffix] alone, not of the *liṅ* and *liṭ* suffixes? [Response: This is not so; let there be no recurrence of the mention of *liṅ* here, yet the elision will occur for any suffix whatsoever without distinction.
When this is the case, nothing undesirable follows; for there is no such suffix...

If there were elision (*luk*) of this [suffix], some undesirable consequence would follow. Even if the reference to the suffix *li* (*ligrahaṇa*) were to continue [from a previous rule], there would be no fault; for when multiple items are to be grasped, a general term is employed, and there is nothing other than *li* that follows *ām* which could be grasped as multiple. Indeed, nowhere else does anything other than *liṭ* follow *ām*.

Since there is such usage, and because of the absence of anything else [to which it could apply], the term *liṭ* itself is what is being referred to. In that case, the vowel *i* (in the suffix *liṭ*) serves no purpose for the sake of grasping the general category, nor does the letter *c* serve the purpose of preventing its obstruction. But is it not the case that in forms such as *pāvayāṅkriyāt*, there is also another *liṭ*? This is not so; [it is included] precisely by virtue of the technical designation (*nipātana*).

That is established. And that [term] must necessarily be treated as an irregular formation (*nipātana*); otherwise, even if the vowel *i* were applied and the letter *c* added to prevent its obstruction, the form *abyutsādayāmi* would not be established. Therefore, the previously stated purpose alone is logical.
We shall demonstrate later how the particle *ca* has the sense of "and so forth.

Now, for what purpose is the *cli* affix introduced and then replaced by *sij* and the rest, rather than simply prescribing *sic* as the general rule (*utsarga*) and then prescribing *ksa* and the others as its substitutes? It is not thus.

It is possible [to argue as follows]: since there is no *cli* suffix in the rule *ṭhśala igupadhādaniṭaḥ ksaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.45), the mention of "non-iṭ" (*aniṭ*) would be understood as a qualifier of the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself—namely, "of a root that does not take iṭ. And in that case, the form *aghukṣat* from the root *guh* would not be established, because that root is marked with the indicatory letter *ū* (*ūdit*).

Because the optionality of the augment *iṭ* is prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.2.44] *svarati-sūti-sūyati-dhūñ-ūdito vā*, there is no absence of *iṭ* (*aniṭtva*). When the suffix *cl* is present, that very suffix is qualified by the mention of "non-*iṭ*"—namely, "of *cl* which is non-*iṭ*. And since the *cl* following the root *guh* has optional *iṭ*, when *eṇ* (the augment *iṭ*) is absent, then...
Because of the absence of the *niṭ* designation for the root *clṛ*, the suffix *ksa* is established.

44. *cleḥ sic* (3.1.44). [The commentary states: "The letter *i* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārthaḥ*). By this, showing that there is no purpose other than pronunciation here, he indicates the absence of the designation *it*. But surely, if the *anubandha* letter *i* were not present...
By the rule *ṭhaniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24), the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) would apply here in the form *āmaṃsteta*;
therefore, why is this [the letter *s*] not considered to have the technical designation *it* for the purpose of prohibiting that [elision]? It is thought thus:
even in the absence of the indicatory vowel *i*, the elision of the nasal must occur for a root ending in *sic* by means of the *anubandha* itself.

This is because of the indicatory marker *k* in the rule *ṭhhana sic* (Pāṇini 1.2.14). For indeed, the purpose of applying the marker *k* to the root *han* is so that the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) may occur in forms such as *āhata*;
if the elision of the nasal were to apply to the *sic* suffix after *han*, [the marker *k* would be unnecessary].

The inclusion of the letter *k* would be purposeless. [The author says: "The letter *c* is for the sake of accent (*svarārtha*). That is, it is for the sake of making [the word] have an acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*). [Objection:
But since the suffix *sic* is devoid of vowels (*anacka*), the purpose of the letter *c* as an accent-marker is not tenable?

[Reply: This is no fault, because once the augment *iṭ* is applied, it becomes possessed of a vowel (*sācka*). [Objection: Even so, in the case of the *luṅ* tense, when the augment *āṭ* has an acute accent...
Since the remaining accent must be the udātta, for what purpose is the letter *ca* [in the rule]?

In that case, its purpose as an indicator of accent (*svarārthatā*) will apply where the augment *aṭ* is prohibited by the rule "na māṅyoge" (Pāṇini 6.4.74). But even there, [the prohibition] applies by the rule "tiṅṅtiṅaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.1.28).

Should there not be elision (*nighāta*)? If so, then in cases where elision is prohibited by the rule *ṭhhi ca* (Pāṇini 8.1.34)—as in examples such as *mā hi lāvīt*—it will serve the purpose of [marking] the accent.

But surely, in that case, the status of being marked with the *cit* designation will result for the substitute (*ādeśa*) simply through its having the nature of a *sthānin* (the original element); what then is the point of [specifying it as] a substitute?

Is the particle *ca* being carried over? He says: "For the unaccented nature of the augment," and so forth. By the rule prescribing that *yāsuṭ* is acute, it will be indicated that the augment is unaccented. And this is prescribed when no other accent has already applied. For instance, regarding those augments that are parts of the base (*prakṛtibhakta*), such as *aṭ*, *āna*, *ka*, and others—

The original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) would apply, and for those suffixal elements such as *iṭ* that are parts of the suffix, the suffix-accent (*pratyayasvara*) would apply; therefore, the unaccented status (*anudāttatva*) of the augment (*ag*) sublates all other accents. Consequently, just as it sublates the suffix-accent, it would likewise sublate the *cit*-accent produced by the principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*).
Therefore, the letter *ca* is also attached to the substitute (*ādeśa*).

The word *hi* means "because," and the word *iti* means "therefore. Since it would thus subvert even the accent of the *cita* suffix, therefore the letter *ca* is attached twice, both to the original base (*sthānin*) and to the substitute. But [one might object]:
For if the āgama were to be anudātta in examples such as *mā hi lāvīt*,
the designation of *cit* for the *cli* suffix would be purposeless due to the absence of any utility; therefore,
by virtue of the force of designating *cli* as *cit*, the *cit-svara* (the accent of the *cit* suffix) shall not be sublated by the anudātta nature of the āgama.
Is the addition of the *c* to the suffix *si* therefore useless? It is not useless, because it serves a purpose in one particular view.

How so? For here, just as the rule "of those that are similar in form, only one remains" (*sarūpāṇām ekaśeṣaḥ*, 1.2.64) was initiated by relying on the view that the individual word-meaning (*vyakti*) is the referent, so too...

The word *vyakti* (individual instance) is connected with the particle *ca* (and), based on the meaning of the word *pada* (word). For, when the referent (*padārtha*) is the individual instance, just as the rule concerning the acute accent (*udātta*) applies to each specific instance, so too does the statement that the suffix *yāsuṭ* is acute serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the fact that the augment (*āgama*) is unaccented (*anudātta*). Consequently, in the form *mā hi lāvīt*, the augment is unaccented.
This has already been indicated by that [rule].

And thus—it must be that as there is a svarita here, so there must also be an anudātta (unaccented) for the *āgama*; otherwise, the indicator (*jñāpaka*) regarding this subject would be purposeless. Furthermore, the simultaneous occurrence of two anudātta vowels is not possible.

There would be an optionality. In that case, the *sthānin* (the original element), the letter *ca*, would be sublated by the fact that the augment (*āgama*) is unaccented in the alternative view. However, when the letter *ca* is repeated twice, although the unaccented form is produced in one alternative view, nevertheless, once it has been produced—
Because of the force of the fact that the marker *k* has been applied twice, the *cit-svara* (acute accent on the final syllable) is produced once again;
therefore, there is no fault.
Regarding the rule "ṭhspṛśamṛśa" and so forth: from the roots *spṛś*, *mṛś*, and *kṛṣ*, [the suffix] *ksa* is applied by the rule "ṭhśala igupadhādaniṭaḥ ksaḥ."

When *kṣa* would [otherwise] apply by rule 3.1.45, and when *aṅ* would apply to the roots *tṛp* and *dṛp* because they belong to the *puṣādi* class, it must be stated—or rather, explained—that *isi* optionally applies. Regarding this, the explanation is as follows:
in the rule prescribing *kṣa*, [the word] "from *vidāṃkurvantu* etc. from rule 3.1.41 [is understood].

The term *anyatarasyām* is carried over by the maxim of the frog's leap from the rule *puṣādi-* (7.2.5), specifically from the phrase *ātmanepadeṣu* (3.1.54). That [optionality] is understood as being restricted (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) in both directions. Consequently, the suffix *ksa* will optionally apply after the roots *spṛś*, *mṛś*, and *kṛṣ*.

But from others [roots] it is always [the case]. From *tṛp* and *dṛp*, the suffix *aṅ* will optionally occur; however, from others such as *puṣ* and so on, it is always [the case]. Therefore, in that alternative where *ksāṅ* is absent, only *sij*, which is prescribed generally, occurs.

Regarding *aspr̥kṣat*: from the root *spr̥ś* (DhP 1422) in the sense of "touching," with the suffix *ksa*, the substitution of *ṣ* by *vraścādi* (8.2.36), the substitution of *k* for *ṣ* and *ḍh* before *s* by *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si* (8.2.41), and the substitution of *ṣ* for the substitute [consonant] by *ādeśapratyayoḥ* (8.3.59). Regarding *asprākṣīt*: [from the root] *anudātasya*... [etc.]

The augment *am* is applied by the rule *cardupadhasyānyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.1.59); then, by the rule *vadavraja* (Pāṇini 7.2.3), there is *vṛddhi*, and the *ṛ*-vowel undergoes the *yaṇ* substitution. Thus, *aspākṣīt*. Here, the suffix is *sic*. When the augment *am* is not present, then the *vṛddhi* occurs for the *ṛ*-vowel itself. Similarly, in the case of *mṛśa* in the sense of touching (*āmarśane*).
The two forms of these two roots—*dhā* (DhP 1425) and *kṛṣ* "to scratch" (DhP 1286)—should also be understood [in this way]. Regarding *atu pat*: *tṛp* "to satisfy" (DhP 1195).
Regarding *atrāpsīt* and *atāpsīt*: as before. Likewise, *dup*.
One should also understand that there are three forms for the root *hṛṣ* (meaning "to rejoice" and "to release") listed as number 1196 in the Dhātupāṭha.

45. *śala igupadhādaniṭaḥ ksaḥ* | (Pāṇini 3.1.45) [The suffix] *ksa* [is applied after a root] ending in *śal*, having *i* as its penultimate letter (*igupadha*), which does not take the augment *iṭ*.
Regarding the form *adhukṣat*: [it is derived from] the root *duh* "to milk" (Dhātupāṭha 1014). By the rule *dāderdhātorghaḥ* (8.2.32), the *d* is replaced by *gh*;
then, by the rule *ekāco baśo bhaṣ* (8.2.37), the *d* undergoes the *bhaṣ*-substitution.

The letter *dh*. By the rule *ṭhkhari ca* (8.4.55), the *cari* substitution of the letter *dh* results in the letter *k*. Regarding the form *alikṣat*: the root *lih* means "to taste" (DhP 1016); by the rule *ho ḍhaḥ* (8.2.31), the letter *h* is replaced by *ḍh*, and as before, the *ṣatva* and *katva* substitutions apply. Regarding the form *adhākṣīt*: the root *daha* means "to reduce to ashes" (DhP 991).

As before, there is the substitution of *ḍha*, *ka*, *ṣa*, *bhaṣ*-bhāva, and *ca* [for *ta*]. Thus, from the root *ṭhakuṣ*—that is, *ṭhakuṣa niṣkarṣe* (DhP 1518)—there is the *guṇa* strengthening of the light penultimate vowel.

46. *śliṣ* [is used] in the sense of embracing. (Pāṇini 3.1.46). Regarding the word "here": it means in the sense of embracing. "This is for the purpose of restriction," because it is commenced even though [the rule] was already established by the preceding [sūtra]. In *aślikṣat*, the substitution of *k* is as before.

"Let the wood adhere (*samāśliṣajjatu*). Here, due to its inclusion in the *puṣādi* group, the suffix *aṅ* is applied. In this context, the meaning of the root *śliṣ* is characterized by proximity (*pratyāsatti*), namely contiguity, and not physical embracing (*āliṅgana*). If this [root] is recited in the *puṣādi* group, how can it serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*)? For a grammatical operation that begins when something is already established serves to restrict it.

And is it not the case that *ksa* is already established by the preceding rule, since *aṅ* would be superseded? [The author] thinks: a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) must be made for "śliṣaḥ. For what purpose? To prevent the application of *aṅ*; thus, only *ksa* occurs, not *aṅ*.
Then, for what purpose is "āliṅgane" (in the sense of embracing)? It is for the purpose of restriction—that is, [only in the sense of] embracing...

In this way, the rule [for *kṣa*] occurs, except in the case of *āreĀ* and so forth. If that were so, then just as the analysis of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "of *śliṣ*" excludes *āreĀ*, it would likewise exclude *ciṇ* by the rule "in the passive and middle voices" (Pāṇini 3.1.66)—as in the example *upāśleṣi kanyā devadattena*? This is not the case.

"Exceptions [apavāda] sublate only those rules immediately preceding them, not those further ahead"—this rule (*ām*) sublates [the *ciṇ*], but not the *ciṇ*. Or alternatively: since the word "ciṇ" is carried over from the rule "ciṇ te padaḥ" (3.1.60) into the rule "ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ" (3.1.66), [it is understood that the *ām* sublates the *ciṇ*].

Furthermore, the purpose of mentioning *ciṇ* again is so that [the rule] may apply only to *ciṇ*, and not to whatever else might otherwise be applicable. Now, why is there no inclusion of this *śliṣ* from the roots *śriṣu*, *śliṣu*, *pruṣu*, and *pluṣu* meaning "to burn" (*dhā.pā.* 701, 704)? [Because its inclusion would apply] only to the sense of embracing (*āliṅgana*).
Because its [the suffix's] occurrence is impossible, and because of the governing rule "of that which does not have the augment iṭ" (3.1.45), this [suffix] possesses the augment iṭ.

47. *na dṛśaḥ* | (3.1.47) [The suffix *liṭ*] is not replaced by *kvasu* after the root *dṛś*. For example, in *adarśat*: the suffix *aṅ* is applied; by the rule *ṛdṛśo’ṅ guṇī* (7.4.16), *guṇa* substitution occurs. In *adrākṣīt*: the augment *am* is added by the rule *sṛjidṛśorjhalyamakiti* (6.1.58). [Also, the rule *vadavraja* (7.2.3) applies.]
By these and other such [rules], there is lengthening; as before, there is the substitution of *ṣ* and *k*.
48. *ṇi-śri-dru-srubhyaḥ kartari caṅ* (3.1.48).

The letter *c* in *caṅ* is for the purpose of specification (*viśeṣaṇārtha*). If, in the rule *caṅ* (6.1.11), the term were stated simply as *aṅ*, then even by the rule *asyativaktikhyātibhyo’ṅ* (3.1.52), which prescribes *aṅ*, there would be reduplication (*dvirvacana*) [of the root].
It would be as follows: *aṭiṭat*, *aṭāṭyat*, *aciṭikarat*, *ajīharat*. By the rule *caṅ* (6.1.11), there is reduplication of the roots *kṛ* and *hṛ*;
by *urat* (7.4.66), the substitution of *u* for the radical *ṛ*; and by *kuhoścuḥ* (7.4.62), the substitution of *c*-sounds for *k* and *h*—namely, *c* for *k* and *jh* for *h*.
Then, by *abhyāse car ca* (8.4.54), the *jha* becomes *ja*.

The letter *jha* becomes *ja*. The remainder is to be understood according to [the rule] *abhyudasīṣadat*. Examples include *ṭhaśiśriyat*, etc. [These derive from] *śriñ* "to serve" (DhP 897), *du* and *dru* "to go" (DhP 944, 945), and *sru* "to go" (940), by means of the rule *aci śnudhātu-* (Pāṇini 6.4.77), etc.

"According to the appropriate application, *iy*, *Ru*, *vaṅ*, and *ai* [are substituted]; [in the form] *ṭhakārayiṣātām*, there is the dual ending of the object (*karmani*), namely *ātām*, followed by the augment *iṭ*, *guṇa*, the *āyādeśa*, and the substitution of *ṣ*. Regarding the statement "there is an addition [of the suffix] after the root *kam*," one might object: "But surely, once the suffix *ṇiṅ* has been applied by the rule *kamerṇiṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.30)..."

Since the root *kam* already possesses the suffix *ṇic*, the formation with *caṅ* (the reduplicated aorist) is already established; therefore, he asks how it is that this is added as a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*). He says: "The roots beginning with *āya*" and so forth. Regarding the form *acakamata*: because the root is *anudātta*-accented, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used, and as before, there is the substitution of *ku* for the semivowel in the reduplicated syllable. Regarding the statement "in the alternative where *ṇiṅ* is absent, there is the treatment as *saṇvat*": no.

He shows this in the view that [the suffix] *ṇiṅ* is included; for the meaning of the rule *sanvallaghuni caṅpare* (Pāṇini 7.4.93) is as follows: when *caṅ* follows immediately after a *ṇi*, that is "having *caṅ* following it" (*caṅpara*); when a stem (*aṅga*) occurs with that [suffix] following it, the operation of *sanvadbhāva* applies to its reduplication (*abhyāsa*). And this meaning [is not applicable here].
This is possible in the case of the neuter gender.

49. *vibhāṣā dheṭ-śvyoḥ*. Regarding "ṭhadadhat": by [Pāṇini 6.4.64] *āto lopa iṭi ca*, there is elision of the vowel *ā*. As before, the *jaś*-substitution for the reduplication results in the letter *d*. Regarding "ṭhadhāsīt": [this is formed with] *luṅ* and *sic*.

By the rule *ṭhyamaramanamātāṃ sak ca ṭa* (Pāṇini 7.2.73), there is the augment *iṭ*, as well as the augment *sak* for the root; by *astisico'pṛkte* (7.3.96), there is the augment *iṭ*; and by *iṭa īṭi* (8.2.28), there is the elision of *sic*. Regarding *aśiśviyat*: the *iyaṅ* substitution occurs as before. It is stated that "here, the augment *aṅ* is also optional."

By the rule *ṭhjṛstambhu* (3.1.58) and others, [the suffix *luṅ* is applied]. Regarding *aśvat*: by the rule *śvayateraḥ* (7.4.18), the substitution of *a* occurs; then by *ato guṇe* (6.1.97), the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is applied. Regarding *aśvayīt*:
when the prohibition of *vṛddhi* is effected by the rule *hyantakṣaṇāśvasa* (7.2.5) and others, the *guṇa* substitute is applied, followed by the *ay*-substitution.

"ṭhadhiṣātām": this is the dual ending for the object (*karmaṇi dvivacanam*), namely *ātām*. By the rule "ṭhsthāghvoricca" (Pāṇini 1.2.17), there is both the *kit* designation and the substitution of *i* for the final vowel. 50. "gupeścchandasi" (Pāṇini 3.1.50).

"This rule applies where the suffix *āya* does not exist," because [the rule] mentions that which does not end in the suffix *āya*. This is because that which ends in the suffix *āya* constitutes a different verbal root (*dhātu*).
[The example is] "he protected" (*agūgopat*), from the root *gup* (DhP 395) meaning "to protect" (*rakṣaṇe*), in the *luṅ* tense.

There is reduplication; by the rule *ṭhtasthastha* (3.4.101) and others, the suffix *tha* is applied, and by the rule *ḍujādīnāṃ dīrgho'bhyāsasya* (6.1.7), there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable. Regarding the form *agauptam*: by the rule *jhalo jhali* (8.2.26), there is the elision of the *sic* suffix; because that [elision] is treated as non-existent (*asiddhatva*), the rule *vadavraja* (7.2.3) and others apply.
*Vṛddhi*: [In the example] *agopiṣṭam*, because the root is marked with *ū* (*ūdittvāt*), the augment *iṭ* optionally applies by Pāṇini 7.2.44 (*svarati-sūti-sūyati-dhūnūdito vā*).

When *iṭ* is present, Pāṇini 7.2.4 (*neṭi*) prohibits *vṛddhi*, and thus the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇaḥ*) occurs. [In the example] *agopāyiṣṭam*, the suffix *sic* follows the root ending in the *āya*-suffix; *iṭ* is added, and then there is the elision of the final *a* (*ato lopaḥ*).
"The three forms" refers to the latter [of the two].
51. [The suffix *ciṇ* is applied] after the roots *ūn*, *dhvan*, *el*, and *ard*, when followed by the affix *ṇic*.
(Pāṇini 3.1.51). This means "after those ending in *ṇic*. [The forms] *ūnayati* and *elayati* are derived from the roots *ūn* and *el* with the *curādi-ṇic* affix.
"By the preceding rule" refers to [the rule] beginning with *śriṇi* (3.1.48). Regarding the form *auṇayīt*: [it is formed with] the *tip* suffix.

Thus, by the rule *ṭhiṭa īṭi* (8.2.28), there is the elision of *sic*; since that [elision] is considered asiddha, when *vṛddhi* would otherwise apply, there is a prohibition by the rule *hmyantalakṣaṇa* (7.2.5). Then the *guṇa* and *ay-ādeśa* [substitutions] occur, followed by *āḍajādīnām*.
(6.4.72) thus *āṭ* is added; by (6.1.90) *āṭaśca*, there is *vṛddhi*. Regarding *āṬninat*:
by (6.1.2) *ajāderdvitīyasya*, there is reduplication. There is the elision of the *ṇi*. Regarding *dhvanayīt*:
in the form *dhvanayīt*, the short *a* [of the suffix] is due to this very irregularity (*nipātana*), and then by (6.4.48) *ato lopaḥ*, there is its elision.

Because of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (acting like the original element), the *vṛddhi* substitution prescribed by "ṭhata upadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.116) does not occur. The prohibition of *aṭ* is due to "bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅyoge 'pi" (Pāṇini 6.4.75). In "adidhvanat," there is the substitution of *i* due to the application of the *sannvadbhāva* rule. In "aililat," [the reduplication is of] "the second [syllable] beginning with a vowel" according to "ajāder dvitīyasya" (Pāṇini 6.1.2).

Thus, there is reduplication of the root *liś*, and the augment *āṭ* is applied as before. Regarding "ārdidat": here too, there is reduplication of the second monosyllabic portion as before; however, the *repha* (the letter *r*) is not reduplicated, due to the prohibition in Pāṇini 6.1.3, which states: "The first elements of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), beginning with *n* and *d*, are not reduplicated. Then follows the augment *āṭ* and the application of *vṛddhi*.
52. After the roots *as* (to throw), *vac* (to speak), and *khyā* (to tell), the suffix *aṅ* is applied.
[The commentary notes: "Or rather, there is the substitute *brū*"; this refers to the rule *brūño vaciḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.53). "Or rather, there is the substitute *cakṣiṅ*";
this refers to the rule *cakṣiṅḥ khyāñ* (Pāṇini 2.4.54). [An example is given: *paryāsthata*.

The ātmanepada ending is applied due to the supplementary rule (vārttika 49): "After a prefix, [the roots] as- and ūh- take [the ātmanepada endings]. [Thus we have] *asyate*. By Pāṇini 7.1.17, "thuk is added after as-," [we have] *avocata*. [Regarding] *avocat*: by Pāṇini 7.4.20, "um is substituted for vac-.
[Regarding] *ākhyat*: as before, there is the elision of the long ā.

53. *lipisicihvaśca* | (3.1.53) [The suffix] *ṭhak* occurs [after these roots]. As before, there is the elision of the vowel *ā*. Now, for what purpose is this division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*)? Why not simply state the single rule: "*ṭhasyativaktikhyātilipisicihvaśca*" [meaning: the suffix *ṭhak* occurs after the roots √as, √vac, √khyā, √lip, √sic, and √hve]? To this he says:

"Separately," and so forth. The purpose of this separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*) is so that, in the subsequent sūtra, the option for the *aṅ* affix (*aṅvikalpaḥ*) may apply only after roots beginning with *lipi* and others in the *ātmanepada*. For if they were in a single rule, there would be a carry-over (*anuvṛtti*) of these [roots] such as *as* and others into the subsequent [sūtra], and consequently, the option would apply to those as well.
It would follow [absurdly] by means of conceptual construction.

54. *Ātmanepadeṣv anyatarasyām* (3.1.54). The *ātmanepada* [ending] is applied after a root marked with a *svarita* accent or a *ñi*. Because the roots *lip* and *sic* are marked with *svarita*, and because *hvā* is marked with *ñi*, we have the forms *alipata* and *asikta*; and [the elision of *s* occurs] by the rule *jhalo jhali* (8.2.26).
There is elision of *s* [by P. 7.2.10]. Since that [elision] is established as valid by P. 6.4.22, the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) would have applied;

however, it does not occur because the suffixes *liṅ* and *sic* are marked with the *k*-sign when used with the *ātmanepada* endings (P. 1.2.11). Furthermore, the substitution of *k* for the palatals (*cuḥ kuḥ*, P. 8.2.30) takes place.
55. *puṣādi-dyautādy-ḷditaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (Pāṇini 1.3.55).
Those whose *ḷ* is *it* are called *ḷdit*. The *puṣādi* group indeed exists as a sub-group within the *bhvādi* class—namely:
*puṣa* (to nourish, DhP 700); *śriṣu*, *śliṣu*, *pruṣu*, *pluṣu* (to burn, DhP 701–704).
Thus, there is a sub-group beginning with *div*— namely, *puṣa* in the sense of "nourishing" (DhP 1182),
*śuṣa* in the sense of "drying up" (DhP 1183), and so forth; and there is also a sub-group beginning with *kryā*—
namely, *puṣa* in the sense of "nourishing" (DhP 1529), *muṣa* in the sense of "stealing" (DhP 1530), and so forth.
Regarding this, he asks whose inclusion [is intended] here, and says: "The *puṣādi* group is included within the *divādi* sub-group," and so forth.

If the *bhvādi* sub-group were being taken, he would not have made a separate mention of the *dyutādi* group immediately after the *puṣādi* group, because they would already have been included by the mention of the *puṣādi* group itself. Therefore...

That [root] is not included; nor indeed is the *ṛk* group included, for only four roots are recited therein: the two previously mentioned, as well as *ṭh khac* (DhP 1531) in the sense of "the manifestation of what has been" and *ṭh grah* (DhP 1533) in the sense of "taking. And if these were intended to be grasped...

If one were to perform these operations for roots ending in *lṛ* (lṛdit), then it would not be necessary to mention *puṣ* and the others [separately]. Therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is understood that the mention of *puṣ* and the others refers to those included within the *div* group and so forth. Now, why were *puṣ* and the others not made *lṛdit*? No; for they are not.

They can indeed be made to have the marker *ḷ*. For if they were marked with *ḷ*, then because they would be read as having both *u* and *i* as markers (*udita* and *ādita*), there would be an absence of the two grammatical operations prescribed by the rules "vā ḷditah" (Pāṇini 7.2.56) and "āditaśca" (Pāṇini 7.2.16). Now, why are *dyauta* and the others not made to have the marker *ḷ*?
For the very same reason that the *puṣ* group has not been made to end with *lṛdita*, the *dyut* group likewise [has not been so made].

For among those as well, some are recited as having an indicatory *u* (*udita*) and others as having an indicatory *ā* (*ādita*). Among them, the *puṣ* group extends up to the completion of the *ādivādi* group; however, after the rule "ṣṇiha prītau" (DhP 1200), there is the mention of "vṛt."

The closure (*vṛtkaraṇa*) is for the purpose of concluding [the section] of *rav* and the others, but not of *puṣ* and the others; such is the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) of the Teachers. The roots beginning with *dyut* extend as far as *kṛpū* in the sense of "capability" (DhP 762); after that comes the closure (*vṛt*); then follows *ghaṭa* in the sense of "exertion."

This is because of the inclusion of the *vṛt* marker [in the Dhātupāṭha, sūtra 763]. Regarding "adyautat": by the rule *dyudbhyo luṅi* (Pāṇini 1.3.91), the *parasmaipada* (active voice) is optionally used. Regarding "aśvatat": from the root *śvitā varṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 742).
Regarding "agamat" and "aśakat": from *gamlṛ gatau* (Dhātupāṭha 982).
The root *śaklṛ* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha (1261) with the meaning "to be capable. Regarding the form *vyadyotiṣṭa*:

because it is marked with an anudātta vowel, the ātmanepada voice is applied. Regarding the form *aluṭiṣṭa*: the roots *ruṭ* and *luṭ* are listed in the Dhātupāṭha (747, 748) with the meaning "to strike back" (*pratīghāte*).

56. *sartiśāstyatibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.56). Regarding *asarat*: [the rule] *ṛdṛśo’ṅ guṇiḥ* (7.4.16) applies. Regarding *aśiṣat*: by the rule *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ* (6.4.34), there is the substitution of *i* for the root vowel, and by *śāsivasi* (8.3.60), there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *ś*.
In *ṭhāra*, as before, there is *guṇa* substitution, then *āṭ* augment because the root begins with *aj*, and finally *savarṇadīrgha*.

Regarding *pṛthak* and so forth: if the rule *puṣādidyautādylṛditsartiśāstyasartibhyaśca* were formulated as a single compound (*ekayoga*), then the *parasmaipada* endings would apply only to the roots beginning with *sarti*.

Not [in the case] of the ātmanepada. Therefore, this separate rule is formulated so that [the substitution] may occur even when these very roots are used in the ātmanepada. Regarding "samaranta": the ātmanepada ending is applied to the root *ṛ* preceded by *sam* by virtue of the rule *samo gamyṛcchi-* (Pāṇini 1.3.29). [The lengthening of the vowel is justified] by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅyoge 'pi* (Pāṇini 6.4.75).

Thus, there is an absence of the augment *aṭ*; this usage is due to its being Vedic (*chāndasa*). Now, one might ask: if *aṅ* occurs even in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), then what is the purpose of the particle *ca* (and), which serves to carry over [the rule] from the active voice (*parasmaipada*)? To this he says: "And that," etc. "That" refers to...

This refers back to the rule *parasmaipadeṣu*. It will find its application in the subsequent [sūtra], for it does not find application here itself; otherwise, the formulation of a separate rule would be purposeless.

*i* and *r* are *ir*; that which has *it* [as its final element] is *irit*. Among these, the vowel *i* receives the designation *it* by the rule *ṭhurajeṣe 'janunāsika it* (1.3.2), and the letter *r* [receives the designation *it*] by the rule *ṭhhalantyam* (1.3.3).

(1.3.3) Thus [it is said]. Alternatively, is the designation *it* applied to the entire group that contains the sound *ir*, and not to each individual constituent? That which has this group *ir* as its *it*-designation is called *irit*.
The fact that the designation *it* applies to the entire group is to be understood from this very statement; for it is not established by any other rule.

The designation *it* is prescribed for this [root]. In the form *abhaitsīt*, there is *vṛddhi* by the rule *vadavraja-* (Pāṇini 7.2.3), and the augment *iṭ* by the rule *astisico’pṛkte* (Pāṇini 7.3.96). In *aruddha* and *abhitta*, the *ātmanepada* occurs because of the *svarita* accent; the elision of *sic* is as before.
58. *jṛ-stambhu-mrucu-mlucu-grucu-glucu-glucu-añcu-śvi-bhyaś-ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.58).
The addition of the marker *ud* to the root *stambh* is for the purpose of qualifying it by [the rule] *udito vā* (7.2.56).
Thus, in the form *astabhat*, there is the elision of the nasal according to *aniditām* (6.4.24). [The form] *aśvat*.
And so forth. The three forms have been explained under the rule *vibhāṣā dheṭśvyoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.49). It is said: "The three forms are established by employing either *gluc* or *gluñc*.
How so? If first *gluc* is employed, then for that [root] there is the augment *aṅ* in the case of *isiC*.
Thus, the two forms *aglucat* and *aglocīt* are established;

however, from the root *gluñci*, with the suffix *sic*, the third form *agluñcīt* is produced. Now, if *gluñci* were to be adopted [as the root], its two forms would be *aglucat* and *agluñcīt* with the suffix *aṅ* and *sic* respectively; but from *gluci* with *sic*—

"Thirdly, [it is said] 'the *maglocī* [is not established]' and so forth. If this is so, for what purpose are both [reasons] adduced? For the three-fold nature (*rūpatraya*) is that which is to be proven (*sādhya*), and that is indeed established even by the adduction of either one.
To this, he says: "Because of the difference in meaning," and so forth. The word "but" (*tu*) is used for emphasis. For the meaning of these two is indeed distinct.

In that case, if only one of the two were taken, then for that very meaning which is not included, the form *aglucat* would not be established. Therefore, because the two meanings are distinct, both are taken. As for the phrase "some say" (*kecid*) and so forth:
since verbal roots have multiple meanings, there is no contradiction in their having non-distinct meanings [in this context].
Therefore, it is established that for both [of them], there is a "lump" (gluñca) of appropriation.

59. *kṛ-mṛ-dṛ-ruhi-bhyaś chandasi* (Pāṇini 3.1.59). [The roots are: *ṭhḍukṛñ karaṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 1472), *ṭhmṛṅ prāṇatyāge* (Dhātupāṭha 1403), *ṭhdṛ vidāraṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 1493), and *ṭhruha prādurbhāve bījajanmani ca* (Dhātupāṭha 1494).

[The roots] *jan* (DhP 859), etc. Among these, for the first three, *sic* would have been expected [by Pāṇini 3.1.44]; for *ruh*, however, *ksa* would have been expected by "śala igupadhād aniṭaḥ" (3.1.45). [The forms] *akarat* and *amarat*: the guṇa substitution is as before. In *amarat*, the parasmaipada ending occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). In common speech (*bhāṣāyām*)...
Thus, the forms *akārṣīt*, *amṛta*, *adārīt*, and *aruksat* come into being.
60. *ciṇ te padaḥ* (3.1.60).

Regarding the phrase "by virtue of the semantic capacity" (*sāmarthyāt*) and so forth: this suffix *ta* exists both as the singular number of the ātmanepada and as the second person plural of the parasmaipada, for which [the substitution] is prescribed.
In this context, because this verbal root (*dhātu*) is marked for the *ātmanepada* voice, the plural number of the *parasmaipada* is not possible;

therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the singular form of the *ātmanepada* is understood. This very principle of elimination constitutes the "semantic force" (*sāmarthya*). [The example is] *udapādi*. [This is derived by applying] *ciṇo luk* (Pāṇini 6.4.104).

Thus, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ta*. Regarding "udapatsātām": [the suffix] *ātām* undergoes *c*-substitution (*cartvam*) by the rule *khari ca* (8.4.55). Regarding "udapatsata": [the suffix] *jhi* undergoes the substitution of *at* by the rule *ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ* (7.1.5). Here, the word *vā* ("or") is no longer in force, because the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is employed in the subsequent rules.

61. After the roots *dīp*, *jan*, *budh*, *pūrī*, *āpyāy*, [the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied] optionally. (Pāṇini 3.1.61) The roots are *janī* in the sense of "manifestation" (Dhātupāṭha 1149) and *budha* in the sense of "understanding" (Dhātupāṭha 1172). By this [sūtra], [it is understood that] *jan* is the root *jan* in the sense of "birth" (Dhātupāṭha 1105), and *budh* is the root *budh* in the sense of "awakening" (Dhātupāṭha 875).

The roots *budha* "to awaken" belonging to the *bhvādi* class (858) and the *divādi* class (1172) are read in exactly this way. Regarding the form *adugdha*: by the rule *śala igupadhādaniṭaḥ ksaḥ* (3.1.45), the suffix *ksa* is applied;
then, with *ksasya* being carried over from the rule *ksasyāci* (7.3.72), there is optionally elision (*lugvā*).
By the rule *duhadiha* (Pāṇini 7.3.73), there is elision (*luk*). By *dāderdhātorghaḥ* (8.2.32), the sound *gh* is substituted;

as before, there is the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*). Thus, we have *adohi*. Here, the suffix *ta* is used in the sense of the pure passive (*śuddhe karmaṇi*), and therefore the suffix *ciṇ* necessarily occurs in this case.

64. *na rudhaḥ* | (3.1.64) This is a prohibition of *ciṇ*, which would otherwise have been applicable through the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule "like the object" (*karmavat*). In the form *aruddha*, there is the elision of *sic* by the rule *jhalo jhali* (8.2.26); because that [elision] is considered as if non-existent (*asiddhatva*), the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) would have been applicable.
By the rule "ṭhliṅsicāvātmanepadeṣu" (1.2.11), [the substitution] does not occur because of the *kit* designation.
As before, there is the substitution of *dh* and *jaś*.

65. *tapo'nutāpe ca* | (3.1.65) By the extension [of rule] *ṭhtapastapaḥ karmakasyaiva* (3.1.88), this is a prohibition of the *ciṇ* affix which would otherwise be obtained by *ṭhciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (3.1.66). Example: *atapta tapas tāpasaḥ* ("the ascetic performed penance").

The ascetic (*tāpasa*) performs (*tapati*) austerity (*tapas*), characterized by fasting and so forth; the meaning is that he causes suffering. Here, austerity is the agent (*kartṛ*) and the ascetic is the object (*karman*). However, when that ascetic—who has become nothing but skin and bone—performs austerity for the sake of heaven, then this is the usage: "The ascetic performed austerity" (*atapta tapas tāpasaḥ*). Now...

"Tapaḥ" is the object and "tāpasa" is the agent. Here, the word *tapaḥ* refers to a specific kind of knowledge that serves as the cause for attaining heaven and other such goals. The root *tap-* also means "to acquire. Thus, the meaning is that the ascetic (*tāpasa*) has acquired this specific knowledge. As it is said: "He was not afflicted by sinful action," which [was mentioned] previously.
The meaning is that he has performed an evil deed and is subsequently tormented and struck down; here, the suffix *lakāra* denotes the object (*karman*).

66. *ciṇ* [is substituted] for [the affixes] expressing the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). (Pāṇini 3.1.66) The phrase "in the senses of the abstract state and the object" is an adjective qualifying the word *ta*. That is, it means "that *ta*-affix which occurs when the abstract state or the object is to be expressed. Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *ciṇ*? For [one might ask]: why is this necessary? Since...
Does the mention of *ciṇ* indeed continue from the rule "ṭhaciṇ te padaḥ" (3.1.60)?

It might be argued as follows: that [mention of *ciṇ*] is connected with the optionality (*anyatarasyām*) in "dīpajana" (3.1.61) and with the prohibition (*niṣedha*) in "na rudhaḥ" (3.1.64); therefore, if it were to continue [from 3.1.60], [it would apply to those rules as well].

It might be argued that [the rule] should follow only that which is connected to it, but this is not the case; for the inclusion of "either one" (*anyatarasyām*) has already been precluded by the two preceding rules, and a prohibition must be preceded by a prior application.
