If there were an application of *ciṇ* in the cases of the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), then...

To prohibit that [application], the word "na" (not) would have to be carried over [from the previous rule]. Furthermore, there is no application of that [affix] to those two [roots] by anything else, because in the rule prescribing *ciṇ*, the word "kartari" (in the sense of the agent) is carried over in all cases. Therefore, he says—"The mention of *ciṇ* is for the sake of clarity"—lest [the rule be applied] otherwise.

If the mention of *ciṇ* were not made, those of dull intellect would experience difficulty in comprehension; therefore, the mention of *ciṇ* is repeated again for the sake of favoring them and to clarify the very meaning already established by logic.

67. *sārvadhātuke yak* (Pāṇini 3.1.67). The phrase "in the sense of the agent and the object" (*bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*) is understood [from the previous rule]; showing that this [phrase] qualifies the *sārvadhātuka* [affix], he says:
"expressing the agent and the object," and so forth. It occurs in the two meanings of the agent and the object.
That which is a *sārvadhātuka* [affix] expresses the state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). The suffix *ṇini* occurs in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*) or necessity (*āvaśyaka*).

Now, why is it not stated thus: "when the *sārvadhātuka* follows, *yaK* occurs when the state or the object are to be expressed"? It is impossible to state it in this way, because [the state and the object] are already expressed by the *sārvadhātuka* itself.
Because it is declared in the treatise [of Pāṇini] that [the suffixes] apply to both the action and the object. If one asks, "Why is this so?

it is because of the statement: "The suffix *l* is used in the sense of the object and in the sense of the action for transitive roots, and in the sense of the action for intransitive roots" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.4.69). But surely, in examples such as *akāri kaṭo bhavatā*, *aśāyi bhavatā*, and *abibhar bhavān*, even in the absence of a *sārvadhātuka* suffix...
Since the object of the action (*karman*) and so forth are perceived [even when the suffixes are absent], it is not tenable that they constitute the meaning of the *sārvadhātuka* suffixes;

for it is not logical that whatever is perceived in the absence of something else should be the meaning of that thing, since the meaning is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)? This is not a fault; for there is no such rule:

[The objection: "Since [the suffix] is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), it must be meaningful; what then? It is a *pratijñā* (a formal assertion). And that [assertion] has been established, as in the case of *kvip* and others. Furthermore, there is the rule *sārvadhātukasya* [which provides the long vowel]; therefore, this [objection] is trivial. [As for the example] *śayyate*: [it is formed by] *ayaṅ yi kṅiti*."
Thus, this is the substitution of *ya*.

Regarding the phrase "in the prescription of *ya*" and so forth: one might object, "Since the *ya* will occur by the very extension (*atideśa*) 'like the passive' (*karmavat*), what is the purpose of this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*)? To this, he says: "Because of the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*)."

And so forth. The scope of *kartari śap* (Pāṇini 3.1.68) is, for example: *śuddhaḥ kartā bhavati* ("the agent is pure"); the scope of *sārvadhātuke yak* (Pāṇini 3.1.67) is, for example: *śuddhaṃ karma*, *pacyata odanaḥ* ("the object is pure," "the rice is being cooked"). In the case of *pacyata odanaḥ svayam eva* ("the rice cooks by itself"), the suffix *yak* occurs due to the treatment as an object (*karmavadbhāva*).
[The suffix] *śap* is obtained; by virtue of the inclusion of the particle *vat*, it may also apply to its own base (*svāśraya*), since the status of being an agent is possible there.
In that case, because it is subsequent, *śap* alone would occur. The rule for *śap* is subsequent to the rule for *yak*;
therefore, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*)—that is, an explanation—is required for *yak* in the case of a reflexive object-agent (*karmakartṛ*).

This must be established; the proof is as follows: by virtue of this indicator (*jñāpaka*), the *yaṅ* affix will occur even in the case of the reflexive object-agent (*karmakartṛ*). What is that indicator? It is the prohibition [stated in] *na duhasnunamāṃ yakciṇau* (Pāṇini 3.1.89). For if the *yaṅ* affix did not occur in the case of the reflexive object-agent, that prohibition would be purposeless.

It may be so. For it was stated—assuming that the substitution of *śap* is stronger due to its status as a scriptural extension (*śāstrātideśa*)—that this is not actually an extension of a rule (*śāstrātideśa*), but rather an extension of an operation (*kāryātideśa*). Indeed, the sūtra concerning the extension of an operation is itself independent regarding the operation of *yaṅ* and so forth.
It is prescriptive, and that [prescription] is supreme; therefore, due to this contradiction, the injunction alone possesses superior force.

68. *kartari śap* (Pāṇini 3.1.68). [The commentary states: "The letter *ṭ* [in *śap*] is for the sake of the accent. This is so that the low-pitched (*anudātta*) quality may apply by the rule *anudātau suppitau* (3.1.4). "The letter *ś* [in *śap*] is for the sake of the designation *sārvadhātuka*."
This is so that the status of being a *sārvadhātuka* may apply by the rule "ṭhtiṅśitsārvadhātukam" (Pāṇini 3.4.113).
It should be understood that this same purpose applies to the letter *ś* in *śyan* and the other affixes as well.

69. *divādibhyaḥ śyan* (Pāṇini 3.1.69). [The commentary states: "This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *śap*. This is because this rule is commenced precisely when that [application of *śap*] would otherwise occur. [The commentary further states: "The letter *n* is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*). This is so that, by the rule *ñnityādir nityam* (6.1.197), the word may have its first syllable acute-accented (*ādyudātta*).
It would be "dīvyati"; the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.77] "hali ca."
70. *vā bhrāśabhlāśabhramutrasitruṭiṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.70).
[The examples given are] *sanoti* and *kṣaṇoti*. [The roots are] *ṣaṇu* in the sense of giving (Dhātupāṭha 1464) and *kṣaṇu* in the sense of harming (Dhātupāṭha 1465).
[Regarding the phrase] "for the sake of restriction" (*niyamārtham*): it is so that this very operation belonging to the *tanādi* class [of roots] may apply [only to these].

The rule "syāt" (it may be so) is intended so that there may be this restriction: that other effects of *tan* and the rest shall not occur in its absence. For if the purpose of the restriction were absent, then just as there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding *sic* after other roots such as *tan*, so too would there be elision (*luk*) of *as*—as in *atata*, *atathāḥ*, *ataniṣṭa*, *ataniṣṭhāḥ*—and likewise [in the case of *as*].

It might also apply to the root *kṛ*. However, when that [substitution] is present, [the substitution of *i* for *ṇal*] does not occur; and in its absence, the elision prescribed by the eighth book—specifically Pāṇini 8.2.27, "after a short vowel, from a base" (*hrasvādaṅgāt*)—does indeed take place: *akṛta*, *akṛthāḥ*. Now, one might object: even if that [substitution of *i*] were present, no undesirable result would arise regarding the operations such as *tan* and so forth.

[Objection: Even in the alternative where the *aluk* [non-elision] applies, would not the elision [of the augment *iṭ*] take effect by the rule "after a short vowel" (*hrasvāt*, 8.2.27)? [Response: This is not so; since the *luk*-elision of *sic* is introduced when the [other] elision has not yet occurred, it must be an annulment of that [earlier elision]. [Objection: One should not entertain this doubt, because the annulment of the elision is improper due to the status of being "not established" (*asiddha*) according to the rule "what precedes is as if non-existent" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*, 8.2.1).

For he will say this: "There is no non-application (*asiddhatva*) in the case of exceptions (*apavāda*), because of the authoritative status of the statement regarding the exception. If, then, another operation belonging to the *tanādi* class is not desired for the root *kṛ*, why then is it recited in the *bhvādi* class itself? Who, moreover, [would argue] thus?

The distinction is based on brevity. Even if it were included in the *bhū* class, it would necessarily have to be mentioned specifically in the rule prescribing its suffix; therefore, this objection is not valid.

80. *dhinvikṛṇvyora ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.80). Since the suffix *śap* would otherwise apply because [the roots] belong to the *bhū-ādi* class, this rule is stated. An *ṭh* substitute occurs; by the maxim *alo'ntyasya* (1.1.52), [this applies to] the final letter. Thus, *dhinoti*. [Then] *ato lopaḥ* [applies].

Now, he explains why the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) does not apply here: "Because of the elision of 'a'," and so forth. Due to the status of the elision of 'a' as *sthānivadbhāva* by the rule "When a subsequent [element] is applied, [the preceding element] is treated as if it were present for the sake of a prior operation" (Pāṇini 1.1.57), the vowel *i* is no longer a light penultimate vowel; therefore, the *guṇa* substitution does not take place. This is for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*).

Although it would have been sufficient to state "of *dhā* and *kṛt*," the mention of them as accompanied by the augment *num* is made for the purpose of indicating that the *num* occurs precisely at the stage of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*). Consequently,
it need not be stated that "the rule regarding the original form (*upadeśivad-vacana*) is required for the sake of achieving the desired accentuation when the *num* is prescribed."
It comes to be.
81. *Śnā* [is the affix] after roots beginning with *krī*. (3.1.81) 82. *Śnu* as well as *śnā* [are the affixes] after the roots *stambhu*, *stumbhu*, *skambhu*, *skumbhu*, and *skuñ*.
(3.1.82) The particle *ca* (‘as well as’) serves to carry forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) the affix *śnā*. [Thus we derive] ‘*stabhnāti*’. First, [the rule] *aniditām...* [applies].

(6.4.24) Thus there is the elision of the nasal. Because these roots are mentioned together with *śnu* and *śnā*, someone might have the misconception that they belong exclusively to the domain of those [affixes]. Therefore, in order to dispel that, he says: "Because of the demonstration of their having *u* as an indicatory letter" (*uditvapratipādanāt*), and so forth. For these [roots] have the vowel *u*—

It is postulated that they possess this designation (udittva); the result of this is the optional application of the augment *iṭ* after the suffix *ktvā*. If these were restricted solely to the domain of verbal conjugational classes (*vikaraṇa*), the inclusion of the marker *u* would be purposeless.
Therefore, from the postulation of the marker *u*, it is determined that they serve all purposes.
This word "artha" denotes an object; the meaning is "the state of having all things as its objects."

83. *halaḥ śnaḥ śānajjhau* (Pāṇini 3.1.83). [Examples: *puṣāṇa*, *muṣāṇa*. [This is] the imperative (*loṭ*) in the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth; by *serhyapicca* (3.4.87), *hi* replaces the suffix *si*; because it belongs to the *kyādi* group, the suffix *śnā* is applied; by this rule [83], that [suffix] is replaced by *śānac*. The letter *ca* is for the purpose of making the final syllable accented (*antodātta*). [From] *ataḥ*...
By the rule *heḥ* (6.4.105), there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *hi*.

Thus we have *krīṇīhi*. By the rule *ī halyaghoḥ* (6.4.113), the substitution of *ī* occurs. Now, since the suffix *śnā* is the subject under discussion, one might think that it alone will be understood here as the substituendum; so what is the purpose of mentioning *śnaḥ*?
Thus he states the explanation: "The mention of *śna* is a reference to the original element (*sthānin*)," and so forth.

The purpose of this mention of *śna* is so that there may be the understanding that this word *śānac* is a substitute (*ādeśa*). But what is the reason that, in the absence of that [mention], there would not be such an understanding?

To this he says: "For [it would be] another suffix," and so forth. That which has all roots—even those read in other groups—as its object is described as such. For if the designation of the *sthānin* (the original element) were not present in the word "śnaḥ," the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the suffix *śnā* would not be known; and consequently, from all [roots]...

This suffix is introduced as an exception to *śānac* after verbal roots ending in consonants, and for that [suffix], there is the substitution of *śānac*; otherwise, the *guṇa* substitution for the root *mid* would not occur. For if this *guṇa* were commenced within the scope of the prohibition, then just as it occurs here in "medhyati," it would likewise occur here as well.

It might be argued that [the rule applies] to *mide*. However, when the *śit* suffix is applied again, the status of being *ṅit*—by the rule "sārvadhātukamapit" (Pāṇini 1.2.4)—is also reinstated. Consequently, although the *guṇa* substitution is prescribed for *mide* even in cases where the prohibition would otherwise apply, it does not occur here.
84. *cchandasi śāyaj api* (Pāṇini 3.1.84). Here too, the purpose of the markers *cit* and *śit* is exactly as previously stated. [Note: This is not found in the Kāśikā.
Regarding the word *gṛhāṇa*: it is the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *graha* (Dhātupāṭha 1533), meaning "to take" or "to seize."

*Sip*; *hiḥ*, then *śnā*; for that [suffix], *śānac*; by *her luk* (6.4.105); and by *grahyādīnāṃ samprasāraṇam* (6.1.16), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). The reading "gṛbhāya" occurs in some places; therein, by the Vārttika *hṛgrahorbhaś chandasi* (8.2.32), there is the substitution of *bha*. "Badhāna": [from] *bandha*.
In the root *bandh* (Dhātupāṭha 1508), there is the elision of the nasal *n* according to Pāṇini 6.4.24 (*ṭhaniditām*). The remainder is as before.

85. *vyatyayo bahulam* (3.1.85). Regarding the term *yathāyatham*: that which is one's own respective domain is *yathāyatham*; the meaning is "in whichever respective domain. He asks: what, then, is this so-called *vyatyaya* (transposition)? He says: [it is]—
"Transposition (*vyatyaya*) is the act of exchanging. To clarify that very transposition, he says:

"Exchange (*vyatihāra*)," etc. By the words "in some cases," etc., he shows another mode of transposition. Regarding the form "bhedati": [this occurs] in the domain of the *śnam* suffix, where the *śap* suffix [would otherwise apply].

The rule [is as follows]: even in the case of *mriyate*, the substitution of *śa* for *śap* and the use of the *parasmaipada* ending occur by way of anomaly (*vyatyaya*). Regarding *mriyate*: as before, there is the augment *riṅ*, and for that, *iyaṅ*.
Regarding *neṣatu*: it is the *loṭ* of the root *nī*, with the ending *tip*; then by *er-uḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.86), *sip* is substituted for it. From that...
The suffix *śap* is added, the root undergoes *guṇa*, and the *s* of *sip* becomes *ṣ*.

An example of the threefold formation (*trivikaraṇatā*) is: *taruṣema vṛtram* (Kāśikā) and *taruṣema dṛṣadam*. Here, from the root *tṛ* ("to cross"), the optative (*liṅ*) is used in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), followed by the suffix *mas*; [the augment] *nityaṃ iṅt* applies.

(3.4.99) Thus, there is elision of the *s* of *asmasi*; [the suffix] *yāsuṭ* [is applied]; because of the rule "in the Veda, both ways" (3.4.117), the *liṅ* suffix is treated as *sārvadhātuka*, from which follows *sip*, and after that, *aṅ*; [then] *guṇa* of the root, *ṣatva* of *sip*, and [finally] "for *a*, *iy*" (ato yeyaḥ).
Thus, there is the substitution of *iy*. By the rule "aṅgasya saha ṭhād guṇaḥ" (6.1.87), there is *guṇa* [substitution].
By the rule "liṅḥ salopo'nantasya" (6.1.79), there is the elision (*lopa*) of *s*. By the rule "lopo vyor vali" (6.1.66), there is the elision of *y*.
Now, why was it not simply stated as "atha vyatyayaḥ" (now, transposition), instead of using the term *bahulagrahaṇa* (the mention of 'often' or 'frequently')?

For, when the word *api* (also) is carried over from the preceding sūtra, the sense is that "in the Veda there is transposition (*vyatyaya*), and by virtue of the word *api*, there is also that which is obtained according to the general rule (*yathāprāpta*). When this connection is made, even without [the use of *bahula*], [the desired result follows].

Since the inclusion of the term *bahula* (often) ensures that everything desired is indeed accomplished, he says: "The inclusion of *bahula*," and so forth. The purpose of *bahula* is so that there may be a deviation—characterized by transposition—from every rule, whether it be one currently under discussion (*prakṛta*) or not (*aprakṛta*). Otherwise, if the inclusion of *bahula* were absent, [the rules would apply without exception].
[The substitution] would apply only to those [suffixes] beginning with *sya* and ending with *śānac*, and not to others such as *śnam* and so on;
yet it is desired that it should apply to them as well. This is obtained only through the inclusion of the term "bahulam" (diversely).
To demonstrate this very point, he says: "su-p-ti-r-upagraha," etc. Thereupon...

There is a transposition of case endings (*supām vyatyayaḥ*): where "in the southern direction" (*dhuri dakṣiṇāyām*) would have been expected, the genitive is used in place of the locative. Regarding verbal suffixes (*tiṅam*): in the example "those who fashion the sacrificial post" (*ye yūpāya takṣati*), the form *takṣanti* would have been expected.
The primary *upagraha* (voice) is a specific action indicated by the substitutes for *l* (the *l*-class suffixes). However, in this context...
The term *upagraha* (grammatical voice) is applied because it is the cause for manifesting those [voices];
what is meant is this: there is a transposition (*vyatyaya*) of the *ātmanepada* and *parasmaipada*. For example:
*sa brahmacāriṇamicchate*, *pratītamanyadagniṃ yudhyati*; *icchati*, *badhyate*.

Where *liṅga* (grammatical gender) is required—such as in "madhostṛptā ivāsate" (*they sit as if satiated with honey*)—*madhoḥ* (genitive singular) is required. Where *puruṣa* (person) is required—such as in "atopacārairdaśabhirviyūyāya" (*having separated [him] by ten expedients*)—in the domain of the first person, the second person is used, as in *viyūyāt*. [The root *yu* is used in the sense of] "mixing" (Dhātupāṭha).

1033), from the root preceded by *vi*, in the sense of benediction (*āśis*), the suffix *liṅ* is applied; then *sip*; then *yāsuṭ*; then, by the rule "ṭhakṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.24), there is lengthening [of the vowel]; then, by the rule "ṭhskoḥ saṃyogādyorante ca" (Pāṇini 8.2.29), there is the elision of *s*. Regarding "of time"—he, by means of one who is about to establish the sacred fires (*ādhāsyamāna*). [This is] the *luṭ* [suffix].

The suffix *luṭ* is used in the sense of an object (*viṣaye*). Here, the word "time" (*kāla*) refers to the *luṅ* and other temporal suffixes because they have time as their domain. Indeed, a transposition of actual time cannot be effected. Regarding *halām*: "the seed of the mouth has blossomed" (*śubhitaṃ mukhabījam*). This form occurs where one might expect *śobhitam*. [This is derived from] the roots *śubha* and *śumbha*, which mean "to shine" (*śobhārthe*).
(Dhātupāṭha 1321, 1322) *niṣṭhā*, *iṭ*, and the replacement of the phoneme *bh* by *ph*. Regarding the vowels (*acām*):

[in the case of] "the pregnant wives shall sing to me" (*upagāyantu māṃ patnayo garbhiṇyaḥ*), where one would have expected "patnyaḥ garbhiṇyaḥ," the long vowel *ī* is replaced by the short vowel *i*. Regarding the accents (*svarāṇām*): by the rule "ṭhanto'vatyā" (Pāṇini 6.1.220), there is the acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable.

Just as it occurs here—*aśvavatīm somavatīm prajāvatīm sūryavatīm dṛṣadam ita*—so too it should be here: *aśvavatī somavatī prajāvatī*. However, when there is a transposition (*vyatyaya*), the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the word *satyāśva* itself occurs. What, then, is the original accent?

The first syllable is acute (*udātta*). For instance, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is grave (*anudātta*) because it is marked with the indicatory letter *p*. The same applies to the possessive suffix *matup*.
Regarding the suffix *kvan*, there is the Daivaṭasūtra:
"From the roots *aś*, *pruṣ*, *laṭi*, *kaṇi*, *khaṭi*, and *viś*, [the suffix] *kvan* [is added]" (Daivaṭa 8.125).

Because it ends in the *kvan* suffix, the word *aśva* has its first syllable acute by virtue of the *nit*-accent. The mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) is for the purpose of indicating any grammatical relation (*kāraka*); the meaning is that there is an interchange of grammatical relations. [The form] *āsādayadbhiḥ* [is used] for both [the agent and the object]; although *āsādayadbhyaḥ* would have been expected, [it is not so because] the recipient (*sampradāna*) [is intended].

The term *karaṇatva* [is used] for the purpose of including the *pratyāhāra* "ṭhyaṅ"—that is, from the *yak* in "sārvadhātuke yak" (3.1.67) up to the *ṅ* in "liṅyāśiṣyaṅ" (3.1.86). The meaning is that there is a transposition (*vyatyaya*) of the affixes beginning with *yak* and ending with *aṅ*. [This applies to the forms] *muṇḍā* and *śuṣmasya*.

Regarding the word *bhedati*: since the suffix *śnam* would otherwise be required, the author of the grammar—Pāṇini—intends a substitution (*vyatyaya*) for these suffixes beginning with *śap*. That [substitution] is also established by means of "variety" (*bāhulaka*). From the word *api*, the substitution of *syat* and so forth is also included. The state of being various is "variety" (*bāhulakam*).
The suffix *vuñ* is applied [after the word *dvandva*] because it belongs to the class beginning with *manojña* (Pāṇini 5.1.133). The word *ca* ("and") indicates the reason (*hetu*).

Since, in this way, the transposition of both the relevant (*prakṛta*) and irrelevant (*aprakṛta*) elements is established by means of the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*), for that reason the term *bahulagrahaṇa* was employed.

86. *liṅyāśiṣy aṅ* (3.1.86). [This is] an exception (*apavāda*) to *śap*. Now, one might object: "The *liṅ* that is prescribed in the sense of benediction (*āśis*) receives the designation *ārthadhātuka* by the rule *liṅyāśiṣi* (3.4.116), and [the designation] *sārvadhātuka* [is also applied to it]."

[Since the suffix] śap is prescribed [by Pāṇini 3.1.68], how can it be an exception (apavāda) to that? To this he says: "In the Veda, both ways," and so forth. With the intention that it is seen here only after roots such as *sthā* and not after others, he says: "sthā-gā-gami," and so forth. Regarding "upastheyam": from the root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *upa*, there is the optative (liṅ) in the sense of a benediction (āśis), with the ending *mip*; of that...

By the rule *ṭhtasthas' (3.4.101)* and others, there is the substitution of *ām*; then *yāsuṭ* is added. Because it possesses both designations (*ubhayasaṃjñātvena*), it is treated as a *sārvadhātuka*, and thus by the rule *ṭhliṅ salopo'nantyasya' (7.2.79)*, there is the elision of the *s*.
In some places, the reading is *ṭhupastheṣam'. In that case, because it is an *ārdhadhātuka*, there is no elision of the *s*.

In *upageyam*, there is the elision of the *yaL* suffix. [The root is] *gai* (meaning "to sound," DhP 917). The substitution of *ā* occurs by the rule *ādeca upadeśe 'śiti* (6.1.45). The remainder is as before. In *gamema*, there is the *mas* ending of the *liṅ* after the root *gam*. The elision of *s* occurs by the rule *nityaṃ ṅtiḥ* (3.4.99).

The *yāsuṭ* suffix and all other elements are as before. Regarding *vocyeyam*: the root *vac* (meaning "to speak," DhP 1842) takes the suffix *sip*, followed by *ām*, then *aṅ*. After *aṅ*, by *vaca um* (Pāṇini 7.4.20), *um* is added to *vac*. For the syllable *yā*, there is *iy* (by *liṅaḥ salopo 'nantyasya*, though not explicitly cited here, it follows from context). In both cases, *ādguṇaḥ* (6.1.87) applies. Regarding *vidyeyam*: the root *vid*...
In *jñāne* (DhP 1064), [the form] is "śaknuyām" (I may be able); this is from *śaklṛ* in the sense of "capacity" (DhP 1261).

In "āruheyaṃ" (I may climb), [it is derived from] *ruha* in the sense of "germination from a seed" or "manifestation"—that is, "birth" (DhP 859)—where the substitution of *iy* and all other operations are as previously described.

Regarding the statement "the suffix *aṅ* should be prescribed for the root *dṛś*": if *aṅ* were applied, then by the rule "for *ṛ* and *dṛś*, *aṅ* [is substituted], and there is guṇa" (Pāṇini 7.4.16), guṇa would occur; and thus the form *dṛśyam* would not be established. However, when *aṅ* is applied, because it is marked with *k* (kit), there is an absence of guṇa. Therefore, *aṅ* must be stated—that is, explained. The explanation is as follows: [The commentary continues: "The suffix *aṅ* is prescribed after the root *dṛś* in the sense of 'to be seen,' provided that it is intended to express a feminine gender ending in *ī*. Why? Because otherwise, the suffix *kyap* would apply. For the suffix *kyap* is prescribed after the roots *dṛś*, *spṛś*, and *mṛś* in the sense of 'to be seen. Since *kyap* is marked with *k* (kit), there is no guṇa; and since it is marked with *p* (pit), there is no feminine *ī*. Consequently, the form *dṛśyam* would not be established. However, because of the continued application of the term "frequently" (bahula), this must be stated as an explanatory rule (vaktavya).

87. *karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.87). Regarding the term *karmavat*: it is derived from *tena tulyaṃ kriyā ced vatiḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.115), and not from *tatra tasyeva* (Pāṇini 5.1.116); this is because the word *tulyakriyaḥ* is presented in the nominative case (*prathamā*). Otherwise, [the rule would have been formulated differently].
Regarding "tulyakriye": one should provide the designation [of this term] in either the locative or the genitive case, as in *tulyakriyasya*.

[The compound] *tulyakriyaḥ* means "one whose action (*kriyā*) is equal (*tulya*). Equal to what? Equal to the object (*karman*). Although it is a dependent compound (*sāpekṣa*), it is formed because its meaning is clear (*gamakatvāt*). This word *tulya* signifies "similar" (*sadṛśa*). And not...

The similarity between the means (*sādhana*) and the action (*kriyā*) is established through the action; for they are absolutely distinct. To explain: the object (*karman*) is a substance that is fully accomplished, whereas action has a nature contrary to that. Therefore, in the phrase "by means of the object" (*karmaṇā*), this word "object" is used figuratively (*gauṇa*) by way of metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*), because it resides in that which pertains to the object.

It occurs in relation to the action, as in the example "the beds cry," where the word "beds" refers to the persons [on them]. This figurative usage (upacāra) is intended so that verbs whose state resides in the object (*karmasthabhāvaka*) and whose action resides in the object (*karmasthakriyā*) may undergo the treatment of being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*), whereas this does not apply to those whose state resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*) or whose action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthakriyā*).

The purpose is so that this [undesirable consequence] does not occur. Having kept all of this in mind, he says: "In the case of an action residing in the object (*karmaṇi*), the action is the object (*karma*).

By this, he explains that this word *karman* denotes an action residing in the object. And regarding the meaning of the sūtra that results when the word *karman* denotes an action residing in the object, [he states it as follows]:

To demonstrate this, he says: "By [an action] residing in the object," and so forth. The meaning of the sūtra being thus established, one who might teach—thinking that this word *tulya* (equal) signifies "common"—might say: "If, by an action residing in the object, the agent whose action is equal [to it], that is, whose action is common, becomes like the object (*karmavat*)."

In that case, the expression "Devadatta cooks rice" would also [be an instance of] this; because here too, with reference to that primary action, all the causal substances proceed, and by means of that action residing in the object, the agent becomes one whose action is common [to all factors].

To the objection that "just as this [action] belongs to other causal factors, so too does it belong to the agent," he replies with the words "in which action" and so forth. By employing the two words *tadvat* and *yathā* in the sense of similarity, he indicates:
"this word *tulya* (equal) expresses similarity, not commonality."

Thus he explains: in a case where an agent, even while remaining in the state of being an agent, is observed to perform such an action as that which was performed while in the state of being an object, that agent becomes "like the object" (*karmavat*).
And since this similarity must be based on some point of difference, it is precisely the unique [action] characterized by placing [the pot on the fire] and so forth [that constitutes the basis].
The specific activity of the agent is grasped, and not the common [activity] characterized by softening and so forth.

And that specific activity of the agent Devadatta—unlike the activities of other factors—is what is expressed in the sentence "Devadatta cooks the rice. Therefore, it is not [the case that the common activity is denoted].

The treatment as an object (karmavadbhāva) occurs. Alternatively, it might be argued that since it is stated "the agent whose action is similar to the action residing in the object is treated as an object," one might think that the word *tulya* (similar) expresses identity and thus raise this objection: "If that were so, then in a case such as 'the granary being split splits the vessels,' [the agent] would also [be treated as an object]."

[The opponent] attains [this conclusion], for indeed, "just as such an action consisting of the division of parts is observed in the receptacles (pātra), exactly the same is observed in the granary (kusūla) acting as the agent"—regarding this prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), he says:
"In which action," and so forth. By the word *sa* ("that"), the same meaning as that expressed by *yasmin* ("in which") is intended.

That very [agent] which was previously specified is now being referred back. By this, demonstrating that an agent who performs an action equivalent to an action residing in the object—by virtue of having a single substance as their substratum—becomes like an object (*karmavadbhavati*), he refutes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). And this is obtained through the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*).
For action is proximate when it inheres in the same substance [as the agent], but it is remote when it inheres in another substance.
Now, it is a view that power (*śakti*) is the causal factor (*kāraka*), yet the power of the object (*karman*) is never [perceived].

It attains the state of being an agent; therefore, it was incorrectly stated: "in which action, even though it has become the agent... [This is because] when the distinction between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) is not intended to be expressed, this refers simply to the substance (*dravya*) which is the substratum of that power; thus, there is no fault. However, this which was stated is incorrect: "In the same way, action... [is not distinct from the agent].
"It is observed as such in the case of an action.

[Objection: Since the very same operation that exists in the state of being an object (*karman*) also exists in the state of being an agent (*kartṛ*), similarity is not tenable, because similarity must reside in a locus of difference?
[Response: This is not a fault, because of the distinction between states (*avasthā*).
Although substance, like a state, is non-different from action due to its identity with it, nevertheless there is a distinction between states:

for the state of being an agent is indeed one thing, and the state of being an object is another. Since there is a difference of action through the difference of states, the similarity exists as that which underlies them.
In this context, extension (atideśa) is of many kinds, based on the distinctions of cause (nimitta), designation (vyapadeśa), scripture (śāstra), and function (kārya).

Among these, here there is no extension of the cause; for it is not possible to extend to the agent that which is the cause of the object—namely, its being "that which the agent most desires to reach" (kartur īpsitatamatva).
Because there is no connection between the properties of one thing and another thing that possesses contradictory properties.

Furthermore, the transfer of designation (*vyapadeśātideśa*) does not differ from the transfer of name (*saṃjñātideśa*). However, in the case of the transfer of name, the fault that will be stated [later] applies, and the mention of the suffix *-vat* would be purposeless. But in the case of the transfer of grammatical rule (*śāstrātideśa*),...
The grammatical rule (śāstra) is extended [by analogy]; when that is extended, the suffixes *ya* and so forth are obtained by those very rules.

Consequently, if this were an extension of the rule (*śāstrātideśa*), then because they are subsequent, the suffixes *śa* and so forth would act as sublaters (*bādhaka*) regarding the agent who is also the object of the action, and a remedy for that situation would have to be provided.

But in the case of the extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*), the *ya*-class suffixes and others are prescribed by this very [rule]. Therefore, since the *śa*-class suffixes and others—which depend on the agent—would otherwise apply to the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*), they are superseded by the *ya*-class suffixes and others due to their higher status; thus, there is nothing further that needs to be addressed. For the extension of the operation is indeed the primary [consideration].
Because those extension rules (atideśa-śāstra) have that [the agent] as their purpose. Therefore, demonstrating that this [tulyakriya rule] is an extension of function (kāryātideśa), he says:

"karmāśrayāṇi" and so forth. Now, one might object: since the word "tulyakriyaḥ" is presented in the nominative case, it would be understood that the extension applies to the agent (*kartṛ*) ending in that suffix, and not to the [action] in the sūtra.
The mention of the *kartṛ* (agent) exists. Although that [term] is under discussion (*prakṛta*), it ends in the locative case;

however, the purpose here is with that which is indicated by the nominative. Therefore, he says "in the agent" (*kartari*) and so forth, to explain how the extension (*atideśa*) can be made without a mention of the *kartṛ* ending in the nominative.

What, then, is the purpose of this extended application (*atideśa*)? He says: "The [rules for] *yak*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*," and so forth. "It is split" (*bhidyate*) is an example of *yak*. "It was split" (*abhedhi*) is an example of *ciṇ*. "It will be done" (*kāriṣyate*) is an example of the *ciṇvadbhāva* (the treatment as if *ciṇ* had occurred). For in the passive (*karmani*), by the rule "before *syas*, *sic*, and *sīyuṭ*" (Pāṇini 6.4.62), etc., [the *ciṇvadbhāva* applies].
The status of being treated like *ciṇ* (ciṇvadbhāva) has been prescribed. However, all of these examples pertain to the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
Regarding the phrase "even that which is inherent" (*svāśrayam api*) and so forth: that which does not occur even in the absence of an extended application (*atideśa*) is "inherent" (*svāśraya*).

The suffix *vat* is employed for the purpose of expressing "it might be as if. For if it were absent, this would be merely a rule for technical designation (*saṃjñāsūtra*), and consequently, an agent whose action is similar to that of an object would receive the designation "object" (*karmasaṃjñaka*).
This being the case, because [the verb] would be transitive (*sakarmaka*), [the rule] *ḷaḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.69) [would apply].

If the suffix *lakāra* were used [in the sense of the agent], it would not occur in the sense of the state (*bhāva*). However, when the suffix *vat* is employed, there is indeed an extension (*atideśa*). By means of that, the grammatical operation (*kārya*) pertaining to the agent—which was previously unobtained—comes to apply to the object, rather than the agency residing in its own substratum.

Thus, the nature of being intransitive (*akarmaka-svabhāvatva*) is removed, because the function (*vyāpāra*) of that [agency] is transferred there [to the object]. By this, for those [verbs] that are intransitive...

The suffix *la* is established in the sense of the action (bhāva)—as in "the granary is being split" (*bhidyate kusūlam*). Now, one might ask: why does the accusative case not occur after the word *kusūla* in the sentence "the granary splits by itself" (*bhidyate kusūlaḥ svayameva*), since this too is an object (*karman*)? To this he says: "In the sense of benediction (*āśis*), the suffix *aṅ* is applied to the root *liṅ*" (*liṅyāśiṣyaṅ*), and so forth. There are two *lakāra*s.
In which [context] there is that mention of two *l* sounds. If it is a mention of two *l* sounds, then he asks "why? and says "in that case," etc. The word "effect" (*kārya*) is to be supplied.
When there is a mention of two *l* sounds, [the rule] from "ṅyāśiṣy-aṅ" (Pāṇini 3.1.86) [applies].

In the case of *lānuvṛtti* (the recurrence of the suffix *la*), only that which is the agent (*kartṛ*) with respect to the action becomes like the object (*karmavat*), but not the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason. Since this is so, the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) does not occur after the word *kusūla*.

Regarding the rule "karaṇādhikaraṇābhyām": if the word "karmaṇā" (by [the action] of the object) were not present, then even by means of an action residing in an instrument or a locus, an agent whose action is equal [to that of the object] would be treated like the object;

however, because this word is present, it does not occur. For example, in the expression "sādhvasiś chinatti" ("he cuts well with the sword"), [the agent is not treated like the object]. This is because of the instrument.

When there is an intention to express agency (*kartṛtva*), even with respect to an action residing in the instrument— characterized here by the entry of the substance to be cut— the sword is the agent because its action is identical [to that of the agent]. In the example "The pot cooks well" (*sādhu sthālī pacati*), when there is an intention to express the agency of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), it is possible because of the action residing in the locus, which consists of supporting (*dhāraṇa*).

The agent is one whose action is equal [to that of the object]. Now, why does this not apply here: "Devadatta cooks rice" (*pacaty odanaṃ devadattaḥ*) and "the rice cooks by itself" (*rādhyaty odanaḥ svayam eva*)? For even in these cases, the agent has an action equal to that which resides in the object; for the action is of the same kind in the rice when it has become the object.

It is observed that the characteristic of moistening (*vikledana*) is present even when [the agent] is the performer, because *pacati* (he cooks) and *ādhyati* (he digests) have the same meaning; thus he says: "Because of the governing rule of the verbal root (*dhātu*)," and so forth.
This word *samāna* is a synonym for "one" (*eka*), as in: "The [wealth] of Devadatta and Yajñadatta is the same."

Regarding the word *mātṛ*: it is understood that there is only one mother. From the rule *dhātor ekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.22), the term *dhātu* (verbal root) is carried over [by anuvṛtti]. Furthermore, words such as "object" (*karman*) and so forth are relative terms (*sambandhi-śabda*); and those which are relative terms present their correlative by its very nature (*prakṛtyā*).

For instance: when it is said, "One should act with devotion toward one's mother," even without the explicit mention of the word "one's own" (*svasyām*), it is understood as "toward one's own mother. Therefore, it brings to mind only that verbal root in relation to which the object possesses the status of an agent; it does not bring to mind any other. And thus—

Since the mention of "root" (dhātu) is being carried over [from a previous rule], this meaning is obtained: when a root is presented with an object, if that same root has that very object as its agent, then this extension (atideśa) applies, and not otherwise. Therefore, in the case of *pacaty odanam* ("he cooks rice"), [the rule does not apply].

In the case of *devadattaḥ, rādhyaty odanaḥ svayam eva* ("Devadatta, the rice cooks by itself"), [the rule] does not apply, because it is impossible for a single rice (*odana*) to be both the object and the agent when two distinct verbal roots (*dhātu*) are involved. Alternatively, the singular number (*ekā saṃkhyā*) attached to the word "root" (*dhātoḥ*) is intended to be significant; therefore, [the rule applies] only when there is a single root.
The treatment as an object (*karmavadbhāva*) occurs.

By the rule beginning with "of those whose action resides in the object" (*karmasthabhāvakānām*), he demonstrates the very meaning established by logic. For instance: the treatment as an object applies to an agent whose action is equivalent to an action residing in the object.
Furthermore, for verbs whose state resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*) or whose action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthakriyā*), there is no such agent [as described].

Although action (*kriyā*) is also included— since both "state" (*bhāva*) and "action" (*kriyā*) are encompassed by the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.126)— nevertheless, because both are mentioned here, there is a distinction in meaning.
It should be understood as follows:

that action which is to be accomplished by means of motion is denoted by the word "action" (kriyā), whereas that which is to be accomplished without motion is denoted by the word "state" (bhāva). This applies to those [roots] whose state resides in the object and whose action resides in the object.

Regarding action (*kriyā*): in order to show examples of those [verbs] for which the state (*bhāva*) resides in the agent and the action (*kriyā*) resides in the agent, he says: "The state of the root *pac* resides in the object" (*karmasthaḥ pacaterbhāvaḥ*). In the case of "the pot cooks by itself" (*pacyate ghaṭaḥ svayameva*), when the cooking having that location as its object is accomplished, [that is the example].

At that time, cooking, which by its very nature is to be accomplished by means of motionless instruments, resides in the agent; however, when the production of cooking occurs in a substance of cooking that is moving to another location, then the action of the root *pac* resides solely in the object, as in the example: "The rice is being cooked" (*pacyata odanaḥ*).

Regarding the rule *karmasthāṭaca bhideḥ kriyā* ("the suffix *aṭac* is applied after the root *bhid* when the action resides in the object"): "The granary splits by itself. For the action of the root *bhid* is characterized by the separation of parts, and that occurs when a change of state (*daśāntaraprāpti*) has taken place; thus, there is a movement (*parispanda*), and by that, the action resides in the object.
"The state of being (bhāva) [expressed by] the root *ās* resides in the agent. The term *āsibhāvaḥ* means the state (*bhāva*) of the verbal root *ās*.

For "sitting" (*āsana*) is indeed a state (*bhāva*), because it is accomplished by means of an instrument that does not involve physical motion (*parispanda*). Thus, when activity has ceased, one uses the expression "he sits" (*āste*). The state of sitting associated with the month is what is meant here.

The compound is formed according to the *śākapārthiva* class (where the middle term is elided), resulting in *māsāsibhāvaḥ*. When does this state of "sitting" (*āsibhāva*) become associated with a month? It occurs when the expression *māsam āste* ("he sits for a month") is employed. Here, the word *māsam* takes the accusative case in the sense of an object (*karman*). The designation of "object," however, is established by the rule: "Time, state, and distance to be traversed are designated as objects when used with intransitive verbs."

Because of the statement [Pāṇini 1.4.51], "The state of being seated (*āsibhāva*) resides in the agent, because it inheres in the one who sits. Therefore, the expression "the month sits by itself" (*asyate māsaḥ svayameva*) does not occur.
And as for the statement, "The action of *gam* resides in the agent": movement (*gamana*) consists of the shifting of the feet, and that is characterized by vibration (*parispandana*).
Furthermore, action is unaccomplishable [by itself], and it inheres in the agent, such as Devadatta, not in the object,
such as the village. Therefore, because there is no action residing in the object, the expression "the village goes by itself" does not occur.

88. *tapas* [takes the genitive] only when it has *tapas* as its object. (3.1.88) Regarding the phrase "only when it has *tapas* as its object": the particle *eva* (only) is for the sake of clarity; for since all sentences have exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) as their result, this meaning is already obtained [by default]. For if it were the case that [the genitive would apply] even when it does not have *tapas* as its object...

It would follow that the mention of "the performance of austerity" (*tapaḥkarma*) would be purposeless. By means of the restriction "not for one whose action is other [than austerity]," he shows what is excluded. "Because of the difference in action" (*kriyābhedāt*);
the meaning is "because of the dissimilarity of the action. For previously, when there was similarity of action, there was the status of being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*).

Since [the term] "vihita" implies dissimilarity (*vaiṣamya*), this [sūtra] is for the purpose of providing an injunction (*vidhi*). For this very reason, because equality with the action residing in the object (*karman*) is not possible, the rule *karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.87) does not apply here. By the phrase "fasting and so forth," he refers to that very same [point].

He demonstrates the distinction in verbal action (*kriyābheda*). By the word "fasting" (*upavāsa*) and so forth, he explains the meaning of the word *tapas*. With the phrase "it causes suffering," he shows that in the state of the object of the action (*karmāvasthā*), the root *tap* has the meaning "to cause suffering. As in the expression "one performs austerity for the sake of heaven," the word *tapas* here refers to the object of knowledge (*jñānaviṣaya*).

By the phrase "it exists as the cause for the attainment of heaven and so forth," and by the gloss "the meaning is 'he acquires,'" [the author] shows that in its state as the agent, the root *tap* (to heat) functions in the sense of acquisition (*arjana*). "The meaning is 'it causes to turn back'" means it does not cause suffering; for since austerity (*tapas*) is insentient, suffering is impossible for it.
In examples such as "he heats gold" (*ṭhapati suvarṇam*), the verb *tap* does not undergo the treatment of an object-like agent (*karmavadbhāva*) because gold is the object of the heating.

89. *na duhasnunamāṃ yakciṇau* (Pāṇini 3.1.89). [The commentary states: "In the case of the reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*), the suffixes *yak* and *ciṇ* are not prescribed. The term "reflexive agent" (*karmakartṛ*) is a qualifier. This refers to the rule: *karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.87).

This prohibition applies to the *yak* and *ciṇ* affixes that are obtained [by rule], but not to the *ciṇvad-bhāva* and the passive (*karman*) affixes. This is for the purpose of showing that it also applies to those two which are obtained when there is a pure passive (*śuddhe karmaṇi*). And this follows the principle: "A rule applies either to what is immediately preceding or to what is otherwise applicable."

This is obtained by the *paribhāṣā* "or there is a prohibition" (*pratiṣedho vā*, Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 19). Regarding the form *dugdhe*: when the *yak* affix is prohibited, the *śap* affix is applied; because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of that [affix]. As before, the changes of *ghatva*, *jhatva*, and *jaśtva* apply. Regarding the form *adugdha*: this is the *luṅ* tense. When the *ciṇ* affix is prohibited, the *ksa* affix is applied; of that...

By [the rule] *ṭhlugvā* (Pāṇini 7.3.73), there is elision (*luk*). Regarding *prasnute*: the root is *pṣṇu* or *snu* in the sense of "flowing" (Dhātupāṭha 1038); as before, there is elision of the *śap* suffix. Regarding *prāsnoṣṭa*: this is the *luṅ* tense. Regarding *namate*: the root is *ṇam* in the sense of "bending" and "sound" (Dhātupāṭha 981).

It should be understood that here the root *nam* (to bow) functions in the sense of the object (*karman*) with the causative meaning (*ṇyartha*) inherent within it. For in this way, the action resides in the object (*karmasthakriya*). Otherwise, because the action would reside in the agent (*kartṛsthakriya*), there would be no possibility [of the application of the rule], and thus the prohibition would be meaningless. However, when the causative meaning is inherent, the action resides in the object.

It occurs as follows: "Devadatta bends the staff" (*namati daṇḍaṃ devadattaḥ*) and "the staff bends by itself" (*namate daṇḍaḥ svayameva*), just as in the state of the causative suffix *ṇic*. Regarding the rule "in the prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ*" (*yakciṇoḥ pratiṣedhe*), etc., when the prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ* is to be applied, there must be an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of that same prohibition to the roots beginning with *śranth* (such as *śranth*, *granth*, *vṛt*, etc.).
The meaning is that the application [of the rule] must be made. However, the application is not [otherwise] established;

therefore, for the sake of achieving the desired result, it must be made by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule). The mention of *ṇi* includes both the causative *ṇic* with a cause (*hetumaṇṇic*) and the other [causative]. Regarding the causative *ṇic*: "Devadatta causes the mat to be made" (*kārayati kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ*).

"The mat causes itself to be made" (*kārayate kaṭaḥ svayam eva*). When the *yak* suffix is prohibited, the *śap* suffix is applied. "The mat caused itself to be made" (*acīkarata kaṭaḥ svayam eva*). When the *ciṇ* suffix is prohibited, the *caṅ* suffix is applied by the rule *ṇi-śri-* (Pāṇini 3.1.48), and the shortening of the penultimate vowel occurs by the rule *ṇau caṅy upadhāyā hrasvaḥ* (7.4.1). [The elision of the *ṇic*] occurs by the rule *caṅ* (6.1.11).

The doubling [of the root] is the operation of reduplication (*abhyāsakārya*). The other suffix is *ṇiṅ*, according to the rule "after the words *puccha*, *bhāṇḍa*, and *cīvara*, the suffix *ṇiṅ* is applied" (Pāṇini 3.1.20). Examples are: "the cowherd shakes the tail of the cow" (*utpuccchayate gāṃ gopaḥ*) and "the cow shakes its own tail" (*utpuccchayate gauḥ svayameva*). Since the *yaK* suffix is prohibited, the *śap* suffix is applied. It should be understood that the same applies in subsequent cases as well. Example: "the cow shook its tail repeatedly" (*udapupuccchata gauḥ*).

"By itself" (*svayameva*). When the *ciṇ* affix is prohibited, the *caṅ* substitute occurs as before; this should be understood to apply in subsequent cases as well. [The roots] *śrantha* and *grantha*, meaning "to string together," are listed in the Curādigaṇa (DhP 1837, 1838). [The rule] "optionally from *ā-dhṛṣ*" (DhP 1805) applies.

"Immediately following [the root]"—this refers to the option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding the causative suffix (*ṇic*). When *ṇic* is absent in those two cases, it is as in the examples; otherwise, the formation is established simply by the suffix *ṇi*. Devadatta knots the knot (*granthi*).
The knot knots itself (*granthaṃ granthate svayam eva*). The knot knotted itself (*agranthiṣṭa granthaḥ svayam eva*). He weaves (*śranthati*).

Devadatta binds the girdle (*mekhalām*); the girdle binds itself (*mekhalā svayameva*). Since the roots *śrantha* and *grantha*—meaning "to bind"—are also listed in the *krī* class and other classes (*dhā.pā.* 1512, 1513), this prohibition applies to them as well:
Devadatta binds the girdle (*śrathnīte mekhalām devadattaḥ*), the girdle binds itself (*śranthīte mekhalā svayameva*).

The substitution of *i* occurs by the rule *ṭhī halyaghoḥ* (6.4.113). The girdle untied itself (*aśranthiṣṭa mekhalā svayameva*). Devadatta ties the knot (*grathnīte granthaṃ devadattaḥ*). The knot ties itself (*granthīte granthaḥ svayameva*). The knot untied itself (*agranthiṣṭa granthaḥ svayameva*). Devadatta tells the story (*brūte kathāṃ devadattaḥ*). The story tells itself (*brūte kathā svayameva*). As before, there is the elision of *śap*.
*luk* [is applied]. *Devadattaḥ avocata kathām* ("Devadatta spoke the story"). *Avocata kathāṃ svayam eva* ("He himself spoke the story").

By the rule *bruvo vaciḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.53), there is the substitution of *vac* for *brū*; by the rule *asyativaktikhyātibhyaḥ aṅ* (3.1.52), there is the substitution of *aṅ* [for the suffix]; and by the rule *vaca um* (7.4.20), the augment *um* is added. This is because the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) is inherent (*antarbhāvita*).

The state of having action residing in the object (*karmasthakriyatva*) is to be understood [from the rule] "of those that are intransitive when used with the middle voice" (*ātmanepadākarmakāṇām*). Those verbal roots which are taken as being intransitive at the time of the prescription of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) are called "those that are intransitive when used with the middle voice. For example: "The Saindhava horses exert themselves by themselves" (*vikurvate saindhavāḥ svayameva*). [This refers to the rule] "in the case of middle-voice endings, [the substitution of *iṭ* does not occur] after a root ending in *a*" (*ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ*, Pāṇini 7.1.5).

This is an instance of *ityādi-ādeśa* (substitution of "etcetera"). In the phrase "the Saindhavas drew themselves apart by their own accord" (*vyakṛṣata saindhavāḥ svayameva*), the use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*)—due to the rule "after the root *kṛ* preceded by *vi*, when it is intransitive" (*vipūrvāt ṭhakarmakācca*, Pāṇini 1.3.35)—establishes its intransitivity. Here too, [it refers] to leaping (*valgana*).
The present form of the verb *karoti* has the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) internalized and functions as a transitive action residing in the object (*karmasthakiya*).

90. *kṛṣi-rañjoḥ prācām śyan parasmaipadaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.90). The mention of *rañj* with the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika*) is for the sake of brevity. [The commentary states: "These are exceptions to the *yak* and the *ātmanepada*. Here, *śyan* is an exception to *yak*; *parasmaipada* [is an exception to the *ātmanepada*].
Regarding the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), as in *rañjate*:

there is the elision of the nasal by the rule *aniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24). [The commentator states: "The mention of the Easterners (*prācām*) is for the sake of optionality. By this, he removes the sense that it is for the purpose of honoring (*pūjārtha*). For if it were for the purpose of honoring, no option would be obtained.

By the phrase "ṭh kuṣyate" and so forth, he demonstrates what is intended when the term *prāk* (before) is used in the sense of an option (*vikalpa*). The phrase "and in the domain of *syādi*" and so forth—by the word *ādi*, there is the inclusion of *tāsi* and the others. [The examples are] "cukuṣe" and "rarañje"; these are in the *liṭ* (perfect tense), *ātmanepada* voice, with the suffix *tap*.
The example for that [root] is *koṣiṣīṣṭa*. Here, the suffix is the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of benediction (*āśis*);

the augment *sīyuṭ* is applied; the augment *suṭ* is added by the rule *suṭ tithoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.107); then the *guṇa* substitution occurs because the penultimate vowel is light, followed by the substitution of *ṣ* and *ṣṭu* (the change of *t* to *ṭ*).

The example *raṅkṣīṣṭa* is formed as follows: there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *ekāca upadeśe'nudāttāt* (Pāṇini 7.2.10), and the change of *c* to *k* occurs by the rule *coḥ kuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.30).
Thus, there is the substitution of *ku*—the letter *ga*. By the rule "ṭhkhari ca" (Pāṇini 8.4.55), there is the substitution of *ca*—the letter *ka*.
[Examples are] "akoṣi" and "arañji," where *luṅ* and *ciṇ* [are applied].

91. *dhātoḥ* | (3.1.91) "Because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) 'of a verbal root' (*dhātoḥ*) in the prescription of *yaṅ*"—this means that the mention of "verbal root" (*dhātugrahaṇa*) which occurs in the prescription of *yaṅ* in [Pāṇini 3.1.22] *dhātorekācaḥ*, is the governing rule here. And this...

The reasoning for the inclusion of the term *dhātu* (root) when it appears to be redundant is stated as: "But [it is] for the sake of the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of *kṛt*-affixes and *upapada*s. This refutes the charge of redundancy. Now, one might object: "Would not the designations of *kṛt*-affixes and *upapada*s be established even by the previous mention of *dhātu*, as in the case of the suffix *syat* in *kariṣyati*?"

By the rule *kṛdatiṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.93), the designation *kṛt* would apply. Consequently, by the rule *kṛt-taddhita-samāsāś-ca* (1.2.46), the designation *prātipadika* would result; and once that exists, the suffixes *sup* would arise. Furthermore, in the rule *cli luṅ* (3.1.43), the rule *tatrōpapadam* (3.1.92) [would also apply].

Otherwise, the designation *upapada* would also apply to the *luṅ* [tense], and consequently, the meaning "when *luṅ* is the *upapada*, there is *cli*" might be presumed. Therefore, the term *dhātu* is mentioned again here so that the designations *kṛt* and *upapada* may apply within the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning verbal roots (*dhātu*), but not in the preceding rules. Now, these two designations are established by means of this governing rule.
If it is argued that these two will receive the designation of *pratyaya* (suffix), and therefore they will not occur in the preceding rule, we say no;

for the logic of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita-nyāya*) also applies. If the rule were established by way of a governing heading (*adhikāra*), they might be possible even in the preceding case, which would necessitate providing an explanation (*vyākhyāna*). And since an explanation is cumbersome, [the simpler method is preferred].
The mention of "dhātu" (verbal root) occurs. Furthermore, the mention of "dhātu" must necessarily be made for another purpose;
being made for that other purpose, it will also serve to clarify the rule regarding the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of a *kṛt* suffix and its *upapada*.
To demonstrate that very necessity for another purpose, he says: "for the sake of the designation *ārdhadhātuka*," and so forth.
The meaning here should be understood as follows: by virtue of the word "ca" (and), the purpose is also to provide for the rule of non-identity of form (*vā'sarūpa*).

Within this governing heading on verbal roots (*dhātvadhikāra*), namely *vā'sarūpo'striyām* (Pāṇini 3.1.94), it is so that a non-identical apavāda (exceptional rule) may act as an annulment [of the general rule], whereas previously it was not.

Therefore, there is no co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the *sic* affix with the *kṣa*-class and others. Now, one might ask: "Since the designation of *ārdhadhātuka* will be established by the previous mention of 'root' (*dhātu*), what is the purpose of the second mention of 'root'?
To this, he says: "By [the rule] beginning with *dhātoḥ*," and so forth. By [the rule] beginning with *dhātoḥ*...

The meaning is that the term *dhātu* is mentioned again in order that the designation *ārdhadhātuka* should apply to that which is prescribed after the utterance of the word *dhātu*. Why, then, is the designation *ārdhadhātuka* stated for that which is prescribed after [the mention of] *dhātu*? He says: "So that it may not occur here. In its absence...
Regarding the second mention of the term *dhātu* [in Pāṇini 3.4.78], in forms such as *lūbhyām* and *lūbhiḥ*, the designation *ārdhadhātuka* would apply.

This is because a suffix follows a verbal root (*dhātu*) here—on the basis of the rule "those ending in *kviP* do not lose their status as roots" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 132). Since the *ārdhadhātuka* designation would thus apply, the augment *iṭ* characterized by the *ārdhadhātuka* rules would have to be inserted.

[Otherwise] it would follow [as an over-extension]. However, when a second mention of the term "dhātu" (root) is made, by virtue of its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), it refers to that which consists of a verbal root and a suffix (*ucchabdapadātmaka*). By this, the following meaning is obtained:
that which is prescribed by means of the designation "dhātu"—that is, by the very expression "of a root"—is termed *ardhadhātuka*.

Thus, in forms such as *lūbhyām*, the status of being an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix does not apply. For in this case, the suffix is not prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*)—what then? It is prescribed after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

92. *tatra upapadaṃ saptamīstham* (Pāṇini 3.1.92). By the phrase "indicated by the locative case" (*saptamyā nirdiṣṭam*), the meaning of "located in the seventh [case]" (*saptamīstham*) is explained. For this is a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) being prescribed for a word; and which word is "located in the seventh"? That [word] of which the locative case...

The explanation is as follows: in the case of "kumbhakāraḥ," once the designation *upapada* is established, there is a compound by the rule *upapadam atiṅ* (Pāṇini 2.2.19). By the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), the final member of the compound retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvaratva*).
Regarding the phrase "the mention of *ṭh* and *sth*" and so forth: that by which something is pointed out is a "pointing-out" (*nirdeśa*).
That which has a pointing-out in the locative case is a "locative pointing-out" (*saptamī-nirdeśa*). The mention of *sth* is for the purpose of understanding that [rule]. This is what is meant:
so that there may be an understanding of that which is pointed out in the locative in the Sūtra as being the technical name (*saṃjñin*).

The term *sthā* is included for this very purpose. To explain what would happen if the term *sthā* were not used, he says: "For otherwise," and so forth. For otherwise, if the term *sthā* were not employed, [the rule] "In a rule prescribing a technical designation (*saṃjñā*), when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, there is no inclusion of that which ends with it" (Paribhāṣenduśekhara 81) would apply.

The locative case would acquire the designation *upapada*. And since a designation is not appropriate for a non-existent designatum, this [designation] would apply only where the locative case is actually heard—such as in "stamberama" and the like. It might be argued:
"This is not a reference to the suffix; rather, what is it? It is a reference to the actual form of the word 'saptamī'."

He states "grahaṇam" (the mention) with the words "yatra" and so forth; the meaning has already been explained. Regarding the words "sthagrahaṇāt tu" and so forth: when the mention of "stha" (the locative case ending) is made, because of the addition of the word *stha*, that which is indicated by the locative case in the sūtra is designated as the technical term (*saṃjñin*); by this, everything is established.
This designation will apply to all those [words] that are indicated by the locative case in the *sūtra*.
For instance, in the rule "stambakarṇayoḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.13), the words *stamba* and *karṇa* are indicated by the locative case in the *sūtra*. Likewise, in "saptamyāṃ janerḍaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.97).

Thus, here too, we have words such as *upasar* and others; and in the rule *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1), we likewise have words such as *kumbha* and others which denote the object (*karman*). Now, a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is established for the sake of brevity; why then is a cumbersome designation being made?
Thus he says: "The designation 'heavy' (guru)," and so forth. The prefix *upa* denotes proximity. The term *upapada* refers to a word uttered in proximity [to another].

The purpose of establishing this designation as "heavy" is so that, when there is an understanding of technical designations for other meanings, the operation of the paribhāṣā rule concerning semantic competency (*samartha*) may take effect.

When the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) regarding semantic capability (*samartha*) is present, he says "Look at the jar," etc., in order to demonstrate what is thereby accomplished. For when a name is based on its literal meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), a suffix (*pratyaya*) dependent on a subordinate word (*upapada*) constitutes a rule concerning words (*padavidhi*). And where there is even a trace of a word (*padagandha*), there [the rule applies].

The technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) "samartha" applies here. Consequently, in the examples "paśya kumbham" and "karoti kaṭam," the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by Pāṇini 3.2.1 ("karmaṇyaṇ") does not occur; for in these cases, the word "kumbha" has no semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) with the verb "karoti," but rather with the word "paśya. Furthermore, the term "pada" here is etymological (*anvartha*), not technical (*pāribhāṣika*).
For instance, at the time when the designation *upapada* is prescribed for the suffix *ṭac*,

the nominal stem (*subanta*) still possesses the status of being a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*); because once the designation *upapada* has been applied, the suffix is prescribed based on that *upapada*, and thus the *upapada-compound* (*upapadasamāsa*)— as in the rule "verbs (*gati*), non-agentive (*akāraka*), and *upapada*s [are compounded] with primary derivatives (*kṛt*)"— is also established.

According to the rule "the statement of a compound occurs prior to the production of the *sup* suffix" (*Vyāḍiparibhāṣāvṛtti* 138), the *sup* suffix ought to be produced [first]. Therefore, this word *pada* is etymological: that by which meaning (*artha*) is reached or understood (*padyate*) is a *pada*.
In that context, the mention of "therein" (*tatra*) serves to establish the status of being a cause for the production of the suffix in relation to that which stands in the locative case.

This is for the purpose that the designation *upapada* (governing word) should apply; for if that [designation] were not included there, the suffix would occur when *karman* is the governing word, whether it is actually present (*upapada*) or not. As for the indication by means of the locative case in the term *karmaṇi*, that applies when [the word] is possible as a locative ending.

Its purpose would be to establish the designation *upapada*; however, the meaning that "the suffix must occur only when that [word] exists" is not thereby obtained. Therefore, the mention of *tatra* is for the sake of the aforementioned purpose. But is it not the case that the mention of *tatra* is for the purpose of indicating the immediately preceding element, namely the verbal root (*dhātu*) and so forth?

Why would it not be so? [One might ask: "In this context of governing rules (*adhikāra*), why is it not the case that the designation *upapada* should apply immediately [to what follows]? This is not the case; for this is established even by virtue of the governing rule itself.
The designation *upapada* will be governed [by a subsequent rule], and by that, the designation will apply to the bases (*saṃjñin*) that are to be mentioned hereafter.

The meaning "it will be" is not the purpose of the mention of "there" (*tatra*) in that context. However, the passage from the *Vṛtti* beginning with "in this [context]" (*etasmin*) is to be interpreted as follows: "In this governing section concerning verbal roots (*dhātu*), that which is indicated by the locative case receives the technical designation 'subordinate word' (*upapada*). And in that regard, the meaning is: 'when there is a cause (*nimitta*) for a suffix.'"
This is obtained because the commentary (*vṛtti*) contains supplementary explanations (*sopaskāra*).

93. *kṛd atiṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.93). [The example] "kartavyam" ("to be done"): when the designation *kṛt* is established, the designation *prātipadika* applies by the rule "kṛt-taddhita-samāsāś-ca" (1.2.46). [The example] "cīyāt": this is the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), according to the rule "liṅ āśiṣi."

(3.4.116) Thus [is established] the designation *ārdhadhātuka*. If "not being a *tiṅ*" (*atiṅ*) were not stated, then even a *tiṅ* would receive the designation *kṛt*; consequently, the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by "ṭhakṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.25) would not occur.
However, because the condition "not being a *tiṅ*" (*atiṅ*) is present, [the designation *kṛt* does not apply], since [in this case] the suffix is not of the form *yak*.

94. *vā'sarūpo'striyām* | (3.1.94) It is a general rule (*utsarga-dharma*) that a general rule does not apply to a domain where an exception (*apavāda*) is operative; however, the application of certain general rules even within the domain of exceptions is desired, and that [is what this sūtra provides].
This [sūtra] is for that purpose, because [the desired result] is not established without this statement.
But even if this were commenced, this objective would still not be accomplished;
for instance, its connection would have to be either with the general rule (*utsarga*), or with the exception (*apavāda*), or with both. In that regard:

If the previous rule (*pūrvakalpa*) were relied upon, then, with the word *vā* serving to present existence and non-existence as alternatives, the meaning would be this: "In the case of a non-feminine [stem], the general rule (*utsarga*) applies optionally; that is, it applies in one alternative, and does not apply in the other. Likewise...
The exception would never apply to its own domain,
for nothing has been done by this [general rule] for the sake of the exception, as there is no connection between them. Furthermore,
when the subverting exception is functioning without any alternative, the general rule cannot operate therein.

If it were the first [alternative], the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) would operate only within its own domain. If, however, it is the second, then the meaning would be this: "An exception (*apavāda*) of a different form applies optionally when not in the feminine.
Even so, the operation of the general rule (*utsarga*) within the domain of the exception is not obtained.

It is said that a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*) may optionally apply to a non-feminine [stem]. Even so, the operation of the general rule is not obtained within the domain of the exception; for the general rule avoids the domain of the exception, because the exception possesses the quality of sublation (*bādhakatva*). And that quality of sublation exists even in this alternative view.

It remains exactly as it was, for nothing has been removed by this; rather, its presence and absence in its own object have been established—that it exists in one case and does not exist in another. And there is no other statement whereby the general rule (utsarga) could override the scope of the exception (apavāda).

If it is argued that in the case where there is no exception (*apavāda*), the general rule (*utsarga*) will prevail even without an enjoining statement because there is no obstruction, this is true regarding the sublation of an effect (*kāryabādhā*); however,
regarding the sublation of a scriptural injunction (*śāstrabādhā*), that which prescribes the effect is itself being sublated by the exception.

It should proceed only by way of avoiding that [exceptional] object; once it has proceeded toward that [general rule], even if one subsequently undergoes the operation of the exception through an alternative application (*vikalpa*), the operation of the general rule (*utsarga*) regarding that same object is not possible,
because the general rule lacks that specific object as its domain.

If it is argued that there must be sublation of the effect [of the injunction], we say no; for that is illogical. Indeed, as long as the enjoining scripture remains unsublated, the sublation of its effect is not tenable. For the destruction of the derivative can only be accomplished by the destruction of its primary cause, and not otherwise. Indeed, while the lamp is not extinguished, its light cannot be extinguished.

Therefore, the exception (apavāda) sublates the general rule (śāstra) itself; and when that [general rule] has been sublated, even in the view that there is an absence of an exception, the general rule would not apply to the domain of the exception.
Now, as for the third alternative, its meaning would be this: "The general rule is non-identical in form (asarūpa), except in the feminine."

[It might be argued that] there is also an exception (apavāda). Even so, there would be an optional application (vikalpa) of those two with respect to their own respective domains, but not of the general rule (utsarga) within the domain of the exception; for the very reason stated previously.
Therefore, even if this [proposition] were made, the intended meaning is not accomplished.

Regarding that which was stated [in the rule], he replies: "A suffix that is a counter-exception (*apavāda*) is a sublater (*bādhaka*) when it is not of the same form [as the general rule]. By this, he shows that the connection is with the counter-exception itself, and that existence and non-existence are not being treated as optional alternatives;
rather, what is shown is that its status as a sublater is contingent upon a particular alternative (*pakṣa*). And thus, in whichever alternative the counter-exception...

It does not act as an obstructor; since there is no impediment regarding that subject matter, the general rule (*utsarga*) proceeds, and thus the coexistence (*samāveśa*) is established. [The statement] "excluding a suffix prescribed under the heading of feminine (*strī-adhikāra*)"—how, then, is this meaning obtained from the expression "not in the feminine" (*a-strīyam*)? It is as follows: [The answer: This is because the word *strī* here refers to the technical grammatical term (*saṃjñā*) "feminine" (*stri*), which is taught in the section beginning with *striyām*. Since the suffixes *ṅīp*, *ṅīṣ*, and *ṅīn* are taught under that heading, they are understood by implication (*arthāt*) to be excluded. Therefore, the meaning is obtained that "the suffixes taught under the heading of feminine are excluded. Thus, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is indeed included. Consequently, the form *kārīṣagandhyā* is derived from *kārīṣagandher apatyaṃ strī* ("the female descendant of Kārīṣagandhi") by applying the suffix *ṅīṣ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.78 (*gāndhāribhyaś ca*). Alternatively, it may be explained as follows: the word *strī* here denotes the actual state of being female (*strītva*), which is the property (*dharma*) residing in the individual (*vyakti*). Since the suffixes *ṅīp*, *ṅīṣ*, and *ṅīn* are taught for the purpose of expressing that property, they are understood by implication to be excluded. Therefore, the meaning is obtained that "suffixes taught for the purpose of expressing the property of femininity are excluded. Thus, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is indeed included. Consequently, the form *kārīṣagandhyā* is derived from *kārīṣagandher apatyaṃ strī* ("the female descendant of Kārīṣagandhi") by applying the suffix *ṅīṣ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.78 (*gāndhāribhyaś ca*). Or again, it may be explained as follows: the word *strī* here denotes the individual (*vyakti*) itself, which is the substratum (*āśraya*) of the property of femininity. Since the suffixes *ṅīp*, *ṅīṣ*, and *ṅīn* are taught for the purpose of expressing that [property], they are understood by implication to be excluded. Therefore, the meaning is obtained that "suffixes taught for the purpose of expressing the substratum of the property of femininity are excluded. Thus, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is indeed included. Consequently, the form *kārīṣagandhyā* is derived from *kārīṣagandher apatyaṃ strī* ("the female descendant of Kārīṣagandhi") by applying the suffix *ṅīṣ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.78 (*gāndhāribhyaś ca*). Or yet again, it may be explained as follows: the word *strī* here denotes the genus (*jāti*) "femininity," which is the universal (*sāmānya*) residing in the individual. Since the suffixes *ṅīp*, *ṅīṣ*, and *ṅīn* are taught for the purpose of expressing that [genus], they are understood by implication to be excluded. Therefore, the meaning is obtained that "suffixes taught for the purpose of expressing the genus of femininity are excluded. Thus, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is indeed included. Consequently, the form *kārīṣagandhyā* is derived from *kārīṣagandher apatyaṃ strī* ("the female descendant of Kārīṣagandhi") by applying the suffix *ṅīṣ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.78 (*gāndhāribhyaś ca*). Or finally, it may be explained as follows: the word *strī* here denotes the individual (*vyakti*) itself, which is the substratum (*āśraya*) of the genus of femininity. Since the suffixes *ṅīp*, *ṅīṣ*, and *ṅīn* are taught for the purpose of expressing that [genus], they are understood by implication to be excluded. Therefore, the meaning is obtained that "suffixes taught for the purpose of expressing the substratum of the genus of femininity are excluded. Thus, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is indeed included. Consequently, the form *kārīṣagandhyā* is derived from *kārīṣagandher apatyaṃ strī* ("the female descendant of Kārīṣagandhi") by applying the suffix *ṅīṣ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.78 (*gāndhāribhyaś ca*). In all these cases, the word *strī* is used in its primary sense (*mukhya-vṛtti*). However, in the case of the word *a-strīyam*, the word *strī* is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇa-vṛtti*) to denote the suffixes *ṅīp*, *ṅīṣ*, and *ṅīn* themselves. Therefore, the meaning is obtained that "suffixes such as *ṅīp*, *ṅīṣ*, and *ṅīn* are excluded. Thus, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is indeed included. Consequently, the form *kārīṣagandhyā* is derived from *kārīṣagandher apatyaṃ strī* ("the female descendant of Kārīṣagandhi") by applying the suffix *ṅīṣ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.78 (*gāndhāribhyaś ca*). Or alternatively, the word *strī* here denotes the property of femininity (*strītva-dharma*), which is the property residing in the individual. Since the suffixes *ṅīp*, *ṅīṣ*, and *ṅīn* are taught for the purpose of expressing that [property], they are understood by implication to be excluded. Therefore, the meaning is obtained that "suffixes taught for the purpose of expressing the property of femininity are excluded. Thus, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is indeed included.
