Consequently, the form *kārīṣagandhyā* is derived from *kārīṣagandher apatyaṃ strī* ("the female descendant of Kārīṣagandhi") by applying the suffix *ṅīṣ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.78 (*gāndhāribhyaś ca*). Or yet again, the word *strī* here denotes the genus "femininity," which is the universal residing in the individual. Since the suffixes *ṅīp*, *ṅīṣ*, and *ṅīn* are taught for the purpose of expressing that [genus], they are understood by implication to be excluded. Therefore, the meaning is obtained that "suffixes taught for the purpose of expressing the genus of femininity are excluded. Thus, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is indeed included. Consequently, the form *kārīṣagandhyā* is derived from *kārīṣagandher apatyaṃ strī* ("the female descendant of Kārīṣagandhi") by applying the suffix *ṅīṣ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.78 (*gāndhāribhyaś ca*). Or finally, the word *strī* here denotes the individual (*vyakti*) itself, which is the substratum (*āśraya*) of the genus of femininity. Since the suffixes *ṅīp*, *ṅīṣ*, and *ṅīn* are taught for the purpose of expressing that [genus], they are understood by implication to be excluded. Therefore, the meaning is obtained that "suffixes taught for the purpose of expressing the substratum of the genus of femininity are excluded. Thus, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is indeed included. Consequently, the
He thinks: "The mention of *strī* (feminine) is intended here as a *svarita* accent; and through a *svarita*, the understanding of a governing heading (*adhikāra*) occurs.

Therefore, having recourse to that which is prescribed under the heading of 'feminine,' a prohibition is understood to apply to those [cases] for which both a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*) have been prescribed. Now, why is it not understood in this way?

Is it that when the feminine gender is to be expressed, a non-homogeneous exception (apavāda) does not act as a sublater (bādhaka)? This cannot be understood in such a way; for if it were understood thus, then in cases such as *lavyā* and *lavitavyā*, the suffix *tavya* would not occur. If that is so, then why is it not understood [in this way]?

By the mention of the word "strī" in the rule *striyām*, that suffix which is prescribed [by rules such as *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*] is what is referred to here by the word "strī. In that case, when a suffix is prescribed by the rule *striyām*, would it not follow that a dissimilar (*asarūpa*) apavāda (exceptional rule) or a bādhaka (sublating rule) does not apply? This cannot be so understood; for if it were understood in this way—

Regarding the forms *vyāvakrośī* and *vyāvakruṣṭiḥ*, the suffix *ktin* would not apply in the domain of the suffix *ṇac*; for since *ṇac* is prescribed by the rule "In the sense of mutual action, *ṇac* [is used] in the feminine" (Pāṇini 3.3.43), and *ktin* is also prescribed for the feminine, the meaning remains exactly as stated previously. If this is so, [then...]

Does the paribhāṣā "ṭhktalyuṭtumunkhalartheṣu" (Pāṇini 3.3.116) not apply here, because those suffixes are prescribed under the heading of the neuter gender (*astrī*)? [For example: *napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ* (3.3.114) and *lyuṭ ca* (3.3.115)—as in *hasitam* and *hasanam*; in the domain of these two, [the rule] "bhāve" [would not apply].

(3.3.18) Thus, the suffix *ghañ* would also apply. Regarding the rule "when there is a common agent, [the infinitive] *tumun*" (3.3.158)—as in "he desires to eat"—would not the suffixes *liṅ* and *loṭ* also apply in that context by the rule "after verbs meaning 'desire,' [the suffixes] *liṅ* and *loṭ*" (3.3.157)? Regarding the rule "after a verbal root ending in *ā*, the suffix *yuc*" (3.3.128)—as in "drinking easily" (*īṣatpāna*)—in that context...

Does [the suffix] *khal* not also apply here by the rule "after the roots *sthā*, *iṣ*, *duḥ*, and *suṣ*, when they mean 'difficulty' (*kṛcchra*) or 'absence of difficulty' (*akṛcchra*), [the suffix] *khal* [is applied]" (Pāṇini 3.3.126)? There is no fault, because the mention of the option (*vāvacana*) is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
[The statement] "the suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc* are the general rule" is because they are prescribed as a general provision (*sāmānyavihitatva*).
"The rule *ṭhigupadhāpīkiraḥ kaḥ* is an exception (*apavāda*)," because it is prescribed as a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*).

The general rule (*utsarga*) is *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1), while the suffix *ka* prescribed by *ātaścopasarge* (Pāṇini 3.1.136) is its exception. Now, one might object: "But surely that [suffix *ka*] is also dissimilar (*asarūpa*) due to the difference caused by its indicatory letter (*anubandha*)."

Thus he says: "Not caused by an *anubandha*," and so forth. In this context, the mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*) in the rule *dadātidadhātyor vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 3.1.139) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*). For if dissimilarity (*asārūpya*) were caused by an *anubandha*, the mention of the option would be purposeless; for [the rule] would already apply simply because of the dissimilarity caused by the *anubandha*.
By the rule *ṣṭhiv-klam-vyadhaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.141), the suffix *ṇa* will optionally occur.
95. *Kṛtyāḥ* before *ṇvul*.

(Pāṇini 3.1.95) The use of the plural form in the term "*kṛtyāḥ*" is due to the multiplicity of the items being designated (*saṃjñin*). Alternatively, the plural is used for the purpose of including all *kṛt* suffixes not explicitly mentioned [in this section]. By means of this, there is the inclusion of *kelimara*.
(Vārttika 121) This [application] need not be performed. For he will state [later], "The suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc* [are applied].

Now, why is it not understood that the *ṇvul* in the rule "ṇvul is frequently used when denoting a disease" (Pāṇini 3.3.108) serves as the limit [for the application of subsequent rules]? Because there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Namely, this [rule]: "The *kṛtya* suffixes and *tṛc* are applied in the sense of 'fitting for'" (Pāṇini 3.3.169).

Having thus mentioned the *kṛtya* suffixes, he mentions the *tṛc* suffix; from this it is understood that [the *tṛc*] does not function as a limit (*avadhi*). Otherwise, since the *tṛc* is also a *kṛtya*, its separate mention would be purposeless. If this is so;

The preceding statement would be purposeless; therefore, by this very indication (*jñāpaka*), this designation will not apply to the *tṛc* suffix? This is not so; for if this [statement] were absent, it would be precisely the *tṛc* suffix that would not have [the designation], whereas the *ṇvul* suffix certainly would. It might be argued: the indication is dependent upon the specific rule (*yoga*).

In this rule (*yoga*), there would be the notion that it is a *kṛtya* suffix— the meaning being indicated by the mention of *tṛc*, whereby the suffix *ṇvul* would also not apply. This might be the case for other suffixes beginning with vowels, but it would result in an excessive complexity of understanding (*pratipatti-gaurava*), because a grammatical indicator (*jñāpaka*) that depends on a specific rule (*yoga*) is difficult to discern.
96. *tavyat-tavya-anīyar* (Pāṇini 3.1.96).

Regarding the statement "the letters *t* and *r* are for the sake of accentuation": the letter *t* serves the purpose of making the vowel *svarita* according to Pāṇini 6.1.185 (*titsvaritam*). The letter *r* serves the purpose of making the penultimate syllable *udātta* according to Pāṇini 6.1.217 (*upottamaṃ riti*).

Regarding the rule "ṭhvasestavyat kartari ṇicca": from the root *vas* in the sense of "dwelling" (DhP 1005), the suffix *tavyat* occurs in the active voice (*kartari*), and that suffix is treated as having the marker *ṇit*. However, this need not be stated, because it is already established by the rule "kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam" (Pāṇini 3.3.113).

"One who dwells" is *vāstavyaḥ*. The *vṛddhi* [strengthening] occurs because of the suffix being marked with *ṇ*. Regarding the statement "the addition of *kelimara* should be mentioned," the word *upasaṃkhyāna* means "explanation" or "demonstration.
This demonstration has already been made previously; however, it is performed once again here—[as part of the rule concerning] *kṛtya* and *lyuṭ* suffixes.

Due to the word "bahulam" (in Pāṇini 3.3.113), the suffix *kelim* will also be considered a *kṛtya* suffix. The letter *ka* is for the purpose of the *kit* operation, and the letter *ra* is for the purpose of the accent (*svara*). "The beans cook by themselves" (*svayameva pacyante pacelimā māṣāḥ*); this is due to the inherent nature of the power of words (*śabdaśaktisvābhāvyāt*) and from the plural number (*bahuvacanāt*).
This occurs only when the object is the agent, and not otherwise.

97. *ato yat* (Pāṇini 3.1.97). The letter *t* [in *yat*] is for the sake of the *p*-suffix [as in *yap*], according to the *Kāśikā*, which states: "It is for the sake of the qualification [in the rule] *yato 'nāvaḥ*," and it is for the sake of making the first syllable acute (*ādyaudāta*). [The example is] *geyam*. [The root is] *kai* and *gai* in the sense of "sound" (Dhātupāṭha 916, 917), and [the rule] *ādeca...* [is applied].
In the *upadeśa* (original form), there is *ā*-vṛddhi by [Pāṇini 6.1.45] *upadeśe'śiti*, *ī*-substitution by [6.4.65] *īdyati*, and *guṇa*.
Thus we have "yāvatā" and so forth. Here, roots are of two kinds: those ending in a consonant (*halanta*) and those ending in a vowel (*ajanta*).
Among these, one desires the suffix *ṇyat* for a root ending in a consonant according to [3.1.124] *ṛhalorṇyat*. Therefore...

The intention is that since [the suffix] would necessarily occur after a stem ending in a vowel (*ac*) even without the explicit mention of *ac* by means of the principle of remainder (*pariśeṣa*), the mention of *ac* is redundant.
Regarding the phrase "from that which was formerly vowel-ending" (*ajantabhūtapūrvāt*): it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both vowel-ending and formerly so."

The mention of *aj* (vowel) is for the purpose that the rule should apply even when [the root] was originally vowel-ending (*ajanta*) but is now consonant-ending (*halanta*). For example: *ditsyam* and *dhitsyam*. Here, the suffix *san* follows the roots *dāñ* and *dhāñ*, followed by reduplication. Then, by the rule *sani mīmā-* (Pāṇini 7.4.54), *i* is substituted [for the penultimate vowel], and by the rule *atra lopo'bhyāsasya* (Pāṇini 7.4.58), there is elision of the reduplicated syllable.
By this [sūtra 7.4.58], there is the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*). By [sūtra] 7.4.49, *ṣaḥ syārdhadhātuke*, there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*.

When the *ardhadhātuka* suffix has not yet arisen but is intended to be the domain [of the rule], there is the elision of the vowel *a* by [sūtra] 6.4.48, *ato lopaḥ*. In this state, if the mention of *aj* were absent, [the desired result] would not occur; because [the stem] would not end in an *ac* vowel (*anajantatvāt*).

But when that [suffix] exists, it occurs by resorting to its having been previously [treated as] ending in *aj*. And this purpose should be understood as being optional. In which case? When the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix is intended to be the domain for the application of the rule "there is elision of *at*" (Pāṇini 6.4.48). When it is an *ārdhadhātuka*, then...

This is not the purpose [of the rule]. Rather, the inclusion of the letter *j* should be understood for the sake of clarity. [Examples include] *taki*, *śas*, and so forth. [The root] *taka* is printed in the Dhātupāṭha as "in the sense of endurance" (117), [the root] *śasu* as "in the sense of injury" (727), and [the roots] *cate* and *cade*.

An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*)— that is, an explanatory rule (*pratipādana*)— must be made for the suffix *yat* after the roots *yāc* (DhP 865, 866), *yat* (DhP 30) in the sense of "effort," and *jan* (DhP 1149) in the sense of "manifestation. This explanation, however, is carried out by relying on the mention of the term *bahulam* ("variously").
It should be formed as follows:

*ṭhhano vā vadha ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.76). This means that the suffix *yat* is applied to the root *han*, serving as an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṇyat*. Because of the mention of the option (*vā*), in the alternative case, *ṇyat* indeed occurs; however, the suffix *yat* follows from that [specific rule].
This is obtained from the word *bahula* (in the sense of "diversely" or "variously"). Whenever [the condition] occurs, then the substitute *badh* is applied for the root *han*.

That too is obtained through the continued application of the term *bahulam* from rule 2.4.39 (*bahulaṃ chandasi*) to rule 2.4.42 (*hano vadha liṅ*). As for *ghātya*, [it is derived] by rule 7.3.32 (*hanastaḥ*).
This is the truth; the substitution of *k* for *h* in the root *han* is applied by the rule "ṭhho hanteḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.54).

98. *poradupadhāt* | (3.1.98) [The suffix *ṇyat*] is applied after a root ending in *p*, provided that the penultimate letter (*upadhā*) is a short vowel. For example: *vākyam* ("speech") and *kopyam* ("to be angered"), *gopyam* ("to be protected"). [The roots are] *kupa* in the sense of "anger" (DhP 1233) and *gup* in the sense of "protection."

Thus, *gup* is listed as "in the sense of hiding and censuring" (DhP 970), and *gup* is also listed as "in the sense of confusing" (DhP 1234). Regarding the term *āpya*: it is derived from *āplṛ*, meaning "to pervade" (DhP 1260).
99. *Śaki-sahaś-ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.99).

100. *Gada-mada-caraya-maś-cānupasarge* (Pāṇini 3.1.100). Regarding the term "without a prefix" (*anupasarge*): by a transposition (*vyatyaya*), the locative case is used in the sense of the ablative. For this very reason, he says:

Regarding the rule "anupasargebhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.75), the meaning is "from those [roots] for which no prefix (upapada) exists. Now, why is it not understood thus: that "anupasarga" means "other than a prefix"? It is impossible to understand it in this way;
for if it were understood thus, the suffix would not apply to simple roots. This is according to the principle "nañ-iva-yukte" (Pāṇini 2.1.60).

If there were a comprehension of a *subanta* word similar to a prefix by means of logical reasoning (*nyāya*), then the repeated mention of *sub* in the rule "ṭhvadaḥ supi kyap ca" (Pāṇini 3.1.106) would be purposeless, because this very [term] "without a prefix" (*anupasarga*) would carry over (*anuvṛtti*) there [from the previous rule]. Therefore, the previously stated meaning alone is correct. [The phrase "for the sake of restriction" (*niyamārtham*) refers to this.]

This is so that [the suffix] may apply only after a root that has no prefix (*anupasarga*), and not after one with a prefix (*sopasarga*). [The rule] beginning with *careḥ* [is stated]; this is for the sake of roots with prefixes—meaning that [the suffix] occurs after the root *car* when *āṅ* is the prefix—and provided that "not heavy" (*aguru*) is what is to be expressed. However, that [result] is established by the very fact of the *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence).

It is not necessary to add [this] as a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyeya*), because he [Pāṇini] provides rules such as *ṭhāścaryamanitye* (6.1.147) and *ṭhsammānanotsañjanācāryakaraṇajñānabhṛtivigaṇanavyayeṣu niyaḥ* (1.3.36). From this, it is understood that the suffix *ṇic* occurs after the root *car-* when preceded by the prefix *āṅ*. Thus, [the term] *ācārya* is established. "The region is the teacher" (*ācāryo deśaḥ*).
The meaning is "one who should go"; "guru" refers to the initiator (upanetā).

101. *Avadya*, *paṇya*, and *varya* [are formed] in the senses of "blameworthy," "to be sold," and "prohibition" respectively. (3.1.101) Regarding *avadyam*: when the prefix *nañ* is present as an upapada to the root *vad*, both *yat* and *kyap* are applicable by the rule *vadaḥ supi kyap ca* (3.1.106). Here, *yat* alone is prescribed as the substitute. Regarding *anudyam*: because [the root *nud*] belongs to the *yajādi* group...
Regarding *saṃprasāraṇa*: by the rule *nalopo nañaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.73), the *n* of the negative particle *nañ* is elided; then, by the rule *tasmānnuḍ aci* (Pāṇini 6.3.74), the augment *nuṭ* is added.

Regarding *paṇyam*: although the suffix *ṇyat* would have applied to the root *paṇ* in the sense of "transaction," the form *paṇya* is here prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). Regarding *pāṇyam*: it means "that which is to be praised."

Regarding the term ‘varya’: although the suffix *ṇyat* would have applied to the root *vṛñ*, this form is established as an irregularity (*nipātana*). By the word ‘in the feminine’ (*striyām*), he demonstrates that the mention of gender in the rule is a governing factor (*tantra*). Regarding ‘non-obstruction’ (*apratibandha*): by this he explains the meaning of the word ‘anirodha’. The meaning is that non-obstruction is the absence of an impact upon one’s movement.

Regarding the term "vṛttyā": it means that which is to be restrained; the sense is that its outward flow must be obstructed. This form is derived from the root *vṛ* with the suffix *kyap* according to Pāṇini 3.1.109 (*etyestṛśāsu*), and the augment *tuk* is applied according to 6.1.71 (*hrasvasya piti kṛti*). In the example "the priests are to be chosen (*vāryā ṛtvijaḥ*"), the root is *vṛṅ*.
This is its form. For there is no prohibition against the rule that "the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) must be distributed wealth";

however, because the feminine gender does not apply here, the suffix *ṇyat* alone occurs. [Objection: But should it not be *kyap* by the rule "after the roots *hi*, *stu*, *śās*, and *vṛ*, [the suffix *kyap* is added]" (Pāṇini 3.1.109)? [Response: This is not so; for in that rule, it is the root *vṛñ* that is intended to be included.
An example of this is as follows.
102. *vahyaṃ karaṇam* (3.1.102).
103. *aryaḥ svāmivaiśyayoḥ* (3.1.103).

Regarding the statement "it should be explained" (*vaktavyam*), the meaning is that it must be commented upon. In this regard, the following is the explanation: here, by means of *tantra* [the term is used twice].

Two forms of this word have been uttered: therein one has the acute accent on the first syllable (ādyaudāta), while the other has the acute accent on the final syllable (antodāta). That which has the acute accent on the first syllable is applied to a Vaiśya; the other, however, refers to a female owner (svāminī).

104. *Upasaryā* [is formed with the suffix *yat*] when meaning "ready for breeding. (3.1.104) The word *kālyā* means "one whose time has arrived" (*prāptakālā*). While the rule *tadasya prāptasya* (5.1.104) is being carried over, the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *kālādyat* (5.1.107). Furthermore, *prajana* means "procreation"; it is derived from the root *jan* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*).

The prohibition of *vṛddhi* [strengthening] is applied by the rule *ṭhjanivadhyośca* (Pāṇini 7.3.35). Regarding the word *upasāryā*, the meaning is "to be approached" (*upasaṃkramaṇīyā*). 105. *ajaṃrya saṅgatam* (Pāṇini 3.1.105).
Regarding the word *jīryate*: it is derived from the roots *jṛṣ* and *jhṛṣ*, meaning "the loss of vitality" (*vayohāni*) [Dhātupāṭha 1130, 1131].

Regarding the word *saṅgamana*: *saṅgamana* is indeed *saṅgati* (conjunction). The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied by the rule *lyuṭ ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.115). By this, in the case of the word *saṅgatam*, the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) in the neuter gender, according to the rule *napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.114).

It shows: "The suffix *yat* is introduced by irregular derivation (*nipātana*) when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [suffixes] such as *tṛc*. For example, in "ajaritā," the suffix *tṛc* [is applied].

106. *vadaḥ supi kyap ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.106). [The word] "after a prefix" (*anupasarge*) is understood [to carry over]. Now, one might object: in the rule *satsūdviṣa-* (3.2.61) and others, he will state that this mention of a prefix (*upasarga*) is for the sake of providing an indication (*jñāpanārtha*), [namely] that elsewhere the mention of a case-ending (*sub-grahaṇa*)...
"The mention of *upasarga* does not occur"; and thus, by that very same indicator (*jñāpaka*), it will not apply when there is an *upasarga*.
So what is the purpose here of the continued reference (*anuvṛtti*) to the non-mention of *upasarga*? Some say it is for the sake of clarity.
In that case, however, the mention of *upasarga* must be made for the sake of providing that indication; here—
Others say that the inclusion of the prefix *anu-* without the suffix *vati* is for the purpose of showing an alternative form. Regarding the term *brahmāedyam*:
it means "the speaking of Brahman. The suffix *kyap* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*), with the semivowel *y* being vocalized (*saṃprasāraṇa*) as before;
then *āṬ* is substituted by *guṇa* (Pāṇini 6.1.87), and finally there is a compound with an upapada.

107. *bhuvo bhāve* (Pāṇini 3.1.107). It is said that *ṭhyat* does not follow [from the previous rule], because it was not carried over (*anukṛṣṭa*) from the preceding sūtra. The example is *brahmabhūyaṃ gataḥ*, which means "he has attained the state of Brahman" (*brahmatvam prāptaḥ*). But is it not the case that [the rule] *tayoreva kṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.70) applies?

By this [rule 3.4.70], the suffixes are prescribed after roots in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*); and since the term "without a prefix" (*anupasarga*) also follows [from the previous rule], and because the root *bhū* is intransitive when without a prefix, by implication it will apply only to the sense of the abstract action and not to the object—so what is the purpose of explicitly mentioning "the abstract action"? To this he says: "By the mention of the abstract action..."
With this intention, he says: "The mention of *bhāva* is for the sake of what follows. By this, he states its utility in the rule *hanasta ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.108):
so that [the suffix] may occur there only when *bhāva* is intended. As in the example *bhavyam*: by *aco yat* (3.1.97), there is guṇa of the root, according to *dhātostannimittasyaiva* (6.1.80).
Thus ends the section on substitutes.

108. *hanasta ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.108). [The examples are] *brahmahatyā* ("the killing of a Brahmin") and *dhātaḥ*. The meaning of *brahmahatyā* is "the act of killing a Brahmin. Regarding *dhātaḥ*, it is the same as in the previous case (*tat-karaṇe*). Why, then, is the suffix *ghañ* cited here as an example and not *ṇyat*? He says: *ṇyati*.

And so forth. He states the reasoning for that very point: "Because of non-denotation. For *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and *samāsa* suffixes are characterized by denotation (*abhidhāna*), yet the state of being (*bhāva*) cannot be denoted by the *ṇyat* suffix prescribed after the root *han*. To explain: when *dhātya* is uttered, only the object (*karman*) is understood, not [the state].
The state of being.

109. *etistuśāsvṛdṛjuṣaḥ kyap* | (3.1.109) [The suffix] *kyap* is applied after the roots *i*, *stu*, *śās*, *vṛ*, *dṛ*, and *juṣ*. Regarding the word *śiṣya*: from the root *śāsu* in the sense of "instruction" (DhP 1075), there is the substitution of *ī* by *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ* (6.4.34), and the change to *ṣ* by *śāsivasi* (8.3.60). Regarding the word *ādṛtya*: [it is derived from *dṛ* with the same suffix].

The root *dṛś* (meaning "to respect") is preceded by the prefix *ā*. Regarding the word *juṣyaḥ*: the root *juṣ* (meaning "to love" and "to serve") is [the source]. Now, for what purpose is the mention of the suffix *kyap*, since the mention of *kyap* already continues from the rule *vadaḥ supi kyap ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.106)? To this [it is replied]:
He says: "While [the rule] *kyapi ca vartamāne* and so forth is in force," and "for the purpose of subverting that which subverts.

To clarify this, he says: "In the sense of necessity (*orāvaśyake*). The scope for the inclusion of *stu* is where necessity is not intended to be expressed—as in *stutya*; thus, the rule *orāvaśyake* (Pāṇini 3.1.125) applies.

This provides scope for another suffix, *avaśyalāvyam*; however, in this case, both [suffixes] would apply—namely *avaśyastutya*—and since it is subsequent, *ṇyat* would be the sublater. But because of the repeated mention of *kyap*, even that is set aside and *kyap* occurs. By the mention of *vṛ* [in the rule], [it refers to] *vṛñ*.

"It is intended that *grahaṇa* [is used], not *vṛṅ*. How so? From the rule *kṛṣirajoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.90), the mention of the *parasmaipada* suffixes (*parasmaipadagrahaṇa*) is understood to carry over here; by this, the word *vṛ* is qualified—namely, "the word *vṛ* which belongs to the *parasmaipada*. And what belongs to the *parasmaipada*?

Regarding the word *vṛ*: that which is observed to be the cause for the *parasmaipada* (active voice) suffixes is seen to belong only to the root *vṛñ*, which is used in both voices (*ubhayapadin*), and not to *vṛṅ*; for the latter is invariably restricted to the *ātmanepada* (middle voice). Therefore, the reference is only to *vṛñ*, and not to *vṛṅ*.

The meaning is that one must explain the rule beginning with "ṭhśaṃsiduhi" etc. as having the sense that the suffix *kyap* optionally occurs after these roots, beginning with *śaṃs*. This explanation, however, should be carried out by relying on that very term *bahulagrahaṇam* (the mention of "diversely"). Regarding the form "śasyam": [it is derived from] the root *śansu* in the sense of "praise."
(dhā.pā. 728), the elision of *n* occurs by the rule "ṭh-an-īditām" (6.4.24). Regarding the word "guhyam": [the root] "guhū" means "to conceal" (dhā.pā.
896). [The form] "aṅ-pūrvād añjeḥ" and so forth; the meaning of the word "upasaṃkhyāna" is "explanation" or "supplementation. And that—
As before. [The root] *ṭhañjū* is listed as "to manifest, to wander, to shine, to go" (*dhā.pā.* 1458).

As before, there is elision of the *n*. And this is a name for clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*). [The question] "How is it to be understood? is the inquiry of one who considers this form to belong to the root *iṇ*. [The answer is] *īṅ*.

Regarding the form "etadrūpa": this form arises from the root *iṅ* in the sense of "motion" (*gatau*, Dhātupāṭha 1143) when the suffix *yat* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.97 (*aco yat*), and not from the root *iṇ*. For if *kyap* were applied to *iṇ*, the form would have to be *upetyam*.
110. *ṛdupadhāccāklṛpicṛteḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.110). [The commentary states:
"Excluding *klṛp* and *cṛt*. [The root] *kṛpū* means "to be capable" (Dhātupāṭha 762);
*cṛtī* means "injury and tying" (Dhātupāṭha 1324).

Having set aside these two [cases]: because the substitution of *l* for *r* is not established (*asiddha*), there is the status of having a short vowel as a penultimate (*ṛdupadhatva*). Thus, "kalpyam": because the substitution of *l* for *r* is not established, the *guṇa* substitution of *a* occurs for the *ṛ*-vowel itself. "ṇyadeva bhavati—kīrtyam": when there is the intention to express an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, the *ṇic* of the *curādi* class [is applied], and by the rule "ṇer aniṭi" [the *yaṅ* is added].

Thus, when the *ṇi*-affix is elided, since the word ends in a consonant (*halanta*), the suffix *ṇyat* alone is applied by the rule *ṛhalorṇyat* (Pāṇini 3.1.124). The lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *hali ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.77). Now, one might object: what is the purpose of the mention of *ac* in the rule *aco yat* (Pāṇini 3.1.97)?

The purpose [of the rule] has been stated: so that [the suffix] may apply even after a root that was previously not ending in a vowel, as in *ditsyam* and *dhitsyam*. If this is so, should there not likewise be the suffix *yat* here after the causative (*ṇic*)? If that is the case, then since the *cur*-class roots are not invariably accompanied by the causative (*ṇi*), the suffix *ṇyat* occurs here after the non-causative form itself; thus there is no fault.

"It is to be stated" (*vaktavyaḥ*) means "it is to be explained. The explanation is as before. A rope that is to be created by the two hands is called *pāṇisargyā rajjuḥ*. This is a compound formed according to Pāṇini 2.2.19: *upapadam atiṅ*.

Regarding the rule "samavapūrvācca": it is connected with the statement that the suffix *ṇyat* occurs after the root *sṛj*. The particle *ca* (and) serves as a conjunction. It is not only when *pāṇau* is the upapada that *ṇyat* must be stated;
rather, it also occurs after [the root *sṛj*] preceded by the prefixes *sam-* and *ava-*.

111. *ī* is substituted for the *kh* of *khan*. (Pāṇini 3.1.111) In the example "kheyam" (*to be dug*), from the root *khanu* (Dhātupāṭha 878) meaning "digging," the *n* is replaced by *ī*, and then *guṇa* substitution applies according to Pāṇini 6.1.87. Now, for what purpose is the long vowel (*ī*) prescribed, given that even the short vowel (*i*) would suffice?

When [the substitution] has been performed, the *guṇa* rule (Pāṇini 6.1.87) ought to apply. And when the *guṇa* has been applied to the short vowel, is there not some distinction? It might be argued: "However, it must be stated that the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is *asiddha* for the purpose of applying the *tuk* augment;
in that case, if a short vowel is prescribed, then once the *guṇa* has been applied to the short vowel..."
Since *tuk* is not established for the application of the rule, *tuk* would apply based on the short vowel; however, it does not apply when there is a substitution of a long vowel.

Therefore, must the substitution of the long vowel be stated? This is not necessary; because it must be stated that this very substitution [of the long vowel] occurring at the end of a word and the beginning of a word is not established (*asiddha*) for the application of the rule regarding *tuk*, but not otherwise.

He says "everywhere": [the sūtra contains] a long-vowel designation (*dīrghanirdeśa*). But for what purpose is the long-vowel designation used so that there may be a contraction (*praśleṣa*) of two *i*-vowels by means of the rule for the lengthening of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*, Pāṇini 6.1.101)? And for what purpose is the second *i*-vowel used, since this could be accomplished with just one?

Since the form *rūpam* is established, he says "therein" (*tatra*), and so forth. This is a compound indication (*praśleṣanirdeśa*) of two *i*-vowels. The purpose of the second *i*-vowel therein is so that there may be an annulment of the substitution of *ā* by the rule "and before *ye*" (*ye ca*, 6.4.109). [This refers to] "optionally before *ye*" (*ye vibhāṣā*, 6.4.43).

This is the scope [of the rule]: *khāyate* and *khanyate*. The scope for this substitute *isi* is that alternative in which the substitution of *ā* does not occur; however, in the alternative where the substitution of *ā* applies, both [rules] would apply.
When both apply, in the absence of a specific prohibition, the substitution of *ā* would take effect because it is *antaranga* (internal). And in this case—
The substitution of *ā* (ātvam) occurs by setting aside the substitution of *i* (itvam);
for the former is internal (*antaraṅga*) because it is prescribed based on the general category of the letter *y*,
whereas the latter is external (*bahiraṅga*) because it is prescribed based on the specific suffix *kyap*.

112. *bhṛño’saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 3.1.112). [The commentary states: "The meaning is 'those who are to be supported' (*bhartavyāḥ*). By this, showing that the word *bhṛtya* is a term denoting an action (*kriyāśabda*), he refutes its status as a technical name (*saṃjñāśabda*). [Regarding the rule] *saṃpūrvādvibhāṣā*: this [suffix *kyap*] applies only when it is not a technical name.
The option for that which is invariably applicable after *kyap* is obtained because this term *vibhāṣā*, which is about to be stated,
functions as a supplement (*śeṣa*) to both rules, and because it is understood as an unsettled option (*avyavasthita-vibhāṣā*).
"Regarding the rule *saṃjñāyāṃ puṃsi*," and so forth. The ellipsis to be supplied is "of the prohibition [contained in] *asaṃjñāyām*.

By this, he states that the purpose of the prohibition is fulfilled in the masculine: since the prohibition is thus rendered effective in the masculine, therefore the word *bhāryā* is not established for you. [The word] *bhāryā* [is not established] for you.

The meaning is that, according to the author of the Sūtra, [the desired form] would not be established. For if the prohibition applied to the masculine were already fulfilled, then the suffix *kyap* ought to apply to the feminine. But surely it is stated "provided it is not a technical term (*asaṃjñāyām*)", and the word *bhāryā* is indeed a technical term; for even when Devadatta is not supporting her, his wife is still called *bhāryā*.

Whence, then, would there be the contingency of *kyap*? We do not say that *kyap* must occur by virtue of this sūtra; what then? [It occurs] by virtue of [Pāṇini 3.3.99]: "In the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*), after the roots *samaja*, *niṣada*, etc. To this, he replies:

"There is the governing rule (*adhikāra*) for the feminine gender and for the abstract state (*bhāva*). By the term "governing rule for the abstract state" (*bhāvādhikāra*) here, [he means the following].

The operation intended here is characterized by the attainment of the status of being denotable by a word (*abhidheyabhāvopagama*), and not the technical "heading" (*adhikāra*) of the grammatical treatise. In the section on feminine suffixes (*striyām*), within the context of feminine gender, when the *kyap* suffix is prescribed by rules such as *saṃjñāyāṃ samajaniṣada-* (Pāṇini 3.3.99), there is indeed an operational heading (*adhikāra*) for the state of being.

This is due to the inherent nature of the expressive power of words (*śabdaśaktisvābhāvyāt*). In that context, the suffix *kyap* is prescribed for the abstract state (*bhāva*) alone, not for the object (*karman*). [As stated in the commentary: "By this, *bhāryā* is established"—the intention is that it would otherwise apply to the object. This is because the scope for the abstract state (*bhāva*) exists in the feminine gender; thus, only the abstract state functions as the expressed meaning (*vācyatvena*), and not [the object].

[The word *bhāryā*] is derived from the sense of "action" (*karman*); thus, the word *bhāryā* is established in the sense of "action. For, under the heading of "abstract state" (*bhāva*) for feminine nouns, the suffix *kyap* should indeed be applied to denote the abstract state; however, in the sense of "action," only the suffix *ṇyat* is applicable.

113. *mṛjer vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 3.1.113). Since the root *mṛj* has *ṛ* as its penultimate letter (*ṛdupadha*), this is an optional rule (*prāptavibhāṣā*). This is because the suffix *kyap* is prescribed by the rule *ṛdudhāccāklṛpicṛteḥ* (3.1.110). Thus we have *parimārgyaḥ*. As before, there is the substitution of *ku*-sounds (*kutva*).
"Vṛddhi [is substituted] for the root √gṛj" (Pāṇini 7.2.114).

114. *rājasūya-sūrya-mṛṣodya-rucya-kupya-kṛṣṭapacya-avyathyāḥ* (3.1.114). By the rule "to be pressed by a king" (*rājñā sotavyaḥ*), he shows that this is a specific grammatical formation (*nipātana*) where the word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyānta*) is the governing word (*upapada*) in the sense of the object (*karman*). This is also indicated by the statement: "or, the king is here being pressed" (*rājā veha sūyate*).

When *rājan* ending in the nominative case is used as an upapada, this is a nipātana (irregular formation) for the locative sense. From the root *ṣuñ* "to press" (DhP 1247), the suffix *kyap* is applied; therein, the absence of the *tuk*-augment and the lengthening of the vowel are both nipātita (irregularly prescribed). Regarding the rule "from *sū* and *sṛ*": *ṣū* means "to impel" (DhP 1408), and *sṛ*...

From these two roots, *gatau* (DhP 935) and [the other], when the suffix *yat* would have applied by Pāṇini 3.1.97 (*ṭhaco yat*), the suffix *kyap* is irregularly prescribed by Pāṇini 3.1.124 (*ṛhalorṇyad*). [The form] "suvati" is used in the sense of the object;
it means "he impels the worlds toward their task. For when that [sun] has risen, for the world...

The engagement in action. [This occurs] "when *yati* is applicable in the alternative case," by the rule *vadaḥ supi kyap ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.106). *Mṛṣā-vadanam* becomes *mṛṣodyam*: the suffix *kyap* is applied, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*), and by the rule *ād guṇaḥ* (6.1.87), a compound with an upapada is formed. [The phrase] "this is pleasing" (*rocate'sau*).
By indicating the meaning through an affix denoting the agent (*kartṛ-pratyaya*), he demonstrates that this is an irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in the sense of the agent.
Since [affixes] such as *tṛc* would otherwise apply, *kyap* is irregularly prescribed here. Regarding "of *gup*":
this refers either to *gup* in the sense of "concealing" (*gopaṇe*, DhP 970) or to *gup* in the sense of "protecting" (*rakṣaṇe*, DhP 395). Regarding "indeclinable" (*avyaya*): [this is the result].

From the root *ṭhvyath* (DhP 7.64), meaning "fear" and "trembling," the suffix *kyap* is introduced as an exception to the suffix *tṛc* when used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). This is a grammatical irregularity (*nipātyate*).

115. *bhidyoddhyau nade* (Pāṇini 3.1.115). [The Vārttika] states: *ujjheś ca*. The root *ujjh* means "to abandon" (*utsarge*, Dhātupāṭha 1304). It is taught that the suffix *kyap* is applied [after this root] when denoting the agent (*kartari*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the application of] suffixes such as *tṛc*.

116. *Puṣya* and *siddhya* are [formed] from the asterisms (*nakṣatra*). (Pāṇini 3.1.116) [The rule states: "From the roots *puṣ* and *sidh*. [The roots are: *puṣa* (Dhātupāṭha 1182) in the sense of nourishing, and *sidhu* (Dhātupāṭha 1192) in the sense of accomplishment. The suffix *kyap* is applied irregularly (*nipātyate*) in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇe*).

Thus [it is said]. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *lyuṭ*. 117. *vipūyavinīyajityā muñjakalkahaliṣu* (Pāṇini 3.1.117). [The rule] "from *pū* preceded by *vi*" refers to *pū* in the sense of "purifying" (*paṅ pavane*, Dhātupāṭha 966). [The rule] "and from *nī*" refers to *nī*.
This refers to the rule "after the prefix *vi-*" (*vipūrvāt*). [The suffix] *ghañ* is applied because all three [roots] end in long vowels (*ajanta*).

That which is decomposed (*vipūyate*) is *vipūya*. That which is led away (*vinīyate*), that is, attains completion, is *vinīya*. A specific medicinal preparation (*auṣadhaviśeṣa*) such as *kalka*, which is to be prepared with oil or ghee combined with substances like the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), etc. [is meant].
Thus it is said: that which is to be conquered is "conquerable" (*jitya*); one who possesses great strength is "Halī."

118. *pratyapibhyāṃ graheśchandasī* (Pāṇini 3.1.118). [The word] *pratigṛhyam*: the semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) is applied by the rule *grahijyā* (6.1.16), and the compound is formed by the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* (2.2.18).
119. *padāsvairibāhyāpakṣyeṣu ca* (3.1.119).

[The example is] *ṭhasvairī*. The root *īr* (in the sense of "motion" and "trembling") is found in the Dhātupāṭha (1018). The suffix *ṇini* is applied here in the sense of habit (*tācchīlika*), meaning "one whose nature it is to move or go by himself (*svena svayam īritum*)."

The vowel *svarī* undergoes vṛddhi by virtue of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). One who is not independent is called *asvairī*. Regarding the term "bāhyāyām," the meaning is "that which is external. The suffix *yañ* is applied according to the supplementary rule (Vārttika 378), "There is also the elision of the final syllable of *bahiṣ*," and in that case, the *ṭi*-portion is elided. Regarding the phrase "and in the sense of *pakṣye*," the word *pakṣya*— [End of excerpt]

He explains the group (*varga*): that which exists in a side is "side-born" (*pakṣya*), by virtue of belonging to the *dig-ādi* class [of words], which takes the suffix *yat*. That which is grasped is a "grasped word" (*pragṛhya*). Here, the meaning of the root *gṛh* is "not being in close proximity. For in that case, the vowels are not brought into close proximity;
they are not placed near one another—this is "non-proximity" (*asannikarṣa*). That which is separated is "separated" (*avagṛhya*).

Regarding the phrase "of which an *avagraha* is made": therein, within a compound word (*samudāyapada*), the constituent words (*avayavapada*) are explained by being separated and divided. Because the constituents are thus separated (*avagṛhya*), it is called *avagṛhya*. [This refers to] the term "those who are to be grasped" (*gṛhyakāḥ*).

The suffix *kan* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.3.76 (*anukampāyām*). Regarding the term "gṛhītakāḥ," it means those who are restrained or made dependent. Regarding the phrase "elsewhere," it refers to both the masculine and neuter genders. The term "vāsudevagṛhyāḥ" is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

120. *vibhāṣā kṛvṛṣoḥ* | (3.1.120) [The rule] "and after the root *vṛṣ*" [is understood]. The root *vṛṣu* is listed [in the Dhātupāṭha] as *vṛṣu*, *pḷuṣu* in the sense of "burning" (DhP 703); and *pḷuṣu*, *mṛṣu* in the sense of "sprinkling" (DhP 706, 707).

121. *yugyaṃ ca patre* (3.1.121). [The word] *patra* [is derived as follows]: "that by which they fly (*patanti*) is *patram*. [This is formed] with the suffix *ṣṭran* according to [Pāṇini 3.2.182] *dāmnīśas-* etc. [The word] *yugyam*: [the root] *yujir* in the sense of "joining" (Dhātupāṭha 1444); that which is to be yoked (*yojanīya*).
The reading "yujyate vāhanena gamanam" is the established text; "gavādikam" refers to a vehicle (yugyam).

122. *amāvāsyadantarasyām* (3.1.122). Regarding the form *amāvāsya*: the inclusion of the indicatory letter *t* (*takāra-anubandha*) is for the purpose of making it known that this is a *nipātana* (irregular formation) ending in the suffix *ṇyat*, and not one ending in the suffix *kyap*; otherwise, [the suffix would be] *kyap*.

Because of the context, one might suppose that this [word] ends in the *kyap* suffix. Moreover, the suffix intended here is *ti*, as in *ṇyat*, and not *yat*; otherwise, the irregular formation (*nipātana*) would be purposeless.
For in the section on *yat*, he would have simply said, "after the root *avas*, optionally. Furthermore, because [the alternative form] would be defective.
Regarding the fault in treating this as a nipāta (irregular formation) ending in the suffix *yat*, that fault will be revealed later.

Furthermore, whatever fault exists in treating it as a nipāta ending in *yat*—namely, the absence of *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution)—would also apply to the form ending in *kyap*; therefore, this nipāta must be understood as ending in the suffix *ṇyat*.
Having considered this, he says: "The suffix *ṇyat* occurs when [the word] *kāla* functions as a locative (*adhikaraṇa*).
By means of the principle of "modification of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtatva*), he demonstrates the purpose of the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) ending in the suffix *ṇyat*.
For it is precisely the word *amāvasyā* that is irregularly derived with the suffix *ṇyat*, which results in the absence of *vṛddhi*. Thus, the word *amāvasyā*—
In this case, [the rule] does not apply under the view that there is no increase [of syllables].
Consequently, according to the principle "that which is modified in one part is treated as non-different," when the word *amāvāsyā* is included, the word *amāvāsyā* is also included. Therefore...

While the rule *pūrvāhṇāparāhṇārdrāmūlapradoṣāvaskarād vun* (Pāṇini 4.3.28) is being carried over, the suffixes *vun* and *aṇ* are prescribed by the rule *amāvāsyāyā vā* (Pāṇini 4.3.30) for the word *amāvāsyā*; thus, the form *amāvasyā* is also established.

"Ṭhamāvaseḥ," and so forth. Although there is only one primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the dual number is used in the designation because a distinction is intended based on the difference between its attributes of being subject to growth and not being subject to growth. [The word] "I" refers to the Self (*ātman*).

By stating "others do it otherwise," he indicates that they act differently. "Of the two ending in *ṇya*" means "of those ending in the suffix *ṇyat*. Regarding "I shall cause [the word] *avṛddhi* to fall [under the rule]," the words "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) are to be supplied. He asks what is accomplished by this and says: "In that way, the status of being a single term applies to those two."

Thus [the word] "is established" (prasiddhyati) is to be connected with what is to be stated hereafter. In some places, the reading is "tathaikavṛttitām"; there, it is to be connected with the contextually relevant "I shall cast down" (nipātayāmi).
And the meaning of "I shall cast down" (nipātayāmi) is "I shall accomplish" (sādhayāmi). [The word] "of those two" (tayoḥ).

The term *amāvāsyā* refers to the reflection (*pratyavamarśa*) upon the two *amāvasyās*. Furthermore, "occurrence" (*vṛtti*) means the production of the suffixes *-vuñ* and *-aṇ*. Those two which have an identical occurrence are "of the same occurrence" (*ekavṛtī*);

the state of being such is "identity of occurrence" (*ekavṛtitā*). That [state], having produced the suffix *-ṇyat*, results in the non-occurrence of *vṛddhi* by virtue of its being a technical irregularity (*nipātana*).

"It is established," because that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original]. "And my *svara* is established" refers to [the rule] *tit svaritam* (Pāṇini 6.1.185). The state of having the final syllable as *svarita* is intended. "It is established" (*sidhyati*):
those who prescribe the *yat* suffix for the root *vas* preceded by *am*, and because of the mention of the option (*anyatarasyām*).

In the alternative view, they desire the suffixes *ṇyat* and *at*. Although for them the form *amāvāsya-* is established, nevertheless, in the case of the suffix *yat*, the correct accent is not achieved;
for by the rule "ṭhyato ’nāvaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.213), the initial udātta of the word *vasyā-* would apply as an exception to the svarita accent.

Even if the compound is formed with the word *amā*, by the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), which assigns the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) to the final member ending in a *kṛt*-suffix, the word *vasya* itself would become udātta on its first syllable. However, it is desired that the svarita be on the final syllable. Furthermore, the previously mentioned *ekavṛttitā* does not apply here either.

It is established; because it is a different word. For while one [form] ends in the suffix *yat*, the other ends in the suffix *ṇyat*; thus, the absence of *vṛddhi* is prescribed as a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*) in the case of *ṇyat*.

123. *chandasi niṣṭarkyadevahūyapraṇīyonnīyoccchiṣyamaryastaryādhvaryakhanyakhānyadevayajyāpṛcchÂayapratiṣīvyabrahmavādyabhāvyastāvyopacāyyapṛḍāni* | (3.1.123) [The word] *ṭhkyapi prāpte* [is used] because [the root] has *ṛt* as its penultimate letter. [The rule] *ādyantaviparyayaḥ* [applies].

The initial *ka* is treated as final, and the final *ta* is treated as initial. Regarding the rule "from the root *hvayati*" and so forth: when the suffix *kyap* is applied to the root *hveñ* (meaning "to contend") [DhP 1008], there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) because it belongs to the *yajādi* class (Pāṇini 6.1.15), and lengthening occurs by the rule "after a consonant" (6.4.2). When...

From the roots *hu* "to give" (*dhā.pā.* 1083) and *hū* "to sacrifice" (*dhā.pā.*), the absence of the augment *tug* and the lengthening [of the vowel] are prescribed as irregularities (*nipātana*). [Thus we have] *devahūvaḥ*, meaning "that in which the gods are invoked.
Regarding *accchivyaḥ*—[the Kāśikā reads] *pucchyiṣyam*—it is derived from the root *śiṣlṛ*.

In the sense of "falling apart" (*viśaraṇa*), [the root] *viś* [is used] (DhP 1451). By the rule *śaś chāe ṭi* (Pāṇini 8.4.63), the letter *ch* is substituted; by the rule *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.40), the *ścutva* substitution [of *ś* for *s*] occurs. [The suffix] *yat* is added after these two [roots]. Since the suffix *ṇyat* would otherwise apply because the root ends in *ṛ*, [the rule] applies in the feminine.

"It is an irregular formation (*nipātana*). Otherwise, the feminine designation "staryā" would be meaningless. Regarding "āpṛcchyāḥ," there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by [Pāṇini 6.1.16] *grahy-ādi*. Regarding "pratiṣīvyaḥ," there is lengthening by [Pāṇini 8.2.77] *hali ca*. Regarding "vader ṇyat," [it occurs] after the root *vad* when followed by a *sup*-ending.

Regarding the rule *kyap ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.106), where both *kyap* and *yat* would otherwise apply, [we have] the forms *bhāvyaḥ* and *stāvyaḥ*. Here, the suffix *ṇyat* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *yat* applied to the roots *bhū* and *stu*. The examples beginning with *niṣṭarkya* and so forth are two summary verses (*saṅgrahaśloka*) intended for the easy comprehension [of the material]. [The word] *vyatyayam*...

Thus; the meaning is "the reversal of the beginning and the end. Regarding the rule *ṇyad ekasmāt*: this fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) occurs due to the elision of the suffix *lyap* (denoting the object). That is to say, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied with reference to the single word *niṣṭarkya*; it means that *ṇyat* is employed in order to derive one particular form. Regarding the rule *caturbhyaḥ kyap*: [this indicates] the sense of being for the sake of that (*tādarthya*).

This is the fourth [instance]. Regarding those four immediately following "devahūya" and so forth, the suffix *kyap* occurs for their sake—that is, for the purpose of their accomplishment—according to the rule: "The suffix *yat* is prescribed after the four beginning with *catur*. This fourth case ending (*caturthī*) also expresses *tādarthya* (the state of being for the sake of that). For the sake of those four immediately following it—the boundaries extending up to *khāni*—[the suffix *kyap* occurs].

Since the rule exists for the sake of establishing that [suffix], it says: "The suffix *ṇyat* occurs after one [root]. For these as well, the ablative case is used in the sense of the object when there is an elision of the suffix *lyap*. With reference to a single word ending in *khānya*, the suffix *ṇyat* occurs;
the meaning is: "in order to derive the word *khānya*. And [the sūtra] says: "and after [a root] ending in *ya*."

The word "ekasmāt" (from one) serves the purpose of attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*). The suffix *ya* occurs with reference to the word *devayajyā*. Regarding the statement "there are two *kyap*s," there are two *kyap* suffixes for the sake of establishing the forms *āpṛcchyā* and *pratīṣīvya*. Regarding the statement "the rule for *ṇyat* applies after *cut*," the meaning is that the suffix *ṇyat* occurs four times. That...
Furthermore, regarding the remaining [roots] such as *brahmavādī* and others;

or alternatively, the rule "ṇyadekasmāt" means "from a single root. Regarding the rule "caturbhyaḥ kyap," it means that the suffix *kyap* occurs after four roots. But is it not the case that *nī* is only one?
[Since] there is only one root (*dhātu*), how is it said "from four roots"?

There is no fault, for by the distinction of prefixes (*upasarga*), a distinction of even a single [root] is intended to be expressed. As it is said: "And after the four, the rule applies to *ya*. Thus, the suffix *yat* [is applied] after those four immediately preceding roots.
The meaning is "the rule. Regarding the statement "ṇyat after one [root]": the suffix *ṇyat* is prescribed after a single root.
Regarding the statement "and the word *ya*": in the word *devayajyā*, the suffix *ya* occurs after a single root. Regarding the statement "two *kyap*s":
for the sake of establishing the words *āpṛcchyā* and *pratiṣīvya*.
The two suffixes *kyap* occur after the roots *ā-pracchi* and *iṣ-vaś*.

124. *ṛhalorṇyat* (Pāṇini 3.1.124). [The statement] "the genitive is used in the sense of the ablative" is by virtue of the rule *vyatyayo bahulam* (3.1.85). But in what sense of the ablative is the genitive used? In the sense of the ablative characterized by connection with a direction (*digyoga*). For in the prescription of suffixes...
Because of the connection with the rule "ṭh paraś ca" (Pāṇini 3.1.2), the ablative case ought to be used.

125. *orāvaśyake* (Pāṇini 3.1.125). [The word] *āvaśyakam* is derived from *avaśya-bhāva* (the state of being necessary) with the suffix *vuñ*, because it belongs to the *manojñādi* group. This very fact is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that for indeclinables (*avyaya*), the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) occurs before any *bha*-affix. In this case, there are two [points].

It is considered that [the word *avaśyaka*] functions as an *upapada* (a subordinate word) because it is necessarily an *upapada*, and it functions as an *upādhi* (a qualifying condition) because it is necessarily that which is to be indicated (*dyotya*). In that regard, if it were understood thus— that [the suffix applies] when *avaśyaka* is the *upapada*—
then [the suffix] would not apply in cases where *avaśyaka* is to be indicated but no *upapada* is present, such as in "lāvyaṃ" and "pāvyam."
He says—"when the sense of necessity (āvaśyaka) is to be indicated"—because it is understood in this way.
And this is obtained through proximity (pratyāsatti). For the qualifier (upādhi) is internal (antaraṅga), since it is to be indicated by the suffix itself;
whereas the connection with the subordinate word (upapada) is external (bahiraṅga), because its meaning is expressed by another word.

Regarding the phrase "the impossibility of the accentual compound" (*svarasamāsānupapatti*): when the word *upapada* is understood in the sense of being necessary (*avaśyaka*), the compound is formed by the rule *upapadam atiṅ* (Pāṇini 2.2.19). And since that [compound] exists, the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139) applies, based on the *upapada*.

There is the accentuation of the original tone of the final member (*uttarapadaprakṛtisvaratva*); the accent of the *ti* suffix does not occur. However, in the view that [the suffix] is merely indicative (*dyotaka*), there would be no compound at all, because the defining condition (*lakṣaṇa*) for it is absent. Even if, somehow, there were a compound other than an upapada-compound, even so the accent based on an upapada-compound would not occur; consequently, the accent of the *ti* suffix [would apply].

It would not be obtained, for there would be the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound. In the case of *avaśyalāvyam*, the *m* is elided by the rule *lumped avaśyamaḥ kṛtye*. [The formation of the compound] is due to its inclusion in the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group, and so forth.

He shows that because the *mayūravyaṃsaka* group is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, words such as *avaśyalāvya-prabhṛti* and *lāvya-prabhṛti* should be understood as included therein. He asks, "How is the accent? and says: "And when there is the original accent of the final member," and so forth. In this regard, the following rule applies: *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139).

In this context, the particle *ca* from the rule "ṣaṭ ca kāṇḍādīni" (Pāṇini 6.2.135) will be understood as carrying over; moreover, it serves the purpose of including that which is not mentioned in the *Ṛgveda*. Consequently, even in forms such as *avaśyalāvyam*, the accent of the base (*prakṛtisvara*) occurs.

126. *āsuyuvapirapilapitrapicamaśca* | (Pāṇini 3.1.126). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffix] *ṭhya*. [The roots] *ṣṛñ* "to press" (DhP 1247) and *yu* "to mix" (DhP 1033) are included because they end in *r*. [Also included are: *ḍuvapa* "to sow seeds or weave threads."

(dhā.pā. 1003), *ṭhrapa lapa vyaktāyāṃ vāci* (dhā.pā. 401, 402), *ṭhtrapūṣ lajjāyām* (dhā.pā. 374), *ṭhcamu adane* (dhā.pā. 469)—because these [roots] have a vowel as their penultimate (*adupadha*) and end in a labial (*pavargānta*). "Dābhyam" [is derived from the root *dabh*].
The root *dabh* exists as a distinct verbal base not even listed among the [standard] roots, just like *culump*.

127. *Ānāyyo’nitye* (3.1.127). [The suffix] *ṭh-ṇya* is prescribed as an irregular formation (*nipātita*). Since the suffix *yat* would otherwise apply, [the author asks]: "If it is prescribed as an irregular formation for the sense of 'non-eternal' (*anitya*), then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to words such as *ghaṭa* and the like, because those too are non-eternal. To this he replies with "established" (*rūḍhaḥ*), and so forth.
Even though they possess a basis for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*), words function with respect to a specific object due to conventional usage (*rūḍhi*),

and not with respect to an unspecified one, just like the word "peacock" (*mayūra*) and others. For not every creature that cries on the earth is called a peacock, nor is everyone who goes [called a peacock].
It is called "cow" (*gauh*); what then? It is specifically a living being. Therefore, the conventional term (*rūḍhi-śabda*) applies only to the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire and not to jars and the like.
Regarding the phrase "because it is never awake," the meaning is that it does not burn constantly; for [the word] refers precisely to burning.

That [fire] remains specifically in the *jāgaraṇa* [state]. To show that it does not abide everywhere—even in the *dakṣiṇāgni*—he says "and which," etc. But does it have a variety of origins (*yoni*) by which it is thus distinguished? He says "for of that," etc. Origin (*yoni*).
The meaning is "the cause. By the words "from the maker of all" (*vaiśvakṛtāt*) and so forth, he demonstrates the variety of wombs (*yonivikalpa*).
Regarding the phrase "if it is argued that the *ānāyya* is non-eternal," the ellipsis is: [this argument] would also apply to jars and other such things.
Regarding the phrase "it would be performed in the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire," this is an irregular grammatical derivation (*nipātana*) for the word "*ānāyya*."

It would be performed specifically in the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire and not elsewhere. The optative suffix (*liṅ*) expresses possibility; the meaning is that this is possible, and not otherwise. Regarding the statement, "And one should know it in that which has a single source": having brought that [fire] denoted by the term *ānāyya*, one should know it in the *dakṣiṇāgni*, which shares the same source as the *āhavanīya*.
The meaning is that one should know [it] thus. The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis—meaning "only in a single womb.

For it is said: "Otherwise, it would be *āneya*. This is because in the case of an impermanent object like a jar, or in the case of the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire which has a different origin than the *āhavanīya*, when the suffix *yat* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.97 (*aco yat*), the form would simply be *āneya*.
It comes to be.
128. *praṇāyyaḥ* [is used] in the sense of *asammataḥ* (not approved).

By showing that this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound through the specific phrase "avidyamānā sammatiḥ" (there is no approval), he dispels the suspicion that it might be a *tatpuruṣa* compound—explaining that "sammatiḥ" means "the state of being approved."
"Sammata" means "honored. The state of being honored is "sammatatā. By this word "sammati," he demonstrates that the meaning here is "one who is honored.
[Regarding the phrase] "If it is so," and so forth: in the case of a thief and others, there is no honor present.

The use of the word *praṇāyya* in the sense of a pupil (*antevāsī*) is not appropriate; for the intention is not that respect (*pūjā*) is absent in a pupil. In the phrase "he should proclaim the *brahman*," the word *brahman* here refers to the Veda. It is also said that "consent (*sammati*) is called desire (*abhilāṣa*). Not [so].

By the word "also" (api) in the phrase "merely worship," he indicates this. "By the absence of that" means by the absence of longing. "By being free from desire" means by being devoid of the longing for the enjoyment of mental states (bhāva).
129. *pāyya-sānnāyya-nikāyya-dhāyyā* [are formed with *kyap*] in the senses of a measure, an oblation, a dwelling, and verses for the *sāmidhenī* [respectively].
Regarding *pāyya*: by [the rule] *āto yuk ciṇ-kṛtoḥ* (7.3.33), [the suffix *yuk* is added]; it refers specifically to particular types of sacrificial oblations (*havir-viśeṣeṣu*).
It remains established only where it has taken root; it does not apply to every mere oblation.
The term *dhāyyā* is formed with the suffix *yuk* as before. It denotes a specific type of *ṛc*. Not all *ṛcs* are designated by the word *sāmidhenī*;
rather, what is meant is the mantra used for placing the fuel-sticks (*samid-ādhāna*). For it is so stated:

The word *sāmidhenī* is derived within the mantra for placing the fuel-sticks (*samid-ādhāna*). However, not every *ṛc* verse is designated as a *sāmidhenī*; rather, he says "in that [context]" and so forth, showing that only a specific one is so called.
But how is it that a derivation made in a general sense comes to apply to a particular case?
Thus he says: "For the word *rūḍhi* is non-etymological (*amama*). The word *dhāyyā* is a conventional term (*rūḍhi-śabda*) denoting a specific type of *ṛc*;
it is that very one which is meant by this [term], and no other. How, then, is it known that this is a conventional term?
To this he says: "And thus," and so forth. If this were not a conventional term...

It might be argued that because the term *dhāyyā* is applied within the *sāmidhenī* verses, it would not be observed in reference to a specific *ṛc* verse in the phrase "he recites the *dhāyyās*," yet it is indeed so observed. Therefore, it is concluded that this is a conventional (*rūḍhi*) word. If, then, it is also observed even outside the *sāmidhenīs*, would the mention of *sāmidhenī* not be redundant?
It is not meaningless, because it serves to indicate a specific conventional usage.

130. *kratau kuṇḍapāyyasañcāyyau* (Pāṇini 3.1.130). [The word] *pibateḥ* [is used]; [the root is] *pā pāne* (Dhātupāṭha 925). [The rule] *adhikaraṇe yat-pratyayaḥ* applies. Since the suffix *lyuṭ* would otherwise be expected, what is the reason for abandoning *ṇyat* and using a form ending in the suffix *yat*?

Why is the word *kuṇḍapāyya* treated as an irregular formation (*nipātana*)? To this he says: "The accent is [governed] by the rule *yato 'nāvaḥ*. For if it ended in the suffix *yat*, the first syllable of the second member would be udātta; however, if it ended in the suffix *ṇyat*, the svarita accent would fall on the final syllable. Thus, [the form is] *kuṇḍapānam*.
In cases other than when it denotes an action (kratu), only the suffix *lyuṭ* occurs.

131. *agnau paricāyyopacāyyasamūhyāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.131). Regarding the rule *saṃpūrvād vaheḥ* and so forth: since the root ends in a consonant (*hal*), the suffix *ṇyat* is already established by rule; however, if that [suffix] were applied, vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) would not occur because [the suffix] is not *akit*. Even if vocalization were applied after the suffix *ṇyat* had been formed...

The lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by *ṭhhalaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.2) does not apply here; for that rule ordains lengthening of an *aṅga* which ends in a *saṃprasāraṇa* occurring after a consonant (*hal*) that is part of the *aṅga*.
This [form], however, is not of such a nature; therefore, both [the elision and the lengthening] are established as *nipātana*s. It is not derived from the root *ūh* preceded by the prefix *sam*.

The suffix *ṇyat* prescribed by the general rule alone suffices; however, [the specific rule] is intended so that *ṇyat* occurs only after the root *vah* when preceded by *sam* with *agni* as the object, and not in cases such as "the Brāhmaṇa is to be carried" (*saṃvoḍhavyo brāhmaṇaḥ*).
132. *cityāgnicitye ca* (3.1.132). [The commentary states:

"By this, the final acute accent (*antodātatva*) occurs. For when there is the introduction of the suffix *yat*, the word becomes finally accented by the accent of the suffix itself; however, if the suffix *ṇyat* were present, [the accentuation would be different].
The svarita accent occurs [therein]. Therefore, the sense is that the suffix *ya* is introduced as an irregularity (*nipātana*), setting aside the original rule.

133. *ṇvul-tṛcau* | (Pāṇini 3.1.133) "The letter *ṭh* is for the purpose of general reference," and so forth. This means that there should be a general reference to both *tṛj* and *tṛn*. For if that [letter *ṭh*] were not present, [the rule would apply only to the one with no *anubandha*, according to the principle: "When a form without an *anubandha* is prescribed, it does not include the one with an *anubandha*."

Thus, there would be no inclusion of the suffix *tṛn*. Now, why is it not for the sake of making [the word] oxytone? Because that is already established by the accent of the suffix itself (*pratyayasvara*).

134. *nandigrahipacādibhyo lyuṇinyacaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.134). Lest it be understood that the word "ādi" (etcetera) is connected only with the root *pac*, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), he says: "with each [root]," and so forth.

Regarding the verse beginning with "nandivāśi" and so forth: the roots are *ṇadi* in the sense of "prosperity" (*samṛddhi*) [DhP 67], *vāśṛ* in the sense of "sound" (*śabda*) [DhP 1163], *madī* in the sense of "joy" (*harṣa*) [DhP 1208], *duṣa* in the sense of "corruption" (*vaikṛtya*) [DhP 1185],
*rādha* and *sādha* in the sense of "accomplishment" (*saṃsiddhi*) [DhP 1262, 1263], and *śubha* and *śumbha*.

From these verbal roots—*śubh* (in the sense of beauty, DhP 1321, 1322) and *ruc* (in the sense of shining, DhP 745)—when followed by the causative suffix *ṇic*, the suffix *lyu* occurs in the sense of a technical name (*saṃjñā*). Examples include *nandana* from *nandayati* (he causes to rejoice), and so forth; and *dūṣaṇa* from *dūṣayati*, according to the rule *doṣo ṇau* (Pāṇini 6.4.90).

Thus [is established] the substitution of *ū*. However, for these roots ending in *aṇ*, when not forming a technical name (*asaṃjñā*), and even when forming a technical name (*saṃjñā*), only suffixes such as *tṛc* and others occur.

The very purpose of including *grah* and others, as well as *nandi* and others, in their respective lists (*gaṇa*) is this: so that their grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) may be maintained in instances characterized by technical names. Otherwise, indeed—
One should list only the verbal roots (*prakṛti*) in this group and, having indicated them by means of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*),

prescribe the suffix; namely, from the roots *sah* (in the sense of endurance, DhP 1809), *tap* (in the sense of heating, DhP 985), and *dam* (in the sense of calming, DhP 1203), as in the rule beginning with *sahitapi*.
The suffix *lyu* is applied after roots ending in *aṇ* when used with the prefix *saṃjñāyām*. Examples include *jalpanaḥ* and so forth. [The roots are:

*japa* and *jalpa* in the sense of "articulate speech" (*dhā.pā.* 397, 398); *ramu* in the sense of "play" (*dhā.pā.* 853); *dṛpa*—[according to the *Dhātupāṭha*: *harṣa-mocanayoḥ*]—in the sense of "exultation and release" (*dhā.pā.* 1196); and *kadi*...

The roots *krad* in the sense of calling out and weeping (*dhā.pā.* 70, 71), *kṛṣ* in the sense of scratching (*dhā.pā.* 990), *hṛṣ* in the sense of delighting (*dhā.pā.* 709), and *ard* in the sense of harming (*dhā.pā.* 1828):
he who harms (*ardayati*) people (*jana*) is Janārdana. Although the suffix *aṇ* would have been expected by rule [Pāṇini 3.2.1], the suffix *lyu* is used here. [The suffix] *yu*...
Regarding the roots *miśra* (in the sense of mixing) and *sūd* (in the sense of flowing, DhP 1033 and 1717):

[the term] *madhusūdana* means "one who causes the honey to flow. Here too, although the suffix *aṇ* would have been expected after an object, the suffix *lyu* is used. Regarding the root *bhī* (in the sense of fear, DhP 1084), when preceded by the prefix *vi-*, [the suffix *ṇic* is applied] by the rule *hetumati ca*.

(3.1.26) Thus, there is the *ṇic* suffix; [the rule] "ṭhbhiyo hetubhaye ṣuk" (7.3.40) applies. Regarding "lavaṇaḥ": [the root] "lūñ chedane" (DhP 1483). "The change to *ṇ* is by way of *nipātana*" means that the inclusion of the form with the *ṇ* substituted in the list of roots (*gaṇa*) constitutes the *nipātana*. [The root] "ṇaśa adarśane" (DhP 1194), preceded by the prefix *vi*, [and] "damu".

The two roots *upaśam* (Dhātupāṭha 1203) are both derived with the causative suffix *ṇic*. "One who destroys the *vita*" is *vitavināśanaḥ*; "one who subdues the family" (*kula*) is *kuladamanaḥ*. The shortening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.92); although the suffix *aṇ* would have been expected after an object [denoted by the first member], the suffix *lyu* is used instead.

Regarding "ṭhgraha" and so forth: the root *grah* means "to seize" (DhP 1533); *ṣah* means "to endure" (DhP 1809), preceded by the prefix *ud*; *tasu* means "to throw" or "to cast away" (DhP 1212)—the *dhuḍ* augment is applied as in the case of *das*, which follows the same rule; and *bhas* means "to revile" or "to shine."
[The root] preceded by *ud*. [From] *sthā* (DhP 928) "to stop moving," with *yuk* added according to Pāṇini 7.3.33: *sthāyī*.
[From] *matri* (DhP 1679) "to speak secretly" (the curādi class ending in *ṇic*), and *mṛd* "to crush."

(DhP 1515) [The rule] begins with *sam*. This is so that [the suffix] may apply only after the root preceded by *sam*, as in *saṃmṛdnāti*. [This refers to the rule] "After the roots *rakṣ*, *śru*, *vas*, *vap*, and *śo*, the suffix *nauc* [is applied]. *Rakṣ* means "to protect" (DhP 658); *śru* means "to hear" (DhP 942);
*ḍuvap* means "to sow seeds or to weave" (DhP 1003); *śo*...

Regarding *tanūkaraṇe* (DhP 1145): when the word *ni-* is used as an *upapada*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied. Thus, "niśāyī" is formed; the derivation is as before. Regarding "yāci" and so forth: *yācṛ* (DhP 863) means "to beg," and *hṛñ* (DhP 899) means "to take"; the latter is preceded by the prefixes *vi-* and *ā-*, and then that same [root] again.

The suffix *ṇini* occurs after these [roots] when they are preceded by *sam*: *vraj* (meaning "to go," Dhātupāṭha 252, 253), *vad* (meaning "articulate speech," Dhātupāṭha 1009), and *vas* (meaning "dwelling," Dhātupāṭha 1005)—provided that they are otherwise prohibited [from taking this suffix]. Regarding the phrase "when they are prohibited": it means "when their meanings are otherwise prohibited."

Since the negative particle *nañ* occurs only with words whose meaning is prohibited, the suffix *ṇini* is understood to follow those preceded by *nañ*. But how can there be the employment of things that are prohibited?
There is no fault here, because they are not prohibited when existing as metaphorical (*upacāra*) entities; for the existence of word-meanings is not solely primary (*mukhya*).

However, even that which is metaphorical (aupacārikī) is another [kind of existence] for entities by way of its meaning, as previously stated. In that regard, it is only the primary (mukhyā) existence that is negated, not the metaphorical existence residing in the intellect; thus, the employment of that [metaphorical term] based upon it is not contradictory.

Regarding "ṭhacām" and so forth: the affix *ṇini* occurs after verbal roots ending in vowels (*ajanta*) that have an unconscious agent (*acit-kartṛka*) and for which [other suffixes] are prohibited. That whose consciousness (*cita*) is non-existent is "unconscious" (*acita*); those whose agent (*kartṛ*) is such are described as "having an unconscious agent. This qualification is applied by way of the meaning (*arthadvāraka*), for it is through the meaning that the agent is unconscious.
The verbal roots denoting those [actions] are figuratively referred to in that way. Regarding the rule *viśayī viṣayī deśe*:
the words *viśayin* and *viṣayin*, ending in the suffix *ṇini*, are grammatically correct when the meaning to be expressed is "country.
[The roots are] *śīṅ* "to sleep" (DhP 1032) and *ṣiñ* "to bind."

Regarding these two [roots] preceded by *vi*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied; the absence of *vṛddhi* is due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*). It is stated: "The word *abhibhāvī* [is used] in the sense of the past. The word *abhibhāvī* is correctly formed with the suffix *ṇini* in the past tense. The suffix *ṇini* is added to the root *bhū* preceded by the prefix *abhi*. One who has overcome (*abhibhūtavān*) is called *abhibhāvī*.

*Uparodhī*, *uparodhī*: from the roots *rādha* and *sādha* in the sense of "accomplishment" (*saṃsiddhau*) [DhP 1262, 1263], and *rudhir* in the sense of "obstructing" (*āvaraṇe*) [DhP 1438], with the suffix *ṇini* after these two preceded by the prefix *upa*.
*Paribhāvī*, *paribhavī*: from the root *bhū* preceded by *pari*; in one alternative (*pakṣe*), there is an absence of *vṛddhi*.

Regarding "ṭhpaca" and so forth: *ḍupacaṣ* in the sense of cooking (DhP 996); *vaca* in the sense of speaking (DhP 1842); *ḍuvap* in the sense of sowing seeds, weaving, and also cutting (DhP 1003); and *vada* in the sense of distinct speech.
(dhā.pā. 1009), *ṭhcala kampane* (dhā.pā. 832), *ṭhśala gatau* (dhā.pā.

843), *ṭhpatlu gatau* (dhā.pā. 845). Regarding *ṭhnadaṭ*: *pṇada*—*nada* [is used] in the sense of indistinct sound (dhā.pā. 54). The suffixal marker *ṭ* is for the purpose of forming the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. *ṭhbhaṣaṭ*—[Kāśikā].
*bhasaṭ*—the root *bhaṣ* is used in the sense of "threatening" (*bhartsane*), and *bhas* is used in the senses of "threatening" and "shining" (*bhartsanadīptyoḥ*) [Dhātupāṭha 1100].

The letter *ṭ* is for the purpose of forming the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. [The roots] *gṛ* in the sense of "swallowing" (*nigaraṇe*) [Dhātupāṭha 1410], *miṣ* in the sense of "rivalry" (*sparddhāyām*) [Dhātupāṭha 1352], *kup* in the sense of "anger" (*krodhe*) [Dhātupāṭha 1233], and *miha* in the sense of "moistening" (*secane*) [Dhātupāṭha 992].
The roots *tṛ* in the sense of floating and crossing (*plavanataraṇayoḥ*) [DhP 969], *cur* in the sense of stealing (*steye*) [DhP 1534],

*gāh* in the sense of agitating (*viloḍane*) [DhP 649], *jṛṣ* and *jhṛṣ* in the sense of loss of vitality (*vayohānau*) [DhP 1130, 1131], *mṛṅ* in the sense of giving up life (*prāṇatyāge*) [DhP 1403], and *kṣamūṣ* in the sense of enduring (*sahane*).

(dhā.pā.442), *tud* in the sense of "to afflict" (dhā.pā.1281), *mṛd* in the sense of "to crush" (dhā.pā.1515), *div* in the sense of "to play" and so forth (dhā.pā.1107), *nṛt* in the sense of "to move the limbs" (dhā.pā.1116), *vraṇ* in the sense of "to bruise the limbs," belonging to the *curādi* group; *dṛśir*...

From the root *prekṣ* (DhP 988) and from *ḍubhṛñ* "to support and nourish" (DhP 1087), with the word *jāra* as an upapada, the suffix *ac* is applied. Thus, one who supports (*bibharti*) a paramour (*jāram*) is called *jārabharaḥ*. From the root *pac*, with *śvan* as an upapada, the suffix *aṇ* is applied for the object (*karman*), and the initial vowel is replaced by *ac*; thus, one who cooks a dog (*śvānam*) is called *śvapacaḥ*.

"It is an *ākṛtigaṇa*," because the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) connected with the *pacādi* group has the sense of "type" (*prakāra*). And by its being an *ākṛtigaṇa*, [words such as] *cakradhara* and others are established.

135. *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ* | (Pāṇini 3.1.135) In the case of *vikṣipaḥ*, because the suffix is marked with *k* (kit), there is an absence of *guṇa*. In the case of *jñaḥ*, by [the rule] *āto lopa iṭi ca* (6.4.64), there is the elision of the vowel *ā*. In the case of *priyaḥ*, [it is derived from] *prīñ tarpaṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 1836).

Regarding *iyaṅ*: [it is derived] from the root *kṝ* in the sense of "scattering" (*kiraḥ*; DhP 1409). By the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.100), there is the substitution of *i*, followed by the substitution of *ra* for the *ṛ*. Now, how are words such as *deva* and others established?
For, since the roots beginning with *div* have a vowel *i* as their penultimate (*igupadha*), when the suffix *ka* is applied, they would result in forms such as *divakaḥ* or *sivakaḥ*.
Should it be so? To this he says: "like a god," and so forth. The word "etc. (ādi) indicates a manner or type.
136. *ātaścopasarge* (3.1.136).

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṇa*. It supersedes what would have been obtained by the rule *śyādvyadha-* (3.1.141), etc. The form *suglaḥ* is derived from the roots *glai* and *mlai*, meaning "to lose one's joy" (*harṣakṣaye*), as listed in the Dhātupāṭha (nos. 903, 904).

137. *pā-ghrā-dhmā-dheṭ-dṛśaḥ śaḥ* | (Pāṇini 3.1.137) *pā* "to drink" (Dhātupāṭha 925), *ghrā* "to perceive odour" (Dhātupāṭha 926), *dhmā* "in the sense of sound and contact with fire" (Dhātupāṭha 927), *dheṭ* "to suck" (Dhātupāṭha 902).

When the suffixes *ka* and *ṇa* would otherwise apply by virtue of the characteristics of the roots ending in long vowels (*ākārānta*), the suffix *śa* is prescribed here. If the term "preposition" (*upasarga*) is understood to carry over [from a previous rule], then *ka* applies; if it has ceased to apply, then *ṇa* applies after non-prepositions (as in the case of *ke prāpta*). For the root *dṛś*, the suffix *ka* applies by virtue of the characteristic of roots ending in *ṛ* or having a penultimate *i*. In examples such as *ṭhu-piba*, the suffix is *śit* because of its *ś*-marker.

When the designation *sārvadhātuka* applies, [the rule] "ṭhkartari śap" (Pāṇini 3.1.68) [prescribes the addition of *śap*]. By the rule "prāghrādinā" (Pāṇini 7.3.78), *piba* and other substitutes are applied as appropriate. [The phrase] "there is a prohibition regarding a technical name (*saṃjñā*)" refers to the suffix *śap*, because it is the subject under discussion; [it refers] to that prohibition.
The rule "with *vyāghra* and so forth" (Pāṇini 2.1.56) is the indicative mark (*liṅga*).

138. *anupasargāllimpavindadhāripārivedyaudejicetisātisāhibhyaśca* | (3.1.138) Regarding *ṭhanupasargāt*: by means of a transposition of case endings (*subvyatyaya*), the singular number stands in place of the plural.

"ṭhlimpaḥ, vindaḥ," and so forth. [The roots] "lipa upadāhe" (DhP 1433) and "vidlṛ lābhe" (DhP 1432). The inclusion of the nasal (num) indicates that the augment *num* occurs only in the state of the original root-form (*upadeśāvasthā*). "Dhṛñ dhāraṇe" (DhP 900) is [used here] with the causative suffix *ṇic*.
Regarding the word *pārayaḥ*: the root *pṛ* (with variants *pāra* and *tīra*) meaning "completion of an action" belongs to the *curādi* group (*dhā.pā.* 1911, 1912).

Alternatively, it is derived from the root *pṛ* meaning "protection and filling" (*dhā.pā.* 1489) with the causative suffix *ṇic*. [The root] *vid* [is used] in the senses of consciousness, narration, feeling, and dwelling (*vedanākhyānanivāseṣu*). (*padamañjarī*)

(dhā.pā. 1708), ending in the causative suffix *ṇic* from the *curādi* class; or alternatively, one of the roots beginning with *vid* (such as *jñā*) meaning "to know" etc., ending in the causative suffix *ṇic*; the root *ṭhejṛ* meaning "to tremble" (dhā.pā.
234), ending in the causative suffix *ṇic*; the root *ṭhcitī* meaning "to perceive" (dhā.pā. 39), ending in the causative suffix *ṇic* from the *curādi* class; [the root] *ṣaha*...
The root *marṣ* (Dhātupāṭha 1809) is either causative (*hetumaṇṇic*) or belongs to the *curādigaṇa*.
