[The forms] *limpaḥ* and *vindaḥ* [are derived as follows]: by the rule *tudādibhyaḥ śaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.77), the suffix *śa* is applied; then, by the rule *śe mucādīnām* (7.1.59), the augment *num* is inserted.

"ṭhpralipaḥ, pnāsti-kāśikā}pravidaḥ" means that the suffix *ka* is indeed prescribed by the rule "igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ. Regarding "nau limpeḥ" and so forth, the meaning is that this should be explained as having the sense: "when the word *ni* is an upapada, the suffix *śa* occurs after the root *limp*. As for the explanation, it pertains to what stands in this very context.

Because the particle *ca* (and) has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned, [the suffix] must be applied. This is indicated by the phrase "in the case of *go*, etc. When words such as *go* and others are the upapadas (governing words), the suffix *śa* occurs when a proper name (*saṃjñā*) is intended.

This is an exception to the suffix *aṇ* prescribed after an object (karma). And that [suffix *śa*] is obtained because the particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.
139. *dadāti-dadhātyor vibhāṣā* (3.1.139).

[This is] an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṇa*. It is an exception to what would otherwise be obtained by the rule *śyād-vyadha-* (3.1.141) and so forth. To which, however, does it not apply as an exception? Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the condition "not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasargāt*). [The resulting forms are] *dadaḥ*, *dadhaḥ*. [This is] *śe*.

In the case of *kṛte*, because it belongs to the class beginning with *juhoti*, there is *ślu* substitution; by the rule *ślau* (6.1.10), reduplication occurs, and by the rule *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ* (6.4.112), the vowel *ā* is elided. Regarding *dāyaḥ*: [the suffix] *yuk* is added by the rule *āto yuk ciṇ-kṛtoḥ* (7.3.33). Regarding *pradaḥ*: [the suffix] *ka* is added by the rule *ātaś copasarge* (3.1.136).

Who [is the agent]? But surely, when the suffix *ac* is applied to the roots *dad* (DhP 17, "to give") and *dadh* (DhP 8, "to hold"), the forms *dado* and *dadhaḥ* will result; and when the suffix *ṇa* is applied to *dā* and *dhā*, the forms *dāyaḥ* and *dhāyaḥ* will likewise result. So what is the purpose of this rule? This is not so; for [the forms] with *ac*...

For if [the suffix] *ṭhak* were present, there would be an udātta accent on the final syllable by rule 6.2.157; however, when [the suffix] *śa* is used, only the accent of the negative particle (*nañ*) occurs—as in *adadaḥ* and *adadhaḥ*.

140. *Jvalitikasantebhyo ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.140). Regarding the term *jvaliti*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those whose beginning is *jval*, *u*, etc. The case-ending is not heard because it has been elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk* (7.1.39).

Regarding the rule *ṭhkasantebhyaḥ* ("after [roots] ending in *ka* or *sa*"): it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "those whose end (*anta*) is *kas*" (*kasa-anta*), where the word *anta* signifies proximity. Alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those for whom *kas* is the end" (*kasa-anta*). In this case, the word *anta* signifies either proximity or a limit (*maryādā*). The root *jvala* (in the sense of "to shine") is listed twice in the Dhātupāṭha (at numbers 804 and 831).

Regarding "from those" (*tebhyaḥ*), which refers both to [the group] beginning with *ghaṭa* and to what follows: if this qualification were absent, a doubt might arise as to "from which ones?"—namely, from among the *jvala*-group? Therefore, in order to exclude that [possibility], the *jvala*-group is specified as "those *jvala*-roots which belong to the *ka*-suffix class. Thus, the sub-group (*antaṅgaṇa*) beginning with *ghaṭa* is not excluded.

It occurs. The mention of *kas* is not for the purpose of excluding those [roots] which are recited later than *kasi*, because they are recited as "having *kas* and having *vṛt*" (*kasamadhītya vṛt*). But surely, the inclusion of the *jvalādi* group among the *ghaṭādi* roots is for the sake of the designation *mit*; in that case, even without the mention of *kas* and *ant*, only those ending in *kas* and *ant* [would be affected].

[If you argue: "Since they will be included [by other rules], this qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) is useless," [we reply: that is not so. For if that [qualification] were absent, the recitation of the preceding roots beginning with *jval* would have a dual purpose—the purpose of the *mit* designation and the purpose of the suffixes—whereas for the others, it would serve only the purpose of the suffixes. Therefore, the mention of *kas* [is necessary].
"It must be formulated as an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ac*, because the roots beginning with *jval* are included within the group ending in *pac*.
It must be stated that there is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the *ṇa* of the root *tan*;
that is, when the suffix *ṇa* is to be prescribed, the *ṇa* of the root *tan* must also be established. This establishment, however, occurs later."
Because the particle *ca* has the sense of including what is not explicitly stated, it must be performed.
141. [The suffix *kvip* is applied after the verbal roots] *śyaiṅ*, those ending in long *ā*, *dā*, *dhā*, and so forth, *vyadha*, *sru*, *ava*, *hrī*, *lih*, *śliṣ*, and *śvas*.

(Pāṇini 3.2.141). *Śyaiṅ* means "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 963). By the phrase "those ending in long *ā*," there is the inclusion of *dā* and *dhā* and others. *Vyadha* means "to strike" (Dhātupāṭha 1181); *sru* means "to flow" (Dhātupāṭha 940).

The root preceded by *ā-*; again, that same root preceded by *sam-*. The root *ṭhiṇ* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*) preceded by *ati-*; the root *ṣo* in the sense of "concluding an action" (*antakarmaṇi*) preceded by *ava-*; the root *hṛñ* in the sense of "taking away" (*haraṇe*) preceded by *ava-*; the root *liha* in the sense of "tasting" (*āsvādane*); [and] *śliṣ*...
Regarding the roots *āliṅg* (DhP 1186) and *śvas* (DhP 1069):

here, from those that are listed with prefixes (*sopasarga*), the suffix occurs only after those with prefixes; however, from the remaining roots, it occurs both after those with prefixes and those without prefixes. Thus, the restriction "provided it is not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasargāt*) is no longer applicable.

"Furthermore, because of the mention of 'not being preceded by a prefix' (anupasarga) later on, and because of the word 'optionally' (vibhāṣā),"—this connects with the phrase "it is withdrawn" (nivṛttam). For the mention of "optionally" is connected with "not being preceded by a prefix"; therefore, when that [mention of the prefix] is withdrawn, its [mention of the optionality] is also withdrawn. "For the purpose of subverting the sublater"—referring to the rule *ātaścopasarge* (Pāṇini 3.1.136).

Because of this rule (Pāṇini 3.1.136), since it is prescribed as a specific exception (*viśeṣavidhi*), the suffix *ka* sublates the suffix *ṇa* which is prescribed as a general rule (*sāmānyavidhi*). Therefore, the inclusion of the root *ava-śya-* must be understood as having the purpose of sublating that [general rule]. Alternatively, its mention is for the sake of restricting the application of the prefix (*upasarga*).
It should apply only after the prefix *ava*, as in "avaśyāyaḥ," by virtue of [Pāṇini 7.3.33] *āto yuk ciṇ-kṛtoḥ*.

142. *dunyor anupasarge* (3.1.142). In the word *dunyoḥ*, the genitive case is used by way of a metrical substitution (*subvyatyaya*) for the ablative sense. Similarly, in *anupasarge*, the locative case is used for the ablative sense. For this very reason, he says: "from the roots *du* and *nī* when they are without a prefix (*anupasarga*)."
Regarding "dāvaḥ": [it is derived from] "ḍu dāp śodhane" (DhP 1256). Regarding "nayaḥ":

[it is derived from] "ṇīñ prāpaṇe" (DhP 901). In the forms "pradavaḥ" and "praṇayaḥ," the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule beginning with "pacādyac," and the augment *ṇatva* is applied by the rule "upasargādasamāse 'pi" (Pāṇini 8.4.14).
The substitution of *ṇ* [occurs].
143. *vibhāṣā grahaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.143). [The commentary states:
"And this is an *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (a restricted option). This is clarified by the rule beginning with *jalacare*.

Regarding the statement "it should be stated that [the suffix] also follows the root *bhū*": this must be explained as meaning that the suffix *ṇa* optionally (*vibhāṣā*) occurs after the root *bhū*. This explanation, however, should be carried out by means of splitting the rule (*yogavibhāga*), namely by treating "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) as a separate rule.

[The commentary says: *ṭhgehe kartari* ("when 'geha' [is used] in the sense of the agent"). By this, he shows that *gehe* is an attribute (*upādhi*) of the agent, which is the meaning of the suffix, and not a governing word (*upapada*). And this [is the case] in *aśvapati* and so forth.

It is understood from the recitation of the word *gṛhapati* [in the rule] that [the suffix applies] "because of its location in them," as in the case of the word *dārāḥ*. The connection is with the word *geham*, which is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*). By this, he indicates that the suffix occurs even when *geha* is used in a figurative sense. And this is obtained through the simultaneous utterance (*tantra*) of the word *geha* twice. [The example is] *gṛham*.
There is vocalization (samprasāraṇa) for [the roots] beginning with *grah* (Pāṇini 6.1.16).

145. *śilpini ṣvun* (3.1.145). [The commentary states: "*ṭh-śilpini kartari*" ("the suffix *ṭhac* occurs when the agent is a craftsman"). By showing that [the word *śilpin*] functions as a qualifier (*upādhi*) as before, it excludes its status as a subordinate term (*upapada*). And this is illustrated by the example: "He gives the garment of a washerman."

This is obtained from the usage of the author of the Bhāṣya; specifically, from the enumeration [of roots] beginning with *nṛt*, *khan*, and *rañj*. And this is further obtained because the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is understood as a *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā* (a restricted option).

Regarding the rule "ṭhrañjeranunāsikalopaśca" (Pāṇini 6.4.24), this too is understood from that very usage of the Bhāṣyakāra. Furthermore, the fact that he teaches the *mit* designation for the root *rañj* in the rule "janījṛṣknasurañjo'mantāśca" (Dhātupāṭha 819 onwards) indicates the following:
Even when there is no suffix marked with *k* (*akṅti*), the elision of the nasal of the root *rañj* occurs; for this is precisely the purpose of its being designated as *mit*:

so that the shortening prescribed by "the short vowel of *mit*-roots" (Pāṇini 6.4.92) may take place. And if this elision of the nasal did not exist, there would be no *vṛddhi*; and if there were no *vṛddhi*, [the desired form would not be achieved].

The penultimate vowel becomes short. Therefore, just as the elision of the nasal occurs for the root *rañj* when followed by the suffix *ṇic*, so too does it occur when followed by the suffix *ṣvan*. Because of this specific enumeration, it does not occur in forms such as *hvātā* and *hvāyaka*.
The addition of the marker *n* to *ṣvan* is for the purpose of making the first syllable udātta; the letter *ṣ* is for the purpose of [triggering] the suffix *ṅīṣ*.

Regarding the term *ṭhgaḥ*: this is a reference to the root *gai śabde* (DhP 917), after having applied the elision of the vowel *ā* by means of Pāṇini 6.4.140 (*āto dhātoḥ*). For this very reason, he says: "of *gāyati*. But [one might object]: [The objection continues: "But surely..."

Should the root *gāṅ* "to go" (DhP 950) also be included under the rule "in the case of taking villages and so forth, there is no distinction" (Vārttika on Pāṇini 3.1.14)? This is not so; because in the word *gāthaka*, the agency of the artisan is expressed specifically through the meaning of "singing," by means of the suffix *thakan*.
It is understood [from this rule], but not in the case of the *gārtha* [suffixes]. The letter *n* in *thakan* is for the purpose of making the first syllable acute (*ādyaudāta*).

147. *ṇyuṭ* also [is applied after verbal roots ending in long *ā*]. (Pāṇini 3.1.147). [The example] "gāyanaḥ" (singer): the augment *yuk* is applied by [the rule] *āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ* (7.3.33). "gāyanī": because it has the marker *ṭ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. [Vārttika: "The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows. That is, for the subsequent [rules].

The inclusion of the letter *ca* is so that only *ṇyuṭ* may be carried over [from the previous rule], and not *thakan*; for if there were a single compound rule such as "ṭhgo ṇyuṭ-thakanau," then *thakan* would also be drawn along [into the present rule].

148. *Haś* [is substituted] for the roots *vrīh* and *kāla*. (Pāṇini 3.1.148) Regarding "after the root *hā*" (*jahāteḥ*): this refers to *ohāk* "to abandon" (Dhātupāṭha 1090). Regarding "and after *jihāti*" (*jihāteśca*):
this refers to *ohāṅ* "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1089). It is intended that this [latter root] be understood here. Of these two...

The letter *k* is specified after the root *jahāti* precisely for the purpose of including it in the general category. For if that [letter *k*] were not present, then this mention of a single *anubandha* would apply only to the root *jahāti* with two *anubandhas*, and not to the root *jahāti* with two *anubandhas* [in other contexts]. However, when the letter *k* is present, [it serves its intended function].

Because both [the rice and the time] possess a continuous connection [to the action], their inclusion as general [factors] is justified by the rule "in the case of *vrīhi*, [a word denoting] time, and the agent" (*vrīhau kāle ca kartari*). By this, he shows that rice and time are qualifiers of the meaning of the suffix; however, he excludes their status as *upapada* (governed words). And this is [the basis for the application of] the rule "also after those ending in *dāman* and *hāyana*" (*dāmahāyanāntācca*, Pāṇini 4.1.27).

This is understood from the grammatical rule: "The term *hāyanāḥ* [is formed] by the application of the augment *yuk* according to Pāṇini 7.3.33 (*āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ*). By the phrase 'because they abandon water,' he shows the ground for the application of the word *hāyana* to rice. [And by the phrase] 'it abandons states of being,' [he shows the etymological derivation]."
"He stands firm regarding all beings"—by this [formula] also, for one year.

149. *pru-sṛ-lvaḥ* with the suffix *vun* when there is frequent repetition (*samabhihāra*). The mention of *pru-sṛ-lvaḥ* is made by applying reduplication (*samabhihāra*). The augment *num* has not been applied even though [the base] is neuter, because the teaching regarding augments is not universally obligatory. "With the suffix *vun* when there is frequent repetition."

Thus [it is said]. Elsewhere, the word *samabhihāra* has meanings such as "repetition" (*paunaḥpunya*) and so forth; one might therefore have the misconception that here too it has that very same meaning. To refute that, he says:
"By the mention of *samabhihāra*" and so on. The meaning is that it is "indicated" (*lakṣyate*), which is to say, "shown."
And this [meaning] is obtained because verbal roots have multiple meanings; others say it is due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *śilpinī*.

A *śilpī* is one who performs well. By stating "the rule for *vun* applies to one who performs well," he demonstrates the result of taking "performing well" as a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*). This is shown by the passage beginning with "even once," and so forth.
This is a clarification of what was stated immediately before.

150. *āśiṣi ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.150). [The commentary says: "When a benediction (*āśis*) is implied," not when it is explicitly expressed. This is because, according to the rule *kartari kṛt* (3.4.67), the agent alone is the meaning expressed by the suffix. [The commentary continues: "From the root alone."

Because the commonality of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is intended to be expressed, because [the specific roots] *pru*, *sṛ*, and *vā* have been set aside, and because no other specific root is relied upon here, it relies on the verbal root in its general sense alone, and not from any particularity whatsoever— as in "may he live" (*jīvatāt*) and "may he rejoice" (*nandatāt*). This is in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*).

By the use of the imperative (*loṭ*), he shows that Jīvaka and Nandā have the same meaning [as the benediction]. He asks, "What, then, is this so-called *āśis* (benediction)? and says: "A benediction is a specific kind of prayer (*prārthanā*).
A prayer for a desired object not yet attained is a benediction. And that [benediction] here—

"Having action as its object": this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has action (*kriyā*) as its object (*viṣaya*). And this meaning is understood from the inclusion of the term *dhātu* (root), because a root denotes action. [The phrase] "of this action" refers to the agent of the action of living and the action of rejoicing.
Thus it is wished: "May your life and your joy increase."
Thus ends the third chapter of the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who was a disciple of the Bodhisattvas.
First Pāda.
Now begins the third chapter.
Second Pāda.
1. *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1). In the rule *karmaṇi*, this is not a reference to the actual form [of the word]; rather, it is governed by the rule *aśabdasaṃjñā* (Pāṇini 1.1.68).

Because of the prohibition. Furthermore, if the essential form (*svarūpa*) itself were understood in the sections concerning *karma*, then the formulation of technical names (*saṃjñā*) would be purposeless; nor is there a grasping of the action (*kriyā*), for if that were grasped, the reference "when intended for the agent" (*kartrabhiprāye*, Pāṇini 1.4.72) would not be tenable, since [the term] refers to the object of the action (*kriyākarmaṇaḥ*).

A suffix must occur when a word expressive of an action (*kriyāvac*) is present as a subordinate element (*upapada*); however, in this case, there is no such subordinate element expressive of an action. Therefore, "object" (*karman*) is understood here according to the rule *kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma* (Pāṇini 1.4.49). To demonstrate its divisions, he says: "threefold," and so forth.

Among these, that which is *nirvartya* (to be produced) is that which arises while being non-existent; for example, "he makes a pot" or "he builds a city. For since the pot and so forth arise while previously non-existent, it is the *nirvartya* object (*karman*). That which is *vikārya* (to be modified) is that of which some modification is prescribed while it already exists; for example, a stalk...

[Examples such as] "he reaps" (lunāti) and "he reaps the city" (nagaraṃ lunāti): because a modification is produced through the reaping of something already existent, such as stalks of grain, it is called the "object as modification" (vikārya-karman). As for the "object to be reached" (prāpya)—neither is there the production of what was non-existent, nor is there the imposition of a modification upon what was already existent; rather, only the mere connection with the action is perceived.

For example: "He studies the Veda" (*vedam adhīte*) and "He practices the *carccā*. Here, by means of the act of studying and so forth, only a relationship with the Veda and the like is perceived; there is no production of something previously non-existent, nor is there a transformation consisting of a change in the characteristics of something already existent. Thus, this is an object to be attained (*prāpya-karma*). Regarding the phrase "in all cases" (*sarvatra*), and so forth:

Because no specific distinction is made regarding the type of suffix. Why would [the rule] "when a verbal root has a word denoting an object as its upapada" not apply? It is because it would be superseded by the rule "kṛt suffixes [denote] the agent" (Pāṇini 3.4.67).
[The sūtra begins with] "śīli-kāmi... etc. The verbal root *śīl* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha under the curādigaṇa in the sense of "to hold firmly."

The root *śīl* in the sense of "concentration" (*samādhi*) is listed in the *Dhātupāṭha* under the *bhvādi* class; *śīl* (DhP 1878) is a *curādi* root with the suffix *ṇic*. The root *kam* in the sense of "desire" (*kānti*) is *kami* with the suffix *ṇiṅ*.
The root *bhakṣ* in the sense of "eating" (*adana*) is a *curādi* root with the suffix *ṇic*. [The root] *car*...

The root *gati* (DhP 5.59) is preceded by the prefix *āṅ*. The letter *i* is for the purpose of indicating the verbal root (*dhātunirdeśārtha*). Since the suffix *aṇ* would otherwise apply to these roots, it must be stated—or rather, explained—that *ṇa* applies instead. In this regard, the explanation is as follows:
by the logic of the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*), [the rule] from *jvalitikasantebhyo ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.140) [is brought forward].
The term *vibhāṣā* is carried over from "vibhāṣā grahaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.143);
thus, both suffixes, *ṇa* and *ṇic*, are prescribed here when the object (*karman*) is the upapada.

Because of the continued application of the term *vibhāṣā* in this context, and because it is understood as a restricted option (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*), the suffix *ṇa* is applied after roots such as *śīla*.
[The suffix] *aṇ* shall apply [to the remaining cases], while *aṇ* alone applies to the rest. However, there is a distinction between these two regarding the feminine gender:

for when *aṇ* is applied, the suffix *ṅīp* occurs, whereas when *ṇa* is applied, the suffix *ṭāp* occurs. The letter *ṇ* in *ṇa* is for the purpose of causing *vṛddhi* by the rule "ṭhaco ñṇiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.115). Furthermore, it serves to ensure that the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) is maintained.

Thus: regarding the rule *gatikārakopapadānāṃ kṛd* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), which prescribes that the final member (*uttarapada*) retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*), it must be stated—or rather, explained—that the initial member (*pūrvapada*) also retains its original accent. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: "In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, [the initial member retains its accent] when preceded by words such as *tulya*."

In the rule *tulyārthaiḥ* (6.2.2), a *yogavibhāga* (separation of the rule) should be made by adding the word *tatpuruṣe*. By this, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member will also apply to words such as *māṃsaśīla*. The word *māṃsa* is udātta on its final syllable.

While the rule *ṭhvṛtṛvadihanikamikaṣiyumucibhyaḥ saḥ* (Daiva 9.21) is being carried over, the rule *manerdīrghaśca* (Daiva 9.23) applies; because it ends with the suffix *sa*, it is accented by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). Thus, the word *kalyāṇa* has its acute accent on the middle syllable (*madhyodātta*), according to the rule *laghāvante*.

By the rule "dvayośca bahvaṣo guruḥ" (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.42). Its meaning is as follows: when a light syllable (*laghu*) follows at the end, or when two light syllables follow at the end, that which is the heavy syllable (*guru*) of the word *bahvac* becomes acute (*udātta*). The term "bahvaṣ" means "having many vowels" (*bahvac*). But [one might object]:...

If one were to form *māṃsaśīla* and so forth by adding the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an object (*karman*) to words such as *śīla*, and then forming a *bahuvrīhi* compound with that [derivative], the desired forms would indeed be established. Why, then, is the rule for *ṇa* prescribed? This is not the case; because when a *bahuvrīhi* is present—as in *bahubhakṣa*—the rule "after *bahu*, like *nañ*, when the final member denotes abundance" (Pāṇini 6.2.175) applies.
Thus, there would be udātta accent on the final syllable of the subsequent member [of the compound]. Furthermore, the suffix *ṇa* must necessarily be stated for the purpose of overriding *aṇ*;
otherwise, when the sentence "he desires meat" (*māṃsaṃ kāmayate*) occurs, *aṇ* would also apply.

Regarding the rule *ṭhīkṣikṣamibhyāṃ ca*: the meaning is that the suffix *ṇa* occurs after these two roots—*īkṣa* (meaning "to see," DhP 610) and *kṣam* (meaning "to endure," DhP 1206)—and this must be explained. The explanation, however, should be performed in the same manner as before.

2. *Hvāvāmaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.2). [The roots] *hveñ* "in the sense of rivalry" and *veñ* "in the sense of weaving" [are included]. Now, why is there not an inclusion of the root *vā* "in the senses of motion and scenting" (Dhātupāṭha 1050)?

Because it is intransitive (*akarmaka*). And here, [the rule] *karmaṇi* (P. 3.2.47) continues to apply. Regarding the statement *māṅ māne*: this is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the root *mā* that possesses the indicatory letter *ṅ*. It is also desired that there be the inclusion of *meṅ praṇidāne* (DhP. 961); for "in the case of the mention of *gā*, *mā*, and so on, there is no distinction."

Because of the statement [in the *Vyāḍipāṭha*]: "(vyā.pa.124). Now, if there is no distinction regarding the inclusion of roots beginning with *gā* and *mā*, then for the two roots *mīñ* "in the sense of injury" (DhP 1476) and *ḍumiñ* "in the sense of throwing" (DhP 1250), once the substitution of *ā* has been applied in the domain of *ej*-roots, would not the form *meti* be produced?
The suffix *aṇ* indeed occurs after these two, as established by the preceding rule. In the example "svargahvāyaḥ," the augment *yuk* is applied according to Pāṇini 7.3.33:
*āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ*.

3. *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ* | (Pāṇini 3.2.3) Regarding the term *anupasarge*: although a locative case (*saptamī*) is used here despite the fact that a fifth case (*pañcamī*) would have been expected by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*), this is an adjective qualifying the verbal root (*dhātu*). For this very reason, he says: "after roots ending in the vowel *ā*, provided they are not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*)."
And [the form] "godaḥ": here, as before, there is the elision of the letter *l*. [The form] "pārṣṇim": [this is derived from] the root *traiṅ* in the sense of "protecting" (Dhātupāṭha 965).
4. *supi sthaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.4).
Because of the mention of *supi*, [the term] *karmaṇi* is not connected [to this rule], and furthermore, because the root *sthā-* is intransitive (*akarmaka*).

In examples such as *samasthaḥ*, when a word ending in the seventh case (*saptamyanta*) is the *upapada*, [the suffix *ka* is applied] by the rule beginning with *atra*. *Supi* is one [separate rule].

Regarding the rule *yogaḥ*, the word *ataḥ* is understood to carry over from the preceding context. By the rule *supi* and so forth, he explains the meaning of this *yoga*. "Then [the suffix] *tha* occurs after that" refers to the second *yoga*. The phrase *sthaśca supi* is its detailed explanation (*vivaraṇam*).

"‘What [is the purpose]? and so forth. This is a question from one who considers [the rule] already established by the preceding [sūtra]. [The purpose is stated: ‘So that it may apply even in the sense of an abstract state (bhāva). By the very force of its commencement, it will certainly not apply in the sense of the agent (kartṛ). Nor is any other meaning specified; in such cases, suffixes whose meaning is not specified [apply] in their own inherent sense (svārtha)."

According to the rule *bhavanti* (Puṣpabhūti-pāṭha 90), it would simply be the abstract state (*bhāva*). For that alone is the inherent meaning (*svārtha*) of verbal roots. Regarding the forms *pākhūtthaḥ* (as in the *Kāśikā*) and *ākhūttham*, the vowel substitution of the preceding sound (*pūrvasavarṇa*) occurs by the rule *udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ pūrvasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.61).

5. *tundaśokayoḥ parimṛjāpanudoḥ* | (3.2.5) Regarding the phrase *parimṛjāpanudoḥ*: the genitive case is used by way of a transposition (*subvyatyaya*) in the sense of the ablative. [The root] *mṛj* (meaning "to clean") with the prefix *pari-* is used; [the root] *nud* (meaning "to impel") is used with the prefix *apa-*. (Dhātupāṭha 1066 and 1426).
The prefix *apa-* [is used here]. Regarding the phrase "of *ālasya*" and so forth: this is a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārthopādhi*). *Ālasyam* means simply *alasa* (lazy).

The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*), according to the rule for words beginning with *cāturvarṇya*. *Āharati* means "he brings"; thus, *āharaṇaḥ* is formed with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), according to Pāṇini 3.3.113 (*kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*). *Sukhāharaṇaḥ* means "one who brings happiness."

The meaning is that this should be explained as having the sense: "Who becomes [the agent] in the bringing about of pleasure by one who causes laziness, and not otherwise? In this regard, the following is the explanation: here too, as before, the mention of the optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) continues, and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).

Thus, between the two agents—laziness (*ālasya*) and the bringing of pleasure (*sukhāharaṇa*)—the suffix *aṇ* occurs only in the latter and not elsewhere. As for the other case, "tundaparimārja," it is formed with *aṇ* in the sense of non-laziness (*anālasya*). [In this case] there is the *vṛddhi* strengthening by Pāṇini 7.2.114. Regarding "śokāpanodaḥ," it refers to one who [removes sorrow] through the instruction of its opposite.
It merely removes [distress], but does not produce happiness; rather, it becomes a refuge in this very state.
Regarding the phrase "in the section on *ṭhak*" and so forth: the fourth case (*caturthī*) is used in the sense of those [categories] beginning with *mūlavibhuja*, etc.;
the word "etc. (*ādi*) expresses a class or type. For the sake of the meaning of *mūlavibhuja* and so forth, words such as *mūlavibhuja* are correct, just as [in the following examples].
The meaning is that the suffix *ka* must be introduced and established for this very purpose.

In this regard, the following is the demonstration: from the rule *hvāvāmaśca* (3.2.2), the particle *ca* ("and") is carried over (*anuvartate*) into the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ* (3.2.3). That *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccayārtha*); therefore—

The suffix *ka* will occur after words such as *mūlavibhuja*. [For example: *mūlaṃ vibhujati* ("it spreads its roots"). [The root] *bhuja* [is listed] in the Dhātupāṭha (1417) with the meaning "to bend. [Another example: *nakhamucāni* ("those which release the nails"). [The root] *muclṛ* [is listed] in the Dhātupāṭha (1430) with the meaning "to release. [And: *kākagṛhāstilāḥ* ("sesame seeds gathered by crows").

Thus: from the root *guhū* "to conceal" (DhP 896), [the word] *kāka-guha* is formed meaning "those who are to be concealed from crows. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffixes *tavya* and others; the suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). [The word] *kumuda* is formed according to the rule "it rejoices in the *ku*" (*kau modate kumudam*);
this is an exception to the suffix *tṛc* and others.
6. *pra* before *dājñaḥ*. (3.2.6) [The commentary states:

"This rule is commenced for the sake of [roots] with prefixes (*sopasarga*), because [the form] is already established by [Pāṇini 3.2.3], *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*, which applies to roots without prefixes (*anupasarga*). [The word] *dadāteḥ* refers to those [roots] whose form is *dā*."

This is an illustration of the verbal roots (*dhātu*); it is intended to include other roots as well ending in *dā*, according to the statement: "In the case of rules concerning the taking of *gā*, *mā*, and *ā*, there is no distinction" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 124). Regarding the phrase "preceded by *pra*": the meaning is "connected with the prefix *pra*. In the sūtra, the term *pra* [is used].

Thus, by means of a substitution of case endings (*sub-vyatyaya*), the locative case is to be understood in the sense of the instrumental; "one who knows the path" (*pathiprajñaḥ*) means one who thoroughly knows the way.

7. *sami khyaḥ* | (Pāṇini 3.2.7) Regarding the example *gāṃ sañcaṣṭe*: by means of this specific rule, there is the inclusion of the substitute *khyāñ* [prescribed] by *cakṣiṅḥ khyāñ* (2.4.54), and not of the root *khyā* in the sense of "speaking" (*prakathane*) found at Dhātupāṭha 1060.
He demonstrates this; and this is understood because the use of the root *khyāti* preceded by the prefix *sam-* is impossible.

8. *gāpoṣṭak* (Pāṇini 3.2.8). According to the maxim *ṭhlugvikaraṇālugvikaraṇayor lukvikaraṇasyaiva grahaṇam* (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 50), "the form with the elided suffix (*luk*) is alone to be understood when there is a conflict between one with an elided suffix and one without"; thus, by the term *pā*, the root meaning "to drink" is intended, not the one meaning "to protect. Even though...

Although it is stated that "there is no distinction in the case of taking up [the roots] beginning with *gā*" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 124), nevertheless, due to its association (*sāhacarya*) with *pibati*, the term *gā* is understood here as the root with the *aluk*-suffix (*gāyati*), and not the root meaning "to go. Thus he says: "of *gāyati* and *pibati*. The *k* in *ṭak* is for the sake of making it *kit*.

The purpose [of the suffix] is elision (*lopārtha*). The addition of the marker *ṭ* is for the sake of [triggering] the feminine suffix *ṅīp*; it is not for the sake of [the rule] "A *ṭ*-marked or *k*-marked element is placed at the beginning or end [of what it qualifies]" (Pāṇini 1.1.46). Why is this so? Because the beginning and the end are parts (*avayava*) [of a whole], and it is not logical for a suffix (*pratyaya*) to be a part, according to the statement "And [a suffix] follows" (Pāṇini 3.1.2). But surely...

Is it intended that this genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in *gāpoḥ* indicates the suffix *ṭak* and its status as a member [of the root]? This is not the case; rather, this genitive has the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe*), or it serves to qualify the agent—meaning "when *gā* and *pā* are the agents.
And this is appropriate, for in this way the requirement of being followed by a suffix (*pratyayaparatva*) is not sublated. Furthermore, regarding the initial position...
Indeed, the inclusion of the marker *ṭ* would be purposeless.

He states "of *surā* and *śīdhu*" (*surāśīdhvoḥ*) and so forth in order to exclude the final vowel of the upapada of the root *pibati*. It has already been established that the root *pibati* is what is intended here, and not the root *pāti*. In this context...

The term "vibhāṣā" (optionally) from rule 3.1.143 is understood here, but it is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*); therefore, [the suffix] will apply when *surā* and *śīdhu* are the accompanying words (*upapada*), and not otherwise. The example "kṣīrapā" (milk-drinker) is given as a feminine illustration in order to demonstrate that there is a specific rule regarding the feminine gender.

Regarding the phrase "bahulam" and so forth: the meaning is that this form [of the rule] should be explained as signifying that the suffix *ṭak* is applied diversely (*bahulam*) to the root *pibati* in the Vedic language (*chandas*). The explanation, however, must be made by relying on the fact that the very same term *vibhāṣā*, which is understood as being carried over from the previous rule, functions as a restricted option (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*). The result of this, however, is [the formation of the word] *surāpā*.
The suffix *ka* occurs in the sense of "on the side of" (*pakṣe*).

9. *harater-anudyamane-ac* (Pāṇini 3.2.9). "Lifting up (*udyamana*) means raising upwards," it is said. This means bringing an object situated below to a higher position. In the example *aṃśaharaḥ*, the meaning is "one who takes a share for oneself," not one who raises it upward.
In the section beginning with "ṭhac-prakaraṇe," the printed reading is "prātipadika-grahaṇe liṅga-viśiṣṭasya.
According to the maxim "liṅga-viśiṣṭasyāpi grahaṇam" (Vārttika 29),
since the inclusion of *ghaṭī* would be established by the mention of *ghaṭa* alone, the specific mention of *ghaṭī* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of this Paribhāṣā.
This is for the purpose of making known its impermanence. Its utility, however, will be explained under the rule *dityadityādityapatyuttarapadāṇṇyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.85).
The word *upasaṃkhyāna* means "an additional statement" (*pratipādana*). In this regard, the following is that additional statement:

In the subsequent sūtra, the word *ca* (and) has the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned; by this, the suffix *ap* will occur after the root *grah* when words such as *śakti* are present as upapadas.

Regarding the phrase "in the sūtra" and so forth: the meaning of *dhāri* is the object to be supported (*dhāryartha*). From the root *grah* used in that sense [of supporting], [the suffix *ap* is applied].
And when *sūtra* is the upapada, an addition (*upasaṃkhyānam*)—that is, a specific rule (*pratipādanam*)—must be made.
That rule is as follows: "In the case of *sūtragrāha*, however, it is otherwise. When one merely takes up the thread (*sūtram*) but does not wear it, the suffix *aṇ* alone occurs.

10. *vayasi ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.10). This rule is commenced for the purpose of excluding the sense of "lifting up" (*udyamana*). For if "lifting up" were not intended, the formation would already be established by the preceding rule. The example *asthiharaḥ* means one who exists at an age capable of lifting a bone.

11. *āiṅ tācchīlye* | (3.2.11) The term "not lifting" (*anudyamana*) is excluded. Therefore, by virtue of there being no distinction, it is understood that this rule applies even in the case of "lifting. But surely, in the case of "not lifting," it is already established by the preceding rule; for *tṛn* is indeed subsequent [to the previous rule].

[Objection: Does [the suffix] *ac* not also occur because of the rule for optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhāna*)? [Reply: This is not so; for he will state this: "In the case of suffixes expressing habitual disposition (*tācchīlika*), suffixes such as *tṛc* do not occur by way of optional forms.
"Habitual disposition" (*tācchīlya*) means "having that as one's nature" (*tatsvabhāvatā*). That, moreover, is a mental quality (*mānaso dharmaḥ*).
Activity is inferred from its independence from a result; by the phrase "one who gathers flowers" and so forth, he illustrates habitual disposition (*tācchīlya*).
12. *arhaḥ* | (3.2.12) [The root text reads:
*striyāṃ viśeṣaḥ*. "There is a distinction in the feminine gender. For if the suffix *aṇ* occurs, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied;
but if the suffix *ac* occurs, the suffix *ṭāp* is applied.

13. *rami-japyoḥ stambakarṇayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.13). Regarding the rule "because *japi* has sound as its object" (*japeḥ śabdakarmakatvāt*), one says "he mutters the *gāyatrī*" (*gāyatrīṃ japati*) or "he mutters a section of the Veda" (*anuvākaṃ japati*); for in these instances, only the usage where sound is the object is observed. [The opponent objects: "An object [in the sense of the action] is not possible."

The intention is that the ear (*karṇa*) does not have sound as its essence. The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*). Precisely because the ear cannot be the object (*karman*) [of the action], the term "in a word ending in a case-suffix" (*supi*) is connected here, and not the term "in the objective case" (*karmaṇi*).

Regarding the rule "hastisūcakayoḥ" and so forth: the mention of "hastin" (elephant) and "sūcaka" (spy/indicator) serves as a qualifier specifically for the agent who is the meaning of the suffix. The meaning is that this prescription of the suffix *ac*—found in the rule "stambakarṇayo ramijapoḥ"—must be explained as having the sense that it applies when the agents are an elephant or a spy.
The explanation, however, should be made by relying on the fact that the term *vibhāṣā*, which is understood from the previous rule,

applies here as a *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā* (restricted option). Thus we have "stamberamaḥ" and "karṇejapaḥ," where there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending according to the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.3.14).
"Sūcakaḥ" means a slanderer.
14. [The suffix *ka* is added] after the root √*śam*, when a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is to be expressed.

(Pāṇini 3.2.14) Regarding the phrase "after any root whatsoever" (*dhātumātrāt*): by using the expression "any root whatsoever," he indicates that the rule applies even in cases where it would otherwise be superseded by an exception (*apavāda*).
For it occurs after any root whatsoever, provided that it sets aside the exception.

This also applies to the domain of that [root]. And this meaning is obtained through the inclusion of the term *dhātu* (root). By demonstrating the purpose of including the term *dhātu* in the rule "śami saṃjñāyām" and so forth, he clarifies the meaning expressed by the root: "śami saṃjñāyām."

This is an elliptical reference to the sūtra; the meaning is "in this sūtra, namely *śami dhātoḥ saṃjñāyām*. Regarding the phrase "in the sense of cause, etc.," the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes the senses of habitual disposition (*tācchīlya*) and compliance (*ānulomya*). [The rule applies] when *śam* is the upapada of the root *kṛ* in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*).

When *hetu* and so forth are intended [as upapadas], the suffix *ṭa* would apply by the rule *ṭhṛño hetutācchīlyānulomyeṣu* (Pāṇini 3.2.20); therefore, the mention of the word *dhātu* is for the purpose of setting aside that [suffix]. As for the rule *śami dhātoḥ*, its scope is restricted to verbal roots other than *kṛ* that can occur with *śam* as an upapada.

Regarding the term *śaṃvada*: this is the scope of rule 3.2.20, *kṛño hetutācchīlyānulomye*, which applies when the root *kṛ* has another word as its upapada—for example, one who performs a *śrāddha* is called a *śrāddhakara*.
However, when the word *śam* is the upapada of the root *kṛ*, both rules apply simultaneously in the case of a proper name (*saṃjñā*), such as *śaṅkara*.

Regarding the word *śakunikā*: since she possesses that nature (*tacchīlā*), she is designated by that name (*tatsaṃjñā*). In this case, because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], the suffix *ṭa* would apply; however, due to the repeated mention of "root" (*dhātu*), the suffix *ṭa*, which is prescribed after a mere root, is superseded, and thus only *añ* occurs.

15. *Adhikaraṇe śeteḥ* (3.2.15). [The word] *supi* is connected [to this rule], because the root *śī* (to lie down) is intransitive. Since it is intransitive, the locative case (*adhikaraṇa*) is possible; therefore, *supi* is connected here, and not the accusative (*karman*).
Regarding the statement "an addition [should be made] for *pārśva* and so forth," this introduction is intended to show that the term is not used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

It demonstrates that *pārśvābhyām* is an accompanying word (*upapada*) ending in the third case; likewise, in the examples *uraḥśayaḥ* and *pṛṣṭhaśayaḥ*, the accompanying words should also be understood as ending in the third case.

Regarding the term *digdhasahaśayaḥ*: the compound is formed by the rule *tṛtīyā* (Pāṇini 2.1.30), which allows for a split in the application of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). First, there is a compound with the word *saha*;
subsequently, before the suffix arises, there is a secondary compound (*upapadasamāsa*) with *digdha*.
Regarding the passage beginning with *girau*: when *giri* is the upapada, the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *śī* in the Vedic domain (*chandas*).

Thus we have *giriśaḥ*. Because the suffix is marked with *ḍ*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*ṭilopa*). All of this is established by the word *bahulam* in the rule *vyatyayo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.1.85).
16. *careṣṭaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.16). [The commentary states:
"The creation of a separate suffix *ṭha* is for the sake of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*; because it is marked with *ṭi*, the suffix *ṅīp* occurs."

17. And [the suffix *ṭhan* is applied] after *bhikṣā*, *sena*, and *ādāya*. (Pāṇini 3.2.17) "This rule is commenced for the sake of the non-locative sense (*anadhikaraṇārtha*)," it is said. For in the locative sense, it would already be established by the preceding rule. Thus: one who moves among alms is a *bhikṣācaraḥ*; one who moves through an army is a *senācaraḥ*. Regarding the word *ādāya*: [it means] "having taken."

This is an exception (*lyabantametat*). In the term *ādāyacaraḥ* (one who moves after taking), the suffix is applied when only the prior time (*pūrvākāla*) is intended to be expressed, because the object to be taken (*ādātavyakarma*) is not intended to be expressed.
That is to say, it means "one who moves after having performed the act of taking. By this [rule],...

This objection—that because there is a lack of syntactic capacity (*asāmarthya*) due to being dependent on something else, the suffix would not be established—is not to be raised. Even if it depends upon an object (*karman*), there is still no fault;
by the force of the explicit statement (*vacana-sāmarthya*), the suffix occurs even when there is a lack of syntactic capacity.
18. *pura-agrata-agreṣu sarteḥ* (3.2.18).
The word *puraḥ* is derived with the suffix *asi* by the rule *pūrvādharāvarāṇāmasi puradhavaścaiṣām* (5.3.39). The word *agrataḥ* is also [derived] in the section on the suffix *tasi*.
The suffix *tas* is added [to *agra*] by the Vārttika "An addition for words beginning with *ādi*" (Vā. 634). Thus, we have *agre*.

The substitution of the long vowel *ai* (*ekāra*) for the final syllable of the word *agra* is prescribed so that the form *agresara* may be obtained. Now, one might object: "Is this not already established even without the elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending? True; when it is established, then...

The suffix [is applied] when a word ending in the locative case (saptamī) is the *upapada*. When it is "he moves ahead" (*yadāgraḥ sarati*) or "he moves by means of the front" (*agreṇa vā sarati*), it would not be established because [the word] does not end in the locative; for that purpose, the form ending in /e/ (*agrai*) is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*).

19. *pūrve kartari* (3.2.19). [The commentary states: "When the word *pūrva* is used as an attendant noun (*upapada*) expressing the agent (*kartṛ*), the suffix is applied. By this, the word *kartari* qualifies the attendant noun, not the agent; thus, the meaning of the suffix is indicated.
Thus he demonstrates this; for that [word "pūrva"] is already indicated by the rule *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67).

The intention is that its mention here is inappropriate. Now, one might object that there is indeed a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*) in the case of *pūrvaḥ sarati*, for instance; to explain: this word *pūrva* expresses a state of relative position (*vyavasthā*).

Or [the word *pūrva*] may denote a part (*avayava*). In the former case, a limit (*avadhi*) must be expected—[as in] "this is prior to that. In the other case, however, the referent is a whole (*avayavin*), as in "the front part of the body" (*pūrvaṃ kāyasya*). Since both cases involve dependence [on another term], would there not be a failure of syntactic competency (*asāmarthya*) and consequently no formation of the compound? This is not so.
This is not a fault; for the word "prior" (pūrva) is a relative term. Indeed, a compound can occur even when there is a requirement for a correlative, as in the example:
"Devadatta’s teacher’s house."

20. *kṛño hetutācchīlyānulomyeṣu* (Pāṇini 3.2.20). These—*hetu*, *tācchīlya*, and *ānulomya*—are not *upapadas*. For if they were *upapadas*, the mention of the word *dhātu* (root) in the rule *śami dhātoḥ saṃjñāyām* (3.2.14) would be purposeless; for that [mention] applies to *kṛñ*.

The mention of "dhātu" (root) is made for the purpose of prohibiting the suffix *ṭa* after [words] such as *hetu*. If these were to function as *upapadas*, there would be no possibility of the suffix *ṭa* at all; thus, the mention of "dhātu" would be redundant.
Therefore, these are neither *upapadas* nor meanings of the suffix; rather, [the suffix *ṭa* applies] in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).

Because of the rule *kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67), the agent (*kartṛ*) is the meaning of the suffix; and it is not proper for these [suffixes] to sublate that, as there is no contradiction. Therefore, it is appropriate that these [suffixes] serve to specify the meaning of the suffix. In that context, when the agent is expressed by a suffix, its specific qualifications—such as being the cause (*hetu*) and so forth—are [conveyed].
They are understood. For this very reason, he says: "when cause (hetu), habitual tendency (tācchīlya), and conformity (ānulomya) are implied.

He explains that "cause" means an unerring cause (*aikāntikaṃ kāraṇam*). By this, he shows that the worldly cause is intended here, not the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) one. The technical cause belongs to [the domain of] independent [syllogisms].
If the instigator of the agent were to be included here [in the rule], then the mention of *kṛñaḥ* (of the root *kṛ*) would not be appropriate;

for the suffix *ṇic* is not produced after a root ending in *aṇ* (*a*-class) in the sense of the instigating agent, but rather the suffix is produced after a root ending in *ṇic* (*ṇi*-class) which already contains the causative meaning within itself. If this is argued, it is not so.

Because the sense of the causative suffix (ṇic) ending in the suffix -ṭ is not perceived [here]. But surely, when a worldly cause is apprehended, the agent is qualified by being its instrumental cause (*nimitta*); and that is incorrect, for there is no such thing as an "instrumentality" belonging to an agent that would need to be excluded by a qualification? This is not a fault.

Since the status of the agent as a cause is already established, the further employment of the word "cause" (hetu) indicates its absolute necessity—that is, that the agent is the absolute cause of that [action]. For this very reason it has been said:
"A cause is an absolute cause. This refers to the state of conformity (ānulomya).
"I am favoring [him]" (*anukūlayāmi*) refers to acting in accordance with one's honored intentions. Regarding the word *yaśaskarī*:
by the rule *ataḥ kṛkami-kaṃsa-* (Pāṇini 8.3.46) and others, the *visarjanīya* is changed to *s*.

*divāvibhāniśāprabhābhāskarāntānantādibahunāndīkiṃkṛlipilibibalibhaktikartṛcitrakṣetrasaṃkhyājaṅghābāhvaharyataddhanuraruṣṣu* (3.2.21). Regarding the phrase "according to the requirements" (*yathāyogam*): the word *divā* is connected with [the rule] *supi*; it refers to that which is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

Because [the agent] is the primary factor, it cannot logically function as the object (*karman*). However, since the remaining factors have substance (*sattva*) as their primary element, they can logically function as objects when connected with the verb *karoti* ("to do"); thus, they are connected by the term "objects" (*karmaṇi*).
The statement "this is begun for the sake of excluding causes and so forth" is made because [the designation of cause and so on] is already established by the preceding rule.

Regarding the word "bhāskaraḥ": how then can there be a *sakāra* here, since for a *sakāra*, by the rule "kupvoḥ ka pau ca" (Pāṇini 8.3.37), it ought to be replaced by either a *visarjanīya* or a *jihvāmūlīya*? To this he says: "of the *sakāra*..."

"By means of irregular derivation (*nipātana*)," and so forth. The very pronunciation of the letter *s* in the word *bhāskarānta* is itself the irregular derivation. Regarding "bahukaraḥ": the word *bahu* denotes abundance. Regarding "ahaskaraḥ": in the word *ahan*, the *n* is replaced by *r* according to Pāṇini 8.2.69, *ro'supi*; of that [substitution],...

The *visarjanīya*. Its substitution by *s* occurs by the rule "ṭhataḥ kṛkami" (8.3.46), as in the examples "dhanuṣkaraḥ" and "aruṣkaraḥ. The substitution by *ṣ* occurs by the rules "isusoḥ sāmarthye" (8.3.44) and "nityaṃ samāse 'nutarapadasthasya" (8.3.45). Now, regarding the mention of the word "ananta" (immediate):
For what purpose? [One might argue: "Since the term *anta* (end) is included, it will apply even to the word *ananta* by means of the rule for *tadanta* (ending in that).

This is not so; for in every rule where a word is prescribed as an *upapada* (governing adjunct), a *tadanta* application is not desired. Thus, indeed, the author of the *Vārttika*, the *Padakāra*, recites: "In rules prescribing an *upapada*, there is the mention of *bhaya*, *āḍhya*, and so forth."

[The Vārttika] states: "It causes the application of the rule regarding the final element" (1.1.72, Vārttika 9). If that is so, then in the case of *nānata-karaḥ* ("one who does not bend") or *ananta-karaḥ* ("one who does not end"), would there not also be a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) with the word *anta*? One should not suspect this; for otherwise, there would be a fault regarding the accent (*svara*). For when [the accent] is subsequently prescribed by the rule "In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, [the first member retains its original accent] when the meaning is similar... (*tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-*), [the desired result would not follow].

By such [rules] as these, the accent of the negative particle (*nañ*) would necessarily apply by the rule for the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Consequently, the word *anantakara* would have its first syllable acute (*ādyaudāta*), because the negative particle is acute according to the rule "particles are acute on the first syllable" (*nipātā ādyaudātāḥ*, Phiṭ-sūtra 4.80); however, [this is not desired], for there is the rule: "a primary derivative (*kṛt*) following a prefix, a kāraka, or an upapada [retains its own accent]."

By the rule *gatikārakopapadānāṃ kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), there is an oxytone accent (*antodātta*) due to the natural accent of the final member of the compound; therefore, the mention of the word *ananta-* must be made.

"What is the purpose of this rule prescribing *aj* for many [suffixes]? and so forth. Since the prescription of *aj* applies when words such as *kim* are used as *upapadas*, how is it that *ṭa* also continues to apply here?
[The answer is: by the principle of the *Māṇḍūkakalpa*, *aj* also [continues]; furthermore, the mention of *vibhāṣā* [also continues].

From the knowledge of the established *vibhāṣā* (optionality) therein, the suffix *ac* occurs after the root *kṛ* when preceded by *kim*, *yad*, *tad*, or *bahu*, but only the suffix *ṭa* occurs when the remaining [words] such as *div* etc. follow. Furthermore, because the commencement [of this rule] is for the purpose of excluding "cause" (*hetu*) and so forth, when specific meanings such as "cause" are not intended to be expressed, then the prescription of *ac* after *kṛ* applies to *kim*, *yad*, *tad*, and *bahu*. In those cases...

In the instances intended here, by the preceding rule, only the suffix *ṭa* occurs. Thus, this usage becomes justified: "This class is a *kiṃkarī*. One who has the habit of doing something is a *kiṃkarī*; [here] she does not do anything at all. That is to say, she is useless.

22. *karmaṇi bhṛtau* (Pāṇini 3.2.22). Regarding the statement, "In the rule *karmaṇi*, there is a reference to the word-form itself," from what does this follow? It follows from the force (*sāmarthya*) of the mention of the word *karman*.
For if the technical definition (*paribhāṣika*) of "object" were intended here, the mention of the word *karman* would be redundant.

It may be so; because of the governing role of the object (*karman*), and since the root *kṛ* is transitive, [the suffix] will be connected with that very object. And thus it was stated previously: both [rules], "in the sense of an object" (*karmaṇi*) and "after a word ending in a case-suffix" (*supi*), are carried over [into the subsequent rules]. Among those, in the case of transitive roots, the rule "in the sense of an object" applies, whereas elsewhere the rule "after a word ending in a case-suffix" applies. Therefore...
This is simply the mention of its own form. "The mention of the object" (*karma-nirdeśa*): the object (*karman*) is the operation (*vyāpāra*), and its mention is the price (*mūlya*).
23. [The suffix *ṇa* is applied] after the words *śabda*, *śloka*, *kalaha*, *gāthā*, *vaira*, *cāṭu*, *sūtra*, and *mantrapada*.
(3.2.23) [This is because] "the suffix *ṭa* is obtained after [words denoting] causes (*hetu*) and so forth," according to [the rule] *kṛño hetutācchīlyānulomyeṣu* (3.2.20).

24. *stamba-śakṛtor-in* (3.2.24). It should be stated: "The suffix *in* [is applied] when referring to rice and a calf. The mention of "rice" and "calf" serves to specify the agent. By this rule, the suffix *in* which is prescribed applies to rice and a calf.
The meaning is that this form, "bhavati" [in the sense of] "the agent," must be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows:
here too the word "vibhāṣā" (optionally) is understood, and it is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, it will apply only when *vrīhi* and *vatsa* are the agents, and not otherwise.
Because it is a permanent [term], the first syllable of the subsequent word has the udātta accent.

25. *harateḥ dṛtināthayoḥ paśau* (Pāṇini 3.2.25). The phrase "when the agent is an animal" (*paśau kartari*) indicates that the mention of "animal" (*paśu*) is an attribute of the agent who is the meaning of the suffix. Its status as the meaning of the suffix follows from the rule *kartari kṛt* ("kṛt-suffixes [denote] the agent").

Because of the statement [Pāṇini 3.4.67]. But how is it determined that this is merely a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix, and not something that sets it aside? To this it is said: because the suffix is prescribed after the verbal root, the suffix expresses that which is connected with the meaning of that [root].

It must be so: the meaning of a verbal root is action (*kriyā*), and its connection is with the means (*sādhana*), not with the essential nature of the object (*vastusvarūpa*). Furthermore, the means is power (*śakti*), not the essential nature of the object. The word "animal" (*paśu*) denotes its own referent by way of the essential nature of the object, not by way of the nature of power. Therefore, in that which is not of the nature of power—

An animal being conveyed [as the object] cannot be the meaning of the suffix. Since it is not the meaning of the suffix, how could it—being incapable [of that function]—sublate this meaning of the suffix? Therefore, it is the meaning of the suffix; by that, the agent is qualified. Thus it was rightly said: "when the animal is the agent. This...
This same principle is to be observed elsewhere as well, in cases where the meaning of the suffix serves as a qualifier.
26. *phalegrahir ātmambhariś ca* (3.2.26). 27. *cchandasi vanasanarakṣimathām* (3.2.27).
[Examples: *brahmavaniṃ tvā kṣatravanim*. [He] desires (*vanati*) sacred knowledge (*brahman*), [he] desires sovereign power (*kṣatra*).
The suffix *in* is applied with the intended meaning "one who desires" (*vanati*). From that form ending in *in*, the second case (*dvitīyā*) is applied;

its elision occurs by the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). From the word *yuṣmad*, for the second case and subsequent cases, the substitution *tvā* is applied by the rule *tvāmau dvitīyāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.23). [The example] *gosanim* means "one who desires a cow" (*gām*).
The suffix *in* has the sense of "one who performs" (*sanati*). When *am* follows a word ending in that suffix, the preceding form (*pūrvarūpatva*) applies.

[The term] *pathirakṣī* means "those who protect the path" (*panthānaṃ rakṣataḥ*); this is a dual form, and the long vowel of the same class as the preceding sound (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghatva*) is applied.
Regarding the expression *havirmathīnām*: having analyzed it as *havīṃṣi mathanti*, the suffix is added; [the plural is formed] from that which ends in this suffix.
The plural number of the genitive case.

By the phrase "from the causative (*ṇyantāt*)," he dispels the doubt that this mention of *ej-* might refer to a different verbal root. But how is it determined that it is the causative? From the suffix *khaś*.
Because of the addition of the marker *śit*. If it were intended to refer to another verbal root (*prakṛtyantara*), the addition of the marker *śit* would be purposeless.

For that [marker] is employed so that, when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix follows, the rule for *śap*—which depends on that [marker]—may apply. And in the case of the root *ej*, whether another root exists or not, there is no *śap*.

There is a specific distinction: if the mention of *ṇi* were not made, the inclusion of the marker *ś* would be purposeless. If that [marker *ś*] were absent, there would be the elision of *ṇi*; but since it exists, when *śap*—which is conditioned by being a *sārvadhātuka* affix—is applied, the elision of *ṇi* does not occur. Some maintain that the elision of *ṇi* occurs because of the status of being an *ārdhadhātuka* affix, but this is incorrect.

Indeed, the inclusion of the syllable *śit* is for the sake of what follows; for if it were not there, in the subsequent sūtra, the substitution of *ā* for *dhā* (√dheṭ) would not occur, nor would the replacement of *dhmā* by *dham*. Consequently, forms such as *stanandhayaḥ* and *nāsikandhamaḥ* would not be established. Therefore, its causative nature (*ṇyantatva*) is to be understood from the very [grammatical] explanation itself.

"This *ṭhak* [suffix] has the sense of 'mum'"; that is, under the governing rule *khityanavyayasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.66), the augment *mum* should occur by the rule *arurdviṣadajantasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.67). "The letter *ś* is for the purpose of the technical designation *sārvadhātuka*"; that is, according to the rule *tiṅśit sārvadhātukam* (Pāṇini 3.4.113).

So that the designation *sārvadhātuka* may apply— as in the example *ṭhaṅgamejayaḥ*— there is the affix *śap*, followed by *guṇa* and *ay-ādeśa*. Regarding the rule beginning with "in the section on *khaś*" (*khaśprakaraṇe*), when words such as *vāta* are used as upapadas, [the root] *aja* (meaning "motion" and "throwing") [is applied].

The addition [of the suffix *khaś*] should be prescribed for these roots— *dhā* (DhP 230), *dheṭ* "to drink" (DhP 902), *tuda* "to pain" (DhP 1281), and *ohāk* "to abandon" (DhP 1090)— within the section on *khaś*. Regarding the word *upasaṃkhyāna*:

The purpose [of this rule] is to provide an exposition. In this regard, the exposition is as follows: in the rule *nāḍīm-uṣṭrayoś ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.20), there is the word *ca* ("and"); that *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccayārtha*).
By means of that, the suffix *khaś* will occur after verbal roots beginning with vowels when words such as *vāta* are used as upapadas. For example: *śunindhayaḥ*.
Thus [it is said]. By the rule "khityanavyayasya" (Pāṇini 6.3.66), there is shortening of the vowel. Regarding "śarddhañjahāḥ":
there is the *ślu* substitution for the *śap* suffix after roots of the *juhotyādi* class; by the rule "ślau" (6.1.10), there is reduplication;
and by the rule "śnābyasatyorātaḥ" (6.4.112), there is the elision of the long *ā*.
29. *nāsikāstanayordhmādheṭoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.29).

By the rule *ṭhstane dheṭaḥ* and so forth, [the author] demonstrates the connection with the respective *upapadas* (governing words) and shows the examples. Regarding *nāsikandhamaḥ*: [this is derived] by the rule *pāghrādisūtreṇa*.
(7.3.78) *dham* is the substitute.

Regarding the phrase "And this," etc., he states the reason for the absence of numerical correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*): for the word *stana* has fewer syllables than *nāsikā*, and thus it ought to be placed first [according to the rule governing the order of words].

This reversal of the usual order of words indicates that the rule for *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence in order) possesses a characteristic non-deviation; just as here the rule governing the prior placement [of shorter words] deviates and does not apply within its own scope,
so too does the definition of *yathāsaṃkhya*.
Therefore, from this sign of the deviation of the definition, the absence of a one-to-one correspondence is obtained.
30. *nāḍīmuṣṭyośca* (3.2.30).

Here too, by the rule beginning with *atra api*, the words *nāḍī* and *muṣṭi* end in the *ghi* designation; for although their prior placement would have been required by the rule *dvandve ghi* (2.2.32), this non-prior placement which has been made [is explained as follows].

This is a mark indicating a deviation from the rule regarding initial placement (*pūrvanipāta*); it also suggests that here, too, there will be no application of the principle of "designation according to number" (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*). Now, each prefix is connected individually with the verbal root, and this is made manifest in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by means of examples alone.

"The particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been mentioned. By this, the suffix *khaś* is applied to the roots *dhmā* and *dheṭ* even when the words *ghaṭī*, *khārī*, and *vāta* are used as upapadas.

If this is so, then because of the very lack of parity (*vaiṣamya*), there will be no application of the rule for corresponding enumeration (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*); therefore, the purpose of that [mention of *ca*] regarding the absence of such enumeration is redundant.

Why is there this reversal of the usual order [of the compound]? It is said: because there are two distinct sentences here. By one sentence, it is meant that the suffix *khaś* occurs after the roots *dhmā* and *dheṭ* when combined with the words "nāḍī" and "muṣṭi.
Therefore, "nāḍīmuṣṭyoḥ" constitutes one sentence.

Because the particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned, there is a second [application]: when *ghaṭī*, *khārī*, or *vāta* are also the subordinate words (*upapada*), the suffix *khaś* occurs after the roots *dhmā* and *dheṭ*. In that case, since there is equality (*samānatva*) in the preceding rule, there would indeed be a correspondence according to number (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*).

31. *udi kūle rujivahoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.31). Regarding the word *udi*: this is a locative case, meaning "when *ud* is present. In that context, the specific application of the two words *ut* and *kūla* should be understood. Because of the rule *te prāgdhātoḥ* (1.4.80), the word *ut* must immediately precede the verbal root.

Therefore, the word *kūla* is the prior [member]. Alternatively—the reading *uditi* is printed as *udīti*—the term *udi* is a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*), meaning that the word *kūla* has the designation of "governing word" (*upapada*) when *ud* follows it.
Now, why does the word *ut* not also receive the designation of "governing word," since each [word] [is individually so designated]?

Is it because of the utterance of the locative case? For this is the style of the Teacher: wherever there is the status of being a subordinate word (*upapada*) for each individual member, he utters the locative case from the aggregate, as in "nāḍīmuṣṭyoḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.30).
But here, the reverse has been done; therefore, the status of being a subordinate word does not apply. Moreover—

Because the roots *ruj* and *vah* are transitive (*sakarmaka*), the rule "after [a root] having an object" (*karmaṇi*) applies here. However, the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is not possible for the word *ucchabda*, because it denotes a non-substance (*asatvavācin*). How, then, could it function as a subordinate word (*upapada*)?
[Examples are: *kūlamudrujaḥ* ("one who breaks the bank"), with the suffix *śa* due to belonging to the *tudādi* class; and *kūlamudvahaḥ* ("one who carries away the bank"), with the suffix *śap*.

32. *vahābhre lihaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.32). [The example is] *vahaṃlihaḥ*. Regarding the root *liha* in the sense of "tasting" (Dhātupāṭha 1016), because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision of the *śap* suffix. Due to the rule *sārvadhātukamapit* (1.2.4), the suffix is treated as having the marker *ṅ*, which results in the absence of *guṇa* substitution.
33. *pacaḥ* [is used] in the sense of a measure (*parimāṇe*). (Pāṇini 3.2.33) Examples:

*ṭhprasthampacā*, *droṇampacā*. Here, the words *prastha* and *droṇa* are applied figuratively (*upacāreṇa*) to rice and other grains that are measured by a *prastha* or a *droṇa*; they do not refer merely to the specific measures themselves.

[The term *prastha*] refers to something made of wood and the like. For here, the root *pac* denotes "moistening" (*kleda*). Now, moistening is not possible for a primary [measure] such as a *prastha*, and therefore its connection [to the action] is not tenable. For this very reason, it cannot be a reference to the essential nature [of the measure]; for the root *pac*, which expresses moistening, does not have a connection with a dimension that has the essential nature as its primary referent.
A connection is possible; for although words such as "prastha" refer to the object measured, their designation as a measure is not contradicted, because they primarily function to denote measurement.
34. *mitanakhe ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.34).

"This [sūtra] is begun for the sake of excluding measurement (*parimāṇa*)," because it would have been established by the preceding rule alone regarding measurement; for the words *mita* and *nakha* do not denote measurement. Indeed, the word *mita* always [denotes a specific measure].
The word *nakha* denotes a limited substance, for it indeed denotes a limb of a living being.

35. *vidhvarūṣostudaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.35). Regarding the example *aruntudaḥ*: after the word *arus*, the augment *mum* is inserted after the vowel *u* by the rule *arurdviṣadajantasya* (6.3.67); then there is the elision of the final consonant of the *saṃyoga* cluster (*saṃyogāntalopaḥ*, 8.2.23); and finally, the *anusvāra* is substituted for *m* by the rule *mo'nusvāraḥ* (8.3.23).
The *anusvāra* is replaced by a homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*) according to the rule *anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.58).

36. *asūryalalāṭayordṛśitapoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.36). [The example is] *asūryampaśyāḥ*. By the rule *prāghrādi-* (7.3.78), there is the substitution of *paśya*. [The commentary states: "Because of the connection of the negative particle (*nañ*) with *dṛśi*. This is the reason for the lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*). For here, it is the act of seeing...

It is the act of seeing that is negated, but not the sun itself. Therefore, the negative particle (nañ) is connected only with the verb "to see" (dṛśi), and not with the word "sun"; thus, there is a lack of semantic competency [between the negative and the noun]. By saying "they do not see the sun," he demonstrates the connection of the negative particle with the verb "to see. When the sun is what is being negated, then the suffix must certainly not occur.

Because it is not so expressed. Furthermore, this compound occurs even in the absence of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*), because it conveys the meaning, or simply because of this very statement. Now, one might object: just as "the king's wives do not see the sun," so too [they do not see] other things such as other men; in that case, it is improper to mention only the sun.

To the objection that this is not so, he says: "And this is primarily for the sake of protection. This statement—that "the wives of the king are not to be seen by the sun"—is primarily concerned with protection, because it is employed for the purpose of establishing such protection. By the words "in this very way," etc., he demonstrates that its primary concern is protection.

37. *ugraṃpaśya-irammada-pāṇindhamaś-ca* (3.2.37). Regarding *ugraṃpaśya*: although *karmaṇyaṇ* (3.2.1) would have applied, the suffix *khaś* is irregularly prescribed (*nipātita*) after the root *dṛś*. As before, there is the substitution of *paśya*. Regarding *irammada*: [it means] "he intoxicates with water" (*irayā mādyati*). [The root is] *madī* in the sense of exhilaration (*harṣe*).

When the suffixes *tṛc* and others would otherwise apply, *khaś* is introduced by irregular derivation (*nipātana*). In that case, since the root belongs to the *divādi* class, the suffix *śyan* would normally apply; its absence is therefore established by irregular derivation. Regarding the form *pāṇindhamāḥ*: when the suffix *lyuṭ* would otherwise apply in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), *khaś* is introduced by irregular derivation. As before, there is the substitution of *dham*.

38. *priyavaśe vadaḥ khac* (3.2.38). The letter *ṭh* in *ṭhcakāraḥ* is for the purpose of specifying [the rule] *ṭhkhaci hrasvaḥ*. If it were stated simply as *khe hrasvaḥ*, it would apply to *khaś* as well. But surely, when there is the mention of a suffix with one indicatory letter (*ekānubandhaka*), there is no application of a suffix with two indicatory letters (*dvyanubandhaka*)?

"Will it not be so? [The author replies: "In that case, since one must rely on a *paribhāṣā*, it is considered simpler simply to employ the letter *ca*. But surely forms such as *priyaṃvadaḥ* and *vaśaṃvadaḥ* are established even by means of the suffix *khaś*; for what purpose, then, is a different suffix prescribed? To this he says:

"The creation of a different suffix (*pratyaya*) is for the sake of what follows. This means that in the rule *dviṣat-parayos tāpeḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.39), so that the shortening may apply to the root *tāp-* when the suffix *khac* follows, and so that the elision of the *ṇi*-affix (*ṇilopa*) and other such operations may occur, a different suffix is prescribed. Why, then, is *khac* not simply prescribed in the subsequent rule itself? [The answer is: because *khac* also occurs here.
This is for the sake of making the meaning clear. By this, the suffix *khac* is established for the root *gam* as well when preceded by a *sup*-ending word.

If it is argued that "there is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of *gam* under the section on *khac* when preceded by a *sup*-ending word" (Vārttika 247), then in that case, another suffix is introduced for the purpose of demonstrating what is meant by the term "addition."
The derivation of this very word should be understood as follows: "vihāyaso viha ca. When the root *gam* (to go) has the word *vihāyas* as its *upapada*, the suffix *khac* is applied;
by virtue of that [suffix], the word *vihāyas* undergoes the substitution *vihā*.

"It should be stated that [the suffix] ṭhak has the marker ḍ. Because of the marker ḍ, there would be elision of the feminine suffix (ṭilopa), since this is recited separately from the rule "vihāyaso viha ca" (Vārttika 248). This is for the purpose of indicating that the presence of the marker ḍ is not universally obligatory; otherwise, the form *vihaṅgama* would not be established.

"ṭhḍe ca," etc. When the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *gam*, there is the substitution of *vihā* for *vihāyas*. Thus, "vihaga. But is not the suffix *ḍa* [normally] absent here? It occurs precisely because of this specific rule. Alternatively, he will state later in the section on *ḍa*: "It is also seen in other cases" (Vārttika 256).

Regarding the rule *dviṣatparayos tāpe* (Pāṇini 3.2.39): "There is the inclusion of both [the causative and the non-causative forms]," because there is no distinction between them in their state as causatives (*ṇyantāvasthā*). "The mention is with two *t*s," meaning that in the mention *dviṣatparayoḥ*, there are two [instances].

Regarding the letter *t*: one of them is a constituent part (*avayava*) of the word *dviṣat*; by means of that, the word *dviṣat* is qualified—namely, that when the word *dviṣat* occurs as an *upapada*, [the suffix applies] to that which ends in *t*. Thus, it does not apply in the feminine;
for there is no word ending in *t* that terminates in a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*). However, if the second *t* were not present...

According to the paribhāṣā *ṭhprātipadikagrahaṇe liṅgaviśiṣṭasyāpi grahaṇaṃ bhavati* (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 29), "when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included," the suffix would also apply to the feminine form. Thus, one would have *dviṣatī* [according to the Kāśikā], with the suffix *ṅīp* applied by the rule *ṭhugitaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.6). The status of being *ugit* for the word *dviṣat* is established by the rule *ṭhdviṣo'mitre* (Pāṇini 3.2.131).
Because it is formed with the suffix śatṛ.

40. *vāci yamo vrata* (Pāṇini 3.2.40). [The word] *śāstritaḥ* [is derived as follows]: having analyzed [the compound] as *śāstre kṛtaḥ* ("done in the treatise"), one adds the suffix *ṇic* after the nominal stem *śāstra* in the sense of the verbal root; then, when the suffix *kta* is added after that [form ending in *ṇic*], it becomes *śāstritaḥ*.

The meaning is "prescribed by the treatises" (*śāstravihita*). Alternatively, *śāstrita* means "followed by those who possess the treatises" (*śāstriṇa itaḥ*), or "arisen from, or set in motion by, those who know the treatises. Or else—the word *śāstra* should be seen as belonging to the *tārakādi* group [of suffixes]. Thus, *śāstrita* means "one for whom the treatise has become manifest" (*śāstram asya sañjātam*). Regarding the term *vācaṃyama*: having analyzed the compound as "one who restrains speech" (*vācaṃ yacchati*), the suffix *khac* is applied.

In the rule *ṭhvācaṃyamapurandarau ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.69), the absence of the augment *mum* for the first member of the compound is prescribed as a nipātana (irregularity). Now, one might object: "The suffix will also be provided by that very same nipātana;

so what is the purpose of this [separate rule]? This is not the case; for if the suffix *ac* is applied in the sense of "one who speaks" (*yacchati*) according to the *pacādi* group, then from that [base] *vāc-*...

If the compound *vācaṃyama* were formed by applying the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*)—that is, from *vācaḥ yamaḥ*—it would indeed be established; however, in that case, the rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*) would be purposeless. Furthermore, if this were so, the compound would not be obligatory with the subordinate word (*upapada*). Therefore, the suffix *khac* must be prescribed, and the irregular derivation must also be performed.

41. *pūḥ-sarvayoḥ dāri-sahoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.41). Regarding the term *dāri*: this is a designation by means of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) for the root *dṛ* (meaning "to tear apart," Dhātupāṭha 1493). Regarding the form *purandaraḥ*: the substitution of *mu* for the initial [of the prefix] is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*) when it occurs as the first member of a compound.

Regarding the statement, "It should be stated that [the suffix] occurs when *bhaga* and *dāra* are the upapadas," the meaning is that this should be explained as having the sense that the suffix *khac* occurs when *bhaga* is the upapada. In this regard, the explanation is as follows:
"And *ugram-paśya*, *irammada*, and *pāṇindham* [are formed with *khac*]. (Pāṇini 3.2.37).

Therefore, the word "ca" (and) is understood here as a carry-over from the previous rule, and not for the purpose of including unmentioned items; by this, when *bhaga* is the upapada, the suffix *khañ* is applied to the root *dṛ*.
42. [The suffix] *kaṣ* is applied after [the roots] *sarva*, *kūla*, *abhra*, and *karīṣa*. (3.2.42) For example:
