*sarvaṅkaṣaḥ*. [The roots] *kaṣ*, *khaṣ*, *śiṣ*, *jaṣ*, *jhaṣ*, *śaṣ*, *vaṣ*, *maṣ*, *ruṣ*, and *riṣ* have the meaning "to injure" (*hiṃsārtha*). (Dhātupāṭha 685–694).

43. *kṛñaḥ* [is used] after *megha*, *arti*, and *bhaya*. (Pāṇini 3.2.43). Regarding the rule "in the prescription of an upapada," etc.: Now, one might object that the word *abhaya* is indeed established through a *nañ*-compound;
however, this cannot be so, because [the suffix] is *satiśiṣṭa* (later applied), as stated in the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-* (Pāṇini 6.2.2).

The initial syllable would have the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member, whereas by the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), ending-accentuation (*antodātatva*) is intended. Therefore, [the suffix] *-khac* must be applied; because it is an exception (*apavāda*), it subverts the application of *-mayaṇ*.
And when there is the intention to express the reason (*hetu*) and so forth, the suffix *ṭa* is also applied because it is subsequent [in the order of rules].

44. *kṣemapriyamadre 'ṇ ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.44). Now, why was it not stated simply as *kṣemapriyamadre vā*; what is the purpose of including the mention of *aṇ*? [One might argue: "It is optional in the case of *khac*, and *aṇ* will occur by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ* (3.2.1) itself. To this, he says:

Regarding the statement "it should be stated as *ṭha*," and so forth: when it is said "optionally after *kṣema*, *priya*, and *madra*," because of the inclusion of the word "optionally" (*vā*), that which is established by default is also accepted. Consequently, when the sense of cause (*hetu*) and so forth is intended, the suffix *ṭa* would apply by the rule "after the root *kṛ*, [the suffixes *ṭa* and *ka* are added] in the sense of cause, habitual action, and so forth" (Pāṇini 3.2.20); therefore, this is for the purpose of setting aside that [suffix]. By means of that—
When there is the intention to express "the cause" (hetu) and so forth, the suffix *aṇ* occurs, superseding the suffix *ṭa*.

45. *āśite bhuvaḥ karaṇabhāvayoḥ* | (3.2.45) Here, *supi* is understood [from the previous rule], not *karmaṇi*; for the root *bhū* is intransitive (*akarmaka*). [The commentary continues: "In the word *āśita*, which ends in a *su*-affix," and so forth. Now, why is the reverse not the case?

Is the meaning of the suffix [the state] when *karaṇa* (instrument) and *bhāva* (existence) are the accompanying words (*upapada*) in the sense of "having eaten" (*āśita*)? No, because that is impossible. By the word *āśita*, the agent of the root *aś* (to eat) is expressed; its connection with the verb *bhū* (to become) is not tenable. For that which is the agent of *aś* cannot possibly be the meaning of the suffix for the root *bhū*.

Therefore, the word *āśita* functions as an upapada (governing word), while the other two [words] function as the meaning of the suffix. In this way, [the suffix *ghañ*] becomes an exception (*apavāda*) to both *ghañ* and *lyuṭ*. By the rule of "optionality of dissimilar forms" (*vā'sarūpa-vidhi*), *lyuṭ* also indeed occurs—as in *āśitabhavana odanaḥ* ("rice that has been eaten"). However, because *ghañ* represents its own form, it is precisely what sublates [the other].
46. *saṃjñāyāṃ bhṛtṛvṛdhārisahitapidamaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.46).

Regarding the phrase "by virtue of being a name" (*saṃjñāvaśāt*): indeed, names are of two kinds—some follow the meaning of their constituent parts, such as *saptavarṇa* ("seven-syllabled"); others, however, are the opposite.

As in the case of *tailapāyikā*. Here, in cases where there is a correspondence with the meanings of the constituent parts—as in *viśvambharaḥ*, *śatruntapaḥ*, and so forth—the term "in the object" (*karmaṇi*) is connected [to the suffix]; thus, one who nourishes the universe is *viśvambharaḥ*. But where there is no correspondence with the meanings of the constituent parts—as in *rathantaram*—[the suffix is not applied in that way].

Regarding "sāma": in order to provide a distinct meaning there, the word "sup" is connected [to the rule]—as in *rathena tarati* ("crosses by means of a chariot") or *rathe tarati* ("crosses on a chariot"). Regarding *patiṃvarā*: from the roots *vṛñ* in the sense of "choosing" (*varaṇe*, DhP 1254) and *vṛṅ* in the sense of "choosing as a husband" (*sambhaktau*, DhP 1509). The analysis is: she chooses a husband (*patiṃ vṛṇīte*) or she chooses a husband (*patiṃ vṛṇute*).

"He conquers the enemy" is *śatruñjayaḥ*. Regarding "dhāri": this is the inclusion of the root *dhṛ* with the suffix *ṇya*. "He bears the yoke" is *yugandharaḥ*; there is shortening of the first member of the compound. "He endures the enemy" is *śatruṃsahaḥ*. "He torments the enemy" is *śatruṃtapaḥ*. "He subdues the foe" is *arindamaḥ*.
Although the root *dam* is intransitive, it will nevertheless become transitive by virtue of having the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) inherent within it;
the meaning is "he subdues the enemy."
47. *gamaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.47). [The example is:
"He whose son is Sautāṅgami. This shows that by means of the designation of the son as "Sautāṅgami," the name of the father as "Sutaṅgama" is inferred; for [only] when the father's [name] exists...

When there is the notion of *sutaṅgama*, the son of *sutaṅgama* is designated by the word *sautaṅgami*; this does not occur when such a notion is absent. Now, for what purpose is the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*)? He says—“The separation of the rule is for the sake of what follows”—meaning that the mention of the root *gam* should have been made in the preceding rule itself.

The purpose is so that the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of *gama* alone may occur in the subsequent [sūtra], while that of *bhṛñ* and the others does not; for if they were in a single compound (*ekayoga*), those too would recur.

48. *Antātyantādhvadūrapārasarvānanteṣu ḍaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.48). [The commentary states: "The letter *ḍ* in *ḍaḥ* is for the purpose of the elision of the *ṭi*. This is so that the elision of the *ṭi* may occur by the rule *ḍiti ṭeḥ* (6.4.155). But how is the elision of the *ṭi* obtained even when the letter *ḍ* is present, given that...
For the elision of the *ṭi* suffix is prescribed for that which bears the designation *bha*, yet here there is no *bha*-designation; thus he says:

"In the presence of a *ḍit* [suffix], even for that which is not *bha*," and so forth. The intention is that if the elision of *ṭi* were not to occur even when a *ḍit* suffix is present, then that [rule] would be rendered useless. But surely it will serve the purpose of making the sound *ca* audible; why then...?

Would there be futility? He thinks as follows: by making this reference to *jan* ending in the suffix *ḍa*—after the elision of *ṭi* has been applied by the rule "prāvṛṭ-śarad-kāla-divāñje" (Pāṇini 6.3.15)—it is understood that the letter *ḍ* is intended for the purpose of non-audibility [of the *ṭi*]. [This is shown by] the words "in all cases," and so forth.

The purpose of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is to provide an exposition. In this regard, the exposition is as follows: the particle *ca* ("and") is carried over from the rule *gamaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.47). Since that particle has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned, the suffix *ḍa* will apply even when there is no governing word (*upapada*), such as in the case of *sarvatra*. Furthermore, the word *sarvatra* here...
It is connected with the word *sup*, and not with the word *karmaṇi*;

for since that [word *karmaṇi*] primarily denotes the power of the locus (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*), it is untenable for it to denote the object (*karman*). However, the word *panna* (fallen), being a qualifier of the action, is connected with the word *karmaṇi*. For this has indeed been established.
In the sūtra "stokālpa... (Pāṇini 2.3.33), etc., that which qualifies the action (kriyāviśeṣaṇa) is treated as an object (karman).
[Regarding the form] "urasaḥ," there is elision (lopa) [of the final letter]; by the rule "alo'ntyasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.52), this refers to the elision of the letter *s*.

Regarding the rule *suduroradhikaraṇe*: the suffix *ḍa* is prescribed as an exception to *lyuṭ*. By the rule of optional non-homogeneity (*vāsarūpavidhi*), *lyuṭ* also occurs—thus we have *sugamana* and *durgamana*.
Why specify "in the sense of locus" (*adhikaraṇe*)? So that it does not apply when [the word] denotes the object (*karman*). This refers to the rule *īṣadduḥsuṣu* (Pāṇini 3.3.126).

By such statements as these, [it is shown that] it becomes like a threshing floor—meaning it is easy to traverse or difficult to traverse. Regarding the rule "nirgo deśe" (nirga- in the sense of a place): when the word *nir* is used as a prefix (*upapada*) to the root *gam*, the suffix *ḍa* occurs when the location (*adhikaraṇa*) is a place. A place in which one goes out from is a *nirga* place. [This applies] elsewhere than in the case of a place.
Lyuṭ-eva—namely, "going forth" (nirgamana).

49. *hanaḥ* [is used] in the sense of benediction (*āśiṣi*). (Pāṇini 3.2.49) The term "in the sense of benediction" (*āśiṣi*) serves to specify the meaning of the suffix. When that [suffix] occurs as a suffix denoting the agent, it is applied in a context where a benediction is understood. For example: *timiṃ vadhyāt* ("May he slay the whale"). This is the benedictive mood (*āśīr-liṅ*).
The citation of the word *prayogavat* is for the purpose of illustrating the term *tim-iha*, since they share the same meaning.
[Examples such as] *dārāvāhana* and so forth; only the substitution of *ṭ* is added as a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*), whereas the suffix *aṇ* [is already established].

This [suffix] is already established by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1). Now, what is the purpose of including the word *anta* ("end")? For, by the rule *alo'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52), it will apply to the final letter. Furthermore, operations prescribed by a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) do not concern the final letter of a word. And here, there is no genitive case [ending] for the root *han*.

[Question: Is this an explicit explanation (*nirdeśa*), or rather [is it understood] through the fifth case (*pañcamī*)? [Objection: But surely, by the force of the meaning, there will be a transformation of the case-ending—would not the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) be obtained for this word *hanaḥ*? [Response: If that is so, then the mention of the word "end" (*anta*) is for the sake of clarity. As in the example "dārvāhanti" (they strike wood); here, the word *dāru*...

It ends in the second case. Because [the suffix] *su* has been elided by the rule "ṭhsvamornapuṃsakāt" (Pāṇini 7.1.23), the second case ending is not heard. Regarding "cārau vā": here too, the substitute is prescribed optionally; however, the suffix *aṇ*...

The suffix *aṇ* is established as obligatory by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1). In the word *cārvāghāṭaḥ*, there is *kutva* (the substitution of *gh* for *h*) by the rule *ho hanter ñṇinneṣu* (7.3.54), and there is *tatva* (the substitution of *t* for *n*) by the rule *hanasta aciṇṇaloḥ* (7.3.32). The statement *karmaṇi sami ca* is merely an elaboration of the rule *karmaṇy upapade*.
The qualifier.
50. *Ape kleśatamasoḥ* (3.2.50).

The rule stated previously regarding the word *ud* being an *upapada* in the sūtra *ṭhudi kūle rujivahoḥ* (3.2.31) should also be understood to apply here to the word *apa*. "This [sūtra] is commenced for the sake of meanings other than *anīśīra*"—that is, in the sense of *āśis* (benediction).
Because it is already established by what precedes.
51. The suffix *ṇini* is applied after [the words] *kumāra* and *śiras*. (Pāṇini 3.2.51) For example:

*kumāraghātī*. As before, there is the substitution of *tat* for *tad*, and by virtue of this very rule (*nipātana*), the word *śiras* becomes *śīrṣa*. It is precisely from the mention of *kumāraśīrṣayoḥ* that the substitution of *śīrṣa* for *śiras* occurs by way of *nipātana*.

The form *śīrṣa-bhāvaḥ* occurs, and not by the rule *ṭhśīrṣaś chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.60). For in that rule, another word *śīrṣan*—which has the same meaning as the word *śiras*—is prescribed as a substitute; otherwise, forms such as *śīrṣa-ghātī* would occur only in the Vedic language (*chandas*) and not in the common language (*bhāṣā*). [This applies also to] the rule *kumāra-śīrṣayoḥ*.

Furthermore, this grammatical designation would not be appropriate, for that [root] ends in *n*, whereas this designation is made with a form ending in *a*, not one ending in *n*. The second *i* in *ṇin* is for the purpose of protecting the *n* from being designated as an *it*, and the *ṇ* is for the purpose of causing *vṛddhi* [vowel strengthening].
52. *lakṣaṇe jāyāpatyoṣṭak* (3.2.52).

That by which something is marked or characterized is a *lakṣaṇa*. "In that which possesses it" means in that which has a *lakṣaṇa*. By this, the word *lakṣaṇa* in the sūtra is understood as ending in the possessive suffix *-a* (*matvarthīya-akāra*).

Thus he demonstrates this; and showing that it is a qualifier of the agent (*kartṛ*) which is the referent (*pratyaya*), he says: "when the agent possesses the characteristic (*lakṣaṇavat*). Now, why does the word *lakṣaṇa* not function as a subordinate term (*upapada*)? Some say: because the root *han* is transitive, the rule "in the case of the object" (*karmaṇi*) applies here; in that context—

If, in this context, the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) were to function as a subordinate term (*upapada*), it would be qualified by the object (*karman*). However, a defining characteristic is not logically possible as the object of the root *han* (to kill), for that root occurs in the sense of violence, and violence pertains to living beings. Since the husband and wife possess the nature of living beings, their status as the object is indeed logical. Thus [he says].

And this is untenable; for the word *lakṣaṇa*, which ends in the possessive suffix *-aka* (*matvarthīya-akāra*), is seen to apply even to a living being. Its status as not being a subordinate member of a compound (*anupapada*) is understood either from the very fact of its being explained [as such] or because of non-usage (*anabhidhāna*). The designation of the husband and wife as the agents is observed, as in the example: "a killer of his wife" (*jāyāghnaḥ*).

Due to its being a *kit* suffix, there is elision of the penultimate vowel by Pāṇini 6.4.98 (*ṭhgamahana...* etc.), and as before, there is the substitution of *k* for *gh*. Thus we have *patighnī*; because of the *ṭi*-marker, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied.

53. *Amanuṣyakartṛke ca* (3.2.53). Regarding the phrase *amanuṣyakartṛke*: that which has a non-human as its agent is so described. And this is a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root; since the meaning of the root belongs to the verb *han* ("to kill"), he says: "of such a kind."
[This line] does not exist in the root text. [The rule begins with: "When the meaning of the verbal root has a non-human agent," and so forth.

Now, why is the mention of "having a non-human agent" (*amanuṣyakartṛka*) not a qualifier of the *upapada* (governing word)? Because the term "in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi*) is understood by anuvṛtti (carrying over from a previous rule), and a connection between the object and a non-human agent is impossible.

For there is a connection with the action of the means (*sādhana*), not with another factor of action (*kāraka*). Why is it not understood that this [agent] is a qualifier of the agent who is the meaning of the suffix?
Because that [action] lacks a non-human agent. Indeed, an agent of an agent is not possible; rather—
[This refers] to the action. But surely the mention of the "agent" (kartṛ) need not be made, for even without it, the suffix would indeed be obtained when the agent is non-human? It cannot be so;
without the mention of the "agent," the mention of "non-human" [would be impossible].
Even when it is employed alone, it is understood as a qualifier of the following word (*upapada*).

Therefore, the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) must be made. When that [mention] exists, it is impossible for it to be a qualifier of the "non-human agent"; hence, it is appropriate that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) itself should be qualified by it.

"Why does the suffix *ṭha* not occur? [The answer is: Because the meaning of the verbal root has as its agent a non-human being, namely an elephant; therefore, it is thought that the suffix *ṭak* alone must necessarily occur here.
54. *śaktau hastikapāṭayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.54). [The commentary states: "When *śakti* (capability) is implied. By this, it negates that *śakti* is an *upapada*.
Furthermore, by the rule "*hastikapāṭayoḥ karmaṇor upapadayoḥ*," [it is shown that] *hasti* and *kapāṭa* are the two *upapadas*.
It is a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix. Now, why is it not understood in this way:

"when *hastin* and *kapāṭa* are the upapadas [denoting] the agents (*kartṛ*), [the suffix applies] in the sense of potentiality (*śakti*)"? For, even though this would be understood by the very force of the rule's formulation, the root *han* occurs in the sense of the verbal root-meaning when *hastin* and *kapāṭa* have a human as their agent. And thus...

If [the rule] were established by the preceding one alone, the commencement of this [rule] would be redundant. However, when those two [words, *viṣa* and *hasta*] function as upapadas (governing words) and their capacity (*śakti*) is understood, it is recognized that the agent is a human being; thus, this fault does not arise.
In the example "he kills the elephant with poison" (*viṣeṇa hastinaṃ hanti*), the word "with poison" (*viṣeṇa*) demonstrates the lack of capacity [on the part of the hand]. For he who...
Being unable to kill him himself, he kills him by means of another method through despondency.

55. *pāṇigha* and *tāḍagha* [denote] an artisan. (Pāṇini 3.2.55) Regarding the rule "pāṇighatāḍaghau": the suffix *ap*, the substitution of *gh* for *h*, and the elision of the *ṭi* portion are prescribed as irregularities (*nipātana*).

56. After the root *kṛ*, when used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), the suffix *khyun* is applied before the words *āḍhya*, *subhaga*, *sthūla*, *palita*, *nagna*, *andha*, and *priya*, provided that these words have the sense of the suffix *cvy-* and do not themselves end in *cvy-*.
[The rule states: "And *ṭha* in place of *cvy*. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound: *na vidyate cviryasmin*—that in which *cvy* does not exist, i.e., *acvyau*. It is also a *tatpuruṣa*.

Or [the word *aci*] means "other than *cv-*"; that is, ending in a suffix other than *cv-*. The term *aci* is an adjective qualifying *āḍhyādi* and so forth. The singular number, however, is connected with each of them individually. By the phrase "in the case of *āḍhya* and so forth," etc., [the author] rejects the interpretation of *āḍhya* and the others as being qualifiers of the agent (*kartṛ*). [The word *aci* refers to] the instrument (*karaṇe*).

By the rule *kārake*, he also excludes the status of the instrument (*karaṇa*) as a co-occurring word (*upapada*). Now, why is it not understood thus: "when the instrument is the co-occurring word, and [the agent] is among those beginning with *āḍhya*"?
Regarding this, some say: "In this context, words such as *āḍhya* are primarily [the meaning of] the word itself (*śabda-pradhāna*), and such [words]..."

The status of being an agent is thus established. Furthermore, their primacy of the word-form is understood from the prohibition "not after those ending in *cvī*" (*acvyanteṣvacvi*); for it is the word itself that becomes something ending in *cvī*, not the meaning. The state of ending in *cvī* belongs to the word alone, not to the meaning. In that case, if these were primarily concerned with the meaning;

The qualification "in the sense of *cvya*" would be untenable, and the prohibition "not when [it means] a horse" (*acvau*) would be purposeless. Furthermore, even the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) would be purposeless; this is not so, for by that very [prohibition], the word *āḍhya* becomes easy to understand, as does the word *subhaga*.

Since agency (*kartṛtva*) is observed in constructions such as *sukhayati* and others, the determination of the meaning [of the suffix] based on the commentary alone is not to be rejected. Because the instrument (*karaṇa*) is indicated as the meaning of the suffix, the rule *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67) does not apply. But surely these...

Words ending in *cv* are necessarily those formed with the suffix *cv*; however, in this context, words such as *āḍhya* and others cannot possibly end in *cv*, so why are they excluded? To this he says: "Because [the suffix] *cv* is prescribed optionally," and so forth. The prescription is indeed optional according to the rule: "From among those that are semantically capable, the first [member] optionally [takes the suffix]."
This is because the term *vā* ("or") is understood to carry over from [Pāṇini 4.1.82]. For example:

*āḍhaḷṃ tailena kurvanti* ("they make the vessel solid with oil," etc.). Indeed, this vessel was not previously non-solid and is made solid by the oil; rather, being already solid, it is anointed with oil. This is because verbal roots have multiple meanings.

In this context, the root *kṛ* (karoti) refers to the act of anointing; therefore, since there is no manifestation of what was previously non-existent (*abhūtaprādurbhāva*), it serves as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*). Alternatively, even if one were to grant that there is indeed a manifestation of what was previously non-existent, he says the following to demonstrate that this counter-example remains entirely appropriate:

Regarding the phrase "when the material cause (*prakṛti*) is not intended to be expressed," and so forth: it is not the case that every manifestation of what was previously non-existent constitutes the meaning of the suffix *cvi*; rather, it is only a specific kind. For in that context, the mention of the "material cause" will be demonstrated. The material cause is the prior state of the effect. Therefore...

Where the effect is dependent [on a cause] and the prior commencement of that effect is intended to be expressed as being in a state of becoming (*bhāvyamānatayā*), there it is "the manifestation of what was previously non-existent" (*abhūtaprādurbhāva*); that alone is the meaning of the suffix *cvī*. This is what is meant:
when the prior state of the effect is intended to be expressed, then the meaning of *cvī* occurs.

"Not when there is a desire to express the manifestation of what was previously non-existent. However, in this case, without referring to or relying upon a prior state, when a product is undertaken that did not exist before, only the mere fact of its becoming what it was not (*abhūtatadbhāva*) is intended to be expressed. Therefore, even though there is the state of "becoming what it was not," the sense of the suffix *cvi* does not apply. Hence...

This serves as a counter-example: "āḍhyīkurvanti. Here, the suffix *cvi* is applied by the rule "abhūtatadbhāve kṛbhvastiyoge" (Pāṇini 5.4.50), and the substitution of *i* for *a* occurs by the rule "asya cvau" (Pāṇini 7.4.32). [The opponent argues: "There ought to be the suffix *lyuṭ*."

Because the suffix *lyuṭ* is prescribed by the rule "ṭhkaraṇādhikaraṇayośca" (Pāṇini 3.3.117), he asks: "If it must be *lyuṭ*, then what [follows]? and replies with "And not," etc. In both cases, the form is identical and the accent is the same. First, the form is indeed undifferentiated, as in both instances there is a compound.

Because it has the sense of "eternal" (*nitya*); for in this way, there must be a compound with the *khyun* suffix and an upapada, whereas with the *lyuṭ* suffix there would be a *gati*-compound. Furthermore, due to the prohibition in [Pāṇini 6.3.66], "ṭhan-avyayasya," the *mum* augment would not occur, so there is no difference in form. Nor does the accent (*svara*) serve as a differentiator; for in the case of *khyun*—
"Wherever there would otherwise be the *nitsvara* accent, the *litsvara* accent will apply even in the case of the suffix *lyuṭ*.
The prohibition [of *lyuṭ*] by the rule *acvau* (Pāṇini 3.2.56) is made for the purpose of excluding the form *āḍhyīkaraṇa*;
thus its exclusion is effected."

If [the suffix] *khyun* occurs when there is liberation (*mukta*), then *lyuṭ* also occurs; otherwise, it would indeed occur. The sense is that since the very same form [would result], the prohibition would be redundant, which is the intended meaning. Regarding "by implication" (*arthataḥ*): not by the literal word (*śabdataḥ*). But the implication is precisely the force of the prohibition. And regarding "for the sake of what follows" (*utarārthaśca*): The sense is as follows: if one were to state the rule simply as *mukte*, then because *khyun* would apply to the word *mukta*, the suffix *lyuṭ* would also apply to it. Consequently, the form *muktakaḥ* would be produced even from the word *mukta*. Since this very same form would also be produced from the word *mucyate* (where *lyuṭ* is applied), the prohibition [of *lyuṭ*] would be useless. Therefore, the mention of *mucyamāna* is for the purpose of excluding the application of *lyuṭ* to the word *mucyate*. Furthermore, the mention of *mucyamāna* is for the sake of what follows. For if one were to state the rule as *mucyamāne*, then because *khyun* would apply to the word *mucyamāna*, the suffix *lyuṭ* would also apply to it. Consequently, the form *mucyamānakaḥ* would be produced even from the word *mucyamāna*. Since this very same form would also be produced from the word *mucyate*, the prohibition [of *lyuṭ*] would be useless. Therefore, the mention of *mucyamāna* is for the purpose of excluding the application of *lyuṭ* to the word *mucyate*. Thus, the mention of both *mucyamāna* and *mukta* is for the sake of what follows. This is the intention. Regarding "by implication": it is not by the literal word. However, the implication is precisely the force of the prohibition. And regarding "for the sake of what follows": if one were to state the rule as *mucyamāne*, then because *khyun* would apply to the word *mucyamāna*, the suffix *lyuṭ* would also apply to it. Consequently, the form *mucyamānakaḥ* would be produced even from the word *mucyamāna*. Since this very same form would also be produced from the word *mucyate*, the prohibition [of *lyuṭ*] would be useless. Therefore, the mention of *mucyamāna* is for the purpose of excluding the application of *lyuṭ* to the word *mucyate*. Thus, the mention of both *mucyamāna* and *mukta* is for the sake of what follows. This is the intention. And regarding "for the sake of what follows": if one were to state the rule as *mucyamāne*, then because *khyun* would apply to the word *mucyamāna*, the suffix *lyuṭ* would also apply to it. Consequently, the form *mucyamānakaḥ* would be produced even from the word *mucyamāna*. Since this very same form would also be produced from the word *mucyate*, the prohibition [of *lyuṭ*] would be useless. Therefore, the mention of *mucyamāna* is for the purpose of excluding the application of *lyuṭ* to the word *mucyate*. Thus, the mention of both *mucyamāna* and *mukta* is for the sake of what follows. This is the intention. And regarding "for the sake of what follows": if one were to state the rule as *mucyamāne*, then because *khyun* would apply to the word *mucyamāna*, the suffix *lyuṭ* would also apply to it. Consequently, the form *mucyamānakaḥ* would be produced even from the word *mucyamāna*. Since this very same form would also be produced from the word *mucyate*, the prohibition [of *lyuṭ*] would be useless. Therefore, the mention of *mucyamāna* is for the purpose of excluding the application of *lyuṭ* to the word *mucyate*. Thus, the mention of both *mucyamāna* and *mukta* is for the sake of what follows. This is the intention. And regarding "for the sake of what follows": if one were to state the rule as *mucyamāne*, then because *khyun* would apply to the word *mucyamāna*, the suffix *lyuṭ* would also apply to it. Consequently, the form *mucyamānakaḥ* would be produced even from the word *mucyamāna*. Since this very same form would also be produced from the word *mucyate*, the prohibition [of *lyuṭ*] would be useless. Therefore, the mention of *mucyamāna* is for the purpose of excluding the application of *lyuṭ* to the word *mucyate*. Thus, the mention of both *mucyamāna* and *mukta* is for the sake of what follows. This is the intention. And regarding "for the sake of what follows": if one were to state the rule as *mucyamāne*, then because *khyun* would apply to the word *mucyamāna*, the suffix *lyuṭ* would also apply to it. Consequently, the form *mucyamānakaḥ* would be produced even from the word *mucyamāna*. Since this very same form would also be produced from the word *mucyate*, the prohibition [of *lyuṭ*] would be useless. Therefore, the mention of *mucyamāna* is for the purpose of excluding the application of *lyuṭ* to the word *mucyate*. Thus, the mention of both *mucyamāna* and *mukta* is for the sake of what follows. This is the intention. And regarding "for the sake of what follows": if one were to state the rule as *mucyamāne*, then because *khyun* would apply to the word *mucyamāna*, the suffix *lyuṭ* would also apply to it. Consequently, the form *mucyamānakaḥ* would be produced even from the word *mucyamāna*. Since this very same form would also be produced from the word *mucyate*, the prohibition [of *lyuṭ*] would be useless. Therefore, the mention of *mucyamāna* is for the purpose of excluding the application of *lyuṭ* to the word *mucyate*. Thus, the mention of both *mucyamāna* and *mukta* is for the sake of what follows. This is the intention. And regarding "for the sake of what follows": if one were to state the rule as *mucyamāne*, then because *khyun* would apply to the word *mucyamāna*, the suffix *lyuṭ* would also apply to it. Consequently, the form *mucyamānakaḥ* would be produced even from the word *mucyamāna*. Since this very same form would also be produced from the word *mucyate*, the prohibition [of *lyuṭ*] would be useless. Therefore, the mention of *mucyamāna* is for the purpose of excluding the application of *lyuṭ* to the word *mucyate*. Thus, the mention of both *mucyamāna* and *mukta* is for the sake of what follows. This is the intention. And regarding "for the sake of what follows": if one were to state the rule as *mucyamāne*, then because *khyun* would apply to the word *mucyamāna*, the suffix *lyuṭ* would also apply to it. Consequently, the form *mucyamānakaḥ* would be produced even from the word *mucyamāna*. Since this very same form would also be produced from the word *mucyate*, the prohibition [of *lyuṭ*] would be useless. Therefore, the mention of *mucyamāna* is for the purpose of excluding the application of *lyuṭ* to the word *mucyate*. Thus, the mention of both *mucyamāna* and *mukta* is for the sake of what follows. This is the intention. And regarding "for the

He demonstrates the utility of the subsequent sūtra: in that case, when *khiṣṇuc* and *khukañ* are excluded, there must be [the application] of *tṛc* and so forth; this is the distinction. In *khyun*, the letter *kh* is for the purpose of the elision of the suffix marker (*mum*), and the letter *n* is for the purpose of the accent (*svara*).

57. *khiṣṇuc* and *khukañ* [are affixes] after the root *bhū* when the agent (*kartṛ*) is the *kāraka*. (Pāṇini 3.2.57). [The word] "when the agent is the *kāraka*" (*kartari kārake*) is used. The mention of the agent (*kartṛ-grahaṇa*) is for the purpose of excluding the instrument (*karaṇa*). Now, one might object:

"Is it not true that because [the term 'agent'] has already ceased [after the previous rule], it would not carry over [to this rule]? This is true; however, even something undesirable [might carry over].

Someone might think that just as [the operations] such as those for the rich (*āḍhya*) follow, so too does the formation of their connection; therefore, the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) is for the sake of the subsequent rule.
[The rule begins with] "because of being acute" (*udāttatvāt*) and so forth. That which is other than acute is grave (*anudātta*); by that [term].

The prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "the *iṭ* augment is not applied to an *ardhadhātuka* suffix beginning with *ṭh* that follows a monosyllabic root which is unaccented in its original enunciation" (Pāṇini 7.2.10) does not apply here. Rather, the *iṭ* must be applied by the rule concerning suffixes beginning with *bal* (Pāṇini 7.2.35); consequently, the status of having an initial *i* is established by that very rule, and thus the suffix *khiṣṇuc* need not be prescribed.

The intended meaning is that [the suffix] begins with the vowel *i*. He states the purpose for making it begin with *i* in the passage beginning with "But in the case of *nañ*" (*nañastu*). If the quality of beginning with *i* were not applied to *khiṣṇu*, then even though it would come to begin with *i* once the augment *iṭ* is added, nevertheless, because that [form] is *lākṣaṇika* (derived through a grammatical rule), [it would not be included].

In the rule *kṛtyokeṣṇuccārvādayaśca* (Pāṇini 6.2.60), there would be no inclusion by the mention of *iṣṇuc*. Consequently, in the form *anādṛḍhabhaviṣṇuḥ*, the final syllable of the subsequent member following the negative particle *nañ* would not be udātta-accented, yet this is desired. Therefore, [the term *iṣṇuc*] is not [included].
The final syllable of the subsequent member [in the compound] is acute-accented; by that means, the suffix *iṣṇuc* is made to begin with the vowel *ī*.
Now, even though it begins with *ī*, one might object that only the *iṣṇuc* prescribed by the rule *alaṃkṛñ-ādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 3.2.136) should be understood here, and not the other.
Because that [suffix] has only one *anubandha*, whereas this [suffix] has two?

There is no fault, for by the power of the pronunciation of the letter *i*, this [suffix] will also be included. The letter *kh* is for the purpose of elision (*mum*); the letter *c* is for the purpose of accent (*svara*); the letter *ñ* is for the purpose of *vṛddhi*.

58. *spṛśo'nudake kvin* (3.2.58). Regarding this, it was stated under *supi sthaḥ* (3.2.4): both *karmaṇi* and *supi* are understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Among those, in the case of transitive verbs, *karmaṇi* applies; elsewhere, [the suffix *kvip* applies].

Regarding the word *supi*: this root *spṛś* is transitive; therefore, when it is stated that "after the root *spṛś*, provided there is a *subanta* [nominal] as an *upapada* other than *udaka*," one might think there is a contradiction with what was previously stated. Anticipating this, he says "But surely... and so forth. The resolution is given by the words "This is not so... and so forth. But how, then, [is the rule applied] when there is the mention of the agent (*kartṛ*)?

Since the sense of accumulation (pracaya) is understood to belong to the agent (kartṛ), he says "in the case of a mere inflected word" (*subantamātre*) and so forth, to show that when an inflected word is the subordinate term (*upapada*), the suffix is obtained. When there is merely an inflected word as the subordinate term, one sense of accumulation occurs with the agent as the subordinate term, while another occurs with the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth as the subordinate term.

In that case, since there is a distinction [between the suffixes], an accumulation of the agent—which is differentiated by the distinction of its connection to them—is obtained. For example, in *ghṛtaspṛk*, [the rule] "the *k* of a *kvip* suffix" (*kvinpratyayasya kuḥ*) and so forth applies. If it were stated simply as "the *k* of a *kvip* suffix" (*kvipratyayasya kuḥ*), there would be the inclusion of the *kvip* suffix as well; therefore, the letter *n* is appended [to the technical name].

The letter *n* in *prakṛti* does not have the meaning of "original" (*ādyaudātta*), because it is a single vowel (*ekāc*) and is already established by its own accent. The letter *k* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa*, and the letter *v* is for the purpose of qualifying [the rule] "ṭhe-rapṛktasya" (Pāṇini 6.1.67).

59. *ṛtvigdadhṛksragdiguṣṇigañcuyujikruñcāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.59). [The suffix *kvip* is applied after the roots] *yaj*, *dhṛ*, *sraj*, *diś*, *uṣṇih*, *añc*, *yuj*, and *kruñc*. [Example: *ṛtau yajati* ("He sacrifices at the proper season"). This means he sacrifices during the seasons such as spring (*vasanta*) and so forth; that sacrifice in which a season is the deity is called an *ṛtu-yajña*, and he performs that sacrifice. Alternatively, it means "he sacrifices impelled by the season. In whichever sacrifice...

"Season (*ṛtu*) is the motivator; one sacrifices being motivated by that season. In this view, the suffix *kvi* is prescribed as being elided immediately after it has been introduced. Regarding "priest (*ṛtvij*)," there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) due to its inclusion in the *yajādi* group (Pāṇini 6.1.15). "It should be understood in whatever way possible" means by any means whatsoever.
He shows that the word must be derived in this manner, and that the meaning of its individual parts is not the governing factor.

[The rule] "the final syllable is shown to be udātta by nipātana" is for the purpose of overriding the fixed accent. Regarding "dadhṛk": there is the substitution of *u* for the radical vowel by Pāṇini 7.4.66 (*urat*), followed by the *halādi-śeṣaḥ* (retention of the first consonant) by 7.4.60.

"The substitution of *jaś* (the voiced unaspirated stop) and the substitution of *ṣatva* (the sibilant) are prescribed as irregularities (*nipātana*). This is because [otherwise], due to the prohibition in the rule "sātpadādyoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.109), these substitutions would not apply. [The word] *uṣṇik* is derived from the root *ṣṇiha* (meaning "affection") with the suffix *kvip*, as in "it causes one to feel affection" (*utsnihyati*). This is established by the statement beginning with "because of its mention together with [other words formed by] irregular prescriptions" (*nipātanaiḥ saha nirdeśāt*).

The mention of these [words] along with the *nipātana*s (irregular formations) is for the purpose that they too should undergo certain non-technical (*alākṣaṇika*) operations. Therefore, in these cases, certain non-technical operations occur. This, however, is the non-technical [operation]: that which occurs even when the verb is transitive (*sakarmaka*), provided only a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) is the attendant word (*upapada*). For example: *prāṅ*.

Thus: by the rule *ugidacāṃ sarvanāmasthāne 'dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.70), the augment *num* is applied; then, by *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* (6.1.68) and *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* (8.2.23), there is elision [of the final consonant]; and for the letter *n*, as before, there is *kutva* (the substitution of *g*). Regarding the word *kevalāt*: even though the object (*karman*) exists, it is under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of *supi*.

It occurs from the root alone, without an *upapada*, because of the rule for *nipātana* stating "with *saha*" (*saheti nirdeśāt*), or by virtue of the power of the prescription of the *kvin* suffix. For if there were an *upapada*, the *kvip* suffix would have to apply by the rule *sadādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.61). [The phrase] "from that which has an *upapada," etc., means that the *kvip* suffix does not occur after *yuji* when it has an *upapada*.
Or rather, there is indeed a distinction: since the substitution of *k* for *c* and *j* by the rule "ṭhcoḥ kuḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.30) is already established,

the prescription of *kvip* is meaningful for the purpose of applying the substitution of *k* to the letter *n* after the augment *num* has been added by the rule "yujerasamāse" (Pāṇini 7.1.71) when there is no upapada.

60. *tyadādiṣu dṛśo'nālocane kañ ca* (3.2.60). Here, "non-observation" (*anālocana*) is intended to mean mere visual cognition. If the root *dṛś-* does not apply there [in the sense of non-observation], then this suffix occurs, and not otherwise. Examples: *tyādṛk*, *tyādṛśaḥ*.

While the rule *dṛgdṛśavatuṣu* (6.3.89) is being carried over, the substitution of *ā* [for the final vowel] in a pronominal stem occurs by the rule *ā sarvanāmnaḥ* (6.3.91). Regarding the statement that "the letter *ñ* in *kañ* is for the purpose of specification in the rule *tiḍḍhāṇañ...*"—if the letter *ñ* were not added to *kañ*, then the letter *n* would have to be added for the sake of making the word oxytone (*udātta*). And thus:

The suffix *kan* must be applied in this way [by the rule *kañ kany-evaṃ* 4.1.15]. Consequently, if it were stated thus, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would also undesirably apply in the case of *yādikā*, derived from *yāvadibhyaḥ kan* (5.4.29); therefore, the letter *ñ* must be included as a qualifier for that [suffix]. Now, one might object: since the root *dṛś* denotes the act of seeing, [the forms] *tādṛk* and *tādṛśa*— [...are formed by the addition of the suffixes *kvun* and *śas* respectively.]

In such instances as these, the action of seeing (*darśana-kriyā*) certainly exists; for, in their etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), teachers establish the suffix by instructing that one sees in such a manner.
The *vṛtti* (the derivative form) has the same meaning as the sentence, and that action of seeing has the sense of cognition (*jñāna*).

To the question, "How then does the root *dṛś* function here in the sense of 'not perceiving'?", he says: "For words such as *tādṛk* and others belong to the class of conventional (*rūḍhi*) words," and so forth. In conventional words, one must not rely on the meaning of the individual parts;
rather, they function by means of the collective meaning of the whole. For this very reason, the meaning of the individual parts is not adopted here.

However, even though the etymological meaning exists, the meaning of the individual components (*avayavārtha*) is not employed [in the conventional sense], as for example in "a tiger" (*vyāghra*) because it "sniffs from afar" (*vyājighrati*), and so forth. Therefore, although the action of seeing is employed in the sentence for the sake of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), nevertheless, that [action] does not exist at all in the derivative formation (*vṛtti*). To explain:

From words such as *tādṛk* and *tādṛśa*, a cognition arises with respect to an object that is similar [to another], but not with respect to the act of seeing; therefore, it is logical that the root *dṛś* functions in the sense of "not perceiving" (*anālocana*).

Regarding the statement, "It should be stated that [the suffixes] also occur after *samāna* and *anya*": the meaning is that this sense—that the suffixes *kvip* and *kan* occur after the verbal root *dṛś-* when the words *samāna* and *anya* are used as accompanying words (*upapada*)—must be explained. In this regard, the following is the explanation: from the previous sūtra, here...

The particle *ca* is understood [from the previous rule], and its function here is that of a conjunction (*samuccaya*). By virtue of this, the two suffixes will apply when the words *samāna* and *anya* are used as upapadas with the root *dṛś*. Thus, we have the form *sadṛśaḥ*;
for while the term *samānasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.84) is being carried over, the rule *dṛgdṛśavatuṣu* (6.3.89) applies.
The intrinsic nature.
61. *satsūdviṣadruhaduhayujavidabhidacchidajinīrājām upasarge 'pi kvip* (Pāṇini 3.2.61).
However, the mention of the word "object" (*karma*) does not apply from this rule onwards, starting from *spṛśo 'nudake kvin* (3.2.58).

"It is engaged in activity" (*vyāpriyate*). Now, one might object: "But there are also verbal roots that are transitive; so why is it not said that [the self] is engaged in activity? The thought is this: in rules such as *spṛśo'nudake kvin* (Pāṇini 3.2.58), the term *kartari* (3.2.57) is understood to follow; that [term] is for the purpose of including a plurality of agents.

It is understood that, by that [rule], the term *sup* is operative, not the term *karman*. For in this way, an accumulation of agents (*kartṛpracaya*) is obtained, and not otherwise. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *upasarga*?
Since prefixes (*upasarga*) are indeed only those ending in *sup*, the mention of *upasarga* is already included by the mention of *sup* itself.

He says, "The mention of *upasarga* [in the rule] is for the sake of making it known that elsewhere, when there is a mention of *sub*, the mention of *upasarga* does not occur. He asks, "Where else, when there is a mention of *sub*, does the mention of *upasarga* not occur?
and he replies, "In the rule *vadaḥ supi kyap ca*. But surely, in the rule *vadaḥ supi kyap*...

In the rule *ca* (3.1.106), the term *anupasarga* ("without a prefix") is understood to carry over from the preceding rule *gadamadacarayamaścānupasarge* (3.1.100). Alternatively, the inclusion of the term *upasarga* here is for the purpose of indicating that the term *upasarga* need not be carried over [into subsequent rules].

Others say that [the mention of *anudake*] must be made for the purpose of demonstrating an alternative interpretation (*vikalpa*). However, on the point of "filling up" (*pūraṇa*), they say: the author of the Vṛtti shows that this is merely an indication of the direction of the purpose of the *jñāpaka*.
But this is clearly the purpose of the *jñāpaka*: namely, [the rule] "after the root *spṛś*, *kvin* is applied when not followed by *udaka*" (*spṛśo'nudake kvin*).

In this context [of rule 3.2.58], because of the governing authority of the term *supi* (3.2.4), if there were no indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the inclusion of the prefix (*upasarga*), it would apply even when the prefix ends in a *sup*-suffix—as in *upaspṛśati* and *saṃspṛśati*. It does not so apply due to this very indicator. As for the phrase "by way of association" (*sāhacaryāt*) and so forth: if this [term] *sū*...

The root *dhā* deviates from being an *adādika* (belonging to the second class), but the root *dviṣ* in the sense of "displeasure" (DhP 1013) does not deviate; therefore, by association with this [latter], the root *sū* belonging to the *adādika* class— specifically *ṣūṅ* in the sense of "the delivery of a fetus by living beings" (DhP 3031)— is understood, and not *ṣū* in the sense of "impelling."
This refers to the root *dhā* belonging to the Taudādika class (Dhātupāṭha 1408). Now, one might object:
"Is it not the case that because of its association with the Taudādika roots, this [root *sā*] is also understood by means of the root *sad*? This is not so;
for just as the root *sū* deviates from being Taudādika, so too does *sad*. Therefore...

Since [the root] is listed among the *bhvādi* roots, how could there be a reference here to the *tudādi* root by virtue of association with it? Regarding the rule "not after *su*" (*na suvateḥ*), this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the verbal root whose form begins with *sū* in the *adādi* class. [The root is] *pṣūṅ* (or *sūṅ*) in the sense of "procreation of living beings" (*prāṇiprasave*).

It is also not appropriate to include this [root] *dā* belonging to the *divādi* class; for the reasoning is the same. [The phrase] "the inclusion of both" is used because no distinction is specified. [The phrase] "not of that which means 'to obtain'" refers to the root *vidlṛ* meaning "to obtain" (*dhā.pā.* 1432). [This applies] to the letter *akāra*.

"Because it was intended to be so stated. Here, the reason for not including the root meaning "to obtain" is that in the rule *vidaḥ*, the pronunciation with the long vowel *ā* (i.e., *vidā*) is intended; therefore, [the rule applies] to the root *vid* ending in *ā* as listed in the *gaṇa*.
From the recitation [of the root], that very one is understood, not the one ending in *ḷ*.
Regarding "śṛciṣat": *pṣad* / *sadḷ* (DhP 854) has the meaning of "falling apart. Regarding "mitradhruk": *druh* (DhP 1197) means "desire to harm" (*jighāṃsā*). Or...

In *druhamuha*, the letter *k* is applied by [Pāṇini 8.2.33]; the substitution of *bhaṣ* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.37], *ṭhekāco baśo bhaṣ*, and so forth. In *godhuk*, [the root] *duha* (meaning "to milk") is used; the substitution of *gh* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.32], *dāderdhātorghaḥ*. In *aśvayuk*, [the substitution of *k* occurs] by [Pāṇini 8.2.30], *coḥ kuḥ*.
(8.2.30) Thus, by *kutva*, the letter *ga* is changed; as before, it becomes *ka*. [The form] is "śatrujit.
[Regarding the rule] "hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk" (6.1.71): [the question] "How is there *ṇatva* here?
[is answered: by the rule "pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām agaḥ" (8.4.3), which prescribes [ṇatva] when a name (*saṃjñā*) is formed.

The sense is that, because it is a *natva* [nasal], there should not be the designation *asaṃjñā* here. Regarding "samrāṭ": from the root *rājṛ* in the sense of "shining" (DhP 822), the substitution of *c* for *ṛ* by *vraścabhrasja* (8.2.36) results in the letter *ṭ*; then the letter *m* is substituted by *mo rājisamaḥ kvau* (8.3.25). The letter *k* in *kvip* [is for the sake of indicating the elision].

The [augment] *guṇ* and *vṛddhi* are prohibited. The letter *p* is for the sake of the *tuk* augment. By the rule "ṭh-veḥ apṛktasya" (Pāṇini 6.1.67), there is the elision of the letter *v*. The letter *i* is for the sake of including the general term "apṛkta" in the rule "ṭh-veḥ apṛktasya."
62. *bhaj* takes the suffix *ṇvi*. (Pāṇini 3.2.62). Thus, *ardhabhāk*. [In this form,] by the rule *ṭherapṛktasya* (6.1.67), there is the elision of the letter *v*.

By the principle of "that which is caused by the elision of an affix" (*pratyayalopalakṣaṇa*), there is the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the penultimate vowel according to *ata upadhāyāḥ* (7.2.116). Furthermore, by *coḥ kuḥ* (8.2.30), [the *j* is changed to *g*].

Thus, there is the substitution of *k* for *t*. The letter *ṇ* is for the purpose of effecting vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*). The letter *i* is for the purpose of including the general category in the rule "when an apṛkta suffix beginning with *ṭh* follows" (Pāṇini 6.1.67).

63. *sahaḥ* [is substituted for *han*] in the Vedic language. (3.2.63) As in *jalāṣāṭ*. By the rule *ho ḍhaḥ* (8.2.31), there is the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha*; this undergoes *jaśtva*—becoming *ḍa*;
and by the rule *vāvasāne* (8.4.56), it becomes *ṭa*.
64. *vahaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.64). [The example is] *pṛṣṭhavāṭ*. As before, there is vṛddhi; then the substitution of *ḍha*, *jaś*-ness (*da*), and *cartva*-ness (*ta*).
The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows, so that the term *bahu* may be carried over (*anuvṛtti*) into the subsequent [sūtra], but not [the term] *sahi*.
For when there is a single compound with *bhūta*, there would be the recurrence of both [terms].

65. The suffix *ñyuṭ* is applied after verbal roots ending in *kavarga* (velars), *pa*, *r*, *ś*, *ṣ*, or *s*, when used in the sense of "the act of" (*parīṣya*) or "one who performs" (*parīṣin*). (Pāṇini 3.2.65) Since the previous rule [3.2.64] would have already applied the suffix *cvī* in these cases, this rule prescribes *ñyuṭ*. The letter *ṭ* serves the purpose of introducing the feminine suffix *ṅīp*; the letter *ñ* serves the purpose of vowel accentuation and the purpose of causing *vṛddhi* strengthening. The suffix is simply *yu*. By the rule *ṭhyuvoranākau* (7.1.1), it is replaced by *ana*. Thus, for example, from the root *kṛ*, we derive *kāraṇam* ("the act of doing"). From *pā*, *pānam*; from *rā*, *rāyaṇam*; from *śās*, *śāsanam*; from *ṣas*, *sāsanaṃ*; from *su*, *sāvanam*. In the sense of "one who performs," from *kṛ*, *kāraṇaḥ*; from *pā*, *pānaḥ*; from *rā*, *rāyaṇaḥ*; from *śās*, *śāsanaḥ*; from *ṣas*, *sāsanaḥ*; from *su*, *sāvanaḥ*. In the feminine, *kāraṇī*, *pānī*, etc., are formed with *ṅīp*. From *dā*, *dānam*; from *dhā*, *dhānam*; from *mā*, *mānam*; from *hā*, *hānam*; from *jyā*, *jyānam*; from *stṛ*, *staraṇam*; from *kṛt*, *kartanam*; from *vṛt*, *vartanam*; from *bhṛt*, *bharaṇam*; from *cit*, *cetanam*; from *yat*, *yatanam*; from *mat*, *mananam*; from *vad*, *vadanam*; from *svap*, *svapanam*; from *jan*, *jananam*; from *han*, *ghātanam*; from *gam*, *gamanam*; from *śak*, *śakanam*; from *labh*, *lambhanam*; from *śuc*, *śocanam*; from *duh*, *dohanam*; from *lih*, *lehanam*; from *pac*, *pācanam*; from *tyaj*, *tyajanam*; from *yaj*, *yajanam*; from *vah*, *vahanam*; from *bhañj*, *bhañjanam*; from *chid*, *chedanam*; from *bhid*, *bhedanam*; from *rudh*, *rodhanam*; from *bandh*, *bandhanam*; from *krī*, *krāyaṇam*; from *mī*, *māyanam*; from *lū*, *lāvanam*; from *pū*, *pāvanam*; from *stṛ*, *stāranam*; 66. *anantaḥpādam* in the sense of *havye* (Pāṇini 3.2.66).
Regarding the rule *ṭhanantaḥpādam*: the word *antaḥ* has the same meaning as the word *madhya* (middle).
Thus, *antaḥpādam* means "in the middle of a foot. [This is an example of] the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti...* (Pāṇini 2.1.6).
By such [rules] as these, there is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of a case-ending: *na antaḥpādam* = *anantaḥpādam*.
And since "of the root *vah*" (*vaheḥ*) is the subject under discussion, this is understood as a specific qualification of that very [root]; therefore, he says:

"provided that *vah* occurs outside the foot (*anantaḥpādaṃ ced vahirvartate*). Because the word "in the Veda" (*chandasi*) is understood from the previous context, the word "foot" (*pāda*) [is understood].
It causes the *ṛk*-pāda to be awakened; the meaning is that no external [element] occurs within the middle of the *ṛk*-pāda.
In the counter-example, because an external [element] occurs within the middle of the pāda, by that very reason, only the suffix *ṇvi* applies according to [Pāṇini 3.2.64]: *vahaśca*.
67. *jana-sana-khana-krām-gamaḥ viṭ* (3.2.67). "The mention of both" [is intended], because no distinction is specified. "In the same way," etc.:
just as there is the mention of both for the two immediately preceding verbal roots, so too for these two.
The meaning is "of both the suffix *sambhava* and the word *artha*. Regarding the statement, "The letter *ṭ* is for the purpose of preventing the general reference [to other suffixes]":

if the letter *ṭ* were not present, then in the rule *ṭhe-r-apṛktasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.67), this [suffix *ṭhak*] alone would be included by means of the paribhāṣā concerning single indicatory letters (*ekānubandha-paribhāṣā*), and not the suffixes beginning with *vij*. However, when the letter *ṭ* is present, this [suffix *ṭhak*] is also included.
The inclusion of all [the suffixes] is justified because they are all followed by a double consonant (*dvayanubandhakatvāt*). And [it is said], "for the purpose of distinction" (*viśeṣaṇārthaśca*):

in the rule *viḍvanoranunāsikasyāt* (P. 6.4.41), the letter *ṭ* is for the sake of distinction; for if it were stated simply as *vinoḥ*, there would be the inclusion of *kvip* and others as well, and likewise...

In such cases as "cākarot" and so forth, there would be elision [of the augment]. Regarding "abjāḥ": it is born in the waters (*apsu*), thus "abjāḥ. Similarly, "gojāḥ. He wins the cow (*gām sanoti*), thus "goṣāḥ"; the sibilant change (*ṣatvam*) occurs by the rule "sanoteranaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.106). He wins a man (*naram sanoti*), thus "nṛṣāḥ. He digs a hole (*vilam khanati*), thus...
"Dadhikrāḥ" means "he who strides through curd. "Agregāḥ" means "he who goes at the front.

In these cases, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending according to *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.3.14). In all instances, the suffix *apṛkta* is elided by *verapṛktasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.67), and the vowel substitution (*ātvam*) occurs by *viḍvanor anuṇām* (Pāṇini 6.4.41).
[The commentary states: "Since it is already established by the preceding rule alone," because the word *kravya* is devoid of meaning [in this context].

[Question: "How then [is the word] *kravyādaḥ* [formed]? [Answer: The intention is that if [the rule] were a statement intended to subvert the *vā'sarūpa* rule (P. 3.1.94), then by the rule beginning with *kṛtavikṛta-* (P. 3.2.42), the suffix *aṇ* is applied when the words *kṛta* or *vikṛta* are the governing words (*upapada*), but not when the word *kravya* is the governing word. [Objection: If, then, the suffix *aṇ* is applied when the words *kṛta* or *vikṛta* are the governing words, how...

The word *kravyāda* is established; one might argue that it ought to be *kṛtavikṛtāda*, to which he replies with "And of that," and so forth. Now, if the suffix *aṇ* is applied when the words *kṛta* or *vikṛta* are the subordinate members (*upapada*), and the form *kravya* is substituted for that subordinate member, the resulting form is [correct]; however, if the suffix *aṇ* is applied when the word *kravya* itself is the subordinate member...
That being so, what distinction is there here such that the suffix *ñ* is prohibited when the word *kravya* occurs as a subordinate term?
To this he says: "cooked or uncooked," and so forth. By this he demonstrates the difference in meaning: for one who eats cooked meat (*pakvamāṃsa*) is indeed a *kravyāda* (meat-eater).
It is said: he who eats raw flesh is called a *kravyād* (flesh-eater).

70. *duhaḥ kabghaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.70). [The suffixes] *kap* and *gha* are added after the root *duh*. Examples: *kāmadudhā* ("yielding desires"), *gharmadughā* ("yielding the sacrificial milk"). [Derivation: She who milks out desire is *kāmadughā*; she who milks out the *gharma* [milk] is *gharmadughā*.

71. *mantre śvetavahokthaśaspuroḍāśo ṇvin* (Pāṇini 3.2.71). [The commentary says: "From these," meaning from the composite bases consisting of the root and the upapada, such as *śvetavah* and so forth. It means that these composite forms of root and upapada are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*). Such forms as *śvetavāḥ* and so on are thus established. What [is the point]?
Furthermore, why are these formed by the combination of a verbal root (*dhātu*) and an affix (*upapada*), rather than being taught as separate affixes and roots? To this he says:
"For the sake of accomplishing non-technical (non-lakṣaṇika) operations," as in the case of *śvetavāh* and so forth, [where the suffix] *ṭhak* [is applied]. *Avayāḥ*.

In the case of *śvetavāḥ* and *puroḍāś*, the substitution of *ru* is prescribed by nipātana. In *ukthaśāḥ*, the substitution of *ru* indeed occurs by the rule *sasajuṣo ruḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.66). Regarding *śaṃsateḥ*: this refers to the root *śaṃsu* (Dhātupāṭha 728), meaning "to praise. The addition of the marker *ṇ* in the suffix *ṇvin* is for the purpose of making the first syllable udātta.
The addition of the marker *ṇ* is for the purpose of [triggering] *vṛddhi*. The letter *i* is for the sake of distinguishing [the suffix] by the rule "ṭhe-rapṛktasya" (Pāṇini 6.1.67).
Regarding the phrase "of *śvetavāha* and so forth": if this is indeed stated, then there is no need for the [separate mention of] "age" (*avayāḥ*).
Is it by means of this statement, "śvetavāḥ puroḍāśca," for the sake of the substitution of *ru*, that its lengthening occurs?

But is it not the case that the lengthening is already established by the rule "ṭhatvasantasya cādhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.14)? [The answer is: It is for the sake of those cases where it is not established by that [rule]. Where, then, is it not established by that?

In the case of the vocative singular (*sambuddhau*): if that is the case, then the suffix *ḍas* need not be mentioned; for by that very irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the absence of the suffix *asant* (i.e., the elision of the final vowel) will be prescribed for words such as *śvetavāh* and others? This is not so;

it has already been stated that in the vocative singular, the lengthening [of the vowel] would not occur. Now, if it is argued that the absence of *asant* will be prescribed by irregular derivation...

It must be stated [that the suffix is *ḍas*]; and if that were so, then in the case of *śvetavobhyām*, the substitution of *u* would occur. Therefore, *ḍas* must be prescribed, and a formal exception (*nipātana*) must also be made.
72. *ave yajaḥ* | (3.2.72) "The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows," it is said; so that in the subsequent sūtra, only *yaj* may continue to apply.

73. *vijupe chandasi* (3.2.73). [The suffix] *upayaḍ* [is applied]. By *vraścādinā* (8.2.36), there is the substitution of *ṣ*; as before, by *jaśtva*, it becomes *ḍ*. [Regarding] *ubhayatva*: when the suffix *tva* follows, by *khari ca* (8.4.55), [the rule applies].

The *ṭ* in *cartvam* is the letter *ṭ*. Now, one might object: since the term "in a mantra" (*mantre*) from Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.210 will be carried over [by anuvṛtti], and a mantra is indeed nothing other than Vedic verse (*cchandas*), for what purpose is the mention of "Vedic verse" (*cchandas*) made? To this he says: "The mention of 'Vedic verse' is for the sake of the Brāhmaṇas. For if the mention of "Vedic verse" were absent, then even by the continued application of the mention of "mantra," [the rule would apply] to the Brāhmaṇas as well.
It would not [apply], for by the mention of "mantra" the Brāhmaṇa is not included; because that is a different type of text.

The word "Brāhmaṇa" applies to a specific type of text consisting of an explanation of mantras, but not to the mantra itself. Therefore, the term "in Vedic (chandas)" was stated so that [the rule] might also apply to the Brāhmaṇa.

Regarding the statement "the addition of the marker *c* [is for the purpose of] making it marked" (*ṭhvicaścitkaraṇam*), etc.: if the marker *c* were not added, this [suffix *kvip*] would have only one marker (*ekānubandha*).

Consequently, in the rule *verapṛktasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.67), by the paribhāṣā concerning that which has a single marker (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 52), only this [suffix *kvip*] would be included, and not *kvip* and the others. But when the marker *c* is added...
Since there is no one who is bound by truth alone, all are included.

74. *āto maninkvanibvanipaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.74). In the suffix *manin*, the letter *n* is for the purpose of making the first syllable udātta. In *kvanip* and *vanip*, the letter *p* is for the purpose of making them anudātta, and the letter *i* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). In *kvanip*, the letter *p* is for the purpose of the grammatical operations pertaining to *pit* suffixes; the letter *c* [is for the purpose of including it in the *caṅ* group].

The particle *ca* serves the purpose of attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*). One who gives well is "Sudāmā"; the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule "sarvanāmasthāne ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.8). One who stands like a horse is "Aśvatthāmā";
the substitution of *ta* for *sa* occurs because the word belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group. One who holds well is "Sudhīvā."

"He who drinks well" is *supīvā*; by Pāṇini 6.4.66, the substitution of *i* occurs for the roots beginning with *dhū*. "He who gives abundantly" is *bhūridāvā*. "He who drinks ghee" is *ghṛtapāvā*. "He who drinks sweet water" is *kīlālapāḥ*.
75. *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante* (Pāṇini 3.2.75). Regarding *suśarmā*: the root *śṛ* (meaning "to injure," Dhātupāṭha 1488) is analyzed as "one who cuts well" (*śobhanaṃ śṛṇāti*).
Regarding *prātaritvā*: when the word *prātaḥ* is the governing word (*upapada*) for the root *iṇ*, the suffix *kvanip* is applied; [the rule] *hrasvasya...* [applies].

The augment *tuk* is applied by [Pāṇini 6.1.71] *piti kṛti*. Thus, "vijāvā. The root *janī* in the sense of "manifestation" (Dhātupāṭha 1149); from *vijāyate*, the suffix *vanip* is added, and by [Pāṇini 6.4.41] *viḍ-vo-r-anunāsikasya*, there is the substitution of *ā* for the nasal. Thus, "agregāvā. The roots *gmlṛ* and *sṛplṛ* mean "to go."

As before, there is the substitution of *ā*. Regarding "ṭhreḍasi": from the root *ṛṣ* (meaning "to injure," DhP 694), as before, there is the substitution of the voiced stop (*jaś*), resulting in the letter *ḍ*. "The mention of *dṛśi* is for the sake of following actual usage"; therefore, when it is understood through usage, wherever they are seen [in the grammatical tradition].

These suffixes, such as *manin* and others, are valid only in those specific instances; therefore, nothing entirely new is being established here. By this, it is implied that these suffixes are not to be applied universally. If they were seen after other roots as well, the preceding sūtra would be rendered useless, since one could simply say that *manin* and the others are seen after all verbal roots.

Is this to be stated? It is not necessary; for those [suffixes] necessarily occur after verbal roots ending in long ā (ākārānta), whereas they occur only optionally after those not ending in ā. Furthermore, the preceding rule applies to the Vedic language (chandas), whereas we [apply it] even to the common language (bhāṣā).

76. *kvip* also. (Pāṇini 3.2.76) [The rule] "after *nṛ*, *ṣṭran*, and [roots] with no prefix (*an-upapada*)"—this is obtained through the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *api*, which signifies the exclusion of all conditions (*sarva-upādhi-vyabhicāra*). Examples: *ukhāsrat*, *praṇardhat*.

Thus: [the roots] *sraṃsu* and *dhvaṃsu* are used in the sense of "falling down" (*avasraṃsane*). By the rule *aniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24), there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*). By the rule *vasusraṃsudhvaṃsvanaḍuhāṃ daḥ* (8.2.72), there is the substitution of *da*. By the rule *vāḍavasāne* (8.4.56), there is the substitution of *ca* (cerebralization). Thus: *vāhābhraṭ*.
The root *bhranśu* means "to fall down" (Dhātupāṭha 1225). By the rule *vraścādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 8.2.36), the substitution of *ṣ* occurs;
as before, there is the substitution of *jaś* (the dental *n*), followed by *cartva* (the retroflex *ṇ*). Then, by the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 6.3.37), a long vowel is substituted.

77. *sthaḥ ka ca* (3.2.77). [The commentary states: "For the purpose of subverting that which subverts," and so forth. The suffix *ac* subverts *ka* and *kvip*; this [suffix *ka*] is for the purpose of subverting even that (*ac*). The subverting power of *ac*, however, is established by the rule *śami dhātoḥ saṃjñāyām* (3.2.14).

In this context, there is the mention of the verbal root (*dhātu*). Indeed, that [mention] is made for the purpose that, even where an exception (*apavāda*) has been prescribed, when *śam* is the attendant word (*upapada*), the suffix *a* alone should occur in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*). And thus, if the rule "after the root *sthā*, when followed by *ka* or *ca*" were not stated, then just as in the case of the root *kṛ* with respect to the causal and other senses...

The mention of the root (*dhātu*) is understood to serve the purpose of prohibiting [the application of suffixes] by *ṭ*, and likewise to override both *kan* and *kvip* even in the case of the root *sthā*. This being so, when *śam* is the upapada and it is a name (*saṃjñā*), only *ac* would apply to *sthā*, and not *kan* or *kvip*. However, when this rule (*yoga*) is present, both [suffixes] occur, overriding *ac*.
In the word "ṭhśaṃsthaḥ," there is the elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule "āto lopa iṭi ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.64).
78. *supyajātau ṇinistācchīlye* (Pāṇini 3.2.78). For example:
*brāhmaṇānām antrayitā* ("one who habitually addresses Brahmins"). [The root] *matri* (meaning "to speak secretly") belongs to the Dhātupāṭha (1679);
by the rule *idito num dhātoḥ* (7.1.58), the augment *num* is added; then the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied (as it belongs to the *curādi* group); from that, the suffix *tṛn* is added.
(3.2.135) Thus, the suffix *tṛn* is used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*). Regarding the rule beginning with *supi*:
one might ask, "Since *supi* (3.2.4) is already being carried over [by anuvṛtti], is the repeated mention of *sub* not redundant? It is not redundant;
for the previous mention of *sub* was connected with the prefix (*upasarga*), and therefore, if that were to be carried over [without modification], [the rule would not apply].
Its recurrence would also occur. Therefore, the term *sub* is mentioned again for the purpose of excluding the prefixes (*upasarga*), as in the rule "after *huta* and *prati*" and so forth.
This is the purpose of the mention of *sub*.

Because [the suffix] is intended to prevent the application of prefixes (*upasarga*), it does not apply when a prefix is present; therefore, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*)—that is, an explanation (*pratipādana*)—must be made regarding the root *sṛ* when preceded by *ut* and *prati*, with *āṅ* as the subordinate word (*upapada*). In this regard, the explanation is as follows: "also from others... (*anyebhyo 'pi*).

From the rule *dṛśyante* (Pāṇini 3.2.75), the word *api* is carried over here as well, signifying that [the application of the suffix] occurs even when there is deviation from all qualifying conditions (*upādhi*); therefore, in the example *udāsāriṇyaḥ*, the suffix *ṇini* occurs after a prefix (*upasarga*).
Regarding the rule "sādhukāriṇi ca" (Pāṇini 3.2.135): this introduction is for the purpose of excluding the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*).
By the word *ca* ("and"), the phrase "upasaṃkhyānam" ("supplementation") is drawn over from the previous rule; its meaning is precisely that of supplementation.

As for the supplementation itself: one should understand it by relying on the particle *api* as before, in the sense of the deviation [of the suffix] from all qualifying conditions (*sarvopādhi-vyabhicāra*).

It must be so understood. Or rather— since the author, having stated "tacchīla" (having that as one's habit) in the rule *tacchīlataddharmatatsādhukāriṣu* (Pāṇini 3.2.134), additionally includes the term "tatsādhukāri" (one who performs it well),
he thereby indicates that the suffix *ṇini* occurs even when denoting excellence (*sādhukārin*), despite the absence of habitual action (*atācchīlya*).

Regarding the rule *brahmaṇi vadaḥ*: this introduction [of the suffix] is either for the purpose of excluding the sense of habitual action (*atācchīlya*) or for the purpose of expressing a genus (*jāti*). It is not for the purpose of preventing the application of the "non-identical" (*vā'sarūpa*) rule, because in the case of habitual action or when not denoting a genus, it is already established by the preceding rule. Thus, one who speaks the Veda is called *brahmavādī*. The letter *ṇ* in the suffix *ṇini* is for the purpose of causing vṛddhi (vowel strengthening).
The second *i* is for the purpose of protecting the *n* from being designated as an *it*.

79. *kartaryupamāne* | (3.2.79) Since suffixes are prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*) after a verbal root, it is understood that the agent expressed by the subordinate word (*upapada*) is the object of comparison; thus he says: "the agent of the subordinate word," and so forth. The agent expressed by the subordinate word is the "agent of the subordinate word" (*upapadakartṛ*).

This is a compound with the middle term elided (*madhyamapadalopī samāsaḥ*), following the *śākapārthiva* class and others. Regarding "ṭhuṣṭrakrośī": the root *kruś* (meaning "to call out" and "to weep," Dhātupāṭha 856). Regarding "ṭhdhvāṅkṣarāvī": the root *ru* (meaning "sound," Dhātupāṭha 1034). This [formation] is begun for the sake of meaning other than habitual action (*atācchīlya*), or for the sake of expressing a genus (*jāti*); for if it were habitual action (*tācchīlya*) and not a genus, [the suffix would be formed differently].
And because it is already established by the preceding [rule].
Regarding "bhakṣayati": the root *bhakṣ* meaning "to eat" belongs to the curādigaṇa (DhP 1557).
Regarding the rule *vrate* (Pāṇini 3.2.80),

the statement "this is a condition pertaining to the entire complex" (*samudāyopādhi*) refutes the suspicion that it might be a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix. For if it were a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix, then [the agent] would have to be restricted to the act of *vrata* alone.

Otherwise, the suffix would apply to Devadatta himself, and not to that which possesses [the root-meaning]. By the rule "dhātūpapada" (Pāṇini 3.1.92) and so forth, he shows that the vow is a condition for the entire complex [of the verbal form]. "When there is the possibility of acting according to one's desire, there is a restriction.
Acting according to one's desire means proceeding according to one's will; when such a possibility exists, there is a restriction.

Since there is no fixed rule, when one has reached the state of engaging in sleeping and eating according to one's desire in a general sense, this [rule] excludes that from other objects and applies to specific cases such as a bare ground (*sthaṇḍila*);
therefore, it is established as a restriction (*niyama*). And here, two kinds of restriction are possible: "one sleeps on the bare ground,"...

Or it may be of such a form as "he eats only what is not *śrāddha*"; or it may be of such a form as "he sleeps only on bare ground and eats only what is not *śrāddha*. In that case, regarding the former restriction (*niyama*), as soon as he does not sleep on bare ground or does not eat what is not *śrāddha*, a breach of the vow (*vratalopa*) would ensue.
Therefore, considering that the second restriction is logical, he says: "When there is a bed," and so forth.

81. *bahulam ābhīkṣṇye* | (3.2.81) "Ābhīkṣṇya is repetition (*paunaḥpunyam*). This means that the state of occurring again and again is "repetition"; for indeclinables, there is elision of the *ṭi* suffix before any *bha*-ending. Its intended meaning is simply "frequent practice."

Thus, that is "repetition" (*abhīkṣṇya*). He clarifies this through two other synonymous terms: "other than [indicating] habituality" (*tācchīlyād anyaḥ*)—as stated in the *Kāśikā* and the *Padamañjarī*. By this, [it is shown that] the suffix is not applied in the sense of repetition by the rule "after a verbal root, when denoting a genus" (*supyajātau*, Pāṇini 3.2.78), etc.

By stating "it succeeds," he demonstrates the fruit of this yoga while pointing out its lack of efficacy [in other contexts] with the words "those who drink decoctions. In whatever place health arises for those who repeatedly drink a decoction (*kaṣāya*), they drink it for that reason, and not because it is their habitual disposition (*tācchīlyāt*).

Regarding the term "milk-drinkers" (*kṣīrapāyiṇaḥ*): they too drink milk out of necessity, even in the absence of a habitual disposition (*tācchīlya*), because of the aforementioned cause or due to the lack of any other drink. Regarding "sauvīra-drinkers" (*sauvīrapāyiṇaḥ*):
here too, the reason for drinking *sauvīra* repeatedly is precisely that which was just mentioned.
In all cases, the augment *yuk* is applied by the rule "ṭhāto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.33).
The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by the rule "ṭhprātipadikāntanum" (Pāṇini 8.4.11), etc. Regarding the form "kulmāṣakhādaḥ," the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "karmaṇyaṇ" (Pāṇini 3.2.1).

82. *manaḥ* | (Pāṇini 3.2.82) [The commentary states: "The inclusion of *manya-ti*. This refers to the root *mana* meaning "to know" (Dhātupāṭha 1176), which belongs to the Divādi class. [The commentary continues: "Not [the inclusion] of *manu-ti*. This refers to the root *manu* meaning "to perceive" (Dhātupāṭha 1471).

In this case, there would be no inclusion of *tān* and the others. Now, is it not the fact that when the suffix *ṇini* is applied to the root *man*, the form *darśanīyamānī* arises, and that very same form arises from the root *manu* as well?
What, then, is the distinction here, such that the inclusion of *man* is desired and not [that of *manu*]?

To address this, he says: "For in the subsequent sūtra," and so forth. Although there is no distinction here, in the subsequent sūtra, however, there is a distinction caused by the *vikaraṇa* suffix; for when *khaś* is applied to *man* there, because it belongs to the *divādi* class, the suffix *śyan* occurs, whereas for *manu*, [it does not].
The suffix *u* is applied because it begins with the letter *t*.

83. *ātmamāne khaś ca* | (3.2.83) [The word] "in the sense of self-pride" (*ātmamāne*). Pride (*mānaḥ*) is the act of thinking (*mananam*), formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). Self-pride (*ātmamānaḥ*) is the pride of the self. The genitive case is applied by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65), and also by the rule *kṛdyogā ca*.
The compound is formed according to the rule "the genitive case is compounded" (Vārttika 83). Now, why does the genitive not denote the agent?

Because of the force of the inclusion of the word *ātman* (self). For it is not possible for the cognition (*mati*) of any entity other than the self to exist, since cognition is a quality (*guṇa*) of that [self]. Now, this word *ātman* does not denote qualities such as pleasure and so forth; rather, what...
If so, [it means] "not being another. That which is not another is the Self (*ātman*);

even so, the mention of "Self" would be purposeless. For in this way, the meaning would be "that which exists in whatever cognition the cognizer has," and that is incorrect, because all cognition [is such].
Even when one considers [the agent] as something else, it remains the agent; therefore, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) applies only to the object (*karman*).

As for the statement, "When the meaning of the suffix is the agent," and so forth—how, then, can this same entity be both the object and the agent? It is due to a difference in capacity (*śakti-bheda*), just as in the expression, "The honey being drunk intoxicates. [This is the function of the] *khaś* suffix.

The letter *kh* is for the purpose of [triggering] elision (*mum*) by the rule "ṭh-ru-rdviṣad-ajantasya" (Pāṇini 6.3.67). The letter *ś* is for the purpose of [providing] the designation *sārvadhātuka*.

84. *bhūte* (Pāṇini 3.2.84). This word *bhūta* has the sense of "past" (*atikrānta*), and it also has the sense of "inherent nature" (*svarūpa*). In that case, it is not known: in what sense of "past" is the suffix [to be applied]? Therefore, for the sake of clarifying this, he says:

Regarding the phrase "And because of the governing context of the verbal root (*dhātu-adhikāra*)," etc.: the word *ca* (and) indicates a reason. Since the term "from a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], it is therefore understood that [the suffix] occurs after a verbal root that has become the meaning of the root (*dhātvarthabhūta*). Now, one might object: since there is a governing context of the verbal root, is it not more appropriate for this qualification (*bhūta*) to apply specifically to the verbal root itself? No; it is not so.

Because of impossibility: for if the verbal root were subordinate when this [meaning] is expressed, the qualifier "bhūta" (past) would be untenable. Therefore, because of that impossibility, it is understood that the qualifier belongs to the meaning of the root itself.

85. *yajaḥ* in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). (Pāṇini 3.2.85) The suffixes *ṇini* and *niṣ* are understood here, but not *khaś*, because only *ṇini* is marked with the svarita accent. To the question "In what sense, then, is sacrifice the instrument? he says: "The *agniṣṭoma* [is the instrument] in the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) directed toward the fruit," and so forth.
