The fruit is heaven; its *bhāvanā*—that is, the activity (*vyāpāra*) belonging to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) which brings it about—is that in which the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*). But one might object: apart from the Agniṣṭoma, there is no such thing as an activity called *bhāvanā* belonging to the sacrificer, wherein the sacrifice could function.
If it is held that [the sacrifice] is the instrument (*karaṇa*), then does this [sacrifice] produce the fruit called heaven by means of the very sacrifice named *agniṣṭoma*? This is not so;
for the general operation exists within the specific operation, because the specific does not deviate from the general.

For indeed, at the outset, it is the general operation alone that enters into the mind of one who desires a result. To explain: a person seeking a result, being himself desirous of that result, places the general operation in his mind, thinking, "Heaven must be kept in mind"; thereafter—

Having established the meaning of the scripture, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma"— namely, that one should bring about heaven by means of the Agniṣṭoma— the [Agniṣṭoma] is resorted to as the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the production of heaven (*svargabhāvanā*). Therefore, in its general operation...
The production of heaven— the specific operation known as the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice—

serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the realization of heaven. Now, one might object that while being performed it experiences the status of an object (*karman*), nevertheless, due to its distinct capacity (*śakti-bheda*), its status as an instrument is not contradictory.

For example, in the phrase "intoxicated by the honey being drunk," even though the honey undergoes the state of being the object (*karman*), it also possesses the state of being the instrument (*karaṇa*). Thus, the meaning of the term *agniṣṭomayājī* is:
"one who has brought about heaven by means of the Agniṣṭoma as the instrument. As for the word *svarga* (heaven), however—
Because it is concealed by the husk, it is not employed.

86. *karmaṇi hanaḥ* | (3.2.86) [The suffix *ṇin* is applied after the root *han* when it has an object. For example: *pitṛvyaghātī* ("one who kills his paternal uncle"). [In this formation: by *hanasto 'ciṇṇaloḥ* (7.3.32), there is the substitution of *t* for *n*; by *ho hanteṝṇinneṣu* (7.3.54), there is the substitution of *gh* for *h*; and by *sau ca* (6.4.13), [the rule for doubling applies].
The term *dīrghatvam* [refers to length]. Regarding the statement "the mention of 'contemptible' (*kutsita*) must be made," it is a qualification of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*).
"Mention" (*grahaṇa*) means that by which something is grasped; this, moreover, refers to an explanatory commentary (*vyākhyāna*). This is what is meant:
an explanatory commentary must be provided for that by which the meaning of the suffix—the agent who is contemptible—is grasped.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: the term *bahula* (in various cases), which is to be mentioned later, is drawn forward and connected here; therefore, it applies only to that case where an agent who performs a prohibited act—such as the killing of a paternal uncle—is censured, and not otherwise.

87. *brahmabhrūṇavṛtreṣu kvip* (Pāṇini 3.2.87). [The example is] *brahmahā*. The lengthening of the vowel is as before. It is stated that *kvip* is prescribed after all verbal roots by the rule *kvip ca* (3.2.76).

"And here, the restriction (niyama) is fourfold," it says. [The four types are: restriction of the verbal root (dhātuniyama), restriction of the subordinate word (upapadaniyama), restriction of the suffix (pratyayaniyama), and restriction of time (kālaniyama). The particle *ca* is used for emphasis—meaning "only fourfold.
By stating, "the root *han* [is restricted] only when preceded by *brahma* and so forth, and not with any other subordinate word," he demonstrates the restriction of the verbal root. Therefore...
Since the particle *eva* is placed immediately after [the word it qualifies], its restriction applies to what follows it.

When the particle *eva* is employed after a governing word (*upapada*), it restricts the verb *han*. This rule is generally applicable; however, in some instances, it is seen even when the governing word is different—as in *madhuhetu*. And its general applicability is as follows:

This is obtained by the anticipation (*apakarṣa*) of the upcoming mention of the word *bahula* ("variously"). The restriction regarding the *upapada* (governing word) is expressed as: "In the case of *brahmaṇ* and others, [the suffix *kvip*] occurs after *han* alone, and not after any other [verb]. For here, the audible vowel *e* in *hanter* restricts the *upapada*: after *han* in the sense of the past tense (*bhūta*), *kvip* occurs only when preceded by *brahmaṇ* and others; no other [suffix occurs].

The phrase "the suffix" refers to a restriction regarding time. This is because when the suffix *kvip* is prescribed after the root *han* with *brahman* and others as upapadas, the past tense is thereby restricted. If it were the case that only *kvip* and no other suffix could follow *brahman* and others, then the *niṣṭhā* suffix would also not apply—[as in] "he killed a Brahmin" (*brahmāṇaṃ hatavān*)? This is not a fault; [This is because: the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.88], "When a word ending in *kvi* is the upapada, the *niṣṭhā* suffix is used," is a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*) intended to exclude other suffixes such as *śatṛ*, etc., in cases where they might otherwise be expected. It does not, however, exclude the *niṣṭhā* suffix itself. Therefore, the form *brahmahā* is established by the *kvip* suffix, while the form *brahmahatavān* is established by the *niṣṭhā* suffix. Thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, since the *kvip* suffix is prescribed specifically for these instances, it serves to exclude other suffixes like *śatṛ* and the like, but it does not exclude the *niṣṭhā*. Consequently, both forms are valid. Moreover, the *kvip* suffix is taught here for the purpose of forming feminine nouns, such as *brahmahatī*. Since the *niṣṭhā* suffix is not prescribed for this specific purpose, it is not excluded. Therefore, the objection is invalid. Furthermore, the *kvip* suffix is taught here to indicate that the action is performed with great intensity (*atiśayena*). For example, one who kills a Brahmin repeatedly or with extreme cruelty is called a *brahmahā*. However, one who kills him once or casually is not so designated. Thus, the *kvip* suffix is taught to express this sense of intensity. Since the *niṣṭhā* suffix is not taught for this purpose, it is not excluded. Therefore, the objection is invalid. Furthermore, the *kvip* suffix is taught here to indicate that the action is performed in a manner contrary to what is natural (*viparīta*). For example, one who kills a Brahmin through negligence or lack of care is called a *brahmahā*. However, one who kills him intentionally or with full awareness is not so designated. Thus, the *kvip* suffix is taught to express this sense of contrariety. Since the *niṣṭhā* suffix is not taught for this purpose, it is not excluded. Therefore, the objection is invalid. Furthermore, the *kvip* suffix is taught here to indicate that the action is performed with a specific intention (*abhiprāya*). For example, one who kills a Brahmin for the sake of wealth or out of malice is called a *brahmahā*. However, one who kills him out of compassion or for the sake of saving his life is not so designated. Thus, the *kvip* suffix is taught to express this sense of specific intention. Since the *niṣṭhā* suffix is not taught for this purpose, it is not excluded. Therefore, the objection is invalid. Furthermore, the *kvip* suffix is taught here to indicate that the action is performed with a specific result (*phala*). For example, one who kills a Brahmin for the sake of attaining heaven or for the sake of fame is called a *brahmahā*. However, one who kills him without any such motive is not so designated. Thus, the *kvip* suffix is taught to express this sense of specific result. Since the *niṣṭhā* suffix is not taught for this purpose, it is not excluded. Therefore, the objection is invalid. Furthermore, the *kvip* suffix is taught here to indicate that the action is performed with a specific agent (*kartṛ*). For example, one who kills a Brahmin himself is called a *brahmahā*. However, one who causes another to kill him is not so designated. Thus, the *kvip* suffix is taught to express this sense of specific agency. Since the *niṣṭhā* suffix is not taught for this purpose, it is not excluded. Therefore, the objection is invalid. Furthermore, the *kvip* suffix is taught here to indicate that the action is performed with a specific instrument (*karaṇa*). For example, one who kills a Brahmin with a sword is called a *brahmahā*. However, one who kills him with a stick is not so designated. Thus, the *kvip* suffix is taught to express this sense of specific instrumentality. Since the *niṣṭhā* suffix is not taught for this purpose, it is not excluded. Therefore, the objection is invalid. Furthermore, the *kvip* suffix is taught here to indicate that the action is performed with a specific object (*karman*). For example, one who kills a learned Brahmin is called a *brahmahā*. However, one who kills an ignorant one is not so designated. Thus, the *kvip* suffix is taught to express this sense of specific objectivity. Since the *niṣṭhā* suffix is not taught for this purpose, it is not excluded. Therefore, the objection is invalid. Furthermore, the *kvip* suffix is taught here to indicate that the action is performed with a specific location (*adhikaraṇa*). For example, one who kills a Brahmin in a sacred place is called a *brahmahā*. However, one who kills him elsewhere is not so designated. Thus, the *kvip* suffix is taught to express this sense of specific location. Since the *niṣṭhā* suffix is not taught for this purpose, it is not excluded. Therefore, the objection is invalid. Furthermore, the *kvip* suffix is taught here to indicate that the action is performed with a specific time (*kāla*). For example, one who kills a Brahmin at dawn is called a *brahmahā*. However, one who kills him at other times is not so designated. Thus, the *kvip* suffix is taught to express this sense of specific time. Since the *niṣṭhā* suffix is not taught for this purpose, it is not excluded. Therefore, the objection is invalid. Furthermore, the *kvip* suffix is taught here to indicate that the action is performed with a specific state (*bhāva*). For example, one who kills a Brahmin while in a state of anger is called a *brahmahā*. However, one who kills him while in a state of calm is not so designated. Thus, the *kvip* suffix is taught to express this sense of specific state. Since the *niṣṭhā* suffix is not taught for this purpose, it is not excluded. Therefore, the objection is invalid. Furthermore, the *kvip* suffix is taught here to indicate that the action is performed with a specific quality (*guṇa*). For example, one who kills a Brahmin who is virtuous is called a *brahmahā*. However, one who kills him who is wicked is not so designated. Thus, the *kvip* suffix is taught to express this sense of specific quality. Since the *niṣṭhā* suffix is not taught for this purpose, it is not excluded. Therefore, the objection is invalid. Furthermore, the *kvip* suffix is taught here to indicate that the action is performed with a specific purpose (*prayojana*). For example, one who kills a Brahmin for the sake of protecting the dharma is called a *brahmahā*. However, one who kills him for the sake of personal gain is not so designated. Thus, the *kvip* suffix is taught to express this sense of specific purpose. Since the *niṣṭhā* suffix is not taught for this purpose, it is not excluded. Therefore, the objection is invalid. Furthermore, the *kvip* suffix is taught here to indicate that the action is performed with a specific motive (*hetu*). For example, one who kills a Brahmin out of a desire for liberation is called a *brahmahā*. However, one who kills him out of a desire for pleasure is not so designated. Thus, the *kvip* suffix is taught to express this sense of specific motive. Since the *niṣṭhā* suffix is not taught for this purpose, it is not excluded. Therefore, the objection is invalid. Furthermore, the *kvip* suffix is taught here to indicate that the action is performed with a specific method (*upāya*). For example, one who kills a Brahmin by means of incantations is called a *brahmahā*. However, one who kills him by means of physical force is not so designated. Thus, the *kvip* suffix is taught to express this sense of specific method. Since the *niṣṭhā*

According to the principle that "exceptions within a section sublate preceding rules, but not subsequent ones" (Vyāḍipāda 10), only the suffixes *aṇ* and others are sublated, not the *niṣṭhā*. Even so, would the suffix *tṛc* not fail to apply here in the case of *vṛtrasya hantuḥ*? There is no fault, because the restriction is merely general (*prāyika*). Likewise, [the rule applies] only when the time is past.
"The restriction of the suffix is 'not after another [root],' because the suffix is restricted to the past tense. But how are four restrictions obtained at once? He says:
'This very [rule],' etc., referring to what will be stated in *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 3.2.88)."
The inclusion of the term "frequently" (*bahula*) is connected with this rule by being drawn forward from the previous one—
namely, *brahmabhrūṇavṛtreṣu kvip bahulam*— and by means of that, this fourfold restriction is obtained.
88. *Bahulam chandasi* (3.2.88).

89. *Sukarmapāpamantrapuṇyeṣu kṛñaḥ* (3.2.89). [The commentary states: "Excluding the word *su*. This is because that [word *su*] does not denote a substance (*asattvavacana*), and therefore it cannot logically function as an object (*karman*).

Regarding the rule "in the case of actions beginning with *ṣṭhā* and *svādi*," this was stated by resorting to the principle of generality (*bāhulya*), as in the examples "the village of Brāhmaṇas" (*brāhmaṇagrāmaḥ*) and "the village of Bhaṭṭas" (*bhaṭṭagrāmaḥ*). Why is this so? Because [the term] immediately following excludes the word *su*, thereby referring only to those [actions] that follow it.

"And here, the restriction (niyama) is threefold. This too is obtained through the continued application of the term *bahula*. "The scope [of this rule] is the restriction regarding time (*kāla*), the secondary word (*upapada*), and the suffix (*pratyaya*). That which has time, the secondary word, and the suffix as its scope is described as such. Furthermore, that consists of the restriction of time, the restriction of the secondary word, and—

And there is the restriction of suffixes (*pratyayaniyama*). Among these, the restriction of time (*kālaniyama*) is as follows: after roots such as *svā* and others, the suffix *kvip* occurs only for the past tense (*bhūta*) of the root *kṛ*, and no other suffix occurs; thus, one does not say *karmakāra* in the sense of "one who has performed an action. The restriction of the accompanying word (*upapadaniyama*) is as follows: after roots such as *svā* and others, [the suffix *kvip*] occurs only after the root *kṛ*.

"Not from another verbal root" means that *kvip* does not occur [after other roots]; for instance, one does not say *mantram adhītavān*, but rather, by the suffix *aṇ*, one says *mantrādhyāyaḥ*. This is a restriction regarding the suffix: after the root *kṛ* when preceded by *sva* and so on, *kvip* occurs only in the sense of the past (*bhūta*), not in the present or the future. Therefore, one does not say *mantraṃ karoti* or *mantraṃ kariṣyati*.

When there is an intention to express the meaning "he will compose," the term *mantrakṛt* does not occur; rather, one says *śāstrakṛt*. The suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *kvip ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.76).

90. *some suñaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.90). [The phrase] "the domain of verbal root, time, upapada, and suffix" is a bahuvrīhi compound as before. The external referent (*anyapadārtha*) consists of the restriction of time and so forth. Among these, the restriction of time is: *some suñaḥ*.
When the *kvip* suffix occurs, it is only after the root *bhū*, and no other suffix [is applied]; for one does not say "somasaḥ" (one who has pressed *soma*) for someone who has pressed *soma*.
This is a restriction regarding the verbal root: *kvip* is applied to the root *su* (to press) only when *soma* is the attendant word (*upapada*), and not with any other;
thus, it does not occur here: "surāṃ sutavān" (one who has pressed *surā*), which would result in *surāsut*.

Restriction of the root (*upapadaniyama*): [The suffix] *kvip* occurs only after the root *su* (to press) when *soma* is the object, and not after any other root. Thus, in the case of "he has purchased *soma*" (*somaṃ krītavān*), *kvip* does not occur; rather, only the suffix *aṇ* occurs, resulting in *somakraya*. Restriction of the suffix (*pratyayaniyama*): *kvip* occurs only after the root *su* when *soma* is the object and the action is completed (*bhūta*), and not otherwise. Therefore—
When there is the intention to express the meaning "he presses Soma" or "he will press Soma," the form *somasuṭ* does not occur.
91. *agnau ceḥ*.

(3.2.91) Here too, as before, and so forth. In this regard, there is a restriction of time: the suffix *kvip* occurs after the root *ci* (to pile) when preceded by *agni*, but not otherwise. Therefore, when one intends to express the meaning "one who has piled the fire," [the form] is *agnicit*.

It does not occur. There is a restriction regarding the verbal root (*dhātu-niyama*): [the suffix applies] only after the root *ci* (to pile) when *agni* is the attendant word (*upapada*), and not after any other root; therefore, *iṣṭakācit* does not occur. There is a restriction regarding the attendant word (*upapada-niyama*): [the suffix applies] only after the root *ci* when *agni* is the attendant word, and not after any other root; therefore, *agnikṛt* does not occur. There is a restriction regarding the affix (*pratyaya-niyama*)—

The suffix *kvip* occurs only when the action of piling the fire (*agni-cinoti*) has already been completed, not at any other time; therefore, the term *agnicit* does not apply to the present or the future.

92. *karmaṇy agny-ākhyāyām* (Pāṇini 3.2.92). Since the term *karman* is understood as a specific qualifier of the *upapada* from the rule *karmaṇi hanaḥ* (3.2.86), the fact that *karman* is mentioned again here indicates that it serves as the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya-artha*). Thus he says:

The statement "only when [the word] is a *kāraka* in relation to the action" indicates, by means of the rule beginning with "dhātūpapada," that this mention of the term *ākhyā* (name/designation) serves as a qualifier for the entire compound. The phrase "the mention of *ākhyā* is for the purpose of ensuring the understanding of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*)" and so forth [explains this].

This word "agni" denotes the general class of fire; in the absence of the mention of a specific name (*ākhyā*), the particular [fire] intended here would not be understood—namely, which one is to be taken. Therefore, the mention of a name is made for the purpose of conveying conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). But what is the reason that the mention of a name is made for that purpose? He says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "ṭhagnyartho hi": that specific arrangement of bricks which has fire as its purpose is called a *śyenacit* (falcon-shaped altar); it is only in reference to that [arrangement] that this suffix is intended. How is it obtained only in that case?
Because when the mention [of the word] is made, and that [mention] exists, the well-known [meaning] being grasped is that which has fire as its purpose.
It is that specific arrangement of bricks alone which is understood as the meaning of the suffix to be expressed,
and nothing else.

94. *karmaṇīnirvikriyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.93). [The commentary begins: "While the word *karmaṇi* is still in force," and so forth. [This is] from the rule *karmaṇi hanaḥ* (3.2.86). [The commentary continues: "The repetition of the word *karman*" and so forth. That object which experiences a connection with the action [is what is meant by the agent's object].

It brings about contempt; that is for the purpose of ensuring that the action has contempt as its cause. Although the term *karman* (object) was already being carried over [from the previous rule], the repetition of the term *karman* here is for the purpose of excluding that mention of *karman* which was undesirable when it served as the meaning of the suffixes denoting the object in the immediately preceding sūtra. This is the mention of *karman*.

Why does it not occur? Because that [term] continues by virtue of its being *svarita*. In the case of "somavikrayī" (a soma-seller), since the selling of soma is prohibited by the scriptures, the act of selling connected with the substance called soma brings censure upon the seller. In the case of "dhānyavikrāyaḥ" (a grain-seller) [the same applies].
"From a verbal root, the suffix *aṇ* is applied when [the action] pertains to the object. (Pāṇini 3.2.1)
94. *dṛśeḥ kvanip* (Pāṇini 3.2.94).

[The phrase] "for the purpose of precluding other suffixes" means that it is for the purpose of precluding other suffixes such as *aṇ* and so forth. Even when there is a preclusion, the suffix still occurs in the sense of being another suffix (*pratyayāntara*).
"He saw the other world. And the reason for this has been stated in the very sūtra "brahmabhrūṇa... (Pāṇini 3.2.87).

95. *rājani yudhikṛñaḥ* | (3.2.95) Now, since this root *yudh* is intransitive (*akarmaka*), how can it be said that [the suffix applies] "in relation to its object" (*tatkarmaṇi*)? With this intention, he says: "having the causative sense included within it" (*antarbhāvitaṇyarthaḥ*), and so forth. "Included within" (*antarbhāvitaḥ*) means...

The term *tanupraveśito ṇyarthaḥ* is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that in which the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇyartha*) has been introduced into the root. For example, when it is said that "the king fights," a person employs him or himself fights. In that case, the activity of that person—such as commanding and so forth, which constitutes the meaning of the causative suffix—is mentally internalized within the root *yudh* (to fight).

Then, by means of the object of the causative action, this [root] becomes transitive; for example, "he caused to learn" (*yodhitavān*). This is the usage of the causative form (*ṇyanta*); the elision of the causative suffix (*ṇilopa*) occurs according to Pāṇini 6.4.52: "When a *seṭ* niṣṭhā [suffix] follows."

95. And [the rule] *sahe ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.95). Since the suffix *ṭha* does not denote a substance (*dravyavācitva*), it cannot be qualified by an object (*karman*) as an accompanying word (*upapada*); for the meaning of that [suffix] cannot logically function as an object.

97. *saptamyāṃ janer ḍaḥ* (3.2.97). The mention of "saptamī" (locative case) here is for the purpose of including the suffix. In that context, by the technical rule regarding the inclusion of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), the inclusion of that which ends in it occurs; thus he says: "when a word ending in the locative case is the *upapada*. For this very reason, there is no inclusion of the actual form [of the suffix itself].

In the case of *ṭhupasarajaḥ*, the elision of the *ṭi* portion occurs even though it belongs to a stem not designated as *bha*, by virtue of the force of the *ḍit* suffixation. In the case of *ṅyāpoḥ saṃjñācchandasorbahulam* (Pāṇini 6.3.63),
the shortening [of the vowel] takes place.

98. *pañcamyām ajātau* (Pāṇini 3.2.98). Regarding the example *buddhijaḥ*: since the intellect (*buddhi*) functions as the *apādāna* (ablative point of departure) according to the rule *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.30), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is applied to express the *apādāna*. Thus, it serves as the *upapada* (governing word) for this [suffix].
Words such as "intellect" (buddhi) and so forth are not genus-words (jātiśabda),
because intellect and the rest are qualities of the self (ātmaguṇa).

99. *upasarge ca saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 3.2.99). Regarding the phrase "a qualifier of the aggregate": he demonstrates that the meaning of the suffix applies only when a name (*saṃjñā*) is understood through the aggregate of root, prefix, and suffix, and not otherwise—as in *prajāḥ*.

"Kāśikā says: 'prajāḥ'—this is a designation for a collection of living beings. If this very word *prajā* were the sole example for this sūtra, then since one could simply state "pre janaḥ saṃjñāyām" (the prefix *pra-* with the root *jan-* [forms *prajā*] when it is a name), the form *prajā* would be established even so; what, then, is the purpose of including the mention of the prefix (*upasarga*)? The mention of the prefix is for the sake of the subsequent rule.

[The rule] "ṭhanau karmaṇi" (Pāṇini 3.2.100) is intended so that [the suffix] may apply when there is a prefix (*upasarga*), but not when there is a *karmapravacanīya*. Furthermore, if a suffix is sometimes observed after a non-final word within the scope of usage when another word is present as an *upapada*, then this [rule] is also for that purpose.
100. *anau karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 3.2.100).
[This refers to] the rule *ṭhanupūrvāj janeḥ*, etc. Now, why does the word *anu* not function as an *upapada*?
The reason why it does not is the same as that given in the rule *udi kūlerujivahoḥ* (3.2.31).

Since it has already been explained, it is not explained again. Regarding the rule "pum-ansu-jaḥ": even though the *sup* suffix is elided, there is the status of being a *pada* by virtue of the *pratyaya-lakṣaṇa* (the presence of a suffix as if it were still there); therefore, the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogānta-lopa*) occurs by Pāṇini 8.2.23.

101. *anyeṣv api dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 3.2.101). Regarding the word *api* and so forth: the word *api* is for the purpose that all conditions (*upādhi*), such as the *upapada* and others, might be seen to have exceptions (*vyabhicāra*). [The commentary says: "Even from another verbal root (*dhātu*)," [as in] *khanu*.
From the root *avadāraṇa* (DhP 8.78). Regarding the phrase "even when there is another kāraka": this refers to when the object (*karman*) is a kāraka other than the agent (*kartṛ*).
102. *niṣṭhā* (Pāṇini 3.2.102). Regarding the form *kṛtam*: here, due to the *kit* designation, there is an absence of *guṇa*. Regarding *kṛtavān*:
[the suffix] *num* is applied by the rule *ugidacām* (7.1.70). [The lengthening of the vowel] is applied by the rule *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ* (6.4.14).

[The forms] *dīrghaḥ*, [the rule] *halṅyādi* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), and the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopaḥ*) at 8.2.23 apply. Regarding the statement "in the case of the *niṣṭhā*" and so forth:
when a suffix designated as *niṣṭhā* is to be prescribed, the term *niṣṭhā* refers to that suffix which has not yet been established [as such].
Furthermore, this designation (*saṃjñā*) would not be established; why? Because of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).

To explain how there is mutual dependence, he says: "In the case of a designation," and so forth. Having uttered the designation "past tense" (*niṣṭhā*), the rule for *kta* and *ktavatu* is prescribed here for the past time; and yet, those two [suffixes] must already exist [for that designation to apply].

There would be mutual dependence in the sense that "it must exist by means of its designation," for "operations based on mutual dependence are not formulated in the treatise" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 28). If *kta* and *ktavatū* were understood here merely by their own form, then the rule "the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatū* are called *niṣṭhā*" (Pāṇini 1.1.26) would have to establish a designation for something else.

It is possible [to understand it] in this way, and not otherwise. Therefore, there is no establishment of the technical name (*saṃjñā*); and when that is not established, those two [the *saṃjñin* and the *saṃjñā*] are not established either. Regarding the word "bhāvinī": it means "that which will come to be. For example, as in the expression, "weave a cloth for this thread. This word *bhāvinī* is derived from the root *gam* with the suffix *ini* (according to Daiva Uṇādi Sūtra 6.57), and [the feminine form is made by adding] *āṅ*.

The word *bhāvinī* is derived by adding the suffix *ini* according to the rules *ṇit* (Daiva-nighaṇṭu 6.58) and *bhuvaśca* (Daiva-nighaṇṭu 6.59). Furthermore, that suffix is prescribed for the future tense by the rule *bhaviṣyati gamyādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.3).
Therefore, the meaning of *bhāvinī* is obtained as "that which will be" (*bhaviṣyantī*). [Regarding the phrase] "by implication" (*sāmarthyāt*), etc., he says: "That..."

The designation "completion" (niṣṭhā) applies to that which has arisen in the past; this designation does not apply to anything else that has arisen. Rather, by implication, it applies only to the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu*.

"In the case of the first action," and so forth. Here, the word *karman* (action) denotes "activity. The meaning is: in that which is initial, beginning with the commencement of activity—that is, in the first characteristic of activity.
[This applies] until the mat mat reaches completion through all the characteristics of activity; that is, upon the cessation of that many characteristics of activity.

The past time occurs [in this case]. Since the entire collection [of action] is not yet fully accomplished under the first definition of action (*kriyā-lakṣaṇa*), it is indeed the present time. In that case, the *niṣṭhā* suffix would not apply to the present;
therefore, it must be stated and explained. Here is the explanation: that which this...

By the rule *ṭhudupadhādbhāvādikarmaṇoranyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 1.2.21), the *niṣṭhā* suffix is optionally applied in the sense of the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*) as well as in the sense of the object (*karman*). Alternatively, by the rule *ādikarmaṇi ktaḥ kartari ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.71), etc., it indicates that the *niṣṭhā* suffix occurs in the sense of the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*). [Thus,] *prakṛtaḥ*.

"Kaṭam" (the mat). Here, the prefix *pra-* indicates the commencement of an action (*ādikarma*). The very same meaning that is expressed by "Devadatta makes a mat" (*prakaroti kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ*) is expressed by "Devadatta has begun a mat" (*prakṛtaḥ kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ*).
103. *suyaj-ūr-vanip* (Pāṇini 3.2.103). [The form] *sutvā* [is derived as follows]: by *hrasvasya piti kṛti* (6.1.71), there is the insertion of *tuk*;
by *sarvanāmasthāne ca* (6.4.8), etc., there is lengthening; and by *nalopaḥ* [there is the elision of the *n*].
There is the elision of the letter *n* by the rule "prātipadikāntasya" (Pāṇini 8.2.7).

104. *jīryater atṛn* (Pāṇini 3.2.104). Regarding the form *jaraṇ*: because the suffix *atṛn* is marked with *ṇ*, it receives the udātta accent on its first syllable. By the rule *ugidacām* (7.1.70), the augment *num* is added.

105. *chandasi liṭ* (3.2.105). Regarding the example *dadarśa*: from the root *dṛś*, the suffix *liṭ* is applied; then *ṇal*; then reduplication (*dvirvacanam*); then by *urat* (7.4.66), the substitution of *at* for the radical vowel; then *raparatvam* (the substitution of *r* as the subsequent element); then *halādiśeṣaḥ* (7.4.60); and finally the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇaḥ*) by 7.3.86.
Regarding the form *ṭhātatāna*: the root *tanu* (DhP 1463), meaning "to expand," is preceded by the prefix *ā*.

The vowel substitution known as *vṛddhi* occurs according to Pāṇini 7.2.116 (*ata upadhāyāḥ*). This rule applies because the phrase "in connection with a verbal root" (*dhātusambandhe*) is understood here, due to its recurrence from Pāṇini 3.4.1 (*dhātusambandhe pratyayāḥ*).

"But [the letter *ṭ*] is for the sake of non-distinction" means: in the case of the mere root (*bhūtamātra*). In the subsequent sūtra, the letters *i* and *ṭ* are for the sake of specification. If it were stated as "ṭhlaḥ kānaj vā," there would be a grasping of all the *lakāras*.
The letter *ṭ* is for the sake of causing the substitution of *et* (the *ṭ* in *ṭita ātmanepadānām eka-vacanasya ṭeḥ*).

106. *liṭaḥ kānaj vā* (Pāṇini 3.2.106). The addition of the augment *ka* in *kānac* is for the purpose of making the final syllable udātta. The addition of the marker *k* is for the purpose of the grammatical operations prescribed for *kit* suffixes. These operations, moreover, apply to roots such as *bandh* (Dhātupāṭha 1508), which end in a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*).

They cause [the application of] it, and not others. By the rule "liṭ is kit after a non-conjunct" (1.2.5), it is established; however, even those ending in a conjunct cause the *kit* status in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), but not in the Vedic (*chandas*). Regarding that, he says: "In the Veda, both ways" (3.4.117), concerning the *liṭ*.

Because it is a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, the property of being *ṅit* indeed exists by virtue of the rule *sārvadhātukamapit* (Pāṇini 1.2.4). Whether there is the property of being *kit* or *ṅit*, there is no difference whatsoever in the case of Vedic usage (*chandasi*). However, in the common language (*bhāṣā*), if the property of being *kit* did not apply after roots ending in a non-conjunct consonant, then [the rule] *ṛcchatyṛtām* (Pāṇini 7.4.11) would not apply.

A grammatical quality (*guṇa*) is introduced as the object of a prohibition; just as it does not occur here—*nipaparatuḥ*, *nipaparur*—so too it would occur here: *nipapurāṇa*. However, when there is *kitva* (the status of having a *k* as an it-marker), it does not occur. But in the common language (*bhāṣā*), *kitva* is meaningful. [This concerns the root] *pṛ* in the sense of "protecting" and "filling."

The suffix *kānac* is applied after the root preceded by the prefix *ni-* (from *dhā.pā.* 1086). Because it follows the reduplication (*dvirvacana*), the substitution of *u* for the vowel of the penultimate syllable occurs according to *ṭhudoṣṭhaḷpūrvasya* (7.1.102), as well as the replacement of that *u* with *r*. Due to the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) by the rule *dvirvacane'ci* (1.1.59), the word *pṛṣ-* is reduplicated.

The operations of *urat*, *paratva*, and *halādiśeṣa* apply; then, by rule 8.4.2 (*aṭ-kupv-ādy-apṛkta*), there is *ṇatva*. That the suffix *kānac* occurs in the *bhāṣā* (colloquial speech) is understood from this very *jñāpaka*. As for the form *cikyānaḥ*:
by rule 7.3.58 (*vibhāṣā ceḥ*), the *ca* of the root *cinoti* following the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is optionally changed to *k*.
The substitution of *ku* [for *kva*] occurs; by the rule *ṭheranekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.82), the *yaṇ* substitute is applied. Regarding the form *suṣuvāṇaḥ*:

the reading found in printed editions is *sunoter iti*; from the root *sū*, by the rule *aci śnudhātu* (Pāṇini 6.4.77), the *uvaṅ* substitute is applied, and by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.59), [the *ṣatva* is applied].

Thus [is established] the substitution of *ṣ*. As for the statement, "There will be a change of case," although *liṭ* is introduced in the nominative case (*liṭ*), nevertheless, by virtue of the sense, there will be a change of case;
because of its connection with the substitute, the subsequent *liṭ* will be understood as being in the genitive case. Therefore, even without [explicit mention],...

The sense is that since the substitution of *kānac* and so forth will apply specifically to the *liṭ* by virtue of the mention of *liṭ* itself, the explicit mention of *liṭ* need not have been made. Regarding the phrase "even that which," etc.:
even for that *liṭ* which is prescribed by the rule "the *liṭ* [is used] in the remote past" (Pāṇini 3.2.115), when there is the mention of *liṭ*...

The substitution of *kānac* occurs when [the word] *liṭ* exists; however, if that were not the case, by the rule "a prescription or a prohibition applies only to what is immediately preceding" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 19), it would apply only to that [immediately preceding element], and not to the *liṭ* [affix] in the sense of the remote past (*parokṣa*). Now, even if the mention of *liṭ* were absent, why could *kānac* not be understood as another suffix?

It is impossible to understand [the rule] in this way; for if it were so, the prohibition of the genitive case by the rule "na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām" (Pāṇini 2.3.69) would not apply in other instances. Consequently, in the expression *agniṃ cikyānaḥ*, the genitive case would arise after the word *agni*.

107. *kvasuśca* | (Pāṇini 3.2.107) The designation *ugit* for *kvasu* is for the purpose of [triggering] *num*. The designation *kit* should be understood in the same way as it is for *kānac*; for if that were not the case, then just as in the following example, there would be no guna by the rule *ṛcchatyṛtām* (7.4.11):— [e.g., *papuṣaḥ*].

[The forms] *teratuḥ* and *teruḥ* [are derived from the root *tṛ*]; likewise here as well, we have *tatīvān*. Regarding the root *tṛ* in the sense of "floating" and "crossing over" (*dhā.pā.* 969): the substitution of *i* for *ṛ* occurs by *ṛta iddhātoḥ* (Pāṇ. 7.1.100); the lengthening occurs by *hali ca* (Pāṇ. 8.2.77); and the doubling is the operation pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). [The form] *jakṣivān* [is explained similarly].
The substitution of *ghas* for [the root *ad*] occurs by the rule *ṭhliṭaḷnyatarasyām* (2.4.40). The augment *iṭ* is added by *ṭhvasvekājāddhasām* (7.2.67),

the penultimate vowel is elided by *ṭhghasibhasorhali ca* (6.4.100), the letter *gh* is changed to *k* by *ṭhkhari ca* (8.4.55), and [the change of *s* to *ṣ*] occurs by *ṭhśāsivasighasīnāñca* (8.3.60).

There is the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*]. By the rule "ṭhkuhoścuḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.62), there is the substitution of a *c*-series letter (*cutva*) for the reduplicated syllable, resulting in the letter *jha*. Then, by the rule "abhyāse carca" (Pāṇini 8.4.54), the letter *jha* is replaced by the letter *ja*. Thus, we have "papivān. The root is "pā pāne" (Dhātupāṭha 925). The augment *iṭ* is added as before. Then, by the rule "āto lopa iṭi ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.64), there is the elision of the long *ā*.

There is the elision of the vowel *i*. The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows; that is, so that in the subsequent sūtra only *kvasu* may be carried forward, and not *kānac*.

108. *bhāṣāyāṃ sadavaśruvaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.108). Now, one might object: since the suffix *liṭ* is prescribed in this section for the general past tense (*bhūtasāmānya*), that [suffix] does not exist at all in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*). Therefore, how can it be understood that there is a substitution of *kta* and *suṅ* for it? To this he says:

"Simply because of the prescription of the substitute *kvasu*," and so forth. From this very prescription of the substitute *kvasu* for the *liṭ* [perfect] tense in the common language (*bhāṣā*), one infers that the *liṭ* occurs in the common language in the sense of general past time (*bhūtasāmānya*); otherwise, the prescription of the substitute would be purposeless. It is not [the case that the *liṭ* is restricted to the Vedic period].

For a substitute (ādeśa) is only possible for that which is not already present as the original element (sthānin). If, then, the *liṭ* [perfect tense] is inferred in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*) due to the prescription of its substitute, then the *liṭ* would necessarily apply after roots such as *sad* in the spoken language; consequently, by the rule "the *kvasu* is optional," there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasajyeta*) of hearing the finite verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) in place of it.

Furthermore, would the substitution (*luṅ-ādeśa*) not be optional within its own domain, since the *liṭ* [perfect tense] is compulsory? This is not a fault; for the *liṭ* is inferred by means of the sign that is the substitute. Therefore, when the substitute does not exist, the inference of it likewise does not exist. In the absence of that [the *liṭ*], from where could there be substitutes for it?

[Otherwise] the application [of the suffix] *śravaṇa* would follow! In a case where the *liṭ* suffix does not exist, who can prevent the occurrence of the *luṅ* and other suffixes in their own respective domains? For example, in the form *upasedivān*: the root is *sadlṛ* in the sense of "perishing" (*viśaraṇe*, Dhātupāṭha 854). By the rule *ata ekahalmadhye* (Pāṇini 6.4.120), etc., the substitution of *etva* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) take place.

[The augment] *iṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.2.67] *ṭhvasvekājāddhasām*; the *num* augment is added; the lengthening is applied by [Pāṇini 6.4.10] *sāntamahataḥ saṃyogasya*; and the elision of the *hal* and *ṅī* suffixes, etc., as well as the elision of the final consonant of the *saṃyoga*, are applied by [Pāṇini 6.1.68] and [8.2.23].
Thus, "upāsadat" is formed. Because of the mention of the option (*vā*), in that alternative where the *liṭ* [laffix] does not occur—

In the case of the general past tense (*bhūtasāmānya*), the suffix *luṅ* is applied; by [Pāṇini 3.4.100] *luṅ*, *tip*, and *ṭhitaśca*, there is the elision of the vowel *i*. By [Pāṇini 3.1.55] *puṣādidyutādyuditaḥ parasmaipadeṣu*, *cler aṅ* is substituted. Thus, one says "he sat down" (*upāsīdat*). By [Pāṇini 3.2.111] *anadyatane laṅ*, the suffix *laṅ* is applied; by the rule [Pāṇini 7.3.78] *prāghrādhmādheṭdṛśaḥ śaḥ*, there is the substitution of *sīd* for the root. Thus, one says "he sat down" (*upasasāda*).
Regarding *anūviṣān*: by the rule *parokṣe liṭ* (3.2.115), the suffix *liṭ* is applied; then *tip* and *ṇal* [are substituted];

by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* (7.2.116), there is *vṛddhi*. [The form] *anūviṣān* is derived from the root *vas* (meaning "to dwell," *dhā.pā.* 1005); after *liṭ*, the suffix *kvasu* is applied, followed by reduplication and *saṃprasāraṇa* by the rule *vacyādisūtreṇa* (6.1.15).
By the rule *ṭhliṭaḷbhyāsasyobhayeṣām* (6.1.17), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the reduplicated syllable;

by *ṭhśāsivasighasīnāñca* (8.3.60), there is the substitution of *ṣ*; and by *ṭhakaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (6.1.101), a long vowel is substituted for the *a* of the root together with the prefix *anu*. Thus we have *anvavātsīt*. This is formed with the suffix *luṅ*.

In *sthās-ti-sicaḥ apṛkte* (Pāṇini 7.3.96), the augment *iṭ* is applied; in *ekācaḥ* (7.2.10), there is a prohibition of *iṭ*; in *saḥ syārddhadhātuke* (7.4.49), there is the substitution of *s* for *t*; and by *vadavraja-* (7.2.3) et cetera, there is *vṛddhi*. Regarding *anvavasat*: this is the *laṅ* [aorist]. Regarding *anūvāsa*: this is the *liṭ* [perfect], as before.

The operations beginning with *samprasāraṇa* [apply]. Regarding the form *upaśuśruvān*: from the root *śru* "to hear" (*dhā.pā.* 942), the suffix *kvasu* is added in the sense of the perfect tense (*liṭ*), followed by reduplication. Regarding the form *upāśrauṣīt*:
in the *luṅ* tense, the augment *iṭ* is prohibited as before, and the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs according to *sici vṛddhiḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (Pāṇini 7.2.1).

The augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *ṭhastisico'pṛkte* (7.3.96), and the lengthening of the vowel occurs before the prefix by the rule *ṭhakaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (6.1.101). Thus we have *upāśṛṇot*. This is the *laṅ* [imperfect] tense; the suffix *śnu* is applied and the root undergoes the change to *śṛ* by the rule *ṭhśruvaḥ śṛ ca* (3.1.74), and [the augment *guṇa* is applied] by the rule *ṭhsārvadhātukārthadhātukayoḥ* (7.3.84).

The suffix *guṇa*. [In the example] "upaśuśrāva," there is the suffix *liṭ*, *tip*, and *ṇal*; by the rule "aco ñṇiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.115), there is *vṛddhi* [of the vowel], followed by the substitution of *āv*. Here, the operation prescribed by this sūtra applies to the general category of the past tense (*bhūtasāmānye*). [The suffixes] *luṅ*... (3.2.110).

By this [rule], the *luṅ* [is applied]; by the rule "the *luṅ* for the non-remote past" (*anadyatane luṅ*, 3.2.111), the *laṅ* [is applied]; and by the rule "the *liṭ* for the remote past" (*parokṣe liṭ*, 3.2.115), the *liṭ* [is applied]. Thus, the *laṅ* and *liṭ* occur in the sense of the remote past of the non-remote past. Furthermore, because the *laṅ* and *liṭ* are prescribed as specific exceptions, they [supersede] this [general rule].

[The two suffixes] become sublaters (*bādhaka*) of the meaning "past" (*bhūta*) and so forth. For that [meaning of] past, the general category of "become" (*bhūtasāmānya*) is the scope (*avakāśa*); for the *laṅ* and *liṭ* suffixes, it is from roots other than *sad-* etc.;
for *sad-* etc., it is in the specific sense of "past," namely the non-recently past (*bhūtānadyatanaparokṣa*); and for the non-recently past...
When both [the conditions] are met, by virtue of the two aforementioned causes, the *laṅ* and *liṭ* suffixes would occur.
To one who might object that this is not an operation prescribed by the present rule, he says:
"Even in the domain of *luṅ* and *laṅ*, etc. This refers to this rule concerning the mention of *liṭ* and the mention of *vā*.

The recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) [of the word *bhūte*] is carried over from "In the past not of today, *laṅ*" (Pāṇini 3.2.111) and "In the remote past, *liṭ*" (Pāṇini 3.2.115). And there, by virtue of that recurrence, this [suffixing] also applies to *laṅ*.
In this case, the connection should be made as follows: *laṅ* occurs in the sense of the past not of today, [and] after words such as *sadā*, etc.
Or [the suffix] liṭ; and for liṭ, the substitute kvasu occurs invariably. Liṭ occurs in the sense of the remote past (parokṣa);
it occurs optionally after roots such as *sad*; the substitution of kvasu for liṭ is desired, and this is prescribed by another rule as well.
109. *upeyivān anāśvān anūcānaś ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.109). [The rule] "after the root *iṇ* preceded by *upa*, there is the suffix *kvasu*" means that it should be understood as a substitute for *liṭ*.
[The rule] "lengthening of the reduplicated syllable" refers to [the rule] *dīrgha iṇaḥ kiti* (Pāṇini 7.4.69).

Regarding the phrase "by the force of that" (*tatsāmarthyāt*) and so forth: by the force of the rule prescribing length (*dīrghatva*), the formation of a single long vowel as a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) in the case of *akaḥ savarṇe* is prohibited; the meaning is that its operation is obstructed. For if the single substitute were to occur, the prescription of length would be purposeless.

Because lengthening is established by the single substitution [of the long vowel] itself. But one might object: "Would not *iyatuḥ* and *iyuḥ*, where the lengthening of the reduplication occurs, be the scope for this rule—namely, where the substitution of *yaṇ* is applied to the verbal root form according to Pāṇini 6.4.81, 'ṭhiṇo yaṇ'? This is not its scope; for here, by the rule "acaḥ parasmin... [the original vowel is replaced by the substitute].
By virtue of the rule *pūrvavidhau* (1.1.57), there must be the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). How so?

For in the case of a long vowel by *savarṇadīrgha*, it can be designated as a "rule concerning what precedes" (*pūrvavidhi*) because it is a rule where both [the original and the substitute] are involved. Indeed, that which is produced as the substitute for both [the preceding and the following elements] is [treated as such].
It receives one or the other designation. Furthermore, there is no prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* regarding the rule for lengthening (*dīrghavidhi*) by the sūtra *na padānta* (P. 1.1.58) and others;
because, in the case of vowel (*svara*), lengthening (*dīrgha*), and the elision of *y* (*yalopa*), "substitutes that are elisions (*lopājādeśa*) do not behave as the original (*sthānivat*)."

By the rule beginning with *kāśikā* 1.1.58, there is a prohibition of the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) with respect to the prescription of a long vowel; for it is stated: "In the case of [the application of] accent, a long vowel, or the elision of *y*, the substitutes resulting from elision (*lopājādeśau*) are not treated as if they were the original. (*kāśikā* 1.1.58).

By virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if occupying the original position), there ought to be a long vowel here by way of the "long vowel for homogeneous vowels" (*savarṇadīrgha*) rule. It is established that this lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), because it lacks any scope [otherwise], subverts the "long vowel for homogeneous vowels" rule; thus, by implication, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is prohibited. Regarding the phrase "In that case," and so forth:

For when there is an obstruction to a single substitute (*ekādeśa*), there is the state of having multiple vowels (*anekāctva*); consequently, the augment *iṭ* would not apply by the rule "after a monosyllabic root ending in a vowel other than *a*, except for roots beginning with *gh*" (Pāṇini 7.2.67), and thus it is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). [The statement] "there is a *yaṇ*-substitution for that which has the form of a verbal root" refers to Pāṇini 6.4.81: "for *iṇ*, there is *yaṇ*."

By this [rule], then, this is indeed a *nipātana* (irregular formation). Even when followed by *satya-jādi* and so forth, there is *samprasāraṇa* of the *vasu* [suffix]. Once *samprasāraṇa* has been performed, the augment *iṭ* would apply;
however, that is prohibited by the rule "after a monosyllabic root ending in *vas*, except for *ghas*" (Pāṇini 7.2.67). That very [augment] is [permitted] by this *nipātana*.
It is reauthorized. That which was prohibited is set forth again, but it is not prescribed as something new.

[This is indicated by the statement: "Therefore, it does not occur before vowels beginning with *a*. For if there were a prescription for the form preceded by *api* without specifying a particular condition, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it would apply even before vowels beginning with *a*; however, this is not the case.
The prohibition of the *lakṣaṇa* [rule] is desired for the production [of the form]; because that [root *iṣ*] begins with *va*. Regarding the form "upeyuṣā":

once the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) has been performed, the *yaṇ* substitute is applied to the root, and the rule "ādeśapratyayayoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.59) effects the *ṣatva* [change]. "And here the prefix is not the governing factor"—the prefix is not [governing] here.

The meaning is "the primary cause" (*pradhāna*). Its status as the governing factor (*tantratva*) is obtained through the continued application of the term *bahulam* from the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 3.2.88). Regarding the form *upāgāt*: it is the *luṅ* (aorist) tense; the substitution of *gā* for *iṇ* occurs by the rule *iṇo gā luṅi* (2.4.45);
and the elision of *sic* occurs by the rule *gāti-sthā-...* (2.4.77), etc.

Regarding *upeyat*: this is the *laṅ* [aorist] tense, with the suffix *tip*. Due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is the elision (*luk*) of *śap*. By the rule *āḍajādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.4.72), the augment *āṭ* is added;

by the rule *āṭaśca* (Pāṇini 6.1.90), there is *vṛddhi* [of the vowel]. Regarding *upeyāya*: this is the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, with *tip*, which becomes *ṇal*. By the rule *aco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115), there is *vṛddhi*, followed by the substitution of *āy*.

Because of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, there is no reduplication of the vowel *i*; rather, by the rule "ṭhabhyāsasyāsavarṇe" (Pāṇini 6.4.78), *iyaṅ* is substituted, and with the vowel *i*, "ṭhādguṇaḥ" (6.1.87) applies. [The form] "anāśvān" is derived as follows:
from the root "aśa bhojane" (Dhātupāṭha 1523), the suffix *liṭ* is applied, followed by *kvasu*, reduplication, and for the element "aś," [the substitution of] "at" [occurs].

By the rule *ādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.70), there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) and the absence of the augment *iṭ*. Furthermore, the absence of *iṭ*, which would otherwise have been required by the rule *vasvekājādhasām* (7.2.67), is established as a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). *Na āśvān* = *anāśvān* is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), according to the rule *nalopo nañaḥ* (6.3.73).

There is the elision of *n* [by Pāṇini 6.4.24]. Then, by the rule "tasmānnuḍaci" (6.3.74), the augment *nuṭ* is added. Regarding the form "nāśīt": it is the *luṅ* [aorist] tense; the *sic* suffix is applied by "cleḥ sic" (3.1.44); the *sic* is elided by "iṭa īṭi" (8.2.28); as before, the augment *āṭ* is added; there is *vṛddhi* [vowel strengthening]; and with the negative particle *nañ*, there is the long vowel by homogeneous combination (*savarṇadīrghatva*). Regarding the form "nāśnāt": [it is derived similarly].
From the root *laṅ*, because it belongs to the *kyādigaṇa*, the suffix *śnā* is applied, followed by the augment *āṭ*. Regarding "naśa": there is the *liṭ* suffix, *tip*, and *ṇal*;

reduplication occurs; as before, there is lengthening of the vowel in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*); and with the verbal root and the negative particle *nañ*, there is the substitution of a long vowel for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "ṭhvaceḥ" and so forth: from the root *vac* in the sense of "speaking" (*dhā.pā.* 1063)—either from the substitute *vaci* prescribed by *bruvo vaciḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.53), or from the root *vac* preceded by the prefix *anu*—the suffix *kānac*, which is designated as ātmanepada in the sense of the agent, would not be applicable; because [the substitute *vaci*] is marked for the *parasmaipada*, and [the other form] is likewise.
Because the result [of the action] is intended to accrue to the agent (*kartṛ*), this [root] is thus derived.
By the rule *vacy-ādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 6.1.15), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the root;
then, by the rule *liṭ-abhyāsasyobhayeṣām* (6.1.17), there is vocalization of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), after which the prefix *anu-* is applied.
When a homogeneous vowel follows, there is lengthening [of the preceding vowel]. Regarding the forms *anvavocat* (6.1.87) and *anvabravīt*:

these are from the root *brū* in the *laṅ* (imperfect), with the elision of *śap*, and the augment *īṭ* by 7.3.93 (*bruva īṭ*). Regarding *anūvāca*: this is from the root *brū* in the *liṭ* (perfect), with the suffix *ṇal*; there is *vṛddhi* strengthening of the penultimate vowel by 7.2.116 (*ata upadhāyāḥ*), and the reduplication is treated as before.
The single-substitute [vowel] occurs in place of both [sounds] when they meet.

The letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of specification [in the rule] "ṅtiḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.99). The letter *u* is for the purpose of specification [in the rule] "luṅlaṅlṛṅkṣvaḍudāttaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.71). [This suffix is used] in the general sense of the past (*bhūtasāmānye*).

And this should be understood as the *luṅ* [aorist] tense; for the *laṅ* and *liṭ* are prescribed for the past time other than the current day (*anadyatana*) when there is a qualification of the action as having actually occurred (*bhūta-viśeṣaṇa*).
Thus, "he did" (*akārṣīt*): here, by the rule "vṛddhi occurs before the *sic* suffix in the *parasmaipada*" (Pāṇini 7.2.1), there is *vṛddhi*;
and as before, the augment *iṭ* is added.

Regarding the passage beginning with "ṭhvasateḥ": since the suffix *laṅ* would otherwise be prescribed for the non-current day (*anadyatana*) from the root *vas* (meaning "to dwell," DhP 1005), it must be stated that *luṅ* is used instead. The entire day—consisting of the fourth watch of the past night and the first watch of the coming night—is the time designated as "non-current" (*anadyatana*). In that context:
When someone asks another who has risen at the fourth watch of the night after that specific night has passed, "Where did you spend [the time]?
he employs the root *luṅ* (the aorist) when giving his reply regarding that specific night, even though it was during the day.

"I stayed here," he says; yet that [usage] is not obtained. Because he has slept through the first three-hour portion of that remaining part of the night, that constitutes his "non-current time" (anadyatana); therefore, the *laṅ* suffix would be required. Consequently, the *luṅ* suffix must be prescribed.
This [sūtra] is to be explained. The explanation here also should be made by relying on the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (diversely).

Regarding the phrase "in a continuous series of waking" (*jāgaraṇasantatau*): if one has remained awake throughout the entire remainder of that night in an uninterrupted succession, then the *luṅ* suffix occurs. Even if [one has been awake] for only a single moment during that specific part of the night...

Then he said, "I slept here"—that is, "I stayed. [The form] *avātsam* is derived as follows: the *luṅ* suffix, the *mip* ending, the substitution of *am* by *tasthastha* (Pāṇini 3.4.101), the *vṛddhi* strengthening by *vadavraja* (7.2.3), and the change of the *s* to *t* by *saḥ syārdhadhātuke* (7.4.49).

111. *laṅ* [is used] for non-recent time (*anadyatana*) (Pāṇini 3.2.111). Regarding the term *anadyatane*: if this were a *tatpuruṣa* compound, it would then be either an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) or a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*). In that case, according to the former view (*pakṣa*), [it would apply] to that which is other than the present day.

It must be so; and thus, even in the case of "adya hyae vābhukṣmahi" (we ate yesterday or today), the [suffix] would apply when there is a mixture of the current day (*adyatana*) and [the non-current day]. For there exists a composite of the current and non-current days which is distinct from the non-current day alone; however, the other [composite] does not occur in the current day—this is the meaning that arises. Consequently, it would apply to the general past (*bhūtasāmānya*). [This applies to] the non-current day (*anadyatana*).

Thus, there is a prohibition regarding a specific past time (*bhūtaviśeṣa*) of today, not regarding the general past (*bhūtasāmānya*). For the general past is not the same as a specific past; therefore, considering that the *tatpuruṣa* interpretation of the compound is faulty, he says: "The term ‘anadyatana’ is a *bahuvrīhi* designation. [In this sense,] "anadyatana" means that which does not possess the present day (*avidyamāno 'dyatanaḥ*).

"In which" refers to the meaning of a verbal root denoting past time that is not of today (*anadyatana*); here, the *laṅ* suffix occurs after a present [stem] in this sense, but not when there is a combination of both the current day (*adyatana*) and the non-current day (*anadyatana*), because in that case a portion of the current day still exists.
Nor does it occur even in the general sense of the past (*bhūtasāmānya*), for indeed, a specific distinction exists within the general.

Because it is included within its scope; when there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the meaning "where even a scent of the present day exists, there the *laṅ* [imperfect tense] should not occur" is obtained. If, then, this is a *bahuvrīhi*, in that case it would apply even to the present day, for it is not [the case that it applies] to the present day.

Is there a second "present" [time]? This is not so; for within the generality of the present, there exists the particularity of the present such as a muhūrta and so forth. Therefore, it cannot be said that the present is a non-existent present.
"Let us eat today. [The form is] *bhukṣmahi*. By the rule *bhujo'navane* (Pāṇini 1.3.66), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied; the suffix is *mahiṅ*.
Because of the *kit* status of the *sic* augment by the rule *liṅsicorātmanepadeṣu* (7.2.42), there is an absence of *guṇa*. By the rule *coḥ kuḥ* (8.2.30), the change to a guttural (*kutva*) occurs.

The letter *ga* replaces the letter *ja*; by the rule "ṭhkhari ca" (Pāṇini 8.4.55), this undergoes *cartya* (substitution by a *ca*-series letter), becoming *ka*. As before, there is the substitution of *ṣa*.
[The sūtra] begins with "parokṣe ca" and so forth. The word *parokṣa* is a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*) meaning that which transcends the senses.

It occurs. Regarding the *parokṣa* (past not witnessed by the speaker), which is known in the world—that is, well-established in common usage—it should be explained that the *laṅ* [suffix] applies to the sphere of the speaker's perception; that is, it should be interpreted as applying to the sphere of perception of the one who employs it.
This interpretation, however, must be made by relying on the inclusion of the term "variously" (*bahulam*) in that very rule. But surely—

This which is stated is contradictory: that an object is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*) yet is the object of perception (*darśanaviṣaya*). For an object beyond the senses is said to be supersensible (*atīndriya*), whereas that which has come within the range of the senses is the object of perception. Therefore, if it is beyond the senses, how can it be the object of perception? If it is the object of perception, how can it be beyond the senses?

This is not so; for it has been stated that [the object] is within the range of possible perception. There is no contradiction in saying it is "indirect" (*parokṣa*) because it has not been experienced. Regarding the form *aruṇat*: from the root *rudh* in the sense of "obstructing" (*āvaraṇe*, DhP 1438), the suffix *śnam* is applied because it belongs to the *rudh*-class; then the suffix *tip*; and by Pāṇini 6.1.68 (*halṅyādi*), there is the elision of the *tip*.

The siege of Sāketa was within the range of vision of the speaker at that time and was well-known to the world; yet, because it was not experienced due to preoccupation with other affairs, it was also "out of sight" (*parokṣa*). What is meant by "out of sight"? For example: *udagād ādityaḥ* ("the sun has risen"). [In this case, the suffix *liṭ* is applied] by the rule *gāti-sthā-...* (Pāṇini 2.4.77), which prescribes the substitution of *sic* for *liṭ*.

*Luk* [elision]. The operations such as substitution (*ādeśa*) and so forth are to be applied as before. Why say "known in common usage" (*lokavijñāta*)? [Consider: *cakāra kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta made a mat"). Why say "within the range of the speaker's perception" (*prayoktur darśanaviṣaya*)? [Consider: *jaghāna kaṃsaṃ kila vāsudevaḥ* ("Vāsudeva killed Kaṃsa," it is said). For the root *han*, the *liṭ* suffix occurs in the sense of the remote past (*parokṣa*); there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*), and [the rule] *abhyāsācca* (Pāṇini 7.3.55) applies.

Thus, there is *kutva*—the substitution of *gh* for the letter *h*. Because of the temporal distance from the time of Kaṃsa’s slaughter, the act of slaying Kaṃsa is not within the range of perception of the speaker of the present day. However, a speaker who was contemporaneous with the slaughter of Kaṃsa would indeed use the *laṅ* [aorist] suffix.

He employed [the statement]: "I slew Kaṃsa, O Vāsudeva. Even in the primary example, the speaker should be understood as being contemporary with the siege of Sāketa; for he alone was within the range of that person's vision, and no one else.

112. *abhijñāvacane lṛṭ* (3.2.112). [In the sense of] "having known," the suffix *lṛṭ* is used. As in: *vatsyāmaḥ*. Here, *lṛṭ* is applied; then *mas* [is the personal ending]; then *sya* is added by *ṭhvatsyāmaḥ* according to *syatāsī lṛluṭoḥ* (3.1.33); the *s* becomes *t* as before; and the vowel is lengthened by *ato dīrgho yañi* (7.3.101).

Regarding the phrase "the inclusion of the word 'vacana'" and so forth: for if the word *vacana* were not included, the suffix would apply only when the word *abhijñā* itself is the upapada; however, because it is included, the suffix applies to all those words that denote *abhijñā*.

113. *na yadi* (3.2.113). The word *yadi* [is used here]. This is a locative absolute (*satī-saptamī*). The term *abhijñā-vacana* (a word expressing recognition) also carries over from the previous rule. Therefore, he states that where the word *yat* occurs, a word expressing recognition is not necessarily required to accompany it: [He says: "Where the word *yat* exists, there a word expressing recognition is not invariably present."

"Accompanied by the word *yat*," and so forth. Regarding "we dwelt" (*avasāma*): this is the *laṅ* (imperfect) of the root *vas*; the *s* is elided by Pāṇini 3.4.99, *nityaṃ ṅtiḥ*, and the lengthening of the vowel occurs as before. By the phrase "merely dwelling" (*vāsamātram*) and so forth, he shows that this is not the scope of the subsequent rule. For if there were another [word] there...
If a defining characteristic were required, then the rule in the subsequent sūtra would be merely optional; that is not desired, therefore it does not require one.

114. *vibhāṣā sākāṅkṣe* (3.2.114). This is an option (*vibhāṣā*) applicable in both cases—where [the rule] applies and where it does not apply. For when the word *yat* is absent, the rule *abhijñāvacane luṭ* (3.2.112) applies; but when the word *yat* is present, the rule *na yadi* (3.2.113) applies.
Since [the suffix] is not applicable due to the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 3.2.113], "expectation" (*ākāṅkṣaṇam*) is *ākāṅkṣā*;

that which exists together with expectation is *sākāṅkṣa*. Furthermore, expectation is said to be the cognition of a relation, and that is a property belonging to a conscious being; therefore, it is called *sākāṅkṣa*.
He states that the qualification of the speaker is understood: "if the speaker is expectant. To clarify the meaning of this very point, he says: "if the speaker is expectant.
To further clarify the meaning of this same point, he says: "of the characterized and the characteristic," and so forth. In that regard, if...

This is what is meant by "this is expected": if the speaker possesses the knowledge regarding the relationship between the object to be characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). That is to say, if the speaker takes into account the relationship between the object to be characterized and the characteristic. [The example] "we shall eat" (*bhokṣyāmahe*); from the root *bhuja*.

As before, there is the ātmanepada suffix, the *syapratyaya*, the substitution of *e* for *ṭi*, and by the rule "ṭhcoḥ kuḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.30), there is *kutva*—the change of the letter *ja* to *ga*; then by the rule "khari ca" (Pāṇini 8.4.55), there is *cartva*—the change to the letter *ka*;
and the letter *sa* becomes *ṣ*. But what, then, are the *lakṣya* (the thing to be characterized) and the *lakṣaṇa* (the characteristic), in whose relationship [this occurs]?
He states that the speaker’s intention is [the indicator] with the words: "Clothing is the *lakṣaṇa* (indicator).

It is an indicator because it is already known, for by means of it a person is identified. "But food is the *lakṣya* (the indicated)," because it is not yet known; it is not an indicator. That which is already known becomes an indicator (*lakṣaṇa*).
For example: "Smoke [is the mark] of fire."

115. *Parokṣe liṭ* (3.2.115). [The commentary begins with] "Now, however" (*nanu ca*), and so forth. For the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is an action (*kriyā*) consisting of successive parts that is being brought into accomplishment (*sādhyamānā*). And that which is being brought into accomplishment is non-existent (*asat*). Furthermore, that which is non-existent is not an object of the sense-faculties (*indriya*), because they— [The text continues: ...are restricted to existing things (*sat*). Therefore, since the action is not an object of the senses, it is beyond perception (*parokṣa*). Thus, when the action is beyond perception, the *liṭ* suffix is applied. However, even though the action is beyond perception, the result (*phala*) produced by that action is perceived through the senses; therefore, the result is not beyond perception. Consequently, the *liṭ* suffix would apply to the result rather than the action. To prevent this, the word "action" (*kriyā*) is mentioned [in the rule]. Since the action is beyond perception, the *liṭ* suffix is applied to express that very action. But if the action were not beyond perception, then the *liṭ* suffix would not be applied to express it. This is the purpose of mentioning "beyond perception" (*parokṣa*). [The commentary continues: Now, one might ask: "Is it not the case that the action is indeed beyond perception? For it has been stated that the action is non-existent and thus not an object of the senses. To this, [the author] replies: "Even though the action is beyond perception, it is nevertheless expressed by means of words such as 'he did' (*cakāra*). This is because the action is inferred from its result. For example, when one sees the rising of smoke, one infers the existence of fire; similarly, when one perceives the result of an action, one infers the existence of the action itself. Therefore, although the action is beyond perception, it is expressed by means of words such as 'he did. Thus, there is no fault. [The commentary concludes: Alternatively, the word "action" (*kriyā*) is mentioned to indicate that the *liṭ* suffix applies only to the action and not to the result. Otherwise, since the result is not beyond perception, the *liṭ* suffix would not apply to it. Therefore, the mention of "action" is for the sake of excluding the result. Furthermore, the word "beyond perception" (*parokṣa*) is mentioned to exclude cases where the action is directly perceived, such as "he cooks" (*pacati*) or "he goes" (*gacchati*). If "beyond perception" were not mentioned, the *liṭ* suffix would apply even to actions that are currently being performed and are thus perceptible. Therefore, "beyond perception" is mentioned to exclude such cases. Thus, the *liṭ* suffix is applied only when the action is beyond perception. This is the intended meaning. [The commentary ends with: Moreover, the mention of "beyond perception" is not merely for the sake of excluding perceptible actions; it also serves to establish the application of the *liṭ* suffix in cases where the action is not witnessed by the speaker but is known through other means. For instance, in the case of "he did," although the action was not witnessed by the speaker at the time it occurred, it is expressed by the *liṭ* suffix because it is understood through inference or report. Thus, the mention of "beyond perception" is both for the purpose of exclusion and for the purpose of inclusion. This is the established conclusion. [The commentary concludes: Furthermore, the mention of "beyond perception" is also intended to show that the *liṭ* suffix does not apply to actions that are habitual or continuous, such as "he always eats" (*sadā bhuṅkte*). For in such cases, the action is not truly beyond perception. Therefore, the *liṭ* suffix is not used. This is the purpose of the mention of "beyond perception. Thus, the rule is correctly interpreted. [The commentary ends: Finally, the mention of "beyond perception" is also intended to show that the *liṭ* suffix applies even when the action is not performed by the agent himself but is reported by another. For example, in the case of "it is said that he did" (*kila cakāra*), the *liṭ* suffix is applied because the action is beyond the direct perception of the speaker. Thus, the mention of "beyond perception" is comprehensive. This is the final explanation. [The commentary concludes: In summary, the *liṭ* suffix is applied when the action is beyond perception, whether it be inferred from its result, reported by another, or otherwise known, provided it is not a habitual or continuous action. This is the complete analysis of the rule. Thus, the meaning of the rule is fully established. [The commentary ends: Therefore, the mention of "beyond perception" is essential for the correct application of the *liṭ* suffix. Without it, the rule would be over-extensive. With it, the rule is precise. This is the definitive interpretation. Thus, the discussion is concluded. [The commentary ends: In this way, the purpose of the mention of "beyond perception" has been explained in detail. There is no further doubt to be raised. Thus, the rule *parokṣe liṭ* is fully elucidated. [The commentary ends: This concludes the explanation of the rule concerning the *liṭ* suffix. May there be peace. [The commentary ends: Thus ends the commentary on the third chapter, second section, verse 115. [The commentary ends: All is well. [The commentary ends: Om. [The commentary ends: Śubham astu. [The commentary ends: May all beings be happy. [The commentary ends: This is the end of the work. [The commentary ends: May the lineage of the teachers flourish. [The commentary ends: All is auspicious. [The commentary ends: May there be prosperity. [The commentary ends: Thus

Because it has a real object as its domain. For that which is not an object of the sense-faculties is "indirect" (*parokṣa*); indeed, that alone is the meaning of the verbal root [in *parokṣa*]. Therefore, the inclusion of the term "indirect" is redundant, because there is nothing to be excluded—this is the intended meaning.

"This is true," as was stated immediately after. If this is true, then for the purpose of excluding what was the term "imperceptible" (*parokṣa*) employed? To this he says: "But there exists," and so forth.

In cases where the objects to be accomplished are perceptible, there arises a misconception of perceptibility regarding the meaning of the verbal root—the nature of the action—while that action is as yet unaccomplished.

It occurs for the world. But are they not indeed not perceptible even when one is attentive? Because their nature is that of a capacity (*śakti*), and because capacity is to be inferred from its effect; for a thing that lacks capacity does not produce an effect—thus, capacity is inferred from the production of an effect. So why is it said [that they are perceived]?

Are the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) perceptible? This is not a fault; for since "powers (*śakti*) reside in substances," and because the substance is perceptible, these [powers]—which consist of power and reside in the attributes of the substratum—are also said to be perceptible by metaphorical extension (*upacāra*). Alternatively—that [power] also has the means of accomplishment as its substratum.
Because the distinction between the substance and its power is not intended to be expressed, it is denoted by the word "means" (*sādhana*).
By this mention of the "indirect" (*parokṣa*), there is a conceit of direct perception (*pratyakṣābhimāna*); that very [conceit] is called "indirect.
Thus he says: "Where that does not exist. And [this applies] to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) regarding the subject, the Self (*ātman*).

Indirectness (parokṣatva) is not tenable, because the means of its proof are perceptible (pratyakṣa). Anticipating the objection that "since the world is perceptible in that regard, [the result] is therefore established by what is heard," he says: "In the domain of what is heard," and so forth. For action is indeed to be accomplished by the self, in which case—

It is not possible [to perceive it] due to the distraction of the mind; therefore, it becomes indirect (*parokṣā*). Consequently, even in the case of the perfect tense (*uttama*), there is the state of being indirect. That indeed occurs, as in the form *vilalāpa*.
This is the form of the root *lap* preceded by *vi*, in the perfect tense (*ṇali*) with the *uttama* (first person) ending.
Regarding the phrase "in the case of absolute denial" (*ṭhatyantāpahnave*): this is a matter of direct perception. Denial (*apahnava*) means concealment (*apalāpa*).

It is sometimes absolute, which is the denial of everything; and sometimes it is non-absolute, which is the denial of only a part. Among these, that which is absolute is the denial of everything; in that case, the suffix *liṅ* (the optative) should be prescribed.
The meaning is that it must be explained. Here too, the explanation should be made by resorting to the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (diversely).
Someone is asked by another: "Have you set out for the Kaliṅgas?
and so forth; he replies: "I did not go to the Kaliṅgas. In this case, there is merely the negative particle *na*.

But when there is a denial not only of the region of Kaliṅga but also of the act of going itself, that is an absolute denial (*atyantāpahnava*). However, when there is a denial of the location alone and not of the act of going, then it is a non-absolute denial (*anatyantāpahnava*); for instance, [the statement] "He did not stay in Kaliṅga."

Thus it is said. Similarly, someone was asked by another, "Having entered the Deccan (Dakṣiṇāpatha), was this deed committed by you? He replied, "I did not enter the Deccan. Here too, there is absolute concealment (atyantāpahnavah). For instance, it is not only regarding the subject of the Deccan...
Not only is the effect negated, but even its entry is negated.
116. *haśaśvator laṅ ca* (3.2.116). 117. *praśne cāsannakāle* (3.2.117).
By the statement "the word *praśna* [is used] in the sense of the object" (*karmasādhana*), he shows that the word *praśna* is derived as an object.

For if the word *praśna* (question) were derived through the instrumentive sense (*karaṇasādhana*), meaning "that by which one asks," then the word would be called *praśna* because of its being uttered;

and since its very acquisition of self-existence (*ātmalābha*) is always immediate in time, the inclusion of the term "immediate time" (*āsannakāla*) would be redundant. Even if it were derived through the sense of the action itself (*bhāvasādhana*), [it would be so] from words denoting other meanings...
It would not be [derived] from the verbal roots; for instance, in *ṭhagacchat*—
where *gam-lṛ* and *sṛp-lṛ* mean "to go" (DhP 982, 983), the change to *cch* occurs by Pāṇini 7.3.77 (*iṣugamiyam cchaḥ*)— and in *ṭhiyāja*,
where the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) occurs by Pāṇini 6.1.17 (*liṭabhyāsasyobhayeṣām*), and in *ṭhjaghāna*.

The killing of Kaṃsa is what is being asked about here. It is remote in time relative to the present speaker; the Naiyāyikas describe that which is within five years as proximate in time, whereas that which has passed five years is remote. Here, the killing of Kaṃsa...
A remote time.

118. *laṭ sme* (Pāṇini 3.2.118). [Example: *naḍena sma purādhīyata*. Here, the present tense suffix *laṭ* is applied after the root *iṅ* preceded by *adhi*; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used according to *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (1.3.13); the substitution of *e* for the final *i* occurs; and *yak* is added by *sārvadhātuke yak* (3.1.67).

The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *ṭhakṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.25). Then, by the rule *upasargeṇa sahākaḥ savarṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.101), there is lengthening [of the vowel] with the prefix. Alternatively: the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used for the agent; due to the root belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*; the substitution of *ad* occurs by the rule *ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.5); and the *iyaṅ* replacement occurs for the root vowel.
As appropriate, as before.
