119. *Aparokṣe ca* (3.2.119). [The examples are] *bravīti* and *kathayati*. Regarding *bravīti*: by the rule *bruva īṭ* (7.3.93), the augment *īṭ* is added. Regarding *kathayati*: the root *katha* (meaning "to compose a speech") is listed at DhP 1851; it belongs to the *curādi* group and ends in a short vowel (*a*). From this, the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied, and then [the elision of the penultimate *a* occurs].

Due to the status of being "as if in the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*)—by the rules "there is elision" (*lopaḥ*, 6.4.48) and "when a subsequent [element] intervenes, it is as if it were not there for a preceding rule" (*acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau*, 1.1.57)—the *vṛddhi* substitution prescribed by "of that which has *at* as its penultimate letter" (*ata upadhāyāḥ*, 7.2.116) does not occur.
Now, for what purpose is this [sūtra] commenced again? Because the previous [rule] prescribes [the suffix] in the remote past (*parokṣa*), it does not apply in the non-remote (*aparokṣa*).

[The suffix] is obtained; therefore, it is for the sake of ensuring that [the rule] applies there as well. Now, one might object: "In the previous rule (*pūrvayoga*), the mention of 'remote' (*parokṣa*) will be withdrawn; once that is withdrawn, [the suffix] will apply by the preceding rule itself, both in the remote and in the non-remote. This is true; however, someone might still raise the following objection: "If..."
The mention of "parokṣa" (out of sight) has been removed; since it is connected with that, the mention of "anadyatana" (not of today) is also removed.
Lest this be misunderstood otherwise, the term "parokṣa" from the preceding sūtra is carried over [as anuvṛtti].
While that is being carried over, this [present rule] must be applied; for otherwise, it would not apply in cases that are not "aparokṣa" (within sight).
120. *nanau pṛṣṭaprativacane* (3.2.120). Regarding the term *pṛṣṭaprativacane*: *pṛṣṭam* means "questioned"; the suffix *niṣṭhā* is used here in the sense of the action (*bhāve*).
A reply preceded by a question is *pṛṣṭaprativacanam*.

This is a compound with the middle term elided (*madhyamapadalopī samāsaḥ*), following the *śākapārthiva* class and others. [The rule] "the [use of the periphrastic future] is for the remote past not of today" (*anadyatane parokṣe*) has ceased to apply, because it is not marked with the svarita accent. "Did you make the mat, Devadatta?"—this is the question.
"Indeed, I am making it, sir"—this is the reply preceded by that question. "You said there..."
"Is Devadatta doing something?"—this is the question. "Indeed, I am doing it, sir"—this is the answer preceded by that question.
"Has he not done it?"—this is an answer that is not preceded by a question; therefore, it occurs only in *luṅ*.
[It] exists. But surely every answer is preceded by a question; therefore, the mention of "asked" is useless, because there is nothing to be excluded [by it]. This is not accepted;
for this word "answer" (prativacana) indeed exists in the sense of a statement following what was asked—that which does not exist without a question.

It exists; it exists in the sense of an *avyayībhāva* compound—namely, "word after word" (*vacanaṃ vacanaṃ*) meaning "in reply" (*prativacanam*), where an *avyayībhāva* occurs in the sense of repetition according to Pāṇini 2.1.6, "An indeclinable [is compounded] in the sense of 'according to'"; and it exists as a term for meditative absorption (*samādhi*), because the root *vac* preceded by *prati* is seen to denote absorption, for so say those who speak.
They say: "That which was not stated by [the opponent] has been employed by me"—the meaning is that it has been refined (*pariṣkṛta*).

Thus, since the word *prativacana* (rejoinder) has multiple meanings, if the mention of "questioned" (*pṛṣṭa*) were not made, it would apply to all those meanings. But when this [mention of "questioned"] is made, it refers to that which is preceded by a question.
The word "response" (prativacana) refers specifically to that [word] alone and not to anything else; thus, there is no pointlessness in your [statement].
121. *nanvor vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 6.3.75).
[The example] *nākarṣam* is formed as before, with the substitution of *am*.
122. *puri luṅ cāsme* (Pāṇini 3.2.122). [The commentary says: "In the word *purā*. By this, he shows that the word *purā* is introduced here as an *upapada* (governing word), and not the word *pur*.
If it were only this [word *purā*], then because it ends in the vowel *ā*, [the form] *purī* would be the locative case ending.

Is the grammatical explanation not tenable? There is no fault, because of the elision of the long *ā* by means of a word-split (*yogavibhāga*) in the rule "āto dhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.140). Alternatively, [the form may be derived] from the root *pṛ* ("in the sense of protecting and filling," Dhātupāṭha 1086) by means of the rule for the *bhrāja*-class (Pāṇini 3.2.177).

Why is it not understood that the word *pūḥ*—which results from the application of the rule "kvipi vihitaṣṭhūdoṣṭhaḷpūrvasya" (Pāṇini 7.1.102), whereby the substitution of *u* occurs followed by *r* as a replacement—is also taken here as an *upapada*? Because its occurrence in the sense of the immediate past (*anadyatana*) is impossible; for the word *purā* functions only in that specific context [of the immediate past].

Thus, it is logical that only this [present tense] is taken [as the subject]. By the particle *ca* in the rule *ṭhluṅ ca*, he shows that *laṭ* is drawn along [by attraction]. "According to their respective domains" (*yathāviṣayam*): this is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to Pāṇini 2.1.7, *yathā’sādṛśye*, used here in the sense of distribution (*vīpsā*). "Others as well": namely, *laṅ* and the rest. "They dwell" (*vasanti*): this is *laṭ*.

"ṭhavātsuḥ": this is the *luṅ* [aorist] tense. By the rule "sijabhyastavidibhyaśca" (Pāṇini 3.4.109), there is the substitution of *jus* for *jhi*. By the rule "vadavraja" (Pāṇini 7.2.3) et cetera, there is *vṛddhi*. As before, there is the substitution of *t* for the *s* [of the suffix]. "ṭhavasan": this is the *laṅ* [imperfect] tense. "ṭhūṣuḥ": this is the *liṭ* [perfect] tense.

By the rule *ṭhparasmaipadānām* (3.4.82), *jhi* is replaced by *jus*; there is reduplication; by the rule *vacyādisūtra* (6.1.15), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) [of the semivowel]; and by the rule *ṭhliṭaḷbhyāsasyobhayeṣām* (6.1.17), there is vocalization of the reduplicated syllable as well; finally, by the rule *ṭhśāsivasighasīnāñca* (8.3.60), there is the substitution of *ṣ*.
123. *laṭ* [is used] for the present (*vartamāne*).

(Pāṇini 3.2.123). "That which has begun but is not yet completed" means: that which has been commenced—that is, set forth to be accomplished—and has not yet reached completion, is called "present. The mention of "present" [is made]...
Since the context concerns verbal roots (*dhātu*), it is understood that the qualification applies specifically to their meaning;

thus he says "in the present" (*vartamāne*), and so forth. For the occurrence of a verbal root is not possible where there is no meaning of a verbal root. The letter *ṭ* in *laṭ* is for the purpose of qualifying [the rule] "for the *ṭit* ātmanepada endings, *ṭer e*" (Pāṇini 3.4.79). The letter *a*...

The vowel *i* is for the purpose of specification, according to the rule "ṭhvido laṭo vā" (Pāṇini 3.4.83); for if the letter *i* were not pronounced, there would be the inclusion of *liṅ* and the other suffixes as well.

124. *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacāvaprathamāsamānādhikaraṇe* | (3.2.124) The *ś* in both *śatṛ* and *śānac* serves to indicate that they are *sārvadhātuka* suffixes. The vowel *ṛ* is for the purpose of triggering operations prescribed for items marked with the technical marker *u*. The term "not having the same referent as the nominative" (*aprathamāsamānādhikaraṇe*) is a restrictive exclusion (*paryudāsa*). This word "nominative" (*prathamā*)...

In this grammatical system, the term *apradhama* is conventionally established as referring to case-endings (*vibhakti*) other than the nominative (*su*), up to and including the accusative (*aujas*). Here, the word *samāna* signifies "common" or "shared," just as in the expression:
"Devadatta and Yajñadatta possess equal wealth."

This word *adhikaraṇa* denotes that which is expressed [by the term]. "That which is common (*samāna*) and that which is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*)" forms a *karmadhāraya* compound. "Not having the same locus as a non-nominative" means *aprathamā-samānādhikaraṇa*.
The compound is formed by the split of the rule *tṛtīyā* (Pāṇini 2.1.30). Then, by the rule *yasya ca bhāvena*...

The locative case [in the rule] "bhāvalakṣaṇam" (Pāṇini 2.3.37) is used because the state (*bhāva*) is indicated by the present participles *śatṛ* and *śānac* through their non-co-referentiality with a word ending in the nominative case. By the function of exclusion (*paryudāsa-vṛtti*), the term "not the first case" (*apratamā*) refers to the second and subsequent cases; thus, by the technical rule regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*), [the suffixes themselves are understood].

He says that the rule for modification at the end of a word (*tadanta-vidhi*) will apply: "If [there is] coreferentiality with a word ending in a case other than the first," and so forth. "'Of that' (*tasya*)" refers to the present tense suffix (*laṭ*). "'Coreferentiality' (*sāmānādhikaraṇyam*)" means having the same denotation (*samānābhidheyam*).
That is, if there is coreferentiality—that is, identity of denotation—with a word ending in the accusative case...

The meaning of the sentence is that the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* occur only in this way, and not otherwise. By explaining it in this manner, it is shown that here an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is intended for that which is not coreferential with the nominative, rather than a simple prohibition (*prasajyapratiṣedha*); for if a simple prohibition were intended, [the following would occur].
If one were to say that there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a word ending in the nominative case,

what would happen if a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) were resorted to? In that case, the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* could not occur when the subsequent member of the compound is not coreferential— for example, [the forms] "bhaktiḥ" (from *bhajyate*) and "kurvan" would not be possible.

*bhaktir asya kurvadbhaktiḥ* (his devotion is that of one who is currently performing devotion), *kurvāṇo bhaktir asya kurvāṇabhaktiḥ* (he whose devotion is that of one who is currently performing devotion). Furthermore, these two [suffixes] would not occur in the case of those secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) which have meanings coreferential with the first member (*prathama-samānādhikaraṇa-vṛtti*), such as in *praśaṃsāyāṃ rūpap* (Pāṇini 5.3.66):
*kurvadrūpam*, *kurvāṇarūpam*; and in *īṣadasamāptau*...

Regarding the rule *kalpaśabdeśyadeśīyaraḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.67), we have the example *kurvatkalpaḥ*. Now, one might object: even in the case of *paryudāsa* (exclusion), the same fault remains; for here, it is not the case that [the suffix] occurs with something other than a word ending in the first case (*apathamāntena*), even when there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a word in the first case. However, in the case of *prasajyapratiṣedha* (absolute negation), the negation...

Furthermore, it is improper to first enjoin that which has been prohibited; for instance, in the example "see Devadatta cooking," [the author] demonstrates coreferentiality with a word ending in the accusative case. In the form "pacatā," [he shows it] with a word ending in the instrumental case, by changing the case-ending and connecting it as "by Devadatta."

But is it not the case that here the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) belongs to the substitute (*ādeśa*) of *laṭ* with what does not end in the nominative case, and not to *laṭ* itself, because the latter does not occur in actual usage? There is no fault, for by metaphorically attributing the property of the substitute to the original base (*sthānin*), the coreferentiality of *laṭ* also becomes figuratively applicable. Now, as for the mention of *laṭ*:

For what purpose [is this], since the term *laṭ* continues to apply from the immediately preceding sūtra? It might be argued: "This [term *laṭ*] is in the nominative case, whereas here the sense requires a genitive indication;
therefore, the term *laṭ* must be mentioned again for the sake of indicating the genitive. But this is incorrect, because even that which is in the nominative case [can serve as a reference].

Since it might be argued that the mention of *laṭ* here is for the purpose of changing the case-ending of its referent so that it is understood as being in the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), he says: "While *laṭ* is still in force," and so forth.

Furthermore, the mention of *laṭ* again is for the sake of [excluding cases where it is] not in grammatical coreferentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇa*) with a non-nominative (*aprathamā*). By means of this, in some instances...

The two [suffixes] occur when not in grammatical agreement with the first word—*kurvan brāhmaṇaḥ* and *san brāhmaṇaḥ*. In *as*, from the root *as* "to be" (DhP 1065), there is elision of *śap* due to its belonging to the *adādi* class.
By the rule *śnasoralopaḥ* (6.4.111), there is elision of the vowel *a*; thus, in all instances such as *vidyamānaḥ*, the word *brāhmaṇaḥ* remains [unchanged].
Thus it is expected. [The root] *vid* in the sense of "existence" (*satāyām*) belongs to the *divādi* class and is *ātmanepada*;
[the suffix] *śyan* is applied. Regarding *juhvat* (Pāṇini 7.1.78):

[the root] *hu* in the sense of "giving" (*dāne*)—some say "taking" (*ādāne*), while the Bhāṣya says "also in the sense of pleasing" (*prīṇane*)—belongs to the *juhotyādi* class; [the suffixes] *hu* and *śnu* [are applied].

The substitution of *yaṇ* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.87] *sārvadhātuke*; the absence of the augment *num* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.1.78] *nābhyastāc chatuḥ*. Thus, "adhīyānaḥ. The root is *iṅ* in the sense of "studying" (DhP 1.1046), preceded by the prefix *adhi*. As before, the substitution of *iyaṅ* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.77] *aci śnu* etc.

Regarding the rule "māṅy-ākrośe" (Pāṇini 3.2.173): when the root *māṅ* is used as an upapada and reproach (*ākrośa*) is understood, the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* are applied to the present tense marker *laṭ*. Examples are "mā pacan" and "mā pacamānaḥ". Now, one might object: should not *luṅ* (the aorist) be used here instead, precisely because of this additional prescription?

Furthermore, because of the inclusion of *laṭ* [in the rule], the fault does not arise regarding verbal abuse (*ākrośa*), for that is the scope (*avakāśa*) of the rule *māṅi luṅ* (Pāṇini 3.3.175), where there is no verbal abuse.
"Some maintain that the term *vibhāṣā* is carried over [from the previous rule]," as in: "There is this Brāhmaṇa. *san*... *brāhmaṇaḥ asti brāhmaṇa*.
The phrase "in such cases as these" is for the purpose of ensuring that the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* may optionally occur;
by the use of the word "some," it is implied that some do not carry them over [from the previous rule].
Their intention is this: if those two were mandatory when coreferential with a nominative case...

In that case, you should not have included the phrase "not co-referential with a word ending in the nominative case" (*aprathamāsamānādhikaraṇa*); rather, you should simply have said "the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac*" (*śatṛśānacau*). Even in that formulation, the meaning would be this: since *śatṛ* and *śānac* are prescribed in general for cases other than those co-referential with a nominative, there is no need for a further mention [of that restriction].
It must be done.

Therefore, by the force of the inclusion of the term "not having the same referent as a word ending in a case other than the first" (*aprathamāsamānādhikaraṇa*), those two [suffixes] are necessarily applied only when they do not have the same referent as a word ending in a case other than the first; in the case of words having the same referent as a word ending in the first case (*prathamāsamānādhikaraṇa*), it is otherwise. If, then...

They maintain that the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) applies here, so that just as in cases such as *san brāhmaṇaḥ*, *asti brāhmaṇaḥ*, *vidyamāno brāhmaṇaḥ*, and *vidyate brāhmaṇaḥ*, [the suffixes] occur optionally; likewise, [one might object that] forms such as *kurvadbhaktiḥ* and *kurvāṇabhaktiḥ* would also be possible. To this, he says: "That..."
And so forth. Regarding the word "therein": this refers to when there is an option fixed by specific rule (vyavasthitavibhāṣā). Regarding "according to observation":

one should infer linguistic usages that correspond to the observation of the actual usage (lakṣya). This is what is meant: it should be like the observation of the usage. In some cases, those two suffixes, *śatṛ* and *śānac*, are obligatory.
It should be understood that [these suffixes] are sometimes optional and sometimes non-existent.
In cases such as *kurvadbhaktiḥ*, *kurvāṇabhaktiḥ*, *kurvataraḥ*, and *kurvatamaḥ*, they are obligatory (*nitya*);
in cases such as *san brāhmaṇaḥ* and *asti brāhmaṇaḥ*, they are optional (*pākṣika*); and [they are absent] when suffixes such as *tarap* and *tamap* follow.

The two others, however, do not exist at all in such cases. For instance, in the form *pacatitarām*: after the word *pacati*, the suffix *tarap* is applied by Pāṇini 5.3.56 (*tiṅśca*), and when the suffix *ām* is added by 5.4.11 (*kimeṭ* etc.), those two [suffixes] do not occur.
125. *sambodhane ca* (3.2.125).

"This rule is commenced for the purpose of [the nominative case] being coreferential with the first case (*prathamā-sāmānādhikaraṇa*)," it is said. Here, a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is to be understood.
For the preceding rule (*pūrva-yoga*) was for the purpose of [the nominative case] not being coreferential with the first case, in certain instances.

And [the previous rule] was for the purpose of being in grammatical agreement with a nominative case; this one, however, is specifically for the purpose of being in grammatical agreement with a nominative case.

If, then, the previous rule also applies when there is agreement with a nominative case, then, that being so, just as those two [suffixes] occur elsewhere even when there is agreement with a nominative case, so too should they occur in the vocative.

Is [the form] *bhaviṣyataḥ* meaningless? It is not meaningless, because it serves as an illustration (*prapañca*). [The example] *he pacan*: due to the prohibition of the elision of *n* by the rule *na ṅsimbuddhyoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.8), there is no elision of *n*. [The example] *he pacamāna*: [due to the rule] *eṅ hrasvāt*...
By the rule "sambuddheḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.69), there is the elision of the suffix *su*.

126. *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.126). [The commentary states: "And this is a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvarthaviśeṣaṇam*)," because of the governing context of "verbal root" (*dhātu*). Now, why do these two suffixes not occur when there is an attendant word (*upapada*)? Because of the explicit mention of "of the action" (*kriyāyāḥ*). If they were to occur when there is an attendant word, then...

The mention of "action" (*kriyā*) would be redundant. For a *upapada* belongs to a verbal root (*dhātu*), and since that [root] expresses action, even without the mention of "action," those two [suffixes] will be understood as having action as their domain by virtue of the definition. Therefore, by the mention of "action," [it is indicated that] those two serve as qualifiers of the meaning of the verbal root.

In some cases, the meaning of a verbal root (dhātvartha) is the cause of a substance, or its defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa); in some cases it is the cause of a quality (guṇa), and in some cases of an action (kriyā). Therefore, the mention of "action" (kriyā) is appropriate for the purpose of excluding substances and the like;
hence the statement "of an action. [The phrase] "having action as their object" means: of an action...

This is the explanation. Those two [verbs] whose objects are actions have been described accordingly. By this, it is indicated that this genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the rule "of the action" (*kriyāyāḥ*) is prescribed in place of the locative case (*saptamī*) through a transposition of case endings (*sub-vyatyaya*). For example: "lying down, they eat" (*śayānā bhuñjate*). Because the root *śīṅ* is included in the *apad* group, there is the elision of *śap*.

By the rule *luk, ṭhśīṅḥ sārvadhātuke* (Pāṇini 7.4.21), there is *guṇa* substitution. Here, lying down (*śayana*) is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), while the act of eating (*bhujikriyā*) is the object (*viṣaya*). For it is by means of that [lying down] that the act of eating is indicated; thus, the root *śīṅ* is employed there.
As in the expression *tiṣṭhanto 'nuśāsanti* ("standing, they instruct"), where, according to the rule *pāghrādhmādheṭdṛśaḥ śaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.78), [the substitute *śa* is applied to the root *sthā*].

The term *tiṣṭha* (staying) is an *ādeśa* (instruction). Here, staying (*avasthāna*) is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), by which the act of instruction (*anuśāsana-kriyā*) is indicated. In the example "He dwells while studying" (*adhyayan arjayann vasati*), it is the act of studying that [indicates].

In cases such as "he cooks" (*pacati*) or "he reads" (*paṭhati*), the relationship of indicator and indicated (*lakṣya-lakṣaṇa-bhāva*) between two actions is not intended. [Regarding] "yaḥ... [the text continues].

"This aśvattha tree trembles. Here, trembling is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); by means of that, the aśvattha is characterized. It is not, however, concerned with an action; rather, it concerns a substance (*dravya*), because the aśvattha is a substance. "That which floats is light."

In this case, the quality known as "lightness" (*laghu*) is indicated by the act of jumping; thus, that [suffix] has a quality as its domain, not an action. Even though in examples such as *varṣatīti dhāvati* ("he runs because it rains") and *hantīti palāyate* ("he flees because he is being struck"), the actions of running and fleeing are indicated by the acts of raining and striking, nevertheless, the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* [are used].

It does not apply to you [the opponent]; for from the rule *ṭhnanvor vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 3.2.121), the term *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (restricted option) is understood to carry over. This is because the use of the particle *iti* indicates that [the rule] functions as a reason. Furthermore, the fact that [a word] appears as the first member [of a compound] is a sign of its non-deviation from the definition. Thus: *dvandve ghi*.
(2.2.32) By this [sūtra], the rule regarding the prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) of a word ending in *dhi* is shown to have exceptions;

that is, even when its own scope (*svaviṣaya*) applies, its [prior placement] is sometimes absent. This specific mention (*nirdeśa*) is the indicator (*liṅga*) of that exception. For if the prior placement of a word ending in *dhi* were without exception, [the sūtra would have been stated simply as] "in the case of cause (*hetu*) and characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)."
One should provide an explanation; for when there is deviation, [statements] such as "smoke and fire" become justified.

127. [Objection: Surely, this designation would apply to the *śatṛ* and *śānac* suffixes simply because they are the subject under discussion; so what is the purpose of explicitly mentioning "those two" (*tau*)? [The author] says: "The mention of 'those two' (*taugrahaṇam*)," etc. [This is done] by way of a limiting condition (*upādhi*).

The meaning is that the mention of *tau* (the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac*) is for the purpose of excluding this specific [condition]. However, the temporal condition (*upādhi*) is the present time, because *śatṛ* and *śānac* are prescribed therein. He asks: when the mention of *tau* is made for the purpose of excluding the temporal condition, what happens?
He says: "of *śatṛ* and *śānac* alone," and so forth.

The inclusion of the term *mātra* (only) is for the purpose of excluding the inclusion of conditions (*upādhi*). For if that [term] were not included, the designation would apply only to those two [roots] exactly as they are in their original form (*prakṛti*). And what are those two? They are those prescribed for the present tense. Consequently, [the designation would not apply] to the substitutes of *lṛṭ*, which are prescribed for the future tense.

The designation *sad* would not apply. [Objection: But surely those two [tenses] are prescribed by the word *sat* in the rule "ṭhluṭaḥ sad vā" (Pāṇini 3.3.14); therefore, by the force of that statement, they will indeed be designated as *sadbhūta*. [Response: We do not say that their prescription is not established; rather, we say that the designation does not apply to them at a time subsequent to their being prescribed.

[The suffix *śatṛ*] is established [as denoting the present tense]. Consequently, in the cases *brāhmaṇasya kariṣyan* ("one who will do for a Brāhmaṇa") and *brāhmaṇasya kariṣyamāṇaḥ* ("one who is being made to do for a Brāhmaṇa"), the prohibition of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) by the rule *pūraṇaguṇa-* (Pāṇini 2.2.11) would not apply.

However, the inclusion of the word *sat* [in the rule] is intended so that [the prohibition applies] only when the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* denote the present tense by means of the word *sat* itself.

It would be for the purpose of prohibiting the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Since the mention of *ta* (the affix) designates the technical name (*saṃjñā*) based on the mere form without regard to the specific distinction between the *śatṛ* and *śānac* suffixes,
the designation is established even for those two [suffixes] which are not connected with the present tense.

128. *pūṅ-joḥ śānan* (Pāṇini 3.2.128). The suffixes *śatṛ*, *śānac*, and so forth, which are prescribed for the present tense (*vartamāna*), are they substitutes for *la* (*lādeśāḥ*) or independent suffixes (*pratyayāḥ*)? In this regard, if the term *laṭaḥ* (of the present tense marker *laṭ*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], then they are substitutes for *la*; however, if it does not carry over, [they are independent suffixes].

Then, regarding suffixes (*pratyaya*): if their substitutes (*ādeśa*) were to be applied [immediately], then the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) would have to be understood as carrying over from Pāṇini 3.2.121, *ṭhnanvor vibhāṣā*; otherwise, one would hear the finite verbal endings (*tiṅ*) in forms such as *pavate devadattaḥ* or *yajate devadattaḥ*. However, this is not the case under the rule of "suffix-characterization" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*).

When *laṭ* occurs by virtue of the rule regarding alternative forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*), then the hearing of a suffix— that is, the hearing of a *tiṅ*— is justified. Furthermore, under the view that [the suffixes] are substitutes (*ādeśapakṣa*), by the rule "after roots denoting action, *laḥ* is used in the sense of the object and,
after intransitive roots, in the sense of the state" (Pāṇini 3.4.69), suffixes such as *śānan* and others would also apply in the sense of the state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*).

[The suffixes] are intended [to apply] only in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). However, in the view that they are affixes (*pratyaya*), by the rule "kṛt [affixes] in the sense of the agent" (Pāṇini 3.4.67), they occur only in the sense of the agent and not in the senses of the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*); this is seen here in the examples "the agent here" (*katīha*) and "adorned here" (*maṇḍayamāna*), where the suffix *cānaś* is applied by the subsequent sūtra.

By the rule "ṭhtāsyanudātenṅdidupadeśāllasārvadhātukamanudātamahnviṅeḥ" (6.1.186), there would be a *nighāta* (anudātta accent) [on the affix], but this does not occur in the view that it is a suffix (*pratyaya*),
because it is not a *sārvadhātuka* affix. Furthermore, for the *cānaś* suffix, [the rule] "ṭhlaḥ parasmaipadam" (1.4.99) applies.

[If it were a suffix], the designation *ātmanepada* would apply by the rule "ṭita ātmanepadānāṃ ṭere" (Pāṇini 3.4.79), and consequently, [the substitution] would occur only after roots that take the *ātmanepada* endings—as in the example: *katīha nighnānāḥ*. However, in the view that it is a suffix (*pratyaya*), there is no possibility of the designation *ātmanepada* because it is a substitute for *la*. Thus, in this way, regarding the view that it is a substitute (*ādeśa*):
Since many faults would have to be remedied, and even in the case of such remedies there would be a burden of understanding them, he resorts to the view of it being an affix (*pratyaya*) and says:
"The affix *śānac* occurs. The letter *ś* is for the purpose of [granting] the designation *sārvadhātuka*. [Thus we get] *pavamānaḥ*.
Thus: from the root *pūṅ* "to purify" (DhP 966), with the suffix *śap*, and by [the rule] *āne muk* (Pāṇini 7.2.82).

Regarding the phrase "if," etc.: this is the question of one who considers that in rules such as *na lokāvyaya* (Pāṇini 2.3.69), the term *tṛn* refers specifically to the suffix *tṛn*. [The answer is: "It is *tṛn*."
"Because of the indication by way of a reference (pratyāhāra)"—as in "somaṃ pavamānaḥ" and "naḍam āghnānaḥ.

This is to be connected with the phrase "prohibition of the genitive" (ṣaṣṭhī-pratiṣedha). If there were a reference to the suffix *tṛn* itself, then, since the meaning of the suffix would apply to *śānan* and the others, [the forms] "somaṃ pavamānaḥ" [would not be established].
In such cases as these, the prohibition of the genitive case would not apply. Nor is there a reference here to the suffix *tṛn*;

rather, it is a reference to a *pratyāhāra* (a grammatical abbreviation). Since *śānan*, *nā* (*naḍ*), and others are included within that *pratyāhāra*, the prohibition of the genitive indeed takes effect.

Regarding the statement, "there is an option for the *śatṛ* [ending] after the root *dviṣ*," since the *śatṛ* prescribed by the rule *dviṣo'mitre* (Pāṇini 3.2.131) is included within this pratyāhāra, there would be a prohibition of the genitive case when that [ending] is used.

Consequently, [the rule] would not apply in the case of *caurasya dviṣan* (one who hates the thief). Therefore, when the present participle (*śatṛ*) of the root *dviṣ* (Dhp. 1013), meaning "to feel aversion," is employed, it should be stated that the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used optionally in place of the accusative (*dvitīyā*).

129. *tācchīlyavayovacanaśaktiṣu cānaś* (Pāṇini 3.2.129). [The example is] "maṇḍayamānāḥ. From the root *maḍi* in the sense of "adornment" (Dhātupāṭha 321); because it is marked with *it*, the augment *num* is added. Then the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied (*hetumaṇṇic*). Thus, "bhūṣayamāṇāḥ. From the root *bhūṣa* in the sense of "ornamentation" (Dhātupāṭha 682).

The suffix *ṇic* is applied to the root *cur* (from the *cur-ādi* class). In the phrase "casting off their armor" (*kavacaṃ paryasyamānāḥ*), the suffix *śyan* is applied because the root belongs to the *div-ādi* class. By that very [suffix], a particular stage of life (*vayaḥ*) is understood; those situated therein cast off their armor. "Armor" (*kavacam*) means a suit of mail or equipment.
In the phrase "bearing the crest-lock" (*śikhaṇḍaṃ vahamānāḥ*), likewise, a similar stage of life is understood wherein...

Those currently existing wear a tuft of hair (*śikhaṇḍa*). *Śikhaṇḍa* means a crest (*cūḍā*). The inclusion of the word "speech" (*vacana*) is for the sake of variety; for even without it, when age is understood, the suffix is indeed obtained, as in the rule *vayasi ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.20). [The example is] *nighnānāḥ*.
It is understood as the power of destruction.
130. *iṅdhāryoḥ śatrakṛcchriṇi* (3.2.130).

[The commentary states: *ṭhakṛcchriṇi kartari*. By this, he shows that *akṛcchriṇi* is an adjective qualifying the agent (*kartṛ*), which is the meaning of the suffix. One for whom [the action] is *akṛcchra*, i.e., easily accomplished, is *akṛcchrin*.
"The meaning of the root is 'that which is effortless' (*akṛcchrin*). The suffix *ini* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.115 (*ata iniṭhanau*).
"Adhīyan": as before, the *iyaṅ* substitution occurs. "Dhārayan": from the root *dhṛṅ* in the sense of "remaining steady" (DhP 1412), with the causative suffix *ṇic*.

131. *dviṣo'mitre* (3.2.131). [The suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *dviṣ* when *amitra* follows. Thus, *amitraḥ* means "an enemy. This is because the word *amitra* is a conventional term (*rūḍha*) derived specifically from the root *dviṣ*. [In the example] *dveṣṭi*, there is the elision (*luk*) of *śap* due to the root belonging to the *adādi* class.

132. *suño yajñasaṃyoge* (Pāṇini 3.2.132). Regarding the term "yajñasaṃyoga" (connection with sacrifice): the word *saṃyoga* is used here in the sense of an object (*karmasādhana*). For this very reason, the author of the Vṛtti says: "in the pressing [of Soma] connected with sacrifice. *Saṃyukta* means "connected," that is, joined with the sacrifice.

"Connected with sacrifice. And when is the pressing connected with sacrifice? When it becomes a constituent part (*yajñāṅga*) of the sacrifice. [The passage begins] "pressing [the Soma]" (*sunvantaḥ*), etc.; [here the suffix] *śnu* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.73 (*svādibhyaḥ śnuḥ*). "All the sacrificers" (*sarve yajamānāḥ*): by the word "pressing," those who are the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) in the sacrificial session (*sattra*) are meant.

He shows that they are designated as "masters" (svāmin), and not as "sacrificial officiants" (yājñika). But how is this meaning obtained, given that just as the sacrificers are the agents of the pressing (abhiṣava), so too are the officiants? To this he says: "The mention of 'connection' (saṃyoga)," and so forth. Here...

It should be understood that [the word "sunoti"] means "in a sacrifice" (*yajñe*); for even if this were stated, the connection with the sacrifice would indeed be obtained for the act of pressing (*abhiṣava*), since the meaning of the root *su* (to press) is understood as having the sacrifice as its domain. Therefore, the mention of "connection" (*saṃyoga*) is not necessary.

Is this to be done? It is performed for the purpose of identifying the primary agent. Those who, having become the performers of the sacrifice, obtain the fruit by pressing the Soma—these are the primary agents;
they, moreover, are the sacrificers (yajamānas), not the officiating priests (yājakas).

133. *arhaḥ* is used in the sense of praise. (3.2.133) 134. *ā kveḥ* [is added] in the sense of one who has that habit (*tacchīla*), one who possesses that quality (*taddharmā*), or one who performs that well (*tatsādhukārī*). [The commentary states: "When the agent (*kartṛ*) has those habits, etc. By this, [the suffixes are applied] to those who have such habits and so forth.
He shows that this [prefix] *āṅ* functions as a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*). He says: "And this *āṅ* is used in the sense of *abhividhi*.

*Abhividhi* means pervasion (*abhivyāpti*). Here, *āṅ* is not used in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*); therefore, this is also the specification of the meaning for the *kvip* suffix that will be mentioned later. That [suffix] also occurs only in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth.

Regarding the passage beginning with "tat" and so forth: the term "dhātoḥ" (from 3.1.91) is understood to carry over, yet it is not possible for a root to be qualified by attributes such as habit (*śīla*) and the like. Therefore, that which is the meaning of the root is indicated by the words "tacchīla" and so on as being the qualifier of those three [categories], namely habit and the rest. That is the meaning of the root.

"One whose character is such" means one who possesses that character (*tacchīla*). "One whose nature is such" means one who possesses that nature (*taddharmā*). "A doer of good" (*sādhukārī*) means one who performs the action denoted by the verbal root in a good manner; this is the meaning of "a doer of good. Regarding the phrase "by way of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*): the sense is that from this [intrinsic nature] proceeds an activity that is independent of the fruit. And "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to the mental factor (*caitasika*).

"Dharma" refers, moreover, to ethical conduct (*śīla*) alone; "independent of fruit" means being devoid of desire for results. Regarding the word "therein": it refers to the meaning of the verbal root. Regarding the phrase "conduct therein": this shows that conduct may differ from [mere] ethical conduct. Regarding the phrase "one who performs the meaning of the verbal root well": here too, it implies [doing so] even without [the formal practice of] ethical conduct.
It is connected [with the word] "sādhu. The meaning is "praiseworthy.
It is neuter because it functions as an adverbial modifier (kriyāviśeṣaṇa).

135. *tṛn* (3.2.135): Regarding the example *muṇḍayitāraḥ*, the suffix *ṇic* is applied according to *muṇḍamiśra* (3.1.21), meaning "those who make [them] shaven-headed. Through the application of the *iṣṭhavadbhāva* rule, the *ṭi*-portion (*a*) is elided. Thus: *muṇḍayitāraḥ*.
The Śrāviṣṭhāyanas shave the bride who has been married—so says the *Kāśikā*.

"The Śrāviṣṭhāyanas shave the bride who has been married": this is their family custom (*kuladharma*). "The Āhvarakas carry off the food once the *śrāddha* ceremony is completed": this is their practice (*ācāra*). He who makes a mat well is... [he is a Kaṭha-kara].
"The agent [is expressed] in *kartā kaṭam*. "He who goes with ease (*kheṭam*) goes well (*sādhu*).
Regarding the rule for the suffix *tṛn*, etc.: this introduction is for the purpose of excluding the sense of habitual action (*ācchīlya*).

In this rule for the suffix *tṛn*, it should be stated that *tṛn* is applied after a verbal root that is not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*), when the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are to be denoted.

"Ṭh-hotā": from the root *hu* "to give, to eat" (DhP 1082); some say "to take"; the Bhāṣya says "also in the sense of pleasing"—[the Dhātupāṭha has] *dāne* (DhP 1083). "Potā": from *pūṅ* "to purify" (DhP 966). "Udgātā": from *kai* and *gai* "to sound" (DhP 916, 917). [In the sense of] "tone."

Regarding the form *vikṣepaḥ*: when the suffix *tṛc* is present, by the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), the word has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) by virtue of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). However, when the suffix *tṛn* is present, while the rule *gatiranantaraḥ* (6.2.49) is still in force, the rule *tādau ca niti kṛtyatau* (6.2.50) applies.

Otherwise, its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) would apply as before, according to the rule *nayateḥ ṣuk ca*. It should be understood that the augment *ṣuk* is applied after the *guṇa* has been effected;
for otherwise, because the penultimate vowel would not be light (*alaghu*), there would be no *guṇa*. Or else, the *guṇa* itself must be explicitly stated here.
The term *ṛtvij* is understood [from the previous rule]. This new rule is also commenced for the sake of meanings other than habitual action (*atācchīlya*).

Regarding the statement "from *tviṣ*, etc.": from the root *tviṣ* (DhP 1001), meaning "to shine," the suffix *tṛn* should be stated when a deity is to be expressed, and the vowel *a* is the substitute for the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*).
[The rule] "there is [the state of] being aniṭ" applies. And since this [rule] is a universal supplement (sarvaśeṣa), the state of being aniṭ is established for *potā* in the form *potā*.
[Regarding the rule] "of *kṣad*" and so forth: *kṣad* is a verbal root belonging to the Sūtra (sautra). [The roots are] *gudh*, *vīpaci*, *vayi*, *yami*, *sad*, and so on.

This is established because the word *hotṛ* and others are included among the *uṇādi* [derivatives], as per the reading of the *Uṇādi-sūtra*: "From the roots *kṣadi* etc., the suffix *traḥ*" (Pañcapāda Uṇādi 4.166). For in that [sūtra] list, it is stated:
"naptṛ, neṣṭṛ, tvaṣṭṛ, kṣattṛ, potṛ, hotṛ, bhrātṛ, jāmātṛ, pitṛ, duhitṛ."
These [words] have been thus set down as irregular forms.
*alaṃkṛñ-nirākṛñ-prajana-ut-paca-ut-pata-unmada-ruci-apatrapa-vṛtu-vṛdhu-saha-car-iṣṇuc*.
(3.2.136) The root *kṛ* preceded by *alam*; again, that same [root] preceded by *nirā*; and the root *jan* in the sense of "manifestation."
Preceded by *pra*; *pac* (DhP 174) "to make manifest";
*pad* (DhP 1898) "to go"—some read it as *paṭ*;
*śal*, *hul*, *patlṛ* (DhP 843, 844, 845) "to go"; *madī*.

The roots *madi* (in the sense of satisfaction, DhP 815) and *madī* (in the sense of exhilaration and stupefaction, DhP)—these roots beginning with *pad* are preceded by the prefix *ut*. [Furthermore,] *ruc* (in the sense of shining and delighting, DhP 745);
and *trapūṣ* (in the sense of shame, DhP 374), preceded by the prefix *apa*; and *vṛtu*... [DhP].
The suffix *iṣṇuc* occurs after the roots *vṛt* (DhP 758, "to turn"), *vṛdh* (DhP 759, "to increase"), *sah* (DhP 1809, "to endure"), and *car* (DhP 559, "to move");
it is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffix] *tṛn*. This is the reading in the *Mugdhabodha* (mu.pāṭha). However, when preceded by the particle *alam*, [it is an exception to *kṛt*].
When *karoti* occurs with the sense of *maṇḍana*, then by the rule "after roots meaning anger and *maṇḍa*, [the suffix] *yuc* [is applied]" (Pāṇini 3.2.151), the suffix *yuc* would apply;

furthermore, a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) must be stated. Otherwise, the suffix *iṣṇuc*—which elsewhere has its own scope—would supersede it due to its posteriority. As for those forms that are listed here with prefixes (*sopasarga*), [they are treated as exceptions].
This [suffix] occurs after those [roots] preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*) alone; however, in other cases, it is not restricted.
137. *ṇeśchandasī* (Pāṇini 3.2.137). [Examples:

*dhārayiṣṇavaḥ*, *pārayiṣṇavaḥ*. [The roots] *dhṛṅ* "to stand firm" (Dhātupāṭha 1412) and *pṛ* "to protect and to fill" (Dhātupāṭha 1086) take the causative suffix *ṇic*; then, by [the rule] *ayāmanta-* (6.4.55), [the penultimate vowel is lengthened].
By such [rules] as these, there is the substitution of *ā*.

138. *bhuvaśca* (3.2.138). [The commentary states: "The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows. This is so that only the word *bhavati* may be carried over (*anuvartana*) into the subsequent sūtra; otherwise, if a single rule were made as *ṇibhūbhyāñca*, then...
The suffix *ṇigrahaṇa* would also be drawn in [from the previous rule]. In examples such as "bhājiṣṇunā," there is common worldly usage (*laukikaprayoga*).
Its presentation is for the purpose of demonstrating that the suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied even in the colloquial language (*bhāṣā*) from this root: *bhrājṛ* (DhP 1.81), meaning "to shine."

139. *glājisthaśca ksnuḥ* (3.2.139). Now, regarding the word *sthāsnū*, he asks why the substitution of *ī* occurs here by means of the rule *ghumāsthāgāpā...* (6.4.66), and answers with the words *piccāyam* and so forth. The substitution of *ī* occurs before an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*. In that regard, [the rule applies] to *dīṅ*.
This is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *yuḍ aci kṅiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.63). Now, this [suffix] is not *kit*, nor is it *ṅit*;

what then? It is *git*. As for the non-hearing of the letter *g*, it is due to its being indicated as having undergone the change to *c* (*cartva*). If, then, this is *git*, the rule for *guṇa* would apply here in the word *jiṣṇu*.

Since the rule "kṅiti ca" (Pāṇini 1.1.5) prohibits *guṇa* substitution when a suffix marked with *k* or *ṅ* follows, and not when marked with *g*, he says: "kṅiti ca," etc. For in the rule "kṅiti ca" (1.1.5), it is not only the letters *k* and *ṅ* that are indicated; rather, the letter *g* is also included.

Since *c* has been substituted for *t*, the *guṇa* substitution does not occur even before a suffix marked with *g*. Now, in the case of *bhūṣṇuḥ*, where the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "śrayukaḥ kiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.11) is being applied, it would not apply before a suffix marked with *g*;
therefore, he says: "In the expression 'śrayukaḥ kiti,' etc., the letter *g* is indicated as having undergone the substitution of *c*."
The connection is with what has been previously stated. "By that" means by the mention of the *ga* sound which has undergone *cartva* (the substitution of *ca* for *k*).
Regarding the phrase "because *kasnu* is marked with *g*" (*gitvāt*), etc.: that which has the *ga* sound as its *it* (indicatory letter) is called *git*; the state of being such is *gitva*.
Therefore, because of this *gitva*, the vowel *i* does not occur in the word *syāt*. However, the vowel *ī* does occur in *tiṣṭhateḥ*.
It occurs. But why does the augment *iṭ* not occur here? He says:

"Because of the teaching that [the suffixes] marked with *k* and *ṅ* are *it*" (*kaṅtoiritvaśāsanāt*), and so forth. In the term *kaṅ*, the letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).
Since it is taught that [suffixes] marked with *k* and *ṅ* are *it*, and this [suffix *ktvā*] is marked with *g*, therefore, in the case of a suffix marked with *k* or *ṅ* (*kṅiti*)...

The substitution of *ī* being prescribed here, the status of being an *it* (indicatory letter) does not apply. If this is so, then in the case of *jiṣṇu*, the *guṇa* substitution would apply; therefore, he says: "the absence of *guṇa*" and so forth. One must remember that the prohibition of *guṇa* applies when the three letters *k*, *g*, and *ṅ* bear the designation *it*.
It must be understood that in the rule *ṭhkṅiti ca* (1.1.5), the letter *g* is specified as having undergone the substitution of *c*.
If this [suffix] were *gi*, then in the case of *bhūṣṇuḥ*, the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *śrayukaḥ kiti* (7.2.11) would not apply; therefore, he says:

It should be understood that the prohibition of *iṭ* applies to a root ending in *ṭh*, *ś*, or *yuk*. If the letter *g* were subject to *cartva* (the substitution of *c*), then by the rule "ṭh-ś-ayukaḥ kiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.11), the prohibition of *iṭ* would not occur;
therefore, he says: "The non-*iṭ* status of what ends in *ṭh*, *ś*, or *yuk," and so forth. The letter *g* as well...
Next,

the exception (apavāda) is pointed out: it should be understood that for both the letters *ka* and *ga*, which possess the designation *it*, there occurs the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* because they are not followed by a consonant (*śrayuk*) and are non-*iṭ* [roots].

If the letter *y* were intended as a substitute for *r* in the rule "ṛt-śaya-uk-aḥ kiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.11), then by the rule "haśi ca" (Pāṇini 6.1.114), the substitution of *u* would apply; however, because that [substitution] is considered *asiddha*, there is no fault.
This is because, according to Vāmana, the mention in the Sūtra is due to its being read without *saṃhitā*.

All of this is undesirable; how it is undesirable has been explained in the rule *ṭhṅiti ca* (1.1.5). Regarding the entry beginning with *daṃśeḥ*: the word *upasaṃkhyāna* here functions in the sense of "providing an addition" [to the rule]. From the root *daṃśa* (DhP 898), meaning "to bite," [the suffix *kvip* is added].

An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made regarding the suffix *kṣnu*; that is, it must be established. Here is the establishment: the particle *ca* is carried over from the preceding rule, and it has the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned;
therefore, it will also apply to the root *daṃś*. Thus we have "daṃkṣṇavaḥ" [by means of *daṃkṣṇavaḥ*], according to Pāṇini 8.2.36 (*vraścādi*).

There is the substitution of *ṣ* [by Pāṇini 8.3.59], and then the substitution of *k* by "ṣṭuaniditām" (6.4.24) does not apply because the suffix *ksnu* is marked with the *g*-sign (*git*). However, for those who maintain that [the suffix] is *kit*, there is a prohibition of the elision of the *n* here, as in the rule "nāñceḥ pūjāyām" (6.4.30).
In this case [of Pāṇini 6.4.30], the word "na" must be separated by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule); or else, they must adopt another effort:
that there is an *anusvāra* for the letter *n*, and for that, a *parasavarṇa* (the following homogeneous sound).

140. *trasigṛdhidhaṣikṣipeḥ knuḥ* | (Pāṇini 3.2.140) [The suffix] *knū* is applied after the roots *tras*, *gṛdh*, *dhṛṣ*, and *kṣip*. {According to the Dhātupāṭha: *tras* in the sense of "trembling" (1741); *gṛdh* in the sense of "desire" (1246); *dhṛṣ* in the sense of "boldness" (1269); *kṣip* in the sense of "impelling"}; *tras* (in the sense of "fear" according to the Dhātupāṭha 1741); *gṛdh* in the sense of "longing" (Dhātupāṭha 1246); *dhṛṣ* in the sense of "boldness" (Dhātupāṭha 1269); *kṣip* in the sense of "propulsion."

Regarding "trasnu": there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule "neḍ vaśi kṛti" (Pāṇini 7.2.8). Regarding "gṛghnu": there is an absence of *guṇa* substitution by the rule "kṅiti ca" (Pāṇini 1.1.5).
141. *ghinuṇ* is added after the eight roots beginning with *śam*.
(Pāṇini 3.2.141) [The roots are: *śamu* "to calm" (DhP 1201), *tamu* "to desire" (DhP 1202), *damu* "to calm" or "to cease" (DhP 1203), and *śramu* "to exert oneself" or "to suffer" (DhP 1204).
(dhā.pā. 1204), *bhramu* "to wander" (dhā.pā. 1205), *kṣamu* "to endure" (dhā.pā. 1206), *klamu* "to be weary" (dhā.pā. 1207), *madī* "to rejoice" (dhā.pā. 1208).
[The mention of these roots] is for the sake of the substitution of *k* (*kutva*) in subsequent cases; thus, in words such as *saṃparkī*, the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇyatoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.52) applies.

"Thus it should be; the letter *ṭh* is for the sake of pronunciation"—this rejects its status as an *anubandha*. If it were an *anubandha*, then in the forms *śaminau* and *śaminaḥ*, the augment *num* would undesirably apply by the rule *ugidacām* (Pāṇini 7.1.70). Furthermore, in the forms *śaminitarām* and *śaminitamām*, [the rule] *nadyāḥ*... [would apply].

While the rule *śeṣasyānyatarasyām* (6.3.44) is in effect, the rule *ṭhugitaśca* (6.3.45) would optionally cause shortening; otherwise, the inclusion of the indicatory letter (*anubandha*) would be purposeless. Therefore, the vowel *u* serves solely for the purpose of pronunciation, and the shortening [occurs] as well.

By the rule *ṭhgharūpakalpacelaḍÂbruvagotramatahateṣu* (Pāṇini 6.3.43), [the suffix] occurs invariably. In the word *śamī*, the vṛddhi [strengthening] prescribed by *ata upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116) does not take place.

Because [the substitution] is prohibited by the rule "ṭhnodātopadeśa" (Pāṇini 7.3.34) and others, there is lengthening by the rule "sau ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.13). Regarding the form "asitā," it occurs with the suffix *tṛn* after the root "asu kṣepaṇe" (Dhātupāṭha 1209).

[The roots] *sampṛc*, *anurudh*, *aṅyām*, *aṅyas*, *parisṛ*, *saṃsṛj*, *paridevi*, *saṃjvar*, *parikṣip*, *pariraṭ*, *parivad*, *paridah*, *parimuha*, *duṣ*, *dviṣ*, *druh*, *duha*, *yuj*, *ākrīḍ*, *vivic*, *tyaj*, *raj*, *bhaj*, *aticara*, *apacara*, *amuṣ*, and *abhyāhan* [take the suffix *ghañ* when used as action-nouns]. (Pāṇini 3.2.142) The root *pṛcī* (meaning "to mix") is preceded by *sam*. The root *rudhir* (meaning "to cover").

*anupūrvaḥ*; *yama* in the sense of "ceasing" (DhP 984); *yasu* in the sense of "exertion" (DhP 1210) preceded by *āṅ*; *sṛj* in the sense of "emission" (DhP 1178); *jvara* in the sense of "disease" (DhP 776) preceded by *sam*;
*kṣip* in the sense of "impelling" (DhP 1285); *raṭa* in the sense of "speaking" (DhP 1286).

(dhā.pā.297), *ṭhvada* in the sense of speaking (dhā.pā.1009), *ṭhdaha* in the sense of reducing to ashes (dhā.pā.991), *ṭhmuha* in the sense of bewilderment (dhā.pā.1198) preceded by *pari*, *ṭhduṣa* in the sense of corruption (dhā.pā.1185), *ṭhdviṣa* in the sense of enmity (dhā.pā.1013), *ṭhdruha*...

The root *jighāṃs* (DhP 1197) [is used] in the sense of "desire to kill"; *duh* (DhP 1014) in the sense of "milking" or "extracting"; *ā-krīḍ* (DhP 350) preceded by *ā* in the sense of "sporting" or "diversion"; *vi-jir* (DhP 1094) preceded by *vi* in the sense of "separation"; and *tyaj* (DhP 986) in the sense of "loss of vigor" or "decay."
The root *rañj* in the sense of coloring (*rāge*) [DhP 999], *bhaj* in the sense of service (*sevāyām*) [DhP 998],

*car* in the sense of motion (*gatyartha*) preceded by *ati*, that same [root] preceded by *anu*, *muṣ* in the sense of stealing (*steye*) preceded by *āṅ*, and *han* in the senses of injury and motion (*hiṃsāgatyoḥ*) [DhP 1012].
The root preceded by *abhi* and *āṅ* is intended; they are specifically indicated as belonging to the *śap*-class (*tudādi*) and the *vṛt*-class (*curādi*), but not those beginning with *ad*.
It is connected with the word "is taken" (*gṛhyate*). Why is the root belonging to the *adādi* class not taken? He says:
because the *adādi* root has a *luk*-suffix (the absence of a suffix), therefore it is not taken. "But *paridevi* belongs to the *bhvādi* class."

The connection is with the word "is grasped" (*gṛhyate*). Now, why is there not a grasping of the causative form of *pari-div*, meaning "to play" and so forth? Because of its association with other [roots] that are not causative (*aṇ-anta*). [The rule] "it is grasped in a general sense" is because there is no distinction [between the specific forms]. [The statement] "there is a grasping of both" is for that very same reason.

Regarding "ṭhnipātanādanunāsikalopaḥ": in the rule *tyajaraja*, the very pronunciation [of the root] without the nasal is the *nipātana* (irregularity). Regarding *samparkī*: there is the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. Regarding *āyāmī*: there is *vṛddhi* by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116).
In the case of *parisārī*, here too there is *vṛddhi* by [Pāṇini 7.2.115] *aco ñṇiti*.
In the case of *abhyāghātī*, as before, there is the substitution of *gh* for *h* and the subsequent *t* substitution.
143. After the verbal roots √kaṣ, √laṣ, √sak, √atth, and √srambh, [the suffix *ghañ* is applied] when preceded by *vi*.

(3.2.143) 144. And also after √laṣ, when preceded by *apa*. (3.2.144) 145. After the verbal roots √lap, √sṛ, √dru, √math, √vad, and √vas, [the suffix *ghañ* is applied] when preceded by *pra*. (3.2.145)
"Pralāpī, prasārī"—[from] *lapa* "in distinct speech" (DhP 402) and *sṛ* "in going" (935).
"Pradrāvī, pramāthī"—[from] *dru* "in going" (DhP 944–945) and *math* "in churning" (DhP 848). [This applies] except for that which has the sense of covering.
Thus; this is not [the case] for the root *vas* in the sense of "covering" (*ācchādane*, Dhātupāṭha 1023).
The suffix *vuñ* is applied after the words *nindā*, *hiṃsā*, *kliśa*, *khāda*, *vināśa*, *parikṣipa*, *pariraṭa*, *parivāda*, *vyābhāṣā*, and *asūyā*.
(Pāṇini 3.2.146)
The root *ṭhṇidi* is used in the sense of contempt (*kutsā*) [DhP 66]; *ṭharda* is used in the sense of injury (*hiṃsā*) [DhP 1828, 1829];

*ṭhkhādṛ* is used in the sense of eating (*bhakṣaṇa*) [DhP 49]; and *ṇaśa* is used in the sense of disappearance (*adarśana*) [DhP 1194]. These are preceded by the prefix *vi-* and are causative (*hetumaṇṇic*). *Kṣipiḥ* is exactly as previously mentioned; likewise for *raṭiḥ* and *vadiḥ*.

The root *pari-pūrva* [is used] with the causative suffix (*ṇic*); *vyāṅ-pūrva* [is used] with the root *bhāṣ* (DhP 612), meaning "to speak clearly. The term *asūya* refers to the root ending in *yaṅ*, belonging to the *kaṇḍvādi* group.
Here, for the root *kliś* in the sense of "affliction" and for *bhāṣ*, [the suffix *ac* is applied] by the rule *anudāteśca halādeḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.149).

When *yuc* was expected, *vuñ* is prescribed; however, for the remaining [roots], *tṛn* is prescribed. But surely, by the rule "and what follows" (*paraśca*, 3.1.2), there ought to be an ablative case based on connection with direction, as in the commentary (*vṛtti*)—“from roots such as *nind* and so forth”—so how is it that the nominative is used in the sūtra? To this, he says:
The statement "the nominative is used in the sense of the ablative" means that there is a substitution of case endings (*sub-vyatyaya*) according to Pāṇini 3.1.85, *vyatyayo bahulam*.

Furthermore, the nominative singular is used for a collective dvandva compound, while the masculine gender is likewise due to substitution. Regarding the form *asūyakaḥ*, [the suffix -aka is added] by Pāṇini 6.4.48, *ato lopaḥ*.
Thus there is the elision of the letter *i*.

Now, for what purpose is the suffix *vuñ* prescribed after verbal roots such as *nind* and others, given that words like *nindaka* and so forth would already be established by the rule of "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*)? For that very same form [would result]. That indeed is the form; that very same...

Regarding accent (*svara*): here, in this very instance, there is a specific difference in accent—namely, in the word *asūyakaḥ*. When the suffix *vuñ* is applied, because it bears the marker *ñ*, the first syllable becomes udātta; however, if the suffix *ṇvul* were applied, the accent would fall on the syllable preceding the *lit* suffix. Therefore, *vuñ* must be prescribed after the root *asūyati* alone, and not after the others.

Regarding the phrase "from *nindā* and so forth," he says: "Since [the suffix] *ṇvul* alone would suffice," and so on. If, by the rule of "non-identical form" (*vāsarūpa*), suffixes such as *tṛc* were also applicable in the sense of "having that habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth, then [the author] would not have prescribed *vuñ* after *nindā* and the others;
yet it has been prescribed. Therefore, the prescription of *vuñ* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Or rather, the rule for dissimilar forms (*asarūpavidhi*) does not apply in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth; therefore, words such as *alaṅkārakaḥ* and *nirākartā* do not possess grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) in the sense of "having that as one's habit" and the like.

147. *devikruśoścopasarge* | (3.2.247) "Ṭhādevakaḥ" means: from the root *div*, in the sense of "to play" (*krīḍā*), with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the suffix *vuñ*. "Ākrośakaḥ" means: from the root *kruś* (Pāṇini’s Dhātupāṭha 856), which means "to call out" (*āhvāna*) and "to weep" (*rodana*); here it is used in the sense of "calling out. [Kṛt-suffix: *Kroṣṭā*.
Thus; the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.36], *vraśca*-ādi.
148. *yauc* [is added] after roots meaning motion (*calana*) or sound (*śabda*), provided they are intransitive (*akarmaka*).

(Pāṇini 3.2.148) Motion (*calana*) is a specific kind of action that causes the attainment of another location. Sound (*śabda*) is an object perceived by the sense of hearing. Examples are *calanaḥ* and *copanaḥ*. [The roots are] *cala* "to shake" (Dhātupāṭha 832) and *cupa* "in the sense of slowness... [Dhātupāṭha 833].

[The root] *gatau* (DhP 403). Regarding "śabdana": [the root] *śabda* with the prefix *upa* means "to manifest" and "to speak"—this is from the curādigaṇa (DhP 1714), meaning "manifestation following a prefix" (*upasargād āviṣkāre*). Alternatively, [it is formed] by the rule *prātipadikād dhātvarthe bahulam* (Gaṇasūtra 1860).

The suffix *ṇic* is applied by the rule beginning with *curādiḥ* 1915; from this *ṇij*-derived form, the suffix *yauc* is applied by the rule beginning with *śabdavairakalaha* 3.1.17. Regarding the word *ravaṇaḥ*: the root is *ru* (meaning "to sound") as listed in the Dhātupāṭha at number 1034.
149. *anudāteśca halādeḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.149). [The examples] *ṭhedhitā* and *ṭhedhitum*: from the root *ṭhedha* (meaning "to increase," *dhā.pā.* 2). [The examples] *jugupsanaḥ* and *mīmāṃsanaḥ*:
by the rule *guptijkidbhyaḥ san* (3.1.5), and by the rule *mānbadha* (3.1.6) etc., the suffix *san* is added, resulting in lengthening of the vowel.

And [the suffix] *kṛt* occurs here. In this case, the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) applied to the parts—namely that the two composite wholes ending in those [suffixes] are anudātta—serves as a qualifier for the whole. Thus, if the mention of "beginning" (*ādi*) were not made, then [the designation] would not apply by means of those two; because, in the absence of the mention of "beginning," [the rule would apply] only to a consonant (*hal*).
The rule of "specification of the end" (tadanta-vidhi) is understood here: [the suffix occurs] after that which ends in a consonant and begins with an unaccented vowel.

Now, the words *jugupsa* and *mīmāṃsā* do not end in a consonant; rather, they end in a vowel. Since the suffix occurs even after those ending in vowels when the word "beginning" (*ādi*) is included, the inclusion of the word "beginning" must be made. And that [inclusion] must be made at that point.

Therefore, when the position is that the elision occurs when an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix follows, and not the position that it occurs when an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix is the governing object (*viṣayabhūta*), then, since the intention to apply an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix would already be understood, the mention of "ending in a consonant" (*halanta*) would be purposeless; for there would be nothing to exclude. Consequently...

By the force of the inclusion of the term *hr* [in the rule], it will be understood as a qualifier of the initial [element]; thus, the inclusion of the word "initial" (*ādi*) need not have been made at all.
Here, the inclusion of the word "initial" should be explained merely for the sake of clarity. Regarding the form *vasitā*: [the root] *vas* [is used] in the sense of "covering" (DhP 1023).

150. [The suffix *yu* is applied after the roots] *ju*, *caṅkram*, *dandram*, *sṛ*, *gṛdh*, *jval*, *śuc*, *laṣ*, *pat*, and *pad*. (Pāṇini 3.2.150). The example is *javanaḥ* ("swift"). *Ju* is a root found in the *sūtra*; some say it means "to go," while others say it means "impulse" (*vega*) as a specific cause. The examples are *caṅkramaṇaḥ* and *dandramaṇaḥ*. [The root] *kramu* [is used] in the sense of "stepping with the feet."

From the roots *dhr̥m* and *ham* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*) [DhP 466, 467], the intensive suffix *yaṅ* is applied by the rule "nityaṃ kauṭilye gatau" (Pāṇini 3.1.23). This results in reduplication. Then, *nuk* is added by the rule "nugato 'nunāsikāntasya" (7.4.85), the vowel *a* is elided by "ato lopaḥ" (6.4.48), and the *y* is elided by "yasya halaḥ" (6.4.49).
By this [rule], there is the elision of the letter *y*. Thus: *jvalanaḥ*, *śocanaḥ*. [The roots] *jvala* and *hvala* mean "to move" (*dhā.pā.* 804, 805); *śuca* means "to grieve" (*dhā.pā.* 183).

Now, one might object: although here [roots like] *jucaṃkramyadaṃdramya* and so forth have the sense of moving, the root *pad* is [specifically] marked as *anudāteta* (unaccented in the *dhātu-pāṭha*).

And [the suffix] *halādi* [is also included]; therefore, since [the suffix] *yuc* is established for these [roots] by application of the two preceding rules as appropriate, he asks: "For what purpose is their inclusion here? He replies with the words "of those meaning 'to move'" (*calanārthānām*), and so forth. If their inclusion here were not made, then [the suffix] would not apply in cases such as *caṅkramaṇo grāmasya* ("the wandering of the village"), and so on; [for the village and other such entities are not themselves moving].
Because [the presence of] an object is intended to be expressed. Therefore, these [roots] are mentioned for the purpose that [the suffix *tṛc*] may apply after transitive roots.

By the words "for the sake of an indicator (*jñāpaka*)" and so forth, he shows another opinion: namely, that "the suffix *tṛn* does not occur after the root *alaṃkṛ*. By this also, [he demonstrates] the nature of the indicator.

The purpose [of the rule] is as follows: one must supply the phrase "it does not become a virtuous person who merely decorates. But how is the mention of the word *pada* (word) an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? He says: "For instance," and so forth.
This is so that there may be no sublation (*bādha*) by *ukañ*, which is prescribed as a specific exception; rather, there should be co-occurrence (*samāveśa*).
The word *pada* is included here for this very purpose:

if the rule of non-identity of form (*asarūpavidhi*) were to apply to suffixes denoting habitual action (*tācchīlika*), then the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) with *ukañ* would already occur simply because of their different forms; consequently, the prescription of *yu* for *pada* would be redundant.

Therefore, this status of being prescribed as a specific rule is solely for the purpose of making known [the existence of the general rule]; for it is prescribed by the general definition "anudātetaśca halādeḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.149). If, then, the absence of the *vā'sarūpa* rule is what is being made known, [then consider] the form *gantā*, which is also derived by "anudātetaśca halādeḥ".

Since the suffix *yuc* is established by [Pāṇini 3.2.149], and because the suffix *dhinuṇ* is prescribed by [Pāṇini 3.2.143] starting with "ṭhvau kaṣa," he says: "And it is mostly so" (*prāyikaṃ ca*), etc. That it is "mostly so" (*prāyikatva*) will be demonstrated in the subsequent sūtra.
151. *krudha-maṇḍārthebhyaś-ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.151).

Since the suffix *tṛn* (by rule 3.2.135) would otherwise apply [to roots meaning "to be angry" and those meaning "to adorn"], the suffix *yuC* is here prescribed. In this case, as well as in subsequent rules, wherever no specific distinction is intended to be expressed, the suffix *tṛn* alone is the exception (*apavāda*) [to be set aside].
It should be understood as "roṣaṇaḥ" [meaning "one who is prone to anger"], from the root *ruṣ* in the sense of "anger" (*ruṣa roṣe*, Dhātupāṭha 1670).

[The word] "by the preceding rule" refers to [the fact that the desired form] is already established by [the rule] *anudātetaśca halādeḥ* (3.2.149), etc. Now, as for the roots *aya*, *vaya*, *raya*, and *ṇaya* in the sense of "motion" (*gatau*) [DhP 474, 475, 482, 480]:

Why is this not understood as being for the purpose of prescribing the suffix *yuc* after this root? It is impossible to understand it thus; because [the form] is already established by rules such as Pāṇini 3.2.149, *ṭhanudātetaśca*. Therefore, this [rule] is for the purpose of prohibition. [The examples are: *knāyitā*, *kṣmāyitā*.
The root *ṭhknūyī* means "to sound" and "to purify" (*dhā.pā.* 485); the root *kṣmāyī* means "to shake" (*dhā.pā.* 486).

153. And [the suffix *ghañ* is applied] after the roots *sūd*, *dīp*, and *dīkṣ*. (Pāṇini 3.2.153) *sūda* (in the sense of "flowing," Dhātupāṭha 25); *dīp* (in the sense of "shining," Dhātupāṭha 1150); *dīkṣ* (in the sense of "tonsure," Dhātupāṭha 609)—[the root *dīkṣ* is listed as taking the meaning of] "tonsure, sacrifice, initiation, and the instruction of rules and vows."
The objection begins with "But surely... (*nanu ca*), and the resolution begins with "By the rule *vāsarūpeṇa*...
(*vā'sarūpeṇa*). It might be argued: "It has been indicated that the rule *vāsarūpa* does not apply; therefore, there is no possibility of the suffix *yuc*.
To this he says: 'That which denotes habit' (*tācchīlika*), etc. And this [suffix] is indeed the one for the majority of cases.

This is the indicative mark (*liṅga*). For if there were an absence of the rule regarding dissimilar forms (*asarūpavidhi*) everywhere, then, because [the general suffix] would already be set aside by the specifically prescribed suffix, the prohibition "in the sense of *yuñj* and *bhaviṣya*" would be purposeless. By the phrase "and so on" (*tathā ca*), [it refers to] the suffix denoting habitual action (*tācchīlika*).

By demonstrating the inclusion (*samāveśa*), he further strengthens the fact that the indicator (*jñāpaka*) is merely occasional (*prāyikatva*). Regarding "kamrā": the suffix *ra* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.167] *namikampi-*. Regarding "kamanā": the suffix *yuc* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.149] *anudātetaśca halādeḥ*. Regarding "kamprā": [the suffix *ra* is applied by Pāṇini 3.2.167] *kapi-*...

The objection begins with *calane* (Dhātupāṭha 275) and continues with *sūdeḥ*, etc.; the resolution begins with *anityam*, etc. It is stated that "it is understood through a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). The proof for this non-eternality is provided by the rule *nayasūdadīpadīkṣa*.

Since a single rule (*ekayoga*) ought to have been formulated, the fact that he performs a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) indicates that there is some distinction between this [present rule] and the preceding prohibition.
That specific distinction is precisely its non-eternality (*anityatva*). Even though the suffix *yuc* would also apply after the roots *dīp* and *dīkṣ*, [the split of the rule is necessary].
It would follow [that it applies], but it does not occur because it is not explicitly stated.

154. *laṣa-pata-pada-sthā-bhū-vṛṣa-hana-kama-gama-śṛbhya ukañ* (3.2.154). [The Kāśikā reads: *upasthāyukāḥ*; the form is] *upasthāyukaḥ*. [The suffix] *yuk* is applied by the rule *āto yuk ciṇ-kṛtoḥ* (7.3.33). [The Kāśikā reads: *pravarṣukāḥ*; the form is] *pravarṣukaḥ*. [The root is] *vṛṣu* (to rain). *mṛṣu*... [etc.]
Regarding the roots *sic* (DhP 706, 707), [we have] the word "kāmukāḥ. From the root *kam* in the sense of "desire" (DhP 443),

although the prohibition of *vṛddhi* would apply by the rule beginning with *nodāttopadeśa-* (Pāṇini 7.3.34), [the form is derived] by the inclusion of *cam, kam, and vam* in the rule *anācamer-* (Pāṇini 6.1.59).

Regarding the statement "it should be said" (vā. 844), only *vṛddhi* occurs [in the formation of *śāruka*]. As for the form *śārukaḥ*—[the variant reading is *kiṃśārukaṃ-kāśikā*]—it is derived from the root *śṛ* in the sense of "injuring" (*śṛ hiṃsāyām*, DhP 1488). From the root *laṣ* preceded by the prefix *apa*, the suffix *dhinuṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.144: *ape ca laṣaḥ*. For it was stated previously regarding suffixes expressing habitual character (*tācchīlika*)...

This is due to the force of the rule *ṭhglājisthaśca ksanuḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.139). Furthermore, the suffixes *kikin* also occur after the root *gam* in the Vedic language by virtue of the rule *ādṛgama...* (Pāṇini 3.2.171), and they occur in the colloquial language as well, according to the Vārttika:
*bhāṣāyāṃ dhāñkṛñsṛjanigaminamibhyaḥ* (Vārttika 284).
This is because of the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*); from the root *kam*, the suffix *ra* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.167, *ṭhnamikampi*, and so forth.

155. *jalpa-bhikṣa-kuṭṭa-luṇṭi-vṛṅaḥ ṣākan* (Pāṇini 3.2.155). *jap* and *jalp* [mean] "in distinct speech" (Dhātupāṭha 397, 398); *bhikṣ* [means] "in begging" (Dhātupāṭha 606); *kuṭṭ* [means] "in cutting" (Dhātupāṭha 607). (Note: *kuṭṭa* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as meaning "cutting" and "threatening").

*(Dhātupāṭha 1558), and ṭhluṇṭa steye* (Dhātupāṭha 1563)—these two belong to the *curādi* class. Regarding *vṛṅ sambhavatau* (Dhātupāṭha 1509): since *jalp* is intended here as intransitive (*akarmaka*), the suffix *yuc* would have applied by the rule *calanaśabdārthādakarmakādyuc* (Pāṇini 3.2.148). [The same applies] to *bhikṣi* as well.

The suffix *yuc* is applied by the rule "ṭh-anudātetaśca halādeḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.149). From the roots *kuṭṭi* and *luṇṭi*, the suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied by the rule "ṇeścchandasi" (Pāṇini 3.2.137). Regarding the root *vṛñ* as well, although the suffixes *kvi* and *kin* would have been applicable by the rule "ādṛgamahana... (Pāṇini 3.2.171), etc., the suffix *ṣākan* is prescribed as an exception to those.
[The form] "ṭhvarākī" [is derived] by adding the suffix *ṅīṣ* because of the presence of the marker *ṣ*.

156. *prajor iniḥ* | (3.2.156) Since the suffix *yuc* would have applied by rule 3.2.150 (*ju-caṅkramya-*, etc.), *ini* is here prescribed. The vowel *i* is for the purpose of protecting the *n* from being designated as an *it*.
157. [The suffix *ka* is applied] after the verbal roots *ji*, *dṛś*, *śri*, *ṇvi*, *mā*, *vyath*, *abhibhū*, and *paribhū*.

(Pāṇini 3.2.157) *ji* in the sense of "to conquer" (Dhātupāṭha 561); *dṛś* in the sense of "to respect" (Dhātupāṭha 1411); *śri* in the sense of "to serve," preceded by the prefix *vi-* (Dhātupāṭha 897); *iṇ* in the sense of "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1045); *ava*... [the root *mā*].
The root *ud-gir* (DhP 8.49), the root *vyath* (DhP 7.64) meaning "fear and trembling" with the prefix *nañ*, the root *am* (DhP 10.172) meaning "disease" with the prefix *abhi*,
and the root *sū* (DhP 5.1408) meaning "impulsion" with the prefix *pra*— it is the inclusion of these that is intended, and not [others].

This refers to the two roots *ṣūṅ* (*prāṇigarbhavimocane*, DhP 1031) and *ṣūṅ* (*prāṇiprasave*, DhP 1132). The intention is that [the rule applies] by means of the technical rule regarding roots without an indicatory letter (*niranubandhakaparibhāṣā*;
VP 53). In the rule *iṇjibhyām*, [it refers to] *iṇ*, *naś*, and *ji*.
By virtue of the rule *kvarap* (Pāṇini 3.2.163), it becomes *kparap*.

158. *spṛhi-gṛhi-pati-dayi-nidrā-tandrā-śraddhābhya āluc* (Pāṇini 3.2.158). [The commentary notes: "These are listed in the *curādi* group as being without the suffix *a* (*adanta*). Therefore, when the elision of the final *a* has been performed, by virtue of the rule *acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau* (Pāṇini 1.1.57), which prescribes that a substitute is treated like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the application of a preceding grammatical operation, neither *vṛddhi* nor *guṇa* takes place.

This is the intended meaning. From these roots, while the suffix *iṣṇuc* would apply according to the previous rule in Vedic usage, and while *kikin* would apply to the roots *drāti* and *dadhāti*, the suffix *āluc* is prescribed. In the example "spṛhayāluḥ," the substitution of *ay* is applied by the rule "ayāmanta" (Pāṇini 6.4.55). Regarding the phrase "in *āluc*," etc., the root *śīṅ* is understood. By which...

This means that the mention of *śīṅ* is for the purpose of providing a further explanation. That explanation must be formulated such that the mention of *śīṅ* also applies when *aluc* is to be prescribed.
In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the particle *ca* from the preceding sūtra is carried over (*anuvartate*) here; it...
And it has the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned; by that, the root *śīṅ* is also understood as being the base form (*prakṛti*).

159. *dā-dheṭ-śi-śad-sad-ām ruḥ* | (3.2.159) The roots *ḍu-dāñ* "to give" (DhP 1091), *do* "to cut" (DhP 1148), and *deṅ* "to protect" (DhP 962)—all three are included here; for there is no distinction among them in the rules concerning the roots *gā*, *mā*, and *dā*.

According to the statement [in Vyāḍipāṭha 124]: "The root *dheṭ* means 'to drink' (DhP 902), *ṣiñ* means 'to bind' (DhP 1477), *śadlṛ* means 'to fall away' (DhP 1428), and *ṣadlṛ* means 'to dissolve, to go, or to perish' (DhP 1427). Now, [as in the phrase] "the calf, desiring milk, [sucks] its mother."
Thus, how can there be an accusative case here, since by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65), a genitive ought to occur? To this he replies: *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhā*.

The letter *u* which follows *uk* is joined with the *ak* [of *uktam*] by means of a long vowel resulting from the combination of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇadīrgha*); therefore, by the rule of "specification by the final letter" (*tadantavidhi*), [the prohibition applies to forms ending in *ukta*].

When a suffix ending in *u* is employed while [the object] is being perceived [as the object], the genitive case does not occur; therefore, only the accusative occurs, and thus there is no genitive. But then, in this case—*kaṭaṃ cikīrṣuḥ* (desiring to make a mat)—the prohibition [of the genitive] would not apply, because the suffix *u* does not end in *u*. [Answer: The suffix *ghinuṇ* also occurs [in such cases].
Since the word *cchandas* ends in the vowel *u*, the suffixes *kikin* also occur by virtue of the rule *ṭhādṛgamahan...* (Pāṇini 3.2.171).

160. After the roots *sṛ* (to flow), *ghas* (to eat), and *ad* (to eat), the suffix *kmarac* is applied [to form nouns denoting the agent]. (Pāṇini 3.2.160) 161. After the roots *bhañj* (to break), *bhās* (to shine), and *mid* (to be glad), the suffix *ghurac* is applied.

(Pāṇini 3.2.161) *bhañja* is listed as "in the sense of crushing" (Dhātupāṭha 1453); *bhāsṛ* is listed as "in the sense of shining" (Dhātupāṭha 624); *ñimidā*... [is listed as "in the sense of being glad"]. (Dhātupāṭha 1454)
[The root] *sniha* [is listed] in the *Dhātupāṭha* as "in the sense of moistening and releasing" (*snehanamocanayoḥ*, DhP 1243). Regarding the word *bhaṅgura*:

the substitution of *k* for *c* and *j* occurs by the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.52). It is said that "the suffix is used in the sense of the reflexive object" (*karmakartari pratyayaḥ*). The meaning is: "it breaks by itself. But how, then, is the suffix obtained in the sense of the reflexive object?
To this he says: "by its very nature. By its very nature, the suffix denotes the reflexive object-agent (karmakartṛ), not the agent alone. Therefore, it applies only to the reflexive object-agent.

162. *vidi-bhid-icchideḥ kurac* (Pāṇini 3.2.162). Regarding the statement "the root *vid* is taken here in the sense of 'knowing'," this refers to the root *vid* meaning "to know" (Dhātupāṭha 1064). It does not refer to [the root] in the sense of "obtaining," namely the root *vidlṛ* meaning "to obtain" (Dhātupāṭha 1432).

This is an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the root *vid* in the sense of "knowing" (*ajñāna*); therefore, it does not include the two roots *vid* in the senses of "existence" (*sat*) and "investigation" (*avicāraṇa*). However, in some places, there is a reading "in the sense of obtaining" (*lābha*) in order to include these two by means of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*). He asks: why, then, is the root in the sense of "knowing" included? He says:

Regarding the phrase "from its own nature" (*svabhāvāt*): by means of the suffix produced after the root *vid*, it is precisely the self-nature that is perceived as the agent of the act of knowing, and nothing else. Therefore, there is the apprehension of the object of knowledge itself, and not of anything other than that. Regarding the phrase "the suffix [is used] in the sense of the object-as-agent" (*karmakartari pratyayaḥ*): this refers to the sense "it cuts itself. In that case—
"From its own nature" refers to the very same reason previously stated.
163. *iṇ-naś-jis-rtibhyaḥ kvarap* (3.2.163).
Regarding "ṭhitvaraḥ": by [the rule] *hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk* (6.1.71), the augment *tuk* is added. Regarding "ṭhitvarī":
by [the rule] *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (4.1.15) and so forth, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied.

165. *jāgarūkaḥ* (3.2.165). Regarding the form *jāgarūkaḥ*: the root *jāgṛ* (meaning "to wake from sleep") [is used]. By the rule of optional non-homogeneity (*vā'sarūpa-vidhi*), [the suffix *ūka* is applied].
The suffix *tṛn* also occurs—as in the word *jāgarita*.
166. *yajajapadaśāṃ yaṅ* (3.2.166).
