Although the elision of the nasal in the root *daṃś*—by the rule *aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti* (6.4.24)—is established even when the *yaṅ* suffix is elided by means of the "characteristic of the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), nevertheless, for the sake of brevity...
The elision of the nasal (*anunāsika*) should be understood as having been indicated [in the rule]. For example, in *yajājūkaḥ*: from the root *yaji*, there is the intensive suffix *yaṅ*;

by the rule *dīrgho 'kitaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.83), lengthening occurs; then by *ato lopaḥ* (6.4.48), the vowel *a* is elided. Similarly for *jañjapūkaḥ* and *dandaśūkaḥ*. [These are derived] by the rule *lupasada* (3.1.24).
By the rule *yaṅ* [Pāṇini 3.1.22] and so forth, and by the rule *japajabhadahadaśabhañjapaśāṃ ca* (7.4.86), the augment *nuK* is added to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

167. *namikampi-smya-jas-kama-hiṃsā-dīpa-raḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.167). The roots *ṇam* (in the sense of bowing and sound; DhP 981), *kapi* (in the sense of moving; DhP 375), *ṣmiṅ* (in the sense of slight laughter; DhP 948), *kam* (in the sense of desire; DhP 443), and *tṛh* (in the sense of injuring; DhP 1029)... [are followed by the suffix *ra*.]
The roots *tṛh* and *his* are used in the sense of "injuring" (*hiṃsāyām*) [DhP 1455, 1456], and *dīpī* is used in the sense of "shining" (*dīptau*) [DhP 1150].

Since the root *kapi* has the meaning of "moving" (*calana*), and since the suffix *yaC* would apply to *kam*, *dīpī*, and others because they are marked with an anudātta vowel, the suffix *ra* is specifically prescribed here. This refers to "the continuity of action" (*kriyāsātatyam*).

The continuous engagement in actions being performed without interruption is "perpetuity of action" (*kriyāsātatyam*). In that regard, the suffix *pratyaya* occurs precisely as part of the word's own form (*svabhāva*).
168. *san-āśaṃsa-bhikṣa-uḥ* (3.2.168).

[The commentary states: "The suffix *san* is understood here"—that is, the one prescribed by the rule *guptijkidbhyaḥ* (3.1.5) and so forth. [It further states: "The root *san* is not [meant here]"—referring to *ṣaṇu* in the sense of "giving" (DhP 1464), as well as *vana* and *ṣaṇa*.

The root *sambhaktau* (DhP 4.63, 4.64) is not intended here. This is understood from the inclusion of the word *jigīṣu* in the *gargādi* group; for that [inclusion] is appropriate when there is a reference to a suffix (*pratyaya*), but not when there is a reference to a verbal root (*dhātu*). [The roots] beginning with *āṅ śāsi icchāyām* and so forth—this too [is understood] together with *āṅ*.

This is understood from the grammatical explanation (*nirdeśa*). For the root *paṭh* is recited with the prefix *āṅ* in the sense of "desire" (*icchā*), not in the sense of "praise" (*stuti*). In the case of the example *āśaṃsu*, *bhikṣuḥ*, although the suffix *yuc* would have been applicable by the rule *anudāteśca halādeḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.149), the suffix *up* is prescribed instead.

169. *vindur icchuḥ* | (3.2.169) [The word] "from the root *vid*" refers to *vid jñāne* (DhP 1064). As for the others, they are not included because they are not denoted [by this rule], or else because of the specific force (*sāmarthya*) of the *nipātana* (irregular formation). [The word] "from the root *iṣ*" refers to...

This refers to the root *iṣ* in the sense of "desire" (*icchā*) from Dhātupāṭha 1351. However, there is no inclusion of other roots such as *iṣ* in the sense of "motion" (Dhātupāṭha 1127) and so forth, as was the case previously.
Thus, [the form] is *icchuḥ*; here the substitution of the letter *cch* is prescribed by rule, and by the rule *che ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.73), the augment *tuk* is applied.
The substitution of *ścu* [for *ṣṭu*] occurs by the rule "ṣṭunā ścuḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.40).

170. *kyāc ca chandasi* (Pāṇini 3.2.170). Regarding the example *mitrayuḥ*: from the sense "he desires a friend" (*mitram icchati*), the suffix *kyac* is applied by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (3.1.8).
By the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* (7.4.25), lengthening would have occurred; however, [this is prevented] by the rule *kyaci ca*.

(7.4.33) Thus, both of these [substitutions] do not occur because of the prohibition in (7.4.35): *na ccchandasyaputrasya*. In the case of *saṃsvedayuḥ*, the suffix *kyaṣ* is applied according to (3.1.13) due to its inclusion in the *lohitādi* group. In the case of *sumnayuḥ*, there is a prohibition by (7.4.38): *devasumnayoḥ*. [The word] *sumna*...

The suffix *kyaṅ* is applied according to the rule "ṭhkartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca" (Pāṇini 3.1.11), meaning "the suffix *kyaṅ* is added after a verbal root ending in *ṭh* [i.e., a consonant] when it denotes the agent acting like another, with the elision of the final *s*."
171. *ādṛgamahanajanaḥ kikinau liṭ ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.171).

Words employed in the sense of another thing convey that meaning even without the suffix *-vat*, just as in the examples: "The Vāhīka is a cow" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*) and "The boy is a lion" (*siṃho māṇavakaḥ*). When it is said, "The Vāhīka is a cow," [it implies he possesses the qualities of a cow].

A word employed in reference to another object—even without the suffix *vati*—is understood to apply to a Vāhīka who possesses a form similar [to a cow], as in the expression "this is like a cow" (*gaur ivāyam*). Here, the term *liṭ* is employed outside its own primary meaning to refer to the *kikina* suffixes; therefore, even in the absence of a connection with *vati*, an extended application (*atideśa*) is understood.

Thus he says: "Those two are like the *liṭ*. The meaning is that they are equal to the *liṭ*, possessing the same properties as the *liṭ*. The sense is that whatever operation belongs to the *liṭ*, such as reduplication (*dvirvacana*) and so forth, that occurs for the *kikin* suffixes.
This is an extension of operations (*kāryātideśa*), not an extension of rules (*śāstrātideśa*); for, in comparison with the extension of operations—

Because the extension of the *śāstra* (the rule) is not primary; the lack of primacy in the extension of the *śāstra*, however, is due to its being a grammatical operation (*kārya*). If, then, this were an extension of the operation, the designation *parasmaipada*—as in "the *l* [suffixes] are *parasmaipada*" (P.
1.4.99)—would also apply to the *kik* and *kin* suffixes.
In that case, would those two [terminations] not fail to occur after roots that take the ātmanepada? This is not a fault;

for the designation *parasmaipada* applies to the substitute (*lādeśa*), not to the letter *l*. Indeed, in the rule "ṭhla," the genitive case is used with reference to the substitutes, meaning that the substitute of *l* receives the designation *parasmaipada*. Furthermore, *kikina* are not such substitutes.

Since there are substitutes for *l*, how could there be any occasion for the designation *parasmaipada*? Well then, why do the *tiṅ* suffixes not occur? Because of the specific power of the rule enjoining those two (*ki* and *kin*). If the *tiṅ* suffixes were to occur, the injunction of *ki* and *kin* would be purposeless—one would simply have enjoined the *liṭ* [perfect] suffix—and yet that is not the case.
Are the suffixes *taci*, etc., prescribed for the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth? They will not occur because they are not so designated.

Why do the suffixes *kvasu* and *kānac* not occur here? Furthermore, the state of meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*) of those two suffixes is not possible in the case of *ki* and *kin*. This is because of the rules: "After the *liṭ* [perfect], *kānac* may optionally [be used]" (Pāṇini 3.2.106) and "and *kvasu*" (Pāṇini 3.2.107).
Is it because the suffixes *kvasu* and *kānac* are prescribed by way of option (*vikalpa*)? They will not occur precisely because of non-expression (*anabhidhāna*);

for by those two, the states of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth are not prescribed, for that very reason of non-expression. [This is established by] *laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.69).

Thus, the *kṛt* suffixes *ki* and *kin* do not occur even in the case of the object (*karman*). For just as by the suffix *ghurac*— produced after the root *bhañj* by the rule "after *bhañj*, *bhās*, and *mid*, [the suffix] *ghurac*" (Pāṇini 3.2.161)— only the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*) is expressed by its very nature and not the agent (*kartṛ*) alone, so it is also with *ki* and *kin*.

"By the very nature of the suffixes produced from a verbal root (*dhātu*), only the agent (*kartṛ*) is denoted, not the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). The letter *d* in [the rule] *ṭha* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation. This is intended to exclude the possibility that it is a *tapara* (a marker indicating that the preceding vowel is short). Therefore he says: "But this is not a *tapara*. What, then, is the reason that it is not desired to be a *tapara*?

Thus he says: "Let it not be," and so forth. In the rule *tapa-ras-tat-kālasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.70), the analysis as a genitive compound (*pañcamī-samāsa*)—meaning "that which follows even from *ta*"—is also adopted. This is for the purpose that, in the rule *vṛddhir-ādaic* (Pāṇini 1.1.1), the designation *vṛddhi* should not apply to the diphthongs *ai* and *au* when they consist of three or four morae (*mātra*). And therefore...

If it were thus [that the term *tapara* applies here], then it would apply to the short *ṛ* as well; consequently, by means of the short *ṛ*, there would be the inclusion of those [vowels] of its own duration that consist of one *mātrā*, but not of the long ones. What fault would there be in that? [The fault is that the rule would apply] only in cases such as *dadhiścakriḥ*.

[Otherwise] *taturiḥ* and *jaguriḥ*, and so forth, would not be possible. Therefore, since this fault must indeed be avoided, the use of the marker *t* (taparatva) is not intended here. [In the example] "papiḥ somam," there is the elision of the vowel *ā* by Pāṇini 6.4.64 (*āto lopa iṭi ca*), followed by reduplication and the treatment of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
It is short. By the rule "na lokāvyayaniṣṭhā" (Pāṇini 2.3.69) and others, the prohibition of the genitive case applies;

thus, from the word *soma*, the second case singular is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). Regarding "dadat": [the root is] *ḍudāñ* "to give" (Dhātupāṭha 1091). Regarding "tatatuḥ": [this is formed] by the rule "bahulaṃ cchandasi" (Pāṇini 7.1.103).

Thus it has been stated, as well as the substitution of *r* for *ra*. By virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) according to Pāṇini 1.1.59 (*dvirvacane'ci*), the word *tṛ* is reduplicated. [Then] by Dhātupāṭha 7.4.66, there is the substitution of *i* for the radical vowel, followed by the substitution of *r* for *ra*, and the application of 7.4.60 (*halādiśeṣaḥ*). Thus, "jaguriḥ" is formed from the root *gṛ* in the sense of "swallowing" (Dhātupāṭha 1410).

Regarding the forms *jañjaniḥ* and *jaghniḥ*: the elision of the penultimate vowel occurs by the rule *gamahana-* (Pāṇini 6.4.98). In *jan*, the substitution of the *ścu*-class sound *ñ* for the nasal *n* occurs by the rule *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ* (8.4.40).
The objection begins with the word *atha*; the resolution is provided by the rule *ṛcchatyṛtām* (7.4.11), and so forth.

"ṭhutsargaścchandasi" and so forth. *Utsarga* means a general rule (*sāmānyena vidhānam*). This is what is meant: the production of the suffixes *kik* and *kin* should be understood as occurring from any verbal root (*dhātumātra*) without specifying a particular base (*prakṛtiviśeṣam anupādāya*). That is to say, they are to be prescribed from any verbal root whatsoever. Why?

He states the reason: "Because they are seen even after [roots] such as *sad*. For the suffixes *ki* and *kin* must be applied as a general rule (*utsarga*) even after roots such as *sad*, which are not included in the [standard] list of roots. Examples are *sediḥ* and *nemiḥ*. [In these cases,] due to the preceding cause, there is the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-lopa*). [The root is] *ṣadlṛ*.
[The root] *viś* [is used] in the senses of "falling apart," "going," and "depression" (*dhātupāṭha* 854); [the root] *ṇam* [is used] in the senses of "bowing" and "sound" (*dhātupāṭha* 981).
By the rule *ata ekahalmadhye'nādeśāderliṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.120), there is the substitution of *e* for the radical vowel and the elision of the reduplicated syllable.

In *dadhiḥ* and *cakriḥ*, there is the elision of the vowel *ā* as before. In *cakriḥ* and *sasriḥ*, there is the substitution of *yaṇ* for the roots *kṛ* and *sṛ*. In *jajñiḥ*, there is the same [elision] as before, along with the substitution of *cut* and the elision of the penultimate vowel. In *nemiḥ*, there is the substitution of *at* and the elision of the reduplication as before.
The forms beginning with *sahivahi* and so forth also occur in the colloquial language (*bhāṣā*). The forms beginning with *sāsahiḥ* and so forth are derived as follows:
the suffix *yaṅ* is added after roots such as *sah*, reduplication occurs, and the elision of the initial vowel and the semivowel *y* takes place as previously described.

172. *svapitṛṣornajiṅ* (Pāṇini 3.2.172). [The suffix] *najiṅ* is applied after the roots *svap* and *tṛṣ*. Thus: *svapnaka*, *tṛṣṇaka*. [The roots are] *ñiṣvapa śaye* (Dhātupāṭha 1068, "to sleep") and *ñitṛṣā pipāsāyām* (Dhātupāṭha 1228, "to thirst"). By the rule *coḥ kuḥ* (8.2.30), the substitution of *k* occurs [for the palatals].

The [root] is *gakāra*. By the rule "ṭhvo'vasāne" (Pāṇini 8.4.58), its *g* becomes *k*, resulting in *kakāra*. In the suffix *nañiṅ*, the *ṅ* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* after the root *tṛṣ*, and the *ikāra* is for the sake of pronunciation.

173. *Śru-vandyor āruḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.173). After the root *śru*, the suffix *āru* is applied; thus, *śrāva* is formed, as also the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by *ṭhag-ṛdara-pada...* (3.2.154) and other rules.
After the root *vand*, although the suffix *yu* would have been expected by *anudātetaś ca* (3.2.149) and other rules, this specific rule [prescribes *āru*].
174. *bhiyaḥ kruklukanau* (3.2.174).

Regarding the statement "krukan also should be mentioned": the meaning is that another suffix, *krukan*, must be stated—that is, it must be explained. In this regard, the following is the explanation: [it follows] from the rule *ādṛgamahana-* (3.2.171) onwards.

The letter *ca* is carried over from the preceding sūtra; it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. Since it includes what has not been mentioned, by that [rule], *kruk* will also occur.

175. *stheśabhāsapikṣasakas* take *varac*. (3.2.175) [The example] "sthāvaraḥ" [is formed with this suffix]. The prohibition of *iṭ* is by the rule "ekācaḥ" (7.2.10). In cases such as "īśvaraḥ," the prohibition of *iṭ* is also by the rule "neḍ vaśi kṛti" (7.2.8). This applies to the root *sthā* (*tiṣṭhati*).

The suffixes *ksnu* and *ukañ*, which were prescribed by the preceding sūtra, also occur here by virtue of this explicit statement (*vacana*). This statement is made because, in the case of the roots *īś* and *bhās*, the suffix *yuc* would have been applicable as before; [this sūtra] supersedes that.
Regarding "ṭhyāyāvaraḥ": as before, there is the elision of the letter *a* and the semivowel (*y*).
177. *bhrājabhāsadhurvidyutojipṛjugrāvastuvaḥ kvip* (Pāṇini 3.2.177). *bhrājṛ* (Dhātupāṭha 181): *bhrāja* in the sense of shining; *bhāsṛ* (624): *bhās* in the sense of shining;
*urvī*, *turvī*, *thurvī*, *dhurvī* (Dhātupāṭha 569, 570, 571, 573): these have the meaning of injury (*hiṃsā*); *dyauta*.

The roots *dīp* (to shine, DhP 7.41), *turj* (to exert strength or give life, DhP 15.49), *pṛ* (to protect or fill, DhP 10.86), *ju* (a root from the Sūtra collection), and *ṣṭuañ* (to praise, DhP 10.43) preceded by *grāvan*. Regarding the form *vibhrāṭ*: [it is derived] by means of the rule concerning the *vraśca*-group.

(8.2.36) *ṣatvam* (the substitution of *ṣ*). As before, there is *jaśtva* and *cartva*. Regarding *dhūḥ*: by *rāllopaḥ* (6.4.21), the *v* is elided; then, by *rṭhvorupadhāyā dīrgha ikaḥ* (8.2.76), the vowel is lengthened. Regarding *pūḥ*: by *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya* (7.1.102), *u*-substitution occurs, followed by *raparatva* (the replacement of *u* by *r*).

The lengthening is as before, according to the rule "There is lengthening for *jū*. How so? Some say that in the sūtra, *jū* should be read with a long vowel. Others, however, say that since it is seen in the subsequent sūtra, it is a remainder (*śeṣa*) of both rules, and its purpose is to include other injunctions.

Therefore, a long vowel is prescribed for the root *ju*. One who praises the pressing-stones (*grāvan*) is a *grāvastut*. [The suffix *kvip* is applied] by the rule "there is *tuk* after a short vowel before a *kṛt* suffix ending in *pit*" (Pāṇini 6.1.71).
The objection beginning with "For what purpose is this? is raised; [the answer is] that it is superseded by suffixes having the sense of habit (*tācchīlika*).
This is the rebuttal. It might be argued: "It will occur somewhere by means of the *vāsarūpa* rule.
To this he says: "And the *vāsarūpa* rule [does not apply here]. This was stated in the context of the sūtra *nindahiṃsa-* (3.2.146).
But surely, in the sūtra *sūdadīpadīkṣaśca* (3.2.153), its applicability is shown to be merely occasional (*prāyikatva*).
The indicative nature [of the rule] has been established; furthermore, he states that the *vāsarūpa* rule does not apply here by saying "of that very [root].
[The suffixes] are formed by rules such as "it is also seen after others" (3.2.75) and "the suffix *kvip* also [occurs]" (3.2.76).

178. *anyebhyo'pi dṛśyate* (3.2.178). Now, one might ask: since the rule would be established by the words *anyebhyo'pi* alone, for what purpose is the inclusion of the word *dṛśi*? [The answer is: The inclusion of *dṛśi* is for the sake of including those cases which are not otherwise covered, as indicated by the phrase "in some instances" (*kvacit*) and so forth. These are the cases...

He shows other rules. Since the inclusion of the term *dṛś* (‘to see’) is for the purpose of encompassing other rules, and having done so, the author of the Vṛtti recites the rule beginning with *ṭhkvibvacipṛcchi* (Vārttika 288). Those very other rules are those included by the mention of *dṛś*.
The intention is "in order to show. But how, by the inclusion of the term *dṛśi* (to see), is there an inclusion of other rules (*vidhyantara*)?
For when *dṛśi* is included, the meaning obtained is: "Just as verbal roots ending in *kvip* are seen [to be treated], so indeed should they be understood. And when that meaning is obtained—

The rules for reduplication and so forth are thus subsumed; in this way, they become consistent with how they are observed. If reduplication and the like are prescribed according to their proper application, then in the case of roots ending in *kvip*, reduplication is seen in some instances, while in others it is not.
It was rightly stated that "vocalization" (*saṃprasāraṇa*) [is the rule]; namely, that "the mention of *dṛśi* is for the purpose of including other rules.
As for the form "vāk," it is derived from the root *vac* by means of the rule *vaci-ādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 6.1.15).

The absence of *samprasāraṇa* is effected [in the case of the root *prach*], as in the form *śabdaprāṭ*. For the root *prach* as well, *samprasāraṇa* occurs by the rule *grahādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.16). By the rule *vraścabhrasjasṛjamṛjayajarājabhrājacchaśām ṣaḥ* (8.2.36), *ṣatva* is applied; then, as before, *jaśtva* and *cartva* follow. From "he praises that which is extended" (*āyataṃ stauti*), the form *āyatastūḥ* is derived. [The root is] *ṣṭuañ*.

In *stuti* (to praise) [from root 1043]. *Kaṭaprūḥ*: from *pruṅ gatau* (root 957, "to move"). *Śrīḥ*: from *śriñ sevāyām* (root 897, "to serve"). *Didyaut*. *Jagat*: the nasal is elided by *gamaḥ kvau* (Pāṇini 6.4.40). *Dadṛt*.

Thus: by the rule *uraṇ* (Pāṇini 1.1.50), substitution of *u*; by *urat* (7.4.66), substitution of *at*; by *rapara* (1.1.51), the substitute is followed by *r*; and by *halādiśeṣaḥ* (7.4.60), the remaining consonant is retained. Thus we have *dhīḥ*.
[The derivation of] *dhyai* is from the root *dhyai* in the sense of "thinking" (Dhātupāṭha 908); the lengthening is by the rule *halaḥ* (6.4.2).
179. *bhuvaḥ saṃjñāntarayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.179).

Regarding the phrase "of the creditor and the debtor" (*dhanikādhamarṇayoḥ*) and so forth: the creditor (*dhanika*) is he to whom a debt is owed; the debtor (*adhamarṇa*) is he who owes it. Between these two, he who stands in the middle, having fallen on the side of one or the other, [is called a *bhū*].

The word *sapratibhū* denotes one who is a cause for confidence (*sampratyayahetu*), not everyone. Therefore, one who stands between two villages is not considered a *pratyaya* (guarantor) in that case. This is understood from the inherent nature of the word's expressive power (*śabdaśaktisvābhāvyāt*), or because of the recurrence of the term *dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 3.2.178). Of this...
If [the term] *pratibhū* is to be understood as a designation (*saṃjñā*) for one who follows after [another], then what is the purpose of including the word *antara*?

Should it not simply be stated that it is a "designation" (*saṃjñā*)? This is not so; for words that are designations (*saṃjñā-śabda*) serve to exclude the status of being a substance (*dravyatva*), and the word *pratibhū* is not like that. Nevertheless, even when Devadatta exists, at some time he...
It does not proceed at all.
180. *ḍaḥ* is added after *vipra*, *saṃ* (*sam*), and *pra* when not forming a proper name. (3.2.180) For example, *vibhuḥ*. By the preceding rule, only *kvip* occurs.
Regarding the statement "there is an addition [of the suffix] after *mita*, *drava*, etc.," it applies without distinction—both in non-proper names and in proper names.

And in the case of *asaṃjñā* (non-technical name). The dative case in *mitadravādibhyaḥ* is used in the sense of "for the purpose of" (*tādarthye*). The purpose [of this rule] is so that words such as *mitadrava* and others, which end in the suffix *ḍu*, may be grammatically correct. The word *upasaṃkhyāna* means "statement" or "explanation. And since the subject under discussion is the suffix *ḍu*, this statement refers to it. In this regard, the following...

Regarding the explanation: the word "also" (*api*) from the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 3.2.178) is understood here as well; therefore, the suffix *ḍu* occurs after words such as *mitadrava* and others, even from other verbal roots, provided that there is another word [in composition].

181. *dhaḥ karmaṇi ṣṭran* (Pāṇini 3.2.181). [The word] "dhayateḥ" refers to *dheṭ pāne* (Dhātupāṭha 902). [The word] "dadhāteḥ" refers to *ḍudhāñ dhāraṇapoṣaṇayoḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 1092). [The phrase] "karmaṇi kārake" means that by this [rule], [the suffix is applied] when there is an object (*karman*).

By demonstrating that [the word *karma*] has the sense of a suffix (*pratyaya*), he refutes its status as a governing term (*upapada*). For if *karma* were indeed an *upapada*, [the author] would have prescribed [the suffix] in this very section, namely under the rule *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1).
In this way, the mention of the word *karma* would not need to be made twice. Now, even if it were mentioned twice...

The mention of *karman* need not be made. Now, even if the mention of *karman* need not be made twice, does it not follow that the mention of *ṣṭran* must be made in the subsequent sūtra? Let it be so; for the mention of *ṣṭran* is indeed lighter than the mention of *karman*. But here—

Because of the continued application of the term "present" (*vartamāna*), the suffix occurs in the sense of the present; however, if [the rule] were formulated there, this would not be obtained? This is not so; even if it were formulated here, the suffix would certainly not occur in the sense of the present. For when "nurse" (*dhātrī*) is mentioned, no specific [time] is understood; what then?

A woman qualified merely by the relation between action and its factors (kāraka) is understood— as in the case of "the *āmalakī* plants bear her for the sake of medicine. Therefore, in this context, the term "in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi*) refers exclusively to the meaning of the suffix,
and not to an *upapada*.

182. *dāmnīśasayuyujastutudasisicamihapatadaśanahaḥ karaṇe* (Pāṇini 3.2.182). Regarding the rule *dāp lavane*: just as in the rule *dādhā ghvadāp* (1.1.20), there is the inclusion of *daip śodhane* (Dhātupāṭha 924), why does the same not occur here as well?

Because it is not so expressed. For by its very nature, the suffix *ṣṭran* in the word *dātram* denotes the instrument of cutting (*lavana*), not that of cleansing (*śodhana*). This is because [the rule] states, "when the agent is the instrument" (*karaṇe kārake*). By thus demonstrating that the meaning of the suffix is the instrument, he refutes [its status as] a subordinate term (*upapada*).
If this [word *daṃṣṭra*] were to have the status of being a secondary derivative (*aupapada*), then its inclusion among the words beginning with *ajā* would not be justified. [Examples:

*yoktram*—here there is the substitution of *k* by rule 8.2.30, *coḥ kuḥ*. *meḍhram*—here there is the substitution of *ḍh* by rule 8.2.31, *ho ḍhaḥ*, followed by the substitution of *dh* by rule 8.2.40, *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ*.

The substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭu* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.4.41], and the elision of *ḍha* before *ḍha* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.3.13], resulting in the form *daṃṣṭrā*. The suffix *ṭāp* is applied because it begins with a vowel (*ajādi*). Regarding the rule "from the root *daṃś*" and so forth: but surely, just as in the case of [the rule] *tyajaraja* (3.2.142)?
In the case of the root *rañj* with the suffix *dhinuṇ*, when there is the mention of its nasalized form, the elision of the nasal occurs in *rāgī*;

likewise, in the case of *daṃś* with the suffix *ṣṭran*, the elision of the nasal will occur. How, then, is its status as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) justified? This is not a fault; for if this mention were [intended] for *daṃś*...

If [the suffix] *ṣṭran* were for the purpose of eliding the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*), then the inclusion of the word *daṃṣṭrā* in the list beginning with vowels (*aj-ādi*) would be contradicted. Therefore, it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Regarding the form *naddhrī*: there is the substitution of *dh* by [Pāṇini 8.2.34] *naho dhaḥ*, and [the rule] *jhaṣas tathordho 'dhaḥ*.

By [Pāṇini 8.2.40], the *t* is changed to *dh*; by [Pāṇini 8.4.53], the *dh* undergoes *jaś*-substitution; and by [Pāṇini 4.1.41], the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. Regarding those verbal roots beginning with *śas* that are *seṭ* (having an *iṭ* augment), [the rule] "ṭhtitutratatha... [applies].
By these and other such [rules], there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*.

183. *halasūkarayoḥ pūrvāt* (3.2.183). The commentary states: "If that instrument is a constituent part (*avayava*) of the plow (*hala*) or the pig (*sūkara*). By this, he demonstrates that the term *halasūkarayoḥ* is a genitive of constituent part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), and not a locative of the thing denoted (*abhidheya-saptamī*).

The "face" (mukha) is said to be [the primary part], as stated in the *Kāśikā* and the *Padamañjarī*: "It is the face itself that is so called," meaning no other limb such as the ear. This is due to the inherent nature of its denotative power (*abhidhānaśakti*).

184. *itra* is added after the roots *arti*, *lū*, *dhū*, *sū*, *khan*, *sah*, and *cara*. (Pāṇini 3.2.184). The inclusion here is of the two roots *dhū* "to shake" (Dhātupāṭha 1398) and *sū* "to impel" (1408). [The roots] *dhūñ* "to tremble" (Dhātupāṭha 1487) and *ṣūñ* (Dhātupāṭha 1408) are also included.

In the case of the roots *sūṅ* (DhP 1031) "to release the fetus of a living being" and *sūṅ* (DhP 1132) "the birth of a living being," there is no inclusion [of these] by virtue of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating that "when a root without an indicatory letter (*niranubandhaka*) is mentioned, one without an indicatory letter is understood, not one with an indicatory letter (*sānubandhaka*)."

185. *puvaḥ saṃjñāyām* | (3.2.185) [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the root *pu* when forming a name. As in *barhiṣpavitram*. It is derived from either *pavate* or *punāti*. By this [suffix], the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is made pure. *Barhiṣpavitram*, moreover, is a modification of *kuśa* grass. [It is held] by the forefinger...
The wrapping of the fingers is so called.
186. [The suffix] *kṛt* is used in the sense of the agent when referring to a Ṛṣi or a deity.
187. After a root ending in *ñī*, the suffix *kta* is applied.

In *kṣviṇṇa*, there is a prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *āditaśca* (Pāṇini 7.2.16). There is the substitution of *n* by the rule *radābhyām* (8.2.42). The same applies to *kṣviṇṇaḥ*. The substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule *aṭkupvāṅ* (8.4.2), etc. Regarding *dhṛṣṭaḥ*, [the rule] *dhṛṣiśasī vaiyātye* (7.2.19) [applies].
Thus there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*; furthermore, by the rule "ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.41), the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭu* takes place.

188. *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca* (3.2.188). [The word] *mataḥ*: from the root *man* (meaning "to know," *dhā.pā.* 1176). There is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by [the rule] *ekācaḥ* (7.2.10), etc., and the elision of the nasal [of the root] by [the rule] *anudātopadeśa* (6.4.37), etc.

Regarding *ṣṭhiṣṭaḥ*: from the root *piṣ*—in the sense of "desire" (*iṣu icchāyām*, Dhātupāṭha 1351)—the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* in the *niṣṭhā* suffix applies by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 7.2.15), because [the addition of] *iṭ* is optional according to the rule *udito vā* (Pāṇini 7.2.56). Regarding *buddhaḥ*: from the root *budh*—in the sense of "understanding" (*avagamane*, Dhātupāṭha 858).

As before, there is the substitution of *dha* for *t*, the substitution of *jaś* for *ta* (yielding *da*), and the substitution of *da* for *dha*. Thus: *pūjitaḥ*, *arcitaḥ*. These are not found in the *bhvādi* class; they are well-known only as belonging to the *curādi* class. "pūja" (meaning worship) is at Dhātupāṭha 1642; "arca" (meaning worship) is at Dhātupāṭha 204 in the *bhvādi* class. These two [roots]...
And regarding *cārita*: when a suffix is applied to roots such as *cur* and others, there is the elision of *ṇi* by the rule "ṭhniṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi" (Pāṇini 6.4.52).
In forms such as *śīlita*, [the root is] *śīla* in the sense of "steadfastness" (Dhātupāṭha 658), and *kṣamuṣ* in the sense of "endurance."
(dhā.pā.442) *kruśa* "in calling out and weeping" (dhā.pā.856); *āhvāne* "in calling" (dhā.pā.856);
*juṣī* "in pleasure and service" (dhā.pā.1288); *ruṣa* "in anger" (dhā.pā.1670);
*hṛñ* "in taking away" (dhā.pā.899); *hṛṣa* "in satisfaction" (dhā.pā.1229); *hṛṣu* "in falsehood."

Of these verbal roots: *tuṣ* (DhP 709) in the sense of satisfaction (*tuṣṭau*), *tuṣ* (DhP 1184) in the sense of contentment, *kam* (DhP 443) in the sense of desire, *yam* (DhP 984) in the sense of cessation, *kaṣ* (DhP 685) in the sense of injury, and *mṛṅ* (DhP 1403) in the sense of giving up life.

These forms follow their respective sequences. Among them, the first two are marked with the *seṭ* designation. Furthermore, for any root here that is marked with *udic* or *ūdic*, there is a prohibition of the *iṭ* augment by the rule "ṭhyasya vibhāṣā" (7.2.15). As for a root marked with *īdit*, for that as well, [the *iṭ* is prohibited] by the rule "śvīdito niṣṭhāyām" (7.2.14).

Thus, there is a prohibition of *iṭ*. For the root *hṛṣ*, the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied by the rule "optionally after *hṛṣ*, *mṛṣ*, *kṛś*, *saṃghuṣ*, and *svan*" (7.2.28), as in "the hair bristled" (*hṛṣitāni loma*) and so forth.
Examples include *kāntaḥ* and *kṣāntaḥ*. [The rule] "of a nasal before *kvip* and a consonant beginning with *jhal*" (6.4.15)...

The long vowel [is applied] by the rule *kṅiti* (6.4.15). In the word *ākruṣṭaḥ*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *vraśca-* (8.2.36). In the word *saṃyataḥ*, there is the elision of the nasal as before. In the word *amṛtaḥ*, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) after roots meaning "to go" and so forth. The phrase "as before" means as in the case of [words like] *śīla* and others.

The meaning is that the *niṣṭhā* suffix occurs in the present tense, and the same applies to the word *amṛta*. In *suptaḥ*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the root *svap*. In *śayitaḥ*, because of the prohibition of *kit*-treatment by the rule *niṣṭhā śīṅ* (Pāṇini 1.2.19), *guṇa* substitution takes place. In *āśitaḥ*, [the root is] *aś*.

The roots *bhuja* (DhP 1523) with the prefix *āṅ*, *lip* (DhP 1433) meaning "to smear," and *tṛp* (DhP 1195) meaning "to satisfy" are included here. Among these, *aś* and *śīṅ* are *seṭ* (taking the augment *iṭ*), while the remaining ones are *aniṭ* (without *iṭ*). The prohibition of *iṭ* applies by the rule "ekācaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.10) and others. Although [roots such as] *śīl* and so forth pertain to the present tense...

Although these [terms] are explained [as denoting the past], nevertheless, in expressions such as *śīlito devadattena*, *rakṣito devadattena*, and *ākruṣṭo devadattena*, the genitive case does not occur by virtue of the rule *ṭh-ktasya ca vartamāne* (Pāṇini 2.3.67).
How it does not occur has been demonstrated in that very [section].
Thus ends the third chapter of the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable Ācārya Jinendrabuddhi, who was a disciple of the Bodhisattvas.
Second Pāda. Now begins the third chapter.
The third quarter [of the third book]:
*iuṇādayo bahulam* (3.3.1).
[This rule] follows from the rule *vartamāne laṭ* (3.2.123), which states "the suffix *laṭ* is used when there is present time."

He shows that the term "present" (*vartamāna*) is understood [from the previous rule]. The phrase "in the sense of a name" (*saṃjñāyām*) is [understood] from the rule *puvaḥ saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 3.2.185).
Regarding the phrase "by way of multiplicity" (*bāhulakam*), etc.: the root *lā* means "to take" (*ādāne*, Dhātupāṭha 1058); thus, one who takes many things is called *bahulā*.
"Abundantly. Regarding the rule *ṭhāto 'nupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3), there are many meanings;
in some cases, these include "occurrence" (*pravṛtti*) and so forth. And thus it has been said:
"In some cases occurrence, in some cases non-occurrence, in some cases an option (*vibhāṣā*), and in some cases something else entirely."
"Having examined the various prescriptions of the rules in many ways, they speak of 'bāhulaka' as being fourfold.

The state of being *bahula* is *bāhulaka*. The suffix *ghañ* is applied here because it belongs to the *manojñādi* group, according to the rule *dvandvamanojñādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 5.1.133). The word *bahula* signifies the taking up of many meanings.

The term *pravṛttinimitta* is used precisely in that context as an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). That [usage] is stated to be frequent because the nature of the base (*prakṛti*) is rarely observed. That word which is employed first, taking the suffix as beginningless, is called the *prakṛti*. It is called *prakṛti* because it is placed before the suffix (*pratyaya*).
Alternatively, it is called *prakṛti* because a cognition (*pratyaya*) is produced from it with excellence and regularity.

Regarding the term "of the *prakṛti*": this is a singular genitive used in the sense of a genus (*jāti*). Regarding "from the sight of the subtle" (*tanudṛṣṭeḥ*): this is a fifth case ending used after a verb of seeing with the elision of the suffix *lyap*; that is, having observed the subtle vision, the rule is stated as being optional (*bāhulaka*). [The rule] "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*).
However, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) does not apply here by virtue of the rule *guṇe 'striyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.25),
because of the prohibition contained in the phrase *astriyām*.
Alternatively, the ablative case should be understood here through a formal split (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule *vibhāṣā guṇe*.

The word *tanu* has both the sense of "body" and the sense of a "quality"; here, however, it denotes the quality known as the "minuteness" of primordial matter (*prakṛti*). *Darśana* means vision, perception, or apprehension;
thus, *tanudṛṣṭi* is the vision of that subtle quality. From that [vision], the quality is eternal.

Because it is understood that [the word *tanu*] requires a possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), a compound is formed with the word *dṛṣṭi* even though *tanu* depends upon its own base (*prakṛti*). This, however, is the meaning: [it refers to] the quality of the base (*prakṛti-guṇa*) and the seeing of those two.

Alternatively, "tanudṛṣṭi" refers to that nature (prakṛti) whose vision is subtle. In this view, although the quality of subtlety is an adjective of vision, it is nevertheless understood as an adjective of both the vision and the nature itself; for it is precisely because the nature is subtle that [the vision is so].
Thus, there is an absence of that [specific] view. In the *Uṇādisūtra* consisting of five quarters (*pañcapādī*), only a few root-forms (*prakṛti*) are seen;

yet suffixes (*pratyaya*) are also seen from other root-forms as well. Therefore, they come into being by virtue of the inclusion of the term "variously" (*bahulam*). For example, as in the rule: *hṛṣerulac* (Pañcapādī 1.98).

The suffix *ul* is attached to the root *ṛṣu* in the sense of "falsehood" (*alīka*) [as per Dhātupāṭha 709]; likewise, it also occurs from the root *śaki* in the sense of "doubt" (*śaṅkā*) [as per Dhātupāṭha 86], resulting in the word *śaṅkulā*. Furthermore, the connection is that those [suffixes] are stated [to occur] even through general inclusion (*prāyasamuccayana*). The word *tat* refers to *bāhulaka* (the principle of diversity).

It is referred to as follows: *prāya-samuccayanam* means the collection, inclusion, or prescription of those *uṇādi* suffixes for the most part (*prāyeṇa*), that is, in their majority. The compound is formed by the split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "the third case" (*tṛtīyā*, Pāṇini 2.1.30). The word *api* is used in the sense of conjunction; it implies that it is not only... [but also].
It is not because the *prakṛtis* (bases) are few that the term *bāhulaka* (variety/diversity) is stated; rather, it is said because of their frequent aggregation (*prāyasamuccayāt*).
Not only are the *prakṛtis* recited as being few, but the *pratyayas* (suffixes) are also mostly aggregated, though not all; for that purpose, the term *bāhulaka* is used.
If those suffixes are prescribed by being inferred even when separated by other elements due to the rule of "bāhulaka" (diversity of application), then for instance,

although the verbal root *ṛ* is listed [in the Dhātupāṭha] in the rule "ṛteḥ kyurucca" (Paṇini 3.2.172), the suffixes *phiṭ* and *phiḍḍa* are not explicitly prescribed there; nevertheless, the words *ṛphiḍa* and *ṛphiḍḍa* are observed in usage.
And those two are also prescribed.
Regarding the phrase "and because of the injunction with a remainder of the task," the word *ca* (and) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Because of these two previously mentioned reasons, that abundance [of usage] has been stated. *Vidhi* means the act of prescribing (*vidhāna*).

The reason is as follows: a rule (*vidhi*) that operates along with a remainder (*śeṣa*) is "with remainder" (*saśeṣa*); that which is both with remainder and a rule is a "rule with remainder" (*saśeṣavidhi*). The "rule with remainder regarding grammatical operations" (*kāryasaśeṣavidhi*) refers to such rules. And because of this, the term *bāhulaka* ("generally") has been stated. This is what is meant: [the suffixes] depend upon the base (*prakṛti*).

Not all grammatical operations have been demonstrated in the *Pañcapādī*; moreover, those not explicitly shown are nevertheless intended [to apply]. Therefore, for the sake of establishing them, the term "bāhulaka" (variety/diversity) has been stated therein. By means of that, the prohibition of *guṇa* substitution is established in cases such as *ṛphiḍa* and *ṛphiḍḍa*. Such is the case, first of all.

An effect dependent upon conditions becomes established. From the root *ṣaṇu* in the sense of "giving" (*dāne*, DhP 1464), the form *ṣaṇḍaḥ* is derived by the rule *ñamantāḍḍaḥ* (Paṅgi Uṇādi Sūtra 1.113). Here, the substitution of *s* for *ṣ*—as prescribed by the rule *dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.64)—does not take place. Or, even if that substitution of *s* were to occur, the substitution of *ṣ* is applied once again.

Thus, even grammatical operations that depend on the *prakṛti* (base) occur by virtue of *bāhulaka* (generalization). "That which arises from *naigama* and *rūḍhi* is indeed very correct. Here, *nigama* means the Veda (*chandas*); those occurring therein are *naigama*. The suffix *aṇ* is applied because they are recited in the *Ṛgveda* and other collections. Or, these belong to the *nigama*, hence they are *naigama*. *Rūḍhi* (conventional usage)... [text ends]

"Established" (*prasiddhi*); "beings" (*bhavāḥ*) are those that exist, established beings. The compound is formed by the split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "the locative case" (*saptamī*, Pāṇini 2.1.40). The meaning is "well-known in the world.
"Naigama" and "rūḍhibhava" form the compound *naigamarūḍhibhavam*. [This is justified by the rule: "Every *dvandva* compound may optionally be treated as a singular. (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 91).
Thus, there is a singular formation (*ekavadbhāva*), and by the rule *sa napuṃsakam* (Pāṇini 2.4.17), it takes the neuter gender.

The word *hi* has the sense of "because. Because this very term *bahulaka* (the suffix -la added to *bahu*) is the means for establishing multiple meanings, therefore that which arises from conventional usage (*rūḍhi*)—namely, the Vedic form—is perfectly correct; this is due to the inclusion of the term *bahula* in grammar.
Because it is a refined (saṃskṛta) word; otherwise, due to its being unrefined (asaṃskṛta), it would be considered incorrect (asādhutva), like words such as *agauḥ* and so forth.
Furthermore, other authoritative persons have also accepted that words arising from common usage (*naigama*) and conventional convention (*rūḍhi*) are to be explained.
To demonstrate this, he says: "And a name is born from a root," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in the Nirukta":
in the treatise known as the *Nirukta*. Regarding the word "name" (*nāma*): it refers to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), for this is another technical term for it used by the Teacher.
It is called "born from a root" (*dhātujam*) because it has arisen from a verbal root (*dhātu*). The mention of the "root" is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).

The suffixes (*pratyaya*), augments (*āgama*), and so forth are also included. The author of the *Nirukta* stated in his own treatise, the *Nirukta*, that a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is derived from a verbal root (*dhātu*); this is because it is etymologically analyzed through the division of roots, suffixes, and so on. The word "and" (*ca*) is used for emphasis and is displaced in its position; thus, it means "only derived from a verbal root."
This should be observed. Śākaṭāyana, the son of Śakaṭa, also maintains that names are derived solely from verbal roots (*dhātu*).

Thus, according to the view of the author of the *Nirukta* and Śākaṭāyana, there are three modes of application for words—namely, genus-words (*jātiśabda*), quality-words (*guṇaśabda*), and action-words (*kriyāśabda*)—and no such thing as arbitrary words (*yadṛcchāśabda*).
Alternatively—words denoting genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*) are also nothing but action-words (*kriyāśabda*), because they are derived from verbal roots (*dhātu*).
Consequently, there is only one mode of application for words: namely, that they are "action-words.
Now, if [a word] has not been etymologically derived by taking up a specific base (*prakṛti*) and a specific suffix (*pratyaya*), [it is still an action-word].

Regarding the form of the word: how is its derivation from a verbal root (*dhātujatva*) to be understood? For it is not possible to ascertain that something is derived from a root without determining the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*).
To this he says: "That which," and so forth. The word *artha* denotes purpose; thus, it means "that whose ultimate purpose is the supreme reality" (*paramārtha*).

That [word] has its meaning in the stem (*prakṛti*) and so forth. But how does the word come to have its meaning in the stem and so forth? Because they are employed with reference to it. For the stem and so forth are employed for the purpose of explaining the word. Why? Because the meaning of the word consists of both the stem and the suffix. Of that...

*Viśeṣa* means a particular category of things (*padārthaviśeṣa*). *Samutthāna* means arising (*samuttha*), that is, manifestation (*prādurbhāva*). According to the rule *supi sthaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.4), by means of a split in the yoga (*yogavibhāga*), the suffix *kap* is applied here specifically to denote the state of being (*bhāva*). That [knowledge] whose manifestation arises from a particular category of things is what is meant.

That which arises from a specific category of word-meanings— if a form of a word is not of such a kind, it must be inferred both from its suffix and from its base. It is also stated by virtue of being derived from a verbal root— that for which the completion [of its formation] is not achieved through specific bases and suffixes mentioned as individual rules.

"The status of being derived from a verbal root (*dhātujatva*) is to be ascertained through the specific nature of the base (*prakṛti*) and the specific nature of the suffix (*pratyaya*). Now, one might object: "But surely, because such specific bases and suffixes are not recognized, it is impossible to ascertain that something is derived from a verbal root. Anticipating this, the opponent has raised the objection; how then [can it be known] by means of the suffix?

Is it not reasonable that what was stated regarding the base (*prakṛti*) should also be inferred for the suffix (*pratyaya*)? This is not a fault; for by saying this, he has effectively stated that first the base and the suffix must be inferred in this manner, and consequently, by implication, that the form of the word arises from those two. For [the form] does not arise from those two when they have not been determined.

What is unreasonable here [in the claim] that it is possible to determine the verbal origin (*dhātujatva*) of something by means of both a base (*prakṛti*) and an affix (*pratyaya*)? For where there is the apprehension of similarity between a certain part [of a word] and another word consisting of a well-known affixal element, one perceives the affix therein.

The remaining portion should be conceived as the *prakṛti* (base). For example, the word "oṣṭha" and others ending in the suffix *than*—as in the rule *uṣikuṣigartibhyasthan* (Pāṇini 5.2.107)—are well-known instances where a suffix is a constituent part; and by means of that [suffix], there is some [connection] with the words *ḍittha* and *vittha*.

There is similarity; for just as in those [other words], so too in these, the phoneme *tha* exists as a constituent part residing in a specific location. In that regard, because of the similarity with the phoneme *tha*—which is designated as a suffix (*pratyaya*)—that is observed in the word-form ending in the suffix *than*, one [perceives] the phoneme *tha* residing in the words *ḍittha* and *ḍavittha*.

Having determined the [specific] condition (*pratyaya*), the remaining portion of those two should then be inferred as a verbal root (*dhātu*) according to the rule *ḍiḍḍavid*. Consequently, the sūtra should be formulated thus:
*ḍīṅ sthaṇ ḍiḍḍvic ca*. From the root *ḍīṅ* [meaning] "to fly" or "to go" (DhP 1135)...
The suffix *than*, as well as the roots *ḍīṅ* and *ḍīḍvid*, undergo the substitutions *ḍit* and *ḍid*. However,

where in a word-form there is some degree of similarity in a particular part with another word whose verbal root-component is already known, one should identify the base (*prakṛti*) and [treat] the remaining portion [as the suffix].
It should be understood as a condition (*pratyaya*), as follows: the form *ṛta* is seen as a well-known constituent of a base (*prakṛti*) in the word-form *śabda*;
by means of that, there exists a certain partial similarity between the word *ṛphiḍa* and the word *ṛphiḍḍa*, because both of them begin with the vowel *u*. In that regard—

In the word *ṛta*, which ends in a suffix (*niṣṭhā-pratyaya*), the element consisting of the vowel *ṛ* is designated as a verbal root (*dhātu*) due to its similarity [to actual roots]. By extension, one should likewise determine that the *ṛ*-vowel in the words *ṛphiḍa* and *ṛphiḍḍa* is a verbal root;
consequently, the remaining portions of those two words, namely *phiḍa* and *phiḍḍa*, should be inferred to be suffixes (*pratyaya*).

And thus the sūtra should be formulated as: "phiḍa and phiḍḍa [are the suffixes] after the root *ṛ*. From the root *ṛ* meaning "to go" (DhP 1098), the suffixes *phiḍa* and *phiḍḍa* occur. Thus we have *ṛphiḍaḥ* and *ṛphiḍḍaḥ*. Guṇa does not occur because of the reasons previously stated. Alternatively—

These two notions alone are to be established: having thus inferred [the existence of] a base (prakṛti) and an affix (pratyaya), one must infer that the form of that word is derived from a verbal root (dhātu). That which conforms to the specific components of the base and the affix does not deviate from being derived from a verbal root.

For example—words such as "kartavyam" (to be done) and "karaṇīyam" (to be performed). Regarding the term "ūhyam" (to be inferred): it means that which is to be authorized. It is not the case that inference is to be made anywhere at all; rather, it must be made only in a specific context.

Showing this, he says: "In the case of technical names" (*saṃjñāsu*), and so forth. Those word-forms which are established as being correct (*sādhutvena nirūḍhāḥ*), in those alone should the addition of a technical name (*saṃjñātaddhita*) be made, and not elsewhere. Regarding "the forms of verbal roots" (*dhāturūpāṇi*), the words "are to be supplied" (*kalpayitavyāni*) are to be understood as the ellipsis. And "the suffixes follow after them."
Thus [the sense is]: "they are to be classified"—this is the ellipsis. From the "effect," that is, from the presence or absence of a suffixal marker (guṇa) and so forth;

one "should know" (vidyāt), i.e., one should understand; the "suffixal marker" (anubandha), such as the letter *k* and others; this refers to the "treatise" (*śāstra*) concerning the *uṇādi* suffixes mentioned immediately above, because it is based upon a treatise or because its subject matter is the treatise.
It has been stated that this is a technical rule (*śāstra*).

If, then, in this sūtra the terms "in the sense of a name" (*saṃjñāyām*, 3.2.185) and "in the present tense" (*vartamāne*, 3.2.123) are understood as being carried over (*anuvartate*), and the term "diversely" (*bahulam*) is also applied, then...

For what purpose is the mention of "present time" (*vartamāna*) in the rule *pṛṣadvṛhajjagacchatṛvacca* (Dhātupāṭha 6.5)? And for what purpose is the mention of "proper name" (*saṃjñā*) in the rule *dhṛṣerdhiṣa ca saṃjñāyām* (Dhātupāṭha 5.27), as well as the mention of "diversely elsewhere" (*bahulam anyatrāpi*) in the rule *bahulam anyatrāpi* (Dhātupāṭha 5.23)?

Why is it formulated? It is for the purpose of removing the doubt that, because of the rule "it is also seen in the past tense" (3.3.2), words such as *pṛṣat* and others might apply even to the past; [the present tense marker] *vartamāna* is included to firmly establish that only the technical term (*saṃjñā*) under discussion is being continued [from the previous rule]. The re-formulation of the technical term is...

Or [the term "bahulam" is used] to dispel the doubt that [the operation] might occur even in cases where there is no notion (asaṃjñā). The repetition of the word "bahulam" is for the purpose of recalling this very same "bahulam"; for in this way, assistance is rendered to those of forgetful nature.

"2.bhūte'pi dṛśyante | (3.3.2)" [The rule] "pūrvatra vartamānāt" [is understood]. Now, why was the mention of "vartamānāt" ("occurring in what precedes") not omitted? Indeed, it would have been proper to omit it there; for instance—in that case—tasmiṃstatra...

If [the rule] has ceased, should this not be performed? This is not so; it must necessarily be performed, because some [grammarians] maintain that [the suffixes] apply even to what has already occurred (*bhūta*). Furthermore, if the recurrence of the mention of the "present" (*vartamāna*) from the preceding rule did not exist here, then the *uṇādi* suffixes would not apply even to the future.

Regarding the rule *bhaviṣyati gamyādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.3), one might understand it as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) meaning that "gamyādayaḥ" occur only in the future tense. Therefore, the mention of the present tense (*vartamāna*) must be carried over from the preceding rule. [The word] *vartma* [is derived] by [the rule] *āto manin* (Pāṇini 3.2.74).

While this [rule] continues to apply, the suffix *manin* is added by the rule "it is seen after others as well" (Pāṇini 3.2.75). There is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule "there is no *iṭ* before a *kṛt* suffix beginning with *vaś*" (Pāṇini 7.2.8). Thus, "bhasma.
[The root] *bhas* [is used] in the sense of "threatening" and "shining" (Dhātupāṭha 1100). Regarding the phrase "the mention of *dṛśi*," etc.:

By the inclusion of the term *dṛśi* (is seen), he demonstrates this meaning: following distinguished usage, a suffix should be applied in the sense of the past only where it is employed by the learned (*śiṣṭa*), and not everywhere.

3.bhaviṣyati gamyādayaḥ | (3.3.3) "Only of the suffix" and so forth. For this [is the case]: *gamyādayaḥ* are correct forms in the future tense (*bhaviṣyati*) only if the future time is prescribed for the suffix itself; but if, however...

If the suffix were of a different time [than the action], your [rules] would not be correct; therefore, by this means, the future tense of the suffix itself is prescribed. In the example "grāmaṃ gamī" ("one who will go to the village"), the suffix *ini* is applied by the rule "gameriniḥ" (Daiva 6.57), and the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule "sau" (Pāṇini 6.4.13).

Since the genitive case is prohibited by the rule *ṭhakenorbhaviṣyadādhamarṇyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.70), the accusative case is applied after the word *grāma* according to *karmaṇi dvitīyā* (Pāṇini 2.3.2). Regarding the form *āgāmī*:
while the suffix *ini* is in force by the rule *gameriniḥ* (Daiva-Uṇādi-sūtra 6.57), the suffix *ini* is added by the rule *āṅ iṇit* (Daiva-Uṇādi-sūtra 6.58).

Due to the suffix being marked with *ṇ*, there is *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel. Examples include *prasthāyī* and so forth. From the roots *sthā* (DhP 928) in the sense of "cessation of motion," *budh* (DhP 1172) in the sense of "awakening," *yuj* (DhP 1177) in the sense of "concentration," and *yā* (DhP 1949) in the sense of "going"—from these, [the suffix] *sūc* is applied when a verbal root begins with a consonant (*supyajātau*).

The suffix *ṇini* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.78 (*ṇinistācchīlye*). In the case of the roots *yā* and *sthā*, the augment *yuk* is added by 7.3.33 (*yāta-tiṣṭhatyor ṭhāto yuk ciṇ-kṛtoḥ*). For the root *yuj*, the substitution of *ku* occurs by 7.3.52 (*ca-joḥ ku-ghiṇ-ṇyatoḥ*). Regarding the form "bhāvī," [the suffix] *iṇ* is applied after the prefix *āṅ*.

While [the rule] *vartamāne* (Pāṇini 3.2.123) is in effect, the suffix *ini* is applied by the rule *bhuvaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.179); because the suffix is marked with *ṇ*, there is *vṛddhi* strengthening.
Regarding the statement "an addition for the non-recent past (*anadyatana*)," what is the reason that [the desired form] is not established?
This indication is made using the *lṛṭ* suffix in the sense of "will be" (*bhaviṣyati*), and therefore, it applies only within the domain of the *lṛṭ*.

It would apply to the general future (*bhaviṣyat-sāmānya*), but not to the immediate future (*bhaviṣyad-anadyatana*); therefore, the *luṭ* suffix would not have its proper scope there, because it is superseded by *lṛṭ*. Consequently, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the immediate future. Here, the word "addition" (*upasaṃkhyāna*) means "explanation" (*pratipādana*). In this regard, the explanation is as follows:
The term *bahulam* ("optionally") is understood here; therefore, [the suffixes] will also apply to the non-immediate future (*anadyatana*).

Furthermore, these [roots] such as *gam-* and so on are superseded by both the *luṅ* and *lṛṭ* suffixes, because they are exceptions (*apavāda*). Their status as exceptions follows the principle of "that which was not previously applicable" (*yenāprāptinyāya*). Now, one might object:

By the rule of *vāsarūpa*, the *luṅ* and *lṛṭ* suffixes would also be applicable, because the phrase "in the future tense, *gam* and so forth" (*bhaviṣyati gamyādayaḥ*) is understood to carry over (*anuvṛtti*) into that rule? True; if you argue that even with this carry-over, [the suffixes] apply only optionally (*pakṣe eva*), this is not so; for if that were the case, the carry-over would be purposeless.

4. *yāvatpurānipātayor laṭ* (Pāṇini 3.3.4). In the example *yāvad bhuṅkte*, the ātmanepada ending is applied by the rule *bhujo 'navane* (1.3.66). The elision of the letter *a* [of the suffix *śatṛ*] occurs by the rule *śnasor allopaḥ* (6.4.111).
"He will eat as much as he gives. Since its measure is that [measure], the suffix *vatup* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.39:
*yatadetebhyaḥ parimāṇe vatup*. While the rule *dṛgdṛśavatuṣu* (6.3.89) is in effect, the rule *ā sarvanāmnaḥ* (6.3.91) applies.

Thus [there is] the substitution of *ā*. Regarding the phrase "purā vrajiṣyati": the root *pṛ* is used in the sense of "protecting" and "filling" (Dhātupāṭha 1489). By the rule *bhrājabhās...* (Pāṇini 3.2.177), the suffix *kvip* is applied;
by the rule *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya* (7.1.102), the substitution of *u* occurs; and the third case singular is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*). Now, [an objection]:...
Furthermore, the two particles *yāvat* and *purā* are indeed un-derived (*avyutpanna*), yet they have been derived [by others];

since they will be included by the very paribhāṣā "that which is taught as a technical term (*lakṣaṇa*) or taught as a word-form (*pratipadoka*)" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 3), for what purpose is the mention of "particle" (*nipāta*) made?

Some say it is for the sake of removing the sense of obligation toward the practice for those of dull intellect; others say it is for the purpose of making known that this technical rule (paribhāṣā) is not universally obligatory (anitya). The purpose of making known its non-obligatory nature, however, will be explained later.

5. *vibhāṣā kadā-kahyoḥ* (3.3.5). Example: *kadā bhoktā* ("when will he eat?"). [This is] the periphrastic future (*luṭ*). Now, one might object: since the word "future" (*bhaviṣyati*) is understood [from the previous rule], this should apply only to the scope of the simple future (*lṛṭ*), not to the periphrastic future (*luṭ*). Therefore, it would be more appropriate to cite the simple future (*lṛṭ*) as the alternative option.

How then is *luṭ* cited [as an example]? He thinks as follows: because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "optionally when *kadā* or *karhi*" from the sūtra "the conditional suffix *luṭ* is used for non-today time" (Pāṇini 3.3.15), there should be an option for *luṭ* in the domain of *lṛṭ*. Thus, in the example "When will he eat? (*karhi bhokṣyate*), *lṛṭ* is used. But surely the word *karhi*—?

The suffix *rhil* is prescribed by the rule *ṭhanadyatane rhil anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.3.21) for times other than the immediate past (*anadyatana*). Therefore, wherever this suffix is employed, the time [indicated] must be as if it were non-immediate past. Consequently, how could there be the application of *lṛṭ*?
By the rule *anadyatane luṭ* (Pāṇini 3.3.15), it should rather be *luṭ* optionally in that case.

This is not so; for the word *bhokṣyate* (he will eat) occurs only in reference to the future time. The understanding of the non-remote past (*anadyatana*) arises from the sentence when the word *karhi* (when) is present. And the *lṛṭ* suffix is not used for a meaning conveyed by the sentence. For in this case, it is the individual word that is being grammatically formed (*saṃskriyate*), and not [the sentence].

In the refinement of words (*padasaṃskāra*), the meaning conveyed by the sentence (*vākya*) is what is employed. Therefore, when a general future tense is intended to be expressed, the suffix *lṛṭ* occurs; and when a specific future not belonging to the current day is intended to be expressed, the suffix *luṅ* occurs.

6. *Kiṃvṛtte lipsāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.6). [The commentary begins with] *kimo vṛtam* and so forth. He asks: what, then, is the *vṛta* (usage/occurrence) of *kim*? He says: by the mention of *vṛta*, and so forth. By the word *tat* (that), the word *kim* is connected; that is, this form of the word *kim*.
One should understand that the inclusion of the word *vṛta* implies [the presence of] a case-ending (*vibhaktyanta*). Furthermore, the two suffixes *ḍatara* and *ḍatama*—

namely, *ḍatarac* [as in] "of two, one [is selected] by means of *kim*, *yad*, or *tad* in the sense of selection" (Pāṇini 5.3.92), and *ḍatamac* [as in] "or *ḍatamac* when asking about one among many regarding a genus" (Pāṇini 5.3.93)— are these two suffixes.

It should be understood that by the mention of *vṛt*, only those [suffixes] connected with the word *kim* are perceived; and by the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa*), only those ending in *ḍatara* and *ḍatama* are perceived here—this is the meaning to be known.
Regarding the phrase "restriction" (*parisaṃkhyāna*), it means a rule (*niyama*). By this, [the forms] *kiṃtarām* and *kiṃgauḥ* [are excluded].

In words such as *kiṃpuruṣaḥ* and the like, [the substitution] does not occur; for those have been excluded by the enumeration of the items beginning with *kim*. In *bhojayanti*, the suffix *laṭ* follows the causative form (*ṇic*) of the root *bhuj*. In *bhojayitāraḥ*, the suffix *jhi* is replaced by *āra* according to Pāṇini 2.4.85: *luṭaḥ prathamasya ḍāraurasaḥ*.

There is the substitution of *ras* [for *ra*], and by the rule "ṭhri ca" (Pāṇini 7.4.51), there is the elision of the letter *s*. [The phrase] "one who desires to obtain asks" is used because, in the examples, the desire to acquire (*lipsā*) is understood.

7. And [the suffix *liṅ* is used] when there is the accomplishment of what is desired to be obtained (*lipsyamāna-siddhi*). (3.3.7) This occurs only when there is a desire to obtain (*lipsā*), not when it is absent.
Therefore, wherever the accomplishment of what is desired to be obtained is understood, there must necessarily be a desire to obtain; and thus:
Since [the desired form] is already established by the preceding rule alone, for what purpose is this new undertaking? To this he says:

"This undertaking is for the sake of the sense of *kiṃvṛta* (interrogative particles). If that is so, why not simply prescribe the suffix in the previous rule itself without employing the term *kiṃvṛta*, so that this present rule would not need to be commenced at all?

This is not so; for just as when the attainment of what is desired is being understood, there occurs both that which is expressed by an interrogative pronoun (kiṃvṛta) and that which is not so expressed (akiṃvṛta), so too it would occur even where the desired object to be attained is devoid of the attainment of what is desired. Yet, in that case, it is accepted that it must be expressed by an interrogative pronoun (kiṃvṛta) alone; therefore—

In the previous rule (*pūrvayoga*), the inclusion of the term *kiṃvṛta* (interrogative pronouns) must be made. And since that is so, this [present] rule for *akiṃvṛta* (non-interrogative pronouns) must also be commenced: "he encourages the giver" (*dātāraṃ protsāhayati*).
The meaning is: he generates encouragement in him regarding the giving of food (*bhakta*).
8. *loḍarthalakṣaṇe ca* (3.3.8).

By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the rule *praiṣādi*, injunction (*vidhi*), invitation (*nimantraṇa*), entreaty (*āmantraṇa*), request (*adhīṣṭa*), and so forth are understood. In the example *āgacchati*, the substitution of *cch* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.3.77]: *iṣugamiyamāṃ cchaḥ*.

Regarding the term *adhyayanapraiṣa*: "adhyayanapraiṣa" is a compound meaning "an injunction (*praiṣa*) concerning study (*adhyayana*)," formed as a *madhyamapadalopa* (elision of the middle member) compound according to the *śākapārthiva*-type group. For example: "Now, you must study the Veda (*chandas*).

Here, the suffix *loṭ* is used according to Pāṇini 3.3.163: "The suffixes *kṛtya* and *loṭ* are used after a root when expressing an injunction (*praiṣa*), a permission (*atisarga*), or that the time has arrived (*prāptakāla*). That [suffix is used].

And the injunction (*praiṣa*) has study as its object; for, depending upon the arrival of the teacher, the injunction "one should study" establishes the arrival of the teacher as the causal condition (*nimittabhāva*) for that injunction.
9. *Liṅ* is used [to express] that which occurs after a *muhūrta*.

(Pāṇini 3.3.9) "The compound is formed by means of a *nipātana*," and so forth. The term *ūrdhvamauhūrtika* is established through a *nipātana* even at the very moment of its utterance. Having analyzed the compound as *ūrdhvam muhūrtāt*, it is established precisely because of this *nipātana*.
This is a compound. Then, by the rule *bahvaco'ntodātāt* (Pāṇini 4.3.67), the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied;

consequently, there is vṛddhi of the penultimate syllable (*ut-tarapada-vṛddhi*), for that indeed occurs precisely because of this specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*). Since "that which is to be" (*bhaviṣyat*) is the subject under discussion, it is understood that the term *ūrdhvamauhūrtika* serves as its qualifier; thus he says:
"And this will be for one who is about to be," and so forth. This word *ūrdhvamauhūrtika* refers to what is proximate to the present; the meaning is "in that which is near the present moment.
[Regarding the form] *āgacchet*: there is the suffix *yāsuṭ*, and by the rule *ato yeyaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.80), there is the substitution of *iy*.
By the rules "ṭhādguṇaḥ" (6.1.87) and "lopo vyorvali" (6.1.66), there is the elision of the letter *y*; by the rule "salopo'nantyasya" (7.2.79), there is the elision of the letter *s*.
10. *tumun* and *ṇvul* are used when a verbal action is intended for the sake of another verbal action.
(Pāṇini 3.3.10) "His matted hair [is worn] because he will beg (*bhikṣiṣye*). [Analysis: This is the *lṛṭ* (future) suffix;
because it is *anudāteta*, the *ātmanepada* ending is applied; specifically, the third person singular (*uttamapuruṣaikavacana*). Then *iṭ* is added, followed by the substitution of *e* for *et*.

By the rule *ṭhato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97), there is substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*). Here, the word *jaṭā* is a subordinate term (*upapada*) for the sake of the action of begging (*bhikṣi*), but the word *jaṭā* itself does not denote an action; for matted locks (*jaṭā*) are substances (*dravya*). [The example is:
"As you run, the staff will fall. [The root] *dhāv* [is used in the sense of] "motion and purification" (Dhātupāṭha 601).

The suffix *laṭ* takes the substitute *śatṛ*, [forming] the sixth case singular. Alternatively, for the root *sṛ* "to go" (*dhā.pā.* 935), there is the substitute *dhāv* by the rule *prāghrādisūtra* (Pāṇini 7.3.78). Here, the action of running (*dhāvati*) is a subordinate element (*upapada*), but it is not for the sake of the action [of the main verb]. For this word *artha*—

The term "purpose" (*prayojana*) refers to that which one acts for; whatever one proceeds toward becomes its purpose. This person does not run toward the falling of the staff; rather, he runs for the sake of some other task. The objection beginning with "Now," etc., [is raised]. [The response is: "It is indeed prescribed in a general sense," and it will apply elsewhere as well.

Because [the suffix] is prescribed without distinction both when the word expressing the purpose of the action (*kriyārtha*) is present as a subordinate element (*upapada*) at the proper time (*kāle*), and otherwise; therefore, the phrase "by *lṛṭ*" and so forth is the solution. He will state "*lṛṭ śeṣe ca*" (Pāṇini 3.3.13), which prescribes *lṛṭ*; thus, it is superseded by that *lṛṭ* which is specifically prescribed. Let there not be the supersession of that [other rule].
Furthermore, it is prescribed here [by Pāṇini 3.3.10]: "Now, the suffix *tumun* is superseded by [the rule for] a word ending in a verbal root used in the sense of another action.
Why was this not stated in the *Kṣamā*? Because their meanings are different. Indeed, there can be no relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) between two things of different meanings;
and the suffixes *ṇvul* and *tumun* have different meanings. For instance: *ṇvul* [denotes] the agent (*kartṛ*), whereas *tumun* [denotes] the action.

Regarding rebirth: how is this known? From the inclusion of the term *tum-artha* in the rule *tum-arthe seseṇa* (Pāṇini 3.4.9). If *tumun* were restricted to the agent by the statement *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67), then *seṣen* and the others would likewise apply only to that [agent].
If [the suffix] were to occur in the sense of "will be," one would not have included the mention of the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*); yet he has included it.

Therefore, from the inclusion of the sense of *tumun*, it is understood that [the suffix] does not occur when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed. Furthermore, no other meaning is specified; in that case, "suffixes whose meaning is not specified [occur] in their own primary sense" (*anirdiṣṭārthāḥ pratyayāḥ svārthe*).
In the statement "bhavanti" (Puṣpabhūti 90), it is understood that the suffix *tumun* occurs only when there is a sense of becoming (*bhāva*).

As for what was said— that [the suffix *tumun*] is superseded by the future suffix *lṛṭ* when accompanied by a word expressing a purposeful action— he says "by the rule of dissimilarity" (*vāsarūpavidhinā*) and so forth, beginning with "if that is so" (*evaṃ tarhi*), in order to demonstrate its status as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

He explains the prescription of the suffix *ṇvul*: for if, when a verbal root meaning an action is the *upapada* [of another action], the suffixes *tṛc* and so on were to apply by the rule of "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpa*), then *ṇvul* would also apply by that same rule of non-identity of form because it expresses the same meaning as *tṛc*; therefore, that is not the case here.

He would have prescribed [the suffix], and indeed he has prescribed it; therefore, by this prescription of the suffix *ṇvul*, it is made known that in this context, by the rule of non-identity of form (*vāsarūpa*), the suffixes *tṛc* and others do not occur. With the words "by that" and so forth, he shows the purpose of this indication. The word "agent" (*kartā*) is formed with the suffix *tṛc*.

Regarding the word *vikṣipaḥ*: [it is derived] by Pāṇini 3.1.135, *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ*. The letter *n* in the suffix *tumun* is for the purpose of making the initial syllable acute (*ādyaudātārtha*), while the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). In the suffix *ṇvul*, the letter *l* is for the purpose of making the vowel preceding the suffix acute (*lit-pratyayāt-pūrvasya-udātārtha*), and the letter *ṇ* is for the purpose of causing *vṛddhi* (guṇa-increment).

11. *bhāvavacanāśca* (3.3.11). Regarding the term *bhāvavacanāḥ*: they are called *vacanāḥ* because they express (*bruvanti*), the suffix *lyuṭ* being used in the sense of the agent due to the presence of the term *bahulam*. Thus, *bhāvavacanāḥ* means "those which express an action" (*bhāva*). Furthermore, their status as "expressing an action" is established within the section governing *bhāva* (Pāṇini 3.3.18).

In order to demonstrate that [the suffixes] are prescribed by rule, he says: "having introduced [the topic] with 'in the sense of a state' (bhāve),' etc. The meaning of "prakṛtya" is "having made the subject matter" (adhikṛtya). "Ghañ-ādayaḥ" (beginning with ghañ)—by the word "ādi" (etcetera), the inclusion of ajap and other such suffixes is intended.
"For what purpose? and so forth is the objection. "By that which is prescribed when there is an accompanying word denoting the purpose of an action," etc.
The rebuttal: It might be argued that those [suffixes] will occur by virtue of the rule *vāsarūpa* (P.

3.1.94). To this he says: "And it has been stated that the rule *vāsarūpa* does not apply here. This was stated in the preceding sūtra. Regarding the words "Now," etc.: only "bhāve" (in the sense of being) need be stated; for if it were stated in this way, then this very [sūtra]—

[Otherwise] it would be a rule prescribing *ghañ* and other suffixes, and consequently, they would apply without distinction to every verbal root (*dhātu*), because no specific restriction has been stated. By the inclusion of the term "vacana" (expression), this meaning is obtained:
those suffixes which are prescribed in the sense of "being" (*bhāva*) function in such a way that they express the "being."

"They come to be. To demonstrate how they become denoters of an entity, he says "And how," etc., preceded by a question. Regarding the phrase "by way of consistency with the name": the meaning is not by way of exclusion (vyatireka), nor by way of lack of restriction (aniyama).

Regarding this, some say: "By those very prescriptive sentences through which their existence is established by the mention of words, they come to be [used] when there is a verbal root as an upapada for the sake of another action; thus they become denoters, and not otherwise. Others, however, say: "This very sūtra is the prescriptive rule."

Because of the force of the mention of the word "vacana" (injunction). By this [word] as well, their prescription occurs in the same way as by their own injunctive sentences. For if that prescription were for the sake of the action itself (*bhāva*), it would not apply to any other object; therefore, it is prescribed again.

12. *aṇ* [is used] also after [roots ending in] a vowel when there is an object (*karmaṇi*). (3.3.12) This refers to rules such as *karmaṇyaṇ*. This has been made known by the rule *tumun-ṇvul-au* (3.3.10): that here the rule regarding alternative forms (*vā-sarūpa-vidhi*) does not apply. Therefore, even though...

Although [the suffix] *ṇin* is prescribed by the rule of qualification (*viśeṣaṇena*), nevertheless, because there is no application of the rule regarding "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*), it is not sublated by *ṇvul* when the accompanying word (*upapada*) has the sense of an action; therefore, it is prescribed once again.
[The statement] "because it is an exception (*apavāda*), it sublates *ṇvul*" applies only when *ṇvul* would otherwise have applied.

Because the suffix *ṇvul* has already commenced [its application] elsewhere, and because it is prescribed as a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*). Regarding the phrase "kādīn" (beginning with *ka*): it is to be connected with the verb "bādhate" (it subverts). By the word "ādi" (etcetera), the inclusion of *ṭak* and others is intended.
The statement "therefore it occurs even in the domain of exceptions" refers to the exceptions (*apavāda*) to the general suffix *aṇ*.

The suffixes beginning with *ka* also occur in that domain. Regarding the rule "ṭhaṇ karmaṇi ca" (Pāṇini 3.2.12), its scope is when the verb has a non-*ā*-ending action as its upapada, as in "kāṇṭalāvo vrajati" (he goes as one who cuts grass).
Regarding the rule "āto 'nupasarge kaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.3), its scope is when the action has an *ā*-ending [word] as its upapada.

—*godā* (one who gives cows). For here both [suffixes] would apply: *godāya vrajati* ("the cow-giver goes"). Because of its higher status, the suffix *aṇ* occurs. Likewise, the scope of *ṭh gha poṣṭak* (Pāṇini 3.2.8)—as in *surāpaḥ*, *śīdhupaḥ*—is the same as that of *aṇ*. Here both would apply: *surāpāya vrajati*, *śīdhupāya vrajati*.
It goes.

13. *lṛṭ* [is used] also in the remaining cases. (3.3.13) Regarding the phrase "and because of the word *ca*" (*cakārāt*), etc.: by this, he shows that the word *ca* is for the purpose of drawing back (*anukarṣaṇa*) the rule "when one action is for the sake of another action" (*kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām*). [Example: *kariṣyāmi*.
Thus; [the augment] *iṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.2.70]: "After [a root ending in] *ṛt* or *an*, [the augment *iṭ* is added] before *sya*."

14. *lṛṭaḥ sad vā* (Pāṇini 3.3.14). Regarding the term "those called *sat*": because they are prescribed by the technical rule *tau sat* (3.2.127), the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* bear the designation *sat*. But how can *śatṛ* and *śānac* occur after the future tense marker *lṛṭ*? To this he says:

Regarding the rule *aprathamāsamānādhikaraṇe* and so forth: just as the *śatṛ* and *śānac* suffixes are optionally applied to the present tense (*laṭ*) when not in grammatical coreferentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇa*) with a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamā*), so too do the suffixes designated as *sat* (participles) apply to the future tense (*lṛṭ*) by way of a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). However, in cases where they are not in coreferentiality with a nominative case, and so on, they apply invariably.
"Behold one who will do," "behold one who will be done"; O you who will do, O you who will be done;
"he dwells intending to acquire"; "devotion to one who will do," "devotion to one who will be done";

"having the form of one who will do," "having the form of one who will be done"—these examples apply when there is no coreferentiality with a word in the nominative case (*aprathamā-samānādhikaraṇe*).
But when there is no coreferentiality with the first case ending (*prathamā-asamānādhikaraṇe*), there is an option: *kariṣyati devadattaḥ* or *kariṣyan devadattaḥ*;

*kariṣyate devadattaḥ* or *kariṣyamāṇo devadattaḥ*. While the term *lṛṭ* was already in force, the repetition of *lṛṭ* here is for the purpose of specifying the substituend (*sthāninirdeśārtham*); otherwise, indeed—

The status of being a distinct condition (*pratyayāntaratva*) would be understood for those [suffixes] designated as *sat*. Or rather, it is for the purpose that it should apply to the mere *lṛt* suffix. By this, it also applies to that *lṛṭ* which occurs in the non-today (*anadyatana*) time—as in "by one who will establish the sacred fires tomorrow" (*śvo'gnīnādhāsyamānena*). However, it does not apply to the rule "the *lṛṭ* is used when there is a statement of recognition" (*abhijñāvacane lṛṭ*, 3.2.112).

[The form] *bhavataḥ* [is derived from the root *bhū*]; this is because of the governing rule [Pāṇini 3.3.15], and because this [suffix] is prescribed for the future tense.
