Furthermore, it should be understood that [the suffix] *lṛṭ* occurs even in the sense of "not today" (*anadyatana*) due to the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) in the sūtra *lṛṅśca* (Pāṇini 3.3.13), which includes the term *anadyatana*. The letter *ṭ* in *lṛṭ* is for the purpose of [triggering] the substitution of *et* [for the final vowel and following consonant of the suffix]; the letter *ṛ* is for the purpose of [including it in] the rule *syatāsī lṛluṭoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.33).
In this context, [the term] has the sense of a specific distinction.

15. *luṭ* [is used] for the non-today (*anadyatana*) [time]. (Pāṇini 3.3.15). The term *anadyatana* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; that is, "that which does not have its occurrence today" is *anadyatana*. By the rule beginning with *tena*, there is recourse to the *bahuvrīhi* compound.

It demonstrates the result. This has been largely explained under the rule *ṭhanadyatane laṅ* (3.2.111), so it should be understood from that very source. Regarding the example "He will go today or tomorrow" (*adya śvo vā gamiṣyati*), the meaning is "He will go both today and tomorrow."

Regarding "ṭhparidevane" and so forth: the *luṅ* suffix, which is prescribed for the future not of today (*bhaviṣyadanadyatana*), does not apply to the general future (*bhaviṣyatsāmānya*), yet it is desired there; for this purpose, the following is stated. "Paridevana" means lamentation or sorrowful grieving. "Śvastanī" is another technical term (*saṃjñā*) for the *luṭ* suffix used by other teachers. "Vaktavyā" means it should be stated [as such].

This must be explained. Here is the explanation: from the rule *lṛṭ śeṣe ca* (3.3.13), the word *ca* ("and") is understood by anuvṛtti; it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. Consequently, in the sense of lamentation (*paridevana*), the *śvastanī* (future-in-the-past) occurs in the sense of the future (*bhaviṣyat*). But this [particle] *nu*—when?

Demonstrating that the *luṅ* suffix occurs only in the sense of non-today (*anadyatana*) time in cases such as "gantā" (he will go), he says: [This applies] in the grammatical treatise (*padam anvākhyāne vyākaraṇe ca*). And that word, such as "gantā" and so forth, refers only to non-today time.
When its application pertains to non-today or to general future time, it is determined by the sense or the context.

The meaning of the sentence remains as "it comes to be. Furthermore, the meaning of the sentence is not the cause for the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the word; rather, it is the meaning of the word itself. Therefore, the rule "the *luṅ* [suffix] is used for what is not of today" is established.
By this same principle, the statement that the *śvastanī* [future tense suffix] is used in lamentation (*paridevana*), and so forth, is correct. This also applies to the *luṭ* [periphrastic future].

The letter *ṭ* is for the purpose of [indicating] the substitution of *ṛt* by *et*; the letter *u* is for the purpose of qualifying [the rule] "for the first of *ṭhluṭ*, there are *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras*" (Pāṇini 7.1.85).
16. *ghañ* is prescribed after the roots *pad*, *ruj*, *viś*, and *spṛś*.

(Pāṇini 3.3.16) The suffix *ghañ* is ordained as an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṇvuṭ* and *tṛc* after the root *pad*; it is an exception to *ka*—which would otherwise be applied by the rule regarding roots with *i* as an upadhā—after *ruj* and *viś*; and it is an exception to *ac* (the *pacādi* group) after *spṛś*. Thus, the form is *pādaḥ*.

The vṛddhi [substitution] occurs by the rule "ṭhata upadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.116). If this is so, would it not follow that the form *padam* is not established? It is certainly not the case that it is not established, because of the nipātana (irregularity) stated in "anudātaṃ padamekavarjam" (Pāṇini 6.1.158).

"It should be stated that *ṣpṛś* [is used] in the sense of 'affliction' (*upatāpa*). The meaning is that this must be explained as having the sense: "the suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *spṛś* when affliction—that is, disease—is present. Regarding this, the explanation is as follows: the word "optionally" (*vā*) from the rule *lṛṭaḥ sadvā* (Pāṇini 3.3.14) is carried over (*anuvartate*), and that...

This is a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (an option that is restricted). Therefore, the suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *spṛś* only when it has the agent (*kartṛ*) as its referent, and not otherwise. "There is a difference regarding the accent (*svara*). For if the suffix *ac* were present, there would be an acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*), whereas with *ghañ*, there would be an acute accent on the first syllable of the word (*ādyudāttatva*). The letter *ñ* in *ghañ* serves both to cause *vṛddhi* and to ensure the initial acute accent.
The letter *gha* is for the purpose of applying the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *gh*) by the rule "ṭhcajoḥ kughiṇṇyatoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.52).

17. *sṛ* [is used] when the agent (*kartṛ*) is stable (*sthira*). (Pāṇini 3.3.17). [The rule begins with] "of the root *sṛ*" (*sarter dhātoḥ*). This refers to the root *sṛ* meaning "to go" (*gatau*, Dhātupāṭha 935). [It continues with] "when the agent is stable" (*sthire kartari*). By this, the mention of "stable" (*sthiragrahaṇam*) is not a qualifier of the agent who is the meaning of the suffix.

He shows that [the word] has an upapada by stating, "the suffix ghañ occurs. This is an exception (apavāda) to the suffixes tṛc and others. He asks, "What, then, is this so-called 'stable' (sthiram)? and replies, "'Stable' means persisting through another time," and so forth. He provides the justification for that very point with, "That [which lasts] for a long time," and so forth. The root *sṛ* has the meaning of "motion" (gati). That...

And this is possible only for an agent who persists through a period of time, not for one who perishes immediately after attaining its own existence. Therefore, it is only an agent who persists through a period of time that is logically fit to be the agent of "going," which is the meaning of the verbal root; it is precisely such an agent who is referred to here by the word "stable" (*sthira*). If...

Motion is possible only for that which persists over a period of time; therefore, the inclusion of the term "stable" (sthira) is redundant, for an unstable entity cannot logically be an agent of motion. This is not redundant, however, because it is intended so that the suffix may apply to an agent who moves with excellence (prakarṣeṇa). For this very reason, he [the agent] is long-lasting...

In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the term "long time" (*ciram*) is employed in the phrase "staying, he traverses another period of time. [The word *candasa*] is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the essence of Vedic meters" (*chandaḥsāraḥ*). Regarding the statement "it should be stated that [the rule applies] to disease, fish, and strength," this introduction is intended for the sake of meanings that are not fixed. In these cases...
The meaning is that this form [of the rule] must be explained as being intended for all three cases, beginning with *vyādhi*.

However, the explanation here should also be made by relying on the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *ca* (and). As in the example "atīsāraḥ," there is lengthening of the vowel according to Pāṇini 6.3.122: *upasargasya ghañyamanuṣye bahulam* ("There is optional lengthening of a vowel in a prefix before a word ending in the suffix *ghañ*, provided it does not refer to a human being").

18. *bhāve* (Pāṇini 3.3.18). [The word] *rāgaḥ* [is formed as follows]: by [the rules] *rañjeśca* (6.4.26) and *ghañi ca bhāvakaraṇayoḥ* (6.4.27), there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*). Now, one might object: this [word *bhāve*] is not [derived] from the root *bhū* with the suffix *ghañ*.
When it is said that "the explanation is being made," the explanation of the meaning of the suffix is made only with reference to the domain of the root *bhū*;

consequently, the suffix would occur only when that which is to be expressed is the state (*bhāva*) of *bhū*, and since that [state] can be denoted by a suffix produced from *bhū* itself, [the suffix] should therefore arise from that very root.
It must be by means of a suffix; how then does [the form] *pāka-*, *tyāga-*, or *rāga-* arise from roots such as *pac*?
To this he says: "denoting action in general," and so forth. For the meaning of the root *bhū* is action in general (*kriyāsāmānya*), which underlies the meanings of all verbal roots. By that—

The intention is that when a definition of meaning (*arthanirdeśa*) is made by means of a term denoting action in general (*kriyāsāmānya*), it pertains to the domain of all verbal roots (*dhātu*); therefore, the suffix occurs even after roots such as *pac* and others. Now, one might object:

the meaning of a root (*dhātvartha*) consists of a sequence of prior and posterior stages and is not yet fully accomplished; therefore, if [the suffix] were to apply there when that meaning is to be expressed...

Since that [suffix] is not a sentient being (asattvabhūta), its connection with gender and number—which are properties of the meaning of a suffix—is not established; therefore, he says: "And the meaning of the verbal root," and so forth. The particle *eva* serves to exclude the suffix.
The meaning of the verbal root is expressed by the verbal root alone, and not by the suffix.

How, then, are the *ghañ* suffixes and others prescribed? To this he says: "Of that," and so forth. Of that meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), there is a property called "accomplishedness" (*siddhatā*) or "perfectedness" (*niṣpannatā*); it is with respect to that [property] that the *ghañ* suffixes and others are prescribed.
Therefore, the connection of the meaning of the suffix with gender and number is logical. Of that [meaning], which...

The meaning is that *dharma* belongs to it because it has become an entity (*satvabhūta*). Regarding the term "bhāva"—this designation is made in the masculine gender and in the singular number. Consequently, suffixes would occur only when the state (*bhāva*) is expressed in the masculine gender and in the singular number; not when it is joined with another gender, nor when it is in another number. And this being the case...

In the rule *ṭhstriyāṃ ktin* (Pāṇini 3.3.94), the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two terms *bhāve* ("in the sense of an action") and *striyām* ("in the feminine") is not tenable; rather, there would have to be a lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). Consequently, the suffix *ktin* would not apply to the sense of an action in the feminine, but would instead apply only to other meanings, such as the object (*karman*) and so forth. And regarding the sense of an action...

In the masculine gender, in the case of *pākau* and *pākāḥ*, there would have to be the singular number. For a nominal stem (*bhāvaśabda*) is capable of denoting a meaning of a certain kind; therefore, it ought to be joined with a suffix expressing that same kind of meaning, and not otherwise. Hence he says: "the masculine gender and the singular number."

And in this regard, it is not the case that [gender and number] are not the governing factors (*tantra*). That which is capable of being connected with all genders and numbers, and which is based on the general meaning of the nominal stem (*prakṛti*), is adopted as the basis for the suffix;
that alone is the primary factor, neither gender nor number. In that context:

Since it is impossible to specify [an object] by means of gender and number without the general meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), their inclusion is due to their being inseparable [from that meaning]. However, once that [general meaning] has been understood,
gender and number have fulfilled their purpose through the general meaning of the nominal stem.

And suffixes indeed occur with other genders as well: *paktiḥ*—this is by *striyāṃ ktin* (Pāṇini 3.3.94) in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). *Pakvam*—this is by *napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.114). *Pacanam*—this is by *lyuṭ ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.115), where *lyuṭ* is applied. Here too, if it is in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*), [the suffix occurs].

The suffix *lyuṭ* would be masculine; consequently, because of the impossibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the [masculine] word and the neuter word "bhāva," there would be a lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). And as a result, the suffix *lyuṭ* would not occur in the neuter sense of "action" (*bhāva*), but rather it would occur only in the sense of another [grammatical category]. Furthermore, regarding the sense of "action":
The presentation of the objection and its resolution is based on the similarity between this case and the masculine form *pacana*;
for otherwise, since the suffix *lyuṭ* is prescribed with reference to a different kind of action (*bhāva*), this would not have been presented here at all. [This applies to] forms such as *pākau*.
In another passage, there is an illustration of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*).

19. *akartari ca kārake saṃjñāyām* | (Pāṇini 3.3.19) The word *prāsaḥ* [is derived as follows]: from the root *asu* in the sense of "throwing" (Dhātupāṭha 1209), with the suffix *ghañ*. The word *prasevaḥ*: from the root *ṣivu* in the sense of "weaving" (Dhātupāṭha 1108). In both cases here, the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). The word *āhāraḥ*: [is derived similarly].

The root *ṛ* in *ṛñ haraṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 899) [is used here]. The term *madhurāhāraḥ* is either a *karmadhāraya* or a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound. Regarding *meṣaḥ*: from the root *miṣ* in *miṣa sparddhāyām* (Dhātupāṭha 1352), with the suffix *ac* added according to the rule for *pacādyac*. It is "to be done" (*kartavyaḥ*).

Thus, [the suffix] *tavya* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). "The letter *ca* is for the purpose of preventing ambiguity regarding the technical name (*saṃjñā*)"—this *ca* is out of its regular order and should be understood immediately after the word *saṃjñāyām*; by that, the meaning of "and" (*ca*) is indicated.

By indicating the meaning of "and" (*ca*) in the rule *saṃjñāyāṃ ca*, this [suffix] serves to prevent deviation from its status as a technical name (*saṃjñā*); therefore, it also occurs even when not a technical name.
If this is so, then one should prescribe the suffix in a general sense without mentioning the word *saṃjñā*; for in that case, too, this is the intended meaning:
Is it not the case that the word "ca" (and) need not be used for the purpose of indicating deviation from the technical name (*saṃjñā*)? This is true;

nevertheless, the mention of the term *saṃjñā* is made to indicate this point: that [the operation] occurs mostly in the case of a technical name, but only occasionally when it is not a technical name. [The word is formed as follows: it is given (*dīyate*).
The term *dāyaḥ* is formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*), with *yuk* applied as before. The term *lābhaḥ* likewise has *ghañ* in the sense of the object.

Regarding the phrase "the mention of *kāraka*," etc.: for if the rule were stated as "not in the sense of the agent" (*akartari*) by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), then even without the mention of *kāraka*, [the suffix would apply] to anything other than the agent according to the maxim of *nañ-iva-yukta* (Pāṇini-vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 65).

Cognition of [the term] occurs only with respect to such a *kāraka* (participant in an action), such as in the case of "non-Brāhmaṇa," which refers to a Kṣatriya or the like who is similar to a Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, since the cognition is obtained as referring only to a *kāraka* even without the mention of the word *kāraka* in the context of *paryudāsa* (exclusion), the mention of *kāraka* need not be made.

But it must be understood as a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), for in that case only the negation of the action is perceived, and not another similar entity. In this regard, if only "in the sense of a name [applied] when not denoting the agent" were stated, the meaning would be understood as "it does not occur when denoting the agent. And thus...

Since there is no other rule prescribing [the suffix], the suffix would not apply to *karman* and the others. Where, then, would it apply? It applies in its own sense (*svārthe*), according to the principle: "Suffixes whose meaning is not specifically prescribed apply in their own sense" (Puṃ.pra. 90). But was it not already prescribed in its own sense by the preceding rule?

This is not so; for it has been stated that "the suffixes *ghañ* and others are prescribed in reference to that property which is called the 'accomplished state' (*siddhatā*) of the root-meaning. Therefore, why is the mention of the "participant" (*kāraka*) made in the case of a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*)? To this he replies: [In the case of] an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the mention of the "participant" is established even without it. That...
Since [the suffix] will be based on this very [kāraka], for what purpose is this mention of "kāraka" made? To this he says:

"That is done," and so forth. If, then, this *nañ*-compound were merely an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the mention of "kāraka" would be useless; for even without it, the suffix would apply only to a kāraka.

[The suffix] is obtained; however, it is only when there is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) that the mention of the term "kāraka" becomes meaningful, for in that case, the suffix is not obtained even without [the mention of] "kāraka. And this is precisely what has been demonstrated immediately prior. Therefore, by the mention of "kāraka," even in the case of a *prasajya-pratiṣedha*,...

It is made known that there is a compound [in the rule]. By this, in the rule *ādeca upadeśe 'śiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.45), a negative compound (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) is obtained; consequently, what was stated—that "the substitution of *ā* is not occasioned by anything else, and the prohibition applies to *śit*-affixes"—becomes logically consistent. But what is the reason for that?

Is a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) intended? For if the substitution of *ā* were applied even before the production of the suffix—being without a cause—the forms *suglaḥ* and *sumlaḥ* would result, so that the suffix *ka* might apply according to [Pāṇini 3.1.136], "And after a verbal root ending in *ā*, when preceded by a prefix. However, if an exclusionary negation (*paryudāsa*) were intended there, it would apply to suffixes other than *śit*, such as *tṛc* and others.

If [the suffix] were to be treated as having the nature of another element (*parabhūta*), then the suffix characterized by the long vowel *ā* would not occur after roots such as *glāyati*. However, the activity of the Teacher indicates that suffixes characterized by the long vowel *ā* do indeed occur after roots ending in *ej* (vowels other than *a*), since he [prescribes the suffix] for the purpose of superseding *kap*.

The rule "ṭh-vāvāmaśca" (Pāṇini 3.2.2) prescribes the suffix *aṇ*; therefore, even if the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "not ending in *i*" (*aśiti*) is adopted, does this not serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that a suffix characterized by an *ā*-ending [is established] for a stem ending in *e*? This is not so; this indicator is understood to apply specifically to cases where a direct object (*karman*) functions as a subordinate word (*upapada*).
Therefore, in the case of the expression *aśiti*, it is proper to rely solely on a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*).

And its existence here is made known by the mention of the term "kāraka. But what is the reason that a simple negation is not established [otherwise], such that this demonstration of its existence must be undertaken?

Incapacity is the cause [for not forming a compound]; for when there is capacity, a compound must occur, and that is not present in the case of a prasajya-pratiṣedha (absolute negation). This is because, in such a case, the negative particle *nañ* is connected with the verb, not with the subsequent word.

20. *parimāṇākhyāyāṃ sarvebhyaḥ* (3.3.20). [Examples: "one *taṇḍulaniścāya*" (a measure of rice). Although *ghañ* would also have applied here by *grahavṛdṛniścigamaśca* (3.3.58), [the rule prescribes *dhañ*]. "two *śūrpaniṣpāvau*" (measures of flattened grain). Here too, although *ap* would have applied by *ṛdorap* (3.3.57) [the rule prescribes *dhañ*].

This being the case, the *visarjanīya* undergoes the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule "ṭhidudupadhasya cāpratyayasya" (Pāṇini 8.3.41), resulting in "dvau kārau. [The root] "kṛ" [is used here] in the sense of "scattering" (dhātupāṭha 1409). But surely, in the expression "dvau śūrpaniṣpāvau," the suffix *ghañ* is applied by the rule "nirabhyoḥ pūlvoḥ" (Pāṇini 3.3.28)?

[The rule] is already established; so for what purpose is this stated here? He thinks as follows: when the term "all" (*sarva*) is employed for other purposes, [the formation] is already established even in the expression of measure (*parimāṇa*) or elsewhere; for the suffix *ap* is indeed appropriate after the prefix *ni-* as well, whereas the rule "after *ni-* and *abhi-*, with *pū-* and *lū-*" (Pāṇini 3.3.28) applies only where...

It is not understood that the designation "measure" (*parimāṇa*) refers to that [specific] space (*avakāśa*). Furthermore, what distinction is there when the suffix *ghañ* is applied to either that [space] or to "wind" (*vāta*)? What principle (*nyāya*) is being explained? None at all. But surely, the general term "root" (*dhātu*) is the governing rule (*adhikṛta*), not a specific root. Even without...

The inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) will ensure that the suffix *ghañ* occurs after the mere verbal root; so for what purpose is the inclusion of "all"? He says: "The inclusion of 'all'," and so forth. Furthermore, what is the reason that, in the absence of the inclusion of "all," the sublation (*bādhā*) of the suffix *ap* would not be established? He says: "In the preceding [rules]," and so forth. "Exceptions (*apavāda*) occurring earlier [sublate] those immediately following..."

"Later rules do not supersede earlier ones" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 9). If the word *sarva* were not present, it would only supersede the suffix *ac* immediately following the *ghañ*, but not the suffix *ap*. However, when *sarva* is present, it supersedes even *ap*.
Therefore, the inclusion of the word *sarva* is so that there may be supersession of *ap* as well.
Furthermore, this word *parimāṇa* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in reference to measures such as the *prastha*, but not in reference to number (*saṃkhyā*).

Therefore, how can this suffix, being prescribed to denote a measure (*parimāṇa*), apply in cases such as *ekaḥ taṇḍulaniścāyaḥ* where number is what is understood? To address this, he says: "The mention of the word *ākhyā*," and so forth.

The inclusion of the term *ākhyā* (name/designation) here is made for the purpose of excluding [the application of the rule] to conventional (*rūḍhi*) usage, so that it may be abandoned [in those cases]. Consequently, when conventional usage is abandoned, number (*saṃkhyā*) is also included. Indeed, by the force of the inclusion of the term *ākhyā*, measurement (*parimāṇa*) is also implied; therefore, its inclusion too is appropriate. This is because, if [the term *sarva*] were not used...

The intention is that this *ghañ* suffix also supersedes [the application of] feminine suffixes; it would even supersede feminine suffixes, and for this reason he says: "But feminine suffixes are not superseded. How, then, is this meaning obtained? From the mention of "from all" (*sarvebhyaḥ*) in the ablative case. When there is a mention in the ablative case...

For the word *sarva* is understood here as being in grammatical apposition with the verbal root (*dhātu*). Consequently, by the inclusion of the term *sarva*, there is an annulment of an exception (*apavāda*) that is based on the verbal base (*prakṛti*), but not of one that is based on the meaning (*artha*).
If, however, it were intended to annul even an exception based on the meaning, then...

In the word *sarvasmin*, one should pronounce the word *sarva* ending in the locative case (*saptamyanta*). Regarding the form *utkṣiptiḥ*: from the root *śriñ* with the prefix *ud*, the suffix *ktin* is applied by Pāṇini 3.3.94 (*striyāṃ ktin*); then, by 8.4.40 (*stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ*), the substitution of *ścu* occurs; and by 8.4.63 (*śaśchāe’ṭi*), the substitution of *cha* for *śa* takes place.
Thus, there is the substitution of *cch*.

Regarding the rule "dārajārau" and so forth: the words *dāra* and *jāra* are treated as irregularly formed (*nipātita*). What is irregularly formed here? From the roots *dṛ* "to tear apart" (DhP 1493) and *jṛṣ* "to lose vigor/age" (DhP 1130), [the forms *dāra* and *jāra* are derived].

When suffixes such as *tṛc* and others follow roots ending in the causal *ṇic*, the agentive case applies; however, when the suffix *ghañ* follows, there is elision (*luk*) of the *ṇic*. Now, if the *ṇic* were indeed elided by the rule "ṇer aniṭi" (Pāṇini 6.4.51), then, because of the rule "janījṛṣknasurañjo'mantāśca" (Dhātupāṭha 817), the root would receive the designation *mit*.

Even when the elision of *ṇi* has been performed, by virtue of the rule regarding the characteristics of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the shortening of the vowels of roots marked with *m* (*mit*) would still apply to the root *jṝ*.

If it is argued: "Let there be the shortening of the *mit* vowels, and then the *vṛddhi* will occur again by virtue of the *ghañ* affix," this is incorrect; for the *vṛddhi* does not apply on account of the *ghañ*, because of the rule: "When a subsequent [element] follows an *ac*... (*acaḥ parasmin*).

In the case of the rule *pūrvavidhau* (1.1.57), because there is the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), the operation is obstructed by the presence of the suffix *ṇic*. However, when *luk* occurs, since that [suffix] does not serve as a cause for the subsequent operation, the status of being like the original does not apply; thus, by relying on the *ghañ* suffix, the *vṛddhi* substitution takes place. Nor does the shortening [of the vowel] result by means of the rule concerning the indication of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*); for [the rule states] "not... [and so forth].
Because of the prohibition of the application of suffixal characteristics (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) by the rule *lumatāṅgasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.63),
it must therefore be stated that there is elision (*luk*).

21. *iṅśca* | (3.3.21) [This is] an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṭhac*. Since *ṭherac* (3.3.56) would otherwise apply, this *ghañ*, being prescribed after a root ending in the vowel *i*, is an exception specifically to *ac*.

It should be understood as follows: the word *adhyāyaḥ* is formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*). Regarding the rule "optionally *ṅīṣ* after that which ends in such [a suffix]," this *ṅīṣ* is to be applied after a word ending in *ghañ* used in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*). In this regard, the following is the explanation: "After a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*) ending in the suffix *vut*, [the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied]. (Pāṇini 4.1.44).

In this context, the rule should be analyzed by splitting the *yoga* (with the word *vā*). By that [splitting], the suffix *ṅīṣ* will apply after a word ending in a *ghañ* affix prescribed for the feminine in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*). And when the connection with a male (*puṃyoga*) is not intended to be expressed, then *ṅīṣ* is to be applied. But when there is a connection with a male, as in "the wife of a teacher" (*upādhyāyasya strī*), [then *ṅīṣ* does not apply].
When that is intended to be expressed, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is established by the rule itself: *pūṃyogād ākhyāyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.48).
She who studies under a teacher is an *upādhyāyī*.
[The root] *śṛ* is used in the senses of "wind," "color," and "protection. [Alternatively,] *śṛ* is used in the sense of "injury" (Dhātupāṭha 1488).

Therefore, when *vāyu* and the others are to be expressed, the suffix *ghañ* is to be applied. This application should be made either by relying on that very particle *ca* as having the sense of an unexpressed conjunction (*anuktasamuccaya*), or by resorting to the term *bahulam* (in various ways) from the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.113). *Nivṛtam* means "warding off" (*nivāraṇam*).

"Prevention" (nivāraṇa) is said to be the cause for the cessation of suffering such as cold; [as in the phrase] "one who has not made a shelter against the cold" (akṛtanīśāraḥ). The meaning is "one who has not created a protection against the cold. The lengthening of the vowel in the prefix is as in the previous case.

22. *upasarge ruvaḥ* | (3.3.22) "This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffix] *ap*. This refers to what was obtained by the rule *ṛdorap* (3.3.57). Furthermore, the suffix *ghan*, which is prescribed by the subsequent rule for verbal roots ending in *u*, is also an exception specifically to *ap*.
It should be understood.
23. *sami yudruduvaḥ* | (3.3.23) 24. *śriṇībhuvo’nupasarge* | (3.3.24) Regarding the phrase "anupasargebhyaḥ": it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those for which no prefix (*upasarga*) exists."

By providing the explanation "from *anupasargebhyaḥ*" using a word in the ablative case, he shows that in the sūtra the term *anupasarga* is in the locative case through a transposition of cases (*subvyatyaya*).
[He asks: "How is it that there is 'the power (*prabhāva*) of the king'? Since the word *anupasarga* is stated [in the rule], the prefix *pra-* here is an *upasarga*.

The sense is that [the suffix] should not occur when there is an *upapada*. As for the question "How then [is it said]: 'kathaṃ nayo rājñaḥ'?", he considers that the suffix *ghañ* should occur here because it is not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*).
25. *vau kṣuśruvaḥ* | (3.3.25) [The example is] *vikṣāvaḥ*. [The root is] *kṣu* in the sense of "sound" (*ṭuakṣu śabde*, Dhātupāṭha 1036).

26. *avodorniyaḥ* | (3.3.26) Regarding the form *unnāyaḥ*: [the rule] *yaro'nunāsike'nunāsiko vā* (Pāṇini 8.4.45) optionally applies the nasalization (*anunāsika*). [Question: "How is it that there is an *unnaya* of the meanings of words? [Answer: [It is so].
The intention is that, because it has "ucca" as its preceding member, the suffix -dhak must be applied here.
27. *pre dru-stu-ruvaḥ* (3.3.27). 28. *nirabhyoḥ pūlvoḥ* (3.3.28).
[The phrase] "the mention is general" is used because no specific distinction is stated.

"The connection with the prefixes is according to their respective order. The prefix *ni-* is connected with the root *pū*, and *abhi-* with *lū*. Now, one might object: "There are three roots—*pūñ*, *pūṅ*, and *lūñ*—but there are only two prefixes;
therefore, due to this discrepancy in number, the rule of correspondence by order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) should not apply."
Since the universal [nature] that has been relinquished is one and the same, there is no inequality; thus, there is no fault.

29. *unnyor grahaḥ* | (3.3.29) This is an exception (*apavāda*) to what would otherwise be obtained by the rule *ṭhAñdor ap* (3.3.57). Even in subsequent [rules], the *hañ* suffix being prescribed after a stem ending in *añ* should be understood as an exception specifically to *ap*. [The commentary states: "There is the inclusion of both."
Because no specific distinction is mentioned.

30. *kṛ* [is used] in the sense of grain (*dhānya*). (Pāṇini 3.3.30) Here, does "grain" (*dhānya*) function as the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*), or does it function as the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*)?
First of all, it is not tenable for it to be the meaning of the verbal root; for grain is a substance (*dravya*), whereas the verbal root [denotes an action].
Because it expresses an action. However, the meaning of the suffix is appropriate for the word *dhānya*;

yet, because it is not expressed by the suffix, the usage of the word *dhānyasya* (of the grain) in the phrase *utkāro dhānyasya* would not be justified. Even if such usage were to occur, [it would still be improper] because [the grain] is already included within the meaning of the suffix.

The genitive case is not appropriate—as in the expression "utkāraḥ dhānyasya" (a heap of grain). There would have to be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word ending in the suffix;

for the meaning of the suffix is realized only when there is coreferentiality with the word ending in that suffix, as in "dṛtihariḥ paśuḥ" (a beast called dṛtihari). Therefore, this is not [the case].
"It is neither the meaning of the suffix nor the meaning of the base, but rather a qualifier of the base-meaning;
thus, it does not refer to the root *kṛ* in the sense of 'injury' (*hiṃsā*) [found at Dhātupāṭha 1496]. He asks, "For what reason? and replies, "Because it is not so expressed (*anabhidhānāt*)."

Due to the inherent nature of the word's power (*śabdaśakti*), the two words *ut* and *kara* denote only the scattering of grain, not violence. It is appropriate to include only that whose meaning is expressed by the suffix, and not anything else—as in the expression "the scattering of grain" (*dhānyasyotkaraḥ*). This refers to scattering.
The meaning is "of another."
31. *yajñe saṃstau* (3.3.31).
By the statement "the place where they praise together," etc., [the author] shows that the word *saṃstāva* has the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
32. *pre stro'yajñe* | (3.3.32) [The example is] *barhiṣprastaraḥ*. The substitution of *ṣ* for the *visarga* is by [Pāṇini 8.3.41]: *idudupadhasya cāpratyayasya*.

33. [The suffix *ghañ* is used] after the root *prath* in the sense of extension (*prathana*), provided it does not mean sound (*avaśabda*). (3.3.33) For example: *tṛṇavistaraḥ*. This means "a covering of grass."

34. And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after the word *cchandas*. (Pāṇini 5.1.134) This word *cchandas* exists indeed in the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas; it also exists in another sense, namely, a specific arrangement of syllables characterized by metrical feet such as the *gāyatrī* and others. Of these two meanings, which one is intended here? To this he says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "ṭhvṛtam," he provides the justification right here: "because of the mention of the name. If the intention here were the *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa*, he would not have mentioned the "name"; he would simply have said "in the *chandas* (Vedic).
For even if it were stated in that way, the inclusion of both *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa* would indeed be obtained, as in the rule "bahulam... [Pāṇini 3.1.85].

In such sentences as "cchandasi" (Pāṇini 2.4.39), the word *chandas* is understood here by virtue of its mention [in that context]. Thus, in the term "viṣṭārapaṅktiḥ," the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs by the rule "cchandonāmni ca" (Pāṇini 8.3.94).
One might have the misconception that the word *viṣṭāra* itself, ending in the suffix *ghañ*, is the name of a meter (*chandonāman*).

To refute that, he says: "The word *viṣṭārapaṅkti* here," and so forth. Therein, regarding the word *viṣṭārapaṅkti*: "it exists as a constituent part"—this should be connected with the phrase "the form of a word ending in the suffix *ghañ*". If the form of a word ending in *ghañ* were not the name of a meter (*chandas*), [then this would not be possible].

However, regarding the word *viṣṭārapaṅkti*, the form ending in the suffix *ghañ* functions as a constituent part [of the compound]. If that is so, how then is it understood as a name of a meter (*chandas*)? For the meaning of this [rule] is that when the name of a meter is to be understood, [the base] becomes a name of a meter by means of a suffix; such is the sense. And thus, the meaning is as follows:
He says that [the objection] does not hold:
"The word *cchandonāmni* is a locative of location (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*).

By this, the meaning here should be understood as follows: the suffix *ya* occurs when the basis of the suffix is a name of a meter (*cchandonāman*) which has itself been derived from a suffix; it is not the case that [the suffix occurs] when "the name of a meter" is merely being implied.
He shows.
35. *udi grahaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.35). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the rule] "grahavṛdṛniścigamaśca" (3.3.58), which would otherwise have applied. [The Vārttika] states:
"In the Vedic language, it is also desired after the prefix *vi-* [in the sense] of lifting up and lowering the sacrificial ladle (*sruc*). Thus [it is established].
The reading of the Vārttika is seen printed as "cchandasi tu" and so forth.
A specific sacrificial vessel by which the oblation is offered is called a *sruk*; its *udyamana* is the lifting upwards, and its *nipātana* is...
The suffix *ghañ* is prescribed after the roots *dhṛ* (to hold) and *hṛ* (to take) when these two meanings are involved in the Vedic domain (*chandas*).

It should be understood that this suffix is obtained by the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.113). In the word *nigrābham*, the substitution of *bh* for *h* occurs because of the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) stating that *h* is replaced by *bh* after the roots *hṛ* and *grah* in the Veda.

36. *sami muṣṭau* | (3.3.36) Since the root *grah* denotes an action and a "fist" (*muṣṭi*) is not of the nature of an action, [the suffix] cannot apply to *grah* in that context; therefore, he says that the scope of the meaning of "seizing with a fist" is what is understood.

"If the meaning of the verbal root *mūṣ* is 'the object of a fist,'" [it is objected]. Indeed, this word *muṣṭi* exists in the sense of a measure—as in "a fistful of vegetables" (*śākasya muṣṭiḥ*)—and it exists in the sense of a particular arrangement of the fingers, as in "he strikes with a fist" (*muṣṭinā hanti*). Therefore, if here [in the sūtra] there were a reference to its usage in the sense of a measure...

Otherwise, the sūtra would be rendered useless, since the desired form is already established by the rule *parimāṇākhyāyāṃ sarvebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.20). Therefore, he states—*muṣṭiraṅgulisanniveśaḥ*—"a fist is a particular arrangement of the fingers"—to show that the term is understood as referring to a specific configuration (*racanāviśeṣa*) of the fingers. Here, *sanniveśa* means a particular arrangement.
"Ṭhaho mallasya saṃgrahaḥ" means the firmness of the fist; for this very reason it says, "firmness of the fist is expressed. 37. pari-ni-āṅ-bhyo nī-ṇī-ud-yama-ūha-vṛtāṃ bhreṣeṣu (Pāṇini 3.3.37).

Regarding the phrase "of the six categories" (*ṣaṇṇām padārthānām*), and so forth: the word *pada* signifies a "thing" (*vastu*). *Apacāra* means a contemptible practice (*kutsitaś cāraḥ*). Its meaning is the non-performance of what ought to be performed.
Just as in the world, the non-performance of what is required is censured as improper, therefore [this is] other than that.
"Tranquil conduct is conduct free from transgression. To clarify this very point by means of another synonym, he says:

"the performance of what has been obtained. The term *yathāprāpta* is an avyayībhāva compound used in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*), according to Pāṇini 2.1.7 (*yathā asādṛśye*). *Karaṇa* means accomplishment or bringing about. This is what is meant: [one should perform] whatever has been obtained.

The non-deviation (*abhreṣa*) is the accomplishment of those things which one attains through reasoning, scripture, or worldly renown. [Regarding the term *bhreṣa*: from the root *bhreṣṛ* in the sense of "going" (DhP 884), *bhreṣa* means "wavering.
*Bhreṣaṇa* is the act of wavering; thus, *bhreṣa* is that wavering from one's own true nature. *Abhreṣa* is the absence of such wavering.]

Non-deviation from the essential nature [of things]. For objects remain unmoved from their own nature only if they do not overstep what has been attained. Regarding the term "parimāṇena": the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule "upasargādasamāse 'pi ṇopadeśasya" (Pāṇini 8.4.14). The word "hanti" means "it obstructs."
"By looking all around"—this is an explanation of the meaning of the term "by means of circumambulation."

38. *parāvanupātyaya* (Pāṇini 3.3.38). [The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *iṇ* when preceded by *parā* in the sense of] "non-transgression" (*anupātyaya*), meaning "not exceeding" (*anatikrama*). [In contrast,] "transgression" (*atipāta*) means "exceeding" (*atikrama*).

39. [The suffix *kvanip* is applied] after the root *śī* (to lie down) following the prefixes *vi-* and *upa-*, in the sense of "turn by turn" (*paryāya*). (3.3.39) "Turn by turn" (*paryāya*) here refers specifically to "succession" (*anupātyaya*). Since the rule would have been established by the continued application of the term "succession" alone, the explicit mention of "turn by turn" (*paryāya*) is for the purpose of overriding any potential exceptions. Furthermore, when there is an intention to express "inclusiveness" (*abhividhi*), it also implies "extent" (*parimāṇa*).

Thus, by setting aside [the rule for] the *ghañ* suffix, it should be as [prescribed]; and in this way, since there is an increase in the word, an increase in the meaning is obtained, and not that this is a synonymous term expressing that same meaning.

40. *hastādāne cerasteye* (Pāṇini 3.3.40). Regarding the phrase "by the mention of *hastādāna*," and so forth: *hastādāna* refers to taking up [an object] by means of the hand, independent of any other means; that is, proximity (*pratyāsatti*). Precisely because of that...

It pertains to an object; therefore, by the mention of "taking with the hand," the proximity of the object to be grasped is indicated, because of the association with the meaning denoted by the term "hand-taking" (hastādāna).
"‘On the top of a tree,’ and so forth. By the mention of ‘the top of a tree,’ he indicates that the object to be taken is not nearby."

41. *nivāsacitiśarīropasamādhāneṣvādeśca kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.41). [The word] *rāśīkaraṇam* ("the act of making into a heap") means the bringing together in one place of that which was scattered. [The word] *cikhallinikāyaḥ*: *cikhalli* is a country; its *nikāya* is its dwelling-place (*nivāsa*). Now, what is the purpose of including the term "and so forth" (*ādi*)?

Let there be no [need for] this meaning. If that is so, why should it be stated as "caḥ kaḥ"? In that case, when [the suffix] is produced from a form ending in *yaṅ-luk*, then by the rule "in the absence of an ultimate [element], [the substitute applies] to that which occupies the position of the ultimate" (*antyābhāve antyasadeśasya*), or "in the modification of the ultimate, [it applies] to that which occupies the position of the ultimate" (*antyavikāre antyasadeśasya*), [the substitution occurs] for the second [consonant].
The inclusion of the word "ādi" (etcetera) is for the purpose that [the rule] should not apply to the letter *ca*.
42. "And [there is no offense] when there is no superiority within the Saṅgha" (3.3.42). Regarding the phrase "by entering into a single dharma," the meaning is "by following a single dharma."

43. *karmavyatihāre ṇac striyām* | (3.3.43) Since there is the governing rule *dhātoḥ* (3.1.91), that which is expressed by the verbal root as its object (*karman*) is understood here, not the object as a grammatical factor (*sādhana*). Thinking that the verbal root does not have its application (*vṛtti*) in that [latter sense], he says: *karmaṃ*.

Regarding the word "kriyā": as for the statement "the letter *ca* is for the purpose of specification," why does the letter *ca* not serve the purpose of making [the word] oxytone? It cannot serve the purpose of making it oxytone, because the suffix *añ* is prescribed after a stem ending in the negative particle *nañ*.
Consequently, by the accent that remains when other accents have fallen away (*satiśiṣṭasvara*), the word ought to be udātta on its first syllable; so how could it be oxytone?

This is the justification. Therefore, the particle *ca* is used solely for the purpose of specification (*viśeṣaṇārtha*). If only "in the feminine" (*striyām*) were stated, then [the suffix] *ṇa* prescribed by "after *prajñā*, *śraddhā*, and *arcā*, the suffix *ṇa*" (Pāṇini 5.2.101) would also apply here in the case of *prājñā*.
[Examples include] *vyāvakrośī* and so forth. [Regarding the root] *kruśa*—[the Dhātupāṭha reads] "to call out and to weep"—and *likha*...

From the roots *akṣaravinyāsa* (DhP 1365) and *has* in the sense of "laughing" (DhP 721), the suffix *ṇac* is applied; then, by the rule *ṇacaḥ striyām* (Pāṇini 5.4.14), the suffix *añ* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*); next, by *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15), the suffix *ṅīp* is applied; and finally, by *na karmavyatihāre* (Pāṇini 7.3.6), the substitution of *aij* is prohibited.

Only the *vṛddhi* substitution of the first vowel occurs; thus, we have "vyatipākaḥ. In that case, because the state (*bhāva*) is masculine, the suffix *ghañ* is employed. Now, why is the suffix *ṇac* not mentioned in this very section [of Pāṇini's rules] under "striyāṃ ktin" (3.3.94)? What [is the reason]?
Furthermore, if this were the case, there would be an advantage: it would not be necessary to mention the word "strī" (feminine) twice.
There is indeed an advantage; however, the rule for optional forms (*vā-sarūpa-vidhi*) would not apply, because of the prohibition [contained in the phrase] *astriyām* ("not in the feminine").
Consequently, since there would be no co-occurrence (*asamāveśa*) of *ktin* and *ṇac*, the form *vyāvakruṣṭiḥ* would not be established. In this regard—

However, [the desired form] is not established when [the suffix *ṇvul*] is applied; because in the rule *vā'sarūpo'striyām* (Pāṇini 3.1.94), the mention of "not feminine" (*astrī*) is understood to apply specifically to the domain of suffixes prescribed under the heading of "feminine" (*strī*), since the term "feminine" (*strī*) is marked with a svarita accent, and thus the prohibition "not feminine" (3.1.94) is understood to pertain only to that context. It does not [apply here].

This applies only to the scope of feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*). Therefore, it is more logical that the forms *vyāvacorī* and *vyāvacarcī* are derived in the same manner as others. From the roots *cur* (meaning "to steal," DhP 1534) and *carc* (meaning "to study," DhP 1712)—both belonging to the *curādi* class and taking the causative suffix *ṇic*—the suffix *ṇi* [is applied] according to the rule *ṇyāsaśrantho...*.

The suffix *yuc* [prescribed by Pāṇini 3.3.107] would apply; however, because it is prescribed as a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*) and because it occurs later in the sequence (*paratva*), it would be the sublater [of other rules]. Nevertheless, in this particular domain, only *ṇa* and *ac* are desired. Thus we have *vyatīkṣā* and *vyatīhā*. [The roots are] *īkṣa* in the sense of "seeing" (DhP 610) and *īh* in the sense of "exertion" (DhP 611).
From these two roots, by the rule *gurośca halaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.103), only the suffix *a* is applied.

It is not possible to apply the suffix *ṇac*, because that [suffix] is intended only in certain cases where there is an obstruction [to the application of *a*], and not everywhere. Furthermore, the fact that the suffix *a* acts as an obstructor should be understood as previously explained.

Regarding the term *vyātyukṣī*: the root *ukṣ* means "to sprinkle" (*dhā.pā.* 657). Here, even in the domain of the prohibitive particle *nañ*, the suffix *ṇa* alone occurs. [The question] "How is this variety obtained? [is answered: not at all;
the sense is that there is no cause for its attainment. [This is because] the suffixes *kṛtya* and *lyuṭ*...
By means of this [sūtra] *bahulam* (3.3.113), he shows that this diversity is thereby obtained.

44. *abhividhau bhāve inuṇ* (Pāṇini 3.3.44). Regarding the form *sāṃkūṭinam*: from the root *kūṭa* (meaning "to torment," or according to others, "to burn") [Dhātupāṭha 1890], the suffix *aṇ* is added in the sense of the word itself (*svārthika*) to the stem ending in *inuṇ*, by virtue of the rule *aṇinuṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.15).

Due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *ṭhinaṇyanapatye* (Pāṇini 6.4.164), the elision of the suffix *ṭi* by the rule *ṭhnastaddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.144) does not occur.
Thus, we have *saṃrāvaḥ*; here, the suffix *ghañ* is applied by the rule *upasarge ruvaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.22). Similarly, we have *saṃdrāvaḥ*.
In this case as well, [the rule] "sami yudruduvaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.3.23) applies.
Now, one might ask: since the term *bhāve* (in the sense of an action/state) is already understood from the context, for what purpose is it mentioned again? To this he says:
"In the sense of an action (*bhāve*)," and so forth. The mention of *bhāve* here is redundant.

That [word "bhāve"] is understood as being repeated for the purpose of excluding the *vāsarūpa* rule; therefore, there is no co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the suffix *kta* with the suffix *ṇa* when used in the sense of an instrument (*hetu*). But surely the word "kārake" (in the sense of an agent) also persists [from the previous rule]; why, then, is the mention of "bhāve" not intended to exclude that? It is thought thus: [the two terms] "bhāve" and "kārake" constitute a pair.

In the present case as well, a restriction is established by virtue of observing the actual usage, just as in the case of the suffix *ṇac*. For although that suffix applies to both [action and agent], it is understood to denote only the action (*bhāva*)—and not the agent (*kartṛ*)—in accordance with what is observed in the linguistic data (*lakṣya*), even without an explicit re-statement; likewise, here too, *inuṇ* will be understood to denote only the action.
Therefore, it is logical that the word *bhāva* is mentioned again specifically for the purpose of excluding the rule regarding optional forms (*vā-asarūpa-vidhi*).

If this is so, then just as there is no co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of *ghañ* and *inuṇ*, there would likewise be none with *lyuṭ*; to this he says: "But with *lyuṭ*," and so forth. The meaning has already been explained. As for the letter *ṇ* in *inuṇ*—
The letter *v* is for the purpose of augmentation; the letter *u* is for the purpose of pronunciation.
45. *ākrośe'vanyor grahaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.45).
This is a statement made because [the suffix] would otherwise have been obtained by the rule *ṭh grahavṛdṛ* (3.3.58), etc.
[The phrase] "due to the force of observed continuity" means by virtue of its presence in usage.

The capacity for the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of *ghañ* is observed [in the previous rule], whereas for *inuṇ* it would have to be inferred. And when two elements with observed capacities are in proximity, it is logical to adopt the one whose capacity is observed. Therefore, some maintain that only *ghañ* recurs. However, this being the case, [the same logic applies] even in rules such as *grahavṛdṛ* (Pāṇini 3.3.58).
The suffix *ghañ* alone continues [from the previous rule], not *ap*. Therefore, it is explained otherwise:

where the capacity for the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the governing term is observed, that is "observed capacity for continued application" (*dṛṣṭānuvṛttisāmarthya*), and in such a case, there is the status of being *svarita*. For it is from that [status] that the word which is the governing element continues in the treatise.

This is observed in terms of capability. What is meant by this is as follows: it is only the suffix *ghañ* that is declared to have the *svarita* accent, not the suffix *inuṇ*. Therefore, because of the *svarita* accent, only *ghañ* is carried over [into the subsequent rule], and not *inuṇ*.
46. The suffix *pre* is used in the sense of desiring (*lipsā*). (Pāṇini 3.3.46) 47. The suffix *pari* is used in the sense of sacrifice (*yajña*). (Pāṇini 3.3.47) 48.
The suffix *ni* is used in the sense of grain (*dhānya*). (Pāṇini 3.3.48)

"An exception to the rule. This refers to what would have been obtained by the rule *grahavṛdṛ* (Pāṇini 3.3.58). "There are grains called *nīvāra*. By this, although this word is derived by means of the general term *dhānya*, nevertheless, it ends in a secondary suffix (*pratyaya*).
He shows that, by the very nature of the word's power (*śabdaśaktisvābhāvya*), it refers specifically to a particular kind of grain.
There is lengthening [of the vowel] according to *upasargasya ghañi* (Pāṇini 6.3.122).
Regarding the form *nivarā*: it is called *nivarā* because it is "held back" (*nivriyate*). Even though it is naturally an *ā*-stem, it occurs in the feminine.

And thus, it should be understood that the statement in the section on gender (liṅgādhikāra) regarding the masculine gender of forms ending in *ghañ*— namely, those ending in *ghañ* and those ending in *gha*— is merely general (prāyika).

49. *udi śrayati-yauti-pū-druvaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.49). [The suffix *ṣṭran*] is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṭhañ* and *ap*. Because the root *śri* ends in an *i*-vowel, it is an exception to *ac*; because *yuti* and the others end in an *u*-vowel, they are exceptions to *ap*. [Question: "How can there be such heights (*samucchrayāḥ*) that end in falling (*patanāntāḥ*)?"

The meaning is that because the word *ut* is used as an upapada (governing word), the suffix *ghañ* must occur here. The phrase "what will be stated," etc., is the refutation. If, then, the mention of *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is connected here, would it not follow that the suffix would also optionally apply to roots such as *yu* and others?
There is no fault, for [the objection] does not apply according to the established rule of optional interpretation (vyavasthitavibhāṣā).
50. *vibhāṣā''iṅ rupluvoḥ* (3.3.50).

Since the suffix *ghañ* is obligatory after the root *ru* when preceded by a prefix by rule 3.3.22 (*upasarge ruvaḥ*), and since the root *plu* also ends in the vowel *u*, this sūtra is commenced [to provide an option].

51. *ave graho varṣapratibandhe* | (3.3.51) Although [the suffix] would also have been obtained by rule 3.3.58 (*grahavṛdṛ...*), this [present rule] is an exception to that; the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed optionally. [The phrase] "due to some cause" means: [Note: This rule prescribes the suffix *ghañ* after the root *grah* when preceded by the prefix *ava*, provided the sense is the obstruction of rain.]
Because it concerns the transgressions of the actions of sentient beings.

52. *pre vaṇijām* | (3.3.52) [The commentary begins: "In connection with merchants (*vaṇik-sambandha*), etc. For a measuring-cord (*tulā-sūtra*) is generally associated with merchants; thus, by way of association (*sāhacarya*), it is characterized by its connection to merchants. It is not [the case] here...
Because of the preeminence of merchants, that very sūtra concerning the balance and so forth is the denotation of the word "other" (tadanya).

53. *raśmau ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.53). [The rule] begins with *ṭhrathādiyuktānām*. But how is this obtained, given that the word *raśmi* is a general term, just as it is used for the purpose of restraining horses and so forth?

Does it likewise occur with the rays associated with the moon, the sun, and so forth? He thinks thus: just as in the rule "nau vṛ dhānye" (Pāṇini 3.3.48), even though the word *dhānya* is used, only a specific kind of grain is understood by means of the suffix.

This is because of the inherent nature of the word's power (*śabda-śakti*), or because it denotes a specific kind of grain; likewise, although the word *raśmi* (ray) is a general term, nevertheless, when followed by a suffix, it refers specifically to a particular kind of rope due to its inherent nature. Therefore, its inclusion [in the list] is appropriate.

54. *vṛṇoti* in the sense of "covering" (*ācchādane*). (Pāṇini 3.3.54) Regarding the mention of *vṛṇoteḥ*: the citation with the *śnu*-suffix is for the purpose of excluding *vṛṅ*. Here too, as before, when it expresses a general sense, it applies elsewhere than in the sense of "covering. Optionally, by [the rule] *grahavṛdṛ* (3.3.58).
It occurs by means of such [passages] as these.
55. *parau bhuvo’vajñāne* (3.3.55).
[Regarding the statement] "The letter *c* is for the sake of specification," even without it, [the rule] *thāthādisūtra* (6.2.144) [would apply].
By the rule *apratyayāt*, there would also be the inclusion of that which is not a suffix (*apratyaya*).

Regarding the phrase "in the prescription of the suffix *ṭhaC*" and so forth, the meaning of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is "presentation" (or "provision"). This presentation, however, must be carried out by relying on the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.113). But another [teacher] says...

Regarding the rule *pañcamī bhayena* (Pāṇini 2.1.37) and the rule *varṣapramāṇa ūlopaścāsyāntarasyām* (Pāṇini 3.4.32), he seeks to establish the formation of words such as *bhaya* through these specific grammatical derivations (*nipātana*), yet that is not correct.
Why is there this mention of the neuter gender forms of the words *bhaya* and *varṣa*? Thus [he asks].
Because of the doubt [regarding] whether these two are masculine, [the author says] "they are to be explained" (*vaktavyau*). This means they must be analyzed.

The explanation, however, should be made by relying on that very mention of the term *bahulam* (in various ways). [The examples are] *javaḥ* and *savaḥ*. [The former is derived] from the root *ju*, which is a root found in the Sūtras (Pāṇini 3.2.150), and [the latter] from *ṣuñ* in the sense of "pressing."
Since [the suffix] *ap* would also have been obtained from this root (*dhā.pā. 1247*) by the subsequent rule, the vowel *a* is used here.
There is a distinction regarding the accent: for otherwise, the word would have been udātta on its first syllable (*api hi stām*), whereas when ending in *a*, it becomes udātta on its final syllable.

57. *ṛdorap* (3.3.57). "The addition of the marker *ṭh* is for the sake of accentuation," meaning that the rule *anudātau suppitau* (3.1.4) may apply so that [the suffix] becomes unaccented (*anudātta*). In the rule *ṛdorap*, the vowel *ṛ* should be followed by the marker *t* (i.e., it should be *ṛt*).
This being the case, since it is stated that "that which has *t* as its marker (*tapara*) is [the name] of its own duration," the letter *u* would also be *tapara* for that [vowel].

Consequently, by the application of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "that which has *t* as its marker is [the name] of its own duration" (Pāṇini 1.1.70), this [substitution] would occur only here—namely in *yavaḥ* and *stavaḥ*—but it would not occur in cases such as *lavaḥ* and *pavaḥ*. However, in the case of the letter *d*, [the rule] "aṇ... [applies].

It includes its own class (*savarṇa*): [as stated in] *bhuvaḥ gṛhṇāti* (Vyāḍipāṭha 66), it occurs even after a long vowel. Therefore, this *u* includes its own class. And here is the evidence for this: the mention [*nirdeśa*] in *bhuvaḥ prabhavaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.31). However, if [the *u*] were followed by *t* (*tapara*), the suffix *ap* would not occur after the root *bhū*; and consequently...
The designation "originating from ṭ" would not be appropriate;

however, since that letter *d* serves the purpose of ease of pronunciation (*mukhasukhārtha*) and no other purpose is possible, having considered all this, he says: "The letter *d* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation."
58. *grahivṛdṛniścigamaśca* (Pāṇini 3.3.58).

The term *vṛ* includes both *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ* generally. The term *dṛ* refers to *dṛṅ* in the sense of "respect" (Dhātupāṭha 1411). [The suffix *ap*] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *niścinauteḥ tavacaḥ*. [The suffix *ap* is added] by the rule *erac* (3.3.56).

[This applies to] that which has been obtained. Now, what is the purpose of including the term *niści*? For even if *aci* were prescribed instead, there would be no difference; indeed, the same form results in both cases. To this he says: "The inclusion of *niści* is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtham*). This means it is for the sake of the *anudātta* (unaccented) tone. But [one might object]: [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the partial nature of the source.]

[Objection: Since the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed for the root *ci* by the rule *hastādāne cerasteye* (Pāṇini 3.3.40), it would not apply [in the case of *niścaya*]; however, since it would also apply after the prefix *nis*, is it not appropriate to include the mention of *ni* (*niścigrahaṇa*) in order to block that? [Response: This is not so; for this *ghañ* applies even after the root *ci* when preceded by the prefix *nis*.

This is desired by means of a prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). Now, one might object that the mention of *ni* is not even necessary for the sake of the accent; nevertheless, when the natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member would apply according to *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), [the rule] *antaḥ* (6.2.143) [is required].

By the rule *ṭhthāthaghañktājabitrakāṇām* (Pāṇini 6.2.144), [the word] ought to have its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). Thus, even when the suffix *api* is present, should it not likewise be unaccented (*anudātta*)? This is not a fault; by the force of the inclusion of the term *niś* [in the rule], the accentuation prescribed for *ṭhātha* and so forth does not apply in that specific case.

When that [suffix] is absent and the subsequent word remains in its original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), because the suffix *ap* is unaccented (*anudātta*) and the verbal root is oxytone (*antodātta*), the word becomes middle-accented (*madhyodātta*) by the accent of the entire word (*kṛtsvara*). However, when the vowel *ac* is present, it is oxytone.
It may be so;

[as stated] in the rule beginning with *vaśiraṇyoḥ*. *Vaś* (in the sense of "desire," DhP 1080) and *raṇ* (DhP 445) have the meaning of sound; *aṇ*, *araṇ*, and so forth, have the meaning of sound (DhP 444–453).
Regarding the *dhātus*: an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the roots *vaś* and *raṇ*, that is, their inclusion (*pratipādana*) must be effected.
Here is the method of inclusion: the particle *ca* is used here in the sense of including what has not been mentioned;
by this, it will apply to *vaś* and *raṇ* as well.

"ṭhghañarthe ka" and so forth. The meaning of *ghañ* is the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object other than the agent; in that sense, the suffix *ka* should be prescribed for the purpose of forms such as *sthā*. However, this is already established by the rule "kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam" (Pāṇini 3.3.113). [The form] "pā" [is derived] by the paribhāṣā regarding the elision of the *vikaraṇa* suffix.

The root *pā* is taken here in the sense of "drinking," not in the sense of "protecting. Regarding *prastha*: there is the elision of the vowel *ā* by Pāṇini 6.4.64 (*āto lopa iṭi ca*). Regarding *praśna*: the root is *ṣṇā* in the sense of "cleansing" (DhP 1052). Regarding *āvidha*: the root is *vyadha* in the sense of "striking" (DhP 1181). [The rule] *grahijyā*... [applies].

By the rule beginning with (6.1.16), there is *samprasāraṇa*. In the word "vighnaḥ," there is elision of the penultimate vowel by the rule beginning with (6.4.98), and the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *gh*) by the rule beginning with (7.3.54). In the word "āyudham," [the root is] *yudh* in the sense of "striking together" (Dhātupāṭha 1173).

59. *Upasarge 'daḥ* | (Pāṇini 3.3.59) "The suffix *ap* is applied after the root *ad* when a prefix (*upasarga*) is present. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ghañ*. From this point onward, even where *ap* is prescribed after roots ending in consonants, it should be understood as an exception to *ghañ*. [Example: *vighasaḥ*.

[The word] *praghasaḥ* [is formed thus]: the substitution of *ghas* [for *ad*] occurs by the rule *ghañapośca* (Pāṇini 2.4.38). Now, for what purpose is the suffix *ap* prescribed after the root *ad*, rather than being prescribed after the distinct root *ghas* itself? What advantage would there be in doing so? [The answer is: even for *ad*, the transformation into *ghas* need not be performed.

Is this so? This is true; nevertheless, [the rule] was prescribed for the sake of what follows—so that [the substitution] might apply to forms such as *naun* and *ṇa* according to Pāṇini 3.3.60, but not to the root *ghas*.

60. The affix *ṇa* is applied after the roots *nau* and *ca*. (3.3.60) 61. The affix *ṇa* is applied after the roots *vyadh* and *jap*, provided they are not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*). (3.3.61) 62.
The affix *ṇa* is optionally applied after the roots *svan* and *han*. (3.3.62)
63. [The suffix *ghañ* is applied] after the roots *upa-ni-viś*, as well as after *yam*.

(3.3.63) 64. [The suffix *ghañ* is applied] after the roots *gad*, *nad*, *paṭh*, and *svan*, when preceded by *ni*. (3.3.64) 65. [The suffix *ghañ* is applied] after the root *kvaṇ*, and also when it refers to the lute (*vīṇā*). (3.3.65)

"The mention of the *vīṇā* is for the sake of including [the suffix] after a preverb. If [the suffix] were to occur even in the case of *vīṇā* only because of a preverb, then the mention of *vīṇā* would be purposeless;
for since it is prescribed generally after a non-preverb (*anupasarga*), the suffix is already established in the case of *vīṇā* as well.

66. *nityaṃ paṇaḥ parimāṇe* (3.3.66). [The suffix] *ṭhañ* [is applied after the word *paṇa* in the sense of] "measured. "Measured" means measured out, delimited; that specific quantity which is bound together as a handful of two, three, or four items such as radishes and the like.
For the sake of conventional usage, that [unmanifested] is denoted by such words as "the root-coin" (*mūlakapaṇa*) and so forth.

67. *mado'nupasarge* (Pāṇini 3.3.67). [The example] "vidyāmadaḥ" (pride in learning): pride by means of learning. The compound is formed by the rule "kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam" (Pāṇini 2.1.32). [The example] "unmādaḥ" (insanity): here too, [the compound is formed] by the rule "kugatiprādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.2.18).

Since the inclusion of *mad* could have been made right there in the rule *ṭhvyadhajaporanupasarge* (Pāṇini 3.3.61), the formulation of the rule *mado'nupasarge* is for the purpose of indicating that this grammatical operation is not mandatory; by this means, the form *māda* is established.

68. *pramada* and *saṃmada* [denote] joy. (3.3.68) Now, since *madaḥ* (3.3.67) is understood as a governing rule (*anuvartate*), one should have stated [the rule] as "after *pra* and *sam*" (*prasaṃbhyām*). Even so, the desired form is indeed established; why then is this [specifically] prescribed? To this he says: "after *pra* and *sam*. (*prasaṃbhyām*)

And so forth. Here, by the term "conventional word" (*rūḍhiśabda*), since nothing other than *pramada* and *saṃmada* is heard, and since these two are indeed conventional words, it is understood that these alone are intended. Furthermore, a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is to be seen here, because all sentences possess an inherent restrictive force (*sāvadharanatva*). Therefore, [it refers to] the conventional meaning.

This is an irregular derivation (*nipātana*). This meaning results precisely in the sense of the words *pramada* and *sammada*. By means of this rule, the purpose of the irregular derivation is so that the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of these two specific conventional words (*rūḍhiśabda*), namely *pramada* and *sammada*, may occur, and not of other words. For if...

If, following the mention of *mad*, one were to state only "after *pra* and *sam*," then even when *mad* occurs after *pra* and *sam* joined together as a compound, the suffix would still apply; likewise,
even when *pra* and *sam* follow another prefix, and *pra* and *sam* themselves are followed by [another element].

In that case, there would also be *madirbhavati*; and consequently, the Sūtra would apply to established words (*rūḍhiśabda*) such as *prasammadaḥ*, *abhiprasammadaḥ*, and *pranisammadaḥ* as well, and not solely to the meanings of *pramada* and *sammada*. However, when the rule of substitution (*nipātana*) is applied, a restriction is understood.
These two [conditions] apply individually, neither collectively nor in conjunction with other afflictions (*upasarga*). Thus, the sūtra attains its conventional meaning (*rūḍha-artha*).
69. *samudorajaḥ paśuṣu* (3.3.69).

70. *akṣeṣu glahaḥ* (3.3.70). [Regarding the latter: "The suffix *ap* after the root *grah* is already established" by the rule *grahavṛdṛ...* (3.3.58), and so forth. If this is the case, [why is it stated here?]
He asks, "For what purpose is this irregular formation (nipātana)? and replies with the words "for the sake of [the substitution of] *l*," and so forth.
71. [The suffix *ghañ* is applied] after the root *sṛ* when preceded by *pra*.

(3.3.71) 72. After the root *hve*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) as well, when preceded by *ni*, *abhi*, *upa*, or *vi*. (3.3.72) [The example is] "nihavaḥ" (calling). [The root is] *hveñ*—[according to the Dhātupāṭha] "in the sense of rivalry and sound"—[here specifically] "in the sense of rivalry."

When the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) has been performed, the *guṇa* and *āv* substitutions [are applied]. Since the four forms beginning with "nihavaḥ" are already established for the root *hu-* itself when preceded by prefixes such as *ni*, this specific rule is intended solely to exclude the suffix *ghañ* from the root *hvayati* when preceded by *ni* and other such prefixes.
73. *āiṅ* in the sense of "calling" (*yuddhe*). (3.3.73) [The form] *āhvāyaḥ* is derived by applying *yuk* according to the rule *āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ* (7.3.33).

74. *nipānam āhāvaḥ* | (3.3.74) The term *nipāna* means "that in which they drink"; thus, the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of a locus according to Pāṇini 3.3.117. To the question of why the word *āhāva* refers to a reservoir for water, he says: "For in that," and so forth.
By this, he shows the ground for the application of the word *āhāva* to a reservoir of water.

75. *bhāve 'nupasargasya* | (3.3.75) Regarding the phrase "the mention of *bhāva*" and so forth: [An objection is raised: But surely, just as in the rule *karmavyatihāre ṇac striyām* (3.3.43), although two [meanings] are presented, the suffix occurs only in the sense of *bhāva* by virtue of observing the usage in the examples (*lakṣyadarśana*).

It will be understood [there]; so it is here as well. Why, then, is there the inclusion of the term *bhāva* (action/state), for the purpose of excluding [the application of] Pāṇini 3.3.19, *ṭhakartari ca kārake*? This is true; however, by the very force of observing the linguistic usage (*lakṣyadarśana*), this meaning is already established. The inclusion of the term *bhāva* is merely stated for the sake of favoring those of dull intellect. Now...

Just as in the rule *inuṇ bhāve* (Pāṇini 3.3.44), where the term "bhāve" (in the sense of an action/state) is already present from the previous context, its repetition is understood to be for the purpose of excluding the *vāsarūpa* principle, why should it not be understood in the same way here? [The answer is:
Because of the observation of actual usage (*lakṣyadarśana*). For we do indeed observe forms such as *hūtam* (which ends in the suffix *kta*).
"Hvānam" and "hūtiḥ"—in these cases, the suffix *ghañ* and others are used by the rule of "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpa*) to denote the abstract state (*bhāva*).

76. *hanaś ca vadhaḥ* (3.3.76). [The commentary states: "And that [substitute] is udātta at the end. This is because the word *vadha* is pronounced with an udātta accent on the final syllable in the sūtra.
By means of the phrase beginning with "therein," he demonstrates what is intended to be established when the substitute *vadha* is udātta on the final syllable.

Furthermore, when the *akāra* is elided by "api kṛte ṭhato lopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.48), the *udātta* accent of the suffix *ap* occurs by the rule "anudātasya ca yatrodātalopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.161). [The word] "dhātaḥ":

the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root in the sense of an object (*karman*) and so forth; the substitution of *t* for *th* occurs by the rule "hanasto 'ciṇṇaloḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.32); [the final *s* is elided] by the rule "haḥ".

The substitution of *k* [for *h*] occurs by the rule "of the root *han*" (Pāṇini 7.3.54), etc. Regarding the phrase "the letter *c* is out of its proper order," etc.: the connection is that the letter *c* is not connected with the substitute (*ādeśa*). Why is it not connected? Because it is out of its proper order. If the sequence of the letter *c* were "of *han*, *vadha* and [the letter *c*]," [then it would be connected].

Because there is no pronunciation immediately after the substitution, and because the order is different—due to this difference in sequence—it is not connected with the substitute; rather, it is connected with the affix under discussion (*prakṛta*). And so, in order to demonstrate this connection with the *prakṛta*, he says "ap ca" and so forth. The affix is *ap*.
The word "and" (ca) is repeated; therefore, that which is obtained [by the previous rule] also applies here. Consequently, the suffix ghañ also occurs.

77. *ghana* [is used] in the sense of "solid form" (*mūrti*). (Pāṇini 3.3.77) Regarding the example "*abhra-ghanaḥ*": this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). It means "the solidity of the cloud. If the word *ghana* is derived in the sense of a solid form—as in "*ghanaṃ dadhi*" (solid curd)—then it refers to that which possesses a solid form.

The designation "curd" would then apply [to the milk]; for how indeed could that which is derived from a specific form (mūrti) function elsewhere? To this he says: "By the word 'dharma,' the possessor of the quality (dharmī) is expressed. This is a metaphorical identification (abhedopacāra) based on the elision of the possessive suffix *matup*, as in the expression "the white cloth."
The meaning is that by the word "white," the white quality [is meant], as in the expression "the white cloth."

78. *antarghano deśe* (3.3.78). Regarding the word *antarghana*: it is derived with the suffix *ap* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), meaning "a place where living beings are hidden. [The commentary states] "it must certainly be understood as having the suffix *ap*"; for the Teacher has taught both ways to his disciples.
79. *praghaṇa* and *praghāṇa* [denote] a porch that is a part of a house.

(3.3.79) 80. *udghana* [denotes] a support placed above. (3.3.80) Regarding the term "support placed above" (*atyādhāna*): the word *ati* here signifies the sense of being "above," while the root *ā-dhā* means "to place."

That upon which something is placed or set down is its *ādhāna* (receptacle). The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇe*). As in the rule "ṭhudghanaḥ," [the suffix] *ap* is used in the sense of the locus when it is said "in this it is piled up" (*uddhanyate'smin*).

81. *apaghana* means a limb (*aṅga*). (Pāṇini 3.3.81). Regarding the form *apaghanaḥ*: it is derived with the suffix *ap* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), as in "that by which one strikes. Thus, *apaghana* means that which is struck (or a part of the body).
82. [The suffix *khañ* is applied] after the words *ayas*, *yu*, and *drus* when they denote an instrument (*karaṇa*).
(3.3.82) 83. After the word *stamba*, [the suffixes] *ka* and *ca* [are applied].

(3.3.83) Regarding "and there" (*tatra ca*): this refers even to what was mentioned immediately prior. Regarding "the substitution of *ghana*": [this occurs] when it denotes a solid mass (*mūrti*), as in *ghana*.

(3.3.77) Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "ghaṇ" from that [preceding sūtra], [we have] *stambaghnaḥ*. As before, there is the substitution of *k* for *g* and the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*).

84. *parau ghaḥ* | (3.3.84) [The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *ghrā* when preceded by the prefix *pari*. Regarding the form *parighaḥ*, there is optionally the substitution of *l* for *gh* according to *pareśca ghāṅkayoḥ* (8.2.22).
85. *Upaghna* means "resting place" (*āśraya*).
(Pāṇini 3.3.85). Regarding the phrase "the word *āśraya*," etc.: resting (*āśrayaṇa*) is "resting" (*āśraya*), that is, service (*sevā*).
And since that [service] occurs where there is proximity (*pratyāsatti*), "resting" (*āśraya*) is that which is accompanied by proximity. Therefore, the word *āśraya* [is used in this sense].

The term *sāmīpya* indicates proximity (*pratyāsatti*), because its meaning is associated with proximity. For example, in the expression *parvatopaghnaḥ*, an object situated near a mountain is expressed.

86. *saṅghodghau* [are used] in the sense of a multitude (*gaṇa*) and praise (*praśaṃsā*). (3.3.86) Regarding the term *saṅghodghau*: *saṃhananam* is a *saṅgha*. That which is raised up (*utkaṭam*) and struck (*hanyate*)—that is, known—is *udghaḥ*. The suffix *ap* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). But how can the root *han* signify "knowing"? Because it has the sense of "going" (*gati*).
Because all verbal roots meaning "to go" have the sense of "knowing."

87. *nigho nimitam* | (3.3.87) The word *nimita* means "measured all around" (*samantānmita*). The sense is that it is equal in height and in circumference on all sides. To demonstrate this single meaning by means of a more well-known term, he says:

"Samārohapariṇāham" means that which possesses equal height and circumference; "āroha" is height, and "pariṇāha" is width. Regarding the term "nighāḥ," it refers to trees; they are called "nighāḥ" because they are struck (hit) or known without distinction. The meaning is that they are equal on all sides. Thus they...
If they are known to be without distinction, being equal in height all around and in circumference, they are identical.

88. *ḍāvitaḥ ktriḥ* | (3.3.88) [The suffix] *ktri* follows a verbal root ending in *ḍā*. In the example *ṭhuptrimam*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) according to *vacisvapi-* (6.1.15) and other rules.
The letter *k* in *ktri* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* substitution.

89. *ṭvito'thuc* | (3.3.89) [The example] "vepathuḥ" [is given]. Trembling (*vepanam*) is indeed "vepathuḥ. Since both of these [roots ending in *ṭu* and those ending in *i*] inherently occur in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*), this [suffix *athuc*] is understood as an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ghañ*. However, the suffix *ghañ* does not apply even by the rule of optional forms (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*).
It occurs; because it is not so designated. Furthermore, the letter *c* in *athuc* is for the sake of accent (*svara*). The letter *c* in *athuc* serves the purpose of accentuation.

90. The suffix *naṅ* is applied after the verbal roots *yaj*, *yāc*, *yat*, *vicch*, *prach*, and *rakṣ*. *yaja* (in the sense of worshiping the gods, etc. [DhP 1002], *yāc* (in the sense of begging) [DhP 863], *yat* (in the sense of effort) [DhP 30], and *vicch* (in the sense of going).

Regarding the roots *pracccha* (DhP 1413) in the sense of "desire to know" and *rakṣa* (DhP 658) in the sense of "protection"— since [the suffix] *naṅ* is inherent [in these cases], and because the word *yāc* and others ending in the suffix *naṅ* function in the masculine, the suffix *naṅ* is not an exception (*apavāda*) to *ghañ*.
