It occurs accordingly; and by the rule of optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhāna*), the suffix *ghañ* also occurs—as in *yāga*.
However, because *yācñā* is by its very nature a word ending in the suffix *naṅ*, it functions in the feminine;
therefore, this [suffix *naṅ*] is an exception to the application of the suffix *ā* that would otherwise be obtained by the rule *gurośca halaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.103).

Because of the rule "kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam" (Pāṇini 3.3.113), the provision for non-identical forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*) does not apply here. The statement "the letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of prohibiting [the substitution of] *guṇa*" means that this is intended so that the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) does not occur in the root *vicch*. But surely, because it is *antaraṅga*, the *tuk* augment prescribed by "che ca" (Pāṇini 6.1.73) would apply first?

In that case, there must be an investigation: since the guna substitution will not occur simply because the root has a non-light (alaghūpadha) penultimate vowel, why should the letter *ṅ* be added for the purpose of its prohibition?
And this addition of *ṅ* to the augment *naṅ* is precisely [the application] of the rule "the teaching regarding augments is not eternal" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 99).

It is an indicator (*jñāpaka*). If, then, because it is not eternal (*anityatva*), the augment *tuṭ* is not applied, then the substitution of *ś* for the *cch* sound—as prescribed by the rule *ṭhcchÂavoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.19)—which is enjoined for the *cch* sound accompanied by the augment *tuṭ*, would not apply to the simple [sound] *cch*. This is not a fault, because:

The notation "cch-avoḥ" contains two *cch* characters; therein, one is accompanied by the *tuk* augment, while the second is alone. Therefore, the substitution of *ś* will occur even for the [second] *cch* that is alone. However, if the notation "cch-avoḥ" were intended as a dual ending containing two *cch* characters, it would not [apply].

[Objection: Does [the fault] not arise because there are many *sthānins*? [Response: Since this is a sūtra-style designation, the dual number will occur by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*) instead of the plural;
thus, there is no fault. Furthermore, the mention of two *ch*s must necessarily be made;
otherwise, in the rule "ṛāllopaḥ" (6.4.21), the elision (*lopa*) would not apply to the solitary [ṛ].
It might be so, because the mere letter *c* cannot be the cause;

rather, the statement [of the rule] must be for the sake of the elision of the letter *v*. Thus, in "yajñaḥ" and "yācñā," by the rule "stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.40), the letter *n* becomes *ñ* through the substitution of *ścu* for *ścu*. In "yatnaḥ," [the rule] "neḍ... [applies].
In *vaśikṛti* (7.2.8), there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*. [Examples are] *viśnaḥ* and *praśnaḥ*;

here, by the rule *cchavoḥ* (6.4.19) and so forth, the substitute *ś* is applied in place of the letter *cch*. In *rakṣṇaḥ*, the letter *ṇ* is substituted for the letter *n* by the rule *ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ* (8.4.41). Now, regarding the root *pracchi*:

One might ask why the *samprasāraṇa* substitution prescribed by the sūtra *grahijyā...* (Pāṇini 6.1.16) does not occur in the word *praśnaḥ*. To this, he says: "of the root *pracch*" and so forth. He asks what the indicator (*jñāpaka*) is, and replies: "and in the case of *praśna*" and so forth.
*upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ* (3.3.92). [The rule states: "The suffix *ki* occurs. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ghañ*. "The purpose of making it *kit* is for the sake of elision (*lopa*)."
This is so that the elision of the vowel *ā* may occur according to the rule "ṭhāto lopa iṭi ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.64).
93. *karmaṇy adhikaraṇe ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.93).

Because the object (*karman*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) are mentioned separately from the locative case [in the rule], neither of them functions as an *upapada*, nor do they constitute the meaning of the suffix; therefore, something else must serve as the *upapada* in that context.

The meaning of the suffix is "something" (*kiñcit*). The object (*karman*) is the *upapada*, while the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the meaning of the suffix. He says—"when the object is the *upapada*" and so forth—stating that this distinction is understood from the explanatory commentaries (*vyākhyāna*) and from observing the usage in the examples (*lakṣyadarśana*). Now, for what purpose is the mention of "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*), given that [the rule] states "and when [the suffix is applied] to a factor other than the agent (*akartari ca kārake*)"?
Is the suffix obtained for the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) solely through the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of this [rule]? To this he says:

"The mention of 'locus' (*adhikaraṇagrahaṇam*)," and so forth. For if the mention of "locus" were absent, the suffix under discussion would apply even to other meanings—such as the abstract state (*bhāva*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and other *kāraka*s; therefore [the mention is necessary].
The term "locus" (adhikaraṇa) is included in order to exclude that [fault].
94. *striyāṃ ktin* (Pāṇini 3.3.94).
[The phrase] "in the sense of bhāva and so forth" (*bhāvādau*): by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of a *kāraka* other than the agent (*akartaḥ*).

[The phrase] "an exception to *ghañ*, *ac*, *ap*, and *am*" (*ghañajapāmapavādaḥ*): among those [roots] ending in *i*, this is an exception to *ac*; as for those [ending in other vowels], it is an exception to *ap*.
Those ending in *ṛ* and those ending in *u*: from these, the suffix *ap*; from the remaining [roots], the suffix *ghañ*.

"It should be stated" (*vaktavya*) means it should be explained. The explanation, however, should be made by relying on the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.113). [Examples such as] *āptiḥ* and so forth; [the root is] *āplṛ*.

The roots *vyāp* (DhP 1260) "to pervade," *rādha* and *sādha* (DhP 1262) "to accomplish," *dīpī* (DhP 1150) "to shine," *sraṃsu* and *dhvaṃsu* (DhP 754, 755) "to fall down," and *ḍulabhaṣ* (DhP 975) "to obtain. [The form] *labhet* [is derived] because of its being marked with the *ṣit* designation.

Since the suffix *aṅ* would otherwise apply by the rule *ṭhṣidbhidādibhyo'ṅ* (Pāṇini 3.3.104), the suffix *ktin* is prescribed instead for the remaining roots—due to their being heavy (*guru*)—by the rule *ṭhgurośca halaḥ* (3.3.103). Thus we have *iṣṭiḥ*. In the case of *vac* and other such roots, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) according to the rule *vacyādisūtreṇa* (6.1.15); hence *kīrṇiḥ*, *gīrṇiḥ*, and *śīrṇiḥ*.
Thus: by the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.100), there is the substitution of *i* for *ṛ*; and by the rule concerning *raṣādi-* (8.4.1), there is the substitution of *ṇ*.

Just as in the form *kīrṇa*, the substitution of *n* for the *t* of the suffix *niṣṭhā* occurs according to the rule *radābhyām* (8.2.42) and others, so too does it occur here for the suffix *ktin*. And just as in the form *lūna* [the substitution of *n* for *t* occurs] according to the rule *lvādibhyaḥ* (8.2.44).
In this case, there is the substitution of *n* for the final *t* of the suffix *niṣṭhā*; likewise, in forms such as *lūniḥ* and *yūniḥ*, the same applies to the suffix *ktin*.

95. *sthā-gā-pā-aci bhāve* (Pāṇini 3.3.95). [The commentary states: "It is an exception (*bādhaka*) to the exception (*apavāda*) regarding *ṭhaṅ*. The meaning is that it subverts the exception (*apavāda*) of *aṅ* which would otherwise apply by the rule *sthādibhyaḥ ṭhaṅ ātaścopasarge* (3.3.106). Example: *paktiḥ*.

This refers to [the rule] *ṭhṣidbhidādibhyo'ṅ* (Pāṇini 3.3.104). Regarding *prasthitiḥ*: by the rule *ṭhdyatisyati* (7.4.40) etc., *itva* (the substitution of *i*) occurs. Regarding *saṅgītiḥ*: by the rule *dhumāsthāgāpājahātisām hali* (6.4.66), *itva* occurs. And here, according to the maxim *gāmādāgrahaṇeṣvaviśeṣaḥ* (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 124), [the root] *gai-*...
In the case of the root *śabda* (DhP 9.17), there is the inclusion of both [roots], namely *gāṅ* "to go" (DhP 9.50).
Regarding *pā*, as before, it is the inclusion of the sense of "drinking," not the sense of "protecting.
The phrase "the inclusion of the abstract state (*bhāva*)" and so forth means that another meaning, excluding the agent (*kartṛ*), is the object (*karman*).
To prevent that [undesired application], the term *bhāva* (abstract state) is included.

As for the question beginning with "How? and so on: if this suffix *ktin* is an exception to an exception of the suffix *aṅ*, then how is the form *avasthā* (state) or *saṃsthā* (arrangement) established? The intention is that it cannot be established in any way.

Regarding the phrase "in the sense of *vyavasthā*," etc.: this very recitation of the word *vyavasthā* ending in the suffix *aṅ* within the Sūtra is itself the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that there is no absolute supersession (*atyantabādha*) by the suffix *ktin*;
therefore, forms such as *avasthā* are also established. Regarding "for the sake of *atyantāya*": this is a word that imitates a form ending in the dative case.
This is a particle, just like [the word] *cirāya*.
96. In the case of *mantre*, [the suffixes] *vṛṣ*, *iṣ*, *pac*, *man*, *vid*, *bhū*, and *vīr* are udātta.

(Pāṇini 3.3.96) *vṛṣu* and *mṛṣu* are in the sense of "to sprinkle" (Dhātupāṭha 706, 707); *iṣu* is in the sense of "desire" (Dhātupāṭha 1351); *ḍupacaṣ* is in the sense of "cooking" (Dhātupāṭha 996); and *mana* is in the sense of "knowing."
(dhā.pā.1176), *ṭhvida* in the sense of "knowledge" (dhā.pā.1064), *ṭhbhū* in the sense of "existence" (dhā.pā.1),
*ṭhvī* in the senses of "motion," "pervasion," "procreation," and so forth (dhā.pā.1048),
and *ṭhrā* in the sense of "giving" and "taking" (dhā.pā.1057). [The rule applies] to both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*).

The dual number is used because there is an intention to express the commonality of the *prakṛti*s; otherwise, since there are many *prakṛti*s, the plural would have been required. [The phrase] "the connection is by means of changing the case-ending" means that the nominative which follows after *vṛṣan* and so forth is, by implication, changed into the ablative. By that—
There is a relationship between the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), for otherwise a relationship would be untenable. [The example] "matiḥ":
by the rule beginning with *anudātopadeśa* (Pāṇini 6.4.37), there is the elision of the nasal.
[The phrase] "in all cases" and so forth: both in mantras and in non-mantras—in all cases, [the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] after words such as *vṛṣan*.

But [the suffix] is prescribed here by the rule *sthāgāpāpaco bhāve* (Pāṇini 3.3.95). If this is so, he asks "For what purpose is this? and replies: "For the sake of the udātta accent. Regarding "of *iṣ*, however," etc.:
he will state the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) of *iṣ* as *icchā*; therefore, the suffix *ktin* is prescribed, otherwise...

This [form] would be established by means of irregular derivation (*nipātana*) alone. The suffix *ktin* itself should be prescribed after roots such as *vṛṣ*. The mention of the acute accent (*udātta*) is for the sake of what follows, so that the suffix *kyap*—as in "the suffix *kyap* is added in the sense of abstract action (*bhāva*) after the roots *vraj* and *yaj*" (Pāṇini 3.3.98)—may be acute.

97. *ūti*, *yūti*, *jūti*, *sāti*, *heti*, and *kīrti* [are formed with the suffix *ktin*]. (3.3.97) The statement "the mention [of these roots] is for the sake of the accent" (*svarārthaṃ vacanam*) means that it is not for the sake of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtham*), because [the feminine form] is already established by the rule *striyāṃ ktin* (3.3.94). Nor is it for the sake of the substitution of *ūṭh*; for that is already accomplished by the rule *jvaratvara-* (6.4.20), etc.

Because [the form] is established: "from *yu*" refers to the root *yu* in the sense of "mixing" (*miśraṇe*) or "not mixing" (*amiśraṇe ca*), according to the Dhātupāṭha (1033). "And from *ju*" refers to the root *ju*, which is mentioned in the Sūtra (Pāṇini 3.2.150). "And lengthening" means that by the word "and" (*ca*), high-pitched accent (*udāttatva*) is also included. The suffix is *ktin*.

It is established by the general characteristic [of the rule] alone. Regarding the statement "from the root *ṣṭhīv*": this refers to the root *ṣo* in the sense of "concluding an action" (*antakarmaṇi*, DhP 1147). It is stated that "the absence of *it* is also a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). Since [the rule] *dyatisyati-* (Pāṇini 7.4.40) and so forth would require the substitution of *it*, its absence is thus prescribed as an irregularity. Alternatively, [it may be derived] from the root *san*.

Thus [it refers to] the root *ṣaṇ* in the sense of "giving" (*dāna*) from Dhātupāṭha 1464. The remainder is that once the substitution of *ā* for the vowel of *jan*, *san*, and *khan* has been applied by Pāṇini 6.4.42, the form *sāti* is established. If this is so, he asks: for what purpose is there a formal rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*)? He replies: "For the sake of the accent," and so forth. For if the irregular derivation were not present...

The word *sāti* would otherwise have its initial syllable accented acute (*ādyaudāta*); this is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) intended so that it may instead have its final syllable accented acute (*antodāta*). [This is explained by the rule] "from the root *han* or from *hi* and *nī*. When it is derived from *han*, the substitution of *e* for the letter *ha* is irregularly prescribed (*nipātyate*), while the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) follows from the rule "the nasal of a root taught with an udātta accent... (*anudātopadeśa...*) [which prescribes the elision of the nasal of such roots when followed by a suffix beginning with *t*].

This is already established by [Pāṇini 6.4.37] and similar rules. However, when [the root] *kṛ* in the sense of "to go" or "to perceive" (DhP 157) is intended, then the *guṇa* substitution is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*), resulting in the form *kīrtiḥ*.

Furthermore, from the root *kṛt* meaning "to sound" (DhP 1653), which belongs to the *curādi* class and takes the causative suffix (*ṇic*), [the form *kīrtanam* is derived] by [Pāṇini 6.1.49]: *ṇyāsa-śrantho yuc*.

Since the suffix *yuc* would otherwise apply by rule 3.3.107 (*yuc*), *ktin* is prescribed as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). By rule 7.1.101 (*upadhāyāśca*), the substitution of *i* occurs for the penultimate vowel, and by rule 8.2.77 (*hali ca*), lengthening takes place.
98. The suffix *kyap* is applied after the roots *vraj* and *yaj* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*).
[The form is] *ijyā*. There is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule *vacyādi* (Pāṇini 6.1.15). If [the accent] is prescribed as udātta, he asks:
"What is the purpose of adding the marker *p*? and replies: "The addition of the marker *p* is for the sake of what follows," and so forth.

99. *saṃjñāyāṃ samajaniṣadanipatamanavidaṣuñśīṅbhṛñiṇaḥ* (3.3.99). "The term *bhāva* is not [here] indicated by its accent" (*bhāva iti na svaryate*), etc. The fact that the mention of *bhāva* was made in the rule *sthāgādisūtra* (3.3.95) is not here treated as having a svarita accent. [This refers to the rule] *bhāve* (3.3.18) and *akartari ca...* (3.3.19).

The governing rule (*adhikāra*) is precisely this: "When [the suffix] *kyaṅ* follows a verbal root denoting an agent, provided it is a name" (Pāṇini 3.1.19). Regarding the word *samajyā*, the substitution of *vī* for the root *aj* does not occur by virtue of the rule "The substitution of *vī* for *aj* occurs except before the suffixes *ghañ* and *ap*" (Pāṇini 2.4.56); this is because of the explicit statement "provided it is a name. For once the substitution of *vī* has been applied, the specific name is no longer understood, as a name consists of a fixed sequence of phonemes.

For there is a notion [of this]. "Nipatyā" means "they fall upon it. [The root] *sad* (DhP 854) [is used in the sense of] "falling apart," "going," and "sinking down"; thus, "they sit down upon it. "Nipatyā" means "they fall upon it. "Matyā" means "they think by means of it."

By the rule *matyā* (Pāṇini 6.1.97), as before, there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*), and by the rule for the short vowel, there is the augment *tuk*. They know by means of that: *vidyā*. They press [the Soma] in that: *sutyā*. They lie down in that: *śayyā*. By the rule *ṭhayaṅ yi kṅiti* (7.4.22), there is the substitution of *ayaṅ*. The act of supporting is *bhṛtyā*. She goes by means of that: *ā u*.
Regarding the term *ayana*:
in the rule *bhṛño'saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 3.1.112), it is said:
"Because [the suffix] is seen in the masculine when it is a name (*saṃjñā*), your *bhāryā* is not established [as a feminine form]."
The suffix expressing abstract state (bhāvādhikara) occurs in the feminine; by that means, the word "bhāryā" (wife) is established.

This has been stated; here it was declared that "the term *bhāva* is not accented" (Kāśikā 3.3.98). Therefore, considering the previously cited statement to be contradictory, he asks: "How? and so forth.
If *bhāve* (3.3.18) is not accented here, then how [is it applied] in the feminine?

It was stated that "there is the governing authority of *bhāva*"; for if the term "*bhāve*" were not being recited [as a governing heading], the existence of the governing authority of *bhāva* here would not be tenable. The resolution is as follows:
"The governing authority of *bhāva* is the operation (*vyāpāra*) of the *bhāvya*," and so forth; by the term "governing authority of *bhāva*," the operation therein [is meant].
It is intended as that which is to be expressed. Furthermore, it is characterized by the attainment of the state of being denoted by the word *bhṛtyatva* (servitude).

For this very reason, it is said: "The state (*bhāva*) itself becomes the denotation of the word *bhṛtya*, which has been derived [as a taddhita formation] by the rule 'saṃjñāyāṃ samajaniṣada... and so forth; it does not [denote the individual servant]."

The *kāraka* [is defined] as being devoid of an agent (*kartṛ*). By this, it is established that when the *kāraka* is the object (*karman*), the form *bhāryā* is derived. However, this is not a scriptural authority (*śāstrīya-adhikāra*), because it does not apply to usage due to the absence of the *svarita* accent; let it not be intended there by the word "state" (*bhāva*). In that [place], they assemble; hence it is called *samajyā*.

Regarding such expressions as "they sit on that seat" (*niṣīdanti tasyāṃ niṣadyā*) or "one knows by means of this knowledge" (*vidantyanayā vidyā*), there is no lack of grammatical correctness (*asādhutva*) because [the suffix -ya] is applied to the *karaṇa* (instrument) and other *kārakas*. But how is it that [Pāṇini’s rule] states: "In the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*), and when not denoting an agent (*akartari*), [the suffix -ya is applied] to a *kāraka*"? (3.3.18, 19).

When [the suffix] *an* applies in all cases, how is it that in some instances the state of being (*bhāva*) becomes the expressed meaning of a word ending in a *kyap* suffix, while in other instances it refers solely to the non-agentive factor (*akartṛkāraka*)? This restriction is obtained by virtue of technical designation (*saṃjñā*).
Where a technical designation is understood through the suffix being produced, there the state of being alone constitutes the expressed meaning.

One engages with one [meaning] while remaining indifferent toward the other. However, where a designation (*saṃjñā*) is understood from a suffix produced for a non-agentive *kāraka*, that [non-agentive *kāraka*] becomes its expressed meaning, while the abstract state (*bhāva*) maintains indifference. This is according to the rule: "And [the suffixes] after a non-agentive *kāraka* when a designation is intended" (Pāṇini 3.3.19).

Thus, while the term "technical designation" (*saṃjñā*) is already understood from the preceding context, its mention here again is for the sake of expressing the abstract state (*bhāva*); for the previous mention of "technical designation" was connected with a grammatical factor (*kāraka*) that lacks an agent (*akartṛka*). Consequently, the designation would apply only to a *kāraka* other than the agent, and not to the abstract state (*bhāva*). Therefore, it is stated [again] so that the designation applies even to the abstract state.

The term "saṃjñā" (name/designation) is mentioned again for the purpose that it may be so [that the suffix applies]. Now, how is it that *bhṛtiḥ*, *matiḥ*, and *āsutīḥ* are formed? It is by means of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). What, then, is this irregular derivation? [It is based on the rules: "after a verbal root meaning 'to hire' when there is an object" (Pāṇini 3.2.22), "and after roots meaning 'intellect', 'understanding', or 'reverence'" (3.2.188), and "after *rajas*, *kṛṣi*, *āsuti*, and *pariṣad*" (3.3.96).
[This is] by [the rule] *valac* (Pāṇini 5.2.112).

100. *kṛñaḥ śa ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.100). It is said here that "a separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must be made. First, there is *kyap* after the root *kṛ*; then, *śa* also [is applied], as well as whatever was already obtained [by previous rules]. Thus, three forms are established. Among them, regarding the rule "after *kṛ*"...

By means of *yoga*, the form *kṛtyā* is established; and by the rule *ṭhśa ca*, the two forms *kriyā* and *kṛtiḥ* are produced. When the word is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), then by the rules *sārvadhātuke yak* (Pāṇini 3.1.67) and *riṅ śayagliṅkṣu* (7.4.24), the substitution of *riṅ* occurs. When...
When the agent is not the grammatical subject (*akartari kārake*), then because there is no *ya*-affix, after the suffix *cha* alone has been applied, the substitute *iṅ* is made for the verbal root;
then, by the rule "ṭhaci śnudhātu" (Pāṇini 6.4.77), the *iyaṅ* substitution occurs for that [root].
The letter *ś* is for the sake of [marking] the *sārvadhātuka* affixes.

101. *icchā* (Pāṇini 3.3.101). The suffix *śa* occurs after the root *iṣ* in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*), due to the inherent capacity of the word’s expressive power, and not in the sense of a grammatical participant (*kāraka*).
[The sūtra also states] "and there is the absence of *ya*. Otherwise, by the rule "yak is applied before a sārvadhātuka suffix" (3.1.67), the suffix *yak* would have occurred.
Therefore, its absence is prescribed [by the rule] *ṭhicchā*. The substitution of *cch* occurs by the rule *ṭhiṣugami* (Pāṇini 7.3.77).
Regarding *paricaryā* and so forth: the root *cara* means "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 559), and *sṛ* means "to go."

From the roots *mṛg* (DhP 965) in the sense of "searching," which is an anudātta-ending root in the curādigaṇa; *aṭ* and *paṭ* (DhP 295, 296) in the sense of "going"—from these, the suffix *śa* is applied in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*). As before, *yaK* is added, and for the root *sṛ*, there is guṇa. For *mṛgayati*, there is no elision of the vowel *a*; however, by the rule *ṇer aniṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.51), there is the elision of the *ṇiC* suffix.

Regarding *ṭhaṭāṭaḷa*: from the root *aṭ*, there is reduplication and the substitution of *t* for the reduplicated syllable. Regarding *jāgarti*: when the suffix *śa* is applied, then by *sārvadhātuke yak* (3.1.67) and *jāgro 'viciṇṇalṅtsu* (7.3.85), there is *guṇa*. When it is *jāgarā*...
The letter *tv*.

Since the governing rule *dhātoḥ* (3.1.91) is in force, the mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*) is understood as a qualifier of the verbal root (*dhātu*); thus he says: "from verbal roots ending in affixes. For example: *cikīrṣā*.

From the word *cikīrṣa*, which ends in the desiderative suffix (*san*), the suffix *a* is applied. Regarding *putrīyā*: by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8), the suffix *kyac* is added; then, by the rule *kyaci ca* (7.4.33), the vowel *i* is substituted [for the final vowel of the stem]. Regarding *putrakāmyā*:
by the rule *kāmyacca* (3.1.9), the suffix *kāmyac* is added. Regarding *lolūyā*: [this is derived] from a root consisting of a single syllable...
The suffix *yaṅ* [is applied] by [the rule] *halādeḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.22).

103. *gurośca halaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.103). Since the governing rule *dhātoḥ* (3.1.91) is in force, it is understood that the mention of *guru-* and the mention of *hal-* serve as qualifiers for that very [root]. Thus he says: "that root which has a heavy vowel (*gurumān*) and ends in a consonant (*halantaḥ*)," and so forth.

But how, when it is said "of the guru," is a verbal root (dhātu) possessing a *guru* [vowel] obtained? By implication (*sāmarthyāt*). For no designation of *guru* has been prescribed for any verbal root ending in a consonant (*halanta*);
yet this term "of the guru" is stated. Therefore, by implication, it refers to that which possesses a *guru*.

It is understood that the word *guru* is used by applying a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) between the element (*dhātu*) and its designation; for it is accepted that, even without the possessive suffix *-mat*, there is a denotation of both the quality and the possessor through metaphorical identification—as in "the white cloth. Now, [this rule] should apply only to the roots beginning with *rudh*.

Why is the reverse interpretation—that the rule applies to roots ending in a consonant (*hal*) that have a heavy vowel (*guru*)—not understood for the sake of preventing [the application] to *kuḍi* and so forth? It is because of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), namely this:
"The second and fourth cases are used for the object of a verb meaning 'motion' when there is physical effort, provided it is not a path" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.12).

Thus, he provides the citation of the word *ceṣṭā*, which does not end in a suffix, and the word *śaṅkā*, [derived] from the root *śaki* in the sense of "doubt" (Dhātupāṭha 86); from this it is known that there is no reversal here. For in the case of a reversal, [the forms] would not be *ceṣṭā* ending in a heavy vowel (*gurvant*), nor would they be *śaṅkā*. [The form] *kuṇḍā*...

And so forth. These are the forms of the following roots: *kuḍi* in the sense of burning (*dāhe*, Dhātupāṭha 270); *huḍi* in the sense of heaping together (*saṅghāte*, Dhātupāṭha 269); *īha* in the sense of movement (*ceṣṭāyām*, Dhātupāṭha 632); and *ūha* in the sense of deliberation (*vitarke*, Dhātupāṭha 648).

104. *ṣidbhidādibhyo'ṅ* (Pāṇini 3.3.104). Regarding the phrase "among those enumerated in the *gaṇa*" and so forth: the roots beginning with *bhid* are listed in the *gaṇa* as already ending in the suffix *aṅ*. If, however, *aṅ* were prescribed here again for nominal stems (*prātipadika*), [it would be redundant].
And that would be incorrect, because the context concerns verbal roots (*dhātu*). Therefore, those bases which constitute parts within them are extracted and set apart;
they are then indicated by the mention of the *bhidādi* group in the rule "after *ṭh*, *sidh*, and the *bhidādi* group, [the suffix] *aṅ*. Furthermore, those [bases]...

*bhid* in the sense of splitting (*vidāraṇe*), *chid* in the sense of dividing into two (*dvaidhīkaraṇe*), *vid* in the sense of knowing (*jñāne*), *kṣip* in the sense of throwing or impelling (*preraṇe*),
*guh* in the sense of concealing (*saṃvaraṇe*), and *ḍudhāñ* in the sense of supporting and nourishing (*dhāraṇapoṣaṇayoḥ*).
(dhā.pā.1092), *ṭhpmidṛ* [in the Dhātupāṭha] means "to injure" (medhāhiṃsanayoḥ); *pmedṛ* [in the Dhātupāṭha] means "also to meet" (*saṅgame ca*);

*medhṛ* means "to injure and to afflict" (*hiṃsāsaṃkleśanayoḥ*) (dhā.pā.868, 869); *ṛ* means "to go" (dhā.pā.1098); *hṛñ* means "to take away" (*haraṇe*) (dhā.pā.899); *hukṛñ* means "to do" (*karaṇe*).

(dhā.pā.1472), *kṣi* in the sense of destruction (dhā.pā.236), or *kṣi* in the sense of dwelling and going (dhā.pā.1407), *tṛ* in the sense of leaping and crossing (dhā.pā.969), *ghṛñ* in the sense of holding (900),
*likha* in the sense of arranging letters (dhā.pā.1365), *cuda*...

*psañcodana* (to impel) [Dhātupāṭha]; *samucchraya* (to rise up) [Dhātupāṭha 1592]; *pīḍa* (to press down or immerse) [Dhātupāṭha 1544]; *ḍuvapa* (to sow seeds, to weave, and also to cut) [Dhātupāṭha 1003]; *vasa* (to dwell) [Dhātupāṭha 1942].

The roots *mṛj* (in the sense of "purification") from Dhātupāṭha 1066 and *krap* (in the sense of "compassion" and "going") from Dhātupāṭha 771 are to be understood [as included]. If, then, the verbal roots (*prakṛti*) are being specified, is the recitation of *bhid* and the others in the list (*gaṇa*) useless? Or, on the other hand, if they are indeed recited...

Is the formulation of the rule [for] suffixes purposeless? The recitation in the *gaṇa* is certainly not purposeless, because it serves to include well-known forms. The inclusion of well-known forms is so that their grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) may apply only where these groups, such as *bhidā* and others, are already established, and not elsewhere.
The purpose is so that [the suffix] may occur. By this, what was stated in the Bhāṣya—namely, "bhidā in the sense of splitting" (Gaṇasūtra 29), and so forth—becomes justified.
Nor is the prescription of the suffix meaningless, because it serves to eliminate ambiguity. For if it were not there, doubt would arise: "In these cases..."

By such other rules as "ṭhigupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.135), are suffixes beginning with *ka* prescribed, or is it only the suffix *aṅ*? If the former position is taken, then when femininity is intended to be expressed, the suffix *ktin* would result; why so?
Because it serves to eliminate doubt, the prescription of the suffix is not purposeless. Regarding "ārā":
[the rule] "ṛdṛśo'ṅ guṇiḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.16) applies.
Regarding "guhā": [the rule] "guhā giryyoṣadhyoḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.105) applies; the word *guhā* occurs only in the sense of a mountain (*giri*) or a medicinal herb (*oṣadhi*).

It is correct [to say *guhā*], and not otherwise. Furthermore, the word *giri* here refers to a single part [of a mountain], according to the principle: "Words used for wholes also apply to their parts" (*Vyākaraṇa-pāṭha-sūtra* 85). By *guhā*, a certain specific part of a mountain is meant. *Guha* is the name of a medicinal herb; [the term is used] elsewhere than in the sense of a cave (*guha*).
The suffix *ktin* occurs—as in *gūḍhiḥ*. [The following rules apply: *ṭhho ḍhaḥ* (8.2.31); *ṭhjhatastathorgho'ghaḥ* (8.2.40);
*ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ* (8.4.41); *ḍho ḍhea lopaḥ* (8.3.13);
*ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho'ṇaḥ* (6.3.111). [Examples are] *hārā*, *kārā*, *dhārā*. When the *guṇa* has been applied...

The lengthening [of the vowel] is an irregularity (nipātana). In the case of *rekhā* and *lekha*, the *guṇa* substitution for the root *likh* is an irregularity; alternatively, there is the substitution of *ra* for the letter *la*. In the case of *cūḍā*, the substitution of *ḍa* for [the final consonant] of the root *cud* is an irregularity, as is the lengthening of the penultimate vowel. The word *ārā* means "an iron bar" (*śastra*). Thus ends the word *ārā*.
It is correct [to derive] *śastrī*; here too, when the suffix *guṇa* has been applied, lengthening is introduced by way of *nipātana*.

Regarding "ṭhārtiranyā": the word *ārti* is formed from the root *ṛ* preceded by the prefix *ā-* with the suffix *ktin*. There is a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) according to Pāṇini 6.1.91, "When a vowel follows a prefix ending in *ṛ*, [the substitute is the long vowel]," and then the substitution of *ra* for the semivowel (*raparatva*). Regarding "ṭhdhārā prapāte": where there is a falling down (*prapātana*).
In that regard, it is maintained as follows: "a stream of water," "a stream of milk."

105. *cintipūjikathikumbacarcaśca* (Pāṇini 3.3.105). [The word] "ṭhcurādiḥ" (belonging to the curādi group) is connected individually with each of the roots beginning with *citi smṛtyām* (Dhātupāṭha 1535). Regarding the phrase "when *yuc* would have been obtained," [the rule is]: "After roots ending in *ṇi*, *āsa*, *sraṃs*, and *śranth*, *yuc* is applied."

By this [rule, 3.3.107]. However, since *kumbi* is listed in the *bhvādi* class, the suffix *a* should apply by virtue of Pāṇini 3.3.103 (*gurośca halaḥ*). And since there is no difference whether the suffix *a* or *iṅ* follows *kumb*, that root does not necessitate its inclusion here.

106. *ātaścopasarge* (Pāṇini 3.3.106). [The rule] beginning with *śradantaroḥ*. "Like an upasarga" means as if it were an upasarga. Whatever operation occurs upon an upasarga—characterized by the production of suffixes—that very same operation occurs for those two [words *śrat* and *antara*] as well. Thus, just as in *pradhā*,...

The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the prefix *upa*, as well as after *śrad* and *antar*, forming the words *śraddhā* and *antardhā*. Nor is this grammatical derivation dependent on a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*), because the word *śraddhā* attains its correctness through its inclusion in the *tārakādi* group [of the *gaṇa* sūtra Pāṇini 3.1.22]. The word *antardhā* also [attains its correctness] by virtue of an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), namely that—

In the rule *antar-dhā-ya-nā-darśa-nam-i-ccha-ti* (Pāṇini 1.4.28), he provides the citation of the word *antardhi* ending in the suffix *ki*; from this it is understood that the word *antar* serves as the cause for the operation of an *upasarga*. Otherwise, if that were not the case, [the rule] *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ* (3.3.92) would apply when that [word *antar*] is the governing term (*upapada*).
Thus, the *kip* suffix would not occur, and consequently, the grammatical reference "in the sense of disappearance" (*ṭhantardhau*) would be untenable.
107. *ṇyāsaśrantho yuc* (Pāṇini 3.3.107).
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṭhak*. It supersedes what is obtained as appropriate by the two rules: *ṭha pratyayāt* (3.3.102) and *gurośca halaḥ* (3.3.103).

"How can there be [the suffix] *asya*?"—in no way at all. The intention is that *asya* would arise from the root *ās*, and by this very rule (*āsaḥ*), it will be joined with *yuc*, and not anything else. The phrase "by the rule *ṛhalorṇyat*" (Pāṇini 3.1.124), etc., is the rebuttal. But surely, by the rule regarding optional forms (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*), the suffix *ṇyat* would also apply; and that—

The rule regarding optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*) does not apply in the feminine, because of the prohibition stated in *ṭhastriyām* (Pāṇini 3.1.94). Therefore, why is it said that the suffix *ṇyat* will occur by virtue of *ṛhalorṇyat* (Pāṇini 3.1.124)? To this he replies: "The rule *vāsarūpa*... and so forth. And this meaning is established in that very same [sūtra].
It has been established.
The term "supplementary addition" (upasaṃkhyāna) means "establishment" (pratipādana). In this regard, the establishment is as follows:
the upcoming mention of the term *bahula* ("in many cases") is a supplement to both rules; by means of it—
The suffix *bhaviṣya* shall apply after roots such as *ghaṭṭi*; this must be stated. The meaning is that it should be explained.
That explanation is to be made by relying on the very mention of the term *bahula*. Regarding the word *anveṣaṇā*: [it is derived from] *iṣ* "to go" (DhP 1127) or *iṣ* "repetition" (?).

108. *rogākhyāyāṃ ṇvul bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.108). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to suffixes such as *kṛt*, *tin*, and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), suffixes like *aṅ* are included. Regarding the phrase "the mention of *ākhyā*," etc.: if the word ending in this suffix is indeed the name of a disease, then this suffix occurs.

The mention of "ākhya" (name/designation) is for the purpose of providing corroboration for the rule "nānyathā" (not otherwise). It does not apply when the disease is expressed by another word—for instance, in the case of *bubhukṣā* (hunger) or *bhasmaka* (a specific digestive disorder). Regarding the phrase "bahulagrahaṇam" (the mention of the term *bahula*), there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that the suffix *ṇvul* is prescribed even outside the context of naming a disease.
The inclusion of the term *bahulam* (diversely) is for that purpose. By means of it, the rule becomes established even when there is a mention of the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*).

Another purpose is this: there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the application of this rule in other instances where it would otherwise apply—specifically regarding the prescription of the suffix *ṇvul* after words denoting diseases—and the inclusion of *bahulam* is for that purpose. By means of it...

By this [rule], everything beginning with "ṭhikśtipau dhātunirdeśe" (Vārttika 319) is included. Regarding "praccchardikā": the root *ccharda* meaning "vomiting" belongs to the curādigaṇa (dhātu-pāṭha 1589).
Regarding "pravāhikā": the root *vaha* meaning "to convey" (dhātu-pāṭha 1004). Regarding "pracarcikā": the root *carca*...

The root *adhyayi* (DhP 1712) belongs to the *curādi* class. Here, while the suffix *ktin* would have been expected after the root *vah*, the suffix *ṇvul* is applied; however, for the other two [roots], the suffix *yuc* is applied. Regarding the term *śiro'sti*: the root *harda* (DhP 1828) means "to injure," while the root *arda* (DhP 55) means "to go" or "to beg."
Or [alternatively]: by *ṭhkhari ca* (8.4.55), there is the substitution of *c*. There is a genitive compound with *śiras*;

by *sasajuṣo ruḥ* (8.2.66), *ru* is substituted; by *ato roraplutādaplute* (6.1.113), *u* is substituted; by *ādguṇaḥ* (6.1.87), *guṇa* is substituted; and by *eṅḥ padāntādati* (6.1.109), these [rules apply].
The suffixes [tiP etc.

are to be prescribed by the rule "ṭhikśtipau. The letter *k* is for the purpose of the operations pertaining to *kit* suffixes; by means of it, in the form *pacati*, the substitution of *śa* occurs, which is conditioned by a *sārvadhātuka* suffix. But [one might object] that when [the suffix] denotes the agent...

The *śap* affix is prescribed for *sārvadhātuka* suffixes; however, in this case, the agent is not the meaning of the suffix. Therefore, how could there be the occurrence of *śap*? [Answer: By virtue of the power of the inclusion of the marker *ś* for the purpose of designating the term *sārvadhātuka*, *śap* will occur even when the *sārvadhātuka* suffix does not express the agent. Otherwise, the inclusion of the marker *ś* would be purposeless.

If this is so, would it not also apply in other cases? It will not apply because it is not so stated. [The rule] says "kāra after a phoneme" (*varṇāt*); in that case, how is *evakāra* not established?
There is no fault, for by virtue of the statement made in proximity to the mention of the term *bahulam* ("diversely"), it will occur in some instances even after what is not a phoneme.

Alternatively, *kāra* is [derived from] the root *kṛ*, and this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the making (*kāra*) of *eva*. According to the rule "the suffix *cha* is added after a word expressing possession" (*matvarthīya*), the elision of the letter *a* must be stated here; for otherwise, it would not apply because the word would not have the designation *abha*. However, the elision of the letter *a* will occur by virtue of the mention of the term *bahula* (in the sense of "diversely"). [This applies] to words such as *iṇ* and *añ*.

(Thus: "The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after [roots] such as *kṛṣi*. This is for the purpose of indicating that which is not a verbal root (*adhātu*). Words such as *ājya* and others should be understood as technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*).
109. *Saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 2.1.49).

[The example is] *uddālakapuṣpabhañjikā*. This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) by virtue of the rule *nityaṃ krīḍājīvikayoḥ* (2.2.17). Furthermore, the genitive case here is governed by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (2.3.65).
The case endings characterized by connection with a *kṛt* suffix [are used].

110. *vibhāṣākhyānaparipraśnayoriñ ca* (3.3.110). In this sūtra, *ākhyāna* is mentioned first and *paripraśna* afterwards; however, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), it says "when *paripraśna* and *ākhyāna* are understood," placing *paripraśna* first.

This presentation consists of a preliminary inquiry followed by an exposition; regarding this, one might raise the objection: "What is the reason that the reverse order has been made in the commentary (*vṛtti*)? To that, he replies: "First, the inquiry," and so forth.
An exposition occurs preceded by an inquiry; therefore, in the commentary...

The intention is that the presentation of the inquiry and its illustration was made first, and the narrative afterwards; for there is no purpose in deviating from the proper sequence. To this, he asks: "In that case, why was the inquiry not specified first in the Sūtra, and the narrative afterwards?"

Regarding the phrase "in the sūtra" and so forth: by means of the sūtra *alpāctaram* (Pāṇini 2.2.34), which prescribes that in a *dvandva* compound the order of the words is fixed, he shows that the word *ākhyāna*, having fewer syllables (*alpāctara*), has been placed first in the sūtra. Regarding "kāṃ kārim": [the suffix] *iñ*. Regarding "kāṃ kārikām": [the suffix] *ṇvul*.
"Which action? (*kāṃ kriyām*). The suffix *śa* is applied by the rule *kṛñaḥ śa ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.100). "Which duty? (*kāṃ kṛtyām*).

Here, the suffix *kyap* is used because of the word *ca* [in the rule]. "Which deed? (*kāṃ kṛtim*). The suffix *ktin* is applied to the root *kṛ* by means of a formal separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*). "Which number? (*kāṃ gaṇim*). The suffix *iñ* is applied. [The root] *gaṇa* [is used] in the sense of counting (*saṃkhyāna*). (Dhātupāṭha 1853).

In the *curādi* (tenth) class, [the root] is read as being without a final vowel (*adanta*). [Examples include: "Whom did you cause to count? (*kāṃ gaṇikām*)—here the suffix *ṇvul* is applied; "whom did you cause to count? (*gaṇanām*)—here the suffix *yuc* is applied.

Likewise: "Whom did you cause to cook? (*kāṃ pācim*), and so forth. [Specifically: "Whom did you cause to cook? (*kāṃ pācimakārṣīḥ*), "whom did you cause to cook? (*kāṃ pācikām*), "whom did you cause to cook? (*kāṃ pacām*); "whom did you cause to sacrifice? (*kāṃ yājim*), "whom did you cause to sacrifice? (*kāṃ yājikām*).
And so forth, regarding the *kāmiṣṭi*: "kāṃ pāṭhim," "kāṃ pāṭhikām," and "kāṃ paṭhitim."
111. *Paryāya-arhaṇa-utpatiṣu ṇvuc* (3.3.111).

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *kṛt*, *ktin*, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [the suffixes] beginning with *a* are intended. [The example] *agragāmikā* means "one who goes to the front. There is a compound (*samāsa*) with the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) characterized by its connection with a *kṛt*-suffix.
"For the sake of the accent" means so that the word may have the udātta accent on its final syllable; for if the suffix *ṇvul* were used, the accent would fall on the syllable preceding the suffix.

112. *nañyaniḥ* after the root *ā-kruś* (3.3.112). 113. *Kṛtya*, *lyuṭ*, and others occur diversely (3.3.113). [The commentary states: "They occur not only where they are specifically prescribed, but elsewhere as well. If this is so, then regarding those two alone—

Does this result in the meaninglessness of the specification of meanings in rules such as *kṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.70)? This is not so; for by virtue of the grammatical rule (*yoga*), the *kṛtya* suffixes and others are intended to denote meanings such as the abstract state (*bhāva*) and so forth, while their occurrence in other kārakas is rare. And that function of theirs occurs in that manner when there is a specification of meaning.

Since it is established [that the suffix is used], how could it be meaningless? In the case of *snānīyam*, the *kṛtya* suffix is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). In the case of *dānīyaḥ*, it is used in the sense of the recipient (*sampradāne*), meaning "to whom it is given. In the case of *apasecanam*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*), meaning "that which is poured out. In the case of *avasrāvaṇam*, [it means] "that which is caused to flow out."

The word *tat* [is derived] from the root *sṛ* "to go" (DhP 935) with the causative suffix *ṇic*, followed by the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the object (*karman*). *Bhojanāḥ* means "those which are eaten"; *ācchādanāni* means "those which are covered. In both cases, *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the object. The expressions *rājño bhojanāḥ* ("the king's meals") and *rājña ācchādanāni* ("the king's coverings") are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
"Praskandana" and "prapatana"—the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*), as in "he leaps forth from it" (*praskandati*) or "he falls down from it" (*prapatati*).
Now, what is the purpose of including the term "bahulam" (variously)? For surely, by the very force of the commencement of this rule itself, [the desired forms would be established].

Since it is already understood that *kṛt* and *lyuṭ* suffixes occur not only where they are specifically prescribed but also in other instances—mostly so—the author says: "Because of the mention of *bahulam*," and so forth. By this, it is intended that other *kṛt* suffixes as well, even when prescribed in one context, are desired in other contexts as well, provided the meaning [is appropriate]. And that...
It is established by virtue of the inclusion of the term "bahulam" (in various cases). Thus, he indicates that the term "bahulam" has been employed.

Regarding the example "pādahārakaḥ": although the suffix *ṇvul* is prescribed in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), it occurs here in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*) due to the inclusion of "bahulam."
114. *kta* [is used] in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) when it is neuter. (3.3.114).

Since the *kta* suffix is already established for the sense of an abstract action by the rule "The *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khalartha* suffixes [are used] only in those two senses" (3.4.70), this present rule is commenced because this *kta* suffix, even when denoting an abstract action in the neuter, would otherwise be superseded by the specifically prescribed *lyuṭ* suffix.
The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows; that is, so that only *lyuṭ* may be carried forward in the subsequent rules, and not *kta*.
116. "From the accumulation of action, through contact, there arises bodily pleasure for the agent" (3.3.116).

[The commentary states: "This statement is for the purpose of making the compound obligatory. That which has an obligatory compound as its meaning or purpose is so described. But how does this statement serve the purpose of making the compound obligatory? To this he says:

"For a compound with an *upapada* is an obligatory (*nitya*) compound. By this rule, since a suffix is prescribed when an *upapada* (an accompanying word) in the objective case is present, there will be an *upapada* compound according to Pāṇini 2.2.19, *upapadam atiṅ*; and that [compound] is obligatory; for in its prescription, [the word] "always" (*nityam*)...

Because of the continued application of the term "constant reproach" from the rule *krīḍājīvikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.17), [the example] is "drinking milk is happiness. But how can this be an example for it? For in this case, happiness does not arise from contact; rather, it arises from consumption. This is not a fault; for all...
For those [factors] such as eating and so forth do not exist without contact (*sparśa*); because it is an invariable concomitant (*nāntarīyakatva*), contact is not required [as a separate cause].
[As in the examples: "The rising from the couch is pleasant," and "In place of *ud-* followed by *sthā* or *stambh*, the former [vowel] is substituted" (Pāṇini 8.4.61).

Thus [is established] the *pūrvasavarṇa* [substitution]. Here, there is physical pleasure for the agent (*kartṛ*), but not for one who is touched by the action (*karman*); what then? It is rather through the *apādāna* called the mattress (*tūlikā*). [As in the example:
"The attending upon the fire-pit" (*agnikuṇḍasyopāsanam*). [The root] √*ās* [is used] in the sense of "instructing" (*upadeśana*) [according to Dhātupāṭha 1021].

[The root] preceded by *upa* [is used here]. In this case, pleasure (*sukha*) arises from not touching (*a-sparśāt*), because that [pleasure] arises precisely for one who is being touched while the fire-pit (*agni-kuṇḍa*) is being worshipped. Regarding the expression "bathing the teacher" (*guroḥ snāpanam*):
the root *ṣṇā* means "cleansing" (*śauce*; DhP 1053); the causative suffix *ṇic* is added. [This applies to the roots] *ṛ*, *hrī*, etc. [as per Pāṇini 6.1.59].

By [the rule] *ityādinā puk* (Pāṇini 7.3.36), the augment *puk* is applied. Now, one might object: "In this case as well, the teacher becomes the agent of pleasure; thus, there is indeed pleasure belonging to the agent. So how can this serve as a counter-example? To this he says: *snāpayaternna guruḥ*. By this he demonstrates that here [in the case of *snāpayati*], the teacher is not [the one who experiences the pleasure].
The agency intended here is not with respect to pleasure; rather, it is with respect to the action.

Furthermore, in this case, the teacher is not the agent of the act of bathing; rather, it is the student, and for him, the teacher becomes the object (*karman*). The designation of "object" for the teacher is established by the rule *gati-buddhi-* (Pāṇini 1.4.52), etc.
In its intransitive sense, even one who has bathed is designated as the agent (*kartṛ*). Regarding the word "pariṣvañjanam":

from the root *ṣvaj* in the sense of "embracing" (*pariṣvaṅge*, DhP 976), the cerebral [ṣ] is substituted by the rule "after a prefix, in the case of *sunoti*" (*upasargāt sunoti*, Pāṇini 8.3.65). Regarding the phrase "mental joy" (*mānasī prītiḥ*): by that...
This demonstrates that the particular joy arising from embracing one’s son is a physical pleasure.

Regarding the word "mardanam": the root *mṛd* (DhP 1515) means "to crush. It is stated that "in all cases, the uncompounded form is cited as a counter-example"; however, this does not mean there is an absence of the suffix *lyuṭ*. For the suffix *lyuṭ* applies everywhere by virtue of the preceding rule.
Because of existence.

117. *karaṇādhikaraṇayośca*. (3.3.117) By the rule "in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) as kārakas," [the author] shows that the instrument and the locus are the meanings of the suffixes. Why, then, do the instrument and the locus not become the *upapada* in this context?

This is because of the very mention [in the rule] "karaṇādhikaraṇayoḥ. For the words *karaṇa* and *adhikaraṇa* end in the suffix *lyuṭ* and have *karaṇa* and *adhikaraṇa* as their respective semantic bases (*sādhana*). In that case, if these two were to have a word as a subordinate element (*upapada*), this specific mention would not be appropriate. If this is so, then given this mention, there must be the prescription of a suffix.
And if that were the case, would it not follow that there is mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*)—namely, that the designation [of grammatical elements] exists only when that [usage] exists? No;
because words are eternal (*nityatva*). For nothing new whatsoever is produced; since words are eternal, it is merely their already existing forms that are explained (*anvākhyāna*).

There would be the consequence of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatā*). Regarding "ṭhidhma-pravraścanaḥ": the root *vraścū* means "to cut" (DhP 1292); thus, "the cutter of fuel-wood" (*idhmānāṃ pravraścanaḥ*) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Regarding "ṭhpalāśa-śātanaḥ":

the root *śadlṛ* means "to fall off" (DhP 1428); with the causative suffix *ṇic* added for the sense of causing [something] to fall, and by the rule "ṭhśaderagatau taḥ," the substitution of *t* for the final consonant occurs.
This is the truth [of the rule]. Regarding the word *godohanī*: the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15).
118. *Gha* is generally used [as a suffix] after a word ending in *puṃs* when a name (*saṃjñā*) is to be expressed. (3.3.118).

Regarding the phrase "if [the name is understood] by means of the aggregate," etc.: this suffix occurs only if the name is understood through the aggregate of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), and not otherwise. [The suffix] *ṭhak* is for the sake of expressing non-totality (*akārtsnyārtham*).

*Akārtsnyam* means incompleteness; that which has a purpose (*prayojana*) as its object is described thus. By this, he demonstrates that the cognition has an incomplete scope. Regarding the word *dantacchadaḥ*: the root *chad* is used in the sense of "covering" (*apavāraṇe*), belonging to the *curādi* class with the suffix *ṇic*; [the form is derived] by the rule *chāder ghe 'dvayupasargasya*.

By [Pāṇini 6.4.96], the vowel is shortened; the compound is formed as before. Regarding "prasādhanam": from the roots *rādha* and *sādha* in the sense of "accomplishment" (Dhātupāṭha 1262, 1263), the suffix *ṇic* is added to denote causation (*hetumaṇṇic*), and by the preceding rule, the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). The compound is formed according to [Pāṇini 2.2.18]: *kugatiprādayaḥ*.

119. *gocara-sañcara-vaha-vraja-vyajāpaṇa-nigamāś-ca* (3.3.119). [The suffix] *gha* is applied in the same sense as in the preceding rule—that is, in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Now, since the suffix *gha* is already established for words such as *gocara* by the previous rule alone, why is this new rule commenced? To this he says:

Regarding the rule "halaśca" and so forth: one might object, "But since the term 'pratyaya' (affix) will be carried over from that [previous rule], the suffix *ghañ* will apply to words such as *gocara* and others. However, this would result in unnecessary complexity (*pratipatti-gaurava*), because the continued application of the term "prāya" (mostly/usually) does not serve as an indicator [that the term "pratyaya" is not being carried over].
120. *ave tṛstrorghañ* (Pāṇini 3.3.120). [The word] "from *stṛṇāti*" refers to the root *stṛñ* "to cover" (Dhātupāṭha 1484).
[The phrase] "due to the recurrence of *prāyaḥ*" and so forth: only when there is the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *prāyaḥ* [does the rule apply] with respect to the *upapada*.

The meaning obtained is that the suffix *ghañ* generally occurs after roots ending in *tṛ* or *sr* when a name (*saṃjñā*) is to be expressed, provided that [the condition] is present as a limiting factor (*upādhi*). Regarding the rule "not when it is a name" (*na saṃjñāyām*),
because this limiting factor is occasional, the suffix sometimes occurs even when it is not a name.

121. *halaśca* (Pāṇini 3.3.121). [The rule] "after the root *viṣṭ*, [the suffix *ghañ* is applied]. [The root] *viṣṭ* is listed as *veṣṭa veṣṭane* (Dhātupāṭha 255). [The word] *mārgaḥ apāmārgaḥ* ("the path; the weed *apāmārga*"). [The root] *mṛj* is listed as *mṛjū* (Dhātupāṭha 1066). By the rule *cajoḥ kughiṇṇyatoḥ* (7.3.52), there is the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *g*).
There is vṛddhi by [Pāṇini 7.2.114] *mṛjer vṛddhiḥ*, and lengthening by [Pāṇini 6.3.122] *upasargasya ghañi*.
122. *adhyāyanyāyodyāvasaṃhārādhārāvāyāśca* (3.3.122). [The commentary states:
"This rule is commenced for the sake of those ending in consonants (*halanta*), because [the suffix] would have been established by the preceding rule alone for those ending in consonants."

123. *udaṅko'nudake* (3.3.123). The objection begins with "But surely... (*nanu ca*), and so forth. The resolution is: "The statement is for the purpose of prohibiting [the application of the suffix] to *udaka*.
The meaning is that if this rule were not commenced, then even in the case of *udaka*, the suffix would apply by virtue of the preceding rule.

Regarding "tailodaṅkaḥ": this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Furthermore, the genitive case here is characterized by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix, specifically in the sense of the object (*karman*). Regarding "udakoñcanaḥ": here the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). As for the question "Why [is] *ghaṅ* [not used]? and so forth, he thinks as follows: since *gha* would have been applicable by the rule "In the masculine, when there is a name" (*puṃsi saṃjñāyām*, Pāṇini 3.3.118), the suffix *ghañ* is employed instead.
It has been prescribed; therefore, it is logical that when that [suffix] is applied to the word *viṣaya*, the suffix *ghan* alone should occur.
This is because "there is no distinction" (*viśeṣābhāvāt*). For there is indeed no difference here whether *ghan* or *gha* follows the root *añc*.
The intention is that if *gha* were also used in the case of *udaka*, the prohibition of the unmentioned (*anukta-pratiṣedha*) would be purposeless.

But surely, if the suffix *gha* were present, the word *udaṅka* would be oxytone by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), whereas if *ghañ* or *aṅ* were present, it would be acute on the first syllable by the accent of the *ñit* suffix. Why, then, is it said that "there is no difference"?
To this he replies: "Even when [the suffix] *ghañ* [is present]," and so forth; [this refers to its being] "by the accent of the *thā-thādi* group."
By means of that which is prescribed by [Pāṇini 6.2.144]: *thāthaghañktājabitrakāṇām*.
*khano gha ca* | (3.3.125) The statement "the suffix *ḍa* should be stated," and so forth—everywhere, the word "should be stated" (*vaktavya*) means "it must be explained."
In this regard, the following is the explanation: the particle *ca* is used here, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccayārtha*).

By means of it, suffixes such as *ḍa* and others will also occur. [Objection: But is the particle *ca* intended for the purpose of carrying over (*anukarṣaṇa*) the suffix *ghañ*? [Response: This is not so; for it is precisely because of its being marked with the *svarita* accent that—

The suffix *ghañ* is prescribed [after the root *sthā*]. Now, for what purpose is the suffix *gh* prescribed after the root *khan*, given that its prescription is for the sake of the substitution of *ku* (i.e., changing *kh* to *k*), and yet no part of the root *khan* consists of the letter *k*? If this is so, then it indicates this: that this suffix occurs after other roots as well. By this, [forms such as] *khalaḥ* and *bhagaḥ* [are accounted for].
Thus, words such as *pada* and others become established.

126. *īṣad-duḥ-su-ṣu* [are used] with words meaning difficulty (*kṛcchra*) [to form adverbs], [and the suffix] *khal* [is applied]. (3.3.126). [The phrase] "in the other two" refers to the words *su* and *īṣat*. But how is a specific [meaning] obtained even when a general statement has been made? To this he says: "because of possibility" (*sambhavāt*). Wherever something is possible, there that [specific application] occurs.
It serves as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). The word *kṛcchra* occurs only in the sense of *duḥ*, not in the sense of *akṛcchra*.

However, in the senses of the other two [prefixes], only *akṛcchra* occurs, not *kṛcchra*. Therefore, *kṛcchra* is a qualifier only for *duḥ*, while *akṛcchra* is a qualifier only for the other two. [Example: *īṣatkaraḥ kaṭaḥ* ("a mat that is easy to make").

"By you": the meaning is that the mat is made by you without difficulty, i.e., without effort. Regarding "easy to do": the suffix *ṇyat* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.124 (*ṛhalorṇyat*). Here, the word *īṣat* functions in the sense of "slightly."
"The letter *ṭh* is for the sake of the vowel" means that the acute accent (*udātta*) of the syllable preceding the suffix marked with *ṭh* should occur, as in the rule "when a suffix has *ṭi*.

But surely, operations such as those denoted by the *khi*-marker—like [the substitution of] a short vowel and so forth—are prescribed by rules such as "in the case of a non-indeclinable ending in *khi*" (Pāṇini 6.3.66) for non-indeclinables; yet, *īṣat* and the others are designated as indeclinables.

For what purpose, then, is the suffix *khit* added? He says: "The addition of *khit* is for the sake of the *mum* augment in subsequent rules. Since the suffix *khal* will be prescribed even when a non-indeclinable (*avyaya*) follows as an upapada, the *khit* is added so that the *mum* augment—prescribed by the rule *arur-dviṣad-ajantasya mum* (Pāṇini 6.3.67)—may occur there.

127. *kartṛkarmaṇośca bhūkṛñoḥ* | (3.3.127) The agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) function as *upapadas*, but they do not constitute the meaning of the suffix. If those two were indeed the meaning of the suffix, the suffix would only occur when *īṣat* and so forth are the *upapadas*; consequently...

The addition of the suffix *khit* would be purposeless, because the operation of *khit* is prescribed for that which is not an indeclinable (*avyaya*), and since words such as *īṣāda* are indeclinables, [the rule] would apply there as well. Therefore, from this also, it is determined that when the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) are the *upapada*, these two are not the meaning of the suffix itself. And in this regard—

The agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), as well as the group beginning with *īṣat*, are not individually the cause for the suffix; what then? It is their collective combination. For by the particle *ca*, a mutual conjunction (*sanniyoga*) is established, whereby the status of being a subordinate element (*upapada*) occurs simultaneously for both the agent and the object, as well as for the words beginning with *īṣat*; it cannot be otherwise.

If this is so, how can there be a simultaneous compound of two secondary words (*upapada*)? But who says that there is a simultaneous compound? For first, having formed a compound with the subsequent secondary word, the compound with the preceding one occurs afterwards. What, then, is the subsequent secondary word here?

The agent and the object [are designated as the first case endings]. Why is this so? Because of the power of the inclusion of the suffix *khit*. Indeed, the inclusion of *khit* is for the purpose of the augment *mum*; and the addition of the augment *mum* is prescribed for that which is not an indeclinable (*anavyaya*). In that regard, if there were immediate succession between the words beginning with *īṣat* and the verbal root, the inclusion of *khit* would be purposeless. [For example: "Become somewhat firm by you" (*īṣadāḍhyaṃ bhavaṃ bhavatā*).

Thus: "Devadatta is made somewhat firm by you" means "Devadatta is made firm by you without difficulty. "Devadatta is made somewhat firm by you" means "Devadatta is made firm by you without difficulty."

Regarding the rule "ṭhkartṛkarmaṇoḥ" and so forth: the meaning of the suffix *cvī* is "the becoming of that which was not [previously] so" (*abhūtatadbhāva*). The sense of this passage is that it must be explained as meaning: "when the agent or the object, which possess that [suffix's] meaning, are used as attendant words (*upapada*), the suffix *khal* occurs. In this regard, the following is the explanation: the mention of "generally" (*prāya*)...

It follows by the maxim of the frog’s leap; therefore, the suffix occurs only when the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) are used in the sense of the *cv*-suffix, and not otherwise. In the example "it becomes sweet" (*svāduḥ bhūyate*), the suffix does not occur because the sense of the *cv*-suffix is not intended to be expressed.
128. *āto yuc* (Pāṇini 3.3.128). 129. *chandasi gatyarthebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.129).
[The example] "sūpasadanam" [is given]. The root *sadlṛ* [is listed] among "those meaning dispersal, motion, and exhaustion" (Dhātupāṭha 854).
The prefix *upa* precedes it.

130. *anyebhyo’pi dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 3.3.130). [The example] "sudohanam" [is given]. [The root] *duh* [meaning] "to milk" (Dhātupāṭha 1014). [The word] "vaktavyaḥ" means "it must be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the word *api* is used here, and it...

This serves to include all irregularities; by this [rule], the following roots are included: *śās* in the sense of "instruction" (DhP 1075), *yudh* in the sense of "combat" (DhP 1173), *dṛśir* in the sense of "seeing" (DhP 988), *ñidhṛṣā* in the sense of "boldness" (DhP 1269), and *mṛṣa* in the sense of "endurance" (DhP 1164).

Thus, the suffix *yuc* also occurs after these [roots] in the vernacular (*bhāṣā*). But how is it determined that the word "also" (*api*) has the sense of including all deviations? From the commencement of the rule itself. For if only the deviation regarding the meaning of "motion" were intended here, this rule would not have been commenced.
Furthermore, one need not include the mention of "the sense of motion" (gatyartha) in the preceding sūtra itself.

131. *vartamānasāmīpye vartamānavadvā* (Pāṇini 3.3.131). If the state of being near the present were to be expressed [as the primary meaning], then that [suffix] would indeed apply; however, in that case, there could be no compound between "the present" (*vartamāna*) and "nearness" (*sāmīpya*), because there is no relationship [between them]. For nearness does not...
The connection is not with the present [time], but rather with its proximity, because that [proximity] is a quality of it.

Therefore, thinking that this [suffix] will occur here in its own primary sense (svārtha), he says: "Proximity itself is *sāmīpyam*. But for what purpose is this formulation made by employing the suffix *ṣyañ* in its own primary sense?
Why is it not simply stated that [the suffix] occurs in immediate proximity to the present tense, since that would result in brevity?
To this he says: "It is made known that *ṣyañ* is used in its own sense (*svārthika*). This means that by this rule, *ṣyañ* may also occur in its own sense;
thus, in order to make known the fact that *ṣyañ* occurs in its own sense, the *ṣyañ* suffix is employed as a *svārthika*.

"‘For the sake of establishing the four castes and so forth’—by this, too, the purpose of the indication is stated. By the word ‘and so forth’ (*ādi*), the four stages of life (*cāturāśramya*) and others are included.
‘I am coming here’—this refers to the meaning of ‘I have come. ‘I have come’ (*āgamam*).”

In the imperative, first person singular, by the rule *ṭhasthasthamipām* (Pāṇini 3.4.101), there is the substitution of *am* for *mi*; by the rule concerning the *puṣādi* group (3.1.55), there is *aṅ* for *cl*. Thus, "eṣa gacchāmi" means "I shall go"—this is what is intended here. [This is based on] the rule *gameriṭ parasmaipadeṣu*.
(7.2.58) Thus [the augment] *iṭ* is applied. [The example is: "I shall go" (*gantāsmi*). [This is derived from] *luṭ*, the suffix *tāsi*, and the ending *mip*.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of the word *vat*? For if it were stated simply as "in the vicinity of the present time, [the suffixes prescribed] for the present," then the suffixes prescribed for the present time would [also apply] in the vicinity of the present time.

The meaning "they become" is indeed obtained; therefore, he says: "the suffix *vat*," and so forth. If the suffix *vat* were not present, only the form of these affixes would be indicated by the present tense, and the base (*prakṛti*) and other factors would not be included; consequently, they would arise from the verbal root alone. But when the suffix *vat* is present...

When there is complete similarity, it is understood; for it is precisely in that case that the suffix *vati* is prescribed, and thus no confusion arises. To demonstrate this very absence of confusion, he says: "By which," and so forth.
For complete similarity occurs in this way: if, by whichever qualifier [the object] exists...

Those [suffixes] prescribed by that very rule occur when there is proximity to the present time, and not otherwise. By the phrase "by means of the root, the upapada, and the upādhi," the word *ādi* includes both the *upādhi* and that which is not directly expressed (*avidheya*). Examples are *pavamānaḥ* and *yajamānaḥ*. This is according to the rule *pūṅyajoḥ śānan* (Pāṇini 3.2.128).

That which is prescribed [by the suffix] occurs even when there is proximity to the present time (*vartamānasāmīpya*), and it arises from those two [roots] alone, not from another root—as in *laṅgariṣṇuḥ*. The suffix *iṣṇuc* is prescribed after the root *kṛ* preceded by *alam* when the agent is characterized by habituality (*tācchīlya*) and so forth; even when there is proximity to the present time, it occurs only after that same [root] preceded by *alam*. In that very case...

In the case of the meaning "in the distant past," as in the example *parud agacchat* ("he went [long ago]"), the *lṛṅ* suffix occurs precisely when there is an intention to express remoteness (*viprakarṣavivakṣā*).
In the case of *varṣeṇa gamiṣyati* ("he will go after a year"), here too, only the *lṛṭ* suffix occurs.
Furthermore, by the statement beginning with *yo manyate*, he refutes the rule for each specific type of cognizer.

Regarding the passage beginning with "But the transition to another time" (*kālāntaragatistu*): "another time" (*kālāntaram*) refers to a past or future time proximate to the present; "its transition" (*tasya yā gatiḥ*) means its cognition (*pratītiḥ*). Even though the word "I am coming" (*āgacchāmi*) pertains to a specific present time, [the listener understands] from this sentence "I am going" (*gacchāmi*) when Devadatta will arrive.

This occurs from the word "gamiṣyasi" (you will go) being employed immediately after [the preceding word]. Even if time were understood through the sentence (*vākya*), its commencement in the *sūtra* would be justified only if it were useful at the time of the phonological refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the words; however, it is not useful there. This is because, according to the treatise (*śāstra*), the refinement is performed upon the word (*pada*), and not [upon the sentence].

When a word within a sentence is being refined, the temporal relation (*kāla*) understood from that very word is employed; therefore, the intention is that it is understood from the sentence as a whole. The particle *iti* serves to refer back to the subject under discussion. This [work] need not even be commenced for one who thinks—that is, understands—in this manner. For what purpose, then, is it commenced?

Because those [suffixes] are already established by the rule *vartamāne laṭ* (3.2.123) and others within the very same grammatical treatise, this sūtra need not have been composed solely on account of the mention of "context" (*prakaraṇa*); rather, rules such as *aśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca* (3.3.132) and others would likewise not need to be begun.

He shows that [the treatise] should not be undertaken with the words "of such a kind" (*tādṛśam*), and so forth. And thus, it is implied that for one who is not such a recipient—that is, for one of dull intellect—it must indeed be undertaken;
for such a person is not capable of understanding it through this method. With the words "and likewise" (*tathā ca*), and so forth, he explains why: because...

In that regard, time understood through the sentence is not utilized at the stage of the grammatical formation (*saṃskāra*) of individual words; and this being so, such expressions as "he will do tomorrow" become possible. For even there, the word "will do" (*kariṣyati*) occurs only in the future tense, and thus the suffix *lṛṭ* is applied by the rule "lṛṭ śeṣe ca" (Pāṇini 3.3.13).

It is established that this time is future and non-remote (*bhaviṣyadanadyatana*). Even if a subsequent time is perceived, it is nonetheless the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) and is therefore not taken into account during the grammatical formation of the word (*padasaṃskāra*). However, if the time understood from the sentence were also relied upon during the formation of the word, then...

Expressions such as "he will do" (kariṣyati) and so forth would not be possible— on the grounds that, according to the rule, the suffix *luṭ* must be used for the future tense when referring to a time other than the current day.

132. *Āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca* (3.3.132). [Examples: *āgamat*—this is the *luṅ* (aorist) suffix. *āgataḥ*—this is the *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle) suffix. The nasal is elided by the rule *anudāttopadeśa...* (6.4.37). *adhīmahe*—this is the *luṭ* (future) suffix with the *mahiṅ* ending after the root *iṅ*.

Due to the rule *adāditvāc chapo luk* (Pāṇini 2.4.72), there is the elision of the *śap* suffix. In the form *adhyagīṣmahi*, the *luṅ* tense is used; by the rule *vibhāṣā luṅlṛṅoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.50), the substitute *gāṅ* is applied for the root *iṅ*. Because the suffix *sic* is marked with the *ṅ*-sign by the rule *gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.1), the *it* augment is applied according to the rule *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām* (Pāṇini 6.4.66).
In a location such as "bhūtavat" and so forth, the *laṅ* and *liṭ* suffixes would also apply; why then do they not occur?

To this he says: "In the case of an extension of a general property," and so on. This is an extension of the general property of being a *bhūta* (past), whereas *laṅ* and *liṭ* are suffixes that denote specific types of *bhūta*. In the case of an extension of a general property...
There is no extension of the specific [rule]; therefore, those two do not apply here.
133. *lṛṭ* [is used] in the sense of quickness (*kṣipra*).
(Pāṇini 3.3.133). [The commentary states: "This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *bhūtavat ca*.
This is because this [rule] is formulated even when the rule *bhūtavat ca* would otherwise have applied.

Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the word *vacana* (utterance)? Since everything would be established by the rule *kṣipre lṛṭ* alone, he says: "The inclusion of *vacana* is for the sake of synonyms. For if the inclusion of *vacana* were absent, the *lṛṭ* suffix would occur only when the word *kṣipra* itself is the attendant word (*upapada*); but since it is present, [the suffix occurs] even with its synonyms.
[The rule] applies to all those [tenses] that denote speed. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *lṛṭ*?

Why not simply say "in [tenses] denoting speed"? Because the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule "as if past" (*bhūtavat*) has as its domain the future tense; when that [past-like status] is prohibited, the present tense (*laṭ*) occurs in the remaining cases.
Is this not already established by [Pāṇini 3.3.13] *ca* itself? To this he says: "It should have been stated that 'not so' (*na*), etc.

Since the mention of *lṛṭ* is made even though it should have been stated that "not so," its purpose is this: so that *lṛṭ* may also occur in the domain of the future time not belonging to the current day (*bhaviṣyadanadyatana*), otherwise—
The *luṅ* [suffix] itself shall apply as an exception to the *lṛṭ* [suffix].

134. The *liṅ* [is used] after a word expressing hope (*āśaṃsā*). (Pāṇini 3.3.134) For example: "I am engaged in the hope that I might study" (*āśaṃse yukto 'dhīyīya*). From the root *iṅ*, the *liṅ* suffix, the *sīyuṭ* augment, the first person singular ending, the *iṭ* augment, and by Pāṇini 3.4.106, the substitution of *at* for the *iṭ* augment.

By the rule *sārvadhātukam apit* (Pāṇini 1.2.4), because it has the marker *ṅ*, there is an absence of *guṇa*. By the rule *liṅsalopo'nantasya* (7.2.79), there is the elision of the *sakāra*. The *iyaṅ* substitution occurs for the root vowel. With the prefix, by the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (6.1.101), a long vowel results. [The sense is expressed as]: "I hope that I may study quickly. In this case:

Although the word *kṣipra* (quickly) is both a *upapada* and a word expressing *āśaṃsā* (expectation), nevertheless, because it is subsequent [in the order of the rules], the suffix *liṅ* occurs and not *lṛṭ*. However, the scope for *lṛṭ* remains where there is no *upapada* expressing *āśaṃsā*—as in: "We shall study quickly."
135. *Nānadyatanavat-kriyā-prabandha-sāmīpyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.135).

By the rule *kālānāṃ sāmīpyam*, it is shown that here proximity related to time (*kāla*) is intended. But why [is this so], given that proximity related specifically to time is [already] expressed by the general statement?

Is the inclusion [of the present tense] obtained? Starting from the rule *vartamānasāmīpye* (Pāṇini 3.3.131), this section is for the most part (*prāyikatvāt*). Why is that? Because words such as "present" (*vartamāna*) and so forth are temporal terms (*kālaśabda*). Furthermore, there is a prohibition regarding the *laṅ* and *luṭ* suffixes, and those two are prescribed by reference to time. Therefore, wherever those two occur, there...

It is understood that here, proximity in time (*kālasāmīpya*) is based solely on that connection. To explain what kind of [proximity] it is, he says: "by something of the same class," and so forth. The mention of "of the same class" is for the purpose of excluding things of a different class. If [the interval] were taken as being separated by mere time, then this—
In examples such as "The full moon day has passed;
on that [day] the teacher kindled the fires," there would be no sense of proximity, because of the intervention of the new moon day and other lunar dates. Therefore...

Non-intervention by a letter of the same class is required [in this context]. In *adāt*, the suffix *sic* is elided by *gāti-sthā-* (Pāṇini 2.4.77). In *adhyāpipat*, the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied by *hetumati ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.26);
then, *ātvam* (the substitution of *ā*) occurs by *krīṅ-jīnāṃ ṇau* (Pāṇini 6.1.48), and [the lengthening] by *arti-hrī-* (Pāṇini 7.3.36), etc.

By the rule *puk, luṅ, cleḥ ṭhṇi śrī* (3.1.48), the suffix *caṅ* is applied; by the rule *ajāderdvitīyasya* (6.1.2), the reduplication of the syllable *pī* occurs; by the rule *āḍajādīnām* (6.4.72), the augment *āṭ* is added; by the rule *āṭaśca* (6.1.90), vṛddhi substitution takes place; and there is the elision of the *ṇic* suffix.

"The full moon day has passed" should be understood as referring to that full moon day which is not separated by another full moon day; for although it is indeed separated from the new moon day and other lunar days,
it is nevertheless [separated] by what is of the same class, namely, by that which is called a full moon day.

Because it is not separated by time, proximity (*sāmīpya*) is not bypassed. In the example "agnīn ādhit," there is the substitution of *i* for the root *dhā* preceded by the prefix *ā-* according to Pāṇini 1.2.17 (*sthāghvoricca*), the *s*-augment of the *sic* suffix becomes *kit*, and the *sic* is elided according to 8.2.27 (*hrasvādaṅgāt*). [The word] "adita" [is used].
The form *dadāte* is as before. Regarding *yakṣyate*: this is the *lṛṭ* (future) suffix after the root *yaj*, with the augment *sya*;
when that [suffix] follows, and *ṣatva* has been applied, *katva* occurs by the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si* (Pāṇini 8.2.41).
In all instances such as *ādhita*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *svaritañitaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.72), and so forth. For what purpose?
A double prohibition is stated; would it not have been sufficient to say simply, "not [used] in the case of continuity of action or proximity as in the case of the present"?
