For indeed, in the cases of continuity of action and proximity, the aorist (*luṅ*) and the conditional (*lṛṭ*) are intended to take the place of the present tense markers.
The *laṅ* and *luṭ* suffixes do not denote the non-immediate past (*anadyatana*). Since those two, *laṅ* and *luṭ*, would indeed be established even by this [general rule] being stated, he says:
"two negations," and so forth. He thinks as follows:

if it were simply stated, "not [used] in the sense of continuity of action (*kriyāprabandha*) and proximity (*sāmīpya*) as in the case of the non-immediate past," then this very sūtra [would suffice].

It would become prescriptive, and consequently, a confusion [of rules] would result—the *luṅ* suffix occurring even in the domain of the *lṛṭ*, and the *lṛṭ* suffix in the domain of the *luṅ*. For no such distinction is adopted here [in the rule]. If it were stated that "the *luṅ* is used for the past and the *lṛṭ* for the future," then this fault would not arise; therefore—
Nothing is prescribed by this rule; rather, only a prohibition of the non-recent (anadyatana) tenses is effected.

When those [tenses] are prohibited, the general rules (utsarga), such as the *luṅ* and others, which are prescriptive in their own right, come into effect in their respective times, being freed from the exceptions. Therefore, it is for the purpose of permitting what is already established [by the general rules].
A double negation is stated.

136. *bhaviṣyati maryādāvacane'varasmin* (3.3.136). [The commentary says: "When there is a statement of a limit (*maryādāvacane*). The inclusion of the word "statement" (*vacana*) is so that [the rule] may apply even in the case of inclusive limit (*abhividhi*). An inclusive limit is indeed a specific kind of limit; it is that very same limit when—

When it is connected with the object of the action (*kārya*), it is called "inclusive" (*abhividhi*); but when it is not so connected, it is called a "limit" (*maryādā*). In this context, because of the inclusion of the word "statement" (*vacana*), no specific distinction is intended;
therefore, it applies merely to the mention of a limit. Even without the inclusion of the word "statement," [the term applies] in the sense of inclusiveness (*abhividhi*).

The prohibition would not apply; for wherever one intends the sense of inclusive limit (*abhividhi*) to be operative, one either employs the term *abhividhi*, as in "āṅ in the senses of limit (*maryādā*) and inclusive limit" (Pāṇini 2.1.13),
or one employs the dual number, as in "āṅ in the expression of limit" (Pāṇini 1.4.89).

Thus, the word "vacana" (mention) is employed so that [the rule] may apply even in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*). "In the latter part" (*avarasmin*) means "further on. "To be traversed" (*gantavya*) indicates the future state of the path. "That which is further on of it" (*tasya yadavaram*) indicates the division of the path; "twice" (*dviḥ*) [is used].

By this as well, there is an absence of obstruction to the action. In the word "bhokṣyāmahe," the ātmanepada suffix is applied by the rule "bhujo 'navane" (Pāṇini 1.3.66); the letter *g* is substituted for the *j* by the rule "coḥ kuḥ" (8.2.30); and the *k* is substituted for the *g* by the rule "khari ca" (8.4.55).

Regarding "adhyaimahi": the suffix *mahiṅ* is applied; by the rule *āḍajādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.4.72), the augment *āṭ* is added; by the rule *āṭaśca* (6.1.90), vṛddhi is substituted [for the *a* of *adhi*]; and by the rule *upasargasya* (6.1.77), the *yaṇ* substitution [of *e* for *i*] occurs. Regarding "apibāma": by the rule *pāghrādhmādheṭdṛśaḥ śaḥ* (7.3.78), the substitute *piba* is applied; and by the rule *nityaṃ ṅtiḥ* (3.4.99), the suffix *am* is applied.
There is the elision of the letter *sakāra*. [The example] "bhoktāsmahe" is formed with the suffix *luṭ*. Regarding this, he will state a specific rule:
"In that case, by the sūtra *an-ahorātrāṇām* (Pāṇini 3.3.137)."

137. *kālavibhāge cānahorātrāṇām* (3.3.137). The compound *kālamaryādāvibhāge sati* is a *dvandva* formed by the conjunction of the two words *maryādā* and *vibhāga*. Consequently, the word *kāla* forms a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound [with *vibhāga*]. [The phrase] "of those" (*teṣāṃ ca*) refers to these.

It is logical that there is a prohibition of division between them [the parts] and those [the whole], because the division is related to them. When there is a division of one thing by means of those [parts], then it is not logical [to say the division is between the parts themselves], for in that case the division is not related to them. What is it related to, then? It is related to the object being divided.

Nevertheless, because the division is made by means of day and night, the relationship [of the name] certainly exists; since there is a connection between the cause (the time) and the effect (the division), there is no fault. If the statement is for the purpose of prohibiting [the use of the name] with respect to day and night, then by implication (sāmarthyāt) a prohibition of the division of time itself will be understood, and not—

Regarding the division of space (*deśavibhāga*): since there is no connection between the division of space and days and nights, he says, "The separation [of the rule] is for the sake of what follows" (*yogāvibhāga uttarārthaḥ*). This is so that [the application of the rule] may occur only in the case of the division of time (*kālavibhāga*) in the subsequent sūtra, and not in the case of the division of space. [For example: "abhuñjmahi" (we did not eat).

By the rule "ṭhśnasorallopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.111), there is the elision of the vowel *a*. Regarding the phrase "an example of the threefold rule": therein, in the first case, there is a division by days and nights of time expressed by another word; in the second case, [there is a division] of that which is expressed as days and nights.

The division [of time] is by means of a time denoted by another word: in the third [case], it is by means of a time denoted as "day-and-night" (*ahorātra*) for that which is denoted as "day-and-night. Regarding the phrase "in every way" (*sarvathā*): it means in every manner.
Whether the division of one thing is by means of days-and-nights, or whether those [days-and-nights] themselves are divided by something else, or even if they are divided by days-and-nights alone.

The meaning of the word *sarvathā* is that there is a prohibition even in this manner for them. Regarding the phrase "contact with day and night" (*ahorātrasaṃsparśa*): it means the connection of days and nights through their division; thus, "contact with day and night.
138. *Parasmin vibhāṣā*. (138)

"One should cite examples for all [tenses] as if they were non-current (anadyatana). Regarding the past non-current: "We applied ourselves there," "We ate rice there"—in all such cases, the *luṅ* suffix should be cited.
Regarding the future non-current, however: "We shall apply ourselves there," "We shall eat rice there."
Thus, the *luṅ* [aorist] should be cited as an illustration in all such cases.
139. *Lṛṅ* [is used] when there is a condition for the *liṅ* [optative] and there is a failure of the action (*kriyātipatti*). (Pāṇini 3.3.139).
"In such cases as these" means that by the word "etc. (*ādi*), rules such as *katham-i liṅ ca* (3.3.143) are included. "Due to some deficiency" means...
"Due to the occurrence of adverse conditions, or due to the deficiency of other causes. Regarding "sthāsyati":

the suffix *syat* is applied by the rule *syatāsī lṛluṭoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.33). The elision of the vowel *i* occurs by the rule *itaśca* (Pāṇini 3.4.100). Regarding "āhvāsyat": [the root] *hveñ* is used in the sense of rivalry and sound.

The root *paryas* is listed as meaning "in competition" (*spardhāyām*) [DhP 3.1.27]; this example, *paryāsiṣyata*, is cited in the *Kāśikā*. The root *ās* is listed as meaning "sitting down" (*upaveśane*) [DhP 2.41] and is *anudātta*. Regarding the phrase "that which is the cause thereof" (*taddhetubhūtam*), it refers to that which serves as the cause in that context—[as noted in the *Kāśikā*].

It is the cause of the cart's overturning. By this, he demonstrates the relationship of cause and effect characterized by the indicative sign (*liṅga*). [The phrase] "having understood the sign and the possessor of the sign" means that after repeatedly seeing the cart not overturn even when previously called by the name "Kamalaka," [one understands] even that which is yet to come.

Having understood, through a logical mark (*liṅga*), that the calling of the *kamala* is the cause of the overturning of the cart; and the logical mark, moreover, is the property (*dharma*) common to the calling of the *kamala*.
Regarding the phrase "and its excess," it refers to the calling of the *kamala* being excessive for the overturning of the cart.
And the transgression of Kamalaka is understood through such signs as his departure for another country;
here, the transgression of the cart is understood through such signs as the loading of heavy cargo onto it. Thus it stands.
Regarding the phrase "from a sentence": this refers to sentences such as "if he were to call Kamalaka.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of "action" (*kriyā*) [in the rule]? It need not be stated that "the conditional suffix *lṛṅ* occurs when the potential suffix *liṅ* is the cause," because even without the mention of "action," [the meaning is established] through the governing context of the verbal root (*dhātu*).

[The opponent argues: "In the phrase 'upon the transgression of the root-meaning' (*dhātvarthasyātipāte*), a specific meaning is obtained; therefore, the mention of 'action' (*kriyā*) is redundant. [The author replies: This is not so; for it is heard [in the sūtra] as "conditioned by the *liṅ*," and because of the connection with the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*), the connection with what is explicitly stated in the text (*śruta*) is stronger.

It is understood that the transgression (*atipatti*) pertains only to that which is caused by the conditional marker (*liṅ*). Consequently, according to the rule *ṭhutāpyoḥ samarthayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.152), the conditional suffix *liṅ* would undesirably apply both when there is a transgression of capability (*sāmarthya*) and when there is a transgression of *uta* and *api*.
Therefore, the explicit mention of "action" (*kriyā*) must be made.
140. *bhūte ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.140).

Starting from *utāpyoḥ* (3.3.141), etc., up to *utāpyoḥ samarthayorliṅ* (3.3.152)—in these rules where *liṅ* is the condition, this prescription of *lṛṅ* applies. Why? Because [the former] refers to the past (*bhūta*).
He says this with the words "previously," and so forth.

Since it will be stated later that "the [suffixes] *vā* or *tāpya*" (Pāṇini 3.3.141) apply, then by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the prescription for the conditional (*liṅ*) in the sense of the past remains restricted only to those rules beginning with "the [suffixes] *vā* or *tāpya*" (3.3.141), and not to cases such as "he has eaten" (*bhuktavān*).
And so forth; he demonstrates the conditional mood (*kriyātipatti*).
141. *votāpyoḥ* | (3.3.141) [The sūtra] states:

*ṭhvā ā utāpyoḥ*. By this, he indicates the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *ā*. If there were an elision of the vowel *o* here, the rule *votāpyoḥ* would not apply, because the *guṇa* substitution would have already taken effect due to its higher priority.
Should there not be a single substitution (*ekādeśa*) with the preceding [element] due to the rule of *vṛddhi*? There is no fault, because this is a Vedic-style (*sautra*) designation.

Since it is an irregular formation (*nipātana*), one shall first perform the single substitution with the preceding element and then apply the *aguṇa* rule (Pāṇini 6.1.87) with the following element. But surely, when used in conjunction with *aṅ*, the rule "the ablative case is used with *apa*, *āṅ*, and *pari*" (2.3.10) applies?

Thus, by this [rule], when the word *āṅ* is joined with a fifth-case form, the fifth case does not occur, because [the resulting form] is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadikatvāt*). Regarding the phrase "in the sense of a limit" (*maryādāyām*) and so forth: if [the term *āṅ*] were used in the sense of inclusive limit (*abhividhi*), then the conditional suffix (*liṅ*) would optionally apply by virtue of the rule *utāpyoḥ samarthayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.152).
It is intended to be eternal. Therefore, this *āṅ* is used in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*), not in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*).
And [the phrase] "as it occurs" refers to the optative (*liṅ*) and so forth, because of the mention of the word "or" (*vā*).
142. *liṅ* is used for censure when *api* or *jātu* occur.

(3.3.142) [The objection] "It would not apply to the general time" indicates that this is a rule for the general time, by implying the continuation of [the word] "future" (*bhaviṣyati*) and so forth, which denote specific times.

He demonstrates this with the words: "prescribed for specific times. The *laṅ* and *liṭ* suffixes are prescribed for the past time, while the *luṅ* and *lṛṭ* are prescribed for the future. The *laṭ*, being prescribed for time in general, supersedes all of those by virtue of its posteriority. For example: "he causes to sacrifice" (*yājayati*).
Regarding the statement "from the causative form of the root *yaj*, the present tense (*laṭ*) [is used] because the conditions for the conditional (*liṅ*) are absent":

although here the non-occurrence of the action (*kriyātipatti*) is intended— since the conditions for the conditional, such as the relation between cause and effect, are absent— the conditional (*lṛṅ*) nevertheless does not occur.

143. *vibhāṣā kathaṃ-liṅ ca* (3.3.143). Regarding the phrase "the mention of *vibhāṣā*" and so forth: the mention of *vibhāṣā* is for the purpose that there may be no sublation of those [tenses] such as *lṛṅ* which have been prescribed for specific times. If this is so, [then...]

The particle *ca* is redundant; for since the rule for the present tense (*laṭ*) is not superseded by the very mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*), it would indeed be established. True, it is established for the present time; however, it is not established for other times. For in those cases, there is no application of the present tense when the word *katham* is used as an attendant term (*upapada*). Therefore, how can that [other time] be established by the mention of the option?
It is established! Therefore, the letter *ca* must be understood as having the sense of the *laṭ* (present tense); thus, "he should cause to sacrifice" (*yājayet*) is the *liṅ* (optative).
"He will cause to sacrifice" (*yājayiṣyati*) is the *lṛṭ* (future). "He caused to sacrifice" (*ayīyajat*) is the *luṅ* (aorist):
the *cli* suffix is replaced by *caṅ*, the penultimate vowel is shortened before the causative suffix *ṇi*, the *ṇi* is elided, and by the rule *caṅ* (Pāṇini 6.1.11), reduplication occurs.
The substitution of *i* [for *e*] occurs by the rule "sanyataḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.79). Regarding the form "ayājayat": [it is derived from] "yājayāñcakāra," which is the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*).
By the rule "kāspratyayāt" (3.1.35), the suffix *ām* is added; by "āmaḥ" (2.4.81), there is elision (*luk*) of the *liṭ* suffix;
because that [suffix] is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), there is elision of the case endings (*sub-luk*); and by the rule "kṛñ ca" (3.1.40), [the suffix *ām*] follows the *liṭ*.

The suffix *ṇal* is applied after the root *kṛ*, followed by reduplication, the operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsakārya*), and the substitution of *ay* by rule 6.4.55 (*ṭhayāmanta*). Since there is a cause for the conditional mood (*liṅ*) here, how can this be considered "censure" (*garhā*)? This [is so] because the conditional mood is prescribed in the sense of censure when there is an intention to express the past.

Since the rule *kriyātipatau lṛṅ* ("the conditional suffix *lṛṅ* is used when there is a non-fulfillment of action") continues [from the previous sūtra] with the addition of *bhūte ca* ("and when [the action] is in the past"), and because of the statement *votāpyoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.141), the conditional suffix *lṛṅ* must necessarily be employed in all cases where there is an intention to express the future— [that is,] it must be used even when [the word] *bhavitavyam* ("it is to be") occurs, as well as when *bhaviṣyati* ("it will be") occurs.
Because of the rule: "The conditional suffix *lṛṅ* is used when there is a condition for the potential suffix (*liṅ*) and there is a failure of the action. (Pāṇini 3.3.139).

144. *Kiṃvṛte liṅlṛṭau* (3.3.144). Regarding the term *kiṃvṛte*: by the inclusion of the word *vṛta*, that which ends in a case-ending [derived from] that [interrogative pronoun] is understood. Why was it not stated simply as "after *kiṃvṛta*, there are *liṅ* and *lṛṭ*, and also after *ḍatara* and *ḍatama*"? For *liṅ* is indeed the subject under discussion.
Then, one might ask: "Since the conjunction *ca* will be understood as conjoining that very same [element], what is the purpose of mentioning the optative (*liṅ*)?

To this he says: "The mention of the optative," and so forth. For if the mention of the optative were absent, just as the optative is conjoined by the conjunction *ca* due to its proximity (*prakṛti*), the present indicative (*laṭ*) would likewise be conjoined.
For that [present tense] is indeed the subject under discussion; therefore, the mention of the optative (liṅ) was made for the purpose of excluding the present indicative (laṭ).

145. *anavaklṛptyamarṣayor akiṃvṛte ’pi* (3.3.145). Here, there are two meanings [for the two terms], and there are likewise two suffixes; consequently, someone might have the misconception that the rule applies according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyena*). Therefore, in order to refute that, he says: "bahvacaḥ" and so forth.
For the word *amarṣa* has fewer syllables than the word *anavaklṛpti*; since the rule "that which has fewer syllables" (*alpāctaram*,
Pāṇini 2.2.34) requires it to be placed first, the fact that the polysyllabic word *anavaklṛpti* is placed first here [in the compound] is [the point under discussion].

He demonstrates that it serves the purpose of showing the deviation from the rule (*lakṣaṇavyabhicāra*). Just as here the rule for prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) does not apply to its own domain because of such deviation, so too is the rule for correspondence in order (*yathāsaṃkhya*). Therefore, there is no correspondence in order. The inclusion of the word "also" (*api*) is so that [the rule] may apply even when *kiṃ* is present; otherwise—
If the mention of *akiṃvṛta* were not made, it would not apply when a *kiṃvṛta* follows.

Just as in the rule *upakādibhyo 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 2.4.69), the mention of *advandva* is for the purpose of terminating the governing context (*adhikāra*) of *dvandva*, so too here the mention of *akiṃvṛta* [serves a similar purpose].

It would serve to exclude the scope of the rule concerning *kiṃ-vṛta* (words derived from interrogative pronouns). Once that [scope] has been excluded, it is explained that both suffixes will apply whether the word is *kiṃ-vṛta* or not *kiṃ-vṛta*. In that case, the inclusion of the term *api* could have been omitted; however, it is included for the sake of clarity.

146. *Kiṃkila* is used when there is the sense of "it is said" (*astyartha*). (Pāṇini 3.3.146). [The commentary states: "The word *kiṃkila* is a composite whole. By this, he rejects the possibility that the words *kim* and *kila* are each individually an *upapada*. Why, then, should they not each individually be an *upapada*?

Because the word *kim* alone cannot function in the senses of impossibility (*anavaklpti*) or intolerance (*amarṣa*), whereas it can do so as part of the compound; and because [the rule] "it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the gender" refers to what was previously obtained by the preceding rule;
and because "there is no cause here for the gender" since only the suffix *lṛṭ* is prescribed.
147. *jātuyadorliṅ* (3.3.147). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *lṛṭ*. It supersedes what was obtained by the rule *anavaklṛptyādi-sūtra* (3.3.145). [The Vārttika] states:
"There is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for *yadā* and *yadi*. This is so that it may apply only with *liṅ*, and not with *lṛṅ*.
The purpose of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is to provide an exposition. In this regard, the exposition is as follows:
from the rule *anavaklṛpty-ādi* (Pāṇini 3.3.145), the word *api* is carried over (*anuvartate*) here as well;
and that [word] has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccayārtha*). Therefore, it will apply to both *yadā* and *yadi*.

148. *yaccayatrayoḥ* (3.3.148). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to what was obtained by the rule *anavaklṛpty-ādi-sūtra* (3.3.145). Now, why was the mention of *yacca* and *yattra* not made in the preceding rule itself? Why is there this separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*)?
To this he says: "The division of the yoga (yogavibhāga) is for the sake of what follows.
This is so that in the subsequent [sūtras] there may be the recurrence of only *yac* and *yat*, and not of *jātu* and *yad*.
"Sequential correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*) is not intended here," because of the very same sign of deviation from the rule mentioned previously.

Furthermore, the fact that the longer member is placed first in every instance within this section is a sign of deviation from the general rule (*lakṣaṇavyabhicāra*), and not a feature restricted solely to that specific sūtra. Alternatively, because there is no *svarita* accent to indicate the sense of "correspondence in order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*), such correspondence does not apply here. For it was stated previously:
"By means of the svarita mark, the correspondence is according to the respective order."

149. And [the conditional *liṅ* is used] in the sense of reproach. (3.3.149) 150. And [it is used] in the sense of wonder. (3.3.150) 151. In the remaining cases, the conditional *lṛṅ* is used when there is no *lad* (present or future). (3.3.151)
By the rule "yaccayatrābhyām," etc., he shows that the remainder depends on *yac* and *yatra*.
The remainder cannot be understood as depending on *citrīkaraṇa* (wondering), because *citrīkaraṇa* is what is being expressed here.
[The example is] "ārokṣyati" (he will climb). [The root] *ruh* [is used] in the sense of the germination of a seed and manifestation.

*ṭhho ḍhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.31); *ṭhṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si* (8.2.41). Regarding the example "it would be a marvel if he were to eat," here a sense of impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*) is understood. Since the future tense (*lṛṭ*) is prohibited when used for the purpose of expressing a marvel, the rule *jātuyador liṅ vidhāne yadāyadyor upasaṃkhyānam* [Vārttika] applies.
(vā. 331) Thus, the suffix *liṅ* is used in the sense of impossibility.

152. *utāpyoḥ samarthayor liṅ* (3.3.152). Regarding the term *samarthayoḥ*: here, grammatical competency (*sāmarthya*) with a verbal root is not intended. This is because such competency is already established by their status as *upapada*s (governing words). Therefore, it refers to mutual competency (*parasparasāmarthya*).

In this context, "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) is understood as that which is expressed by the word. Furthermore, neither of the two definitions—namely, that characterized by mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) nor that characterized by unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*)—is possible here;
for both of those would function as subordinate elements (*upapada*) alternatively. Therefore, in this case, capacity is defined as having a common meaning (*samānārtha*).
Because it is expressed by the word "samartha" (capable/competent), he says: "these two have the same meaning.

Regarding the form *kuryāt*: when the suffix *u* is applied, there is *guṇa* substitution and the replacement of *r* (*raparatva*); then, by the rule *ata ut sārvadhātuke* (Pāṇini 6.4.110), there is the substitution of *u*, and by the rule *ye ca* (6.4.109), there is the elision of the vowel *u*.
153. *Kāmapravedane 'kaccit* (3.3.153). For example: "I wish that you would eat. By this, one makes known one's own intention to another.

154. *sambhāvane’lamiti cetsiddhāprayoge* (3.3.154). [The commentary states: "The determination of capability (*yogyatādhyavasānam*). Capability (*yogyatā*) is capacity (*sāmarthya*); its determination (*adhyavasāna*). That by which it is determined or ascertained is the determination of capability; that is, knowledge (*jñāna*).
This is called "sambhāvanā" (conviction). In order to clarify that very same meaning through another synonym, he says:
"śaktiśraddhānam" (conviction in capacity). "Śakti" means capability; that knowledge by which it is believed is "śaktiśraddhānam. "Tat" refers to "sambhāvanā. "Paryāptyā" means...

By this [use of] capacity (*sāmarthya*), he shows that the word *alaṃ* is understood here as occurring in the sense of "sufficiency" (*paryāpti*), and not in the sense of "ornamentation" (*bhūṣaṇa*) and so forth. Regarding the term "sufficient" (*paryāpta*):
it means capable, that is, competent to accomplish its own function. Its own function, moreover, is...
The determination of an object that is contrary [to reality]. "Not false" (*avitatha*) means because its object exists.

By this, it is accepted that this [term] has the sense of sufficiency (*paryāpti*). For it is only when it is not false—because its object exists—that it becomes contrary to that [unreal] object, and not otherwise. "Sufficient" (*alam*).

Regarding the word *alaṃ*: why is this so? Because by means of the particle *iti*, the word *alaṃ* is displaced from having "meaning" (*artha*) as its referent (*padārtha*) and is established as having "the word itself" (*śabda*) as its referent. The meaning of *alaṃ* is not appropriate as a qualifier for "possibility" (*sambhāvana*), and therefore, as it has been stated—"Now, this is sufficient for the purpose... [and so forth].

Is it not the case that [the rule] "it is qualified" (viśeṣyate) is contradicted? This is not a fault; the word *alam* will be repeated (*āvṛti*). Therein, one instance of it will have the meaning of the word *artha*, because it has not fallen away from being the meaning of the word *artha* due to its connection with the particle *iti* after it has been repeated.

And here, the status of being the meaning of the word is understood from the sense or from the context. [The *Kāśikā* says: "But it is not employed"—meaning it is not actually used—because its meaning has already been understood. [The *Kāśikā* says: "In such a case, where there is the condition of this kind of possibility..."

Regarding the phrase "conditioned by the possibility of an action" (*kriyāsambhāvanopādhike*): that whose specific condition (*upādhi*) is the possibility of an action is so described. As in the example, "He might even split a mountain with his head.
As before, there is the elision of the *a* of *śna* and *as* according to Pāṇini 6.4.111. Here, that which pertains to the object of splitting the mountain—

The capacity of a man is conjectured as being "only his knowledge"; because this is not false, the conjecture is sufficient. In the expression "he will probably go," there is a conjecture here understood from the word *prāyaḥ* (mostly/probably), but there is no sense of sufficiency (*alam-artha*); therefore—
When there is an intention to express the future tense, only the *lṛṭ* (the periphrastic future) occurs, and not the *liṅ* (the optative).
155. *vibhāṣā dhātau sambhāvanavacane 'yadi* (3.3.155).

[The *Kāśikā* states: "And in the future tense (*bhaviṣyati kāle*). This is understood in relation to the word *iṣyate* ("is desired"). But how is it that both the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) and the future tense are obtained here, given that...?
Is there a future tense even without the mention of *vibhāṣā* in the Sūtra? To this he says:
"Because the mention of *vibhāṣā* continues [from the previous rule]. By that, the *liṅ* suffix is obtained optionally (*vibhāṣā*).
This is because, while *liṅ* is still in force from the Sūtra beginning with *utāpyoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.152),...

The mention of *liṅ* is repeated here so that the future tense may be obtained. The purpose of this repetition of *liṅ* is to ensure that [the rule] applies specifically to the future time. Consequently, in examples such as "he kills" (*hanti*) or "he flees" (*palāyate*), when there is an intention to express the present tense, [the rule does not apply].

The same applies here: in this case, "killing" is the cause (*hetu*) and "fleeing" is that which possesses the cause (*hetumat*). Regarding the form "palāyate," the substitution of *l* for *y* occurs by the rule "upasargasyāyatau" (Pāṇini 8.2.19).
157. *liṅloṭau icchārtheṣu* (Pāṇini 3.3.157).

[The example] *bhuṅktām*. When the substitution of *e* for *ṭi* has been made, [the suffix] *ām* is applied. It should be stated: "in the sense of making known one's desire. That is, when making known (*pravedane*) a desire (*kāmasya*), i.e., a wish (*icchāyāḥ*).
The meaning is that this form of the rule—namely, "these two [suffixes] *liṅ* and *loṭ* occur in the sense of 'informing' (*prakāśane*)"—must be explained.

The explanation here is as follows: the term "informing one's desire" (*kāmapravedana*) is carried over from the rule "ṭhkāmapravedane 'kacciti" (Pāṇini 3.3.153); therefore, these two [suffixes] occur only in the sense of informing one's desire. In this regard...
What is the purpose of mentioning *liṅ*? Why not simply say "and *loṭ* [is used] after [roots] having the sense of desire (*icchārtha*)"?
Even though *liṅ* would be brought forward by the particle *ca*, it would still be the *liṅ* under discussion. This is not so;
for it has been stated that [the use of *loṭ*] is optional (*vibhāṣā*) regarding the future tense. Therefore, if that [previous *liṅ*] were to follow here, there would be an optionality.
It might be so; therefore, the term *liṅ* is mentioned again specifically for the purpose of excluding that [possibility].

158. *samānakartṛkeṣu tumun* (Pāṇini 3.3.158). Since the suffixes *liṅ* and *loṭ* were obtained by the preceding rule, *tumun* is now prescribed. [The commentary states: "It depends precisely upon the verbal root (*prakṛti*) from which *tumun* is derived. Therefore, from whichever verbal root *tumun* is applied...

Due to proximity, the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) is understood as being dependent on that very [proximity]—namely, that the agent of the base of the *tumun* suffix is the same as the agent of the verbs having the sense of desire (*icchārtha*). As in "he wishes to eat" (*icchati bhoktum*):
the one who is the agent of the root *iṣ* here is indeed the same as the agent of *bhuj*; thus, there is here [an instance of] identity of agent among those [verbs].

The *liṅ* and *loṭ* [suffixes] would also apply by virtue of their higher status; therefore, for the purpose that they should not occur— and likewise for the purpose that the *ṇvul* suffix should not occur— [the rule is stated].

"‘He desires Devadatta while he is eating. Here, Devadatta is the agent (*kartṛ*) of the root *bhuj* (to eat), whereas for the root *iṣ* (to desire) he is something other than that; thus, there is no identity of agent (*samānakartṛkatva*).
Therefore, when the present tense is intended, only the suffix *laṭ* occurs. This is because of the principle ‘due to non-mention’ (*anabhidhānāt*); for in this case..."

The intended meaning can be expressed by that which is produced [by the suffix]; and derivatives (kṛt), secondary formations (taddhita), and compounds (samāsa) are characterized by such expression. Alternatively, it means "due to non-expression" (*anabhidhānāt*);
the sense is that there is an absence of expression such as "one desiring to act. For indeed, among those things well-known in the world...
In the treatise, a formal exposition is provided; however, such things as "one who desires to act" and so forth are well-known in common worldly usage.

159. *liṅ ca* (3.3.159). [The example given is: *bhuñjīyād adhīyīta*. [In this form,] *iṭo 't* (3.4.106) applies. But for what purpose is this stated, since the optative (*liṅ*) would occur here by the rule of non-identity of forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*) alone?

This is not the case; since the *liṅ* and *loṭ* [moods] are exceptions (*apavāda*) that would otherwise apply, the suffix *tumun* is prescribed for the purpose of setting those aside. Therefore, just as the *loṭ* does not occur because it has been set aside, so too the *liṅ* would not occur.

Therefore, this is stated for the purpose of prescribing the optative suffix (*liṅ*); [the phrase] "the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows" means that in the subsequent sūtra, only the optative (*liṅ*) should continue to apply, and not the infinitive (*tumun*).

160. *icchārthebhyo vibhāṣā vartamāne* (3.3.161). Regarding "instigation" (*preraṇa*), it means "command" (*niyoga*). Regarding "invitation" (*nimantraṇa*), it means "the act of commanding. Even in the absence of desire, because there is the production of merit (*dharma*) from non-performance, [the action] occurs by necessity—that is, with certainty.

The "making" (karaṇa) is that invitation. Regarding the phrase "the making of acting according to one's will" (kāmacārakaraṇa): "acting according to one's will" (kāmacāra) means moving about according to one's desire. That which is the making by means of that [will] is the invitation. This is what is meant:
if it is performed solely through desire and not through lack of desire, even in the case of non-performance [of other duties].

Because there is no fault [in this], that is the intended meaning. In this context, would this meaning—beginning with the injunction (*vidhi*)—be a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), or the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), or a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix? Among these, if the first alternative were adopted, then where there is only the base...

If one were to explain meanings such as injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth [as being expressed by the suffix], it would not be established—[meaning] that one "should perform" (*vidadhyāt*), "should invite" (*nimantrayeta*), "should address" (*āmantrayeta*), or "should study" (*adhīcchet*). For in this case, there would be no injunctions and so forth existing as qualifiers distinct from the meaning of the verbal root; thus, this fault would have to be addressed.
Even if that [first position] were accepted, there would be a burden on the understanding. Now, as for the second [position]:

if it were held that the optative and other suffixes are the denoters of the meanings of the bhāva (action), karma (object), and kartṛ (agent) affixes—having seen these faults in these two [positions], he states the third alternative:

"‘The optative and so forth,’ etc.: those very things which are the meanings of the suffixes—namely, the state of being (*bhāva*), the object (*karman*), and the agent (*kartṛ*)—are what is meant. Since the suffix is prescribed for these by the rule *‘laḥ karmaṇi ca’* (Pāṇini 3.4.69) and others, considering that this meaning beginning with the optative is their qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), he says: ‘in those qualified by the optative and so forth.’"

And so forth. By this word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of *nimantraṇa* and other such [meanings] is intended; by the second [word], the inclusion of the *bhāva* (abstract action) and *karman* (object). Regarding "āsīt": due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix according to Pāṇini 2.4.72.
Regarding "adhyāpayet": as before, there is the substitution of *ā* and the elision of the *śap* suffix.

If the *loṭ* [suffix] occurs only in the sense of injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth, for what purpose is this rule split (*yogavibhāga*)? He says: "The split of the rule is for the sake of what follows. This refers to the *loṭ* in the subsequent sūtra.
This is so that there may be *anuvṛtti* [of the rule], lest it apply to the optative (*liṅ*). Regarding "karotu":
it is stated that *eruḥ* [is substituted] by 3.4.86. Regarding "adhyai": *āṭ* is applied by 3.4.92, *āḍuttamasya piñca*;
then, when *eḥ* has been changed to *etva*, *eta ai* (3.4.93) applies; and finally, *vṛddhi* is applied by 6.1.90, *āṭaśca*.
The substitution of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* occurs for the *prakṛti*.

163. *Kṛtya* affixes are also used in the senses of command (*praiṣa*), permission (*atisarga*), and the arrival of the proper time (*prāptakāla*). In the example "kāryaḥ" (to be done), the suffix *ṇyat* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.124] *ṛhalorṇyat*. In the example "kṛtyaḥ" (to be done), the suffix *kyap* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.120] *vibhāṣā kṛvṛṣoḥ*.

"What is the purpose of this? and so forth is the objection (*dveṣya*). "Because it is prescribed for a specific [instance]" and so forth is the rebuttal (*parihāra*). For the *kṛtya* suffixes are prescribed generally, whereas the imperative (*loṭ*) is prescribed for a specific meaning such as "command" (*praiṣa*) and the like.
Therefore, by that which is specifically prescribed, the *kṛtya* suffixes would be superseded in the domain of "command" and the rest.

It is further prescribed [that the rule] refutes the resolution [offered] by the rule *vāsarūpa* and others. With the words *evaṃ tarhi* ("if that is so, then"), he demonstrates that the prescription of the *kṛtya* suffixes for the *preṣa* (commands) and other such meanings serves as an *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence).
Now, an *jñāpaka* occurs only when there is no other purpose; but here there is indeed a purpose—what is it?

[Objection: Is it because of a restriction that [the suffixes] kṛtya occur after [roots] such as *pra-iṣ*, and not elsewhere? [Response: This is not so, because it is undesired. For kṛtya suffixes are indeed seen elsewhere—as in *tṛṇena śoṣyam* ("to be dried by grass") and *budhena bodhyam* ("to be awakened by a wise man"). And that would not be established if there were such a restriction, for in these cases there are no [meanings such as] *praiṣ* (command) and so forth.

[The suffixes] are understood [to apply]. Therefore, no restriction is intended here, nor is it logical for a grammatical operation (*praklṛpti*) to be prescribed in the treatise without its purpose being specified (Bhoja’s Pāṇinisūtra 107). Consequently, it is appropriate that this is merely an *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence), because the prescription of the *kṛtya* suffixes is necessarily required. By the inclusion of the word "necessarily" (*avaśyam*), [it is shown that] not in any case...

This shows that [the suffix] occurs. And this rule regarding dissimilar forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*) is obtained even beyond the scope of feminine suffixes (*stradhikāra*), because it is established by the formal agreement (*pratijñāna*) regarding the *svarita* accent. Therefore, when words such as *kāla* are present as upapadas, the suffix *lyuṭ* also occurs by the rule of dissimilar forms—e.g., *kālo bhojanasya*. However, if...

In every respect, the rule of *vā-asarūpa* (the optionality of non-identical suffixes) would not apply; consequently, by the rule *kāla-samaya-velāsu tumun* (Pāṇini 3.3.167), the suffix *tumun* alone would be obligatory. By the statement "some say," it is implied that others do not accept a distinction between these two views.
164. *Liṅ* is used for an action occurring after a moment (*ūrdhvamauhūrtika*).
(Pāṇini 3.3.164). [The rule] "and as otherwise applicable" (*yathāprāptaṃ ca*) implies that *loṭ* and the *kṛtya* suffixes are also used.
165. *sme loṭ* (Pāṇini 3.3.165).
[This is] an exception (*apavāda*) to the *liṅ* and the kṛtya suffixes; that is, it supersedes those [suffixes] prescribed by the immediately preceding rule.

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffix] *liṅ*. It applies to that which was obtained by the rule concerning injunctions (*vidhi*) and so forth. In the example *adhyāpaya*, there is the substitution of *hi* for *si* (by 3.4.87), and its elision (*luk*) occurs by *ato heḥ* (6.4.105).
"Perform the sacrifice"—here, the substitution of *dhi* for *hi* occurs by the rule "hujhalbhyo herdhiḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.101).

167. *kālasamayavelāsu tumun* (3.3.167). [The commentary states: "The mention of *praiṣa* and so forth is connected here. The intention is that if *praiṣa* (an order) and the like are not understood here, then [the suffix] does not occur there; for instance, when it is said, "It is time for eating" (*kālo bhojanasya*), [the suffix does not apply]. Its beginning...

The injunction "let your honor break it" (*bhaṅktāṃ bhavān*) is understood as a command (*praiṣa*). Consequently, even though the mention of "command and so forth" (*praiṣādi*) continues to apply, [the author] says—"Why does [the suffix] not occur here?"—with the intention that it would indeed follow in this case. This might be argued: [it does not occur] because there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the application of the *kṛtya* suffixes to commands and the like.
Because the section on feminine endings (*stryadhikāra*) follows, even beyond that there is no application of the rule regarding optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*); what then?

It is *anitya* (non-obligatory). Consequently, it occurs only in certain instances. And this has already been stated previously by the passage beginning with "In that case, this makes it known" (*evaṃ tarhetañjñāpayati*, 3.3.163, Kāśikāvṛtti).
168. *liṅ* when *yadi* [is used]. (3.3.168) This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *tumun*; it supersedes what was obtained by the preceding rule.

169. *Arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca* (Pāṇini 3.3.169). Regarding the example *voḍhavya*: [the derivation is as follows: by *ho ḍhaḥ* (8.2.31), *jhaṣastathordho’dhaḥ* (8.2.40), *ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ* (8.4.41), *ḍho dhe lopaḥ* (8.3.13), and *sahivahorodavarṇasya*.

These rules [Pāṇini 6.3.112 onwards] must be applied. The objection beginning with "Now" (*atha*) and so forth is the point of contention; the response beginning with "This which... (*yo'yam*) and so forth is the resolution. It has already been stated that the rule regarding optional forms of different types (*vāsarūpavidhi*) does not necessarily apply after the section on feminine suffixes (*strī-adhikāra*).

170. The suffix *ṇini* is used after a verb when [the action] is necessary (*āvaśyaka*) or when it denotes a debt (*adhamarṇya*). (Pāṇini 3.3.170) Regarding "it is necessary" (*āvaśyakam*): the suffix *vuñ* is applied because the word belongs to the *manojñādi* group. Regarding "this is a qualifier" (*upādhi*): the meaning is that it qualifies the sense of the suffix itself. Regarding "not an *upapada*" (*nopapadam*): if it were an *upapada*, however...

The intention is that the form would not be *kārī* or *hārī*. It has already been established in the rule *ṭhori avaśyake* (Pāṇini 3.2.125) that "necessity" (*avaśyam*) is an *upādhi* (condition), not an *upapada* (governing word); therefore, here too, one must state that "necessity" functions as an *upādhi* in the same manner. Together with that...

If one were to think that because it is explicitly taught [as a separate category], even *ādhamarṇya* (the state of being a debtor) is merely an *upādhi* (condition) and not an *upapada* (governing word),
and that if an *upādhi* is necessarily not an *upapada*, then the compound formed by *upapadam atiṅ* (Pāṇini 2.2.19) would not occur—
since there is no other rule by which such a compound could be formed here— [we reply as follows].

He replies to that: "The compound is formed according to the *mayūravyaṃsaka*-class," as in the example "one who gives a thousand" (*sahasraṃ dāyī*). Since the genitive case is prohibited by the rule "the sixth [case] is not used after words ending in *akan* or *in*, when expressing the future or a debt" (*akenorbhaviṣyadādhamarṇyayoḥ*, Pāṇini 2.3.70), the accusative case alone is employed.
171. *kṛtyāśca*.

(3.3.171) The objection beginning with "For what purpose" (*kimartham*) and so forth; the resolution beginning with "By that which is prescribed as a specific rule" (*viśeṣavihitena*); and the refutation of that resolution beginning with "In the sense of the agent" (*kartari*).
With the words "some," etc., the support of the [author's] own position is established according to the view of others.

Regarding the term "bhavyageya": since it is said that "words applied to wholes also apply to their parts" (Śābarabhāṣya 85), words such as *bhavyageya* [apply] to those things which constitute the parts.

They occur here in the sense of "action" (kṛtya). [The phrase] "denoting the agent" is because these words are optionally prescribed as denoting the agent by the rule *bhavyageyādi*. The separation of the sūtra (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows.

172. *śaki liṅ ca*. (3.3.172) This [suffix] is a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*). This is stated for the purpose of excluding the status of being a co-occurring word (*upapada*), as intended by the preceding rule.
"May he live"—here, there is the elision of *s* by [Pāṇini 8.2.29] *skoḥ*. Now, for what purpose is the mention of the optative (*liṅ*)?
It would be established simply by [Pāṇini 3.3.162] *loṭ ca*, since the optative (*liṅ*) will apply here as well when being drawn along by the word "and" (*ca*). This cannot be so; for just as...
By the word "ca" (and), the *liṅ* [optative suffix] is drawn forward; likewise, the *kṛtya* [gerundive suffixes] might also be drawn forward.
But surely the *kṛtyas* will be excluded; once they are excluded, the *ca* will serve solely for the purpose of drawing forward the *liṅ*? This is true; however, if that were the case for them...
If it were understood that there is cessation even when the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is present, then cessation would occur [there too].
If it is argued that this will follow by virtue of the commentary, even so, there would be an excessive burden on the understanding.
Therefore, for the sake of avoiding such a burden on the understanding, it is proper to follow the original arrangement (*yathānyāsam*) itself. In this regard:

Why was the mention of *āśis* (benediction) not made in the very sūtra for injunctions and so forth (3.3.161)? For in that way, the mention of *liṅ* and *loṭ* would not have been necessary. This is not possible;

because if it were read in the sūtra for injunctions and so forth, it would be superseded by rules such as "after *sma*, [there is] *loṭ*" (3.3.165), due to their higher status [in the order of the rules].

In this case, however, since this rule [P. 3.2.178] is subsequent, it will sublate those [previous rules], and thus this undesirable consequence does not arise. Furthermore, the mention of *āśis* ("benediction") must necessarily be made for the sake of the subsequent rule—so that [the suffixes] *kta* and *ktavatu* may occur in the sense of benediction according to "kticktau ca saṃjñāyām" (P. 3.3.174).
174. *kticktau ca saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.174).
"By the whole" (*samudāyena*) means by the combination of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*).
By this, he shows that the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is a qualifier of the whole. "The string" (*tantih*) [is derived from] *tanu*.

In the case of the root *vistṛ* (Dhātupāṭha 1463), here [in the formation of *visti*], the rule *ṭhanunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ kṅiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.15) would require lengthening, and the rule *ṭhanudātopadeśa...* (Pāṇini 6.4.37) and so forth would require the elision of the nasal; however, both of these are precluded by the rule *ṭhna ktici dīrghaśca* (Pāṇini 6.4.39).

It is prohibited [by the rule] "sāti. [The word] "sāti" is derived from the root *ṣaṇu* (DhP 1464, meaning "to give"), with the substitution of *ā* by the rule "janasanakhanāṃ sañjhaloḥ" (6.4.42). [The word] "devadattaḥ" is formed from the root *ḍudāñ*; in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), there is the substitution of *dad* for *dā* by the rule "do dad ghoḥ" (7.4.46), and [the doubling of the *t*] by the rule "khari ca" (8.4.55).
The state of being a chariot.
175. *māṅ* [is used] in the sense of the future tense (*luṅ*). (Pāṇini 3.3.175). As in *mā kārṣīt*. Due to the rule *na māṅyoge* (6.4.74), there is an absence of the augment *aṭ*.
176. *smottare laṅ ca*.
That which has the word *sma* following it as an addition to *māṅ* is described as such.
Thus ends the third chapter of the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable Master Jinendrabuddhi, who was a disciple of the Bodhisattvas.
The Third Chapter:
Now begins the third chapter.
The Fourth Pāda.
1. *dhātusambandhe pratyayāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.1).

[The word] "dhātu" [is used here] in the sense of "the meaning of a verbal root" (*dhātvarthe*). This is done by applying a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of the signifier (*abhidhāna*) to the signified (*abhidheya*).

He shows that here the word "dhātu" (root) is used to indicate the meaning of the root (*dhātvartha*). This word "dhātu" applies only to [the list of roots] beginning with *bhū*; for there would be no connection between the word "dhātu"—which is subordinate as it functions in its own sense—and another word. Therefore, this word "dhātu" applies only to the meaning of the root, and not [to the root-form itself].

[This occurs] among the *bhvādi* [roots]. Consequently, he states that the phrase "connection with a verbal root" (*dhātusambandha*) is understood to mean "connection with the meaning of a verbal root" (*dhātvarthasambandha*), saying: "The connection of the meanings of verbal roots is 'dhātusambandha'. But how is this connection defined? He says:
"The relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*). [And: "That which is expressed at an improper time..."
"Api" and so forth. "Yasya kālaḥ" means one's own time. The term *yathākāla* is an avyayībhāva compound formed with the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*) according to Pāṇini 2.1.7, *yathā'sādṛśye*.

Those spoken at the proper time are called *yathākāloktāḥ*. The compound is formed by the application of the rule for the locative case (Pāṇini 2.1.40) through a split in the yoga (*yogavibhāga*). It is not [the case that the compound is formed otherwise].

"Those used at the proper time" and "those used at an improper time"— this is what is meant: suffixes which have been prescribed by their respective prescriptive rules for this or that specific time become grammatically correct even when employed at a time other than that.

He shows examples such as "one who has performed the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice" (agniṣṭomayājī). In all these cases, the meaning expressed by the verbal suffix (tiṅanta) is the qualificand (viśeṣya), while the meaning expressed by the nominal suffix (subanta) is the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa).
Regarding the example "agniṣṭomayājī," [it means] "one for whom past time exists"; this is a bahuvrīhi compound.

The state of being in the past time [is established] because of the prescription of the suffix *ṇini* in the rule "karaṇe yajaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.85), which occurs within the section on the past tense (*bhūta*). As for the statement "janitā refers to future time," this is simply a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has future time. The state of being in the future time, however, pertains to that which is in the future but not of today (*bhaviṣyadanadyatana*).

Because of the prescription of the *lṛṭ* [future tense suffix]. Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): this is the locative case used for specification (*nirdhāraṇa*). Between those two—past time and future time—that which is past time becomes grammatically correct when connected with future time. For example: *agniṣṭomayājī*.

Even when connected with the future tense as in "will be produced" (*janitā*), that which is past becomes future. In the second example as well, "done" (*kṛtaḥ*) is past, because the *niṣṭhā* suffix is prescribed for the past; "will be" (*bhavitā*) is future, just as before. In that case:

The past tense, when connected with the other [suffixes] as well, is grammatically correct. In the third case too, "bhāvī" refers to the future tense, according to the rule "gamy-ādayaḥ in the sense of the future" (Pāṇini 3.3.3).
"Āsīt" refers to the past tense, because the *laṅ* suffix is prescribed for the past not of today. In that regard:
The future tense, even when connected with the past tense, becomes grammatically correct.

For example, in the sentence "the son of one who has performed the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice will be born," the past tense, though connected with the future tense, results in a future sense. Thus, this is the meaning understood here:

"He is his son who will sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma"—and a future time, when connected with a past time, does not attain the status of being past; for this meaning is not understood here: "He is his son who has sacrificed with the Agniṣṭoma."

In the other two examples as well, the qualifier attains the time of the qualified, because there the following meaning is understood: "that mat which will be made is what will exist tomorrow," and "that action which did not exist was what occurred. How does this come about? Why is the reverse not the case?

Does this occur? He says: "The qualifier," and so forth. For a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is a subordinate factor (*guṇa*), meaning it is not the primary element (*apradhāna*), because its purpose is for the sake of another. And by that [qualifier], assistance must be rendered to the time of the primary element, which is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Yet, without abandoning that primary element, it does not [retain] its own time.

Since that which does not conform to the time of the principal act is incapable of performing the action that assists the principal, it obstructs whatever time belongs to the principal. For the qualified object (viśeṣya) is the principal because it is that which is to be assisted; and it is not logical for the principal to fall under the time of its subordinate elements (guṇa), otherwise—
If the time of the subordinate element (*guṇakāla*) were to coincide with the time of the principal element (*pradhānakāla*), then its status as a subordinate element would be lost;
therefore, such a reversal does not occur.
Now, for what purpose is the mention of "affix" (*pratyayagrahaṇa*) made, since the term "affix" (*pratyaya*) continues [from the previous rule]? To this he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "In the section concerning the suffix *ṭ*," etc.: the previous mention of the term "suffix" (*pratyaya*) was connected with the heading on verbal roots (*dhātu*).

Therefore, when that [term] is relied upon here, it serves to ensure the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of those suffixes prescribed under the heading of verbal roots. However, in this subsequent mention of "suffix," every suffix whatsoever is included; for that purpose, [the rule is stated] again...

The term *pratyaya* (condition) is mentioned. Regarding the phrase *kālabhede* ("in a difference of time"): this means at a specific time, that is, at a time other than the present one. In the example *gomān āsīt* ("the owner of cows was"), the form *gomān* refers to the present time;
for the suffix *matup* is applied by the rule *tad asya* (Pāṇini 5.2.94) and others, based on the existence [of the cows] in the present time.
Because it is so prescribed; that [action], being connected with the past and future times, becomes correct.

2. *kriyāsamabhihāre loṭ loṭo hisvau vā ca tadhvamoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.2). [The commentary states: "And this [sūtra] qualifies the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*). By this, it rejects [the interpretation of the suffixes as] being in apposition (*upapadatva*). For the intention is that if they were in apposition, [the forms] would not arise from the simple verbal root alone, and so forth. In this regard...
There are two positions: that *hi* and *sva* may be substitutes for the *tiṅ*-suffixes, or they may be substitutes for the *loṭ*-suffix.

But surely there is no occasion for even suspecting the first position, since it is stated "for the *loṭ*" (*loṭaḥ*); so how could such a suspicion arise? [The answer is: because they occupy the place of the *loṭ*, they are indeed its substitutes (*ādeśa*).

It is reasonable to suspect that it attains the designation of the *loṭ* [imperative] mood; for in that case, if the former view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) were adopted, then in the example "bhuṅkṣva bhuṅkṣvety evāhaṃ bhuñje" ("I eat saying 'eat,
eat'"), by the rule "āḍ uttamasya piñca" (Pāṇini 3.4.92), because [the suffix] is marked with *pi*, there is no *ṅtva* (the substitution of *ṅ* for *n*), and consequently—

The elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule "ṭhśnaṣorallopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.111) would not occur; furthermore, both [the suffixes] would apply indifferently to both parasmaipada and ātmanepada endings, because there is no cause for restriction. [This would happen] in place of the general *tiṅ* suffixes.
How can this be obtained when two [suffixes] are being prescribed?

For, in the case of the *parasmaipada* suffixes, there must be substitution by *hy*, while for the others, there must be substitution by *sva*. Therefore, considering this position to be faulty, he states the second alternative, beginning with "And of that *loṭ*," and so forth—[referring to] the position in which there is a fault.

"It follows that this will be countered [by the rule]: 'Or let there be the substitution of *tad* and *dhvam*. The term *loṭ* is required [in this context]. *Ta* and *dhvam* are *tadhvam*; that *loṭ* for which these two are to occur is *taṣvambhāvī*.
By this, it is shown that the *loṭ* itself is the substitute (*sthānin*) for such a meaning; because of its being for that purpose (*tādarthyāt*), as stated in the Sūtra."

He shows that the word *ta* is designated as the substitute for *t* and the word *dhvam* as the substitute for *dhva*. Now, why are *ta* and *dhvam* themselves not understood as the substituenda (*sthānin*)? For it is impossible to understand them as substituenda; if they were also substituenda, then *hi* and *sva* would likewise be substitutes for the *luṅ* (aorist) affixes.

[They] might [be so]. Now, if it is argued that we shall qualify *ta* and *dhvam*—namely, "those which are *ta* and *dhvam* of the *loṭ* [imperative]"—then this fault would not arise; even so, there would be an excessive burden on the understanding (*pratipatti-gauravam*).
It is more appropriate that the status of being a substitute belongs to the *loṭ* itself as that which undergoes the state of *ta* and *dhvam*, rather than to *ta* and *dhvam*.

If, then, the substitutes *hi* and *sva* belong to the imperative (*loṭ*), they would not belong to *tiṅ*-suffixes alone; and in that case, by the rule "that which is called *l* is the *parasmaipada*" (Pāṇini 1.4.99), those two would receive the designation *parasmaipada*.

Consequently, by the rule "from the remainder, when [the agent] is the *kartṛ*, there is *parasmaipada*" (Pāṇini 1.3.78), both [substitutes] would apply only after roots that are inherently *parasmaipada*.

[The two suffixes] would [be included]; and because of their placement within *tiṅ* suffixes, that which ends in them would not be considered a *tiṅ* suffix, and consequently, the elision (*nighāta*) prescribed by "A *tiṅ* [is elided] after a *tiṅ*" (Pāṇini 8.1.28) would not occur. Therefore, he says:
"And there is a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*)," and so forth. "[After the word] *loṭ* alone"—by this, in the second rule...

He shows the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *loṭ* [from the previous rule] in the phrase "those having the properties of *loṭ*" (*loḍ-dharmāṇau*), and so forth. Those two have the properties of *loṭ* because they possess the properties of *tiṅ*, such as being verbal suffixes (*ākhyātatva*), just like *loṭ*. Now, one might object: "The property of being a *tiṅ* suffix and so on belongs to the substitutes (*ādeśa*) of *loṭ*, not to *loṭ* itself. [We reply: It is through the medium of the substitute that [the property is attributed].

There is no fault, because even the *sthānin* (the substitute) possesses properties such as being a *tiṅ* (verbal suffix), which belong to the *loṭ* (imperative). But how, when there is a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), do those two come to possess the properties of the *loṭ*? When there is a split of the rule, the word *loṭ* is carried over (*anuvartate*) into the second rule.

Therefore, by virtue of the sense, there occurs a transformation of the case ending; for *hi* and *sva* are qualified by that which has attained the state of being in the genitive case—namely, "those *hi* and *sva* which are substitutes of the *loṭ* [imperative].
Consequently, in place of the *sip* and *thās* which are substitutes of the *loṭ*, those *hi* and *sva* [are applied] by the rule *serhyapicca* (Pāṇini 3.4.87), and so forth.

They will be prescribed by the grammatical treatise (śāstra); those very two [forms], having their respective specificities already acquired, are prescribed here in place of the imperative (loṭ), and not as something previously non-existent. By this, the meaning that "those two possess the properties of the imperative" is indeed obtained. Regarding the phrase "by that," etc.: for this very reason, in the manner already described, *au* [is used].

The *hi* and *sva* suffixes, which possess the properties of the imperative (*loṭ*), occur in place of the imperative; therefore, the status of being *parasmaipada* (active voice) and *ātmanepada* (middle voice) is established separately according to their respective domains. Among these, the status of *parasmaipada* is established in the case of the suffix *hi*.

Because the *hi* belonging to the imperative (*loṭ*) is designated as *parasmaipada*, the designation *ātmanepada* is established for the word *sva*; this is because the word *sva* belonging to the imperative is designated as *ātmanepada*. Furthermore, both [the *hi* and the *sva*] possess the property of being a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*).
Because both of those [suffixes] related to *loṭ* are themselves *tiṅ* (verbal suffixes). Now, one might object:
"Those two are related to the substitutes *sip* and *thās*, because they are their substitutes, not to *loṭ*;
so how can they be designated as being related to *loṭ*? [The answer is: by way of their substitutes.

Since the state of being related to the *loṭ* [imperative] exists for those two as well, there is no fault. If, then, they possess the properties of the *loṭ*, in that case, the designation "singular" (*ekavacana*) would apply, as well as the designation "second person" (*madhyamapuruṣa*), because those two also possess the properties of the *loṭ*; consequently, [the forms] occurring in other numbers and occurring in other persons [would also be affected].

Would not the *loṭ* [imperative] endings be absent? This is not a fault; for if the singular number and the second person were also designated by these two names, this rule would be purposeless, because the second person singular and dual endings *hi* and *sva* would already be established even without this rule.

"Cut! Cut!"—here there is reduplication according to the rule *kriyāsamabhihāre dvau bhavataḥ* (Vārttika 886). Then, by the rule *ī halyaghoḥ* (6.4.113), the substitution of *ī* occurs. In the form *lunanti*, there is the elision of the long *ā* by the rule *śnābhyastayorātaḥ* (6.4.112). Alternatively, as indicated by the words "or rather" (*atha vā*) and so forth, [the form is explained] optionally...
And he demonstrates the result of including the mention of *tadhvam* [in the rule] with the example *alāvīt*. Here, there is *vṛddhi* by the rule *sici vṛddhiḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (7.2.1),
the augment *iṭ* by the rule *ārdhadhātukasyeḍ valādeḥ* (7.2.35), and [the substitution of *ī* for *as*] by the rule *astisico 'pṛkte* [7.3.96].

By [Pāṇini 7.3.96], the augment *iṭ* is added; by [Pāṇini 8.2.28], there is the elision of *sic* when followed by *īṭ*. Thus, "alāviṣṭām": by [Pāṇini 3.4.101] and the following rules, *tas* is replaced by *tām*. "Alāviṣuḥ":
by [Pāṇini 3.4.109], *jhi* is replaced by *jus* after *sic*, a reduplicated stem (*abhyasta*), and *vid*. Thus.
"Even by way of being woven into the middle [of the text], it should be cited from the *Kāśikā* and the *Padamañjarī*:
'Lunīhi lunīhi (Cut! Cut!)—thus you have cut, you two have cut, and you all have cut; or else: lunīta lunīta (Cut! Cut!)—thus you all have cut.'"
"Cut! Cut!"—in this way I have cut; we two have cut; we have cut.
The same should be cited for the middle and the last persons as well:
"Cut! Cut!"—in this way you will cut, you two will cut, you all will cut.
You will reap; or rather—by saying "reap! reap! you will reap. By saying "reap! reap! I will reap, we two will reap, and we all will reap.
Regarding "adhīyāt": [the substitution of] *iyaṅ* [occurs]. Regarding "adhīyate": [this is governed by] Pāṇini 7.1.5, "ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ."
This is the substitution [of *it*]. This should be illustrated for all *lakāra*s—[as stated in] the *Kāśikā* and the *Padamañjarī*:

"It should be illustrated for all *lakāra*s"—such as in the case of *laṅ*: "Cut! Cut! (lunīhi lunīhi), yet he cut (alunāt), these two cut (alunītām), these [many] cut (alunan). Cut! (lunīhi) [etc.]...

"Cut!"—saying this very thing, you cut; "you two cut!"—saying this, you two cut; "you all cut!"—saying this, you all cut. Or alternatively—"May he cut! May he cut!"—saying this very thing, you all cut.
"Cut! Cut!"—saying this very thing, I cut; "we two cut!"—saying this, we two cut; "we all cut!"—saying this, we all cut.

"Study! Study!"—saying this very thing, he studied; these two studied; these [many] studied. "Study! Study!"—saying this very thing, you studied; you two studied; you all studied. Or rather—"Study! Study!"—saying this very thing, you all studied.

"Study, study!"—thus I studied (*adhyaiṣi*), we two studied (*adhyaiṣvahi*), and we all studied (*adhyaimahi*). Regarding the other *lakāra*s (tenses/moods), I do not provide examples here for fear of excessive prolixity; one should understand them by oneself following this same method.

Now, regarding the expression "lunīhi lunīhi" (cut, cut), how is there a doubling [of the word] here, since the repetition of the action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*) is already understood by the verbal root itself?
For the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) is prescribed after a verbal root that expresses an action qualified by that very repetition. Or rather—[it is understood]...

If it is argued that reduplication occurs when that [intensive suffix] is present, then would there not also be reduplication for a root ending in *yaṅ*? To this he says: "In the manifestation of the repetition of action," and so forth.
Although the imperative (*loṭ*) occurs after a verbal root that denotes an action qualified by the repetition of action, nevertheless...

The manifestation of that [action] through repetition (kriyāsamabhihāra) is not expressed by the verbal root (dhātu); rather, it is expressed by the imperative suffix (loṭ). And that [suffix] is capable of effecting that [manifestation] only when accompanied by reduplication, not alone, because its [the reduplication's] prescription is not made in that context. For that [prescription] belongs to the imperative (loṭ), according to the rule "laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve... [Pāṇini 3.4.69].

By the rule *cākarmakebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.69), [the suffix *loṭ*] is prescribed for the objects and other [grammatical relations], but not for the intensification of action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*). Therefore, since the *loṭ* suffix itself is incapable of manifesting that [intensity] when it ought to be manifested, it requires reduplication; thus, there is reduplication of that which ends in it.
That which comes into being is called a *bhāva* (action/state). To the question, "In dependence upon what is the reduplication (*dvirvacana*) prescribed?", he says:

"In the sense of the intensification of action" (*kriyāsamabhihāre*), and so forth; and "the *yaṅ* affix, moreover," and so forth. For the *yaṅ* affix is indeed prescribed only in the sense of the intensification of action; therefore, it [the reduplication] occurs there.
Since that which is being prescribed is itself capable of manifesting [the reduplication], it does not require a reduplication [of the whole];
thus, the meaning is that there is no reduplication of the entire complex ending in that [suffix].
3. *Samuccaye 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 3.4.3).

Regarding the phrase "the bringing together (*adhyāhāra*) of multiple actions": the meaning is the accumulation (*cīyamānatā*) of several actions. By this, he shows the distinction between *samuccaya* (conjunction) and *samabhihāra* (repetition/intensity). *Samabhihāra* also...
Repetition (*paunaḥpunyam*) or intensity (*bhṛśārtha*) can only occur with respect to a single action;
whereas conjunction (*samuccaya*), however, pertains to multiple actions.
[In the example] *bhāṣṭramaṭa*, there is elision (*luk*) by the rule *ato heḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.105). In this case...
There is a combination (*samuccaya*) of various actions of wandering through many forests belonging to those who have attained distinction through the diversity of means (*sādhana*).

Regarding the phrase "or else" (*atha vā*) and so forth: by the first occurrence of "or else," he demonstrates the option (*vikalpa*) established by the mention of "or" (*vā*) in the rule *vā ca tadhvamoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.2); by the second, [he indicates] *anyatarasyām*.
(3.4.3) This has been established by the act of grasping.

4. *Yathāvidhy-anuprayogaḥ pūrvasmin* (Pāṇini 3.4.4). By the words "from whichever root," etc., he clarifies the meaning of the sentence beginning with "in the preceding injunction of the *loṭ* [mood]," and so forth. [He explains] "in connection with a verbal root," and so on.

Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *dhātusambandhe* (Pāṇini 3.4.1), the prescription of the imperative (*loṭ*) occurs only when there is a connection with a verbal root (*dhātu*). Therefore, the subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) [of the root] is already established, for without it, there can be no connection with a verbal root; since that [connection] resides in two things (*dviṣṭhatva*). If this is so, for what purpose is this statement? To this he says:

Regarding the phrase "but for the sake of indicating the specific manner [of application]," why does it not serve to exclude either the separated usage or the preceding usage, as in the rule "the root *kṛ* is also employed after [another verb] when the *liṭ* suffix follows" (Pāṇini 3.1.40)? It is not so, because both of those are indeed intended. For the separated usage is indeed accepted.
"Reap, reap!"—saying this, Devadatta reaps.
The prior application (*pūrvaprayoga*) is also accepted—as in "Devadatta reaps; [someone says] 'Reap, reap!
Therefore, it is logical that this [repetition] serves only the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*). But [one might object]: "Is it not for the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*)?"

Since the rule *sāmānyavacanasya* (3.4.5) permits the employment of another root having the same meaning, the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) will occur according to the prescribed rule in the case of the intensification of action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*); so what is the purpose of this [present] rule? This is not so, for it is indeed a case of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

There would be a restriction [to the specific root used]; however, in the case of the intensive repetition of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), there should be the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) according to the rule of the original form, and also of another verbal root having the same meaning. Therefore, this [sūtra] must be commenced.
5. *samuccaye sāmānyavacanasya* (Pāṇini 3.4.5). [The commentary states:

"This is for the purpose of preventing the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of all specific [verbs]. If this rule were not commenced, then the subsequent application would apply only to as many roots as the imperative (*loṭ*) had been prescribed from.

[Otherwise] it would follow [as an over-extension]; therefore, this [rule] is for the purpose of excluding that. But surely, even without this statement, the subsequent application of the general term alone will occur due to parsimony (*lāghava*). For if every specific term were to be subsequently applied, one would have to say: "Eat this rice, drink the groats, eat the parched grains."

In this way, since one would say "he eats," "he drinks," or "he chews" [of trees], then the term *taru* alone would be used for all [trees], while terms such as *vanaspati* would be eliminated; but this is not the case.
Therefore, in the usage of worldly language, there is no concern for the relative weight or brevity of words. But surely—

In examples such as *bhrāṣṭramaṭa*, there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of the factors of action (*kāraka*) alone—namely, the frying pan and so forth—and not of the action itself, because that action is singular. Furthermore, "residing in multiple substrates" is a universal (*sāmānya*); since an action is unitary, this [multiplicity] is impossible for it. Therefore, how can the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of a word expressing a universal be justified?
Thus he says: "Enter the furnace," and so forth; the meaning has already been explained.
6. *chandasi luṅlaṅliṭaḥ* | (3.4.6) [The commentary says:

"According to their respective [domains] (*yathāyatham*)" means "according to each one's own" (*yathāsvam*). The meaning is: that which is the specific domain of a particular [suffix], it occurs there.
Regarding "he did" (*akarat*), by the rule *kṛmṛdṛruhibhyaśchandasi* (3.1.59), *aṅ* is substituted for *cli*.

Regarding *aṭṛdṛśo'ṅ guṇiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.16): [the example] is *akārṣīt*. [The form] *am* is the substitute for *mip*. Regarding *avṛṇīta*: this is the *laṅ* [augment] of the root *vṛñ*; because it belongs to the *krī-ādi* group, there is the *śnā* suffix; the substitution of *ī* is as before. Regarding *mamāra*: this is the *liṭ* [augment]; by the rule *mriyater luṅliṅoś ca* (Pāṇini 1.3.61), the *parasmaipada* [ending] is applied.

After *ṇal*, there is *vṛddhi*; by the rule "rapara" [the substitute is followed by *r*]; then, because of the status as a substitute for the original place (*sthānivadbhāva*) according to Pāṇini 1.1.59 (*dvirvacane 'ci*), the element *mṛ* is reduplicated; then, by Pāṇini 7.4.66 (*urat*), *u* is substituted for *ṛ*; then *rapara* applies again; finally, the *halādiśeṣa* [remains].
7. *leṭ* is used in the sense of the *liṅ* (optative). (Pāṇini 3.4.7) As in *neṣat* and *takṣiṣat*. From the roots *nī* and *takṣ*, the suffix *leṭ* is applied; then *tip*;
then the elision of the *i* by "the elision of the *it* [augment] occurs in the case of *parasmaipada* endings" (3.4.97); and then *sib* is added frequently.
In *leṭi* (Pāṇini 3.1.34), the suffix *sip* is applied; by *leṭo ’ḍāṭau* (3.4.94), the augment *āṭ* is added.
In *takṣiṣat*, the augment *iṭ* is added by *ārdhadhātukasyeḍ vaḷādeḥ* (7.2.35).
Examples such as *joṣiṣat* and others are cited under the rule *sib bahulaṃ leṭi* (3.1.34).
These have been explained.

8. And [the affix *niṣṭhā* is used] after [roots meaning] "agreement" (*upasaṃvāda*) and "suspicion" (*śaṅkā*). (3.4.8) "Agreement" (*upasaṃvāda*) means "negotiation" (*paribhāṣaṇa*) or "a binding agreement regarding what is to be done.
These two are synonyms for the word *upasaṃvāda*. [For example: "If you [would do this] for me..."

By the words "ityādi" (and so forth), he shows the nature of that objection; by "kāraṇataḥ" (from the cause) and so forth, he shows the nature of the doubt. "Anusaraṇam" means following after, that is to say, inference (*anumāna*). "Tarka is *utprekṣā*"—these two are synonyms for doubt (*āśaṅkā*).

"Ṭhahameva," and so forth. The gods said to Paśupati, "Slay Tripura. He replied, "I alone am the Lord (Īśa) of the bound souls (paśus). When told, "Take a share of the sin of Brahman-slaughter," Āditya said this: "Your cups shall be drawn first; your deities shall be mine alone."

The forms *pātrāṇy ucchīṣai* and *gṛhyāntai* are explained as follows: Regarding *ucchīṣai*: from the root *īś* in the sense of "lordship" (*aiśvarya*) [DhP 1020], the third person singular ending (*uttama-puruṣa-ekavacana*), the augment *iṭ*, the substitution of *e* for *ṭi* (the final vowel of the suffix), and then by Pāṇini 3.4.93, the substitution of *ai* for *e*. Regarding *gṛhyāntai*: from the root *grah* in the sense of "taking" (*upādāna*) [DhP 1533], the third person singular ending *jhi* is replaced by *antaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.3], and this occurs in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*).

By the rule *sārvadhātuke yak* (Pāṇini 3.1.67), the suffix *yak* is added; by the rule concerning *grah* and others (6.1.16), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). The remainder is established as before. Regarding the form *ucyante*: from the root *vac* in the sense of "speaking" (Dhātupāṭha 1063), there is vocalization by the rule concerning *vac* and others (6.1.15). The remainder is as before.

Regarding "ṭhpatāma" — the root *patlṛ* means "to go" (*dhā.pā.* 845); *mas* is the first person plural ending; and *āṭ* is added by the rule *leṭo'ḍāṭau* (Pāṇini 3.4.94). With the words "by crooked conduct," etc., he demonstrates the previously mentioned definition of doubt (*āśaṅkā*) through an illustration. [He concludes: "This is indeed a *liṅ* suffix."

The relationship of cause and effect. How so? First, regarding agreement (*upasaṃvāda*): "If you would do this for me, I too shall give this to you"—such is the definition characterized by a mutual stipulation. In that case, it is logical that performing the action is the cause (*hetu*) and the giving is the effect (*hetumat*).
Agreement (*upasaṃvāda*) is the meaning of the inferential mark (*liṅga*). Suspicion (*āśaṅkā*) also consists in following after an effect on account of its cause.

In that case as well, the cause is the reason (*hetu*), and the following after the effect is that which possesses the reason (*hetumat*); thus, suspicion too is indeed the meaning of the inferential mark.
If this is so, since it is already established by what preceded, for what purpose is this stated? To this he says:
"The statement is for the sake of making [the rule] obligatory. This might be so;
however, thinking that it would be obligatory by the preceding rule alone, he says: "In the previous sūtra," and so forth.
9. *tum-arthe ses-enase-asen-kasen-adhyai-adhyaik-adhyaik-adhyain-śadhyai-śadhyain-tavai-tavenaḥ* | (3.4.9) [Question:
"How is this known? [Answer: Because of the statement *kartari kṛt* (3.4.67), it is only the agent (*kartṛ*) [that is expressed].

He considers that the meaning of *tumun* is [not] necessarily the agent; this is expressed by the words "by the force of the statement" (*vacanasāmarthyāt*), and so forth. If the agent alone were the meaning of *tumun*, then the mention of "the meaning of *tumun*" would be purposeless, for suffixes such as *ktvā* and others would already apply to the agent by their very nature. Therefore, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) provided by the inclusion of the term "the meaning of *tumun*," *tumun* does not denote the agent.
It occurs; it is set aside; it is removed—meaning that it does not occur when [the agent] is the referent.
This might be argued: "Its meaning will be [one of] the object (*karman*) and so forth," to which he replies with "And not," etc.
