"In another" means in the object and so forth. Thus, since there is no specification regarding the object and so forth, it does not occur.

The same would not apply even in the case of an existing entity (*bhāva*). He states that even when an entity exists, the suffix *tumun* is not prescribed [by this rule], saying: "those whose meaning is not specified" (*anirdiṣṭārthāḥ*), and so forth. Because another meaning has been specified, the base (*prakṛti*) which is employed as the cause for the suffixes is understood to apply only to that [base] due to the proximity (*pratyāsatti*) of its own meaning; thus, they are called "those whose meaning is not specified."
Suffixes (*pratyaya*) occur in their own meaning (*svārtha*), and here, moreover, that "own meaning" is the state of being (*bhāva*). Why is this so?

Because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning verbal roots (*dhātu*), and because a verbal root expresses the state of being. If this were the case, one should simply have used the term "state of being" (*bhāva*) [in the sūtra], for it would be more concise. This cannot be done; for if "state of being" were used, [the suffix] would apply to the agent (*kartṛ*) as well.

By virtue of the rule *kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67), the suffix *tumun* would apply only when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed. However, since the inclusion of the term *tum-artha* ("having the sense of *tumun*") implies that even for *tumun*, the meaning is indeed the abstract action (*bhāva*) itself, there is no fault whatsoever. [Regarding the form] *vakṣe*: from the root *vac* "to speak" (Dhātupāṭha 1063), with the suffix *se*, and by the rule *coḥ...* [the substitution of *ś* occurs].
The substitution of *ku* [for *k*] occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.30]: *kuḥ*. Regarding "in *preṣe*": this is the suffix *sen* added to the root *iṇ*. Regarding "in *jīvase*":
the root is *jīv* in the sense of "sustaining life" (Dhātupāṭha 562). This very same example applies to both suffixes;
however, their accents differ. Regarding "in *preṣe*": from *iṇ* preceded by *pra*, there is the suffix *ksa*; [then] *ād guṇaḥ* [applies].

Regarding "śriyase": from the root *śriñ* "to serve" (DhP 897), [the suffix] *ksen* is applied, resulting in *iyaṅ*. Regarding "upācaradhyai": the root *car* "to move" (DhP 559) is preceded by the prefix *upa*. These are examples of both suffixes; however, they differ due to their distinct accents.

Regarding "ṭhāhuvadhyai": from the root *pā* "to drink" (DhP 925), with the suffix *śadhyai*; by the rule *prāghrādisūtra* (Pāṇini 7.3.78), there is the substitution of *piba*. Regarding "mādayadhyai": from the root *madī* "in exhilaration" (DhP 815)—[the Dhātupāṭha reads] "in exhilaration and intoxication"—with the causative *ṇic*, the suffix *śadhyai*, and the [substitution of] *guṇa* and *ayādeśa*. Regarding "pātavai": [from the root *pā*].

Thus: *pibateḥ tavai*, *sūtave*. Regarding *ṣūṅ prāṇigarbhavimoce* (Dhātupāṭha 1031), the suffix *taveṅ* is applied; because of the marker *ṅ*, there is an absence of guṇa. Examples such as *gantave* and others follow the roots *gam*, *kṛ*, and *hṛ* respectively.
10. *prayai rohiṣyai avyathiṣyai* (3.4.10). Regarding *prayai*: by the rule *ato lopa iṭi ca* (6.4.64), there is the elision of the vowel *a*.

11. *dṛśe vikhye ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.11). Regarding *dṛśe*: the suffix *ke* is applied to the root *dṛś*. Regarding *vikhye*: the suffix *ke* is irregularly prescribed (*nipātyate*) after the root *cakṣiṅ* or *khyāti*, preceded by the prefix *vi*.

12. *śaki ṇamulkamulau* | (3.4.12) Regarding the example *vibhājamam*: the suffix *ṇamul* is applied to the root *bhaj* preceded by the prefix *vi*. Regarding the example *apalupam*: from the root *lup* meaning "to cut" (*dhā.pā.* 1431), the suffix *kamul* is applied.

13. *īśvare tosun-kasunau* (Pāṇini 3.4.13). [The examples] *abhicaritoḥ*—here, the suffix *tosun* is applied to the root *car* preceded by the prefix *abhi*. [The examples] *vilikhaḥ*, *vitṛdaḥ*—[these are derived from] the roots *likh* and *tṛd*; *tṛd* [is listed] in the Dhātupāṭha with the meaning "to injure" or "to give."
And from this [root] *dhā* (DhP 1446), the suffix *kasun* is applied.

14. *kṛtyārthe tavaikenkenyatvanaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.14). [The commentary states: "The meaning of the *kṛtya* suffixes is the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*)," because it is prescribed that *kṛtya*, *kta*, and those having the sense of *khal* suffixes apply only to these two—abstract state and object—as in *tayoreva kṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ* (3.4.70). [The rule continues with] *antetavai*.

*anupūrvādiṇastavai*: from the root *iṇ* preceded by *anu*. *paridhātavai*: from the root *dhā* preceded by *pari*. *paristaritavai*: from the very same [root] *stṛñ* meaning "to cover" (DhP 1252), preceded by *pari*. *avagāhe*: from the root *gāh* meaning "to stir" (DhP 649), preceded by *ava*.

Regarding the form *didṛkṣeṇya*: from the root *dṛś*, the suffix *san* is applied; there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*); the substitution of *u* for the radical vowel (*uratvam*); the substitution of *ra* for the *u* (*raparatvam*); the substitution of *i* for the radical vowel by the rule *sanyataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.79); the absence of *guṇa* strengthening by the rule *halantācca* (1.2.10); the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *vraścādi-sūtra* (8.2.36); and the substitution of *k* for *ṣ* by the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si* (8.2.41).

When *didṛkṣā* is established, the suffix *kenya* is applied; by the rule *ato lopaḥ* (6.4.48), the final vowel is elided. In the case of *śuśrūṣeṇyaḥ*: the desiderative suffix *san* is added to the root *śru*; by the rule *ajjhanagamāṃ sani* (6.4.16), there is lengthening of the vowel; the reduplication and the operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsakārya*) take place; when *śuśrūṣa* is established, the suffix *kenya* is applied. [The form] *kartvam*.

Thus [it is said]: "The suffix *tvam* is prescribed after the root *kṛ*; the suffix *tavai* is also prescribed in the rule beginning with *sayādi*. The rule for *sayādi* is the *sayādi-sūtra*, by which *sa* and the others are prescribed; in that [rule] as well, the suffix *tavai* is prescribed.
[Regarding the phrase] "of that which has the sense of *tum*" (*tasya tumarthāt*), etc.: if, however, that [suffix] has only the sense of *tum* in the abstract sense (*bhāve*).
The rule would be purposeless, as [the desired meaning] is already established by this very [rule]. Therefore,

although it is stated there that the suffix denotes the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*), nevertheless, one should understand that the suffix *tavya* is prescribed elsewhere for the object (*karman*) and other factors (*kāraka*), such as the agent (*kartṛ*).
15. And it is stated:
"The suffix *ṭha* is prescribed [after the root *cakṣ*]. The addition of the marker *ś* is for the purpose of assigning the technical designation *sārvadhātuka*.
Consequently, that which is prescribed for an *ārdhadhātuka* [suffix] does not apply when a *sārvadhātuka* [suffix] follows, such as in the rule "for *cakṣiṅ*, substitute *khyāñ*" (Pāṇini 2.4.54).
Thus, the substitution of *khyāñ* does not occur.

16. *bhāvalakṣaṇe stheṇkṛñvadicarihutamijanibhyastosun* (Pāṇini 3.4.16). Regarding the rule *āsaṃsthātoḥ* and so forth: by the word *āsaṃsthātaḥ*, completion (*samāpti*) is expressed; the sitting upon the altar (*vedyāṃ sadanam*) is indicated. [An example is: "It should be established before the rising of the sun."

In this case as well, the act of *ādhāna* (establishing the sacred fires) is [indicated] by the rising of the sun; in passages such as "before the calves are driven away," the sitting is indicated by the driving away of the calves; in passages such as "before the [fire] is kindled," the offering is indicated by the kindling; and in passages such as "before the [sacrificial food] is served," the offering itself is indicated by the serving.
In the two subsequent examples, there is an impossibility of being carried across by means of the Āhavanīya fire.
17. *sṛpitṛdoḥ kasun* (3.4.17).
18. *alaṃkhalvoḥ pratiṣedhayoḥ prācāṃ ktvā* (3.4.18). [The commentary states: "Of those expressing negation"—this is an explanation of the term *pratiṣedhayoḥ*. By this...

He shows that because they express negation, the words *alam* and *khalu* are designated by the term "negation" (*pratiṣedha*) in the Sūtra. For a designation based on expressing that [meaning] does indeed occur; for example, in the rule "small creatures" (*kṣudrajantavaḥ*, 2.4.8), where the words *yūka*, *likṣā*, and so forth, are used because they denote small creatures.
They are referred to by the term "small creatures" (kṣudrajantu).

Regarding the word "alaṅkāraḥ": the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). In this context, the word *alam* signifies "ornament" (*bhūṣaṇa*), as in the expression "enough with weeping" (*alam vāle rodanena*). Here, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). [If it is argued: "But surely there is the rule regarding optional forms (*vā-sarūpa-vidhi*)?"
Thus, even without the mention of "prāk" (before), the option (*vikalpa*) is indeed obtained;

for if you think that a dissimilar exception (*asarūpa-apavāda*) is what sublates [the general rule], then in that case, the mention of "prāk" [is necessary] because it refers to what precedes the section on feminine (*strī-adhikāra*). Or rather, there is no rule of non-similarity (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*) after that point.
Having kept this in mind for the sake of the conceptual analysis, the mention of "prior" was stated.

19. *udīcāṃ māṅo vyatīhāre* (3.4.19). [The example is] *upamitya*. There is the substitution of *ā* by [Pāṇini 6.1.45]: *ādeca upadeśe 'śiti*. There is a compound by [Pāṇini 2.2.18]: *kugatiprādayaḥ*. And there is the replacement of *ktvā* with *lyap* by [Pāṇini 7.1.37]: *samāse 'nañpūrve ktvo lyap*.
Thus, by [Pāṇini 7.1.37], *lyap* is substituted; by [Pāṇini 6.4.70], *it* is optionally applied;

and by [Pāṇini 6.1.71], *tuk* is inserted after a short vowel before a suffix beginning with *pit*. Now, one might object: the suffix *ktvā* occurs here precisely by [Pāṇini 3.4.21], "when two actions have the same agent, [the suffix is used] for the earlier time," for that rule applies here as well.

There is identity of agent (*samānakartṛkatva*). To explain: since the very same person who is the agent of "driving away" (*apamayati*) is also the agent of "begging" (*yācate*), for what purpose is [the suffix] prescribed? He says: "Because there is no priority of time," and so forth.
For he first begs and afterwards drives away; thus, there is no priority of time.

Therefore, the suffix *ktvā* is prescribed precisely when [the action] has not yet been reached [by another rule]. Let it be prescribed; however, this is the objection: at the very moment that *ktvā* arises from the root *mā* due to this rule, would it not also arise from the root *yāc* due to the rule "for two actions having the same agent"? This is not a fault; [because the former rule is more specific].
Since the phrase "of the Northerners" (*udīcām*) from rule 3.4.19 is understood in the rule "when two [actions] have the same agent" (3.4.21),
and that [phrase] constitutes a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), therefore, when the suffix *ktvā* occurs after the root *mā*,
the suffix *ktvā* will not occur after the root *yāc*. This is because of the mention of "the Northerners," and so forth.
The mention of "the northerners" (*udīcām*) here is for the purpose of providing an option; by means of that, what is [otherwise] established also occurs in the alternative case. [Examples include:
the *ktvā* suffix after the root *yāc*, and the *laṭ* and other suffixes after *mā*.
This reference as *māṅ* is [intended] for the root *māṅ* in the sense of "measuring" (*māne*), according to the Dhātupāṭha (1142).

Someone might have this doubt; therefore, in order to refute it, he says: "This is a reference to *meṅ* after the substitution of *ātva* has taken place. But how is this understood? From the inclusion of the term *vyatīhāra*. Only *meṅ* occurs in the sense of *vyatīhāra*, not *māṅ*; therefore, [it refers to] *meṅ*.
It is understood that this is indeed the intended explanation. But for what purpose was this formulation made?
If [the rule] were formulated such that doubt might arise, then instead of "na meṅ," it should have been stated unambiguously as "meṅ" alone.
To this he says: "For the sake of making known (jñāpanārthaḥ). This means that although the formulation could have been simply "meṅ,"...
This mention of the form with the *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) along with its *anubandha* is made for the purpose of providing an indication (*jñāpana*).

By that, this is indicated: "The state of not ending in a vowel (*anejantatva*) is not caused by an *anubandha*. With the words "by that" and so forth, he demonstrates the purpose of the indication. If this meaning were not indicated, then...

Because [the root *dā*] ends in a consonant (*hal*), it would not possess the property of ending in the vowel *e* (*ejanta*). What is the fault in that? The term *dāp* would not include *daip*, because they are different forms. Consequently, in the rule *dādhā ghu adāp* (Pāṇini 1.1.20), there would be no prohibition of *daip*. However, when this meaning is made known [by the following *jñāpaka*], [the fault is avoided].
It comes to be.
20. And [the suffix *ṭac* is applied] after [a word ending in the seventh case] when used in connection with "the further" (*para*) and "the nearer" (*avara*).

(3.4.20) Here, these two words, *para* and *avara*, are relative terms (*sambandhiśabda*). One becomes "further" in relation to what precedes it, and "nearer" in relation to what follows it; and relative terms are necessarily [dependent].

They bring the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) to mind; therefore, although a specific application is not indicated in the sūtra, nevertheless, it is understood that the connection of *para* and *avara* occurs only with what precedes and follows them.
Thus he says: "of the preceding by the following," and so forth. [The mountain is connected] by its connection with the distant river.

"It is distinguished" (*viśiṣyate*). For instance, when it is said "the mountain not having reached the river," the mountain is understood as being distinguished by its connection with the river that lies beyond it. Or, "the river is distinguished by its connection with the lower mountain. This is because when it is said "the river having crossed the mountain," [it is understood] by means of the lower [mountain].
When there is a conjunction of a mountain and a river, the river qualified by that [conjunction] is understood.

21. *samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle* (Pāṇini 3.4.21). Since the governing topic is "roots" (*dhātu*), it is understood that the state of having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) pertains specifically to the meanings of the roots; thus he says: "those two root-meanings which have a common agent," and so forth. This genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).

This word *samāna* signifies "one and the same. Now, an objection is raised: "The *kāraka* is the capacity (*śakti*), whereas the prior action is something else; so how is it understood that they have the same agent? To this he says: "Of the capacity and the possessor of capacity," and so forth. "Capacity and the possessor of capacity" are the two referred to as *śakti-śaktimantau*. And that which...

The substratum of the capacity and the capacity itself—their distinction is not intended here. Therefore, Devadatta alone, as the substratum of the capacity, is the agent; and since he is one and the same for both actions, it is logical that there is a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*). Regarding "having drunk" (*pītvā*): the substitution of *ī* [for *ai*] is as in the previous case. Here...

The dual ending has been employed in the expression "samānakartṛkayoḥ" (of two [actions] having the same agent); therefore, only two actions will be presented, not many. Consequently, [the suffix would apply] only when two actions are presented, not when there are many? To this he says: "the dual ending."
And so forth. Because this designation is primarily concerned with the action, the dual number is not the primary factor here;

rather, it is used because [the action] is inseparable from it. Thus, the designation is made by means of the dual number. Since a designation must necessarily be made by some grammatical number or another, the dual number is therefore not a restrictive factor (*atantrāt*).
It indeed occurs even when there are many actions, as in:

*bhuktavati brāhmaṇe vrajati* ("When the Brāhmaṇa has eaten, [Devadatta] goes"). Here, the Brāhmaṇa is the agent (*kartṛ*) of the action of eating, whereas Devadatta is the agent of the action of going; thus, there is an absence of a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*). [The word] *vrajati*...
And he says, "jalpati" (he speaks). Here, because of simultaneity, there is no anteriority of time for the action.
"Vyādāya": this is a form of the root *dā* preceded by the prefix *vi-ā*. "Sammīlya":
this is from the root *mīla*, *smīla*, or *kṣmīla* in the sense of "closing the eyes" (Dhātupāṭha 517, 519, 520), preceded by the prefix *sam-*.

[This applies] to a causative (*hetumaṇṇic*) ending. But for what reason is it not established? He says: "Because it does not precede" (*apūrvakālatvāt*). The meaning of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is "provision" (*pratipādana*). In this regard, the provision is as follows: the word *ca* (and) from the preceding rule (*pūrvayoga*) is carried over (*anuvartate*), and that...
And it has the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned; therefore, in cases such as "he sleeps with his mouth open," the suffix will apply even though there is no prior sequence of time.

22. *abhīkṣṇye ṇamul ca* (3.4.22). Regarding the phrase "accompanied by reduplication" and so forth: indeed, it is only when the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are accompanied by reduplication that they have the capacity to express frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*), not when they are used alone.

This is due to the inherent nature of the expressive power of words (*śabdaśakti*). Therefore, the intention is that reduplication (*dvirvacana*) must be prescribed. To the question "By what means, then, is there reduplication here?", he says: "In the sense of frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*)," and so forth. [The form] *pāyampāyam* [is derived] by [the rule] *āto yuk* (Pāṇini 7.3.33).
23. *na yadyanākāṅkṣe* (3.4.23). Regarding the term *anākāṅkṣe*: that which has no *ākāṅkṣā*—that is, no expectation or requirement—is so described.
Regarding the phrase *ktvā tu pūrvasūtravihito 'pi*: by the word *api*, it is indicated that even that which was prescribed by the immediately preceding rule [is included].

It is logical that what is prescribed by the immediately preceding sūtra is prohibited, on the principle that "a rule or a prohibition applies to what is nearest" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 99). But how can there be a prohibition of that which was prescribed by the previous sūtra? [The answer is: because the prohibition is formulated with reference to the specific context.

This prohibition is made with reference to the section on the prior time (pūrvakāla-prakaraṇa), in the sense that "whatever [suffix] would otherwise apply according to the section on the prior time does not occur. Therefore, it is logical that there is a prohibition even of that which was prescribed by the preceding rule.

24. *vibhāṣāgreprathamapūrveṣu* (3.4.24). [The word] *ābhīkṣṇye* does not carry over [from the previous rule]. This is the reasoning for the statement: "This is an option where there was no prior application" (*aprāptavibhāṣā*).

But is it not more appropriate that this be an option where there was already an application (*prāptavibhāṣā*), since the suffix *ktvā* would otherwise have applied by default when the suffix *ṇamul* is used?
Is this [rule] begun because it would otherwise be superseded by Pāṇini 3.4.21, *samānakartṛkayoḥ* etc.?

This is not so; for, having taken over the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* prescribed by the immediately preceding sūtra, this is stated to be an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) where [the suffixes] were otherwise not required. As for that which...

Since the suffix *ktvā* alone is prescribed by the rule "samānakartṛkayoḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.21) and so forth, the mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*) need not be made with respect to it; for the meaning established by that [suffix] is already accomplished by the rule regarding non-identical forms (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*). [Objection: But surely...
By the words "ityādinā" and so forth, he refutes the purpose of the inclusion of the term *vibhāṣā* mentioned immediately prior.

[The text continues with] "ṭhktvāṇamulī yatra" and so on. Since the forms such as the present tense (*laṭ*) and others would already be established in alternative cases by the rule of non-identity of form (*vāsarūpavidhi*) alone, the fact that the term *vibhāṣā* is employed for that purpose indicates that [the option applies] where both the absolutive suffix *ktvā* and the gerundive suffix *ṇamul* occur.
In that case, since two operations are prescribed simultaneously, it is indicated that the rule regarding "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpa*) does not apply.
What is the purpose of this indication? He says: "By that," and so forth;
"the compound with an *upapada*," and so forth; namely, the *upapada*-compound according to Pāṇini 2.2.20: *amaivāvyayena*.

He asks why that [result] does not occur and says: "It has been stated," and so forth. It was previously stated [in Kāśikāvṛtti 2.2.20]: "That upapada which is prescribed by the same rule as *am* is compounded with it.
The upapadas *agne*, *bhṛti*, and so on, are prescribed by the same rule as *am* and another *ktvā* suffix.
Therefore, they are not compounded.

25. *karmaṇyākrośe kṛñaḥ khamuñ* (Pāṇini 3.4.25). [The example] "ṭhcaurāṅkāram" [is formed as follows]: by the rule *arurdviṣadajantasya mum* (Pāṇini 6.3.67), the augment *mum* is added. Thus we have "ṭhcaurakaraṇam" and so forth. Here, the verb *kṛ* denotes the action of uttering.

In the abusive statement "You are a thief," the utterance of the word "thief" is for the purpose of accomplishing the abuse itself; for without it, the abuse cannot be conveyed. It is not the case that "he is made into a thief," because that is impossible. Nor...
Even by saying "you are a thief" a hundred times, one cannot produce the state of being a thief in a person.

26. *svādumi ṇamul* (3.4.26). Regarding the statement, "In *svādumi*, there is a reference to the meaning," one might object: "But surely, according to the rule *svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasyāśabdasaṃjñā* (1.1.68), there ought to be a reference to the word's own form (*svarūpa*) alone? This is not so.

Since the term "of the word" (*śabdasya*) is already established by the very context of the introduction to the *Śabdānuśāsana* (the science of grammar), the explicit mention of "word" (*śabda*) has been made for the purpose of making it known that: where a designation refers to the word itself, its own form (*svarūpa*) is understood, and not when the designation refers to the meaning (*artha*). In this case, however, the designation refers to the meaning; therefore, only the meaning is to be taken.

This is correct; however, that the instruction is intended for the actual meaning is understood from the uninterrupted tradition of the teachers' lineage. And since the actual meaning is being grasped, the suffix is obtained even when synonyms are used; thus he says: "in the sense of 'delicious things'," and so forth.

Now, regarding the rule *atha ṭhsvādumi*: for what purpose is the final *m* (makārāntatva) prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*)? If it is argued that it is so that the upapada ending in *m* may be heard [as such], we say no; if this were the intended purpose, the irregularity should not have been prescribed, because the suffix *khamuñ* is taught in the immediately preceding rule.

Since that [suffix] is the subject under discussion, it alone will be prescribed. And once it has been prescribed, the fact that the upapada ends in *m* will follow by the very rule for *mu*; in order to dispel this objection, he says: "in the sense of *svādumī*" and so forth.

By this he shows the following: although the status of ending in *m* (*makārāntatva*) is established when *khamuñ* is present, the prohibition of the vowel *ī* (*īkārapratiṣedha*) is not established; consequently, from the word *svadu* as an upapada, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would be applied by the rule "ṭhvoto guṇavacanāt" (Pāṇini 4.1.44), and thus an undesired form would result.

It would be so; for if it were prescribed as ending in *m*, since the condition (*nimitta*) would already be established, there would be no possibility of the application of the suffix *ṅīṣ*. Therefore, even by one who prescribes *khamuñ*, it must necessarily be prescribed as ending in *m* in order to prohibit the vowel *ī*.

Although it might be argued by another that "once *khamuñ* is prescribed, the status of ending in *m* will be achieved simply through *muṭ*," he says "of that which ends in *cvī*" (*cvyantasya*) and so forth to indicate that this is not the case everywhere.
By this, he shows that if the status of ending in *m* were not treated as an irregularity (*nipātana*), then...

Even though *khamuñ* exists, the suffix *mum* would not apply to an upapada ending in *cvī* because that [suffix] is indeclinable (*avyaya*); furthermore, in the rule prescribing *mum*, there is the governing heading "when *khiti* follows, provided it is not an indeclinable" (Pāṇini 6.3.66). Therefore, even by one who prescribes *khamuñ*, [the same restriction must be observed].

The irregularity (*nipātana*) regarding its ending in *m* must be prescribed. If that is so, let only this irregularity regarding the ending in *m* be performed, while the suffix *khamuñ*, which is the subject under discussion, should be enjoined? It is impossible to enjoin *khamuñ*; for if the suffix *khamuñ* were applied, the irregularity regarding the ending in *m* would be necessary for the sake of making it an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

It is understood [that the suffix is *ṇamul*]; consequently, by the rule "ṭhcvau ca" (Pāṇini 6.3.64), lengthening (*dīrghatva*) would indeed occur. However, when *ṇamul* is present, it should be understood as an exception (*apavāda*) to all other rules; therefore, even lengthening does not take place.
Furthermore, *ṇamul* must necessarily be prescribed for the sake of subsequent rules, and when it is prescribed for those subsequent cases, [the objection does not apply].
There is brevity [of expression], nor is there any prolixity here.

To the question, "In what sense, then, do these suffixes occur?", he says: "And because of the governing rule for the sense of 'tum' (infinitive)," and so forth. "'These' refers to those which are prescribed under the governing rule for the sense of 'tum'. 'If this is so'..."
The meaning is that [the suffix] occurs when there is the sense of "you" (*tum-arthe*). Regarding the phrase "by the suffix of *bhuj*" and so forth:

although the agent is not expressed by the suffix *ṇamul*, nevertheless, because it is expressed by the suffix *laṭ* of the root *bhuj*, the third case ending should not occur. Now, one might object: the agent is characterized by its capacity (*śakti*), and this [capacity] is distinct [from the action].

There is one power (śakti) whose object is the act of making [food] sweet, and another power whose object is the act of eating; in that case, even though the power whose object is the act of eating has been expressed by the present tense suffix (*laṭ*), because the other power is not expressed as having the designation "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*), [the designation would] follow— this is the reading as it appears in the printed text.

He states that the third [case ending] is indeed obtained: "And not in this," and so forth. For here, in the section concerning a common agent (*samānakartṛka*), the distinction between the capacities (*śakti*) is not intended to be expressed because they are identical; therefore, the possessor of the capacity, Devadatta, is the agent, and he is expressed as being one and the same.
How, then, can there be the contingency of a third [case ending]? For what reason is the distinction not intended to be expressed?

To this he says: "For when there is a common agent," and so forth. Even while conceding the intention to express a distinction, he states another resolution: "When the primary power is denoted," and so forth.
But what determines the primary and subordinate status of the agent and the capacity [of the action] here? It is determined by the action (*kriyā*);
for the act of making delicious (*svāduṅkāra*) is subordinate because it exists for the sake of the act of eating.
The act of eating, however, is primary because it is that which is assisted by the former. Furthermore, this is because the action possesses the nature of both the subordinate and the principal.

Even for the two potencies of the agent (*kartṛ-śakti*) that have those [two] as their objects, there exists a relationship of primary and subordinate. In that case, when the primary potency has been expressed, the subordinate potency, because it is already expressed, shines forth—that is, it manifests—since subordinate factors follow the primary one. Therefore, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) does not [apply].
That which comes into being is "bhāva" (an entity).

27. *anyathā-evaṃ-katham-ittham-su siddhāprayogaś-cet* | (3.4.27) Regarding the term *siddhāprayogaḥ*: that whose non-usage (*aprayoga*) is established (*siddha*) is so described. "Because of being meaningless," and so forth; [this means] because of the absence of a denotable object (*abhidheya*) or because of the absence of a purpose (*prayojana*).

"Uselessness" (*nirarthakatvam*). "In this very way" means precisely that it is useless. By the phrase "he eats otherwise," etc., having kept that very uselessness in mind, he demonstrates the status of being an unestablished usage (*siddhāprayogatām*). The meaning conveyed by "he eats otherwise" is exactly the same as when the verb *karoti* ("he does") is not employed.
The same meaning is understood when the verb *karoti* is not employed as it is when it is employed in the form "he eats otherwise" (*anyathākāraṃ bhuṅkte*).
Therefore, the verb *karoti* is redundant. But how can it be redundant while it is actually being employed?

Otherwise, these [words] such as *anyathā* are expressive of a manner (*prakāra*). When they express the manner that constitutes the meaning of the verb used in subsequent application (*anuprayoga*), then the root *kṛ* (in *karoti*)—being qualified by them—expresses that very manner; since this manner is already understood from elsewhere, [the use of *karoti*] would be redundant. If this is so, then because its meaning is already understood...
Does its application not follow? It is not so; for even when the meaning is already understood, usage is observed—as in "Bring two cakes" or "I am cooking.
In the expression "He eats while holding his head otherwise," by the word *anyathā*, [the modification] of another word [is indicated].

The manner [in which] the head is eaten is expressed; that [manner] is not understood without the verb *karoti* (to do). For if *karoti* were not employed, the manner pertaining to the act of eating would be perceived as having a different characteristic, rather than one pertaining to the head. Indeed, only the fact that the head is being eaten would be understood.
Therefore, the verb "to do" (karoti) is not used here as a completed action.
28. *Yathātathayorasūyāprativacane* (3.4.28).

Regarding the phrase "asūyāprativacane": a reply arising from malice is an "asūyāprativacana" (a reply of malice). For example, "yadi asūyan," and so forth. Here, *asūyan* is a present participle (*śatṛ*-affix) derived from the root *asūya*, which belongs to the *kaṇḍv-ādi* group and takes the suffix *ya*.
The connection is with the word *prativakti*. "He answers" (*prativakti*) means he speaks back;
the sense is that he utters a reply. Regarding the word *pṛcchati*: this is in the locative case.
When [someone] is asking (*pṛcchati*), if one answers while being envious (*asūyan*), meaning manifesting envy, then in that case, regarding what is asked—
A reply that is characterized by malice is a "malicious reply. Regarding the phrase "in whatever manner," etc.:
when one asks the question, "How will you eat? in such a manner, it is a malicious reply, [expressed] as "in whatever manner," etc. When one asks the question, "How will you eat? in such a manner...
This is not a response born of malice, such as "you shall see what I will do before I eat. Rather, it is an explanation of that [statement].

29. *karmaṇi dṛśividoḥ sākalye* (3.4.29). The commentary states: "When the object (*karman*) is the upapada, provided it is qualified by totality (*sākalya*). By this, he demonstrates that the mention of "totality" is an adjective qualifying the object. [As in: "Whichever Brāhmaṇa he knows... (*Kāśikā*). Whichever... [yaṃ]... [yaṃ]... [brāhmaṇaṃ jānāti].

"Whatever one knows, acquires, or deliberates upon"—by this, he shows that the roots *vid* (to know), *lābha* (to acquire), and *vicāraṇā* (to deliberate) are included. But why is the root *as* (to exist) not included? Because it is intransitive (*akarmaka*), whereas [the rule applies to] "in the presence of an object" (*karmaṇi*).
Because of grasping.
30. *yāvati vindajīvoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.30). [The word] *vindateḥ* refers to the root *vidlṛ* in the sense of "obtaining" (Dhātupāṭha 1432).
31. After the roots *car* and *dṛ*, [the suffix *ṇa* is applied] to *pūr*.

(3.4.31) [The word] "of *pūrayati*" indicates that this refers to the causative form (*ṇyanta*) of the root. Here, the term "object" (*karman*) from the previous rule continues to apply. Furthermore, an object is not possible for the non-causative (*aṇyanta*) *pūr*, for it is intransitive (*akarmaka*).
The verbal roots ending in the causative suffix *ṇic* are transitive; therefore, this reference is understood to apply to the root when it ends in *ṇic*.

32. *varṣapramāṇa ūlopaścāsyānyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 3.4.32). Regarding the phrase "by the aggregate": this refers to the aggregate consisting of the base (*prakṛti*), the suffix (*pratyaya*), and the subordinate word (*upapada*). By this, he demonstrates that the measure of years functions as a qualifier for the aggregate.

"What is the purpose of mentioning *ṭha*?"—the intention is that, because *pūrayati* is the subject under discussion, its elision will be understood even without the statement "of this (*asya*). [The objection is: "Let it not apply to the *upapada*. If "of this" were not stated, then just as [the rule for] the measure of rain (*varṣapramāṇa*)...

The elision of *ū* is understood as a condition pertaining to the entire complex; likewise, the elision of *ū* should also be understood as a condition pertaining to the entire complex. That is to say, the elision occurs of that which ends in *ū* belonging to a complex consisting of a base (*prakṛti*), an affix (*pratyaya*), and an upapada; consequently, it would apply to the upapada as well. Therefore...
Lest this fault should occur, the rule "of *ṭha*" is stated.

33. *cela-ṣṇuk* (3.4.33). [The rule] "after a root ending in ṇi" (*ṭhṇyantāt*) is a reference to the form including the augment *puk*. And since *puk* occurs only after a suffix beginning with *ṇa*, as stated in [Pāṇini 7.3.36] "*arti-hrī-* etc., it follows that for this very reason..."
The causative nature (*ṇyantatā*) is understood from the grammatical instruction (*nirdeśa*). Regarding the phrase "in the sense of *cela*":
this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those whose object (*artha*) is *cela*. By this, he shows that the word *cela* is taken in its sense (*arthagrahaṇa*).

And as for the reasoning regarding the inclusion of the sense (*arthagrahaṇa*), that same reasoning which was stated under the rule "with *svādumī* [the suffix] *ṇamul*" (Pāṇini 3.4.26) applies here as well to the inclusion of the sense.

It should be understood as follows: in the word *celaknopam*, there is the elision of the *y* in *vali*; then, by the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya* (Pāṇini 7.3.86), there is the *guṇa* strengthening; finally, there is the elision of the suffix *ṇi*.

34. [The suffix *khaś* is applied] after the root *kaṣ* when it takes the prefixes *ni-* and *sam-*. (3.4.34) Regarding the mention of "after *kaṣ*": the root *kaṣ*, along with *śiṣ*, is recited in the section of verbal roots meaning "to injure" (hiṃsārtha) in the Dhātupāṭha (685, 687).
35. *Piṣ* [takes the suffix *ṇamul*] after words meaning "dry," "powder," and "rough. (3.4.35). Regarding "of *piṣ*": the root *piṣlṛ* means "to grind into powder" (*sañcūrṇane*). (Dhātupāṭha 1452).

36. *samūlākṛtajīveṣu hankṛñgrahaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.36). Regarding the form *samūlaghātam*: the substitution of *gha* for *han* occurs by the rule *ho hanter ñṇinneṣu* (7.3.54), and the substitution of *t* for *n* occurs by the rule *hanasta aciṇṇaloḥ* (7.3.32).

37. *hanaḥ* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). (Pāṇini 3.4.37) This rule is begun for the purpose of [denoting] non-injury (*ahiṃsā*). For [the formation of a word meaning injury] would already be established by the upcoming rule *hiṃsārthānām* (3.4.48). [The phrase] "for the sake of making it an obligatory compound" (*nityasamāsārthaḥ*)—the remainder [of the thought] is that this applies even to [the root *han*] when it has the sense of injury.
This rule is commenced so that there may be an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*) by the rule *ṭhupapadamatiṅ* (2.2.19). However, when a suffix (*pratyaya*) follows,
there would instead be an optional compound by the rule *ṭhṛtīyāprabhṛtīnyanyatarasyām* (2.2.21).

"And for the purpose of employing [the root] according to its specific rule," as stated in *Kaṣādiṣu yathāvidhyanuprayogaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.46). This means that the employment (*anuprayoga*) must be of that very root after which the suffix *ṇamul* was prescribed;
otherwise, by that suffix, there would be an employment of a different root.
But surely, since the root *han* has the meaning of "killing" (*hiṃsā*), then by virtue of its subsequent position, the rule for that [root] alone should apply;

so how is it appropriate for this introduction of the root *han*—which has the meaning of killing—to serve the purpose of forming a compulsory compound and the purpose of applying the suffix according to the prescribed rule? To this, he says:
"By means of the prior prohibition," and so forth.
38. *pipaḥ* [is used] in the sense of *snehana*. (3.4.38) By the phrase "in the sense of *snehana*," he explains the meaning of the term *snehane*.
39. *haste vartigrahoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.39).
Regarding the statement "*vartiḥ ṇyantaḥ*" (the root *vṛt* is followed by the causative suffix *ṇi*), the fact that *vṛt* is followed by *ṇi* is understood from the very wording of the rule itself.

40. *sve puṣaḥ* | (3.4.40) Regarding the form *svapoṣam*: when the word *sva*, signifying "self," is the *upapada*, this suffix [is applied]. Regarding *gopoṣam*: when it signifies "one's own. Regarding *dhanapoṣam*: when it signifies "wealth. Regarding *pitṛpoṣam*.
Thus, [the suffix] *kta* is used in the sense of what has been known.
41. The suffix *kha* is applied after [the roots] *naś* and *vah* when used with the word *adhikaraṇa* (locus).

(3.4.41) 42. [The suffix *kha* is applied after the same roots] when used with a word that serves as a name (*saṃjñā*). (3.4.42) 43. [The suffix *kha* is applied after the roots] *naś* and *vah* when used with the words *jīva* or *puruṣa* as the agent (*kartṛ*). (3.4.43)

In *naṣṭaḥ*, the substitution of *ṣ* for *n* occurs by the rule *vraścādi-* (Pāṇini 8.2.36); the augment *num* prescribed by *masjinaśorjhali* (7.1.60) is elided by *aniditām-* (6.4.24), and so forth.
In *puruṣeṇoḍhaḥ*, the semivowel *v* of the root *vah* is replaced by its corresponding vowel (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule *vacyādi-* (6.1.15).
The substitution of the preceding vowel [for the semivowel] occurs by *samprasāraṇācca* (6.1.108); then *ho ḍhaḥ* (8.2.31),
*jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* (8.2.40), *ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ* (8.4.41), *ḍho ḍhea lopaḥ* (8.3.13),
and finally the lengthening by *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho'ṇaḥ* (6.3.111).

44. *ūrdhve śuṣi-pūrauḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.44). [The sūtra states: "*ūrdhvam pūryate*" (it is filled upwards). The meaning is: "it becomes filled from above. Because the root is *anudātta*, the *ātmanepada* ending is applied; furthermore, it belongs to the *divādi* class, hence the suffix *śyan*.
45. [The suffix *khyun* is applied] after a word denoting a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) when it functions as the object (*karman*).
(Pāṇini 3.4.45) As in the example "a vessel for ghee" (*ghṛtanidhāya*), the derivation is formed in the same manner as previously explained.

46. *Kaṣādiṣu yathāvidhyanuprayogaḥ* (3.4.46). 47. *Upadaṃśas tṛtīyāyām* (3.4.47). In examples such as "he eats with a radish" (*mūlakenopadaṃśaṃ bhuṅkte*), the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used for the instrument (*karaṇa*); that which ends in this [third case]— [The rule applies when it is followed by the verb *bhuj* or *ad*, provided it is not used in the sense of eating. The term *upadaṃśa* refers to the act of biting or nibbling at the side of something while eating. In the example given, the radish is the instrument of the action of eating. Thus, the word *mūlakena* takes the third case ending. When this [word ending in the third case] is followed by the verb *bhuj* or *ad*, the aforementioned rule applies. However, this does not apply if the meaning is simply "eating" (*bhojana*). For instance, in "he eats with radishes" (*mūlakena bhuṅkte*), the root *bhuj* is used in its primary sense of consuming food, and therefore the rule does not apply here. Furthermore, the rule does not apply when the object of the action is expressed in the accusative case (*dvitīyā*). For example, in "he eats the radish while nibbling on it" (*mūlakam upadaṃśaṃ bhuṅkte*), the word *mūlakam* takes the second case ending because it is the direct object (*karman*) of the action. In such instances, the rule is not applicable. The mention of the word *upadaṃśa* in the sūtra is intended to include the verb *ad* as well. This is because the word *upadaṃśa* is derived from the root *daṃś* with the prefix *upa*, and since the roots *bhuj* and *ad* share the same meaning, the inclusion of *upadaṃśa* serves to extend the application of the rule to the root *ad*. Therefore, the rule applies to both verbs. Consequently, in examples such as "he eats with radishes" (*mūlakenopadaṃśaṃ bhuṅkte*) or "he eats with radishes" (*mūlakenopadaṃśam atti*), the verb *bhuj* or *ad* is subsequently employed according to the specific grammatical rules (*yathāvidhi*). This is because the subsequent employment of the verb is restricted by the specific conditions of the original rule. The mention of the word *anuprayoga* ("subsequent employment") in the sūtra is intended to exclude cases where the verb is used independently or in a different construction; thus, the rule applies only when the verb is employed immediately following the word ending in the third case. Therefore, in examples such as "having eaten with radishes, he goes" (*mūlakenopadaṃśaṃ bhuktvā gacchati*), the rule does not apply because the verb *bhuj* is not employed immediately after the word ending in the third case. The mention of the word *tṛtīyāyām* in the sūtra is intended to indicate that the rule applies only when the third case ending is present. Therefore, in examples such as "he eats with radishes" (*mūlakena bhuṅkte*), where the third case is not used, the rule does not apply. The mention of the word *upadaṃśa* in the sūtra is intended to specify the particular type of action; therefore, the rule does not apply to other actions such as "he eats with radishes" (*mūlakena khādati*) or "he eats with radishes" (*mūlakena carvati*). The mention of the word *bhuj* in the sūtra is intended to restrict the scope of the rule; therefore, the rule does not apply to other verbs such as "he eats with radishes" (*mūlakena ghasati*) or "he eats with radishes" (*mūlakena grasati*). The mention of the word *ad* in the sūtra is intended to further restrict the scope; therefore, the rule does not apply to other verbs such as "he eats with radishes" (*mūlakena jakṣiti*) or "he eats with radishes" (*mūlakena jagdhvā*). The mention of the word *anuprayoga* in the sūtra is intended to exclude cases where the verb is used in a different sequence; therefore, the rule does not apply to examples such as "having eaten with radishes, he eats" (*mūlakenopadaṃśaṃ bhuktvā bhuṅkte*). The mention of the word *yathāvidhi* in the sūtra is intended to ensure that the subsequent employment of the verb follows the specific requirements of the original rule. Therefore, the rule does not apply to cases where the verb is employed in a manner that deviates from those requirements, such as "he eats with radishes" (*mūlakena bhuṅkte*) where the verb is used independently. The mention of the word *kaṣādiṣu* in the sūtra is intended to provide a comprehensive list of the relevant verbal roots; therefore, the rule does not apply to other roots such as *pac* or *pācayati*. The mention of the word *upadaṃśa* in the sūtra is intended to clarify the specific nature of the action; therefore, the rule does not apply to other actions such as "he eats with radishes" (*mūlakena bhakṣayati*) or "he eats with radishes" (*mūlakena prāśnāti*). The mention of the word *tṛtīyāyām* in the sūtra is intended to specify the grammatical condition; therefore, the rule does not apply to cases where the third case is not used, such as "he eats with radishes" (*mūlakena bhuṅkte*) where the third case is absent. The mention of the word *anuprayoga* in the sūtra is intended to exclude cases where the verb is used in a separate clause; therefore, the rule does not apply to examples such as "having eaten with radishes, he goes" (*mūlakenopadaṃśaṃ bhuktvā gacchati*). The mention of the word *yathāvidhi* in the sūtra is intended to ensure that the subsequent employment of the verb is governed by the specific rules of the original formation. Therefore, the rule does not apply to cases where the verb is employed in a way that contradicts those rules, such as "he eats with radishes" (*mūlakena bhuṅkte*) where the verb is used in a general sense. The mention of the word *kaṣādiṣu* in the sūtra is intended to define the scope of the rule; therefore, the rule does not apply to other roots such as *khād* or *carv*. The mention of the word *upadaṃśa* in the sūtra is intended to specify the type of action; therefore, the rule does not apply to other actions such as "he eats with radishes" (*mūlakena bhakṣayati*) or "he eats with radishes" (*mūlakena prāśnāti*). The mention of the word *tṛtīyāyām* in the sūtra is intended to specify the grammatical condition; therefore, the rule does not apply to cases where the third case is not used, such as "he eats with radishes" (*mūlakena bhuṅkte*) where the third case is absent. The mention of the word *anuprayoga* in the sūtra is intended to exclude cases where the verb is used in a separate clause; therefore, the rule does not apply to examples such as "having eaten with radishes, he goes" (*mūlakenopadaṃśaṃ bhuktvā gacchati*). The mention of the word *yathāvidhi* in the sūtra is intended to ensure that the subsequent employment of the verb is governed by the specific rules of the original formation. Therefore, the rule does not apply to cases where the verb is employed in a way that contradicts those rules, such as "he eats with radishes" (*mūlakena bhuṅkte*) where the verb is used in a general sense. The mention of the word *kaṣādiṣu* in the sūtra is intended to define the scope of the rule; therefore, the rule does not apply to other
The root *mūlaka* and others function as the subordinate element (*upapada*). And would that subordinate element be the instrument (*karaṇa*) of either *udaṃś* or *bhuj*?

In that regard, it is first of all not tenable for it to be the subordinate element of *upa-daṃś*; for when one thing is being pointed out (*upadiśyamāna*) while another is being pointed out (*upadaṃśyamāna*), there exists a separate instrument, whereas here, it is that very same [thing].

Only *mūlaka* and so forth are designated as "upapada," and nothing else. However, with respect to the act of eating (*bhuji*), the status of being an instrument (*karaṇabhāva*) certainly applies; yet, there would be no designation of "upapada," and in its absence, there would be no upapada-compound (*upapadasamāsa*).
This is because the designation "upapada" is established by means of a technical term (*mahatī saṃjñā*) for the purpose of the paribhāṣā concerning semantic compatibility (*samarthaparibhāṣā*).

For the sake of its application, when that [term] is present here, the designation *upapada* must apply to that which has the capacity with respect to whichever [verbal root] it concerns. Thus, the designation *upapada* must apply to the verbal root *bhuj* (to eat) with respect to *mūlaka* and so forth.

Anticipating the objection that there is no semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) with the *upadaṃśi* (the act of nibbling), he says: "And *mūlaka* etc., in the sense of *upadaṃśa*," and so forth. Although *mūlaka* and the like function as instruments (*karaṇa*) with respect to the act of eating (*bhuji*), nevertheless, their semantic connection with the *upadaṃśi* is indeed established; for they are its object (*karman*). Nor...
When there is a connection with *bhujin* (the root √bhuj), the connection with *upadaṃśin* (the root upa-√daṃś) ceases;

for there is no contradiction [between them]. Therefore, the status of being an *upapada* (governing word) is indeed established, and when that exists, there is an *upapada-samāsa* (compound with a governing word).

Regarding the phrase "when there is a difference between actions" (*kriyābhede sati*): by the mention of the "difference between actions," he indicates the domain of the suffix *ktvā*. That which possesses both the temporal sequence (*paurvāparya*) of actions and a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) is the domain of the suffix *ktvā*. And both of these [conditions] exist only when there is a difference between actions.

The scope of the *ktvā* suffix is indicated by the expression "when [something] exists, [something else] comes to be," as in: "He eats while eating with radishes" (*mūlakenopadaśya bhuṅkte*). Here, the elision of the nasal is applied according to the rule *aniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24).

48. And [the suffix *ktvā* is used] after roots meaning "to injure" (*hiṃsā*) when they have the same object (*samānakarmaka*). (Pāṇini 3.4.48) Because of the governing rule regarding the connection with a verbal root (*dhātusambandha*), there must be an auxiliary verb (*anuprayoga*), since [the relationship of having the same object] resides in two [roots]. In that case, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the state of having the same object is understood specifically in relation to the auxiliary verb; thus he says:

"By means of the root *anu-prayuj*," and so forth. Regarding "he causes time to pass" (*kālayati*): [the roots] *kala* in the sense of "instruction regarding time" (some say *kāla* is a separate root)—*dhā.pā.*;
and *kala* in the sense of "neglect"—*dhā.pā.*; and *kāla* in the sense of "wasting"—*dhā.pā.* 1880.
Regarding "striking with the teeth" (*danta-tāḍam*): *taḍa* in the sense of "striking"—*dhā.pā.* 1579.

It is precisely the *curādi* [group of roots] [that is intended]. In the example "having struck with a staff," etc., the thief is the object (*karman*) of the root *han*, whereas the cow is the object of the subsequently applied (*anuprayoga*) root; thus, because there is an absence of a common object (*samānakarmakatva*), only the suffix *ktvā* occurs. Regarding the form "having struck" (*āhatya*), [the rule] *anudātopadeśa...* (Pāṇini 6.4.37) applies.
By these and other rules, there is the elision of the nasal; and by "ṭhhrasvasya piti kṛti tuk" (Pāṇini 6.1.71), the augment *tuk* is added.

49. *saptamyāṃ copapīḍarudhakarṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.49). [The commentary states: "The word *upa* is connected with each [of the following roots]. This is so that [the suffix *lyuṭ*] may apply only after the roots *rudh* and *kṛṣ* when preceded by *upa*. For example: *pārśvopapīḍam*. [The root] *pīḍ* [is listed as] "avagāhane" (in the sense of pressing or submerging; Dhātupāṭha 1544).

The *curādi* group: "of *karṣati*" and so forth. The root *kṛṣ* "to scratch" is listed both in the *bhvādi* class (DhP 990) and in the *tudādi* class (DhP 1286). Here, the *bhvādika* one is intended, not the *taudādika* one;
this is because of the mention [of the root] with the *śap* suffix. That mention with *śap* belongs to it.
It is obtained by the pronunciation of the [syllable] *kṛta* with its inherent quality (*guṇa*).

50. *samāsataḥ* | (3.4.50) Regarding the phrase *yuddhasaṃrambhāt*: *saṃrambhaḥ* is a specific modification of speech and body preceded by mental agitation; *yuddhasaṃrambhaḥ* is the agitation for the sake of battle, from which [it follows] excessively.
They are brought near; that is to say, they draw close.

51. And in the case of *pramāṇa*. (Pāṇini 3.4.51). [The word *pramāṇa* here] means "length" (*āyāma*). This is because of the statement: "Length (*āyāma*), however, should be *pramāṇa*. Thus, by means of another word whose meaning is more commonly known—namely, "length"—the very meaning of the word *pramāṇa* [is indicated].
He clarifies this with the phrase "an increase of two finger-breadths" (*dvyaṅgulotkarṣam*).

The term *dvyaṅgulam* is a collective compound (*samāhāra*) meaning "the combination of two fingers," formed according to the rule *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.86), which prescribes the suffix *ac*. By means of that measure of two finger-breadths, the length of the *khaṇḍikā* and so forth is determined.

52. [The suffix *lyap* is used] after a word denoting the point of departure (*apādāna*) when there is a sense of haste (*parīpsā*). (3.4.52) For example, in the expression "śayyotthāyam" ("rising from bed"). [In this case, the substitution of the preceding vowel is governed by] the rule "udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ pūrvasya" (8.4.61), which prescribes the substitution of the homogeneous preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*).
By the rule *ṭhāto yuk* (Pāṇini 7.3.33), he demonstrates urgency through the word *evam* and so forth.
"Drawing away from the opening" (*randhrāpakarṣam*) means that she hastens so much that she does not even wait for the vessel;
rather, drawing the milk directly from the opening of the breast, she drinks it with her mouth. "Drawing away from the frying pan" (*bhrāṣṭrāpakarṣam*).
Thus, he is indeed so hurried that he does not even wait for a vessel to be given,
but instead takes [the food] directly from the frying pan and eats it with his hand.

53. And [the suffix *khañ* is applied] after the second [case ending]. (3.4.53) 54. After a word denoting a limb of one's own body (*svāṅga*), provided it is not liquid (*adhruva*) and so forth, [the suffix *khañ* is applied]. (3.4.54) The definition of a "limb of one's own body" (*svāṅga*), as well as the exclusion of things such as liquids (*adrava*), will be stated in the fourth [chapter]. [An example is: *akṣiṇikāṇam*. [The root] *kaṇ*... [is used here]. (Ṭhakṣinikāṇam iti | Ṭhkaṇa)

The root *nimīlana* (Dhātupāṭha 1715) belongs to the *curādi* class and is preceded by the prefix *ni*. "That limb upon whose being cut a living being does not die is called *dhṛta*" refers to the hands, feet, and so forth. Its impermanence (*adhruvatva*), moreover, arises because it is occasionally absent even while the living being is alive, as when a limb is severed. Upon the severing of which limb the living being... [does not die].
That [body] certainly dies, starting from the head; its permanence, however, consists in its constant presence within a living being.
55. *parikliśyamāne ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.55). [The commentary states:

"Affliction (*parikleśaḥ*) is oppression from all sides (*sarvato vibādhanam*). By the word "from all sides" (*sarvataḥ*), he explains the meaning of the prefix *pari-*; and by the word "oppression" (*vibādhana*), he explains the meaning of the verbal root *kliś-*.

56. *viśi-pati-padi-skandām vyāpyamānāsevyamānayoḥ* (3.4.56). [The commentary states: "By the words 'with *viśi* etc., as actions etc. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the triad beginning with *pati* is included. "Without parts" (*anavayavena*) means "in its entirety" (*sākalyena*). "Of the objects" (*padārthānām*).

"The meaning [of the suffix] is 'repetition' (*tātparya*) regarding houses and so forth. The sense is that "frequency" (*ābhīkṣṇya*) refers to the repetition of actions. By the statement "pervasion (*vyāpti*) regarding substances," etc., he demonstrates the distinction between the objects of that which is being pervaded and that which is being practiced. If [it is] being pervaded...

When an object is being attended to, a cognition arises; and this being the case, since both of those objects possess permanence (*nityatā*) and distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), there ought to be a doubling by means of the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.4).
Why, then, does this not occur? To this he says: "By that which is identical," and so forth. Even though...

A compound of those two meanings is not prescribed; this has already been established previously, as the author of the Bhāṣya will say: "And so he will state. Because of the statement "repetition (*vīpsā*) occurs in the case of *sup*-suffixes," it is implied that "there is reduplication of a word denoting a substance when there is the sense of pervasion (*vyāptimātratā*)."

Because of the statement "the state of being constant (nityatā) is [implied] immediately," it is said that "there is reduplication of a word denoting an action when it is being restricted. For example:
*gehaṃ-geham* ("house after house"). This is the reduplication of a word not denoting a substance (*dravya*).

Regarding the phrase "entering the house again and again," this refers to the expression of an action. With the words "But surely... and so forth, he raises an objection from another's perspective—namely, that [the suffix] *ktvā* is used for the purpose of excluding repetition—and then refutes it with the words "for the purpose of excluding *ktvā*" and so forth.
It might be argued that both *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are prescribed by the rule "In the sense of frequency, *ṇamul* and [the rest]" (Pāṇini 3.4.22).

Both [suffixes] are prescribed; in that case, if *ṇamul* were to be prescribed again for repetition (*āsevā*) after roots such as *viś*, then the suffix *ktvā* would also occur. Therefore, is it said that *ṇamul* is stated again in order to exclude that? This is not so, because it is desired. For it is indeed desired in the case of repetition.
Regarding the rule *viśiprabhṛtibhyaḥ ktvā* (Pāṇini 3.4.26), one might say: "having repeatedly entered the house, he sits.
Therefore, it is incorrect [to claim that the rule is unnecessary]; for the sake of excluding that [usage], the term *ṇamul* is mentioned again.
As for the phrase "for the purpose of having a word ending in the second case as an upapada," and so forth: if it were not employed for the purpose of excluding the *ktvā* suffix...

In that case, the repetition [of the word "second-case"] is for the purpose of assigning the technical designation *upapada* to that which ends in the second case. By this, because of the governing rule *dvitīyāyāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.53), the suffix is prescribed when an item ending in the second case is the *upapada*; thus, the status of being an *upapada* is obtained for that which ends in the second case. For what purpose?
Is it intended that a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyānta*) should function as an *upapada*? To this he says: "The compound with an *upapada*" (*upapadasamāsa*), and so forth.

The mention of the alternative view (*pakṣagrahaṇa*) is because the formation of a compound is prescribed optionally by the rule "The third case and those following may optionally [be compounded]" (*tṛtīyāprabhṛtīnyanyatarasyām*, Pāṇini 2.2.21). It might be argued that by that same rule, the suffix *ṇamul* is also prescribed.

Since the designation *upapada* will [otherwise] apply, he says: "For by that," and so forth. For by that [word], the suffix *ṇamul* is not prescribed in connection with an *upapada*, because there is no word whatsoever situated in the locative case (*saptamī*). Therefore, in the prescription of *ṇamul* by means of that [word]...
There would simply be an absence of the non-existence of a co-occurring word.

57. *Asyati-tṛṣoḥ kriyāntare kāleṣu* (3.4.57). Regarding *asyati-tṛṣoḥ*: *asu* (to throw) is found at Dhātupāṭha 1209; *tṛṣ* (to thirst) is found at Dhātupāṭha 1228. Regarding *kriyāmantarayati* and so forth: *antara*...

The suffix *ṇic* is applied by the rule "that which performs that" (*tatkaroti*, Vārttika 200). [In the case of] "one who intervenes in an action" (*kriyāmantarayati*), the suffix *aṇ* is added according to the rule for the object (*karmaṇyaṇ*); there is the elision of the *ṇic*. Showing that the word *antara* here functions in the sense of "intervention" (*vyavadhāna*), he says: "an intervener in the action" (*kriyāvyavadhāyaka*). [The example] "he causes to drink" (*pāyayati*)—[the root] *pā*...

From the root *pā* (Dhātupāṭha 925), with the suffix *ṇic*; then by [Pāṇini 7.3.37], *yuk* is added. [The phrase] "the act of drinking by the cows is interrupted by the act of driving away and by thirst" means that both this present drinking and the drinking that will occur after two days have passed [are interrupted].

Because [the verb] *pāyayati* occurs in the middle of those two [verbs], *āsana* (seating) and *tarpaṇa* (satisfying), the phrase "having caused them to drink today" (*adya pāyayitvā*) and so forth explains the meaning of "he causes the cows to drink for two days.
Following this logic, the meaning of other instances is also understood; therefore, they have not been individually explained.
Regarding the expression *dvyaham upoṣya*: [the root] *vas* (meaning "to dwell," DhP 1942) undergoes *saṃprasāraṇa* by virtue of the rule *vacy-ādi* (Pāṇini 6.1.15);
the suffix *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap*; and the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 8.3.60).
Here, the root *vas* functions in the sense of "fasting" (*upavasana*), with the act of eating (*bhujikriyā*) serving as the intervening factor. In this context...

If it were not stated that "the [root] *as* and *tṛṣ* [are excluded]," then this [rule] would apply here as well—namely, the rule stating "movement (*gati*) is not separated [by an intervening element]. Just as in the example of *mala*, the act of drinking (*pāna*) is separated by the intervening acts of "not being" (*atyasana*) and "thirsting" (*tarṣaṇa*), movement is not [separated] in this case. In that regard:
And from the word *ahar* (day), the accusative case is applied by the rule *kālādhvanoratyantasaṃyoge* (Pāṇini 2.3.5).
Since the entire day is pervaded by the shooting of arrows, the word *iṣu* (arrow) takes the accusative in the sense of the object (*karman*) itself. For example:

*yojanam atyasya gāḥ pāyayati* ("He makes the cows drink [water] after having shot them for a distance of one yojana"). Here, the word denoting a path (*adhvan*) is the subordinate term (*upapada*). In some cases...
The meaning is that after having made [the horse] drink at a watering place (srughna) and so forth, one makes it drink after it has traversed a distance of one yojana.
Both terms—*adhvakarmakam* and *na kālakarmakam*—are bahuvrīhi compounds.
58. *nāmny-ādiśo grahoḥ* | (3.4.58) Regarding "ādiśeḥ": [the root] *diś* meaning "to bestow" (*atisarjane*) from the Dhātupāṭha (1283), preceded by the prefix *āṅ*.
59. After the root *kṛ*, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are used when expressing something contrary to what was intended (*avyaye'yathābhipretākhyāne*).
Regarding the phrase "when expressing something contrary to what was intended": "yathābhipreta" means that which is intended or desired;
it is an *avyayībhāva* compound formed with the distributive sense (*vīpsā*) according to Pāṇini 2.1.7, *yathā'sādṛśye*. It is not [the *avyayībhāva* meaning "as"]...

"According to one's wish" (*yathābhipreta*) means "not according to one's wish" (*ayathābhipreta*), which signifies something unpleasant. Regarding the form *ācakṣe*: it is the present tense (*laṭ*) of the root *cakṣiṅ* preceded by the prefix *ā*. By the rule *thāsaḥ se* (Pāṇini 3.4.80), *thās* is replaced by *se*; by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyor antec* (8.2.29), the letter *k* is elided; and by the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si* (8.2.41), [the *ṣ* is changed to *k*].
Thus, there is the substitution of *k* [for *kh*], and by the rule "ṭhiṇkoḥ ṣṭu" (8.4.41), there is the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*].
It is said: "It has been stated. Where was it stated? In the rule "upadaṃśas tṛtīyāyām" (3.4.47).
And it is also stated that this statement is for the purpose of forming a compound with an *upapada*. Furthermore, in the rule "ktvā ca" (2.2.22) [it is stated].

By this [rule], the *upapada* compound may optionally occur. But why does the compound occur with that *ktvā* which is prescribed by this [rule], and not with that which is prescribed by [the rule] "of two actions having the same agent" (3.4.21), etc.? To this he says: "For thus," and so forth. *Ktvā*...
In this rule (Pāṇini 2.2.22), the phrase "beginning with the third case" (2.2.21) is understood by way of anuvṛtti.

Therefore, by this [rule], compounding occurs only optionally with that *ktvā* which is prescribed [by 3.4.21], but not with others; for the *ktvā* suffix is prescribed when words beginning with the third case function as *upapadas*. Now, as for the mention of *ṇamul*:

"For what purpose? Since the rule for *ṇamul* continues [from the previous sūtra], should one not simply say 'and *ktvā*'? To this he replies: "In the section on *ṇamul*" and so forth. "Equal status" means having equal force. "By that," etc., he demonstrates the purpose of the indicator (*jñāpaka*). If [the rule were] "and *ktvā*..."

If this were said, then the *ṇamul* suffix, though intentionally drawn forward by the particle *ca*, would not carry over to what follows, because there would be no further effort [to do so]. Just as it is understood that the *ktvā* suffix is being mentioned as a secondary addition (*anvācaya*) by that [particle], and consequently, due to its lack of primacy, it would not carry over to what follows. [Therefore,] the *ṇamul* must be mentioned again.
Since they are mentioned together, there is no relationship of subordinate and principal between the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul*; therefore, both continue to apply.
60. *tiryacy-apavarge* (Pāṇini 3.4.60). [The example is] *tiryakkṛtvā*. [Derivation: From *tiras* + *añcati*, the suffix *kvin* is applied by the rule *ṛtvig-ādinā* (3.2.59).
When the letter *ca* is changed to *ja* by the rule *jhalāṃ jaśo'nte* (8.2.39), [the form becomes *tiryañc-*]. [Then, regarding the suffix *kvin*...]

By the rule *kuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.62), there is the substitution of *k* for *g*; furthermore, by the rule of *carv-*, that *k* becomes *k*. By the rule *tirasas tiryallope* (6.3.94), there is the substitution of *tiri* for *tiras*. [The root text reads: *tiryakkṛtvā kāṣṭhaṃ*].
"He has gone across the stalk," meaning having made it non-straight, i.e., sideways.
The meaning is "having done so.

Now, as for this mention of *tiryaci*: since the designation *bha* applies, when the elision of the vowel *a* is performed by Pāṇini 6.4.138 (*acaḥ*), the form ought to be *tiraścī*; therefore, he says:

Regarding the phrase "in the case of animals" (*tiryaci*) and so forth: in all cases, a word that functions as an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is an imitation of the very form of the word itself. However, there is this distinction:
in some instances, there is an imitation of the word as the referent (*śabdapadārtha*), while in others, there is an imitation of the meaning (*artha*).

In that context, although it would have been sufficient to say merely "imitation" (*anukaraṇa*), the inclusion of the term "word-form" (*śabdarūpa*) is for the purpose of making known that this imitation pertains solely to the form of the word, devoid of meaning.
This is what is meant: [it refers to] that which has sound as its referent (*śabdapadārthaka*).
This is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of that animal sound, but it is not the sound itself.
Therefore, because it is a different word (*śabdāntara*), the elision of the vowel *a* does not occur; this is the intended meaning. [Objection:
Even so, according to the rule "an imitation is like its original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇaṃ bhavati*), [the elision] ought indeed to occur here.

Is it by means of the effect of the *prakṛti* through the elision of the letter *ā*? To this he says: "And not," and so forth. He provides the justification for this very point: "Because of the consequence of the destruction of the form being imitated. If there were an effect of the *prakṛti* here, then [the form] of the imitation, such as the word-form *tiryak*, would be destroyed.
Destruction would result in non-perception;
the meaning is that one would not perceive that which is intended to be imitated as something whose original form has not been lost.
Since this defect arises when there is an imitation of the original (prakṛti), therefore it is not the case here.

An imitation must be like its original (*prakṛti*). However, the scope of the rule "an imitation is like its original" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 113) should be understood as applying where there is an imitation of a word whose meaning is a referent (*arthapadārtha*). And where does an imitation occur as being like its original? He says: "after *etad*, [the suffix] *aś*."
And so forth. Both *etado* and *adaso* are imitations (*anukaraṇa*) of words whose referents are the words themselves.

If there were also *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) for that which is an imitation of a word as its own referent, then, after the primary grammatical operations such as the substitution of *yat* for *tyad* and so on had been applied, the forms would have been *etasya* and *amuṣya*.
It may be that just as the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) does not occur here, so it is also in the case of the word *tiryacī*.

61. *svāṅge tas-pratyaye kṛ-bhv-oh* (Pāṇini 3.4.61). It is stated here that "correspondence according to order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) is not intended. But how is it that it does not occur even though it is intended, given that there are two bases and likewise two suffixes? [The answer is: it exists...

What is the reason for obtaining the respective order [of application]? It is because of the indication in the rule *kṛbhvoḥ*, which serves as a non-deviating mark (*lakṣaṇa*). Since a suffix (*pratyaya*) is being prescribed here, there must be an ablative case (*pañcamī*) characterized by direction (*digyoga*), due to its connection with the rule *paraśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.2). Therefore...

Regarding the statement "kṛbhūbhyām," although the ablative case (*pañcamī*) should have been employed, the use here of the form "kṛbhvoḥ" serves as a sign of deviation from the general rule (*lakṣaṇavyabhicāra*). In this context, when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is being prescribed, it ought to be in the ablative case characterized by separation (*digyogalakṣaṇā*), based on its connection with the rule *paraśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.2). In that regard:

Regarding the statement "kṛbhūbhyām," although a locative case (*pañcamī*) should have been employed, the fact that it is presented here in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) as "kṛbhvoḥ" is a sign of deviation from the rule; by this, it should be understood that there is no correspondence according to the respective order (*yathāsaṃkhya*). [The word] "mukhataḥ" [is derived] by [the rule] "apādāne cāhīyaruhoḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.45).
Regarding the form *tasiḥ*:

in the phrase *mukhīkṛtya*, the word *mukha* ends in the suffix *cvi*. The suffix *cvi* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.4.50 (*abhūtatadbhāve*), and the change of the vowel to *i* occurs according to 7.4.32 (*asya cvau*). [The meaning is] "it extends toward the face" (*mukhe tasyati*).

Thus: from the root *tasu* in the sense of "wasting away" (*upakṣaye*), [the suffix] *kvip* is applied by Pāṇini 3.2.178 (*anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*). By Pāṇini 6.1.68 (*halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...*), there is elision of the *su* [case-ending], followed by the substitution of *ru* and *visarjanīya*. Here, the word *tast* is a verbal root (*dhātu*), not a suffix (*pratyaya*). Therefore, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* do not apply to that which ends in it when it is designated as such.
In your view, by the rule "samānakartṛkayoḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.21), only the suffix -ktvā is applicable.

62. *nādhārthapratyaye cvyarthe* (3.4.62). [The commentary explains: "The meanings of *na* and *dhā*. That which is accompanied by the suffix *na* is called *nā*, and that which is accompanied by the suffix *dhā* is called *dhā*. A suffix whose meaning is *nā* is called a *nārtha* suffix.

The suffix *dhā* has that meaning as its purpose which is expressed by the word *dhārtha*. Regarding "having divided into two" (*dvidhākṛtya*): [this is derived] from the rule *saṃkhyāyā vidhārthe dhā* (Pāṇini 5.3.42). Regarding "having made into two parts" (*dvaidhaṃ kṛtvā*): [this is derived] from the rule *dvitryośca dhamuñ* (Pāṇini 5.3.45), which prescribes the suffix *dhamuñ*. Regarding "having divided into two ways" (*dvedhākṛtya*): [this is derived] from the rule *edhācca* (Pāṇini 5.3.46), which prescribes the suffix *edhāc*.
"Having separated," "having made distinct"— if the term *pratyaya* (suffix) were not mentioned [in the rule],
then since the words *hiruk* and *pṛthak* have the sense of "separation" (*asaha*), they would lack the status of being verbal roots (*dhātu*).
Consequently, even when these two are used as *upapadas*, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* would still apply, precisely because of the preceding sūtra.

Since the rule would have been established by the continued application of the previous mention of "pratyaya," the repetition of "pratyaya" here is for the sake of easy understanding; for the previous mention of "pratyaya" might have been understood as applying only through effort, being a part of a compound. [Example: *nānākṛtvā kāṣṭhāni gataḥ* ("having split the wood pieces, he went").
Thus, there is no sense of the *cv* suffix here, because a state different from the original form is not intended to be expressed.

Regarding the phrase "the mention of *artha* is for the sake of [excluding] the *dhā* suffix": that for which the suffix *dhā* is the meaning or purpose is described as such. For there are many suffixes whose purpose is the *dhā* suffix; therefore, if the word *artha* were not mentioned, it would refer only to the *dhā* suffix.

There would be the inclusion [of the word *artha*] for that specific meaning, but not for other meanings. However, when there is an inclusion [of the word *artha*], there is an inclusion of those [other meanings] as well. Now, why is it that the inclusion of the word *artha* does not also include the meaning itself? To this he says:
"But here, it is only one. For the inclusion of the word *artha* is made in a case where many things are to be included.

[The suffixes] arise; however, the single [suffix] *apratyaya* does not [arise], and since its establishment occurs without the mention of "meaning" (*artha*), the mention of "meaning" is not for its sake. But surely, by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original), even *ghañ*, *muñ*, and so forth will be included by the mention of "dhātu" (root); therefore, is it not improper to include the mention of "meaning" even for the sake of *dhātu*? This is not so.

There is a fault; for there is also a suffix *gha* with the meaning of *dhā*, according to the rule: "The suffix *ḍa* is seen after a stem ending in *ghañ* in the sense of the same [action]" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 610). Therefore, the mention of the word *artha* must be made in order to include the meaning of *dhā*.

We, however, say: the mention of the word "artha" must indeed be made even for the sake of its meaning. For instance, there are two [roots] that are not suffixes (*apratyaya*): one is without an *anubandha*, and the second is with an *anubandha*.

In that case, if the mention of "artha" were absent, the rule "when there is a mention of that which lacks an *anubandha*, it does not include that which possesses an *anubandha*" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 53) would apply.

Thus, there would be the inclusion of only that which lacks a suffixal marker (*apratyaya*), and not that which possesses a marker (*sānubandhaka*) or the negative particle *nañ*. However, when there is the mention of the meaning (*arthagrahaṇa*), its inclusion also occurs.

63. *tūṣṇīmi bhuvaḥ* (3.4.63). Now, one might ask: since the mention of *bhū* continues from the rule *svāṅge taspratyaye kṛbhvoḥ* (3.4.61), for what purpose is *bhuvaḥ* stated here? To this he replies:
Regarding the phrase "the mention of *bhū*," etc.: previously, the mention of *bhū* was connected with the root *kṛ*;

therefore, if that were to carry over [into the present rule], its [connection with *kṛ*] would also carry over. Consequently, the mention of *bhū* is repeated here in order to prevent that [connection].

64. *anvacyānulomye* | (3.4.64) The mention of *anvac* is explained by [the rule for] *tiryac*. The form *anvagbhūya* is derived as follows: after the suffix *kvip* has been applied as before, and the *jaś*-substitution has been applied to the final consonant of that stem, the resulting form is obtained.
"Having become a follower (anvaga-bhūtvā)" means that he remains as an attendant (anucara).

65. *śak-dhṛṣa-jñā-glā-ghaṭa-rabha-labha-krama-saha-arhāḥ astyartheṣu tumun* (3.4.65). Now, one might object: since *tumun* is already established by the rule *tumun-ṇvulau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām* (3.3.10) when words such as *śaka* and others are used as attendant words (*upapada*), for what purpose is this new rule commenced? To this he says:

"This undertaking is for the purpose of [including] non-verbal meanings. This undertaking is made so that the suffix *tumun* may occur even after verbs such as *śak* (to be able) where there is no verbal action [as a subordinate element]. For in examples such as *na hi śaknoti bhoktum* ("he is not able to eat"), a verbal action is not understood as a subordinate element (*upapada*). What then? It is a different meaning altogether. Here...
In such cases as "he is able to eat," "he is capable of eating," or "he knows how to eat," proficiency is understood. In "he is weary of eating," inability is understood;
in "he prepares to eat" or "he deserves to eat," mere fitness is understood. [And in] "he begins..."

In the expressions "he sets out to eat" (*bhoktum prakramate*) and "he begins to eat" (*bhoktum prakramate*), there is another action of commencement (*ādyavasthāna*) belonging to the very act of eating (*bhuji*).
