In "he obtains to eat" (*labhate bhoktum*), there is a refusal (*pratyākhyāna*). In "there is [the possibility] to eat" (*asti bhoktum*) and similar cases, there is merely a possibility (*sambhava*).

66. [The suffix *kṛt* is applied after verbal roots] following words expressing "sufficiency" (*paryāpti*) when they have the sense of "being capable of" (*alam*). (3.4.66) "Sufficiency" (*paryāpti*) means "not being deficient"; that is to say, "completeness. "In words characterized by the sense of 'being capable of'" (*alamarthaviśiṣṭeṣu*):
although words such as *bhūṣaṇa* ("adornment") and others also possess the sense of "being capable of," nevertheless, in this context, it refers to words expressing sufficiency.

Since capacity alone is possible, that alone is understood—either through the observation of usage, through the comprehension of the meaning, or through grammatical explanation (*vyākhyāna*). Therefore, the meaning becomes "in those [words] qualified by the sense of 'sufficient'. If this is so, why is it not stated simply as "in capacities" (*sāmarthyeṣu*)? It cannot be stated thus; for if it were stated in that way...

[Otherwise], there would also be [the undesirable application] in cases such as *sāmarthyena bhuṅkte* (he eats by means of ability) and *balena bhuṅkte* (he eats by means of strength). But according to the established rule (*yathānyāsa*), there is no fault; for in these instances, "sufficiency" (*paryāpti*) is not observed. What then? It is "ease" (*saukarya*).
The meaning is that this is easy to perform. Only the mere possibility of its occurrence is intended here.
The meaning is that the production of such a thing is indeed possible.
67. *kṛt* [suffixes] are used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
(Pāṇini 3.4.67) For what purpose is this stated? So that suffixes such as *tṛc* and others may occur in the sense of the agent. Where, then, would they otherwise occur?
Suffixes whose meaning is not specifically prescribed [occur] in their own sense (*svārthe*) (Puṣpavarga-pāda 90). But surely, where [a suffix occurs] in its own sense...

When one desires a specific condition (*pratyaya*) therein, one employs the term "bhāva" (state/abstract action), as in the rule for the suffixes *ghañ* and others: "in the sense of bhāva. Yet these suffixes, such as *ghañ*, do not apply to the [action] itself in its own right; rather, they apply to its property known as "accomplishment" (*siddhatā*). Likewise, in the rule for the verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) and others: "the suffix *la* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) and in the sense of bhāva."

In the sūtra "cākarmakebhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.69), even the *lakāra*s are not prescribed in their own sense; what then? They are prescribed for its property called "sādhyatā" (the state of being to-be-accomplished). Although there is a prescription of the *ghañ* suffixes and the *lakāra*s in the sense of "bhāva" (abstract action), nevertheless, due to the inherent nature of the power of words (*śabdaśakti*), this is so.

The distinction between their respective domains is obtained. For suffixes such as *ghañ* and others have the capacity to express only the completed state (*siddhatā*) of the verbal root's meaning, whereas the *lakāra* suffixes express only its state of being in process (*sādhyatā*). Thus, since suffixes whose specific meanings are not explicitly stated function according to their own inherent sense, it follows that suffixes such as *tṛc* and others do so as well.
They would apply only to that [specific instance]; therefore, this [treatise] is commenced so that they may apply to the agent alone.
And in this regard, there are two possibilities: either this [work] is a supplement (śeṣa) to the rules concerning the origin of verbal roots (kṛd-utpatti-vākya).

Is it that [the suffixes] *ṇvul* and *tṛc* are prescribed for the agent (*kartari*), as in "from *nandi*, *grahi*, *paci*, etc., [the suffixes] *lyu*, *ṇini*, and *ac* are prescribed for the agent"? Or is it a prescription of meaning (*arthādeśa*)? That is to say, would the meaning be assigned by this [rule] subsequently to those *kṛt* suffixes already prescribed by their respective independent prescriptive rules—those which have not been formed by other grammatical rules?

It is stated that these [suffixes] occur when the agent (*kartṛ*) is to be expressed. In that regard, if the second alternative were adopted, then just as the meaning of the agent is conveyed by this rule for suffixes such as *tṛc* and others, so too would it be for suffixes such as *khyun* and others; because no distinction is specified, those [suffixes] would also apply to the agent.
Since the agent and other factors are included within their own respective prescriptive statements, this applies even to the *kaṇādi* [roots].
Although it is impossible for a single suffix (*pratyaya*) to apply simultaneously to both the agent and the instrument,
nevertheless, by the force of the grammatical rule, they may occur alternately as the agent and as the instrument.
Therefore, considering that this position is faulty, he first adopts the initial position and says:
"Of the sūtras on the origin of kṛt-affixes," and so forth. By this, he asserts their syntactic unity with this [sūtra].
If this were the case, then this [sūtra] should also apply to the sūtras concerning the *khyun* suffix and others, for this is a supplement to them as well.
Having considered this, one might ask: "In that case, would the fault that applies to the second position not also apply to this [first] position?
To this, he says: "Among those... and so forth. He provides the reason for that very point: "Because they require a further object (arthākāṅkṣatvāt)," for [the word *śeṣa*] is indeed their remainder.

Those [words] which, because they are incomplete, require a meaning— and not others— therefore, since a meaning is not indicated in those very sentences that possess expectancy, it is logical that this [supplementation] serves as their remainder (*śeṣa*).
Only the rules prescribing suffixes such as *-tṛc* and so forth are expectant of meaning, because they do not indicate meanings themselves.

For instance, when it is stated, "The suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc* occur," there arises an expectation for a specific meaning—namely, "In what sense do these two occur? Therefore, this [rule] is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to those very [rules], and thus it applies specifically to them. [This is expressed by the phrase: "But not in the rules concerning *khyun* and so forth"; [and the word] "it applies" (*upatiṣṭhate*).
The connection is indeed with what has been previously stated: "directly" (*sākṣāt*), and so forth. This is the reason for its non-application:

sentences such as those containing the suffix *khyun* do not possess a requirement for further meaning, because in them the meanings such as the instrument (*karaṇa*) are directly specified. Therefore, this [rule] is not a supplement (*śeṣa*) to them.
It presides over them; therefore, this undesirable consequence does not arise.
68. *bhavya-geya-pravacanīya-upasthānīya-janya-āplāvya-āpātyā* vā.

(Pāṇini 3.4.68) Among the words beginning with *bhavya*, the forms *geya*, *pravacanīya*, and *upasthānīya* are transitive; therefore, since the [kṛt] suffix would otherwise apply to their object, this rule prescribes their application to the agent (*kartṛ*). For the remaining intransitive ones, the suffix applies to the abstract state (*bhāva*).

And in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Regarding "bhavyaḥ": by [Pāṇini 3.1.97] *aco yat*, there is *guṇa* substitution, and by [Pāṇini 6.1.80] *dhātostannimittasyaiva*, there is the substitution of *av*. Regarding "geyaḥ": by [Pāṇini 6.4.65] *īdyati*, there is the substitution of *ī*, and then *guṇa*. Regarding "sāmnām": this is a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) characterized by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix in the sense of the object (*karmani*).

Regarding "sthāpanīyaḥ": the suffix *anīyar*. Regarding "janyaḥ": in the rule *aco yat* (Pāṇini 3.1.97), the suffix *yat* is applied by the vārttika *taki-śasi-yati-cati-jani-nām upasaṃkhyānam* (Vārttika 213).
Regarding "āplāvyaḥ": from the root *plu*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied by the rule *orāvaśyake* (Pāṇini 3.1.125), followed by *vṛddhi* [of the vowel].
As before, there is the substitution of *ā*; [the suffix] *āp* is to be applied, according to the rule *ṛ-halor ṇyat* (Pāṇini 3.1.124).

69. *laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ* | (Pāṇini 3.4.69) Since the letter *l* was designated as having the technical name *kṛt* by the preceding rule, it would apply only to the agent (*kartṛ*) and not to the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). Therefore, this [sūtra] is commenced so that it may also apply to those two. *La-*...

"Thus, having discarded the indicatory letters (*anubandha*)," and so forth. Having set aside the specific indicatory letters of the ten *lakāra*s beginning with *laṭ*, the general term "laḥ" is taken.
And this [term] ends in the nominative plural; [this is stated] to rule out the suspicion that it might be in the ablative or genitive singular.
[The author] refutes [this]. For if [the word *para*] were in the ablative case, the meaning indicated would belong only to that which follows the *lakāra*;

consequently, the *lakāra* would apply only to the agent (*kartṛ*), and in this [fifth case], the characteristic of immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) would have to be understood as belonging to the sixth [case, i.e., the object]. And thus, regarding the *lakāra*—

The meaning would be specified for that which is immediately preceding; and consequently, the same fault that occurred in the fifth [alternative] would arise here as well. Is the genitive case understood here in relation to the substitutes (*ādeśa*)? Even so, since the meaning of the substitutes of the *lakāra* is being specified by this [sūtra], this very point remains the subject matter.
It would have been specified [as such]. But surely, there is no usage of the *lakāra* at all;

how then can its meanings be "object" (*karman*) and so forth? There is no fault, because by implication these meanings will be understood as belonging to its substitutes (*ādeśa*). [The rule] "they do not occur in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) after transitive verbs" implies "after intransitive verbs."
Because of the scriptural statement; otherwise, it would be purposeless.
70. "The *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khalartha* [affixes] apply to those two alone" (Pāṇini 3.4.70). [The commentary says:

"To those two alone, namely the action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). By this, he shows that the term "to those two" (*tayoḥ*) refers back to the phrase "action and object" (*bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*). Now, one might object regarding the immediately preceding rule...

There are two statements: "The [suffixes] *la* occur in the sense of the object and the agent" is the first statement; "And they also occur in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) after intransitive roots, and in the sense of the agent" is the second.
Therein, by the word "those two," only the agent and the abstract state mentioned in the immediately preceding statements are intended.

Is this retrospective reference (*pratyavamarśa*) logical? This is not a fault. Since the author employs the term "in the agent" (*kartari*) in the subsequent sūtra (Pāṇini 3.4.71), it is understood from that that the retrospective reference applies only to the passive and impersonal (*bhāva-karman*).
For if the retrospective reference were intended for the agent (*kartṛ*) alone, the mention of the "agent" would be redundant.

It would [be unnecessary], because the agent is already established by this very [rule]. For in that case, it would have been more appropriate to say "and in the object" (*karmaṇi ca*), since [the suffix] might not have applied to the object by some [other rule]. However, when there is here a reference to both the state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), then the mention of the agent (*kartṛ*) is appropriate, as [the suffix] would not otherwise apply to the agent.

It should be as follows: [the suffixes] occur according to what is obtained in the case of the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). Therefore, it is logical that there is a reference only to the abstract action and the object. By the words "the particle *eva*" and so forth, the purpose of the particle *eva*—namely, exclusion (*vyavacchedya*)—is for the sake of drawing down [the focus] or for the sake of cessation (*nivṛtti*).
In *śayitam*, there is *guṇa* [substitution] because the prohibition of *kit* status applies by the rule *niṣṭhā śīṅ* (Pāṇini 1.2.19).
In *īṣatkaraḥ* and *sukaraḥ*, the suffix *khal* is applied by the rule *īṣadduḥsuṣu* (Pāṇini 3.3.126).
Regarding the rule *ṭhīṣadāḍhaḷṃbhavam*, here too [the suffix *kha* is applied] by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇośca bhūkṛñoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.127).

71. *Ādikarmaṇi ktaḥ kartari ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.71). Regarding the phrase *ādikarmaṇi*: it is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) consisting of *ādiḥ* (beginning) and *karma* (action), meaning "the beginning which is an action. Regarding the term *kriyākṣaṇaḥ* (moment of action): by this, the word *karman* denotes the action itself, not the instrument (*sādhana*).
He shows that [the word] "karma" [means] action. But how is it determined that "kriyā denotes karma"?

It is because of the qualification by the word "ādi" (beginning). Since there is a state of beginning, middle, and end among many moments of action, the term "beginning" excludes those moments of action that have no beginning; thus, it refers to that which constitutes the initial moment.

It is appropriate to establish that the moment of action (*kriyākṣaṇa*) is the "initial action" (*ādikarma*). However, by using the term "initial," it is not possible to qualify the "means" (*sādhana*) as being "only one action" and so forth;
for the word "initial" (*ādi*) depends on the existence of something prior to it, and thus it cannot apply there [in the case of the means].

Because there is nothing to be excluded [from the scope of the rule]. And showing that [the suffix] is prescribed by the very rule "niṣṭhā" (Pāṇini 3.2.102), while the rule "in the sense of the past tense" (bhūte, 3.2.84) is still in force for the beginning of an action, he says "tasmin" and so forth. For the first moment of an action, because it has reached completion, becomes "past" (bhūta).

It is appropriate that [the word *kṛta*] is intended to be expressed in its state of being a past participle (*bhūtatva*). In the expression "Devadatta has made the mat" (*kṛtaḥ kaṭo Devadattena*), the suffix *kta* denotes the agent; since the agent is already expressed by that very suffix, the third case ending does not occur after the word *Devadatta*.
However, because the object (*karman*) is not expressed, the second case ending certainly occurs after the word *kaṭa*.

In the example "ṭhprakṛtaḥ kaṭo devadattena" (The mat was made by Devadatta), the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). Because the object has already been expressed by that very [suffix], the accusative case does not occur. Since the agent (*kartṛ*) has not been expressed, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) occurs after the word "devadatta. [The word] "prakṛtam" [is also explained as follows:]...

[The example is] "devadatena" (by Devadatta). Here, the suffix *kta* denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*). In all cases, the prefix *pra-* indicates the commencement of an action (*ādikarma*). Now, it might be argued that at the time when the initial action is capable of beginning, the mat (*kaṭa*) has not yet been produced;
at that time, only the weaving and other [actions] that constitute the causes of the mat exist, and the mat does not exist in that state.

The mat is in that state; it is a mat. How then is there grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word "mat" and the word "prepared," which denotes a past time? The word "mat" applies to that specific modification produced in the *vīraṇa* grass and other materials by the first moment of the action, because [the grass] is for the sake of that [mat]; and that [modification]...
Since it is indeed real, there is no fault.

72. *gatyarthākarmakaśliṣaśīṅsthāsavasajanaruhajīryatibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 3.4.72). Regarding *upasthitaḥ*: by *dyatisyatimāsthāmiti kiti* (7.4.40), there is *it*-substitution [of the *ā* of *sthā*]. Regarding *anūṣitaḥ*: by *vacyādinā* (6.1.15), there is *samprasāraṇa*; and by *vasatikṣughoḥ* [the substitution of *u* for the root vowel].
(7.2.52) thus there is the augment *iṭ*; (8.2.36) by the rule "and [the substitution of] *ṣ* for [the *s* of] *śās*, *vas*, *ghas*, and *si*," there is the substitution of *ṣ*.

Regarding "anujātaḥ": by the rule (6.4.42) "of *jan*, *san*, and *khan*, [there is] *āt* before *saṅ* and *jhal*," there is the substitution of *āt*. Regarding "ārūḍhaḥ": by the rule (8.2.31) "for *h* [comes] *ḍh*," and by the rule (8.2.40) "after a *jhaṣ* [consonant], for *t* and *th*, [there is] *ḍh*, except after *adhaḥ*," there is the substitution of *ḍh*. By the rule (8.2.40), there is the substitution of *dh*.

Regarding *ṣṭhūanā ṣṭuaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.41), *ṭh ḍho ḍhea lopaḥ* (8.3.13), and *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho 'ṇaḥ* (6.3.111), there is lengthening [of the vowel]. Regarding *anujīrṇaḥ*: from the root *jṛ* in the sense of "loss of vitality" (Dhātupāṭha 1494), there is the substitution of *i* for *ṛ* by *ṛta iddhātoḥ* (7.1.100), and then lengthening by *hali ca* (8.2.77).

And by the rule *ṭhradābhyām* (8.2.42), there is the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*. Now, one might object: "Since roots such as *śliṣ* are inherently intransitive (*akarmaka*), the desired form is already established; what then is the purpose of including them [in this list]? To this, he says: "*śliṣādayaḥ*" etc., and "*tadartham*" ("for that purpose").
The meaning is that it has the sense of being transitive (sakarmaka).

73. *dāśagoghnau sampradāne* (Pāṇini 3.4.73). Regarding *goghna*: this is the same [root] *han*, with the suffix *ac* (from Pāṇini 3.1.134). The suffix *ac* is applied irregularly (*nipātita*) when the recipient (*sampradāna*) is expressed, and there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*). Alternatively, the suffix *ak* is applied irregularly, and there is elision of the penultimate vowel.
The form is already established by the rule *ṭhgamahana* (Pāṇini 6.4.98), and the substitution of *k* for *h* is achieved by the rule *ṭhho hanteḥ* (7.3.54).

If the word *goghnaḥ* were prescribed as an irregular formation (*nipātana*) when [the cow] is the recipient (*sampradāna*), then it would follow that even a *cāṇḍāla* or similar person could be designated by that term; for [the cow] belongs to them as well.
Since they too are considered virtuous when they kill for the sake of giving to one who has arrived, he says:

"By the force of the grammatical substitution (*nipātana*)," and so forth. For just as in this case, by the force of the grammatical substitution, some non-technical (*alākṣaṇika*) operation is obtained, so too is a specific meaning. Therefore, even though...

Although the term *goghna* is established as an irregular formation (*nipātana*) without qualification, it nevertheless applies only to a specific case. By this, it denotes a priest (*ṛtvij*) and others, but not anyone else such as a *caṇḍāla*. [Objection: In that case, when a cow is killed for the purpose of giving it away, the term *goghna* would not apply to that person; therefore, he says: "even though [the act of killing] does not exist [in the sense of being for one's own sake]."

And so forth. For just as one who does not currently cook is nevertheless called a "cook" by virtue of his fitness [for the task], so too is one called a "cow-killer" even in the absence of an actual killing of a cow.

74. *bhīmādayo'pādāne* | (3.4.74) [The *Kāśikā* states: "These end in *uṇādi* suffixes"—meaning these are formed by *uṇādi* suffixes. Those whose suffixes are *uṇādi* are thus described. But what, then, are those *uṇādi* suffixes?
Therefore, he says: "After roots ending in *śī*, *ā*, *dhū*, and *sū*, [the suffix] *mak*," and so forth. By the word "etc.

(*ādi*), the inclusion of *maṅku*, *van*, and others is intended. If, then, these are *uṇādi* suffixes, this being the case, since *uṇādi* suffixes are conventional words (*rūḍhi-śabda*) and thus lack a relationship between action and its factors (*kriyā-kāraka-sambandha*), [the rule regarding] the ablative case (*apādāne*)...

Is it not the case that such a formation is simply impossible? This is not a fault; for even among words that are conventional by usage (*rūḍhiśabda*), some indeed possess a relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakasambandha*), as in the case of *tailapāyikā* ("oil-drinker") and similar terms. Therefore, this objection is not to be raised. [Regarding the phrase] "by those two" (*tābhyām*) and so forth: but surely, if this rule (*sūtra*) did not exist...
This reference "by those two" (tābhyām) would not be appropriate, because the ablative case has not been introduced [in the context];
therefore, how could there even be an occasion for its exclusion? This is not a fault, for this serves a single purpose.
For if this were not so, the sūtra would have to be formulated in that very manner: [i.e., *na yvābhyāṃ padāntābhyām*].
Therefore, the rule "uṇādayaḥ" applies elsewhere than from the apādāna [kāraka]. And thus, if this were not stated, there would indeed be an exclusion (paryudāsa).
75. *tābhyām anyatra uṇādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.75). Now, for what purpose is there this reference to the *sampradāna* and *apādāna* cases by means of the word *tābhyām*?
One might simply say: "elsewhere than these [two], *uṇādi* [suffixes occur]"; for indeed, [the two cases] are already under discussion by virtue of the context.
Would the *uṇādi* suffixes be understood as occurring elsewhere than after those two? Therefore, he says:
"For the purpose of referring back to those two," and so forth; and "Otherwise," and so forth.
The meaning is: if a reference to those two were not made by means of the phrase "after those two" (*tābhyām*).

Regarding the phrase "because of proximity" (*anantaratvāt*), etc.: according to the maxim "a rule or a prohibition applies to that which is proximate" (*anantarasya vidhir vā bhavati pratiṣedho vā*; Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 19), there would be an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the ablative case (*apādāna*) alone, were it not for the specific mention of "by those two" (*tābhyām*). [The example] "kṛṣiḥ" [is formed by the rule] "the suffix *ik* is added after *kṛṣi* and others. (*ik kṛṣyādibhyaḥ*).
(vā. 324) Thus [the suffix] *ik*.
Regarding "tantu": the suffix *tun* is applied by the rule "sitanigamimasisacyāvidhāñkruśibhyas-tun" (Daiva Uṇādi Sūtra 1.122).
Regarding "carma": the suffix *manin* is applied.
76. *kta* [is used] in the sense of locus (*adhikaraṇa*) after roots whose meanings involve staying still (*dhrauvya*), motion (*gati*), or consuming (*pratyavasāna*).

Now, one might object: "This is not a well-known convention in the world—that roots meaning 'staying still' are intransitive (*akarmaka*), and that roots meaning 'consuming' are non-transitive (*avyavahārin*)—so how is this meaning obtained? To this [it is replied]:...
He said: "Established in one's own school" (*svanikāyaprasiddhiḥ*). One's own school (*svanikāya*) is the community of grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇasaṅgha*);

in that [community], this is the established doctrine: "In the case of the agent, the action, and the locus. Regarding the action and the object, it is by the rule beginning with *tayoreva* (Pāṇini 3.4.70). "This belongs to them" (*idameṣām*).

The genitive case [is used] by the rule *adhikaraṇavācinām* (Pāṇini 2.3.68). Regarding "how," etc.: [the examples are] "the Brahmins have eaten" (*bhuktā brāhmaṇāḥ*) and "the cows have drunk" (*pītā gāvaḥ*). Here, the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) denotes the agent;
otherwise, since the agent is not already expressed [by another word], the agent would be required from the words *brāhmaṇa* and *go*.
The third [alternative] would be as follows: no one has prescribed the suffix *kta* in the sense of the agent after roots meaning "to consume" (*pratyavasānārtha*).
Therefore, why is this not recited immediately after that rule? If this were so, there would be one advantage:
the mention of *kta* need not be repeated twice. Thus, it should be stated: "The first [suffix is applied] in the sense of *maṇi*."
[The rule] "ktaḥ kartari ca" (Pāṇini 3.4.71), then "śliṣa-śīṅ-sthā-āsa-vasa-jan-i-ruha-jīryatibhyaś-ca" (3.4.72),

and then "adhikaraṇe ca dhrauvya-gati-pratyavasānārthebhyaḥ" (3.4.76)— if this were the case, would it not mean that the mention of *kta* twice and the mention of "roots meaning motion and intransitive roots" would not need to be made? But it is impossible [to achieve this] in such a way.

To explain: if it were stated in this way, then just as the suffix *kta* occurs after roots meaning "stability" (*dhrauvya*) when denoting the agent (*kartṛ*), it would likewise occur after roots meaning "consumption" (*pratyavasāna*), which is not desired.
Therefore, let it remain exactly as it was originally formulated.
"77. Regarding *lasya*: the letter *ṭh* is for the purpose of pronunciation. By this, he dispels the suspicion that it is an *anubandha*.
For if this were an *anubandha*, there would be a grasping (*grahaṇa*) of only those *laṅ* and *laṭ* suffixes that are specifically characterized by the *anubandha* letter *a*.
"Not for others such as the *liṅ* and so forth. Regarding "in a specific meaning," it refers to the agent, the object, and so on.

Regarding "in a specific time," it refers to the present and so on. Regarding "like the traditional enumeration of phonemes" (*akṣarasamāmnāya*), it is just as the phonemes beginning with *a* appear in sequence within the traditional enumeration of phonemes (*pratyāhāra*).
The meaning is "it is said, in that same way.

[An objection is raised: "Why then is there not a grasping of the mere *lakāra*? The intention is that no specific distinction is provided. [The example given is] "cūḍālaḥ," [derived from the rule] "prāṇisthād ātaḥ... [and so forth].

The suffix *lac* is applied by the rule *lajanyatarasyām* (5.2.96). Regarding the heading "under the jurisdiction of the verbal root" (*dhātvadhikāra*): the word *dhātoḥ* (3.1.91), ending in the fifth case, is carried over [as an adhikāra], and by it the letter *l* is qualified—meaning, "the *l* prescribed after a verbal root. Then there is the rule: *laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ* (3.4.69).

In this context, those meanings—namely the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*karman*), and the state (*bhāva*)—which were specified in the preceding section continue to apply here; and by means of these, the *l*-suffix is qualified—as in "of the *la* prescribed for the agent and so forth.
Consequently, only that *l*-suffix which is thus qualified is understood, not every instance of it.
The state of being.

78. *tiptasjhisipthasthamibvasmastātāṃjhathāsāthāṃdhvamiḍvahimahiṅ* | (Pāṇini 3.4.78) The letter *ṭh* is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*). [It is] unaccented (*anudātta*) by the rule *anudātau suppitau* (3.1.4).

So that it may be as follows: "The augment *iṭ* has the phoneme *ṭ* [as its marker]," and so forth. Now, even if this purpose of the qualification were absent, nothing undesirable would result; for in the rule *iṭo't* (Pāṇini 3.4.106), the substitution of *at* is prescribed for the *iṭ* that is a substitute for a verbal suffix (*liṅ*), and not for any other.

Because it is impossible for the *ik* [the phoneme *i*] to be a substitute (*ādeśa*) for a *liṅga* [an affix]. If it is argued that there exists an *ik* which is a constituent part of *ti* and so forth, we say no;

for that is not a substitute for *l*. For *ti*, etc., as a whole, are substitutes for *l*, and the *ik*s such as *i* are not constituents of those [whole forms]. This is because of the rule "when a meaningful element is mentioned... (*arthavadgrahaṇe*).

If the vowel *i* were understood through its technical designation (*paribhāṣā*) as being meaningful, there would be the undesirable consequence that it would include [the suffix] *kṛt*, *tas*, and so on, which are parts [of verbal forms].

For these are not meaningful, since only the composite units such as *tiP* and the others possess meaning. Therefore, the marker *ṭ* should certainly not be applied? True, it need not be applied, for one who is capable of understanding in this way—

As for one who is incapable [of performing the ritual], it must indeed be performed for him. Now, why is the letter *ṭ* not understood as being for the purpose of ensuring that this [augment]—which has become an *āgama* (an augment)—is prescribed in a specific location by the rule "ṭ- and k- markers [indicate] the beginning and end" (Pāṇini 1.1.46)? To this, he says: "by means of *tiP* and so forth."

And so forth. "Tulyatva" means similarity; that [similarity] exists because they are taught in connection with the same rule (*ekayoganirdiṣṭatvena*). When that is the case, by the rule *tasya* (Pāṇini 3.4.77), all the suffixes beginning with *tiP* become connected with the genitive case. In the second view, however, it is connected with *iṭ* alone. In that regard, whichever position is adopted—

Since it is that [suffix] alone which is fit to be resorted to as it provides favor to all, this must be accepted as a locative of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). Furthermore, because it is an *ādeśa* (substitute) for *iṭ*, the letter *ṭ* is not added for the purpose of indicating the accent (*anudātta*) as would be the case with a substitute for a place (*deśavat*). Or else—

The fact that [the suffixes] beginning with *tiP* are equal to [the suffixes] beginning with *tiP* because they are taught as being in a single grammatical rule (*ekayoganirdiṣṭatvena*) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of their association (*sāhacarya*). "Because of equality with those beginning with *tiP*" means "because of association with them.
Through association, there is the determination of a doubtful meaning, as in the example: "a cow with its calf" (*savatsā dhenur iti*).

Likewise, here too a doubt arises: "Is this a substitute (ādeśa) or an augment (āgama)? Nevertheless, because of its association with *tiP* and others whose status as substitutes is beyond doubt, it is determined that this is indeed a substitute. Therefore, the letter *ṭ* does not serve the purpose of indicating a location (*deśavidhi*). If this is so, [then...]

In the rule *ṭhphalipāṭinamimanijanāṃ guk paṭinākidhataśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.103), would the augment *guk* also be considered an "adeśa" (substitute) because it is similar to the substitutes *paṭi*, *laṭi*, and so on? This is not a fault; for the term *saṃjñāyām* ("when [the word] is a name") is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*) from that context, and a substitute cannot be a name.
It is understood, however, by means of an *āgama* (augment). Therefore, it should be known that the status of being an *āgama* belongs to the *guṇa*.

In that regard, when even a single genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is connected with a substitute (*ādeśa*), it is a genitive of the locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*); but when it is connected with an *āgama*, it is a genitive of a part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). For example, "the letter *ṅ* [is the augment] of *mahiṅ*" and so forth. Now, as for the purpose of the letter *i*...
Why does [the augment] *ṅ* not occur? Because that is already established by the rule *sārvadhātukamapit* (Pāṇini 1.2.4).

7.3.79. *ṭita ātmanepadānāṃ ṭere*. [Question: Why does this not apply here [in the case of *śānac*]? And so forth. Since *śānac* is also connected to a *ṭit* *l*-suffix and is designated as *ātmanepada*, therefore for that too, by virtue of being *ṭe*, [the substitution of *e* would occur].
The intended meaning is that [the rule] must apply. Regarding the phrase "among those introduced" (*prakṛtaiḥ*) and so forth:
among the *tiṅ* suffixes and others that have been introduced, the *ātmanepada* suffixes are specifically distinguished here by the words "those which are *ātmanepada*.
Therefore, this fault does not arise; for the *śānac* suffix is not included among the *tiṅ* suffixes and the rest.

Although one could have simply said "ṭhṭitaḥ taṅām" for the sake of brevity, the statement "ṭhātmanepadānām" is intended for stylistic variety (*vaicitrya*). Now, one might object: if "taṅām" were stated, would there not be the inclusion of a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated term) by means of the letter *t* in "tas"? [The answer is: No, because of the paribhāṣā (metarule) regarding the inclusion of only those [elements] that possess meaning (*arthavat*).
It will be so. But then, would it not apply to that [suffix] which is prescribed in place of *tha*? No;

the term *tiṅ* shall be understood as referring to those [suffixes] included within *tib* and the rest. Or rather, by proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the inclusion of the entire *pratyāhāra* (abbreviation) shall be understood through the word *ta*, which belongs to the *ātmanepada*.
But the pervasion has no substratum [other than the subject], because it must conform to the existence of the locus to be defined.

80. *thāsaḥ se* (3.4.80). [In the example] *ṭhpeciṣe*, there is *liṭ* [the perfect tense]; by [the rule] *ṭhata ekahalmadhve'nādeśāderliṭi* (6.4.120), there is *etva* [the substitution of *e* for *at*] and the substitution of *o* for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). [In the example] *ṭhpaktāse*, there is *luṭ* [the periphrastic future]; [the suffix] *tāsi*; [and by the rule] *ṭhtāsastyorlopaḥ* [there is the elision of the *s*].

(7.4.50) Thus, there is the elision of the letter *s*. Regarding "pakṣyase": this is the *lṛṭ* [future tense suffix]; by the rule "coḥ kuḥ" (8.2.30), there is the substitution of *k*—that is, the letter *k*. Now, why does the substitution of *s* not occur for the letter *th* alone—as in "thaḥ sa"—such that when *s* is substituted for *th*, the subsequent portion would undergo the substitution of *e* for *i*?

Is it not the case that what is truly desired is indeed accomplished? This is not possible; for in this way, the same would apply even to the *takāra* belonging to the word *arthāt*. If you argue that it does not occur because of the qualification "prescribed after a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*)—since the context is that of verbal roots (*dhātu-adhikāra*)—we say no; because such a thing is impossible. For there is no such *takāra* [that fits those criteria].
[The augment] is prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*). Now, would it be specified as "after that which immediately follows a verbal root"?
Even so, the [augment] would apply only to the subsequent [element], and not to the other *vikaraṇas*, because of the intervention;

therefore, let it remain exactly as in the original formulation (*yathānyāsam*). Since the ending in /e/ is already established by the substitution of /e/ for /ṭi/, [there is no need for further rule].

The fact that the substitute is made to end in the vowel *e* is for the purpose of indicating that the substitution of *e* for the final *ṭi* does not occur in the case of substitutes for *tiṅ* suffixes. Consequently, the substitution of *e* for the final *ṭi* does not occur in forms such as *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras*—
as in *paktā*, *paktārau*, and *paktāraḥ*.
81. *liṭas tajhayoḥ eś irec* (Pāṇini 3.4.81). [The commentary states:

"The letter *ś* is for the sake of making [the substitute] a replacement for the whole. If that were not the case, because of the governing rule for verbal roots (*dhātvadhikāra*), the rule *tasmād ity uttarasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.67)—which prescribes a substitute for what follows—would result in the substitution applying only to the following *t* sound.

But when *śakāra* is present, it applies to the whole [stem] by virtue of the rule "that which has more than one *al* or is marked with *ś* replaces the whole" (Pāṇini 1.1.55). Now, why is it not stated as *śe*? It cannot be so; for if it were *śe*, it would receive the technical designation *pragṛhya*. And in this case, in the word *vyatipapa*, there would be the substitution of *piba*. But in *eśi*...
When there is *sati*, it does not occur; for this will be stated: "One should know that whatever [substitution] would apply to a vowel, that applies to the beginning of that [vowel]."

82. For the *parasmaipada* [terminations], *ṇal*, *atus*, *us*, *thal*, *atha*, *us*, *ṇal*, *vam*, and *maḥ* [are substituted]. (3.4.82) Regarding "papaktha": there is an absence of *iṭ* by virtue of the rule "for that which has *at* in the original instruction" (7.2.62). Regarding "pecitha," this is a reading found in some places; there, *iṭ* occurs by the restriction "after *ṛt*, according to Bhāradvāja" (7.2.63).

By the rule *ṭhthali ca seṭi* (6.4.121), there is the substitution of *e* for the root vowel and the elision of the reduplication. Thus, we have *peca*. Because of the governing context of *dhātoḥ* (3.1.91), and by the rules *tasmādityutarasya* (1.1.67) and *ādeḥ parasya* (1.1.54), the letter *th* is replaced by the letter *a*. Then, between the two *a*s, the rule *ato guṇe* applies.

(6.1.97) There is substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*). Alternatively, because of internal similarity (*āntaratamya*), it is logical that the substitute *ā*, which has a plural referent, should replace a base (*sthānin*) that likewise has a plural referent; thus, it applies to the entire aggregate [of the stem and suffix], as in *peciva* and *pecima*. The augment *iṭ* is applied here by the rule governing roots beginning with *krī*.
83. *vido laṭo vā* | (3.4.83) [The root] *vid* means "to know. By this, only the *vid* whose meaning is "to know" is intended, not others.
He thinks as follows: *vidaḥ* is in the ablative case; therefore, by the rule *tasmād ity uttarasya* (1.1.67), [the suffixes prescribed after *vid* replace those that would otherwise follow].

Thus, there ought to be the substitution of the immediately following *ti* and other suffixes. Furthermore, it is not possible for the *parasmaipada* suffixes to follow any other [root] than *vid*, because they are separated by the *vikaraṇa* affixes;
and since *vicāra* and *satā* are *ātmanepada* roots, the occurrence of *parasmaipada* suffixes is untenable. Therefore—
The apprehension is of the object itself as it is known.

84. *bruvaḥ pañcānāmādita āhau bruvaḥ* | (3.4.84) [The word] "five" (*pañca*) and so forth. Now, one might object: there is no second mention of "five" here, nor is there a mention of "beginning with" (*ādi*) to specify the substitute; therefore, how can it be that the substitute takes the place of the first five?
Since all [substitutes] beginning with *ṇal* must occur in turn, how is the meaning "only five substitutes, beginning with *ṇal*, occur" obtained? To this he says:
"Because of the connection with the substituend (*sthānin*)," and so forth. For here, only the first five substituends have been specified.
And by the paribhāṣā "among those [substitutes], the most similar one [is chosen] in place of [the original]" (1.1.50), a connection with only the first five is possible, not with the others.
For instance, similarity (āntaratamya) exists only among the first five, because they have the same meaning; it does not exist for the others.

By way of contrast: therefore, because of the connection with the substituends (*sthānin*), it is logical that even in the case of the substitutes (*ādeśa*) there is understood both "fiveness" and "being the first"; thus, *ṇal* and the others are indeed five substitutes. [The form] *āttha*: by the rule *āhasthaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.35), the *ha* is replaced by *tha*; then, by the rule *khari ca* (8.4.55), [that *tha* becomes *ta*].
Thus, *cartvam* refers to the letter *t*. Regarding the rule "he says" (*bravīti*), [the augment] *īṭ* is applied by Pāṇini 7.3.93: *bruva īṭ*.

Regarding the term "of the subsequent ones" (*pareṣām*), it refers to the suffixes beginning with *th*. Now, for what purpose is this [word] *bruvaḥ* stated again, since there is already the word *bruvaḥ* ending in the fifth case?

He says—"The word *bruvaḥ* is stated again"—and so forth, meaning that there will be a transformation of the case-ending for that same object, and it should be understood as being in the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*). For when a related term is not explicitly heard, a transformation of the case-ending is appropriate; here, however, the term *parasmaipadānām* [is explicitly stated].

Since the *tiṅ* suffixes and others, which are the subject under discussion, are already in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) as the related members, a change of case ending is not appropriate. If, however, the word "of *bruvaḥ*" were not stated, then just as the *ṇal* and other suffixes belong to the *parasmaipada* endings, so too would this designation [of *bruvaḥ*] apply. Therefore...
The term "bruvaḥ" is stated again for the purpose that the substitution [of *śnā*] should apply specifically to the root *brū*.

[The commentary says: "For it would otherwise apply only to the parasmaipada endings. This is the implied meaning: if "bruvaḥ" were not stated again. And this is the reason for the repetition of "bruvaḥ."
The word *hi* has the sense of "because. Because, in the absence of the repetition [of the rule],
the substitution of *āh* would apply only to the *parasmaipada* forms, therefore the repetition of the word "bruvaḥ" must be made.
85. *loṭo laṅvat* (3.4.85).
[The suffixes] beginning with *tām*—those which are prescribed by the rule *tasthasthamip* (3.4.101)—[are applied].
And [the rule] *salopaśca* ("and there is elision of *s*") applies that which is prescribed by the rule *nityaṃ ṅtiḥ* (3.4.99).

Regarding "ṭhaḍāṭau" and so forth: by the rule "ṭhluṅlaṅlṛṅkṣu" (Pāṇini 6.4.71), the augment *ṭ* is prescribed; by the rule "āḍajādīnām" (Pāṇini 6.4.72), the augment *āṭ* will be prescribed as an operation for the *laṅ* tense; and by the rule "laṅ śākaṭāyanasyaiva" (Pāṇini 3.4.111), there is the substitution of *jus* for *jhi*. Furthermore, there is no distinction here [between the two views].

It is applied; therefore, since that effect occurs by virtue of the extension (*atideśa*), the intention is that it must likewise occur by the effect of *laṅ*, according to the rule "ṭhāḍajādīnām" (Pāṇini 6.4.72). There is elision [of the *i*] by "itaśca" (3.4.100), and the substitution of *am* for *mip*. This is a point of instruction (*deśya*). From those two, [the suffix] *ṭheḥ* becomes *uḥ*.

Because the substitution of *u* (as in *ityutva*) and the substitute *ni* for *ṭhmer* (in *ṭhmerniḥ*) are both about to be prescribed as exceptions [to the present rule], [the author] says: "And that [substitution] is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). By this, he considers that only the substitute beginning with *tām* occurs, and not one beginning with *aḍ*.

86. *eruḥ* | (3.4.86) Regarding the rule beginning with *ṭhhinyoḥ*: *hinī* refers to *hi* and *ni*; a prohibition of the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* must be stated for these two, otherwise forms such as *lunīhi* and *pacāni* would not be established. [Objection: "No, because of the force of the pronunciation [of the rule]."
Thus: if, once the vowel *i* has been employed, there ought to be the vowel *u*, then one should have pronounced *u* itself;
for this is the more concise means for the derivation of words.
Furthermore, the brevity of the sūtra does not result from the pronunciation of *i*; rather, it results from [the pronunciation of] *u*.
If one pronounces the vowel *i* when the [vowel *u*] ought to be pronounced, the purpose of this is so that the substitution of *u* (*utvam*) does not occur.
87. *serhyapicca* (3.4.87). Regarding the example *lunīhi*: since the *pit*-designation is prohibited, the *ṅtva* (ṅ-it designation) applies by the rule *sārvadhātukamapit* (1.2.4);
consequently, *ītvam* (the substitution of *ī*) occurs by the rule *ī halyaghoḥ* (6.4.113), which is based upon that [ṅ-it designation].
Regarding *rāghnuhi*: the root *rādh* (and *sādh*) is listed as "to accomplish" (*saṃsiddhau*) at Dhātupāṭha 1262 and 1263;

because it belongs to the *svādi* group, it takes the suffix *śnu*. Here too, as in the previous case, when the augment *ṅ* is present, there is no *guṇa* substitution. Now, for what purpose is this heavy (*guru*) rule formulated? Why not simply say *se rhi ṅcci* instead?
This cannot be so; for if this [suffix] were prescribed as having the marker *ṅ*, then by virtue of its being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), it would indeed possess the quality of being *pit*.

Consequently, there would be the prohibition of *guṇa* and other operations required by the marker *ṅ*, and due to its being *pit*, it would also be unaccented (*anudātta*). Therefore, let it remain exactly as it was originally formulated.

88. *vā chandasi* (3.4.88). "The substitution of *ṭha* is made optional," it is said. [This refers to] the rule "the substitute is *ṭha*. Because that [substitution of *ṭha*] is immediate, it is applied. However, the substitute [of *ṭha*] is not immediate because it is separated by that [rule], and thus it is made optional.

Regarding *yuyodhi*: the root *yu* (DhP 1033) means "to mix" (*miśraṇe*) as well as "not to mix" (*amiśraṇe*). By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 2.4.76), there is *ślu*-elision of the *śap* suffix; by the rule *ślau* (6.1.10), reduplication occurs. Here too, because [the penultimate vowel] is *pit*, it does not possess *ṅtva* status; therefore, *guṇa* [substitution applies].

It does not occur. By the rule *ṭhaṅtiśca* (Pāṇini 6.4.103), there is the substitution of *ghi*. [The example is] *prīṇīhi*. [The root] *prīñ* [is listed] in the Dhātupāṭha (1474) as meaning "to satisfy" and "to desire. Because it belongs to the *kryādi* class, the suffix *śnā* is applied.
Here too, since the suffix is *apit*, the substitution of *ī* occurs as before.

89. *merniḥ* | (3.4.89) This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the [substitution of] *ṭh* and the elision of *u*. It applies respectively to those [operations] obtained through the extended application (*atideśa*) of *ṭheruḥ* (3.4.86) and *loṭo laṅvat* (3.4.85). And [it applies] to the elision of the vowel *i* in the case of the *liṅ* [optative].

Its application occurs through extended application (*atideśa*) by virtue of the rule "ṭhitaśca" (Pāṇini 3.4.100). In the form "pacāni," the augment *āṭ* is applied by the rule "āḍajādīnām" (Pāṇini 6.4.72), which is understood as "āḍ ajādīnām pi ca."
90. *āmetaḥ* | (3.4.90) Here, there are two positions: either the imperative (*loṭ*) is qualified by the vowel *e*, or the vowel *e* is qualified by the imperative.
If the first position were adopted, then because *e* would be the qualifier, and by means of a qualifier—

The fault to be addressed is this: if the rule of "specification of the end" (tadantavidhi) applies, then the suffix *ām* being prescribed for the imperative (*loṭ*) ending in *e* would be a replacement for the whole word because it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*). However, in the second view, the vowel *e* itself is the primary element because it is the qualificand. It is not...

And since the rule regarding the final element applies to the principal member, this will apply to the single vowel *e* alone; thus, there is nothing further to be addressed. Therefore, relying on the second alternative, he says: "of the *e* belonging to the *loṭ* [imperative]," and so forth. In the form *pacatām*, once the substitution of *etva* (the change to *e*) has been made, the suffix *ām* follows. Here...

Even though, in expressions such as *pacāveda* and *yajāveda*, the *guṇa* substitution is included by the mention of the imperative (*loṭ*) due to the application of the principle that "the end of the preceding and the beginning of the following are treated as one" (*antādivadbhāva*), nevertheless, according to the maxim "that which is external is weaker than that which is internal" (*bahiraṅgam antaraṅge*), the internal substitution of *ām* must first be applied.

Because the external *guṇa* substitution is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the replacement by *ām* does not occur. The external nature of the *guṇa* is due to its dependence on two words, whereas the internal nature of *ām* is due to its dependence on a single word.

91. *Savābhyāṃ vāmau* (3.4.91). In *pacasva*, after the substitution of *se* for *thās* has been made by [Pāṇini 3.4.80], the letter *v* is substituted. In *pacadhvam*, after the substitution of *e* for *at* has been made, the substitution of *am* occurs.

92. *āḍuttamasya piñca* (Pāṇini 3.4.92). [The commentary states: "And that *āṭ* is the first person (*uttamapuruṣa*), and it is *pi*. Now, why is the *pit* designation not applied to *āṭ* itself? Because it would be purposeless. For the *pit* designation would either serve the purpose of making [the vowel] unaccented (*anudātta*), or...

Or [it may be] for the sake of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. In that case, the fact that *āṬ* is unaccented is established simply by virtue of its being an augment (*āgama*); however, it is not at all the cause of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, because it is not an affix (*apratyaya*). Therefore, since the status of being a *pit* (which causes *guṇa*) would be useless with respect to *āṬ*, it is prescribed as belonging to this very [augment] itself—as in "karavāṇi."

Since there is no *ṅt* suffix after the root *pā*, the *guṇa* substitution occurs. Thus, "karavai" [is formed]: by [Pāṇini 6.1.88] *eta ai* and [6.1.90] *āṭaśca*, the *vṛddhi* substitution takes place.
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ām* [prescribed by] 3.4.90. As in *pacāvedaṃ yajāvedam*, when the *s*-suffix is elided according to 3.4.85, *loṭo laṅvat*.
The vowel *vṛddhi* [substitution] occurs by the rule "ṭhādguṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.90).

94. *leṭo’ḍāṭau* (3.4.94). [The commentary says: "By way of alternation (*paryāyeṇa*). Now, why do these two not occur simultaneously? He thinks as follows: these two are prescribed as having the marker *ṭ*; and the status of being marked by *ṭ* is for the purpose of applying the rule regarding initial elements (*ādividhānārtham*). And...

Two [sounds] cannot simultaneously occupy the status of being initial, because a single point of articulation (*ādideśa*) is occupied by only one; therefore, simultaneity is not tenable. Examples such as *joṣiṣat* have been explained under the rule *sibbahulaṃ leṭi* (Pāṇini 3.1.34), and they are explained here as well.

Regarding *ṭhjoṣiṣat*: from the root *juṣ* in the sense of "pleasure" and "service" (*juṣī prītisevanayoḥ*, Dhātupāṭha 1288); the *i* in *sip* is for the sake of pronunciation; by this [rule], *aṭ* is added; then, by the rule *itaśca lopaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (Pāṇini 3.4.97), there is the elision of the *i*; and by the rule *ārdhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ* (7.2.35), the augment *iṭ* is added.

The *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel [occurs], and by the rule "before the suffix *ṣa* and a suffix beginning with *ṭha*" (Pāṇini 8.3.59), there is the substitution of *ṣ*. Regarding the form *tāriṣat*:

from the root *tṛ* (meaning "to float" and "to cross over," Dhātupāṭha 969), the vowel of the root is replaced by [guṇa] by the rule "before *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes" (7.3.84), applied here by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*).

The vowel is long; the rest is as before. Regarding "like *manda*": the root *madi* (in the sense of praise, joy, intoxication, sleep, beauty, and motion; DhP 1.3) takes the augment *num* because it is marked with *i* (Pāṇini 7.1.58).
Regarding "foot-soldier" (*padāti*): the root *pad* (in the sense of going; DhP 10.169) belongs to the *divādi* class and is anudātta.

The *parasmaipada* ending is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*), as is the *śap* suffix. By the rule *aṭā sahākaḥ savarṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.101), there is lengthening of the vowel; the *tip* ending follows. Here, the elision of the *ik* [of *śap*] does not occur, because in the rule prescribing that elision, the word "optionally" (*vā*) from *vaito'nyatra* (Pāṇini 3.4.96) is understood to carry over. Thus, one says "he causes to move" (*cyāvayati*). The roots are *cyuṅ* and *jyuṅ*.
The roots *pruṅ* and *pluṅ* mean "to go" (*gatau*) [Dhātupāṭha 955–958]; they take the causative suffix *ṇic*.

95. *āta ai* (Pāṇini 3.4.95). Regarding the rule *mantrayate*: the root *matri* (Dhātupāṭha 1679) means "to speak secretly"; it takes the *ṇic* suffix of the *curādi* class, followed by the *śap* suffix, and then the *guṇa* and *ayādeśa* substitutions [are applied]. This is the reading in the *mu.pāṭha*. Thus, the *guṇa* and *ayādeśa* substitutions occur.

"Why does [the augment] *āṭ* not occur in cases such as *padātyavidyat*? [The answer is: "Because of the force of the rule prescribing [the augment] *āṭ*. [The author] thinks that if *āṭ* were to undergo the change to *ai*, one would simply have prescribed the augment *ai*;
in this way, there is economy of procedure (*prakriyālāghava*).

96. *vaito'nyatra* | (3.4.96) Regarding *śāsa*: this is the first person singular (*uttamapuruṣaikavacana*) with the augment *iṭ*, and the substitution of *e* for *ṭi*. Examples such as *īśai* and others have been explained under the rule *upasaṃvādāśaṅkayoḥ* (3.4.8).
Regarding "dadhas": the root is *ḍudhāñ* in the sense of "holding and nourishing" (DhP 1092). By Pāṇini 3.4.80, *thās* is replaced by *se*.

There is *ślu*-elision of the *śap* suffix, followed by reduplication according to 6.1.10. Then there is the augment *aṭ*, and the elision of the vowel *a* by 7.3.70, which states that the *a* of *ghu* roots is optionally elided in the *leṭ* mood.

97. *itaśca lopaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (Pāṇini 3.4.97). Regarding the phrase "the mention of *parasmaipada*," etc.: [An objection] might be raised: "Since the substitution of *e* for *i* will serve as an exception (*bādhaka*) to the augment *iṭ* and others, what is the purpose of mentioning *parasmaipada*? This is not so.

The scope for the substitution of *ṭeretva* is in other *lakāra*s and so forth, while the scope for the elision (*lopa*) of *it* is in the *parasmaipada*s; when both would apply simultaneously, the elision of *it* would occur because it is the subsequent rule.
98. *sa uttamasya* (3.4.98).
[The example is] *ṭhkaravāva*. [The augment] *āṭ* is applied by [the rule] *ṭhleṭo'ḍāṭau* (3.4.94). Regarding the phrase "the mention of *uttama*" and so forth:
if, then, the mention of *uttama* is for the purpose that [the augment] should not occur in other persons...
Is it being done? No; one should simply employ the mention of *vas* and *mas*. Here too, this is the meaning:

the mention of *s* need not be made, for the elision of *s* occurs by the very rule regarding the final letter (*alo’ntyaparibhāṣā*). [Objection: It is impossible to employ the mention of *vas* and *mas*; for when that [mention] exists, whenever...
If, by this transposition, those two [suffixes] were to occur in the place of another person (puruṣa), then there would still be elision;

and when *thas* is substituted in the place of the first person (*uttama-puruṣa*), then there would be no elision. Only when the term "first person" (*uttama*) is explicitly mentioned does this fault not arise, by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*).

When the designations "middle" (madhyama) and "highest" (uttama) both occur, because of the governing rule of a single designation, there is no coexistence; rather, the middle designation is superseded by the highest designation. Furthermore, if the inclusion of the letter *s* were not made, then when the highest [vowel] undergoes substitution in other rules, there would be the elision of even another phoneme.
Let it be so; therefore, let it remain exactly as it was originally stated.
99. *nityaṃ ṅtiḥ* | (3.4.99) [The forms] *ṭhapaca-avāpaca-avāpama* are derived from the *laṅ* [tense]. The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *ato dīrgho yañi* (7.3.101).

100. And for this reason as well: (3.4.100) *ṭhapacāt*—this is the *laṅ* [aorist] suffix. *ṭhapākṣīt*—this is the *luṅ* [aorist] suffix; by the rule *ṭhvadavraja* (7.2.3) et cetera, there is *vṛddhi*, and by the rule *ṭhastisico'pṛkte* (7.3.96), there is *iṭ*.
101. *tasthasthamipāṃ tāntantāmaḥ* | (3.4.101) [The forms are] *tā*, *anta*, *tām*. As before, there is vṛddhi; and by *jhalo jhali* (8.2.26), there is the elision of the suffix *sic*.

102. *Liṅ* takes the suffix *sīyuṭ*. (3.4.102) In forms such as *pacet*, the *liṅ* suffix is applied by the rule "vidhinimantraṇa... (3.3.161), the *sakāra* is elided by "liṅ salopo'nantasya" (7.2.79), and [the vowel *e*] undergoes *guṇa* substitution with the *śap* suffix by "ādguṇaḥ".
(6.1.87) *vali lopaḥ* (elision of *v*). In forms such as *pakṣīṣṭa*, the suffix *liṅ* is used in the sense of benediction (*āśis*).
By the rule *coḥ kuḥ* (8.2.30), there is the substitution of *k* for the *c*; then by *iṇkoḥ* (8.3.57), there is the substitution of *ṣ* [for the *k*].
103. *yāsuṭ* is acute (*udātta*) in the *parasmaipada* endings when followed by a suffix marked with *ṅ*.

(Pāṇini 3.4.103). The phrase "belonging to the domain of the *parasmaipada*" indicates that this locative case in *parasmaipadeṣu* is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*), not a locative of contiguity (*para-saptamī*). Indeed, it is not a locative of contiguity.

It is possible; for the *liṅ* [augment] cannot occur in the *parasmaipada*. Regarding the statement "when the unaccented nature of the augments (*āgama*) is about to apply," from what source is it determined that the augments are unaccented? Precisely from this very fact: because of the explicit statement that *yāsuṭ* is accented. For if the augments were unaccented, [the rule would not be necessary].

In that case, the rule stating that [the suffix] is udātta would be purposeless; for since *yāsuṭ* is a portion of an affix, its initial syllable would already be established as udātta by the accent of the affix itself. [Objection: But surely the rule stating it is udātta must be for the sake of those instances where it is designated as *pit*; for since they are *anudātta*, the portion belonging to them—

Would *yāsuṭ* be necessarily anudātta if it were not stated that it is udātta? This is not so; for if this were the intended purpose, he would have simply said "api. Therefore, this mention of *udātta* is merely an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the augment (*āgama*) is anudātta. In that case...
"Because [the suffix] ṅt is impossible for all [verbal bases]," such is the intended meaning. Why is this so?
Because in the case of the form *duṣyāt*, the *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization) that occurs by the rule *grahijyā-ādi* (Pāṇini 6.1.16) is possible when the *yāsuṭ* suffix is present with a *ṅit* marker.
For the *samprasāraṇa* is indeed dependent solely upon the *ṅ* marker.

Because no specific distinction is made [in the rule]. In that context, if the *ṅt* designation were prescribed for *yāsuṭ*, then only the single case of the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the root *grah* would be favored. However, since the *ṅt* designation is prescribed for the *liṅ* [optative], the favoring of the entire scope of *ṅt*-operations occurs precisely through the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*; thus, it is the *liṅ*.
In this way, the suffix *ṅt* is prescribed; that is, "of those operations which have *ṅt*.

The meaning is: "of those operations [that apply] when there is a *ṅt* suffix. Regarding the form *kuryāt*: there is the *guṇa* substitution for the root based on the *vikaraṇa* suffix, the substitution of *ut* by [Pāṇini 6.4.110] *ata ut sārvadhātuke*, and [the substitution of *i*] by [Pāṇini 6.4.109] *ye ca*.

Thus, there is the elision of the vowel *u*. In the case of "kuryuḥ," there is the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) according to Pāṇini 6.1.96: *usyapadāntāt*. In "acinvam," the *m* replaces the *mi* suffix; here, because of the absence of the marker *ṅ*, there is *guṇa* substitution.
And this is the purpose of the indicator (*jñāpaka*).

104. *kidāśiṣi* (Pāṇini 3.4.104). [The commentary states: "This *kit*-status applies only to the suffix *ṭha*. If this is so, does it not contradict the rule that the *yāsuṭ* augment added to the *liṅ* in the sense of benediction (*āśis*) becomes *kit*? There is no contradiction.

The mention of *yāsuṭ* is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *liṅ* [optative] itself. Therefore, by means of its constituent part (*avayava*), it is the *liṅ* itself that is prescribed as having the *kit* designation by this rule; for the *liṅ* possesses *yāsuṭ* as its constituent part. Regarding the phrase "of the augment *na*" (*nāgamasya*), here too it should be understood to mean "of the augment *na* alone."

"Because there is no purpose [for it]"—the sense is that this is not because there is an absence of purpose for *kit* in every instance. Why? Because by the rule *vacy-ādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 6.1.15), the *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) that applies to the roots *vac* and *svap* is possible even when the suffix *yāsuṭ* is present, provided it is *kit*. For the *samprasāraṇa* is prescribed for any *kit* suffix whatsoever.

Because there is no specific distinction [between them]. If the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is exactly the same, then what is the distinction between the property of being marked with *ṅ* (*ṅtva*) and the property of being marked with *k* (*kitva*), such that when the former is applicable, the latter would be prescribed?
To this he says: "Samprasāraṇa," etc. [The rule] regarding *ṅtva* is by the sūtra beginning with *vici-ādi* (Pāṇini 6.1.15), whereas [the rule] regarding *kitva* is...

The *samprasāraṇa* substitution would not occur for the root *didhī*. The *guṇa* [substitution] prescribed by the rule "jāgro 'viciṇṇalitsu" (Pāṇini 7.3.85) results in the form "iṣyāt. The elision of the *s* is effected by the rule "skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca" (Pāṇini 8.2.29).

Regarding "vacyāt": because the suffix is not *kit*, there is no vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the root *vac*. Regarding "jāgṛyāt": by the preceding rule, the suffix is *ṅit*; therefore, there is no *guṇa* strengthening.
In both cases, the *śap* is elided because they belong to the first class (*adādika*).
105. *ra* replaces the final letter of the root *jha*. (Pāṇini 3.4.105).
Thus, "kṛṣīran. This is the *liṅ* (optative) in the sense of benediction (*āśis*).

106. *iṭo't* (3.4.106). [The example] is "kṛṣīya. This is the *liṅ* [mood] in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*). [The objection: "This [substitute] is not a part of the original element (*ādeśāvayava*)," because it is the substitute for the vowel *a* alone. [The response: If that is so, then this substitute *a* is being prescribed as the replacement.
Would [the vowel *u*] be a grasper (*grāhaka*) of its own homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*) by virtue of the rule "ṭhaṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.1.69)?
It will not be so, because of the metarule "bhāvyamāno’ṇ savarṇān na gṇāti" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 35).
Or, even if there were grasping of homogeneous sounds, by the principle of closest proximity (*antaratamya*), it would result in a vowel of exactly one mora (*mātrika*).

Now, as to why the augment *iṭ* in the form *lāviṣīṣṭa* does not undergo the substitution of *akāra*, he says: "The augment *iṭ* is not included [in the application of this rule]. He states the reason for this: "In the case of the inclusion of that which possesses meaning (*arthavat*), [the augment is not included]," and so forth. But surely even augments possess meaning; for instance:
Is the meaning of the *liṅ* suffix expressed only when accompanied by *yāsuṭ*, and not by it alone?
This is not so; for in other *lakāra*s, the meaning is seen even without that [augment], whereas for augments (*āgama*s), it is never the case. Therefore, they (the augments) do not possess meaning.
107. *suṭ* is applied to *ti* and *tha*.

(Pāṇini 3.4.107) Now, is the *liṅ* stem qualified by the letters *t* and *th*—meaning "the *liṅ* which has *t* or *th* as its substituend"? Or rather, do they [the letters *t* and *th*] belong to the *liṅ*—meaning "the *t* and *th* that are related to the *liṅ*"? Regarding this:

If the first alternative were adopted, then, because it is the qualified element (*viśeṣya*), the optative suffix (*liṅ*) would possess predominance (*prādhānya*). Consequently, since grammatical operations apply to the predominant element, the augment *suṭ* would be attached to the optative suffix itself. And in this way, because it is both subsequent and specifically prescribed, *suṭ* would supersede *sīyuṭ*. Therefore, this [first alternative] is defective.
Regarding the second alternative, he says: "of those related to the *liṅ*.

To clarify the meaning of what was stated—that the augment *suṭ* occurs after the letters *t* and *th*—he says: "the letters *t* and *th* are the bases (*āgaminau*)," treating them as the subjects (*viśeṣya*).

The meaning is "because of its predominance. Regarding what was stated—"of the *liṅ* and that which is connected to it"—he says the following in order to clarify its meaning: "the *liṅ* is its qualifier" and "the augment *sīyuṭ*, however, is the substitute for *liṅ*. By the particle *eva*, the letters *t* and *th* are excluded. "By that..."

And so forth. Since the *takāra* and *thakāra* [of the suffixes] are the substitutes for *suṭ*, whereas *sīyuṭ* is substituted only by *liṅ*, they occupy different positions; therefore, *sīyuṭ* is not superseded by *suṭ*. Moreover, a relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) between two elements occupying different positions is not logical, because there is no contradiction between them. [Thus one forms: *kṛṣīṣṭa*.

The forms for the singular [optative] are "kṛṣīṣṭhāḥ. For the dual, they are "kṛṣīyāstām" and "kṛṣīyāsthām," due to the suffixes *ātām* and *āthām*. In all these cases, the *liṅ* (optative) is used in the sense of benediction (*āśis*); because the suffix is *kit* by rule 1.2.32 (*uśca*), there is an absence of *guṇa* substitution.
[In the example] *paceyuḥ*: by *ato yeyaḥ* (7.2.80), there is the substitution of *iy*; by *ād guṇaḥ* (6.1.87), there is the resulting single substitute (guṇa);
and [by the rule of] *pararūpa*, there is the subsequent form.

109. *sijabhyastavidibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 3.4.109). By the mention of *vetteśca*, it is shown that only the root belonging to the *lug-vikaraṇa* class is intended here. For only that [root] can have *jhi* immediately following it, and not the other roots of the *vidi* group.

Because of the intervention by the *vikaraṇa* suffixes; since the roots *as* (to be) and *cārya* (to investigate) take the *ātmanepada* endings, the occurrence of *jhi* is impossible, and therefore it is logical to understand that only those [roots] with a *luk*-type *vikaraṇa* are intended.
As for the statement, "The mention of *abhyasta* and *vidi* is for the sake of *asi*": if the mention of *abhyasta* and *vidi* is indeed for the sake of *asi*, [then...]

This being the case, the substitution of *jus* would also apply to the *jhi* that follows *laṭ* and other suffixes; therefore, he says: "The word *ṅti* also carries over. By this, the meaning is that *jus* will occur only for the *jhi* associated with the letter *ṅ*, and not for others—namely, in the forms *abibhayuḥ* and *ajihrayuḥ*. [The root is] *ñi bhī* (to fear).

From the roots *ṭhhrī* in the sense of "shame" (*lajjāyām*) (DhP 1085) and *ṭhjuji* (DhP 1084), there is *guṇa* substitution by Pāṇini 7.3.83 (*juji ca*). For the roots beginning with *juhoti*, there is *ślu*-substitution for *śap* by Pāṇini 2.4.75, and doubling occurs by Pāṇini 6.1.10 (*ślau*). Regarding the form *ajāgaruḥ*: due to its inclusion in the *adādi* group, there is *luk*-elision of *śap*; this applies to the root *jāgarti*.
The designation "abhyasta" (repeated) is applied by the rule "ṭhjakṣityādayaḥ ṣaṭ" (Pāṇini 6.1.6).

110. *ātaḥ* | (Pāṇini 3.4.110) By stating that the *jhi* which follows an *akārānta* [root] after the suffix *sic* is replaced by *it*, it is effectively stated that the *jhi* must be immediately following both [the root and the suffix]. However, such immediate succession (*ānantarya*) with respect to both is not possible, because of the intervention of *sic* after the *ā*.
Thinking that there is an intervention [between the root and the suffix], he asks: "How," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "when there is the elision (*luk*) of *sic*":

when the elision of *sic* is effected by the rule *gāti-sthā-* (Pāṇini 2.4.77) and others, then, by means of the technical designation of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), [the augment] occurs immediately after *sic*. And [it is said]: "by direct statement (*śruti*) from a stem ending in long *ā*."

Because it is heard immediately after that; "by direct audition" (śrutyā) means by the perception accomplished through the sense organ of hearing. Thus, since the immediate sequence is established by both [the context and the direct audition], it follows by implication from the word *ataḥ*, which ends in the *sij* suffix.
It is stated that *jherjus* occurs; for when the suffix *sic* is actually heard, proximity (*ānantarya*) between two [sounds] is not possible.
[The rule states] "the letter *t* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation," because there is nothing to be excluded. Indeed, a suffix *sic* cannot occur after either a short or a protracted vowel.

Regarding the phrase "even though it is already established by the preceding rule itself": even when the *sic* suffix is elided, because the *jhi* ending is immediately preceded by *sic* according to the rule of *pratyayalakṣaṇa*, he shows the purpose of the restriction [in the present rule] by means of the form *abhūvan*. The augment *vuk* is applied by the rule "bhuvo vuk luṅliṭoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.88). Now, one might object: "But surely this is not [the case] here by the preceding rule..."

[The objection: "It would obtain [the suffix *jus*], for here there is no immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) of the *jhi* [ending] with respect to the *sic* [augment]; so what is being prohibited? To this he says: "By the characteristic of the affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*), etc. For when [the *sic*] is elided, there is immediate sequence by virtue of the characteristic of the affix; therefore, it would obtain [the suffix *jus*] by the preceding rule. [This is prevented] by the restriction regarding *jus*.

It is being refuted. If, then, this [rule] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), then [the form] *ṭh akārṣuḥ* would also not occur, because here the suffix *jhi* does not follow a root ending in *at* with the elision of *sic*. To this he says:
"of the same class," and so forth. This *jus* is for the purpose of restriction after a root ending in *at* with the elision of *sic* that belongs to the same class.

It is prescribed; and that restriction depends on what is of the same class, and therefore it excludes only that which is of the same class. And what is of the same class? [The reading *anyaḥ psijalugantaḥ* is a corrupt reading;
it should be] *sijlugantaḥ* (that which ends in the elision of *sic*). Nor is there a form ending in the elision of *sic* preceding *jhi* in the case of *akārṣuḥ*.
Thus, this is not the domain of that restrictive rule; therefore, the *jus* suffix indeed occurs.
111. *Laṅḥ śākaṭāyanasyaiva* (3.4.111).
[The forms] *ṭhayuḥ*, *avuḥ*—as before, there is the elision (*luk*) of *śap*, and as before, there is the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatvam*).
"In *laReĀva*" and so forth: the substitution of *jus* for *jhi* belonging to that [stem] is to be prescribed.
This was stated with reference to the *tiṅ* suffixes. Why is this so?

Because it is possible for both the *laṅ* and *liṅ* [suffixes] to follow immediately after a stem ending in *ā*. However, the substitution of *jus* for those [suffixes] related to them is prescribed by the grammatical rule itself, namely *ṭhjherjus* (Pāṇini 3.4.108), and so forth.

This is not stated with reference to that [case]. However, the particle *eva* serves to exclude the *lṛṅ* (conditional), because the suffix *syapratyaya* intervenes between the root and *jh*. And it should be understood that this applies to that for which the state of being like *laṅ* does not occur by way of extension (*atideśa*). For, in the case of that for which the state of being like *laṅ* has been prescribed by way of extension—
That [suffix] is called *laṅ* by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). In the ultimate sense, however, it is indeed *loṭ*, not *laṅ*.

Regarding the phrase "by the state of being like *laṅ*," it is connected with *laṅ*. The mention of *laṅ* is made so that there may be a reference to the primary *laṅ* itself, lest there be a confusion with what is merely similar to *laṅ*.

But by what means does the treatment as *laṅ* (*laṅvadbhāva*) occur? He says: "The *loṭ* [tense] is treated like the *laṅ*" (Pāṇini 3.4.85). For by this rule, when the operations of the *laṅ* are extended to the *loṭ*, it acquires the status of being like the *laṅ* due to its connection with the operations of the *laṅ*. Consequently, it becomes similar to the *laṅ*.

It is designated as *laṅ* by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). The meaning here is this: if the mention of *laṅ* were not made for the purpose of including the primary *laṅ*, then—due to the extended application (*atideśa*) in the rule "the *loṭ* is like the *laṅ*" (Pāṇini 3.4.85)—just as the operations of the *tām*-suffixes and so forth apply to the *loṭ*, this [operation] would likewise apply.

Therefore, the mention of *laṅ* is made for the purpose of excluding this fault; let there be no such *jus* [substitution] here due to the effort of mentioning *laṅ* for the *loṭ* [imperative]. However, that which is prescribed by the rule "sijabhyastavidibhyaśca" (Pāṇini 3.4.109) shall apply in cases such as *bibhyatu*, *jāgratu*, and *vidantu*.

"Why does it not occur? Is there not some other effort involved there? To this he says: "In the rule *sijabhyasta*," and so forth. But how is it that, without further effort, the *jus* of the preceding [rule] does not apply to the imperative (*loṭ*)?
To this he says: "For it is merely the state of being *jus*," and so forth. For this [imperative *jus*] is not the same [as the one previously mentioned].

The *laṅ* [augment] is distinguished by its primary [form]; what then? It is merely the state of being *jus*. Whatever *jus* is prescribed in this section belongs only to the primary *laṅ*, not to any other.
Therefore, the preceding *jus* also does not occur. [The mention of] "the single *k* is for the sake of the subsequent [rule]"—now, for that purpose...

Why is there the particle *eva*? Because its function is that of an injunction (*vidhi*). For the meaningfulness of the particle *eva* is not tenable in a sentence whose purpose is an injunction; rather, it is employed for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*), and not for the purpose of an injunction. Nor is this [sentence] for the purpose of restriction; for an injunction is commenced only when [the matter] is already established.
It serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), for this [sūtra] is not commenced when [the desired form] is already established.

Therefore, the particle *eva* is indeed for the sake of what follows. [Objection: Should the particle *eva* here be intended so that it applies only according to the opinion of Śākaṭāyana, and not according to the opinions of others? [Response: No; by him...
Because this rule is established even without it; for if it were not so according to the opinion of others, the mention of Śākaṭāyana would be purposeless.
112. *dviṣaśca* (Pāṇini 3.4.112). Regarding the term *dviṣu*: because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*.

113. *tiṅśitsārvadhātukam* | (Pāṇini 3.4.113) As in "bhavati" and "nayati": when the designation *sārvadhātuka* is applied to *tiṅ* suffixes, the *śap* affix is introduced for the agent (*kartari*) based on that designation; and because that *śit* [affix] is also *sārvadhātuka*, the rule "*sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ*" [applies].

By [Pāṇini 7.3.84], there is *guṇa*. In "roditi," as before, there is the elision of *śap*, and by [Pāṇini 7.2.76], there is *iṭ*. In "pavamānaḥ" and "yajamānaḥ," by [Pāṇini 3.2.128] there is *śānan*; because that [suffix] is a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, there is *śap*.
Since that [suffix] is also sārvadhātuka, there is guṇa substitution for the root vowel.

114. "The remainder [of affixes] are *ārdhadhātuka*. (Pāṇini 3.4.114). In the example *lavitā*, there is the suffix *tṛc*; the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule "The *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant receives the augment *iṭ*" (7.2.35). In the example *vṛkṣatvam*, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are applied by the rule "The suffixes *tva* and *tal* denote the state (*bhāva*) of that" (5.1.119). In the example *lūbhyām*, [the suffix *bhyām* is applied].

From the root *lū* with the suffix *kvip*, [the form] *lūbhyām* [is derived]. Regarding *jugupsate*: by the rule for the *gup*-class (Pāṇini 3.1.5), the suffix *san* is applied; because the suffixes beginning with *tva* are not considered *ārdhadhātuka*, there is an absence of the augment *iṭ*. As for *vṛkṣatvam*, it is given as a counter-example, because the suffix *tva* is not prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*). [The example] *lūbhyām*...
This and so forth is incorrect, because of the maxim "those ending in *kvip* do not lose their status as verbal roots" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 132);

for the suffix *myam* is prescribed only after a verbal root, and the suffix *san* is also [prescribed] after a verbal root, since *gup* and others possess the status of verbal roots? This is not so; for it is precisely to avoid this very fault that...

It was stated that [the suffix] is prescribed by means of the word "dhātu" (root). And this is its meaning: that which is prescribed in such a manner as "from a root" (dhātoḥ), that is to say, that which is prescribed after uttering the word "dhātu. That for whose prescriptive definition the mention of "dhātu" exists—yet *bhv-ādayaḥ* and *asan* are not prescribed in this way.

Because in this two-fold rule, neither the governing context of "dhātu" (root) nor the explicit mention of "dhātu" (root) is possible. But how is the meaning "that which is prescribed by the designation 'dhātu'" obtained,
given that only one mention of "dhātu"— namely, the word *dhātoḥ*— is carried over [from the previous rule], and that [mention] serves to exclude suffixes that are not roots?

Since its purpose has already been fulfilled, is it not incapable of expressing anything further that is more specific? He thinks thus: from either the rule prescribing the *yaṅ* affix (Pāṇini 3.1.22) or from the rule "after the root *śam*, when a name is to be formed" (3.2.14), the mention of "the second verbal root" (*dvitīyadhātu*) is understood to carry over; therein, by means of one verbal root...

The non-verb-root affix (*adhātupratyaya*) is excluded; by another [rule], the verb-root affix (*dhātupratyaya*) is specified as "that which is prescribed after a verb root" (*dhātoḥ*). Why is the term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) mentioned? So that it does not apply to *tiṅ* and *śit* affixes; otherwise, since there would be no governing authority for a single designation, [the rule] would be like that of the designations "affix" (*pratyaya*) and so forth.
There would be absorption.
