115. *liṭ ca* (3.4.115). Regarding the form *śekitha*: because the *liṭ* suffix is an *ārdhadhātuka*, the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *ṛto bhāradvājasya* (7.2.63). In that rule, the augment *iṭ* is applied after a root ending in *ṛ* only according to the opinion of Bhāradvāja, and not according to others.

The meaning intended here is "of the roots. By the rule *ṭhthali ca seṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.121), there is the substitution of *e* for the root vowel and the elision of the reduplication. Thus we have *jagle* and *mamle*. Because these are *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes, the vowel *ā* is elided by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64).

Now, he refutes what was stated in the passage beginning with "But [it might be argued]..."—namely, that [the present rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the designation *sārvadhātuka* (Pāṇini 3.4.115)—by stating: "Because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) regarding 'one designation at a time,' there is no co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) elsewhere, as is the case with the designations such as *pratyaya* and so forth. It is not [the case here].

Furthermore, since there is no governing rule (adhikāra) here for a single designation, the intention is that it is incorrect to regard this designation as *sārvadhātuka* as an exception (*apavāda*). With the words "This is true," etc., he establishes that it is indeed an exception.

116. *liṅaśiṣi* | (3.4.116) [The variant reading "plaviṣīṣṭhā" is found in the manuscript; it should be "laviṣīṣṭa"]. [In the form] *thās*, there is the augment *suṭ* by the rule *suṭ tithoḥ* (3.4.107), followed by the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*, and the substitution of *ṣṭ* for *t*.

117. *cchandasy ubhayathā* (Pāṇini 3.4.117). The printed reading is *svastaye*; [another reading is] *svastaye*. [The root] *as* [is used] in the sense of "being" (Dhātupāṭha 1065); the suffix *ktin* is applied in the feminine. Because it is treated as *sārvadhātuka*, the substitution of *bhū* for *as* does not occur.

In the form *śuśruvire*, because the *liṭ* [perfect] affix is treated as a *sārvadhātuka* [affix], there is the application of the *śnu* affix and the substitution of *śṛ* for the root *śru* by the rule *śruvaḥ śṛ ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.74).
In the form *sunvire*, the *śnu* affix is applied by the rule *svādibhyaḥ śnuḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.73).
"ṭhupastheyāma" [is derived as follows]: from the root *sthā*, the suffix *liṅ* is applied; then *yāsuṭ*; then *mas*; and by the rule "ṭhatherliṅ" (7.4.24), the substitution of *e* for *th* occurs.
Now, one might object: is not all of this already established by the rule "vyatyayo bahulam" (3.1.85)?
To the question "For what purpose is this undertaking?", he says: "Of this very [rule], 'vyatyayo bahulam'. The meaning has already been explained.
Thus ends the third chapter of the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who was a teacher of the Bodhisattvas.
The fourth quarter.
And the third chapter is completed.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
1. *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* (4.1.1).
"This is a governing rule (adhikāra)," because it is not marked with the svarita accent.

"Up to the end of the fifth chapter," by this he shows the limit of the governing rule; beyond that, it does not continue, because it lacks the svarita accent. "In the words beginning with *su* and ending with *kap*."

He explains the irregularity of the governing rule (*adhikāra*): "The term *ṅī* is a general designation for *ṅīp*, *ṅīṣ*, and *ṅīn*," and so forth. By disregarding the specific indicatory letters (*anubandha*), that which is the common element *ṅī* alone is what is understood here. [Likewise,] "the term *āp* is a general designation for *ṭāp*, *ḍāp*, and *cāp*. It is taken generally.

The term "grahaṇam" (the act of grasping) is to be connected with what precedes. Now, one might object: since the suffixes beginning with *ṅī* are plural in number, the plural case-ending ought to be used; how then can there be a reference by means of the singular form "ṅyāpprātipadikāt" (Pāṇini 4.1.1)? To this he replies with the words "teṣām" and so forth.

The meaning is that here, this designation of the *ṅī* suffixes and so forth is made by means of a collective (*samāhāra*) *dvandva* compound. For if it were an associative (*itaretarayoga*) *dvandva*, there would have to be a plural ending; however, this is not an associative *dvandva*, but rather a collective one. And since that [collective] has a single referent, the use of the singular number alone is appropriate.
The statement "this is a collective designation" (samāhāranirdeśaḥ) is intended to exclude the sense of mutual conjunction (itaretarayoga) and to exclude other types of compounds; for otherwise,
a genitive compound such as "the nominal stem of *ṅī* and *āp*" (*ṅyāpoḥ prātipadikaṃ ṅyāpprātipadikam*) would also be possible.

One might suspect [this objection]. Therefore, since the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) from which [the suffixes] would arise is that which ends in *ṅī* or *āp* within a compound, it would apply to forms such as *rājakumārī* and the like, but not to *kumārī* and the like when they are used alone.
Furthermore, by the very rule for their prescription, the nominal stem would be the base (*prakṛti*). Therefore—
This designation is by means of a collective *dvandva* compound. In that context, however, the three [suffixes] are taken as the base forms (*prakṛti*), and thus it applies in all cases.
Now, how then is the analysis (*vigraha*) here? Some say: "The feminine suffix *ṅī* and the suffix *āp*..."

"And it is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Now, one might object: since the technical designation "nominal stem" is prohibited by the rule *ṭhapratyayaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.45), the suffix *ṅīp* would not arise, and consequently, the formation of case-endings would not occur. To this it is replied: this is not a suffix (*pratyaya*), but rather an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of a suffix. Even so, [the objection remains].
Would there not indeed be a prohibition [of the *samprasāraṇa*] by the rule "an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is like its original form" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 113)?
This is not a fault, for imitation is of two kinds: that of meaning and that of the mere sound-form.
This was indicated by the Teacher through his twofold instruction in the rule "after *pari*, *vi*, and *ava*, the root *kṛ*" (*parivyavebhyaḥ kṛñaḥ*).

(1.3.18) Because of the optional application or non-application of the substitution of *iy* for *ji* by the rule "after *vi* and *parā*, [the root] *ji*" (1.3.19), only the sound-form is imitated here, not the form accompanied by its meaning.
Therefore, in this case, the prohibition stated in "the suffix *ap*" (1.2.45) does not apply at all.

The extended application (*atideśa*) is like that of the original form (*prakṛti*), provided the imitation is meaningful. [Objection: But even so, shouldn't there be elision of the *hal* and *ṅī* suffixes according to Pāṇini 6.1.68? It is said in reply: the elision of *su* occurs after a stem ending in *ṅī*, not after the mere suffix *ṅī*. If it is argued that this could occur by virtue of the principle of "treatment as if possessing a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), we say no.

It is stated [in the *Śākapārthivādhikāra*] that "the status of being like that which has a designation (*vyapadeśavadbhāva*) does not apply when [the word] is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadikena*)," and this [word *pūrva*] is indeed a nominal stem. Therefore, [the suffix] *ṅīṣ* applies by the rule "and *ṅīṣ*" (*ṅīśca*). Now, this is a governing rule (*paribhāṣā*) concerning the domain of the prescription of suffixes, as seen in the rules "from *pūrva*, [the suffix] *ini*" (Pāṇini 5.2.86) and "also from that which is preceded by something else" (Pāṇini 5.2.87).
Is it because [the suffix] has already been made known? This is not a rule for the addition of an affix; what then? It is a rule for elision (*lopa-vidhi*).

Therefore, the *paribhāṣā* does not apply, and since the designation of the whole as being like its parts (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*) indeed exists, the rule for elision (*lopaśāstra*) proceeds from that. Consequently, there must be elision of the *su*-suffix by the rule "when *ṅī* follows" (*ṅī ceti*).
Based on the general application of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), the analysis is *ṅīśca*.

However, another says: "In actual usage, as in the words *kumārī*, *gaurī*, and so forth, that which is the vowel *ī* is precisely what is being referred to here, with its case-ending elided; therefore, it becomes simply *ṅī*. If this is the case,"
Why is the marker *ṅ* attached for the purpose of denoting the general category?

But surely, since it possesses meaning through the meaning of that which is being imitated (*anukriyamāṇa*), the production of a case-ending would again follow; and consequently, by the rule *ṅīp*, the form should be *ṅī*. This is not so; [the suffix] belongs to the preceding time.
Because that which is a case-ending (*vibhakti*) relies upon the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* [rule], and thus the prohibition in *apratyaya* (Pāṇini 1.2.45) applies.

Now, it might be argued: "By the *jñāpaka* [indicative mark] in *na ṅsimbuddhyoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.8), the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) is not prohibited by the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule [via 1.2.45]."

This is incorrect; this *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) pertains specifically to the domain of the rule for the elision of *n*. Therefore, it is established that in this case there is no prohibition of the designation "nominal stem" (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) by means of the rule concerning suffixes (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*).
But surely, if they are suffixes, then by the statement "and [suffixes] follow" (*paraśca*, Pāṇini 3.1.2), they must occur after [the base]?

The affixes beginning with *svādi* (the case-endings) occur by implying a preceding base (*prakṛti*); for otherwise, their status as "subsequent" (*para*) would not be tenable, since that status of being subsequent is dependent upon a prior element, and no base other than those ending in *ṅī*, etc., is possible. In that regard, even without the explicit mention of the term "*ṅyāpprātipadika*" (a nominal stem ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, or a prātipadika), [the rule functions].

By the principle of elimination, this very [set] is obtained as the *prakṛti* (base); for indeed, the other types of *prakṛtis* are the verbal root (*dhātu*), namely that which ends in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) and the sentence (*vākya*). As for the suffixes (*pratyaya*), they are those beginning with *su*, those beginning with *ṭāp*, and those beginning with *aṇ*. Among these, first of all, the verbal root cannot be followed by suffixes beginning with *su*, because they...

When [case-endings] are prescribed for meanings such as singularity and so forth, they imply a word that possesses those [meanings]. And a verbal root does not possess singularity and so forth. Even if they are produced without qualification, a restriction is nevertheless made regarding those already produced; even so, it is not logical that their production should originate from the verbal root.
Because the suffixes *sva* and others, which are prescribed generally,
are superseded by the suffixes *tavya* and others, which are prescribed specifically; if it is argued that, in that case,
the suffixes *ṭāp* and others would then apply to the verbal root (*dhātu*), this might be so— provided that [the general rule] were not [superseded].

When there is the mention of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *ṅī* or *āp*, the suffix *ṭāp* would apply by Pāṇini 4.1.4 (*ataḥ*), [namely] after verbal roots ending in *a* such as *jugupsā* and others; the suffix *ṅīp* would apply by Pāṇini 4.1.6 (*ugitaśca*), [namely] after roots ending in *ap* such as *vañcu* and others;
and [the suffix] *ṅīṣ* would apply by Pāṇini 4.1.5 (*ṛnnebhyo...*) after stems ending in *n* such as *man* and others.

Is it that the suffix *ṅīp* [is applied] by the rule "ṅīp" (Pāṇini 4.1.5)? This is not the case; for the suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth are prescribed for the feminine gender, whereas a verbal root (*dhātu*) denotes an action (*kriyā*).
And because an action is of a non-substantial nature (*asatvabhūta*), it has no connection with gender; such is its character.

Because they possess the nature of a substance (*dravya*). By this, the derivation of suffixes such as *ṭāp* from finite verbs (*tiṅanta*) and from sentences (*vākya*) is refuted, since both of those are primarily concerned with action (*kriyā*). Furthermore, the derivation of suffixes such as *aṇ* from a verbal root (*dhātu*) is likewise untenable; for they are prescribed only when there is a connection with a meaning such as "offspring" (*apatya*).

Since the meaning expressed by a nominal stem (*dhātu*) is an abstract entity (*asattvabhūta*), just as its connection with femininity is impossible, so too is its connection with meanings such as "offspring" (*apatya*). By this, the production of suffixes such as *aṇ* from verbal endings (*tiṅanta*) or from sentences (*vākya*) is refuted; for the meaning of those [verbal endings and sentences] is likewise [abstract].

Because that which has action as its primary element lacks a connection with [nouns such as] "offspring" (*apatya*) and so forth. Even though a connection exists in the case of "the offspring of him who cooks for Devadatta," it does not occur because of the *jñāpaka* rule *ṭhtiṅśca* (Pāṇini 5.3.56). Those secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) are prescribed when there is a connection with meanings such as "offspring."

If it is argued that, by the principle just stated, let that not be so, but rather that those [suffixes] which are prescribed for their own sake must necessarily be joined [to the root], this is a trivial objection; for just as the suffixes *sva* and others, though prescribed generally, are sublated by the suffixes *tavyat* and others which are prescribed specifically, so too is it here.

That [suffix] cannot arise; likewise, even for those [suffixes] prescribed generally as *svārthika* (denoting the same meaning as the base), it is simply not possible because they are superseded by *tumun* and other *svārthika* suffixes that are prescribed as specific exceptions (*viśeṣavidhi*).

If it is asked, "In that case, what [suffixes] would occur after a *tiṅanta* (a verbal form ending in a personal ending)?"—they will not occur, due to an *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence). Namely, this...

In some instances, he includes the mention of *tiṅ* (verbal suffixes) in the formulation of a *taddhita* rule— namely, "atiśāyane tamabiṣṭhanau" (Pāṇini 5.3.55) and "tiṅśca" (5.3.56); and in other instances of *taddhita* formulation, he likewise includes the mention of *tiṅ*— namely, "atiśāyane tamabiṣṭhanau" (5.3.55) and "tiṅśca".

By this [rule], it is indicated that secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) do not occur after a word ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). If it is argued that they might then occur after a sentence (*vākya*), we reply: they will not occur because of non-usage (*anabhidhāna*).

For when it is said, "Devadatta’s little horse" (*devadattasyāśvakaḥ*), the meanings such as "unknown" (*ajñāta*) and so forth, which reside in the meaning of the sentence, are not expressed by the suffix *ka*.
They are not illuminated [by the suffixes]; rather, they are inherent in the word "aśva" itself.

Furthermore, there should likewise be no occurrence of *svādi* (the case-endings) after a *tiṅanta* (verb ending in a verbal suffix), for their meanings—such as singularity (*ekatva*) and so forth—are already expressed by the *tiṅ* suffixes themselves. And there is no application of suffixes whose meaning has already been expressed.

It is appropriate [not to use them], because of the statement: "There is no employment of words whose meaning has already been expressed" (Vyāḍipāṭha 60). But surely, the employment of words even when their meaning has been expressed is observed, as for example: *ekaḥ*, *dvau*, *bahavaḥ*?
In this case, the employment is justified because of the inclusion of the word "vacana" (number/gender). For in the sūtra beginning with "prātipadika," etc., [the term *vacana* is understood].
This [rule] applies to them because of the mention of the word "vacana" (number); for that reason, this *paribhāṣā* (metarule) is present there.
Consequently, the operation of a pronoun (*sarvanāma*) is established even for those [words] beginning with *sarva-* when they are qualified by gender suffixes (*liṅga*).
If this is so, could one not avoid the mention of the suffixes *ṅī* and *āp* by relying on this very principle?

This is not the case; for the designation *prātipadika* cannot apply to a meaningful verbal form qualified by gender, because of the prohibition in Pāṇini 1.2.45 (*arthavad adhātur apratyayaḥ prātipadikam*). Furthermore, in the rule prescribing the *prātipadika* designation, it is not possible [to list] all meaningful items as designata by their own forms.

[This is] in order to show [the application]; because they are infinite. If this is so, then this paribhāṣā would not apply even in the case of the rule "ṇāviṣṭhavat prātipadikasya" (Vārttika 813), since there is no mention of the specific form [of the stem]; and consequently, the treatment as if it were an iṣṭhan-suffix (iṣṭhavadbhāva) would not occur for forms qualified by gender.

What is the fault here? [One might argue that] in the case of *kumārīmācaṣṭe* and *kumārīyati*, the elision of the *ṭi* suffix would not occur. This is not a fault; for the application of the *iṣṭhan*-like behavior is desired extensively (*bahulam*), and thus it is stated in the *Cura-ādi-gaṇa-sūtra* (186): "The suffix *ṇic* is added after nominal stems (*prātipadika*) in the sense of verbal action, and the *iṣṭhan*-like behavior applies extensively."
Thus, because of the use of the plural number [in the rule], the *iṣṭhavan* behavior will apply even to that which is qualified by a feminine suffix (*liṅga-viśiṣṭa*).
Furthermore, with the words "and moreover" (*kiñca*), he adds another purpose. The word "that" (*tad*) refers to the feminine suffixes *ṅī* and *āp*.

The mention of *ṅī* and *āp* [in Pāṇini’s sūtra] is for the purpose that the formation of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) may occur from stems ending in *ṅī* and *ā*. For example, in the form *kālitarā*:

the suffix *ṅīp* is applied to the word *kāla* by the rule governing names of regions and so forth (4.1.42); then, from that stem ending in *ṅī*, [the suffix *tarap* is added] by the rule beginning with "when a dual or a distributive word is the upapada" (5.3.57).
The short vowel [is substituted] by the rule *tarap-ṭhag-hrasva-kalpa* (Pāṇini 6.3.43). Regarding the form *hariṇitarā*:

from the word *harita*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *varṇādanudātāt topadhāto naḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.39), whereby the letter *t* is replaced by *n*. If the mention of the suffixes *ṅī* and *āp* were not present in the rule *aṭ-ku-pv-āṅ* (Pāṇini 8.4.2), [the substitution would not apply].

[Otherwise,] it would be more powerful due to its subsequent status. But this being the case, since the feminine suffixes *ṅī* and *āp* are relied upon as the base (*prakṛti*) when a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is prescribed, they must occur first;
thus, the prescription of the secondary derivative from that which ends in them is established. Now, one might object: "The feminine suffix is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*)."

The external factors (*bahiraṅga*) are those such as lightning; for instance, because of the governing rule "from [words] that are semantically capable, optionally after the first [case-ending]" (Pāṇini 4.1.82), [suffixes] arise after words ending in case-endings (*vibhakti*). Case-endings, moreover, depend upon [grammatical relations] such as the object (*karman*);
and since objects and so forth are external factors because they are caused by external actions, therefore, [the suffixes] depend upon that cause.

Because they depend on external factors, even secondary nominal suffixes (*taddhita*) are indeed dependent on what is external; however, since gender does not depend on another related element, it is internal (*antaraṅga*), and therefore the feminine suffixes such as *ṭāp* and others, being caused by that [gender], are also internal. Consequently, precisely because they are internal...

[Objection: Since the suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth must first apply, and only afterwards the secondary (*taddhita*) suffixes should apply to that which ends in them, the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* is useless? [Response: This is not so;

for in the statement "the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* is for the purpose of introducing secondary suffixes after that which ends in them," by the mention of "secondary suffixes" (*taddhita*), [it is implied that the rule applies even when a secondary suffix has already been added].
Only those secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) that are used in their own sense (*svārthika*) are intended here. To indicate this very point,
the suffix *tarap* is cited in its own sense after feminine suffixes in the examples "kālitarā" and "hariṇitarā."

Furthermore, among the suffixes that denote the same meaning as the base (*svārthika*), the rule *samarthānām* (Pāṇini 4.1.82) does not apply. For the author of the Vṛtti states: "This governing rule extends up to the limit of the *svārthika* suffixes, reaching as far as *prāgdiśo vibhaktiḥ* (5.3.1); for it has no utility among the *svārthika* suffixes."

And this being the case, since the suffixes expressing the same meaning (*svārthika*) ought to arise from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself without depending on the production of case-endings, how can those [suffixes] be considered *bahiraṅga* (external)? But even so, forms such as *kālitara* would not serve as examples; for the *tarap* suffix is *bahiraṅga*. For it...
Even if it does not depend on the production of a case-ending (*vibhakti*), it certainly depends upon an external object as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*);
however, since the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) does not depend on any such counter-correlate, is it not therefore *antaraṅga* (internal)?
This is not a fault; this direction of examples was merely shown by the author of the Vṛtti.

These examples should be shown here: *enikā*, *śyenikā*, and *rohiṇikā*. For in this case, if the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) were applied first, then from the words *eta*, *śyeta*, and *rohita*, when there is a desire to express meanings such as "unknown" (*ajñāta*), the suffix *kap* would be added.

By the rule "ṭhvarṇādanudātāt topadhāt to naḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.39), the suffixes *ṅīp* and *nakāra* would not occur. If, then, the mention of *ṅy-āp* is for the purpose of prescribing secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) after words ending in *ṅī* or *āp*, then the compound-ending suffixes (*samāsānta*) would also have to occur after those very same endings; and consequently, [in the case of] *bahavaḥ*...

One might think that because there are cows (*gomantaḥ*) in this city, after forming a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the suffix *ṅīp* would apply by the rule *ṭhugitaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.6), and subsequently, the suffix *kap* would apply by the rule *nadyutaśca* (Pāṇini 5.4.153), resulting in the form *bahugomatīkā*. Yet, the desired form is *bahugomatkā*. This is not so.

This is a fault; for suffixes added at the end of a compound (*samāsānta*) do not arise from the compound itself. What then? They arise from the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) even before the compound has been formed. For the author of the *Vṛtti* will state in the rule *na kapi* (Pāṇini 7.4.14):
"Even this shortening [prescribed] by *gostriyor upasarjanasya* (1.2.48) does not apply when *kap* follows."
"It occurs because, when the suffix *kap* is applied to the final member (*uttarapada*) for the sake of forming a compound, the compound must subsequently be formed;

thus, the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in a feminine suffix does not yet constitute a compound. Furthermore, in the sentence "In this city there are many who possess cows" (*bahavo gomanto 'syāṃ nagaryām*), the final member is not for the purpose of forming a compound.
The rule "it occurs in the feminine" must apply first, followed by the compound, and then the feminine suffix; thus, through this sequence of suffixes, *bahugomatī* is established.
If, however, the compound has not yet been formed, the compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) would apply to the final member [of the compound] because of its meaning.

In that case, the commentary (*vṛtti*) on *Pāṇini* 5.4.71, which states, "The compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) prescribed hereafter for words such as *ṛc* do not occur after a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *nañ*," would be contradicted; for [according to your view], those compound-final suffixes would not occur after those *tatpuruṣa* compounds whose meanings are derived from those [words].
Should it not be said that they "become"? Because the negative particle (*nañ*) is the subject under discussion, it is precisely that which is understood.

Furthermore, in the rule *tatpuruṣāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.71), the word *tatpuruṣa*—by virtue of its purpose (*tādarthyāt*)—refers to a compound whose final member has the sense of a *tatpuruṣa*. In that context, however, [the suffix applies] after *ṛc* and so forth.

Because it is so heard [in scripture], it is understood that *ṛk* and the others are indeed [the referents]; furthermore, the two ablative case-endings in *tadantāt* and *tatpuruṣāt* are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*). Therefore, the meaning is as follows: from that *tatpuruṣa* compound which has those words beginning with *ṛk*—which follow the negative particle (*nañ*) and are situated near that negative particle—as its final member, [the suffix *aṇ* is applied].

The compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) does not occur. Alternatively—the word *anta* denotes a constituent part; thus, both ablative endings are in apposition [to *tatpuruṣāt*], because they serve that purpose. That which ends in *ṛc* and so forth is precisely the second member for the sake of the *tatpuruṣa* compound. Therefore, it is stated: "from that which ends in such [a word] for the sake of the *tatpuruṣa*."

Therefore, this is the meaning: the compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) do not occur after an *uttarapada* that constitutes the sense of a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *ṛc* and so forth, when these follow a negative particle (*nañ*).

Furthermore, that [ending] refers to the sense of a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in those [words]. By virtue of syntactic competency (*sāmarthya*), the *uttarapada* is understood to be precisely *ṛc* and so forth.

In that case, would there not be a contradiction with this commentary on the rule *bahuvrīhau saṃkhyeye ḍajabahugaṇāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.73): "The suffix *ḍac* occurs after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in a word other than *abahu* or *gaṇa*, which functions [to denote] a numerable object (*saṃkhyeya*)"? No, there is no contradiction.

There is a contradiction here; for it has been stated that in this case the final member (*uttarapada*) itself is the meaning of the *bahuvrīhi* because it exists for its sake, and thus it is called a *bahuvrīhi*. Therefore, the meaning is this: the suffix *ḍac* occurs after that final member which stands as the meaning of the *bahuvrīhi* when it refers to the object to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*).
In this manner, other contradictions of a similar kind should also be resolved.
Thus, it remains established that the mention of *āp* (the feminine suffix) is for the purpose of prescribing *taddhita* suffixes after it;
[and] because of the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the mention of *ṅy-āp* is for the purpose of prescribing *taddhita* suffixes.
Regarding the statement "the taddhita suffix is stronger":
if this is so, why is the inclusion of *tyūṅ* not understood for the two rules *ṭhyunastiḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.77) and *ūṛtaḥ* (4.1.66), such that a taddhita suffix would arise from a word ending in those?

It might be asked: why not [form] *yuvatitarā* or *brahmabandhūtare*? The shortening by the optional application of *ūṅ* according to Pāṇini 6.3.44, "nadyāḥ śeṣasyānyatarasyām," need not be performed;

for the mention of *hyām* [in that rule] is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). This is because [the suffixes] are introduced under the heading "striyām" (Pāṇini 4.1.3), for those [suffixes]...

The mention of *ṅī* and *āp* here is for the purpose of indicating that [the rule applies to all such suffixes]. Therefore, it should be understood that the inclusion of *tyūṅ* is already effectively accomplished here.
If the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* were merely for the sake of indication (*upalakṣaṇārtha*), then only one of them should have been mentioned.

For is it not the case that feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*) are indeed observed even with a single [vowel]? True; however, both are mentioned for the sake of variety. But by the rule "the suffix *kan* after *śyāva* and others" (5.4.29), "after *lohita* when referring to a gem" (5.4.30), and "also when the color is non-permanent" (5.4.31)—by means of this optional, pleonastic (*svārthika*) suffix—[the forms are derived].

The sublation of the feminine suffix is intended [in this context]. In that regard, when there is sublation, then after the suffix *kan* has been added to the word *lohita* and the suffix *ṭāp* has been applied, and the change of *i* to *e* (*cetva*) has occurred, it should be *lohitikā*. However, when there is no sublation, then by the rule "ṭh, from a color-word ending in an unaccented vowel with a non-penultimate *u*, there is *na*" (Pāṇini 4.1.39), there is the addition of the suffix *ṅīp* and the replacement of *t* with *n*.

Since the shortening [of the vowel] would occur by the rule "kani ca ṭhke'ṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.13), the form should have been *lohinikā*. Therefore, this must indeed be stated: "or there is a sublation of the gender based on the word *lohita*."
*svaujasamauṭchaṣṭābhyāmbhisṅebhyāmbhyasṅasibhyāmbhyasṅasosāmṅyossup* (Pāṇini 4.1.2).
Regarding the statement "the letters beginning with *ṭ* are *anubandhas*," and so forth: therein, the letter *u* belongs to the nominative singular case-ending (*su*).

They are for the purpose of correct pronunciation. Why is it not understood that [the *j* in *jas*] is for the sake of distinguishing [it from other sounds], according to the rule "ṭha-naha-sau" (Pāṇini 7.1.93)?

Because there is nothing to be excluded [by such a distinction]. The *j* in *jas* is for the sake of unambiguous pronunciation; for if it were absent, once the substitution of *au* for *ā* had been made, a doubt would arise as to which [sound] it refers.

Regarding the statement "the utterance of the suffix," an explanation must be provided there. Now, why is it not understood as being for the purpose of qualification in the rule *jasaḥ śī* (Pāṇini 7.1.17)?
[Because] even if it were stated as *asaḥ śī*, there would be no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). [Furthermore,] the letter *ṭ* in *āṬ* is for the sake of [identifying] *suṭ*.

"The purpose [of the letter *ś*] is for the sake of including [the *ś*] in the *pratyāhāra*. This passage, however, does not exist in the *vṛtti*; it ought to be there, but it has now disappeared due to the error of a scribe or similar causes. The letter *ś* in *śas* is for the sake of unambiguous pronunciation, as it is subject to the substitution of *c* by the rule "ṭhkhari ca" (Pāṇini 8.4.55).
The letter *ś* is for the purpose of removing doubt; otherwise, if it were stated as *aiḍas*, there would be a doubt:

"Is this the pronunciation of the letter *ṭ*, or of the letter *ḍ*? In that case, because of the pronunciation of *ḍ*, there would be the elision (*lopa*) of the *ṭi* suffix. But surely, even when the letter *ś* is present...

There must indeed be doubt: "Is this the utterance of the phoneme *ḍ* for the *t* that has been substituted, or is it the phoneme *ṭ*? This is not so; for if it were the phoneme *ḍ*, the utterance of the phoneme *ś* would be purposeless. [Furthermore, consider] the rule: "From that [stem], *śas* becomes *naḥ* in the masculine" (Pāṇini 6.1.103).
Thus, in that context, the purpose is for the sake of specification in the rule *ṭāṅsiṅsāminātsyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.12).

In rules such as *supāṃ suluk* (7.1.39), there is a phonetic insertion (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *ā* in the sequence *supāṃ suluk pūrvasavarṇa ā āt śe*; for if the marker *ṭ* were not present there, that [vowel *ā*] would also be included [in the scope of the rule].

"Number, case-role (*karman*), and so forth"—and so on. Number is prescribed for the meanings of *svādi* [suffixes] by another rule of the science, such as "the plural is used when there is multiplicity" (Pāṇini 1.4.21). Case-roles such as the object (*karman*) are prescribed by rules such as "the second case is used for the object" (Pāṇini 2.3.2). "It forms a single syntactical unit with that" means: [it forms a single statement with those other rules].

When there is plurality of the object (*karman*), the plural suffix *śas* is used; when there is duality or singularity of the object, the dual suffixes *au* and *ḍam* (or *auṭ* and *śas*) are used. In this same way, a single unified statement (*ekavākyatā*) should be understood in other cases as well.
If, then, this [rule] forms a single unified statement with that [other rule], then it is appropriate [to say]: "The plural is used for the plural."
In this regard— namely, [the statement] "this instruction applies where number is possible;

however, for indeclinables, which are devoid of number, the case-endings (svādayaḥ) prescribed by general rules certainly exist"— that would be contradicted, for if there were syntactic unity (ekavākyatā), [the suffixes would apply] only to a specific meaning.

Since the suffixes beginning with *su* (the case endings) are prescribed for [grammatical categories] such as singularity (*ekatva*) which are connected to the object of the action (*karman*) and so forth, it is not tenable that they are "prescribed generally" (*sāmānyavihitatva*).

Furthermore, regarding what was stated there: "The suffixes beginning with *su* are applied after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in a feminine marker (*ṅī*) or a long vowel (*āp*), and the suffixes beginning with *ti* are applied after the verbal root (*la*)."

As for the claim that "the plural number was prescribed [by the rule], and by this [subsequent rule] it is further enjoined as having the numerical category of plurality as its denotation," that too is certainly contradictory; for it is not logical to enjoin the denotation of the numerical category of plurality after the plural number has already been prescribed within a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*).

By combining this [rule] with the end of that treatise, since the plural number is prescribed only for the count of plurality, there is first of all no contradiction. For even in the case of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), just as the general prescription of the suffixes *svādi* is established, so too [is it established] "in the case of many."

The plural number has already been explained in this very context [under Pāṇini 1.4.21]. Furthermore, the second contradiction that was raised does not exist at all; for the plural number is prescribed by the rule "svādayo bahuvacanam" (Pāṇini 1.4.21), which states that after a verbal root (dhātu), a nominal stem (prātipadika) ending in a vowel or a consonant (hyāp-prātipadikāt), the suffixes beginning with *su* (the case endings) and those beginning with *ti* (the verbal endings) are applied when there is a plurality (*bahuṣu*).

The intended meaning there should be understood as follows: [the word *bahuvacanam*] has attained syntactic unity with the rule *bahuvacanam* (Pāṇini 1.4.21). By this present sūtra, the number "plurality" (*bahutva*) is prescribed as the denotable meaning;
in this regard also, [the same applies] by virtue of the rule *svādi-sūtra* (4.1.2) and the rule *lasya* (3.4.77), etc.

This intention should be understood as follows: [the word "plural"] has attained syntactic unity with the treatise (śāstra). And thus, the plural number is prescribed only by way of aggregation; since its plurality is enjoined as the expressed meaning only through aggregation, how can there be any contradiction? Now, one might object: "But [the term] 'plural'..."

(1.4.21) Is this one single treatise (*śāstra*), such that its syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the rule *svādi-* (Pāṇini 4.1.2) is not possible through another rule such as *ṭh-lasya* (Pāṇini 3.4.77)? Or, if there is syntactic unity with that [latter rule], then its unity with the *svādi-* rule (4.1.2) is not possible?

There is no fault at all; for these two utterances are pronounced *tantra*-wise (simultaneously), such that one has syntactic unity with the rule *svādyutpattiḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.2), while the other has unity with another rule of the science, namely *lasya* (1.4.21).

Alternatively—the absence of contradiction is demonstrated in another way. For here, would the *svādi* suffixes be prescribed by this sūtra independently of the rules beginning with "the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is used for the object" (Pāṇini 2.3.2), or would they be prescribed in dependence upon those rules, thereby attaining syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with them? Thus there are two [alternatives].
There are two positions. Regarding the first position, it is held that *svādi* suffixes are prescribed without distinction;

however, for those thus prescribed, a restriction (*niyama*) is established by another rule of the science, such as: "Where number is possible, the plural suffix is used when there are many" (Pāṇini 1.4.21), and so forth.

In the first view, [the suffix] is prescribed as denoting numbers such as singularity and so forth, which are related to the object (karman) and other factors; however, in the case of indeclinables (*avyaya*) that lack number, the case-endings (*svādi*) prescribed by general rules simply exist.
But in the second view, [the suffixes] apply specifically to meanings characterized by plurality and so forth, which are related to the object and other factors.

The case endings (*svādi*) are prescribed. In that regard, the first alternative—that "the plural number is used for many" (Pāṇini 1.4.21)—and so forth, was adopted; however, here the second [alternative] is adopted, and thus there is no contradiction, because such a statement is made by resorting to the other alternative. Now, in the second alternative, how can case endings arise from indeclinables (*avyaya*), since...

If there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), how can the derivation of case endings (*svādi*) from words devoid of meanings such as number, action, and so forth be justified? This is not a fault; it will occur by virtue of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). That this [Pāṇini] teaches the elision (*luk*) of the case ending (*sup*) produced after an indeclinable (*avyaya*) in the rule "after an indeclinable, the elision of *āp* and *sup*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.82), indicates—
The derivation of case endings occurs from indeclinables.
Regarding "kumārī": the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "vayasi prathame" (Pāṇini 4.1.20). Regarding "gaurī":
the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule "ṣidgaurādibhyaśca" (Pāṇini 4.1.41). Regarding "śārṅgaravī": [the suffix *ṅīn* is applied].

[The suffix] *ṅīn* [is applied] after the *yañ* [suffix] following stems such as *śārṅgarava* (Pāṇini 4.1.73). [The word] *khaṭvā*: [the suffix] *ṭāp* [is applied] by [the rule] *ajādyataṣṭāp* (4.1.4). [The word] *bahūrājā*: [the suffix] *ḍāp* [is applied] by [the rule] *ḍābubhābhyāmanyatarasyām* (4.1.13). [The word] *kārīvagandhyā*: the smell (*gandha*) is like the smell of dried cow-dung (*karīṣa*).

Regarding the word *yasya*: by the rules *gandhasyedutpūtisusurabhibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.135) and *upamānācca* (5.4.137), the substitution of *i* for the final vowel occurs. In the formation of *karīṣagandher apatyam*, the *a* is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca* (6.4.148), and [the subsequent lengthening] follows from the rule *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ* (7.2.117), and so forth.
The substitution of *ṣyaṅ* is applied by the rule "vṛddhiḥ, ṭhaṇiñor anārṣayor gurūpotamayoḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.78),
and the feminine suffix *cāp* is applied by the rule "ṣyaṅś cāp" (Pāṇini 4.1.74).

3. *striyām* | (4.1.3) "Because [the suffixes] *ṭāp*, *ṅīp*, and *āp* are prescribed by this very rule," thus, by means of this, he states that when a suffix is prescribed under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of *striyām*, there is an absence of a base (*prakṛti*) ending in *ī* or *ā*. And this...

This is the reason why, in this context, only the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is connected [to the suffix]. For if a base ending in *ṅī* or *āp* were possible here in this context, then *ṅī* and *āp* would also have been connected; however, that form consisting of *ṅī* or *āp* is not possible here, and therefore those two are not connected.
These two are connected.
Here, regarding femininity, there is a difference of opinion among the teachers; furthermore, in some views, a fault is observed. In that regard, the view of certain [teachers] is as follows:
"A woman is one who possesses breasts and hair; a man is said to be one who possesses hair [on his body]. That which is the interval between these two, in the absence of both, is the neuter.

Regarding the term "possessing breasts and hair" (*stanakeśavatī*), the suffix *matup* is used here in the sense of abundance or excellence. The same applies to the word "possessing hair" (*lomaśaḥ*).

The suffix *śa* is applied by the rule *lomādipāmādisūtreṇa* (Pāṇini 5.2.100). The phrase "the interval between both" means that which is similar to both—namely, female and male. Furthermore, that similarity consists in possessing grammatical gender (*liṅga*). If this is so, then that which possesses both [genders] combined is the neuter (*napuṃsaka*).

[The objection] arises: since the form of the aggregate (*samudāya*) is indeed similar to the forms of the constituents (*samudāyin*) by virtue of being characterized by them, he says—"in the absence of that. That in which both of these [masculinity and femininity] are absent is "neuter" (*napuṃsaka*). Therefore, this fault does not occur. If, in the absence of that...

If it were said that "this is the neuter," then indeclinables and even verbal forms (tiṅanta) would also possess neuter gender. Even if it were stated that "the neuter is that which is the difference between both [genders]," this would still apply to compounds such as *kukkuṭamayūryau* (a cock and a peahen), which are considered to be a collection of genders.

It would follow that collections [of words] would necessarily be neuter. Therefore, both [the alternatives] have been stated: "that which is the interval between the two" and "the absence of those two. Thus, that thing which is neither female nor male, yet possesses gender, is called neuter; from that [it follows that] indeclinables [are neuter].

This means it is stated that neuterhood does not apply to words ending in verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*) or to those ending in *ān*. In this view, the suffix *ṭāp* would undesirably apply to the word *bhrūkuṃsa*, for in that case, a connection with breasts and hair is perceived. A *bhrūkuṃsa* is a male dancer who wears female attire; he is called a "man. And as for [the application of the rule to] *khaṭvā* and so forth...

In the absence of breasts and hair, femininity would not exist; furthermore, because trees and the like lack body hair, they would result in a lack of masculinity, whereas donkeys, huts, and so forth, due to their possession of hair, would possess masculinity.
Consequently, in the case of the phrase "paśya kharakuṭīḥ" ("look at the donkey-huts"), [the rule] "tasmāc chaso naḥ puṃsi" (Pāṇini 6.1.103) would apply.
Otherwise, it would not attain the state of being a "nature" (bhāva).
However, the view of others is that there are three: contraction (*saṃstyāna*), procreation (*prasava*), and persistence (*sthiti*).
Contraction is femininity (*strītva*) by nature, characterized by decrease; that object in which this exists is a female (*strī*). Procreation...

Masculinity consists of the nature of accumulation; that in which this exists is a male. Neutrality is the state consisting of that condition which is devoid of both accumulation and depletion; that in which this exists is a neuter. In this view as well, the triad beginning with contraction (saṃstyāna) is present everywhere.
Otherwise, every single entity would result in being simultaneously female, male, and neuter.

Femininity occurs only when there is the intention to express contraction (*saṃstyāna*); masculinity occurs only when there is the intention to express procreation (*prasava*); and neuterness occurs only when there is the intention to express persistence (*sthiti*). Therefore, this is not a fault.

If [it is argued that gender is determined by increase or decrease], this is incorrect; for instance, when it is said "the girl grows" (*upacīyate kumārī*), the girl remains a female (*strī*) and not a male (*pumān*). Likewise, when it is said "the tree diminishes" (*apacīyate vṛkṣaḥ*), even when there is an intention to express diminution (*saṃstyāna*), the tree remains a male only and not a female. Similarly, "the bowl increases" (*upacīyate kuṇḍam*) or "the bowl diminishes" (*apacīyate*).
Even when there is an intention to express either an increase or a decrease, the word *kuṇḍa* remains neuter alone,
being neither masculine nor feminine.
Thus, because of these differing views among the teachers regarding its femininity and because of the perceived defects [in those views], he asks:

Regarding the statement "it is said [to apply] to the feminine," [the question is asked]: "What is this 'feminine'? and so forth. The author of the *Vṛtti*, however, having understood the intended meaning, speaks from the perspective of another philosophical system, saying: "The generalities and the particulars," and so forth.
That is to say, they are both generalities (*sāmānyāni*) and particulars (*viśeṣāḥ*). Likewise, they are generalities and...

Because they are common to things of the same class, and because particularities (*viśeṣa*) are distinguished— that is, excluded— from one another and from things of different classes, they are called "general-particulars" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*). [The phrase] "femininity and so forth,
like cowness and so forth" means that just as general-particulars such as cowness and the like [reside] in distinct [individuals],...
Likewise, femininity and the rest are also the causes of non-differentiated cognition and designation with respect to their own substrata.
For just as "cowness" and the like subsist in all members of the same class and exclude those of different classes, so too do "femininity" and the rest. Therefore:

In that very same way, those [categories] are also generalities and particularities. But surely, since generalities and particularities pervade all individual instances, even in this view the same undesirable consequence follows—that there would be all genders everywhere. Why then abandon another view for this one?

He states that [the universal] is dependent upon manifestation (*darśana*), saying: "The individuals (*vyakti*) are of many kinds. They are called "individuals" because they are manifested (*vyajante*);

they are the substrata (*āśraya*) of the generalities and particularities (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*). Those generalities and particularities which have individuals of many kinds are described as such. By this, he indicates the following:

Because the manifestors that serve as the substrata for universals and particulars are diverse, only a certain universal or particular is manifested by a certain substratum, and not every one by every one;
this is because the potencies of word-meanings have restricted domains. In that regard, by whichever meaning femininity itself [is manifested]...

Neither masculinity nor neuter-ness is manifested; she is indeed a woman, not a man, nor a neuter. That by which masculinity alone is manifested is a man indeed; that by which neuter-ness is manifested is a neuter indeed. But he who is the manifester of two or three [sexes]—

It is accepted as having two genders or three genders—as in *ardharcaḥ* / *ardharcam*, *padmaḥ* / *padmam*, *taṭaḥ* / *kaṭī* / *taṭam*. Therefore, in this view, there is no occasion for the aforementioned defect. As for that which is the substratum of a general property and its particularity, and the manifester—[it is not so].

How does that [being] become a woman, a man, or a neuter through connection with those [qualities]? To this he says: "In some cases," and so forth. For among ether, space, and the like, general properties such as femininity and so on are manifested in some instances by mere verbal instruction alone, and not manifested by their substratum.

Because their substrata are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). In this regard, that [substratum] in which femininity is manifested through instruction is "female," as in: "this is a female donkey" (*iyam āśā*); where masculinity is [manifested], that is "male," as in: "this is the self" (*ayam ātmā*); and where neuterness is [manifested], that is precisely "neuter," as in—

"This is space. To explain how femininity and so forth are sometimes manifested by mere instruction, he says "Just as," and so on. For there is no such substratum for Brahminhood, Kṣatriyahood, and the like, which could manifest them [directly].
Because the ether and other such substances, which are the substrata of general and particular properties, are beyond the reach of the senses,

the manifestation of [qualities] such as Brahminhood— which depend upon those substrata— occurs elsewhere only through similarity and by means of instruction alone; and just as it is for them, so it is in some cases.

Regarding "femininity" (*strītvam*) and so forth: what, then, is this femininity? Is it the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*), or is it a qualifier of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)? To this he says: "And femininity," etc. When the word *strī* (woman) denotes femininity even without a suffix expressing the abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*), then, when the feminine gender is to be expressed...

Since the suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth occur, femininity (*strītva*) becomes the meaning of the suffix. For just as the word *go* (cow) refers to "cowness" (*gotva*) even when devoid of an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) in the view that the word denotes a universal (*jāti*), so too does the word *strī* (woman) refer to "femininity. However, when femininity is taken as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to that which possesses it...

When the word "strī" (female) also applies to a substance (*dravya*), then this alternative view also holds: "The suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth occur after that nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which applies to a female"; thus, "femaleness" (*strītva*) becomes a qualifier of the base. [It is said: "In both ways it is appropriate. But how, indeed, is it appropriate in both ways?

To the extent that, if *strītva* (femaleness) were the meaning of the suffix, *strītva* would become the primary element; consequently, a genitive case expressing a relation of distinction (*vyatireka-lakṣaṇā*) would result—as in "the femaleness of Devadattā"—and thus there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "Kumārī Devadattā" (Devadattā the girl). This would also apply in the case of the dual number.
Furthermore, in the plural, the forms *kumāryau* and *kumāryaḥ* would not occur, because femaleness (*strītva*) is a single entity;
nor would multiple suffixes be possible, as in *gārgāyaṇī*, *kārīṣagandhyā*, and *kālitareti*, because femaleness is one and because that [femaleness] is...

Because it has already been stated by the *ṣphāṣyaṅ* and other [suffixes] produced at the very first [stage], the vowel *ī*— as in "strī"— does not apply; for in the printed recension of the *Daśapādya-uṇādi-sūtra*,
it is seen that the rule is simply "styāyateḥ ṣṭran" (*Pañcapāda-uṇādi* 4.165).
It is denoted by a word ending in a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*), because otherwise there would be a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) characterized by distinction [between the two].

Why? Because the distinction between universals (*sāmānya*) and particulars (*viśeṣa*) based on their substratum is not denoted by a word ending in a feminine suffix, which would result in a genitive case characterized by distinction.
But why is it not denoted? Because of the inherent nature of the word's expressive power (*śabdaśaktisvābhāvyāt*).
Furthermore, the dual and plural numbers are also applicable;
because even when the general and the particulars are one, [the word] is not denoted [in those numbers], it is due to the inherent nature of the word's expressive power.

The dual and plural number endings are also applicable; for even when the general and particular [qualities] are one, the words denoting them take on the number of their substrata due to the very nature of the power of words. Thus, because the substratum is manifold, the dual and plural endings occur.

In forms such as *gārgyāyaṇī*, femininity is expressed by two feminine suffixes; it is not expressed by a single one. Thus, even though there are multiple suffixes, such as *ṣyaṅ* and others, they are indeed appropriate. Alternatively, in the case of *gārgyāyaṇī*, regarding the suffix *ṣpha* prescribed by the rule "prācāṃ ṣpha taddhitaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.17)—
By virtue of the inclusion of the letter *ṣ* [in the rule], the suffix *ṅīṣ* will occur, as in "kārīṣagandhyā.
By virtue of the statement "ṣyaṅ and cāp" (Pāṇini 4.1.74), the suffix *cāp* will occur after a stem ending in *ṣyaṅ*, as in "kālitarā.
[The form] "kālitarā" [is derived] by means of the suffix *ṅīṣ* prescribed by the rule "jānapadādi" (Pāṇini 4.1.42).

Femininity (*strītva*) has been stated as not qualified by excellence, and not as qualified by excellence; therefore, since it is not expressed [by the suffix], the *ṭāp* suffix will occur after a word ending in the superlative suffix *tara*. This is either due to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule "striyām" (Pāṇini 4.1.3), which states "in the feminine," or due to the capacity of the inclusion of the marker *ṭi*.

[The suffix] will not arise. However, in the view where the base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) is the qualifier, the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) expresses the substance itself as qualified by femininity, while the *ṭāp* and other suffixes are merely indicators (*dyotaka*).
In that case, since there is no distinction [between the base and its qualifiers], the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) does not apply; for the same reason, the dual and plural numbers also do not occur.

Since the substance is manifold, it is indeed logical that even multiple suffixes may occur. For just as the feminine suffixes *ṭāp* and others occur in words such as *khaṭvā*, even though the feminine nature has already been expressed by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), so too do multiple suffixes such as *ṣpha* occur in words like *gārgyāyaṇī*. By this very [reasoning]...
Since the state of being female has been indicated, it is rightly said: "It is appropriate in both ways."

4. *ajādyataṣṭāp* (Pāṇini 4.1.4). [The rule states: "From that which begins with a vowel other than *a*, and from that which ends in *a*. This means "from that which ends in the vowel *a*. Now, why is it not understood as a reference to the word-form itself—as in "from words ending in the word *ac*, such as *śarat* and *darat*"? Because of the [subsequent] indicative mark (*liṅga*). What [is that mark]?

What is the indicator (*liṅga*)? It is the fact that rules such as *tadādyācikhyāsāyām* (P. 2.4.21) and *yakapūrvāyāḥ* (P. 7.3.46) provide such indications; for if [the letter *p*] were taken as referring to its own form (*svarūpa*), those [rules] would not be possible. [The statement] "the letter *p* is for the purpose of a general reference" [is made] because, in the absence of [the letter *p*], [the rule] *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* (P. 4.1.1) would not apply.
Otherwise, there would be no inclusion of this [suffix] in the form *hi*. "The letter *ṭ* is for the purpose of preventing the obstruction of general inclusion" (so it is said).

For if the letter *ṭ* were absent, then according to the rule "when a suffix with one indicatory letter (*ekānubandhaka*) is mentioned, a suffix with two indicatory letters (*dvy-anubandhaka*) is not included" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 52), there would be the inclusion of only *ṭāp*, and not of *ḍāp* and *cāp*.

Because it involves a connection with two [factors]. [The example is] "śubhaṃyāḥ kīlālapāḥ" (those who go for the auspicious, those who drink the sweet liquid). The suffix *vic* is applied by the rule "anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante" (Pāṇini 3.2.75). What would happen, however, if *ṭāp* were also applied here? To this he says: "halṅyābhyaḥ," etc.

Regarding "characterized by genus" (*jātilakṣaṇe*): this refers to [the rule] *jāter astrīviṣayādayopadhāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.63). Regarding "characterized by connection with a male" (*puṃyogalakṣaṇe*): this refers to [the rule] *puṃyogād ākhyāyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.48). Regarding "characterized by having 'flower' or 'fruit' as the final member of the compound" (*puṣpaphalottarapadalakṣaṇe*): this refers to [the rule] *puṣpaphalottarapadāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.64).
"From [words ending in] *pakva*, *karṇa*, *parṇa*, *puṣpa*, *phala*, *mūla*, and *vāla* as the final members [of a compound]" (4.1.64);
"in the sense of a mark of age" (*vayolakṣaṇe*); "in the first stage of life" (*vayasi prathame*) (4.1.20); "in the sense of a mark" (*ṭillakṣaṇe*);
"after [stems ending in] *ṭi*, *ḍha*, *āṇ*, or *añ*" (4.1.42).

"Also *śūdrā* when not preceded by *amahat*," and so forth. Now, one might object: "Since [the rule] *āmanmahataḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.46) applies here, there ought to be a substitution of *ā*; therefore, it should have been stated as *amahāpūrva*.

This is not so; for that substitution of *ā* is prescribed when the word is used in its primary sense (*arthapradhāna*), whereas this [word *śūdrā*] is used primarily as a formal expression (*śabdapradhāna*).

That which has "mahat" as its prior member is called *mahatpūrvā*. [The rule] "there is a prohibition for that which has *mahat* as its prior member" explains the meaning of *amahatpūrvā*. Here too, the word *jāti* (genus) is connected; thus, the prohibition applies to a word denoting a genus. Let it not be so here: *mahatī śūdrā* (a great Śūdra woman).

Regarding the term *mahāśūdrā*: here, the word *śūdra* as the final member of the compound refers to the [social] caste (*jāti*), not the collective form consisting of the two words *mahatī-śūdrā*. But how is it that the application of the [prohibition] is obtained for a word preceded by *mahat*, such that a prohibition is stated when it is said "regarding the caste"? To this he says: "The word *mahāśūdra*..."
[The word *mahāśūdra*] expresses the name of a specific class (*jāti*) among the Ābhīras. For it is the entire composite form that denotes the genus;

for this very reason, in the form *mahāśūdrī*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *jāter astrīviṣayād ayopadhāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.63). [Objection: Even so, there is no possibility of the application of the suffix *ṭāp*, because the suffix is added to the word *śūdra*.
To the question, "How does [the suffix] arise from *mahāśūdra*?", he says: "In that case, there is no rule of inclusion of what ends with that (*tadantavidhi*)," and so forth.

To the question, "How could there be a rule of inclusion of what ends with that?"—he thinks: "Not at all; for there is a prohibition of the rule of inclusion of what ends with that when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is accompanied by a suffix that causes its own inclusion" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 89).

"Ṭhatidhīvarī" and "ṭhatipīvarī. [These are derived] from the roots *dhā* and *pā* with the suffix *kvun* according to Pāṇini 3.2.74 (*āto maninkvanivvanipaśca*), and the substitution of *ī* for the vowel by the rule 6.4.66 (*ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām hali*). [Thus, they mean] "one who has surpassed the wise man" (*dhīvān*) and "one who has surpassed the fat man" (*pīvān*).

The compound is formed by *kugatiprādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18). Since it is made known here that the rule of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies, the suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ* prescribed by *vanorac* (4.1.7) do not occur. If, however, the extension to what ends with that were not made known, then *vanaḥ* would be a reference to the suffix itself; and in the case of a reference to a suffix...

Because of the rule stating, "Since that [element] has been prescribed, there is the inclusion of everything from its beginning to its end" (*pu.pa.vṛ.* 44), these two [suffixes] would apply only here— namely, *dhīvarī* and *pīvarī*; however, they would not apply in cases such as *atidhīvarī*,
*atipīvarī*, *atibhavatī*, or *atimahatī*.

The word *bhavat* alone is listed among the *sarvādi* group, while *mahat* is listed in the *gaurādi* group; if this indicator (*jñāpaka*) did not exist, the feminine suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ*— which are prescribed by the rules for stems ending in an *ugit* vowel and those beginning with *gau-* respectively— would apply only to the words *bhavat* and *mahat* themselves.
However, in the cases of *atibhavatī* and *atimahatī*, these two [suffixes] would not occur; yet, when there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*), they do occur.

If this is so, then in the case of *pañcājī*—the collective compound of five goats—the suffix *ṭāp* would also apply to the *dvigu* by means of the rule for "that which ends in" (*tadantavidhi*). This is not a fault, because [the application of *ṭāp*] is governed by the rule "after words beginning with *aja* when [denoting] the feminine."

We shall provide a qualification: since the genitive case in "ajādyataḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.4) is used, the connection must be made in this way—that is, "for that which is feminine among those beginning with 'ajā'," or "for that femininity which resides by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) in the meaning expressed by words beginning with 'ajā', there [is] the suffix *ṭāp*. And it is not...

In the word *pañcājī*, when the meaning of the word *ajā* (goat) is intended to be expressed, femininity (*strītva*) is inherent; however, what is actually being expressed is the collective aggregate (*samāhāra*). [Examples include] *pūrvāpahāṇā* and *aparāpahāṇā*. This is because [the suffix] *-i* is applied by the rule *ṭit*, since it ends in the suffix *lyuṭ*. *Kaka*.

Regarding the term "prākpuṣpā": those which face forward (prāñcanti) are *prāñci*; [the suffix] *kvin* is applied by the rule "ṛtvigdadhṛk... (Pāṇini 3.2.59). That which has flowers facing forward (*prāñci*) is *prākpuṣpā*.

5. *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* (Pāṇini 4.1.5). [The commentary states: "The letter *ṅ* in *ṅīp* is for the purpose of general reference. For if that were not present, in the rule *ṅy-āpprātipadikāt* (4.1.1), the mention of *ṅī* would only include *ṅīṣ* and *ṅīn*.
It would be so; [but] not of the suffix *ṅīp*.
6. *ugitaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.6).

Regarding the phrase *yathākathaṃcit*: "in whatever manner possible. Whether it is a phoneme (*varṇa*) that is *ugit*, or a suffix (*pratyaya*), or even a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), in every case [the designation applies].

"Wherever any one of these occurs, that word-form ending in *u* or *i* is [the subject]"— by this, he shows that the qualification applies to the word-form ending in *u* or *i*, and not to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). If it were a qualification of the nominal stem alone, it would apply only in cases such as *bhavatī* and *mahatī*.

However, [the designation *ugit*] would not apply in the case of *arvatī*, because by the rule "ṭharvaṇastrasāvanañaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.127), the replacement of the letter *n* with *tr* has been performed; thus, it is only the phoneme *t* that is *ugit*, not the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Furthermore, it would not apply in the case of *gomatī*, for here too it is only the suffix *matup* that is *ugit*, not [the stem].

The term is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*); therefore, the intention is that it is appropriate for it to qualify the word *ugit* itself. And since that form of the word *ugit* is the qualifier of the nominal stem, and a rule involving "that which ends in" (*tadanta*) applies by means of a qualifier, he says: "from that which ends in that," and so forth. If...

If it were the case that the feminine suffix *ṅīp* occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in a vowel (*u*, *i*, or *ṛ*) denoted by the term *ugit*, then the form *bhavatī* would not be established; for in this instance, there is no nominal stem ending in a vowel denoted by *ugit*, since there exists no other nominal stem ending in *ugit* than the one ending in the word *bhavat*. [Response: This is not so.

This is a fault; [the desired form] will result from that which ends in [the suffix], by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). But is it not the case that, according to the rule "the principle of behaving like that which possesses a designation does not apply when [the element] is not a nominal stem" (*vyapadeśivadbhāvo 'prātipadikena*), this principle of behaving like that which possesses a designation should not apply here? This is not so; for [the term] *ugit*...
It is not merely the mention of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*); rather, it is the mention of both nominal stems and non-nominal stems,
because the term *ugit* is understood to include both vowels and suffixes— as in the examples *pacantī* and *yajantī*,
where the feminine suffix *ṅīp* follows a present participle ending in *śatṛ*.
"The prohibition [applies] to a root ending in an *ugit* vowel"—this is the remainder of the statement; it means that the application [of the rule] is being established.
"And there must be an addition for the root *añc*"—the meaning is that the suffix *ṅīp* must be prescribed for the root *añc*. In this regard, the following is the establishment for both cases:

In the sūtra "pādo 'nyatarasyām" (4.1.8), the term "anyatarasyām" will be treated as a separate rule through yogavibhāga; and this [term] is a supplement to all three rules: "ugitaśca" (4.1.6), "vano ra ca" (4.1.7), and "pādo 'nyatarasyām" (4.1.8).

And that is a rule of fixed optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, the suffix *ṅīp* invariably occurs after a nominal stem ending in a vowel other than *u*, as well as after verbal roots and words ending in the suffix *uG*; however, it does not occur at all after any others.
Others, however, provide a different explanation: *ukhāsrat*, *parṇadhvat*.
It is intended merely to express the relationship between the action and its factors (*kriyākārakasambandha*), not femininity; therefore, the suffix *ṅīp* does not occur.
However, the perception of femininity arises through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "strī" (woman). And [the rule] "in the feminine" (*strīyam*)...

In this regard, the position that [the word *prācī*] is in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a feminine noun is established. However, in words such as *prācī*, the feminine gender is intended to be expressed; therefore, the suffix *īkāra* occurs here. For example: *ukhāsrat*, *parṇadhvat*.

[These are derived from the sentences] "he slips out of the pan" (*ukhena sraṃsate*) and "the leaves fall" (*parṇāni dhvaṃsate*), according to the rule "they are seen after other [roots] as well" (*anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante*).

By the rule (3.2.75), the suffix *kvip* is applied; by the rule "it is also seen in other cases" (6.3.137), there is lengthening of the *ukha* portion. In the word *prācī*, the suffix *kvip* is added to the root *añc-* preceded by *pra*;
by the rule "of *ac*" (6.4.138), there is elision of the vowel *a*, and by the rule "before *ca*" (6.3.138), there is lengthening of the prefix.

7. *vano ra ca* | (Pāṇini 4.1.7) The term *vanaḥ* here refers to the inclusion of the two suffixes *kvanip* and *vanip*. Now, [the forms] derived from the roots *vana* and *ṣaṇa* in the sense of "possibility" (Dhātupāṭha 463, 464), and *vanu* in the sense of "requesting" (Dhātupāṭha 1470)—[these are also included].

When the suffix *vic* is applied by the rule *ṭhanyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante* (Pāṇini 3.2.75), the form *vat* is produced; why is that not accepted [as the basis for the term *vati*]? If *vij* were seen after those two [roots], it would be so, but it is not seen; because of non-usage (*anabhidhānāt*). [The word] *śarvarī*: [from the root] *śṛ* in the sense of "killing" (Dhātupāṭha 1488).
The suffix *vanip* is applied by the rule *ṭhanyebhyo'pi dṛśyante* (Pāṇini 3.2.75); there is *guṇa* substitution and the replacement of *v* with *r*.
Thus, we have "paralokadṛśvarī. The suffix *kvanip* is applied to the root *dṛś* by that same rule (3.2.75).
Regarding the statement "vanona haśaḥ," the word "somewhere" (*kvacid*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. This refers to the case where *vanip* follows *haś*.

The suffix *ṅīp* and the substitution of *repha* (*ra*) at the end do not occur after a nominal stem ending in a verbal root that has been prescribed with the suffix *kvanip*. For example: *sahayudhvā*.
[Root] *yudh* (DhP 1173) "to fight"; [affix] *kvanip* after *dṛś* (Pāṇini 3.2.94); [context] *rājani*...

By the rules *yudhikṛñaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.95) and *sahe ca* (3.2.96), the suffix *kvanip* is applied; then, by *nopadhāyāḥ* (6.4.7) and *sarvanāmasthāne* (6.4.8), the vowel is lengthened, and finally, by *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* (8.2.7), the final *n* is elided. In some instances, however, this prohibition does not apply at all.

In *śarvarī*, the suffix *vanip* follows a root ending in *r* that has a penultimate *ha*-class consonant (*haś*); in *avāvarī*, although *vanip* is prescribed here as well after a root ending in *ha*, the prohibition nevertheless does not apply. From the root *ṭhuṇṛ* (DhP 4.54) meaning "to remove," *vanip* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.75: "It is seen [to occur] after other [roots] as well."

The substitution of *ā* [for the final vowel] occurs by the rule *ṭhviḍÂvanoranunāsikasyāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.41), followed by the substitution of *ava*. The printed reading—"*na ca vano na haśa ityeva vaktavyam kartavyam*"—is incorrect;
for it ought to be stated that "*pādaḥ anyatarasyām*" (Pāṇini 4.1.8) [applies here].

Thus, the mention of "within" (*antarasyām*) is also a supplement (*śeṣa*) to this rule (*yoga*). And that [mention] is understood as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*); therefore, where the suffixes *ṅīp* and *repha* (the *ṝ* vowel) are not desired, they will not occur.
8. *pādo 'nyatarasyām* (4.1.8).

It is stated that "the word *pāda*, which has the samāsānta suffix [applied], is what is being indicated here. Now, from the root *pad* (meaning "to go," DhP 1169), with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), [the form *pāda* is derived] according to the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*.

When the *kvip* suffix is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.2.178], the form *yat-pād* is produced. Why is it not understood that this very form is what is being referred to? It would be so understood if the *kvip* were seen after the root *pādayati*, but it is not seen; for there is no such linguistic usage (*anabhidhānāt*). Thus we have "dvipāt" and "dvipadī."

The term *dvipadī* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has two feet. While the rule *pādasya lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.138) is in force, the elision of the vowel *a* occurs by the rule *saṃkhyāsupūrvasya* (5.4.140), and the substitution of *pad* for *pāda* occurs by the rule *pādaḥ pat* (6.4.130).

9. *ṭābṛci* | (4.1.9) [The commentary states: "The mention of *ṛci* is a specification of the thing to be designated (*abhidheya-nirdeśa*). This refutes the suspicion that it might be a specification of the scope (*viṣaya-nirdeśa*). For if it were a specification of the scope, then [the suffix] would apply to the subject matter of the *ṛk*, namely, that which is in the *ṛk*-text (*ṛggrantha*).

The meaning would be that the suffix *ṭāp* occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in the word *pāc*; in that case, it would apply only to the *Ṛgveda* and not elsewhere. However, the intention is that when the object denoted (*abhidheya*) is specified, the suffix applies everywhere.

10. *na ṣaṭsvasrādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.10). "Whatever [suffix] would otherwise apply [after these stems], all of that is prohibited"—this was stated in order to dispel the doubt that this prohibition applies specifically to the suffix *ṅīp* because it is the one immediately preceding. But surely, in this case...

In the rule *ṭābṛci* (Pāṇini 4.1.9), it is only *ṭāp* that is immediate; therefore, how can there be immediacy for *ṅīp*? Because [the former] is not marked with svarita. It is more appropriate that this *ṭāp* follows immediately after *ṅīp*. But surely, those termed *ṣaṭ* are number-words (*saṃkhyāśabda*), and number-words convey only the differentiation of a substance (*dravya*), not [the substance itself].

Femininity (*strītva*) exists; however, that cognition of its femininity arises through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with another word, and the position that it is coreferential with a feminine noun is not maintained in the rule *striyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.3); thus, the application of a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) follows from those [words] alone.

Is the negation "it does not exist" meaningless? This is not so; for number is a quality (*guṇa*), since it is recited in the Vaiśeṣika *Guṇasūtra* (1.1.6): "Number, dimensions, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction. And for words denoting qualities, the gender and number [of the word] follow from their substratum (*āśrayataḥ*).
[The suffixes] occur as follows: *śuklā śāṭī* (a white cloth), *śuklaḥ kambalaḥ* (a white blanket), *śuklaṃ vastram* (a white garment);

*śuklaḥ*, *śuklau*, *śuklāḥ*. That being the case, if there were a prohibition [of the feminine suffix], then just as the feminine suffix occurs after words such as *śukla*, it would also occur after those designated by the technical term *ṣat* (the numerals one through five), as in *pañca* (five).

Regarding *brāhmaṇī*: by the rule *ṣaḍbhyo luk* (Pāṇini 7.1.22), there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *jas*. Regarding *svasā*: by the rule *anaṅ sau* (7.1.93), the substitution of *anaṅ* occurs;
as before, there is lengthening by the rule *nopadhāyāḥ* (6.4.7).
The words *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* are also recited among the *svasṛ*-type stems; for what purpose is their inclusion there?

To the extent that, when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) follows, [the forms] *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* must occur by the rule "for *tri* and *catur*, *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* in the feminine" (Pāṇini 7.2.99), in that case, if these two were to serve as the cause for the suffix *ṅīp*— which is characterized by ending in the vowel *ṛ*— the immediate sequence with the case-ending would be obstructed by them.
And this has been stated [in the Vyāḍiparibhāṣā]: "A rule characterized by a combination [of causes] is not the cause for the destruction of that combination.

Therefore, since the feminine suffix *ṅīp* will not occur by the very maxim of "a rule characterized by a combination," what is the purpose of the prohibition? If this is so, then this [prohibition] indicates that this maxim is not universal (*anitya*). Consequently, *yā*...

Thus it is established. For here too, in the case of the case-ending (*vibhakti*), the substitution of *at* for *tyad* and so forth would not be the cause for the feminine suffix *ṭāp*; for if *ṭāp* were present, the immediate sequence with the case-ending would be obstructed.
However, by virtue of the non-universality (*anityatva*) of this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), *ṭāp* does indeed occur.

Regarding the passage beginning with "of the six designations" (*ṣaṭsaṃjñānām*), etc.: in cases such as *pañcabrāhmaṇyaḥ*, since the rule "an operation applies to what is immediately preceding, or there is a prohibition thereof" (*avantarasya vidhirbhavati pratiṣedho vā*) results in the prohibition of the suffix *ṅīp* that is immediately preceding, the *nakāra* [is applied] by the rule "the elision of *na* at the end of a nominal stem" (*nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*).

When the state of ending in a *satya*-suffix has been elided, why should the suffix *ṭāp* not arise? It would indeed arise, because its cause is present. If it is argued that it would not arise because the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), this is not so; for [the rule] states: "The elision of *n* is [treated as non-existent] in the application of case-endings (*sup*), accent (*svara*), technical names (*saṃjñā*), and the rules for *tuṅ* and *kṛt* suffixes" (Pāṇini 6.4.24).

Thus, the non-validity (*asiddhatva*) of the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is stated only with respect to those rules specifically enumerated therein. And since the rule for the suffix *ṭāp* is not enumerated there, how could the non-validity of the elision of *n* apply there?
Demonstrating that the rule for *ṭāp* is indeed enumerated there as well, he says: "Because of the pratyāhāra."

And so forth. The term *cāp* indicates the *pakāra* belonging to *cāp*. This is what is meant by the expression *sub*: therein, the *pratyāhāra* is not taken by means of the *pakāra* belonging to *sup* (the seventh case plural), but rather by means of the *pakāra* belonging to *cāp* [in the rule] *ṭhyaṅśca cāp* (Pāṇini 4.1.74).

Therefore, the rule for *ṭāp* is indeed a "good" rule (*subvidhi*), since *ṭāp* is also included within the pratyāhāra [ṭā]. Consequently, even in the application of the rule for *ṭāp*, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) must be treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), and thus everything desired is established. It is indeed established. [As stated: "But there is a fault in the case of *it* and *atve*."

The compound *bahucarmā* is a *bahuvrīhi* meaning "in this city there are many hides" (*carmaṇi*). The suffix *kap* is applied by the rule *śeṣādvibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 5.4.154), followed by the feminine suffix *ṭāp* and the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*). Now, one might expect that the rule *pratyayasthātkāt* (Pāṇini 7.3.44) would apply here to produce the desired form *bahucarmikā* by substituting *ī* for the *a* of *ṭāp*; however, that is not the case.

[The rule] applies, for here the vowel *a* does not precede *kā*; a compound ending in all case-terminations (*sarvavibhaktyanta*) has been resorted to for the sake of establishing its validity. "A rule concerning *sup*" (*subvidhi*) means either a rule regarding *sup*, or a rule [prescribed] in the presence of *sup*. And if *ṭāp* were also a *sup*, then [the rule] would apply there as well.

If it were argued that "being situated elsewhere" (*paratrāvasthita*) is what is meant by [the term *para*], then that too would be a rule for after a case-ending (*sup*), since it is a rule prescribed when a *sup* follows. Consequently, even in that case, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would be treated as non-existent (*asiddha*). Furthermore, the formation of the pratyāhāra *cāp* would be improper. Therefore, it is said: "Therefore, not both. Because it is so...

In the case of *cāp*, there is a fault when it is combined with *pratyāhāra*; therefore, both *ṭāp* and *ṅīp* are prohibited and do not occur. Why, then, is the meaning "in the feminine" (*striyām*) required here?
