Because regarding this meaning, it is stated that [the suffix] occurs; and since both *ṅīp* and *ṭāp* are prescribed for the sense of the feminine (*stryarthe*), both of them indeed occur.

11. *manaḥ* | (4.1.11) Regarding the forms *vāmā* and *pāmā*: from the roots *dā* (to give) and *pā* (to drink), the suffix *manin* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.74], *āto maninkvanibvanipaśca*. As before, the lengthening of the vowel of the penultimate syllable is applied by [Pāṇini 6.4.7], *nopadhāyāḥ*. Now...

*samīmā*, *sīmānau*, *sīmānaḥ*; *atimahimā*, *atimahimānau*, *atimahimānaḥ*—in these cases, why is there a prohibition? For the term *man-* in the rule is a reference to the meaningful suffix *man-*. It is not the case that, as in *dāmā* or *pāmā*, the suffix *man-* possesses meaning through the sense of the derivative suffix (*pratyaya-artha*), in the same way [as here].

In such expressions as *sīmā*, there is no meaningfulness with respect to any referent whatsoever; for the word *sīmā* is an underived nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and its meaningfulness belongs to that [stem] alone, not to the *manas* which constitutes its constituent part. Likewise, in the expression *atimahiman*, the *manas* likewise possesses no meaningfulness.

For—when one intends to express the meaning "the state of being great" (*mahato bhāvaḥ*), the suffix *imanij* is prescribed after the word *maha-* by the rule *pṛthvādibhya imanic* (Pāṇini 5.1.122). In that case, the meaningfulness belongs to *imanij* as a whole, not to its constituent part *man*.
Therefore, he says: "The mentions of *ani*, *as*, and *man*" (*aninasmangrahaṇāni*), and so forth. This is the statement [of the Vārttika].
When the author of the Vārttika uses the terms *an*, *in*, *as*, and *man* in his citations, the paribhāṣā "the mention of a meaningful element" (*arthavadgrahaṇaparibhāṣā*) does not apply.
Consequently, there is the inclusion of even those that are meaningless; and by these [terms], both the meaningless and the meaningful are included.
Thus it is stated that the designation of the final element (tadanta-vidhi) occurs; consequently, the prohibition is established even in cases such as *sīmā* and *atimahimā*.

12. *Ano bahuvrīhiḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.12). [The commentary states: "In this context, *anupadhālopa-bahuvrīhi* is the example. But how is this obtained, since no specific distinction is mentioned here? To this he says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "ṭhupadhālopino hi": since [Pāṇini] will state an option for a *bahuvrīhi* compound whose penultimate vowel is elided in the rule "ṭhana upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām" (4.1.28), therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), this [present rule] provides scope for a *bahuvrīhi* compound whose penultimate vowel is not elided.

Thus; and its example is "suparvā" and so forth. [The analysis is: "one whose joints (*parvan*) are beautiful" or "one whose hide (*carman*) is beautiful"—this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. And here, by the rule "na saṃyogādvamantāt" (Pāṇini 6.4.137), the elision of the suffix *aC* does not occur.

Regarding "ṭhatirājī": this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound formed by the rule "kugatiprādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.2.18), according to the Vārttika "atyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe dvitīyayā" (Vārttika 91), which prescribes that words such as *ati* form compounds with a word in the accusative case in the sense of "having surpassed" (*krānta*) and so forth.

13. *ḍāb ubhābhyām anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.13). Here, the purpose of including the term *anyatarasyām* might be either that, when both [the suffix *ḍāp* and the prohibition] are set aside, a prohibition should also optionally apply; or else, that when both the suffix *ḍāp* and the prohibition are set aside, [the feminine suffix *ṭāp* should apply].

Or is it so that the suffix *ṅīp* might also occur? Regarding this, the first [alternative] is untenable; for both the suffix *ḍāp* and the prohibition are stated, and both will occur by the force of the explicit statement (*vacana*).
The second [alternative] is also untenable; for by the mention of the option (*anyatarasyām*), [the rule would apply] either to those not having a penultimate vowel-elision (*anupadhālopin*)...

Is the suffix *ṅīp* prescribed for the *bahuvrīhi* optionally, or for that which has a penultimate vowel elision (*upadhālopin*)? Of these, the first alternative is not tenable; for if the suffix *ṅīp* were prescribed here even in the case of that which does not have a penultimate vowel elision, the statement of the prohibition would be purposeless. The second [alternative] also...

This is not tenable, because the suffix *ṅīp* will be prescribed optionally by the specific rule *ṭhan upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.28). Nor is it appropriate to assume that the mention of *anyatarasyām* here is for the purpose of performing the mention of *anyatarasyām* in that [other rule], thinking "we shall not employ that *anyatarasyām*"; for that [mention] is indeed necessary.

This must be done so that, when the *ṅīp* suffix is excluded for words whose penultimate vowel is elided (*upadhālopinaḥ*), both the *ḍāp* suffix and its prohibition may apply— as in *bahurājñyau*, *bahurājānau*, and *bahurāje*. Otherwise,
the *ḍāp* suffix and its prohibition would find their scope only in cases like *suparvā* and others where the penultimate vowel is not elided.

Because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], the suffix *ṅīp* would sublate [the application of *ṅīṣ*]. Therefore, even though it will be stated later, the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* must indeed be made;
having kept all of this in mind, he asks:
"What is the purpose of including *anyatarasyām*? The sense is that it is redundant. [He then cites] "In a *bahuvrīhi*," etc., and "of *van*, *ra*..."

The mention of *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") in this context is redundant; for even regarding the grammatical operation prescribed by the rule *ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.7), there should already be an option within the *bahuvrīhi* compound. Whatever is applicable must be presented as an alternative. [In this case,] the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the *repha* (*ra*) are not applicable, whereas the suffix *ṭhan* is.

Because of the prohibition [stated] in *Pāṇini* 4.1.12, "of a *bahuvrīhi*," the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") must be employed for the sake of prescribing that [suffix]. How so, with respect to *anyatarasyām*?
A split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is made here; in that [first part], the mention of *bahuvrīhi* is carried over, and [the suffix] *van* is [prescribed]. *Ra*...

And the rule *ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.7) is also applied here by the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*). By this, after a Bahuvrīhi compound ending in *van*, the suffix *ṅīp* is optionally obtained, as well as the replacement of the final syllable with *repha* (the sound *r*). Thus, forms such as *bahupīvā*, *bahudhīvā*, *bahupīvarī*, and *bahudhīvarī* are established.

Others, however, say: because of the mention of "either one" (*anyatarasyām*) from among the two [options], the suffixes *ṅīp* and *repha* are obtained after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *van*. In the rule "from both" (*ubhābhyām*, 4.1.13), this is not a fifth case (*pañcamī*); what then? It is a third case (*tṛtīyā*).

When explaining [the rule], it must be made clear by the speaker that in a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *vān*, femininity is to be conveyed by both suffixes—namely, by the feminine marker *ṅīp* and by the *repha* (*ra*). But is not the purpose of including the mention of "both" in the rule *ḍāb ubhābhyām* simply for the sake of the nominal stems ending in *man* and those ending in *an*? It is thus.
He thinks: "Precisely because of the *svarita* accent, the suffix is obtained from both [roots] even without the statement 'from both' (*ubhābhyām*, Pāṇini 4.1.13)."

14. *anupasarjanāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.14). Here, does this [sūtra] establish a rule (*vidhi*) for what follows—meaning that *ṅīp* and other suffixes occur after what is not an *upasarjana* (i.e., after something other than an *upasarjana*)? Or is it a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*)?

Or [one might ask]: "Does it not occur after an *upasarjana*? In that case, if the first alternative were adopted, the form "kukkuṭīpādaḥ" would not be established; for the first member of the compound would be an *upasarjana*.
Its status as an *upasarjana* follows from its being introduced in the nominative case in the rule for compounds, "ṣaṣṭhī" (Pāṇini 2.2.8). This applies to the word "kukkuṭī" as well.

It would not be established; for the *pradhāna* (the principal) is that which is not subordinate (*anupasarjana*), and here the genus (*jāti*) is not the principal. Indeed, something becomes principal only in relation to what is non-principal, and there is nothing here that is non-principal in relation to which the genus could possess primacy. Therefore, this position favoring [the word as] an injunction (*vidhi*) is flawed.

Considering this, he adopts the position of prohibition and says: "In the subsequent sūtras, he effects a prohibition regarding the *upasarjana*. [The example is] *kurucarī*. From the analysis *kuruṣu carati*, the suffix *ṭa* is applied by the rule *careṣṭaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.16). Then, by the rule *upapadam atiṅ* (Pāṇini 2.2.19), there is a *tatpuruṣa* compound.

Because the latter member (*uttarapada*) is predominant in this [compound] and because it is not specified by the first case (*aprathamānirdiṣṭa*), the word *cara* is not an *upasarjana* here according to the rules of compound formation (*samāsa-śāstra*). Thus, [the example] is "bahukurucarā," meaning "in which there are many Kurucaras.

Because this [compound] has the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) as its predominant element and is specified by the first case, [it is not an *upasarjana*] according to the technical treatise.

In this context, within compound words, the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) is [the first member]. Regarding the suffix *ṅīṣ*, the *Kāśikā* states: "The suffix *ṅīṣ* after a genus-word" (*jāterṅīṣ*), according to the rule: "The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after a genus-word that does not denote a female and has a non-*y*-vowel as its penultimate letter" (Pāṇini 4.1.63). The example "bahukukkuṭā" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; here too, as before, it is a word denoting a genus.
[It is] a subordinate element (*upasarjana*).
But surely, in the case of *bahukurucarā*, it is the entire aggregate (*samudāya*) that functions in the feminine gender, not the individual member; and the aggregate does not end in *ṭi*.
What then? It is the individual member. In that case, by what [rule] is the *īkāra* prescribed for that which ends in *ṭi*?

Furthermore, would it not follow that [the suffix] does not apply after a collective compound? Even in the case of *bahukukkuṭī*, the collective compound refers to a female [animal], not its individual parts. Moreover, the collective compound does not denote a genus (*jāti*); what then?
It is the individual part that does. In that case, how could a suffix prescribed after that which denotes a genus be applied to that which does not denote a genus?

Thinking that this [rule] is stated for the purpose of prohibiting [the application of the suffix] from a collective whole (*samudāya*), he asks: "How? and so forth. The response is: "By the rule of *tadantavidhi*. In this regard, one might object:
"The rule of *tadantavidhi* is prohibited when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is accompanied by a suffix that itself possesses a suffix" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 89).

Therefore he says: "And it has been made known," and so forth. In the rule *śūdrā cāmahatpūrvā jātiḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.4), by the phrase "not preceded by a word meaning 'great'" (*amahatpūrvā*), it is made known that in this section the rule of extension to the end of a compound (*tadantavidhi*) applies. "And thus" (*tathā ca*) means: such being the case.

Since it has been indicated previously that the rule of "specification by the final element" (*tadantavidhi*) exists in this section, and since this sūtra prohibits *tadantavidhi* only when [the word] is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), and not when it is not a subordinate member—
it being the case that *tadantavidhi* certainly occurs with respect to the principal member— therefore, [the form] *kumbhakārī* [is established].

The form *nagarakārī* is established. For in that case, the word *kāra*, ending in the suffix *aṇ*, is the principal member; consequently, from the compound ending in that [suffix], the feminine suffix *ī* would indeed occur by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15). Now, one might object: in the term *aṇ* [within the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*], there is a reference to a *kṛt*-derived suffix; and therefore, in a reference to a *kṛt*...

By this very *paribhāṣā*, "The inclusion of even that which has a word denoting a direction (*gati*) or an agent (*kāraka*) as its prior member" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 126), the long vowel *ī* is established after the word *kumbhakāra* because it ends in *kāra*;
therefore, this [example] is not a purpose for making known the rule of "specification by the final letter" (*tadantavidhi*). To this, he says: "And not," and so forth.

How is it not so? He says: "The *aṇ* suffix is also included [as a *kṛt*]. It is also understood here; otherwise, the form *āpagavī* would not be established. Therefore, this is not a mention of only *kṛt*-suffixes, but rather a mention of both *kṛt* and *akṛt* suffixes. In that case, if the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) were not indicated, then [the *aṇ*] would be... [the form *āpagavī* would not be established].

The mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*) is for the purpose of applying the rule: "When there is the mention of an affix, the term refers to that which begins with the element from which that affix is prescribed and ends with the affix itself" (Paribhāṣenduśekhara 44).

Consequently, [the designation *gāp*] would apply here—*aupagavī*—but it would not apply here—*kumbhakārī*. For in this case, the affix *aṇ* is prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*), and that which ends in it is feminine.

It does not apply, because the word *kāra* is never used in that sense alone; or, that feminine form which exists [in the sense of "doing"] is a compound (*upapada*), and no suffix has been prescribed after it. However, once the rule of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) is made known, the long vowel *ī* is established even from words ending in *kāra*.
15. *ṭiḍḍhāṇañdvayasajdaghnañmātractayapṭhakṭhañkañakvarapkhyunām* (Pāṇini 4.1.15).
[The word] *sarvatra* [is understood] in the section concerning feminine suffixes (*strī-prakaraṇa*). But is it not the case that [the rule] *patyurno yajñasaṃyoge* (4.1.33) [also applies]?

In rules such as *ṭhito manuṣyajāteḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.65), [the word *ataḥ*] does not carry over, because since that [word *ataḥ*] is impossible there, its qualification is not tenable; thus he says, "when that exists," and so forth. A qualification applies where it is possible, but where it is not possible...
In that case, [the rule] follows for the sake of the subsequent meaning. Why does it not apply here in the word *pacamānā*?

The intention is that since the affix *śānac* possesses the property of being *ṭit* (having *ṭ* as its indicatory letter) by virtue of *sthānivadbhāva*, the suffix *ṅīp* ought to occur even after a stem ending in that. [The answer is: "Because the present tense marker (*laṭ*) has two indicatory letters (*dvyanubandhakatvāt*). By that...

By means of this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), "In the case of the inclusion of that which has one indicatory letter (*ekānubandhaka*), there is no inclusion of that which has two indicatory letters (*dvyanubandhaka*)" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 52), he shows that there is no inclusion of *laṭ* here; for its second indicatory letter is the vowel *a*.

"How is it [applied] in the case of *lyuḍ* and the others?"—the remainder of the sentence is "the vowel *ī* occurs. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), rules such as *gāpoṣṭak* (Pāṇini 3.2.8) are included.
Since *lyuḍ* and the others also possess two indicatory letters (*anubandha*), they ought to be included by the mention of *ṭit*; therefore, the suffix *ṅīp* does not apply to those ending in them.
If that were the case, then the designation *kṛt* would not apply, and consequently, forms such as *sāman-gīti* would not be established. [The author says:

"By virtue of the purpose of making them *ṭit*. If even those [suffixes] were not included by the mention of *ṭit*, then the act of making them *ṭit* would be useless, since no other purpose is possible. Therefore...

Even though there is the status of being a double-cause (dvyanubandhaka), there is no fault because the *lyuṭ* suffixes and others are understood by virtue of the power of the marker *ṭ*. If it is argued that the present tense (*laṭ*) should likewise be included by virtue of the power of its *ṭ* marker, he says: "In other cases [the marker ṭ is for the sake of the feminine suffix]," for in the case of *laṭ*, the purpose of the *ṭ* marker is [to form the feminine] by the rule "ṭita ātmanepadānāṃ ṭere" (Pāṇini 3.4.79).

The substitution of *e* for the *ṭi* of the ātmanepada endings [is] the result [of the rule] "ātmanepadānāṃ ṭere" (Pāṇini 3.4.79). Therefore, even if there were no inclusion [of the ātmanepada endings], the employment of the *ṭi*-marker would not be rendered useless.
Consequently, by the force of the *ṭi*-marker, forms such as *lyuṭ* are included; thus, there is no fault. This also applies to the present tense (*laṭ*).
In that case, one might argue that it must be understood as referring to the *laṭ* by the very power of the inclusion of the marker *ṭ*; to this he says: "But elsewhere [the marker] *ṭ*.

For in the case of *laṭ*, the purpose of applying the marker *ṭ* is the substitution of *e* for the *ṭi* of the *ātmanepada* endings, according to the rule *ṭita ātmanepadānāṃ ṭere* (Pāṇini 3.4.79). Therefore, even though this [present context] does not constitute a reference to that [marker *ṭ*], nevertheless, it is not at all [the case that the *laṭ* is meant].
Otherwise, the purpose of the marker *ṭ* would be rendered useless. Therefore, since the marker *ṭ* has already served its purpose, it is incorrect to include this [root] under its heading.
[In the example] "the science has been studied" (*paṭhitā vidyā*), the question "how? (*katham*) is also connected here. For, regarding the augment *iṭ*—
Since the suffix (*pratyaya*) possesses the *ṭi*-designation because it is a portion of the suffix, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* ought to apply;

how then does this form *paṭhitā* arise? [The answer is: "The *ṭi*-designation of the augment (*āgama*) is not the cause [for the application of *ṅīp*]. Because the subject under discussion is the suffix, it is understood that *ṅīp* [is what would apply]. How so?
It is understood that this [suffix] is *animitta* (not a cause for grammatical operations); thus he says: "ṭyu-ṭyuḷu-lau," and so forth.

Since the form would already be established by the addition of the augment *ṭi* in the case of *tuḍ*, the fact that the suffixes *ṭyu* and *ṭyuḷu* are prescribed again in the rule "sāyaṃ-ciraṃ-prāhṇe... (Pāṇini 4.3.23) as "ṭyu-ṭyuḷu-lau" serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)—that is, it indicates that [the suffixes in question] do not function as causes for grammatical operations.
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule for the feminine (*āgamaṭitvam animittvam*). For example:

*soparṇeyī*, *vainateyī*. [These are derived] from the word *suparṇī*, which ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* denoting a genus (*jāti*), and from the word *vinatā*, which ends in the suffix *ṭāp*. [This is established] by the rule *strībhyo...*.

The suffix *ḍhak* [is applied] by [Pāṇini 4.1.120]. The substitution of *ey* [for *a*] occurs by means of the rule [Pāṇini 7.1.2], "āyanādi. Now, one might object: since it is a principle that "when a term without an *anubandha* is mentioned, a term with an *anubandha* is not included," there should be no application here because of the mention of *ḍhak*. To this, he says: "the word *ḍha* is without an *anubandha*," and so forth. But surely...
And is this [suffix] without a subsequent marker (*niranubandhaka*), as in the rule "ḍha after *sthālī*"? This is not so;
for by its very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*), this [suffix] occurs in the neuter gender. Then there is this [other suffix], by virtue of its inherent nature—as printed in the text:
"ḍha after *sabhā* in the Veda" (Pāṇini 4.4.105)—namely, the suffix *ya*.

Regarding [the rule] *ṭhḍhaścchandasi* (Pāṇini 4.4.106), this word also does not occur in the feminine, because the word *sabheyī* is never seen used in the Veda (*chandas*) in the feminine. Therefore, since the word *ḍha* with its marker (*n-anubandhaka*) does not exist in the feminine, the paribhāṣā concerning the "unmarked" (*niranubandhaka*) does not apply here; otherwise, indeed—

Otherwise, the mention of the suffix *ḍha* would be purposeless. Regarding the rule "also when *ṇa* follows": it is stated that whatever operation is performed when *aṇ* follows, that same operation occurs sometimes even when *ṇa* follows, and sometimes it does not. But where, then, does an operation performed when *aṇ* follows also take place when *ṇa* follows?

Regarding words expressing a habitual disposition (*tācchīlika*): for this has been made known in the rule *kārmastācchīlye* (Pāṇini 6.4.172)—namely, that even after the suffix *ṇa*, the grammatical operation prescribed for the suffix *aṇ* takes place. How so?

For the word *kārmā-* is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) intended for the elision of the suffix *ṭi* when expressing a habitual disposition. If the operation prescribed for *aṇ* did not apply even after *ṇa*, [the form *kārmā-* would not be established].

The *nipātana* [the specific grammatical prescription] would be purposeless; for once the suffix *ṇa* is applied by the rule "after words meaning 'umbrella' and the like, the suffix *ṇa* [is added]" (Pāṇini 4.4.62), the elision of the final vowel is already established by the rule "in a *taddhita* suffix, the final vowel of *naḥ* is elided" (6.4.144). It might be argued that it is not established because of the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule "before the suffix *an*" (6.4.167).
If you ask why this is not so: it is because *aṇ* is said to undergo its original form (*prakṛtibhāva*).

In that context, the term *aṇ* is understood to carry over from the rule *ṭhinaṇyanapatye* (Pāṇini 6.4.64). Thus, since it has been indicated that "even when the suffix *ṇa* is used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*), the operation prescribed for *aṇ* takes place," the operation performed for *aṇ* occurs in that very instance.

It occurs [only] in these cases and not elsewhere: *caurī* and *tāpasī*. Because her habit (*śīla*) is thievery (*curā*) and her habit is asceticism (*tapas*), the suffix *ṇa* is applied according to *cchatrādibhyo ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.62). Since the suffix *ṇa* is treated as if it were *aṇ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. [The examples] *dāṇḍā* and *mauṣṭā* mean "one whose weapon is a staff" (*daṇḍaḥ praharaṇam asyāḥ*) and "one whose weapon is a fist" (*muṣṭiḥ praharaṇam asyāḥ*).
In the word *krīḍāyām*, the suffix *ṇa* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.2.57: *tad-asyām praharaṇam*.

Now, why is there not a reference (*pratyāhāra-grahaṇa*) to the entire sequence beginning with the letter *a* of *aṇ* and ending with the letter *ṇa* of *laṇ*? Because of the subsequent mention of *ti* and the other suffixes. For if there were a reference to the entire sequence, those [suffixes] would [be included].
The mention [of the suffix] would be redundant, since [the desired forms] are already established from those ending in *aṇ* alone—as in *ṭhāṬtsī* and *āṬdapānī*.

[In these cases], the suffix *añ* is applied according to *ṭhutsādibhyo'ñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.86), as in "this belongs to a spring (*utsa*)" or "this belongs to a well (*udapāna*). Now, regarding the rule *ṭhśārṅgaravādyaño ṅīn* (Pāṇini 4.1.73):
For what purpose is the word *punaḥ* ("again") used [in the rule], since the desired result is already established by this very [previous] rule?

For that is indeed the same form (*rūpa*) and that is indeed the same accent (*svara*). To illustrate: when the suffix *ṅīn* is present, [the first syllable] becomes udātta by the rule "that which begins with *ñ* or *ṇ* is always [udātta]" (Pāṇini 6.1.197).

Does the same initial udātta accent remain when *utsa*—which is already udātta on the first syllable by the accent of the *ñi*-suffix added after the word ending in *añ*—is followed by the feminine suffix *ṅīp* in the form *autsī*? To this he says: "After *añ* in the sense of *śārṅgarava*, etc.
[Pāṇini 4.1.73]. Since she is the female descendant (gotra) of Bida, [the rule] "from *Bida* and others, the suffix *añ* is applied when not denoting immediate descent" [Pāṇini 4.1.104] applies.

When the suffix *añ* has been applied [by 4.1.104], since that [term] is a genus (*jāti*) according to the rule "the lineage (*gotra*) together with the *caraṇas* [are genera]" (Kāśikāvṛtti 4.1.63), the suffix *ṅīṣ* would apply by the rule "after a genus term that does not denote a feminine and has a non-*y* as its penultimate vowel" (4.1.63). To prevent that, the rule "for *añ* after *śārṅgarava* and so on, there is *ṅīn*" (4.1.73) is stated again.

In this [sūtra], the mention of *añ* is made. If that is so, then the mention of *añ* here need not be made, since by that very [mention] forms such as *autsī* would also be established. This is not the case; for the mention of the genus (*jāti*) follows from [the previous rule] *ṭhitaḥ manuṣyajāteḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.65).

By the rule "ṭhpuṃyogādākhyāyām" (Pāṇini 4.1.48), the suffix *añ* is applied [to form *baida-*]; thus, the wife of a *baida* is called *baidī*. In this case, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is desired to express connection with a male (*puṃyoga*). Therefore, in that context, the mention of "jāti" (generic class) must be understood as being carried over [from the preceding rule]. And while that [mention of *jāti*] is being carried over—

In the case of *āṬtsī*, when the suffix *añ* is applied with the intention of expressing the meaning "this is from a spring (*utsa*)," the long vowel *ī* would not apply there because it is not a genus (*ajāti*). Therefore, the mention of *añ* must indeed be made here as well.
The pronunciation of the indicatory letters (*anubandha*) for *dvayasaC* and the others is for the purpose of including the suffixes themselves.

There are also nominal stems (*prātipadika*) beginning with *dvi*, *as*, and so forth; if the indicatory letter (*anubandha*) were not pronounced, they too would be understood as being included. Furthermore, the word *taya* is the vowel-ending form of the root *tay* from the verbal roots *ṭhaya*, *vaya*, *taya*, *pṇaya*, and *naya* in the sense of "motion" (*gati*). (Dhātupāṭha 474, 485, 479, 480).
Since the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is possible [in this context], the pronunciation of the letter *pakāra* is for the purpose of excluding that [possibility].

This applies to examples such as *ūrudvayasī*. In the sense of "her thigh is the measure" or "her knee is the measure," the suffixes *dvayasaC*, *daghnac*, and *mātrac* are applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.37: *pramāṇe dvayasajdaghnañmātracaḥ*.
Regarding "ṭhpañcatayī": the suffix *tayap* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.42, *saṃkhyāyā avayave tayap*, meaning "that which has five parts.

Regarding "ṭhākṣikī, śālākikī": [the suffix *ṭhak*] is applied by the rule *tena dīvyati* ("he plays with that"). Thus, one who plays with dice (*akṣaiḥ*) is an *ākṣika*, and one who plays with counting-sticks (*śalākābhiḥ*) is a *śālākika*.

By the rule *dīvyati-khanati* (Pāṇini 4.4.2), the suffix *ṭhak* is applied; for the *ṭha*, there is the substitution of *ikā*. Thus we have *lāvaṇikī*. [The derivation is as follows: because salt (*lavaṇa*) is her merchandise (*paṇya*), the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule *lavaṇāt-ṭhañ* (4.4.52). Now, for what purpose is *ṭhak* and *ṭhañ* mentioned separately? Is it not [the case that they could be subsumed]?

One might object that, having set aside the specific suffixes with their continuations (*anubandhas*), the inclusion [of the suffixes] should be made by means of the general term *ṭh* alone; therefore, he says "by distinction" (*bhedena*), and so forth. If there were inclusion by the general term *ṭh*, there would also be the inclusion of *an* and the others; hence, to exclude those, the inclusion is made by means of distinction.

The word "ādi" (and so forth) is for the purpose of including suffixes such as *ñiṭha*; therefore, when the suffix *ṭhan* is applied according to the rule "ṭhata iniṭhanau" (Pāṇini 5.2.115)—as in the case of "daṇḍo 'syāsti" (he has a staff)—the form does not become *daṇḍikī*. Likewise, when the suffix *ñiṭha* is applied according to the rule "kāśyādibhyaṣṭhāññiṭhau" (Pāṇini 4.2.116)—as in the case of "kāśiṣu bhavaḥ" (born in Kāśī)—[the same applies].

The form *kāśikī* does not occur. The inclusion of the indicatory letter *k* in the suffix *ka* is for the purpose of excluding rules such as *ṭhāto 'nupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3). For example: *yādṛśī*, *tādṛśī*. [This applies] by the rule *tyadādiṣu dṛśeranālocane*...

The suffix *kañ* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.3.12] *kañ ca*; the substitution of *ā* for the *y* and *t* of *yat* and *tat* is by [Pāṇini 7.2.102] *ṭhā sarvanāmnaḥ*. The pronunciation of the indicatory letter (*anubandha*) in *kvarap* is for the purpose of excluding *varac*, which is prescribed by [Pāṇini 3.2.175] *stheśabhāsa-* and so forth. If this is so, then only one indicatory letter should have been pronounced, since even with one—

Is it not the case that cessation (*nivṛtti*) is established by the word *vara* alone? True, this is so; nevertheless, the mention of the two suffixes (*kvarap* and *kvanip*) is for the sake of easy comprehension by those of dull intellect.
[The examples are] *ṭhitvarī* and *naśvarī*. [The rule is: *iṇ-naś-ja-sarti-bhyaḥ kvarap* (Pāṇini 3.2.163); there is the augment *tuk* after a short vowel.

The mention of the suffix *khyun* is for the sake of brevity; otherwise, if the genitive plural were used, there would be a cumbersome pronunciation due to the addition of the augment *nuṭ* and the lengthening of the vowel in the *nām* group. [The example] "āḍhyaṅkaraṇī" is formed by the rule "āḍhya-subhaga...
(Pāṇini 3.2.56), meaning "that by which one who is not wealthy (*anāḍhya*) is made wealthy (*āḍhya*)."
*Khyun*, *ṭharuḥ*, *dviṣadajantadasya mum* (Pāṇini 6.3.67);

*nañ-snañ-īkak-* etc. The word *upasaṃkhyāna* means "an additional statement" (*pratipādana*). Herein is that additional statement: in the subsequent sūtra, the particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been mentioned; by means of that—

"It will also occur after *nañ* and other [affixes]," as in *straiṇī* and *pauṃsnī*. [These are derived] from the sense "this belongs to a woman" (*striyā iyam*) and "this belongs to a man" (*puṃsa iyam*), by the rule *strīpuṃsābhyāṃ naṅsnañau bhavanāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.87), which prescribes the affixes *nañ* and *snañ*. [Examples are] *śāktīkī* and *yāṣṭīkī*, meaning "one whose weapon is a spear" (*śaktiḥ praharaṇam asya*) or "one whose weapon is a staff" (*yaṣṭiḥ praharaṇam asya*).

Regarding the examples *taruṇī surā* and *talunī surā*: here, the suffix *ṅīp* is to be understood after the words *taruṇa* and *taluna* when followed by *surā* and other such terms; for *surā* and the like possess no age (*vayas*), since that is a property of living beings (*prāṇin*). In the case of *surā* and the others, there is merely the state of being new (*abhinavatva*).

This is understood from the words *taruṇa* and *taluna*. However, when age (*vayas*) is intended to be expressed, then by virtue of their inclusion in the *gaurādi* group, the suffix *ṅīṣ* must be applied. In that case, there is a difference in accent:

for the words *taruṇa* and *taluna*, [the suffix] *unan* is added according to the rule *ṭhp-kṛ-vṛ-dā-ribhya unan* (Uṇādisūtra 5.52), and [the word *taluna* is derived from the root *tṝ* with the substitution of *ra* for *ṝ*].

The two words [loka and loka] are derived with the suffix *unan* according to Pāṇini 5.4.101 (*lo vā*), and thus, by the accentuation rule for *nit* suffixes, they have the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable. In that case, when the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied, the acute accent remains on the first syllable; however, when the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied, the word has the acute accent on the final syllable due to the accentuation rule for suffixes.

16. And [the suffix] *yañ* [is applied after the words *garga*, etc. (Pāṇini 4.1.105). [Examples: *gārgī*, *vātsī*. From the words *garga* and *vatsa*, when denoting a female descendant, the suffix *yañ* is applied by [the rule] "from *garga* and others, *yañ*" (4.1.105); then the feminine suffix *ṅīp*; and finally, by [the rule] "and that which has *y* as its [initial] vowel" (6.4.148), there is the elision of the vowel *a*.

There is elision [of the *y*] by the rule "ṭhhalastaddhitasya" (Pāṇini 6.4.150). Regarding the statement "the mention of 'apatya' (descendant) must be made": that by which a descendant is grasped is "apatyagrahaṇam.
This is what is meant by the explanation—it should be explained in such a way that the suffix *yañ* [is not elided].

The qualifier "apatyam" (offspring) should be understood here. Regarding this, the following is the explanation: the mention of "prācām" (of the Easterners) in the subsequent sūtra for the purpose of providing an option is also connected with this rule; furthermore, that [option] is understood as a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (a restricted option). Consequently, the suffix *nitya* (always) applies to a word ending in *yañ* which has been prescribed in the sense of offspring.

As for the claim that [the suffix] *dant* does not apply to the sense of "born from" (*jāta*) and so forth because it follows the word *dvīpa*: now, what is the purpose of this *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule)? It is not the case that the mention of *añ* should have been made in the preceding rule itself;
therefore, he says: "The *yogavibhāga* is for the sake of the subsequent [rule]. This means that in the subsequent rule, the suffix *ṣpha* applies only after a stem ending in *yañ*.
So that it might be so, [the rule] "from those ending in ṬI and others" should not apply.

17. *prācām ṣpha taddhitaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.17). [The commentary states: "The letter *ṣ* in *ṣpha* is for the sake of [triggering] *ṅīṣ*. This is so that *ṅīp* might apply by the rule *ṣid-gaurādibhyaś-ca* (4.1.41). But one might object: even if the letter *ṣ* were present, *ṅīṣ* should certainly not occur.
Since femininity is already manifested by the suffix *ṣpha* itself, he says "by two suffixes," and so forth. For the suffix *ṣpha* alone is not capable of manifesting femininity;
thus, it requires *ṅīṣ*. Femininity is manifested only by those two together, and therefore [the suffix] *ṅīṣ* [is applied].

It must be so. Regarding the phrase "the mention of *taddhita*," etc.: the mention of *taddhita* is for the purpose that the designation *prātipadika* should apply by virtue of the rule "and [that which ends in] a *kṛt*, *taddhita*, or compound" (Pāṇini 1.2.46).
However, the designation *prātipadika* is for the purpose that the suffix *ṅīṣ* should apply. But surely, even without...
By the very power of the designation *ṣit*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* will indeed occur;

otherwise, the designation *ṣit* would be purposeless, as there would be no other motive for it. Furthermore, there is no over-extension [of the rule] to the root *trapūṣ* (DhP 3.74, meaning "to be ashamed"), because [the suffix *ṅīṣ*] would not apply from that root either.

Is it not to be suspected that [the mention of *taddhita*] is redundant, because the addition of the marker *ṣ* to the root serves its purpose in the rule for the suffix *aṅ*, namely Pāṇini 3.3.104 (*ṣidbhidādibhyo 'ṅ*), and because the word "from this" (*ataḥ*) is a governing heading (*adhikāra*)? True, this is so;
however, there would be an excessive burden on the learner (*pratipattigaurava*). Therefore, the mention of *taddhita* is for the sake of easy comprehension.
Regarding the phrase "the inclusion of the word *sarvatra*," and so forth: the inclusion of the word *sarvatra* in the subsequent sūtra is redundant.
That [inclusion] is made for the purpose of ensuring that [the rule] applies according to the opinion of all teachers;
however, this is unnecessary, because by virtue of the term not being marked with the *svarita* accent, the preceding inclusion already applies according to the opinion of all.
It must be so. Therefore, the inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) in the subsequent sūtra is redundant;
hence, it is drawn back here. He asks, "For what purpose? and replies: "In order to override that which overrides.
This explains the very meaning of the statement, "He will state [the suffix] *āvaṭaḷac* and *cāp*," and so forth.

He clarifies this: *āvaṭaḷac-cāp-avakāśaḥ*—according to the opinion of the northerners (*udīcām*), from the word *avaṭa*, which ends in the suffix *iñ* belonging to the *garga*-class, the suffix *cāp* is applied [to form *āvaṭaḷā*];

the scope (*avakāśa*) of the rule "the suffix *ṣpha*, a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), for the easterners" (Pāṇini 4.1.17) is, for example, *gārgyāyaṇī*; thus, when both would apply according to the easterners (*prācām*), [the former takes precedence].

And because it is subsequent [to the previous rule], the suffix *ap* would apply. However, due to the inclusion of the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*), only the suffix *ṣpha* will occur—as in *āvaṭyaḥ*.

18. [The suffix *ṭhak* is applied] everywhere after words such as *lohita*, etc., ending in *kata*. (Pāṇini 4.1.18) "Independent" (*svatantra*) means that which does not constitute a part of anything else; thus, the word *kata* alone is an independent nominal stem (*prātipadika*). However, that which is a constituent part of the compound *kurukata*— [Note: The text provided ends abruptly.]

The word *kata* has no independence (*svātantrya*) of its own, because it is dependent upon a composite whole (*samudāya*). What, then, is this word *kata* that is an independent nominal stem (*prātipadika*)? To this he says: "from the word *kapi*" and so forth. [Examples are] *Lauhityāyanī* and *Śāṃsityāyanī*.

From the words *lohita* and *śaṃsita*, the suffix *yañ* is applied according to the rule for the *garga*-class (*gargādi*). Regarding the form *vābhravyāyaṇī*: here too, from the word *babhru*, the suffix *yañ* is applied by the rule *madhubabhruvor brāhmaṇakauśikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.106);
then, by *orguṇaḥ* (6.4.146), the *guṇa* substitution occurs, and by *vānto yi pratyaye* (6.1.79), the substitute *vānta* (the sound *au*) is applied.

The suffix *ṣpha* is applied after words ending in *yañ*. [As in] *kāṇvāyana*, and so forth. It is intended that the word *śakala* precedes the word *kaṇva*, and the word *kata* follows it. To the question, "What happens when this is the case? he says: "The preceding and the following," and so forth.

This being the case, the preceding and following groups have that as their final and initial elements respectively. By the word *tat*, the word *śakala* is referred back. Those two preceding and following groups, of which the word *śakala* is respectively the final and the initial element, are "those having that as their final and initial elements. [The first group is] *lohitādi*.

The *pūrva* (first) group ends with the word *śakala*, while the subsequent *uttara* group, belonging to the *kaṇvādi* class, begins with the word *śakala*. What, then, is the purpose of these groups ending and beginning with that word? He says: "The purpose therein is [the application of] the suffixes *ṣpha* and *aṇ*. This refers to the first group.

If the *gaṇa* ends with *śakala*, the suffix *ṣpha* is the purpose [of its inclusion]; if the subsequent [member] begins with *śakala*, the suffix *aṇ* is the purpose. "The reading in the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) is otherwise," as in: *kapikata*, *kurukata*, *anaḍuh*, *kaṇva*.

The reading among the nominal stems (prātipadika) is "śakala"—this sequence must be established. It should be established by the sequence shown in [the passage] beginning with "But Kaṇva is prior to Śakala. Therefore, this is what is meant: *kurukata*.

The two words *anaḍuh* and [the others] should be recited in another place, while the word *śakala* should be recited between the words *kataka* and *kaṇva*. Regarding the statement "it is thought (*manyate*) thus," the author of the Ślokavārttika says: "But how, when the recitation is in this manner, are the suffixes *ṣpha* and *aṇ* established from the word *śakala*? To this he replies:

Regarding the rule beginning with *ṭhkatantebhyaḥ*: *katasyāntaḥ* is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the end of *kata*. The form *katantebhyaḥ* results from the application of a *nipātana* (irregular grammatical substitution) which effects the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*). Those words such as *lohita* and others that have the word *kata* at their end are called *katantāḥ*; this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Furthermore, the word *śakala* is also a *katanta*.

Regarding the expression "katantāśca lohitādayaḥ," there is a single-remainder (ekaśeṣa) of similar forms [meaning] both "those ending in *kata*" (*katantāḥ*) and "those beginning with *lohita*" (*lohitādayaḥ*). By the phrase "in the same way" (*tathā*) and so forth,

it is indicated that just as there is a single-remainder of both the *bahuvrīhi* and *tatpuruṣa* types in the case of "from those ending in *kata*" (*katantebhyaḥ*), the same applies here in the case of "from *kaṇva* and others" (*kaṇvādibhyaḥ*).
[The author] demonstrates this: "Kaṇvādi" means those beginning with Kaṇva; the word *śakala* is the same as the word *kaṇva*.

Those [names] such as Gokakṣa and others that have *kaṇva* as their first [member] are "the Kaṇvas and so forth" (*kaṇvādayaḥ*). Then, by the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) as before, we have "the Kaṇvas and so forth" (*kaṇvādiśca kaṇvādayaśca kaṇvādayaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "not included under the operation of a *tatpuruṣa*," this refers to the rule "after those ending in *kta*" (*katantebhyaḥ*).

In the rule *ṭhkaṇvādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.111), by means of the function of a *tatpuruṣa*, that is, by means of a *tatpuruṣa* compound. [The example is] *madhyāpīta*. This refers to the two groups [of surnames] beginning with *kata* and *kaṇva*. "Two suffixes" refers to the suffix *ṣpha* and the suffix *aṇ*. "Attains" means he acquires them.
For when it is included by means of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the meaning of this sūtra arises as follows:
after the word *śakala* ending in *kat*, and likewise after words beginning with *lohita* that end in *yañ*, the suffix *ṣpha* occurs in the feminine. By this, one obtains the suffix *ṣpha*.

The word *śakala*. Regarding the form *śākalyāyanī*, even in the rule *kaṇvādibhyo gotre* (Pāṇini 4.2.111), since the word *śakala* is included there by way of its occurrence as a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the meaning is as follows: [the suffix is applied] after words beginning with *kaṇva* that end in *śakala* and consist of a *gotra* suffix, from among those beginning with *kaṇva*.

The suffix *aṇ* occurs after words ending in *gotra* and *pratyaya* in the sense of secondary derivatives (*śaiṣika*). By this rule, the word *śākala* also acquires the suffix *aṇ*: "these are the pupils of Śākalya" = *śākalāḥ*.

19. And [the suffix] after *kauravya* and *māṇḍūkya*. (4.1.19) [Question: "How is it that there is *kauravī*? This question is raised by one who thinks that the suffix *ṅīp* is prescribed here from the word *kauravya* itself. [Answer: Here, *ṅīp* is prescribed from the word *kuru* itself, which ends in the suffix *aṇ*.
Showing this, he says: "tasyedam" and so forth;

"kauravyamāṇḍūkayoḥ" and so forth. Whatever grammatical operation is prescribed for *kauravya* and *māṇḍūka* by this rule, there is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*)—that is, a formal application—of that same operation to *āsuri* as well.
It must be performed; that is to say, the suffix *ṣpha* must also be applied after the word *āsuri*. In this regard, the following is the demonstration:
the letter *ca* is inserted here, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned;
therefore, the suffix *ṣpha* will also occur after the word *āsuri*. Thus, [the form] "Āsurāyaṇī" is derived.

The word *asura* forms its feminine derivative [meaning "daughter of an Asura"] by the rule *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95); from that form ending in *iñ*, the suffix *ṣpha* is applied. Regarding the statement "since the suffix *aṇ* would otherwise apply by the rule *ṭhiñaśca*" (4.1.120), one must perform a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) as follows: "In the case of words ending in *prastha*, those having *uttara-pada*, and those beginning with *paladyādi*, the suffix *aṇ* does not apply. By this, even from the word *āsuri*, the application of *aṇ* is prohibited; consequently, the suffix *cha* applies by the rule *vṛddhācchaḥ* (4.2.114).
By this rule (Pāṇini 4.2.114), it will be *cch* itself—the *āsurīya* ritual manual (*kalpa*) taught by Āsuri.
20. *vayasi prathame* (4.1.20). [The commentary says:

"‘yauvanādiḥ’—the word ‘ādi’ (and so forth) is for the purpose of including old age and the like. [It further says: “*śrutyā vartate*”—that nominal stem which, by mere hearing alone, functions independently of context and the like.

It causes the first stage of life to be understood; thus it functions here by way of direct scriptural statement (śruti), as in the word "maiden" (*kumārī*). But is it not the case that this word *kumārī* does not denote the first stage of life? Where, then, does it apply? It applies to the absence of union with a male;
for indeed, it is used even for an old woman—as in the expression "an old maiden" (*vṛddhā kumārī*).

This is not so; for the word *kumārī* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) only in reference to the first stage of life. As for its application even to an old woman, that is due to her similarity (*sādharmya*) with a maiden, and not because of the absence of union with a male. For a thing may receive the name of another through similarity to it, as in the following example: [text fragment].

Regarding the example *gaur vāhīkaḥ*: the meaning of this sūtra's commentary is that the suffix *ṅīp* occurs when it is "not the last" (*acarame*), which means "when it is not final" (*anantye*). This is the explanation here: [The rule] *vayasyacarama-* [is interpreted as follows]: the suffix *ṅīp* occurs when [the word] is not the last—that is, when it is not final. This is the explanation of this sūtra.

The mention of "the first stage of life" (*prathamavayaḥ*) here is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the final stage of life as well; therefore, the suffix *ṅīp* occurs even in other cases outside of the final stage of life. But what is the reason that it would not be established if only the first stage of life were taken, such that the meaning of the sūtra must be explained in this way? To this, he says:
"These two [words] refer to age," and so forth. Here, some maintain that there are four stages of life (*vayaṃsi*):
childhood (*kaumāra*), youth (*yauvana*), middle age (*madhyatva*), and old age (*vṛddhatva*). Thus they say:
"What was not studied in the first stage of life, nor wealth acquired in the second..."
"In the third [stage] no austerity was practiced; what will the fourth do?
Others desire three [stages]: childhood, youth, and old age. And so they say:
"The father protects in childhood; the husband protects in youth."
"But a son, in his state of old age, [is dependent]; a woman does not deserve independence.
Some, however, maintain that there are three stages—childhood, youth, and old age—and as they say:
"One should be considered a child until the age of sixteen, so long as one subsists on milk and rice."

"The middle [age] lasts up to seventy years; beyond that, one is called old. Among all these [ages], youth constitutes the second stage of life. Now, an objection might be raised: since the words *vadhūṭī* and *ciraṇṭī* denote the first stage of life, [the suffix] would not apply here; therefore, [it applies] to the final stage of life.
Some explain that "the first stage of life" (*prathamaṃ vayaḥ*) here should be understood as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).

However, as for the one who thinks, "Some maintain that there are only two stages of life," [he holds that] all those states which possess intelligence are gathered together and established as the first stage of life.

All those states characterized by decline, taken together, constitute the second stage of life. And so it has been said: "As long as one increases by means of food, so long should one continue to increase; thereafter, one will be joined with decay.
It is by relying on this very perspective that this aphorism was composed. By that...

In the case of *vadhūṭī* and *ciraṇṭī*, the suffix *ṅīp* also occurs; therefore, these two denote the second stage of life. One must strive to ensure that this does not contradict the statement that "a woman who has attained youth" is being designated [by these terms]. For in this view, youth is not included within the second stage of life; rather, it is the state of youth itself.

Because it possesses growth. Now, as for how she is "lying on her back with red feet"—since childhood is understood here, for it is only a child who lies on her back with red feet; therefore, this [state] must indeed exist.

To this he says: "These are not words denoting age. The meaning is that these are not terms expressing age. Here, first of all, by the mere hearing of the nominal stem *utānaśayā*, only a general relationship between an action and its factors is perceived—namely, "she who lies on her back" (*utānā śete* = *utānaśayā*).

While the term *ac* is being carried over from the rule "after the root *sthā*, when not meaning 'exertion', [the suffix *kvip* is added]" (Pāṇini 3.2.9), the suffix *ac* is applied here by virtue of the supplementary rule "in the case of the roots *śī* and *sthā*, when the agent is among those beginning with *uttāna*" (Pāṇini 3.2.15). Then, by the rule "a feminine word is treated like the masculine" (Pāṇini 6.3.34), [the feminine form is replaced by the masculine].

[The rule of] masculine equivalence (*puṃvadbhāvaḥ*). When it is said, "Every woman lies on her back," and it is further stated, "She is a 'back-lying woman' (*utānaśayā*)," a restriction is understood there. Otherwise, since she would be incapable of lying [in any other way], one understands that she who lies only on her back is a "back-lying woman. Even when this restriction is understood, doubt remains: is she...?

Is she a child or an old woman? For even an old woman might sometimes be unable to lie down otherwise and may indeed lie on her back. Therefore, when there arises the cognition of a restriction—that she lies only on her back—and the absence of old age is determined from some context or other source, [the inference proceeds].

In that case, the state of being a child (*bālya*) is understood. Regarding the expression "one with red feet" (*lohitapādikā*), here too, from the word *tat* (in the compound), only the referent of another word—the fact that her feet are red—is initially perceived. However, when, through context or other means, it is understood that her feet are naturally red and not due to lac-dye or similar substances, [the meaning of the suffix is established].
When such a cognition arises, she is understood to be a "child" (*bālā*). The word *iti* has the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*);
the meaning is that these Vedic verses are not of such a kind. How [is she] a child?
[The form] *vatse* will be derived with the suffix *ṭāp* because it belongs to the *ajādi* group. But surely, by the force of the rule itself, the suffix *ṅīp* would also apply here?
Does it apply? This is not the case; for that [term] has its purpose fulfilled elsewhere, as in examples such as *kumārī* (maiden) and *kiśorī* (mare).

21. *dvigoḥ* | (4.1.21) [The example] "ṭhpañcapūlī" (a bundle of five bundles): this is a collective compound (*samāhāra*) of five bundles. It is a collective *dvigu* compound by virtue of the rule "taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca" (Pāṇini 2.1.51).

The feminine gender is applied because of the rule: "A *dvigu* compound whose final member ends in the letter *ṭha* and which has a vowel as its penultimate syllable is expressed in the feminine" (Vārttika 156). Thus, "triphalā" means "a collection of three fruits. As before, it is a *dvigu* compound.

22. *Aparimāṇa-vistā-cita-kambalyebhyo na taddhitaluki* (Pāṇini 4.1.22). The phrase "when there is elision of the *taddhita* suffix" (*taddhitaluki sati*) indicates that the locative case in *taddhitaluki* is a locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*). It is not appropriate to take this as a locative of sequence (*parasaptamī*), because elision (*luka*) is of the nature of non-existence, and [the rule] would apply to a non-existent thing.

And because there is no priority or posteriority [in this case]. "Dimension (*parimāṇa*) is measurement from all sides (*sarvatas*). The word *pari* signifies "from all sides. That by which something is measured—that is, delimited—both in terms of height and in terms of circumference is dimension, such as a *prastha* and so forth.

Regarding "five horses" (*pañcāśva*): it is a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). The suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.1.37, *tena krītam* ("purchased with that"), as an affix denoting value (*ārhīya*). Then, by Pāṇini 5.1.28, *adhyardhapūrvād dvigor luk*, there is elision (*luk*) of the *ṭhak* after a *dvigu* preceded by *adhyardha*. [The reason for this is that] time and number are not measures (*parimāṇa*), for by them one is not measured in terms of height or circumference.
Furthermore, it is established by an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that these two do not possess the status of "measure" (*parimāṇa*).
For, although the rule *ṭhparimāṇāntasyāsaṃjñāśāṇayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.17)— which prescribes the vṛddhi of the subsequent member— is already established,
the specific mention of "number" (*saṃkhyā*) and "year" (*saṃvatsara*) in the rule *saṃkhyāyāḥ saṃvatsarasaṃkhyasya ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.15) serves as that indicator.
This indicates that time and number do not constitute *parimāṇa*.
Furthermore, "extent" (*vistādi*) and so forth must be understood as specific types of *parimāṇa* alone. Therefore, the commentary states:

"The mention [of the word] is for the purpose of including *parimāṇa*. Alternatively, if the *kāṇḍa* (section) itself is considered a *parimāṇa*, then [the application of the rule follows] by the subsequent sūtra.

The status of [the rule] as being for the sake of restriction (*niyamārthatā*) is not contradicted. If this is so, does it not contradict what was stated under *kālāḥ parimāṇinā* (Pāṇini 2.2.5)—namely, that by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), words denoting time (*kālaśabda*) which express a measure (*parimāṇavacana*) are compounded? There is no contradiction; for in that other case, [the word] is used figuratively (*upacāreṇa*) as denoting the object of measurement (*parimāṇin*).
Because [the suffix] is prescribed by a *subanta* (nominal stem). For here, the primary status of time as a measure (*parimāṇa*) is denied;

for it has been stated—by one who says "time-words are measures" (*kālāḥ parimāṇanam*)—that words expressing time are used as measures only by resorting to a figurative (*aupacārika*) status of time as a measure.

The status of words for time as denoting measure (parimāṇa) becomes applicable; for without that, the designation of the subsequent member of the compound as "that which possesses a measure" (parimāṇin) would not be possible in relation to the measure itself. Furthermore, time does not possess primary measurehood; therefore, by implication, it is figurative.

It is understood that [time] is based on measurement (*parimāṇa*). The cause for its being figuratively designated as such is simply its being the cause of delimitation; this is the common characteristic with measurement. For time—such as months and so forth—makes known the movement of the sun associated with birth and other events; thus it comes to be [so designated].

It is the cause of delimitation; therefore, by virtue of its similarity to measurement (*parimāṇa*), it is appropriate [to speak of it as such], and there is a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the term "measurement" in that context, as in "two years old" (*dvivarṣā*) or "three years old" (*trivarṣā*). This is by means of the suffix *ṭhak* prescribed by the rule *samadhīṣṭo bhṛto bhūto bhāvī* (Pāṇini 5.1.80), [in the sense] "having lived for two years."

The elision (*luk*) [of the suffix] by the rule *ṭhvarṣālluk* (5.1.88) is optional. However, when the meaning of the suffix is intended to be expressed as "possessing" (*citavati*), the elision is obligatory by the rule *citavati nityam* (5.1.89). In the case of *dve varṣe pramāṇamasyāḥ* ("two years are its measure"), the feminine suffix *lo* is applied by the Vārttika *pramāṇe lo dvigornityam* (Vārttika 558, 559).

The elision (*luk*) is always [of the suffix]. In the case of *dviśatā* and *triśatā*, since the suffix *ya* would otherwise be expected by the rule *paṇapādamāṣaśatādyat* (Pāṇini 5.1.34)—meaning "the suffix *yat* is applied after *paṇa*, *pāda*, *māṣa*, *śata*, etc., when they mean 'bought for'"—there is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) to the rule *śāṇādvā* (5.1.35): namely, that "it should be stated that [the suffix *yat* is also applied] after *śata*. By this [addition], [the forms *dviśatā* and *triśatā* are established].

From the word *śata*, in the alternative case, the suffix *kan* is applied by the rule "after a numeral ending in *ati* or *śat*, [the suffix] *kan* [is added]" (Pāṇini 5.1.22); its elision (*luk*) occurs as before.
Regarding "two *bista*s": one who cooks two *bista*s [of grain]. This is according to the rule "one who is capable of, one who gathers, or one who cooks" (Pāṇini 5.1.52).

By this [rule], the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "worth" (*arha*), and as before, there is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix]. In the case of "he cooks for two *ācit*s," one says *dvayācita*. While the rule *āḍhakācitapātrātsakho 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.1.53) is in force, the suffix *ṣṭhan* is applied by the rule *dvigoḥ ṣṭhañ ca* (Pāṇini 5.1.54); as before, there is elision of that [suffix].

"Purchased for two *kambalyas*": *dvikambalyā*. By the rule "purchased with that" (*tena krītam*, 5.1.37), the suffix *ṭhak* is applied; as before, there is elision (*luk*). "Two *āḍhakas*" (*dvyāḍhakī*): she cooks two *āḍhakas*.

While the rule *ṭhāḍhakācitapātrātkho 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.1.53) is in effect, the rule *dvigoḥ ṣṭhañ ca* (Pāṇini 5.1.54) applies; thus, in one alternative, the suffix *ṣṭhan* is added, and its *luk*-elision occurs. The form *pañcāśvī* is derived as follows:
as before, there is a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*).
Here, two prohibitions are stated, of which one is capable of being omitted. How so?

The formulation of the sūtra will be made thus: *parimāṇāntāt-taddhita-luki*. Since this is already established by the preceding rule, this [new formulation] is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtham*): the suffix *ṅīp* occurs only after a word ending in a measure-term when there is elision of a *taddhita* suffix.
Not from any other [word]. Therefore, [the suffix] occurs only in cases such as *dvyāḍhakī*, and not in cases such as *pañcāśvā*;

after that, the phrase *na taddhitaluki* ("not when there is elision of a taddhita suffix") is carried over, [meaning that the suffix is applied] even after measures such as *bista* when there is elision of a taddhita suffix.

Why does the suffix *ṅīp* not occur? It cannot be said so; for a contrary restriction might also be possible—that *ṅīp* occurs only when a *taddhita* suffix is elided after a word ending in a measure (*parimāṇa*), and not otherwise.
Consequently, in the case of "the collection of two *kuḍava*s" (*dvikuḍavī*), the suffix would not occur.
Therefore, let it remain exactly as it was originally arranged.

23. *kāṇḍāntātkṣetre* (Pāṇini 4.1.23). [The commentary states: "The suffix *ṭhañ* is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*)," meaning that it should apply only when the word ends in *kāṇḍa* and the object is a field (*kṣetra*), and not otherwise. Now, what is the purpose of including the word *anta* ("end"), since the rule of taking that as the final element (*tadantavidhi*) is already obtained by the very force of the context?

As in the previous sūtra: "Is it not the case that the designation *dvigu* has not been prescribed for the word *kāṇḍa* alone by anyone? This is true; however, if the term *asatya* were not included, the word *kāṇḍa* itself would be qualified by *kṣetra*—that is, only the word *kāṇḍa* which [occurs] in relation to a field.

[The word *kāṇḍa*] occurs [in this sense]; therefore, there would be a prohibition here: "a mare bought for two fields designated as *kāṇḍas* is called *dvikāṇḍī*. But here it would not apply: "a field-division whose measure is two *kāṇḍas* is a *dvikāṇḍā* field-division. However, when the final sūtra exists...
The word *kṣetra* is not an adjective for the word *kāṇḍa*; because it [the field] is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) to the *dvigu* compound.

24. *puruṣāt pramāṇe 'nyatarasyām*. (Pāṇini 4.1.24) "When the word *puruṣa* occurs in the sense of a measure (*pramāṇa*). Although the word *puruṣa* also denotes a genus (*jāti*), [it is used here in the sense of a measure].
When it is connected with the word "pramāṇa" (valid cognition), then it refers to the means of valid cognition residing in a person.

A word may function to denote another meaning through its connection with another word, just as in the case of "The boy is a lion. Although the word "lion" denotes a genus (*jāti*), [it is used here to signify the boy].
Due to the proximity of the word *māṇavaka*, it expresses the quality characterized by the measure of a teacher. Regarding the term *dvipuruṣī*:
the suffix *dvayasaC* prescribed by [Pāṇini 5.2.37] *pramāṇe dvayasac* is elided by the Vārttika [558, 559] *pramāṇe lo dvigornityam*.

"Because a prohibition would otherwise apply due to the suffix having a fixed limit," [referring to] the rule *ṭhaparimāṇavistāc ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.22). Thus, "purchased for two *puruṣas* is *dvipuruṣā*. As before, the suffix *ṭhak* [is applied] in the sense of being worthy of (*ārhīya*).
[The suffix] *luk* [is applied];

this is because of the rule "when there is *luk* of a *taddhita* suffix" (*taddhitaluki*). In the case of *pañcapuruṣī*, since the compound is formed from words denoting a measure (*pramāṇa*) and an object (*artha*), there is no deficiency of two members [of the compound].
25. *Bahuvrīher ūdhaso ṅīṣ* (Pāṇini 4.1.25).

[The commentary states: "When the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) *anaṅ* has been applied to *ūdhas*. Even before the compound has actually been formed, for the sake of the *bahuvrīhi*, the subsequent member must first undergo the compound-ending suffix; thus, the compound-ending suffix itself occurs prior to that.

There occurs [the formation of the feminine], then the *bahuvrīhi* compound, and then the feminine suffix—this is precisely the sequence. Regarding the rule "ṭhano bahuvrīheḥ" and so forth: the word *iti* has the sense of "and so on. The meaning is: by another grammatical rule such as "ṭhano bahuvrīheḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.12). In that context, by the rule "ṭhano bahuvrīheḥ,"...

When a prohibition would have applied by the preceding rule, the suffix *ḍāp* is introduced by the rule "ṭhḍābubhābhyāmanyatarasyām" (4.1.13). Thus, we have "kuṇḍoghnī. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose udder (*udhas*) is like a pot (*kuṇḍa*"); the vowel *a* is elided by the rule "allopo'naḥ" (6.4.134).

In the word *prāptodhaḥ*, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule *prāptāpanne ca dvitīyayā* (Pāṇini 2.2.4). The lengthening of the vowel is by the rule *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.14).
Regarding the phrase *ana upadhālopinaḥ* and so forth, this refers to the rule *ana upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.28).

By this [rule], it is intended that this *ṅīp* which is being prescribed here is a sublater (*bādhaka*) of the *ṅīp*. But how does what is stated here become a sublater of that? Through the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) from the subsequent rule. For if there were no recurrence from the subsequent rule, it would follow the principle: "Exceptions (*apavāda*) in the middle sublate preceding rules."

(Vyā.pa.10) Thus, this [rule] subverts only the prohibition of *ṅīp* and *ḍāp*, but not the *ṅīṣ* of that which has a penultimate vowel elision (*upadhālopin*). Consequently, because it is subsequent [to the rule for *ṅīṣ*], that very [suffix *ṅīṣ*] would occur in the alternative case. Therefore, its recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) occurs in the rule "after a word ending in *taddhita* suffix *ṭhan*, provided it does not have a penultimate vowel elision" (Pāṇini 4.1.28).
They must be applied. Therefore, even for a word ending in *ūdhas* that undergoes elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopin*), only the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs.

This is because of the rule "the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) occurs only in the feminine. However, the non-universality (*anityatva*) of this rule regarding compound-final suffixes is established by the fact that there exists a compound with the word *ūdhas* ending in *s*, which lacks a compound-final suffix.
It is understood from the qualification [in the rule]; for if it were eternal, the designation would have been "bahuvrīher ūdhaso ṅīp."

26. *ṅīp* [is applied] after numerals and indeclinables [ending in *ūdh-*]. (Pāṇini 4.1.26). Examples include *dvyūdhnī* and so forth. The analytical explanations (*vigraha*) are: "she who has two udders" (*dve ūdhasī asyāḥ*), "she who has three udders" (*trīṇyūdhāṃsyasyāḥ*), "she from whom the udder has not departed" (*abhigatamūdho'syāḥ*), and "she from whom the udder has gone out" (*nirgatamūdho'syāḥ*).

"What is the purpose of including the word *ṭha*? [The author] thinks as follows: one should simply say "after a numeral (*saṃkhyā*) or an indeclinable (*avyaya*)," for the rule *bahuvrīherūdhaso ṅīṣ* (Pāṇini 4.1.25) is still in effect;
there, the connection will be made in this way: "that which follows a numeral or an indeclinable..."

The word *ūdhas* [is mentioned] so that the suffix *ṅīp* occurs after a bahuvrīhi compound ending in it; thus, the inclusion of the word "beginning with" (*ādi*) in [the rule for] *niṣphalā* and others is unnecessary, because the desired form is established even without it—as in the example "dvividhōghnī" and so forth. For if the inclusion of the word "beginning with" were not made, then [the rule] "after a numeral or an indeclinable... would apply.

Due to the mention of the fifth case (pañcamī-nirdeśa), [the suffix] would apply only to that which ends with the word *ūdhas* immediately following a numeral; however, where there is an intervention, it would not apply. But because of the inclusion of the word "beginning" (*ādi*), it does apply even in those cases. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "one whose udder is of two kinds. In this context, when the word "beginning" is included, by means of the word *vidha*, [the formation is justified].
It occurs even when there is an intervention.
27. *Dāmahāyanāntācca* (4.1.27).
The rule *ūdhasaḥ* has ceased to apply, because a different base (*prakṛti*) is introduced.
"The mention of 'numeral' (*saṃkhyā*) continues, but not the mention of 'indeclinable' (*avyaya*)," it is said; for [the application] belongs specifically to the mention of 'numeral'.
Because of the *svarita* accent. Regarding the phrase "when the optional application of the prohibition of *ḍāp* has been reached":

since *ḍāp* would have applied by the rule "ḍāb ubhābhyām anyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 4.1.13), there is the prohibition by the rule "anaḥ bahuvrīheḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.12); and [there is] the optional application by the rule "ana upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 4.1.28).

And in the case of this alternative [stated in 4.1.28]: "she who has two cords" is *dvidāmnī*; "she who has two years" is *dvihāyanī*. [The rule] "the word *hāyana* is prescribed [as a suffix] in the sense of age" refers to the base form (*prakṛti*), which is the understood remainder [of the sūtra]. Of what is it the base form?

Because *ṅīp* is the subject under discussion, it refers to that very suffix. Since this occurs within the governing rule (*adhikāra*) for *bahuvrīhi*, it is understood here that this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *hāyanā*. What is meant is this: the teachers have recorded that a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *hāyanā* is the base for the application of *ṅīp* when age is being expressed. Therefore—

If "vayas" (age) is understood [as the meaning], then the suffix *ṅīp* occurs, and not otherwise. This is obtained because the mention of the word "anyatarasyām" (optionally) in the subsequent sūtra functions as a supplement to both rules, and because of the understanding that this is a fixed option (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*). Now, regarding the forms from "tricaturbhyām":

Since *hāyana* is also included [in the list], just as the substitution of *ṇ* occurs in *trihāyanī* and *caturhāyaṇī*, why does it not also occur in *trihāyanā śālā* and *caturhāyanā śālā*? To this he says: "The substitution of *ṇ* also," and so forth. For that too...

The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* is traditionally recorded by the Teachers as applying only to the word *vayas*; since "age" (*vayas*) cannot belong to a building (*śālā*), because it is a property of living beings, the substitution of *ṇ* does not apply here.
The inclusion of the term "end" (*anta*) is for the sake of clarity, for [the application of the rule] follows from the governing context of *bahuvrīhi* by virtue of its inherent capacity.
The rule of "specification of the final element" (tadantavidhi) is thus obtained; for the designation of *bahuvrīhi* has not been prescribed by anyone for the words *dāman* and *hāyana* alone.

28. *ana upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.28). Regarding the term *upadhālopī*: that [base] for which the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) is possible when the suffix *ṅīp* follows is called *upadhālopī*.
Regarding the passage beginning with "nanu" and so forth: the prohibition [of the feminine suffix] by the rule *ano bahuvrīheḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.12) is established;

the suffix *ḍāp* is applied by the rule *ḍābubhābhyām anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.13), and because of the inclusion of the phrase *anyatarasyām*, the suffix *ṅīp* optionally occurs in the alternative case. If, then...

By the rule "ṭhḍābubhābhyāmanyatarasyām," the suffix *ṅīp* is also prescribed; would it then not also apply in cases such as *dāmā* and *pāmā*? It will not apply, because the mention of "anyatarasyām" (optionally) is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). [The sūtra] begins with "anupadhālopinaḥ" etc. If this were not stated, [the following would occur].

The suffix *ṅīp* would apply even to those [stems] that do not drop their penultimate vowel (*anupadhālopinaḥ*). Therefore, this [rule] is stated so that *ṅīp* may apply only to those that do drop their penultimate vowel (*upadhālopinaḥ*) and not to those that do not. For example, in "bahurājā," there is a prohibition of *ṅīp* by the rule "sarvanāmasthāne ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.8).
The penultimate vowel is not lengthened. In the case of *bahurājñī*, there is the suffix *ṅīp*, and by *allopo'naḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.134), the *an* is elided.

In the case of *bahurāje*, there is the suffix *ḍāp*; by *āṬṅ āpaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.18), the *śī* replacement occurs, and by *ādguṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.97), the single substitute *e* is formed. The mention of the dual number is for the purpose of making the suffix *ḍāp* manifest; for in the singular, [it would not be so].

There is no difference between the suffix *ḍa* and the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), for in both cases the form is identical. In some instances, there is a reference using the plural, as in "bahurājāḥ"; the purpose of that [plural] is also the same [as the singular]. [Examples include] "bahumatsyā" and, by the rule "sūryātiṣyāgastyamastyānāṃ ya upadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.149), [the forms sūryya-, tiṣya-, agastya-, masty-].

Thus, because of the prescription of elision (*lopa*), the term *upadhālopī* is a bahuvrīhi compound. In the case of *suparvā*, this is not an instance of elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*), because of the prohibition of such elision by the rule *na saṃyogād vamantāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.137).

29. *nityaṃ saṃjñācchandasoḥ* | (4.1.29) The mention of *nityam* (always) is for the sake of clarity. For by the preceding rule alone, the suffix *ṅīp* would have been established as optional; since this [present] rule is commenced, by its very force, *ṅīp* will necessarily occur. Otherwise, this...
The statement would be meaningless.
30. [The suffix *cha* is applied after the words *kevala*, *āmāka*, *bhāgadheya*, *pāpa*, *apara*, *samāna*, *ārya*, *kṛta*, *sumaṅgala*, and *bheṣaja*.
(4.1.30) Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the word *māmaka*, since the suffix *aṇ* would already apply by [Pāṇini 4.3.120], *tasyedam* ("this belongs to that")?
When the substitution of *māmaka* occurs by the rule "the forms *tavaka* and *māmaka* are used in the singular" (Pāṇini 4.3.3), the word *māmaka* is formed;

and since the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would then be established by the rule "after [stems ending in] *ti*, *ṭi*, *ḍha*, *āṇ*, and *añ*" (Pāṇini 4.1.15), this is indeed true. Nevertheless, the mention of the word *māmaka* is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*).
This is so that [the rule] may apply to *saṃjñā* and *chandas*, but not elsewhere.
31. *rātreścājjasau* (Pāṇini 4.1.31). Regarding the phrase "*ajjasau*": this is a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*), not a locative of posteriority (*parasaptamī*). Why?
Because the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) is internal (*antaraṅga*), and thus there is no contradiction in its being subsequent to *jas*; therefore, it is a locative of domain.

He states the fault [in the rule] with the words "because it has *jaś* as its object," and so forth. The meaning is that one must explain the rule in such a way that it conveys: "it should be stated that [the suffix] occurs after *rātri* in the case of *aj-as* and so on"; that is, the suffix *ṅīp* occurs after the word *rātri* in instances other than those governed by *jaś* and so on. In this regard, the following...

Explanation: Here, for the sake of brevity, although one could have said "ṭh-ajasi," it is stated as "ajasau"; this is intended to indicate that because of the increase in syllables (mātrā), there is an increase in meaning. Consequently, the suffix *ṅīp* occurs in the case of *ajas* and so forth.
By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the inclusion of *ām* and others is intended.

"‘How’ and so forth; ‘rātryaḥ’—this is the usage of the word *rātri* in the *jas* case-ending. For only in this way, when the rule ‘dīrghāj jasi ca’ (Pāṇini 6.1.105) prohibits the lengthening of a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*), does the substitution of *yaṇ* become applicable, and not otherwise. If, however, this were the usage of the word *rātri*, then..."
The intention is that if the *guṇa* substitution were applied by the rule *ṭhjasi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.109), followed by the *ayādeśa*, the form would be *rātrayaḥ*.
Furthermore, a feminine stem *rātri-* ending in the vowel *ī* is not possible, because the suffix *ṅīp* is prohibited by the rule *ajādyatas* (Pāṇini 4.1.4).
Consequently, the usage *rātryaḥ* would be untenable. [This refers to the statement] "this is *ṅīṣ*" and so forth.

Now, an objection is raised: "The word *rātri* is listed among the *bahv-ādi* group; therefore, how can the suffix *ṅīṣ* occur after it by virtue of the *bahv-ādi* rule? To this, he says: "For in that case," and so forth.

[He refers to the rule] "After a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix containing the vowel *i*, except for those ending in *ktin*. Here, *kṛd-ikāraḥ* means the vowel *i* belonging to a *kṛt*-suffix; the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after words ending in such a vowel.

It occurs [after roots ending in long *ī*]. According to the rule *vṛdṛbhyāṃ vin* (Uṇādi-sūtra 1.23), we have *varvī* and *darvī*. However, it does not occur after a word ending in *ktin*—as in *striyāṃ ktin* (Pāṇini 3.3.94)—such as *kṛtiḥ* and *hṛtiḥ*.
Regarding the statement "some say [it applies] after every [root] except for those ending in *ktin*," some teachers maintain that it applies after every [root] except for those ending in *ktin*.
They say that the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after words ending in the vowel *i*, whether that *i* is part of a *kṛt* suffix or not; thus, from *rāji* we have *rājī*.

In the view that the word *rāji* is not derived through grammatical formation (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*), it does not end in the vowel *i* belonging to a *kṛt* suffix. Regarding the rule "after a word that does not have the sense of a *ktin* suffix" (*aktinnarthāt*):
a word for which there exists no *ktin* suffix is "one that does not have the sense of a *ktin*"; after such a word, the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs universally.

However, it does not occur after a word ending in a *ktin* suffix—such as *kṛtiḥ* or *hṛtiḥ*. Regarding the rule "In the sense of reviling, *ani* is added after *nañ*" (Pāṇini 3.3.112), we have *akaraṇiḥ* and *aharaṇiḥ*. Furthermore, according to the view that this word *rātri-* is derived through etymological analysis (*vyutpatti-pakṣa*), it ends in a vowel other than *ik*, being formed from the root *rā* (meaning "to take," Dhātupāṭha 1057) with the suffix *ni* according to the rule "after *rā* and *śad*, [the suffix *ni* is applied]"...

The word *trip* (from Daiva 1.36) means "night"; therefore, in the view that it is a derivative, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied to form *rātrī*. However, in the view that it is not a derivative (*avyutpatti*), it does not end in the vowel *i* of a *kṛt*-suffix; consequently, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *sarvato 'ktinnarthāt* (Gaṇasūtra 51).

32. *antarvat-pativator nuk* (Pāṇini 4.1.32). [The commentary states: "But that [suffix] is already established by the fact that [the word *antarvat*] ends in the letter *n*, namely by [the rule] *ṛn-nebhyo ṅīp* (4.1.5). [It continues with: "By the force of its being a *nipātana*," and so forth. For just as...
By the force of the rule for elision (*nipātana*), some other non-technical (*alākṣaṇika*) operation occurs;
likewise, there is application (*vṛtti*) even in a specific sense (*arthaviśeṣa*). In which specific sense, then, does the application occur?
To this he says: "as in *antarvat* and *pativat*," and so forth. This refers to the term *antarvat* respectively.
The term *vṛtti* [is used] in connection with pregnancy (*garbhasaṃyoga*), and [the term *patipadī*] is used in connection with a husband (*bhartṛsaṃyoga*).
