[The rule] "and there is the substitution of *ṇ* for *d* after [the prefix] *ācārya*"— this need not be stated as something new, because it is already included among the *kṣubhna*-type words.

"This rule applies only to its own primary meaning (*svārtha*). By the use of the particle *eva*, connection with a male (*puṃyoga*) is excluded. For if this rule were to apply to connection with a male, then even a Śūdra woman who is the wife of a Kṣatriya would be called "Kṣatriyāṇī. Therefore, this rule applies only to its own primary meaning—that she is a Kṣatriya herself.

Regarding the term *kṣatriyāṇī*: "In the case of connection with a male (*puṃyoga*), however, it must be formed with the suffix *ṅīṣ* alone" [by] the preceding rule. [The rule] "and *li*"—of what is that *lit*-ness? Of the *ānuk*. For instance, the word *mudgalānī* is recited in the second accentuation in the *Āmnāya*; whereas if *ṅīṣ* were *lit*, it would have the third accentuation.
It may be so.
50. *krītāt karaṇapūrvāt* (4.1.50).

By the analysis "that in which the instrument (*karaṇa*) is prior," etc., he shows that both the mention of "instrument" (*karaṇa*) and the mention of "purchased" (*krīta*) are qualifiers of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
This word *pūrva* signifies a "part" (*avayava*). The meaning is: that in which the instrument (*karaṇa*) is the part.
Now, why is the term *karaṇapūrva* not understood as a qualifier of the word *krīta* itself?
Because it is impossible. For the word *krīta*, having taken the word *pūrva* as signifying a part—

Is it to be qualified as "the instrument in the preceding [member]"? Or is it the word *vyavasthā* (distinction/limitation), as in "the instrument prior to this"? Of these, the first alternative is not possible; for here, no other word denoting an instrument can logically function as a constituent part (*avayava*) of the word *krīta*. However, the second alternative is possible, yet—

This fault would also apply to a sentence—for example, in *aśvena krītaḥ* ("bought for a horse")—because here, prior to the word *krīta*, there exists the instrument (*karaṇa*). However, when the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is being qualified, this fault does not arise; for *aśvena krītaḥ* is not a nominal stem that ends in the word *krīta* with the instrument as its constituent part. What then? It is a sentence.

This is the sentence. Therefore, the base noun (*prātipadika*) under discussion, which is a general term, is qualified by the word *pūrva* (preceded), which denotes a specific constituent part. By the word *krīta* (bought) as well, that very same base noun is intended as being preceded by an instrument (*karaṇa*).
Consequently, when that [base] is being qualified, the rule of "extension to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies by virtue of the inherent capacity of the words.
He says that [an undesirable consequence] would follow: "from the nominal stem *krīta*. [Examples are: *vastrakrītī*, *vasanakrītī*.
In this case, there is the rule regarding the compounding of preverbs (*gati*), agents (*kāraka*), and subordinate words (*upapada*) with *kṛt*-derived stems.

Regarding the words *vastra* and *vasana* as instruments [of action], the compound with the word *krīta* occurs prior to the production of case-endings (*sup*), by virtue of the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32), which states that a word denoting an agent or an instrument is compounded with a *kṛt*-suffix ending, "frequently" (*bahulam*), even before the arising of case endings. Thus, it is said: *prāk subutpatteḥ* (Vyāḍipāda-vṛtti 138).

Regarding the forms *sukrītā* and *duṣkrītā*: because *gati* (indeclinables) function as upapadas, the compound occurs by the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18) prior to the generation of the case-ending (*sub*). In the word *duṣkrītā*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs according to the rule *idudupadhasya cāpratyayasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.41).
Regarding the rule "a compound is formed with that which ends in ṭāp," it should be understood that this applies only to two [words] ending in *sub*-suffixes (*sup*).

This is because once the suffix *ṭāp* has been applied, the status of being a *kṛdanta* (ending in a *kṛt* suffix) is established. Here, should *ṭāp* be applied first, or the case-ending (*vibhakti*)? Because it is *antaraṅga* (internal), *ṭāp* is applied first; subsequently, the external (*bahiraṅga*) [case-ending] follows.

The term "vibhakti" refers to a compound of two words ending in case endings. The status of being *antaraṅga* (internal) and *bahiraṅga* (external) regarding the two case endings, *ṭāp* and *ṅī*, has been explained in the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.1). To the question, "Once *ṭāp* has been applied, why does *ṅīṣ* not occur?", he says: "from *at*" (*ataḥ*).

And so forth. But how is the compound established with a word ending in *ṭā* (the feminine suffix), given that the rule "gati, kāraka, and upapada [words] are compounded with *kṛt*-derived forms before the occurrence of case-endings" (*Vyāḍīya-paribhāṣāvṛtti* 138) dictates that the compounding must take place only when the status of being a *kṛdanta* has already been attained? To this [it is replied]:
He says: "Of *gati*, *kāraka*, and *upapada*," and so forth. But how is that [compounding] stated to be "frequently" (*bahulam*)?

To this he replies: "The agent (*kartṛ*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*," and so forth. For by the rule "The agent and the instrument are frequently compounded with *kṛt*-derivatives" (Pāṇini 2.1.32), there is compounding of *gati*, *kāraka*, and *upapada* with *kṛt*-suffixes.

It is prescribed; and because of the inclusion of the term *bahulam* ("in various cases"), it occurs sometimes in the state of being a *kṛt*-derivative even before the production of case-endings (*sup*), and sometimes otherwise. Therefore, the rule "the statement regarding the compounding of prepositions (*gati*), case-words (*kāraka*), and subordinate words (*upapada*) with *kṛt*-derivatives takes place before the production of case-endings" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣāvṛtti 138) is [to be understood] as *bahulam*.
To this, the teachers say: the intention is that, for that reason, a compound is sometimes obtained even with a word ending in the feminine suffix *ṭāp*.
51. *ktād alpākhyāyām* | (Pāṇini 4.1.51) [The example is] *abhra-viliptī*. From the root *lip* (meaning "to smear," Dhātupāṭha 1433), the suffix *kta* is applied.
When there is the intention to express the meaning "smeared with few clouds," as in the previous case, [the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added] before the occurrence of the nominal suffix (*sup*).

This is a compound. However, the word "alpa" (small) is not employed because its meaning is already understood [from the context]. For example, in the phrase "candanānuliptā" (smeared with sandalwood paste), the meaning is "smeared with abundant sandalwood paste."

52. And [the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] after a *bahuvrīhi* compound that has an acute accent on the final syllable. (Pāṇini 4.1.52) For example: *śaṅkhabhinnī*. The substitution of *n* for *t* occurs by the rule "after *ra* and *da*" (8.2.42). Although the rule "the past passive participle" (2.2.36) would have required the word ending in the past passive participle to be placed first in the compound, it is not so because of the rule "after words denoting genus (*jāti*), time, or *sukha*, etc. (2.1.57).

The rule *paravacanam* (Vārttika 116) does not apply here. For words such as *śaṅkha* denote a genus (*jāti*). It is precisely for this reason that the final syllable has the udātta accent, according to the rule *jātikālasukhādibhyo 'nācchādanāt kto 'kṛtamitapratipannāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.170).
Regarding "ṭhgalakotkṛtī": the suffix *kta* is applied to the root *kṛtī* (DhP 1435), meaning "to cut.
Regarding "ṭhkeśalūnī": this means "one who cuts hair" (*keśān lunāti*). [The author] raises an objection concerning the substitution of *na* for *n* according to Pāṇini 8.2.44, *lvādibhyaḥ*.

Regarding the term *pādapatitā*: it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32), which results in the acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable. Regarding the phrase *antodātājjātapratiṣedhaḥ*: this refers to the prohibition of the suffix *ṅīṣ* after a *bahuvrīhi* compound that has an acute accent on its final syllable.

The prohibition [of the suffix] after a word ending in *jāta* is obtained precisely by the inclusion of the term "end" (*anta*) [in the sūtra]; therefore, it need not be stated. Here, the inclusion of "end" should indeed not be made; even without it, just as in the rule *varṇād anudātāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.39), it is understood as "ending in an unaccented vowel."
In this case as well, will it be understood that [the rule applies] only to that which has the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*)? It is formulated for this purpose:

so that [the suffix *cha*] may apply after a *bahuvrīhi* compound that is always (*nityam*) acutely accented on the final syllable, but not after one that is optionally (*vikalpena*) acutely accented on the final syllable. And in this regard, [it applies] in cases such as *dantājātā* and *stanajātā*.

By the rule *ṭhvā jāte* (Pāṇini 6.2.171), there is an optional elision of the final vowel; therefore, this [specific] rule will not apply. Alternatively—the word *vā* ("optionally") in the subsequent sūtra is a remainder (*śeṣa*) for both rules, and it is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*); thus, it will not apply to words ending in the stem *jāta*. However, in this case...

It should be understood that the mention of "extreme cases" (*antagrahaṇa*) in the commentary is solely for the sake of clarity. Regarding the rule "for words such as *pāṇigṛhītī* in specific meanings," the word "for the sake of establishment" (*siddhaye*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
For the sake of establishing forms such as *pāṇigṛhītī*, the suffix *ṅīp* occurs only in specific instances, not everywhere.

This is also obtained through the established *vibhāṣā* (optional rule). However, the specific meaning of the term *pāṇigrahaṇa* (taking of the hand) should be understood as follows: she whose hand is taken for the purpose of becoming a wife, preceded by the presence of fire as witness, is called *pāṇigṛhītī*. Regarding the phrase "in whatever manner," it refers to [the case] other than what has been stated.
The meaning is: "in some manner other than [the one previously mentioned].

Regarding the rule *abahunañ* and so forth, the meaning is that this should be explained as having the sense that the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not occur after words such as *bahu* when they precede [a feminine noun]. As for the explanation, however, it pertains to that very mention of the word *vā*.
This should be done by relying on the fact that the *vibhāṣā* rule is fixed (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). This applies to rules such as "jāti-kāla-sukha-ādi" (Pāṇini 2.1.49).

In the case of *bahukṛta*, the final syllable is udātta according to "bahor nañvat uttarapadabhūmni" (6.2.175). In the cases of *akṛtā* and *sakṛtā*, [the accentuation is governed] by "nañ-subhyām" (6.2.172).

Thus, in expressions such as "māsajātaḥ" ("born after a month"), the suffix *kta* is applied according to Pāṇini 6.2.170: "The suffix *kta* is used after words denoting genus (*jāti*), time (*kāla*), pleasure (*sukha*), and so forth, provided they do not denote clothing."

53. *asvāṅgapūrvapadādvā* (Pāṇini 4.1.53). Regarding the rule *ṭhasvāṅgapūrvapadāt*: "not a body-part" (*na svāṅgam*) is *asvāṅgam*; that which has such a non-body-part as its prior member (*pūrvapada*) in a *bahuvrīhi* compound is described as such. For example: *sāraṅgajagdhī*. [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. *Ada-*... [text fragment]

In the word *bhakṣaṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 1011), the substitution *jagdhi* occurs according to the rule *ṭhado jagdhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.36). Then, by the rule *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* (8.2.40), the *t* is changed to *gh*. Following this, the *gh* is elided by the rule *jharo jhari* (8.4.65). Thus we have *palāṇḍubhakṣitī*. [The root] *bhakṣa* is listed as *bhakṣa adane* (Dhātupāṭha 1557).
The suffix *ṇic* is applied according to the *cur-ādi* class. In the form *surāpī*, the substitution of *i* for the vowel is by the rule Pāṇini 6.4.66 (*ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām hali*).
In all these cases, the acute accent on the final syllable of the second member of the compound is by the rule Pāṇini 6.2.170 (*jātikālasukhādibhyo ’nācchādanāt*), etc.

Regarding the forms *vastracchannā* and *vasanacchannā*: from the root *chad*, meaning "to cover" (*apavāraṇe*), which belongs to the *cur*-class and takes the suffix *ṇic*, the word *cchanna* is derived by adding the *kta* suffix and is established as a nipātana (irregularly formed word) by the rule *vā vānta-śānta-pūrṇa-* (Pāṇini 7.2.27). This is further supported by the rule *anācchādanāt* (Pāṇini 6.2.170).

Thus, when the prohibition of the acute accent on the final syllable of the final member applies, and the *prakṛtisvara* (original accent) has been applied by the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, the first member retains its original accent" (Pāṇini 6.2.1), the remainder becomes *anudātta* (unaccented) according to the rule "a word is unaccented except for one [syllable]" (Pāṇini 6.1.158); therefore, in this case, there is no acute accent on the final syllable. Regarding the first member:

Thus, here today [the accentuation] is explained: one [word] by the *nit*-accent, the other by the *lit*-accent. From the root *ṭhtha* in the sense of "covering" (*ācchādane*, DhP 1023), with the suffix *ṣṭran*, we get *vastra*. From the root *vas* in the sense of "clothing," with the suffix *lyuṭ*, we get *vasana*.
By the rule beginning with "bahulam," [these forms are used] frequently in the Veda as technical names (*saṃjñā*).

The meaning is that this form, having such a sense, must be explained [as follows]: since the mention of the word *vā* (or) in that rule is a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (a restricted option), the suffix *ṅīṣ* will occur abundantly (*bahulam*) in both technical names (*saṃjñā*) and Vedic usage (*chandas*). Now, one might object:
since this very rule [P. 4.1.52] applies to *avasyā*, which is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the suffix *ṅīṣ* will occur [there] by that rule alone; for what purpose [is this further statement]?
If one asks, "Then what is this? he says: "And [the word] *pravṛddhā*," and so forth. He demonstrates a *tatpuruṣa* compound by means of a specific analysis [of its members]:
54. *svāṅgāccopasarjanādasaṃyogopadhāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.54).

Regarding "candramukhī": this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose face is like the moon. Here, by the rule "that which is designated in the nominative" (Pāṇini 1.2.43), the word *mukha* receives the technical designation of *upasarjana* (subordinate member). Regarding "atikeśī": this is a compound formed by the rule "kugatiprādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.2.18). [The rule] "eka-vibhakti ca" (Pāṇini 1.2.44) [also applies].
Thus, the word *keśa* has the status of an *upasarjana*.

Regarding the term *aṅga*: the meaning is that it must be explained as having the form "the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after [words] such as *aṅga* when they are *upasarjana*s. For what purpose? Because [the word *keśa*] has a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) as its penultimate letter, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would not otherwise apply.
This is obtained; for that purpose, this form of explanation must be provided. This is the explanation:

in the subsequent sūtra, the particle *ca* (and) serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; by means of it, the suffix *ṅīp* occurs after [stems ending in] *aṅga* and so forth, when they have a conjunct consonant as their penultimate letter.
Regarding the term "solid-fluid" (*ṭhadrava*): the air that issues forth through the mouth and nose is *prāṇa*;

one who possesses this *prāṇa* is *prāṇin*. That which resides therein is "residing in a living being" (*prāṇistha*). The mouth and so forth are called one's own limbs (*svāṅga*). If this were the case, then phlegm (*kapha*) would also be a limb, and consequently—

One might ask: "In the case of *bahukaphā*, would not the suffix *ṅīṣ* be applicable? To this he says: "provided it is not liquid" (*adrava*). Because of the inclusion of this qualification, this contingency does not arise, since phlegm (*kapha*) is liquid by nature.
Even so, one might argue that "knowledge" (*jñāna*) could be considered a "limb of the self" (*svāṅga*), because it resides in a living being and is not liquid; and consequently—
One might ask: "Would the suffix *ṅīṣ* also apply here in the case of *bahujñā*? To this he says: "possessing form" (*mūrtimat*).

That which is the dimension—such as shortness and so forth—of those substances that are not all-pervading is "form" (*mūrti*); that which possesses this is "possessing form. And [it is not the case that...].

It exists even in its absence [of cognition], because it is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*). Furthermore, since qualities belong to cognition as its own attributes, there is no possibility of it being a limb of itself. Even according to those for whom "form" (*mūrti*) is a specific kind of touch, such as hardness and so forth, [the same applies] to cognition.

It becomes embodied, for knowledge has no tactile contact. Even so, a swelling (*śopha*), which is designated as *śvayathu*, necessarily attains the status of being one's own limb (*svāṅga*), because it is characterized by the aforementioned qualifications. Consequently, in the word *bahuśophā*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied.

Since this [undesirable] consequence would follow, he says: "not born of transformation" (*avikāraja*). "Transformation" (*vikāra*) means an imbalance of the humors (*dhātu*), that is to say, a disturbance of the elements (*bhūta*); what is born from that is "born of transformation.
That which is not born of transformation is "not born of transformation. Thus, by the force of the qualification [applied] to the swelling (*śopha*), the same applies to the swelling as well.

It would not attain the status of being a "limb of one's own" (svāṅga). If a limb of one's own must reside in a living being, then in that case, hair fallen on a road or similar place would not have the status of being a limb of one's own; consequently, the form *dīrghakeśī rathyā* ("a street with long hair") would not be established. Therefore, he says: "residing therein," and so forth. [That is,] in that living being...

That which stays [in something] is "tatstha" (located therein); that which is not located therein is "atatstha," meaning not located in the body. Even so, hair and the like constitute a "limb of one's own" (*svāṅga*) provided they have been previously seen on a living being.
In that case, however, the facial features and other parts of a statue would not possess the status of being limbs of one's own.

One might ask: "Since [the face] does not reside in a living being (*aprāṇisthatvāt*), would the suffix *ṅīṣ* not be absent in the case of the expression 'dīrghamukhī pratimā' (a long-faced image)? To this he says: "And that of him in such a way. That which is a limb of that living being (*tasya prāṇinaḥ tat svāṅgam*) is connected by means of a particular configuration (*saṃsthānaviśeṣeṇa*) in whatever manner (*yathā*) it is joined; [the suffix applies] in that very way (*tathā*).

Even if it is connected to something that is not a living being, in such a manner, it still possesses the status of being its own limb (*svāṅga*). Alternatively— if this [limb] belongs to that living being and is joined to it in the same way as it is to a living being— it is likewise considered its own limb.

There is another reading: "tena cet tathā yutam. This means that if it is connected with that non-living thing (*aprāṇin*) in the same manner—as it was connected with that living being (*prāṇin*) through a particular configuration and so forth—then even in this case, it is considered its own limb (*svāṅga*). Alternatively: "by that [non-living thing], such as its mouth and so forth..."

If it is joined or connected in such a way as [the limbs] of a living being, even so it is a "limb of one's own" (svāṅga). Or else, if by that limb— such as a mouth or the like— that substance which does not reside in a living being is joined in the same manner as a substance belonging to a living being, even so it is a "limb of one's own."

It is so. The meaning is this in every respect: if a face or other limb belonging to a living being is of such a nature, then if it belongs to one who is not a living being, it is likewise considered a limb (svāṅga) only if it is of that very same nature.
55. [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] after *nāsikā*, *udara*, *oṣṭha*, *jaṅghā*, *danta*, *karṇa*, and *śṛṅga*. (4.1.55).

Regarding the phrase "when [the word] has many vowels" (*bahvac-lakṣaṇe*), etc.: for *nāsikā* and *udara*, this statement is made because a prohibition would otherwise apply by the rule "not after *kroḍa* and so forth when [the word] has many vowels" (4.1.56), which prohibits [the suffix *ṅīṣ*] when [the word] has many vowels. As for the remaining [words], [the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] by the general rule.
Regarding the phrase "from that which has a conjunct consonant as its penultimate" (Pāṇini 4.1.54), this refers to the indication of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*).
It is said: "However, the prohibition indeed applies to those preceded by *saha*, *nañ*, *vidyamāna*, or a *lakṣaṇa*.
Now, as for this rule concerning *nāsikā* and *udara*, [the principle is that] "exceptions stated earlier [in the text] supersede those immediately following them."

"Rules [of one type] subvert those that follow them, not others" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 9); thus, immediately thereafter, it subverts the prohibition characterized by the presence of many vowels (*bahvaj*), but not that characterized by *sa* and so forth. Furthermore, regarding *oṣṭha* and other such cases, "intermediate exceptions subvert preceding rules" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 10); thus, it subverts the preceding rule first.

The characteristic [of the suffix] is based on its connection with the following word; therefore, it becomes thus: *sahanāsikā*, *anāsikā*, and *vidyamānanāsikā*. Regarding "bimboṣṭhī": she whose lips are like the *bimba* fruit is *bimboṣṭhī*; [this is formed] by the rule:
"In a compound, the single substitute for both *o* and *uṣṭha* may optionally be stated" (Vārttika 687).

Thus, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is an optional addition (*aupasaṃkhyānika*). However, those who read the vowel *au* in the word *bimbauṣṭhī* apply the *vṛddhi* substitution according to the rule "vṛddhir eci" (Pāṇini 6.1.88).
[Regarding the suffix *ṅīṣ*,] it should be stated: "Also after a nominal stem ending in *puccha*"; thus, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after a nominal stem that ends in *puccha*.

The meaning is that this form of the word *bhavati* should be explained [in such a way]. For what purpose? So that [the suffix] may also apply after words ending in *puccha*, even when preceded by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*). However, the explanation must be made by relying on the fact that the particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. An example is *kalyāṇapucchī*.
One asks about its auspiciousness:
"kabara," and so forth. The suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after words ending in *puccha* that follow *kabara* and others.
This [suffix] also follows from that very [rule], either by virtue of the particle *ca* ("and") or by the inclusion of the word *vā* ("or").
This is obtained because the rule is one where the *vibhāṣā* (optionality) is fixed (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Thus, "that which has a tawny tail" is *kabarapucchī*;

likewise, *maṇipucchī*, *viṣapucchī*, and *śarapucchī*. By the rule "In a *bahuvrīhi*, when there is a locative case or a qualifier" (2.2.35), the word *puccha* does not undergo initial placement [as a prior member]; this is because of the [restriction] regarding the locative case.
This is because of the rule: "In the case of *gaḍu* and others, there is a statement [to the effect] that [the compound] is placed after [the word it qualifies]" (Vārttika 115).
Regarding the rule "after a word meaning 'resemblance', and after *pakṣa* and *puccha*," the word "always" (*nityam*) is understood to apply here.
This is also obtained from the two reasons previously mentioned. Furthermore, it is stated: "It should be said: 'and after *puccha*'. (Vārttika 364).

Since this [suffix] is already established by the preceding rule, the inclusion of the word *puccha* here again is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*), or for the sake of establishing its permanence (*nityārtha*).
That which has a tail like that of an owl is called *ulūkapucchī*.
56. *na kroḍādibahvacaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.56).
[The example] "kalyāṇakrīḍā" (auspicious play): the word *krīḍā* is feminine. [As stated:
"kroḍā, ghāṭā, jihvā, śirodharā, saṅga, kula, āspṛhā, māyā."
Because of the reading in the *Liṅgakārikā*. The analysis of the compound is: "she whose lap (*kroḍa*) is beautiful (*kalyāṇī*).

The masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is applied by the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat* (Pāṇini 6.3.34). The shortening of the final vowel of the second member (*uttarapada*) is effected by the rule *gostriyoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.48), etc. Then...

By this [sūtra], there is a prohibition of the suffix *ṅīp* which would otherwise have been applicable by the rule "ṭhsvāṅgāccopasarjanāt" (Pāṇini 4.1.54); consequently, the suffix *ṭāp* is applied. Thus we have "mahālalāṭā," where the substitution of *ā* for *tva* is effected by the rule "āmanmahat" (Pāṇini 6.3.46).

57. [The suffix *ka* is applied] after a word preceded by *saha* or *vidyamāna*. (Pāṇini 4.1.57) For example, *sa-keśaḥ*. This means "existing together with hair. The compound is formed by Pāṇini 2.2.28: *tena saheti tulyayoge* ("with that, in the sense of equal connection"). By Pāṇini 6.3.82: *vopasarjanasya*, the substitution of *sa-* for *saha-* occurs.

Regarding the example *a-keśaḥ*: "one whose hair does not exist" (*avidyamānāḥ keśā asya*). According to the Vārttika 102, *naño'styarthānāṃ bahuvrīhir uttarapadalopaś ca* ("with words having the sense of 'existent,' there is a bahuvrīhi compound with *nañ*, and the elision of the final member"), the word *vidyamāna* is elided.
Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *pūrva* [in the rule]? One might simply say *saha-nañ-vidyamānāt*; for by this [rule],...
Is it not the case that when a body part (*svāṅga*) is qualified by the fifth case (*pañcamī*), the requirement of being preceded by *saha* and so forth is indeed obtained?

This is not so; for the fifth case would qualify the body part as being "subsequent" (*para*)—that is, "the body part which follows after *saha* and so forth. And therefore, [the rule applies] to what follows after *saha* and so forth.
The analysis [of the compound] is: "she whose face is auspicious even for another by means of her own limb," or alternatively:
"he whose face is present is 'vidyamānamukhaḥ'; she whose auspicious one is 'vidyamānamukhaḥ'. This is because, when the word *pūrva* is employed, it denotes a constituent part (*avayava*).

Since the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is qualified by having "saha" and so forth as its prior member, when it is understood that [the rule applies] from a nominal stem ending in a word for a body part (*svāṅga*) which has "saha" and so forth as its constituent, there is no prohibition in this case; for this [stem *kalyāṇapāda*] does not have "saha" and so forth as its constituent. What then? It has the word "kalyāṇa" as its constituent.
Thus, there is no occurrence of an undesirable consequence.

58. [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] after [the word] *nakha* when it occurs at the end of a compound that is a proper name (*saṃjñā*). (Pāṇini 4.1.58) For example: *śūrpaṇakhā*. Here, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by the rule "In a proper name, [the *n* of] *nakha* following a preceding word [is replaced by *ṇ*, except when preceded by *ga*]" (8.4.3). Now, how is it that the Rākṣasī is called *śūrpanakhī*? It is because she is not a proper name (*asaṃjñātvāt*). It is stated [in the sūtra] "when it is a proper name," but...
And this is merely a designation. For instance, by the rule "pūrvapadāt" (Pāṇini 8.4.3) and so forth, the substitution of *ṇ* does not occur.
However, this is an etymological designation for her, based on her connection with nails shaped like winnowing baskets (*śūrpa*);
that is, she whose nails are like a winnowing basket is called Śūrpanakhī.

59. *dīrghajihvī ca cchandasī* (Pāṇini 4.1.59). Now, for what purpose is this substitution of the long vowel *ī* prescribed? Why not simply say, "In the Veda, [the word] *dīrghajihvā* [is formed]"? If it were stated in that way, then because of the context of prohibitions (*pratiṣedha-prakaraṇāt*), it would result in a prohibition.

If it is argued that [the rule] should be understood as an injunction (*vidhi*), we say no; because there is no possibility of attainment due to the suffix being a *saṃyogopadha*, and because prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*) are preceded by the possibility of attainment.
Therefore, he says—"The *nipātana* (irregular formation) is for the sake of making [the form] obligatory"—on account of its being a prescribed exception (*kalpita*).
Although this [suffix] ṅīṣ would be understood as optional here as well according to the general rule, it becomes compulsory by virtue of this specific grammatical derivation (nipātana).

60. *dik-pūrva-padān ṅīp* (Pāṇini 4.1.60). Regarding the statement "the rule for the suffix and the prohibition," etc.: the scope of the rule (*vidhi-viṣaya*) consists of a word denoting a bodily limb (*svāṅga*) that is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), ends in a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga-upadha*), and is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) such as *nāsikā* and others.
The scope of the prohibition concerns a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that has a conjunct consonant as its penultimate letter (*saṃyogopadha*),
as indicated by the rules "na kroḍādibahvacaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.56) and "sahanavidyamānapūrvācca" (4.1.57).
By this, he indicates [the application of] the rule "svāṅgāccopasarjanāsaṃyogopadhāt" (4.1.54).

The prescriptive rule beginning with (4.1.54) applies here, as does the prohibitive rule beginning with (4.1.56), "not after *kroḍa* and so forth when [the stem] has many vowels. Therefore, the suffix *ṅīp* must be prescribed only in those cases where *ṅīṣ* has been enjoined; however, in those cases where *ṅīṣ* is prohibited, [it is not applied].

"Even the *ṅīp* is prohibited. By the statement beginning with "where *ṅīṣ* is prescribed," he demonstrates the result in relation to the scope of the rule. But what is the difference between *ṅīp* and [the other suffix], since the form is the same in both cases? To this he says: "There is a difference in accent (*svara*). Regarding *ṅīp*—

For by the rule *hi-pit-ādanudātatvam* (the suffix is unaccented when preceded by a root marked with *hi* or *pit*), the [first syllable] becomes unaccented; however, for the suffix *ṅīṣ*, the first syllable is acute by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).

Regarding the word *prāṅmukhī*: the suffix *kvin* is applied to the root *añc* by the rule *ṛtvig-ādi* (Pāṇini 3.2.59), there is the elision of the nasal by the rule *aniditām* (6.4.24), and [the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added] by the rule *ugitaśca* (4.1.6).

The suffix *ṅīp* [is applied as follows]: *prācī*. In the sense of "having the face toward the eastern direction," the suffix *astāti* is added by the rule *dikśabdebhyaḥ saptamīpañcamī* (Pāṇini 5.3.27); then, by the rule *añcer luk* (5.3.30), there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix; and by the rule *luk taddhitaluki* (1.2.49), there is also elision of the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*).

The status of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is established by the rule *taddhitaś cāsarvavibhaktiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.38), and the elision of the case-ending (*sup*) follows from *avyayād āpsupaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.82). That which has its face turned toward the east is *prāṅmukhī*;
the nasalization of the letter *ṅ* is applied according to *yaro 'nunāsike 'nunāsiko vā* (Pāṇini 8.4.45). [Thus, the form] *prāṅmukhā*.

Thus [the suffix] *ṭāp* [is applied]. Now, one might object: "When *ṅīp* is excluded, should not *ṅīṣ* apply by the rule 'ṅīṣ after a word denoting a limb of the body that is an upasarjana' (Pāṇini 4.1.54)? This is not so;
the activity of the Teacher indicates that where there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) between a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*), the exception prevails.

The release of the suffix does not proceed [as a general rule], because here [Pāṇini] employs the word "or" (*vā*) in the rule *pīlāyā vā* (A 4.1.118). If, in this case, the suffix *aṇ* were optional, then once it is released, the suffix *ḍhak* [from the rule] *strībhyo ḍhak* (A 4.1.120) would necessarily apply; what then would be the purpose of employing the word "or"?

Therefore, by this mention of "or" (*vā*), the following is made known: where even a general rule (*utsarga*) is optional (*vibhāṣā*), there the general rule does not apply when it is set aside by an exception (*apavāda*). But how is a general rule optional? By means of the Great Option (*mahāvibhāṣā*). For instance, the suffix *aṇ* [prescribed] by "the suffix *aṇ* after [a stem ending in] *prāgdīvyat*" (Pāṇini 4.1.83) is a general rule.

The suffix *ḍhak* [is prescribed] by the rule "ṭhstrībhyo ḍhak" (Pāṇini 4.1.120); this is an exception (*apavāda*) to that. Even if the general suffix *aṇ* were to apply when that [ḍhak] is set aside, what would be the purpose of including the mention of *vā*? One should say: "No," for its purpose is to exclude the default suffix *aṇ*. By stating "it does not occur here," etc., he demonstrates the result of the requirement for a prohibition.

"Prākkroḍā, prāgjaghanā"—for here, because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *na kroḍādibahvacaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.56), the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not occur. "Prāggulphā"—here too, [the suffix *ṅīp* applies] because of the rules *asaṃyogopadhāt* (4.1.63) and *vahaśca* (3.2.64), which provide for the suffix *ṇvi*. From *ṇvi*...

The elision (*lopa*) removes everything [except the final phoneme]; by the rule "the penultimate vowel of a stem ending in *ṭh* or *t* is subject to *vṛddhi*" (Pāṇini 7.2.116), *vṛddhi* is applied; then the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added; and by the rule "for *vāh*, *ūṭh*" (Pāṇini 6.4.132), the *u* of *vāh* becomes *ūṭh*, which is designated as *saṃprasāraṇa*; this follows from the rule "there is *saṃprasāraṇa* for *vas*" (Pāṇini 6.4.131).

Because of the continued application of the term *samprasāraṇa*: the letter *ṭha* is for the purpose of specification in the rule "ṭhetyedhatyūṭhasu" (Pāṇini 6.1.89). By the rule "samprasāraṇācca" (6.1.108), there is substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*);
and by the rule "ṭhetyedhatyūṭhasu" (6.1.89), there is a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for the vowel *ā* of the preceding word, which is a *vṛddhi* [strengthening].

62. *sakhyaśiśvīti bhāṣāyām* | (Pāṇini 4.1.62) Regarding the word *sakhī*: it is formed by adding the suffix *ṅīp* to the word *sakhi*. By means of the supplementary statement "she has no child" (*nāsyāḥ śiśurasti*), [the author] indicates that this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; thus, for that *bahuvrīhi* which contains the word *aśiśu*, the form is *aśiśvī*.

It is elided; however, he shows that this is not a *tatpuruṣa* compound in the sense of "that which belongs to him. For in a *tatpuruṣa*, [the form] would not become *aśiśuḥ* from *na śiśuḥ*. Regarding the word *sakhā*: the substitution of *anaṅ* occurs by the rule *anaṅ sau* (Pāṇini 7.1.93), and [the lengthening of the vowel] occurs by the rules *nopadhāyāḥ* (6.4.7) and *sarvanāmasthāne ca* (6.4.8).

The word *dīrgha* [is used]. Although it could have been stated simply as "after *sakhi* and *śiśu*," the fact that this specific formation (*nipātana*) is employed has this purpose: so that it may apply to another word having the same phonetic form; thus, she who exists together with a friend (*kha*) is called *sakhī*.

63. *Jāteḥ astrīviṣayādayopadhāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.63). Since it is impossible for the term "from a *jāti*" to be in grammatical apposition with "from a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*), the word "nominal stem" here refers by metaphorical designation (*abhidheyopacāra*) to that nominal stem which expresses a genus (*jāti*).

It is expressed by the word "jāti" (genus); for this very reason, the commentary (*vṛtti*) says: "that nominal stem which denotes a genus," and "not having [only] the feminine as its domain. The word "domain" (*viṣaya*) is used even when something does not exist elsewhere; for this very reason, the commentary says: "and provided it does not apply to the feminine alone."

Regarding the term "niyata" (restricted): it is not that whose existence is restricted to the feminine gender alone; rather, that which exists in the feminine as well as elsewhere is "not restricted to the feminine" (*astrīviṣaya*).
It is called a "jāti" (genus/class); but what is this so-called *jāti*?

He provides the answer to the question with the words "ākṛtigrahaṇāt" and so forth. That by which something is made manifest (*ākriyate*) is called *ākṛti*; it refers to configuration (*saṃsthāna*). For instance, a bad *ākṛti* is said to be a bad configuration, and a good *ākṛti* is a good configuration. [The suffix -ti] is used in the sense of that by which something is grasped (*gṛhyate*).

*Grahaṇa* [is formed] with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of instrument (*karaṇe*). That whose apprehension (*grahaṇa*) is its form (*ākṛti*) is "form-apprehending" (*ākṛtigrahaṇā*), meaning that which is manifested by configuration (*saṃsthāna*). Now, one might object:
since the word *grahaṇa* occurs in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *ākṛti*, it functions in the feminine gender.

[One might object: "By the rule *ṭhṭhiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15), the suffix *ṅīp* should be applied; once the compound is formed with that [word ending in *ṅīp*], the suffix *kap* is added by the rule *nadyutaśca* (Pāṇini 5.4.153). Consequently, one would obtain the form *ākṛtigrahaṇīkā*. Is this not a fault? This is not a fault; for the word *grahaṇa* was previously derived in the sense of a general instrument (*karaṇasāmānya*).
It is subsequently connected with a specific [gender]. In that case, when another word is in proximity, whatever connection it has with a specific gender is considered *bahiraṅga* (external);
therefore, the compound is formed by first constructing the sentence with the *antaraṅga* (internal) general gender alone.
For example, as in the rule: "A sound articulated through the mouth and nose is nasal" (Pāṇini 1.1.8).
By this definition, it is stated that a *jāti* (universal) is a general form, such as "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth.
For cowness and the like are apprehended through their configuration (*ākṛti*), because they are manifested by the specific arrangement of features such as horns and the rest.
By this definition, specific castes such as Brahminhood and others are not included.

For these are not manifested by configuration (*saṃsthāna*); because the configuration of their substratum is indistinguishable. Indeed, whatever the configuration of a Brahmin may be, the configuration of a Kṣatriya and others is exactly the same. Therefore—

He states the second characteristic with the words "and of genders," etc. Even that genus which does not possess all genders, and which is manifested by non-configuration (asaṃsthāna), such as Brāhmaṇahood and so forth— it indeed possesses both the feminine and masculine genders, as in "brāhmaṇī" and "brāhmaṇaḥ."
It is [the word] "brāhmaṇī," and not the neuter gender; thus, it does not possess all genders.

Even in the case of "brāhmaṇatva" and so forth, one must rely on its being manifested by a specific designation (uddeśa); otherwise, since [the name] Devadatta takes two genders—as in "Devadattaḥ" and "Devadattā"—it would also have to be a genus (jāti) in this case as well. And this is not [the case].
It is not intended as a genus-term (*jāti-śabda*); rather, it is a technical name (*saṃjñā-śabda*). This is for the purpose of a rule (*vidhy-artha*).

Therefore, even those [words] that possess all genders (*sarva-liṅga-bhāj*) have the status of a genus (*jātitva*) by the preceding definition, such as *taṭaḥ*, *taṭī*, and *taṭam*. It is called "possessing all genders" (*sarva-liṅga-bhāk*) because it takes on all genders.

When *karman* is the upapada, the suffix *ṇvi* is applied by the rule *ṭhbhajo ṇviḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.62). Now, one might object: since the word *sarva* depends on gender, the suffix *ṇvi* would not apply when *sarva* is the upapada, because [the suffix] relies upon the upapada, and furthermore, there can be no compound with an upapada due to a lack of semantic capacity (*asamarthatvāt*). This is not a fault; for just as...

For in the case of "devadatasya gurukulam" (Devadatta’s teacher's family), the compound occurs even though there is no semantic connection (*asāmarthya*), because it is intelligible (*gamakatva*); in the same way, both [the general property and the individual] will be present here.
And that general property (*jāti*) is "to be grasped by being mentioned once" (*sakṛdākhyātanirgrāhyā*). "Once" (*sakṛt*) means one time.

"Expressed" (ākhyātā) means taught; "to be apprehended" (nirgrāhyā) means to be grasped with certainty. By this, he demonstrates the characteristics of the universal (jāti), namely: its manifoldness, its eternity, and its complete presence in each individual instance.
For it is expressed all at once in a single instance, whether it be a black or a white cow-individual.

It is indeed perceivable even in a cow-individual that is distinct from that [other individual]; for this very reason, it is eternal and fully present in each [individual]. For if it were not one, then when "cow" is expressed once, it would not be apprehended in another individual. And if it were not eternal, then upon the destruction of the individual, its [destruction] would follow.

Furthermore, it would not be perceived by another lump even after its destruction. And if it were not fully present in each [lump] in its entirety, then it would not be perceived in its entirety even in that very lump where it was described, let alone in another lump! For if it were present only partially, [the aforementioned difficulties would follow].
Only the portion that is real (*satya*) is grasped, not the genus (*jāti*). The genus-portion does not itself become the genus, because that would entail the fallacy of [the genus] being manifold.
He states the third definition of genus with the words "and lineage" (*gotraṃ ca*), etc. [The definition is: "Offspring beginning with the grandson... (*apatyaṃ pautraprabhṛti*).

Regarding the term *gotra* [in Pāṇini 4.1.162], it has a technical (*pāribhāṣika*) meaning; however, in this context, even the worldly (*laukika*) sense of *gotra*—meaning simply offspring—is intended. *Caraṇa* is of many kinds according to the differences in Vedic recension. *Gotra*, together with *caraṇa*, constitutes a caste (*jāti*). *Gotra* refers to [lineages] such as Nāḍāyana and so forth, although [the status of] being a Nāḍāyana and so on...

The universal (sāmānya) is postulated just like the lineage (gotra); nevertheless, it is not manifested by configuration (saṃsthāna). Furthermore, because it exists in all genders—as "Nāḍāyana is a man," "Nāḍāyanī is a woman," and "Nāḍāyana is a neuter"—therefore, for the purpose of establishing that lineage possesses the status of a genus (jāti), [the following is stated].

And it has been stated that this refers to the *gotra*. However, because the word *caraṇa* is applied by virtue of its connection with the act of Vedic study, it is strictly an action-word (*kriyāśabda*) rather than a genus-word (*jātiśabda*). Therefore, in order to establish that its referent is indeed a genus, it was said "together with the *caraṇas*."

"Kukkuṭī, śūkarī, mayūrī"—these are examples of a genus (*jāti*) apprehended through its form. "Brāhmaṇī, vṛṣalī"—these are [examples] not possessing all genders. "Nāḍāyanī, cārāyaṇī"—these are examples of a genus characterized by a lineage (*gotra*). [The suffix] *phak* is applied after the words *naḍa* and *cara* according to Pāṇini 4.1.97: *naḍādibhyaḥ phak*.
In the sense of "daughter of a Phak," [we have] *ṭhkaṭhī* and *bahvṛcī*; these are based on the characteristic of a Vedic school (*caraṇa*).

[The word] *muṇḍā* is used because of the connection with the quality of being shaven (*muṇḍaguṇa*). It is not restricted to females—such as *muṇḍo devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta is shaven")—because the word *muṇḍa* is applied even to a male. But not... [the others].

Is it a word denoting a genus (*jātiśabda*)? No; rather, it is a word denoting a quality (*guṇaśabda*). As for "fly" (*makṣikā*): because it is always restricted to the feminine gender, the word *makṣikā* has the feminine as its referent. As for "Kṣatriya woman" (*kṣatriyā*): here, "genus" (*jāti*) refers to a lineage (*gotra*).
This is because [the suffix] *-ya-* is applied to "Kṣatra" by Pāṇini 4.1.138 (*kṣatrād dhaḥ*) to denote a descendant of a lineage.

Because it is prescribed by a specific rule and because it possesses the characteristic mark of a genus (*jāti*), it is a *jāti* term. Furthermore, since the word "kṣatriya" applies even to a male—as in the case of "a kṣatriya"—the word *kṣatriya* does not have the feminine as its exclusive domain.
However, regarding a word with *y* as an upadhā, [the rule] "in the prohibition concerning words with *y* as an upadhā... [applies].
"There is no prohibition for *hayā*, *gavayā*, *mūkā*, *tsyā*, and *manuṣyā*. How, then, is this obtained?

Because the particle *ca* in the subsequent sūtra has the sense of including what was not explicitly mentioned. For by that [subsequent rule], since the suffix *ṅīṣ* is prescribed after *hayā*, *gavayā*, and so on, this prohibition does not apply. Thus, we have "matsī."
In the case of *sūryatiṣyāgastyamatsyānām* (Pāṇini 6.4.149), there is the elision of the *yat* suffix. Regarding *manuṣī*:
by the rule *manorjātāvañyatau ṣuk ca* (4.1.161), the suffix *yat* is applied and the augment *ṣuk* is added.
Furthermore, the status of these—such as *puruṣa*, *haya*, *gavaya*, and so forth—as generic classes (*jāti*) should be understood from their being grasped through their form (*ākṛtigrahaṇāt*).

64. *pākakarṇaparṇapuṣpaphalamūlabālotarapadācca* (Pāṇini 4.1.64). [The suffix] *ṭhañ* [is applied after a word ending in *pāka*, etc., when it is the final member]. For example: *odanapākī*. This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the cooking of rice. However, this [formation] is made merely for the sake of etymological derivation; no actual meaning of the individual parts exists here, for this is indeed a conventional whole.
It exists in a certain genus (*jāti*). In this same way, it should be understood in the case of "ṭhśahkukarṇī" and so forth as well.
65. From this [class] of human beings: (Pāṇini 4.1.65).
[The examples are] *āvantī* and *kuntī*. By means of the words *āvantī* and *kuntī*, in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*), [the suffix] *ñyaṅ* is applied according to (Pāṇini 4.1.171):
*vṛddhet-kośalājādāñ-ñyaṅ*.

By the rule *ṭhstriyāmavantikuntukurubhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.176), there is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix], and then the suffix *ṅīṣ*. Thus: *dākṣī*, *plākṣī*. By the rule *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95). For in all cases, *gotra* is indeed a genus (*jāti*). [Examples: *viṭ*, *darat*. Regarding the offspring of the *viś* [clan], [the suffix] *añ* is applied by the rule *janapadaśabdātkṣatriyādañ*.

(4.1.168) | *Dārada* [is derived] by the rule *dvyañmagadhādi-sūtra* (4.1.170), which prescribes the suffix *aṇ*; by the rule *ataśca* (4.1.177), there is elision (*luk*) of these two [suffixes] in the feminine. Here too, "lineage" (*gotra*) is a "class" (*jāti*). Regarding *titiri*:
here, the class is defined by the apprehension of form (*ākṛtigrahaṇā jātiḥ*). Regarding *audameyī*: here, "lineage" (*gotra*) is [derived] by the rule *ata iñ* (4.1.95).

"Jātiḥ | ṭhiña upasaṃkhyānam" (Vārttika). This means that an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the suffix *ṅīṣ* after words ending in *iñ*. For what purpose? To include cases where it is not a genus (*ajāti*). That is, so that [the suffix] may apply even to words ending in *iñ* that do not denote a genus. In this regard, the following...

Regarding the explanation: here a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule) is made for the word "sthitāḥ," whereby [the suffix] will also apply after a feminine stem ending in *iṅ* that does not denote a genus (*ajāti*). Following that, the second rule, "manuṣyajāteḥ" (after a genus name denoting a human), is intended to indicate that the preceding rule is not mandatory (*anityatva*). By means of this—

In the case of a specific genus (*jāti*), [the suffix] is used invariably; elsewhere, however, it is according to what is observed—only in certain instances, not everywhere. "Sautāṅgami" and so forth are examples. It might be argued: since the suffix *iñ* is prescribed by the rule *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95) specifically for a descendant in the line of a clan (*gotrāpatya*), and a clan is indeed a genus (*jāti*), then...
What is being said? [Namely,] that there is a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the suffix *iñ* in order to exclude its application when [the base] denotes a genus (*jāti*).
To this he says: "From *sutaṅgama* and so forth," etc. [The example is: "A city established by Sutaṅgama.

Here, because it belongs to the *sutaṅgama*-class, the suffix *iñ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.2.80, *vuñ-chaṇ-kvāḍ-ya-javidakakaṭhacañyañ-nika-ṭhaka-ṭhañ-ñiṅ-ñakañ-kvarapaḥ*. [The form] *itaḥ* [is derived from the word *it*].
The application of *tap* (the long vowel marker) is for the purpose of preventing lengthening. Therefore, this [lengthening] does not occur in the case of *avantī*.

When one desires *avantī*, by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8), the suffix *kyac* is added; then, by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* (7.4.25), lengthening occurs. With the form *avantīya* thus established, the suffix *kvip* is applied, and by the rule *ato lopaḥ* (6.4.48), the final vowel is elided.

Thus, there is the elision of the letter *a*. Because the term "elision" (*lopa*) was mentioned previously, the elision of *y* occurs first by the rule "the elision of *y* and *v* before *v*al" (6.1.66), and subsequently the elision of the *v* by the rule "the elision of an uncombined (*apṛkta*) suffix ending in *v*" (6.1.67). Then, when the form *avantī* is established, if the specification of the long vowel *ā* (*taparakaraṇa*) were not made, [the following would occur].

From this [suffix] as well, [the suffix *ap*] would arise; consequently, by the rule "ṭh-ḍha-l-ṅ-y-āp-bhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.68), the elision of the case-ending *su* would apply, and thus the form "Avantī" would not be established.
66. *ūrūtaḥ* | (4.1.66) Regarding "ṭhkurūḥ": the feminine descendant of Kuru—[formed by] *kurunādibhyo ṇyaḥ* (4.1.172);
[then] by *striyām avanti-kurubhyaś ca* (4.1.176) and so forth, there is the elision (*luk*) of that [suffix]. Here, "lineage" (*gotra*) means "caste" (*jāti*).

Regarding the term *brahmabandhūḥ*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose relative is a Brahmin" (*brahma bandhuḥ asyāḥ*) or "one whose relative is a hero" (*vīraḥ bandhuḥ asyāḥ*). The words *brahmabandhū-* and *vīrabandhū-* refer to a specific caste (*jāti*). Its status as a *jāti*, moreover, is due to its not possessing all genders; for those two [words] exist only in the feminine and masculine genders, and not otherwise.

These two are neuter genders. In the rule *utaḥ*, the use of the *tapara* (long vowel marker) is for the sake of ease of pronunciation, not for the purpose of excluding the long vowel (*dīrgha*); this is because there is no word denoting a human genus that ends in a long *ū*.
In the example *ṅkāraḥ* and so forth: if the *ṅ* were not attached to *ūṅ*, then...
Even in the case of the rule *nodhātvoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.175), [the addition of the marker *ṅ*] would not need to be prescribed;

for there exists no other *ū*-vowel besides that which possesses the *ṅ*-anubandha. Consequently, if it were stated simply as *nodhātvoḥ*, then even in forms such as *yavāgvā* and *yavāgvai*, [the rule *udāttayaṇo...*] would apply.

By the rule *halpūrvāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.174), there would be a prohibition of the acute accent (*udāttatva*) that would otherwise apply to the third case-ending and subsequent cases. Now, one might object: since the vowel *ū* is specified as being meaningful (*arthavat*), the principle *arthavadgrahaṇe nānarthakasya* (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 1)—which states that when a meaningful element is mentioned, an element lacking meaning is not included—will prevent this from occurring; for the word *yavāgū* [is indeed meaningful].

The word *āgūḥ* is derived from the rule "ṭhsṛyuvacibhyo'nyujāgūjaknucaḥ" (Dhātupāṭha 10.4), being formed with the suffix *āgūc*. In that case, is it not the case that the word *āgūc* alone is meaningful as the sense of the suffix, while the vowel *ū* is entirely meaningless? This is not so; for this grammatical maxim (*paribhāṣā*) is not established to apply in the case of the mention of individual phonemes (*varṇa*).

This [term] is a mention of the phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*); therefore, it does not apply. But if it were to apply, even so, there would be a mention of the suffix *ū* [in the rule] "from the roots *kṛṣ*, *cam*, *tan*, *dhani*, *sarj*, and *kharj*, the suffix *ū*" (Daiva-Uṇādi 1.164). Consequently, a prohibition would undesirably follow in cases such as *kharjvā* and *kharjve*.

Therefore, the marker *ṅ* must be applied for the sake of specification. Now, what is the purpose of the long vowel pronunciation? Should it not simply be stated as *uRē*, since by the rule "a short vowel followed by a homogeneous vowel becomes long" (Pāṇini 6.1.101), the long vowel is indeed included within the designation of the short vowel? To this, he says: "The pronunciation of the long vowel," and so forth. If...

If the long vowel were not pronounced, then, by virtue of the subsequent rule *ṭhaśiṣādvibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 5.4.154), the suffix *kap* would optionally apply; therefore, the long vowel is pronounced in order to preclude that. But how does the pronunciation of the long vowel effect the exclusion of *kap*? [In the case of] *brahmā bandhūrasya*.

Immediately after the formation of the compound, should *ūṅ* be applied, or *kap*? In that case, because it is subsequent in order, *kap* would apply; for by the explicit utterance of the long vowel, there is an elision (*praśleṣa*) of the short *u*. A restatement [of the rule] applies when both [suffixes] are simultaneously eligible; since it is a suffix added for its own sake (*svārthika*), it pertains specifically to the application of *kap*, which belongs to the same class.

It causes [the suffix] to be replaced, but not the rule for *svādi* [suffixes]. However, *svādi* suffixes do indeed occur after a stem ending in *ūṅ*, because *ūṅ* is also included in the scope of the rule, or else because of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), namely the mention in Pāṇini 1.2.71: "The father-in-law [is called] *śvaśura* by virtue of his wife" (*śvaśrū*). Therefore, in the word *brahmabandhūḥ*, it remains invariably ending in *ū* alone, and not—

Sometimes [the form] is *kabantaḥ*, as in "adhvaryuḥ. [The derivation is as follows: from the root *ad* with the suffix *u*, the desiderative suffix *kyac* is applied in the sense of "one who desires sacrifice" (*adhvara*), followed by the suffix *up* according to Pāṇini 3.2.170 (*kyāc chandasi*). Then, the vowel *a* is elided according to Pāṇini 7.4.39 (*kavyaghvarapṛtanasyarci lopaḥ*).

"Ṭhāprāṇijāteśca" and so forth. The meaning is that this rule must be explained as having the sense: "The suffix ūṅ occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting a genus of non-living beings. In this regard, the explanation is as follows:
in the rule "paṅgośca" (Pāṇini 4.1.68), the particle *ca* (and) serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned.

Therefore, due to the absence of aspiration (*apraṇijāti*) and because it is devoid of [the quality of] being a rope and so forth, there will be the forms *alābūḥ* and *karkandhūḥ*. What, then, is the difference between this [form] having the vowel *uṅ* and not having it, since in both cases the form is the same and the accent is the same? For instance, the word *alābū*.
In the *Uṇādisūtras*, that which ends in the suffix *u* is derived as follows:

from the rule "from the roots *kṛṣ*, *cam*, *tan*, *dhani*, *sarji*, and *kharji*, the suffix *ū* [is added]" (*Daiva Uṇādi Sūtra* 1.164), and while the condition *pit* is in effect, the rule "the suffix is *ṇit*" (*Daiva Uṇādi Sūtra* 1.168) applies; furthermore, from the rule "after the root *lamb*, when preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, there is also elision [of the *m*]" (*Daiva Uṇādi Sūtra* 1.170), it is derived from a base preceded by *nañ*.

The reading should be "from the root *ḷab* in the sense of 'slipping down' (*avasraṃsane*), the suffix *ū* is applied. Thus, according to the rules "in the present tense, with the augment *ṇit*" and "with the prefix *nañ*, from *laṃb*, there is elision of *na*," the suffix *ū* is applied to the root *ḷab* (*labi avasraṃsane*, Dhātupāṭha 379) preceded by the negative particle *nañ*.

By the rule *ṭhito num* (Pāṇini 7.1.58), the augment *num* is prescribed for a form ending in *ṭh*, and the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *n* is also ordained. Furthermore, the word *karkandhū* is derived while the rule *nṛtiśṛdhyoḥ kūḥ* (Daiva Uṇādi Sūtra 1.174) is in effect, [along with] the rule *andūdṛnbhūjambūkaphelūkarkandhūdidhiṣūḥ*.
Since [the word *alābū*] has been derived as ending precisely in the vowel *ū* [by the rule *ūṅ ṇoḥ*], for what purpose is the suffix *ūṅ* prescribed?

It is so that in forms such as *alābvā* and *alābvai*, there may be the prohibition of the acute accent on the beginning of the case-ending by the rule *noṅdhātvoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.175). For if that [suffix *ūṅ*] were not present, as [in the case of other words],...
Just as [the substitution] does not occur in *khalapv-au* and *khalapvaḥ*, so too it would not occur here either.
67. [The suffix *cha* (i.e., *īya*) is applied] after words ending in *bāhu* when a name (*saṃjñā*) is formed. (Pāṇini 4.1.67) 68. [The suffix *cha* is applied] also after *paṅgu*.
(Pāṇini 4.1.68) [And there is the rule: "In the case of *śvaśura*, there is the elision of the phonemes *u* and *a*. However, this [form] is *śvaśuraḥ śvaśruvā*.
(1.2.71) It should not be stated that [the form] is established solely by means of this irregular derivation (*nipātana*).

69. *ūrūtarapadādaupamye* | (4.1.69) [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after a word ending in *ūru* when it is the second member of a compound, provided that the comparison is with something round. Regarding the example *vṛtoruḥ*: the printed reading is *vṛtāv ūrū*.
She whose thighs (*ūrū*) are round (*parimaṇḍala*) is called *vṛtoruḥ*. For the sake of brevity, it should have been stated as "after a word ending in *ūru*" (*ūrvantāt*).

It was stated [in Pāṇini 5.4.96] "when *ūru* is the final member [of a compound]"— this is for the sake of ensuring that the rule applies where the word *ūru* alone is the final member; otherwise, if it were stated as "after *arvant*," then it would also apply in a case such as *hastisvāmyūrūḥ*, meaning "she whose husband's thighs are like those of an elephant" (*hastina iva svāmina ūrū yasyāḥ sā*).

It might be so; for this is indeed a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *ūrū*. However, there is no fault in the mention of "the latter member" (*uttarapada*), because this is not a nominal stem that has *ūrū* as its latter member; rather, it is a nominal stem that has *svāmyūrū* as its latter member.
70. *saṃhita-śapha-lakṣaṇa-vāmā-deḥ* (4.1.70). Regarding the example *saṃhitorūḥ*: the word *saṃhita* signifies "joined together"; thus, the meaning is "one whose thighs are joined together."

The meaning is that this should be explained as follows: "It should be stated that [the suffix] *ūṅ* occurs after the word *uru* when it follows either *sahita* or *saha*. This means that one must explain the rule in such a way that *ūṅ* is applied to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in the word *uru* which is preceded by these two words, *sahita* and *saha*. Regarding this, the following is the explanation: the letter *gh* is inserted here; that...
And it has the sense of "collecting what is not [otherwise] joined"; by that, it will also apply with *sahita* and *saha*.

The inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the Sūtra is a sign for the continuation (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "the subsequent member is *ūru*" (*ūruttarapada*). Otherwise, the meaning would be understood as: "the suffix occurs only after nominal stems (*prātipadika*) such as *saṃhitā* and so forth."
For if the suffix were indeed carried over by virtue of its being *svarita*,

then even when this intermediate word exists, the suffix would still be attached only to that which follows these [words], namely to the word *ūru* in *saṃhitasvāmyūru*, and not to the word *ūru* in *saṃhitoru*.
Because it functions as a subordinate attribute (guṇabhāva), the word "thigh" (ūru) could not possibly serve as a qualifier here.
71. *kadrukamaṇḍalvoś chandasi* (Pāṇini 4.1.71).

The word *kadru* denotes a particular color; from it, although the suffix *ṅīṣ* would have been applicable by the rule *ṭhvoto guṇavacanāt* (4.1.44), its prohibition is applied by the Vārttika *kharusaṃyogopadhayoḥ* (Vārttika 349).
This statement is made because, although the base noun (*prātipadika*) has already been employed, there was no prior expression [of the feminine];

furthermore, since the word *kamaṇḍalu* does not denote a living being, the suffix *ūṅ* would have applied by the rule "after words denoting non-living beings, except for *rajju* and others" (Vārttika 369). Therefore, this is for the purpose of restriction in the Vedic language (*chandas*). Alternatively—this...
Since [the prohibition] applies to the rope and so forth, the statement is intended to establish the attainment [of the rule].
72. [The suffix *ṅīp* is applied] after [a stem ending in] *saṃjñā*.

(4.1.72) 73. [The suffix] *ṅīn* is applied after the *yañ* [suffix] in the case of [stems] beginning with *śārṅgarava*. (4.1.73) Examples: *baidī*, *aurvī*. [These are derived] from the words *bidu* and *urva* by means of [the suffix] *ṭhak* according to [Pāṇini 4.1.104]: *anṛṣyānantarye*. (4.1.104)

By such [rules] as these, the suffix *añ* is applied; since that which ends in it does not belong to the *agotra* class, and because it is a genus (*jāti*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* would otherwise be required by the rule for genera, but *ṅīn* is prescribed instead. There is a difference in accent.
These words end in *aṇ*. From the word *gotama*, in the sense of a descendant, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to *ṛṣy-andhaka-vṛṣṇi-* (Pāṇini 4.1.114).

By these and other rules, the suffix *aṇ* [is applied]; however, for the remaining cases, [the rule] "tasyāpatyam" (Pāṇini 4.1.92) applies. From the word *gautama*, because it is included in the *gaura-ādi* group, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* also occurs. [The statement] "these end in *ḍhak*" is due to their belonging to the *śubhra-ādi* group. [The form] "kāmaṇḍaleyaḥ" [is derived by applying] "ḍhea lopo 'kadr̥vāḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.147).

Thus, there is the elision of the vowel *u*. This is a rule [stated] because the suffix *ṅīp* would otherwise apply to these by [Pāṇini 4.1.15], *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*. Regarding "Vātsyāyana": from the word *vatsa*, which ends in the *yañ* suffix belonging to the *garga*-class, the suffix *phak* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.101], *yañiñośca*. Regarding "Mauñjāyana": from the word *muñja*.

The suffix *phak* is applied by the rule *ṭhañādibhyaḥ phak* (Pāṇini 4.1.99). [The word] "jāti" refers to the characteristic of a *gotra*. For even in common usage, what is conventionally termed a *gotra* is included there; and even a *yuvan* (descendant in the fourth generation and beyond) is called a *gotra* in the world, as speakers say: "He is a Gārgyāyaṇa by *gotra*. [The phrase] "ending in *ḍhak*" [is used].
Because the word *kekasa* belongs to the *śubhrādi* group, [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied; furthermore, [the suffix] *tāp* is applied even after a word ending in *añ* or *ñyaṅ*.

From the words *kapi* and *śibi*, when the sense is "descendant" (*apatya*), the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied by the rule *vṛddhet kośalājādāñ ñyaṅ* (Pāṇini 4.1.171). Since [the feminine suffix] *cāp* would also have been applicable by the rule *ñyaṅśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.74), this statement [is made as an exception]. [Thus: *ehi*.
"Search! [This is derived] from the root *īh* meaning "to strive" (Dhātupāṭha 632), with the prefix *ā-* and further the prefix *pari-*.
According to the *uṇādi*-sūtra *pin*, [the suffix *in* is added]; however, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), it is observed that the suffix *in* occurs after all roots—namely, "after all roots."

Thus, there is the suffix *in*. Since the suffix *ṅīṣ* would otherwise apply by virtue of the reading in the *Gaṇasūtra* 50, "after words beginning with *bahu*, and after a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix vowel, except for *ktin*," this statement is made [to prevent that]. Regarding the term "ending in *yañ*": because [the word *gārgī*] belongs to the *Gargādi* group, both the suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṣpha* would apply by Pāṇini 4.1.16 (*yañaśca*) and 4.1.17 (*prācāṃ ṣpha taddhitaḥ*). [This rule prevents those.]
Regarding the word *āṬdapānaḥ*—the printed reading is *pudapānaḥ*.

[The form] *āṬdapānaḥ* is derived by the rule *śuṇḍikādibhyo’ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.3.76), meaning "coming from a well" (*udapāna*). Since this word is listed among the *utsādi* group, when the suffix *añ* is applied there, there is no difference whether one uses the feminine suffix *ṅīp* or *ṅīṣ*.

For in both cases, one must consider that [the suffix] ought to be udātta by virtue of the rule *ṭhñnityādir nityam* (Pāṇini 6.1.197); having this in mind, he says: "The word ending in *aṇ*, beginning with *śauṇḍika*, serves as the motivator. As for the term "jāti" (genus): because *arāla* and *caṇḍāla* do not possess all genders (*asarvaliṅga*), they possess the status of a genus (*jātitva*).
This statement is made because the suffix *ṅīṣ* would otherwise apply to *vataṇḍa* by virtue of its being listed among the words beginning with *gaura*.

By the rule "the feminine suffixes *ṅīṣ* and *ṣpha* supersede [those that would otherwise apply] when a *taddhita* suffix follows" (4.1.16), and specifically by the rule "for the descendants of the Easterners, the *taddhita* suffix *ṣpha* [is added]" (4.1.17), there is a supersession of both *ṅīṣ* and *ṣpha*.
The feminine descendant of *vataṇḍa* is formed with the suffix *yañ* according to the rule "from *vataṇḍa*, [the suffix *yañ* is applied]" (4.1.108); this *yañ* is then elided.
There is elision (*luk*) by [Pāṇini 4.1.109] *striyām*.

Regarding [the rule] *bhogavadgaurimatoḥ saṃjñāyām*: when a name (*saṃjñā*) is understood, the suffix *ṅīn* occurs after the words *bhogavat* and *gaurimat*. Because they end in the suffix *mat*, [the suffix *ṅīp* would otherwise apply] by [Pāṇini 4.1.6] *ugitaśca*.

(4.1.6) This statement is made because the suffix *ṅīp* would otherwise apply. Now, the word *bhoga* ends in the suffix *ghañ*, and the word *gauri* ends in the suffix *iñ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.95;

thus, both of these are acute on the first syllable (*ādyaudātta*) due to the accent of the *ñit* suffixes. The suffix *matup* added to them is unaccented (*anudātta*) because it is marked with *p*. And so:

Since there is no difference whether the suffix *ṅīp* or *ṅīṣ* is prescribed after words ending in *bhoga* and *gaura*, for what purpose is the suffix *ṅīn* prescribed after them? To this he says: "In order to ensure the constant shortening [of the vowel] in the case of *gha*-class suffixes," meaning that in rules such as *gharūpakalpa* (Pāṇini 6.3.43), the shortening is constant.

The rule for the suffix *ṅīn* is prescribed by those two [sūtras] as in *bhogavatitarā* and *gaurimatitarā*. However, if the suffix *ṅīp*, characterized by the presence of an *uṅit* vowel, were applied instead, then— while the phrase "optionally for the remainder of a nadī-stem" (*nadyāḥ śeṣasyāntayatarasyām*) from 6.3.44 is still in force— the rule "also after that which ends in an *uṅit*" (*ugitaśca*) from 6.3.45 would apply.

Thus, by this alternative rule, there would be shortening. Now, even with this [suffix] *ṅīn*, why does shortening not optionally occur by the rule "ṭhugitaśca" (Pāṇini 6.3.45), given that this [suffix] occurs after bases ending in *ug* such as *bhogavat* and *gaurimat*? To what extent is there optional shortening for bases ending in *ug*?

It occurs thus. Furthermore, that [suffix] which is prescribed by this sūtra is not considered to be prescribed by the designation *nadī* or *ugit*; for there is no reliance on the status of being an *ugit*. Why is it said "when it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*)"? [Consider] *bhogavatī*, *gaurimatī*. Here, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭhugitaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.6). And here, among the *ghādi* group...
The very act of conceptualization (*vikalpanā*) itself becomes the feminine suffix *hrasva*—namely, *bhogavatitarā*, *bhogavatītarā*, *gaurimatitarā*, and *gaurīmatītarā*.

Regarding the word *nṛ*, [the rule] "there is also *vṛddhi* for *nṛ* and *nara*" applies; and for the word *nṛ*, [the rule] "after words ending in *ṛt* or *n*, the suffix *ṅīp*" (Pāṇini 4.1.5) applies.

This statement is made because [the suffix] *ṅīp* would otherwise apply. Since the word *nara* would take the suffix *ṭāp* by the rule "ṭhājādyataḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.4), or alternatively the suffix *ṅīṣ* because it denotes a genus (*jāti*), the status of being a genus arises from its being apprehended through its generic form (*ākṛti*). Furthermore, the *vṛddhi* strengthening occurs for those two [suffixes], and that [strengthening] applies to the word *nṛ* according to the paribhāṣā "alo'ntyasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.52).

It occurs in place of the *ṛ* sound. When the elision (*lopa*) of the *ya* in the word *nara-* has been performed by [Pāṇini 6.4.148], it is in place of the *akāra*. But is it not the case that, according to the maxim "in the absence of a modification of the final, [the substitute] belongs to what is in the vicinity of the final" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 63), it ought to belong to the *repha* itself? This is not a fault; for in this context, the original form (*prakṛti*) is that which precedes the *vṛddhi*.
Regarding the genitive case: where there is a genitive, the vowel *a* is understood as the substitute for the locus (sthānin), according to the rule "where there is a genitive, there is a substitute.

Some read the word *putra* here; however, since that [word] does not by itself denote a female, this is taken as ending in a compound-affix (*samāsānta*). And when it occurs with a compound-affix, it is [replaced] by the word *duhitṛ*.
Being of the same meaning, it becomes feminine—as in *pradyotaputrī* (daughter of Pradyota) and *śailaputrī* (daughter of Śaila). "According to the application" means according to what is possible.

74. *yañca-ap-*. Here, the letter *p* in *ap* serves the purpose of including the general category [of prātipadikas] in the rule *ṭiṅyāpprātipadikāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.1), while the letter *c* in *yac* serves the purpose of preventing that exclusion. Thus, both [the *p* and the *c*] function elsewhere as well.

Since the two [suffixes] have already fulfilled their purpose, the rule *citaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.163), which prescribes that the final syllable of a word ending in a *cit* suffix is udātta, takes precedence over the rule *anudāttau suppitau* (3.1.4) by virtue of its posteriority; thus, the feminine suffix *cāp* becomes udātta. This [mention of] *ñyaṅ* and *ṣyaṅ* is a general reference, having set aside the specific indicatory letters (*anubandha*).
This is the apprehension of that which is the commonality (*sāmānya*) consisting merely of the element *yaṅ*. But how is the apprehension of a commonality appropriate here?

For it would be more appropriate to apprehend only the element *ñyaṅ*; for instance, since this [element] being prescribed in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*) is incapable of expressing femininity, it requires a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*), but not—

[Objection: Is it not the case that [the suffix] *ṣyaṅ* is prescribed only for the feminine? [Reply: This is not so; for if there were no general inclusion (*sāmānyagrahaṇa*), the addition of the marker *ṅt* to *ṣyaṅ* would be purposeless. Indeed, the sole purpose of that marker in this rule is for the sake of general inclusion, and nothing else. Therefore...
By the force of the mention of *ṅt*, there is also the inclusion of *ṣyaṅ*. For example, *āmbaṣṭhyā* and so forth.

From the words *āmbaṣṭha*, *sauvīra*, and *kosala*, in the sense of a descendant (*apatya*), the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied by the rule *vṛddhetkosalājādāññyaṅ* (Pāṇini 4.1.171); and from that which ends in *ñyaṅ*, the suffix *āp* is added.
*Ṭhkārīṣagandhyā*: this is derived according to the rule *svādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 4.1.2). *Ṭhvārāhyā*: from the word *varāha*, [the suffix] *iñ* is applied by *ata iñ* (4.1.95). *Ṭhbālākyā*:
from the word *balākā*, the suffix *iñ* is applied by the rule for the *bāhv-ādi* group. In both cases, [the feminine suffix] *ṅīṣ* is applied by *aṇ-iño-r-anārṣayoḥ*.
By [the rule] beginning with (4.1.78), the substitution *ṣyaṅ* is applied, and from that which ends in this [substitute], the suffix *cāp* is added.
Thus, "Śārkarākṣyā" and so forth; [these forms arise] from the words *śarkarākṣa*, *pūtimāṣa*, and *gorakṣa*, which end in the suffix *yañ* belonging to the *garga*-class, followed by *cāp*.
75. *Āvaṭya* and so forth. (Pāṇini 4.1.75). "When *ṅīp* was expected" means by [the rule] *ṭhyañaśca* (4.1.16).

"Derivatives (taddhita) are those [suffixes] beneficial for them. By the word "them" (tad), both worldly and Vedic words are referred back, because they are the subject under discussion as things to be explained. Therefore, the suffixes beginning with *aṇ* occur only there; and wherever they occur, they are beneficial to those [words], and not elsewhere.

Therefore, it is established that the secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) have the characteristic of denotation. Now, why is the section on secondary suffixes not placed at the very beginning of the section on feminine suffixes? What would be gained by doing so? It would result in the term "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) being applicable to the secondary suffixes as well, because there is no end to the secondary suffixes.

In the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* (4.1.1), the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* need not be made; likewise, in the rule *prācāṃ ṣpha taddhitaḥ* (4.1.17), the mention of *taddhita*, and in the rule *yasyeti ca* (6.4.148), the mention of the vowel *i* [need not be made], because [the desired forms] would be established simply by the term *taddhita*. [Objection: This is impossible.

[This rule] should be formulated in this way; for if it were formulated thus, the purpose previously stated for the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* would not apply there, because the *it*-designation of the *ṅ* in *ṅīp*, *ṅīṣ*, and *ṅīn* is prohibited by [Pāṇini 1.3.8], "In the absence of a taddhita suffix. And in this case, [in the word] *paṭvī*, [the rule] "guṇa for *o*" [would not apply].
Thus, by [Pāṇini 6.4.146], there would be *guṇa* substitution; therefore, let it remain exactly as in the original arrangement.

77. *yūnas tiḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.77). [The commentary states: "This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṅīp*. This is because, due to the word ending in *nakāra*, the suffix *ṅīp* would otherwise apply by the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* (4.1.5). Now, why does the suffix *ṅīṣ* not apply instead by the rule *itaś ca manuṣyajāteḥ* (4.1.65), since the word ends in the vowel *i*?
Is it so? Because it belongs to the class of non-human beings. For the word *yuvati* (young woman) does not denote the human species;
what then? It denotes a stage of life. Indeed, it applies only to the state of youth, not to the states of childhood or old age. Nor are such words [denotative of] species (*jātiśabda*), for they...
In all states and conditions, [words] function based on genus (jāti), just like the word "cow" and others.
78. *aṇiñoḥ anārṣayor gurūpotamayoḥ ṣyaṅ gotre* (Pāṇini 4.1.78).

Here, does the term *aṇiñoḥ* refer merely to the suffixes themselves, or to the entire word-form ending in them? If the first alternative were adopted, then the qualification "having a heavy syllable as the penultimate" (*gurūpotamayoḥ*) would [not apply].

[The designation *guru*] would not be applicable; for it is impossible for the vowels *a* and *i* (the *aniñ*) themselves to possess the quality of being "heaviest" (*gurūpotama*). To what, then, does it apply?

It applies to the entire aggregate ending in those [suffixes]. Therefore, considering that the second alternative is the appropriate one to adopt, he says: "In the case of the *gotra* [lineage], regarding those two suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ* which are prescribed [after a *pratyaya*] that is not an *ārṣa*, [the designation *guru* applies] to those ending in them."

Regarding the phrase "of the two nominal stems": if this were a reference to the entire aggregate consisting of that which ends in *aṇ* and that which ends in *iñ*, then the qualification "of those [suffixes] other than *ṭhak* and *ārṣa*" would not be applicable; for the entire aggregate is prescribed only after the name of a seer (*ṛṣi*). However, this qualification is indeed applicable to the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ* themselves.

Because one or the other of those two is prescribed by rule, the qualification "in the *gotra*" is also properly applicable only to the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ*, and not to the entire group; for in this context,
the technical term *gotra* is defined by the rule "the offspring from the grandson onwards is the *gotra*" (Pāṇini 4.1.162).

It is understood that in that context, only the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ* are prescribed, not the entire aggregate. This is not a fault; since these two cannot function as qualifiers of the aggregate, they are understood by implication to refer to the two constituent parts, namely *aṇ* and *iñ*. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Vṛtti*: "In the case of a lineage (*gotra*)."

"Regarding the statement *yāvaṇiñau vihitāvanārṣau* (the suffixes *ya* and *aṇ* are prescribed [after *yuvan*] when not used in the Veda)," one might ask: in this case, should this be a substitute (*ādeśa*) for *ṣyaṅ*, or a suffix (*pratyaya*)? Now, since it is indicated by a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī-nirdeśa*), it must undoubtedly be a substitute; therefore, is not the suspicion regarding the second alternative (that it is a suffix) improper? This is not so.

Even in the case of the prescription of suffixes (*pratyaya*), the use of the genitive case is observed, as for example in *gāpoṣṭhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.8) and *vrīhiśālyorḍhak* (Pāṇini 5.2.2). Therefore, the suspicion that [the term] refers to a suffix is indeed appropriate.
In that regard, if it were a suffix, the form *audameghīya* would not be established.
