The feminine descendant of Udamegha—by the rule *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95), the suffix *iñ* is added; from that form ending in *iñ*, the suffix *ṣyaṅ* is applied by this [present rule];
there is the elision of the vowel *i* by *yasyeti ca* (6.4.148); then *cāp* is substituted for *ṣyaṅ* by *ṣyaṅścāp* (4.1.74), resulting in *audameghyā*.
Her descendant is formed by *strībhyo ḍhak* (4.1.120), where *ey* is the substitute for *ḍhak*. In that [context]:

Regarding the word *ṭhāpatya*, the elision (*lopa*) of the *y* is desired by the rule "ṭhāpatyasya ca taddhite'nāti" (Pāṇini 6.4.151), yet that does not apply here because the *y* is not part of a patronymic suffix (*apatyapratyaya*). If it is argued that this is covered by the rule "halastaddhitasya" (6.4.150), we say no; for the term "īti" is understood to carry over from that rule. Furthermore, in the view that [the *y*] is a substitute (*ādeśa*), the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ* are indeed patronymic.

Since the substitute *ṣyaṅ* also possesses the status of "offspring" (*apatyatva*) by virtue of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, the elision of *y* (*yalopa`) is established. Therefore, with the intention that the view of substitution alone is correct, he says: "The substitute *ṣyaṅ* occurs. But even in the view of substitution, [the form] *auḍulomyā* would not be established.

The word *loman* is listed among the *bāhv-ādi* group [of nominal stems]. Since there is no occurrence of the simple word [by itself] in connection with a patronymic suffix (*apatya*), the entire complex ending in it is taken; thus, for the feminine descendant of *Uḍuloman*, when the suffix *iñ* is applied due to its being in the *bāhv-ādi* group, that [suffix] undergoes the substitution of *ṣyaṅ*. In this regard, [the rule] "ṇas-taddhite" [applies].

According to [Pāṇini 6.4.144], the elision of the *ṭi* is desired, yet it does not occur because of the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by [Pāṇini 6.4.168]: "And in the case of *tyad* and so forth, when they do not denote an abstract quality (*bhāva*) or an action (*karman*). However, in the view that [the suffix] is a secondary derivative (*pratyaya*), because the *iṇ* is separated [from the *ṣyaṅ*], there is no preservation of the original form for the *ṣyaṅ*, and thus the elision of the *ṭi* takes place. [Objection: But what about [the rule] "and of *ya*"?

When the elision [of the *ṭi*] has been performed by [Pāṇini 6.4.148], there is no intervention. By [the rule] "when a subsequent element is present, for a preceding grammatical operation" (1.1.57), once the elision [of the *ṭi*] by [6.4.148] has been performed, there is no intervention. By [the rule] "when a subsequent element is present, for a preceding grammatical operation" (1.1.57), [this applies to] the elision.

It certainly exists by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). There is no fault even in the view that it is a replacement (*ādeśa*); for it is established through its sequential order. For in this case, the status of having a heavy penultimate syllable (*gurūpotamattva*) is not possible until the elision (*lopa*) has taken place. In that regard, first there is the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) in the *iñ* suffix before the *ṣyaṅ* [is applied], and then follows the state of having a heavy penultimate syllable. After that—

The non-establishment [of the desired form] occurs due to the sequence of the suffixes. If it is argued that this is a fault in the view of substitution—namely, that because [the substitute] consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it would result in a total replacement (*sarvādeśa*) according to P. 1.1.55, and thus by P.
1.1.53 it would replace the whole ending? This is not so; for the total replacement is prevented by the prohibition of the exception.

[The question arises: "Does [the substitution] apply? Should an *antādeśa* (substitution for the final phoneme) be made by the rule *ṅcci* (Pāṇini 1.1.53), or rather, because it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), should it be a *sarvādeśa* (substitution for the whole)? In that case, because it is subsequent (*paratva*), the *sarvādeśa* applies—just as in the rule *tuhyaestātaṅṅaśiṣyanyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 7.1.35)? From this...

He says: "Of that which is being pointed out," and so forth. Just as the substitute *pad* is understood to apply to the word *pād* itself, and not to a composite whole ending in the word *pād*, so too this [substitution] is understood to apply only to the specific *aṇ* and *iñ* that are being pointed out. Then, where would there be a substitution for the whole?
Is it necessary? [It is] where the genitive case is uttered from a composite form, as in *tuhya-eh* [from *tvad-asmad*].

[In this context], the letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of general inclusion; for if it were not there, in the rule *ṅyaḥ cāp* (Pāṇini 4.1.74), only the suffix *ñyaṅ* from the rule *vṛddhetkosalājādāññyaṅ* (4.1.171) would be understood.

It would be so for *ṣyaṅ*, but not for *ñyaṅ*. [In the rule] "The letter *ṣ* is for the purpose of preventing its [the *ṣyaṅ*] interference," for if there were no mention of a single *anubandha*, there would be a reference only to that which has two *anubandhas* (*ṣyaṅ*), and not to *ñyaṅ*.

This word *uttama* exists both as a derivative nominal stem ending in the suffix *-tamap* and as an underived (avyutpanna) word. In that regard, if this were a reference to the derivative form, then [the formation] *vārāhyā* would not be established; for the derivative word *uttama* is restricted to [denoting] four or more [items].
For just as the suffix *tamap*, which denotes excellence, is prescribed after the word *udgata* (risen) when it signifies superiority—

since something becomes "risen" only in relation to what is "not risen," and among three things there are two that are risen and one that is not risen— it is not the case that this [suffix] is applied to two things that have both risen.

Thus, when there is the intention to express that this has risen to a higher degree than these two, the suffix *tamap* arises; for it is not sublated by the suffix *tarap*, which is specifically prescribed [for comparison between two]. However, among four, three have risen and one has not risen; therefore, with respect to those three that have risen, this one has also risen. This...
When there is an intention to express the meaning "this has risen to an extreme degree," the suffix *tamap* is produced;

consequently, it would apply only to the four [classes]. Since the word *uttama* (highest) is established by its own form (*svarūpa*) therein, the form *vārāhyā* would not be established. For in this case, there are not four [classes].

Having considered that "they exist," he says "the word *uttama* by its own nature," and so forth, showing that the word *uttama* is understood here as being unlearned (*avyutpanna*). For the word *uttama*, by its very nature, denotes the last among three or more when it is unlearned, but not when it is learned (*vyutpanna*). For that [learned usage]...

By stating "the last of those beginning with four," and so forth in the passage beginning with "therefore the word utama is [formed] by its own nature," it is shown that here the word *uttama* is understood in its unanalyzed (avyutpanna) form.
Thus, when the unanalyzed form is accepted, the form *vārāhī* is also established.

"The rule *ṭhṭhiḍḍhāṇañ* etc. results only in the suffix *ṅīp*"—this is a faulty reading. For just as in the case of *baidī*, where the suffix *ṅīn* occurs after the word ending in *añ* because it denotes a genus (*jāti*) by the rule *śārṅgaravādyaño ṅīn* (Pāṇini 4.1.73), so too here it ought to be *ṅīn* alone. As for its being a genus...
Because it belongs to the *gotra* [lineage] class; therefore, the reading "from this point on, by the rule *śārṅgaravādyaño ṅīn*, only *ṅīn* occurs" is what should be observed here. [Examples are:
*vāsiṣṭhī*, *vaiśvāmitrī*. [The suffix] *iṇ* is applied by the rule *ṛṣyandhaka-* (4.1.114), etc.

*Ṭhāṭpagavī*, *kāpaṭavī*: from the words *upagu* and *paṭu*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the general rule (*autsargika*), and the *guṇa* substitution occurs according to Pāṇini 6.4.146. *Āhicchatrī*, *vaiśvāmitrī*: here the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.3.25, "born there."
79. *gotrāvayavāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.79).

That which is both a *gotra* (a lineage name) and a part (*avayava*) of it is called *gotrāvayava*. Here, however, by applying a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) from the denoted object to the word itself, the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that denotes such a [lineage] is referred to by the term *gotrāvayava*. But is this not so?

In a compound, because the word for the "member" (*avayava*) functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), it would—like the word "blue" in the case of "blue lotus"—be required to appear first. However, because the *rājadanta* group is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*), the qualifier will instead appear last. Furthermore, in this context, "lineage" (*gotra*) is understood in its worldly sense, and not [in its technical grammatical sense].

This is a technical term. In common usage, the primary progenitor who bestows a name upon the lineage of offspring originating from himself is called a *gotra*. For instance, there was a certain primordial and preeminent person named Bharata; by him, all those who preceded him [were designated].

Sons, grandsons, and so forth are designated as "Bharatas. This word *avayava* (part) exists in the sense of a single portion; by virtue of that connection, the whole (*avayavin*) is called a "collection" (*samudāya*). And it also exists in the sense of separation—*avayuti* means *avayava*, in the sense of being separated (*pṛthagbhūta*).

Although the root *yu* is recited in the sense of "mixing," nevertheless, because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the prefix *ava-* conveys the sense of "separation" (*pṛthaktva*). It is used in the sense of being subordinate (*apradhāna*), as in: "this is a member of a family," or "this is a member of a community. That is to say, this person is subordinate to the family or the community.
It is understood as follows: in that case, if [the word *gotra*] were taken as denoting only a part, then the inclusion [of the word *gotra*] would be purposeless;

one should simply say "from *gotra*" (*gotrāt*). For even a part of a lineage (*gotra*) is indeed a lineage (*gotra*), just as a part of milk is called milk. Furthermore, if it were to exist separately, apart from a lineage...
Even so, [the suffixes] *aṇ* and *iñ* are prescribed after [names such as] Puṇika and others;

however, this is undesired. Therefore, regarding the word *vākya*, which denotes a part of that [whole] or a separate existence, the fault lies therein; thus, only that which expresses the subordinate element is accepted [as the base]. This is stated in the rule: "The parts of a lineage (*gotra*)."
This is a qualification of the *śrutis* such as *puṇika* and others; the meaning is that they denote non-principal *gotras*.

Regarding the phrase "considered to be *gotras*," this means they are well-known in common usage as denoting *gotras*, being considered as such, but not because they are recited in the chapter on *gotras* (*gotrādhyāya*). For this very reason...

These [names] are secondary because they are not listed in the *Gotrādhyāya*. Regarding the term "designations of families" (*kulākhyāḥ*): "family" (*kula*) means lineage (*gotra*); "designations" (*ākhyā*) means those by which something is named, such as "by lineage" (*gotreṇa*), and so forth.
Regarding the word "thence" (*tataḥ*): it refers to names such as *Puṇika* and others that are distinguished by the aforementioned qualifiers. If...

In that case, since *ṣyaṅ* would indeed occur after the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ* prescribed for the *gotra* [lineages], this rule (*yoga*) would be purposeless, as it is already established by the preceding one. To this, he says:
"The commencement [of this rule] is for the sake of excluding *ṭhak*, *guru*, *potu*, and *am̐śa*. [Examples include] "pauṇikī" and so forth.

From words such as *puṇika*, *bhuṇika*, and *mukhara*, by [Pāṇini 4.1.95] *ṭhañ-iñ-au*, there is the suffix *iñ*; and for that which ends in *iñ*, as well as for [stems ending in] *ṣyaṅ*, there is the feminine suffix *cāp*.
80. *Krauḍy-ādibhyaś-ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.80). [The rule states:

"The suffix *ṣyaṅ* occurs after [the group of words] beginning with *krauḍi*, when denoting a female. Now, since the view that [the suffixes] belong to the base (*prakṛti-pakṣa*) was previously adopted, for what purpose is the view that they belong to the suffix (*pratyaya-pakṣa*) adopted here?

The purpose [of this rule] is to demonstrate that even when resorting to that [previous rule], there is no fault here. Regarding the statement "the commencement [of this rule] is for the sake of those whose penultimate syllable is not heavy (*agurūpotama*)," etc.: for those [words] listed here ending in *iñ* or *añ*, this commencement is for the sake of those whose penultimate syllable is not heavy; however, for others, it is for the sake of the suffixes *aṇ*, *ini*, and *ña*.
Among these, the first group begins with *krauḍi* and others ending in *iñ* prior to the word *caupayata*;
however, from *caupayata* onwards, up to the word *saudhātaki*, they end in *aṇ*. As for the word *saudhātaki*, it is formed by [Pāṇini 4.1.97]: *sudhātor akaṅ ca*.

Thus ends the section on words ending in *iñ*. Regarding the rule "after *sūta*, when meaning a young woman": after the word *sūta*, the suffix *ṣyaṅ* occurs when referring to a young woman who has attained youth—*sūtyā*;
otherwise, only the suffix *ṭāp* occurs—*sūtā*. Regarding the rule "after *bhoja*, when meaning a Kṣatriya":
after the word *bhoja*, the suffix *ṣyaṅ* occurs when the Kṣatriya caste is to be expressed. [This applies] to that which is characterized as a genus (*jāti*).

This is an exception to the suffix *ṅīṣ*—in the case of *bhojyā*, the suffix *ṭāp* alone occurs elsewhere, as in *bhojā*. Those following that [up to] the word *gaukakṣya* end in the suffix *iñ*; furthermore, that [suffix *iñ*] itself ends in *yañ* from the *garga* group.
81. *Daivayajñi-śaucivṛkṣi-sātyamugri-kāṇṭheviddhibhyo 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.81).

Regarding the rule "In the case of a gotra [patronymic], [the suffix] is obligatory by the preceding [sūtra]," etc., when the secondary derivative (*apatya*) refers to a descendant from the grandson onwards, the suffix *iñ* is applied.

In that case, when [the suffix] is prescribed by the rule "ṭhañ-iñau" (Pāṇini 4.1.78) and so forth, it is an optional alternative to what is otherwise obligatory; however, when it refers to a descendant of the immediate generation, it is prescribed as an option where it was previously not applicable at all.

82. *samarthānāṃ prathamādvā* (Pāṇini 4.1.82). "This governing rule (*adhikāra*) extends up to the suffixes that do not alter the meaning of the base (*svārthika-pratyaya*). Those which occur in the sense of the base itself—that is, in the sense of the original form—are called *svārthika*. The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied here according to the list beginning with *adhyātma* (Vārttika 456). These are the *svārthika* suffixes.

"Avadhi" means a limit; thus it is so described. [The phrase] "up to the point where 'prāgdiśo vibhaktiḥ' [applies]" indicates that this refers to the sūtra *prāgdiśo vibhaktiḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.1), from which point onwards the suffixes having their own meaning (*svārthika*) function as limits.

He explains that this governing rule (*adhikāra*) applies [only] prior [to that point]. But what is the reason that this governing rule does not also apply to *svārthika* (suffixes used in their own sense)? He says:
"In the case of *svārthika* suffixes," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of those that are capable" (*samarthānām*), the meaning is "of those whose meanings are connected."
Furthermore, the state of having a connected meaning arises from being dependent on two [terms], which occurs only when there is a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).

However, in the case of suffixes used in their own right (*svārthika*), no distinct meaning other than that of the base (*prakṛti*) is possible, for the sake of conveying which another word would have to be employed, and in relation to which there could be semantic capacity (*samarthatā*). Therefore, [the suffix cannot be *svārthika*].

Since there is no capacity [for composition] among those suffixes that denote their own meaning (*svārthika*), the rule "of those that are semantically connected" (*samarthānām*) is not applicable here. For this very reason, because of the absence of a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), the rule "from the first [word]" (*prathamāt*) is likewise not applicable. For if there were another word as a counter-correlative, then such a doubt would arise.

It might be asked: does the cognition arise from the first [word], or from the second? Consequently, for the sake of excluding that [possibility], the continued application of the rule "from the first" would be meaningful. However, in the absence of a second correlative, its continued application would be of no use. Furthermore, there is also the possibility of an option (*vikalpa*).

Regarding the phrase "not fixed" (*anavasthita*) therein, the meaning is "unrestricted. For some [suffixes] are invariably *svārthika* (denotative of their own base meaning). Thus, in the rule *ṣaḍakṣāśitaṅgvalaṃkarmālam* (Pāṇini 5.4.7), the author of the Bhāṣya will provide an enumeration: "Which, then, are the invariable ones?"

What are the suffixes? They are: those beginning with *tamap* up to *kā*; those beginning with *ñya* up to *vun*; those beginning with *ām* up to *mayaṭ*; and the compound-ending suffixes (*samāsānta*) after the word *bṛhatī* and words denoting a genus (*jātyanta*). Among these, the suffixes beginning with *tamap*—as prescribed by "the suffixes *tamap* and *iṣṭhan* are used in the sense of excellence" (Pāṇini 5.3.55)—and those beginning with *ka*, as prescribed by "the suffix *ka* is used like *prāgivāt*" (Pāṇini 5.3.70), [are included].
(5.3.70) All [suffixes] prior to this are compulsory (*nitya*). Likewise,
from the suffix *ñya* in "pūgāññyo 'grāmaṇīpūrvāt" (5.2.112) up to "pādaśatasya saṃkhyādervīpsāyāṃ vun malopaśca" (5.4.1).

Those suffixes which occur prior to *vun* are compulsory (*nitya*). Likewise, those suffixes which occur from *ām* onwards—starting from *ṭh kim-et-iṅ-vyaya-ghād ām* (Pāṇini 5.4.11) up to *tat-prakṛta-vacane mayaṭ* (Pāṇini 5.4.21)—are compulsory. The same applies to that which is prescribed by *bṛhatyā ācchādane* (Pāṇini 5.4.6).

The suffix *ka* [in *kapratyayaḥ*], the suffix *ya* [in *jātyantācchaḥ* and *bandhuni*], and all those compound-ending suffixes (*samāsānta*) such as *ḍa* and others—all these are obligatory (*nitya*). Therefore, optionality (*vikalpa*) among the *svārthika* suffixes is not established; consequently, even the mention of the word "optionally" (*vā*) in that context is itself not established.
It is stated that [the application] occurs in some cases and not in others.

Here, does the qualification "from the first" refer to the sentence of usage (*prayoga-vākya*) or to the defining sentence (*lakṣaṇa-vākya*)? If it is the former, then there is no fixed rule regarding the employment of words in an ordinary sentence.
Because of the usage "bring the vessel" (*pātram āhara*) and "bring [it], the vessel" (*āhara pātram*),

when the expression "the offspring of Upagu" (*apatyam upagoḥ*) is employed, the suffix would then arise after the word *apatya* due to its connection with the nominative case. But is it not the case that this is already covered by the word *tasya*, which is included in the rule as a word of imitation (*anukaraṇa*)?

By means of the first word ending in the sixth case, the word that follows—even though it is mentioned later—is repeated as being inherent in the extraordinary (alaukika) sentence; because it is the first [in that context], it receives the designation "first. Therefore, even when the ordinary sentence *apatyam upagoḥ* ("the offspring of Upagu") is employed, [it is understood].

In that case, the suffix will arise from the word *upagu* itself, because it receives its primary designation (*prathamavyapadeśa*) in the very manner already described; it will not arise from the word *apatya*. If it is argued that there is no fault even when the first alternative (*pakṣa*) is adopted, this is a mere pretense; for when the primary [meaning] is possible as the first, [the secondary cannot be accepted].

The inclusion of the secondary [meaning] is appropriate. Therefore, even though the word *upagu* has primacy in a secondary sense, the suffix should arise only from the primary first member, which is the word for "offspring" (*apatya*), and not from the word *upagu*. Furthermore, this avoids the burden of a complex interpretation (*pratipadigaurava*). However, in the second alternative, the fault does not even arise.

Because the employment of words in defining statements (*lakṣaṇavākya*) is fixed, he says "defining statements," etc., relying upon that [fact]. Among the capable [words], the first is determined as the base (*prakṛti*) for the suffix, just as in the example:
"Kṛṣṇā is the most abundant in milk among cows"—that is, among cows.

The word *kṛṣṇā* [is used] because the cow possesses the highest degree of milk (*sampannakṣīratamatva*). If, then, the suffix occurs after the first among those that are semantically capable, this being the case, in the rule *tasyāpatyam* (Pāṇini 4.1.92),
the word *tasya* is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) which is mentioned first as denoting a general sense.
The suffix would apply only to that which expresses a general meaning, not to that which expresses a specific meaning;

for [in the case of] a nominal stem such as *upagu* and so forth, that [specific meaning] is not first mentioned in the defining rule (*lakṣaṇavākya*). To this he says: "of that," and so forth, namely, "for the purpose of indicating the specific."

The meaning is that it is for the purpose of indicating a specific distinction. For if "of that" (*tasya*) were not for the purpose of indicating a specific distinction, then its capacity [to function] would not exist; for this term "of that" does not, independent of context and so forth, settle upon specific instances. Nor...

No benefit whatsoever is conferred upon the offspring by this [term] when it is not restricted to specific instances; for the term "offspring" (apatya) already conveys the general relationship, since it is a word denoting a relative.
Consequently, in the absence of such a benefit, there would be no functional capacity [for the genitive]. And yet, this is stated: "of that" (tasya).

Therefore, by implication, its purpose is to indicate specific qualifiers (*viśeṣa*). Thus, those specific qualifiers which are indicated—that is, expressed—become beneficial because they convey the related entity as qualified by the exclusion of other related entities; this is logically established by them.
It possesses a functional capacity; therefore, this general term should be understood as being for the purpose of indicating its specific instances.

By means of that [general term], the priority belonging to it is recognized as pertaining to its specific instances, such as the word *upagu* and others. Consequently, the suffix occurs only from that [specific instance] and not from the general term itself.
"In 'Kambala is the offspring of Upagu, [the son] of Devadatta,'" the word *upagu* is connected with *kambala*, not with *apatya* (offspring);

and the word *apatya* is connected with the word *devadatta*, not with the word *upagu*. Therefore, since there is no connection between the word *upagu* and the word *apatya*, it does not follow from that [connection].
It becomes a condition [for the application of the suffix],
so that "even a sentence" may occur. For if the mention of "a word" (vāk) were absent,
since the designation of a descendant by means of a sentence would be possible, [the suffix] being prescribed for that meaning...
The grammatical rule (*pratyaya*) should set that aside. But surely, when the meaning is the same,

that which is governed by a formal rule (*śāstrānvita*) sets aside that which is not governed by a formal rule (*aśāstrānvita*), just as, for example, by the rule *gamer ḍoḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 2.11), the word *go*, being governed by a formal rule, sets aside [the form derived from] that which is not governed by a formal rule.

The word *gāvī* has the same meaning as [the word *go*,] but not a different meaning such as *ḍittha* and so forth. Nor is the meaning the same for the compound (*vṛtti*) and the sentence (*vākya*), for in a compound there is semantic integration (*ekārthībhāva*) as its capacity (*sāmarthya*), whereas in a sentence there is mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*). This is not so; for even though this difference in meaning exists, the primary meaning is not...

It is distinguished as follows: for instance, when it is said, "Bring Upagu’s offspring," the very same object that is qualified by the relationship of being an offspring is brought; and when it is said, "Bring the son of Upagu (Aupagava)," that very same object is brought. And it is only with respect to the primary element [the meaning] that a word governed by grammatical rules (*śāstrānvita*) is considered to have the same meaning as one not so governed (*aśāstrānvita*).
It excludes [the other], for otherwise even the word *go* would not exclude the word *gāvī*.

Indeed, there is a difference in meaning between those two as well; for instance, the word *go* denotes "cowness" (*gotva*), whereas the word *gāvī* denotes that same thing as well as its ungrammaticality (*aśāstrīyatva*). Therefore, in the absence of the mention of the word *vāk* (speech), just as...

Just as the word *go* excludes the word *gāvī* because their primary meanings are identical— even though there exists a difference in their secondary meanings— so too a nominal suffix (*taddhita*), when accompanied by a formal rule (*śāstra*),
should exclude a sentence (*vākya*) that is not so accompanied. Therefore, the term "word" (*vāk*) is employed [in the definition] so that the sentence may also be included.

"If this is so," and so forth. If, by the inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*), the existence or non-existence of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is made dependent on the existence or non-existence of the sentence, then when the sentence does not exist, the secondary derivative must necessarily occur. In that case, the compound formation (*samāsa-vṛtti*) such as *upagvapatyam* would be sublated by the secondary derivative formation (*taddhita-vṛtti*).
"This is not a fault," and so forth; the meaning has already been explained.

83. *prāgdīvyato’ṇ* | (4.1.83) This reference, "before *dīvyataḥ*," is incorrect; for [the sūtrakāra] will later state *dīvyati* (4.4.2), and not *dīvyat*. In that case, the word *dīvyati* is taken as the limit (*avadhi*).
Should there not have been the indication "of the root *div*"? To this he says:

"A part of that," and so forth. If the entire word *dīvyati* were taken as the limit (*avadhi*), this indication would not be appropriate; however, it is not the entire word that is taken, but rather—
Thus, there is no fault regarding the word *dīvyat*, which is a part of that [compound]. Now, for what purpose are both the mention of *dīvyat* and the mention of *prāk* [in the sūtra]?
Why not simply make the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "naṇ" alone? It cannot be done in this way;
for if it were so made, then by another governing rule such as "strībhyo ḍhak" (Pāṇini 4.1.120), etc., [the desired application would fail].
In rules such as *tena raktaṃ rāgāt* (Pāṇini 4.2.1), where the suffix *aṇ* has been interrupted [by other rules],
the mention of *aṇ* would have to be repeated. Since the scope of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) is defined by its limit,
and this [suffix] is permitted for all meanings falling within that limit, the mention of *aṇ* would have to be repeated.

It does not occur. Therefore, the term *dīvyat* must first be employed in order to indicate the extent of the scope (*adhikāra*). The term *prāk* must also certainly be employed for the purpose of indicating that very [term *dīvyat*] as the limit. For if that were absent, [the rule would be] "after *dīvyat*, the suffix *aṇ* [is applied]."

When this is stated, the suffix *aṇ* would be understood as applying even where the word *divya* occurs. [This is addressed by] "In all three views," and so forth. But how is it that the application of this *aṇ* is obtained while avoiding the scope of exceptions, given that such a governing rule (*adhikāra*) exists?
Because [the suffix] *aṇ* is prescribed for every individual case, it would also apply even in the domain of exceptions— such as in the rule "from *at*, *iñ* and *aṇ*" (*ata iñ aṇ ca*)—
for otherwise its mention there would be purposeless.
Even under the view that this is a *paribhāṣā* (a general metarule), since it is stated without distinction that "*aṇ*" applies to meanings prior to "divya" (*prāgdīvyataḥ*), [the objection remains].

How could a general rule (*paribhāṣā*), while operating, avoid the domain of an exception? Even regarding a positive injunction (*vidhi*), if all those bases (*prakṛti*) that occur prior to the suffix *-dīvyat* were brought together here and the suffix *aṇ* were prescribed for them, it would apply everywhere; otherwise, the prescription [of *aṇ*] for all cases would be purposeless.

He thinks as follows: "It will not apply in the domain of an exception (*apavāda*) on account of an indicator (*jñāpaka*); for this reason, [Pāṇini] employs the term 'optionally' (*vā*) or 'alternatively' (*anyatarasyām*) in certain instances—such as *pīlāyā vā* (4.1.118) and *udaśvito'nyatarasyām* (4.2.19)—which indicates that the suffix *aṇ* does not apply in the domain of an exception."

It is so. But in the case of a positive injunction (*vidhi*), there is a greater way of avoiding this difficulty. For the suffix *aṇ* is not enjoined after those bases (*prakṛti*) that occur before the word "prādīvyataḥ"; rather, it is enjoined for those meanings that occur before "prādīvyataḥ.
In that case, since the suffix *iñ* would be produced from a specific base within that same meaning, it will sublate (*bādhiṣyate*) the suffix *aṇ*. Now...

For what purpose is this specific limit adopted? Why not simply say "before *ṭhak*," meaning "before the *ṭhak* [suffix] prescribed by the rule *prāgvahateṣṭhak* (4.4.1)"? This cannot be done; for [the suffixes] such as *dadhnaṣṭhak* (4.2.18) would also [otherwise] have *ṭhak* as their limit.
It is understood [as follows]: "In that case, one should rather say:

'After *kaṃsīya* and *paraśu*, there is the suffix *yañ* and *añ*, and elision (*luk*),' [Pāṇini 4.3.168]; the meaning would then be 'before that which is the word *kaṃsīya*. Even so, it is impossible to state [it] thus."
By the rule "dvigorluganapatye" (Pāṇini 4.1.88), the suffix *ka* would also arise after *kaṃsīya*;
consequently, in the case of "dvikaṃsaḥ," meaning "a modification of two *kaṃsīyas*," the elision (*luk*) would not occur. Therefore, let it remain exactly as it was originally stated.
84. And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after words such as *aśvapati* (Pāṇini 4.1.84).

85. The suffix *ṇya* is applied after words ending in *diti*, *aditi*, *āditya*, and those having *pati* as their final member (Pāṇini 4.1.85). Regarding the rule "and after that which has *pati* as its final member," the word *uttarapada* (final member) is connected only with the word *pati*.
He shows that [the suffix] does not occur after others such as *diti* and so on. And this is obtained either from the explanation of *pratyāsatti* (proximity) or from the statement:
"It should be stated that [the suffix occurs] also after *yama*. This means that the suffix *ṇya* occurs after the word *yama*.

This must be explained. Here is the explanation: although it would have been sufficient to say "after the word *pati*" for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*), the expression "after a word ending in *pati* as its final member" (*patyuttarapadāt*) is intended to provide an additional rule. For an expansion of the text serves to expand the scope of the meaning. Consequently, the suffix *ṇya* will also apply after the word *yama*. Alternatively—

The particle *ca* ("and") is carried over from the previous rule; therefore, because its purpose is to include what has not been explicitly mentioned, it will apply here as well. Regarding the phrase "of *vāṅmat*, *pitṛmat*, etc.": the meaning of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is "presentation" (*pratipādana*). This presentation must be made either by adding more text—thereby implying an addition of meaning—or by relying on the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the particle *ca* in the sense of including what was not stated. In the case of *yāmya* and so forth, the suffix *ṇya* is applied according to the requirements, in senses such as "descendant" (*apatya*) and others belonging to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group.
Regarding the rule "from *pṛthivī*, the suffixes *ña* and *añ*": these suffixes beginning with *ña* are called *taddhita* by the rule "these are *taddhitas*" (Pāṇini 4.1.76).

Since the inclusion of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) not explicitly mentioned is achieved by means of the plural number, it need not be stated separately. In that regard, when the suffix *ñ* follows the word *pṛthivī*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied, resulting in *pārthivā*; however, when the suffix *añ* follows, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.15 (*ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*), resulting in *pārthivī*. [Likewise,] for the word *bahiṣ*, there is both the elision of the sixth case ending and the application of the suffix *ṭilop*.

And so forth. Now, one might object: "Since the elision of the *ṭi* suffix is already established by the rule 'The elision of the *ṭi* of indeclinables occurs before any suffix beginning with *bh*, for the sake of forms such as *sāyaṃprātika* and others' (Vārttika 802), why is this stated again?
To this he replies: "The mention of the elision of the *ṭi*," and so on. [This results in] the form *ārātīyaḥ*.

The purpose of making known its impermanence is as follows: [in the case of] *ārāt* [as the first member], the suffix *cha* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.2.114 (*vṛddhāc chaḥ*). Regarding the rule "the [suffix] *aka* after *sthāman*," since the word *sthāman* alone is never used in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*), it should be understood that the suffix *aka* applies to that which ends in *sthāman*. It is just like [the formation of] *aśvaka*.
In *sthāmāsyā*, [the word] *aśvatthāmā* [is used]; due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group, the letter *s* is replaced by *t*.

From *aśvatthāman* comes *aśvatthāmaḥ* [as a patronymic], with the elision of the suffixal *an* according to *ṭhnastaddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.144). Regarding the rule "in the sense of a descendant of *loman*": the word *loman* is listed among the *bāhvādi* group; of that [word...]

Since there is no connection of the suffix with the base alone, it is understood that the rule applies to that which ends in [the base]. Here, when the intention is to express "offspring" (*apatya*) and the suffix *iñ* would otherwise apply in the plural, the vowel *a* is prescribed as an exception to that. Thus, the many offspring of Uḍuloman are called *uḍulomāḥ*.

"Everywhere" means both in the sense of offspring (*apatya*) and elsewhere. Alternatively, it means that the suffixes beginning with *aj* (such as *yañ*) would apply both in the sense of *prāgdīvyatīya* (relating to what comes before *divya*) and in other senses. "The application of a suffix beginning with *aj*" refers to its occurrence or attainment.
In that case, the suffix *yat* occurs after the word *go* everywhere. If this is so, [one might object] that *yat* is prescribed by the rule "from *go*, *uṣṭra*, etc., *yat*."

(5.1.2) In this context, what is the purpose of including the mention of *go*? It is for the sake of elaborating upon this very point. [The example is] *gavyam*, meaning "the offspring of a cow" (*gor apatyam*) or "that which moves by means of a cow. Whether the suffix *aṇ* or *ṭhak* applies, wherever there is occasion for its application after a word beginning with *aj* and so forth, the suffix *yat* occurs there and not elsewhere. [Examples are] *gorūpyam* ("cow-silver") and *gomayam* ("cow-dung").
From words ending in *hetu*, *manu*, and *āya*, the suffix *rūpya* is optionally applied (Pāṇini 4.3.81), as is *mayaṭ* (4.3.82).
Regarding the phrase "the *ṇya*-class, etc.": the word *lakṣaṇa* signifies a cause or a mark.
That which has a specific meaning as its mark (*lakṣaṇa*) is called *arthaviśeṣalakṣaṇa*; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*. Therefore...

By the principle of prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the suffixes beginning with *ṇya* take effect. Nor need this be stated, because the word "para" signifies that which is desired, and thus [the desired result] is already established by that alone. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), suffixes such as those prescribed by *ṭh-utsādibhyo 'ñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.86) are included. In that regard:

The scope for [the application of] ṇya is as follows: *daityaḥ* (a descendant of Diti) and *vānaspatyam* (that which pertains to a tree). Since this suffix ṇya is prescribed in all senses such as "offspring" (*apatya*) and so forth, it is a general suffix;
therefore, it is not restricted to a specific meaning. The scope for the exception (*apavāda*) of the suffix *aṇ*, which is restricted to a specific meaning, is as follows:
From *diteḥ apatyam* ("the offspring of Diti"), by [Pāṇini 4.1.122] *ṭhitaścāniñaḥ ṭhaḥ*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied, resulting in *dauleyaḥ*.
Since this *ḍhak* is prescribed specifically for a particular meaning within the general sense of "offspring," it serves as a marker for that specific meaning.
In this case, both [suffixes] would apply: *diteḥ apatyam* results in *daityaḥ*, and "a collection of trees" (*vanaspatīnām samūhaḥ*)...

Or, the suffix *ṇya* occurs in the sense of "produced from a tree" (*vānaspatya*) by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). Why [is it said] "because it is prescribed for a specific meaning"? That which is an exception to the suffix *aṇ*, being prescribed for a specific meaning rather than a general meaning, is [the one intended].
Because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], it indeed overrides *ṇya* and the others. A leaf is called *uṣṭrapati*.
When there is the intention to express "this belongs to that *uṣṭrapati*," the suffix *añ* is applied by the rule *ṭhpatrādhvaryupariṣadaśca* (Pāṇini 4.3.133), resulting in *auṣṭrapatyam*.

This [suffix] *añ* is indeed an exception (*apavāda*) to that [general rule] whose characteristic is "his" (*tasya idam*), and not to that which has the specific meaning of "offspring" (*apatya*) and so forth as its characteristic. For meanings such as "offspring" are specific meanings; however, the meaning of "his" (*tasya idam*) is a general meaning, not a specific meaning.

"How then is *daiteya* formed? [The answer is: If the suffixes beginning with *ṇya* (such as *ṇya*) occur by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) to the *aṇ* suffix which is prescribed for specific meanings, then *daiteya* would not be established; for in this case too, the suffix *ṇya* alone ought to apply—this is the sense. [The text continues with] "from the word *diti*," and so forth.

When this word *diti* is derived from the root *ḍudāñ* (or *ḍo*) in the sense of "cutting" (*avakhaṇḍane*, DhP 1148), with the suffix *ktic* by rule *kticktau* (Pāṇini 3.3.174), and the vowel substitution *itva* by rule *dyatisyati* (Pāṇini 7.4.40) and so forth, then the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the *gana-sūtra*: *kṛdikārādaktinaḥ* (Gaṇasūtra 50).

If, however, the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is not yet derived [by suffixation], then one follows the rule: "Some say that [the suffix *ṣyaṅ*] comes after every [nominal stem] except for those ending in a feminine suffix" (Gaṇasūtra 51).

Now, one might object: according to the principle that "when a nominal stem is mentioned, it includes the form qualified by gender as well," the mention of the word *diti* would also include the word *ditī*.

And since, just as the suffix *ṇya* occurs after the word *diti* by means of the "prior counter-exception" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), it should likewise occur after the word *ditī*, he says: "The maxim regarding words qualified by gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*) is non-eternal. Furthermore, its non-eternality is as follows:

In the section on *ṭhak*, it should be understood from the Vārttika "An addition [to the rule] regarding the roots *grah* and others when used with the words *śakti*, *lāṅgala*, *aṅkuśa*, *yaṣṭi*, *tomara*, *ghaṭa*, *ghaṭī*, and *dhanus*" (Vārttika 235) that the word *ghaṭa* is included among those [words] signifying a vessel.

86. *utsādibhyo'ñ* (4.1.86). [The phrase] "and of those that are exceptions to it" refers to the suffixes beginning with *iñ*. The word *vaṣkaya* is recited in the list (*gaṇa*). Its meaning is as follows: the suffix *añ* occurs after the word *vaṣkaya*, provided that there is no *as*—that is, when it is not in a compound.

The ancient teachers established the technical designation "sa" for a compound. For example, *vaṣkaya* is the offspring of *vaṣkaya*, hence *vāṣkayaḥ*. Why [is the condition] "asa" stated? [Consider] *gauvaṣkayiḥ*; here, by the rule "ata iñ" (Pāṇini 4.1.95), only the suffix *iñ* occurs. Regarding the rule "udasthānāddeśe": when a location is to be expressed, the suffix *añ* occurs after the word *udasthāna*.

The place where one stands up is *udasthāna*; [the suffix *añ* is applied] after this word *udasthāna*. Why [is the word] "place" (*deśa*) mentioned? [Consider: there is a certain man named Audasthāna; his descendant is *Audasthāniḥ*. [Regarding the rule] "after *pṛṣadaṃśa*": the suffix *añ* occurs after the word *pṛṣat* when "part" (*aṃśa*) is to be expressed. *Pṛṣada-aṃśaḥ* becomes *Pārṣadaḥ*. [The word] "part" (*aṃśa*)...
What [is the problem]? There is another [view] regarding the *pārṣada*. It is precisely because of this that the word *kuru* is recited here;

otherwise, when one intends to express its descendant (*apatya*), the form *kaurava* would not be established, because the suffix *ṇya* is prescribed by the rules "ṭhkurvādibhyo ṇyaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.151) and "ṭhkurunādibhyo ṇyaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.172).

[The suffix] *añ* is obtained. For the suffix *añ* is prescribed as a general rule (*sāmānyavihita*), whereas the suffix *ṇya* is prescribed as a specific rule (*viśe�ṣavihita*). And is it not the case that what is prescribed as a general rule is superseded by what is prescribed as a specific rule? This is not a fault; this rule (*yoga*) will follow after those two rules; and even there, in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*).

Since the word *kuru* has no other scope [for the suffix *aṇ*], the suffix *añ* will apply there as well. Alternatively, when the sense of "offspring" is intended, but one wishes to express the sense of "belonging to that" (*tasyedam*) according to Pāṇini 4.3.120, the form *kaurava* will result.
It should be stated: "After *grīṣma*, the suffix *ac* applies in Vedic usage. Thus, after the word *grīṣma*, the suffix *ac* is applied when the Veda is the subject matter.

The meaning is that the form *bhavatī* must be explained as having this specific sense. He asks, "For what purpose? and says: "So that it may not occur here," and so forth. This is for the sake of ensuring that when *triṣṭubh* and the like are to be expressed in Vedic (*chandas*), the suffix *ṛtvaṇ* alone—as prescribed by the rule *saṃdhivelādi-* (Pāṇini 4.3.16)—is applied, and that the suffix *añ* does not occur. By this [rule], [the word] *graiṣmī* [is formed].

The suffix *añ* does not occur after *triṣṭubh*. Regarding this, the following is the explanation: the word *vā* ("or") is understood [from the previous rule], and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Consequently, when the Vedic language (*chandas*) is to be expressed, the suffix *añ* does not occur after the word *grīṣma*. As for the statement "the *vṛt* [suffix] is taken," that refers here to those specific cases such as *triṣṭubh*, *jagatī*, and so forth.
Therefore, the *chandas* (meter) is understood here, not the *veda* (Vedic scripture).
87. *Nañ* and *snañ* are substituted for [the suffix *aṇ*] after *strī* and *pumān*, respectively, when [the word *bhavana* follows].

(4.1.87) Here, first of all, there is the mention of the actual form of the word *strī*, and not of a word ending in a feminine suffix such as *ṭāp*. For, subsequently, he will state [the rule] "after *strī*, [the suffix] *ḍhak*" (4.1.120).

By association with that [feminine form], the masculine word is also understood as having that same property; its own form is likewise grasped, as in *pauṃsnam*. Here, the elision occurs by the rule *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.23).

If the suffixes *nañ* and *sa-nañ* were to occur after the words "strī" and "pums" prior to the mention of the term *bhavana*, they would also apply in the sense of the *vati*-suffix; consequently, forms such as *strīvat* and *puṃvat* would not be established. Therefore, he says: "The feminine [word] like the masculine," and so forth. Since this [sūtra] states "like the masculine in the feminine" (*striyāṃ puṃvat*), [it follows that the rule applies specifically in this context].

By making this specific mention (*nirdeśa*), it is understood that the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* do not occur in the sense of the suffix *vati*. Now, one might argue that from this mention it is possible to understand that the suffix *snañ* does not occur in the sense of *vati*, but not that the suffix *nañ* does not occur; consequently, [one might form] *strīvat*.

[If one asks,] "Is it not established?"—to this he says: "And dependent on a rule" (*yogāpekṣaṃ ca*), etc. Because of the mention [in the sūtra] as *puṃvat*, this rule does not apply in the sense of the suffix *vati*;
for this reason, this is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that is dependent on a rule, and not dependent on the suffix *snañ*. Therefore...
This [argument] "like a woman" is also established.
88. *dvigor lug anapatye* (Pāṇini 4.1.88).

[The rule] "before *prāgdīvyataḥ*" [is understood here]. Because that [word *prāgdīvyataḥ*] is marked with the svarita accent. [The rule] "not after *bhavana*" [is understood here] because of the reversal [of the sequence]. Is this [word] *dvigoḥ* in the ablative case (*pañcamī*) or in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*)? In that regard, if...

The fifth [interpretation] would mean this: "There is elision (luk) of the suffixes *ana* and *ap*, when they follow a *dvigu* compound and occur before the suffixes *prāg-dīvyat* and *yat*. Consequently, just as there is elision of that which is caused by the designation (*saṃjñā*) of a *dvigu*—as in "a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) prepared in five potsherds (*kapāla*)" is called *pañcakapāla*—[so too would it apply here].

Likewise, this would also apply to that which is not marked by two horns— for instance, regarding a *puroḍāśa* cake made from five potsherds (*pañcakapāla*), one might say "this is a portion of it," and by applying the suffix *aṇ* according to Pāṇini 4.3.120 (*tasyedam*),
it would result in the form *pāñcakapālam*. Having observed this flaw in the case of the fifth alternative (*pañcamīpakṣa*), [the author proceeds...]
Relying on the position that the genitive case is used [in the rule], he says: "The genitive [is used] after *dvigu*," meaning "that which is related to *dvigu*.

That *taddhita* suffix for whose meaning the *samāhāra-dvigu* compound is prescribed by the rule *taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca* (Pāṇini 2.1.51) is what is "related to *dvigu*"; this is so by way of the meaning, because it belongs to that meaning.

Because it is related to a *dvigu* compound; that [word] also becomes related to the *dvigu* by means of that [compound]. By the phrase "by way of being the cause," he shows that the elision (*luk*) occurs for that relationship which exists through the relation of cause and effect (*naimittika*), and not for that which exists through a relation of temporal sequence (*paurvāparya*). And this...
Because the relationship between the cause (nimitta) and the effect (naimittika) is internal, it is obtained;

for that is indeed the primary connection of the *dvigu* with the secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Therefore, that [internal relationship] is grasped. However, the state of sequence (paurvāparya) occurs even at a later time and is thus external (*bahiraṅga*); hence—

There is no inclusion of that [in the list]. In the case of *pañcakapālaḥ*, the compound is formed by *taddhitārtha* (Pāṇini 2.1.51), meaning "prepared in five potsherds. It receives the designation of *dvigu* by *saṃkhyāpūrvo dviguḥ* (2.1.52). The suffix *aṇ* is applied by *saṃskṛtam* (4.4.3), and there is its elision (*luk*). In the case of *dvivedaḥ*:
The compound *dvau vedāv adhīte* is formed as previously described; the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to *tad adhīte tad veda* (Pāṇini 4.2.59).
Regarding *dvaidevavatiḥ*: it means "the offspring of two Devadattas," and the suffix *iñ* is applied according to *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95).

In the case of *pāñcakapālam* [meaning] "this belongs to the five-pot-sherd," the very first suffix that arises in the sense of being prepared (*saṃskṛta*) is the cause for the *dvigu* compound; it is not the suffix that arises subsequently when there is the intention to express the sense "this belongs to it" (*tasyedam*). For [the *dvigu* status] does not depend on that [subsequent] sense being the object.

It is not prescribed for a *dvigu* compound; rather, it is prescribed for that which is formed for the sake of a derivative (*saṃskṛta*) meaning. Therefore, because it is not caused by a *dvigu*, the elision (*luk*) does not occur here for that [suffix] which is prescribed by the rule *tasyedam* (Pāṇini 4.3.120). As for the phrase "Or else" (*atha vā*), etc., previously...

The elision (*luk*) was prescribed for that *taddhita* suffix which is caused by a *dvigu* compound; now, however, it is being prescribed specifically for the *dvigu* itself—this is the distinction. But how is it that the elision occurs specifically for the *dvigu*? To this he says: "The word 'dvigoḥ' is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*)."

With the words "But surely... and so forth, he refutes the explanation just stated. By the rule *pratyayasya luk-ślulupaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.61), these technical terms—*luk*, *ślu*, and *lup*—are prescribed for the non-appearance (*adarśana*) of an affix. Therefore, when *luk* is mentioned here [by the rule *dvigor lug anapatye*], it is not capable of effecting the elision of the affix of a *dvigu* compound alone.
The intention is "in order to establish [this]. Regarding the statement "This is true," which was said immediately after;

if this is so, how is the elision (*luk*) for the *dvigu* compound obtained through the technical designation (*saṃjñā*)? To this he says: "But by way of metaphorical usage" (*upacāreṇa tu*), and so forth. This refers to a thing that is not actually so.

That specific cognition which consists of a superimposed state of being is metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). That by which something is indicated is indication (*lakṣaṇā*); moreover, in this context, that [indication] is indeed metaphorical usage itself.
For by this, a non-dvandva compound is indicated as having the form of a dvandva; just as in the expression "the platforms cry," those who are not actually platforms [are indicated].

Just as men are perceived through the form of a chariot, so too here the *taddhita* suffix, though not itself a *dvigu*, is [perceived] as having the form of a *dvigu*. The basis for this metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) is its being the cause of a *dvigu*;
as it has been said: "The suffix itself, when it serves as the cause of a *dvigu*, is [called] a *dvigu*. For indeed, it occurs.

The term for the effect is applied metaphorically to the cause, as in the expression "clarified butter is life. Regarding the phrase "even that which has a double cause," etc.: that which has a double cause is called "dvigu-nimittaka. Here, the word *guṇa* (quality) is intended to signify that property which serves as the basis for the metaphorical application. The conceptual construction based on such qualities is...
The conceptualization based on a quality (*guṇanimittakalpanā*) should be understood as being essentially metaphorical (*aupacārikī*).

If, by way of metaphor, the suffix which is the cause of the *dvigu* compound is also called a *dvigu*, then why is that [suffix] whose cause is the *dvigu* not also called a *dvigu* through this same figurative conceptualization?

For indeed, the word for the cause is even used figuratively for the effect; as in the expression, "all this ancient karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious, is being experienced. Regarding the term *pāñcakapālam*:
it is derived with the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of "this is a fragment of the five-plate sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*)," and that [suffix]...

The intention is that [the suffix] arises because of the *dvigu* compound; thus, "having the *dvigu* as its cause" is the meaning. It is not the case that being a *dvigu* is the cause for that [suffix]. Since the *dvigu* is already established when the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is produced, being a *dvigu* is not the cause; what then? It is the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). For it is said: "This is not a *dvigu* in this way..."

What is prescribed? It is not that [the suffix] is prescribed after the word *dvigu*, but rather after the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Therefore, even though the state of being a *dvigu* is present, it is not the cause for the suffix; nor can the suffix itself be designated as a *dvigu* through figurative usage. "But the other" refers to the *taddhita* suffix, which...

In the primary example, elision (*luk*) is shown by the statement: "It is the cause of *dvigu*-ness alone. By the word "alone" (*eva*), the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is excluded—meaning it is the cause of *dvigu*-ness alone, and not the cause of being a nominal stem;
for the *dvigu* compound is prescribed for the sake of that [number], and not for the sake of [being] a nominal stem.

There is a distinction, namely that [the term] "prātipadikatva" (nominal stem-ness) exists [only in the former case]. Consequently, the designation "dvigu" occurs only in that which is the cause of the dvigu, by way of metaphorical application (upacāra), but not also in that which arises from an already completed dvigu.

"If it is so," and so forth. If the *taddhita* suffix which is the cause of the *dvigu* compound is here called "the *dvigu*" by metaphorical designation because of its causality, then its elision (*lopa*) occurs. This being the case, how is there elision here in the example "pañcakapāla" (prepared in five pots)? For in this instance—

When the compound *pañcānāṃ kapālānāṃ samāhāraḥ* ("the collection of five potsherds") has been formed as a *samāhāra-dvigu*, the subsequent application of a *taddhita* suffix does not have the *dvigu* as its cause. The refutation begins with "Not so here," and so forth. To the question "Why is it not produced?", he says: "For there would be threefoldness of expression (*traiśabdyam*)."

And so forth. *Traiśabdyam* means "only three words. The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of the base itself, according to the rule beginning with *cāturvarṇyādi*. Here, we must establish *traisabdyam* [as the correct form].
Since the word *pañcakapālī* is established even without the production of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), it does not follow from that [word].

A *taddhita* suffix is produced; by the rule beginning with "prepared in five potsherds" (*pañcasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtaḥ*), he demonstrates the threefold terminology. Regarding the phrase "of two words," etc.: both the word *pañcakapālī*, which occurs in the sense of a collective compound (*samāhāra*), and the word *pañcakapāla*, which occurs in a compound within the scope of a *taddhita* meaning—these two...

Both [terms] have the same meaning; however, since the analysis (vigraha) is performed with the former alone, it should be understood that the secondary derivative (taddhita) does not arise from it. Rather, "its arising is from the latter," namely from the word *pañcakapāla*. This is according to the analogy of the sheep (*avi*) and the goat (*avya*); just as in the case of "the flesh of a sheep" (*āvikam*), the word *avi* [is used].
The analysis (*vigraha*) is as follows: the word *avi* produces a suffix, and it is the same here as well.

[The question] "Why does it not occur here? and so forth [is raised]. For even in the case of the suffixes *-rūpya* and *-maya*, they are caused by a *dvigu* compound; therefore, the intention is that there should also be elision (*luk*) of those two.
The word "vā" (or) is understood [from the previous rule], following from "samarthānāṃ prathamādvā" (Pāṇini 4.1.82).

Now, one might object that even so, an optional elision (*luk*) would apply everywhere; therefore, he says "sā ca" and so forth. The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*); because that [elision] is understood as a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (a restricted option).
Therefore, in cases such as *pañcakapāla*, elision (*luk*) occurs invariably; however, in cases such as *pañcagargarūpya*, it does not occur at all.

89. *gotre’lug aci* (4.1.89). Regarding the phrase *ṭhaci*: if this were a locative case (*parasaptamī*), a mutual dependency (*itaretarāśrayatā*) would result in the application of the rule for the suffix *cha*. How so? [Consider] "the many descendants of Garga," which takes the suffix *yañ* by *gargādibhyo yañ* (4.1.105); of that [suffix],...

If there were *luk* elision, the suffix *cha* would not occur. Even if that [suffix] were elided, one might argue that by the rule "when a suffix is elided, the operations conditioned by the suffix still take place" (Pāṇini 1.1.62), the designation *vṛddha* should apply. However, because of the prohibition against suffix-conditioned operations when a suffix is marked with *lumat*—stated as "not when a suffix is marked with *lumat*" (Pāṇini 1.1.63)—there would be no occurrence of *vṛddhi*, and consequently, the designation *vṛddha* would not be established. And thus...

The characteristic of being *vṛddha* would not exist [in that case]. Therefore, for one who desires the *vṛddhi* status of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there should be non-elision (*aluk*) of the preceding [case-ending]. And if that non-elision occurs when *cha* follows, then *cha* is conditioned by the non-elision (*alug-nimitta*).

And because that [suffix] is caused by it, there is clearly a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). Therefore, seeing this fault in the locative absolute (*parasaptamī*), he says— showing that this is a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*)—
"when a suffix beginning with *ṭha* belonging to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group is the domain," meaning when it is present as an object of cognition even though it has not yet been produced.
This is the meaning. Regarding the form *gārgīyāḥ*: there are many descendants of Garga; [the suffix] *yañ* is applied by virtue of [Garga] belonging to the *gargādi* group (Pāṇini 4.1.105).

When there is a desire to express the meaning "the pupils of the Gargas," and before the suffix *añ* (which would apply by Pāṇini 4.2.113) has been produced—[that is,] while the object [of the suffix] is present as a mental construct—the elision (*luk*) of *yañ* and *iñ* occurs by the rule *yañiñośca* (Pāṇini 4.1.101).

This [suffix] would apply to that [word], and its prohibition is made by this [rule]; consequently, when the initial *vṛddhi* has been applied, and the designation *vṛddha* based upon that [designation] has also occurred, the suffix *cha* is applied by the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.114);
then the substitution of *īya* occurs; then the elision of the vowel *a* occurs by the rule *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148); and [finally] the elision of the *apatya* [suffix].

In the case of a *taddhita* suffix beginning with *an-*, the *y* [is elided] according to Pāṇini 6.4.151. Thus, we have "vāstīyāḥ. This is similar to the previous example. Regarding "ātreyīyāḥ": there are many descendants of Atri. The suffix *ḍhak* is applied by 4.1.122 (*itaścāniñaḥ*), which is then elided by 2.4.65 (*atribhṛgukutsavasiṣṭhagotamāṅgirobhyaśca*).

When *chātrāḥ* is obtained [as a form] for the [patronymic] *atrīṇām*, there is a prohibition of that [substitution] when it is the domain of *cha*. [The example is] *ṭhkhārapāyaṇīyāḥ*: the many descendants of Kharapa. There is the elision (*luk*) of that [suffix] which was applicable by the rules "naḍādibhyaḥ phak" (Pāṇini 4.1.99) and "yañādibhyo gotre" (Pāṇini 2.4.63).
In the case of *kharapāṇāṃ chātrāḥ*, there is a prohibition when the domain of *cha* is present. [Examples:

*ṭhakauvalam*, *vādaram*. The words *kubalī* and *badarī* end in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* (gaurādi); they are oxytone (*antodātta*) by the accent of the suffix, and the remainder is unaccented (*anudātta*). Therefore, in the case of *kubalyā-*...

When there is the intention to express the meaning "the fruit is a derivative of the *vadara* tree," as in "the fruit is a derivative of the *vadara*," the suffixes prescribed by Pāṇini 4.2.44 (*anudātāder añ*) and 4.3.163 (*tasya phale luk*) would apply; however,
when there is the intention to express the meaning "this belongs to the *kubala*" or "this belongs to the *vadara*," [the suffix] beginning with *aj* applies.

A prohibition does not apply when [the suffix] has become the object of the domain [of the rule]; because of the mention of "gotra" (lineage). There should be a prohibition of *luk* elision for that suffix which exists as a designator within the *gotra*; however, this suffix *añ* does not exist as a designator within the *gotra*, but rather in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*), therefore its—

The suffix *añ* indeed becomes *lug* (is elided). When that [suffix] exists, by the rule "luktaddhitaluki" (Pāṇini 1.2.49), there is also the elision (*luk*) of the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*). Since the *vṛddhi* [vowel] does not occur when *añ* is elided, the status of being "vṛddha" (having a *vṛddhi* vowel in the first syllable) does not exist; therefore, only the suffix *aṇ* applies, and not *ccha*. Thus, we have "gargarūpyam" and "gargamayam."
The suffixes *mayaṭ* and *yañ* are as previously explained. If there were no elision (*aluk*) here, we would have forms such as *gārgyarūpyam* and *gārgyamayam*;
however, [the correct form] is *gārgīyam*. This is derived by adding the suffix *cha* according to Pāṇini 5.1.5 (*tasmai hitam*) and 5.1.1 (*prāk krītāc chaḥ*).
Yet, this *cha* does not belong to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group, because it occurs after the word *dīvya*.

"From the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.93]: *gotrasya*," meaning "of the gotra-suffix. "In the case of that which has elision when there is plurality" (*bahuṣu lopinaḥ*): that suffix for which elision is prescribed when it arises in the sense of plurality is called "one that has elision in the plural.
"When there is the application of that which ends in the plural number" (*bahuvacanāntasya pravṛtau*): "application" (*pravṛtiḥ*) means the transition to another meaning.

This is what is meant: [the rule applies] when there is a transition to another meaning for that which ends in a plural suffix. And that "transition to another meaning" should be understood to occur when a secondary suffix (*pratyaya*) is produced after that [plural form] in reference to a youth (*yuvan*); at that time, it concerns the end of the lineage (*gotra*).

Regarding the rule *pravṛteḥ* [from Pāṇini 2.4.63], the phrase *dvayekayoḥ* means that when a patronymic suffix (*gotrapratyaya*) is produced from a base signifying one individual or two individuals among the descendants (*yūni*), then, upon the transition to another meaning, the elision (*aluk*) does not occur. For example:
"the many descendants of Bida" (*bidasyāpatyāni bahūni*). This is according to the rule *anuṣyānantarye bidādibhyo’ñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.104).

Thus, because the suffix *ṭhyañ* and *añ* are subject to elision (*luk*) when denoting a plurality according to Pāṇini 2.4.64, they are dropped in the plural; then, when the intention is to express the youth (*yuvan*) derived from that [base], whether in the singular or the dual, the suffix *iñ* is applied by 4.1.95 (*ata iñ*), and once the *luk* of that has been effected by the rule for *ṇya*, *kṣatriya*, etc. (2.4.58), [the form is established].

When that [derivative] ending in the *gotra* suffix undergoes a shift to another meaning (*arthāntarasaṃkrānti*), the suffix *añ*, which is the *gotra* suffix, also becomes applicable here even when it has been produced in the plural. But why does it not occur?
For, since there is no scope for *aluk*, the suffix *iñ* prescribed by Pāṇini 4.1.85 (*prāgdīvyato’ṇ*) applies instead, as it is not a *jāti*.

And there is the paribhāṣā: "The characteristic of a suffix [applies] when it has been introduced" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 96). For example, in the case of *go-hitam* ("beneficial for a cow"), which is a fourth-case compound (*caturthī-samāsa*), once the case-ending (*sup*) has been elided, the substitution of *ava* for the *ai* of the word *go*—by the rule "for *eC*, there is *ay, av, āy, or āv*" (*eCaḥ ayavāyāvaḥ*)—does not take place by relying on the presence of the fourth-case suffix through the characteristic of the suffix (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*).

It occurs; because it depends on the phoneme (*varṇa*). Its dependence on the phoneme, however, arises from its being prescribed with respect to a vowel (*ac*). And just as there is the paribhāṣā, "There is no *pratyayalakṣaṇa* [effect] when [an operation] depends on a phoneme" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 96), so too in cases such as *baidaḥ* and *baidau*, should there not likewise be an absence of [the application of the rule] due to its dependence on a phoneme, even though there is no elision (*aluk*)?

This is not so; for here the *aluk* is not dependent on a vowel (*varṇa*), but rather on a secondary suffix (*taddhita*). In this rule, however, the term "before a vowel" (*aci*) is stated as a qualifier. For this very reason, it is said in the *Vṛtti*: "a suffix belonging to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group that begins with a vowel. Therefore, regarding that *paribhāṣā*...
If this state [of being a *yuvan*] were not present, the rule "ṭhgotre'lugaci" would apply; however, by this very [rule], the elision of the suffix (*aluk*) is established here.

Furthermore, so that this [elision] does not occur when there are many *yuvan* descendants, the addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "only in the case of two or one" is made. In that case, the form remains simply "bidāḥ."

Regarding the phrase "of that which ends in the singular and dual," and so forth: when a *gotra* suffix ending in the singular or dual is applied—that is, when it has shifted its application—to refer to many individuals who are designated as *yuvan*, elision (*luk*) must be stated. In that context, *baidaḥ* is the *gotra* form ending in the singular.
*Baidayoh* is a dual form. Here, as before, the suffix *añ* is applied;

then, when there is a desire to express the plurality of the young descendants (*yuvāpatya*) of those two, the suffix *iñ* is added by the rule *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95). When the elision (*luk*) of that [suffix] has been performed by the rule *ṇyakṣatriyādibhyaśca* (2.4.58), the *gotra* suffix *añ* is also [elided].

It will be elided (*luk*). But that [elision] does not apply here; therefore, it is added as a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*). What, then, is the reason it does not apply? To this he says: "For in this case," and so forth. By the rule *yañañośca* (Pāṇini 2.4.64), elision is prescribed when [the suffixes] *yañ* and *añ* have been produced in the plural; however, *añ* has not been produced in the plural here. Why? [Because...]
What then? [It applies] when there is one or two; therefore, it does not apply [in the case of many]. Thus, it is established that in every way, when there are many, it must be "bidā" (plural).

90. *yūni luk* (4.1.90). Regarding the word *yūni*: the locative case (*saptamī*) is used in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), according to the rule *vyatyayo bahulam* (3.1.85). For this very reason, the author states in the commentary: "of the suffix denoting youth" (*yuvapratyayasya*). This is intended when a suffix beginning with a vowel (*ajādau*) is desired to follow.

By the words "buddhisya" and so forth, he demonstrates that the locative case [in *aci*] is a locative of object (*viṣayasaptamī*). His intention is that if this were a locative of co-occurrence (*parasaptamī*), then even in cases where the suffix *cccha* is not desired, it would still apply, because the word ending in the *yuvan* suffix is already considered a *buddha* (formed) word.
"Phāṇṭāhṛtarūpya, phāṇṭāhṛtamaya. If there were elision (*luk*) here, "phāṇṭāhṛtarūpya" and "phāṇṭāhṛtamaya" would not occur. "Bhāgavitikīya":
the suffix *cha* (as prescribed by 5.1.1, *prākkrītīya*) is applied as before.
91. *phakphiñor anyatarasyām* (4.1.91). [Examples:

*gārgīyāḥ*, *vātsīyāḥ*. There is the elision of the *k* and *y* of the preceding member. While the word *vā* (4.1.82) is still in force, the mention of *anyatarasyām* indicates that the rule in the preceding sūtra was obligatory (*nitya*).
For the purpose of making it known.

92. *tasyāpatyam* (4.1.92). [The word] "connected with suffixes both preceding and following" [is understood here]. Among these, it is first connected with the preceding [suffixes], such as *aṇ* and others, because they are prescribed without being joined [to a specific base]. If this [word *apatyam*] were not connected with the preceding [suffixes],...

One might have formulated this as a single rule, "the suffix *iñ* occurs after that which has [the word] *apatya* [as its final member]. However, because he separates the rule "after that which ends in *at*, the suffix *iñ*" (4.1.95) from the rule "that which has [the word] *apatya* [as its final member]" (4.1.92), it is understood that, due to this separate formulation, the present rule pertains to the preceding subject matter. Thus...

It is connected with the preceding [words] as well as with the subsequent ones, because it is marked with the *svarita* accent among them. As for the word "tasya" (of that), it is specified in the masculine gender and in the singular number. Therefore, its derivation would occur only from a masculine base and only when ending in the singular number.

It would not occur after a feminine noun or a neuter noun—for instance, in cases such as *devadattāyā apatyam* ("the offspring of Devadattā") or *kulasyāpatyam* ("the offspring of the family"). Nor would it occur after words ending in the dual or plural numbers—for instance, in cases such as *dvayormātrorapatyam* ("the offspring of two mothers") or *tisṛṇāṃ mātṛṇāmapatyam* ("the offspring of three mothers"). Now, [if one asks...]
Is this indication made using the neuter gender so that it would not apply to the feminine or masculine genders? Furthermore,
since the term *apatyam* (offspring) is used here in the singular, the suffix would apply to only one offspring,
and not to two or many— for instance, [the suffix would not apply] in the case of "the two offspring of Upagu" (*aupagavau*).

Regarding the example "the offspring of Upagu are the Aupagavas," the author states this [objection] in the form of a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): "qualified by the meaning of the base" (*prakṛtyarthaviśiṣṭa*), and so forth. This is to be connected with the word "is apprehended" (*gṛhyate*), which will be mentioned later.
The "meaning of the base" (*prakṛtyartha*) is the referent of words such as *aupagava*; [the object] is qualified by that.
The meaning of the genitive case here is the relationship between offspring and that which possesses offspring. Now, one might object:

"In this context, the word *tasya* (of him/it) is understood as denoting a general category, whereas [in the specific case of] *kṛta*, there is a particular meaning such as 'Upagu’s son' (*upagava*), by which the genitive meaning is qualified. There is no fault here, because the word *tasya* serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the particular instance.

Furthermore, its status as a specifier of a particular (viśeṣopalakṣaṇatva) has already been established previously. Therefore, the base-meaning (prakṛtyartha) is indeed the particular, such as Upagu and so forth. Regarding the phrase "and merely offspring" (apatyamātraṃ ca), the word *mātra* serves to exclude anything additional, such as gender (*liṅga*) and so on.

"Gender, number, and so forth"—by the word "and so forth" (ādi), time is included. For this indication is made by means of the present tense. As it has been said: "Even where another verbal action is not explicitly heard, there the verb 'to be' (asti) is understood, with the present tense suffix."

"Even when the first person is not explicitly employed, it is understood that it exists. In that case, if there were an intention to express the present tense, it would not apply to other times. Furthermore, what is the reason that gender, number, and so forth are not intended to be expressed? Because they are subordinate. For necessarily, by that [which is primary]...
The indication must be made by some mark (*liṅga*) or the like, because [the secondary element] is invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyakatva*).

Its inclusion here is, for example, like the inclusion of straw and such things by one seeking grain, even though they are not the primary object. The rule "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*, Pāṇini 4.3.120) and so forth applies even in the sense of offspring (*apatya*).

It applies; for one who is the offspring of Upagu can indeed be designated as "this is his [Upagu's] offspring. These—offspring, collection, residence, and modification—are indeed the specific instances of the rule *tasyedam* (Pāṇini 4.3.120). Therefore, by that rule...

By this very [rule], the suffix *aṇ* is established even for the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*); so for what purpose was the rule *tasyāpatyam* (4.1.92) composed? [The answer is: "It would have been composed for the sake of sublation (*bādhanārtham*). That is to say, it serves to sublate the suffix *cha*, which is prescribed by the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ* (4.2.114) as an exception to the *aṇ* prescribed by the rule *tasyedam* (4.3.120).

Thus, the suffix *ccha* would apply; this [present rule] is made in order to block that. It is so that there may be a blocking of the suffix *ccha* by the *aṇ* prescribed by this sūtra. But how does a non-śaiṣika [suffix] block a śaiṣika?

The scope of the secondary suffixes (*śaiṣika*) other than those beginning with *apatya* and ending with the four meanings [of the fifth case] is sixfold. And this [sixfold scope] does not exist at all within the domain of the *cha* suffix after *apatya*. Therefore, since that [scope] is absent, how could this [rule] set aside the *cha* suffix? To this he says: "This is indeed a general rule (*utsarga*) for the remainder (*śeṣa*). If this rule did not exist...

This is the intended meaning. By the word "asau" (this), because it is the subject under discussion, the sense "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*) is referred back. Although the suffix *aṇ* has been produced by the general rule (*utsarga*), that same meaning is expressed through association with the general rule. And its association with the general rule is as follows:
In that case, because the general rule (*utsarga*) beginning with *aṇ* and so forth is prescribed; here too, when this rule "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*,

Pāṇini 4.1.92) is being applied, since it falls under the scope of the rule "belonging to him" (*tasyedam*, 4.3.120), it becomes a "remainder" (*śeṣa*) in the same way as any other specific [suffix] not otherwise assigned.

The same applies to the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*). This [sense] also possesses a distinctness based on its specific requirement, because it is not included among those ending with the four senses [of the *taddhita* suffixes]. Consequently, due to its being a "remainder" (*śeṣa*), the suffix *ccha* would apply in the sense of offspring. However, in this rule [Pāṇini 5.1.16], under the heading of "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*, 4.3.120)...

It does not enter into the remainder, because it has already been employed. Consequently, since there is nothing remaining, there is simply no possibility for the suffix *ccha* to apply to the word *apatya*. That very non-occurrence is what is expressed by the term "sublation" (*bādhana*). Now, what is the purpose of this [term] in the sense of sublation?

He states the purpose [of the rule]: "The purpose of this [rule] is for the sake of the *vṛddhi* [vowels]. The *vṛddhi* vowels in nominal stems (*prātipadika*) are the purpose of this grammatical operation. Thus, in the cases of *bhānor apatyam* ("the offspring of Bhānu") resulting in *bhānavaḥ*, and *śyāmagor apatyam* ("the offspring of Śyāmaga") resulting in *śyāmagavaḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* becomes established. However, if this [rule] were not present, [it would not be so].
If the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*) were the remainder (*śeṣa*) according to the previously mentioned method, then the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.114),
which prescribes the suffix *cha* after bases containing a *vṛddhi* vowel, would consequently apply there as well.

93. *eko gotre* (4.1.93). According to the maxim *kṛtrimākṛtrimayoḥ kṛtrime kāryasaṃpratyayaḥ* (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 6), "between the technical and the non-technical, the application of an operation is understood to pertain to the technical one," only the technical *gotra* is intended here. This is also because the term *gotra* is employed within the governing context (*adhikāra*) of offspring (*apatya*).

For "lineage" (gotra) in common usage refers merely to offspring; if the inclusion of that [usage] were intended here, he would have said simply "one" (eka), since the worldly sense of lineage as offspring is already understood from the context. Therefore, because of the mention of "lineage," he states that the technical (paribhāṣika) sense is what is meant: "offspring..."
"The lineage begins from the grandson onwards. Regarding the phrase "by distinction," etc.: by distinction means by division;

that is, with respect to each successive offspring (*apatyam apatyam prati*). When there is the contingency—that is, the possibility—of suffixes arising even for all those offspring that are possible, [the rule is stated].

The meaning is "it being so. Since the offspring of any one among Garga, Gārgi, Gārgya, and Gārgyāyaṇa— the offspring of all— is the offspring of all, the suffixes that denote the immediate *gotra* from the ultimate base (*paramaprakṛti*) would consequently apply [to all].

Whatever is the offspring of Garga belongs to all those who are Gārgis, Gārgyas, and Gārgyāyaṇas.
