For although here the analysis is performed with the word *garga* as "the offspring of Garga" (*gargasyāpatyam*), nevertheless this restriction is not obtained—that the suffix must arise from the word *garga* alone; rather, [it arises from any of the forms].
There is freedom of application (*kāmacāra*). Consequently, when the suffix arises from the word *garga*, then by [Pāṇini 4.1.105] *gargādibhyaḥ yañ*, the suffix *yañ* is applied;
when it arises from the word *gārgi*, then by [Pāṇini 4.1.101] *ṭhyañiñośca*, the suffix *phak* is applied;
and even when it arises from the word *gārgya*, that same *phak* is applied; and when it arises from the word *gārgyāyaṇa*.

Then [the rule] *ṭhañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95) applies. Thus, when it would follow that multiple suffixes are produced for each offspring through division, this restriction is established by the present rule: "only one suffix occurs. By this, he demonstrates that it is a restriction regarding the suffix (*pratyayaniyama*). Furthermore, the restriction regarding the suffix consists in the singularity expressed by the word *eka*.

This is understood from the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "condition" (*pratyaya*). Furthermore, in this rule, the word "one" (*eka*) should be understood as denoting a number, as in: "one," "two," or "many. By the particle *eva*, the exclusion of two or more is effected: there is only one condition, not two, nor...

Regarding the word "many" (*bahavaḥ*): that single suffix, being produced, is understood by implication to arise from the ultimate base itself because of the mention of "one" (*eka*). For if it were produced from the word *gārgi*, there would be two suffixes—*iñ* and *phaṅ*—and not one. Or if it were from the word *gārgya*, even then there would still be two.

Regarding *yañ* and *pha*: otherwise, from the word *gārgyāyaṇa*, there would be three [suffixes]—*yañ*, *phan*, and *iñ*. Therefore, by employing the mention of "one" (*eka*), it is stated by implication that the suffix for the lineage (*gotra*) arises only from the original base form (*mūlaprakṛti*). Thus, when the suffix is produced from the original base itself, only one suffix is established.
But surely it is the progenitor alone who is connected with the offspring; for thus it is observed in the world:
seeing a child sitting on his grandfather’s lap, someone asks, "Whose is this? and he replies, "Devadatta’s. By that [reply], one understands the progenitor.

[If it were so that] one does not designate oneself [as the agent], then, because there would be no connection with the offspring for all [members of the family], the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that a distinct cognition would arise for each individual offspring simply does not exist; thus, since there is nothing to be excluded, this [rule] was not commenced for the sake of restriction. To this, he says: "All [are designated] by means of the offspring."
"They are joined.

Regarding this very point, he states the justification: "Because of not falling, it is offspring. For that by means of which one does not fall into sins becomes one's offspring because of that non-falling. Therefore, [that which is] separated...

That [intermediate offspring] which has been produced is also the offspring of the meaning expressed by the ultimate source (paramaprakṛti), because it does not fall away from that [ultimate source] either. Furthermore, the mention of the "ultimate source" should be understood as an illustration;
for even the meaning expressed by another source (itaraprakṛti) is indeed the offspring when produced immediately [from it].

Furthermore, as for what was said— that when it is asked "Whose is this?", one points to the progenitor and not to oneself— it cannot thereby be established that the offspring belongs to the progenitor alone. For in that case, it would not be the person from whom the descent originated who is being sought to be known.

What then? It is that which designates the progenitor, not itself. If, however, by that [designation] the non-falling [of the lineage] were intended for someone, then it would certainly designate itself as well. And if all were not connected through offspring, then "offspring beginning with the grandson is the *gotra*."

Thus, this co-referential designation (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the terms "offspring" (*apatya*) and "grandson and so forth" (*pautraprabhṛti*) is not tenable; for, relative to that person from whom they derive the designation of "grandson" and so on, those [descendants] are not considered offspring. Therefore, even from this designation—
It is known from scripture that "all are joined with offspring," as in the example: "His son is also a Gārgya.
By the use of the word "also" (api), his grandson and so forth are also included. What, then, is the reason why even his son is called a Gārgya?
To this he says: "In all [of them]," and so forth. Even in the case of the form *gārgyāyaṇa*, by means of one...

Since the offspring of a lineage (*gotrāpatya*) produced through an intervening [generation] also takes the suffix *yañ* from the word "Garga," his son as well is called Gārgya. By the phrase "from the word Garga," he shows that this occurs from the original base (*paramaprakṛti*). And it has been stated that this is understood from the mention of the singular [in the rule].
By the words "ṭha tha vā" and so forth, he demonstrates the rule regarding the *prakṛti* (base).
This rule of *prakṛti*, however, is obtained through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "one" (*eka*).
It should be understood that the word "one" here functions in the sense of a restriction to the first [letter] of each group; for example, [the rule applies to] the groups (*varga*).

The first and second [consonants] are produced with the throat closed (*saṃvṛtakaṇṭha*), have breath as their secondary cause (*śvāsānupradāna*), are voiceless (*aghoṣa*), and some are "slightly aspirated" (*alpaprāṇa*) while all the others are "greatly aspirated" (*mahāprāṇa*). Here, it is understood that the first [category] consists of those that are slightly aspirated.
This is the explanation of the word *eka* (one/some): "the first original form" (*prathamā prakṛtiḥ*). And what is the first? That which...

The "original base" (*prakṛti*) is that which ends in a suffix other than a secondary suffix (*apratyayānta*), such as *garga* and *naḍa*. It is stated that "the original base is restricted": only a word in the nominative case (*prathamā*) produces a suffix, not one in any other case. Thus, words such as *gārgi*, *gārgya*, and *gārgyāyaṇa* end in suffixes.

The descendant of Garga is Gārgya; his son also is Gārgya. The descendant of Naḍa is Nāḍāyana; his son also is Nāḍāyana. In all cases, even when the offspring of a lineage (gotra) is removed by one generation, the first base form produces the suffix.
94. *gotrād yūni striyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.94). [The commentary states:
"This rule is also a restriction (*niyama*). By the word *api* ("also"), he shows that it is not only the previous one [that is a restriction].

For when all [terms] are joined with a descendant (*apatya*), [the suffixes are restricted] even after those that are the immediate original base (*paramaprakṛti*), as well as after the *yuvan* [suffixes].

When there is a desire to express a descendant who is young, [the suffix] would apply; therefore, a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is established to exclude that. "Only from a *gotra* [stem]" means "only from that which ends in a *gotra* suffix. By this, he shows the nature of the restriction. With the words "not from a further [descendant]" (*na parama*), etc., he indicates what is excluded by the restriction.

In the case of *gārgyāyaṇaḥ* and *dākṣāyaṇaḥ*, the suffix *phak* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.1.101], *yañiñośca*, because these forms end in the *yañ* and *iñ* suffixes prescribed for the *gotra* lineage. In the case of *aupagaviḥ* and *nāḍāyaniḥ*,
the suffix *iñ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.1.95], *ata iñ*, because these forms end in the *aṇ* and *phak* suffixes prescribed for the *gotra* lineage.

Regarding the term ‘ṭhdākṣī’’: it is the feminine of the fourth descendant of Vatsa. [The suffix] *iñ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.95], and *ṅīṣ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.65] because it is a word denoting a human species. [The question] “What, then, is being prohibited here? refers to the fault that would arise if everything were prohibited.
He thinks thus; in order to reveal that very fault, he says "yadi" (if), etc. The meaning is:

"there would result a lack of restriction regarding the feminine"; that is to say, even after words ending in *parama*, *prakṛti*, *anantara*, and *yuvan*, the *yuvan* suffix would result in the feminine. [This is so] because of the designation *gotra* being [superseded] by the designation *yuvan*.

"Because it is sublated. In the rule "But when a descendant is living, [the suffix] yuvan [is used]," the word *tu* is employed for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇārtha*). By that, the designation [of the younger generation] would not be obtained. "Therefore," and so forth; and precisely because there is a fault in the prohibition of both the restrictive rule and the *yuvan* suffix, [the author proceeds].

Therefore, in order to exclude that [undesired application], a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must be made. In this regard, "from *gotra*, [the suffixes] up to *yuvan*" is the first rule; by this, a restriction (*niyama*) is established, as he says: "From *gotra*, a suffix occurs in the sense of *yuvan* (descendant). Then, "except for *astrī* (feminine)" is the second rule. And by that—
In the rule concerning *yūni*, a prohibition is made of that operation which was previously stated;

as it says: "That which was stated regarding *yūni* in the feminine does not take place. [Another view holds: "The designation *yuvan* itself is prohibited. How so? For in the rule *astriyām*, the term *yūni* is carried over (*anuvartate*), and thus—

It is understood that the operation prescribed for the *yuvan* [stage] does not apply to the feminine; and since the technical designation *yuvan* is applied only to the *yuvan* [stage], it is that very designation which is prohibited. By the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "the *yuvan* designation only," the restriction excludes both the *yuvan* suffix and the suffixes [of the *yuvan* stage]. Therefore, the feminine...
"It will be designated by means of the *gotra* [suffix]. This is because, once that designation as *yuvan* has been prohibited, the designation as *gotra* remains unshaken.

25. *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95). By the word *ataḥ*, the previously mentioned nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is qualified; and because a rule involving a qualification applies to that which ends with it (*tadantavidhi*), he says: "from a nominal stem ending in the letter *t*."
Why is it not understood that *athātaḥ* is the inclusion of the root *at* (meaning "continuous movement," *dhā.pā.* 34) with the suffix *kvip*? Because of the rule *śivādibhyo 'ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.1.112).
That [rule] is indeed formulated for the purpose of superseding the suffix *iñ*. And if there were a reference to the actual form (*svarūpagrahaṇa*) here, [the rule would be unnecessary].
Since there is no possibility [of application] from roots such as *śiva* and others, the prescription of the suffix *aṇ* for the purpose of superseding them would be useless,
because roots like *krauḍi*, which end in *iṇ*, are listed [in the relevant section]. Therefore, this refers only to that which ends in the vowel *a*.

If this is so, then in the case of *asyāpatyam* ("his offspring"), [the suffix] *ira* would not apply because it does not end in the vowel *a*. This objection is without fault, because by the principle of "behaving like that which possesses the designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), it is considered to end in *a*. Thus we have *śubhaṃyāḥ* and *kīlālapāḥ*, derived from the roots *yā-* and *pā-* by the rule *āto maninkvanibvanipaśca*.
For in this rule (3.2.74), *vij* is drawn forward by the particle *ca* from the preceding rule (3.2.73): *ṭhvijupeścchandasi*.
[The question] "How? and so forth [is raised]. From the word *daśaratha* as well, there ought to be the suffix *diñ* after a stem ending in *a*; therefore—
The point is that the usage of *dāśarathāya* as a form ending in the suffix *aṇ* is not tenable.

Regarding the phrase "when there is a desire to express the remainder" (*śeṣavivakṣāyām*), etc.: by this, the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed here when there is a desire to express the meaning "this belongs to Daśaratha," and not [in the sense of] "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*).

This indicates that [the suffix] is used when one intends to express that meaning. However, when one intends to express "the offspring of Daśaratha," then the suffix *iñ* indeed occurs—namely, *dāśarathiḥ*.

96. *Bāhvādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.96). [The example] "bāhaviḥ" [is formed as follows]: by the rule *orguṇaḥ* (6.4.146), [the vowel *o* is replaced by its guṇa substitute]. [The word] "kvacit" [means] in the case of those ending in *ajīgartāviṣkāra*. [This applies to] *bāhu* and the others.

The recitation [of these names] is for the purpose of obtaining [the suffix *cha*], because all words ending in *vaṭāku* and so forth terminate in the letter *a*. Furthermore, in the case of the word *cūḍā*, since the suffix *ḍhak* would otherwise apply by the rule "dvya-caḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.121), [the mention of *cūḍā* is necessary]. As for the group beginning with *vṛkala* and ending before the word *puṣkarasat*, the suffix *aṇ* applies by the rule "avṛddhābhyo nadīmānuṣībhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.113).
The sense of "attainment" (*prāpti*) applies to the words beginning with *puṣkarasat* and ending with *loman*, because they do not end in the vowel *a*. [This is indicated by] the rule:
"After *amita* and *ojas*, there is the suffix *iñ* and the elision of *s*. Thus, the suffix *iñ* occurs after the word *amitaujas*, and there is also the elision of the *s*.

Regarding *āmitaujiḥ*: it is read as *udañc* [in the root list]; therein, the letter *c* of the root *añc* is to be understood. This, however, does not end in the vowel *a*; rather, what is it? It ends in the suffix *kvip*, and due to a specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*) at the time of the suffix's application, the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) does not occur.

The offspring of one who faces north is *audañciḥ*. The word *śiras-* necessitates an application of the rule concerning suffixes added after a final member (*tadanta-vidhi*), because the neuter form alone cannot be connected with "offspring. Thus, the offspring of *hastiśiras-* is *hāstiśīrṣiḥ*, according to the rule *ṭhye ca taddhite* (Pāṇini 6.1.61).

The letter *ca* serves to include that which has not been explicitly mentioned: "the offspring of Ūrdhvaloman" is *Āurdhvalomiḥ*. Since for [names] beginning with Ajīgarta and ending before the word Udaṅka, the suffix *aṇ*—which subverts [the application of] *iñ* by the rule "ṛṣyaṇḍhakavṛṣṇi...
(Pāṇini 4.1.114)—would otherwise apply, [the sūtra] states: "Udaṅkaḥ in the sense of a proper name. Thus, there is a certain person named Udaṅka.
His offspring is Audañki. Regarding the rule "sambhūyo'mbhasoḥ salopaśca" (Pāṇini 4.1.86):
the suffix *iñ* is applied after the words *sambhūya* and *ambhas*, and there is the elision of the letter *sa*.

Thus, [the forms] *sāmbhūyiḥ* and *āmbhiḥ* are derived. Regarding the phrase "in the group beginning with bāhu": by the word *prabhṛti* ("beginning with"), it is indicated that from this point onward...

Those which will be mentioned are included [in this rule]. Regarding the statement, "The view is that their status is in the worldly *gotra*": "view" (*darśana*) here means established usage (*prasiddhi*). "Status in the worldly *gotra*" (*laukike gotre bhāvaḥ*) means the state of being designated as such.
Those for whom there is established usage regarding their status in the worldly *gotra*—their inclusion is among the *bāhu*-class [of stems].

It should be understood that "the prohibition of them applies elsewhere than that. That is to say, the prohibition should be known to apply to those for whom there is no perception of the worldly state of lineage (*gotra*), but rather perception of something other than that. By this, it refers to a certain primordial person named Bāhu, who, by virtue of having established a designation...

It is well known that men who fall within the lineage of one's offspring receive the designation "Bāhu" (descendant of Bāhu), and from that very fact the suffix *iñ* occurs [to form the patronymic]. However, for someone named Bāhu who is not a descendant of that [lineage], only the suffix *aṇ* occurs—thus, "Bāhavāḥ. And this...

This is understood through the recurrence of the word "vā" and by recognizing that the option is fixed (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Furthermore, regarding the grammatical operation prescribed for relative terms such as *śvaśura* ("father-in-law") and others, there is a prohibition [of that operation] based on their similarity [to other relatives].
Here too, the previously stated reason should be understood. This refers to the rule *rāja-śvaśurād yat* (Pāṇini 4.1.137).

Thus, the suffix *yat* in the word *śvaśurya* occurs only after a relative term (*sambandhi-śabda*), not after a proper name (*saṃjñā-śabda*). Therefore, if there is someone named Śvaśura, his offspring is *śvāśuri*, formed only with the suffix *iñ*.
This is according to the rule "of a Śvaśura who is a proper name. One who is a Śvaśura by virtue of being a proper name is not [necessarily] so by virtue of a [matrimonial] relationship.
He whose father-in-law was Saṃjñā.

97. *sudhāturakaṅ ca* (4.1.97). Regarding the rule beginning with *ṭhvyāsavaruḍa*: the meaning is that this must be explained as having the sense that the suffix *iñ* is applied after [names such as] Vyāsa and others, and by virtue of its co-occurrence (*tatsanniyogena*), the substitution of *akaṅ* occurs. In this regard, the explanation is as follows:
The particle *ca* from the preceding sūtra is carried over (*anuvartate*) here, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been mentioned;

by this, [the suffix] will also apply to Vyāsa and others, as in "Vaiyāsakiḥ. [In this case,] the prohibition of *aij*-vṛddhi is applied by the rule "na yvābhyām" (Pāṇini 7.3.3), etc. Alternatively, one might read the word *sudhātṛ* itself among the *bāhv-ādi* group.

And why was that specific region (the *ākaṅ* suffix) not applied there, as it is recited in the list [of roots] in the rule "amitaujaḥ salopaśca"? Or [why was it not applied] in the sūtra? For in that case, no particular advantage in terms of brevity (*lāghava*) is obtained; thus, this [objection] is trivial.

98. *gotre kuñjādibhyaś cphañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.98). [This is] an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṭhiñ*; for the words beginning with *kuñja* end in the vowel *a*. "The letter *c* is for the sake of specification. If the letter *c* were not used here, then...

Even in the rule *ṭh-vrāta-cphañ-or-astriyām* (5.3.113), this [suffix] is not applied at all, because the suffix *cphañ* does not exist. Consequently, if it were stated as *ṭh-vāta-phañ-or-astriyām*, there would be the inclusion of *aśvādibhyaḥ phañ* (4.1.110) as well. [For example: *kauñjāyanyaḥ*.

Regarding "kauñjāyanyau": following the rule "pūgāññyo 'grāmaṇīpūrvāt" (Pāṇini 5.3.112), while the suffix "ñya" is being carried over, the suffix "ñya" is applied in its own sense by the rule "vrātacphañorastriyām" (5.3.113). Thus we have "kauñjāyanāḥ," according to the rule "ñyādayastadrājāḥ" (5.3.119).

Because it is designated as a *tadrāja* [patronymic], there is elision (*luk*) by the rule "of a *tadrāja* [suffix], when many [descendants are denoted]" (Pāṇini 2.4.62). Now, in this case, should the accent be determined by the *ñit* accent or by the *cit* accent?

To this he says: "In the singular and dual," and so forth. First, in the singular and dual... [provided that]... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on Pāṇinian grammar. The ellipsis indicates the sentence is incomplete in the original.)

In that case, when the suffix *ñya* is subsequently prescribed after a *cit*-accented stem, the accent resulting from the *ñit* designation becomes "remaining" (*satiśiṣṭa*), and thus it alone ought to apply. However, in the case of the plural number, once *ñya* has been set aside and its application is reached, it is desired that the *cit* accent alone should prevail, even though [the conditions for] it have ceased. How so?
If it is argued that even when [the suffix] is desired to be marked with *ñ*, it is obtained by virtue of the *ñ* designation, we say no;

for by virtue of the *ñ* designation, the accent (*ñitsvara*) is also obtained. If that is so, then a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made regarding the prescription of accents: first, this [sūtra] exists—“*citaḥ*” (Pāṇini 6.1.163); then...
Regarding the rule *taddhitasya* (6.1.164), the term *citaḥ* continues to apply there.

For what purpose is this [rule]? Because of its subsequent position, the rule *ñnityādir nityam* (6.1.197) would otherwise apply, prescribing that the first syllable is acute; this [present rule] is for the purpose of overriding that. Thereafter, the rule *kitaḥ* (6.1.165) [applies].
Thus, furthermore, the final syllable of a secondary derivative (taddhita) is acute-accented.

99. *Naḍādibhyaḥ phak* (Pāṇini 4.1.99). Among the *naḍādi* group, it is recited: "*Ṭhaśalaṅku śalaṅkañ ca*. This is its meaning: the word *śalaṅku* produces the suffix [phak] and undergoes the substitution of *śalaṅka*. By that—

The form *śālaṅkāyana* occurs. Regarding the mention of "among the *pailādi*s": the word *śālaṅki*, ending in the suffix *iñ*, is listed among the *pailādi*s so that the elision (*luk*) of the secondary suffix (*yuvan-pratyaya*) produced from it may occur—as in:
"Śālaṅki is the father; Śālaṅki is the son. For in that case...

From the sūtra beginning with *ṭhṇyakṣatriyārṣañitaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.58), the phrase *yūni luk* is also understood as a governing rule (*anuvartate*). Therefore, the inclusion of the word *śālaṅgi* there [in the list of *naḍādyaḥ*] is not appropriate;
for, since it is read among the *naḍādi* group, the suffix *phak* ought to occur [by Pāṇini 4.1.99]. How then can it be there [in the sūtra] ending in *iñ*?

The objection is: "It is recited [in the text]. He states the resolution for that: "In a specific lineage," and so forth. Regarding the lineage *Kauśika*, the teacher prescribes the suffix *phak* after the word *Śalaṅku* specifically in that context;
however, elsewhere, only the suffix *iñ* occurs, and thus there is no fault. That [suffix] is *iñ*.

[The suffix] is obtained because [the group beginning with] *bāhu* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*. Even granting that the suffix *phak* is prescribed for the mere sense of lineage (*gotra*), he states another solution, beginning with "Or rather" (*atha vā*). The mention of the state of having the suffix *iñ* is an illustration; for even the fact that the state of being a *Śalaṅka* is included in the list of *Paila* and others is itself the indicator [of this].

Even in the previous explanation, this very [rule] should be understood as its indicator: "In the Vṛṣagaṇa [gotra], [the suffix] Phak is applied after Agniśarman. From the word *agniśarman*, when the Vṛṣagaṇa gotra is intended, the suffix *phak* occurs—thus, *āgniśarmāyaṇaḥ*.
In other cases, only *aṇ* occurs—thus, *āgniśarmaḥ*. It is read as "of that person" (*amuṣya*).
In that case, due to an irregularity (nipātana), there is no elision (aluk) of the case-ending: *āmuṣyāyaṇa*. Regarding the rule "kṛṣṇaraṇau brāhmaṇavāśiṣṭhayoḥ":
the words *kṛṣṇa* and *raṇa* produce the suffix *phak* when the meanings to be expressed are respectively a Brāhmaṇa and a Vāśiṣṭha. Thus: *kārṣṇāyanaḥ* for a Brāhmaṇa; *rāṇāyaṇaḥ* [for a Vāśiṣṭha].

*Vaśiṣṭha*: this means one belonging to the *vaśiṣṭha* gotra. In other cases, only the suffix *iñ* occurs—as in *kārṣṇiḥ* and *rāṇiḥ*. It is stated that "the word *kroṣṭu* [becomes] *kroṣṭṛ*"; the word *kroṣṭu* produces the suffix *phak* and undergoes the change to *kroṣṭṛ*—thus, *krauṣṭāyanaḥ*.

100. *haritādibhyo’ñaḥ* | (4.1.100) The objection begins with "And not [the suffix] *ṭhak*," etc. The resolution is stated as "This is true," etc. From those [names] beginning with *harita* that end in the *añ* prescribed for the *gotra* [lineage], the suffix *phak* is applied; and not...
Another suffix conditioned by *gotra* (a clan name) can occur following [a word] conditioned by *gotra*.

In that case, by implication (*sāmarthya*), even though the governing topic is *gotra*, the suffix is understood to apply to the *yuvan* (descendant) degree. If this is so, what is the purpose of the governing topic of *gotra*? To this he says: "The governing topic of *gotra* is for the sake of what follows."

101. *yañiñośca* | (4.1.101) Now, regarding the *yañ* prescribed by the rule *dvīpādanusamudraṃ yañ* (4.3.10), as well as the *iñ* prescribed for *sutaṅgama* and others by the rule *vṛñcchaṇ* (4.2.80) etc., [the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied].

"Why does [the suffix] not occur after that [word *dvīpa*]? For no specific distinction has been stated here. To this, he says: "After *dvīpa*, the suffix *yañ* [is applied] according to the ocean," and so forth. For by the mention of *gotra* (lineage), *yañ* and *iñ* are specified here—namely, "those *yañ* and *iñ* which occur in the sense of *gotra*. And [this is not the case for] "after *dvīpa*" (Pāṇini 4.3.10).
By such statements as these, it is shown that the suffix *yañ* is not prescribed after [names like] *gotra*, but rather after specific meanings such as "born from" (*jāta*).

Nor is the suffix *iñ* prescribed after [names like] *sutaṅgama* and others in the sense of *gotra*; rather, it is prescribed in four senses beginning with "that which exists in this place" (*tad asminn asti*) according to Pāṇini 4.2.67 and 70. Therefore, the suffix does not occur after those [words] ending in them.

If, then, *yañ* and *iñ* are qualified here by the mention of "clan" (*gotra*), and not by the meaning of the suffix itself, then it would not be understood where this suffix occurs; therefore, he says "from that which ends in that," and so forth. Why does he say "that"? He replies: "because of the statement 'yaūni after a clan [name]'."

102. *Śaradvac-chunaka-darbhād Bhṛgu-vatsāgrāyaṇeṣu* (4.1.102). [The word] "in a gotra" (*gotre*) [is understood here]. If, then, "in a gotra" is indeed the governing term, it would not be possible for the meaning of the suffix to be qualified by *Bhṛgu* and *Vatsa*, which are themselves root-primitive bases (*mūlaprakṛti*).

For it is only by means of those two—the *gotra* and the *pratyaya*—that the meaning of the *apatya* (descendant) can be qualified as the sense of the *pratyaya*; therefore, it would indeed be appropriate to say "among the Bhārgavas, Vātsyāyanas, and Āgrāyaṇas. This [is not the case].

This is a fault; for, by virtue of the governing power of the *gotra* (lineage), it is only those [suffixes] that denote the offspring of a *gotra* which are understood here, having applied a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of the cause to the effect. To demonstrate that very application of those two to the offspring of a *gotra*, it is stated in the commentary (*vṛtti*) "in the *vṛtti*"—namely, "he becomes a Śāradvatāyana."
If he is a Bhārgava, he becomes a Śaunakāyana; if he is a Vātsya, [he becomes a Śaunakāyana].

103. *droṇaparvatajīvantād anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.103). [The commentary asks: "How is this so? and so forth. If the suffix *-phak* occurs after *droṇa* and others to denote a descendant in the *gotra* lineage, then how is it that in usages such as *drauṇāyanaḥ* ("the son of Droṇa") and *droṇataḥ prati* ("in opposition to Droṇa"), Aśvatthāman is referred to by the immediately preceding [form]?

Why is this said? [The answer is: "Not indeed here. This means that the present-day Droṇa is not the one referred to here by the patronymic suffix *phak* as *Drauṇāyana*; what then? It is "beginningless" (*anādi*).
This was stated for the purpose of showing the possibility of its being heard in scripture. By which reason Aśvatthāman is called *Drauṇāyana*...

Thus it is said; he now demonstrates this with the words "the present-day," and so forth. The phrase "the present-day, however," and so on, should be understood as referring to the exclusion of the ancient Droṇa. For the Droṇa of the *Mahābhārata* is certainly not a present-day person, because he belongs to the distant past. Even though an object belongs to the distant past, it [remains] in the mind...
Being thus contemplated, it attains the state of being present; for example: "Let Kaṃsa be killed today.

Furthermore, the designation of Aśvatthāman as "Droṇāyana" by means of a patronymic suffix (*gotra-pratyaya*) from Droṇa—who is [only] contemporary—occurs through superimposition (*adhyāropa*), since [the status of being his son] does not actually exist [at that time].
In this context, "superimposition" (adhyāropa) means non-attachment [to the distinction]. To what is there superimposition? To the lineage (gotra).

The phrase "due to the commonality of the name" (*śrutisāmānyāt*) states the reason for the superimposition. There is a common name, "Droṇa," for both the beginningless Droṇa, whose name is Aśvatthāman, and the father Droṇa. Therefore—

Due to the similarity of sound, those whose intellects are unsettled superimpose upon Aśvatthāman— the son of Droṇa, who is a descendant of Bharata— the status of being a *gotra*, which is the property belonging to the lineage of the beginningless Droṇa; by means of that superimposition, they apply the designation "Droṇāyana" to him.
It proceeds.

104. *anṛṣyānantarye bidādibhyo’ñ* (4.1.104). Regarding the phrase "those words here which are not names of seers (*anṛṣiśabda*)," and so forth: [An objection is raised: But surely, in the sūtra, the word *ānantarya* is employed with an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*); therefore, it should be explained in this way: those...
Furthermore, in this context, do the words *ṛṣi* and so forth denote sons and others, such that the suffix occurs only when there is immediate succession (*ānantarya*) of offspring?

This is not the case; for this suffix *ṣyañ* is not prescribed in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), but rather in its own primary sense (*svārtha*), just as in the word *cāturvarṇya*. Otherwise, the suffix would have to be applied in the sense of the "duty" (*dharma*) of offspring or in the sense of "immediate succession."
The suffix would apply [to the grandson], not to the immediate descendant, yet it is intended to apply there.

But how, when the context concerns *gotra* (lineage), is it obtained that the suffix applies only to the immediate descendant after words denoting *ṛṣis*? In this case, the mention of *gotra* is set aside; after words denoting *ṛṣis*, the suffix applies only to the immediate descendant.
To this he says: "This [is the meaning] of the rule *anṛṣyantarya*," and so forth; "If this is the meaning," and so forth.
For if this were the meaning, the rule *anṛṣyantarya* would have a specific scope;
because the suffix is prescribed for a descendant immediately following one who is not a *ṛṣi*. And therefore, [it applies to] the offspring of a non-*ṛṣi*.
He says that the prohibition regarding immediate succession (*ānantarya*) would not have been established:

"The word *ṛṣi* here refers to the genus *ṛṣi* or the state of being an *ṛṣi*; 'immediate succession' [is understood] with respect to the offspring. The compound is formed by the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "the locative case" (Pāṇini 2.1.40).

The compound *paścādṛṣerapatyanairantaryam* is a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound. In that case, the meaning is as follows: the prohibition of the suffix *añ* would not have been made regarding the continuity of the status of being a seer (*ṛṣitva*) among the offspring.
Alternatively: "seers" (*ṛṣi*) and "offspring" (*apatya*) together form "seer-offspring" (*ṛṣyapatya*); [the compound refers to] their continuity.

The meaning is that, regarding that subject, the suffix *añ* should not be prohibited [from forming the word] *kṛta*. What, then, would be the fault? He says: "In that case, this," and so forth. There were seven *ṛṣi*s of the Kāśyapa lineage who were mutually related through the connection of offspring and descendants, among whom was one named Mitrahū.

Kāśyapa is the seventh; among their descendants there is continuity. In that regard, regarding the continuity of the descendants of the ṛṣis, the suffix *añ* is desired to be prohibited, so that the form "kāśyapānām" may occur. If *añ* were present, [the form would be different] when there are many.

Because there would be no elision (*lopābhāvāt*), the form *kāśyapānām* would result; however, since that prohibition [of the suffix] applies when this meaning [of non-remoteness] is present, it does not occur, and thus *kāśyapānām* is not established.
Therefore, the meaning of the rule *ṭhanṛṣyānantarye* is that [the suffix] does not occur when there is an uninterrupted lineage of descendants from a seer (*ṛṣyapatyanairantaryeṇa*).

The intended meaning is that [the person] is understood as such. "Only in the form of an immediate descendant" (*anantarāpatya*): here, what is intended is not a descendant in the sense of a lineage (*gotra*), but rather an immediate descendant.
Therefore, it is only in the form of an immediate descendant that the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ*, prescribed by Pāṇini 4.1.114 (*ṛṣyandhakavṛṣṇikurubhyaś ca*), applies.

The designation "Kāśyapas" will come into being. To strengthen this very point, he says: "And necessarily," and so forth. That prohibition whose scope is the uninterrupted succession of the offspring of sages is described as such.
It refers to the uninterrupted continuity of the state of being a sage among the offspring, or of the offspring themselves who are sages.
The meaning is: "when a negation is understood. [For example: "Kauśika is corrupted by being called Viśvāmitra.

What is the reason? Viśvāmitra performed austerities [thinking], "May I not be one who is not a seer (*anṛṣi*)," and thus he became a venerable seer; yet when he again performed austerities [thinking], "May I not have a son who is not a seer," [he was corrupted].

Thinking, "May I [become one]," the venerable Gādhi also became a seer (ṛṣi); he again performed austerities, thinking, "May I not have a grandson who is not a seer," and the venerable Kuśika also became a seer.
Thus, there is an uninterrupted continuity of seership among the descendants, [beginning] from the offspring of seers.

Or [it refers to] immediate succession. Consequently, if it were understood that this does not occur when there is no immediate succession between a seer (*ṛṣi*) and his offspring, then the form *kauśika* as *viśvāmitra* would not be established.
[In the rule] "after *parastrī* and *paraśu*," the word *parastrī* causes the suffix to arise.
And he attains the state of another; the offspring of another's wife is a Pāraśava.

105. *gargādibhyo yañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.105). [Question: How is it that there is the form *mānavī prajā* ("the progeny of Manu")? Since [Manu] is included among the *gargādi* group, the suffix *yañ* ought to apply; consequently, the form *mānavī* would not be established. [Answer: For, by the rule for the *lohitādi* group, the suffix *ṣpha* applies after a stem ending in *yañ*.
The intention is that when [the patronymic] Mānavya is prescribed, it ought to be *mānavī*. "Gotra" is what is being referred to here;

for the suffix *yañ* is prescribed in relation to a *gotra*, not in relation to offspring (*apatya*) in general. Therefore, in that case, the general suffix *aṇ* will apply, resulting in *mānavī*. As for the question "How? and so forth: if...

It is called a *gotra*; therefore, just as the suffix *yañ* does not occur after the word *garga* when referring to the immediate descendant, so too it should not occur after the words *jamadagni* and *parāśara*.
How then can there be the suffix *yañ* in such cases as "Rāma, the son of Jamadagni" (*jāmadagnya*) and "Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara" (*pārāśarya*), which refer to immediate descendants?
Does it occur? It will occur "by the superimposition of the form of a lineage" (*gotrarūpādhyāropeṇa*).

When the forms of the lineages belonging to the two immediate descendants, Rāma and Vyāsa, are intended to be expressed, then the superimposition of the form of a lineage is performed; in that case, [the suffix] *yañ* [is applied].
Thus, there is no fault. Furthermore, it is not conceivable that the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) regarding a non-existent thing is improper;
for the intention to speak even regarding a non-existent thing is observed, as in the cases: "The Vindhya is a vardhitaka" and "The ocean is a water-pot.
When, then, there is an intention to speak of the immediate offspring, by what [is it designated]?
He says that [the suffix] must occur: "But when there is a desire to express an intermediate offspring," and so forth.
Regarding "vājā'se": the word *vāja* causes the suffix *yañ* to arise. "In *ase*" means in a non-compound (*asamāsa*).
Why [is it said] "in a non-compound"? [Consider] *sauvājiḥ*.
106. *madhubabhvror brāhmaṇakauśikayoḥ* (4.1.106).

If, then, the word *babhru* is already established [by the application of the suffix] due to its inclusion in the *gargādi* list, and its mention here for the sake of restriction applies only to the *kauśika*, then there is no purpose for its inclusion in the *gargādi* list.

[Kumārila asks: "O Kauśika, let the inclusion [of the word *lohitaka*] be for the sake of the suffix itself; why not for this [the feminine suffix]? To this he replies: 'The reading in the Gargādi list, etc. The reading in the Gargādi list must also be made so that the internal-group operation *ṣpha* may apply by the rule 'sarvatra lohitaka-' (Pāṇini 4.1.18). Now, the list..."

Why was the mention of *kauśika* not made? What advantage would there be in doing so, such that the mention of *babhru* would no longer need to be made in the Sūtra? This is true; it is because the *gaṇa* is non-Pāṇinian. However, Pāṇini does not deserve censure for failing to do so.
For what has not been done by the author of the *Gaṇa*? It was for the sake of variety; indeed, the composition of the *Gaṇa* by the author of the *Gaṇa* is diverse.

107. *kapibodhād āṅgirase* (Pāṇini 4.1.107). [The example] "kāpeyaḥ" is formed with the suffix *ḍhak* by the rule *itaścāniñaḥ* (4.1.122). If the word *kapi* is read in the *gargādi* group, its inclusion here is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtham*); thus...
Since the inclusion of *Satyāṅgirasa* is for the very purpose of applying the rule [of elision], what is the need for its recitation among the *Garga*-type names?
To this he says: "And for the sake of the grammatical operations pertaining to the *lohita*-type," and so forth.

108. *Vataṇḍācca* (4.1.108). For what purpose is this? The meaning is that this is purposeless. He asks, "What is the reason? and says, "Insofar as... and so forth. By the words "Even in the *Śivādi* [list]," etc., he demonstrates the utility [of the rule]. If this...

If it were not stated [in the rule], then, because of the inclusion of "Garga" and others in the list, just as the suffix *yañ* occurs for the descendant of Aṅgiras, so too would the suffix *aṇ* occur for those such as Śiva due to their inclusion in that same list.

Therefore, the repetition is for the purpose of ensuring that the suffix *yañ* for the descendant of Aṅgiras supersedes the suffix *aṇ* for Śiva and others. Now, [if it is argued] that [the desired result] follows simply from the inclusion in the Garga-list...

[Objection: Since [the result] is already established, why was it not stated that this is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*) regarding the descendant of Aṅgiras? [Reply: It is impossible to say so;
for a rule serves the purpose of restriction only when there is no other motive. But here there is a motive, and that has indeed been shown.
109. *luk* in the feminine (*striyām*).
(Pāṇini 4.1.109) [The example is] *vātaṇḍyāyanī*. [This is formed by] the suffix *ṣpha*, which is conditioned by [the word] *lohita* and others.

110. *aśvādibhyaḥ phañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.110). Regarding the phrase "but here, in the case of *ṭhya*" and so forth: because of the rule *eko gotre* (4.1.93), which states that there is only one [descendant] suffix in a lineage (*gotra*), it is not possible for another *gotra*-suffix to follow a word already ending in a *gotra*-suffix. In that regard...

By implication, even though the context concerns those who do not belong to a *gotra*, when words ending in the *gotra*-suffixes are recited, it is understood that the suffix [denoting] a *yuvan* descendant applies to them by the rule "ṭhak after a *gotra* word, except for *yuvan*" (Pāṇini 4.1.94). Regarding the entry "śapa ātreye": from the word *śapa*, if the descendant is Ātreya, the suffix *phañ* is applied, resulting in *śāpāyana*.
Ātreya; elsewhere, Śāpi. The word *vailya* ends in a *gotra* suffix; therefore, it occurs in the masculine. There was a royal seer named Vili; his descendant is a *gotra*.
According to Pāṇini 4.1.171, *vṛddhetkosalājādāñ ñyaṅ*, [the suffix] *ñyaṅ* is applied, resulting in *vailyaḥ*. His descendant...

*Vaiyāyana* is a youth. The word *ānaḍuhya* also ends in a *gotra* suffix because it belongs to the *garga-ādi* group due to its *yañ* ending; from that [base] as well, *phañ* is applied specifically for a youth—thus *ānaḍuhyāyana* is a youth. In the feminine, only *ḍhak* occurs:
the offspring of *jātā* is *jāteyaḥ*. [This is governed by the rule] "In the case of *ātreya*, [it refers to] a descendant of Bhāradvāja."

From the word *Ātreya*, the suffix *phañ* is applied if the descendant belongs to the lineage of Bhāradvāja; thus, one who is both an Ātreyāyaṇa and a Bhāradvāja. Otherwise, it is *Ātreyi*. This is according to the rule: "Bhāradvāja [is used] when [the descendant is] an Ātreya.
From the word *Bhāradvāja*, the suffix *phañ* is applied when the descendant is a specific type of Ātreya; thus, *Bhāradvājāyana*.
Ātreya says: elsewhere, [the suffix] is ṛṣyaṇ.
111. *bhargātraigarte* (4.1.111).
"As appropriate" (*yathāyatham*) means according to each one's own [rule]. Whichever [suffix] belongs to which [base], [that is applied].
The suffix *iñ* and others are [already] one's own [established] affixes; therefore, *aṇ* is prescribed for those [names] not included therein. Now, what is the purpose of mentioning *aṇ*?

Why not simply say "from Śiva and the rest"? If only "from Śiva and the rest" were stated, it might be thought that the affixes such as *iñ* prescribed elsewhere should not apply here, but rather only *aṇ*.

If it is argued that this is for the purpose of ensuring that [the suffix] occurs exactly as it should, this is not so; for with respect to the suffixes *iñ* and others as prescribed, this statement would be redundant, since that result is established even without it.
Therefore, even in the absence of the mention of *aṇ*, only *aṇ* will occur. But surely, if the mention of *aṇ* were not there...
Is it not the case that, because *phañ* is the subject under discussion, the rule is understood to apply to that [suffix] alone? This is not so;

for if it were intended to prescribe *phañ* after *Śibi* and the others, then one would have listed them among the *aśvādi* group itself. What, then, is the purpose? It is this: the word *Auṣṭriṣeṇa*.

Since *śiva* and others are recited [in the list], the suffix *ṇya* would apply to them by the rule *senāntalakṣaṇakāribhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.152). In that case, if the mention of *aṇ* were not present, this subsequent prescription would serve to set aside that [suffix *ṇya*], and consequently, only the *iñ* prescribed [by 4.1.95] would occur, and not *aṇ*; therefore, it is indeed *aṇ*.
The inclusion of the suffix *aṇ* is so that [the rule] may apply;
[it is said] "in order to override the *iñ* of the Northern grammarians. By the rule "udīcām" (Pāṇini 4.1.153), the suffix *iñ* would otherwise be applicable;
therefore, the word *takṣan* is recited here in order to override that. If that is the case, then...

Since the word *takṣan* is listed here, the suffix *iñ* is superseded; likewise, there arises the problem that the suffix *ṇya* prescribed by the rule *senāntalakṣaṇakāribhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.152) would also be superseded. Consequently, the form *tākṣaṇyaḥ* would not be established? To this, he says: [of the suffix] *ṇya*.
"But sublation is not accepted [in this case]. How is it that even though it is not accepted, it does not occur?

Because of its association with words such as *supiṣṭa*. Here, the word *takṣan* which is recited together with *supiṣṭa* and the others—namely, in the sequence *supiṣṭa-mayūra-khara-dūra-takṣan*—is just like [the following example]: [text fragment]...just as...

If the recitation of these [words] here is for the purpose of supplanting *iñ*, then by association with them, this [recitation] also will be understood as being solely for the purpose of supplanting *iñ*. In that regard, the mention of *śiva* and the others prior to the word *bhūri* is for the purpose of supplanting *iñ*;
for these—*bhūri*, *saṃdhi*, and *muni*—[the suffix *aṇ* applies] by the rule "after a word ending in *ṭh* or *it*, except when *iñ* follows" (Pāṇini 4.1.122).
When *ḍhak* is applicable— namely, for *kuṭhāra*, *anabhimlāna*, and so forth, starting with *kakutstha*— it is for the purpose of setting aside *iñ* which follows the word *jaraṭkāru*.
[The suffix *ḍhak* applies] to the words beginning with *jaraṭkāru* and ending before the word *supiṣṭa*, by virtue of the rule "from feminine stems, *ḍhak*" (Pāṇini 4.1.120).

Thus, when *ḍhak* was expected [to apply], [the rule] "before *takṣan*, from *supiṣṭa* and so on" applies. The suffix *iñ* for *takṣan* is characterized by the sense of an agent according to the Easterners (*udīcām*). This is for the purpose of setting aside the suffix *ṇya* prescribed after *ṛṣṭiṣeṇa*—which ends in *senānta*—and also [the suffixes] prescribed after words ending in *lakṣaṇa*. As for the two words *gaṅgā* and *pāṭa*, their inclusion here occurs in a case where [another suffix] had not yet been established.

It has been explained by the author of the *Vṛtti* himself: when the suffix *iñ* would otherwise apply before the word *bhūmi* following [the group] beginning with *yaska*, the suffix *ḍhak* applies to the word *bhūmi* by the rule "ṭhitaścāniñaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.122). Likewise, for the word *ilā*, the suffix *ḍhak* applies by the rule "dvyacaśca" (Pāṇini 4.1.121), which is part of the rule "padyacaḥ. It is exactly the same in this case.

For the word *sapatnī* as well, the suffix is indeed *ḍhak*, by the rule *strībhyo ḍhak* (Pāṇini 4.1.120). Regarding the rule *dvyaco nadyāḥ*: the suffix *aṇ* occurs after two-syllable words that denote rivers; for example, from *saṃdhyā* comes *sāṃdhya*, and from *kulyā* comes *kaulya*. But is it not the case that the *aṇ* derived from a proper name (*tannāmika*) already exists here?

It is true that [the suffix] exists; however, it is superseded by the suffix *ḍhak* according to Pāṇini 4.1.121 (*dvya-caḥ*). Therefore, this statement is for the purpose of superseding that [suffix]. Regarding the rule "triveṇī and trivaṇaṃ," the word *triveṇī* produces a secondary suffix and becomes *trivaṇa*. The offspring of Triveṇī is *traivaṇaḥ*.
113. [The suffix ṅīṣ is applied] after feminine river-names that are non-vṛddha and whose names are identical [to those of the rivers].

Although there is another technical definition of *vṛddha* given in other treatises—namely, "that which has an intermediate descendant is *vṛddha*"—there is also a definition of *vṛddha* provided within this very treatise.

Regarding the rule "That [word] whose first vowel among its vowels is *vṛddhi* is *vṛddha*" (Pāṇini 1.1.73), a doubt might arise concerning this prohibition of *vṛddha*: of which *vṛddha* is there a prohibition here— is it the prohibition of that which has been defined by this very technical definition (*paribhāṣā*), or rather of that which is designated as *vṛddha* by another rule?

Is it defined [by a technical term] in that [treatise]? Therefore, in order to refute that, he shows by means of the rule *vṛddhir yasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.73) and others that this is a prohibition of whatever has been defined as "vṛddha" within this very science. But how is it determined that what is defined here as "vṛddha" [is the one intended]?
He shows that this is a prohibition of that [which was previously stated]. But how is it determined that this is a prohibition of that which was defined as "vṛddha" in this context?
Because it is impossible for the name of a river or a female human being to end with a *gotra* suffix. This is so because of the mention of the word "nadī" (river).
In this case, however, only a worldly river is understood, and not one that is technical (paribhāṣika). Why is this so?

Because of the association with the word *mānuṣī*, which functions in its worldly sense. Now, why does the literal form (*svarūpa*) itself of the words "river" (*nadī*) and "human woman" (*mānuṣī*) not [apply here]? Because of the prohibition regarding the term *vṛddha*. If there were a grasping of the literal form...
For otherwise, the prohibition regarding the plural would be purposeless, as there would be no occasion for its application.

Furthermore, because of the use of the plural number in the reference, the actual forms [of the words] are not being grasped. For if the actual forms were being grasped, since the words *nadī* and *mānuṣī* are duals, one would have referred to them using the dual number alone.

[Otherwise] the rule "ṭha-vṛddhābhyām" would be a property of words (*śabdadharma*). If, then, this is a property of meaning (*arthadharma*), how is it that by the rule "nadīmānuṣībhyaḥ" the base forms (*prakṛti*) are indicated? For in this way, only a property of meaning is indicated, not the base forms. To this he says: "By that," and so forth.

Therefore, by way of figurative application based on a difference in meaning, verbal bases (*prakṛti*) denoting rivers and human females are indicated. In the expression "the base of an affix" (*pratyayaprakṛti*), it is a genitive compound meaning "the base of an affix. [The phrase] "an exception to *ḍhak*" refers to [the suffixes prescribed for] rivers and human females that do not begin with a vowel-lengthening diphthong (*avṛddha*).
Because these names end in feminine suffixes: "vaitastaḥ" and "nārmadaḥ" are derived from the words *vitastā* and *narmadā* with the suffix *aṇ*. "Śaikṣitaḥ" is derived from the word *śikṣitā*.
"Suparṇeyaḥ" and "vainateyaḥ"—the words *suparṇā* and *vinatā* are names of female birds.

It does not refer to a river or a human female. Regarding the term "śaubhaneya," the word *śobhanā* occurs as the meaning of "river" or "human female," but not as a proper name (*saṃjñā*); rather, it functions as an adjective (*viśeṣaṇa*).

114. *ṛṣy-andhaka-vṛṣṇi-kurubhyaś-ca* (4.1.114). [The sūtra states: "This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṭhiñ*. Now, one might object: since *ḍhak* and other suffixes would apply after words ending in consonants that do not end in *a*—provided they are not among those beginning with *at-*, *strī*, etc.—it would be more logical for this rule to be an exception to those very suffixes. To this, he says:

Regarding the rule "from *ṭhaktṛ* and so forth," etc.: by the first word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the *ṛṣya* suffixes such as those applied to Jātasena and others, as well as *ugrasena* and others occurring among the Andhakas and so on, are included;
by the second [word], the suffixes beginning with *ṇya* are included. In that regard, the scope of the *ṛṣya-ṇ* suffix is, for example, *vāsiṣṭhaḥ*.

The scope of the suffix *ḍhak* [by the rule] "ṭhitaścāniñaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.122) is, for example, *dauleyaḥ*. When both [suffixes] would apply after the word *atri*, *ḍhak* occurs by virtue of its higher priority:

*ātreyah*. The scope of the suffix *aṇ* [after the name of] a seer (*ṛṣyaṇ*) is that same case; the scope of the suffix *ṇya* [after words ending in] *senānta* or *lakṣama* is as follows: [e.g., *saineyaḥ*].

*Kāriṣeṇyaḥ*, *hāriṣeṇyaḥ*; the sage named Jātasena—when both [suffixes] are applicable, the suffix *ṇya* occurs by virtue of its later position: *jātasenyaḥ*. This is the scope for the suffix *aṇ*: Vāsudeva; for *ṇya*, it is the same. Śūrasena, Viṣvaksena—the name of a Vṛṣṇi.

Therefore, when both [suffixes] are applicable, the suffix *ṇya* occurs by virtue of its subsequent position: *śaurasenyaḥ*, *vaiṣvaksenyaḥ*. The scope of the suffix *aṇ* is: *nākulaḥ*; for *ṇya*, it is the same case. There is an Andhaka named Ugrasena; when both are applicable, *ṇya* occurs by virtue of its subsequent position: *āugrasenyaḥ*.

The scope of *vṛṣṇyaṇ* is: Vāsudeva; the scope of *ṇya* is the same. There is a Vṛṣṇi named Śūrasena or Viṣvaksena; since both [suffixes] would apply, *ṇya* occurs by virtue of its higher status—resulting in *śaurasenyaḥ* and *vaiṣvaksenyaḥ*. The scope of *kurvaṇa* is: Nākula; the scope of *ṇya* is the same.
There is a Kuru named Bhīmasena; since both [suffixes] are applicable, the suffix *ṇya* occurs by virtue of its higher status, resulting in *bhaimasenyaḥ*.
The objection beginning with "But how... and so forth is the challenge. The response to that challenge begins with "Some say... and so forth.
"Kākatālīyam" means occurring by chance, without prior intention. "Saṅkalitāḥ" means accumulated.
"Nityā eva" (eternal indeed) is because the lineages of Andhaka and the others are beginningless.

115. *mātuḥ utsaṅkhyā-sambhadra-pūrvāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.115). [The example] *dvaimāturaḥ*: first, the *dvi* is applied in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), and afterwards the *taddhita* suffix is added.
[The example] *sāmmāturaḥ*: first, there is a *prādi*-compound, and afterwards...
[The example] "bhādramāturaḥ" [is explained as follows]: first there is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*), and then the secondary suffix (*taddhita*).

Now, why is the statement not made regarding the meaning of the suffix? To this he says: "But the suffix... and so forth. [It is formed] by the general rule itself, namely "tasyāpatyam" (Pāṇini 4.1.92). But surely...

The status of being preceded by a numeral and so forth is a qualifier of the word *mātṛ*; in that context, when the designation is made with reference to the word *mātṛ*, it is seen only in the masculine gender. Therefore, how can there be a designation in the feminine gender as in "saṃkhyāsambhadrapūrvāyāḥ"? To this, he says:
"The mention in the feminine gender is with reference to the meaning. This mention is made with reference to the meaning of the word *mātuḥ*, and that meaning is feminine.
Therefore, the mention was made in the feminine gender. By the words "by that" (*tena*) and so forth, the result of [the mention] being with reference to the meaning is shown.

[The author] demonstrates this: for when a feminine gender designation depends on the meaning, it must be understood as referring only to that whose meaning is feminine; therefore, there is no inclusion of the *dhātrī* (wet-nurse). For its meaning is not feminine; what then? It is masculine.
A hired laborer who measures grain is called a *dhānyamātr*.
In the term *saumātra*, it is first a *prādi*-compound; from that, the general suffix *aṇ* is applied.

116. [The suffix] *kanīna* is also applied after the word *kanyā*. (4.1.116) 117. After *vikarṇa*, *śuṅga*, and *cchagala*, [the suffixes are applied] when [the descendants are] Vatsa, Bharadvāja, and Atri respectively.
(4.1.117) In this context, the words *vatsa*, *bharadvāja*, and *atri* refer to the specific lineages (*gotra*) known as Vātsya, Bhāradvāja, and Ātreya.
"They have obtained their functions (vṛtti) when they are taken up. For this very reason, it says: "If he is a Vātsya, he becomes a Vaikarṇa;
if he is a Bāradvāja, he becomes a Śauṅga; if he is an Ātreya, he becomes a Cāgala.
Furthermore, that function of theirs regarding the offspring of the lineage (gotrāpatya) is to be understood through the metaphorical attribution of the cause to the effect.

"And both of these are valid means of knowledge. Anticipating the objection, "But how can even mutually contradictory things be valid means of knowledge? he says: "For this sūtra was composed by the Teacher in both ways; therefore, what contradiction is there?"
118. Or [the suffix] *pīla* [is applied after the word *vatsa*].
(4.1.118) 119. And [the suffix] *ḍhak* [is applied] after *maṇḍūka*. (4.1.119) 120. [The suffix] *ḍhak* [is applied] after feminine bases (*strī*). (4.1.120)
"By the mention of *strī* (feminine), words ending in feminine suffixes such as *ṭāp* and others are understood.

Now, why is there not a reference to the word-form itself (*svarūpagrahaṇa*)? Because of the use of the plural number in the indication. For if it were a reference to the word-form itself, since that [form] is singular, one would have made the indication using the singular number alone. [Therefore,] it is a reference to the mere meaning of "female" (*stryartha*).

Why does it not occur? Because the word *vimātṛ*, which has the meaning of "female," is listed among the *śubhra* group. If, in this context, the word *strī* were intended to denote the mere sense of "female" in general, its inclusion in the *śubhra* group would be purposeless, since the suffix *ḍhak* would already be established by this very rule. [Examples: *ṭhaiḍaviḍaḥ*, *dāradaḥ*.

Thus, in the case of *iḍaviḍa-apatyam* and *varada-apatyam*, only the suffix *aṇ* occurs. While the suffix *ḍhak* was already under discussion, its mention again here is for the sake of making it obligatory (*nitya*).
Regarding the rule "after *vaḍavā*, when the meaning is 'bull' (*vṛṣa*)": he who deposits seed in her womb is the bull.

It is said, "The suffix *ṭhak* is prescribed after [the words] *krauñca* and *kokila*"; the word *vṛṣa* is not required [in this context]. This is a rule specifically for the formation of a descendant (*apatya*), and it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ḍhak*.

121. *dvyacaḥ* | (Pāṇini 4.1.121) [This is] an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ* prescribed for those names (*tannāmika-aṇ*). For those two-syllable words ending in feminine suffixes which are names of rivers or human beings, the suffix *aṇ* is specifically ordained because it is taught as a particular rule (*viśeṣavidhi*).
It occurs; therefore, the suffix *ḍhak* is prescribed in order to supersede that [suffix].
122. And [the suffix *iñ* is applied] after [words] other than those ending in *i*. (4.1.122) 123. And [the suffix *iñ* is applied] after [words] beginning with *śubhra*.
(4.1.123) "According to the requirements," and so forth. First, for those [words] ending in *a*, this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *iñ*.

From the words *śalākā*, *kurekā*, *ambikā*, *aśokā*, *khaṭvā*, *piṅgalā*, and *khaṇḍonmatā*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied [to form feminine nouns]. From the word *vidhavā*, the suffix *ḍhrak* is applied as a characteristic of a low-born woman (*kṣudrā*). [The following are examples: *kiṃkasā*, *rohiṇī*, *ajavasti*, *śakandhi*, *kṛkalāsa*, *sudata*, and *paridhi*.

From these [names], the suffix *ḍhañ* applies to those characterized by the four feet (*catuṣpād*). From the word *godhā*, the suffix *ḍhrak* is applied; by the force of the explicit statement (*vacana-sāmarthyāt*), that [suffix] indeed occurs as well. For the remaining [names], the general suffix *aṇ* applies—this is the meaning according to the respective application. [The rule] "In the case of Vasiṣṭha, [the suffixes apply] to *lakṣaṇa* and *śyāma*" refers to *lakṣaṇa* and *śyāma*.

The suffix *ḍhak* occurs after these two [names] when the specific descendant is a Vāsiṣṭha: *lākṣaṇeyaḥ* as a Vāsiṣṭha, whereas another is *lākṣaṇi*; *śyāmeyaḥ* as a Vāsiṣṭha, whereas another is *śyāmāyanaḥ*. [In the latter case, the suffix] *phañ* is applied because they belong to the *aśva* group.

124. After *vikarṇa* and *kuṣītaka*, [the suffix *cha* is applied] when *kāśyapa* follows. (4.1.124) 125. And *vuk* is substituted for *bhrū*. (4.1.125) 126. For *kalyāṇī* and others, *inaṅ* is substituted [for the final vowel and following consonant]. (4.1.126)

127. Or [the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] after *kulaṭā*. (Pāṇini 4.1.127) She who wanders among families (*kulān*) is a *kulaṭā*. Now, one might object that since the rule for lengthening a vowel before a homogeneous vowel (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*) applies, the form should be *kulāṭā*; therefore, he says: "The subsequent form" (*pararūpam*), etc. [He says: "By the preceding [rule]"—that is, by the rule *strībhyo...*. (Pāṇini 4.1.120)
By this very rule, *ḍhak* (Pāṇini 4.1.120), the designation "prior" (*pūrva*) applies even when there is an intervening element, just as one says, "Pāṭaliputra is prior to Mathurā.
[In the example] *kaulaṭeraḥ*, once the substitute *ey* has been applied, there is the elision of *y* by virtue of the rule *vali yalopaḥ*.
128. *airak* is the [substitute] for *caṭakā* [in the sense of offspring].

(Pāṇini 4.1.128) Thus, "the female offspring of a *caṭakā* is a *caṭakā*" (*caṭakāyā apatyaṃ strī caṭakā*). When the elision (*luk*) has been applied by the rule "there is elision (*luk*) when a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is elided" (1.2.49), the feminine suffix *ṭāp* must be applied again. This is indeed desired even after a masculine stem.
Luk. Thus the rule was originally "ṭh caṭakāder ak," but now, due to an error, the reading has become "ṭh caṭakāyāḥ."
129. *Godhāyā ḍhrak* (Pāṇini 4.1.129).
[The form] *ṭhgodheraḥ* [is derived from this rule]; as before, there is the elision of *y*.
130. *Ārag udīcām* (Pāṇini 4.1.130).

[The commentary states: "The mention of *ācārya* is for the sake of honor (*pūjārtham*). Now, one might object: if the mention of *ācārya* were not present, this rule would be obligatory (*nitya*), and in that case, there would be no co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) with the suffix *ḍhrak* prescribed by the preceding rule, as in the form *ārakaḥ*.
It might be asked: "Why is the mention of the Teacher (Ācārya) not intended for the sake of that very option?
To this he says: "By the force of the statement. For both *ḍhra* is mentioned and *āra* is mentioned;
therefore, by the force of the statement, there will be a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of both. Therefore...

The mention of *ācārya* is solely for the purpose of honor. As for the statement beginning with "but it is an indicator" (*jñāpakam tu*), since [the form] is already established by the suffix *rak*, the specific mention of *āraṅ* is for the sake of providing a technical designation (*saṃjñāpanārtha*). By this, it is understood that this [suffix] occurs after other roots as well; otherwise, the mention of *āraṅ* would be redundant, since it is already established by *rak*. Therefore...
The offspring of a *jaḍa* is *jāḍāraḥ*, and thus *pāṇḍāraḥ* is established; for this is not accomplished by [the suffix] *rak*.

131. Or from words meaning "mean" (*kṣudra*). (Pāṇini 4.1.131) [The rule] states: *ṭharthadharmeṇa*. Because the object (*artha*) is mean, the base words (*prakṛti*) that denote it are also designated as "mean" by metaphorical extension (*upacāra*).
132. *pitṛṣvasuś chaṇ* (4.1.132).

133. *ḍhaki lopaḥ* (4.1.133). [Question: "But how [is this so]? and so forth. [Answer: Because in the rule prescribing the suffix *ḍhak*, there is the inclusion of feminine suffixes such as *ṭāp* and others.

And because the word *pitṛṣvasṛ* ends in a suffix that is not feminine (*astrīpratyaya*), there arises a question for one who considers the application of the suffix *ḍhak* to be impossible: "This very [point]" and so forth. This very reliance upon the word *pitṛṣvasṛ* as the cause for the suffix *ḍhak*—this is [the basis] for that [suffix] from the word *pitṛṣvasṛ*.
It makes known an existent state; for the status of being a cause is not possible for that which is non-existent.

134. *mātṛṣvasuśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.134). [The commentary] states: "This refers back to *pitṛṣvasuḥ*. Here too, according to the principle that "a rule or a prohibition applies only to what is immediately preceding," only the elision (*lopa*) is the immediate predecessor.

[The suffix] *cha* is not obtained [after *pitṛṣvasṛ*], because it is separated [by the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*]. Both of these [results] are desired; therefore, he shows the reason why both are obtained by means of the word "pitṛṣvasuḥ.
This [word] is understood here as being in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), as is required in this context, just as in the rule for elision (*lopavidhi*).
And there is the genitive case in *pitṛṣvasuḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.132); by this, the following meaning is established:

whatever was prescribed for the father’s sister (*pitṛṣvasṛ*) applies to the mother’s sister (*mātṛṣvasṛ*) as well; thus, both the suffix *chaṇ* and the elision (*lopa*) of the *ḍhak* are obtained. For both of these [suffixes] were indeed prescribed for the father’s sister.
135. *ḍhañ* after words meaning "four-footed" (4.1.135).

Regarding the rule *ṭhcatuṣpādbhyaḥ*: those [animals] which have four feet are thus designated. There is elision [of the final syllable] according to *pādasya lopo hastyādibhyaḥ* (5.4.138). Here too, it is by virtue of the property of the object (*arthadharma*) [that the designation applies].
The *prakṛtis* (bases) that denote these [suffixes] are now specified. For this very reason, it says:

"from the *prakṛtis* denoting the four feet. The use of the plural number is for the purpose of excluding the rule regarding the specific form (*svarūpavidhi*). Regarding the phrase "of *aṇ* and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes *ḍhak* and the others.
The inclusion [of these words] is as in "kāmaṇḍaleyaḥ" and so forth.
The words *kamaṇḍalu*, *śaunti*, *bāhu*, and *jambu* denote species of four-footed animals; in them, the vowel *u* is elided by the rule "ḍhea lopo 'kadravāḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.147).

136. *gṛṣṭyādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.136). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffixes *aṇ* and others. By the word "and others" (*ādi*), the suffix *ḍhak* is included. The use of the plural number (*bahuvacana*) is intended to indicate that these two [suffixes] are distinct due to the difference in their respective bases (*prakṛti*).

In this context, [the suffix] *aṇ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the words *aja*, *vastimant*, and *ayu*; for the remaining [words], the suffix *ḍhak* applies by virtue of the rule "after those ending in *ṭi* and after [stems] other than those ending in *ini*" (Pāṇini 4.1.122).

137. *rāja-śvaśurād yat* (4.1.137). [The commentary states: "If it refers to the Kṣatriya caste. This suffix occurs provided that the Kṣatriya caste is understood by means of the word ending in the suffix; that is, when it denotes one who is indeed the offspring of a king, and not merely someone related to a king.

In that case, the *kṣatriya* caste is generally the one [denoted]. And this is obtained through the understanding that the rule *vā* (Pāṇini 4.1.131), which is extended here, is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Thus we have *rājanyaḥ*. [In the formation of] *rājanyaḥ*, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *ye cābhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.168). [And thus we have] *rājanaḥ*.
Here too, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *ṭhan* (Pāṇini 6.4.167).

138. *kṣatrād ghaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.138). It should be understood that the suffix *gha* itself is intended here, and not the comparative and superlative suffixes *tarap* and *tamap*. But how is this obtained, given that the rule simply states *ghaḥ*?

Is it not the case that since these are technical names (*saṃjñā*) for the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap*, and because a name brings about the understanding of the named object (*saṃjñin*) as soon as it is uttered, it is only logical to take those two [suffixes] themselves? This is not a fault; for in a rule prescribing an affix (*pratyaya-vidhi*), where the expression "ṭhak" or "ṭhañ" is heard, there is a reference to the actual form (*svarūpa*) of the word itself, due to an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Since this...
It teaches the substitution of *iy* for the letter *gh* following an affix (*pratyaya*) and so forth;

this indicates that wherever *gh* is heard in an affix rule, it is the actual phonetic form (*svarūpa*) itself that is intended. For it is not possible for a *gh* following an affix to exist through the mention of two technical designations (*saṃjñin*).

139. *kulāt khaḥ* (4.1.139). Regarding the phrase "in the subsequent sūtra," etc.: for in the subsequent sūtra, because there is a prohibition concerning the preceding word (*pūrvapada-pratiṣedha*), that technical term (*paribhāṣā*) which contains the mention of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-śruti*) does not apply here; such is the meaning.

It is understood [from this]. For if it were *upasthita*, then, because of the prohibition of the rule regarding the inclusion of what follows (*tadantavidhi*) when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in a suffix is present (Pāṇini 1.1.72), that [suffix] would not occur after a preceding member; thus, the prohibition "not after a preceding member" (*apūrvapadāt*) would be redundant.

Furthermore, an indicator (*jñāpaka*) depends upon a general rule; therefore, these two *paribhāṣās*—namely, "the designation of a thing as being like itself does not apply when [the base] is not a nominal stem" (*Pāṇini 1.1.56*) and "an operation involving a nominal stem that includes a specific suffix is not desired to apply to a compound ending in that [nominal stem]" (*Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 89*)—do not apply here either. Consequently, and...
A nominal stem ending with the word *kula* is understood as the word *kula*.

140. After a word that does not end in *pūrva*, the suffixes *yañ*, *ḍhak*, and *kañ* may optionally [be applied]. Now, the word *pūrva* denotes a constituent part (*avayava*); however, it is not logical for the word *kula* to have another word as its constituent part, because [such a word] would be separate and because it does not constitute the beginning [of the compound]. Therefore...

Has it not been stated that because there is no possibility of separation, this is a qualifier of the word *kula* [meaning] "prior member" (*pūrvapada*)? To this he says: "belonging to a compound," and so forth. This occurs when a compound exists—namely, the distinction between "prior member" and "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*). Therefore, it belongs to a compound.
The word *kula* is qualified by the absence of a preceding member (*pūrvapada*): that is, it is that for which no preceding member related to the compound exists. Of what is it non-existent?
It is of that which does not form part of a compound—the solitary word *kula*; therefore, from the solitary [word].

It is thus stated that this rule applies to words such as *kula*. Now, why is the word *pūrva* not accepted as signifying "established" (*vyavasthā*)? Because it is impossible. For if that were accepted, a word from which a preceding member (*pūrvapada*) does not exist would be called "a word without a preceding member" (*apūrvapadaśabda*) by that term; and consequently, [the rule would apply to] *devadattaḥ*.

In the sentence "kulyo devadattaḥ" or "kauleyakaḥ," the suffixes *yañ* and *ḍhak* would not apply, because here "devadatta" exists as a prior member (*pūrvapada*). [The author asks: "Why is there a mention of the word 'pada'? [The answer is:
Why was it not simply stated as "apūrvāt" (provided it is not preceded by anything)? For even so, the desired result would be established, and the rule would be more concise.
It is thought that [the word *pada*] is used so that [the suffix] may also apply when a *bahuc* is the prior member.

If it were stated as "from what is not preceded" (*apūrvāt*), then the suffix would not apply after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that has *bahuc* as its prior member—that is, one that is prior to the formation of *bahuc*—because that [stem] would not be "not preceded. However, since the term *pada* is employed, [the suffix applies] even from such a case.

It occurs because it is not preceded by another word. In the case of *bahukulyaḥ*, since a family (*kula*) is only slightly incomplete, the suffix *bahuc* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.3.68: *vibhāṣā supo bahuc purastātu*.
[Thus] *bahukula* means "one whose family is nearly complete," and *bahukulyaḥ* is the offspring of such a one.
141. From *mahākuḷa*, the suffixes *añ* and *añkhañ* [are applied].
(4.1.141) 142. From *duṣkuḷa*, the suffix *ḍhak* [is applied]. (4.1.142) 143. From *svasuḥ*, the suffix *ch* [is applied]. (4.1.143)
144. *bhrātṛvyacca* (4.1.144). [The commentary states:
"The letter *t* is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*)," meaning that the circumflex accent (*svaritatva*) should apply according to the rule *tistvaritam* (6.1.185).

145. *vyaṅ sa-patne* (Pāṇini 4.1.145). Now, one might object: since it is established by the rule *ṭh-nityaṃ sapatny-ādiṣu* (4.1.35) that the word *sapatnī* alone is derived as feminine, how is the masculine usage *sapatna* justified?

Thus he says: "The word *sapatna* is a synonym for 'enemy' (*śatru*)," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in the sense of *iva*": the meaning of *iva* is similarity. For just as a co-wife (*sapatnī*) is a cause of suffering, so too is an enemy; thus, one who is like a co-wife is called a *sapatna*.

146. *Revatyādibhyaṣṭhak* (4.1.146). Regarding "according to the requirements" (*yathāyogam*) and so forth: among those [names], because the first four end in feminine suffixes, this [suffix] is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ḍhaka*; for *vṛkañcin*, it is an exception to *aṇ*; and for the remaining ones, because they do not end in the letter *a*, it is an exception to *iñ*.
147. *Gotrastriyāḥ kutsane ṇa ca* (4.1.147).
"The term *gotra* is understood here as the offspring beginning from the grandson onwards," it is said. It does not refer to mere worldly offspring;
for if that were the case, the mention of *gotra* would be redundant, since [the context] is already under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning offspring (*apatya*).
The meaning is that the non-grasping of that [suffix] has already been established. Regarding the phrase "when the father is unknown" (*piturasaṃvijñāne*):

this refers to when he is not well-known. By means of the designation made by the mother for the purpose of indicating that the father is unknown, there arises a sense of contempt, as in: "Gārgya is a rogue; he is a Gārgika."

From the word *garga*, which belongs to the *gargādi* group and ends in the suffix *yañ* used for the *gotra* lineage, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭhyañaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.16). When the *y* is elided by *halastaddhitasya* (6.4.150), the form *gārgī* is established. [From this,] the suffixes *ṇa* and *ṭhak* are applied, resulting in *glaucukāyanaḥ* and so forth. This refers to the female descendant (*apatyam*) in the *gotra* lineage of Glucaka.

From [the word] *kāraka*, the suffix *phin* is applied by the rule *ṭhprācām avṛddhāt phin bahulam* (Pāṇini 4.1.160). Then, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *ito manuṣyajāteḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.65), and subsequently the suffixes *ṇa* and *ṭhak*. Thus, "Kārikeya" [is derived]. This word *kārikā* is formed from the stem *kāraka* with the suffix *ṇvul* and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. This is the word *kārikā*.

If it does not refer to a *gotra*, then only the suffix *ḍhak* occurs; for example, "aupagaviḥ. This means the male descendant in the *gotra* line of Upagu; from the base [Upagu] with the suffix *aṇ*, the suffix *iñ* occurs after that which ends in *aṇ*. In this case, contempt should be understood as resulting from some improper conduct or similar act by that person. For example: "gārgeyo māṇavakaḥ" (the young boy Gārgya). In this instance...
When the father is already known, there is no censure in the mother being designated by her [own] maternal uncle for the sake of identifying her; therefore, the suffix *ḍhak* occurs.

148. *Vṛddhāt ṭhak sauvīreṣu bahulam* (Pāṇini 4.1.148). Regarding the statement "In the case of *sauvīreṣu*, it is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti-viśeṣaṇam*)," the meaning is: among the Sauvīras, that which is *vṛddha*—that is, that *vṛddha* [patronymic] which denotes a lineage (*gotra*) of the Sauvīras. [The examples are] *bhāgaviteyaḥ*, etc.

The lineage (*gotra*) is the offspring of Bhāgavita. From [the base] *bhāgavita*, by [Pāṇini 4.1.95] *ata iñ*, we have the suffix *iñ*; from that which ends in *iñ*, by the suffix *ṭhak*, we derive *bhāgavitika*. By [Pāṇini 4.1.101] *yañiñośca*, we derive *phak* [to form *bhāgavitāyana*]. The offspring of Tṛṇabindu is formed with the general suffix *aṇ*, yielding *tārṇabindavaḥ*; from that, by the suffix *ṭhak*— [The resulting forms are: *bhāgavitikaḥ* and *bhāgavitāyanaḥ*; and *tārṇabindavaḥ*. From that, by *ṭhak*— [the resulting form is *tārṇabindavīyaḥ*].]
The suffix *ṭh* in *tārṇabindavikaḥ*: Since the suffix *ṭhak* was drawn forward from the previous sūtra, it does not carry over here;

therefore, the mention of *ṭhak* again is for the purpose of excluding the suffix *ṇa*. For the mention of *ṭhak* preceded by *vā* is connected with the suffix *ṇa*; thus, if that were to carry over, *ṇa* would also carry over.

"‘bhāga’ as the prior member [forms] *vṛtti*, etc."—those words from which the suffix *ṭhañ* is prescribed by this rule are enumerated in this verse. That word *vṛtti* which has *bhāga* as its prior member is described thus. This, first of all, is one instance of *bhāgavitti*.

The second is Tārṇabindava, and the third is Ākāśāpeya—these are the three words [derived from] "from that [gotra]," according to the rule *gotre ṭhag bahulaṃ tataḥ*. From a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting a Sauvīra gotra, the suffix *ṭhak* is frequently prescribed; it [is applied] from those very [stems].
The meaning is that [the suffix] occurs after the three beginning with *bhāgavitti*, and not after others.
Now, for what purpose is the mention of *vṛddha* (vṛddha-grahaṇa),
since the term *gotra* is understood from the preceding sūtra by virtue of the mention of *sauvīra* itself?

We shall provide a specification: since the nominal stem *bhāgavitti* and others belonging to the Sauviro-gotra are already *vṛddha*, the mention of *vṛddha* would be useless because there is no possibility of its exclusion. To this he says: "The mention of *vṛddha*" and so forth. For that mention of *gotra*...

The term *strī* (feminine) is a qualifier; therefore, while it continues [from the previous rule], there would be a continuation of the qualified object, which is the feminine. Consequently, the mention of *vṛddha* (grown/elder) is for the purpose of excluding that.
Only the mention of *gotra* (lineage) will continue, because it alone possesses the svarita accent, and not the word *strī*.
This is what must be explained: by way of this explanation, the inclusion of *vṛddha* alone is sufficient.
