[The example is] "aupagaviḥ," which is formed with *iñ* after a stem ending in *aṇ*. But surely an enumeration (*parigaṇana*) has been made; how then can there be the possibility of *ṭhak* from the word *aupagava*, given that the mention of *sauvīra* is present?

This is the enumeration [of the relevant cases]. For instance, Bhāgavitti and others are enumerated as designating the Sauvīra lineage. In that context, if the mention of "Sauvīra" were absent, the suffix *phak* would apply even from the word *ĀṬpagava*, resulting in the form *Bhāgavittāyanaḥ*. [The suffix *phak* is applied] as in the previous case.

Now, what is the purpose of including the term *bahulam* (optionally)? Could one not simply use the term *vā* (or), since by that alone forms such as *bhāgavittika* and *bhāgavittikāyana* would indeed be established? To this he says:
"The inclusion of *bahulam*," and so forth. From the use of *vā*, only an option (*vikalpa*) is obtained, but not...

The diversity of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). However, by the inclusion of the word "frequently" (*bahula*), even that [diversity] is intended. Therefore, the inclusion of the word "frequently" is for the purpose that there may be a diversity—that is, a manifold variety—of the specific limiting adjuncts.
To demonstrate that very diversity of limiting adjuncts, he says: "In the case of a woman of the *go* lineage... (*gotrastriyāḥ*)...
Beginning with "ityārabhya" and so forth; this is easy to understand.

149. *pheśca ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.149). [The rule] beginning with *yamundaśca*. This verse provides an enumeration of those words for which the suffixes *cha* and *ṭhak* are prescribed by this sūtra; that [enumeration] is obtained precisely through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *bahulam* ("diversely").

Thus should this be understood; regarding *yamunda*, the author of the Vṛtti himself has shown the example. Now we shall show the examples for the other two: the descendant of *suyāman* with the suffix *phiñ* is *sauyāmāyani*; his descendant is *sauyāmāyanika*. The descendant of *vṛṣan* with the suffix *phiñ*—his...

Vārṣyāyaṇi; his descendant is Vārṣyāyaṇīya or Vārṣyāyaṇika. These words, beginning with Yamunda, are recorded as having the suffix *phiñ*; they are understood to end in *phiñ*. There are four rules beginning with "ṭh gotrastriyāḥ kutsane ṇa ca" (Pāṇini 4.1.147). Among them, the first applies only in the sense of censure (*kutsana*).
The last [accent] occurs only among the Sauviras; however, a knower of words should remember—that is, know—that the middle two occur both among the Sauviras and among the Kutsas.
150. *Phāṇṭāhṛti* and *Mimata* take the suffixes *ma* and *phiñ* respectively. (Pāṇini 4.1.150).

Regarding the rule "the shorter [member] comes first" (*ṭhālpāctarasya*), etc.: the word *mimata* has fewer syllables; thus, although its placement before [the other member] would have been required by the rule "the shorter [member] comes first" (2.2.34), the fact that it appears after [the other member] is due to...

This indicates that the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is subject to deviation (*avyabhicāra*). Just as this characteristic of prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) deviates—that is, it does not apply within its own scope—so too does the characteristic of "according to order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*);
thus, there is no application of "according to order. For this very reason, two suffixes are established for each individual [root].

151. *Kuru-ādibhyaḥ ṇyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.151). Regarding the form *kauravyaḥ*: [the rule] *orguṇaḥ* (6.4.156) and *vānto yi pratyaye* (6.1.79) provide exceptions to this. [The sūtra] begins with *kurunādibhyaḥ ṇyaḥ*. But for what purpose [is this stated]?

One might ask: "Will there not be another suffix *ṇya* after the word *kuru*, since the desired form is already established by this very [suffix], and both the phonetic form and the accent would be identical? To this he says: "But that [is derived] from a Kṣatriya.
By this, he demonstrates a difference in meaning; for that [suffix *añ*] is prescribed [by Pāṇini 4.1.168] as "the suffix *añ* after a word denoting a country when it refers to a Kṣatriya."
Because of the governing rule (adhikāra) [stated as] "(4.1.168)," [the suffix] occurs after the word *kṣatriya*; however, this [present case] is other than that.

Consequently, one is the offspring of a *kṣatriya*, while the other is the offspring of one who is not a *kṣatriya*; thus, the difference in meaning is indeed clear. Furthermore, showing that there is also a difference in form (*rūpa*) in many instances, he says:

Regarding the phrase "designated as *tadrāja*," and so forth: since that [suffix] is designated as *tadrāja*, there ought to be elision (*luk*) in the plural according to the rule "of a *tadrāja* suffix, when many [are meant]" (Pāṇini 2.4.62), as in the case of *kuravaḥ*. However, here it is actually heard as *kauravyāḥ*.

The word *rathakāra* is recited here; in that regard, the word *rathakāra* indeed exists as a term denoting a caste (*jāti*), and it also exists as a term denoting an artisan (*kārin*). Therefore, which of these two is recited here? To this he says:
"The word *rathakāra* is recited here," and so forth. Now, why is it not [recited] as the term denoting an artisan?
Why is it recited? He says: "But for the agent," and so forth.
For since the word *rathakāra* is already [included] in the list of *vacana* words, the suffix *ṇya* is established by the very subsequent rule; what, then, is the purpose of its separate recitation?
[The answer is: "The masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) does not occur. This refers to that which is prescribed by the rule *bhasyāḍhe taddhite* (Vārttika 731).

The substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would apply, but it does not occur for the word *keśinī*. If it were to occur, then after the elision of the final vowel by the rule *ṭhnastaddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.144), the undesired form *kaiśyaḥ* would result. Why does it not occur? To this he says: "Because of the force of the explicit mention of the feminine suffix."

Thus [it is said]. For if there were *puṃvadbhāva* (the substitution of the masculine form), this mention of it by means of a feminine suffix would be purposeless; he would have recited it simply in the masculine gender. Even if it were recited in the masculine, the suffix is established from the word *keśinī* as well, by virtue of the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the rule that a grammatical operation applies to a word qualified by its gender). But [an objection may be raised]:...
And would the mention of the word ending in a feminine suffix be for the purpose of excluding the masculine gender? This is not so;

for it will not apply to the masculine gender simply because it is not so designated. As for the statement, "of that [the suffix], as in the case of Kaṇva and others," this is an extension (*atideśa*) occurring within the section on offspring (*apatya*).

It is understood from the mention of Kaṇva and others ending in patronymic suffixes that Kaṇva and the rest fall within the *garga-ādi* group; therefore, whatever operation applies to the *kaṇva-ādi* stems ending in *yañ*, that same operation applies to Vāmarathya, with the exception of the accent. Regarding the phrase "the elision (*luk*) and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) [includes other operations].

The suffixes *ṅīp* and others are included. According to Pāṇini 2.4.64, *kaṇva* and so forth undergo elision (*luk*) of the plural marker when followed by a patronymic suffix (*apatyapratyaya*) such as *ṭhyañ* or *añ*. In the feminine, according to 4.1.16, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Furthermore, according to 4.1.17, the suffix *ṣpha* is applied in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) for those belonging to the Easterners (*prācām*).
Only in the feminine. [The suffix] *phak* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.101]: *ṭhyañiñośca*. In the sense of secondary derivatives (*śaiṣika*), [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.111]:

*kaṇvādibhyo gotre*. When there is a desire to express the sense of "belonging to this" (*tasyedam*) by [Pāṇini 4.3.120], [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.127]: *saṅghāṅkalakṣaṇeṣvañyañiñām*.

The suffix *aṇ* [is applied]. Just as these grammatical operations apply to Kaṇva and the others, so too do they apply to Vāmarathya. The examples for these, such as "Vāmarathāḥ" and so forth, follow their respective order. [Regarding the statement] "The initial acute accent is not extended," it is just as in the case of Kaṇva and the others, who end in the suffix *yañ*.
The initial syllable is acute by virtue of the three accents (trisvara), but it is not so for Vāmarathya;

rather, by the accent of the suffix (pratyayasvara), it becomes oxytone. Regarding the rule "samrājaḥ kṣatriye" (after *samrāj*, the suffix *ṇya* occurs when a Kṣatriya is meant): after *samrāj*, the suffix *ṇya* occurs, as in *sāmrājyaḥ*, meaning "the descendant of *samrāj*. In other cases, only the suffix *aṇ* is used.
Of the universal monarchs.

152. *senāntalakṣaṇakāribhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.152). Here, because of the prohibition against a rule applying to that which ends with a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) when that stem itself is specified as the basis for the operation (*grahaṇavatā*), the word *lakṣaṇa* is taken in its own form (*svarūpa*). For this very reason, he says: "from the word *lakṣaṇa*."

Thus, the term "kārin" (doer) is used to signify the meaning [of the action]. Since there is no grammatical operation (*kārya*) upon that meaning itself, he states—"and from words expressing the doer"—to indicate that the suffix is understood as applying to that which denotes the doer. Why is it that, just as the word *lakṣaṇa* is taken in its own form (*svarūpa*), the word *kārin* is not likewise taken? [Because] in the list beginning with Śiva, the form *takṣan* is given.

Because of its recitation [in that list]. For its recitation there is intended to set aside the *iñ* suffix characterized by the agent (*kārin*). And if, in this context, there were a literal apprehension of the word *kāri*, then since it would be impossible for the suffix to apply from words such as *takṣan*, the general suffix *aṇ* alone would have to occur; therefore, it [the word *kāri*] is included among the *śiva*-type words.

The recitation [of the rule] would be purposeless; however, if the term "meaning" (artha) is included, the recitation there is appropriate for the purpose of subverting the suffix *iñ* which would otherwise be obtained by that [general rule].
[The commentary] says, "By the force of the statement," and so forth. Both *ṇya* and *iñ* are mentioned;
by the force of the statement itself, their co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) is established even without the explicit mention of the Teacher (*ācārya*).
The mention of the teacher (*ācārya*) is made for the sake of variety.
This meaning is obtained because the mention of the teacher is superfluous;

it is on the principle that an increase in the text results in an increase in the meaning. But [one might object]: [Note: The provided text fragment ends with "But [one might object]: (nanu ca). As the instruction requires providing only the translation and no further commentary, the response reflects the available portion.]

Could the mention of *ācārya* be for the sake of honor? This is not so; for if that were the case, the mention of the Easterners (*prāc*) would also have to be made. For they too remember the suffix *iñ* after words ending in *senānta*.
By the phrase "the word *takṣan*," etc., he demonstrates the variety [of forms]. "Of *tākṣṇaḥ*"—this is by the *aṇ* suffix [prescribed] after the group beginning with *śiva*.

In the case of *tākṣṇyaḥ*, there is elision of the final vowel by Pāṇini 6.4.135, *kṛte ṭhṣapūrvahandhṛtarājñāmaṇi*. Thereafter, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by Pāṇini 6.4.168, *ye cābhāvakarmaṇoḥ*.

154. *phiñ* after *tiki* and others. (4.1.154) "The word *kauravya* is recited," and so forth. This word *kauravya* indeed exists as a designation for a Kṣatriya lineage (*gotra*), [formed] by the rule "from *kuru*, *nada*, etc., *ṇya*" (4.1.172).

It ends in the suffix *ṇya*; here, the former of those two is understood. Why is this so? Because of its association with the word *āuṣa*. This word *āuṣa* ends in the suffix *añ* by the rule "From a word denoting a country, [if it denotes] a Kṣatriya, [the suffix] *añ* [is added]" (Pāṇini 4.1.168); therefore, it expresses a Kṣatriya.
Due to its association with that [term], the word *kauravya*—which denotes a Kṣatriya because it ends in the Kṣatriya suffix—is understood as referring specifically to that [Kṣatriya lineage].
As for the phrase "but he who," etc.: he who [is derived] by the rule *kurvādibhyo ṇyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15).

A word ending in the *ṇya* suffix denotes a *gotra* such as "Brāhmaṇa" and the like; therefore, by the rule *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95), there ought to be only the suffix *iñ*. To this, one might object: "This is merely your own arbitrary fancy. To this he replies with the words "And thus," etc. Since it is so—that [the word] denoting a *gotra* such as "Brāhmaṇa" and the like [is formed] only with *iñ*—[the following applies].

It must be so; for indeed, in the rule *ṇyakṣatriyādi* (Pāṇini 2.4.58), even the earlier commentators cited the examples: "the father is a Kauravya" and "the son is a Kauravya. If the suffix *phiñ* were applied here [to form *kauravyāyaṇī*], that example would not be appropriate; for...
The elision (luk) of *phiñ* prescribed after a word ending in the *ṇya* suffix is stated to occur when [the derivative refers to] the grandson (*yuvan*), but it applies specifically to *aṇ* and *iñ*.
155. "And [the suffix] after *kauśala* and *karmāra*" (4.1.155).

It is intended that this suffix is applied only to the original base (*prakṛti*). That is, from the word *kauśala* and from the word *karmāra*. The word *eva* [in the rule] [is used to exclude the application of the suffix] by [the rule] "After a word ending in a long vowel, and after *kośala*, *āja*, etc., [the suffix] *ñyaṅ* [is applied]" (4.1.171).

This is for the purpose of excluding the word *kauśalya*, which ends in the suffix *ñyaṅ*, and the word *karmārya*, which ends in the suffix *ṇya* characterized by the agent (*kārin*) according to Pāṇini 4.1.152 (*senāntalakṣaṇakāribhyaśca*).
If it is intended [to apply] only to the root-primal matter (*mūlaprakṛti*), how can this modified form (*vikṛta*) be relied upon as having the nature of the primal matter (*prakṛtirūpa*)?

Thus he says: "In connection with the suffix," and so forth. Nor is this his own invention; rather, showing that this is the very opinion of the teachers beginning with the author of the Bhāṣya, he says:
"And likewise," and so forth. What, then, is the distinction between [the suffix] *vat* when applied to the ultimate source (*paramaprakṛti*) and when applied to that which ends in a suffix?

When there is production from the supreme *prakṛti*, the suffix is obtained for the mere offspring (*apatya*); however, when there is production from that which ends in a suffix, the specific distinction is "in the case of a young descendant" (*yūnyapatye*), according to the rule *gotrād yūni* (Pāṇini 4.1.94). Regarding the phrase *yuḍ vādiṣṭasya*: the inclusion of the word *ādiṣṭa* is intended to refer to the case where the substitution of *āyan* has been performed.
This is for the purpose that it should be so; otherwise, because [the word] would be beginningless (*anādi*), the substitution of *āyan* would not occur.
In the case of "dāgavyāvaniḥ," once the *guṇa* substitution has been applied by Pāṇini 6.4.146 (*orguṇaḥ*), the substitution of *av* occurs by Pāṇini 6.1.79 (*vānto yi pratyaye*).

156. *Aṇ* [is applied] after a stem ending in *aṇ* that consists of two syllables. (Pāṇini 4.1.156) Regarding "Kārtrāyaṇi": the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "the offspring of Kartṛ," resulting in *Kārtra*; from that, the suffix *phiñ* is applied. Regarding "Dākṣāyaṇa": from the word *Dākṣi*, which ends in the suffix *iñ*, the suffix *yaūn* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.101 (*pañiñoś ca*).
The refutation, the demonstration, and so forth are easy to understand.

157. *udīcāṃ vṛddhādagotrāt* (4.1.157). Regarding the term "vṛddhāt" [in this sūtra], it is the technical definition of *vṛddha* that is understood here, not what is well-known in other systems of grammar, because of the prohibition [contained in the phrase] "agotrāt. [This applies] from the word *kāri*.
And so forth. The scope for the suffix *iñ* characterized by the sense of agency is, for example, *tāntuvāyi*;
the scope for *phiñ* is, for example, *āmraguptāyani*. In the case of *nāpitāyani*, both would apply; however, because of its higher status in the order of rules (*paratvāt*), only *phiñ* occurs.

158. *vākinādīnāṃ kuk ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.158). Regarding the statement "here, that which is *vṛddha* is not a *gotra*": this refers to the group beginning with *vākina* and ending with *ikaka*. It is stated that "this rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to *iñ* and others"; by the word "others" (*ādi*), the suffix *aṇ* is included. In that regard:
This is an exception to the suffix *aṇ* applied to the words *carman* and *varman*, while for the remaining [words], the suffix *iñ* applies.

Regarding the rule "In *carmin* and *varmin*, there is also elision of the *n*," the suffixes *kuk* and *phiñ* are applied to these two forms, *carmin* and *varmin*, and there is elision of the *n*. When *kuk* has been applied...
Since the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) does not end in the letter *n*, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would not apply here; therefore, it is prescribed:
*cārmikāyaṇiḥ*, *vārmikāyaṇiḥ*.
159. *putrāntād anyatarasyām* (4.1.159).

Regarding the phrase "by that" (*tena*) and so forth: by virtue of this statement, even the augment *kuk* is optionally prescribed by this [sūtra] for that *phiñ* suffix which was optionally prescribed in the previous sūtra according to the opinion of the Northerners (*udīcām*). Consequently—
There are three forms.

160. *prācām avṛddhāt phin bahulam* (Pāṇini 4.1.160). [The word] "for the sake of option" (*vikalpārtha*) means for the purpose of providing an alternative. [The phrase] "it is accomplished by one alone" is because it serves the purpose of an option; since "option" (*vikalpa*) is the subject under discussion, it is understood that this refers to an option. And here, for what purpose...

The phrase "the inclusion of all" (*sarveṣām grahaṇam*) is to be supplied [as the subject]. The subsequent portion beginning with "therein" (*tatra*) follows. Both the mention of the Northern grammarians (*udīcām*) and the mention of the Eastern grammarians (*prācām*) are for the sake of honor (*pūjārtham*). As it is said: "The frequent use of the term *bahulam* is for the sake of variety. By the principle of remainder (*pāriśeṣyāt*), the mention of *anyatarasyām* [is understood].

It is stated that this is for the sake of providing an option (*vikalpa*). By the words "in some cases" (*kvacit*) and so forth, he demonstrates that the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (variously) serves the purpose of indicating diversity.

161. *manorjātāv añyatau ṣuk ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.161). [The commentary begins with] "And likewise," and so forth. Since the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*) is not present here, and because this is the case, the elision (*luk*) does not occur in the plural form *mānuṣāḥ*. However, if the sense of offspring were present, then by the rule *yañañoś ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.64), [elision would apply].

The elision (*luk*) would apply excessively in many cases, such as in the rule "the suffix *ṭhak* is used for a descendant when [the ancestor] is contemptible" (*apatye kutsite*). This verse is intended to provide a supplementary rule regarding the cerebral nasal (*mūrdhanya*).
When there is a desire to express a descendant, the suffix *aṇ* is established by the very rule "his descendant" (*tasyāpatyam*, Pāṇini 4.1.92).

But is it not the case that the cerebral [substitution] is already established even by the continued application of the term "bahulam" (diversely)? If this is so, then the meaning obtainable from the continued application of "bahulam" is stated by means of this verse.
Furthermore, that cerebral substitution occurs only in specific cases—such as in the sense of a descendant of a fool (*mūḍha*) and the like—and not everywhere.

One who is ignorant because he has not studied the Vedas is a fool; and because of that very foolishness, or because of his practice of prohibited acts, such a contemptible person belonging to the Brāhmaṇa caste is called a *māṇava*.
162. *Apatyam* [meaning offspring] from the grandson (*pautra*) onwards is called *gotra*.

(Pāṇini 4.1.162) The word *prabhṛti* has the sense of the word *ādi* (beginning with). It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that of which the grandson is the beginning. If offspring starting from the grandson is designated as *gotra*, then even the [offspring of] Garga would receive the designation *gotra*.

He indeed becomes a *pautra* (grandson) with respect to someone else. Anticipating the objection that "if the designation *gotra* applies, then a suffix for a descendant one generation removed from the *gotra* would not be obtained," he says: "Because it is a relative term (*sambandhiśabda*)," and so forth. For the designation *gotra* [applies] to a descendant...

[The designation] is prescribed starting from the grandson (potra) onwards. And since that term "descendant" (apatyam) is a relative word, it necessarily requires one who possesses a descendant. Therefore, the technical name "gotra" is prescribed with reference to whatever is his descendant. And for one whose grandson is Garga, he [is not so designated].
It can be designated as "this is Garga's descendant" (gargāpatyam), because the state of being a descendant (apatyatva) does not manifest therein.

Its non-manifestation is due to the fact that the suffix *taddhita* is not intended to express that [specific relation]. For even that state of being a descendant which exists there is not expressed in its actual form, as it is not intended to be conveyed.

Therefore, [the designation] "descendant" (apatya) is prescribed for those beginning with the grandson (pautra). Consequently, that which appears in its own form [as Garga] does not incur the application of the technical name "lineage" (gotra) for Garga.

[In the phrase] "the descendant of Garga beginning with the grandson," the offspring beginning with the grandson who is related to Garga is [designated] Gārgya; and when the technical name "lineage" applies, [the suffix] *gotre* [is used].
Following the rule *kuñjādibhyaś cphañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.98), the term *gotra* is understood to carry over [into the subsequent rules].
Thus, by the rule *gargādibhyo yañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.105), the suffix *yañ* occurs to denote a *gotra* descendant.

Regarding the statement "this is the designation *apatya* (descendant)," the word *saṃjñinaḥ* ("of the named entity") is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. And that [designation] is [explained] in the subsequent sūtra.

This is the intended meaning. However, in this context, since the status of being an offspring (*apatyatva*) is never absent in the case of a grandson (*pautra*), that which is the offspring of him [the grandson] alone is understood by means of the suffixes; therefore, there is no purpose in including the term "offspring" (*apatya*) for the sake of designating the named object (*saṃjñin*).

But in the subsequent sūtra, this term "beginning with the grandson" (*pautraprabhṛti*), ending in the genitive case, is transformed [to the nominative], [meaning] "of the grandson and those following."
The designation "yuvan" (younger generation) is intended for the offspring of a relative; however, that [designation] cannot be obtained without the mention of "offspring" (apatya).

For there are other relatives besides the offspring—such as those starting from the grandson—and in those cases, it would not be known whose [descendant] this designation is. Therefore, for the purpose of identifying the bearer of the designation in those instances, [the word "apatya" is included].
Some say that the inclusion of the word "offspring" (apatya) is appropriate.

However, we see that the inclusion of the word "offspring" here is appropriate for the purpose of specifying the term to be defined (saṃjñin). For if the word "offspring" were not included, then—as it has been stated—the word "offspring" would [be understood] as a relative term (sambandhi-śabda), and so forth.
Otherwise, that [rule] would fail to achieve its purpose in dispelling the objection; consequently, even the name *garga* itself would incur the designation of a *gotra*.
Therefore, here too, the mention of "offspring" (*apatya*) must necessarily depend upon the named entity (*saṃjñin*), so that the designation may apply to that which appears in the form of offspring.

[The objection: "Let it not apply to anything else. [The response: But surely, since that very term *apatya* (offspring) is already present in the context (*prakṛta*), that same word will serve as the designation for the thing to be named (*saṃjñin*); so what is the use of another mention of *apatya*?
[The reply: This is not so; for how can that which was introduced as the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya-artha*) serve as the designation for the thing to be named?

It might be argued: "Even though that [term] was employed for the sake of its own specific meaning, nevertheless, since it continues here [in the present rule], its purpose is no longer there; therefore, it will be understood as a designation for the named object. But this is not so, because it is for the sake of what follows.
The recurrence of the governing topics (*adhikāra*) is observed, and the explanation would have to be made in this manner;

however, since a direct statement (*vacana*) is simpler than an explanation, the term "offspring" (*apatya*) must be employed [in the rule]. For example: *kauñji-gārgiḥ*. Since there is an absence of the designation "lineage" (*gotra*) for that which is immediately preceding, [the rule] applies to "lineage" (*gotre*).
Furthermore, that *yañ* which is prescribed for the *gotra* [lineage] by the rules "kuñjādibhyaś cphañ" (Pāṇini 4.1.98) and "gargādibhyo yañ" (Pāṇini 4.1.105) does not apply here.

163. *jīvati tu vaṃśye yuvā* (Pāṇini 4.1.163). [The commentary states: "The lineage (*abhijana-prabandha*). Here, *abhijanāḥ* refers to the ancestors, such as the grandfather and so forth; *prabandhaḥ* means a continuous succession (*santāna*). That which exists therein is called *vaṃśya*; the suffix *yat* is applied because it belongs to the *dig-ādi* group. [The commentary further states: "The descendant beginning from the grandson" (*pautra-prabhṛti-apatyam*).

This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Regarding the rule "and [the term] *pautraprabhṛti*," etc.: if the word *pautraprabhṛti* were to qualify *apatya* (descendant) through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—that is, if it meant "a descendant beginning with the grandson"—then the designation *yuvan* (young/younger generation) would apply starting from that point. However, that is undesirable. Therefore, this is not the case.
Is the offspring (*apatya*) qualified by grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)? No;

rather, when the case-ending is changed according to the sense of the word, it becomes a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), and thus [the qualification] occurs through grammatical non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*): "that offspring which begins with the grandson (*pautra*). This being so, that which is desired is accomplished.

To demonstrate this, he says "by that" (*tena*), and so forth. Since, when the case-ending has been thus changed, the word *apatyam* (offspring) is qualified by *pautraprabhṛti* (starting from the grandson) in the genitive case, the technical designation *yuvan* (younger descendant) is prescribed beginning from the fourth generation; and the cause for that change of case-ending is the offspring (*apatyam*).

For the word *apatya* (offspring), being a relative term, requires a correlative such as a cause (*hetu*) and so forth; in that context, the genitive case functions as the cause. And because of its proximity, it requires only "of him" (*tasya*) starting from the grandson (*pautra*) onwards; therefore, it establishes the genitive case precisely there. If, then, [the genitive] is [assigned] due to the incapacity [of the term] to denote offspring...
The change to the genitive case occurs for "pautra" and those following; why does it not also occur in the preceding sūtra?
Because in that [preceding] case, the nominative has no scope. For in the preceding sūtra, the nominative has its purpose unfulfilled;
therefore, it is not possible to change it to the genitive. Here, however, its purpose is fulfilled.

It can be transformed into the state of a genitive [case ending]. In the case of "Gārgyāyaṇaḥ," since the designation *yuvan* applies here, the suffix *yaūn* occurs after a *gotra* suffix according to Pāṇini 4.1.94 (*gotrād yaūni striyām*). The word "tu" is for the purpose of restriction.

Furthermore, what fault is stated regarding the coalescence of designations (*saṃjñāsamāveśa*)? [Consider] the form *śālaṅki*: the patronymic descendant of Śālaṅka who is a youth takes the suffix *phak* by the rule "ṭhyañiñośca" (Pāṇini 4.1.101). [Consider] the form *pailīya*: the patronymic descendant of Paila who is a youth takes the suffix *phiñ* by the rule "ṭhaṇo dvyacaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.156).
Regarding these two, [the prohibition applies] by the rule "pailādibhyaśca" (Pāṇini 2.4.59).

It is said: "Śālaṅki is a youth, Paila is a youth. And if there were a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the technical designations "gotra" and "yuvan," then, when one intends to express the meaning "the pupils of the youth Śālaṅki," and a suffix beginning with *a* (such as *añ*) belonging to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group is to be applied, [the designation "yuvan" would apply].

Since [the suffix] *yaūn* would otherwise undergo non-elision (*aluk*) according to Pāṇini 4.1.89, *gotrādibhyaśchaḥ*, the word *tu* is employed for the sake of restriction, so that the designation *gotra* does not apply to that [descendant] from which [the suffix is added].

164. *bhrātari ca jyāyasi* (Pāṇini 4.1.164). Since the word *bhrātṛ* ("brother") is a relative term, it implies as its own referent that very brother in relation to whom the state of being a "brother" exists. The term *jyāyas* denotes one who is more praiseworthy or older.

And since his seniority is due either to qualities or to age, and this occurs in relation to a younger competitor, it is that very person who is presented as the "competitor" by the word *jyāyān* (the elder). Thinking that, therefore, the designation [of "younger"] will be understood as referring specifically to the younger brother, he says: "the younger brother."

"He becomes one who perceives [them] as grass. By the words "those born before" (*pūrvajāḥ*) and so forth, he establishes that the purpose of this undertaking concerns those who are not of the same lineage (*avaṃśya*). By the phrase "because of being no cause" (*akāraṇatvāt*), he also shows that a brother is not of the same lineage.
For whoever is a cause, either directly or through a succession of generations, is one of the same lineage; and a brother is not a cause.

Therefore, he does not belong to that lineage. "While Gārgya is living" means while his brother is living. In the same way, it should be understood that while Vātsya is living, Vātsyāyana is his younger brother;
while Dākṣa is living, Dākṣāyaṇa is his younger brother.

165. "Or while another sapinda who is older is living" (4.1.165). Regarding the phrase "having the seventh person as their limit": those sapindas for whom the seventh person is the limit are so described. They are called *samānapiṇḍāḥ* (those sharing the same funeral cake); the substitution of *sa-* [for *sama-*, resulting in *sapiṇḍa*] occurs by nipātana (irregular formation), according to the rule *samānasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.84).
Or rather, it is due to a split in the grammatical rule (*yogavibhāga*). This is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of that split:

by means of it, those who are *sapiṇḍas* according to the scriptures are [defined] up to the seventh person; beyond that, they are not called *sapiṇḍas*. The word "of whom" (*yeṣām*) is a governing term (*adhikāra*), and thus it connects with what follows.
"In both cases" means at birth and at death. "In such [occasions] as these": by the word "etcetera," activities such as cessation (*nivṛtti*) and so forth are included. And thus it has been said:
"In both cases, for ten days, the food of the family is not to be eaten."
"Giving, receiving, sacrifice, and Vedic study cease. Thus [it is said].

The word "jīvati" is the singular locative case. The locative has been prescribed in place of the nominative by means of a transposition of case endings (sub-vyatyaya); for this very reason, he says "jīvadeva.
Regarding the phrase "the mention of the suffix -tara," etc.: for if the mention of -tara did not exist...

From the word *sthavira*, only the excellence of age is understood; however, by the suffix *-tarap*, the excellence of position is also understood. Therefore, the suffix *-tarap* is employed to express the superiority of both. As it is said: "In the case of a paternal uncle, a grandfather, and a brother"—both of these two are superior by virtue of their position.

In this context, the word *sthāna* denotes a specific relationship, because verbal roots have multiple meanings. [The example] "Gārgya alone exists" means he is not a Gārgyāyaṇa; for if the designation *yuvan* (younger descendant) were absent, the suffix *phak*, which is the marker of the *yuvan* descendant, would not arise. [The term] "when dead" refers to a more senior *sapiṇḍa*.
Regarding the phrase "or dead," here the meaning of "dead" includes even one who has died as a grandson or later descendant.

166. And [the term] *vṛddha* is used in the sense of "reverence" (*pūjā*). (4.1.166) This indicates that what is designated as *vṛddha* by another technical rule of the science, beginning with "that which is an offspring separated [by generations]" (*apatyam antarhitam*), is what is intended here; it is not, however, that which is defined by the technical definition within this very treatise.

But from what is it understood that "seniority" (*vṛddhatva*) as defined in another treatise is what is intended here? It is understood from the context of the section on offspring (*apatya*). Since it is impossible for that which consists of sound (i.e., a word) to be an offspring, [the meaning of seniority is determined].
[The rule states: "when honor (*pūjā*) is implied. But what kind of honor is intended here?

It is youthfulness itself; for that is desired by all living beings in the world. But is it not the case that here the word *yuva* does not have "age" as its referent? This word *yuva* will apply to a lineage (*gotra*).
By the statement beginning with "by virtue of its being a technical term (*saṃjñā*)," he demonstrates the purpose of formulating this technical designation.

Although the *gotra* [suffix] has already been expressed by the *gotra*-suffix itself, the *yuvan*-suffix is prescribed again by the force of the technical name (*saṃjñā*), as in "Gārgyāyaṇa. Now, for what purpose is the genitive case used in the expression "of the *vṛddha*" (*vṛddhasya*), rather than indicating it in the nominative case as "the *vṛddha*" (*vṛddham*)? For if it were so...
"Why is the sūtra concise? To this he says: "Of the *vṛddha*," and so forth. The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).
Since the composition of the sūtra is varied (*vicitrā*), therefore the genitive case is employed in the word *vṛddhasya*.
The intention is that by composing the sūtra in this way, such variety becomes possible. "In that regard, your honor... [and so on].
"Gārgyāyaṇa"— by the use of the honorific word *tatrabhavat*, which signifies respect, it conveys veneration.

167. *yūnaśca kutsāyām* (4.1.167). Now, it may be objected that the designation *yuvan* (youth) has already been established previously, as indicated by the rule "*yūnaśca*. For this specific mention would not be appropriate if that designation were non-existent; therefore, that [designation] must have been already established.

Furthermore, since a positive injunction by means of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is untenable, he says: "Conceptual construction has cessation as its primary focus. This conceptual construction does not have injunction as its primary focus;
rather, the meaning is that it is intent upon establishing a negation. Once the designation of "lineage" (*gotra*) has been established and then negated...

They must be stated [as exceptions]; otherwise, there would be no designation of a youth by means of the *gotra* suffix. Therefore, he says: "In the case of the technical name *yuvan*," and so forth. The technical name *yuvan* is the opposite (*pratipakṣa*) or adversary (*pratyanīka*) of the technical name *gotra*. If that [name *yuvan*] is set aside, then the technical name *gotra* itself prevails, because of the absence of its opponent.
Therefore, the sense is that it should not be stated [in that way]. Regarding the phrase "Gārgya is a fool" (*jālma*):

by the use of the word *jālma*, which is a term of reproach, it conveys contempt. Furthermore, the contempt here arises precisely because designating a youth as "old" is itself undesirable. For this very reason, [the rule applies] when there is no reproach, as in the case of "youth."

A word is explained with reference to the meaning of a sentence; and as for that censure—or whatever else it may be—no specific distinction is required, just as in the case of Devadatta and others when referring to bad food and the like.

168. *añ* [is added] after a word denoting a *janapada* [country] that denotes a *kṣatriya*. (4.1.168) A word denoting a *janapada*, such as *Pañcāla* and others, has been stated to be a *janapada*; however, it is called a *kṣatriya* when it signifies a *kṣatriya* by metaphorical transfer (*abhidheyopacāra*) from the name to the person, or through association (*sāhacarya*). But [one might object]: "Are not *Pañcāla* and the others..."

Regarding these words: when a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is formed according to the rule *tasya nivāsaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.69), and then that suffix is elided by the rule *janapade lup* (4.2.81), they come to denote a country (*janapada*).
How then can eternal Kṣatriya-denoting words be qualified by the status of being "country-names," which is a property belonging to a later time? Furthermore, how...?

A learned person ought to state that these [people] reside in the countryside because of their connection with Kṣatriyas; for the author of the Sūtras has established the treatment as "possessing that" (*yuktavat*) in the rule: "That [is the name of the country], because the name is authoritative, since the connection is not commonly perceived" (Pāṇini 1.2.53–54).

Furthermore, by rejecting the theory of elision (*lup*), it is stated that the application of the word "Pañcāla" and others occurs naturally, just as it does among the Kṣatriyas in a country; since the country (janapada) Pañcāla and so forth are eternal just as words are eternal, how could the status of being a designation for a country be of later origin? [Thus, one says] "Pāñcālaḥ."

And so forth. Words such as *pañcāla* and others, while denoting regions, are by their very nature also expressive of the Kṣatriyas residing there; from these, the suffix *añ* is applied in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*). [The example] "*aikṣvākaḥ*" [is formed thus]: in the rule beginning with *dāṇḍināyanahastināyana* (Pāṇini 6.4.174), there is the elision of the letter *u* in the word *ikṣvāku*.
It is declined as *drauhyavaḥ*. The word *drahyu* denotes a Kṣatriya specifically and is not a name for a country; therefore, the suffix *aṇ* alone is applied. [Examples are given:
*pāñcāliḥ*, *vaidehiḥ*. Here, the words *pañcāla* and *videha* occur.

The two words *janapada* and *śabda* do not denote a Kṣatriya; rather, they denote a Brāhmaṇa, and therefore the suffix *iñ* alone occurs [by Pāṇini 4.1.96]. As for the rule "from a word denoting a Kṣatriya" (*kṣatriyasamānaśabdāt*) and so forth, it is a word denoting a Kṣatriya that is used here by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāreṇa*).

Regarding the statement "kṣatriya" and the word "janapada": that whose name is identical to the word for a *kṣatriya* is thus described. Therefore, it must be stated that from this [base] ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī-samartha*), when a king is to be expressed, a secondary suffix (*pratyaya*) is produced just as in the case of a descendant (*apatya*).

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *vuñ* which would otherwise apply by the rule "after a word ending in a long vowel, even if it is a *vṛddhi*-derived base, when it denotes the plural" (4.2.125). Just as one says *pāñcālaḥ* in the sense "the descendant of Pañcāla," so too one says *pāñcālaḥ* in the sense "the king of the Pañcālas. Likewise, [one says] *māgadhaḥ*.
From the word *Māgadha*, the suffix *aṇ* occurs [to form *Māgadha*] by the rule "dvyañmagadha" (Pāṇini 4.1.170), and likewise in the case of "tadrājāḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.172).

169. And [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] after *sālveya* and *gāndhāri*. (4.1.169) 170. The suffix *aṇ* is applied after [names ending in] two vowels (*dvyañc*), as well as after *madha*, *kaliṅga*, and *sūramasa*. (4.1.170) 171.
The suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied after [names ending in] a *vṛddhi* vowel, as well as after *kośala* and *āja*. (4.1.171)

By the mention of "vṛddha" here, the term defined by Pāṇini’s rule *vṛddhir yasyācām ādis tad vṛddham* (1.1.73) is intended; for it is only that which possesses this status that can possibly be a name for a country (*janapada*) and denote Kṣatriyas, not what is defined by other grammatical systems. For example: *āmbaṣṭhyāḥ sauvīryaḥ*.

From the words *āmbaṣṭha* and *sauvīra*, the suffix *ñyaṅ* [is applied]. From the words *avanti* and *kunti*, [the suffix] *ñyaṅ* [is applied], as in "one from Avanti" (*āvantyaḥ*) and "one from Kunti" (*kauntyaḥ*). In the case of "one from Kumāra" (*kaumāraḥ*), the suffix *añ* occurs. It should be stated that [the suffix] *ḍaḷṇ* [applies]; this is an exception to the *ñyaṅ* for *kṣatriya* [names], and the letter *ḍ* is for the purpose of eliding the *ṭi* (the first vowel). That...

And [the option] "or" (vā) is obtained through the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "or" from the rule *ca ṭhvānyasmin sapiṇḍe* (Pāṇini 4.1.165), according to the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūakapluti*). If that is so, does this not lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? It will not, because it is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*); for example, in the expression *anyasmāt pāṇḍavaḥ*.
The word *pāṇḍu*, which refers to a Kṣatriya, becomes *pāṇḍava* when the general suffix *aṇ* is applied.

172. *Kurunādibhyo ṇyaḥ* (4.1.172). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to both *añ* and *aṇ*. However, in the case of the word *kuru*, it is an exception to *aṇ* characterized by having two syllables (*dvyac*). The suffix *ṇya* was previously prescribed after the word *kuru* for the sense of "descendant" (*apatya*) by the rule *kurvādibhyo ṇyaḥ* (4.1.151). Of that [suffix], which...

The term *janapada* does not refer to a Kṣatriya; that is the scope [of the rule]. However, in the case where the term *janapada* refers to a Kṣatriya, because it follows [the previous rule], the suffix *añ* would apply, and by virtue of having two syllables (*dvyac*), the suffix *aṇ* would be its exception.
Therefore, the suffix *ṇya* is prescribed again in order to set aside that [suffix *aṇ*].

173. Regarding the rule *sālvāvayavapratyagrathakalakūṭāśmakādiñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.173), it is stated that "the suffix *ṭhañ* is also desired. This is a characteristic [rule] based on their names. How is this known? From the fact that *sālva* is a *nipātana* (an irregularly formed word). Those [names] which denote parts (*avayava*) of the Sālva territory are the common designations for the Kṣatriyas of those regions.
Therefore, they too receive the designation of "Sālva" in a figurative sense.

174. *te tadrājāḥ* (4.1.174). [The commentary states: "Because it is separated by the section concerning the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of *gotra* and *yuvan*. For this very purpose was the section on the designations of *gotra* and *yuvan* inserted as an intervening interruption. Therefore, those...

The elements beginning with *aṇ* mentioned previously are separated [from the current context]; thus, [the author] says "so that there may be no reference by means of the pronoun in the rule *tadrājāḥ*," for it has been illustrated in that very manner. Furthermore, in the rule *tadrājasya bahuṣu tenaivāstriyām* (Pāṇini 2.4.62), an example was given based on the grammatical operation (*kārya*). But here, however—
In this context, it is that which has form as its basis.
175. *kambojāl luk* (4.1.175):

[The suffix] *luk* [is applied after the word *kamboja*]. Thus, *colaḥ* and *śakaḥ*. [In these cases,] there is *luk* of the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by 4.1.170 (*dvyañmagadha*), and [in the case of *kerala*], there is *luk* of the suffix *añ*.

176. *Striyām avantikuntikurubhyaś ca*. (4.1.176) [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after the bases *avanti*, *kunti*, and *kuru* when forming feminine nouns. Examples: *āvantī* and *kuntī*. When the *taddhita* suffix has been elided (*luk*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *ṭhito manuṣyajāteḥ* (4.1.65). The form *kurūḥ* is derived by the rule *ūṅ* (4.1.66).
177. And for this reason:

"The letter *t* is for the sake of clarity. For if the letter *t* were not present, the rule would have to be stated as *ṭhasya*; and because of the similarity of that statement, there would be ambiguity.

Is this a designation of the phoneme *a* itself, or rather of the demonstrative pronoun *idam*? However, when the letter *t* is present, this fault does not arise; for the term "followed by *t*" (*tapara*) is well-established as referring only to phonemes.
Nor is the letter *t* intended for the purpose of excluding the long vowel, since a long vowel is impossible [in this context].

Regarding "Sūrasenī" and "Madrī": from the word *sūrasena*, the suffix *añ* is applied; from the word *mada*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by virtue of its having two syllables (*dvyac*). When these two suffixes have been elided (*luk*), the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added according to Pāṇini 4.1.63: "The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after a genus name (*jāti*) that does not refer to a female [by nature], provided it has a vowel other than *ya* as its penultimate letter. Regarding "Darat": [The suffix *aṇ* is applied to form the name of the country. When the suffix *aṇ* is subsequently elided, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.175: "The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after a word ending in *a* which denotes a country and is not a name. Thus, the forms *sūrasenī* and *madrī* are derived. As for *darat*: [the same process applies].
From the word *darat*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *aṇ* (Pāṇini 4.1.170), which is characterized by having two *añ* suffixes.

If [in that rule] the term *ataḥ* were a reference to the phoneme *a*, then, since a reference to a phoneme triggers the application of the rule for "that which ends with it" (*tadantavidhi*), this case would also apply: namely, *āmbaṣṭhyaḥ* and *sauvīryāḥ*. Therefore...

He says: "There is elision (*luk*) after *Avanti* and so forth. If there were here an application of the rule for *tadanta* (i.e., if the suffix were elided after words ending in *Avanti*, etc.), then the explicit mention of elision after *Avanti* and so forth would be purposeless, as the result would already be established by this very [general] rule.
Since the result is not established merely by the mention of the vowel *a* when the *tadanta* rule does not apply, [the rule specifies] "after *Avanti* and so forth."
The word of a sheep is meaningless.

178. Not after *prācya* [eastern] names such as *bharga* etc., nor after *yaudheya* etc. (4.1.178). Examples: *pāñcālī*, *vaidehī*. [The suffix] *añ* is applied by the rule "from words denoting a country" (4.1.168) etc.
Then, the suffix *ṅīn* is applied by the rule "after *aṇ* [denoting a gotra] from *śārṅgarava* etc. (4.1.73). Examples: *āṅgī*, *māgadhī*.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.170] *dvyañmagadha* etc.;
the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.63] *jāter astrīviṣayād ayopadhāt*.
From the words *bharga* and *śālva*, the suffix *aṇ* characterized by *dvyañmagadha* [4.1.170] is applied; from the remaining [words], however, the suffix *añ* is applied.
In *bhārgī* and similar forms, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied as before. Regarding *yaudheyī*, *śaukreyī*, and *śaubhreyī*:

from the words *yaudheya*, *śaukreya*, and *śaubhreya*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*) by the rule "From *parśu* etc., and from *yaudheya* etc., [the suffixes] *aṇ* and *añ*" (Pāṇini 5.3.117). This applies in the case of *bhārgī* and the others.
The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied as before.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Of whom, moreover," he reveals the intention with which he asked by means of the passage beginning with "How. Regarding the passage beginning with "Parśvādi": Parśu was a Kṣatriya.

It shares the same phonetic form as a word denoting a country (*janapada*); its feminine descendant is formed with the suffix *aṇ* by the rule "dvyañmagadha" (Pāṇini 4.1.170), which is then elided by "ataśca" (4.1.77).
It is also [formed] by the suffix *ya* according to the rule "parśvādiyaudheyādibhyo 'ṇañau" (5.3.117).
The suffix *aṇ* is added in its own sense (*svārthika*), and that too is elided (*luk*). Thus [we have] "rakṣāḥ.

From the word *asūra*, being a word denoting a country (*janapada-śabda*), the suffix *añ* is applied according to the rule beginning with "janapada-śabdāt," and from that [derivative], as before, the suffix *aṇ* is added in its own sense, with the elision of *ya*. The phrase "and likewise" (*tathā ca*) and so forth serves merely as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
He confirms this by means of the author of the Bhāṣya.
Thus ends the first quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇa-pañjikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who was a teacher of the Bodhisattvas.
Now begins the fourth chapter,
the second quarter.

1. *tena raktaṃ rāgāt* (Pāṇini 4.2.1). This root *rañj* indeed exists in the sense of passion or attachment—as in "attached to the king" (*deve raktaḥ*) or "attached to a woman" (*striyāṃ raktaḥ*). It also exists in the sense of a particular color—as in "red cow" (*rakto gauḥ*), meaning "reddish"; and it exists in the sense of white.

Regarding "bringing about another color" (*varṇāntarāpādane*): as in "the cloth is red," the meaning is that having removed the white, another color such as red has been brought about. Here, [the term] is understood in its third sense, as he says:
"of the white," and so forth. This word *rāga* is indeed used as a noun denoting an action (*bhāvasādhana*), and it is...
And [the suffix] is formed by means of the instrument (*karaṇasādhana*); here, the second [meaning] is intended, as it says:
"that by which one is colored is *rāga*. By the mention of *rāga*, the object is grasped, not the essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Therefore, the suffix is understood to be applied to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that denotes a specific kind of passion (*rāgaviśeṣa*), and not [to the word for passion in general].
To the objection that [the rule] applies to the word *rāga* itself, he says: "from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting a specific kind of passion.

Now, why does this not result in the taking of the word's own form (*svarūpa*)? Because the mention is intended to convey meaning (*arthaparatva*). Where a mention is intended to convey the word-form itself, there the own form is taken; but where a mention is intended to convey meaning, it is not so—this was stated previously.

This has already been established. Furthermore, that the instruction is intended for a specific purpose is understood from the unbroken lineage of oral transmission from teacher to teacher. If, then, [the author] says "How? with the intention of showing how a white [substance] is brought to another color:

The refutation begins with "from analogy" (*ṭhupamānāt*) and so forth. Just as in the expression "the Vāhīka is an ox" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*), the word "ox" (*go-śabda*) applies to the Vāhīka—a different object—by way of analogy, so too here the words "kāṣāya" and so forth apply to the "donkey-ears" (*gardabhakarṇa*) and the like; such is the intended meaning.

2. *lākṣārocanāśakalakardamāṭṭhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.2). Regarding this, [the suffix] *aṇ* is also prescribed after the words *śakala* and *kardama*. And that [suffix *aṇ*] is obtained through the recurrence of the word "optionally" (*vā*) by means of the "frog-leap" maxim (*maṇḍūakapluti*), from the rule *vānyasmin sapiṇḍe* (Pāṇini 4.1.165). It is not [otherwise].
And this being so, there would be an over-extension [of the definition], because the *vibhāṣā* is established as having fixed distinctions.
3. Time conjoined with a lunar mansion.

(4.2.3) Here, some maintain that time has the nature of action (*kriyā*), while others hold that it has the nature of a substance (*dravya*), comparable to space (*ākāśa*) and so forth. Both of these views [are presented].

And it is improper to rely on this here. When the former view is adopted, would the conjunction with the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) belong to the action residing within the substance of the sun and so forth, or to that residing in the self? First of all, the former is not possible, because [the action] does not inhere in a different object.

Otherwise, even space and the like would possess action. For there could be no connection of a substance with an action that inheres in a different entity. However, while there exists a connection of an action residing in the self with a constellation, the qualification "connected" (yukta) is not tenable [as applied to the asterism].

Because there is no [time] to be excluded. For it is never possible for time, which abides in the Puṣya constellation and so forth, to be conjoined with the Puṣya constellation and so forth; thus, the inclusion of the term "conjoined" (yukta) would serve no purpose as an exclusion. Therefore, it is improper to adopt here the view that "time is action" (kriyā kālaḥ).

The second [position] is also indeed untenable; because here, what is intended by "yoga" is the cause for determining a specific time. For instance, in common usage, terms such as "Pauṣī" are employed precisely for the purpose of determining a specific time. And such a yoga belongs only to those two.
It is said that for those two between which there exist proximity and remoteness— such as, for example, the Puṣya constellation and the moon—
there is sometimes proximity and sometimes remoteness; however,
there is never any proximity or remoteness between the lunar mansion and time.
Having kept in mind that these two [the asterism and the moon] are eternal, he says: "How, moreover... and so forth.

The intention is that it is not possible in any way [to speak of their conjunction]. Indicating that the word "asterism" (nakṣatra) is employed in the Sūtra as referring to the moon when it is situated near an asterism, he says: "situated near Puṣya and the others," and so forth.

For just as the word "Ganges" is applied to the region near the Ganges in the expression "the hamlet on the Ganges" due to proximity, so too here the words denoting specific constellations such as Puṣya are applied to the moon when it is in proximity to Puṣya and the others.

Therefore, those situated right there produce a cognition [of it]. Consequently, a conjunction with the moon situated near Puṣya and so forth is possible as the cause for determining specific divisions of time,
because the moon in that state occurs only occasionally when situated near Puṣya.
The meaning is that [the moon] is conjoined with the moon (*candramas*); for the word *puṣya* is applied when the moon is in that state.
Regarding the form *pauṣī*: in the rule *sūryatiṣyāgastyamastyānāṃ ya upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.149), there is a variant reading in the manuscript: *tiṣyapuṣyayornakṣatreṣu yalopaḥ*.
The elision of *ya* occurs by virtue of the rule: "In the case of *tiṣya* and *puṣya*, [the suffix] *nakṣatra* [is applied]" (Vārttika 808).
4. *Lubaviśeṣe* (Pāṇini 4.2.4).

If the elision (*luk*) occurs when there is no specific distinction (*aviśeṣa*), then it would also apply here in the cases of *pauṣī rātriḥ* ("the night of the month of Pauṣa") and *pauṣamahar* ("the day of the month of Pauṣa"), for in these instances too, the absence of a specific distinction is indeed understood. To explain:
When it is said, "the night of Pauṣī," no specific distinction such as "today" or "tomorrow" is understood; therefore, he says:

"And not [if it refers] to that which is joined with a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*)," and so forth. He thinks as follows: the rule *nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.3) continues to apply, and by that, it does not become a specific instance of that [general time].

Regarding the phrase "the distinction of night and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes such distinctions as the *muhūrta* and the *lava*. Regarding the phrase "as much as" (*yāvān*) and so on, he clarifies the very meaning just stated: for how long a duration of time is a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) conjoined? It is one day and night (*ahorātra*).

Thus, when a certain duration of time is conjoined with a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), if that [time] is not understood in its entirety, but rather as a portion of it—whether of the night or of the day—this is not the domain of the elision (*lup*). If this is so, how can even the suffix have a "portion" as its domain? [It does so] by way of the whole, since that portion is included within it.

[The parts] are grasped. Because even a single part [of the whole] is joined [with the name], the production of the suffix by the preceding rule is established. Furthermore, in this case, a single part of the constituent member is the domain for elision (*lup*). In that case, however, it would apply here:
*pauṣo 'horātraḥ* ("the day-and-night belonging to the month of Pauṣa"), because as much time as is conjoined with a lunar mansion [is designated by its name].

Its lack of distinction is understood; for when "day and night" is mentioned, it is not known whether it refers to the past, the future, or the present. This is not a fault; "lack of distinction" here is a simple negation (prasajya-pratiṣedha). Therefore, it refers to that specific time which is conjoined with a lunar mansion.
It is understood that there is no elision (*luk*) in cases such as *rārtya* and so forth; however, it is not the case that elision occurs wherever there is no distinction.

5. *saṃjñāyāṃ śravaṇāśvatthābhyām* (Pāṇini 4.2.5). [Question: "Why does the treatment as if endowed with the gender and number of the original (*yuktavadbhāvaḥ*) not occur when there is *lup*? [Answer: If it were to occur, the word *śravaṇa* would have to be masculine. The resolution is provided by the rule beginning with *nipātanāt*. The meaning has already been explained.

6. *dvandvāc chaḥ* | (4.2.6) The mention of *nakṣatra*, which was introduced [in the previous rule], is here understood as being in the genitive case by virtue of the sense; thus, it is explained that the suffix is understood to follow from a *dvandva* compound of lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). Therefore, he says:

Regarding the rule "from a dual of lunar mansions" (*nakṣatradvandvāt*) and the rule "both when there is a distinction and when there is no distinction" (*viśeṣe cāviśeṣe ca*): since the mention of "no distinction" (*aviśeṣagrahaṇa*) has been withdrawn [in this specific context], [we have] the example "today is the day of Rādhānurādhīya. Now, one might object: "In the case of no distinction, there ought to be elision (*lup*); so how is it that the suffix is heard? To this he says: "elision (*lup*)."
"Because it is subsequent, it sublates [the former]."

7. *dṛṣṭaṃ sāma* | (4.2.7) 8. *kalerḍhak* | (4.2.8) [The suffix] *tīya* is applied by the rule *tīyāt* [meaning "from the third"]. [The suffix] *tīya* is applied by the rule *dvestīyaḥ* (5.2.54). And [the suffix] *samprasāraṇa* is applied to *tri-* by the rule *treḥ samprasāraṇañca*.

(5.2.55) Thus he will state [the suffix] *tīya*; after that which ends in it, the suffix *īkak* should be stated in the sense of the base itself (*svārtha*). "Not after *vidyā*"—when expressing *vidyā*, *īkak* does not occur after *tīya*.
"Like *aṅka* from *gotra*"—just as when the meaning "its mark" (*tasyāṅkaḥ*) is intended to be expressed.

A secondary derivative (*pratyaya*) is formed from a *gotra* [name] when the sense expressed in Pāṇini 4.2.7, "a *sāman* seen by him," is intended; this is exactly what is desired in the case of "a *sāman* seen by one of the Āupagava lineage. The word *āupagava* ends in a *gotra* suffix according to 4.1.92, "his descendant" (*tasyāpatyam*). [The rule] "from a *gotra* or a *caraṇa*, the suffix *vuñ*" [applies].

"It occurs. Just as from the word *aupagava*, which ends in a *gotra* suffix, the suffix *vuñ* occurs in the sense of "the lap" (*aṅka*)—as in *aupagavaka* meaning "this is the lap of Aupagava"—so too does it occur in the case of "the *sāman* seen by him. But [one might object]: in the rule *gotracaraṇād vuñ* (Pāṇini 4.3.126),...
The meaning of "like a numeral" (*aṅkavat*) has not been explicitly stated; how then, when it is said "like a numeral," does the suffix *vuñ* occur?

This is not a fault; for by the expression "like a numeral" (*aṅkavat*), what is intended here is the meaning "belonging to this" (*tasyedam*). Thus, it is desired that a suffix be applied after a word ending in a *gotra* suffix in this sense, according to the rule "this belongs to it" (*tasyedam*, Pāṇini 4.3.120).
The meaning is that it was seen by him in that same manner even here; "when the *sāman* has been seen" is the summary. Its meaning is already explained.
9. *vāmadevāḍ ḍyaḍḍyaḷau* (Pāṇini 4.2.9). [Note:
The two examples are not present in the root text; instead, only *vāmadevyam* is seen.
*Vāmadevyam*, *vāgamadevyam*. One of these has an *anta-svarita* accent by virtue of its own inherent accent (*titsvara*).
The second [syllable] is udātta by virtue of the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).

As for the question, "What is the purpose of making it marked with *ṭ* and *ṅ*?", one considers the marking with *ḍit* to be useless because the elision is already established by the rule *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148)—as in the case of *ḍaḷ*, *ḍuḍḍaḷ*, and so forth. It is not [useless].
Regarding the expression *vāmadevyam-avāmadevyam*: here, while the word *nañ* is being carried over from the rule *naño guṇapratiṣedhe sampādyarhahitālamarthāstaddhitāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.155),
the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) is acute by virtue of the rule *yayatoścātadarthe* (Pāṇini 6.2.156).

The addition of the marker *ḍit* is for the purpose that these two [suffixes] should not be included when the rule is being formulated. If they were not included there, the accentuation would belong to the negative particle *nañ* alone, and that, moreover, would be acute (*udātta*), according to the statement: "Particles are acute on the first syllable" (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.80). Now, when [the marker] is applied...

Why is there no inclusion of these two [suffixes] when *ḍit* is mentioned? To this he says: by the paribhāṣā "when a suffix without an *anubandha* is mentioned, one that with an *anubandha* is not included," the exclusion of both *ḍaḷ* and *ḍaḷ* is also effected. Even when *yat* is mentioned, [the rule] "when a suffix with only one *anubandha* is mentioned... [applies].

[The substitution occurs] from that [suffix] by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "of that which has two *anubandhas*" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 52). And the very fact of making this [suffix] marked with the *ḍit* marker is the proof for the existence of these two technical rules;
[this is indicated] in the *Saṅgrahaśloka* by the phrase "in the sense of not that" (*atadarthe*), referring to Pāṇini 6.2.156: "after *ya* and *yat*, when not in that sense."
This refers to the rule that is obtained; that is, within this sūtra. Regarding the phrase "nañ-svare":
*nañ-svara* means the accent (*svara*) of the negative particle *nañ*. The remainder has already been explained.

10. *parivṛto rathaḥ* | (4.2.10) Regarding the word *cārmaṇaḥ*: because of the rule *an* (6.4.167), which causes the stem to remain as it is (*prakṛtibhāva*), the elision of the *ṭi* suffix does not take place.
Furthermore, by the rule *na saṃyogād vamantāt* (6.4.137), the elision of the final vowel (*allopa*) does not occur.
Now, why does it not occur here: "a chariot surrounded by students"? To this he replies:
"completely encircled," and so forth. This root *vṛ* (in *parivṛta*) signifies "encircling";
by the prefix *pari*, its state of being on all sides is indicated. Therefore, it applies only to that which is encircled on every side.

The suffix must be applied [in this way], but it is not the case that the chariot is surrounded on all sides by students; therefore, there is no occasion for the application of the suffix there. As for the usage "the chariot surrounded by students," that is figurative (*aupacārika*), based on the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of the state of being surrounded upon [the chariot]. And this is so because the primary sense (*mukhya*) exists.
When there is a surrounding context, it is appropriate to understand the secondary sense as that which is superimposed.
11. *pāṇḍukambalādiniḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.11). Regarding the form *pāṇḍukambalī*: the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *sau ca* (6.4.13).
As for the statement "it is already established by the suffix expressing possession (*matvarthīya*"): for that which is completely enveloped by something is [considered to possess it].

It exists [in that rule]. Therefore, since the suffix *ini*—prescribed by "ṭhata iniṭhanau" (Pāṇini 5.2.115)—would have already established the meaning of the matup-affix (*matvarthīya*), this specific statement is for the purpose of excluding the suffix *aṇ*. If it were obtainable [by the general rule], this statement would not have been commenced.
For if this statement did not exist, then [the form] "parivṛto rathaḥ" (a chariot covered around) [would be derived by *aṇ* under Pāṇini 4.2.10].

Otherwise, the suffix *aṇ* would apply, and consequently the form would be *pāṇḍukambala*; however, *pāṇḍukambalī* is what is intended. Therefore, the rule is stated for the purpose of excluding *aṇ*.
12. *dvaipavaiyāghrādañ* (Pāṇini 4.2.12).

Regarding the rule "the modification of a leopard (*dvīpin*) or a tiger (*vyāghra*)" and so forth: when there is the intention to express the meaning "the hide which is the modification of a leopard" or "the hide which is the modification of a tiger," [the suffix] *añ* is applied by the rule *prāṇirajatādibhyo 'ñ* (4.3.154).

Because the words *dvaipa* and *vaiyāghra* end in the suffix *-añ*, they here denote the hide as being a modification (*vikāra*) of the leopard and the tiger respectively. It is only by means of a hide that is a modification of a leopard or a tiger that the covering of the chariot is possible, and not otherwise.
By the phrase "by mere modification," it is understood that what is intended here by the words *dvaipa* and *vaiyāghra* are two pieces of leather.
13. *Kaumārāpūrvavacane* (4.2.13). Regarding the phrase *apūrvavacane*: "the statement of what has not occurred before" means "the designation of what was not previously [designated].
To the question "Of what is there a statement of what has not occurred before? he says: "Of the taking of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*)" and so forth. And this...

Even though [the term] is stated in a general sense, it is obtained through the force of the specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*). For just as some other non-technical (*alākṣaṇika*) operation is obtained through the force of a specific rule, so too is this one. [This applies to rules such as] "in both cases, when feminine" (*ubhayataḥ striyām*), and so forth. If [the word] *kaumāra*...

A male is denoted [by the suffix]; even so, its status as *apūrva* (unprecedented) occurs when it serves as a qualifier for the woman alone and not for the man—meaning it is applied in this way and not otherwise. In the example "apūrvapati," it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "she whose husband was not previously [married]," i.e., she who has no prior husband. It refers to her who is together with a husband.

The taking of the hand (marriage) has been completed; she is one whose husband was not previously obtained. The meaning is that her husband has approached and attained her. Regarding the term "apūrvapatiḥ" (one whose husband was not previously obtained), this is also a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
[In the rule] "kaumārāpūrvavacane" and so forth, the word *kaumāra* is treated as an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) term.

Regarding the statement "in the case of *apūrva*": what, then, is prescribed here as a *nipātana* (irregular formation)? He says: "The suffix *aṇ* is prescribed for *kumārī*. The meaning is that the suffix *aṇ* is irregularly applied to the word *kumārī*. When? He says: "when there is *apūrvatva* (the state of being previously unmarried) on her part. For in this case, by means of the *nipātana*, either a male or a female is denoted; therein—

In both cases, there is novelty [of the rule]. The meaning is that this nipātana (irregular formation) applies when it is a qualifier of that woman and not of a man; it does not apply otherwise. By the statement "or it occurs after *kumārī*," this grammatical rule (*yoga*) is rejected. For he who has attained the state of a *kumāra* (a young man) in that context—

It occurs. Consequently, the word *kaumāra* would be derived as ending in the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava*), according to the rule *tatra bhavaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.53). Then, when the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by virtue of its being a masculine *yañ*-stem, the form *kumārī* is established. There is indeed no difference in accent. For instance:

Even when the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied, after the elision [of the final vowel] by "ṭhyasyeti ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.148), the suffix *ṅīp* ought to be udātta according to "anudātasya ca yatrodātalopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.161). However, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is indeed udātta on its first syllable due to the accent of the affix (*pratyayasvara*). But if this is the case...

Would it not follow that any other woman who is the cause for the designation "boyhood" (kaumāra) would also be called "Kaumārī"? This is not a fault; for by virtue of proximity, she alone who is proximate to him will be his Kaumārī. Which one, then, is proximate to him? She who—

The cause for the designation "Kaumāra" is that very [marriage] in which one becomes a *kaumāra*, and not any other. Although Vyāsa and others also become [husbands] of a maiden (*kumārī*), nevertheless,
the suffix *aṇ* will not apply to them, because of non-usage (*anabhidhāna*).
And this non-mention must necessarily be resorted to; for otherwise, even if the formation were made, the suffix *aṇ* would still apply by the rule "tatra bhavaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.3.53).

14. [The suffix *cha* is applied] after [the word *uddhṛta*] when it occurs in a compound with a word denoting a vessel (*amatra*). (4.2.14) 15. [The suffix *cha* is applied] after [the word *sthaṇḍila*] when it means one who sleeps there as part of a religious observance (*vrata*).

(4.2.15) By the phrase "and by the whole [compound]" (*samudāyena ca*), etc., he shows that the religious observance (*vrata*) serves as a condition for both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*).
The word "śāstritaḥ" is derived [and explained] in the rule "vāci yamo vrate" (Pāṇini 3.2.40).

16. *saṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.16). Regarding the word *saṃskṛtam*: here, because the word *saṃskṛta* is a general term, it takes the neuter gender and the singular number. Regarding the word *bhakṣāḥ*: [it is] the particular...

Because of its nature as a word, the term *bhakṣa* possesses the masculine gender and the plural number. This word *bhakṣa* is derived with the suffix *ghañ*; it is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) specifically for that which is solid and distinct and is consumed.
Thus he says: "solid and distinct," and so forth. This is easily understood.
17. *śūlokhādyat* (4.2.18). 18. *dadhnaṣṭak* (4.2.18).
He will state [the suffix] *ṭhak* by means of the rule "that which is prepared" (4.4.3). [The desired form] is established by that very [suffix].

Thus, the intention is that what is prepared in curd is indeed prepared by means of curd. "In this case, the curd is the locus, serving as the substratum," just as a spit is for meat being prepared on a spit. For no transformation whatsoever is produced in the meat by the spit itself.
Rather, it is by means of salt and so forth. The meat merely serves as a substrate for the *śūla* (spit).
If, then, the curd is solely the substrate, by what means is the seasoning (*saṃskāra*) performed therein? To this he says: "by another substance," and so on.
19. udaśvito 'nyatarasyām. (Pāṇini 4.2.19) [The variant reading *udaśvitvam* is found in the manuscript. The form is *audaśvitkam*. [This is derived by applying] Pāṇini 7.3.51: *isusuktāntāt kaḥ*.
20. *kṣīrāḍ ḍhañ* (Pāṇini 4.2.20). Regarding the form *kṣaireyī*: the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by [the rule] *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15).

21. *sāsmin paurṇamāsīti saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 4.2.21). Regarding the statement "if there is a desire to express [the meaning] from that," the word "from that" (*tataḥ*) refers to that which ends in a suffix. This is what is meant: if in common usage there is a desire to express this [meaning] from that which ends in a suffix, in this manner...

The meaning is that [the designation] occurs only in this way and not otherwise. By the rule "pratyayāntena ca" and so forth, he clarifies that the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is a qualifier for the entire complex. "eṣā saṃjñā" means that which is understood through a word ending in a suffix. For example, "pauṣī"; here, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.2.3).

"The feminine suffix *ṅīp* does not apply to those ending in that [suffix], because the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not understood here. For neither the term *daśarātra* nor *bhṛtakamāsa* is a technical name formed with such a suffix. What, then, is the equivalent result? He says:
Regarding the phrase "following the usage" (*prayogānusaraṇam*): the meaning is that "following the usage" refers to the indication of usage.

For this is done for the purpose of grasping the technical designation (*saṃjñā*): having indicated the usage, wherever that usage is observed—in the case of *māsa*, *ardhamāsa*, and *saṃvatsara*—there the suffix should be produced, but not otherwise.
In cases such as *bhṛtakamāsa*, this very same thing is accomplished by means of the particle *iti*. For instance:

if there is a desire on the part of the world to express a meaning derived from a suffix, then the suffix must be produced in that way and not otherwise; it is for this purpose that the particle *iti* is employed, and consequently—

The worldly intention (*lokavivakṣā*) concerns months, fortnights, and years; thus, it does not concern wages for a month and so forth. Therefore, there is a pursuit of the primary sense (*prayogānusaraṇa*), and the result is indeed the same for both. Regarding the phrase "a technical term" (*saṃjñā*) and so on: [an objection] is raised, "But just as a word that is a technical term..."

It is well known in the world that [the suffix *kṛt*] has the result of following actual usage (*prayogānusaraṇaphalatva*), and the same applies to the formation [of technical terms]. Why, then, is its identity with that [usage] made known here? To this he says: "For this is not," and so forth. For instance, in the world, this term is a conventional designation (*saṃjñāśabda*) by virtue of having the result of following actual usage.

The sense is that it is not performed in the same manner as it is commonly established; therefore, its similarity to that [commonly established form] is made known. By the words "for the purpose of technical designation" (*saṃjñārthatve*) and so forth, he demonstrates the purpose of this making known.
That whose meaning is equivalent to a technical designation is "having a meaning that is a technical designation" (*saṃjñārtha*). This is because it is understood through the compound.

The word *tulya* (equal) is not employed; the sense is that in the rule *ṛcyarthānām* (Pāṇini 1.4.33), [the term used] is *samāna* (same) rather than *tulya*. The state of being for the sake of a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is "being for the sake of a technical name" (*saṃjñārthatvam*).
Furthermore, this word *artha* signifies purpose. [The phrase] "that becomes established" means: because of that very [reason].

The term *saṃjñā* (name/designation) indicates that it has the same meaning as the particle *iti*. Therefore, wherever the particle *iti* is used for the sake of following the actual application [of a word], it is said that from each such instance the intended meaning (*vivakṣā*) arises— namely, that it becomes appropriate— because the purpose of the particle *iti* is to serve as a designation.

Regarding the rule *pūrṇamāsādaṇ*: the term *pūrṇamāsa* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound in the sense of "that lunar day (*tithi*) on which the moon is full. From this very word, by means of the suffix *aṇ*, [we derive] *paurṇamāsī*, meaning "belonging to the full moon" (*pūrṇamāsasyeyaṃ*).
This *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *tasyedam* (Pāṇini 4.3.120). This is the technical name for a specific lunar day (*tithi*). As for its etymological derivation:
They should be performed by whatever means possible.
22. [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the words] *āgrahāyaṇī*, *aśvattha*, and *aṣṭakā*. (4.2.22) 23.
[The suffix *aṇ* is applied] optionally after *phālgunī*, *śravaṇā*, *kārttikī*, and *caitrī*. (4.2.23) 24. [The suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of] "this has that as its deity. (4.2.24)

"In that which is denoted" means in the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and so forth, for which the deity who is the recipient of the sacrifice is the owner. And this specific thing denoted is obtained through the recurrence here of the word "even" (*api*), despite its being stated in a general sense. [The rule applies to] the state of being limited by *ādi* and so forth.
Regarding "bārhaspatyam": the suffix *ṇya* is applied according to the rule *dityadityādityapatyuttarapadāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.85). Here, the deity of the sacrifice is intended;
thus, in the usage "an Aindra mantra," it refers to a certain sacrificial offering such as a *puroḍāśa*.

Because the deity does not exist, Indra lacks the status of a recipient (*sampradāna*).
