Therefore, it is thought that the suffix *devatā* (forming *devatā*) should not occur here [in the case of *indra*]. [The rule] "that which is praised by a mantra" means that just as a deity is worthy of worship, so too is an object praised by a mantra; therefore...

Because of its similarity to a deity, the learned metaphorically designate it as a "deity" (devatā). And since Indra is the object of praise in the mantra, they metaphorically designate him as a deity even though he is not [in this context] the recipient of an offering;
the meaning is that they apply the metaphorical designation of "deity" to him there. But even so—

"One should not assume a secondary sense here, because when the primary sense is possible, it is improper to resort to a secondary one. This is not a fault; for just as in the expression "the white horse runs," someone might use the same effort [for both words] through *tantra* (simultaneous application).

He utters two sentences; likewise here too, two sentences have been uttered by the Teacher through *tantra* (a single utterance serving multiple purposes). Among them, one will have the primary meaning, and the other the secondary meaning.
[The question] "How so? and so forth: for fire (*agni*), there is neither a primary nor a secondary status as a deity (*devatātva*). In that regard—

The primary [application] does not exist here, because, due to the absence of anything to be given, it does not function as a recipient (*saṃpradāna*). Nor does the secondary [application] exist, because, due to the absence of the word "mantra," it is not presented as being equal to a mantra. Therefore, the sense is that a suffix (*pratyaya*) should not occur here. [Objection: "It will occur by way of comparison (*upamāna*)."

In this case, only the suffix *devatāsvāminīka* is appropriate as a derivative meaning. As for the application of another suffix in the sense of a different object, that will occur by way of comparison (*upamāna*), just as in the case of "āgneya" [derived from *agni*] being used like "āgneya" [derived from *agnidevatā*].
For example: "kāṣāyau gargabhasya karṇau" (the two reddish ears of Gargabhā). But surely, in the phrase "sāsmin..."?

"Paurṇamāsī" refers to that very same subject under discussion. Why, then, is the locative case (samarthavibhakti) specified here once again? To this they say: "Since 'that' (sā) is the subject under discussion," and so forth.
This "that" which is the subject under discussion is connected with a technical name (saṃjñā); therefore, [the locative case is used] for the purpose of its recurrence (anuvṛtti).

The mention of the term *saṃjñā* (name) would also have continued [from the previous rule]. Therefore, in order to exclude that, the case-ending indicating the semantic capacity (*samarthavibhakti*) is stated here once again.

25. *kasyet* (Pāṇini 4.2.25). The letter *t* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation, not for the purpose of excluding the long vowel; for when a vowel is being taught (*bhāvyamāna*), it does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*). Even if there were inclusion of the homogeneous vowels, by virtue of "nearest proximity" (*āntaratamya*), a short vowel would [replace] a short vowel.

Thus it will be, and not long [in duration]. [The suffix] *ṭha* is the designator of Prajāpati. By this, he shows that this [word] is not a pronominal (*asarvanāman*). The elision of the vowel *i* does not occur by virtue of the rule *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), because of the force of the specific prescription. [The form is] *kāyam*.
The augment vṛddhi and the ādeśa (substitute).
26. *śukrād ghan* (4.2.26).
27. *aponaptrāpānnaptṛbhyāṃ ghaḥ* (4.2.27). [The suffix] *gha* is applied after *aponapāt* and *apānnapāt*, provided that these are names of deities (*devatānāmadheya*). *Aponapāt*, *apānnapāt*.
How is this nature (prakṛti), which is distinct [from the soul], heard of in the Sūtra? To this he says: "But of those two, through conjunction with the intellect (pratyaya)," and so forth.

28. *ccha ca* | (4.2.28) Now, for what purpose is this division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) made? Why is it not simply formulated as a single rule: *ṭhaponaptṛ-apānnaptṛbhyāṃ ghacchāṬ*? To this he says: "The division of the rule," and so forth.

For if there were a single rule (*ekayoga*), there would be two bases (*prakṛti*) and likewise two suffixes (*pratyaya*); because they are equal in number, there would be an application according to numerical correspondence (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*).
Therefore, to prevent that, a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is made:
"In the section on *cha*, etc. [This means] "in the section on *cha* following Paiṅgākṣīputra and others."
An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the suffix *cha*. Here is the justification for it:
the letter *ca* is added here, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned;
by means of that, the suffix *cha* occurs after [names such as] Paiṅgākṣīputra and others.
29. *mahendrād gha-ña-au ca*.

(4.2.29) Now, why was it not simply stated as *mahendrād aṇ ca*? Because of the word *ca*, the suffixes *ghac* and *chaṬ* would also be understood to follow; however, if it were stated in that way, one might also understand that only *cha* follows immediately after.
The letter *ca* is drawn in here [from the previous rule] as "it is performed" (*kriyate*). Therefore, the mention of *gha* is made so that it should not be understood in that way.
30. *somāṭ ṭaḷṇ* (Pāṇini 4.2.30). Regarding the form *saumī*: there is the elision of *y* by [the rule] *halas taddhitasya* (6.4.150).

31. *vāyvṛtupitruṣaso yat* (Pāṇini 4.2.31). [Examples: *vāyavyam*, *ṛtavyam*. [In these cases,] by *orguṇaḥ* (6.4.146) and *vānto yi pratyaye* (6.1.79), there is the substitution of *av*. [The example] *pitryam*: by *rīṅtaḥ* (7.4.27), there is the substitution of *rīṅ*.
The elision [of the genitive suffix] occurs by the rule *yasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.49).
"32. [The suffix *cha* is applied] after *dyāvāpṛthivī*, *śunāsīra*, *marutvat*, *agnīṣoma*, *vāstoṣpati*, and *gṛhamedha*.
(4.2.32)" This is an exception (*apavāda*) to both the suffix *ṭhañ* and the suffix *ṇya*. From the word *vāstoṣpati*, [the suffix *cha* is applied] by the rule "after *diti*, *aditi*, etc. (4.1.85).

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṇya* prescribed by [Pāṇini 4.1.85] and other rules; however, for the remaining [words], the general suffix *aṇ* applies. "Lord of the site" (*vāstoṣpatiḥ*): the neuter word *vāstu* takes a masculine gender, and there is no elision (*aluk*) of the sixth case ending.
[The form] is derived through irregular derivation (*nipātana*). The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule "ṣaṣṭhyāḥ patiputrapṛṣṭha...
(Pāṇini 8.3.53). In the case of "dyāvāpṛthivyau," the substitute *dyāvā* is applied by the rule "divo dyāvā" (Pāṇini 6.3.29).
In the case of "śunāsīrīyam," the substitute *ānaṅ* is applied by the rule "devatādvandve ca" (Pāṇini 6.3.26).
In the word *āgnīṣomīyam*, there is the substitution of *ī* by [Pāṇini 6.3.27] *īd agneḥ somavaruṇayoḥ*;
and there is the substitution of *ṣ* by [Pāṇini 8.3.82] *agneḥ stutstomasomāḥ*.
33. *agner ḍhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.33). 34. *kālebhyo bhavavat* (Pāṇini 4.2.34).
By the use of the plural number, the acceptance of the word-form itself is excluded; [the suffix is applied] after words denoting specific divisions of time.
He says that the suffix *pratyaya* is understood [in this context]: "from those expressing specific times," and so forth;

"the inclusion of *vat*," and so forth. The purpose of the inclusion of *vat* is so that the similarity of everything may be grasped. If it were stated simply as "that which arises from times" (*kālebhyo bhavaḥ*), then...

Is the mention of "time" (*kāla*) connected with the suffixes conditioned by "existence" (*bhava*)? If those suffixes prescribed after words denoting time were intended for the sense of "this is its deity" (*sāsya devatā*, Pāṇini 4.2.24), then the base word [denoting] the deity would remain unspecified. And thus...

Otherwise, suffixes would apply without distinction to nominal stems (*prātipadika*) that denote deities alone. Or, if the mention of "time" is connected with the bases denoting deities, then those suffixes which are prescribed [by rules] beginning with *bhave* would apply to times as well as to deities. Furthermore, if it were for both...

Because of proximity, because of the distinction of the qualified object, and because of the resulting split in the sentence, [the suffixes] would have to be connected both with the affixes and with the bases—

[meaning that] those affixes which are prescribed after words denoting time in the sense of "occurring at that time" would instead come after words denoting deities? Even so, any affix whatsoever whose base is a word for time...

From whatever time it may be—from a deity, from the seasons, or even from the *muhūrta*s and so forth—it would apply. However, when the suffix *vat* is present, because it prescribes similarity, there is an inclusion of all forms of similarity. Therefore, from whichever bases (*prakṛti*) and by whichever...

By means of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), those suffixes (*pratyaya*) which are prescribed for the sense of "belonging to the season" (*bhava-artha*) will also apply here; since those very same suffixes occur after those same bases (*prakṛti*) by that same qualifier, there is no occurrence of an undesired consequence (*aniṣṭa-prasaṅga*). [As in: *vāsanta*—[according to the Kāśikā]—"belonging to the spring."
The suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *sandhivelādi* (Pāṇini 4.3.16), as in the example from the *Kāśikā*:
*prāvṛṣeṇya*. [This is derived] by the rule *prāvṛṣa eṇyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.17).
35. [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied after *mahārāja* and *proṣṭhapada*.
(4.2.35) 36. The forms *pitṛvya*, *mātuḥ*, *mātāmaha*, and *pitāmaha* [are formed with the suffix *yañ*].
(4.2.36) Regarding *pitāmahī* and *mātāmahī*: the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule "after roots ending in *ṣit* and after the *gaura*-group" (4.1.41).
37. "A collection thereof" (4.2.37).

[The examples are] *kākam*, *śaukam*, and *bākam*. The words *kāka*, *śuka*, and *baka* have the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable, according to the rule: "Of living beings whose names begin with *ku*" (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.30).
This is its meaning: for words denoting specific living beings, the initial consonant from the *ka*-group (the gutturals) becomes udātta.

38. *bhikṣādibhyo’ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.2.38). Now, for what purpose is the mention of *aṇ*? Why not simply say that [the suffix] prescribed by rule applies after the words *bhikṣā* and so on? To this he says: "The mention of *aṇ*, etc. This word *bhikṣā* [is included in the *guru-bhṛgu-ṛṣi* group].

Because [the word] ends in the suffix *a* by virtue of Pāṇini 3.3.103 (*halaḥ*), it is oxytone. In that case, the suffix *añ* prescribed by 4.2.44 (*anudātoderañ*) would apply as an exception to *aṇ*; therefore, the mention of *aṇ* is for the purpose of subverting that subverting rule. Now, one might object: what if *aṇ* were applied here?

Would the repetition be purposeless? This is not so; because it is subsequent, the suffix *ṭhañ*, which has the characteristic of being unaccented (*acita*), would apply. Therefore, the repetition is for the purpose of setting that aside. However, the suffix *añ* would indeed still occur; since there is a specific mention of *aṇ*, the rule "again, only *aṇ*" does not apply, and thus this fault does not arise. [The example is] *gārbhiṇam*.

Thus: [the word] *garbhīṇīnām* is a collection [denoted by the suffix *aṇ*]. By the rule *bhasyāḍhea taddhite* (Vārttika 731), and because [the base form] is already established (*siddhatvāt*) at the time of the prescription of the suffix according to *puṃvadbhāvena* (Pāṇini 6.3.35), there is the removal of the feminine suffix. Then, the suffix *aṇ* is applied;
in that case, the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopaḥ*) would be required by the rule *nastaddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.144). However, this is precluded by the rule *inaṇyanapatye* (Pāṇini 6.4.164).

Because of the rule "prakṛtibhāva" [6.4.164], this does not occur. Regarding the phrase "tasya-grahaṇa": if the word *yuvati* does not undergo the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), then, since it would end in a suffix, the suffix *añ* would apply by [Pāṇini 4.2.44] "anudātādeḥ."

In order to preclude that [substitution], the mention of *aṇ* here is purposeful; for if the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) were to apply, then it would be redundant. To explain: by the statement "and it is established when a suffix is prescribed" (Vārttika 4.2.38), the substitution of the masculine form occurs through the mental presence of the suffix even before the suffix has actually been produced.

It must be so; for the word *yuvan*, which ends in the suffix *kanin* according to Pāṇini’s rule *ṭhkaninyuṛṣitakṣirājidhanvidyaupratidivaḥ* (Uṇādisūtra 6.51), has its first syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*) by virtue of the *nit*-accent. In that case, if there were *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like substitution)...

If the rule were established by the general characteristic (*utsarga-lakṣaṇa*) alone, then the explicit mention [of the word *yuvan*] here would be purposeless. Therefore, so that this [mention] does not become meaningless, by the very force of its mention, the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment) does not occur;
thus, the form *yauvatam* is established.

39. *gotrokṣoṣṭrorabhrarājarājanyarājaputravatsamanuṣyājād vuñ* (4.2.39). [The commentary states: "Since this occurs outside the governing context of *apatya* (offspring), 'gotra' is understood here in its worldly sense. If this is so, [then...]
Is the mention of *rājanya* and *manuṣya* redundant because this [result] is already established by the inclusion of the term *gotra*?
This is not so; for those two do not end in a *gotra*-suffix, since the meaning of the suffix is "birth" (*jāti*).
If that is the case, then the elision (*lopa*) does not even apply; in that regard, it was said: "by the original form (*prakṛtyā*) in the case of *ake*..."

[If it were so,] the elision of *y* in the rule "rājanyamanuṣyayuvānaḥ" (Vārttika 814) would not occur, and thus that [rule] would be rendered purposeless? However, this was stated by relying on the opinion of certain authorities; for some teachers maintain that *rājanya* and *manuṣya* end in patronymic suffixes.

Therefore, there is no fault in saying that this was stated by relying on that view. [Objection: In that case, according to that view, the mention of *rājanya* and *manuṣya* would be purposeless? [Response: No, because it is for the sake of providing information (*jñāpanārtha*).
By this, the following is made known: that some [suffix] dependent on the offspring (*apatya*) follows the *yakāra* of *rājanya* and *manuṣya*.
It does not become a *kārya* (an operation). What, then, is that? It is the designation of *apatya* (offspring).

Therefore, in the cases of *rājanyakam* and *mānuṣyakam*, the elision of *y*—which would otherwise occur by the rule "and [the *y*] of *apatya* in a *taddhita* suffix other than *ān*" (Pāṇini 6.4.151)—does not take place. Likewise, it is included in the very wording of the sūtra.

It should be understood that the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) for the words *rājanya* and *manuṣya* is taught by the Vārttika: "The forms *rājanya*, *manuṣya*, and *yuvan* remain in their original state before the suffix *aka*" (Vārttika 814). Furthermore, it should be stated: "Also after a word denoting an elder (*vṛddha*)," whereby the suffix *vuñ* is applied to a word denoting an elder.

The meaning is: "it occurs for this purpose. Regarding this, the following is the explanation: here, moreover, the particle *ca* is carried over from the subsequent sūtra by way of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*) maxim;
and that [particle] serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly stated. By means of it, the suffix *vuñ* occurs after the word *vṛddha*. And this is a *yoga* (rule).
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rules concerning *ma* and *ṇa*, applied as appropriate.

40. *kedārādyañ ca* (4.2.40). [The commentary states: "The suffix *yañ* should also be stated after *gaṇikā*. The meaning of "should be stated" (*vaktavyaḥ*) is that it should be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: here too, the particle *ca* ("and") is carried over from the subsequent rule; it...

And [the particle] *ca* has the sense of including what has not been mentioned; by this, the suffix *yañ* also occurs after the word *gaṇikā*, while *vuñ* does not occur, because of the lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*).
41. *uñ* [is applied] after *kavacin*.
(4.2.41) The word *kavacin* ends in the possessive suffix *ini*; it is udātta on the final syllable by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
Since the suffix *añ* would otherwise apply by the rule "after that which begins with an anudātta" (4.2.44), this statement is made.
42. *brāhmaṇa-māṇava-vāḍavād yan* (Pāṇini 4.2.42).

Regarding the statement "an addition [should be made] for the word *pṛṣṭha*," the meaning is that an explanatory supplement (*upasaṃkhyāna*)—that is, an explanation—must be provided for the suffix *yan* after the word *pṛṣṭha*. This is the explanation: from the preceding sūtra, it is carried over here...

The particle *ca* is understood here, and it serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; therefore, the suffix will also apply after the word *pṛṣṭha*. In the form *ahīnaḥ*, there is the elision of the *ṭi* portion [of *ahan*] by the rule *ahnaṣṭakhoreva* (Pāṇini 6.4.145).
In the form *āhnaḥ*, there is the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *allopo'naḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.134). Now, one might object:
Since the suffix *ṭhak* ought to occur by virtue of the characteristic [of the word] being listed in the *cācitalakṣaṇa*, how is it that the form *āhnaḥ* arises? To this he says:

"In the *khaṇḍika*-group," and so forth. It should be stated that there is the suffix *ṇa*. The letter *s* is for the purpose of specification [in the rule] *siti ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.16). By means of that...
In this case, because there is no status as a *bha* [suffix] in the word *pārśvam*, the rule "ṭhorguṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.146) does not apply.

43. *grāmajanabandhusahāyebhyas tal* (Pāṇini 4.2.43). Regarding the word *grāma*, since the suffix *ṭhak* would otherwise apply by virtue of its denoting a non-hereditary settlement (*acita*), this rule provides for *tal*. The word *jana* has its first syllable acute (*udātta*) by virtue of the *nit*-accent, because it ends in the suffix *ghañ*. Likewise, the word *bandhu* also has its first syllable acute by virtue of the *nit*-accent; for it is as follows: [the derivation of *bandhu* is] *bandh + u*.
While the rule *dhānye nit* (Dhātupāṭha 1.94) is in effect,
[the suffix -in] is applied by the subsequent rule *pṛṣṛsvṛsnihitrapyasidasidhṛñsṛjvaripavargādibhyaśca* (Dhātupāṭha 1.95).
The word *sahāya* is derived by adding the suffix *u*, which results in its initial syllable being udātta; thus, since the suffix *aṇ* would otherwise have applied, [the suffix *tal* is prescribed].

Furthermore, the word *sahāya* has its middle syllable udātta according to the rule "when the final syllable is light and there are many vowels, the heavy syllable [is udātta]" (*Phiṭ-sūtra* 2.42). In that case, since the suffix *añ* would have applied because it begins with an anudātta vowel, the prescription of *tal* is made.

The phrase "it should be stated that [the suffix] also [comes] after *gaja*" means that it must be explained that the suffix *tal* occurs after the word *gaja*. And this explanation here should be made by relying on the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the particle *ca* ("also").
44. *anudātāder añ* (Pāṇini 4.2.44). For example:

*kāpotam*, *māyūram*. The words *kapota* and *mayūra* have the acute accent (*udātta*) on the middle syllable, according to the rule *laghāv ante dvayoś ca bahvaṣo guruḥ* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.42). [And] *taitaram*.

The word *titiri* ends in the *kit* suffix [by Pāṇini 3.2.174, *titiriśabdaḥ kit*]. According to the rule "the root *tṛ* [takes the suffix *kvip*] like *psan*" (*tarateḥ psanvalluk*), and by the rule "the reduplication [is treated] like *san*" (*sanvatuk cābhyāsasya*), it is udātta on the final syllable due to the accent of the suffix. But surely, because of the treatment as *san*, the initial syllable should be udātta?

Because of the word "bahulam" (variously) in the rule *ṭhuṇādayo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.1.3), the treatment as having the augment *saN* (*sanvadbhāva*) will not occur in the case of the accent; thus, there is no fault.

45. *Khaṇḍikādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.2.45). [The commentary states: "This rule is for the sake of making the first syllable udātta and for the sake of excluding the sense of 'not a multitude' (*acita*). If this rule did not exist, the suffix *aṇ* would apply after words with an udātta on the first syllable, and the suffix *ṭhak*—which characterizes a multitude—would undesirably apply after words that do not denote a multitude. [For example, regarding the group] *kṣudrakāścamālavāśca*.
Regarding the compound *kṣatriyadvandva*: the descendants of many *Kṣudraka*s are formed by *añ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.168 (*janapadaśabdāt kṣatriyādañ*), as are the descendants of many *Mālava*s.
By 4.1.171 (*vṛddhetkośalājādāññyaṅ*), the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied. For these two, [the elision of the final vowel and consonant] follows from 2.4.62 (*tadrājasya*).

Thus, there is elision (*luk*) in the case of many [members], followed by a *dvandva* compound. Then, since the suffix *añ* is established by the preceding rule, and once the final acute accent of the compound has been applied, the *dvandva* compound begins with an unaccented vowel; therefore, this specific statement is made for the purpose of overriding the *vuñ* suffix prescribed by the rule "gotrokṣoṣṭrorabhra... (Pāṇini 4.2.39).
The suffix *vuñ* would apply by virtue of the rule for "lineage" (*gotra*); its reading here in this group [of *kṣudraka* and *mālavaka*] is for the purpose of overriding that.
As for the phrase beginning with "But surely," etc.: since the suffix *añ* will override *vuñ* precisely because it is subsequent, there is no need [for the specific mention].
The meaning is that this statement is intended to express the sense of "obstructing" (*bādhanārtha*).

And this was stated while accepting the status of being a *gotra*; now, in order to show that there is no such thing as the status of being a *gotra* at all, he says: "And not," and so forth. This is a collective enumeration of *gotras*. And not...

A collection of clans (*gotra*) is not grasped by the term "clan," just as a collection of districts (*janapada*) is not grasped by the term "district. For example, the Kāśis and the Kośalas are called "the Kāśi-Kośalas";
those who dwell among them are "the inhabitants of Kāśi-Kośala" (*kāśikośalīya*). This is because [the collection] lacks the status of being a single district.
Regarding the rule *janapada-tadavadhyoś-ca* (Pāṇini 4.2.124), the suffix *vuñ* does not apply; rather, only *cha* applies by virtue of the rule *vṛddhāc-chaḥ* (4.2.114). This might be argued:
although a collection of lineages (*gotra*) is not itself a lineage (*gotra*), its constituent parts are.

Is it not the case that since the word *kṣudrakamālavaka* is a component (*avayava*) of a *gotra*, the suffix *vuñ* would apply even after a *samudāya* (composite) that is not a *gotra* by means of the rule for suffixes following what ends in such a word? To this he says: "And not," etc. For not every instance of a suffix following what ends in such a word occurs; as it is said: "By which..."

Regarding the rule *vidhistadantasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.72), it has been stated there: "There is a prohibition regarding the prescription of compounds and suffixes," with the exception of those involving the mention of *ugit* and vowel-classes (Vārttika 12 and 13). And this [rule concerning the suffix] is a prescription of a suffix (*pratyayavidhi*).
Furthermore, those cases where the inclusion of the ending (*tadantavidhi*) is desired therein are specified right there by the mention of *bhaya* and the like (Vārttika 303).

By such statements [the suffixes] are enumerated, and this [suffix *cha*] is not included therein; therefore, the rule for "final element" (*tadantavidhi*) does not apply. [The author says: "If that is so," and so forth. The fact that he includes the mention of "Kṣudra-Mālavaka" for the purpose of setting aside the suffix *vuñ* indicates that a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) applies to *vuñ*, and not [to *cha*].

There is a counter-exception (*paravipratiṣedha*) regarding collective formations (*sāmūhika*): "In the case of collective suffixes, there is the rule of *tadanta-vidhi* (the suffix applies to a word ending in that). He asks: "What is the purpose of this indication? and replies: "The forms *āupagavakam* and *kāpaṭavakam*.
This is the purpose for indicating the priority (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) of the suffix *vuñ*. For if this indication did not exist, [the desired forms would not be established].

By way of mutual exclusion, the suffix *añ* would apply according to Pāṇini 4.2.44 (*ṭhanudātāder añ*). However, the scope for the suffix *vuñ* is where there is an acute accent on the first syllable—as in *glaucukāyanakam*.
For the word *glucukāyana* [is derived] by [the rule] 4.1.160 (*prācām avṛddhāt phin bahulam*).

Because it ends in the suffix *phin*, it is acutely accented on the first syllable by the rule for *nit* suffixes. [The examples] "vānahastikam" and "gothenukam" serve as the purpose for making known the application of the rule to that which ends in those [suffixes]. If this rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) were not made known, then according to the rule "after *aci*, *hasta*, and *dhenu*, the suffix *ṭhak*" (Pāṇini 4.2.47), [the suffix would apply] from the words *dhenu* and *hasti*.

The suffix *ṭhak* being prescribed, it should not [be applied] after that which ends in *-a*. [Regarding the form] *kṣudrakamālavakāt*: in the *Kāśikā* and the *Padamañjarī*, it is stated [that this form is derived by adding] *ṭhak*.
In the list (*gaṇa*), the rule "from *kṣudrakamālava* when denoting an army" (*ga.sū.* 82) is recited; therein—

If this were a single *yoga*, then both the indication (*jñāpana*) and the restriction (*niyama*) could not be obtained by means of a single effort. Therefore, a division of the *yoga* (*yogavibhāga*) must be made here. In that regard, "after *kṣudraka*, *mālā*, etc.
is one *yoga*, and "in the sense of an army (*senā*) when it is not a technical term (*asaṃjñāyām*)" is the second. Therein, the former *yoga* is for the purpose of indication.

The subsequent [rule] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). "Of this very [suffix]" means of this very rule (*yoga*), namely *kṣudrakamālavāt*. Regarding "kṣaudrakamālavī," the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15). Regarding "another [place] called kṣaudrakamālavaka," the suffix *vuñ* occurs here by means of the rule for extension to that which ends in such a suffix (*tadantavidhi*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "ṭhañ-siddheḥ": from the word *kṣudrakamāla*, the suffix *añ* is already established by the rule *anudātāder añ* (Pāṇini 4.2.44). Therefore, what is the meaning or purpose of its inclusion in the *gaṇa* list? The meaning is that there is no purpose whatsoever. This might be argued: [what about] the suffix *vuñ* which characterizes a *gotra*?
One might ask: "Is this reading intended to exclude that [application]? To this he says: "The suffix *vuñ* is prescribed after a *gotra*.
Now, the word *kṣudrakamālava* is not a *gotra*; therefore, how could there be the application of *vuñ* from it?
[He replies with the words] "from that which ends in [a *gotra*]," and so forth. Even though the word *kṣudrakamālava* is a collection of *gotras*, it is itself a *gotra*.

It does not exist [as a whole], but its constituent part exists; therefore, by that rule concerning what ends in [a specific element], it would indeed apply. [Regarding the phrase] "and not after every [suffix]": the rule concerning what ends in [a specific element] does not apply everywhere. It is desired that the rule concerning what ends in [a specific element] applies only to those operations that have been specifically enumerated, and this [case] is not enumerated among them.

How then could the suffix *vuñ* be obtained by the rule of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*)? [The author replies: "It would be an indicator (*jñāpaka*)," and so forth. Indeed, this mention of *kṣudraka-mālava* must be for the purpose of providing an indication. It indicates that in the case of collective suffixes (*sāmūhika*), there is an extension to what ends with that.
By doing so, the rule even for one who is not a Piśali becomes logically established.
That by which something is prescribed is a *vidhi*. This, moreover, is the rule: "After the word *dhenu*, when not preceded by a negative particle" (*dhenor anañaḥ*, Vārttika 423).

For this is that sūtra. Its meaning is as follows: the word *dhenu* produces the suffix *ṭhak* in the sense of a collection (*samūha*), provided that the word *dhenu* does not follow a negative particle (*nañ*).

That is to say, it does not have "nañ" (the negative particle) as its prior member. If, in that context regarding collective formations (*sāmūhika*), the rule of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) were not applied, then the statement "after [a word] other than 'nañ'" (*ṭhanañaḥ*) would be untenable. In the absence of such an extension to what ends with that, what occasion would there be for a suffix to be prescribed after the word *dhenu*?

If [the suffix] were to occur after the word *adhenu*, then this statement "provided it is not preceded by the negative particle *nañ*" (*anañ*) becomes meaningful only if the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) applies to collective formations (*sāmūhika*), and not otherwise.
He states another purpose with the words "in the case of an army" (*senāyām*), etc.; [this applies] only when it is the technical name (*saṃjñā*) for an army.

The purpose of its inclusion in the *gaṇa* is so that this restriction—that the suffix *añ* occurs after the word *kṣudrakamāla*—should apply. Regarding the phrase "just as," etc.: the particle *ca* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Its inclusion in the *gaṇa* is for the purpose that, by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the suffix *vuñ* should supersede the suffix *añ*.

The reading [from] the *Kāśikā* on *Pāṇini-sūtra* 5.2.115 is "khaṇḍika. The word *khaṇḍika* ends in the possessive suffix *ṭhan*, and by virtue of the accentuation rule for *nit*-stems, it is udātta on its first syllable. [The root] *val* [is used] in the sense of covering and moving.

From the root *vaḍ* (in the sense of "covering," according to Dhātupāṭha 491), by applying the suffix *avan* according to Pāṇini 3.3.1 (*uṇādayo bahulam*), and by the traditional rule that *ḍa* and *la* are identical, the letter *la* is replaced by *ḍa*;
then, with the addition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, the form *vaḍavā* is derived. Similarly, the word *bhikṣuka* is used when there is a desire to express contempt.

Because it ends in a *kan* suffix, the first syllable of the preceding word is udātta. Furthermore, for the words *śuka* and *ulūka*, the initial syllable is udātta according to the *Phiṭ-sūtra* 1.30: "For living beings, those preceded by *ku* [are udātta]. As for the word *śvan*, it is derived from the root *śvi* with the suffix *kanin*, while the mention of *kanin* continues from *Dhātu-pāṭha* 6.51: "The suffix *kanin* is applied after roots ending in *yū* and *ṛṣi*."

The word *maghavan* is listed among the *nipātita* (irregularly formed) words ending in the suffix *kanin* in the rule: "ṭhśvannukṣanpūṣanplīhankledantasnehanmūrdhanmajjannaryamanviśvapsanparijmanmātariśvanmaghavan" (Uṇādi-sūtra 6.55). Therefore, it is also acutely accented on the first syllable, as in the previous cases. The meaning of the compound *yugavaratra* is not [merely] the sum of its parts; rather, they explain the inclusion of both *yuga* and *varatra* as referring to the meanings of the two words taken together and separately—namely, *yaugam*, *vāratram*, and *yogavaratram*.

46. *caraṇebhyo dharmavat* (Pāṇini 4.2.46). [The commentary says: "Starting from *gotracaraṇād vuñ*. Now, one might object: "But since the word *dharma* is not mentioned there, how can this extension (*atideśa*) 'like *dharma*' be applied? To this he replies: "In that regard, this... and so forth.

This very statement, "as if [it were] dharma" (*dharmavat*), serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) that leads to the understanding that the rule "from *caraṇa*, [the suffix *vat* is used] in relation to *dharma* and *āmnāya*" (Vārttika 4.3.120) is a supplementary rule (*śeṣa*). For without that [supplementary rule], the designation [of *vat*] would not be possible. [The Vārttikakāra says: "The suffix *vat* has the sense of similarity. For if *vat* did not exist...

If the term *caraṇa* is connected with the suffixes that denote *dharma*, such that those suffixes which will be taught after *caraṇa* occur in the sense of "a collection thereof" (*tasya samūhaḥ*, Pāṇini 4.2.37), then the base for the formation of the collective would not be specified. And if this were the case here...

[If the suffix were applied] from the base *prakṛti* alone, it would follow that [the suffixes] are conditions for *dharma*. Now, if *prakṛti* is connected [to the word *dharma*], then those suffixes which will be prescribed after *dharma* are what occur. Even if [the rule] "after words denoting conduct (*caraṇa*), [the suffix -yañ denotes] a collection" were intended in this sense, even so, the suffixes conditioned by *dharma* would not be specified.
Furthermore, those suffixes (*pratyaya*) which would be prescribed for *dharma* even from the perspective of conduct (*caraṇa*), they too would here fall under the category of conduct.

Moreover, if both [conduct and *dharma*] were present, both would be qualified; thus, by effecting a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), [the suffixes] would be connected with both the bases (*prakṛti*) and the suffixes—[namely], with the bases "from conduct" and with the suffixes "for *dharma*. Then, as for those suffixes...

Would they not be prescribed for a collection [of things] by means of the suffixes *caraṇebhyaḥ*? Even so, some suffix whose base is a *caraṇa* might occur after any [word] whatsoever denoting a *caraṇa* in the sense of a collection;
thus, by the rule *ṭhkaupiñjalahāstipadādaṇ* (Pāṇini 4.3.132), it would also apply after words such as *chāndoga*.

However, because the suffix *vatu* is prescribed for similarity (*sādṛśya*) in general, it encompasses all forms of similarity. Therefore, whatever suffixes have been prescribed after certain bases by means of a specific grammatical branch (*caraṇa*), those same suffixes occur here as well after those same bases by that very same specification; thus, there is no [need for further rule].

Something undesirable would follow; therefore, for the sake of including all similarities, the suffix *vat* must be applied. For example: *kāṭhakam*, *kālāpakam*—[derived] by [Pāṇini 4.3.126] *gotracaraṇād vuñ*. Also: *chāndogyam*, *aukthikyam*.
The suffix *ñya* is applied by the rule *chandogokthikayājñikabahvṛcanatāññyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.129).

Regarding the term *ātharvaṇam*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied and the *ika* portion is elided by the rules *kaupiñjalahāstipadādaṇ* (4.3.132) and *ātharvaṇikasyekalopaśca* (4.3.133). These [are the forms].
Just as conditions arise for a phenomenon from its constituent parts, so too do they arise for the collection.
47. *acita-hasti-dhenor-ṭhak* (4.2.47). Regarding the term "acita": because the designation is based on meaning, this refers to the sense [of the word], not to its formal phonetic shape (*svarūpa*).
Therefore, he explains that the suffix *ṭhak* is understood to apply after words expressing the sense of "acita" by stating: "after words denoting 'acita'."
Thus [it is said]. And because the indication of the words *hasti* and *dhenu* is primarily concerned with the word-forms themselves, there is a grasping of their own forms (*svarūpa*).
For this very reason, it says "by the two words *hasti* and *dhenu*.

The reading of the Vārttika is: "It should be stated that [the suffix *ṭhak* applies] after *adhenūḥ* (i.e., after a word other than *dhenu*) when not preceded by the negative particle *naÑ*. Hence, [the example is given as] *adhenūḥ*.

"It must be stated" means that this form of meaning—namely, that the suffix *ṭhak* occurs after the word *dhenu* when it is not preceded by a negative particle (*nañ*)—must be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows:
the term "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*), which is to be mentioned later, is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to both rules.

It is understood from the established *vibhāṣā* rule that the suffix [ṭhañ] occurs only after the word *dhenu* when it is not preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, and not when it is preceded by *nañ*. Thus, in the form *ādhenavam*, the suffix *añ* is applied according to *utsādibhyo 'ñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.86).
But surely the word *dhenu* is listed there [in the *utsādi* group]?

How then does it arise from the word *adhenu*? Because even in that case, the rule of "application to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) is possible. How is this understood? From the prohibition against the word *vaṣkaya* in a compound—as seen in the form *vaṣkayāsaḥ*. For the suffix is prescribed after the word *vaṣkaya*; it would not apply after the word *go-vaṣkaya*. Why? [Because of the aforementioned prohibition.]
Is it by way of prohibiting compounds? From this prohibition, it is understood that the rule of "specification of what ends in that" (tadantavidhi) applies there.
48. *keśāśvābhyāṃ yañchāv anyatarasyām* (4.2.48).

This rule is formulated because the suffix *ṭhak* would otherwise apply after the word *keśa*, and the suffix *aṇ* would apply after the word *aśva*. By the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally"), the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *aṇ* also occur [alongside *yañ* and *cha*].
49. *ya* after *pāśa* and others. (4.2.49) This rule is stated because [the suffix] *kaṭhi*, which is characterized by having a non-cit vowel as its penultimate, would otherwise have applied.

50. *khalagorathāt* (Pāṇini 4.2.50). Since the suffix *aṇ* would otherwise apply after the word *go*, this rule provides for the suffix *ṭhak*—characterized by the addition of *ic*—after the words *khala* and *ratha*. Why was *khala* and the others not included directly in the list beginning with *pāśa*? To this he says:

"The non-inclusion of *pāśa* and others [in the list] is for the sake of what follows"; that is, so that the suffixes *ini*, *tra*, and *kaṭyac* prescribed by the subsequent sūtra may apply only after words such as *khalādi*, and not after words such as *pāśādi*.
51. *ini-tra-ṭac-ca* (Pāṇini 4.2.51). The statement "the suffix *ini* should be prescribed after words such as *khalu*" means that it must be stated—that is, explained. Here is the explanation:
the letter *ca* is used here, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned; by means of it...
The suffix *ini* will be applied after [the words] beginning with *khala*. This word "beginning with" (*ādi*) is used in the sense of "type" (*prakāra*);

thus, the meaning is "those of the type of *khala*. But what are those types of *khala*? They are those after which the suffix *ini* is observed. If, then, *ini* occurs after *khala* and so forth, would there not be a lack of correspondence due to the inequality [in number], such that the rule of "respective order" (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) would not apply?
Because there is a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), this is not a case of "one-to-one correspondence" (*yathāsaṃkhya*). There are two sentences here:
one sentence is "the suffixes *ini*, *tra*, and *kaṭac* occur after the words *khala*, *go*, and *ratha*";
and the second sentence is "the suffix *ini* occurs after *khala* and so forth," with the particle *ca* serving to include what has not been explicitly mentioned.
In the second sentence, however, it should be understood that the word *khala* serves there as an indicator of the manner [of action],
but not as the base form (*prakṛti*).

52. *viṣayo deśe* (4.2.52). [The meaning is: "That which is an object (*viṣaya*) becomes [the name] if it is a location (*deśa*). Now, one might ask: since whatever is an object is necessarily a location, what is the purpose of the specific qualification "if it is a location"? To this he says:
"This word [denotes] an object," and so forth. "Extremely practiced" means thoroughly habituated.
53. *rājanyādibhyo vuñ* (Pāṇini 4.2.53).
"And this is a *ṭhākṛtigaṇa*," [he says], thereby showing that the list beginning with *rājanya* is not exhaustive; furthermore, this word "etc. (*ādi*) has the sense of "type" (*prakāra*).

54. The suffixes *vigha* and *bhakta* are added after [words] such as *bhauriki* and [words] such as *aiṣukārī*. (4.2.54) 55. The suffix *cha* is added after a word denoting the *Chandas* when it means "this is its beginning," provided it refers to *pragāthas*.

(4.2.55) Regarding the term "*chandasah*" [in the rule], it does not refer to the actual form [of the word *chandas*], nor does it refer to the *mantras* and *brāhmaṇas*. To what, then, does it refer?

The word *chandas* exists as a term denoting the measure of syllables, of which *jagatī* and others are specific varieties; this [term] is what is being referred to here. For it is only this [word] that has a connection in such instances as *pragātha*, and not the other [meaning].
By this, it is stated that the suffix occurs after *paṅkti* and the other [metres].

Regarding the phrase "by means of a *pragātha*," [the commentary] says "by means of a *pragrantha*" (a pre-eminent composition). This is because it is a qualification of the act of recitation, meaning either "due to its excellence (*prakarṣa*) over other compositions" or "due to its being sung (*gāyana*) as something pre-eminent. By this, he demonstrates the action that serves as the cause for the word *pragātha*. As for this word *pragātha*, when it is used according to the rule "the suffix *ṭha* is applied to denote an agent or another *kāraka*, provided it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*),"...
(3.3.19) Thus, it is derived with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*): "that which is sung forth is a *pragātha*.

Due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group, there is the elision of both the *repha* (the letter *r*) and the nasal (*anunāsika*). In that case, it is based on the action of composing (*pragranthana*). However, when [the root] is *kai* or *gai* in the sense of "sound" (*śabda*), [it is derived differently].

From this root [dhā.pā. 916, 917], by the rule *ṭhuṇādayo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.1), the word *pragātha*, ending in the suffix *than*, is derived; in that case, it is based on the action of singing (*gāyanakriyā*). "In the neuter," and so forth: in the neuter gender, it is used in its own primary sense (*svārtha*) according to Vedic usage.
There is an addition [to the rule] regarding the suffix (*pratyaya*). Here is the explanation:

the particle *iti* is intended to express the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). Therefore, wherever there is an intention on the part of the learned to use a form ending in a suffix, there a suffix must be applied. Furthermore, that [intention] occurs even in the neuter gender and in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).
Therefore, even in that case, the suffix occurs. And this must necessarily be understood:
for one who thinks that "the exclusion of all over-extension is effected by the particle *iti*," for him that particle would be entirely useless.
Because all over-extensions have been excluded by means of non-limiting adjuncts (anupādhi).
56. [The suffix *cha* is applied] after words denoting the cause (*prayojana*) and the combatants (*yoddhṛ*) when [the battle] itself is the object of the derivative (*saṅgrāme*).

(Pāṇini 4.2.56) In this rule, "in the battle" (*saṅgrāme*) indicates the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*), because it ends in the locative case. "After the cause and the combatants" (*prayojanayoddhṛbhyaḥ*) is an indication of the base (*prakṛtinirdeśa*), because it ends in the ablative case; and therefore—

This contradicts the rule "samarthānāṃ prathamādvā" (Pāṇini 4.1.82), because the first [word] is taken as the meaning of the suffix and the second as the base (*prakṛti*). To refute this objection, he says: "The case-ending of the related word is that which expresses 'this belongs to him' (*so'sya*)."

"And the meaning of the word *pratyaya* (suffix) also carries over. By this, he demonstrates the following: because the word *saḥ* (that) from the preceding rule itself follows here for the sake of [the rule] "from *prayojana*, *yoddhṛ*, etc.," that [word] is first carried over here; however, "from *prayojana*, *yoddhṛ*, etc. serves as its qualifier.

The term "pratyaya" (suffix) from the preceding sūtra also carries over here; "saṃgrāma" is its qualifier, and thus there is no contradiction, because the suffix is prescribed based on that very element which was designated in the nominative case in the preceding sūtra.

57. The suffix *ṇa* is applied after [a word denoting] a weapon in the sense of "this is his sport" (*praharaṇam asyāṃ krīḍāyām*). (Pāṇini 4.2.57) 58. The suffix *ñ* is applied after a word ending in *ghañ* in the sense of "this is his activity" (*sāsyāṃ kriyā*).

(Pāṇini 4.2.58) Regarding the statement, "The word 'activity' (*kriyā*) is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti-viśeṣaṇam*)," it means that in this context, that which ends in *ghañ* must denote an action (*kriyā-vāci*).

"If it exists" (cedbhavati). By this, it is stated that the suffix occurs after a word ending in *ghañ* which denotes an action (*bhāva*). But is not that very *ghañ* which denotes an action already expressive of an action by virtue of being so formed? Because the property called "accomplishment" (*siddhatā*) belongs to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).

It was stated previously that [the suffixes] *ghañ* and so forth must occur; since the distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) is not clearly delineated, there is no fault in the fact that even the property of action (*kriyādharma*) is expressed by the word "action" (*kriyā*). [The rule] "the suffix *ṭi* is for the purpose of expressing the intended meaning" [is relevant here]. But surely—

The particle *iti* is understood to carry over from the previous sūtra; why, then, is it mentioned again here? It is mentioned again to show that the particle *iti* has no governing authority (*anadhikāratā*) in this particular section. By means of this [repetition], the rule "one who studies that or knows that" (Pāṇini 4.2.59) [is applied].

Regarding this, some say that because the particle *iti* does not recur here, and because there is no restriction on what is intended to be expressed, the suffix is established for any mere student or knower.
Others say that the inclusion of the particle *iti* is for the sake of variety. [The example is] *śyenampātā*. [The rule is] *śala*...

The root *patlṛ* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*) [is listed at Dhātupāṭha 843, 844, 845]. With the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), the term *śyenapātaḥ* ("the flight of a hawk") is formed as a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). When the suffix *ñi* is prescribed, the augment *mum* is applied according to the rule *śyenatilasya pāte ñe* (Pāṇini 6.3.71).

Regarding the word *prākāraḥ*: from the root *kṛ* preceded by *pra*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) by the rule *akartari ca kārake saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.19). The lengthening of the vowel in the prefix *pra* is according to the rule *upasargasya ghañy amanuṣye bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.3.122). Thus, this is a word ending in *ghañ*; it does not denote an action.

The wall [is mentioned] because it is a substance (*dravyatvāt*). "Now," and so forth, is the objection (*codya*). "By the word 'in play' (*krīḍāyām*), this is connected to that," and so forth, is the resolution (*parihāra*). This might be the case: let "play" continue to apply; and if this [is intended] in that context...
Since it is intended that there be no counter-argument, he says: "And in a general sense," and so forth.

59. *tad adhīte tad veda* (Pāṇini 4.2.59). [The example is] *vaiyākaraṇaḥ*. By the rule *nañ-yv-ābhyām* (7.3.3), etc., there is a prohibition of *vṛddhi*, and the substitution *ai* is applied as an augment (*āgama*).

Regarding the phrase "The mention of 'twice that'" (*dvistaddagrahaṇam*), and so forth: if it were stated simply as "he studies or knows that" (*tadadhīte veda*), then a combination would be understood for the meaning of the suffix when it is in grammatical apposition with a word in the second case;

consequently, the suffix would apply only in cases where one both studies and knows that [text]. However, it would not apply in the case of one who merely studies but does not know, or one who knows but does not study.

Or, if one does not study [the Veda] exclusively, there would be no [application of the suffix] in that case. However, by taking the word "that" (tat) twice, because of the resulting split of the sentence, the suffix is established for each case—both for one who studies and for one who knows. It is for that purpose that "that" is taken twice. This, however, is not the purpose of taking it twice; for just as...

In the rule *ṭhite na dīvyati khanati jayati jitam* (Pāṇini 4.4.2), although the case endings expressing semantic competency (*samarthavibhakti*) are employed only once, a conjunction with the four meanings of the suffixes via the third-case-competent [word] is not understood; likewise here too, it will not be understood. Therefore, just as...

[Objection: "In cases such as *divyati* and others, the suffix occurs; likewise here too, it will occur both when one studies individually and when one is learned (*vidvas*). [Response: We do not say that. Why? Because the mention of 'twice' (*dvis*) right here is for the purpose of prescribing [the suffix] separately for the student (*adhīyāna*) and the learned man (*vidvas*). [Question: "From where then [does this distinction arise]?"

[This would apply] in the rules "ṭhak after words ending in *kratu*, *uktha*, etc. (Pāṇini 4.2.60) and "ṭhak after *vasanta*, etc. (Pāṇini 4.2.63). What is the reason that it would not apply there? The word *kratu* is a name for a ritual action (*karman*), and *vasanta* and the others are names of seasons; their study is not possible.
It would apply to the text associated with that [Veda], and since that [text] is used there figuratively (*gauṇa*), it is not accepted.

Because a primary sense (*mukhya*) is possible for the term *veda*, the suffix should be understood from those [Vedas] by way of its learned meaning, not from the student. However, because of the repeated mention of "that" (*tad-*) in the rule, even the figurative sense is included.
In this case, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied individually to both the student and the learned man.
60. The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after words ending in *kratu*, *uktha*, and so forth, as well as after sūtras.

(Pāṇini 4.2.60) The word *kratu* is a name for a ritual action (*karman*); since two types of learning—namely, the act of studying and the act of knowing—are not possible for it, its referent is taken to be the text [bearing that name] by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), and not because there exists a ritual named *kratu*.
The specific forms of that [sacrifice], such as the Agniṣṭoma and others, are understood here as the "chariot" which is the text; regarding this, he says:
"from words denoting specific sacrifices. The phrase "he has studied the Agniṣṭoma" means that he has studied the text associated with the Agniṣṭoma, which deals with its subject matter.
Regarding the statement "it is desired from the *sūtrānta*, from that which is not a *kalpa*, etc.," is it indeed desired? If so, then it is not praised; yet it is obtained. Why?
Because of the recurrence of the word "or" (*vā*), which indicates the understanding of an optionally fixed rule (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). What then? It is the definition of *sāman*.

Regarding the phrase "while the *Āuṭṭhikya* is being recited": the *Āuṭṭhikya* is a commentary (*vyākhyāgrantha*) that explains the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the *sāmans* designated as *ukthas*. The suffix *ñya* is applied according to the rule *chandogaukthikya* (Pāṇini 4.3.129). Thus, it refers to one who is engaged in that *Āuṭṭhikya*, the treatise on the characteristics of the *sāmans*.
The word *uktha* produces a derivative suffix. Why is this so? Because it is mentioned together with the word *kratu* in a figurative sense.

The application of the word *uktha* in the term *aukthikya* occurs because of its being for that purpose (*tādarthya*). And there is indeed the designation of something by the name of that for which it exists due to such purposiveness; for example, a jasmine flower intended for a lamp is called "the lamp."
Regarding the question, "How should it be in the case of one who studies the *Āuṭṭhikya*?"—to this it says:
"And from the word *āuṭṭhikya*" [Pāṇini 4.2.60]. He states the reason for that very point: "Because of non-mention" [in the *Gaṇasūtra*].
[This refers to] the *Gaṇasūtra*: "After words denoting branches of knowledge (*vidyā*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and ritual manuals (*kalpasūtra*)" (Gaṇasūtra 84).

He states an exception to this overly broad application with the words "and *vidyā*," etc. The meaning is that the word *vidyā* produces a suffix only when preceded by the three [terms] beginning with *anaṅga*, *kṣatra*, and *dharma*, and not when preceded by *aṅga* and the others. Thus, "one who knows the three sciences" (*traividyaḥ*): a science (*vidyā*) consisting of three parts (*tryavayavā*).
This is a compound with elision of the second member (*uttarapadalopin*), following the *śākapārthiva* class and others. One who studies the three Vedas is a *traividya*.
One who studies the narrative of Yāvakrīta is a *yāvakrītika*. One who studies [the treatise on] *priyaṅgu* is a *praiyaṅgavika*. One who studies the narrative of Vāsavadattā is a *vāsavadattika*.
"One who studies the *Sumanottara* is called a *saumanotarikaḥ*," according to the rule:

"After a word beginning with *sarva*, and after a *dvigu* compound, there is *la*. The meaning is that the suffix *ṭhak* which has arisen after a word beginning with *sarva* or after a *dvigu* compound undergoes elision (*lopa*). But [one might object]: is this not already covered by the rule "There is elision of the patronymic suffix after a *dvigu*" (Pāṇini 4.1.88)?

[Is this] established? This is true; however, in this context, some [grammarians] prescribe a suffix for every individual word by means of rules such as *vidyā-lakṣaṇa-kalpa-sūtrāntāt* (Pāṇini/Gaṇasūtra 84). Consequently, even that which is undesirable would arise.
Since there is no elision (*luk*) due to the prescription for each specific word, the explicit statement of elision (*lug-vacana*) is therefore necessary.

Regarding the rule "ṭhanusūrlakṣyalakṣaṇe ca": the word *anusū* causes a suffix to arise; furthermore, the words *lakṣya* and *lakṣaṇa* cause a suffix to arise when they take the form of words. [The example is] *ānusukaḥ*.
Here, the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule "isusuktāntāt kaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.51), and the vowel is shortened by the rule "ke'ṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.13).
"In many instances, [the suffix] is added after the latter member of a compound. Here, "that which has the word *pada* as its latter member" is what is meant by that expression.
[The rule] "after *pathin* following *śata* and *ṣaṣṭi*, the suffix *ṣikan* [is applied]" means that [the suffix is applied] after the word *pathin* when it follows the words *śata* and *ṣaṣṭi*.
The suffix *ṣikan* occurs. The letter *ṣ* is for the purpose of [triggering] the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*, and the letter *n* is for the purpose of accentuation.

All of this is established simply by the recitation [of the word] among the *ukthādi* group. Even that which is not explicitly recited here is included by virtue of the mention of "variously" (*bahulagrahaṇena*). Furthermore, the suffix *ṣikan* is applied variously even within the *ukthādi* group.
And it is recited as "padottarapadācca."

61. *Vun* is added after *krama* and others. (4.2.61) 62. *Ini* is added after *anubrāhmaṇa*. (4.2.62) "An *anubrāhmaṇa* is a text similar to the *Brāhmaṇa*. This refers to an *avyayībhāva* compound used according to its actual meaning (*yathārtha*).

[The author] shows [the purpose]. Now, one might object: "For one who studies the *Anubrāhmaṇa*, the *Anubrāhmaṇa* belongs to him"—this is already established there by the suffix *-in* itself, which expresses possession (*matvarthīya*). So what is the purpose of this [sūtra]? It is for the sake of precluding the suffix *aṇ*. If this were not stated, the suffix *aṇ* would apply by the rule "one who studies that or knows that" (Pāṇini 4.2.59).
63. *Vasantādibhyaṣṭhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.63). [The *Kāśikā* explains: "A book associated with spring is called *vasanta*;
a book associated with spring is called *vasanta*. That which is recited in spring, or that in which spring is prescribed [as the time], [is so named].

He is described as being accompanied by spring. Regarding the term "varṣāśaradam": *varṣā* and *śarat* form the compound *varṣāśaradam*. The suffix *ṭac* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.4.106, "After a *dvandva* compound ending in *c*, *u*, or *ṣa*, when it denotes a collective (*samāhāra*). The reference is made using this compound-ending suffix.

64. *proktālluk* (Pāṇini 4.2.64). This formulation is appropriate if there exists a treatise named *prokta*, such as a work on grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) and so forth; however, such a work does not exist. To avoid the fault that [the suffix] might follow after something else for some other purpose, he says:

Regarding the passage beginning with "proktasahacaritaḥ" and so forth: by means of association (*sāhacarya*), he shows that the suffix applied to the sense of "proclaimed" (*prokta*)—through the metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) of "this is that"—is expressed by the word *prokta*. For example, in the case of "pāṇinīyaḥ": from [the base] ending in that [suffix], according to "vṛddhāc chaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.2.114), and then [applying] "tad adhīte tad veda" (Pāṇini 4.2.59).

(4.2.59) *it-aṇ*. There is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix]: *pāṇinīyaḥ*. When there is the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of "taught by Āpiśali," there is elision of that [suffix]: *āpiśalaḥ*. But what is the specific difference in meaning here when there is elision, since the form remains the same? To this he says: "In the feminine," and so forth. If there were no elision...
By the rule *ṭhṭhiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15), the suffix *ṅīp* would apply; this [suffix] is *udātta* on the final syllable due to the accent of the *aṇ* suffix.
However, when there is elision (*luk*), the suffix *ṭāp* occurs, and by its accent, it becomes *udātta* on the middle syllable.
In the case of the word *āpiśali*, once the elision has occurred, there is no difference in the accent. For even though...
The final syllable ought to be udātta due to the elision (*luk*). However, in the case of the feminine, the previously mentioned distinction applies:

for when there is *luk*, the suffix *ṅīp* does not occur; even though the suffix *aṇ* is present, there is a prohibition because of the governing rule "not [after] a non-principal element" (*anupasarjanāt*) at 4.1.14.
And because the suffix *aṇ*, prescribed for the meaning already stated [by the rule], is here a subordinate element (*upasarjana*).

65. *Sūtrācca kopadhāt* (Pāṇini 4.2.65). Because of the statement "from that which has *ka* as its penultimate letter" (*kopadhāt*), it is understood that the rule does not apply to the actual form [of the word] itself; therefore, he says—"[from a base] denoting a *sūtra*"—to indicate that the reference is to words expressing a *sūtra*.

Regarding the word *aṣṭakam*: its measure consists of eight chapters (*adhyāya*). While the rule *tadasya parimāṇam* (Pāṇini 5.1.57) is in force, and also the rule *saṃkhyāyāḥ saṃjñāsaṅghasūtrādhyayaneṣu* (5.1.58), the suffix *kan* is applied by the rule *saṃkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan* (5.1.22).

"It should be stated that [the elision occurs] after a suffix whose base is a numeral. A suffix whose base (*prakṛti*) is a numeral is a "numeral-base" (*saṃkhyāprakṛti*). The meaning of this statement—that the elision (*lup*) occurs after a word ending in such a suffix which has *ka* as its penultimate letter (*kopadha*)—is that it must be explained (*vyākhyeya*). This is the explanation thereof: the word "optionally" (*vā*) is understood to carry over (*vartate*), and that...
And because this is a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (an option restricted by rule), it will apply only to the base word *saṃkhyā* (numeral) and not to anything else. Thus:
*cātuṣṭayaḥ*—as in the *Kāśikā*; *catuṣṭayaḥ*—as in the *Padamañjarī*; and *cātuṣṭayam*.

In the word *caturtha*, since it consists of four parts (*catvāro 'vayavā asya*), the suffix *tayap* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.42 (*saṃkhyāyā avayave tayap*). Then, by Pāṇini 8.3.99 (*hrasvāt tādau taddhite*), the retroflex *ṭ* is substituted [for the dental *t*], resulting in *ṭha*. This word ends in the suffix *tayap* with the numeral as its base, and it is not a word ending in *ka*; rather, it is a word ending in *ya*.

66. "And the *chandas* and *brāhmaṇas* that have them as their subject matter" (4.2.66). [The word] *prokta* ("proclaimed") is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. And here, by virtue of the sense, it is understood to be in the nominative case (*prathamānta*) for the sake of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the term *cchandobrāhmaṇāni*; therefore, he says—*chandāṃsi*.
"And the *brāhmaṇas* are those that end with the suffixes called *prokta*. Here, there is no inclusion of the actual word-forms [of the suffixes].

For instance, the term *prokta* is carried over here [from the previous rule], and the words *chandas* and *brāhmaṇa* do not themselves end with the *prokta* suffixes. Therefore, those which denote the *chandas* and *brāhmaṇas*...
Words ending in the suffixes mentioned [by Pāṇini] are understood here. But for what purpose is this stated?

Here, words ending in the suffix *prokta* are seen to have various forms. For instance, in some cases, independence is observed for that which ends in such a suffix, as in: "The science taught by Pāṇini is the Pāṇinian [grammar]."

The function (*vṛtti*) of the word *prokta* is precisely its stated meaning: independence. And here, the function of the word *pāṇinīya* is precisely its stated meaning. In some cases there is connection with a further attribute (*upādhi*), as in: "the great *pāṇinīya* has been prescribed for you.
In some cases it is a sentence: "he has studied the *pāṇinīya*. In some cases it is a function (*vṛtti*).

Regarding the term *pāṇinīya*: this is stated so that the suffix here may apply to those who study or know the *chandas* (Vedic texts) and the *brāhmaṇas*, and not to other types of persons. Thus it says "adhyetṛveditṛ" (those who study or know). This means that the suffixes [denoting] "one who studies" or "one who knows" have these [texts] as their objects.

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. [As stated in] the *Kāśikā* and the *Padamañjarī*: "The meaning of 'elsewhere' (*anyatra*) is the sense of 'domain' (*viṣaya*). Just as in the expression "water is the domain of fish," the word "domain" (*viṣaya*) is used here in the sense of "not being elsewhere" (*ananyatrabhāva*), so it is here as well. By this, although...

The word *viṣaya* has its application in meanings such as a collection of villages (*grāmasamudāya*) and so forth; nevertheless, he shows that here it is understood as functioning in the sense of "not existing elsewhere" (*ananyatrabhāva*). By the words beginning with "by that" (*tena*), he demonstrates the result of the term functioning as "not existing elsewhere. For in this way, there is the absence [of the object] elsewhere.

If independence and so forth do not exist, then there is a connection with another qualifier (*upādhi*), such as being related to the specific [teacher] Kaṭha by means of "greatness" (*mahattva*) and so on. [In the case of the word *kāṭhaka*, it is derived from] "proclaimed by Kaṭha" (*kaṭhena proktam*). According to [Pāṇini 4.3.104], "the suffix *ṇini* is applied after [words denoting] Kalāpin, Vaiśampāyana, and those who are their pupils," the suffix *ṇini* is used here. Of that [suffix]:

From *kaṭha* and *caraka*, there is elision [of the suffix] by *ṭhkaṭhacarakālluk* (Pāṇini 4.3.107). Then, by *tataḥ kaṭhena proktam adhīte tad veda* (4.2.59), there is again the suffix *aṇ*; for that too, there is elision by *proktālluk* (4.2.64).
Thus we have *maudāḥ* and *paippalādāḥ*. [The suffix is applied] also from the pupils of Kalāpin and Vaiśampāyana.
By [Pāṇini 4.3.104], the suffix *ṇini* is applied, [forming] *modena proktam*. Then, by [Pāṇini 4.3.108], *ṭhkalāpino’ṇ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied;
from that which ends in *aṇ*, by [Pāṇini 4.2.59], *tadadhīte tadveda*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied again;
and for that, by [Pāṇini 4.2.64], *proktālluk*, there is elision (*luk*). [The form] *ārcābhinaḥ* is derived from *ṛcābhena*.
Regarding the word *proktam* (proclaimed): the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule *ṭhkalāpivaiśamyāyanāntevāsibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.3.104);
from that form ending in *ṇini*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *ṭhtadadhīte tadveda* (Pāṇini 4.2.59). Thus we have *vājasaneyinaḥ*.
[The derivation is: "proclaimed by Vājasaneya. The suffix *aṇ* is applied here by the rule *ṭhśaunakādibhyaścchandasi* (Pāṇini 4.3.106).
The suffix *ṇini* is applied; from that form ending in *ṇini*, the suffix *aṇ* is added by the rule "one who studies or knows that" (Pāṇini 4.2.59), which then undergoes elision (*luk*).

Thus we have "tāṇḍinaḥ. From the word *tāṇḍya*, which ends in *yañ* according to the *Garga*-class (Pāṇini 4.1.105), the suffix *ṇini* is applied in the sense of "proclaimed" (Pāṇini 4.3.105) because it refers to a Brāhmaṇa or Kalpa text proclaimed in ancient times.

In the case of *ṭhāpatya*, there is the elision of *y* by the rule *taddhite'nāti* (Pāṇini 6.4.151). From that, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *tadadhīte tadveda* (4.2.59), which is then elided (*luk*). Thus we have "the Bhāllavins. From the word *bhāllavi*, which ends in the suffix *iṇ*, the suffix *ṇini* is added in the sense of "proclaimed" as before; from that [form ending in *ṇini*], the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "one who knows that."

(4.2.59) *ity-aṇ*, its *luk* elision. Regarding "of a Śāṭyāyanin": from the word *śāṭya*, which ends in *yañ* by virtue of belonging to the *Garga*-class (4.1.105), there is the suffix *phak* by (4.1.101) *ṭhyañiñoś-ca*. From that, in the sense of "proclaimed by" (*prokta*), there is *ṇini* as before; then, from that [form] ending in *ṇini*, [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] by the rule "one who studies that or knows that" (*tad-adhīte tad-veda*).

(4.2.59) *ity-aṇ*, its *luk* elision. Regarding the form ‘aitareyiṇaḥ’: from the word *aitareya*, which ends in the *ḍhak* suffix belonging to the *chubhrādi* group (4.1.123), the suffix *ṇini* is applied as before; then, by (4.2.59) *tad adhīte*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied, and there is *luk* elision of that.

"For the purpose of understanding the specific Brāhmaṇa": the "specific Brāhmaṇa" refers to its being proclaimed by the Purāṇas. The mention of "Brāhmaṇa" is for the sake of ensuring that there be such an understanding (*pratipatti*).
Regarding the term "Yājñavalkyāni": it is derived from the word *yājñavalkya* with the suffix *yañ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.105, as it belongs to the *garga*-class.

The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to *Pāṇini 4.2.111*: *proktārthe ṭhkaṇvādibhyo gotre*. Thus, *saulabhanī* means "those proclaimed by Sulabha. As before, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to *Pāṇini 4.3.108*: *kalāpino’ṇ*. Here, independence [of the author] is established; for in this case, there is no status of being "proclaimed in the past" (*purāṇaproktatva*), as it was proclaimed by someone in the present.

Because it has been stated [in the sūtras]: "Kāśyapinaḥ, Kauśikinaḥ. [This means] a ritual manual (*kalpa*) taught by Kaśyapa, and one taught by Kauśika. [The suffix] *ṇini* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.3.103, "From the seers Kaśyapa and Kauśika, [the suffix] *ṇini*";
from that which ends in this [suffix], the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to 4.2.59, "He studies that," and there is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix].

"Pārāśariṇaḥ, Śailālinaḥ. These refer to the Sūtra taught by Pārāśarya and the Sūtra taught by Śilālin; by the rule "pārāśaryaśilālibhyāṃ bhikṣunaṭasūtrayoḥ" (Pāṇini 4.3.110), the suffix *aṇ* is applied, which is then elided (*luk*). [Examples: "Karmandinaḥ, Kṛśāśvinaḥ," [referring to those] by Karmanda.

The word *sūtra* is formed as "the *sūtra* proclaimed by Kṛśāśva," according to Pāṇini 4.3.111 (*ṭh karmandakṛśāśvādiniḥ*). From that [form ending in *-ini*], the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to 4.2.59 (*tad adhīte tad veda*), which is then elided (*luk*). Thus we have "the *paiṅgī kalpaḥ*" (the ritual manual proclaimed by Piṅga), according to 4.3.105 (*purāṇaproktāḥ*).
By such [rules] as these, the suffix *ṇini* is applied; therein there is only autonomy, and not the state of being its object.

67. *tadasminnastīti deśe tannāmni* (4.3.67). [The word] "named after that" (*tannāmā*) refers to a name ending in the suffix *ṭha*. If, then, the suffix applies when the place is named after that, the particle *iti* is redundant; for by the very mention of "named after that," the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would already be excluded?

This is not so; for a name is indeed of two kinds: the conventional (*saṅketita*) and the recurring (*anuvṛta*). The conventional is that which has not yet entered the path of common usage; as for the recurring name, it is with respect to that that this [present] application occurs. And the recurring name is that which is used in worldly transaction (*vyāvahārika*).
The particle *iti* is employed for the purpose of indicating that [the preceding word] is the object of comprehension, and for the purpose of delimiting specific items such as villages and the like.
If this is so, then let only the particle *iti* be used; what is the use of the phrase "that which is its name" (*tannāmnī*)? This too need not be stated;
for [the particle *iti*] sets aside even those contrary notions, however powerful they may be, regarding the status of being a name (*nāmadheyatā*).

[The suffix *matup*] is sublated. How so? When this rule (*yoga*) is commenced, it sublates *matup* because it is an exception (*apavāda*) to it. However, when there is a conflict with its own exceptions such as *ini*, *ṭhan*, and so on, by the principle of "the prohibition of an exception" (*apavādavipratiṣedha*), only *ini*, *ṭhan*, and the like would apply. [This is the case] when there is the mention of the name [of the base].

But when there is a deliberation even by means of stronger [arguments], the conviction arises that "that which brings about the status of being a name is indeed that which belongs to the fourth [chapter]. Therefore, it is precisely that [which is the name].
68. *tena nirvṛtam* (Pāṇini 4.2.68). Regarding the phrase *caturṣv api*: this refers to the immediately preceding rule, as well as to the two rules that are about to be stated.

Regarding *kartari ca*: depending on the specific grammatical example (*lakṣya*), [the suffix] is applied sometimes in the sense of the cause (*hetu*) and sometimes in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).

In the phrase "by a thousand," the word *hetu* (cause) is used in the sense of an instrumental cause (*hetu*), while in "by Kuśāmba," it is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). When it is used in the sense of a cause, since the root *vṛt* is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) in *nirvṛtaḥ* denotes the agent.

When it is used in the sense of the agent, because the causative meaning (*ṇyartha*) is implicitly contained within the root, the participle denotes the object (*karman*). Even intransitive roots may have the causative meaning implicitly contained within them.
They become transitive.
69. *tasya nivāsaḥ* (4.2.69). 70. *adūrabhavaśca* (4.2.70).

"According to their respective [meanings]" (*yathāyatham*) means "according to each one's own. In that regard, in the first case, it is used after a word joined with a case-ending having the sense of the first case;

in the second, after a word joined with a case-ending having the sense of the third case; and in the third and fourth cases, after a word joined with a case-ending having the sense of the sixth case. As for the feminine suffix *nadi*, however, because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], only the suffix *matup* occurs.
By the rule "nadyāṃ matup" (Pāṇini 4.2.85).
72. *matośca bahvajaṅgāt* (Pāṇini 4.2.72).
[The example] "mālavatam" is given. If [the rule] applies when there are many syllables (*bahvac*), then there is no fault at all.
73. [The suffix *cha*] is applied after words with many vowels when they denote wells.

(4.2.73) 74. And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after the word *udaka* when it follows *vipāś*. (4.2.74) 75. And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after the group of words beginning with *saṅkala*. (4.2.75)
76. [The suffix *cha* is applied after words denoting] Sauvīra, Śālva, and Prācya when referring to women. (4.2.76) 77. The suffix *aṇ* is applied after [words beginning with] Suvāstu.

(4.2.77) [This applies] to those ending in *u*, by the rule "for that which is characterized by the suffix *ṭha* ending in *u*" (*ṭhūvarmāntalakṣaṇasya*), etc.; for those ending in *u*, [the suffix] *rañ* is applied by the rule *ṭhorañ* (4.2.71).

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *añ* [suffix] that would otherwise apply; and it is an exception to the suffix characterized by *kūpa*, which would apply to the remaining [bases] by the rule "after polysyllabic [names], when [the place is] in wells" (*bahvacaḥ kūpeṣu*, 4.2.73). Now, what is the purpose of mentioning *aṇ*? It might be argued that for [places] such as Subāstu, the suffix *yat* alone is prescribed. The repetition [of *aṇ*] is for the sake of those [suffixes] which are prescribed but do not [otherwise] apply.

This is understood from that very [sūtra]. Furthermore, since [the suffix] *aṇ* is prescribed, it would not apply [to the case in question], because it is sublated by an exception (*apavāda*). To show that it will indeed apply, he says: "The mention of *aṇ*" and so forth. For if the mention of *aṇ* were absent, the principle would hold that "exceptions sublate preceding rules, but not subsequent ones."

(Vyāḍipāda 10) Thus, if the *samprasāraṇa* were to occur together with the *nadī-matup*, the *nadī-pamatup* would apply because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. However, due to the mention of *aṇ*, only *aṇ* occurs. Therefore, the mention of *aṇ* is for the purpose of setting aside *matup*.

78. *roṇī* | (4.2.78) [Question: "What is this mention of *ṭhak*? [Answer: The meaning is that this mention is contemptible. It is contemptible because it transgresses the grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*). To demonstrate precisely that transgression of the rule, he says:

The phrase "as far as" (*yāvatā*) and so forth is stated for the purpose that the understanding of both the simple [suffix] and that which ends with it may occur by virtue of being the subject under discussion (*prakṛtatvena*). If the indication were made by [the rule] "of *droṇī*" (*droṇyāḥ*) and so forth, then [it would follow that] by a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) accompanied by a suffix...

According to the principle *tadantavidhir na* (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 89), [the suffix] would apply only to the base itself, not to that which ends in it. Here, by the mention of *roṇī* without reference to a specific rule (*śāstra*), independence from a rule is expressed;
because this paribhāṣā is not required here, the suffix is established as applying even to that which ends in [the base].

But surely, the rule of extension to that which ends with [a specific element] (*tadantavidhi*) is prohibited when the item containing it is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and this is not a nominal stem because it ends in a feminine suffix. Now, if it is argued that "when a nominal stem is mentioned,
that which is qualified by gender is also included" (Vyāḍipāda 29), [then it is still not a nominal stem].

Since that which is prohibited by the rule regarding the inclusion of the final element (tadantavidhi) is also prohibited for that which ends in a feminine suffix, and since it was previously established that this paribhāṣā applies specifically to cases where there is a mention of the actual form of a nominal stem (prātipadika), [the author] now shows that this explanatory principle (jñāpana) is merely general in its application.

Therefore, even when the actual form [of the word] is not being grasped in some instances, this paribhāṣā operates. Consequently, in the example *kumārayati* (he treats as a girl), the status of being like the superlative suffix (*iṣṭhavadbhāva*)— as prescribed by the Vārttika *jātiṣṭhavad iti prātipadikasya* (Vārttika 813)— is established.
79. [The suffix *cha* is applied] after a word ending in *kopadha*. (4.2.79) 80.

The suffixes *vuñ*, *chaṇ*, *kaṭhac*, *ilac*, *seni*, *raḍ*, *ḍhañ*, *ṇya*, *ya*, *phak*, *phiñ*, *iñ*, *ñya*, *kak*, *ṭhak*, and *ka* are respectively applied after the following groups of words: *arīhaṇa*, *kṛśāśva*, *ṛśya*, *kumuda*, *kāśa*, *tṛṇa*, *prekṣā*, *aśman*, *sakhi*, *saṅkāśa*, *bala*, *pakṣa*, *karṇa*, *sutaṅgama*, *pragadin*, *varāha*, and *kumuda*. (4.2.80)
"Even the general rule (*autsargika*) is desired there. If this is so, then its hearing [in the text] would follow;
therefore, he says: "And of that," etc., and "And thus it has been said," etc.
He confirms that very point: "It is simply *autsargika*. [The word] *śirīṣāḥ* means those produced not far from *śirīṣa* trees.

That his forest was the Śirīṣa Forest is understood from the statement of the author of the Bhāṣya; for there should not be elision (lup) of suffixes prescribed by specific rules. Therefore, it is understood that the general elision (lup) occurs here.

81. The suffix *lup* is applied [to a word denoting a country] when it signifies a country (*janapada*). (4.2.81) 82. And [the suffix *lup* is applied] after words beginning with *varaṇa*. (4.2.82) 83.
After the word *śarkarā*, [the suffix *lup* is applied] optionally. (4.2.83)

"By the force of its recitation," and so forth. If the *lup* were obligatory (*nitya*), its recitation in the two [Gaṇapāṭha] lists would be purposeless.
