Therefore, he says "In that case, then," and so forth, providing an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the mention of the word *vā*. This indicates that by the very force of its recitation, there will be optional hearing (*śravaṇa*) [of the suffix].

He demonstrates this with the example "śarkarā" (gravel/sugar), where there is the elision (*lup*) of the suffix by the general rule. With "śārkaram," there is the audible presence of that same suffix in one alternative view. With "śarkarakam," the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied because it belongs to the *kumuda* group. With "śārkarakam," the suffix *kak* is applied because it belongs to the *varāha* group. [Finally,] "śārkarikam" and "śarkarīyam."
By the subsequent sūtra, the suffixes *ṭhak* and *chaṬ* [are applied].
84. *ṭhakchāṬ ca* (Pāṇini 4.2.84). 85. *nadyāṃ matup* (Pāṇini 4.2.85).
[The example is] *udumbarāvatī*. [In this case, the suffix] *matup* is applied according to [the rule] *matau bahvaco'najirādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.3.119).
Long.
86. *madhvādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.2.86). 87. *kumudanaḍavetasebhyo ḍmatup* (Pāṇini 4.2.87).
[This rule applies] when the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ṭhak* would otherwise be applicable after the word *kumuda*; likewise for the word *naḍa*.

[The suffix] *valac* is prescribed by [Pāṇini 4.2.88] *ṭhañ-ṇaḍa-śādāḍ-ḍvalac*, and [the suffix] *kuk* is prescribed by [Pāṇini 4.2.91] *ṭhañ-ṇaḍādīnāṃ kuk ca*. When this rule is applicable, the suffix *matup* is also prescribed after the word *vetasa*. [The sūtra] beginning with *mahiṣācca* means that the suffix *matup* is prescribed after the word *mahiṣa*. This is the intended meaning.
The meaning is that this must be explained. Here is the explanation:
the particle *ca* is carried over from the preceding sūtra, and it serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned. By means of it, [the suffix] will also apply after the word *mahiṣa*.
88. The suffix *ḍvalac* is added after *naḍa* and *śāda*. (4.2.88) 89. The suffix *valac* is added after *śikhā*. (4.2.89) 90.
The suffix *cha* is added after words beginning with *utkara*. (4.2.90)
91. *Naḍādīnāṃ kuk ca* (Pāṇini 4.2.91). [The Vārttika states:
"And for *kruñcā*, there is shortening. The suffix *kuk* is applied to the word *kruñcā*, and there is shortening of the vowel:
*krauñcakīyam*. [Another Vārttika states: "For *takṣan*, there is elision [of the final *n*] as well. The suffix *kuk* is added to *takṣan*.
The elision of *n* also occurs—as in *takṣakīyam*.
92. *Śeṣe* (Pāṇini 4.2.92).
"That which is other than what has been employed is the remainder (*śeṣa*)"—this is the explanatory statement (*grahaṇakavākya*). That very [statement]...

He explains this with the words beginning "from *apatya* and so forth. For *apatya* (offspring) and the others, up to and including *cāturarthya* (the four senses), have been employed in the rules prescribing suffixes;
therefore, any meaning other than those—such as *jāta* (born) and so on—is the *śeṣa* (remainder). But [it may be objected]: offspring and the others have already been excluded.
Since suffixes such as *gha* and others are prescribed for meanings like "born from them" (*jāta*) and so forth, they would not at all apply to meanings such as "offspring" (*apatya*).
Therefore, what is the purpose of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) for the sake of excluding those? To this, he says:
"‘tasyedam’ (of that, this)," and so forth. For meanings such as "born from him," the meaning "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*) is taught.

And that [suffix] is common to offspring and the rest. When a rule is prescribed for a general category, it is also prescribed for its particular instances, because the general category serves as an indicator (upalakṣaṇa) of those particulars. Therefore, since this [suffix] is a particular instance, the suffixes *gha* and so on would apply to offspring and the rest when they fall within the scope of "born" (*jāta*) and other such terms. Consequently—

The heading "the remainder" (śeṣādhikāra) is established so that they [the subsequent rules] do not apply to those [cases]. Furthermore, by the words "Moreover," etc., he demonstrates another purpose: for if the heading "the remainder" were absent, then since the suffixes beginning with *gha* would experience a connection only with the meaning of the nominative case, their function would be fulfilled right there.

It would be understood as follows: in that case, regarding the second and subsequent meanings, only suffixes such as *aṇ* and others—those taught in the section beginning with *prāgdīvyatīya*—would apply, and not suffixes such as *gha* and others. However, the word *śeṣa* (remainder), by unifying meanings such as "born" (*jāta*) and so forth under the category of being "other than what has been employed," is capable of expressing them; thus, suffixes such as *gha* and others are established in all cases. Therefore, [the word *śeṣa*] is used for the sake of completeness.

The statement regarding the remainder: "Both a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and a governing heading (*adhikāra*). Here, because it functions as a prescriptive rule, it is called a "definition" in the sense that "it defines by means of this"; whereas in what follows, it is a "governing heading" due to the presence of the *svarita* accent. In that regard, when it serves as its definition, terms such as *cākṣuṣa* ("perceived by the eye") and so forth are established. When...

If [the suffixes] *gha* and so forth occur when there is one's own domain (*svādhikāratā*), then they would occur in all meanings such as "born" (*jāta*) and so on. If, then, this very definition of "remainder" (*śeṣa*) applies here— such that just as the suffix occurs in meanings like "grasping" (*grahaṇa*) and so forth,
it will likewise occur in "born" and so forth— then is the enumeration of "born" and so forth useless?

No; because it is intended for the purpose of prescribing exceptions. However, those [sūtras] which do not have the purpose of prescribing exceptions—such as "those born, ceased, acquired, or purchased are virtuous" (jāta-nivṛtta-labdha-krīta-kuśalāḥ)—should be understood as a detailed elaboration (*prapañca*) of the very term "the remainder" (*śeṣa*).

93. *rāṣṭrāvārapārād-ghakhau* (4.2.93). From the word *rāṣṭra*, since the suffix *cha* would apply by [Pāṇini 4.2.114] *ṭh-vṛddhāc-chah*, the suffixes *gha* and *kha* are prescribed [instead]. From the word *avārapāra*, the suffixes *gha* and *kha* are ordained. The compound *avārapāram* is a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound meaning "the far shore of the near shore" (*avārasya pāram*).
Because it is observed in cases such as *rājadanta* (king-tooth), the form *pārāvāra* also occurs in that sense.

It is obtained from both the analyzed (*vigṛhīta*) and the reversed forms. This indeed must be stated. Alternatively, a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) will be understood; therein, one will be the meaning of the whole (*samudāyārtha*), while the other will be the meaning of the parts (*avayavārtha*).

Even in the case of words that are contrary [in meaning], the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) is not contradicted by the rule "of words having the same referent, even if they are dissimilar" (1.2.64, Vārttika 23); for example: *thā*—*vakradaṇḍaśca kuṭiladaṇḍaśca kuṭiladaṇḍau*, and likewise *yaṅlukau*. But surely its bases (*prakṛti*) are thus five?

Since there is a discrepancy—namely, that there are words such as *rāṣṭra* and so forth, whereas there are only two suffixes—the application of elements according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) would not be established. This is not a fault; for correspondence according to order depends upon the specific mention [of the elements]. Since the mention concerns only two [suffixes], correspondence according to order applies to the present case in relation to those two. Thus, there is no difference regarding the five [suffixes] and so forth.

It arises, yet it does not sublate [the rule] according to numerical correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*). Just as in the case of suffixes such as *vuñ* and others, which operate according to numerical correspondence with respect to the *gaṇa*s; for although at the time of the production of the suffix by means of numerical correspondence, the forms of the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) within the *gaṇa*s may be unequal in number, so too here, according to numerical correspondence—

It does not fail [to apply]. From what, then, is it understood that this is an *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one)? From the commentary: "merely by the mention of a specific base" (*prakṛtiviśeṣopādānamātreṇa*). The word *mātra* is for the purpose of excluding the mention of case endings (*vibhakti*) and meanings such as genus (*jāti*), and so forth.
94. *grāmādya-khañau* | (4.2.94) This rule is stated because the suffix *cha*, which would otherwise apply by virtue of the definition of "vṛddha," is [here] superseded.

95. *kattryādibhyo ḍhakañ* | (Pāṇini 4.2.95) Since the suffix *cha* would apply to those [words] among the *kattryādi* group that are marked with a vṛddhi-vowel, and the suffix *aṇ* would apply to the remaining [words], this rule is commenced. Furthermore, the word *katri* is a *tatpuruṣa* compound: "three who are contemptible" (*kutsitās trayaḥ*). [The substitution of *ku-* for *tri-* occurs by the rule *koḥ...*].

The suffix *ka* occurs by means of the split (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule *kat* (Pāṇini 6.3.101). Precisely for this reason, it is also a *bahuvrīhi* by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*): "she who has three contemptible [sons] is *kattri*.

Regarding the statement "from *kuḍa* and *jña*, the suffix *ḍhañ* occurs and there is elision of *ya*": the suffix *ḍhañ* is applied after the words *kuḍa* and *jña*, and there is elision of the *ya*.
—Kauḍeyaka.
However, for those who read "kulyāyā yalopaśca" (and there is elision of the *ya* of *kulyā*), the form is *kauleyaka*.

96. After *kula*, *kukṣi*, and *grīvā*, [the suffix *ṭhak* is applied] in the sense of "one who eats" (*śvāsya*) and "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*). This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the application of] *ṭhaṇ*.

97. *ḍhak* after [words denoting] rivers and the like. (4.2.97) This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *aṇ* suffix which would otherwise apply to those [names] that are non-vṛddha, and to the *cha* suffix which would apply to vṛddha names such as *vārāṇasī*. For some [grammarians], it applies after a word ending in *ṭha* or having *ra* as its penultimate letter (*upadha*).

Since the suffix *vuñ* would have applied by the rule *prācām* (Pāṇini 4.2.123), the suffix *ḍhak* is now introduced. Thus we have *pāureya*, meaning "that which exists in the city" (*puri bhavam*). Similarly, *vāneya* means "that which exists in the forest" (*vane bhavam*), and *gaireya* means "that which exists on the mountain" (*girau bhavam*). Both of these views are authoritative; for the Teacher has [taught] in both ways.
Because it is taught for the sake of the students:
the term *nadī* here is intended as a reference to its own form (*svarūpa*), not for the purpose of referring to a technical designation (*saṃjñā*).
For if it were a reference to a designation, the recitation of *mahy* and the others would be purposeless.
98. *dakṣiṇāpaścātpurasastyak* (4.2.98).

Because *paścāt* and *purastāt* are indeclinables (*avyaya*), by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), the word *dakṣiṇā* is also understood here as being exclusively that which ends in the suffix *añ*, namely the form derived from *dakṣiṇādāc* (5.3.36). And thus, [the rule] *avyayāttyap* (4.2.104) applies.
Since [the suffix] *tyap* is not included in this enumeration, there is no possibility of its application; therefore, this rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the [suffix] *aṇ*.
99. *kāpiśyāḥ ṣphak* (4.2.99). Since the suffix *cha* would apply by virtue of [the rule] *vṛddhāc chaḥ* (4.2.114), the suffix *ṣphak* is prescribed after the word *kāpiśī*.
The phrase "from *bāhli*, etc. means that the suffix *ṣphak* occurs after words such as *bāhli* and others.

The meaning is that it must be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the word "ca" (and) from the subsequent sūtra is carried over here by the maxim of the lion’s glance (*siṃhāvalokita-nyāya*), because its purpose is to include what has not been explicitly mentioned;
thus, the suffix *ṣpha* occurs after words such as *bāhlika* and others as well.

100. *raṅkoramanuṣye ca* (4.2.100). This is a rule [providing for the suffix *vuñ*] when the suffix *ṭhañ* [would otherwise apply] by *ṭhorddhaśe ṭhañ* (4.2.119), or when *vuñ* [would apply] as a characteristic of a country by *ṭhjanapadatadavadhyośca* (4.2.124), or when *aṇ* [would apply] by *kopadhādaṇ* (4.2.132); this statement [is made] regarding [the word] *raṅku* when it does not refer to a human being.
Because of the inclusion [of *kaccha*] in the list beginning with *kaccha*, the suffix *aṇ* is also established for non-human [derivatives], as stated in both the *Kāśikā* and the *Padamañjarī*:

"The suffix *aṇ* is established by the inclusion in the *kaccha*-group. This is because, in the rule *kacchādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.2.133), the suffix *aṇ* from the preceding rule *kopadhādaṇ* (4.2.132) is carried over by anuvṛtti.
"By the maxim of that which is joined with *nañ* and *iva*"—when joined with *nañ* and when joined with *iva*, there arises a cognition of something similar to that [original object].

Here, the word "man" (*manuṣya*) is joined with *nañ*; therefore, here it is not the negation of the man himself that is being effected. Furthermore, its application is directed toward a living being similar to a man.

Therefore, the suffixes *ṣpha* and *gaṇa* occur when the referent is a living being similar to a human; however, in the case of a non-living being, only the suffix *aṇ* occurs because of its inclusion in the *kaccha*-group, and not *ṣpha*—as in the example "a woolen blanket from Rāṅku" (*rāṅkavaḥ kambalaḥ*).
[The phrase] "by that which is prescribed for a specific case," etc., means: if *aṇ* were not applied here as well, then [the rule] *ṣphakacchādibhyaśca*...

Such is the sūtra. Since the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by "from *kaccha* and others, *aṇ*" (4.2.133) has its scope in cases such as *rāṅkavaḥ kambalaḥ* ("a woolen blanket from Rāṅku"), it would be superseded by the suffix *ṣphak*, which is specifically ordained for living beings (*prāṇin*). Therefore, so that this fault does not occur, *aṇ* is also applied here.

101. *dyauprāgapāgudakpratīco yat* (4.2.101). This rule prescribes the suffix *yat* where the suffix *aṇ* would otherwise have applied. Words such as *prāk* and so forth acquire their form when the suffix *kvip* is added to the root *añc-* by virtue of the rule *ṛtvig...* (3.2.59). And these...

They are of two kinds: those designated as indeclinables (*avyaya*) and those not designated as indeclinables. When they end in the suffixes *astas* and *atip*, they are designated as indeclinables because of the rule "A taddhita suffix that does not take all case-endings is also an indeclinable" (Pāṇini 1.1.38); otherwise, they are not designated as indeclinables.

Since no distinction is made among them here, both types are included. [The forms] *prācyam*, *apācyam*—this is the reading in the *Kāśikā* and the *Padamañjarī—and *udīcyam* [are derived as follows]:
there is elision of the vowel *a* by rule 6.4.138 (*acaḥ*), and lengthening by rule 6.3.138 (*cau*). [The form] *udīcyam*.
Thus, by the rule *uda īt* (Pāṇini 6.4.139), the vowel *ī* is substituted. Regarding the term *prāktanam*:

from the word *prāk*, the suffix *astāti* is applied according to the rule *dikśabdebhyaḥ saptamīpañcamīprathamābhyo dik* (5.3.27); this suffix is then elided by *añcer luk* (5.3.30), after which [the present rule] applies.
When [the word] *yati* is reached, the suffixes *ṭa*, *ḷuṭ*, and *ḷul* occur by virtue of the rule *sāyaṃ-ciram-...* (Pāṇini 4.3.23).
However, that which denotes time (*kālavācin*) is the scope (*avakāśa*).
102. *kaṇṭhād yaṣṭhak* (4.2.102). This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*.

103. *Varṇau vuK* (Pāṇini 4.2.103). [The word] *ṭhvarṇuḥ* refers to a river (*nadī*). Since a *kanthā* (a coarse woolen garment) cannot exist within the current of a river, it is understood as a locative of proximity (*sāmīpika-adhikaraṇa*); therefore, he says: "the region near that..."
"Varṇuḥ. From the word *varṇu*, in the sense of "located not far from" (Pāṇini 4.2.70), the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "suvāstvādibhyo’ṇ" (4.2.77).

When the elision (*lup*) of that suffix is performed by the rule "janapade lup" (4.2.81), the form *varṇuḥ* results. But is it not the case that [this would not apply] because of the specific prescription [of the rule]?

Why does there not occur elision (*lup*) of the suffix? It is not so; for the reading of *suvāstu* and others has already fulfilled its purpose when applied to a meaning other than a country—such as "the village Vārṇava" or "the city [Vārṇava]"—and not when it refers to a country. In that case, however, elision (*lup*) must occur by virtue of the subsequent rule.

Regarding the phrase "tadviṣayārtha" (having that as its object): by the inclusion of the word *viṣaya* (object), he shows that the locative case in the term *varṇāt* is a locative of object (*viṣayasaptamī*). That which has the region of the letter (*varṇudeśa*) as its object is "tadviṣayārthaḥ. Furthermore, that [operation] is indeed the *kārya* (grammatical effect) itself.
104. *avyayād ap* (Pāṇini 4.2.104). [The examples] beginning with *ṭhameha* constitute an exhaustive enumeration (*parigaṇana*).
And this is understood to apply to both rules [98 and 99] because of the mention of the word *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") in the subsequent sūtra.

This is also understood from the rule regarding the *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (restricted option). The word *amā* signifies "nearness," and its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is established by its inclusion in the list beginning with *svar*.
By the rule *taddhitaś cāsarvavibhaktiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.38), [the suffix *yat* is applied] to words such as *iha*. Thus, one who exists near (*amā*) is an *amātya* (minister).

Regarding the form *upariṣṭāt*: when the suffix *aṇ* is applied to the sense "being above" (*upari bhavati*), the elision of the *ṭi* (the *ri*) occurs by the rule "the elision of the *ṭi* of indeclinables should be stated when a nominal stem ending in *bh* follows" (Vārttika 842). Similarly, *pārastāt* means "being on the other side" (*parato bhavaḥ*).
The word *parataḥ* ends in the suffix *asuc*, according to the rule "optionally after the words *para* and *avara*" (Pāṇini 5.3.29).
In the case of *ṭhārātīyaḥ*, the elision of the *ṭi* portion does not occur; for it has been indicated that the rule *bahiṣaṣṭilopaśca* (Vārttika 378) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).
Regarding the rule *tyabnerdhruve*: when the word *ni-* is used to express something stable (*dhruva*), the suffix *tyap* occurs. [Thus, *niyata*].

Existence at all times is "nitya" (eternal). Regarding the word *niṣṭha*: by the rule *niḥśabde gate* [Pāṇini 4.2.104], the suffix *tyap* is applied when the meaning "gone" (*gata*) follows the word *nis*. Thus we have *niṣṭhaḥ*. The retroflex substitution [of *ṣ* for *s*] occurs by the rule *hrasvātādau taddhite* (8.3.99). In the same way, *ādaviṣṭhaḥ*.
This also applies here.

105. *aiṣamo-hyaḥ-śvaso ’ntarasyām* (Pāṇini 4.2.105). The nominal stems *aiṣamas*, etc., which denote time, are indeclinables (*avyaya*). This rule is stated because, although the suffixes *ṭa*, *ṭyu*, and *ṭyul* would otherwise apply by virtue of the subsequent rule *sāyaṃ-ciram* (4.3.23), this present sūtra supersedes them.
In the word *ṣaustika*, the augment *ai* is applied by the rule *dvārādīnāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.4).

106. *tīrarūpyotarapadādaññau* | (4.2.106) Now, why was it not stated simply as *tīrarūpyotarāt*? For in that way, the sūtra would have been more concise. To this he replies: "From [a compound] ending in *tīra* or *rūpya*, etc. If here...

The term *tīrarūpyānta* would be applicable [to a compound ending in *tīra*], and it would also apply even when preceded by *bahu*—as in *bahutīre jātaḥ* ("born on many banks"), for this is indeed a case where *tīra* is the final member (*anta*). However, if the term "final member" (*uttarapada*) were not mentioned, this over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would not occur; for this [compound *bahutīra*] does not have *tīra* as its final member, since that status only occurs when a compound has been formed.
According to the maxim that "the prior member [is subordinate] to the subsequent member," this is not a compound.

107. *Dik-pūrvapadāt asaṃjñāyāṃ ñaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.107). [Example: *paurvaśālaḥ*. That which exists in the eastern hall (*pūrvasyāṃ śālāyāṃ bhavaḥ*) is *paurvaśālaḥ*. The compound is formed in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) according to the rule *taddhitārtha-* (2.1.51) et cetera; thereafter, the suffix is applied.
Now, for what purpose is the mention of the word *pada*? Why not simply say "not after a word preceded by a direction" (*na dikpūrvāt*)? To this he says:
"The mention of *pada*, etc. For if the mention of *pada* were absent, there would be a reference to the actual form (*svarūpagrahaṇa*).
And in that case, [the prohibition would apply to] *diggajaḥ*, *dignāgaḥ*, *digdāhaḥ*, and so forth.
The base form (*prakṛti*) is understood [as the referent]. However, when the word *pada* (member) is included, a specific direction is grasped; how so?

By the force of including the word *pada*, a *bahuvrīhi* compound with different case-roles (*vyadhikaraṇa*) is understood: "that which has a directional term as its first member. Furthermore, the genitive case in the word *diśaḥ* (of direction) is understood in relation to the denotative word (*vācaka*). Therefore, in this instance...
The word "pūrva" and others, which denote those directions, are taken here.

108. *madrebhyo 'ñ* (Pāṇini 4.2.108). [The example is] *paurvamadraḥ*. As before, there is a compound in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) according to 2.1.51; from that, the suffix *aṇ* is applied.
When [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied by the rule "also from a non-vṛddha [base], when the meaning is plural" (Pāṇini 4.2.125), and when *vṛñ* is applied,
the suffix *kan* is prescribed by the rule "after *madra* and *vṛji*, [the suffix] *kan*" (Pāṇini 4.2.131).
109. [The suffix *cha* is applied after a name of a village in the north that consists of more than two syllables and has its accent on the final syllable. (Pāṇini 4.2.109). Examples:
*ṭhaśaivapuram*, *māhānagaram*. The words *śivapura* and *mahānagara* have their accents on the final syllable by virtue of the accentuation rule for compounds (*samāsasvara*).

Regarding "ṭhmāthuram": the word *mathurā* is oxytone (antodātta) by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). However, in the case of a village in the Middle Country (*madhyadeśa*), the suffix *aṇ* alone is applied. Regarding "ṭhdhvājam": the word *dhvajī* ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* because it belongs to the *pippalyādi* group; for the *pippalyādi* words are included among the *gaurādi* group.

Since it is so read, it is consequently acute on the final syllable by virtue of the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). A village of the North is one that ends in a polysyllabic word; [in this case], the word *dhāna* is acute. This is because, according to the rule *gatikārakopapadāt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtibhāva*) for the word *dhāna*, which ends in the suffix *lyuṭ*.

110. *Prastha-uttarapada-ādya-dika-upadhāt aṇ* (4.2.110). [This rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *añ*, which characterizes villages of the Northern people (*udīcya-grāma*), because villages such as those beginning with "prastha" belong to the Northern people. Examples: *mādrīprasthaḥ*, *māhakīprasthaḥ*.

Thus [it is said]. Here, the base (*prakṛti*) is oxytone by virtue of the accent of the compound (*samāsasvara*). Now, for what purpose is the mention of "the second member" (*uttarapada*)? Could it not simply be stated as "after [a word] ending in *prastha*"? It cannot be so; otherwise, this would also apply here: *ūṣakakarṇīprasthaḥ*. Even in that case, it does not occur because of the mention of "the second member. For it is not the case here...
The word *prastha* is not the final member [of the compound]; rather, it is the word *karṇīprastha*.

This is an exception to the rules for the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha* as prescribed by the rule "vāhīkagrāmebhyaśca" (Pāṇini 4.2.117). Now, for what purpose is the word *vāhīka* recited here, given that...

Is the suffix *aṇ* established simply because [the word] has *k* as its penultimate letter (*kopadha*)? To this, he says: "The word *vāhīka*, etc. If the word *vāhīka* were not recited here [in the list of *kopadha* words], then by virtue of its being subsequent, the suffix *ccha* would apply according to Pāṇini 4.2.114 (*vṛddhāccchaḥ*).
However, for a word with *k* as its penultimate letter, such as *nilīka*, there is scope [for *aṇ*] when the base is not *vṛddha*. Therefore, even though *ccha* is subsequent, [it is superseded].
In order that the suffix *aṇ* should apply by superseding [other rules], the word *vāhīka* is also listed as having a *ka* as its penultimate letter (*kopadha*).

Now, what is the purpose of mentioning *aṇ*? For could it not simply be stated "as prescribed"? No; because of this re-statement, it is understood that only *aṇ* occurs. This is because when an exception (*apavāda*) is being prescribed...

He states that the re-enactment [of the rule] is purposeless with the words "the mention of *ṭha* and *ja*" (*ṭhajagrahaṇam*), and so forth. In this case, since the village is a *vṛddha* [name], when the suffix *aṇ* would apply by the rule "after *prāgdīvyat*, *aṇ*" (4.1.83), the suffix *cha* applies by the rule "after a *vṛddha* [name], *cha*" (4.2.114). Regarding that [suffix *cha*], [the rule] "and from the villages of the Vāhīkas" (4.2.117) [would apply].

Thus, [the suffixes] *ṭhañ* and *ṭhiṭha* exist; since they are subsequent, they would override [the rule for *aṇ*]. If the mention of *aṇ* were not made here, then by virtue of being restated, only *cha* would apply. It is precisely because of the mention of *aṇ* that it occurs—as in "that which exists in *goṣṭha*" (*gauṣṭhalyam*). Therefore, even overriding what overrides [it], only *aṇ* applies as intended.
The inclusion of the suffix *maṅ* is for the sake of the word *syāt*. Here, the mention of the *ka*-upadhā [words] is for the purpose of excluding those that denote a *janapada* (country).
This is already established by the rules *janapadatadavadhyośca* (4.2.124) and *ṭhakopadhādaṇ* (4.2.132).
The word *yakṛlloman* is listed among the *paladyādi* group; its *n*-elision (*nalopa*) is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*), otherwise—
If there were the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *ṭhan* (Pāṇini 6.4.167), then the form *yākṛlloma*— meaning "born in Yakṛlloman"— would not be established.

111. *Kaṇvādibhyo gotre* (Pāṇini 4.2.111). [The commentary states: "In this rule, the mention of *gotra* is not for the purpose of the affix-meaning. This is because of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of *śeṣa*. For if it were for the purpose of the affix-meaning, the heading of *śeṣa* would have been stated. And so says the *Kāśikā*: [text fragment].
And [the author of] the *Padamañjarī* says: "It is not a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*), because it is impossible.

For it is not possible that the names Kaṇva and others, which are themselves the ultimate base forms, could have the meaning of a lineage (*gotra*). Therefore, he asks with the words beginning "In this way" (*evam*) for the purpose of showing that the mention of "lineage" (*gotra*) would indeed be connected [to the rule].

Having shown that the mention of *gotra* is a qualification of the rule for suffixes (*pratyaya-vidhi-viśeṣaṇa*), he demonstrates by means of it that the suffix *aṇ* occurs after those belonging to the *kaṇva* group and others who end in a *gotra* suffix. [This is] "an exception (*apavāda*) to *cha*, because those *kaṇva* group members ending in a *gotra* suffix are *vṛddha*."

"Kāṇvāḥ, Gaukakṣāḥ. From the words *kaṇva* and *gokakṣa*, the suffix *yañ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.105 (*gargādibhyaḥ yañ*) for the sense of a descendant in the *gotra* lineage; from that form ending in *yañ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied. Then, by the rule "the elision of the *apatya* [suffix]" (6.4.151), there is the elision of the *ya*. Regarding "Kāṇvaḥ," the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.2.24 (*sāsya devatā*).

From words ending in *iñ*, such as *dākṣya* and others—derived from *dākṣi* etc. by the rule *ṭhañ-iñaḥ* (4.1.95)—the suffix *aṇ* is applied. Thus, we have *sautaṅgamīyam*. This is formed by adding [the suffix *cha*] according to the rule *vuñ-chaṇ-karap-ca* (4.2.80), meaning "produced by Sutaṅgama."
The suffix *iñ* is applied after the word *sutaṅgama* in the four senses [of the fourth case].

113. *Na dvyacaḥ prācyabharateṣu* (Pāṇini 4.2.113). Examples of Eastern (*prācya*) gotras: *paiṅgīyāḥ*, *prauṣṭhīyāḥ*. Examples of Bharata gotras: *kāśīyāḥ*, *pāśīyāḥ*. [The question] "How? and so forth.
The objection is: "This is not so. The rebuttal is: "Both of these [cases] are included; that is the illustration.

And both of these follow the intended meaning. Now, since the Bharatas are indeed Easterners (*prācya*), they will be included by the very mention of "Easterners"; for what purpose, then, [is there a separate mention]?
Why is there the explicit mention of these [suffixes] by their own names? To this he says: "Except where there is an indicator," and so forth.
Where else? In the rule: "The suffix *iñ* is not applied after a word with many vowels when referring to the Easterners or the Bharatas" (Pāṇini 2.4.66).

114. *vṛddhāc chaḥ* | (Pāṇini 4.2.114) [The suffix] *cha* [is applied] after a word containing a *vṛddhi* vowel in its first syllable. [This applies] to cases such as "born on the bank" (*tīra*). Among these, it sets aside the rule for indeclinables (*avyaya*): that which is near (*ārāt*) is *ārātīya*. The rule [for the suffix *cha*] applies specifically to words ending in *tīra*; thus, that which is born on the bank of the Vāyasa is *vāyasatīrīya*.

In the case of a word ending in *rūpa* as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the suffix *vuñ* characterized by the presence of *y* as an upadhā—according to Pāṇini 4.2.121, *ṭhdhanyayopadhād vuñ*—occurs, overriding [the previous rule]. For example: that which exists in *maṇirūpya* is *māṇirūpyaka*. This overrides the rule for villages of the Northern regions (*udīcyagrāma-vidhi*): that which exists in *vāḍavākṣa* is *vāḍavākṣīya*, and likewise in *sāḍalapura*.

The suffix *bhava* occurs after the word *sāḍalapurī*. Regarding those [suffixes] prescribed after words ending in the *kopadhā* (having *k* as a penultimate letter)—such as *audakīyaḥ*, meaning "born in water" (*audaka*), and *caullukīyaḥ*, meaning "born in Cauluka"—the scope for those rules is limited to cases where the vowel is not *vṛddhi*.
115. *bhavataṣṭhakchasaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.115). [Vārttika:

"The letter *ṭh* is for the purpose of the technical designation *pada*. This is so that the designation *pada* may apply by the rule *siti ca* (1.4.16). And when that [designation] exists, [the substitution of] *jaś* occurs for *jhal* sounds at the end [of a word] in the form *bhavadīyam* by the rule *jhalāṃ jaśo'nte* (8.2.39).
Thus, the substitution of *jaś* occurs. Regarding "bhāvatkaḥ": [the suffix] *ka* is applied by Pāṇini 7.3.51, *iśusuktāntāt kaḥ*.
Regarding "from one that is not *vṛddha*, from *bhavat*": this refers to [the base] ending in the present participle suffix *śatṛ*.

116. *kāśyādibhyaṣṭhañ-ñiṭhau* | (Pāṇini 4.2.16) From the words *kāśi* and *cedi*, when the suffix *vuñ* would otherwise apply by virtue of [the rule] *janapadalakṣaṇe* (4.2.124), and when the suffix *aṇ* would apply by virtue of *sājāteṣṭhiñaśca* (4.2.112), and from the group beginning with *saṃvāha* when the suffix *cha* for the *vṛddha* [lineage] would apply by virtue of *vṛddhācchaḥ* (4.2.114), [the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha* are respectively prescribed].

Regarding the word *hastikarṣu*, when the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule "ṭhañ after [words denoting] a place" (4.2.119), and the suffix *aṇ* is applied to the remaining words by the rule "aṇ from here up to prāgdīvyat" (4.1.83), this [present sūtra] is commenced. But how is there a distinction when the marker *ñ* alone is made an *anubandha* in a reversed position? To this he says: "In the case of a feminine suffix... (*strīpratyaye*).

[The answer is: "There is a distinction. For when the suffix *ñ* is present as an *anubandha* at the end, the suffix *ṅīp* occurs by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15). But if it were present at the beginning, only the suffix *ṭāp* would occur.

[Objection: "The word *vṛddhāt* is understood here [from the previous rule]. [Reply: If that is so, then [the suffix *ṅīp*] should apply to those [names] which are recited as *vṛddha* in this context.
Why does [the suffix] not occur after *ptyaya*? To this he says: "In the rule *hyetvavṛddhāḥ*," and so forth.

If, then, the suffix occurs even after non-*vṛddha* [names] by virtue of the authority of the explicit statement (*vacana*), the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *vṛddhāt* would be purposeless; therefore, he says: "The word *devadatta*," and so forth.

For the designation *vṛddha* applies to the word *devadatta* only when it refers to the eastern region (*prāgdeśa*), and not to a village of the Vāhīkas. In that case, if the term *vṛddhāt* were not carried over [from the previous rule], then the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭh* would apply even from a word denoting a Vāhīka village. Therefore—
The intention is that the designation *vṛddha* becomes meaningful for the purpose of excluding those [other cases]. With the words "How?

and so forth, the author refutes the example provided by the Bhāṣyakāra—namely, *devadatīyā*—in his presentation regarding the technical term *vṛddha*, and then establishes it with the words "In that regard, they explain as follows," and so on.
Regarding the rule "from *kāla* preceded by *āpad* and so forth": those words beginning with *āpad* are called *āpadādi*. That which has these as its prior member (*pūrvapada*) is *āpadādipūrvapada*.
From such a *kāla* [compound], the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭh* occur. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), words such as *ūrdhva* and others are included.

117. And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after [words denoting] villages of the Vāhīkas. (4.2.117) 118. [The suffix *cha* is applied] optionally after [words denoting] the Uśīnaras. (4.2.118) 119. In the sense of a country (*janapada*), the suffix *ṭhañ* [is applied]. (4.2.119)

"ṭhnaiṣādakarṣukaḥ| śāvarajambukaḥ|" [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied after the words *niṣādakarṣū* and *varajambū*. By the rule "ṭhisusuktāntāt kaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.51), the final vowel is replaced by *k*; then, by the rule "ke'ṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.13), the vowel is shortened. Now, one might object: since *ṭhañ* is already the subject under discussion, it is simply being carried over (*anukṛṣyate*) here; so what is the purpose of explicitly mentioning *ṭhañ* again? To this [the author replies]: [The answer follows: ... [The explicit mention of *ṭhañ* serves to indicate that the suffix applies even when the word ends in a consonant, which would otherwise not be covered by the previous rule.]
He says: "Regarding the rule ‘ṭhañ-ñiṭhayoḥ’. For just as *ṭhañ* is the subject under discussion, so too is *ñiṭha*.
In that case, since both are present in the context, it would not be possible to conclude that *ṭhañ* alone continues to apply while the other does not.
Therefore, the mention of *ṭhañ* is made again in order to exclude *ñiṭha*. But surely—

And will not the suffix *ñiṭha* cease to apply simply because it lacks the *svarita* accent? This is true; however, the mention of *ṭhañ* is made specifically to indicate that very absence of the *svarita* accent.
And that absence of the *svarita* accent is explained for the benefit of those of dull intellect.

120. *vṛddhāt prācām* | (4.2.120) [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after a *vṛddha* [patronymic] stem denoting people of the eastern regions. Example: *ṭhāḍhakajambukaḥ*. As before, there is the substitution of *ka* for the final syllable and the shortening of the vowel.

121. *ghaṇvayopadhād vuñ* (Pāṇini 4.2.121). The word *dhanvan* is taken here in its sense [of "desert" or "arid land"], not in its own form (*svarūpa*), because of the governing rule concerning *vṛddha* [words]. For the word *dhanvan* itself is not *vṛddha*. [Examples: born in *pāredhanvan* is *pāredhanvakaḥ*, by the rule *naḥ taddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.144).
By [Pāṇini 6.4.144], there is the elision of the *ṭi* suffix. One born in Airāvata is called an *airāvatataka*.

122. *prasthapuravahāntācca* (4.2.122). [The commentary states: "Only after *vṛddhāt*. If, then, *vṛddhāt* is indeed being carried over, then since the term *vṛddha* is understood from its governing context (*adhikāra*) and there is no mention of its own form (*svarūpa-grahaṇa*), how can there be an application of the rule regarding that which ends in it (*tadanta-vidhi*)? For it is not so.
The status of being "vṛddha" (possessing a vṛddhi vowel in the first syllable) is possible for *prastha* and the like only when they stand alone; what then? It applies to that which ends in them.

Why, then, is there the mention of the suffix (*anta*)? Do not say so; for even though the heading "vṛddha" is in effect, just as the mention of "vṛddha" in the rule *dhanve ca* serves as a qualifier for the place (*deśa*), so too would it be here.
The term "extreme" (anta) was employed for the purpose of excluding that [view].

123. *ropadhetoḥ prācām* (Pāṇini 4.2.123). [The rule continues with] "and from that which ends in *ṭhīka*. How, then, is it known that this is a reference to the long vowel (*dīrgha*) and not the short (*hrasva*)? By virtue of the contextual necessity (*sāmarthya*). For the mention of "of the easterners" (*prācām*) is a qualification of the region.
The term "vṛddha" is understood to carry over from the previous rule; however, there is no word ending in the vowel *i* that is designated as *vṛddha* when referring to a region in the east.

Therefore, it is understood that this refers to the long vowel [in the word *ekacakrā*]. As for the word *ekacakrā*, its designation as *vṛddha* is established by the rule "ṭheṅ prācām" (Pāṇini 1.1.75).
Now, for what purpose is the addition of the long vowel marker *ā* (the *tapara* rule)? Since there is nothing here that needs to be excluded by it, he says:

"The addition of the *tapara* is for the sake of clarity. For if that were not present, then after the form *ropadha* was established and the *guṇa* substitution had been applied, the reference in the rule would have been *ropadhayoḥ* when the case ending (*vibhakti*) was added.

In that very case, there might be doubt: does this refer to a word ending in *ra* as its penultimate letter (*ropadha*), or to one ending in *i* with *ra* as its penultimate letter? However, when the *tapara* (the *t* following the vowel) is employed, no doubt arises.
It was not stated as "from a word ending in *ī* with *ra* as its penultimate letter" (*īropadhāt*) for the sake of variety.

124. *janapadatadavadhyośca* (Pāṇini 4.2.124). Regarding the phrase "of that limit as well" (*tadavadher api*) and so forth: in the rule *janapadatadavadhyośca*, because of its proximity, the word *tat* refers specifically to the *janapada* (country/region). Furthermore, this is not a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

For if it were a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), then even for that which is not a country (*ajanapada*) but serves as a limit (*avadhi*), the suffix *vuñ* would undesirably apply. However, only the suffix *cha* is intended for such a case—for example, Mauñjī is the name of a village that serves as a limit for the Vāhīkas; that which exists there is called *mauñjīya*. Therefore, this compound must indeed be a descriptive determinative compound (*samānādhikaraṇa*). That very [point is established].
"Janapada" means a boundary or limit; "tadavadhi" means having that as its limit. Therefore, only those things whose limits are the countryside (janapada) are included, not a village.
[Question: "For what purpose, then, is the mention of 'having that as its limit'? [Answer: If even that which has it as its limit is indeed the countryside itself.

[The suffix] is applied; however, its inclusion would then be purposeless, for the intended meaning is that one should have stated only "and from a name of a country" (*janapadācca*). [Regarding the phrase] "for the sake of subverting what subverts":
the suffix *cha*, which will be prescribed after a compound whose final member is *garta*, is the sublater, because it is subsequent and because it is specifically ordained.

The mention of "that limit" (tad-avadhi) is for the purpose of setting aside that [suffix]. For, by means of that [mention], in the case of *traigartaka*—derived from *trigarteṣu bhavaḥ*—the suffix *cha* prescribed by the subsequent rule (*gartottarapadāc cha*) is set aside, and only *vuñ* occurs.
125. "Even from a non-vṛddha [base], when it is the domain of the plural.
(4.2.125) This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṭhañ* and *cha*. Specifically, it is an exception to *aṇ* after a non-vṛddha base, and an exception to *cha* after a vṛddha base.
Now, what is the purpose of including the term "domain" (*viṣaya*)? Even without it, the distinction would indeed be obtained. How so?

In this context, because of the coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatva*) with the words "country" (*janapada*) and "its limit" (*tadavadhi*), the word "plural" (*bahuvacana*) is not understood as technical (*pāribhāṣika*); rather, it is etymological (*anvartha*). That is to say, it refers to that country and its limit which express many objects (*arthānām vacanaḥ*). And that which expresses many objects [expresses] those objects...
Does it not follow by implication alone that when many [villages] are mentioned, the scope is plural? To this he says:

"The mention of the word *viṣaya*," and so forth. The mention of *viṣaya* is for the purpose of ensuring that the meaning is restricted exclusively to this (i.e., a group of villages). Why is such exclusive restriction desired? He says: [it is to indicate] a part of a country (*janapada*).

It is formed as follows: *vartanī*, *vartanī*, and *vartanī* become *vartanyaḥ*; this [term] denotes many [instances]. Consequently, if the mention of "object" (*viṣaya*) were not made, then the suffix *vuñ* would apply in the sense of "existing in the paths" (*vartanīṣu bhavaḥ*). However, when the mention of "object" is present, it does not apply, because [the word] does not exist elsewhere.

This is the subject matter. By this it is understood as follows: the plural number (*bahuvacana*) does not deviate [from its primary sense] in the case of that which is not a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one).

However, that which is a *ekaśeṣa* does deviate from the plural number, because even when plurality is intended, there is only one word remaining; furthermore, because [the two meanings] sometimes do not occur together.

"Regarding the inclusion of *api*": the inclusion of *api* is made for the purpose that [the suffix] should also apply after a *vṛddha* [name]. Since the suffix is already established by the preceding rule even after a *vṛddha*, what is the purpose of including *api*?
[The answer is: "By way of the analogy of the curd and Kauṇḍinya. Just as when it is said, "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas, and buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya..."

Just as the general rule for giving curd, which applies to [the gift] for Kauṇḍinya, is set aside by the specific rule for giving buttermilk, so too here, the preceding rule, which generally applies to the domain of the plural number,
is set aside by this [present rule] which applies specifically to the domain of the plural number.
The obstruction [of the rule] is understood through the application of the yoga-rule; therefore, by means of the word "api," it is joined so that [the result] may also occur from a *vṛddhi* vowel.

126. [The suffix *cha* is applied] after [words ending in] *kaccha*, *agni*, *vaktra*, and *garta*, when they are the final members [of a compound]. (4.2.126) Because of the mention of "the final member" (*uttarapada*), this refers to the meaning of the word *kaccha*; for that [word *kaccha*] occurs even by itself to denote a region.
However, since the others cannot denote a region when used alone, [the application of the suffix] follows from their very capacity (*sāmarthya*).
Since the rule of "specifying the final element" (*tadanta-vidhi*) is obtained [by implication], the mention of the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) with respect to the others is redundant.
The expression "ending in *kaccha*, *agni*, *vaktra*, or *garta*" was not stated so that [the suffix] would not apply after a compound beginning with *bahu*.
For when there is a similarity of quality between one region and another region, such as the *kaccha* region, [the suffix denotes] something that is slightly incomplete.

Regarding the term *kaccchadeśa*: when the suffix *bahuc* is applied to the word *kacccha*, the resulting term *bahukacccha* denotes a country (*deśavacana*). However, if the mention of "the end" (*anta*) were included [in the rule], the suffix would apply even after that [compound]. It does not occur because of the mention of "the final member" (*uttarapada*), as in the example *dārukaccchaḥ*, where *kacccha* is the final member.

‘Vṛddha’ (vṛddha) is an example; ‘paippalīkaccchakaḥ’ is an example of ‘avṛddha’ (non-vṛddha). The same applies to other suffixes beginning with ‘aya’. ‘Ekavṛddha’ (ekavṛddha) is an example; another instance of ‘vṛddha’ should be understood.
127. *Dhūmādibhyaśca* (4.2.127).
[This is] an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṭhaṇ* and the others. By the word "and others" (*ādi*), the inclusion of *kaccha* and so forth is intended.
Among those, for place-names beginning with *dhūma* that are not *vṛddha*, this is an exception to the suffix *aṇ*. However, as for those...

From those [villages] that are *vṛddha*, the suffix *cha* is applied; from those villages of the North (*udīcya*), the suffix *aṇ*; and from those villages of the Bāhīkas, the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ṭhiṭha*. Since the suffix *vuñ* is already established for these by the rule "ṭhasya yopadhatvādeva vuñi siddhe" (Pāṇini 4.2.123), which refers to the rule "dhanvayopadhād vuñ" (4.2.121), the suffix *vuñ* applies here by virtue of the word being characterized as a *janapada*.

Regarding the word *siddha*: [the suffix] is applied by the rule beginning with *avṛddhād api* (Pāṇini 4.2.125). Regarding *kūlāt sauvīreṣu*: the suffix *vṛñ* occurs after the word *kūla* when referring to the Sauvīras. If he is a Sauvīra, he is called *kaulaka*; otherwise, he is called *kaula*.

128. *Nagarāt* [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] in the senses of "despising" and "skillfulness. (Pāṇini 4.2.128) Example: *nāgarā brāhmaṇāḥ* ("Brahmins skilled in [or: despisers of] the city"). This is by means of the suffix *aṇ*. But surely, since the word *nagara* is listed among the *kattry-ādi* group in the rule *nagara-māhiṣmatī* (4.2.95), the suffix *ḍhakañ* ought to apply; how then is this so?

He says that "nāgarāḥ" is cited as a counter-example, stating: "in the case of *kattrī* and so forth. The word *nagara* is of two kinds: one denoting a genus (*jāti*) and one denoting a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Between these two, in the list beginning with *kattrī*, the word denoting a proper name is recited because of its association with the word *māhiṣmatī*. In that context:

The word *nāgara* is cited as a counter-example for a word denoting a genus (*jātiśabda*); however, for a word denoting a proper name (*saṃjñāśabda*), one should cite *nāgareyaka* as the counter-example.

129. *araṇyān manuṣye* (Pāṇini 4.2.129). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṇya*, which is introduced by the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) *araṇyāṇ yaḥ* (Vārttika 437). [The rule applies] to these words beginning with *pathin*, *adhyāya*, and *nyāya*. In the case of these words beginning with *pathin*:
The meaning is that the form of this [sūtra], "vuñ bhavati," must be explained. Here is the explanation:
the particle *ca* from the sūtra "dhūmādibhyaśca" (Pāṇini 4.2.127) is carried over [by anuvṛtti];
and since it has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccayārtha*), the suffix *vuñ* occurs after words such as *pathin*.
Regarding the phrase "or in *gomaya*": when *gomaya* is the object to be expressed, the suffix *vuñ* occurs.

This is obtained because that very particle *ca*, which has the sense of an unexpressed conjunction (*anuktasamuccaya*), is carried over (*anuvṛtti*), and because the upcoming mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*) serves as a supplement to both. If, then, [the rule] is to be stated...

Is the inclusion of the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) intended as a supplement to both rules, so that the application would also be optional in the case of *pathyā* and others? This is not a fault; for that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, the rule applies optionally after *gomaya*, but it applies invariably (*nityam*) in the case of *pathyā* and others.

130. *vibhāṣā kuruyugaṃdhārābhyām* (4.2.130). [The commentary states: "This optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) is for the sake of *yugaṃdhara*, not for the word *kuru*. In that case, because *kuru* is included in the list beginning with *kaccha*, the suffix *aṇ* must necessarily apply even without this mention of an optional rule. [Objection: But surely...

Even from the word *yugaṃdhara*, since the suffix *vuñ* would necessarily apply by rule 4.2.125—"after a word ending in *aṇ*, even if it is not a *vṛddha* [stem], when it refers to the plural"—this statement will serve to restrict that necessity. For if *vuñ* were already mandatory, a further rule would be purposeless; therefore, the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) does not apply even for the sake of *yaugaṃdhara*.

Would it not follow [that this is redundant]? This is not so; for this new undertaking cannot be justified by means of the opposite [interpretation]. That *vuñ* which is prescribed by the rule *janapadalakṣaṇo vuñ* (Pāṇini 4.2.124) is optional (*vibhāṣā*), whereas this [present rule] is compulsory (*nitya*). Therefore, for the sake of [the word] *yugandhara*, the mention of the term "optional" (*vibhāṣā*) must be made here.

However, in the case of *manuṣya* and *tatstha*, the suffix *vuñ* occurs invariably after the word *kuru*, due to the force of its inclusion in the *kacchādi* group. Otherwise, since *vuñ* and *aṇ* would already be established by this very option (*vibhāṣā*), the reading in the *kacchādi* list would be purposeless; for it [the *kuru* rule] would have no scope [otherwise].
131. *kan* [is added] after *madra* and *vṛji*.

(4.2.131) This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *vuñ* prescribed for country names. It supersedes what would otherwise have been obtained by rules such as "even from a non-*vṛddha* [stem]" (4.2.125).

Regarding the statement "the suffix *kan* after *madra* and *vṛji*," the word ending in *ñi* is placed last in the compound according to the rule "in a *dvandva*, a *ghi*-stem [comes first]" (2.2.32).
This is for the purpose of indicating that this rule is not obligatory; by means of this, forms such as *dhūmāgnī* and so forth are established.

132. *kopadhādaṇ* (Pāṇini 4.2.132). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *vuñ* prescribed for [names of] regions (*janapada*). It supersedes what was previously applicable. But why is it not desired when [the word] refers to something other than a region, even though it occurs in a region? To this he says: "In another place," and so forth.

Regarding the word "pūrveṇa": it is by means of the rule *prasthotarapadāt* (Pāṇini 4.2.110). Now, what is the purpose of mentioning the suffix *aṇ*? Why not simply say "as prescribed" (*yathāvihita*) for words having *ka* as an upadhā? If it is argued that if "as prescribed" were stated, the suffix *vuñ* would apply as an exception (*apavāda*) to *aṇ*, [the answer is]: no.
For if the suffix *vuñ* were prescribed [in this context], the explicit statement [of the rule] would be purposeless, since *vuñ* would be established even without it.

Therefore, by the force of that very statement, only the suffix *aṇ* applies. Even though it might be sublated by another [suffix], for this very reason, only *aṇ* will occur; for that [suffix *aṇ*] is indeed prescribed by the rule "Before *prāgdīvyat*, [the suffix] *aṇ*" (Pāṇini 4.1.83).
Since [the suffix] *vuñ* would both be prescribed and sublated [by other rules], he says "the mention of *ṭhañ*" and so forth.

Regarding the example "born among the Ikṣvākus": from the word *ikṣvāku*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applicable by Pāṇini 4.2.119 (*or-adeśe ṭhañ*) because it denotes a region; that [suffix] is sublated by *janapada-vuñ* (Pāṇini 4.2.125). If the mention of *aj* were not made here, then—
Due to the repetition [of the rule], only the suffix *vuñ* occurs; due to the mention of *aṇ*, only *aṇ* occurs. Thus, "Aikṣvākaḥ.
In the rule "dāṇḍināyana-hāstināyana... (Pāṇini 6.4.174), the elision of the vowel *u* in the word *ikṣvāku* is prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation).
133. *kacchādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.2.133). [The sūtra states:

"An exception to *vuñ* and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), *ṭhañ* is included. Among those [bases], for those that refer to pluralities of inhabited regions (*janapada*), this is an exception to the application of *vuñ*.

Regarding the rule *sindhu-varṇu-śabdābhyām ordeśe ṭhañ* (Pāṇini 4.2.119), [the author] states: "The word *kaccha* is not the object of the plural number. By this, he demonstrates that since the exception *vuñ*—introduced by the rule *avṛddhād api* (4.2.125) and others—is not applicable, the suffix *aṇ* is established as a general rule.

If this is so, for what purpose is its recitation? He says: "of that," etc. The purpose of the recitation of *kaccha* here is so that the suffix *vuñ* may apply after [the word] *manuṣya* and *sthala* by means of the subsequent rule;
it is not without purpose. [The objection] "the suffix *aṇ* is already established [after *kaccha*] by virtue of having *ka* as an upadhā" refers to the preceding rule.
"The mention of *sthita* is for the sake of what follows," meaning so that the suffix *vuñ* may apply in the subsequent sūtra.
134. *manuṣya-tatsthayor vuñ* (4.2.134).
135. *apadātau sālva-āt* (4.2.135). Regarding the word "Sālva": because it is listed in the *kaccha-* group, the suffix *aṇ* is applied.
136. *goyavāgvośca* (4.2.126). 137. *gartotatrapadāccchaḥ* (4.2.137).
This statement is for the sake of excluding [the application of] *vṛddhi*. However, in the case of *vṛddhi*, it is already established by the rule *vṛddhāccchaḥ* (4.2.114).
"Success! Even when *vṛddhi* [vowel lengthening] would otherwise apply, this [suffix] must occur by virtue of its higher priority.

It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṭhan*, because this rule is initiated even when that [suffix *ṭhan*] has not yet become applicable. And as for the phrase "and that which characterizes a Vāhīka village," etc.: from that which has *garta* as its final member and denotes a Vāhīka [place], [the suffix *cha* is applied].

Since the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭh*, which characterize the villages of the Vāhīkas, are superseded by *cha* due to its higher priority, *cha* alone occurs; its scope is when "garta" is the final member of the compound. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "final member" (*uttarapada*)?
Why not simply say "from that which ends in *garta*"? To this he says: "The mention of 'final member'... and so forth. If...

If it were said "ending in *gartā*," then [the suffix] would also apply after *bahugarta*, because this too ends in *gartā*. However, when there is the mention of the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*), it does not apply, for this does not have *gartā* as its subsequent member; for this [designation of ending in *gartā*] occurs only when there is a compound (*samāsa*).
The preceding word and the subsequent word.

138. *gahādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.2.138). [The commentary states: "This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṭhaṇ* and the others. By the word "and others" (*ādi*), *vuñ* is included. In that regard, from the word *kāmaprastha*, it is an exception to the *vuñ* prescribed by the rule *ṭhprasthapuravahāntācca* (4.2.122).
"But for the remaining [bases], there is the general suffix *aṇ*. 'The qualification depends on possibility (*sambhavāpekṣam*).

That which depends on possibility is 'dependent on possibility. This qualification applies only to those, such as *gaha*, whose occurrence is possible both in their own region and elsewhere. Both of these [points] also...
The qualifiers themselves are remembered by the learned for their meaning. By the phrase "of the middle of the earth," and so forth, he demonstrates that specific qualification.
Regarding the phrase "by connection with the *caraṇa*":
the connection with the meaning (*artha*) of the *caraṇa* is "connection with the *caraṇa*"; by means of that, the word *vāṇ* comes into being. Of what kind is it?

"Nivāsalakṣaṇaḥ": that whose characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is residence (*nivāsa*) is so described. How is it characterized by residence? That which arises from the word *madhya* (middle) when it exists as a place of residence within the earth is indeed characterized by residence. This is what is meant: his residence is in the middle of the earth.

Regarding the word *caraṇasya*: when this meaning is understood, then the suffix *aṇ* occurs, and not otherwise. Therefore, when one intends to express "the foot that has come from the middle of the earth" as simply "the foot," then only the suffix *cha* occurs—[resulting in] *mādhymīya*. But how is it that a specific [meaning] arises even when there is a general statement?
Is it obtained? Because even when there is a general designation, the perception of a specific instance is observed.
Just like the flow of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), that [term], though taught without distinction, settles specifically upon clarified butter and the like.
Therefore, even when there is a general statement, the word "middle" (*madhya*) refers specifically to the center of the earth.

It attains a middle state. Furthermore, regarding the suffix *caraṇa* in the sense of a derivative (*pratyaya*), the suffix *aṇ* occurs only in the sense of "dwelling" (*nivāsa*), and not in all senses such as "born from" (*jāta*) and so forth.
[The rule] "there is elision of the *tas* in *mukha* and *pārśva*" means that there is elision of the *tas* belonging to the words *mukha* and *pārśva*.

The elision occurs by virtue of its connection with a grammatical condition (*pratyaya*). And because of the rule *alo’ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52), that elision applies to the final [letter]. The statement regarding this elision is for the purpose of making known the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the maxim *avyayānāṃ bhamātre ṭilopaḥ* (Vārttika 842); therefore, it does not apply in the case of *ārātīya*.

"mukhatīyam, pārśvatīyam. [In these forms,] by the rule "apādāne cāhīyaruhoḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.45), the suffix *tasi* is applied after the words *mukha* and *pārśva*. Then, by the vārttika "ādyādibhya upasaṃkhyānam" (Vārttika 634), when the *s* of the augment *sa* is elided, the *a* [of the stem] is also elided by the rule "yasyeti ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.148).
Thus, there is elision [of the final vowel].

Regarding the statement "it should be stated that [the suffix] *kuk* applies after the word *deva*," the meaning is that it should be explained that the word *deva* takes the suffix *kuk*. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: "after a word ending in *p* or after a country name (*janapada*), [the suffix] *kuk* [is applied]."
In the rule *kugjanasya parasya* (Vārttika on Pāṇini 6.2.41), the particle *ca* is understood from the preceding context;
it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. Consequently, the suffix will also apply after the word *devadatta*.

[The suffix *cha* is applied] after a word denoting a person of the East that contains a *vṛddhi* vowel in its first syllable, provided it does not end in *ekeka* or have *kh* as its penultimate letter. (4.2.141)

The meaning is that it should be stated simply as "from that which has *ka* as its penultimate letter" (*kopadhāt*).

142. [The suffix *cha* is applied] after words ending in *kanthā*, *palada*, *nagara*, *grāma*, *hṛda*, and *otarapada*. [This is stated] because of the rule "of that which characterizes a village of the Vāhīkas. Regarding the rule "and after [stems ending in] *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭh*": since this is already established by the mention of the final element (*anta*) alone, the mention of the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) is for the sake of variety.
144. *vibhāṣā'manuṣye* (4.2.144).
[The example is] "pārvatīyāni phalāni" ("mountain fruits"). Now, as for the word *amanuṣya*:

The term [amanuṣya] is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) specifically for *rakṣas*, *piśāca*, and so forth; for instance, regarding the rule "A compound ending in *sabhā* preceded by a non-human (*amanuṣya*) [is a tatpuruṣa]" (Pāṇini 2.4.23), one asks: "Why does it not apply here in the case of *kāṣṭhasabhā*?
To this, it is stated: "The word *amanuṣya* is used in its conventional sense (*rūḍhirūpeṇa*) only for *rakṣas*, *piśāca*, and the like."

[If it is argued: "Since [the suffix] occurs [only in those cases]," how then does it apply when *amanuṣya* is stated [as the condition], while fruits (*phala*) and the like are the objects to be denoted? This is not a fault; for there are two meanings of the word *amanuṣya*: the conventional (*rūḍha*) and the etymological (*vyutpanna*). Among these, in the rule *sabhā rājāmanuṣyapūrvā* (Pāṇini 2.4.23), the conventional word is taken; here, however...
But for the other, that which exists as something different from a human being.
145. *Kṛkaṇaparṇād bhāradvāje* (Pāṇini 4.2.145). [The commentary states:

"The word *bhāradvāja* also refers exclusively to a region (*deśa*), not to a lineage (*gotra*)," because the application of the word *kṛkaṇaparṇa* is possible only when *bhāradvāja* denotes a region.
Thus ends the second quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇa-pañjikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who was a teacher of the Bodhisattvas.
[Blank]
Now begins the fourth chapter, third quarter:
1. *yuṣmadasmador anyatarasyāṃ khañ ca* (Pāṇini 4.3.1). [The suffix *cha*] and optionally [the suffix] *khañ* are applied after the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*.

"In this regard, there is a lack of correspondence [between the number of rules and the number of items], because there are two bases (*prakṛti*) whereas there are three suffixes (*pratyaya*). But surely only *KaÑ* and *cha* are prescribed by this [rule],
while the suffix *aṇ* is merely permitted as it was already established by the inclusion of the term "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*).

Does the irregularity (*vaiṣamya*) arise from the treatise itself? In that case, even *cha* is prescribed by that very same [treatise], for the particle *ca* in that rule is indeed an authorizer (*abhyanujñāpaka*). Does that [suffix *cha*] also arise solely from its own treatise, namely from this rule "after a word ending in *vṛddhi*, *cha* [is applied]" (Pāṇini 4.2.114)? Even so...
There is a discrepancy; in no way does the consequence of following the numerical order arise.
2. *tasminnaṇi ca yuṣmākāsmākau* (Pāṇini 4.3.2).

Regarding the word *tasmin*, it is stated that "the suffix *khañ* directly prescribed [by the preceding rule] is indicated. When *tasmin* is mentioned, the cognition arises immediately regarding that very [suffix] alone. The reason for this, moreover, is as follows:

Because it is directly prescribed and because of its immediate proximity, the suffix *khañ* is rightly applied to that [word] alone. But is it not the case that in the previous rule, by the word "and" (*ca*) in "KaÑ ca," the suffix *cha* is drawn forward, and since a part of the expressive [word] is itself the expressed, *cha* is indeed immediately prior to *khañ*? It would be immediately prior if the letter *ca* were the expressive [indicator] of that [suffix], but it is not.

And this [letter *cha*] is not its denoter; for it merely expresses the assistance of another proximate word-meaning. Once the letter *ca* has ceased after expressing that assistance, that assistance is understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*) as belonging specifically to *cha*. Therefore, the letter *ca* is not the denoter of *cha*.
It is not the case that he is such [a person].

Regarding the phrase "the immediate sequence of the two causes produced by that," and so forth: for there are two causes—*kha* and *ṇa*; and there are likewise only two substitutes. Therefore, because they are equal in number, there is a correspondence here according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyena*).

The question is: "It must be so. The answer begins with "By means of a division of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*)," etc., and provides the examples "yauṣmadīyaḥ" and "āsmadīyaḥ. [The objection is: If it were not stated that "in that case, and also before the suffix *aṇ*," then just as these two substitutions (*ima* and *asma*) occur for the suffixes *khañ* and *aṇ* prescribed by the preceding rule, they would likewise occur before the suffix *cha*.
They might exist; however, when that [other] exists, they do not come to be.

3. *tavakamamakāvekavacane* | (4.3.3) Since *yuṣmākā* and *asmākā* would have been obtained by the preceding rule, the substitutes *tavaka* and *mamaka* are prescribed for *tva* and *mama* respectively when they occur in the singular, both as suffixes (*pratyaya*) and as subsequent members of a compound (*uttarapada*), by the rule *ṭhpratyayotarapadayośca* (7.2.98).
Regarding the phrase "of the singular and the subsequent": those two [rules] are so described because the singular number follows them.

Regarding the phrase "but of the two causes," and so forth: just as in the previous rule itself, by means of a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules), there is no correspondence according to order (*yathāsaṃkhyatva*) with respect to the substitutes for the two causes.

So it will not be here either. And the reason for the absence of *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence by order) in that case is precisely the *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) in the preceding sūtra. For by that, once the cause in the previous instance has ceased and *yathāsaṃkhya* has been applied, it therefore continues to apply here as well; those two, having ceased, continue only as *yathāsaṃkhya*.
Because the designations (adhikāra) do not abandon their inherent properties, therefore here too,

due to the prior analysis of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), there is the absence of the number "one" (*asaṃkhyabhāva*). Since the rule for elision (*luk*) is stronger than all rules of application (*vidhi*), once the elision of the singular suffix has been performed...

Since the status of being followed by the singular number of the second person (*yuṣmad*) or the first person (*asmad*) is not possible [in this context], it must be justified through the principle of "the indication of the elision of an affix" (*pratyayalopalakṣaṇa*). To refute even that indication of the elision of an affix—which itself functions as a prohibition—[the author] says: "But surely... and so forth. The rebuttal begins with: "...because of the statement," and so forth.

The intention is that if this were not a case of indicating the elision of a suffix (*pratyayalopa-lakṣaṇa*), then this statement would be purposeless. Now, one might ask: for which [word] is it possible for there to be a state of being followed by the singular number (*ekavacana-paratā*), such that the singular number would serve as a qualifier? To what does this possibility of being followed by the singular number apply?

Regarding the *nimita*, such as *khañ* and so forth: if the *nimita* were qualified by the condition of being followed by a singular number (*ekavacana*), then [the suffixes] would apply only in these cases—*yauṣmākaḥ putraḥ* (your son) and *āsmākaḥ putraḥ* (our son)—for here there is indeed the state of being followed by a singular number, since that [suffix] is appropriate for it; but in this case, they would not apply: *tāvakāḥ*.

"O sons, my sons"—is it not the case that here the condition of being followed by a singular suffix (*ekavacana*) for the cause [of substitution] is impossible? This is not so; in the preceding rule, *yuṣmad* and *asmad* were qualified [by the number of the following word].
For instance, in the rule "after *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when *khañ* and *aṇ* follow," those two [pronouns] are followed by *khañ* and *aṇ*.
For this very reason, the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are specified. Therefore, here too, they follow as being of that same nature;

since the governing rules (*adhikāra*) do not abandon their inherent properties, it is appropriate that the qualification "being in the singular" applies to those two alone. Alternatively, because *tavaka* and *mamaka* are the primary elements as the objects to be enjoined, [the qualification applies to them].

This qualification is appropriate for those two alone. That qualification, applying to those two, occurs precisely by way of the substituends (*sthānin*). If the substituends are followed by a singular suffix, then the substitutes (*ādeśau*) likewise become followed by a singular suffix due to their being *sthānivadbhūta* (behaving like the substituend). Thus, by this method as well—
It is appropriate that the singular number (*ekavacana*) qualifies *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, but not in any way the affixes such as *khañ* which serve as the cause [of the application of the suffixes].
As for the passage beginning with "Or rather" (*athavā*), it was previously explained by relying on the technical (paribhāṣika) sense of the singular number.
Now, however, relying on the present tense, he explains: "That by which a single object is expressed is the singular number.
In this explanation, however, the term "in the singular" (*ekavacane*) is not the locative case singular;
rather, it is the nominative dual ending.
4. *ardhād yat* (Pāṇini 4.3.4). 5. *parāvarādhamottamapūrvācca* (Pāṇini 4.3.5).
"There is no rule for a suffix to apply to that which ends with a nominal stem when that stem is accompanied by a [specific] suffix" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 89).

Thus, because of the prohibition of the *tadanta-vidhi* (the rule applying to forms ending in those words), this [rule] is commenced since [the suffix] would not otherwise be obtained by the preceding rule.

In that context, the words *adhama* and *uttama* denote censure and praise respectively; since the suffix *aṇ* would apply to them by the preceding rule, this [present rule] is commenced. As for the words *para* and *avara*, which are *yāvad-vṛtti* (denoting extent) words, even when preceded by them, only *aṇ* applies. Those two...

But the two words *dik* (direction) and *śabda* (sound) [form their derivatives] by means of the suffix *ṭhañ* and the suffix *yat*, according to the subsequent sūtra. But how, when it is stated "from *para*, *avara*, *adhama*, and *uttama* with the suffix *ṭha*," can the state of being preceded by *para*, *avara*, etc., be understood? To this he says: "the word 'from *ardha*' is understood," and so forth. For here...

The term "from the preceding sūtra" (pūrvasūtrāt) continues [into this rule]. In that context, when it is specified that "the word *ardha* which follows *para*, *avara*, *adhama*, or *uttama*," the fact that it is preceded by *para*, *avara*, and so on, will be understood through the very force (*sāmarthya*) of the word *ardha* itself; so what is the purpose of including the word "preceded" (*pūrva*)? This is addressed by the word "therein" (*tatra*).

Regarding the words *para* and *avara*, which denote direction: [the intention is that] by the subsequent rule, the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *yat* would apply. The meaning is that this would occur if the mention of *pūrva* were not made. [The phrase] "from this," etc., serves precisely to ensure that [the suffixes] apply only when preceded by *para*, *avara*, and so forth.

The purpose of including the word "pūrva" [in the rule] is this: it indicates that by means of it, the operation occurs first, and not later. Therefore, even in the view that these are words denoting direction (*dik-śabda*), only that which is "para," "avara," "pūrva," and so forth, undergoes the operation.

6. *dikpūrvapadāṭ ṭhañ ca* (4.3.6). [The example] "paurvārddhikam" means "born in the eastern half. There is a compound by [the rule] *taddhitārtha-* (2.1.51), etc., and then the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is applied. Now, for what purpose is the mention of the word *pada*?

Would it not simply be said that "the directions beginning with East" [are meant]? To this he says: "The mention of the word *pada*," and so forth. For if the mention of *pada* were absent, it would be a rule concerning the actual form (*svarūpavidhi*), and consequently, it would apply only in cases such as *digarddhe jātaḥ* ("born in the half of the direction"). But when the mention of *pada* is present, any word whatsoever that is related to a direction and stands as a prior member (*pūrvapada*) [is intended].
Its apprehension becomes logically established.

7. *grāmajanapadaikadeśādañṭhañau* (4.3.7). These two [suffixes] are exceptions (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ya* [prescribed by 4.2.106]. They supersede what was obtained by the preceding rule [4.2.106]. For example, *paurvārdhāḥ*.
The compound is formed as before. Now, one might object: "In this case, [the meaning is] 'in the eastern half of the village' (*grāmasya*)."

Is it not the case that because the word *ardha* lacks the capacity [to function] when dependent on *grāma*, a compound is not possible? This is not a fault; for *ardha* functions as a mere principal (*pradhāna*) element. That a compound is formed even when the principal element is dependent—this has been established in the rule *upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ sāmānyaprayoge* (Pāṇini 2.1.56).
It has been made known.

8. *madhyān maḥ* | (4.3.8) The word *madhya*, which is listed among the *gahādi* group in the sense of "the middle of the earth" by the rule *madhyamadhyamañcāṇ caraṇe* (Gaṇasūtra 99), undergoes this grammatical operation [of substituting *ma* for *ya*] precisely from that [list].
But it should be understood that the inclusion here refers to another [type] than that.
9. *sāmpratike* | (4.3.9) He explains the meaning of the word *sāmpratika* by means of synonyms such as "proper" (*nyāyya*) and "suitable" (*yukta*): *sāmpratikam*—proper, suitable.

"Appropriate (*ucita*) means 'proper' (*sāmpra-tika*); 'fitting' (*nyāyya*) means 'right' (*sāmpratika*). For instance, the usage is seen as follows: "One should not act in such a way that what is external has been obtained; this is improper (*asāmprata*). In this context, the prohibition is appropriate (*nyāyya*).

It is understood as "sāmpratikam," meaning "just now" or "immediate. Because [the word] *vinaya* belongs to the class of *ākṛtigaṇa* words, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.4.34: *vinayādibhyaśca*.
10. *dvīpādanusamudraṃ yañ* (4.3.10). Regarding the term *anusamudram*: *samudraṃ samayā* means "alongside the ocean.
This is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to Pāṇini 2.1.15, *aṇuryatsamayā*. It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffixes *aṇ* and *manuṣyavuñ*.
Of the *aṇ* suffix prescribed by "ṭhkacchādibhyaśca" (4.2.133), and of the *vuñ* suffix prescribed by "ṭhmanuṣyatatsthayorvuñ" (4.2.134).

11. *kālāṭ-ṭhañ* (Pāṇini 4.3.11). Regarding the phrase "denoting a specific time": by this, there is a reference to the meaning (*arthagrahaṇa*) of "time" (*kāla*), not to its formal expression (*svarūpa*). For if it were a reference to the formal expression itself, [the rule] *saṃdhivelādi* (4.3.16) would apply.

The prescription of the suffix *aṇ* by means of this rule would be purposeless, since it is already established by the rule "ṭhañ prāgdīvyataḥ aṇ" (Pāṇini 4.1.83). However, in this case, because the mention of the word "artha" (meaning) serves the purpose of superseding the suffix *ṭhañ*, that [suffix] becomes purposeless. Therefore, this is indeed the mention of "artha."

In this world, some words denote time by their primary (mukhya) function— such as "month" or "fortnight"— while others do so by secondary (gauṇī) function: for instance, time is called "kadamba-flower" due to its association with the kadamba flower, and time is called "rice-husk" due to its association with rice husks.
The inclusion here is of both these categories. For this very reason, he says: "in whatever way.

This means by any manner whatsoever. By saying "even by figurative application" (*guṇavṛttyā*), he clarifies the meaning of the phrase "in whatever way. Figurative application (*vṛtti*) is that which is metaphorical (*aupacārikī*).

The meaning is that the function (*vṛtti*) is not primary. By the word "also" (*api*), it is implied that this applies even to the primary function. But is it not improper to include the secondary (*gauṇa*) when the primary (*mukhya*) exists, because of the rule: "In cases of both the secondary and the primary, the application of the grammatical operation is understood to pertain to the primary" (Vārttika 4)? This is not a fault; for the activity of the Teacher (*ācārya*) makes this known: [The text continues: *na vā vṛddhisaṃjñāyāṃ jñāpakaṃ bhavati yadayaṃ vṛddhirādaijadeṅguṇa iti sūtre 'daijadeṅ' iti pratyāhāraṃ karoti.* [Or rather, there is no fault, for the Teacher provides an indicator (*jñāpaka*]: "In the definition of the technical term *vṛddhi*, there is an indicator, namely that he forms the abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*) 'adaijadeṅ' in the sūtra *vṛddhirādaijadeṅ guṇaḥ*."*] *Note: The bracketed portion represents the continuation of the original Sanskrit commentary.*

There is also the inclusion of time in its secondary sense, since in the sūtra *sandhivelādi* (Pāṇini 4.3.16), he qualifies the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) by means of the term "time" (*kāla*) which is under discussion. For it is not logical for time in its primary sense to serve as a qualifier of the lunar mansions, because the status of being primary time is impossible in their case.

12. *śrāddhe śaradaḥ* (4.3.12). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffix] *ṛtvaṇ*. It supersedes what would have been obtained by the rule *sandhivelādi-sūtra* (4.3.16). The original reading seen is: "In the word *śrāddha*, the word *karman* (action/rite) is not understood. However, [some read]: "*śrāddha* is the action."

It is understood [from the *Padamañjarī*]: "The term *śrāddha* does not denote an object (*karman*). A certain specific ritual action (*kriyāviśeṣaḥ*) to be accomplished by means of the procedure prescribed in the scriptures is what is grasped by the mention of *śrāddha*, and not a person possessed of faith (*śraddhāvān*). Why is this so? Because that [person] is not denoted by the suffix (*pratyaya*).
