For, by the very nature of the denotative power of the word "autumnal" (śāradika), it denotes the action alone, not the person.

13. The suffix *vibhāṣā* is applied after the words *roga* and *ātapa*. (Pāṇini 4.3.13) 14. And [the suffix *vibhāṣā*] is applied after the words *niśā* and *pradoṣa*. (Pāṇini 4.3.14) 15. After the word *śvas*, the augment *tuṭ* is also inserted. (Pāṇini 4.3.15)

The root text and the *Padamañjarī* read "tasya ptyaś ceti" (and [the suffix] after that which has the augment *ptu*). [The suffix is] *ṭhañ*. Why is this so? Because it is the primary element due to being what is prescribed for that [base], and because grammatical operations apply to the primary element. And that augment *tuṭ* occurs once the substitution of *ik* has been made.

It should be understood as follows: [An objection is raised: "But surely, because it is taught as being conditioned by the co-occurrence [of the augment], the *tuṭ* augment must first occur, and only afterwards, once the designation of the *aṅga* (base) has been established, should the substitution of *i* take place?
This is not so; for once the substitution of *i* has been made even at the stage of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*), the [augment] should not occur.

Because of the indicator [the letter *k*]. For this reason, in the rule *ṭhvuñ-chaṇ-kaṭhac* (Pāṇini 4.2.80), he employs the indicatory letter *k* for the sake of the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).

This is because, by virtue of the co-occurrence (*sanniyoga*) with the technical designation of a suffix (*pratyayasaṃjñā*), once the accent of the suffix has been applied, the substitution of *ik* occurs subsequently.

The fact that the final syllable is acute (udātta) is established by some specific operation; therefore, it is understood from that specific operation that the substitution of *ik* occurs even before those [suffixes] prescribed in conjunction with others. Consequently, the mentions of the suffix *ṭhak* indicate only the *ik* which has become part of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of the stem (*aṅga*); thus, the augment *tuṭ* also belongs to that very same [stem].

It is understood that [the suffix] will occur; thus, "by these two," and so forth. This word *śvas* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) denoting time. Therefore, when the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *tyap* do not occur, then by the rule *sāyañciram* (Pāṇini 4.3.23), the suffixes *ṭaḷu* and *ṭaḷul* also occur.

16. *Sandhivelādyṛtunakṣatrebhyo’ṇ* | (4.3.16) This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṭhañ*. It supersedes what would have been obtained by *kālāṭṭhañ* (4.3.11). Now, for what purpose is the mention of *aṇ*? One might say that it should be stated exactly as prescribed [by the previous rule]; however, if it were stated in that way alone, then—
One might suspect that [the suffix] is obtained; however, if *ṭhañ* were to apply, the restatement would be purposeless.

Therefore, by the authority of the statement, that which was prescribed [by another rule] does not apply, because it has been superseded by the *ṭhañ* suffix. [If it is asked,] "Will that very [suffix] occur?"—to this he says:

Regarding the phrase "the mention of *aṇ*," etc.: in the list beginning with *saṃdhivelādi*, the word *paurṇamāsī* is recited as having the designation *vṛddha*; likewise, *svāti* is a *nakṣatra* word that is *vṛddha*. In that case, if the mention of *aṇ* were not made, then because they are subsequent [rules], the suffix *ṭhañ* would supersede the suffix *cha*, and by virtue of the repeated statement, *cha* alone would apply.

Therefore, the word *aṇ* is mentioned again so that, even after setting aside that [suffix], the suffix *aṇ* alone from the *vṛddha* base may apply; for example, *taiṣam* and *pauṣam*. From the words *tiṣya* and *puṣya*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.3] *nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ*; then, by [Pāṇini 4.2.4] *lubaviśeṣe*, there is elision (*lup*) of that *aṇ*.

Thus, there is elision (*lup*); then, by this [sūtra], the suffix *aṇ* is applied; and by the rule "the *ya* of *tiṣya* and *puṣya* is elided when referring to lunar mansions" (Vārttika 808), the *ya* is dropped.
Regarding the rule "from *saṃvatsara*, [the suffix *aṇ* occurs] in the sense of fruit and festival": the suffix *aṇ* occurs after the word *saṃvatsara* when it denotes a fruit or a festival.
And [the suffix -ika] is used for the object denoted: *sāṃvatsaram phalam* (the fruit of a year) or *sāṃvatsaram parva* (a yearly festival);
*sāṃvatsarikam* is something else.

17. *prāvṛṣ-eṇyaḥ* (4.3.17). Now, for what purpose is the cerebral [ṇ] prescribed in the suffix? It might be asked: "Why is it taught here, since the substitution of ṇ will occur by the rule *ṭh-ra-ṣābhyām* (8.4.1) alone? This cannot be so; for in this case, [the substitution] would not occur in *prāvṛṣeṇi*.
Because it is at the end of a word.
18. *varṣābhyaṣṭhak* (4.3.18).

Now, for what purpose is the suffix *ṭhak* prescribed? Since it is already established by *kālāṭ ṭhañ* (4.3.11), as the form would be identical in both cases, one might ask why this rule is necessary. It is not so; for when *ṭhak* is used, there is final acute accent (*antodātatva*) by virtue of the accent of the suffix itself.
If, however, the suffix *ṭhañ* were present, the initial syllable would be acute by virtue of the rule "a word beginning with *ṭh* or *ñ* is always acute" (Pāṇini 6.1.197).
19. In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), [the suffix *cha*] is applied after [the word *vasanta*] to form *vāsantī*. (4.3.19) 20. And also after [the word *vasanta*]. (4.3.20) 21.
And also after [the word *hemanta*]. (4.3.21)

"The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows. He will state [later], "In all cases, [the suffix] *aṇ* and the elision of *tar*," and that should apply only to the word *hemanta*, not to *vasanta*. If the single rule "from *hemanta* and *vasanta*" were made, then [the suffix] would also apply to *vasanta*.
It may be so; for that [term] continues to recur subsequently.

22. *sarvatra* and the elision of the suffixal *tal*. (4.3.22) Since the previous rule would have applied the suffix *ṭhañ* in the Vedic language (*chandas*), this is stated for both the Vedic and the common language (*bhāṣā*) when the suffix *ṛtvaṇ* is applicable. By the words "the mention of *sarvatra*" and so forth, [the author] explains the purpose of mentioning *sarvatra*. In the Vedic language...
With the words "And in the spoken language," etc., he demonstrates the purpose of ending the governing rule (*adhikāra*) for *chandas*. [He raises the objection: "But surely," etc.

The intention is that since [the word] is not *svarita*, the term *chandasi* will not carry over [from the previous rule]; therefore, there is no need for the mention of *sarvatra* (everywhere) for the purpose of ending the governing rule for *chandas*. [The author replies: "That very same..."

By the phrase "ityādinā," that which is non-continuation (*ananuvṛtti*) due to the absence of the *svarita* accent is indicated by the expression "that very [non-continuation] applies everywhere. He asks, "For what purpose? and replies with "by the excess of effort" (*prayatnādhikyena*), and so forth. This very [excess of effort] is expressed by the word; for that reason, [the rule] also applies to the preceding sūtra.

The word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) is expressed by the word [in the sūtra] for the purpose that its connection [to the preceding rule] may occur. But why is the inclusion of the term "everywhere" desired as being connected even to the previous sūtra? To this he says:
"For [it is said] *haimantikam*," and so forth. The word *hi* indicates a reason. For the Teacher...

They maintain that the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs in the sense of "belonging to the winter season" (*haimantika*) in common usage (*bhāṣā*). And this [suffix] is established even in common usage provided that the mention of "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) is connected to the preceding rule as well. For if that were the case, the meaning of the preceding rule would be: "also after *hemanta*, everywhere, in the Vedic language (*chandas*)."

"In common usage (*bhāṣā*) as well, the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs. [Question: "But what is the difference between these two (*ṭhak* and *ṭhañ*) compared to *aṇ*? [Answer: The sense is that there is no difference at all. He demonstrates the distinction with the words "for when *aṇ* follows *ṛtu*," and so forth.
Regarding "Haimantī": the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15). "Thus, therefore," and so forth.
Since the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs by the preceding sūtra and this [sūtra] provides *aṇ* along with the elision of the *tal*, there are thus three forms.
23. *sāyaṃ-ciraṃ-prāhṇe-prage-avyayebhyaṣṭaḷuṭaḷulau tuṭ ca* (Pāṇini 4.3.23).

Since the suffix *ṭhañ* would otherwise apply by the rule *kālāṭṭhañ* (4.3.11), the suffixes *ṭaḷu* and *ṭaḷul* are prescribed after the words beginning with *sāyam*, and the augment *tuṭ* is added to them. Furthermore, *ṭaḷu* and *ṭaḷul* serve as exceptions (*apavāda*) to *ṭhañ*.
Since the suffix *ṭhañ* itself subordinates *ccha*, there is no further deliberation regarding *ccha* by these two [suffixes].
Therefore, even after a word ending in *vṛddhi*, only *ṭaḷu* and *ṭaḷul* occur—as in the example "prāktanam. Regarding the phrase "of those two" (*tayośca*) and so forth:
if the augment *tuṭ* were to occur when the two suffixes have not yet been prescribed (*anādiṣṭayoḥ*), then those two suffixes would not possess the form *yu*.

Thus, there would be no designation (*ādeśa*). Therefore, the augment *tuṭ* applies to those two when they have been designated—that is, when the designation has already taken place. And this is understood from the rule *ghakālataneṣu kālanāmnaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.17). For if the *tuṭ* were prescribed for [the words] before they had been designated, the word *tana* [would not be possible].
[This] is established. Now, for what purpose is the *ṭi*-marker applied to the augment (*tuṭ*)?

Why not simply recognize that the *ṭi*-marker [of the suffix] also applies to the augment because it is included by the mention of that [suffix], rather than applying the *ṭi*-marker to the augment itself? This is not correct; for it is logical that the properties of a suffix should apply to an augment.
Because they are subordinate to the suffix (*pratyaya-bhaktatvāt*), the properties of the base (*āgaya-dharma*) do not apply to the suffix.

Therefore, for the sake of the grammatical operation (*kārya*) dependent on the *ṭi* marker, the status of being *ṭit* is attributed to the suffixes as well. This refers to the root *syati* in the sense of "ending" (*antakarmaṇaḥ*), specifically the root *ṣo* in the sense of "ending" (*antakarmaṇi*, DhP 1147). [The examples are] *prāhṇe* and *prage*.

"Thus, [the word] ending in -e is [an irregularity]," meaning it is an irregularly formed (nipātita) form. Now, one might object: since the non-elision (aluk) of the locative case is already established by the rule "ghakālataneṣu kālanāmnaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.17), this irregular formation is purposeless. To this we reply: the irregular formation is for the sake of those cases where the locative sense is not present.

*grāhaṇaḥ saḍho 'sya prāhṇetanaḥ*, *pragaḥ soḍho 'sya pragetanaḥ*. For here, since the suffix is prescribed after a word in the nominative case by the rule *tad asya soḍham* (Pāṇini 4.3.52), there is no sense of the locative case; and because that [locative sense] is absent, the locative case [ending] also [does not apply].
It does not exist at all.

Regarding the statement "it should be stated that *tna* follows *cirapara*, *parāri*, and *parāri*," the meaning is that it must be explained. However, the explanation has already been provided under the rule *taddhitāḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.76). It should be understood in the same way for subsequent cases as well.

Because the word *cira* is included in the sūtra, the suffixes *ṭyaP* and *luc* also occur [after it]. The connection is with the phrase "it should be stated" (*vaktavya*). The meaning of the word *vaktavya* is the same as that [of the preceding rule]. However, according to the commentary, here too [the suffix] *thāl* occurs after *pratna*, *pūrva*, and *viśva* in the Vedic language (*chandas*), as in: "ṭhpragasya ccchandasi galopaśca" (Pāṇini 5.3.109); the word *vaktavya* has that very same meaning. By virtue of the explanation, here too [the suffix] *thāl* occurs after *pratna*, *pūrva*, and *viśva* in the Vedic language.

(5.3.111) This must be done by relying on the inclusion of the particle *iti*. [The meaning of] "it should be stated that [the suffix applies] after a word ending in *anta*" is that this form *ārta*—meaning that the suffix *ḍāḍimac* occurs after the word *anta*—is to be explained.
However, the explanation has already been provided. Regarding the suffix *ḍimac*, the purpose of its being marked with the *ḍi*-indicator is as follows:

The word "paścāt" is mentioned for the purpose of eliding the *ṭi* suffix. Now, one might object: is this not already established by the rule "the elision of the *ṭi* of indeclinables should be stated when a *bha*-affix follows" (Vārttika 842)? It is not so established; because that rule is not universally applicable (*anityatva*). Just as the elision does not occur in the case of *ārātīya*, so too it does not occur here.
Someone might have the misconception that [the suffix] belongs to something else; therefore, the addition of the marker *ḍit* is made in order to dispel that.
24. *vibhāṣā pūrvāhṇāparāhṇābhyām* (Pāṇini 4.3.24).

[The Kāśikā states: *pūrvāhṇetanaḥ*. The compound *pūrvāhṇa* is a part-whole compound (*ekadeśisamāsa*) according to the rule *pūrvāparādharottarāt* (2.2.1), meaning "the former part of the day. [The suffix] *ṭac* is applied by the rule *rājahaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac*.

By [Pāṇini 5.4.91], the suffix *ṭac* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*); by [Pāṇini 5.4.88], the substitution of *ahna-* for *ahan-* occurs; and by [Pāṇini 8.4.7], the change to *ṇ* (ṇatva) takes place. When the suffix is applied after a word ending in *-apatya*, then the form should be *pūrvāhṇatana-*, because there is no occurrence of the locative case [in that context].
But the seventh case [ending] does not occur, because the secondary derivative (taddhita) is produced from that which is capable of governing the first case.
Regarding the rule *tatra jātaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.25):

"The suffixes beginning with *ṭhaṇ* and those beginning with *gha," etc. By the first word "etc. (*ādi*), the general suffixes such as *aṇ* and others are included; by the second, the suffixes beginning with *gha*, which are prescribed under the heading of the "remainder" (*śeṣādhikāra*).

"Sraughnaḥ" and "māthuraḥ": [these are formed] by *aṇ* according to *prāgdīvyato’ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.1.83). "ĀṬtsaḥ" and "āṬdapānaḥ": [these are formed] by *añ* according to *utsādibhyo’ñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.86). "Rāṣṭriyaḥ" and "avārapārīṇaḥ": [these are formed] by *gha* and *kha* respectively according to *rāṣṭrāvārapārādghakhau* (Pāṇini 4.2.93). "Śākalikaḥ" and "mālavikaḥ": [these are formed by *ṭhañ*].

From the rule *ṭhvāhīkagrāmebhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.2.117), the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭh* are applied; thus we have *kāttreyakaḥ* and *āṬmbheyakaḥ*. This is because of the rule *ṭhkattryādibhyo ḍhakañ* (Pāṇini 4.2.95).
26. *prāvṛṣaṣṭhaḥ* (4.3.26). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffix] *eṇya*; it applies to that which was obtained by the rule *prāvṛṣa eṇyaḥ* (4.3.17).

27. *saṃjñāyāṃ śarado vuñ* (Pāṇini 4.3.27). [The commentary states: "If the name is understood through the whole. By this, he shows that the name functions as a condition for the whole. The meaning is: if the name is understood by means of the combination of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*).

If this is so, then the use of the word *darbha* in the expression "autumnal *darbhas*" (*śāradakā darbhāḥ*) would not be possible, because [the meaning] has already been expressed by the suffix? This is not a fault; for just as the word *śāradaka* is the name of a specific type of *darbha*, so too is it the name of a specific type of *mudga*. In that case, when [the specific type] is absent...

Since the word *darbha* is applicable to multiple meanings, there would be a doubt as to whose name [is intended]—that is, what meaning is intended by the word *śāradaka*. Therefore, the word *darbha* is employed to eliminate this doubt. Regarding the phrase "the section on technical names" (*saṃjñādhikāra*) and so forth, some say:
By this statement, it is meant that some do not turn back from falsehood.

28. From *pūrvāhṇa*, *aparāhṇa*, *ārdrā*, *mūla*, *pradoṣa*, and *avaskara*, the suffix *ṭhañ* [is applied] to form *pūrvāhṇikaḥ* and *aparāhṇikaḥ*. As before, the formation of the *ekadeśi-samāsa* and other operations must be applied according to the rule: "The suffix *ṭhañ* is optional after *pūrvāhṇa* and *aparāhṇa*" (Pāṇini 4.3.24). In that regard:

And there is the rule for *ṭaḷu* and *ṭaḷul*: "ṭhārdrakaḥ, mūlakaḥ. The meaning of the suffix [ṭhak] arrived at by the rule "ṭhnakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.2.3) is subsequently elided by the rule "lubaviśeṣe" (4.2.4), after which *vun* is applied.
[The example] "niśāpradoṣābhyām" refers to the prescription of the suffix *ṭhañ*. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), it is meant that only *ṭhañ* and the others [are intended].
The forms *ṭaḷu*, *ṭaḷula*, and so forth are included.
29. *pathaḥ* and *pantha* [are substitutes for *pathin*] (4.3.29).

30. Optionally [the substitution occurs] for *amāvāsyā* (4.3.30). [The rule] "of that which has undergone modification in one part" (*ekadeśavikṛtasya*), etc., applies here. Regarding the rule *amāvāsyad anyatarasyām* (3.1.122): [it means that the word *amāvāsya*, derived from *amāvāsyā*, is optionally formed].

Only the substitution of *ṇyat* and the absence of *vṛddhi* are prescribed as a *nipātana*. Since the absence of *vṛddhi* constitutes a modification (*vikāra*) by virtue of becoming a single substitute for *vṛddhi*, the term "partially opened" (*ekadeśavivṛta*) is applicable to the word *amāvāsyā*. However, for those who recite the *sandhivelādi* group with a short vowel in the penultimate syllable, there is no inclusion of a form with a long vowel in the penultimate syllable.
[The word] attains [the long vowel], for a modification does not take on the form of its original; therefore, the reading with the long vowel alone is appropriate.
31. *a ca* | (4.3.31) Now, for what purpose is this word-splitting (*yogavibhāga*)? One might ask: why not simply say "na ṭhamāvāsyā a ca vā"?
In that case, the particle *ca* would serve to carry forward the suffix *vun*.
And the word *vā* is for the purpose of providing an option for both [suffixes]; by that, even when those two are excluded, the suffix *aṇ* will also occur.

This is true; however, if there were a single rule (*ekayoga*), someone might mistakenly think that only the suffix *kan*—as in "sindhvapakarābhyāṃ kan" (Pāṇini 4.3.32)—is optional. Therefore, to prevent that misconception, [the word *vā* is used].
For when there is a separation [of rules] through the division of the yoga, it is understood that the *kan* suffix is optionally [applied].
32. *kan* [is added] after *sindhu* and *apakara*.
(Pāṇini 4.3.32) The connection is that this is a rule prescribing the suffix *kan* when the general suffix *aṇ* would otherwise have applied after the word *apakara*.

33. *aṇañau ca* (Pāṇini 4.3.33). The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of establishing a correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*). If the single rule *sindhvapakarābhyāṃ ca kan-aṇ-ñaḥ* were made, then, due to the inequality [in number], three suffixes would apply to each individual base.
They may be.
*Śraviṣṭhā*, *Phalgunī*, *Anurādhā*, *Svāti*, *Tiṣya*, *Punarvasu*, *Hasta*, *Viśākhā*, *Āṣāḍhā*, and *Bahulā* undergo elision [of the suffix].

(4.3.34) Since the suffix would have applied to these names of lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) by virtue of the rule "optionally after [names of] lunar mansions" (*nakṣatrebhyo bahulam*), the present sūtra declares that their elision (*luk*) occurs. But is it not already established by the rule "*nakṣatrebhyo bahulam*"?

"Will the elision (*luk*) occur by this very rule [4.3.37]?"—this is true; however, this [present rule] is an elaboration (*prapañca*) of that very same principle. It should be understood that the two subsequent rules are also elaborations of that same principle. Furthermore, regarding these [names] beginning with *śraviṣṭhā*, the suffix *aṇ*—which would otherwise be introduced by the rule "A time joined with a lunar mansion" (4.2.3)—is elided by the rule "The suffix *aṇ* is elided when there is no distinction" (*lub aviśeṣe*).

(4.2.4) Thus, it should be understood that [the suffixes] ending in *lup* are intended; for even in the case of a feminine suffix, elision (*luk*) occurs by the rule "elision of a feminine suffix when a *taddhita* suffix is elided" (1.2.49).
The meaning is that this is an explanatory supplement (*upasaṃkhyāna*) concerning those [words] which end in feminine suffixes.
And that will be explained later on. In the case of *citrā*, after the elision (*luk*) of the feminine suffix *ṭāp* has been effected, *ṭāp* is applied again;
this is according to the rule "due to being listed in the *gaura*-group, there is *ṅīṣ*," as in the examples *revatī* and *rohiṇī*.

"Regarding [the suffixes] *ṭha* and *pha*, it should be stated that *ṭā* and *na* are substituted for them after the words *phalgunī* and *aṣāḍhā*. The word "in the feminine" (*striyām*) is understood here. However, because of the specific force of their prescription, elision (*luk*) does not occur. The *ṭ* in *ṭā* is for the sake of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*;
the *n* in *ana* is for the sake of making the first syllable udātta. The word "it should be stated" (*vaktavya*) refers to what is to be explained. The explanation, however, is as follows:

And it has already been established: "The suffix *chaṇ* should also be stated after the words *śraviṣṭhā* and *āṣāḍhā*. In this context, the mention of "in the feminine" (*striyām*) is not appropriate.
The letter *ṇ* is for the purpose of [triggering] vṛddhi; the word "should be stated" (*vaktavya*) has that very same meaning. This is also the explanation.
And it shall be done; it is as good as already done.
35. *Sthānāntagośālakharaśālācca* (Pāṇini 4.3.35).
Because *gośālā* and *kharaśālā* are listed with short final vowels, they are understood here as being neuter.
Their neuter gender, however, is established by the rule *vibhāṣā senāsurā* (2.4.25), and so forth. Even though...

Although there is the mention of the two neuter genders, nevertheless, by the principle that "when a nominal stem (*pratipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included," the elision (*luk*) occurs even after the two feminine stems.
In the example as well, there is the elision of the default *aṇ* suffix.
36. *vatsaśālābhijidaśvayukśatabhiṣajaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.36).

The word *vatsaśāla* is understood here as being in the neuter gender. Why is this so? Because of the pervasion [of the rule]; for if the neuter gender were not taken [as intended], [the rule would fail to apply].

Even from the feminine form, elision (*luk*) is not established by the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim that a word qualified by gender includes its gender-variant); however, it is not [precluded] when there is the inclusion of the feminine form from the neuter.
"This is an elaboration of the mention of *bahulam*. Although the words *vatsa* and *śāla* denote constellations, [they are used here in their primary sense].

Although it does not occur [in that specific case], nevertheless, by virtue of the frequent use of the word "bahula" (diversity), the elision will occur even from that [suffix]; such is the intended meaning.

37. *Bahu-lam* after the names of lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). (Pāṇini 4.3.37) In examples such as *ṛohiṇaḥ*, there is optionally (*pakṣe*) elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṅaṇ* [denoting "born under"] after the names of lunar mansions. Thus we have *mṛgaśirāḥ*.
[The lengthening of the vowel occurs] by the rule *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ* (6.4.14). [Similarly] *mārgaśīrṣaḥ*. And [the suffix is also elided] when followed by *ya*.

In the rule *taddhite* (6.1.61), because the letter *ca* has the sense of an "inclusion of what is not explicitly stated" (*anuktasamuccayārtha*), the substitution of *śīrṣa* for *śiras* occurs. Now, what is the purpose of including the term *bahulam*? Will the particle *vā* not simply continue to apply from the preceding sūtra? This is the purpose: so that in some cases something else entirely may occur, as follows—
Thus, by that [rule], the suffixes *ṭā* and *ṅīp* are established after the words *phalgunī* and *aṣāḍhā*;
and by the rule "after *śraviṣṭhā* and *aṣāḍhā*, the suffix *chaṇ*," [the suffix *chaṇ* is established].

38. *kṛtalabdhakrītakuśalāḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.38). Now, as for the phrase "But surely... and so forth: the meaning of the word *jāta* is a thing that has come into existence (*janman*). Since even that which is *kṛta* (made) possesses existence, therefore whatever is made there is also considered *jāta* (born/come into being) in that context. And [the same applies to] what is *krīta* (bought).
And so forth. "Obtained" (*prāpta*) means acquired. Even that which is purchased is indeed obtained;
therefore, what is purchased is also considered obtained. This is because there is no difference in the meaning of the word.
The meaning of the word *jāta* ("born") is the state of being an agent experienced at the time of its own birth. This refers specifically to the word *jāta*.
The meaning of the word *krta* (made) is the operation of another person characterized by a specific [purpose] toward the accomplishment of one's own birth.

The meaning of the word *labdha* (obtained) is the general state of attainment (*prāptisāmānya*). The meaning of the word *krīta* (bought) is a specific attainment, that attainment of which has its primary cause [in exchange]. Furthermore, there is no identity of referent between the general and the specific.

It is logical that the word and its meaning are distinct, lest there be the undesirable consequence of synonymy. [The phrase] "by the mere thing" (*vastumātreṇa*) means that when there is a mere thing serving as the substratum for both what is purchased and what is obtained, because that [thing] has an undifferentiated form, it becomes both purchased and obtained. The inclusion of the term "mere" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of excluding the word and its meaning. For this very reason, he says:
"But the meaning of the words *krīta* and *labdha* is indeed distinct. For it is not by the same form that the object is signified by the word *krīta* as it is by the word *labdha*.
Thus, while the words *jāta* and *kṛta* are non-different in terms of the actual entity (*vastu*), they are [different] by way of their respective words and meanings.
It is indeed a difference in meaning; for that object is signified by the word "born" (jāta) in one form, and by the word "made" (kṛta) in another.
39. *prāyabhavaḥ* | (4.3.39) "The mention of *prāyabhava* is purposeless.
This is said to be purposeless because there is no other meaning [for it] than variety (*vaicitrya*). However, by way of variety—
It is indeed meaningful. Why, then, is it meaningful? Because "it has already been accomplished by [the rule] *tatra bhavaḥ*.
The sense is that what was to be established by the rule *prāyobhavaḥ* has already been established by the rule *tatra bhavaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.53). For one who generally resides in a kingdom—

In that case, he certainly exists there; and since his inclusion within that state of existence is already accomplished by the rule *tatra bhavaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.53), what is the purpose of including the term *prāyabhava* ("mostly existing there")?
With the words "an eternal existence" (*anityabhava*) and so forth, the opponent anticipates the following objection: "This might be the case—"

[One might object: "Is it not the case that [the intermediate state] is an impermanent existence (*anityabhava*), whereas [the state of] birth (*prāyabhava*) is a permanent existence (*nityabhava*), and therefore, since it is not included therein by virtue of being a 'being there' (*tatra bhavaḥ*), [the definition] is not established? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "It is equivalent to that which has abandoned doubt. That by which doubt has been released—that is, abandoned—is "that which has abandoned doubt" (*muktasaṃśaya*).

That which is determined as "this being [bhava] there is proper" is equivalent to that. For instance, Devadatta, who exists in Srughna, is called *sraughna*; yet he does not exist in Srughna at all times, for he inevitably departs for the northern regions and so forth at some point, and yet the suffix denoting existence there (*tatra-bhava*) is still applied.

[The suffix *cha*] occurs. And if [the meaning] "that which exists there" (*tatra bhavaḥ*) were [always] "existence therein" (*nityabhava*), then in the case of *jihvāmūlīya*—meaning "the phoneme existing at the root of the tongue"—the suffix *cha* prescribed by the rule *jihvāmūlāṅguleścchaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.62), which falls under the governing heading *tatra bhavaḥ* (4.3.53), would not apply; for a phoneme is not...

It always occurs at the root of the tongue. Therefore, since *prāyabhava* is included within *kakakakakakakakakaka*, it does not exceed [the scope of] *tatra-bhava*; thus, the mention of *prāyabhava* is redundant.

40. *upajānu*, *upakarṇa*, *upanīvi* (Pāṇini 2.1.40). [The forms] *jānoḥ samīpam* (near the knee), *karṇasya samīpam* (near the ear), and *nāvyāḥ samīpam* (near the hip)—these are *avyayībhāva* compounds by virtue of the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti-* (Pāṇini 2.1.6). [The form] *upajānukaḥ*—[as stated in] the *Kāśikā*.
In the word *upajānukaḥ*, [the suffix] *ka* is applied according to Pāṇini 7.3.51: *ṭhisusuktantāt kaḥ*.
41. *sambhūte* (Pāṇini 4.3.41).

[The rule] beginning with *ṭha-vaklṛptiḥ*. *Avaklṛptiḥ* means possibility (*sambhāvanā*). It is the non-excess of measure (*pramāṇānatirekaḥ*), that is, the state where the measure of the contained (*ādheya*) does not exceed the measure of the container (*ādhāra*), given which—

The flowing [element] enters into that which is to be filled, the receptacle; thus it is said, "it comes into being in Srughna. That which is conceived as being in Srughna does not exceed the dimensions of Srughna; because of its entry into that, an object such as an army and so forth is described in this way.
42. *kośāḍḍhañ* (Pāṇini 4.3.42).
[The example given is] "kauśeyaṃ vastram" ("silk cloth"). Now, it might be argued that silk (*kauśeya*) cannot belong to the cloth, but rather to the silkworm;
therefore, the suffix should apply only to the silkworm and not to the cloth. Furthermore—

Since no specific distinction is stated, it would follow that the suffix could also apply to the sheath belonging to a sword; therefore, he says: "This is a conventional usage," and so forth. For a word based on convention (*rūḍhi*) is derived in whatever way possible; in such cases, the meaning of the individual parts need not necessarily be taken into account.

In some cases, because the meaning of the individual parts is impossible; for instance, the word *tailapāyikā* is derived as "one who drinks oil," yet in that case the meaning of the individual parts need not necessarily be expected, because in some instances the meaning of the parts is impossible. For instance, [the word] "one who drinks oil" (*tailaṃ pibati*)...

The word *tailapāyikā* is etymologically derived [as "one who drinks oil"], yet it refers in certain cases to a particular kind of living being even when devoid of the act of drinking oil. Therefore, although it does not apply to a worm, what fault is there in its application to a sword emerging from its scabbard, such that a suffix would not be desired there? It is simply that the sword is not denoted [by that specific word].

[The opponent argues: "He indeed attains [the state of being a garment], for he is produced therein. [The proponent replies: In that case, when a cognition arises from another sheath as well, the designation "garment" would apply to the worm too, for he too is produced therein. Now, if you say that even in that case the designation "garment" applies to the cloth by virtue of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and not to the worm, then [the same logic applies] to the other case as well.

Why is there a designation for the cloth arising from the *kośa* (cocoon), but not for the sword? He thinks as follows: although the suffix *ḍhañ* is prescribed after *kośa* in the sense of "arising from" (*sambhūta*), nevertheless, from the word *kauśeya*, the meaning of "arising from" is not understood; rather, the meaning is "modification" (*vikāra*), due to the force of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). [Thus,] *kauśeya*.
The modification (*vikāra*) of a sheath (*kośa*) made of cloth means "cloth. And so it has been stated by the author of the *Vārttika*:

"The suffix *ḍhañ* is applied after *kośa* in the sense of a modification; [this is] because the literal meaning is untenable" (*sambhūtārthānupapattiḥ*; Vārttika on Pāṇini 4.3.42). And as for the modification...

From the word *kauśeya*, the cocoon of a silkworm is understood, not the sheath of a sword; this is due to conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). Therefore, the suffix *yañ* is applied only to that word whose modification is understood from the word *kośa*, and not to any other.

43. *kālāt sādhupupyatpacyamāneṣu* (Pāṇini 4.3.43). The term *kālāt* is reiterated [from the previous rule] in order to qualify the subsequent bases (*prakṛti*). For if it were taken as referring to its own form (*svarūpa*), the subsequent bases could not be qualified; this is because a word's own form is unique and non-common.

Therefore, this is indeed for the purpose of grasping the meaning. Consequently, he says "from those expressing specific times" and so forth, so that the suffix is understood to be applied after words denoting particular times. For example, *hemanaḥ* ("winterly") is derived by [the rule] *sarvatrāṇ ca talopaśca* (Pāṇini 4.3.22). In cases such as *śaiśiraḥ* ("pertaining to the cold season"), [the suffix is applied] by the rule *sandhivelādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 4.3.16).
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the word *ṛtu*.
44. *upte ca* (Pāṇini 4.3.44). [The author] says:

"The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows. This is so that the suffix *vuñ* may apply only after the word *upta* in subsequent rules, and not after words such as *sādhu* and others.

45. *āśvayujyā vuñ* (Pāṇini 4.3.45). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṭhañ*. It supersedes what would otherwise be obtained by *kālāṭ ṭhañ* (4.3.11). But surely *ṭhañ* is prescribed after words denoting time; and since the word *āśvayujī* does not denote time, how could *ṭhañ* apply here?
Having raised this doubt, he says "joined with the two Aśvinīs," etc., in order to demonstrate that the word *āśvayujī* denotes a time.

46. [The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied] optionally after the words *grīṣma* and *vasanta*. (4.3.46) 47. [The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied] after the word *deya* when it refers to a season (*ṛtu*). (4.3.47) 48. [The suffix] *vuñ* is applied after the words *kalāpī*, *aśvattha*, and *yavabusa*. (4.3.48)

But how do words such as *kalāpa* and others denote time, given that their usage is well-established in reference to peacocks and the like? To this he says: "Words such as *kāla*, *apyā*, etc. He clarifies this very point with the passage beginning "at which time," and so on. Here, the word *aśvattha* [is used].

The word is conventionally established as referring to a specific tree; therefore, since it is connected with all time, no specific time is indicated by means of that [tree]. Consequently, he says—"because there are no horse-ears"—in order to show that the word *aśvattha* (horse-ear) applies to the time associated with the fruiting of the *aśvattha* tree.
Regarding the passage beginning with "phalanti": although the word *aśvattha* refers to the tree, it nevertheless also refers to its fruit.
49. *grīṣmāvarasamād vuñ* (Pāṇini 4.3.49).

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṭhaṇ* and *ṭhañ*. It is an exception to *ṛtvaṇ* after the word *grīṣma*, and to *kālāṭ ṭhañ* after the word *avarasama*. [The compound] *avarasamā* means "a later year" (*avarā cāsau samā ca*).
50. After *saṃvatsara* and *āgrahāyaṇī*, there is also *ṭhañ*.

(4.3.50) This statement is made because [the suffix] *ṭhañ* would otherwise be required by the rule "after a word denoting time, *ṭhañ*" (4.3.11). Therefore, it need not have been stated that *ṭhañ* is used;
for since *vuñ* is optionally prescribed, even without the mention of *ṭhañ*, *ṭhañ* itself will apply in its alternative case as required by the general rule.

This is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "the mention of *ṭhañ*," and so forth: if the mention of *ṭhañ* were not made here, then in rules such as *sandhivelā* (Pāṇini 4.3.16), because of the reading *saṃvatsarāt phalaparvaṇoḥ* (Gaṇasūtra 104), the suffix *aṇ* would apply to words beginning with *sandhivelā*; and since *aṇ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṭhañ*, [the desired form] would not occur in the sense of time.
When the suffix *vuñ* is intended to be applied, it would otherwise be replaced by *aṇ*; however, because of the specific mention of *ṭhañ*, even *aṇ* is superseded and *ṭhañ* alone occurs.
51. *vyāharati mṛgaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.51). [The examples are:
*naiśikaḥ*, *naiśaḥ*; *prādoṣikaḥ*, *prādoṣaḥ*. [In these cases,] the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied by [the rule] *niśāpradoṣābhyām* (4.3.14).
In the alternative view where that [suffix] is not applied, only the suffix *ṛtvaṇ* occurs.
52. *tadasya soḍham* (Pāṇini 4.3.52). The term *kālāt* ("from time") is understood [as a governing word] from the previous rule; however, time itself is not conquered.
Therefore, in this context, "study" (*adhyayana*), which is invariably associated with time, is used in a figurative sense (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*).
It is understood that [the word "night"] is denoted by such expressions as "niśā" (night) and so forth. For this very reason, it is said: "Study associated with night is called 'niśā'."
53. *tatra bhavaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.53). 54. *digādibhyo yat* (Pāṇini 4.3.54).

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffixes] *ṭhañ* and *cha*. Regarding the *yat* [suffix] applied to words such as *dik* (direction), or to words like *vāpī* (pond) which are "vṛddha" (belonging to the Vṛddha class): [it is used to denote that which exists there].
Consequently, there is an exception for *śas*, whereas for the remaining [words], the suffix *aṇ* applies when the meaning is "belonging to that" (*prāgdīvyatīya*).

Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of *mukha* and *jaghana* among the *digādi* group, since by the subsequent rule (4.3.55), which deals with parts of the body, the desired forms will be produced from those two anyway? To this, he says:

Regarding the phrase "of the mouth and the hips": for those words "mouth" and "hips" which denote parts of an army do not denote parts of a body. Indeed, a body has the nature of limbs such as hands and feet, but an army is not of such a nature; rather, it consists of a collection of chariots and so forth.

Regarding the rule "udakāt saṃjñāyām" (Pāṇini 4.1.109): when a name is to be understood from the word *udaka*, the suffix [ṭāp] occurs—thus *udakyā* refers to a woman who is menstruating (*rajasvalā*). And here, neither the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) nor the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) exists [in that sense]. That non-existence of those two meanings is indicated by the mention of the word "name" (*saṃjñā*).
It is understood that in another case of a name—such as "a fish in water"—the elision does not occur.
55. *Śarīrāvayavācca* (4.3.55).

[This is] an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṭhañ*. Because this rule is commenced even though that [suffix *ṭhañ*] would otherwise have applied. However, as for [the suffix] *yat*, which applies after words such as *pāda* that undergo vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*), it subverts both [the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *cha*] because it is subsequent in the order of rules.

56. *dṛtikukṣikalaśivastyastyaherḍhañ* (Pāṇini 4.3.56). Since the suffix *yaT* would apply to *dṛti* and *kukṣi* by virtue of their being parts of the body (*śarīrāvayava*), and since the word *kukṣi* is also listed among the *dhūma*-group words, the suffix *vuÑ* would apply to it by rule 4.2.127 (*dhūmādibhyaśca*); [this sūtra prescribes *ḍhaÑ* instead].

[The suffix] *aṇ* is prescribed for the remaining [roots], while *ḍhañ* is prescribed [for others]. Lest the word *asti*—which ends in a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*)—be understood [as falling under this rule], he says "the word *asti*" and so forth. It is designated as a particle (*nipāta*) because of the rule: "Those which resemble case-endings or accents are particles."

This nominal stem (*prātipadika*) resembles a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), but it is not a verbal suffix. Furthermore, it has the same meaning as a verbal suffix, as in "the Brāhmaṇī woman who possesses milk" (*astikṣīrā brāhmaṇī*); yet it also has a different meaning, as in "he who possesses wealth" (*astimān*), from which "wealthy" (*dhanavān*) is understood. Thus, in this case...
Since no distinction is specified, both are understood.
57. *grīvābhyo’ṇ ca* | (Pāṇini 4.3.57) Because of the mention in the plural, the suffix must be applied after a word ending in the plural;
otherwise, someone might have the misconception that the rule should have been stated in the singular. Therefore, [the author] addresses that [misconception].
In order to refute this, he says: "The word 'neck' (grīvāśabdaḥ) [is singular]," and so forth.
He shows why there is an indication in the plural number due to the plurality of objects, and not as if it were simply because the word itself ends in the plural suffix.

58. *gambhīrāññyaḥ* (4.3.58). The meaning is that this rule, beginning with *bahirdeva*, must be explained as having the sense that the suffix *ñya* occurs after the words *bahudeva* and *pañcajana*. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the particle *ca* ("and") is understood here; by means of it—
The suffix *ñya* will also occur after words such as *bahiḥ*.

59. *Avyayībhāvācca* (Pāṇini 4.3.59). [The commentary begins with] "What then? and so forth. But how is it that the suffix, which is prescribed generally by the rule "after an *avyayībhāva*," applies only after *parimukha* and the others? To this he says: "And of *parimukha* etc.," and so forth.

The word *ca* (and) indicates the reason. For there is no ultimate purpose for the inclusion of [the term] *parimukha* and so forth in the list of gaṇas. Even if this [specific rule] were not present, its inclusion would still serve the purpose of a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*). Therefore, it occurs only after *parimukha* and the others, and not after every *avyayībhāva* compound. If that is the case, [then...]
He says "of those" (*teṣām*) and so forth to explain that it should be stated as "beginning with *parimukha*.

For if it were simply stated as "beginning with *parimukha*," then, in the absence of the mention of *avyayībhāva*, the suffix would apply even to *tatpuruṣa* compounds beginning with *parimukha*; however, when that [mention of *avyayībhāva*] is present, it does not.

It occurs as follows: *parimukham* is a *prādi-samāsa* (compound with a prefix), meaning "that which has the face encompassed"; that which exists there is *parimukha*. Here, the suffix *aṇ* alone applies. Furthermore, the mention of the *avyayībhāva* compound must certainly be made for the latter half [of the rule], namely: *antaḥpūrvapadāt ṭhañ* (Pāṇini 4.3.60) and *grāmāt paryanupūrvāt*.

(4.3.61) [The suffix *ya*] is applied so that it may form an *avyayībhāva* compound, as in *pārihanavyam*. [In this case,] by Pāṇini 6.4.146 (*orguṇaḥ*), there is *guṇa* substitution, and by 6.1.79 (*vānto yi pratyaye*), there is the substitution of *av* for *au*. [An example is] *āpakūlam*.
This is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to 2.1.6 (*avyayaṃ vibhakti...*) and so forth. And this—

Since [the word] is not recited among *parimukha* and the others, only the suffix *aṇ* occurs. Here, how is *parimukham* an *avyayībhāva* compound? For [according to the rule] *apaparibahirañcavaḥ pañcamyā* (Pāṇini 2.1.12), these are compounded with a word in the fifth case; and the fifth case occurs after *pari* when it is used as a *karmapravacanīya*.

The designation *karmapravacanīya* [for *pari*] would apply by virtue of the rule "ṭhapaparī vardane" (Pāṇini 1.4.88); however, in the case of *parimukha*, exclusion (*varjana*) is not understood—what then? It is the sense of "on all sides" (*sarvatobhāva*). If that is so, then by means of a split of the yoga-rule (*yogavibhāga*), it will be an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule "avyayam" (Pāṇini 2.1.6).

However, as for those avyayībhāva compounds here such as *parihāṇu* and so forth, they are formed by the rule *upa-apari-bahi-rañcavo pañcamyā* (Pāṇini 2.1.12). Even in those cases where exclusion (*varjana*) is not understood, they are still [governed] by the rule *avyayam* (2.1.6).

[This is] precisely by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule). However, those compounds beginning with *upa*, such as *upasīra*, [are formed] by [the rule] 2.1.6: "That which begins with *upa* is an indeclinable when meaning proximity," and so forth. In the case of *anugaṅgam*, there is the status of an indeclinable by [the rule] 2.1.16: "And that whose length [is measured]. But others say that those beginning with *anu*, such as *anusīra*, [are formed]...
By the rule beginning with "paścādarthe 'vyayam" (an indeclinable used in the sense of 'afterwards').

60. *antaḥ pūrvapadāt ṭhañ* (4.3.60). [The word] ending in *ṭha* is compounded with a word expressing a case-meaning (*vibhakty-artha*), according to the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti-* (2.1.6) et cetera. Now, the "case-meaning" (*vibhakty-artha*) here refers to the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
Because the word *antaḥ* primarily denotes a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

[The rule] "the suffix *ṭhañ* should be stated after words ending in *samāna*"—the word *vaktavya* (should be stated) refers to what is to be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: although the desired form would be established by the rule *antaḥpūrvāt* alone, the additional mention of the word *pada* [is for a specific purpose].
This is done for the purpose of showing that in this case, the suffix *iñ* occurs even from a word that is not identical [to those previously mentioned], such as *samāna*. By this,
it is established that the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after *adhyātma* and other such words, after *ūrdhvadaṇḍa*, after *ūrdhvadeha*, and after a compound whose final member is *lokottara*.

It should be understood as "internal" (*ādhyātmika*). Regarding the term "internal": *ātmani adhi* means "with reference to the self," forming an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of a case ending. By the rule *anuśatikādīnāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.20), there is vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) for both members of the compound. It is said that "this is a class-based group (*ākṛtigaṇa*) beginning with *adhyātma*. If this is so, [then...]

Is the statement "the suffix *ṭhañ* should be prescribed after words ending in *samāna*" (Vārttika 454) and so forth useless, since it is already established by the rule "after *adhyātma* and others"? It is not useless, because it serves to provide a detailed exposition (*prapañca*) of that very rule. Indeed, the group beginning with *adhyātma* is what is being elaborated here. [Objection: But surely [the word] ends in *-ā*.
Regarding the word *ūrdhva*, one might ask: "How has it come to have the form ending in -m here? To this he says:
"By the word *ūrdhva*," and so forth. [The forms] *aihalaukikaḥ* and *pāralaukikaḥ* [are derived] with the vṛddhi strengthening of both members as in the previous cases.

[The forms] *mukhatīyam* and *pārśvatīyam* [are derived as follows]: the suffix *tasi* is applied by the rule *apādāne cāhīyaruhoḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.45), or alternatively, it is the suffix prescribed by the supplementary rule (*vārttika*) *ādyādibhya upasaṃkhyānam* (Vārttika 634). The elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) is effected by the rule *avyayānāṃ bhamātre ṭilopaḥ* (Vārttika 842).
"And the suffixes -īya and -ya should be stated," [referring to the rule] "from the word *madhya*..."—this refers to the word *madhya*.

[The rule] "from *madhya*, [the suffixes] -madhya and -dinaṇ [are applied]" means that the word *madhya* undergoes the state of becoming *madhyam*, and the suffix *dinaṇ* is applied after it. [The rule] "from *sthāman*" means from a word ending in *sthāman*.

From the nominal stem (*prātipadika*): "He whose strength (*sthāma*) or power (*bala*) is like that of a horse (*aśva*)" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; by virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group, the letter *s* is replaced by *t*. [The derivative] *aśvatthāman* means "born from Aśvatthāman," formed with the suffix *aṇ*, which is then elided (*luk*).
Regarding the rule "ṭhājināntācca": the word *luk* (elision) is understood here. In the example "vṛkājinaḥ," there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *aṇ*.
Regarding the rule "samānasya": this is a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) characterized by immediate sequence. It is intended that the suffix *ṭhañ* follows immediately after the word *samāna*.
This is the meaning.

Regarding the phrase "of *samāna*": this is a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) characterized by immediate succession. The meaning is that the suffix *ṭhañ* is desired immediately after the word *samāna*. Regarding the phrase "in *adhyātma* and so forth": this is the locative case (*saptamī*) used in the sense of a sphere (*vaiṣayika-adhikaraṇa*).

The meaning is that the suffix *ṭhañ* is desired when [the words] *adhyātma* and so forth are the objects. Regarding the rule "ṭhuk after *jana* and the following," the word "and" (*ca*) implies that the suffix *īya* is also applied. Regarding the rule "after *ūrdhva*, *dama*, and *deha*," the meaning is that the suffix *añ* is desired after the word *ūrdhva*, after the word *dama*, and after the word *deha*. [The suffix] *īya*...
"Then the suffix *iya* is to be applied after the middle [term]. The word *atha* (then) signifies conjunction.

The meaning is that the suffix *iya* is to be applied immediately after the word "middle. Regarding the phrase "the suffixes *maṇ* and *īya* likewise," the word "after the middle [term]" is to be understood as the required reference.
The suffixes *maṇ* and *īya* are to be placed after the word "middle. Regarding the phrase "likewise from *ajina*," [the same applies].
The meaning is that elision (*luk*) should be stated [to apply] to the end of the word *ajina*.

61. *paryanupūrvāt* (4.3.61). [The example is] *pārigrāmikam*. According to the *Kāśikā*: "From an *avyayībhāva* compound ending in the word *grāma*, [the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after] *pari*. That is, from *pari-grāmāt*. [This is governed by the rule: *apara-pari-bahirañcavaḥ pañcamyāḥ* ("[The suffixes *ṭhañ* and *khañ* are applied] after *apara*, *pari*, *bahis*, and *añcu* when [these are] in the fifth case").
(2.1.12) Thus ends the section on *avyayībhāva* compounds. Regarding the example "ānugrāmikam," here too [the suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule "anuryatsamayā" (2.1.15).
62. *jihvāmūlāṅguleścchaṭhaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.62).
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffix] *ṭhya*. It supersedes what would otherwise be obtained by the rule *śarīrāvayavācca* (4.3.55).
63. *vargāntācca* (4.3.63).
64. *aśabde yatkhāvanyatarasyām* (4.3.64). [The phrase] "when *cha* would otherwise have applied" refers to the preceding rule.
65. [The suffix *kan* is applied after the words *karṇa* and *lalāṭa*] when a decorative ornament is meant.

(Pāṇini 4.3.65). The word *karṇikā* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as denoting a specific type of ornament. And in the case of conventional words, it is not necessarily required that there be a connection with the ear.
66. *tasya vyākhyāne* (Pāṇini 4.3.66). [The portion of the sūtra is: *tasya vyākhyāne*. "Its exposition" (*tasya vyākhyānam*).

It is called an "exposition" (*vyākhyānam*) because it is explained by means of it; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). By virtue of the word *ca* ("and"), [the rule also applies to] that which occurs therein (*tatra bhave*).

And [regarding] "ca": Now, since the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is what is being explained, and the particle *ca* is heard in proximity to it, it is logical that by it only those of the same class as the meaning of the suffix should be drawn forward (*anukarṣaṇa*), and not even the case-ending (*vibhakti*) expressing the capacity (*samartha*); for the particle *ca* effects a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of things belonging to the same class.

It acts as follows: in the rule *kedārād yañ ca* (Pāṇini 4.2.40), by the letter *ca* situated near the suffix (*pratyaya*), the suffix itself is conjoined; as in *ṭhañ kavacinaś ca* (4.2.41). Since the case ending expressing the governing relation (*samarthavibhakti*) from the preceding rule is thereby suspended, [the suffix applies] even in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava*).

The suffix is appropriate precisely because of the force of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*); therefore, what was said [by others] is incorrect—that one should say *tatra bhave ca* or *tasya bhave ca*. To this, he replies with the words beginning with "near the meaning of the sentence" (*vākyārthasamīpe*).
By the use of the particle *iti* here, the sense of "this is the explanation of that" is recalled.
But it is not for the purpose of providing an explanatory cognition.

Therefore, the word "ca" (and), uttered immediately after the particle "iti," being heard in proximity to the very meaning of the sentence just touched upon by that [particle], [conjoins] only a sentence-meaning of an identical class.

He collects [the points]. By that, the locative case (*saptamī*) is employed precisely for the sake of expressing "being there" (*bhavārtha*); otherwise, he would have said simply, "and in its explanation" (*tasya vyākhyāne ca*). He asks, "What then is this sentence-meaning?
and says: "In that which exists there" (*tatra bhave*).
"But the word *pāṭalīputra* is not the name to be explained. [Objection: But surely *pāṭalīputra* is explained by means of *sukośalā*;
it must necessarily be that which is to be explained, otherwise its explanation, *sukośalā*, would not exist. Regarding that explanation...
The sense is that the word "Pāṭaliputra" is the name of that which is to be explained? This is not so;
the sense is that if what is intended here as the subject to be explained were [the city], this would not be its name.
Furthermore, what is intended here as the subject to be explained? That which is recognized in the world as being the subject to be explained.
It is more well-known. Why is this so? Because of the mention of the name of that which is to be explained.
For in this context, the mention of the name of that which is to be explained need not even be made for the sake of explaining its meaning;
because even without it, the cognition of the very name of that which is to be explained is established. Thus, [in the phrase] "of that," [the word "that" refers to...].

The counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) has been introduced [as the referent]. And that [introduction] is possible only for that which is to be explained, not for anything else. Therefore, it is understood that whatever is to be explained is taken up by the word "of that" (*tasya*), expressed with the genitive case-ending, precisely because of its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*). Consequently, even without [explicit mention],...
Since the mention of the name of the commentary itself will result in the cognition of that which is to be commented upon,

what is the purpose of mentioning the name of the subject to be explained? It is done so that the cognition may refer specifically to that which is well-known in the world as being the subject to be explained, just as [in the case of the word "grammar"].

The word "syāt" (might be) is for this purpose: specific texts such as grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) and so forth are well-known in the world, whereas [cities like] Pāṭaliputra and so forth are not. Even so, the mention of the name [of the specific work] need not be made;
for by the very force of mentioning that which is to be explained (*vyākhyātavya*), [the reference] is understood from among those things most commonly known as being worthy of explanation.

Is the suffix (pratyaya) indeed obtained? This is not so; for when the meaning of the suffix is [already] established by the very act of explanation itself from the word expressing that which is to be explained, then—by the force of the further mention of "that which is to be explained" (vyākhyātavya)—[the suffix applies] only to those things well-known as being "to be explained."

The suffix is obtained, but not from that [specific] *bhū* (to become); because there is a lack of expressive power (*sāmarthya*) therein. Even when the meaning is *bhava*, since those [words] are more well-known as explained [by grammarians], it is desired that the suffix be applied only to those that denote it, and not to just anything. Therefore, under the heading of *bhava*, for the purpose of including conventional (*rūḍhi*) words—
The mention of the name must be made.
Now, for what purpose is the simultaneous governing rule (*adhikāra*) of "existence" (*bhava*) and "explanation" (*vyākhyāna*) established? To this he says:
"Of existence and explanation," and so forth.
The simultaneous introduction of these two [rules] is for the purpose of stating that "I shall hereafter explain the exceptions (*apavāda*) to the suffixes beginning with *ṭhañ*.

Now, one might ask: why is it said "for the purpose of prescribing exceptions," when the intention is rather that there should be a specification of the meanings of the suffixes already under discussion, such as *aṇ* and the rest? To this he says: "For [the meanings] have already been specified..."

Regarding the word *tau*: those two meanings have already been specified; one is [the sense of] "born there" (*tatra-bhava*), and the other is [the sense of] "belonging to that" (*tasyeda*). This is because the explanation is a specific instance of the latter.
67. *Bahvaco'ntodātāṭ ṭhañ* (Pāṇini 4.3.67).

[The examples given are] *ṭhaṣātvaṇatvikam* and *nātānatikam*. In both cases, the suffix is applied after a *dvandva* compound. "The bases are oxytone by virtue of the accent of the compound," according to the rule *samāsasya* (6.1.223).
The use of the plural number [in the rule] is with reference to other bases (*prakṛti*) of this same class.
He will state [the suffix] *ṣṭhan* after two-syllable bases in the rule "dvyajṛdbrāhmaṇa" (Pāṇini 4.3.72), and so forth. The terms "sopam" and "taiṅm" are [examples of] the words *sup* and *tiṅ*.

[The word *pratyaya*] is udātta on the final syllable by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). [It is also] "udātta on the first syllable by the accent of a *gati*" according to the rule *gatiranantaraḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.49). The inclusion of the term *anta-* (end/final) is for the sake of clarity, since a nominal stem that is entirely udātta is impossible. This follows from the very force of the context.
The rule of "specification by the final element" (*tadantavidhi*) will apply here, just as in the case of the rule: *varṇādanudātātopadhāt to naḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.39).

Furthermore, since the mention of the term *udātta* as a specific phoneme (*varṇa-grahaṇa*) necessitates that rule of specification by the final element in all such instances, the application of *tadantavidhi* is indeed logical.

68. *kratuyajñebhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.3.68). "The rule is commenced for the sake of making the suffix *ṭhan* have an udātta accent on its final syllable. If this is so, then these two examples alone—*rājasūyika* and *vājapeyika*—are appropriate.

In the case of the words *rājasūya* and *vājapeya*, because they have a *kṛt*-derived suffix as their final member, they possess a middle-acute accent (*madhyodātta*) by virtue of the accent of the base (*prakṛtisvara*). However, in this context, the final member has an initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*): one [word] due to the accent of the *kṛt* suffix because it ends in a primary derivative suffix (*vyāp*), and the other by the rule "the vowel *y* following a non-vocalic [suffix] is acute" (*ṭhyato 'nācaḥ*, Pāṇini 6.1.213). And when the compound has been formed...

By the rule *gatiranantaraḥ kṛdantāt* (Pāṇini 6.2.49), the preceding member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) due to the status of being a *kṛt*-derivative; thus, in examples such as *āgniṣṭomikaḥ*, *nāvayajñikaḥ*— [as noted in the Kāśikā] *āgniṣṭomikaṃ nāvayajñikam*— the word remains accented on its first syllable.

This pair of examples is incorrect, because by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), the words *agniṣṭoma* and *navayajña* are oxytone (*antodātta*), and [the rule] does not apply here. Indeed, there is no difference whether the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied by the preceding rule or by this one. It has been cited here because of its association with *kratu*; a word functions through association.
Thus it is known.
39. [The suffix *ṇya* is applied after words ending in *ṛṣi*] in the sense of "belonging to" (*adhyāyeṣu*). (4.3.69) 70. [The suffix] *ṣṭhan* is applied after *pauroḍāśa* and *puroḍāśa*.
(4.3.70) [In the compound] *puroḍāśasyedaṃ*, [the word *pauroḍāśa*] is oxytone (*antodātta*). From that [word], which is polysyllabic (*bahvac*) and oxytone, the suffix *ṭhañ* [is applied].

(4.3.67) When [the suffix] *aṇ* would otherwise apply, [the suffix] *ṣṭhan* is prescribed. For [the word] *puroḍāśa*, the accent falls on the middle syllable according to the rule: "But in *puroḍāśa*, if the final syllable is light, or if there are two [light syllables], the heavy syllable [is acute]" (*Phiṭ-sūtra* 2.42). Since *aṇ* would have applied from this [base], *ṣṭhan* is ordained. The letter *v* is for the purpose of [triggering] *ṅīṣ*; the letter *n* is for the purpose of making the first syllable udātta. The *mantra* is that which effects their consecration (*saṃskāra*).

Regarding the term *pauroḍāśa*: it means "that which is associated with the *puroḍāśa*. By virtue of its capacity or through association, the word *puroḍāśa* applies to the mantra by which the *puroḍāśa* cakes are consecrated, and not to the *puroḍāśa* cakes themselves.
Why is this so?
This is because the mention of the name of that which is to be explained continues; for the *puroḍāśa* cakes are not more widely known as being the subject to be explained.
71. After *cchandas*, [the suffixes] *ya* and *aṇ* [are applied].
(4.3.71) 72. After words consisting of two syllables ending in *ṛt*, after *brāhmaṇa*, *ṛk*, *prathama*, *adhvara*, *puraścaraṇa*, a proper name, and a verb, [the suffix] *ṭhak* is applied.

"An exception to *ṭhan*. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), *ṭhañ* is included. In that context, for those polysyllabic words ending in *ṛ*, such as *udgātṛ* and others which have the acute accent on the final syllable, this is an exception to *ṭhan*.
It is also an exception to *ṭhan* after the words *brāhmaṇa*, *prathama*, and *adhvara*; these too are polysyllabic.

They are udātta on the final syllable by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Even when derived from nouns or verbs that form part of a compound, the same applies; that [suffix] also has many vowels, and it is udātta on the final syllable by the accent of the compound (*samāsa*).
From the remaining [bases], the suffix *aṇ* [applies], as in "pāṃśukam" and "pāñcahotṛkam."

According to *ṭhisusuktāntāt kaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.51), the suffix *ka* is added. In the case of the words *pañcahotṛ* and *caturhotṛ*, by the rule *dvigau* (6.2.29), the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member prevails, making the initial syllable acute (*udātta*). For the first member is indeed acute according to the *Phiṭ-sūtra* *nraḥ saṃkhyāyāḥ* (2.28).

The word *puraścaraṇa* ends in the suffix *lyuṭ*; by the rule *kṛdutarapadaprakṛtisvareṇa* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), it is udātta on the middle syllable. The verbal form [in *puraścaraṇam*] is udātta on its first syllable by the rule *gatiranantaraḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.49). Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of including both the collective and the individual meanings," that is obtained by resorting to the compound with *ekaśeṣa*.
It should be understood.
73. *Aṇ-ṛgayanādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.73). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffixes *ṭhak* and *ṭhañ*. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the suffixes *ṭhak* and *cha* are also included.

Among those [words in the list], for those consisting of more than two syllables that have the udātta accent on the final syllable, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied; this applies to the words *vidyā*, *nyāya*, and *śikṣā*.

The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after a word denoting a "pair" (*dvyajlakṣa*). After the word *vyākaraṇa*, which ends in a *vṛddhi* vowel, the suffix *cha* is applied. For what purpose is the mention of *aṇ*? It might be argued that [the suffix] should simply be stated as being prescribed after words such as *krīta* and *ayana*;
and if that were so, it might be suspected that the exceptions beginning with *ṣṭhan* would not apply. For [the rule] concerning the prescription of exceptions...

[The rule] would be rendered useless. Therefore, by virtue of the authority of the statement, that which is prescribed and does not otherwise obtain—because it is sublated by another—will indeed occur; and will that [suffix] be *aṇ*? To this he says:
"The mention of *aṇ*" and so forth. In that context, if the mention of *aṇ* were not made, then whatever here is a *vṛddha* [stem] with an udātta on the final syllable...

Since the suffix *ṭhañ* would otherwise supersede it, the suffix *cha* alone will apply by virtue of the preceding rule. Therefore, the mention of *aṇ* is for the purpose of setting aside that which supersedes *cha*. By this, the form *vāstuvidya* is established.
The word *vāstuvidyā* is *vṛddha*, and as a compound, its final syllable is udātta.

Regarding "ṛgayana" and so forth: as for the term *ṛgayana*, the word *ṛgayana* is derived in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva-sādhana*), meaning "the study (*ayana*) of the *ṛc*s. Although the suffix *lyuṭ* is prescribed in the sense of an action, it nevertheless applies—by way of metaphorical designation (*abhedopacāra*)—to the treatise (*grantha*) that possesses that action when it is to be explained; and that [suffix] is expressed in the rule "after the root √an, [the suffix *lyuṭ* is added] in the sense of an action or an object" (Pāṇini 3.3.117). Furthermore, [the suffix] *ṭhañ* is prescribed in the sense of an action or an object (Pāṇini 5.1.119).

Thus, it has an acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*). However, for those who derive the word *ārṣeya* by applying the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), that word would have an acute accent on the middle syllable (*madhyodātta*) due to the original accent of the first member of the compound (*kṛduttarapada-prakṛtisvara*); in their view, its inclusion in the list [of *gotra* names] would serve no purpose, as the desired form is already established by the rule *prāgdīvyato’ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.1.83).

The word *padavyākhyāna* is oxytone by virtue of the rule *ṭhmanktinvyākyānaśayanāsanasthānayājakādikrītāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.151). [Note: This is not found in the *Kāśikā* or the *Padamañjarī*. Regarding the form *māna*: when the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *man*, then by the rule *ṭhthāthaṣañktājavitrakāṇām* (Pāṇini 6.2.144), it becomes oxytone.

(6.2.144) Thus, [the word] is oxytone. Now, if [the suffix] *lyuṭ* is applied to the root *mināti*, then by (6.2.150) "after [a verbal root], *ṭhan* expresses the sense of the action or the object," it is oxytone. Regarding the phrase "the state of being a Vedic meter" (*chandobhāva*), it is oxytone by the accent of a *kṛt*-suffix according to (6.2.139) "after a prefix, a kāraka, or an upapada."

The word *bhāṣāśabda* is derived with the suffix *a* [in the sense of an action] by the rule *gurośca halaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.103). The word *cchandoviciti* has its final syllable accented acute (*antodātta*) by the rule *manktin* (Pāṇini 6.2.151), etc. The word *punarukta* has its final syllable accented acute by the rule *thāthaghañktājavitrakāṇām* (Pāṇini 6.2.144). *P*... [text continues]

In the *Kāśikā*, [the word] *nirukta* is explained as being oxytone by the rule *saṃjñāyām anācitādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.2.146); the word *vyākaraṇa*, ending in the suffix *lyuṭ*, is middle-accented; and the word *nigama* is derived with the suffix *gha* by the rule *gocarasañcara-* (Pāṇini 3.3.119) and so forth.

By the rule *pratyasvareṇāntodātaḥ*, the word *vāstuvidyā*—along with *aṅgavidyā*, *kṣattravidyā*, *kṣatriyavidyā*, and so forth—is accented on the final syllable according to the accent of the compound (*samāsasvara*). [See *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī*. Furthermore, *utpāta* and *utpāda* [according to the *Kāśikā*] are likewise accented on the final syllable.
The words *udapāda*—these two are oxytone (accented on the final syllable) by the rule Pāṇini 6.2.144 (*thāthādisūtra*). Regarding *saṃvatsara*:

since it is derived according to the rule *vaser saṃpūrvāc cit* (Daiva Upādhyāya 8.51, 52), with the word *sara* following from the rule *aśeḥ sara* (Daiva Upādhyāya 8.50), the word *saṃvatsara* is oxytone.
From the root *mṛh*, the suffix *kta* is applied; with the augment *ūr* added after the *kta*, the word *muhūrta* is thus oxytone (having the acute accent on the final syllable).
The word *nimita* also [is oxytone] by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). Regarding *upaniṣat*:
from the root *sad* preceded by the prefixes *upa* and *ni*, the suffix *kvip* is applied; it is oxytone by the accent of the *kṛt* suffix.

74. "Then he has come from [there]. (Pāṇini 4.3.74). Now, regarding the example: "Having gone from Sṛughna, he has come from the foot of a tree"—why does the suffix not occur here after the word *vṛkṣamūla*? To this, he says: "The primary," and so forth. The primary (*mukhya*) is that which is principal (*pradhāna*).

That which is intended [to be expressed] is what is accepted here; however, the primary element that is invariably concomitant is not [accepted], for when the primary is present, it is not proper to accept the other as non-primary, since the comprehension of the effect occurs through the primary.

75. *ṭhag āyasthānebhyaḥ* | (4.3.75) 76. *śuṇḍikādibhyo 'ṇ* | (4.3.76) "The suffix *aṇ* [is prescribed] as an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffixes *ṭhañ*, *āyasthāna*, and *ṭhak*. This is stated because of its general prevalence; for [otherwise],...

The word *kṛkaṇa* is recited here; for in that case, it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *ccha* suffix prescribed by the rule "after *kṛkaṇa* and *parṇa*, [the suffix *ccha* is added] when [the patronymic] Bhāradvāja [is meant]" (Pāṇini 4.2.145). Furthermore, the word *tīrtha* is recited here among the *dhūma*-group;
consequently, it is an exception to the *vuñ* suffix prescribed by the rule "and after the *dhūma*-group" (Pāṇini 4.2.127). Now, as for the mention of *aṇ*:

For what purpose [is this rule stated]? Why should it not simply be said that [the suffix] is applied as prescribed after words such as *śauṇḍika*, and why should one not fear that if it were recited in this way, it would result in nothing but an exception (*apavāda*)? For if an exception were being enjoined, the statement would be redundant; therefore, even without the explicit mention of *aṇ*, *aṇ* itself will certainly occur.

Therefore, he says: "The mention of *ṭhaN*," and so forth. The word *udapāna* is recited here as a designation for a place of water (*āyasthāna*), whereas it is recited among the *utsa*-group [of suffixes]; in that case, if the mention of *ṭhaN* were absent, the *añ* suffix prescribed by *utsādibhyo 'ñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.86) would apply, thereby subverting the *ṭhak* suffix [prescribed] for places of water. Therefore, for that [word],...
The mention of *aṇ* is for the purpose of subverting that which would otherwise supersede it; by this, the suffix *aṇ* is established in the case of *udapāna*.
77. *Vun* is added [to denote a descendant] after words signifying a relationship through learning (*vidyā*) or birth (*yoni*).

(4.3.77) 78. *Ṭhañ* is added [after a word ending in short *ṛ*]. (4.3.78) Regarding the statement, "The use of the long vowel *ṝ* (in *ṛtaḥ*) is for the sake of ease of pronunciation," one might ask: why does it not serve to exclude the long vowel?

Because it is impossible; for among those related by the ties of learning (*vidyā*) or birth (*yoni*), there is no nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in the vowel *ṛ* for which the letter *t* could serve to exclude [the application of the suffix].

79. *pituryat* (Pāṇini 4.3.79): [The example] is *pitryam*. By [the rule] *rīṅ ṛtaḥ* (7.4.27), *rīṅ* is substituted for *ṛ*; then, by *yasyeti ca* (6.4.148), there is elision [of the final vowel and consonant of the suffix].
80. *Gotrādaṅkavat* (4.3.80).

If it is stated that "if a suffix is prescribed after a *gotra* [name] as if it were an *aṅka*," then only the extension (*atideśa*) of *aṇ* would apply, not of *vuñ*. This is because the mention of the term *aṅga* occurs only in the rule prescribing *aṇ*.

Regarding the rule for the suffix *vuñ* in sūtras such as *saṅghāṅkalakṣaṇa* (Pāṇini 4.3.127), one might ask: does this also apply to the rule *gotracaraṇād vuñ* (4.3.126)? To this he says: "By the inclusion of the word *aṅka*," and so forth.
This is just as in the case of the expression, "Let the curd be protected from crows."

The mention of *kāka* is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the general category of *upadhāta*; likewise here, the mention of *aṅka* is an illustration of [the rule] *tasyedam* (Pāṇini 4.3.120). Therefore, this is the meaning of the sūtra:
just as a suffix occurs in the case of *tasyedam* (4.3.120), so too [it occurs] in the case of *tata āgataḥ*.
This also applies here [in 4.3.74]. By this, the extension (*atideśa*) of the suffix *vuñ* is likewise justified.

But even so, the extension of *aṇ* would not apply, for in its rule of prescription there is no mention of "lineage" (*gotra*). There is no such fault, because the term "non-lineage" (*agotra*) is carried over from the preceding sūtra.
He shows the specific sūtra by which the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed, namely *ṭha-saṅghāṅka-lakṣaṇāt* (Pāṇini 4.3.127).
81. *hetumanuṣyebhyo 'nyatarasyāṃ rūpyaḥ* | (4.3.81) "samādgatam" means that which has come from the cause that is the *samā*. But why is the ablative case (*pañcamī*) used here?
Precisely because of the indicator (*jñāpaka*), since this [sūtra] prescribes an affix after a word ending in the fifth case, it follows that [the word *samā*] must be in the ablative.
It is understood that the ablative case occurs when expressing the cause.
82. *mayaṭ* ca.

(4.3.82) [The commentary states: "The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the purpose of avoiding a correspondence between the elements (*yathāsaṃkhya*). Now, one might object: since the optional suffix (*anyatarasyām*) permits the general rule (*autsargika*), how can there be a lack of correspondence (*vaiṣamya*) that would necessitate avoiding *yathāsaṃkhya*?
Is it not the case that [the application of] the rule itself does not exist? This is true;

however, for one who might think that there is a correspondence in order (*yathāsaṃkhyatva*) with respect to what is being prescribed because the two [suffixes] *rūpya* and *mayaṭ* are unprecedented, a separation of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) is made for his sake.
83. *prabhavati* (4.3.83).

[The *Kāśikā* states: "First" means "is first perceived. By the word *prathama*, he explains the meaning of the prefix *pra*; by the word *upalabhyate*, he also explains the meaning of the root *bhū*.

Since roots have multiple meanings, the root *bhū* here functions in the sense of "perception" (*upalabdhi*). In the expression "it originates from the Himavat," the Himavat receives the designation of *apādāna* (ablative point of departure) by virtue of the rule *bhuvaḥ prabhavaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.31).

84. *vidūrāñ ñyaḥ* | (4.3.84) [The suffix] *ñya* [is applied after the word *vidūra*] in the sense of "it is refined there. The word *tu* is used for emphasis. It means that it is indeed refined (*saṃskriyate*) in that city of Vidūra, but it does not originate (*prabhavati*) from there.

Regarding the statement, "The word *vālavāya* and *vidūra*": it is the word *vālavāya* alone that produces the cognition [of the source], not the word *vidūra*. The meaning of the word *prabhavati* is "is first perceived.
And it is first perceived on Mount *Vālavāya*. Therefore, the word *vālavāya* denotes that from which [the river] originates.

The base form is implied by its very nature. For instance, although only *viśravaṇa* and *ravaṇa* are recited in the list beginning with *śiva* and so on, because of the governing rule concerning "descendants" (*apatya*), that very word which establishes the relationship between them as descendant and ancestor is implied as the base form; thus, the descendant of Viśravas is Vaiśravaṇa.

Rāvaṇa: Or rather, the word *vidūra* refers to a different kind of origin (*prakṛtyantara*) in the case of woolen cloth (*vālavāya*). Its meaning is that it "comes from afar," that is, it originates from the mountain Vālavāya. This being the case, whoever...
One might say: "The word *vidūra* is not well-known in that sense [of 'far'] among the Vālavāyas. To him, he replies:
"One should apply it like *jitvarī*. Just as only merchants pronounce the city of Vārāṇasī as *jitvarī* for the sake of auspiciousness, and not ordinary people, so too do the grammarians.

In this very way, they pronounce [the word] *vālavāya* as *vidūra*. By the phrase "like *jitvarī*," he explains that even conventional designations (*rūḍhi*) have restricted regions and persons as their objects.

85. *tad gacchati pathidūtayoḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.85). Since the path (*pathin*) is devoid of action, the status of being the agent (*kartṛtva*) for the root *gam* (to go) is not logically possible; therefore, he says: "in those situated upon it" (*tatstheṣu*), and so forth. He demonstrates that the movement residing in the person is metaphorically attributed (*upacaryate*) to the path. "Or else" (*atha vā*).

And so forth. Here, the root *gam* (to go) signifies "attainment. And for Srughna and the others, there exists an attainment characterized by immediate succession (*ānantarya*) on this very path, which is indeed accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

86. *Abhiniṣkramati dvāram* | (4.3.86) But how can the door, which is well-known as an instrument (*karaṇa*), be intended [here] as an independent agent? To this he says: "Just as," and so forth. Just as a sword is an instrument in the act of cutting...
Even though it is well-known [to be inanimate], it is intended here as independent. Now, it might be argued:
