[The rule] "uṇ [is added] after *ṭha*, *bilva*, etc. (4.3.136). Now, for what purpose is the mention made with the suffix *matup*? Why not simply say "after *nodvadhrabilva*" (4.3.151)? To this he says: "the mention with *matup*. If it were stated as "after *nodvadhrabilva*,"...

In this case, there would be a mention of the *varṇa* (phoneme) itself. Since the mention of the *varṇa* here applies the rule of "ending-in-that" (*tadantavidhi*) everywhere, the mention of the suffix *matup* is made in order to prohibit that. To the question, "What fault would arise if the rule of 'ending-in-that' were applied? he says: "Only here," and so forth. By the use of the particle *eva*...
He shows that [the suffix] would not apply after words such as *muñja* by saying "vaiṣṇavī";
[here] the suffix *aṇ* is applied because [the word *viṣṇu*] belongs to the *bilva* group.

152. *tālādibhyo’ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.3.152). [The commentary states: "This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *mayaṭ* and the others. By the word "and the others" (*ādi*), *añ* is included. Because of the difference in their bases (*prakṛti*), the plurality of those two is intended; therefore, the dual number is used for both. In that regard:

The suffix *mayaṭ* prescribed by the rule for denoting "characteristic of an elder" (*vṛddhalakṣaṇa*) is superseded by the words *tāla* and *śyāmāka*. Furthermore, the word *barhiṇa*—derived from *barhin* with the suffix *añ* according to the rule *ṭhañ prāṇirajatādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.154)—also ends in a suffix denoting a modification or a part; therefore, the suffix *añ* [is applied] after that word, as well as after those ending in *ñit*.
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *añ* prescribed by [Pāṇini 4.3.155] *tat-pratyayāt*.
However, from the remaining roots such as *indrāliśa* and others, the suffix *añ* is applied according to the rule for those beginning with an unaccented vowel (*anudātādi*).
In the case of the roots *liś* and *dṛś*, when *indra* is the upapada, [the suffix *ka* is applied] in the section concerning the suffix *ka* for words such as *mūlavibhuja*.

The suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *upasaṃkhyānam* (Vārttika 232). Lengthening occurs by the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 6.3.137). By the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), the word *indrāliśendrādṛśa* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) due to the accent of the *kṛt*-suffix; [so too does] the word *indrāghu*.

By the accent rule for compounds (*samāsasvara*), [the word] is *antodātta* (accented on the final syllable). From the root *cap* in the sense of "consoling" (*sāntvane*) [DhP 3.99], with the suffix *ac* [by Pāṇini 3.1.134], the word *capa* is *antodātta*. The word *pīyūkṣā* is *madhyodātta* (accented on the middle syllable) by the rule beginning with "when a light syllable is at the end" (*laghāvante*, Phiṭ-sūtra 2.42). Even though the suffix *ṭāp* is added to this [word], by the rule "when a light syllable is at the end" (*laghāvante*, Phiṭ-sūtra 2.42)...

It does not exist [thereafter], but previously the suffix *ṭāp* certainly existed; in that very state, the middle syllable becomes udātta. It is read as "tālāddhanuṣi" (the suffix *aṇ* occurs after the word *tāla* when meaning 'bow'). Thus, the suffix *aṇ* occurs after the word *tāla*.

Regarding the statement "it is to be designated as *dhanus*": [the word] *tāla* is *dhanus*, while others consist of *tāla*. Now, for what purpose is the mention of the suffix *aṇ*? Could it not simply be stated "as prescribed"? This cannot be done;

for from the word *bārha*, by the rule "after a word ending in *vr̥ddhi*, there is *mayaṭ*" (Pāṇini 4.3.143), and by the rule "and after a suffix marked with *ñ* or *ṭ*," (4.3.155), [the suffix *mayaṭ* would otherwise apply].

Thus, [the suffix] *añ* is superseded. In that case, by virtue of the capacity of the initial formation (*ārambha-sāmarthya*), only *mayaṭ* would apply. The word *śyāmāka*, according to the rule "when a light syllable is at the end" (*phi.sū.* 2.42), etc., has the middle vowel as the udātta accent. From that [word], by the rule "after a word with an anudātta-initial vowel, *añ*" (4.2.44), [the suffix *añ* would apply]; however, it is superseded by *mayaṭ*, which is characterized by the presence of a vṛddhi vowel and is of higher priority.
Thus, by the force of the renewed undertaking, it would indeed be *aṅ* itself; because of the mention of *aṇ*, it becomes only *aṇ*.
153. *jātarūpebhyaḥ parimāṇe* (4.3.153).

[The commentary begins with] "Because of the mention in the plural," and so forth. The sense is that if the intention were to grasp the actual form (*svarūpa*) [of the word], one would have made the mention in the singular alone, since that [form] is a single entity.

Regarding the phrase "of *mayaṭ* and the rest": the word "and the rest" (*ādi*) includes *añ*. The plural number is as before. Among those [words], for the *vṛddha* ones such as *hāṭaka*, *jātarūpa*, and so forth, there is an exception to *mayaṭ*; but for those such as *tapanīya* which begin with an *anudātta* vowel, there is an exception to *añ*.
Regarding the word "tāpanīyam": by the rule "laghāvante" (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.42), etc., the word *tapanīya* has its middle syllable accented acute (*madhyodātta*).

154. *prāṇirajatādibhyo’ñ* (Pāṇini 4.3.154). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffixes] *ṭhaṇ* and the others. By the word "and the like" (*ādi*), the suffix *mayaṭ* is included. The plural number is as before. Among those, for words denoting living beings (*prāṇin*) that have the acute accent (*udātta*) on their first syllable, this [suffix] *añ* is an exception to *aṇ*. As for those...

However, among those [words], *mayaṭ* is selected for the [words] beginning with *vṛddha*. Even in the case of *rajata* and others, *mayaṭ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to *aṇ* when the first syllable is udātta; whereas for those beginning with *anudātta*, it is an exception to *mayaṭ*. For since *añ* would already be established for those [words] by the rule "ṭhanudātādeśca" (Pāṇini 4.3.140), the repetition [of the rule] is so that *añ* alone [may apply].

It might be argued that [the suffix] *mayaṭ* should not apply by virtue of the rule "mayaḍvaitayoḥ" (Pāṇini 4.3.143) and so forth; for that purpose, [the word] *rajatam* is acutely accented on the final syllable because it is listed among the words beginning with *ghṛta*. As for *sīsam* and *loham*, they are acutely accented on the first syllable by the rule "nabviṣayasyānisantasya" (Phitsūtra 2.26).

This is its meaning: for a word denoting a neuter [noun] that does not end in -i, the first syllable becomes udātta. *Nab* is the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for the neuter. While the rule "before the final [syllable]" (*antyāt pūrvam*) is understood to carry over, there is the exception:
*śiśumāra, udumbara, balīvarda, uṣṭra, ārapura, and purūravas* (Phiṭ-sūtra 3.64).
Thus, in the word *udumbara*, the syllable preceding the final one is acute (*udātta*).

In the case of *nīladāru*, *rohitabibhītaka*, and so forth, there is lengthening of the middle syllable according to the rule beginning with *ṭhlaghāvante* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.42). Some also recite the word *pītadāru*. That...
The word *tri* is acutely accented on the first syllable because it ends in the suffix *ḍri*, according to the rule *tarater ḍriḥ* (Pañcapādikā Uṇādisūtra 5.66).

The term *trikaṇṭaka* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has three thorns. According to the rule *ṭhna-bviṣayasyānisantasya* (Phiṭsūtra 2.26), it is acutely accented on the first syllable. Thus, the first syllable of the entire compound is acute by the accent of the initial member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*).

According to the rule *bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā pūrvapadam* (Pāṇini 6.2.1), the word *trikaṇṭaka* has its initial syllable accented (*ādyaudāta*). [The derivation is as follows: from the root *kaṇṭ*, with the prefix *tri-*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of an object (*karmaṇi*), yielding *trikaṇṭaka*. The word *kaṇṭakāra*—derived from the root *kaṇṭ* with the suffix *āra*—has its final syllable accented (*antodāta*) by the rule governing the accent of primary derivatives (*kṛtsvara*).

155. *Ñitaśca tatpratyayāt* (Pāṇini 4.3.155). [The commentary states: "This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *mayaṭ*. This is because everything characterized by *vṛddhi* that ends in a *ñit* suffix is itself *vṛddha*. [The question is raised: "Are these suffixes [intended] to be included? However, [one might object] by means of the paribhāṣā regarding single indicatory letters (*ekānubandha*).

Does the inclusion of *ṣṭlan* not follow? This is not a fault; for in the rule *ṭhñitaśca*, the word *ca* (and) serves to include that [suffix] as well. Thus, its inclusion will also occur by virtue of the mention of *orañ* (Pāṇini 4.3.139), which [is governed by] *ṭhanudātadeśca* (4.3.140) and *palāśādibhyo vā* (4.3.141).
(4.3.141) It should be understood that this rule is included [in the previous one]; because they are not distinct,
the very same suffix *añ* which was prescribed by the rule *ṭhorañ* (4.3.139) is carried over into these two rules by means of the phrase "the modification or part of *daivadāra*," and so forth.

He demonstrates the examples and so forth of these conditions as appropriate: "kāṃsyam pāraśavam" (bronze, iron). [The derivation is as follows: from *kaṃsa* with the sense of "beneficial for," by Pāṇini 5.1.1 (*prāk krītāc cha-*), we get *kaṃsīyaḥ*.
From *paraśu* with the sense of "beneficial for," by Pāṇini 5.1.2 (*ugavādibhyo yat*), we get *yat*; thus, [the form] *pāraśavya*.

Regarding the rule "vikāro'vayavo veti kaṃsīyaparaśavyayoryañañau luk ca" (Pāṇini 4.3.168), the suffixes *yañ* and *añ* are applied respectively, and there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *cha* and *yat*— resulting in *kāṃsya* and *pāraśavaḥ*. By this same rule [4.3.134], the suffix *añ* is applied to denote "a modification or a part of those two," as in "bailvamayam."

The word *bilva* ends in the suffix *aṇ* by [Pāṇini 4.3.136] *ṭhbilvādibhyo'ṇ*. From that, by the rule for *vṛddha* [denoting a descendant], only the suffix *mayaṭ* occurs, as in *vaidamaya*. However, by [Pāṇini 4.1.104] *anṛṣya* etc., the suffix *añ* occurs—namely *vaida*. This suffix *añ* is marked with the indicator *ñ*, but it does not denote a modification (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*); therefore...
It becomes as if made of illusion (māyā).

156. *krīta-parimāṇāt* (4.3.156). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffixes beginning with *ṭhaṇ*. By the word "beginning with" (*ādi*), the inclusion of suffixes such as *añ* and others is intended. It is stated that "number (*saṃkhyā*) is also included by the mention of 'measure' (*parimāṇa*). But how is this obtained, given that...?

Is the word *parimāṇa* (measure) restricted by convention to measures such as the *prastha* and so forth, and not used for number? This is not a fault; for just as the *prastha* and so forth are the means of delimiting [an object], so too is number. Therefore, by way of analogy, the word *parimāṇa* will also apply to number, in the sense that "number is like a measure."
But surely, if the primary meaning exists, it is improper to take the secondary sense? This is the fault here:

for in this *tantra* system, two words denoting measure (*parimāṇa*) are uttered by way of *tantra*; therein, the second word is accented acute (*udātta*), and by that, number (*saṃkhyā*) is also included. [The example is] "naiṣkikam" (worth one *niṣka*). [This is formed] by adding *ṭhañ* after a word ending in *prāgvatīya* (Pāṇini 5.1.18).
‘ṭhśatyaḥ’, ‘śatikaḥ’—[these are formed] by [Pāṇini 5.1.21]: *śatācca ṭhanyatāvaśate*. ‘Sahasram’—[this is formed] by [Pāṇini 5.1.27]:
*śatamānaviṃśatikasahasravatanādaṇ*. When the suffix *vatu* is applied in the sense of similarity according to [Pāṇini 5.1.28]: *adhyardhapūrva* and so forth, that which is desired [is obtained].
He shows that [it] is accomplished. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of *prakṛti* and so forth. Regarding "two thousand" (*dvisahasram*):

it is a *dvigu* compound used in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), meaning "a modification of two thousands. This is according to the rule: "Before suffixes beginning with *vat*, there is the extension of the rule to include what ends in that [numeral], provided the preceding member is a numeral and the elision (*luk*) has not occurred" (Vārttika on Pāṇini 5.1.20).

The rule regarding the inclusion of the final element (*tadantavidhi*) is permitted here as well, just as in the case of the suffix *ṭhañ* in the sense of "purchased from," according to *Pāṇini 5.1.29*: "after *śatamāna*, *viṃśati*, *sahasra*, and *vasana*. Consequently, in this instance too, there is optionally elision (*luk*), resulting in the form *dvisāhasram*.
Furthermore, by the rule *Pāṇini 7.3.15*: "of a numeral preceded by *saṃvatsara*," there is vṛddhi substitution in the final member of the compound.

Regarding the term *dviniṣka*: just as the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after the word *niṣka* in the sense of "purchased for" according to Pāṇini 5.1.18 (*prāgvateṣṭhañ*), and that suffix is optionally elided by 5.1.30 (*dvitripūrvānniṣkāt*), so it is here as well. Thus, we have *dviniṣkikam*. [This is governed by] the rule *parimāṇāntasyāsaṃjñānnāṇayoḥ*.
(7.3.17) Thus, there is a vṛddhi of the subsequent member.

157. *uṣṭrād vuñ* (4.3.157). 158. *umorṇayor vā* (4.3.158). The word *umā* refers to a grass-corn (according to *Phiṭ-sūtra* 2.27); it is not acute-accented on the first syllable. The word *ūrṇā* is also [not acute-accented on the first syllable].

The word [ending in *pratyaya*] is udātta on the final syllable by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*); since the suffixes *aṇ* and *añ* would apply to those two respectively, the optional *vuñ* is now introduced.

159. *eṇyā ḍhañ* (4.3.159). [The commentary states: "In this case, the form *pums-tva* occurs because of the suffix *añ*. If *ḍhañ* were applied here to the word *pum̐s*, he would have made the reference in the masculine gender alone.
For if the reference were in the masculine gender...

Since the inclusion of the gender-qualified form also occurs when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, the suffix is indeed obtained even from the word *eṇī*. Therefore, by the very mention of the feminine gender, the suffix *añ* applies to the masculine,
and not *ḍhañ*.

160. *gopayasoryat* (Pāṇini 4.3.160). It is stated [in the commentary] that "it is prescribed in the scope of *mayaṭ*. Because of the statement "when there is the contingency of [suffixes] beginning with *aj*," since *mayaṭ* does not begin with *aj*, it would not apply in its scope; therefore, in that case...
From the word *go*, [the suffix] is prescribed. However, the word *payaḥ* ends in the *asun* suffix added to the root *pā* (to drink);

by virtue of the *nit*-accent, it has an udātta on its first syllable. Consequently, the rule "after a word ending in a long vowel, the suffix *aṇ* is applied" (Pāṇini 4.1.83) would apply. Therefore, this [suffix] which is being prescribed serves as an exception to that.

161. *dro* [is substituted for *dvayasaj*] when expressing a measure (*māna*). (Pāṇini 4.3.161) 162. *vaya* [is substituted for *dvayasaj*] when expressing a measure. (Pāṇini 4.3.162) 163. There is elision (*luk*) of [the suffix *kan*] after *kala*. (Pāṇini 4.3.164)

Regarding the phrase "in that domain": it refers to the domain of products (*vikāra*) and parts (*avayava*). Regarding the word "āmalakam": by the rule *nityaṃ vṛddhaśarādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.144), the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied, which is then elided (*luk*). The elision of the feminine suffix is as before. Now, one might object: a fruit is neither a product nor a part of a tree. A product...

It occurs in two ways: either it subsumes the material cause, as in "the *khadira* tree is ashes"; or it provides a designation for the material cause, as in "the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is made of *khadira* wood. Furthermore, it does not remove the fruit from the tree, nor does it produce a different designation for that which is already possessed of the fruit. Now...
And its modification as well as its fruit would likewise [be so]. This might be argued:

"The sprout arises by taking on the state of budding of the tree; therefore, it is logical that it is a modification and a constituent part of that [tree]. The fruit also [arises] by taking on the state of bearing fruit of the tree..."

When the fruit arises, it is indeed logical that it possesses the state of being a modification of that [tree]. As for what was also said—that "it is not a part because it does not initiate [another part]"—that too is incorrect; for the fruit, as it is produced, initiates a distinct and specific part of the tree, with the assistance of parts such as the branches and so forth. For example:
Just as a sprout, by initiating a distinct composite whole, becomes a constituent part, so too should it be understood that the fruit does likewise.
164. *Plakṣādibhyo 'ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.3.164). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṭhañ*.
Among those [words], in the case of the words *ikṣu* and *karkandhū*, it is an exception to *añ*, which is characterized by having a final *u*-vowel.

But for the remaining [words], the rule applies by virtue of having an initial anudātta accent; for all of them are anudātta-initial because they have an udātta accent on the final syllable. Among them, the words *plakṣa*, *nyagrodha*, and *aśvattha* have an udātta on the final syllable by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*).
However, the words *iṅguda* and *bṛhatī* end in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* according to the *gaurādi* group.

The two words are oxytone by virtue of their suffixal accent. [The phrase] "by the force of the rule" (*vidhānasāmarthyāt*) and so forth means: if there were elision (*luk*) of the *aṇ* suffix, the statement [of this rule] would be purposeless; for once the elision of either the *aṇ* or the *vāñ* has been effected, there is no difference whatsoever. [The example] "naiyagrodham" [is formed] by [the rule] "and [the substitution of *a* for the final vowel] of *nyagrodha* when it is not compounded with anything else. (*nyagrodhasya ca kevalasya*)
(7.3.5) Such indeed is the sacred tradition.

[The suffix] *ṭhañ* indeed occurs [after *jambu*]. However, if its *luk* elision were to take place, the rule would be rendered purposeless because it would not be heard [in the form]. [In the case of] *jambūni*, once the *luk* has been applied, the gender of the expressed meaning [remains].
It becomes neuter. By the rule "ṭhhrasvo nupaṃsake prātipadikasya" (1.2.47), [the final vowel of the stem] is shortened;
by "ṭhjaśśasoḥ śiḥ" (7.1.20), *śi* is substituted for *jas* and *śas*; *num* is added; and by "ṭhnopadhāyāḥ" (6.4.7), lengthening of the penultimate vowel occurs.
166. *lup ca* (Pāṇini 4.3.166). What, then, is the distinction when *lup* occurs, such that this [rule] is prescribed even though *luk* is already in force?
To this he says: "The distinction is the state of being like that which is joined" (*yuktavadbhāva*). When *lup* occurs, there is the state of being like that which is joined.

Regarding the rule "when *lup* [elision] occurs, the gender and number are like those of the joined element" (Pāṇini 1.2.51), it is precisely when *lup* is present that this distinction applies. For example, in the case of "the fruit is a *jambū*," by virtue of the treatment as if joined with the base (*yuktavadbhāva*), the gender remains that of the original base; therefore, the neuter gender does not apply.
Regarding the passage beginning with *ṭhlupprakaraṇe* and so forth: "those that wither through the ripening of their fruit" are called *phalapākaśuṣaḥ*.
The suffix *kvip* is applied according to *ṭhanyebhyo'pi dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 3.2.178). Examples include *vrīhayaḥ* (rice) and *mudgāḥ* (mung beans);
here the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by *bilvādibhyo'ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.3.136) is elided (*lup*). Examples include *yavāḥ* (barley) and *māṣāḥ* (beans). From this [it follows...]
The suffix *aṇ* is the general rule (*utsargika*). These [words] have their first syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*) by the rule beginning with "ṭhṛṇadhānyānām" (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.27).
[And] regarding the rule "puṣpamūleṣu bahulam": when flowers and roots are to be expressed, [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] diversely (*bahulam*).

It becomes *lubbhavati*. In the case of *mallikā*, *vanamallikā*, *jāti*, *vidārī*, *aṃśumatī*, and *bṛhatī*, there is elision (*lup*) of the suffix *aṅ* characterized by an initial anudātta vowel. The words *mallikā* and *navamallikā* have the middle syllable as udātta according to the rule: "In a word ending in a light syllable, or having two [light] syllables, the heavy syllable [among those preceded by a light one] is udātta" (Phiṭsūtra 2.42).

The word *jāti* is oxytone because it ends in the suffix *ktic*, according to Pāṇini 3.3.174 (*jātiśabdaśca ṭhkvicktau ca saṃjñāyām*). The words *badarī* and *bṛhatī* are also oxytones because they end in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* from the *gaura*-class. The word *aṃśumatī* [is oxytone] by virtue of Pāṇini 4.1.6 (*ugitaśca*).

Thus ends the section on words ending in *ṅīp*. Since the word *aṃśu* is oxytone by virtue of its nominal stem accent (*prātipadika-svara*), [the compound] is middle-accented (*madhyodātta*). Regarding "pāṭalāni": the suffix *aṇ* is applied because it belongs to the *bilva*-class. Regarding "śālvāni mūlāni": [the same applies].

Regarding the form *śālvāni*, it is derived by the rule *anudātāder añ* (Pāṇini 4.2.44). The word *śālva* is oxytone (*antodātta*) by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). It is well known that *śālva* means "a kind of grass" (*uśāka*).
According to the principle "sometimes even something else [occurs]," the operation of *lup* occurs in other instances as well. Thus, the effect of *lup* sometimes applies elsewhere too.

And there is the absence of both *tatpuruṣa* [compounding] and *luk* [elision]. In examples such as "kadambakam," there is *luk* elision of the suffix *añ*, which would otherwise be characterized by an *anudātta* accent. Words such as "kadamba" have the middle syllable accented (*madhyodātta*) according to the rule "laghāvante" (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.42). In the case of "balvāni," there is the absence of both [suffixes]. [This is derived from] the rule "bilvādibhyo 'ṇ."

(4.3.136) This entire matter is established by the very recitation of the *harītaky-ādi* group; thus, nothing new need be stated. For among the *harītaky-ādi* words, those for which there is drying caused by the ripening of the fruit (*phalapāka-nimitta*) are listed under the rule "puṣpamūleṣu bahulam" (4.3.167).
167. *Harītakyādibhyaśca* (4.3.167).

Among the *harītakyādi* group, the words *kaṇṭakārikā*, *gargārikā*, and *śephālikā*—because they end in the suffix *kan* by rule 5.3.75 (*saṃjñāyāṃ kan*)—have their first syllable acute by virtue of the *nit-svara*. By that very [rule],...

From those [words], there is the elision (*lup*) of the default suffix *aṇ*; however, from the remaining ones, there is the elision of the suffix *añ* characterized by having an initial low-pitched vowel (*anudātādi*).

All of them have the high-pitched accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*), and therefore they are "beginning with an unaccented vowel" (*anudātādi*). Among them, those that are recited before *kālā*, *drākṣā*, and *dhrākṣā* have the high-pitched accent on the final syllable because they end in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*; among these is *śvetapākī*.
*Arjunapākī*—these two [words] end in *ṅīṣ* by virtue of the rule *ṭhpākakarṇaparṇa* (Pāṇini 4.1.64).
From the remaining [words], however, [the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] because they belong to the *gaurādi* group, according to the rule *gaurādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.41).
From the words *kālā*, *drākṣā*, and *dhrākṣā*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied, as these are oxytone (*antodātta*) by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
There is lengthening by *savarṇadīrgha*, and by the rule "the single substitute for [a vowel] with an acute [vowel] is acute" (*ekādeśa udātenodātaḥ*), it acquires an acute accent.
Therefore, *kāla* and the others are also oxytone.

168. *kaṃsīyaparaśavyayoryaññau luk ca* (Pāṇini 4.3.168). Regarding *kaṃsīya*: in the *Uṇādi* [section], the word *kaṃsa* is derived with the suffix *sap*. The word *paśu* is also derived from the roots *pṛ*, *dhṛ*, *vi*, *pad*, *dhṛṣ*, and *hṛṣ* with the suffix *ku* (as stated in the *Dhātupāṭha*).

While this [rule] is being carried over, [the rule] "after *khan* and *śṛ*, with *ṭha* and *aṅ* following, there is *ṣṭu*" (Daiva-Uṇādi 1.108)—where the reading in the Prācya-munyāsa is "and *ti*"—is followed by "there is *ṇi*" (Daiva-Uṇādi 1.118), [forming a word] ending in the *ku*-suffix.
Why then does elision (*luk*) not also occur here for both the root and the suffix? To this he says:

"Because of the governing rule [adhikāra] concerning nominal stems (prātipadika)," and so forth. The term "from a nominal stem" (prātipadikāt) is understood [from the previous sūtra]; therefore, elision (luk) occurs for that [suffix] which is prescribed after a nominal stem. Now, these two [suffixes] are not prescribed after a nominal stem; rather, they are prescribed after a verbal root (dhātu). Consequently, elision does not apply to them.
"Simply because of its being *anudātta*. For the word *paraśavya* has a svarita accent on its final syllable by the rule "ṭitsvaritam" (Pāṇini 6.1.185).
"Therefore, it begins with an *anudātta* [syllable]. This is because the term "īti" is understood to carry over there from the rule "yasyeti ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.148).
Thus ends the third quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇa-pañjikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who was a teacher of the Bodhisattvas.
Now begins the fourth chapter,
the fourth quarter.

1. *prāgvahateṣṭhak* (Pāṇini 4.4.1). Now, what is the purpose of the mention of *prāk* ("before")? It is so that the suffix *ṭhak*, which has been set aside by another suffix as an exception (*apavāda*) for a specific meaning, may be reinstated in a subsequent section of the treatise. For example:

The word *syāt* is used for this purpose. For example: in the specific sense [of "born in"], after the suffix *aṇ* has been set aside by [the rule] *kulatthakopadhāt* (Pāṇini 4.4.4), it is [reinstated] later in another sense, namely in the sense of *tarati* (Pāṇini 4.4.5).
"Furthermore, so that there may be a subsequent application (punarupasthāna), [the rule] beginning with 'in the section on the suffix ṭhaṭ' [is stated].

Regarding the word 'tat': after words denoting an action, the suffix *ṭhak* is added in the sense of 'he says this,' provided they are preceded by the word *mā* and others; this is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) to the rule. This prescription of the suffix applies to a complete sentence (*vākya*).

Thus, since that alone is the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), it has not been overlooked as having attained the status of an action (*karman*). Therefore, it is pointed out by the phrase "it says": "the cognition arises from the very sentence that expresses that [meaning]. For a sentence is indeed a collection of words (*padasamudāya*). And regarding the word *mā* and the word *śabda*, whatever... [of the word]... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragmentary commentary on grammatical philosophy, likely from a work such as the *Vākyapadīya-bhūṣaṇa*. The ellipsis indicates a missing portion of the original Sanskrit sentence.)
The collection [of words] is that sentence. This should be understood in other cases as well.

But how can there be an injunction for an affix from a sentence when the governing rule is *prātipadika* (nominal stem)? To this he says: "from *prabhūta* and so on. Because of the repetition; for if by this [rule] also [the affix were applied] only from a nominal stem...
If this were the case, the rule for the conditional suffix *ṭhyap*— namely,

the supplementary statement (*vārttika*) "after *prabhūta* and others, [the suffix is added] before *āha*" (*prabhūtādibhya āhau*)— would be rendered useless, as the desired form would already be established by this very [proposed rule]. For even words such as *prabhūta* will be included among those beginning with *mā*.
And those [words] produce a cognition as denoters of objects (*karman*) alone,
because they denote adverbs (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). For the status of being an object (*karmatva*) for adverbs will be established in the rule *tatpratyanupūrvamīpalomakūlam* (Pāṇini 4.4.28).

It says, "The meaning of the suffix *pratyaya* is also 'he says' (*āha*). Therefore, because of the repeated statement "from *prabhūta* and so on," it is understood that the rule for the suffix is applied specifically to the sentence itself.
[Regarding the phrase] "from an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇāt*)," this refers to words such as *prabhūta*.
Since it expresses a qualifier of the action, the term "action-qualifier" (kriyāviśeṣaṇa) is stated by applying a metaphorical designation (upacāra) of the denoted object to the denoting word itself.
2. *tena dīvyati khanati jayati jitam* (Pāṇini 4.4.2).

The word *tena* ("by that") is connected with each [verb] individually. Since "the third case is used everywhere for the instrument" (*sarvatra karaṇe tṛtīyā*), in forms such as *dīvyati*, the *lakāra* suffix denotes the agent; thus, because the agent is already expressed by that very suffix, [the third case is not applied].

The instrumental case is not appropriate in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Therefore, the instrumental occurs only in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). Now, why does the instrumental not occur in the sense of the cause (*hetu*)? Because it is not so expressed (*anabhidhānāt*). Although the instrumental is possible in the sense of the agent as well—since in the word *jitam*, the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is prescribed in the sense of the object—it is nevertheless [not used there].
Due to its association with words such as *dīvyati* ("he plays"), the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is understood to denote the instrument (*karaṇa*) alone.
In the example *devadattena jitam* ("victory was won by Devadatta"), the third case denotes the agent (*kartṛ*); therefore, this is simply a sentence, not a derivative suffix (*pratyaya*).

In this sūtra, by means of the word "divyati" and so forth ending in the singular number, there is an indication of a single number for the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) and of the present tense. Consequently, the suffix would apply only when the meaning of the suffix is one, and not in the case of two or many; likewise, it would apply only in the present tense, and not otherwise.

To one who might object regarding the past and the future, he says: "In the meaning of the suffix, there is no intention to express number or time. However, the non-intention to express those two arises because they are inseparable;
for necessarily, a designation must be made by some number and at some time.
"It must be performed. These two [number and time] are not the primary elements, nor is there an intention to express them.

If, then, number and time are not intended to be expressed, does it follow that the means [the sacrifice] is also not intended to be expressed, since they belong to the same context? This is not a fault; for without the intention to express one, the second— [cannot be expressed].
The utterance of a word would otherwise be purposeless; therefore, it must necessarily be intended [to convey its meaning].

If only the etymological sense were intended in cases such as *divyati* and so forth, the utterance of a second word would result in being purposeless; thus, it is not logical to claim that even the grammatical factor (*sādhana*) is not intended to be expressed.

In cases such as "he plays here" (*iha dīvyati*), according to the principle that "the verb (*ākhyāta*) has action as its primary meaning," it is the action alone that is expressed by the word as the principal element, while the agent is subordinate; however, in the case of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) such as *ākṣika* ("a gambler"),
it is the agent alone that is expressed here as the principal element, while the action is subordinate— and this [position] is incorrect.

If someone were to object that just as this [action] is expressed by means of a suffix produced after a verb (ākhyāta), so too it ought to be expressed when joined with a suffix at the end of a nominal stem, he says:
"And even though the action is primary," and so forth. And this is the very nature of linguistic expression, by which...
Even though the suffix (taddhita) follows the predominance of the action, it becomes predominant with respect to the agent;
therefore, the state of being an agent must be understood here. For even one's own nature does not deserve to be questioned.

3. *saṃskṛtam* | (4.4.3) The division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows: [the rule] *kulatthakopadhādaṇ* (4.4.4) is an exception (*apavāda*) intended so that it applies only to the sense of "prepared" (*saṃskṛta*), and not in cases such as "he plays with" (*dīvyati*). This is the purpose.
The analysis of the yoga.
4. The suffix *ḍaṇ* is applied after *kulattha* when it is used as a deceptive measure (*upadhā*). (4.4.4) 5. The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after [a word ending in] *tarati*.
(4.4.5) 6. The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after *gopuccha*. (4.4.6)

"There is a distinction regarding the accent. For if the suffix *aka* were used, the word would have its final syllable accented acute (*antodātta*) by the rule "the [suffix] *kit* [is treated as having an indicatory *k*]" (Pāṇini 6.1.165). If the suffix *aṇ* were used, however, the initial syllable would be accented acute due to the indicatory letter *ñ*.

7. *naudvyacaṣṭhan* (4.4.7). In this section, in some instances a *ṣakāra* is seen as part of a *saṃhitā*, while in others it is merely an *anubandha* of an affix; therefore, within this context of the rule for *ṭhak*, it is not known which [is intended].

"Is it *sāṃhitika*? What is the *pratyaya-anubandha*? For this reason, a systematic enumeration has been made to eliminate doubt. He provides this by means of the verse beginning with "ṭhākarṣātparpādibhyaḥ":
"ṭhākarṣāt ṣṭhal" (Pāṇini 4.4.31) and "pargādibhyaṣṭhan" (Pāṇini 4.4.10).

There are these six [suffixes] derived from *vit*: namely, *ṭhan* by "ṭhbhastrādibhyaṣṭhan" (Pāṇini 4.4.16), *ṣṭhan* and *ṣṭhac* by "ṭhkasusīdadaśaikadaśāt ṣṭhanṣṭhacau" (4.4.31), *ṣṭhal* by "ṭhāvasathāt ṣṭhal" (4.4.74), and *ṣṭhan* by "ṭhkiśarādibhyaḥ ṣṭhan" (4.4.53). Now, one might object: "But does not [the rule] 'ṭhanyato ṅīṣ' (4.1.40) [apply here]?"

There are indeed other [suffixes] marked with *ṭ* besides these; why then is it said that "these six" are meant? To this, he says: "In the section on *ṭhak*, etc. Since *ṭhak* is the subject under discussion, he shows that only those suffixes marked with *ṭ* which fall within that specific section are intended to be included.

"But even if this is so, would there not still be seven [rules], because two *ṣit* affixes are prescribed in the rule *kusādibhyaḥ saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 4.4.31)? To this he says: "But the number six is in relation to the prescriptive statements (*vidhivākya*)," because there are seven *ṣit* affixes. By this very [rule], the *yogāḥ* (formations) ending in *ṣit* are employed.
The meaning is that these six yogas have the sense of the suffix -ṣit.
8. *carati* (Pāṇini 4.4.8). 9. *ākarṣāt ṣṭhal* (Pāṇini 4.4.9).
"The letter *ṭh* is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*). By the rule *liti*, the syllable preceding the suffix marked with *l* becomes udātta, as follows: [example].

It may be that the letter *ṣ* is for the sake of [forming] the suffix *ṅīṣ*; thus, by the rule *ṣid-gaurādibhyaś-ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.41), the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs, as in the word *ākarṣikī*. It is said that "a touchstone (*nikaṣopala*) is so called because it is used for the purpose of testing gold. This is because gold is drawn across it (*ākṛṣyate*).

10. *parpādibhyaḥ ṣṭan* (Pāṇini 4.4.10). In the list beginning with *parpa*, it is recited that "for *pāda*, there is *paddh-*". This is its meaning: after the word *pāda*, the suffix *ṣṭhan* occurs, and by virtue of its connection [with that suffix], the substitute *pad-* is applied [to *pāda*]. Thus, *padikaḥ*.

[The opponent asks: "If this is so, why is the substitution of *pad* for *pād* prescribed by the Vārttika ‘*padbhāva ike caratāv upasaṃkhyānam*’ (Vārttika 740) under the rule ‘*padyaty atadarthe*’ (Pāṇini 6.3.53)? [The author replies: This is not a fault, because the rule ‘*pādaḥ pat*’ (Pāṇini 6.4.130) is not of ancient (Pāṇinian) origin.

11. *śvagaṇāṭ ṭhañ ca* (Pāṇini 4.4.11). [The example given is] *śvāgaṇikaḥ*. A group of dogs is a *śvagaṇaḥ*. Now, since the word *śvan-* is recited among the *dvārādi-* group, by the prohibition of vṛddhi according to *dvārādīnāṃ ca* (7.3.4), [the form would be established] simply through that rule. To this he says: "In the case of *śvan* etc., when *iñ* follows, [the suffix] *ṭa* [is applied]," and so forth. And since the operations pertaining to the *dvārādi* group are prohibited, only the initial *vṛddhi* occurs.
12. [The suffix *cha*] is added after words such as *vetana* to denote one who lives by means of them. (4.4.12) 13. [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is added after *vasna*, *kraya*, and *vikraya*.
(4.4.13) Regarding this, it is said: "The inclusion of *kraya* and *vikraya* is for the sake of both the compound and its separated forms. Here, [the rule applies] by virtue of the *tantra* method.

The words "purchase" (kraya) and "sale" (vikraya) have been uttered; therein, it should be understood that for one [word] the meaning is taken as a compound, while for the other, the meaning is taken in its analyzed form.

14. Also [the suffix *kan*] after the word *āyudha*. (Pāṇini 4.4.14) 15. [The suffix *kan*] after words such as *utsaṅga*, when meaning "he carries. (Pāṇini 4.4.15) 16. [The suffix] *ṣṭhan* after words such as *bhastrā*. (Pāṇini 4.4.16)

In the rule *bhastrādibhyaḥ ṣṭhan* (Pāṇini 5.2.39), the word *śīrṣebhāra* is recited. In that context, the substitution of *śīrṣan* for *śiras* occurs by virtue of this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*). The compound is formed through a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) *saptamī* (Pāṇini 2.1.40). Furthermore, the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending occurs optionally by the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.3.14).

17. *vibhāṣā vivadhavīvadhāt* (4.4.17). [The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied] in the sense of "carrying around" (*paryāhāre*). It is called "carrying around" (*paryāhāra*) because it is carried all around; it refers to a circular arrangement (*maṇḍala*) and the like.

18. The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the word *kuṭilikā*. (Pāṇini 4.4.18) 19. The suffix *aṇ* is applied after words such as *akṣadyūta* when meaning "completed. (Pāṇini 4.4.19) 20. The suffix *mam* is always applied after a word ending in the suffix *tri*. (Pāṇini 4.4.20)

"In the rule *ṭhḍivataḥ ktriḥ*, this word *tri-* is understood [as a technical suffix], not the numeral word. Why is the numeral word not understood? Because it would not convey the intended meaning; for by merely saying "three times" (*tris*), the intended sense is not communicated. [The example is] *uptrimam*. [This is derived from the root *tṛ* with the suffix *ktri*, according to the rule *vacisvapiyajādīnāṃ kiti*.]
(6.1.15) Thus there is *samprasāraṇa*.

"The mention of *nitya* is for the purpose of precluding independence (*svātantrya*). Independence refers to the usage of the suffix *tri* alone, without the suffix *map*; the mention of *nitya* is for the purpose of precluding that.
By the phrase "when the word *nitya* is used for the purpose of excluding independence," [the author] demonstrates the meaning that results; and by the phrase "in another domain," etc.,
he explains that which is excluded by the particle *eva*.
That which has an object other than the meaning of the suffix *maya* is a different [suffix], where no suffix occurs;
it should be understood that the mention of "eternal" (*nitya*) is for the purpose of excluding that [different suffix].

21. *Apamitya* and *ayācita* [are used] in the sense of *kakka* and *nau*. (4.4.21) Regarding the word *apamitya*: it is formed by the suffix *ktvā* according to Pāṇini 3.4.19, *udīcāṃ māṅo vyatīhāre*, and when the substitution of *lyap* is applied to that *ktvā*, the form *apamitya* arises. Furthermore, by the rule *ktvāsosunkasunaḥ*... [it is treated as indeclinable].

(1.1.40) Thus, this is designated as an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Consequently, although there is a governing rule for the third case (*tṛtīyā*) ending, the suffix is prescribed from this very word even though it is devoid of any case-ending.

22. *saṃsṛṣṭe* | (4.4.22) Now, one might object: since the suffix will apply to "that which is mixed" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*) by the rule itself, namely *saṃskṛtam* (4.4.3)—for that with which something is mixed is indeed "prepared" (*saṃskṛta*) by it—is this not so? This is not correct; for... [the suffix applies] to that which exists...

Refinement (*saṃskāra*) is the production of excellence, while conjunction (*saṃsarga*) is the state of being one with another. And in that case, there ought not to be excellence; rather, upon contact with a substance that is pure in its own nature, only its own natural pre-eminence occurs, not excellence [brought about by the other].
Only the mere fact of contact is intended as the cognition [of the suffix]; therefore, it must simply be said "conjoined" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*); this alone [is correct].

Let it be done; what is the purpose of the rule "saṃskṛtam" (Pāṇini 4.4.3)? Even in the absence of a connection (*saṃsarga*), the suffix is desired where there is that which has been refined (*saṃskṛta*)—as in *vaidyika* ("medical"), for a connection with knowledge (*vidyā*) is not possible here; a connection occurs only between two substances (*dravya*), such as between a staff and a person.

Because that property belongs to what possesses form (*mūrtimant*), whereas knowledge (*vidyā*) does not possess form. For the sake of prescribing [the suffix] after *kulattha*, *kola*, and *dhānya* (Pāṇini 4.4.4), the mention of "refined" (*saṃskṛta*) must be made. For the suffix is not intended merely for that which is mixed together;
rather, it is intended when a quality has been imparted by that [mixing].
23. *cūrṇādibhya iniḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.23).

Now, one might object: since those things which are mixed with flour (*cūrṇa*) possess that flour, the desired form is already established by the suffix *-in* used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*); therefore, this rule is redundant. This is not so.

If there is the intention to express mere existence, the formation would be established by means of a suffix denoting possession (*matvarthīya*); however, if there is the intention to express a state of being mixed, it is not established, for in that case the suffix *ṭhak* would be required. Since its purpose is to set aside the application of *ṭhak*, how could this [suffix] be devoid of meaning?

24. *lavaṇālluk* (Pāṇini 4.4.24). Regarding the phrase "denoting a substance" (*dravyavācī*) and so forth: this word *lavaṇa* is indeed a quality-word (*guṇavacana*) when it refers to a specific taste (*rasaviśeṣa*), because taste is a quality (*guṇa*). It is also a substance-word (*dravyavācana*), as for example in the expression "five *lavaṇas*."

Regarding the term *lavaṇāni*: therein, that which is a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*) does not necessitate the elision [of the feminine suffix]. For although a substance (*dravya*) is not physically mixed with its qualities, nevertheless, words denoting qualities apply to the substance through a relationship of non-difference, expressed as "this is that" (*so 'yam*), just as in the cases: "the white cloth" (*śuklaḥ paṭaḥ*) and "the alkaline salt" (*kṣāraṃ lavaṇam*). Thus it is established.

The reading is: "shaving" (*kṣaura*) and "sour curd" (*amla-dadhi*); likewise, the word *lavaṇa* will also function [as a name]. What then is the use of elision (*luk*)? It must necessarily be understood in this way; otherwise, elision would have to be prescribed even after words such as "sweet" (*madhura*). However, in other cases, words denoting substances (*dravya-śabda*) do not [function as names], because their identity is established through the cognition "this is that very thing."
They exist; therefore, the word *lavaṇa*, when denoting a substance, causes the elision [of the feminine suffix].
25. *mudgādaṇ* (Pāṇini 4.4.25). 26. *vyañjanair upasikte* (Pāṇini 4.4.26).
Regarding the phrase "*vyañjanaiḥ ra*" [in the rule], the use of the plural number is intended to exclude the application of the rule to the word-form itself.

By the word "tena" (by that), because it is already established by the governing context (*adhikāra*), the mention of the third case (*tṛtīyā*)—which is already present as the governing case-ending (*samarthavibhakti*)—is for the sake of easy comprehension. While the term "saṃsṛṣṭe" (in contact with) from [Pāṇini 4.4.22] is still in force, this [mention of "tena"] serves the purpose [of specifying] "mixed with" (*upasikta*);
so that [the suffix] may apply to cases such as *odana* (rice), etc., but not here [in the following example]: [Example omitted in source]

"A pot mixed with soup," or "rice sprinkled with water. Water is not a *vyañjana* (condiment/sauce), because the word *vyañjana* is conventionally restricted to things such as soup. [Objection: But surely that which is sprinkled with *vyañjanas* becomes prepared (*saṃskṛta*) by them; in that case, it is indeed *saṃskṛta*.

[Objection: It is not established; for refinement (*saṃskāra*) is the enhancement of that which already exists, and such [enhancement] is not possible when [the object] is saturated with everything. To explain: when rice and other foods, whose sweet flavors have vanished, are saturated with substances possessing flavor, there is only a diminution [of the original state], not an enhancement.
It is also desired [to be included] even when merely sprinkled; therefore, its separate commencement is made prior to that.

27. *ojaḥ sahombhasā vartate* (Pāṇini 4.4.27). Regarding the word "vartate": it means "exerts itself" (*ceṣṭate*). The phrase "it is a qualifier of that process" (*tatprakriyāviśeṣaṇam*) and so forth indicates by this very [sūtra] that the action denoted by the root *vṛt* must be performed. The form "vartate" expresses the sense of performing the present action (*vartamānam karoti*).
For that [word], being connected as something to be performed for the sake of the verbal activity (*vṛtti*), becomes an object (*karman*).

And because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [object], its qualifier is also construed as something to be performed; thus, it too follows as an object. This is so even in the case of an intransitive root, provided it is a qualifier of an action.

The state of being an object (*karmatva*) has been explained. Although the second case (*dvitīyā*) is already obtained by the word *tat* (meaning "that") through its capacity as a governing case, the bases (*prakṛti*) are here specified with the second case ending for the sake of clarity; otherwise, since the fifth case is the logical one in the formulation of suffixes (*pratyaya-vidhi*), they would have been specified with that [fifth] case-ending alone.

28. *tatpratyanupūrvam īpalomakūlam* (Pāṇini 4.4.28). [The example is] *prātīpikaḥ*. [This is derived as follows: *pratigatā āpaḥ asmin* ("water has gone back toward this") is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The suffix *a* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmānakṣe* (Pāṇini 5.4.74). And thus...
In the first case, there is the substitution of *ī* by rule 6.3.97 (*dvyantarupasargebhyo'pa īt*).
In the other case, however, by rule 6.3.98 (*ūdanordeaśe*), there is the substitution of *ū* for *ap* when the word does not mean a place; from that [base], the suffix *ṭhak* is added.
Thus we have *prātilomikaḥ* and *ānulomikaḥ*—as stated in both the *Kāśikā* and the *Padamañjarī*.

"Prātilomika" and "ānulomika": these are *bahuvrīhi* compounds meaning "one whose body hairs go against [the grain]" (*pratigatāni lomāny asya*) and "one whose body hairs follow [the grain]" (*anugatāni lomāny asya*). The suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule *ṭhac pratyanu* (Pāṇini 5.4.75) and others, serving as the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*).

29. *Parimukham* (4.4.29). [The word *pari* takes] the fifth case (*pañcamī*) by the rule *apaparibahirañcavaḥ pañcamyā* (2.1.12), forming an *avyayībhāva* compound; from this, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied. It means "facing oneself."
A servant who attends [to his master] by avoiding [other tasks] is *pārimukhika*. Alternatively, the prefix *pari-* is used in the sense of "on all sides" (*sarvatobhāve*);

thus, by the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18), it forms a *prādi*-compound. A servant who attends [to his master] from whichever direction the master's face is turned—[that is, following him everywhere]—is [a *pārimukhika*].
That which pertains to the face.

30. *pyaccchati garhyam* (Pāṇini 4.4.30). [The example is] *dviguṇam*. By this, he shows that the word for the purpose applies to the thing itself (*tādarthyāt tācchabdyam*). What is the intention of one who, having applied the word *dviguṇa* to an object intended for the sake of a double [debt], forms a suffix there?

He thinks as follows: "A 'dvaiguṇika' refers to a creditor (*uttamarṇa*), and he does not give back double [the principal]; rather, having let [the debt] accumulate, he takes double. For otherwise, if the opposite were the case, it would indeed be praiseworthy, not censurable. When there is a single purpose..."

Because it serves that purpose, the word "twofold" (*dviguṇa*) is used; for when one gives even a single thing for the sake of a twofold purpose, it becomes "twofold," and thus it is censurable (*garhya*). Furthermore, "censure" (*garhā*) here should be understood as the fact that what is given, though prohibited by the scripture, is a cause of demerit (*pratyavāya*). [The term *dviguṇa*] is a different primary form (*prakṛtyantara*).

Thus, he rejects even this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*). Even in that case, because it serves that purpose, that which is given for the sake of interest is expressed by the word *vṛddhi*. But surely, if that [supplementary rule] were rejected, then when a suffix is added after the word *vṛddhi*, the form *vārdhika* would also result? This is not a fault; [The text continues: ...because the word *vṛddhi* here refers to the principal (*mūladhana*) as well, since it is the source from which interest arises. For the word *vṛddhi* is applied to both the principal and the interest, just as the term "mother" is used for both the mother herself and the grandmother. Therefore, the form *vārdhika* does not occur. Or rather, let it occur; there is no contradiction with usage, for the word *vārdhika* is indeed attested in the sense of "one who lives by interest. Furthermore, the word *vṛddhi* is applied to the principal because it is the cause of interest, just as the word "lamp" is applied to the wick because it is the cause of light. Thus, the objection is refuted. Alternatively, the word *vṛddhi* may be understood as referring to the principal through its connection with the action of lending, just as the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) is used for the sacrificer. Consequently, the form *vārdhika* is not produced. Or again, let it be produced; there is no contradiction with usage, for the word *vārdhika* is indeed attested in the sense of "one who lives by interest. For, according to the analogy of the sheep and the ewe (*avyavika-nyāya*), by the word *vṛddhi* there is only a sentence;
whereas by the word *vṛdhuṣi*, there is both a sentence and a function (*vṛtti*).
31. *kusīda-daśaikādaśāt ṣṭhan-ṣṭhacau* (Pāṇini 4.4.31).

In this rule as well, having applied the word *daśaikādaśa* to a thing that is the object of a loan (*kusīda*) and to the ten items that constitute the "ten-plus-one" (*daśaikādaśa*), the suffixes are added from that base. In all cases, the intended meaning is as previously explained.
It should be understood that "ten and eleven" (*daśa ca ekādaśa ca*) is a coordinate compound (*sāmānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*). Now, one might object:
"Is it not the case that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not possible between two things that have different referents?
[The answer is: The word "ten-and-eleven" (*daśaikādaśa*) also functions through metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*) to mean ten, with respect to those eleven objects.
Thus, there is no fault. One who gives ten and one—that is, eleven—is called "daśaikādaśa. The form *daśaikādaśāt* is established by the rule as having a final vowel *a*;
for what purpose? So that the final vowel *a* may be heard even in a sentence, as in *daśaikādaśān*.
"He bestows."
32. *uñchati*.
(Pāṇini 4.4.32) Regarding the word "uñchati," it means "he gathers [grain] by shaking [the stalks]."
33. *rakṣati* (Pāṇini 4.4.33).
34. *śabdadarduraṃ karoti* (Pāṇini 4.4.34). Since the accusative case-ending is already obtained by the word *tat* itself, [the rule] *śabdadarduram* [is stated].

The second mention is for the purpose of illustrating a worldly sentence. "He makes a sound like a frog" is a common worldly sentence. This indicates that the suffix occurs where there is usage in the world, and not elsewhere; therefore, [the suffix is applied] to *śabda*.

In the case of *karoti ravaraḥ*, [the suffix] does not occur. In the world, he is called a "grammarian" (*śābdika*) who knows the word (*śabda*); it is only the grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*) who knows the word, and therefore the suffix occurs only there, not in *ravara*. Furthermore, that grammarian knows every word by means of the suffix, the base (*prakṛti*), and so forth.

35. *pakṣimatsyamṛgān hanti* (Pāṇini 4.4.35). It is desired that there be the inclusion of the actual forms (*svarūpa*), their synonyms (*paryāya*), and their qualifiers (*tadviśeṣaṇa*). But how is it that the inclusion of synonyms and so forth is obtained, even though it is merely desired?

Because the designation is primarily concerned with the meaning. For it has been established previously that when a designation is primarily concerned with the word-form (*śabda*), there is a grasping of the form itself, whereas when it is primarily concerned with the meaning (*artha*), this is not the case. If, then, synonyms are also to be included, then [the rule would apply] even in cases such as *ajihmān hanti* and *animiṣān hanti*.

Does it follow [that this is a fault]? This is not a fault; for although the case-ending capable of governing a second case (dvitīyāsamarthavibhakti) has already been obtained here, the repeated mention of the case-ending capable of governing a second case is for the purpose of illustrating the usage of common worldly sentences (*laukikavākya*). This is the summary: the suffix occurs where there is the linguistic usage of common worldly sentences.

This is for the purpose of indicating the meaning "not elsewhere"; therefore, the suffix does not occur in cases such as *ajihmān hanti* (he kills the straight). When there is an intention to express the meaning "he kills the straight" or "he kills the unblinking," there is no usage in common worldly practice of the forms *ājihmikaḥ* or *ānimiṣikaḥ*. In that regard—

Among birds, "pākṣikaḥ" is an example of the actual form [of the word], while "śākunikaḥ" is an example of a synonym. "Māyūrikaḥ" and "taitirikaḥ" are examples of specific types. Among fish, "mātsyikaḥ" is an example of the actual form, while "mainikaḥ" is an example of a synonym.

Regarding fish, "śāpharikaḥ" and "śākulikaḥ" denote specific types; "mārgikaḥ" denotes the general nature [of a hunter]; "hāriṇikaḥ" denotes a synonym [for deer-hunter]; and "saukarikaḥ" and "sāraṅgikaḥ" denote specific types.
36. *paripanthañca tiṣṭhati* (4.4.36).

Just as in the case of *parimukham*, where the word *parimukha* possesses both the status of an avyayībhāva compound and a tatpuruṣa compound, so too here the word *paripantha* should be understood to possess those two [statuses]. Regarding the word *tat*:

"From that which is not in apposition with a second [case ending]. Now, one might object: "But this root *sthā* (to stand) is intransitive; how then can it have a connection with a second case? This is not a fault; for even in the case of intransitive roots, time (*kāla*), state (*bhāva*), and distance (*adhvan*) receive the designation of "object" (*karman*). [This is the reading of the established text. Time, state, and distance receive the designation of "object."

They proceed [in this manner]. And so it has been said: "Time, state, and the distance to be traversed are designated as *karman* for roots that are otherwise *akarman*" (Vārttika 1.4.51). The term *pāripanthika* ("waylayer") is an *avyayībhāva* compound. It refers to a thief who stands having obstructed the path.
It is expressed by the word *pāripanthika*. However, according to the *tatpuruṣa* interpretation, one who stands obstructing the path is called a *paripanthika*.
Regarding the phrase "the letter *ca*" and so forth: in the expression "and he stands" (*tiṣṭhati ca*), the letter *ca* occurs immediately after the meaning of the suffix has been established.
It must be understood that [the particle *ca*] effects a conjunction of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) itself, specifically with that which is of the same class.
Now, why is it not understood as a conjunction of the base (*prakṛti*) alone? Because the status of being an object (*karman*) would be untenable;
for in that case, the accusative case, which is the governing case-ending (*samartha-vibhakti*), would follow, yet the root *sthā* is intransitive (*akarmaka*).
The status of being an object (*karmabhāva*) is not applicable to the natural objects (*prakṛti*) such as fish;
for it is only time, state, and distance that are desired to receive the designation "object" when used with intransitive verbs, but not fish and the like.
He says this second utterance of *karoti* in order to demonstrate its usage in common speech.

The word *paripatha* is a synonym for *pathin*—[as stated in] the *Kāśikā*: "it is a synonym for *paripatha*. He asks: "What is the purpose of making this known? and replies with the words "In another scope," etc. For if this rule of notification were not present, the base (*prakṛti*) being indicated in conjunction with the suffix *ṭhak* would [not apply] due to the absence of that suffix.
[This] would follow [as an undesirable consequence]. But when there is a making known [of the meaning], even in a case where a suffix does not occur, the usage is justified.

37. *māthottarapadapadavyanupadaṃ dhāvati* (Pāṇini 4.4.37). *Daṇḍamātha* means a straight path; one who runs along it is called *dāṇḍamāthika*. *Śulkamātha* means the collection of tolls; one who runs after that is called *śaulkamathika*. [Likewise for] *padasya*...

The term *anupada* is an *avyayībhāva* compound meaning "afterwards" or "subsequently. In the phrase *anupadaṃ dhāvati*, the suffix *ṭhañ* (forming *ānupadikaḥ*) is applied. The meaning is that he runs in close pursuit. Since the second case (*dvitīyā*) was already established as the governing case (*samarthavibhakti*), the explicit mention of the second case again is so that the suffix may apply when the word ending in the second case follows a word beginning with *iṣṭādi*.

This is for the purpose that [the rule] "it shall not be undesirable" (*aniṣṭāt mā bhūt*) may apply. Therefore, the compounding of the word *anu* with the rules such as *tena yuktamalpākhyam* (P. 2.1.15), *yatsamayā* (P. 2.1.16), and *kugatiprādayaḥ* (P. 2.2.18) does not take place.

38. *ākrandāṭṭhañ ca*. (Pāṇini 4.4.38) [The example is] *ārtāyanam*. That which is gone to (*ayana*) for the sake of protection is *ayana*; that which is the *ayana* of those who are distressed (*ārtānām*) is *ārtāyanam*. The meaning is "refuge."

39. *padottarapadaṃ gṛhṇāti* (Pāṇini 4.4.39). By the mention of the word *pada*, only the word-form itself is understood, not a *pada* ending in a nominal suffix (*sup*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). For this very reason, he says:
"that which has the word *pada* as its *uttarapada*. And this [occurs] in the second [case].
This is understood because it is intended to illustrate a worldly sentence and because there is no mention of the second [technical] term.
"It takes up a word following another word" is the worldly sentence. By illustrating this, it is indicated that there is the taking up of a worldly word, not a technical (pāribhāṣika) one.

Now, why was it not simply stated as "from the end of a word" (*padāntāt*)? To this he says: "It was not stated as 'from the end of a word,'" and so forth. The meaning has already been explained. [The rule] should apply from that which has a word as its subsequent member (*uttarapada*). However, some hold that here the word *pada* refers to a quarter-verse of a *śloka*.

40. *pratikaṇṭhārthalalāmañca* | (4.4.40) *pratikaṇṭham* means "towards the throat" (*kaṇṭhaṃ kaṇṭhaṃ prati*). This is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of "corresponding to" (*yathārthe*), or else [it is formed] in the sense of "facing," according to the rule *lakṣaṇenābhipratī ābhimukhye* (Pāṇini 2.1.14). Thus, it means "facing the throat."

*Pratikaṇṭham* means "facing the throat" (*kaṇṭhasya abhimukhyam*). One who seizes everyone by the throat, or one who seizes [someone] directly by the throat, is called *prātikaṇṭhika*. Furthermore, in the section concerning words formed with the second case ending, the mention of the base form ending in the second case is intended so that it may apply to desired instances, and not to undesired ones.

Because [the compound] "pratigataḥ kaṇṭham" (gone toward the throat) is a *tatpuruṣa* according to the rule "kugatiprādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.2.18), the word *pratikaṇṭha* does not [arise] from that [specific formation].
41. *dharmañcarati* (4.4.41).

[The rule] "the root *car-* [is used] in the sense of repeated practice (*āsevā*)" applies here; for "repeated practice" means doing something again and again. [The Vārttika] "it should also be stated [after the word] *adharma*" means that after the word *adharma*, [the suffix *aṇ* is added] in the sense of "practicing."
The meaning is that the form of this rule, "ṭhag bhavati," must be explained. Here is the explanation:

the particle *ca* (and) is carried over (*anuvartate*) from the preceding sūtra; it should be understood as having the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccayārtha*).
Therefore, [the suffix] will also occur after the word *adharma*.

42. *pratipatham eti ṭhañ* (Pāṇini 4.4.42). [The example is] *prātipathikaḥ*. As before, this is an *avyayībhāva* compound used either in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*) or in the sense of facing toward (*ābhimukhya*). *Pratipatham* means "toward each path" (*panthānam panthānam prati*). In the sense of facing toward: "facing toward the path."
*Pratipatham*: he who goes along all paths, or goes toward a path, is called *prātipadika*.
43. *samavāyān samavaiti* (Pāṇini 4.4.43). [The commentary states:

"The term *samavāya* refers to a collection (*samūha*), not to *samprasāraṇa*. Why is this so? Because in that context, it would be inappropriate for the meaning of the suffix in *samavaiti* [to refer to *samprasāraṇa*]. Rather, it means "having come together, one becomes a part of that."

The meaning of the word *samavaiti* is as follows: deliberation (*sampradhāraṇā*) is formless (*amūrti*), a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*), and it cannot become a constituent part of that [deliberation]. Therefore, the meaning of the word *samavāya* is simply a collection (*samūha*), not the sense of "going" (*eti*). For while "going" (*eti*) refers to the present tense, "he comes together" (*samavaiti*) [refers to the act of uniting].

The statement is for the purpose of understanding the specific meaning. "It goes" (eti) means it performs mere reaching; "it enters into union" (samavaiti) means that having arrived, it becomes a constituent part of that.

44. The suffix *ṇya* is applied after the word *pariṣad*. (4.4.44) 45. Or, it is optionally applied after the word *senā*. (4.4.45) 46. The suffix *ṇya* is applied to form a name when [the agent] looks at the *lalāṭa* or the *kakudī*. (4.4.46)

"The purpose is to restrict the denotation. This means that there is a restriction regarding the suffix when the denoted object is a specific type of servant, so that the word may apply only in that sense. "But not for the sake of conventional meaning," because the words *lālāṭika* and *kaukkuṭika* are already established through convention (*rūḍhi*) as singular entities.

Regarding the passage beginning with "tadanena" and so forth: since the forehead is seen at a distance from all other limbs, therefore, by this seeing of the forehead, the lack of close contact (*anupaśleṣa*) of the servant toward the master is obtained. However, in this case, there is neither the meaning of "forehead" nor the act of "seeing. And as for the kind of non-contact that [is implied]—
What is intended [by this] is shown by the phrase "not being present at one's duties.

Regarding the expression "also by the word *kukkuṭī*," etc.: for the flight of a cock (*kukkuṭa*) has a limited spatial range. Thus, by this, the smallness of the space covered by the cock’s flight is indicated; however, it is not [the case] here that...
And there exists a region called Kukkuṭārtha.

47. [The suffix] *dharmya* [is applied after a word ending in *ṅīp*]. (4.4.47) 48. The suffix *aṇ* [is applied] after words such as *mahiṣī*. (4.4.48) 49. The suffix *añ* [is applied] after a word ending in *ṛt*. (4.4.49)
50. *avakrayaḥ* | (4.4.50) 51. *tadasya paṇyam* | (4.4.51) One for whom cakes (*apūpa*) are the merchandise is called *āpūpikaḥ*.

Now, why is the word *paṇya* not employed in the *vṛtti* (compound) in the same way as it is employed in the *vākya* (sentence)? To this he says: "The word *paṇyam*," and so on, "the qualifier," etc. Now, for one who, upon such consideration, includes the meaning of *paṇya* within the *vṛtti*, the word *paṇya* is not used because its purpose has already been served (*gatārthatvāt*).
It is applied.
52. [The suffixes] *ṭhañ* and *aṇ* are added after *lavaṇa*. (Pāṇini 4.4.52) 53.
[The suffix] *ṣṭhan* is added after *kiśara* and others. (Pāṇini 4.4.53) 54. [The suffix *ṣṭhan* is added] optionally after *śalālu*. (Pāṇini 4.4.54)
Regarding the word *ṭhśalālukaḥ*: [the suffix] *ka* is applied by the rule *isusuktāntāt kaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.51).

55. *Śilpam* (Pāṇini 4.4.55). The term *śilpam* means "skill. It refers to a specific kind of knowledge preceded by the practice of an action. For example: "The playing of the *mṛdaṅga* drum is his *śilpa*. That is, the *mṛdaṅga* is played by means of that skill (*śilpa*).

Regarding the term *tanmṛdaṅgavādanam*: surely, when the suffix is produced by analyzing the compound as "one whose craft (*śilpa*) is the playing of the mṛdaṅga drum," it would apply only to the word *mṛdaṅgavādana*, and not to the word *mṛdaṅga*; consequently, it ought to be *mārdaṅgavādanika*. How then [is the form *mārdaṅgika* justified]?
"How does one become a *mārdaṅgika*? To this he says: "The playing of the *mṛdaṅga*," and so forth.

It is the sound of the *mṛdaṅga* itself that produces the suffix (*pratyaya*), and that [sound] occurs in the act of playing the *mṛdaṅga*, not in the *mṛdaṅga* [instrument] itself. In this case, the inherent nature of the power of words (*śabdaśaktisvābhāvya*) is the reason. Nor is this...

The rule (niyama) is this: by whatever word a compound is analyzed (vigraha), from that very word the suffix must be formed. For example, in the case of "this is the meat of a sheep" (*āvikam māṃsam*), where the analysis is made using the word *avi*, the suffix occurs from the word *avika* itself; so it is here as well.

The conflict is resolved by the sound of the drum-playing itself, while the cognition arises from the word "mṛdaṅga" (drum); therefore, the intention is that since the meaning is already conveyed therein, the word "śilpa" (art/craft) is not employed.

56. *maḍḍuka-jharjhara-ādayaḥ* optionally [take the suffix *ṭhak*] (Pāṇini 4.4.56). 57. [The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after a word denoting] a weapon (*praharaṇa*) [to form a word meaning "one who uses that as a weapon"] (Pāṇini 4.4.57).

In the example "dhānuṣkaḥ" ("an archer"), there is the substitution of *kā* [for the final syllable], and the visarga [of the original *iṇ* suffix] is replaced by *ṣ* according to Pāṇini 8.3.39 (*iṇaḥ ṣaḥ*).
The substitution of *ṣ* [occurs].
58. And [the suffix] *aṭṭhañ* is added after *paraśvadha*. (4.4.58) 59. [The suffix] *īkak* is added after *śakti* and *yaṣṭi*.
Now, for what purpose is the long vowel (*ī*) pronounced? Why could it not simply be stated as *ikak*, since even with *ikak* [the desired form would be obtained]?
If the rule for lengthening homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*) is applied, would *śāktīkaḥ* and *yāṣṭīkaḥ* not be established? They are not so established;

for by the rule "of the *i* and of that which ends in *ṭh*" (*ikaḥ kāśe*, Pāṇini 6.4.148), elision (*lopa*) ought to occur. Why, then, would there be lengthening of the homogeneous vowel? It is precisely because of the force of the pronunciation of the *i* that the elision will not take place.
But would not the purpose of the *ikāra* be the prevention of the *avagraha*? This is not so;

for if this were its purpose, the commencement of the rule (*sūtra*) would be useless, since the absence of the *avagraha* is already established even by the letter *ṭh*. It is not useless, because it serves the purpose of preventing [the application of] the entire sentence (*vākya*). Even so—

The mention of the suffix *pratyaya* would be redundant, for the suffix *ṭhak* is already in force; in that case, one should simply have said "after *śaknoti* and *yaṣṭi*. However, this [repetition] will serve to terminate the application of the previous rule. What, then, is the purpose of prescribing the suffix *ikak*? Therefore, by the very force of the mention of *ikak*, there is no elision (*lopa*).

It will be so. Even though the non-elision (*alopa*) would be established by the very fact that *ṭhak* [is present], such that there would be no *anavagraha* (non-separation) due to the absence of elision according to *ṭhyasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), the inclusion of *hīk* is understood as being for the purpose of an additional rule.
By that, the elision according to *ṭhyasyeti ca* (6.4.148) does not occur; just as [the elision] does not occur from *akaḥ*.
Since even the long vowel would not occur by [the rule] *savarṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.101), the form would be heard as being split apart;
therefore, the augment *īk* must be stated.

60. *astināstidiṣṭamatiḥ* | (4.4.60) [The Kāśikā explains: "What then? He whose opinion is that 'the other world exists'—[this is the meaning of] *matiryasya*. But how is this obtained when no specific term has been mentioned? To this he says: *tadetad*.

And so forth. This is obtained through the inherent nature of the expressive power [of words]. Now, one might object: "asti" is a verbal form (*tiṅanta*), whereas "nāsti" is a sentence; therefore, the suffix would not be applicable by these two, because of the governing rule that the context concerns nominal stems (*prātipadika*) [Pāṇini 4.1.1]. To this, he says: "the words *asti* and *nāsti*."
And so forth. Even while conceding both the status of being a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) and the status of being a sentence (*vākya*), he states another solution:
"The cognition [of the meaning] arises from the word, from the verb, and from the sentence."

61. *Śīla* | (4.4.61) [The example is: "He whose habit (*śīla*) is the eating of cakes and bread. This designation is made thus because of the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the term *śīla* to the object [of the habit]. The act of eating and the habit directed toward that object are both included within the formation of the secondary derivative (*taddhita-vṛtti*). Therefore...
The point is that, because [the meaning] is already understood there, the words "habitual eater" (*bhakṣaṇaśīla*) and "word" (*śabda*) are not employed.
62. *ṇa* [is added] after *chatra* and others.
(Pāṇini 4.4.62) In order to demonstrate that the disciple possesses the character (*śīla*) of a *chatra*, he says:
"A *chatra* is so called because of covering (*chādana*) and because of warding off (*apavāraṇa*)," and so forth. By the term *apavāriṇāt*...
He clarifies the meaning of the word "cchādanāt" (from covering):

for that which covers is called a "chatra" (umbrella); by this, even a disciple who is devoted to the teacher's business is fit for that [role], being engaged in the act of concealing those faults of the teacher which he seeks to protect.
"One who performs actions accompanied by truth becomes one whose character is truthful.

Here, the root *sthā* is recited, and it is understood as being preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*). Consequently, because the suffix *aṅ* has already been applied to it according to the rule *ātaścopasarge* (Pāṇini 3.3.106), [the suffix *ac* is not applied].

However, the reading of the root alone is for the purpose of including all prefixes. It is read as "curā," where, by way of irregular derivation (nipātana), there is the suffix -a and the absence of guṇa.

63. *vṛta* [is used] in the sense of "occupied with" (*karmādhyayane*) [Pāṇini 4.4.63]. That which is being reached by an action, whether it be most desired (*īpsitatama*) or least desired (*anīpsitatama*), is the object (*karman*). In this context, however, the "least desired" is understood. For this very reason, he says: "of one who is engaged in study," and so forth. Not...

For indeed, when someone who is engaged in study recites at the time of examination, there occurs that which is desired in the form of a faltering recitation. The word *adhyayana* is either an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*) or an object noun (*karmasādhana*). [Thus,] "studied" (*adhītam*), "is studied" (*adhīyate*), or "the act of studying" (*adhyayanam*). It is chosen.
"Bhūta" means "arisen.

Regarding the phrase "one is different," and so forth: the meaning should be understood differently in view of the correct reading, namely, "dvaiyanyikaḥ; traiyanyikaḥ. [This refers to the rule] "na yvābhyāṃ padāntābhyām" (Pāṇini 7.3.3).

The augment *ai* is applied [to form *adhyai*]. The statement, "All this—namely, that the object [of the action] is the act of studying—is included within the formation of secondary derivatives (*taddhita-vṛtti*)"—means that, for that reason, the word *adhyayanavṛta* is not employed there because its meaning is already understood. This is the intended sense.

64. *Bahvac-pūrvapadāt-ṭhac* (Pāṇini 4.4.64). [The example is] "dvādaśānyikaḥ" (one who owes twelve coins). Here, the word *dvādaśa* has a multi-syllabic (*bahvac*) prior member. It is a *dvandva* compound consisting of "two" (*dvi*) and "ten" (*daśa*). [This is governed by the rule: *Dvyaṣṭanaḥ saṃkhyāyām-abahuvrīhyaśītyoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.47).
Thus there is the substitution of *ā* (by *ātaḥ sthaḥ*); then, having analyzed [the compound] as *dvādaśa-anya*, there is a compound by [Pāṇini 2.1.51], *taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca*.

But surely, once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, because the prior and subsequent members of the compound no longer exist, the prior member is not "possessing many vowels" (*bahvac*), nor does the status of being "as if prior or posterior" (*antādivadbhāvaḥ*) apply—[since it would have to be] on both sides...

Regarding the objection that "in a compound, [the substitution] does not apply to the final or initial [element] as if it were external" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 51), this fault does not arise; for, by the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) of the rule *nendrasya parasya* (Pāṇini 7.3.22), the suffix is applied before the replacement of the stem. Thus, in the example *tatrodaśānyikaḥ*:
*trayaśca daśa ca* (three and ten) forms a *dvandva* compound, and the word *trayaḥ* is substituted [for *tri*] by the rule *trestrayaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.48).

Since the word *anya* here refers to a wrong reading (*apapāṭha*) in contrast to the correct reading (*samyak-pāṭha*), he says: "The fourteen wrong readings," and so forth. But how is it known that the word *anya* refers to a wrong reading? To this he says: "In the *udāta*," and so forth. In the *udāta*...

The use of the anudātta accent where an udātta ought to be used is a faulty reading (apapāṭha). In that context, when someone uses an anudātta where an udātta should be used, they are told, "You are making it something else.
From this, it is understood that the word *anya* refers to a faulty reading.

65. *hitaṃ bhakṣāḥ* | (4.4.65) Now, one might object that when used in conjunction with the word *hita*, the dative case ought to occur, because of the supplementary rule (Vārttika 123): "The dative case occurs in connection with *hita*," as in the rule *tasmai hitam* (Pāṇini 5.1.5).

Is it because of the explicit statement? [The answer is: "By virtue of the semantic force (*sāmarthya*), there will be a transformation of the case-ending. Furthermore, that very same supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) constitutes the semantic force. And as for the indicative mark (*liṅga*): an action whose purpose is benefit is included within the formation of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*); therefore, it is not used [as a separate word].

66. That which is fixed for him is given to him (*tadasmai dīyate niyuktam*). (4.4.66) Now, one might object: since the word *tat* from the rule "that which is his merchandise" (*tadasya paṇyam*, 4.4.51) will be understood as the governing case-ending (*samarthavibhakti*) in the nominative, this [repetition of *tat*] here is redundant.
The employment of the case-ending of the first [case] is [thereby] rendered meaningless; likewise, the meaning of the suffix in "ṭhasmai" is also entirely purposeless.

For indeed, the word "ṭhasya" (Pāṇini 4.4.51) is carried over [into this rule], and since there is a connection with the phrase "dīyate" (it is given), it ought to function as a recipient (*sampradāna*). Consequently, [the rule would apply to that].

When the remaining relationship has ceased, the fourth case ending (*caturthī*) is transformed here; therefore, should one not simply say "that which is given as an assignment" (*dīyate niyuktam*)? To this it is replied:
first, the employment of the case-ending for the "capable" (*samartha*) in the preceding rule was intended to specify that particular capable case-ending.
This is for the purpose of indicating that the suffix is not applied when it does not produce a derivative meaning. Therefore, the following do not occur:

*duḥkham asyādhyayane vṛtam* ("suffering is encountered by him in study") and *ajayo 'syādhyayane vṛtaḥ* ("defeat is encountered by him in study"). For the suffix is desired only after the word *vṛta* when it functions as a past passive participle (*apapāṭha*).
