Is that [suffix] also prescribed by way of an option (*vibhāṣā*) in the present context? To this it is said: the mention of *ṣyañ* must necessarily be made for the sake of subsequent rules. Whether it is done there [in the subsequent rule] or here [in the present one], there is no difference. In the case of "śuklimā," the elision of *ṭil* occurs as before. In the case of "draḍhimā,"...
There is the substitution of *ra* for the initial *pūrvadṛk* [of *pūrvadṛś*].
[The suffix] *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule "ṣid-gaurādibhyaś-ca" (Pāṇini 4.1.41), as in the examples "ṭhāṬcitā" and "yathākāmī.
The elision of *ya* occurs by the rule "halas-taddhitasya" (Pāṇini 6.4.150).

The reading is *ṭhveyatilābhamatimanaḥśāradānām*. Its meaning is as follows: suffixes occur after the word *vi* when followed by *yāta* and the others. Thus: *viyātatvam*, *viyātatā*, *viyātimā*, *vaiyātyam*; *vilābhatā*.
*vilābhatva*, *vailābhya*, *vilābhimā*; *vimatitva*, *vimatitā*, *vaimatya*, *vimatimā*; [the suffix] *aṇ* by [Pāṇini 5.1.131] *ṭhigantāt*, [forming] *vaimata*;
*vimanastva*, *vimanastā*, *vimanimā*, *vaimanasya*; *viśāradatva*.

*viśāradatā*, *vaiśāradya*, *viśāradimā*. Regarding the rule "the suffix *sam* is applied after the words *mati* and *manas*": the suffix *sam* becomes the affix for the latter two, *mati* and *manas*. Thus: *saṃmatitā*, *saṃmatitva*, *saṃmatimā*, *sāṃmatya*; *saṃmanastva*; *saṃmanastā*, *saṃmanimā*.
Harmony.

124. *guṇavacanabrāhmaṇādibhyaḥ karmaṇi ca* (Pāṇini 5.1.124). Since the secondary suffixes (*śaiṣika*) prescribed by *tasyedam* (4.3.120) would otherwise apply here, this rule prescribes the suffix *ṣyañ* in the sense of "action" (*karmaṇi*), and by the force of the word *ca*, also in the sense of "state" (*bhāve*). In this context, the word *karma* denotes "action" (*kriyā*).

He dispels the doubt regarding [the word] *karma* as denoting the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). For those words such as "insentient" (*jaḍa*) and so forth, which are qualities (*guṇa*), as well as those denoting qualities, and [words like] "Brāhmaṇa" and so on—for these, a connection with the means of accomplishment is impossible because they lack the capacity to denote an action (*kriyā*). Therefore, the word *karma* is exclusively a word for action.

"The group beginning with *brāhmaṇa* is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class)," because it has not been specifically enumerated (*avṛtkṛtatvāt*). "The word *ādi* (beginning) signifies 'type' (*prakāra*)," according to the *Kāśikā* and the *Padamañjarī*. Thus, the word *ādi* indicates its status as signifying a type, for the purpose of showing that the suffix *ṣyañ* occurs after words of this type. If this is so, then...

Would the mention of "words expressing qualities" (*guṇavacana*) and the enumeration of *brāhmaṇa* and so forth among the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) be purposeless? It is not purposeless; for that is intended as an elaboration (*prapañca*) and for the sake of prescribing [the suffix] in its own meaning (*svārtha*). In that regard, since the word *brāhmaṇa* denotes a genus (*jāti*), the suffix *añ* would apply by the rule "after words denoting living beings and genera" (Pāṇini 5.1.129).

The suffix *ṣyañ* is prescribed for the purpose of superseding those [other rules]. Regarding *māṇava* and *vāḍava*, the suffix *vuñ* applies when they denote a lineage (*gotra*). [In the case of *arhat*], there is the rule: "After *arhat*, [the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied] and there is also the augment *num*. The reading of this [sūtra] for the sake of the *num* augment is: *arhantya*.
When *cora* and *dhūrta* are used, since they belong to the *manojñādi* group, the suffix *vuñ* would otherwise apply. [The forms] *ārādhaya* and *virādhaya* [are derived accordingly].

From these words beginning with *aparādhaya*, when there is a desire to express offspring (*apatya*), the suffix *añ* is applied by the rule "from a word denoting a country, if it denotes a Kṣatriya" (Pāṇini 4.1.168).

For that [suffix], there is elision (*luk*) by the rule "elision after *kamboja*" (4.1.175). Then, when the suffix *vuñ* for a lineage (*gotra*) would have been applicable, this recitation [is made] for the sake of the primary meaning (*svārthe*) of the group beginning with *ekabhava* and ending with *anyabhāva*.

For the purpose of prescription: when the prohibition [by Pāṇini 5.1.121] *nañpūrvāt* would have applied to the word *akṣetrajña*, and when the suffix *aṇ* would have applied to words such as *kuśala*—preceding the word *bāliśa*—due to their belonging to the *yudādi* group;
and when the suffix *añ* would have applied to the word *bāliśa* because it denotes age (*vayas*).

Since the word *anīśvara* would be subject to the prohibition [of the suffix *ṣyañ*] by the rule "not after a compound beginning with *nañ*" (Pāṇini 5.1.121), the bahuvrīhi compound *alasa* produces the suffix *ṣyañ*; however, in the case of a tatpuruṣa, the prohibition "not after a compound beginning with *nañ*" (5.1.121) ought to apply. Regarding that...

The recitation [of these examples] is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*). Since the suffix *yaK* would otherwise apply to the word *rājan* because it belongs to the *purohitādi* group, [these examples are given];
furthermore, the purpose of the rule regarding words preceded by *naÑ* applies to such forms as *saṃvādin*, *saṃveśin*, *bahubhāṣin*, *śīrṣaghātin*, *sayastha*, *paramastha*, and *duṣpuruṣa*.

This is the recitation (*pāṭha*). Regarding *gaṇapati* and *adhipati*, the suffix *yak*—which is prescribed by the rule for words ending in *pati*—would otherwise apply; this [list] serves to exclude that. For *gaḍula*, *dāyāda*, and *viśasti*, it serves to prevent the application of the suffixes *tva* and *tal*.
For the remaining items, it serves as an elaboration (*prapañca*). One group consists of adjectives (*guṇavacana*), while the second group consists of *brāhmaṇa* and the others.
From those two [words], it would follow that [the suffixes] apply respectively to the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*); why, then, does this not occur?

Because the word *brahmādi* is placed last despite having fewer syllables (*alpāctara*). For that [rule] indicates the independence of the grammatical indicator (*lakṣaṇa*), and thereby makes known the independence from the rule of "respective order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*). Therefore—
There is no correspondence according to the respective order.
125. *stenādyanalopaśca* (5.1.125). 126. *sakhyuryaḥ* (5.1.126).
[The sūtra] *dūtavaṇigbhyāṃ ca* and so forth; this has the sense that the suffix *ya* occurs after the words *dūta* and *vaṇij*.

The meaning is that this must be explained. Here is the explanation: the particle *ca* ("and") from the preceding sūtra is carried over (*anuvartate*) here, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned—namely, "also from a messenger (*dūta*) and a merchant (*vaṇij*)" and so forth.
Thus, [the suffix] also occurs after the words *dūta* and *vaṇij*.
127. *kapi-jñātyor ḍhak* (Pāṇini 5.1.127).
This rule is prescribed because, in the case of the word *kapi* and those ending in *ṭha*, the suffix *aṇ* would otherwise apply by virtue of [Pāṇini 5.1.131]: *ṭha-igantāc ca laghu-pūrvāt*.

Regarding the phrase "according to their respective order" (*yathā-saṃkhyam*), and so forth: therein, [the suffix applies] after words denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*) and after the *brahmaṇa*-class, etc.
In this context, the absence of *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence according to order) has been established; here too, it is now being established.

This is the demonstration: the particle *ca* ("and") recurs here, and it combines the prescription of the suffix *ḍhak* for both the sense of "becoming" (*bhāva*) and "object" (*karman*) from a single base. Therefore, there is no correspondence according to order.

It does not apply; for otherwise, a collective application (samuccaya) would not be possible. Alternatively, because there is no *svarita* accent, there will be no correspondence according to numerical order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*), for it was established previously that "correspondence according to numerical order occurs by virtue of the *svarita* accent. And here, there is no *svarita* accent for the purpose of indicating numerical correspondence.
It is being asserted.
128. *patyantapuruhūtādibhyo yak* (Pāṇini 5.1.128).

After words ending in *pati*, since the suffix *aṇ* would have applied as before, and after the group beginning with *purohita*, since the suffix *ṣyañ* applies due to their inclusion in the *rājanyādigaṇa* (which is a sub-division of the *brāhmaṇādigaṇa*), [the suffix *yak* is prescribed].

In the remaining cases, however, the suffixes *ya* and *tva-tal* are prescribed [by Pāṇini 5.1.126]. Regarding the rule "rājāse" (Pāṇini 5.1.128): after the word *rājan*, when not in a compound (*ase*), the suffix *ya* occurs—thus, *rājyam*. But in a compound, because it belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class (Pāṇini 5.1.124), only the suffix *ṣyañ* occurs—thus, *ādhirājyam*. Now, one might object: what about the word *kevala*?

The word *rājan* is recited in the list beginning with *brāhmaṇa*; how then [is it applied] from the word *adhirāja*? By means of the rule for "that which ends in" (*tadanta-vidhi*). This very point is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the statement "in the case of *as*": namely, that within this section, the word *rājan* functions by the rule of "ending in. Here, in the rule *patyanta-purohitādibhyaḥ*, there are two [words].

Since both *rāśī* and *arthau* denote two things—namely, the state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*)—a correspondence according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) would result due to this similarity;
however, because that [rule] is not marked as *svarita*, it does not apply here, just as in the previous case.
129. [The suffix] *añ* is applied after words denoting a class of living beings (*prāṇabhṛt-jāti*), age (*vayas*), sound (*vac*), color (*chāya*), parts of the body (*udra-gātra*, etc.).
"Living beings" refers to those possessed of breath; the meaning is "the class of such living beings.

For words expressing that [class], provided that it is not possible [to apply other suffixes], the suffix *añ* is prescribed in place of *tva*, *tal*, and so forth. This is because of the inclusion of the term "living beings" (*prāṇabhṛt*).

It does not occur after words such as *tṛṇa* (grass), as in *tṛṇatva* or *tṛṇatā*. Because it is specified that [the suffix applies] to a genus (*jāti*), it does not occur after words such as *Devadatta*, as in *Devadattatva* or *Devadattatā*. However, if a word ends in *i* or *u* and has a light vowel (*laghu*) preceding that final syllable, the suffix *aṇ* occurs by virtue of its higher priority [in the rules].

Regarding the term *vayas-tiraḥ*: even though suffixes such as *tva* and *tal* would apply according to their respective rules after a word denoting age (*vayaḥ*), this rule prescribes the suffix *añ*.

The inclusion of the word "denoting" (*vacana*) is for the purpose of excluding a rule that applies to the specific form [of the word itself]; otherwise, the suffix would apply only after the word *vayas*.

In that regard, for *udgātṛ*, *unnatṛ*, and *adhvaryu*—since these denote officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the suffix *cha* would otherwise apply by the rule *hotrābhyaś chaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.135); therefore, their inclusion here is for the sake of the suffix *añ*. As for *suṣṭhu*, *duṣṭhu*, and *vadhū*:

Even though the previous rule [Pāṇini 4.1.120] would have applied as well, [the author] says: "In the case of *subhaga* when it refers to a mantra. This means that the word *subhaga* produces the suffix *añ* when its object is a mantra—as in *mahate saubhāgyāya*. For it is said: "All rules are optional in the Veda" (*Puṣpavṛtti* 56). [This is also supported by] Pāṇini 7.3.19: *hṛdbhagasindhvanta-*.

Thus, there is no vṛddhi of the subsequent syllable. Why [is] "mantra" mentioned? [To exclude cases such as] *saubhāgyam*, because it belongs to the *brāhmaṇādi* group. The reading of the remaining [words] here is for the purpose of providing exceptions (*śeṣa*) where the suffixes *tva* and *tal* would otherwise apply.

130. *hāyanāntayuvādibhyo’ṇ* (Pāṇini 5.1.130). This rule prescribes the suffix *aṇ* after words ending in *hāyana*, since the suffixes *tva* and *tal* would otherwise have been applicable. Now, one might object: is not the suffix *aṇ* already established for words ending in *hāyana* by the rule *tasyedam* (4.3.120)? It is not so established; for [the present rule] is subsequent [to that].
[The suffix] *tv* and *tal* are superseded [by the suffix *aṇ*]: from *āṣāḍha-hāyaṇa*, in the sense of "the state" (*bhāva*) or "the action" (*karman*), the form would be *āṣāḍha-hāyaṇa*;
otherwise, by the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.114), the suffix *cha* would apply. Therefore, the prescription of *aṇ* after words ending in *hāyana* is correct.
In the word *yauvana*, there is the preservation of the original stem-form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *an* (Pāṇini 6.4.167). [This occurs] among the *yuvan*-class [of words].

In the case of the word *yuvan*, since it would otherwise denote age, the suffix *vuñ*—which applies to words beginning with *manojña*—would be required; its inclusion [in this list] is therefore for the purpose of preventing that. In the case of the word *sthavira*, the suffix *añ* applies because it denotes age.
For the word *hotṛ* as well, the suffix *añ* alone applies because it belongs to the *udgātṛ* group.

Regarding the rule *puruṣāda-samāse*: the suffix *aṇ* occurs after the word *puruṣa* when it does not form a compound. For example: *pauruṣam*. Why "not in a compound"? [Consider] *rājapuruṣatvam*. This is stated because [the suffix *tva*] would otherwise apply by the rule *prāṇabhṛjjāti* (Pāṇini 5.1.129).
Since the word *kamaṇḍalu* already ends in the vowel *ī*, the suffix *aṇ* would have been established even without this rule; however, its purpose here is to set aside the suffixes *tva* and *tal*.

The reading is: "In *hṛdayāse*. The suffix *aṇ* occurs after the word *hṛdaya* when it is not part of a compound. Thus, *hārda*. The substitution of *hṛd* for *hṛdaya* is according to Pāṇini 6.3.50: "In place of *hṛdaya*, [the substitute *hṛd*] occurs before *lekha*, *aya*, *an*, and *āsa*. Why specify "*āse*" [in the rule]? Because the suffix *aṇ* occurs after the word *hṛdaya* when it is not part of a compound; thus, *hārda*. [The substitution of *hṛd* for *hṛdaya* applies here as well.]

In the rule *hṛd-lekha-yadaṇ-lāseṣu* (Pāṇini 6.3.50), there is the substitution of *hṛt* for *hṛdaya*. Why does it say *asaḥ*? [To exclude cases like] *paramahṛdayatvam*. Since words beginning with *kuśala* and ending with *kṣetrajña* belong to the *brāhmaṇādi* group, the suffix *ṣyañ* would otherwise apply; their inclusion here serves to block that. For the remaining words, however, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* apply. But surely, by the principle of *grahaṇavatā*...
Since there is no rule for *tadanta* (extension to what ends with that) based on a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the suffix *aṇ* would not apply at all after a compound;

therefore, is the prohibition regarding "puruṣāsa" and "hṛdayāsa" useless? It is not useless, for this is a locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*): it applies precisely when a compound is intended to be formed.

Regarding the words *puruṣa* and *hṛdaya*: if the prohibition were not stated, then when there was a simultaneous possibility of both the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) and the abstract suffix *aṇ*, the latter alone would apply because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. However, due to the prohibition, the compound occurs first; thereafter, for that which...
That which has a cause for its abstract suffix (bhāvapratyaya) arises. And what is that [cause]? The suffixes *tva* and *tal*: *apuruṣatvam*, *apuruṣatā*; *ahṛdayatvam*, *ahṛdayatā*.
Here, [the group] ending in *hāyana* is the first, and the *yuvan*-class is the second; the meanings also [differ].

There are only two [factors]: the agent and the object; therefore, by implication, one might expect them to correspond respectively [to the agent and the object]. However, that [correspondence] does not occur because the word *yuvan* and others, having fewer syllables, do not undergo the rule for posterior placement (*paranipāta*) due to the indicative mark of deviation from the general rule, or because they are not marked with the *svarita* accent.
131. *igantācca laghupūrvāt* (5.1.131). Regarding the term *igantāt*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has *iK* as its final element.

The base word (*prātipadika*) is the external referent (*anyapadārtha*). Regarding the phrase "in the case of the mention of *laghupūrva*" and so forth: why is [the suffix] not applied after a base ending in *iK* alone?

Why is it qualified? Because, being subordinate to the sense of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, it is impossible to establish a connection with a qualifier. Furthermore, this word "prior" (*pūrva*), being a term of relative determination, requires something else that is posterior.
And since no such posterior element has been specified here, it is not known—prior to what is the [substitute] light?
In order to understand that, he asks: "But from what [cause] is this former [element] light?

Relying on the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), he says: "Because of its vicinity," and so forth. Here, in this sūtra, the "iK" (the vowel *i*) is [the one intended], because it is explicitly mentioned in the text.

Regarding the phrase "by that": the inclusion of the term *ekānta* (standing at the end) by means of the word *laghupūrva* being understood as included within it is redundant, because it would serve no purpose. For when it is stated "from that which has a light vowel preceding," since the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) applies to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), its status as being at the end is obtained by the very force of the context itself.

Thus, the mention of "the end" (anta) is redundant in this interpretation. However, in the previous formulation, if the mention of "the end" were absent, the rule would be understood as simply "laghupūrvād vataḥ," and consequently, even an *ik* that is not at the end would be subject to the operation. Therefore—
The inclusion of the word "anta" (end) is for the purpose of preventing the application of the suffix even after words such as *laśuna* and * lakuṭa*.

[An objection is raised: "How is *kāvyam* [formed]?"—the intention is that otherwise [the suffix would apply], because the word *kavi* has a light penultimate vowel (*laghupūrva*) and ends in a long vowel (*oganta*).
132. *yu*-upadhāt *gurūpottamād vuñ*.

(5.1.132) When suffixes such as *tva* and *tal* would otherwise apply, *vuñ* is prescribed. Here, the word *uttama* is understood as an underived nominal stem (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*); by its very nature, it denotes the last member of a group of three or more.

Having considered this, he says: "The final [vowel] of those beginning with *tri*, etc. However, if there were a reference to that which ends in the suffix *tamap*, then the fault stated regarding *sutāra* in the rule *aṇiñoḥ anārṣayoḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.78) and so forth should be understood here as well, following that same logic. *Upotamam* means "near the highest" (*utama*); it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
This is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to [Pāṇini 2.1.6] *vibhaktisamīpa*.
133. *Dvandvamanojñādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 5.1.133).

When suffixes such as *tva* and *tal* would otherwise apply after a *dvandva* compound, the suffix *vuñ* is prescribed. In the case of words belonging to the *manojñādi* group that denote a quality (*guṇavacana*), the suffix *ṣyañ* applies; furthermore, it applies after the words *caura* and *dhūrta* because they belong to the *brāhmaṇādi* group.

[The suffix] *ṣyañ* alone [is applied]; after the word *yuva*, because it begins with *yav* etc., the suffix *aṇ* is applied; but after the remaining [words], the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are applied. In the expression "the son of such-a-one" (*amuṣyaputraḥ*), the non-elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending occurs by way of an irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Here, in the group beginning with *dvandva* and *manojña*, there are two groups [of bases], and the meanings of the suffixes are also only two—namely, the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*)—so that a correspondence according to order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) would result.
That does not occur because, as before, it lacks the svarita accent.

Alternatively, the particle *ca* here is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). Since there is nothing else to be conjoined by it, it conjoins the rule for the suffix *vuñ* itself with each of the two: the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*).
Therefore, from a single group [of words], the suffix *vuñ* occurs in both the sense of "origin" (*bhāva*) and "object" (*karman*), but not according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*);
for otherwise, a collective conjunction (*samuccaya*) would not be possible.
134. *Gotra* and *caraṇa* [are used] in the sense of praise and contempt regarding those [persons] and their derivatives.

(Pāṇini 5.1.134) A designation based on offspring is called *gotra*, and it is recited in the *Pravarādhyāya*. Furthermore, that which denotes persons engaged in the study of the Veda is the designation of the word *caraṇa*. And *gotra*...

In the rule "caraṇaiḥ saha" (Mahābhāṣya 2.225), the technical definition establishes that both *gotra* and *caraṇa* are considered *jāti* (classes). Thus, although the suffix *añ* would have been expected by the rule "prāṇabhṛjjāti...
(Pāṇini 5.1.129), the suffix *vuñ* is specifically prescribed here. In this context, there are two nominal stems (*prātipadika*) denoting *gotra* and *caraṇa*.

There are also only two meanings; in that case, one might expect them to apply respectively [to each], but that does not occur because the first member of the compound has a svarita accent. For this very reason, he says: "respectively for the two meanings of the abstract state (bhāva) and the object (karman)," and "when *ślāghā* and the others function as the objects. Likewise...

For an entity (*bhāva*) cannot be any one of [the qualities] such as praise (*ślāghā*) and so forth. An entity is the ground for the application of a word (*śabdapravṛttinimitta*). And praise and so forth do not constitute the ground for the application of words denoting lineage (*gotra*) or school (*caraṇa*). Nor does action (*karman*) possess the nature of praise and so forth; for indeed—

The acts of praising and so forth regarding lineages and conduct are conventionally established as objects (*karman*), just as heat and so forth are of fire, because they possess the nature of an action (*kriyā*). The suffix *vuñ* occurs when [the lineage or conduct] is the object (*viṣaya*) of the meaning of the suffixes denoting the state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*) by virtue of being that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Regarding the rule "one who knows that, one who has attained that," the root *iṇ* is used here.

Because it has the sense of "going" (*gati*). Regarding the phrase "or known by that": since the root *i* preceded by *ava* can also function in the sense of "knowing," the word "that" (*tat*) here refers back to the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the action (*karman*) related to the lineage (*gotra*) and the school (*caraṇa*). For example: "by means of Gārgikā. And [the rule applies] to the offspring (*apatya*).
There is elision of *ya* by the rule "taddhite'nāti" (Pāṇini 6.4.151).
135. *hotrābhyaś chaḥ* | (5.1.135) When *tva* and *tal* would otherwise apply, *cha* is prescribed [in place of them].
136. *brahmaṇastvaḥ* | (5.1.136) [The commentary states: "It should have been stated as *na*. Even though the suffix *cha* is prohibited by this exception (*apavāda*), the suffix *tva* occurs;
thus, it is established simply by [the rule] *tasya bhāvastvatalau* (5.1.119). Therefore, it should indeed have been stated as *na*.

This statement is for the purpose that the suffix *tala* may be sublated by the suffix *tv*. If it were not stated, then when *cha* is prohibited, *tala* would apply just as *tva* does. However, by the explicit mention of *tva*, the sublation of *tala* is established.
Thus ends the first quarter of the fifth chapter in the *Kāśikāvivaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who is like a Bodhisattva.
Now begins the fifth chapter,
second quarter.

1. *Khañ* [is used] after [words denoting] grains in the sense of "place of origin" (*bhavana*) and "field" (*kṣetra*). (Pāṇini 5.2.1) The word *bhavana* is explained as: "that in which things *bhavanti*, i.e., are born (*jāyante*). This is derived with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
The meaning is "they are born" or "they arise. By this, the verb *bhavati* is understood here in the sense of "origination," not in the sense of "existing."

For if that [the field] were understood as the locus of grasping, then the rule for placing things elsewhere after they have been produced—namely, where they are subsequently placed—would also apply there. If the verb *bhavati* (to exist) were taken in the sense of "arising," then the mention of the "field" would be purposeless; for in the case of "the existence of mung beans in a granary," [the field would not be required].

It is done for this purpose: that there be no [application of the rule] to the verb *bhū* (to be) when it is understood as a term denoting origination (*utpatti*). For if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its application to a granary (*kusūla*), since a granary is not the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the origination of mung beans and the like, but rather of their existence (*sattā*). This is not so; for if the term "field" (*kṣetra*) is included...

In this context, the verb *bhavati* signifies "origination. How so? For this word *kṣetra* denotes the substratum for the origination of grains; therefore, since it is the field of those [grains] that exist, it is logical that the earth receives the designation *kṣetra* (field) with respect to their origination, and thus the verb *bhavati* applies to that origination.

Thus, if the word "field" (kṣetra) were not used, the term "existence" (bhava) would also be understood as denoting that which exists; consequently, it would also apply to a granary. Furthermore, the word "existence" is also conventionally used to denote a house, and that too would be excluded by the word "field. Now, how is the genitive case [to be explained]?

A case-ending expressing the sense of capability (*samartha-vibhakti*) is employed; however, since the genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī-samartha-vibhakti*) continues from the rule "The suffixes *tva* and *tal* occur after [a word] in the genitive sense" (Pāṇini 5.1.119), the desired form is established by that very rule. If this is so, then this [usage] indicates that the suffixes previously mentioned do not necessarily follow a word in the genitive sense.

By that [rule], namely *ṭh hotrābhyāś chaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.135), the suffix *cha* is established in its own sense (*svārthe*) after the word *hotrā* when it is in the nominative case: *hotrā* itself becomes *hotrīyam*. And in this way, the suffix *ṣyañ* is established in its own sense after words such as *caturvarṇa* when they are in the nominative case.

2. The suffix *ḍhak* is applied after the words *vrīhi* and *śāli*. (5.2.2) 3. The suffix *yat* is applied after the words *yava*, *yavaka*, *ṣaṣṭika*, and so forth. (5.2.3) 4. After the words *tila*, *māṣa*, *umā*, *bhaṅgā*, and *aṇu*, the suffixes are optionally applied. (5.2.4)

Regarding the statement, "When *khañ* is applicable, this rule [provides] an option, and thus it also occurs," it is logical that *khañ* should optionally occur after *tila*, *māṣa*, and *aṇu*, because these are grains (*dhānya*).
However, since *umā* and *bhaṅgā* are not grains, it is not logical for *khañ* to be optional after them. For indeed, that which...

In Vedic passages such as "sesame seeds are mine, barley is mine," and so forth, that alone is considered grain which is recited in the mantra—namely, barley and the like—and not māṣa beans and mudga beans. If those two were also grain, they too would have been recited; therefore, it is understood that they are not.

Since those two [the *khañ* suffix] are for grains (*dānya*), and thus the *khañ* suffix does not apply after them, because that [suffix] would also occur optionally, he says: "in the case of *umā* and *bhaṅgā*" and so forth. According to the Smṛti, there are seventeen types of grains, including *śaṇa*; among those, *umā* and *bhaṅgā* are also considered grains.

Since these two are enumerated [among the grains], their status as grain is indeed established. As for their non-recitation in the Veda, that is due to their lack of utility in Vedic rituals. Therefore, the intention is that they do not cease to be grain simply because they are not recited there.

5. *sarvacarmaṇaḥ kṛtaḥ khakhañau* (Pāṇini 5.2.5). Here, the meaning of the suffix is "made" (*kṛta*). In that context, the leather (*carman*) would function either as the instrument (*karaṇa*) or as the agent (*kartṛ*).
If it functions as the instrument, then, because the instrument is fixed [as the factor], the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) characterized by the instrument would necessarily apply.

It must be so. Now, since the genitive case is prohibited by the rule "na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām" (Pāṇini 2.3.69), the third case ending alone is used to express the sense of the agent. Therefore, the third case ending, obtained through the force of the meaning of the suffix, is the governing case (samartha-vibhakti).
Having considered this, he says: "From that which is in the third case. And that indication, *sarvacarmaṇaḥ*, was made by forming a compound of the word *sarva* with the word *carman*.
Therefore, for one who thinks that its connection is only with *carman* and that no other [word] can form a compound [with it], [the author] says...

He replies with the words, "And here the word *sarva*," and so forth. If this is so, would not a compound be impossible due to a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*)? To this he says, "In that case, this [is the rule]," and so forth; the intention is that it is due to this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Now, why is the connection not understood as being with *carman* alone?

Thus he says: "The whole was made from leather. For here, the secondary derivative (taddhita) formation is intended to apply to the meaning of the sentence. Indeed, it is this very meaning of the sentence that is perceived as being conveyed by the secondary derivative.
And in this sense, the secondary derivative formation is obtained for the meaning of the sentence only if the word "whole" (sarva) [is connected] with "made" (kṛtena).

It is not connected with *carman* (skin). If the word *sarva* were connected with *carman*, there would have to be either a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) or a descriptive determinative compound (*karmadhāraya*), as in *sarvacarmaṇā*. In that case, if it were a genitive compound, the meaning understood from the derivative suffix (*taddhita*) would be "made by skin belonging to the whole."

In the case of a *karmadhāraya* compound, however, the meaning is "made with the whole hide. This [meaning] is not of two kinds—that which is understood from a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)—but rather only this: "made with the whole hide.
Therefore, since it is impossible to understand the connection of the word "whole" (*sarva*) with "hide" (*carman*), [the compound must be analyzed] only with "made" (*kṛta*).
The connection is logical.

6. *yathāmukhasammukhasya darśanaḥ khaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.6). Regarding the word *darśanaḥ*: "it is seen in this, thus it is a *darśana*" (*dṛśyate 'sminn iti darśanaḥ*). The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*). Regarding *yathāmukham*:
it is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) according to Pāṇini 2.1.7, *yathā'sādṛśye*. It means "resembling the face" (*mukhasya sadṛśam*).

"Yathāmukham. What, then, is that? It is a reflection based on a mirror. [Objection: But surely, because of the prohibition "not when there is dissimilarity" (*asādṛśye*), a compound should not be formed here? To this he says: "By virtue of being a *nipātana*," and so forth. Furthermore, this compound is one in which the meaning of the first member is predominant.

Since the first member (*pūrvapada*) is a word denoting a non-substance (*asatvavacana*), the suffix is properly formed from that which is already in the nominative case (*prathamāsamartha*). Alternatively, because of the *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) in the rule "nāvyayībhāvādato'mtvapañcamyāḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.83), it is understood that cases beginning with the accusative (*dvitīyā*) occur after an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*). Therefore...
The suffix *kha* is justified by the force of the second [case ending]; as in the example "yathāmukhaṃ yatāmukhīnaḥ" (one who looks according to the face).

[This means] "one whose seeing is similar to the face. Here, the sixth case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). That mirror or other surface in which the entire face is seen is so described.

7. *tatsarvādeḥ pathyaṅgakarmapatrapātraṃ vyāpnoti* (Pāṇini 5.2.7). Now, for what purpose is the base form (*prakṛti*) uttered in the accusative case in this sūtra? It is so that the suffix may occur by virtue of the power of the accusative case in the word *tat*. Now...

Or rather—the word "pathyaṅgakarmapatrapātram" does not take this second case ending (*dvitīyā*), for *pathya* and the others are not connected with the action of pervading (*vyāpnoti*). What then? It is *sarva* [that is connected]. Therefore, the status of being the object (*karmatva*) belongs to that alone, and not to *pathya* and the others which are its parts. Why is that? Because... [the rest of the sentence is missing].

That [word *pariśiṣṭam*] is the second [member of the compound]; by means of a transposition of case endings (*sub-vyatyaya*), the nominative is used in place of the ablative. Therefore, because the collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) is neuter, the substitution of *am* prescribed by Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.83 (*ato 'm*) has been applied. Regarding the word "pariśiṣṭam," [the rule] applies: "After words beginning with *sarva*, [the suffix *aC* is added] to *pathin*, *aṅga*, *karman*, *patra*, and *pātra*."

And this is as follows: pathy- and the others do not occur at the beginning of a nominal stem (prātipadika) that begins with *sarva*. Therefore, by virtue of the logical necessity (*sāmarthya*), it is understood that the rule applies to those [stems] ending in them; thus he says: "ending in *pathin*, *aṅga*, *karman*, *patra*, or *pātra*. For example: *sarvapathīnaḥ*.

The compound *sarvapatha* is formed by the rule *pūrvakāla-* (Pāṇini 2.1.49), etc., and the suffix *a* is added as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmānakṣe* (Pāṇini 5.4.74). Now, one might object:

"Once the compound-final suffix has been applied, the word no longer ends in *pathin*; how then can that which ends in *pathin* be the basis [for the application of the suffix]? [The answer is: that which ends in *pathin* here is indeed the basis.

Thus, there is no fault, as it becomes *vidhari*. But surely, due to the intervention [of other elements], it would not apply? No, because by the inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*), the compound-final suffixes are understood to be included within the mention of the "compound" (*samāsa*); therefore, there is no intervention.
8. "He reaches up to the toes" (āprapadaṃ prāpnoti).
[This is formed] by the rule "An avyayībhāva compound is formed with those two" (Pāṇini 2.1.6), and by the rule "The prefix āṅ is used in the senses of limit and inclusion" (2.1.13).
Thus, the measurement of even a cloth that is not connected to the body is expressed.
For it is on account of its fitness for attainment that he is said to be "capable" of reaching the body down to the tips of his toes.

Now, what is the distinction between pervasion (*vyāpti*) and attainment (*prāpti*), such that when one says "he pervades," it is stated that "he attains"? Attainment is merely a connection; pervasion is that very connection in its entirety.
The distinction is simply that it is called "pervasion" (vyāpti).

9. *anupada-sarvānnāyānayaṃ baddhābhakṣayatineyeṣu* | (5.2.9) [The rule begins with] *anu āyāme*, etc. When it means extension (*āyāma*), then there is a compound by [Pāṇini 2.1.16] *yasya cāyāmaḥ*. When it means similarity (*sādṛśya*), then by [Pāṇini 2.1.7] *yattadetebhyaḥ parimāṇe vatup* and [Pāṇini 5.2.37] *tadantāt saṃkhyāyāḥ saṃjñāsaṅghasūtrādhyayaneṣu khaḥ*, and [Pāṇini 1.1.37] *avyayam*, [the word *anupada* is an indeclinable].

By the rule "vibhakti" (Pāṇini 2.1.6) and so forth. Just as a foot is long, so too [the word] *anupadīnā* is explained as "one whose sandals (*baddhopānat*) are according to the foot. In the sense of similarity, it means "that which is spread out according to the foot";
the meaning is "measuring the foot. Even when *anu* is used in the sense of similarity, this is the meaning.

It should be understood that similarity consists precisely in having an equal measure. Regarding the phrase "movement to the right" (*pradakṣiṇamaya*): *aya* means movement; thus, movement toward the right is called *aya*. Regarding the phrase "non-movement to the left" (*anaya*): that which is contrary to *aya*, namely movement to the left, is called *anaya*. Such is the meaning of the individual components.

Having shown the meaning of the individual components, he says "of those moving clockwise and counter-clockwise," and so forth, in order to demonstrate the purpose of the plural number. If the dice move both clockwise and counter-clockwise, then victory and defeat are possible; not otherwise. In that regard, one's own [dice]...

The arrows of one's own side fly clockwise, while those of the enemy fly counter-clockwise; when those arrows moving in such a manner reach their respective positions, through that specific mode of movement consisting of clockwise and counter-clockwise flight,
they are countered by the opposing forces.

The non-occupation of the *śāra* squares, the non-seating, and the non-advancing—this is called *ayānaya*; it does not consist merely in moving clockwise or counter-clockwise. This *ayānaya* of such a nature is to be understood as occurring when the squares are stepped upon by the *śāra* pieces of equal rank.
For indeed, the positions of arrows that possess assistants cannot be occupied by others;
however, those that are without assistants can certainly be so occupied. "Standing at the head of the board" (*phalakaśirasi sthitaḥ*):
on that board where they play with dice, the place which is the head of that board belongs to the *kiṃtavān*s.
It is well known that one who stands there is called *śāra-ṭhayānayīna*, because the word *ayānayīna* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in that very sense.
Others, however, [explain it as]: *neya* means "to be led," and *na nītaḥ tataḥ* means "not led away from there"; thus, he is "one who stands upon the head" (*śirasi sthitaḥ*).

They say that because the meaning [as previously stated] is untenable, the text should read: "it is placed upon the surface of the board" (*phalakaśirasi sthāpyate*). Alternatively, *nītaḥ* (brought) may be understood as *neyaḥ* (to be brought), since the former serves as an indicator for the latter.

It is expressed by means of a future state. Even though all [the items] are connected to both "bringing" (*āya*) and "not bringing" (*anāya*), [the distinction] arises solely from the qualified object (*viśeṣya*).

The production of the suffix *pratyaya* has already been stated. Nevertheless, even though the second case (*dvitīyā*) is already under discussion, the second case is mentioned again for the purpose that the suffix should apply specifically from a word ending in the second case. Consequently, the suffix is applied from the word *anaya*, which ends in the second case and signifies a specific meaning.

It is so, not merely because of the words of the *neyārtha* (provisional meaning). That very [method] which proceeds clockwise and counter-clockwise is what has been shown by the passage beginning with "the method (*naya*) that goes...
Now, as for the word "others" (*anya*), if this is a *dvandva* compound in the sense of a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*), then of that—

Should it not be *ayānaya* because of its neuter gender? Or, if it were a *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction), it would have to be *ayānayaḥ* because it has a dual meaning? This is not a *dvandva*; what then?
It is a *tatpuruṣa* because it belongs to the *mayūravyaṃsaka*-class and so forth—namely, *ayānaya* as "an *anaya* accompanied by *aya*. Now, if...

Regarding the expression *baddhābhakṣayatineyeṣu*, how can there be a *dvandva* compound of forms ending in verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*)? Who, moreover, says that this is a *dvandva*? If it is not a *dvandva*, how is there the plural form *neyeṣu*?
[The answer is: because the formulation is Vedic (*sautra*), or because of a transposition of case endings (*sub-vyatyaya*), where the singular stands in place of the plural in the Vedic language.

The plural number is appropriate. Now, one might object: "Is it not stated that in the Vedic language there is a transposition of case endings (*sub-vyatyaya*), yet this is not the Veda? There is no fault here, because of the rule: "The Sūtras are like the Veda" (*cchandovat sūtrāṇi bhavanti*). Alternatively, this is simply a *dvandva* compound and not a verbal form (*tiṅanta*); for this word *bhakṣayati* is not a verbal form. Why? [Because...]

What then? It is a particle (*nipāta*) that resembles a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) and has the same meaning as a verbal suffix, just like the word "exists" (*asti*) in the expression "the Brāhmaṇī woman possesses milk" (*astikṣīrā brāhmaṇī*).

10. "One experiences [the results] through one's sons and grandsons, in succession, from one to another" (Pāṇini 5.2.10). But how is it possible for a nipātana (irregular formation) to appear without a suffix when it is prescribed in conjunction with a suffix? To this he says: "That should be regarded as a different word altogether."

11. *avārapārātyantānukāmam gāmī* (Pāṇini 5.2.11). Regarding the word *gāmī*: the suffix *ṇini* is applied here in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*), according to Pāṇini 3.3.170 (*āvaśyakādhamarṇyayor ṇiniḥ*). Furthermore, this word *gāmī* refers to a future time.

As he says: "One who will go is a *gāmī*. And that future state (*bhaviṣyadvṛtti*) is obtained by the rule "the [words] *gamī* and so forth [denote] the future" (Pāṇini 3.3.3). Thus he says: "in the future," and so on.
"By the rule 'after [a word ending in] *akan* or *u*, there is a prohibition of the genitive case when denoting the future or a debt' (Pāṇini 2.3.70), the genitive is prohibited. By this...

The intention is that the second case (dvitīyā) is established as being incapable [of applying]. For the sixth case (ṣaṣṭhī) resulting from connection with a *kṛt*-suffix is an exception (*apavāda*) to the second case; therefore, when the sixth case is prohibited, there must necessarily be the second case.
In the example "avārapāram," this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the further shore of the near shore" (*avārasya pāram*). And "vā" [indicates]...
It should be stated that the sixth member [of the compound] takes the prior position; by this, *pārāvāram* also occurs as an alternative.
[The rule applies] "even from a separated [compound]"—this is the reading in the printed edition—and "also from the reverse order."

But how is it that, although the second case-ending is already obtained here by virtue of the governing context (*adhikāra*), the word "second" (*dvitīyā*) is mentioned again? By this, it is indicated that the rule applies to something additional to that [context]. Consequently, the suffix is validly applied after a compound as well as after its opposite (i.e., a non-compound). [The example is: *atyantam*.

Thus: "the absence of an end" or "the transcendence of an end. It is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti* (Pāṇini 2.1.6), and so forth. Alternatively, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule *kugati* (Pāṇini 2.2.18), meaning "that which has transcended the end. This functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), meaning "one who goes intensely."
Thus [it is said], because in common usage the word *atyanta* is well known in the sense of "excessive. Regarding the term *anukāmam*:
*anukāmam* means "similar to desire" (*kāmasadṛśam*), that is to say, "in accordance with desire. This is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of "according to" (*yathārthe*).
This, too, is strictly an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) of the action.

12. *samāṃsamāṃ vijāyate* (Pāṇini 5.2.12). Regarding the expression *samāṃ samām*: the reduplication is for the sake of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), according to the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ* (8.1.4). Therefore, he says: "The expression *samāṃsamām* is a distributive repetition."

"A collection of nominal stems (*subanta*) is the base (*prakṛti*)," because of the force of the statement made under the governing rule for nominal stems (*prātipadika*). "The meaning is 'she bears a fetus,'" because verbal roots have multiple meanings.

Regarding the rule "it should be stated that there is non-elision (*aluk*) of the *sup* [case-ending] in the preceding member": once a *taddhita* suffix has been produced, the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) applies by the rule "kṛt, *taddhita*, and compounds" (Pāṇini 1.2.46).

Consequently, the elision of the *sup* [case-ending] would apply by the rule "there is elision of *sup* after a verbal root or a nominal stem" (Pāṇini 2.4.71); [this is the objection to which the following sūtra is a response].
An objection must be stated:
"They say that the root *vijani* also occurs in the sense of 'delivering a fetus'.
To this, he thinks as follows: when it occurs in the sense of "conceiving a fetus," the accusative case ending alone is used here to express absolute connection (*atyantasamyoga*).
It is not the seventh [case-ending]. In the sense of "deliverance from the womb," the seventh case occurs in the word *vijanī*.

[The rule] says "merely the elision of the suffix" (*ṭhyalopamātram*); for since the entire year (*samā*) is not pervaded by the act of deliverance from the womb, the word *mātra* indicates that there is no elision of the entire case-ending.
Regarding the phrase "of the remainder": this refers to the word *ām*.

Regarding the phrase "in the case of non-occurrence": this refers to the secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Regarding the phrase "and of the final member": by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), it should be stated that there is elision of the prior member; thus, the elision of the letter *y* occurs in conjunction with the suffix.
On the view that an elision being prescribed does not apply in the absence of that [condition], this supplementary rule (upasaṃkhyāna) is stated.
13. *adyaśvīnāvaṣṭabdhe* (5.2.13).
Regarding the rule *avaṣṭabdhe vijane āsanne prasave*: here, the meaning of the two preceding words is explained respectively by the two following words.
14. *āgavīnaḥ* (5.2.14). 15. *anugvalaṅgāmī* (5.2.15).
16. *adhvano yat-khau* (5.2.16).
17. *Abhyamitrāc cha ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.17).

Regarding the term *abhyamitrāt*: "facing the enemy" (*amitra*) is *abhyamitram*. This is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to [Aṣṭādhyāyī] 2.1.14, *lakṣaṇenābhipratī ābhimukhye*. And this is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). Therefore—
Only the second case ending is the capable (samartha) vibhakti.

18. *khañ* is added after *goṣṭha* when expressing "that which formerly was [a cow-pen]. (5.2.18) Since the suffix *caraṭ* would otherwise apply by the rule *bhūtapūrvaṃ caraṭ* (5.3.53), *khañ* is prescribed here. [The derivation is as follows: "That in which cows stand is a *goṣṭha*. Here, the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *supisthaḥ* (3.2.4).
The cerebral [ṇ] is substituted by [Pāṇini 8.3.97], *ṭhambāmbagobhūmi*, etc.

Regarding the term *bhūtapūrve*: that which was previously existing (*pūrvaṃ bhūtaḥ*) is "formerly been" (*bhūtapūrvaḥ*). This is a compound formed according to [Pāṇini 2.1.4], *supsupā*. The mention of *bhūtapūrva* is a qualifier of that very [suffix]. It qualifies it through its meaning.

It should be understood that, for example, in the sūtra beginning with "dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ samānakartṛkāt" (Pāṇini 3.1.7), there is the status of being an object (*karmatva*) and the status of having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*).
19. *aśvasyaikāhagamaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.19).

[The word] *ekāhagamaḥ* means "that which is reached in one day" (*ekāhena gamyate*). The suffix *ghañ* is applied by the rule *akartari ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.19), and due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is no *vṛddhi* strengthening of the vowel. [The compound is formed] by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32).

This is the compound [analysis]. Regarding the phrase "having fallen [from the sky] and traveled a hundred *āśvīna*s": the meaning is that having gone a hundred of those *yojanas* which are traversed in a single day (*ekāha*). The word "hundred" (*śata*), while denoting a number to be counted, by its very nature functions only in reference to its own count. Therefore, [the term] "*āśvīna*s" [is used].

In the expression "a hundred [horses]," although the word *āśvīna* refers to many objects and thus involves grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a plural sense, it is employed only in the singular number.
20. *śālīna* and *kaupīna* [are used] in the senses of "timid" and "improper," respectively.

(5.2.20) [The word] *yathākathaṃcit* means "in whatever manner. He shows that one should not insist upon the meaning of the individual parts [of the compound], stating: *utarapadalopaśca*. The latter member of the compound (*utarapada*)...

The words *praveśana* (entering) and *avataraṇa* (descending) undergo elision [of their final vowel and following consonant]. Regarding the term *śālīna*, it means "dull-witted. For such a person, although capable of giving even a reply due to his dullness, when being respected by noble persons, he is unable to remain there—thinking, "the people are watching"—and therefore he deserves only entry into a hall (*śālā*). Thus, he is called *śālīna*.
In this context, the word *śālā* signifies a small hut (*kuṭīra*). Regarding the expression "the *kaupīna* is evil":

because it is censurable and improper in the world, it is called *akārya*; thus it is said that it deserves (*arhati*) to be cast down into or entered into a well (*kūpa*) in the world. By implication, [the term refers to] a part of the body.

A certain thing is designated by the word *kaupīna*. Furthermore, even the garment intended for covering that particular part of the body is called *kaupīna* by association with it, as in the case of wandering mendicants and others.

21. *vrātena jīvati* (Pāṇini 5.2.21). [The commentary explains: "Of various kinds" (*ṭhnānājātīyāḥ*) means of many different castes (*anekajātīyāḥ*). "Of irregular livelihoods" (*ṭhaniyatavṛtayaḥ*) means of uncertain occupations (*aniyatakriyāḥ*). "Their work is *vrāta*" (*ṭhteṣāṃ karma vrātam*); by association with *vrāta*, that [work] also [is so called].

It is called *vrāta*. Alternatively, when there is the intention to express the meaning "this belongs to the *vrātas*," although the suffix *cha* would have been expected, the suffix *aṇ* occurs by virtue of this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Furthermore, that [action] is work such as carrying loads and so forth. Regarding the statement "it is not desired therein," how is it that it is not desired even though it is intended, given the context?
Because the *Mahāvibhāṣā* is a work that establishes the various doctrinal positions (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).

22. *Sāptapadīnaṃ sakhyam* (Pāṇini 5.2.22). Regarding the statement "the form *sāptapadīna* is thus prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*)," what exactly is being prescribed here? It is the suffix and the meaning of the suffix, which are already under discussion. Furthermore, the meaning of the suffix *khañ* is "attainment" (*avāpti*). [The compound is formed] by means of seven...
The compound is formed in the sense of a secondary derivative (taddhita), meaning "that which is obtained by means of steps. From the word *saptapada*, the suffix *khañ* is then applied.

Regarding the phrase "How," etc.: [the question is] whether *sakhyam* refers to the state of being a friend (*sakhitva*) or to the action of a friend (*sakhyuḥ karma*). In that case, if *sāptapadīnam* were to be derived as a ready-made form (*nipātana*), there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *sakhi*.
[He] attains [it], for the intention of the questioner is that a friend does not become a friend merely by being a friend.

Regarding the phrase "that which has a quality as its primary element" (*guṇapradhāna*), etc.: that of which the quality (*guṇa*)—whether it be a state (*bhāva*) or an action (*karman*)—is the primary element is thus described.
And when that [word] functions toward the mere quality by means of its primary function (*mukhyayā vṛttyā*), then it is "that which has a quality as its primary element."

It should be understood that "at that time, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word 'friend' (*sakhi*)," because both [words] function with respect to a single referent. As for the phrase "but when," etc.: *lakṣaṇā* is metaphorical usage (*upacāra*).

Through the metaphorical usage of non-difference between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), by means of secondary application (*gauṇī vṛtti*), [the suffix] *taddhita* [is applied] to that which possesses number.

When it refers to the person (*puruṣa*), then it stands in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with that very [word for the person]. Just as when the word "white" (*śukla*) refers solely to the quality (*guṇa*), it does not stand in apposition with a word for a substance (*dravya*)—
as in "the white of the cloth" (*paṭasya śuklaḥ*)— but when it [refers] to the cloth through its connection with the word "you" (*tvam*).
When they coexist, there is grammatical coreferentiality—as in "a white cloth"; it should be understood that the same applies here as well.
23. *haiyaṅgavīnam* in the sense of a specific designation. (Pāṇini 5.2.23) The rule states: "In place of *hyas-godoha*, there is the substitute *hiyaṅgu*.
This means that the word *hiyaṅgu* is the substitute for *hyas-godoha*. *Hyas-godoha* means "the milking of yesterday"; [it is formed] by the rule *sup-supā* (2.1.4).

This is a compound. The suffix *khañ* is applied in the sense of "modification" (*vikāra*). It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *tasya vikāraḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.134), which would otherwise have applied.

24. *tasya pākamūle pīlvādikarṇādibhyaḥ kuṇabjāhacau* (Pāṇini 5.2.24). These two suffixes, *kuṇap* and *jāhac*, are exceptions (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*. Since the suffix *aṇ* would otherwise apply by rule 4.3.120 (*tasyedam*), these suffixes are prescribed instead. Because the letter *j* serves no purpose [as a marker], the designation *it* does not apply to it by rule 1.3.7 (*dhuṭ*).
It comes to be.

25. *pakṣātiḥ* | (5.2.25) Regarding the rule "of those mentioned in a single yoga," there is the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of words beginning with *ādi* by virtue of their being marked as *svarita*.

Because it is bound by the formal declaration (*pratijñā*) of the *svarita* accent: even for those elements taught within a single grammatical rule (*ekayoga*), the *svarita* occurs only where its declaration is made, and not elsewhere. Consequently, the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of even a single part of what was taught in a single rule is logically established.
26. *tena vittaścuñcupcaṇapau* (Pāṇini 5.2.26). [Examples:
*vidyācuñcuḥ*, *vidyācaṇaḥ*. Now, why does the letter *c* not receive the technical designation *it* by the rule *cuṭū* (1.3.7)? This has already been explained.
The reason for this is precisely that: the formulation of a separate rule (yoga) is intended to indicate that this procedure is not mandatory (anitya).

27. *vinañbhyāṃ nānāñau nasaha* (Pāṇini 5.2.27). [The commentary states: "The suffixes *nān* and *añ* occur in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*)," because of the rule: "Suffixes whose meaning is not specifically prescribed occur in the sense of the base itself" (Siddhāntakaumudī 125). The letter *ñ*, however, is for the purpose of making the initial vowel udātta (accented).
28. *veḥ śālacchaṅkaṭacau* (Pāṇini 5.2.28).

Regarding the statement "from that which expresses an action together with its means" (*sasādhanakriyāvacanāt*), and so forth—it has been stated that prefixes (*upasarga*) are of such a nature that wherever a word expressing an action is employed, [the prefix functions accordingly].

They say that [the word *upasarga*] is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). Where it is not employed, [the suffix applies] to an action together with its means (*sasādhanakriyām*). Here, no word denoting an action (*kriyāvācī śabdaḥ*) is employed; therefore, the suffix occurs after a prefix (*upasarga*) which denotes an action together with its means. And that [suffix], being applied, [is one] whose meaning is not specifically indicated by the rule (*ṭhanirdiṣṭārthāḥ pratyayāḥ*).
Because it is not specified otherwise, [the suffix] occurs in its own sense, according to the rule *svārthe bhavanti* (Sīpa 125).

In the phrase "when the horns have fallen off" (*vigate śṛṅge*), this demonstrates that the word *vi-* functions with respect to the action of falling off (*vigamana-kriyā*) which has the horns as its instrument (*śṛṅga-sādhana*).

If the suffix were applied to an action accompanied by its instrument (*sādhanā*), then forms such as *viśālo gauḥ* ("a broad ox") and *viśaṅkaṭo gauḥ* ("a wide ox") would not be established; for here, "going" (*vigamana*) is not the instrument [of the action], but rather what is it?
It is the horns. Therefore, he says: "Because of connection with that," and so forth. Just as...

Because of its connection with parts such as the dewlap, the cow is called "dewlap" by means of a property belonging to its parts; likewise, because of its connection with large and broad horns, the cow is called "horned. As for the phrase "But in the ultimate sense," and so forth: the collective whole exists for the purpose of etymological derivation. Therefore, in this context, there is not merely an action accompanied by its instruments.

There is no [proof], nor even a means of proof. Therefore, words for qualities such as *viśāla* and others are established in the world from the perspective of ultimate reality, just like words such as *śukla* (white) and so on. Consequently, one should not insist upon a distinction between the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) in these cases, such as *viśālī*. Thus it is.

In the ultimate sense, they are meaningless. It is stated that even the suffixes *śāla* and *chaṅkaṭac*, which are prescribed after the root *vi*, are likewise meaningless. Regarding the word "these" (*ete*): the plural number is used by taking into account *saṅkaṭa* and the others which are about to be derived, for they too are indeed words expressing qualities (*guṇaśabda*).

29. *saṃ-prod-acaḥ kaṭac* (Pāṇini 5.2.29). It should be understood that everything is exactly as before: the suffix *kaṭac* is added in its own sense (*svārthe*) after a prefix (*upasarga*) that expresses an action together with its means (*sasādhanakriyā*).

"Ṭhalābūtilomā" and so forth. An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the suffix *kaṭac* after words such as *alābū* when "dust" (*rajas*) is to be expressed. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffixes denoting a modification (*vikāra*); for the dust of things like the *alābū* is indeed a modification of them.

Regarding the phrase "ṭhgoṣṭhādayaḥ" and so forth: the word "ādi" (and so on) indicates a class or type. The names of animals begin with the word *go* (cow); from these, when words such as *sthāna* (place) and others are to be expressed as the referents, suffixes such as *goṣṭha-ja* and others are to be prescribed. This occurs when one intends to express the sense of "belonging to this" (*tasyedam*, Pāṇini 4.3.120) in relation to places and the like.

Words such as *goṣṭhaja* are prescribed. [Objection: But is not everything, including *kaṭaja* and so forth in the sense of a collection, already included by the plural number in the rule "taddhitāḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.76)? [Response: True;
this is an elaboration (*prapañca*) of the very sentence just mentioned. Regarding the word "avikaṭam": here, [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] to that...

The suffix *kaṭaṭ* is applied in the sense of a collection according to [Pāṇini 4.2.37] *samūhaḥ*. Thus, *avipaṭam* refers to the expanse of scattered sheep. Two camels are called *uṣṭragoyugam*. Six elephants are called *hastiṣaṅgavam*.
The oil of *iṅguda* is *iṅgudataila*. The juice of sesame is *tilataila*.

Regarding the phrase "in the place" (*bhavane*) or "in the field" (*kṣetre*), and so forth: the place or field for sugarcane is *ikṣuśākaṭa* or *ikṣuśākinam*. The place or field for roots is *mūlaśākaṭa*.
The *mūlaśākinī*.
30. *avāt kuṭārac* (5.2.30).

31. *nate nāsikāyāḥ saṃjñāyāṃ ṭīṭañ-nāṭaj-bhraṭacaḥ* (5.2.31). [The word] *natam* is derived from the root *nam*; he shows that the suffix *niṣṭhā* is used here in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*). [The rule applies] to the nose...

Regarding the phrase "sambandhinī" (belonging to): by this [term] as well, the genitive case in "nāsikāyāḥ" (of the nose) is a genitive of relation (*sambandha-lakṣaṇā*). If these suffixes are to be applied when there is a curvature belonging to the nose, how then can both the nose and the person be denoted by this [word]? To this he says: "tadyogāt" (due to connection with that).

32. *nerbiḍajbirīsacau* (Pāṇini 5.2.32). [Question: "How is it that [the word] *nibiḍāḥ* [is formed]? [Answer: There is no application of that [rule] here. Therefore, the intention is that such a designation is not justified because of the absence of that connection. [Objection: "It will arise from a comparison (*upamāna*)."
The hair and the garments are equal to the nose in their density;
therefore, by way of comparison, both of them shall be denoted by the word "nibiḍa" (dense).
33. *tyakan* is used after two limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) denoting "not near" (*anāsanna*) and "ascended" (*ārūḍha*). (Pāṇini 5.2.33). [The commentary says:

"And because of the governing rule on technical names (*saṃjñā*). This is because the governing rule on technical names continues from the preceding sūtra, *nate nāsikāyāḥ* (5.2.31), etc. [The commentary says: "It has a restricted scope."

The sense is that only that which has already ascended (*ārūḍha*) is understood as being "near" (*āsanna*) to the mountain; therefore, in expressions such as *vṛkṣasyāsannam* ("near the tree") or *plakṣasyārūḍham* ("ascended on the *plakṣa* tree"), this does not occur. Now, why does the substitution of *i* not take place in *upatyakā* and *adhityakā* by virtue of the rule *pratyayasthāt kāt pūrvasya* (Pāṇini 7.3.44)?

Therefore, he says: "from *kā* [following] a suffixal *t*. If there were *it*-strengthening here, the technical name (*saṃjñā*) would not be established; that is, the technical names such as *naupatyikā* and *adhityikā* would not be formed. Consequently, because this falls under the governing rule for technical names (*saṃjñā-adhikāra*), there is no *it*-strengthening.

35. *karmaṇi ghaṭo’ṭhac* (Pāṇini 5.2.35). By the word "in *karmaṇi*," [the author] shows that there is a reference to the actual form (*svarūpa*) of the word *karmaṇi*. Why, then, is there not a reference to the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) sense of "object" (*karman*)? Because such a thing is impossible.

But [the suffix] *asambhava* is not possible because the root *ghaṭ* is intransitive. The pronunciation of the vowel *a* in the suffix *ṭhañ* is for the purpose of preventing the substitution of *i* for *ṭha*.
36. *tad asya sañjātaṃ tārakādibhya itac* (Pāṇini 5.2.36).

In the list of *tārakādi* words, the terms *bubhukṣā* and *pipāsā* are recited. What is the purpose of their inclusion, since [the forms] *bubhukṣitaḥ* and [the like] can be derived from the desiderative (*sannanta*) roots by adding the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) along with the augment *iṭ*?

Is it the case that "Devadatta is thirsty" (*pipāsito devadattaḥ*) is [formed] by this rule? True; because the suffix is prescribed after a past participle (*bhūta*), it would not be established for the present tense. However, by this [rule], it is established even for the present. Therefore, the recitation of those two [rules] is logical. Regarding the rule *garbhād aprāṇini*: the suffix *itac* occurs after the word *garbha* when a non-living being (*aprāṇin*) is to be expressed.

"Garbhitāḥ śālayaḥ" (the rice grains are filled with embryos). Why say "not pertaining to a living being"? [Consider: "garbhaḥ sañjāto'syāḥ" (an embryo has been produced in her), "garbhiṇī gauḥ" (a cow that is pregnant).

37. *pramāṇe dvayasaj-daghnañ-mātracaḥ* | (5.2.37) Since the word *pramāṇa* (measure) is a relative term, the meaning of the suffix is understood [as that which possesses the measure]. [The examples are] "the first" and "the second," and so forth. The suffixes *dvayasaC* and *daghnaC* are intended for vertical measurement (*ūrdhvamāna*). [Regarding the rule: *upari...*

That in which something is placed and measured, neither obliquely nor all around, is *ūrdhvamāna* (vertical measurement). Regarding the phrase "without distinction": whether it be *pramāṇa*, *parimāṇa*, or *unmāna*, the suffix *mātraC* occurs everywhere without distinction; thus, one also says "a measure of a *prastha*" (*prasthamātram*).

Because of the word *api*, it also occurs as "only two spans" (*vitastimātra*). [The rule] "the elision of *mātraC* when expressing a measure" (*pramāṇe loḥ*) applies here. This elision (*luk*) is a technical term established by the ancient teachers. This elision is prescribed for the suffix *mātrac* that has been produced; it does not apply to *dvayasaC* and *dadhnaC*, because those two are prescribed for measuring height (*ūrdhvamāna*).

In this matter, even the possibility of [the application of] the rule does not arise. This is because, according to the rule *dvigornityam*, a *dvigu* compound cannot function as a measure (*apramāṇatvāt*). Furthermore, even if it were to end in a measure-word, there is no occurrence of the suffix *taddhita* ending in that [measure-word]. Therefore, the elision (*luk*) is stated precisely because it was already applicable by the preceding rule. The inclusion of the word "nityam" (always) [is for the sake of restriction].

"What is [the purpose]? Indeed, optionality (*vikalpa*) is not the subject under discussion such that the term "obligatory" (*nitya*) would be employed for the sake of its exclusion. Nor is it appropriate to employ the term "obligatory" here in order to indicate that the preceding rule operates optionally; for the intention is that this [rule] is not intended to be optional (*vibhāṣā*).

With the words "In case of doubt," etc., he states the purpose of including the term *nitya*. The root *śru* takes the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) by virtue of the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.113); thus, *śrāva* means "the act of hearing. That which possesses this [hearing] is called *śrāvī*. Furthermore, that which is about to be mentioned—the suffix *mātrac*—is spoken of here in connection with the notion of measure (*pramāṇa*).

Regarding the rule "ṭhstome ḍaṭ" and so forth: [the word] *pañcadaśaḥ* means "that sacrifice whose measure is fifteen days. [The word] *pañcadaśī* [is formed similarly]; because of its *ṭi*-nature, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied.
Regarding the rule "śanśatorḍiniḥ," this rule applies without distinction both to the *stoma* and elsewhere. [The word] *viṃśaḥ*...

"Śinaḥ"—the suffix *ḍini* is applied; by the rule "ṭi-viṃśater-ḍiti" (Pāṇini 6.4.142), there is the elision of the *ṭi*-portion, and then the elision of the vowel *ya* by the rule "yasyeti ca. "Śamamātram" and "diṣṭimātram" are two examples of measure (*pramāṇa*). "Prasthamātram," "kuḍavamātram."

Regarding measure: "fivefold" (*pañcamātra*) and "tenfold" (*daśamātra*) refer to number. Where it is not determined whether there will be peace or not, there the term "mere peace" (*śamamātra*) is employed.
In other cases as well, it should be understood accordingly.

38. [The suffix] *aṇ* is also applied after *puruṣa* and *hastin*. (5.2.38) Regarding *hāstinam*: there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule "before the suffix *yañ*, when not denoting a descendant" (6.4.164).
Regarding *dvipuruṣī*: [it is derived] by the rule "after *puruṣa*, when denoting a measure, optionally" (4.1.24).
In the case of *dvihastinī*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied here by the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* (Pāṇini 4.1.5).

39. *Yat-etebhyaḥ parimāṇe vatuP* (5.2.39). Regarding the form *yāvān*: [the suffix] *vatuP* is applied after *yad* and the others when denoting measure. By *ā sarvanāmnaḥ* (6.3.91), the vowel *ā* is substituted [for the final *a*]. By *ugidacām* (7.1.70), the augment *num* is added. By *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ* (6.4.14), the long vowel [is substituted for the penultimate *a*].

[The rules regarding] the elision of *hal* (consonants) and the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) [apply here]. One might raise an objection, thinking that the words *pramāṇa* and *parimāṇa* are synonyms: "Why is the term *parimāṇa* mentioned here, since the term *pramāṇa* is already being carried over [from the previous rule]? In response to him, he says: "In the sense of *pramāṇa*."

Regarding the passage beginning with "in the present," that distinction between these two—measurement (*pramāṇa*) and dimension (*parimāṇa*)—has already been explained previously: "Dimension, however, is on all sides; length, moreover, should be measurement."

"Because of the distinction in meaning for those ending in *ḍā* and *vat*" (*ḍāvatāvarthavaiśeṣyāt*). This reference is made with respect to the technical designations established by earlier teachers; for they indeed created the suffixes *ḍā* and *vat* from these [roots]. That which is distinguished is a "distinction" (*viśeṣa*); [the compound] is of the distinction...
"Bhāva" means distinction (*vaiśeṣya*). "Distinction of the object" means the specific quality of the object; that is the meaning.
The word *pramāṇa* has one meaning, while the word *parimāṇa* has another;
thus, these two have different meanings. Therefore, because of this distinction in meaning, the suffixes *ṅa* and *vat* must be prescribed.

The separate mention of the word *parimāṇa* (measure) is stated. "Is stated" means "is performed. For what purpose is this separate mention made? He says: "In order to prevent [the application of] *mātra* and so forth. Since a difference in meaning is established by the separate mention, there is no sublation (*bādhā*) of *mātra* and the others.

He says that the separate mention is made for this purpose: "it exists" (*bhūti*). However, when there is identity (*ekatva*) in the general form (*prakṛtisāmānya*), the suffixes *mātraj* and others being prescribed are general rules (*utsarga*);
whereas the suffix *vatup*, being prescribed from a specific form (*prakṛtiviśeṣa*), is an exception (*apavāda*).
If it were the case that the general rule (*utsarga*) is set aside by the exception (*apavāda*), then suffixes such as *mātra* and so forth would not apply after these [words];
consequently, forms such as *tatpramāṇam asya tanmātram* would not be established.
However, since there is no relationship of general rule and exception when there is a difference in meaning, this undesirable consequence does not arise.
Furthermore: "The formation of a noun (*bhāva*) from [stems ending in] *ḍā* and *vatu* is established. The term "*ḍāvatoḥ*" is in the ablative case.
When there is a difference in meaning, the derivation of suffixes such as *mātrac* and others from those ending in the suffix *vatup* is established.
The suffix *vatup* occurs in the sense of measure: that which is its measure is "as much" (*yāvān*).

After that [suffix], when denoting measure (*parimāṇa*), suffixes such as *mātra* and others occur— as in *yāvanmātram*, meaning "that which has such a measure. However, in the case of singularity (*ekatva*), because of the principle "there is no employment of what has already expressed its meaning" (*uktarthānām aprayogaḥ*), these suffixes such as *mātra* would not occur after that [suffix], since this meaning has already been expressed by the possessive suffix *matup*.

In *ṭhvāvataḥ* and *māvataḥ*, the substitutes *tvā* and *mā* are applied to the forms of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* ending in *mat* by the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca* (7.2.98), and as before, the substitution of *āt* [for the final vowel] occurs.

40. *Kim-idam-bhyām vo ghaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.40). [The examples are] *kiyān* and *iyān*. By the rule *idaṃ-kimoḥ īś-ka* (6.3.90), *kim* becomes *kī*; by the rule *idama īś* (5.3.3), [the suffix] *īś* is applied; then by the rule *yasyeti ca* (6.4.148), there is elision [of the final vowel and consonant]. But by what [suffix] is this formed?
Is the substitution of *gh* for the *v* of the suffix *vatup*, which is prescribed after the words *kim* and *idam*, being enjoined?
To this he says: "Or rather," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "or by means of a division of the rule" (*yogavibhāgena vā*):
having first prescribed the suffix *vatup* by the rule consisting of just "after *kim* and *idam*," and then [the subsequent rule] "after *idam*... [is applied].
By the rule "ghaḥ," the substitution of *gh* for the *v* of the suffix *vatup* is prescribed.

Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *v* [in the rule], since by the rule "ādeḥ parasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.54), the substitution of *gh* would apply to the *v* alone? Is it not the case that, because it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it must be a substitute for the whole [suffix]?

Does he obtain [the result]? This is not a fault; for here the letter *a* is merely for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), being simply a phoneme (*varṇamātra*) and not a substitute (*ādeśa*). But how is this to be understood? From the commentary (*vyākhyāna*). If so, since the letter *va* is more concise (*laghīyas*), it is proper that it should be taken as the substituendum (*sthānin*). Regarding the letter *va*:
Although the substitute occurs in place of the entire complex when the affix is added to *tvat*, there is nevertheless no fault;
for the single-substitute form (*pararūpa*) will apply to the two *a* sounds.

41. *kimaḥ saṃkhyāparimāṇe ḍati ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.41). [The commentary explains: "The measure (*parimāṇa*) of a number. This is a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) characterized by its connection with a verbal derivative (*kṛt*), signifying the object (*karman*). "Measure" (*parimāṇa*) means the act of measuring; the meaning is the delimitation (*pariccheda*) of a number. Regarding the term "delimitation" (*pariccheda*)...

The suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an action (*bhāve*). Regarding the statement "from that which exists in the delimitation of number" (*saṃkhyāparicchede vartamānāt*), the intended meaning is "from that which exists in a number qualified by delimitation.
For this very meaning of this statement will be made explicit later on. Of that...
Regarding the substitution of *gh* for *v*: this is due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "ṭhvo ghaḥ. Regarding the phrase "because it is being asked":

when the word *kim* functions to delimit a number, then it is used. And when does it function thus? When the number itself is being questioned. For [the word *kim*] is not used when the number is not being questioned.

Determination (*pariccheda*) is established. And when it is being questioned, the word *kim* functions with respect to a determination characterized by that questioning; therefore, because it is being questioned, the suffix is applied to *kim* when it denotes a number that brings about such determination.

It is understood that [the suffix] *bhavati* occurs. That which has "delimitation" (*pariccheda*) as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)—that is, having delimitation as its qualifier—is called *paricchedopādhikā*. This means that the intended meaning of the word *kim*, when it functions in the sense of the delimitation of number, is [as follows].

It has been made manifest. Regarding the word "kati": there is elision (*luk*) of the *jas* suffix by the rule "ṣaḍbhyo luk" (Pāṇini 7.1.22). As for the phrase "or rather," and so forth: in this interpretation, the compound is a *karmadhāraya* based on the expression "saṃkhyā-parimāṇe";
due to a formal irregularity (*nipātana*), this subordinate member (*upasarjana*) appears at the end of the compound. Furthermore, the word *parimāṇa*...

"By this it is measured," thus [the word *parimāṇa*] is derived in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*). With the words "of such a nature," he clarifies its meaning by means of the phrase "having the nature of delimitation. That by which something is delimited is "delimitation" (*pariccheda*); that which has this as its nature is described as such. By the words "wherein," etc., [he explains] for what purpose.
The specific number is qualified by the apprehension of its measure; this he demonstrates.

It might be argued: "There is no such distinction at all where the nature of the number's delimitation does not exist, so this qualification is useless. To this he says: "For in the case of censure," and so forth.

"What is the number of these ten?"—here, number is not intended as a defining characteristic. For there is no definition here; rather, the sentence is intent upon censure. The word "what" (kiṃ) is used here in the sense of censure, not in the sense of an inquiry.
42. *tayaP* is added [to a word denoting] a number to express a part thereof. (5.2.42) For example, in the word *catuṣṭayī*: the *r* of *catur* becomes *s* by the rule *visarjanīyasya saḥ* (8.3.34);
that *s* is then changed to a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) by the rule *hrasvātādau taddhite* (8.3.99).
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "ṭhṭhiḍḍhāṇañ" (Pāṇini 4.1.15), etc.

43. *dvitribhyāṃ tayasyāyaj vā* (Pāṇini 5.2.43). For what purpose is the mention of the suffix *tayap* [in this rule], since that very suffix is already understood by way of anuvṛtti from the preceding context? To this he says: "The mention of *tayap*, etc. If the mention of *tayap* were not made, then...

This suffix *ayac* should be understood as something entirely different from the suffix *tayaP*, rather than being a substitute for *tayaP*.
