What would be the consequence if it were a separate suffix? The operations specific to *tayaP* would not apply to *ayac*. What is that [operation]? It is the optional application [of the feminine suffix *ī*] before the nominative plural ending *jas*, according to the rule "prathama-carama... (Pāṇini 1.1.32).
Regarding the designation *sarvanāman*: [in the case of] *dvaya*, [the forms are] *dvaye* and *dvayāḥ*;

with the suffix *ṅīp* by [Pāṇini 4.1.15] *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*, [we get] *dvayī*. Now, one might object: since that [designation] was already prescribed by the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*), its recurrence here should be understood as being for the purpose of an *ādeśa* (substitute), as there is no other purpose.

Regarding the rule "dvitribhyām" [Pāṇini 5.2.43]: the mention in the ablative case will, by the rule "tasmād ity uttarasya" (1.1.67), be converted into a genitive ending. Therefore, even without the explicit mention of *tayap*, the status of *tayap* as the substitute is indeed obtained. This is not so; for if the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of *tayap* were for another purpose...

It would not [apply]; therefore, by virtue of its continued application (*anuvṛtti*), the status of *tayap* as the element to be replaced (*sthānitva*) would be understood. However, its continued application serves a further purpose: in the rule "ṭhbhādudāto nityam" (Pāṇini 5.2.44), *tayap* must be prescribed through a separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*). And that which is being continued cannot [be applied] in this way.
Since this would apply even when the subsequent rule is being carried over (anuvṛtti), it is improper for *tayap* to be the substitute; therefore, the mention of *tayap* is made.

44. *ubhādudāto nityam* (Pāṇini 5.2.44). [The commentary states: “By the force of the statement,” and so forth. If it were [already] udātta at the end, the mention of *udātta* would be purposeless. Furthermore, when *ayac* is applied, by the accent of the *cit* suffix itself, the rule "the accent that remains is stronger" (*satiśiṣṭasvaro balīyān*) [would apply].

Because the final acute accent (*antodātatva*) is already established by [Pāṇini 6.1.158], the initial acute accent (*ādyaudātatva*) would otherwise not be established; thus, that which is being prescribed for its sake becomes a meaningful statement. "If it is a worldly number" means like *dvitrādi* ("two or three," etc.). By the preceding rule (*yoga*), the suffixes *tayap* and *tay* are prescribed.

By another rule, the substitution of *ayac* for *ubha* is prescribed as permanent: "In the case of *ubhaya*, both gods and humans. Those whose two parts (*avayava*) are [the constituents] are called "both" (*ubhaye*). How can there be two parts when there is a plurality of gods and humans? Even though there is plurality here, duality (*dvitva*) also exists.

However, it certainly exists between the two nominal stems; for here there are two groups which are parts of the aggregate— one group consisting of the gods and the other consisting of humans— and thus there is no fault.
45. *tadasminn adhikam iti daśāntāḍ ḍaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.45).

Regarding the rule *ṭh-pratyayārthena ca*, etc.: if the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is of the same kind as the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), then the suffix *vati* is applied; it is not otherwise. [This occurs] by means of the meaning of the suffix.
He presents an example to show that the meaning of the base (prakṛti) belongs to the same class [as the meaning of the suffix]: "eleven kārṣāpaṇas.
Since the meaning of the base is also "eleven kārṣāpaṇas," the meaning of the base [is homogeneous] with the meaning of the suffix.

"Of the same class (*samānajātīya*): but not here," and so forth. For in this case, "one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*" is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*), whereas the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is "eleven *māṣas*. And since those [eleven *māṣas*] are of a different class from the *kārṣāpaṇas*, the suffix does not apply. It is desired [only] in the case of "hundred" and "thousand," as in the rule "that [is] in this" (*tadasmin*).
And in that case, the suffix is desired after a hundred or a thousand, but not after thirty and so forth.

But how is it obtained from the Sūtra that it applies only when there is no addition (*anupātama*)? To this he says: "The formation [of the compound] is for the purpose of expressing the intended meaning," and so on. "How? and so forth: if [the number] is greater than a hundred or a thousand...
The suffix must be applied; however, in this case, the suffix does not apply in the expression "one hundred and eleven thousand" (*ekādaśaṃ śatasahasram*).

For here, there is another number added to the hundred-thousand, and the intention is that it is neither merely a hundred nor merely a thousand. [The example] "of hundreds," etc., serves to indicate the hundred-thousand by this [rule].

It excludes another numerical value: when the word *śata* (hundred), ending in the genitive case, is compounded with the word *sahasra* (thousand), then the compound *śatasahasra* denotes a thousand of hundreds. But when the word *sahasra*, ending in the genitive case, is compounded [with *śata*], then it denotes a hundred of thousands.

It is expressed by the term *śatasahasra*. Now, one might object: "In a compound where the word *sahasra* ends in the genitive case, shouldn't it be *sahasraśatam*? There is no fault here, because its placement at the end [of the compound] will occur due to its inclusion in the group beginning with *rājadanta* (Pāṇini 2.2.31). Thus, it is established that the form is simply *śatasahasrayoḥ*.
Thus [it is said], because a meaning expressed by a hundred thousand is included within those very two [categories of] hundred and thousand.

Regarding "in the case of an excess" and so forth: in common usage, when there is an excess belonging to the same class as the meaning of the suffix, the grammatical operation known as a suffix is desired only for the numbers hundred and thousand. However, when the excess belongs to a different class—
If [the word] *bhavati* occurs, and neither "hundred" (*śata*) nor "thousand" (*sahasra*) is intended in the sense of a multiplier (*pratyaya*), then [the suffix] is not desired.

Now, in the case of *ekādaśaṃ śatasahasram*, when there is an excess of what should the suffix *ḍa* be applied? To this he says: "of which," and so forth. *Saṃkhyā* means numbering; that is, counting. Of which...

Regarding the numeral: when there is an addition to it, the suffix *ḍa* must be applied. And of what does the number belong? It belongs to that of which the state of being additional is counted. When hundreds are being counted, then—as in "a thousand of hundreds"—it is "a hundred-thousand" (*śatasahasram*);
in that case, *ḍa* must be applied due to the addition of a hundred. [As in: "in this, eleven are additional."

"One hundred thousand" (*śatasahasram*) means "the eleventh [unit] of a thousand. However, when thousands are being counted—as in "one hundred of thousands," which is "hundred-thousands" (*sahasraśatam*)—then the suffix *ḍa* must be applied when there is an excess of thousands. Thus, "one hundred thousand" means that eleven thousand are added to it. Now...
Why is the nominative case-ending (*prathamāsamarthavibhakti*) employed [in the sūtra] for the word *tat*?

For since the phrase *tad asya sañjātam* (Pāṇini 5.2.36) continues to apply, should not the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) itself be specified here by the word *asmin*? It cannot be so; for if that [phrase from 5.2.36] were to continue, then [the word *asya*] would be connected to that [suffix].
Otherwise, the recurrence of the meaning of the base (*pratyārtha*) would also follow as a consequence. Nor is there a contradiction between the meanings of the genitive and locative cases;

for, because of the indication "in this" (*asmin*), the preceding meaning of the base does not cease. However, if that [meaning] were to recur, the suffix would also apply in the sense of the genitive. Therefore, [the word *asya* is used] for the purpose of excluding that [genitive sense].

Furthermore, the word *tat* is employed here with the first case ending (*prathamā*) as its governing factor. If this is so, then because the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*), namely "of this" (*asya*), has been excluded, the suffix prescribed by the rule *saṃkhyāyā guṇasya nimāne mayaṭ* (Pāṇini 5.2.47)—which occurs in the sense of the genitive—would not apply. Even though [the meaning] has been excluded here...

There is no fault, for the recurrence [of the term] will occur by way of the "frog-leap" maxim (*maṇḍūkapluti*). Others, however, explain that as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the word *tad*. He says *tad*—referring to that which is under discussion—and this indicates that in the rule *tadasya sañjātam* (Pāṇini 5.2.36) and others, whatever is specified [is intended].
Therefore, since it does not attain the status of a subordinate member (*aṅga*) even while being present here, the suffix [denoting] the sense of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*) does not occur.
46. *śadantarviśateśca* (5.2.46).

Now, in rules such as *ṭhpaṅkti* (5.1.59), words like *triṃśat* and others end in the suffix *śat*; therefore, by the very paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), the suffix [should be added] after that which ends in it.

[The objection is: "Since [the desired result] is obtained, what is the purpose of including the mention of 'end' (anta)?"; to this he says: "In the case of the mention of *śat*, there is the inclusion of the word 'end'," and so forth.

If the mention of 'end' were not made, then by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyaya-grahaṇa*), [the operation] would apply only to that which begins with the element from which the suffix is prescribed, and not to anything more than that. Therefore, [the mention of 'end'] is for the sake of [including] even what is more than that.

The mention of the word "anta" (end) is for the purpose that it should be so. If, then, the mention of "anta" is intended to mean "beginning with that from which the suffix is prescribed," it would not apply to a solitary [word]. This is not a fault;
for the particle *ca* is used here, and it serves to include what has not been explicitly stated; by means of it, [the rule applies] even to a solitary [word].

"It will be so. And the term 'numeral' (*saṃkhyā*) must be included. That by which a numeral is grasped is "the inclusion of the numeral," and that must be done. But what must be done? An explanation.
The explanation there is as follows: from the rule "the suffix *tayap* occurs after a numeral in the sense of a part" (Pāṇini 5.2.42), [the word] "numeral" (*saṃkhyāyāḥ*)...
This [rule] continues [from the previous sūtra]; therefore, it will apply only when preceded by a numeral (saṃkhyā), and not when preceded by anything else.

Regarding the phrase "and from *viṃśati*," etc., the meaning is that this form of the rule must be explained as follows: the suffix *ḍa* occurs after the word *viṃśati* and after nominal stems ending in *viṃśati*.

In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the suffix occurs both directly from the word *viṃśati* as it is explicitly mentioned in the sūtra, and also from that which ends in it; for the particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been stated.
In the passage beginning with "and the mention of the word 'number' (*saṃkhyāgrahaṇam*)," the meaning is exactly as before, and the explanation is also precisely as before.
47. *mayaṭ* [is used] after a numeral when there is a measure of a quality (*guṇa*). (Pāṇini 5.2.47). "A quality by which something is measured" means that it is exchanged or sold.
"That too," etc.: for without its being a portion, it could not simply be called a "quality" of the thing to be measured.

It is possible to determine that something possesses the status of a "part" (bhāga) only when it has been specified; for indeed, if the root [of the term] does not possess the status of a part, the designation "part" does not apply at all. Therefore, even though the status of being a part of the measure (*nimāna*) was not explicitly stated, it is nevertheless understood through implication. [As in: "two parts of barley."

"Of this there is the exchange (*nimāna*). Now, although there is indeed an exchange in both cases, nevertheless, the word *nimāna* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) only in the sense of "price. Therefore, only that which is intended as the price becomes the *nimāna*, and nothing else. Regarding the phrase "of barley grains" (*yavānām*), the genitive case is used in relation to the portion. If this is so, [then...]

If the word *udaśvit* were dependent on something else, the application of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix would be contradicted. Now, the suffix is applied to the portion that is curdled milk (*udaśvit*), not to the word *udaśvit* itself; so how can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *udaśvit* for that which ends in a suffix, such that one says "curdled milk consists of two [parts]"? To this [it is replied]:
He says: "But even in the case of a part," and so forth. Here, moreover, the reason is the inherent nature of the denotative power (*abhidhāna-śakti-svābhāvya*).

Just as [suffixes] such as *aṇ* and others, although prescribed in relation to the connection between offspring and the progenitor, denote the related party primarily due to the inherent nature of their denotative power—as in the case of *aupagavaḥ*.

Regarding the term *dākṣi*: likewise, this [suffix] also, when prescribed after a part (*bhāga*), denotes that which possesses the part, such as curd (*udaśvit*) and so forth. As for the statement "the singular number in *guṇasya* is intended to be significant," the singular number in the word *guṇasya* is indeed intended to be significant. But is it not the case that [the rule] *taddhitāḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.76) [applies]?

Even though it has been stated that "in this case, although there is such an indication, the plural number is not authoritative because it is not intended to be significant," how is it appropriate here to intend the singular number? This is not a fault;
for in this instance, one should form a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) and then apply the diminutive suffix (*guṇanimāna*), for in this way the sūtra remains concise.
It is so. Since this must be stated in such a way, the fact that he utters the singular form *guṇasya* indicates that singularity is intended here;
by the words "by that" (*tena*) and so forth, he demonstrates the fruit of intending singularity. For when singularity is intended, this [is the case].
The purpose [of this rule] is so that [the suffix] may occur when there is a comparison (*nimāna*) of a single quality (*guṇa*), as in:
"two parts of barley, three of buttermilk. In this case, since the word *dvi-* ("two") occurs in comparison with three parts, the suffix does not apply.

But even if there is an intention to express oneness (*ekatva*), the suffix *-tama* should certainly not occur here, because of the rule stating: "The suffix is desired after a number that expresses a plurality.
For in this case, the word *dvi-* (two) does not denote a plurality. If that is so, then [it refers to] those two parts of barley which...

In this context, those two are intended to be expressed as the objects to be measured (*nimeya*). Those three portions of *udaśvit* are intended as the means of measurement (*nimāna*). In that case, if there were no intention to express singularity, then the suffix would apply based on the three qualities of *udaśvit*. This is also the case for the rule "and when [the number] is greater" (*bhūyasaśca*).

A suffix is desired to express the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) when that meaning is more extensive than the meaning of the suffix itself, and not otherwise—as in the case where it is said, "it does not occur here. This is because [the meaning] is not expressed [by the suffix], or because the particle *iti* is understood as carrying over from the preceding sūtra, "tadasminn adhikam" (5.2.45). If [the meaning] were more extensive...

Is it not the case that for a verbal number, [the rule] "this has two parts as its measure" (*yavānāṃ dvau bhāgau nimānam asya*) would not apply? To this he says: "And because of the word *bhūyas*," and so forth.
For even in this way, the following would apply: "two barley-corns and half a ladle of buttermilk," since such a thing exists here.
Why is there an excess of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) over the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*)? To this he says: "The word *guṇa*, etc.
For this word *guṇa*, while denoting a part (*bhāga*), also expresses the equality of that part; and by the word *ardha*, an equal part is not expressed.

"And it is also seen in the word *ṭhnimeya*. By what, then, is it prescribed that it is seen? By this very [sūtra]. How so? There are two sentences here; in one of them, the word *nimāna* is derived by means of the instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*)—*nimānam* being that by which something is measured (*nimīyate'neneti nimānam*); but in the second...
*Nimāna* is that which is measured (*nimīyate*); the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) according to Pāṇini 3.3.113 (*kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*).
When it is derived as an instrument (*karaṇa*), then the genitive case *guṇasya* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*);
but when it is derived as the object (*karman*), then [the genitive] is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). For the quality (*guṇa*)...

The instrument of the act of exchange (*nimāna*) is intended to be expressed as the agent (*kartṛ*). For indeed, there is an intention to express the instrument as the agent, as in the example: "the axe cuts" (*sādhyasiś chinatti*). In that case, by means of a single sentence, the suffix is prescribed for the object of exchange (*nimeya*), which is the thing to be expressed, when the number residing in the act of exchange is [intended].

By another [interpretation], when *nimaya* is present, the suffix is also stated even when *nimāna* is the meaning to be expressed. And the basis for the inclusion of the word "number" (*saṃkhyā*) in the case of a split in the sentence is derived from the rule "the suffix *tayap* occurs after a number in the sense of a part" (Pāṇini 5.2.42). And thus...

The mention of "number" (saṃkhyā) continues [from the previous rule]. This is the second [instance] here. In that case, if there were only one sentence here, the second mention of "number" would be purposeless; however, when two sentences are formed based on the inference from the Sūtra, it becomes meaningful. Therefore, there are two sentences here.

Regarding the expression "two *vrīhi* and *yava* [for one *udāśvit*]," etc.: here, two *vrīhi* and *yava* are not intended as the measure for a portion of the *udāśvit*; rather, they are the measure for the *udāśvit* itself. Similarly in "two qualities," etc.;
here, that which is expressed by the first case-ending functions as the measure of the quality (*guṇa*). For it is not [intended] that [the quality] exists by means of two portions of milk.

A portion of oil is measured out. The addition of the suffix *mayaṭ* with the augment *ṭi* is for the sake of [forming] the feminine suffix *ṅīp*—as in "two parts of molasses and one part of grape-juice" (*dvimayī drākṣā*).
48. *ḍaṭ* is used for its completion (*pūraṇa*).

Here, two mentions of "number" (*saṃkhyā*) are carried over [from previous rules]. Among them, by the first, which states "from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting a number," the base (*prakṛti*) is specified. By the second, however—
In order to specify the meaning of the suffix, he says "by which" (*yena*), and so forth.

By pronouncing the word *saṃkhyāna*, he demonstrates that the meaning of the suffix is specified by the word *saṃkhyāna* as a term denoting number. For the word for number (*saṃkhyā-śabda*) is of two kinds: that which denotes the act of counting (*saṃkhyāna-vacana*) and...

And there is the term *saṃkhyeya* (countable). In that context, if the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is qualified by the word *saṃkhyeya*, then the meaning would be this: that by which a countable object, such as a fistful (*muṣṭi*) and so forth, is completed—that is, made complete by another substance and no longer deficient—is the "completer" (*pūraṇa*). Consequently, [the suffix would apply] to "five" and so on.

In that case, [the suffix] would also apply in an expression such as *muṣṭikānāṃ ghaṭaḥ* ("a jar of handfuls"). Therefore, it is proper to qualify the meaning of the suffix by means of a word expressing a number (*saṃkhyāvacana*) alone. By the word *sampadyate*, he explains the meaning of *pūryate* ("is filled").
By this, he shows that the meaning of the suffix is [qualified] by a word expressing a number.

It is specified [as follows]: the completion of a number is not the addition of a further substance to substances, as in the case of a handful of beans; rather, it is simply their aggregation (*sampatti*). "In this case, it does not occur," and so forth. For when a jar is produced, the number five does not become aggregated in the handful of beans. Why?
What then? In that case, there is an excess of precisely five [factors] by means of another substance.

49. *nāntādasaṃkhyādermaṭ* (Pāṇini 5.2.49). [The commentary states: "The augment *maṭ* occurs after the suffixes *ṭhaṅ* and *ḍaṭ*. Now, why does the suffix *maṭ* itself not occur after a stem ending in *n*, rather than being an augment? It is not fit to be a suffix; for if it were a suffix, [the following rule would apply:]...

The recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of *ḍaṭ* would be purposeless, for it has already been prescribed previously; and the recurrence of what has already been prescribed is not appropriate for the purpose of further prescription. Furthermore, that [recurrence] is understood to serve the purpose of indicating an augment (*āgama*).
But surely, in cases such as "pañcama" and so forth, there is no distinction between *maṭ* being an augment and its being an affix (*pratyaya*).

Or rather: that very thing is the *rūpa* (form), and that indeed is the *svara* (accent); what is the use of the *anu* suffix? Let the status of being an affix (*pratyayatva*) belong to *maṭ* alone. True, there is no distinction here [in the case of *pañcama*]; however, a distinction exists in cases such as *viṃśatitama*. For it is said: "The suffix *tamaṭ* is optionally applied after words beginning with *viṃśati*" (Pāṇini 5.2.56).

The suffix *mat* (the printed reading is *mayaṭ*) would apply. Words beginning with "twentieth" (*viṃśatitama*) would have the middle syllable accented by the accent of the suffix. However, when the suffix *ḍaṭ* is present, since its first syllable is made acute and the augment (*āgama*) is unaccented, they become oxytone (having the final syllable accented).
Therefore, since it continues for the sake of the subsequent meaning, it is understood here as well that *ḍaṭ* alone possesses the status of an affix (*pratyaya*).

But how can the augment *maṭ* be prescribed for *ḍaṭ*, given that the mention of *ḍaṭ*— which is the subject under discussion— is indicated in the nominative case, whereas the purpose here is indicated by a genitive?

And so forth—starting with "nāntāt" and so on. Although the mention of *ḍaṭ* in the nominative case (*prathamānta*) is the subject under discussion, nevertheless, because *ḍaṭ* is connected with an augment (*āgama*), this ablative case (*pañcamī*) "nāntāt" (from that which ends in *n*) is interpreted as a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*)—"of that which ends in *n*"—in relation to the nominative "ḍaṭ," according to the rule "tasmād ity uttarasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.67). Thus, there is no fault.

"In the fifth [case], the elision of *ṭi* does not occur here; for once the suffix *maṭ* has been applied, it possesses the designation *abha*. But surely, by virtue of its higher status (*paratva*), the elision of *ṭi* ought to take place first? This is not so; for the augment (*āgama*) is internal (*antaraṅga*), since it..."

It is stated [by the rule] in connection with the suffix (*pratyaya*). However, the elision of *ṭi* occurs after the suffix has been produced; since the designation *bha* exists when both base and suffix are present, it is *bahiraṅga*.
[The example is: "the eleventh, which completes eleven" (*ekādaśānāṃ pūraṇa ekādaśaḥ*). But how can there be the application [of the suffix] from this [word], given that...

The mention of "number" (saṃkhyā) continues [from the previous rule], for even a collection of numbers is included by the mention of "number"—since it is so called because "one counts by means of it. And this must necessarily be understood in this way;
otherwise, there would be no application of the term "not ending in ten" (adaśatayā).
50. *thaṭ ca chandasi* (Pāṇini 5.2.50).

51. *ṣaṭ-kati-katipaya-caturāṃ thuk* (Pāṇini 5.2.51). [The commentary states: "In this context, [the suffix is added] after the locative case," and so forth. For this [suffix] is prescribed within the section concerning ordinal numbers (*pūraṇa*).

This is prescribed in connection with the suffix *ḍaṭ*. Although there is no locative case (*saptamī*) present there, it is nevertheless understood as being subsequent to *ḍaṭ*. Therefore, by implication, there occurs a transformation of the case-ending; thus, that which was stated as "after *ḍaṭ*" is here transformed into the locative. Furthermore, the word *katipaya* is not a numeral (*saṃkhyā*).

Thus, because it lacks the status of being worldly (*laukika*), it is not a number (*saṃkhyā*); for it is not recognized as a number in common usage (*loka*). Nor is it a technical number according to the treatise (*śāstra*), because the designation "number" is not prescribed for it in the *Śāstra*. If it is not a number, how can the suffix *ḍaṭ* apply to it, in which case...

Is *thuk* prescribed when *ḍaṭ* follows? To this he says: "of that," and so forth. From the very fact that *thuk* is prescribed for certain words when *ḍaṭ* follows, it is determined by that very indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the suffix *ḍaṭ* occurs after this [word]. In the form "ṣaṣṭhaḥ" (sixth), there is the substitution of *ṣṭ* [for *ṣṭh*]; here, the elision of the *ṭi* portion does not take place.
This is due to the force of the rule's formulation (*thugvidhānasāmarthyāt*). The making of the beginning of the preceding element (*pūrvāntakaraṇa*) is for the sake of the designation *bha*.

If it were made the beginning of the following element (*parādi*), then the designation *bha* would not apply; and that being absent, the designation *pada* would apply by the rule "in the presence of *svādi* suffixes other than those called *asarvanāmasthāna*" (Pāṇini 1.4.17). Consequently, [the sixth case...]

In this case, the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaś*) would apply. [Consider] "caturthaḥ"; here, the substitution of *s* for the visarga of the letter *r* occurs by the rule "visarjanīyasya saḥ" (8.3.34). However, if the preceding final form (*pūrvānta*) is accepted, then because the technical name (*saṃjñā*) [of the word ending in *r*] applies, [the substitution of *s*] does not take place.

52. *Bahupūgagaṇasaṅkhaśatam̐ tithuk* (Pāṇini 5.2.52). [The commentary states: "Because the words *pūga* and *saṅgha* are not numbers (*asaṃkhya*). In this regard, how can there be a suffix? For indeed, the words *pūga* and *saṅgha* are neither worldly numbers nor technical numbers according to the grammatical treatise; so how [can they take a suffix]?

From those two, the suffix *ḍaṭ* is applied; when that suffix follows, the augment *tithuk* is prescribed for them, and there is also a rule for its application in the case of *ḍaṭ*. To this, he gives the following answer: "This very [fact]," and so forth. This very prescription of *tithuk* for those two when *ḍaṭ* follows indicates that [the suffix] occurs after them.
Regarding the suffix *ḍat*: for that which is non-existent cannot logically function as a cause (*nimitta*) with respect to the augment *tithuk*.
53. *vatorathuk* (Pāṇini 5.2.53). [The example is] *yāvatithaḥ*. [The derivation is as follows: from *yat*, *etad*, and *tad*, the suffix *vatup* is applied in the sense of measure (Pāṇini 5.2.39);
then, by Pāṇini 6.3.91, *ā* is substituted for the final vowel of the pronominal stem.
54. *dvestīyaḥ* | (5.2.54) [The rule states:

"The suffix *tīya* occurs after the word *dvi*. Now, why is it that the substitution of *tīya* for the suffix *ḍaṭ* following the word *dvi* does not simply take place by this very rule? Because it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). For this [author] [states] "in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi*)...

By providing the designation *dvitīyā* (2.3.2) with the suffix *ṭāp*, he indicates that this is not a substitute (*ādeśa*). If this is so, is the formulation of the suffix (*pratyaya*) useless since it is already established by this very [rule]? No; it is for the sake of the accent (*svara*). For, due to the irregularity (*nipātana*),...

[The word] would be oxytone by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). However, with the suffix *tīya*, it becomes middle-accented (*madhyodāta*) by the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*). Furthermore, if the suffix were not prescribed, then even the suffix *ḍaṭ* might occur, according to the principle that "even exceptions (*bādhaka*) arise from irregular derivations (*nipātana*). If...

Furthermore, if this were the substitution of *ḍaṭ*, what would happen? By the accentuation rule for *ḍaṭ*, the word *tīya* would be udātta on its final syllable; moreover, because it would end in a *ṭi*-suffix, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would apply, and consequently, the form *dvitīyā* as used in the grammatical rule would be untenable.

55. *treḥ samprasāraṇañca* (5.2.55). The word *ṭhaṇ* is understood there [in this sūtra] from the previous rule. [The word *aṇ*] is understood from *ṭhḍhūalope pūrvasya dīrgho'ṇaḥ* (6.3.111). Now, one might object: since the *aṇ* is qualified by the subsequent *ṇ*, would not the vowel *ṛ* also be considered an *aṇ*?
To this he says: "And by the preceding [rule]," and so forth.
Why was it not stated here simply as "and for the three"? It is impossible to state it in this way;
for if it were stated thus, there would be doubt: "Is this a substitute (ādeśa), or is it an affix (pratyaya)?"
56. *viṃśatyādibhyastamaḍanyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.2.56). [The commentary begins:

"After *viṃśati* and so forth," and so on. Now, an objection is raised: since the suffix *ḍaḍ* intervenes between [the word] and the suffix *tīya*, how can the augment *tamaḍ* be understood [to apply]? Therefore...

He says: "Because of the governing rule concerning ordinal numbers. Since the suffix *tamap* is prescribed for that which is ordained in the sense of an ordinal following words such as *viṃśati* and so forth, and since no other [suffix] than *ḍaṭ* is possible in this context, it is understood to be *ḍaṭ* itself.

"The worldly number-words beginning with *viṃśati* are included," because of the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Thus, those [numbers] beginning with *viṃśati*, *ekaviṃśati*, and so forth, become included. What, then, would happen if [this were not the case] in the rule for *paṅkti* and so on (Pāṇini 5.1.59)?
Because they are not included [in the previous list].
57. *nityaṃ śatādimāsārdhamāsasaṃvatsarācca* (Pāṇini 5.2.57).
Regarding the phrase "the mention of 'śatādi' etc.": from words beginning with numerals such as 'śata' (hundred) and so forth, just as...

The mention of "hundred" and so forth is for the sake of the word *syāt* (it may be). Now, what is the purpose of the mention of *nitya* (constant/obligatory), since by the very force of the commencement [of the rule], the injunction will necessarily be constant? It might be so from the force of the commencement in the case of "hundred" and so forth.
However, because the term "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) recurs from the rule for *māsa* and so forth, there would be an optionality. [Objection:

But surely the term "optionally" will be excluded simply because it is not marked with a svarita accent? [Response: In that case, the explicit mention of "necessarily" (*nitya*) is for the sake of clarity.

58. And [the suffixes] *ṣaṣṭha*, etc., after a numeral beginning with *asaṃkhya*. (Pāṇini 5.2.58) Those beginning with *ṣaṣṭha* are to be understood as applying before one hundred (*śata*); for the suffix *tamaṭ* is prescribed for words beginning with "one hundred" by their own specific rule.
59. *Chha* is substituted for *matup* when expressing a *sūkta* or a *sāman*.

(Pāṇini 5.2.59) The term "in the sense of *matup*" (*ṭhmatau*) refers to the possessive sense (*matvartha*), by virtue of association (*sāhacaryāt*). [The commentary] says "by the possessive sense" (*matvarthena*), etc.
The case ending of the governing word (*samarthavibhakti*) is the nominative (*prathamā*); it is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*)—namely, existence (*astitvam*).

The meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*)—namely "this belongs to that"—is all implied by the mention of the possessive suffix *matup*; this means it is brought near, or presented. It is appropriate that the meaning of the suffix is implied when *matup* is mentioned, because its scope is precisely that. [This applies to] the case endings used for the governing relation (*samarthavibhakti*), and so forth.
How is it implied? Through association with the meaning.

Alternatively, because subordinate elements (guṇas) follow the principal element (pradhāna), when the meaning of the suffix is presented as the principal element, that [meaning of the base] which has become subordinate is also necessarily presented by the power of the suffix. In this case, a word such as *asyavāma* is a sentence (*vākya*) because it consists of multiple words. Of the sentence...

If someone were to object that because the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) regarding meaningful aggregates, these [imitative words] lack the designation of *prātipadika*, and therefore the suffix does not apply to them due to their not being *prātipadikas*, he says in response: "And imitative words (*anukaraṇaśabda*)," and so forth.

Furthermore, by the mention of "imitation" (*anukaraṇa*), [the author] rejects the status of being a sentence (*vākyatva*) for words such as *evam* and *āma*. For imitation-words do not possess constituent parts that are words (*pada*);

how then could they have the status of a sentence? [Otherwise], the designation of nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) would not apply to them. [Therefore, it is said: "they have their own form alone as their primary meaning."

By this, he demonstrates that they possess meaning (*arthavattva*). For if they were meaningless, they would not have the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), since the designation "nominal stem" is prescribed only for those that possess meaning; and consequently, the very absence of suffixes would follow [for them]. The word *mātra* is for the purpose of excluding other meanings; [it indicates] merely the essential form (*svarūpa*).
Those for whom the primary element (pradhāna) is the denotable object (abhidheya) are described as such. The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of "because.

Because imitation-words (anukaraṇaśabda) produce a suffix while having their own form alone as the primary element, therefore the grammatical operation known as a suffix is established even from multiple [sounds]; this is because they possess the status of nominal stems (prātipadika).

Furthermore, the status of not being a nominal stem (*aprātipadikatva*) would arise either from being a sentence (*vākya*) or from being meaningless (*anarthaka*). Now, these words beginning with *asyavāmam* do not constitute sentences, because they are words of imitation (*anukaraṇa*).
Nor are they meaningless, because they possess meaning by virtue of their own form alone. If...
In cases such as *hyasyavāma*, there exist many words as constituent parts (*avayava*) by means of the word "imitation" (*anukaraṇa*);

how then is it said that [the suffix] is established even from that which consists of multiple words? [The answer is: this is according to the established usage of others regarding the word. *Asyavāma* and so forth are likewise; their multiple constituents are well-known.

Therefore, it was stated in that way precisely because of its conventional usage [in that context], and not because multiple words actually exist there. Now, how is it that imitative words (*anukaraṇa-śabda*) provide merely their own form,
given that for them the object being imitated (*anukārya*) alone is the denotation, and thus that alone is the primary form?

This is not so; for here, a suffix is prescribed after a word in the nominative case that is coreferential with the verb *asti*. And imitation-words (*anukaraṇa-śabda*), although they possess meaning through the object being imitated, are nevertheless perceived as mere words by means of the particle *iti* or by the word "word" (*śabda*).

The words standing in the nominative case (*prathamā*) are coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇa*). For it is not possible for those that have become subordinate (*guṇībhūta*) in meaning to possess the status of being nominative-qualified (*prathamāsamarthatva*) and to function as limiting adjuncts (*upādhikatva*);
for instance, when it is said "this *asvāma* exists in this," it is precisely the original object of imitation (*anukārya*), as conveyed by the imitative form (*anukaraṇa*), [that is intended].

In the case of *śatṛ*, its initial incapacity and its status as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) are understood, but this is not the case for an imitative word (*anukaraṇa-śabda*). Therefore, there must necessarily be a reflective reference (*pratyavamarśa*) by means of the particle *iti* or by the word "word" (*śabda*). [The analysis is: "In this [expression] 'asyavāma', the word 'vāma' exists," or "in this [expression], 'vāma' exists."

The status of being a referent object (*padārthatā*) that is imitated through its differentiation (*bheda*) ceases, and only the status of being a referent object as its own essential form (*svarūpa*) arises. But if this is so, the possessive sense (*matvartha*) is not justified; for the words of the Vedic tradition (*āmnāya*) exist as the objects to be imitated (*anukārya*) in the case of *sūkta* and *sāman*, whereas the worldly words and others used as imitations (*anukaraṇa*) do not. This is not so.

This is the fault: because of the presence of the particle *iti* and other markers that serve as the cause for syntactic independence (*vākya-svātantrya-hetu*), imitative words (*anukaraṇa-śabda*) possess their own meaning when they are referred back by that [particle]; however, in a *vṛtti* (compound or derivative formation), they possess meaning only through the original object of imitation (*anukārya*), because in that case the particle *iti* and the like—which are the causes of syntactic independence—are absent.

Since it is precisely the *vṛtti* (the individual words) that are intended to be expressed as meaningful through their coalescence, and not the *vākya* (the sentence as a whole), what here is not logically consistent? The word *asyavāma* exists in this [hymn], thus it is the *Āsyavāmīya*;
the words *kayā śubhā* exist in this [hymn], thus it is the *Kāyāśubhīya*. And this is the etymological derivation (*yoga*).
This is an exception to [the rules concerning] suffixes expressing possession (*matvarthīya*).

60. *adhyāyānuvākayor luk* (5.2.60). Since the preceding rule prescribed the elision of *cch* only for *sūkta* and *sāman*, and since it has not been ordained elsewhere in another context for *adhyāya* and *anuvāka*, he asks: "By what [means] then?"
And so forth. For the elision (*luk*) of that [suffix] is not possible if it is non-existent; yet this very [rule] prescribes its elision.
Therefore, this very mention of elision indicates that there is a prescription for *cha* in the case of chapters (*adhyāya*) and sections (*anuvāka*).
Regarding the phrase "and optionally" (*vikalpena ca*), the word *ca* is used in the sense of restriction; the meaning is "only optionally. How?

Is it obtained through an alternative interpretation? Because of the continued application of the term *anyatarasyām* from the rule *ṭiṃśatyādibhyastamaḍanyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.2.56). If that is so, would not the rule also apply optionally in the preceding case?
There is no fault, for the continued application will occur according to the maxim of the frog’s leap (*bhaṇḍkapluti*).

61. *Vimuktādibhyaḥ-aṇ* (Pāṇini 5.2.61). Since the suffix *cha* would have applied by the preceding rule, and its optional elision (*luk*) would also have been applicable, the suffix *aṇ* is here prescribed after words beginning with *vimukta*.

62. *goṣadādibhyo vun* (Pāṇini 5.2.62). Since the suffix *cha* [which would otherwise apply] is subject to elision (*luk*) by the rule "elision of the suffixes [denoting] chapters and sections" (5.2.60), the suffix *vun* is introduced after words beginning with *goṣada*.
63. *kuśalaḥ* [is used] in the sense of "path" (*pathin*). (5.2.63) Since the suffix *aṇ* would otherwise apply by the rule *kṛtalabdhakrītakuśalāḥ* (4.3.38), the suffix *vun* is prescribed here.

64. *kan* is added after *ākarṣa* and others. (Pāṇini 5.2.64) Since the suffix *cha* would apply to words like *ākarṣa* that contain a *vṛddhi*-vowel, while *aṇ* applies to the remaining ones, the suffix *kan* is prescribed here.
The reason for employing a different suffix is this: so that *guṇa* does not occur for those among these [words] that end in the vowel *u*.

This is for the purpose that, in the case of that which ends in /e/, the elision [of the final vowel] prescribed by the rule *ṭhyasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148) should not occur; however, if the suffix *vuñ* were applied, both of those [undesirable consequences] would follow. Furthermore, from that, an ungrammatical form (*aśiṣṭa*) would result here. But if either *vuñ* or *kan* is applied to it, [that fault does not arise].
Since there is no distinction [between them], it does not necessitate another cognition.
65. *dhanahiraṇyātkāme* (Pāṇini 5.2.65). [The example is] "desire for wealth" (*dhane kāmaḥ*). The meaning is: a wish directed toward wealth.

66. *svāṅgebhyaḥ prasite* (5.2.66). Regarding the word *prasite*: although this root *si* is listed in the sense of "binding" (*bandhane*) as *ṣiñ bandhane* (Dhātupāṭha 1477), nevertheless, because roots have multiple meanings, it is used here in the sense of "attachment. [Examples: *keśeṣu*...

Regarding the word *prasitaḥ*: the locative case is used here according to Pāṇini 2.3.44, *prasitotsukābhyāṃ tṛtīyā ca*. Furthermore, attachment (*āsakti*) is a property whose object is an action; therefore, the action residing in the locus of the hair and so forth is expressed by the words "hair" and so on. For this very reason, he says: "engaged in the arrangement of the hair and so forth."
"It is stated thus:

'The plural number [is used] so that it may apply even to a collection of one's own limbs. For if that [rule] were not present, just as a collection of districts is not grasped by the term 'district,' so too [would it be here]."

If it were not for the inclusion of "one's own limb" (*svāṅga*) [in the definition], then [the term] would not apply to a collection of one's own limbs; however, since that [term] exists, it does apply. Otherwise, there would be no purpose for it.
If it is argued that its purpose is to exclude the prescription of the word-form itself (*svarūpa-vidhi*), we say no; because of the rule *adrava* ("not liquid").
Because "one's own limb" (*svāṅga*) has been defined by [the rule] beginning with *Kāśikā* 4.1.54, a rule concerning its own form (*svarūpavidhi*) is impossible.

67. *udarāṭṭhañ gādiṣv alpīyasi* (Pāṇini 5.2.67). Since the suffix *kan* would have applied by the preceding rule, *ṭhañ* is prescribed here. [The rule] "after *ṭha*, etc., there is *ūna* when not meaning 'desirous of conquering'" (*ṭhād yaūno’vijigīṣau*) applies;

for by the rule "*vi* is substituted for *vī* when not meaning 'desirous of conquering'" (*vivo’vijigīṣāyām*, 8.2.49), the substitution of *vi* occurs only when it does not mean "desirous of conquering."
Because the substitution of *na* for the final *ta* is prescribed, "udarakaḥ" is formed by the suffix *kan* according to the preceding rule.
68. *sasyena parijātaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.68).
In the rule *sasyena*, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used either to indicate association (*sahayoga-lakṣaṇa*) or to indicate a characteristic mark (*itthambhūta-lakṣaṇa*).
It is said that "this word *sasya* denotes a quality. For this word *sasya* is indeed used to denote grain as well.

For example, as in "rice is a crop" and "barley is a crop"; this was stated—"this is a designation"—so that its inclusion [under the term *sasya*] might not be understood [as being included by the rule for *sasya* itself]. The word *sasyaka*, however, ends in the suffix *kan*.

69. *Aśaṃhārī* (Pāṇini 5.2.69). [The commentary states: "In the case of the object (*karman*), only the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) occurs. Since the second case ending would have applied to the object, this sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*), characterized by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix, is introduced as an exception to it. And this applies when the suffix *ṇini* is used in the sense of necessity (*avaśyaka*).
There is a prohibition [of the accusative case] by the rule "ṭhako 'norbhaviṣyadādhamarṇyayoḥ" (Pāṇini 2.3.70). Consequently, because it is free from any exception, only the accusative case applies.
70. *tantrāt acirāpahṛte* (Pāṇini 5.2.70). Regarding the example *acirāpahṛtam*: the word *acira* signifies a short period of time.

By means of the word *apahṛta*, [the compound] *acirāpahṛta* is formed according to the rule *kālāḥ parimāṇinā* ("time-denoting words [are compounded] with a word denoting that which possesses the measure"). This means "that from which a short time has been taken away" (*apahṛtaḥ gataḥ kālaḥ asya*).

(2.2.5) Thus ends the compound. Regarding the phrase "from that which is in the fifth case-ending" (*pañcamīsamarthāt*): this is understood precisely from the explicit mention (*nirdeśa*) itself. For no case-ending is being carried over (*anuvartate*) here as a subject of discussion; rather, the mention of the fifth case is directly heard. Therefore, it is understood from the very mention that the suffix is applied after that which is in the fifth case-ending. Furthermore, that [fifth case]—
Since the root *apahṛ* (to take away) denotes a state of misfortune (*apāya*), that with which one is connected by means of it becomes the ablative (*apādāna*) itself;
thus, it should be understood as characterized by the ablative case.

71. *brāhmaṇakoṣṇike saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 5.2.71). But for what purpose is this [rule] stated, since it is derived (*vyutpādyate*) in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*), and *brāhmaṇaka* and *uṣṇika* are indeed names? No; because they apply even in other domains. That very domain [is as follows]:...
To demonstrate this, he says "where," and so forth; the meaning has already been explained.

72. [The suffix *ṇini* is applied] after [the words] *śīta* and *uṣṇa*, when they denote an agent (*kāriṇi*). (Pāṇini 5.2.72). Regarding the phrase "from an adverb" (*kriyāviśeṣaṇāt*): for it has been established that an adverb functions as the object (*karman*). Regarding the word "agent" (*kāriṇi*): the suffix *ṇini* is used here in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*). And when this [suffix] is employed...

The sixth case (genitive) is prohibited; therefore, the second case (accusative) alone must be used for the object. It is understood that the suffix is applied after words such as *śīta* ("cold") when they function as adverbs of action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) and are capable of taking the second case. Consequently, the words *śīta* and *uṣṇa* are not used here in the sense of "touch" (*sparśa*).

[The suffix -ṇini] produces a cognition [of necessity]. Where, then? In slowness and speed; for the suffix -ṇini occurs [only] when there is necessity (avaśyaka). There is no such entity that necessarily produces the sensations of cold and heat, since even frost and sunlight do not necessarily produce them, as an obstruction may occur.

However, since the capacity of entities to act is restricted, it is indeed necessary that this capacity— regarding their agency— is determined by some specific cause; for otherwise, one would inevitably have to explain why one agent acts slowly while another acts quickly.
73. *Adhikam* (5.2.73). [The rule states:

"There is elision of the final member of the word *adhyārūḍha*. That is to say, the elision of the final member, the word *ārūḍha*, is prescribed by nipātana (irregular derivation). But how can there be the form *adhiko droṇaḥ khāryām*, where the word ending in the nominative case (*adhikaḥ*) is used?
Why is the word *droṇa* used [as a noun], and why is there the use of the instrumental case ending in *adhikā khārī droṇena* ("an excess of a khārī by a droṇa")?

To this he says: "In the sense of the agent and the object," and so forth. By the rule *gatyarthakarmakaśliṣa-* (Pāṇini 3.4.72), the suffix *kta* is prescribed for the root *ruh* in both the senses of the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*); therefore, in the sense of the agent...

The word *adhyārūḍha* functions in both the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*); consequently, when the word *adhika* is etymologically derived as having that same meaning, it also becomes a synonym for those two very meanings. Among these, when it functions in the sense of the agent, then...

From the word *droṇa*, the nominative case occurs, not the instrumental. When it functions as the object (*karman*), then, because the agent (*kartṛ*) is not expressed, the instrumental case occurs after the word *droṇa* due to the word *adhika*.
However, because the object is already expressed, only the nominative occurs after the word *khārī*, not the accusative.

"An *adhika* [measure] is a *khārī* plus a *droṇa*. Now, one might object: since the *droṇa* is the object (*karman*) in the sense "an additional *droṇa* is in this *khārī*," and because it has not been expressed by a case ending, shouldn't the second case (*dvitīyā*) apply to the word *khārī*? This is not a fault; for there are these two rules: "that from which something is greater" (Pāṇini 2.3.9) and "that which is greater in this" (Pāṇini 5.2.45).
And by making this specific instruction, he indicates that when joined with the word *adhika*,
only the fifth and seventh case endings (*pañcamī* and *saptamī*) occur.

74. *anukābhikābhīkaḥ kamitā* | (5.2.74) [The suffix] *ṭhanuka* is added. From the word *anu*, the suffix *kan* is applied. [The forms] *abhikaḥ* and *abhīkaḥ* are likewise derived; here too, they are formed from the word *abhi*.
75. *pārśvenānvicchatī* (Pāṇini 5.2.75). Since the third case ending is obtained from the very wording of the rule itself, he says: "from the word *pārśva*, when it is in the third case."

76. *Ayaḥśūla-daṇḍājina-bhyām ṭhak-ṭhañ-au* (5.2.76). Regarding the rule *ayaḥśūla-daṇḍājina-bhyām*: since the nouns are presented in the third case (*tṛtīyā*), the third case as the governing case-ending (*samartha-vibhakti*) is obtained by implication; thus he says: "from these two [words] standing in the third case."
77. *tāvatithaṃ grahaṇam iti lug vā* (5.2.77).

This is a general reference to those words ending in ordinal suffixes (*pūraṇapratyaya*). Why then is it not a reference to the actual form [of the word] itself? Because this reference has meaning as its primary focus; for if the reference were primarily concerned with the word-form itself...
It has been stated that there is the apprehension of the word's own form (*svarūpa*). How does a suffix (*pratyaya*) occur in its own sense (*svārtha*)?

It is because it is established that "suffixes whose meaning is not specifically prescribed occur in their own sense" (Pāṇini 5.3.27). Thus, [we have] *dvikam* and *trikam*, where there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *tīya*; and *catuṣkam*.

There is elision (*luk*) of the ordinal suffix *ḍaṭ* and of *sathuk*; then, by the rule "the *ṣ* replaces the *ṭh*-visarga of a word ending in four *ṛ*s" (Pāṇini 8.3.34), and subsequently by the rule "there is *ṣ* for that [suffix] which has *ṭh* or *id* as its penultimate, provided it is not a suffix" (Pāṇini 8.3.41), the substitution of *ṣ* occurs.
Thus, we have "tāvatithena" and so forth. This is derived from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in an ordinal suffix.

It should be stated that the suffix *kan* occurs after a word ending in the third case (instrumental) in the sense of "he takes. Furthermore, there is always elision (*luk*) of the ordinal suffix. Thus, [from *ṣaṣṭha*] we have *ṣaṭkaḥ*. Here, the *ṣ* undergoes the change to the voiced unaspirated sound (*jaś*), becoming *ḍ*; then the *ḍ* undergoes the change to the voiceless unaspirated sound (*car*), becoming *ṭ*. And in this instance, there is the elision of the suffix *ḍaṭ* along with its inherent *sathuk*.

Regarding the rule "ṭh-pañcakaḥ," here too [the suffix] ḍaṭ [is intended]. Now, why does it not apply in this case: "he grasps a staff with his second hand"? To this he says: "The inclusion of the letter *ṭ* is for the sake of indicating the intended meaning (*vivakṣārtha*)," and so forth.
This is easy to understand.
78. *sa* [is used] in the sense of "their leader" (*grāmaṇī*).
(5.2.78) 79. *śṛṅkhala* [is used] in the sense of "its tether" (*bandhana*) when referring to a young camel (*karabha*).
(5.2.79) But surely a young camel is not bound by a chain alone; what then? By means of a rope and so forth.

And [one might ask]: "How then is the chain called a bond? To this he says: "Even though," and so forth. Even though there is also something else there, such as a rope and the like, nevertheless the chain indeed serves as the instrument for making that [chain] the string; for it does not become that [string] by means of that [rope]. Therefore, the chain...
It is called a bond. Even if a rope or the like constitutes a bond, let it be so! For in this context, it is not restricted to the idea that "only a chain" is a bond.
80. *utka* [expresses] the act of going (*unman-ga*). (Pāṇini 5.2.80).

Regarding the phrase "from that which expresses an action together with its instrument" (*sasādhanakriyāvacanāt*): the "instrument" (*sādhana*) is the mind (*manaḥ*); the "action" (*kriyā*) is the act of going (*gamanam*);
"together with that" means the action of going accompanied by it. Thus, the meaning is: from that which denotes the act of going along with its instrument.

Regarding the phrase "tadvati" (possessing that): by the word "tat" (that), the action is referred back; the meaning is "possessing an action together with its means. Regarding "utsukaḥ" (eager): the meaning is "one who has been drawn upward [or excited]."

81. *kālaprayojanādroge* (Pāṇini 5.2.81). [The commentary begins: "The meaning is obtainable," and so forth. "Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and other such factors. By this, even though not explicitly stated here, the case endings beginning with the seventh (locative)—the case endings that express the governing relation—are obtained. "Purpose" (*prayojana*)...

The mention of "time" (kāla) by the word "cause" (kāraṇa) should not be made separately [as a distinct factor], because time is also a cause of disease. This is not so; for time is not necessarily a cause of disease.
In that regard, even when it is not a cause of disease, nevertheless, from that [time]—just as...
The mention of "time" (kāla) is for the sake of this very meaning: "that which occurs on the second day is 'dvitīyaka'.
In that case, regarding a fever arising from some other cause such as wind (vāta), time is intended merely as the locus (adhikaraṇa-bhāva), and not as the cause (hetu-bhāva). But how [is this so]?

The suffix occurs after words such as *dvitīya* and others when they denote something other than time; for these are not well-known as words for time. Indeed, these are general terms, and it is only through the proximity of another word that their application to time is understood. This is not a fault, for in the sentence...

In the proximity of another word, there is a restricted application (kalivṛtti); and the meaning of the base (prakṛtyartha) contained within that application serves as a qualifier for the suffixes because of its immediate proximity, not that which belongs to the sentence, due to remoteness. For example: "produced by poison-flowers" (*viṣapuṣpair janitaḥ*), where the third case ending is used; and "heat is its effect" (*uṣṇaṃ kāryam asya*). In this [latter] case...

The relationship between cause and effect is intended here. Since that [relationship] is expressed by the genitive case arising from the word *idam* itself, the nominative alone occurs after the word *uṣṇa*. In this context, the suffix is prescribed after words expressing time, purpose, and specific qualities, but not [after others].

[The suffix] *bhavan* occurs after words expressing specific times, in the sense of the agent of an action, when used with the word *jvara*; [the suffix] *prayojana* occurs after words expressing specific purposes;
and when there is an intention to express cause and effect, it occurs in relation to the effect. Nor is this a restrictive rule regarding the types [of formations].

It is stated in the Sūtra; how, then, is this obtained? To this he says: "In this [context], the mention of 'technical term' (saṃjñā) from the subsequent Sūtra is drawn back [into the present one]. By that, when that [condition] exists, the meaning becomes: if it ends in an affix and is a technical term, and when that meaning exists, [it refers to] that which ends in an affix.
If a term is indeed a technical name (*saṃjñā*), then it arises only in this manner and not otherwise.
Because of the proximity of the mention of "technical name," this restriction is obtained here in all its aspects;
for a suffix does not become a technical name by any other means than that. But is it not so in the subsequent rule?

The mention of "saṃjñā" (name) is supplementary to that very [rule]; how then can it be separated from it? This is not a fault; for it is supplementary to both rules. How so? A division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made:
first, "tadasminn annaṃ prāye," and then "saṃjñāyām. By this...
The mention of "notion" (saṃjñā) will be understood as a remainder for both.
82. *tadasminn annaṃ prāye saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 5.2.82). [The commentary states: "If the food (*anna*) is the subject of 'mostly' (*prāya*). That which has "mostly" as its scope is thus described.

By the inclusion of the word "scope" (*viṣaya*), it is shown that in the expression "mostly" (*prāye*), the locative case functions as a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*). [The suffix] is applied...

[The word] *bhavati* [is used]. Otherwise, in the case of the intention (*vivakṣā*) that "jaggery-cakes are generally food," the case-roles (*kāraka*s) [of the cakes] arise; because the object of the generalization (*prāya*), being intended as the instrument (*karaṇa*), the third case ending [is applied].
[In the formation of] *guḍāpūpikā*, [the rule] *pratyayasthāt kāt pūrvasyātaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.44) [applies].
Thus [is established] the substitution of *it*.
Regarding the statement "the suffix *ini* should be prescribed after the word *vaṭaka*," the meaning is that it must be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows:
since the mention of a "technical term" (*saṃjñā*) here functions as a condition for the presence of a suffix ending, wherever there is a suffix ending...

In that case, there must be a technical name (*saṃjñā*) [for the word *vaṭaka*] for the suffix to apply. However, the word *vaṭaka* ending in the suffix *kan* is not the technical name of anything; therefore, the suffix *kan* will not occur after it.
And since that [suffix *kan*] is absent, the possessive suffix *ini* will occur, resulting in the form *vaṭakinaḥ*.
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied after [stems ending in] *ṛt* and *nabha*. (Pāṇini 4.1.5)
83. *kulmāṣādañ* (Pāṇini 5.2.83).

Since the previous rule [5.2.114] would have provided for the suffix *kan* by virtue of it being a technical name (*saṃjñā*), and since the possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya*) such as *matup* would otherwise apply when expressing the sense of possession through a periphrastic construction, this rule is stated to supersede them. Thus we have *kaulmāṣī*, [formed] by *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* [4.1.15].
(4.1.15) Thus, the suffix *ṅīp* [is applied].

84. *śrotriyaḥ* means "one who has studied the Veda" (*chando'dhīte*). (Pāṇini 5.2.84). [The commentary states: "The letter *ṇ* is for the sake of the accent. Now, one might object: "An accent is prescribed when *nit* follows—that is, when *n* is the final element of that which precedes it. But since *n* is a marker (*anubandha*) of the entire suffixal complex (*samudāya*), there is no state of being 'followed by *nit*' (*nitparatva*) here. This is not so.

There is a fault; it is not so, for this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Therefore, since the letter *n* bears the designation *it*, the vowel of the preceding element will receive the accent when [the suffix] follows. What, then, is prescribed here? He says: "one who studies the *Chandas*" (*cchando'dhīte*). In the sense of this sentence, [the term] is *śrotriya*.

It is treated as an irregular formation (*nipātyate*). Regarding the rule "optionally in the Veda" (*chandaso vā*) and so forth: previously, in the sense of a sentence-meaning, a word was treated as an irregular formation without the division of base and suffix; now, however, both the base and the suffix are treated as irregular formations in the sense of "having studied that. Although [the root] *ni* is mentioned here...
It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; nevertheless, the accent is indeed established, because the suffix *ghan*, which follows a *nit* [marker], is present.
Regarding the phrase "How so? and so forth: if the word *cchabdaḥ* is a substitute for the word *śrotra*, and *ghaṃ* is [the suffix].

The term *pratyaya* is prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation) in the sense of "one who studies that"; the intention is that because this meaning is already covered by the nipātana, the suffix *cha* (as in *cchāndasa*) would not otherwise apply here.

85. *śrāddham anena bhuktam iti iṭhan-au* (Pāṇini 5.2.85). Regarding the phrase "the word *śrāddha*" and so forth: the term *śrāddha* is the designation for a particular ritual act (*kriyā-viśeṣa*) that is to be accomplished according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures. This is a noun (*karman-śabda*) denoting an action. It is that in which there is faith (*śraddhā*).

The word *śrāddha* exists as a *karma* (object); the suffix *ṇa* is applied according to the rule "prajñā-śraddhā-arcā-vṛtibhyo ṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.2.101). Regarding the phrase "in that which accomplishes it" (*tatsādhane*), etc.: since the state of having been eaten (*bhuktatvam*) cannot function as a qualifier of the *karma*, the word *śrāddha* functions by referring to that which accomplishes it—namely, the food and so forth.

It is understood that [the sense organ] produces the condition (pratyaya). Its function, however, lies in its accomplishment of that [condition], because it exists for that purpose; just as, for example, the word "lamp" is applied to a jasmine flower when it is intended for a lamp.
Regarding the phrase "grasping at the same time": that by which a common time is grasped [is meant].
The simultaneous apprehension of those [two] must be explained; this is the meaning. For what purpose? He says:

"if one has eaten today," and so forth. On the very day that the *śrāddha* was eaten by him, he would be designated as a *śrāddhika*; it is for the sake of preventing this from applying when he has eaten today but [the designation is intended for] tomorrow. In that regard, this...

The explanation: here too, the word "or" (vā) is understood from the previous rule, and that is a restricted option (vyavasthitavibhāṣā); therefore, it is desired that [the food] be eaten on the very same day the śrāddha was consumed, and not on another day.

86. *pūrvādiniḥ* (5.2.86). [The examples] "gone before," "drunk before," and "eaten before" are given. Since the word *pūrva* here functions as an object (*karman*) by virtue of being an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), it is understood that the suffix is applied after a word in the second case (*dvitīyāsamartha*). Thus, [the form] *pūrvaḥ* [is derived].
The long vowel [ā] is substituted [by Pāṇini’s rule] "sau ca" (6.4.13).

87. *Sapūrvācca* (5.2.87). The word *saha* signifies "existing" (*vidyamāna*). For this very reason, it says: "that which has a preceding [element] existing. The substitution of *sa-* for *saha-* occurs by the rule *vopasarjanasya* (6.3.72). [The example is: *kṛtapūrvaḥ kaṭam*.
But is it not the case that, because the object (*karman*) has already been expressed by the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), the accusative case ending should not occur here?

This is not a fault; this [participle] is not used in the sense of the object, but rather in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*). Even when it is used in the sense of the object, there is still no fault; for by the *niṣṭhā*, the object is expressed only in its general sense, and not—

[This refers to] a specific action (*viśeṣakarma*). Therefore, because that specific action has not been expressed [by another word], the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) will occur. But is this not a sentence, since it consists of multiple word-components such as "previously done" (*pūrvaṃ kṛtam*)? And since the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) is for the purpose of restriction—namely, that the designation "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) applies only to meaningful collections [that are compounds]—the nominal stem designation would not apply here.

[The objection: "It does not exist. How, then, can there be a grammatical derivation (*pratyaya*) from this? To this he says: "By the rule *sup-supā*," and so forth; "and by two applications of the rule (*yogadvayena*)," and so forth. If this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), namely *vyapadeśivadbhāvo 'prātipadikena* (Śākaṭāyana Paribhāṣā 65), did not exist, then...
One might instead form a single rule: *sapūrvātpūrvādiniḥ*. What is the purpose of this separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*)?

For if there were a single rule, the suffix would apply even after a simple [word] by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which has a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). Thus, since the result is established through a single rule, why is it stated as *pūrvādiniḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.86)?

He makes a separate rule [Pāṇini 1.1.27] to indicate that there exists this technical maxim (*paribhāṣā*): "The designation of one thing as being like itself applies even when it is not a nominal stem" (*vyapadeśivadbhāvo 'prātipadikena*; Śākaṭāyana Paribhāṣā 65). Alternatively, if such maxims as "that which possesses a [specific] mention" (*grahaṇavatā*; Vyāḍi Paribhāṣā 89) did not exist, [the sūtra] *sapūrvācca* [would have been unnecessary].

One should not formulate this rule [that the suffix *ini* occurs after a word ending in *pūrva*]. For even in cases such as *kṛtapūrvī*, the suffix will occur by means of the rule *pūrvādiniḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.86) itself through the principle of "extension to that which ends in [the specified stem].

Thus, since the suffix is already established from the word *pūrva* by the previous rule alone, the inclusion of the phrase *sapūrvācca* (Pāṇini 5.2.87)—"also after a word preceded by another"—is intended for a specific purpose.

By performing this application [of the rule], he indicates that there exists this metarule: "A nominal stem (*prātipadika*) accompanied by a suffix does not undergo the extension of a grammatical operation to what ends with it" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 89).

88. *iṣṭādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 5.2.88). [The rule] *iṣṭo yajñe* [is cited]. But how can there be a locative case here, since the sacrifice (*yajña*), being the object, ought to take the accusative? To this he says: *ktasyenviṣayasya*, etc.

89. *chandasi paripanthi-paripariṇau paryavasthātari* (Pāṇini 5.2.89). What, then, is being irregularly formed (*nipātyate*) here? Having established the word *paryavasthātṛ*, in one case the substitution of *panth* for the constituent part *avasthātṛ* is made, and in the other, that very same [substitution] is applied.
The word *pari* [is used], and the suffix *ādin* [is applied].

90. *anupadyenveṣṭā* (Pāṇini 5.2.90). Regarding the form *anupadī*: *anupadam* means "behind the foot" (*paścāt padasya*), an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) used in the sense of "behind. From this [base], the suffix *ini* is prescribed as a formal irregularity (*nipātana*).

91. *sākṣāddraṣṭari saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 5.2.91). Regarding the phrase "the mention of *saṃjñā*" and so forth: the restriction of the meaning (*abhidheyaniyama*) is that the application of the suffix ending [in this case, *ṇini*] occurs only when a specific denotatum is intended; thus, there is the elision of the *ṭi* portion [of the stem]. [The rule contains] the mention of *saṃjñā*.

And so forth. For if the term *saṃjñin* (the designated) were not mentioned, then just as the one who receives and the one who observes are called "witnesses" (*sākṣin*), so too the giver and the receiver would have to be called witnesses, since they too are certainly observers. By the mention of *saṃjñin*, however, only the observer is meant [to be the witness], and not the giver or the receiver.

He who is another observer nearby is the *upadraṣṭṛ*. Now, one might object: "Will not the word *sākṣin* be established as correct simply by the rule of irregular formation (*nipātana*) stating 'the master, lord, ruler, heir, and witness' (Pāṇini 5.2.39)? Furthermore, its restriction of meaning is also established because it is a worldly term."

[Objection: This [rule] would be understood as merely a worldly convention regarding the word *pada*; therefore, it is useless. [Response: This is not so. For when that elision (*nipātana*) occurs, it is impossible to determine that the word *sākṣin* ends in the letter *n*, because there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for such a determination. In common usage, when its own denoted meaning is being perceived, there is no cognitive burden for the listener.
It might be so; therefore, this is stated for the purpose of avoiding the difficulty of understanding that [the word] ends in the letter *n*.

92. *kṣetriya* [means] "to be treated in another's field" (Pāṇini 5.2.92). The suffix *kṛtya* in *cikitsya* is used in the sense of possibility (*śakyārtha*). Regarding the phrase "in the sense of the sentence" (*vākyārthe*) and so forth: the word *kṣetriya* is used in the sense of the sentence "to be treated in another's field" (*parakṣetre cikitsyaḥ*).
The word *pada* is treated as an irregular formation (*nipāta*) in which the division between stem and suffix does not exist.

The particle *ca* is for the purpose of making it have an udātta accent on the final syllable. Regarding the phrase "or from *parakṣetra*," etc.: the word *vā* indicates an alternative method. Alternatively—from the word *parakṣetra*, [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] when it is in the seventh case-ending (locative), meaning "in that."
In this sense, the suffix is applied as a nipātana (irregular formation), and there is the elision of the word *para*.

Regarding the statement, "The 'other field' (*parakṣetra*) is the body of another birth," he demonstrates the meaning of the word *para* by means of the phrase "incurable" (*asādhya*), because [that body] is different from the body belonging to this world.
For a field that has been prepared for the sake of grain becomes a "foreign field" to the weeds because those weeds do not grow there.
And [the phrase] "all this is authoritative" is used because everything has been established by the Teacher.
93. *Indriya* [is derived] as "the mark of Indra," "seen by Indra," "created by Indra," "beloved by Indra," or "given by Indra" (Pāṇini 5.2.93).
By the phrase "this is a conventional term (*rūḍhiḥ*)," [the author] causes one to abandon the etymological meaning of its parts. How, then, is this known?

Is this a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*)? To this he says: "And thus," and so forth. If this were not a conventional usage, there would be no lack of restriction regarding etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*); for in the case of non-conventional words, the meaning is precisely restricted.
However, in the case of this conventional word, a lack of restriction regarding derivation is appropriate. For, in the case of conventional words...
The etymological derivation is made in some manner by means of an imagined meaning of the constituent parts. But how can the self be inferred by means of instruments such as the eye?
To this he says: "It is not without an agent," and so forth. By this, he demonstrates the invariable concomitance (avinābhāva).

The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Since the activity or cessation of the instruments and other factors depends upon an agent, therefore, wherever those factors exist, there must necessarily be an agent. The self (*ātman*) is inferred by means of the eye and other instruments, which serve as its inseparable marks (*aliṅga*). But how, then, [is this] through that self?
He asks: "Is it served? and answers with the words "by means of that," and so forth. For, by means of the door [of the senses], knowledge of the self arises regarding objects.
Therefore, in order to know objects, the self serves the senses, such as the eye and the rest. "According to their respective [functions]" means according to each one's own [nature]. Whoever...

"The object of whichever sense-organ is given to that [organ]; the particle *iti* has the sense of 'manner' (*prakāra*). Thus, the particle *iti* indicates the sense of manner, signifying that the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) should also be performed in this other way; for this very reason, he says: "sat..."

Regarding the passage beginning with "sambhave": when possible, one should provide an etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) such as "it is called *indriya* because objects (*viṣaya*) are led toward or connected [to the self] by means of it (*indreṇa nīyante sambadhyante*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "the word 'vā'": for if the word "vā" were not present, [there would be no distinction between] "the mark of Indra" (*indraliṅga*) and so forth...

The dependence of the various types of conceptual constructions should be understood; for it is only through their mutual dependence and combination that they constitute the cause of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*).
The word "or" (*vā*) connects with [the notions] "this is Indra's mark" and "this is seen by Indra," and thus relates to them.
It demonstrates independence; thus, each individual mode functions as a constituent of proficiency independently of other modes.

94. *tad asyāsty asminn iti matup* (Pāṇini 5.2.94). Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the suffix": now, it may be argued that whatever belongs to someone exists in that person, and whatever exists in something belongs to that thing—just as, for example, a branch is in a tree, and [one speaks of] "the branch of the tree."
In that case, it would be established by the mention of either one alone; for what purpose, then, are both mentioned?
This is not so; for there is no necessary co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) between the meanings of the genitive and the locative cases.
For instance, "cows are in the Ganges"—they are there, yet they do not belong to it; likewise, even one who has gone to another country [is still related to his former home].

He is the son of Devadatta, yet he does not reside there; therefore, both [the father and the son] must be specified. [The statement] "the word *asti* is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*)"—but surely the relationship of qualified and qualifier occurs only when there is both possibility and deviation, as in the case of "blue lotus"? No.

Furthermore, there is no deviation from existence, as it has been said: "An entity does not deviate from being existent. Is this qualification therefore useless because there is nothing to be excluded?
This is not so; for by the very power of employing the qualification, it is precisely that which is qualified [as existent] [that is intended].

It is understood that [the term] is employed as a qualifier, and not as mere existence (*sattāmātra*). Furthermore, that qualified existence is precisely "present existence" (*sampratisatā*). And since there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from that, the relationship between the qualified and the qualifier necessarily follows. But what, then, is present existence?

Is it included as a qualifier so that the suffix (*pratyaya*) may apply only to that [present state], and not to past or future existence? For this reason, [suffixes] do not occur in such cases as *gāvo 'syāsan* ("he had cows") or *gāvo 'sya bhavitāraḥ* ("he will have cows"). But would it not [apply] in *gomān āsīt* ("he was cow-possessing")?

Having prescribed the suffix *matup* in the sense of existence in the past and future—as in "one will become possessed of cows" (*gomān bhavitā*)—how is it employed? This is not a fault; for since the grammatical correctness of suffixes even when stated out of their proper time is ordained when there is a connection with a verbal root (*dhātusambandha*), it is thus employed; it is not [employed] solely in the sense of existence in the past or future.

"Because of the prescription of the suffix [matup]"; the meaning is: "if it exists as something characterized by the sense of 'being' (asti-artha). That is to say, if it exists there as qualified by present existence. Regarding the form *gomān*:

the augment *num* is applied by the rule *ugidacām* (Pāṇini 7.1.70); then, the elision of the final consonant (*hal-ṅy-ādi*) and the elision of the final member of the conjunction (*saṃyogānta-lopa*) take place.

The lengthening [of the vowel] is according to Pāṇini 6.4.14: "And for that which ends in -ṭh or -as, provided it is not a verbal root. In the form "vṛkṣavān," the substitution of *v* for *m* is according to 8.2.9: "Also for [the *m*] following a long vowel or a short vowel preceded by a short vowel, when followed by *t*, *th*, *d*, or *dh*. Regarding the phrase "restriction of scope" (*viṣayaniyama*): the occurrence of the suffix within its specific domain is what is meant by "restriction of scope."

Showing further that this [object] has a distinguished scope, such as "earth" (*bhūmi*) and so forth, he says: "The praise and censure of *bhūman*," and so on. *Bhūman* is the state of being much (*bahu*). [The suffix] *iman* is applied by the rule *pṛthvādibhya imanic* (Pāṇini 5.1.122). The substitution of *bhū* for *bahu* occurs by the rule *bahorlopo bhū ca bahoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.158).
And there is the elision of the vowel *i*. One who possesses many cows is called "gomān" (possessor of cows). Even if one or two cows are present, one is not designated as "gomān.
