In the sense of censure—as in "kakudāvartī" (one with a hump)—he is censured because of its fruitlessness. In the sense of praise—as in "praśastam" (praiseworthy)—it is excellent.

One who possesses form (*rūpa*) is called "possessing form" (*rūpavān*). In the sense of constant connection (*nityayoga*), as in "these trees have milk," they are called "milk-bearing trees" (*kṣīriṇo vṛkṣāḥ*); those whose connection with milk is constant are so described. In the sense of excess (*atiśāyana*), as in "the girl has a large belly" (*udariṇī kanyā*); she who has an excessively large belly is thus called.

In the expression "one with a staff" (*daṇḍī*) in the context of contact, it is the contact with a staff that is denoted. Therefore, even though a staff exists and remains in the house, one is not called "one with a staff" [merely by its presence].

95. *rasādibhyaśca* (5.2.95). "For the purpose of excluding *ṭhan*" means that its purpose (*artha*) or motive (*prayojana*) is the exclusion of other possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya*), such as *ini* and so forth; thus it is so described. [The question] "How? and so on refers to [the derivation from] *rasa* and the others.

The repetition is for the purpose of excluding others; the intention is that, [without it], forms such as *rūpiṇī kanyā* would not be established. Regarding the phrase "generally" (*prāyika*) and so forth:
the meaning of "generally" is the frequent exclusion of others; thus, it is more appropriate to say "it generally possesses this."
"It exists.

[The question is: Since it is generally characterized by the exclusion of others (anyanivṛtti) in cases such as "rūpaṇī" (feminine suffix -ī), how is it that another [suffix] also occurs in some instances? To this he says: "the maker of the locative case-ending (*ṭhitikaraṇaḥ*)."

And so forth. Here, the particle *iti* functions to indicate the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*) and continues [its application]. Therefore, in cases where the world’s intention arises specifically from a word ending in the suffix *matup*, exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti*) is effected by that [suffix];
this does not apply everywhere.
"Or [it is] 'ṭhatha'," and so forth. This is another solution.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is the inclusion of the sense organs such as the eye. The term "guṇa" is recited in the *gaṇa* list;

moreover, the mention of "guṇa" is a qualifier for all [objects] beginning with taste (rasa). Therefore, those [objects] which are perceivable by the sense organs such as the tongue (rasana) [are included].

"This reading belongs to those very [grammarians]. By this, the exclusion of those [qualities] other than those graspable by the senses such as the tongue—which end in qualifying words—is effected, and not others.
It might be argued that even in cases such as *rūpī* and so forth, the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) applies to those qualities which are graspable by the senses.

"Has it arisen? To this he says: "of one possessing form (rūpin), of one who is formal (rūpika)," and so forth. In the cases of *rūpiṇī* and *rūpika*, what is understood is the quality of beauty (*śobhā*), not the form (*rūpa*) perceivable by the eye. In the case of "the actor is *rasika*," too, what is understood is the quality of emotional state (*bhāva*), not the quality perceivable by the sense of taste (*rasanendriya*). These are the *bhāvas*.
The erotic, the heroic, the loathsome, and so forth, are properties of composition.

Regarding the rule "ṭhekācaḥ": "from that which has one vowel" (ekākṣarāt) means from that which possesses a single *ac* (vowel); from such a base, only the suffix *matup* occurs—as in *dhīmān* (wise) and *svavān* (possessing one's own).
96. *prāṇisthād ato laj anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.2.96). Regarding the example "kaṇikālaḥ": this word *kaṇikā* and others denote a limb of a living being, not a particular type of ornament.
Since it is desired [that the suffix] be applied only to words denoting parts of living beings, he says: "It should be stated that [the rule applies] 'to a part of a living being' (prāṇyaṅgāt).

The meaning is that this must be explained as having the sense that the suffix *laC* occurs after a word ending in *a* precisely because it denotes a part of a living being (*prāṇyaṅgatvāt*). In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the particle *iti*...

The intended meaning follows [the rule]; therefore, it will apply only to the limbs of living beings (*prāṇyaṅga*) and not to anything else. Or rather, due to the lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*), it will not apply to non-living limbs.

But surely, since the suffix *lac* consists of a single vowel (*ekāc*), its final acute accent is already established by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*); so for what purpose [is this rule stated]?

What is the purpose of the particle *ca*? To this he says: "By the accent of the suffix" (*pratyayasvareṇaiva*), and so forth. When the word *asi* follows the word *cūḍālaḥ* in the nominative singular, it receives the *nighāta* (elision of accent) by the rule *tiṅṅtiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28). Furthermore, for the word *saḥ*, [the substitution of] *ru* occurs by the rule *sasajuṣo ruḥ*.

By [Pāṇini 8.2.66], there is the substitution of *r*; by [Pāṇini 6.1.113], there is the substitution of *u* for *roḥ* when not preceded by a protracted vowel and followed by a non-protracted vowel; by [Pāṇini 6.1.87], there is the *guṇa* substitution; and that [resulting vowel] receives the acute accent (*udātta*) by [Pāṇini 8.2.5];
and [the elision of the final *e*] occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.109].

The single-substitute is the form of the subsequent element. However, in the absence of the letter *c*, there would be a circumflex (*svarita*) accent according to the rule "svarito vānudāte 'padādau" (Pāṇini 8.2.6). Therefore, the letter *c* is employed in order to set aside that [circumflex accent].
97. *Sidhmādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 5.2.97).
If the suffix *lac* were optional by virtue of the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām*, then in the alternative case, it would follow exactly what was previously established;
consequently, the suffixes *ini* and *iṭhan* would apply to *sidhma* and other words ending in *a*. Therefore, [the author] addresses this fault:
To provide a solution, he says: "By the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām*," and so forth.
Because particles have multiple meanings, here *anyatarasyām* functions as a conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Thus it has been stated by the author of the Vārttika: "The term *anyatarasyām* denotes a conjunction. The possessive suffix *matup* is used here...
Some say that because it is marked with the *svarita* accent, only that which is contextually proximate is conjoined here, and not another suffix as might otherwise be expected. Others, however, say:

"The mention of *anyatarasyām* is solely for the purpose of providing an option (*vikalpa*). Both the suffixes *ini* and *iṭhan* are not applied simultaneously, precisely because of the *mahāvibhāṣā*."
Because [the suffix] is already established, is another suffix then prescribed as an alternative? That too is not the case;
because of the proximity of what is present, it is *matup* alone that is intended to bring about what has been obtained.
Thus, when the term "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) is used, it is *matup* alone that is made optional.
With this intention, it was stated that [the suffix] is conjoined by means of the mention of *anyatarasyām*;

however, "it is not the case that the suffix is made optional. But surely the meaning is that the presence and absence of the *lac* (the suffix) are being effected. As for the passage beginning with "tasmāt" (therefore), since it is thus through the mention of *anyatarasyām* that the *matup* [suffix is applied].

The suffix is accumulated [added], but the suffix is not optionally chosen; therefore, the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* do not occur after those words which are here read with a final long vowel (*ākāranta*).
Regarding the rule "pārṣṇi-dhamanyor dīrghaś-ca" (Pārṣṇi and dhamani take the long vowel), it refers to the two words *pārṣṇi* and *dhamani*.
The suffix *lac* occurs after these two with the augment *dīrgha*: *pārṣṇīlaḥ* and *dhamanīlaḥ*.

According to the rule "after *vāta*, *danta*, *bala*, and *lalāṭa*, there is also *ūṅ*," the suffix *lac* follows *vāta* and the others, and *ūṅ* is added to it. Thus: *vātūlaḥ*, *dantūlaḥ*, *balūlaḥ*, *lalāṭūlaḥ*. [Also] *jaṭāghaṭākalāḥ*.
When reproach (*kṣepa*) is implied: *jaṭālaḥ*, *ghaṭālaḥ*, *kalālaḥ*. Why "when reproach"? [As in:

*jaṭāvān* ("one who possesses matted hair"). Regarding the rule "and from small creatures and afflictions" (*kṣudrajantūpatāpācca*): "small creature" refers to a weasel and the like; "affliction" refers to a disease of the chest.

98. [The suffix *matup* is applied] after the words *vatsa* and *aṃsa* when the sense is "possessing desire" (*kāmavat*) and "possessing strength" (*balavat*). By the mention of the forms ending in *mat*, he indicates that the words *kāma* and *bala* are understood here as ending in the vowel *a* according to the rule beginning with *arśa-ādi*.

But surely, the words *vatsa* and *aṃsa* do not denote desire and strength; what then? They denote a particular stage of life and a particular part of a living being. So how can one who possesses desire or strength be expressed by them? To this he says: "In the domain of the derivative meaning (*vṛtti-viṣaye*)," and so forth. How is this known?

Thus he says: "For here... and so forth. The meaning is that the specific meaning well-known for the word *vatsa* (calf) as denoting a particular stage of age, and the scope of the word *aṃsa* (shoulder) as denoting a limb of a living being, do not exist—that is, they are not understood—here in this commentary (*vṛtti*).

Alternatively—"does not exist" means "is not. By this, the absence of those two meanings which are well-known in common usage—namely, age and a specific part of a living being—is shown within the word.
Now, in order to show the existence of those two meanings which are intended [here], he says: "vatsalaḥ" (affectionate toward calves).
And so forth. Regarding the term "snehavān" (possessing affection): the meaning is "possessing desire.

Thus, since in the sentence the meanings of "vatsa" and "aṃsa"—namely, age and a limb of a living being—do not exist [in the intended sense], therefore, by the words *vatsala* and *aṃsala*, one who possesses the aforementioned affection and one who is strong are expressed respectively.

From this it is understood that the words *vatsa* and *aṃsa*, when occurring in the scope of a derivative formation (*vṛtti*), produce a cognition directed toward that which possesses those qualities, provided they refer to desire (*kāma*) and strength (*bala*).
In this entire section, the mention of the option (*anyatarasyām*) serves to include the suffix *matup* everywhere.
To one who thinks that there must therefore be a possessive suffix (*matup*), he says: "And this is not," and so forth.
By this very reason, it should be understood that even a sentence does not exist;
for this meaning is simply not possible in the case of a body (*kāya*).
*lomādipāmādipicchādibhyaḥ śanelacaḥ* | (5.2.100) In the list of *pāmādi* words, "from *aṅga*" (*aṅgāt*) is recited; therein—

The inclusion of the word *kalyāṇa* is a qualification of the word *aṅga*. A woman (*aṅganā*) is so called because she possesses beautiful (*kalyāṇa*, i.e., *śobhana*) limbs (*aṅga*). Why [include] *kalyāma*? [To exclude forms such as] *aṅgavatī*. [According to the rule] "For *śīka*, *palāla*, and *idrā*, there is shortening," the suffix is applied to *śāki* and others, and there is also shortening: *śākinaḥ*.
*Palālinaḥ* refers to those suffering from ringworm (*dadru*). Some say that *śākī* means "great vegetable" and *palālī* means "great straw.

Alternatively, *śākī* is a collection of various kinds of vegetables, and *palālī* is a collection of straws. Regarding the rule beginning with *ṭhviṣvak*: the suffix is not applied after the word *viṣvak*.

There is [the elision of the suffix], and there is also the elision of the subsequent member (*utarapadalopa*). And that [elision] occurs before the sandhi has been applied, that is, before the *yaṇ* substitution has taken place.

When the word *viṣu* is used as an *upapada* in the sense of "moving in various directions" (*viṣvañcati*), the suffix *kvin* is applied by the rule *ṛtvig-ādi* (Pāṇini 3.2.59), followed by the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*). Thus, when the form *viṣuaac* is established, [the elision applies] to *viṣvañc*.

In the case of *yasya santīti na pratyayaḥ*, there is the elision of the second member (*uttarapadalopa*) before the suffix *na* has undergone the *ayaṇ* substitution; thus, it becomes *viṣuṇa*. This word *viṣuṇa* is treated as an irregular formation (*nipātita*). It occurs in the sense of "various" (*nānārtha*). [The rule] "lakṣmyā acca" means that the suffix *na* is added to the word *lakṣmī*, and the letter *a* is substituted for its final vowel.

"Lakṣmaṇa" means "one who possesses *lakṣmī*. Regarding the rule beginning with "*jaṭā-ghaṭa*" and so forth: the suffix *ilac* is applied after words such as *jaṭā* when contempt (*kṣepa*) is implied. Examples are *jaṭilaḥ*, *ghaṭilaḥ*, and *kalilaḥ*. Why specify "contempt"?
[To exclude cases like] *jaṭāvān*, *ghaṭāvān*, and *kalāvān*.
101. After *prajñā*, *śraddhā*, *arcā*, and *vṛti*, the suffix *ṇa* [is applied].

(5.2.101) Since the suffix *matup* would apply after the word *prajñā* due to its inclusion in the *picchādi* group, and *ilac* would also apply [to the others], the suffix *ṇa* is prescribed after these [four] words following the suffix *matup*.
102. *tapaḥ sahasrābhyāṃ vinīnī* (Pāṇini 5.2.102).
In this sūtra, two bases (*prakṛti*) are introduced; likewise, two meanings for the suffixes (*pratyayārtha*) follow from the two preceding bases. Thus, it is said: *vatsāṃsābhyāṃ kāmabale* (5.2.98).

Regarding those who believe that the rule of "correspondence according to order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*) should also apply to certain grammatical operations such as *sikatāśarkarābhyāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.104), the author says in response:
"But [this applies] to the meanings of the suffixes. Why, then, is this not accepted even when desired?

Does it occur? It does, because in the rule *vatsāṃsābhyāṃ kāmabale* (Pāṇini 5.2.98), the word *aṃśa* appears as the subsequent member (*paranipāta*), serving as an indicator (*liṅga*) that there is no deviation from the general rule. For if the word *aṃsa* were to be placed first according to *ajādyadantam* (Pāṇini 2.2.33), then the word *bala* would also have been placed first according to the principle that "the word with fewer syllables (*laghvakṣara*) is placed first."

(Vārttika 108) Since this [conclusion] has been reached, this subsequent placement (*paranipāta*) demonstrates independence from other defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇāntara*), thereby showing that in this section concerning the possessive suffix *matup*, the correspondence of order (*yathāsaṃkhya*) is subject to deviation. Consequently, in all cases within the section on *matup*, there is no correspondence of order between the affixes and their respective meanings.
It occurs. From what [source] does this "in the context" (prakaraṇe) derive?

From the fact that the sign of deviation from the definition depends upon the context. And from what [source] does even that derive? From the commentary; or else, from the employment of both signs of deviation from the definition.

If, however, there were a dependence on grammatical derivation (*yogāpekṣatā*), one would have to adopt only one of the two [options], namely: "because of its being *asan*. Since the word *tapaḥ* ends in *as*, the suffix *vin* is established by rules such as "after words ending in *as*, *āma*, *eṣas*, and *sraj*, the suffix *vin* is added" (Pāṇini 5.2.121). Furthermore, since the word *sahasra* ends in *a*, the suffix *ka* is applied.

Since the suffix *ini* would already be established by the rule "ini-ṭhanau" (Pāṇini 5.2.115), this further prescription is for the purpose of preventing its being superseded by the *aṇ* suffix that will be mentioned later. Regarding the examples beginning with "sahasrāt," since the suffix *an* would also apply by the rule "ata ini-ṭhanau" (5.2.115), that too is superseded. By this...
By the word "thousand," he shows that this is a restatement intended to set aside the suffix *ṭhan*.
103. *aṇ* also.

(5.2.103) In the section concerning *ṭhaṇ*, etc., *jyotsnādi* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*. Those from which the suffix *aṇ* is seen to occur in the sense of the possessive suffix *matup* should be understood as the *jyotsnādi* group. And this word *upasaṃkhyāna* [indicates that]...

It is employed for the purpose of providing an exposition. In this regard, the exposition is as follows: in the subsequent sūtra, the particle *ca* (and) serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; by means of it, [the suffix] will also apply after words such as *jyotsnā*.
Regarding the example "kauṇḍalaḥ": one who is worthy of earrings (*kuṇḍala*) is so called. But another [says]:
It becomes simply "Kuṇḍalī."
104. *Sikatāśarkarābhyāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.104).
"The substitution of *ṭha* is the example here," [it is said], because the suffix *lu* and *ilac* will be prescribed for the word *deśa* by the subsequent rule.
105. *deśe lubilacau ca* (5.2.105).
106. *danta unnata urac* (5.2.106). Since the suffixes *ini* and *iṣṭhan* would otherwise apply because [the word] ends in the vowel *a*, [the rule] *tundādiṣu* (5.2.117) [is introduced].
Because of the reading "ṭhsvāṅgāt," the suffix *urañ* is prescribed after the word *danta* when the suffix *ilac* follows.

107. *ūṣasuṣimuṣkamadho raḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.107). The suffix *ra* is prescribed after *ūṣa*, *suṣi*, *muṣka*, and *madhu*, where the suffixes *matup* and *iniṭhan* would otherwise apply according to the circumstances. For example, *madhuraḥ*. Here, the word *madhu* refers to a specific kind of taste (*rasaviśeṣe*).
"In the section beginning with *ṭhra-prakaraṇe*," etc. The word *upasaṃkhyāna* (supplementation) here functions in the sense of "explanation" or "establishment.
In this regard, the following is the explanation: the particle *ca* ("and") from the rule *deśe lub-ilacau ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.105) is carried over (*vartate*) here;
and that *ca* serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned (*anukta-samuccaya*). By means of that, [the suffix] *ra* is also applied after words such as *mukha*.

It occurs. Regarding the rule *ṭhnagapāṇḍupāṃśu* (i.e., *ṭhnagapāṃśupāṇḍubhyaḥ kāśikāṭ*), the meaning is that one must explain this form as having the sense "the suffix *ra* occurs after words such as *naga*, *pāṃśu*, and so forth.
This explanation, however, should be made by relying on the very recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the particle *ca*.

108. *dyaudrubhyāṃ maḥ* | (5.2.108) From *dyau* and *dru*, when the suffix *matup* would [otherwise] apply, *ma* is prescribed. Thus, from *dyaumaḥ*—meaning "one who has heaven"—the substitution of *u* for *div* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.131]: *ṭhdiva ut*.

Some say: "The word *dyau* is a separate verbal root (*prakṛti*) which is a name for *ahan* (day); from that, this suffix is prescribed. [They add: "In the case of conventional (*rūḍhi*) words, however, the suffix *matup* is not optionally applied," because the meaning of a conventional word is not expressed by *matup*.

109. *keśād vo 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.2.109). This is commenced in order to introduce the suffix *matup*, since *ini* and *thañ* would otherwise have been applicable. But surely the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is already present in the governing rule; why then is this repeated?

Thus he says: "But surely, [the topic] under discussion," and so forth; "in the section on *v*," and so forth. The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*). Just as the suffix *vap* occurs after the word *keśa*, so too is the suffix *vap* seen after other words as well;
therefore, it must be stated—that is, explained. Such an explanation must be provided.
The meaning is that it occurs after these as well as after others. Regarding this, the explanation is as follows:
here too, that same particle *ca* (and), which serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned, is understood to carry over; therefore, the meaning is that it also occurs after others.
110. *gāṇḍī-jagāt saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 5.2.110).
"It occurs even after a short [vowel]," it is said. But how can it occur even after a short vowel when there is a mention of a long one? [The answer is:

"For in that case, they are indeed equal," and so forth. Just as the *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) of a long vowel is observed here, exactly the same is seen even when there is a mention of a short vowel. Therefore, the inclusion of the short vowel here is not contradictory.

This is the state of affairs. In this regard, one might think: "Even though the *saṃhitā* is the same, nevertheless, since this is a single word in which the *yaṇ*-substitution has been applied, there ought to be an inclusion of either [the long or the short vowel] as its own form (*svarūpa*). In that case, if the long vowel is included, it would not [apply] to the short."
[If it were otherwise,] the short [vowel] would be included, but the long one would not be obtained; therefore, he says "in both ways.
For the rule was composed by the Teacher in two ways. Consequently, there is no fault, as both are indeed included.

Now, what is the purpose of including the word "saṃjñā" (name), given that by the continued application of the particle *iti*, it will not apply when it is not a name— just as the suffix *map* does not apply after *dyu* and *drabhi*? If this is so, then the inclusion of the word "saṃjñā" should be understood as an elaboration (*prapañca*) of that very particle *iti*.
111. *kāṇḍāṇḍād īrannīracau* (5.2.111). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan*.

112. *rajaḥ-kṛṣi-sūti-pariṣada-valac* (Pāṇini 5.2.112). After the word *rajas*, since the suffix *vini* would otherwise apply by the rule *ṭhasmāyāmedhāsrajo viniḥ* (5.2.121), the suffix *valac* is prescribed instead; however, after the other words [in the list], *valac* is prescribed in place of the suffix *matup*.

Regarding the passage beginning with "in the section on *ṭhvalac*," this has already been largely explained by the explanation of the suffix *vap*. Why does the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by "before *val*" (Pāṇini 6.3.118) not occur here?
Because the term "proper name" (*saṃjñā*) is understood to carry over from the preceding rule, "in a proper name for *vana* and *giri*" (Pāṇini 6.3.117).
113. *dantaśikhātsaṃjñāyām* (5.2.113).
Regarding the word *danta*, since the suffixes *ini* and *thañ* would otherwise apply, the suffix *valac* is prescribed.
Regarding the word *śikhā*, the suffix *ini* will be taught in the rule *vrīhyādibhyaśca* (5.2.116).

"An *ini* suffix is to be prescribed after words such as *śikhā*" (Mahābhāṣya 2.398). The mention of *śikhā* is for the sake of non-locative (*adeśa*) meanings, so that [the form] *śikhāvalā sthūṇā* ("a pillar possessing a crest") may be formed. However, in the sense of location (*deśa*), it is already established by the rule "after *śikhā*, the suffix *valac*" (Pāṇini 4.2.89), which belongs to the fourfold set of meanings (*cāturarthika*). If this is so, then this very [rule]...
It must be stated: what is the use of that? This is not so;

for that too must indeed be stated, so that [the designation] may apply to meanings such as "ceased" (nirvṛta) and so forth. Here, too, the mention of the term *saṃjñā* is for the purpose of restating that very meaning.
Because the restriction of the subject matter is established through the continued application of the particle *iti*.
*jyotsnātamisrāśṛṅgiṇorjasvinnūrjasvalagominmalinamalīmasāḥ* (5.2.114).
"The femininity is non-essential" means it is subordinate, because it is not intended to be expressed;
however, the mention of the feminine gender is for the sake of stylistic variety.

115. *ata iniṭhanau* (Pāṇini 5.2.115). Here, by the rule *ataḥ*, the letter *a* followed by the marker *t* is understood. For this very reason, he says: "from that which ends in the letter *t*," and so forth.
Now, why is it not understood as a reference to the actual form of the word *at*—that is, [the suffix] from the word *at*?

Regarding the phrase "from a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*): it is incorrect to assume that this is a reference to the word's own form (*svarūpa-grahaṇa*). For if it were a reference to its own form, the prescription of the suffix *matup* after words such as *rasa* would be purposeless.
That suffix is prescribed for the purpose of superseding the suffixes *ini* and *iṭhan*; and if there were a reference to the word's own form here, those two [suffixes] would not apply after them.
Since the two suffixes [matup and vatu] would apply [in any case], what is the purpose of prescribing matup by that rule?

Why is the vowel *a* made long in the sūtra (*taparakaraṇam*)? [To exclude forms like] *śraddhāvān*. But surely, since words such as *mālā* ending in long *ā* are listed in the *vrīhy-ādi* group, they will serve a restrictive function—[namely, to indicate that these specific words take *vatu*] from among those [listed].

Is it only from those ending in the vowel *a*? This is not so; such a restriction would apply only to those of the same class [ending in *a*], and thus *ini* and *iṭhan* would necessarily follow after words ending in *ḍāp* and *āp*. Therefore, the letter *a* must be followed by the marker *t* (to indicate its shortness). [The example] "kāryī" is formed with the suffix *ini*. [The example] "taṇḍulikaḥ" is formed with *ini* and *iṭhan* according to the rule for denoting a genus (*jāti*).

116. *Vrīhyādibhyaś-ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.116). [The rule] beginning with *śikhādibhyaḥ* [is also mentioned]. In both cases, the word *ādi* (etc. signifies "of the same class. Those words after which only the suffix *-in-* is observed in the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) should be understood as the *śikhādi* group; for indeed, the suffix *-ṭhan-* is applied to those [other words].
[They] have prescribed [it]. This division of subject matter, however, is understood solely through the recurrence of the particle *iti*.

Regarding the word "to be expressed" (*vācya*), its meaning is "that which is to be explained. In the phrase "in *yavakhada* and so forth," the locative case indicates the scope of application (*viṣayasaptamī*).

"If that is so," and so forth. Since the word *vrīhi* is included among the *tuṇḍa*-type words as a reference to its own form (*svarūpa*), its inclusion here would be understood as purposeless; therefore, by implication, it is understood that in that [list] the inclusion of *vrīhi* refers to the meaning (*artha*). When there is a reference to the meaning, that which is desired is established.
To demonstrate this, he says: "One who has *śāli* [rice] is *śālikaḥ*" and so forth.

Regarding the rule "after *nañ*, [the suffix] *śīrṣan*": the suffix *śīrṣan* occurs after the word *nañ*. By means of a formal irregularity (*nipātana*), there is the substitution of *śīrṣa-* for *śiras-*—thus: *aśīrṣī*, *aśīrṣikaḥ*. Others, however, [interpret] *śīrṣan*...

They recite it as a separate word. However, its inclusion [in the list] is for the purpose that it may also occur in the vernacular (*bhāṣā*). Otherwise, because of the rule "śīrṣan in the Veda" (Pāṇini 6.1.60), forms such as *aśīrṣikaḥ* and *aśīrṣavān* would not be possible in the vernacular.

117. *tundādibhya ilac ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.117). This rule is commenced because the suffixes *matup* and others might otherwise apply according to their respective scopes. [The commentary states: "By the word *ca* (and), the suffixes *ini*, *iṭhan*, and *matup* [are included]. By this, four suffixes—*ini*, *iṭhan*, and *matup*—as well as *ilac*, are added after words such as *tuṇḍa*.

Regarding the rule *ṭhsvāṅgādvivṛddhau*: a suffix occurs after a word denoting a limb of the body when that limb is in a state of enlargement. When his two ears are enlarged—that is, large—he is called *karṇilaḥ*, *karṇikaḥ*, *karṇī*, or *karṇavān*.

118. *ekagopūrvāt ṭhañ nityam* | (5.2.118) Since suffixes such as *matup* would otherwise apply, *ṭhañ* is here prescribed. And that [suffix] occurs after a *tatpuruṣa* compound beginning with *eka*, provided it has *go* as its prior member, but not after every [such compound].

[The suffix *ṭhan*] is applied after [a compound] whose first member is *eka*. This is obtained through the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the particle *iti* from that rule. *Eka* and *śata* together form *ekaśatam*; one who possesses that is *aikaśatikaḥ*. In a genitive tatpuruṣa compound, it is *ekaśatavān*.
As for the question "How [is this so]? and so forth: if the word *ataḥ* (from 5.2.115) were to recur here, [the desired forms would not be obtained].

The point is that [the suffix] is not established after the word *gośakaṭī*, because it does not end in the vowel *a*. The phrase "it will occur from that" means that it will occur from that which ends in such [a word]. This is the meaning: the suffix *ṭhañ* is prescribed after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *a* that has *eka* or *go* as its prior member.

It is obtained by implication (*sāmarthyāt*). Alternatively, there is no fault [in the rule] because [the word *ataḥ*] will be understood from that cause [of the context]. As for the passage beginning with "and necessarily" (*avaśyaṃ ca*), if the recurrence of *ataḥ* were not present, then the suffix would also apply after words such as *citra*, *kala*, and *lāṭikā* in connection with the rules concerning *dvandva*, *upatāpa*, *garhya*, and so forth (Pāṇini 5.2.128; 5.2.115).

Regarding the passage beginning with "The mention of 'nitya' (always)": for if the mention of *nitya* were absent, the mention of *anyatarasyām* (optionally) would follow everywhere as being intended to include the suffix *matup*, and thus [the suffix] *vati* would also occur alongside *matup*. Therefore, the mention of *nitya* is for the purpose of precluding that. As for the question, "How [can there be a commonality], since they reside in a single substance (*ekadravyavattvāt*)?"—if...

The inclusion of the word *nitya* is for the purpose of setting aside the suffix *matup*. Thus, he considers that in the case of *na hyaeka-dravyavattvāt*, the suffix *matup* is established from the word *dravya* preceded by *eka* [by the rule *tad asyāstyasminn iti matup*].

[He then provides] the example beginning with "by one," etc.; since the word *eka* possesses the quality of being a substance (*dravyavattva*), [the compound is formed] by the rule *sup-supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4).
The meaning is that, having formed a compound, its grammatical correctness (sādhutva) must be demonstrated.
119. [The suffix *kan* is applied after a word ending in *śata-sahasra*] to denote a *niṣka*.

(5.2.119) 120. [The suffix] *yaP* is applied after the word *rūpa* to denote "struck" (*āhata*) or "praise" (*praśaṃsā*). (5.2.121) Regarding the statement "it is called *āhata*": *āhata* means *āhanana*, which signifies "striking. Therefore...

The form of a person (*puruṣa*) and so forth is already accomplished; nevertheless, that too is called "produced" (*āhata*) by means of metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*) of the cause to the effect. Regarding the rule *yap-prakaraṇe*, it should be stated that [the suffix] *yaP* is seen after other roots as well.
Since this [rule] is identical to that [preceding one], its explanation should be performed in exactly the same manner.
The word "ca" (and), however, is carried over here from the rule "śatasahasrāntācca niṣkāt" (Pāṇini 5.2.119).

121. *asmāyāmedhāsrajo viniḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.121). [Examples: *yaśasvī*, *tapasvī*, *payasvī*. Because of the rule *tasau matvarthe* (1.4.19), these are treated as *bha*-stems; due to this *bha*-status, the substitution of *jaś* does not occur. By the rule for *jaś*-substitution, one might expect the letter *s* to be replaced by *d*.
That does not exist.

122. *Bahulam chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.122). [Examples include] *dvayobhaya-hṛdayāni*, and so forth. A restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is to be understood here: only *dvaya* and the others cause the lengthening of the vowel, not the others, because those others are already long by their very nature.

The intention is that the phrase "all this is accomplished by means of the inclusion of the word *bahula*" is intended to mean that the word *vaktavya* (to be stated) is used in the sense of providing an explanation (*vyākhyāna*).
123. *ūṛṇāyā yus* (Pāṇini 5.2.123). Regarding the example *ūrṇāyuḥ*: because it is treated as a *pada*, it lacks the designation *bha*; therefore, the elision of *y* (*yasyeti ca*) does not occur.
124. *vāco gminiḥ* | (5.2.124) Now, why is it not simply stated that [the suffix] is *min* alone? For once *jaś*-substitution has been applied, the form *vāggmī* would be established.
But surely, by the rule *ṭhyaro'nunāsike'nunāsiko vā* (8.4.45), there would be an optional nasalization [of the *g*]?
Does it not follow [that this fault arises]? This is not a fault; for it should be understood as a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
In that case, by adding the letter *ga*, he indicates this: "this is *gmini*.
Even in the case of one who is properly and extensively devoted (*bahubhāvate*), there [the suffix] would override the *vālaja* and *aṭac* suffixes which are to be mentioned later.

It occurs only with the suffix *gmini*. For it is thus stated in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*: "If it occurs even in the domain of an exception (*apavāda*), it is [this one] alone and no other. And so, it should be understood that *alaj* and *aṭac* occur only in that case where one expresses contempt for something by saying it exists excessively, according to the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*).

125. *Ālaj* and *āṭac* [are added] after the word *vaktavya* when it means "one who speaks much. (Pāṇini 5.2.125). The intention is that the word *kutsite* ("when there is contempt") is to be supplied; however, the word *vaktavya* itself functions in its explanatory sense [as "one who ought to be spoken to"].
Regarding the form *vaktavyam*: the suffixes *ālaj* and *āṭac* occur when one speaks much in a contemptible manner.
The meaning is that this form of the sense must be explained; the explanation has already been provided in the preceding sūtra.

126. *svāminnaiśvarye* (5.2.126). Since the word *sva* is listed among *rasa* and others in 5.2.95 under the rule *ṭhakācaḥ*, the suffix *matup* would otherwise apply; therefore, this [sūtra] is commenced. Regarding the phrase "denoting sovereignty": the word *sva*, which primarily denotes wealth, here signifies sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). Thus...

The possession of wealth (ca-dhana-yoga) is called sovereignty (aiśvarya); thus it is said, "one who possesses property" (svavān). The word *sva* is used here with reference to something other than the self, such as wealth.

127. *arśaādibhyo’c* (Pāṇini 5.2.127). The suffix *ac* is prescribed [after the words in this class] in place of *matup* and other suffixes as far as possible. It is stated that "this is an *ākṛtigaṇa*" because it has not been closed by a final limit (*avṛtkṛta*). Furthermore, this word *ādi* (beginning) signifies "type" or "kind," as in the rule *svāṅgāddhīnāt*.
The suffix *ac* occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that denotes a deficient limb—such as "one whose foot is lame" (*khañjaḥ pādaḥ*). [An example is] *śuklaḥ*.

Now, since the word *śukla* is an expression for a quality (*guṇavacana*), would this not be established even through the metaphorical treatment of identity (*abhedopacāra*) between the quality and the substance? If that is so, then [the suffix] applies even when it denotes a substance (*dravyavṛtti*).

The mention of *varṇa* (color) was made for the purpose that [the suffix] should apply to nominal stems (*prātipadika*) expressing color. For example: "white" (*śukla*) refers to palaces endowed with the quality of whiteness; "the city is white" (*śuklaṃ nagaram*) means that the city possesses those [palaces].

Since the final acute accent (*antodātta*) would already be established by the accent of the suffix itself, the letter *c* [in the rule] is intended to indicate that [the suffix applies] in the sense of "one who has hemorrhoids" (*arśas*), resulting in the circumflex accent (*svarita*).
The rule *vānudāte'padādau* (8.2.6) is intended to set aside the svarita accent.

128. *dvandvopatāpagarhyāt prāṇisthād iniḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.128). Regarding the phrase *tadviṣayebhyaḥ*: by the word *tat*, only "affliction" (*upatāpa*) and "censurable" (*garhā*) are referred to. The term *tadviṣayāḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those for which affliction and censurability are the objects. [This applies] to words denoting things residing in living beings (*prāṇistha*).
This is a qualification for all [suffixes], such as *dvandva* and the rest:
"it is not desired after words denoting parts of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*). But how is it that it does not occur even though it is desired?
Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *ca*. [The rule] "the suffix having been established" refers to "the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* after *at*" (Pāṇini 5.2.115).

By this very [rule], [it is stated]: "For the purpose of excluding *ṭhan* and the rest. This repetition is for the sake of ensuring that only *-in* occurs, so that *ṭhan* and the rest do not occur; by the word "and the rest" (*ādi*), *matup* is included. From this point onward, the rules (*yoga*) should be understood as being for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).

129. *vātātisārābhyāṃ kuk ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.129). Regarding the phrase *vātātisārābhyām*: although it is in the ablative case, there is nevertheless a change of case by virtue of the sense; for when connected with an augment (*āgama*), it takes the form of the genitive.
It undergoes modification. For this very reason, it is said: "And by its application, there is the augment *k* for those two.

Now, why does the augment not belong to the suffix itself? Because the meaning would not be expressed by the suffix when accompanied by the augment *k*, and because its own form would not be established.

The phrase "it should be stated that [the suffix] *ini* also occurs after the word *piśāca*" means that this rule must be explained as having the sense that the suffix *ini* occurs after the word *piśāca*. Regarding this, the explanation is as follows:
[it is understood] from the rule "diversely in the Vedic language" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*, 5.2.122).
The mention of "bahula" (optionally) continues [from the previous rule]; therefore, it will also apply after the word *piśāca*.

130. *vayasi pūraṇāt* (Pāṇini 5.2.130). [The commentary states: "When age (*vayas*) is to be indicated. But how, then, is age indicated, if words such as *pañcama* ("fifth") and so forth produce the suffix while functioning in the sense of time (*kāla*)? Precisely for this reason, they [function] in the sense of time.

In order to demonstrate the restrictive rule (*vṛti*), he says: "The fifth month belongs to him," and "Since [the suffix] is already established," and so forth. Since the suffix *ini* is already established because the ordinal suffixes end in the vowel *a*, this further statement is understood to be for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Thus, it means: "Only *ini* occurs."
He shows the essential nature of the observance (niyama).
131. *Sukhādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 5.2.131). It is stated that "the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ini* are restricted [to these]. This restriction is to be understood as being like the previous one.
Regarding the phrase "tadiha" and so forth: since the word *mālā* is recited among the *vrīhyādi* group, therefore, in this case...
The repetition of the word *mālā* in the rule for the sense of "contempt" (*kṣepa*) is for the purpose of excluding the suffix *matup*, and not the suffix *ṭhan*;

for it is not stated that [the suffix applies] "after *sukha* and so on," since [that possibility] has already been precluded by this very [repetition]. For the word *mālā* is included among the *śikhā*-group, and from within that group, [the suffix *matup*] is excluded by the mention of "contempt" (*kṣepa*). Thus, [the suffix *matup*] does not occur elsewhere [than in the specific cases provided].

And because [the word] belongs to the class beginning with *śikhā*, the suffix *matup* is also applied; since *matup* has been optionally combined [with other suffixes] by the mention of "either one" (*anyatarasyām*), we have both *mālī* and *mālāvān*.

132. [The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after words ending in *dharma*, *śīla*, and *varṇa*. (5.2.132) 133. [The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after the word *hasta* when it denotes a genus (*jāti*). (5.2.133) In the case of *hastena*, what is understood is the measure "one cubit" (*hastamātra*), not a genus; for the word *puruṣa* is employed [in the subsequent rule].
The human species is understood.

134. *varṇādbrahmacāriṇi* (Pāṇini 5.2.134). [The Vārttika states: "If the term *brahmacārin* is used with reference to the whole [set of qualities]. By this, he shows that *brahmacārin* functions as a qualifier for the entire collection [of attributes]. When one is initiated (*upanīta*) for the purpose of acquiring knowledge, from that point on, [the conduct] must be observed.

That specific discipline is *brahman*; one who practices that is a *brahmacārī*. The suffix *ṇini* is used here in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*). Regarding that practice of specific discipline, only the three castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa have the qualification, not the Śūdra; thus he says: "By the term 'brahmacārī,' a member of the three [upper] castes is intended. Within the three castes...
Because he is included therein, he is a member of the three *varṇas*. What, then, is the reason that he alone is intended?
To this he says: "For he," and so forth.
135. *puṣkarādibhyo deśe* (Pāṇini 5.2.135). Why does [the suffix] not apply here: "In this region there are *puṣkara*s, that is, lotuses"?
Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the particle *iti*.
Regarding the phrase "and [the suffix is used] for an object that is not present (*arthāccāsannihite*)," there is a contradiction if one accepts its existence while it is designated as "not present.
For if an object is not present, it does not exist; and if it exists, how can it be not present?

Therefore, because of the employment of this qualification, the qualifier "exists" is set aside, and the suffix is prescribed based on the object through the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of non-presence. Furthermore, this follows from the inherent nature of the denotative power (*abhidhāna-śakti*). As for the term "one who desires" (*arthī*), it refers specifically to one who possesses longing (*abhilāṣavat*).

Not every object that is not present is necessarily denoted by a suffix ending in *t* because of the reflection (*vimarśa*) upon it; therefore, must a suffix be stated? It need not be stated. How, then, is it obtained without being explicitly stated? By means of the term *bahulam* ("diversely") from the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 5.2.122). Just as the grammatical operation prescribed in such rules as *aṣṭrāmekhalādvayobhayarajāhṛdayādīnāṃ dīrghaśca* (Bālakāśikā 586)—which effects lengthening and other changes—is accomplished through the inclusion of the word *bahulam*, so too is this case. [The sūtra] begins with *tadantācca*. The word *asannihitam* ("not present") is understood to carry over [from the previous context].

The meaning is that the form *arthādi* is to be explained in such a way that the cognition of "objects and so forth" arises even when the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is not present; however, the explanation has already been largely provided. 136. *balādibhyo matub anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.2.136).

If, by the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally"), the suffix is made optional—meaning that after words such as *bala*, there is an option for the *matup* suffix—then, when the *matup* is not used, both *ini* and *iṭhan* would occur according to their respective rules; yet only *ini* is desired. How, then, is only *ini* obtained?

If one were to think: "Is *ini* optionally added by the mention of *anyatarasyām*, rather than *matup*?"—having considered this, he says: "By the mention of *anyatarasyām*," and so forth. But surely, if both *ini* and *iniṭan* were to apply, the formulation of the rule would be purposeless.

Since the suffix *pratyaya* is established even without this [rule], does this [rule] cause a fault for the optional application of the suffix *matup*? This is not so; by the force of its commencement, the meaning obtained is that "one of the two, *ini* or *thañ*, occurs," and not that *ini* alone [occurs].
Therefore, the term "anyatarasyām" must be included for the purpose of expressing an option (viniścaya).
137. *saṃjñāyāṃ manmābhyām* (Pāṇini 5.2.137).
[The examples are] *prathiminī* and *dāminī*. From the bases *prathiman-* and *dāman-*, the suffix *ini* is applied;
then, by *naṣtaddhite* (6.4.144), there is elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*), and by *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* (4.1.5), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added.
The suffix *ṅīp* [is also included here]. Here too, the mention of "technical term" (*saṃjñā*) is merely an elaboration of the particle *iti*.

138. *kaṃśaṃbhyāṃ babhayustitutayasaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.138). [The commentary states: "The word *udaka* (water) and *sukha* (happiness) are the meanings. According to their respective order, *kam* denotes *udaka*, and *śam* denotes *sukha*. Regarding the form *śaṃyuḥ*: by rule *mo'nusvāraḥ* (8.3.33), the *m* becomes an *anusvāra*; for that [anusvāra], there is an option (*vā*).

"By the rule *padāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.59), there is a *parasavarṇa*; the nasalized (*anunāsika*) counterpart of *m* is *y*. Thus, the *anusvāra* and the *parasavarṇa* are established. This is because those two are prescribed under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "word" (*pada*). However, if the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "word" did not exist, then in its absence—
Because of the absence of the anusvāra and the parasavarṇa [substitutions] based on the position of the word, the undesirable forms *kamyuḥ* and *śamyuḥ* would result.

139. *tundibalivaṭerbhaḥ* | (5.2.139) From the word *tundi*, since it is listed among the *tundi*-group in [Pāṇini 5.2.117] *svāṅgādvivṛddhau*, the suffixes *ilac*, *ini*, and *iṭhan* would be applicable; however, after *bali*, since it is listed among the *pāma*-group, the suffix *matup* is applied.
For you, O Vāta, this [offering] is ordained just as for Manu.

140. *ahaṃśubhamoryus* (Pāṇini 5.2.140). Regarding the statement "the word *aham* is a different [independent] word": after the substitution of *tvāhau sau* (Pāṇini 7.2.94) for *asmad* and the application of the *tyadādi* replacement (*yatva*), the form *yah* is produced; however, *aham* is indeed something other than that, being an unanalyzed (irregularly formed) word.

Having thus shown the difference in sound by stating "it is not *tat* (that)," he says "it exists in *ahaṅkāra*" in order to show a different meaning [of the suffix]. In the examples "ahaṃyuḥ" and "śubhaṃyuḥ," the anusvāra and the subsequent homogeneous letter (*parasavarṇa*) are applied as before.
Thus ends the second quarter of the fifth chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who was a teacher of the Bodhisattvas.
Now begins the third quarter of the fifth chapter.

1. *prāgdiśo vibhaktiḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.1). [The commentary states: "Those [suffixes] should be understood as having the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) 'vibhakti'. That is to say, those for which the word *vibhakti* is the designation are so described. Now, one might object: the word *vibhakti* is the designation for *su*-affixes and *tiṅ*-affixes, and a designation...

If a word uttered in specific rules were to convey its own designatum (*saṃjñin*), then the prescription of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for *su*- and *tiṅ*-suffixes would be purposeless. Just as the word *vṛddhi*, although subordinate to its own expressed meaning in common usage, functions as a designation for the sounds *ā*, *ai*, and *au*, so too [is it here].

It should be understood that the word *vibhakti* (case-ending) is also a technical name (*saṃjñā*) with respect to the suffixes beginning with *tasil*. Now, why is it not stated right there [in Pāṇini 1.1.38]: "The *sup* [suffixes] are called *vibhakti*, as well as those beginning with *prāg-diś*"? If this were done, it would not be necessary to mention *vibhakti* again [in Pāṇini 2.4.71]. This cannot be so; for if such were the case in the formulation...

Since the word *sati* exists, it is not known from where the *prāgdiśīya* suffixes begin. Furthermore, because the term *dig* occurs multiple times in the treatise—such as in "from *dik* etc., [the suffix] *yat*" (Pāṇini 4.3.54) and "in the same direction as that" (4.3.112)—the very limit (*avadhi*) would be subject to doubt. [This is also true for the rule] "from *kim*, all pronouns (*sarvanāman*), and *bahu*" (5.3.2).

And for the sake of showing the limit of such forms beginning with *ityevaṃ*, one would have to state again here: "after *prāgdiś* [the suffix] *ṭha*. Therefore, the traditional formulation (*yathānyāsam*) alone is correct. [The forms] *tataḥ* and *yataḥ* [are derived as follows]: while the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.2.84) is still in force, [the rule] *tyadādīnām aḥ* (7.2.102) [applies].
[The suffix *kutaḥ* is derived as follows: by [Pāṇini 5.3.7], the suffix *tasil* is applied;

by [Pāṇini 1.3.4], the prohibition of the *it*-designation for the letter *s* applies because it occurs in a case-ending (*vibhakti*); and by [Pāṇini 1.1.38], because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), there is elision (*luk*) of the case-ending. Thus, "from where" (*kutaḥ*). [The form *kutaḥ* is derived] by [Pāṇini 7.2.104]: "After *kim*, [the substitution of *ku* occurs] before *ti* and *haḥ*."
The substitution of *ku* for *kimaḥ*.

The rule "the operations pertaining to *tyadādi*" applies here; that is, the rules concerning *tyad* and so forth are dependent upon case endings (*vibhakti*). The example "tataḥ" illustrates the [substitution] of *atva* (the replacement of *kim* by *tat*) under the rule for *tyadādi*. The example "iha" illustrates the accentuation of the case ending of *idam*.

From the word *idam* ending in the locative case, the suffix *ha* is applied by the rule "ṭhidamo haḥ" (5.3.11), and the substitution of *iś* is applied by the rule "ṭhidama iś" (5.3.3). Thus, when it is a case-ending (*vibhakti*), the acute accent (*udāttatva*) for what follows *idam* is established by the rule "ūḍidampadādyappumraidyaubhyaḥ" (6.1.171). However, in this case...

The initial acute accent (*ādyaudātta*) is established by the accent of the suffix itself (*pratyayasvara*). Therefore, this has been shown merely as an illustrative direction. However, the following example is more appropriate here: *itaḥ*. Here, the suffix *tasil* is added to *idam*, and *diś* is substituted as before. For, if it were not a case ending (*vibhakti*), the suffix would have the *lita*-accent [by P. 6.1.193].

The acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) would apply to the first syllable of the preceding word. However, in that case, by rules such as *ūḍidamparaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.171), the acute accent on the initial syllable of the suffix *tas* following *idam* is established. But even if this were so...
Since it is a case-ending (*vibhakti*), should not the accent of the *lit* suffix apply by virtue of its being subsequent? This is not a fault;

for in the rule *liti* (Pāṇini 6.1.193), the preceding rules beginning with *ūḍidam* (6.1.171) will be carried over (*anuvartate*) in order to set aside the accent of the *lit* suffix. But even so, would the acute accent of the case-ending still not be established?

For in that context, the mention of "the third case and those following" (*tṛtīyādigrahaṇa*) is carried over from the rule *sāvekācastṛtīyādivibhaktiḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.168); however, the suffixes beginning with *tasil* are not included by that mention of "the third case and those following. [This applies] starting from the singular of the third case (*tṛtīyaikavacana*).

From the conclusion of the fifth chapter onwards, every suffix (*pratyaya*) designated as a case-ending (*vibhakti*) beginning with the third case is [governed by] "ataḥ param" and so forth. For "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) indeed means the state of having a relation (*sambandha*); and that—
Co-occurrence (*ekārthībhāva*) occurs only when there is a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), and not otherwise. Priority (*prāthamya*) also depends entirely upon a counter-correlative;
for it is only in relation to a second [item] that something is called "first. Hereafter follow the suffixes (*pratyaya*).
Since [the suffixes] occur only when the meaning is that of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), there is no possibility of a second counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) for that [base];

and because of its absence, there is likewise no possibility of "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) or "primacy" (*prāthamya*), as these two depend upon a counter-correlative. And since this is so, therefore [the rule] "under the heading of capacity" (*sāmarthyādhikāraḥ*) [is stated].

The mention of "the first" (prathama) is also not required; thus, both [the mention of "the first" and the mention of "the last"] are eliminated. If this is so, does it not follow that the mention of the option (vāvacana) is also eliminated, since it is prescribed in the same single rule (ekayoganirdiṣṭa)?
To this he says: "But the mention of the option (vāvacana) indeed persists. The intention is that this is because it is marked with the svarita accent.
"By that alternative," and so forth; by this, he demonstrates the result of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "optionally" (*vā*) from the subsequent sūtra.

2. *kiṃsarvanāmabahubhyo 'dvyādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.2). Regarding the word *kutra*: [it is formed] by *saptamyās tral* (5.3.10); the substitution of *ku-* occurs as before. Regarding *prakṛtiparisaṃkhyānam*: it means an enumeration of the base forms (*prakṛti*).

Regarding "ṭhvaiyākaraṇapāśaḥ": by the rule "ṭhyāpye pāśap" (Pāṇini 5.3.47), the suffix *pāśap* is applied. And since this [suffix] follows the limit *vyas*, it occurs after other bases as well. Regarding the statement "it is established simply because of its being a pronominal (*sarvanāman*)," the status of being a pronominal for *kim* arises from its inclusion among the words beginning with *sarva*. The phrase "the mention of *kim*" and so forth [follows].

Since this word *kim* is recited among the "dvi" group and so forth, it is excluded by the rule "from *dvi* and the others. Therefore, even though it is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), it is mentioned by its own specific name [in the rule].
If that is the case, the word *kim* should be recited before the word *dvi*; for in this way, its—

Is it not the case that the separate mention [of *kimaḥ*] should not have been made at all? True, this is so; however, since the author of the Sūtras does not provide a formal list of word-groups (*gaṇapāṭha*) here, he does not deserve censure. Furthermore, according to the rule "among the words beginning with *tyad*, whichever follows remains," when there is a desire to express [the combination of] *kimaḥ* together with all the words beginning with *tyad*, [the form] *śeṣa* [would result].

It is accepted [by some] that [the forms] *tvaṃ ca kaśca* and *bhavāṃśca kaśca* should be *kau*; however, since this is not established by the reading [of the rule as it stands], let it remain exactly as it was formulated.
Regarding the statement "in the mention of 'many' (*bahu*), there is the mention of 'number' (*saṃkhyā*)," how then are the words beginning with *sarva* designated as pronouns (*sarvanāman*) here?

Why are they designated as *saṃjñins*? Because they are taught together with those [technical names], it is understood that by the rule *bahu-gaṇa-ādi* (Pāṇini 1.1.23), which prescribes the technical name *saṃkhyā* for the word *bahu*, it is precisely that [word] which possesses the name that is grasped as the *saṃjñin*. As in the example: *bahoḥ sūpāt*.
In this context, the word "bahu" signifies "extensive."

3. *idama iś* (Pāṇini 5.3.3). [The commentary states: "The letter *ś* is for the sake of making it a substitute for the whole word (*sarvādeśa*). For if that were not the case, [the rule] *alo'ntyasya* (1.1.52) would apply; then, when the elision of *id-rūpa* is performed by *hali lopaḥ* (6.4.113), [the form *iś* would result].
By the rule *ṭhādguṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.87), the undesirable forms *etaḥ* and *eha* would result. Now, one might argue:

"But surely, once the substitution of *yat* for *idam* etc. has been applied by *tyadādyatva* (7.2.102), and then the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) by *ato guṇe* (6.1.97), and finally the elision of the final vowel, the forms *itaḥ* and *iha* are indeed established? This would be established only if...

First, the substitution of *tyadādi* (the *yatva*) would be obtained; however, that is not what is obtained here, for the substitution of *it* (the *itva*) is indeed more *antaranga*. For the *itva* is *antaranga* because it depends only upon the suffixes beginning with *tasil*, whereas the *tyadādi-yatva* depends upon the designation of the stem (*aṅga-saṃjñā*), the subsequent suffix, and its being a case-ending (*vibhakti*).
And because it depends [on something else], it is "external" (bahiraṅga); therefore, the suffix śākaRA should be applied.

4. *etetau rathoḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.4). In the rule *rathoḥ*, there is a reference to the two phonemes *ra* and *tha*. In that context, according to the maxim *yasmin vidhis tadādāvalgrahaṇe* (Vārttika 14), the grammatical operation applies to that which begins with *repha* (*ra*) and that which begins with *thakāra* (*tha*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "it is understood" and continuing with "at the beginning of *repha*," etc.: how is it known that the vowel *a* [in the word *repha*] is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*)? Because there is no *repha* containing the vowel *a* following the pronoun *idam*.

5. *etado'ś* (Pāṇini 5.3.5). [The commentary states: "The letter *ś* is for the purpose of making [the substitute] an all-replacement (*sarvādeśa*). Now, if that [substitute] were to apply to the final [phoneme], would it not follow that if it occurred when the substitution of *t* for *tyad* and so on has not yet taken place, then its application to the letter *d* would be rendered purposeless?

For even by virtue of the substitution of *tyad* and so forth, its form as the vowel *a* is indeed obtained; however, once the substitution of *tyad* and so forth has been applied, the [substitution of *a*] occurring in place of that *a* would result in being entirely purposeless, since there is no need to state the vowel *a* for the vowel *a*, and it has already been established. Therefore, by virtue of the explicit statement, it is a substitute for the whole (sarvādeśa) even in the absence of the letter *ś*.

Will it occur? This is not so; for there is a purpose in stating the letter *a* as *a*. What is it? To ensure that, in this case [of the word *atre*], whatever else might otherwise apply does not take effect. But what is that? [The rule] "the syllable preceding an affix marked with *l* is acute" would apply. Therefore, the letter *ś* must be employed.

Regarding *ṭhthamuḥ*: this suffix *thamu* must be added as a supplement (*upasaṃkhyeya*). As for the statement in the *Kāśikā*, "it must be added as a supplement," that is because [the suffix] is not found [in the original rule]. The meaning of "must be added" is that it must be established.
In this regard, the following is the proof: these very [suffixes] are the statement of substitutes beginning with the letter *th*.
It indicates: "This [suffix] *tham* occurs after *asti*. But from what indeed does this follow? From an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

The suffix *tham* will occur, and not the suffix *tha* itself—which, being prescribed without distinction by the rule "the suffix *thāl* in the sense of 'kind'" (Pāṇini 5.3.23), would be a substitute for that very [suffix *tha*] beginning with *tha*. This is not a fault.

This [suffix] is intended to be a specific marker such as *tha* and so forth. For even in the rule "ṭha etadaḥ," the phrase "of this [word] beginning with *e*" (*edamaḥ*) is understood to carry over; and that [carry-over] is not for the purpose of prescribing a substitute, because the substitute has already been prescribed previously.
Therefore, it is understood as a specifier of the suffix (*pratyaya-viśeṣaṇa*). Consequently, by this, [the suffix] begins with *tha*.

We shall provide a distinction: that which is prescribed by the word *idam* itself—namely, that which begins with the letter *th* and so forth—is indeed prescribed as *thamu*, and not as *thāl*. Thus, the statement of the substitute (*ādeśa*) is rightly said to indicate that this [suffix] exists even when it is not *thamu*.

6. *sarvasya so'nyatarasyāṃ di* (Pāṇini 5.3.6). The term *dīti* is a locative case ending in the letter *d*. Since there is no prāgdiśīya suffix consisting of the mere letter *d*, the rule *yasmin vidhis tadādāvalgrahaṇe* (Vārttika 14) applies.

Therefore, he states that the rule is understood to apply when the suffix begins with the letter *d*, saying: "in the case of a suffix beginning with *d* belonging to the *prāgdiśīya* group," and so forth. For example: *sarvadā brāhmaṇī*. [The derivation is as follows: by the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3), the suffix *ka* is applied;
from that, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added.

7. *Pañcamyās tasil* (Pāṇini 5.3.7). [The sūtra states: "The suffix *tasil* occurs. Why are these substitutes, beginning with *tasil*, not applied directly in place of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) and the others? For if this were so, they would not have the designation of "case endings" (*vibhakti*).

Is it to be performed? These substitutions cannot be carried out; for if they were indeed substitutions (*ādeśa*), then by [Pāṇini 4.2.104] *tyap*, and subsequently by *tya*—as in the forms *yatastyaḥ* and *yatastyaḥ*—there would be elision (*luk*) by [Pāṇini 2.4.71] *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*. Indeed, they do obtain [this result].

By virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the substitutes for *su* and so forth undergo operations dependent upon *su*. Thus, in *tataḥ*, [the suffix] is unaccented by the rule "anudāttau suppitau" (Pāṇini 3.1.4). In *kutaḥ*, there is *guṇa* substitution by the rule "dheṅiti" (Pāṇini 7.3.111). In *etarhi*, there is lengthening by the rule "supi ca" (Pāṇini 7.3.102). In *tatra*,...

In the case of the plural ending *jhal*, there is the substitution of *et* by [Pāṇini 7.3.103]. Where is this? In the form *atra*, there is the substitution of *aut* for *ghis* by [Pāṇini 7.3.119]. Then, in the case of *tatra*, there are the substitutions *smāt* and *smin* for *ṅsi* and *ṅi* respectively by [Pāṇini 7.1.15]. Therefore, these are not substitutes of the base (*nādeśa*). If this is so, [then...]

From the root *upa-kṣi* (Dhātupāṭha 1212), in the case of the form *tasyan* [derived from] *tasya*, the substitution *tasil* would apply by the rule *taseśca* (Pāṇini 5.3.8). This is not a fault; for these suffixes beginning with *tasil* are understood to be *svārthika* (added without changing the original meaning). Indeed, these suffixes such as *tasil* are *svārthika*.

The substitution *tasil* being prescribed in that context is understood in such a way that, when applied in its own sense (*svārtha*), it does not deviate from the nature of a suffix used in its own sense (*svārthika*). Thus, the *tasil* which occurs as a substitute for that *ṭha*— itself a *svārthika* suffix prescribed by the rule "ṭhapādāne cāhīyarūhoḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.45)— is likewise [understood].

It is indeed *svārthika* (denotative of its own meaning). However, since the verbal root (*dhātu*) occurs in a different sense from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the suffix *tasil*, being a substitute for that [root], is not *svārthika*.
8. *taseśca* (Pāṇini 5.3.8).

[In the example] "kuta āgataḥ" ("from where has he come?"), because the suffix *tas* [of the ablative case] is applied by the rule *apādāne cāhīyaruhoḥ* (5.4.45) due to its higher priority, the suffix *tasil* is then applied to that *tas* by this present rule (*taseśca*). But surely, even when *tasil* is applied, it is that very same [suffix *tas*]?

Regarding the word *rūpam*, for what purpose is it mentioned? To this he says: "The statement 'from the [suffix] tas, [the suffix] tasil is used in the sense of 'like'" (Pāṇini 5.1.116), and so forth.

9. *paryabhibhyāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 5.3.9). It is intended [that this rule applies] when [the words] *pari* and *abhi* signify "all" (*sarva*) or "both sides" (*ubhaya*). Therefore, it does not apply here in the cases *pariṣiñcati* ("he sprinkles around") and *abhiyāti* ("he goes toward"). And the reason for this is non-mention [of these specific senses]. Since [the word *ataḥ*]...

Or rather— the term *anyatarasyām* from the sūtra beginning with *sarvasya* (5.3.6) is understood to carry over, and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Consequently, [the suffix] occurs only when [the words] *sarva* and *ubhaya* are present, and not otherwise.
10. After [the word] *saptamī*, the suffix *traL* is added. (5.3.10) 11. After *idam*, the suffix *ha* is added. (5.3.11) 12. After *kim*, the suffix *at* is added. (5.3.12)

Regarding the word *kva*: by the rule *kvāti* (Pāṇini 7.2.105), the substitute *kva* takes the place of *kim*. Since the prohibition [of *it*-designation] stated in *na vibhaktau tusmāḥ* (1.3.4) is shown to be non-universal (*anitya*) by the presence of the vowel *u* in *idamasthamuḥ* (5.3.24), the letter *t* receives the designation *it*. However, for the suffix *dānīm*, there is no *it*-designation because of that very prohibition.
And because of the absence of purpose.
13. *vā ha ca chandasi* (Pāṇini 5.3.13).

14. *itarābhyo 'pi dṛśyante* (Pāṇini 5.3.14). Regarding [the term] *itaratva*, it is said: "The state of being *itara* is relative to the fifth and seventh cases. Immediately after that [occurs the mention of] the word *itara*.

Because [the object] is already known. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *dṛśi* (to see), since the rule would be established by the words "also from others" (*itarābhyaḥ*) alone? To this he says: "The mention of *dṛśi*" and so forth. The mention of *dṛśi* is for the purpose that the rule may be understood as being general (*prāyika*). When that is present, however—

When following the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), the meaning obtained is that [the rule] applies where it is observed [in their usage], and not elsewhere; by this, the optional nature (*prāyikatva*) of the injunction is established. Regarding the phrase "by that" (*tena*) and so forth: however, when the word *dṛśi* ("is seen") is included, it means wherever the usage of the learned is observed among other [forms].

From those [words] alone, suffixes such as *tasil* and others ought to occur. Since they are seen occurring only after words beginning with *bhavat*, the rule for them is prescribed specifically for those cases. For if *tasil* and the other suffixes were to occur after other words as well, then the previous prescription [of them] after the fifth (*pañcamī*) and seventh (*saptamī*) case endings would be purposeless. This is not so.

For [the suffix] is necessarily intended by those two in the case of connection with *bhavat* and so forth, while [it is used] for other [words] in the case of connection with *bhavat* and so forth. And since both are obtained when this preceding rule and this [present] one exist, how can there be pointlessness?

15. *sarva-eka-anya-kim-yat-tadaḥ kāle dā* (5.3.15). The phrase "of the seventh case" (*saptamyāḥ*) is understood [from the previous rule], because it is marked with the svarita accent. [The phrase] "but not from the others" (*na tvitarābhyaḥ*) follows from its opposite. [The phrase] "an exception to *tral* and so forth" (*tralāderapavādaḥ*) applies as far as possible. In that regard:

This is an exception to the suffix *āt* which would otherwise be obtained from the word *kim* by Pāṇini 5.3.12 (*kimo't*). According to the opinion of some, it is also *taral*. From the word *tat*, the suffixes *dā* and *hil* are applied according to 5.3.20 (*tayordādhilau ca chandasi*). From the remaining words, however, the suffix *trala* is applied. In the form *kadā*, there is the substitution of *kā* for *kim*.

16. *idamo hil* (5.3.16). [This is] an exception (*apavāda*) to [the rule] *hasya* [which follows from 5.3.7]. It supersedes what was obtained by *idamo haḥ* (5.3.11). "The letter *l* is for the sake of the accent" means that, by the rule *liti* (6.1.193), the syllable preceding the suffix receives the acute accent (*udātta*).

It might be so. But surely, just as in the case of *itaḥ*—where the accent of the case-ending (*vibhaktisvara*) occurs by the rule "ūḍidampada... (Pāṇini 6.1.171)—so too here it ought to be the same? This is not so;
for while it is appropriate that the accent of the case-ending occurs in *itaḥ*, this is because of the *lit*-designation of the suffix *tasil*.

Since the terms *paritaḥ* and *abhitaḥ* have already fulfilled their purpose [by being included elsewhere], the inclusion of the *liṭ* suffix here would otherwise be rendered meaningless. Therefore, if it were overridden by the accent of the case-ending (*vibhaktisvara*), that inclusion would be purposeless. Consequently, the accent of the *liṭ* suffix alone prevails.
The separation of this rule (*yogavibhāga*)—namely, the addition of *dānīm*—is for the sake of what follows: namely, in the rule *tado dā ca* (5.3.19).
So that it may be exactly as it is now, let there not be the suffix prescribed by the preceding sūtra.

19. *tado dā ca* (Pāṇini 5.3.19). [The commentary states: "The suffix *ṭhan* is meaningless. This is for the sake of variety (*vaicitrya*). Since there is no other [suffix] [to apply here], being meaningless [in this context], it becomes meaningful precisely through its variety. [The commentary says: "Because it has already been prescribed," by means of [the rule] *sarvaikānya-* (5.3.15), etc.

20. *tayoḥ dārhilau ca chandasi* (Pāṇini 5.3.20). [The suffixes] *dā* and *rhil* are added to those two (*tad* and *idam*) in the Vedic language. From *idam*, by *idama iś* (5.3.3), we get *iś*. Likewise, through the transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyaya*), the letter *d* becomes *dh*.
Thus, *idānīm* and *tadānīm*. These are examples of the suffix *dānīm*.

21. *anadyatane rhilanyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.3.21). When the suffixes beginning with *tasil* would otherwise apply, the suffix *hil* is optionally prescribed. [The form] *kahi* is derived as follows: by *kimaḥ kaḥ* (7.2.103), *kim* becomes *ka*;
then, by *sarvaikānyakiyatadaḥ kāle dā* (5.3.15), the suffix *dā* is added to *ka*, resulting in *kadā*. Similarly, one obtains *yadā* and *tadā*.
22. *sadyas*, *parut*, *parāri*, *aiṣamas*, *paredyavi*, *adya*, *pūrvedyus*, *anyedyus*, *anyataredyus*, *itaredyus*, *aparedyus*, *adharedyus*, *ubhayedyus*, and *uttaredyus*.
(Pāṇini 5.3.22)

Regarding the rule "sadyaḥ" [meaning] "on the same day": this is a grammatical irregularity (nipātana) for the word *sadyas* when both the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*naimittika*) occur on the same common day (*samāne ahani*). For example: "striking a vital point (*marman*) is immediately life-taking.
The meaning is that on whichever very day there is a strike at a vital point, on that very same day there is the taking of life.
And [the word] *udārī*. *Udāri* is derived from *ucca* and *āri*.
According to the rule "after *para*, *edyavi*," the suffix *edyavi* occurs after the word *para* when a day is to be expressed.

23. The suffix *thāl* is used in the sense of expressing a "manner" (*prakāra*). (Pāṇini 5.3.23) [The *Kāśikā* explains: "A 'manner' (*prakāra*) is that which distinguishes a particular instance from a general category.
24. The suffix *thamu* is used after the word *idam*. (Pāṇini 5.3.24)

25. *kimaśca* | (5.3.25) "The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows," it says; for he will state [the next rule] as *thā hetau ca* (5.3.26). This [separation] is so that the suffix may apply only to *kim*, and not to *idam*.
26. *thā* is used for the sense of cause (*hetu*) in the Vedic language (*chandas*).

(Pāṇini 5.3.26) 27. From words denoting direction (*dik-śabda*), the suffix *astāti* is added after those in the seventh, fifth, and first case endings, when referring to direction (*diś*), place (*deśa*), or time (*kāla*).
(Pāṇini 5.3.27)

"Regarding those existing in direction, place, and time. But how is it that the words for directions exist in place and time? By their very nature (*svabhāva*). For just as they exist in directions by their very nature and not from any other cause, so too it is with respect to place and time. If this is so, then in all three...

How can those [words] currently existing [denoting directions] be designated by the phrase "from words denoting direction" (*dik-śabdebhyaḥ*)? How, then, should it be designated? Should it be "from words denoting direction, place, and time" (*dig-deśa-kāla-śabdebhyaḥ*)? This is not so; for such a designation would have this result: that [the suffix] would not apply in a case such as *aindraḷaṃ diśi nivasati* ("he dwells in the eastern quarter").

It is appropriate to designate this [number] by means of even one of these [directions], so that the sūtra becomes concise through such designation; and by designating it by direction, it becomes concise because the word for "direction" has fewer syllables. Thus, it is designated by means of the directions. Even so...

Since the word *dik* (direction) occurs in the sense of "direction," the qualification [“in the sense of direction”] is inappropriate; for a word denoting direction necessarily refers to a direction. In that case, it should have been stated as “in the sense of place and time. This is not so; for if it were stated in that way, the word *dik* would merely serve as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), whereas it should rather be [understood as] a synonym (*paryāya*).

[The suffix] would arise only from the divisions of space (*deśa*) and time (*kāla*), but not from the divisions of direction (*diś*); however, when "direction" (*dig*) is included [in the rule], it arises from those as well. Here there are three case-endings (*vibhakti*) and three meanings, beginning with "direction" (*dig*); therefore, due to their correspondence, they are applied according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*).
Someone might have the misconception that [the rule] must apply [in this way];
therefore, in order to dispel that, he says: "In this case, the correspondence of numbers (yathāsaṃkhya) is not intended.
How then can there be a plural designation here when a singular designation ought to be made? [The answer is: with respect to each [individual].

This is intended to indicate that the suffix should be applied after a word ending in various case-terminations (*bahulavibhaktyanta*) when it denotes direction (*digvṛtti*). Thus, this suffix is applied after a word ending in various case-terminations only if it denotes direction— namely, when it ends in the seventh, fifth, or first case— and likewise when it denotes place (*deśavṛtti*).

Also for that which expresses time. Alternatively, the particle *ca* is carried over from "ṭhaḥ pratinā mātrārthe, hetuhetumator ca" (Pāṇini 5.4.46); and that particle conjoins only what has been heard [in the rule].
Consequently, the suffix occurs after words expressing direction and so forth, when they are used individually in the locative, ablative, or nominative case.

There is no correspondence according to the order of enumeration (*yathāsaṃkhyam*). For if there were correspondence according to the order of enumeration, the conjunction (*samuccaya*) would be contradicted.

Alternatively, it has been stated that "correspondence according to the order of enumeration occurs when the *svarita* accent is present," and since the *svarita* accent is not here intended for the purpose of correspondence according to the order of enumeration, there will be no correspondence according to the order of enumeration.

Regarding the expression "purastād adhastāt": the suffix *astāti* is applied to the words *pūrva* and *adhara*. By the rule that will be stated later, *astāti ca* (Pāṇini 5.3.40), the forms *pur-* and *adha-* are respectively the substitutes for the words *pūrva* and *adhara*.

"In the eastern direction dwells Indra. The word *aindrī* generally denotes any object related to Indra; however, in proximity to the word "direction," it refers specifically to the direction. Therefore, it is not the case that this [word] is not well-known in the world as a term for direction.

An example is: *pūrvaṃ grāmaṃ gataḥ* ("He went to the village previously"). Here, the word *pūrva* refers to a location because the village is of the nature of a place; it does not end in the seventh (locative) case or similar, but rather ends in the second (accusative) case. In the phrase *pūrvasmin gurau vasati* ("He dwells with the teacher previously"), the word *pūrva* here...
The Guru resides in that which is characterized by the directions and so forth, but not in the directions and so forth themselves.
28. *dakṣiṇottarābhyāmatasuc* (5.3.28).

The letter *ṭh* is for the purpose of specification (*viśeṣaṇārtha*). If the vowel *a* were not used here, then the rule *ṣaṣṭhī tasarthapratyayena* (2.3.30) would have to be formulated; and this being the case, [the following would occur].

In that case, there would also be the inclusion of the suffix *tasil*; consequently, even in the expression *tato hetunā*, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would supersede the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*). Therefore, the vowel *a* must be included for the sake of specification.
Furthermore, when the words *dakṣiṇā* and *uttarā* refer to the directions, so that the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is heard...

Why does the vowel *a* not serve the purpose of [forming] *bhū*? Because the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is already excluded by the rule "in all simple compounds, a feminine noun becomes masculine" (Vārttika 104). Now, one might argue that if *a* were not present, the accent would be established by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), and thus the letter *c* would also not need to be added.
In that case, since the rule "when a suffix with one *anubandha* is mentioned, there is no [application of] a suffix with two *anubandhas*" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 52) applies,

would there not be no mention of *tasil*? Even so, there would be a mention of either [the suffixes] in the rules "the suffix *tasi* after the fifth case-ending when used with *prati*" (5.4.44), "the suffix *tasi* after [a word ending in] *tena* when meaning 'in the same direction'" (4.3.112), and "also the suffix *tasi*" (4.3.113).
It might be so; therefore, the particle "ca" (and) must be employed for the purpose of specification.
