29. [The suffix *ṭhañ* is optionally applied] after the words *para* and *avara*. (5.3.29) 30. There is elision (*luk*) of the suffix after the root *añc*.

(5.3.30) Because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "from words denoting direction" (*dik-śabda*), and because the simple root *añc* does not denote a direction, [the suffix] *ṭhañ* is [applied]. (5.3.31)
Thus, this is understood as a reference to a word ending in *añcu*; for this very reason, he says:

"from those ending in *añcu*," "from words denoting direction (*dikśabda*)," and "he dwells in the east (*prāgvasati*). In the case of *pra-añcu*, the suffix *kvin* is applied by the rule beginning with "the *ṛtvij* etc.
(Pāṇini 3.2.59).

By the rule *ṭhañcateścopasaṃkhyānam* (Vārttika 336), the suffix *ṅīp* is added; by *ṭhacaḥ* (6.4.138), there is elision (*allopa*) of the *ṭha*; and by *ṭhau* (6.3.138), there is lengthening—thus, with *prācī* established, the suffix *astāti* is applied, which is then elided (*luk*), and by *kvinpratyayasya kuḥ* (8.2.62), there is the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *k*); thus, *pratyak*.
Thus; the suffix [is applied] after the word *pratīcī*, and that [suffix] is to be explained as before.
31. *upary-upariṣṭāt* (Pāṇini 5.3.31).
The suffixes *ṭhri*, *lri*, *ṣṭātil*, and *atil* are prescribed as substitutes [for the locative suffix], and they serve as exceptions (*apavāda*) to the suffix *astāti*.

32. *paścāt* (5.3.32). [The rule] "and the suffix *āti*"—this also is an exception (*apavāda*) to *astāti*. Examples include *dakṣiṇapaścāt* and *uttarapaścāt*, as in: "he dwells in the south-western direction."
In the same way, *dakṣiṇapaścāt* and *uttarapaścāt* [are formed].
According to the rule *ṭhardhotarapadasya ca*, the word *aparasya* (of the latter) is connected [here].
Furthermore, it is stated that "the status of being *paścāt* should be expressed even without the preceding member."

The phrase "of another whose final member begins with a vowel" (aparasyārddhotarapadasya) must be connected with what has been previously stated. In all these instances, the word *vaktavya* ("it should be stated") occurs in the commentary (*vyākhyāna*). Here is that commentary:

by the method of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*), the particle *ca* ("and") from the subsequent rule is understood here; and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.
By this, the grammatical operation whereby the word *apara* following a directional term as its prior member undergoes the substitution of *paśca*, and so forth, becomes established.
33. *paśca* and *paścāt* [are used] in the Vedic language (*chandas*).
(5.3.33) 34. After *uttara*, *adhara*, and *dakṣiṇa*, the suffix *āti* is applied.
(5.3.34) [Note: After *uttara* and *dakṣiṇa*, the suffix *atasuc* is also applied by rule 5.3.28: *dakṣiṇottarābhyām atasuc*.
By the application of these rules— *ṭhenabanyatarasyāmadūre'pañcamyāḥ* (5.3.35), *dakṣiṇādācĀ* (5.3.36), *āhi ca dūre* (5.3.37), and *utarācca* (5.3.38)—
the suffixes *atasuc* and others would have been applicable; however, by this [present rule], the suffixes *astāti* and *āti* are prescribed even after the word *adhara*.
Its number is indeed sublated; however, *suj* and the others do occur optionally by virtue of an explicit statement (*vacana*).

And here, although there is a triad of both the suffixes—namely the seventh case endings and so forth—and the conditions—namely *diś* and so forth—nevertheless, there is no correspondence according to numerical order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*). Why? Because of its meaning (*tadarthasya*).

Because the quality of being *svarita* has not been formally asserted; and because the word *adhara*, having a light syllable (*laghu*), is placed first— which serves as a sign of deviation from the general rule— he demonstrates that this [rule] is independent of other definitions, showing that the definition of "correspondence" (*yathāsaṃkhya*) is not required here.

This indicates that, for that reason, there is no correspondence according to the number of case-endings; however, with respect to the qualifiers, this is because the word *dakṣiṇa* cannot function to denote time.
35. *enab anyatarasyām adūre 'pañcamyāḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.35). [The Vārttika states:

"If *adūra* (not far) is the limit (*avadhimān*), it relates to that which possesses the limit (*avadhimat*). But how is such a distinction obtained, given that the word *avadhi* (limit) is not heard in the sūtra, nor is *avadhimān*?

The operation of words such as *dika* (directional) occurs with reference to a limit (*avadhi*). Since a person who possesses a limit exists only in relation to a limit, this specific distinction is obtained by implication even though it is not explicitly stated.
For example, in the phrase "he dwells below" (*adhastād vasati*), the suffix *astāti* is applied according to the rule *astāti ca* (Pāṇini 5.3.40), which will be mentioned later.

The word *adhará-* undergoes substitution [by *para-*] from what follows. This refers to what will be stated [in Pāṇini 5.3.39]: "Before *asi*, there is the substitution of *pura-*, *adhara-*, and *avara-* for these.
According to the opinion of those who hold that the suffix is applied after any word denoting direction (*dikśabda*) in general, [the rule applies] by the preceding [sūtra].

The form *vasati* and so forth also occurs. If the suffix were to arise from the mere word *dik* (direction), then it would also occur after *atyanta*. Let it be so; will there not be elision (*luk*) by the rule *añceḥ luk* (5.3.30)? This is not the case; for "exceptions (*apavāda*) [operate] in the middle, [blocking] preceding rules."

By this [rule], there is elision (*luk*) here specifically of the root *as* (in *asta*), and not of any other. If that is so, then the term *anyatarasyām* (optionally) constitutes a fixed option (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*). Consequently, it will not apply to words ending in *añc*.
The letter *pakāra* is for the purpose of distinguishing [the rule] by "ṭhena prathamāʼd dvitīyā" (Pāṇini 2.3.31), and it is also for the sake of the accent (*svara*).
36. *dakṣiṇād āc* (Pāṇini 5.3.36). [The commentary states:

"The letter *ca* is for the sake of specification (*viśeṣaṇārtha*). For if that were not present, since the word *paścāt* is prescribed as ending in the vowel *ā*, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) would also occur when used in conjunction with it.
But the purpose of the particle *ca* is not tenable, since the desired accentuation is already established by the accent of the suffix itself.
37. *āhi ca dūre* (Pāṇini 5.3.37). 38. *utarācca* (Pāṇini 5.3.38).
[The suffixes] *ṭhañ* and *āhin* are prescribed after the word *bhakta*. Now, one might object: "On account of proximity (*anantarya*), wouldn't it follow that only *āhin* applies?"
"Nana"; the particle "ca" (and) is employed here, for it conjoins even that which is separated [by other words].
Therefore, there will also be [the suffix] āṬ.

39. *pūrvādharāvarāṇām asi puradhavaś caiṣām* (Pāṇini 5.3.39). Since the suffix *tāti* would have applied after *pūrva*, and *tāt* would have applied after *avara* as well, this rule beginning with *atasuc* is commenced optionally.
Now, for what purpose is it stated "of these" (*eṣām*), given that [the suffixes] are already included among *pūrva* and the others?

That very sixth [case-ending], having established a condition, is understood as a genitive in place [of another]; and because of the difference in relation, there is a difference in the meaning of the genitive? This is true; nevertheless, it was stated "of these" for the sake of easy comprehension.

40. And [the suffix] *astāti* [is used after words denoting direction]. (5.3.40) Now, one might object: "Since [words like] *pūrva* and others have already been negated by the suffix *asin*, the suffix *astāti* should not apply to them. To this, he says: "This very [sūtra]," etc. The meaning has already been explained.
41. *vibhāṣā 'varasya* (Pāṇini 5.3.41). 42. *saṃkhyāyā vidhārthe dhā* (Pāṇini 5.3.42).
[This is] an exception (*apavāda*) to [the rule] *ṭhak-prakāravacane ca jātīyar* (Pāṇini 5.3.69).

Regarding the statement "the suffix *thāl* is used in the sense of 'manner' (*prakāra*)" (Pāṇini 5.3.23), that manner also exists as a specific property (*guṇa*) of a substance (*dravya*). If that [property] were also included [in the definition],
then because substances and properties are connected with gender (*liṅga*) and number (*saṃkhyā*), the word ending in that suffix would be devoid of gender and number.

It would not [be so]; and in that case, its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) would not hold, yet that is desired. For it is recited among the indeclinables: "the *dhā* suffixes, beginning with *tasil* and ending with *edhāc*, are taddhita [suffixes]. However, there is no fault if it is understood in the sense of action (*kriyā*), because action is always...
Having kept in mind that [the term] is not connected with gender and number, he says "And that," and so forth.
The action is the meaning expressed by the verbal root, such as "moistening" and the like; since that is its object, it is described in that way.
But how is the apprehension of a particular instance obtained when there is a statement of a general category?

For this is precisely the purpose of including the word *artha* (meaning): so that there may be a specification of the manner (*prakāra*). Otherwise, he would have simply said "in the sense of 'mode' (*vidhā*)". If, then, the manner is understood as pertaining to action (*kriyā*), why does [the suffix] not apply in cases such as *navadhā dravyam* (ninefold substance) or *navadhā guṇaḥ* (ninefold quality)?
This is not a fault; here too, the action must be supplied: "Substance is ninefold, and quality is established as ninefold," thus it is analyzed.
43. And [the suffix *dhyam* is applied] after *eka* when there is a shifting of the locus (*adhikaraṇavicāla*). (5.3.43) 44. After *eka*, the suffix *dhyamuñ* is optionally applied.
(5.3.44) "Make it into a single entity" (*ekadhyaṃ kuru*)—this is an example for the shifting of the locus (*adhikaraṇavicāla*). "He eats all at once" (*aikadhyam bhuṅkte*).

Thus [it is said]. Regarding the sense of "injunction" (vidhi): here, the mention of *dhā* is carried over (*anuvartate*), yet an occurrence in the sense of an injunction was not appropriate there, because it had already been prescribed previously. Therefore, by the force of this carry-over, the suffix *dhā* possesses the status of a substitute (*sthānitva*).

He says, "It is understood from the context itself," meaning that the status of being the substitute for the *dhā* suffix is obtained [from the context]. But what is the reason that [the rule] does not apply to that which is prescribed in the sense of 'prevention' (*vidhā*) when the mention of *dhā* is absent? He says: "For [the rule applies] only to the immediately preceding," and so forth. For if the mention of *dhā* were not repeated...
According to the principle "a rule applies to what is immediately preceding" (*vyā.

pa. 19*), [the substitution] would apply only to that which is prescribed for the purpose of restriction (*adhikaraṇavicāla*), and not to that which is prescribed for the purpose of prevention (*vidhāra*). However, when the word *dhā* is mentioned again, the substitution is established for every instance of *dhā*.
It comes to be.

45. *Dvitryos ca dhamuñ* (5.3.45). [The examples are] *dvaidham*, *tridham*, and *dvaidhāni*. Now, one might object: since suffixes added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthika*) retain the grammatical properties of the base, there should not be [variation in] gender and number here. This is not a fault; for [such suffixes] indeed transcend those properties.
Sometimes suffixes used in their own sense (svārthika) follow the properties of their base (prakṛti), as for example: "the four castes" (cāturvarṇya).
46. *edhācca* (Pāṇini 5.3.46).
47. *yāpye pāśap* (Pāṇini 5.3.47). This word *yāpya* is used in the sense of that which is to be sent away—as in "he is to be sent away from another village."
In the case of "incurable" (*aśakyapratīkāra*), there is the expression "this is a palliative disease" (*yāpyo roga*);

in the case of "despised" (*kutsita*), it is understood that "this is despised" (*yāpyo 'yam*). Since a word ending in the suffix *pāśa* is understood to denote something despised, the word *yāpya* itself is included here precisely because it expresses that [sense of being despised].

This is most appropriate; for this very reason he says: "The term *yāpya* is said to mean 'despised'. It is called *yāpya* because qualities are *yāpyante*—that is, they are removed from it. The suffix *kṛtya* is used here in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*) according to Pāṇini 3.3.113: *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*.

Regarding the question, "Why does it not occur there?"—the intention is that although he is proficient in grammar, nevertheless, because of his bad character (*duḥśīlatva*), [the rule] must indeed apply there. As for the phrase "of whom" (*yasya*) and so forth: a quality (*guṇa*) is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and a substance (*dravya*) is the qualified (*viśeṣya*); and although there may be many qualities in that substance...

Even so, when a word applies to or resides in a substance due to the presence of a certain quality, by virtue of proximity, that very quality must be what is expressed by the word in its state of being censured. However, for a grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*), bad character (*duḥśīlatva*) is not the ground for the application of the term; rather, it is [the study of] grammar.
It means thorough understanding or study; nor should one here be characterized by immoral conduct as a condition.

48. *pūraṇādbhāge tīyād an* (Pāṇini 5.3.48). This refers to "the suffix *tīya* which is a *pūraṇa*-suffix. It is so called because it is prescribed under the governing rule for *pūraṇa* [suffixes] in 5.2.48 (*tasya pūraṇe ḍaṭ*), or because its denoted meaning is a *pūraṇa*. [The word *pūraṇa* is used here] by metaphorical extension (*upacāra*).

The ordinal suffix *tīya* is also called *pūraṇa*. Regarding the word "in the sense of a part" (*bhāge*), the meaning is "a portion" (*aṃśa*). But for what purpose is this [rule] stated, since even when it is not applied, the form remains the same? To this he says: "The statement is for the sake of the accent" (*svarārtham vacanam*).
This is so that, in the sense of a division (*vibhāge*), the word may have the acute accent on the first syllable by virtue of the *nit*-accent rule.

"The mention of *pūraṇa* (ordinal) is for the sake of what follows" means that the suffix [under discussion] should apply after a word ending in a *pūraṇa*-suffix in the subsequent rule. And since that [subsequent application] is being delimited, the mention of *pūraṇa* here would also be purposeful;
however, because that [subsequent application] does not exist, its purposefulness here is not tenable. But surely—

One might ask: "Is there also [the form] *pārśvatīyaḥ*—as in *mukhapārśvataserīyaḥ*—even though it is not a ordinal number (*apūraṇa*)? To this he says: "*mukhatīyādiranarthakaḥ*" ("*mukhatīya* and so on are meaningless").
By the paribhāṣā regarding the inclusion of meaningful elements (*arthavadgrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), only a meaningful *tīya* suffix is understood here; and [in these cases], it is not [meaningful].
The word *mukhatīya* and others are meaningless; therefore, even though the term "pūraṇa" (ordinal) is mentioned [in the rule], its inclusion will not occur—this is the intended meaning.
49. Before eleven [in the sense of "parts"], the suffix *añ* is applied in Vedic usage. (5.3.49) 50. After the words *ṣaṣṭha* and *aṣṭama*, the suffix *ñ* is also applied.

(5.3.50) For if there were a correspondence according to the order of enumeration (*yathāsaṃkhya*), then after *ṣaṣṭha* the suffix *añ* would be obtained; and it is not established by the preceding rule alone.
Thus, the mention of the sixth sense-organ would be purposeless; therefore, both [the object and the sense] produce both [the cognition and the contact].

51. After the words *māna* and *paśvaṅga*, there is optionally the substitution of *kan* or *luk*. (Pāṇini 5.3.51) By virtue of the word *ca* ("and"), the rule "as otherwise obtained" (*yathāprāptam*) also applies.
52. *ekād ākinic cāsahāye* (5.3.52).

It is understood that there is an optional elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ākinic*, which is [a substitute] for *kan*; this is due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*). However, it does not apply to that which is prescribed in another context, because of the remoteness (*viprakarṣa*). If [the rule] "and that" (*sa ca*), etc., were mandatory...

In that case, the prescription would be purposeless; therefore, by the force of the prescription itself, it occurs optionally. But what is the reason for including the term "alone" (*asahāya*) in order to exclude numeral words?

Thus he says: "For if that [restriction] were not adopted," and so forth. If the mention of "non-existent" (*asatya*) as an auxiliary were not included, there would be the inclusion of the word *eka* even when it denotes the number one.
But when that [mention] is present, it would not apply to two or many; for the number one does not exist in two or in many.

However, even for a hundred [people], there can be a state of being without a companion (*asahāyatā*), because of the absence of another of the same kind—hence the expression "a hundred without a companion. Therefore, by adopting the sense of "being without a companion," the suffix is established even for two or many. Now, why is *ākinic* taught [separately] instead of [merely using *in*]?

If it were said that [the vowel] is not elided (*akṛti*), would the desired form still be established here by means of *savarṇadīrgha*? It is not established; for both *pararūpa* (by Pāṇini 6.1.97, *ato guṇe*) and the elision of the final vowel (*lopa*, by 6.4.148, *yasyeti ca*) would apply. Would it not be the case that these do not occur due to the force of the explicit utterance of the letter *a*? This is not so.

Indeed, there is a purpose for the pronunciation of the letter *a*: what is it? It is so that, in the context of the technical name *bha*, there may not be another *avagraha* (word-separation) based on the technical name *pada*. Therefore, the suffix *ākinic* alone should be prescribed.

53. *bhūtapūrve caraṭ* (Pāṇini 5.3.53). But for what purpose are these two words of identical meaning taught [separately], rather than just one of them being taught? It is not possible [to do otherwise]; for here, in a sense qualified by a past time—

The present tense is intended [to be understood] from the word *vartamāna*, yet that time has already passed; thus, when only one of the two [terms] is mentioned, it is not grasped. For instance, the word *bhūta* can refer even to the present meaning, as in "he was" (*bhūtavān*); however, the word *pūrva* refers also to direction and location.
Therefore, when one of the two [words] is mentioned, that which has passed away in time is not understood.

For this very reason, he says: "The word *bhūtapūrva* expresses that which has passed away in time. Now, why does the designation *it* not apply to the letter *ca* by the rule *cuṭ* (Pāṇini 1.3.7)? Because that rule is non-obligatory (*anitya*).
But impermanence has been established in that very same place.

54. And [the word] *rūpya* [is used] after a genitive [ending]. (Pāṇini 5.3.54) Here, that which ends in the genitive case and serves as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is subordinate (*apradhāna*) because it exists for the sake of another;
the other, however, being assisted by that very [qualifier], is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and is primary (*pradhāna*). And with the primary...
Since the understanding of the object of the action (*kāryasaṃpratyaya*) occurs when a suffix is prescribed after a word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*),
the suffix is understood to apply to the primary correlate (*pradhāna*) which ends in the sixth case, and not to the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*); likewise,
the mention of "having previously existed" (*bhūtapūrva*) is understood to refer to that [correlate] alone, and not [to the base].
Having considered the phrase "of the meaning of the base" (*prakṛtyarthasya*), he says: "from that which ends in the genitive," and so forth.
However, the meaning of the suffix should be understood as that which is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of the word ending in the genitive.

55. *atiśāyane tamabiṣṭhanau* (Pāṇini 5.3.55). Regarding the word *atiśāyanam*: it is derived from the root *śī* with the suffix *lyuṭ*. Although the root *śī* by itself denotes "sleeping," here, due to its association with the prefix *ati*, it functions in the sense of "excellence" (*prakarpa*). Therefore, he says: "excellence. Now, [an objection:]...
Should it not rather be *atiśayanam*? To this he says: "The lengthening occurs by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*).

But how is the word *atiśāyana* understood as correct through such an irregular derivation? It is for the purpose of making its grammatical correctness known. And this [term] is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*), in order to preclude the suspicion that it might be a suffix (*pratyaya*).

He refutes [this]: it need not be stated that for secondary suffixes (*svārthika*) the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) serves as the indicator (*dyotya*); for that [meaning] is already expressed by the base itself. For example:
*paṭiṣṭhaḥ*, *laghiṣṭhaḥ*. Here, the elision of the *ṭi* portion occurs by the rule *turiṣṭhemeyassu* (Pāṇini 6.4.154).

In the word *gariṣṭhaḥ*, the substitution of *gara-* for the word *guru-* occurs by the rule *priyasthirasphirorubahulaguru-*(Pāṇini 6.4.157). There should not be another suffix following a suffix that already expresses excellence (*prakarṣa*); [excellence] is expressed by one [suffix] alone.
To the one who thinks that "the suffix of comparison (*pratyaya*) has already been indicated," he says: "And when...

Where the suffix expressing excellence (*ātiśāyanika*) is prescribed for the first degree of excellence, let there not be a second suffix of excellence, since it has already been indicated by that very [first] one. This is the case when there is another degree of excellence.

The meaning is that it is only logical for a word ending in a superlative suffix to be followed by another superlative suffix, because [the quality] has already been expressed by the former. When *iṣṭhan* follows, "praśasyasya śraḥ" (Pāṇini 5.3.60) applies, and with the preceding [suffix], "ād guṇaḥ" (6.1.87) applies. [This occurs] after a word ending in the suffix *iṣṭhan*.

This is the suffix *tamap* expressing excellence (*prakarpa*). Here, the excellence that is relative to a counterpart (*pratiyogin*)—an excellence greater than a previous excellence—is indicated by the suffix *iṣṭhan*. Now, one might object:
there is no specific rule (*vākya*) for prescribing this superlative suffix (*atiśāyika*), by which it would be enjoined when that [excellence] is present.
If another suffix of excellence (*ātiśāyanika*) were prescribed after that [suffix], this would indeed be a single sentence;

for in that case, while the suffix of excellence is being prescribed by this very rule, a base ending in that [suffix] is impossible, so how could there be the occurrence of a further suffix of excellence after a suffix of excellence? This is incorrect.

This is not a fault; for here, due to the difference in the suffixes being prescribed, there are two distinct sentences: by one, the suffix *iṣṭhan* is prescribed, and by the other, the suffix *tamap* is prescribed after that [which ends in *iṣṭhan*].

56. *tiṅśca* (Pāṇini 5.3.56). [The suffix *tamap* is added after] a *tiṅ*-ending [word]. For example: *pacatitamām*. Here, the suffix *ām* is applied by the rule *kimetiṅvyayaghādāmvadravyaprakarṣe* (5.4.11).

Regarding the passage beginning with "ṭhguṇavacane" and so forth: the reason why the suffix *iṣṭhan* is not cited as an example is that there is a restrictive rule stating "aj-ādi [suffixes] are applied only after words denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*)" (Pāṇini 5.3.58); therefore, it must necessarily occur only from such words. Furthermore, a word ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) is not a *guṇavacana*; hence, it is not cited as an example.
57. *dvivacanavibhajyopapade tarabīyasunau* (Pāṇini 5.3.57). [The commentary states:

"The expression 'dvivacanam' means 'the speaking of two things'. By this, he shows that the term *dvivacana* is taken in its etymological sense (*anvartha*), and not in its technical (*pāribhāṣika*) sense; for if it were the technical sense...

If the term "dual" were taken [in its technical sense], then in the sentence "Between my Devadatta and Devadatta's [son], Devadatta's is more handsome," the suffix would not occur; for there is no occurrence of the technical dual there. However, when it is taken in its etymological sense (*anvartha*), the status of the subordinate term (*upapada*) as having a dual meaning is established. Likewise...

For by the word *asmākam* ("of us"), one meaning is expressed, since the plural number is prescribed for the pronoun *asmad* when it refers to a single entity according to the rule *asmado dvayośca* (Pāṇini 1.2.59). And by the word *devadattasya* ("of Devadatta"), a second meaning is expressed; thus, that secondary term (*upapada*) is indeed appropriately termed "dual" in accordance with its meaning.

Thus, since the term is understood according to its etymological meaning (*anvartha*), it is established in all cases; therefore, he considers this application [of the rule] to be appropriate. "To be distinguished" (*vibhaktavya*) means "to be made separate. Furthermore, that which is being surpassed (*atiśayyamāna*) functions as the subordinate element (*upapada*), not the agent of surpassing (*atiśayitṛ*); hence...

Because of the specific prescription [of the suffix]. But surely, when the suffix *ṇyat* is applied by the rule "ṛ-halor ṇyat" (Pāṇini 3.1.124), the form should be *vibhājya*; how then is the citation *vibhajya* justified? To this he says: "It occurs by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Here there are two subordinate words (*upapada*), and likewise two verbal roots (*prakṛti*).

Since there are only two conditions as well, someone might have the misconception that they must correspond [to the two causes] respectively; therefore, in order to dispel that, he says: "respectively" (*yathāsaṃkhyam*), because of the indicator of the sequence. For that...
By demonstrating independence from other defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), he indicates that even the characteristic of "respective order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*) need not be relied upon here.
Regarding the term *paṭīyān*: as before, there is the elision of the *ṭi* suffix; furthermore, by the rule *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.14), [the lengthening of the vowel occurs].
Thus, [the vowel] is long, and there is the elision of the *hal* and *ṅī* suffixes as well as the final consonant of the *saṃyoga*.

In the expression "The people of Mathurā are more wealthy than the people of Pāṭaliputra," the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used according to the rule *pañcamī vibhakte* (Pāṇini 2.3.42). In this instance, "from the people of Pāṭaliputra" (*pāṭaliputrakebhyaḥ*) is the *upapada* [governing the ablative].

For the people of Pāṭaliputra are distinguished—that is, made separate—from those of Mathurā. But is this not already established by the rule "when a word in the dual number is the upapada"? Indeed, there is a dual word as the upapada here; for instance, there is one heap of the Mathuran people, and another...

[Objection: Since the two [the father and the son] are expressed by a dual ending for the inhabitants of Pāṭaliputra, is the inclusion of the term "separately" (vibhajya) therefore useless? [Response: This is not so; for although there is a duality here in relation to the group (rāśi), nevertheless that [duality] is not conveyed by the word itself. What then?

This is a distinction of parts; for this very reason, there is the plural form in "the people of Mathurā [are more delicate] than the people of Pāṭaliputra. Here, even with respect to a collection (*rāśi*), there is no twofold referent—as in the case of "the people of Mathurā are more delicate than both the people of Sāṅkāśya and the people of Pāṭaliputra."
Therefore, even the mention [of the word] by way of analysis must be performed.

58. [The suffixes] *aj* and so forth [denote the agent] only after words expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*). (Pāṇini 5.3.58) For example, in "pācakataraḥ" (a better cooker), this word "pācaka" denotes a substance (*dravyavacana*), because it expresses a substance that possesses the capacity of an agent (*kartṛśaktimat*).

Now, for what purpose is the particle *eva* used, since a rule being commenced when [the desired result] is already established becomes restrictive even without it? To this he says: "The particle *eva*," and so forth. For if the particle *eva* were absent, a contrary restriction would be understood—namely, that [the suffix] occurs only after words denoting qualities that begin with vowels (*ajādī*)—and consequently...

Since the restrictive particle *eva* occurs [after the base], the restriction would apply to something other than that; thus, by the natural rule, because the word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*) is restricted to those beginning with *ajādi*, the suffixes *tarap* and so forth would not follow from it. However, when the particle *eva* is uttered immediately after the base, this becomes a restriction on the meaning of the suffix.

The rule *prakṛtiniyamaḥ* (restriction to the base form) implies that the forms *paṭutaraḥ* and *paṭutamaḥ* are established. To establish these two as well, the sūtra *guṇavacanādibhyaḥ iṣṭhanīyasunau* was not composed. Since those two [suffixes] would then serve as original injunctions (*vidhi*), they would act as exceptions (*apavāda*) to the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap*, thereby precluding them; thus, in the absence of those [suffixes], [the desired forms are obtained].
Otherwise, forms such as *paṭuataraḥ* and *paṭuatamaḥ* would not be established.

59. *tuccchandasi* (Pāṇini 5.3.59). Regarding the example *kartṛṣṭhaḥ*: from the word *kartṛ*, which ends in the suffix *tṛn*, the suffix *iṣṭhan* is added; by the rule *turiṣṭhemeyassu* (6.4.154), the syllable *tṛ* is elided. Regarding the example *dohīyasī*.

From the word *dogdhrī*, which ends in the suffix *tṛn*, the suffix *īyasun* is added; when the syllable *tṛ* is elided, the substitution of *gh* and other such changes cease because their cause no longer exists, and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ugitaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.6).

60. *praśasyasya śraḥ* (5.3.60). Now, since *ajādī* is in the nominative case, how can it be understood that the substitute occurs when followed by words beginning with *aja*? To this he says: "in *ajādī* [which is] *itac*"; [and] "having that as its scope. That word *praśasya*...

That which has such an object is "tadviṣayaḥ" (having that as its scope). By this, he shows that the restriction established by the rule "ṭhajādī guṇavacanādeva" (5.3.58)—which stipulates that suffixes beginning with ṭha or ja must follow only words expressing a quality—does not apply in that specific scope.
This applies "likewise to the subsequent rules," namely to those beginning with "vṛddhasya ca" (5.3.62) and so forth. This [is the case] for these two.
In the case of the suffix *īyasun* with the word *dvivacana* as its *upapada*, [the form is] "this one is better than these two";
whereas when the word *vibhajya* is the *upapada*, [the form is] "this one is better than this. In the former case, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used according to Pāṇini 2.3.41;
in the latter, the ablative (*pañcamī*) is used according to 2.3.42.

61. *jya ca* | (Pāṇini 5.3.61) This separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the purpose of avoiding a correspondence between the elements in order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*), and for the sake of what follows. In the subsequent rules, it is intended that only the substitute *jya* should apply to the word *vṛddha*, and not the substitute *śra*.

62. *vṛddhasya ca* (Pāṇini 5.3.62). The phrase "of the word *vṛddha*" means "of this word *vṛddha*. By this, he shows that there is a reference to the actual form (*svarūpagrahaṇa*) of the word *vṛddhasya*. Now, one might object: but the word *vṛddha* is a technical term (*saṃjñā*).
[Objection: Has [the term] "vṛddha" been formed by the rule *vṛddhir yasyācām ādis tad vṛddham* (Pāṇini 1.1.73)?

Therefore, only that which is designated by that [term] should be understood as the named object (*saṃjñin*), and not its own form (*svarūpa*), because of the statement *svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasyāśabdasaṃjñā* (Pāṇini 1.1.68). [Reply: This is not a fault, because of the [rule] *praśasyasya...* [etc.].

This [term] recurs here; by it, the word *vṛddha* is qualified—namely, "of that which is excellent (*praśasya*) and old (*vṛddha*). If there were a literal apprehension of the form, excellence would be appropriate for a word-meaning denoting advanced age, but not for a technical (*pāribhāṣika*) apprehension. Alternatively, by the rule of "the most similar in place" (*sthāne 'ntaratama-paribhāṣā*, 1.1.50).

Regarding the word *jya*, that which is its most similar (*antaratama*) is understood to be its [substitute] base; and for this [word *jya*], the word *vṛddha* alone is the most similar. Therefore, it is proper to take that [word *vṛddha*] alone. As for the phrase "and of those two," etc., it is just as in the rule "for *praśasya*, [the substitute] *śra*" (Pāṇini 5.3.60), where, due to the absence of a restrictive rule, [the substitutes apply] to the suffixes beginning with vowels (*ajādī*).

The existence [of the rule] has been made known; likewise here too it is made known. However, the absence of restriction regarding the substitution of *aja* and so forth after [the suffix] *para* is to be understood precisely from the fact that the substitutes are prescribed as before.
63. *antikabāḍhayornedasādhau* (5.3.63).

Regarding the phrase *ṭhnimittayoḥ* and so forth: these are two suffixes (*pratyaya*) that serve as causes; for it is after them that the substitutions are prescribed. Why, then, is [the substitution] not desired [in other cases]? Because [the original form] has fewer syllables (*alpāctara*).

Because of the suffix -āt. For that [suffix] expresses independence from any other defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Therefore, even the rule of "correspondence according to order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*) is not required here. If this is so, would it not follow that correspondence according to order would also not apply between the substituend (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*)? Let there be no correspondence according to order; rather, the determination shall be based on "proximity" (*āntaratamya*).

It will be so. But surely, if no other defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇāntara*) is required to establish the rule, then the maxim *sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.50) would not apply either? This is not the case; for it is precisely this that is meant: there is no fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) established by the author of the instruction (*nirdeśakṛtā*) regarding a different mode of application (*nirveśānyathātva*).

It brings about an understanding [of the meaning], yet it does not subvert the established order based on purpose. Furthermore, for the sake of correctly comprehending the instruction, this paribhāṣā—"ṣaṣṭhī sthāne yogā" (P.
1.1.49)—must necessarily be relied upon; and "sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ" (P. 1.1.50) is a supplement to that.
How could it be possible not to take the conventional designation into account?

64. *yuvālpayoḥ kananyatarasyām* | (5.3.64) Here too, the correspondence according to order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) between the two causes [of the suffix] is not intended; for otherwise, by the rule *ajādyadantam* (2.2.33), the word *alpa* would have been placed first [in the compound].
Because of the suffix being applied in its secondary sense (*paranipāta*) and independently of the primary definition, the term *cihnin* is understood;

thus, "yuvan" is intended as a designation for one's own form (*svarūpa*), not as a quality of the lineage. Why? Because here too, the rule "praśasyasya" (Pāṇini 5.3.60) continues to apply, and by that, the word *yuvan*—

It must be qualified as "of a praiseworthy youth. For praise is applicable when the word's meaning is understood according to its own nature (*svarūpa*)—that is, in connection with the age known as youth, which is esteemed by all the world—but not when it is understood according to a technical (*pāribhāṣika*) definition. Alternatively, [this is explained] by the rule *sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.50).

It is understood that among the substitutes for *kan*, only that which is the most similar (*antaratama*) takes its place, and the word *yuva* alone is the most similar. Therefore, it is proper to take the actual form itself [of *yuva*]. Here, the inclusion of the term "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) serves only to apply to the word *alpa*, and not to the word *yuva*, since even without that [term], [the substitution of *yuva*] occurs.

The alternative is indeed established by the rule: "In place of *sthūla*, *udara*, *yuvan*, *hrasva*, *kṣipra*, and *kṣudra*, when followed by a semi-vowel (*yaṇ*) and so forth, there is the substitution of the *guṇa* vowel for the preceding portion" (Pāṇini 6.4.156). For if the substitution were permanent, it would be impossible for the following semi-vowel and so forth to be elided, nor could the preceding portion be the locus of the *guṇa* substitution.
In the words *sthaviṣṭhaḥ* and *yavīyān*, by the rule *sthūladūrādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.156), the portion beginning with the *yaṇ* [the semi-vowel] is elided,
and the *guṇa* substitution occurs for the preceding vowel.
65. *vin-matoluk* (5.3.65).

Due to its association (*sāhacarya*) with *matup*, only the suffix *vin* used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) is understood here—namely, *vin* in the rule *tapaḥ-sahasrābhyāṃ vinīnī* (5.2.102) and *asmāyā-medhā-srajo viniḥ* (5.2.121).

Thus; by these two examples, this very statement regarding the elision (*luk*) makes known that [the suffix] *vin* occurs after roots beginning with vowels other than *a*. For instance: "sragviṇau" (two wearing garlands), where *vin* is applied by the rule *asmāyāmedhāsrajo viniḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.121). And "srajiṣṭhaḥ" (most garlanded), where there is no elision of the *i* due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) according to the rule *prakṛtyaikāc* (Pāṇini 6.4.163).

66. *rūpap* is used in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*). Regarding the statement "and those which have their own meaning as their object" (*svārthikāś ca*), etc.: praise and so forth are qualifiers of the meaning of the base word (*prakṛtyartha*); the suffixes that indicate these are *svārthika* (those whose meaning is inherent in themselves), but they are not denoters of a different meaning.

If the suffix -rūpa- is prescribed when [the base word] is used in the sense of praise, it would not apply when it is used in the sense of censure—as in "this man has the form of a vṛṣala" (vṛṣalarūpo 'yam) or "this man has the form of a thief" (caurarūpo 'yam). For words such as *vṛṣala* always express censure; they never occur in the sense of praise, just as...
Why are words such as *kāka* (crow) [used in this way]? To this he says: "Of the meaning of the base," and so forth.

The "qualification" (*vaiśiṣṭya*) of the meaning of the base is its completeness (*paripūrṇatva*); when that exists, praise occurs. And thus, when even for words such as *vṛṣala* (outcaste), there is completeness of the referent (*padārtha*), then those [words]—

Since they occur in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*), the suffix also occurs after them. When the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is fulfilled by the eating of onions and the drinking of liquor, then they occur in the sense of praise;
therefore, the suffix also occurs after them. [Regarding] the eating of onions...

And by the mention of drinking liquor (*surāpāṇa*), he demonstrates the fulfillment of the essential meaning [of the term]. For the word *vṛṣala* has "Śūdra" as its denotation; when he consumes even such things as onions—which are censured by virtuous people—then his Śūdra-ness reaches full completion.
"A Śūdra is one who eats everything and sells everything. Furthermore, the meaning of the word *caura* (thief) is fully realized through the stealing of well-guarded objects.
Now, it may be argued that "secondary suffixes (*svārthika*) follow the gender and number of their base form" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 74).

The meaning is that whatever gender and number belong to the meaning of the base (prakṛti) also belong to that which ends in a svārthika suffix. Consequently, one might ask: "In cases such as *pacatorūpam* and *pacantirūpam*, should there not be dual and plural endings? To this he says: "the action is primary" (*kriyāpradhānam*).

And so forth. Although both the action (*kriyā*) and the means (*sādhana*) are denoted by a verb (*ākhyāta*), nevertheless, the action alone is its primary meaning (*pradhānārtha*). And since gender and number ought to follow the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) which is primary, it is proper that they should conform to the [action] through the addition of suffixes expressing their own meanings (*svārthika*). Furthermore, the action is singular and primary.
[This is] an action (*kriyā*). Therefore, the dual and plural endings do not occur after a verbal noun ending in the suffix *rūp*.
[Objection: In that case, would it not also lack neuter gender, since an action is devoid of gender? To this he says: "But [it has] the neuter gender," and so forth. In that very same [work]:

He states the reason: "Because the indicator (liṅga) has recourse to the world. If, then, the action is indeed one, how are the dual and plural numbers not established in forms such as *pacataḥ* ("they two cook") and *pacanti* ("they cook")? This is not a fault;
for although the action is one, the means (sādhana) are many, and therefore the dual and plural numbers apply based on those [means].

[The suffixes] will occur [after a word ending in a kṛt affix]. But then, would they not also occur after a word ending in a pratyaya (secondary suffix) such as *rūpa*? They will not occur, because [the meaning] has already been expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*).
However, the singular number will occur, because that is the general rule, according to the statement: "The singular number shall be used as the general rule."

67. The suffixes *kalpa*, *adeśya*, and *adeśīya* are used in the sense of "slightly incomplete" (*īṣadasamāpti*). (Pāṇini 5.3.67) 68. Optionally, the suffix *bahuc* is added after a nominal stem (*sup*), but it is placed before [the word].
(Pāṇini 5.3.68) By the mention of the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) here, it is the suffix *bahuc* that is connected [to this rule], not the phrase "but it is placed before"; therefore—

Since the state of being "preceded by many" (bahucaḥ pūrvatvam) is not subject to optionality, it is always the case; for this very reason, he says: "But that [is] only from what precedes. By means of the word *eva*, he shows that the word *tu* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇārthatā*). If, however, the word *tu* were not used for the sake of restriction, then... [it would not be so].

It is understood: with what is the mention of "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) connected—is it with *bahuc*, or is it this [rule] beginning with "from here onwards" (*purastāt*)? However, by the word *tu* (but), which has the sense of restriction, once it is determined that [the optionality] applies to this rule beginning with "from here onwards," then by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), [it must apply] to the statement of the optional rule.

It is understood that [the suffix] *bahuc* is generally connected [to this rule]. It is said: "The marking with *cit* is for the purpose of making the final syllable udātta. But of what does the final syllable become udātta by virtue of the *cit*-marking? Of the entire complex including its base (*saprakṛti*), according to the Vārttika: "The *cit*-marked [suffix], along with its base, is for the sake of [words ending in] *bahu*, *ac*, and *ka*" (Vārttika on Pāṇini 6.1.163).

Because of the statement [of the rule]. If this is so, when *paṭavaḥ* is produced from the nominal stem (*subanta*) ending in *jas*, would the acute accent not apply to *jas*? This is not a fault; for when the suffix *bahuc* has been produced, once the designation of nominal stem (*prātipadika*) has been applied by the rule "That which is meaningful, not a verbal root, and not a suffix, is a nominal stem" (Pāṇini 1.2.45), then [the rule] "sup... [is applied].
First, the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*) is applied by the rule *dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.71).
Once that has been performed, the subsequent assignment of the acute accent (*udāttatva*) applies to the vowel *u* in the word *paṭu*.
However, as for that [accent] which would apply after the designation of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) has been made and the elision of the case-ending has occurred...

A different accent arises [in the compound], and its being udātta cannot be denied, for it is not a part of the original base (*prakṛti*). But surely, since the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) serves as a restrictive rule for meaningful aggregates, a form preceded by *bahuc* should not receive the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)?

This is not a fault; the restriction applies to those of the same class. And what is "of the same class"? It refers to those whose composition [is of the same type]. Of what kind is their composition? It is that of things possessing distinctness and connection. And distinctness and connection occur only in the case of things that have separate meanings.

And [the substitution] of those [suffixes] that indicate distinct meanings is not possible. Now, why is the elision of the *su*-affix (*subluk*) performed first, followed by the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*), when—given the principle of priority (*paratva*)—it would be more logical for the acute accent on the final syllable to occur first? This is not so.

For elision (*luk*) is indeed permanent, because it applies whether [the condition for it] has been fulfilled or not. For that elision occurs both when the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) has been applied and when it has not; whereas the final acute accent, however, would apply to one thing once the elision of another has occurred, but to a different word when the elision of that other has not yet occurred.
The rule is non-eternal; therefore, the elision (*luk*) is indeed performed first.

[As in the example] "bahuguḍā drākṣā" (grapes with abundant jaggery). But how is there "incompleteness" (*iṣadasamāpti*) here, since the word *guḍa* denotes either the genus (*jāti*) of jaggery or the substance (*dravya*) which is its substratum? In that case—

First, a genus (jāti) is a single entity and, being partless, is fully present in every locus; likewise, whatever substance is connected with it is also fully present because it is entirely pervaded by it.
Therefore, is it not the case that the qualification "partially unmanifested" (īṣadasamāpti) is inappropriate here, due to its impossibility?

Furthermore, [in the case of] *sāmānādhikaraṇya* (grammatical coreferentiality), as in the expression *bahuguḍā drākṣā* ("grapes with much molasses"), it would not be obtained through the word *drākṣā*, because its meaning is different [from that of the compound]. Also, the feminine gender would not be justified by the rule "derivative suffixes (*svārthika*) follow the gender and number of the base" (*Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā* 74)? This is not so.

This is a fault: here, from a word that is uttered, two things are perceived—the word and the meaning, as well as the genus and the substance; furthermore, qualities, though not themselves the meaning of the word, are understood through their connection with the denotable object.
Where both of these [the word and the meaning] are present, there is completion; however, where either one is absent, in that case here—

The word *guḍa* (molasses) applies to a substance that is deficient in the genus *guḍa* or deficient in qualities such as sweetness; thus, a slight incompleteness [of meaning] is established, and grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is indeed possible. How so?
First, when [the word *guḍa*] refers to something like grapes (*drākṣā*) by virtue of some common property (*sādharmya*), even though that thing lacks the genus [of molasses].

When the word *guḍa* functions by producing a derivative suffix (*pratyaya*), it then stands in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *drākṣā*, because both function with respect to the same object. But when it refers to something devoid of that quality, namely to one who is merely like molasses (*guḍajātīya*), even then there is grammatical coordination, as in the case of "the Vāhīka is an ox" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*).

Thus, just as it is so, it will be the same even for the word "guḍa" (molasses) when it is devoid of its [usual] qualities. Since "guḍa" is expressed by the term "bahuguḍa" (abundant molasses), and since the grape is similar to that, it too shall be denoted by the term "bahuguḍa. Furthermore, the feminine gender is also appropriate for it.

Because [the suffix] depends upon the world [for its usage]. Furthermore, the rule "secondary suffixes (*svārthika*) follow the gender and number of the base" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 74) is merely a general tendency;
therefore, they sometimes even deviate from it, as in the cases of *kuṭīraḥ* and *śamīraḥ*.
The suffix *ra* is also [taught] by the rule "ṭhkuṭīśamīśuṇḍābhyo raḥ" (Pāṇini 5.3.88) as a suffix expressing the same meaning (*svārthika*).
By the statement beginning with "vibhāṣāvacanāt," he explains the purpose of including the term *vibhāṣā*.
For if the term *vibhāṣā* were not included, the suffixes such as *kalpa* and others, which have already found their scope of application among *tiṅ*-endings, [would otherwise be restricted].

Otherwise, they would be superseded by the suffix *bahuc*, which is prescribed specifically for that [word ending in a case-suffix]. However, since that [suffix *bahuc*] exists, those [other suffixes] also occur in that alternative view. Now, one might object: "Since *bahuc* occupies a different position [in the word-formation process], there is no conflict with them;
so how could there be any supersession? Even if such supersession did not exist, [the other suffixes would still apply] even after *bahuc* has been applied.
"Must they necessarily [be the Bahvṛcas], because the other state (the state of being Taittirīyas) is not occupied? This is not so;
for the contradiction between the general and the particular is not necessarily caused by location alone. What then?
It is also caused by the subject matter (*artha*). And since the subject matter is the same for the Bahvṛcas and those beginning with the Kalpas, they are "Bahvṛcas."

Since that meaning has already been expressed, the suffixes *kalpa* and so forth will not occur; for there is no further expression of what has already been expressed, just as there is no further denotation of what has already been denoted.
Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *sub* (case-endings), since the mention of *prātipadika* (nominal stem) continues to apply? It is not [the case that it is unnecessary].

Is there any distinction when *bahu-c* is produced from either a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) or a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*)? To this he says: "The mention of *sub*," and so forth. For if the mention of *sub* were not present, the suffix would arise from that [verbal root] because of the topicality of the rule "and after a verbal root" (*tiṅ-ś-ca*, 5.3.56). Therefore, for the purpose of excluding that, [the mention of *sub* is made].
The inclusion of the word "sub" [is for the purpose of] restriction.

69. *jātīyar* [is used] in the sense of expressing a manner (*prakāra*). [The phrase] "in the expression of that" (*tasya vacane*) means in the statement or the indication [of it]. By the words "and this [suffix] is also [used] in that which possesses the manner" (*prakāravati ca*), [the author] shows the difference in scope between *thāl* and *jātīyar*. Since there is a difference in scope...
Even by that which is specifically prescribed, the suffix *tātil* does not exclude the suffix *jātīyar*;
for *jātīyar* is established after bases ending in the suffix *thāl*, as in the example *kathaṃjātīyaḥ*.

70. *prāgivāt kaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.70). This suffix is not desired after a word ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). [Rather,] *ṭhak* and *kañ* are desired. But how are the presence and absence of these two obtained? To this he says: "The phrase *tiṅśca* is understood [from the previous rule]."
"Thus, etc. By the restrictive particle *eva* in the subsequent [sūtra], he shows that although [the word] is carried over here, it must be connected with the suffix *kap*.
And that [suffix], even though the term *vacana* is being carried over from the preceding sūtra, [is applied] by that [word] from which [the suffix] is produced...
The suffix *ka* is introduced to express a meaning such as "unknown" (*ajñāta*) and the like; therefore, it must occur in that very context.

Furthermore, even though the suffix *ka* is produced after a verbal form ending in *tiṅ*, that meaning cannot be indicated by it, whereas it can be indicated by *akac*. Therefore, [the rule] "after a *tiṅ*-ending [as well]" (Pāṇini 5.3.56).
This [rule] is carried over and should be connected with the subsequent sūtra by means of the suffix *akac*, not here with the suffix *kap*.
The mention of "prāk" (before) is for the sake of indication, while the mention of "iva" is for the sake of defining the limit;
otherwise, the extent of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) would not be known.

71. *avyaya-sarvanāmna-akac-prāk ṭeḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.71). [The commentary states: "This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ka*. Now, one might object: since they apply in different locations, there is no conflict (*virodha*) between *ka* and *akac*; and in the absence of conflict, there can be no relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*). Therefore, how [can this rule be an exception]?

To whom is this an objection? This is not a fault; for it has been stated that contradiction does not necessarily arise only from location, but also from meaning—as in the rule "the same meaning [is expressed] by the suffix *thak* and the suffix *ac*.
Since that meaning has already been indicated by *akac*, the suffix *kap* will not apply to it.

If, because of the recurrence of the word *prātipadikāt* (from the nominal stem), the suffix *akac* were prescribed before the final vowel (*ṭi*) of the nominal stem, forms such as *tvayakā* and *mayakā* would not be established. Alternatively, if [the suffix] were prescribed before the final vowel of the case-ending (*sup*), even so, the form *yuṣmakābhiḥ* would not be established. Therefore—

He says: "From the nominal stem (prātipadika), the case endings (sup) [are applied]," and "both" and so forth. Now, even though both are carried over [into subsequent rules], why is this restriction not obtained—that in some cases the suffixation occurs before the *tiṅ* endings only for that which has a case ending (*subanta*), while in other cases it occurs for the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)? To this he says: "In that regard," and so forth.

The mention of "vacana" (number) is carried over here for the purpose of restriction. Therefore, wherever the expression of meaning can be accomplished by an affix produced before the case-ending (*sup*) of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there it occurs before the case-ending of the nominal stem; wherever the expression of meaning can be accomplished by an affix produced after a word ending in a case-ending (*subanta*).

In order to achieve this, the suffix *su* alone [is affected]. The addition of the marker *c* to *akac* is for the purpose of making it *udātta* at the end; for that [accentuation] applies to the entire complex including its base (*saprakṛti*).
And thus he will state: "The *cita* accent applies to the whole complex including its base, for the sake of *bahu-akac*" (Vārttika on Pāṇini 6.1.163).

"The suffix *kā* should be stated after the root *tūṣṇīm*, in the sense of censure and so forth, as far as possible. The particle *ca* (and) is for the purpose of including other rules. Regarding the rule "the suffix *ka* [is added] after a word denoting habit (*śīla*), with the elision of the final *m*," by "habit" (*śīla*) it is not only natural disposition (*svabhāva*) that is meant; what then?

Restraint is also [a factor]. For instance, one who maintains perfect restraint is called a "virtuous monk" (*śīlavān bhikṣuḥ*). Therefore, even one who restrains speech through devotion to restraint is also said to be "silent."

72. *kasya ca daḥ* (5.3.72). Regarding the phrase "by way of the simultaneous application (*sanniyoga*) with *ṭhak* and *ac*," etc.: how is this specific distinction—that it is by way of the simultaneous application with *ac*—obtained, given that it is not stated in the sūtra? To this he says: "The letter *c*," etc.
The purpose of this very *cakāra* (the letter 'ca') is as follows: the intention is that, by virtue of its association with *akac*, the letter 'ka' should be replaced by the letter 'da'.

73. *ajñāte* (5.3.73). [The word] *ajñāta* means "that whose specific nature is unknown. If that which is entirely unknown were to be called *ajñāta*, then in the case of a total absence of cognition regarding an object, the base (*prakṛti*) itself would not even exist.

For an object that is entirely unknown does not deserve to be the subject of a formal application (prayoga); therefore, it is understood that what is intended here by "unknown" is that which, though known in its own form, has its specific attributes (dharmāntara) unknown—namely, "unknown" means having its particularities unperceived. This is the meaning of this very [statement].

To make this clear, he says "by its own" and so forth. Its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is [the universal] such as "horseness" (*aśvatva*), while its specific form (*viśeṣarūpa*) is [the particular] such as the relationship between owner and owned.

74. [The suffix *kan* is added after a word] denoting something contemptible. (5.3.74) 75. [The suffix *kan* is added] when it forms a name (*saṃjñā*). (5.3.75) 76. [The suffix *kan* is added] when expressing compassion (*anukampā*). (5.3.76)

"By compassion," and so forth. *Abhyupapatti* means simply favor or assistance. Regarding the forms *svapitaki* and *śvasitaki*: the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule "after roots beginning with *rud*, before an *sārvadhātuka* suffix" (Pāṇini 7.2.76), and the elision of the *śap* suffix occurs because the root belongs to the *adādi* class.

77. And [the suffix *cha*] occurs after the word *nīti* when joined with that [suffix]. (Pāṇini 5.3.77). "Policy (*nīti*) consists of means such as conciliation (*sāma*), bribery (*dāna*), and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), dissension (*bheda*) and force (*daṇḍa*) are included; however, these two are not possible in the sense of compassion (*anukampā*).
The policy beginning with conciliation and bribery is understood as being one and the same; [this is expressed by] the form *ṭhehaki*.

From the root *iṇ* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, in the second person singular imperative (*loṇmadhyamapuruṣaikavacana*), there is the substitution of *hi* according to *ṭhserhyapicca* (Pāṇini 3.4.87). Now, one might object: "Is not the suffix already established here by the preceding rule? To this we reply: "In this case, there is compassion."
It is indeed understood; therefore, he asks "for what purpose? and says "by the former alone," and so forth.
That [person] for whom there is a proximate relationship of compassion toward the one being compassionate is described as such.
This proximity, however, refers to the relationship with all those who are objects of compassion.

Since compassion has that [the preceding word] as its basis, when it is prescribed, it is logical to prescribe it from that very [word] with which there is a proximate connection through compassion; therefore,
the suffix is prescribed after the immediately preceding word that is the object of compassion, and not after one that is separated by an interval.
[The rule applies] again to *dhānā* and so forth. Therefore, this [sūtra] is for the purpose that it may also apply from that [preceding rule] at present.

"From a separated [word]" (*vyavahitāt*) means "from a remote [word]" (*viprakṛṣṭāt*). Remoteness is due to compassion not having that as its basis; for in that [compassion], *dhānā* and so forth are not the basis.
What then? Devadatta and others are being shown compassion.

78. *Bahvaco manuṣyanāmnaṣṭhajvā* (Pāṇini 5.3.78). [Examples: *ṭhdevikaḥ* ("belonging to Devadatta"), *ṭhyajñikaḥ* ("belonging to Yajñadatta"). When the word *datta* is elided by the rule *ṭhājāvūrdhvaṃ dvitīyādacaḥ* (5.3.83), the vowel *a* is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca* (6.4.148).

In every counter-example (pratyudāharaṇa), it should be understood that *ka* alone [is applied]. For instance, "madrabāhukaḥ. One whose arms are Madra is *madrabāhuḥ*. This is not a personal name; what then? It is an adjective (*viśeṣaṇa*).

What is the purpose of including the mention of "manuṣya" (human)? So that it does not apply here: *devahastako hastī* ("the elephant Devahastaka"). [The word] *nāma* [indicates that the rule applies to names].
For what purpose is the inclusion [of the word "mṛga"]? So that [the suffix] does not apply in cases such as *mṛgakaḥ* and *matsyakaḥ*.

79. *ghanilacau ca* | (5.3.79) [The suffixes] *ghan* and *ilac* [are also applied]. Regarding "ṭhdeviyaḥ": with *ghan*, there is elision as before. Regarding "ṭhdevilaḥ": with *ilac*. Regarding "ṭhdevikaḥ": with *aṇ*. Regarding "ṭhdevadatakaḥ": with *ka*.

80. *prācām upāder aḍajvucau ca* (Pāṇini 5.3.80). The suffixes *aḍac* and *vuc* are added after words beginning with *upa*, such as in the case of *upendradatta*. Why is the mention of *prāk* (before) not intended to signify optionality (*vikalpa*)? To this he says:
"For [the word] *vā* itself [is understood]" and so forth. Here, the word *vā* (or) is carried over from the previous rule.
Therefore, since conceptual construction has already been accomplished by that very [means], the apprehension of that object is not tenable.

81. *kan* [is the suffix] after a word denoting a genus (*jāti*) or a name (*nāman*). (Pāṇini 5.3.81). Regarding the mention of "name" (*nāmagrahaṇam*): for if the mention of "name" were not there, there would be the grasping of the actual form of the genus itself.
Therefore, the mention of "genus" (*jāti*) is for the purpose that there should not be the grasping of the actual form [of the genus].
82. *ajināntasyottarapadalopaśca* (Pāṇini 5.3.82). [The example is:

"A certain person named Vyāghrājina. [This means: the skin (*ajina*) of a tiger (*vyāghra*), i.e., one whose skin is like the skin of a tiger, is *vyāghrājinaḥ*. [This applies] when the word is preceded by a locative case or a word used in comparison (*upamāna*).

By the rule "bahuvrīhi with elision of the final member" (Vārttika 99), when the elision of the final member (*uttarapada-lopa*) is applied to a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the word *vyāghrājina* is formed. Now, why was it not stated simply as "elision of *ajina*," rather than using the term "elision of the final member"? It cannot be done in that way, because [the forms] *vyāghra* and *mahājina* would [otherwise] result.

There is a certain [objection]: "He has been shown compassion"—in this case, if the elision of the word *ajina* were prescribed [for *māghraka*], there would be no removal of the word *mahat*. However, when the elision of the *uttarapada* (the second member of the compound) is prescribed, it occurs. Therefore, let it remain exactly as in the original formulation: *mahadajinaṃ*.

*Mahājinam*: it is like the great skin (*mahājina*) of a tiger; thus, *mahājina* belongs to him—this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with elision of the final member as previously explained, followed by the suffix *kan*.

83. *ṭhājādāvūrdhvaṃ dvitīyādacaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.83). [The commentary begins with: "In this section," and so forth. By this rule, in this section, those suffixes beginning with *ṭha* or *ā* that are prescribed undergo elision; however, those which are prescribed in other sections do not undergo such elision.
[The author] demonstrates this. And this [fact] is obtained here through the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the two [terms], *oṣṭhya* and *aja*, which are prescribed in this very context.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of "after" (*ūrdhva*)? Since the ablative case in "after the second vowel" (*dvitīyādacaḥ*) is used, therefore, even without the mention of "after," by the rule "from that, the following" (*tasmādityuttarasya*), [the meaning] is understood as "after."

[An objection is raised: "Will there not be elision (*lopa*) of that very form which contains the word *yat*? To this, he says: "The mention of *ūrdhvam*," and so forth. If the mention of *ūrdhvam* were absent, then by the rule "of what follows, beginning with the first letter" (*ādeḥ parasya*, Pāṇini 1.1.54), there would be elision of the initial [letter] of that which follows the second vowel; but when that [mention of *ūrdhvam*] is present, everything [from that point onward] is set aside. Therefore...
The mention of "ūrdhvam" (after) is for the purpose that the elision (*lopa*) of everything [following] may occur.

Now, what is the purpose of mentioning "ṭha"? Since it would be established by the rule "ajādau" (when an *ac* begins) once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) of "ṭha" has been applied? To this he says: "The mention of 'ṭha'," and so forth. This is because, while the *uk* [of *ṭhak*] remains in its second position, it has not yet been...

The mention of *ṭh* [in Pāṇini 7.3.51] is for the purpose that the rule prescribing *ka*—namely, "after [a stem ending in] *ṭh*, *su*, *uk*, or *t*, there is *ka*"—should apply even when the substitution of *iK* has already taken place and the portion following the second vowel has been elided.
In this regard, the following objection might be raised: once the substitution of *iK* has occurred, [the stem] is characterized as beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*).

And [one might ask]: "Since the letter *ṭha* is included by the mention of *ṭha* due to its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* when there is elision of what follows the second [letter], will the substitution of *kā* (i.e., *ka*) take place? To this he says: "For in the case of the definition of [suffixes] beginning with *ṭha*, etc.
Here, in the rule prescribing the substitute, the mention of *ṭha* would refer either to the individual phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*) or to the entire group (*saṅghātagrahaṇa*).
In that case, regarding the mention of the phoneme (*varṇa*), the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* is not possible because it is not a rule concerning an *al* (phoneme).

Even if it were possible regarding the mention of the whole cluster (*saṅghāta*), nevertheless, according to the maxim "a rule characterized by a specific configuration [of elements] is not the cause for the destruction of that very configuration" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 12), [the substitution would be blocked].
Thus, since the *u* [of *uk*] is produced by the conjunction of the status of being preceded by *aja* and so forth (*ajāditva*), and because there is immediate succession with the suffix *ṭha*,

that [suffix] should not cause the destruction of the status of being preceded by *aja*. And therefore, just as in the case of *māthitikaḥ*— meaning "one whose merchandise is churned milk" (*mathitam paṇyam asya*)— where, even though the *ya* has been elided by *yasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), [the status of being preceded by *aja* remains intact] due to the *ta*.

If there were no substitution for the single substitute (ekādeśa) when *ṭha* follows immediately, then forms such as *vāyudataḥ* and *vāyukaḥ* would not be possible. Therefore, the mention of *ṭha* is for the purpose of prescribing the letter *ka* when *u* is the second element.
[The rule] "after a vowel (*uvarṇāt*), *la*" means that its [the *ṭha*'s] elision (*lopa*) occurs; and that [elision] occurs only for the initial [element], not otherwise.

Of the whole; or rather—this *l* is simply a substitute (*ādeśa*), and since it is prescribed for every instance of *l*, and because it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it replaces the whole. Regarding the rule "from the second vowel" (*dvitīyādacaḥ*): when the elision of the second [vowel] is to be performed, the diphthong (*sandhyakṣara*) possesses the status of being the second.
It should be stated that when [the suffix] *bhavati* occurs, there is elision (*lopa*) of the phonetic form beginning with that [suffix].
Although elision of what follows a diphthong (*sandhyakṣara*) would also apply,

there is elision of what follows the second vowel in words such as those where the preceding member consists of a single syllable, according to the rule beginning with *sandhyakṣarasyaikākṣarapūrvapadānām*.
This has been stated as an exception to that [rule].

Regarding the term "ekākṣara": this word *akṣara* also applies to a syllable (*ac*). For those compounds whose prior member consists of a single syllable (*ekākṣara*) or a single vowel (*ekāc*), the elision of the subsequent member (*uttarapadalopa*) must be stated. For example: *vāgāśīḥ*.

Considering that *vāc* is the object of the blessing (*āśis*), a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed despite the lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). Having analyzed the compound as *anukampita-vāg-āśīḥ*, when the suffix *ṭhak* is applied, there would be elision of everything from the second vowel onward.
When that occurs, the form *vāca-aika-* remains; then, once the elision by rule 6.4.148 (*yasyeti ca*) has been applied...

Due to the rule "ṭhacaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau" (Pāṇini 1.1.57), which prescribes the status of being like the original (sthānivadbhāva), the designation *pada* would not apply. Therefore, by relying on the internal case-ending (*vibhakti*), the designation *pada* is established, and by the rule "coḥ kuḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.30), there is the substitution of *k*—thus [the form] would be *vāgika*. This applies to the word *āśīḥ*.

When the elision (*lopa*) has taken place, because that [elided element] is not a substitute for a vowel (*aj-ādeśa*), the status of being "as if occupying the original position" (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply;

thus, the designation *bha* indeed occurs. Consequently, once the designation *pada* is negated by that [designation *bha*], the *kutva* substitution and other such operations dependent upon the *pada* designation do not take effect, and thus the form *vācika* is established.

Regarding the passage beginning with "How so? (katham): if it is stated that there is elision of the second member (*uttarapada*) when the first member (*pūrvapada*) consists of a single syllable, then the form *ṣaḍika* would not be established. For even here, once the elision of the second member has occurred, the designation *bha* has not yet arisen; consequently, the designation *pada* remains in force (having not been superseded), and by the rule "jhalāṃ jaśo 'nte" [Pāṇini 8.2.39], [the final consonant would become a voiced unaspirated stop].
Thus, when the *jaś*-substitution is applied to the *ṣ* of *ṣaṣ*, the form *ṣaḍika* is not established.

84. *Śevala*, *supari*, *viśāla*, *varuṇa*, *aryaman*, and so forth [lose their final vowel] after a third [vowel] (Pāṇini 5.3.84). Regarding the statement "and that [occurs] when no vowel-sandhi has been applied": if the elision occurs precisely when there is no vowel-sandhi, then it is established; otherwise, it is not. Therefore, the elision applies only to *śevala* and the others when no vowel-sandhi has been applied.
It should be stated that "it exists."
[The term] "short" (*hrasva*) is that which has a "long" (*dīrgha*) as its counterpart. Furthermore, that [short vowel] is in relation to which the other becomes long.
It should be understood [as follows]. But is it not the case that when there is a diminution of length, there is shortness;

and since there is smallness wherever there is a diminution of length, is this not already established by the previous rule? It is not so established; for there is no such necessity—that wherever there is a diminution of length, it must necessarily be due to smallness—and likewise...
For— even when there is a decrease— that object which is endowed with the quality of greatness becomes indeed "not great," and not merely "small."
87. *kan* is added after a word expressing a name [of a village].

(5.3.87) 88. *ra* is added after *kuṭī*, *śamī*, and *śuṇḍā*. (5.3.88) [Examples: *kuṭīraḥ*, *śamīraḥ*. These suffixes are applied in the sense of the base itself (*svārthika*), following the gender and number of the original form.

Since gender and number follow the base [word], should there not be the feminine gender belonging to the base itself, rather than the masculine gender? To this he says: "Even though it is svārthika," and so forth.
89. After the word *kuts*, the suffix *ḍupac* [is applied] to form feminine nouns.

(Pāṇini 5.3.89) 90. After the words *kāsū* and *goṇī*, the suffix *ṣṭarac* [is applied]. (Pāṇini 5.3.90) 91. After the words *vatso*, *ukṣan*, *aśva*, and *ṛṣabha*, the suffix *ṣṭarac* is applied when expressing their smallness. (Pāṇini 5.3.91)

If the suffix were prescribed after words such as *vatsa* (calf) and others in the sense of "thinness," then the suffix would undesirably apply without distinction even to those calves and so forth that are thin in body, since no specific qualification has been provided.
Therefore, he says: "of which quality," and so on. A "quality" (*guṇa*) is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), [and] the qualified (*viśeṣya*)...

Substance (*dravya*). The ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of words such as "calf" (*vatsa*) is a particular stage of age (*vayoviśeṣa*) and so forth. When that [ground] exists, words such as "calf" apply—that is, they function—toward the substance as the qualified object (*viśeṣya*).
It is precisely when that ground for the application of the word "calf" and so forth becomes attenuated (*tanutva*) that the suffix occurs, and not otherwise.

[The suffix occurs] merely because of its attenuation; furthermore, that [attenuation] is due to proximity. When a suffix is prescribed after bases such as *vatsa* and others, no other basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is proximate; therefore, it is logical that the suffix should occur precisely because of that [base's] attenuation.

"‘Its attenuation’ means the attainment of the second stage of life. At the time of attaining the third stage of life, there remains only the certain attenuation of the basis for the application of the term ‘bull’ (ukṣan) belonging to the second stage of life. "‘Its attenuation’ means having another father."

The meaning is "born from a donkey as a father. In that case, one born from a donkey and a mare is called an *aśvatara*. Regarding the statement, "Its thinness consists in having little strength for carrying burdens," one who would not be capable of carrying a burden is called an *ṛṣabhatara*. But when his—
When the capacity for bearing the burden becomes weak and diminishes, then there occurs attenuation.

92. *kiṃ-yad-tado nirdhāraṇe dvayor ekasya ḍatarac* (Pāṇini 5.3.92). [The sūtra states: "The suffix is applied to those things being singled out (*nirdhāryamāṇa*). From where is it understood that [the suffix applies] to words denoting "those being singled out"? It is because, once the suffix has been produced from that very [base], the act of singling out (*nirdhāraṇa*) is implied.

Regarding "Mahāvibhāṣā" and so forth: [the rule] "samarthānāṃ prathamāt niṣṭhāntāt" (Pāṇini 4.1.82) applies here. This is so that the suffix may occur when there is such a context. As for the statement "dvayor iti samudāyān nirdhāraṇavibhaktiḥ," this refers to either the genitive or the locative case; furthermore, that [suffix] belongs to it.

And by the rule *ṭhyataśca nirdhāraṇam* (Pāṇini 2.3.41), the mention of "of one" (*ekasya*) is a mention of that which is being singled out; this is so that [the operation] may apply when a single entity is being singled out. Now, one might object: "Is not *nirdhāraṇa* (singling out) the separation of a part from a whole?"
By the word "of two," a collection of parts is indicated from which a single part is to be singled out;
and when a single part is to be singled out, only one such part is possible.
Therefore, even without the explicit mention of the word "one" (*eka*), the singling out will apply to only one.

Is the mention of "one" (eka) purposeless? It is not so; for if that were absent, the genitive case in "dvayoḥ" would be understood as a *karma-ṣaṣṭhī* (genitive of object), meaning "if two are extracted from somewhere," and consequently, the suffix would also apply here: "in which village... [kau].
[Otherwise, one would have to say] "Devadatta-Yajñadatta. Therefore, the mention of the singular must be made.

93. *Vā bahūnāṃ jātiparipraśne ḍatamac* (Pāṇini 5.3.93). [The commentary says: "From those words which have as their object an inquiry regarding a genus (*jāti*). Those for whom an inquiry regarding a genus is possible are described in that way. For example: "Which mat among yours is it? [And: "A lineage (*gotra*) together with its branches (*caraṇa*)" (Mahābhāṣya).

(Thus, according to Bhāṣya 2.225,) its status as a genus (*jāti*) is established. And is that *kaṭha*-genus being inquired about by means of the word "what" (*kiṃ*)? Here, the word "what" has the inquiry regarding a genus as its object, as in: "Let whichever Kaṭha among you is such-and-such come here. In this context, the words "whichever" (*yatas*) and "that" (*tatas*) refer exclusively to the genus, and not [to the individual].
It becomes the object of an inquiry: "Which among you is Kaṭha? Let that one come.

Here, the words *yatas* and *tatas* refer exclusively to the genus (*jāti*), not to the object of an inquiry; for such an inquiry is impossible through them. Why? Because the inquiry is actually made by means of the word *kim*. For this very reason...

He will say: "The mention of *paripraśna* is a qualification of *kim* alone, not of *yad* and *tad*, because [the latter] are impossible [in that context]. And: "The statement 'optionally' (*vā*) is for the sake of *akac*; so that *akac* may also occur in its place. If this were so, the sentence would not be established, for when *ḍatamaj* is not [applied]...
"Is it necessarily the case that [the suffix] must occur? To this he says: "The *Mahāvibhāṣā*, etc. And here, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* follows for the purpose of providing an option regarding the suffix;

when the suffix is optionally applied by means of it, the sentence will also occur as an alternative. Furthermore, "the mention of the genus (*jāti*), however, is connected with all [the preceding rules]."
