The genus (*jāti*) occurs everywhere; in that case, when the word is qualified by the genus and so forth, is its status as the object of inquiry obtained through the very force of the context? This is not so;

for it [the genus] also functions in the sense of censure (*kṣepa*). In that regard, if the term "inquiry" (*paripraśna*) were not mentioned, then whenever the genus functions in the sense of censure—
Then there would be a cognition.

94. *ekacca prācām* (Pāṇini 5.3.94). [The commentary says: "In its own domain" (*svasmin viṣaye*) means in its own sphere. Therein, the domain of the suffix *ḍataraC* is the selection of one out of two; the domain of *ḍatamaC* is the selection of one out of many.

The particle *ca* serves the purpose of attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*). For if it were not present, then by the rule "A rule applies either to what is immediately preceding or to what is excluded" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 19), only the suffix *ḍatamaC* would occur; because [the sūtra] continues with "of two, for the selection of one among two, the suffix *ḍatarac*," whereas for many...

Because the rule "ḍatamac" continues [from the previous sūtra] in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). Why then is the mention of "prāk" (before) not intended for the purpose of option (*vikalpa*)? To this he says: "The option indeed continues. It was stated that there is an option because the word "vā" (or) continues from the immediately preceding sūtra.

By that very [rule], the alternative regarding the condition is established. Therefore, the mention of "prior" (prāk) is solely for the sake of honoring [the preceding rule], not for the sake of providing an option.

95. *kan* [is added] after a word meaning "contempt" (*avakṣepaṇa*). (Pāṇini 5.3.95) Examples include *vyākaraṇakena* ("with contempt for grammar"), and so forth. But how can grammar be an object of contempt, since its study is prescribed by the scriptures because it is an auxiliary of the Vedas (*vedāṅga*)? Nevertheless, in cases where there is a lack of reverence...
He concludes that [the suffix] *kan* expresses disparagement (*avakṣepaṇa*); its status as expressing disparagement toward that [object] is justified because it is the cause of a fault.
This is established by the rule "after [a word denoting] another," etc., which prescribes the suffix *kan* in the sense of disparagement according to Pāṇini 5.3.74.
He shows the division.

96. *iva* [is used] in the sense of a likeness (*pratikṛti*). (Pāṇini 5.3.96) [The commentary states: "The mention of *pratikṛti* is for the purpose of qualifying that [similarity]. This is so that the usage occurs where there is similarity pertaining to a likeness. In the case of *gaur iva gavayaḥ* ("A gavaya is like a cow"), there is similarity; however, [it is not a likeness].
But [the term "pratikṛti"] has as its object a likeness; for a cow is not a likeness of a gavaya. Indeed, that which is a representation made of wood and so forth is called a *pratikṛti*.
97. And in the case of *saṃjñā* [the elision of the suffix occurs]. (5.3.97) 98. There is elision (*lup*) when it does not refer to a human being.
(5.3.98) The word *cañcā* refers to a straw figure of a man. Because of its similarity, a human being is also called *cañcā*. [This applies] when there is *lup* [of the suffix].

By the rule *yuktavad vyaktivacane* (Pāṇini 1.2.51), the gender of the base itself is maintained. Now, one might object: "But does not the status of being treated like the original (*yuktavadbhāva*) fail to apply here because of the statement *manuṣyalūpi pratiṣedhaḥ* (Vārttika 21)? This is not so; that prohibition applies to qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), not to that which ends in a *lup* suffix.
99. [The suffix *cha* is applied] after a word meaning "for the sake of livelihood," provided it is not for sale.

(5.3.99) 100. [The suffix *cha* is applied] also after [words beginning with] *devapatha*. (5.3.100) Regarding the form *devapadya*: it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the path of the gods" (*devānāṃ panthā*). [The suffix *yañ* is applied here] by [Pāṇini 5.4.74]: *ṛk-pū-ra-bdhū-pathām-anaṅ-kaḥ-samāsāntāḥ*. (Note: The text cited as *ṛkpaḥ* is an abbreviation for this rule.)
By [the rule] beginning with *ityādinā*, the suffix *kan* is applied as a compound-final (*samāsānta*) suffix; its [subsequent] case-ending is *sup*.

101. *vaster ḍhañ* (Pāṇini 5.3.101). From this point onward [the rule] "starting from *itaḥ*" and so forth applies. In that regard, since the suffix *kan* would otherwise apply by the rule "*pratikṛtau ḍivaḥ*" (5.3.96) when referring to an image (*pratikṛti*), the suffixes beginning from here are introduced. However, when not referring to an image, and when it is not a conventional name (*saṃjñā*)...

Since it would follow that [the suffix] is expressed by the word itself, [the rule specifies that] for a name, however, when it refers to a replica or something not the original, only the suffix *ḍhañ* is used; thus, *vāstī* means "a modification of a dwelling. In the form *vāsteyī*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15).

102. After *śilā*, [the suffix] *ḍha* [is applied]. (5.3.102) 103. After *śākhā* and the following, [the suffix] *yat* [is applied]. (5.3.103) 104. And *dravya* [is used] in the sense of "suitable for" (*bhavye*). (5.3.104)
105. *kuśāgrāc chaḥ* (5.3.105).
106. *samāsācca tadviṣayāt* (5.3.106). [The commentary explains: "From a compound whose meaning is that of the word *iva*. The meaning of the word *iva* is *ivārtha*, namely, similarity (*sādṛśya*).

That which has such a scope is described as "tathokta" (so-called). If the suffix *śā* were prescribed after a compound whose scope is the sense of "as if" (*iva*), would it not also apply in cases such as *śastrīśyāmā* ("dark like a knife") and *puruṣavyāghra* ("tiger-like man")? This is not a fault, for in these cases the compound does not function in the sense of "as if"; rather, what does? The prior member and the subsequent member [function independently].

Or, as in "The woman is like a knife" (*śastrīva śyāmā*) or "This man is like a tiger" (*puruṣo'yaṃ vyāghra iva*). Even though the compound is said to express the sense of "like" (*iva*) because it functions in the sense of a single part [of that comparison], nevertheless, since the meaning has already been expressed by the compound itself, the suffix will not occur. As for the compound, in what sense does it function as "like"?

This suffix is prescribed where there exists a meaning similar to that of a compound, as in the expression "this is as if in another. This is because of the governing word "as if" (*iva*). "Unexpectedly arrived" means having presented itself without prior intention.
"Citrīkaraṇa" means causing wonder. "How so?"—by what manner does this cause for wonder arise unexpectedly?
He asks about this matter with the words beginning with "How so? (tat katham).

"‘And this is a compound,’ etc.: from the very fact that a suffix is prescribed after a compound whose object is the sense of *iva*, one understands by that very indicator (*jñāpaka*) that a compound occurs. But how is this an indicator? He says: ‘For not of this,’ etc.; [it refers] to that which has the sense of *iva* as its object."

There is no general definition for "compound" (samāsa). Therefore, the very fact that suffixes are prescribed after such [elements] serves as the justification for understanding that they possess the status of that [which they replace]. Alternatively, one might ask: what is the reason that the status of being that [original element] is established by means of an indicator (jñāpaka)? He says: "No..."
Regarding the passage beginning with "hyasya" and so forth: the phrase "and that [cognition] has precisely such an object" means that its object is precisely the sense of the particle *iva*.
107. The suffix *aṇ* is applied after words such as *śarkara* [to denote "made of" or "abounding in"].

(5.3.107) 108. The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after words such as *aṅguli* [to denote "pertaining to" or "belonging to"]. (5.3.108) 109. After the word *ekaśālā*, the suffix *ṭhac* is optionally applied. (5.3.109)

Regarding the phrase "by the mention of *anyatarasyām*" and so forth: since [the suffix] *ṭha* alone is immediately preceding due to being prescribed by the previous rule (5.3.108), the mention of *anyatarasyām* serves the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Therefore, according to the principle "by that [mention], there is either an injunction or a prohibition for what is immediately preceding" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 19), [the suffix *ṭhak* is also included].
That very thing is attained.
110. *Karkalohitādibhyaḥ kāṅ* (Pāṇini 5.3.110). 111. *Pratnapūrvaviśvebhyasthāl chandasi* (Pāṇini 5.3.111).
Regarding the term *timatha*: there exists another base, *ima*, which has the same meaning as *idam*. From that [base], this [suffix is applied].
The destruction of conditions.

112. [The suffix *cha* is applied] after a word denoting a multitude (*pūga*), provided it does not begin with the word *agrāmaṇī*. (Pāṇini 5.3.112) Regarding the term "beginning with" (*pūrvāt*): the word *pūrva* here signifies a constituent part. That which has *agrāmaṇī* as its first part is called *agrāmaṇīpūrva*. And by means of this prohibition, it is understood that the actual form [of the word *agrāmaṇī*] is what is being referred to.

When the word *pūga* is understood in its own form (*svarūpa*), there is no possibility of application [of the suffix] after a word preceded by *grāmaṇī*, because of the prohibition of the rule of "taking what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) for a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that already possesses [the suffix] as its constituent (Pāṇini 4.1.89).
In the example *lohaṣvajāḥ*, the suffix *kan* is applied. Here, the word *devadatta* is not a constituent part of the preceding *grāmaṇī*.
The condition.

113. *vrātacphañor astriyām* | (Pāṇini 5.3.113) [The sūtra states: "from words denoting a *vrāta*. Now, why is there not a reference to the actual form (*svarūpa*) itself? Because of the rule regarding the posterior placement of the suffix *cphañ*, which has fewer vowels; for that [suffix]— [Note: The provided fragment ends mid-sentence. The full sūtra is *vrātacphañor astriyām*, meaning "the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply after a word ending in *vrāta* or a word formed with the suffix *cphañ*."]

He expresses the independence from other defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇāntara*). By this, even the rule "one's own form [is the name] of a word" (Pāṇini 1.1.68) is not required here; thus, there is no mention of "one's own form" (*svarūpagrahaṇa*). [The example is] *kauñjāyānyaḥ*.
From the rule "the suffix *cphañ* is applied after *kuñja* and others in the sense of a lineage" (Pāṇini 4.1.98), [we derive] *kauñjāyanaḥ*.

The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *jāter astrīviṣayāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.63). Its status as a genus (*jāti*) is established by the statement: "A lineage (*gotra*) together with the Vedic schools (*caraṇa*s)" (Mahābhāṣya 2.2.25).

114. *āyudhajīvisaṅghāññyo vāhīkeṣvabrāhmaṇarājanyāt* (5.3.114). Regarding the phrase *vāhīkeṣu*: the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) according to Pāṇini 2.3.41. Thus, it means "among the Vāhīkas, that group which subsists by arms. And selection applies only to members of the same genus.

The guild of weapon-bearers is also understood to be specifically Vāhīka. Alternatively, since the word *vāhīka* denotes a country, this locative case is used in the sense of location itself: the guild of weapon-bearers dwells in a particular region of the Vāhīka country.

"In the case of the word *brāhmaṇa*, there is the apprehension of its specific [meaning]. Now, why does the apprehension of the word's own form (*svarūpa*) not occur? Precisely because of this prohibition. If there were an apprehension of the word's own form, the prohibition of the word *brāhmaṇa* would be purposeless. For a prohibition must be preceded by a prior application [of the rule]. [This concerns] the word *brāhmaṇa*.
Since no community of weapon-bearers exists among the Vāhīkas, what is the purpose of the prohibition against Brāhmaṇas?

However, there are words such as "cowherd" (*gopāla*) and others that denote specific types of Brāhmaṇas, and the communities of weapon-bearers denoted by those terms do exist among the Vāhīkas; therefore, if a prohibition were not made in that regard, then—

It would apply to them as well; therefore, the prohibition regarding the mention of specific [sub-varieties] is purposeful for the sake of excluding that [undesired application]. Consequently—it is said: "In the case of a Brāhmaṇa, there is the mention of his specific [sub-division], but in the case of a Rājanya, there is no mention of his specific form at all. This refers to the community of weapon-bearers denoted by that term among the Vāhīkas.

Because of its existence [as a technical term], and because of the statement: "The own form of a word is not designated as a word" (Pāṇini 1.1.68). Regarding the phrase "by that," etc.: since the letter *ṭ* has been added here for the sake of the suffix *ṅīp*, the term "not in the feminine" (5.3.113) does not follow. If that were to follow, a word ending in the suffix *ñyaṭ* would not exist in the feminine.

The addition of the marker *ṭ* would be purposeless for the sake of forming the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. Therefore, the phrase "not in the feminine" (*astriyām*) is no longer operative; consequently, [the suffix] occurs even in the feminine, as in *kauṇḍībṛsī* and *kṣaudrakī*. In these cases, there is the elision of the letter *y* by the rule *halastaddhitasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.150).

115. *vṛkāṭ-ṭeṇyaṇ* | (5.3.115) If the word *vṛka* denotes a guild of weapon-bearers among the Vāhīkas, then, although *ñyaṭ* would otherwise be expected, this rule prescribes a different suffix (*ṭeṇyaṇ*) for that very same [guild], whether it be obtained or not obtained [elsewhere].
It should be understood as follows: "like two wolves. Here, the word *vṛka* denotes a species.
116. *Dāmanī* etc., with *trigarta* as the sixth, take the suffix *cha*.

(5.3.116) Regarding these, there is this traditional text (*smṛti*): "the *trigarta-ṣaṣṭhāḥ* are remembered"; it is called a *smṛti* because by it they are remembered or known. That [text] is: "They say the *trigarta-ṣaṣṭhāḥ*."

This very verse was composed by a trustworthy authority (*āpta*): among these six Trigarta names, the first and the fifth end in the suffix *aṇ* derived from Śiva (i.e., *śaiva*), while the remaining ones end in the suffix *iñ*. Some read the fifth name as ending in a non-taddhita suffix; for them, the patronymic suffix *cha* is applied directly to the word *brahmagupta* itself.

117. *parśv-ādibhyaḥ aṇ*, *yaudheya-ādibhyaḥ añ*. (5.3.117) For what purpose, however, are the *yaudheya* and others listed here, since they have already been enumerated in the fourth [chapter] for the sake of prohibiting elision (*luk*), and it is those very same ones that are understood here?

This is true; for the work of the authors of the *gaṇas* is indeed diverse, and thus [the word] has been read again. In the *parśvādi* group, the word *satvacch-* is recited; and that should be understood as a derivative formed from the word *satvacch-*, ending in the suffix *matup*.
118. After *abhijit*, *vidabhṛt*, *śālāvat*, *śikhāvat*, *śamīvat*, *ūrṇāvat*, and *śarumat*, the suffix *yañ* is applied [to form patronymics]. (5.3.118) [The example is:
"The descendant (*apatyam*) of *abhijit*"—here the suffix *aṇ* is applied. [This is because] "the suffix *aṇ* is applied before the [section on] *dīvyati*" (4.1.83).
This is the general rule; the same applies elsewhere as well.

It is intended that "the suffix *aṇ* denoting a *gotra* is what is understood. How then does [the term] "of a name for a genus" (*jātināmnaḥ*) continue to apply? By that, only that which is a name for a genus ending in *aṇ* will be taken. And whoever...

A name for a lineage (*gotra*) is applied only to that which ends with it, because of its status as a *jāti* according to the rule: "The *gotra* [is used] together with the *caraṇas*" (Mahābhāṣya 2.225). For example: "the moment of Ābhijit" (*ābhijitaḥ muhūrtaḥ*) and "the *sthālīpāka* offering of Ābhijit" (*ābhijītaḥ sthālīpākaḥ*). In one case, this is by the rule: "Time joined with a lunar mansion" (Pāṇini 4.2.3).
In this case, the suffix *aṇ* [is applied], whereas in the other case, [the rule] "that which has this as its deity" (*sāsya devatā*, Pāṇini 4.2.24) applies.
119. "The suffixes beginning with *ñya* are called *tadrāja*.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the venerable Ācārya Jinendrabuddhi, who was a disciple of the venerable Bodhisattva.
The third quarter.
Now begins the fifth chapter,
the fourth quarter.

1. *pādaśatasya saṃkhyādervīpsāyāṃ vun lopaśca* (Pāṇini 5.4.1). The term "from a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*) is understood [from the previous rule]; the mention of "of *pāda* and *śata*" (*pādaśatasya*) is a qualifier for that.
Since a rule involving a qualifier applies to that which ends with it, he says: "of that which ends in *pāda* or *śata*."

The word "ādi" (and so forth) signifies a constituent part (*avayava*). However, it is not logical for a numeral to be a constituent part of the words "pada" and "śata," because they exist separately and do not constitute a composite whole. Indeed, it is not possible for something that exists separately and does not initiate a new entity to be a constituent part of another word, just as the word "jar" cannot be a constituent part of the word "cloth. This would be the case if the opposite were true.

However, this is appropriate, just as they say that the cause of a cloth— which is of the nature of a composite whole— is its parts, such as the threads, which occupy the same location. Therefore, he says "of number and so forth" (*saṃkhyādeḥ*) etc., to indicate that this [suffix] is understood to apply to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and not to the words *pāda* and *śata*.

And this sixth [rule] has the characteristic of immediate sequence (*ānantarya*), as in the case of *gāpoṣṭakam* (Pāṇini 3.2.8), where the suffix *ṭhak* occurs after the roots *gā* and *pā*; the word "immediately" (*anantaram*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the rule]. And [the phrase] "and by its conjunction" (*tatsanniyogena ca*): because the particle *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*sanniyoga*). [The word] "of that" (*antasya*).

By the paribhāṣā "alo'ntyasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.52). [The word] "punaḥ" and so forth: that which occurs because of a cause is *naimitika*; [the suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied according to the rule for the *adhyātmādi* group (Vārttika 456). That which is not *naimitika* is *anaimitika*. This is for the purpose of ensuring that there would be elision (*lopa*).

The mention of "elision" (*lopa*) once again is for the following reason: even when elision is prescribed along with the suffix *vun*, it does not depend on a subsequent cause and thus becomes non-contingent (*anaimitika*). This refers to the elision [of the final vowel and consonant] by the rule *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148).
As for the statement "it has a subsequent cause," this is because that [elision] is prescribed when a subsequent cause exists, namely a *taddhita* suffix or the phoneme *ī*.

Because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), by virtue of the rule "when a subsequent element [is involved], in a rule concerning what precedes it" (Pāṇini 1.1.57), the form of the word *pāc* is treated as prescribed through the status of the elision (*lopa*) being a substitute. For the word-form *pāc*, which is devoid of vowels (*anacka*), is the original element (*sthānin*) that is introduced; and its vowel-less nature persists when the status of being a substitute applies.

It is elided. The point is that because this [elision] is not occasioned by a specific grammatical cause (*anaimitikatvāt*), it does not undergo the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*); therefore, the substitution of *pad* occurs. Regarding the phrase "two feet each," the reduplication occurs due to the sense of distributive repetition (*pīpsā*).
2. *Daṇḍavyavasargayośca* (Pāṇini 5.4.2). "Restraint is *daṇḍa*. Now, one might object: "Does this word *daṇḍa* not also apply to a staff and so forth?
True; nevertheless, it is appropriate here to take the word as referring to restraint, for it is restraint alone [that is intended].

Because [the meaning] is understood through the addition of a suffix. As it is said: "giving is relinquishment. If this is so, then that which was cited as an example in the preceding rule—namely *dattam* (given)—is only possible if this rule serves to provide an additional prescription and is not an exception (*apavāda*); therefore, this [present] rule is unnecessary.

Regarding the question "by means of yoga?"—it is for this reason that he says: "the sense of repetition" (*avīpsārtha*), and so forth. By that [rule], the suffix *vun* occurs after the mere word "giving" (*dāna*); however, when there is a repetition of giving, it indeed occurs again by the preceding rule.

3. *kan* is added after words such as *sthūla* in the sense of expressing a variety (*prakāra*). [The commentary states: "This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *jātīya*. By this, he shows that just as *jātīya*, which is prescribed in the sense of expressing a variety, applies to that which possesses the variety and not to the variety itself, so too does this suffix (*kan*). Otherwise, [the rule would be redundant].

Indeed, this exception (*apavāda*) based on a difference in scope is not tenable. Now, for what reason is *kan* not prescribed immediately after "ṭhak-prakāravacane jātīyaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.3.69) in the rule "ṭhak-prakāravacane jātīyaḥ" (5.3.69)? What would be achieved by that? [The answer is: the statement that *kan* expresses a kind (*prakāra*) would not need to be stated.

Is this so? It cannot be thus; for when there is a simultaneous desire to express both the suffixes *sthūla* and so forth, as well as *ajñāta* and so forth, since the latter takes precedence, once *kan* has been applied, how could *k* not occur? This is because they are distinct words. Furthermore, even if that were the case, in forms such as *sthūlaka*, the acute accent (*udātta*) would apply to the first syllable; however, here, [the accentuation] of *kan*...
Because of its subsequent position in the rule, after the *kan* suffix has been applied by the rule *kṛti*, the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) is established by the rule *ka*.
[This applies to] "cañcadbṛhataḥ" and so forth. However, that [accentuation] does not apply to words such as *sthālī* and others, because *cañcat* and *bṛhat* are not included among them.

[The desired form] is obtained. Therefore, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*)—that is, a formal justification (*pratipādana*)—must be made. Here is that justification: the particle *ca* ("and") from the preceding sūtra is carried over (*anuvartate*) here;
it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccayārtha*). By means of this, [the suffix] will apply even to *cañcat* and *bṛhat*.

Regarding the rule "ṭh sthālāṇumāṣeṣu": some explain that these four [suffixes] belong to the base [prakṛti], namely: *sthūlakaḥ*, *aṇukaḥ*, *māṣakaḥ*, and *iṣukaḥ*. Others, however, say that the words *sthūla* and *aṇu* are the bases, while the term *māṣeṣu* is an indication of the limit (*tapādhinirdeśa*). Still others [hold a different view].
Because of proximity, they state that the word *aṇu* itself is qualified by the mention of *māṣa*. The first view alone is logical; for instance—*sthūlaka* and so forth are its qualifiers.
"Black sesame seeds" (*kṛṣṇakāstilāḥ*). Regarding "barley among rice-grains" (*yavo vrīhiṣu*): *yava* is the base term, while *vrīhiṣu* [is the qualifier].

That is its qualifier: "barley-rice" (*yavaka-vrīhi*). Regarding the rule *pādyakālavadātāḥ surāyām*, others, however, say that because of immediate proximity, the word *avadāta* qualifies the term *surā*, and does not function as a qualifier for *pādya* and *kāla*. [The rule continues: *gomūtrād ācchādane*.

Regarding the rule "gomūtre ācchādane" (Pāṇini 5.2.97), as stated in the Kāśikā: the word *gomūtra* is the base (*prakṛti*), and *ācchādane* is its qualifier. A covering of the type of cow-urine is called *gomūtraka*. Regarding the rule "surāyā ahau" (Pāṇini 5.2.98), as stated in the Kāśikā: *surā*...
The word *ahi* (snake) is qualified by *prakṛtiḥ*; thus, *surāvarṇo'hiḥ* means "a snake with the color of wine" (*suraka*).
Regarding the phrase *jīrṇaśāliṣu*: the two word-forms *patra* and *mūla*, whether used together or separately, produce a suffix—namely, *patrakam* and *mūlakam*.

4. *Anatyantagatau ktāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.4). [The commentary states: "The connection with the remainder" (*aśeṣasaṃbandhaḥ*). This means that there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the remainder by its own related elements, such as the act of splitting (*bhedana*). [The example is] *bhinnakam*; but not that which is split in its entirety.
Although there is a relation [between the whole and its parts], it is nevertheless said that "one part is different from that" (*tadbhinna*).

In this context, by the term "different" (*bhinnam*), the complete relation [of the action of dividing] is understood. If a jar or similar object is entirely pervaded by the action of dividing, it is designated as "different from that."

5. *na sāmivacane* (Pāṇini 5.4.5). Regarding the term *sāmivacane*: that by which "a portion" (*sāmi*) is expressed is called *sāmivacana*. In the example *sāmikṛtam*, there is either a *bahuvrīhi* compound or a *viśeṣaṇasamāsa* (descriptive compound).

"Because it is already expressed by the base form (*prakṛti*)"—this is the reason for the prohibition being purposeless. The suffix *kan* is prescribed in order to convey the sense of "not reaching the end" (*anatyantagati*). However, since that sense is already conveyed by the word *sāmi* itself, there is no possibility at all for the application of *kan*. Therefore, the prohibition is redundant. [For] *kan* applies merely in its own primary sense (*svārtha*).
Thinking that there exists a rule that prescribes [the suffix], he says, "By what, moreover... and so forth.

This very statement of prohibition makes known that the suffix *kan* occurs in its own sense (*svārthe*); otherwise, the statement of prohibition would be meaningless. [The word] *ardhakṛtam* [is thus explained].
It was made by Nemi.

6. *bṛhatyā ācchādane* (Pāṇini 5.4.6). [The word] *kan* is understood [from the previous rule], because it is marked with the svarita accent. [The phrase] "there is no prohibition" [is understood] because of the reversal [of the context]. [The form] *bṛhatikā* [is derived as follows]: by the rule *ke’ṇaḥ* (7.4.13), there is shortening [of the vowel].

7. *Aṣaḍakṣāśitaṅgvalaṅkarmālampuruṣādhyutarapadāt raḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.7). [The commentary states: "The term *aṣaḍakṣi* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning 'that in which six eyes do not exist'. From that, by [the rule] *bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇoḥ* (5.4.113), the suffix *ṣac* is applied.
The seventh case [locative] follows from the word *rājan*. Having analyzed [the compound] as *rājani arthaḥ*, there is a compound by the rule *saptamī śauṇḍaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.40).
Regarding the phrase "beginning with *tamap*," this refers to the rules such as *atiśāyane tamabiṣṭhanau* (Pāṇini 5.3.55).

"Prior to *kana*" refers to [the rule] "The suffix *kan* may optionally be used for *yuvan* and *alpa*" (Pāṇini 5.3.64). "The suffixes beginning with *ñya*" refers to [the rule] "The suffix *ñya* is added after a group-name (*pūga*) that does not have a leader (*agraṇī*) as its first member" (Pāṇini 5.3.112), and so forth.
"Prior to *vr̥n*" refers to [the suffixes] prescribed by the sūtra beginning with "Of a hundred feet" (Pāṇini 5.4.1).
"Ṭhāmādayaḥ" refers to [the rules] beginning with "kimetiṅvyayaghādām" (Pāṇini 5.4.11). "Prāṅ mayaṭaḥ" means up to the rule "tatprakṛtavacane mayaṭ" (Pāṇini 5.4.21).
"Bṛhatījātyantāḥ" refers to the sūtra "bṛhatyā ācchādane" (Pāṇini 5.4.6).
What does he indicate? He indicates that even by the term *jātyanta* [in Pāṇini 5.4.9], the rule *jātyantāc cha bandhuni* is intended.
This use of the plural number is for the purpose of including those [suffixes] not prescribed in the *aṣaḍakṣa-* sūtra and others.
8. The suffix *cha* is optionally applied after a word ending in *añc*, provided it does not denote a direction or a feminine noun.
(Pāṇini 5.4.8) 9. The suffix *cha* is applied after a word ending in *jāti* when it denotes a class or kind (*bandhu*).
(Pāṇini 5.4.9) 10. The suffix *cha* is optionally applied after a word ending in *sthāna*, provided that the compound is a *sa-sthāna* (having the same location). (Pāṇini 5.4.10)
Regarding the phrase "by way of position" (*ṣaṣṭhānena*): this is the instrumental case used in the sense of an instrument.
By "position"—that is, by the meaning expressed as a position, which is synonymous with "similarity"—if that which ends in *sthāna* is indeed meaningful, then the suffix occurs;
otherwise it does not. But how is similarity expressed by the word "position"?

Thus he says: "samānam" and so forth. That which has an identical place (*sthāna*) is called "having the same place" (*sasthāna*). And that which is of such a kind, in relation to whatever its place is identical, becomes equal to that [thing]. "Pitṛsthānīyaḥ" means a place like the place of a father.
In the word *yasya*, there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*), according to the rule *saptamyupamāna* (Vārttika 99).
The form *goṣṭhānam* is a genitive *tatpuruṣa*; for this [word] indeed ends in *sthāna*.

It is the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and not the *sthāna* (base), that is meaningful for the purpose [of the suffix]; for just as a suffix occurs after a *sthāna*, so too, when the meaning is presented by the word *svasthāna* within a *tatpuruṣa* compound,
the suffix must arise from that *sthāna* which is meaningful by virtue of that meaning.

Because no specific distinction is made, one might object that the *pratipadika* ending in *-stāna* is therefore equivalent [to the word *sthāna*], being meaningful through the meaning expressed by the word *sthāna*. To such an objector, he says:

"The use of the particle *iti* is for the sake of indicating intention (*vivakṣārtha*). For here, the particle *iti* is employed for the purpose of indicating intention; by this, the following meaning [is established].

If it is argued that the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) arises from that [suffix], then the intention of common usage arises when a suffix is produced after a meaningful base in the sense of a *bahuvrīhi*, and not after one in the sense of a *tatpuruṣa*. Therefore,
it is only the *bahuvrīhi* that can produce the meaning of that [final] member.

It produces the meaning of the word "sthāna" (place), but it is not a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Therefore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Regarding the statement, "the word *cet* is for the purpose of connection": the word *cet* is used so that the suffix *sa* may have a connection with the final element of the *sthānin*; otherwise, [it would apply] only in relation to the affix.

Because of the mention of "the end of the fifth" (*pañcamyāḥ sthānāntasya*), there would be no connection between that which ends in the fifth case and the sixth case; for it is not possible to establish a connection with that [fifth case] by means of the fifth case itself.

However, in the case of the word *cet*, the expression "if that [suffix] is meaningful by virtue of its position" (*sthānena arthavān*) is logically consistent, yet this does not constitute a grammatical connection.
"Between two optional rules (vibhāṣās), the permanent rules (nityavidhi) [take effect]. If these were not permanent,
the preceding option would carry over to the subsequent rule, and thus the mention of "option" (vibhāṣā) in the latter rule would be purposeless.

11. *kimetihvyayaghādābhvadravyaprakarṣe* (5.4.11). Regarding the phrase *adravyaprakarṣe*: But surely there is no excellence (*prakarṣa*) of a substance (*dravya*); for it has been stated in the Bhāṣya, "Indeed, there is no excellence of a substance. Therefore, is this prohibition not purposeless?

To this he says: "Even though," and so forth. Furthermore, the metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*) of the qualities of the contained (*ādheya*) to the container (*ādhāra*) is observed, as in the expression, "The platforms are crying. Therefore, excellence (*prakarpa*), which is a quality of the action or attribute belonging to both the container and the contained, when it is metaphorically attributed to the substance that serves as the container, is then [regarded] as a quality of the substance by way of metaphor.

It is a property of a substance; therefore, this prohibition is made: "only [the excellence] of action and quality," and so forth. When the excellence of an action or a quality is not transferred to a substance—that is, when the excellence belongs only to the action or the quality—the suffix occurs there. However, if it is transferred to a substance...

This follows from the statement "the excellence of the substance" (*dravyaprakarṣa*). Regarding the form *kiṃtarām*: there are many specific qualities of an object; in that context, the meaning of the word *kim* is the question itself. Regarding *pūrvāhṇetarām*:
the non-elision (*aluk*) of the genitive case ending occurs by the rule *ghakālataneṣu kālānāmnaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.17). But surely—

The time "forenoon" (*pūrvāhṇaḥ*) is a substance (*dravya*), and since a suffix [denoting degree] should not occur when there is excellence of a substance—on account of the prohibition "not when there is excellence of a non-substance" (*adravyaprakarṣe*)—is this not a fault? No, there is no fault at all; for in this case, it is not the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) that functions in the sense of excellence, but rather the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*), and that is merely a quality (*guṇa*).

This is because the case-factors (*kāraka*s) consist of the nature of substance (*dravya*) and power (*śakti*). Alternatively, it occurs when there is an extension of time, by virtue of the force of the grammatical statement itself; for no suffix *gha* occurs after a single vowel other than one denoting time.
This is because the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending is prescribed [by Pāṇini] in the rule "after a word denoting time" (*kālanāmnaḥ*).
"Higher still."
12. *amu* [is substituted for *adas*] in the Veda (*chandas*). (5.4.12) 13. The suffix *ṭhak* is added after *anugādin*. (5.4.13) Regarding the form *anugādī*:

it means "one who follows behind" (*anugadati*). The suffix *ṇini* is applied here because the word belongs to the *grahādi* group; alternatively, it may be used in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*).
Or it may denote habitual action (tācchīlya), and this is also due to this very irregular derivation (nipātana).
14. *ṇacaḥ striyām añ* (Pāṇini 5.4.14). Regarding the form *vyāvakrośī*: from the root *kraś* in the sense of "calling out" (Dhātupāṭha 856), the suffix *ṇac* is applied;

there is *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*), and then the suffix *añ* is added after the stem ending in *ṇac*. And this [application of *añ*] occurs by virtue of the technical rule concerning the mention of *kṛt* suffixes (*kṛdgrahaṇaparibhāṣā*).

It occurs from that which possesses a motion (*sagatika*). Therefore, in this context, only that which possesses a motion receives the designation of a nominal stem (*pratipadika*), and not the reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*) itself; thus, by the very prohibition [of *vṛddhi*], only the initial *vṛddhi* takes place. By the rule "ṭiṅḍhāṇañ" (Pāṇini 4.1.15), the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Thus: *vyāvahāsī*. [From] *ata*...
The vowel *vṛddhi* [substitution] occurs by the rule *upadāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116).

Regarding the word "from that" (*tataḥ*), it means "from a word ending in the negative particle *nañ*. This is because, as the Jaiminīya-Paribhāṣāvṛtti (95) states: "Svārthika suffixes follow the gender and number of their base. [Objection: "If that is so..."

By the words "ityādinā" (by such [words]), he shows the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) consisting in the mention of the feminine gender. By the words "tena" (by that), he shows the purpose of the indicative mark. "Ativartante 'pi" (they even go beyond) means they even deviate from [the rule]. From the word "api" (even), it follows that they also continue [to apply] to the primary suffix (*aṇ*). If [it were the case that] for primary derivatives (*svārthika*) there is [no deviation] from the base form...

The deviation from the concordance of gender and number is indicated; therefore, suffixes such as *kalpa* and others occur in their own sense after words like *guḍa*, which follow the masculine gender and so forth.
Their masculine gender and number would likewise occur at that very time, and thus forms such as *guḍakalpā drākṣā* (grapes that are "almost" molasses) and the like are established.
This is not tenable; however, when that [the suffix -ya] is indicated, another grammatical indicator (liṅga) also occurs.
By this, all of this becomes established. By the word "etc. (ādi), there is the inclusion of such forms as *tailakalpā*, *cāturvarṇyam*, and *trailokyam*.
15. *aṇinuṇaḥ* | (Pāṇini 5.4.15) Regarding the word *sāṃrāviṇam*: from the root *ru* meaning "to sound" (Dhātupāṭha 1034), the suffix *inuṇ* is applied;
by the rule *aco ñṇiti* (7.2.115), there is *vṛddhi* [of the vowel]; then the suffix *aṇ* is added after the stem ending in *inuṇ*. And that [suffix *aṇ*] is treated as before.
It occurs only with *sagatṛ*. There is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule "ṭhinaṇyanapatye" (Pāṇini 6.4.164).

Regarding the form "sāṃkūṭinam": [it is derived from] "kūṭa dāhe" (Dhātupāṭha 1890); [and from] "mṛjūṣ śuddhau" (Dhātupāṭha 1066), where there is the vṛddhi [strengthening] by the rule "mṛjervṛddhiḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.114); [and from] "śamityaṣṭābhyaḥ... [etc., Pāṇini 7.3.74].

Regarding the suffix *ghinuṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.141): although *inuṇ* occurs when the letter *gh* is elided, nevertheless, the suffix *aṇ* does not follow from it; this is because the particle *iti*, which serves to indicate the intended meaning (*vivakṣārtha*), is understood to carry over from the rule "optionally after words ending in *sthāna*" (5.4.10).

16. *visāriṇo matsye* (Pāṇini 5.4.16). Regarding the word *visārī*: the suffix *ṇini* is applied as before. Regarding *vaisāriṇaḥ*: the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is as before.
17. *Kṛtvasuc* is added after a numeral when counting the repetition of an action.

(Pāṇini 5.4.17). Regarding the statement "repetition (*abhyāvṛti*) is frequency (*paunaḥpunya*)," here, by association with that [frequency], actions of the same kind performed by a single agent are indicated; therefore—

Thus he says: "of those having a single agent," and so forth. In the expression "ekakartṛkāṇām" (of those having a single agent), the quality [of being] added (*upasaṃkhyāta*) which is drawn along with the thing to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*) applies to that alone. For this very reason, the genitive case occurs in the word for number (*saṃkhyā-śabda*) as being based on distinction (*vyatireka*). The counting of actions is indeed repetition (*abhyāvṛtti*).
"In 'he eats five times,' the meaning is that he performs five occurrences of the action. [In] "he eats many times," if the mention of "number" (*saṃkhyā*) were not made,
then just as the suffix occurs after number-words such as *pañca* and so on, so too [would it occur after other words].
The suffix *kṛtvasuc* would also apply after words such as *bhūri*; however, it does not occur because of the inclusion of the term "number" (*saṃkhyā*) [in the rule].

As in the statement: "Repetition (*abhyāvṛtti*) is possible only for an action. But surely it is also possible for substances and qualities—as in "one who is repeatedly a staff-bearer" (*punaḥ punardaṇḍī*) or "repeatedly stout" (*punaḥ punaḥ sthūla*)? This is not so.

In this context, by implication, there is the repetition of an action—such as "he becomes a staff-bearer again and again" or "he becomes stout again and again. Therefore, repetition is possible only for an action, not for substances or qualities. In the expression "again and again a staff-bearer," the action is obtained through implication.

The mention of "action" (*kriyā*) need not be made [in the rule], as in the passage beginning with "of one [thing], once," and so forth. For by the word "one" (*eka*), only a single individual instance of action is denoted.
And repetition (*abhyāvṛtti*) is not possible within a single instance of action; rather, it occurs across multiple instances.
Regarding the manifestation of actions (*kriyāvyakti*), it was stated previously: "of those having a single agent," and so forth.

Therefore, only a single action is counted as one, not its repetition. Consequently, if the word *kriyā* (action) were not included [in the rule], the suffix would not be obtained when counting actions based on the word *eka* (one).

Therefore, for the sake of the subsequent rule, the mention of "action" (kriyā) must be made. If only "in the counting of actions" (kriyāgaṇane) were stated, this [suffix] would also apply here in the case of "five cookings" (pañcapākāḥ), for there is indeed a counting of actions here; for repetition (abhyāvṛtti) occurs among actions that take place at different times.

In this case, however, only simultaneous acts of cooking (*pāka*) are counted; therefore, that [non-simultaneity] is excluded. But surely, even action (*kriyā*) does not exist here at all, since the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed when the property called "accomplishment" (*siddhatā*)—which is the meaning of the verbal root—is present? This is not a fault; for that accomplishment also [functions as an action] in those instances where action is the subject of discussion.
It is indeed included by the mention of "action" (*kriyā*), because the distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the possessor of the property (*dharmī*) is not intended here.

Otherwise, in examples such as *kārakasya gatiḥ* ("the going of the agent") or *kārakasya vrajyā*, the suffix *ṇvul* would not apply according to the rule *tumunṇvuṇau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.10). [The phrase] "if it were not stated," etc., [follows].
The suffix shall occur only after words denoting numerable things that themselves denote numerable things.
For example: *śataṃ vārān bhuṅkte* (he eats a hundred times), which becomes *śatakṛtvo bhuṅkte*.
Here, by way of the connection "this is that," the word *śata* (hundred) refers to the number of repetitions of the action.

For this very reason, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). To show that [the suffix] would not apply when "hundreds of times" (*śataṃ vārān*) is being counted, he says: "It would not occur here. Why is this so? He says: "Because it functions only with respect to counting" (*saṃkhyānamātravṛttitvāt*). The word *mātra* [indicates] the thing to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*).
"Having abandoned a hundred [other] ways," so it would be.
18. *dvitricaturbhyaḥ suc* (Pāṇini 5.4.18).

[The example is] *caturbhuktam*. By [the rule] *rāt sasya* (8.2.24), there is the elision of the *sakāra*. [It is said] "The *cakāra* is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*)," meaning that the base (*prakṛti*) should have the udātta accent on its final syllable. As for the affix (*pratyaya*), however...

The letter *ca* cannot serve the purpose of indicating accent (*svarārtha*), because it is without a vowel (*anacka*). The status of the *ca* as serving for accent applies only with respect to the word *catuḥ*, which is the subject under discussion, and not to the other two [words]; for those two are already acute (*udātta*).
As for the word *catuḥ*, it is derived from the root *cat* with the suffix *uran* (Pāṇini Daivamudgala 8.78).
Thus, because it ends with the suffix *uran*, it has the acute accent (*udātta*) on its first syllable by virtue of the *nit* accent rule.
19. *ekasya sakṛcca* (5.4.19).

[The suffix *kṛt* is applied after the word *eka* in the sense of "once," as in] *sakṛdbhuktam* ("eaten once"). The elision of the suffixal *s* is by [the rule] *saṃyogāntasya* (8.2.23). The inclusion of the particle *ca* is for the purpose of making the word *udātta*-accented at the end; for if that were not present, [the accentuation would not apply].
Since the word *eka* ends in the suffix *kan* by the rule "ṭiṇbhīkāpāśalyatimarcibhyaḥ kan" (Uṇādi-sūtra 3.21), it is acutely accented on the first syllable (*ādyaudāta*) due to the *nit*-accent;

therefore, by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, the substitute (*ādeśa*) would also necessarily be acutely accented on the first syllable. However, because [the suffix] is marked with the indicator *cit*, it is acutely accented on the final syllable (*antodāta*).
[The compound] occurs. Now, why does it not occur in the case of *ekaḥ pākaḥ* ("one cooking"), since there is indeed a counting of actions here?
To this he says: "In 'ekaḥ pākaḥ'... and so forth.
20. *Vibhāṣā bahordhā’viprakṛṣṭakāle*.
The word *bahu* [is used] in the sense of generality alone, as it also functions in the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*).
In that regard, it is first of all logical that the non-interruption (*aviprakarṣa*) of the repetition of multiple actions is intended, and this depends upon context and other such factors.
Even the suffixes *kṛtvasuc* and others are not able to function in this domain;
therefore, the mention of the term *vibhāṣā* need not be made.

21. *mayaṭ* [is used] in the sense of "made thereof" (*tatprakṛtavacane*) when that which is introduced as the subject (*prakṛta*) is intended. [The commentary states: "That which is introduced predominantly is 'the subject' (*prakṛta*). But how is this distinction obtained, since the word *prakṛta* signifies merely that which is introduced? [The answer is: because of the inclusion of the word *vacana* ("expression") here.

Although it would have been sufficient to say "in the original sense" (*prakṛte*), the inclusion of the word "mention" (*vacana*) is for this purpose: that the suffix *mayaṭ* should apply only where a mention of the original base ending in *mayaṭ* is observed in common usage with a derivative form.
And in common usage, words such as *rannamaya* and others ending in the suffix *mayaṭ* express the abundance of the original base.
The distinction is obtained precisely from the inclusion of the word "iti.

As for the phrase beginning with "apare tu," here the suffix denotes a meaning entirely different from the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). By the word *prakṛta*, only that which is under discussion (*prastuta*) is expressed, and not that which is characterized by abundance (*prācurya*).
"This is the distinction: 'it is the subject under discussion. Regarding "in both ways," etc., the meaning is that the sūtra was composed for this purpose in either manner.
22. *Samūhavacca bahuṣu* (5.4.22).

[The example is] *ṭhmaudakikam*. Just as in the case of a collection, the suffix *ṭhak* occurs after words such as *modaka* by virtue of the rule *acittahastidhenoṣṭhak* (4.2.47); so too here, it occurs from the word *modaka*.
Since the suffix *ṭhak* is prescribed in its own sense (*svārtha*) after masculine bases as well as feminine bases and so forth,

and because it is stated that "suffixes used in their own sense follow the gender and number of the base" (Vyāḍipāda 74), the resulting form ought to possess the very gender and other properties belonging to the base; how then is this [so]?
Why is there another gender, namely the neuter, and another number for this suffix?
To this he says: "even though they overstep," and so forth. And this has been made known under the rule "ṇacaḥ striyām" (Pāṇini 5.4.14).
23. *anantāvasathetihabheṣajāññyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.23).

[The word] *itiha* occurs in the sense of "tradition" (*upadeśapāramparya*). This is because we observe its usage only in such instances as *ha smopādhyāyaḥ kathayati* ("Thus, indeed, the teacher used to say") and *iti ha sma pitā kathayati* ("Thus, indeed, the father used to say").

24. *devatāntāt tādarthye yat* (Pāṇini 5.4.24). [The sūtra states: "From a word ending in the fourth case in construction. it is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) consisting of "Agni" and "deity" (*devatā*), meaning one who is both Agni and a deity.

Regarding the rule *ṭhcchabdasya*: from the word *ccha-pada*, which denotes a collection of seven syllables, the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). Thus, *cchāyā* means "a collection of seven syllables."
Regarding the statement "there is no elision (*aluk*) of the second-case plural ending":

when the suffix *yat* is applied after the word *ap* in its second-case plural form, the case-ending (*sup*) is elided by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.71), and then... [all]... This is done on the basis of the rule: "In the Vedic language, the objects [of grammatical operations] are optional" (Puṣpavṛtti 56).

Regarding the statement "An addition [to the sūtra] is made for *āmuṣyāyaṇa* and *āmuṣyaputrīka*," this further addition is for the purpose of preventing the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending, not for the sake of the meaning of the suffix itself.

Regarding the term *āmuṣyāyaṇa*, the word *amuṣya* is listed among the *naḍādi* group; when the suffix *phak* is added to it, although the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending would normally apply, it must be stated that there is no such elision (*aluk*). This non-elision will occur by virtue of the fact that the word is listed in the *naḍādi* group together with its case-ending. As for the form *amuṣyaputrikā*:

Since the word *tvaṃ* is listed among the *manojñādi* group, when the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending would otherwise apply, it must be stated that there is non-elision (*aluk*). Alternatively, it is established by its inclusion in the *manojñādi* list; thus, it need not be explicitly stated [as an exception].
In both cases, the substitution of *mat* and *ut* occurs according to Pāṇini 8.2.80: *adaso'serdādu do maḥ*.

29. *kan* after *yava* and others. (Pāṇini 5.4.29). Regarding the rule beginning with "in the sense of a season" (*ṛtau*): the word-forms *uṣṇa* and *śīta* take the suffix *kan* when a season is to be expressed—thus, *uṣṇaka* season, *śītaka* season. In other cases, they remain simply *uṣṇaḥ* and *śītaḥ*.

It occurs [as follows]: "In the sense of 'an animal,' the words *lūna* and *viyāta* produce the suffix *kan*—that is, when an animal is the object denoted: *lūnakaḥ paśuḥ* (a castrated animal), *viyātakaḥ paśuḥ* (a castrated animal).
Other than in reference to an animal, [the forms are] *lūnam*, *viyātam*. And: "The word *aṇu* [produces the suffix *kan*] in the sense of 'skillful. Thus, the word *aṇu*...

The suffix *kan* produces the form *putraka*: "little son. In other cases, it is simply *putra*. Regarding the rule "the word *snāta* [is used] upon the completion of the Vedas," the word *snāta* produces the suffix *kan* when the completion of the Vedas is intended to be expressed. One whose Veda is completed is called a *snātaka*.
What is the purpose of [the rule] "even at the end of a Vedic word"? [Example: *nadyāṃ snātaḥ* ("bathed in a river"). Regarding the rule "for *śūnya* when meaning 'empty'":

the word *śūnya* takes the suffix *kan* when its expressed meaning is "empty"—that is, *śūnyakaḥ*, meaning "slightly empty. In other cases, it is simply *śūnyam*. Regarding the rule "for *dāna* when meaning 'contemptible'": the word *dāna* [takes the suffix *kan*] when contemptible...
It forms *kan*: from *dānīya* (meaning "to be given"), *dānakam*; elsewhere, however, it is simply *dāna*.
From the word *tanu*, *kan* is formed according to the rule "in the sense of 'sūtra'," resulting in *tanukam* (a thin sūtra);
elsewhere, it is *tanu*. According to the rule "and after *īyas*," *kan* occurs after a stem ending in the suffix *īyas*, as in *śreyaskaḥ*.
Regarding the phrase "and the playthings of young girls": those things which are the playthings of young girls produce joy—namely, the ball.

30. [The suffix *kan* is applied] after the word *lohita* when it denotes a gem (*maṇi*). (5.3.30) 31. [The suffix *kan* is applied] after the word *lohita* also when [the color] is not permanent (*anitya*).
(5.3.31) For example: "He is red with anger" (*lohitakaḥ kopena*). This means that the color expressed by the word *lohita* occurs when anger is present.
[The word *lohitaka*] exists. Furthermore, since Devadatta remains stationary even when his anger has subsided and then departs, [the word *lohitaka*] would be non-eternal.
Now, for what purpose is the mention of *varṇa* (color), given that the word *lohita* (red) refers only to color?
This is not so; for this [word] also refers to a substance (*dravya*) when caused by a gem, and in that case, if [the mention of *varṇa*] were absent...

If the term "color" (varṇa) were not mentioned, the mention of "non-eternality" would be understood as a qualifier of the substance (dravya); consequently, there would be no such cognition as "the atoms of earth are red," because those [atoms] are eternal. However, when the term "color" is present, the mention of "non-eternality" is understood as a qualifier of the color itself.

Thus, the suffix is established as applying to that which is eternal. Furthermore, the word *lohita* (red) refers only to blood by way of its primary characteristic (*varma-nimitta*), and since that [blood] is everywhere non-eternal, it is stated—by virtue of the power of employing the qualification—that a specific effect is denoted as being non-eternal. That, moreover, is...

[The quality] exists only when its substratum is present; sometimes it occurs, and sometimes it does not. Therefore, it would apply only to that which is the menstrual blood (*ārtava*) of women. Consequently, the mention of *varṇa* (color) must be made [in the rule].
[This is illustrated by the examples: "a red cow" (*lohito gauḥ*) and "red blood" (*lohitaṃ rudhiram*).
Color is not impermanent because it persists as long as its substratum exists.

But is this [color] not indeed impermanent, since it perishes through the destruction of its substratum? This is true; for every color is of such a nature. However, it is called "impermanent" by virtue of the force of employing that specific qualification.

By that excellence, it is understood as "the last"; moreover, that [suffix] occurs only when there is a basis (āśraya), for it is only that which, having not existed, comes into being, and having existed, passes away, that can truly be said to "be.

That *pratyaya* is expressed by the word "liṅga" figuratively; it must be stated that its application is set aside by the word "lohita. Otherwise, when there is a simultaneous desire to express both femininity and a non-eternal color, [the suffix] *naḥ* prescribed by the rule "varṇādanudātātopadhāto naḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.39) from the word "lohita"— [The text continues: ...would arise. Therefore, it must be said that the word "liṅga" here refers to the *pratyaya*. And since the word "lohita" is a *varṇa-śabda* (a word denoting a color), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is not applied. When the shortening prescribed by "in place of *aṇ* after *ke*" (7.4.13) is effected, the form *lohinikā* arises.

32. *rakte* (Pāṇini 5.4.32). [The suffix *yañ* is applied] "when [the object] is dyed with lac and so forth. Now, one might object: since the red color imparted by lac and such is impermanent, this is already established by the preceding rule (*an-āvaśyake*). For when those...

Through a particular kind of yoga, such stability arises that it does not abandon its own substratum; at that time, because of its permanence, one does not [otherwise] attain it—for this reason, this is said.
33. [The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied] after [words denoting] time. (5.4.33) 34. [The suffix] *ṭhak* is applied after [the group of words beginning with] *vinaya*.
(5.4.34) [The rule] "after *upāya*, there is also shortening" means that it produces the suffix *ṭhak* after the word *upāya*, and there is also shortening [of the final vowel].
He practices—that is, he is one who acts accordingly.

35. [The suffix *ṇini* is applied] after a word denoting speech (*vāc*) when the meaning is that which has been uttered (*vyāhṛta*). (Pāṇini 5.4.35) The term "uttered" (*vyāhṛta*) means "spoken. The phrase "by another" (*anyena*) refers to the sender of the message. For that speech was not previously commanded by itself; rather, it becomes a message-speech (*sandeśavāk*) by virtue of being previously commanded by the one who sends it, through which [speech]— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.]
The matter to be communicated is expressed, and that is called the message.

36. *tadyuktāt karmaṇo 'ṇ* (Pāṇini 5.4.36). Regarding the phrase "from the word *karman*": by this, he shows that there is a reference to the actual form (*svarūpa*) of the word *karman*, and not to that which is the most desired object (*īpsitatama*). But surely, [this refers to] the word *karman*...

Is it not the case that, because it is a term denoting a name (*saṃjñāśabda*), it is proper to understand only that which is most desired (*īpsitatama*) [as the object], and not its own form (*svarūpa*)?

This is not so; for here, the particle *iti* is carried over from the preceding sūtra, "After a word ending in *sthāna*" (Pāṇini 5.4.10), and by means of it, this meaning is obtained: if there is a desire to express that [meaning].

It occurs as follows: when a suffix is produced after a word denoting an object (*karman*), there is an intention to express [the object] in common usage, not from that which is "most desired" (*īpsitatama*). For it is not possible to indicate the object by means of the *aṇ* suffix produced from that [word denoting the most desired], since its meaning would already have been expressed;
however, it can be indicated by the suffix produced after a word denoting the object. Therefore...

The apprehension of the essential nature alone is appropriate, as in the term "kārmaṇam"; here, the original form [of the stem] is maintained by the rule *an* (Pāṇini 6.4.16). Regarding the phrase "in that very way": it means in the same manner as it was set forth by speech whose meaning has been articulated—that is, "this must be done"—by that very method.

Regarding the passage beginning with "in the section on *ṭhan*," etc., the word *upasaṃkhyāna* means "an explanatory addition" (*pratipādana*). In this regard, the explanation is as follows: since the group beginning with *prajñā* is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class), words such as *kulāla* and others should be understood as included therein. Consequently, by the rule "and from *prajñā* and so forth" (*prajñādibhyaśca*, Pāṇini 5.3.38), the suffix *aṇ* will apply.

If this is so, would it not also apply in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*)? This is not a fault; for from the rule "optionally after *bahu*" (Pāṇini 5.4.20) and others, the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) is understood to carry over, and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) which will apply only in Vedic language (*chandas*), not in the spoken language.

Regarding *sānnāya* [as seen in the *Sānnayya-kāśikā*, *Padamañjarī*, etc.]: *sānnāya*, *anujāvara*, *anuṣūka*, *anuṣṭubha*, *cātuṣprāśya*, *rākṣodhva*, *vaiyāta*, *vaikṛta*, *vārivaskṛta*, *āgrayaṇa*, *āgrahāyaṇa*, and *sāntapana* are desired [to be formed] both in the Vedic language (*chandas*) and in common speech (*bhāṣā*). Therefore, there are *sānnāya* and the others. Their bases (*prakṛti*) should be understood as being included precisely within the *prajñādi* group. And here, in the case of *āgrayaṇa* and *āgrahāyaṇa*, the suffix is applied to the forms ending in long *ī*—namely the words *āgrayaṇī* and *āgrahāyaṇī*—rather than to the forms ending in short *a* such as *anujāvara* and the rest.

And here, the word *sānnāyya* is taken in the sense of having the accent on the final syllable; its form, however, is established by the rule *pāyyasānnāyya* (Pāṇini 3.1.129) itself through nipātana. 37. *oṣadher ajātau* (5.4.37): [The suffix *yañ* is applied after the word *oṣadhi* when it does not denote a genus]. For example: *oṣadhaṃ pibati* ("he drinks the medicinal herb"). This suffix is applied after the word *oṣadhi* when it refers to a fruit or similar object.

And [the word] *jāti* does not occur [in this context], because the defining characteristic [of *jāti*], such as "a *jāti* is the apprehension of a common form" (*kāśikā* 4.1.63), is absent. Herbs grow in a field; in this case, the *jāti* ends with the ripening of the fruit.
In that context, the word "oṣadhi" (herb/medicine) is employed.
38. *Prajñādibhyaśca* (5.4.38).

[The example is] "one who understands is *prajñaḥ*" (*prajānātīti prajñaḥ*). This is derived by *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ* (3.1.135). But surely, for one who understands, there exists understanding (*prajñā*), and thus [the suffix] *aṇ* should apply by *prajñaśraddhārcāvṛtibhyo'ṇ* (5.2.101)?

Since the suffix *ṇa* itself already conveys the sense of possession (*matvartha*), for what purpose is the suffix *aṇ* prescribed after the word *prajñā*? To refute this objection, [the author], showing the specific distinction regarding the feminine gender, says:
"In the feminine, *prājñī*," and so forth. [He specifies] that there is the inclusion of the present participle (*śatṛ*) form of the root *vid*, and not [the simple root] *vid*.
"From *śatṛ*, [the suffix] *vasu*" (Pāṇini 7.1.36), and so forth.

Regarding "in the body": when the word *śrotra* occurs in reference to the body, the suffix *aṇ* is applied to it—thus *śrautra*; elsewhere, it is *śrotṛ*. Regarding "one who sacrifices" (*juhvat*): from the word *juhvad*.
The suffix *aṇ* occurs after the word *kṛṣṇa* when it refers to a black antelope—namely, *jauhva*. Elsewhere, it is simply *juhvad*.

Others read "kṛṣṇa mṛge" as separate words; the suffix *aṇ* occurs after the word *kṛṣṇa* when a black antelope is to be expressed—as in *kārṣṇo mṛgaḥ* (a black antelope)—but elsewhere it is simply *kṛṣṇa*.
In this reading, the suffix is applied without distinction to the word *juhvad*. Regarding the term *satvantu*:
the word *sat* which ends in the possessive suffix *matup* refers to those who possess *sattva*; thus, he is a *Sātvata*.
This [list] beginning with *prajñā* is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class); it is precisely because of its status as an *ākṛtigaṇa* that...
The particle *ca* has been employed here for the purpose of indicating an unexpressed collection (*samuccaya*), so that the suffix *aṇ* is established after words such as *kulāla* and *kukkuṭa*.
39. *mṛda-stikan* (Pāṇini 5.4.39).

But for what purpose is this [suffix] prescribed again, instead of simply prescribing *tak* itself? For this feminine suffix is obligatory; thus, once the *ṭāp* has been applied, the desired form would be established by the rule "ṭh-pratyayasthāt kāt" (Pāṇini 7.3.44) through the substitution of *ī*. [Objection: In that case, where the elision (*luk*) of the suffix is performed, there [the form] would not be established.

It would be established thus: "purchased for five clods of earth" is *pañcamṛtika*. For in that case, when the suffix *ṭhak*—prescribed by the rule *ṭhaṣyarddhaparvadvigoḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.28)—is elided by the rule *luk taddhitaluki* (Pāṇini 1.2.49), the feminine suffix is also elided.

[The suffix] *luk* [is applied]. In that case, if *takan* were prescribed, then because of the absence of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, the vowel *i* would not be heard; furthermore, there would be the fault of unnecessary complexity (*prakriyā-gaurava*), since the addition of the suffix *ikak* is already prescribed by another rule of the grammar.

40. The suffix *san* is used in the sense of praise. (Pāṇini 5.4.40) 41. After the words *vṛka* and *jyeṣṭha*, the suffixes *tila* and *tātil* are respectively applied in the Vedic language. (Pāṇini 5.4.41) 42. After a word denoting much or little, when it functions as a kāraka, the suffix *śas* is optionally applied. (Pāṇini 5.4.42)

Regarding the phrase "ṭhityevamādīni," the word "ādi" (and so forth) includes the technical rules (*paribhāṣā*) concerning examples of the ablative (*apādāna*), instrumental (*karaṇa*), and other cases—for instance: *bahubhya āgacchati* ("he comes from many"), *bahuśa āgacchati* ("he comes many times"), *alpaśa āgacchati* ("he comes few times"), and *bahuśo nidadhāti* ("he places [it] many times"). In the example *bahūnāṃ svāmī* ("the master of many"), the word *bahu* expresses the remaining relation (*śeṣa*) rather than denoting a specifically intended grammatical case (*kāraka*).

It occurs [due to the rule] beginning with "because of the inclusion of the word *artha*. For if the inclusion of the word *artha* were absent, the suffix would occur only after the words *bahu* and *alpa*; but since it is present, it occurs even after synonyms.

Regarding the phrase "from words meaning 'much' or 'little'," etc.: when a suffix is to be prescribed after words meaning "much" or "little," an auspicious statement (*maṅgalavacana*) must be made. And here, by "auspicious statement," an explanation (*vyākhyāna*) is meant, because [the suffix] is explained (*vyākhyāyate*) by means of it. But how can there be an auspicious statement regarding a grammatical cause (*kāraṇa*)?

"What is to be done? To this he says: "In which," and so forth. Herein is the explanation: the term *praśaṃsā* (praise) is understood here by way of anuvṛtti; a suffix must be employed when there is praise, and that occurs in the context of auspicious rites (*śrāddhas*). He gives much, not little—in this way, praise is established.

This very word [is used] frequently in the world in the context of giving for auspicious occasions (*ābhyudayika*); because another [word] is not understood due to the recurrence of that [particle], the suffix does not occur when it refers to an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*). Alternatively—because of the recurrence of the particle *iti* here as well, it occurs only in the case of an auspicious rite, and not elsewhere. [This concerns] the suffix *śas*.
The letter *s* does not receive the designation *it*, because there is no purpose for it.
43. *Saṃkhyaikavacanācca vīpsāyām* (5.4.43).
By the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ* (8.1.4), which prescribes reduplication (*dvirvacana*), this [suffix] *śas* is ordained as an exception (*apavāda*).
"That by which a single object is expressed is called a singular (*ekavacana*). By this...

The intention is that [the compound] consists of words ending in the singular number when they have a single referent (*sahārtha*). Now, one might object: "By taking the term *anvartha* (‘having a meaning according to its etymology’), it would indeed apply; for there is a singular form because it functions with reference to a single referent. This is not so; for in the formulation of a grammatical rule (*pratyayavidhau*), the singularity of the referent of a sentence (*vākya*) is not relied upon. What then? It is the singularity of the referent as it exists in the compound formation (*vṛtti*). Not in the sentence.
And when the case-ending has been elided, words such as *ghaṭa* (pot) and so forth remain in the singular number;

for they are genus-words (*jātiśabda*). Genus-words do not apply to only a single individual that serves as the locus for a single genus, but rather to many individuals as well. Thus, their application to a single referent [is established].

Number is understood only when resorting to case-endings (*vibhakti*) in a sentence (*vākya*), not in a derivative form (*vṛtti*), because the case-ending has ceased to exist there. Regarding the phrase "and *kārṣāpaṇa* and so forth," it was stated that "words such as *kārṣāpaṇa* denote measures. They are denoters of a specific measure (*parimāṇaviśeṣa*).

Thus, when there is an increase in the referent (*artha*), their occurrence [as separate words] is not possible. However, when they are used in a sentence—as in "two *kārṣāpaṇas*" (*kārṣāpaṇau*) or "many *kārṣāpaṇas*" (*kārṣāpaṇāḥ*)—there is the cognition of multiple referents; that case-ending does not belong to them [individually]. But in a compound (*vṛtti*), that case-ending is absent, and therefore they become a single referent (*ekārtha*).

It has been stated that in the formulation of grammatical rules (*pratyaya-vidhi*), the state of having a single meaning (*ekārthatā*) is relied upon as it exists in a compound (*vṛtti*), not as it exists in a sentence (*vākya*).
For example, in the expression "he gives a jar, a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ ghaṭaṃ dadāti*), words such as *ghaṭa* do not possess a single meaning in a compound;
this has already been demonstrated. However, when words like *ghaṭa* are etymological (*anvartha*) and accompanied by context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth—
When words denoting genus (*jātiśabda*) have a single referent, then the suffix *śas* must necessarily occur; otherwise,

regarding what will be stated under the rule *ṭhjaśśasoḥ śiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.20)— namely, that there is an inclusion of *śas* as it co-occurs with *jas*, and thus it does not apply in cases such as "he gives *kuḍavaśas*" or "he enters *śataśas*"— [that statement would be contradicted].
That [objection] is refuted; for even words such as *kuḍava* are genus-words (*jātiśabda*).

44. *pratiyoge pañcamyāstasiḥ* | (5.4.44) As in: "Pradyumna is the counterpart (*prati*) of Vāsudeva. Here, the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is applied by the rule *pratinidhipratidāne ca yasmāt* (2.3.11), and from that [fifth case], the suffix *tasi* is added. The vowel *i* in *tasi* is for the sake of [forming] *mukhamukha*. Now, one might object:
Is it for the purpose that the letter *s* [in *sat*] should not receive the designation *it*? This is not so;

for precisely because there is no purpose, it will not receive the designation *it*. [The rule] "there is an addition [of the suffix *tasil*] after *ādi* and the rest" means: there is an addition of *tasil* after *ādi* and the rest, excluding *sat*.

The meaning is that this must be established. This is the demonstration: in the subsequent sūtra, the particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been mentioned; by it, the suffix *tas* will apply after words such as *ādi*.
Regarding the particle *ca* having the sense of including what has not been mentioned, [the rule] "In that [word], the first half-mora is acute" (1.2.32) [is relevant].
Such is the definition.

45. And [the fifth case ending is used] in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*), except for the roots *hī* and *ruh*. (Pāṇini 5.4.45) For example: *grāmād āgacchati* ("He comes from the village"). The designation *apādāna* is applied by the rule *dhruvam apāye 'pādānam* (Pāṇini 1.4.24). For example: *caurebhyo bibheti* ("He fears the thieves"). [The designation *apādāna* is applied] by the rule *bhītrārthānāṃ bhayahetuḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.25).

(1.4.25) Thus: "He fails because of his studies" (*adhyayanāt parājayate*). [This is governed by] *parājer asoḍhaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.26). "He deserts the caravan" (*sārthād dhīyate*). [The root] *ūhāk* (Dhātupāṭha 1090) means "to abandon"; [the suffix] *laḥ* [is applied].
The *ātmanepada* suffix is used because [the root] is *karmavācya*; the *yak* affix is applied, and by the rule *ghumāsthā* (Pāṇini 6.4.66), the vowel *i* is substituted.

Now, one might object: "But there is no object that lacks an agent," according to the statement *kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma* (Pāṇini 1.4.49); and in this case, the caravan is not the object (*karman*), but rather the point of departure (*apādāna*). This is not so.

This is a fault; for in the definition of the term *karman*, the mention of the agent (*kartṛ*) is intended as an indicator of independence (*svātantrya*). Why is this so? Because it functions as a qualifier of the action. And in the case of the agent, two things exist: independence and the technical designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*). Of these, [the mention of the agent serves] for the sake of the designation...

The status of being an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇatva*) is not tenable. For that which is the cause of an action is precisely what is fit to qualify it. And the designation "agent" (*kartṛ*) is not the cause of that [action]; what then?
It is independence (*svātantrya*), because that constitutes the very nature of an agent. This occurs when, with respect to an action...
The state of being a cause; and since the action is not qualified by the object, the meaning here is this:

that which is most desired by the action, which possesses independence, receives the technical designation "object" (karman). Even for the caravan leader, he is designated as such by Devadatta. Of him—

If that [the act of abandoning] were not present, even the ablative case (apādāna) would not exist at all. Therefore, Devadatta is the object (karman). It is precisely for the sake of the meaning of the root *hā* (to abandon) that there must be an ablative; and therein, although the ablative exists, it is by the very intention to express the independence (*svātantrya*) of the agent in the act of abandoning that Devadatta [is designated as the object].
The designation "karma" (object) occurs.
Now, for what purpose is the suffix *yak* employed in the instruction; why not simply say "ṭhhāruhoḥ"?
To this he says: "the indication of a modification," and so forth. That is called a "modification" (*vikāra*) in which the form is transformed.

"Vikāraḥ" (modification); furthermore, in this context, it refers specifically to the [substitution of] "hi" [for "jahāti"]—because, according to the sūtra *dhumāsthāgāpājahātisām* (Pāṇini 6.4.66), the form of the root *jahāti* is modified by the substitution of the vowel *e* for *i*. Alternatively, "vikāraḥ" means "vikṛtiḥ" (transformation); the indication is made by means of that transformation. How?

What is the purpose [of the specific mention]? It is so that the rule may apply to *jahāti* (the root *hā*), and not to *jihīte* (the root *hī*); for otherwise, there would be the inclusion of *jīhīte* as well.

However, when there is a reference to a specific grammatical form (*vikāranirdeśa*), the inclusion applies only to that which possesses such a form. Thus, it is not [the case that *jihīte* is included].

This contingency arises: [the objection] that "it rises from the ground" (*bhūmita ujjihīte*). Since *jihīti* is not included here [in the rule for the substitution of *i*], the substitution does indeed occur from the apādāna related to it. Because of the marker *ṅ* in *hāṅ*, there is the ātmanepada;
by *bhṛjāmit* (Pāṇini 7.4.76), there is the substitution of *i* for the reduplicated syllable; and by *ī halyaghoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.113), [the long ī is substituted].
The substitution of *ī* occurs for the root-vowel (*dhātu*).

How is it that [the Vedic passage] says, "How can a mantra be deficient in accent or in phoneme"? The intention is this: when a prohibition is made regarding the root *hā*, then [the substitution] does not apply to that [mantra]. This is not a fifth case (ablative).

Thus [it is said]: because the ablative case (pañcamī) is not prescribed [here], the suffix *tasi* is used figuratively (*upacāreṇa*); it has been stated that this is not the ablative. What then? It is the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*). Since the instrumental is prescribed here as well, the suffix *tasi* is stated to be [added] after the instrumental. By this, he indicates that this *tasi* is not [added] here by this very rule.

It is not prescribed by the fifth case-suffix (*pañcamī*) in the sūtra; rather, while the phrase "after the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*), when [the sense is] taking, non-agitation, or enduring" (5.4.46) is being carried over, the rule "and also when connected with that which is being abandoned or that which is evil" (5.4.47) prescribes the third case. And that third case should be understood as denoting either the cause (*hetu*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*).
46. *Atigrahāvyathanakṣepeṣvakartari tṛtīyāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.46).

"Having surpassed (*atikramya*)"—by this he shows that the word *ati* here functions in the sense of "surpassing. "Non-trembling is *avyathana*"—[this is stated] because [the root] *vyath* [is listed] as "in the sense of fear and trembling" (Dhātupāṭha 764).
It is recited; here it denotes the function (vṛtti) in its movement. The third case ending in "vṛtena" is used either in the sense of cause (hetu) or instrument (karaṇa).

47. And [the third case ending is used] because of connection with that which is being abandoned (*hīyamāna-pāpa-yoga*). (5.4.47) In the examples "he is abandoned by virtue" (*vṛtena hīyate*) and "the wicked person is abandoned by virtue" (*vṛtataḥ pāpaḥ*), when there is a connection between virtue (*vṛta*) and the wicked person who is being abandoned, the third case ending is used either in the sense of cause (*hetu*) or as the instrument (*karaṇa*).
"Why does this not serve as an example when there is an intention to express censure (kṣepa)? To this, he says: "And of censure," and so forth.
48. [The sixth case ending is used] in relation to the locus (*vyāśraye*).

(5.4.48) 49. [The sixth case ending is used] after a word denoting a disease (*roga*) when it signifies removal (*apanayana*). [As in the example] "from dysentery" (*pravāhikātaḥ*): the sixth case ending is employed after the word *pravāhikā* with reference to the remedy (*pratīkāra*).
Then, the suffixes tasi and the others [are applied].

50. *Cvi* is applied after a word [ending in a case-affix] when it denotes the attainment of a state not previously possessed, provided it is in construction with a verb meaning "to make" (*kṛ*), "to be" (*bhū*), or "to exist" (*asti*), and the agent is the subject of the attainment (*sampadyakartṛ*). (Pāṇini 5.4.50).

The phrase "of a cause that has not yet come to be in the form of an effect" means: the "cause" (*kāraṇa*) is the primal material (*prakṛti*), and its subsequent different state is the "effect" (*vikāra*). By this—

The meaning is: "of that which has not come into being" (*abhūta*) by way of modification, that is, of that which is unborn (*ajāta*). But from where is this specific distinction of "becoming what was previously non-existent" (*abhūtatadbhāva*) obtained? It is obtained from the inclusion of the term *abhūta*;

for here, "coming into being" (*bhāva*) refers either to birth (*janman*) or to existence (*sat*). For if it were existence of that which already exists (*sat*), then [the term] would be synonymous with "being" (*asti*) itself.
There would be a connection with the root *as* (to be), but not with *karoti* (to do). For that which is being produced is not [already] existent.

Furthermore, since all three roots are employed, when a meaning is grasped such that there is a connection with all three roots, it is proper to adopt that very meaning; and that is birth alone, not existence.

This specific distinction is obtained from the inclusion of the word *kṛt*: "the becoming [of something] by means of that. By the word *tat* (that), the modification (*vikāra*) is referred to; it is that very modification which is the *ātman* (self/nature).
