Thus, "having become that modification as its own nature" refers to the state of having become that [modification]. However, this applies only to a cause that has already attained existence.

It is stated that *abhūtatadbhāva* (the becoming of what was not previously so) is the attainment of a state of modification at a later time by something that had not previously undergone modification. Therefore, where the original material (*prakṛti*) is not intended to be expressed, the suffix does not occur, as in the counter-example "he makes white" (*śuklaṃ karoti*). For in this case, the original material is not [intended].
When such a state of "becoming that which it was not" (abhūtatadbhāva) is intended to be expressed, it is understood;

by the word *tat*, the intention to express the non-difference between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*) is conveyed. Therefore, the suffix occurs only where the material cause, while undergoing the form of a modification, is intended to be expressed as non-different from it.

It occurs; however, it does not apply where a distinction between cause and effect is intended to be expressed. But where there is such a distinction—as in "he makes a cloth" (*paṭaṃ karoti*)—it does not apply there. [This is the case with] the rule: "The agent of *sampad* is the *sampadyakartṛ*.
But how can there be a compound with a word ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), and how can there be the elision of the *tiṅ* suffix? It is because this is a Vedic (or sūtra) usage.

Because there exists an explicit explanation (*nirdeśa*), all of this is logically established. Alternatively—by deriving [the word] from the root *pad* preceded by the prefix *sam*, precisely through this irregular formation (*nipātana*), the suffix *yat* is applied; this is a non-compound (*asamāsa*) characterized by that [suffix]. When forming a commentary (*vṛtti*) on that verbal form (*tiṅanta*), however, only the demonstration of its meaning has been performed; it is not...

Furthermore, this is an analytical statement (*vigrahavākya*): where one should have said "in *sampatti*," it is stated as "*sampadyakartari*" for the sake of variety, as in the example "*śuklīkaroti*. Following the rule "*asya cvau*" (Pāṇini 7.4.32), the substitution of *i* occurs;
then, by the rule "*cvau*" (Pāṇini 7.4.26), lengthening takes place. Because that which ends in *cv-* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

There is elision of the *s* (sorlopaḥ). [The objection is: "In this case, the original form (*prakṛti*) is not intended to be expressed. [The reply is: Because only the modification (*vikāra*) is intended to be expressed. And where the original form is not intended to be expressed, the transition from one state to another (*abhūtatadbhāva*) is not understood there; therefore, [the rule] does not apply.

The suffix *pratyaya* [is used] because it is already understood through the force of the expression "the becoming of that which was not previously so," and so forth. For that which, having existed in an unmodified form,
comes to exist as a modification, necessarily attains that modified state.
The statement "it becomes the agent" implies that it becomes so by means of another form;

however, with the intention that it does not necessarily follow that it must retain the designation of "agent," he says: "lest there be [the application of the term] upon its becoming another kāraka," as in the example "adevagṛhe."

And so forth. Here, since the temple (*devagṛha*) was previously non-existent as a place for the propitiation of a deity, and subsequently attains the nature of being that [deity-receptacle] through its connection with the deity to whom it is dedicated, this is an instance of *abhūtatadbhāva* (the becoming of what was not before); however, this pertains to the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), not to the agent (*kartṛ*). Likewise...
For even when it attains another form (*tadrūpāntaram*), it does not receive the designation *kartṛ* (agent);

rather, it receives the designation *adhikaraṇa* (locus) itself; otherwise, the seventh case-ending (*saptamī*) would not occur. In the suffix *cvī*, the letter *i* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). The letter *c* is for the sake of making the original base (*prakṛti*) have an udātta accent on its final syllable. As for the letter *v*...
The elision [of the *y*] occurs by the rule "ṭh-lopaḥ for what is not followed by a vowel" (6.1.67).
51. *Arur-manas-cakṣuś-cetas-raho-rajasām lopaś-ca* (Pāṇini 5.4.51).

Here, [the commentary] begins with "due to the connection with the qualifiers" (*viśeṣaṇasaṃbandhāt*). All the qualifiers, such as "becoming that which it was not" (*abhūtatadbhāva*) and so forth, are carried over (*anuvartante*) from the preceding sūtra. Therefore—

Since the suffix is already established by the preceding rule for words such as *aruṣ* and others due to their connection with all qualifying attributes (*viśeṣaṇa*), that suffix is not prescribed here; however, the mere elision (*lopa*) does not apply. Therefore, this statement is made for that purpose.
If, on the other hand, the prescription of the suffix were to occur by this very rule alone, then [in cases] such as *durmanīkaroti*, etc., [the desired form would not be obtained].

The suffix would not apply; for there is a prohibition against the rule of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself contains [the element] to be grasped (Pāṇini 1.1.72, Vārttika 89). However, by the preceding rule, it does apply even after such a form ending in that [element], because in that case there is no nominal stem containing the element to be grasped—as in examples such as *unmanīkaroti*.
The suffix [is applied] after a bahuvrīhi compound.

52. *vibhāṣā sāti kārtsnye* (5.4.52). "The mention of *vibhāṣā* is intended to bring about [the application of] *cvi*; this is because it has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). Its having the sense of conjunction is due to the fact that an indeclinable (*nipāta*) has multiple meanings. If this is so, then [the particle] *ca* alone [would suffice]."
Why is it not to be inferred? Because of the diversity of the composition of the Sūtras.
Now, why is the term *vibhāṣā* not taken to mean "only for the purpose of an option regarding the affix"? To this he says: "But as for the option regarding the affix," and so forth.

53. *abhividhau saṃpadā ca* (Pāṇini 5.4.53). [The commentary states: "But that [suffix] occurs only in connection with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*. This is because, by the phrase "only in connection with *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*," the very same condition of connection (*yoga*) is understood to carry over here. [This refers to] *abhividhi*, which signifies totality (*kārtsnya*).
And there must necessarily be a distinction; otherwise, the commencement of two sūtras would be fruitless, since [the desired result] would be established by one alone.
Since that distinction is not known, he asks: "atābhividheḥ."

And so forth; "as in this army," and so forth. Now, in the case of the remaining weapons, what is intended to be expressed is merely a connection with a part of their own self, and not an assumption of a state of modification through their entire self—as in: "In the rainy season, all salt becomes water. Here too, [the same principle applies].

What is intended here is merely the connection of all individual instances of salt with a transformation into the nature of water by way of a single part; it is not that one [instance] undergoes a transformation into the form of a change in its entirety. This is expressed in the passage beginning with "But [in the case of] totality," etc.; for where even a single substance undergoes a transformation into the form of a change in its entirety, [it is not so here].

[The term *kārtsnya* applies] only by way of a single part, yet in that context it constitutes totality (*kārtsnya*). In that regard, if the former rule (*yoga*) were not commenced, then where totality refers to a specific single substance, there the subsequent rule would not apply, because of the absence of "inclusiveness" (*abhividhi*). Now, if this [present] rule were not commenced, then where all the base forms (*prakṛti*)...
If they were to undergo modification only in part, it would not be possible; therefore, both must be produced from a new beginning.

54. *tadadhīnavacane* (Pāṇini 5.4.54). [The compound] *tadadhīnam* means "dependent on that" (*tadāyattam*). [It is analyzed as: *tasyāyattaṃ tadāyattam*. By the word *tat*, the general category of the master (*svāmi-sāmānya*) is expressed; by the word *adhīna*, the general category of the one who is subject to control (*īśitavya-sāmānya*) is expressed.
In order to clarify the very point just mentioned, he says: "The meaning is 'having that as its owner'.

That which has him as its master (svāmī) is "tatsvāmikam" (having that as its owner). Here too, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound because the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is predominant. [This refers to] the object to be ruled.

Furthermore, because it is the meaning of another word (anyapadārtha), that [the object] holds the status of the primary element (pradhānabhāva), whereas the owner (svāmin) holds the status of a subordinate element (guṇabhāva) since he serves merely as a qualifier for it. Regarding the phrase "the generality of owners" (svāmisāmānya) and so forth: "the generality of owners" means the generality of lords (īśvara).

The object of lordship (*īśitavya*) and the lord (*īśvara*)—these two together are expressed by the word *tadadhīna*. How so? Here, by the rule "adhi in the sense of lordship" (*adhir īśvare*, 1.4.97), the word *adhi* receives the designation *karmapravacanīya*;

when used in conjunction with that, the locative case is applied by the rule "the seventh case [is used] for that which is superior (*adhika*) and for that which is the lord (*īśvara*)" (*yasmād adhikaṃ yasya ceśvaraḥ*, 2.3.9). That...

Since this Īśvara is dependent upon that which is to be ruled (*īśitavya*), by implication the term "that which is to be ruled" is expressed through the use of the word *adhi* in conjunction [with it]. Furthermore, this word *adhi* is listed among the *śauṇḍādi* group; when a compound is formed there according to the rule *saptamī śauṇḍaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.40), the meaning of the preceding member is its own general sense.

It occurs because the latter member [of the compound] shares the commonality of being that which is to be ruled (*īśitavya*). When the suffix *kha* is applied by the rule *avaḍakṣādi* (Pāṇini 5.4.7), it results in this very same meaning: "because he is the master of that. Having established it thus, the commonality of being a master and the commonality of being that which is to be ruled are expressed by the word *tadadhīna*. In that regard:

Since the general concept of "owner" (svāmisāmānya) is the meaning of the verbal root (prakṛtyartha), whereas the general concept of "one to be ruled" (īśitavyasāmānya) is the meaning of the suffix (pratyayārtha), he says: "of that which expresses a specific owner," and so forth.
55. *deye trā ca* (Pāṇini 5.4.55).
Regarding the rule "from *rājasa-* comes *rāṣṭra-*," by the preceding [sūtra] only *sāt* occurs.
56. [The suffix *sāti* is applied] after *deva*, *manuṣya*, *puruṣa*, *puru*, and *martya*, in the sense of the second or seventh case endings, diversely (*bahula*).
Now, what is the purpose of the mention of "diversely" (*bahulagrahaṇa*), since it has already been stated that "the *sāti* suffix is optional when expressing completeness"?

In this regard, [one might ask: "Will the word *vibhāṣā* continue to apply here so that the suffix will occur optionally? To this he says: "Because of the mention of *bahula*, it is obtained even elsewhere.
Therefore, since the topic of *vibhāṣā* is already under discussion, the fact that the term *bahula* is employed indicates that it applies even in other instances.
The intention is that it should be so.
57. *Avyaktānukaraṇāt dvyajavarārdhād anitau ḍāc* (Pāṇini 5.4.57). "The imitation of an indistinct sound is 'avyaktānukaraṇa'.
Although in an imitation the specific phonemes do not manifest in their formal shape, nevertheless, due to the similarity of the resonance (*dhvani*), [the imitation is recognized].

Because it is imitated by way of similarity with that [original] alone, it is also called an "imitation" (*anukaraṇa*) of it. A suffix occurs after that which has at least two syllables as its second half; that is, it must not have fewer than two syllables in its second half, such that it becomes a monosyllable even after that. This applies if, before reduplication (*dvirvacana*), it possesses the quality of having at least two syllables in its second half.

From that, it is understood that [the rule applies] when "bhavati" follows; therefore, [the rule] would not apply to forms such as *paṭadi*. For one does not consider that "half [of the word] consists of at least two syllables" in this context; having kept this in mind, he says: "And of that which... and so forth. But if this were the case, then when *ḍāc* follows and reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is performed based upon it—

There would be the condition of having at least two vowels as the minimum, and if that were the case, a circular dependency (*itaretarāśraya*) involving the suffix *ḍāc* would result. Since operations based on mutual dependence are not admitted in the grammatical treatise, he says: "In the case of *ḍāc*, [the substitution is] variously applied," and so forth. If this were a locative case referring to what follows (*parasaptamī*),...
This might be considered a fault; however, this is not a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*), but rather a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*).

In the case of "he makes the sound *paṭat*," when the suffix *ḍāc* is intended—that is, while it is present as the object of operation and resides in the intellect, even before it has actually arisen—the reduplication of the word *paṭat* is first performed.

When that [suffix] has been applied, and the condition of having at least two syllables (*dvyajavarārdhatā*) has arisen, there is the elision of the *ṭi* by the rule *ṭhnityamābhreḍite ḍāci* (Pāṇini 6.1.100). Consequently, the substitution of *pararūpa* occurs for the preceding *t* sound, resulting in the form *damadamākaroti*. This is the case with the word *vamad*.
As before, there is doubling of the word, and then the suffix *ḍāc* is applied.

Regarding the example "he makes a clatter" (*dṛṣatkaroti*), here too, once the doubling has been performed, it results in a word consisting of two syllables with the second half being fewer syllables. This is not an imitation of an indistinct sound. Regarding the example "he makes a crackling sound" (*śratkaroti*).

This is an imitation of an indistinct sound (*avyaktānukaraṇa*), not one consisting of two syllables with the latter half having at least two morae (*dvyajavarārddha*). For even when reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is applied here, it results in a half-verse (*ardha*) consisting of only one syllable, as in the example *kharāṭ-kharāṭākaroti*. In this case, the imitation of the sound *kharāṭ* is treated like the imitation of the sound *paṭat*.

As before, there is the addition of *vṛddhi*, and from that, the suffix *ḍāc*. If only "consisting of two syllables and having a second part" (*dvyajarddham*) were stated, the suffix would not apply here, for in this case there is no state of having two syllables and a second part.
However, when the term "lower part" (*avaragrahaṇa*) is included, it applies here as well; for in that case, [the rule applies] to that which has a second part consisting of two syllables.

Since the suffix *ardha* is even shorter than that, the elision must occur by that very rule; however, it must certainly occur from all other [suffixes]. Otherwise, the mention of the term *avara* would be entirely purposeless, and one would simply have said "after a dissyllabic [stem] ending in *ardha*" (*dvyañ-ardhāt*). [The example is] "he makes the sound *paṭit*. This is governed by the rule *avyaktānukaraṇasyāta itau* (Pāṇini 6.1.98).

Thus, there is the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) for the word *itya*. If *ḍāc* were present here, then after that which ends in *ḍāc*, the root *kṛ* would have to follow immediately after the word "param" is uttered; however, it does not follow "param," and that is undesirable.

Now, for what purpose is the letter *ca* [in the rule]? Since the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) of the word ending in *lat* is already established by the accent of the suffix itself, he says "the letter *ca*" and so forth. When *paṭapaṭā asi* is situated, the elision (*nighāta*) of the word *asi* is effected by the rule *tiṅṅtiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28).

By the rule *svarito vānudāte 'padādau* (Pāṇini 8.2.6), a svarita single-substitute would result [in cases such as *kumāry-au*], yet a svarita is not desired there; for that purpose, the letter *ca* is included.
It is to be understood as having its own meaning (*svārthika*), because there is no distinct additional meaning. But by what [is it so understood]?
Is the letter *y* pleonastic (*svārthika*)? It is so by this very rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
58. *Kṛñaḥ* [the suffix *ḍāc* is applied] after the second and third syllables of words meaning "seed," when used in connection with agriculture (*kṛṣau*).

(5.4.58) Now, since the word *karoti* ("to do") is understood from the previous rule *kṛbhvastiyoge*, for what purpose is the mention of *kṛñaḥ* here? To this and other such questions, [the answer is: three verbal roots (*dhātu*) were introduced [in the preceding rules]; in that context, if the mention of *kṛñaḥ* were absent—
Just as it occurs for the root *kṛ*, so too would it occur for *bhū* and *as*; therefore, the mention of *kṛ* is for the purpose of excluding *bhū* and *as*.
59. [The suffix *kan* is added] after a numeral ending in a *guṇa* vowel.

In the rule "after a numeral" (*saṃkhyāyāḥ*), the genitive case is used in the sense of proximity. In the rule "ending in a *guṇa*" (*guṇāntāyāḥ*), by the phrase "of a word denoting a number," it is indicated that the numeral word itself stands in the genitive case.

He demonstrates this: the word *anta* also signifies a "part" (*avayava*). If it were taken here in that sense, there would be no connection with the word for number (*saṃkhyā-śabda*), for a "part," which is a substance (*guṇa-śabda* in the sense of a quality-part), is not logically applicable to a word denoting a number. Thinking thus, he maintains that this word *anta* signifies "proximity."

Showing this, he says: "The word *guṇa* [is used] at the end, in the sense of 'nearby'. By the word "where," the base (*prakṛti*) is indicated. By "that" and so forth, the meaning is: that base, which is a number, is expressed by means of a word ending in *guṇa*. That which has the word *guṇa* at its end is described as such.

By the phrase "from such as that" (*tādṛśāt*), the meaning is: from a word for number (*saṃkhyā-śabda*) that is of such a nature, that is, from a word for a quality (*guṇa-śabda*) situated in proximity. Now, one might object: in a word ending in a term expressing proximity, the distinction of whether the quality (*guṇa*) precedes or follows the number cannot be determined; and thus...

"Would it not also exist where that [proximity] was previously [located]? This is not a fault; for this term, while denoting proximity, expresses only that proximity which is restricted to a specific location or dependent on another, and not proximity in general—just as a term denoting a part does not denote the mere part itself, but rather [the whole]. What...
In that case? It is precisely because of the specific dress and so forth that it is said, "he performs a double scratching."
60. [The suffix *ḍāc* is added] after the word *samaya* in the sense of "passing time" (*yāpanā*). (Pāṇini 5.4.60) 61.

[The suffix *ḍāc* is added] after *sapattra* and *niṣpattra* in the sense of "causing extreme pain. (Pāṇini 5.4.61) *Sapattraḥ*: that which is together with a wing (*pattra*) is *sapattra*. *Niṣpattraḥ*: from which a wing has gone out is *niṣpattra*.
Excessive oppression means excessive affliction.
62. *niṣkulān niṣkoṣaṇe* (Pāṇini 5.4.62). [The example is] *niṣkulān karoti*. One whose family (*kula*) has been pointed out [and removed] is *niṣkula*.
Here, the word *kula* refers to kinsmen (*bandhu*).
63. Regarding the phrase "conformity with the mind through affection for happiness and compliance":
by performing what is not desired or by failing to perform what is desired, [one causes] the mind of the master or others [to become disturbed].
Oppression is suffering; it is the state of being contrary [to one's will]. That too is a property belonging solely to sentient beings.
64. *Duḥkhāt prātilomye* (Pāṇini 5.4.64).
[The rule] states: *ṭhsvāmyādeścitapīḍanam*.
This refers to the mental affliction (*cita*) resulting from the performance of what is undesirable or the non-performance of what is desired by one's master (*svāmin*) and others.
Oppression is suffering that is contrary to one's will; that too is a property of sentient beings alone.
65. [The suffix *ṇic* is applied] after the word *śūla* in the sense of "cooking" (*pāka*). (Pāṇini 5.4.65). For example: *śūlākaroti māṃsam* ("he cooks the meat"). The meaning is "he cooks."

66. After *satya*, [the suffix *ṇic* is applied] in the sense of taking an oath. (5.4.66) 67. After *madrā*, [the suffix *ṇic* is applied] in the sense of performing a ritual shaving. (5.4.67) Regarding "madrākaroti": it means he performs a shaving preceded by auspicious rites.

Regarding the statement "it should be stated that [the suffix] also [occurs] after *bhadra*": the meaning is that this form of the rule—that the suffix *ḍāc* occurs after the word *bhadra*—must be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the particle *ca* ("and") is carried over from the rule "after *samaya*, in the sense of 'delaying'" (Pāṇini 5.4.60); and that particle serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned. By means of it...
"It will come from Bhadra as well."
68. *Samāsāntāḥ* (5.4.68).

The phrase “*samāsāntāḥ*” is a governing heading (*adhikāra*). By means of the rules to be stated hereafter, such as *bahuvrīhau saṃkhyeye ḍajabahugaṇāt* (5.4.73), [the suffixes] are applied by virtue of being *bahuvrīhi* compounds and so forth.

They will be prescribed according to the specific type of compound; even where there is no explicit mention of "bahuvrīhi" and so forth, the compound as a whole is indicated as the base. For example, in the rule *ṭhac pratyanvavapūrvāt sāmalomnaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.75), it follows that by the very force of the context, the suffixes forming compound-final elements (*samāsānta*) are [intended].

[The forms] will be understood; so what is the purpose of including the term "compound" (*samāsa*)? [It is for cases] where neither of these two [conditions] exists—such as in the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmānakṣe* (Pāṇini 5.4.74).
For that purpose, the inclusion of the word "suffix of a compound" (*samāsānta*) is made. This word *anta* also has the sense of "proximity" (*sāmīpya*), if...

Thinking that its mention here would be redundant—since the proximity [of the suffixes] such as *ḍac* and others is already established by their status as "following an affix" (*pratyayaparatva*) alone, which would render the word *anta* meaningless—he says:
"The word *anta* is understood here as denoting a 'part' (*avayava*)," and showing this, he says: "the parts..."
Thus, in order to explain its formation by way of an alternative method, he says: "ekadeśāḥ" (parts).

By employing the word *ekadeśa* here, it is meant that the suffixes to be mentioned later occur after the final member of the compound—which is the meaning of the compound—prior to the rule for forming the compound itself; only afterwards does the compoundation take place. For it is thus [that the formation occurs].
They become parts of the compound if they were to exist prior to the formation of the compound;

having first applied the compound suffixes (*samāsānta*), the compound is subsequently formed with that which ends in them. And thus, since the designation "compound" applies to them as well, it is established that the *ḍac* suffixes and others are constituents of the compound.

Therefore, this must be understood as follows: for one who thinks that when a compound has been formed, the suffixes *ḍa* and so forth must apply, the author of the Vṛtti will say regarding the rule *na kapi* (Pāṇini 7.4.14): "For when the suffix *kap* has been added to the final member (*uttarapada*) in the sense of the compound, subsequently [the rules for the compound] apply."
[If it is argued that] "it must be analyzed as *bhaktavyam*," that contradicts [the rule].

Now, even in this alternative view—where the suffixes such as *ḍaC* are first applied to the final member (*uttarapada*) of the compound, and only afterwards is the compound formed with that resulting form—the same fault remains; for [the rule] states, "optionally after *pathin*."

In such cases as (Pāṇini 5.4.72), would not the grammatical instructions—stating that "after a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in the word *pathin* which follows the negative particle *nañ*, there is optionally an affix at the end of the compound"—be contradicted? This is not so; for their non-contradiction is established in the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* (4.1.1).

Because it has already been established [that they are included]. By the statement "they are included by the mention of that," the compound (*samāsa*) is referred back by the word "that" (*tat*). Since they are constituent parts of the compound, the designation of that [compound] applies to them as well.
Therefore, they are included by the mention of the compound. Now, regarding their being constituent parts of the compound...

"What is the purpose of the suffix *pratyaya*? To this he says: "The purpose," and so forth. [Examples are] *adhirājam* and *uparājam*. In these cases, respectively, the *avyayībhāva* compound is formed in the sense of a case ending (*vibhaktyartha*) and in the sense of proximity (*sāmīpya*). [This is governed by the rules] *avyayībhāve śaratprabhṛtibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.107) and *anaśca* (Pāṇini 5.4.108).
Because the form ending in *ṭac* is included by the mention of *avyayībhāva*,
there is no elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending according to the rule "nāvyayībhāvādato 'm tv apañcamyāḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.83), and the suffix *am* is applied at the end.

The compound *dve purī samāhṛte* ("two cities combined") is formed by the rule *taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca* (Pāṇini 2.1.51). This is then designated as a *dvigu* by the rule *saṃkhyāpūrvo dviguḥ* (2.1.52),
because the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathām* (5.4.74)— which prescribes the suffix *a*— specifically mentions the term *dvigu*.

The suffix *ṅīp* is established by the rule "dvigoḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.21) following a word ending in the locative case (*grahaṇāvakārāntāt*). Regarding the term *kośaniṣadinī*: *kośa* and *niṣad* form a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*).
Then, by the rule "dvandvāccudaṣahāntāt samāhāre" (Pāṇini 5.4.106), the suffix *ṭac* is applied to it.

Because it is included by the mention of *dvandva*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.5 (*ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*) to form *kośaniṣadmanī*, based on the rule 5.2.128 (*dvandvopatāpagarhyāt*), which prescribes the suffix *matup* for the sense "possessing this," provided the word refers to a living being and so forth. The form *sraktvacinī* is similar to the preceding case.

In the words *ṭhvidhuraḥ* and *pradhuraḥ*, the compound is a *prādi-tatpuruṣa* according to Pāṇini 2.2.18 (*kugatiprādayaḥ*), meaning "one whose burden has departed" (*vigato dhuraḥ*) and "one who has gone before the burden" (*pragato dhuraḥ*). As in the previous case, because the term *tatpuruṣa* is included here [in the rule], the elision of the vowel *a* occurs within this *tatpuruṣa*.

By the rule "tulyārtha-tṛtīyā" (Pāṇini 6.2.2) and others, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member is established. Furthermore, the first member is the particle *itarat*, which is udātta on its initial syllable. However, if the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) were not present, the final syllable would be udātta by the accent of the suffix. [Thus we have] *uccairdhuraḥ*.

Regarding the term *nīcairdhuraḥ*: the forms *uccairdhūrasya* and *nīcairdhūrasya* are *bahuvrīhi* compounds. As before, there is the suffix *-a-*; because this is included by the mention of *bahuvrīhi*, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada*) applies according to the rule *bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā pūrvapadam* (Pāṇini 6.2.1). Thus, the first member retains its original accent.
In this case, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) is replaced by an acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*).

The words *sanutar*, *uccais*, *nīcais*, *śanais*, *ṛdhak*, *ṛte*, *yugapat*, *ārāt*, and *pṛthak*— these beginning with *sanutar*— are acutely accented on the final syllable when listed among the *svarādi* (the group of particles beginning with *svara*).
From the recitation.
69. *na pañcamyāḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.69).

[Examples: *surājā*, *atirājā*. Having analyzed [the compounds] as "an excellent king" (*śobhano rājā*) and "a preeminent king" (*atiśayito rājā*), the compound is formed by *kugatiprādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18). [Example: *sugauḥ*. The compound is formed in the same manner as before.
In this case, the suffix *ṭac* would otherwise apply by the rule *ṭhgorataddhitaluki* (5.4.92); however, due to this specific statement, it does not occur.
Thus we have *paramarājaḥ* and *paramagavaḥ*. The compound is formed according to the rule *sanmahat* (2.1.64).
Regarding the form *susakthaḥ*: the suffix *ṣac* is applied by the rule *bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇoḥ svāṅgāt ṣac* (Pāṇini 5.4.113).

70. *kimaḥ kṣepe* (Pāṇini 5.4.70). Regarding the example *kiṃrājā*: having analyzed [the compound] as "a censured king" (*nindito rājā*), the compound is formed by the rule *kiṃ kṣepe* (2.1.64). In the case of *kiṃrāja*, however, the word *kim* is used in the sense of a question (*praśna*) and not in the sense of censure (*kṣepa*); thus, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). But is this not so?

According to the rule "Between that which is defined by its specific technical form (*lakṣaṇa*) and that which is stated as a specific word (*pratipadokta*), only the specifically stated one is to be accepted" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 3), only that compound of *kim* which is specifically prescribed by the rule "In the sense of reproach (*kṣepa*)," namely Pāṇini 2.1.64, will be understood [as the one intended here].
Therefore, would the inclusion of the term "reproach" (*kṣepa*) not be redundant? If that is so, then by the inclusion of the term "reproach,"...

This very point makes it known: that this technical rule (paribhāṣā) does not hold. By this, the prohibition is established even in the case of a Bahuvrīhi compound—such as *ninditā dhūryasya* (one whose yoke-pole is censured), resulting in *kindhuraṃ śakaṭam* (a cart with a faulty pole), or *nirdharaṃ śakaṭam* (a cart without a pole).

71. *Nañ-statpuruṣāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.71). Regarding the example *arāja*: this is a *tatpuruṣa*. In the cases *anṛco māṇavakaḥ* ("the boy who has no Ṛgveda verses") and *adhuraṃ śakaṭam* ("the cart without a yoke"), both are *bahuvrīhi*s.
The letter *a* is as before.
72. *patho vibhāṣā* (5.4.72).
In the word *apatha*, the vowel *a* is substituted as in the previous rule. Its neuter gender is established by the rule *apathaṃ napuṃsakam* (2.4.30).

73. *Bahuvrīhau saṃkhyeye ḍaj-abahugaṇāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.73). In the word *bahuvrīhau*, the locative case is used by transposition (*subvyatyaya*) in the sense of the ablative. This refers specifically to that *bahuvrīhi* compound which is formed by rules such as *saṃkhyāvyayāsanna* (2.2.25) and so forth. Of that [compound], [the suffix *ḍac* is applied].

The application [of the suffix] is to the numbered object (*saṃkhyeya*). But then, why does it not apply in cases where it occurs in the sense of "or" (*vā*), as in *dvitrāḥ* ("two or three") and *pañcaṣāḥ* ("five or six"), and where it occurs in the sense of the suffix *-suC*, as in *dvidaśāḥ* ("twelve") and *tridaśāḥ* ("thirty-three")? This is not a fault;
for even those two occur in the sense of a numbered object, since the meaning of "or" and the meaning of the suffix *-suC* are themselves [conceived as] numbered objects.

And because it is so designated: *upadaśāḥ* means "near ten"; *upaviṃśāḥ* means "near twenty. In *upaviṃśāḥ*, there is the elision of the suffix *ti* by the rule *tiviṃśaterḍiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.142), and for both *a* sounds, the single substitute of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) applies by the rule *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97).

"Near to ten" is *āsannadaśāḥ*; "not far from ten" is *adūradaśāḥ*; "more than ten" is *adhikadaśāḥ*. "Two or three" is *dvitrāḥ*; "five or six" is *pañcaṣāḥ*. In all these cases, [the compound is formed] by the rule beginning with *saṃkhyāvyayāsannādūrādhika-saṃkhyāḥ saṃkhyeye* (Pāṇini 2.2.25).
The *bahuvrīhi* [compound] is, for example, *citraguḥ*. [In this case], the short vowel [of the final member] occurs by the rule *gostriyor upasarjanasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.48). Now, one might object:

"But surely, according to the maxim of the exclusion of *nañ*, *iva*, and so forth (*nañ-iva-yukta-nyāya*), there should be a prohibition of the application of the term 'many' (*bahu*) and 'countless' (*gaṇa*)."

By means of a cognition similar to that, the *bahuvrīhi* compound will be understood only when a numeral is the final member; and since, in cases such as *citragu* ("possessing brindled cows"), there is no possibility [of the application of the rule] at all, what is the purpose of mentioning "numeral"?
This would be so if the word *bahu* were exclusively a term denoting a thing to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*); however, it is not.

There is also the word *vaipulya*. Therefore, if the term *saṃkhyā* (numeral) were not mentioned, there would be no mention of a subsequent member that is a numeral. [The examples] *upabahavaḥ* and *upagaṇāḥ* are *bahuvrīhi* compounds, as previously explained. Regarding the passage beginning with "here" (*atra*), etc.: whether the suffix *ḍāc* is present or absent in the case of *upagaṇāḥ*, there is no difference in the resulting form; however, there is a difference in accent (*svara*).

But it does exist—for if *ḍac* were present, there would be an acute accent on the final syllable; since that is absent, the first syllable becomes acute by virtue of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) of the preceding member.
Regarding the rule "of a numeral" (*saṃkhyāyāḥ*), etc.: the meaning of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is "an additional statement" (*pratipādana*). Of the *tatpuruṣa*...

The meaning is that the suffix *ḍac* must be prescribed after a final member (*uttarapada*) that expresses a numeral. The proof for this is as follows: the word *ca* from the rule "after a numeral ending in *guṇa*" (5.4.59) is carried over [by *anuvṛtti*], and it serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; therefore—
The suffix *ḍac* will occur after a numeral in a *tatpuruṣa* compound; this is for the sake of forms such as *nistriṃśa*.

The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) indicates a class or type. Thus, in the base form *nistriṃśaḥ*, *nistriṃśāni*, or *nistriṃśaḥ*, the rule *mūlapāte pade ṭi* applies. This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18).

The addition of the marker *ḍac* is for the purpose of making the final syllable udātta; otherwise, because the suffix is part of a compound, its accent would be superseded by the accent of the *bahuvrīhi* compound.
74. *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathām ānakṣe* (Pāṇini 5.4.74).

Regarding the phrase "by virtue of semantic capacity" (*sāmarthyāt*): that which has a relationship with something else serves as its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). And it is only with *dhur* that there is a connection with *akṣa*, not with the others. Therefore...
By implication, this qualification "not pertaining to a lunar mansion" (*anakṣa*) is understood to apply to that [suffix] alone, and not to the *ṛc* and so forth.
Furthermore, in the expression "in the case of *anakṣe*," the locative case is used in the sense of the genitive by means of a metrical substitution (*subvyatyaya*).
For this very reason, he says: "pertaining to what is not connected with a lunar mansion," and so on. The connection with the die (*akṣa*) is characterized by the relationship between part and whole.
The term *akṣamabandhinī* means "that which is bound to the axle"; it does not apply to that [wheel] which has such a yoke-pole (*dhur*).
Now, why is it not understood in this way—that [the suffix] does not occur when the axle itself is the object denoted? It is impossible to understand it thus;
for if it were understood in this way, the prohibition would apply only here—namely, in the case of *dṛḍhā dhūr asyākṣasya*.

Regarding the term *dṛḍhadhūr-akṣa*: here, however, it would not apply to *akṣasya dhūḥ* = *akṣadhūḥ*. If that is so, then it is understood as follows: [the prohibition applies] when *akṣa-* is the prior member. Even so, it is impossible to understand it in that way; for if it were understood thus, the prohibition would apply only here—namely, to *akṣadhūḥ*—but not here [in the case of *dṛḍhadhūr-akṣa*].

It may be "dṛḍhadhūrakṣaḥ. Just as it was explained by Vṛttikāra, so it is in both cases, because the compound ends with the word *dhūḥ* which is related to the axle (*akṣa*). Regarding "ardharcaḥ": it is a compound formed according to Pāṇini 2.2.2, "ardhaṃ napuṃsakam," meaning "half of a ṛc" (*ṛco 'rdham*). [The word] "ardharca-"...

And by the rule *puṃsi ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.31), there is also the neuter gender. Regarding the word *bahvṛcaḥ*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one who has many *ṛc*s. Regarding the word *lalāṭapuram*:
this is a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound; or alternatively, it is an *upamita* [compound] meaning "that which fills (*pūri*) the forehead (*lalāṭam*)."

The compound is formed by [the rule] "vyāghrādibhiḥ" (Pāṇini 2.1.56). Regarding the term "nāndīpuram," it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Although this form is established when the word *pura* ending in the vowel *a* is compounded, nevertheless, if the compound were made with the word *pūr* ending in a consonant, then—

The mention of *pura-* is for the purpose of preventing the hearing of [the suffix] at the end of a consonant; for example, *dvīpam*, *antarīpam*, and *samīpam*. These are *bahuvrīhi* compounds meaning "in which water has gone twice," "in which water has gone within," and "in which water has come together," respectively.
In *rājadhūrā*, the substitution of *ī* occurs by Pāṇini 6.3.97 (*dvyantarupasargebhyo'pa īt*).

It is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). In *mahādhuraḥ*, it is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*); the substitution of *ā* occurs by Pāṇini 6.3.46 (*ānmahataḥ*), and the masculine form is applied by Pāṇini 6.3.34 (*striyāḥ puṃvat*) and so forth.

The compounds *sthala-pathaḥ* and *jala-pathaḥ* are genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compounds; alternatively, they may be locative (*saptamī*) compounds due to the split (*yogavibhāga*) of rule 2.1.40. Regarding the *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *ṛc* that has a negative particle (*nañ*) as its prior member, it denotes only a *māṇavaka*.

It is shown that a suffix is desired [only] when it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with many preceding members ending in the vowel *ṛ*, and that such a suffix is desired only in the sense of "Vedic school" (*caraṇa*)— as indicated by the rule "anṛco māṇavako jñeyaḥ" and so forth.
And this [is understood] from the rule "patho vibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 5.4.72).

It should be understood that because the term *vibhāṣā* is carried over [from the previous rule], an optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) is observed; thus we have *anṛkkaḥ* and *bahuvṛkkaḥ*. Here, the suffix *kap* is applied by the rule *śeṣādvibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 5.4.154), and the substitution of *k* for *c* occurs—specifically, the letter *c* is changed to *k*—by the rule *coḥ kuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.30).

75. *ac* [is substituted] after *prati*, *anu*, and *ava*, when followed by *sāman* and *loman*. (5.4.75) The example is *pratisāmam*. *Pratisāmam* means "gone toward the *sāman*"; it is a *prādi*-compound (*avyayībhāva*). Alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi* meaning "one for whom the *sāman* has gone [toward it]. In the case of the *bahuvrīhi*, the word *gata* is not used because its meaning is already conveyed [by the prefix].

It is applied [as follows]: Alternatively, *sāmapratī* is an avyayībhāva compound formed by *avyayaṃ vibhakti-* (Pāṇini 2.1.6) and so forth, meaning "in accordance with the pitch" (*yathārthe*). Or, it is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that which has followed the pitch. *Avasāmam* is similar to the former [example]. In *anulomam* and so forth, it is [treated] according to the former [rule].
It is the same. In the case of "ṭh valomam" and so forth, the *prādi* compounds and other such formations should be understood as before.
Regarding the rule "kṛṣṇodakpāṇḍupūrvāyāḥ": this refers to a feminine word preceded by the words *kṛṣṇa*, *udaka*, or *pāṇḍu*.
The suffix *ac* is prescribed after the word *bhūmi* [when it denotes a region]. For example: "In this region the land is black" (*kṛṣṇā bhūmir asmin deśe*) becomes *kṛṣṇabhūmo deśaḥ*;

"In this region the land faces north" (*udīcī bhūmir asmin deśe*) becomes *udagbhūmaḥ*; "In this region the land is pale" (*pāṇḍur bhūmir asmin*) becomes *pāṇḍubhūmaḥ*. Furthermore, the suffix *ac* is prescribed after the words *godāvarī* and *nadī*. These...
The words *nadī* ("river") and *godāvarī* ("Godāvarī") become neuter when they follow a numeral. For example, the collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) of five Godāvarīs is expressed as *pañcagodāvaram*;
likewise, the aggregate of five rivers is *pañcanadam*. In these cases, the *avyayībhāva* compound is formed according to the rule "nadībhiśca" (Pāṇini 2.1.20).

Regarding the phrase "even from *bhūmi*" and so forth: it is not only desired [as a compound] after *nadī* and *gīdāvarī*, but also after *bhūmi* when it is preceded by a numeral. In examples such as *dvibhūmaḥ*, it is in all cases a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Regarding the passage beginning with "tat," the teachers establish this— even the word *kṛṣṇabhūma* and others— by means of a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*).

76. [The suffix *ka* is applied] after the word *akṣi*, except when there is non-visibility (*adarśanāt*). (Pāṇini 5.4.76) The prohibition "except when there is non-visibility" is established. Examples are *kabarākṣam* and *gavākṣam*. These two are conventional terms (*rūḍhiśabda*); one should not insist upon the meaning of their constituent parts here. *Kabarākṣam*...

The intention is that the term *gavākṣa* is not established [by this derivation]. This might be argued: "This is established by the prohibition of 'seeing' (*darśana*), because [the suffix -aṇ] occurs in the sense of 'that by which one sees'; yet it is not 'seeing,' nor is anything seen by means of a *kabara-akṣa* (a variegated eye), nor even by means of a *gavākṣa* (a window). To this, he says: "By that also," and so forth.

This word "darśana" is well-known in the sense of the eye, which is a part of a living being; for instance, one uses the expression "darśana" even for that which is perceivable by the eye. Therefore, by virtue of its conventional usage, the word "darśana" is a synonym for the eye, and it is this meaning that is accepted here.

*acatura-vicatura-sucatura-strī-puṃsa-dhenu-anaḍuh-ṛksāma-vāṅmanasa-akṣi-bhruvad-āra-gava-ūrvaṣṭhīva-padaṣṭhīva-naktandiva-rātrindiva-ahardiva-sarajasa-niśśreyasa-puruṣāyuṣa-dvyāyuṣa-tryāyuṣa-ṛgyajuṣa-jātokṣa-mahokṣa-vṛddhokṣa-upaśuna-goṣṭhaśvāḥ* | (5.4.77) [The rule] "in a compound, even when there is a restriction (*vyavasthā*)" and so forth.
The rule for the formation of compounds and the restriction regarding non-compounds— such as that in some cases there is only a *bahuvrīhi* and in others a *dvandva*,
and so forth— is to be understood from *nipātana* (specific grammatical irregularity) alone,
because there is no other basis for such a distinction. By the word "also" (*api*), other operations such as the elision of the *ṭi* suffix are likewise implied.
This must be understood from the very fact of its being a *nipātana* (an irregular formation).

For, by the rule beginning with "saptamyarthavṛttayoḥ," a compound is prescribed for two indeclinables (*avyaya*) that function in the sense of the locative case and where the substratum (*ādheya*) is the predominant factor.

Therefore, it should be understood that this occurs solely by virtue of the irregular derivation (nipātana). Because of the word "api" (also), the compound as well exists solely by virtue of irregular derivation. [The example] is "ahardivam. In this, the letter *n* is replaced by *r* according to Pāṇini 8.2.69, "ro'supi. As for the phrase beginning with "nanu ca," the employment of words is indeed for the sake of conveying meaning.

Since the meaning has already been expressed by one synonym, the employment of a second is not possible; *ahar* and *divā* are synonyms, so how could there be a *dvandva* compound of these two? The sense is that it is not possible in any way. However, the employment of what has already been stated is not contradictory when intended to indicate distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).

Thinking thus, he says: "In the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*)," and so forth. Since a *dvandva* compound arising in the sense of "and" (*cārtha*) would not apply in the sense of repetition, it is therefore prescribed as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). One [example] is the *avyayībhāva* compound.
"In the sense of totality (*sākalya*)"—this is by the rule beginning with "An indeclinable [compounded] with a case-ending" (Pāṇini 2.1.6). An example is *sarajasaṃ*.
In the case of *niḥśreyasa*, there is the substitution of *sa* for *saha* according to Pāṇini 6.3.81 (*avyayībhāve ca kāle*).

The form *niḥśreyasa* is a *prādi-samāsa*. The form *niḥśreyaska* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one by whom the highest good is certain," with the suffix *kap* added according to Pāṇini 5.4.154 (*śeṣād vibhāṣā*).

"Confused regarding the *ṛc* and the *yajus*": one who, due to being deluded, considers the *ṛc*s and the *yajus*s [to be something else] is expressed by the term *ṛgyajuḥ* using a *bahuvrīhi* compound. "Then there is the *avyayībhāva*":
this refers to proximity according to the rule beginning with *avyayaṃ vibhakti* (Pāṇini 2.1.6). "Absence of the elision of the *ṭi*" and so forth; as in *upaśuna*.

In this context, the absence of *ṭi*-elision [of the final vowel] in the word *maghavat* is due solely to a formal irregularity (*nipātana*), according to the rule "ṭhnastaddhite" (Pāṇini 6.4.144). Since the rule "śvayuvamaghonāmataddhite" (Pāṇini 6.4.133), which prescribes semivowel-vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) for the words *śvan*, *yuvan*, and *maghavan* when a *taddhita* suffix does not follow, would otherwise not apply in the case of a *taddhita* suffix, that very vocalization occurs here only by virtue of the formal irregularity.

"It occurs," [referring to] "in the section on *caturoc*" and so forth. The meaning is that an addition (*upasaṃkhyānam*)— that is, an explanatory rule (*pratipādanam*)— must be made for the vowel following the word *catura* when it follows the words *tri* or *upa*.
Therefore, as before, one should proceed by resorting to a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*): "three or four" is *tricaturaḥ*;
"near four" is *upacaturāḥ*. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to [Pāṇini 2.2.25] *saṃkhyāvyayāsannadūrādhikasaṃkhyāḥ saṃkhyeye*.
In that regard, [the rule] *bahuvrīhau saṃkhyeye*...
Since the suffix *ḍac* would have applied by the rule "ḍajbahugaṇāt" (Pāṇini 5.4.73), the suffix *ac* is here prescribed instead.

78. [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the words] *brahman* and *hastin* when followed by *varcas*. (5.4.78) Examples: *brahmavarcasam*, *hastivarcasam*. These are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). This word *varcas* signifies "splendor" or "brilliance."

It should be stated that [the suffix] also occurs after the words *palya* and *rājan*. The meaning is that this should be explained as having the sense that the suffix *ac* occurs after the word *varcas* when it follows the word *palya* or the word *rājan*.
And its explanation should be made precisely as before, by resorting to the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*).

79. *avasamandhebhyastamasaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.79). Regarding the form *avattamasam*: this is either a *prādi*-compound meaning "that from which darkness has departed" (*avahīnaṃ tamasā*) or "that which has departed from darkness" (*avahīnaṃ tamaḥ*). Likewise, [the forms] *saṅgatatamasam* and *saṅgatam* [are explained similarly].

*Tamaḥ*—it is "thick darkness" (*santamasa*). From the root *andh*, with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) because it causes blindness, we have *andhayati*; from that [denominative base], we have *andham*. That which is both blindness (*andha*) and darkness (*tamaḥ*) is "blinding darkness" (*andhatamas*). It is called such because it makes the darkness blind.

80. *śvas* [is compounded] with *vasīyaḥ* and *śreyasaḥ*. (Pāṇini 5.4.80) Examples: *śvovasīyam*, *śvaḥśreyasam*. Having analyzed [the compounds] as *śvovasīyaḥ* and *śvaḥ śreyaḥ*, the compound is formed because they belong to the *mayūravyaṃsaka*-class. Regarding the phrase "and by its very nature" (*svabhāvācca*), etc.: although...

Although the word *śvas* refers elsewhere to a specific point of time, here, in a compound, it conveys praise or eulogy directed toward the object denoted by the final member of the compound as a subject of benediction. Why? Because of its inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
For the denotation of meaning by words is innate; in this case, that very nature is the cause.
"This is a synonym for *ṭhśvovasīyasam*"; by the word "of this" (*asya*), the term *śvaḥśreyasam* is indicated.
81. *anvavataprādrahasaḥ* | (5.4.81) [The word] *anurahasam* [is formed as follows]: this word *rahaḥ* occurs in the sense of "secrecy" (*aprakāśe*).

[The compound] *anurahasam* means either "that which has entered into secrecy" (*anugataṃ rahasaḥ*) or "that which has entered into seclusion" (*anugataṃ rahaḥ*), being a *prādi*-compound. Alternatively, it means "that in which secrecy has entered" (*anugataṃ raho'smin*).

Or it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound: *ṭhavarahasam*. It is either a *prādi* compound meaning "that from which secrecy (*rahas*) has been removed" (*avahīna-rahas*), or a *bahuvrīhi* meaning "in which secrecy has been removed. Furthermore, *taptarahasam* is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) meaning "that which is both heated and secret. This refers to the secret [act] that has arisen when the hair is shaved.
It is not perceived by anyone; therefore it is called *taptarahasa*. It is "heated" (*tapta*) as if by heat; for just as that which is heated by fire cannot be perceived by anyone, so too is this.
82. [The suffix *ka* is applied] after *prati* when it follows a word standing in the seventh case (*saptamī*).

(5.4.82) Regarding the term "standing in the seventh case" (*saptamīstha*): that which stands in the seventh case is *saptamīstha*; the suffix *kap* is added by [Pāṇini 3.2.4] *supi sthaḥ*. Thus, that which exists in the sense of the seventh case is likewise called *saptamīstha*.
He says that it occurs in the sense of the locative case (*saptamī*): "pratyuraḥ" means "that which has gone toward the chest. The compound is formed by the rule:
"Words beginning with *ati* are compounded with a word in the accusative case when they have the sense of 'surpassing' and so forth" (Vārttika 91).

83. *anugavamāyāme* (Pāṇini 5.4.83). [The commentary says: "When extension (*āyāma*) is to be expressed. Extension means length. This word ends in the suffix *a*, which has the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). The meaning is: "when extension is the thing to be expressed."

Otherwise, there would be no grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "the carriage follows the cows" (*anugavaṃ yānam*). Here, "carriage" (*yāna*) means "motion" (*āyāma*). Thus, "the carriage follows the cows" means that the motion of the carriage is just like that of the cows.

Regarding the expression *gavāṃ paścāt*: this is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti-* (Pāṇini 2.1.6) and others, used here in the sense of "behind. As in the previous case, there is shortening of the vowel in the word *go*. When the suffix is to be prescribed after the word *anu*, the specific form *anugavam* is taught as a *nipātana* (irregular formation); this is for the purpose of including well-known usage. By means of that—
Whatever is external to the cows and equal to the cows exists in that very place, and not elsewhere.
84. *dvistāvā* and *tristāvā* are [forms of] the sacrificial altar (*vedi*).

(5.4.84) *dvistāvā*, *tristāvā* *vediḥ*. (6.4.148) When the elision [of the suffix] has been made, the elision of the *ṭi* of the word *tāvat* is prescribed as a grammatical anomaly (*nipātana*). By the rule "and it is a compound" (*samāsaśca*), the forms of the words *dvi* and *tri* are prescribed as anomalies.
By the words "as many as are in the archetype" (*yāvantaḥ prakṛtau*), etc., he demonstrates the purpose of the rule of non-elision (*na-pātana*).
The terms *prakṛti* (archetype) and *vikṛti* (ectype) denote specific types of ritual actions;
for among the various ritual acts, one called a sacrifice (*yāga*) is designated by the word *prakṛti*, while another is designated by the word *vikṛti*.

85. *upasargād adhvanaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.85). Regarding the form *prādhvam*: it is a *prādi*-compound. In that context, the compound *prādhvam* is formed by the rule "Words beginning with *ati* are compounded with a word in the accusative case in the sense of 'having traversed,' etc. (*atyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe dvitīyayā*, Vārttika 91). [The form] *niṣkrāntam adhvanaḥ* ("gone out from the road") is [formed by the rule] "*nirādayaḥ*... [with the fifth case].

Regarding the rule "after [words] such as *krānta*, the fifth case ending [is used] in the sense of 'path'" (Vārttika 95), the term *prādhvam* is equivalent to this [term *adhyam*]. Furthermore, in this context, the prefix (*upasarga*) is not an indicator of motion (*gati*). Why is that?
Because there is an absence of connection with an action (*kriyā*).

86. *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ saṃkhyāvyayādeḥ* (5.4.86). [The rule] "there is elision of *mātrac*" refers to that which is prescribed by [the rule] *pramāṇe dvayasac-dhanañ-mātracaḥ* (5.2.37) and so forth. The form *niraṅgulam* is equivalent to *niradhvam*.
The term "ṣaḍaṅgula" (six-fingered) is similar to this [previous example].
The term "pañcāṅguli" (five-fingered) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

87. [The suffix *cha* is applied] after *ahan*, after words meaning "all," "one part," "numbered," and "meritorious," and after *rātri*. (Pāṇini 5.4.87) "The mention of *ahan* is for the sake of forming a *dvandva* compound"—this is the intended rule (*iṣṭi*). It is not for the sake of a *tatpuruṣa* compound; for a *tatpuruṣa* is impossible in its primary sense [of "day-night"]. In the case of a *dvandva*, the basis is each individual member of the compound. Thus: [The examples follow: *ahardivam*, *sarvāhnam*, *pūrvāhṇam*, *saṃkhyātāhnam*, *puṇyāhnam*, *rātryahar*, *dvyahar*, *tryahar*, etc.]
For— whether the night, characterized by the day, is expressed by the word "day," or the day, characterized by the night,

is expressed by the word "night" through a figurative construction, then a tatpuruṣa compound in apposition (sāmānādhikaraṇya) consisting of "day and night" is indeed possible. Therefore, this is the intended interpretation.

This much would have been said: "A dvandva compound is desired. And here is the evidence for this—the rule "hemantaśiśirāv ahno-rātre ca chandasi" (Pāṇini 2.4.28), which prescribes the substitution of the word *rātra* for the final member of a dvandva compound, as in the example "ahorātraḥ" (day and night).

The masculine gender [of *sarvarātraḥ*] is established by Pāṇini 2.4.29: *rātrāhnāhāḥ puṃsi*. By Pāṇini 8.2.68: *ahan*, and the Vārttika 924: *rūparātrirathantareṣūpasaṃkhyānam*, the *n* is replaced by *r*, resulting in guṇa. Thus, "sarvarātraḥ" [is formed]. [This is governed by] Pāṇini 2.1.49: *pūrvakālaika-sarva-*.

By the rule beginning with "ityādinā," this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). In the case of "dvirātraḥ," it is a *dvigu* compound for the sake of collective aggregation (*samāhāra*), according to the rule "taddhitārthottarapada" (Pāṇini 2.1.51); furthermore, by the rule "dviguśca" (2.1.23), it receives the technical designation of *tatpuruṣa*. As for "atirātraḥ," it is [formed] by the word "atyadhvam."
This is the same as in the case of *nīrātraḥ*. There is elision of the *repha* by [Pāṇini 8.3.14] *roḥ*.
The lengthening is by [Pāṇini 6.3.111] *ḍhralope pūrvasya*.
88. *ahno'hna etebhyaḥ* (5.4.88). [The commentary says:

"He will state the suffix *ṭac* in the rule *ṭhrājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac*. Now, why is it that this substitute is not understood as applying only when the suffix *ac* has already been added by another rule? It is impossible for this to be understood in that way; for [the substitute] cannot [be applied] there.
Since the suffix *ṭac* is prescribed after a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in the word *hyah* by some [rule], how could it be the cause for the substitution [of *hy-ah*]?

Or, if *ṭac* is prescribed by means of a split (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule "after *hyah*, *ṭac*" (Pāṇini 5.4.89), even so, this statement would be purposeless; for once the vowel suffix *ac* has been applied, [the form] would be governed by "the *l* of *alpa* and *apo* is replaced by *na*" (Pāṇini 6.4.134).

Since the substitution [of *ahan*] for *ahar* is established by this very rule, one should not think that the elision of the *ṭi* suffix (*ṭilopa*) would apply; for there is the restrictive rule: "The elision of the *ṭi* occurs only before the suffixes *takh* and *kha*" (Pāṇini 6.4.134). Therefore, this [substitution] is indeed an exception (*apavāda*) to the elision of the *ṭi*. But why is this substitution improper? What, then, is that [which makes it improper]?

What is the capacity [of the word] by which the word *ahan* is not accepted as being prior? To this he says: "For not from the word *ahan*," and so forth. Regarding the form *dvyahnaḥ*: the compound is formed by the rule "taddhitārtha" (Pāṇini 2.1.51), meaning "that which occurs in two days" (*dvayor ahnoḥ bhavaḥ*); then the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "tatra bhavaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.3.53).

In the case of *taddhita* [suffixes], there is elision (*luk*) by the rule "dvigor lug anapatye" (Pāṇini 4.1.88). Regarding "atyahnaḥ": this is a compound (*samāsa*) with the word *adhyana* as the first member. Regarding "nirahnaḥ": here too, it is a compound with the word *adhvana* as the first member. Regarding "sarvāhṇaḥ": this is a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*).
He will state the prohibition [to the effect that] "and [the suffixes] having a sense other than those [already mentioned]" (Pāṇini 5.4.90).
89. *Na saṃkhyādeḥ samāhāre* (5.4.89). In the case of "dvyahaḥ," there is elision of the suffix *ṭi* by the rule *ahnaṣṭakhoreva* (6.4.145).

90. *Utamaikābhyāṃ ca* (5.4.90). [The word] *puṇyāham* [is derived as follows]: the compound is formed by [the rule] *viśeṣaṇam* (2.1.57), etc. [The word] *ekāhaḥ*: here too, [the compound is formed] by *pūrvakālaika-* (2.1.49).

By such statements as these, one might ask: "How, then, is the prohibition [of the feminine suffix] obtained from the word *puṇya* by the rule *ṭhutamaikābhyām*? To this he says: "The word *ṭhuta* signifies the final [element]," and so forth. This is because, in the sūtra *ahaḥsarvekadeśa-* (Pāṇini 5.4.87) and others, the word *puṇya* is seen at the end [of the list]. [The suffix] *ṭhak* is added to words ending in *ṭh*.

Thus, even though the word *uttama* is present, the term *antya* (final) is employed here for the purpose of negation. Therefore, he expresses the word *puṇya*. Now, why was the mention of *puṇya* alone not made, so that the sūtra would be more concise? To this he says: "The mention of *puṇya* alone," and so forth. For there is indeed variety [in the usage].

This is accepted by the author of the Sūtra, and that [acceptance] is realized when there is the mention of "excellent" (uttama). For the mention of "excellent" was made for the sake of variety, and not for the sake of mentioning "merit" (puṇya).
Regarding the passage beginning with "some," etc.: although the mention of "merit" ought to have been made, the mention of "excellent" was instead employed.

The purpose of that [mention]—some explain it as follows: so that there may be an understanding of the prohibition even for the word *uttama* when it is used in the plural. There is a transfer of the designation [of the primary term] to something else due to proximity, as in "the hamlet on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*) and so forth. Therefore, it is capable...
Their intention is that the word *uttama* (highest) denotes the word *upottama* (penultimate) by virtue of proximity.
By the words "by that" (*tena*) and so forth, he demonstrates the result of the prohibition through the understanding of the word *upottama*.

91. *rājāhassakhibhyaṣṭac* (5.4.91). [Examples: *paramāhaḥ*, *uttamāhaḥ*. These are *karmadhāraya* compounds according to the rule *sanmahatparamottamotkṛṣṭāḥ pūjyamānaiḥ* (2.1.61). [Example: *madrarājaḥ*. This is a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound. But how is it that the word *rājan* is included [in this rule]?
Why does the designation *rājñī* not [apply]? To this he says: "by the paribhāṣā concerning gender," and so forth.

The "paribhāṣā concerning gender" is simply this: "When there is the mention of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the mention includes that which is qualified by gender as well" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 29). [The rule] "of the short vowel" (*ladhv-akṣarasya*)...

That whose purpose or objective is the formation of a long vowel by the rule of *savarṇadīrgha* is described as such. Here, since the rule "a short syllable is placed first" applies, when it would have been appropriate for either *sakhi* or *ahan* to be placed first, the fact that the word *ahan* is placed last serves the purpose of enabling the *savarṇadīrgha* with the word *rājan*. The actual usage is as follows:
In some instances, this does not indicate that the suffix *ṭac* occurs only after the word *rājan* when it possesses the vowel *a*;
for it does not occur after a word ending in *ī*, since a long vowel resulting from the combination of *ī* with *a* as a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) vowel is impossible.

92. *gorataddhitaluki* (Pāṇini 5.4.92). In the case of *pañcagavam*, there is a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhitārtha*), according to Pāṇini 2.1.51. In *pañcaguḥ* as well, [the *go* stem is used] in the sense of a secondary derivative. In *rājagavam*, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). [The elision of the case-ending occurs] by *supo...* [Pāṇini 2.4.71].

By the rule *dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.71), there is elision (*luk*) of the *sup* [case-ending]. In the form *rājagavīyati*, the suffix *kyac* is added by *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (3.1.8); there is elision of the *sup*, and by *kyaci ca* (7.4.33), the vowel is changed to *i*. There is indeed elision here, but it is of the *sup*, not of the *taddhita* [suffix]. This is due to a transposition of the word order (*paravyatyaya*).
The locative case is used in the sense of the ablative. How is this known? From its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *go* ending in the fifth (ablative) case.
93. *agra-ākhyāyām urasaḥ* (5.4.93).

This indicates that the word *uraḥ* [chest/front] must be a designation for "the foremost" (*agra*). Thus, *aśvora-sam* ("the foremost among horses") is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*), meaning "the chief of horses. Similarly, *hastyura-sam* ("the foremost among elephants").
"Between the two chariot-horses."
94. *ano'śmāyassarasāṃ jātisaṃjñayoḥ* | (5.4.94) Regarding *upānasa*: it is a *prādi*-compound meaning "that which has approached" (*upagatam anaḥ*). Regarding *mahānasa*:
it is a *karmadhāraya* compound according to the rule *sanmahatparamottamotkṛṣṭāḥ pūjyamānaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.61), meaning "great fire" (*mahad anaḥ*).

"Ṭhamṛtāśmaḥ" (stone from the ṭhamṛta region) and "piṇḍāśmaḥ" (ball-shaped stone) are examples of descriptive compounds (viśeṣaṇasamāsa). Similarly, "kālāyasam" (black iron) and "lohitāyasam" (red iron) are [descriptive compounds]. "Maṇḍūkasarasam" (frog-pond) and "jalasarasam" (water-pond) are examples of genitive compounds (ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa).
Regarding the term "sadanaḥ": it is a compound (samāsa) similar to that of "mahānasa" (a kitchen).
95. *grāmakauṭābhyāṃ ca takṣṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.95). [The commentary states:

"The meaning is 'one who is common to many'. This is because the word *grāma* is used here in the sense of a collection of districts (*janapada*). The form *kauṭatakṣaḥ* is derived through compounding in the same manner as before.
96. After *ati*, [the word] *śvan* [is treated as if ending in the nominative case].
(5.4.96) Thus, "atiśvaḥ" is a *prādi*-compound.

97. [The suffix *kan* is applied] after a word denoting a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), when it refers to something inanimate. (Pāṇini 5.4.97) In the example "ṭhākarśaśvaḥ" ("like a dog"), the dog (*śvan*) is the standard of comparison.
In the example "ṭhaśvā loṣṭaḥ" ("a clod of earth like a horse"), the word "horse" (*aśva*) refers to the clod of earth, which is inanimate; it does not refer to an animal.
This is an example [of a compound]. "A monkey-dog" (*vānaraśva*): this is a compound formed according to Pāṇini 2.1.56, *upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ*.
Here, the word "monkey-dog" (*vānaraśva*) refers to a living being.

98. And [the suffix *ṭac* is applied] after *uttara*, *mṛga*, and *pūrva* when they are in composition with *sakthi*. (5.4.98) The form *uttarasaktham* is derived as follows: the compound *uttaraṃ sakthnaḥ* is formed by the rule *pūrvāparādharottaramekadeśinaikādhikaraṇe* (2.1.57). Alternatively, it is a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) meaning "the northern thigh. Similarly, *mṛgasaktham*.
Thus, this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). "Pūrvasaktham" is equivalent to "uttarasaktham. "Phalakasaktham" is a compound formed by [the rule] "viśeṣaṇam" (Pāṇini 2.1.57), etc.

99. *nāvo dvigoḥ* | (5.4.99) [The suffix *ṅīp* is applied after the word *nau* when it is the final member of a *dvigu* compound. Examples: *dvināvam*, *trināvam*. Here, the *dvigu* compound is formed by rule 2.1.51, *taddhitārthottarapada...*. [In the case of] *dvināvadhanaḥ*: once the *bahuvrīhi* compound "one whose wealth consists of two ships" (*dve nāvau dhanaṃ yasya*) has been formed...
By that same rule, a *dvigu* compound is formed with the subsequent word following the two preceding words; for example, *pañcanāvapriya*.

This is similar to the previous case: *dvināvarūpya* and *dvināvamaya*. By that same rule, a *dvigu* is formed when a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) meaning is intended; as before, the suffixes *rūpya* and *mayaṭ* are applied.

In the case of *rājanauḥ*, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). In the case of *pañcanauḥ*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṭhak* prescribed by rule 5.1.19 (*ārhīya*), according to rule 5.1.28 (*adhyardhapūrvam...*) and so forth.

100. *ardhācca* (5.4.100). [The suffix] *ṭhañ* [is added after *ardha* when compounded with *nau*]. Now, one might object: since it is stated that "in a *dvandva* and a *tatpuruṣa*, the gender is that of the final member" (2.4.26), this word ought here to be feminine. To this he says: "the gender is not that of the final member..."
"It comes to be," and so forth.
101. *khāryāḥ prācām* (Pāṇini 5.4.101). [Examples: *dvikhāri*, *trikhāri*. As before, there is shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upasarjana-hrasva*).
In some places, the reading is *ardhakhārī*. Here, once the shortening of the penultimate vowel of the *aic* diphthongs has been applied, [the rule follows].

The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied because the word is read in the *bahv-ādi* group [of the Gaṇapāṭha], according to the rule: "Some [teachers] hold that the feminine suffix is applied after every [word] ending in a short vowel, except for those denoting an object. (Gaṇasūtra 51).

102. [The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied] after the words *dvau* and *trayaḥ* when followed by *añjali*. (Pāṇini 5.4.102). For example: "bought for two *añjalis* is *dvyañjali*" (*dvābhyām añjalibhyāṃ krītaḥ dvyañjaliḥ*). As before, there is elision (*luk*) of the *arhīya* suffix. For example: "one who is fond of two *añjalis* is *dvyañjalipriyaḥ*. As before, there is a *dvigu* compound with the subsequent member.
103. *anasantān-na-puṃsakāt chandasi* (5.4.103).
[The forms] *hasticarma* and so forth are genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compounds.
Regarding *sutrāmāṇam*: *su-trāmā* is a *prādi*-compound; [the rule applies] "for others as well... [is understood].
In *vṛśyate* (6.3.137), there is lengthening of the first member;
in the second case singular, there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca* (6.4.8), etc.;
and in *anehasām*, there is the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* by the rule *aṭ kupvāṅ* (8.4.2), etc. Thus ends [the section on] *anehasām*.
The word *anehas* is in the masculine gender, and this is the genitive plural.

The phrase "the mention of the option (*vāvacana*)" is understood as the remainder [of the rule]. By the term *vāvacana*, the mention of *prāk* (before) is intended here; by that, they are stated as optional, meaning that the suffix (*pratyaya*) is made known or expressed by it.
Having done so, this is what is meant: "The term *prāk* (before) is understood from [the rule] *khāryāḥ prācām* (5.4.101).
As for the fact that the term *prāk* is understood, he shows what is thereby established as desired by means of the example "brahmasāma."
Regarding the term "ṭhdevaccchandaḥ," in both cases it is a genitive compound (ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa).

104. *brahmaṇo jānapadākhyāyām* (5.4.104). Regarding the phrase *jānapadākhyāyām*: here, the word *jānapada* has the sense of an abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*). For this very reason, the commentary (*vṛtti*) states: "If the status of being a *jānapada* is expressed by means of a compound with *brahman*. It occurs [as follows].

For indeed, even without an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), there can be an expression where the state of being (*bhāva*) is the primary meaning, as in the rule: "The dual and singular endings are used for two and one" (Pāṇini 1.4.22). But how is it possible to qualify the "locality" (*jānapadatva*) of Brahman, since there is only a single mention of "Brahman" here? By that [mention]...
And why is the compound specified? This is not so; by means of *tantra* (the principle of simultaneous application), two instances of the word *brahman* are uttered.

Therein, by one it is the compound that is specified, and by the other, the status of being a name of a region (*jānapadatva*) is specified—that *tatpuruṣa* compound whose first member is a word denoting a region.
The compound is as before.
105. *kumahadbhyām anyatarasyām* (5.4.105). 106. *dvandvāc cudaṣahāntāt samāhāre* (5.4.106).
"Speech and skin" (*vāk ca tvak ca*) becomes *vāktvacam*; "ladle and skin" (*sruk ca tvak ca*) becomes *sruktvacam*.
*Śrī* and *sruk*—*śrīsruk*; *vāk* and *ūrk*—*vāgūrjam*; *samit* and *dṛṣat*—*samiddṛṣadam*; *sampad* and *vipad*—*sampadvipadam*; *vāk* and *tviṣ*—*vāktviṣam*; *vāk* and *vipruṣ*—*vāgvipruṣam*.

An umbrella and sandals are "umbrella-and-sandals" (*cchatropānaham*). An umbrella and sandals are "umbrella-and-sandals" (*cchatropānaham*). A female cow and a milkman are "female-cow-and-milkman" (*dhenugoduh*).
"Five-words" (*pañcavāk*) is a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a collective. "Speech-restrained" (*vāksamit*).

This [word] ends in the letter *dh*. By the rule "jhalāṃ jaśo'nte" (Pāṇini 8.2.39), the *jaś*-substitution for the letter *dh* occurs, resulting in the letter *d*; then, by the rule "vāvasāne" (Pāṇini 8.4.56), the *car*-substitution occurs, resulting in the letter *t*.

107. *Avyayībhāve śaratprabhṛtibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.106). [The example] is *upaśaradam*. This is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of proximity (*sāmīpya*). [The example] *pratiśaradam* is an *avyayībhāva* compound formed by the rule *lakṣaṇenābhipratī ābhimukhye* (Pāṇini 2.1.14), meaning "toward" (*ābhimukhya*) the autumn.
"ṭhupavipāśam, parativipāśam"—this is as before.

Here, for what purpose are those [roots] ending in *jh* recited, since the suffix is established after those [bases] by the rule "ṭhjhayaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.111) which is to be stated later? To this he says: "those..."

Regarding the passage beginning with "tvatra" and so forth: if these were not mentioned here separately, then the suffix *ṭac* would optionally apply by virtue of the rule *jhayaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.111). Therefore, they are listed separately among those ending in *jhay* so that [the suffix] may apply invariably (*nityam*).

Regarding the rule "ṭhjarāyā jaraśca": after the word *jarā*, the suffix *ṭac* occurs in an *avyayībhāva* compound, and the substitution of *jaras* also takes place—as in *upajarasam*, meaning "near old age.
Regarding the rule "prati-pari-samanubhyo 'kṣṇaḥ": after the word *akṣi*, following the prefixes *prati*, *pari*, *sam*, and *anu*...
The suffix *ṭac* is applied after these [words] *anu*, *pra*, *ati*, *ava*, *sa*, *ni*, *vi*, and *ud*; thus we have *pratyakṣam* and *parokṣam*.
The substitution of *u* for *o* in *parokṣa* occurs by virtue of the rule *parokṣe liṭ* (Pāṇini 3.2.115), which is a specific grammatical injunction (*nipātana*).
Similarly, we have *samakṣam* and *anvakṣam*.
[The examples] "ṭhuparājam" and "pratirājam" are *avyayībhāva* compounds, similar to "upaśaradam" and "pratiśaradam. [The example] "ṭhavyātmam" means "with regard to oneself" (*ātmani adhīti*).
Regarding the meaning of the case ending: "pratyātmam" (individually) is used in the sense of direction, as explained previously.
109. *napuṃsakād anyatarasyām* (5.4.109). 110. *nadī-paurṇamāsī-āgrahāyaṇībhyaḥ* (5.4.110).
By the mention of *nadī*, the actual form [of the word] is understood, not the technical designation (*saṃjñā*). If the designation were understood [here],...

One should not include *paurṇamāsī* and *āgrahāyaṇī* [in the rule]. But would this not be for the purpose of restriction—that [the suffix ṅīṣ] occurs only after *paurṇamāsī* and *āgrahāyaṇī*, which end in long ī and are feminine (nadī)?
This is not so; for if this were the intended purpose, [it would have been formulated differently].
One should say "paurṇamāsī-āgrahāyaṇī"; therefore, there is the mention of the svarita accent. In the word "upanadi," the short vowel occurs by the rule "gostriyor upasarjanasya" (Pāṇini 1.2.48).

111. *jhayaḥ* | (5.4.111) 112. *gireśca senakasya* | (5.4.112) The form *ṭhantargiram* is an *avyayībhāva* compound meaning "within the mountain" (*giraḥ antar*), used in the sense of a case ending. The word *antaḥ*...

Indeed, because it functions with the sense of the locative case, it occurs in the sense of a case ending. Why then does the mention of *Senaka* not serve the purpose of providing an option (*vikalpa*)?

To this he says: "The option (*vikalpa*) indeed continues [to apply]. This is because its purpose is to provide an option; or rather, that [option] is determined by this [mention of Senaka]. The mention of *anyatarasyām* is an option.

Thus it has been stated; here, [the term] from "optionally after a neuter" (5.4.109) is understood by anuvṛtti. Therefore, since the option is already established by that very rule, the mention of Senaka is stated solely for the sake of honor, not for the sake of providing an option. But surely—
"Between two *vibhāṣā* rules, the permanent (*nitya*) rules take effect" (Kātantra Paribhāṣā-vṛtti 11).

Would the mention of Senaka then be for the sake of an option (*vikalpa*), in order to establish the permanence of the preceding rule? This is not so; for if the preceding rule were indeed permanent, [the forms] ending in *jhay*...

The mention [of Senaka] in the rules beginning with "śarat" would be purposeless, as the desired form is already established by the rule "jhayaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.111). Therefore, the mention of Senaka is not for the sake of providing an option; it is solely for the sake of honor.

113. *Bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇoḥ svāṅgāt ṣac* (Pāṇini 5.4.113). Here, "limb" (*svāṅga*) refers to that which is defined technically [by Pāṇini] as "that which is not fluid, possesses form, and is fixed," and so forth (Mahābhāṣya 2.222, Kāśikā 4.1.554). [The example is] *duḥśliṣṭavibhaktiḥ*. [This means] with difficulty...
Those compounds in which the case-endings (*vibhakti*) are joined or connected with difficulty are called *duḥśliṣṭavibhakti*.

And thus—there ought to be a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) due to the connection with a suffix (*pratyaya*), as in the rule "tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.86). [This applies] here by the mention of *sakthi*, *akṣi*, and *pragadha*.

Because the bahuvrīhi compound is intended to be qualified by that which ends in [the word *sakṛt*], it is proper that the case and number of the bahuvrīhi should be the same as those of the word from which it is derived. However, in this instance, the bahuvrīhi ends in the locative singular; whereas from the words *sakṛt* and *akṣi*, the genitive dual would be expected.
Or it may be the dual of the locative case. The mention of "one's own limb" (*svāṅga*) here serves as a qualifier in apposition with *sakthi* and *akṣi*;

consequently, a qualifier in apposition that possesses the same case-ending as the case-endings of the words *sakthi* and *akṣi* is established. By means of such words with their respective case-endings...

Someone, joined with difficulty and hardship, understands the meaning only by relying on the case-endings; therefore, those [words] have ill-fitting case-endings. For what purpose, then, were those words composed? For the sake of variety.

"‘A cart with long poles’ (*dīrghasakthi śakaṭam*), ‘sugarcane with thick joints’ (*sthūlākṣirikṣuḥ*)"—in these cases, the words *sakthi* and *akṣi* do not denote a limb of a living being (*svāṅga*). Rather, a certain part of the cart and of the sugarcane is designated by those terms respectively. However, the definition beginning with "that which is non-fluid and possesses form" (*adravaṃ mūrtimat*, Mahābhāṣya 2.222) does not apply there.

The characteristic of its own member (*svāṅgalakṣaṇa*) exists. Now, since all of this is established even by the suffix *ṭac* under the current rule, for what purpose is another suffix, *ṣac*, introduced? To this he says: "When *ṭac* is applicable," and so forth. [The example is] *dīrghasakthī*.

In the case of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, the *ṅīp* would be anudātta; however, when the suffix *ṣap* is present, the *ṅīṣ* established by "ṣidgaurādibhyaśca" (Pāṇini 4.1.41) becomes udātta.
