Now, one might object that even with *ṅīp*, since it is anudātta, it becomes udātta by the rule of "the accent of the displaced udātta" (*udātanivṛttisvara*). Therefore, [the rule] is not even for the sake of the accent.
Is another condition to be adopted? To this he says: "from *sakthi* and from that which ends in *ā*.

Since the word *vibhāṣā* is understood to carry over from the rule *vibhāṣotpucche* (Pāṇini 6.2.106), by the rule *sakthañcākrāntāt* (Pāṇini 6.2.198), the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) is optionally acute.

It is prescribed as follows: in that case where [the vowel] is acute, when the suffix *ṅīp* follows, after the elision of the acute *a* by rule 6.4.148 (*yasyeti ca*), the suffix *ṅīp* ought to become acute by rule 6.1.161 (*anudātasya ca yatrodyatalopaḥ*). Therefore...

There is no contradiction regarding the suffix *ṅīp*. In that alternative where an acute accent (*udātta*) is not possible, there is no "accent of the disappearance of the acute" (*sty-udāta-nivṛtti-svara*) in *ṅīp*, and thus the acute accent is not applied. However, when *ṅīṣ* is present, the acute accent is established everywhere, because the suffix *ṅīṣ* itself has an acute accent on its final syllable.

114. *aṅgulerdāruṇi* (Pāṇini 5.4.114). That which has two fingers is [called] *dvyaṅgulam*. Since the primary fingers cannot logically have a connection with the wood—which is the meaning of the compound—the term [is applied] by implication (*sāmarthyāt*) to things resembling two fingers.
Thinking that the word *aṅguli* (finger) is applied to the parts of wood when a compound is employed, he says: "having parts similar to fingers," and so forth.
But [one might object]: "In cases such as *dve aṅgulī pramāṇam asya dāruṇaḥ* ('this wood has two fingers as its measure'),..."

There is a connection with the primary fingers; since the connection is with the primary fingers, and this is possible in the case of the primary, is it not improper to take the secondary meaning? To this he says: "But for that which...
and so forth. Because the term *bahuvrīhi* is understood as being carried over [from the previous rule], a suffix is here prescribed after a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

When one intends to express the single meaning "that whose measure is two fingers," a *tatpuruṣa* compound must be formed for the sake of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Once that has been formed, the suffix *ac* must necessarily be applied by the rule "In a *tatpuruṣa*, after *aṅguli* preceded by a numeral or an indeclinable" (Pāṇini 5.4.86). And it is precisely this figurative word *aṅguli* [which is intended].
By the very force of the context, it is stated that this is the object of yoga.
115. *dvitribhyāṃ ṣa mūrdhnaḥ* (5.4.116).

Now, for what purpose is *ṣa* prescribed as a separate suffix, rather than simply prescribing *ṣac*, which is the subject under discussion? [The answer is: so that there may be an option regarding the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*). [This is] by the rule *vibhāṣotpucche* (6.2.196).

Therefore, while the term *vibhāṣā* continues to apply, because of the mention of the word *mūrdhan* ending in *n* in the rule *dvitribhyāṃ pāddanmūrdhasu bahuvrīhau* (Pāṇini 6.2.197), the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) for a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the word *mūrdhan* ending in *n* follows *dvi* or *tri* is optional.

It is prescribed [that the word *mūrdhan* takes the suffix *ṣac*]; otherwise, if the word *mūrdhan* ending in the vowel *a* were intended to have the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound, he would have specified it as already having the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*). In that case, if the suffix *ṣac* were prescribed, then by the power of the marker *c*, there would be a constant acute accent on the final syllable, overriding the optional final accentuation.

It may be so. However, the rule prescribing the option for an acute accent on the final syllable (*vibhāṣāntodāta*) finds its scope where there is no compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*). But in this case, once another suffix has been applied as a compound-ending, the optional acute accent on the final syllable is established. Now, one might object that because of the mention of the form ending in *n* (*nakārānta*), it must refer to a word ending in *n*.
For indeed, the word *mūrdhan* [is such that], when it occurs as a final member of a compound, it ought optionally to be oxytone;
how then could this [accentuation] arise from a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*)? This is not a fault; for he will state:
"Even where a compound-ending suffix is applied, because it functions as an operation of the *bahuvrīhi* and because it is a part of that [compound]."

"The acute accent on the final syllable of the compound indeed occurs. Now, for what purpose is the word *mūrdhan* with a final *n* possible after *dvi* and *tri* in a *bahuvrīhi*, given that it must always be accompanied by a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*), and there is no mention of an option (*vibhāṣā*) in the rule? This is not so.
This is a fault; for that very mention with a final *n* [in the rule] indicates that the compound-ending suffix does not apply optionally.

116. *Appūraṇī-pramāṇyoḥ* (5.4.116). Regarding the phrase "those ending in affixes denoting ordinal numbers": by association with those [affixes] prescribed in the section beginning with *tasya pūraṇe ḍaṭ* (5.2.48), which are employed in the sense of ordinal numbers, [the term *pūraṇa* here refers to them].
They are called by the term *pūraṇa*. Those words which end in a *pūraṇa* suffix are "those ending in a *pūraṇa* suffix.
Regarding the statement "even when the primary feminine *pūraṇī* is intended," it means that even when a suffix beginning with *t* is to be prescribed, that which is the primary [feminine]...

Its inclusion must be made as a *pūraṇī* (a feminine ordinal), so that the application occurs only from that [specific form] and not from any other. But where does its predominance lie? To this he says:
"In which," and so forth. Where the *pūraṇī* enters into the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) as the thing to be expressed, and not merely...

The referent of the compound is indeed the referent of the constituent member that forms part of the compound; in that case, the ordinal suffix (pūraṇī) is predominant, as in "the nights with the auspicious one as the fifth" (*kalyāṇīpañcamā rātrayaḥ*). For here, the analysis (*vigraha*) is not performed by means of a single constituent alone, but rather it is the nights themselves that are expressed by the suffix.

The term *sahapañcamīka* means that which is joined with a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*), namely the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) formed by the combination, rather than a distinct meaning conveyed by those [case-endings] themselves. For example, in the expression *kalyāṇapañcamīkaḥ pakṣaḥ* ("the fortnight having the auspicious fifth day"), the meaning of the compound is not a collection of separate parts; rather, it is the whole aggregate (*samudāya*) designated as a "fortnight" (*pakṣa*) which is initiated by them.

Regarding the term *pūraṇī* (a feminine ordinal): [the example is] "the fortnight containing the auspicious fifth day" (*kalyāṇapañcamīkaḥ pakṣaḥ*). The meaning of the compound is not its individual constituent parts; rather, it is the aggregate (*samudāya*) formed by them which is designated as the "fortnight" (*pakṣa*). However, the ordinal (*pūraṇī*), being a constituent part of the compound, is not explicitly denoted [as the primary referent]; thus, because it enters into the compound as a subordinate element (*anyapadārtha*), it lacks predominance (*aprādhānya*) here.

"Even when there is a prohibition of *puṃvadbhāva*," and so forth. This applies not only here, but also in cases where the *puṃvadbhāva* is prohibited by the rule "striyāḥ puṃvad bhāṣitapuṃskādanūṅ" (Pāṇini 6.3.34), and so on. It is not only here, but also in the case of the feminine [suffix].

Regarding the phrase "even when there is a prohibition of the *puṃvadbhāva* by the rule beginning with *puṃvadbhāṣitapuṃskādanuṅ* (Pāṇini 6.3.34)," and so forth: not only here, but because of the word *striyām* ("in the feminine"), only the primary ordinal (*pradhānapūraṇī*) is understood. Regarding the phrase "but here," and so forth: the suffix *ap* [is applied].

In the case of *kalyāṇapañcamīkaḥ pakṣaḥ*, the masculine form is not applied [by Pāṇini 6.3.34], and thus the suffix *kap* is added by the rule *śeṣādvibhāṣā* (5.4.154). Regarding the word *netuḥ* and so forth: the meaning of the term *upasaṃkhyāna* is "presentation" or "addition. As for that which pertains to a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*)...

The meaning is that since the word *netṛ* occurs [in the rule], one must provide for the suffix *ap* after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in it. This provision, however, should be made by relying on the particle *ca* in the subsequent sūtra as having the sense of an "unexpressed conjunction" (*anuktasamuccaya*). Thus, [the form] *devadattanetṛkāḥ* is derived.
(Thus,) by [Pāṇini 5.4.153] *nady-utaś-ca*, the suffix *kap* is applied.

Regarding "in the Vedic language" (*chandasi*) and so forth, and "from *māsa*" (*māsāt*) and so forth: that suffix which is prescribed in the sense of "wages" (*bhṛti*) is called "wages" (*bhṛti*) here due to its association with wages; that which has such a suffix [expressing wages] is [referred to as] *bhṛti-pratyaya*.

A *bahuvrīhi* compound whose prior member (*pūrvapada*) is based on "wages" (*bhṛti*) is called "one having wages as its prior member. From such a [compound] ending in the word *māsa*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is prescribed. The addition of the marker *cit* is for the purpose of subverting the accent of the *bahuvrīhi*. [An example is: *pañcamāsika*, meaning "five months are his wages," according to the rule *so'syāṃśavasnabhṛtayaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.56).

By the rule *saṃkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan* (Pāṇini 5.1.22), [the suffix] *kan* is applied, resulting in *pañcakaḥ*. When there is a month (*māsa*) consisting of five [days], it is called *pañcakamāsikaḥ*. Regarding the addition of the marker *p* after the word *ap*, where the rule for the acute accent on the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) in a *bahuvrīhi* compound is initiated, [therein...]

In order to prevent that [undesired accentuation]: *supañcamāḥ* means "those nights for which a fifth is auspicious," while *apañcamāḥ* means "those nights for which a fifth does not exist. For in this case, if the suffix *pit* were not present, the rule *nañsubhyām* (Pāṇini 6.2.172) would cause the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) to be udātta.

117. [The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied] after the words *antar* and *bahiḥ*, as well as after *loman*. (5.4.117) 118. [The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied] after *nāsikā* when it forms a name (*saṃjñā*), and [the word *nāsikā* is replaced by] *nas*, provided it does not follow *sthūla*.
(5.4.118) Regarding the statement "‘When it is a name’ is a condition (*upādhi*) for the whole [compound]," by this, if—

He demonstrates that a collection of base and suffix constitutes the technical name (*saṃjñā*) of something, and thus becomes a suffix, and not otherwise—as in the example "druṇasaḥ. Here, the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule "pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām agaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.3).
A female belonging to the Vardhra class is "vārdhrī"; he whose nose is such [a one] is [the referent].

Regarding the term "vārdhrīṇasaḥ": there is a prohibition of the masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) by the rule "and [the feminine base] of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) whose cause is a *vṛddhi* increment, when it does not denote a color or a modification" (Pāṇini 6.3.39). A *gonasa* is one whose nose is like that of a cow (*go*). The addition of the *c*-marker (*cit*) after the suffix *ac* is for the purpose of subverting the accent of the *bahuvrīhi* compound.

In the words *ṭhkharaṇāḥ* and *khuraṇāḥ*, there is lengthening by the rule *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.14). One whose nose is white is *śitināsaḥ*; [by eliding the final vowel and the following consonant] it becomes *śitināḥ*. One whose nose is like that of a snake is *ahirnāsaḥ*; [by the same process] it becomes *ahināḥ*. One whose nose is like that of a *arcā* is *arcanāsaḥ*; [by the same process] it becomes *arcanāḥ*. [This is according to] the rule *ṅyāpoḥ saṃjñācchandasorbahulam* (Pāṇini 6.3.63).
Thus ends the section on short vowels.

119. *upasargācca* (Pāṇini 5.4.119). The mention of *upasarga* is intended as an illustration for *pra* and the other prefixes; [the suffix *ḍīp* does not apply here] because there is no connection with an action directed toward the nose (*nāsikām prati*).

"It should be stated that [the substitution] occurs after the word *vi*. It should be stated that the word *gra* is the substitute for *nāsikā* when it follows the word *vi*. Thus: *vigraḥ*. The suffix is added only when there is no vowel (*aj*).
120. *suprāta-suśva-sudiva-śāri-kukṣa-catura-aśra-uṇīpada-aja-pada-proṣṭhapadāḥ*.
(5.4.120) Regarding the phrase "the elision of the *ṭi* [vowel] and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the word *su*, which functions as an adverbial modifier of the action.
"His morning [sacrifice] is excellent (*śobhana*). Here, the word "excellent" is an adjective qualifying the ritual action (*karman*). The meaning is:

"His ritual action at the time of morning is excellent. In the same way, it should be understood that in the subsequent examples as well, the word "excellent" is an adjective qualifying the ritual action.
121. *nañ-duḥ-subhyo halisakthyor anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.4.121).

There is also a word *hala* ending in the letter *ṭh*; when the compound is formed with that [word], it will be *hala*, but when it is formed with the one ending in the vowel *i*, it will be *halī*. Therefore, [the mention of] that [ending in *ṭh*] is purposeless.

Why is the mention of *hali* (the consonant) not purposeless? Because it serves a different purpose. By that [mention], when the sense of *hali* as "one who possesses great power" (*mahaddhalaṃ haliḥ*) is intended to be expressed, the form *ahala* would not be established. When *ahala* is formed as a compound with a word ending in long *ā*, then, as before, the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) applies, resulting in the acute accent on the first syllable.
If it were so intended, the suffix *kap* would apply by the rule "ṭhśeṣādvibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 5.4.154). Therefore, the inclusion of the term *halin* is appropriate.
122. *nityam asi ca prajā-medhayoḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.122). [Objection:

"In that case, by the inclusion of the word 'always' (*nityam*), it is indicated that [the suffix] occurs elsewhere as well. This is because one assumes that an increase in the wording implies an increase in the meaning. [Response: The addition of the *c*-marker to *asi* is for the sake of [accentuation], as in *duṣprajāḥ*.
The rule [Pāṇini 6.2.173] *durmedhāḥ* is intended so that the final syllable may be udātta; however, in cases such as *aprajāḥ*,
there is no purpose served by the marker *c*, because the udāttatva of the final syllable of the second member is already established by the rule *nañ-subhyām* (6.2.162).
123. *bahuprajāśchandasi* (5.4.123).
124. *dharmādanic kevalāt* (5.4.124). Regarding the phrase *ṭhasamastaḥ*, it does not appear in the *Kāśikā*. The meaning is that it is formed as a non-compound (*asamāsa*).
"Supreme own-duty (paramasvadharma)": this is one's own duty (*svadharma*), being both "own" (*sva*) and "duty" (*dharma*);
and being both "supreme" (*parama*) and "own-duty," it is "supreme own-duty. [Regarding the phrase] "If it were so," and so forth:
if *dharma* were not qualified by the inclusion of the word "only" (*kevala*), such that it were not "supreme own-duty," then it would have to be "supreme own-brahman" (*paramasvabrahma*).

Regarding the phrase "from a preceding member that is alone": this means from a preceding member that is not accompanied by anything else [i.e., not part of a compound]. Regarding the phrase "not from a collection of words": this connects with the current topic, "supreme dharma" (*paramo dharma*). In this interpretation, the rule does not apply in the case of a three-membered *bahuvrīhi*.

This is a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*); for the word *dharma* [in the compound] is supreme when derived from the entire collection of words, not from the preceding member alone. The addition of the marker *c* [to the suffix *an*] is intended so that, by overriding the original accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*), the word shall have an acute accent on its final syllable (*antodātta*).
125. *jambhā suharitatṛṇasomebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.125).

By the mention of *jambha*, the analysis (*vigraha*) should be performed as "his jaw (*jambha*) is like grass" (*tṛṇam iva jambho 'sya*) or "his jaw is like the Soma plant" (*soma iva jambho 'sya*). [Objection: But surely it should be analyzed as "grass is his jaw" (*tṛṇaṃ jambho 'sya*) or "Soma is his jaw" (*somo jambho 'sya*)?

The compound should be analyzed as *tṛṇajambhaḥ* and *somajambhaḥ*, for [in these cases] it is not the act of chewing grass or Soma that is intended. However, when the act of eating (*abhyavahāra*) is meant—as in "grass is his food" (*tṛṇaṃ jambho 'sya*) or "Soma is his food" (*somo jambho 'sya*)—then the analysis must indeed be performed in this way;
for in those instances, grass and Soma are intended for consumption.
126. *dakṣiṇermā* in the sense of being wounded by a hunter (*lubdhayoga*). (Pāṇini 5.4.126) 127. The suffix *ic* [is applied] in the sense of mutual exchange of action (*karmavyatihāra*).
(Pāṇini 5.4.127) It is stated that "this *bahuvrīhi* compound, [defined] by the rule *tatra tenedam iti sarūpe*, is what is intended here. Of this very [compound]...

When the sense of mutual striking (*karmādhyatihāra*) is intended, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule *keśākeśi*; the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 6.3.137). Because this form is listed among the *tiṣṭhadgu*-type compounds, it receives the designation of *avyayībhāva*; and since a compound designated as *avyayībhāva* is itself termed an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

The meaning is that by this [rule], *sub-luk* (the elision of the case-ending) occurs. The inclusion of the marker *c* in *ic* is for the sake of distinction; for if the letter *c* were not used here, then in the list beginning with *tiṣṭhadgu*, only the vowel *i* would be recited, and consequently, there would be the apprehension of the vowel *e* as well.
It may be so.

128. *dvidaṇḍy-ādibhyaś-ca* (Pāṇini 5.4.128). Regarding the statement, "The word *dvidaṇḍy-ādibhyaḥ* is in the dative case in the sense of *tādarthya* (being for the sake of that)," and so forth: since the items beginning with *dvidaṇḍi* are listed in the *pratipadika* (nominal stem) lists as already ending in the suffix *ic*, it is not necessary to prescribe the suffix *ij* again from them.

It is possible [to argue] that even if it were enjoined, it would be purposeless; therefore, this is not a *pañcamī* (ablative) case, but rather a *caturthī* (dative) in the sense of "for the sake of" (*tādarthye*). By stating that the suffix *ic* occurs for the sake of things such as *dvidaṇḍi*, he demonstrates this sense of being for the sake of something. This is the meaning of this very [rule].

To make this clear, he says: "It becomes thus," and so forth. By speaking in this way, it is stated that "the suffix occurs after *dvidaṇḍi* and the like, but not after *dvidaṇḍa* and the like. In this manner they are established; not otherwise. Now, for what purpose are these compounds cited in their pure, unaltered forms as *nipātana*s?

Is the suffix prescribed after having recited the bases (*prakṛti*) among the nominal stems (*prātipadika*)? To this he says: "And because of the compounding of the whole," and so forth. Having recited the bases among the nominal stems, only the suffix is prescribed after them; from that, the restriction [follows].
It may be argued: because these [compounds] are formed by the inclusion of the whole collection (*samudāya*), they qualify only that specific object for which they are well-known;

the meaning is that they apply only in that context. For example, in "he strikes with a *dvidaṇḍi*," it refers to a striking instrument consisting of two sticks. As for the phrase "it occurs here": [this refers to the following].
The meaning is that this word-form *dvidaṇḍī* is not correct (*sādhuh*) in this sense.
Because the governing rule (*adhikāra*) pertains to *bahuvrīhi*, no suffix would ever be prescribed after a *tatpuruṣa*.
However, due to the specific formation (*nipātana*) of the whole compound, it occurs even after a *tatpuruṣa* in certain cases; when—
When [the suffix] is elided, the designation of *avyayībhāva* applies; since [the rule] would then not apply, he says: "by means of the characteristic of a suffix," and so forth.

129. *prasambhyāṃ jānunorjñuḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.129). [The commentary states: "The substitute *jñu* occurs in place of the word *jānu*. But how is it known that this is a substitute (*ādeśa*) and not an affix (*pratyaya*)? If it were an affix, [the rule would have been stated] using the singular form *jānunaḥ*.
One should provide an explanation: the indication has been made by means of the genitive dual itself.

Therefore, it is understood that this is an *ādeśa* (substitute), not a *pratyaya* (suffix). The indication by means of the genitive dual is made for the sake of avoiding ambiguity—so that its status as a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) may be beyond doubt.
It should be understood thus: when "of the knee" (jānoḥ) is uttered, a doubt may arise—whether this is a genitive case or a ablative case.
130. *ūrdhvādvibhāṣā* (5.4.130). 131. *ūdhaso'naṅ* (5.4.131). [The question is: "This *anaṅ* is a substitute (*ādeśa*). How, then, is it understood that this is a substitute and not [something else]?

Regarding the term *pratyaya* (condition): if this were a *pratyaya*, the addition of the marker *ṅ* would be purposeless; for it is only when [the suffix] is an *ādeśa* (substitute) that the *ṅ*-marker serves a purpose by ensuring that the substitution applies to the final letter. Therefore, it is understood that this substitution occurs precisely because it is marked with *ṅ*. For example: *kuṇḍodhnī*.

By [Pāṇini 6.1.97], *anaṅ* being applied, there is substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*). By [Pāṇini 4.1.25], *bahuvrīherūdhaso ṅīṣ*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added, and by [Pāṇini 6.4.134], *allopo'naḥ*, the *a* is elided.

Regarding the statement "the mention of 'feminine' (*strī*) must be made": it means that by which [word] the feminine gender is understood through the necessity of its being the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*), from that [word].

The mention of "strī" (feminine) must be made. This is what is meant: the explanation should be formulated in such a way that *anaṅ* occurs when the feminine is the object denoted. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: [the rule] from "ūrdhvādvibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 5.4.130)...
The term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) continues to apply, and that is an irregularly restricted option (*vyasthitavibhāṣā*); therefore, it occurs only in the feminine and not elsewhere.
The inclusion of the letter *ṅ* in *anaṅ* is for the sake of subsequent rules; here, however, the desired result is achieved even without it.

132. And [the substitution of *anaṅ* occurs] after the word *dhanus*. (Pāṇini 5.4.132). As in the example "Śārṅgadhanvā" (the one whose bow is made of horn). Once *anaṅ* has been applied, the substitution of *yiṇ* takes place, and by the rule "sarvanāmasthāne ca" (6.4.8), lengthening of the vowel occurs.
133. Or [the suffix *cha*] is applied when *saṃjñā* follows.
(5.4.133) 134. For *jāyā*, the substitute *niṅ* is used.
(5.4.134) "Let *niṅ* be the substitute"—its status as a substitute is established here as before, precisely because of its *ṅ*-marker.

It is understood as *yuvajāniḥ*. There is the elision of *y* by the rule *lopo vyor vali* (Pāṇini 6.1.66). There is the substitution of the masculine form [for the feminine] by the rule *striyāḥ pumvat* (Pāṇini 6.3.34).
135. *gandhasyedutpūtisusurabhibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.135).

[The rule states: "The substitute *ṭhak* occurs. But how is it known that this is a substitute (*ādeśa*) and not an affix (*pratyaya*)? Because of the mention of the genitive case in the word *gandhasya*. For if it were an affix, [the genitive would not be used].

To ensure that the meaning is not ambiguous, one would have made the reference by means of the ablative case, as in *gandhāt*; however, the reference is made by means of the genitive case. Therefore, it is understood that this is a substitute (*ādeśa*).
[The rule] begins with *gandhasyetve* and so forth. Smell (*gandha*) is of two kinds: smell as a quality (*guṇa-gandha*), and...

In that case, it would not be exclusively an external object. However, in the expression "a perfumer (*sugandha āpaṇikaḥ*) whose fragrance is excellent," the word "fragrance" refers to the substance of the fragrance; and that [substance] constitutes a part of the perfumer. In that context, [the rule is stated] so that it may apply to the fragrance as a quality (*guṇagandha*).

In order that [the rule] "dravyagandhe" (in the case of a substance possessing fragrance) should not apply, when the suffix *it* is to be prescribed for the word *gandha*, the term *tadekānta* must be employed. By the word *tat*, the sense of a *bahuvrīhi* compound is indicated by implication. Its *ekānta*—meaning a single part, a quality, or a constituent member—is what is grasped as *tadekānta*. That by which this *tadekānta* is grasped [is the basis for the designation].

This must be done. What is meant is this: such an explanation must be provided by which even a trace (*gandha*) of the rule for *it* [the substitution of *it* for *in*] remains here from the sense of another word-component; therefore, that [explanation] should be resorted to. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: [the rule] starting from "or, when a name is designated" (*vā saṃjñāyām*, 5.4.133).

It follows the usage of speech, and that [usage] is established as optional (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, the substitution of *it* occurs only where the word "fragrance" (*gandha*) constitutes a part of another referent, and not elsewhere. Alternatively, there is this word "fragrance" (*gandha*) which denotes a substance—as in "he sells fragrances"—and there is...

An example of a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*) is "the earth possesses fragrance" (*gandhavatī pṛthivī*). In this context, the term *guṇavacana* is intended [by Pāṇini], not a word denoting a substance (*dravyavacana*). Therefore, a word denoting a substance occurs in the plural only when it refers to a substance—as in "he sells fragrances" (*gandhān vikrīṇīte*) or "fragrances are his merchandise" (*gandhāḥ paṇyam asya*). Here...

The indication is made by the singular form "of the odor" (gandhasya). Therefore, it is determined that this is a reference to a word expressing a quality (guṇavacana). When there is a reference to a word expressing a quality, the quality—namely, the odor—becomes a part of the referent of the other word (anyapadārtha); consequently, [the rule applies] only to that which is entirely composed of that [quality].
This is the nature of fragrance.
136. [The suffix *kan* is applied] after a word denoting a small quantity.

(5.4.136) 137. [The suffix *kan* is applied] also after a word expressing a standard of comparison (*upamāna*). (5.4.137) 138. The word *pāda-* is elided [when followed by a suffix beginning with *ka*, provided it does not follow words such as *hastin-*]. (5.4.138)

"The elision of *ṭh* occurs as a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*). But what would happen if it were not a compound-final suffix? [The substitute] would apply only to the initial [sound], according to the rule "of that which follows, the first" (Pāṇini 1.1.54). When it is a compound-final suffix, however, this word *anta* denotes a constituent part whose position is fixed; therefore, the elision applies only to the final [sound].

And thus the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) occurs only if [the elision] applies to the final [element], and not otherwise. Now, one might object: "Since elision (*lopa*) is of the nature of non-existence, how can a compound-ending suffix be applicable?
To this he says: "by way of the substituendum" (*sthānidvāreṇa*), etc. [This refers to] the vowel *a*, which is the substituendum.
He shows that because it is a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*), even the elision (*lopa*) is called a "compound-final suffix" by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

139. And in the case of *kumbhapadī* and others. (Pāṇini 5.4.139). It is said: "Words such as *kumbhapadī* are listed as complete compounds in which the [final] syllable *pāda* has already been elided. If this is so, how is the following [example] to be explained? To this he says: "In that case, thus," and so forth. In that regard...

The meaning is that when words such as *kumbhapadī* and others—which have undergone the elision of the suffix *pāda*—are recited, they should be explained in this manner; that is, one should explain how forms such as *kumbhapadī* and so forth come into being. But for what purpose are these groups [of words] recited as wholes, rather than [the individual components]?

Having listed words such as *kumbhapada* in the list of nominal stems (*prātipadika*), would the elision of the word *pāda* following them be prescribed? To this he says: "And because of the reading of the compound," and so forth.
If that elision of *pāda* after *kumbha* and the others were stated, then [the forms] with the elision of *pāda* already accomplished—

The restriction that "the compounds themselves shall not be recited" would not be obtained; consequently, they would apply to all three genders, yet they are intended for the feminine alone. When there is a recitation of the compound, the suffix *ṅīp* occurs only when the feminine gender is the domain [of application]. "Not otherwise" refers to the example *kumbhapadī*.
When the suffix *ṅīp* is applicable by the rule *ṭhpādo 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.8), there is the elision of *pāda*;

then the suffix *ṅīp* is added, and by the rule *ṭhpādaḥ pat* (6.4.130), the substitution of *pad* occurs. Regarding the phrase "where [the word] is preceded by a standard of comparison" (*yatra copamānapūrvam*), examples include *kumbhapadī*, *jālapadī*, and so forth.

Regarding the rule "and that which has a numeral as its prior member": examples include *ekapadī* (one-footed) and *śatapadī* (hundred-footed). Regarding the phrase "when that [suffix] is established":
since a compound preceded by a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is already established by the preceding rule, this [present rule] applies to those preceded by a numeral.
The form *aṣṭāpadī* is cited there; in that case, the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) is for the sake of lengthening the vowel.
Or [it is formed] by [the rule] "ṭhaṣṭanaḥ saṃjñāyām" (Pāṇini 6.3.125).
140. *saṃkhyāsupūrvasya* (Pāṇini 5.4.140).
This [sūtra] is for the purpose of excluding the case of a comparison (*anupamāna*).

141. *vayasi dantasya datṛ* (Pāṇini 5.4.141). Regarding the form *dvidan*: because the vowel *ṛ* serves the purpose of triggering the operations of the *ugit* markers, the augment *num* is applied by *ugidacām* (7.1.70); then, the elision of the final consonant (*halṅyādi*) and the elision of the final member of the cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) apply, resulting in *sudantaḥ*.
"Southern" (dākṣiṇātyaḥ) is used here; what is understood is excellence, not age.
142. *chandasi ca* (Pāṇini 5.4.142).

This rule is for the sake of the Veda (*avaya-artha*) and for the sake of cases where the preceding member is not a numeral (*asaṃkhyā-pūrva-padārtha*). The form *ubhayatodataḥ* is taught by this very rule.

143. *striyāṃ saṃjñāyām* | (5.4.143) This is for the purpose of excluding the Vedic (*acchandaḥ*). [The example is: "She whose teeth are like arrows" (*aya-iva dantā asyāḥ*) is *ayodantī*. This is an instruction (*śāsanam*).
In the word *samadantī*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *nāsikodara-* (Pāṇini 4.1.55).

144. *vibhāṣā śyāvārokābhyām* (Pāṇini 5.4.144). The term *strīyām* ("in the feminine") is no longer in force. *Rokaḥ* means shining, radiance, or light. [It is derived from] the root *ruca* (Dhātupāṭha 745) meaning "to shine," with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), and the substitution of *k* for *c* and *j* before suffixes ending in *ṇi* or *nya* according to Pāṇini 7.3.52.
