Thus [is explained] the substitution of *k* for *r*. Having kept in mind the etymology of the word *aroka* as "that which has no light" (*avidyamāna-roka*), he says—"*Aroka* means lacking radiance"—in order to demonstrate its meaning.

145. [The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied] after the words *agra*, *anta*, *śuddha*, *śubhra*, *vṛṣa*, and *varāha*. (5.4.145) 146. There is elision (*lopa*) of the syllable *kakuda* when it denotes a state (*avasthā*).
(5.4.146) Regarding the phrase "produced by time, etc. (*kālādikṛta*), the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes food (*āhāra*) and other such factors.

147. *trikakut-parvate* (Pāṇini 5.4.147). This [rule] is for the sake of avoiding an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). When "mountain" (*parvata*) is the external referent (*anyapadārtha*), the primary meaning of "hump" (*kakuda*) is not possible;
yet this is stated as "*trikakut-parvataḥ*" (the three-humped mountain). Therefore, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), it refers to that which has the shape of a hump.

The word *kakuda* is applied to a mountain peak by virtue of its similarity [to the hump of an animal]; if that were what was being referred to here, then the designation *trikakuda* would apply to every such thing that possesses peaks shaped like humps. To this, [the author says] "And not," and so forth. This is to be connected with the word "it is said" (*ucyate*) from the context. [It is said: "This is a technical name (*saṃjñā*)."
And so forth. By this, he demonstrates that for whomsoever this designation exists, they are expressed by the word *trikakud*.

And this is obtained through the rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), because of the continued application of the term "designation" (*saṃjñā*) from [Pāṇini 5.4.143], which states: "In the feminine, when it is a designation. Now, one might object: is not the restriction of the meaning also obtained from that very same source?

Should the mention of "mountain" (*parvata*) not be made because [the meaning] is already obtainable? This is not so; it is the style of this Teacher that he explains the cause for the denotation even in those [terms] which are eternal, such as in the rule *puṣyasiddhyau nakṣatre* (Pāṇini 3.1.116); how much more so in a case where...
There is no established proof; that [proof] is merely worldly.

148. *udvibhyāṃ kākudasya* (Pāṇini 5.4.148). [The forms] *ṭhūt-kākut* and *vikākut* are derived as follows: when the final [phoneme] has been elided, the substitution of *c* by *ṭ* occurs according to *vāvasāne* (8.4.56). Now, one might object that by the rule *ādeḥ parasya* (1.1.54), [the elision should apply to the initial phoneme].

It must be so; how then does it apply to the final [element]? For the word "final" (antya) also denotes a "member" (avayava), and it has been stated that it expresses a member located in a specific position. In that case, if [the suffix] were to apply to the beginning (ādi), the status of being a compound-final element (samāsānta) would not be possible.

149. After *pūrṇa*, there is optional [application of the suffix]. (5.4.149) 150. *Suhṛd* and *durhṛd* are used in the senses of "friend" and "enemy" respectively. (5.4.150) 151. After words beginning with *uras*, the suffix *kap* is applied. (5.4.151)
Since the suffix *kap* would already be applicable by the rule *śeṣād vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 5.4.154), this statement is made for the purpose of making it obligatory.
Thus we have *priyasapiṣkaḥ*; here, the letter *ṣ* replaces the visarga according to the rule *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.39).
One by whom shoes have not been removed is called *avamuktopānatkaḥ*; here, *dha* replaces *na* according to the rule *naho dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.34).

Thus, for the letter *dh* that has been prescribed, there is the substitution of a *jaś* sound by the rule "ṭhjhalāṃ jaśo'nte" (Pāṇini 8.2.39), resulting in *d*; for that *d*, there is the substitution of a *car* sound by the rule "ṭhkhari ca" (Pāṇini 8.4.55), resulting in *t*.
But what is the purpose of reciting these words with their case-endings? To this he says: "In that regard..."

And so forth. By the word "therein" (tatra), the reading of the words ending in case-terminations is referred back. Regarding the rule "after *artha* when preceded by *nañ*": the suffix *ka* occurs after a *bahuvrīhi* compound that ends in the word *artha* when *nañ* follows it. For example, "that which has no purpose" (*na asti artho asya*) is *anarthakaḥ*.

152. *inaḥ striyām* | (5.4.152) This rule is also like the previous one; although [the suffix] *kap* would have been established [by the preceding rule], this is for the sake of making it obligatory. Thus, "bahudaṇḍikaḥ. The elision of the *n* is by [Pāṇini 8.2.7]: *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*.
153. And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after words ending in *nadī*. (5.4.153) 154. Optionally [the suffix *cha* is applied] from the remainder (*śeṣa*).
(5.4.154) The term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) may be understood either in relation to the suffix *kap*—that is, that *bahuvrīhi* compound after which *kap* has not been prescribed—or...

Regarding the term "remainder" (*śeṣa*): does it refer to that which depends on a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*)—that is, a remainder is that *bahuvrīhi* compound for which no compound-ending suffix has been prescribed? In that case, if "remainder" were dependent on the suffix *kap*, then [the suffix would apply] even in cases such as *anṛcaḥ*, *vyāghrapāt*, and *sugandhi*; for in these instances, the suffix *kap* has not been prescribed by anyone.

Thus, having observed the fault in [interpreting] "remainder" (*śeṣa*) as referring to the *kapa* suffix, he says—showing that "remainder" refers to [the compound] with respect to the *samāsānta* (compound-final) suffixes—"That bahuvrīhi compound for which no *samāsānta* suffix occurs is the 'remainder'.
How is it known that "remainder" refers to [the compound] with respect to the *samāsānta* suffixes? Because of the mention of the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*). In that case, if...
The suffix *ka* would be understood as being for the remainder (*śeṣa*), and the mention of "remainder" (*śeṣagrahaṇa*) would be purposeless;
for by the very force of its commencement, the option will apply only to the domain of the remainder.

Otherwise, if *ka* were prescribed even from those [bases] for which it has already been enjoined by previous prescriptive rules, then this [present rule] would provide an option (*vibhāṣā*) even for those.

[If it were not so] prescribed, the injunctions would fall into meaninglessness. Therefore, because of the mention of "the remainder" (śeṣa), the "remainder" is understood as being in expectation of a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*). In the case of *bahūkhaṭvakaḥ*, there is shortening by the rule *āpo'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 7.4.15). It is the same in the case of *bahukhaṭvaḥ*.

Regarding the rule *gostriyor upasarjanasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.48), the question "How? and so forth arises. The intention is this: if "remainder" (*śeṣa*) were dependent upon the presence of a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*), then the suffix *kap* would not be established in cases such as *anṛkkaṃ sāma* ("a Sāman that does not have Ṛc verses") and *bahvṛkkaṃ sūktam* ("a hymn containing many Ṛc verses"). [The answer is: "That [suffix] is desired in a specific case."

For that suffix *a* (akāra), which serves as a compound-final (*samāsānta*), is intended to apply specifically to the word *māṇava* when it denotes a Vedic school (*caraṇa*); thus, the suffix *a* is prescribed there. Nor is that specific [suffix] prescribed only in that instance;
rather, it applies to other domains—as well as to *sāman* and *sūkta*. In those cases, it depends upon the compound-final suffix of a *bahuvrīhi*.

This is the remainder (*śeṣa*). And by that [remainder], in the case of *priyapatha* and *priyamadhura*, the suffix *a* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) according to the rule "ṛkpūrabdhūḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.74), etc. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *śeṣa*?
For surely, those very bases from which compound-final suffixes are prescribed will themselves serve as exceptions (*bādhaka*) to [the general rule]?

This is not so; for the [general] rules regarding the scope will be superseded by those that have no other occasion [for application], whereas the suffixes forming compounds (*samāsānta*) have their own occasions. What is their occasion? They are the base forms introduced word-for-word; those from which the compound-forming suffixes are prescribed word-for-word with respect to specific meanings and specific compounds.

That [absence of an occasion] is not the case; for when there is an occasion arising from specific bases and both [suffixes] would apply, the suffix *ka* would occur by virtue of its being subsequent [in the order of rules]. Therefore, the mention of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) must be made.
155. *Na saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 5.4.155).
156. *Īyasaśca* (Pāṇini 5.4.156). [The commentary states:
"Every application [of the suffix] is prohibited. Now, an objection is raised: "Is it not the case that a rule applies only to what immediately precedes it (*anantarasya*)?"

Does the prohibition [in the rule] *pratiṣedho vā* (Vyākaraṇa Paribhāṣā 19) result in the prohibition of the *kap* suffix specifically as defined by the rule *śeṣāt*? This is not a fault; for here *kap* is what is being carried over (*anuvartate*), not the word *śeṣāt*. Therefore, this will be a prohibition of *kap* in general. As in: *bahavaḥ śreyāṃsaḥ*.

By the rule *dvivacanavibhajyopapade* (Pāṇini 5.3.57), the suffix *inayasun* is applied; by the rule *praśasyasya śraḥ* (5.3.60), the substitution *śra-* occurs. Regarding the statement "even the shortening does not take place": although shortening would apply by the rule *gostriyor upasarjanasya* (1.2.48), that too does not occur. Why does it not occur?

Thus he says: "By [the rule] *īyasaḥ bahuvrīheḥ*," and so forth. Here, the intention is not the removal of the feminine suffix by means of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment); rather, because this occurs in the section concerning short vowels (*hrasvatva*), its absence [is intended]. This is what is meant: just as when *puṃvadbhāva* applies, the long *īkāra* [is replaced by a short vowel].
Just as [the substitution] does not occur for a short vowel, likewise it does not occur for a feminine suffix that follows an *īyas* affix.

157. *vandite bhrātuḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.157). This is a prohibition of the *kap* suffix which would otherwise have applied by rule 5.4.153 (*ṭhnadyautaśca*). Although the root *vad* (Dhātupāṭha 11), meaning "to speak," occurs here in the sense of "saluting" (*abhivādana*), [the rule still applies].
Nevertheless, in this context, he is understood as being engaged solely in praise; for this very reason, it says: "He who has been saluted and praised."
158. *ṛtaś chandasi* (Pāṇini 5.4.158). This rule also, like the preceding one, is a prohibition of the suffix *kap*, which would otherwise have applied.

159. *nāḍī-tantryoḥ svāṅge* (5.4.151). This is a prohibition of the suffix *kap*, which would otherwise have applied by rule 5.4.153 (*nady-utaś-ca*). Here, "limb" (*svāṅga*) is understood in its technical sense. In the example *bahunāḍiḥ*, the shortening of the penultimate vowel occurs as in the previous case, because it is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*).

In the case of *bahutantrīḥ*, shortening does not occur; this is because of the statement: "A prohibition must be stated for [stems ending in] *kṛt* suffixes when feminine. And so it has been said: "The mention of 'feminine' will be accented" (*Mahābhāṣya* 1.2.48).
160. *Niṣpravāṇiśca*.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who is like a Bodhisattva.
The fourth quarter.
And this fifth chapter is completed.
The sixth chapter.
First Pāda.
1. *ekāco dve prathamasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.1).
Here, some rules apply only to their own specific meaning (*svārtha*), and not to the general meaning of the word (*padārtha*).

For example, in the rule *ṭhaṇ kuṭilikāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.18), the suffix *aṇ* prescribed after the word *kuṭilikā* serves its own meaning (*svārtha*). However, some suffixes serve both their own meaning and the meaning of another;
for instance, in the rule *padarujaviśaspṛśo ghañ* (Pāṇini 3.3.16), the suffix *ghañ* [is applied] after words such as *pada*.

That which is being prescribed is for its own sake (*svārtha*), whereas that which continues to apply in subsequent rules due to the connection with a *svarita* accent-mark is for the sake of another (*parārtha*). However, some governing rules (*adhikāras*) are indeed only for the sake of another and not for their own sake, such as "samarthānāṃ prathamādvā" (Pāṇini 4.1.82). That...
Is this [the suffix] for one's own benefit alone? Or is the qualification for the benefit of both? Or is it for the benefit of another alone?
To remove such doubt and to demonstrate that it is indeed for the benefit of another, he says: "and [the rule] *ekācaḥ*," etc.
This is the summary statement (*grahaṇaka-vākya*), and its [detailed] explanation begins with "after *it*" (*ita uttaram*), etc.

[This is] the commentary. By the logic of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*), the governing rules (*adhikāra*) also continue to apply to what precedes; therefore, their cessation should be understood from the fact that they are not marked as *svarita*. But for what [word] does the rule "of a monosyllable, there are two [become]" apply?

Is this how it should be understood? Therefore, if this genitive were in apposition with the verbal root itself, then reduplication would apply only to *pac* and the like, and not to *jāgarti* and the like; for in those cases, [the condition] "having a single vowel" (*ekāc*) does not exist—thinking thus, [the author] says: "this is not [a case of] having a single vowel."
The genitive case [in the rule] "of a root having a single vowel" (*dhāto-rekācaḥ*) is one of apposition;

however, to show that it is rather a connection by way of being a constituent part—as in "that which is a constituent part of the root having a single vowel"—he says: "of a constituent part of the root. This refers to the form *jajāgāra*.

The word *jāgṛ* is stated twice: the root *pac* occurs in the example *papāca*; in the former case, there is *vṛddhi* by [Pāṇini 7.2.115] *aco ñṇiti*, and in the latter case, by [Pāṇini 7.2.116] *ata upadhāyāḥ*.
As for *iyāya*: the root *iṇ* means "to go" (*gartau*, Dhātupāṭha 1045); here too, the *vṛddhi* is by [Pāṇini 7.2.115] *aco ñṇiti*.

When the *vṛddhi* substitution has been applied, by virtue of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* according to Pāṇini 1.1.59 (*dvirvacane 'ci*), the vowel *i* is reduplicated; then the *āy* substitute is applied, and by Pāṇini 6.4.78 (*abhyāsasyāsavarṇe*), the *iyaṅ* substitution occurs. Regarding the form *āra*:
from the root *ṛ* (meaning "to go," Dhātupāṭha 1098), there is the reduplication of *ṛ*, and then the *urat* substitute is applied.

(7.4.66) Thus, there is the substitution of *i*, followed by the substitution of *ra* for the final element (*raparatva*), the lengthening of the vowel according to (7.4.70) "ata ādeḥ," and the lengthening of the homogeneous vowel (*sarvarṇadīrghatva*). Alternatively, this [compound] *ekāc* may be a *tatpuruṣa*: namely, that which is both "one" (*eka*) and a "vowel" (*ac*) is *ekāc*.

Or is it a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has one *añ* suffix"? In that regard, if this were a *tatpuruṣa* compound, reduplication would occur only for roots beginning with *i*, such as in *iyāya* and *āra*; however, it would not occur for roots beginning with *p*, such as in *papāca*, because those consist of a combination of vowels and consonants (*ajjhal-samudāya*). This is what [the author] has in mind.

Having done so, he said: "The term *ṭhekāca* is an indication of a *bahuvrīhi* compound. An "indication" (*nirdeśa*) is the mention or description of the meaning intended by the *bahuvrīhi*. An "indication of a *bahuvrīhi*" (*bahuvrīhinirdeśa*) is either the mention, the description, or the utterance of a *bahuvrīhi*. Why?

Furthermore, this has been determined: that this is a designation of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, based on such indicative marks as "the remaining [consonant] begins with a *hal*" (Pāṇini 6.1.68), "the *khay* consonants preceded by a *śar* are elided" (6.1.66), and so forth. But is there not also an indicative mark for a *tatpuruṣa* compound, namely, "there is lengthening of *iṇ* before a *kit* suffix" (7.4.69)?

Is this the prescription of lengthening for the reduplicated syllable of the root *iṇ*? This is not so; for even in this Bahuvrīhi compound, since the designation [of the whole] applies to its parts (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the prescription of lengthening for the reduplicated syllable of *iṇ* is indeed possible, but not in this Tatpuruṣa compound.

The grammatical operations such as *halādiśeṣa* (the retention of the first consonant) are possible [only if it is a bahuvrīhi], because for [words] beginning with *pac*, which are collections of vowels and consonants (*ajjhal-samudāya*), reduplication is impossible. Therefore, there is evidence for a bahuvrīhi compound alone, not for a tatpuruṣa; thus, this is indeed a designation of a bahuvrīhi. If this is so;

Since the *bahuvrīhi* compound primarily denotes the meaning of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*), and since it expresses that pure external referent alone as being devoid of any qualifying attributes (*upalakṣaṇa*), it follows that reduplication would apply only to that very external referent which is qualified by a member [of the compound], and not to anything else.

Even in the case of that which serves as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), it does not serve as a factor for the actual effect. For instance, when it is said, "Let the owner of brindled cows be brought," it is he alone who possesses the brindled cows who is brought, but the brindled cows themselves, being merely indicators, are not brought. Therefore, in order to exclude that [possibility],...

Showing that this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the qualities [of the members] are understood (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*), he says "there," etc. "The aggregate is the meaning of the compound" means that the aggregate itself, together with that member which serves as a qualifier (*upalakṣaṇa*), is the referent of the other word (*anyapadārtha*). "And included within that" means contained therein.
This is the meaning. The word *ca* (and) is used for emphasis; the meaning is "only within. The particle *iti* indicates the reason:

because a constituent part is included within the whole—that is, within the meaning of the compound—therefore, reduplication occurs only of that which possesses a consonant (*sāckasya*). Even in common worldly usage, [this is seen] in some cases as a characteristic mark (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Because it is included within a compound, its utility for grammatical operations is clearly observed;

just as when it is said, "Bring the one with white clothes," he is brought along with the white clothes themselves. In the case of *paci*, by that very same monosyllabic (*ekāc*) collection which includes the vowel *a*, the constituent element *ac* is also included.

And because it is called *paśabda* (the word *pac*), double application (*dvirvacana*) would consequently apply to each of its constituent parts (*avayava*) individually. Just as by that very hand which is a part, the arm becomes "possessing a hand," and by that same [hand], Devadatta also becomes "possessing a hand"; likewise, in the verbal root *pac*, by whichever form...
The word *acchabda* is a composite (*samudāya*) consisting of a single vowel (*ekāc*); by that very fact, its individual components—the sound *ac* and the sound *pa*—are also called *acchabda*.

Consequently, reduplication (*dvirvacana*) applies to each of these components as well. And since reduplication pertains to a single-vowel element (*ekācaḥ kāryiṇaḥ*), this follows from the general designation. Thus, it would apply to the composite as well.

Furthermore, if the single-vowel (ekāc) parts were reduplicated separately, an undesirable form would result; therefore, in order to avoid this objection, he says "tatra" and so forth. Among those single-vowel groups, the single-vowel parts are not reduplicated individually. What then? Only the single vowel of the entire group is reduplicated.

The compound *avayavaikāj* is a *karmadhāraya*. [The phrase] *samudāyaikāc* is also indeed a *karmadhāraya*. But from what source is this specific meaning obtained when there is a general designation? To this he says: "In that way..."

Regarding the passage beginning with "hi," etc.: although both the whole (samudāyin) and the part (avayava) consist of a single vowel (ekāc), nevertheless, doubling is properly applied to that [whole] by whose doubling the benefit of all [the constituent parts] is achieved. In this way, there is no violation of the grammatical treatise (śāstra), because the operation prescribed by the treatise is accomplished for all of them.
This alone is the benefit: the accomplishment of the task prescribed by the treatise.

When the doubling is performed of the entire collection itself, there is benefit for all [the constituent parts]. Just as a tree, when moving, moves together with its parts, so too, through the single operation of the treatise, the entire collection [is affected].

When it is repeated twice, it is repeated together with its constituent parts, for a composite whole cannot be pronounced twice without its parts, since the whole is of the nature of those parts. However, the repetition of the constituent parts cannot be accomplished for all of them by a single act of pronunciation; thus, when that [whole] is repeated, [the parts are repeated].

There is favor shown to all. How so? For the reason that they are designated as "ekāc" (having one vowel) is simply because there is one vowel (*eka-aC*) in them all. In that case, when a particular vowel is designated as the single constituent part (*avayava*) by which it is called "ekāc," then, since that [designation] is already accounted for by that very [vowel], another [vowel] cannot be [designated as] "ekāc."

It must be specified. Consequently, when the reduplication of a single *ekāc* [monosyllabic root] is intended to be prescribed, then at that time, only that specific portion which possesses a vowel (*ac*) would undergo reduplication, and not the other [consonantal] portion, because it lacks a vowel (*anackatvāt*). To this, one might object: "In the rule *ekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.1), [the term *ekācaḥ*] refers to all [roots] in the genitive case..."

Since it has been taught that all of them [the suffixes] must undergo reduplication, and since that cannot occur simultaneously, one performs it for one first. Once it has been performed for one, it will be performed for the other as well through a subsequent application? This is not so; for that which...

Since the reduplication of the constituent element has already been performed previously, it is not proper to perform its reduplication again with another constituent element, because the vowel has already been reduplicated. For reduplication is applied to that which has not yet been reduplicated, not to that which has already been reduplicated; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress. [This is the meaning of the rule] "anabhyāsasya" (of that which is not a reduplicate).

Because of this statement, it is indeed improper to perform a reduplication of another member when one member has already been reduplicated. Therefore, when there is a reduplication of only one member, the inclusion of all members is not possible; in that case, for that [member] whose reduplication is not possible, there would be a violation of the grammatical rule (*śāstrahāni*).
That is incorrect, because there would be a double articulation of each individual member.
Now, if it is argued that a simultaneous double articulation of these members is impossible,
and therefore it will be done alternately in a subsequent usage to avoid the previously mentioned fault— even so, when...

If there were reduplication of the root *pac*, then forms such as *papāca* would not be established. Furthermore, from the root *ṇijir* (DhP 1093), meaning "purification and nourishment," there is the present indicative suffix *laṭ*; then *jhi*; then *śap*; then, because it belongs to the *juhoty-ādi* class, there is *ślu*; [and then] *ślau*.

(6.1.10) Thus, there is a doubling [of the suffix]. In that case, if the doubling is applied to the mere sound *ni*, then by the rule "for the three roots beginning with *ṇi*" (7.4.75), a *guṇa* substitution occurs. Now, in this instance, the substitution of *at* is desired by the rule "after a reduplicated stem" (7.1.4)—thereby the form *tenijatīti* is produced.

The purpose [of the rule] would be for this [substitution] to occur, but it does not apply here because it is separated by the letter *j*. For the designation *abhyasta* (reduplicated) does not belong to the letter *j*, but rather to the word *ni*; this is because *ni* is reduplicated (*dvirukta*), whereas the letter *j* is not. As in the form *anenijuḥ*—here, [the substitution applies] to *jhi*, which is the substitute for *laṅ*.

The substitution *jus* would not apply by the rule *ṭhsijabhyastavidibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 3.4.109), for the very same reason [as previously stated]. Furthermore, in the case of *nenijat*, the prohibition of the augment *num* by the rule *nābhyastācchatuḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.78) would not occur, for that same reason. Nor can it be argued...

To say: "By the power of the verbal instruction, it will apply even when there is an intervention"—this is so because that instruction has scope when the reduplication applies to the entire cluster. However, when the reduplication applies to the letter *j* together with the vowel *i*, as in *nenijati* and so forth, [the rule does not apply].
The form itself would not exist; therefore, the doubling of the parts is incorrect. Consequently, the whole alone must be doubled.
Now, how is there doubling in *papāca*, given that [the rule] "of a single-syllable root, the first part is doubled" applies?

Thus it is said; yet here there is no designation of "the first" for that which consists of a single vowel (*ekāc*), because the word "first" (*prathama*) is dependent upon what is not first, being a relative term (*sambandhiśabda*). That which has nothing before it among many is "the first"; however, that which is alone does not receive the designation "the first."
[If it were so], one would obtain [the result] here, and since there is only one *ekāc* (monosyllabic) element here, reduplication (*dvirvacana*) would not occur;

it would only occur in cases such as *jajāgāra*. But how then could there be reduplication in *iyāya* and *āre*, given that reduplication is prescribed for an *ekāc*, and yet here there is no status of being *ekāc*, because there is no vowel (*anac*) other than the *aj* (vowel)?

Because there is an absence of a reason for the designation "single" (*ekāj*), he says: "In the case of *papāca*, etc. A designation is based on a connection with a vowel delimited by the number one; that which possesses such [a designation] is "designated" (*vyapadeśī*). In verbal roots such as *jāgarti* and others, there is the designation "jāg" and so forth. "Equal to that... [the rule applies].
By the rule *vartate* (Pāṇini 5.1.115), there is the status of being "like that which has a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*).

Its state is "the state of being like that which has a designation. Because of the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "also the state of having a single vowel," it also implies "the state of not being doubled.
Therefore, by this [rule], just as in the case of *jajāgāra*, when there is actual primacy for the element *jāg*, [the rule applies].

The doubling of a single vowel (*ekāc*) belonging to the first [syllable] occurs; likewise, even though it is not actually the first in ultimate reality, the doubling of the single vowel of the word *pac* occurs in the form *papāca* by virtue of the treatment as if it were designated as such (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). Similarly, in *iyāya* and *āre*, even though there is no actual status as a single vowel or as the second [vowel], [the rule applies].

The doubling occurs by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*); as for example, in *aṭiṭiṣati*, although in reality [the root] consists of a single vowel, the doubling applies to the second syllable, namely the word *ṭi*.
Nor should it be said that this [principle] does not apply to forms such as *pac* when they are not the first member [of a compound].
"By the principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (acting as if possessing a designation), reduplication occurs. In this regard,

the rule "for the reduplicated syllable of the *liṭ* [perfect], of both classes" (Pāṇini 6.1.17) serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*), showing that even when there is no actual status of being a single vowel (*ekāctva*) or a second member (*dvitīyatva*), reduplication still takes place by virtue of *vyapadeśivadbhāva*.

There is reduplication for *ceṅ* and the others. In this regard, the rule *dīrgha iṇaḥ kiti* (Pāṇini 7.4.69), which prescribes lengthening for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Here, because "numbers from one up to ten denote the thing numbered (*saṃkhyeya*) and not merely the act of numbering," the word *dvi* (two) here refers to the thing numbered.

It proceeds [as follows]: And that which is to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*)—is it the form of the word (*śabdarūpa*), or is it the act of utterance (*uccāraṇa*)? In that regard, if the form of the word were what is to be numbered, then by the word "two" (*dve*), two instances of the word-form "dvi" would be indicated as being brought about (*bhāvyamānatayā*). Consequently, for the rule *ekācaḥ* [in the context of the substitute *san*], [the same logic would apply].

The relationship is one of conjunction (*yogalakṣaṇa*); therefore, the position "doubling occurs in place of [the single consonant]" is adopted. In that case, the genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) arises in the rule *ekācaḥ*. However, if the repetition itself were the object to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*), then the relationship between the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*) would not exist.

Utterance (uccāraṇa) is a property (dharma) that follows from sound. If this [property] were to cease, then the substituend (sthānin), which possesses the property of cessation, would also cease; consequently, there would have to be a cessation of the substituend of the word *ś* [in *śit*], and therefore utterance itself would not occur, because that [utterance] is its property.

Therefore, since reduplication is not possible when [the term] *uccāraṇa* (utterance) is the object to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*), the position that "reduplication is the double employment [of the word]" (*dviṣprayogo dvirvacanam*) must be accepted. Consequently, in the rule *aikācaḥ*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), according to *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65). That [genitive]...

Because it is most desired to be pervaded by the act of pronouncing the sound *hy-*, it becomes the object (*karman*). In that case, if the position "doubling in place [of the original]" were adopted, then in the form *jighāṃsati*, the substitution of *gh* for *h* (*kutva*) would not occur; for the entire reduplicated root ending in the desiderative suffix (*sannanta*) would be the substitute for the entire original root ending in the desiderative suffix.
In that case, if [the substitution] were applied when [the suffix] was already present, then the change of *h* to *gh* in the root *han* in the form *jighāṃsati* would not occur;
for the substitute is the entire desiderative complex (*sannanta*) in place of the entire original complex, and once that has been done,
the distinction that "this is the suffix" and "this is the base" no longer exists because of the ambiguity.

Seeing that under the view where there is reduplication of the *sthānin* (the original element), the *han* of the root *han* would be destroyed and thus the *kutva* substitution for the *h* of *han*— prescribed by the rule *ṭhabhyāsācca* (Pāṇini 7.3.55)— would not occur, he states the following, adopting the alternative view that "reduplication is the doubling of the utterance": "And [it is] the double utterance."
And so forth. The word *ca* (and) is used for emphasis; the meaning is "only in the case of double usage.

It does not mean that there is a double usage in place [of the original]. Now, one might ask: how is it that this fault does not occur when there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*) consisting of double usage?
To this he says: "For the number refers to the repetition," and so forth. Again...

Repetition (*āvṛtti*) is utterance again. That [repetition] is prescribed for a verbal root that is already established by a specific number. Regarding the phrase "by that" and so forth: since repetition is prescribed for a verbal root established by a specific number, therefore that very same word, being established, is uttered twice, and not [any other].
But since another word is prescribed in its place, how could there be any occasion for the previously mentioned fault?
If, then, this position— that reduplication is the double usage [of the same word]— is rejected, and this being so:

In the rule *ṭhvasvekājādghasām* (Pāṇini 7.2.67), having cited *ādivān*, *āśivān*, *pecivān*, and *śekivān*, he will state: "When a single-substitute replacement has occurred between the root and the reduplication, [the elision of the reduplication takes place]..."
The claim that "these [roots] do not become single-vowel (ekāc) once reduplication has been performed" is incorrect;

for even when the single-substitute (ekādeśa) of the root and the reduplicated syllable has not yet occurred, and even before the substitution of *ai* (*aitva*) and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) have taken place, these [roots] remain single-vowel (ekāc) despite having undergone reduplication. This is because [the original form] existed in its place (*sthāne*).

For if there were a doubling [of the word], another distinct word altogether would be designated as having "more than one vowel" (anekāc); thus, those words which have undergone doubling would possess the status of being "anekāc," but not under the view that there is a double utterance of the same word. For in that case, it is that very same word which is uttered twice; and even if it were uttered a hundred times, it would still remain the same.
It abandons its state of having a single vowel sound, how much more so when it is pronounced twice?

Furthermore, as for that which he will later introduce—such as "bibhidvān" and so forth—in order to show what is excluded by the restrictive rule (*niyama*), that too is entirely untenable; for [the exclusion] applies only to *bhid* and the like, precisely because of what has already been stated.

Because even those [bases] that have undergone reduplication possess only a single vowel (*ekāc*). Furthermore, what he will state—that the mention of *ā* (in Pāṇini 6.4.57) is for the sake of those with multiple vowels (*anekāc*)—is also incorrect; for by that very same reason, it is impossible for bases ending in *ā* that have undergone reduplication to be considered *anekāc*.

Therefore, the position that [doubling] occurs in place of the original must also be accepted. If that is so, it is explained otherwise: here, the two previously mentioned positions are possible. Among them, which is adopted—is it the position that doubling consists in the double application [of the word], or is it the position that doubling occurs in place [of the original]?—thus [the question].

On the occasion of the question, he says: "And the double application is reduplication. The word *ca* ("and") indicates this meaning: that there is reduplication in place [of the original]. Now, one might object: since the rule "The genitive case [indicates] a connection with a substitute" (Pāṇini 1.1.49) establishes the principle of substitution, the view that reduplication occurs in place [of the original] is already established here. [The reading *dvirvacanapakṣe nātra* is printed in the edition.]
The reading ought to be [as follows]; how then is even the position of double usage (dviḥ-prayoga-pakṣa) justified?

To this he says: "For the number of repetitions," and so forth. If another word were prescribed in place of that [original], then, regarding the relationship between the original (sthānin) and the substitute (ādeśa), there would be doubling for every instance of the original.

It has been stated that "the side arises. However, when the number of repetitions is prescribed, then the other side comes into being. This too was established previously. Therefore, when the position of double performance is intended to be accepted, then the number of repetitions is prescribed as "two," by which that [is accomplished].
The word *eva* is uttered twice, but no other word is substituted in its place;
therefore, the position that the doubling consists in the double employment [of the same word] must also be accepted.
Now, how can this position—that the doubling occurs in place [of the original]—also be resorted to, given that...

Regarding the statement that "in *jighāṃsati*, the substitution of *gh* for the *h* of the root *han* does not occur," this is not a fault. It is stated as follows: "The substitution of *gh* occurs for *han* even when it is not preceded by a reduplication" (*Pāṇini* 7.3.55). And once another word has been substituted in place of that [root], the root *han* no longer exists there. In that case...
By the force of the statement, the word *hanti* will be understood as a substitute (*ādeśa*) that is a partial form (*ekadeśa*) resembling *hanti*.
However, the faults that might be suspected regarding these two positions have already been raised and addressed in the Bhāṣya itself.
These have been refuted; however, they are not written here for fear of excessive prolixity.

2. *ajāder dvitīyasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.2). [The commentary states: "This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the first doubling. Now, one might object: by the rule *ekāco dve prathamasya* (6.1.1), the doubling of the first monosyllabic element is prescribed.

But by the rule "ṭhajāderdvitīyasya" (Pāṇini 6.1.2), it applies to the second [syllable]; so how could this, being stated for one thing, be a sublater of another? Indeed, there is sublation only when coexistence is possible, and here there is the possibility that both [rules] might apply.

It might be argued: "This genitive case in the word *dhātoḥ* cannot logically be connected with either the second [word] or the first [word]; therefore, the possibility of both [connections] does not exist. But this is not so;
for one sentence prescribes the doubling of the first [vowel], and another [sentence] [prescribes it] otherwise.

Regarding the second doubling: since there is a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) in that case, why would the connection not be possible? Therefore, it was stated that even when the second doubling has occurred, the first doubling is indeed possible; [this constitutes] an annulment (*bādhana*). This is not a fault; for instance, in the word *dvīpam*.

In the word *antarīpam*, the substitution of *ī* [for *ap*] occurs by the rule "after two [vowels], after *antar*, and after a preposition, *ap* becomes *īt*" (Pāṇini 6.3.97). Although the rule "of the final [element]" (1.1.52) would have resulted in the substitution applying to the final *a* of the stem ending in *an*, the rule "of that which follows, [the substitution applies] to the beginning" (1.1.54) prescribes it for the initial [sound]. In that case, even though...

In a case of conflict, a final modification subverts a non-final modification; likewise, the second doubling will subvert the first doubling. If, then, the doubling of the first *ekāc* (single-vowel) syllable is subverted by this rule, then the doubling of a consonant belonging to the first doubling would also be subverted.
Just as there is the application [of a rule] to that which is exactly as it is, so too does the cessation of reduplication occur for that which is exactly as it is.

And to what kind of first reduplication is there such application? To that which possesses a consonant. In that case, just as the reduplication of a single vowel (*ekāc*) does not occur, so it is for that which is designated as having a single vowel.

"Would this [rule] not also apply to a consonant? This is not a fault; for when the author teaches the prohibition "na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.3), that indicates that the doubling of a consonant does not cease to occur. Otherwise, there would be no point in the prohibition of *n*, *d*, and *r*.

The prohibition of reduplication would be purposeless, because there is no possibility [of it occurring] in cases such as *aṭiṭiṣati* and *aśiśiṣati*. Here, when the augment *iṭ* has been added to the roots *aṭ* and *aś*, the forms *ṭiṣ* and *śiṣ* are reduplicated. [Furthermore,] in *aririṣati*, [it is derived] from the root *ṛ*.
When the suffixes *san* and *yaṅ* have been applied, the word *riṣ* is reduplicated.

[An objection is raised: "The status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) would apply. By the rule *sanyaṅoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.9), reduplication is prescribed for that which ends in *san*, and the augment *iṭ* is also attached to it. Therefore, this [augment] belongs to the reduplication.

The intended meaning is that it is the *nimitta* (the cause). And if the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) were to apply, then when the reduplication of the *iṣ*—which is devoid of the letter *r*—is performed, and the long vowel by rule of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇadīrghatva*) follows, the undesirable form *arīṣati* would result.
Regarding the term "kāryī": reduplication itself is the *kārya* (the grammatical operation); that which possesses this is called *kāryī*.

It might be argued: "Even though he is the agent of the action, he is nevertheless [the cause] with respect to the effect. To this, he says "And not," and so forth. But how is it known that he, as the agent of the action, is resorted to as the cause? To this, he says "Thus..."

"hi" and so forth. "Tathā hi" means "because. The particle *iti* indicates a manner. Since the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* caused by *kṅit* suffixes, as prescribed in Pāṇini 1.1.5 (*kṅiti ca*), does not apply in cases such as *śayitā*, it is therefore known that—[not].

For the effect (*kāryin*) is indeed resorted to as the cause (*nimitta*). If it were so resorted to, then because the root *śīṅ* has the marker *ṅ*, and because of the rule "before an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*" (Pāṇini 1.1.5), which prescribes the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* caused by a *tiṅ* affix,
there would result a prohibition of *guṇa* in the form *śayita*, and likewise in *śāyaka*.

And there is the prohibition of *vṛddhi*. Now, an objection is raised: that without which something does not occur is the cause (*nimitta*) of that thing, just as a cloud is the cause of rain; and just as *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* do not occur without an affix (*pratyaya*), so too they do not occur without an effect (*kārya*). Therefore, why is there no prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* for the root *śīṅ* here?

Does it occur? To this he says: "For [the cause] does not belong to that which has the effect," and so forth. Here, the word *āśrīyate* ("is resorted to") is to be supplied. It is true that even the effect (*kārya*) is the cause for the root *śīṅ*; its quality, namely *vṛddhi*, is to be understood [as the reason]. The particle *iti* indicates the nature of this immediate refutation.
[The author] demonstrates this. How, moreover, is it known that "the possessor of the effect (kāryin) is not resorted to as the cause (nimitta)"?

For if [it were], then since the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* with respect to the effect would already be established by the rules "dīdhī-vevī-ṭām" and "kṅiti ca" (Pāṇini 1.1.6 and 1.1.5), the prohibition of *guṇa* for those two [roots] would be redundant.

Regarding this, some maintain that the ablative case ending (*pañcamī*) in the rule *ajādeḥ* is derived from a *karmadhāraya* compound, as in: "That which is both *ac* and *ādi* is *ajādi*; from that *ajādi*. Describing it thus, they intend the ablative to be taken from a *karmadhāraya*. If, then, this ablative is indeed from a *karmadhāraya*, [then...]

For them, the mention of the second [case] is purposeless, because there is no possibility at all of a third [case]. For those for whom this sixth case is intended after a *bahuvrīhi*, if the mention of the second [case] were not made, there would be no possibility whatsoever of reduplication even for a third [case]. For those...

This genitive is intended for the bahuvrīhi; if the mention of "the second" were not made, reduplication would result even for a third [element], and thus the mention of "the second" is appropriate for the purpose of excluding that. Furthermore, for those who consider this [genitive] to belong to the karmadhāraya and so forth, it is the fifth [case-ending].

The second mention [of the word *teṣām*] is purposeless; for by the rule "tasmād ity uttarasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.67), it will apply only to the immediately following second [element], and not to the third, because it is separated. To this, he says: "teṣām," etc.
3. *na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.3).

Regarding the phrase "because they are included therein" (*tadantarbhāvāt*): this means that because the parts are contained within the whole, there is inclusion therein. Regarding the phrase "being constituent parts" (*avayavabhūtāḥ*): [this refers to] the word "beginning" (*ādi*).

Because they denote specific locations and parts, the meaning should be understood as "having become specific locations and parts. Regarding *diṇḍiṣati*: from the root *undī* (meaning "to moisten," Dhātupāṭha 1457), with the desiderative suffix (*san*) and the augment *iṭ* added, there is reduplication of the word *diṣ*. Regarding *aḍḍiḍiṣati*: from the root *aḍḍa* (meaning "assault" or "attack").

In this context, the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) begins with the letter *d*; by the rule of *ṣṭuan* (Pāṇini 8.4.41), the *d* is replaced by *ḍ*. However, the application of *ṣṭuan* is considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*) when there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*). Therefore, once the augment *iṭ* has been added in the desiderative (*san*), the word *viṣ* is reduplicated, and only then does *ṣṭuan* apply. Thus, [the form] *arciciṣati* is derived from the root *ṛc*.

In the case of the root *pūjāyām* (DhP 204), there is reduplication of the syllable *ciṣ*. Thus, one says *īcikṣiṣate*. When the suffix *san* is added to the root *īkṣa* in the sense of "seeing" (DhP 610), and the augment *iṭ* has been applied, there is reduplication of the syllable *kṣiṣ*.
Then, by the rules *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* (7.4.60) and *kuhoścuḥ* (7.4.62), [the appropriate substitutions are made].

The state of being a *cutva* [is illustrated] by "prāṇiṇiṣati. [This is derived from] the root *śvas* "to breathe" (DhP 1069) with the suffix *ana* (DhP 1070), preceded by *pra*. [The form] "didrāsati" [is derived from] the root *drā* "to go in a contemptible manner" (DhP 1054).

"Some say 'of *aja* and so forth," etc. According to their view, the meaning of the sūtra is that those *n* sounds and others which follow *aja* and so forth and constitute the beginning of a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*) are not doubled. What, then, is the purpose of carrying that [condition] over? To this he says: "Of that," etc.

Since the letter *da* is indeed pronounced twice, if there were a continuation of the genitive-fifth-case (*pañcamyanta*) *karmadhāraya* compound, then by the rule "tasmādityutarasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.67), a prohibition of doubling would have to apply only to the immediately following letters, beginning with *na*.

Because the inclusion of the term "nirdiṣṭa" (explicitly mentioned) serves the purpose of indicating immediate sequence (*ānantarya*). Although the letter *d* there is the initial member of the conjunction consisting of *r* and *d*, it is nonetheless separated by the letter *n*.
Therefore, the letter *d* is indeed doubled as well. [The example is] *indidrīyiṣati*, derived from the word *indra*.
In some cases, there is the substitution of *i* by [Pāṇini 7.4.33] *kvaci kṛte ṭhkyaci ca*;
from the root ending in *kyac*, there is the suffix *san*, followed by *iṭ*, and the elision of the vowel *a* by [Pāṇini 6.4.48] *ato lopaḥ*. Thus we have *ubjijiṣati*.
The root *ubj* is listed as *ubja ārjave* (Dhātupāṭha 1303). When it is taught with *ba* as its penultimate letter, then this [is the form].

A prohibition must be stated [for the doubling of the consonant]. However, if the letter *d* is taught [in the root], it need not be stated, because it is already established by the rule "na ndrāḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.3). But then, the substitution of *b* for the *d* must be prescribed so that forms such as *ubjita* and *ubjijiṣati* may occur. That too [is necessary] in cases where the substitution of *b* and the absence of *kutva* apply.
It must be prescribed [as such]; otherwise, forms such as *abhyudgaḥ* and *samudgaḥ* would not be established.

The reading with the letter *da* as the penultimate is indeed appropriate. Should only the substitution of *ba* for *va* be stated? That too need not be stated, because of the rule: "The words *bhujam* and *nyubjam* [are used] in the sense of the hand and affliction, respectively" (Pāṇini 7.3.61).

The substitution of *ba* for *ku* is obtained solely through the rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Furthermore, this would not undesirably apply to forms such as *abhyudgaḥ* or *samudgaḥ*, because an irregular derivation has scope only where the [regular] substitution of *ku* does not occur; thus, the substitution of *ba* is understood to apply only where *ku* is absent, and not in the domain where *ku* applies.

Regarding the phrase "of that which follows the letter *ṭh*," and so forth: the meaning is that this should be explained as having the sense that the prohibition [of the substitution of *ṛ* for *ṝ*] would not apply to that after which the letter *y* follows. In this regard, some explain it as follows:
the letter *r* is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*), according to the rule "there is *guṇa* [substitution] for *ṛti* and for that which begins with a conjunct consonant" (Pāṇini 7.4.29).

By the rule *ṭhyaṅ ci* (Pāṇini 7.4.30), the *guṇa* substitution prescribed for the *aṅga* is *bahiraṅga* because it depends on the *yaṅ* suffix; the *repha* (*r*) that relies upon it is likewise *bahiraṅga*. Consequently, it is non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the *antaraṅga* [operation], and therefore there is no prohibition of reduplication (*dvirvacana*) for it.
[It] becomes so. If this is the case, then in the form *indidiṣati*, the prohibition would not apply even to the augment *num*.
This is not a fault; for he will state this:
"The statement that [the base] is like its original form of instruction (*upadeśivad-vacana*) applies to the domain of *num*."

The Naiyāyikas, however, explain it otherwise, citing [Pāṇini 6.1.3]: "The *n*, *d*, and *r* at the beginning of a conjunct (*saṃyoga*) are not doubled. What have they stated? They say that the *n* and other letters preceding a conjunct are not reduplicated if that conjunct ends in *y*.
Therefore, in the case of *ārāryyate*, because the conjunct [ends in *y*], [the rule does not apply].

Because it ends in the letter *ya*, the prohibition does not apply; thus we have "arāryyate. By the rule "yaṅci" (Pāṇini 7.4.30), there is *guṇa* substitution and the replacement of *ra* with *ra*; then the word *rya* undergoes reduplication, followed by "halādiśeṣaḥ" (7.4.60) and "dīrgho'kitaḥ" (7.4.83), which effects the lengthening of the vowel. Now, one might object: [The objection follows: "But..."

One might object: "Since *arti* begins with a consonant (*halādi*), the suffix *āyaṅ* should not apply; for that [suffix] is prescribed only for roots beginning with a consonant by the rule *dhātor ekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.22). To this, he says: "Of *arti*, etc."

Regarding the rule "of the consonant" (*vyañjanasya*): when the reduplication of the monosyllabic root *īrṣyati* is to be performed, that which constitutes the consonant is the letter *y*. Once the augment *iṭ* has been applied, the reduplication must be made of the entire syllable including that consonant.
Regarding the example *kaṇḍūyiṣate*: [the suffix] *san* is added. When *iṭ* is applied, the third element becomes a single vowel (*ekāj*).

When reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is performed on that, the substitution of *i* occurs by the rule *sanyataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.79). Then, depending on each preceding *iṇ* vowel, the *ṣatva* (change to *ṣ*) is applied to all the *s* sounds. Thus we have *kaṇḍūyiṣate*. Similarly, *asūyiṣati*.
The roots *kaṇḍū* and *asū* are listed among the *kaṇḍvādi* group; from them, [the suffix] *yak* is applied by the rule *kaṇḍvādibhyo yak* (Pāṇini 3.1.27).
Regarding the statement *vā nāmadhātūnām*: a nominal base (*subanta*) functioning as a verbal root is designated here as a *nāmadhātu*.

Regarding "aśvīyiyiṣati": from the word *aśva*, after the addition of the *kyac* suffix and the *san* suffix with the augment *iṭ*, there is reduplication of the syllable *yiṣ*. Regarding "āśiśvīyiṣati": there is reduplication of the syllable *śvī*, shortening of the vowel, and the application of *halādiśeṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.60).
"According to one's wish" means that whichever among the first [cases] and so forth is desired,
for that it should be performed.

4. *pūrvo 'bhyāsaḥ* | (6.1.4) This word *abhyāsa* is well-known in common usage as signifying repetition (*āvṛtti*). Since such repetition does not apply to the first [occurrence], when it would otherwise follow that the subsequent [element] is to be understood in the rules concerning *abhyāsa*, there is instead the taking of the preceding [element].

The designation "prior member" (*pūrvapada*) is prescribed for that [word] for the purpose of ensuring that [the compound] occurs as such. The word *pūrva* denotes a constituent part (*avayava*), as in the examples "the front of the body" or "the front of the animal.
And while constituents belong to a whole (*avayavin*), although that whole is not explicitly mentioned here, nevertheless—
Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "dve" (6.1.1), only that meaning expressed by that term is understood as being "prior";

thus he says: "The word 'dve', which occurs in the nominative case, is what is carried over," and so forth. Now, one might object: the word "dve" occurs in the nominative case, whereas here the required sense is in the genitive; for otherwise, it could not be connected with the word "pūrva."
Since the relationship can be demonstrated, he says "tadarthāt" (from its meaning), etc.
It is said that "the change of case-ending occurs by virtue of the meaning. Thus, in this context, the sense is that [the word] ends in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*).
Now, however, does the genitive here express the relationship between a part and a whole (*avayavāvayavi-lakṣaṇā*), as in the example "the branch of the tree"?

Even so, if—due to the recurrence of the word "two" (*dve*)—the designation of *abhyāsa* were prescribed for that which is the first of two [elements], then in the context of [Pāṇini 8.1.1] *sarvasya dve*, the designation of *abhyāsa* would also apply to that which is the first of the two elements prescribed there; therefore, he says: "In that case... (*tatra*).

And so forth. Regarding the phrase "the preceding member" (*pūrvo 'vayavaḥ*): since the word *pūrva* can also denote a fixed position or order, the term *avayava* (member/part) is included to exclude that meaning. Thus, in the case of *papāca*, once the designation of "reduplication" (*abhyāsa*) is established, the shortening of the reduplicated syllable occurs by Pāṇini 7.4.59 (*hrasvaḥ*), followed by the replacement of all consonants except the first by the first consonant alone by 7.4.60 (*halādiśeṣaḥ*).

In *prakṛticaraḥ*, the change to *car* occurs because they are *prakṛticara*s. In *pipakṣati*, as in *juhoti*, there is the change of the letter *h* to *c* according to the previous rule; that [c] becomes *c* again by *abhyāse car ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.54). In *apipacat*, the suffix *caṅ* is applied after the root *pac* when it is followed by the causative marker (*ṇi*) and the suffix *cli*.

There is the elision of *ṇi* [by P. 6.4.51]; then, by "ṇau caṅy upadhāyā hrasvaḥ" (P. 7.4.1), there is reduplication; by "sanvallaghuni" (P. 7.4.93), there is the substitution of *i* for the penultimate vowel; and by "dīrgho laghoḥ" (P. 7.4.94), there is lengthening. These are all the purposes served by the designation of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
5. *ubhe abhyastam* (6.1.5).

Here, the mention of *ubhe* ("both") is made for the purpose of indicating the technical name (*saṃjñī*). Now, since the term *dve* ("two") from [sūtra 6.1.1] is understood by continuity (*anuvṛtti*), that indication of the technical name could indeed be established even without the mention of *ubhe*; so for what purpose is it [stated]?

Why is the mention of "both" (*ubhe*) made when "two" (*dve*) is already being carried over from the previous rule? To this he says: "When 'two' is being carried over," and so forth. If the mention of "both" were not made, then the designation of *abhyasta* (repeated) would apply to each one individually; for that designation applies to each of them separately.

[The designation] indeed applies [to the individual members]. For instance, when it is said, "one should bring two," by bringing each one individually, those two are brought. Therefore, so that the application of the designation may occur with respect to the collection as a whole, [the rule] is not for each one individually.

The mention of "both" is for the purpose that [the rule] should apply only where both [halves] exist. "In combination" (samudite) means when they are joined together or have come into a collective state. But surely, [the rule] should apply only where the reduplication is actually heard, and not where it is not heard; [otherwise, it would undesirably apply] in cases such as *īpsanti*, *īpsan*, and *aipsan*. [This objection is addressed as follows: No. In those instances, the reduplication is indeed present. How so? Because the augment *iṭ* is inserted after the root, and then the entire form ending in *iṭ* is reduplicated. Thus, since the reduplication is heard there as well, the rule applies. However, in cases like *īpsati*, *aipsīt*, and *īpsitavya*, the reduplication is not heard because the augment *iṭ* is elided by the rule *ārdhadhātuke* [Pāṇini 7.2.35], which causes the elision of *iṭ* before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. Therefore, since the reduplication is not heard there, the rule does not apply. Furthermore, the word "both" (*ubhe*) is used to indicate that the rule applies even when the two parts are separated by intervening elements. For example, in *īrtsati*, the reduplication occurs despite the intervention of the augment *iṭ*. If the word "both" were not used, the rule would only apply when the two parts are directly adjacent, and would not apply in cases like *īrtsati* where an element intervenes. Thus, the mention of "both" is intended to ensure the rule's application even when there is an intervention. Alternatively, the word "both" is used to indicate that the rule applies to the two halves of the verbal root itself, and not to the two halves of a compound. If it were not so, one might think the rule applied to the two members of a compound, such as in *adhyagīṣata*, where the two parts *adhi-aga-* appear to be combined. To prevent this, "both" is specified to show that the rule concerns the two halves of the verbal base. Or again, the word "both" is used to indicate that the rule applies to the two halves of the root even when they are separated by other elements, such as in *ajīgaṇat*, where the reduplication occurs despite the intervention of the augment *iṭ*. If the word "both" were not used, the rule would not apply in such cases. Therefore, the mention of "both" is necessary to ensure the rule's application across these various scenarios. As for the statement "in combination," it means when the two parts are joined together or have become a unified whole. Now, an objection is raised: surely the rule should apply only where the reduplication is explicitly heard, and not where it is not heard; in domains such as *īpsanti*, *īpsan*, and *aipsan*, [the rule should not apply]. Thus, since the reduplication is heard there as well, the rule applies. Therefore, since the reduplication is not
Would the inclusion of the word "both" (*ubhe*) be for the purpose of ensuring that [the designation applies] even where [only one part] exists? This is not the case;

for the term "repetition" (*abhyāsa*) is understood by way of anuvṛtti, and the connection is made thus: "both receive the designation *abhyasta* provided that there is a repetition. And this being so, even without the inclusion of the word "both," wherever a repetition is heard, [the designation applies].

It will occur in that very case, and not elsewhere. Therefore, the purpose for including the term "both" (*ubhe*) as shown by the author of the *Vṛtti* alone is correct. Regarding the example "dadati": this is the root *dā* with the suffix *laṭ*, followed by *jhi* and *śap*; then, by the rule "juhotyādibhyaḥ śluḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.75), there is *ślu*-elision, and by the rule "ślau" (Pāṇini 6.1.10), reduplication occurs.

Here, when the designation *abhyasta* is established, there is elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule *ṭhśnābhyastayorātaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.112), and the substitution of *at* for *jhi* by the rule *ṭhadabhyastāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.4). Thus we have *dadhātu* (or *dadhatu*, as in the Kāśikā); this is the imperative (*loṭ*), with the substitution of *ur* for *jhi* by the rule *ṭheruḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.86).

[The purpose is] "so that the acute accent (*udāttatva*) may belong to the entire aggregate. For if the mention of *ubhe* were absent, the designation of *abhyasta* would apply to each [syllable] individually; consequently, even the initial acute accent prescribed by "the beginning of *abhyasta*s" (Pāṇini 6.1.189) would apply to each one separately. Furthermore, [there is the rule]: "A word is unaccented except for one [syllable]."
Thus, there is no possibility of simultaneity; even so, might it [the operation] occur by way of alternation?

Therefore, the mention of both [in the rule *ubhe*] is for the purpose that the operation prescribed by "the first of those that have been elided" (*hamyastānām ādiḥ*, 6.1.189) should apply to the entire aggregate, and not to each [element] individually by way of alternation.

6. *Jakṣityādayaḥ ṣaṭ* (Pāṇini 6.1.6). Regarding the phrase "jakṣityādayaḥ": this is an illustration; even when the word *ādi* ("etcetera") forms a *bahuvrīhi* compound with *jakṣi* ending in *śtip*, it remains so even when [the compound] is a *dvandva*—that is, when...
And a *dvandva* compound is formed with words such as "jakṣeranajantasya" and so forth. Even in a sentence,
when there is the employment of both of these [terms] just mentioned,
if a *bahuvrīhi* is being understood therein, then if this [compound] is one where the qualities are cognized (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*),...
If a *bahuvrīhi* were resorted to, then there would be no inclusion of *vevīṅ*;

if, on the other hand, this were a *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna* [bahuvrīhi], then there would be no inclusion of *jakṣ*. Having seen this defect in resorting to the *bahuvrīhi*, [the author] [proceeds] with the other two [types of compounds].
Relying on one of the two positions, he says: "‘This root *jakṣ* [is included], and so forth’," and so on.

Here, the word *iti* refers back to what has just passed. Since this root *jakṣ* was mentioned immediately prior, it is that very one which is referred back by it. Those for which *iti* is the beginning are "those beginning with *iti*"; that is, those beginning with *jakṣ*.

This is the meaning. Furthermore, those [roots] beginning with *jāgr* and ending with *vevī*—namely, the six beginning with *jāgarti* as indicated by *jakṣ*, and the seventh, *jakṣiti* itself—these seven verbal roots receive the designation *abhyasta*. From among them...
Regarding that which is specified separately:

[one might object] that in forms such as *dīdhyate* and *vevyate*, the substitution of *ā* for the root vowel is already established by the rule *ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.5), and the remaining operations pertaining to reduplicated bases (*abhyasta*), such as the elision of the long *ā*, would likewise follow.

The designation *abhyasta* (repeated) is simply impossible for the roots *dīdhī* and *vevī*: first, the elision of the vowel *ā* is impossible because the vowel *ā* does not exist [in these roots] there; furthermore, the substitution of *jus* is impossible due to the absence of the suffix *jhi*; and the prohibition of the augment *num* is also impossible because the suffix *śatṛ* is marked with *ṅ* and is *ātmanepada*. Therefore, what is the purpose of assigning the designation *abhyasta* to these two?
"How is this prescribed? he asks, and replies with "dīdhyate" and "vevyate," and so forth. By the rule "dīṣyat iti ca śatari" and others, he also demonstrates another purpose:
that because these two roots are ātmanepada, the present participle suffix *śatṛ* cannot occur without a transposition [of the class].
The mention of "vyati" [is for the purpose of] grasping.

7. *tujādīnāṃ dīrgho'bhyāsasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.7). This word *ādi* exists both in the sense of "restriction" (*vyavasthā*) and in the sense of "type" (*prakāra*). If it were taken here in the sense of restriction, then [the rule would apply only to] *tuja* and *pija* in the meaning "to injure."

If [the rule] were to begin from this point [dhā.pā. 1566, 1567], only those [roots] read therein would be included; and in that case, the long vowel would not occur for those roots mentioned in the Sūtras or those read in other Gaṇas.
Having considered this, he says "of *tuji* and the rest," etc. The word "beginning" (*ādi*) here signifies "type" (*prakāra*).
Thus [it is said]. Since that manner has not been specified, it is not understood; therefore, he asks: "And what is the manner?
He shows that it has the sense of "manner" by means of the phrase "the lengthening of *tuja*, etc.
[He says] "those which have become such," meaning those which have attained the manner just described. "Lengthened..."

"It becomes correct. By this, he shows that only the correctness of the existing long vowel is established by this rule, and not that a new long vowel is created. [The example is] "tūtujānaḥ," which is formed with the *liṭ* suffix.
And this is obtained through the inclusion of the word "ādi" (etcetera), which expresses a class, followed by the suffix *kan*.
Regarding *māmahāna*: the root *maha* is used in the sense of "worship" (*pūjāyām*) [Dhātupāṭha 730]; the rest is as before. Regarding *dadhāna* [this example is not found in the Kāśikā]:
the root *ḍudhāñ* is used in the senses of "holding" and "nourishing" [Dhātupāṭha 1092]. Regarding *mīmāya*: the root *ḍumiñ* is used in the sense of "throwing" (*prakṣepaṇe*).

In the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, *ṇal* is the suffix; thus, "he held" (*dadhāra*). The root is *dhṛñ* in the sense of "holding" (DhP 900). Regarding "he crossed over" (*tūnāva*), *tu* is a verbal root found in the *sūtra* tradition, as it is listed in the rule beginning with *turustuśamyamaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.95).

By the rule "dīrghaścaiṣām" (and for these, the long vowel [is substituted]), the correctness of that which already exists is established by this [sūtra]; moreover, that long vowel is seen only in the Veda (*chandas*), not in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*). Even there, within the domain of the Veda, it occurs specifically in the context of suffixes such as *kānac* and others, not in the context of suffixes in general. Thus, "it does not occur elsewhere than that."

The meaning is that [the substitution] does not occur elsewhere than in the aforementioned context. Since the suffix *kānac* is observed after the root *tuj* in Vedic (chandas), it does not occur elsewhere—namely, in the secular language (*bhāṣā*), nor even in Vedic when other suffixes such as *kānaC* follow.
And because this is so, its operation does not extend elsewhere; by this rule, there is merely the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the long vowel where it already exists.
It is prescribed; and there is no other long vowel (*dīrgha*) elsewhere for which its correctness (*sādhutva*) could be prescribed by this rule.
And this is understood from the word *ādi* (and so forth), which expresses a class. The example "tutoja" is an usage in the colloquial language (*bhāṣā*).
If, then, the correctness of a long vowel already existing in the Vedic language (*chandas*) is [merely] established by this [rule]...

Is this [statement] redundant, since a substitution of case-endings (*sub-vyatyaya*) has already been prescribed by the rule "vyatyayo bahulam" (Pāṇini 3.1.85)? It is not redundant; for that [rule] is intended as a general elaboration (*prapañca*) of this very point.
8. *liṭi dhātoranabhyāsasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.8).

The phrases *ekāco dve prathamasya* (6.1.1) and *ajāder dvitīyasya* (6.1.2) are understood [as governing this rule]. The genitive case in *dhātoḥ* is one of part-to-whole relation (*avayava-yoga*). For if it were in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), [the meaning would be different].

Furthermore, the connection between "of the first" and "of the second" is not tenable; moreover, it is because of the prohibition [contained in the rule] "not of a reduplicated [root]. For if there were grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), the prohibition would be purposeless, since a root consisting of a single vowel that undergoes reduplication cannot possibly exist. [The phrase] "according to the application" refers to [roots] beginning with a consonant.

The meaning according to the application [of the rule] is that the first monosyllabic constituent is doubled, whereas for that which begins with a vowel, it is the second; thus, in *prorṇunāva*, since the root *ūrṇuñ* (meaning "to cover") begins with a vowel, the word *nu* is doubled by the rule *ajāder dvitīyasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.2). However, the doubling of the *repha* (the letter *r*) does not occur.

[The substitution] does not occur because of the prohibition [stated in] *na ndrāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.3). Now, one might object: since the root *ūrṇoti* begins with *ij*, when the suffix *ām* is added by *ijādeśca gurumato'nṛccchaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.36), there is elision of the *liṭ*-suffix by *āmaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.81);
and then, by *kṛñcānuprayujyate liṭi* (Pāṇini 3.1.40), the root *kṛ* is employed after it.
There would be the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of a root ending in *liṭ*, and consequently, the form would be *prorṇuvāñcakāra*;
so how then can there be *prorṇanāva*? To this he says: "The [suffix] should be stated for *ūrṇu*" and so forth.
Just as by virtue of being treated like *nu* (the *nu*-substitute), the *ām* augment does not occur after *nau*, so it is also the case for *ūrṇu*.

He shows this with the word "viśrṛṇvire. [The root] *śru* is used in the sense of "hearing" (*śravaṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 942). The form *viśrṛṇvire* is derived from the perfect tense (*liṭ*) by applying the suffix *irec* according to Pāṇini 3.4.81:
*liṭastajhayoreśirec*. Furthermore, the application of the perfect suffix is justified by Pāṇini 3.4.117: *chandasyubhayathā*.

There is the status of being a *sārvadhātuka* suffix; consequently, by the rule "śruvaḥ śṛ ca" (Pāṇini 3.1.74), there is the *śnu* affix and the substitution of *śṛ*. Then, by the rule "huśnuvoḥ sārvadhātuke" (Pāṇini 6.4.87), there is the *yaṇ* substitution [of u for v]. Thus we have "sunvire.
[The root] "ṣuñ abhiṣave" (Dhātupāṭha 1247). Because of the mention of the "root" (*dhātu*) here, there is reduplication of the *vikaraṇa* [affix].

It does not occur. Some say that it does not occur there because the verbal root is separated by its suffix (*vikaraṇa*). Others say it is due to the nature of Vedic usage (*cchandasatvāt*), according to the principle: "All rules are optional in the Veda" (*sarve vidhayaś chandasi vikalpyante*). And this is also supported by the statement: "Some say it does not occur because it is separated."
Others say it is because of its being *chandas* (Vedic), according to the principle: "All rules are optional in *chandas*" (*Puṣpavārttika* 35).

And this is obtained from the inclusion of the term *bahulam* ("variously") in the rule *vyatyayo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.1.85). Having established this, [regarding] the section on reduplication (*dvirvacana-prakaraṇe*)...
The rule *chandasi vā* (Vārttika 656) need not be stated. Regarding the form *ṇonāva*:

from the root *ṇu* "to praise" (Dhātupāṭha 1035), there is the intensive suffix *yaṅ*, reduplication, the substitution of *guṇa* by *guṇo yaṅlukoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.82), resulting in *ṇonūya*. At this stage, [the form *ṇonāva* arises].

By the rule *yaṅe'ci ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.74), there is elision (*luk*) of the *yaṅ* suffix; [the following suffix is] *liṭ*. Because of the prohibition in *amantre* (Pāṇini 3.1.35), [the substitution of *sa* for *liṭ*] does not occur. Thus we have *sasmimikṣuḥ*. The root *miha* (meaning "to sprinkle," Dhātupāṭha 992) is preceded by the prefix *sam*; from this, the desiderative suffix *san* is added. By *ho ḍhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.31), there is the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha*, and by *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si* (Pāṇini 8.2.41), there is the substitution of *ka* for *ḍha*.

By [Pāṇini 8.2.41] *si*, there is the substitution of *k*; by [Pāṇini 7.2.10] *ṭhekācaḥ*, there is the prohibition of *iṭ*; because of the *kit* designation by [Pāṇini 1.2.10] *halantācca*, there is no *guṇa* [substitution]; then follows reduplication and the substitution of *ṣ*.
When *sammimikṣa* is thus established, the suffix *liṭ* applies; however, by the prohibition [in Pāṇini 3.1.35] *amantre*, the suffix *ām* is applied.

It does not occur. [In the case of] *jhi*, there is *us* by the rule *tasya us* (6.4.48), and then *ato lopaḥ* (6.4.48). Thus we have *jāgāra*. [The form] *dāti* is due to *liṭ*; [the form] *dadāti* is due to *ślu*. Because of the statement "optionally" (*vā*), both *jajāgāra* and *dadāti* also occur as alternative forms.

9. Is this word *sanyoḥ* in the locative case (*saptamyanta*) or in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*)? If it were in the locative, then the meaning would be "after *san* and *yaṅ*"; and since the augment *iṭ* is a part of *san*, it would be included by the mention of *san*. And here, regarding *san*...

Because [the augment] *iṭ* would be caused by reduplication (*dvirvacana*), and because that which is the cause cannot be the subject of the grammatical operation (*kāryin*), reduplication would not apply to *iṭ*;

consequently, forms such as *aṭiṭiṣati* would not be established. However, when this [term *san*] is in the genitive case, the rule regarding the inclusion of the suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*, Pāṇini 1.1.72) applies, and once that which ends in it is brought forward, the meaning is as follows:

It is argued that for a root ending in *saN* or *yaṅ*, reduplication occurs of that which is either the first or the second monosyllabic element (*ekāj*) [of the stem], and thus forms such as *aṭiṭiṣati* are established. Having considered this, he says: "In the rule *sanyaṅoḥ*, this is a genitive form. In this regard:

And the separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). For if the term "after *san*, *yaṅ*, and [the suffixes]" (*sanyaṅeḥ*) were in the locative case, one would have composed a single rule as "after *ślu*, *san*, and *yaṅ*" (*ślusanyaṅḥ*). But surely there is an indicator even when there is no purpose? And here there is indeed a purpose for the separation of the rules; what is it?

Is it by virtue of that [contextual] capacity so that there may be a correspondence according to order—namely, "of the first [root] when *san* follows," and "of the second [root] when *yaṅ* follows"? This is not the case; for if correspondence according to order were intended here, then [the rule] would have stated "of the reduplication of *vañc* and the others" by means of the rule *nīgvañcu* (Pāṇini 7.4.84) regarding the elision of *yaṅ*.

The prescription of the augment *nīg* is not tenable [if taken as a separate rule]. For if there were a correspondence according to order (*yathāsaṃkhya*), then since these [roots] do not undergo reduplication, one would not have prescribed the augment *nīg*. Therefore, it is determined that this is the genitive case ending [of the compound] due to the division of the rule.
Regarding "ṭhaṭāṭālyate":

the *yaṅ* suffix is applied by the Vārttika rule "There is an addition [to the list] for *sūci*, *sūtri*, *mūtri*, *aṭ*, *laṭ*, *arti*, and *śūrṇoti*," which provides for the *yaṅ* suffix. Regarding "prarṇonūyate": [the lengthening of the vowel occurs] by the rule "akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.25).
The form *jugupsiṣate* is derived from the root *gup* with the suffix *san* by the rule *guptijkidbhyaḥ san* (Pāṇini 3.1.5);

then, from that form ending in *san*, the suffix *san* is added again to express desire by the rule *dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ samānakartṛkāt icchāyām vā* (Pāṇini 3.1.7). The form *lolūyiṣate* is derived from the reduplicated (*yaṅ*) stem.
He is the Good.

10. *Ślau* (Pāṇini 6.1.10): "When *ślu* follows. Now, *ślu* is the non-appearance of a suffix, and that is of the nature of an absence (*abhāva*). Since there can be no sequence (*paurvāparya*) in an absence, what has been stated is incorrect.

Regarding the phrase "when *ślau* follows": since [the reduplication] follows the original base (*sthānin*), it is appropriate to state this by taking the relative priority (*paurvāparya*) of *t* as well in a figurative sense through that [reduplication]; thus, there is no fault.

11. *caiṅ* (Pāṇini 6.1.11). For example, *apīpacat*, etc. [The derivation is as follows: from roots such as *pac* followed by the causative suffix *ṇic*, there is the *luṅ* tense; the augment *aṭ*; the suffix *cli*; and by the rule *ṇiśri* (3.1.48), the suffix *cli* is replaced by *caṅ*. Now, in this instance, reduplication (*dvirvacana*) occurs.
The elision of the *ṇi* affix also occurs; since both operations apply whether [the other] has been performed or not, they are both obligatory (*nitya*).
Consequently, because the two have equal force, the elision of the *ṇi* takes place by virtue of its being subsequent.
In the case of "āṭiṭat," even when the elision of the *ṇi* has occurred, reduplication still takes place precisely because the elision of the *ṇi* is treated as if it were present (*sthānivadbhāva*).
The status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), however, is established by the rule *dvirvacane 'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59).
