The elision of the suffix *ṇi* is also obligatory; it must occur whether the reduplication has not yet taken place or even when it has. Nor does this result in the acquisition of a different word-form, for reduplication consists in the double employment of the same word.
Having performed [the substitution], reduplication is not accepted here in its place; this is because it must conform to the observed usage (*lakṣya*).

Consequently, between these two rules of equal force, the elision of *ṇi* (*ṇilopa*) applies by virtue of being subsequent. Once that has been performed, both reduplication and the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhāhrasva*) become applicable; since both of these also apply whether [the other rule] has been performed or not, they are considered obligatory (*nitya*).
For reduplication applies both when shortening has not yet occurred and when it has already occurred.

Nor is there the attainment of a different word-form, because of the rule: "That which is modified in one part is treated as non-different [from the original]" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 16). Shortening also applies both when reduplication has occurred and when it has not. Nor...

It is the attainment of another form of the word, on the grounds that the very same word is uttered twice. However, the doubling [of the phoneme] in place (*sthāne dvirvacanam*) is not accepted here, because it must conform to the observed linguistic usage (*lakṣya*).
In that case, since both [rules] possess equal force, shortening (*hrasvatva*) occurs by virtue of its being subsequent; thereafter, doubling takes place.

The operations [prescribed by] "sanvallaghuni" (Pāṇini 7.4.93), which causes the treatment as if it were the suffix *saN*, and "dīrgho laghoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.94), which causes lengthening—these operations must be performed. For this very reason, it is stated in the Vṛtti:
"of the roots beginning with *pac*" (*pacādīnām*), and so forth. But what is the reason for the application of the grammatical rule in such a manner?

"How is it done so that this sequence of operation for these grammatical effects occurs? To this he says: "And thus," and so forth. "Because of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (substitute-like), it is not prohibited"—the sense is that [the cause] is absent. And this is a fifth case (*pañcamī*) used in the sense of cause (*hetu*), as in: "That [is] not to be prescribed... (*tadaśiṣyam*).

Regarding the rule *saṃjñāpramāṇatvāt* (1.2.53): for here, the substitution of *sandad* (the reduplication of *san*) prescribed by the rule *sanvallaghuni* (7.4.93) when a light radical syllable follows is prohibited on the grounds that [the original] short vowel would otherwise be considered as its *sthānin*; and when that [prohibition] occurs, the lightness [of the syllable] ceases to exist.
Having accepted this, since the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is not possible under this sequence,
the treatment as *san* (*sanvadbhāva*) is not prohibited, because the cause for obstruction is absent.
But how is it that, this sequence being in effect, the status of being a substitute does not apply to the operations?

He says that [this] is possible, beginning with the words "yo hy anādiṣṭāt... and so forth. Regarding the rule *acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau* (Pāṇini 1.1.57), the established meaning of the sūtra is this: when an operation (*vidhi*) concerns what precedes an *ac* (vowel) that has not been directly enjoined (*anādiṣṭa*), there occurs the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element). And this is not the case in this sequence.
In this context, the practice regarding what has not been specifically prescribed belongs to the preceding [rule], but rather to that which is specifically prescribed.
Therefore, when its own operation (*vidhi*) is to be performed, the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) does not apply to the short vowel;
thus, its lightness (*laghutva*) is not revoked. Consequently, by the rule "as if preceded by *san*" (*sanvat*, 7.4.93), etc., [the desired result follows].

The designation of *saṇvadbhāva* (the treatment as if having *saṇ*) being prescribed on account of a light syllable is not contradicted. However, if the operation of shortening (*hrasva*) and so forth were to be prescribed after reduplication has already taken place, then the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) would precede a vowel that has not been subject to the original rule (*anādiṣṭāt*). Consequently, when that [reduplication] is to be prescribed, for the short vowel—

The status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) would indeed occur. Thus, once the designation "heavy" (*guru-saṃjñā*)—whose nature is established by the rule *dīrghaṃ ca* (P. 1.4.12)—has superseded the designation "light" (*laghu-saṃjñā*), the application of the treatment as if preceded by *san* (*sannvadbhāva*) would have no scope here. What, then, is its scope? It is in forms such as *aśīśamat*, for in this case, [the condition applies] in relation to the causative suffix (*ṇi*).
The substitution of a short vowel for a long vowel already established (*sthita*) is prescribed by the rule *parabhūte prāgeva sthitām hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.92).

If this is indeed the sequence of operations, then in the case of *āṭiṭat*, once the suffix *ṇi* has been elided, reduplication of the second monosyllabic element *ṭiś* would not apply; would it not be absent because of that?

To this he says: "In the case of *āṭiṭat*, [the rule] 'after reduplication, before a vowel' (*dvirvacane'ci*) applies," and so forth. Now, for what purpose are these three rules formulated separately—as "in the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*)," "before the suffix *ślu*," and "before *caṅ* (the aorist marker)"—rather than having them made into a single rule as "in *liṭ*, *ślu*, and *caṅ*"?

In this regard, there is also this meaning: the case-ending (vibhakti) should not be uttered again and again, as in the case of the *liṭ* and *ślau* suffixes where reduplication (*dvirvacana*) occurs. The separate employment [of the rule] is for the purpose of making known that this [rule regarding repeated utterance] is not universal (*anitya*). Therefore, in examples such as "those who wake are desired by the Ṛg-verses" (*yo jāgāra tamṛcaḥ kāmayante*), and "he gives dear things" (*dāti priyāṇi*), "he bestows dear things" (*dhāti priyāṇi*), [the repetition does not occur].
There occurs reduplication, and consequently, the rule "In the section on reduplication, optionally in the Vedic language" (Vārttika 656) need not be formulated.

12. *dāśvān*, *sāhvān*, and *mīḍhvān* (6.1.12). [The commentary states: "They are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*) without distinction," because no specific distinction is mentioned. And regarding the statement "and the absence of *iṭ*": since the rule *vasvekājādghasām* (7.2.67) would require the addition of *iṭ*, their absence [is therefore established].

[The root] is treated as having a short vowel. But surely, the augment *iṭ* will be prescribed for monosyllabic roots that have undergone reduplication, whereas this [root] remains a monosyllable even before reduplication; since it has not yet undergone reduplication, is it not improper to prescribe the absence of *iṭ* (*aniṭ*) by means of a technical designation (*nipātana*)? This is not so; for in the case of the *liṭ* [perfect tense]...

In that [rule], the mention of "that which has undergone reduplication" (kṛtadvirvacana) was made for the purpose of indicating a root that is heard as having a single vowel (ekāc). And since there is indeed the state of being heard as a single vowel here in the case of the periphrastic perfect (liṭ), what is improper about this? [The objection is raised: "It is a parasmaipada.
Because the root sah takes the ātmanepada, it is not a parasmaipada.
Because [the desired form] is obtained, that [term] is introduced as a nipātana (an irregularly formed word).
What, then, is its purpose? He says: "The *halādiśeṣa* (the rule for the retention of the first consonant) applies," and so forth.
If the *halādiśeṣa* were to apply, then in that case he would have prescribed only the substitution of the vowel *ā*; for when the *halādiśeṣa* applies, [the result is not achieved].
There is a specific purpose for the mention of the elision (*luk*) of *ṇi*, as opposed to its elision (*lopa*).

Although the elision of *ṇi* is already established by the rule "ṇer aniṭi" (Pāṇini 6.4.51), the explicit statement of *luk* is for the purpose of preventing the strengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhāvṛddhi*) by means of the technical designation of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). For if there were merely an elision (*lopa*), [the condition for the application of that rule would remain].

Otherwise, there would be an increase in the vowel length (*upadhāvṛddhi*) due to *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations conditioned by a suffix); however, when there is elision (*luk*), it does not occur because of the prohibition stated in Pāṇini 1.1.63: "There is no [application of an operation] to a stem (*aṅga*) when a suffix is elided."
13. *ṣyaṅḥ saṃprasāraṇaṃ putrapatyostatpuruṣe* (6.1.13).
The term *saṃprasāraṇa* has been prescribed as a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for the vowel *iK* which is the substitute for *yaṇ*, and it refers to the meaning of the sentence [of the rule].
This "meaning of the sentence" is that which is expressed by *igyaṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.45).

If it were characterized by a relationship between a substitute and its original (sthānyādeśa), then this would have been stated there: "In a restatement (anuvāda), a phoneme presents itself, but in an injunction (vidhi), it is the meaning of the sentence [that presents itself]. However, this is an injunction; therefore, it is the meaning of the sentence alone that presents itself. Thus he says: "In place of *yaṇ*," and so forth. And from that also...
[The suffix] is prescribed by [Pāṇini 4.1.74], *ṭyaṅśca āp*. "Ibhya-putraḥ":
[the word] *ibhya-* is derived from *ibham arhati* ("one who deserves an elephant") by [Pāṇini 5.1.66], *daṇḍādibhyo yaḥ*. "Kṣatriya-putraḥ":
[the word] *kṣatriya-* is derived from *kṣatrasyāpatyam* ("the offspring of a kṣatra") by [Pāṇini 4.1.138], *kṣatrād dhaḥ*, which prescribes the suffix *dha*.

This [reference] "ṭh-ṣyaṅ" is a mention of an affix (*pratyayagrahaṇa*); because the paribhāṣā concerning the mention of an affix (Puṣpavṛtti 44) applies there, the rule "from that which it is ordained,
beginning with that and ending with that" would apply here only in cases such as *kārīṣagandhīputraḥ*, but not in this case.

It might be argued: "How can there be [the form] *paramakārīṣagandhīputra*? For the suffix *ṣyaṅ* is prescribed after the word *kārīṣagandha*, not after the word *paramakārīṣagandha*. Therefore, in order to remove this objection, he says: "'*ṣyaṅ*' is a mention of a feminine suffix," according to [Pāṇini 4.1.3] *striyām*.

Because this is prescribed with reference to [the preceding rule]; and the feminine nature of *ṣyaṅ* is established through the principle of "as if being the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), as well as its status as an affix—for otherwise, its status as a feminine affix would not be tenable—and because the view that it is a substitute (*ādeśa*) has been adopted there. If this is indeed the mention of a "feminine affix," then what follows from it?

In that case, there would be no restriction regarding the initial [element]; for there might be the inclusion of even more than this, or else there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Indeed, if there were no restriction, then just as here we have *paramakārīṣagandhīputra*, so too would it be here.
It might be argued that [the form] *atikārīṣagandhyāputraḥ* would be incorrect; therefore, he says: "And not when there is a feminine suffix," and so forth.

This is an exception (*apavāda*) made to the paribhāṣā concerning the mention of "suffix" (*pratyaya*), namely: "Not when there is a feminine suffix, provided it is not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*)" (Puṃvadbhāva-vṛtti 45). Consequently, wherever [the feminine suffix] is not a subordinate member...

In this case, because the word *strī* (feminine) is a suffix (*pratyaya*), the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) concerning the mention of a suffix does not apply; therefore, there is no restriction that the compound must begin with that [word]. Consequently, in the case of *paramakārīṣagandhīputra*, the formation indeed occurs.
For here, by the rule *sanmahatparamottamotkṛṣṭāḥ pūjyamānaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.61), [the compound] *paramā cāsau kārīṣagandhyā ca* is formed.

In this compound, the feminine suffix is predominant; thus, by the rule *striyāḥ pumvat* (Pāṇini 6.3.34) and others, the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) applies. However, where the feminine suffix is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), this paribhāṣā indeed applies because of the statement *anupasarjanāt*. Therefore, in this case, it certainly occurs.

This is the rule regarding initial [members]. Consequently, it does not apply here in the case of *atikārīṣagandhyāputra*. For in this instance, *atikrāntaḥ kārīṣagandhyām* ("one who has surpassed Kārīṣagandhyā") is a *prādi*-compound (*avyayībhāva*). Here, that which is "surpassed" (*atikrānta*) is the principal (*pradhāna*), while Kārīṣagandhyā is the subordinate (*upasarjana*). Precisely for this reason...

By the rule *ṭhgostriyor upasarjanasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.48), the short vowel [of the feminine suffix] occurs. However, there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the substitution of semivowels (*samprasāraṇa*) for the words *putra* and *pati* when they stand at the beginning of a compound; this would undesirably apply even here in the case of *kārīṣagandhyāputrakula*. For it is stated: "for *putra* and *pati*" [in the rule].

The seventh [case-ending] expresses immediate succession (*ānantarya*) with respect to the agent (*kāryin*); consequently, it is indistinguishable [from the sixth case-ending] when applied to two pure [elements] or at the beginning of that [compound]. Even if, for some reason, it were not used at the beginning of that, there would still be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) here as well, according to the rule "that by which an operation is prescribed applies to what ends with it" (Pāṇini 1.1.72), because it would apply to the end of that [compound].

One obtains [the form] "karīṣagandhyā-paramaputra" (the son of Karīṣagandhyā, the supreme). When three factors—the rule, the recipient of the rule, and the application—are present, the internal rule takes effect.
And these are present here: the rule is *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution), the recipient of the rule is *ṣyaṅ*, and the application is...

The words *putra* and *pati*. And here, because it is invariably present in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the final member (*uttarapada*) which has been brought to mind is qualified by the words *putra* and *pati*; and since an internal rule applies by means of a qualifier, [the suffix is applied] when the final member ends in the word *putra* or ends in the word *pati*.
Someone might have the misconception that "vocalization (samprasāraṇa) occurs" [independently];

in order to refute this, he says: "of putra and pati," and so forth. He thinks as follows: here, the *tatpuruṣa* compound consisting of "putra" and "pati" is indicated as the locus for the suffix *ṣyaṅ*, and thus it possesses the status of being a constituent part (*avayava*) of that *tatpuruṣa*.
It indicates [the relationship] between the son and the wife, as for example: "a branch on a tree.

When the tree is indicated as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the branch, it makes known that the branch is a constituent part (*avayava*) of the tree, because of their proximity (*pratyāsatti*). In that case, within the *tatpuruṣa* compound, only that which possesses the constituent part where the suffix *ṣyaṅ* applies remains.
In the case of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, only those two constituent parts that are "son" (*putra*) and "wife" (*pati*) are intended to be grasped;

however, when the words "son" and "wife" occur as subsequent members (*uttarapada*) in compounds such as *putrapatī*, they are not considered constituents of that specific *tatpuruṣa* which would trigger the application of the suffix *ṣyaṅ* to the preceding member. Rather, they belong to other, different *tatpuruṣa* compounds.

Therefore, there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) at the beginning of those [words] *putra* and *pati*. Nor does it occur at their end either; for here, the mention of *putra* and *pati* refers to the qualifier-qualificand relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) between those two and the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) which has been joined with them by means of a *tatpuruṣa* compound.

There is freedom of action here. In that regard, if the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) were qualified by the words *putra* and *pati*, then the rule for inclusion of what ends with those (*tadantavidhi*) would apply, on the principle that "inclusion of what ends with [a term] occurs through its qualification.
However, in this case, the subsequent member is not qualified by those two; rather, it is those two themselves that are qualified by it. And therefore—

Since there is no rule for [a compound] ending in that [suffix], this qualification applies only to the two [words] by themselves; how then could there be the over-extension of being "ending in that"? But surely, if the son and the husband are qualified by the subsequent word, then by that [qualification] their status as ending in that is understood, and consequently, it would apply only to the end of the subsequent word.

Is it not the case that there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the beginning of those [words] because the suffix is not applied to the two alone? This is not so; for the words *putra* and *pati* cannot possibly end in a subsequent member (*uttarapada*).
This is because this word *anta* denotes a constituent part (*avayava*), and [the words *putra* and *pati*] do not [end in such a part].

In the words *putra* and *pati*, the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) is not a constituent part; rather, it belongs to the compound (*samāsa*), yet these two are not compounds. Therefore, it should not be understood as "of those two words *putra* and *pati* which have subsequent members"; rather, it refers to the words *putra* and *pati* themselves when they function as subsequent members.
Regarding the phrase "of the two alone":

by the rule *yena vidhis tadantasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.72), which governs that which ends with [the element specified], it is understood here that the *samprasāraṇa* applies to that which ends in *ṣyaṅ*; consequently, even in the case of *vārāhīputra*, [the substitution applies] to the letter *va* as well.

Since [the vowel] would undergo *samprasāraṇa*, he says: "And when followed by ṣyaṅ," and so forth. He states the reason for that very point: "Of that which is being specified," and so forth. The mention of *samprasāraṇa* is for the sake of what follows; for it is indeed established even by the mention of the word *ati*.

And we shall demonstrate that very fact of being for the sake of what follows in that very place. Indicating that same fact of being for the sake of what follows, he says: "The *samprasāraṇa*," and so forth.

14. *bandhuni bahuvrīhau* | (Pāṇini 6.1.14) "The mention of *bandhunī* is in the neuter" and so forth. The meaning is that the mention is made in the neuter gender with respect to the word-form (*śabdarūpa*) *bandhunī*. But what is the reason for doing so?
How is this explained? He says: "This [word] is denoted in the masculine gender," and so forth.
Now, why was the reference not made using the masculine gender alone in the case of *bandhau* (in the locative singular)? [It is] so that it does not apply to the synonyms.
For if it were done in this way, the reference would be understood as being primarily concerned with the meaning (*arthapradhāna*), and so on.

And consequently, this would also apply to the case of synonyms. It has been stated that when a designation is made with the meaning as the primary factor, the technical definition of the word-form itself does not apply.
[Consider] the rule *mātaC* and so forth. Now, one might object: "But the word-form *mātaj* does not exist at all; for its..."

Since the independent use [of the word *samprasāraṇa*] is not found anywhere, how can the substitution of semivowels (*samprasāraṇa*) be effected there? To this he says, "Precisely for this reason," and so forth; and "In that case," and so forth. And if the accent of the *bahuvrīhi* compound were governed by the rule "In a *bahuvrīhi*, the first member retains its original form" (Pāṇini 6.2.1).

[If this were not the case,] the employment of the term *cit* would be purposeless. Therefore, so that its purposelessness does not occur, the force of employing *cit* sets aside the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) prescribed by the rule "of a *cita* [word]" (Pāṇini 6.1.163), which is the accent of a Bahuvrīhi compound.

But surely, the word *mātṛ* cannot possibly function as a final member (*uttarapada*) in a bahuvrīhi compound, because by the rule "ṭhnadyautaśca" (Pāṇini 5.4.153), the suffix *kap* must necessarily be applied; so how can the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of *ṣyaṅ* be justified there in the final member of a bahuvrīhi? To this he says: "And [the substitution applies] in the case of both *mātṛ* and *mātṛka*."
And so forth. Furthermore, if the *kap* suffix were obligatory (*nitya*), the author would not have made a separate mention of both *mātṛ* and *mātṛka*; yet he has done so.
Therefore, because of this separate mention, the *kap* suffix is applied optionally, and not exclusively.
The meaning of the word "also" (api) is that [the substitution] occurs even when [the vowel] is produced by the rule *mātajādeśaḥ*.

15. *vacisvapiyajādīnāṃ kiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.15). This word *ādi* ("etcetera") is connected only with *yaji*, not with each of the roots beginning with *vac*. For if a connection with each individual root were intended, [the rule would have been formulated differently] regarding the root *vac* (meaning "to speak," Dhātupāṭha 1063).
Having studied thus, let "ṭhñiṣvap śaye" (DhP 1068) be studied; since [the rule] "vacyādīnām" (6.1.15) would apply to *svap* as well, its separate mention [in that rule] would not need to be made.
But if this were so, why is there a mention of *svap* in the rule "rudaśca pañcabhyaḥ" (7.3.98)?
Could this be so? This is not a fault; for it is possible to teach *svapi* first among the *rud*-class verbs and then formulate the rule as *svapaś ca pañcabhyaḥ*.
Therefore, what was stated is correct: that [the suffix] is connected only with *yaji*, and not with *vac* along with *svapi*.

The letter *i* is for the purpose of indicating the verbal root through its association (*sāhacarya*), not for the sake of qualification. By means of that, there is the inclusion of only the substitute *vac*;

thus he says: "In the sense of speaking (*paribhāṣaṇe*), [the roots] *vac* and *brū* become *vac*. [The form] "spoken" (*uktaḥ*) is derived by [the rule] "and after a *samprasāraṇa*" (Pāṇini 6.1.108).
The state of being *parapad* (belonging to another word). Regarding "ṣṭhiṣṭaḥ":
the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by Pāṇini 8.2.36 (*vraśca-* etc.), and from that, the substitution of *ṣṭu* occurs. Regarding "ūḍhaḥ":
the substitution of *ḍha* occurs by 8.2.31 (*ho ḍhaḥ*), the substitution of *ṣṭu* occurs by 8.4.41 (*ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ*), and the elision of the letter *ḍha* occurs by 8.3.13 (*ḍho ḍhea lopaḥ*).
In the case of *uṣitam*, there is lengthening according to Pāṇini 6.3.111: "When ṭh, ḍh, or r are elided, the preceding vowel is long if it is an aṇ.
Regarding *saṃvītaḥ*, *āhūtaḥ*, and *śūnaḥ*, there is lengthening of the *i* by Pāṇini 6.4.2:
"After a consonant [the augment iṭ is added]. In the case of *śūnaḥ*, [the rule] "and after a root ending in an ūṭh-vowel" applies.
(8.2.45) The substitution of *ṇ* for the final letter of the *niṣṭhā* suffixes.

Now, why does this not occur here: in *vācamicchati* (he desires speech), *vācā tarati* (he crosses by means of speech)—where the suffix *ṭhak* applies—resulting in *vācyati* or *vācikaḥ*? Even though [the rule] *ṭhkvibvacipracchayāyatastukaṭaprujuśrīṇām* applies to the root *vac*.

Alternatively, a long vowel may have been applied by the Vārttika "dīrgho'saprasāraṇañca" (Vārttika 288); nevertheless, since there is the principle that "that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original]," the application [of the rule] remains possible. Thus he says: "dhātoḥ" (of a root), etc.—where the root is not taken up by the word "dhātu" as a general term, but rather...

However, by the very use of the word "dhātoḥ" (of the root), it is understood that the operation applies only to that affix which is prescribed after a root in the context of that [specific] suffix. And by making the irregular form *bhrauṇahatya* a nipātana (an irregularly formed word), he indicates that this nipātana is for the purpose of establishing its status as a taddhita derivative. And if [it were not so], from the root...

If the word were used to denote its own form (*svarūpa*), the very cognition of that [word] would not be understood as the grammatical effect; consequently, the specific nipātana [of *t* for *th*] would be purposeless, since the substitution of *t* is already established by the rule *hanasto'ciṇṇaloḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.32). As for the example "vācyati" and "vācikaḥ," although words ending in *kvip* do not lose their status as verbal roots (*dhātu*), [the substitution of *t* would still apply].

(Vyā.pa.132) Thus, even so, this suffix has not been prescribed as being [added] "after a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*). For instance, in one case the suffix is prescribed as being after a nominal ending (*sup*), namely in *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8), while in the other case it is prescribed as being after a nominal stem (*prātipadikāt*).

Because of the governing rule *ṅy-āpprātipadikāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.1), since the verbal root *vac* is taken here in its own form (*svarūpa-grahaṇa*), there is no "cognitive inclusion" (*saṃvijñāna*) of the operation [of the suffix] only when that suffix is present.

16. [The substitution of *ī* for the vowel of] the roots *grah*, *jyā*, *vayi*, *vyadhi*, *vaṣṭi*, *vicati*, *vṛścati*, *pṛcchati*, and *bhṛjjati* occurs before an affix marked with *ṅ* as well as before *liṭ*.
(Pāṇini 6.1.16) In the example "gṛhītam," the lengthening [of the vowel] is by [the rule] *graho 'liṭi* (7.2.37). [In the example] "jarīgṛhyate,"...
Thus: there is a *yaṅ* [intensive suffix], a *samprasāraṇa*, and reduplication; then, by the rule *rīgṛdupadhasya* (Pāṇini 7.4.90), there is the augment *rīg*.
This very root *vayi* exists as an *ātmanepada* verb—namely, *aya vaya gatau* (Dhātupāṭha 474, 475)—and it also [exists as a parasmaipada].

Regarding the rule *vetro vayiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.42), one might ask: "In that context, since it occurs alongside roots such as *grah*, which are not *ātmanepada*, is this *vayi* also understood as not being *ātmanepada*?
To this he says: *vayir liṭi*, etc. And therefore, for the *liṭ* [affix] following that, [the substitution of *kvasu* applies] by the rule *asaṃyogālliṭ kit*.
One might ask: "Should [the substitute] be treated as having the *kit* designation by virtue of rule 1.2.5? To this, he says: "Of that," and so forth.

"If this is so" means: if there is the inclusion of *vay*, which is the substitute for *veñ*. "Because *veñ* is recited among the roots beginning with *yaj*"—and therefore, by the preceding rule itself, its status as a *sthānin* (original element) is maintained.

The intention is that the *samprasāraṇa* is established. "It cannot be understood in this way"—the word "to understand" (*vijñātum*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The meaning is: by this reasoning, it is not possible to understand that the mention of *vay* is purposeless. For what reason? He says: "In the case of the *liṭ* [affix], of that," and so forth.
It might be argued: "Because of the contradiction between affirmation and negation, there will be affirmation alone in one place, not negation. To this, he says: "In this case, since...
and so forth. It might be argued: "Because of the contradiction between affirmation and negation, there will be affirmation alone in one place."
Is it not a negation? To this he says: "In this case, just as... and so forth.
If there is an impossibility of [two things] being in one place due to contradiction, let there be alternation (paryāya);
however, because both would find their fulfillment elsewhere, it follows that there must be only one, and not the other—this is the meaning obtained.
Such are the [objectionable] states. [Response: "This is not a fault. How is this not a fault? To this he says: "In the case of *liṭ*," and so forth.

The prohibition of *saṃprasāraṇa* for the *yakāra* in the rule "in *liṭ*, [the *v* of] *vay-* becomes *ya*" (*liṭi vayo yaḥ*) is an *upalakṣaṇa* (indicative mark) for the fact that by the mention of *veñ* in the rule for *vidh-*, there is also the inclusion of *vayi*.

Since an acquisition is impossible in the absence of a rule for its application, a prohibition would be meaningless. In the case of the rule *veñaḥ*, the fact that the mention of *vyeñ* does not occur when there is a prohibition serves as the very evidence for this statement regarding the prohibition. For if the mention of *veñ* were present, [the rule] would be accomplished by *veñaḥ* itself.

Since the prohibition [of *vay*] is already established by the rule "in the *liṭ*, *vay* becomes *ya*" (6.1.38), he reiterates the point just mentioned. If this is indeed the case, then for what purpose is the mention of *vay*? To this he says: "This very... and so forth. By that, it is for the sake of clarification.

He explains that this is the inclusion of the verbal root *vyadh*. In the form "vidhyati," the suffix *śyan* is applied because it belongs to the *divādi* class. In the form "uṣṭaḥ," this is the form ending in the suffix *tasa*; the *śap* is elided because it belongs to the *adādi* class, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *vraścādi* (Pāṇini 8.2.36), and the substitution of *ṣṭu* follows. In the form "vicati," the suffix *śa* is applied because it belongs to the *tudādi* class.

In *vṛkṇa*, the substitution of *n* for *t* occurs as before, and there is elision of *s* by the rule *skoḥ* (8.2.29). The point is that the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) does not begin with a *jhal* sound; therefore, the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur here, because that [substitution] is prescribed only when a *jhal* or *ac* follows—specifically from the rule *jhalo jhali* (8.2.26).

Because of the continued application of the term *jhal*; for it is said that "when *kutva* is to be applied, that [the preceding rule] is indeed not established. For it is not the case that the established status (*siddhatva*) of the *niṣṭhā* substitute is asserted in the same way as it is for *ṣatva* and so on;
rather, by that [non-establishment], *kutva* indeed proceeds. "He cuts" (*vṛścati*): the suffix *śa* is applied as before. "He cuts repeatedly" (*varīvṛścyate*).

The augment *rīk* is applied according to the Vārttika (880): "It should be stated that [the augment *rīk* is added] after the root *pṛ*. Thus we have *pṛṣṭaḥ*. The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs as before. Why does vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) not occur in the word *praśna*, where the suffix *naṅ* is prescribed by the rule "yajayāca... (Pāṇini 3.3.90)? To this he says: "In the case of *naṅ*, etc. [And thus we have] *bhṛṣṭaḥ*.

Thus [it is said]. As in the previous case, there is the substitution of *ṣ*. In "bhṛjjati," as before, there is the suffix *śa*. In "barībhṛjyate," as before, there is the augment *rīk*. Regarding the phrase "of that which has the same time," etc.: [one might object] that by the rule "skhoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca" (Pāṇini 8.2.29), its [the *s*'] elision ought to occur?
This is not so; it is stated that [the substitution] occurs before a *jhal* consonant and at the end of a word.

17. *liṭ-abhyāsasya ubhayeṣām* (Pāṇini 6.1.17). Regarding the form *uvayitha*: the augment *iṭ* is first required by the rule governing roots beginning with *krī* (7.2.13), but it is prohibited by the rule *upadeśe 'tvataḥ* (7.2.62). However, due to the restrictive rule *ṛto bhāradvājasya* (7.2.63), it occurs once again.

"There is no difference between [the roots] *ṭhgrah* and *ṛ*. This is because, when there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*), after the application of "remainder of the consonant" (*halādiśeṣa*, Pāṇini 7.4.60), the *repha* is removed;

thus, the form that results from *grah*—namely *jagrāha*—is exactly the same even when vocalization has occurred, provided that the substitution of *urat* (Pāṇini 6.4.142), the subsequent addition of *rapara* (Pāṇini 1.1.51), and "remainder of the consonant" have all been performed.

Regarding "jijyau": by [Pāṇini 7.1.34], *āta au ṇalaḥ*, the substitution of *au* occurs. Regarding "jijyatha": by [Pāṇini 6.4.64], *āto lopa iṭi ca*, there is the elision of the vowel *ā*. As for the statement, "Whether there is a connection [with another rule] or not, there is no difference in the case of *vṛścati*": if the connection were commenced for the sake of another meaning and not for the sake of the meaning of *vṛścati*, then...
The meaning of this statement— that "this [substitution] does not occur for the root *vṛścati* even when this other rule exists"— is that even though this other rule exists,

there must still be no vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the reduplicated syllable of *vṛścati*. For the intention is that without such a specific rule to that effect, vocalization cannot be justified by any means whatsoever.
Therefore, even if this rule were non-existent, the form *vavraśca* would be exactly the same as it is now;
thus, there is no distinction for the root *vṛścati*. This has been stated according to the opinion of the author of the Vṛtti.
However, according to the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya, he says "when the yoga is commenced," and so forth. His intention is as follows: when [the rule] exists...

When the meaning of *vac* is being applied [to another root], it also possesses the meaning of *vṛścati*; for *vṛścati* is included among the roots beginning with *grah*. Consequently, since this rule (*yoga*) is commenced for that purpose as well, there ought to be vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) even for its repetition; such is the implication of the word *tu*.
He shows the distinction from the opinion of the author of the *Vṛtti* with the words, "If, without performing the *samprasāraṇa*," and so forth.

But surely he will state the purpose of including both [terms] as follows: "So that the *samprasāraṇa* itself may take place, even overriding the subsequent *halādiśeṣa* (P. 7.4.60). How then can this position [be maintained]?

"Is there a possibility?"—the intention is that this occurs when the *yoga* (grammatical operation) is devoid of the mention of both [elements]. "Now, regarding the *repha*," etc.—the sense is that this occurs when the *yoga* is accompanied by the mention of both. "Because of the status of being a *sthānivat* for the substitution of *uradattva*"—by what, then, is there the status of being a *sthānivat*? [By the rule] *acaḥ*...

Regarding the rule *parasmin vidhau pūrvasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.57): what is this [that is "subsequent"]? It is the suffix (*pratyaya*) that follows a vowel (*ac*), by reason of which the substitution of *am* for *au* would occur. When it is understood that "the reduplication belongs to the base (*aṅga*"), the suffix is necessarily resorted to by implication; for without that suffix, there can be no designation of a base.

The opinion of the author of the Vṛtti must be accepted; otherwise, because both [the *r* and *v*] would not be grasped there, the *r* would be eliminated by the rule *halādiśeṣaḥ* (P. 7.4.60) even before the *samprasāraṇa*, and consequently, the *samprasāraṇa* of the *v* would occur. As a result, the undesirable form *uvraśc* would arise.

"‘ṭhapṛcchati’ and ‘bhṛjjati’ have no distinction [from the forms with ṭu]"; this should be understood as being like the case of the root *grah*. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the *kit* suffix," etc.: what, then, is the reason that this must be explained for the sake of the *kit* suffix?
To this he says: "when a *kit* suffix follows," etc.; because when a *kit* suffix follows, the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) occurs by virtue of its higher priority.

Since it is understood that the rule applies again even after a semivowel has been vocalized (*samprasāraṇa*), once reduplication has been performed, forms such as *ūcatuḥ* are established even without this specific statement.
Therefore, this [rule] is not for the sake of the *kit* affixes, but rather solely for the sake of those that are not *kit*.
Now, for what purpose is it stated "of both" (*ubhayeṣām*),

given that by the very connection with the *svarita* accent, the term "of both" will naturally carry over (*anuvṛtti*)? And if there were such a carry-over, would not the *samprasāraṇa* [substitution] apply even to the roots beginning with *vac* when followed by a *ṅit* suffix?

Nor should it be suspected that [the rule] applies here; for if *samprasāraṇa* were to occur for *vraśc* and the others as well when followed by a *ṅit* suffix, the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) would be purposeless. Alternatively, the recurrence of *vraśc* and the others will take place by the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti-nyāya*);
so how could there be any occasion for this objection?

Thus he says: "By the very context," and so forth. Since the inclusion of both [types of vowels] is already established by the context alone, the fact that "both" (*ubhayeṣām*) is mentioned again constitutes a restatement (*punarśruti*). And the purpose of this restatement is as follows: where both a *samprasāraṇa* and something else would otherwise apply, [the rule applies].

This is so that there may be *samprasāraṇa* alone, and nothing else. Consequently, in forms such as *vivyādha* and *vivyadhitha*, *samprasāraṇa* occurs even by setting aside the subsequent *halādiśeṣa* (P. 7.4.60); otherwise, because [the latter rule] would apply first due to its higher status (*paratva*), [the desired result would not follow].
Once the substitution of *y* has been effected by the rule *halādiśeṣaḥ*, the *v* would undergo *samprasāraṇa*; consequently, undesirable forms such as *uvyādha* and *uvyadhitha* would result.
18. *svāpeścaiṅ* (6.1.18). Regarding the term *svāpeḥ*: since the root *āplṛ* (meaning "to pervade," DhP 1260) also has a form with a single *i*, its mention here as *svāpeḥ* is possible.
Therefore, in order to dispel the doubt regarding the inclusion of that [root], he says: "The inclusion is of the causative (*ṇyanta*) form of *svap*.
And the inclusion of the causative form is understood from the mention of *caṅ*, for a *caṅ* affix cannot occur after a non-causative (*aṇyanta*) root.

[The example is] *asūṣupat*. The causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied by the rule "And when there is a motive" (*hetumati ca*, Pāṇini 3.1.26). [The reduplication follows] from the doubling [of the root].

"Here, the *samprasāraṇa* [occurs] first," because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. In "svāpyate," the *lakāra* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), and *yak* is added by Pāṇini 3.1.67 (*sārvadhātuke yak*).
In "svāpitam," the *ṇi* is elided by Pāṇini 6.4.52 (*niṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi*). But is it not the case that [the rule] from the *grahyādi* group (Pāṇini 6.1.16) [would apply]?

[The objection: "The term *ṅt* continues [from the previous rule], and since there is no other *ṅt* besides *caṅ* in the context of sleep (*svāpa*), it will apply to *caṅ* alone by virtue of its capacity; therefore, the mention of *caṅ* need not be made. To this, he says: "The *ṅt* is merely... and so forth. For in the sūtra beginning with *grah-*, both [the *ṅt* and the *caṅ*] are present.

Regarding the proximity [of the terms]: there is the mention of *kit* and the mention of *ṅit*. Since both are present without distinction, it is difficult for those of dull intellect to understand why only the mention of *ṅit* is carried forward (*anuvartate*) and not the mention of *kit*. Therefore, for the sake of easy comprehension by those of dull intellect, the mention of *caṅ* is made.
The state of being.
19. *yaiṅ* is substituted for the *yaṅ* of *svapi*, *iṇ*, and *vyeñ*. (Pāṇini 6.1.19). Regarding the form *svapnaka*: [it is derived] by the rule *svapitṛṣornajiṅ* (3.2.172).
*cāyaḥ kī* | (6.1.21) Now, for what purpose is the long vowel [of *cāy*] pronounced, given that even when a short substitute is applied...

Is it not already established that *cekīyate* is formed by the lengthening [of the vowel] according to the rule *ṭhakṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.25)? To this he replies: "The utterance of the long vowel," and so forth. But how, when it is stated that *yaṅ* is added [by the rule] *yaṅ ci* (7.4.30), can there be an *ādeśa* (substitution) in the case of *yaṅ-luk* (the elision of *yaṅ*)? [It occurs] by means of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations as if a suffix were present).

It might be so. But even if the rule "na lumatāṅgasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.63), which prohibits the application of suffix-based operations (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), were to apply here, we would still understand from the very fact of the pronunciation of the long vowel that this occurs when there is elision of the *aṅga* suffix; otherwise, that [long-vowel pronunciation] would be purposeless.
Regarding "ṭhcekītaḥ": this ends in the suffix *tasa*. There is elision (*luk*) of the *yaṅ* by [Pāṇini 2.4.74], "after *yaṅ*, when *aci* follows."
22. *Sphāyaḥ sphī niṣṭhāyām* (Pāṇini 6.1.22). [The example is] *sphātiḥ*. By the rule *striyāṃ ktin* (3.3.94), the suffix *ktin* is applied; then by *vali* (6.1.66), there is the elision of *y*.
[The example is] *sphātībhavati*. When the suffix *cvi* is added to the root *sphāy-* ending in the *niṣṭhā* suffix, by the rule *as ya cvau* (7.4.32), the *a* is replaced by *ī*.

Thinking that this form occurs when the substitution of *it* has taken place, someone might object: "But how is this form *sphātībhavati* possible, since even here, if this substitution were applied in the past participle (*niṣṭhā*), it ought to be *sphītibhavati*? To him [the author replies]:...

He replies: "Even this [expression] 'it becomes sphāti'... and so forth. This too is the very form of the word ending in *ktin*, because when the suffix *cvi* is applied after the word *sphāti* ending in *ktin*, the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *cvau ca* (Pāṇini 7.4.26). Therefore, this undesirable consequence does not arise.
23. *styaiḥ prapūrvasya* (6.1.23). [The commentary states:

"There is a general inclusion. Since the substitution of *ā* has been applied to both [roots], and because the form is identical due to the application of *s* to the initial of the root by *dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ* (6.1.64), [the rule applies].

Furthermore, the paribhāṣā "the rule as stated by its specific technical name [takes precedence]" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 3) does not apply here, because both rules are defined by their own specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇika*). Now, one might ask: why does the substitution of *ṇ* for the final letter of the suffix *niṣṭhā* (Pāṇini 8.2.43), which applies to roots beginning with a conjunct consonant and ending in a vowel followed by *yaṇ*, not occur here? To this, he says: "in the case of *samprasāraṇa*."

And so forth. However, because this [substitution] is *asiddha* with respect to what precedes it, the *samprasāraṇa* is performed first; and once that has been done, since there is no longer a *yaṇ*, the substitution of *na* does not occur. [The author says:
"It is established simply as *prastya*. But surely, if this were stated, [the rule would apply to] the word *pra* as well?

There would be *samprasāraṇa*, and consequently the form would be *prastīta*; why then is it said that [the form] is established by [the rule] *prastya* alone? He thinks: "This fault does not arise because of the principle *anantyavikāre 'ntyasadeśasya*" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 63). [He adds: "So that this may also apply here."
Thus [it is asked]: why, then, does it not apply? Because it is separated by the word *saṃ*.

Is it that when the term *pūrva* (preceding) is employed, the very meaning of the word becomes such that it applies here as well? Or rather, with the intention of indicating that an increase in the text suggests an increase in the meaning, he says: "That..."

"How so? To show the first alternative, he says: "Of that which is preceded by *pra*. [This is explained as follows: "The *bahuvrīhi* compound is used in the sense of the genitive case. Since this word *pūrva* denotes a constituent part (*avayava*), the *bahuvrīhi* occurs in the sense of the genitive. When the word *pūrva* denotes a constituent part, the verbal root (*dhātu*) becomes the external referent (*anyapadārtha*).

This is not tenable; for this prefix *pra* is not a constituent part (*avayava*) of the verbal root (*dhātu*), but rather a constituent part of the combination of the root and the prefix (*dhātūpasarga-samudāya*). Therefore, he says—"that which has *pra* as its prior member," and so forth—stating that it is that very [combination] which is logically the referent of the other word (*anyapadārtha*). Regarding the phrase "of its constituent part" (*tadavayavasya*): that which is a part of it is "its constituent part" (*tadavayava*).

This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). By the word "tat" (that), the aggregate of the root and the prefix is referred to. Regarding the phrase "a genitive of different substrata" (*vyadhikaraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*), and the phrase "preceded by *pra*" (*prapūrvasya*): the genitive here expresses the relationship of part and whole (*avayavāvayavisambandha*) with respect to the constituent parts of the prefix; however, this [genitive] in the word "of *styā*" (*styaḥ*)...

Regarding the relationship that exists in dependence upon the constituent parts of a compound: because [the referents] are different due to that [relationship], the two genitive cases in *satyaḥ* and *prapūrvasya* are in different grammatical relations (vyadhikaraṇa). This might be so; however, in the case of *prasaṃstīrṇa*, the word *styā*, which is a constituent part of the aggregate preceded by *pra*, is not possible [to exist independently]. Therefore...
He said: "In that regard," and so forth.

24. *dravamūrtisparśayoḥ śyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.24). [The commentary states: "*dravamūrtau dravakāṭhinye*" ("in the case of *dravamūrti*, it means the solidity of a liquid"). By this, he explains the meaning of the term *dravamūrti*.
Here, it refers to a specific subsequent state of a liquid known as solidity (*kāṭhinya*).
It is expressed by the term "liquid form.

Regarding the phrase "and in touch": touch is said to be a quality that co-exists with color and the other [sensory qualities]. As in the expression "the water is cold," how then can there be grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) here, given that...?
The word "cold" (*śīta*) denotes a specific quality (*guṇaviśeṣa*), whereas words such as "wind" (*vāyu*) denote a specific substance (*dravyaviśeṣa*);
therefore, he says: "in the case of a mere quality," and so forth. For example, words such as "white" (*śukla*) sometimes refer to a mere quality, as in "the white of a cloth"; but at other times...

In the case of a substance possessing that quality, the expression "this is that" (*so 'yam*)—such as "the white cloth" (*śuklaḥ paṭaḥ*)—arises either through the relation of non-difference (*abheda-sambandha*) or because of the elision of the possessive suffix *matup* (*matub-lopa*), resulting in a form ending in the possessive suffix *a*. The same applies to the word *śīta* ("cold"). Therefore, when it refers to a substance possessing that quality, since both [words] are applied to the same substance, their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established; this is the intended meaning. In the form *saṃśyānaḥ*, the substitution of *n* for *s* occurs by the rule *saṃyogādeḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.43).
25. *prateśca* (6.1.25). 26. *vibhāṣābhyavapūrvasya* (6.1.26).

"This is a *vibhāṣā* (optional rule) in both cases," it is said. Since the [application of the suffix] was already established by the preceding rule regarding the objects of fluidity, form, and touch, [the present rule provides an option].

[This rule applies] where [the preceding rule] does not otherwise apply. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "pūrva" (preceding)? Why not simply say "vibhāṣā abhyavābhyām"? To this he says: "Of the mention of 'pūrva'," and so forth. He asks: even when the mention of "pūrva" is made, why does it not occur here? To this he says: "It is indeed not," and so forth. For this...
Neither the compound *samudāya* preceded by *abhi* nor that preceded by *ava* [is intended];

rather, it is preceded by *sam*. Therefore, because of the inclusion of the word "preceded" (*pūrva*), [the rule] does not apply here. Thinking that [the rule] would indeed still apply even if the word "preceded" were included, he used the word *kila* to indicate his lack of approval.

Demonstrating that very application (*prāpti*), he says "yo'tra" and so forth. Why does the option not apply based on that collection of root and prefix which follows the word *sam*? For indeed, since this [prefix] is preceded by *ava*, the application exists. To this he replies: "Another effort must be undertaken."
The term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is employed here, and it is understood as a *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā* (a restricted option);
therefore, [the rule] does not apply here, which is another effort [of the author]. Furthermore, "another purpose for the mention of *pūrva* must be stated";
that [purpose], moreover, is [to form] *abhisaṃśīnam* and *abhisaṃśyānam*.

It should be understood that this [rule] is intended so that there may likewise be an option in cases such as *avasaṃśīnam* and *avasaṃśyānam*. Furthermore, since this result is achieved when the word *pūrva* is included, in the rule *styaḥ prapūrvasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.23),
the term *prapūrvasya* is a bahuvrīhi compound used in the sense of a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*).
This has been explained by [the passage] beginning with "ityādi" (and so forth).

27. *śrutaṃ pāke* (Pāṇini 6.1.27). This refers to the rule for the root *śrā* in the sense of "cooking. The root *śrā pāke* (Dhātupāṭha 1053) is listed among the roots beginning with *ad* (the second class), and it is also listed among the roots beginning with *ghaṭ* (the seventh class) for the purpose of assigning it the designation *mit*. Some authorities also list it among the roots beginning with *cur* (the tenth class).

The root *śrai* meaning "to cook" belongs to the *bhvādi* class (DhP 919); therefore, its inclusion here would have been expected without distinction. For even the form derived from *śrā* (with the substitution of *ā* for *ai*) indeed possesses this very form. Furthermore, due to this specific grammatical convention (*nipātana*), the paribhāṣā concerning "that which is taught by a rule versus that which is taught explicitly" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 3) does not apply as a restriction.
"Of that which ends in ṭhūṇ and that which ends in aṇ," because no specific distinction is mentioned. And thus it has been said: "In the case of śrā and śrap, [the form is] śr̥ta.
If the word *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is understood to carry over, then even in the case of *kṣīra* (milk) and *havis* (clarified butter), there would optionally be the form *śrāṇa*.

[If one were to say] "it has been cooked" (śrapita), then by those [two rules], even in the other case, the form "cooked" (śṛta) would undesirably follow. To this he says: "This is a restricted option" (vyavasthitavibhāṣā).
[He explains] "even when," etc. The activity of the instigator (prayojaka) consists of commanding, requesting, and so forth, with respect to the action to be performed.

By employing a metaphorical designation of the cause (*kāraṇopacāra*), it is expressed by the word "prompter" (*prayojaka*). For that [prompter] stands outside of the primary meaning (*prākṛtārtha*), because it is not included therein. In that case, when a second *ṇic* affix is produced by the rule "and in the sense of having a cause" (*hetumati ca*, Pāṇini 3.1.26), even then—
This elision is not desired even for *kṣīra* and *havis*;

this is understood precisely because of the rule of "optionally fixed" (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). And so it has been said: "The form *śṛtam* [is used] for the root *śrā*, except when there is a cause (*hetu*). The meaning is: "except when there is a causal suffix *ṇic*. The mention of the second [word, *havis*], is when there is only one [instance].
Since that is desired, [the example] "the milk was cooked by Devadatta with Yajñadatta" is given;

because of the word *ca* ("and") in the rule *tatprayojako hetuśca* (Pāṇini 1.4.55), the designation of agent (*kartṛ*) is prescribed for both Devadatta and Yajñadatta, and thus the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used for both in the sense of the agent. This refers to the form "śrapitam."
When the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied to *śrā*, the augment *puk* is added by the rule *arti-hrī-...* (Pāṇini 7.3.36), and the vowel is shortened by *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* (6.4.92).

Thus, we have *kṣīraṃ svayameva śrāti sma*. When this is used with Devadatta as the agent, the first *ṇic* is applied by the rule *hetumati ca* (3.1.26). When he, in turn, causes [the milk] to be cooked...

At that time, it was employed by Yajñadatta as a second [object]; by the rule "ṭhṇeraniṭi" (Pāṇini 6.4.51), there is the elision of the preceding *ṇi*, and then, with milk (*kṣīra*) as the object of the causal action (*prayojya*), the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is applied—thus "śr̥tam.
Since it has been asserted that "both the form ending in *ṇic* and the form ending in *aṇic* are prescribed as irregular forms (*nipātita*)," this is correct.

This is also a nipātana (irregular formation) for the causative form—this being the accepted view of those who maintain that the root *śrā* is recited even in the *curādi* group. However, for those who do not admit its inclusion in the *curādi* group, how can this nipātana apply to the causative? Nor can it be argued that [it applies] for them as well.

If someone should object that this formation [of *śrāta*] is appropriate through the intervention of a causal *ṇic* suffix— citing the statement of the author of the Bhāṣya, "The word *śṛta* [is used] after the root *śrā*, except when a cause is intended"— the author replies to him with the words "This [root] is *śrāti*" and so forth. Even when the meaning has attained the status of an object (*karman*), because of its ease (*saukarya*), it is treated as independent (*svātantryeṇa*).
That is intended to be designated as a *karmakartṛ* (an agent that is also the object), on the basis of the principle that "the object becomes the agent.
It is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) meaning "that which is both an object and an agent"; the domain of such [an agent] is the *karmakartṛviṣaya*.
And this qualification—namely, that the root *pac* has as its domain the *karmakartṛ*—is mediated by the meaning [of the action].

It should be understood as follows: when its meaning consists merely in the act of softening by one who is the agent of the cooking process, then this root *śrā* occurs as intransitive (*akarmaka*). But when it takes the causative suffix (*ṇic*), then it expresses the original meaning of *pac* (to cook). "Prākṛta" means that which exists in the base form (*prakṛti*); furthermore, it refers to that which belongs to the base form of the causative.

The meaning of the root *pac* (to cook) should be understood here as the process of softening, gathering [the ingredients], and so forth, having the agent who cooks—such as Devadatta—as its performer; that is to say, he expresses the ordinary action called "cooking" which has such an agent as its performer. In that regard, it is accepted that "it is cooked" (*śṛtam*) applies to both [the object and the agent] when the causative form *śrāpayati* functions with respect to the agent-as-object (*karmakartṛ*).

In this case as well, a root having the same meaning as *pac* (to cook) is intended; even when it is a causative (*ṇyanta*) that expresses the basic meaning of *pac*, it is intended there too. In that regard, "the milk was cooked by itself" (*śṛtaṃ kṣīraṃ svayameva*) is an example of the first [type], while "the milk was cooked by Devadatta" (*śṛtaṃ kṣīraṃ devadattena*) is an example of the second. But surely, according to the rule "after the root *śrap*, the form *śṛta* occurs elsewhere..."?

It is stated in the Bhāṣya, "except for [the sense of] cause" (*hetoḥ*); how then is this intended to apply to both [the *ṇic* of causation and the *ṇic* of the denominative]? He thinks as follows: regarding that which is stated in the Bhāṣya—"the word *śṛta* [is used] after the root *śrī*, except for [the sense of] cause"—therein, by the phrase "except for [the sense of] cause," there is no exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of every *ṇic* with a causal sense.

If it were intended otherwise, this would be contradictory; for if *śrā* were not included in the *curādi* class, and *śrap* were instead treated as a nipātana (irregular formation) resulting in *śṛta*, how could there be an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of it elsewhere by the rule "except when caused by an agent" (*anyatra hetoḥ*)? Or, if there is an exclusion elsewhere by the rule "except when caused by an agent," then [the inclusion of *śrā* in *curādi*] cannot be the case.

The grammatical derivation of *śṛta* from the root *śrap* is thus justified. For, since the root *śrā* is not listed in the *curādi* (tenth) class, there exists no other causative suffix (*ṇic*) after it than the one added in the sense of causing another to act (*hetumaṇṇic*). Therefore, that very [root] for which the causative suffix in the sense of causing another to act cannot be justified as being merely expressive of its own primary meaning (*svārthika*) in any way whatsoever, is precisely [the one intended].

That which is intended by the author of the Bhāṣya as the object of exclusion (paryudāsa) is to be understood as that second *ṇic* affix which arises when there is an external instigator (*prayojaka*). However, that [ṇic] for which self-referentiality (*svārthikatva*) can be established in some manner is not the object of exclusion intended by the author of the Bhāṣya.

This derivation of it is indeed desired. Furthermore, that [root] which, when produced, expresses the meaning of the root *pac* (to cook) in its natural state (*prākṛta*) is to be understood as such; for since it has the same meaning as the sense of the base form (*prakṛtyartha*) of *pac*, its status as a suffix expressing its own meaning (*svārthika*) can be designated by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). Thus, in this case—
Even according to the reading in the *curādi* class, this substitution is indeed appropriate for the causative form (*ṇyanta*) of the root *śrāti*.

28. *pyāyaḥ pī* (6.1.28). [The form] "pīnam" [is derived thus]: by [the rule] *oditaśca* (8.2.45), there is the substitution of *ṇatva* for the *niṣṭhā* [suffix]. Regarding "even here," etc.: by the word *api*, it is indicated that not only is the same option (*vibhāṣā*) [applied] as in the preceding rule...

He shows that this is also a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (an option restricted by specific conditions), as indicated by the words "api tveṣāpi" (but even this). He asks, "What is established by this? and answers with the words beginning with "tena" (by that). He states an exception to the rule that [the suffix] does not occur after a root preceded by a prefix, using the words beginning with "āṅpūrvasya" (of that which is preceded by *āṅ*).
This substitution of *pī* for *andhū* and *ūdhas* is permanent; it is indeed a case of fixed optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
29. *Liṅyaṅośca* (6.1.29).
[The word] *vibhāṣā* has ceased [to apply]. This is because the word *vibhāṣā* is mentioned again in the subsequent sūtra;
otherwise, since this very [word] would have continued to apply there, he would not have done so. Therefore...

Thus it is said: "Those rules which occur between two rules expressed in different languages are considered eternal (nitya). Furthermore, the word *ca* ("and") draws in [the rule] "pyāyaḥ pī" [P. 6.1.28]. For otherwise, since the term *samprasāraṇa* is the subject under discussion, one might understand that the *samprasāraṇa* applies to *pyāy* in the context of the *liṅ* and *yaṅ* suffixes. But when the word *ca* is present...

The connection with the substitution of *pī* is easily understood as occurring immediately after the [substitution of] *satya*. However, someone might have the apprehension that since the doubling (*dvirvacana*) has not yet occurred when the substitution of *pī* is prescribed, the latter would therefore constitute an exception (*bādhaka*) to the former. To dispel this doubt, he says: "Because it is subsequent (*paratvāt*)."
And so forth. For sublation (*bādha*) would occur only if there were a contradiction; however, in this case, there is no contradiction.

Therefore, since the rule for *pībhāva* applies later, by the principle that "what has already occurred is not subject to recurrence" (*punaḥprasaṅgavijñānāt*), the doubling (*dvirvacana*) is established as valid.

30. *vibhāṣā śveḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.30). Regarding *śuśāva*: when the *liṭ* suffix *ṇal* is applied, after the vowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) has taken place, the *vṛddhi* and *ā* substitutions occur. Regarding *śiśvāya*: when there is no vowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*), then the *vṛddhi* and *āy* substitutions occur.

[The forms] *śuśuvatuḥ* and *śiśviyatuḥ*: when there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*), then *ovaṅ* occurs; otherwise, *iyaṅ*. [The phrase] "not obtained" means because it has not been prescribed by anything [else]. In the rule *liṭaḷbhyāsasyobhayeṣām* (P. 6.1.17), because the word *ubhaya* is used in both [the sūtra and its commentary], it is something else [than what was previously mentioned].
The purpose of including both [groups] has been stated so that, setting aside the operation currently in progress, there may be only the *samprasāraṇa* of the practice; consequently,
someone might have the misconception that this [rule] would also necessarily result in *samprasāraṇa* alone, overriding the optionality.
Therefore, in order to refute that [view], he says "And when," and so forth.

Here, it is stated that the *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) for the root *śvi* is optional; if at any time there is no *samprasāraṇa* for the root, then it would apply to the reduplication (*abhyāsa*), and consequently, the *samprasāraṇa* of *śvi* would not be merely occasional (*pākṣika*).

[The objection: "It would be so. This might be the case: this operation is prescribed optionally for the root *śak* when followed by *liṭ*, and that [root] certainly exists [in both instances]. [Response: This is incorrect; for when there is a double application (*dvirprayoga*) due to reduplication (*dvirvacana*), it is merely the action (*kriyā*) that differs, not the form of the verbal root (*dhāturūpa*). Therefore, how [could there be a distinction] between the preceding and the following?

Is there a distinction with respect to the connection with the grammatical operation? Therefore, when it does not apply to the verbal root (dhātu), then it certainly does not apply to the reduplicated stem (abhyāsa) either.

31. *ṇau ca saṃścaṅeḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.31). The locative case endings in *ṇau ca saṃścaṅeḥ* refer to different substrata: [the meaning is] "after *saṃ* and *caṅ*, when there is a *ṇi*-affix," and "when there is a *śvi* [root] followed by a *ṇi*-affix. For example: *śuśāvayiṣati*.

From the root *śvi* with the causative suffix *ṇic*, the desiderative suffix *san*, vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*), vṛddhi, and the substitution of *āv* for *ā*; then reduplication of the syllable *śu*. Thus, *aśūśavat*. [This is formed] with the aorist marker *luṅ*, the *caṅ* substitute for *cli*, vocalization and so forth, the elision of the *ṇi* augment as before, and the shortening by the rule *ṇau caṅ* (Pāṇini 7.4.1).

There is reduplication, and by the rule *dīrgho laghoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.94), a long vowel is substituted. Now, one might object: when the suffix *ṇic* is added to the root *śvi*, and the suffix *san* is subsequently added to that form, and then the *caṅ* is applied, the internal (*antaraṅga*) operations—namely the substitution of *vṛddhi* and the replacement by *ā*—must take effect first, followed by the *samprasāraṇa*. And thus [the form would be incorrect]. To this it is replied:

When the suffix *san* follows, as in the form *śuśuyayiṣati*, it ought to be [the result] after a causative (*ṇi*) preceded by *san*; however, when followed by *caṅ* (the reduplication of the aorist), it should be *aśūśuyat*. How then is it that *śuśāvayiṣati* and *aśūśavat* are cited as examples? To this he says: "The *samprasāraṇa*," and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the substitution of *āy* is intended.

It is accepted that here, by virtue of being dependent on a *samprasāraṇa*, the substitution of the preceding vowel with the subsequent one (*parapūrvatva*) applies according to Pāṇini 6.1.108: *samprasāraṇācca*. It is further stated that even by this, the *vṛddhi* and other operations are superseded. Now, even if this were so, once the *vṛddhi* and the substitute *āv* have been applied, would not the doubling (*dvirvacana*) of the element *śau* still apply? No.

By whom was the status of being "as if the original" (sthānivadbhāva) prescribed for the element *ṇau*? To this he says: "In the rule *thoḥ puyaṇjyapare*," etc. We shall demonstrate in the commentary (*vṛtti*) how this very point serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) in that specific context.

32. *hvaḥ samprasāraṇam* | (6.1.32) In the case of *juhāvayiṣati*, here too, as before, because it is more powerful, the *samprasāraṇa* occurs prior to the *vṛddhi* and other operations; [and] for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), [the rule] *kuhoścuḥ* (7.4.62) applies.

*Cutvam*: the substitution of *jh* for *h*. By the rule "in reduplication, *car* [is substituted] for *ca*" (Pāṇini 8.4.54), there is the substitution of *jaś*—namely, *j*—for that [sound]. Now, why is it that in this case the augment *yaṅ* does not occur prior to the *samprasāraṇa* by the rule "after *sā*, *chā*, *śā*, and *hvā*" (Pāṇini 7.3.37)? To this he says: "of the *samprasāraṇa*..."
And so forth.

Now, one might ask: since the mention of *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) is indeed still in force, for what purpose is *samprasāraṇa* stated again? To this he says: "Regarding *samprasāraṇa*," and so forth. [This refers to] the preceding...

For the mention of *samprasāraṇa* is connected with the word *vibhāṣā*; therefore, when that [word *vibhāṣā*] is carried over [into the subsequent rule], this [mention of *samprasāraṇa*] would also be carried over. Consequently, it is stated "again *samprasāraṇa*" in order to cause the cessation of that [*vibhāṣā*].

Now, why is a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) performed, given that even with a single rule—"there is *samprasāraṇa* for *hu*, and for the reduplicated (*abhyasta*) [root]"—forms such as *juhāvayiṣati* are indeed established? For here too, the root *hvayati* is indeed related as the cause of the reduplication; thus, by the rule "for a monosyllabic [root], there is reduplication," [the form is achieved].
Is that very [first element], being reduplicated by the rule "of the first" (6.1.1), indeed the cause for the reduplication?

To this he says: "the *samprasāraṇa* of *hvṛ*, etc. If this were established by a single rule alone, the fact that a separate rule is formulated would not convey this meaning; therefore, this [meaning] would indeed apply here.
There is *samprasāraṇa*. For here too, the word *hvapati* is the cause for the reduplication (*abhyasta*).

From the word *hvāyaka*, ending in the suffix *ṇvul*, there is the addition of *kyac*; by the rule *kyati ca* (Pāṇini 7.4.33), there is the substitution of *i* for the vowel; from the form ending in *kyac*, there is the addition of *san*, then *iṭ*, and then the elision of the final *a* by *ato lopaḥ* (6.4.48), followed by reduplication.
33. *abhyastasya ca* (6.1.33). The particle *ca* is for the purpose of drawing back [the word] *hvaḥ*; therefore he says: "The term *hvaḥ* is understood.
If this term *hvaḥ* were not understood here, then [the substitution] would apply to the entire reduplicated form (*abhyasta*) alone. In that case, [the rule regarding] *hvaḥ*—
If there were coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word *anuvartamānasya* and the word *abhyastasya* [in the rule], then,

once reduplication (*dvirvacana*) has occurred and the designation "repeated" (*abhyasta-saṃjñā*) has arisen, the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) would take place; and in that case, by the rule "there is no semivowel-vocalization for a semivowel-vocalized element" (*na samprasāraṇe samprasāraṇam*, 6.1.37), the semivowel-vocalization of the reduplicated syllable would be prohibited.

It would not [be so]. Even though there is an intervention by another form (*harūpa*), nevertheless, because of the inclusion of "having the same member" (*samānāṅga*), this prohibition applies here even when there is such an intervention,
as in the case of *yūnā*— this is the fault in the alternative view regarding grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Observing this, he says: "By the phrase 'of that which is practiced,' there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (vyadhikaraṇa).

This means that the referents are distinct. By stating "the act of calling belonging to that which is practiced," and so forth, he demonstrates that very lack of coreferentiality by indicating a genitive case based on the relation of connection (sambandha-lakṣaṇā). Therefore...

What is established [by this]? He says: "By that," and so forth. Regarding the form *juhāva*: because of the status of being a *sthānivat* (as if occupying the original position) for the *vṛddhi* and *āv* substitutions following the *samprasāraṇa*, there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*) of the root *hu*.
34. *Bahulam chandasi* (6.1.34).
35. *Cāyaḥ kī* (6.1.35). Regarding the form *nicikyuh*: the substitution of *yaṇ* [for *i*] occurs by the rule *eranekācaḥ* (6.4.82), etc. [The form] *nicāyya*.
Thus [it is said]. This is a form ending in the suffix -lyap. The long vowel is pronounced for the sake of hearing the long vowel in the word *cikīrvān*; this is a form [ending] in the suffix -kvasu.

36. *apaspṛdhethām*, *ānṛcuḥ*, *ānṛhuḥ*, *cicyuṣe*, *tatyāja*, *śrātāḥ*, *śritam*, *āśīr*, *āśīrtāḥ*. (6.1.36) "And there is the elision of the letter *ṭh*. By this rule, there is the elision of the vowel *a* which is a constituent part of the verbal root, due to its being a specific grammatical substitution (*nipātana*).
In *ṭhapāspaddhaithām*,
there is the substitution of a long vowel for two homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*) by [Pāṇini 6.1.90] *āṭaśca*.
[The phrase] "he desires a distinction of scope" is understood through the force of the irregular formation (*nipātana*).

It should be understood as follows: if the absence of *śrā* is observed anywhere even once, then for that purpose another effort must be undertaken. For this is not established by the term *śrātāḥ* alone, because of the use of the plural number in the sūtra. Therefore, he says: "of that," and so forth.

37. *Na samprasāraṇe samprasāraṇam* (Pāṇini 6.1.37). Since it has been stated that for certain [roots] there is *samprasāraṇa*, this prohibition is now undertaken because it would otherwise follow that *samprasāraṇa* would apply to all the *yaṇ* sounds that are possible. Now, one might object: [is this not already established?]
[Objection: By the rule *cālo'ntyasya* (P. 1.1.52), [the substitution] will apply only to the final [consonant], not to a non-final one.

[Response: This is not so; for this paribhāṣā cannot be brought to bear here, because it is impossible for a semivowel (*yaṇ*) to be the final element of the roots *vic*, *svap*, and those beginning with *yaj*. If that is the case, then...

Regarding the rule "ṭhanantyavikāre'ntyasadeśasya" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 63), will the operation apply to that which is in the vicinity of the final [element]— that is, will the operation apply only to that *yaṇ* which is in the vicinity of the final, and not to any other? This is not a universally accepted paribhāṣā.
Because there is no purpose [for it]. As it has been said: "There are purposes for that Paribhāṣā. Therefore, this Sūtra must be formulated.
But is it not the case that the Samprasāraṇa is characterized by a single grammatical operation (*ekayogalakṣaṇa*) applying to both the preceding and the following [sounds]? Consequently, if...

When that [subsequent] has been produced, then the former has already been produced as well; and it is not possible to effect the cessation of what has already been produced, nor is it logical to rely upon what has not yet been produced as a cause. Therefore, from this very statement of prohibition, it follows that...

First, [the rule] is applied to the subsequent [vowel]; once that has been performed, even though [the substitution] would have applied to the preceding one as well, it is prohibited. Now, since "samprasāraṇa" is being carried over [from the previous sūtra], for what purpose is "samprasāraṇa" stated again? To this he says: "samprasāraṇam" and so forth. If, however, [it were] not...

Regarding the mention of *samprasāraṇa*, according to the rule "In the case of a mention of *samprasāraṇa*, there is either an operation or a prohibition for what is immediately preceding" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 19), there would be a prohibition only of the *samprasāraṇa* under discussion,
and not of that situated in a different location. Therefore, there must be a prohibition even of that situated in a different location which is prescribed in a different context.
The term *samprasāraṇa* is mentioned again for the purpose that it should occur [in this specific case]. As in the example *yūno yūnā*:
when *samprasāraṇa* has been applied, and the substitution of the preceding vowel (*parapūrvatva*) has also been applied, the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.101) applies.
Now, one might object: even if the mention of *samprasāraṇa* is made again, would there not still be a prohibition in that case?

[One might ask: "Could it be that, because of the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) regarding the preceding rule for *savarṇadīrgha*, [the vowel] is separated by the letter *u*? To this, he says: "Precisely by the force of the mention of *samprasāraṇa*," and so forth. If there were indeed *sthānivadbhāva*, [the mention of *samprasāraṇa*] would be purposeless once again.
The intention is that there should be the mention of *samprasāraṇa*. Having granted this for the sake of argument, he states another solution, beginning with "sati vā" (or, even if...).
By the very force of the mention of *samprasāraṇa*, [the rule applies] here even though it is not heard in another recension (*śākhāntara*).

When an *ac* vowel has attained the status of a *sthānivadbhāva* and acts as an intervention, an intervention consisting of that alone shall not be considered [as a valid separation]; this is so that the mention of *samprasāraṇa* in the rule might not be rendered meaningless. But is it not the case that there are rules such as "yūnaśca kutsāyām" (P. 4.1.167) and "vṛddho yūnā" (P. 1.2.65)?
[Objection: Since it is established by irregular derivation (*nipātana*) itself, there will be no vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) in the case of *yūnaḥ* (genitive singular of *yuvan*);
so why is there a further mention of "vocalization" (*samprasāraṇa*) for the purpose of excluding that? [Response: This is not so;
for it has been stated that irregular derivations can also be non-obstructive (*abādhaka*). Moreover, this very point is the subject at hand.

The elision (*nipātana*) is understood; and thus, in the forms *yūnaḥ*, *yūnā*, and *yūnī*, the vowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) would indeed occur. Regarding the form *ārevān*: the suffix *matup* is added because he possesses wealth (*rayi*).
Once the vowel substitution has been performed, *ādguṇaḥ* (P. 6.1.87) applies, and by *chandasi iraḥ* (P. 8.2.15), the substitution of *v* for *r* takes place.

38. *liṭi vayo yaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.38). Regarding the root *vī*, there are two semi-vowels (*yaṇ*); since the prohibition of *samprasāraṇa* for the first [vowel, *v*] would have applied by the preceding rule, this sūtra prohibits the *samprasāraṇa* of the letter *y* when the *liṭ* suffix follows. That being prohibited...

The letter *ya* does not undergo *samprasāraṇa*; rather, *samprasāraṇa* occurs for the letter *va*, both in the root and in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Among these, that of the root is by the rule *grahyādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.1.16), and that of the reduplicated syllable is by the rule *liṭi abhyāsasyobhayeṣām* (Pāṇini 6.1.17). Now, for what purpose [is this stated]?

As for the mention of *liṭ*: since there is no possibility of the substitution of *vay* occurring anywhere other than in the *liṭ* [tense], and because the mention of *liṭ* from the rule "optionally in the *liṭ*" (2.4.40) continues by anuvṛtti into this rule, will [the substitution] not occur in the *liṭ* simply by the force of that [mention]? To this [it is replied]:
He says: "The mention of *liṅ* is for the sake of what follows. The mention of *liṅ* is for this purpose: so that the prohibition [stated] in "of *veñ*" (6.1.40) may apply in the case of *liṭ*.

39. The substitution of *va* for the root *vyeñ* optionally occurs before an affix beginning with *k*. (6.1.39) 40. [The substitution of *va* for the root] *vyeñ* [occurs before an affix beginning with *k*]. (6.1.40) 41. [The substitution of *va* for the root *vyeñ* occurs] also before the suffix *lyap*. (6.1.41)
[The commentary states: "The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows. Thus, in the subsequent [sūtras], the optional *samprasāraṇa* applies only to the root *vyeñ*.
The separation of the rule (yogavibhāga) is for the purpose that [the substitution] should apply where it ought to, but not in the case of the word *jyā*.
44. *vibhāṣā pareḥ* (6.1.44). 45. *ādeca upadeśe’śiti* (6.1.45).
[The word] "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*) is understood [here], as it follows from [the rule] *liṭi dhātoranabhyāsasya* (6.1.8).

And this [suffix] is a qualifier for the root itself by the rule *aic ca*; and because of that qualification, the rule of "ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies, as he says: "the root which ends in *ej*. Regarding the term *upadeśe*:
the meaning is "in the initial pronunciation," that is, in the recitation of the list of roots (*gaṇapāṭha*). Examples are *cetā* and *stotā*. Now, one might object: [...]
"In this case [at *vyāpa.* 3], it will not apply by the very technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding 'that which is taught as a specific form' (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*);
