so what is the purpose of including the term 'instruction' (*upadeśa*)? If that is so, then the inclusion of the term 'instruction' indicates this: that this technical rule is not eternal (*anitya*). By this, [the rule] *artihrī*..."

In the rule beginning with (7.3.36), since even the *ā* that is obtained through a technical definition (*lākṣaṇika*) is included, the augment *puk* is established even in forms such as *krāpayati*. Furthermore, regarding the term *śit*, it means "that which has *ś* as its *it*"; and that which is the substitute *eś* for the *liṭ* suffixes *ta* and *jha* according to (3.4.81), that too [is included].

Consequently, when the prohibition is applied to the *śit* [affix], the substitution of *ā* for *e* would not occur even there. Thinking that, once the *ayādeśa* has been performed, the form *jaglāya*—resulting from the reduplication of the root *glai* by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva*—would be an undesirable outcome; thus he considers:

He asks: "How so? and so forth. In roots such as *glai*, there is the elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64). The rebuttal is given with the words "Not so" and so forth. When it is understood that *ś* itself is *it*—that is, *śit*—then the mention of *al* (vowel) becomes necessary. In that context, [the rule applies] to that which...

By the paribhāṣā "vidhistadādāvalgrahaṇe" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 127), there ought to be a prohibition [of the substitution] when a suffix beginning with a *śit* follows; however, *aiś* does not begin with a *śit*. What then? It ends in *śit*, because it is pronounced as ending in *śit*. Therefore, the prohibition does not apply here to *aiś*.

Is "aśiti" (not-śit) a paryudāsa (exclusion) or a prasajyapratiṣedha (absolute negation)? If it were a paryudāsa, then [the term] would depend on a cause other than śit belonging to another tense (ārdhadhātuka).
And in that case, as long as it is not the cause for ātva (the substitution of ā), it ought to undergo udātta (high pitch).

Because it does not end in the vowel *ā*. Thinking that, in cases such as *sugalaḥ*, the suffix *kap*—which is characterized by [the condition of] ending in *ā*—would not apply, he says "in the case of *aśiti*" and so forth. What is established by this?
He says: "By this," and so forth. For, in the case of a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), there would be a prohibition of the substitution of *ā* when followed by a suffix marked with *ś*.

It is performed, but since no specific cause (nimitta) is relied upon, it is considered "causeless" (anaimitika). Therefore, the substitution of *ā* occurs even before the production of the suffix, whereby the suffix characterized by having a final vowel *ā* is established; thus, forms such as *suglaḥ* and others are proven. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), [other examples are implied].
This includes forms such as *suglaḥ* and *suglā*; for in those cases, when [the suffix] is feminine, the suffix *aṅ* applies by the rule *ātaścopasarge* (Pāṇini 3.3.106).

46. *na vyo liṭi* (Pāṇini 6.1.46). [The root] *vyeñ* means "to cover. Now, why is it not understood as *athāliṭi* ("but not in the *liṭ* [perfect]")? For is not the *saṃhitā* (phonetic combination) the same? This is not so; for if that were the case, there would be a restrictive rule (*niyama*) stating *liṭi vyaḥ* ("in the *liṭ*, [the substitution applies] to *vyi*").

Thus it would be established that the substitution of *ā* occurs only after the *liṭ* suffix and not elsewhere. And by virtue of the established usage of the linguistic data (*lakṣya*), there will be a contrary restriction: whether or not the *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute) and the *ātva* (substitution of *ā*) occur following the *samprasāraṇa* in the dual and plural, there is no difference [in the resulting form].

Thus, the form ending in the singular number has been illustrated as *saṃvivyayitha*. Regarding the suffix *thala*, there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*—which would otherwise be required by the rule *valādy-ārdhadhātuka-*—by the rule *ekāca upadeśe'nudāttāt* (Pāṇini 7.2.10). Furthermore, the restriction imposed by the rule *krādiniyama* (Pāṇini 7.2.13) would again apply, but that too is precluded by the rule *acastāsvat-thaly-anit* (Pāṇini 7.2.61).
Although [the substitution] is prohibited, since an option would otherwise arise by the restrictive rule "ṭhṛto bhāradvājasya" (Pāṇini 7.2.63),
it is made obligatory by the rule "ṭhiḍartivyayatīnām" (Pāṇini 7.2.66).
47. Regarding *sphurati* and *sphulati* with the suffix *ghañ*:

(Pāṇini 6.1.47) [the forms] "ṭhvisphāraḥ" and "visphālaḥ" [are derived]. [The suffix] *ghañ* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*), or, by [the rule] "halaśca" (3.3.121), in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) or a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
48. *krīṅjīnāṃ ṇau* (Pāṇini 6.1.48).

[The roots] *ṭhḍukrīñ* "to exchange goods" (Dhātupāṭha 1473), *iṅ* "to study" (Dhātupāṭha 1046), and *ji* "to conquer" (Dhātupāṭha 561): this rule is commenced for the sake of preventing the substitution of *upadeśa* [vowel lengthening]. [This applies] when *ātvam* [the substitution of *ā* for the penultimate vowel] occurs in forms such as *krāpayati*.

The suffix *puk* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.3.36], *kṛte ṭhartihrī*. Why is this stated? It is not [the case that the forms] from *krapa* (DhP 771) "to move with contempt," *japa* and *jalpa* (DhP 397, 398) "to speak clearly," or *ā-plu* (DhP 1260) "to pervade" preceded by the prefix *adhi* [would suffice].
When the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied, forms such as *krāpayati* are established.
One might ask: since verbal roots have multiple meanings, will *krap* and other such roots function in the sense of "buying" (*krīṇāti*) and so forth? It is said in reply:
[this is] for the purpose of precluding other usages of *krīṇāti* and the like when the causative suffix is present. Now, regarding the root *kṛ* (to do), there is *īṅ*.

Why is it not understood that the root *gatau* (DhP 1143) is being referred to here? It is said in reply: first of all, it cannot refer to the root *kṛ*, because of the governing rule *ecaḥ*. For this very reason, the author of the Vṛtti has continued [the application of] the term *ecaḥ*. Or rather, by the force of the statement itself, for that [root *kṛ*] would indeed have its *ā*-vowel substitution through the process of *vṛddhi* alone.

Is it established? This is not so; for [the rule] would be for the sake of restriction—meaning that there is only the substitution of *ā*, and not the substitution of *ra-paratva*. This is not so; according to the principle "when both a general injunction (*vidhi*) and a restrictive rule (*niyama*) are possible, the injunction alone is superior" (Vyāḍipāṭha 130), there is the inclusion of *krīṇāti* alone, and not of *karoti*. For that [latter],...

Because [the former rule] serves a restrictive purpose (*niyamārthatva*), whereas the root *krī* serves a prescriptive purpose (*vidhyarthatva*). Furthermore, the inclusion of the root *iṅ* (meaning "to go," DhP 1143) is not possible, due to its association with *jayati*, which ends in a short vowel. Thus, *iṅ* will be understood as ending in a short vowel, not as ending in a long one.
Because of the prohibition based on the literal sound [of the term]. There is association with the root *ji* (to conquer), not with the root *krī* (to buy).
Or rather, the distinction is to be understood from the commentary.
49. [The substitution of *siddha* for *sādhya* occurs] after the root *sidh* when it does not refer to the next world. (Pāṇini 6.1.49)

"Food is accomplished" (*annaṃ sādhyati*) means "he produces food. For here, the root *sidh* refers to a specific kind of knowledge regarding matters pertaining to the next world. He clarifies its meaning with the example, "The ascetic succeeds" (*tāpasaḥ sidhyati*), and so forth. "In the conclusion" (*upasaṃhāre*) means "while producing."

"Why does it not constitute *sthiti* (stability)? and so forth. They think as follows: "He who prepares food with the intention, 'I shall give this to the Brahmins,' attains in another birth the fruit characterized by prosperity (*abhyudaya*); therefore, there is accomplishment here regarding a goal pertaining to the next world."

It must be understood through the method of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) that "it exists. By stating that "the meaning of the root *sidh* here is 'accomplishment' (*niṣpatti*)," he shows its relevance to this world.
"Its purpose is food" means it is undertaken with a view toward food. "Of it" refers to food.
"Nor, again, is there success alone"—thus, having changed the gender, one should connect it as:
"nor, again, is there success alone pertaining to the next world.
"Success" (siddhi) means accomplishment (niṣpatti). The particle *iti* indicates a reason; because [the goal] is already accomplished...

The verbal root (*dhātu*) occurs [in this context]. Here, the accomplishment (*siddhi*) does not pertain to the next world; therefore, the substitution of *āt* is not excluded here. It might be argued: even if the verbal root itself does not directly have the next world as its purpose, it certainly does so indirectly; therefore, there ought to be a prohibition [of the substitution of *āt*].

Thus he says: "Directly," and so forth. If the meaning of the word *siddhi* were such that it refers only to that which accomplishes the purpose of the next world directly, without mediation, then the expression "pertaining to the next world" (*pāralaukika*) would not have fulfilled its purpose;
therefore, it should also apply to that which functions toward the purpose of the next world even through a succession of steps—lest...
[Otherwise] the statement [of the author] would be useless. However, this [inference] fulfills its purpose regarding a specific cognition that is directly established for the sake of the next world;
therefore, it is simply not capable of penetrating such a subject. It is unable to establish a restriction regarding a subject of this kind.
The meaning is "to proceed.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *siddhyati* with the suffix *śyan*, rather than simply saying *sidheḥ*, since in this way the sūtra would be more concise? To this he says: "of *siddhyati*," and so forth.
50. *mīnāti-minoti-dīṅāṃ lyapi ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.50).

Since the term *upadeśe* (from 6.1.45) is understood to carry over [into this rule], it follows that the substitution of *ā* must occur even before the suffix arises; therefore, at the time when the substitution of *ā* is being prescribed, the condition of "following *lyap*" is not possible.
Therefore, he says— "in the domain of *lyap*"— to indicate that this is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*).

Although *ec* was previously a qualifier of the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*), nevertheless, here, because of the governing context of "instruction" (*upadeśa*), [it refers to] the roots beginning with *mīnāti*.

Since *ec* is impossible in the state of being taught (*upadeśāvasthāyām*), he says—“in the domain of *ec*” (*hecaśca viṣaye*)—because by implication (*sāmarthyāt*) it is understood as a qualifier of the domain. He explains the meaning of “in the teaching” (*upadeśe*) by means of [the words] “prior,” etc. [He gives the example] “having measured” (*pramāya*), [citing] Pāṇini 7.1.37: *samāse 'nañ*.
Regarding the *lyap* suffix:

what purpose is served by prescribing the substitution of *ā* (*ātvavidhāna*) at the very stage of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*), such that the substitution of *ā* is made at the stage of the original instruction? To this, he says: "At the very stage of the original instruction," and so forth.

The suffix *ac* is prescribed by the rule *ivarṇāntalakṣaṇaḥ ṭherac* (Pāṇini 3.3.56), and the suffix *yuc* is prescribed by the rule *ākārāntalakṣaṇaḥ ṭhāto yuc* (Pāṇini 3.3.128) for words ending in *ā*. Since the substitution of *ā* for the vowel occurs precisely at the stage of the original instruction (*upadeśa*), the suffix *ac* is established as having been applied based on that [original form]. Consequently, the general rule *ghañ* [is applicable] by the rule *bhāve* (Pāṇini 3.3.18). Thus, the suffix *ghañ* is established.

It occurs thus: by the rule *āto yuk ciṇ-kṛtoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.33), the suffix *yuk* is applied; and by the rule *īṣad-duḥ-su-ṣu kṛcchrākṛcchrārtheṣu khal* (Pāṇini 3.3.126), the suffix *khal* is applied. Thus, in the state of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*), the suffix *yuc*—which is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ātvam*—is established.
51. *vibhāṣā līyateḥ* (6.1.51).

"The mention of both [roots] by means of the letter *y* is recorded as a traditional teaching (*smṛta*) by the Teachers (*ācāryaiḥ*). Now, why is this not understood as a mention by means of the suffix *śyan* belonging to the *divādi* class? Precisely for this reason.

Because of the specific mention [in the rule]. If it were intended here that only the root beginning with *div* (i.e., *līṅ*) should be mentioned, one would have made the mention using the technical marker (*anubandha*), namely as *līṅ*.
Therefore, the mention of both is made by means of the common, adventitious letter *y*. As in the example: "īṣatpramayaḥ."

The suffix *khal* is applied by the rule *ṭhīṣad-duḥ-suṣu* (Pāṇini 3.3.126). [In the case of] "a barter (*nimaya*) takes place," the suffix *ac* is applied by the rule *erac* (Pāṇini 3.3.56). However, in this case, the form is established through the understanding of a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) regarding the root *lī*. [Thus, the word is] *liyaḥ*.

This is merely an illustration; the [substitution] is indeed established for the other two as well, because the mention of *vibhāṣā* (optionally) connects with the preceding rule too. Due to the understanding that this is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the substitution of *āt* occurs invariably when the causative suffix *ṇiC* follows the roots *pralambhana* and *śālīnīkaraṇa*.

This is understood precisely from the established *vibhāṣā* rule [Pāṇini 1.3.69]. In the cases of *ullāpayate* and *apalāpayate*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *liyaḥ sammānana-śālīnīkaraṇayoḥ* (1.3.70).

52. *khidic chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.52). Regarding the form *cikhāda*: the vowel *ā* is the result of the *guṇa* substitution prescribed by *pugantalaghūpadhasya* (7.3.86). If the root *khād* also occurs in the sense of the root *khid*, then this rule [of 6.1.52] applies.
It can be made [into *khād*]; for *khād*, it will be *cakhāda*, but for *khid*, it will be *cikheda*.
53. *apaguro ṇamuli* (Pāṇini 6.1.53). [The example is] *apagāram-apagāram*. By the rule "there is reduplication when there is frequency" (Vārttika 887), there is doubling.
54. *cisphuror ṇau* (6.1.54).
This rule was not stated in the specific context of *ṭhkrīṅjīnāṃ ṇau* (6.1.47); its purpose is to ensure that [the substitution] does not occur invariably there.
55. *prajane vīyateḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.55).

If this root *vī*, meaning "to go" or "to scent" (*vā gatigandhanayoḥ*, Dhātupāṭha 1050), is used in the sense of procreation (*prajana*), then the application of the rule can indeed be stated; for from the root *vā*, the form *vāpayati* will result.
But for *vī* [the form] is *vāyayati*, meaning "he causes to blow."

56. *bibheti* [is used] with the cause of fear (*hetubhaye*). Regarding the term *hetubhaye*: this is a genitive compound (*pañcamī-samāsa*) according to the rule *pañcamī bhayena* (Pāṇini 2.1.37). He explains this by saying "the fear which arises from that" (*tato yad bhayam*). But what, then, is that?

"What is that fear? he asks, and says: "That [fear] of which... and so forth. Now, why does the augment *ṣuk* not occur in this alternative case (*athātvapakṣe*)? For here too there is an occasion for its application, according to the rule: "That which is modified in one part is treated as non-different from the original" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 16). To this he replies: "And that... and so forth. [The rule is: *bhiyo hetubhaye ṣuk*.

For in this [sūtra], there is an indication made by means of the vowel *ī* joined in *praśleṣa* with the root *bhī*—that is, the suffix *ṣuk* should apply only to that which ends in *ī*, and not to that which ends in *ā*. Likewise, there is the mention of the root *lī*; for that too, in the alternative view where *ātvam* occurs, [the rule] "ṭhlīlornuklukāvanyatarasyām" applies.
The augment *nuṭ* does not occur [in the case of *snehavipātane*] by virtue of the very fact that the rule is stated with the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *ī*;
this has been explained incidentally.
57. [The suffix *ṇic* is applied] after the root *smi* (*smayate*) when used in the sense of "fear" (*bhaya*).

(Pāṇini 6.1.57). Regarding the statement "because of the similarity of the meaning of the verbal root with the word 'fear' (*bhayaśabda*)," etc.: the meaning of the root *bhī* (*bibheti*) and that of *smi* (*smayate*) are both similar, because both consist in a modification of the mind (*cittavikāra*) by their very nature. Both of these—

The two [states] are characterized by agitation of the mind; therefore, that which is common to both is their similarity (*sādṛśya*). Consequently, the meaning of "astonishment" (*smaya*) is expressed here by the word "fear" (*bhaya*). For it is observed that words function with reference to another object due to similarity, as in the expression: "The boy is a lion."

But what is the reason for explaining it in this way? To this he says: "For not," and so forth. The rule *hetubhaye* (Pāṇini 6.1.56) is understood to carry over. And this qualifier is stated; however, the root *smi-* does not apply to actual fear. Therefore, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), [the word *bhaya*] must refer to something through some similarity.
It is understood that here the word "fear" (bhaya) actually denotes the object of fear itself.

58. *sṛjidṛśorjhalyamakiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.58). [Examples: *sraṣṭā*, *draṣṭā*. When the augment *um* is applied, there is the substitution of *yaṇ*; then, by the rule *vraścādi* (8.2.36), there is the substitution of *ṣ*. [The commentary states: "This [augment] is an exception to the *guṇa* of the light penultimate vowel," and so forth. Now, one might object: if [the augment were not present],...

An obstruction occurs when there is a possibility [of conflict], and there is indeed the possibility that both might occur. In that case, would the augment *am* apply once the *guṇa* substitution has been made? This is not so; for the *guṇa* is prescribed as a general rule (*sāmānya*), whereas the augment *am* is prescribed as a specific rule (*viśeṣa*), and a specific rule [takes precedence over] a general rule.

It becomes an annulment (*bādhaka*), as for example: "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas, and buttermilk to Kauṇjinya. Just as the specific injunction to give buttermilk annuls the general injunction to give curd, so too here the annulment of the quality by the scripture is logical.
In the forms *adrākṣīt* and *adrākṣīt*, there is the substitution of *ṣ* by [Pāṇini 8.3.59] *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*;
the augment *iṭ* is added by [Pāṇini 7.3.96] *asti sico 'pṛkte*; the *vṛddhi* vowel is substituted by [Pāṇini 7.2.3] *vadavrajahalantasyācaḥ*;
and the substitution of *k* for *ṣ* and *ḍh* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.41] *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si*. Thus, the *vṛddhi* takes place when the suffix *am* follows.
Thus [it is asked]: "Why then does the *vṛddhi* not occur even earlier? To this he says: "But the former is sublated.

For just as the general rule for *guṇa* is sublated by the specifically prescribed *am*-augment, so too is the *vṛddhi*, which is also generally prescribed, sublated once the *am*-augment has been applied subsequently.

Furthermore, because it is established through the cognition of recurrence (*punar-prasaṅga-vijñāna*), that [rule] also applies. However, when *ām* has been applied, the *guṇa* substitution does not occur, because the cause [for it] has been prescribed. For when *ām* has been applied, the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) cannot be considered light (*laghu*) such that it would be subject to *guṇa*.

Now, why does this not occur here—namely, in *rajjusṛṅbhyām* and *devadṛgbhyām*? Even though there is the governing rule for verbal roots (*dhātvadhikāra*), since it is stated that "words ending in *kvip* do not lose their status as verbal roots" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 132), one might argue that by relying on the suffix *bhyām* as being attached to a verbal root, the augment *ām* would apply. To this, he says: "of a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*).
And so forth.

59. *anudātasya cardupadhasyānyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.1.59). [The word] "in the original teaching" (*upadeśe*) is understood [from the previous rule]. This is for the purpose of qualifying "unaccented" (*anudātasya*). Therefore, although in the case of *traptā*, when the suffix *tṛn* is prescribed, the verbal root becomes udātta by virtue of the *nit*-accent, [the rule still applies optionally].
Nevertheless, in the state of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*), this augment *am* is established as being applied to what is unaccented (*anudātta*).

And here, in the case of *vardheta*, although the verbal root becomes unaccented once the suffix *tṛc* has been added, nevertheless, because it is not unaccented at the stage of the original instruction, this augment *am* does not apply. For what purpose [is this stated]?

Furthermore, it is stated that [the rule applies] "to a root ending in an unaccented vowel" (*anudāta*); why not simply say "to a non-iṭ root" (*aniṭ*)? For in this way, the sūtra would be more concise. To this, he replies: "tṛpa prīṇane," etc.

Since for the roots *tṛp* and *dṛp*, the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied by the rule "radhādibhyaśca" (Pāṇini 7.2.45), if [the rule] were stated as applying only to non-iṭ roots, [the desired result would not be achieved].

In that case, because [the vowels] are optionally iṅ, they would not be considered iṭ by virtue of being non-iṭ, and thus the augment am would not apply to those two. Alternatively, if the augment am were to apply because those two are iṭ due to the optional presence of iṅ,
then it would also apply to the root *vṛhū* (meaning "exertion," DhP 1347), since this too is marked with ūdit.

Because there is an optional occurrence of *iṭ*, it does not become *aniṭ*; therefore, the intention is that one cannot say it is *aniṭ*. If, then, *iṭ* is optional for these two, what is the purpose of designating them as having an *anudātta* (low-pitched) vowel in their original statement (*upadeśa*)? That [designation] is made for this very purpose: [to apply the rule] "after a root with an *anudātta* vowel... (*anudāttāt*).

(7.2.10) This is so that there may be a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*. If, then, *iṭ* is optional for these two, what is the purpose of this [rule]? To this he says: "But the designation *anudāttopadeśa* is indeed for the sake of *am*. [The example is] *varddha*. [In this case,] by *ho ḍhaḥ* (8.2.31) and *ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ* (8.4.41)...

(8.4.41) "When ṭh or ḍh follows ḍh, there is elision [of the preceding ḍh]" (8.3.13). One might ask: "Even though this root is taught as having an udātta accent, does not iṭ still apply here? To this he says: "Because of its being marked with u," and so forth. By the rule "svarati-sūti... (7.2.44), etc., iṭ is optionally applied because this root is marked with u; therefore, even when the udātta quality is present, in one alternative case—
The substitution of *iḍ* does not occur. The letter *ca* is for the purpose of carrying over (*anukarṣaṇa*) [the previous rule]; therefore, its recurrence does not take place in what follows.

60. *śīrṣan* in the Veda (*chandas*). Why, then, is this not desired as a substitute (*ādeśa*)? He says: "For that too," and so forth. Since the word *śiras* is also employed in the Veda, this [word *śīrṣan*] is therefore not used as a substitute.

For if there were only a substitution (*ādeśa*), the word *śiras* would not be used in Vedic contexts, because the original element (*sthānin*) possesses the property of being replaced. If, however, the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is understood to carry over here, then there is no fault even with respect to the substitution. Thus, "śīrṣā": the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by Pāṇini 6.4.7, *nopadhāyāḥ*.

In some places, "śīrṣṇā" is read; that should be understood as ending in the instrumental case. The elision of the vowel 'a' occurs by the rule "allopo'naḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.134). The form "śīrṣṇaḥ" is [the genitive] singular.

61. *ye ca taddhite* (Pāṇini 6.1.61). If another base (*prakṛtyantara*) is understood even when the *taddhita* suffix begins with *ya*, then if a *taddhita* suffix beginning with *ya* were to arise from the word *śiras*, its [final *s*] would result in being heard; however, it is not so.
Because this [suffix] is intended [to be applied], he says: "This is intended as a substitute (ādeśa).
With the intention that a substitute is not appropriate here either because the original element (ādeśin) has not been mentioned, he asks:
"How can that be? [He answers with] "For it is a taddhita," and so forth; because here [the suffix] beginning with *ya* is a taddhita.

A suffix is applied by taking a base (*prakṛti*), and a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) does not arise without taking a base; yet it is not logical that the word *śīrṣan* itself be the base, because it is impossible [for it] in the common language (*bhāṣā*). For that [word] is prescribed as an irregular form (*nipātita*) in Vedic [language], whereas this [usage] pertains to the common language. Therefore, [the suffix arises] from another base.

When a secondary derivative (taddhita) beginning with the letter *y* is prescribed, this [substitution] is understood as the substitute for that base which is implied by it. For even when a substitute is understood, it is not understood as belonging to just anything; rather, it belongs specifically to the word *śiras*. Because that secondary derivative [requires] a base corresponding to it...

It implies the base *śiras* itself as the most closely related [word] both phonetically and semantically for that suffix; thus, [the form] *śīrṣaṇyaḥ*. The substitution of *ṇ* occurs by virtue of Pāṇini 8.4.2 (*aṭ-ku-pv-ādi*).

Regarding the form *śirasyati*: [it is derived] by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8). Regarding the statement *vā keśeṣu*: the meaning is that when "hair" (*keśa*) is the object denoted, the substitution *śīrṣan* for the word *śiras* should be stated as an option; that is, it must be explained as being optional. In this regard, the following...

The explanation is as follows: the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], and it is recognized as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Consequently, the substitution of *śīrṣan* for *śiras* will occur in the sense of "hair" or "on the head."

62. *aci śīrṣaḥ* | (6.1.62) As in *ṭhsthaulaśīrṣam*. [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied by [the rule] *ṭhtasyedam* (4.3.120). But for what purpose is a different substitute prescribed here, rather than the substitute *śīrṣan* which is already under discussion?

"Let it be prescribed"? Even there, since the desired form is indeed established once the *ṭi*-elision has been applied by [Pāṇini 6.4.144] *naṣtaddhite*, he says: "In the case of the substitution of *śīrṣan*," and so forth;
"when the substitution of *ṣyaṅ* has been made," and so forth; [and] by [Pāṇini 4.1.78] *aṇiñoḥ anārṣayoḥ*, etc.

Because the word *śiras* is included within the term *śīrṣan*, by virtue of the rule for "that which stands in the place of another" (*sthānivadbhāva*), the substitution of *śīrṣan* would apply [to the form *śīrṣa*]. This occurs precisely by the rule *ye ca taddhite* (Pāṇini 6.1.61). As for the phrase beginning with *tatra*, the application of the *prakṛtibhāva* (original form retention) is governed by the rule *ye cābhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.168).

By this [rule], [the forms] *hāstiśīrṣaṇyā* and *hāstiśīrṣyā* are derived. [The suffix] *cāp* is applied by the rule *yaṅścāp* (Pāṇini 4.1.74). How then [is the form] *hāstiśīrṣyā* [justified]? This means: how is the desired form established? "An effort must be made here"—that effort, moreover, is as follows: [the derivation of] *śirasyāḥ*.
For the sake of establishing this [term] *keśā*, that very [word] which was under discussion must be understood.

For, by means of the established option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) itself, since the word *śīrṣan* is included within the word *śiras*, the substitute *śīrṣan* will not occur; therefore, [the form] is simply *hāstiśīrṣyā*.
"It occurs, but not from *astiśīrṣaṇya*. Regarding the phrase "or from that which ends in *ṭhaṇ* or *iñ*," and so forth:

in the rule *ṭhaṇiño'nārṣayor* (Pāṇini 4.1.78), there are two positions. One position is that the suffix *ṣyaṅ* is prescribed as a substitute (*ādeśa*) in the place of *aṇ* and *iñ*; the other position is that the suffix *ṣyaṅ* follows after a word ending in *aṇ* or *iñ*.

The second [view] is that "it becomes. In that regard, regarding the view of substitution (ādeśapakṣa), this fault arises: one must resort to *ṣyaṅ* after a word ending in *aṇ* or *iñ*; thus, the view of suffixation (pratyayapakṣa) must be resorted to—this is the meaning.
Regarding the view of substitution, "the effort (*yatna*) must be made" [is said]; or, the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of an option. Now, even there...

When the suffix *pratyaya* is adopted [as the substitute], why does the substitution of *śīrṣan* for *śiras* not occur? To this he says: "In that case," and so forth. When the suffix *ṣyaṅ* follows, then regarding that elision of *iṅ* by the rule *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), which occurs when that [suffix] follows, [the elision] is subject to the preceding rule (*pūrvavidhi*).

The meaning is that because of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if occupying the original position) regarding what is to be performed, there is no intervention; therefore, since the *taddhita* suffix beginning with *ya*, which is the cause for the substitution of *śīrṣan*, is intervened upon, the substitution does not apply.
63. *paddannomāshṛnniśasanyūṣandoṣanyakañcchakannudannāsañcchasprabhṛtiṣu* (Pāṇini 6.1.63).
Here too, the suffixes beginning with *śas* are taken as the cause [of substitution], and they cannot exist without a base (*prakṛti*).

The meaning is that they do not arise. When those [suffixes] are prescribed from a different *prakṛti*, the substitutes such as *pada* and so forth are understood to be enjoined. Nor does this result in the undesirable consequence of substitutes being applied without the mention of their original bases (*sthānin*), because when those [substitutes] are being enjoined, [the original bases are implied].
He states that *śas* and the following [case endings] imply their own base (*prakṛti*) ending in *pād* and so forth, according to the appropriate form—namely, "pāda, danta, nāsikā," etc.
In the examples beginning with *pada*, the forms *padaḥ* and *dataḥ* end in *śas*. [Also] *yūṣṇaḥ*, *doṣṇaḥ*.

*yaknaḥ* and *śaknaḥ* are nominative singular forms ending in the sixth case. The vowel *a* is elided by the rule *ṭhallopo’naḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.134). *Māsi*, *niśi*, and *āsani* are locative singular forms. In the word *āsani*, the elision of the vowel *a* does not optionally take place according to the rule *vibhāṣāṅśyoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.136).

[The word] *bhavati* [is used]. The remaining [words] end in the third case singular. *Pādau* and *nāsike* end in the nominative dual. But why do they continue to apply the rule *anyatarasyām*? To this he says: "By that..."

"‘Pādādayo’pi’ and so forth: because words such as *pāda* are also employed, they maintain the application of the term *anyatarasyām*. When the word *prabhṛti*, which denotes a limit or starting point, is relied upon, the substitute occurs elsewhere than after [words beginning with] *śas*."
With the intention that [the form] is not established, he says: "The word *prabhṛti* has the sense of 'and so forth' (*prakāra*). Regarding the form *doṣaṇī*:

some say that in the first dual, there is the substitution of *doṣan*, and the substitution of *śī* for *auṭ*. Others, however, say that *doṣaṇī* ends in the feminine suffix *ṅī*; when *ṅīp* is the applicable context, there is the substitution of *doṣan*.

Then, from [the words ending in] *ṭhan* and *ne*, [the suffix] *ṅīp* is applied by Pāṇini 4.1.5, resulting in *nasyam*. For the sense of "beneficial to," [the suffix] *yat* is applied by Pāṇini 5.1.6, resulting in *nastaḥ*. The suffix *tasi* is applied by Pāṇini 5.4.45 in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*), resulting in *naḥkṣudraḥ*. [The word] *nāsikā*...
The term *kṣudrāyasya* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Regarding the expression "a nasal sound" (*nāsikyo varṇaḥ*), the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava-artha*) according to Pāṇini 5.1.6, *śarīrāvayavāt*.
In the expression "the city of Nāsikya" (*nāsikyaṃ nagaram*), the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of "beneficial for" (*hita-artha*).

64. *dhātvādeḥ paḥ saḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.64). Regarding the form *ṣiñcati*: the augment *num* is applied by the rule *śe mucādīnām* (7.1.59). Regarding the form *ṣoḍaśa*: it means "one who has six or ten," and [the compound] is formed by the rule *saṃkhyāpūrvo dviguḥ* (2.1.52) and *dvigur ekavacanm* (2.4.1), with the elision of the final member by *dvigurekavacane* (2.4.1), and the substitution of *ṣaṣ* for *ṣaṭ* by *ṣaṣṭhāṅgasya* (6.3.47). The form *ṣoḍaśa* is derived from *ṣaṣ* and *daśa* by the rule *ṣaṣo 'ti* (6.3.48), which substitutes *ṣaṣ* for *ṣaṣ* before the word *ati*, and then applies *ṣaṣṭha* to the resulting form. Alternatively, one may derive it as *ṣaṣ* and *daśa* combined, where the *ṣaṣ* is changed to *ṣoḍaśa* by the rule *ṣaṣṭho 'ti* (6.3.48), which replaces *ṣaṣ* with *ṣoḍaśa* when followed by *ati*. The form *ṣoḍaśa* is thus established. Regarding the form *ṣoḍaśan*: it means "one who has sixteen," and the *ṣaṣ* is changed to *ṣoḍaśa* by the rule *ṣaṣṭho 'ti* (6.3.48), which applies to the number-word *ṣaṣ* when followed by *ati*. The form *ṣoḍaśa* is derived from *ṣaṣ* and *daśa* by the rule *ṣaṣṭho 'ti* (6.3.48), which substitutes *ṣoḍaśa* for *ṣaṣ* before *ati*. The form *ṣoḍaśa* is derived from *ṣaṣ* and *daśa* by the rule *ṣaṣṭho 'ti* (6.3.48), which substitutes *ṣoḍaśa* for *ṣaṣ* before *ati*. The form *ṣoḍaśa* is derived from *ṣaṣ* and *daśa* by the rule *ṣaṣṭho 'ti* (6.3.48), which substitutes *ṣoḍaśa* for *ṣaṣ* before *ati*. The form *ṣoḍaśa* is derived from *ṣaṣ* and *daśa* by the rule *ṣaṣṭho 'ti* (6.3.48), which substitutes *ṣoḍaśa* for *ṣaṣ* before *ati*. The form *ṣoḍaśa* is derived from *ṣaṣ* and *daśa* by the rule *ṣaṣṭho 'ti* (6.3.48), which substitutes *ṣoḍaśa* for *ṣaṣ* before *ati*. The form *ṣoḍaśa* is derived from *ṣaṣ* and *daśa* by the rule *ṣaṣṭho 'ti* (6.3.48), which substitutes *ṣoḍaśa* for *ṣaṣ* before *ati*. The form *ṣoḍaśa* is derived from *ṣaṣ* and *daśa* by the rule *ṣaṣṭho 'ti* (6.3.48), which substitutes *ṣoḍaśa* for *ṣaṣ* before *ati*. The form *ṣoḍaśa* is derived from *ṣaṣ* and *daśa* by the rule *ṣaṣṭho 'ti* (6.3.48), which substitutes *ṣoḍaśa* for *ṣaṣ* before *ati*. The form *ṣoḍaśa* is derived from *ṣaṣ* and *daśa* by the rule *ṣaṣṭho 'ti* (6.3.48), which substitutes *ṣoḍaśa* for *ṣaṣ* before *ati*. The form *ṣoḍaśa* is derived from *ṣaṣ* and *daśa* by the rule *ṣaṣṭho 'ti* (6.3.48), which substitutes *ṣoḍaśa* for *ṣaṣ* before *ati*. The form *ṣoḍaśa* is derived from *ṣaṣ* and *daśa* by the rule *ṣaṣṭho 'ti* (6.3.48), which substitutes *ṣoḍaśa* for *ṣaṣ* before *ati*. The form *ṣoḍaśa* is derived from *ṣaṣ* and *daśa* by the rule *ṣaṣṭho 'ti* (6.3.48), which substitutes *ṣoḍaśa* for *ṣaṣ* before *ati*. The form *ṣoḍaśa* is derived from *ṣaṣ* and *daśa* by the rule *ṣaṣṭho 'ti* (6.3.48), which substitutes *ṣoḍaśa* for *ṣaṣ* before *ati*. The form *ṣoḍaśa* is derived from *ṣaṣ* and *daśa* by the rule *ṣaṣṭho 'ti* (6.3.48), which substitutes *ṣoḍaśa* for *ṣaṣ* before *ati*. The form *ṣoḍaśa* is derived from *ṣaṣ* and *daśa* by the rule *ṣaṣṭho 'ti* (6.3.48), which substitutes *ṣoḍaśa* for *ṣaṣ* before *ati*. The form *ṣoḍaśa* is derived from *ṣaṣ* and *daśa* by the rule *ṣaṣṭho 'ti* (6.3.48), which substitutes *ṣoḍaśa* for *ṣaṣ* before *ati*. The form *ṣoḍaśa* is derived from *ṣaṣ* and *daśa* by the rule *ṣaṣṭho 'ti* (6.3.48), which substitutes *ṣoḍaśa* for *ṣaṣ* before *ati*. The form *ṣoḍaśa* is derived from *ṣaṣ* and *daśa* by the rule *

The compound is a *bahuvrīhi* formed by the rule beginning with "ityādinā. The suffix *ṅc* is applied by the rule "saṃkhyeye ṅc" (Pāṇini 5.4.73). Regarding the form "ṣoḍan": this is a *bahuvrīhi* meaning "one who has six teeth" (*ṣaṭ dantā asya*).

By the rule "vayasi dantasya datṛ" (Pāṇini 5.4.141), the word *danta* is replaced by the substitute *datṛ*. [Furthermore,] by the rule "ṣaṣa utvam... [the substitution of *u* for the final vowel of *ṣaṣ* occurs].

According to the Vārttika 765, "In the case of *datṛ* and *daśan*, there is the substitution of *u* for the penultimate vowel, and the change of the initial letter of the following word to a *ṣṭu*-sound," there is the substitution of *u* for the vowel of *ṣaṣ*, and the change of the initial letter of the following word to a *ṣṭu*-sound, namely, the letter *ḍ*. Thus, we have *ṣaṇḍaḥ*;
this is a base (*prātipadika*) that is unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*). [The form] *ṣaḍikaḥ* refers to one who is pitied.

In the word *ṣaḍaṅgulidata*, the suffix *ṭhac* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.3.78 (*bahvaco manuṣyanāmnaṣṭhac*), and the word *aṅgulidata* undergoes elision according to 5.3.83 (*ājādāvūrdhvaṃ dvitīyādacaḥ*).
Now, one might object that the term "root" (*dhātu*) from 6.1.8 (*liṭi dhātoḥ*) will be understood here by anuvṛtti [from the previous rule].

In that case, what is the purpose of mentioning *dhātu* here again? It is to indicate this: that [the previous rule] has ceased to apply. For if that were to continue to apply, then even the elision prescribed by *lopo vyor vali* (P. 6.1.66) would be understood as applying only to the constituent parts of a verbal root (*dhātu*). [As in the case of] *knūyī*.

In the case of *knūtaḥ* from the root *knū* (DhP 4.85) with the suffix *kta*, and *kṣmātaḥ* from the root *kṣmi* (DhP 4.86) with the suffix *kta*, [the rule] would apply exactly here; however, it would not apply in cases such as *gaudharaḥ* or *paceran*. Now, even so, the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) is indeed redundant, because the term "original instruction" (*upadeśa*) is already understood [from the previous rule], and it is not...

Is it the instruction (*upadeśa*) of nominal stems (*prātipadika*)? To whom, then, does the instruction belong? To verbal roots (*dhātu*)? This is not so; for within the governing context of "instruction" (*upadeśādhikāra*), by the mention of "instruction," the letter *ṣ* is specified, and the letter *ṣ* of the word *ṣaṣ* is indeed an instance of instruction. [As stated in Pāṇini 6.1.63: "The substitution of *u* occurs for the final vowel of *ṣaṣ* before the words *datṛ*, *daśan*, and *dhā*, as well as for the initial letter of a following member."

Because of this reading in the Sūtra (vā. 765), the term *dhātu* (root) must be included. [The examples are] "kaṣati" and "laṣati. The root *kaṣ*, meaning "to injure," is recited in the class of roots beginning with *bhū* (*bhvādi*) in the group starting with *kaṣa-sidh* etc.; and for "laṣati," there is the root *laṣa* in the sense of "desire" (*kāntau*) at DhP 888. In these two cases, the inclusion of the initial letter [of the root] occurs.

But surely, by the very force of this specific instruction (*upadeśa*), [the substitution] will not occur here; otherwise, the instruction would be purposeless? This is not so; for there is another purpose for the instruction. What is that? It is for the sake of [the rule]: "In the remaining cases, optionally, when the upadeśa does not begin with *ka* or *kha* and ends in *v*, [the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs]" (Pāṇini 8.4.17).
[The inclusion of] *ṣ* [in the root *liṣ*] is so that there may not be the application of *k*; for instance, so that the substitution of *ṣ* may occur in forms such as *leṣatuḥ* and *leṣuḥ*.

But for what purpose are *ṣ* and the others taught, rather than *s* and the others being taught? For if they were taught as *s*, this sūtra would not need to be composed. To this he says: "In place [of a dental] and in an affix... (*ādeśapratyayoḥ*).

And so forth. "The rule for *ṣatva*" refers to the restriction regarding the substitution of *ṣ*. By means of the sūtra *ṣātpadādyoḥ* (8.3.59), this is intended so that the rule for *ṣatva* may apply specifically to *sah* and the others;
otherwise, some [sounds] beginning with *ṣ* would have been taught [in the root lists], and a separate effort would have been required for the sake of the *ṣatva* of *sah* and the rest.

It would have to be done; and the intention is that this [process] is cumbersome. Even though there is no doubt regarding those roots beginning with *ṣ*, there certainly is regarding those beginning with *s*. For here it is not known whether these are indeed *ṣopadeśa* roots which have had their *ṣ* changed to *s* by the rule "ṣ at the beginning of a root is replaced by s" (Pāṇini 6.1.64).
Having raised the doubt—whether [the term *upadeśa*] refers to those [sounds] as they are uttered, or only to those beginning with *ṣa* and so on—he asks: "Which, then, are these? [The answer is:
"Those as they are recited. Because of their proximity, those which are recited beginning with *ṣa* are to be understood as *ṣopadeśas*.
[This is stated in the rule] "those preceded by a vowel (*ac*) or a final dental (*dantya)," and so forth; that is, those for which a vowel or a final dental follows.
"Of those"—this refers to the *ac* vowels and the dental *d*. Here, the word "para" (subsequent) is used in the sense of a constituent part (*avayava*).

Since that status of being subsequent to the *ac* and *d* must be understood in relation to another constituent part, it is understood—by virtue of proximity—to be in relation to the letter *s*. [The rule applies to] *smi*, *sviḍ*, *svañj*, and *svap*.
Thus: the roots *ṣmiṅ* "to smile slightly" (DhP 948), *ñiṣvidā* "to perspire" (DhP 1188),
*ṣvanj* "to embrace" (DhP 976), and *ñiṣvap* "to sleep" (DhP 1068) are taught by their own forms.
Because the letters *m* and *v* are neither vowels (*ac*) nor final consonants (*antya*), some read *svad* in place of *svid*—
namely, *smi*, *svad*, *svad*, *svañj*, and *svap*— and for them, the root is *svad* [the Dhātupāṭha reads *ṣvad*] in the sense of "tasting" (*āsvādane*). (Dhātupāṭha 1.818–819).
Thus, *svadi* is also indeed a root taught with an initial sibilant (*ṣopadeśa*), according to the rule: "With the exception of *sṛp*, *sṛj*, *stṛ*, *styai*, *sekṛ*, and *sṛ*.
[The roots are: *gamlu* and *suplṛ* in the sense of "going" (DhP 982, 983); *sṛj* in the sense of "emission" (DhP 1178); *stṛñ* in the sense of "covering" (DhP 1252); and *styai*...
Excluding the roots *śabda* and *saṅghāta* (DhP 911,

910), as well as *sekṛ*, *sreka* (DhP 81, 82, 84, 85)— which belong to the group of roots meaning "to go"— and *sṛ* (DhP 935), those other roots ending in a consonant preceded by *a* or *i* are termed *ṣopadeśa*.

"Subdhātu," etc. A *subdhātu* is one that ends in *kyac* or other such affixes. Regarding the roots *ṣṭhiv* (meaning "to eject") and *ṣvakka*, as well as certain roots not found in the standard *Dhātupāṭha*—namely *vukka*, *makkatikka*, *ṭikka*, *ṭīkka*, *vagi*, and *lagi*, all meaning "to go"—a prohibition [of the application of *kyac*] must be stated for these.

The meaning is that it must be explained. Here is the explanation: first, in forms such as *ṣoḍīyati*, the initial *ṣ* is not the beginning of a verbal root (*dhātu*), because the "beginning" is a constituent part (*avayava*).
And a constituent part is something that initiates; however, a nominal stem (*subanta*) is initiated by a nominal suffix (*sub*) and by the *kyac* affix. Nor...

Since it is also preceded by another letter, namely the letter *ṣ*, how can it have the status of beginning with *ṣ*? However, words such as *saha* and others are indeed formed from letters beginning with *ṣ*; therefore, it is logical that they begin with *ṣ*.

As for the root *ṣṭhivu*, it does not [begin with *ṣ*] because of a specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*). What is that exception? It is the rule: "In the case of the roots *ṣṭhivu*, *klamu*, and *cam*, [the *ṣ* is changed to *k*]."

Regarding the rule *śiti* (Pāṇini 7.3.75): for that which undergoes the substitution of *satva*, this [treatise] pronounces it as already having undergone *satva* in the specific rules (*pradeśa*), just as in the rule *sthādhvoricca* (1.2.17).
Because [the substitution] of *v* in *svak* is also excluded by the rule *aj-dantyaparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.3), it does not occur. As for the *v* [in *svak*]...

Because [the letter] *ṣ* belongs to the *ṭu*-pratyāhāra (which includes the dentals and the labial), it is not included by the mention of "dentals" (*adantyau*). Alternatively, because of the mention of *yā* [in Pāṇini 6.1.66], it will not apply to the roots *ṣṭhivu* and *ṣvak*. Furthermore, the letter *y* is not heard [in pronunciation] because it has been elided in the traditional formulation (*luptanirdiṣṭatvāt*). Or else, the phrase "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) is understood to carry over here, and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
It is understood from this that [the substitution] does not apply to the root *ṣṭhivu* and others. Regarding "ṣaṣṭhīvati":

there is lengthening by the rule "ṣṭhivuklamucamāṃ śiti" (Pāṇini 7.3.75). Regarding "ṣvakkate": the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs because the root is marked with an *anudātta* accent. Now, is the second letter of the root *ṣṭhivu* the letter *ṭha*?

Is it intended as *ṭha*? Or is it *tha*? If it is *ṭha*, then [the form] *teṣṭhīṣyate* is established, but *teṣṭhīvyate* is not established; for, according to the rule "ṭhabhyāse carc" (Pāṇini 8.4.54), since *ṭha* is the most similar [substitute], only *ṭa* would be obtained in place of *ṭha* in the reduplicated syllable. But if it is *tha*, then...

The established conclusion is as follows: the form *teṣṭhīvya* is not established; that is, in the form *teṣṭhīvya*, because of proximity (*āntaratamya*), a *t* would result in place of the *th* being prescribed. Therefore, he says:
"of this root *ṣṭhivu*" and so forth, so that there may be a twofold form for the root *ṣṭhiv*.

Some teachers instructed their students that "this is the letter *ṭha*"; others, however, led them to understand this point by saying, "this is the letter *tha*, which is heard as *ṭha* due to the rule of *ṣṭuan*. Both of these are for a specific purpose. Others, moreover, say that [the root] *ṣṭhivu* also occurs among the roots beginning with *div*.
It is studied again; therein, for one [reading] it is the form *ṭha*, while for the other it is the form *ṭha*.
Regarding the form *teṣṭhīvyate*, the remainder [of the rule] is *ṭh-śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.61).

65. *ṇo naḥ* | (6.1.65) "This [suffix] *na* is also not desired after a verbal root ending in *su*, because of the same reason as before. [The rule] beginning with *upasargādasamāse’pi* [is cited]. Here, according to the preceding [context], this constitutes the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

It is to be understood as follows: *nṛtī-nandi*, etc. *nṛtī* (in the sense of "moving the limbs") [Dhātupāṭha 1116], *ṭuanadi* (in the sense of "prosperity") [Dhātupāṭha 67], *nard* and *gard* (in the sense of "sound") [Dhātupāṭha 56, 57], *nakka* and *vakka* (or *dhakka* according to the Dhātupāṭha) (in the sense of "destruction") [Dhātupāṭha 1593, 1594], and *naṭ*.
In *avasyandane* [reading *avaspandane* in the Dhātupāṭha (DhP 1545)], it is derived from the curādi class with the causative suffix *ṇic*;
in *nāthṛ* and *nādhṛ*, meaning "request, affliction, sovereignty, and blessing" (DhP 6.7); and in *nṛ*, meaning "to lead" (DhP 809, 1495).
66. *Lopo vyor vali* (6.1.66).
For one who considers that the term *dhātu* from [the rule] *liṭi dhātoḥ* (6.1.8) is also carried over here by virtue of its observed scope of application (*dṛṣṭānuvṛtti-sāmarthya*).

Someone might have the misconception that this elision of *vy* is prescribed specifically for the verbal root (*dhātu*) when followed by *val*; therefore, in order to dispel that, he says: "The word 'dhātoḥ' (of the root) which was under discussion," and so forth. "Didivān" is the form of the root *div* with the suffix *kvasu*. "Ūyī" [is the form of] the root *ūyī*.

In *tantusantāne* (DhP 4.83), [the suffix] *ṭhknūyaḥ* is applied; in *knūyī śabde* (DhP 4.85), [the form] *gauderaḥ* is derived. In *godhāyā ḍhrak* (4.1.129), the substitution of *ey* for *ḍha* occurs, followed by the elision of the letter *y*. In *paceran*, there is the elision of the *y* of the *sīyuṭ* augment. In *jīveḥ*, [the suffix *kan* is applied].

This is from the root *jīv* in the sense of "sustaining life" (Dhātupāṭha 562). Regarding *sriveḥ*: this refers to the root *srivu* in the sense of "motion and drying" (Dhātupāṭha 1109). Regarding *āsremāṇam*:
this suffix *manin* is derived from the *Uṇādi* [list]. But how can this be an example here, since...

Since the rule "a stem-formation (*āṅga*) is stronger than that which depends on a vowel (*vārṇa*)" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 39) applies due to its superior force, should not the substitution of *ūṭh* by the rule "for *cch* and *śu*, there is *ūṭh* and *ūḍ* before a nasal" (P.
6.4.19) and so forth take effect here? To this, he says: "The *uṇādi* [suffixes]..."

Regarding the phrase "bahulam" and so forth: because the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (optionally) serves the purpose of allowing exceptions to all grammatical rules (*sarvavidhivyabhicārārthatvāt*), this undesirable consequence (*doṣaprasaṅga*) does not arise. This is so even when the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *p* is subsequently applied after the letter *p*.

It must be pronounced with a duration of one and a half *mātrās*, for a syllable such as *aka* has a duration of one *mātrā*, whereas a *visarjanīya* is shorter by half a *mātrā*. However, if the elision (*lopa*) were applied first, it would result in a pronunciation of two *mātrās*; this is because the vowel *o* consists of two *mātrās*. In that case—

For the sake of brevity, it would have been more appropriate to mention the elision (*lopa*) later; why, then, is it mentioned first? To this he says: "First," and so forth. Another [view] holds that it is proper to mention the element undergoing the operation (*kāryin*) first, and the operation (*kārya*) afterwards; therefore, when the mention of *v* and *y* was to be made first, for what purpose...

He explains the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the mention of *lop* (elision) is made; however, that is incorrect because, in the rule *ṭhlugaṇiñoḥ* (2.4.58), the operation (*kārya*) itself is mentioned first. [This is seen] in the rule *verapṛktalopāt* and so forth. When the suffix *kvip* is applied to the roots *kaṇḍū* and *lolū*, [the final *u* is elided] due to the elision of the semivowel (*vali lopa*).

Because it is subsequent, because it applies both to what has been and what has not yet been performed, and because it is eternal (*nitya*), the elision of the *apṛkta* vowel after *vi* would occur first.

This being the case, due to the absence of the cause [for the subsequent rule], there would be no elision of *val* (consonants) by virtue of the absence of the designation of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) when depending on a phoneme; therefore, the mention of "elision" (*lopa*) is placed first.

It is stated: "The elision of *val* must occur first, so that it happens as before. For if "elision" (*lopa*) were mentioned first [in the rule], this meaning would be indicated: "Due to the elision of *vi*, the elision of *val* must be performed first. In the example *kaṇḍūaḥ*, there is the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.48).

By the rule "kvilugupadhātvacaṅaparanirhrāsakutveṣu na sthānivat" (Vārttika 2 on Pāṇini 1.1.58), the status of being *sthānivadbhāva* does not apply to the letter *a*; thus, there is no elision (*lopa*) of the *v* before a *val*. Now, why is there no elision of the *vakāra* and *gakāra* in the words *vraścakaḥ* and *vraścanaḥ* when followed by the *val* *repha*?
Thus he says: "of *vraśca* and so forth," etc. If there were also elision (*lopa*) for these [roots], the pronunciation of the letter *v* would be purposeless.
Therefore, by virtue of the power of its pronunciation, there is no elision of *vraśca* and the others when a *val* [consonant] follows.

It might be argued: "In forms such as *vṛścati* and *vavraśca*, since there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) and the substitution of the remaining initial consonant (*halādiśeṣa*), the letter *v* is indeed heard; so how can the instruction [of the rule] be purposeless?
To this he says: "In *vṛścati*, etc. Just as there is the possibility of elision (*lopa*) in cases such as *vraścaka*, so too...

Even in cases such as *vṛścati*, although operations such as *samprasāraṇa* have been performed, they are considered non-existent (*asiddha*) because they are extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). In that context, *samprasāraṇa* is extrinsic because it depends upon the suffix *ṅt*;
likewise, in the rule for *halādiśeṣa*, [the substitution] is extrinsic because it depends upon the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), and [the elision] before a consonant (*vali*) is extrinsic.

However, the elision of *y* (yalopa) is *antaranga* because it depends solely on a phoneme (*varṇa*). Therefore, the elision of the letter *v* would apply to the root *vraśc* in every instance. Yet, its original form is taught [in the grammatical tradition]; thus, by virtue of the authority of that original teaching (*upadeśa*), the elision will not occur—this remains established.

67. *verapṛktasya* | (6.1.67) [The rule begins with] *ṭhveḥ* etc. Since there is no other element beginning with *vi* that possesses the designation *apṛkta*, only those beginning with *kvip* are understood. But how is it that when *vi* is mentioned, [the elements] beginning with *kvip* are included?

The general inclusion is justified; however, since these possess specific qualifiers (*viśeṣa*) as their adjuncts (*anubandha*), such as *prakāra* and so forth, this was stated in order to dispel that objection:
"having set aside the specific qualifiers and adjuncts," as in the examples "brahmahā" (slayer of a Brahmin) and "bhrūṇahā" (slayer of an embryo).

In the word *ghṛtaspṛk*, there is a long vowel by [Pāṇini 6.4.13] *sau ca*; and there is the substitution of *ku* by [Pāṇini 8.2.62] *kvinpratyayasya kuḥ*. In the word *ardhabhāk*, there is the substitution of *ku* by [Pāṇini 8.2.30] *coḥ kuḥ*.

In cases such as *darvi* and others, it could be argued that the elision does not occur precisely because of the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various ways) in the rule *uṇādayo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.1); therefore, the mention of *apṛkta* is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*), or for the sake of variety (*vaicitrya*).
68. *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* (Pāṇini 6.1.68).

If the word "elision" (*lopa*), which is being carried over here [from the previous rule], were meaningful only in its technical (*śāstrīya*) sense, then it would be connected with *hal*, which ends in the nominative case, through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

This is not tenable; for the meaning of the technical term *lopa* (elision) taught in the treatise is the absence of perception—that is, non-appearance—and yet there is no perception of the consonant (*hal*).
Nor can the ablative case in *hal-ṅy-ābbhyaḥ* be interpreted as a genitive case for the nominative *hal*.
One may postulate that [the word *hal*] will be supplied by implication, or that there will be a transformation of *hal* into its genitive form (*halaḥ*),
so that the genitive-ending [word] can be connected with the word *lopa*;
for the nominative case ending cannot be considered to have fulfilled its purpose [in this context].
Having considered that the use of the genitive case would otherwise be untenable, he says "tadiha" (therefore, in this case), etc.

"Lupyate" (it is elided) means "lopaḥ" (elision); [the suffix] *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*). By this, he demonstrates that the word "lopa" possesses meaning according to its worldly sense. "Lupyate" means "is obstructed" (*nirudhyate*). Thus, it possesses meaning by virtue of its worldly sense.

Through the term *lopa*, which functions as the means of the operation (*karmasādhana*), the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) with the word *hal* is established. For by the word *lopa*, only the phoneme (*varṇa*) being elided is denoted—as in the rule "A single consonant (*apṛkta*) consisting of *ṭh*, *su*, *ti*, or *si* is called *hal*. And by this [word *lopa*], that very [consonant] is further specified. [This applies also to the word] *dīrghāt*.

Thus [it is said]. And this [suffix] is a qualifier of *ṅī* and *āp* alone, because of their possibility and non-deviation; it is not, however, a qualifier of that which ends in a consonant (*halanta*), because of its impossibility. For example: *ukhāsrat*, *parṇadhvat*. [The roots] *sraṃsu* and *dhvaṃsu* mean "falling down" (*adhaḥpatane*; Dhātupāṭha 754, 755). [Thus, *ukhāsrat* means] "one who falls from a pot," and [*parṇadhvat* means] "one who causes leaves to fall."

In the case of *kvip*, by the rule "ṭhaniditām" (Pāṇini 8.4.56), there is the substitution of *c* for *t*—that is, the letter *t*. Thus we have "kumārī. The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule "vayasi prathame" (4.1.20). In the case of "gaurī," the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule "ṣidgaurādibhyaśca" (4.1.41). [And] "śārṅgaravī."

By the rule *ṭhśārṅgaravādyaño ṅīn* (Pāṇini 4.1.13), the suffix *ṅīn* is applied; thus we have *kārīṣagandhyā*. By the rule *hyaṅścāp* (Pāṇini 4.1.74), the suffix *cāp* is applied. [Regarding the form *kārīṣagandhyāyanī*:
"The elision of *ti* and the elision of *si* occur only after a stem ending in a consonant. Now, [one might object: by the word *ekāraṇa* ("by the vowel *e*") in the rule *ṅyābantāt*...

[The author] demonstrates this, for the suffixes *ti* and *si* cannot follow a feminine suffix ending in *ṅī* or *āp*, since those two are prescribed only after a verbal root (*dhātu*). [Examples: "abibhar bhavān" (you carried); here, after the *guṇa* substitution and the replacement of *a* by *r* (*raparatva*), there is the elision of *ti*. "ajāgar bhavān" (you were awake).
The guṇa substitution [of o for av] occurs by the rule *jāgro 'vicinnalṅitsu* (Pāṇini 7.3.85).
The auxiliary verb *bhavān* is used for the purpose of manifesting the root *as*. Regarding the form *abhinaḥ*:
it is the *laṅ* [aorist] of the root *bhid*, with *ru*-substitution [for *s*] by the rule *daśca* (8.2.75), and [the lengthening of the vowel] by the rule *ato ror aplutād aplute* (6.1.113).

Thus, there is *utva* [of the *u* in *anu*]. Then, by [Pāṇini 6.1.87] *inaṇyākāreṇa saha ṭhād guṇaḥ*, and by [Pāṇini 6.1.109] *ṭheṅḥ padāntādati*, there is the formation of the single substitute [the *guṇa* vowel *o*]. Thus, "grāmaṇīḥ. [The word] "grāmaṇīḥ" is derived from "he leads the village" (*grāmaṃ nayati*) by means of the suffix *kvip* according to [Pāṇini 3.2.61] *satsūdviṣa...* etc. [The word] "niṣkauśāmbiḥ" [is formed similarly].

In the word *nirgataḥ kauśāmbyāḥ*, it is a *prādi-samāsa* (compound with a prefix); the shortening [of the final vowel] occurs by the rule *gostriyor upasarjanasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.48). In the word *atikhaṭvaḥ*, the compound is formed as "one who has transcended the bed" (*khaṭvām atikrāntaḥ*) as before, and the shortening occurs [by the same rule]. In the word *abhaitsīt*, [the substitution of *ai* for *a-a* occurs] by the rule *vadavraja* (Pāṇini 7.2.3).

Thus [is established] the *vṛddhi* [substitution]; [the augment] *iṭ* is applied when [the suffix] is *apṛkta*. Now, one might object: since the term *sī* is mentioned in general, the root *sic* is also included; therefore, this counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) is not appropriate.
To this he says: "of that which is accompanied by *tiṅ*" and so forth. By virtue of association (*sāhacarya*) with the word *tiṅ*, [the term refers to] *tiṅ*.
If it is so, why is it improper here to say "of *siC*, not of *ser*"? [Consider] *bibheda*:

here the vowel *a* of *ṇal* occurs as a non-conjunct (*apṛkta*), but since it is not a consonant (*hal*), it is not elided. [The objection] "it is already established by the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*)" refers to examples such as *rājā*.

[This is] the remainder. But why, then, is it not established? To this he says: "The king (*rājā*), the carpenter (*takṣā*)," and so forth. Just as in the case of *pacan*, because the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) does not occur;
likewise, it would not occur in *rājā*, *takṣā*, and so on. And the non-existence of the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct in this context [is due to the following rule].

It is an indirect cause (*pāramparyeṇa hetu*). For when that [suffix] exists, the preceding word does not receive the designation "pada" by virtue of the prohibition in Pāṇini 1.4.17, *asarvanāmasthāne*. And when that designation is absent, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*)—which is prescribed for a "pada"—would not occur; and if the elision of *n* did not occur...

The form *rājā* and others would not be established. Regarding the phrase "the substitution of *d*" (*datvam*), it must be connected with the word "it would not" (*na syāt*) from the preceding context. For even the substitution of *d* would not occur, because the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), and thus the designation of a "word" (*pada-saṃjñā*) would not exist. Now, if...
Or rather— the elision of the final member of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) does not apply here at all;

since the elision of the initial member of a conjunct (*saṃyogādilopa*), prescribed by the rule "of *ṣ* and *k*, when they are the first members of a conjunct or at the end [of a word]" (Pāṇini 8.2.29), is an exception (*apavāda*) to it, that alone would take effect, as in *kāṣṭham*.

[The word] *kāṣṭhataṅkṣitṛ* [is derived from the root] *takṣ*, meaning "he fashions. Since that [suffix] is present, the substitution of *ru* and the subsequent visarga (*visarga*) would apply to the *s* of the case-ending; how then could there be the substitution of *d*? [The objection is raised: "There would not be the substitution of *ṭ*," because even this [substitution of *d*] is rendered non-existent due to the fact that the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is considered as if it had not occurred (*asiddha*).

For one who has not yet acquired the designation [of being a *saṃyogānta*], [the rule] would not apply. This is because of the restriction [imposed by] "rātsasya" (Pāṇini 8.2.24). Since [the desired result] is already established by "saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.23), [the former rule] serves as a restriction [stating that the elision occurs only after a consonant following an *r*]. Thus, by the restriction of "rātsasya," [the elision is restricted to the case where *s* follows *r*]. [This is further supported by] "saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ."

Since this is already established by that very rule, the present rule—"ṭh rātsasya" (Pāṇini 8.2.24)—is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*): namely, that the elision of *s* should occur only after a *ra*, and not after anything else.
Consequently, in the form *abibhar bhavān*, there would be no elision of the *t* at all. Therefore...
Since [the result] is not established by the elision of the final member of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*), the elision of the final consonant (*halantāllopa*) is stated.

For the sake of easily grasping this very point, the verse from the *Saṃgraha* beginning with "for when there is the elision of the final of a conjunct" (*saṃyogāntasya lope hi*) is cited. The word *hi* is used in the sense of a reason; because...

If the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) were relied upon, operations such as the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would not be established. Furthermore, for you who advocate the elision of a final consonant cluster, there would be no elision at all of the *t* following the *r* in forms such as *bibharti*, *bibharbhavān*, and *ajagrabh-vān*.
Therefore, the elision of the suffixes *su*, *ti*, and *si* is prescribed after that which ends in *val*.

69. *eṅhasvātsambuddheḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.69). [The word] *ca* from "and after a consonant" (*haliti ca*) is understood to carry over. If *hal* were not carried over, then in the case of *he kuṇḍa-asu*, since the substitution of *am* (*ambhāva*) would apply because it is subsequent to the elision (*lopa*), [the form would be incorrect]. Therefore, [the rule for] the initial [portion]...
The intention is that, with the elision of the letter *a* by [Pāṇini 1.1.54] *parasya* and the lengthening of the vowel by [Pāṇini 7.3.102] *supi ca*,

the undesirable form *he kuṇḍam* would result. "The term *apṛkta* is not governed here" means that if *apṛkta* were to carry over (*anuvarteta*) from this context, then there would be no elision in the case of *he kuṇḍa*.

It might be so; the sense is that because the designation *apṛkta* (uncombined) does not exist [in this context]. But how is it known that the term *apṛkta* does not carry over here? To this he says: "And thus," and so forth. The word "and thus" (*tathā ca*) indicates a reason. Since the mention of *apṛkta* was made in the preceding rule, it is understood that it does not apply here.

The term *apṛkta* is understood to carry over into this section (*prakaraṇa*); for otherwise, since the term *apṛkta* would already have carried over from the rule "ṭhe-r-lop-a-pṛktasya" (Pāṇini 6.1.67), the term *apṛkta* would not have been mentioned again in the preceding sūtra. [The phrase] "if that [elision] occurs in the case of the vocative (*sambuddhi*)" means: if...
The meaning is that it becomes connected with the vocative case ending (*sambuddhi*).

By this, he shows that the word *sambuddheḥ* has a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) ending. [Examples: "O Agni," "O Vāyu"—[here] by [Pāṇini 7.3.108] *hrasvasya guṇaḥ*. [Examples: "O River," "O Daughter-in-law."

The shortening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *ṭhambārthanadyorhrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.107). The elision of the *m* that consists of a *hal* [consonant] occurs because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *hal*. In the case of *he katarat*, once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, since there is a *hal* following the vocative suffix after a short vowel, its [elision follows].

Why does elision (*lopa*) not occur? To this he says: "In *he katarat*, etc. Because in the rule *adḍḍatarādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.25), there is the mention of two *ḍ*s, the substitute is the word *adḍ* with the marker *ḍ*. Due to its being marked with *ḍ* (*ḍit*), the *ṭi*-portion is elided; thus, because there is no short vowel remaining, [the substitution of *hrasva*] does not take place.
[The rule for] elision [is established].

Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *eṅ* (the vowels *e* and *o*), given that even in cases such as *he agne*, elision should not occur because [the word] is already short prior to the *guṇa* substitution caused by the vocative case ending (*sambuddhi*)? To this [it is replied]:

He says: "The mention of *eṅ*," and so forth. Because it is both obligatory (*nitya*) and subsequent (*para*), the substitution of *sambuddhi*-elision (*ślu*) is stronger; therefore, that [elision] must first take place. Once that has occurred, since there is no consonant (*hal*) following a short vowel (*hrasva*) after the *sambuddhi*, the elision [of the final *s*] would not apply. For this reason, the mention of *eṅ* [is made].

It is being formulated. But surely it will be understood as a qualifier of what is prescribed—that is, [the elision occurs] after a vocative case ending *sambuddhi* that is prescribed following a short vowel? This is not so; for this is a single ablative (*pañcamī*), and if it were understood as a qualifier of "prescribed after a short vowel," then it would also be understood [to apply] after those ending in *eṅ*. And thus—*he*...
This would also apply here in the case of "gauh"; therefore, the mention of eṅ must be made.

70. *Śi* is frequently substituted [for the case endings] in the Vedic language. (Pāṇini 6.1.70) This rule prescribes the elision of that *śi* substitute which is ordained by the rule "The substitute *śi* takes the place of *jas* and *śas*" (Pāṇini 7.1.20). For example:

*yā kṣetrā*, *yā vanā*. When the elision of *śi* has been performed, [the preceding form is treated as the original stem] by means of the principle of "reappearance through the original characteristic" (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*).

The augment *num* is applied by the rule "ṭhnapuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ" (7.1.72); lengthening occurs by the rule "sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau" (6.4.8); and the elision of the *n* occurs by the rule "nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya" (8.2.7).

The inclusion of the term *bahulam* ("in various ways") when prescribing what ought to be done is for the purpose of allowing exceptions to all rules; thus, the statement "therefore, all rules are optional in the Veda" (Puṣpavṛtti 56) becomes logically established.

71. *hrasvasya piti kṛti tuK* (Pāṇini 6.1.71). Here, by the term *kṛt*, a primary suffix (*pratyaya*) is brought to mind, and that very suffix is qualified by the word "short" (*hrasva*). Furthermore, since the rule of "ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies, it is understood that a verbal root (*dhātu*) ending in a short vowel is the item to which the augment (*āgama*) *tuK* is added.

Thus he says: "of a root ending in a short vowel," and so forth. Regarding "agnicit": the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *agnau ceḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.91). Regarding "somasut": the suffix [kvip] is applied by the rule *some suñaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.90); in both cases, there is a compound with an upapada. In "prakṛtya" and similar forms, there is a *prādi*-compound.
In the case of a compound where the negative particle *nañ* does not precede, the suffix *lyap* is applied by Pāṇini 7.1.37 (*samāse 'nañpūrve ktvo lyap*).

Now, regarding the example "the Brāhmaṇa family is a *grāmaṇi*": once the shortening of the neuter stem has been applied, why does the augment *tuk*—which depends on a short vowel—not occur here? To this he replies: "the Brāhmaṇa family is a *grāmaṇi*."

And so forth. For shortness (*hrasvatva*) is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*), as it depends upon a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that functions in the neuter sense; whereas the *tuk* augment is intrinsic (*antaraṅga*), because it depends solely upon a phoneme (*varṇa*).
According to the principle "that which is extrinsic is considered non-existent with respect to that which is intrinsic" (*asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam antaraṅge*), the *tuk* does not apply here.
72. *saṃhitāyām* (Pāṇini 6.1.72).

The term "*saṃhitāyām*" here is a locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*). Therefore, if the *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) constitutes the domain for both the element undergoing the operation (*kāryin*) and its cause (*nimitta*), then only the operation to be described hereafter takes place.
It should be understood that [the rule] does not apply to anything else.
Regarding *che ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.73): although this locative case (*saptamī*) refers to the letter *ch* when it possesses the vowel *a*, it nevertheless refers specifically to the *cc* sound.

The *tuk* augment alone is the cause [of the substitution]; however, the letter *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation. This is understood from the prohibition of the *ām* suffix in the rule "ijādeśca gurumato 'nṛcchaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.36). For if the letter *ch*, accompanied by the letter *a*, were the cause of the *tuk* augment, then—

Since there is no *tuk* augment due to the absence of *ṛccha*, there is no possibility for the *ām* augment when the root is heavy; therefore, one would not have formulated the prohibition [of *ām*]. [The form] "icchati" is derived as follows: by the rule "iṣugamiyamāṃ chaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.77), *cha* is substituted [for the root-final], and then *tuk* is applied, followed by the substitution of *cu*-class sounds (*cutva*).

However, regarding the previous rule for the substitution of *tug*, since a short vowel was the augment (*āgamī*), someone might have the misconception that this very same [short vowel] is the augment here as well. To dispel that, he says: "only the short vowel," and so forth. He thinks as follows: the particle *ca* is used here for the purpose of carrying over the short vowel—so that only the short vowel is the augment, just as before.

It might be argued that the *ca* is for the purpose of ensuring that [the rule] does not apply to that which ends in a short vowel; otherwise, because of the svarita accent and its immediate proximity, the same augment (*āgama*) that was understood in the preceding sūtra would be understood here as well, making the *ca* redundant. If only a short vowel were the augment, what desired result would be accomplished?

For what reason is this effort made? To this he says: "By that," and so forth. If *tuk* were to occur after a short vowel, then in forms such as *cic-chidatuḥ*, because that [short vowel] would be included by the mention of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), its removal would occur via the rule *halādi-śeṣaḥ*. However, when the augment is applied after a short vowel...

This is not a fault, for [the rule] "na hy ayam abhyāsasya haL" does not apply here. But how is it that the short vowel (*hrasva*) in the augment (*āgama*) *tuk* is included by the mention of "repetition" (*abhyāsa*)?
To this he says: "nāvayavāvayavaḥ," etc. The particle *iti* indicates the reason (*hetau*). Because of the [principle] regarding the part...

That which is a part is not a part of the whole; therefore, when the short vowel is the augment *tuk*, it is not included by the mention of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). This is because a part of a part does not become a part of the whole. This is the point here.
The intention [of the author] must be understood as being established by the Sūtra itself.
For if, without distinction, a part were not a part of the whole,
then in the case of *śerate*, the substitution of *jha* for the *ru* of the root *sad*, which belongs to a sārvadhātuka affix, would not be a part of that [affix].

Thus, that [augment] would also not be a part (*avayava*) of the *sārvadhātuka* as a whole; consequently, the rule "there is *guṇa* substitution for *śīṅ* before a *sārvadhātuka*" (Pāṇini 7.4.21) would not apply, because the *sārvadhātuka* would be separated by the *ruṭ* augment. For that [augment] has been stated to be a part; it would therefore only separate that very [part] which it is intended to qualify. That...
But the aggregate certainly does not intervene. Therefore, the intention of the author of the Vṛtti must be understood as exactly what was stated previously.
Why, then, is this part-of-a-part prescribed by the Satra considered a part of the aggregate?

Does it not occur? [It does] because of the power of the inclusion of the letter *ca* for the purpose of carrying forward the short vowel (*hrasva*). That *ca* is indeed made for the purpose of carrying forward the short vowel with this intent: lest, when a short vowel alone is the augment (*āgama*), there be an exclusion by the rule *halādiśeṣa* due to the non-inclusion of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) within the *tuK* augment. If...

If even a part belonging to a part were to become a part of the whole as prescribed by this sūtra, then, when a short vowel is the augment *tuk*, that [short vowel] would also be included by the mention of "repetition" (*abhyāsa*) as a part of that [augment];
consequently, it would have to be eliminated by the rule of "remainder after consonants" (*halādiśeṣa*). Therefore, the letter *ca* [is used].

The purpose of drawing in the short vowel [by the previous rule] would be rendered fruitless. Therefore, this very *tuṅ* (the augment *t*) is not a constituent part (*avayava*) of the whole (*samudāya*), whereas another [part] certainly is. And this is logical;
for instance, the hand, which is a constituent part of the arm, is indeed also a constituent part of Devadatta; otherwise, it would not be so.

The usage "hastāvan devadattaḥ" would not be possible. Regarding rule 6.1.74, *āṅmāṅośca*: here, the letter *ā* is marked with the mute indicator *ṅ*; he explains that this [letter] occurs in the sense of "slight" (*iṣat*) and so forth—[referring to the form] *āṅ*. [Note: The manuscript reading *aṅḥ* appears to be a corruption of *āṅ*.]

*Kāśikā*, *Padamañjarī*, *caṭ*, and so forth. The word *mā* also ends in a *ṅt* (ṅit), and since it also functions in the sense of prohibition, he says: "And [the rule applies] after *māṅ*, which expresses prohibition. Examples include "he covers" (*ācchādayati*), etc. The root is *cchad* (meaning "to cover" or "to conceal") [Dhātupāṭha 1935].

The root *caur-*, etc. [is used here]. In this context, since the action of covering (*chādana*) is qualified by the prefix *āṅ*, it occurs in connection with that action. Regarding the phrase "of the covering" (*ācchāyāyāḥ*): the prefix *āṅ* is used in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*). The meaning is "having turned around the limit of the covering. Furthermore, the prefix *āṅ* is used in the sense of a limit according to Pāṇini 1.4.89.

In connection with a term bearing the designation *karmapravacanīya*, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is employed according to Pāṇini 2.3.10: *pañcamy apāṅparibhiḥ*. Regarding the expression *ācchāyam*: the meaning is "extending as far as the shadow. This is an *avyayībhāva* compound formed with an indeclinable ending in the ablative case, according to Pāṇini 2.1.13: *āṅ maryādābhividhyoḥ*.

By the rule *ṭhnāvyayībhāvādato'mtvapañcamyāḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.83), there is elision of the case-ending (*vibhakti-luk*) and the substitution of *am*. In the example *mā chidat*, the substitution of *aṅ* for *cli* occurs because the root has the indicatory letter *iṭ*. In the examples *ācchāyā* and *ācchāyā*, the vowel *ā* here functions as a mnemonic marker (*smaraṇa*), and in that context, it possesses the indicatory property of *ṅ*.

It does not exist; for there is the statement: "The [augment] *ṭh* occurs between the word and the recollection. Therefore, in this case, the option provided by Pāṇini 6.1.76, "optionally after a word-final [visarga]," applies.
[The example is] "pramācchandaḥ. [The root] *māṅ* in the sense of "measuring" (DhP 1142) is preceded by *pra*.

The suffix *aṅ* is applied by the rule *sthā-ā-taś-ca-upasarge* (Pāṇini 3.3.106), and in the feminine gender, *ṭāp* is added by the rule *ajādyataṣṭāp* (4.1.4). Now, one might object: "Since this [form] is derived from a technical definition (*lākṣaṇika*), the [suffix] will not apply here. This is not so;
