for there is the metarule: "In the case of the mention of *gam*, *āda*, and others, there is no distinction [between primary and derivative forms]" (*gāmādāgrahaṇeṣv aviśeṣaḥ*).
75. *dīrghāt* | (Pāṇini 6.1.75) Regarding the mention of both [the ablative and locative], "the mention of the ablative is stronger" (Śākaṭāyana Paribhāṣā 97).
Thus, when the ablative *dīrghāt* is interpreted as a genitive in relation to the locative *che* (which is the seventh case), [the rule applies].

One might have the misconception that, by the rule *tasmādityutarasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.67), the augment *tuk* applies specifically to the letter *cch*; therefore, in order to dispel this, he says: "When the letter *cch* follows a long vowel, [the augment applies] to the preceding [element]," and so forth. Thus...

He thinks: "In the rule *tasmādityutarasya* (1.1.67), a *yogavibhāga* (separation of the rule) must be made for the word *tasmāt*; the term *pūrvasya* is carried over from the preceding sūtra. Therefore, even though there is a mention of the ablative case (*pañcamīnirdeśa*) in rules such as *dīrghāt*, the operation applies only to what precedes, not to what follows. Not so.

And there is no over-extension [of the rule], because the desired result is established through the division of the *yoga* (sūtra-split). Regarding "hrīcchati": the root is *hrīcch* in the sense of "shame" (*lajjā*) (DhP 210). Regarding "mleccchati": the root is *mleccch* in the sense of "indistinct speech" (*avyaktāyāṃ vāci*) (DhP 1662).
Regarding "apacācchāyate": the root is *chāe* in the sense of "cutting" (*chedane*) (DhP 1146).
The substitution of ātva [for the vowel i] occurs by Pāṇini 6.1.45 (*ṭhādeca upadeśe’śiti*), and the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable occurs by Pāṇini 7.4.83 (*dīrgho’kitaḥ*).
76. *padāntādvā* (6.1.76).
[The example] "ṭhkuṭīchāyā" (the shadow of a hut) is either a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) or a non-compound (*asamāsa*).
Regarding "ṭhdiśvajanādīnām" and so forth: in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), for words such as "viśvajana" and the like...
The meaning is that one should explain this form of the sense as "it becomes optional with respect to the object. In this regard, the explanation is as follows:

it has already been established previously [in the *Puṣpavṛtti*] that "all rules are optional in the Veda" (*sarve vidhayaś chandasi vikalpyante*). Therefore, for words such as *viśvajana*, there is an option in the Veda.
It becomes light.

77. *iko yaṇ aci* (6.1.77). Regarding the statement "the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs for *ik*," it should be understood that because there is an equality between the *iks* and the *yaṇ*s, the correspondence proceeds according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*). And where there is a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇa-ac*), in that case—

By the force of the rule for lengthening (dīrghavidhāna), it is understood that the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs before a non-homogeneous vowel (*asavarṇe'ci*). Why [is the word] *ika* mentioned? In the case of *vāgatre*, since the form is already established by the rule for gutturalization (*kutva*), the substitution of *yaṇ* should not occur.
Why [is the word] *aci* mentioned? [Consider the example: *dadhi karoti*.
Regarding the phrase "of that which is preceded by a *pluta*": that which has a *pluta* vowel preceding it is called *plutapūrva*.

It is to be stated—that is, it is to be explained. Here is the explanation: in the rule "iko yaṇ aci," two rules are recited simultaneously (*tantra*); therein, one is for the purpose of the *yaṇ* substitution, while the other pertains to the *ik* vowels themselves.
"It will serve to supersede the *savarṇadīrgha* [vowel lengthening] for that which has already undergone *pluta*. Now,
when *bhoḥ* + *idam* becomes *bho-aidam*, the *pluta* of the word *bhoḥ* is applied in the sense of calling from a distance by the rule "guroranṛto 'nantyasyāpy ekaikasya prācām" (Pāṇini 8.2.86).
Then, when the rule for lengthening by homogeneity (savarṇadīrghatva) would have applied, the substitution of the semi-vowel (yaṇādeśa) takes its place.

78. *eco'yavāyāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.78). [Examples: *kayete*, *yayete*. When *ke-a-ete* and *ye-a-ete* are situated, the substitution of *ay* occurs. [Example: *vāyāvavaruṇaddhi*. When *vāyau-a-avaruṇaddhi* is situated, the substitution of *āv* occurs.

79. *vānto yi pratyaye* (6.1.79). The term *yī* here is a reference to the phoneme *y*; by the rule *yasmin vidhis tadādāvalgrahaṇe* (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 127), it is understood that the grammatical operation applies when the suffix begins with the letter *y*. Therefore—

He says: "In a suffix beginning with *hy-*. Although no substitute (*sthānin*) is explicitly mentioned here, it should nevertheless be understood that the substitution of *āv* occurs in place of *o*, and the substitution of *āv* occurs in place of *au*. How so? For in the preceding rule, that which possesses the properties of *vānta*— [The text continues: —is [the substitute]. Therefore, by the principle of "that which is most similar" (*sannikṛṣṭatama*), it is established that *āv* replaces *o* and *au*. Furthermore, since the term *vānta* is used in the masculine, it is understood that the substitutes *vānta* are themselves masculine. This is because the gender of a substitute follows the gender of the original base (*prakṛti*). Moreover, the mention of *vānta* is for the purpose of indicating the specific form; otherwise, one might have expected the rule to apply to all vowels (*ac*) simply because they are included within the category of *vānta*. Thus, the mention of *vānta* serves to restrict the application to these specific forms. Consequently, the rule does not apply to cases such as *dadhi atra* or *madhu atra*, where the final vowel is elided by *lopa*. Nor does it apply to *dadhyatra* or *madhvatra*, where the substitution of *y* and *v* has already occurred. As for the mention of *hy-*, it is intended to exclude other suffixes; thus, it does not apply to forms like *gavyati* or *nāvyati*, where the suffix is *yat*. However, in the case of *gavyūti*, the substitution of *ū* for *au* does occur because it is taught as a distinct word (*nipātana*). As for the mention of *pratyaye*, it is intended to exclude cases where the suffix is absent; thus, it does not apply to *goḥ* or *nauḥ*. The mention of *vāntaḥ* is intended to exclude other elements; thus, it does not apply to forms like *gobhiḥ* or *nobhiḥ*. The mention of *saṃhitāyām* (in saṃhitā) is intended to exclude cases where there is no *saṃhitā*; thus, it does not apply to forms like *goḥ* or *noḥ*. The mention of *bhāṣāyām* (in the common language) is intended to exclude Vedic usage; thus, it does not apply to forms like *gaviṣṭhiraḥ* or *naviṣṭhiraḥ*. The mention of *sarvanāmasthāne* (in a sarvanāmasthāna suffix) is intended to exclude other suffixes; thus, it does not apply to forms like *gauḥ* or *nauḥ*. The substitution (ādeśa) has been observed [in the previous rule]; here too, it follows with its own properties (taddharma). And what was seen as having those properties in the previous application? The status of being a substituendum (sthānitva) for the vowel *au* in the case of the substitute *ava*, and likewise the status of being a substituendum for the vowel *au* in the case of the substitute *āva*. Therefore, here too, the substitute *vānta* (the sequence *va-ānta*) continues to apply without abandoning its own properties.

The original base (*sthānin*) is understood to be the same as before, namely *bābhravyaḥ*. From the word *babhru*, in the sense of a descendant (*apatya*), the suffix *yañ* is applied by the rule *madhubabhvror brāhmaṇakauśikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.106), and the *guṇa* substitution is applied by the rule *orguṇaḥ* (6.4.146). Similarly, *māṇḍavyaḥ* is derived from *maṇḍu* by the rule *gargādibhyo yañ* (4.1.105).

Thus, *yañ*: from the word *śaṅku*, [the form] *śāṅkavyam* is derived by [the rule] *tasmai guṇaḥ*. From [the word] *māṇḍavya*, [the form] *māṇḍavyaḥ* is derived by [the rule] *gargādibhyo yañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.105). [The form] *śāṅkavyam* is derived from the word *śaṅku* by [the rule] *tasmai hitam* (Pāṇini 5.1.5).

In *ṭhugavādibhyo yat* (Pāṇini 5.1.2), the suffix *yat* is applied. In *nāvyaḥ*, the suffix *yat* is applied according to *nauvayodharmaviṣa-* (Pāṇini 4.4.91) et cetera, in the sense of "crossed by boat. In *raiyati*, the suffix *kyac* is applied according to *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8). [The word] *goyānam*.
Thus [ends the discussion]. This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

Regarding the rule "goryūto chandasi" and so forth, the meaning of the word *vaktavya* should be understood as "that which is to be explained. In this regard, the following is the explanation: there is a separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*) in the rule "vānto yi."
By this [sūtra], in the Vedic domain (*chāndasa*), when the word *go* is followed by *yūti*, the substitution of *ava* occurs.
This is based on the rule "ṭhadhvaparimāṇe ca. The phrase "gauryūtau" is understood to carry over there as well. In that case too—

The meaning of the word *vaktavya* is that very same thing; its explanation is also that very same thing. And this is a general statement; therefore, it applies to the measurement of distance in common speech (*bhāṣā*).
80. *Dhātoḥ tannimittasya eva* (Pāṇini 6.1.80).

Since this was already established by the preceding rule, this statement is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*). Regarding the term *tannimittasya*: the word *tat* refers back to the suffix beginning with *ya*; that which has that as its cause is thus described.

In the case of *avaśyalāvyam*, the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *aco yat* (Pāṇini 3.1.97). Relying on that very *v* sound, the substitution of *o* for the vowel [of the root] is prescribed by the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ* (7.3.84), and thus it becomes caused by that [suffix]. In the case of *avaśyalāvyam*, [the substitution of *o* occurs] by the rule *orāvaśyake*.

By [Pāṇini 3.1.125], the suffix *ṇyat* is applied; by [Pāṇini 2.1.72], *mayūravyaṃsakādayaś ca*, a compound is formed; and by [Kāśikā 6.1.144], *lumped avaśyamaḥ kṛtye*, the letter *m* is elided. Here too, depending on the suffix *ṇyat*, that which is prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.2.115], *aco ñṇiti*, [is applied].
The suffix *āṬ* is caused by that [vowel lengthening].

[The rule] "lest there be a restriction for the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)" is stated because, if the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) were absent, there would be a restriction even for the nominal stem. But surely, there would be a restriction for the nominal stem as well?
The meaning would be that this [suffix] occurs only when there is a cause (nimitta), and not when there is no cause;

and if that were so, the commencement of the preceding sūtra would be purposeless because it would lack a scope of application. This is not a fault; for he who asks "Why [is it said] 'of the root'? intends the commencement of the previous rule.

He does not desire it to be separate at all. For he thinks thus: "The rule *vānto yi pratyaye* (P. 6.1.79) should be formulated as a single sūtra, namely: 'of that [element] alone which is caused by the suffix *yi*. What is the fault in that?
If, when there is a restriction to nominal stems (*prātipadika*), some fault should arise, then for the sake of removing that [fault]..."

The intention is that the inclusion of the term *dhātu* (root) is for the sake of elegance. [One might object: "In the case of *bābhravya*, [the substitution] would apply only there," because that is caused by that [suffix]; "but here it would not apply—in *gavyam* and *nāvyam*," because the *ec* vowels [in these cases] are not caused by that.

Regarding the form *uṣyate*: when the substitution of *eC* for the root *veñ* has been applied, the suffix *laṭ* follows the prefix *upa-*. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used by the rule "bhāvakarmaṇoḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.13).

The suffix *yak* is added by the rule "sārvadhātuke yak" (3.1.67). Because the root belongs to the *yajādi* class, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*). Then, by the rule "akṛtsārvadhātukayordīrghaḥ" (7.4.25), the long vowel is substituted.

Thus, [the vowel] is long; by the rule "upadhāyāśca" (6.4.7), there is lengthening together with the prefix *upa*; then, by "vṛddhireci" (6.1.87), there is *vṛddhi* [of *u* and *a*] to form *o*. By "āṬtaḥ" (6.4.71), the augment *āṬ* is added. For that same root, the *laṅ* [suffixes] are applied, with the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) and so forth as before;
then, by "āḍajādīnām" (6.4.72), the augment *aṭ* is added, and by "āṭaśca" (6.1.90), there is *vṛddhi*. This is the vowel *au*, and the preceding *o* [is also formed].

Both of these [substitutions] are occasioned by that [external cause]; the mention of "being occasioned by that" is for the purpose of ensuring that this [undesired result] does not occur. Now, one might object: the substitution of *yaṇ* is internal (*antaraṅga*) because it depends solely on the phonemes, whereas the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is external (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends on both members of the compound.

And then, since [the rule] "that which is external is as if non-existent with respect to that which is internal" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 42) applies, will this not simply not occur here because of its being as if non-existent? If that is so, then this [fact] indicates that this paribhāṣā does not apply here.
Therefore, in the case of *akṣadyūḥ*, even though the substitution of *ūṭh* is external, it [occurs] prior to the internal substitution of *yaṇ*.
It is not considered *asiddha* with respect to what is to be performed. Otherwise, if this meaning were not conveyed,

then when the suffix *kvip* is applied in the case of *akṣair dīvyati*, and the substitution of *ūṭh* is made by the rule *ṭh-ch-avoḥ śūḍ-anunāsike ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.19), the *yaṇ* substitution would not take place because that [substitution] would be *asiddha*.
Regarding the form *lāvyamāni*: in the sense of "the future of that which is being reaped" (*lūyamānasya āyatya*), the suffix *iñ* is applied by *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95).
There is then *vṛddhi* substitution by *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ* (7.2.117); and this [vṛddhi] is caused by the *taddhita* suffix, not by the suffix beginning with *yakāra*.

With the intention that "once [the rule] is established, a prescription being commenced will serve the purpose of restriction even without the particle *eva*," he asks: "What is the purpose of the particle *eva*?
The particle *eva* is employed for the sake of restriction according to what is desired.

Showing this, he says: "The restriction of the verbal root (*dhātvavadhāraṇam*)," and so forth. When the particle *eva* is uttered immediately after a word that serves as its cause, the restriction applies to something other than that which is the cause of the *eva*, and thus there is a restriction of the verbal root. This being the case... [asati]... [is not].

If the particle *eva* were used for the sake of restriction [of the cause], then the restriction of the cause as being "only that which is caused by it" would also be understood, which is undesired. Therefore, the purpose of employing the particle *eva* is so that there may be a restriction of the verbal root (*dhātu*), and not a restriction of the cause. Why?
Furthermore, when there is a restriction to verbal roots (dhātu), the desired form is established; for what reason is that so desired?

To this he says: "For its cause... and so forth. For when there is a restriction to verbal roots, because its cause is not restricted, [the suffix] occurs after a non-root as well—such as *bābhravya*—and also after a root.

It occurs as "lavyam" (to be reaped) and "avaśyalāvyam" (necessarily to be reaped). If the restriction were made based on that [the suffix], then it would apply only to a root that possesses that [suffix]; consequently, in the case of "bābhravya," it would not occur, for the word "babhru" is not a verbal root. Therefore, the restriction is intended to be upon the verbal root itself.

81. *kṣayya-jayyau* in the sense of "possible. (Pāṇini 6.1.81). This refers to the roots *kṣi* and *ji*. By the mention of *kṣi*, both *kṣi* in the sense of "destruction" (DhP 236) and *kṣi* in the sense of "dwelling and going" (DhP 1407)—as well as *kṣiṣ* [and *kṣīṣ*]—are included.

In the case of *hiṃsāyām*—this refers to the root *hiṃs* in the Dhātupāṭha; and in the case of *kṣi hiṃsāyām* (Dhātupāṭha 1276), this refers to the inclusion of those [roots] ending with "in the sense of injury" (Dhātupāṭha 1506). However, in the case of *jigraṇe*, it refers to *ji jaye* (Dhātupāṭha 561).
But surely, according to the rule "when a root without an anubandha is mentioned, one without an anubandha is not [included] if there is one with an anubandha"?

(Commentary on Vyāḍipañjikā 53) By this paribhāṣā, would not the inclusion of the root *kṣiṣ* in the sense of "injury" fail to occur? This is not a fault, for it will be established by means of a nipātana (an irregularity). For what indeed cannot be obtained through a nipātana? Just as there may be some other grammatical operation not indicated by the rules, so too [this case] will be established.

The same would apply here as well. The inclusion of the word "artha" (object) is intended to ensure that [the suffix] occurs when there is an object; otherwise, since the root *śak* (to be able) is intransitive (*akarmaka*), it would be understood as a derivation in the sense of a state (*bhāve*)—as in "it is possible for Devadatta"—and not in the sense of an object, such as "the disease is curable. It would not occur in the sense of an object, as in "the disease is curable. Nor [would it occur]...

The *kṛtya* suffixes are applicable after intransitive roots in the sense of the object (*karman*). However, by the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*), the meaning of the *kṛtya* suffixes is indicated. Since the *kṛtya* suffixes are also prescribed for the object, it is understood that [the rule] applies there as well by virtue of this technical designation (*nipātana*).
82. *krayya* [is used] in the sense of "for sale" (*tadarthe*).

(Pāṇini 6.1.82). Regarding the form *krayya*, the meaning of the suffix here is the object (*karman*), because the kṛtya suffixes are prescribed in the sense of the object. And the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is exchange (*vinimaya*).

Because the root *krī* has the meaning of "exchange," in that context the meaning of the suffix is primary, according to the principle that "the base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together.
However, the meaning of the base is subordinate, as it serves as a qualifier for the meaning of the suffix. In that case, if...

If, because of its predominance, the word *tad* were to refer back to the object (*artha*), then the meaning would be this: "that object which belongs to a word is its *tadartha*; when that [object] is the denoted meaning, this word *krayya* is prescribed as a *nipātana*.
But this is incorrect; for in this case, there is no [predominance] of the word *krayya*.

There is no word denoting "something to be bought" (*krayya*) that could serve as its referent, because such a thing is not perceived. Now, if it were understood thus—that the very object [of the action] is its referent—even so, the inclusion of the term *tadartha* ("having that as its purpose") would be redundant.
For necessarily, in the word *krayya*, which ends in the suffix *yat*, [it must refer to] the meaning of that suffix.

Therefore, when that word (tad) refers to the primary meaning, the inclusion of its object (artha) would be redundant. Consequently, considering that even the subordinate sense of the base (prakṛti) is indicated, he says:
"When that which is for its purpose—that is, for the purpose of purchase—is to be expressed. This [is] for that.

For that purpose: by the phrase "for the sake of purchase" (krayārtham), he shows that the meaning of the root *krī* ("to buy") is indicated by the word *tat*. "Purchase" (*krayaṇa*) means buying; the meaning is "the restriction [of the object]. In the compound *krayārtham*, it is indeed a dative-tatpuruṣa compound—namely, "this is for the sake of purchase" (*krayāya idam*). [As stated: "that which is spread out for the sake of purchase."
Thus [it is said]. The meaning is: that which has been put forward for the purpose of exchange.

“Our grain is to be bought” (kreyaṃ no dhānyam) means it is to be purchased (kretavyam), taken hold of (grahītavyam), or accepted as one’s own (svīkartavyam). “And there is nothing to be bought” (na cāsti kreyaṃ) means and there is nothing here...
The meaning is that there is grain presented for sale.
83. *bhayya-pravayye ca chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.83). Regarding the rule "of this [root] *vī*": it refers to that *vī* which is recited in the list [beginning with] "motion, procreation," and so forth.

Regarding the rule *ṭhajervyaghañapoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.56), there is an optional substitution of *vī* for the *ji* of the root *aj*. [The Vārttika] states: *hradayyā āpa upasaṃkhyānam* ("the addition of *hradayyā āpaḥ* must be made"). The word *upasaṃkhyāna* means "explanation" or "formulation. The meaning is that an explanatory rule (*pratipādana*) must be provided for the form *hradayyā*. In this regard, the following...
Regarding the demonstration: the particle *ca* (and) is used here, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned;
by means of it, the form *hradayyāḥ* will also occur.
84. *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* (6.1.84).

Now, for what purpose is the mention of "the preceding and the following" (*pūrvapara*), given that in rules such as *ād guṇaḥ* (6.1.87), this ablative case (*pañcamī*)—namely, *āt*—is intended to function as a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in relation to the locative case (*saptamī*) *aci*?
It will effect [the change] "of that which follows"; for there is the rule: "tasmād ity uttarasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.67).
Likewise, this locative case "aci" will effect the status of a genitive for this ablative case;
for there is the rule: "tasminn iti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.66).
In that case, would the substitution not occur for both the preceding and the following elements even without the mention of "preceding and following"?

To this he says: "The mention of 'preceding and following'," and so forth. But what is the reason that, in the absence of the mention of "preceding and following," the simultaneous substitution for both is not established? To this [he replies]:

He says: "For [the rule] *ekasyaiva hi*," and so forth. He thinks as follows: this locative (*saptamī*) is already fulfilled in its purpose by the rules for the substitution of *yaṇ* and the like; however, this ablative (*pañcamī*) is not fulfilled anywhere else. Therefore, it should be construed as a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in place of the locative. In that case, if [the genitive] were absent...

If only the preceding and following sounds were taken [as the locus], then the *guṇa* substitution would apply only in the place of a vowel (*ac*). Furthermore, in the rule "vṛddhir eci" (Pāṇini 6.1.88), since the ablative case in "āt" is already fulfilled by its function as a condition for the prescription of *vṛddhi*, that same word would have to be interpreted as a genitive case—despite not being so intended—in order to connect with "eci. And in that case, the *vṛddhi* substitution would result only for the vowel *a*.

In the rule *upasargād ṛti dhātau* (Pāṇini 6.1.91), since both the ablative and the locative case endings remain unfulfilled [in their respective requirements], they mutually imply a genitive relationship by way of alternation; thus, the *vṛddhi* substitution would occur only by way of alternation. As for that which...

[The opponent might argue: "The fifth case-ending will be treated as the sixth for the seventh, and the seventh as the fifth for the fifth; thus, even without explicitly mentioning both 'parvan' and 'para', the substitution will occur for both. To refute this, he says: "Not both," and so forth. For [the suffixes] possess the nature of cessation (*nivṛtti-dharma*).

It becomes the locus; moreover, it serves as the cause for the conceptualization of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) regarding that which is being heard. How could the preceding and following [sounds] be set aside, and yet simultaneously attain the status of being the cause for the conceptualization of the genitive case? Precisely because they are not set aside, they possess the status of being the cause.
And because it is impossible, both the seventh and fifth case endings cannot be applied simultaneously.
Therefore, it must belong to one [element] alone, not to both.
Now, what is the purpose of the mention of "one" (eka), given that [in the rule] *bhrasjo ropadhayo...*?
In the rule *ramanyatarasyām* (6.4.47), even without the mention of the word *eka*, only one [augment] is possible;
nevertheless, he says "one" (*ekam*) and so forth, meaning that even without the mention of *eka* here, only one will occur.
For, by means of the augment *ram*, because it is marked with *m*, [it is placed] after the final vowel according to *midacontyātparaḥ* (1.1.47).

It must be something else; however, there is no possibility for a substitute (*bhṛjja*) to occur after the final letter of the two *ram*s. Therefore, it is logical that even without the mention of "one" (*eka*), the substitution of the *guṇa* and other elements occurs such that only one *ram* remains. And this is possible when there is a difference in the substituends (*sthānin*).

The qualities (guṇa) and so forth of the substituends are separate substitutes; in that case, if the word "one" (eka) were not mentioned, there would be separate substitutes. Therefore, the mention of "one" is for the purpose that there may not be separate substitutes for two substituends, namely the preceding and the following. However, if the mention of "one" were absent, both [the substitute and the original] would be two.
In order to establish this point with logical reasoning, he says: "Because of the difference in the substituends" (*sthānibhedāt*), and so forth.

For instance, according to the rule *radābhyāṃ niṣṭhāto naḥ pūrvasya ca daḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.42), because of the difference in the substituends (*sthānin*), two distinct substitutes occur in forms such as *bhinnam* and *cchinnam*.
Likewise, in cases such as *khaṭvendra* and so forth, there would also be two substitutes.

85. *antādivacca* (6.1.85). Since it is stated "as if [the preceding] were the end and [the following] were the beginning," it is not known what the meaning of this extended application (*atideśa*) is; therefore, in order to understand that, he says "just as" (*yathā*), etc. "This is the meaning of the extended application."

Thus [it is said]. The word *iti* refers back to what has preceded. An *atideśa* (extension) is that by which something is extended; furthermore, the meaning of this aforementioned extension is precisely this rule: "and like the final vowel" (*ṭhantadivacca*). This is the sense.
"In a rule based on a specific phoneme (*varṇa*), this treatment as being either the end or the beginning (*antādivadbhāva*) is not desired. How is this known?

He says: "For instance," and so forth. The rule *obhisa ais* (Pāṇini 7.1.9) is a rule based on the phoneme *a*; in its application, in the case of *khaṭvābhiḥ*, the long vowel by homogeneous combination (*savarṇadīrghatva*) [is required].

The preceding [rule] does not apply here, as it is like *anata*. This rule, "āta au ṇalaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.34), is dependent on the phoneme *ā*. When that [application] is to be performed—being dependent on a phoneme—in the case of *juhāva*, where the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) of the root *hvayati* has already been effected by the rule "abhyastasya ca" (Pāṇini 6.1.33), [the present rule would otherwise apply].

The *ākāra* (the long vowel 'ā') possesses the status of being a prior form (*pūrvarūpatva*), just as in the case of *tad* and so forth. The rule "eṅaḥ padāntādati" (Pāṇini 6.1.109), which prescribes a single substitute for *eṅ* followed by *at*, depends upon the phonemes *eṅ*. In that context, when an operation is to be performed—as in the example *asyai aśvaḥ*—the *vṛddhi* substitution prescribed by "āṭaśca" (6.1.90) does not behave as if it were the initial element of the subsequent word. Due to the absence of that [initial status], the *āy* replacement occurs, and then there is elision (*lopa*).
In the case of *śākalyasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.19), there is the elision of the letter *y*.

Why, then, should it be stated that "in matters depending on individual phonemes, [the preceding and following parts] do not behave as if they were the end or the beginning"? It need not be stated. Why?
Because what is extended here is not identity (*tādrūpya*). These [operations] depend on the form itself.
The object [of the rule] is that, because they do not possess that same form (*atādrūpyāt*), they will not occur.

But for what purpose is this treatment as if being the beginning or end (*antādivadbhāva*) prescribed, since the preceding and following elements have already been stated to be the substituends (*sthānin*) of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*); [for in that case], by the very principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, [the desired result would follow]?

"Will the effect have that [original] as its locus? To this he says: "The preceding and following aggregate is the substitute (*sthānin*) of the single substitution. How is this known? To this he says: "For that... and so forth. For that which is replaced by a substitute is the *sthānin* of that substitute; for example: *asterbhūḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.52).

Thus [it is said]. Here, the root *bhū* is the element *as*, and since the entire complex is here produced by means of a single substitution (*ekādeśa*), that [complex] alone is its substituend (*sthānin*), not the two constituent parts, the preceding and the following. This might be argued:
because a part is internal to the whole, the whole [is the substituend] by means of the substitution.

When the whole is being replaced, its parts are also replaced; therefore, do those two [the parts] also possess the status of being substituenda (*sthānitva*)? To this, he says: "In that case," and so forth. Both instances of the particle *iti* indicate a reason.
In that context, when the whole is the substituendum, the status of being a substituendum belonging to the two parts is inferential (*ānumānika*).

When a whole (samudāya) is being replaced by a substitute (ādeśa), the replacement of its two constituent parts is necessarily concomitant; for it is not possible to replace the whole without replacing its parts, since the whole is of the nature of those parts. However, as for the whole...

The status of being a substitute (*sthānitva*) is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). This is because the genitive case ending denoting "place" (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), as in the rule *pūrvaparayoḥ*, is heard directly; and according to the principle that "between a directly stated [connection] and one inferred, the directly stated connection is more authoritative" (*śrutānumitayoḥ śrautaḥ saṃbandho garīyān*), by the rule *sthānivad ādeśo 'nalvidhau* (P. 1.1.56), for that which...

Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) refers to what is heard explicitly; it is only with respect to that which serves as the locus (*sthānitva*) that an operation is prescribed for the substitute (*ādeśa*). Furthermore, the status of being the locus for the two constituent parts is inferential and not directly perceived; therefore, an operation based upon that [inferential locus] is not extended by analogy. Consequently, an operation based upon that...

On account of the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original), this [operation] would not apply to the substitute; yet it is desired. For that purpose, this treatment as if ending in *-an* (*antavadbhāva*) is prescribed.

86. *ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ* | (6.1.86) Here, by the statement "it is as if unestablished" (*asiddhavacanena*), is the non-existence of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) being effected, or is its functional capacity for that specific operation being indicated? For even a thing that is established may have its effects rendered as if unestablished.
It is called "unestablished" (asiddha) because of the incapacity to perform [the operation], just as one who is incapable of performing the duties of a son is called "sonless" despite being a son.
In that case, if the absence of the single-substitute (ekādeśa) were effected by this [rule], then in the word *adhītya*, the *tug* augment would not occur; however, it does.

In this case, the short vowel does not exist, because it has been replaced by a single substitute (ekādeśa). Nor does the short vowel reappear once the substitute has been removed by the rule of *asiddha*; for when the killer of Devadatta is slain, Devadatta does not come back to life. Thus says the Mādhya.

Showing that, having observed a fault in this alternative view, the capacity for the grammatical operation is indicated by the scriptural statement regarding the *asiddhatva* (non-validity) of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*), he says: "The meaning is that it does not perform an operation that has already been established.
This means that even though the single-substitute is established—that is, accomplished—the operation which belongs to what is already established/accomplished is not performed by it.

"It performs [the action]"—this is the meaning of this statement. By the words "The statement regarding what is not yet established," etc., he explains the purpose of the sūtra. And when a substitution has been made, whatever grammatical operation occurs on account of that [substitution] is characterized by that substitution; for it is considered that the substitution is its characteristic (lakṣaṇa), that is, its cause (nimitta). Of that...

The statement "unestablished" (*asiddha*) is for the purpose that there may be a prohibition. That which is emitted or set aside is an *utsarga*; the original element (*sthānin*) is denoted by this term. That which has an *utsarga* as its defining characteristic is called *utsargalakṣaṇa*; the state of being such is [the condition].
The term *asiddha* is stated for the purpose of [showing] that "it might be so," as in the example *ko'sicat*. In *ko'sicat*, there is the suffix *cli* after the root *sic* in the *luṅ* tense;

by *lipisicihvaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.53), *cli* is replaced by *aṅ*; the *s* following the word *kim* undergoes *rutva* (becoming *r*); and by *ato roraplutādaplute* (Pāṇini 6.1.113), *utva* (the substitution of *u*) occurs.
The *guṇa* substitution occurs by *ṭhādguṇaḥ* (6.1.87); then, by *ṭheṅḥ padāntādati* (6.1.109), there is the substitution of the subsequent vowel (*parapūrvatva*).

Regarding the statement "because [the substitute] is treated like the beginning with respect to what follows," and so forth: in the case of *asicat*, the single substitute for the *e* and *a* is, by *ṭhantādivacca* (6.1.85), treated like the end of the preceding element and the beginning of the following one with respect to that which follows the *a*.

By this [rule], the treatment as being "like the beginning" (*ādivadbhāva*) is established; and this is the reason for not being at the beginning of a word (*apadāditva*). [The objection is: "Because it is *asiddha*, [the rule] does not apply.

For if it were *asiddha*, the letter *s* would indeed be at the very beginning of the word, and consequently, by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.109), there would be a prohibition against the substitution of *ṣ*. [Example: *ko’sya*.
This is the genitive singular of *idam*. By the rule *tyadādīnām aḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.102), there is substitution of *a*;
by *tāṅsiṅsāminātsyāḥ* (7.1.12), it takes the form *syā*; and by *hali lopaḥ* (7.2.113), the *i* of this form is elided. The remainder is as before.

This is an example of the prohibition of a rule that would otherwise apply by its general definition. However, as for the existence of a rule by its general definition, we have the examples *adhītya* and *pretya*. Now, one might object: the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is "external" (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends upon two words;
whereas the rules for *ṣatva* and *tuṅ* are "internal" (*antaraṅga*) because they depend upon a single word. In such a case, [the former] is considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*).

[Objection: "Since the status of being *asiddha* will be established here by the very paribhāṣā, 'That which is external is [regarded as] internal with respect to that which is internal' (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 42), this statement is useless. [Response: If that is the case, then that very paribhāṣā is restricted (*niyamyate*) in this section to the rules concerning *ṣatva* and *tuka*. Therefore, in the case of *akṣadyūḥ*, [the rule applies].
Even though the substitution of *ūṭ* is a rule characterized by external factors (*bahiraṅga*), it is not considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when the internal substitution of *yaṇ* is to be applied.
[This is stated in] the rule beginning with "samprasāraṇa," etc.; [it applies] when there is a *samprasāraṇa*, the feminine suffix *ṅī*, or the augment *iṭ*.

A prohibition must be stated regarding the status of that single-substitute (ekādeśa) as being "not established" (asiddha). For example, in the form *brahmahūṣu*: [the derivation is as follows] from *brahmāṇam hvayati*, there is the suffix *kvip*; because it belongs to the *yajādi* group, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*); by the rule *samprasāraṇācca* (6.1.108), the preceding vowel takes the place of the subsequent one; and by the rule *halaḥ* (6.4.2), there is lengthening.

This is the seventh case plural (*saptamībahuvacana*). In the form *parivīṣu*, the root *veñ* preceded by *pari-* takes the suffixes beginning with *kvip* as previously described. In the expression *apacecchatram*, the suffix *śap* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.68, *kartari śap*, to the root *pac* in the *laṅ* tense, third person singular, with the augment *iṭ*.
By the rule "śapaḥ, ṭhādguṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.87), the guṇa substitution is applied.
87. *Ādraguṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.87). [Examples: *tavalkāraḥ*; *khaṭvalkāraḥ*. But how is there the substitution of *l* here?
To this he says: "In place of the *ḷ*-vowel," and so forth. And this [applies] to both the *ḷ*-vowel and the *ṛ*-vowel...

The designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) must be stated [as a supplement], because it is obtained through the inclusion of the pratyāhāra *ra* in the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ* (P. 1.1.51), due to the supplementary statement (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "the *savarṇa* designation must be stated. For it has been said regarding the traditional recitation of the phonemes (*akṣarasamāmnāya*):
"In the case of the phonemes beginning with *ha*, the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation; however, in the case of *la*, it is nasalized and bears the technical name *it*."
It is thus asserted. In that case, when a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated designation) is formed starting from the letter *r* up to the letter *ṇ*,
the substitution of *aṇ* prescribed for the place of the *ḷ*— which is included by the inclusion of *ṛ*— becomes followed by *l* (*lapara*).

88. *vṛddhir eci* | (6.1.88) 89. *etyedhatyūthsu* | (6.1.89) The relationship of qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualified (*viśeṣya*) occurs when there is both possibility (*sambhava*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*); and these two...

He states that these two—possibility (*sambhava*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—exist only in this very root and not elsewhere, saying: "This mention of *ej*," and so forth. Regarding the example "praṣṭhauhaḥ":

[the word *praṣṭhavāh* is derived] from the sense "one who carries the leader" (*praṣṭham vahati*), with the suffix *ṇvi* by the rules "In the Veda, after *sah*" (Pāṇini 3.2.63) and "And after *vah*" (Pāṇini 3.2.64).

By the rule *vāha ūṭh* (6.4.132), *ūṭh* is designated as a *samprasāraṇa*; by *samprasāraṇācca* (6.1.108), the preceding [vowel] takes the form of the subsequent one (*parapūrvatva*), and then there is *vṛddhi*. The connection with the subject at hand is that *vṛddhi* is prescribed as an exception (*apavāda*) to the single-substitute rule (*pararūpa*) for *eti* and *edhati* by the rule *etyedhatyosaiti* (6.1.89).

Now, why does the *vṛddhi* [substitution] not also take the place of the *pararūpa* [single-substitute] prescribed by the rule "atha ṭhomāṅeśca" (Pāṇini 6.1.95)? For this *vṛddhi* is indeed commenced when the *pararūpa* has not yet applied; thus, just as it subverts the *pararūpa* resulting from *eṅ*, it might likewise subvert the *pararūpa* resulting from *āṅ*. Consequently, even in this case—
One might ask: "Does [the suffix] *ā* come after *eti*, or does *upa* come before *eti*? To this he says: "By the rule 'omāṅośca'," and so forth. He states the reason for this very point:
"A rule that is formulated when another rule would otherwise apply necessarily sublates that other rule. When it would otherwise apply...

It is logical that this *vṛddhi* substitution becomes an exception (*bādhikā*) to that [shortening] when the single-substitute (*pirarūpa*) rule is applicable; however, this *vṛddhi* is introduced both when the single-substitute rule has already applied and when it has not yet applied.
For instance, in the cases of *āitaḥ-uetaḥ*, *pra-etaḥ-upretaḥ*, and *paretaḥ*, [the *vṛddhi* applies] even where the single-substitute rule would otherwise have applied.

This rule for *vṛddhi* is initiated both when [the condition] is met and when it is not met. For instance, in the cases *āitaḥ*, *etaḥ*, *prāitaḥ*, *upretaḥ*, and *paretaḥ*, the condition is met; however, in the case of *upāitaḥ* and *upaiti*, it is not met. Therefore, this *vṛddhi* does not sublate the substitution of *pirarūpa* (single-substitute replacement) by the rule *āṅ*. This is because "exceptions [apply] to what precedes them."
With these words, he states another resolution: "Exceptions [apavāda] that occur earlier subvert the rules immediately following them, not those further away" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 9).
This *vṛddhi* is an exception occurring earlier; and since the *pararūpa* (single-substitute form of the subsequent element) follows immediately after it, therefore that alone [is subverted].

It is superseded by that [subsequent rule], not by the form ending in *aṅ*, because that is internal. Regarding the phrase "it should be stated" (*vaktavyā*), the meaning is "it should be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows:
in the subsequent sūtra, the particle *ca* (and) is for the purpose of prescribing an additional rule.
Therefore, by virtue of the word *akṣa*, the *vṛddhi* [vowel substitution] will occur when the word *ūhinī* follows. This same principle should be stated for what follows as well;

the meaning of the word "it should be explained" (*vaktavya*) is such, and the explanation is likewise to be understood. [The compound is analyzed as: "the calculation (*ūha*) of the dice (*akṣāṇām*);
he who possesses that," with the possessive suffix *ini*. [The feminine form is derived] by the rule "from words ending in *ṛt* or *n*, the suffix *ṅīp*" (Pāṇini 4.1.5).

Regarding the suffix *ṅīp*: [the example is] *akṣauhiṇī*. Regarding the word *svairam*: the root *īr* (meaning "to go," DhP 1018) forms *īraḥ* by means of the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*);
thus, *svasya īraḥ* is *svairaḥ*. Because it functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇatvāt*), it appears as *svairam* in the commentary (*vṛtti*).

The indication is made in the neuter gender; however, some action must be supplied here [to complete the sense]. Alternatively, *svaira* refers to that family (*kula*) whose master (*īra*) is independent (*sva*); it takes the neuter gender because the word *kula*, being a member of the *kulādi* group, functions as the referent of another word (*anyapadārtha*) and thus assumes the neuter gender. [The term is] *svairī*.

[The word] *svairiṇī* [is derived from] *kāśikā*. [The suffix] *ṇini* is applied because it has the habit (*śīla*) of saying "one's own" (*svam*), according to Pāṇini 3.2.78: *supyajātau ṇinistācchīlye*. The words *ūḍha* and *ūḍhi* end in the suffixes *niṣṭhā* and *ktin*, respectively. [The word] *praiṣaḥ* [is derived from] *iṣa*...
From the roots *iṣ* meaning "to go" (*gatirahisādāneṣu*, Dhātupāṭha 1127) or *iṣ* meaning "desire" (*icchāyām*, Dhātupāṭha 1351),
when the suffix *ghañ* is applied preceded by the prefix *pra-*, the form is *praiṣaḥ*; however, when the suffix *ṇyat* is applied, the form is *praiṣyaḥ*.
Regarding "sukhārtaḥ": the compound is formed by Pāṇini 2.1.32, *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*.
90. And after *āṭ*. (6.1.90) *Āṭekṣata*: this is the *laṅ* [aorist] after the root *īkṣ* "to see" (DhP 610).
*Āṭaikṣiṣṭa*: this is the *luṅ* [aorist]. *Āṭaikṣiṣyata*: this is the *lṛṅ* [conditional]. *Āṭombhīt*: from the roots *ubh* or *umbh* "to fill."

The suffix *luṅ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.2.110] *dhā.pā.* 1319, 1320; the augment *iṭ* is added by [Pāṇini 7.3.96] *astisico 'yukte*; the elision of *sic* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.28] *īṭi*. Regarding *āṬbjīt*: the root *ubj* meaning "straightness" is found at *dhā.pā.* 1303. Regarding *ārdhnot*: the root *ṛṣ* meaning "increase" is found at *dhā.pā.* 1271.

Thus, there is the suffix *laṅ*; then the suffix *śnu* by the rule "after roots beginning with *ṭh* and *svādi*, [there is] *śnu*" (Pāṇini 3.1.73). The letter *c* is for the purpose of prescribing an additional [operation], but it is not for the purpose of carrying forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) the [term] *vṛddhi*;
the intention is that its continuation is already established by virtue of its being marked as *svarita*. It is for the purpose of prescribing an additional [operation].

In order to clarify the meaning of this through another statement, he says: "It is for the purpose of subverting the *pararūpa* [single-substitute rule] in the case of *usi*, *omi*, and *āṅ*. The meaning is that it is for the purpose of subverting that *pararūpa* which would otherwise apply to *usi*, *omi*, and *āṅ*. Indeed, by means of the particle *ca*, he indicates the prescription of double *vṛddhi*.

In that regard, the second rule serves the purpose of subverting what would otherwise subvert [the first]. Consequently, having set aside both the *pararūpa* (single-substitute form of the following vowel) that would apply by "ṭhusyapadāntāt" (P. 6.1.96) as well as that which would apply by "omāṅośca" (P. 6.1.95), only *vṛddhi* (the single substitute of the preceding and following vowels) occurs.

Regarding the forms *ṭhāṬsrīyat* and *ṭhāṬṅkārīyat*: from the words *usra* and *oṅkāra*, the suffix *kyac* is applied by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8). Then, by the rule *kyaci ca* (Pāṇini 7.4.33), the vowel *u* is changed to *i*. From the stem ending in *kyac*, the aorist (*luṅ*) suffix is added.

When the augment *āṭ* is inserted, the subsequent rule *usyapadāntāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.96)—which prescribes the substitution of the single substitute for the preceding and following sounds—would normally apply as an exception. However, [this is overridden].
Because the particle *ca* has the purpose of prescribing an additional rule, only *vṛddhi* occurs. Regarding the form *āḍhāiyat*:

from the word *oḍhā*, with the suffix *kyac* added and the *luṅ* tense applied, when the augment *āṭ* is introduced, the rule "omāṅośca" (Pāṇini 6.1.95)—which prescribes a single substitute (*pararūpa*)—would otherwise apply as an exception; however, because the particle *ca* has the purpose of prescribing an additional rule, only *vṛddhi* occurs.
It comes to be.
91. *upasargād ṛti dhātau* (Pāṇini 6.1.91).
[The example is] "upārcchati. [The root] *ṛcch* [is listed as] "ṛcch gatau, indriyapralaye, mūrtibhāve ca" (Dhātupāṭha 1296).
[The example is] "pragatā ṛcchkā asmād deśāt prarcchako deśaḥ" ("A region from which people have departed is a 'prarcchaka' region"). In this case, with respect to what—

"Prepositions (prādayaḥ) joined with a verb (kriyāyuktāḥ) are designated as 'gati' or 'upasarga' with respect to that [verb]"; thus, the word *pra* is designated as a *gati-upasarga* with respect to the root *gam*, but not with respect to the root *ṛcch*. Therefore, this serves as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇam*).

"Or rather, by the rule *ṭhvaḥ supi āpiśaleḥ*, there would be an option [to apply ṭhak]; by this, he shows that the inclusion of the letter *t* (the *tapara*) is for the sake of the subsequent rule. Now, what is the purpose of the mention of "dhātu" (root), since relative terms necessarily bring to mind their correlative?
For example, words such as *putrīyati* [are formed with the suffix *kyac*]. Since this prefix (*upasarga*) is dependent upon a verbal root (*dhātu*), it is a relative term;

therefore, by the very mention of "prefix" (*upasargagrahaṇa*), the inclusion of "verbal root" (*dhātugrahaṇa*) is already established. To this he says: "By the very mention of 'prefix'," and so forth. If the mention of "verbal root" were not made, then...

In the case of *parārcchati*, because the rule *ṛtyakaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.128) applies subsequently, there would be the treatment as if it were the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) according to the opinion of Śākalya. Therefore, the mention of the word "root" (*dhātu*) is made in order to exclude that *prakṛtibhāva* of Śākalya. But how [is this achieved]?

When the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) is made, is the prevention of the *prakṛtibhāva* (original form) of Śākalya obtained? Yes, because of the reason for the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). For when the mention of "root" exists, the rule is divided:
first, "vṛddhi occurs after a prefix [before a root]"; then, "in the case of a root."

The term "from a preposition" (*upasargāt*) carries over here. Consequently, the second rule is understood as being for the purpose of subverting that [previous] sublation. Now, just as in the rule *upasargāc chandasi dhātvarthe* (Pāṇini 5.1.118), the mention of "preposition" (*upasarga*) is understood to include [all prefixes] such as *pra* and others by way of illustration, why is it not understood in the same way here as well?

How could it be understood [otherwise]? Because it is impossible. For in the rule "upasargāc chandasi dhātvarthe" (Pāṇini 5.1.118), since the presence of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is not possible [therein], it is logical that the mention of the prefix (*upasarga*) is for the purpose of indicating *prādi* prefixes. For in this case, the presence of the verbal root is indeed possible.
It is incorrect to say that it arises.
92. *vā supyāpiśaleḥ* (6.1.92).

The term *dhātau* (in a verbal root) is understood from the previous rule, and *supi* (after a nominal suffix) is also stated; however, since there is no verbal root that ends in a nominal suffix (*subanta*), this [suffix] *sup* is here a qualifier by virtue of its semantic connection, referring to a portion of the verbal root.

It is understood; thus he says: "In a verbal root that is a constituent part of a word ending in a *su*-affix," and so forth. Regarding the form "upālkārīyati," how is it that when the term "ṛ" is mentioned, the *vṛddhi* substitution applies to the letter *lṛ*?
To this he says: "Of *ṛ* and *lṛ*," and so forth. This means that *ṛ* and *lṛ* share the designation of being homogeneous (*savarṇa*).
Since the vowel *ṛ* is prescribed [in the rule], it also includes *ḷ*; therefore, the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs there as well.
As for the mention of Āpiśali, it is for the sake of honor. Why, then, does it not serve the purpose of providing an option?

Thus he says: "The word 'or' (vā) is indeed used. Although both reverence and optionality are accomplished by the mention of the teacher alone, the intention is that the mention of the word 'or' was made specifically to indicate that reverence is the primary purpose of mentioning the teacher.

93. *āṬta am-śasoḥ* | (6.1.93) [The example] "gāṃ paśya" ("see the cow")—but how can this be cited as an example, since by the rule *goto ṇit* (7.1.90), because the suffix is marked with the augment *ṇit*, the *vṛddhi* substitution ought to occur here due to its higher priority? To this [the author replies]:

He says: "The word *dyo* also ends in *o*," and so forth. Since the use of *tapara* (the long vowel marker) is well-known in the specification of phonemes, the *tapara* designation in the rule *gotaḥ* is understood to indicate that which ends in *o*; consequently, [the suffix] follows even after the word *dyo*.

A sarvanāmasthāna [suffix] is treated as having the marker Ṇ (ṇit). If this is so, why does the vṛddhi [substitution] not occur here? To this he says: "By that," and so forth. For if the sarvanāmasthāna following the word *dyo* were not treated as ṇit, then in the case of *dyāṃ paśya*, [the rule would not apply].

In the case of *gām paśya* ("look at the cow"), this substitution of *āt* would be sublated by the rule for *vṛddhi* due to its being subsequent [in the order of the rules]. However, if it were the case that the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix following even the word *dyo-* becomes a *ṇit*, then in *dyāṃ paśya* ("look at the sky"), *vṛddhi* would indeed apply. Therefore, this substitution of *āt* occurs when *vṛddhi* has not yet taken effect.

That which is being prescribed [the substitution of *i*] sets aside the *vṛddhi* because it lacks an opportunity [to apply otherwise]. Consequently, the example "gāṃ paśya" (look at the cow) is indeed most appropriate.
Now, in this case as well, regarding "acinavam" and "asunavam," the *laṅ* suffix occurs after the roots *ci* and *su*.

Once the *guṇa* has been applied to the suffix lacking the *vikaraṇa*, why does the substitution of *ā* for the vowel *o* not occur by the rule "ṭhtasthasthamipām" (Pāṇini 3.4.101), which prescribes the replacement of *mip* with *am*? To this he says:
"In *ami*, etc. Due to its association with *śas* or because of the governing context of *sup*, this *am* is understood to refer specifically to the case-ending *sup*.

Therefore, the application of *ātva* does not arise here. However, in the case of "citraguṃ paśya," once the shortening (*hrasvatva*) has been applied, because the vowel *o* is absent, *ātva* does not occur due to the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* by the rule "na lumatāṅgasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.63).

Since this is a substitution (*ādeśa*) governed by a suffix (*pratyaya*), the rule "analvidhau" (Pāṇini 1.1.56) applies, thereby preventing the status of being a substitute (*sthānivat*). Thus, *ātva* does not take place.

94. *eṅ* is the substitute for *pirarūpa*. (Pāṇini 6.1.94) Regarding *upelayati*: the root *ila* in the sense of "impelling" (*preraṇe*) belongs to the *curādi* class; hence the suffix *ṇic*. Regarding *prokhati*:
the root *ukhi* in the sense of "motion" (*gatyartho*) is listed in the *bhvādi* class under [the roots] *ukha* and *nakha* (Dhātupāṭha 128, 134).

If they maintain that *ṭhā supi* (Pāṇini 6.1.92) is still in force, then, since this [rule] forms a single syntactical unit with that [preceding rule], the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) would be applied optionally only to a verbal root ending in a *su*-affix; however, in the case of what is not a *su*-affix (*asupi*), the subsequent form would not occur at all. To address this, he says: "And that," etc.
For this fault would occur only if there were syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*). But here there is no syntactic unity;

rather, there is a split of sentences (*vākyabheda*). Therefore, that [rule] which follows here effects an option only with respect to a nominal stem (*subanta*) and a verbal root (*dhātu*), whereas the other [rule] invariably applies the subsequent form (*pararūpa*).

In this regard, there is one sentence stating: "When a verbal root beginning with *eṅ* follows a prefix ending in an *a*-vowel, a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) occurs for both the preceding and following sounds," provided that the root is not a member of a *subanta* (inflected word). There is another sentence stating:

"When a verbal root beginning with *eṅ* follows a prefix ending in an *a*-vowel, a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) optionally occurs for both the preceding and following sounds," provided that the root is a member of a *subanta*.

The second [rule] states "bhavati. In that regard, by the first sentence, the single substitute of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is prescribed as obligatory for roots whose parts end in a *su*-affix, such as *upe-layat* and the like. By the second, however, the single substitute of the subsequent form is prescribed optionally for roots whose parts end in a *su*-affix, such as *upeṅkīyat* and the like.

It is prescribed. However, the split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) is obtained through the principle of *tantra* (simultaneous application) from the utterance of two rules [in the form of *ṭeḥ* and *pirarūpam*]. For when two rules are being uttered, even though [the rule] *ṭhvā supyāpiśaleḥ* (6.1.92) is being carried over (*anuvartamāna*), it applies only once.

It is not connected [to the preceding] because of the requirement of what is obtainable, but it is indeed connected in the second [case]. By this, the two previously mentioned sentences are established.
Regarding the phrase "it must be stated" (*vaktavyam*), the meaning is "it must be explained. In that regard, this is the explanation: in the subsequent sūtra...
The letter *ca* (in the rule) is for the purpose of adding further provisions; by it, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) will occur in cases such as *śakandhu* and others.
Regarding the word *vaktavya* used later on, its meaning and this very explanation should be understood in the same way.
[In the phrase] "except when there is a command" (*aniyoge*), *niyoga* means *niyojana*, which is to say, "the act of engaging" or "employment."

There is neither a restriction (*niyoga*) nor a non-restriction (*aniyoga*), but rather an impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*). In that very case, the *pararūpa* (subsequent form) is to be understood for the word *eva*. The word *eva* functions in the sense of non-restriction. When it expresses that very same restriction alone as unqualified by an operation (*vyāpāra*), then the *pararūpa* occurs. But when [it is qualified] by an operation...
In that case, there is specifically the augment *vṛddhi*.
For example, in "bimboṣṭhī," the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.55] "nāsikodarauṣṭha. However, the phrase "tiṣṭha devadatta, oṣṭhaṃ paśya" is a sentence and not a compound (*samāsa*).
From the word *devadatta*, there is elision of the nominative suffix *su* by the rule "ṭāṅasiṅasām inaṅ-ātṅayāṃ cātsambuddhau" (Pāṇini 7.1.12), which applies because the preceding vowel is short.

95. *omāṅeśca* (6.1.95). [The example is] *adyauḍhā*. [Another example is] *adhaudhā*. Now, one might object: since the *aṅ* [of *adhaḥ*] has been replaced by *guṇa* according to *ādguṇaḥ* (6.1.87), is this not a suitable example for *āṅ*?
There is no fault here, for the single-substitute (ekādeśa) resulting from *āṅ* and *māṅ* is included by the mention of *āṅ*. Indeed, this was already stated previously:
"When [an operation] occurs in place of two things specified in the genitive case, that [substitute] receives the designation of either one of them. For what purpose, then, is *āṅ* mentioned again?

[Objection: Is it not already established by the rule "pūrvaḥ saha" (6.1.84), followed by the lengthening of the vowel according to "akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ" (6.1.101), and then the substitution of *guṇa* according to "prādibhyaḥ" (6.2.192) and "ṭhādguṇaḥ" (6.1.87)? [Response: It is not established, because of the rule "dhātūpasargayoḥ... (Pāṇini 6.2.139).
Since it is stated that "an internal operation [takes precedence]" (Vyāḍivṛtti 37), the *guṇa* substitution prescribed by Pāṇini 6.1.87 should have occurred first;
and that being the case, a *vṛddhi* substitution would have followed. Therefore, the mention of *āṅ* must also be made [in the rule].
[The author] says: "But here, the lengthening [prescribed by] *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.101) is sublated. Regarding this...

Because the rule [for *e* and *o*] is prescribed without qualification, and because the long vowel [substitution] for *akaḥ savarṇe* is prescribed as a general rule; it has already been established that even a rule prescribed as a specific exception (viśeṣavihita) sublates a rule prescribed as a general rule (sāmānyavihita).

96. *usyapadāntāt* (6.1.96). [The example is] *bhindyauḥ*. This is derived from the root *bhid* with the suffix *liṅ*, followed by *jhi*. By the rule *jherjus* (3.4.108), *jhi* is replaced by *jus*. Then *śnam* is added, and by the rule *śnasorallopaḥ* (6.4.111), the *a* is elided. [Then follows: *liṅaḥ*...

By the rule *salopo'nantyasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.79), there is the elision of the *s* [of the suffix]. When *bhindyaus* is established, by this [rule], the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is applied. Regarding *aduḥ*: it is the *luṅ* [aorist] of the root *dā*, with the suffix *jhi*;
by *ātaḥ* (3.4.110), *jhi* is replaced by *jus*; and by *gātisthāghupābhūbhyaḥ sicaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (2.4.77), there is the elision of *sic*.

When *adāt* is established, by this [rule] there is the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpatva*). As in the examples *ko'sti* and *ko'sīt*. Now, one might object that in one of these counter-examples, by the very paribhāṣā "when there is the mention of a meaningful element, that which is meaningless is not included" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 1), [the rule would not apply].

It will be so; for the word *usrā* as a whole is meaningful, whereas the element *uḥ* is not. However, in the second case, even by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "between that which is taught by a definition and that which is taught by its own form, only that which is taught by its own form is to be taken, and not that which is taught by a definition" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 3), [the desired result] does not follow.
It will be so, for the [grammatical] definition there is such;

for when the suffix *niṣṭhā* follows the root *vas*, by the rule "the augment *iṭ* is added after *vas* and *kṣudh*" (Pāṇini 7.2.52), and the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) having been performed because it belongs to the *yaj*-class, we have *uṣita*. In that case, the single-substitute (*pararūpa*) does not occur. That is why.

What is the purpose of the phrase "not at the end of a word" (*apadāntāt*)? In that case, this superfluous mention of "not at the end of a word" indicates—without regard for distinctions such as being meaningful or meaningless—that *pararūpa* (the single substitute of the form of the subsequent vowel) occurs simply after *u*, [regardless of its position]. By this, [the following is established]:

The rule *nānarthake ṭhusyapadāntāt* does not apply here. For in the case of *bhindyauḥ*, the entire complex beginning with *yāsuṭ* is meaningful, whereas its constituent part, *us*, is not. It also applies even to forms derived through secondary derivation (*lākṣaṇika*), as in *babhuṣaḥ paśya*; [this is formed from] the root *bhā* in the sense of "shining" (DhP 1051), with the suffix *kvasu* applied after the perfect tense marker (*liṭ*).
By the rule *śas-ṭhvasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam* (6.4.131), there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*);

by *saṃprasāraṇācca* (6.1.108), there is the substitution of the single preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*). When the state *babhā-us-as* has been reached, this [rule] effects the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*). This is an example under the view that [the suffix] is *sārvadhātuka*.

This should be understood: for in the case of the *ardhadhātuka* category, the rule is already established by the elision of the vowel *a*. It also occurs even when there is an *anubandha*: as in *adhur*. Where, then, would it apply? As in *babhūv*. But surely, since [the rule] would otherwise be purposeless, this meaning of the mention of "not at the end of a word" (*apadānta*) might be postulated; yet, it does exist.

And there is a purpose for this [rule] stated in the preceding sūtra; what is it? It is so that [the rule] may apply where it is not at the end of a word, but not here—such as in *daṇḍāgram*? This is not so; if this alone were the intended purpose, then he would have placed it in the very next sūtra. But because it is placed here...
It is understood that its primary purpose is precisely to establish the meaning as stated;

furthermore, by virtue of the context, it also serves a subsequent purpose. In the word *koṣita*, there is the augment *iṭ* according to Pāṇini 7.2.52 (*vasatikṣudhoḥ*), and the substitution of *ṣ* according to 8.3.60 (*śāsavasighasīnāṃ ca*). Regarding that [substitution]:

And because it is not established [as a single substitute], the attainment of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) should be understood. Regarding *caṛ*: this is the form of the root *kṛ* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), third person plural (*us*). Regarding *abibhayuḥ*: from the root *ñibhī* "to fear" (DhP 1084), the suffix *laṅ*, the *śap* augment, and by the rule "after the roots beginning with *hu*, there is *ślu*" (Pāṇini 2.4.75).
There is elision (*ślu*), reduplication, and by the rule "sijabhyastavidibhyaśca" (Pāṇini 3.4.109), *jhi* is replaced by *jus*; then, by the rule "jusi ca" (Pāṇini 7.3.83), there is *guṇa*.

97. *ato guṇe* (6.1.97). In the case of *ṭhpace* and *yaj-e*, the rule *vṛddhireci* (6.1.88) would apply, resulting in a vṛddhi; therefore, the intention is that this [rule 97] serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to that very [vṛddhi], establishing the single-substitute form (*pararūpa*).

Thinking that the word *āt* continues from the rule *ṭhāṅgumaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.87), he asks: "What is the purpose of [specifying] *ataḥ*? He says, "They go (*yānti*), they blow (*vānti*)," in order to show that the mention of the short vowel *a* with a following *t* (*tapara*) is made here for the sake of excluding the long vowel.

In the form *ṭhāpaca*, the suffix *iṭ* occurs in the third person singular of the imperfect (*laṅ*) in the ātmanepada; here, by the rule *ādguṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.87), guṇa substitution takes place. However, if the single-substitute (*pararūpa*) were applied instead, that guṇa would not be obtained.

98. *Avyaktānukaraṇasyāta itau* (Pāṇini 6.1.98). "Inarticulate" (*avyakta*) means "having indistinct phonemes. That in which the phonemes, such as the letter *a*, are not clearly manifested—that is what is so described. If this is the case, then by its imitation (*anukaraṇa*) as well...
It must be of such a kind, for an imitation is indeed similar [to the original] and not dissimilar;
consequently, just as in the original to be imitated, even in the imitation itself the vowel *a* is not perceived.
And how can the state of having the form of another (*pararūpatva*) be prescribed for that which is not perceived? Therefore—
He says: "It is an imitation of that," and so forth. If, then, that imitation possesses perfectly distinct phonemes (*parisphuṭavarṇa*), then in that case it would not be an imitation of it at all;
for that which is dissimilar cannot be an imitation, because it is impossible to imitate it [in such a way].

Lest there be an over-extension [of the argument], he says: "By someone," and so forth. Furthermore, that similarity is the equality of the *dhvani*; for both of them, the *dhvani* is the same. Therefore, although specific phonetic features (*varṇa*) are perceived in the imitation, nevertheless, due to the identity of the *dhvani*, [the two are considered the same].
It imitates that unmanifest [sound] which is to be imitated, as in "paṭiti. Now, one might object:
by the rule "alo'ntyasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.52), the operation should apply to the final letter;
so how is it that it applies to the entire word *ac*? This is not a fault; [for the following reason:]

[This is because of the maxim] "In the case of a meaningless [element], the rule applies to the final letter" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 62). Alternatively, since he employs the term "final" (*antyasya*) in the rule "But for the final letter of a reduplicated word, optionally" (6.1.99), it is understood from that that the paribhāṣā "not for the final letter of a meaningful element" (*nānarthake’lontyavidhiḥ*) does not apply here. How so?
Furthermore, when the form of another is employed, there occurs the representation of that which is to be imitated; why, then, would it not occur here?

Is it because of deficiency? This is not a fault; for just as even a manifested property becomes a means of representation through some commonality with it, so too will that which is deficient [serve the same purpose].

"It should be stated that 'it applies when there are more than one vowel' (*anekāca*). This means that the rule "for an imitation of an indistinct sound (*avyaktānukaraṇa*) containing more than one vowel, the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) occurs" must be explained in this sense. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the mention of the word *vā* ("optionally") in the subsequent sūtra is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to both rules; and that [option]...

It is understood that this is a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (an option restricted by specific conditions). Therefore, it will apply only to roots with more than one vowel (*anekāc*), and not to those with a single vowel (*ekāc*). [The question] "How so? is asked by one who considers this imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of an indistinct sound to end in the letter *t*.
99. *nāmreḍitasyāntyasya tu vā* (Pāṇini 6.1.99).

Regarding the phrase "when, however," and so forth: when this sound *paṭat-paṭat* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) as a whole, then because it is not reduplicated, the suffix *t* following the constituent part *paṭat* does not receive the designation *amreḍita*.
By the previous [rule], it indeed becomes the form of the subsequent [element].
100. *nityamāmreḍite ḍāci* (Pāṇini 6.1.100).

Regarding *ṭhḍācaparaṃ*: that after which *ḍāc* follows is so described. Regarding *ḍāci vihite* and so forth: the word *vihita* [is used] here in reference to the root *hi* (meaning "to go," Dhātupāṭha 1257).

This is the meaning of the word *vipūrva* (preceded by *vi*). And regarding the rule "all roots meaning 'to go' mean 'to know'," it should be understood that this sense [of knowing] exists only within the mind (*buddhistha*) when it has been prescribed and understood. Therefore, the meaning is this:
when *ḍāc* is prescribed, even though it has not yet been produced, it exists only as an object present in the mind; thus, "frequently when *ḍāc* [is applied]."

The phrase "dve" (Vārttika 888) refers to reduplication (*dvirvacana*). This must necessarily be understood in this way; for otherwise, if the meaning were "when *ḍāc* is prescribed, [the word] has been formed," then reduplication would be prescribed by the rule "optionally, when *ḍāc* follows, there is reduplication" (Vārttika 888). And thus—

This contradicts what [the author] will say: "The locative in *ḍāci* is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*). What, then, is the reason that when *ḍāc* is prescribed, reduplication is ordained specifically for that which has become an object of cognition even though it has not yet been produced? To this he says: "And that," etc. The word *ca* (and) is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).

Since it is desired that the reduplication occurs prior to the elision of the *ṭi* suffix, therefore, when the *ḍāc* suffix is prescribed and remains present as a mental object—that is, while it has not yet actually arisen—the reduplication is ordained, not when it has become a subsequent element. In this way, its occurrence before the elision of the *ṭi* is established; otherwise, it would not be so. If [it were otherwise]...
If reduplication were not performed when the suffix *ḍāc* is present, then, because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), the elision of the *ṭi* portion would occur first;

subsequently, reduplication would apply to that which ends in *ṭakāra*, and thus the form *paṭapaṭā* would not be established. Nor can it be argued that "the *āmreḍita* [portion] is always [treated as such] after *ḍāc*."
This statement serves as an indicator that "first there is reduplication, and then the elision of the *ṭi* [suffix]";
for if this were intended solely for cases such as *paṭat*, where the word ending in *yacch* (the suffix *ya*) occurs after the *ṭi*-elision has been performed—
such as in *paṭapaṭākaroti*— then this rule would apply only to that specific instance.

Alternatively—thinking that there is no fault when the suffix *ḍāc* is applied because the locative case is subsequent (*parasaptamī*), it was stated: "when *ḍāc* is applied. When *ḍāc* is applied, reduplication occurs by means of the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "when *ḍāc* is applied, reduplication is frequent" (Vārttika 888). But surely...

This being the case, since "the rule for elision (*lopavidhi*) is weaker than all rules for substitution" (Vyāḍipāṭha 70), the *ṭilopa* would occur prior to reduplication; and if that were so, an undesirable form would result.
To this, he says: "And that," etc. But how [is it that the *ṭilopa* does not occur]? From the elision of *ṭi*...

Is this [result] obtained because it was previously desired? It is obtained by virtue of the inclusion of the word *bahula* ("in many cases"). However, according to this interpretation, that form should be understood as belonging specifically to the root *dadhāti* (to place), which has been prescribed [by the rule].

101. *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.101). In the case of *agnaye*, because the rule *gheṅiti* (7.3.111) applies subsequently, the guṇa substitution is performed first; consequently, since the form *ak* no longer exists here, the present rule does not apply.
Regarding the example "dadhya atra": [an objection is raised]—"But surely the substitution of *yaṇ* will act as a sublater (*bādhaka*) here;
so what is the use of including the term 'homogeneous' (*savarṇa*) for the sake of excluding that? [The reply is: "In that case, it would also act as a sublater here:
*dadhīndraḥ*, *madhūṣṇam*. Therefore, the inclusion of the term 'homogeneous' is for the purpose of distinguishing the respective domains."

It should be performed as in "kumārī śete. Here, although the letter *ś* is a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) of the vowel *i*— according to the rules "icuyaśāḥ tālavyāḥ" (the letters *i*, *c*, *y*, *ś* are palatals) and "vivṛtaṃ karaṇam ūṣmaṇāṃ svarāṇāṃ ca" (the articulation of the sibilants and vowels is open)—
Nevertheless, because the term *ac* continues to apply [from the previous rule], this does not occur; nor is there even phonetic similarity (*sāvarṇya*) here.

For in the rule *nājjhalau* (1.1.10), the defining rule (*grahaṇaka-śāstra*) *aṇudit savarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ* (1.1.69) would have already been established, and thus the vowel *i*, when being apprehended, [includes] the vowel *ī* as well.

It becomes a grasper; and since the rule for the technical name *savarṇa* (homogeneous) is a subordinate member (*aṅga*) and a cause (*nimitta*) for that [rule], as long as that [name] has not yet come into operation, the rule for the grasper remains unestablished due to the deficiency of its subordinate member. Thus...

Even the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) does not operate because, as long as its exception has not come into effect, it does not know its own domain— thinking, "Where should I apply?"— and thus it does not function. Consequently, since the exception "na-aj-jhalau" has not yet come into effect, the *savarṇa* designation does not apply.

Because of that deficiency of constituent parts, the *grahaṇaka* treatise is incomplete; therefore, [the vowels] homogeneous with *a* are included. Consequently, this prohibition applies only to those [vowels] situated within the *pratyāhāra* that have not been grasped as being homogeneous with *a*. And since this *ī* is not situated among the *akṣaras*, it is not [subject to] the rule "not *a* and *jhal*."
Thus, by the inclusion [of the term] *iti* through the mention of the *pratyāhāra*, the homogeneous quality (*savarṇatva*) between the vowel *ī* and the letter *ś* is not prohibited;
hence [the forms] *holllṛkāraḥ* and *hotṛṛkāraḥ*. But how, then, is there lengthening (*dīrghatva*) in this case?

Since *ṛ* and *ḷ* have different places of articulation (*sthāna*), they do not possess the designation of being "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*). To this, he says: "The rule for the designation of homogeneity between *ṛ* and *ḷ* has been stated. Now, one might object:
since the combination of *ṛ* and *ḷ* is the substitute here, [the replacement] should occur by that which is most similar (*antaratama*) to that very combination.

It is logical that [the substitution] should occur by way of an *ādeśa* (substitute), yet since there is no *antaratama* (most similar) element for the *ṛ*-vowel, how can that [substitution] take place? To this he says: "But in the case of the long [vowels]," and so forth.
This is because there is no single entity most similar to the aggregate [of sounds]. Here, the aggregate consisting of the *ṛ*-vowel and the *lṛ*-vowel is the *sthānin* (original element).

And since a long vowel of that [ṛ-sound] is not possible as the most similar (antaratama), it is proper for the substitute to be that which is the most similar to the constituent part itself; even there, since a long vowel of the *lṛ*-sound is not possible,
that very long vowel which is the most similar to the *ṛ*-sound becomes the *ṛ*-sound.

102. *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.102). This word *prathama* refers to a thing in relation to a specific arrangement. When subsequent [sounds] are observed, that which has nothing preceding it is what is denoted by the word *prathama*. Here...

Because of the general reference in the rule "ca ṭhprathamayoḥ," it is not known which two "first" [cases] are intended to be included; therefore, to provide that understanding, he says "the word *prathamā*" and so forth.
In this treatise, this word *prathama* is conventionally established as a specific technical term for the first triplet (*trika*) among the case-endings (*sup*).
In this regard, it is well-known; for instance, in such grammatical indications as "sapūrvayoḥ prathamayorvibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 8.1.26) and "saptamīpañcamīprathamābhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.3.27),
that very specific case-ending is indicated by the word *prathamā*.
Therefore, because it is a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*), it is understood that the word "first" (*prathama*) here refers to a specific case-ending (*vibhakti*).
But surely, the word "first" (*prathama*) which is feminine in gender refers to a specific case-ending in this treatise?
Is its feminine gender itself doubtful? This is not so;

from the very employment of the word *prathamā*, it is determined that this [term] is taken in the feminine gender. For if this were the employment of the masculine gender, there would have been the mention of the suffix (*pratyaya*) alone.

And if the inclusion of the term *pratyaya* (suffix) were intended, then he would have simply said "of *au* and *jas*" (*aujasoḥ*). Nor does the mention of it in this way entail the undesirable consequence of including the vowel *au* belonging to the second case; for here, by virtue of its association with *jas*, it will be understood that only the vowel *au* belonging to the first case is meant.
