Therefore, there is no doubt that this is the mention of the feminine gender. Now, if this word *prathamā* is a conventional term (*rūḍha*) in this science for a specific case-ending (*vibhakti*), then in such a case, since it refers to a single specific case-ending, it ought to appear in the singular alone; so how [is the plural used]?
To the question, "Why is there a dual number in the word *prathamayoḥ*? he says: "Because of association with that," and so forth.

By virtue of its association (*sāhacarya*) with that specific case-ending called the first (*prathamā*), the second (*dvitīyā*) case-ending is also termed "first"; and therefore, because of this duality, the dual number alone is appropriate. This is what is meant by this [statement].
By saying "of the first two," he shows that this mention of *gar* refers to the two case-endings (*vibhakti*), and not to the two [sounds] beginning with *pra*.

[The examples are] "vṛkṣāḥ" and "lakṣāḥ. How can this be cited as an example, given that by the rule "ato guṇe" (Pāṇini 6.1.97), a single substitute of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) ought to occur here; for that [substitution] would indeed apply?

One might ask: "Just as [the rule] *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* sublates the lengthening [prescribed by *iko yaṇ aci*], would it not likewise sublate the lengthening [prescribed by] *ṭhprathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ*? To this he says:
"*ato guṇe*" and so forth. He provides the justification for this very point with the words "*purastāt*" and so forth. The particle *iti*...

Regarding the reason: because of the rule "exceptions [stated] earlier sublate the rules immediately following them, not those further ahead" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 9), the *pararūpa* substitution prescribed by "ato guṇe" (6.1.97) sublates the lengthening prescribed by "akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ" (6.1.101); for that very reason...

Because it follows immediately after that [the substitution of the long vowel is not barred]; for the lengthening by the rule "in the case of the first two [cases], the preceding sound is the same" (Pāṇini 6.1.102) is not set aside, due to the reverse order [of application]. Regarding the example "agnī" and so forth: if the mention of "the preceding" (*pūrva*) were absent, then in the case of "agnī," the composite of the preceding and following sounds would be the *sthānin* (the element to be replaced), and the most similar (*antaratama*) substitute for that would be the long vowel.
Since there is no specific injunction [to the contrary], the substitute must be that which is most similar to the constituent part (*avayava*). And here there are two constituent parts:

the preceding and the following. In that case, a restriction—that it must belong to the preceding part alone—is not obtained because there is no rule establishing such a restriction; therefore, the substitute occurs alternately for those two in one instance.

The substitute might otherwise be a *parasavarṇa* (homogeneous with the following sound). Therefore, the mention of "preceding" (*pūrva*) is for the purpose of excluding that. However, the mention of "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*) is for the purpose of removing any contradiction; for if that were absent, while the term "long" (*dīrgha*) continued to apply, a contradiction would arise in the case of *agnī*, if the [substitute] were not the preceding one.

[The vowel] *dīrgha* [is long]; now, if it is long, it is not "prior" (*pūrva*); if it is prior, it is not long. Furthermore, if by the word "prior" the prior form (*pūrvākṛti*) were intended, then the genitive case in "of the prior" (*pūrvasya*) would have to be understood as following from [the word] "long" (*dīrghāt*). And in that case, the mention of "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*) could have been omitted.
Or rather, that [mention of "long"] should be understood as being for the sake of easy comprehension.

[As stated in the commentary: "The mention of 'long' [is made] because the substitute would otherwise be three-moraic when the original element (sthānin) is three-moraic," and so forth. When *agni* and *au* stand [in juxtaposition], if the mention of "long" were not present, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) being applied would be three-moraic due to the closest similarity (*āntaratamya*) to the original element.

[The substitute] is obtained; for the original (sthānin) consists of three morae. To explain: in this case, the original consists of the aggregate of the vowel *i* (of the word *agni*), which has one mora, and the vowel *au* (of the word *āuṣadhe*), which has two morae.
Therefore, when the original consists of three morae, the most similar substitute (*antaratama*) must also consist of three morae.
The mention of "long" (dīrgha) is for the purpose of ensuring that [the substitution] does not occur.

For when the long vowel is mentioned, the substitute is thereby qualified such that the undesirable consequence of a three-moraic substitute does not arise; this is because the designation "long" (dīrgha-saṃjñā) is prescribed only for a two-moraic vowel.

103. *tasmāc chaso naḥ puṃsi* (Pāṇini 6.1.103). [The commentary says: "From that [which is] a long vowel homogeneous with the preceding" (*tasmāt pūrvasavarṇadīrghāt*). By this, he shows that by the word "from that" (*tasmāt*), the internal long vowel homogeneous with the preceding is indicated. [It refers to] the *sakāra* which is a constituent part of *śas*.

Thus, by this [rule], the genitive case in *śasaḥ* is a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) with respect to the letter *s* as a constituent of the suffix; or else, it is a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix in *puṃsi*, meaning "if the suffix *śas* has been produced in the sense of the plural number of males. Alternatively, it is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*), meaning "if [the base] is the word *pum*."

Regarding the rule *paraḥ śas* (Pāṇini 1.4.98): therein, when the meaning of the suffix is intended as a qualifier [of the base], the following is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) for the passage beginning with "all these": forms such as *vṛkṣān* and *agnīn* are appropriate examples, because the suffix *śas* is produced here in the sense of the plurality of males (*puṃsām*). [As in] *ṣaṇḍakān*.

Regarding the word *paṇḍakān*: these two examples are incorrect; for the suffix *śas* does not arise here because of a plurality of males (*puṃs*), but rather because of neuter nouns (*napuṃsaka*). To this he says: "All these," and so forth.
By the inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*), it is indicated that not only words such as *vṛkṣa* [occur] in the masculine gender.
They do not express their own referent as qualified by a general property and a particular property;

rather, he shows that even the words *ṣaṇḍaka* and *paṇḍaka* [do so]. Furthermore, their own referent is a substance such as a tree, delimited by the general property and particular property of masculinity. Thus, since all...

These [words] denote meanings qualified by the masculine gender; therefore, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)—that the suffix *śas* arising after them occurs only in the sense of the plurality of males—is refuted. However, when it is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*), then this...

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: An example such as *vṛkṣān* is appropriate, for in that case the suffix *śas* follows the word *puṃs*; however, these two examples—*sthūrān* and *ararakān*—are not appropriate. For instance, [the forms] *sthūrāyā apatyāni* and *ararakāyā...* [would require different grammatical operations].

Regarding the term *apatyāni* ("descendants"): the suffix *yañ* is applied by the rule *gargādibhyo yañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.105). When the elision (*luk*) of both *yañ* and *añ* is effected by the rule *yañañośca* (2.4.64), the feminine suffix is also elided by the rule *luktaddhitaluki* (1.2.49). Thus, from these two feminine words, *sthūrā* and *ararakā*, the [patronymic] *atri* is produced.
Why is it that [the suffix] śas follows words denoting feminine (*strī*), but not words denoting neuter (*napuṃsaka*)?

To this he says: "All these," and so forth. For here, the base itself, ending in a *taddhita* suffix with elision (*luk*), occurs in the sense of the suffix; and that sense of the suffix is qualified by the masculine gender. Therefore, it is not merely...

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position— that words such as *vṛkṣa* denote their own referents (*svārtha*) as qualified by the masculine gender, and not even words such as *sthūla* and *arara*— is thereby refuted.
In that case, this is the fault in the view that the suffix-meaning is qualified: *cañcā iva cañcā pumāṃsaḥ* ("men like a wooden doll").

When the suffix *kan* is applied by the rule *ṭhiva pratikṛtau* (Pāṇini 5.3.96), and then elided by *lummanuṣye* (5.3.98), and when the suffix *śas* is produced in the plural number of males from the word *cañcā* which ends in that elision (*lup*), then—
One might ask: why does the substitution of *n* not occur in the word *cañcāḥ paśya*? To this he says: "But here," and so forth.

For in this case, the suffix *śas* has not been produced in the sense of a masculine plural; rather, it is produced in the sense of a feminine plural. Since even a masculine [noun] is treated as feminine through the extension (*atideśa*) of femininity by virtue of being joined with that [suffix], the substitution of *n* does not take place here.

The mention of "long" (dīrgha) is understood from the context; since that [term] is present here in the ablative case by virtue of the sense, he says "but here," etc., with the intention that even without the explicit statement "from that" (tasmāt), the substitution of *n* for *śas* will occur after a long vowel alone. For indeed, in this case, there is no plurality of the masculine.

The suffix *śas* has not arisen here; rather, it arises when there is a plurality of females. Even for a masculine [noun], because the status of being feminine is extended to it by virtue of its behaving like the feminine (*yuktavadbhāva*), the substitution of *n* does not occur here. The term "long vowel" (*dīrgha*) is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*), and it is presented here in the genitive case (*pañcamyantā*) according to the requirements of the sense.

With the intention that, even by means of another rule, this word *tasmāt* would ensure that the substitution of *na* occurs for the *śas* following a long vowel, he asks: "What is the purpose of *tasmāt*? [The answer is: "These cows grazing—*etān gāścarataḥ paśya*. Here, the substitution of *ā* [for *o*] is applied by the rule *āṬto'mśasoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.93).

If that which is immediately followed by a long vowel were to be referred to by the word *tat*, then the substitution of *ṇatva* being prescribed without distinction for every long vowel, it would also apply in the case of "etān gāścarataḥ paśya" (look at these cows grazing),
for this vowel *ā* is indeed long. Therefore, there is no fault in using the word *tat*.
For this aspect is not prescribed by the immediately preceding sūtra.

104. *nādici* (6.1.104). Regarding *khaṭve*: by the rule *āṬṅ āpaḥ* (7.1.18), there is the substitution of *śī*. Regarding *kuṇḍe*: here too, by the rule *napuṃsakācca* (7.1.19), once that [substitution] has been made, *ādguṇaḥ* (6.1.87) applies.
The quality.

105. *dīrghāj jasi ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.105). The term *ṭhāt* does not carry over [from the previous rule]; therefore, this is a prohibition of the *pūrvasavarṇa* [substitution] after a long vowel [only]. Now, how is it that in the case of *khaṭvāḥ*, there is the *pūrvasavarṇa* [substitution] by [the rule] *ṭhprathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ* (6.1.102)?

Why is there lengthening [of the vowel]? The statement "from a long [vowel]" is for the sake of clarity. But would it not follow that [the rule] would apply even in the case of *vṛkṣāḥ* if that [statement] were absent? This is not so; for if it were to apply here as well, then the mention of *ici* in the preceding sūtra would be purposeless. What then [is the purpose] here?

It might be argued: "What about *agnaye*? There is no fault here because it is desired; for in this case, by the rule *jasi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.109), the guṇa substitution alone occurs due to its subsequent position. If it is then asked: "In that case, it must be for the sake of the following rule—so that the long vowel may optionally occur by *vā chandasi* (6.1.106)? This is not so; because the mention of *vā* (optionally) in that [rule]...

This is understood from the rule of *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (optional application based on established usage): [the substitution] will occur only after a long vowel, not after a short one. Furthermore, the rule *jasi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.109) is for the sake of clarity alone. But surely, if this rule *jasi ca* did not exist, there would be a prohibition even regarding the suffix *śas* in cases such as *yuvatīḥ paśya* ("see the young women") and *paddhatīḥ paśya* ("see the paths").

Could it be so? It will not be so, because of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Since this [author] makes the mention of "masculine" (*puṃs*) in the rule *tasmāc chaso naḥ puṃsi* (Pāṇini 6.1.103), that indicates: "the prohibition does not apply after *śas*.

For that [mention of "masculine"] is solely for the purpose of excluding the feminine, since in the neuter gender the substitution of the long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghatva*) is impossible.

[The rule] is being formulated. Furthermore, if this prohibition were to apply even in the case of feminine forms—as in "yuvatīḥ paśya" (look at the young women) and so on—then, due to the absence of the long vowel resulting from the homogeneous preceding sound (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghatva*), the substitution of *n* would not occur at all;

so what is the purpose of including the mention of the masculine (*puṃgrahaṇa*)? [One might argue: "Then the mention of *jas* is for the sake of the subsequent rule. This is not so, because of the mention of the option (*vāgrahaṇa*).
In that case, because the *vibhāṣā* rule is established as restricted (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*), the suffix *jas* will not occur elsewhere.

[The example is] *mārutīḥ*. Since the Maruts are their deities (*marud-devatā āsām*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied by *sāsya devatā* (4.2.24), and then *ṅīp* is applied by *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (4.1.15); there is lengthening of the homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatvam*).

Regarding *vārāhī*: [according to the *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī*, the suffix] *caṭ* is applied; then the suffix *aṇ* is added by [Pāṇini 4.3.135], "The suffix *aṇ* is used for a product (*vikāra*) and for a part (*avayava*) [of something] belonging to living beings, plants, or trees," and as before, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Regarding *upānahī*: [the suffix] is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.41], "The suffix *ṣyaṅ* is applied after roots ending in *ṣit* and after [words beginning with] *gaura*."
The feminine suffix ṅīṣ.

This rule is stated because the substitution of a long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) would otherwise apply. The word "long" (*dīrgha*) is understood here [from the previous sūtra]; for otherwise, this rule would be purposeless.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of "prior" (*pūrva*) made, given that the very same "prior" mentioned in the preceding context will simply carry over here? To this he says: "The mention of 'prior,'" and so forth.
It is for the sake of ensuring that it remains of the same kind as the prior one was.

The mention of "pūrva" (the preceding) is for this purpose. To show what is excluded by the particle *eva*, he says: "lest there be that which is both homogeneous with the preceding (*pūrvasavarṇa*) and most similar (*antaratama*). This is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both homogeneous with the preceding and most similar. For if the mention of "pūrva" were absent—

The mention of "preceding" (*pūrva*) at the beginning must be carried forward by that very same [term]; and while that is being carried forward, the mention of "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*), which is connected to it, would also be carried forward. And thus, by the rule *sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ* (P. 1.1.50), that which is homogeneous with the preceding [element]—

In this way, [the rule] would be over-extended. But what undesirable consequence would there be if this were so? If it is argued that in cases such as *vṛkṣam*, the substitute for the two-mora (*dvimātra*) original would itself be two morae, this is not the case;
for if it were so, this statement [of the present sūtra] would be purposeless, given the rule "for the first two [cases], the preceding homogeneous vowel" (6.1.102).
Since this is established by this [rule], he says: "For in the case of *kumārim*, etc.

In the word *kumārī*, the vowel *ī* has two morae (*dvimātra*), while the *a* of the suffix *am* has one mora (*mātrika*). The substitute here consists of that entire combination; therein, the *pūrvasavarṇa* [is applied].

If [the rule] were being prescribed without the mention of *pūrva*, then for a substitute of three morae (*trimātra*) being enjoined, the most similar (*antaratama*) would necessarily be one of three morae;
however, when the term *pūrva* (preceding) is included, the substitute becomes two morae (*dvimātra*), being of the same nature as that which immediately precedes it.

Regarding the passage beginning with "or [it is] in the Veda" (*vā chandasi*), and so forth: if *vā chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.106) is indeed being carried over (*anuvartate*), then, because this [present rule] forms a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatā*) with that [previous rule], would it not follow that the substitution of the preceding letter (*parapūrvatvam*) is not established in the secular language (*bhāṣā*)? This is not so; for that [rule] which is being carried over here...
As before, by means of a split in the sentence, it establishes an option only in the Vedic language, not in the colloquial language.
108. *samprasāraṇācca*.

(6.1.108) This rule ordains that the preceding vowel [of the *samprasāraṇa*] shall take the place of both [the *samprasāraṇa* and the following vowel], for the purpose of preventing the substitution of a *yaṇ* for the *samprasāraṇa*.
For if the *yaṇ* substitution were to occur here, then...

The prescription of *saṃprasāraṇa* would otherwise be purposeless; therefore, by the very force of the prescription of *saṃprasāraṇa*, the substitution of *yaṇ* will not occur. [An objection is raised: "If that is so, for what purpose is this [substitution] prescribed? To this he says: "By the force of the prescription of *saṃprasāraṇa*."

And so forth. By the force of the rule prescribing *samprasāraṇa*, the substitution of *yaṇ* would not occur; consequently, one would have to hear the separated form (*vigṛhīta*) without the *saṃhitā*-operation having been applied. Therefore, in order that this fault may not arise, the substitution of the preceding vowel (*parapūrvatva*) is prescribed.
Regarding the rule *ṭhVā cchandasīty eva* and so forth: here too, as before, a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) should be understood;
otherwise, [the substitution] would not occur in the secular language (*bhāṣā*). As for the form *yajyamānaḥ* (or *yajyamānau* according to the Kāśikā):
in the alternative where the preceding vowel does not become the single substitute (*parapūrvatva*), the *yaṇ* replacement occurs. But how can there be a *yaṇ* replacement here, given that...

One must indeed understand [the rule] as applying to the separated form (*vigṛhīta*), for it was just stated: "Since the hearing of the separated form would otherwise result from the very force of the prescription for *samprasāraṇa*, the substitution of the preceding vowel with the following one (*parapūrvatva*) is prescribed. To this, he says: "In the prescription of the substitution of the preceding vowel with the following one," and so forth.

For if *parapūrvatva* (the substitution of the preceding vowel with the following) were not applied, one would necessarily hear only the separated [vowels], lest the *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) be rendered useless. But since *parapūrvatva* does exist—wherever *parapūrvatva* occurs, as in *iṣṭam* and so forth—there the *samprasāraṇa* is purposeful. Therefore...

In the view that there is no "preceded by another" (*parapūrva*) condition, the substitution of *yaṇ* certainly occurs. Now, why does it not occur here in the case of *śakahvau* and *śakahvartham*? For in this instance, [the derivation is as follows]: from *śakam hvayati*, the suffix *kvip* is applied;

because it belongs to the *yajādi* group, there is *samprasāraṇa*; then there is the "preceded by another" (*parapūrva*) condition; and according to the rule *ag-tādivat ca*, [that *parapūrva* form is treated like a verbal root].
Because of the inclusion [of this case] by the mention of *samprasāraṇa* in (Pāṇini 6.1.85),
the single substitute for both the *samprasāraṇa* and non-*samprasāraṇa* vowels receives the designation of *samprasāraṇa*; thus, when the vowel *au* and the word *artha* follow, [the rule applies].
One might ask: "Does not [the rule] *samprasāraṇācca* (Pāṇini 6.1.108) require that the preceding vowel take the place of the following one? To this he says:

"And when the vowel is internal (*antaraṅga*)," and so forth. This long *ā* which is prescribed in place of the *ec* of the root *hvayati* is an internal (*antaraṅga*)—that is, more proximate—element of the *samprasāraṇa*.

Because both [the vowel *au* and the substitute *ā*] are included within a single *dhātu*. The form *āu* and the form of the word *artha* are distant (*viprakṛṣṭa*). They are distant in terms of space and in terms of time; as it says, "external" (*bāhya*). That which is a constituent part (*avayava*) of a *dhātu* undergoing *samprasāraṇa* is "external" because it is not included therein. And in terms of time:

As he says: "when [the vowel] has subsequently come together. The meaning is that it is present at a time subsequent to the time of the prescription of the *pūrvarūpa* (the single-substitute form). In that context, between two vowels—one proximate and one remote—this rule applies to the vowel which is *antaraṅga* (internally conditioned) due to its proximity; therefore...

The term "having accomplished its purpose" means that once [the operation] has taken effect in a remote instance such as the vowel *ā* and so forth, it does not subsequently apply when [the same condition] is proximate.
109. *eṅḥ padāntādati* (6.1.109). In the example *agne atra*, the *guṇa* substitution [of *e* for *e* + *a*] is applied by the rule *sambuddhau ca* (7.3.106).

110. *eṅi ca* (6.1.110). "When *eṅ* follows," and so forth. The meaning is: when the suffixes *ṅsi* and *ṅsu* follow, provided that *eṅ* is the subsequent [element] and they are related parts of that [word], and when the phoneme *at* is present immediately before them. For example: *agner āgacchati*.

Thus [it is said]. By the rule *eṅiṅiti* (Pāṇini 7.3.111), there is *guṇa*. Now, why does the correspondence of numbers (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) not apply here, since there are two *eṅ* vowels and also two *ṅsi-ṅs* suffixes? This is not a fault, for here an operation is not prescribed as following after *ṅsi* and *ṅs*; what then?

Regarding the phrase "belonging to that [relation]," that [relation] is indeed one and the same. Even if there were a distinction based on the difference in the related entities (*sambandhin*), there would still be no fault; for here, the particle *ca* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). And thus, there is a conjunction [of rules] provided that, when each individual *iṅ* (the vowels *i* and *ī*) is followed by *ṅsi* and *ṅs* respectively, the substitution of the preceding letter [with the following] occurs.

It occurs [only] thus, and not otherwise. The indications in the rules *agner ḍhak somāruṇayoḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.27) and *or āvaśyake* (Pāṇini 3.1.125) inform us of its absence [in other cases]. Alternatively, it is determined by the sign of deviation from the general rule (*lakṣaṇavyabhicāra*). By the fact that the genitive suffix *ṅsi* of the shorter word is placed last, the absence of a correspondence between the order of words and their meanings (*yathāsaṃkhya*) is understood.

111. *ṛta ut* (6.1.111). [The sūtra states: "In place of two [sounds] specified in the genitive case," and so forth. But what undesirable consequence would arise in examples such as *hotuḥ* if *raparatva* (the substitution of *r* for *ṛ*) were not applied? None whatsoever.
Something [is required]; however, by logical necessity (*nyāyataḥ*), the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* also follows, and that must necessarily be performed.
To demonstrate that very logic, it is stated: "In place of two [elements] specified by the genitive case.
The inclusion of the marker *t* in the word *ṛtaḥ* is for the purpose of excluding the long vowel. By this, [the rule] *unyor graḥ* [applies].

(3.3.29) It does not apply in cases such as *pra-stro'yajñe* (3.3.32). Furthermore, the addition of the *t* in *ut* (*udit*) is solely for the purpose of excluding the long vowel; because of the principle of closest proximity (*āntaratamya*), a long [vowel] would naturally result in place of a long [vowel]. Now, one might object that "an *aṇ* which is undergoing substitution does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*)."

Since the rule *gṛhṇāti* (Pāṇini 1.1.69) would not result in the inclusion of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa*), what is the purpose of adding the *tapara* marker (the short *u*) for its exclusion? If this is so, then it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that in this context, a vowel being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) does include its homogeneous counterparts. Therefore, in forms such as *amū* and *amūbhyām*, [the long *ū* includes the short *u*].
By the rule "ṭhadaso'serdādu do maḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.80), a long *ū* is substituted in place of the long vowel [of the stem].

112. *khyatyāt parasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.112). Regarding the rule *khyatyāt*, it is said: "This refers to the words *khi* and *khī*, as well as the words *ti* and *tī*, when the substitution of *yaṇ* has been applied. This remains the same once the substitution of *yam* has been made.
Because there is no distinction [in the form] "rūpam. Now, why is it that here only those forms ending in the vowels *ā*—namely the words *khya* and *tya*—are not included?
If you argue that this is because the words *khya* and *tya* do not exist in isolation, we say: no; for even if they do not exist in isolation, [the rule applies to] those which end in them.
In that case, let there be the inclusion of the primary [meanings] such as *go* and *saṃkhyā*, as well as their derivatives such as *gārhapatya* and so on?
This is not so; for if it were thus, the two grammatical indications—namely, *sakhyurasambuddhau* (Pāṇini 7.1.92) and *patyurno yajñasaṃyoge* (Pāṇini 4.1.33)—would be untenable.

"‘Sakhaḥ’ means ‘one who exists together with [another]’ (*saha khena vartate*). This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to Pāṇini 2.2.28, *tena saheti tulyayoge*; the substitution of *sa-* for *saha-* is applied by 6.3.82, *vopasarjanasya*. Regarding "‘Sakhīyati’": the substitution of *i* for *ya* occurs by 7.4.33, *kyaci ca*. Regarding "‘Sakhīḥ’": [the suffix] *kvip* is applied.

By the rule *ṭhato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.48), there is the elision of the vowel *a*, and by *ṭhlopo vyor vali* (6.1.66), there is the elision of the *y*. Thus we have *lūnam*. Furthermore, by *ṭhlvādibhyaḥ* (8.2.44), the suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past participle suffix *kta*) becomes nasalized (*ṇatva*). Now, one might object: "This is not the word *tī* [meaning 'crossing over']; so how can this be an example of it? To this, [the author replies]: [The text continues: ...[the word *tī*] is indeed present here as part of the root *tṛ* [in the form *taritvā*]. Therefore, this is a valid example. However, since the word *tī* is not explicitly present here, how can it be cited as an illustration? To this, [the author replies:]... [the word *tī* is indeed present here as part of the root *tṛ* [in the form *taritvā*]. Therefore, this is a valid example. (Note: The provided source text appears to contain a fragmentary or repetitive section regarding the derivation of *lūnam* and the status of the word *tī*. The translation above reflects the core grammatical arguments presented.)
He says: "The status of being a final element," and so forth.

Now, why does this not apply here in cases such as *ataḥkheḥ āgacchati* ("he comes from the owner of the horse") and *senāpateḥ āgacchati* ("he comes from the commander of the army"), since the word *khi* and the word *ti* are also present there? To this he replies: "Because of the mention of the modified form," and so forth.

This very purpose is served by this distorted formulation (vikṛtanirdeśa), made by applying the *yaṇ* substitution to the word *khyāti* as if it were an adventitious form: that [the rule] should apply only where there is the *yaṇ* substitution. Since there is no *yaṇ* substitution here, it does not occur; for otherwise, [it would].

The specific mention of *vikṛta* (the modified form) would be purposeless. But surely it serves the purpose of brevity (*laghu*), for otherwise, if it were stated as "from *khit*, *khī*, and *tī*," there would be prolixity (*gaurava*). He thinks thus: if [the suffix] must occur even where a *yaṇ* substitution does not take place, then it should be stated simply as "from *khī* and *tī*."
One might say: "But if this were stated, it would not apply to those ending in short vowels; for [the forms] are already established by the two specific rules:

*sakhyuryaḥ* (5.1.126) from the word *sakhī*, and *patyurno yajñasaṃyoge* (4.1.33) from the word *patnī*. For here, the words *sakhi* and *pati* themselves are what are being referred to, not [their feminine forms]."
Regarding the two words *sakhī* and *pati*: for here the word *pati* has no connection with sacrifice (*yajña*);

nor is the suffix produced from the word *sakhī*—which is derived by such means as "he who exists together with a friend" (*saha khena vartate*)—capable of denoting the meaning of its own base (*prakṛti*).
It occurs; for *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and *samāsa* suffixes are indeed characterized by their verbal expression.
Therefore, the purpose of the modified statement is exactly as previously stated.
Now, why does the substitution of *yaṇ* not occur here, in the presence of which [substitution] there would be [the condition for] *utva*?
If it is argued that [the substitution] ought to occur because it is barred by the *guṇa* [substitution] prescribed by "gher ṅiti" (Pāṇini 7.3.111), we say no;
for there is a prohibition of the technical designation *dhi* by the rule "śeṣo dhyasakhiḥ" (Pāṇini 1.4.7). To this, he says:
"of the word *sakhī*" and so forth. And in this context, [the principle applies]: "By a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which possesses a specific [technical] designation..."
The prohibition "there is no rule of *tadanta* [application]" (Vyāḍipāda 89) is the reason.

Why is the word "of the subsequent" (*parasya*) used? So that [the rule] does not apply to both the preceding and the following. From this point onward, the phrase "of the preceding and the following" (*pūrvaparayoḥ*) does not recur.

113. *ato roraplutād aplute* (Pāṇini 6.1.113). Regarding the phrase "of that which has the phoneme *ṭh* as its *anubandha*": if the word *ru* were the entire composite (*samudāya*) to be substituted, then in the case of *mahātaruvanam*, the substitution of *u* by rule *haśi ca* (6.1.114) would undesirably apply.
Furthermore, the inclusion of the marker *u* in the rule "sasajuṣo ruḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.66) would be purposeless;

for there, the letter *u* is employed as a qualifier of this rule, yet here, within the entire complex that serves as the substituendum, it becomes meaningless. Therefore, this [term *ru*] is understood as being possessed of the marker *u*.

But surely, when the substitution of *u* (utva) is to be applied, the substitution of *r* (rutva) is "not established" (*asiddha*) by the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* (8.2.1); therefore, how can the substitution of *u* be prescribed for an *r* that does not exist? To this he says: "The substitution of *r* is also established by virtue of its basis. For if the substitution of *r* were unestablished, [the rule for utva could not apply].

In that case, the recourse to the *ru* (the substitute for *visarjanīya*) as the *sthānin* would be purposeless, because no *ru* characterized by the indicatory letter *u* is possible. Therefore, it follows simply from this dependence [on the *sthānin*] that the *ru* is not non-existent (*asiddha*).

Regarding the phrase "of that too": even in cases where the substitution of *u* for *ru* is prescribed after [a vowel], there occurs the protracted (*pluta*) vowel by the rule *dūrāddhūte ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.84), as in *susrotā 3 atra*; and also in *devadatā 3 atra*, where it occurs by the rule *guroḥ anṛto ’nantasyāpy ekaikasya prācām* (Pāṇini 8.2.86).

Now, for what purpose is it stated "from a non-protracted [vowel] to a non-protracted"? For if the letter were indicated by the addition of *ta* (as in *at*), would it not follow that [the substitution] would apply when something follows a protracted vowel, or when a protracted vowel itself follows? To this he says: "of the protracted," and so forth. But surely the protracted vowel is already established?

In the rules concerning vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*), why does he teach the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) in the rule "ṭhplutapragṛhyā āci" (Pāṇini 6.1.125)? He thinks as follows: this [rule] would be an indicator (*jñāpaka*) precisely for the preservation of the original form. Even if, however, it were somehow an indicator regarding the domain of vowel-sandhi, the same would apply to the quality of *r* (*rodatva*).

The euphonic combination (*svarasandhi*) does not occur. Even if the *saṃhitā* were to serve as an indicator for the scope of its operations, nevertheless, the substitution of *u* for *ru* is not a *saṃhitā*-operation. For that by which phonemes are joined together is a *saṃhitā*-operation, and the phonemes are not joined by means of the substitution of *u*.
They do so because they still depend on the substitution of *guṇa* for *ā* and other such operations.

114. *haśi ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.114). Because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "from what precedes" (*pūrvatra*), the substitution of *u* for *r* would not have applied before a *haś* sound; therefore, this rule prescribes it. The particle *ca* is for the purpose of carrying over (*anukarṣaṇa*) the rule *ṭhaplutāt* (6.1.113). Consequently, it does not apply here.
It becomes: "Susrotā 3 vehi."

115. *prakṛtyā antaḥpādam avy-apare* (Pāṇini 6.1.115). Regarding *prakṛtyā*: this is the instrumental case used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe tṛtīyā*). Regarding *antaḥpādam*: this is a locative form. An indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) is formed in the sense of a case ending, and from that, the locative case is applied.

In that [rule], the substitution of *ām* is applied by the rule "the substitution of *ām* occurs diversely for the third and seventh case endings" (Pāṇini 2.4.84). Regarding the phrase "of *eṅ*" (*eṅaḥ*) and so forth: a connection with the word "remains in its original form" (*prakṛtyā bhavati*) is not possible if [the genitive] *eṅaḥ* were taken as ending in the fifth case.
Therefore, here, by implication, the mention of *eṅ* arises as a nominative form. This is shown by the words "original form" (*prakṛtiḥ*) and so forth.

He explains the word *prakṛti*: for in common usage, the word *prakṛti* is employed in the sense of "intrinsic nature," as in the expression "nature is difficult to abandon"; it is also used in the sense of a "material cause," as in "milk is the *prakṛti* of curd. Therefore, in this context as well, that same meaning is understood for it.

"Antaḥ" is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) functioning as a locative (*adhikaraṇa*). For this very reason, the compound *antaḥpādam* is an *avyayībhāva*. Regarding the phrase "by the word *pāda*" and so forth: how, then, is the inclusion of only the *ṛk*-verse quarter obtained, given that the word *pāda* is a general term? He thinks thus: "Or [it is] in Vedic meter (*vā chandasi*)."
From this point [Pāṇini 6.1.106], the term *chandas* (Vedic) is carried over here by the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*);

therefore, it is understood that only the foot of a Vedic verse (*ṛkpāda*) is intended. Furthermore, prior to the sūtra "sarvatra vibhāṣā goḥ" (6.1.122), it is understood that the grammatical operation applies only to the Veda. For thus it is stated there:
The inclusion of the term "universal" (sarvatraga) becomes meaningful if there is a prior rule in the Vedic language (*chandas*).

Having thus explained the meaning of the individual components, he states the meaning of the whole through the phrase beginning with "the letter *v* and the letter *y*," etc. That [word] is so described because its *v*-sound and *y*-sound are non-existent [in that context].

Regarding the passage beginning with "by its own nature" (*svabhāvena*): when the word *prakṛti* is understood as referring to "own-nature," then this is the meaning: the *eṅ* [vowels] exist by their own nature. For it is not possible for the operation of *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) to occur while abandoning one's own nature. However, when the word *prakṛti* refers to a cause...

The meaning of "parigraha" (appropriation) here is this: *eṅ* becomes by means of its causal nature. Since the cause of the effect *eṅ*—namely, the state of having *para* as its predecessor—is its very essence (*ātman*), it is said that *eṅ* becomes by means of that very essence;
that is to say, it exists by means of that same form which *eṅ* possessed prior to the application of the rules of *saṃhitā*.

"It remains as that. In order to clarify the two points just mentioned, he says: "it does not undergo modification. For it exists by its own nature (*svabhāva*) only if a state of modification, characterized by something other than its own nature, does not arise. Thus, in this way...

It exists even as the cause, provided it does not undergo the state of modification; that is to say, provided it does not transform into the form of the effect. [This is stated in the rule: "If not, then there are the *nimita* and *kārya*.

Here, *nimita* refers to the letter *a* characterized by posteriority (*paratva*). For in that case, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) when [the subsequent element] follows.

It is prescribed [that the *prakṛtibhāva* applies] to *eṅ*. For *eṅ* is that which undergoes the grammatical operation (*kāryin*), since its operation is indeed *prakṛtibhāva*. As in the example: "ṭhte agre aśvam āyuñjan. In the middle of this *ṛc*-verse, the *eṅ*—namely the vowel *e* in the words *te*, *agre*, and *aśvam*—undergoes *prakṛtibhāva* immediately following it by the rule "ṭheṅḥ."
By the rule *padāntād āti* (Pāṇini 6.1.109), the single-substitute *pūrvarūpa* does not occur, nor does the *ay*-substitution.
In the example *upaprayanto adhvaraṃ*, here too,
because the word *prayanta* follows immediately after the word *adhvara*, the *pūrvarūpa* does not apply to the vowel *ai* of the word *prayanta*.

[The substitution of] *ava* occurs [for *e*]. Likewise, in cases such as "sujāte aśva," one should understand that due to *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form), there is an absence of the grammatical operation resulting from the single-substitute (*pūrvarūpa*) rule. In the example "ete arcayanti," in the word "ete," the *eṅ* which is the phoneme *e* occurs at the end of a word.
However, the *at* [augment] immediately following that occurs at the beginning of a word, not in the middle of a word—as in *ṭhṭhe'tevadan*.

Here, the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) does not apply to the *eṅ* sound in the word *te*; this is because the *at* immediately following it is followed by the letter *v*. As for *avadan*, it is the *laṅ* [aorist] form of the root *vad*.

This is the third person plural ending. In the example "te 'yajān," even here, the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) does not occur for the *eṅ* sound in the word *te*, because the vowel *a* immediately following it is followed by the letter *y*.
In "anv agni," etc., everything [required for the rule] is present, yet the vowel *u* in the word *anu* is not an *eṅ*; this is not its case.
The state of original form (*prakṛtibhāva*).

Regarding the phrase "some [teachers]" and so forth: if they read the rule as *nāntaḥpādam avyapare*, then in that case, the prohibition would apply only to that which is preceded by another vowel (*parapūrva*), and not to *ay* and *av*.

For instance: since *para-pūrvatvam* (the substitution of the subsequent vowel) was prescribed immediately before [by the rule] *eṅi pararūpam*, he says: "In *saṃhitā*, etc. If this prohibition were made with reference to the specific condition that the substitution of the subsequent vowel is a *saṃhitā*-operation, then this fault would arise. But when—
Their view is that if the prohibition is enjoined with reference merely to whatever operation is prescribed under the heading of *saṃhitā*,
then it is logical that the prohibition applies to every single operation prescribed under that heading of *saṃhitā*.

116. *avyād-avadyād-avakramur-avratā-yam-avantv-avasyuṣu ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.116). Regarding *ṭhno avyāt*: from this [word] *asmat*, in the second case plural, by [the rule] *bahuvacanasya vasnasau* (8.2.21), *nas* is substituted; then, after the *ru*-substitution, by *ato ror aplutād aplute* (6.1.113), [the *r* is changed to *u*].

Thus, having applied the *guṇa* substitution according to "ṭhādÂ guṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.87), the form becomes *no*. From the root *ava* in the sense of "protection" (Dhātupāṭha 600), in the optative (*liṅ*) used for benediction (*āśis*),
with the suffixes *yās*, *iṭ*, and *tip*, the *ikāra* is elided by "itaśca" (3.4.97), and [the *v* is elided] by "skoḥ saṃyogādyorante ca" (8.2.29).

When the elision of *sakara* (the *sa* of *sasajuṣo ruḥ*) has been performed, it becomes *ṭhavyāt*; [and] *ṭhavadhyāt*. This word *avadya* ends in the nominative singular. *Ṭhavakramuḥ*: this is the form of the root *kram* preceded by *ava* in the *liṭ* (perfect) with the suffix *usi*. Others, however, explain it as *luṅ* (aorist)—[according to the rule] "bahulam... [Pāṇini 3.1.85].

By the rule *chandasi* (2.4.76), there is *ślu*-elision of the suffix *cli*; by the rule *ślau* (6.1.10), there is reduplication; and the substitution of *jus* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). Regarding the form *avantu*: it is the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *av*, with the replacement of the suffix *jhi* by *ant*, and the substitution of *u* for *e* according to *er uḥ* (3.4.76). Regarding the form *avasyavaḥ*: [it is derived] from the root *av*.

From the rule *sarvadhātubhyo'sun* (Dhātupāṭha 9.49), the suffix *asun* is applied, resulting in *avas*. Then, by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8), the suffix *kyac* is added. From that form ending in *kyac*, the suffix *u* is applied by the rule *kyācchandasi* (Pāṇini 3.2.170). Then the nominative plural suffix *jas* is added; by the rule *jasi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.109), the *guṇa* substitution occurs, resulting in the vowel *o*.
The substitution of *ava* is applied by the rule "ṭhēco'yavāyāvaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.78).

117. *Yajuṣyuraḥ* (6.1.117). As in the example *uraḥ antarikṣam* ("The chest is the intermediate space"). There is the substitution of *u* for the vowel of the word *uras*, and then the *guṇa* substitution according to the rule *ād guṇaḥ*. [According to the Kāśikā, the word *uras* ends in the vowel *o*, whereas the word *urus* ends in the consonant *u*.]
Regarding the statement "they study [the form] ending in the vocative," when the *guṇa* substitution is applied to the word *uru* by the rule *sambuddhau ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.106), it becomes *uro*.

118. *āpo juṣāṇo vṛṣṇo varṣiṣṭhe ambe ambāle ambike pūrve* (Pāṇini 6.1.118). All these words beginning with *āpaḥ* are indeclinable imitations (*anukaraṇa*), because the case-endings produced after them have been elided by rules such as *supāṃ suluk...* (Pāṇini 7.1.39).
In this context, *āpaḥ* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the nominative plural; *juṣāṇaḥ* is [the imitation] of the nominative singular;
*vṛṣṇaḥ* is [the imitation] of the genitive singular; *vaṣiṣṭhe* is [the imitation] of the locative singular;
and these are the qualifiers for the two [words] *amba* and *ambāle*.
The compound *ambikepūrve* is formed from the word *ambike*, preceded by *pūrve*; the compound is possible precisely because of this specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*).

Now, one might object: is this not an imitation of the vocative ending *ambe*? And if so, then by the rule "the short vowel is substituted for [the final of] *amba* and a river-name" (Pāṇini 6.3.107), there ought to be the substitution of a short vowel as an exception to the change to *e*.
In that case, why is there the substitution of *itva* (the short *i*) in the word *ambe*? To this he says: "Precisely for this reason," and so forth.

However, the substitution of *itva* in *ambāle* and *ambike* is indeed appropriate; for he will state in the rule concerning the prescription of short vowels: "If [the base] consists of two syllables and has the sense of 'mother' (*ambā*)," (Vārttika 7.3.107).
119. "And in *aṅga* etc. (6.1.119). [The commentary says:

"And in *ṭhaṅga* etc. By means of the particle *iti*, the word *aṅga* mentioned previously is referred back. [The phrase] "and when there is an *a* at the beginning of that" contains two locative case endings in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*).
By the word *tat*, which refers back to what has preceded, he explains the meaning of the particle *iti*—namely, "at the beginning of that.

This means "at the beginning of the word *aṅga*. Regarding the phrase "whatever precedes," it is connected with the term *eṅ*. The particle *ca* (and) indicates that when the vowel *a* occurs at the beginning of the word *aṅga*, the preceding *eṅ* [is replaced by *ai*] when followed by that *a*.
The particle *ca* (and) is used for the purpose of conjunction so that the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) may occur [in both cases].
For if it were not so, the original form would apply only to the *eṅ* of the word *aṅga* when followed by the word *aṅga*;
however, in the case where the *eṅ* of a word other than *aṅga* is followed by the word *aṅga*, the original form would not occur there.

"ṭhprāṇo aṅge," etc. Here, in the word *prāṇaḥ*, the *eṅ* [vowels *e* and *o*] remains in its original form (*prakṛti*) before the vowel *a* of the word *aṅge*. [Example: "ṭhaṅga aṅge adīdhyat. Here, in the word *aṅga*, the *eṅ* that occurs remains in its original form before the vowel *a* of the word *aṅge* and before words such as *adīdhyat*.

120. *anudāte ca kudhapare* (6.1.120). Regarding the term *kudhapare*: this is a qualifier for the letter *a*. That [letter] after which *ku* and *dha* follow is thus described. In the word *dha*, the letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation. As in: *ayaṃ so agniḥ* ("this is that fire"). Here, the word *agniḥ* [is the example].
The word *adhvara* is derived from the root *dhvar* with the suffix *ni*, according to the rule *ṭhanerṇilopaśca* (*aṅgernalopaśca*—Durgasiṃha’s commentary on Uṇādisūtra 1.20).
Thus, by the accent of the suffix, it is antodātta (accented on the final syllable);
since the *śaṣ* (the suffix *ni*) is anudātta, the vowel *a* is also anudātta. "This is that sacrifice."

The word *adhvara*, by the accent of its nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*), is udātta on the final syllable; consequently, the initial vowel *a* is also anudātta. [However,] it is prescribed as being udātta on the first syllable by the rule: "It is prescribed as having the first syllable udātta" (*ādyaudāto nipātyate*). This is according to the rule: "Ṛk, aj, indra, agra, vajra, vipra, kuvra, cuvra, kṣura, khura, bhadra, ugra, bhera, bhela, śūkara, śukla, gaura, vanara, irā, and malā" (Daiva 8.46). Regarding the phrase "this very one" (*so'yam*): the word *ayam* is udātta on the final syllable by the accent of its nominal stem, and its initial syllable is anudātta.
121. *Avapathāsi ca*.
(Pāṇini 6.1.121) As in: *yad rudrebhyo 'vapathāḥ*. This word *avapathāḥ* has its initial vowel [accented] by virtue of the accent of the suffix *aṭ*.
122. *sarvatra vibhāṣā goḥ* (6.1.122). 123. *avaṅ sphoṭāyanasya* (6.1.123).
[The word] "ṭha" is discontinued. Even if [the word] "iti" were to follow, then [the substitution would not apply] in cases such as *gavaudana*.

It might be so; therefore, because the word *atīti* lacks the svarita accent, it is discontinued. But then would [the substitution] not also apply before a consonant (*hal*)? To this he says: "The word *aci* is repeated again. This is from [sūtra 6.1.77], *iko yaṇ aci*; its repetition, moreover, occurs according to the maxim of the frog's leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*).
It should be understood that for those rules following "samprasāraṇācca" (Pāṇini 6.1.108) but preceding this present rule, there is no continuation (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "ati.
Thus it was stated previously: "And this [term] *aci* is a governing heading (*adhikāra*) from [the rule] *samprasāraṇācca* (6.1.108)."
Regarding the examples "gavāgram" and "gavājinam": these are either *bahuvrīhi* compounds or *tatpuruṣa* compounds.

"Gavoṣṭram" is a *dvandva* compound. As for the statement "this [compound] has its initial syllable acute," and so forth: here, when the *bahuvrīhi* analysis "gāvo 'gram asya" (of which the cows are foremost) is formed, there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member.

[The suffix] *prāpnoti* occurs, as does the substitution of *avaṅ*; therein, because it is *antaraṅga*, *avaṅ* takes effect. And that [substitution], when occurring, would—by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*)—be necessarily udātta on the final syllable of the word *go*, since it replaces [the final vowel of] *go* which is itself udātta on the final syllable due to internal proximity (*āntaryataḥ*). That being so, subsequently...

If the natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*) were applied, the final syllable of the first member would become udātta, whereas an initial udātta is desired; therefore, this substitute is prescribed as being udātta on the first syllable by way of a nipātana (irregularity). If that is so, would not that same nipātana-accent apply even in cases such as *tatpuruṣa* compounds? To this he says: "But elsewhere," and so forth.

"In other cases" means in the *tatpuruṣa* and *dvandva* compounds. Since this is a substitute for the word *go*, it is precisely the other word connected with it that is overridden by the accent of the *nipātana* (irregular formation), not the accent of the compound as a whole.
Therefore, in cases other than the *bahuvrīhi*—namely, in the *tatpuruṣa* and so forth—the final syllable of the compound is acute due to the rule governing compound-final accents.

The accent of the *nipātana* (irregular formation) is set aside [by this rule], as it is said: "The mention of Sphoṭāyana is for the sake of honor. But what is the reason that it does not serve to provide an option (*vikalpa*)? To this he says: "For the term *vibhāṣā* itself continues to apply.
For what purpose, then, is *avaṅ* prescribed? Why should not *ag* alone be prescribed? In that case as well—

Is it not established simply by the substitution of *hy*? It is indeed established; however, by the rule *ṭheṅḥ padāntādati* (6.1.109), the formation of a single preceding form (*pūrvarūpatva*) would result. But surely, once the augment *ak* has been applied, the word no longer ends in *eṅ*?
No, because the augment is included within the term "that" (*tadgrahaṇena*). For the substitution of *aikāra* had not yet taken effect at that point.
It cannot be said that there is no status as being at the end of a word.

124. *Indre ca nityam* (6.1.124). [The commentary says: "In that which resides in the word *indra*. That which resides in the word *indra* is "that which resides in *indra*"; furthermore, it should be understood as that which is a constituent part (*avayava*) residing within the word *indra*. By the preceding rule, the option was already established; [this rule makes it] obligatory.

In this case, since the status of [the action] as obligatory is already established by the very force of its commencement, the explicit mention of "obligatory" (nitya) is for the sake of what follows.

125. *plutapragṛhyā aci* (6.1.125). As in: *devadattā 3 atra tv asi*. The protracted (*pluta*) vowel is applied by the rule *dūrāddhūte ca* (8.2.84). Now, one might object: since the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* (8.2.1) declares that what precedes is as if non-existent, the protracted vowel is non-existent; how then [can it be subject to the following rule]?
Can the state of being a *prakṛti* (original form) be prescribed? To this he says: "By virtue of its basis," and so forth.

"Basis" (*āśraya*) means the act of taking as a basis (*āśrayaṇa*). This refers to the taking as a basis of the protracted vowel (*pluta*), which is the subject of the operation, in order to prescribe this effect of *prakṛti*-status. It is precisely because of this that the protracted vowel is established here when *prakṛti*-status is to be applied; otherwise, [it would not be].
Its adoption as the object of the operation would be purposeless. [The examples] "agnī" and so forth:

here, the designation *pragṛhya* applies by virtue of the rule "īdūded dvivacanam" (P. 1.1.11). Now, for what purpose is the word "acī" [stated], since the word "acī" already continues [from the previous rule]? To this [it is replied]:

He says: "While 'ac' is being carried over," and so forth. The purpose of the repeated mention of *ac* is so that the vowel (*ac*) which is the cause of the substitute may be understood as being the cause for the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). In this context, the substitute occurs where there is the preservation of the original form before a vowel—as in *jānū asya*.

In the case of *rujati jānū atya rujati*, there is indeed no causal relationship for the long vowel resulting from the homogeneous combination (*savarṇadīrghatva*) between the *u* in the word *jānu* and the following *a*, because that *u* is marked as *pragṛhya*. And here, it is not [the case].

It occurs as follows: *jānv-asya rujati* ("the knee of him hurts"). Although the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for the two preceding and following *u*-sounds is included under the term *pragṛhya* by virtue of the rule "as if belonging to the end and the beginning" (*antādivacca*, 6.1.85), nevertheless, the substitution of *yaṇ* [for the *u*] takes place when an *a*-sound follows.
It indeed occurs. For even here, the vowel *a* is not the cause for the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) operation.

However, if the letter *aj* were not mentioned again for the purpose of including a specific [vowel], then the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), being prescribed for all vowels (*añ*) in general, would certainly apply here as well. [This refers to the] designation of *pragṛhya*.
Furthermore, by the rule *nipāta ekājanāṅ* (Pāṇini 1.1.14), the vowel *u* preceded by *a* [in *vāyū*] is a particle (*nipāta*).

Regarding the phrase "the mention of *nitya*," etc.: if the mention of *nitya* were to carry over here, then because this rule would have already fulfilled its purpose in cases such as *agnī-aiti*, it would not apply in cases such as *vāyū-atra*.
Because it is subsequent, the rule of Śākalya would apply; therefore, the mention of "nitya" (invariable) is carried over here so that the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) alone may occur.

126. *Āṅe 'nunāsikaś chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.126). [The word] *āṅaḥ* means "of *āṅ*. This is the inclusion of the phoneme *a* as qualified by the marker *ṅ*. This is so that the reference may apply specifically to that [particle] which is used in the sense of "slightness" (*īṣadartha*), in connection with a verb (*kriyāyoga*), and in the senses of "limit exclusive" (*maryādā*) and "limit inclusive" (*abhividhi*).

This is for the purpose that [the substitution] of that [anusvāra] in the case of *vākya* and *smaraṇa* should not occur. For if the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-substitution) were not prescribed, even though the rule for the nasalization (*anunāsikatva*) of the prefix *āṅ* had been enjoined, *svarasaṃdhi* would still take place;
however, the prescription of nasalization would then serve only to ensure that the substitute itself is nasalized—this is what is kept in mind.
Having formed [the word], he says: "And it does not exist by its own nature. Regarding "ātarat":

this is the *laṅ* (imperfect) suffix after the root *tṛ* preceded by the prefix *ā*; there is the augment *aṭ*, and with that *aṭ*, there is the lengthening of the homogeneous vowel (*savarṇadīrghatva*).

127. *iko'savarṇe śākalyasya hrasvaśca* (Pāṇini 6.1.127). [The commentary states: "And for that *ik*, there occurs a short vowel in place of it. If this is so, the particle *ca* ("and") need not be employed to carry forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) the rule *prakṛtyā* (6.1.115); for indeed, by the very force of the prescription of the short vowel, [the original form is understood].

Will there not be vowel-sandhi (svarasandhi)? To this it might be argued: "Because of the force of the rule prescribing short vowels for those that are already long, there will be no vowel-sandhi [for them]; however, it would certainly occur for short vowels, for they do not become short [again]. This is because there is no purpose [in doing so]. But this is not the case.

For even in the case of short vowels, a short vowel indeed occurs for the purpose of preventing the application of vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*). This grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) certainly effects what has not yet been accomplished, like a rain-cloud; it does not effect what is already accomplished, like a fire. If that is so, then this is indicated by the letter *ca*: in certain instances, such as *īṣā-akṣa* and the like, there is simply the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*).
"Not shortness. Therefore, that which was stated—that in the case of *amīṣām* and so forth, there is merely the presence of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*)—need not be said.
Why is the mention of Śākalya not intended for the purpose of providing an option (*vikalpa*) with respect to the *yaṇ*-substitution?

Thus he says: "Precisely because of the capacity for the commencement [of the rule]," and so forth. For the domain of the *yaṇ* substitute is only a vowel (*ac*) that is non-homogeneous (*asavarṇa*); however, in the case of a homogeneous vowel, the long vowel is prescribed by the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (P. 6.1.101). This [short vowel] is also prescribed as the Śākala shortening. Therefore, in this [case]...

Since the optionality of this rule with respect to the *yaṇ* substitution is established by the very capacity of the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and the commencement (*ārambha*), the mention of the Teacher (*ācāryagrahaṇa*) is not for that purpose.
Regarding the rule "in the case of *sin*, a permanent compound (*nityasamāsa*), etc.": although the locative case (*saptamī*) is one, it is divided into two ways.
This is due to a difference in perspective: with respect to *sic*, it is a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*);

with respect to *nityasamāsa*, it is a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*). *Sic* and *nityasamāsa* form a copulative compound (*dvandva*): that which has *sic* is "that which has *sic*" (*sit*); a compound prescribed under the governing heading of "eternal" (*nitya*) is an "eternal compound" (*nityasamāsa*). This rule belongs to Śākalya.

Śākalaḥ: By [Pāṇini 4.2.111] *kaṇvādibhyo gotre*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied; by [6.4.148] *yasyeti ca*, there is elision of the vowel *a*; and by [6.4.151] *āpatyasya ca taddhite'nāti*, there is elision of the letter *ya*. "The prohibition of Śākala" (*śākalapratiṣedha*) means the prohibition regarding Śākala. [The word] "should be stated" (*vaktavya*)...

The meaning is that it must be explained. Here is the explanation: the term *vibhāṣā* ("optionally") is understood to carry over from the rule "sarvatra vibhāṣā goḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.122). And that [optionality] is to be understood as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Consequently, the prohibition of the *śākala* [substitution] will apply in the case of the suffix *sin* and in eternal compounds (*nityasamāsa*).

Regarding "ṛtviyaḥ": since the season (*ṛtu*) has arrived for him, [the suffix] *ghas* is applied by the rules *ṛtoraṇ* (Pāṇini 5.1.105) and *chandasi ghas* (5.1.106). Regarding "vyākaraṇam": the compound is formed by the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* (2.2.18);
for here, [the application of the rule] follows from *nityaṃ krīḍājīvikayoḥ* (2.2.17).

Because of the continued application of the term "nitya" (obligatory), this is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*). Regarding the example "kumāryartham": "this is for the sake of the girl" means "belonging to the girl. According to the Vārttika: "The statement that there is a compound with the word *artha* [results in] all genders," this too is indeed an obligatory compound. This applies in all cases.
When the Śākala rule is prohibited, the substitution of *yaṇ* still takes place.

128. *ṛtyakaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.128). [The commentary states: "This rule is for the sake of [preserving] the homogeneous (*savarṇa*) vowel and for the sake of preventing the substitution of *i*. This is because elsewhere [the result] would already be established by the preceding rule. If this rule is indeed for the sake of the homogeneous vowel, how then is *khaṭvarśyaḥ* given as an example? It is not [an example of that].

In this case, there is no vowel (*ac*) following a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) vowel; this is not so. What was stated [in the rule] "and for the sake of *ṭhaN*" is its illustration. For this very reason, "ak" is employed in the sūtra; otherwise, "ik" would have to be carried over [from a previous rule]. When this rule exists, even for the purpose of denoting a homogeneous vowel, the substitute "ak" occurs by this very [rule].
The introduction of this subsequent example is intended to demonstrate that the substitution of the short vowel takes effect due to its priority.

129. *aplutavad upasthite* (6.1.129). That which exists in the Veda of the seers (*ṛṣi*) is called *ārṣa*; other than that is the worldly, non-*ārṣa*. "From the whole" means from the sentence. Why is this so? Because a sentence devoid of words is never employed.

And because a sentence consists of a collection [of words], the term "having separated" (avacchidya) means "having made distinct. The phrase "is established in its own form" (svarūpe vyavasthāpyate)—as the *Kāśikā* reads "established in its own form"—means that it is established in the state of being a word-unit consisting of sound. The term "as if unprotracted" (aplutavat) [is used].
It "behaves like" (*vartate*) that which is "like *apluta*" (*aplutavat*); in order to show the property by virtue of which it becomes "like *apluta*," he says: "the effect of *pluta*," and so forth.
By this, it is shown that there is a prohibition of the effect of *pluta* with respect to its purpose, but not of the *pluta* itself.
It occurs as "suślokā3" [with a protracted vowel]. According to the rule *dūrāddhūte ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.84), there is a protraction (*pluta*).

In the case of "suślokā," because the grammatical operation of protraction is not actually performed, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) certainly takes place. But should it not also fail to occur by virtue of the single-substitute rule itself, since that too is subject to the same operation of protraction?

This is not the case; for if it were so, the statement would be rendered purposeless. Therefore, by the very mention of the *pluta* [vowel], there is a prohibition only of that specific operation prescribed for a *pluta*, and not of every operation pertaining to a *pluta*. Furthermore, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is not prescribed in this manner.

"What is the purpose of using *vat*? [The answer is: The use of *vat* is for the sake of ensuring that the *pluta* (protracted vowel) is heard even when there is a prohibition of every grammatical operation (*kāryamātra*). Furthermore, even though the *prakṛtibhāva* (original form) is a specific operation, by the very prohibition of every operation, the hearing of the *pluta* ought to occur through a partial application (*ekadeśena*).

Because [the rule] has already been revoked. The intention is: "Why is a prohibition not made specifically for the *pluta* vowel? Having kept in mind the fault that will be stated regarding the prohibition of the *pluta*, he says: "If it were said 'in the case of a *pluta*'," and so forth. "What fault would there be in that? That which...

The sense is that when the suffix *vat* is employed, [the original quality] does not occur. Regarding the phrase "when there is reliance on a *pragṛhya*" and so forth: if there were a substitution (*prati* = *pratiṣedha*) based on reliance upon a *pragṛhya*, then in the case of a *pluta* vowel bearing the designation *pragṛhya*, its audible pronunciation would not take place if only the *pluta* itself were prohibited. However, since the suffix *vat* is employed...

This prohibition applies to the *pluta* vowel that has undergone the operation, not to the *pluta* vowel itself. In that case, although the *prakṛtibhāva* (original form retention) based on the *pluta* vowel is prohibited, since the *pragṛhya* status is not prohibited, there is no fault regarding the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) itself—as in the example "agnī iti. This is because of the rule *idūdeddvivacanam* (Pāṇini 1.1.11).
By such rules as these, the designation *pragṛhya* is established; and by rules such as *guroranṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.86), the *pluta* vowel lengthening is prescribed.

130. *ī 3 cākravarmaṇasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.130). [The commentary states: "When *ṭhaC* follows. By this, it indicates that the rule "*ṭhupasthite*" has been superseded, because [the former] lacks the *svarita* accent. [The example given is: *astu hī 3*. [The root is] *asU* in the sense of "throwing."

The suffix *loṭ* with the ending *sip*. By the rule *ser hy apicca* (Pāṇini 3.4.87), *si* is replaced by *hi*, which is also indicatory (*apit*). Due to the transposition [of the root], there is *ślu*-elision. By the rule *kṣiyā-āśīḥ-praiṣeṣu tiṅākāṅkṣam* (Pāṇini 8.2.104), there is the protracted (*pluta*) vowel.

"In order to prevent [the application] when it has already occurred"; for in that case, the state of being treated as *apluta* would have been obligatory by the preceding rule. "In order to bring about [the application] when it has not yet occurred"; for in that case, it would not have been obtained by any other rule.

"From *ṭhīkārāt*," and so forth. But how is this absence of the treatment as a protracted vowel (*aplutavat*) obtained even elsewhere than after the vowel *i*, even though it is desired there? [It is obtained] because of the word *ikaḥ* which is carried over (*anuvṛtta*) from [Pāṇini 6.1.127]: "In place of *ika*, when followed by a non-homogeneous vowel, according to Śākalya, there is also a short vowel."
Because the particle *ca* has the sense of including that which is not explicitly mentioned.

131. *diva ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.131). [The commentary says: "Because it possesses an *anubandha*. Of which verbal root (*dhātu*) is this immediately after? Because it is the subject under discussion, it is that very one. The verbal root *dīv* is with an *anubandha*, but the nominal stem (*pratipadika*) is...

This [term] *divi* is without an indicatory letter (*niranubandhaka*), and it is the one without an indicatory letter that is employed in the sūtra; therefore, according to the principle "when there is the mention of a form without an indicatory letter, that which has an indicatory letter is not included" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 53), this is the mention of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), not of the verbal root (*dhātu*). [Thus, the example is] *dyaukāmaḥ*.

*Divikāmaḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose desire is heaven," or "one who desires heaven. The suffix *ṇa* is applied according to the rule: "The suffix *ṇa* should be stated after [roots ending in] *śīli*, *kāmi*, *bhikṣā*, and *cari*" (Vārttika 229). Regarding *dyumān*: it means "one who possesses heaven" (*dyauḥ asyāsti*), by applying the suffix *matup* according to the rule: "*tat-asyāsti-asminn-iti-matup*" (Pāṇini 5.2.94).

Regarding "ṭhvimaladyau dinamÂ": this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which the sky (*dyau*) is clear (*vimalā*). Regarding "ṭhakṣadyaūbhyāmÂ, akṣadyaūbhiḥ": when the word *akṣa* is used as an *upapada*, the root *div* takes the suffix *kvip*;
then, by the rule "ṭhcchÂaṣoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.19), the substitution *ūṭh* occurs.
Now, for what purpose is the use of the marker *t*? For although it has been indicated by the rule *ṛta ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.111)—

specifically by the use of the marker *t*— that "even a vowel being taught [as a substitute] includes its homogeneous counterparts" (*bhāvyamāno 'py ukāraḥ savarṇān gṛhṇāti*), nevertheless, in this case, by virtue of proximity (*antaryataḥ*), [it would apply only to that which shares] a duration of half a mora (*ardhamātrākāla*).
"Will [the substitution] apply only to the short vowel of the semi-vowel substitute, and not to the long one?

To this he says: "The rule for the formation of the nominative case," and so forth. Even though by this [rule] the long vowel does not obtain, by another rule (lakṣaṇāntara) the substitution of *uṭ* would obtain in cases such as *dyaubhyām* and *dyaubhiḥ*; therefore, that [long vowel]...
The addition of *t* (the *tapara* marker) is for the purpose of ensuring that [the substitution] does not occur. One might object:

"But surely there is no possibility of *ūṭh* at all; what then is the use of adding *t* to exclude it? To this he says: "dyaubhyām, dyaubhiḥ. "For here," and so forth. The scope of the substitution of *u* (*utva*) is where a *kvip* suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant follows.
The [substitution] *ūṭh* does not occur—[as in] *vimaladyau dinam* ("the day with a clear sky") and *akṣadyaūbhyām* ("by two dice").

In cases such as *dyaubhyām*, where both [rules] would apply, *ūṭh* would prevail due to its higher status [in the order of rules]; however, because of the inclusion of the long vowel marker *Ṭ* (taparakaraṇa), only the substitution *ut* takes place. If, then, this is for the purpose of precluding the application of *ūṭh*...
The addition of the long vowel marker (*tapara*) is made for this purpose; for if that were not the case, then regarding the rule *ṭhcachÂavoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca* (P.

6.4.19), when the objection is raised as to how one obtains forms such as *dyaubhyām* and *dyaubhiḥ*, he will state: "Once *ūṭh* has been applied, by virtue of the subsequent rule *ṭhdiva ut* (P. 6.1.131), there will be a substitution of *ut* having the duration of one mātrā."

That is contradictory; does this mean that once *ṭhūṭ* has been applied and [the *ṭ*] has been replaced, the letter *u* will take its place for the duration of one *mātrā*? There is no contradiction; for the connection of the passage "once *ṭhūṭ* has been applied" is with the preceding passage containing the objection (*codya*), and not with the subsequent passage containing the resolution (*parihāra*).
In this regard, when the alternative view is presented that "some do not carry forward [the condition] *kṅti* here," the objection is raised:
"How [can there be] *dyaubhyām* and *dyaubhiḥ* once *ūṭh* has been applied? The intention of the objector here is as follows: if *kṅti* were not carried forward, then in the case of *dyaubhyām*...
The form *dyobhiḥ* must indeed be accomplished by means of the substitution of *au*; for once that substitution has been made, how can *dyobhyām* and *dyobhiḥ* be established?

Since [the expected forms] would have to be *dyūbhyām* and *dyūbhiḥ*, this objection is resolved by the fact that in the rule "diva aut," the vowel *u* is marked with the *t*-pratyāhāra (taparatva), which ensures that the duration will be one mātrā. Thus, it is so.
The rebuttal: Here too, this is the intention of the respondent—the very purpose of the inclusion of *ta* (the long *t*) is precisely so that *ūṭh* shall not occur; otherwise, it would be useless.
Therefore, only *utva* (the substitution of *u*) should be applied, and not the state of *ūṭh*. As for those [who argue] regarding "before *kṅit*"...
They continue [the application] in this way; for them, the inclusion of *t* (the *tapara*) is for the sake of clarity.

132. *etadadoḥ sulopo’ko’nañsamāse hali* (6.1.132). [The commentary states: "In a *nañ*-compound, these two [words] do not occur. By this, showing the connection with the action, he demonstrates that *anañsamāse* is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (an absolute negation). For, in the case of a *paryudāsa* (an exclusionary negation),...

By the logic of "the presence of *nañ*" (*nañivayukta-nyāya*) [Pāṇini-vyākaraṇa-pariśiṣṭa 65], [the designation of *saṃpradāna*] would apply to those two words occurring in a compound other than a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), as in *paramaiṣa dadāti* ("this best person gives") or *paramasa dadāti*; however, it would not apply in cases such as *eṣa dadāti* ("this one gives") or *sa dadāti* ("that one gives"). Now, [regarding the rule] *sa saṃpradānam* (Pāṇini 1.4.32):
Does this kind of instruction indicate that [the suffix] occurs even when there is no compound (*asamāsa*)? It is said:

even so, this would not apply to the word *etad*. However, the intention is that if one were to rely on the indicator (*jñāpaka*) as being dependent on a specific grammatical rule (*yoga*), there would be an excessive burden on the learner (*pratipatti-gaurava*). [The rule states: "Of those two, the word *su*... By this...

He explains that this genitive case in the rule *ṭhetatadoḥ* is one denoting a relationship (*sambandhalakṣaṇā*) with respect to the word *su*. If this is so, then because the word *su* is dependent [on another], it lacks syntactic independence (*asāmarthya*), and thus its composition (*samāsa*) with the word *lopa* would not be possible. [To this, he replies: Because it conveys the meaning (*gamakatva*), composition is possible even for that which is dependent.

There is no fault, for it will come to pass. Or else—since there is no identical designation (*asamānanirdeśa*), a compound with the word *lopa* would not be possible; however, because it is expressive (*gamaka*), a compound may occur even when there is a dependency, so there is no fault. Or else—this is precisely a non-identical designation, but [the word] *ṣaṣṭhī*...

"It is not heard [in the grammatical operation] because it has been elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). And which *su*-word belongs to those two?"—thus he thinks: either the *su*-word would be related to these two (*etad* and *tad*) by way of a relationship characterized by immediate proximity, or by way of their meaning; for in that case...
In the former view, there would also be the inclusion of the locative plural;

for that [plural] is indeed related to *etad* and *adas* by way of the relationship characterized by immediate proximity (*ānantarya*). In the other view, however, the very prohibition "in a non-compound with *nañ*" (*anañ-samāse*) would be rendered useless—as in the case of *aneṣo dadāti*.

"‘Asau’ gives [the result]. For here, by means of the compound, the word *su-* is related only to the compound itself, and not to *etad* or *adas*. But surely, because it possesses an *anubandha*, the locative plural should not even be suspected? This is not so; for even the nominative singular— [...is not excluded. Why? Because the *anubandha* is merely for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), and therefore it does not prevent the application of grammatical operations (*kārya*). Furthermore, the *anubandha* is not applied to the form that undergoes the operation; rather, it is applied to the item (*padārtha*) that serves as the cause (*nimitta*) for the operation. And since the nominative singular is indeed the cause for the substitution of *adas* with *tadoḥ*, the nominative singular is certainly included. Moreover, the *anubandha* is not applied to the entire word-form (*sarvādeśa*), but only to the portion that is being replaced (*ādeśya*). Therefore, the nominative singular is not excluded.
