In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the quality [of the subordinate member] is understood (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*), it refers specifically to that which has a single *anubandha*.

This should be understood with reference to the rule "when there is the mention of that which has a single *anubandha*, [there is no application of] that which has two *anubandhas*" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 52), wherein the mention of that which has a single *anubandha* occurs.

In that case, if the *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (non-inclusion of the qualifier) is accepted, this statement would not be tenable; for there is no such thing as the word *su* apart from its *anubandha*, but rather the word *sa*. However, there is this distinction: for one [form], the letter *p* is the *anubandha*, while for the other, it is the letter *u*. Therefore, [the rule applies] to both.
Because it possesses a continuous connection (*sānubandhakatva*), one might also reasonably suspect that the locative plural ending (*saptamī-bahuvacana*) is intended.

However, keeping in mind that "I shall refute later whatever fault exists in the second alternative," he says: "that which has a connection with the purpose of that. By speaking thus, [he indicates] the nominative singular (*prathama-ekavacana*).

It is stated that [the suffix] belongs to those two. How so? For the words *etad* and *tat* are nominal stems (*prātipadika*). Here, the view that "the meaning of a nominal stem consists of three factors" (*trika*) has been adopted.
For instance, in the rule "the plural is used for many" (*bahuṣu bahuvacanam*, Pāṇini 1.4.21), the plural occurs when there are many.

It exists; the meaning is that plurality (*bahutva*) is to be expressed as indeterminate (*asandigdha*). By stating in [Pāṇini 1.4.21], "Action (*karman*) and others are also among the meanings of the case-endings (*vibhakti*)," it is shown that number and action, etc., are the meanings expressed by the case-endings; and by implication, the state of being a triplet (*trikatva*) [is also established].
Since it is established that "the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of its own referent, substance,
and gender," when there is singularity of that meaning of the nominal stem, only the nominative singular case ending occurs,
not the locative plural. The locative plural occurs only when there is plurality belonging to a different grammatical coreferent (*vyadhikaraṇa*).

Therefore, through the meaning of the two words *etad* and *adas*, it is only the nominative singular that is connected [to the verb], not the locative plural. In the example "he gives this" (*eṣa dadāti*), the substitution of *s* occurs by the rule "the *t* of *tad* becomes *s* before the nominative singular suffix when it is not final" (Pāṇini 7.2.106).

The substitution of *yat* for *tyad* and so forth occurs; then, by the rule "ādeśapratyayayoḥ" (8.3.59), there is the substitution of *ṣ*. Thus, we have "eṣakaḥ. By the rule "avyayasava-nāmnām akac prāk ṭeḥ" (5.3.71), the suffix *akac* is added.
Now, one might object: since these two forms, when accompanied by *akac*, have different shapes, they are not *etad* and *tad*; therefore, why [is this rule applied]?
Is it not because of the prohibition "not after *ṭha* or *ka*" (*ṭhakoḥ*)? To this he says: "That which falls in between them" (*tanmadhyapatitaḥ*), and so forth.

And the very existence of this Paribhāṣā (Vyā.pa. 21) is indicated by this prohibition "not after *ṭha* or *ka*" (*ṭhakoḥ*), as well as by [the rule] "not for *idaṃ* and *adas*, except after *ṭha* or *ka*" (*nedamadasorakoḥ*, 7.1.11).
But surely, once a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) has been formed, the suffix *su* (nominative case ending) belongs to a different word;

this is not a fault, and therefore there is no occasion for the objection—so what is the purpose of the prohibition "not in a negative compound" (*nañ-samāse*)? To this he says: "Because the meaning of the final member is predominant," and so forth. Even though...

The negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) is a distinct word; nevertheless, because it has the meaning of the final member as its predominant sense, and because the pronouns *etad* and *tad* function as the final members, the suffix *su* is produced precisely with respect to the number associated with them, and thus the *su* occurs only for those two.

Therefore, the negation "there is attainment" (prāpti) is established. Why [is it said] "in a compound" (samāse)? So that the negation does not apply to a sentence—such as "he does not give this," or "he does not see that."

133. *syaś chandasi bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.1.133). The term *syaḥ* is the nominative singular of *tyad-*; this is its citation form (*anukaraṇa*). The genitive case ending that arises from it is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk...* (Pāṇini 7.1.39), etc.

There is simply no production of it, because the distinction between the original object of imitation (*anukārya*) and the imitation itself (*anukaraṇa*) is not intended to be expressed, as in the expression "He says 'go'. However, in the actual example, the grammatical operations such as *satva* (substitution of *s*) and so forth apply just as before.
134. *so'ci lope cetpādapūraṇam* (Pāṇini 6.1.134).
The rule *so'ci* is as before; it is an imitation of that [word] ending in the nominative singular.
"Fulfillment of the verse" (*pādapūraṇa*) means the completion of the metrical line.

But surely, by the very force of the rule's formulation, it is understood that [the substitution occurs] before a vowel, since it would already be established before a consonant; so for what purpose is "before a vowel" (aci) stated? To this he says:
"The word 'aci' is for the sake of clarity."
"Some desire [this]," they say; however, they do not carry over the mention of "desire" (icchā).

135. *suṭ* is substituted for the letter preceding *ka*. (Pāṇini 6.1.135) In the word *saṃskartā*, the substitution of *s* occurs for the *m* of *sam* either by the metarule (*vārttika*) "there is *s*-substitution for *sam*, *puṃs*, and *kān*" (Vārttika 936), or by the indicative statement (*nirdeśa*) "for *sam* when *suṭ* follows" (Pāṇini 8.3.5).
In this context, by the rule *ṭhānunāsikaḥ pūrvasya tu vā* (Pāṇini 8.3.2), the preceding vowel *ā* may optionally become nasalized.

Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of "preceding *k*" (*kātpūrva*)? For, since *suṭ* is indicated by its initial letter and the root *karoti* begins with the letter *k*, even without the mention of "preceding *k*," [the rule would apply] because of the principle that "an augment is both at the beginning and at the end."
One might ask: "Will not *suṅ* occur precisely before the *k* by virtue of the rule *ṭakitau* (1.1.46)? To this he says:

"The mention of 'before the *k*' (*kātpūrvagrahaṇam*)," and so forth. Furthermore, what desired result is established if [the augment] is not a part of the word (*abhakta*), such that an effort is made toward the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of that fact? To this he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*).

And so forth. [The opponent asks: "But what is desired to be established when there is non-devotion [to the teacher], such that an effort is made toward its indicator? To this he says: "For instance," and so forth. Regarding the form *saṃskṛṣīṣṭa*: it is the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), with the suffix *sīyuṭ* and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*); [the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs] by the rule *uśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.12).
Because it is *kit*, there is no *guṇa* substitution; by the rule *suṭ-tiyoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.107), the augment *suṭ* is added after the letter *t*.

This *suṭ* precedes the *k*. If this were a part (*bhakta*) of the root *kṛ*, then because it would be included by the mention of *kṛ*, the root *kṛñ* would become "beginning with a conjunct consonant" (*saṃyogādi*), and consequently [the rule] *ṛtaśca*... [would apply].

The augment *iṭ* would apply [to the root] by the rule "after a consonant cluster, etc. (*saṃyogādeḥ*, 7.2.43). In the form "saṃskriyate," the present tense marker *laṭ* is used in the passive voice with the middle ending (*ātmanepada*), followed by the suffix *yak*; then, by the rule "riṅ for *śya*, *yac*, and *liṅ*" (*riṅ śayagliṅkṣu*, 7.4.28), there is the substitution of *riṅ*. In that case, if *suṭ* were a part of the root *kṛ*, then...

If the augment *suṭ* were part of the root *kṛ*, then because it would begin with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogāditva*), the rule "there is guṇa for roots beginning with a conjunct or the root *ṛ*" (Pāṇini 7.4.29) would apply, resulting in guṇa. However, if it is not part of the root (*abhaktatve*), then because *suṭ* does not begin with a conjunct, neither the augment *iṭ* nor guṇa occurs. [This is shown by the rule] "a finite verb form [is unaccented] after another finite verb form" (Pāṇini 8.1.28), and so forth, provided that it is not part of the root.

When *suṭ* is applied, as in the case of *saṃskriyate*, the *nighāta* accent prescribed by *tiṅṅtiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28) is not established because the *pada* [containing the verb] is separated from *suṭ*. Nor can *suṭ* itself be considered a *pada* such that the rule applies to it; for, due to the governing heading *padāt* (Pāṇini 8.1.17), *suṭ* does not possess the status of a *pada*.
The phrase "in a rule concerning vowels," etc., is the solution.

By the rule *ṛtaśca saṃyogādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.43), a *guṇa* is prescribed for a verbal base (*aṅga*) ending in *ṛ* that begins with a conjunct consonant when followed by the *liṭ* suffix; and this [guṇa] applies when the *suṭ* augment is not present.
Thinking that [the augment] *suṭ* is not applicable because the root *kṛ* begins with a non-conjunct consonant (*asaṃyogādi*), he says "sañcaskaratuḥ" and so forth.
[The question] "How is there guna? means "In no way. [The answer] "tanmadhya" and so forth:
once reduplication has been performed, there are two instances of the root *kṛ*, and this *suṭ* occurs in between them.
Therefore, according to the principle that "that which falls within [the scope of] a term is included by the mention of that term" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 29),
it is indeed included by the mention of *karoti*; consequently, the intention is that for the root *kṛ*, there is no status as being "not preceded by a conjunct consonant" (*asaṃyogādi*).

But surely, on the view that "doubling is the double usage [of a word]," only the utterance differs while the verbal root remains one and the same; how then can there be a doubling of the root *kṛ*? This is not a fault, for although the root is undivided, its distinction is nevertheless based on the distinction of the utterances.

This is because of the rule "ṭhaṅbhyāsavyavāye’pi" (Pāṇini 6.1.136). For if there were no distinction [between the presence and absence of an intervening element], there would be no intervention at all, and thus the mention of "repetition" (abhyāsa) would be purposeless. Even if, by some means, that [intervening element] were included by the mention of that term, even so, the guṇa substitution would certainly still occur.

Showing this, he says: "saṃyoga," etc. For if there were the inclusion of the term "saṃyogopadha" (having a conjunct as its penultimate), then—by means of the quality of having a conjunct as its penultimate, namely "that which has a conjunct as its penultimate"—the vowel *ṛ* would first be qualified, and subsequently, by that [quality], the stem (*aṅga*) would be qualified, meaning "of a stem ending in that. In that case, although...

The root *kṛ* does not have a conjunct as its penultimate letter (*upadhā*), but it does have the vowel *ṛ*; therefore, the *guṇa* substitution certainly occurs. If that is so, then *suṭ* is not a part [of the root].
For what purpose is the marker *ṭ* applied? It is indeed for the sake of making it a part of that [root], because by virtue of having *ṭ* as its initial [marker], it becomes a constituent part of it.

It is done for this very purpose. If *suṭ* were not a *bhakta* (an augment attached to the beginning), then the employment of the marker *ṭ* would indeed result in being purposeless; therefore, he says "the employment of *ṭ*" and so forth.
If it were stated as "after *su*, *stu*, and *savañj*," then [the rule would apply] to the word *su* in forms such as *sure*.

If [the rule] were to apply to that which is also "approachable" (upasarya), then the substitution of *ṣ* would undesirably follow even in cases such as *atisusthiraḥ* and *atisusthitaḥ*. Therefore, the addition of the marker *ṭi* is for the purpose of specification.

136. *aḍabhyāsavyavāye’pi* (6.1.136). [The sūtra reads: "even when there is intervention by *aṭ* or by the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). *Vyavāya* means intervention or separation. Because of the word *api* ("also"), it applies even when there is no intervention. If the word *api* were not present, it would apply only when there is intervention.

Regarding "samaskarot": this is the *laṅ* [aorist] tense. Regarding "samaskārṣīt": this is the *luṅ* [aorist] tense; the *cli* suffix is replaced by *sic*, and by the rule "vṛddhi before *sic*" (Pāṇini 7.2.1), there is *vṛddhi* [of the root vowel]; by the rule "and after [a root ending in] *it*" (3.4.100), there is the elision of the *ikāra*; and by the rule "the augment *iṭ* is applied after *asti* and *sic*" (7.3.96), the *iṭ* augment is added. [The form] "sañcaskaratuḥ" [is derived similarly].
Thus: [regarding] the *liṭ* suffix.

If the verbal root (*dhātu*) is first joined with its grammatical factor (*sādhana*), then, once the *l*-suffix has been applied to denote that factor, the augment *aṭ* and the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) must occur by virtue of being caused by it; and consequently—

Since the suffix *suṅ* would not apply when there is an intervention by that [prefix], its formulation is appropriate for that purpose. Furthermore, the verbal root is not first joined with the grammatical factor (*sādhana*), but rather with the prefix (*upasarga*). For if the root were first joined with the factor and only afterwards with the prefix, then [the form] would be *anubhūyate kambalaḥ*.
In the case of *devadattena*, the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) would not occur in the sense of the object (*karman*), because the root *bhū* is intransitive (*akarmaka*).

However, when the prefix (*upasarga*) is first connected with the verbal root, this fault does not arise at all; for even intransitive roots become transitive (*sakarmaka*) when accompanied by a prefix. Therefore, [the prefix must be connected] first...

A verbal root is joined with a prefix, and therefore the operation concerning the root and the prefix is internal (*antaranga*); for the root and prefix, which are the causes of that [operation], are applied even before the augment *aṭ* and the reduplication, because there is no distinction between them as causes. However, the augment *aṭ* and the reduplication are external (*bahiraṅga*).
Because it depends on specific conditions that arise at a later time, and because *suṭ* is an operation pertaining to the verbal root (*dhātu*) and the prefix (*upasarga*),
since it is caused by them;
therefore, due to its being "internal" (*antaraṅga*), the application of the root and the prefix occurs immediately.

It must be so; for one who has not yet produced the cause [of the augment] will not even employ the arising of the suffix *la*, let alone the [augment] *aṭ* or reduplication (*abhyāsa*). With this intention, he says: "But for what purpose is this stated? and so forth. The other [teacher], however, [holds that] this [augment] *suṭ* does not apply at all where it has not been prescribed.

It is commenced for the purpose of attainment. What then? It is said—"the word 'pūrvam' and so forth"—in order to demonstrate that [the augment] *suṭ* should occur when there is an intervention by *aṭ* and reduplication (*abhyāsa*) after they have already been applied, but it should not occur when they have not yet been applied; the particle *iti* signifies a reason. In that context, of the root...
The prior connection with the prefix (*upasarga*) is the cause for the insertion of *suṭ* when it has already become internal; that is, the reason for performing the insertion of *suṭ* first.

Furthermore, [the rule] "after that, the augment *aṭ* and the reduplication (*abhyāsa*)" implies that these two must be performed. Since the verbal root (*dhātu*) is joined with the prefix first, the operation [applies] between the root and the prefix.

"Does no undesirable consequence follow at all? To this he says: "It has been stated that *suṭ* is not a suffix (*abhakta*)," and so forth. For it was already established previously that *suṭ* is not a suffix;
therefore, since it is not included by the mention of the root *kṛ*, the two [suffixes] occurring after it arise from the letter *s*.

The intention is that if the *parā* and *avaḍ* substitutions were to occur in an undesirable place, then the desired form would not be established. Now, [the author] asks: even if this [substitution] exists, how is it that this fault does not arise?
He says: "But when this [rule] exists, truly indeed," and so forth. In this sūtra, however, "truly indeed" (*satyata eva*)...
As long as there is no intervention by the augment *aṭ* or the reduplication (*abhyāsa*), the augment *suṭ* must certainly be applied.

Therefore, *aṭ* and the reduplication should be performed first; then, when there is that intervention, the rule "the augment *suṭ* comes before the root-initial consonant" (Kāt pūrvaṃ suṭ) ensures that everything desired is accomplished.
137. [The suffix *kṛt* is applied] after the roots preceded by *sam*, *pari*, and *upa*, when used with the verb *kṛ* in the sense of adornment.

(Pāṇini 6.1.137). Regarding the statement, "In some cases, even when not in the sense of adornment, it is desired for the root preceded by *sam*," how is this desired application obtained? It is obtained from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the Teacher’s practice, namely the rule: "The word *saṃskṛta* [is used] in the sense of prepared foods" (Pāṇini 4.2.16).
138. *samavāye ca*.

(6.1.138) "Samavāyaḥ" means "a collection" (*samudāyaḥ*). From the root *i* preceded by *sam-ava*, the suffix *ac* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to Pāṇini 3.3.56 (*erac*). Thus, "samavāya" means a "conglomeration" (*saṅghāta*); it means "assembled" (*samudita*).
Firm resolve regarding existence.
139. *Upāt* [is used] in the senses of effort (*pratiyatna*), transformation (*vaikṛta*), completion of a sentence (*vākyādhyāhāra*), and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "of that which has acquired existence" (*sataḥ*) and so on: when another quality (*guṇāntara*)—distinct from the qualities previously produced—is brought about or generated for an object that has already attained existence, by means of that [action], it is called *upaskāra*.

This is the "imparting of another quality" (*guṇāntarādhāna*). For what purpose is this? He says: "for the sake of excellence," and so forth. What is that? He says: "effort" (*samīhā*). Thus, for the sake of the excellence—that is, the increase—of an existing entity, and for the maintenance of that very state of increase once it has increased.

The application of another quality for the sake of non-decline through a specific effort and exertion is called *pratiyatna* (polishing/refinement). "Altered" (*vikṛta*) means that a transformation has occurred.
"Of a sentence whose meaning is already understood in its own form" [is said because] words applied to wholes [function in that way].
The meaning perceived according to the rule "words also apply to their constituent parts" (*Vyāḍi-pāṭha-sūtra* 85)— namely,

that the word "sentence" (*vākya*) refers to a single portion of a sentence due to context and so forth— is the "supplying of a sentence" (*vākyādhyāhāra*). This consists in the explicit mention of the form of a meaning even when it is already implied, for the sake of easy comprehension.

140. *kiratau lavane* (Pāṇini 6.1.140). Regarding the phrase "in the context of cutting" (*lavanaviṣaye*), etc., this indicates that "cutting" (*lavana*) is not a qualifier of the root *kṛ* (*kirati*) by way of being its denotation (*abhidheyatayā*), but rather that it is the state of being the domain (*viṣayabhāva*) for the meaning of that [root]. By what [is this shown]?

Furthermore, the suffix *ṇamul* is used here; for by the rule "The suffix *ṇamul* [is applied] when there is frequency" (Pāṇini 3.4.22), etc., that suffix is prescribed even in senses such as frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*). Yet, neither is that sense intended to be expressed here, nor is it perceived; thus he says: "The suffix *ṇamul* here," and so forth. [Regarding the word] "it should be stated."

The meaning is that it must be explained. Regarding that, the explanation is as follows: it will be established by virtue of the word "bahulam" (diversely) from the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.113).

141. *hiṃsāyāṃ prateśca* (6.1.141). Regarding the phrase "in the sense of injury" (*hiṃsāyāṃ viṣaye*), this shows that injury is not a qualifier of the root *kṛ* (to scatter) by way of being its expressed meaning; rather, it qualifies the meaning of that root by way of being its scope (*viṣaya*).

Regarding the word *pratiskīrṇam*: there is the substitution of *i* for the root vowel by *ṛta iddhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.100), followed by the replacement of *ṛ* with *ra*; then, the substitution of *ṇ* for the final *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix by *radābhyām* (8.2.42) and other rules; and finally, the lengthening of the vowel *i* by *hali ca* (8.2.77). By the phrase "in that manner" (*tathā*) and so forth, [the author] indicates that the meaning of the root *kṛ* (kirati) pertains here to the domain of injury (*hiṃsā*).
"He shows" means "he follows"; the sense is that he goes after.

142. *apāccatuṣpācchakuniṣvālekhane* (Pāṇini 6.1.142). Regarding the phrase "in that context" (*tasmin viṣaye*), etc.: by this [sūtra] as well, he demonstrates that "scratching" (*ālekhanam*) is not a qualifier of the root *kṛ* (kirati) by way of its denotation (*abhidheyatayā*), but rather as the objective domain (*viṣayabhāvena*) of its meaning.

Regarding "ṭhapaskirate": the suffix *śa* is applied by the rule "tudādibhyaḥ śaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.77); as before, there is the substitution of *i* for the root vowel and the replacement of *r* with *ra*. By the phrase "having written" (*ālikhya*) and so forth, he demonstrates that writing constitutes the object-domain of the meaning of the root *kṛ* (here, *kirati*). "Having written" (*ālikhya*) means "having drawn out" (*ākṛṣya*).

Since the term *ālekhana* (scratching) is mentioned in a general sense as a means for quadrupeds and birds, it would follow that this [term] applies here as well—as in the expression "he scatters a ball of boiled rice.
Therefore, he states this qualification of *ālekhana*: "for joy and livelihood," and so forth. *Harṣa* means intense delight.
*Jīvikā* means the means of sustaining life; *kulāya* means a dwelling or hermitage.

But what is the reason that the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) occurs after *harṣa*, *jīvikā*, and *kulāya*, yet not in this counter-example? To this he says: "Only when [the action] consists of joy, livelihood, or making a dwelling," and so forth.
143. *kustumburu* [is used] for *jāti* (a genus).

(Pāṇini 6.1.143) Now, since the term is indicated in the sūtra in the neuter gender, it should apply only to the neuter gender when referring to a genus of fruits (*phalajāti*), and not to other genders, such as a genus of medicinal herbs (*oṣadhijāti*).
It must occur only in the plural and not elsewhere, because it is indicated by the plural number.
To the question, "How then does it occur in the masculine gender and in the singular in the word *kustumburu*? he says:
"In the indication of the sūtra," and so forth. The mention of the neuter gender is merely illustrative.

For even the plural number is indeed non-essential (atantra) in the Sūtra. And so it has been said: "In the Sūtra (i.e., in the grammatical reference to a Sūtra), the neuter gender is not intended to be significant; likewise, gender and number are non-essential because they are not intended to be significant" (Kāśikā and Padamañjarī). [The citation from the Kāśikā is not present here.]
Thus [it is said].

144. *aparaspara-* [is used] in the sense of continuity of action. (Pāṇini 6.1.144). Regarding *aparasparāḥ*: it is a *dvandva* compound meaning "others and others. When the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is applied to the word *santata*, it becomes *sāntatyam*.

With the intention that [the state] must come to be, he says "What is this? and so forth. Showing that this abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) has arisen from the word *satata* itself, he says "The state of being constant" (*satatasya bhāvaḥ*) and so forth. To the question "How is it constant?", he thinks as follows: first, here there is a rule for the elision of the letter *m*.

It is not found in the treatise. Now, if one were to assume that *sātatyam* itself is an irregular formation (*nipātana*), intended to indicate the meaning "the elision of the *m* of *sam-* occurs when followed by the word *tataḥ*," then in that case, the form *santatam* would not be established. To this he says: "In the case of *samtata*, [the elision] is optional."

And so forth. The intention here is as follows: by uttering the word *sātatyam*, which is well-known through the definitions of the ancient masters (*pūrvācārya*), the definition of those ancient masters is also being adopted.
Therefore, by that [definition], the elision of the letter *m* is prescribed here as being identical to it. And this...
By doing so, the elision of [the suffix] *kṛtya* and others even in the case of words such as *avaśyam* becomes established.
Therefore, he shows that very definition of the ancient teachers (pūrvācārya) with the rule beginning "lumpet" (*lumpet*);
the word "final" (*antya*) is to be understood as the remainder. One should elide the final [syllable] of the word *avaśyam* when followed by a *kṛtya* suffix.

The meaning is that one should effect the elision of its final [vowel]. This must necessarily be done; even for a word ending in the *tumun* suffix, one should elide the final [vowel] when followed by the words *kāma* and *manas*—as in *kartukāmaḥ*, meaning "one who has the desire to do," and *hartumanāḥ*, meaning "one whose mind is set on taking."
Intending to remove [the *sa-* prefix]:

one may optionally elide the final syllable of the word *sam* when followed by the two words *hita* and *taya*—namely, *sahitam*, *satatam*, and *santatam*. This is according to the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18).
The compound:

one should elide the final letter of the word *māṃsa*, in what context? In the case of the verbal root *paci*. Specifically, in this root *ḍupacaṣ pāke* (DhP 996), provided it is characterized by the suffixes *yuṅ* and *ghañ*.

The meaning is: when the suffixes *lyuṭ* or *ghañ* follow, [the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs] in that which is called *pacis*. Here too, the mention of the option (*vā*) is connected. Thus: *māṃspacanam*, *māṃsapacanam*; *māṃspākaḥ*, *māṃsapākaḥ*. The compound is formed according to the rule: "And a genitive case ending is compounded with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix" (Vārttika 86).
This elision in a compound is the intention of the ancient teachers (pūrvācāryas) and applies within *saṃhitā*; therefore, it does not occur in a sentence when the words are recited separately.

145. *goṣpadaṃ* [is formed] in the sense of "frequented" (*sevita*) and "unfrequented" (*asevita*), as well as in the sense of "measure" (*pramāṇa*). (Pāṇini 6.1.145). Regarding the rule "and there is *ṣ*-ness for that": since the *s* of *suṭ* is neither a substitute (*ādeśa*) nor part of an affix (*pratyaya*), the change to *ṣ* would not apply; therefore, this form is also established by nipātana (irregular derivation). [The word *goṣpada* refers to] a place, as in "cows walk here," and so forth.

[The author] shows that [the word *goṣpada*] signifies "being frequented" (*sevitatva*). As for the passage beginning with "in what is not frequented" (*asevite*), one might ask: "But the word *goṣpada* is mentioned in the sūtra; why then is 'not frequented by cows' (*agoṣpada*) and so forth cited as an example?
To this he says: "In what is not frequented," etc. But surely the word *goṣpada* is mentioned in the sūtra... [the rest of the sentence follows].

Why is "agoṣpadādīni" (words such as *agoṣpada*) cited as an example under the rule for what is not frequented (*asevita*)? To this he says: "In [the case of] 'not frequented,' etc. This mention of "not frequented" (*asevita*) is made, yet the word *goṣpada* is not possible there [in that sense]; therefore, it is understood that the irregular formation (*nipātana*) is for the sake of the meaning "not frequented by cattle" (*agoṣpada*).

"If this is so," means: if the irregular formation (*nipātana*) is for the sake of [denoting] a place not traversed by a cow's hoof. "There is no need for this" refers to the inclusion of the term *asevita* ("not traversed"). How is it established without that? He says:
"Because of the prohibition regarding *goṣpada*," and so forth. "This is indeed true."

He states the truth of what was said beginning with "because of the negation of a cow’s footprint," but this is not the meaning of the phrase "there is no purpose by this. If, then, this is indeed true, for what purpose is the mention of *sevitam* (the practiced) made here? To this he says: "But where... and so forth.

In the negative compound *agoṣpada*, this *tatpuruṣa* by its very nature expresses a meaning similar to that of the subsequent member, just like *abrāhmaṇa*. Consequently, when the *tatpuruṣa* "not a cow's footprint" (*na goṣpadam agoṣpadam*) is formed, [it denotes] a place where there is neither the act of treading nor the one who has trodden.
"The application [of the rule] exists in that very case where there is the possibility of the term *agoṣpada* occurring; nevertheless, it does so.
The word *api* (even/also) indicates that this meaning applies not only where there is the possibility of the term *sevatā*, but also where *agoṣpada* occurs. Why?
Furthermore, because of the inclusion of the term "not practiced" (*asevita*) here, and since [the rule] would apply even in that case, he says: "For those which...

and "In this way. The manner indicated by the inclusion of the term "not practiced" is what is being referred to. For if the term "not practiced" were not included, this *bahuvrīhi* compound would become redundant; therefore, it is used.

It will be understood through the word *āsevita* as a noun denoting the action (*bhāvasādhana*). Furthermore, since a *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "that in which service (*sevita*) does not exist"—is possible even in the case of absolute non-existence, those forests where the presence of cows is absolutely impossible are designated by the term *āsevita*. And thus:

In that case as well, there occurs the expression *agoṣpadam*. [An example is] *goṣpadapūram*. Here, the suffix *ṇamul* is applied by the rule *varṣapramāṇa ūlopaś cāsya anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 3.4.32). Now, one might object: this *goṣpadam* is actually a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), and of that—

Furthermore, the word "goṣpada" (cow's footprint) has as its meaning that which is connected to a cow, but it is not itself a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, how can examples such as "the field is only the size of a cow's footprint" be applicable to a *pramāṇa*? To this, he says: "Not here," and so forth.
For in this case, the term "cow's footprint" is not employed solely for the purpose of conveying its own primary meaning. What [is it used for]?

What then? It is for the purpose of delimiting the extent of a field and so forth. Therefore, because the extent of a field and so forth is delimited—that is, measured—by it, it becomes a *pramāṇa* (means of valid cognition). And here, by the word *pramāṇa*, length is not meant; what then? Merely the act of delimitation. Why is this so?
Because of the force of the irregular derivation (*nipātana*); for an irregular derivation admits even that which is not established as a fact.
146. *Āspadaṃ pratiṣṭhāyām* (Pāṇini 6.1.146). Regarding the phrase *ātmayāpanāya*: "sustaining the self" (*ātmayāpana*) means the maintenance of life.
That which is a support (*sthāpana*) for that purpose is called *pratiṣṭhā*. Regarding the word *āspadam*: [it is derived] from the root following the prefix *āṅ*.

The suffix *suṭ* is applied as an irregular form (*nipātana*) to the word *pada*. In the expression *āpadam*, the particle *āṅ* is designated as a *karmapravacanīya* by the rule *āṅ maryādāvacane* (Pāṇini 1.4.89). When used in conjunction with such a term, the ablative case is employed according to *pañcamy apāṅparibhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.10). Furthermore, the compound is formed with that [ablative] ending according to *āṅ maryādābhividhyoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.13).
Thus ends the section on *avyayībhāva* compounds.

147. *āścaryam anitye* (6.1.147). If the word *āścarya* is prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation) when referring to something impermanent (*anitya*)—that is, something non-eternal (*aśāśvatika*)—then one might object that it would also apply to things such as jars (*ghaṭa*). Desiring to avoid this fault, he says: "by way of impermanence" (*anittyatayā*), and so forth.

The marvelous (*adbhuta*) is called the extraordinary (*citra*). That which is marvelous in the world is the extraordinary; its state is "marvelousness" (*adbhutatva*). And because that [marvelousness] does not exist elsewhere, impermanence becomes its object, for it cannot possibly occur anywhere other than there. Therefore, by means of that [impermanence]—

The state of being a wonder (*adbhutatva*) is indicated by that which has become the object [of the verb]. In the expression "it would be a marvel if he were to eat," the optative (*liṅ*) is used in the sense of impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*), according to the rule *anavaklṛptyamarṣayorakiṃvṛte’pi* (Pāṇini 3.3.145). Thus, the eating [is impossible].
Because it has never been seen before by anyone at a particular distinguished time, it becomes a marvel in that situation.

148. *avaskaraḥ* [is formed] in the sense of *varcas*. (6.2.148) [The example is: "contemptible *varcas* is *varcaska*. The mention of the suffix *kan* by way of the term "in the sense of contemptible" (*kutsite*) is for the purpose that [the suffix] should not apply in the sense of "splendor" (*dīpti*). For the word *varcas* is indeed used even in the sense of splendor.

In that case too, it might be argued: if the word *avaskara* is prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation) specifically for excrement (*varcaska*), then it would not apply to the place associated with it; yet the word *avaskara* is used for that place as well in common worldly usage.
Therefore, he says: "Because of its connection with that," and so forth. It is just as when one says, "Bring in the sticks."
Just as men are also called by the word "staff" due to their connection with a staff, so too a place is called by the word "refuse" due to its connection with refuse.

149. *Apaskara* means a part of a chariot (*rathāṅga*). By this [sūtra], he explains that the word "part" (*avayava*) is understood from the term "beginning with" (*ādi*) in the rule "a part of a chariot" (*rathāvayava*).

150. *viṣkiraḥ śakunir vā vikiro vā* (6.1.150). Now, one might object: since the desired form is established by the rule *viṣkiraḥ śakunau vā* alone, what is the purpose of including the term *vikira* there? To this, he says: "The word *vikira* [is used] only when it refers to a bird (*śakuni*)."
The mention of "scattering" (*vikira*) is for the purpose that the application [of the rule] should occur here and not elsewhere.
151. [The suffix] *suṭ* is applied before the word *candra* when it occurs after a verbal root (*hava*) within a mantra. (Pāṇini 6.1.151).

It was previously stated that *suṭ* is not a part of the word (*abhakta*) because of the mention of "preceding" (*pūrva*) in the rule regarding what precedes a *k*. However, in this case, being "preceded by a *k*" is not possible; furthermore, it possesses the marker *ṭ*, which is a characteristic of an augment (*āgama*). Therefore, *suṭ* is indeed an augment.

He says that it is understood thus: "the augment *suṭ* occurs. And when it occurs, since there is a mention of both [bases], according to the principle "in the case of a mention of two [bases], the ablative mention is stronger" (*Śākaṭāyanaparibhāṣā* 97), the genitive is substituted for the locative in both "after a short vowel" (*hrasvāt*) and "when *candra* is the uttarapada," and thus it applies to the word *candra* itself.

[The word] *suścandraḥ* [is formed] as a *prādi-samāsa* (prepositional compound). [The word] *sūryācandramasau* [is formed] as a *dvandva* (copulative compound), with the substitution of *ānaṅ* by the rule *devatādvandve ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.26). Now, why does this not occur here in *śuklam asi candramasi*? For even here, the word *candra*, which is the final member (*uttarapada*), follows after a short vowel. To this [it is replied]: [The answer is: Because the rule applies only when the word *candra* is the final member of a compound. Here, *candra* is not the final member of a compound; rather, it is a separate word in apposition with *asi*. Therefore, the substitution does not take place. Furthermore, the rule is restricted to cases where the entire compound is a name (*saṃjñā*) or a specific designation (*viśeṣaṇa*). Since *śukla-candra* is not established as a conventional name or a specific designation, the substitution does not apply. Thus, the desired form is not obtained. Therefore, one must state the following: "In the case of *candra*, the substitution of *ānaṅ* occurs when it is the final member of a *dvandva* compound denoting deities, provided that the preceding member ends in a short vowel. This is how the rule should be formulated. Alternatively, one may say: "The substitution of *ānaṅ* for *candra* occurs when it is the final member of a *dvandva* compound denoting deities, provided that the preceding member ends in a short vowel and the entire compound is a name. By this formulation, the desired result is achieved. However, since the word *candra* is not a name in the examples *śukla-candra* and *kṛṣṇa-candra*, the substitution does not occur there. Consequently, the forms *śuklacandreṇa* and *kṛṣṇacandreṇa* are not produced. Therefore, the following must be stated: "The substitution of *ānaṅ* for *candra* occurs when it is the final member of a *dvandva* compound denoting deities, provided that the preceding member ends in a short vowel and the entire compound is a name. By this, the desired forms are correctly derived. But if one asks why the forms *śuklacandreṇa* and *kṛṣṇacandreṇa* are not produced even though the word *candra* is the final member of a compound ending in a short vowel, the answer is: because the word *candra* is not a name (*saṃjñā*) in those instances. Since the word *candra* is not a name in *śukla-candra* and *kṛṣṇa-candra*, the substitution of *ānaṅ* does not take place. Therefore, the forms *śuklacandreṇa* and *kṛṣṇacandreṇa* do not arise. Hence, it is necessary to state: "The substitution of *ānaṅ* for *candra* occurs when it is the final member of a *dvandva* compound denoting deities, provided that the preceding member ends in a short vowel and the entire compound is a name. By this, the desired results are correctly obtained. But if one asks why the forms *śuklacandreṇa* and *kṛṣṇacandreṇa* are not produced even though the word *candra* is the final member of a compound ending in a short vowel, the answer is: because the word *candra* is not a name (*saṃjñā*) in those instances. By this, the desired results are correctly obtained. Since the word *candra* is not a name in *śukla-candra* and *kṛṣṇa-candra*, the substitution of *ānaṅ* does not take place. Therefore, the forms *śuklacandreṇa* and *kṛṣṇacandreṇa* do not arise. Hence, it is necessary to state: "The substitution of *ānaṅ* for *candra* occurs when it is the final member of a *dvandva* compound denoting deities, provided that the preceding member ends in

He says: "The subsequent word," and so forth. In the sentence *śuklam asi* (you are white) or *candram asi* (you are the moon), the word *candra* is certainly not included by the mention of "subsequent word" (*uttarapada*) here; because the term "subsequent word" is well-known only in the context of a compound (*samāsa*).

152. *pratiṣkaśaśca kaśeḥ* (6.1.152). [The word] *pratiṣkaśaḥ* [is formed with the suffix *ka* after the root] *kaś*. [An example is: *pratigataḥ kaśāṃ pratikaśo'śvaḥ* ("a horse that has gone against the whip"). This is a *prādi*-compound. Now, one might object: the word *kaśā* is also derived from the very same root *kaś* by adding the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class); therefore, in this case as well—

It must be *suṭ*. To this he says: "Even though," and so forth. The mention of the root *kaś* itself is for the purpose that there may be an understanding (*pratipatti*) of the prefix *prati* as belonging specifically to that *kaś*. And *prati* is not a prefix to *kaś*; rather, what is it? [It is a prefix to the root *su*].

Then what? [The suffix is applied] after the root *gam*. 153. *Praskaṇva* and *Hariścandra* are seers (*ṛṣi*). (Pāṇini 6.1.153). Regarding the rule "praskaṇva-hariścandrau": one whose *kaṇva* is excellent (*prakṛṣṭa*) is *praskaṇva*.

"Hariścandra" means "he whose moon is Hari"; this is formed merely for the sake of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), but there is no meaning derived from its constituent parts (*avayavārtha*) here. For these two are conventional (*rūḍhi*) words, in which the meanings of the parts have subsisted, and they refer only to a particular seer (*ṛṣi*). Now, as for Hariścandra...

Since the augment *suṭ* is already established by the rule "ṭhhrasvāccandrottarapade" (Pāṇini 6.1.151), for what purpose is the mention of *hariścandra*? To this he says: "The mention of *hariścandra*" and so forth. Regarding "prakaṇvaḥ": one from whom Kaṇva has departed is *prakaṇvaḥ*; [it means] like Hari.
He whose moon is [the moon] is Haricandra.

154. *maskara* and *maskarin* [are formed] from *veṇu* and *parivrājaka*. (Pāṇini 6.1.154). Regarding *parivrājaka*, it is stated that "the suffix *ṭhañ* and also *tvin* [apply]. This implies that [the forms] are irregularly derived (*nipātyate*). What, then, is the reason? Because [otherwise] they would not be obtained, due to the absence of the meaning of the suffix *mātra*. Even for one who possesses no *maskara* (staff), [the form *maskarin* applies].
The wandering mendicant is called *maskarī*; this is because the word *maskarin* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in that very sense.

They also apply the suffix *ac* by means of a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*), for although the suffix *ac* is prescribed in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), it does not apply here in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*);
thus they apply the suffix *ac* as an irregularity. And if the word *maskara* here refers to a bamboo flute...
If one falls [into a pit], one does not incur the punishment; yet even in that case, the term is used in common parlance.

To this he says: "The mention of the bamboo," and so forth. The mention of the bamboo is for the purpose of indicating that which prevents [the fall]; since one is also prevented by means of a staff, the term applies there as well.
Regarding the phrase "because of being a denier of action" (*karmāpavāditvāt*): action is that which bears worldly fruit.

One whose nature (*śīla*) is to set aside—that is, to deny—that [action] is a "denier of action" (*karmāpavādī*); the state of being such a person is "the quality of being a denier of action" (*karmāpavāditvam*).
By the words "for he," etc., [the author] demonstrates that very quality of being a denier of action.
155. *kāstīra* [is derived] from the city of *rajatunda*. (6.1.155) 156. *kāraskara* is a tree.
(6.1.156) Regarding the phrase "some [readers]" (*kecit*): if, then, some do not study this sūtra, how [is it explained]?
Is the word *kāraska* established as denoting a tree? To this he says: "In the list beginning with *pāraskara*," and so forth.

157. *Pāraskaraprabhṛtīni ca saṃjñāyām* (6.1.157). Words such as *pāraskara* and others are conventional terms (*rūḍhiśabda*) that may be etymologically derived in some way or another; one should not be overly insistent on the meaning of their individual components. [For example,] *pāraskara* is derived from "he makes the other side" (*pāraṃ karoti*), by the rule *kṛño...* [and so forth].
The suffix *ṭa* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.20 (*hetutācchīlyānulomyeṣu*). One who protects a chariot is a *rathaspā*.

According to Pāṇini 3.2.3 (*ātonupasarge kaḥ*), the suffix *ka* is applied; from the root *kṛ*, the suffix *ḍu* is added, and there is a substitution of *kir* for *kārya*—thus, *kiṣkuḥ*. One who places something within is derived from the root *dhā*.
As before, *kaḥ* [is formed], with the doubling of *kim* and the elision of the preceding *m*—thus, *kiṣkindhā*.
Regarding the rule beginning with "of *tat* and *bṛhat*": for these two, namely *tat* and *bṛhat*, respectively...

When the words *kara* and *pati* follow, the suffix *suṅ* is applied when the referent is either a thief (*caura*) or a deity (*devatā*), and there is the elision of the final *t* sound. Thus, regarding "he does that" (*tat karoti*), the rule "when *kim*, *yat*, or *tat* [are followed by a word ending in a case-suffix] among many" (Vārttika 242) prescribes the addition of *aj*. Hence, a thief is called *tasakaraḥ*, while another is called *tatkaraḥ*.

Bṛhaspati is the deity of *bṛhatām patiḥ*, while *bṛhatpati* is another [term]. Now, for what purpose is the qualification "of a thief and a deity" (*caura-devatayoḥ*) employed, since its inclusion is already established by the mention of the term "name" (*saṃjñā*) alone? For are the words *taskara* (thief) and *bṛhaspati* not names of anything else? To this [it is replied]: [The answer follows: ... [the qualification is used] because otherwise, in cases such as *taskaraḥ* and *bṛhaspatiḥ* where the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *tasyedam* ("belonging to him"), the feminine form would result in *taskarī* and *bārhaspatī*. However, the intended forms are *taskarī* and *bārhaspatyā*. Therefore, the qualification is stated to exclude such unintended applications. Furthermore, the word *taskara* is a name [only] when it refers to a thief, and *bṛhaspati* is a name [only] when it refers to the deity; they are not names in other contexts. Thus, the qualification is necessary to ensure that the rule applies only when these are used as proper names. Finally, the word *bṛhatpati* is a name [only] when it refers to the deity Bṛhaspati, whereas *bṛhatām patiḥ* is a different compound. Hence, the qualification is required to restrict the application of the rule.
He says: "The mention of *saṃjñā*," and so forth;

"in *prātumpati*," and so forth. According to the roots *tupa* and *tumpa* in the sense of "satiation" (*tṛptau*), the suffix *suṅ* occurs after the prefix *pra-* when *go* is the agent: *prastumpati*.

The word *gauḥ* [is included]. As stated in the Bhāṣya: "Another [word] certainly satisfies [the requirement]," namely *pratumpati*. If, then, the group beginning with *pāraskara* is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (a class-based group), then the preceding rule starting with "and *pratiṣkaśa* from the root *kaś*" (Pāṇini 6.1.152) need not be recited, since that too would be included by this very [rule]?
This is true; however, it must be recited for the sake of elaboration.

158. *anudāttaṃ padamekavarjam* (Pāṇini 6.1.158). Regarding the phrase *ekavarjam*: it means "excluding one. The suffix *ṇamul* is applied by the rule *dvitīyāyāṃ ca* (3.4.53). If this [sūtra] were intended as a governing heading (*adhikāra*), then the accentuation would apply only to the sixth chapter (*ṣāṣṭhika*).

[If this were the case,] only those [accents] would be included; however, other vowels such as those in the *Saptādhyāyī*—namely, "the vowel following *samānodare śayitaḥ* is udātta" (P. 4.4.108) and "in *asthi*, *dadhi*, *sakthi*, and *akṣi*, the *an* is udātta" (P. 7.1.75), and so forth—would not be included. [This is why it is stated] in the *paribhāṣā*:

For even they are included within this [Paribhāṣā]; for although it resides in only one part [of the grammar], it illuminates the entire treatise, just as a lamp illuminates a house—having considered this, he says: "This is a Paribhāṣā. And this [Paribhāṣā] is a subsidiary member of the rules (vidhi).

For a general rule (*paribhāṣā*) functions as a supplement (*śeṣabhāva*) to the operational rules (*kāryavākya*). In any case where an *svarita* or *udātta* accent is prescribed for a particular word-element, the remainder (*śeṣa*) therein becomes *anudātta*.
Regarding the phrase "having the prescription of accent as its scope" (*svaravidhiviṣayā*): the analysis of the compound is "that whose scope (*viṣaya*) is the prescription of accent (*svaravidhi*)."
Regarding the phrase "where there is another": this "otherness" is in relation to the *anudātta* (unaccented vowel). Regarding the phrase "therein the word is *anudātta*":

one might object that the term *anudātta*—by the rule "the low [pitch] is *anudātta*" (Pāṇini 1.2.30)—is conventionally established as denoting a specific phonetic quality (*guṇa*), whereas a "word" (*pada*) is characterized by vowels and consonants (*ac* and *hal*).

The meaning of the word *pada* is that [syllable]. How, then, is there grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) here? This is not a fault; for what is intended here by "anudātta" is a *pada* consisting of a single non-udātta vowel. Therefore, the word "anudātta" refers to the *pada* itself. How so? Because it ends in the suffix -a, which expresses the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). That is to say, it means "that which has a non-udātta [vowel]."
The word *santi* is unaccented (anudātta). Because the class beginning with *arśas* is an open-ended group (*ākṛtigaṇa*), the suffix *ac* is applied here.
It has been stated that "with the exception of one," but it is not known which one is to be excluded;
therefore, in order to clarify this, he asks: "Which one, moreover? and so forth. And for that [one] whose accent is udātta...

Or rather, that very [vowel] which is prescribed is excluded. For if even this were not excluded, its prescription regarding accentuation would be purposeless—as in "gopāyati" and "dhūpāyati. [The roots are:
"gupū" in the sense of protection (DhP 3.95), and "dhūpa" in the sense of heating (DhP 3.96); [the rule applies to] "gupū-dhūpa..."

By the rule *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.32), that which ends in the suffix *āya* receives the designation "root" (*dhātu*). Furthermore, by the rule *dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.162), the root has its final syllable as udātta; thus, for that which ends in the suffix *āya*, the vowel *ā* of the final *y* possesses the accent of the root. [The rule] *dhātusvaram*...

"The acute accent (*udātta*) sublates [the other], because it is *satiśiṣṭa* (remaining after others have been applied), and that which is *satiśiṣṭa* is stronger. For it has been stated: "It should be said that the *satiśiṣṭa* accent is stronger" (Vārttika on Pāṇini 6.1.168). As in the examples "lunāti" and "punāti," [which belong to] the *pv-ādi* class...

The vowel is shortened by [Pāṇini 7.3.80] *hrasvaḥ*. Furthermore, the first syllable of the suffix *śnā* is acute by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). Regarding the phrase "the accent of *śnā*," it is connected with the verb "it subverts" (*bādhate*). Now, one might object: since the *tiṅ* suffixes and so forth apply later, the verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*) ought to occur after they have been applied; therefore, when the accent of the *sārvadhātuka* suffix is present...

Because the *śna*-accent is being specifically prescribed, it possesses the status of being "later-prescribed" (*satiśiṣṭa*); and thus, it is logical that the accent of the root [the *titsvara*] should be sublated by that very *śna*-accent. This is the view held regarding what follows from the rule "the affix *tās* is followed by an unaccented vowel when taught with the marker *ṅ*" (Pāṇini 6.1.186).

The fact that [the suffix] is treated as *sārvadhātuka* teaches this: even the accent of a *vikaraṇa* is superseded by the accent of a *sārvadhātuka*. For example, in "lunītaḥ" and "punītaḥ," there is the substitution of *ī* by rule 6.4.113 (*ī halyadhoḥ*). This is what is meant by the phrase "the accent of the suffix supersedes the accent [of the base]. It supersedes it.

The connection [is as follows]: the reason for its being sublated is precisely its being *satiśiṣṭa* (later-remaining). In the example "lunītastarām," the suffix *taraP* is applied by the rule *tiṅśca* (5.3.56), and from that which ends in *ta*, the suffix *ām* is added by the rule *kimetiṅvyayaghād ām* (5.4.11).
But for what purpose is this rule that an accent belongs to the word with the exception of one [element] prescribed? To this he says:

"Of the augment," and so forth. The accentuation of the augment and the others is prescribed as being unaccented (*anudātta*) throughout the word, with the exception of one [element], so that their individual accents might not be heard. The accent of the augment [supersedes] the accent of the base (*prakṛti*).
"It obstructs. When this [rule] exists, the word retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) except for the single [substituted] syllable.

If it did not exist, the accent of the substitute (*parakṛti*) and that of the augment (*āgama*) would each remain distinct. In the case of "catvāraḥ," the original accent is the acute (*udātta*) on the first syllable; for thus it is stated: "The suffix *urana* follows the root *catur*" (Dhātupāṭha 8.78).

Thus, the word *catuḥ* is derived by adding the suffix *uran*; consequently, by the accent rule for *nit*-suffixes, it becomes udātta on its first syllable. Regarding the rule "ṭhanaṅvāhaḥ," the word *anuḍuh* is also derived in this same manner: from the root *an* (meaning "to breathe") [DhP 1070], the suffix *asun* is added according to the rule "ṭhsarvadhātubhyo'sun" [Dhātu-upasarga-kośa 9.49].
Because it ends in the suffix *asun*, the word *anaḥ* has its first syllable acute by virtue of the *nit*-accent rule. [In the derivation of *anaḥ*:
from the root *vah-* with the prefix *an-*, there is the suffix *kvip* [by Pāṇini 3.2.64], and then the suffix *asun* is added by the rule "after *an-* there is *asun*" (Daiva-Uṇādi-sūtra 9.49).
Thus, because it ends in *asun*, the word *anaḥ* has its first syllable acute by virtue of the *nit*-accent rule. *Ano*...

By the rule *bahaṭor anasi vahaḥ kvip ṭuścānasaḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 9.107), when *anas* is the upapada, the root *vah* takes the suffix *kvip*, and the vowel *a* of *anas* is replaced by *ū*. Since *vah* belongs to the *yajādi* group, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). Then follows the formation of an upapada compound (*upapadasamāsa*), according to the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-* (Pāṇini 6.2.2) and so forth.

The first member of the compound retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Therefore, even for *anuḍuh* analyzed in this way, there would be an acute accent on the first syllable. A *vikāra* is a substitute (*ādeśa*). [This refers to the rule] "the accent of *anaṅ* applies to the base.
Thus, the words *dadhi* and *asathi* have an acute accent on the first syllable; for instance, [the root] *asu* in the sense of "throwing" (*kṣepaṇe*) [is used].

Because it ends in the *kthin* suffix according to the rule *ṭhasisañjibhyāṃ kthin* (Daiva Upajīvyaka 1.10), the word *asthi* has its first syllable udātta by virtue of the *nit-svara*. The word *dadhi* also has its first syllable udātta because it ends in the *kin* suffix; for the root *dhā*, the suffixes *kikin* are applied according to the rule *ādṛgamahanajanaḥ kikinau*.

By the rule *liṭ ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.171), there is the *kin* suffix; when reduplication has been performed there and the vowel *ā* has been elided, the form *dadhi* arises. By the rule *asthidadhi* (Pāṇini 7.1.75) and so forth, the substitution *anaṅ* is made, and its accent must also be applied; for even that [accent] would not exist in the absence of this [rule], in the case of the words *asthi*, *dadhi*, and *adhi* with the substitution *anaṅ*.

However, there would be a separate acute accent (*udātta*) [on the *ā* of *āya*]. But this being the case, only *anaṅ* occurs. Regarding the phrase "of the base" (*prakṛteḥ*), etc., in the examples "he protects" (*gopāyati*) and "he fumigates" (*dhūpāyati*), since the suffix *āya* begins with an *ā*, the final syllable of the base—namely, of *gup* and *dhūp*—would be acutely accented by the rule "of a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*, Pāṇini 6.1.162). Furthermore, the initial *ā* of the suffix *āya* would also [be acutely accented].

The acute accent (*udātta*) arises from the affix (*pratyaya*). Even in the case of the words *gopāya* and *dhūpāya*, once the designation "root" (*dhātu*) has been applied by the rule "those ending in *san* and so forth are roots" (Pāṇini 3.1.32), the rule "after a root" (Pāṇini 6.1.162) would result in the final syllable being acutely accented.
Thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of two separate accents.
The vowel of the verbal root itself becomes the svarita accent, not that of the *gup* or *dhūp* roots,

nor that of the vowel of the suffix. In the case of "ṭhkartavyam," although both the final udātta of the root and the initial udātta of the suffix would otherwise apply, only the initial udātta of the suffix prevails, and not [the other].

[The rule concerns] the accent of the *dhātu*. Now, why does the exclusion of a single vowel not occur without restriction? For no cause for such a restriction (*avyavasthā-hetu*) is mentioned in this sūtra, nor can that [exclusion] be obtained without a cause for restriction. To this he says: "The subsequent, the obligatory, the internal," and so forth. Where there are subsequent vowels (*para-svara*), etc.

[They] attain [their application], as do their opposites; however, because others (para) and so forth are stronger in that context, one avoids them for that very reason, while the others are set aside. But where, even when there is a conflict with the subsequent, the permanent, the internal, or the exception, the desired result is not achieved, in that case—

The determination is made by that which remains after others have been set aside (*satiśiṣṭa*), for its superior strength has been stated. Therefore, when there is the possibility of obtaining either a *satiśiṣṭa* accent or another, only the *satiśiṣṭa* is excluded, not the other. But how is there no determination when a *satiśiṣṭa* [accent] is present? To this he says: "For he who... and so forth.
How is this known? To this he says: "For thus," and so forth. Regarding the word "gopāyati":

here, by the accentual rule for suffixes (*pratyayasvara*), the first syllable has the acute (*udātta*) accent. And although that accent is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*), once the designation of "verbal root" (*dhātusaṃjñā*) has been applied to the form ending in the suffix *āya*, [the root-accent prevails].
Furthermore, it is superseded by that accent which remains as a remainder:

in the case of *kārṣṇo-tarāsaṅga-putraḥ*. Having first formed a *bahuvrīhi*, the *tatpuruṣa* compound should then be made. This is because of the rule "the accent of the *bahuvrīhi*" (*bahuvrīhi-svara*), specifically by the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, [the final member] retains its original form" (*bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā*, Pāṇini 6.2.1).
This has been stated by such [rules] as these.
Having taken the preceding [rule] as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the mind, he says: "But the accent of the *vikaraṇa*," and so forth;
"from the accent of the case-ending (*vibhakti*)," and so forth; and "particles (*nipāta*) have the acute accent on the first syllable" (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.80).

The negative particle *nañ* is udātta. In that case, once the *tatpuruṣa* compound has been formed, by the rule "In a *tatpuruṣa*, [the first member retains its] original accent" (6.2.2), etc., the udātta accent itself prevails over the original accent. However, when the accent of the case-ending would apply instead of the accent of *nañ*, and the accent of *nañ* is desired—

Therefore, it must be stated that the accent of the case-ending (*vibhaktisvara*) is stronger. When it is stronger, what happens? To this he says: "In the case of *atistaraḥ*, etc. By the rule *tisṛbhyaḥ jasaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.166), the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the case-ending is prescribed. Because of its greater strength...

Even that which remains after the application of the *nañ-svara* (the accent assigned to a word preceded by the negative particle *nañ*) is superseded [by the following rule]. However, for the accent of a case-ending (*vibhakta-svara*), the scope is limited to forms such as *tisraḥ* and *triṣu*.
This is according to the rule beginning with "and from the accent caused by a case-ending" (*vibhakti-nimitta-svarācca*). That accent of which the case-ending is the cause is the *vibhakta-svara*.
The accent caused by a case ending (*vibhakti-nimitta-svara*). This refers to the rule "of that for which the case ending is the cause of the *ām* [suffix].

The fact that the *ām* has a case ending as its cause is due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "sarvanāmasthāna" from the rule "for *pathin* and *mathin*, [the substitution of *āt* occurs] before a sarvanāmasthāna" (Pāṇini 6.1.199). Its acute accent (*udāttatva*) is established by the rule beginning with "that which [is substituted] is acute" (*yad udāttam*), and so forth.
He demonstrates the result of its greater strength: regarding the accent caused by case endings—*catvāraḥ*, *anaṅ vāhaḥ*—this is the scope [of the rule].
As for the passage beginning with "for in a sentence" (*vākye hi*), the word *devadatta* has its first syllable acute by virtue of the vocative accent.

For the word *go* is oxytone by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*); its replacement vowel *ā*, according to the rule "the *ā* [of the nominative-accusative dual] after [a stem ending in] *ṭhā* or *Ṭ* is [treated as] *am* and *śas*" (Pāṇini 6.1.93), is likewise acute by virtue of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). Similarly, even when there is a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with the case-ending, it remains acute because of the rule "a single substitute for [a vowel] preceded by an acute [vowel] is acute" (Pāṇini 8.2.5).

The word *abhi* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). According to the rules "Particles have their first syllable accented" (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.80) and "Prepositions, with the exception of *abhi*, [have their first syllable accented]" (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.81), since it is excluded from the prescription of initial accentuation, it retains the accent of the nominal stem itself. Thus, by the accentuation rule for prepositions, it is accented on the first syllable.
However, this [form] *ajitī* ends in the imperative suffix (*loṭ*), and is therefore unaccented by the rule *ṭhtiṅṅtiṅ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28).
Since the word *śukla* is acutely accented on the final syllable by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*),
when the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is formed according to the rule *ekādeśa udātenodātaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.5), it remains acutely accented on the final syllable.
It occurs. This should be understood as being like the case of *ami-pūrva*.
Thus, because of the mention of the word "pada" (word), in each individual word within a sentence, the accent remains distinct;
provided that a word is unaccented with the exception of one [circumflex], this is so as long as the designation "pada" has not yet been established.
In that case, with the exception of one [vowel], the remainder ought to be *anudātta* (unaccented);

consequently, in the word *kauvalam*, meaning "a product of *kuvalī*," the suffix *añ* prescribed by the rule *anudātādeśca* (Pāṇini 4.2.140) would not apply. This is because this word *kuvala* belongs to the group beginning with *grāma*.

The first syllable [of *gaurī*] is udātta. He says, "And this is for the sake of defining the measure," etc., because even when the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied due to its inclusion in the *gaura*-group, the designation of being a *pada* is absent, and thus the quality of having an udātta on the first syllable is not relinquished. Here, "word" (*pada*) is intended in a secondary sense, not the primary one; otherwise—

If the topic of "word" (*pada*) were already established, the repeated mention of the word "word" would be redundant. Therefore, it should be understood that what is intended here by "word" is that which will subsequently receive the designation of "word.
Without the mention of "word," it would not be known how many vowels are to be considered *anudātta* (unaccented).

However, when there is the mention of "pada" (word), it is understood that for as many vowels (*ac*) as there are in a single *pada*, that many become unaccented (*anudātta*); therefore, this [term] is for the sake of the supreme purpose (*paramārtha*). It is not, however, for the purpose of denoting a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) or a verb ending (*tiṅanta*). Consequently, even before...

Since it must be unaccented by virtue of being a *pada-vyapadeśa* (designation as a word), the aforementioned fault does not arise. This might be argued: even if the term "word" (*pada*) here does not denote the primary word, nevertheless, by virtue of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning words, that [primary word] is brought into proximity; thus, the situation remains the same.
Is there indeed this fault? To this he says: "It effects the cessation of the governing authority of the word (*pada-adhikāra*).

This mention of the word (*padagrahaṇa*), by conveying a secondary meaning, brings about the cessation of the governing authority of the primary word. What is intended by this? He says: "By that," and so forth. And thus...

Thus; and this being the case, the meaning is that even before the designation of the two words, the remaining portion becomes unaccented at the very same time as the rule for accentuation is applied.
To strengthen this very point, he says: "garbhiṇī," etc. The suffix *ini* is used in the sense of "she who has a fetus."

The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭhṛnnebhyo ṅīp* (Pāṇini 4.1.5). This word *garbha* is acutely accented on its first syllable, just like the word *kuvala*. In that case, if the state of being unaccented (*anudātta*) were to occur simultaneously with the acute accent (*udātta*) of the suffix *ini*, then...

Since the word *garbhiṇī* begins with an unaccented vowel, the suffix *añ* would apply by the rule *anudātatāder añ* (Pāṇini 4.2.44); therefore, its inclusion in the *bhikṣādi* group is appropriate for the purpose of overriding that rule.
However, once the designation *pada* has subsequently arisen for it, the remaining portion [of the stem] remains unaccented.

It would be so; if that were the case, the word *garbhiṇī* would have its initial syllable acute-accented (*ādyaudāta*). Consequently, it would not be listed among the *bhikṣā-* group [in Pāṇini 4.1.49] for the purpose of subverting the application of the suffix *aṇ*; yet it is indeed listed there. Therefore, it is understood from this that [the designation of a "word" (*pada*)] occurs even prior to the technical designation of a "word."
The intention is that the remaining [syllable] becomes unaccented (anudātta) at the very same time as the rule for accentuation [of the first syllable] takes effect.

But what is the reason that, when the designation "word" (pada-saṃjñā) has already been obtained and the unaccented nature is being prescribed for the remainder, the suffix *vañ* is not established after the word *kuvala*, and how [is it established]?
The inclusion of *garbhiṇī* in the *bhikṣādi* group is for the purpose of overriding the suffix *añ*, which is characterized by having its first syllable unaccented (*anudātta*);
this is because the remaining portion becomes unaccented at the very time the rule for accentuation applies, even before the designation of the two words has taken place.

What is the indicator [of this]? He says: "The words *kuvala* and *garbha*, etc. For if these two were acute on the first syllable (*ādyaudātta*), then, given that they would possess the designation of a "word" (*pada*), the remainder would necessarily be unaccented (*anudātta*). Consequently, the word *kuvalī* would also be so, and thus the suffix *añ* would not occur after *kuvalī* in the sense of a derivative product (*vikāra*).

Since the word *garbhiṇī* has its initial syllable accented acute (*ādyaudātta*), the suffix *añ* would apply; therefore, it should not have been listed among the *bhikṣādi* group [which prevents that suffix] if it were already a pada. Yet it is listed there. From this, it is concluded that the remaining portion becomes unaccented even before the designation "pada" occurs.

159. *Karṣātvato dhaño’nta udāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.59). Regarding the term *karṣātvataḥ*: it is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) consisting of *karṣa* and *ātvat*. That which possesses the vowel *ā* is called *ātvat*. [The phrase] "of the root *karṣ*" refers to the root *kṛṣ* in the sense of "plowing" or "tilling."

This is connected with [the word] "possessing the vowel *a*" from rule 1286 (*dhā.pā.*). Because of its association with the root *karṣati*, even though it is a suffix (*dātv*), it is understood as referring specifically to a verbal root (*dhātu*). Since "of *ghan*" (*ghañaḥ*) is a mention of a suffix (*pratyaya-grahaṇa*), it is understood through the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix that the grammatical operation applies to that which ends in it; thus he says: "of that which ends in *ghan*."

Thus [it is said]. And this [term] is a coreferential qualifier of *karṣati* and of that which has the augment *āt*. [In the examples] "pākaḥ" and so forth, the root possesses the vowel *ā* once the vṛddhi [strengthening] has been applied by [Pāṇini 7.2.116] *ata upadhāyāḥ*. [In the examples] "dāyaḥ" and "dhāyaḥ," [the suffix] *yak* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.67] *āto yak ciṇkṛtoḥ*.
(7.3.33) Thus, [the suffix] *yuk* is applied.

But for what purpose is the modified form (*vikṛta*) mentioned in this context instead of simply saying "after *kṛṣ*" (*kṛṣātaḥ*)? To this he says: "The mention of *karṣa* is a reference to the modified form," and so forth.

The root *kṛṣ*, meaning "to plow," is recited both in the *bhū* class (the first class) and in the *tud* class (the sixth class). In this context, it is intended that only the *bhū* class root is to be understood—specifically that one for which a modification consisting of *guṇa* occurs when a *vikaraṇa* suffix follows—and not the other. And this is obtained when there is an indication by means of a modified form (*vikṛtanirdeśa*).

Therefore, the modification [of the root] is taught so that there may be the exclusion of the *kṛṣati* belonging to the *tudādi* class. But why is the exclusion of the *tudādi* [root] desired? To this he says:
"Of the *tudādi*," and so forth.

Now, for what purpose is the indication made by means of the possessive suffix *matup* (in the form *ākāra-vat*), rather than simply saying "after *karṣati*" and so on? It is not possible to do so, because there would be understood a reference to the vowel *ā* as a qualifier of that which is prescribed—namely, "that which is prescribed after [a stem] ending in *ā*. And if that were the case, [the rule would apply] only to forms such as *dāya*, but not to forms such as *pāka*.
It might be so; however, when the mention of *matup* is present, there is no fault.
The mention of "final" (*anta*) is for the sake of what follows, for in this case [the rule] "of the final [element]" (1.1.52) will apply.
160. And [the suffix *ghañ* is applied] after *uñch*, etc. (6.1.160):
namely, *uñchaḥ*, *mlecchaḥ*, *jañjaḥ*, and *jalpaḥ*. [The roots are: *ucchi uñche* (DhP 295), *mleccha avyaktāyāṃ vāci* (DhP 1662), and *jaja jaji yuddhe* (DhP 242, 243).

The roots *jap* and *jalp* mean "in distinct speech" (*dhā.pā.* 397, 398). The absence of *kutva* in *jañja-* is due to a specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*). Regarding the statement "the suffix *ap* is added to *vyadh* and *jap*," therein, the suffix *ap* is applied by the rule *vyadhajaporanupasarge* (Pāṇini 3.3.61). For the word *badha* [is derived] from the root *han*.

Regarding "vadhaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.3.76): "The accent of the verbal root would have applied to those two. [This refers to] the acute accent [prescribed] by "dhātoḥ" (6.1.162). Regarding "vyadhaḥ": "vyadha" is in the sense of "striking" (Dhātupāṭha 1181). Here too, by the rule "vyadhajapor... (3.3.61), the suffix -aṅ is applied; as before, the accent of the verbal root would have applied. [This is used] in reference to a specific time.
Thus [it refers to] the Kṛta, Dvāpara, and so forth. Regarding the rule "rathādyaupakaraṇe ca," the word "ādi" (and so forth) includes the plow and other such implements.
Regarding the word "garaḥ":
from the root *gṛ* (DhP 1410) meaning "to swallow," it ends in the suffix *ap* by the rule "ṛdorap" (3.3.57). By the word "viṣam," [the corruption of] the word *dūṣya* is indicated.
He shows the application [of the suffix] in a specific case: "elsewhere it is indeed ādyudātta" (i.e., udātta on the first syllable). This is due to the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*).

[The examples are: *veda*, *vega*, *veṣṭa*, and *bandha*. [The roots are: *vid* in the sense of knowing (DhP 1064), *vic* in the sense of separation (DhP 1442), *veṣṭ* in the sense of encircling (DhP 255), and *bandh*.

[The roots] *bandh* (DhP 1508), etc.; from these, as appropriate, when preceded by prefixes such as *pari*, *ādi*, and *upa*, the suffix *kvip* is applied, and there is no composition with *pra*. [It is stated: "Elsewhere, it has the udātta accent on the middle syllable.
For the word *vartani* is derived from the root *vṛt* according to Uṇādisūtra 1.2 (*arti-sṛ-ghṛ-*).

Thus, while the suffix *ani* is being carried over, [the word] is derived from the root *vṛt* (DhP 758, meaning "to turn") by applying the suffix *ani* according to the rule *vṛteśca* (DhP 3.1.6). Consequently, due to the accent of the suffix, it becomes *madhyodātta* (accented on the middle syllable). Regarding the word *daraḥ*: [it is derived from] the root *dṛ* (meaning "to split").

Because it ends in the vowel *ṛ*, it is a word ending in *-an*. Regarding the rule "The suffixes *sām* and *tāp* are used in the sense of reproach for a state of being": [the word] *sāmbaḥ* means "one who exists together with his mother (*ambā*)," and by the rule "In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the first member retains its original accent" (Pāṇini 6.2.1), it has its original accent.

Since the word *saha* would normally be accented on its first syllable by the rule "particles (*nipātāḥ*) have the acute accent on the first syllable" (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.80), the rule here prescribes that it has the acute accent on the final syllable when used in the sense of censuring an action (*bhāvagarhā*). For example: *sāmbho bhikṣate*. Here, the act of begging is censured. The word *tāpaḥ* (heat) is derived from the root *tap* (to heat, Dhātupāṭha 985) with the suffix *ghañ*.

This rule is stated because the initial acute accent (*ādyaudātta*) would otherwise apply. Why [is it said] "the distress of bandits toward the righteous, expressing contempt for their state"? [Consider: *sāmbastiṣṭhati* (Samba stands) and *tāpo mahān grīṣmasya* (the heat of summer is great).
In these two cases, there is only the initial acute accent.

Regarding the rule *ṭhutamaśaśvatamau*: these two [words] end in the suffix *tamap*. Since the suffix is marked with the indicator *p*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*); consequently, by the rule *nipātā ādyudātāḥ* (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.80), the word *ucch-* would be accented on its first syllable. Thus, the word *utama-* is used here to ensure that it is accented on the final syllable (*antodātta*), thereby overriding the initial accent that would otherwise apply.

It is recited [with this accent]. The word *śaśvat* is also acute on the final syllable by the accent of the nominal stem (*pratipadika-svara*); therefore, since a middle-acute accent would otherwise result, it is recited specifically for the sake of having the final acute. Regarding the term "everywhere" (*sarvatra*):
it applies both in cases of censuring an action (*bhāvagarhā*) and elsewhere.

"Ṭhbhakṣa--mantha' etc. [refers to]: "bhakṣa in the sense of eating" (DhP 1557), [also "bhakṣa in the sense of devouring" (DhP)], "mantha in the sense of churning" (DhP 42), "bhuj in the sense of crookedness" (DhP 1417), [also "bhuja" (DhP)], and "diha in the sense of growth" (DhP 1015). Now, an objection:
Since *bhakṣ* belongs to the curādigaṇa, it takes the suffix *ṇic*; therefore, by rule 3.3.56 (*ṭherac*), it ought to take the suffix *ac*.

How then can it end in *ghañ*? To this he says: "Even though *bhakṣ* is followed by *ṇic*," and so forth. He states the reason for this very point: "of those [roots] ending in *ac* that follow *ṇic*."
161. And [the final vowel of] an unaccented word [is elided], where there is the elision of an acute accent.

(6.1.161) For example, *kumāryau*. Here, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *vayasi prathame* (4.1.20), and the elision of the vowel *a* occurs by the rule *yasyeti ca* (6.4.148). It is stated that "the word *kumāra* is oxytone."

By the accent of the nominal stem (*prakṛtisvara*). In the same way, the state of being oxytone (*antodātta*) should be understood in subsequent cases as well. Regarding "ṅīp": [it is] "anudāta" (unaccented) because it is a *pit* suffix. Regarding "prāsaṅgyaḥ": the suffix *yat* belonging to the *prāgghita* group is applied by the rule "tadvahati" (Pāṇini 4.4.76).

Regarding the passage beginning with "the word *prasaṅga*," etc.: the word *prāsaṅga* is derived by adding the suffix *ghañ* to the root *ṣanja* (meaning "to adhere," DhP 987). Then, by applying [the rule] *gatikārakopapadāt* (6.2.139) and subsequently *tatpuruṣe* (6.2.123), [the required accentuation is established].

By the rule *varatamāne ṭhthāthaghañktājabitrakāṇām* (Pāṇini 6.2.144), an udātta accent on the final syllable is prescribed; therefore, that [word] is udātta on the end. "This is not so" is a negation of what was stated [previously], namely, "the udātta is elided. Why is this not the case? He says: "For in the case of a svarita..."

And so forth. Since the remaining portion becomes unaccented at the very same time as the rule for the accent is applied, this is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Therefore, when a circumflex (*svarita*) is being prescribed, the remainder must necessarily be unaccented. So, how could there be an elision of an acute (*udātta*)? It cannot.
The meaning is "from what [reason]? Regarding the passage beginning with "tad etat":
