since no counter-example for the mention of the anudātta (low-pitched vowel) is possible in this manner, therefore the mention of the anudātta is for the purpose of ensuring that the initial anudātta [of a word] becomes udātta (high-pitched).
The word "syāt" (it may be) is for this very purpose; otherwise, it would indeed be meaningless.

But what is the reason that the udātta accent is not established for an initial anudātta [vowel], such that the mention of "anudātta" is made for its sake? To this he says: "For [if it were] 'at the end' (ante)," and so forth.

Only restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is to be understood here; the meaning is that it would apply only to the final syllable, not to the initial. But where is the mention of *anudātta* made for the sake of making the initial syllable acute?
To this he says: "mā hi dhukṣātām," and so forth. [This is] from the root *duh* in the *luṅ* tense, in the Ātmanepada, with the suffixes *ātām* and *āthām*. And then...
By the rule *ṭhśala igupadhādaniṭaḥ ksaḥ* (3.1.45), there is the substitution of *ksa* for *cli*;
by the rule *ṭhtāsyānudāta* (6.1.186) and others, the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix is unaccented;
by the rule *ṭhksasyāci* (7.3.72), there is the elision of the letter *a*; and the vowel *a* of the *ksa* suffix is acute by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).

By the rules *ṭhdāderdhātorghaḥ* (8.2.32) and *ṭhkhari ca* (8.4.55), there is the substitution of *c* for [the letter *j*], whereby the letter *gh* becomes *k*, followed by the substitution of *ṣ*. In this context, if the mention of the term *anudātta* (unaccented) were not present, the initial vowel of the affixes *ātām*, *āthām*, and *ā* would not be unaccented; however, since it is present, [it is so].

In this case, the initial syllable of the word *ākāra* would have to be udātta. Furthermore, when the particle *hi* is employed, the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent by the rule *hi ca* (Pāṇini 8.1.34) would not apply. For if the *nighāta* were applied, the elision of the udātta [of the verbal suffix]—which occurs when a finite verb lacks the *nighāta* accent—would not take place. Likewise, the employment of *māṅ* [as a prohibitive particle] would prevent the augment *aṭ*.

This is so that the prohibition [of the elision of *m*] by the rule *māṅyoge* (Pāṇini 6.4.74) may apply. For if the augment *aṭ* were present, because it is udātta, the remainder would become anudātta; and if that were the case, the elision of the vowel *a* would occur when it is anudātta, but not when it is udātta.

Regarding "bhṛgavaḥ": the descendants of Bhṛgu are formed with the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ* by the rule "ṛṣy-andhaka-vṛṣṇi... (Pāṇini 4.1.114); this suffix is elided in the plural by the rule "atribhṛgukutsa... (Pāṇini 2.4.65). Now, one might object:
even here, when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) arises, there is the elision of the high-pitched vowel (*udātta*); therefore, in this case as well—

"Must it necessarily be so? To this he says: "Prior to the production of the case-ending," and so forth. For in the rule prescribing the elision (*luk*) of the secondary suffix (*gotra-pratyaya*), the case-ending is not accepted as the cause (*nimitta*). Therefore, the elision of the secondary suffix occurs precisely prior [to the application of the case-ending]; consequently, there is no status of being a restatement (*anuvādatva*) here. [Thus,] *baidī*...
Regarding "Āṭrvī": she is the female descendant of Bida; [the masculine form] being "Urvī," the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15).

The suffix *añ* is added by the rule *bidādibhyo 'ñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.104), which applies when the descendant is not the immediate offspring of a non-ṛṣi. Due to the accentual rule for *ñit* suffixes, the first syllable is udātta.
Finally, the suffix *ṅīp* is added according to *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (4.1.15).
162. *dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.162). [The example] "he runs" (*dhāvati*): due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.
163. *citaḥ* | (Pāṇini 6.1.163) In examples such as *bhaṅguram*, final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) is prescribed as an exception to the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
In the case of *kuṇḍināḥ*, however, there is the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) with respect to the accent.

This is a substitute for the word *kuṇḍina*, and since that [substitute] is middle-accented (*madhyodāta*) by virtue of the accent of the suffix, its substitute must likewise be middle-accented. [The derivation is as follows: from the sense "one who possesses a *kuṇḍa*," the suffix *ini* is applied;
then, from that form ending in *ini*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.5 (*ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*), resulting in *kuṇḍinyā*.

"Many offspring" (*apatyāni bahūni*): by virtue of belonging to the *gargādi* group, the suffix *yañ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.105; when there is plurality, this suffix is elided (*luk*). For the remaining portion, the substitution of *kuṇḍina* occurs. [This is governed by] the rule "when a suffix beginning with a *cit* [element follows]," and so forth. But how is this so?
How is it that the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) is obtained for the entire aggregate consisting of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*)?

It is explained as follows: here, in the expression *citaḥ*, this genitive case refers to a part in relation to the whole. That is to say, the final acute accent belongs to that aggregate which is related to the "cited" (*cit*) part.

The meaning is that it becomes [so]. Alternatively, *citaḥ* is a form ending in the possessive suffix *ac*; thus, *citaḥ* means "that which has consciousness (*cit*)"; the meaning is that its final syllable becomes udātta.
By this, the fact that the final syllable of the entire combination of base and suffix is udātta is established.

If, then, *citaḥ* ends in the suffix *ac* (the *matvarthīya* suffix *a*) denoting possession, then, by means of a transposition of case endings (*sub-vyatyaya*), the nominative will occur in place of the expected genitive. As in the example *bahupaṭavaḥ*: "those who are slightly less than clever," where the suffix *bahuc* is added before the nominal ending according to the rule *vibhāṣā supo bahuc purastāt*.
By [Pāṇini 5.3.68], the suffix *bahuc* is applied; thus we have "uccakaiḥ. By [Pāṇini 5.3.72], "akac" is added after indeclinables and pronouns before the suffix *tasil*; thus [we have "uccakais"].
164. *Taddhitasya* (6.1.164).

[The example is] "Kauñjāyanāḥ. This is derived from a word ending in *cphañ*—by the rule *Kuñjādibhyaś cphañ* (4.1.98)—to which the suffix *ā* has been added by the rule *Vrātacphañor astriyām* (5.3.113).
There is elision (*luk*) by the rule "of a *tadrāja* [patronymic] suffix, when there are many [descendants]" (2.4.62).

The question "For what purpose? is asked by one who thinks that the matter is already established by the preceding rule alone. The phrase "even the subsequent," etc., refers to the fact that the letter *c* in *cphañ* is [present] in the rule "after *vrāta* and *cphañ*, in the non-feminine" (5.3.113).

The purpose is served by the qualification. The letter *ñ* also serves the purpose of [indicating] the *vṛddhi* vowel. If this were not stated, then, because it is subsequent, the accent of the *ñit* suffix would apply; therefore, it is done for the sake of ensuring that the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) occurs, thereby overriding even that [accent].

165. *kitaḥ* | (Pāṇini 6.1.165) This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accent of an affix (*pratyayasvara*). Examples are *ākṣikaḥ* and *śālākikaḥ*. The affix *ṭhak* is applied in the sense of "he plays with that" (*tena dīvyati*), according to Pāṇini 4.4.2.

166. *tisṛbhyo jasaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.166). [The example is] *tisras tiṣṭhanti*. The substitute *tisṛ* is applied by the rule *tricaturor striyāṃ tisṛcatasṛ* (7.2.99), and the substitution of *r* for the vowel *ṛ* is applied by the rule *aci ra ṛtaḥ* (7.2.100).

Regarding the rule *ṭhudātasvaritayoḥ* and so forth: the word *tri-* is oxytone by the accentual rule for nominal stems (*prātipadika-svara*), and thus its substitute *tisṛ-* is also oxytone. In that case, the *ra* prescribed as a substitute for the oxytone *ṛ*-vowel does not become an *udātayaṇ*. Consequently, for the following *jas*...

By the rule "ṭhudātasvaritayoḥ" (8.2.4) and others, a svarita accent would result; therefore, this [present rule] is an exception to that. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *jas*? If it is argued that it is so that [the svarita] does not occur here even in the case of *tisṛka*, [the answer is as follows].

It might be argued: "If the suffix *kan* were applied to the word *tri* to form a name, and if the substitution of *tisṛ* were applied there according to the Vārttika 'the addition of *kan* when *tisṛ* occurs' (Vārttika 837), then the form *tisṛkā* would also result even in the absence of the mention of *jas*. But this is not so; for here the accent of the *nit* suffix will be the sublater [of the *tisṛ* substitution]."

If it is argued that, since the *ni*-accent is not applied when another accent intervenes, and that it begins with the third accent—just as it sets aside the accent prescribed by "the *su* and *ti* affixes are unaccented" (Pāṇini 3.1.4)—it likewise sets aside the *ni*-accent, this is not so; because an exception applies only to that which would otherwise necessarily apply (*yena nāprāpte*). And [in this case], it does not apply when [the other rule] has not yet necessarily applied.
The accentuation of *tisṛ* is commenced under the rule "ṭhanudātau suptitau" (Pāṇini 3.1.4),

even though the *nit*-accent would otherwise apply— whether it has already been applied or not. Alternatively, according to the principle that "intermediate exceptions supersede preceding rules" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 10), the accentuation of *tisṛ* supersedes the *ṭha*-accentuation.
This [rule] will supersede *suptiṅ* (P. 3.1.4), but it will not supersede the *nit*-accent.

If it is argued that the mention of *jas* is for the purpose of excluding [the accentuation of] *śas* and the following cases, this too is not the case; for in the case of *śas*, there must necessarily be an udātta on the final syllable by virtue of P. 6.1.174 (*udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt*).

Thus: all other plural forms beginning with a consonant (*hal*) [are included]; regarding those, [the rule] "after *ṣaṣ*, *tri*, and *catur*, [the nominative/accusative plural ending] beginning with a consonant" (Pāṇini 6.1.174) applies. All other plural forms beginning with a consonant [are included]; regarding those, [the rule] "after *ṣaṣ*, *tri*, and *catur*, [the nominative/accusative plural ending] beginning with a consonant" (Pāṇini 6.1.179) applies.
Thus, by the rule *ṭhjhalyupotamam* (Pāṇini 6.1.80), [the vowel] ought to be udātta;
furthermore, because the word *tisṛ* has the plural as its domain, the dual and singular do not exist for it.
In that case, even without the mention of *jas*, [the substitution] would occur only after *jas*; therefore, he says: "The mention of *jas*..."

And so forth. "Some" refers to the authors of the Bhāṣya and others. They maintain that if the mention of *jas* were not made, then after forming the *prādi*-compound *atisṛ* (meaning "beyond three"), the rule would undesirably apply even in a case such as *atitistr-au*; therefore, they accept the mention of *jas* in order to exclude this fault for the sake of compounds.

167. *caturaḥ śasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.167). Because the word *catuḥ* ends in the suffix *uran*—according to the rule *cateruran* (Uṇādi-sūtra 8.78)—it is udātta on its first syllable. For this sūtra prescribes that its final syllable becomes udātta when followed by the case-ending *śas*.

Now, why does this not occur here: "catasraḥ paśya"? Even when the substitute *catasṛ* has been applied, [the acute accent] would not apply due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*. To this, he says: "The substitute *catasṛ*," and so forth.

Once the substitute *catasṛ* has been made, the initial acute accent (*ādyaudātta*) will be prescribed by way of a specific rule (*nipātana*); that is the accent resulting from the specific rule (*nipātanasvara*).

Since *śas* is a sublater (*bādhaka*) of the vowel accent, by virtue of this prescribed substitution of the acute accent (*audātatva-nipātana*), this accent does not apply here in the case of *paśyeta*. Alternatively, since the substitution of *r* for *ṛ* has already been effected by *aci ra ṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.100) prior to the application of the accent rule, the accent cannot apply to the *ṛ*-vowel; nor can it apply to the *a*-vowel, because of the rule *acaḥ*.

According to the rule *parasmin vidhau pūrvasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.57), when there is an intervention by the vowel *ṛ* due to the substitution of *yaṇ*, the [vowel lengthening] ought not to occur at all. But is it not the case that this is prohibited in rules concerning vowels by the sūtra *na padāntadvirvacanavareyalopa...* (Pāṇini 1.1.58)?

Is there the application of the rule *sthānivadbhāva*? This is not so; for it has been stated therein that "in the case of vowel (*svara*), long vowel (*dīrgha*), and *y*-lopa, a substitute for a deleted element (*lopājādeśa*) is not treated as the original (*na sthānivat*)," and this is not a substitute for a deleted element.
168. *sāvekācastṛtīyādirvibhaktiḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.168).
Does the term *sāu* here refer to the nominative singular, the locative plural, or both? If it were to refer to the nominative singular, [the forms would be] *tvāyā* and *tvayi*.

This [undesirable consequence] would also apply here. For when the word *yuṣmad* undergoes the substitution of *tvā* by the rule "tvāhau sau" (Pāṇini 7.2.94), it possesses the property of being a monosyllable (*ekāctva*) when followed by the nominative singular case-ending.
This fault persists even if both [the singular and plural endings] were intended by the general term. However, this is not the case if the locative plural ending is what is intended to be included.
Having kept all this in mind—that a fault would follow [if the rule were applied as stated], and that the word *yuṣmad* in the form *yuṣmāsu* consists of more than one vowel (*anekāctva*)—he says:
"The term *sā* is the inclusion of the locative plural. [He gives the example: "*yādbhyām*."

From the word *rājan* ending in the suffix *śatṛ*, the third case [instrumental] occurs, as in "to the king" (*rājñe*). When the word *rājan* follows a base designated as *bha*, the [nasal] elision is applied, and it becomes monosyllabic (*ekāc*), unlike in the nominative singular where one has *rājān-su*. In that case, because it is polysyllabic (*anekāctvāt*), the forms *vāktara* and *vāktama* occur by means of the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap*. Thus it is.
It refers to the third case-affix and others, but not to the case-affix itself.
Now, why is the locative plural mentioned?

To this he says: "of the locative plural," and so forth. [The examples are] *tvayā* and *tvayi*; [this is because] for the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, [the substitute *tvad* and *mad* apply] to that which ends in *map*. (Pāṇini 7.2.91).
The substitution of *tvā* is by the rule "ṭhtvamāvekavacane" (Pāṇini 7.2.97); for the remainder, the substitution of *ya* is by the rule "ṭhyo'ci" (Pāṇini 7.2.89).

169. *antodātād uttarapadād anyatarasyām anityasamāse* (Pāṇini 6.1.169). If that which is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*) due to the absence of an analytical statement (*vigraha*) were included here by the term "obligatory compound," then [the rule] would also apply optionally in cases such as *avācā* and *suvacā brāhmaṇena*.
Having kept this in mind, he says: "The word *nitya* is marked with the svarita accent.
The meaning is that its svarita quality is applied. What follows from this? He says: "By that," and so forth.
For by means of the svarita accent, there occurs the understanding of a governing heading (*adhikāra*). By that [svarita], the governing heading of *nitya*—which...

A compound has been prescribed; and since that compound is not one prescribed under the heading of obligatory compounds (*nitya-adhikāra*), it is an optional compound (*anitya-samāsa*). In the example "suvācaḥ," the compound is formed by the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18).
[In this case,] the original accent of the initial member applies because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya-pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*) in a *tatpuruṣa* compound.

According to the rule *tulyārthaiḥ tṛtīyā-saptamy-upamānāvyayam*, there is the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member [of the compound]; thus, in *kāśikāṭ*, that [first member] is acute (*udātta*). This is because of the rules *nipātā ādyudāttāḥ* and *upasargāś cābhivarjam* (Phiṭ-sūtras 4.80, 81).

Because of this statement: just as there is no final acute accent (*antodātatva*) for the subsequent member here, so too there is no obligatory composition (*nityasamāsatva*); for even in rules such as *kugatiprādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18), the term "obligatory" (*nitya*) is understood to carry over. This being the case, [the rule] *mayūravyaṃsakādayaś ca* (Pāṇini 2.1.72) [is established].
By this [statement], the compound should be understood here; for *maravyūyaṃsaka* and so forth belong to the class of words formed according to their general appearance (*ākṛtigaṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "otherwise, indeed": if the mention of the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) were not made, then the mention of "monosyllabic" (*ekāj*) would qualify the compound itself. What would be the fault in that? To this he says: "In that case..."

And so forth. The word *ūrj* ends in the suffix *kvip* because it belongs to the *saṃpad-ādi* group. In the examples "fire-kindler" (*agnicit*) and "Soma-presser" (*somasut*), the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rules *agnau ceḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.91) and *some suñaḥ* (3.2.90). [The commentary states: "This compound is prescribed within the scope of the section on obligatory (nitya) compounds."

In this context, because of the continued application of the term "nityam" from the rule *nityaṃ krīḍājīvikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18), the word "tatra" and so forth [is used]. By the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member (*uttarapada*) is prescribed. And as for that final member...
By the accent of the stem (*dhātu-svara*), the final syllable is udātta; therefore, the word *cic* becomes udātta. The same applies to the word *somasut*.
Regarding the phrase "but that which... and so forth, it refers to what was stated [in the Kāśikā]: "The word *nitya* is accented" (Kāśikā 6.1.169).

He shows the purpose of this [sūtra] by means of the examples "ṭhavācā" and "suvācā. Here, a grammatical analysis (vigraha) with the preceding word "a-" and the word "su-" is not possible, because those two are not employed here; therefore, these two are not *nitya*-compounds, but rather they are so because of the rule established under the heading of *nitya*.

170. *añceśchandasyasarvanāmasthānam* (Pāṇini 6.1.170). As in the example: *indro dadhīcaḥ*. [The word] *dadhyañc-* is formed by the suffix *kvin* according to *ṛtvig-ādinā kvin* (Pāṇini 3.2.59), followed by the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*). This is the singular genitive case; [the final *-c* is replaced by *-a*] by *acaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.138).
There is the elision of the vowel *i*, and by the rule *ṭhcau* (Pāṇini 6.3.138), there is lengthening.

Regarding the phrase "beginning with the third case," etc.: if the term *sarvanāmasthāna* were employed [in the sūtra], then the suffix *śas* would not be [subject to this rule], because it does not begin with the third case. Furthermore, even if the mention of "beginning with the third case" [is made]...
Let it be withdrawn; even so, [the rule] would still apply even in the case of a *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix], as in "pratīcaḥ," which is similar to the previous example.

171. *ūḍidampadādyappumraidyaubhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.171). [The example is] *praṣṭhauhaḥ*. [The suffix] *ṇvi* is applied by [the rule] *vahaśca* (3.2.64); *ūṭh* is substituted by *vāha ūṭh* (6.4.132); and the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs by *etyedhatyūṭhṣu* (6.1.89).

Regarding the phrase "the mention of *upadhā* [is for the sake of] *ūḍ*": the meaning is that one must provide the explanation, "that by which *ūḍ*, being an *upadhā*, is grasped is the 'mention of *upadhā*'. For what purpose? To this he says:
"so that it may not apply here. In that regard, the explanation is as follows: "from that which is oxytone (*antodātāt*)."

From the sūtra beginning with (6.1.169), the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is understood to carry over here; moreover, that is understood as a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (a restricted option). Therefore, since [the suffix] must occur only when [the word] has a penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), it is appropriate to take that very [word] as the referent. Thus: *akṣadyūḥ*. [The derivation is: *akṣair dīvyati* ("he plays with dice"), [forming the stem] by means of the suffix *kvip*.

By the rule *ṭhcchÂañoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.19), the *uṭ* augment is applied to the *v* of *ya*, resulting in the *yaṇ* substitution [to form *yu*]. Thus we have *ābhyām*. Here, the substitution of *at* for *idam* (as in the *astyadādi* group) occurs, and by the rule *hali lopaḥ* (7.2.113), the form *id-* is elided. Thus we have *atho ābhyām*. By the rule *idamo'nvādeśe'śanudātastṛtīyādau* (Pāṇini 2.4.32), the substitute *aś* is applied to *idam* when it follows a prior mention (*anvādeśa*) in the third case and subsequent cases.
(2.4.32) Thus, there is the substitution of *aś*.

[The statement] "here, those ending with *niś* are included" is also obtained through the previously mentioned *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (restricted option); for when that exists, the [substitution] must occur only after those ending with *niś*. Of these very [words]...
It is logical that they alone are understood [by the mention of their substitutes]. "Ni-padaḥ": when *śas* follows, there is the substitution of *pada* for *pāda*.
"Dataḥ": here too, there is the substitution of *dad* for the word *danta*. "Āsann":
here, in the locative singular, there is this substitution of *āsann* for the word *āsana*. "Udan": [likewise].

Here, in the word *ap*, the substitution of *ud* for *apa* occurs; then, by the rule "adbhiḥ," the letter *p* is changed to *t*, which undergoes *jaś*-tva to become *d*. Then, by the rule "rābhyām," the substitution of *ā* for *rā* occurs according to "rāyo hali" (Pāṇini 7.2.85).
172. *aṣṭano dīrghāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.172). [Examples include] *aṣṭābhiḥ*, and so forth. The substitution of *ā* for *aṣṭan* occurs by the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (7.2.84).
[The form] *aṣṭasu*. But surely, here too, the substitution of *ā* ought to occur; for indeed, that [substitution] was prescribed [by the aforementioned rule].
Is there a statement that establishes an alternative interpretation, nor is it the subject under discussion? To this he says: "This very [statement]," and so forth.

For if *ātva* were permanent (*nitya*), the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) here would be purposeless, because there would be nothing from which to exclude it; and [one might ask] why the designation *ṣaṣ* applies to that which has already undergone *ātva*. This very [point] is indeed [the reason].
The inclusion of the term "long" (*dīrgha*) should be understood as indicating [the rule] regarding the word *aṣṭan*. But how does it indicate this? To this he says:
"For otherwise," and so forth. Indeed, the inclusion of the term "long" is made for this purpose:
so that this accent (*svara*) may not occur where the substitution of *āt* (for *aṣṭan*) does not exist. If, however, the substitution of *āt* were applied to *aṣṭan*...

If the designation *ṣaṭ* were not [to apply], then, in the view that [the rule] applies to the short vowel (*tadātva*), since the designation *ṣaṭ* would be absent, the rule "acute on the vowel of *aṣṭan*" (*aṣṭanaḥ svaraḥ*) would have its scope; however, even there, the acute accent of *ṣaṭ* would still apply. Therefore, if the mention of the long vowel (*dīrghagrahaṇa*) were not made, then, because it would lack scope in the view that [the rule] applies to the short vowel, [the rule for] *aṣṭan*...

The [short] vowel does not occur; therefore, this would also apply in the other alternative. Consequently, the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) is purposeful for the sake of excluding that [short vowel]. When *aṣṭan* has undergone the change to *ātva*, it receives the technical designation "ṣaṣ" (six)—as in the case of *aṣṭānām*, where the augment *nuṭ* is applied by the rule *ṣaṭcaturbhyaśca* (Pāṇini 7.1.55).
He becomes accomplished.

173. *śaturanumo nadyajādī* (Pāṇini 6.1.173). [Examples: *tudatī*, *nudatī*. Because they belong to the *tud-ādi* class, the suffix *śa* is applied. [Examples: *lunatī*, *punatī*. By the rule *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ* (6.4.112), there is elision of the long *ā*. [The accentuation is] by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).

In this context, the form ending in the present participle suffix *śatṛ* should be understood as having its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). Regarding the phrase "of that" (*tasya*) and so forth: how is it that [the desired application] does not occur even though it is intended? It is because of the separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*) in the sūtra *na mu ne* (Pāṇini 8.2.3), where the word *na* is treated as a separate rule.

Regarding the rule "bṛhanmahatoḥ" and so forth: the word *upasaṃkhyāna* means "addition" or "supplementation. Here, the supplementation is as follows: from the rule "ḍaḷaśchandasi" (Pāṇini 6.1.178), the term *bahulam* ("optionally" or "diversely") applies by way of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*) maxim; thus, the suffix also occurs after the words *bṛhat* and *mahat*.

174. *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt* | (6.1.174) This rule is stated because [the previous rule] *udātasvaritayoryaṇaḥ svarito'nudātasya* (8.2.4) would otherwise apply. [The word] *tṛnantaḥ* is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable) by virtue of the *nit-svara* (the accentuation of a suffix marked with *n*). [The example is] *bahutītavā*.
Thus: *bahutitavā* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has many *titava*s. This word *titau* is oxytone by the rule *bahoṛ nañcaduttarapadabhūmni* (Pāṇini 6.2.175).
Regarding the statement "the mention of the letter *n* must be made": that by which the letter *n* is grasped is called "the mention of the letter *n*."
The meaning is that an explanation must be provided. In this regard, the explanation is as follows:

here too, as before, the term *bahulam* ("optionally" or "in various cases") is understood to follow. By virtue of that, [the substitution] will not occur even after a *n* that stands in the place of an udātta vowel. Alternatively—[it concerns] the *n* here.

Regarding *praśleṣa* (the combination of letters): [it applies] by the rule "ṅ- and n- are substituted for the final letter of a word ending in a consonant, except when followed by a verbal root" (Pāṇini 6.1.75). Thus, the meaning becomes:

"from that which has an udātta vowel as its *yaṇ*-substitute, and from that which has an udātta *n*. By this, it will also apply to that which has an udātta *n*. For example: *vākpatnī*. Here, the word *pati*...

It is udātta on the final syllable by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). In that case, there is the substitution of *na* for the final vowel according to *vibhāṣā sapūrvasya* (Pāṇini 4.1.34), and the suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* (Pāṇini 4.1.5).

175. *noṅdātvoḥ* | (6.1.175) [The example] "brahmabandhvā" is formed by analyzing it as a *bahuvrīhi* compound: "one whose relative (*bandhu*) is a Brahmin (*brahmā*). From that, the suffix *ūṅ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.66] *ūṅ utaḥ*. [The commentary states: "That single substitute which occurs together with that [suffix] is also acute."

This is because of the rule: "A substitute for a circumflex vowel is circumflex" (8.2.5). Regarding the term *svaryate*: the meaning is that it is made circumflex (*svarita*). Regarding the phrase *kuduttarapada* and so forth: here, the vowel *ū* is oxytone (*antodāta*) by virtue of the accent of the verbal root; this [accent] is [governed by] the rule "After a prefix, a kāraka, or an upapada" (6.2.139).
Thus, having been extended, it remains with its natural accent.

176. *hrasvanuṅbhyāṃ matup* (Pāṇini 6.1.176). Since the suffix *matup* would otherwise be *anudātta* (unaccented) by virtue of its being marked with the *pit* indicator, this rule is commenced. In the example *akṣaṇvantaḥ*, the suffix *matup* is applied in the sense of "possessing eyes" (*akṣam asyāsti*). By the rule *chandasy api dṛśyate* (7.1.76), the substitution *anaṅ* is applied [to the final vowel of *akṣan*], and then *n* is elided.
The augment *nuṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 8.2.13], and the preceding *n* is elided by [Pāṇini 8.2.7]: "There is elision of a *n* at the end of a nominal stem. Regarding the form *śīrṣaṇvatā*:

the word *śīrṣan* is derived from the word *śiras* by the rule "In the Vedic language, *śīrṣan* [is substituted for *śiras*]" (6.1.60). It is thus established as an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) term.
"The word *vasu* has its first syllable udātta.
For that [word] is derived while the rule "after the roots *bhṛ*, *mṛ*, *śī*, *tṛ*, *car*, *tan*, *tan*, *dhani*, *mi*, and *masj*, the suffix *u*" (Daiva-Uṇādi 1.92) is in force,
[and] because of the mention of *niṭ* in the rule "in the sense of grain, [the suffix *u* is] *niṭ*" (Daiva-Uṇādi 1.94).
It is derived by the rule *ṭhśṛsvṛsvihitrapyasivasihaniklidibandhimanibhyaśca* (Dhātupāṭha 1.95). Consequently, by the accentuation of the *nit* suffix, it becomes udātta on its first syllable.
Now, why does this [suffix] not occur here in the case of *marutvān*, meaning "one who possesses Maruts," where the word *marut* also [occurs]?

If it is argued that, because [the word] *mṛgerutiḥ* ends in the suffix *ut* (by *da.u. 6.1*), it is oxytone by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), and thus there is an occasion for [the application of the rule], but that it does not occur here because of the intervention of the letter *n*—[we reply: no, because that [suffix] has been elided. Or, even if the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) for the sake of establishing the accent, even so—

Is there no intervention [of the consonant], on the basis of the rule "in a rule prescribing a vowel, a consonant is as if non-existent" (Vyāḍipāda 37)? To this he says: "In a rule prescribing a vowel," and so forth. But how is it known that [the consonant] is not taken into account? From the mention of *nuṅ*. For this *nuṅ* augment is indeed the suffix *matup*.

Since [the word] *bhakta* is understood by that very mention [of the term], if this *paribhāṣā* were relied upon, then because the consonant *n* would not exist [as a distinct entity], the rule would be established simply by the words "after a short vowel" (*hrasvāt*), and one would not have made the mention of *nuṅ*; yet it has been made. Therefore, it is known that this *paribhāṣā* is not relied upon here.
"It is to be stated" (vaktavyaḥ) means "it is to be explained. This same meaning applies to the word *vaktavya* in subsequent instances as well.
However, the explanation should be carried out as before, by relying on the continued application of the term *bahulagrahaṇa* ("the mention of 'in various ways'").

177. *nāmanyatarasyām* (6.1.177). [The word] *nām* refers to the genitive plural form of *namas* together with the augment *nuṭ*. But what is the reason that the short vowel is qualified by *matup*? To this he says: "Otherwise, indeed..."
And so forth. "Present" (*sāmpratika*) means belonging to the present; the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied according to the rule for the group beginning with *adhyātma*.

Regarding the word "of three" (*tisṛṇām*), here the long vowel is prohibited by the rule *na tisṛcatasṛ* (Pāṇini 6.4.4); thus [the form] is *sāmpratika*, with the suffix *ṭhañ* applied according to the rule for the group beginning with *adhyātma*.

Regarding the phrase "of the three" (*tisṛṇām*): here, because the prohibition of lengthening by the rule *na tisṛcatasṛ* (Pāṇini 6.4.4) applies, only the current short vowel exists. When the current [short vowel] is present, it is not logical to resort to a former state [of length]. In this context, if the short vowel were not qualified by the suffix *matup*, then here—

It would not apply in the case of *agnīnām*—for once the lengthening prescribed by *nāmi* (Pāṇini 6.4.3) has been applied, it would no longer apply because the short vowel is absent. Therefore, for the purpose that the short vowel should apply even when it was previously present, the short vowel is qualified by the suffix *matup*. [This is illustrated in] *dhenvām*, *śakaṭyām*.

Thus: if the inclusion of the form with the augment *nuṭ* were not made, then there would be the inclusion of the genitive plural ending *ām* even for the substitute [of the dative], and consequently it would also occur in forms such as *dhenvām*. However, when the inclusion of the form with *nuṭ* is made, it does not occur; for that [substitute] is absent in that case.

In the case of the words *dhenu* and *śakaṭi*, which are oxytone by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*), when the final vowel undergoes the *yaṇ* substitution, the resulting form becomes invariably oxytone by virtue of the rule "udāttayaṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.174).
Regarding the rule "ṭhtrapūṇām": the word *trapu* is acutely accented on its first syllable, just like the word *vasu*.
178. *ṅyāś chandasi bahulam* (6.1.178).
179. *ṣaṭtricaturbhyo halādiḥ* (6.1.179). [Note:
"The rule *ṭhantodātāt* has ceased to apply. If this were to continue [from the previous sūtra], then [the acute accent would apply] to *pañcānām*.

In the case of "of seven" (*saptānām*) and "of four" (*caturṇām*), [the rule] would not apply; for, since words such as *pañca* and *śabda* are acute-accented on their final syllable by the rule *nraḥ saṃkhyāyāḥ* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.28), the term *nraḥ* refers to the inclusion of numeral words ending in the phonemes *r* and *n*.

180. *jhalyupottamam* (Pāṇini 6.1.180). Regarding the statement "the last among three or more is called *uttama*," the word *uttama* here is taken as an underived (*avyutpanna*) term. And it is because that word, by its very nature, denotes the final member among three or more that this is so.
"In its vicinity" (*tatsamīpe*) is called *upotamam*; this is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule "an indeclinable [preceded by] a case-ending," etc. (Pāṇini 2.1.6).
181. *vibhāṣā bhāṣāyām* | Since the preceding rule would have made [the substitution] obligatory, this statement is for the purpose of making it optional in common speech (*bhāṣā*).

182. *na go-śvan-sāv-avarṇa-rāḍ-aṅ-kuṅ-kṛt-bhyaḥ* (6.1.182). Regarding the term *sau*: does this refer to the *su* of the nominative singular (*prathamaikavacana*), or to [the suffix] *su* in the locative plural (*saptamī bahuvacana*)? In that regard, if it were the reference to the locative plural, [the rule would apply to forms such as *goṣu*, *aśveṣu*, etc., but not to the nominative singular].

In the case of *kebhyaḥ* and *tebhyaḥ*, [the substitution] would not occur, because when the seventh-case plural (*saptamī-bahuvacana*) follows the words *ka-* and *ta-*, it is impossible for them to end in the vowel *a*; for even if the substitution of *yatva* (i.e., *ya* for *tyad*-class stems) were applied, the rule "in the plural, before *jhal*, *e* is substituted" (Pāṇini 7.3.103) prescribes the substitution of *e*. However, if the first-case singular (*prathamaikavacana*) is what is being referred to...

This [exception] also applies here. Therefore, considering that it is logical to take the rule as applying only when the seventh case (locative) is not present, he says: "that which ends in *a* in the nominative singular.
Since there is nothing else to be prohibited immediately following this, this prohibition applies to every vowel belonging to the sixth case (genitive).

He says, "It is understood thus: 'that which was stated regarding these [words] does not occur. In the case of *suguḥ*—meaning "one who has beautiful cows"—the short vowel is applied by the rule *gostriyoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.48), and the final syllable of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is accented on the last vowel by the rule *nañsubhyām* (Pāṇini 6.2.172).

In *śunā*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule *śvayuvamaghonāmataddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.133). Regarding "the application is as before": in cases such as *śunā* and *śvabhyām*, the application [of the rule for lengthening] occurs by the rule *sāvekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.168), and so forth. In *paramaśunā*, here too—

The acute accent on the final syllable, as in *rājā* and *paramarājaḥ*, is due to the accentual rule for compounds (*samāsasvara*)— specifically, Pāṇini 6.1.169, which prescribes an acute accent on the final syllable of a compound whose second member ends in an acute accent. Here too, the application is as previously explained.

"ṭhañ is [the suffix] ending in kvin. If this is so, then there should not be an elision of the letter *n* in that case; rather, the inclusion of that very [suffix] with its *n* must be made. For what purpose is the inclusion of the one with *n*? He says: "of that," and so forth. And for what purpose is even this?

Thus he says: "In this case," and so forth. Now, one might object: since elision (*lopa*) must occur everywhere, how can there be an absence of the elision of *n*? To this he replies: "Not after *añc*," and so forth. Regarding "prāñcā": as before, the root is *prāp* (from *pra* + *añc*). From the sense "he moves forward" (*prāñcati*), the suffix *kvip* is applied. Regarding "prācā": [the same applies].
As before, there is the elision of *u* and the lengthening of the vowel.

Regarding the word "kruñcā": from the roots *kruñc* and *kruñc*, meaning "crookedness" and "becoming small" (*kruñca-kruñca kauṭilyālpībhāvayoḥ*; Dhātupāṭha 185, 186), the suffix *kvin* is applied, resulting in *kruñc*.

The absence of *nalopa* (elision of the nasal) occurs by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). In the case of "paramakruñcā," there is final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) due to the accent of the compound. In the case of "paramakṛtā," it is the same here as well; [the word] "kṛti" is derived from the root "kṛtī chedane" (DhP 1435).
184. *nṛ cānyatarasyām* (6.1.184). [The rule *sāvekācaḥ* (6.1.168) applies] after the word *nṛ*, and [the rule *na gośvansāvarṇa* (6.1.182) also applies].
And since a permanent prohibition would otherwise apply, this optional rule (vibhāṣā) is commenced.

185. *titsvaritam* | (6.1.185) In the examples "cikīrṣyam" and "jihīrṣyam," this optional rule is introduced because the constant prohibition established by "na gośvansāvarṇa" (6.1.182) would otherwise have applied.

186. *tāsyanudātenṅdidupadeśāllasarvadhātukamanudātamahanviṅeḥ* | (6.1.186) The mention of *tāsi* and the others is by way of a collective dvandva compound. [The phrase] "from that which is taught with a non-udātta vowel" (*anudātopadeśāt*) [is used].

It is called *upadeśa* because it is taught (*upadiśyate*); the meaning is that which is first uttered among the sentences of the Śāstra and in the *khilapāṭha*. This [term] *adupadeśa* is a compound consisting of "a" and "upadeśa. The word *upadeśa* is employed here either as a noun denoting the object (*karmasādhana*) or as a noun denoting the action (*bhāvasādhana*); it is not by this [word]...

Because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would otherwise be untenable. In the rule *ṭhasārvadhātukam*, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). In the rule *adupadeśāt*, as before, there is a descriptive determinative compound (*karmadhāraya*) with the word *upadeśa* used in its objective sense. The mention of the "phoneme" (*varṇagrahaṇa*) [in these rules] applies the principle of inclusion of what ends in that (*tadantavidhi*) everywhere.

The meaning is: "because it is taught with a final long *ā* in the form *prayojayati*. Regarding the word *kartā*: it is the periphrastic future (*luṭ*) of the root *kṛ*, in the first person singular of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*); for that [suffix], there is the substitution of *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras*. In the singular, there is the elision of the *ṭi* (the *a* of *ḍā*).
In the dual and plural, by the rule *ri ca* (Pāṇini 7.4.51), there is the elision of the *s* [of *ras*].

In forms such as *tiṣṭhate* and ending with *śete*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap* because they belong to the *adādi* (second) class of roots. *Vaste*: from the root *vas* in the sense of "covering" (DhP 1023). *Sūte*: from the root *ṣūṅ* in the sense of "the delivery of the fetus by living beings" (DhP 1031). *Śete*.

There is *guṇa* substitution by the rule "śīṅḥ sārvadhātuke guṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.21). Thus we have *tudataḥ* and *nudataḥ*; these end in *tas*. Similarly, *pacataḥ* and *paṭhataḥ* are also [examples]. Now, one might object: in its original form (*upadeśa*), this suffix *śap* ends in a consonant, not in the letter *n*. Therefore—
How does the lack of acute accent (anudāttatva) occur here? To this he says: "of the *anubandha*," and so forth.
"Exclusive" (*ekānta*) means a single part; "non-exclusive" (*anekānta*) means that which is not exclusive, that is to say, it is grasped by the inclusion of that [part].
The state of being non-exclusive is "non-exclusiveness" (*anekāntatva*). From that...

The meaning is that the suffix *śap* is taught as ending in the vowel *a*, not as ending in a consonant; therefore, in forms such as *pacate*, the state of being unaccented (*anudātatva*) occurs. However, the status of ending in *a* for the letter *ś* of *śap* is due to its treatment as if it possessed the designation [of the preceding element] (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). Examples include *pacamānaḥ* and *yajamānaḥ*.
[The suffix] *śānac* [is introduced]. But how is there lack of udātta here, given that there is an intervention by the augment *muk*?

To this he says: "If in this case," and so forth. Is this augment *muk* for the vowel *a* alone, or for the stem ending in *a*? In that regard, if it were for the vowel *a* alone, then [the rule] would be covered by the mention of "being taught with *a*" (*adupadeśa*).
Its inclusion [in the rule] occurs immediately after *las*, *sarvadhātuka*, and *adupadeśa* because there is no intervention; for a constituent part of itself does not constitute an intervention.
Therefore, by virtue of being *antaraṅga* (internal), the *nighāta* (elision of the accent) is established. By the words "Now," etc., [the author addresses] the second alternative.
Because the application of the *nighāta* (accentual suppression) is not established, he demonstrates this with the words "even so" (*tathāpi*). This means "even under such circumstances.
The connection is with what will be stated later: that the *nighāta* of the *sarvadhātuka* suffix ending in *l* is established.
The word "unestablished" (*asiddha*) also refers to the current topic, namely the *muk* augment. The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason.

This is the meaning: since the *muk* augment is not established due to its being *bahiraṅga* (extrinsic) when the *sārvadhātuka* suffix is unaccented (*anudātta*), therefore even in this case, the *sārvadhātuka* suffix remains unaccented. However, the *muk* is *bahiraṅga* because it depends on many factors; for it relies upon a stem (*aṅga*) qualified by the vowel *a*, as well as the *āna* augment.

[The cause is] a specific condition (*pratyaya-viśeṣa*): the enclitic accent (*nidhāta*) applies to a *lasārvadhātuka* suffix that follows a verbal root (*aṅga*) taught with a low-pitched vowel (*anudātta-upadeśa*). Therefore, this [enclitic accent] is internal (*antaraṅga*). Furthermore, it is because it is a rule concerning accent; for it has been stated in the Bhāṣya that a rule concerning accent possesses the status of being internal. But surely, in the first alternative (*pakṣa*), once *muk* has been applied, the enclitic accent [would apply]?

"It is not established, because of the instruction [of the rule] *adupadeśāt* due to the inclusion of the *tapara* marker, and because once *muk* is applied, the duration of time becomes excessive. This is not a fault; even if it becomes greater by half a mora (*ardhamātrā*) when this is done, it is nonetheless established precisely because of the mention of "instruction" (*upadeśa*).
Because in the grammatical instruction (*upadeśa*), only that which possesses the marker *m* is pronounced— as in the rule "the acute accent (*citsvara*) also applies by this [rule]," and so forth—
the scope for the *citsvara* is, for example, in the case of *yauc* derived from roots meaning "motion" or "sound" when they are intransitive,
as in *calanam* and *copanam*. The scope for the grave accent (*anudātta*) applied to the suffixes beginning with *tās* is, for example, in *āste* and *śete*.
In this case, both [rules] would apply: "pacamānaḥ" and "yajamānaḥ.

Because it is subsequent, the rule prescribing the anudātta accent for *sārvadhātuka* suffixes prevails, overriding the *cit*-accent. As in "cinutaḥ" and "cinvanti," [the suffix] is [treated as] *apit* by the rule "sārvadhātukam apit" (Pāṇini 1.2.4).
"But, O Goddess, even if there is *ṅt*, how is this counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) justified?

To this he says: "By the rule *ṅdīyam*," and so forth. By the rule *sārvadhātukamapit* (Pāṇini 1.2.4), the operation of the preceding [element] is extended, not that of the subsequent one. And thus it has been said: "But it is established..."

"Because of the extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*) to the preceding [element]. Therefore, with respect to the operation of the preceding element, the status of being marked by *ṅ* (*ṅtvam*) applies, but not to the subsequent one; what here is not justified? [The answer begins with] "And in this case," etc. For in the forms *pacāvaḥ* and *pacāmaḥ*, once the lengthening has been applied by the rule "lengthening of *at* before a *yañ*" (Pāṇini 7.3.101), [the subsequent *as* is not treated as having the *ṅ* marker].

This would be the case if the mention of "instruction" (*upadeśa*) were not present. But since it is present, even though the letter *ś* is taught as having only one mora (*mātrika*), and although it subsequently becomes long, nevertheless it does not undergo the *nighāta* (unaccented) designation. [The author says: "And let it not be so here"—as in *hataḥ* and *hathaḥ*. In these cases, [the rule] "anudātopadeśa... [applies].

By [the rule] beginning with (6.4.37), when the nasal is elided, the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix follows that which is "from the point of instruction" (*upadeśāt*). If the mention of "from the point of instruction" were not there, this [suffixal status] would also apply here [in the case of *hanti*]. But since it is present, it does not apply;
for the root *han* is not taught as ending in a vowel (*avarṇa*), but rather as ending in a consonant (*vyañjana*). [As in: *pacamānāḥ*.

Thus [it is said]. By the rule *tācchīlyavayovacanaśaktiṣu cānaś* (Pāṇini 3.2.129), the suffix *cānaś* is introduced; however, this is not a substitute (*lādeśa*), but rather an affix (*pratyaya*). Consequently, it does not possess the status of being a *sarvadhātuka* ending following *la*. As for the form *śiśye*, it is the Ātmanepada form of the root *śīṅ*, derived by the rule *eranekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.82).

The substitution of *yaṇ* [occurs]. By the rule "and after the *liṭ*" (Pāṇini 3.4.115), this is an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. In the form "śiśyāte," this is the form of the *liṭ* with the *ātām* ending. There is no low-pitched (*anudātta*) accent, because the designation *asārvadhātuka* is prescribed for it. In "hrāute, yad adhīte," there is the *ṅ* [augment] after *hrā*.

The use of the word *yat* with the roots *apa-nī* (DhP 1082) and *sthā* in the sense of "studying" (*adhyayana*) (DhP 1046) is intended so that the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent may apply by the rule *nipātaiyadyadi* (Pāṇini 8.1.30).

187. *ādiḥ sico'nyatarasyām* (6.1.187). [Examples: *mā hi kārṣṭām*. The purpose for the employment of *hiḥ* and *māṅ* has already been stated previously. "The other [syllable] is udātta at the end": this is by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). "The other... [is the remainder].

"Madhyodātaḥ" (middle-accented). [This occurs] precisely by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). But surely, the suffix here begins with a *val* sound, and the augment (*iṭ*) is an addition (*āgama*), and additions are unaccented; therefore, even here it ought to be finally accented. So how is there middle accentuation?

Thus he says: "Because of the *cit* designation of *sic*," and so forth. Since the non-acute (*anudātta*) nature [of *sic*] is set aside by the *cit* designation, the acute accent (*cit-svara*) alone prevails; thus, the acute accent on the middle syllable is logical. "The initial syllable of *sic* is acute," and so forth. When the initial syllable of *sic* is to be made acute, [it applies] to that *sic* which exists after a root that does not take the augment *iṭ*.
It must be stated that the following member of a compound which is a conditional particle (pratyaya) has an acute accent (*udātta*). For example: *mā hi kārṣam*.

This is for the purpose of ensuring that, in the alternative case, the entire word does not become entirely unaccented (*sarvānudāta*). In that alternative case, when the acute accent is absent, the word remains entirely unaccented.
188. *svapādi-hiṃsām acyaniṭi* (6.1.188).

Regarding the phrase "the mention of *sārvadhātuka*," etc.: the term *aci*, being in the locative case, is a coreferential qualifier (*samānādhikaraṇa*) of the *lasārvadhātuka*, and not [a qualifier] of that which ends in the nominative.

Grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established with that which ends in the locative case. Therefore, because of its connection with the word "in *ac*" (*aci*), and due to the relationship between qualifier and qualified, he says: "The locative ending arises [from the rule], and 'beginning with *svap*' is up to the marker *vṛt*. Even though this is so, nevertheless, only those roots—namely *ñiṣvap* "to lie down" (DhP 1068), *śvas* "to breathe" (DhP 1069), and *ana* "to breathe" (DhP 1070)—are included here by the term "beginning with *svap*."

Furthermore, regarding those other roots such as *jakṣ* that bear the designation *abhyasta*, because of their subsequent position, the initial syllable always receives the acute accent (*udātta*) by the rule "the beginning of *abhyasta*s" (Pāṇini 6.1.189). In the form *hiṃsanti*: the roots *tṛh* and *his* (Dhātupāṭha 1455, 1456) mean "to injure. Because they belong to the *rudh*-class, the suffix *śnam* is applied; the vowel *a* is elided by the rule "elision of *a* in *śna* and *śnu*" (6.4.111), and the following *n* is elided by the rule "elision of *n* after *śnā*" (6.4.23). In the form *svapyāt*: this is the optative (*liṅ*) with the elision of *śap* due to the root belonging to the *adādi* class. In the form *svapitaḥ*: the augment *iṭ* is added by the rule "after *rudh*-class roots before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix" (7.2.76).

189. *abhyastānām ādiḥ* (6.1.189). When the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) would otherwise apply, this rule provides an exception (*apavāda*) by prescribing that the acute accent falls on the first syllable of reduplicated (*abhyasta*) roots.
In forms such as *dadhati*, there is the elision of the long *ā* by the rule *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ* (6.4.112); [the remaining portion of the sūtra is] *ubhe*.

The designation *abhyasta* is [applied] by [Pāṇini 6.1.5] *abhyastam*. [Examples are] *jakṣati* and *jāgrati*. Here too, by [Pāṇini 6.1.6] *jakṣityādayaḥ ṣaṭ*, the substitution of *at* for *jhi* occurs everywhere by [Pāṇini 7.1.4] *adabhyastāt*. [In the form] *jakṣitaḥ*, the augment *iṭ* is applied as before. Now, what is the purpose of including the word "beginning" (*ādi*)?
Does the word *ādiḥ* ("beginning") continue to apply from the rule *yāvataṣṭhādissico 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.1.187)? To this he says: "While *ādiḥ* is being carried over," and so forth.
For the previous mention of *ādiḥ* was connected with the mention of *anyatarasyām*; therefore, when that [word *anyatarasyām*] no longer applies...
There would also be the recurrence of that [rule]. Therefore, the word "ādi" (beginning) is mentioned again for the sake of making it permanent.

190. *anudāte ca* (6.1.190). This [rule] is for the sake of cases beginning with non-vowels (*anaj-ādi*). For in the case of an affix beginning with a vowel that is *anudātta*, the result is already established by the preceding rule [6.1.186]. As in *jihīte* and *mimīte*; here, [the *sārvadhātuka* accent] is applied by the rule *tāsyanudātet* (6.1.186), etc.
The *sārvadhātuka* affix is unaccented (*anudātta*). By the rule "ṭhbhṛñāmit" (Pāṇini 7.4.76), there is the substitution of *i* for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
The term "anudāte" here is a reference to that which is technically defined as unaccented within the grammatical system.
Someone might have the misconception [that *anudāta* is a simple compound], and therefore, in order to dispel that, he says:

"The term *anudāta* is a *bahuvrīhi* designation. That is, *anudāta* means "that in which an acute (*udāta*) vowel does not exist. But for what purpose is this *bahuvrīhi* designation? He says: "It is for the sake of [triggering] elision (*lopa*) and substitution (*ādeśa*)."

[The mention of] *sma* is for the purpose that even when the elision (*lopa*) and the substitution of *ayana* (*ādeśa*) have been applied, the initial vowel (*ādy-udāttatvam*) should remain [accented], as in the example *mā hi sma dadhāt* (from *dadhāti*). Here, the use of the word *sma* is so that the *laṅ* suffix may occur after a root ending in *sma*.
In this context, if this were a technical grammatical reference (*śāstrīya-nirdeśa*), [the rule] *itaśca* (Pāṇini 3.4.100) would apply.
If the elision of the vowel *i* were performed and the *yaṇ*-substitution applied, the [resulting] syllable would not be udātta,
because there is no udātta vowel prescribed by the grammatical rules (*śāstra*) present here. Furthermore, when the term is presented as a bahuvrīhi compound, the rule applies even in this case,
since an udātta vowel is absent here.
191. *sarvasya supi* (Pāṇini 6.1.191). Having introduced [the suffix] with *ṭhiṣśībhyāṃ van* (Daiva-Uṇādi-sūtra 8.126), [the sūtra states]: *sarvanīdhṛdhariṣvalaṣvaśivapaṭvapreṣvā asvatantre*.

By the rule *sarvanidhṛṣvariṣvaliṣpaśipahrasvapadvapraheṣvā atantre* (Pāṇini 6.2.127), the word *sarva* is prescribed as having its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). Consequently, the rule prescribes that its first vowel (*ādyudātatva*) is accented when it is followed by a case-ending (*sup*). However, the prescription of its being *antodātta* applies to the word *sarva* [in general].
In the case of *vikāraḥ sārvam*, so that [the suffix] *añ* prescribed by "after a word beginning with an unaccented vowel, *añ*" (Pāṇini 4.2.44) may apply, [it is said]:

"even by means of the technical designation of the affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*), and so forth. But how is this desired result obtained, given that in the case of *sarvastomaḥ*, [the suffix] is elided by "of the sup [case-ending], after a verbal root or a nominal stem" (Pāṇini 2.4.71)?

[Objection: Since [the suffix] is elided by *lumat*, there ought to be a prohibition of the designation "suffix" (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*) by the rule *na lumatāṅgasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.63). [Response: This is not a fault;
the word *ca* ("and") is carried over from the preceding sūtra, and it has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). By means of that—

This accent will also apply to the domain of negation, as in the rule "the accent of *sarva* applies when there is no *akac*" (*sarvasvaro 'nakackasya*), and so forth. The meaning is that this accent which is prescribed for the word *sarva* occurs when that [word] is not accompanied by *akac*; thus the rule must be explained in this sense. In that regard, this...

The explanation is as follows: from the rule "ādiḥ sico 'nyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 6.1.187), the term "anyatarasyām" is carried over here by the maxim of the frog-leap; and that [option] is a restricted option (vyavasthitavibhāṣā), whereby [the augment] occurs for that which does not have the augment *anakac*.

192. *bhī-hvī-bhṛ-hu-mada-jana-dhana-daridrā-jāgarām pratyayāt pūrvam pi ti* (Pāṇini 6.1.192). When [the rule] *anudāte ca* (6.1.190) would have caused the initial syllable to be udātta, this sūtra prescribes that the vowel preceding the affix is udātta when followed by a *ti*-ending affix.
An acute accent (*udātta*) is prescribed for the roots *bhī*, *hrī*, and so forth.
193. *liti* (Pāṇini 6.1.193). Regarding the phrase "that which has *l* as its *it*-marker": that whose *it*-marker is the letter *l* is described in that way.

Regarding the term ‘ṭhcikīrṣakaḥ’ [one who desires to do]: it is formed by adding the suffix *ṇvul* to the desiderative stem (*sannanta*). In that case, after the elision of the vowel *i* by the rule ‘ato lopaḥ’ (Pāṇini 6.4.48), the vowel *i* preceding the suffix *ṇvul* receives the udātta accent. Regarding the term ‘bhaurikividham’: it is formed by the rule ‘bhaurikyādyaiṣukāryādibhyo vidhalbhaktalau’.

The suffix *vidhal* [is applied] according to [Pāṇini 4.2.54]. Since Bhauriki is a region (*deśa*), [the suffix] *bhakta* is applied by the rule "aiṣukāribhaktam" (Pāṇini 4.2.54), as in "aiṣukāribhaktam," meaning "the region whose inhabitants are Aiṣukāris. The suffix *bhakta* is applied by that very preceding rule.

194. *ādirṇamulyanyatarasyām* | (6.1.194) When the accent of the *liṭ* suffix would otherwise apply, the rule prescribes that when *ṇamul* follows, the acute accent (*udātta*) falls on the first syllable optionally. Consequently, when this option is not exercised, the accent of the *liṭ* suffix still occurs. Furthermore, for verbal roots consisting of more than one vowel (*anekāc*), there is an option.

They employ [the suffixes]. However, for those [roots] consisting of a single syllable (*ekāca*), there is no distinction between this [suffix] and the *liṭ* accent; as in "lolūyaṃ lolūyam" and "popūyaṃ popūyam. When the suffix *ṇamul* follows a [root] ending in *yat*, it is doubled according to the rule: "In the sense of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇa*), there are two [instances]. (Vārttika 887).
The word is reduplicated; by the rule "anudāttaṃ ca" (Pāṇini 8.1.3), the reduplicated portion is unaccented.

195. *acaḥ kartṛyaki* (6.1.195). Regarding the term "kartṛyaki": that which is called "kartṛ" refers to a sārvadhātuka suffix; this is because the designation [of the suffix] is applied to the thing designated [the action], by way of metonymy (*abhidheya-upacāra*). In this context, the *yak* that occurs when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed is "kartṛyak."

The compound is formed by a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) from the rule "the seventh case" (Pāṇini 2.1.40). [The example is: "The field mows itself. Devadatta mows the field; because the field is the most desired object to be pervaded by the act of mowing, it is the *karman* (object). However, when, due to ease of the task, that very [field]— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the partial nature of the source.]

When agency (*kartṛtva*) is intended to be expressed, then it becomes the agent; by the extended application (*atideśa*) of Pāṇini 3.1.87, *karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ*, there is the passive suffix *yak* and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). Thus, "it is strewn" (*stīryate*). [The root] *stṛ* [in the sense of] "covering" (DhP 1252) [is used]; [the form] ends in *ān*.

By [the rules] *iddhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.100) and *hali ca* (8.2.77), there is lengthening of the vowel *i*. When the non-sārvadhātuka accent has been applied, "only the accent belonging to the root as taught in the *adupadeśa* [list] remains. This is by way of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* [rule].
Now, how does it happen here that [the forms] *jāyate*, *sāyate*, and *khāyate* occur as being "produced by itself," "cooked by itself," and "eaten by itself"?

For since the substitution of *ā* (by Pāṇini 6.4.43, *ye vibhāṣā*) has been applied, the roots *jan-* and the others subsequently become those ending in long *ā* (*ajanta*), and not [roots ending in short *a*] in their original instruction (*upadeśa*).

Thus he says: "of *jan* and so forth," and so on. For when the rule for the substitution of *ā* is prescribed for *jan* and the others, the term "having an anudātta vowel in their original enunciation" (*anudātopadeśa*) is understood to follow. Therefore, the substitution of *ā* must be seen as applying to them only at the stage of their original enunciation. [As in the example: "it is born by itself. But how can there be an agent who is not an object (*akarmakartṛ*)?
As for the objection that the root *jan* (to be born) is intransitive: there is no fault, because it becomes transitive when the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) is included within its meaning.

Regarding the example "the field is being sown by Devadatta" (*lūyate kedāro devadattena*), since the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is prescribed here for the simple object (*śuddhakarma*), the passive marker (*yak*) does not occur for the agent (*kartṛ*).

196. *Thañ ca seṭ īḍantaḥ vā* (6.1.196). While the phrase *anyatarasyām* (6.1.194) is being carried over, the inclusion of the word *vā* ("or") is for the purpose of providing an option regarding the operation (*kāryin*). By the mention of *anyatarasyām*, the operation itself is made optional; however, by the mention of *vā*, [the suffix] is optionally [treated as having an indicatory letter].

The grammatical operations apply to the *kāryin* (the element undergoing the operation). Therefore, the augment *iṭ* and others are applied alternately to the operation. In the form *lulavitha*, *iṭ* is added by the rule *krādiniyamāt*. In the form *yayātha*, there is an optional prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *acastāsvatthalyaniṭo nityam* (Pāṇini 7.2.61).
197. *Nityādinityam* (6.1.197). Regarding the example *vāsudevakaḥ*: it means "one who has devotion (*bhakti*) toward Vāsudeva," with the suffix *vuñ* applied in this sense.

Now, in the case of *gargāḥ* and *vidāḥ*, when the elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *yañ* and *añ* is performed according to *yañañośca* (2.4.64) because they denote many members of a lineage, [the following applies].

Why does [the rule] not apply here in *cañceva cañcā*, where the suffix *kan*—produced by the rule *ṭhivaḥ pratikṛtau* (Pāṇini 5.3.96)—is elided by the rule *lummanuṣye* (Pāṇini 5.3.98)? For even when a suffix is elided, there is the possibility [of its application] due to the principle *pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam* (Pāṇini 1.1.62). To this [it is replied]: [The answer follows: ... [the text continues with the explanation regarding the specific conditions for the application of the rule].

He says: "The definition of *pratyaya* (affix) is not accepted here. How then is it not accepted? From the *jñāpaka* (indicative mark) that will be stated in the rule *saṃjñāyām upamānam* (P. 6.1.204). Or rather, by the rule *na lumatāṅgasya* (P. 1.1.63), whatever [operation] pertains to the *aṅga* (stem)...

The operation (*kārya*) is indeed prescribed under the heading of "constituent elements" (*aṅga-adhikāra*); therefore, here the designation of "having a suffix as its cause" (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*) need not be accepted for the purpose of the prohibition. In this way, the absence of the designation "having a suffix as its cause" should be understood in subsequent cases as well. [In the phrase] "when *ṭyaÑ* and *kan* have been elided," the word "and" (*ca*) implies [the case] when *avidādhañ* has also been elided.

198. And [the substitution of *e* for *o* occurs] after that which is addressed (*āmantrita*). (6.1.198) Example: *devadata*. [This is derived from] the root *dā* with the suffix *kta* in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), according to Pāṇini 3.3.174: *kticktau ca saṃjñāyām*; then, by 7.4.46: *vo vad ghoḥ*, the root *dā* undergoes the substitution of *dad*.

The compound *dataḥ* with the word *deva* is formed according to *Pāṇini 2.1.32*: *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* ("A word ending in a *kṛt* suffix [denoting] an agent or an instrument is frequently compounded with another word"). In the form *sapiḥ āgacchat*, the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending occurs by *Pāṇini 7.1.23*: *svamornapuṃsakāt* ("The case-endings *su* and *am* are elided after a neuter noun"). In the form *sapta āgacchanti*, the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending occurs here as well by *Pāṇini 7.1.22*: *ṣaḍbhyo luk* ("The case-endings are elided after the six numerals beginning with *ṣaṣ*").
And so it is said.

199. *pathimathoḥ sarvanāmasthāne* (Pāṇini 6.1.199). Regarding the rule "the words *pathin* and *mathin*, etc.": since the suffix *ini* is present [from the rule] *gameriniḥ* (Daiva Uṇādi Sūtra 6.57), and the suffix *ini* is also applied [by the rule] *manthaḥ* (Daiva Uṇādi Sūtra 6.62), the word *mathin* [is derived].

It is explained as follows: because the term *kit* is carried over from the rule "parame kit" (Daiva-Upaniṣad 6.61), there is the elision of the nasal in the root *manath*. Furthermore, since the word *pathin* is also derived with the suffix *ini* according to the rule "patastha ca" (Daiva-Upaniṣad 6.63), these two [words] are formed by that [suffix].

The two words are accented on the final syllable by virtue of their suffixal accent (*pratyayasvara*). Regarding the form *panthāḥ*: by the rule *pathimathyṛbhukṣāmāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.87), there is the substitution of the vowel *a* for the final element; by *ito't sarvanāmasthāne* (7.1.86), the *i* is replaced by *ā*; and by *tho nthaḥ* (7.1.87), the *th* is replaced by *nth*.

"Look at the path. Here, by the rule "the elision of *ṭi* of a *bha*-stem" (Pāṇini 7.1.88), there is the elision of the suffix *ṭi*. Once that has been applied, the final syllable becomes udātta by the rule "and [the word] ending in an unaccented vowel, where an udātta is elided" (Pāṇini 6.1.161).
In the case of "pathipriyaḥ," it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one for whom the path is dear. [The rule applies] "optionally in the case of *priya*" (Pāṇini 6.2.171).
Thus, in this case, the word *priya* is placed at the end of the compound.

200. *antaśca tavai yugapat* (Pāṇini 6.1.200). Regarding *kartavai*—[the Kāśikā and Padamañjarī read *kartavai*]—the suffix *tavai* is applied by the rule *kṛtyārthe tavaikenkenyatāvanaḥ* (3.4.14). But what is the reason [for this]?
"Why is an effort made to exclude the alternative? To this he says: "Except for *heka*," and so forth.
201. *kṣayo nivāse* (6.1.201). Regarding the word "kṣayaḥ": this is the form of the root *kṣi*, meaning "to dwell" and "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1407).

202. *jayaḥ karaṇam* | (6.1.202) Regarding the word *jayaḥ*: this is the form of the root *ji* (or *jri*) in the sense of "conquering" (*abhibhave*), according to Dhātupāṭha 946 and 947. In the example *jayo brāhmaṇānām*, the suffix *erac* (3.3.56) is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
203. And [the suffix *kan* is applied] after *vṛṣa* and others. (Pāṇini 6.1.203) [The examples are:

*vṛṣan*, *janaḥ*, *jvaraḥ*, *grahaḥ*, *hayaḥ*, *gayaḥ*. [The roots are: *vṛṣu* and *mṛṣu* in the sense of "to sprinkle" (Dhātupāṭha 706, 707); *janī* in the sense of "manifestation" (Dhātupāṭha 1149); and *jvara* in the sense of "disease."

The roots *ṭhgraha* in the sense of "seizing" (*upādāne*) [DhP 776], *ṭhhi* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*) [DhP 1257], and *kai* and *gai* in the sense of "sound" (*śabde*) [DhP 916, 917]—all these end in the suffix *ac*. This is because they belong to the *pacādi* group. By this, he shows that these are listed [in the Dhātupāṭha] even though the acute accent on the final syllable (*cit-svara*) would otherwise have applied.

"ṇayaḥ, tayaḥ, ayaḥ, aṃśaḥ, vedaḥ, sūdaḥ, aśaḥ. Regarding these: from the root *ṇīñ* "to lead" (DhP 901), and *tāyṛ* "continuity and protection" (DhP 489). In some places, instead of *tayaḥ*, the reading *cayaḥ* is found; this should be understood as derived from the root *ci* "to gather. [And] *iṇ* "to go."

Or else, [it is derived] from the group beginning with *aya*, *vaya*, *maya*, and *caya* (DhP 4.74–4.78). [It may also come from] *aṃśa* in the sense of "resolution" (DhP 6.1918), *vid* in the sense of "knowledge" (DhP 2.1064), *sūda* in the sense of "protection" (DhP 4.1717), or *aś* in the sense of "eating" (DhP 2.1523). As for *sūdaḥ*, it is formed according to the rule *ig-upadhāt kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.135).

This refers to [the suffix] ending in the *kap* affix. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to what was previously stated regarding "these also. Regarding "guh": the root is *guhū* (DhP 896), meaning "to conceal.
Regarding "śama-raṇau saṃjñāyām": the root is *śam* (DhP 1201), meaning "to pacify," and *raṇa*.

This is the meaning of the word according to the *Dhātupāṭha* (444, 445). In cases other than when it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*), [the suffixes] occur only after a word that is udātta on the final syllable. Regarding the rule "In the sense of consent (*sammata*) for the [meanings of] state (*bhāva*) and object (*karman*)," the term "from the roots *śam* and *ram*" (*śamaraṇāt*) is understood to carry over. When the sense of consent is intended to be expressed, the roots *śam* and *ram* become respectively udātta on the first syllable in the meanings of state and object. For example: *mantraḥ*.

Thus [it is said]. Regarding the root *mantr* (DhP 1679), "to speak secretly," some read: "In the sense of agreement, when the action or object is involved, [the suffix *ghañ* is applied] to *mantr*, resulting in *mantra*. Its meaning should be understood as "that which has become the subject of counsel. Regarding "śāntiḥ": from the root *śam* (DhP 1201), "to be pacified."

The suffix *ktic* is applied by the rule *ṭhkticktau ca saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.174), as in the examples *kāmaḥ* and *yāmaḥ*. [These are derived from] the roots *kamu kāṅkṣāyām* (Dhātupāṭha 443) and *yama uparame* (Dhātupāṭha 984). Regarding the statement "ending in *ghañ*," although the rule *karṣātvato ghaño 'nta udāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.159)—which prescribes that the final syllable of a word ending in *ghañ* is acute when preceded by *karṣa* or a vowel—is applicable here, [the following applies]:

The reading is "kalpaḥ. [The root] *kṛpū* means "to be capable" (DhP 7.62). The word "pādaḥ" [is derived from] *pad* meaning "to go" (DhP 10.1169). "The *vṛṣādi* group is an *ākṛtigaṇa*"—that is precisely it.
The letter 'ca' has been added to indicate that this is an open-ended class (ākṛtigaṇa).

204. *saṃjñāyām upamānam* (6.1.204). [The commentary says: "If it is thus. If this means that there is elision (*lup*) of the suffix *kan*, then even though *kan* is elided, their initial acute accent (*ādyaudātatva*) is established by the very rule for the presence of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), because of the accent of the *nit* [marker].

The intention is that this [rule] is purposeless. Regarding the passage beginning with "this very [point]," etc.: for if *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the status of being a suffix) were to apply in some instances regarding the prescription of accents (*svaravidhi*), then this statement would indeed have to be made;
yet since it is established by *pratyayalakṣaṇa*, it has already been done.

Therefore, this makes it known: the rule regarding the characteristics of a suffix (pratyayalakṣaṇa) would apply; this statement ought indeed to have been made, because [the desired form] would have been established by the rule regarding the characteristics of a suffix, yet it has been specifically stated.
Therefore, this makes it known: in this context, regarding the prescription of accents (svaravidhi), the rule regarding the characteristics of a suffix does not apply.

The mention of "in some cases" (*kvacid*) and "in others it occurs" (*kvacit tu bhavati*) is for the purpose of demonstration; for it has been stated under [Pāṇini 6.1.191] *sarvasya supi* that this accent is also desired by means of the technical designation of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*).
With the words "And thus," etc., he states the purpose of this indication.

In the expression "The boy is fire" (*agnir māṇavakaḥ*), the word "fire" functions as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*); for it is understood that he is indeed fire, and it is not a name (*saṃjñā*) for the boy.

205. *Niṣṭhā* [is formed] after two vowels. (Pāṇini 6.1.205) *Guptaḥ*: from the root *gup* (*gupū rakṣaṇe*, Dhātupāṭha 395). *Buddhaḥ*: from the root *budh* (*budha avagamane*, Dhātupāṭha 858). *Devah*: the word *deva*.

[The word *bhīma*] is udātta on the final syllable because it ends in the suffix *ac* added after the root *bhī* (according to the rule *pacādyac*). The word *bhīma* is also [derived] with the suffix *mak*; having introduced [the rules] beginning with *iṣiyudhi* (Daiva 7.31), it is derived as ending in the suffix *mak* by the rule *bhiyaḥ ṣug vā* (Daiva 7.35). Regarding [the example] "cintitaḥ": [it is derived from] the root *cit* in the sense of "recollection" (*smṛti*).

[The root] *dhā* (DhP 1535) belongs to the *caurādika* group; there is the elision of the *ṇi* suffix by [the rule] *ṭhniṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi* (6.4.52). Thus, "protected" (*rakṣitaḥ*). [The root] *rakṣa* (DhP 658) means "to protect. "Saved" (*trātaḥ*) and "attained" (*āptaḥ*): [the root] *traiṅ* (DhP 965) means "to protect," and *āplṛ* (DhP 1260) means "to pervade."

206. *śuṣka-dhṛṣṭau* | (6.1.206) Regarding *śuṣkaḥ*: from the root *śuṣa* in the sense of "drying up" (*śoṣaṇe*; DhP 1183), there is the substitution of *ka* for the suffix *kta* by the rule *śuṣaḥ kaḥ* (8.2.51). Regarding *dhṛṣṭaḥ*: from the root *ñidhṛṣā* in the sense of "boldness" (*prāgalbhye*; DhP 1269).
The substitution of *ṣṭu* occurs; since the substitutions of *ka* and *ṣṭu* are considered *asiddha*, it should be understood here that the word ends in the suffix *niṣṭhā*.
"This [rule] is commenced for the sake of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*)," because the designation is already established by the preceding rule.

207. *āśitaḥ kartā* (Pāṇini 6.1.207). [The word] *āśitaḥ* is derived from the root *aś* (meaning "to eat," *dhā.pā.* 1523), with the suffix *kta* applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). This is contrary to the rule *gatyarthākarmaka-* (3.4.72) et cetera, which prescribes the suffix in the sense of the object (*karmani*) as in the previous case.
The suffix *kta* [is applied] "in the preceding case"—according to the *Kāśikā*, by the rule "of those two only" (3.4.70), etc.;
and "in the subsequent case, in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*)," according to the rule "the suffix *kta* in the neuter, in the sense of the abstract state" (3.3.114).

208. *rikte vibhāṣā* (6.1.208). Regarding the word *riktaḥ*: the root *ric* (Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 1441) means "to empty" or "to purge. When the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) would otherwise apply, this rule prescribes that the initial syllable may optionally be acute (*udātta*). This applies when [the word] forms a name (*saṃjñā*), and so forth; as does the rule for the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*).

The scope of [the rule] *dvyajanāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.205) is, for example, *dataḥ* and *guptaḥ*. The scope of this [present rule] when not used as a technical term (*asaṃjñā*) is, for example, *rikto ghaṭaḥ*. However, when the word *rikta* is a name (*saṃjñā*) of something, both rules apply; in that case, by the principle of priority (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), [the present rule takes effect].

By the rule *ṭhniṣṭhā ca dvyajanāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.205), the word is invariably udātta on its first syllable. Nor is it necessary to state a prior exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), because the word *para* signifies "desired" (*iṣṭa*).

209. *Juṣṭārpite ca chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.209). Regarding *juṣṭaḥ*: the root *juṣī* (Dhātupāṭha 1288) means "to please" or "to serve. Regarding *arpitaḥ*: from the root *ṛ*, with the suffix *ṇic*; the augment *puk* is applied according to the rule *arti-hroḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.36).

210. *nityaṃ mantre* (Pāṇini 6.1.210). Regarding the phrase "some here," etc.: what, then, is the reason they continue to apply [the rule] only to the word *juṣṭa*? To this he says: "of the word *arpita*," etc. What is the reason for this as well?

Thus he says: "Even [a word] having the udātta accent on the final syllable," and so forth. To show that very mantra which has the udātta on the final syllable, he says: "In that [sacrifice], together with three hundred," and so forth. Since its obligatory nature (*nityatva*) is already established by the very force of the initial statement, the inclusion of the word "obligatory" (*nitya*) is for the sake of clarity and for the sake of what follows.

211. *yuṣmadasmadoRÇĀsi* (Pāṇini 6.1.211). [The commentary states: "The words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* end in the suffix *madik*. This is because the suffix *madik* is applied to the roots *yuṣ* and *as*, according to the rule *yuṣyasibhyāṃ madik* (Dhātupāṭha 6.50), thereby producing those two forms. By this...
He demonstrates that *yuṣmad* and *asmad* have the acute accent on the final syllable (*āntodātta*) by virtue of the accent of the suffix.

According to the rule *tava-mamau ṅsi* (Pāṇini 7.2.96), *tav-* and *mam-* replace the forms of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* up to the *maparyanta* portion; then, when the elision (*lopa*) of the remainder has been applied by the rule *śeṣe lopaḥ* (7.2.90), the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpatvam*) occurs by the rule *ato guṇe* (6.1.97).

Because the substitute for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* possesses the status of the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), it is oxytone. Thus, when a single substitution (*ekādeśa*) occurs together with the substitute [of the pronoun], that single substitution is also necessarily acute according to the rule "a single substitution is acute when [the other element] is acute" (Pāṇini 6.1.161). Since the accent of the case-ending would thus apply by this sequence, the following is stated.

212. *ṅyi ca* (Pāṇini 7.2.92). [The forms] *ṭhubhyam* and *mahyam* [are derived as follows]: by the rule *reĀ prathamayoram* (7.1.28), the substitution of *am* occurs; then, by the rule *tubhyamahyau ṅyi* (7.2.95), the substitutes *tubhya-* and *madya-* are applied to the stems *yuṣmad-* and *asmad-*.

For what purpose is this rule formulated as a separate *yoga*? To this he says: "The formulation of a separate *yoga*," and so forth. For if they were in a single *yoga*, since the two things to be operated upon (*kāryin*) and the two causes (*nimitta*) would be identical in number, someone might suspect that the application of the rule would follow their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhya*). Therefore, a separate *yoga* is formulated.

This is for the purpose of demonstrating that the rule of "correspondence according to order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*) is to be rejected. Consequently, because the [preceding rule] lacks the *svarita* accent, correspondence according to order will not occur. Since this might be suspected by someone of dull intellect, the separate formulation of the rule is intended to dispel that doubt.
