This [new rule] is also to be understood in the same manner as the previous one.
This is an exception to [the rules concerning] case-endings and accents.

213. *yata* after *nāu*. (Pāṇini 6.1.213) Examples: *kaṇṭhyam*, *oṣṭhyam*. [In these cases,] the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is used in the sense of "state" (*bhāva*). Regarding *nāvyam*: in the sense of "that which is to be crossed by boat," the suffix *yat* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.4.91], *nau-vayo-dharma-...*. In this context—

When the substitution of *ava* for *avāntaḥ* before the suffix *yi* has been made by rule 6.1.79, since a consonant is considered non-existent for the purpose of vowel rules, the prohibition is made so that [the *vṛddhi*] does not apply to what precedes that [consonant]. As for "lalāṭyam," the suffix *yat* is applied by rule 5.1.6, "The suffix *yat* after words denoting parts of the body."

214. [The suffix] *ṇyat* is applied after the roots *īḍ*, *vand*, *vṛ*, *śaṃs*, and *duh*. (Pāṇini 3.1.125) *īḍ* (in the sense of "praise") [Dhātupāṭha 1667]; *vad* (in the sense of "salutation" and "praise") [Dhātupāṭha 11];
*vṛ* (in the sense of "partaking" or "choosing") [Dhātupāṭha 1509]; *śaṃs* (in the sense of "praise") [Dhātupāṭha 728].

From these verbal roots—*śaṃs* (DhP 1013), *duh* (DhP 1014) meaning "to fill," and so on—the suffix *ṇyat* is applied by the rule *ṛhalorṇyat* (Pāṇini 3.1.124). But in what case does this [present rule] begin to apply? To this he says: "Because of having two indicatory letters (*anubandha*)," and so forth. Now, how [is this so]?

Regarding the form *vāryam*, why is the suffix *ṇyat* used here, when one would expect the suffix *kyap* prescribed as a specific rule by [Pāṇini 3.1.109], namely *hetistuśāsvṛdṛjuṣaḥ kyap*? To this he says: "vāryam," etc. But surely, even for the root *vṛṅ*, there ought to be *kyap* alone; for [the root is] *vṛ*.
Because of the general indication [of the rule], he says: "For in the prescription of *kyap*, etc."

215. *vibhāṣā veṇvindhānayoḥ* | (6.1.215) "Ending in the suffix *ṇvu*" means that in the rule prescribing that suffix, the mention of *ṇu* is carried over from the rule *stho ṇuḥ* (Daiva-Uṇādi-sūtra 1.147). "And if ending in *ānaś*" refers to the *Kāśikā* reading *yadā*.
[The suffix] *cānaś* is applied by the rule *ṭhtācchīlyavayovacanaśaktiṣu cānaś* (Pāṇini 3.2.129).
[Next is] that which ends in *śānac*, according to the rule *ṭhlaṭaḥ śatṛśānacau* (Pāṇini 3.2.124), etc.
"When the anudātta accent has been applied to the *lasārvadhātuka* [suffix]" refers to the rule *ṭhtāsyanudātenṅidadupadeśāllasārvadhātukamanudāttam ahnyanye* (Pāṇini 6.1.186).
By such [rules] as these. Regarding "indhāne": because this [root] is anudātta (unaccented), [the suffix receives the accent]. Regarding "by the udātanivṛtti-svara":
by the rule "anudātasya ca yatrodātalopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.161).
Regarding "veṇuḥ" and so forth: by the rule "saṃjñāyām upamānam" (Pāṇini 6.1.204).
This is the scope for [the rule]: *cañcā*, *varghrikā*. This is the scope for the optional alternative (*vibhāṣā*):
*anupamāno veṇuśabdaḥ*, *śuṣko vane veṇur iti vā*.
When the word *veṇu* is used as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), such that "like a bamboo" becomes the name (*saṃjñā*) of someone, then—
By the rule *saṃjñāyām upamānam* (Pāṇini 6.1.204), its initial syllable is intended to be udātta; and that is obtained through a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).

216. [The suffix *ya* is applied after the verbal roots] *tyaja*, *raga*, *hasa*, *kuha*, *śaṭha*, *śvaṭha*, and *kratha*. (Pāṇini 6.1.216) *kuha* (in the sense of "to cause amazement," Dhātupāṭha 1901) and *śaṭha* and *śvaṭha* (in the sense of "speaking correctly," Dhātupāṭha 1854, 1855)—these two belong to the curādigaṇa (the tenth class). *Śratha*, *ślatha*, and *kratha* have the meaning "to injure."
218. *caṅy anyatarasyām* (6.1.218). For example: *mā hi cīkaratām*. [This is governed by] *sanvallaghuni caṅpare 'naglope* (7.4.93).

Thus, there is the substitution of *it* for the *abhyāsa*. Regarding the phrase "when the *aṭ* augment is prohibited": if there were a prohibition of the *aṭ* augment, then the accent would belong only to that which follows it, namely the vowel of the root (*dhātu*). [In this case], by the rule "hi ca," there is "anudātta" (low pitch). This depends on the word "pratiṣiddhe" (when prohibited). If the *nighāta* (low pitch) were not prohibited, then...

There would indeed be an absence of the *caṅ* suffix for the root *dhā* when it is udātta, as in "mā hi dadhat. This is because the *caṅ* suffix is applied to the *cli* suffix by the rule "vibhāṣā dheṭśvyoḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.49).

219. *matoḥ pūrvāt saṃjñāyāṃ striyām* (6.1.219). [The example is] *udumbarāvatī*. The suffix *matup* is added in the four senses (*cāturarthika*) because "there are *udumbara* trees in it. The lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *matau bahvaco 'najirādīnām* (6.3.119).
Regarding the example *śarāvatī*: here [the rule] *śarādīnāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.120) applies. Why is *matau* mentioned?

Consider the example *gavādinī*. If *matau* were not stated, then even the mention of *pūrva* connected with it would not be stated; thus, there would be the acute accent (*udātta*) on the mere vowel *a* of the technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*).

[Otherwise] it would follow [that the rule applies everywhere]. The inclusion of the word "pūrva" (preceding) is so that this [suffix] may apply immediately after the suffix *mat*, as in [the case of *śyāmāvatī*]; let it not apply here in *sānumatī*. Furthermore, by the maxim regarding "that which is expressed by its own technical definition" (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā*), it would apply only in cases such as *śyāmāvatī* and *udumbarāvatī*, and not elsewhere. This is due to the inclusion of the word "pūrva."
It belongs to the preceding alone.

220. *Anto'vatyāḥ* (6.1.220). [Examples: *ṭhajiravatī*, etc. As before, the suffix *matup* is applied. "The status of being unaccented (*anudātta*) is obtained because [the suffix] is marked with *ṭh*"—this is the remainder [of the commentary], meaning that this [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to that. Now, if it were stated as *avatyaḥ*...
It does not apply after *rājavatī*, for even when the *n* has been elided, this [word] still ends in the word *avatī*. To this he says: "In a rule concerning vowels," and so forth.
How can this be an example, since the substitution of *vat* for *mat* is *asiddha* (not yet established), and therefore here the word does not end in *avatī*?

Is it not so? To this he says: "But as for *vatvaṃ*," and so forth. By the word "but" (*punaḥ*), he shows the distinction from the elision (*lopa*). For the elision is non-existent (*asiddha*), whereas *vatvaṃ* (the substitution of *v*) is established (*siddha*). Why? Because of its basis (*āśrayāt*).
The meaning is that the "basis" (*āśrayaḥ*) refers to being adopted as the cause (*nimitta*) in the rule concerning accentuation (*svaravidhi*).

By one who states that the word *avatī* has an udātta accent on its final syllable, the substitution of *v* (vatva) is relied upon; therefore, by virtue of that reliance, its established status (*siddhatva*) is maintained. Otherwise, the rule would be meaningless. For, without the established status of the substitution of *v*, there exists nothing whatsoever ending in the word *avatī*.

221. *īvatyāḥ* | (6.1.221) This [rule] also is an exception (*apavāda*) specifically to the [term] *anudātta-pit*. Examples include *ahīvatī*, and so forth. The lengthening [of the vowel] is by [Pāṇini 6.3.120] *śarādīnāṃ ca*, and the substitution of *va* for *ma* is by [Pāṇini 8.2.11] *saṃjñāyām*.

222. *Cau* (Pāṇini 6.1.222): This [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *anudātta-nivṛtti-svara*. For example, in *dadhīcaḥ*: [the word] *dadhyañc-* is formed with the suffix *kvin* [after the root *añc-*], according to [Pāṇini 6.2.139] *gati-kāraka-upapadāt*.
Thus, by the *prakṛtisvara* (original accent) of the final member of the compound, the vowel *a* of the suffix *añc* is acute (*udātta*).
When the *a* is elided by rule 6.4.138, "in the case of a case-ending beginning with a vowel that is not a *sarvanāmasthāna*,

there is elision of the *ṭha*," the *anudātta* (grave) accent of the suffix is replaced by the *udātanivṛtti-svara* (the accent of the disappearance of the acute) according to rule 6.1.161, "and [there is the grave accent] for that which was grave where an acute has disappeared."
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to that [general rule].

Regarding the phrase "before a *taddhita* suffix" (*cāvataddhite*), etc.: the meaning is that this rule prescribing that the penultimate syllable of the root *añc* be udātta must be explained as having the sense that "this occurs when a *taddhita* suffix follows."

And this is the explanation: the mention of "optionally" (anyatarasyām) is understood [from the previous rule], and that is a restricted option (vyavasthitavibhāṣā); therefore, it will not apply in the case of a taddhita suffix.

223. *samāsasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.223). In examples such as *rājapuruṣaḥ*, when various accents would otherwise apply to the constituent members of the compound, this rule is commenced; that [accent] is now being explained. First, regarding the word *rāja*:

Because it ends with the suffix *kanin* according to the rule *ṭhkanin yuvṛṣitakṣirāji* (Daiva Up. 6.51), it has the acute accent on the first syllable by virtue of the *nit*-accent. The same applies to *puruṣa*, for it is derived as ending in the suffix *kuṣan* according to the rule *puraḥ kuṣan* (Daiva Up. 6.51). [The word] *brahmaṇaḥ* [is used in the sense of] "this belongs to Brahman."
The word *brāhmaṇa* ends in the suffix *aṇ* according to Pāṇini 4.3.120 (*tasyedam*), and it is oxytone by the accent of the suffix.

The word *kambala* [is derived] from the root *kam* with the suffix *buk*, according to the *Uṇādisūtra* 8.107 (*kala-stṛpaś-ca*) and 8.109 (*bṛṣādibhyaś-cit*), due to the rule of diversity (*bahulavacanāt*).
It is derived [in this way], and therefore, by that *cit*-accent, this word is udātta on the final syllable. The word *kanyā* has a svarita on the final syllable;

it is established as such by the rule *ṭhadhnyādayaśca* (Daiva-Uṇādi 8.14). Alternatively, it is derived from the root *kanī*—[the Dhātupāṭha reads *kana*]—meaning "to shine, to be beautiful, or to move" (Dhātupāṭha 460).

The suffix *ṇyat* is applied by the rule *ṭhṛhalorṇyat* (Pāṇini 3.1.124). Due to the irregularity (*nipātana*) stated in *kanyāyāḥ kanīna ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.116), there is an absence of *vṛddhi*. By the accentuation of the *tit* suffix, this word becomes *svarita* on its final syllable.
The word *svana* ends in the suffix *ap*, according to the rule *svanahasorvā* (Pāṇini 3.3.62).

The first syllable is udātta by virtue of the accent of the root (*dhātu-svara*). The word *paṭaha* has its final syllable udātta because it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group, derived from the sense "it sounds (*paṭat*) or it makes a sound (*paṭad*). The word *śabda*, ending in the suffix *dan* according to *Uṇādisūtra* 6.48 (*śāśapibhyāṃ dadanau*), has its first syllable udātta by virtue of the *nit-svara*. [It is listed] among the *pacādi* roots.

The word *nadī* is read as ending in *ṭh*. Consequently, when the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15), and the vowel *a* is elided therein by the rule *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), the word *nadī* becomes oxytone (*antodātta*) by the accent known as *udātanivṛtti-svara*. As for the word *gho*:

Because it ends in the suffix *ghañ*, [the word *pṛṣat*] is acute on the first syllable by virtue of the accent of the *ñit* suffix. The words *pṛṣat* and *samit* are acute on the final syllable by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*).
Now, in the case of *rājapṛṣat* and *brāhmaṇasamit*, how can the accent fall on the final syllable, given that [the rule] here—?

Is it not the case that the final vowel of the compound does not participate in the accent, while the vowel preceding it is separated from the *t* by [the consonant]? To this he says: "In the rule concerning vowels," and so forth. "Even at the end of a *hal*" (consonant) is a qualifier of the compound. "The quality of being oxytone" refers to those vowels (*ac*) within the compound.

In relation to that [preceding vowel], the subsequent vowel should be understood as being final (*anta*). Therefore, this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule concerning the accent of non-identical words (*nānāpadasvara*). For in a compound, the constituent words would otherwise retain their individual accents.
If this were not stated, then the accent of distinct words (*nānāpṛthakpadānām*) would consequently apply.
Therefore, this exception to that [rule] is now stated.
Thus ends the first quarter of the sixth chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who is like a Bodhisattva.
Now begins the sixth chapter,
second quarter.
1. *Bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā pūrvapadam* (Pāṇini 6.2.1).

Regarding the phrase "the mention of the first member" (*pūrvapadagrahaṇa*), and so forth: here, the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is appropriately prescribed for that [first member] which would otherwise undergo a modification characterized by being unaccented (*anudātta*). And not...

This [designation] would apply to the entire collection of vowels and consonants (*ajjhal-samudāya*) of the preceding member; what then [would it apply to]? It applies to that which is circumflex (*svarita*) or acute (*udātta*). In that case, if the mention of "preceding member" (*pūrvapada*) here were restricted solely to the preceding member itself, this statement would be entirely meaningless. Therefore, the accent of the preceding member is [understood to be] acute (*udāta*).

It is understood that the mention of the "prior member" (*pūrvapada*) applies even when [the compound] has a circumflex accent (*svarita*). For there is indeed a designation based on location (*tātsthya*), as in the expression "the benches cry out.
[The phrase] "it remains in its own nature" (*svabhāvenāvatiṣṭhate*) expresses the meaning of the word "it exists by its original form" (*prakṛtyā bhavati*).
To clarify that very point through another statement, he says: "The modification undergoes the state of being unaccented (*anudātta*).

But how does a modification characterized by the unaccented tone arise, such that this *prakṛtibhāva* (original form) is commenced for its prevention? To this he replies: "For when there is the final acute accent (*antodātta*) of the compound..."

And so forth. "This is an exception to the rule regarding the acute accent on the final syllable of a compound" (samāsāntodātatva), because this [new rule] is initiated before that [general rule] has already become applicable. "Kṛṣṇo mṛgaḥ" (the black deer): because of its being the color black (kṛṣṇaguṇatvāt). "It has the acute accent on the first syllable" (ādyaudātaḥ):
by virtue of the accentuation of the suffix -ñi.

Regarding the passage beginning with "And there," etc.: there, from the rule "In the case of *stu*, there is lengthening" (*da.u* 7.4), the mention of "lengthening" (*dīrgha*) is understood by anuvṛtti. Also, from the rule "After *su* and *śṛ*, the suffix *nic* [is added]" (*da.u* 7.6)—where the *da.u* commentary reads *sṛśṛbhyāmūrca*—the word "and *nic*" (*nicca*) is understood. Thus, it is said: "By that, the first syllable is udātta."
By the accent of the *kṛt* suffix: "the word following a *kṛt* suffix" (*kṛdutarapada*), etc. In the case of *brahmacārī*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.80] *vrate*;
this is an *upapada* compound. Therein, by [Pāṇini 6.2.139] *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt*, the word *brahmacārī* has its final syllable accented acute (*antodātta*) due to the accent of the *kṛt* suffix.

The word *snātaka* ends in the suffix *kan*. According to the *Kāśikā*, the form *snāta* is established by the rule *kṣatriyaś chandaso dīvyati* (Pāṇini 5.2.74); thus, due to the *niṭ* accent, it is udātta on its first syllable.

"Regarding the statement *manuṣya-śabdaḥ titsvaritaḥ*: [this is so] because it ends in the suffix *yat*, according to [Pāṇini 4.1.161] *manoḥ jātāv añyatau ṣuk ca*. Regarding the phrase *udātagrahaṇam* and so forth:
therein, the mention of *udāta* [is for the purpose of applying] Pāṇini 6.1.159, *karṣātvato ghaño 'nta udātaḥ*."
Thus, the term "svarita-grahaṇam" (the mention of *svarita*) continues [from the previous rule], from "tit svaritam" (Pāṇini 6.1.185). What is established by this? He says: "by that," and so forth.
For this is precisely the purpose of the continued application of the terms *udātta* and *svarita*: wherever there is an *udātta* or a *svarita*...
Indeed, it exists right there so that it may be [so];
for the word *sama* is derived from the root *su* with the suffix *ḍamap*,
and thus, when the *ṭi*-portion of the root has been elided, because the suffix is *pit*, [the vowel becomes udātta].
It becomes entirely unaccented.

2. *tatpuruṣe tulyārthatṛtīyāsaptamyupamānāvyayadvitīyākṛtyāḥ* | (Pāṇini 6.2.2) [The first member of a *tatpuruṣa* compound retains its original accent when it has the sense of "equal to," or when it ends in a word formed with a third-case suffix, a seventh-case suffix, a word used as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), an indeclinable (*avyaya*), a second-case suffix, or a *kṛtya* suffix. [This applies] by the rule *yato 'nāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.213), which prescribes that the initial syllable is acute (*udātta*), and by the rule *nauvayodharmaviṣamūlamūlasītātulābhyas tārthyakrayastulyaprāptāpannāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.91).

Because the word *tulya* ending in a *pratyaya* has been etymologically derived as "that which is measured by a scale" (*tulayā sammitaṃ tulyam*), [the rule applies] to the word *sadṛśa* and so forth. Regarding the rule *tyādādiṣu dṛśo'nālocane kañ ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.60), there is the Vārttika: *samānānyayoś ceti vaktavyam*.

Thus, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) has been made; by that, the word *sadṛś* ends in the suffix *kan*. According to the rule *dṛgdṛśatuṣu* (Pāṇini 6.3.89), there is the substitution of *sa* for *samāna*. [The phrase] "the word *sadṛśa* also," etc., requires the application of the rule regarding the original accent of the final member of a compound ending in a *kṛt*-suffix (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*).
The suffix is *ṭhi*. [That is, the suffix *ik*—as stated in the *Kāśikā*:

"the suffix *i*"]. This is because the suffix *ik* is carried over from the rule "here, *i*" (*da.u.* 1.67). Regarding *kit*: the mention of *kit* is carried over from the rule "after *bhuj*, it is *kit*" (*da.u.* 1.71).

"The word *akṣa* ends in the suffix *sa*. This is because, in the rule *aśerdevane* (Dhātupāṭha 9.24), the suffix *sa* is understood to carry over from the preceding rule *vṛtṛvadihanikamikaṣibhyaḥ saḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 9.21)—[the Dhātupāṭha reads *kamikaṣiyumucibhyaḥ*]. Thus, there is the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the suffix *sa*.

"Of that which has the neuter gender as its scope" means "of that which has the neuter case-ending as its scope. "And the middle-udātta accent" refers to the rule "and of *nyagrodha* when it is alone";
this is connected with the phrase "by way of an irregular derivation (*nipātana*)."
In *a-brāhmaṇaḥ*, it is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*). In *ku-brāhmaṇaḥ* and similar forms, it is by the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18).

[The words] "these indeclinables have the acute accent on their first syllable" is because of the statement *nipātā ādyaudātāḥ* (Phiṭ-sūtra 80), and because these are indeed indeclinables (*nipāta*). Among those, in the case of the two words beginning with *ku-*...
The status of *ca* and the other particles as *nipātas* is due to their inclusion among the *cādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.57);
however, for the words *ni* and *ati*, it is due to their inclusion among the *prādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.58).
Regarding the phrase "in an indeclinable," etc.: when the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is to be applied because the preceding member is an indeclinable.
This meaning—that [the substitution] occurs only for *nañ* and so forth—must be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows:
the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is carried over from the rule "caṅyanyatarasyām" (P. 6.1.218); and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), by which...
It will be [an example] of the negative particle (*nañ*) and indeclinables alone. Regarding "ṭhsvātvākālakaḥ":
it is a compound by virtue of belonging to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group (Pāṇini 2.1.72), and the first member is an indeclinable by virtue of the rule "ṭhktvātosunkasunaḥ" (1.1.40).

In expressions such as *muhūrtasukham*, the accusative case is applied by the rule *kālādhvanor atyantasaṃyoge* (Pāṇini 2.3.5). Regarding the statement "the word *sarvarātra* also ends in the suffix *ac*": when *sarvā* and *rātriḥ* are compounded according to the rule *pūrvakāla-eka-* (Pāṇini 2.1.49), the form *sarvarātra* is derived by the rule *ahaḥ sarvaika-* (Pāṇini 5.4.87).
And because the suffix is prescribed by such rules as these.
3. *varṇo varṇeṣvanete* (Pāṇini 6.2.3).
[The rule] *ṭhruhe raśca lo vā* [is cited]. Here, because *itan* from *ṭhhṛśyābhyāmitan* (Daiva-Uṇādi-sūtra 6.12) is understood to follow. [In the example] *paramakṛṣṇaḥ*, here...
The accentuation remains that of the final syllable of the compound.

4. *gādhalavaṇayoḥ pramāṇe* (Pāṇini 6.2.4). Regarding the example *śambagādham*: it is called *gādha* because one stands firm (*gādhyate*) in it; from the root *gādhṛ*, meaning "to stand firm" or "to desire to obtain" (Dhātupāṭha 4), and according to some recensions, also "in a book. It belongs to the *ardharca*-class of nouns.
(2.4.31) In one alternative, there is neuter gender. By the partial citation "artilūdhūsū," the rule *artilūdhūsūkhanasahacara itraḥ* (3.2.184) is indicated.
"Acute on the middle syllable" (*madhyodātaḥ*) is due to the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). [The mention of] "aśūpruṣi" [is for the purpose of excluding other roots].

The rule *ṭhaśūpruṣilaṭikaṇighaṭiviśibhyaḥ kan* (Daiva-Uṇādi 8.125)—[corrected to *aśūpruṣipluṣilaṭikaṭikaṇikhaṭiviśibhyaḥ kvan*]—indicates the suffix *kvan*. Now, length (*āyāma*) is a measurement; for length is indeed a measurement.

Because of the statement "it may be"; and because a *tatpuruṣa* compound such as *śambagādham* and so forth does not denote a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but rather denotes a measure (*iyatā*). To this he says: "the means of valid cognition," and so forth.
*Iyatā* is the state of being so much; that by which it is delimited is the delimitation of measure (*iyatāpariccheda*), and that alone is what is intended here.
It should be understood as "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*), and not merely as "length. How so?

Here, the word *pramāṇa* is taken as a verbal noun meaning "that by which something is measured," rather than as a conventional term; this is because it must conform to its intended referent. Therefore, that by which a certain amount is delimited [is the *pramāṇa*].

"All [these] are authoritative. Regarding the phrase "and manifested by accent" (*svaravyaṅgyaṃ ca*): the meaning is that it is manifested—that is, made manifest—by that *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) which is prescribed for the accent. Regarding the word "of these" (*eteṣām*):
it refers to *śambagādha* and the others.

5. *dāyādyaṃ dāyāde* (Pāṇini 6.2.5). *Dāyaḥ* means a portion, that is to say, a share. One who takes (*ādatte*) the inheritance (*dāya*) is an heir (*dāyāda*). The suffix *ka* is applied here because the word belongs to the class beginning with *mūlavibhuja* (Vārttika 232). The action of an heir (*dāyāda*) is *dāyādya*. What [is it]?
What, then, is that? It is *dāya* itself; for when it is being taken (*ādīyamāna*), that *dāya* becomes the object (*karman*).
And [the rule] "it does not apply to that which is *udātta*" follows from the sūtra beginning with "ṛtvyavāstvyavāsvya... (4.3.72), specifically from the sūtra "mantre vṛṣa... (3.3.96).
But surely the verbal root in the sūtra is preceded by the prefix *ni-* and is *udātta*; how then can it apply to the simple [root] alone?

Thus he says: "Because of the plural statement," and so forth. If the sixth case (ṣaṣṭhī) is prescribed by the rule "svāmīśvarādhipati" (Pāṇini 2.3.39), then why is the seventh case alone to be prescribed and not the sixth, since the sixth is already established by the rule "śeṣe" (2.3.50)? To this he replies: "But of that..."

And so forth. If only the locative case were prescribed, then, because it would be specifically ordained, it would be understood as superseding the genitive; however, it should not be understood in that way. Therefore, by this very rule, the genitive characterized as "remainder" (śeṣa) is permitted, but it is not being newly prescribed.

Therefore, because it is not prescribed by that specific rule, the compound indeed occurs; as in "paramadāyādaḥ" (the supreme heir). Here, the first member of the compound expresses honor, and does not express the sense of inheritance.

6. *pratibandhi* [is used] with *ciram* and *kṛcchram*. (6.2.6) It is called *pratibandhi* because it obstructs or destroys the accomplishment of an effect (*kāryasiddhi*). The suffix *ṇini* is applied in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*) or necessity (*āvaśyaka*).
[The rule states: "When a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) has been formed. Now, one might ask: is this not already a descriptive compound?

It occurs in a state of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya); yet this is not coreferentiality. How, then, does the first member of the compound function as a negation here? To this he says: "gamanam" and so forth.
When the act of going has occurred at a recent time, the accomplishment of the task is achieved. And [it is said to be] "connected with difficulty."

"Kṛcchra" means suffering; when one who travels engages in such a journey, the traveler, being struck by suffering while seeking the object to be attained, does not reach it. Therefore, a journey that occurs after a long time or is associated with hardship becomes an obstacle to the accomplishment of the task.

7. *pade'padeśe* (6.2.7). [The word] *vyājaḥ* means "a pretext" (*cchadma*). [The example] *mūtrapadena* means "under the pretext of urine. [The word *apadeśa*] ends in the suffix *ṣṭran*; [this is according to] *sivimucyoṣṭerūcca* (Daiva Uṇādi Sūtra 8.83).

[In the rule] *ṣivimucyoṣṭerū ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.24), because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *ṣṭran*, [the form] *mūtrayateḥ* is derived from the root *mūtra* (Dhātupāṭha 1909) meaning "to urinate. The word *uccāra* is also formed with the suffix *ghañ*. This is according to the rule *ṭhthāthādi* (Pāṇini 6.2.144) and so forth, because it ends in *ghañ*.

8. *nivāte vātatrāṇe* | (6.2.8) [The commentary] says: "In the case of *kuḍya-ādi-hetuke*, etc. They exist when the cause is the wall (*kuḍya*) and so forth; this is because the effect is metaphorically attributed to the cause. There is also a metaphorical attribution of the effect to the cause, as for example: "All this..."

"One experiences past karma. Regarding the word *kava*: from the root *ku* meaning "to sound" (*dhā.pā.* 1042). It is "acute-accented on the first syllable" by the rule *ādyaudātaḥ*. It is [acute-accented] by the rule *yato'nāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.213).
Others say that it is "acute-accented on the final syllable" because it ends in the suffix *ḍuḷc*; they derive it as *kavater ḍuḷc*.
Thus the aphorism is studied.
9. *śārade'nārtave* | (6.2.9) [The compound] *rajjūśāradam*, *dṛṣacchāradam* [the Kāśikā reads *dṛṣacchāradāḥ*].
This is a compound formed by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule). It is said that "this word *śārada* denotes 'freshness' (*pratyagra*)."

"Fresh" (*pratyagra*) means new, that is to say, existing for a short time; by this he demonstrates the polysemous nature of the word *śārada*. "A compulsory compound" (*nityasamāsa*): because the previously introduced *mahāvibhāṣā* (the great option) is here a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). "Unimpaired": [unimpaired] by dusts.
"Unimpairedness," however, is due to its being freshly extracted. Regarding the statement "ending in the suffix *u*":
this refers to the rule *sṛjerasuṃ ca* (Dhātupāṭha 1.100), which follows from the preceding rule *bhṛmṛśītṛcaritsaritanidhanimimasjibhya uḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 1.92).

This is because of the continued application of the suffix *uka*. Thus, it is stated: "ending in the suffix *ṭha* [or *adi*, as per the printed *Kāśikā*; *ādi*, as per the printed *Nyāsa*]. Furthermore, regarding the rule "to the root *dṛṇāti*, the augment *ṣuk* and shortening [of the vowel] occur" (*Daiva-Upaniṣad* 6.45), there is the mention of "the suffix *adi* for the roots *śṛ*, *dṛ*, and *bhās*."

Because the suffix *a* (aṅ) follows from this [rule], as in "paramaśāradam. Here, *śārada* means "that which occurs in autumn" (*śaradi bhavam*). This suffix is produced by the rule *sandhivelādyṛtunakṣatrebhyo 'ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.3.16).
Sound.

10. *Adhvaryu-kaṣāyayoḥ jātau* (6.2.10). [The commentary states: "Words denoting a genus (*jāti*) have a restricted scope (*niyataviṣaya*). The analysis of the compound is: "those whose scope is restricted" (*niyato viṣayo yeṣām*). Their having a restricted scope, however, is because they function only with respect to specific genera.

Because [the term *kaṭha*] belongs to the category of *caraṇa*, it possesses the status of a genus (*jāti*) according to the rule *gotrañ ca caraṇaiḥ* (Kāśikāvṛtti 4.1.63). It ends in the suffix *yat*; this is by the rule *dyauprāgapāgudakpratīco yat* (4.2.101). The word *kaṭha* is derived from the root with the suffix *ac* (belonging to the *pacādi* group). [The word *kaṭha*...]

From the root *kṛcchrajīvane* (Dhātupāṭha 333). Regarding the phrase "tadevam" (thus, in this way): since this word *kālapa* ends in the suffix *aṇ*, it is udātta on the final syllable by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). Regarding the statement "it is udātta on the final syllable when *ṭhak* is present": this is by the rule *kitaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.165).

11. *sadṛśa-pratirūpayoḥ sādṛśye* | (6.2.11) [The word *sadṛśa* is treated as a *gati* when used in the sense of similarity. For example, in the phrase *pitṛ-sadṛśaḥ* ("resembling his father"), the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*) case endings are applied by the rule *tulyārther tṛtīyā-ṣaṣṭhyau* (2.3.72), and the compound is formed by the rule *pūrva-sadṛśa-samo...* (2.1.31).
"The words *pitṛ* and *mātṛ* are prescribed as having the udātta accent on the final syllable among the uṇādi suffixes," as stated in [Uṇādisūtra] 2.3:
"naptṛ-neṣṭṛ-tvaṣṭṛ-hotṛ-potṛ-bhrātṛ-jāmātṛ-pitṛ-duhitṛ."

Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the word *sadṛśa* (resembling), since [the forms] *mātṛsadṛśa* and *pitṛsadṛśa* would already be established by the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha* (Pāṇini 6.2.2)? To this he says:
"And for the sake of the genitive compound," and so forth. For when used in the sense of "equal to" (*tulyārtha*), there is also the possibility of the genitive case.

It is prescribed [by the rule]. In that context, when the compound *mātṛsadṛśaḥ* is formed as a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound, the inclusion of the word *sadṛśa* (resembling) is for the purpose that this [specific formation] should also occur. However, if this [new rule] were to be introduced, the inclusion of *sadṛśa* would have to be made even in the case of a third-case (*tṛtīyā*) compound; therefore, he says "here," etc.

In the examples *dāsyāḥ sadṛśaḥ* ("resembling a female slave") and *vṛṣalyāḥ sadṛśaḥ* ("resembling a low-caste woman"), the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is formed after applying the rule *ṣaṣṭhyā ākrośe* (Pāṇini 6.3.21), which prescribes non-elision (*aluk*) of the genitive case-ending when used in an abusive sense. This requirement for non-elision necessitates the inclusion of the term *sadṛśa* ("resembling"); for if elision were to occur, the specific form [required by the compound] would not exist. If the inclusion of *sadṛśa* here were solely for the sake of forming the genitive compound...

It is performed; a third-case compound (*tṛtīyāsamāsa*) should not be made because there is no distinction [in meaning]. This is not so; for it must indeed be made even in that case where the sense of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī-artha*) does not exist, as in *vidyāsadṛśaḥ* ("similar to knowledge"). For here the sense of the sixth case is not found; what then? It is the sense of the third case.

The meaning is that it is similar to the cause, which is knowledge (*vidyā*). Regarding the phrase "here," and so forth: in that context, the suffix *ṅīp* in the word *dāsī* serves the purpose of making the final syllable udātta by means of the "anudātta-nivṛtti-svara" rule. [The root] *daśi* is used in the sense of "serving" (DhP 1786)—[the Dhātupāṭha reads *dasi* in the sense of "nourishing"]—and according to the Unādisūtra rule "from *daṃś*, the suffix *ṭan* is added, and *na* is substituted for *ā*" (UnS 9.103).

The suffix *ṭa* is applied, with the substitution of *ā* for the *n*; by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added; by *yasyeti ca* (6.4.148), there is elision of the *i*; and by *anudātasya ca yatro dātalopaḥ* (6.1.161), the [final syllable] becomes udātta. As for the word *vṛṣalī*, it is formed by the rule *jāter astrīviṣayāt* (4.1.63).
Thus, the word ending in the suffix *ṅīṣ* is udātta on its final syllable by virtue of the accent of the suffix.
12. *dvigau pramāṇe* (Pāṇini 6.2.12).

[The word] *prācyasaptaśamaḥ* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). [In this compound,] the word *prācya* has its first syllable acute (*ādyaudāta*), because it ends in the suffix *yat* [according to Pāṇini 4.2.98], and thus [it is governed by] *yato 'nāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.213). [Likewise,] the word *gāndhāri*.

"Because [the word] belongs to the *kardama*-group, it is either udātta on the first syllable or udātta in the middle. In the rule *kardamādīnāṃ ca* (Phiṭ-sūtra 3.10), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) from the previous rule is understood to carry over.
Therefore, when the udātta is prescribed for the first syllable, it becomes udātta on the first syllable; but when it is prescribed for the second, then...
The middle [syllable] is udātta.
13. *gantavya-panyaṃ vāṇije* (6.2.13).
*Gantavya* means that which is to be gone to; *panya* means that which is to be traded. [Examples: *madra-vāṇijaḥ*.

Thus it is said: "He who deals in the Madra country is so described. This is a locative compound (*saptamī-samāsa*), according to the rule *saptamī* (Pāṇini 2.1.40), which is split off as a separate yoga-rule.
It ends with the suffix *rak*, according to the rule *sphāyitañci* (Dhātupāṭha 3.8.31).
Because [the term] has been explained by means of such passages as these, having established its derivation within the *made* section.

14. *mātropajñopakramacchāye napuṃsake* | (6.2.14) It is said that [the compound] "refers to something of equal measure" (*tulyapramāṇe vartate*). [The variant reading in the manuscript is *tulyapramāṇam*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that which has an equal measure" (*tulyaṃ pramāṇaṃ yasya*). Why is this not considered a *svapadavigraha* (an analysis using its own constituent words), given the rule that it should be an *asvapadavigraha* (an analysis not using its own constituent words)?

For indeed, a sentence should be constructed in such a way that its condensed meaning (*samāsārtha*) is understood—as in "bhikṣāmātram" (merely alms). And the meaning of this is "that which has the same measure as alms. Nor can this be conveyed by means of an analysis using its own constituent words (*svapadavigraha*), because of the word *mātra*.

Because it functions with an equal measure [of meaning]. For that [compound] alone functions with an equal measure, not the sentence. Therefore it has been said: "This word *mātra* refers to the domain of syntactic function (*vṛtti*)," and so forth.
Here, "syntactic function" (*vṛtti*) refers specifically to compound function (*samāsavṛtti*). [The rule] "that which does not end in a suffix is udātta."

[Regarding the reading "apratyayāntodātaḥ" as printed in the Kāśikā: it is because, together with the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, one part is udātta and the other part is anudātta. 15. [The word *sukha* takes the suffix *yat*] in the sense of "beneficial," when it refers to *priya*. (Pāṇini 6.2.15)

Regarding the passage beginning with "In that context, the words *sukha* and *priya*," the word "that" (*tat*) refers back to *sukha* and *priya*. The cause of those two, *sukha* and *priya*, is that which produces pleasure in the future, namely in another birth. In that case, the words *sukha* and *priya* are employed. For what reason is it explained in this way? To this he says: "For that..."

"Hitam" and so forth. "Hi" means "for that reason. In this *tatpuruṣa* compound, the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is prescribed. For this *tatpuruṣa* expresses "beneficial" (*hita*) only if the words *sukha* and *priya*, standing as the prior members (*pūrvapada*), signify "benefit" (*hita*). And what is beneficial?
When it produces pleasure in the future, how then do the words "pleasant" and "unpleasant" apply to that cause?
It is by metaphorically applying the name of the effect to the cause, just as one says "the water of the reed-bed causes foot-disease."

16. And [the suffix *khañ* is applied] when pleasure (*prīti*) is expressed. (6.2.16) Now, for what purpose is this inclusion of "when pleasure" (*prītau*), given that pleasure is invariably concomitant with happiness (*sukha*) and what is dear (*priya*)? Will it not suffice that the suffix occurs whenever pleasure is understood? To this [the author replies]:...
He says: "In the case of *sukha* (pleasure) and *priya* (the beloved), there is *prīti* (affection)," and so forth.

Even though [the state] is established without the mention of *prīti*, since *prīti* is invariably concomitant with pleasure (*sukha*) and the beloved (*priya*), if *prīti* is mentioned here, it is for the sake of [indicating] that which is an intensified form of *prīti*. As for example:

The word "syāt" is used for this purpose: [to indicate that] "the words *brāhmaṇa* and *chātra* are oxytone by the accent of the suffix. The word *brāhmaṇa* ends in the suffix *aṇ*. The word *chātra* ends in the suffix *ṇa*, according to Pāṇini 4.4.62 (*cchatrādibhyo ṇaḥ*). "The word *kanyā* is circumflex-accented on its final syllable," as it is listed among the *adhnyādi* group (Daiva-nighaṇṭu 8.14).

Because it is read exactly as such: "rājasukham" means "dear to the king. Although in this case *prīti* (affection) is understood because pleasure (*sukha*) and what is dear (*priya*) are never separated from affection, nevertheless, that which is affection in its highest degree— [The remainder of the sentence continues: —that is [expressed by the suffix -matup]. For example, *rājamatam* means "highly esteemed by the king," and *rājamataḥ* means "highly favored by the king. In these cases, although the suffix -matup is prescribed for words ending in the sixth case, it is not applied here because the word *rājan* is included among those ending in the first case. Furthermore, since the suffix -matup is prescribed for words ending in the third case, it is not applied here either, because the word *rājan* is included among those ending in the second case. Moreover, since the suffix -matup is prescribed for words ending in the second case, it is not applied here, because the word *rājan* is included among those ending in the first case. And since the suffix -matup is prescribed for words ending in the first case, it is not applied here, because the word *rājan* is included among those ending in the second case. Therefore, the suffix -matup is not applied at all. Consequently, the forms *rājasukham* and *rājaprīyam* are established through the application of the suffix -yat. As for the statement that "the suffix -yat is applied after words ending in the sixth case when expressing 'dear to' (*priya*)," this is merely a restatement of what has already been established; it does not serve as a restrictive rule. Otherwise, it would follow that the suffix -yat could not be applied even to words like *rājñaḥ priyam* (the king's favorite), because the word *rājan* is included among those ending in the first case. However, since the suffix -yat is indeed applied there, the aforementioned restriction is not valid. Thus, the suffix -yat is applied after words ending in the sixth case when expressing "dear to. This is the meaning. Now, regarding the statement "the suffix -yat is applied after words ending in the second case when expressing 'pleasure' (*sukha*)," this too is merely a restatement of what has already been established; it does not serve as a restrictive rule. Otherwise, it would follow that the suffix -yat could not be applied even to words like *rājñaḥ sukham* (the king's happiness), because the word *rājan* is included among those ending in the first case. However, since the suffix -yat is indeed applied there, the aforementioned restriction is not valid. Thus, the suffix -yat is applied after words ending in the second case when expressing "pleasure. This is the meaning. Now, regarding the statement "the suffix -yat is applied after words ending in the third case when expressing 'beneficial' (*hita*)," this too is merely a restatement of what has already been established; it does not serve as a restrictive rule. Otherwise, it would follow that the suffix -yat could not be applied even to words like *rājñā hitam* (beneficial for the king), because the word *rājan* is included among those ending in the first case. However, since the suffix -yat is indeed applied there, the aforementioned restriction is not valid. Thus, the suffix -yat is applied after words ending in the third case when expressing "beneficial. This is the meaning. Now, regarding the statement "the suffix -yat is applied after words ending in the fourth case when expressing 'for the purpose of' (*tadartham*)," this too is merely a restatement of what has already been established; it does not serve as a restrictive rule. Otherwise, it would follow that the suffix -yat could not be applied even to words like *rājñe hitam* (beneficial for the king), because the word *rājan* is included among those ending in the first case. However, since the suffix -yat is indeed applied there, the aforementioned restriction is not valid. Thus, the suffix -yat is applied after words ending in the fourth case when expressing "for the purpose of. This is the meaning. Now, regarding the statement "the suffix -yat is applied after words ending in the fifth case when expressing 'fear of' (*bhaya*)," this too is merely a restatement of what has already been established; it does not serve as a restrictive rule. Otherwise, it would follow that the suffix -yat could not be applied even to words like *rājño bhayam* (fear of the king), because the word *rājan* is included among those ending in the first case. However, since the suffix -yat is indeed applied there, the aforementioned restriction is not valid. Thus, the suffix -yat is applied after words ending in the fifth case when expressing "fear of. This is the meaning. Now, regarding the statement "the suffix -yat is applied after words ending in the seventh case when expressing 'located in' (*adhikaraṇa*)," this too is merely a restatement of what has already been established; it does not serve as a restrictive rule. Otherwise, it would follow that the suffix -yat could not be applied even to words like *rājani bhaktiḥ* (devotion to the king), because the word *rājan* is included among those ending in the first case. However, since the suffix -yat is indeed applied there, the aforementioned restriction is not valid. Thus, the suffix -yat is applied after words ending in the seventh case when expressing "located in. This is the meaning. Now, regarding the statement "the suffix -matup is applied after words ending in the sixth case when expressing 'possessing' (*tadasyāsti*)," this too is merely a restatement of what has already been established; it does not serve as a restrictive rule. Otherwise, it would follow that the suffix -matup could not be applied even to words like *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the king's man), because the word *rājan* is included among those ending in the first case. However, since the suffix -matup is indeed applied there, the aforementioned restriction is not valid. Thus, the suffix -matup is applied after words ending in the sixth case when expressing "possessing. This is the meaning. Now, regarding the statement "the suffix -matup is applied after words ending in the second case when expressing 'having as one's nature' (*tadasya svabhāvaḥ*)," this too is merely a restatement of what has already been established; it does not serve as a restrictive rule. Otherwise, it would follow that the suffix -matup could not be applied even to words like *rājā svabhāvo 'sya* (this has the king as its nature), because the word *rājan* is included among those ending in the first case. However, since the suffix -matup is indeed applied there, the aforementioned restriction is not valid. Thus, the suffix -matup is applied after words ending in the second case when expressing "having as one's nature. This is the meaning. Now, regarding the statement "the suffix -matup is applied after words ending in the third case when expressing 'produced by that' (*tadasya saṃjātam*)," this too is merely a restatement of what has already been established; it does not serve as a restrictive rule. Otherwise, it would follow that the suffix -matup could not be applied even to words like *rājñā saṃjātam asya* (this has been produced by the king), because the word *rājan* is included among those ending in the first case. However, since the suffix -matup is indeed applied there, the aforementioned restriction is not valid. Thus, the suffix -matup is applied after words ending in the third case when expressing "produced by that. This is the meaning. Now, regarding the statement "the suffix -matup is applied after words ending in the fourth case when expressing 'deserving that' (*tadarhati*)," this too is merely a restatement of what has already been established; it does not serve as a restrictive rule. Otherwise, it would follow that the suffix -matup could not be applied even to words like *rājānam arhati* (he deserves the king), because the word *rājan* is included among those ending in the first case. However, since the suffix -matup is indeed applied there, the aforementioned restriction is not valid. Thus, the suffix -matup is applied after words ending in the fourth case when expressing "deserving that. This is the meaning. Now, regarding the statement "the suffix -matup is applied after words ending in the fifth case when expressing 'fleeing from that' (*tato 'petaḥ*)," this too is merely a restatement of what has already been established; it does not serve as a restrictive rule. Otherwise, it would follow that the suffix -matup could not be applied even to words like *rājño 'petaḥ* (departed from the king), because the word *rājan* is included among those ending in the first case. However, since the suffix -mat
"It is not understood" serves as a counter-example.
17. *sva* [is substituted for the genitive] when the word *svāmin* follows.

(6.2.17) 18. *pati* [is substituted for the genitive] when expressing sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). (6.2.18) [The word *dhānyamantaḥ* has a svarita accent on the final syllable] because it ends in the suffix *ṇyat*; this is due to the *titsvara* rule. [In the case of *vṛṣalyāḥ*...]
The meaning is "husband"; that is to say, the lover of a Śūdra woman.
19. *nabhūvākciddidhiṣu* (Pāṇini 6.2.19).

The word *bhū* is acutely accented on the final syllable by the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*), due to the suffix *kvip* [added] by the rule *bhuvaḥ saṃjñāntarayoḥ* (3.2.179). The word *vāk* is likewise [accented], [being derived] from the root *vac-* with the suffix *kvip* by the rule *kvibvacipracchi-*.

By means of [the rule] *da.u.* 10.2, etc., the suffix *kvip* is applied. Regarding the word *cit*: from the root *citī saṃjñāne* (DhP 39), the suffix *kvip* is applied according to *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 3.2.187).
This is stated under the governing rule *nṛtiśṛdhyoḥ kūḥ* (*da.u.* 1.174).
In the *Daiva* (1.176), it is stated: "The word *didhiṣū*, ending in the suffix *kū*, is udātta on the final syllable."

20. Or *bhūvana*. (Pāṇini 6.2.20) 21. In the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*), [the suffix *kyaṅ* is added] after [roots expressing] apprehension (*āśaṅkā*), affliction (*bādhana*), and distance (*nedīyas*).
(Pāṇini 6.2.21) Regarding the root *śaki* in the sense of apprehension (*śaṅkā*) [as listed in Dhātupāṭha 86], [the suffix *ap* is added] by the rule *gurośca halaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.103).

(3.3.103) Thus, there is the suffix *it* (*akāra*). Some, however, explain that this refers to the word *śaṅku*, which ends in the suffix *ghañ*. From the root *bādhṛ* (meaning "to press") with the prefix *āṅ* and the suffix *ghañ*, we have *ābādhaḥ*. [The form] *nedīyaḥ* means "very near"; it is derived from the word *antika*.
In the word *nedasādhau*, the substitute *nedas* occurs by Pāṇini 5.3.63 (*ṭhantikabāḍhayornedasādhau*) when the suffix *iyasun* follows.

Regarding the phrase "ascertainment of existence" (*astitvādhyavasāya*), the meaning is "certainty that [something] exists. In the phrase "fear of departure" (*gamanāśaṅkam*), it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Because it functions as an adverb (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), it takes the neuter gender.
Or rather, because the gender is based on worldly usage.
22. *pūrvo bhūtapūrve* (Pāṇini 5.3.53).
[The suffix] *ṭhañ* [is applied after the word *pūrva* when it means] "having been previously. One who was previously wealthy (*āḍhya*) is expressed in this way.
Because the meaning is already understood through the compound, the word *bhūta* is not employed [in the example], just as in *dadhyodana*.
In this context, the word *upasikta* [is used].

Regarding "paramapūrvaḥ," here there is a compound according to the rule *sanmahatparamottamotkṛṣṭāḥ pūjāyām* (Pāṇini 2.1.61). As for the statement, "here the compound is 'this is both supreme (*parama*) and prior (*pūrva*')," the particle *iti* is used for the purpose of indicating the meaning.

The meaning is that in this counter-example, there is a compound for that sentence-meaning characterized by being honored, namely "this is both supreme and prior. However, [there is no compound] in "paramo bhūtapūrvaḥ.
The word *tu* (however) serves to emphasize. This refers to the sentence-meaning: "one who was previously supreme."
The meaning is that this compound belongs to the category characterized by the time "prior to the ultimate" (*paramapūrvakāla*). Why is this so? He says:

"And thus," and so forth. The word *ca* here has the sense of *hi* (for/indeed). This [specific] compound does not occur. This being the case, this becomes merely an illustrative example (*udāharaṇa*), not a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*).
This is because the word *pūrva* signifies "that which existed previously. As for the reading commonly found in manuscripts here— namely,

that the analysis is "this is both supreme (*parama*) and previously existent (*bhūtapūrva*)" rather than "the supreme one who was previously existent"— that should be understood as a mistaken reading, since [the intended meaning] applies in both sentences.
Because the two previous [states] are being understood as having occurred in the past.

23. *savidha-sanīḍa-samaryāda-saveśa-sadeśeṣu sāmīpye* (Pāṇini 6.2.23). *Savidha* means "in the vicinity" (*saha viṣayā*). It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to [Pāṇini 2.2.28] *tena saheti tulyayoge*. The substitution of *sa-* for *saha-* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.3.82] *vopasarjanasya*. Similarly...

It should be understood that even in cases such as *sanīḍa* and others, there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound and the substitution of *sa-* for *saha-*. Words such as *savidham* are genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compounds.
Now, one might object: words such as *savidha* are derived in the sense of "in the vicinity of" (*saha viṣayeṇa*) and so forth.
How, then, is there usage [of these words] in proximity? To this he says: "‘Together with the object,’ and so forth.

By the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is the inclusion of such expressions as "together with the nest" (saha nīḍena) and "together with the boundary" (saha maryādayā). The particle *eva* is for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), serving to exclude other possible meanings.
He says: "It serves solely as a cause for grammatical derivation, not as a denotable meaning.
Regarding the statement, "But these [words] denote proximity," here too the word *tu* (but) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) alone;
it means that they denote only proximity, and not words whose sentence-meaning consists of such expressions as "together with" (*saha*) or "with" (*vidhi*).
Thus [it is said].
24. *Vispaṣṭādīni gaṇavacaneṣu* (6.2.24). Regarding the example *vispaṣṭakaṭukam*: from the word *kaṭu*, the suffix *kan* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.147] *saṃjñāyāṃ kan*.
Then, by [Pāṇini 2.1.4] *sup supā*, a compound (*samāsa*) is formed.

Now, regarding the rule "A qualifier [is compounded] with a qualified object in various ways" (2.1.57), why is a *karmadhāraya* compound not formed in the case of *vispaṣṭakaṭukam*, by analyzing it as such?
To this he says: "For *vispaṣṭa* and so forth are here," and so on. For the *karmadhāraya*...
Co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) exists when it occurs; however, such co-referentiality does not exist here.

Therefore, in this context, words such as "pungent" (kaṭuka) function as qualifiers of the property—such as pungency—that serves as the ground for the application (pravṛttinimitta) of the word "pungent," and not of the substance possessing that property. And by means of words such as "pungent"...

By means of words, a substance possessing a quality—such as that which possesses the quality characterized by pungency (or, according to the printed reading: "that which has the characteristic of being pungent")—is designated as "possessing that quality" (*tadguṇavat*).
Consequently, because there is a difference in grammatical substratum (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), a karmadhāraya compound is not possible. Therefore, it must be according to the method already stated.

The compound must be formed as *vispaṣṭaḥ* [the word *vispaṣṭa*—Kāśikā]. This is derived from the root *spaś* (DhP 887), meaning "to afflict" or "to touch," in its past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) form, according to the rule:
"In the case of *dasta*, *spaṣṭa*, *cchanna*, and *jñapta*... [Vārttika].

The word *spaṣṭa* is established by the Pāṇinian sūtra *dānta-śānta-pūrṇa-dasta-spṛṣṭa-cchanna-jñaptāḥ* (7.2.27); it forms a *gatapūrva-samāsa* with the prefix *vi*. Regarding the phrase "the word *vicitra*," and so forth: the root *cit* (meaning "to decorate" or "to make variegated") belongs to the *curādi* class (numbered 1917); from this root, the suffix *ghañ* is applied.

*Viśeṣeṇa citram vicitram*: this is a *prādi-samāsa* (prepositional compound). [The accentuation] is by means of the "accent of an indeclinable" (*avyayasvara*), which is prescribed by the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-* (Pāṇini 6.2.2), etc. Furthermore, the word *vi-* here is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), and its initial syllable is udātta (acute-accented) according to the rule *nipātā ādyudāttāḥ* (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.80).

Regarding the expression "ṭhvicitaśabdam": from the root *citī* (meaning "to perceive," Dhātupāṭha 39), the form *citam* is derived in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). A *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed meaning "one from whom perception has departed" (*vigataṃ citam asya*). The phrase "by the accent of the *bahuvrīhi*" refers to this same root *citī*, where *citam* is the past passive participle; [the compound] is "one from whom perception has departed."
"Citamas-ya" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. "By the accent of the *bahuvrīhi*" means by that which is prescribed in *Pāṇini* 6.2.1:

"In a *bahuvrīhi*, [the first member] remains in its original form (*prakṛtyā*). Regarding "the word *vyakta*," and so forth: when the root *añj* preceded by the prefix *vi-* takes the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*), the *gati* accent is acute; therein, the *yaṇ* substitute that occurs in place of the vowel *i*.
There occurs an acute accent (udātta) on the vowel [of the suffix], and consequently, the following unaccented (anudātta) *a* becomes circumflex (svarita).

Regarding the phrase "the word *sampanna*" and so forth: the word *sampanna* is derived from the root *pad* preceded by the prefix *sam*, with the suffix *niṣṭhā* [in the sense] of the agent (*kartari*).
As for the words *paṭu* and *paṇḍita*, they [bear their accents] according to the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).

The term *antodāta* (ending in an acute accent) should be understood by modifying the singular form that was previously mentioned; thus, the connection should be made as "those [roots] ending in an acute accent. Regarding the root *pāṭ*, [the rule] states:
"For *phal*, *pāṭ*, *nam*, and *jan*, there is the suffix *guk*, and for *pāṭ* there is also the suffix *nākin*."

[Regarding the forms *paṭu* and *paṇḍita*: from the root *phaṇ* (DhP 1.549), by the rule *phalipāṭinamimanijanāṃ gukÂpaṭinākidhataśca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.103), the suffix *u* is applied and *paṭi* is the substitute—thus *paṭuḥ*. From the root *paḍi* meaning "to go" (DhP 281), in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), we have *paṇḍitaḥ*. Regarding *kuśalaḥ*: it means "one who takes up (*lāti*) the *kuśa* grass," from the root *lā* meaning "to take up."]
From the root [√dhrā] (DhP 1058), the suffix *ka* is applied by Pāṇini 3.2.3 (*āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*).

This forms a compound with an upapada. By Pāṇini 6.2.139 (*gatikārakopapadāt kṛt*), the original accent of the final member (*uttarapada*) is maintained. Regarding the word *capala*, it is stated that "it has an acute accent on the final syllable" (*antodātta*) due to the *cit* accent.

Thus he considers [this]: "How is this word [citta] udātta at the end by virtue of the *cit*-accent? To this he says: it is derived with the suffix *kala* from the rule "the suffix *kala* after the root *tṛp*" (*Daiva-Upaniṣad* 8.107).
In that context, the mention of *cit* from the rule "the suffix *cit* after *bṛṣṛ* and others" (*Daiva-Upaniṣad* 8.109) is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). By means of that—

The word *citsvara* means "accented on the final syllable. Regarding the phrase "the word *nipuṇa*," and so forth, the term "accented on the final syllable" (*antodāta*) is connected to the subject under discussion. As for the form *puṇeḥ*, it is derived from the root *puṇa* (DhP 1333), meaning "to purify," with the suffix *ka* added according to Pāṇini 3.1.135:
*igupadhājñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ*. Thus, the suffix *ka* is applied.
25. *śrajyāvamakanpāpavatṣu bhāve karmadhāraye* (Pāṇini 6.2.25). In the example "gamana-śreṣṭham" (the best going), the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.115] *lyuṭ ca*;
it is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). That which is most praiseworthy is *śreyas*. [The form *śreṣṭha* arises] from the suffixes *dṛṣṭhan* and *īyasun* applied to the word *praśasya*.

By [Pāṇini 5.3.60], *śra-* is the substitute. Regarding "the eldest in speech" (*vacanajyeṣṭham*): here too, when those same two suffixes follow, the word *praśasya-* undergoes the substitution of *jya-*. Regarding "the youngest in movement" (*gamanakaniṣṭham*) and "the younger in movement" (*gamanakanīyaḥ*): when the suffixes *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun* follow, the word *yuvan-* and the word *alpa-* [undergo their respective substitutions].
The substitution *kan* is applied by the rule *ṭhyuvālpayoḥ kananyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.3.64). Now, one might ask:
how is it that [the term] *śrajyakanām* is used here? The particle *iti* is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
Because here there is a mention of the substitutes [of *yuvan* and *alpa*], namely *śra* and *jya*, and these [substitutes] occur before an affix beginning with a vowel (*ac-ādi*).
Since [the suffixes] are prescribed for *praśasya* and so forth, their occurrence alone is impossible; therefore, by implication, a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) similar to them is understood.

26. *kumāraśca* (Pāṇini 6.2.26). Regarding the example "kumāraśramaṇā," since the rule states that "when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 21), the word *kumārī* is compounded here. For it is thus [that the compound is formed].
The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the feminine form of the word *śramaṇā* is thus established; otherwise, it would not be possible.

As for the statement "the word *kumāra* has its final syllable accented," this is because it is derived from the root *kumāra* (DhP 1877, meaning "to play") with the suffix *ac* according to the rule Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*).

"But some [say]... and so forth. But how, when the paribhāṣā "that which is taught by a technical definition [takes precedence over that which is taught by a word-form]" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 3) exists, is it obtained that [the rule applies] "without distinction"? He thinks as follows: the particle *ca* is used here; and it serves to conjoin this very injunction. Therefore, it applies everywhere without distinction.

[The particle *ca*] occurs [in this sense]. For in this way there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*), and not otherwise. However, those who maintain that the compound [is formed] only in the rule "a boy [is compounded] with *śramaṇa*, etc. (Pāṇini 2.1.70), explain the letter *ca* here as having the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) with respect to the preceding rule.

27. *ādiḥ pratyenasi* (6.2.27). [The word *pratyenas* means] "one who has turned toward (*pratigata*) sin (*enas*). By this, he shows that the word *pratyenas* forms a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule: "Words beginning with *ava* form a compound with a word in the third case when they have the sense of 'reviled' (*kruṣṭa*), etc. (Vārttika 92). Alternatively, it means "one whose sin has turned back (*pratigatam eno yasya*)."
Thus, by this [rule], it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. In the case of "kumārapratyenasah," there is lengthening according to Pāṇini 6.4.14: "atvasantasya cādhātoḥ.
Now, one might object: since the mention of the acute accent (*udātta*) does not exist in this rule, how is the acute accent obtained?

Thus he says: "The word *udātta* is used here," and so forth. But what is that capacity (*sāmarthya*)? He says: "The preceding member [of the compound]," and so forth. For it is not a different accent that is being prescribed other than the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*);
rather, it is the original accent itself, because the term *prakṛtyā* (by its original form) continues to apply.

In this context, the connection is made as follows: that accent which would have been obtained for the word *kumāra* by virtue of its being a base-form (*prakṛtibhāva*) becomes the accent of the initial syllable. And thus, by implication, it is understood to be acute (*udātta*), for that indeed is the accent of the word *kumāra* by virtue of its being a base-form.
28. Optionally [the suffix *cha* is applied] after words ending in *pūga*.

(6.2.28) 29. [The suffix *cha* is applied] after a *dvigu* compound ending in a word with a short vowel (*ik*), or in *kāla*, *kapāla*, *bhagāla*, or *śarāva*. (6.2.29) [This is governed by the rule] "After a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), the suffix *yap* is applied," and by "After *māsa*, [the suffix *kan* is applied] when expressing age. (5.1.81)

While this [rule] continues to apply, the suffix *yaP* is introduced by the rule *dvigor yaP* (5.1.82). Then, by the rule *ṭhaño luk*, there is elision of the *ṭhaÑ* suffix belonging to the *prāgvatīya* group. Thus we have *pañcakapālaḥ*. In the sense of "a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) prepared in five potsherds (*kapāla*)," the suffix *aṆ* is applied by the rule *saṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ* (4.2.16); of that [suffix], there is elision by the rule *dvigoḥ*.

By [the rule] beginning with (4.1.88), there is elision (*luk*). "These are compounds" refers to those starting with *pañcakapāla* and ending with *daśaśarāva*. "Those in which the suffix *aṇ* has been elided" means those in which the suffix *aṇ* has undergone elision; they are described as such.
In this context, the words *pañca* and *daśa* are udātta-accented according to the rule *ṭhgraḥ saṃkhyāyāḥ* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.28).

Regarding the form *pañcāśvaḥ*: it is a compound (*samāsa*) in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). The suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule *ārhādagopucchasaṃkhyāparimāṇāṭ ṭhak* (Pāṇini 5.1.19), and its elision (*luk*) occurs by the rule *adhyardhapūrvād dvigor lug anapatye* (Pāṇini 5.1.28). [Thus,] *pañca*...

The term *śarāvāṇi* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those which have bowls in them. Now, how does it work in this case: *pañcāratnyaḥ*, *daśāratnyaḥ*? Since the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs after *yava* and the *guṇa* substitution has been applied, the final member (*uttarapada*) does not end in *ā*. To this he says: *pañcāratnyaḥ*, etc.
Since the *yaṇ* and *guṇa* substitutions occur when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) beginning with a vowel follows, these two are considered "external" (*bahiraṅga*) in this context,

whereas the accent (*svara*) is "internal" (*antaraṅga*), because it exists prior to the production of the case-ending. According to the principle that "what is external is as if non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to what is internal," this applies even in the case of *pañcāratnayaḥ*.

"The accent characterized by having a penultimate *i* (igantalakṣaṇaḥ) applies by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāvāt*). Regarding the rule "In place of a vowel, when a subsequent [element] is applied, for a preceding operation" (1.1.57), the *guṇa* substitution which is to be performed for the sake of the preceding accent proceeds by way of the status of being a substitute as if it were a penultimate *i*. But is it not the case that in rules concerning accent...?
Is the status of being like the original (sthānivadbhāva) prohibited by the rule *padanta* (Pāṇini 1.1.58)? This is not so;

for it has been stated (*kā. 1.1.58*) that "in the case of vowel [substitution], lengthening, and the elision of *y*, a substitute for an elided element (*lopājādeśaḥ*) is not treated as if it were the original. Furthermore, the *yaṇ* and *guṇa* substitutions in [the formation of] *pañcāratnyaḥ* are not substitutes for an elided element. *Pañcāratnyaḥ*.

Thus [it is said]. Here, the word *aratni* ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*, because it is listed among the *bahu*-group [of words] by the rules "after a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix with a long vowel other than *ktin*" (Gaṇasūtra 50) and "some say, after any word ending in a suffix other than *ktin*" (Gaṇasūtra 51). In this case as well, as before, there is a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), but [the suffix] *mātrac*—
Elision.

30. *bahvanyatarasyām* | (6.2.30) Since the previous [rule] would have necessitated the constant preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) for the word *bahu* when followed by suffixes such as *-in*, this optional rule is now stated. For example: *bahuratniḥ*. As before.

"Beginning with *samāsa* [and] *bahumāsyah*. As before, there is the suffix *yaP*. Compounds such as *bahukapāla* and others—here too, even though the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) has been applied, the elision of the suffix *aṇ* is to be understood according to Pāṇini 4.2.16, *saṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ*. "The word *bahu* is oxytone (*antodātta*). For that indeed...

While the rule *kurbhraśca* (Dhātupāṭha-Uṇādi 1.107) is being carried over, [the word] is derived from the root *bṛh/mah* in the sense of "growth" (Dhātupāṭha 633, 634). By applying the suffix *ku* according to the rule *landhirbrahyaernalopaśca* (Dhātupāṭha-Uṇādi 1.114), it is thus etymologically explained; consequently, by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), it is oxytone (*antodātta*). Where...
"The substitution of *yaṇ* [occurs]"; this refers to the case of *bahvaratniḥ*.

31. And [the suffix *kan* is applied] after *diṣṭi* and *vitasti*. (6.2.31) This rule is commenced for the purpose of excluding the meaning "many. For example: *pañcadiṣṭiḥ* ("five *diṣṭis*"). This is equivalent to the expression *pañcāratniḥ* ("five *aratnis*").
32. *saptamī siddha-śuṣka-pakva-bandheṣv-akālāt* (Pāṇini 2.1.41).
[The example is] *sāṅkāśya-siddhaḥ*. The compound is formed by the rule *siddha-śuṣka-pakva-bandhaiś-ca*.
[It is stated that] "the words *sāṅkāśya* and *kāmpilya* end in the suffix *ṇya*," [referring to] *vuñ-chaṇ-ṇya-yaña-ṇaka-tañ* (Pāṇini 4.2.80).
Because [the word] has been derived by prescribing the *cāturarthika* suffix characterized as *saṅkāśa*, etc., according to the rule beginning with (Pāṇini 4.2.80).
Regarding the phrase "the word *ūka*," etc.: under the governing rule "The suffix *ka* is applied after the roots *kṛ*, *ādhāra*, *arc*, and *kali*" (Daiva Uṇādisūtra 3.18),...

By the rule *sṛdṛbhūśuṣimuṣibhyaḥ kak* (Uṇādi Sūtra 19), the suffix *kak* is prescribed as having the *kit* designation; since this applies even to the root *av*, the word *tanoka* ends in the suffix *kak*. By the rule *jvaratvara-* (Pāṇini 6.4.20) and others, the augment *ūṭh* is applied to *vat*. [The word] *nidhana*...
"By the rule *nighāñaḥ kyupratyaye madhyodāttaḥ*, this word *nidhana* is derived from the root *dhā* with the suffix *kyu* [according to Daiva 5.26:
*kṛpṛvṛjimandi nidhāñaḥ kyuḥ*; the printed reading in the Daiva is *nidhāñbhyaḥ*].
In the locative singular, the augment *num* is applied by the rule *iko'ci vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.1.73)."
Having formed [the compound], it should be understood as neuter gender with respect to the form of the word.
The meaning is that within this verbal form *kyu*, that which is designated as an affix [is intended].
"The words *kumbhī* and *kalasī* end in *ṅīp*"—by this, the intention is that they are oxytone (accented on the final syllable).

The fact that [the word *bhrāṣṭrī*] ends in the suffix *ṅīṣ* is to be understood from the rule "ṅīṣ after a genus-word (*jāti*) that does not refer to a female" (Pāṇini 4.1.63), etc., by means of the *ṅīṣ* prescribed therein. As for the statement "the word *bhrāṣṭra* ends in the suffix *ṣṭran*," this is because while the rule "ṣṭran" (Dhātupāṭha 8.79) is in force, there is the rule: "There is *vṛddhi* [of the root vowel] for the roots *bhrasj*, *gam*, *nam*, *han*, *viṣ*, and *aś*."
[The printed reading of the Nyāsa is "ṭhviśyaśāṃ"].

34. *rājanyabahuvacanadvandve'ndhakavṛṣṇiṣu* (Pāṇini 6.2.34). When there is a dvandva compound consisting of multiple words denoting *rājanya* (kṣatriyas), provided they belong to the Andhaka or Vṛṣṇi clans, [the final vowel of the first member takes the udātta accent]. Those words denoting *rājanya* which are uncompounded, end in the plural number, and constitute the members of such a compound...

That is called a *dvandva* consisting of many words denoting *rājanya*s; as in the example "śvāphalkacaitrakarodhakāḥ. This is a *dvandva* compound meaning "the Śvāphalkas, the Caitrakas, and the Rodhakas. In that compound, the word *caitraka* has the status of the prior member (*pūrvapada*) in relation to the word *rodhaka*, and [the word *rodhaka* has the status of the posterior member] in relation to the word *caitraka*.

There is also the *prakṛtibhāva* (absence of sandhi) for the word *śvāphalka*. For this very reason, he says "the word *śvāphalka* and the word *caitraka*" and so forth, in order to demonstrate the accentuation (*svara*) of both of them. [He states] "the word *śini* is udātta on the first syllable. For that [word] is derived from [the rule] "from the roots *vī*, *yaj*, and *jvar*, the suffix *ni*" (Daiva Uṇādi Sūtra 1.18).

While the suffix *nip* is being carried over, by the rule "ṭhvahi-śri-śru-dru-glā-hā-ātvaribhyo nit" (Dhātupāṭha 1.21), which prescribes the addition of *nip*, it applies to the root *śīṅ* as well. Furthermore, due to the mention of "bahula" (diversity/optionality), the shortening of the vowel also occurs from that very same source; thus, it is udātta on the first syllable.

"It will be with a *nitsvara* accent. Regarding the phrase "in his descendants" (*tadapatyeṣu*), the meaning is: "in those who are the offspring of that Śini, the Kṣatriya. Regarding the phrase "without distinction" (*abhedena*), the meaning is: "by way of metaphorical attribution" (*upacāreṇa*).
Regarding the form "Haimāyanāḥ," the suffix *phak* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.101] "after *yañ* and *iñ*. But surely...

This word *rājanya* denotes the Kṣatriya caste; as it has been stated: "In the case of a descendant of a king, there is the inclusion of the caste" (Vārttika 392); thus, one becomes a *rājanya* if he is a Kṣatriya.
Furthermore, the dvandva compound that occurs among the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis consists exclusively of words denoting Kṣatriyas.

Because the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis are Kṣatriyas, the phrase "the Dvaipyas and Haimāyanas" was stated as a counter-example. For this too is a dvandva compound of words denoting only Rājanyas, since they reside among the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis; therefore, he says: "The Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis," and so forth.

Since the inclusion of Kṣatriyas is already established by the mere mention of "among the Ṭhandhakas and Vṛṣṇis," the fact that the term "Rājanya" is specifically employed has this purpose: so that those who belong to a consecrated lineage may be included. [This applies] whether by learning or by birth.

The lineage (*vaṃśa*) of living beings is characterized by a single characteristic; however, here it is intended as that which is characterized by a single birth. One who belongs to that [lineage] is "of the lineage" (*vaṃśya*), according to Pāṇini 4.3.54, because [the word] belongs to the *dig-ādi* group. Now, one might ask: are not the Dvaipyas and Haimāyanas also Kṣatriyas belonging to an inaugurated lineage (*abhiṣiktavaṃśya*)?
Therefore, he says: "And these," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva": this is a *dvandva* (copulative) compound of the two words *saṅkarṣaṇa* and *vāsudeva*, both ending in the singular number. [He also mentions] "the Vṛṣṇi princes."

This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound: "Kuru-Pāñcālāḥ. Although all the conditions [for the application of the rule] are present here, it nevertheless does not occur because of the specific mention of the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis; for there is no exclusion in that case.

35. *saṃkhyā* | (6.2.35) Regarding "ekādaśa": this is a *dvandva* compound meaning "one and ten. Regarding "dvādaśa": by the rule *dvyaṣṭanaḥ saṃkhyāyāmabahuvrīhyaśītyoḥ* (6.3.47), the substitution of *ā* occurs [for the final vowel and consonant of the first member].

36. "The pupil is preceded by the teacher" (6.2.36). That [compound] is so called whose subordinate member (*upasarjana*) is the teacher (*ācārya*), who is the principal (*pradhāna*). An "antevāsī" is one who dwells near (*ante vasati*).
This designation is figurative (*gauṇa*). It refers to those which are the constituent members of a *dvandva* compound.

These [words] denote the pupil with the teacher as a subordinate element. Therefore, because they denote the pupil, the referent is expressed by means of the two words "teacher" and "pupil" through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) as having the teacher as a subordinate element.
Even a part of that [compound] is called "the pupil with the teacher as a subordinate element," according to the property of being a part of a *dvandva* compound.

"The teacher is Āpiśali"—[this is derived] by [the rule] *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95). Or, "the students themselves are the Āpiśalas"—[this is derived] by the suffix *aṇ* as before. Regarding the phrase "in both ways" and so forth: even when derived in either of the two manners, the student remains subordinate (*upasarjana*) to the teacher. For instance—*ubhayatara*.

It is the disciples alone who are the primary subjects referred to in this way; the teacher, however, being a qualifier of them, is subordinate. The word *āpiśala* is oxytone because it ends in the suffix *aṇ*. [The name] *pāṇinīya* is derived from the sense "proclaimed by Pāṇini" according to the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.114).

By the rule *tad adhīte* (Pāṇini 4.2.59), the suffix *aṇ* is applied, which is then elided (*luk*). Thus, the word *pāṇinīya* has its middle syllable accented (*madhyodātta*) by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
Regarding the phrase *pāṇinīyarauḍhaiyāḥ*: *rauḍhi* is the descendant of *roḍha*, formed by the suffix *iñ* according to *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95).

In the case of *rauḍherācāryasya chātrāḥ*, when the suffix *aṇ* would have been applicable by *ṭhiñaśca* (Pāṇini 4.2.112), the prohibition *ṭhna dvyacaḥ* (4.2.113) is applied, and then *vṛddhāccchaḥ* (4.2.114) applies. Alternatively, *rauhiyam* is that which was taught by Rauḍhi; from that, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by *tadadhīte* (4.2.59).

As before, there is elision of the suffix *aṇ*: *rauḍhāyāḥ*. The word *rauḍhāya* is also middle-accented (*madhyodātta*) as before. [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "proclaimed by Kāśakṛtsna," and those who study that [work] are called *kāśakṛtsnāḥ*; as before, there is elision of the suffix *aṇ*.

Regarding the expression "ṭhchāndasavaiyākaraṇāḥ," this is a *dvandva* compound of pupils (*antevāsinaḥ*), but it is not one where the teacher (*ācārya*) is subordinate. For here, only the pupils are denoted by the terms *chāndasa* and *vaiyākaraṇa*, and they do not have the teacher as a subordinate element.

Those who study the *Chandas* are called *Chāndasas*; those who study grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) are called *Vaiyākaraṇas*. In that regard, they are the pupils (*antevāsinaḥ*) of whichever teacher from whom they study.
Regarding the phrase "in the treatises of Āpiśali and Pāṇini": that which was proclaimed by Āpiśali is the *Āpiśala*; that which was proclaimed by Pāṇini is the *Pāṇinīya*.

Regarding *pāṇinīyam*: in that treatise where [the rule] is stated as primary, the Teacher (*ācārya*) is the principal entity because the suffix is prescribed there; he is so because he qualifies that [treatise]. His status as a teacher here depends upon the teaching (*śāstra*). For the status of being a teacher does not depend solely on a pupil (*antevāsī*), but rather—
There is also dependence on scripture.

37. *kārtakaujapādayaśca* (6.2.37). [The commentary states: "These two end in the suffix *ṭhañ*. The meaning is that, by virtue of the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), they are oxytone (*antodātta*).
It should be understood that in subsequent cases as well, those ending in *aṇ* possess this same oxytone quality.

Regarding "sauvarṇiriñantaḥ" [the Kāśikā reads "sāvarṇiḥ"], the intention is that it is acutely accented on the first syllable by virtue of the *ñit* accent. In the same way, it should be understood that subsequent forms ending in *iñ* are also acutely accented on the first syllable.
