The word *māṇḍūakeya* ends in the suffix *ḍhak*, according to the rule "ḍhak ca maṇḍūakāt" (Pāṇini 4.1.119).
Regarding the passage beginning with *ṭhavanteḥ*: since there are many descendants (*apatyāni*) of Avanti, the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied according to *vṛddhet kośalājādāñ ñyaṅ* (Pāṇini 4.1.171).
By the rule *tadrājasya* (Pāṇini 2.4.62), this suffix is elided (*luk*). Thus, [the word] refers to the country that is the residence of the people of Avanti.

The suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *tasya nivāsaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.69). For this [suffix], *lup* is applied by the rule *janapade lup* (Pāṇini 4.2.81), as in "the Avantyas" and likewise "the Aśmakas. Just as [the form] "Avantyas" is formed, so too is "Aśmakas" formed here; in these cases, there are both words denoting Kṣatriyas and words denoting the country (*janapada*).

Regarding words: when a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) denoting descendants occurs in the plural, the suffix ending in that word is elided (*lup*) when the meaning refers to their place of residence, according to the rule for the fourfold meanings (*cāturarthika*). This same principle applies here in the case of *aśmakāḥ* as well. Only this much is extended [by analogy]: "the many descendants of Aśmaka," [formed with the suffix] *sālvāvayava*.

By [the rule] *ityādineñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.173), the suffix *iñ* is applied; its elision (*luk*) is as before. For their dwelling place, the suffix *aṇ* is applied, and its elision (*lup*) is likewise as before. Some say that the word *Avanti* is oxytone because it belongs to the *ghṛtādi* group;
others say it is due to the accent of the *cit* suffix, for they cite the rule *bhuvo jhic* (Pāṇini 3.2.178).
They explain that because of the word "bahula" (diversity), the suffix *jhic* also occurs after the root *ava*.
The phrase "this is a *yuvan*-dvandva" means that this is a *dvandva* compound of two suffixes ending in those designated as *yuvan*.
Regarding "phailaḥ," the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "pīlāyā vā" (Pāṇini 4.1.118). [The term] "śyāvarṇaśabdaḥ... [is used].

Regarding "bidādi": because of that [list], when there is no intention to express the feminine gender (*apatyavivakṣā*), the suffix *añ* occurs, resulting in *bhavāḥ*. Regarding "strī": [the form] *śārṅgaravī* is derived by the rule "ṅīn for *añ* after *śārṅgarava* etc. (Pāṇini 4.1.73). Regarding *śyāparṇeyaḥ*: [it is derived] by the rule "ḍhak for feminine stems" (Pāṇini 4.1.120). Regarding "the plural number is not intended": this is because it is not intended to be expressed. Regarding "tena": [this refers to the aforementioned reason].
By the words "ityādinā" (and so forth), he demonstrates the result of not intending the plural number [to be significant].
"The word *kapi* is udātta on the final syllable"—this is by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). "By that," etc.:
because this word *kapi* ends in a *luk* elision, the plural number is indeed resorted to here. "By *ṛṣyaṇ*"—[the suffix *aṇ* is applied after *ṛṣi*].

By the rule *ṭhṛṣyandhaka-* (4.1.114), etc.; by the rule *yūni ya iñ* [referring to 4.1.93]; and by the rule *ata iñ* (4.1.95). Regarding *pāñcālī*: the suffix *añ* is applied by the rule *janapadaśabdāt kṣatriyādañ* (4.1.168); from that [base ending in *añ*], the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied as before. [The form] *pāñcāleyī* [is derived similarly].

[Pāñcāleyaḥ: From *Kāśika*, as before, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied. The same applies in the case of *Vārcalī*. Regarding *Śākalyaḥ*: by virtue of belonging to the *Garga*-class (Pāṇini 4.1.105), the suffix *yañ* is applied. The word *Śākalya* has its first syllable accented acute (*udātta*) due to the *ñit*-accent (Pāṇini 6.1.197).

Regarding "ṭhśaṇakabābhravāḥ": [the word] *śaṇaka* is derived from the root *śaṇ* (meaning "to make sound") in the sense of "one who makes a sound" (*śaṇaṃ karoti*), using the suffix *ka* by the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3). Thus, by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), the word *śaṇaka* is oxytone (*antodātta*). Regarding *bābhrava*: [it is formed] by the rule *orguṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.146).
Regarding "ṭhārcābhinnaḥ": the suffix *ṇini* is applied in the sense of "proclaimed" (*prokta*), from which the suffix *aṇ* is added for the one who studies it;

this [suffix *aṇ*] is then elided by the rule "proktālluk" (Pāṇini 4.2.64). In the same way, in subsequent cases as well, the elision of the suffix denoting the student (*adhyetṛ*) after a suffix denoting what was proclaimed (*prokta*) should be understood. [Thus: *mudgalaḥ*.
"Kaṇvādiḥ" refers to the subgroup beginning with Garga. Regarding "tadapatyasya" (of his descendant), as in "maudgalāḥ":

from the word *maudgalya*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "kaṇvādibhyo gotre" (Pāṇini 4.2.111), and the vowel *a* is elided by "yasyeti ca" (6.4.148). Then, [the final *ya*] is elided by "āpatyasya ca taddhite 'nāti" (6.4.151).

Regarding the letter *ya*: the word *ārcābhi* is oxytone due to the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). [Examples include] "kunte surāṣṭrasya" and so forth. From the root *kam* (meaning "desire," DhP 4.43), the suffix *ktic* is applied as before; by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bahulavacanāt*), the change to *u* occurs. Thus, *kunti* means "beautiful."
He whose kingdom is [there] is *surāṣṭraḥ*. The descendants of Kunti are many;

[the suffix] *añ* is applied by the rule *vṛddhet-kośalājād-añ-ñyaṅ* (Pāṇini 4.1.171). The descendants of Surāṣṭra are many; [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied by the rule *janapada-śabdād-in-āñ-aṇ-au* (Pāṇini 4.1.168). Of those two, [the elision of the patronymic suffix is governed by] *tadrājasya* (Pāṇini 2.4.62).

By such means, there is elision (*luk*) in many instances. Then, [the form] *kuntīnām nivāsaḥ* ("the inhabited country of the Kuntīs") takes the suffix *aṇ* in the four senses according to Pāṇini 4.2.69, *tasya nivāsaḥ*; subsequently, this suffix is elided by 4.2.81, *tasya janapade lup*.
Thus, *kuntayaś ca surāṣṭrāś ca* becomes *kuntisurāṣṭrāḥ*. In the same way...

Regarding the many offspring of Kunti and Surāṣṭra in their respective inhabited territories (*janapada*), this dual form arises. The word *kunti* is oxytone due to the *citsvara* accent; thus it is stated: "The *cinti-surāṣṭrāḥ*.
The word *cinti* is likewise oxytone; that too [is derived] from the root *cit* in the sense of "accumulation" (*samṛddhi*).

[The word *Avantī*] is derived from the root [√av] (DhP 1535). It ends in the suffix *ktic*. Some derive the words *Avantī* and *Kuntī* as ending in the suffix *ktic*, according to the rule "In the case of a name, the suffixes *ktic* and *kta* [are used]" (Pāṇini 3.3.174).

Regarding the phrase "ending in the *pacādyac* suffix": from the root *haḍi* (meaning "joy," Dhātupāṭha 280), both in its simple form and preceded by the prefix *ava*, the *pacādyac* suffix is applied. According to the rule "Bhāguri [allows] the elision of the vowel of the prefix *ava* and of *api*," there is the elision of the vowel *a* of the prefix *ava*.

"The elision (*luk*) of *ṭhyañ* is performed," according to *ṭhyañañośca* (Pāṇini 2.4.64). Regarding "avimatakāmaviddhā": from the root *mad* meaning "joy" (Dhātupāṭha 1208), preceded by the prefix *vi*, the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is formed as *vimata*; thus, "not *vimata*" is *avimata*. [This occurs] in a *tatpuruṣa* compound.

When the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) of the first member is applied by the rule *tulyārtha* (Pāṇini 6.2.2), the word becomes acutely accented on the first syllable due to the accent of the negative particle *nañ*. Regarding the term *bahvacaḥ*:
by this partial citation of a sūtra, he indicates the full rule *bahvaca iñaḥ prācāṃ bharateṣu* (Pāṇini 2.4.66). [The example is] *śālaṅki*.
"And *śalaṅka*. This is read among the *naḍa*-class [of suffixes]. Its meaning is this: the word *śalaṅku* produces the suffix *phak* and undergoes the substitution of *śalaṅka*.
"The Bābhravas and Dānacyutas. *Bābhrava* is the descendant of Babhru; it ends in the suffix *aṇ*.

In *dānacyutaśabdādiño bahvaco luk*, the elision (*luk*) is as previously explained. Regarding *kaṭhakālapāḥ*: the word *kaṭha* is oxytone because it is derived from the root *kaṭh* with the suffix *ac* (according to Pāṇini 3.1.134). *Laukākṣi* is the descendant of Lokākṣa; his pupils are *laukākṣāḥ*. Regarding *strīkumāram*.

From the root *satya-ayati*, by [Pāṇini 3.2.165] *satyāyater ḍraṭ*, the suffix *ḍraṭ* is applied; from that form ending in *ḍraṭ*, by [Pāṇini 4.1.15] *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added.

Therein, by the accentuation of *pratyaya* (the suffix), the final vowel *ā* is udātta; its elision occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.148] *yasyeti ca*. Then, by [Pāṇini 6.1.161] *anudātasya ca yatro dātalopaḥ*, the *ṅīp* is also elided.
When the acute accent (*udātta*) has been applied, the word *strī* is indeed acute.

From this [comes] "their students are the Mīdas"; by the rule *iñaśca* (Pāṇini 4.2.112), the suffix *aṇ* is added. Likewise, "the Paippalādas": Pippalādi is the descendant of Pippalāda; his students [are the Paippalādas].
The Paippalādas read "vatsajarat". [In this compound,] from the root *vad*, the suffix *sa* is applied according to *vṛtṛvadihanikamikaṣibhyaḥ saḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 9.21).
By this rule, the word *vatsa* has its final syllable udātta. From the root *jṛ*, the suffix *atṛn* is applied according to *jīryateratṛn* (Pāṇini 3.2.104), resulting in *jarat*.

The copulative compound (*dvandva*) of those two is "sauśrutapārthavāḥ. "Sauśrutāḥ" means the students of Suśruta; "pārthavāḥ" means the students of Pṛthu. In both cases, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.120] *tasyedam*. "Jarāmṛtyu" [is derived] from the root *jṛṣ* by [Pāṇini 3.3.104] *ṣidbhidādibhyo’ṅ*.

By [Pāṇini 3.3.104], the suffix *aṅ* is applied; thus, *jarā*. By virtue of the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), it has an udātta on the final syllable. From the root *mṛ*, by [Dhātupāṭha 1.135] "from *bhṛj*, *ḍimṛṅ*, and *mṛṅ*, the suffix *tyuk* is added," we have *mṛtyuḥ*.
38. The word *mahat* [takes the suffix *aṇ*] before *vrīhi*, *aparāhṇa*, *gṛṣṭi*, *iṣvāsa*, *jābāla*, *bhāra*, *bhārata*, *hailihila*, *raurava*, and *pravṛddha*.

"The word *mahat* has its udātta accent on the final syllable. This is because it is listed as having the udātta on the final syllable among the *uṇādi* derivatives in the rule "In the sense of existing, [the words] *pṛṣat*, *bṛhat*, *mahat*" (Uṇādisūtra 6.5). Now, why does this [rule] not apply here in the case of *mahato vrīhiḥ* > *mahad-vrīhiḥ*? To this he says: "Of that," and so forth. And this...

This is obtained by the technical rule *lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā* (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 3). Now, for what purpose is the word *pravṛddha* recited here, since it ends in a *niṣṭhā* suffix; for in that case, the desired result would already be established by the rule to be stated later, *karmadhāraye 'niṣṭhā* (Pāṇini 6.2.46)? To this [it is replied]:

He says: "In a *karmadhāraya*, [the rule] 'not with a past passive participle' (*aniṣṭhā*), etc. For indeed, by that very technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), this compound is formed by the word-form specified in the sūtra "śreṇyādayaḥ kṛtādibhiḥ" (Pāṇini 2.1.59). In that regard, by the rule "in a *karmadhāraya*, not with a past passive participle" (6.2.46), there is a prohibition of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). And it is not...

The term *mahāpravṛddha* is a *karmadhāraya* compound formed with a word ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix as explicitly prescribed by the rule. In that regard, if the word *pravṛddha* were not recited here, the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) would not occur before the subsequent member.
Therefore, its recitation is made here. Furthermore, this rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of compounds.

39. *kṣullaka* in the sense of "one who belongs to the Vaiśvadeva" (Pāṇini 6.2.39). [The derivation is as follows: "He takes away hunger (*kṣudh*) is *kṣulla*. The suffix *ka* is applied by the rule "after a verbal root ending in *ā*, when no upasarga precedes, the suffix *ka* is used" (3.2.3). The substitution of the homogeneous following sound (*parasavarṇa*) occurs by the rule "for *t* before *l*" (8.4.60).
40. *uṣṭraḥ* [is formed] from the roots *uṣ* and *vah*.

(Pāṇini 6.2.40). While the suffix *ṣṭran* is being carried over from the rule *sarvadhātubhyaḥ ṣṭran* (Pañcapādī Uṇādi Sūtra 4.158), [the rule] *uṣikhanibhyāṃ kit* (Pañcapādī Uṇādi Sūtra 4.161) applies.
Because it has already been explained.

41. *gauḥ sādasādisārathiṣu* (Pāṇini 6.2.41). By the supplementary rule *ṭhgoḥ sādaḥ*, the word *gosādaḥ* is shown to be a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Furthermore, according to the Vārttika in the Kāśikā, it is explained as *gāṃ sādayati* ("he causes the cow to sit").

By this also, it is established that [the root] has the sense of "falling apart" (*viśaraṇa*); because the root *sū* has the meaning of "falling apart," when the word *go* is used as an object (*karma*) in composition, the form *gosāda* arises. This is because the word *go* ends in the suffix *ḍo*, according to the rule *gameḍoḥ* (Daiva Uṇādi Sūtra 2.11).
It is accented with the udātta on the final syllable by virtue of its being a pratyaya-svara.

42. [The suffix *cha* is applied after] *kurugārhapata*, *riktaguru*, *asūta*, *jaratī*, *aślīla*, *dṛḍharūpa*, *pārevaḍava*, *taitilakadrū*, and *paṇyakambala*, as well as after words denoting the loads of female slaves (*dāsībhāra*).
(Pāṇini 5.1.20) In this rule, all the items beginning with *kurugārhapata* and ending with *paṇyakambala* are compound words (*samāsa*). Among them:

*kurugārhapata* and *riṣataguru*—these two are without case endings (*avibhaktika*). The others, however, such as *asūta*, *jaratī*, and so forth, end in the nominative singular. That nominative should be understood as standing in the place of the genitive by way of a substitution of case endings (*sub-adhyaya*). [This is indicated] by the rule "dāsībhārāṇām."
The plural number is for the purpose of indicating the class [of words]. For this very reason, he says: "and of *dāsabhāra* and so forth.

[He states] that "the word *kuru* ends in the suffix *ku*," because, under the heading "ku" from the rule *kurbhraśca* (Daiva 1.107), the rule *kṛgrorucac* (Daiva 1.109) prescribes it as ending in the suffix *ku*.
Because it has already been explained:

"It should be stated that in the case of *kuru* and *vṛji*, when *gārhapata* follows, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) of the words *kuru* and *vṛji* when *gārhapata* is the subsequent member.
Thus, in the case of the words *kuru* and *vṛji*, there is the preservation of the original form when *gārhapata* is the subsequent member.

The meaning is that this form of the word *bhavati* must be explained; in this regard, the explanation is as follows: first, the form of the word *kuru* will be established by the very rule *kurugārhapata* (Pāṇini 6.2.42). As for the word *vṛji*, it is also...
Because the particle *ca* here has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. [The word] *vṛji* is acutely accented on the first syllable;
this is because it is derived by the rule *vṛjerin* [Uṇādi Sūtra 359], which is explained as *igupadhāt kicca* [Uṇādi Sūtra 1.48].

Regarding the phrase "ṭhriktaguruḥ," [the author] demonstrates that the word *riktaguru* is a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇasamāsa*). Similarly, by the example "ṭhasūtā jaratī," he shows that this same applies to the compound *asūtajaratī*. By the example "ṭhaślaulā dṛḍharūpā," he shows that it applies to the compound *aślīladṛḍharūpa*. Furthermore, the word *asūtā* (not born) is also [to be understood as such].

The first syllable is udātta due to the accent of the negative particle *nañ*. The word *aślīla* is formed in the same way: "not *ślīla*" (*aślīla*). [This is justified] because *sidhma* and so forth belong to the *ākṛtigaṇa*, and thus the suffix *lac* is applied according to the rule *sidhmāderākṛtigaṇatvāl lac* (Pāṇini 5.2.97), which is derived from the rule *prāṇisthādāto lajanyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.2.96).

"Because of its occurrence after *lajita*, and because of the substitution of *la* due to belonging to the *kapilaka*-group. This is because, in the rule *kṛpo ro laḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.18), there is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the substitution of *la* via the Vārttika: *kapilakādīnāṃ copasaṃkhyānam* (Vārttika 915). But how is it known that [the word] *śrī* exists?

Why is it called by the word *aślīla* (indecorous)? To this he says: "of indecorous and firm form," and so forth. The meaning of the word *aślīla* is established as that which is not *ślīla* (decorous). In that context, if the word *ślīla* did not have the meaning "one who possesses beauty" (*śrī*), then [the term] *aślīladṛḍharūpā* would not be applicable here.

It should not be said that it is devoid of beauty (*niḥśrīka*), yet it is so described; therefore, it is understood that the word *ślīla* refers to an object possessing beauty. [The phrase] "beautiful by its mere configuration" (*saṃsthānamātreṇa śobhanā*) is used because of the firmness of the configuration; and because it is devoid of beauty, it is called "beautiful by its mere configuration. The word "mere" (*mātra*) [indicates this].
The word *śrīmatāyāḥ* is an exclusionary term (*vyavacchedaka*). By the phrase "devoid of loveliness" (*lāvaṇyarahitā*), he clarifies the meaning of "bereft of beauty" (*niḥśrīkā*).
[Regarding the compound] "pāre vaḍavā iva pārevaḍavā": by what [rule] is the compound here formed? It is not in the sense of *iva*.
There is a certain characteristic of a compound; nevertheless, how could it be a compound?
Even so, why does the elision of the case-ending not occur by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.71)? To this he says: "Precisely because of its being a *nipātana*," and so forth.

By the rule "the offspring of Titilin," he shows here the derivation of a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) from the word *titiliñ* in the sense of offspring. Or, as stated in the *Kāśikā*: "The student is *taitila*. This refers to *titilana*. By this [rule] as well, [the suffix is applied] in the sense of "belonging to him" (*tasyedam*).
In this sense, the form is *taitilāḥ*. As before, there is the elision of the suffix *ṭi* by means of an *upasaṃkhyāna* (supplementary rule).

[The statement] "because it ends in *yat*" refers to the fact that it is a *nipātana* (irregular formation) of a stem ending in *yat* according to Pāṇini 3.1.101 (*avadyapaṇya*). [The statement] "acute-accented on the first syllable" is due to the rule 6.1.213 (*yato ’nāvaḥ*).

Regarding the statement "it should be stated that *paṇyakambalaḥ* [is so] when it is a name" (the printed reading is "it should be stated when it is a name"), the meaning is that this rule must be explained as having the sense that the word *paṇyakambalaḥ* retains the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) when it is a name.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: from the rule *pūgeṣv anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.2.28), the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is carried over by the principle of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*); furthermore, that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Thus, the word *paṇyakambala* is used [with the long vowel] only when it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*).

The original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member applies here, and not elsewhere; for it is said that "elsewhere, there is simply the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound. Now, one might object: this word *paṇya* ends in a *kṛtya* suffix, and by the rule *tatpuruṣe* (Pāṇini 6.2.2) and others, in such a case where it is something to be bartered (*paṇitavya*), the first member [should have its own accent].
It must be that [the compound] is inherently svarita; so how can there be an udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound?

To this he says: "For when [the compound] is explicitly stated," and so forth. Regarding the *kṛtya* compound which is explicitly stated by the rule "A word denoting a gerundive (*kṛtya*), when not a genus-name, forms a compound with a word ending in a case-affix" (Pāṇini 2.1.68), in that case [the rule] "The second member [is udātta] after a *kṛtya*" (6.2.2) applies.
The preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) of the first member has been prescribed. However, this is not a compound formed by a specific rule (*pratipadokta*);

rather, it is prescribed generally by the rule *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.57). Why is this so? Because the word *kambala* is a generic term (*jātiśabda*). This is [established] by the rule *dvitīyā-kṛtyā*.

By means of a portion of the *sūtra*, he indicates the rule beginning with "in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, when the meaning is 'equal'" (*tatpuruṣe tulyārtha*). [The example is] "the load of a female slave" (*dāsībhāraḥ*). The word *dāsī* has the accent mentioned previously. [The example is] "invocation of the gods" (*devahūtiḥ*); because it ends in the suffix *ac* added after the root *hve* (of the *pacādi* class), it is oxytone. [The example is] "the word *oṣa*"; because it ends in the suffix *ghañ*. [The root is] *uṣa* in the sense of "burning."

Because this [word] is derived with the suffix *ghañ*, [it is formed]. According to [the rule] "In the sense of 'moon,' after the root *māṅ*, the suffix *asi* is added as *ḍit*" (*candre mo ḍit*; cf. *da.u.* 9.88;
the reading printed in the Kāśikā is *candre mo'siḥ*), this word ends in the suffix *asi*. And in the sense of "pair" (*mithuna*), it is formed with *asi* as before.

Because the suffix *as* is understood from the rule "sarvam" (Daiva 9.82); and because the word *candra*, ending in the suffix *rak*, is derived by the rule "sphāyitañci" (Daiva 8.31), which prescribes the suffix *rak*. That [word] occurs in the *dāsībhāra* group and so forth.
"It should be seen," [it is said], because the group beginning with *dāsībhāra* is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class).

43. *caturthī tadarthe* (Pāṇini 6.2.43). Regarding the term *tadarthe*: "for that purpose" (*tasmai idam*), [referring to] a word ending in the dative case; the meaning is "that which has that as its purpose. But how is the word *yūpa* (sacrificial post) udātta on its first syllable? To this he says: *kusuyubhyāñca*.

And so forth. While the suffix *pa* is being carried over from the rule "from *pāni* and *viṣi*, *pa*" (Daiva-Uṇādi 7.2), the word *yūpa* is derived by the rule "also from *ku* and *yu*" (Daiva-Uṇādi 7.5)—where the printed reading is *kuyubhyāñca*. In that context, [the rule] "after *su* and *śṛ*, with the augment *nic*" applies.
Because of this, the term *nid* continues [from the previous rule]; therefore, [the suffix] is udātta on the first syllable.

As for the lengthening of the vowel, it occurs because the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) from the rule "for *stu*, there is lengthening and [the suffix is *nid*]" (*paṃ.u. 3.25*) is understood to carry over. Regarding the phrase "ending in the suffix *kalap*," [it refers to the fact that the suffix is] *cit* after roots such as *vṛṣ*.
In this context [of Daiva 8.109], because the suffix *kala* is understood from the previous rule "ṭhkalastṛpaśaca" (Daiva 8.107);
and [the statement] "the word *ratha* has its first syllable udātta" is understood from the rule "hanikuṣinīramikāśibhyaḥ kthan" (Daiva 8.107).
Because of the recurrence of the suffix *kal*. [The rule] "the word *ratha* has its first syllable acute" follows from the recurrence of the suffix *kal* from [Uṇādisūtra 8.107]:
"The suffix *kthan* is applied after the roots *han*, *kuṣ*, *nī*, *ram*, and *kāś*. Thus: "the word *ratha* has its first syllable acute."

Because it ends with the suffix *kthan* according to the rule *ṭhāñ-kuṣi-nī-rami-kāśibhyaḥ kthan* (Uṇādisūtra 6.27); and as for the word *vallī*, it is stated that "it is oxytone due to the accent of the suffix *ṅīṣ*.
However, the suffix *ṅīṣ* should be understood [as applied] by virtue of its belonging to the *gaurādi* group (Pāṇini 4.1.41).

Regarding the phrase "in the case of the relationship between the original material and its modification" (*prakṛtivikārabhāve*), etc.: how, then, is this understood to apply specifically to the relationship between the original material and its modification when it is stated in general terms? It is because the option (*anyatarasyām*) from the preceding rule continues to apply;
and because that option is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), as indicated by the forthcoming evidence.
44. *arthe* (Pāṇini 6.2.44):

"The words *mātṛ* and *pitṛ* have the udātta accent on the final syllable," because they are prescribed as being formed with the suffix *tṛc* in rules such as *naptṛ-neṣṭṛ-tvaṣṭṛ-kṣattṛ-hotṛ-potṛ-bhrātṛ-jāmātṛ-mātṛ-pitṛ-duhitṛ* (Daiva Upajīvyaka 2.3). [In the case of *mātṛ-pitṛ-artha*], it has the udātta accent on the middle syllable by virtue of the *li*-accent.

Thus [it is said]. Because it ends with the suffix *tal* by the rule "from a deity, *tal*" (5.4.27). But for what purpose is this [stated], since it would already be established by the rule "the fourth case [is used] in the sense of 'for that'" (6.2.43)?
For even the word *artha* becomes a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) precisely in the sense of "for that. To this he says: "The specific types of things for its sake... (*tadarthaviśeṣāḥ*).

"Thus," and so forth. He thinks as follows: even the word *artha* (object/purpose) denotes a specific [instance] within its class (*vṛtti*). And this is logical. For when "for the sake of a measure" (*mātrārtham*) is said, one understands a specific object—a distinct entity—that is excluded from things such as a "measure" (*mātra*) itself. [As in the example: "a horse-stall" (*aśvadhāsaḥ*).
By these and other such statements, he demonstrates the purpose of the indicator (jñāpaka).
45. *kte ca* (Pāṇini 6.2.45).

[The word] *aśva* is acute-accented on the first syllable because it ends in the suffix *kvan*. [The word] *manuṣya* is circumflex-accented on the final syllable because [it is derived from] *manu* with the suffixes *añ* and *yat*, and the augment *ṣuk*.
Because it ends with the suffix *yat* according to [Pāṇini 4.1.161], [the rule] states: "The remainder has the udātta accent on the final syllable.
Now, that [remainder] consists of the word *go* and the word *tāpasa*. Among these, the word *go* ends with the suffix *ḍo*, according to [Uṇādi-sūtra 2.11]:
*gamer ḍoḥ*. Thus, because it ends with the suffix *ḍo*, it is the word *go*.

It is accented on the final syllable by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). The word *tāpasa* ends in the suffix *aṇ*, for it is derived by the rule "from *tapas* and *sahasra*, [the suffixes] *vinīn* and *aṇ*" (Pāṇini 5.2.102–103). Now, how can *gorakṣitam* be an example of this?

As for the statement "gobhyo rakṣitam" (protected from cows), the dative case is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthya*); for in that case, there ought to be a connection with a subsequent word. To this he says: "gobhyo rakṣitam," etc.
For here the intended meaning is not "protected for the sake of the cows"; what then? It means "protected from the cows."

The word "is given" (*dīyate*) must be supplied here. Therefore, this fourth case ending (*caturthī*) is used in the sense of the recipient (*sampradāna*); how, then, could it express the sense of "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*)?

46. *aniṣṭhā* in a *karmadhāraya* compound. (Pāṇini 6.2.46) Examples include *śreṇikṛtāḥ* and so forth. The compound is formed by the rule *śreṇyādayaḥ kṛtādibhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.59). It is stated that "the word *śreṇi* has its first syllable acute (*ādyudātta*). This is due to the accent of the *nit* suffix; for [the suffix] *ni* is prescribed after the roots *vīj*, *yaj*, and *jvar*.

Thus, while the term *ni* is understood from the preceding rule (Daiva 1.18), it is derived by the rule "from *vah*, *śri*, *śru*, *yud*, *rud*, *glā*, *hā*, *at*, and *ari*, with the suffix *ni*" (Daiva 1.21); therefore, it is udātta on its first syllable. Consequently, the word *pūga* is said to be udātta on its final syllable.

By virtue of the word "bahula" (in the rule *mudi-gror-gagau*, Daiva-nighaṇṭu 3.66), the suffix *gak* is also applied after the root *pū*. Consequently, it is udātta on the final syllable due to the accent of the suffix.
Regarding the term *kṛtākṛtam*: it is both *kṛtam* (done) and *akṛtam* (not done), [forming a compound] with a *kta*-suffix.

The compound is formed according to Pāṇini 2.1.60, *nañ-viśiṣṭenā-nañ*, [meaning "with that which is qualified by the negative particle *nañ*"]. Because one part has been performed, it is "done" (*kṛta*); because at that very same time another part has not been performed, it is "not done" (*akṛta*).

47. *ahīne dvitīyā* (Pāṇini 2.1.47). *Hīna* means abandoned; *ahīna* is that which is not abandoned. [The word] *kaṣṭa* is cited as being udātta on the final syllable, because it ends in the *kta* suffix, by virtue of the accent of the suffix. [This is according to] Pāṇini 7.2.22: *kṛcchragahanayoḥ kaṣa*.

Thus, there is a prohibition of the *iṭ* augment. [The word] "bahuvrīhisvareṇādyaudātaḥ" [means]: for the word *tri-* is oxytone by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). In that case, when the original accent (*prakṛti-svara*) is applied according to Pāṇini 6.2.1, "in a bahuvrīhi, [the first member retains its] original [accent]," the word *triśakala-* becomes acutely accented on the first syllable by the accent of the bahuvrīhi compound.

The word *grāma* is also acutely accented on the first syllable (*ādyaudātta*). For it is derived as follows: while the suffix *man* is being carried over from the rule "ṛstistusuhusṛdhukṣi" (Daiva 7.26), it is formed with the *man* suffix by the subsequent rules "avateṣṭilopaśca" (Daiva 7.27) and "grasaterā ca" (Daiva 7.28).
Regarding the phrase "one who has passed beyond the wilderness" (*kāntārātītaḥ*): it means one who has gone beyond the wilderness, that is, one who has abandoned it.
In this context, the word *kāntārātīta* functions as a synonym for the word *hīna* (devoid of).

It is stated: "It should be specified that [the suffix -kta] follows a second-case form when there is no prefix. This refers to a word ending in the second case followed by a *kta*-suffix that lacks a prefix (*anupasarga*).

The meaning is that the statement "it becomes its original accent" (prakṛtisvaraṃ bhavati) must be explained in this sense. The explanation here, however, should be made by relying on the recurrence of that very same option (*anyatarasyām*) and its status as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
48. The third [case ending] is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*).

(6.2.48) Although this is already established by the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha* (6.2.2), and since the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*) would be superseded by the accent of the whole compound (*kṛtsvara*) according to *thāthādisvareṇa* (6.2.144), this [sūtra] is intended to establish that [original accent].
The word is *ahihataḥ*. The compound is formed by Pāṇini 2.1.32, *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*.
It is stated that *ahi* is udātta on the final syllable when derived [from the root *han*].
This is because, while the rule *janighasibhyām iṇ* (Daiva-ukta-sūtra 1.58) is in effect, [the suffix] *ḍit ca* is added to the root *han* preceded by *āṅ*.

The word *ahi* is derived by the rule "And by the roots *ṣṭhā*, *ṅi*, *śri*, and *han*, with a short vowel" (Daiva Uṇādi Sūtra 1.66). Regarding the statement "some desire [the word] to have the udātta accent on the first syllable," they also carry forward the mention of the udātta from the rule "In the case of the root *khyā* preceded by *samāna*,
that [suffix] is udātta" (Pāṇini Uṇādi Sūtra 4.136).
"Ending in the suffix *ṭhrak*"— because it is derived as ending in the suffix *rak* by [Pāṇini’s] rule *sphāyitañci* (Dhātupāṭha 8.31), etc. "The word *mahārāja* ends in the suffix *ṭac*"—
[this is stated] because [the base *mahat*] would otherwise end in the suffix *rak* by [Pāṇini’s] rule *sphāyitañci* (Dhātupāṭha 8.31), etc.
Because it has already been explained: "The word *mahārāja* ends with the suffix *ṭac*.
This is because it ends with the suffix *ṭac*, according to the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac* (Pāṇini 5.4.91).
Regarding the example "cut by the reaper" (*dātralūnā*), the rule *dhaḥ karmaṇi ṣṭran* (Pāṇini 3.2.181) is being carried over.

The word *dātra* is derived by means of the suffix *ṣṭran* according to the rule "ṭhdāmnīśasÂ" (Pāṇini 3.2.182), and because of this, it is acutely accented on its first syllable. In all instances, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) according to the rule "ṭhtayoreva kṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.70).

49. *gatiranantaraḥ* (6.2.49). Regarding the example *prakṛtaḥ*: this is a compound formed by *kugatiprādayaḥ* (2.2.18). Since the particles beginning with *pra*, excluding *abhi*, are listed as having the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyaudāta*) in the list of *nipātana*s, the word *pra* has the acute accent on its first syllable.

Regarding the phrase "ṭhabhyudÂdhṛtaḥ," here [the rule] does not apply to the immediately preceding word *abhi*. In this case, one must first form a compound of the word *ucca* with the word ending in the *kta* suffix, and subsequently form a compound of the word *abhi* with the word *uddhṛ*. Now...

Or—since the mention of *sub* (inflected words) has been removed from the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18), a compound may occur even with multiple members. Regarding the example *samudāhṛtaḥ*: here too, [the rule] does not apply to the internal [members] of *sam-ud*. [The rule] begins with *kārakapūrvasya tiḥ* and so forth. [Example: *dūrād āgataḥ*.

In this case, when the *aṅ* [prefix] has been compounded as a *gati*, by this rule the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) applies, and thus it becomes acute (*udātta*). Then, the compound with the fifth case-ending [in *dūrād āgataḥ*] is formed according to *stokāntika-* (Pāṇini 2.1.39) and so forth; once that is formed, [the rule] *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* [applies].

While this [rule] is in effect, by the rule *ṭhthāthaghañ* (Pāṇini 6.2.144) and others, the final acute accent (*antodātta*) of the subsequent member is prescribed. Since that [accent] is prescribed when the *gati*-accent is present, by virtue of being the more authoritative (*śiṣṭatva*), that [latter] alone prevails. [As in: *pañcamyāḥ stokādibhyaḥ*.
(6.3.2) Thus ends the section on *aluk*.

Now, how is the counter-example "samudghṛtaḥ" and so forth justified, given the rule: "When a *kṛt* suffix is mentioned [in a grammatical operation], that which is preceded by a *gata*-type word (*gata-kāraka*) is also included"? (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 126).

In this context, "going" (gati) is understood by the very mention of "conclusion" (niṣṭhā). And so, [one might ask: "Is the word *sam-* present in *samuddhṛta* as well as in *samudāhṛta*? To this he says:
"By the force of the mention of 'immediate' (*anantara*). For by the mention of "immediate," the following meaning [is established].

It is stated [in the rule] "samuddhṛtam" and so forth, so that [the rule] might not apply there. For if this technical definition (paribhāṣā) were adopted here, then in cases such as "uddhṛtaḥ," since the rule "a preverb [is compounded] with what immediately follows" would already exclude [any other element], the inclusion of the word "immediately following" (anantara) would be redundant due to the absence of anything to be excluded.

"The mat is being made by Devadatta"—here, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), according to the rule "The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the beginning of an action and in the sense of the agent" (Pāṇini 3.4.71).
Thus, the suffix *kta* indeed denotes the agent.

50. *tādau ca niti kṛtyatau* (Pāṇini 6.2.50). Regarding the example *prakartum*, this is the suffix *tumun*. Regarding *prakartā*, this ends in the suffix *tṛn*; thus he refutes the suspicion that it might end in *tṛc*. The phrase "for the purpose of subverting the accent of *kṛt*" and so forth [is explained as follows].

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of indeclinables (*avyayasvara*). Since the accentuation of a *kṛt*-suffix (*kṛtsvara*), prescribed by the rule "after a *gati*, a *kāraka*, or an *upapada*, [the suffix] *kṛt* [is udātta]" (Pāṇini 6.2.139), would otherwise apply, this statement is made to set that aside. Regarding the word "prajalpākaḥ":

the suffix *ṣākan* is applied according to the rule "after the roots *jalp*, *bhikṣ*, etc. (Pāṇini 3.2.155). Regarding the phrase "ending in *tṛc*": [this refers to the formation of the word *prajalpakaḥ*].
[The author] dispels the suspicion that [the suffix] *tṛn* [is intended]. Now, what is the purpose of including the word "ni" (*nid*) in the rule?

If it is argued that it is so that forms such as *prakṛṣṭamṛṣṭamṛtikā* (excellent clay) do not occur, this is not the case; for indeed, prefixes (*prādayaḥ*) are used in relation to that [action] which is connected with the verb.

[The prefixes] receive the designations of *gati* and *upasarga*. Since this word *mṛtikā* is a noun (*nāmadheya*), it does not denote an action; therefore, it does not have the designation *upasarga* with respect to that [verb]. To this, he says: "The mention of *kṛt*," and so forth. By the term "in the case of a *kṛt* [suffix],"...

The time of connection with the technical name *kṛt* is indicated; therefore, at the very moment the name *kṛt* is applied, the meaning "that which begins with *ta*" is established. Thus, the mention of *kṛt* serves the purpose of referring to that which begins with *ta* in the original instruction (*upadeśa*), because the time of the comprehension of the name *kṛt* is identical to the time of the instruction. Therefore...

He says "here," etc., because an effort is made for the sake of that [suffix] beginning with *t* during the subsequent instruction (*punarupadeśa*). If the inclusion of that [suffix] in the subsequent instruction were not made for the sake of what begins with *t*, then [the form] *pralapitā* would not occur; for in that case, the status of beginning with *t* would be obstructed by the augment *iṭ*. And when that [subsequent instruction] exists, [the root] indeed becomes one that begins with *t* through that very subsequent instruction.
Even though it is subsequently destroyed by being struck, it nevertheless exists. [The term] ‘āgantuka’ [is derived as follows]:
the suffix *tan* is applied according to the rule ‘sitanigamimasi-’ (Dhātupāṭha 1.122).

51. *tavantū ca yugapat* | (6.2.51) "The final syllable ending in *-t* or *-ant* is acute. But how is it obtained that [the final syllable] becomes acute, since there is no mention of "acute" (*udātta*) here? For no entirely new accent is being prescribed here; what then?

By the rule *ṭhtikārakopapadatÂ kṛtÂ* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) applies, whereby the accent that would otherwise fall on the first syllable does not occur; how then can it be said that [the rule] "continues from" *prakṛtyā*? In this regard, the connection is made as follows: that which would apply to [a word] ending in a suffix other than *tavat* becomes the accent of the final syllable. That...

The term *udātta* is obtained by implication from the word *codāta* itself. The inclusion of the word *yugapat* ("simultaneously") is for the purpose of excluding successive occurrence (*paryāya*). [The form] *anvetavai* [is derived] from the root *i* preceded by *anu*, according to the rule *kṛtyārthe tavai-ken-kenyatvanaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.14).

This suffix is *pratyaya*, and it is a *guṇa*. [The forms] *paripātavai* (paripātavai—Kāśikā) and *abhicaritavai* (abhicaritavai—Kāśikā) are derived from the roots *pā* preceded by *pari* and *car* preceded by *abhi*. [The rule] "the final syllable is udātta" applies because of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
52. *aniganto'ñcatau vapratyaye* (Pāṇini 6.2.52). Regarding the phrase *v-pratyaye*: that which has the phoneme *va* as its suffix is so described. Examples include *prāṅ* and so forth.
In the word *prāṅ*, the suffix *kvin* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.59 (*ṛtvik* etc.), and that [suffix]...

It is merely the letter *va*; for the letters beginning with *ka* are *anubandhas* (indicatory markers), and they are not invariably present. [In the case of the word *suvāk*: by *ugidacām* (Pāṇini 7.1.70), the suffix *num* is added;

in the singular, by *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* (6.1.68) and *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* (8.2.23), [the final *k* is elided]; and by *kvinpratyayasya kuḥ* (8.2.62), [the *k* of the suffix *kvip* is changed to *g*].

By the rule *kuhoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.62), the *k*-sound of the nasal (*n*) becomes the *ṅ*-sound (*ṅkāraḥ*). In the dual and plural, however, by the rule *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ* (8.4.40), the *c*-sound (*ścutvam*) results in the *ñ*-sound (*ñakāraḥ*). Together with the vowel *a* of the prefix (*upasarga*), the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (6.1.101) applies. Thus, in forms such as *parāṅ*, the word *para-* is udātta on its first syllable.
Therefore, this rule—"svarito vānudāte padādau" (or as printed in the Nyāsa, Kāśikā, and Padamañjarī: "svarite vā'nudāte'padādau")—does not apply. (Pāṇini 8.2.6)
Regarding the example *praty-añc*: here, because the word *prati* ends in the vowel *i*, the status of being a *para-kṛti* (a suffix applied after another element) does not apply.
Now, one might object: "Once the *yaṇ* substitution has been made, isn't this [the resulting form] also no longer ending in *i*?

[The answer is: even when the *yaṇ* substitution has been performed, the designation "ending in *i*" still applies by virtue of the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated as the original).

[The objection is: "There will be no fault [in the case of] *bhaviṣyati* and so forth. If you argue that the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if occupying the place of the original) is prohibited in rules concerning accent (*svara*), this is not so; for it has been stated: "In rules concerning accent, lengthening (*dīrgha*), and the elision of *y*, the substitute for an elided element (*lopājādeśa*) is not *sthānivat*, whereas any other substitute is indeed *sthānivat*" (Kāśikāvṛtti 1.1.58).
In the word *ṭhudañcanaḥ*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied; here too, the natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member of the compound prevails.
Regarding the rule *ṭhcoraniganto'ñcatau* and so forth: by the mention of *coḥ*, this refers to the final acute accent (*antodātatva*) prescribed by the rule *ṭhcau* (Pāṇini 6.1.222).
The scope for *coritaya* is *dadhīcaḥ*, where there is no [substitution of] *gati*;
the scope for *anigantasavaras* is where the letters *a* and *n* of the root *añc* are not elided—such as in *parāṅ* and *parāñcāt*; here both [rules] would apply—[as in] *parācaḥ*.
In the case of *parāc* ending in a non-consonant (*aniganta*) followed by *vati*, the accentuation [of the former] prevails by way of prohibition;
the word "prohibition" (*pratiṣedha*) must be supplied there.

53. *nyadhī ca* | (Pāṇini 6.2.53) This rule is commenced for the sake of [stems] ending in an *ik* vowel. [It applies to those stems] such as *udātata-svaritayoḥ*. [The word *ni*] is *anudātta* (unaccented) according to the *Phiṭ-sūtra*: "Prepositions (*upasarga*) are unaccented, with the exception of *abhi*" (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.81). Therefore, that which [is substituted] in place of the vowel *a* of that [preposition]...

The *yaṇ*-substitute is an udātta-vowel. Therefore, by the rule "udātasvaritayoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.4) and so forth, the vowel *a* of the following *añcati* becomes svarita. However, forms such as *adhyaṅ* and others do not occur [as svarita]; this is because the substitute is udātta from the beginning, and thus the *yaṇ*-substitute is not an udātta-vowel.

54. *īṣad-anyatarasyām*. This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation rules governing compounds (*samāsa-svara*). For example, in the case of *īṣat-kaḍāraḥ* ("slightly tawny"), there is a compound according to *īṣad-a-kṛtā* (Pāṇini 2.2.7). When this *prakṛti-bhāva* (original form retention) does not occur, then...
The udātta accent of the final syllable of the compound alone occurs;
in cases such as *īṣadbheda*, the accent of the kṛt-affix (*kṛtsvara*) alone occurs—this is the sense, based on the principle of "priority" (*paratvāt*).
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), examples such as *īṣatkara* are included. [This refers to the rule] *īṣadduḥsuṣu*.
By [the rule] beginning with (3.3.126), the suffix *khal* is applied.

55. *hiraṇyaparimāṇam* [is used] in the sense of wealth (*dhana*). (Pāṇini 6.2.55) "A measure of gold" means gold that possesses a measure; however, in this context, the word-form expressing that [measure] is taken. For example: *dvisuvarṇadhanaṃ*. Here, the word *suvarṇa-*...

It denotes a specific measure of gold. The compound *dvisuvarṇaka* is formed according to Pāṇini 2.1.51 (*taddhitārtha*), meaning "that whose measure is two *suvarṇas*. Then, by Pāṇini 5.1.57 (*tadasya parimāṇam*), the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied according to 5.1.18 (*prāgvateṣṭhañ*). Subsequently, the suffix is elided by 5.1.28 (*adhyardhapūrva*) and so forth. Thereafter...
The term *dvisuvarṇa* is a *karmadhāraya* compound with the word *dhana*. It is oxytone (*antodātta*) by virtue of the accent of the compound itself.

Regarding the phrase "even in a *bahuvrīhi*" and so forth: alternatively, one may analyze it as a *bahuvrīhi*, namely, "one whose wealth consists of two *suvarṇas*. Even that [analysis] results in an option because of its posteriority [to the preceding rule], and not because of the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, [the first member retains] its original accent" (6.2.1).

Thus, this is the eternal rule. Regarding the example "prasthadhanam": this too is either a *karmadhāraya* compound or a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The word *prastha* denotes a measure (*parimāṇa*), but not of gold; what then? Of grain and the like.

Regarding the term "kāñcanadhanam": if the mention of "measure" (parimāṇa) were not made, then the word "hiraṇyam" being stated here would also apply in this case, because the word *kāñcana* denotes gold (*hiraṇya*). However, since [the rule] specifies that which denotes a measure, it does not apply even to that which denotes gold, as gold itself is not a measure.
This undesirable consequence follows; this rule is also an exception to the accentuation of a compound.

56. *prathama* [is used] in the sense of "not long since ordained" (*aciropasampatau*). (Pāṇini 6.2.56). Regarding the phrase *aciropaśleṣaḥ*: the meaning is "connection with a recent time. To demonstrate the meaning of this very term by means of a more commonly known word, he says: "novelty" (*abhinavatvam*).

"First grammarian" (*prathamavaiyākaraṇaḥ*): [this is] a compound by means of [the rule] *pūrvāpara-* (Pāṇini 2.1.58), meaning "first" and "grammarian. In that context, "grammarian-ness" (*vaiyākaraṇatvam*) consists in being a student of grammar (*vyākaraṇasyādhyetṛtvam*). By this, the student's recent connection [with the study] is understood.
By the phrase "abhinavavaiyākaraṇādinā," he shows in the example that there is a recent attainment [of proficiency].

By the words "ṭhādyo mukhyo yaḥ saḥ," he also indicates that in this counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), the word *prathama* has a different meaning and, in one view, lacks the sense of "recent attainment. This too—
This rule is an exception to the accentuation rules for compounds; the same applies to the subsequent rules as well.

57. *katarakatamau karmadhāraye* (6.2.57). The words *katara* and *katama* are derived by the rules *kiṃyatado nirdhāraṇe dvayor ekasya ḍatarac* (5.3.92) and *vā bahūnāṃ jātiparipraśne ḍatamac* (5.3.93), which respectively form the terms for "one of two" and "one of many" in the context of selection.

Therefore, those two [words] are udātta at the end by means of the *citsvara* accent. In the example "katarakaṭhaḥ," there is a *samānādhikaraṇa* compound according to the rule "katarakatamau jātiparipraśne" (Pāṇini 2.1.63).
Why, then, is the mention of *karmadhāraya* not applied here as well? To this he says: "But here," and so forth.

For regarding the words *kataraka-* and *katamaka-*, that which is a *pratipada-samāsa* (a compound formed by a specific rule) is understood precisely through the maxim *lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 1.1.2). And that [compound] is indeed a *karmadhāraya*.
Therefore, it is precisely because this compound is *pratipadokta* (stated by a specific rule) that its status as a *karmadhāraya* is established.
Therefore, the mention of a *karmadhāraya* compound for this purpose is not tenable.

58. [The suffix *cha* is applied] after the words *ārya* and *brāhmaṇa* [in the sense of "belonging to"]. (Pāṇini 6.2.58). For example: *āryabrāhmaṇaḥ*. This is a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) meaning "one who is both noble (*ārya*) and a Brahmin (*brāhmaṇa*).
It is stated that "the word *ārya* ends in the suffix *ṇyat*. This is because the suffix *ṇyat* is applied by the rule *ṛhalorṇyat* (Pāṇini 3.1.124).

Because it has been explained [by the rule] "the final syllable is svarita" (Pāṇini 6.1.173) by means of the accent of the *tit* suffix; however, in the counter-example, there is simply the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound.
59. *rājā ca* (Pāṇini 2.2.59).
[The compound] *rājabrāhmaṇaḥ* (as cited in the Kāśikā) is a compound formed as previously described.
The counter-examples are also to be understood as before. [In these cases,] the word *rāja-* [is not compounded].
Because it ends in the *kvan* suffix, it is acute-accented on the first syllable.
"The formulation of a separate rule is for the sake of what follows" means that the subsequent prescription should apply only to the word *rājan*,
and not to the word *ārya*.
60. The sixth case [ending] is retained in *pratyenasi*.
(Pāṇini 6.2.60) As in the example *rājñaḥ pratyenāḥ* ("a king's adversary"), there is no elision (*aluk*) of the case ending by virtue of the rule *ṣaṣṭhyā ākrośe* (Pāṇini 6.3.21).
61. *kte nityārthe* | (6.2.61) The word *nitya* [in this rule] refers to frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*), not to immutability (*kūṭastha*). Why is this so? Because the suffix *kta* is mentioned;
and *kta* is prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*); and a verbal root denotes action (*kriyā*). Furthermore, immutability is incompatible with action.

It is not tenable [to speak of repetition] because action is momentary (*kṣaṇika*). However, its frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*) is logical in view of its recurrence. This is a genitive compound (*dvitīyā-samāsa*) according to the rule *kālāḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.28). The use of the accusative case, however, is by the rule *kālādhvanoratyantasaṃyoge* (Pāṇini 2.3.5). Now...

Or rather, [the word *nitya*] refers to the object (*karman*) itself; for the designation "object" is applied by the rule: "Time, state, and the distance to be traversed are designated as the object when used with intransitive verbs" (Mahābhāṣya 1.4.51). Regarding the phrase "the word *nitya*," etc.:
by this, the word *nitya* is derived according to the Vārttika: "The addition of the suffix *ka* after the root *dhru* [is prescribed]" (Vārttika 434).

It ends in *tyap*. Consequently, because *tyap* is unaccented due to its being a *pit* suffix, and because *niṣ* is acutely accented, the word becomes acute on the first syllable. As for the statement—"When *sattatam* is derived with the suffix *kta* in the sense of the object (*karman*), it is acute on the final syllable by the rule *thāthādi-svara*"—this reading is incorrect. For when it is *kta* in the sense of the object, [the accent is governed] by the rule *gatiranantaraḥ*.

Since, according to the rule (Pāṇini 6.2.49), there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) of the verbal root *gam*, the word *satata* ought to be acutely accented on its first syllable. Therefore, one should understand that the faultless reading in this context is: "When [the suffix] *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*), then by virtue of Pāṇini 6.2.144, [the word] *satatam* is acutely accented on the final syllable. Likewise...

For even the word *satata* is oxytone by the rule regarding the accent of *thā-thādi* compounds (Pāṇini 6.2.144). It has been stated that when this *niṣṭhā* suffix occurs in the sense of a state (*bhāva*), the accent of a *gati* [prefix] does not apply. However, when the *kta* suffix occurs in the sense of an action (*karmaṇi*), then by the accent of a *gati*, the word *satata* becomes acutely accented on its first syllable. This is according to the rule: "The prefix *sam* is optionally [accented] before *hita* and *tata*."
By [Pāṇini 6.1.144], there is the elision of the *m* in *sama*.

In the example "muhūrtaprahasitaḥ," only the accent of the *thāthādi* group (6.2.144) applies to *prahasita*; here, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) after the root *has* when it is intransitive. This is the accent of the compound.

Since the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) is superseded by the second [rule], the accent of *thā-thādi* would then apply; therefore, this rule is formulated as a conjunction (*yoga*) beginning with "at" (*at-padādi*).

62. *grāmaḥ śilpini* (Pāṇini 6.2.62). The phrase "stated in the locative case" (*saptamīnirdiṣṭa*) is understood to follow from the previous rule. Therefore, *śilpini* is taken as a reference to the meaning [of the word], whereas *grāma* is taken as a reference to its own form (*svarūpa*).
"Grāma-nāpitaḥ": this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation rules for compounds.
The same applies to the subsequent cases as well.

63. *rājā ca praśaṃsāyām* (Pāṇini 6.2.63). [The rule begins with] *karmadhāraye* and so forth. Regarding the example *rājānāpitaḥ*: is this a *karmadhāraya* compound or a genitive *tatpuruṣa*? In that case, when it is a *karmadhāraya*, then for the word *rājan*...
The barber is [designated] by way of metaphorical application (*upacāra*). Metaphorical application, however, is based on the attribution of royal qualities;

therefore, by that very means, praise is bestowed upon the latter member of the compound. But how is it that the barber is expressed by the term *rājanāpita* through a genitive compound? To this he says: "By virtue of being worthy of a king."

"Of him," and so forth. For he, being proficient in his own craft, is fit for the king; therefore, he is called "the king's barber" (*rājñaḥ nāpitaḥ*) by means of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). In this view, the praise of the final member [of the compound] should be understood as being due to the fitness of that very person.

64. *Ādir udāttaḥ* (6.2.64). By the rule *ādiḥ*, etc., he shows the limit of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning "the beginning" (*ādi*). By the rule *udāttaḥ*, etc., he likewise shows the limit of the governing heading concerning "the acute accent" (*udātta*).
65. *saptamī-hāriṇau dharmye 'haraṇe* (Pāṇini 6.2.65).

The suffix *ṇini* is applied after *hārī* in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*). Because of its association with *saptamī*, the term *dhārī* is not understood here as a formal expression (*svarūpa-grahaṇa*). For this very reason, it is said: "The preceding word denotes one who takes (*hāri-vācin*)."
In the case of the word *dharmye* as well, there is no grasping of the word's own form (*svarūpa*), because of the prohibition [contained in the rule] *aharaṇe*.

For this very reason, he says: "in that which expresses *dharma*. Regarding the phrase *ācāraniyatam*, it means "restricted to conduct" (*ācāre niyatam*); for it does not exist elsewhere than in conduct. Alternatively, it means "fixed by conduct" (*ācāreṇa*).

"Fixed by custom" (*ācāraniyata*) means that which must necessarily be performed due to the force of custom is "fixed by custom. But how is it said that this duty fixed by custom is *dharma*? To this he says: "For *dharma* is followed," and so forth. "Followed" (*anuvṛta*) means established (*vyavasthita*). "Therefore," [he says].

"Not departing from *dharma*" means "conforming to" it. "By that" means by *dharma*. "Obtained" means "attainable. In both senses of the meaning, the suffix *yat* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.4.91 (*nau-vayo-dharma-*, etc.).
The particle *iti* and the word *hi* indicate the reason; for *dharma* is a specific kind of conduct.
It is said: that which does not deviate from that dharma, or that which is to be attained by it, is *dharmya*.

Therefore, that which is regulated by right conduct (*ācāra*) is called *dharmya*. [This is] a locative compound according to Pāṇini 2.1.44, *saṃjñāyām*. If this is so, would there not be the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending? To this [it is replied]: [The text continues: "If it were thus, the elision of the case-ending would follow. To this [it is replied]:...
He says: "And in the case of [names] denoting the cause," and so forth. In examples such as *yājñikāśvaḥ*, however, there is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

By the words "in some cases" and so on, he demonstrates—in examples such as *stūpeśāṇaḥ*—that since the behavior of the *śāṇa* (the grinding stone) and other such items is restricted, the final member of the compound denotes the property-bearer (*dharmī*).

He shows this with the words: "the horse and so forth for the sacrificial priests and others. This [phrase] "established in this practice" is connected both with the preceding [statement] and with the words "it should be given. For the sacrificial priests and others are takers;
they take possession of the horse and other such things that are to be given.
Regarding the term *stamberama*: by the rule *stambakarṇayo ramijapoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.13), the suffix *ac* is applied;

this is an *upapada-samāsa*, and by the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.3.14), there is non-elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending. Here, in the word *stamberama*, the element *stamba* is in the locative case.

But the word *rama* does not denote the substratum (*dharmin*). In the expression "the laborer’s *vardhitaka*," the laborer is the one who takes it, for he accepts the *vardhitaka*; however, the word *vardhitaka* does not denote the substratum. For nowhere is there such a fixed rule that the *vardhitaka* belongs to the laborer.

"It should be given. [The word] *vāḍava* [is derived as follows]: "This belongs to a *vaḍavā* (mare)," thus *vāḍava*. The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.3.120 (*tasyedam*). Regarding the phrase "from the pouring of seed": the *bījaniṣeka* is the impregnation of the womb. In this context, the *vāḍava* horse is the *hārī*; for he takes possession of the *haraṇa*, that which is to be given. *Haraṇa* means that which is to be given.

It is consistent with dharma. In some cases, this practice is established: "When a mare is impregnated by a horse, after the emission of the seed, suitable food and so forth must be given for the sake of nourishing its body. Therefore, the word *haraṇa* (taking) here signifies that which is consistent with dharma.

Nevertheless, because of the prohibition "not in the case of *aharaṇa*," this [suffix] does not apply. Consequently, when the accent of the whole (*kṛtsvara*) would otherwise have applied, the word ending in *lyuṭ*—namely the final member [of the compound]—becomes udātta in its final syllable by the rule "the suffix *ṭhan* expresses the sense of the abstract action or the object" (Pāṇini 6.2.150).
Now, one might object: "Since this accent is subsequent [in the order of rules], it will simply prevail; so what is the point of [mentioning] 'not in the case of *aharaṇa*'?"

To [answer] the objection regarding the prohibition, he says: "The other as well," and so forth. With the words beginning with "by that," he demonstrates the purpose of the indication. Regarding the term "vāḍavahāryam": by the rule "ṛhalorṇyat" (Pāṇini 3.1.124), the suffix *ṇyat* is applied to the root *hṛ*, resulting in *hāryam*; this, moreover, refers to that very same act of grasping. Of the submarine fire (*vāḍava*).

[The suffix] -ya is subject to elision by the rule *vāḍavahārya*. In that regard, if the prohibition of elision were not made for the sake of making known the meaning just mentioned, then—because it is subsequent—the final syllable of the second member would become circumflex (*svarita*) by the accent of a *kṛt*-suffix according to Pāṇini 6.2.139: *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt*.
But in this case, this very [rule] becomes the *hārisvara* (the accent on the first member). In examples such as *stūpeśāṇaḥ*,

where the first member ends in the locative case (*saptamyanta*), the rule *samāsasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.223) is set aside by the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-* (6.2.2), which results in the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member being applied.
As before, this is called "acute on the first syllable" (*ādyaudāta*).

Furthermore, the preceding members [of these compounds] are generally oxytone (*antodāta*); for instance, the word *stūpa* is derived from the root *ṣṭūapa* "to pile up" (DhP 1672), belonging to the *cur*-class, by adding the suffix *ac* (the *pacādi* group).
Therefore, this [term] is oxytone (*antodātta*). When one part [of the compound] is replaced together with the locative case ending, it remains oxytone, according to the rule:

"A single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for [a vowel] preceded by an udātta is udātta" (Pāṇini 6.1.102). From the root *maki* in the sense of "adornment" (Dhātupāṭha 89), [the suffix] is applied by the rule "uṇādayo bahulam" (Pāṇini 3.3.1).

Thus, by virtue of its being an *uṇādi* formation, there is the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*), and consequently, the word *makuṭa* has its first syllable acute (*ādyaudāta*). From the root *hala* in the sense of "scratching" (*vilekhane*) [DhP 837], the suffix *gha* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.3.125, *khano gha ca*; since the inclusion of the marker *ghit* indicates that the suffix *gha* occurs after other roots as well, the suffix *gha* is employed here. By means of this—

The word *hala* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). It is derived from the root *dṛ* in the sense of "tearing" (*vidāraṇe*) [DhP 1493] by means of the suffix *adi* according to *Uṇādisūtra* 6.42, and the form *dṛṣat* is derived by applying *Uṇādisūtra* 6.45, which states that *ṣuk* is added to the root *dṛ* and the vowel is shortened; therefore, that word (*dṛṣat*) also has its final syllable accented.

‘ṭhyājñikāśvaḥ’ and so forth are genitive (ṣaṣṭhī) compounds. In these cases, when the accent of the compound would otherwise apply, this [rule] is intended so that the first syllable of the preceding member, which denotes a horse, shall be acute (udātta).
And here, the accent which belongs to the preceding and succeeding members in their non-compounded state [is maintained].

It is not stated [as a separate rule], because once the compound has been formed, that [substitution] is included within its very application. Nor is there any possibility of its occurrence when the compound has already been formed. It is stated for the purpose of demonstrating this meaning: "Since that [substitution] would have occurred by virtue of the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of suffixal operations), this [present rule] is commenced. And for this very reason...
In the preceding case as well, it was not explained.
66. *yukte ca* (Pāṇini 6.2.66). *Yuktaḥ* means concentrated (*samāhita*), one who is intent upon a task. For example: *goballavaḥ*.
This is a name for an office; because he possesses that [office], [the suffix *aṇ*] is seen after other words as well in the section on *vaḥ* (Vārttika 580).

Thus, there is the suffix *vapra*; "gavāṃ ballavaḥ" (the cowherd of cows) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Here too, although the accent of the compound itself would have applied, the acute accent on the first syllable of the prior member is prescribed. [The example] "gomaṇindaḥ": [it is derived from] "he gives a jewel" (*maṇiṃ dadāti*), by the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3); then, by the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.3.14).
(6.3.14) Thus, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending; then, *gavāṃ maṇindā* forms a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

Since the accent of the compound itself would have applied here as well, this specific rule is established. [The example] *gosaṃkhyaḥ*: from *gāṃ sañcaṣṭe* ("he enumerates the cows"), the suffix *ka* is added by the rule *sami khyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.7); it is an upapada compound formed by the rule *gatikārakopapadāt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139).

Since the accent of the *kṛt*-suffix would apply by rule 6.2.139, this statement is made here in order to ensure that the first member of the compound bears the acute accent (*udātta*). [Objection: But surely, because it is subsequent in the sequence of rules, the accent prescribed for suffixes beginning with *tha* and *tha* (6.2.144) should apply;

therefore, how can this statement apply to cases such as *goballava*, since the accent of the *yuk* suffix (6.2.144) should prevail? [Response: It is precisely the accent of the *kṛt*-suffix that applies.
Would it not sublate [the previous rule]? If that is the case, then a prior prohibition (pūrvavipratiṣedha) must be stated;
for the word *para* signifies "desired" (*iṣṭa*).
Thus, all compounds such as *goballava* and others denote that which is joined (*yuktavācin*).

Showing this, he says: "‘Yukta’ means ‘samāhita’" and so forth. By this, he demonstrates that the form *yukta* is derived from the root *yuj* (meaning "to concentrate," Dhātupāṭha 1177) in its past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) form.

67. *vibhāṣā’dhyakṣe* (6.2.67). The word *adhyakṣa*, when occurring in a compound, expresses only that which is joined [with another]; since the preceding rule would have necessitated a compulsory acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable, this optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) is commenced. Thus, it is released from the compulsory acute accent on the first syllable.
Only the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound occurs; "gavām adhyakṣaḥ" (the overseer of cows) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

68. *pāpaṃ ca śilpini* (Pāṇini 6.2.68). In the word *pāpam*, there is a reference to the actual form (*svarūpagrahaṇa*). In the word *śilpini*, there is a reference to the meaning (*arthagrahaṇa*). For what purpose is the reference to the meaning? [One might ask: since the term *śilpi* is well-known as referring to the meaning in the example *grāmaśilpinī* due to the mention of *śilpi*, why is the reference to the meaning stated here?

Is the inclusion of the word "artha" (meaning) understood here as well? Since the accent of the compound would always apply by default, the rule prescribes that the first member of the compound optionally takes the udātta accent on its initial syllable; thus, when that option is not exercised, the accent of the compound itself remains.
Now, why does this not apply here in the case of *pāpasya nāpitaḥ* ("a barber who is wicked")? To this he says: [because] of the word *pāpa*.
"It is explicitly stated [in the rule]. Therefore, the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) does not occur.

For when a compound is explicitly stated by a rule, by the maxim "that which is taught by a specific rule takes precedence over that which is taught by a general characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa-pratipadokta-paribhāṣā*), only that [specifically taught compound] will be understood, and not any other.

69. *Gotrāntevāsimāṇavabrāhmaṇeṣu kṣepe* (Pāṇini 6.2.69). It has been stated [in the Kāśikāvṛtti on 4.2.39]: "Because the governing topic is *gotra*, when the word *gotra* is used elsewhere, the worldly *gotra* is understood. And in common usage, this is well known as referring simply to offspring; therefore, in this context [it refers to that].

The reference here is to that very [meaning], and not to the technical (pāribhāṣika) term. "Antevasin" means a student (śiṣya). In that context, by the mention of "antevasin," the meaning is understood as well-known. Therefore, here too, only the meaning is taken, not the formal word-form (svarūpa). In the case of "māṇava" and "brāhmaṇa," it is indeed the word-form itself. A "māṇava" is one who belongs to Manu; for this very reason...

The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). According to the principle that "irregular derivations also serve as exceptions" (Puṣpavṛtti 99), the form *mānava* also occurs. That which belongs to Brahmā is a *brāhmaṇa*. As for the rule: "The suffix *aṇ* is traditionally taught as the general [suffix] for *manu* when denoting a contemptible or foolish descendant" (Kāśikāvṛtti 4.1.161).

The word *māṇavaka* is being etymologically derived; and as for the word *brāhmaṇa* in the sense of "the offspring of Brahmā," both of these are already established by the inclusion of the term *gotra*. "Censure" (*kṣepa*) means reproach. [The example is] "Jaṅghāvātsya. This is a compound formed according to Pāṇini 2.1.4 (*sup supā*). But how is there censure here? To this he says: "He who..."

Regarding the passage beginning with "jaṅghādāna": *jaṅghādāna* refers to something that must be given as prescribed by custom; one who gives such a thing does so with the intention, "I am giving this. Thus, he becomes a *vātsya*. One who accepts [the gift] thinking, "I am a *vātsya*," is censured as a *jaṅghāvātsya*.
Even though he was not a descendant of Vātsya, he accepted the status of being a Vātsya with respect to the gift of his leg.

This word "Vātsya" belongs to the *gargādi* group [of gotra names]. Regarding the phrase "bhāryāsauśrutaḥ": "sauśruta" means the offspring of Suśruta, formed with the suffix *aṇ*; thus, "bhāryāsauśrutaḥ" means one for whom a Sauśruta woman is the primary wife.

The compound is formed by the rule: "In the section on compounds with a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*), there is an addition [to the list] for *śākapārthiva* and similar terms, along with the elision of the final member" (Vārttika 83). Here, the compound is formed with the word *suśruta*, which functions as a term of common substratum, in the sense of "one for whom a wife is the primary thing."
He demonstrates this by means of the example *suśrutasyāpatyam* (the offspring of Suśruta), which shows that the word *sauśruta* ends in the suffix *aṇ*.

[The rule] "after *vaśā*, *brāhmaṇa*, and *kṛta*, the suffix *ya* [is applied]" applies; by that very supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*), the compound is formed. Here too, because *vaśā* is the predominant factor, there is an exclusion of the offspring of *brahmakṛt*.
In the expression "kumārīdīkṣāḥ," there is a compound according to Pāṇini 2.1.4, "supā supā" (a case-inflected word with another case-inflected word).

The same applies to "kambalacārāyaṇīyāḥ. The term "dākṣa" refers to the treatise taught by Dakṣa; the suffix *aṇ* is applied here by Pāṇini 4.2.112, "iñaśca. Then, the suffix *aṇ* is applied again to form "dākṣam adhīyate" (one who studies that) or "tad vetti" (one who knows that). Of that [the following applies].

There is elision (*luk*) by the rule *ṭhproktālluk* (4.2.64). The word *cara* belongs to the *naḍādi* group; the descendant of *cara* is *cārāyaṇa*. That which was taught by him is *cārāyaṇīya*. [The suffix] *cha* is applied by *vṛddhāccchaḥ* (4.2.114), and then *aṇ* is applied as before by *tadadhīte* (4.2.59). That which was taught by Pāṇini is *pāṇinīya*.

Then, as before, there is the suffix *aṇ* for the agent, and its elision (*luk*); thus: "those desiring the acquisition of a *kambala*, etc. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of *odana* and so forth is intended. Here too, the compound is formed by *sup supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4). Or, by that same supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*), [the form] *kumārīlābhakāmāḥ* is also derived.
"Dākṣāḥ" means those who desire a maiden (kumārī-dākṣāḥ).
"Bhikṣāmāṇavaḥ"—the compound is formed as before; a young student (māṇava) desiring alms (bhikṣā) is a "bhikṣāmāṇava. "Dāsībrāhmaṇaḥ"—a Brāhmaṇa who desires a female slave (dāsī).

[Examples include] *dāsībrāhmaṇaḥ* ("a Brāhmaṇa who has a female slave") and likewise *vṛṣalībrāhmaṇaḥ* ("a Brāhmaṇa who has a Śūdra woman"). Because of the word "frequently" (*bahulam*) in the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32), this compound occurs even though it is not formed with a *kṛt*-suffix; or alternatively, it follows from the separation of the rule *tṛtīyā* (2.1.30) [into two distinct rules].
Regarding the term "dāsīśrotriyaḥ": this is equivalent to "dāsībrāhmaṇaḥ". This rule is an exception (apavāda) to the accentuation of compound words.
70. *Aṅgāni* [are used] in the sense of *maireya*. (Pāṇini 6.2.70) This word *aṅga* denotes a cause; that which initiates [the process] is called an *aṅga*.
The plural number (*aṅgāni*) is for the purpose of excluding a rule regarding the specific form [of the word itself]. [This applies] to everything except *surā*.

The term *madhu-maireya* is explained as follows: [the compounds] *guḍa-maireya* and *madhu-maireya* are examples. This is a non-compound (*asamāsa*). [In the analysis: "Of the *maireya* which is a derivative of molasses (*guḍa*), the molasses is a constituent part (*aṅga*)," because it is the cause of that [beverage]. This rule is also an exception (*apavāda*) to the accent of the compound.

71. *bhaktākhyāḥ tadartheṣu* (Pāṇini 6.2.71). The inclusion of the term *ākhyā* ("designation") is for the purpose of excluding a rule that would apply to the word-form itself (*svarūpavidhi*). [Objection: But surely, because of the plural number (*bahuvacana*), a rule applying to the word-form itself will not occur? [Response: This is not so; for the plural number here refers precisely to this meaning.

One might argue that plurality is intended because the word *bhakta* has multiple referents. Furthermore, since the injunction regarding the specific form [of the offering] is set aside by the plural number, those very things denoted by the word *anna* (food)—which are synonymous with the collective meaning of the compound *bhakta*—would be understood, and not terms like *bhikṣā* (alms) which denote specific types of food. However, if the term *ākhyā* (name/designation) were used...
When the literal form [of the word] is set aside by the application of the plural number, the inclusion of its specific instances is thereby accomplished.
Therefore, this [sūtra] is for that purpose. By the word *tat* (that), the meaning of the term *bhakta-ākhyāna* (the naming of food) is indicated;
examples such as *bhikṣākaṃsaḥ* ("a vessel of alms") fall under the rule *caturthī tadarthārtha-* (Pāṇini 2.1.36).

Regarding the fourth-case compounds (*caturthī-samāsa*): Now, it might be objected that the mention of "original material" (*prakṛti*) and "modification" (*vikṛti*) is enjoined there [in Pāṇini 2.1.36], and yet here there is no relationship of original material and modification. This is true; however, this very statement is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that a word in the dative case is compounded with another when it denotes merely the purpose for something, even in the case of what is called "food" (*bhakta*).

"Equal eating is 'samaśana'. From the root *aś* (meaning "to eat," Dhātupāṭha 1523)—specifically *aś* in the sense of eating—with the prefix *sam*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied to denote the abstract state (*bhāva*). Thus, it is said that "mere action" is expressed; by the word *mātra*, he excludes the notion of food (*bhakta*). Here...

Regarding the rule "the first member [of a compound] has its final syllable udātta": the word *bhikṣā* is derived from the root *bhikṣ* by adding the suffix *ap* according to Pāṇini 3.3.103 (*gurośca halaḥ*), while the word *śrāṇā* is derived from the root *śrā* (meaning "to cook," DhP 919) with the suffix *kta*. Thus, both [words]...

By the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), they would be oxytone; however, by the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, [the first member retains] its original form" (*bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā*, Pāṇini 6.2.1), they remain oxytone due to that state of original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the general accentuation of compounds (*samāsasvarāpavāda*).
72. *gobiḍālasiṃhasaindhaveṣūpamāne* (Pāṇini 6.2.72).

This word *upamāna* (standard of comparison) is connected individually with each of the words beginning with *go*; otherwise, there would be a grammatical mismatch (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between a singular form and plural forms.

Otherwise, the relationship between the qualified and the qualifier (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇabhāva*) would not be possible. Alternatively, due to a transposition of case endings (*subvyatyaya*), this singular number should be understood as standing in place of the plural. In the example *dhānyagavaḥ*, the suffix *ṭac* is added as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) by the rule *gorataddhitaluki* (Pāṇini 5.4.92). Here, since the acute accent of the *cit* suffix (*citsvara*) would otherwise apply, [the following rule is introduced].

The acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) is prescribed in cases such as *bhikṣābiḍālaḥ* (a "begging-cat") within the context of compound accentuation. The phrase "even when it has the sense of a standard of comparison" (*upamānārtho 'pi*) and so forth means that whatever sense of a standard of comparison is possible in this example, that should be applied there. And [this applies] "according to established usage" (*yathāprasiddhi*).

Whatever object of comparison is well-known in the world, that should be applied accordingly. To show therein just a mere indication of how the object of comparison is to be applied, he says: "having the form of a cow" (*gavākṛti*) means the configuration of a cow; by that, it is arranged.

That which is established and arranged in the form of a cow is designated by the term *dhānyagava* (grain-cow); this is because of its identical shape. In other cases as well, whatever similarity exists should be applied in the same way; just as there is a specific arrangement of parts in a cow, so it is here.

The gold belonging to him is that "gold" which is expressed by the term *hiraṇyagarbha*. Just as cats are small in size, so too is the alms-food; or just as cats exist only in certain places and not everywhere, so too is the alms-food. Such is the similarity between the porridge (*śrāṇā*) and the cat.

It should be applied as follows: grass arranged in the form of a lion is a "grass-lion" (tṛṇasiṃha). Just as salt from Sindh is white, so too is barley-meal [white] a "barley-meal-Sindh" (saktusaindhava), and likewise a "drinking-Sindh" (pānasaindhava).

73. *Ake jīvikārthe* (Pāṇini 6.2.73). The mention of *ṭhaka* here refers to the suffix (*pratyaya*). In that context, by the technical rule regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), it is understood that the form ending in that suffix is what is intended; thus he says: "when the word ending in the suffix *ṭhak* is the second member (*uttarapada*)."
Regarding the phrase "denoting a livelihood" (*jīvikāvācini*): this means that which expresses a livelihood (*jīvika*).

For the word *jīvikā* is included in the sūtra ending in the suffix *-a*, by virtue of its belonging to the *arśa-ādi* group (an open-ended class) which takes the possessive suffix *-a*.
