It is for this very reason that it is stated in the commentary (*vṛtti*) that those whose livelihood consists of scraping teeth and so forth are described in this manner.

Thus he says: "dantalekhalaḥ. [The suffix] *ṇvul* is applied after the root *likh*, followed by a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). The genitive case here is according to Pāṇini 2.3.65, *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*, used in the sense of the object (*karman*). Regarding "avaskaraśodhakaḥ": the root *śudh* is used in the sense of cleansing (*śaucakarmaṇi*) [or "in the sense of purity," as per the Dhātupāṭha].
In this way, [the word *ramaṇīyakāraka*] is derived from the causative form (*ṇyantāt*) of the root with the suffix *ṇvul*. In the case of *ramaṇīyakārakaḥ*, it is likewise from the root *kṛ*.

[The alternative form] *ramaṇīyakartā* is formed as before by means of a compound (*samāsa*). Here, by the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtibhāva*), whereby the final syllable of the second member of the compound is acute.

Regarding "ṭhikṣubhakṣikām" and so forth: the suffix *ṇvuc* is applied to the root *bhakṣ* by the rule "paryāya-arhaṇa-utpattiṣu ṇvac" (Pāṇini 3.3.111). Here, the compound is formed solely by the general definition of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī*, Pāṇini 2.2.8). In this case as well, as before, the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) is udātta. This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of the kṛt-suffix (*kṛtsvara*).
The same applies to the subsequent cases as well.
It should be understood that this [rule] is an exception to the *kṛtsvara* (the accentuation of the suffix *kṛt*), extending from here up to the rule "yuktārohyādayaśca" (Pāṇini 6.2.81).

74. *prācāṃ krīḍāyām* (Pāṇini 6.2.81). [The commentary explains: "The play of those residing in the eastern region. By this, he shows that the mention of "the east" (*prāc*) here is not for the sake of an option (*vibhāṣā*), but rather as an adverbial modifier of the action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).

In *ṭhuddālakapuṣpabhañjikā* and so forth, the genitive case is used for the object (*karman*) in connection with a primary derivative suffix (*kṛt*). In *jīvaputrapracāyikā*, here too, the suffix *ṇvul* is added to the root *chid* preceded by *pra* to form a technical name (*saṃjñā*).
The compound is formed as before; by the accent of the *lit*-suffix, the final member of the compound has the acute accent on its middle syllable.

In the compound "tava puṣpapracāyikā" (your flower-gatherer), the compound is formed by the rule "ṣaṣṭhī" (Pāṇini 2.2.8) itself. By the accentuation rule for the *cit* suffix, the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) is acute (*udātta*).
75. *aṇ* is applied after [the word] *niyukta*. (Pāṇini 6.2.75). For example: *chatradhāraḥ* ("an umbrella-bearer"). This is by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ* (3.2.1).
But for what purpose is this [rule], since the suffix *aṇ* is already intended to apply [by that rule], yet it does not express that which is joined (*yukta*)?

Regarding the passage beginning with "ṭhniyukto'dhikṛtaḥ" and so forth: by the rule "yukte ca" (Pāṇini 6.2.66), the first syllable of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) is prescribed as acute-accented (*udātta*) when it denotes one who is "engaged" (*yukta*)—that is, one who is attentive to what is to be done. Consequently, this does not apply to the word *adhikṛta* when it expresses the sense of "authorized. Therefore, in cases such as *adhikṛtacchattrādi*, that which...

The term *niyukta* here is intended in the sense of "appointed," yet one who is intent on some other task, such as holding an umbrella, does not possess the status required for a compound like *chattradhāra* ("umbrella-bearer") under the rule *yukte ca* (Pāṇini 6.2.66).

This is because the word *yukta* in that rule is understood to mean "appointed" (*niyukta*), as defined by the phrase "one who is appointed is one who is authorized" (*niyukto 'dhikṛtaḥ*). Thus, the word expressing such [a mere attendant] is not what is intended there.
He shows that the form *niyukta* is derived from the root *yujir* in the sense of "joining" (*yoge*) [Dhātupāṭha 1444] when used with the suffix *niṣṭhā*.
As for the example *kāṇḍalāvaḥ*, here only the agency (*kartṛtva*) with respect to the action of cutting the stalks (*kāṇḍalavana*) is understood.
It is not produced by the nose; therefore, this vowel does not occur.

76. *Śilpini cākṛñaḥ* | (Pāṇini 6.2.76) This statement is made to specify that [the suffix] is not applied after the root *kṛ*. It is also for the purpose of stating a prohibition regarding specific artisans (*śilpin*). For example: *tantuvāyaḥ* ("a weaver"). [The root is] *veñ* in the sense of "weaving" (*tantusantāna*).
Thus [it is stated in] the Dhātupāṭha (1006). From the root *ve* (to weave), the suffix *aṇ* is applied by Pāṇini 3.2.2 (*hvāvāmaśca*), and the augment *yuk* is added by 7.3.33 (*āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ*).
Regarding the word *ayaskāraḥ*, the visarga is substituted [for the final *r*] by the rule beginning with 8.3.46 (*ataḥ kṛkami*).
The suffix *sakāra* [is included]; in the counter-examples, the accent remains that of the entire word (*kṛtsvara*).
77. And [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] after the word *saṃjñā*. (6.2.77) 78. [The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after *go*, *tanti*, and *yava* when followed by *pāla*.

(6.2.78) [Example: *gopālaḥ*. [Analysis: From the root *pā* in the sense of "protecting" (*rakṣaṇe*; DhP 1056), the suffix *aṇ* is applied as before. [This applies] in the sense of one who is not appointed [to a specific office].

Regarding the word *ārambhaḥ*: since this is already established by the rule *niyukte ṭhaṇi niyukte* (Pāṇini 6.2.75), [the mention of *ārambha* here is for the sake of illustration]. Regarding *gorakṣaḥ*: the root *rakṣ* is used in the sense of "protecting" (*pālane*) [Dhātupāṭha 658].
79. *ṇiniḥ* | (Pāṇini 3.2.78) In the example "pūṣpahārī" ("one who takes flowers"), the suffix *ṇini* is applied either by [sūtra] 3.2.80 (*vrate*) or by 3.2.81 (*bahulam ābhīkṣṇye*).

80. *Upamānam* [is restricted] only when it is the base (*prakṛti*) of a word-meaning. (6.2.80) Regarding the phrase *śabdārthaprakṛtau*: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which the word-meaning is the base.

Regarding the statement "*upamānam niyamyate*" ("the standard of comparison is restricted"): since the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) applies to what follows the particle *eva*, here [the restriction applies to the condition of being the base]. In this case...

The particle *eva* has the sense of restriction (*prakṛti*) regarding the meaning of the word; therefore, a restriction of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) occurs, and thus that [comparison] is restricted. In the example "ṭhuṣṭrakośī," [the suffix *kvun* is applied] after the root *kruś* (meaning "to call out" or, according to the Dhātupāṭha, "to call out and to weep") by means of Pāṇini 3.2.79: *kartaryupamāne*.
Thus, the suffix *ṇini* is applied. Since similarity is already expressed by the suffix *ṇini* itself, the word *iva* is not employed in the compound.
In the example "dhvāṅkṣarāvī" (*one who cries like a crow*), the suffix *ṇini* is applied according to the previous rule [Pāṇini 3.2.78] to the root *ru* (meaning "to sound," Dhātupāṭha 1034).
In the example "kharanādī" (*one who makes a harsh noise*), the root is *ṇad* (meaning "an indistinct sound," Dhātupāṭha 54).

Regarding the phrase "the inclusion of the word *aupamya*," etc.: if the inclusion of the word *aupamya* were not made, then the distinction between the scope of the preceding rule and that of this one would not be known.
Even if another scope were to be inferred by virtue of the power of making this division of rules (*yogavibhāga*), nevertheless, the desired [result]—

Otherwise, the distinction between their respective objects would not be known. However, when the mention of comparison (*upamāna*) is made, the distinction between their objects is determined: the object of the former [perception] is the universal (*sāmānya*), whereas the object of this [comparison] is the particular (*viśeṣa*) that serves as the standard of comparison.
Therefore, the mention of comparison is for the sake of distinguishing their objects.
Regarding "vṛkavañcī": the root *vañcu* is used in the sense of "deceiving" (*pralambhane*, DhP 1703). Regarding "vṛkaprekṣī":

the root *īkṣ* is used in the sense of "seeing" (*darśane*, DhP 610), preceded by the prefix *pra*. In these cases, the accent of the *kṛt*-suffix alone occurs. As for the phrase "the base form itself," etc.: if the mention of the "base form" (*prakṛti*) were not made, then...
Would it not be understood that the suffix *ṇini* which follows a word denoting sound (*śabda*) is one that ends in a subsequent member of a compound?

Consequently, [the suffix] would also apply in cases such as *gardabhoccārī* ("one who makes the sound of a donkey") and *kokilābhivyāhārī* ("one who utters the cry of a cuckoo"), for here too, the suffix *ṇini* follows a word denoting sound consisting of a combination of a verbal root and a prefix.

Therefore, since that [word] ends in that [suffix], the subsequent word would not be included; hence, the mention of the "prakṛti" (base form) is made so that it does not occur here. Consequently, it does not apply in this case. When the *prakṛti* is mentioned, it refers to where the meaning is independent of a prefix (*upasarga*), because of the sense of "going" in the case of *gati*, and because of the sense of "carrying" in the case of *harati*. Or rather, it refers to the lexical meaning (*śabdārtha*) found here.
This is a combination of a root and a prefix; the suffix *ṇini* is not prescribed after such a combination.

If the rule is for the sake of restriction (*niyama*) when it is already established by the preceding [sūtra], then since a rule being commenced when [the matter] is already established serves as a restriction, is the use of the particle *eva* (only) indeed purposeless?

Thus he says: "The employment of the particle *eva*," and so forth. For if the particle *eva* were not present, there would be a restriction such that [the word] would refer only to the simile (*upamāna*) within the context of the nature of the word and its meaning; consequently, only the nature of the word and its meaning would be restricted—namely, that if [something] occurs in the nature of the word and its meaning, it occurs only as a simile.
"Not in the case of that which lacks a point of comparison. Consequently, [the suffix] would not occur in the case of something without a point of comparison.

Therefore, the particle *eva* is employed so that there may be a determination of the point of comparison. For what reason? He says: "But in the case of the primary form of the word's meaning," and so forth. The word *tu* (but) indicates a reason.
Therefore, in the case of the *prakṛti* (base form) of the word-meaning, both the simile (*upamāna*) and the non-simile (*anupamāna*) are acutely accented at the beginning.

For that reason, the particle *eva* is employed for the purpose of determining the simile. Indeed, when there is a restriction regarding the simile, since the base form of the word-meaning is not restricted, otherwise [if there were no such restriction], everything would be acutely accented at the beginning without distinction.

The form *siṃhavinardī* is an example of [the suffix] following a word that is a standard of comparison (*upamāna*). The form *puṣkalajalpī* is an example of [the suffix] following a word that is not a standard of comparison. In the case of *puṣkalajalpī*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied either by Pāṇini 3.2.80 (*vrate*) or 3.2.81 (*bahulam ābhīkṣṇye*).

81. *Yuktārohyādayaśca* (Pāṇini 6.2.81). In the group beginning with *yuktārohin*, where the final member (*uttarapada*) is a *kṛt*-derived word, this rule provides an exception to the accent of the *kṛt* suffix. In other cases, however, it provides an exception to the accent of the compound (*samāsa*). This applies to *yuktārohin* and the others in that list.

Regarding the forms *āgataprahārī* and so forth: in the case of the roots *ṣṭhivu* (to spit) and *ruha* (to grow/arise) [DhP 859], *yudh* (to fight) [DhP 1173], *vañc* (to deceive) [DhP 1703], and *ṭuaṇadi* (to prosper) [DhP 67]... [ṭua]

Regarding the abundance of rivers: from the roots *hr̥* (DhP 899, *hr̥ñ* "to carry") preceded by *pra*, and from these other roots as appropriate—specifically those preceded by *yukta*, *āgata*, and *pūrva*—the suffix *ṇini* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.78 (*supyajātau ṇinistācchīlye*). If these words end in *ṇini*, then...

"For what purpose are these read here, since [the desired form] is already established by the rule *ṭhṇini* (Pāṇini 5.2.79)? To this he replies: 'They are read here for the sake of providing examples specifically for [the suffix] *ṇini*.
According to the opinion of some, by the rule *pūrvottarapada-* (Pāṇini 7.3.10), [the forms would otherwise be derived differently]; therefore, they are read here [to show the correct application]."

He shows another purpose [for the rule]: those compounds for which there is a restriction on the preceding and following members are so described. This is so that [the rule] may apply only where *yukta* and others are the preceding members and *ārohī* and others are the following members; it should not apply here—namely, in *dhvāṅkṣārohī*.

In *vṛkṣārohī*, the first member (*pūrvapada*) is different; in *yuktādhyāyī*, the second member (*uttarapada*) is different. [The suffix] *ṇini* is applied to the root *ṭhiṅ* in the sense of "studying" (*adhyayane*). [The term] *āgatamatasya* is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). [The term] *kṣīrahotā*.

Thus: *kṣīrasya hotā* ("the priest of the milk"). This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) due to this very rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), or else [it is derived] from the root *hu* with the suffix *tṛc* because it belongs to the class beginning with *yājaka* (Pāṇini 2.2.9). As for *bhaginībhartā* ("the husband of the sister"), this too is a genitive compound as previously explained; it is formed from the root *bhṛ* with the suffix *tṛc*.
In the word *grāmagodhuk* ("one who milks the village cows"), the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *duh*. By the rule *dāderdhātorghaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.32), the initial *d* becomes *dh*.
Then, by the rule *ekāco baśo bhaṣ jhaṣantasya sdhvoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.37), the *d* is replaced by *dh*.
Next, by the rule *jhalāṃ jaśo'nte* (Pāṇini 8.2.39), the *dh* becomes *g*. Finally, by the rule *vāvasāne* (Pāṇini 8.4.56), that *g* optionally becomes *k* at the end of a word.
Thus ends the section on the letter *ka*. Regarding the term "trirātraḥ": since three nights (*tisraḥ rātrayaḥ*) are combined, it is a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a collective (*samāhāre*).
By the rule "ahaḥ-sarva-ekadeśa... (Pāṇini 5.4.87), the suffix *ac* is added as the final member of the compound.

Regarding the form *ekaśitipāt*: by the rule *pādasya lopo'hastyādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.138), there is the elision of the vowel *a*. Now, one might object that this word *eka* ends in the suffix *kan* according to the rule *iṣbhīkāpāśalpatimarcibhyaḥ kan* (Uṇādi-sūtra 3.21), and thus, by the accentuation of the *nit*-suffix, it would be udātta on its first syllable. In that case, [the word] *ekaḥ*...

The term "śitipādaḥ" is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "one whose foot is white. Since this form is already established by the rule for *prakṛtibhāva* (preservation of the original form), the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) would be achieved even without this specific entry; therefore, one might ask: what is the purpose of its inclusion here? To this, he says: "One white foot belongs to him. This fault would apply only in the case of a two-word bahuvrīhi, not otherwise.

And this [compound] is not two-worded; rather, it is three-worded. Here, because the word *pāda* occurs as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the rule "taddhitārthottarapada" (Pāṇini 2.1.51) applies, whereby the final syllable of the preceding members—namely, the word *ekaśiti*—would have been expected to be udātta. Therefore, the rule "samāsasya" (Pāṇini 6.1.223) [is applied].

By this [sūtra]—(Pāṇini 6.1.223)—the particle *iti* indicates the reason (*hetu*). Since its final syllable would have been udātta by that rule, its initial syllable is therefore prescribed as udātta. Thus, the intention is that the recitation of the word *ekaśitipāt* is not purposeless. Why?

Furthermore, its final acute accent (antodāttatva) would again result; for, by the accent of the *bahuvrīhi* compound itself, the final acute accent ought rightly to prevail by virtue of being subsequent, thereby subverting [the other].
To this he says: "Because the accent of the cause is stronger" (*nimitasvarabalīyastvāt*). The word "cause" (*nimitta*)...

A *dvigu* is a three-membered *bahuvrīhi*. For when it is formed, [the accentuation] occurs in the two preceding members when the *dvigu* is the subsequent member. And that in whose presence something occurs is the cause (*nimitta*) of that [occurrence]; the accent of the *bahuvrīhi* belonging to that cause is the "cause-accent" (*nimittasvara*).
Therefore, "the strength of the cause" means the strength of the accent of the cause. The compound is formed by the division of the rule *pañcamī* (Pāṇini 2.1.37). This is what is meant:
that because of this [rule], the final acute accent of the compound supersedes the accent of the bahuvrīhi.

[Objection: "It must be stronger; therefore, that [accent] prevails. [Response: But its strength is due to its being *satiśiṣṭa* (remaining after others have been applied). For that [strength] occurs when the *bahuvrīhi* has received its initial udātta accent.
Therefore, it is said that what remains after others have been applied (*satiśiṣṭa*) is stronger. Or else, it is because of the forthcoming indicator (*jñāpaka*).
"The indicatory letter (*n*) has greater force than the accent.

[This refers to the rule] beginning with "even so" (*evam api*). Even so, even when a three-word *bahuvrīhi* is being postulated, [the author says] "there is no purpose served by this. There is no purpose here for the word *ekaśitipād*. Why? Because...

Thus he says: "ending in *iK*," and so forth. For in a three-word *bahuvrīhi*, the compound of the two words *eka* and *triṃśat* as the final member is designated a *dvigu* by the rule "a *dvigu* is that which has a numeral as its first member" (Pāṇini 2.1.52), and it ends in *iK*. Consequently, [the following applies].
The initial udātta accent is established by the rule *ṭhiganta-dvigau* (Pāṇini 6.2.29), and therefore there is no purpose for this [present rule].

With the words "If that is so, then... and so forth, he demonstrates that the reading of the word *ekaśitipād* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). What, then, does it indicate? He says: "This," and so forth; and with the words "By that," and so forth.

He demonstrates the purpose [of the rule]: if this meaning were not made known, then, having formed a three-membered *bahuvrīhi* compound as *asya dvau śitī pādau*, and since there would be a *dvigu* with respect to the two preceding members when followed by the final member, the rule "ṭi-antāt dvigoḥ" (Pāṇini 5.1.29) [would apply].

If the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) were applied, the word *ti* would be acute in the example *dvi-ṣaṣṭi-pād*. However, when this meaning [of the rule] is made known, the accent prescribed by the rule "the final syllable of a *samāsānta* ending in *ig*, and of a *dvigu*" (Pāṇini 6.2.29) does not apply.
And since that [accent] is absent, the word *ti* becomes acute by the accent of the compound (*samāsasvara*).

Otherwise, the greater force of the accent of the *nimita* (the cause) would not prevail. Consequently, in a three-word *bahuvrīhi*, because it is subsequent, the accent of the compound (*samāsa-svara*) would set aside [the accent of the cause], and the accent of the *bahuvrīhi* itself would occur;
since this would then be established by that very rule, the reading of the word *ekaśitipāt* here would not be necessary.
And it has been established; therefore, that very [sūtra] makes known the fact that the accent of the cause (nimitta) is stronger.

82. *dīrghakāśatuṣabhrāṣṭravaṭamuje* (Pāṇini 6.2.82). This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of the suffix *kṛt*. Regarding the example *kuṭījaḥ*: the suffix *ḍa* is applied by the rule *saptamyāṃ janer ḍaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.97), meaning "born in a hut" (*kuṭyāṃ jātaḥ*).
83. *antyāt pūrvam bahvacaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.83).
This rule is also an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of the whole word (*kṛtsvara*).
In the example *dagdhajāni*, the accentuation of the whole word (*kṛtsvara*) alone occurs.

84. *grāme'nivasantaḥ* | (Pāṇini 6.2.84). This word *nivasantaḥ* is understood as being derived from the *uṇādi* suffix *jhac*, according to the rule *jṛviśibhyāṃ jhac* (Uṇādisūtra 6.17), which applies in the context of the present tense.
According to the rule *tṛbhṛvṛdhivasibhāsisādhigaḍimaṇḍijinandibhyaśca* (Dhātupāṭha 6.19), the suffix *jhac* is applied to the root *vas* preceded by the prefix *ni*.
Thus, those who dwell [there] are called *nivasantaḥ*. Some, however, [derive it] from the causative form (*channanta*).
They explain that the word *vasat* (dwelling) is included [in the compound], as in "Mallagrāmaḥ" (the village of the Mallas). This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

In the case of "Devagrāmaḥ" (the village of the gods), the word *grāma* refers to a collection of houses enclosed by a fence; therefore, the meaning is "one whose master is the gods. By this, the relationship of ownership between property and owner is what is intended here.

This shows that the genitive case is compounded, but not when there is a connection with the act of dwelling (*nivasana*); the intention is that otherwise the word *deva* would function solely as a prior member (*pūrvapada*) signifying "dwelling.
This is illustrated by the counter-example: "in which the descendants of Dakṣa and others dwell," and so forth.
This demonstrates that the first member of the compound has the sense of "dwelling."

85. *Ghoṣādiṣu ca* (6.2.85). This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of compounds (*samāsa-svara*). The same applies to the subsequent rules as well. One should understand that those rules which follow the sūtra beginning with *na bhūtādhika-sañjīva* (6.2.91) are exceptions to the accentuation of compounds.

"Ṭhdākṣīghoṣaḥ" and so forth are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). "Ṭhyānayatra" and so forth. But how is this obtained, given that "not residing" (*anivasanta*) is the subject under discussion? To this he says: "not residing. "Others," and so forth; according to their opinion, those which here...
Among them, the names of dwellings are also used to denote those who reside therein.

86. *chāttryādayaḥ śālāyām* | (6.2.86) [The commentary begins: "When ending in *śālā*, etc. Now, by the rule *vibhāṣā senāsurā* (2.4.25), it has been stated that a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *śālā* optionally takes the neuter gender; and here [in this rule]...

The feminine form of the word *śālā* is what is being referred to here. Just as a compound in that context does not become neuter, so too, by the rule "In a *tatpuruṣa*, when the final member is *śālā* and the compound is neuter" (Pāṇini 6.2.123), the accent should be on the first syllable of the final member because this rule is subsequent [to others].

Someone might have a misconception; therefore, the passage beginning with "when [the compound] ends in *śālā*" is introduced in order to dispel that. This is the scope for that [rule] which is a neuter-gender *tatpuruṣa* compound not ending in *śālā*: namely, *chātriśālā* and *ailiśālā*. But as for that which...

A neuter *tatpuruṣa* compound whose prior member is not *chātra* or similar words is the scope of [Pāṇini 6.2.123], which states: "In the neuter gender, [the final vowel of] *śālā* becomes short [after such a word]"—for example, *brāhmaṇaśālam* and *kṣatriyaśālam*.
In the case of *chātriśālam*, however, both rules would apply; by the principle of priority (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), this very rule [of 6.2.123] takes effect.
It becomes the tone.
87. *prasthe 'vṛddham akarkyādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.2.87).

If the word *prastha* is derived [by adding the suffix *ka*] according to the Vārttika: "The suffix *ka* is prescribed in the sense of *ghañ* for the purposes of *sthā*, *snas*, *pā*, *vyadh*, *han*, and *yudh*" (Vārttika 306), then it falls under the accentuation rule for *thā-tha*-type words (*thāthādisvara*).

(6.2.144) [This rule applies] when [the suffix] is applicable. Now, if it is not derived [by this rule], then, by virtue of the udātta accent on the final syllable of a compound, forms such as ‘indraprasthaḥ’ are genitive compounds (ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa).

88. And [the elision of the case-ending] occurs after *mālā* and so forth. (6.2.88) 89. After *amahan* and *nava*, [the case-ending is not elided] before *nagara* when the word does not belong to the Udīcya dialect.
(6.2.89) Expressions such as *suhyanagaram* are also indeed genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). For what purpose is the restriction "of the Easterners" (*prācām*) stated?

It is not said [that it would apply]; for the statement "of the ancients" (*prācām*) is [intended] because of the statement "not of the northerners" (*anudīcām*). This cannot be so; otherwise, in the case of *virāṭanagara-* [as a name] for a city in the Middle Country (*madhyadeśa*), [the rule] would not apply when the acute accent on the first syllable of the prior member is required.
A negation is expressed; it does not necessarily constitute a compound itself.
90. *arme cāvarṇaṃ dvyactryac* (6.2.90).

91. *na bhūtādhikasañjīvamadrāśmakajjalam* (6.2.91). Regarding the phrase "the mention of *madra* and *aśma*," etc.: in both cases, [the words] consist of two or three syllables (*dvyac* and *tryac*).

The attainment [of the desired forms] exists. Therefore, the statement is for the sake of both the compound (saṅghāta) and the uncompounded (vigṛhīta) meaning. But how is the status of being both compound and uncompounded obtained? It is obtained by making a single-remainder (ekaśeṣa), as indicated by the form *madrāśma*. The single-remainder is formed as *madrāśmā ca madrāśmānau ca* ("Madrāśma and Madrāśmans"). When the single-remainder is applied...
The prohibition of the word *madra* alone, as well as the prohibition of the compound containing the word *madra*, is thus justified.

"The section concerning the initial acute accent" (*ādyaudātaprakaraṇam*) means that the section on the initial acute accent has been introduced. In that context, the form of the rule is: "In the Vedic language, [names] such as Divodāsa and others have the initial syllable as acute."

The meaning is that it must be explained. As for the explanations: in rules such as *yukte ca* (Pāṇini 6.2.66), one should proceed by assuming that any of the *ca*-particles occurring in this section has the purpose of including what has not been explicitly stated (*anuktasamuccaya*).
92. *antaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.92).
93. *saṃrva guṇakārtsnye* (Pāṇini 6.2.93). Regarding the term *guṇakārtsnye*: *guṇakārtsnya* means the total absence of a quality (*guṇa*) everywhere.

Regarding the term "sarvaśveta" ("all-white"): it is a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇasamāsa*) according to the rule "pūrvakālaika... (Pāṇini 2.1.49). In this case, the quality of being "all" (*sarva*) pertains to the whole aggregate; it does not apply to each individual part. Thus, the word "sarva" functions here to denote the totality of the quality.

Regarding the phrase "supremely white" (*paramaśveta*): how, then, does the word *parama* here signify the totality of qualities (*guṇakārtsnya*), given that it denotes excellence (*prakarṣa*) and excellence is one thing while the totality of qualities is another?
To this he says: "by pervading the substratum," and so forth. The particle *iti* is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).

Because supremacy (*paramatva*) occurs through the pervasion of the entire substratum (*āśrayavyāpti*), and not otherwise; for its excellence is established only if it pervades the whole substratum. Therefore, in this context, the word "supreme" (*parama*) refers to the totality of qualities (*guṇakārtsnya*). [As in the example: "entirely golden" (*sarvasauvarṇaḥ*).

Regarding the phrase "from all silver" (*sarvarājataḥ*): *sauvarṇa* is a derivative of gold, and *rājata* is a derivative of silver. Here, "entirety" (*kārtsnya*) does not refer to the entirety of qualities; rather, it refers to the entirety of the derivative substance as characterized by its genus. For every derivative substance pervades [its cause] by way of being its material cause (*prakṛti*).

In this case, "entirety" refers to the substance (*dravya*), whereas in that [other] case, the word "all" (*sarva*) applies to the quality (*guṇa*). For example: "He is whiter than all [others], thus he is 'all-white' (*sarvaśvetaḥ*). Here, the entirety pertains to the quality. But how is the compound formed here, given that by the rule "pūraṇaguṇasuhita... (Pāṇini 2.2.11), a genitive compound with a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*) is prohibited?

Is it prohibited? Or even if, for some reason, a compound were possible, even then, once a compound with the word *śvetatara* has been formed, would one have to say *sarva-śvetataram*? To this he says: "A compound [is formed] with a comparative (*tara*) following a quality," and so forth.
Here, the addition of the suffix *tarap* and the elision of the *tarap* are both based on specific supplementary rules (*upasaṃkhyāna*).

[The author] demonstrates: this rule is an exception to the accent of compounds (*samāsasvara*). The same applies to the subsequent rules as well. It should be understood that this is an exception to the accent of compounds prior to the rule *na hāstinaphalakamārdeyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.101).
94. *saṃjñāyāṃ girinikāyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.94).

Compounds such as *añjanāgiriḥ* and others are genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compounds. In the words *añjana* and *bhañjana*, there is lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *ṭhan-giryoḥ saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 6.3.117).
The words *ṭhśāpiṇḍin* and *mauṇḍin* end in the suffix *iñ*; the word *cikhillin* ends in the possessive suffix *ini*.

95. [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] after a word denoting age when it refers to a young girl (*kumārī*). (6.2.95) For example: *vṛddhakumārī*. This is a compound formed by the rule "the qualifier [is compounded] with the qualified" (2.1.57).
Also, for example: *jaratkumārī*. This is a compound formed by the rule "that which is prior in time [is placed first]" (2.1.49), meaning "she who is both old and a young girl."
The compound is formed by these and other such rules. In both cases, the masculine form is applied according to the rule *puṃvat karmadhāraye* (Pāṇini 6.3.42).
Now, one might object that the word *kumārī* refers to the first stage of life; for it is said, "in the first stage of life... [and so forth].

Since the suffix *ṅīp* is prescribed here by [Pāṇini 4.1.20], and the words *vṛddhā* and *ajaratī* refer to an advanced age, how can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in this case? To this he says: "The word *kumārī* is employed by taking as its sole ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) the mere fact of not being joined with a male."

Non-association means non-connection. A word that functions as a constituent part of a collection whose activity and cessation pertain solely to that [general property] operates with respect to the universal (*sāmānya*). For example, when the word "maiden" (*kumārī*) is qualified by words such as "old," which denote specific stages of age, it then becomes a term of common apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with them.

"Age-distinction" refers to the final stage of life. But how can a term expressing a specific distinction be used in a general sense? It is by virtue of the inclusion of the word "age. If the compound *vṛddhakumārī* were to refer to the first stage of life, the mention of "age" would be redundant; for it is precisely because the word *kumārī* is employed [in the compound] that this is understood.

Since it denotes the first stage of life, age is necessarily understood therein; so what is the purpose of explicitly mentioning "age"? Therefore, by the force of the mention of "age," it functions with respect to the general category of age in the manner described. For by the mention of "age," this [term] is removed from that specific [instance].

A general application is resorted to, as in the statement: "And that age is understood here. That which is currently occurring and stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with words denoting specific stages is what is understood by "age" (*vayas*).
By the word "and" (*ca*), other stages such as youth and so forth are included; thus, the meaning is not merely the first stage of life, but childhood itself.
Regarding the term *paramakumārī*: here, the state of being honored (*pūjyamānatā*) is derived from the compound; and this state of being honored arises because she is beautiful to behold.
Thus, the meaning is "a maiden who is beautiful to behold. For in this case, the compound does not intend to denote age; nor does the final member of the compound refer to age in a general sense.

96. *udake'kevale* (Pāṇini 6.2.96). [The word] *miśram* means "mixed with another substance. In the example *guḍamiśram*, it is a compound in which the second member is elided, following the rule for *śākapārthiva* and similar compounds (Vārttika 83).

In the compound *ṭhśītodakam* (cold water), it is a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). Here, the first member denotes water with "coldness" as its subordinate attribute (*guṇopasarjana*), while the second member likewise has "water-ness" (*jāti*) as its subordinate attribute. In this very way, a single object is expressed by both a genus and a quality.
The compound consists solely of words denoting water.
97. *dvigau kratau* (Pāṇini 6.2.97).

[The forms] *gargatrirātra* and so forth are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). The combination of three nights (*tisṛṇāṃ rātrīṇāṃ samāhāraḥ*) is *trirātraḥ*. The compound-ending suffix *ac* is applied by the rule *ahaḥsarvekadeśa-* (Pāṇini 5.4.87) and others.
"Ṭhatirātraḥ": this is a *prādi* compound meaning "one who has passed beyond the night."

98. *Sabhāyāṃ napuṃsake* (Pāṇini 2.4.23). Compounds such as *gopālasabham* and others are genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compounds; they are neuter by virtue of the rule *sabhārājāmanuṣyapūrvā*. [Examples include: *rājasabhā*, etc.
In the case of *brāhmaṇasabhā*, because of the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 2.4.23] "not when preceded by a non-human [word]," the neuter gender does not occur.
Now, why does it not occur here: *ramaṇīyā sabhā asya brāhmaṇakulasya* (the assembly of this Brahmin family is beautiful), resulting in *ramaṇīyasabham*?

To this he says: "that which is explicitly stated" (*pratipadoktam*), and so forth. By the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) concerning that which is explicitly stated versus that which is indicated by a grammatical definition (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā*, Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 3), that neuter gender which is explicitly stated is what is understood here;
however, such a neuter status does not exist here. In this case, however, the gender and number [of the word] are like those of the thing denoted (*abhidheyavat*).

In the rule *bhavanti* (Vyāḍi-pāṭha 73), because the word *brāhmaṇakula*, which is the designated referent (*abhidheya*), is neuter, that [neuter gender] is not [to be understood as] explicitly stated by the rule itself (*pratipadokta*).
99. *pura* [is used] in the sense of the eastern grammarians.
(6.2.99) Examples such as *lalāṭapuraḥ* are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

100. And [the word] *pūrva* [is compounded] with *ariṣṭa* and *gauḍa*. (6.2.100) [The examples are] *ariṣṭapuraṃ* and *gauḍapuram*. These two are also indeed genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). [The question is: "What is the purpose of including the mention of *pūrva*? He thinks thus: [it is to indicate that the rule applies to] *ariṣṭa* and *gauḍa*.

It must be said: even when this is stated, the word *pura-* as a final member (*uttarapada*) in *ariṣṭapura* and *goḍapura* would indeed result in being oxytone (*antodātta*). [The sūtra says] "so that it may also be so here.
If the mention of *pūrva-* were not made, then [in the case of] one who has resorted to *ariṣṭa* (*ariṣṭaśrita*), [the rule would not apply].

Regarding the expression *ariṣṭaśritapura*: the two words *gauḍa* [in the compound] refer to the servants of the Gauḍas. However, if the term *pūrva* (preceding) were included, a *bahuvrīhi* compound would be obtained—namely, *ariṣṭagauḍapūrva*, meaning "that compound in which *ariṣṭa* and *gauḍa* are the preceding members. By that [analysis], one arrives at *ariṣṭaśritapura*.

In the case of *gauḍabhṛtyapura* as well, that which is the final member (*uttarapada*) likewise possesses an udātta accent on its final syllable. For here too, the words *ariṣṭa* and *gauḍa* precede;
and this preceding term denotes a constituent part (*avayava*).
101. *na hāstinaphalakamārdeyāḥ* (6.2.101). 102. *kusūlakūpakumbhaśālaṃ bile* (6.2.102).
Compounds such as *kusūlabilam* and others are genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compounds. This [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation rules for compounds.

This is the application [of the rule]. Thus, all subsequent rules prior to "viśvaṃ saṃjñāyām" (Pāṇini 6.2.106) in the section on *bahuvrīhi* compounds should be understood as exceptions (*apavāda*) to the accentuation rules for compounds.

103. Words denoting directions [form a compound] with names of villages, districts, *cānara*, and *rāṭi*. (6.2.103) Example: *pūrveṣukāmaśamī*. The compound is formed by Pāṇini 2.1.50: "Directional words and numerals [form a compound] when they constitute a name. The same applies to *apareṣukāmaśamī*. Example: *pūrvakṛṣṇamṛtikā*. [The word] *pūrvā*...

And since this is "black clay" (*kṛṣṇamṛttikā*), a compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.58] *pūrvāpara-* and so forth. The same applies to examples such as *aparakṛṣṇamṛttikā*. A work composed concerning Rāma is called *ādhirāmam*; [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.87] *adhikṛtya kṛte granthe*. Now...
Since the form *cānarāṭ* is included [in the list], why does it not also occur in cases such as *grāmādi*?

Because the reference (*nirdeśa*) has the meaning as its primary focus. For it has been stated that when a reference has the word-form (*śabdarūpa*) as its primary focus, there is an inclusion of the actual phonetic form. And here, in the case of *cānarāṭ* alone, the reference has the word-form as its primary focus.
In the case of villages and the like, [the direction] is indeed determined primarily by the object.
Now, for what purpose is the mention of "word" (*śabda*) made; why is it not simply stated as "direction" (*dik*)? To this he says:
"The mention of 'word'," and so forth. For if the mention of "word" were absent, [the rule would apply to] *pūrvādhirāmam*.

In the case of the word *pūrvayāyātam*, [the rule] would not apply. Why? Because here the word *pūrva* denotes time. When there is the mention of a word denoting direction (*dig-vācin*), it refers only to words denoting direction. Therefore, for the purpose of ensuring that even a word denoting time which is a directional term is included, [the word "direction" is used].
The mention of "sound" (śabda).

104. *Ācāryopasarjanaś cāntevāsini* (6.2.104). [The word] *ācāryopasarjanaś ca* [is used]; by the rule *supāṃ suluk...* (Pāṇini 7.1.39), the nominative singular replaces the locative singular. This [term] is an adjective qualifying *antevāsī*.

Regarding the rule *ṭhācāryopasarjanāntevāsinītyuttarapade*: that whose *antevāsī* (pupil) has the *ācārya* (teacher) as its *upasarjana* (subordinate element) is so described. An *antevāsī* who has the *ācārya* as his *upasarjana* is an *ācāryopasarjanāntevāsī*; [the compound] refers to him.
When *śīla* is the final member of a compound, it denotes a pupil who has that [teacher] as his preceptor;
for example, *pūrvapāṇinīyāḥ*. By the rule *pūrvāpara-* (Pāṇini 2.1.58) and others, there is a compound:
the pupils (*antevāsinaḥ*) of the teacher Pāṇini are the *pāṇinīyāḥ*; here, the pupils are [the referents].

They are expressed primarily by means of a word ending in a suffix; however, because the teacher (*ācārya*) serves as a qualifier, he is in a subordinate (*upasarjana*) position, and thus the subsequent member of the compound denotes the pupil qualified by the teacher. For example: *pūrvakāśakṛtsnāḥ* ("the former followers of Kāśakṛtsna"). These belong to Kāśakṛtsna, hence they are *kāśakṛtsnāḥ*; the suffix *aṇ* is applied here according to the general rule (*autsargika*). Another example is *pūrvapāṇinīyaṃ śāstram* ("the earlier Pāṇinian treatise"). That which was proclaimed by Pāṇini is *pāṇinīyam*.

In this context, the compound has as its final member the word denoting the teacher (*ācārya*) as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*), and not the word denoting the pupil (*antevāsī*) who is subordinate to the teacher.

105. *sarvaṃ ca* (6.2.105). Regarding the phrase *utarapadavṛddhau*: "vṛddhi in the case of the subsequent member" (*utarapadavṛddhi*) refers to the vṛddhi prescribed under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "the subsequent member" (*utarapada*); however, in this context, that which possesses such a subsequent member is understood. This very point [is explained as follows]:

To demonstrate this, he says: "The subsequent word [is marked] by means of the acute accent (*udātta*)," and so forth. But how can this meaning be understood when it is stated that "in the case of the operation of the subsequent word"?
To this it is replied: the subsequent word is marked with the acute accent (*svarita*), and by the acute accent, the governing scope (*adhikāra*) is indicated.

First, it is understood that this refers to the *vṛddhi* substitution which has been prescribed under the governing rule *tenottarapadasya*. Now, this final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) is being prescribed for the *pūrvapada*.
And since the term *pūrvapada* is a relative term, it brings to mind the *uttarapada*. Nor does [the rule] refer to *vṛddhi* in general.

The phrase "the subsequent member (uttarapada) is applicable" implies, by virtue of its context and association with the term *vṛddhi*, that it indicates the subsequent member as being characterized by *vṛddhi*. Consequently, it is understood that under the governing rule concerning the subsequent member (*uttarapadādhikāra*), this accent occurs when the subsequent member possesses *vṛddhi*. For example: *sarvapāñcālakaḥ* and *pūrvakālaika*.

The compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.49] and so forth. In examples such as *pūrvapāñcālakaḥ*, it is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.58] and so forth. [Regarding the suffix *vṛñ*,] it is said: "The suffix *vṛñ* is applied to denote a country (*janapada*). [And regarding the suffix *vuñ*,] it is stated: "The suffix *vuñ* is applied after a word ending in *dhanvan* or having *ya* or *va* as its penultimate letter" (4.2.121).

While this [suffix] is being carried over from the rule *ṭhjanapadatadavadhyośca* (4.2.124), and while the term *janapada* is also being carried over, the suffix *vañ* is applied by the rule *avṛddhād api bahuvacanaviṣayāt* (4.2.125). [This applies to] the examples beginning with *susarvārddhāt*; for instance, *sarvapāñcālakaḥ*.

In *susarvārdhāj janapadasya* (Pāṇini 7.3.12), there is vṛddhi of the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*). However, in cases such as *pūrvapāñcālakaḥ*, the rule *diśo 'madrāṇām* (7.3.13) applies. This [vṛddhi] is prescribed under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "the second member" (*uttarapada*), because the term *uttarapadasya* is understood to carry over (*anuvṛtti*) into that context.

But what is the reason for understanding that the mention of "the subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) indicates the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of the subsequent member? To this he says: "Because the governing rule is indicated," and so forth.
If the governing rule of the subsequent member were indicated by the mention of "the subsequent member," then...
It would have been stated that when the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) possesses only the quality of being accented (*udātta*), this substitution of *hyu* for *vuñ* occurs;

and if that were so, it would also apply in cases such as *sarvabhāsaḥ* and *sarvakārakaḥ*. However, under the definition provided by the governing context (*adhikāra-lakṣaṇa*), it does not occur, for it has been stated that the *udātta* accent does not apply here. And thus, [in the case of] *sarvabhāsaḥ*,...

In the case of *sarvakāraka*, [the vṛddhi] would also occur here; however, it does not occur when the characteristic of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) is present, for the vṛddhi is not prescribed under the governing rule for the final member (*uttarapada*). [The word] *bhāsa* is derived from the root *bhāsṛ* (DhP 624) in the sense of "shining" (*dīpti*); it means "that which shines," formed with the suffix *ac* according to the *pacādi* class. [The word] *kāraka* is derived from the root *kṛ* with the suffix *ṇvul*; [the vṛddhi substitution of *ai* for *a* + *e* occurs] by the rule *aco ñṇiti*.
Thus, there is *vṛddhi* [substitution], and that is not prescribed under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning the second member of a compound (*uttarapada*).
106. *viśvam* [is treated as the first member] in a *bahuvrīhi* compound when it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*). (Pāṇini 6.2.106) [Objection:

"Since [the rule] *pūrvapadakṛtisvaratvena ādyudāttatvam prāptam* ('by the accentuation of the first member, the acute accent on the initial syllable is obtained'), [this would apply here]. [Response: By the rule *bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā* (Pāṇini 6.2.1), etc., [the first member retains its original accent]. Thus, *viśve ca te devāḥ* = *viśvadevāḥ*.

This is a *viśeṣaṇasamāsa*, which is a type of *tatpuruṣa* compound. In this case, the accentuation is solely that of the final member of the compound (*samāsāntodātta*). In the word "viśvadevaḥ," however, the accentuation is solely that of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*), which is acute on the first syllable.
This is because the word "viśva" ends in the suffix *kvan*, and by the rule regarding *nit*-suffixes, it is acute on the first syllable.

"Viśvāmitraḥ. The scope for the acute accent on the final syllable of the first member, according to *viśvaṃ saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 6.2.106), is exemplified by *viśvadevaḥ* and *viśvayaśāḥ*. [The scope for the rule] *saṃjñāyāṃ mitrājinayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.165) is as follows: ... [the word] *viśvāmitraḥ*.
Thus, the scope for the acute accent on the final syllable of the second member is, for example, *kulamitram* and *kulājinam*; however,

in cases such as *viśvāmitraḥ* and *viśvājinaḥ*, both rules would apply, and by the principle of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the rule "in a name, [the acute accent falls] on *mitra* and *ajina*" (Pāṇini 6.2.165) prevails.

107. *udarāśveṣu* | (6.2.107) "He whose belly (*udara*) is like that of a wolf (*vṛka*)" is *vṛkodaraḥ*. "He who has a rope (*dāman*) around his belly" is *dāmodaraḥ*. "He whose horse (*aśva*) is tawny (*hari*)" is *haryaśvaḥ*. "He whose horse is youth (*yauvana*)" is *yauvanāśvaḥ*.
Those whose color (*varṇa*) is beautiful are *suvarṇa*; those arrows (*iṣu*) whose nocks (*puṅkha*) are *suvarṇa* are *suvarṇapuṅkha*;

he who has arrows with *suvarṇapuṅkha* is *suvarṇapuṅkheṣuḥ*. He who has great arrows (*maheṣu*) is *maheṣuḥ*. The substitution of *ā* [for the final vowel of the first member] occurs by the rule *ānmahataḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.46). In this case—

In the case of the preceding words, there is *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) by the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, [the first member remains] in its original state" (Pāṇini 6.2.1). This rule is commenced when the accent of the suffix *yat* would otherwise apply; that [suffix] is now explained. While the word *kaḥ* is being carried over from the rule "the suffix *ka* [is added] after roots ending in *ṛt*, after *ādhāra*, *arc*, and *kali*" (Uṇādisūtra 3.40), [the rule continues with] "after the roots *aj*, *i*, *vṛ*, and *rī*, [the suffix *ka* is added] and it is also *nit*."

Therefore, in the case of *nigrahaṇa*, the word *vṛka* is derived by the rule "after the roots *sṛ*, *vṛ*, *bhū*, *śuṣi*, and *muṣi*, the suffix *kak* [is added]" (*Pañcapāda Uṇādi Sūtra* 3.41); because it ends in the suffix *kak*, this word has its initial syllable accented acute (*ādyaudāta*). The word *dāman* is likewise [acute-accented on the first], because it ends in the suffix *manin*.
From this root *hṛ*, by the rule "the suffix *in* is added after all roots" (*sarvadhātubhya in*), the word *hari* has its first syllable accented acute (*ādyaudāta*).

108. [The suffix *aC* is applied] after the root *kṣip* [to form a name]. (Pāṇini 6.2.108) Regarding the example "ṭhkuṇḍodaraḥ": while the rule "ṭhśakiśamyornit" (Pañcapāda 1.111) is in effect, and following from the mention of "kit" in "ṭhkvādibhyaḥ kit" (Pañcapāda 1.114), there is the root "kuḍi dāhe" (to burn).

From this root [√kuṇḍ], by applying the suffix *ḍa* according to the rule "after a word ending in *ṭha*, there is *ḍa*" (*Pāṇini* 5.2.113), we have *kuṇḍam* with the acute accent on the first syllable. Regarding the term *ghaṭodaraḥ*: since this word *ghaṭa* is derived from the root √*ghaṭ* ("to strive") with the suffix *ac* (by the rule *pacādyac*), it has the acute accent on the final syllable.

Therefore, since the desired result is already established by the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*), the author of the Vṛtti— considering that if this [rule] were commenced for another purpose, then by virtue of being an exception (*apavāda*), it would be more appropriate for the word ending in *pacādyac* to have a final acute accent (*antodātta*)— also cites this example: "kaṭukāśvaḥ."
*kaṭuakāśvaḥ* means "one whose horse is *kaṭuaka*. From the word *kaṭua*, the suffix *kan* is applied by the rule *saṃjñāyāṃ kan* (Pāṇini 5.3.87);

thus, the word *kaṭuaka* has its first syllable as the udātta accent. *Spānditāśvaḥ* means "one whose horse is *spāndita*. The suffix *kta* is applied to the root *spadi* ("to move slightly," Dhātupāṭha 14). By that [suffix],...

The word *syandita* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) by the accentual rule for secondary suffixes (*pratyayasvara*). [The compound] *anighāteṣuḥ* means "one whose arrow is not struck down" (*anighāta-iṣuḥ*).
That by which something is struck down is called *nighāta*; it is formed with the suffix *ghañ* according to Pāṇini 3.3.121 (*halaśca*).
*Anighātaḥ* is the negative compound (*nañ-tatpuruṣa*) meaning "not a strike," according to Pāṇini 6.2.2 (*tatpuruṣe tulyārthe*).

By such rules as these, because of the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) of the indeclinable (*avyaya*), the word *anighāta* is udātta on its first syllable. [The compound] *calācaleṣuḥ* means "one whose arrow is moving and unmoving. Regarding the root *cala* (to shake, DhP 832), when it takes the suffix *ac* by the rule *pacādyac*, there is optionally reduplication according to the Vārttika: *caricalipativadīnāṃ vā dvitvamacyākcābhyāsasya*.

There is reduplication and the augment *ag* is added to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). By this, the word *calācala* is udātta on its final syllable. Regarding the rule *anudāttaḥ* and so forth: the scope (*avakāśa*) of the rule *udarāśveṣuṣu* (Pāṇini 6.2.107) and *kṣepe* (6.2.108) is, for example, *kuṇḍīdaraḥ* and *ghaṭodaraḥ*; whereas the scope of the rule *nañsubhyām* (6.2.172) is as follows: [the examples are provided].

Thus, the scope for [the rule] prescribing acute accent on the final syllable of the subsequent member (*uttarapadāntodāta*) is, for example, *ayavaḥ* and *suyavaḥ*; however, in the case of *anudaraḥ* and *sūdaraḥ*, both rules would apply. By way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the rule *nañsubhyām* (Pāṇini 6.2.172) takes precedence.

109. *nadī bandhuni* (6.2.109). Regarding the term *bandhuni*: the neuter gender is used here with reference to the word-form itself; otherwise, since the word *bandhu* is masculine, one would have formulated the rule as *bandhau*.
In the expressions *gārgībandhuḥ* and *vātsībandhuḥ*, the suffix *yañ* is applied to the words *garga-* and *vatsa-* by virtue of their belonging to the *gargādi* class (Pāṇini 4.1.105).
From these forms ending in *yañ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added according to Pāṇini 4.1.16.
Thus, the words *gārgī* and *vātsī* have their first syllable accented acute (*udātta*) due to the accentuation rule for suffixes marked with the indicator *ñit*.

In the case of *brahmabandhuḥ*, the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) of the preceding member indeed occurs. This word *brahman* is derived by adding the suffix *manin*—as per the rule *bṛherno’cca* (Dhātupāṭha 6.74), which follows the rule *manin* (Dhātupāṭha 6.73)—and is therefore udātta on its first syllable. [Similarly,] in *gārgīpriyaḥ*.
The word *gārgī* also remains acutely accented on its first syllable due to its status as a nominal stem (*prakṛtibhāva*).

110. *niṣṭhopasargapūrvam anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.2.110). [The example is] *prakṣālitapādaḥ*. From the root *kṣal* (meaning "to cleanse," Dhātupāṭha 1597), with the suffix *ṇic*, the suffix *kta* is applied. The word *pakṣālita-* is [governed by] *gatir anantaraḥ* (6.2.49).

Thus begins the section on *audāta* [vowels]. Regarding the example "pradhautamukham": from the root *dhāv* in the sense of "motion" and "cleansing" (*dhā.pā.* 601), the suffix *kta* is applied. By the rule "cchavoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.19), *ūṭh* is substituted;
then, by "etyedhatyūṭh-su" (6.1.89), *vṛddhi* is applied.

Regarding the passage beginning with "yadi mukhaśabdaḥ": this word *mukha* can denote one's own limb (*svāṅga*). In that case, if it denotes a limb here, then by this [rule], the final syllable of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) would be udātta. In the alternative view, however, by the rule "mukhaṃ svāṅgam" (Pāṇini 6.2.167), the first syllable of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) becomes udātta. Here...

Because the rule *anyatarasyām* is understood to carry over from the preceding sūtra *niṣṭhā-upasarga-pūrvaṃ*, when the word *mukha* has its final syllable udātta, then the rule *gatir anantaraḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.49) applies. Consequently, when the word *mukha* denotes a limb of one's own body (*svāṅga*), there are three possible accents: by this [present rule], the final syllable of the first member is udātta; [and by the following rule,] *mukham*...

By the rule *svāṅgaṃ* (Pāṇini 6.2.167), the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) is udātta; however, due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *gatiranantaraḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.49), the first syllable of the first member (*pūrvapada*) is udātta. Regarding the phrase *na cet* and so forth:
if the word *mukha* here does not denote a limb of one's own body (*svāṅga*), then [the rule for *mukham* applies].

Since this is not the domain of the rule *svāṅgam* (6.2.167), the prescription of *gatiranantaraḥ* (6.2.49) applies once [the former] has been set aside. Consequently, when the word *mukha* denotes a limb of one's own body (*svāṅga*), there are two accents: the first syllable of the preceding member receives the acute accent (*udātta*), and [the final syllable of the compound] also receives the acute accent.
Regarding *ṭhprasecakamukhaḥ* (as cited in the Kāśikā):

here, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) alone remains. *Prasecakaḥ* means "that which is poured out" (*prasicyate*); it is formed with the suffix *ṇvul* in the sense of the object (*karman*), according to Pāṇini 3.3.113 (*kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*). [The compound is then formed] according to 2.2.18 (*kugatiprādayaḥ*).

This is a compound (*samāsa*). By the rule "In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, when the meaning is that of 'equal' (*tulyārtha*)" (Pāṇini 6.2.2), etc., there is the prakṛtibhāva (original form retention) of the indeclinable. Consequently, the word *prasecaka* has its first syllable as udātta (accented). In the case of *śuṣkamukhaḥ*, by the rule "For the root *śuṣ*, [there is] *ka*" (Pāṇini 8.2.51), the substitute *ka* takes the place of the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*). Due to the accent of the suffix, the word *śuṣka* has its final syllable as udātta.
In a bahuvrīhi compound, by virtue of its original form, it is always oxytone.

111. *utarapadādiḥ* | (6.2.111) 112. *karṇau varṇalakṣaṇāt* | (6.2.112) *Varṇa* refers to [words] such as *śukla* (white) and so forth; *lakṣaṇa* means that by which something is characterized, i.e., a mark (*cihna*); and *varṇa*...

The term *lakṣaṇa* here refers to the characteristic of color (*varṇalakṣaṇa*). The compound is treated as a singular (*ekavadbhāva*). The mention of *artha* (meaning) here applies to both color and characteristic, because the presentation [of the rule] is primarily concerned with the meaning. Examples are *śvetakarṇaḥ* (white-eared) and *kṛṣṇakarṇaḥ* (black-eared).
The words *śveta* and *kṛṣṇa* are oxytone (accented on the final syllable). For it is said: *śvitā varṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 742).

Thus, from this [root], the word *śveta* is derived by adding the suffix *ac*, as prescribed in the *pacādi* group. The word *kṛṣṇa* is also derived from the root *kṛṣ* in the sense of color (*varṇe*), while the suffix *nak* is applied according to the rule *iṇsiñcidīṅyuṣyavibhyo nak* (Dhātupāṭha 5.35), with the word *varṇe* being understood from the subsequent context.

In the case of the suffix *nak*, as in *dātrākarṇaḥ* ("having ears like sickles"), the suffix *ṣṭran* is applied by the rule *dāmnīśas-* (Pāṇini 3.2.182), while the rule *dhaḥ karmaṇi ṣṭran* (3.2.181) is still in force. Consequently, the word *dātra-* has its first syllable udātta. As for *śaṅkūkarṇaḥ* ("having ears like pegs"), [the suffix *u* is applied] by the rule *kṛgrorucca* (Daiva 1.109).

While the rule *kṛgrorucca* (Dhātupāṭha 6.118) is being carried over, the word *śaṅku*, ending in the suffix *ku* according to *kharu-śaṅku-pīyu-nīlaṅguli-* (Dhātupāṭha 1.120), is prescribed as having its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).
This is stated under the governing rule *dhā-pṛ-vasy-aj-yati-bhyo naḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 5.39).

The word *karṇa* is derived from the rule "ṭhṛvṛñcchasisidrupanyanisvapibhyo nit" (Daiva Upādhyāya 5.42)— that is, from the roots *kṛ*, *vṛ*, *jṛ*, *sic*, *dru*, *pan*, *ni*, and *svap*, with the suffix *nit*—
according to the rule "bhinnacchinnadrasruvasvastikasya" (Pāṇini 6.3.115).
The sūtra indicates [the following]:
"śvetapādaḥ" (white-footed), and so forth. The original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member of the compound remains.
Now, why does this not apply here in the case of "sthūlakarṇaḥ" (thick-eared)? For even by means of a thick ear, one is characterized.

Is it then established by that very definition [of *lakṣaṇa*] alone? To this he says: "For the purpose of making known the distinction among animals," and so forth. The intention is that, therefore, it does not apply in a case such as *sthūlakarṇaḥ* ("one with thick ears").
But how is the inclusion of a specific instance obtained when the statement was made in general terms?

This is because the mention of "phoneme" (*varṇa*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). If it were intended here that only a general definition (*lakṣaṇa*) should be understood, the mention of "phoneme" would not have been made; for a phoneme is indeed a definition, since it too defines [something]—as in the case of the word *kṛta*. Therefore, that very mention indicates that only a specific kind of definition is intended here.

Regarding the term "guhyataḥ": furthermore, that which is distinguished by its specific etymological explanation should be understood. In the case of *śvetapādaḥ*, the word *śveta* is derived from the root *śvit* (meaning "color," DhP 7.42) with the suffix *ac* (by the rule *pacādyac*), and thus this word is oxytone (*antodātta*). In the case of *kūṭaśṛṅgaḥ*:

Regarding *kūṭa* in the sense of "burning" (*dāhe*; some say "tormenting," *paritāpe*, according to the Dhātupāṭha 1890), the suffix *ka* is applied by rule Pāṇini 3.1.135 because it has a penultimate *i*.
Therefore, the word *kūṭa* is indeed oxytone (*antodātta*). [The example is] "one with beautiful ears" (*śobhanakarṇaḥ*). [The root is] *śubha* or *śumbha*.

From the root *śubh* (DhP 1321, 1322), the suffix *yuc* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.149 (*ṭanudātetaśca halādeḥ*). Due to the accentuation rule for *cit* suffixes, the word *śobhana* is also udātta on its final syllable.
The application of the rule regarding the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*) occurs at the beginning of the compound. The same applies to the subsequent compounds as well.
This applies prior to the designation [of compounds] as *avyayībhāva*. Therefore, in all counter-examples, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member should be cited.
113. And [the suffix *a* is applied] after the roots *saṃjñā* and *upamā*. (Pāṇini 6.2.113) Examples: *kuñcikarṇaḥ*, *maṇikarṇaḥ*. [The root *kuc* is listed as] *kuci śabde tāre* (Dhātupāṭha 184);
[and the roots] *aṇa, raṇa, vaṇa, bhaṇa, maṇa* (Dhātupāṭha 444–448).

The root *maṇ* is listed in the *bhū* class [of roots]. From these two [roots], by the rules "the suffix *in* after all roots" (*Pāṇini* 3.1.117) and "after a root with a penultimate *i*, *u*, or *ṛ*, the suffix *in* is *kit*" (*Pāṇini* 3.1.135), the suffix *in* is applied, and it is *kit*.
Consequently, the words *kuñci* and *kuñcimaṇi* have their initial syllable accented acute (*ādyaudātta*). Regarding "gokarṇaḥ": it is like a cow (*go*).
The analysis of the compound is *karṇo 'sya* ("the ears of this one"). The word *go-* has its vowel [the first syllable] stated to be udātta.

In the case of *kharakarṇaḥ*, the analysis is *khara-sya* and so forth. Since it possesses a *kha* (hole), the suffix *ra* is applied by the rule *raprakaraṇe khamukhakuñjebhya upasaṃkhyānam* (Vārttika 577); therefore, the word *khara-* is udātta on its final syllable.

114. *kaṇṭhapṛṣṭhagrīvājaṅgham* (Pāṇini 6.2.114). Because it ends in the suffix *ṭha* according to the rule *kaṇeṣṭhaḥ* (Pañcapādī Uṇādi-sūtra 1.105), the word *kaṇṭha* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).
According to the rule *ḍityapṛṣṭhagūthayūthaprothāḥ* (Daiva Uṇādi-sūtra 6.37; Pañcapādī Uṇādi-sūtra 1.106)... [the word *pṛṣṭha* is derived].

The word *pṛṣṭha* is derived as a nipātana (irregular formation) with the udātta accent on the final syllable. While the suffix *van* is being carried over from the rule "from the roots *ṭhiṇ* and *śī*, the suffix *van*" (Daiva-Uṇādi 8.126), the word *grīvā* is derived as a nipātana with the udātta accent on the final syllable by the rule "*ṭh*, *śeva*, *vaha*, *jihvā*, *grīvā*, *pva*, and *mava*" (Daiva-Uṇādi 8.128). It is struck excessively.

The suffix *yaṅ* is applied to the root *han* in the sense of "he goes" (*gacchati*), followed by reduplication. By the rule *nugato 'nunāsikāntasya* (Pāṇini 7.4.85), the augment *nuK* is added; then, by *abhyāsācca* (7.3.55), the substitution of *kuT* occurs. When the form *jaṅghanya* is established, the suffix *ac* is added as per the *pacādi* group, and the *yaṅ* is elided by *yaṅo 'ci ca* (2.4.74). Finally, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied.

The word *jaṅghā* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) by virtue of the *cit* accent. Alternatively—by the rule *ṭhhanteracÂ jaṅgha ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.74), there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *yaṅ*; then the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added, and the word *jaṅghā* has its final syllable accented by the *cit* accent. Or again—by the rule *ṭhhanteracÂ jaṅgha ca* (Pañcapādikā Upaniṣad 5.31).

The word *jaṅghā* is derived either by the rule *ṭhac tasya jaṅgha ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.97)— meaning that the suffix *ac* is applied to the root *han*, and the word *jaṅghā* is substituted for it— or else the word *jaṅghā* is explained in this manner. The term *kaṇṭhādi* refers to a *dvandva* compound denoting the collection of these [parts], beginning with the throat.

Regarding the term *śitikaṇṭhaḥ*: while the rule *sarvadhātubhya in* (Pāṇini 3.2.75) is in effect, the rule *kramitamiśāḍistambhāmata icca* (Pāṇini 3.2.141) applies; thus, by the word *śiti*, which is acutely accented on its first syllable, [the form *śitikaṇṭhaḥ* is derived]. Regarding *nīlakaṇṭhaḥ*: [the root] *nīla* is used in the sense of "color" (Dhātupāṭha 522).

Regarding *nīla-varṇe*—from this root [√nīl], the suffix *ghañ* is applied; thus, the word *nīla* is also udātta on its first syllable. Regarding *kharakaṇṭhaḥ*: the analysis of the compound is "one whose throat (*kaṇṭha*) is like that of a donkey (*khara*). The suffix *ra* is applied because of the supplementary rule (Vārttika 577): "In the section concerning the suffix *ra*, there is an addition for the words *kha*, *mukha*, and *kuñja*," since he possesses *kha* (a hole). Therefore...

The word *khara* is udātta on its final syllable. Regarding the form *uṣṭrakaṇṭhaḥ*: since the rule *uṣṭramukham* (Daiva 8.79) is in effect, the suffix *ṣṭran* is applied by the rule *uṣikhanibhyāṃ kit* (Daiva 8.82) to the root *uṣa* (Dhātupāṭha 696) meaning "to burn," with the suffix being *kit*. Thus, the word *uṣṭra* [is derived].
The first syllable is udātta.

In the word *kāṇḍapṛṣṭhaḥ*, the word *kāṇḍa-* is udātta on its first syllable according to the rule *nabviṣayasyānisantasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26), meaning "that which has the sense of *nañ* [negation] and does not end in *ani*. In the word *nākapṛṣṭham*:

Because of the rule *na bhrātṛ* (Pāṇini 6.3.75), which prescribes the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), there is no elision of the *n* in the word *nāka*. Furthermore, by the rule *nañsubhyām* (Pāṇini 6.2.172), which ordains that the final syllable of the second member is acute when preceded by *nañ* or *su*, the word *nāka* has its final vowel accented. Thus, [the compound] *gopṛṣṭham* [is explained].

"Go-iva-pṛṣṭham asya" means "his back is like that of a cow"; here the word *go* bears its [original] accent. Regarding "ajapṛṣṭham": "his back is like that of a goat (*aja*). From the root *aja* in the sense of "going" or "throwing" (DhP 230), the suffix *ac* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*).
Because the word *aja* is listed among the *ajādi* group, the substitution of *vī* for *aja* does not occur.
The word *aja* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) due to the *citsvara* rule.

In the case of *sugrīvaḥ*, because it means "one whose neck (*grīvā*) is beautiful (*su*)," the word *su* is accented on its first syllable (*ādyaudātta*) according to *Phiṭ-sūtra* 4.80: "Particles (*nipātāḥ*) are accented on the first syllable. In the case of *nīlagrīvaḥ*, [the word *nīla* is...]*nīlā*... [accented on its first syllable].*
In the word *grīvāsyeti* (meaning "whose neck"), the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *nīl* (in the sense of "blue color," Dhātupāṭha 522).

Consequently, the word *nīla* is acutely accented on its first syllable. In the word *daśagrīvaḥ* ("ten-necked"), the word *daśa* is acutely accented on its first syllable according to the rule *nraḥ saṃkhyāyāḥ* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.28). In the word *aśvagrīvaḥ* ("horse-necked")...

"Aśvasyeva grīvā asya" (his neck is like that of a horse). Both the word *go* and the word *aśva* have their [initial] vowel stated as udātta. In "nārījaṅghaḥ" (one whose shanks are like those of a woman), it means "one whose shanks are a woman's. Since "nṛnarayośca" (and for *nṛ* and *nara*) is recited among the *śarṅgarava*-class words (Gaṇasūtra 57), by that rule the first syllable is udātta. "Tālajaṅghaḥ" (one with palm-tree-like shanks).

Thus: "one whose shanks are like palm trees" (*tālo-jaṅgha*). From the root *tala* in the sense of "establishing" (*pratiṣṭhā-karaṇe*)—it belongs to the *curādi* class—and with the suffix *ac* according to the rule for words beginning with *vac*, the word *tāla* is oxytone. "One with shanks like a cow" (*go-jaṅgha*): this means one whose shanks are like those of a doe (*eṇī*).
The word *eṇī* ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.63 (*jāter astrīviṣayāt*),
and therefore it is udātta on its final syllable.

115. And [the suffix *kan* is applied] to the root *śṛṅga* in the sense of state (*avasthā*). (Pāṇini 6.2.115) [The example is] "one whose horns have emerged" (*udgataśṛṅgaḥ*). Under the governing rule "of *gam*, *i*, and *ya*" (Pañcapāda Uṇādi 1.122), and by the rule "after *bhṛñ*, there is *ki* with the augment *nuṭ*" (Pañcapāda Uṇādi 1.124), and [the rule] "and after *śṛṇāti*, there is shortening" (Pañcapāda Uṇādi 1.125).

Thus, the word *śṛṅga* is derived with the suffix *gan*; therefore, it is acute-accented on its first syllable (*ādyaudāta*). The word *udgata*, by virtue of the accent rule for words beginning with *atha* (Pāṇini 6.2.144), is acute-accented on its final syllable (*antodāta*). [The example is] "dvyaṅgulaśṛṅgaḥ" (a horn two fingers long).
In the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), a *dvigu* compound is formed meaning "that of which the measure is two fingers," according to the rule "pramāṇe dvayasac-" (Pāṇini 5.2.37).

There is elision of the suffix *mātrac*, which is prescribed by [Pāṇini 5.2.37] and others. By the rule "In the case of measure, *lo* is always substituted for *mātra* after a *dvigu*" (Vārttika 558, 559), and by the rule "The compound-final suffix *ac* is added to a *tatpuruṣa* ending in *aṅguli* when preceded by a numeral or an indeclinable" (5.4.86), the suffix *ac* is applied as a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*). By that [suffix],...

The word *dvyaṅgula* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). [The compound] *dvyaṅgula-śṛṅgaḥ* means "one whose horn is two fingers long. This is the same as the previous case. Regarding the phrase "here" (*atra*) and so forth: by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of *dvyaṅgulāvi-* is intended. [The example] *ṛṣyaśṛṅgaḥ* means "one whose horn is that of a deer."
The word *ṛṣya* is derived as an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) word with an initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*) by the rule "ṭhardhyādayaśca" and so forth. Regarding the example "meṣaśṛṅgaḥ":

it means "one whose horns are like those of a ram. From the root *miṣ* in the sense of "shining" (*svardhāyām*, Dhātupāṭha 1352), the suffix *ac* is added according to the rule "pacādyac. Consequently, the word *meṣa* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).
In the word "sthūlaśṛṅgaḥ," the word *sthūla* is udātta on its final syllable by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*).

116. *nañaḥ jaramaramitramṛtāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.116). Regarding *ajaraḥ*: "jara" means the act of aging (*jaraṇam*). [The suffix] *ap* is applied by [the rule] *ṛdorap* (3.3.57). Thus, this word is udātta on its first syllable due to the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*). [The compound] *avidyamāno jaro 'syeti* ("that which has no aging") results in *ajaraḥ*. Regarding *amaraḥ*: "mara" means the act of dying (*maraṇam*). [The suffix] *ap* is applied by [the rule] *ṛdorap* (3.3.57). Thus, this word is udātta on its first syllable due to the accent of the verbal root. [The compound] *avidyamāno mero 'syeti* ("that which has no death") results in *amaraḥ*. Regarding *amitraḥ*: "mitra" means a friend (*mitram*). [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied by [the rule] *sālvādibhyo 'ṇ* (4.2.135). Thus, this word is udātta on its first syllable due to the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadikasvara*). [The compound] *avidyamāno mitro 'syeti* ("that which has no friend") results in *amitraḥ*. Regarding *amṛtaḥ*: "mṛta" means dead (*mṛtaḥ*). [The suffix] *kta* is applied by [the rule] *niṣṭhā* (3.2.102). Thus, this word is udātta on its final syllable due to the accent of the *kta*-suffix (*ktasvara*). [The compound] *avidyamāno mṛto 'syeti* ("that which has no one who is dead") results in *amṛtaḥ*. In all these cases, the negative particle *nañ* is elided by [the rule] *nalopo nañaḥ* (6.3.73), and the resulting form is *uttarapadaprakṛtisvaraḥ* (the natural accent of the subsequent member). However, when the subsequent member is a *pūrvapadārthapradhāna* (where the meaning of the prior member is predominant), such as in *anudarā kanyā* ("a girl with a small belly"), the accent of the negative particle itself remains. This is because the *nañ* here is not included among those [words] beginning with *jara* mentioned in the sūtra. Why? Because it is not a *paryudāsa* (exclusion) but rather a *prasajyapratiṣedha* (absolute negation). In the case of *paryudāsa*, since the negative particle is connected with the subsequent member, it is included among those beginning with *jara*. But in the case of *prasajyapratiṣedha*, since the negative particle is connected with the action (*bhāva*), it is not included among those beginning with *jara*. Therefore, in the case of *prasajyapratiṣedha*, the accent of the negative particle itself remains. For example, in *abrāhmaṇaḥ* ("one who is not a Brāhmaṇa"), the word *brāhmaṇa* is derived from the word *brahmāṇaḥ* with the suffix *aṇ* by [the rule] *tasyedam* (4.3.120). Thus, this word is udātta on its final syllable due to the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadikasvara*). [The compound] *avidyamāno brāhmaṇo 'syeti* ("that which has no Brāhmaṇa") results in *abrāhmaṇaḥ*. Here, the negative particle *nañ* is elided by [the rule] *nalopo nañaḥ* (6.3.73), and the resulting form is *uttarapadaprakṛtisvaraḥ* (the natural accent of the subsequent member). However, when the subsequent member is a *pūrvapadārthapradhāna*, such as in *anuccāryaḥ śabdaḥ* ("a word that should not be uttered"), the accent of the negative particle itself remains. This is because the *nañ* here is not included among those [words] beginning with *jara* mentioned in the sūtra. Why? Because it is not a *paryudāsa* but rather a *prasajyapratiṣedha*. In the case of *paryudāsa*, since the negative particle is connected with the subsequent member, it is included among those beginning with *jara*. But in the case of *prasajyapratiṣedha*, since the negative particle is connected with the action (*bhāva*), it is not included among those beginning with *jara*. Therefore, in the case of *prasajyapratiṣedha*, the accent of the negative particle itself remains. For example, in *anuccāryaḥ*, the word *uccārya* is derived from the root *car* with the suffix *ṇyat* by [the rule] *ṛhalor ṇyat* (3.1.124). Thus, this word is udātta on its final syllable due to the accent of the *ṇyat*-suffix (*ṇyatsvara*). [The compound] *avidyamāna uccāryo 'syeti* ("that which has nothing to be uttered") results in *anuccāryaḥ*. Here, the negative particle *nañ* is elided by [the rule] *nalopo nañaḥ* (6.3.73), and the resulting form is *uttarapadaprakṛtisvaraḥ* (the natural accent of the subsequent member). However, when the subsequent member is a *pūrvapadārthapradhāna*, such as in *anudarā kanyā* ("a girl with a small belly"), the accent of the negative particle itself remains. This is because the *nañ* here is not included among those [words] beginning with *jara* mentioned in the sūtra. Why? Because it is not a *paryudāsa* but rather a *prasajyapratiṣedha*. In the case of *paryudāsa*, since the negative particle is connected with the subsequent member, it is included among those beginning with *jara*. But in the case of *prasajyapratiṣedha*, since the negative particle is connected with the action (*bhāva*), it is not included among those beginning with *jara*. Therefore, in the case of *prasajyapratiṣedha*, the accent of the negative particle itself remains. For example, in *anudarā*, the word *udara* is derived from the root *udira* with the suffix *ap* by [the rule] *ṛdorap* (3.3.57). Thus, this word is udātta on its first syllable due to the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*). [The compound] *avidyamānam udaram asyā iti* ("she whose belly does not exist") results in *anudarā*. Here, the negative particle *nañ* is elided by [the rule] *nalopo nañaḥ* (6.3.73), and the resulting form is *uttarapadaprakṛtisvaraḥ* (the natural accent of the subsequent member). However, when the subsequent member is a *pūrvapadārthapradhāna*, such as in *anudarā kanyā* ("a girl with a small belly"), the accent of the negative particle itself remains. This is because the *nañ* here is not included among those [words] beginning with *jara* mentioned in the sūtra. Why? Because it is not a *paryudāsa* but rather a *prasajyapratiṣedha*. In the case of *paryudāsa*, since the negative particle is connected with the subsequent member, it is included among those beginning with *jara*. But in the case of *prasajyapratiṣedha*, since the negative particle is connected with the action (*bhāva*), it is not included among those beginning with *jara*. Therefore, in the case of *prasajyapratiṣedha*, the accent of the negative particle itself remains

*Maraḥ*: [The suffix] *ap* is applied by the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.113). Therefore, this word is also acutely accented on the first syllable, as before. *Amitraḥ*: [The suffix] *ktra* is applied to the roots *am*, *ci*, *mi*, and *śas* (Daiva Uṇādi-sūtra 8.86). Thus, the word *mitra* is acutely accented on the final syllable. *Amṛtaḥ*: [The suffix] *kta* is applied to the root *mṛ*. Thus, the word *mṛta* is acutely accented on the final syllable. Consequently, *amṛta* is acutely accented on the first syllable.

The root *mṛṅ* (meaning "to die," Dhātupāṭha 1403) gives rise to *mṛta*. The suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) when used as a neuter noun (Pāṇini 3.3.114). Consequently, the word *mṛta* has its udātta accent on the final syllable.
In the compound *brāhmaṇamittraḥ*, the word *brāhmaṇa* has its udātta accent on the final syllable because it ends in the suffix *aṇ*. In this case...

The original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) alone remains. For example, in *aśatruḥ*: the word *śatru*, being formed with the suffix *krun* by the rule *ruśātibhyāṃ krun* (Daiva Upādhyāya 1.159), has its first syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*). This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *nañ-subhyām* (Pāṇini 6.2.172), which prescribes that a compound ending in a negative particle (*nañ*) or a word beginning with *su-* has its final syllable accented acute. The same applies to the subsequent rules as well, up to [the end of the section].
These are to be understood from the rule *kūlatīratūla* (Pāṇini 6.2.121).

117. *sormanasī alomoṣasī* (Pāṇini 6.2.117). Regarding the example *sukarmā*: [the suffix] *manin* is applied after the roots *kṛ*, *ṛ*, and *car*. (Dhātupāṭha 6.73; the reading in the Dhātupāṭha is simply *manin*; the reading in the Pañcapādī is *sarvadhātubhyo manin*—4.144).

The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.8). Regarding the form *suprathimā*: the state of being broad (*pṛthu*) is *prathimā*; this is derived from the suffix *iman* by the rule *pṛthvādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.122). The substitution of *ra* for the *ṛ*-vowel occurs by the rule *ra ṛto halāderlaghoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.161).
