Regarding the form *supayāḥ*: [it is formed from *su-paya-as*, with the elision of the final *as*].
While the rule *ṭhasun* (Daiva-nirukta 9.49) is in effect, the word *payaḥ* is derived by the rule *ṭhpibatericca* (Daiva-nirukta 9.50). Consequently, this word is udātta on its first syllable.
The lengthening occurs by the rule *atvasantasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.14). Regarding the word *suyaśāḥ*: the root *aś* means "to eat."
(Dhātupāṭha 1523) [The reading *ṭhaśū bhojane* is printed; however, according to *ṭhaśardeavane yuṭ ca* (Daivamuktāvalī 9.24;

Pañcapādī Uṇādi 3.65), the form *yaśas* is derived from the root *aśū* itself, as the phrase *yuṭ ca* does not appear in either the Pañcapādī or the Paribhāṣāvṛtti-Uṇādi. Therefore, this word has its initial vowel as the udātta accent.]

The vowel is long as before. Regarding "susrotāḥ": while the rule *asun* after all roots (*sarvadhātubhyaḥ-asun*, Pañjikā 4.188) is in force, the rule *srūribhyāṃ tuṭ ca* (Daivapadīya 9.62) applies. Thus: *susrat*, *sudhvat*.

From the roots *sransu* and *dhvan*, the suffix *kvip* is applied; by the rule *vasusraṃsu-* (Pāṇini 8.2.72), the substitution of *d* occurs for the *s*. Because that [substitution] is considered asiddha (not yet established), the condition of ending in *vas* does not apply. Examples are *surājā* and *sutakṣā*; *rājan* and *takṣan* end in the suffix *kanin*. An example is *sulomā*.

Thus [it is said]: "from the root *lū* with the suffix *manin*, [we have] *loma*" [Pāṇini 5.2.100]. Regarding "sudhā": from the root *uṣ* in the sense of "burning" (Dhātupāṭha 696), while the rule "the suffix *asi* occurs in the sense of 'pair'" (Pañcapādī Uṇādi 4.222) is in force, the suffix *kit* is applied by the rule "after *uṣ*, [the suffix *asi* is] *kit*" (Pañcapādī Uṇādi 4.234). Now, how is it that there is *suprathimā*? [It is derived from] *susrotas*, *susrat*.
In these [compounds] such as *sudhvat*, the first syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) is udātta;

however, since the technical terms *manas* and *mānas* are included here by the paribhāṣā "the mention of meaningful items includes those that are meaningful," and these two are not themselves meaningful [in this context], he says: "an-in-as-man," etc. [The rule is: *an-in-as-man*.

By stating that "grahaṇas [of suffixes] cause the application of the rule *tadanta-vidhi* (the designation of a word-form ending in that suffix) even when they are themselves meaningless or accompanied by a meaningless element," the author of the Vārttika has declared that there is indeed the inclusion of even meaningless elements such as *an*, *in*, and *asman*.

It occurs; otherwise, this [rule] would merely serve to demonstrate that the designation of the end of a word applies even in other cases. As for the statement "but *k*ap, because it is subsequent," and so forth: the scope of the rule *sormanasī* (Pāṇini 6.2.117) is, for example, *sukarmāḥ* and *suvayāḥ*; whereas the rule *kapi pūrvam* (6.2.173) applies to cases such as *sukarmakaḥ*.

This is the scope [of the rule]: *ayavakaḥ*, *suyavakaḥ*—here the suffix *kap* is applied by the rule *śeṣādvibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 5.4.154). In cases such as *sukarmakaḥ* and *susrotaskaḥ*, both [suffixes, *ka* and *kap*,] would apply; however, by the principle of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the rule *kapi pūrvam* (Pāṇini 6.2.173) takes effect.
118. *kratvādayaśca* (6.2.118).

From the root *kṛ*, the word *kratu* is formed; by that [rule], due to the *nit*-accent, *kratu* has its first syllable udātta. The words *dṛśīka* and *pratīka*, as well as those beginning with *ṭha* and *r̥dhi*, have their first syllables udātta. [The word *sukratu*] is derived from *su* + *tvarati* with the suffix *ktin*; and [the rule applies] when *tādi* follows.
By the rule *niti kṛtyatau* (Pāṇini 6.2.50), the word *pratūrti*—which is listed among the *kratu*-group words such as *prapūrti* in the *Kāśikā*—is acute-accented on its first syllable;

furthermore, by the rule *jvaratvara* (Pāṇini 6.4.20), the suffix *uṭh* is applied. From the root *hu*, the suffix *yat* is applied by *aco yat* (3.1.97), and by *yato 'nāvaḥ* (6.1.213), it is acute-accented on its first syllable.

The word *bhavya* exists. [It is derived] from the root *bhaj* with the suffix *gha*, according to the rule "ṭh-ṣaṇau gha ca. For here, by the inclusion of the marker *ghit*, it is indicated that the suffix *gha* occurs after other roots as well. Because the word *bhaga* belongs to the *vṛṣādi* group, it has an acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyaudātta*).

119. *ādyadāttaṃ dvayac chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.2.119). By the accentuation of the *ṭh*-suffix and the *niṭ*, the words *aśva* and *ratha* have the acute accent (*udātta*) on their first syllable. As for the word *aśva*, it ends in the suffix *kvan*, according to the rule *aśipuṣi...* (Pañcapāda Uṇādi 1.151) [or *aśūprupi...* (Pañcapāda Uṇādi)].

Because it has been explained [as such]; for the word *ratha* also ends in the suffix *kthan*, according to [Uṇādi Sūtra] 6.27: "The suffix *kthan* is applied after the roots *hani*, *kuṣi*, *nī*, *rami*, and *kāśi*.
It is stated that "the word *bāhu* is oxytone by virtue of the accent of its suffix," according to [Uṇādi Sūtra] 1.107: "*kur* and *bhra* [take the suffix *u*]."
Therefore, while the suffix *ku* is being applied, [the rule] "after the roots *arji*, *dṛśi*, *kamya*, *mi*, *paśi*, *bādh*, *mṛj*, *tug*, *dīrgha*, and *hakāra*" (Daiva-Uṇādi 1.112) applies.
[Note: The variant reading *arjidṛśikamyamipaśibādhāmṛjitugdhugdīrghahakāraśca* is also recorded in the Daiva-Uṇādi.]

Because that which ends in the suffix *ku* has already been explained [as being oxytone]; for example, in "suhiraṇyaḥ," the word *hiraṇya* is acute on its first syllable according to the rule "nabviṣayasyānisantasya" (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26).

120. *vīra* and *vīrya*. (Pāṇini 6.2.120) The word *vīra* is derived by adding the suffix *rak* with the augment *ak* [to the root] according to the rule *sphāyitañci-* (Uṇādisūtra 8.31). Consequently, it is udātta on the final syllable. Alternatively, [it is derived from] the root *vīra* in the sense of "valour" (Dhātupāṭha 1903).

This is because [the word] is derived from the root *pac* with the suffix *ac*; and as for "vīryam," it ends in the suffix *yat*. [The derivation is: "good for a hero" (*vīre sādhuḥ*), where the suffix *yat* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.4.98, *tatra sādhuḥ*, which belongs to the *prāg-dhita* group. Alternatively, it is derived from the root *vīra* itself, belonging to the *cur-ādi* class, by means of this very irregular formation (*nipātana*) according to the rule *aco yat*.

(3.1.97), [the word] *vīryam* ends with the suffix *yat*. This being the case, would not the rule "the first syllable of that which ends in *yat*, excepting *āvaḥ*" (6.1.213) result in its initial syllable being udātta? To this he says: "In that case," and so forth. How, then, is the mention of *vīrya* an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? To this he says: "For in that case," and so forth. If [it were] udātta on the first syllable...

In that case, the desired result would already be established by the rule *ādyaudātaṃ dvyac chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.2.119). Consequently, the author would not have included the mention of the word *vīrya* here; yet he has done so. Therefore, this very fact indicates that even for the word *vīrya*, when it ends in the suffix *yat*, the acute accent does not fall on the first syllable.
In its absence, by the rule "ṭhitisvaritam" (Pāṇini 6.1.185), there is simply the circumflex accent (svarita) on the final syllable.
121. *kūla-tīra-tūla-mūla-śālā-akṣa* in an *avyayībhāva* compound [take the suffix *ṅīp*]. (Pāṇini 4.1.51) The roots are:

*kūla* in the sense of "covering" (*saṃvaraṇe*) [Dhātupāṭha 525], and [according to another reading] *kūla* in the sense of "obstructing" (*āvaraṇe*); *pāra* and *tīra* in the sense of "completion of an action" (*karmasamāptau*) [Dhātupāṭha 1911, 1912]; *tūla* in the sense of "extracting" (*niṣkarṣe*) [Dhātupāṭha 527]; and *mūla*... [the root *mūla*].

From the roots *prati-ṣṭhā* (DhP 5.29) and the others, the suffix *ghañ* is applied; therefore, these words beginning with *kūla* have the acute accent (*udātta*) on their first syllable. From the roots *śul*, *hul*, and *patlṛ* meaning "to go" (DhP 6.843, 844, 845), the suffix *ghañ* is applied. The word *śālā* also has the acute accent on its first syllable. Its feminine gender is established by the rule *tatpuruṣe śālāyām*.

This is due to the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) [of the word *vasu*] according to the rule (Pāṇini 6.2.123). Furthermore, according to the rules "from the roots *vṛ*, *tṛ*, *vad*, *han*, *kam*, and *kas*, the suffix *sa* is applied" (Daiva Uṇādi 9.21; Pañcapādī Uṇādi 3.62)—[the Daiva version reads *vṛ*, *tṛ*, *vad*, *han*, *kam*, *kaṣ*, *yu*, *muc*;
the Pañcapādī reads *vṛ*, *tṛ*, *vad*, *ni*, *kam*, *kaṣ*—the suffix *sa* is applied]—and "from the root *aś* in the sense of eating" (Daiva Uṇādi 9.24).

And thus, because it ends in a suffix with an indicatory *pratyaya*, the word *akṣa* is udātta on its final syllable. Furthermore, even that word *akṣa* which is derived by adding the compound-final suffix *ac* according to the rule "after *akṣi*, [the suffix *ac* is added] when there is no seeing" (Pāṇini 5.4.76), is also udātta on its final syllable due to the *cit*-accent; this too is included here. [The root] *ṣam*.
From the root *sam* (meaning "absence of deficiency," as per Dhātupāṭha 829), the suffix *ac* is added according to the rule *pacādyac*;

thus, *sama-* is udātta on its final syllable. As for the word *sama-* found among the *sarvādi* group, it is listed there as anudātta; however, that too is included here. In the example *upakūlam*, it means "near the bank."

The compound *parikūlam* is an *avyayībhāva* according to the rule *ṭhavyayaṃ vibhakti* (2.1.6), etc. In the word *parikūlam*, the word *pari* is designated as a *karmapravacanīya* by the rule *ṭhupaparī varjane* (1.4.88). Due to its connection with that [designation], the ablative case is used after *kūla* by the rule *ṭhpañcamyapāṅparibhiḥ* (2.3.10).

The compound *ṭhaparibahirañcavaḥ pañcamyā* (Pāṇini 2.1.12) forms an avyayībhāva. In examples such as *suṣamam*, the substitution of *ṣ* is applied by the rule *suṣamādiṣu ca* (Pāṇini 8.3.98); however, because that [substitution] is considered *asiddha* (not yet established), this remains simply the word *sama*. These [words] are recited among the *tiṣṭhadgu*-type compounds; therefore—

By the rule "ṭhṭiṣṭhadguprabhṛtīni ca" (Pāṇini 2.1.17), he shows that these are avyayībhāva compounds. Regarding "upakumbham": here, there is only the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound. Regarding "paramakūlam" and "utamakūlam": these are bahuvrīhi compounds meaning "that which has the highest bank" and "that which has the most excellent bank," respectively.

In this case, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member alone occurs. As for the two *tatpuruṣa* compounds *paramakūla* and *utamakūla*, they will not [be subject to this rule] precisely because of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of *bahuvrīhi*;
therefore, the mention of *avyayībhāva* for the purpose of excluding those is inappropriate.

Regarding the rule *paryādibhyaḥ* and so forth: the scope (*avakāśa*) of the rule *pari-prati-upa-apa varjyamāna-ahorātrāvayaveṣu* (Pāṇini 6.2.33) is where words such as *kūla* do not occur. For example, in *pari-trigartam*, whereas the scope for the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyaudāta*) of words such as *kūla* is where words beginning with *pari* do not occur.

[The suffix] *vidyante* [is applied] as in *apakūlam*; however, in the case of *parikūlam*, both [rules] would apply, and there, by the principle of mutual exclusion (*vipratiṣedha*), this very [rule for] initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) takes effect.
This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of compounds (*samāsa*). The same applies to the subsequent rules, such as "not after *ācārya* or *rājan*" (Pāṇini 6.2.133).
Prior to this sūtra.
122. *kaṃsa-mantha-śūrpa-pāyya-kāṇḍaṃ dvigau* (Pāṇini 6.2.122).
From the rule *ṭhvṛtṛvadihanikamikaṣibhyaḥ saḥ* (Pañcapādī Uṇādi-sūtra 3.62), the suffix *sa* is applied to the root *kam*;
thus, *kaṃsa* is udātta on the final syllable. From the root *manth* (in the sense of "churning," Dhatupāṭha 42), [the suffix *sa* is applied] in the sense other than the agent (*akartari*).
The suffix *ghañ* is applied by the rule *kārake saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.19); therefore, *mantha* is udātta on its first syllable.

While the rule *pānīviṣibhyaḥ paḥ* (Pañcapādī Uṇādi 3.23) is in effect, the rule *suśṛbhyāṃ nicca* (Pañcapādī Uṇādi 3.26) applies to the root *śṛ*, resulting in the suffix *pa* with the augment *ni*. Due to the principle of multiplicity (*bāhulaka*), there is also the substitution of *ū* for *ṛ*. Now...

Or: [the word] *śūrpa* is derived with the suffix *ghañ* from the root *mā* (DhP 1612), *śūrpa māne*; therefore, the word *śūrpa* has its first syllable udātta. The word *pāyya* is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) with the suffix *ṇyat* according to Pāṇini 3.1.129, *pāyyasānnāyya*;
therefore, this [word] has its final syllable svarita. The word *kuṇḍa* has already been stated to have its accent previously. [The compound] *dvikaṃsaḥ*.

The compound "dvābhyāṃ kaṃsābhyāṃ krītaḥ" (bought for two *kaṃsas*) is a compound formed in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Then, because it is accepted that the rule of inclusion of the final element (*tadantavidhi*) applies to items preceded by a numeral before the suffix *vat*, the suffix *ṭiṭhan* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.1.25, "kaṃsāṭṭiṭhan. Furthermore, by the rule beginning with 5.1.28, "adhyardhapūrva," [the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added].

*Luk* [is applied]; *ṭh-trikaṃsaḥ*—this is the same as the previous case. *Dvimanthaḥ*—the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule *ārhādagopucchasaṅkhyāparimāṇāṭ ṭhak* (Pāṇini 5.1.19). The remainder, such as the compound formation and so forth, is as before. *Dviśūrpaḥ*—here the suffix *añ* is applied by the rule *śūrpād anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.1.26).

The remainder is as before. Regarding "dvipāyya": the suffix *yaṣṭhañ* is applied as previously mentioned; the rest is as before. Regarding "dvikāṇḍam" (or "dvikāṇḍaḥ" according to the Kāśikā): since its measure is two sections (*kāṇḍa*), the suffixes *mātraJ* and so forth are applied by the rule "pramāṇe dvayasac-" (Pāṇini 5.2.37).
In these cases, there is elision [of the final vowel] by the rule *ṭhpramāṇe lo dvigornityam* (Vārttika 558, 559), and the compound formation is as previously described.
In the example *paramakaṃsaḥ*, only the accent of the compound itself applies.

123. In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, when the word *śālā* is in the neuter gender: (Pāṇini 6.2.123). The word *śāla* has the accent prescribed in [Pāṇini] 6.2.121 (*kūlatīra*). In the examples *brāhmaṇaśālam* and *kṣatriyaśālam*, the word *brāhmaṇa* is oxytone because it ends in the suffix *aṇ*. As for the word *kṣatriya*, however—

The word *madhyodātaḥ* [is so called] because it ends in the suffix *gha*, according to Pāṇini 4.1.138: *kṣatrād dhaḥ*. Regarding the example *dṛḍhaśālam*: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; therefore, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member (*pūrvapada*) alone occurs. And the first member, being a word ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix, is oxytone (*antodāta*). But surely...
By the technical rule *lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā* (Paribhāṣenduśekhara 3), that neuter gender which is explicitly prescribed by the rule *ṭhvibhāṣā senā* (Pāṇini 2.4.25) will be understood here;
for in the case of *dṛḍhaśālam*, there is no neuter gender prescribed by an explicit rule, but rather [neuter gender] occurs by virtue of the meaning (*abhidheya*).
"It is stated that the gender and number [of a compound] are like those of its referent" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 73).

Therefore, is this mention of *tatpuruṣa* for the purpose of excluding that [general rule]? If so, then the mention of *tatpuruṣa* is for the sake of what follows: "In the sense of reproach, *cela*, *kheṭa*, *kaṭuka*, and *kāṇḍa* [form a compound with a word ending in the genitive]" (Pāṇini 6.2.126).

By this [rule], the compound *dadhi-kaṭukam* occurs precisely when *dadhi* (curd) and *kaṭuka* (pungent) are combined; for example, *dadhi-kaṭukam* and *udaśvit-kaṭukam*. However, since that [term] is employed for the sake of what follows, it also serves to establish clarity of meaning.
The technical rule regarding the application of a term according to its specific form (lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā) should not be relied upon here;
it is for this purpose that "dṛḍhaśālam" is presented as a counter-example to the mention of the term *tatpuruṣa*.

124. *kanthā* (6.2.124). From the root *kath* [meaning] "to afflict" (*kliśane*), by the rule *gurośca halaḥ* (3.3.103), the suffix *a* is added; thus, *kanthā* has its final syllable accented acute (*antodātta*). For example: *sauśamikantham*. [In this compound,] *śuśamaḥ* means one whose tranquility (*śama*) is beautiful (*śobhana*).
The suffix *iñ* is applied by virtue of the rule *tasyāpatyam* (Pāṇini 4.1.95). Consequently, the word *sauśami* is udātta on its first syllable.

Regarding *āhvakantham*: from the root *hvayati* preceded by the prefix *ā*, the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *ātaścopasarge* (3.1.136); thus, the word *āhva* is udātta on its final syllable due to the accentuation of the *atha*-group (6.2.144).
Regarding the word *cappakaṇṭham*: from the root *cap* in the sense of "consoling" (*sāntvane*;
DhP 3.99), the suffix *pa* is applied according to *pānīviṣibhyaḥ paḥ* (Dhātuupādāna 7.2); because of the word "bahulam" (variously), *pa* is also applied to *cap*.
Thus, the word *cappa* has its udātta accent on the final syllable.

125. *ādir ṛd-ahaṇādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.2.125). Since the acute accent on the final syllable of the second member was already established by the preceding rule, this [new] rule is commenced for the purpose of making the first syllable of the first member acute.
From the root *ci* with the suffix *kvip*, we have *cit*; from the root *han* with the suffix *pacādyac*, we have *hanaḥ*. This is due to a specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*).

The elision of the *ta* and the substitution of *ṇa* [occur] in the word *cihaṇa*. From the roots *mala* and *malla*, meaning "to hold" (Dhātupāṭha 493, 494), the suffix *ra* is applied; by means of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is the elision of the *la* and the substitution of *ṇa*, resulting in *cihaṇaḥ*. From the roots *mala* and *malla*, meaning "to hold" (Dhātupāṭha 493, 494), the suffix *ra* is applied; by means of irregular derivation, [the elision of the *la* and the substitution of *ṇa* occur].

There is the substitution of *ḍ* for *t*. The words *maḍara* and *maḍaḍara* are acutely accented on the first syllable (*udātta*). "Vitulā" means that which has departed from comparison (*tulā*); one who possesses that is *vitula*, and his [descendant] is *vaitula*.

Because it ends in the suffix *aṇ*, it is acutely accented on the final syllable (*antodātta*). [The word *vaitulaka* is derived as follows: from the root *kai* or *gai* meaning "to sound" (DhP 916, 917), with the suffix *ka* added after a verbal root ending in *ā* when no upasarga is present (Pāṇini 3.1.136): *paṭat* [he] sounds. Thus, *vaitulaka*.

*Paṭatka* means "white within. From the root *lā* meaning "to take" (*dhā.pā.* 1058), preceded by the prefix *ā*, the suffix *ka* is applied by this very rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), resulting in *citāla*.
His descendant is *caitāli*, formed by the suffix *iñ* according to *Pāṇini* 4.1.95; he is the performer of that [action].

*Caitālikarṇaḥ*. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, which is acute-accented on the first syllable by virtue of the original accentuation of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*). For the first member is indeed acute-accented on its first syllable by the rule governing suffixes ending in *ñi* (*ñit-svara*). Others, however, read the entire form as *caitālikarṇiḥ*, ending in the suffix *iñ*. [The root] *kuk* and *vṛk* [are used] in the sense of "seizing."

From this [root] *dhā* (DhP 91, 92), the suffix *kvip* is applied along with the augment *kuk*, resulting in *kuk*. From the root *kuṭ* in the sense of "crookedness" (DhP 1366), the suffix *ka* is applied by virtue of its having an *iṅ* vowel as its penultimate letter (*igupadhāt kaḥ*), yielding *kuṭaḥ*. Thus we have *kukaḥ* and *kuṭaḥ*; from these, *kukkuṭaḥ* is formed. It is oxytone (*antodātta*) due to the accent of the compound. From the root *ci* ("to gather"), *kvip* is applied, yielding *cit*. From the root *kaṇ*, the suffix *yac* is applied by virtue of belonging to the *pacādi* class.

*Kaṇaḥ*, *citaḥ kaṇāśca* (which becomes *cikkiṇaḥ*), where the letter *t* is changed to *k* by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Others read *citkaraṇaḥ*. It is recorded in tradition that these, beginning with *cihaṇa*, are names for eunuchs (*muṣya-nāmadheyāni*).

Now, what is the purpose of including the word *ādi* (beginning), since *ādi* is already being carried over [from a previous rule]? To this he says: "While *ādi* is being carried over," and so forth. For the previous mention of *ādi* was connected with the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). [This present mention, however, pertains to] the prior members (*pūrvapada*).

The initial acute accent (ādy-udātta) is desired for words such as *cihaṇa* and others; therefore, the mention of "beginning" (*ādi*) is repeated so that those words, when they function as the first member of a compound, may likewise have their initial syllable acutely accented.
126. The words *cela*, *kheṭaka*, and *kaṭuka* are used in the sense of reproach (*garhā*).

(Pāṇini 6.2.126) From the roots *velṛ*, *celṛ*, and *kelṛ* meaning "to move" (*calane*) [Dhātupāṭha 535, 536, 537], the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of a technical name (*saṃjñā*), resulting in *cela*, which refers to a garment (*vastra*). The root *khiṭa* means "to terrify" (*utrāsane*) [Dhātupāṭha 302].

From the root *tras* (to fear), the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) according to Pāṇini 3.3.18, yielding *kheṭa*; this is a name for grass. Due to the accent of the *ñit*-suffix, the words *celakheṭa* have an acute accent on their first syllable. From the word *kaṭu*, the suffix *kan* is applied in the sense of a proper name (Pāṇini 5.3.75);
this is a term denoting a quality with an acute accent on its first syllable. It has also been stated that *kāṇḍa* likewise has an acute accent on its first syllable.

"By means of similarity with cloth (*cela*) and so forth, there is a censure (*garhā*) of sons and the like. For example, just as cloth is produced by a weaver of low birth (*akulīna*), so too a son born of one of low birth is called "cloth-son" (*putracela*). Just as a stalk (*kāṇḍa*) causes pain to living beings, so too...
It is also *bhūta*. In that word, the suffix *putra* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) by the accent of the suffix itself.
For, while the rule *ṭhamicimidiśasibhyaḥ kyaḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 8.86;
Pañcapādī 4.163) is still in force, the rule *puro hrasvaśca* (Dhātupāṭha 8.87; Pañcapādī 4.164) [reading *pūño hrasvaśca* in the Daiva-pāṭha and *puvo* in the Pañcapādī] applies.

And *hrasva*—the word *putra*, ending in the *kta* suffix (*paṃ.u.ṭ*), is derived [as follows]: the word *bhāryā* has a circumflex accent on its final syllable because it ends in the suffix *ṇyat* according to Pāṇini 3.1.124 (*ṛhalorṇyat*). From the root *ṇaha* "to bind" (DhP 1166), preceded by the prefix *upa*, the suffix *kvip* is applied, and [the lengthening occurs] by Pāṇini 6.3.116 (*nahivṛti*).

By these and other rules, there is lengthening of the preceding vowel; by the rule *naho dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.34), the letter *n* is replaced by *dh*, which then undergoes *cartva* (substitution by *t*). The word *upānat* is oxytone (*antodātta*) due to the accent of a *kṛt*-derivative suffix.

[The formation of] *nagara* is explained by the rule *nagarāt kutsanaprāvīṇyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.128): "the suffix *aṇ* is added after *naga* when contempt or skill is expressed. This means that because trees (*naga*) exist in this place, it is called a *nagara*.

Thus, from this very rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the suffix *rap* is applied; therefore, *nagara* is udātta on its final syllable. *Dadhi* is derived from the root *dhā* with the *kvin* suffix by the rule *thādṛgama-* (Pāṇini 3.2.171); therefore, it is udātta on its first syllable. *Udaśvit* means "swollen by water" (*udakena śūyate*); [it is formed] with the *kvip* suffix. [This is according to the rule] *kvibvacipracchi-*.

Because of the frequent occurrence of such forms as in *da.u.10.2*, the long vowel does not occur here. By the rule *udakasyodaḥ saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 6.3.57), there is the substitution of *uda-* for *udaka-*, and by the accent of a *kṛt*-derivative, the final syllable is acute (*udātta*).
The word *bhūta-* is also acute on the final syllable because it ends in a *niṣṭhā* suffix. As for the word *prajā-*, [it is governed] by the rule *upasarge ca...* [Pāṇini 3.2.99].

The word [celaka] ends in the suffix *ḍa* according to Pāṇini 3.2.99 (*saṃjñāyām*), and thus it is oxytone due to the accent of the suffix *kṛt*. In the example "paramacela," honor is understood, not censure.
127. *cīra* is an *upamāna*.
(Pāṇini 6.2.127) While the rule *su-sūdā-gṛdhibhyaḥ kran* (Dhātupāṭha 8.42; Pañcapādī 2.25) is in force, [the Vārttika] *śusicimīnāṃ dīrghaśca* applies.

The word *cīra* ends in the suffix *kran* [according to Pāṇini 3.2.176], and therefore it is udātta on its first syllable. In the compound *vastra-cīram*, the compound is formed as before because it belongs to the *vyāghrādi* group. From the root *vas* in the sense of "covering," the suffix *ṣṭran* is applied to form *vastra*; thus, it is udātta on its first syllable.
Regarding the term "kambalacīra," the word *kambala* is oxytone (accented on the final syllable) according to the rule "ghṛtādīnāñca" (Phiṭ-sūtra 1.21).

128. *palalasūpaśākaṃ miśre* (Pāṇini 6.2.128). [The root] *pala* [in the sense of] "to protect" (Dhātupāṭha 839), or [the root] *pala* [in the sense of] "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 840); with [the suffix] *kala* present [according to] *kalastṛpaśca* (Daiva-Uṇādi-sūtra 8.107), [the form *palala* is derived]; then, by *vṛṣādibhyaścit* (Daiva-Uṇādi-sūtra 8.109), [the suffix *ac* is added].

Because the suffix *kal* is *cit*, the word *pala* has an udātta accent on its final syllable. While the rule "ṛ-ud-ebhyo ṇiluk ca" (Dhātupāṭha 8.39) applies, the elision of the *ṇi* suffix occurs here by virtue of the word "bahulam" (in various cases) in the rule "bahulam anyatrāpi saṃjñā-chandasoḥ" (Dhātupāṭha 8.40). [The suffix] *pa* is added after the roots *pā*, *nī*, and *viṣ* (Dhātupāṭha 7.2).
With reference to this, the word *sūpa* is derived by adding the suffix *pap* according to the rules "ṭhstuvo dīrghaśca" (Dhātupāṭha 7.4) and "suśṛbhyāṃ nicca" (Dhātupāṭha 7.6);
therefore, it is acute-accented on the first syllable. Furthermore, [the word *sūka*] is derived from the roots *iṇ*, *bhī*, *kṛ*, *pā*, *śal*, *yat*, and *arci* with the suffix *kan*.

Because of the frequent usage [of suffixes] as stated in *da.u.* 3.21, the suffix *ka*—characterized by the rule for roots ending in *i* or *u* (*ig-upadhāt-kaḥ*)—is applied to the root *śo* (meaning "to thin," *dhā.pā.* 1270). Consequently, the word *guḍa* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). Furthermore, from the root *dhṛ* (meaning "to flow," *dhā.pā.* 1096), the suffix *kta* is applied according to *da.u.* 6.9 (*añci-dhṛ-sibhyaḥ ktaḥ*), and thus...
*Ghṛta* is udātta at the end. According to the rule *mudi-gror g-gau* (Daiva-Upaniṣad 3.66), the suffix *gak* is applied to the root *mud*; therefore, *mudga* is udātta at the end.

129. *kūlasūdasthalakarṣāḥ saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 6.2.129). The word *kūla* has its accent as previously stated. From the root *ṣūda* in the sense of "flowing" (*dhā.pā.* 1717), by the rule *igupadhāt kaḥ* (3.1.135), the word *sūda* is derived; thus, it is udātta on the final syllable. [The root] *sthala* is used in the sense of "standing" (?).

Because of this, by the rule *pacādyac*, the word *sthalam* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). The word *karṣa-* is accented on the final syllable by the rule *karṣātvato ghaño 'nta udāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.159). In examples such as *dākṣikūlam*, the words *dākṣi-* and *māhaki-* are accented on the first syllable because they end in the suffix *iñ*. The word *deva-*...

Because it ends in the suffix *ac* added after a root beginning with *pac*, it is udātta on its first syllable. The word *bhājī* is udātta on its final syllable because it ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* according to the rule *jānapadādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 4.1.42). The word *dāṇḍāyana* ends in the suffix *phak* because it belongs to the *naḍādi* group (Pāṇini 4.1.99); therefore, by the rule *kitaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.165), it is udātta on its final syllable.

But surely the word *sthala* is employed in the Sūtra; how then can the word *sthalī* be cited as having its first syllable udātta when it serves as the final member of a compound? To this he says: "The mention of *sthala*, etc."

130. *rājyam* [is formed] when it is not a *karmadhāraya* compound. (Pāṇini 6.2.130) *Rājyam* means the state or the action of a king (*rājan*). Because it ends in the suffix *ṣyañ*, its first syllable is udātta. The words *brāhmaṇa* and *kṣatriya* have their accents as previously stated.

Regarding the phrase "ṭhcelarājya" and so forth: the scope for the accent [of the first member] as in *bhāryācela* ("the wife’s garment") and *brāhmaṇarājyam* ("the kingdom of the Brahmins")—which is prescribed by the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-* (Pāṇini 6.1.2) and so on—is exemplified by *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* ("one who has departed from Kauśāmbī"); here, however, both [rules] would apply simultaneously, as in *kucelaḥ* ("badly clothed").

Regarding the term "kurājyam," it becomes a svarita accent by means of the prior prohibition; by the word "ādi" (and so forth), there is the inclusion of the svaritas belonging to the *vargya* class and others.

131. *vargyādayaśca* (Pāṇini 6.2.131). The words beginning with *vargya* and ending with *digādi* have the suffix *yat*. Among them, those consisting of two syllables are accented on the first syllable by the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ* (6.1.213). The remaining ones, however, are circumflexly accented (*svarita*) by the rule *tit svaritam* (6.1.185).

Thus, these [words] have a svarita accent at the end. The word *vāsudeva* has the udātta accent on the final syllable because the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *ṛṣyaṇḍhaka-* (Pāṇini 4.1.114), signifying the descendant of Vasudeva. [The word *arjuna* is derived] from the root *arja* meaning "to earn" (Dhātupāṭha 224), which belongs to the curādigaṇa and takes the causative suffix *ṇic*; from this, the suffix *un* is applied by the rule *ajerṇiluk ca* (Daiva Uṇādisūtra 5.57).

Thus, the suffix *uṇ* is applied; by that, *arjuna* is oxytone (having the acute accent on the final syllable). Regarding the phrase "and so forth (*ityevamādayaḥ*)," the word "and so forth" includes those suffixes which are recited after the word *pakṣa*.

132. *putraḥ pumbhyaḥ* (6.2.132). [The word] *putra* [retains its accent when following] masculine [words]. For example: *ṭhkaunaṭiputraḥ*. The word *putra* has its stated accent (*uktasvara*). *Kaunaṭi* is the descendant (*apatya*) of *Kunaṭa*;
therefore, this [word *kaunaṭi*] is udātta on the first syllable. The words *dāmakamāhiṣaka* are also udātta on the first syllable because they end in the suffix *kan*.

Regarding "Gārgīputraḥ" and "Vātsīputraḥ": from the words *gārgya* and *vātsya*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṅyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.16). Consequently, the words *gārgī* and *vātsī* have their first syllable as udātta due to the accent of the *ñit* suffix. In all these counter-examples within this section on Tatpuruṣa compounds, the rule *samāsasya* (6.1.223) applies.
Thus, its being udātta at the end is to be understood.
133. Not [after words] denoting an *ācārya*, a king (*rājan*), an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), or those designated as kinsmen (*jñāti*).

(6.2.133) Since the preceding rule would have resulted in the initial syllable of the word *putra* being acute even when following words such as *ācārya* and the rest, this prohibition is stated. Consequently, the final syllable of the compound alone becomes acute.

Regarding the phrase "due to the mention of the word *ākhyā*," etc.: the mention of the word *ākhyā* is connected individually with each [term], such as *ācārya* and so forth. Thus, since the mention of *ākhyā* is not set aside, there is the inclusion of synonyms for that *ācārya* and so on, as well as its qualifiers; for example, "the son of the teacher" (*ācāryaputraḥ*).

An example of the essential form (*svarūpa*) is "the son of the teacher" (*upādhyāyaputra*); an example of a synonym (*paryāya*) is "the son of Śākaṭāyana" (*śākaṭāyanaputra*); an example of a specific term (*viśeṣa*) is "the son of the king" (*rājaputra*). An example of a synonym is "the son of the Lord" (*īśvaraputra*); an example of a specific term is "the son of Nanda" (*naṇdaputra*).

"Son of a priest" (*ṛtvikputraḥ*) refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*). "Son of a sacrificer" (*yājakaputraḥ*) refers to a synonym (*paryāya*). "Son of a *hotṛ* priest" (*hotuḥputraḥ*) refers to a specific instance (*viśeṣa*). "Son of one who is joined" (*saṃyuktaputraḥ*) refers to the essential nature.
"Son of a relative" (*sambandhiputraḥ*) refers to a synonym. "Son of a maternal uncle's brother" (*syālaputraḥ*) refers to a specific instance.

In the term *jñātiputraḥ*, it is the essential form (*svarūpa*) [that is intended]; in *bhrātuṣputraḥ*, it is the specific [form]. Regarding the rule *kasyādiṣu ca* (Pāṇini 8.3.48), there is the substitution of *ṣ*. In that context, the word *ācārya* has a circumflex accent (*svarita*) on its final syllable due to the accent of the entire formation (*kṛtsvara*).
For it is derived from the root *car* with the prefix *āṅ* and the suffix *ṇyat*.

The word *upādhyāya* has its accent on the final syllable (*antodāta*) by virtue of the rule *sthāthādisvareṇa* (Pāṇini 6.2.144); it is derived with the suffix *ghañ* according to the rule *ṭiṅśca* (3.3.21). The word *rājan* has its accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāta*), because it ends in the suffix *kanin*. The word *īśvara* has its accent on the final syllable (*antodāta*), by virtue of the rule *stheśabhāsa-* (3.2.175) and others.
Because it ends in a *varac* suffix, the word *nanda* is also oxytone (*antodātta*), as it ends in a vowel. The word *ṛtvij* ends in the *kvin* suffix by the rule "ṛtvig-dadhṛk... (Pāṇini 3.2.59);
it is oxytone due to the accent of the *kṛt* suffix. The word *yājaka* ends in the *ṇvul* suffix, and therefore—

The word *lit* is acute on the first syllable by virtue of its accentual class (*udātta*). The word *hotṛ*, ending in the suffix *tṛn*, is acute on the first syllable. The word *saṃyukta* is acute on the first syllable according to Pāṇini 6.2.49, *gatir anantaraḥ*. From the root *syal* (meaning "to deliberate" or "to go")—which belongs to the curādi group and takes the causative suffix *ṇic*—the word *syāla* is derived with the suffix *ac*; thus, it is acute on the final syllable. [The root] *jñā*...

Therefore, by the rule *kticktau ca saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.174), the word *jñāti* has its final syllable udātta. Furthermore, having introduced the rule *tṛnstṛcau śaṃsikṣadādibhyaḥ* (Daiva-Uṇādi-sūtra 2.1), the word *bhrātṛ* is derived as ending in the suffix *tṛn*; consequently, it has its first syllable udātta.

This word *saṃyukta* exists as both a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*) which refers to brothers-in-law, fathers-in-law, and so forth, by virtue of a relationship established through marriage, and as an action-based term (*kriyāśabda*) which applies everywhere based on some kind of connection; here, it is the conventional term that is intended. Why is this so?

Because the wives of teachers (ācāryānī) are mentioned separately; for if there were a mention of the word "action" (kriyā), then since [the prohibition] would already be established by the mention of those who are "associated," one would not have made a separate mention of the teachers and so forth. For they too [are associated] through a connection established by learning and the like.

They are indeed connected. Therefore, there is the inclusion of a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*). Consequently, the prohibition does not apply to that which is a verbal noun (*kriyāśabda*) which is a connected word.

134. *cūrṇādīny aprāṇiṣaṣṭhyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.134). From the root *cūrī* "to burn" (Dhātupāṭha 1158), the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is applied; thus, *cūrṇa-* is udātta on its final syllable.
[The word] *kariṇa-pāti* ("protecting elephants") is derived from the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ* (3.2.3); in this case, the letter *pa* optionally becomes *va*.

It is applied as a suffix: *karipaḥ*, *karivaḥ*. By the accent of the *kṛt* suffix, or by the accent of the *thā-thādi* group, it is oxytone (*antodātta*). According to [Pāṇini 3.2.168] *maha itraṇ ca*, and because of the word *bahula*, it also occurs after the root *śak*: *śākinam*; by the accent of the suffix, it is madhyodātta. [The suffix] *aṭac* is applied after *śaka* and others.

(From *Daivātmanuśāsana* 5.2; *Pañcapādikā* 4.81) [The suffix *aṭan* is applied after words such as *śaka*—see *Pañcapādikā* ṭīkā: *śakaṭam*. That which carries it is *śakaṭavāh*, and from that comes *śākaṭam*. It is udātta on the final syllable by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
*Drākṣā* is so called because it withers quickly (*drāg drutaṃ kṣīyate*); this is due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group. This word is udātta on the final syllable.

The word is *śabda*. From the verbal roots *tuṣa*, *hrasa*, *hlasa*, and *rasa* in the sense of "sound" (*śabde*)—[Dhātupāṭha 710, 711, 712, 713]—the suffix *tan* is applied after these, by virtue of the rule of frequent usage (*bahulavacanāt*), according to the *Daiva-kośa* (6.7) and *Pañcapādī Uṇādi-sūtra* (3.86): "From the roots *hasi*, *mṛg*, *ṛṇ*, *vam*, *dam*, *mil*, *ū*, *pū*, *dhūrv*, and *vī*, the suffix *tan* is added. [Note: The variant reading *hasimṛgriṇvamidamitamilūpūdhūrvibhyastan* is cited from the *Daiva-kośa*].

The word *hasimṛgaraṇvāmidamūlapūrvibhyas tan* (Pāṇini 3.2.168) prescribes the suffix *tan*. Due to a specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*), there is also lengthening of the vowel; thus, *tūsta* is udātta on its first syllable. Regarding the derivation of *kutsitam dunoti*, the rule *kvib avaci praccchi* etc. (Vārttika 288) contains a split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) by taking *kvip* as a separate rule.

From the root *du* in the sense of "affliction" (*upatāpe*, Dhp 1256), the suffix *kvip* is applied; due to the rule of diversity (*bahulavacanāt*) or because the teaching of augments is not universal (*anityatvāt*), there is an absence of the *tuk* augment. Furthermore, by virtue of the same rule of diversity, the *mum* augment is added to the preceding word—thus *kuṇḍu*. Then, from the root *māṅ* in the sense of "measuring" (*māṅ māne*), [the suffix *kvip* is applied] as in *tanmimīte*.
From this [root *kund*] with the suffix *ka*, *kunduma* is udātta on the final syllable.
By the rule "uṣikuṭidalikacikhajibhyaḥ kapan" (Daiva Uṇādi 7.9), *dalapa* has the udātta on the first syllable.
By the rule "atyavicamitaminami" (Daiva Uṇādi 9.44) and so forth, the suffix *asac* is applied—thus *camasa*; from that...

The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.63 when denoting a genus (*jāti*). From the root *cam* in the sense of "to satisfy" (*tṛpti*) [DhP 783], the suffix *kavip* is added, resulting in *cak*. From the root *kan* in the sense of "shining, beauty, or motion" [DhP 460; variant: *kana* in the sense of shining, beauty, or motion], the suffix *ac* is added, resulting in *kanaḥ*. Thus, *cakakanaḥ*.

*Caulaḥ* is the offspring of *cola*; the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.170 (*dvyañmagadha* etc.). These are *cūrṇa* and the others. Regarding *mudgacūrṇam*: by the rule *mudi grorgaggau* (Daiva Upādhyāya 3.66), *mudga* is oxytone. Regarding *masūracūrṇam*: [the suffix] *ūran* is applied to *masi*.

(Pradīpa on Daśapādī Uṇādisūtra 8.95) *masūra* is udātta on the first syllable. In the example "matsyacūrṇam," the word *matsya* is udātta on the final syllable by the accentuation rule for nominal stems (*prātipadika-svara*). Regarding the statement "in that case, the form ending in the genitive is indeed [meant] by the mention of *u*," this indicates an identity of meaning [between the two].
He shows this in the two sūtras. But how is it that only that which ends in the genitive case is understood by the term *upagraha*?

To this he says: "by the usage of the ancient teachers" (*pūrvācāryopacāreṇa*). For the ancient teachers used to employ the term *upagraha* for that which ends in the genitive case. Therefore, here, by reason of the usage of the ancient teachers—
The term *upagraha* is understood here as being in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*). This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation rules for compounds;
the same applies to the three subsequent rules as well.
135. And six [words] beginning with *kāṇḍa*.
(6.2.135) The six words beginning with *kāṇḍa*, which are included in the four rules starting with "celakheṭakaṭukakāṇḍam" (6.2.126), are understood here. If this is so, then by those very [rules]...

The initial acute accent (*ādyaudātatva*) for these is already established by the *yogavibhāga* rule; why, then, is this [sūtra] stated? It is for the purpose that [the suffix] should apply even where it is not prescribed by those [rules], as in *prāṇiṣaṣṭhaḥ*, and so that it does not occur after the word *ṣaṣṭhī*. For example, in *darbhakāṇḍam*, the suffix *bha* is applied according to the rule *dṛḍhalibhyāṃ bhaḥ* (Paṅktipāṭha 3.151).

The word *darbha* has its acute accent on the final syllable; alternatively, this is according to the *Phitsūtra* rule: "And for grasses and grains consisting of two syllables" (*tṛṇadhānyānāṃ ca dvyakṣarāṇām*, PhiSū 2.27).

As for the word *śarakāṇḍa*, the word *śara* also has its acute accent on the first syllable by that same aforementioned rule "for those consisting of two syllables. The same applies to the word *kuśa*. Likewise, the word *tila* also [has its acute on the first syllable].

The words *palala* and *mūlaka* have the accents already stated. The word *nada* is listed among the *pacādi* group; because it is marked with the *ṭi*-sign (*ṭit*), the suffix *ṅīp* is added after the word *nada*, and by the rule "of that which ends in *ṭi*" (*ṭyasyeti ca*, 6.4.148), there is the elision of the final vowel *a*.

Furthermore, by the rule "and [the first syllable] of an unaccented [word] where an acute accent is elided" (*anudātasya ca yatrodātalopaḥ*, 6.1.161), the *ṅīp* receives an acute accent. By this [rule],...

The word *nadī* has its acute accent on the final syllable. According to the *Phiṭ-sūtra* (1.2), "of *pāṭala*, *pālaṅka*, *ambā*, *sāgara*, and their synonyms," the word *samudra* has its acute accent on the final syllable by virtue of the *Phiṭ* rules. Regarding the term *rāja-śūda*:
the word *śūdra* is listed after the six [classes]; therefore, in this case, there is only the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound.
It occurs; and all those [compounds], such as *darbhakāṇḍa* and so forth, are genitive (ṣaṣṭhī) compounds.

136. *Kuṇḍam* means a forest (*vanam*). (Pāṇini 6.2.136). Regarding the word *kuṇḍa*, it is said that here it refers to a forest by way of similarity to a *kuṇḍa*. Just as a *kuñja* is a shelter for water and such things, so too is a forest. Therefore, it is used here through its similarity to a *kuñja*.

The word *kuṇḍa* occurs in the sense of "forest. For indeed, a thing may receive the name of another through similarity, as in the case of "the fire-gem" (*agnimaṇi*) or "the crow" (*baka*). [In the example] *mṛtkuṇḍam*, the word *kuṇḍa* here refers to a particular shape in a modification of clay, not to a forest.
Therefore, it retains its status as having the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound.
137. *prakṛtyā bhagālam* | (6.2.137) The mention of *bhagālam* here is for the sake of the meaning (*arthagrahaṇam*); for the indication is governed by the primary importance of the meaning.

Indeed, it has been stated that when an indication is governed by the primary importance of the meaning, there is no apprehension of the formal word itself (*svarūpagrahaṇam*). And since the meaning is being apprehended...
This grammatical operation is understood to apply to words expressing that [meaning]. For this very reason, he says: "when expressing *bhagāla*, etc.

In the example *kumbhībhāgālam*, the word *kumbhī* is oxytone because it ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.63 (*jāterastrīviṣayādayopadhāt*). It is stated that "words such as *bhagāla* are middle-accented."
This is because Phiṣ 2.42 states, "In ṭha, la, gā, and ante, as well as in the two [cases] and in bahula,
the vowel is acute," thereby prescribing the acute accent for the vowel *ā* in these words.

138. *śiti-nitya-bahvaj-bahuvrīhāv-abhasat* (Pāṇini 6.2.138). [The example is] *śitipādaḥ*. The word *śiti* is acute on its first syllable by the rule *varṇānāṃ taṇatinitāntānām* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.33). [The examples] *aṃsauṣṭha-śabdau*, etc., [are given]. [The root] *am* [is used] in the sense of disease.

From the root *as* (DhP 1720), the word *asa* is derived with the suffix *san* according to Pāṇini 3.1.5; the word *oṣṭha* is also derived with the suffix *than* according to Dhatupāṭha 6.29. Thus, these two [words are formed].
Because the suffix *nit* is [marked with *n*], it is acute on the first syllable.

In the example "darśanīyapādaḥ," the word *darśanīya* ends in the suffix *anīyar*; therefore, by the rule "upottamaṃ riti" (Pāṇini 6.1.217), it is acute on the penultimate syllable. Consequently, in this case, [the accent of] the preceding member...

It retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) alone; the same applies to the subsequent counter-examples. But how is it that the word *kakuda* is not always polysyllabic? To this he says: "There is elision of *kakuda* when [denoting] a state," and so forth. Regarding the example *śitilalāṭaḥ*: the root *lala* is used in the sense of "desire" (*īpsā*).

From this [root], the suffix *āṭ* is applied by the rule "ṭhuṇādayo bahulam" (Pāṇini 3.3.1); therefore, the word *lalāṭa* has its first syllable udātta. Regarding "śitipādaḥ": in the compound "śiteḥ pādaḥ," only the accent of the compound (*samāsasvara*) occurs. Regarding "śitibhasat": [the suffix] *i* is applied by the rule "śṛdṛbhasodiḥ" (Daiva Upādhyāya 6.42).
Thus the word *bhasat* is etymologically derived; consequently, it is udātta on its final syllable.

139. *kṛt* [suffixes] come after a word denoting a direction (*gati*), an agent (*kāraka*), or a subordinate word (*upapada*). For example, in *prakārakaḥ* and *prahārakaḥ*, the suffix is *ṇvul*. In *prakaram* and similar forms, the suffix is *lyuṭ*. In *īṣatkaraḥ* and similar forms, the suffix is *khal* by virtue of the rule *īṣadduḥsuṣu* (Pāṇini 3.3.126).
In this case, where there is an indeclinable as the first member of the compound, the compound is formed by Pāṇini 2.2.17, *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha*.

As for the rule *kārakāt*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) should be understood as referring to the object (*karman*) among the kārakas, according to Pāṇini 2.3.65, *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*. For *idhma* and the others are indeed [the objects] of the action of cutting (*vraścana*).

Because they are most desired to be pervaded, they undergo the status of the object (*karman*). However, in examples such as *īṣatkaraḥ*, there is a compound by the rule *upapadam atiṅ* (Pāṇini 2.2.19). In that case, the word *pra-* is acute-accented on its first syllable according to the rule *upasargāś cābhivarjam* (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.81). For the word *idhma-*...

[The word *palāśa*] is oxytone because it ends in the suffix *mak*, according to the rule *ṭhiṣiyudhīndhi-* (Uṇādi Sūtra 7.31). [The root] *śo* [is used] in the sense of "making thin" (Dhātupāṭha 1.145). [The word *palāśa* is derived as follows: that which "becomes thin" (*śyatoti*) is *pala-*. Then, by the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3), the suffix *ka* is added. Thus, *palāśaḥ* [is formed]; its accent is determined either by the *kṛtsvara* (the accent of the suffix *ka*) or by the *thāthādisvara* (the accent of the group beginning with *tha*).

(6.2.144) It has an udātta accent on the final syllable. When the suffix *ṇic* is added to the root *śad*, the substitution of *t* for *ś* is applied by the rule *śaderagatau taḥ* (7.3.42), resulting in *śātanaḥ* when the suffix *lyuṭ* follows.
When the substitution of *l* for *ś* is applied to the root *śri* with the suffix *ḍan* in the sense of "in *śman*" according to *śmani śrayaterḍan* (Daiva 1.161), the form *kalpanaḥ* results.

The word *īṣat* has its final syllable acute (antodātta), because it is read as such among the words beginning with *svar-*. The words *su-* and *dur-* have their initial syllables acute (ādātta), because they are read as such among the prepositions (*prādayaḥ*). "In all these cases, the accent is that of the *liṭ*-suffix"; furthermore, that [accent] arises from the suffix itself.
The first member [of the compound] has the udātta accent.

By stating "‘Devadattasya’ is a genitive case characterized by the *śeṣa* (remainder) relation," he rejects the possibility that it is a genitive of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*). For if this were a genitive of the object, Devadatta would necessarily be a *kāraka* (participant in an action) in this context; and so...
And thus, the counter-example is not tenable.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *kāraka* (the factor of action)? If it is argued that it is so that [the suffix] might not apply in cases such as *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* ("one who has gone out from Kauśāmbī"), this is not so; for indeed, those particles (*prādayaḥ*) which are connected with an action [denote the *kāraka*].

The terms *prati*, *gati*, and *upasarga* are technical designations (*saṃjñā*). Now, since the word *kauśāmbī* does not denote an action, how could *niḥ* have the designation of *gati* with respect to it? To this, he says:
"The mention of *kṛt* [suffixes] is for the sake of clarity. If, then, there is the mention of *kṛt*...

[The suffix] *kriyate* [is applied]; however, in the case of *prapacatitarām*, the *para-kṛti-svara* (the accent of the final syllable of the preceding word) would not be obtained. Consequently, setting aside the compound accent (*samāsa-svara*), the accent of the indeclinable (*avyaya-svara*) alone would result. To this, he says: "In *prapacatitarām*," and so forth. For here, from the word *pacati*, there is the desire to express excellence (*atiśaya*).

The suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* [are applied]. Then, by the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18), the word *pra* enters into a compound (*samāsa*) with *śabda*. Once the compound is formed, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member applies according to the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-* (Pāṇini 6.2.2). Subsequently, [the suffix *kvi* is applied] by the rule *kimetiṅvyaya-* (Pāṇini 5.4.11).

By these and other such rules, the suffix-accent (pratyayasvara) prescribed by Pāṇini 6.1.163—"and that which ends in ām is udātta"—would apply; however, since this is an indeclinable accent (avyayasvara), it is "later-remaining" (satiśiṣṭa).
And it has been stated that that which is later-remaining possesses greater force. Therefore, even though this [rule] is made when there is the mention of a *kṛt* suffix for the ending in *ām*—

Even though the *prakṛtisvara* (the accent of the base) would apply when [the suffix] *sati* is present, nevertheless the *āmsvara* (the accent of the suffix *ām*) indeed occurs, because it is *satiśiṣṭa* (remaining after others have been applied). Now, how then can there be a compound with that which ends in *tarap* and so forth? And why should it not be so?
[Because of the rule: "The statement regarding the compounding of *gatis*, *kārakas*, and *upapadas* with *kṛt*-derived forms occurs prior to the application of case-endings (*sup*)."
Is this not so because of the statement [in the *Haiyaṅgavīnapāda*, 88]? This is not a fault; for in this regard there are two views:

one view is that a compound occurs only with *kṛt*-suffixes after a *gati*, a *kāraka*, or an *upapada*, and that moreover, it occurs prior to the production of the nominal suffix (*sup*); the other view is that *gatis*, *kārakas*, and *upapadas* [compound] without distinction.

A compound occurs; however, with *kṛt*-suffixes, it occurs prior to the production of the case-ending (*sup*), which is the second view. In that regard, in both these views, a compound with a word ending in *tarap* and so forth is indeed appropriate. In this context, the mention of *kṛt* is connected with the phrase "for the sake of clarity. Some teachers [hold that] the mention of *kṛt*...
The meaning is that they explain [the word] precisely for the sake of clarity.

Regarding the phrase "but *prapacati* is for the sake of *deśya* and so forth," the word *tu* (but) is used to highlight the distinction from the previous explanation. That which has *prapacati-deśya* as its beginning is...

"prapacatideśyādiḥ. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the inclusion of *prapacatideśīya* is intended. *Prapacatideśyādyartham* means that for which the purpose or objective is something beginning with *prapacatideśya*.

[This is because] it is observed that there is a mention of *kṛt*-affixes [in the rule]. Likewise, [the rule] "the affixes *kalpa*, *deśya*, and *deśīya* are used in the sense of 'not quite complete'" (*īṣadasamāptau kalpabdeśyadeśīyaraḥ*).

In this context [of rule 5.3.67], because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of "tiṅśca" from rule 5.3.56, the suffixes *deśya* and *deśīya* are added after the word *prapacati*. Furthermore, when a *gati*-compound is formed with the prefix *pra-* and that which ends in those suffixes, the term *kṛt* would not be applied [to exclude the case where the suffix is not a *kṛt*]. Thus, in forms such as *prapacatideśyaḥ* and *prapacativeśīyaḥ*, the same applies to the final member (*uttarapada*).

The accent would be that of the original form (*prakṛtisvara*), which is not desired. Therefore, the mention of *kṛt* [in the rule] is indeed seen for the purpose of preventing this from occurring here. Consequently, this is not for the sake of clarity; rather, the intention is that it serves to prevent [the application of the rule] in cases such as *prapacatideśya*.

140. Both [words] in the case of *vanaspati* and others [are udātta] simultaneously. (6.2.140) The word *vana* is udātta on the first syllable by the rule "that which does not end in *ani* and is the subject of the *na*-suffix" (*Phiṭ-sūtra* 2.26). The word *pati* also [is udātta] by the accent of the suffix; it is derived from the root *pā* with the suffix *ḍati* according to the rule "from *pāti*, *ḍati*" (*Daiva-nighaṇṭu* 1.27).

It ends with the suffix *ḍati*. Regarding the statement "the word *bṛhat* has its accent on the final syllable," and so forth: although the word *bṛhat* is prescribed as being exclusively oxytone by the rule "In the sense of the present tense, [the words] *pṛṣat*, *bṛhat*, *mahat*, *jagat* are treated like the present participle" (*Daiva Upādhyāya Sūtra* 65), nevertheless...
In the word *bṛhaspati*, [the author] establishes that the first syllable has the udātta accent.

He states: "The suffix *ū* is applied to the root *tan* according to the Uṇādi rules. By the rule *kaṣicamitaniṣanisarjikharjibhya ūḥ* (Pāṇini Uṇādisūtra 1.82), the word *tanū* is antodātta (accented on the final syllable). It does not protect... [text ends].
By the word *pālayati*, he shows that the form *anapāt* is derived as a nipātana (irregular formation) from the root *pā rakṣaṇe* (DhP 1056). By the word *na pātayati* [he shows] the same.
[Otherwise], by the rule *nalopo nañaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.73), the elision of the *n* of the negative particle *nañ* would apply, [as in the case of] *nabhrāṇnapāt*.

By [the rule] beginning with (6.3.75), the *prakṛtibhāva* (absence of sandhi) does not occur. [The example is: "narā asminnāsīnāḥ śaṃsanti" ("Men seated here praise"). By this, he shows that the word *śaṃsa* has the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) as its grammatical agent (*sādhana*). Likewise, by the form *śaṃsanti*, it also has the object (*karman*) as its agent. [The root is] *śaṃsa* in the sense of "praising" (Dhātupāṭha 728).

Therefore, by the rule "ghañ is used in the sense of the agent and other kārakas" (Pāṇini 3.3.19), there is the suffix *ghañ*. [The word] "ending in *ghañ*" is [derived] by the rule "after roots ending in *ṛ* or *u*, there is *ap*" (Pāṇini 3.3.57). [Regarding] "Śunaḥśepaḥ": this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Consequently, in this case, the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) of the first member [is maintained].

Regarding the statement "when [the suffix] is present, [there is] the rule 'ubhau dvyudāttau'": therein, the word *śvan* is derived by means of the suffix *kanin* according to the rule *śvannukṣan* (Dhātupāṭha 6.55). The word *śepa* is derived from the roots *vṛṅ* and *śīṅ* by means of the suffix *puṭ* with the augment *c*, according to the rule *vṛṅśīṅbhyāṃ rūpasvāṅgayoḥ puṭ ca* (Dhātupāṭha 9.61).
Thus, [the word] ending in the *asun* suffix is derived; therefore, both of them are indeed udātta-accented on the first syllable.
Regarding the words "śaṇḍa" and "parka": from the root *śaḍi* (meaning "to injure," DhP 279), the form *śaṇḍa* is produced with the suffix *ghañ*.
From the root *pṛcī* (meaning "to mix," DhP 1462), the form *parka* is likewise produced in that same manner.

Thus it is so. [The rule] states: "The word *tṛṣṇā* has its initial syllable acute. For it is derived from the root *tṛṣ* with the suffix *niṣṭhā*. Therefore, by the rule "And *niṣṭhā* [suffixes] following a base consisting of two consonants" (Pāṇini 6.1.205), it has its initial syllable acute.
Regarding the word *ṭhvambaśabdaḥ* (the word *vamba*): it is derived from the root *lavi* (or *labi*) in the sense of "falling down" (*avasraṃsane*), according to Dhātupāṭha 379.
Since it is formed with the suffix *ac* by the rule *pacādyac*, the substitution of *va* for *la* occurs here by virtue of this specific irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
Regarding the word *viśvavayaḥśabdaḥ* (the word *viśvavayas*): it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose age (*vayas*) is universal (*viśva*). In that case...
In the rule "bahuvrīhau viśvaṃ saṃjñāyām" (Pāṇini 6.2.106), the word *viśva* has its final syllable accented. Regarding the phrase "of those two," it refers to the words *vamra* and *viśvayaśas*.
[Regarding the root *mṛṅ*, there is the suffix *vic*; according to the Kāśikā, it is *mṛñaḥ*, while according to the Padamañjarī, it is *mṛḍaḥ*.]
Since *vij* is being carried over from "ṭhvi-jupe cchandasi" (Pāṇini 3.2.73), the suffix *vic* is applied by the rule "ṭhanyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate" (Pāṇini 3.2.75)— as noted in the Kāśikā as *dṛśyante*.
Thus, the word *mṛtyu* is udātta on its final syllable, according to the rule "bhujīmṛṅbhyāṃ yuktyukau."
This is because [the word *dvandva*] ends in the suffix *tyuK* [as per Pāṇini 4.1.79].
Regarding the phrase "of *dvandva*s," etc.: the reading here refers to those *dvandva* compounds that do not have deities as their referents;
for in the case of a *dvandva* of deities, the form is already established by the rule "and in a *dvandva* of deities" (Pāṇini 6.2.141).

[The rule] "ṭhanudatādyautarapadārthaśca" is a listing of Dvandva compounds. For if their listing were not present here, then by the prohibition [stated in] "notarapade'nudātādau" (Pāṇini 6.2.142), the final syllable would instead be udātta.

141. *Devatādvandve ca* (Pāṇini 6.2.141). [The example is] *indrāsomau*. In the rule *devatādvandve ca*, the substitution of *anaṅ* occurs for the first member. [This is seen in] *ṛjrendra*, etc. [The suffix] *ran* [is added] after the roots *vṛdhi* and *vap* (according to Daiva 8.45). From that...

In the commentary on the rule *ran* (Uṇādisūtra 2.29), which continues from the previous context, it is stated that the word *indra* is derived with the suffix *ran*, as in "ṭhṛjrendraḥ" (Uṇādisūtra 8.46);

therefore, it is acutely accented on the first syllable. Regarding the statement "the word *soma* ends in the suffix *man*," the intention is that it too is acutely accented on the first syllable for that very reason. Furthermore, its ending in the suffix *man* is established by [the rule] "ṣuñ... [Uṇādisūtra 1.138].

Because [the word *abhiṣava*] is derived from the root *abhiṣava* (DhP 1247) by adding the suffix *man* according to the rule *artistusuhusru-* (Daiva-Upaniṣad 7.26), [it is explained as such]. As for the statement "Varuṇa ends in the suffix *unan*," it is because of the rule *kṛvṛdāribhya unan* (Pañcapādikā-Upaniṣad 3.53). Indeed, the word *bṛhaspati*...

It is recited among the *vanaspati* group, and therein the initial acute accent (*ādyaudātta*) is prescribed for both the preceding and following members simultaneously; thus, there are two acute accents. As in "tenendrābṛhaspatī," where [the rule] states "therein [the words] are acute," referring to the word *indra* and others. In "plakṣanyagrodhau," however, there is only the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound (*samāsāntodātta*).
It occurs thus even in the case of "evam agniṣṭomaḥ. This is a genitive compound (ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa), and this rule is an exception to the accentuation of compounds.

142. *nottarapade'nudātādāvapṛthivīrudrapūṣamanthiṣu* (Pāṇini 6.2.142). [The rule] "the words *agni* and *vāyu* are udātta on the final syllable" is stated; the word *agni* is derived by the rule "from the roots *vī*, *jyā*, and *jvar*, the suffix *ni*" (Dhātupāṭha 1.18), while the rule "there is elision of the *n* of *aṅga*" (Dhātupāṭha 1.20) is also in effect.
The word *vāyu* ends in the suffix *uṇ*. According to the rule *kṛvāpāj...* (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.86), it is formed with the suffix *uṇ*;
therefore, by the accent of the suffix, both words are oxytone (*antodātta*).
Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*), given that [the rule] states "when the initial member begins with an anudātta"?
[An objection is raised: "Will not the locative case itself here indicate that [a word] beginning with an unaccented vowel is not a *pada*?

To this he says: "The mention of 'the subsequent member' (*utarapada*)," and so forth. For in this section, the *dvandva* compound is indicated by the locative case, not the subsequent member. In that context, the locative in the expression "beginning with an unaccented vowel" (*anudātādau*) refers specifically to the *dvandva*.

It becomes a qualifier—namely, "in a Dvandva compound beginning with an unaccented [word]. However, if the term *uttarapada* (final member) were not mentioned, then when the locative case is prescribed for a Dvandva, the phrase "beginning with an unaccented [word]" would become a qualifier of the final member. Therefore, let this be a qualifier of the final member; let it not be a qualifier of the Dvandva.
The mention of the "subsequent word" (*uttarapada*) is for the purpose of ensuring that [the rule] applies only where it is appropriate.

Regarding the phrase "in a word beginning with an unaccented vowel" (*anudātādau*): if this qualification were absent, both the injunction and the prohibition would apply to a *devatā-dvandva* (compound of deities) without distinction; consequently, there would be no differentiation between their respective domains. And thus...

Otherwise, an option (*vikalpa*) would result because the scope of application (*viṣaya*) would be identical. However, when the rule "anudātādau" is present, the prohibition applies where the first member of the compound is anudātta and the second member is a dual deity-name (*devatādvandva*); for all other cases, the positive injunction (*vidhi*) applies. Thus, there is a clear distinction between the domains of the injunction and the prohibition.
Therefore, for the sake of distinguishing the scope [of the rule], it is stated that "it begins with an unaccented vowel (*anudātta*).

As for the statement "the word *pṛthivī* ends in the suffix *ṅīṣ*," this is because it is listed in the *gaurādi* group. Regarding the statement "after the root *rud*, there is elision of the *ṇi* [suffix]," the root is *rudir* (DhP 1067), meaning "to shed tears."

Thus, from this root with the *ṇi* affix, following the rule *sphāyitañci* (Dhātupāṭha 8.31) and so forth, while the word *drak* is being carried over, the suffix *rak* is applied by the rule *roderṇiluk ca* (Dhātupāṭha 8.39); hence *rudra* is udātta on its final syllable.
Regarding the term *śukrāmanthinau*: the word *śukra* ends in the suffix *ran* according to the rule *ṛjendra-* (Dhātupāṭha 8.46), and by that rule, it is udātta on its first syllable.
143. *antaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.143).

144. *thāthaghañktājabitrakāṇām* (Pāṇini 6.2.144). [The commentary states: "In this case, by virtue of the rule regarding the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the secondary member (*kṛduttarapada*), the final syllable of the secondary member (*uttarapada*) would be acute (*udātta*)."
The sense is: "If this [sūtra] were not commenced.

Regarding the statement "the suffix *ath* is applied after the root *vas* when preceded by a prefix," there, the suffix *ath* is understood from the rule "after the roots *śīṅ*, *śapi*, *rug*, *ami*, and *vañci*" (Daiva-Uṇādi 6.38), as that rule continues to apply.
By virtue of the *kṛdutarapadaprakṛtisvara* rule, the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) would be udātta.

In the case of *dūrādāgataḥ*, the suffix *kta* is applied to the root *gam*, and by the rule *anudātopadeśa* (Pāṇini 6.4.37), there is the elision of the nasal. Then, with the word *āgata*, [the compound is formed] according to *stokāntikārtha* (Pāṇini 2.1.39).
The compound is formed by these and other such rules; there is no elision of the case-ending (*aluk*) due to the rule *pañcamyāḥ stokādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.2).

Regarding *śuṣkaḥ* (or *viśuṣkaḥ*, as noted in the Kāśikā and Padamañjarī), the substitution of *ka* occurs by the rule *śuṣaḥ kaḥ* (8.2.51). In both instances here, the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) denotes the object (*karman*). In that regard, the rule *gatiranantaraḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.49) applies.
When [the rule] (6.2.49) applies, its exception—the acute accent on the final syllable of the second member—is prescribed.

However, when the suffix *kta* denotes the agent (*kartari*), then by the accent of the *kṛt*-suffix (*kṛtsvara*), since the second member retains its original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), the acute accent on the final syllable is already established. But surely, [the root] *śuṣ* has an object; how then [can it denote the agent]?

Regarding the question "What is the completion (*niṣṭhā*) in the sense of the object (*karman*)?"—there is no fault, because a transitive verb (*sakarmaka*) retains its transitivity when the causative meaning (*ṇyartha*) has been internally absorbed (*antarbhāvita*).
Thus, [the form] *ātapaśuṣkaḥ* (dried by the sun)—as stated in the *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī*—is a compound formed according to Pāṇini 2.1.32:
*kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* ("An agent or an instrument is frequently compounded with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix"). In this case, within the *tatpuruṣa* compound...
By the rule *tulyārtha* (Pāṇini 6.2.2) and others, the first member of the compound would take its original accent (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*).

Furthermore, in this case, because the first member ends in the suffix *ac* added after the root *pac* (i.e., *pac-aja*), it is *udātta* on the final syllable by the accent rule for primary derivatives (*kṛt-svara*).
Thus, [the forms] *prakṣayaḥ* and *prajayaḥ* [would result]. [One might object: "But [does not the rule] *er-ac* (3.3.56) [apply]?"

One might ask: "Will not the acute accent on the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) be established here simply by the rule that the original accent of the second member is retained in a *kṛt* compound?

To this, he says: "When *kṣayaḥ* means 'dwelling' (*nivāsa*), etc. That is to say, when the words *kṣaya* and *jaya* are accented on their initial syllables by the rules "kṣayo nivāse" (Pāṇini 6.1.201) and "jayaḥ karaṇam" (Pāṇini 6.1.202).

In that case, there would be a universal accent (*kṛtsvara*) with the middle syllable being udātta, as in *pralavitram* and *prasavitram*. [The suffix] *itra* is applied by the rule *artilūdhūsūkhana* (Pāṇini 3.2.184). Since the universal accent would apply here, the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) would prevail; by that, the final member of the compound (*uttarapada*)—

The middle syllable would be udātta [in the word] *govṛṣaḥ*. [This is derived from] the roots *pṛṣu*, *vṛṣu*, and *mṛṣu* in the sense of "to sprinkle" (*dhā.pā.* 705, 706, 707). Here, there is a compound by *upapadam atiṅ* (Pāṇini 2.2.19), and [the suffix -aC is added] by *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139).
(6.2.139) Thus, the acute accent (*udātta*) would apply to the beginning of the final member of the compound.

In the case of *sustutam*, the terms *su* and *ati* receive the designation of *karmapravacanīya* by the rules "suḥ pūjāyām" (1.4.94) and "atiratikramaṇe ca" (1.4.95). In this instance, only the accent of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) applies.
Thus [it is stated] by the rule "In a tatpuruṣa compound, when the sense is that of 'equal' (tulyārtha)," etc. (Pāṇini 6.2.2).

145. *kta* [is used] after a word ending in a *su*-suffix. (6.2.145) For example, *supītam*. The change to *i* is by the rule *ghumāsthā* (6.4.66). For example, *vṛkāvaluptam*. The root *lup* is listed as *luplṛ chedane* (DhP 1431).
Regarding "ṭhśaśaplutam": [the roots] *cyuṅ*, *jyuṅ*, *pruṅ*, and *pluṅ* mean "to go" (*gatau*;
DhP 955, 956, 957, 958). Regarding "siṃhavinarditam": the root *nard* means "sound" (*śabde*; DhP 56).
In all these cases, the compound is formed according to Pāṇini 2.1.32: *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*.
The analysis of the compound begins with "as if leaped upon by wolves," and so forth.

146. *saṃjñāyām anācitādīnām* (6.2.146). Regarding "upahūtaḥ": this is the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) of the root *hveñ*; there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to 6.1.15, and lengthening according to 6.4.2. Regarding "parijagdhaḥ": [this is from] the root *ad*.

The substitute *jagdhi* is applied according to Pāṇini 2.4.36 (*jagdhir lyapti kiti*). The change to *gh* occurs by Pāṇini 8.2.40 (*jhaṣas tathor dho 'dhaḥ*). Regarding the statement "the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi ktaḥ*), since the root *bhū* is intransitive, the formation of a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) in the sense of the object is not possible; therefore, [the word] is *sambhūta*.
Someone might have the misconception that this [term] *niṣṭhā* refers to the agent (*kartṛ*);

therefore, in order to dispel that, he says "sambhūtaḥ. Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *bhū* here functions in the sense of "attainment" (*prāpti*). And those [roots] which have the meaning of attainment necessarily [imply] attainment itself.

Verbal roots become transitive through their object, such as ṇīñ "to lead" (DhP 901) and others. Therefore, in the word *sambhūta* ("produced"), the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object after the root *bhū*, which here has the meaning of "attaining."

What, then, is the reason that the suffix *kta* is desired after an object (*karman*)? He says: "In the rule *gatiranantaraḥ*, the word *karmani* is understood. What follows from this? He says: "And this [present rule] is for the purpose of setting aside that [previous rule]. For in the rule *gatiranantaraḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.49), the word *karmani* is indeed understood.
And this sūtra is for the purpose of subverting only that [rule] which states "the immediately preceding member [retains its accent] in the case of a gati" (Pāṇini 6.2.49).
In this way, it becomes a subverter of the accent of a gati, provided that the suffix *kta* is prescribed in the sense of the object (*karman*).
By this [sūtra], the final acute accent (*antodātatva*) is ordained for the subsequent member ending in that [suffix], and not otherwise. Therefore...
The intention here is that in the word *sambhūta*, the suffix *kta* is to be understood as having the sense of the object (*karman*). Regarding the example *dhanuṣkhātā*:
from the root *khan* in the sense of "digging" (*avadāraṇe*; DhP 8.78), the suffix *ātva* is applied by Pāṇini 6.4.42 (*janasanakhanām*).
Then, the compound is formed by Pāṇini 2.1.32 (*kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*). Thus...

Even from [the compound] *kuddālakhātā* and so forth, the word *dhanuḥ* has its initial syllable acute according to *nabviṣayasyānisantasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26). The word *kuddāla* has its middle syllable acute according to *laghāvante* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.42) and so forth. Regarding *hastimṛditā*: [the root] *mṛd* means "to crush."

The word *hasti* [is derived from the root] *dhā* (DhP 1515). Because it ends in the suffix *ini* by the rule *hastājjātau* (Pāṇini 5.2.133), it is oxytone (*antodātta*). Regarding the form *āsthāpitam*: [it is derived] from the root *sthā* with the suffix *ṇic*, [and the vowel lengthening occurs] by the rule *artihrī* (Pāṇini 7.3.36), etc.

"Enveloped by the *puk* [augment]. (Thus. "The root *grah* takes a long vowel in the *liṭ* [perfect tense]. (Pāṇini 6.4.37). "Expounded. (Thus. From the root *vac* in the sense of "speaking" (Dhātupāṭha 1842), there is *saṃprasāraṇa* by the rule "vacisvapi... (Pāṇini 6.1.15), and *k* is substituted for *c* by "coḥ kuḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.30). "Accepted. (Thus.)
Thus: from the root *pad* "to go" (DhP 1169), the substitution of *n* [for *d*] occurs by Pāṇini 8.2.42 (*radābhyām*).

Regarding "praśliṣṭam": from the root *ṣliṣ* "to embrace" (DhP 1186). Regarding "upadrūtam": from the roots *du* and *dru* "to go" (DhP 944, 945). Regarding "sthitam": [from the root *sthā*, as in] *dyatisyati-*...
By [the rule] beginning with (7.4.40), *itvam* [is applied]. Regarding "saṃhitā," there is the substitution of *hi* for the root *dhā*.

147. And [the word] *pravṛddha* etc. (Pāṇini 6.2.147). This rule is stated because the accent of a *gati* [particle] would otherwise apply. In the case of *pravṛddham*, [it is derived from] the root *vṛdhu* (Dhātupāṭha 759) meaning "to grow.
In the case of *prayutāḥ* [or *prayuktāḥ* as in the Kāśikā], [it is derived from] the root *yu* (Dhātupāṭha 1038) meaning "to mix."
Regarding "avahitam": as before, there is the substitution of *hi* for the root *dhā*.
Regarding "khaṭvārūḍhaḥ": from the root *ruh* in the sense of "germination from a seed" (DhP 859); [the application of] Pāṇini 8.2.40, *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ*;
8.3.13, *ḍho ḍhe lopaḥ*; and [8.2.77], *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho'ṇaḥ*.

(6.3.111), the compound *khaṭvā-kṣepe* (2.1.26). Since the rule *ahīne dvitīyā* (6.2.47) would have required the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member, this specific entry is made here. In the case of *kavi-śastaḥ*: the root *śasu* (meaning "to injure," DhP 727) is used; [the compound is formed] by *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (2.1.32).
Thus ends the compound (*samāsa*). For this as well, by the rule *ṭṛtīyā karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 6.2.48), there is precisely the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member.
Regarding the phrase *yānādīnām*: by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of *vṛṣa* and others is intended.

The recitation here of words such as *yāna* and so forth is for the purpose of demonstrating that usage which occurs predominantly—that is, most frequently—in the sense of "vehicle" (*yāna*) and so on among the meanings of *pravṛddha* and the rest. However, it does not follow that *pravṛddha* has an udātta accent on the final syllable when used in the senses of "vehicle" (*yāna*) or "Vṛṣala. This concerns the word *prayukta*.
In examples such as *saktuṣveva*, the purpose is to restrict the scope (*viṣayaniyamārtha*). He asks, "What will result from that?

and replies with "even elsewhere than after *yāna* etc. [This refers to the rule *yānādibhyo'nyatrāpi*. Regarding the statement "some say it is for the purpose of restricting the scope," according to them, by this [rule], [the suffix] should not occur elsewhere than after *yāna* and so forth.
"This undertaking is for the purpose of providing a technical name (saṃjñā)," [he says], because it is already established by the preceding rule.

"And the *pravṛddha* group should be regarded as an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class). Why is this so? Because the particle *ca* is used here to include what has not been mentioned, in order to indicate that it is an *ākṛtigaṇa*.

To demonstrate what is established by its being an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class), he says: "punarutsyūtaṃ vāsaḥ" (a garment mended again), and so forth. [The root] *ṣivu* (to sew, Dhātupāṭha 1108) takes *ūṭh* by the rule "cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.19), followed by the *yaṇ* substitution. [The example] is "punarniṣkṛtaḥ" (renewed).
The substitution of *ṣ* for the *visarjanīya* is applied by the rule "ṭhidudupadhasya cāpratyayasya" (Pāṇini 8.3.41).

148. [The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after a word denoting an agent (*kāraka*), only when it is combined with *datta* or *śruta*, in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*). (6.2.148) [Example: *devadātaḥ*. While the rule "In the sense of a benediction, the *liṅ* and *loṭ* [moods are used]" (3.3.163) is applicable, the suffix *kta* is applied by the rule "And *kta* and *ktavatu* [are used] in the sense of a name" (3.3.174). [Furthermore, the substitution of *da* for *dā* occurs] by the rule "For *dā* [ending in] *ghu*, there is *da*" (7.4.46).

Thus, there is the substitution of *dada*; as before, there is a compound with the third case (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*). The word *deva*, because it ends in the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class), is oxytone by virtue of the *cit*-accent. The word *viṣṇu* also [is oxytone] by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). It has been stated that the word *brahman*, because it ends in the suffix *manin*, is ādyudātta (acute on the first syllable).

Regarding the statement "sambhūto rāmāyaṇaḥ": if the word *kārakāt* ("from a kāraka") were not mentioned, then because of the governing rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), the restriction would apply only to a *kāraka*, and thus it would also apply to a *gati*. However, when *kārakagrahaṇa* ("the mention of kāraka") is present, [this does not happen].
[The word *gati*] exists [as a technical term]. Therefore, for a subsequent *gati*, the rule "in a compound denoting a name, provided it does not begin with *anācita*, etc.

(Pāṇini 6.2.146) would indeed result in an udātta accent on the final syllable. However, when this [present sūtra] is stated, this case does not arise; because it has been excluded by the restrictive rule (niyama). [This refers to the application of] "the third case ending [is elided] when expressing the object" (Pāṇini 6.2.48).
