The original accent (prakṛtisvara) of the first member [of the compound] alone occurs. As for the purpose of employing the particle *eva*: since the rule is being formulated even though [the desired result] is already established, it serves as a restrictive rule (*niyama*) even without the employment of *eva*.

The intention is that [the action] will come to be. Regarding the phrase "the restriction of the *kāraka*," and so forth: for if the particle *eva* were not present, there would also be a restriction such as "only from the *kāraka*.
Consequently, since the particle *eva* effects a restriction elsewhere than that, the restriction would apply to what is heard immediately following it (*datta-śruta-avadhāraṇa*).

It might be argued: "The rule applies only when [the word] follows immediately after a *kāraka*. In this way, when the rule is applied immediately after a *kāraka* followed by *datta* or *śruta*, the restriction to the *kāraka* is achieved as desired, whereas the restriction to *datta* or *śruta* is not desired. For that reason, the particle *eva* (only) was employed. But what is the reason [for this]?

Is it intended that the agent (*kāraka*) is restricted [by the suffix], and not that the word *datta* is restricted by the hearing [of the suffix]? To this he says: "For even from a non-agent," and so forth. In the example "a trench dug by the gods" (*devakhātā*), no benediction (*āśis*) is present; therefore, because of the rule regarding "benediction" (*āśiṣi*), the restriction does not apply. And thus...
The final acute accent (*antodātatva*) indeed occurs by the rule "saṃjñāyām" (Pāṇini 6.2.146). It is said:

"The restriction 'only after a *kāraka* [term] before the words *datta* and *śruta* when used in a benediction (*āśis*)" also applies here. But how can two restrictions be obtained from a single rule, given that this is but one rule?
For just as someone might utter two parts of a sentence together in a compound manner, saying "the white one is running," so too has the Teacher here uttered the sentence in a compound manner.
In that regard, by one yoga (rule), there is a restriction that the suffix *āśis* occurs only after the roots *dā* and *śru* when they function as the agent (*kartṛ*); but by the other [yoga],...

By the rule "only in the sense of benediction [is the suffix used] after the word *datta* following a *kāraka*," the suffix does not apply in the sentence "Devadatta, being struck, cries out" because it is not a benediction. By showing that Devadatta is a proper name (*yadṛcchā-śabda*)— specifically, that "Devadatta" is the name of a certain conch— the author makes it clear that the suffix *datta* is not used here in the sense of a benediction.
149. *itthambhūtena kṛtam iti ca* (Pāṇini 6.2.149). The use of the particle *iti* here is for the purpose of indicating the meaning [of the rule]. Regarding *āpannaḥ*, the meaning is "attained.
Regarding *suptapralapitam*, [the root] *rap* and *lap* [are used] in the sense of "distinct speech" (Dhātupāṭha 401, 402).

In this case, the state of being asleep (*suptatva*) has become a qualifying attribute (*prakāra*); by that [attribute], the act of prattling (*pralapita*) was performed, and thus a compound occurs there: "the prattle of a madman" (*unmatta-pralapitam*). Here too, the state of being mad (*unmattatva*) has become a qualifying attribute; by that [attribute], the act of prattling was performed. "The song of one intoxicated" (*pramatta-gītam*): here too, the state of being intoxicated (*pramattatva*)...

He made the song reach a state of *prakāra*. [The root] *gai* (to sing) [is listed] in the Dhātupāṭha (916, 917); by the rule *ghumāsthā* (Pāṇini 6.4.66), the substitution of *i* occurs. Regarding the phrase *vipannaśrutam*: here too, he made the hearing reach a state of *vipanna* (ruined/failed). This applies in all cases.

The compound is formed by Pāṇini 2.1.32: *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* ("An agent or an instrument [is compounded] frequently with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix"). In this compound, the word *supta* is oxytone (*antodātta*) due to the accent of the suffix. As for the word *pralapita*, if it is a *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle) in the sense of the object (*karman*), then it is acute on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) by Pāṇini 6.2.49: *gatiranantaraḥ* ("A *gati* [prefix] that is not separated [by another word] has the accent of the *gati*"); however, if it is in the sense of the action (*bhāva*), [it is otherwise].

The word *tatastha* is *antodātta* (accented on the final syllable) by the rule *thāthādisvareṇa* (Pāṇini 6.2.144). Likewise, words such as *āpanna*, *vipanna*, and others formed in this manner are also *antodātta* by the same *thāthādi-svara* rule.
However, the rule *gatiranantaraḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.49) does not apply here; for in that [rule],...

Because of the continued application of the term "in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi*). Here, since the suffix *kta* cannot occur in the sense of the object after an intransitive root (*akarmaka-dhātu*), the words *gīta* and *śruta* have their final syllable accented (*antodātta*), just like the word *supta*. Now, how are these examples to be understood, given that [the rule] is stated as "by one who is thus characterized" (*itthambhūtena*)?

In this context, the word "done" (*kṛta*) refers to that which is to be accomplished; however, this meaning is not possible here, because [actions such as] prattling and so forth do not have "being done" as their purpose. This is because the root *kṛ* does not apply to the act of prattling and the like in the present case; for the root *kṛ* functions only with respect to the manifestation of what has not yet come into being. It does not [apply to these].

Regarding the objection, "Why is it not produced by speaking and so forth?", he says— "‘Produced’ (kṛta) refers to action in general"— in order to refute this. For the root *kṛ* does not denote merely the manifestation of what was previously non-existent.
Does it apply [only] there? Rather, it applies even to the general sense of action (*kriyāsāmānya*).

And that general sense of action exists even in the case of "pralapan" (speaking). By means of that [general sense], even the act of speaking and so forth becomes something performed. [This refers to the rule] "the third case-affix [is used] when the object is expressed" (*tṛtīyā karmaṇi*). Thus, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member [of the compound] is maintained.
With the words beginning with "yadi," he demonstrates its uselessness when the sense of the suffix *niṣṭhā* is that of existence (*bhāva*).

150. *ano bhāvakarmavacanaḥ* (6.2.150). The term *kārakāt* (from 6.2.148) continues [in this rule]. By the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), it is understood that the word ending in that suffix is intended; thus he says: "ending with the suffix *an*."

And so forth. In all instances such as "odanabhojanam" (rice-food), there is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). The genitive case here is characterized by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix, denoting the object (*karman*). However, in cases such as "rājabhojanāḥ" (those who eat for the king), it denotes the agent (*kartṛ*). The word "odana" has its initial syllable acute-accented (*udātta*) according to the rule "laghāvante" (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.42). As for "bhojana" and the like...

The subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is acute on the first syllable by virtue of the *lit*-accent. The word *payaḥ* is acute on the first syllable according to the rule *nabviṣayasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.42). Furthermore, the subsequent members such as *bhojana* are acute on the first syllable by virtue of the *lit*-accent. The word *payaḥ* [is also acute on the first syllable] according to the rule *nabviṣayasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26).

Thus, the word *audāta* itself is accented on the first syllable. The compound *candanapriyaṅgukā* is a *dvandva*; therefore, by the accentual rule for compounds (*samāsasvara*), it is accented on the final syllable. Regarding the form *lepanam*: this is the form derived from the root *lip*, meaning "to smear" or "to cover" (*upa-deha*)—as listed in the Dhātupāṭha (1433)—while *rāja* refers to the word "king."
The aforementioned sound [is as follows]: the word *ācchādana* is a form derived from the root *chad* in the sense of "covering" (*apavāraṇe*, Dhātupāṭha 1935).

By means of a single rule alone—namely, "and [the suffix] *lyuṭ* [is used] when the object [is expressed]" (*karmaṇi ca yena*)—he demonstrates that the suffix *lyuṭ* expresses both the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*).
Regarding the term *hastahārya*: the word *hasta* [is derived] from the rule *hasimṛgriṇavāmidamipūdhurvībhyastan* (Daiva 6.7; Pañcapādikā 3.86). [The full sūtra reads:
*hasimṛgriṇvamidamitamilūpūdhūrvibhyastan*.]

The word *hasimṛgrīṇvāmidamalūpūdhūrvibhyastan* (Paṇini 3.2.168) prescribes the suffix *tan*; being formed with that suffix, it is udātta on its first syllable. The word *hārya*, however, ends in the suffix *ṇyat* according to *ṛhalorṇyat* (3.1.124); by the accent of that suffix (*titsvara*), it is svarita on its final syllable. Regarding the term *dantadhāvanam*: [it is derived from] *dhāvu*...

The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) to the root *gatiśuddhi* (Dhātupāṭha 601). The word *danta* has its first syllable acute (*ādyudātta*) by the rule *svāṅgaśiṭām* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.29). Regarding the term *nidarśanam*: the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied to the root *dṛś* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). Regarding the term *avalekhanam*: here too [the same applies].
"Write: 'In all counter-examples,' and so forth. By this, he shows that this [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *gatikārakopapadānāṃ kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139)."
151. *mank-tin-vyākhyāna-śayana-āsana-sthāna-yājaka-ādibhiḥ krītaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.151).

The mention of *mank-tin* here refers to the suffix (*pratyaya*). In this context, by the technical rule regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), it is understood that the word ending in that suffix is what is being referred to; thus he says—*mannantam*.

Regarding the rule "ktinnantaśca": *rathavartma* and so forth are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). It has been stated that the word *ratha*, ending in the suffix *kthan*, is udātta on its first syllable. From the root *vṛtu* (DhP 748, meaning "to turn" or "to proceed"), the suffix *manin* is applied; thus, the word *vartma* is udātta on its first syllable. The words *śakaṭa* and *payaḥ* [are also treated similarly].

The first syllable is udātta because it is the initial [syllable] of a compound. The words *pāṇini* and *āpiśali* end in the suffix *iñ*. The word *kṛti* also ends in the suffix *ktin*. Furthermore, this word *vyākhyāna* is derived from the root *kṛ* with the suffix *lyuṅ* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*), and it is middle-udātta by the accent rule for *kṛt* suffixes. The word *cchandas* is formed by the suffix *asun* added to all roots.
(Pañcapādikā 4.188) [The sūtra is simply "ṭhasan": the mention of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is "ṭ" (as in *da-u-ṭ*).

When that is applied, [the word] is acutely accented on the first syllable because it ends in the suffix *asun* by the rule "ṭhcanderādeśca ccchaḥ" (Pañcapādikā 4.218). [The term] *ayanam* means "that by which they go"; thus, *ṛcām ayanam*. In the expression "of the ṛcs" (*ṛcām*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).
The word *ṛgayana* has its first syllable acute by the rule of the whole-word accent (*kṛtsvara*). Regarding "the king’s bed" (*rājaśayanam*) and so forth:

it is called a "bed" (*śayanam*) because one lies down upon it, and an "assembly hall" (*āsanam*) because one sits in it; with these two, there is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) with the words *rājan* and *brāhmaṇa*. The words *rājan* and *brāhmaṇa* have the accents already mentioned.

The words *śayana* and *āsana* have their first syllable acute by virtue of the *lit*-accent. Here, as before, the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) due to its connection with a *kṛt* suffix. The same applies in the case of "cow-pen" (*go-sthāna*) and "horse-pen" (*aśva-sthāna*). The words *go* and *aśva* have the accent already mentioned. [The word] *sthāna* is derived from the root *sthā* with the suffix *lyuṭ*, meaning "that in which one stands."

In *lit-svareṇa*, the first syllable is udātta. In examples such as *brāhmaṇa-yājyaḥ*, the genitive case is used for the object (*karman*) by virtue of its connection with a *kṛt* suffix. Among those listed under the *yājakādi* group that end in the suffix *ṇvul*, those that are without prefixes—namely *yājaka*, *pūjaka*, and *snāpaka*—have the udātta on their first syllable; however, those which...

Regarding those with prefixes—*pariveṣaka*, *adhyāpaka*, *udvartaka*, *utsādaka*—these have the acute accent on the middle syllable by virtue of the accent of the entire suffix (*kṛtsvara*). The words *hotṛ* and *bhartṛ* employ the suffix *tṛn*; however, as for those two that end in *tṛc*, their having the acute accent on the final syllable is established by the accent of the entire suffix (*kṛtsvara*). For example: *gokrītaḥ*, *aśvakrītaḥ*.

And so forth. These two compounds are formed by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā* (Pāṇini 2.1.32). The word *krīta* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) by virtue of the accent of the primary suffix (*pratyayasvara*). "This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of the *kṛt*-suffix. This applies to words other than *krīta*.

In the case of *mankti-tanv-*, etc., [the rule applies]; however, in the word *krīta*, by the rule "the third case [ending] in the sense of the object" (Pāṇini 6.2.48), there is the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member. Regarding this, it is said: "The mention of *vyākhyāna*, *śayana*, *āsana*, and *sthāna* includes cases where they do not have the meaning of 'absence' or 'object'."

Because this is already established by the rule *bhāvakarmavacanasyānantasya ṭhano bhāvakarmavacanaḥ* (6.2.150), [the accent is not in question here]. In the examples "prakṛtiḥ" and "prahṛtiḥ," the first member of the compound retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) by the rule *tulyārtha* (6.2.2) et cetera; these two are compounds formed with a *gati* particle.

152. *saptamyāḥ puṇyam* (Pāṇini 6.2.152). [The examples are] *adhyayanapuṇyam*, etc. The word *adhyayana* ends in the suffix *lyuṭ*; by the accent rule for *kṛt*-suffixes (*kṛtsvara*), it is middle-accented (*madhyodātta*). The word *puṇyam*, by the rule *nabviṣayasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26), has its first syllable accented (*ādyudātta*).
"Veda" is derived from the root *vid* with the suffix *ghañ*, meaning "that by which [something] is known. Consequently, the word *veda* is acute-accented on its first syllable.

This was stated based on the view that "in a *tatpuruṣa* compound [beginning with] words meaning 'equal' (*tulyārtha*), etc.," and so forth, while adhering to the position that "the *uṇādi* formations are underived nominal stems" (*uṇādayo'vyutpannāni prātipadikāni*). Now...
Relying on the perspective of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), he says: "But of *puṇ* and so forth," and so on.

For according to the theory of derivation, the word *puṇya* is derived as ending in the suffix *yat*, by the rule "from *puñ*, [the suffix] *yaṇ* and *ṇuk*, and shortening" (Paṅkajākara Uṇādisūtra 5.15). In that regard, if this [present sūtra] were not commenced, then...

By the rule *ṭhgatikāraka* (Pāṇini 6.2.139), the word *puṇya* would have its first syllable acute (*ādyaudāta*) in cases such as *adhyayana-puṇyam*, due to the accentuation of a *kṛt*-suffix. Therefore,
the intention is that this rule for the final acute (*antodāta*) applies when it is not in compound (*apadāda*).

Regarding "Vedic merit" (*vedapuṇya*), it means "merit by means of the Veda" (*vedena puṇyam*). In the view that the word is derived (*vyutpattipakṣe*), the compound is formed by the rule of *yogavibhāga* ("the third case," Pāṇini 2.1.30), and it takes the accent of the original form of the first member (*pūrvapadakṛtisvaratva*).

In the view that the word is non-derived (*avyutpattipakṣe*), the compound is formed by the rule "the agent or instrument with a primary derivative suffix" (*kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā*, Pāṇini 2.1.32), and it takes the accent of the suffix (*kṛtsvara*).
And the word *puṇya* has its first syllable acute-accented (*udātta*).

153. *Ūnārthakalahaṃ tṛtīyāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.30). [The compound] *māṣonaḥ* ("less by a māṣa") is formed by the rule *pūrvasadṛśa-* (2.1.31), etc., which prescribes a compound with a word in the third case. The same applies to *kārṣāpaṇonaḥ* ("less by a kārṣāpaṇa"), and so forth. [The roots] *kaṣa*, *khaṣa*, *śiṣa*, *jaṣa*, *jhaṣa*, *śaṣa*, *vaṣa*...

From the root *maṣ* (Dhātupāṭha 685–692), the suffix *ghañ* is applied; thus, the word *māṣa* has its initial syllable accented (*ādyaudāta*). From the rule "from *iṇ*, *siñji*, *dīṅ*, *uṣi*, and *ava*, the suffix *nak*" (Daiva Uṇādi Sūtra 5.36), the word *ūna* has its final syllable accented (*antodāta*). A *kārṣāpaṇa* is the coinage of one *karṣa*. This is the word *kārṣāpaṇa*.

By the accent rule for compounds (*samāsasvara*), it is *antodātta* (accented on the final syllable). In the sense of "one from whom the *kala* (defect/limb) has departed," it is *vikala*. In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, by the rule regarding the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratva*), the word *vikala* is *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable). [This is stated] in the rule "ṭhasikalahaḥ";
while the rule "aca iḥ" (Daiva-Upaniṣad 1.67) is in effect, [the suffix *i* is applied] by the rule "khanikaṣyañjyasi" (Daiva-Upaniṣad 1.68), etc.

The word *sintodātaḥ* [is explained as follows]: from the root *kala* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*, Dhātupāṭha 1865), the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule *pacādyac*. Thus, that which moves is *kalaḥ*.

Then, from *kalaṃ hanti* ("he strikes *kala*"), the suffix *ḍa* is applied according to the rule *anyeṣv api dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 3.2.101). By this, the word *kalaha* has its accent on the final syllable (*antodātaḥ*).

Regarding the phrase "In this regard, some [say]... and so forth: if "tarhi" (then) were taken as referring to the word-form (*svarūpa*), then in the case of the word *ūna* as well, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasajyeta*) of taking it as its own form; and consequently, other words having that same meaning would not be included. To this, he says: "By the word *ūna* itself," and so forth.

The word *ūna* indicates a distinction from other doctrines. For others indeed maintain that when there is the apprehension of a meaningful [word], there is no apprehension of those that are meaningless.
However, some hold that its purpose is the indication of meaning by means of the very word *ūna* itself for the sake of indicating meaning.

Thus it has been stated: "For when a designation is primarily concerned with the word-form (*śabda*), it is said that the word-form itself is what is grasped" (the printed reading is *svarūpaṃ grahaṇam*).
However, here the designation *una* is one where the meaning (*artha*) is primary. Therefore, they say: "The word *una* is intended for the purpose of indicating the meaning."

Therefore, in that very context, there is the inclusion of those words which have that meaning. The particle *iti* is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Since the inclusion of those having that meaning is achieved by the word *ūna* itself for the purpose of indicating the meaning, some here desire the inclusion of the actual form [of the word] as "meaning" (*artha*). For example: "one who has grain as his object" (*dhānyārthaḥ*). [This is an example of] the third case...

The compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.30] *tatkṛtārthena*. From the root *dhā* (DhP 1104) meaning "to place" or "to hold," the suffix *ṇyat* is applied; thus *dhānya-* has its final vowel circumflex-accented (*svarita*). Alternatively, *dhānya-* means "suitable for storage" (*dhāne sādhū*), with the suffix *yat* added according to [Pāṇini 4.4.75] *prāgdhitādyat*; consequently, by [Pāṇini 6.1.213] *yato 'nāvaḥ*, it retains the acute accent on the first syllable.

The word *dhānya* has its first syllable acute (*ādyaudāta*). In this case, the word *artha* has its first syllable acute by virtue of the rule *prāmādīnāṃ ca* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.38). For what purpose is the mention of the third case [ending]? It is so that [the accentuation] does not apply in examples such as *anūnam* and *akalaha*.
If you ask why, it is not so;

for here, according to the technical rule (paribhāṣā) "the specifically mentioned takes precedence over the general" (Vyāḍi 3), when there is a conflict between a specific mention and a general rule, only that compound which is specifically mentioned is accepted. Therefore, what is the need for [the word] *anūmaka* in order to exclude *kalaha*?

Why is the third [case-ending] mentioned? To this he says: "That which is explicitly stated," and so forth; the meaning has already been explained. 154. *miśraṃ cānupasargamasandhau* (Pāṇini 6.2.154).
In the example "guḍamiśrāḥ" (mixed with molasses), the compound is formed as before by the rule *pūrvasadṛśa...* (Pāṇini 2.1.31) and so forth.

The word *guḍa* is derived from the root *guḍ* "to protect" (*guḍa rakṣāyām*, Dhp 1370) with the suffix *ka* according to Pāṇini 3.1.135, *ṭhigupadha*; therefore, it is udātta on the final syllable. Furthermore, although the suffix *ra* is prescribed by the rule *sphāyitañci-* (Dhātupāṭha-Uṇādi 8.31) and others, it occurs after the root *miś* as well due to the presence of the term *bahulāt* ("by virtue of diversity"); therefore—

The word *mitra* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). The word *tila* has its initial syllable accented (*ādyaudātta*) by the rule "and for grasses and grains that have two syllables" (*tṛṇadhānyānāṃ ca dvyakṣarāṇām*, Phiṭ-sūtra 2.27). [Otherwise,] the forms *pramiśram* and *sanmiśram* would result; therefore, the mention of "without a prefix" (*anupasarga*) is made to exclude those cases.

Why is this done? He says: "here," and so forth. Alternatively, since a third-case compound (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*) is being expressed by the word *miśra*, how is it understood when it is accompanied by a prefix (*sopasarga*)? He says: "here," and so forth. If, in this case, the inclusion of [the word] without a prefix (*anupasarga*) is made, then in other instances where the word *miśra* is employed, [it would apply to] that which is accompanied by a prefix (*sopasargasya*).

If there were no inclusion [of the prefix], then the inclusion of the term *anupasarga* (non-prefix) here would be purposeless. [The text says] "by that," etc., which demonstrates the purpose of the indication (*jñāpana*).
[The example is] "the king who is mixed with Brāhmaṇas" (*brāhmaṇamiśra rājā*); this compound is formed by [the rule] *pūrvasadṛśa* (Pāṇini 2.1.31), etc., alone.

By the phrase "united with the Brahmins," he demonstrates the absence of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) in the counter-example. The phrase "having attained a single purpose" clarifies the very meaning just mentioned.

That which has a single (*eka*), i.e., undivided (*abhina*), object is "single-purposed" (*ekārtha*); the state of being that is "single-purposedness" (*aikārthya*). Having attained that is "having attained a single purpose."
The meaning is "attained.
But how is it known that this is the meaning of the word *saṃdhi*? To this he says: "saṃdhiḥ" and so forth.
A *paṇabandha* is a formal agreement—an undertaking such as: "If you would do this for me, then I too..."

"‘I shall do this for you’—an agreement of this kind; when there is a single purpose through such a binding of a wager, that is called *saṃdhi* (union/alliance). Therefore, when there is *saṃdhi* in the counter-example, the meaning understood is: ‘He has entered into a union with the Brāhmaṇas, having attained a single purpose. Some [hold this view]."

They say again, "and so forth. Some say that *saṃdhi* (euphonic junction) is that proximity (*pratyāsatti*) in which a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*) is perceived; [the rule] would apply only in such a case. Since this kind of *saṃdhi* does not exist in the counter-example, he says: "here, two Brāhmaṇas together with the king."

And so forth. Although there is proximity—that is, spatial nearness—between the king and the Brahmins, nevertheless, even when that [proximity] exists, a distinction of form (mūrtivibhāga)—that is, a specific difference in form—is perceived between the king and the Brahmins. The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*). Since this is so, for that reason...

"The king is cited as an example [of a mixture] because he is mixed with Brahmins; in these examples, there is indeed no loss of distinction. By this, he demonstrates the absence of *saṃdhi* (phonetic coalescence) in cases such as *gūḍhamiśrāḥ* ("mixed secretly"), for just as grains and the like become mixed when they have dissolved, [so too is the case here].

Likewise, its constituent parts (guḍas) are such that no division of their forms is perceived; yet, in that case, there is no occurrence of the non-distinction of the joints (sandhi). Non-distinction is not [the same as] division; "its occurrence" means its attainment. When a joint consists of a single purpose through a binding agreement (paṇabandha), then its absence should be understood in the examples cited.

For that [term] is characterized by the specific quality of being censured; and this quality does not exist in insentient roasted grains mixed with molasses, because it is a property belonging only to sentient beings.
155. *naño guṇapratiṣedhe sampādyarhahitālamarthāstaddhitāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.155).

Regarding the phrase *sampādyādyarthās taddhitāḥ*: this refers to secondary suffixes (*taddhita-pratyaya*s). Therefore, by the paribhāṣā concerning the mention of a suffix (Puṣpavṛtti 44), it is understood that the rule applies to forms ending in those suffixes (*tadantavidhi*).

Regarding the phrase "in the negation of a quality": that meaning of the sentence for which a secondary derivative (taddhita) is produced is prescribed as the basis for the application (pravṛttinimitta) of that derivative—as it has been stated: "That which assists and is already established is a subordinate member (aṅga);
that which is to be accomplished and does not assist is the principal (aṅgin). These two, *aṅgin* and *guṇa*, are synonyms.

"Guṇapratiṣedhaḥ" means the negation of a quality (*guṇa*). This is a qualifier of the negative particle (*nañ*); the meaning is that the negative particle applies when there is a negation of a quality. [The example is] "kārṇaveṣṭakikam," which means "it is beautified by two ear-ornaments made of bricks. [This is derived] from the rule "sampādini" (Pāṇini 5.1.99).
Regarding the rule *ṭhak prāgvateṣṭhañ* (Pāṇini 5.1.18), in the example *na karṇaveṣṭakikam akārṇaveṣṭakikam*,

the negative particle *nañ* functions as a negation of that quality which serves as the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) in the sense of "that which is accomplished by means of two ear-ornaments" (*karṇaveṣṭakābhyāṃ sampadyate*). That, moreover, is the ground for the application.

*Chaidikaḥ*: [The suffix] *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule *ārhādagopuccchasaṅkhyāparimāṇāt ṭhak* (Pāṇini 5.1.19), meaning "he deserves cutting. *Vatsīyaḥ*: [The suffix] *cha* is applied according to the rule *prākkrītāc chaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.1). *Sāntāpikaḥ*:
[The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied according to the rules *tasmai prabhavati santāpādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.101) and *prāgvateṣṭhañ* (Pāṇini 5.1.18).

Regarding the form *ṭhvigārdabharathikaḥ* (*not a donkey-cart driver*): the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule *tadarhati* (Pāṇini 5.1.63) in the sense of "one who deserves that. The word *vi-* forms a *prādi*-compound [with *gārdabharathika*]. Here, the word *vi-* functions as a negation of the quality expressed by the term *gārdabharathika*. In this context, [the elision of the first member] occurs by the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-* (Pāṇini 6.2.2), etc.

The original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member (*pūrvapada*) alone occurs; likewise in subsequent cases as well. When *nañ* is not present, even in this counter-example, that which is the first member should be cited as having its original accent: "one who is other than a Gārdabharathika is an *agārdabharathika*. In this case—

The negative particle (*nañ*) occurs here in the sense of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), meaning "other than a donkey-cart," and not as a prohibition of the state of being a donkey-cart. Regarding the statement, "The quality (*guṇa*) is the basis for the application of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*)," and so forth:
the "meaning of the secondary derivative" refers to the sense of the sentence such as "one who is equipped with two ear-rings," and therein that which...

The basis for the application (*pravṛtinimitta*) of a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix—such as "being accomplished" (*sampādita*) and so forth—is called its "quality" (*guṇa*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), qualities such as "being worthy of that" (*tadarhatva*) are included; thus, both a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix and its meaning are encompassed. Regarding the phrase "the negation of that" (*tatpratiṣedha*) and so on: it refers to a compound in which the negation of that [quality] is expressed.
In this regard, the following is the rule: How is the negation of that quality expressed? To this he says:

"The face is not equal to the two ear-rings. By all of this, [the author] demonstrates that this rule concerns a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) and not a *paryudāsa* (relative exclusion), as seen in the term *agārdabharathika*.
Thus, in this counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), he demonstrates the absence of this rule.

[In the case of] "pāṇinīyam," [it is derived by] "vṛddhāc chaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.2.114). [In the case of] "apāṇinīyaḥ," the final member of the compound is that which ends in a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) used in the sense of one who studies (*adhyetṛ*). It is not [the case here].
Those *taddhita* suffixes which convey meanings such as "fit for," "worthy of," or "beneficial to" are called *taddhita*. Regarding the form *voḍhā*:

as before, the substitution of *dh* for *h*, the substitution of *ḍh* for *d*, the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭh*, and the elision (*lopa*) of *ḍ* must be applied; furthermore, by the rule *sahivahor odavarṇasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.112), the substitution of *o* for the vowel *a* occurs.
Regarding the form *avoḍhā*: here, the suffix *ya* has the sense of the root *ah* (to carry). Since this is a *kṛt* suffix, [the following applies].
This is a subsequent word (*uttarapada*). Because of the mention of *taddhita* [suffixes] therein, the final acute accent (*antodātta*) does not apply to the subsequent word;

rather, the original accent of the initial member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) alone remains. This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the original accent of the initial member. The same should be understood for the subsequent rules as well. This [section] precedes the section on *bahuvrīhi* compounds.
This is because of such rules as (Pāṇini 6.2.162).

156. *yayatoścātadarthe* (6.2.156). Regarding *pāśyā*: by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), it has the udātta on the final syllable. Regarding *adantya*: by *yato’nāvaḥ* (6.1.213), it has the udātta on the first syllable. Likewise—*ākarṇyam*.
This [term] *audāta* is also derived in the same manner as that.
Regarding *pādyam*: the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *pādārdhābhyāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 5.4.25).
Regarding *adanīyam*: here, the negative particle *nañ* occurs in the sense of "other than dental" (*dantyāt anyat*), and not [in the sense of "not eating"].

This is a prohibition against that which ends in *tad*. As in the example "it should be given" (*adeyam*), the suffix *yat* is applied here in the sense of "worthy of" according to Pāṇini 3.3.169, *arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca*, and the substitution of *ī* for *ya* occurs according to 6.4.65, *īdyati*. Now, why does this not also apply here:
"the *sāman* seen by Vāmadeva is the *vāmadevyam*"? To this [the author replies]:
He said: "That which is without a suffixal marker," and so forth; the meaning has already been explained.

157. *aṅgāvaśakte* (6.2.157). Regarding *apacaḥ*: [the suffix] *ac* is applied by *pacādyac*. Regarding *avikṣipaḥ*: [the suffix] *ka* is applied by *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ* (3.1.135). Regarding *apaco’dīkṣitaḥ* and so forth: in the technical treatise (*śāstra*), the terms *dīkṣita* and *parivrājaka* [are used].
They do not cook because it is prohibited, not because they are incapable; therefore, in this case, a vow is understood, not incapacity.

158. And in the case of abuse (*ākrośe*). (6.2.158) Here, "abuse" refers to the statement of a fault. The rule is stated so that [the suffix] may apply even when incapacity (*aśakti*) is not explicitly expressed.

159. *saṃjñāyām* (6.2.159). [The example is] *devadatto 'pajñadattaḥ*. The words *devadatta* and *yajñadatta* are oxytone by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). He who, being Devadatta, does not perform that duty [is called] *apajñadattaḥ*.
It should be understood that this same [explanation] applies here as well in the case of "evaṃ ṭhaviṣṇumittraḥ," where he is thus addressed.
160. *kṛtya-ukeṣṇuc-cārvādayaś-ca* (Pāṇini 6.2.160).

The mention of the suffixes *kṛtya*, *uka*, and *iṣṇuc* is intended as a reference to the suffixes themselves. In this context, by the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), there occurs the substitution of those [suffixes] with their respective endings (*tadanta*). The group beginning with *cāru* [is also included].

[The forms] are indeed nominal stems (*prātipadika*). Regarding "it should be done" (*kartavyam*): when it ends in the suffix *tavyat*, the word *kartavya* has a circumflex accent (*svarita*) on the final syllable; when it ends in *tavya*, it has an acute accent (*udātta*) on the middle syllable. Regarding "it is not to be done" (*akaraṇīyam*): because it ends in the suffix *anīyar*, [the rule] "the penultimate syllable is acute in a *rit*" applies.
By the rule (6.1.217), the word *karaṇīya* has its middle syllable accented (*madhyodātta*) due to the accent of the *rit* suffix.

Regarding the words *anāgāmṛkam* and *anapalāṣukam*: the suffix *ukañ* is applied by the rule "laṣapatapada" (3.2.154) et cetera. The words *āgāmuka* and *apalāṣuka* have their middle syllables accented (*madhyodātta*) by the accent of the *kṛt* suffix. [The example continues with] *analaṅkariṣṇuḥ*.

Thus, by the rule *alaṃkṛñ* (Pāṇini 3.2.136), the suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied. The word *alaṅkariṣṇu* is udātta on its final syllable due to the accent of the *cit* suffix. The word *nirākariṣṇu* is likewise. By the paribhāṣā concerning the inclusion of that which has only one indicatory letter (*ekānubandhakagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), when *iṣṇuc* is mentioned...

Someone might have the misconception that there should be no inclusion of *khiṣṇuc* because it has two indicatory letters (*dvy-anubandhaka*); therefore, in order to dispel that [misconception], he says: "In the rule 'When *khiṣṇuc* follows, [the suffix *kvip* is applied] after the root *bhū* in the sense of the agent' (Pāṇini 3.2.57), there is an inclusion of *khiṣṇuc* even though it possesses two indicatory letters."
The connection is with what will be stated [later], namely "it occurs. He states the reason for this very point: "by virtue of the capacity of the rule for prescribing [affixes] beginning with *i*.
This is precisely the purpose of prescribing *khiṣṇuc* and so forth as beginning with *i*: that there may be a general inclusion of them in this sūtra.

So that it may be [correct]; otherwise, it would be meaningless, because due to the acute accent (*udātta*) on *bhavat*, the subsequent suffix *khiṣṇuc* begins with the vowel *i* (due to the presence of *i* in *iṭ*).
[Examples such as] *dhācāruḥ* and so forth; [the suffix] *ñuṇ* is applied after the roots *dṛs*, *nij*, and *car* (Daiva Upādhyāya 1.88).

[The suffix] *ñuṇ* is applied after the roots *dṛś*, *nij*, *car*, *caṭ*, and *rahi*—according to the *Daiva* and *Pañcapāṭha-ṭīkā*. By that rule, the word *cāru* has its acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable.
The word *sādhū* has its acute accent on the final syllable; this is according to [Pāṇini 3.1.135] *kṛvāpāj...* (Daiva 1.86).
This is because [the word] ends in the suffix *uṇ*. *Yaudhikaḥ* (one who lives by fighting) is derived from *yudhā carati*;

by the rule "prāgvahateṣṭhak" (Pāṇini 4.4.1), the suffix *ṭhak* is applied, and by "kitaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.165), it is oxytone (having the acute accent on the final syllable). Regarding "anaṅgamejayaḥ," it is ādyudātta (having the acute accent on the first syllable) due to the accent of an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Here, in the second case, it is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*).

The rule regarding the acute accent on the final syllable of a compound (samāsāntodātatva) would thus apply to a negative compound (nañsamāsa). Regarding the phrase "in this case also" and so forth: because the rule prescribes that a word following the negative particle *nañ* has its first syllable acute, here too, by means of a second negative compound, there is an acute accent on the final syllable. This applies to words such as *vartamāna*, *vardhamāna*, and others.

Because they end in the suffix *śānac*, they are oxytone (accented on the final syllable). A word signifying a modification [of something] is oxytone by virtue of the accent of the compound (*samāsasvara*).
The word *gṛhapatika* is acute on the first syllable because it ends in the suffix *kan* according to Pāṇini 5.3.87 (*saṃjñāyāṃ kan*).
The word *vadānya*—derived from the root *vad* with the suffix *ānyat* (Daiva Uṇādi Sūtra 8.9)—is middle-acute (accented on the middle syllable) by virtue of the accent of the suffix.
161. *vibhāṣā tṛnn-anna-tīkṣṇa-śuciṣu* (Pāṇini 6.2.161). The mention of *tṛn* is a reference to the suffix; therefore, as before, that which ends in it is brought to mind.
*Anna* and the others are nominal stems (*prātipadika*). [The example is] *akartā*; here *tṛn* has the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*). By this—
The word *kartṛ* has its initial syllable acute (*udātta*) by virtue of the *nitsvara* rule. The word *anna* also [has its initial syllable acute] by the *phiṭ-sūtra* 2.26: *nabviṣayasya*.
The word *tīkṣṇa* has its final syllable acute, according to the rules *kṛtyasūbhyāṃ kṣnaḥ* (Daiva-Uṇādi 5.49) and *tijerdīrghaśca* (Daiva-Uṇādi 5.50). [The suffix] *in*...
While [the rule] "da.u.1.46" is in effect, [the rule] "ṭhigupadhātu kitÂ" (da.u.1.48) applies; by that, the word *śuci* has its first syllable udātta.

162. *bahuvarīhāvidametatadbhyaḥ prathamapūraṇayoḥ kriyāgaṇane* (Pāṇini 5.4.162). Regarding the rule "in the sense of 'first' and 'ordinal'," the term "first" (*prathama*) is taken in its own form (*svarūpa*), whereas in the case of the term "ordinal" (*pūraṇa*), it refers to the category.
Those suffixes that are prescribed in the sense of "filling" (pūraṇa) are understood here, because of their association with the word *prathama* (first).

Alternatively, the mention of *pūraṇa* is marked with a circumflex accent (*svarita*); and by means of a circumflex accent, the governing scope (*adhikāra*) is extended. Consequently, this refers to those suffixes that are prescribed under the heading of *tasya pūraṇe ḍaṭ* (Pāṇini 5.2.48).

The inclusion [of these forms] occurs as follows: "idam-prathamaḥ. Here, *prathama-* is udātta on the final syllable because it ends in the suffix *-amac* by the rule *pratheramat* (Daiva-Uṇādi 7.46). Words such as *idam* are prescribed in the *tyadādi* group as being udātta on the final syllable;
thus we have examples such as "idam-dvitīyaḥ" and "idam-tṛtīyaḥ. [The suffixes] *-tīya* after *dvi-* and *tri-* [are applied by Pāṇini 5.2.54].
Because they end in the suffix *tīya*, the words *dvitīya* and *tṛtīya* have the middle syllable as their udātta accent according to Pāṇini 5.2.55 (*samprasāraṇaṃ ca*).
[The word] *prathama* is formed by [the suffix] *ṭhañ* in the sense of "this is the first of this," as in *prathamaḥ*. In this case, [the rule] *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-* (Pāṇini 6.2.2) applies.

By such rules as these, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member (*pūrvapada*) alone remains. Regarding the term *yatprathamaḥ*: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those for whom 'yat' is the first. Here, by the rule *bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā* (Pāṇini 6.2.1), the original accent of the first member alone occurs. The same applies to the subsequent examples in this [section].

This is to be understood as a counter-example within the section on *bahuvrīhi* compounds; the meaning is "those for whom this is primary. By this, he demonstrates that in the aforementioned counter-example, the word *prathama* denotes "primary" and not "the number one," thereby showing the absence of a plurality.

Regarding the phrase "of the subsequent member" (*uttarapadasya*) and so forth: in this sūtra, the mention of the subsequent member is made with reference to the two case endings [the nominative and the ordinal], and not with reference to the *bahuvrīhi* compound itself.
Consequently, the status of being the recipient of the grammatical operation belongs to the subsequent member alone, and not to the *bahuvrīhi*. Therefore, when...
When it is produced, then by the rule *kapi pūrvam* (Pāṇini 6.2.173), the preceding member becomes udātta;

for the suffix *kap*, being prescribed under the heading of compound formation (*samāsādhikāra*), occurs at the end of the compound itself, not at the end of the final member (*uttarapada*). Indeed, the final member...

This is a compound; therefore, by the rule "it is grasped in the manner of the pigeon’s foot" (*kabutarapadakrama*), the final acute accent (*antodātatva*) being prescribed does not apply to the second member (*uttarapada*), but rather to the first. [The formation is as follows:

from *idam-prathama*, the suffix *ka* is added by the rule "the remaining ones optionally" (*śeṣādvibhāṣā*, Pāṇini 5.4.154). Then, by the rule "in a bahuvrīhi, after a word ending in a kṛt-suffix" (*bahuvrīhau parakṛtyā*, Pāṇini 6.2.1), [the accent is determined].
Thus ends the two rules which constitute exceptions to the original accentuation of the preceding member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*).
In this same manner, the subsequent rules within this section on *bahuvrīhi* compounds are to be understood.
163. *stana* after a numeral. (6.2.163) Examples: *dvistanā*, *tristanā*. The words *dvi* and *tri* are oxytone by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*).
The root *stan* (and *gad*) in the sense of "making a divine sound" belongs to the *curādi* class and ends in *a*.
Therefore, [the suffix] ghañ is applied; by that, the word *stana* has its first syllable udātta. Regarding the phrase "four-breasted" (*catuḥstanā*):
because the word *catur* ends in the suffix *uran* (according to Daiva 8.78), it has its first syllable udātta.
The word *darśanīya* ends in the suffix *anīyar*, [and its accentuation is governed by] Pāṇini 6.1.217: *upottamaṃ riti*.
The middle [syllable] is udātta, as in the word *dviśirāḥ*. According to the rule *nabviṣayasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26), the word *śiras-* has its first syllable udātta.
164. *vibhāṣā chandasi* (6.2.164).
165. *saṃjñāyāṃ mitrājinayoḥ* (6.2.165). For example: *devamitraḥ*, *brahmamitraḥ*. The words *deva* and *brahma* have the accent [prescribed] as stated [in the preceding rule].

The word *mitra* is oxytone by the rule *ṭhamicimidiśasibhyaḥ ktraḥ* (Uṇādisūtra 8.86). Regarding the term *vṛkājina*: since the distinction between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*) is not intended to be expressed here, the word *vṛka* is used in this context to denote a product of the wolf. Thus, *vṛkājinaḥ* means "one who has a wolf-skin [as his garment]. This refers to the word *vṛka*.

In the case of words for living beings (*prāṇin*) preceded by *ku*, [the suffix] is udātta according to Phiṭsūtra 2.30 (*ṭh prāṇināṃ kupūrvam*). Under the governing rule *śyā-asty-āhveñ-ava-bhya inac* (Daivam 5.12), the substitution of *inaC* is applied by *ajer aja ca* (Daivam 5.14).
Therefore, *ajina* has its final vowel accented (*antodāta*). Regarding the example "kūlājinaḥ": *ku* is a particle (*nipāta*);

with that as an upapada, from the root *lā* (meaning "to take," DhP 1058), the suffix *ḍa* is applied by Pāṇini 3.2.101 (*anyeṣv api dṛśyate*), and [the lengthening of the vowel] is applied by Pāṇini 6.3.137 (*anyeṣām api dṛśyate*).
There is lengthening of the first member [of the compound]. By that, *kūla* has its final syllable udātta. Regarding *kṛṣṇājina*:

under the heading "The suffix *na* is added after the roots *iṇ*, *siñj*, *dī*, *ru*, *ṇī*, and *ava*" (*Daivamukha 5.35*), [the rule] "After the root *kṛṣ*, when meaning color" (*Daivamukha 5.37*) applies *na*. Therefore, *kṛṣṇa* has its final syllable udātta.

Regarding "priyamitra": it is called *priya* because it pleases (*prīṇāti*), with the suffix *ka* added by the rule *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.135). Thus, *priya* has its udātta accent on the final syllable. Regarding "mahājina": [the word *mahat* is derived] by the rule *nartamāne pṛṣadbṛhanmahajjagacchatṛvacca*.
In this [section], the word *mahat* has its final syllable accented with the udātta.
166. After a word meaning "sexual union," [the suffix *aC* is applied] to express an interval.
(6.2.166) 167. The word *mukham* ("mouth") when it denotes a part of one's own body [is included in the scope of this rule].
(6.2.167) For example: *gauramukhaḥ*. [The form *gaura-* is derived] from the root *gurī* (meaning "to lift up") with the suffix *aC*. (DhP 1396)

Because *prajña* and other such terms do not undergo *vṛddhi*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *parajñādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 5.4.38); thus, *gaura* has its final syllable udātta. Having introduced the rule *udi dṛṇāterajalau pūrvapadāntyalopaśca* (Pañcapādikā 5.19), the suffix *ḍit* is applied.

Regarding the rule *khanermuṭ ca udāttaḥ* (*Pañcapādikā Upaniṣad* 5.20), the two suffixes *ra* and *jala* are applied after the root *khan*, and these two are marked with the *ḍi*-sign; furthermore, the augment *muṭ* is acute-accented (*udātta*). Consequently, the word *mukha* has its initial syllable accented as acute.
Thus we have the form *bhadramukhaḥ*, according to the rule *ṛjrendra-* (*Daiva*) 8.46.

The word *bhadra* is derived [as follows]: by that [derivation], *bhadra* is oxytone (antodātta). Regarding the phrase "a long-mouthed hall" (*dīrghamukhā śālā*), the word "mouth" (*mukha*) here refers to the doorway of the hall.
As for the statement "here, a limb (*svāṅga*) characterized by being non-fluid is taken," this means "a limb that is non-fluid and possesses form."

The sense is that what has been defined [in the Kāśikāvṛtti 4.1.54] as a "limb of one's own body" (*svāṅga*) characterized by being non-fluid (*adrava*) and so forth is what is intended here; therefore, the [suffix *ṅīṣ*] does not apply in the case of *dīrghamukhā śālā* ("a long-faced house").

168. *nāvyaya-dik-śabda-gomahat-sthūla-muṣṭi-pṛthu-vats-ebhyaḥ* (6.2.168). This prohibition is stated regarding the final acute accent (*antodātta*) which would otherwise have been obtained by the preceding rule. For example: *uccairmukhaḥ*. The word *uccaiḥ* is listed among the *svarādi* group; these [words] are prescribed (*nipātyante*) as having the final acute accent.

Regarding "prāṅmukhaḥ": the word *prāṅ* is formed with the suffix *kvip*, which is udātta on its first syllable; in this case, by Pāṇini 6.2.52 (*aniganto'ñcatau vapratyaye*), the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member remains.
Regarding "pratyaṅmukhaḥ": here, the original accent of the subsequent member (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*) applies. Regarding "gomukhaḥ"...

Regarding "mahāmukhaḥ": it has been stated that the words *go* and *maha* have the udātta accent on the final syllable. Regarding "sthūlamukhaḥ": the root *sthūl* (DhP 1904) means "to grow large" and belongs to the curādigaṇa; from it, the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule for pacādyac. Thus, the word *sthūla* has the udātta accent on the final syllable. Regarding "muṣṭimukhaḥ": [it is derived] from the root *muṣ*.

[The suffix] *ktic* [is applied]. By that, the word *muṣṭi* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). Regarding "pṛthumukhaḥ": under the heading of *kurbhraśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.23), the suffix *ku* is applied to the roots *prath*, *mrad*, and *bhrasj*, with vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) and the elision of the *s*.
By that, *pṛthu* has its final syllable accented. Regarding "vatsamukhaḥ": [the same applies].

By the rule *ṭhvṛtṛvadibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 6.2.40), etc., that [suffix] is applied; by that, *vatsa-* has its final syllable udātta. In examples such as *gomuṣṭi*, even that [accent] which would apply to a prior member ending in a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) or the like—characterized by being a standard of comparison—is also [precluded] by this [rule].
It is set aside. The scope for this prohibition is where *go* and so forth are the objects of comparison (*aupamāna*);

for instance, in the cases "one whose face is like a cow," "one whose face is like a fist," and "one whose face is like a calf," in all instances *go* and so forth are the things compared (*aupameya*), not the standards of comparison (*upamāna*). [This is established] by the subsequent sūtra.

There is scope for the option characterized by the upamāna [suffix] when the first member of the compound is *niṣṭhā* (a past passive participle) and so forth, provided that the cow or other such thing has something else as its point of comparison— such as *siṃhamukhaḥ* ("lion-faced") or *vyāghramukhaḥ* ("tiger-faced"). However, where the cow or other such thing is itself the point of comparison— that is, where it constitutes the first member of the compound— then, since both [rules] would apply, the rule characterized by the upamāna [is preferred].
This very prohibition sets aside the previous prohibition.
169. *niṣṭhopamānād anyatarasyām* (6.1.169).
Since the rule *mukhaṃ svāṅgam* (6.2.167) would have applied obligatorily, this statement provides an option (*vikalpa*). [The commentary begins:
"When this final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) is udātta," and so forth.
Because of the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām*, this rule prescribing the acute accent on the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) is applied optionally. Therefore,
when this does not take effect, then by the alternative view of Pāṇini 6.2.110 (*niṣṭhopasargapūrvapadasyānyatarasyām*), [the acute accent falls on the final syllable of the compound].

The acute accent (*udātta*) falls on the final syllable of the first member (*pūrvapada*). Since this is also prescribed as an optional rule, when the *yadādy-ādeśa* (the substitution of *yad* etc. does not occur, then by the application of *gatiranantaraḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.49), which prescribes the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) for the first member, the accent of the *gati* itself remains. Consequently, the acute accent falls on the initial syllable. Since this is so...
From this, there are three examples:

one is the prescription of the udātta accent on the final syllable of the subsequent member by this very sūtra; the second is [the application of] *ṭhniṣṭhopasargapūrvād anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.2.110).

By the rule *niṣṭhopasargapūrvam anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.2.110), the acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable of the first member is prescribed; by the rule *gata-ranantaraḥ* (6.2.49), the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the prefix *gata-* is prescribed. Thus, in the word *siṃhamukhaḥ*, the word *siṃha-* [is treated accordingly].

It is udātta on the final syllable because it ends in the suffix *ac* added after the root *pac* (and others). Regarding the word *siṃha*: from the roots *tṛhi* and *hiṃsi*, both meaning "to injure" (*dhā.pā.* 1455, 1456)—the form *tṛha* being the reading in the Dhātupāṭha—one who injures (*hinasti*) is a *siṃha*; the transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyaya*) occurs due to its belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group. Regarding the term *vyāghramukha*: [from the root] *ghrā*...

From the root *gandhopādāne* (Dhātupāṭha 926), preceded by the prefixes *vi* and *ā*, the suffix *ka* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.136 (*ātaścopasarge kaḥ*). Therefore, the word *vyāghra* is also oxytone (having its final syllable accented).

170. *Jāti-kāla-sukhādibhyaḥ anācchādanāt ktaḥ akṛta-mita-pratipannāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.170). For example: *śāṅgarajagdhaḥ*. [This is derived] from the root *śam*, either from *guṇati* or *iti*, by the rule *śami dhātoḥ saṃjñāyām*.
(3.2.14) Thus, from *śaṅkara*, [the suffix] *ac* is applied; furthermore, because [the word] belongs to the *prajñādi* group—an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*)—the suffix *aṇ* is applied.

By that, the word *śāṅgara* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). Regarding the example "eaten by a *palāṇḍu*": from the root *pala* in the sense of "going" (DhP 839), the suffix *āṇḍu* is applied according to the rule "uṇādayo bahulam" (3.3.1). By that...

The word *palāṇḍu* has its accent on the middle syllable. Regarding the term *surapīta*: according to the rule *su-sū-dhā-gudhibhyaḥ kran* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.42), the word *surā* has its acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable. Regarding the term *māsajāta*: from the root *masī* in the sense of "measuring" (or "transforming," according to the Dhātupāṭha 1221), the suffix *ghañ* is applied; thus, [the word *māsa* is derived].
The first syllable is udātta. Regarding the word *saṃvatsarajātaḥ*, under the governing rule *aśeḥ saraḥ* (Daiva Up. 8.50)—[the form] *saran* being derived from Daiva Up.
Pañcikā 3.70—the rules *vaseśca* (Daiva Up.
8.51) and *sampūrvāccit* (Daiva Up. 8.52) apply. Consequently, *saṃvatsaraḥ* has its final syllable as udātta.
Regarding "dvayahajātaḥ" and "tryahajātaḥ": it has been stated that the words *dvi* and *tri* have the udātta accent on the final syllable.

Regarding "sukhajātaḥ": from the root *khan*, preceded by *su*, the suffix *ḍa* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.101 (*anyeṣv api dṛśyate*). By this rule, the word *sukha* has the udātta accent on the final syllable. The word *duḥkha* should be understood in the same way.

Therefore, the word *tṛpra* has its udātta accent on the final syllable. Regarding the word *kṛcchrajāta*: according to the rules "from the root *kṛ*, *icch* is the suffix and *krū* is the augment" (*Daiva-kośa* 8.38; *Pañcapādikā* 2.21)—specifically, "from *kṛ*, *icch* is the suffix and *krū* is the augment"—the word *kṛcchra* has its udātta accent on the final syllable. From the root *asu* in the sense of "to breathe" (*Dhātupāṭha* 1209)...

By the rule *bahulam anyatrāpi* (Dhātupāṭha 8.40), the suffix *rak* is applied; therefore, *asram* has its final syllable udātta. By the rule *vṛtṛ-vad-ahani-kami-kaṣibhyaḥ saḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 9.21)—[the variant reading being *kaṣi-yu-mucibhyaḥ* according to the Dhātupāṭha]—the suffix *sa* occurs after the root *am* as well, due to the word *bahula*. *Aṃsaḥ* has its initial syllable udātta because it belongs to the *vṛṣādi* group.

Regarding the word *ṭhalaka*: from the root *al*, the suffix *gha* is applied "mostly in the masculine when a name is formed" (Pāṇini 3.3.118); thereafter, the suffix *kan* is added, so the word *aplaka* ends in *kan*. Consequently, it has the acute accent (*udātta*) on its first syllable. Regarding *karuṇa*: [it is derived] by the rule "from *kṛ*, *vṛ*, *dṛ*, etc., the suffix *unan*" (Pañcapādī Uṇādi-sūtra 3.53); thus, the word *karuṇa* has the acute accent on its first syllable. Regarding *rañjeḥ kvun*: [this refers to the rule] "from the root *rañj*, the suffix *kvun*."

Because of the word "bahula" (variously), this also occurs after the root *kṛp*. Therefore, *kṛpaṇam* has its initial syllable udātta. The form *soḍhaḥ* ends in a *kta* suffix; therefore, it has the udātta accent on its final syllable. As before, the changes of *gh* to *ḍh* and so forth must be applied. Regarding *pratīyam*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "in which water has gone toward."

By the rule *ṭhṛkpūḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.74), the suffix *a* is added as a compound-final (*samāsānta*), and by *ḍvyantarupasargebhyo 'pi īt* (6.3.97), the substitution of *ī* occurs. Regarding the example *putrajātaḥ*:
here, only the accent of the *bahuvrīhi* applies. [The suffix] *ktra* is added after the roots *am*, *ci*, *mid*, and *śas* (Daiva Uṇādi-sūtra 8.86).

By the rule *ṭhpuvo hrasvaśca* (Pāṇini 6.2.134), the word *putra* is oxytone. But how can there be the subsequent placement (*paranipāta*) of the word *jāta*, when by the rule *niṣṭhā* (Pāṇini 2.2.36), the former placement (*pūrvanipāta*) ought to occur here? To this he says: "Because it belongs to the class beginning with *āhitāgni*."

And so forth. This word *putrajāta* is included among the group beginning with *āhitāgni*; therefore, by the rule *vāhitāgnyādiṣu* (Pāṇini 2.2.37), there is the optional posterior placement of the word *jāta*.
Regarding the phrase *vastracchannaḥ*: *vastra* means "covering," based on the derivation that it is that by which something is covered (*ācchādyate*).
The word *vastra* has the aforementioned accent. The word *cchanna* is derived from the causative (*ṇyanta*) of the root *chad* in the sense of "covering" (*apavāraṇe*;
DhP 1833), with the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*), and is thus irregularly formed (*nipātita*) by Pāṇini 7.2.27, *vā dantaśānta*, etc.
Thus, in the expression *vasanacchannaḥ*: the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied to the root *vas* in the sense of "covering. By that [suffix],...

The word *vasana* has its first syllable udātta. Regarding the example *kuṇḍalakṛtaḥ*: this word *kuṇḍa* has its first syllable udātta by the rule *nabviṣayasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26). Regarding the example *kuṇḍamitaḥ*: [it is derived from] the root *māṅ* in the sense of measuring (Dhātupāṭha 1142); the substitution of *it* occurs by the rule *dyatisyati* (Pāṇini 7.4.40).

Now, one might ask: why is there no prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) of the word ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix in these *bahuvrīhi* compounds, contrary to the rule "the *niṣṭhā* [is placed first]" (Pāṇini 2.2.36)? To this he says: "In these," and so forth.
Because this has been done, the rule prescribing the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*) for words following [terms denoting] genus (*jāti*) and the like is established.

Precisely because of this indicator, the word ending in a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) does not undergo prior placement; otherwise, indeed, this teaching regarding its final acute accent (*antodātta*) would be untenable.

Since the word *jāta* also ends in the suffix *kta*, this option is stated so that, although it would otherwise necessarily have an udātta accent on the final syllable by the preceding rule [6.2.169] when following words such as *jāti*, it may optionally do so. For example: *dantajātaḥ*.
By the rule *ṭh-si-mṛ-g-riṇ-vam-i-da-mi* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.155), the suffix *tan* is applied; thus, the word ends in *tan*.
Consequently, this [word] has its initial syllable udātta. Regarding the term *stanajātaḥ*: the word *stana* has the accent already mentioned. 172. *nañ-subhyām* (6.2.172).

"ṭhayavaḥ deśaḥ" and so forth. In "yava-vrīhi-māṣāḥ," the first syllable is udātta according to the rule "tṛṇadhānyānāṃ ca dvy-aṣām" (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.27). Regarding "samāsasya" and so forth: here, "compound" (samāsa) is the subject under discussion, as is the "subsequent member" (uttarapada). In that regard—

If this final acute accent were to belong to the subsequent member of the compound (*uttarapada*), then in the case of *anṛcaḥ* and *bahvṛcaḥ*, once the compound suffix *aC* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.4.74 (*ṛkpūrabdhūḥ*), the rule would result in the final syllable of the subsequent member—
the word *ṛc*— being acutely accented. This would apply to the entire compound.
The acute accent (*udātta*) being prescribed [by the rule] applies only to the letter *a*, because that [suffix] is a constituent part of the compound (*samāsa*);
its status as a constituent part of the compound follows from its being prescribed under the governing heading of "compound-final suffixes" (*samāsāntāḥ*, Pāṇini 5.4.68). Therefore...

This final acute accent (*antodātatva*) is desired for the member of the compound. But how is that which is merely desired obtained? It is obtained from the mention of the word "prior" (*pūrva*) in the rule *kapi pūrvam* (Pāṇini 6.2.173).
For that mention of "prior" serves to indicate that the final acute accent being prescribed by this [rule] applies to the member of the compound.

This is done for the purpose that the suffix *kap* itself should not occur. For if this were the case where the word consisting of both members (*ubhayapada*) had this final acute accent (*antodātta*), then—even without the mention of "preceded by *kapi*" (*kapipūrva*)—the suffix would apply to the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) preceded by *kapi*, and not to *kapi* itself; for it is not [the case that]...
The suffixes of the *kapotapada* compound are [part of the whole], and therefore the mention of "the preceding member" (*pūrva*) is redundant.

This was stated by accepting the view that "the suffixes forming the end of a compound (*samāsānta*) are parts of the compound itself, not of the final member (*uttarapada*). Now, however, [it is maintained that] those suffixes are parts of the final member as well.

Relying on this view, he says: "And [the suffixes] forming a compound-final" (*samāsāntāś ca*), etc. The word "and the latter member" (*uttarapadaṃ ca*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. The connection with the context is that this final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) is intended. The particle *iti* is used in the sense of a reason. Alternatively, it is intended that this final acute accent belongs specifically to the latter member. Why?

Because the compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) become constituent parts of the final member (*uttarapada*), for that reason, in the case of *anuc-* and *bahvṛc-* when the compound-final suffix has been applied, the oxytone quality (*antodātatva*) occurs; and that [oxytone quality] would belong to the final member. It belongs to that very compound-final suffix itself.

The intended meaning is that because it is a constituent part of the final member [of the compound], the acute accent (udātta) occurs at the end of the suffix *sān*. That [accent] would belong to the final member; rather, it belongs to that very compound-suffix (*samāsānta*), because it is a constituent part of the final member—this is the intended meaning. For if it were a compound-suffix...

If they were not constituents of the *uttarapada*, then the rule prescribing that the final syllable of the *uttarapada* constituent be acute would not apply to the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*). For when compound-final suffixes are [treated as] constituents of the *uttarapada*, it is precisely that [suffix] which becomes the final syllable of the *uttarapada*. But how [is this so]?

Is the status of the *samāsānta* suffixes that of being constituents of the final member (*uttarapada*) [of the compound]? Yes, because the *samāsānta* suffix is prescribed before the final member which constitutes the meaning of the compound, and subsequently the formation of the compound is prescribed with that [final member] as its ending. For instance, regarding the rule *na kapi* (Pāṇini 7.4.14), he will state: "Of the feminine [ending] and of a word ending in *go*, when they are *upasarjana*" (1.2.48).

Furthermore, this [suffix] *kap* is not short (*hrasva*). For when *kap* is applied to the final member (*uttarapada*) in the sense of a compound, the subsequent compounding must occur with that which ends in *kap*; thus, the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) of the compound does not end in a feminine suffix. And by means of a word ending in a compound-final suffix (*samāsāntapratyaya*)...

If a compound (*samāsa*) is formed, then, according to the rule "those that fall in the middle of it are included by its mention" (*vyā.pa.* 21), the suffixes at the end of a compound (*samāsānta-pratyaya*) become constituent parts of the final member (*uttarapada*). If this is so, would it not follow that their status as constituents of the compound is untenable? This is not the case; for even that which is a constituent of a constituent (*avayavāvayava*) [is indeed a constituent].
The whole becomes the part; for instance, when it is said, "Let all the limbs of Devadatta be adorned," even the parts of the limbs of Devadatta, such as the fingers and so forth, are adorned.

173. *kapi pūrvam* (6.2.173). Since the preceding rule would have resulted in the acute accent (*udātta*) falling on the suffix *kap* itself, this rule prescribes that the acute accent falls on the preceding member when *kap* is present. Examples include *ṭhakumārīkaḥ* and so forth. Here, *kap* is applied by the rule *śeṣādvibhāṣā* (5.4.154).

The word *kumārī* is oxytone by virtue of the *anudātta-nivṛtti-svara*. The word *vṛṣalī* is also [oxytone] due to the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* which characterizes a genus (*jāti*). The word *brahmabandhūḥ* is also [oxytone] because it ends in the suffix *ūṅ*, by virtue of the accent of that suffix.

174. *Hrasvānte’ntyātpūrvam* (Pāṇini 6.2.174). [The commentary begins: "That which has a short vowel as its final member," and so forth. By this, he demonstrates that for the bahuvrīhi compound *hrasvānta* itself, the referent of another word (*anyapadārtha*), the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), or the entire compound is intended. [Example: *ayavaka*.

Regarding the term *deśaḥ*: here, when *kapi* follows, the word *yava-* ending in a short vowel constitutes the second member of the compound; or alternatively, this is the compound *ayava-*. In that case, the syllable preceding the final *va*, namely the syllable *ya* (the *yakāra* and *akāra*), becomes udātta. In this manner, other instances should be understood.

Now, what is the purpose of the mention of "pūrva" (before), since the word "pūrva" already continues from the rule *kapi pūrvam* (6.2.173)? To this he says: "While 'pūrva' is continuing," and so forth.
For if a second mention of "pūrva" were made, there would be a difference in application due to a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*).

By virtue of the inclusion of the word "pūrva" (preceding), otherwise it would be purposeless. In that regard, by one application [of the rule], it is ordained that when a short vowel (*hrasva*) ends [the stem], the syllable preceding the final one is *udātta*; by another [application], however, there is a restriction that when a short vowel ends [the stem], the syllable preceding the final one is not *udātta*. Therefore, in the case of *kapi*—

Previously, the penultimate syllable was not acute. If there were no restriction by the rule beginning with "tena" (Pāṇini 2.3.29), then, since there would be no acute accent on the syllable preceding the final one here, the *kap* suffix would cause the penultimate syllable to become acute. However, when the restriction "kapi pūrvam" (Pāṇini 6.2.173) is applied, this does not occur.
Therefore, by the rule *tena ṭhañ-sucbhyām* (Pāṇini 6.2.172), it is precisely that which ends in the suffix *ka* which becomes udātta on its final syllable;
how this occurs has been demonstrated right here.
175. *bahornañvadutarapadabhūmni* (6.2.175).
This rule is intended so that whatever accentuation is prescribed for a word following *nañ* by rules such as *nañsubhyām* (6.2.172) may also apply when *bahu* follows. It is "like *nañ*" (*nañvat*).
The suffix *matup* is replaced by *iman* according to Pāṇini 5.1.122 (*nañvat*). The word *bhūman* means "the state of being much" (*bahorbhāvaḥ*);
the suffix *imanic* is applied because it belongs to the *pṛthvādi* group, and the substitution of *bhū* for *bahu* occurs according to Pāṇini 6.4.158 (*bahorlopo bhū ca bahoḥ*).

Thus, there is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the *bhūman* of the final member. Now, what is the purpose of this extended application (*atideśa*), since [the rule] "after *nañ*, *su*, or *bahu*, when the final member ends in *bhūman*" would already suffice?

Thus it might be said; however, when the *yoga* is applied in this way, the rule *naÑsuorapyutarapadabhūmnī* does not become a qualifying condition for that [preceding rule], because this [latter rule] depends on the possibility [of its application]. For it is just as in the case of *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.68).

In this case, the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) is a qualifying term based on possibility, applying only to *ṅī* and *āp*, and not to *hal*; likewise, this [mention of "many"] will apply only to *bahu* and not to *nañ* and *su*, for the existence of plurality in the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is not possible for those two. If that is so, then even that which...

The rule for the accentuation of a Bahuvrīhi compound marked by the negative particle *nañ* when it stands at the end of a word located outside [the compound] is also intended to apply here through this extension; for this reason, this extension is formulated so that [the rule] may likewise take effect.
Consequently, even the rule "after *nañ*, the first syllable of *jara*, *mara*, *mitra*, and *mṛta* is udātta" (Pāṇini 6.2.116) applies.
The term "bahu" is extended [to other cases] as in "bahumanāḥ. Here, however, the word "bahu" does not signify plurality with respect to the final member of the compound.

176. *na guṇādayo'vayavāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.176). Since the previous rule would have led to an over-extension (*atiprasakta*), this rule prohibits [the designation of] qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth as parts (*avayava*). For example: *bahuguṇā rajjuḥ* ("a rope with many strands"). The meaning is "having many parts. [The root] *guṇ* is used in the sense of addressing (*āmantraṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 1894).

It belongs to the *curādi* group; therefore, the suffix *ghañ* is applied. By this, the word *guṇa* has its first syllable udātta. According to the rule "ṭhaśeḥ saraḥ" (Daiva 8.50) [also cited as "saran" in Daiva (Pañjikā 3.70)], the word *akṣara* has its final syllable udātta.
That by which the *chandas* is measured is *cchandomāna*. In the word *cchandomāna*, the accent is determined by the *kṛt* accent.

The word *māna* has its initial vowel accented acute (*ādyaudāta*), because it ends in the suffix *ghañ*. *Sūktam* means "well-spoken"; it is a *prādi* compound. By the rule for the accent of words ending in *tha*, *thā*, etc. (Pāṇini 6.2.144), the word *sūkta* has its final vowel accented acute (*antodāta*). *Adhyāyaḥ* means "that from which [the Veda] is studied"; it is derived with the suffix *ghañ* by the rule *iṅśca* (Pāṇini 3.3.21).
A chapter that contains a hymn (sūkta) has its final syllable accented acute (udātta).

177. *Upasargāt svāṅgaṃ dhruvam aparśu* (Pāṇini 6.2.177). It should be understood that "upasarga" here is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for words such as *pra* and others. This is because a member of one's own body (*svāṅga*) lacks connection with an action [independently]. However, the term "prādi" was not explicitly used [in the rule] for the sake of variety.
This word *dhruva* exists in the sense of a "part" (*avayava*), as in the rule *dhruvam apāye 'pādānam* (Pāṇini 1.4.24);

it also exists in the sense of "unchanging in nature" (*ekasvarūpa*), as in the expression *dhruvam asya śīlam*. Therefore, he says—showing that it is taken here in the sense of being unchanging in nature—"The term *dhruva* denotes that which is of a single, uniform nature."

And so forth. By the phrase "constantly" (*satatam*) and so on, he demonstrates the permanence of the *pṛṣṭha*. The word *pṛṣṭha* is oxytone (accented on the final syllable), because it is derived from the root *pṛṣu*, *mṛṣu*, or *vṛṣu* in the sense of "sprinkling" (*secane*) with the suffix *thak*.

Regarding the term *darśanīyalalāṭaḥ*: the word *darśanīya* has its middle syllable udātta according to Pāṇini 6.1.217 (*upottamaṃ rit*). From the root *lala* in the sense of "desire" (DhP 1687), the suffix *āṭ* is applied by Pāṇini 3.3.1 (*uṇādayo bahulam*), whereby the word *lalāṭa* has its middle syllable udātta. Thus, [the compound] *darśanīyalalāṭaḥ* is a *karmadhāraya*. In this case, because the first member ends in a long vowel, the final syllable of the entire compound becomes udātta by Pāṇini 6.1.223 (*bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā pūrvapadam*). However, since this is a *tatpuruṣa*, the rule Pāṇini 6.2.2 (*samāsasya*) applies, which prescribes that the final syllable of the compound is udātta; consequently, the penultimate syllable of *lalāṭa* becomes udātta. Therefore, the word *darśanīyalalāṭaḥ* has its penultimate syllable udātta. Alternatively, one may consider that the word *lalāṭa* itself has its penultimate syllable udātta due to the application of the suffix *āṭ*. In this view, the word *darśanīyalalāṭaḥ* would have its penultimate syllable udātta by virtue of the rule Pāṇini 6.2.172 (*antodāttād uttarapadād anyatarasyām anityasamāse*), which allows for the penultimate syllable of the second member to be udātta when the compound is not necessarily permanent. Thus, the word *darśanīyalalāṭaḥ* has its penultimate syllable udātta. Alternatively, one might argue that the word *lalāṭa* has its penultimate syllable udātta by the application of the suffix *āṭ*, and thus the word *darśanīyalalāṭaḥ* has its penultimate syllable udātta by the rule Pāṇini 6.2.172. Or again, one might hold that the word *lalāṭa* has its penultimate syllable udātta by the application of the suffix *āṭ*, and therefore the word *darśanīyalalāṭaḥ* has its penultimate syllable udātta by the rule Pāṇini 6.2.172. Or yet again, one might maintain that the word *lalāṭa* has its penultimate syllable udātta by the application of the suffix *āṭ*, and thus the word *darśanīyalalāṭaḥ* has its penultimate syllable udātta by the rule Pāṇini 6.2.172. Or finally, one might assert that the word *lalāṭa* has its penultimate syllable udātta by the application of the suffix *āṭ*, and therefore the word *darśanīyalalāṭaḥ* has its penultimate syllable udātta by the rule Pāṇini 6.2.172. Or else, one might say that the word *lalāṭa* has its penultimate syllable udātta by the application of the suffix *āṭ*, and thus the word *darśanīyalalāṭaḥ* has its penultimate syllable udātta by the rule Pāṇini 6.2.172.
