Or yet again, one might maintain that the word *lal

[The word] *praśākhā* means "a tree with spreading branches. According to the rule *uṇādayo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.1), the suffix *kha* is applied to the root *śo* (meaning "to thin" or "to sharpen," Dhātupāṭha 1145); then the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added, followed by the lengthening of the homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*), and finally, by the rule *ekādeśa udātenodātaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.5), the resulting single substitute vowel is acute. By that [process],...

The word *śākhā* is udātta on its final syllable. Regarding the example "udbāhuḥ krīśati": here, because the state of the arms being of one form does not exist, there is the quality of being raised (*udhruvatvam*). For he does not suffer with his arms always raised; rather, at times his arms are even lowered. Regarding "utparśuḥ": [this is derived] from the root *svṛś*.
The word *parśu* ends with the suffix *śun*, according to the rule *śvaṇśunau pṛ ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.96;
note that the reading *śvaṇ śuno pṛ ca* is found in the Mu-pāṭha). Consequently, it is udātta on its first syllable.
178. *vanaṃ samāse* (Pāṇini 6.2.178).

Regarding the phrase *samāsamātre* ("in every compound"): by the inclusion of the word *mātra* ("mere"), it indicates the exclusion of the *bahuvrīhi* [compound]. Regarding the example *pravaṇe*: when this is a *bahuvrīhi*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that for which the forest (*vana*) is preeminent (*pra-*)" or "the forest which has been made excellent (*prakṛta*)".

When, however, it is a *tatpuruṣa*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is either "an excellent forest" (*prakṛṣṭaṃ vanam*) or "a forest gone beyond" (*pragataṃ vanam*). Regarding the term *nirvaṇe*: here too, when it is a *bahuvrīhi*, the analysis is "one from whom the forest has departed" (*nirgataṃ vanam asya*); but when it is a *tatpuruṣa*, it is "gone out from the forest" (*niragato vanāt*), which is the *tatpuruṣa*.

Regarding the rule *ṭhkugatiprādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18): what would be the consequence if the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) were not made for the purpose of including all types of compounds? To this he says: "For it would apply only to the *bahuvrīhi*.
[The suffix] *kyun* is added after the root *rañj* (Dhātupāṭha 5.24; Pañjikā 2.80). Because of the irregularity (*bahula*) of the application, [the form *raṅku* is derived].
It also occurs from the root *ṭhvan* in the sense of "requesting" (Dhātupāṭha 1470). By that [suffix], *vana* is udātta on its first syllable.

179. *antaḥ* | (6.2.179) The word *antaḥ* is prescribed as an initial-accented (*ādyudātta*) nipātana within the group of words beginning with *svarādi*. For example: *antarvaṇo deśaḥ* ("a forest region").
This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which there is a forest," because the word *antaḥ* is included in the *śauṇḍādi* list [governing the locative case].

(2.1.40) Or it is a locative compound (*saptamīsamāsa*). The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] is according to Pāṇini 8.4.5, *pra-nir-antare*, etc. "The rule is commenced for the sake of cases where there is no prefix (*anupasarga*)," because in the case of a prefix (*upasarga*), it is already established by the preceding rule.
180. *antaśca* (Pāṇini 6.2.180).
The word *antaḥ* is acutely accented on its first syllable because it ends in the suffix *tan*, according to the rule *ṭhasisṛgriṇvamidamilūpūdhurvibhyastan* (Daiva Upādhyāya 6.7).

181. *na nivibhyām* (6.2.181). Since the preceding rule would have resulted in the acute accent on the final syllable even for words preceded by *ni* and *vi*, this prohibition is stated. [The commentary says: "When the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) has been applied. When...

When it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) according to the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, the first member retains its original accent" (Pāṇini 6.2.1). But when it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound, [the accent is determined] by the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa*, [the first member retains its accent] when it has the meaning of 'equal' (*tulyārtha*)" (Pāṇini 6.2.2), and so forth.

182. *parermukha-lalāṭa-bhruvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.182). [The forms] *parimukham*, *parilalāṭam*, and *paribhruvam* are examples. Regarding *parimaṇḍalam*: the words *kūla* and *tīra* have the aforementioned accents in the rule *kūlatīratūlamūla-* (6.2.121), etc. [The form] *parimaṇḍalam*.

On all sides, that is, everywhere, is the circular maṇḍala. From the root *maṇ* in the sense of "adornment" (*bhūṣā*), the suffix *kala* is applied by virtue of the rule *kalas tṛpaś ca* (Dhātupāṭha 3.21) and the general principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*), as well as by the rule *vṛṣādibhyaś cit* (Daiva-Uṇādi-sūtra 8.109). By means of that [suffix].

The word *maṇḍala* has its final syllable accented (*antodāta*). Regarding the statement "this is a *bahuvrīhi*," and so forth: when it is a *bahuvrīhi*, [the analysis is] "that which has its bank (*kūla*) all around" or "that which has its shore (*tīra*) all around";
therefore, *maṇḍala* has its final syllable accented. Regarding the statement "this is a *bahuvrīhi*," and so forth, when...

In that case, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; its analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which has its bank (*kūla*) all around" or "that which has its shore (*tīra*) all around. But when it is a *prādi-samāsa*, then it is "the bank encompassed" or "the shore encompassed. Furthermore, when it is an *avyayībhāva*, then it is "around the bank" or "around the shore."

The *avyayībhāva* compound is formed by the rule "ṭhapaparibahirañcavaḥ pañcamyā" (Pāṇini 2.1.12). In the expression *pari kūlāt*, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) occurs due to the application of the term *karmapravacanīya* according to the rule "pañcamyapāṅparibhiḥ" (Pāṇini 2.3.10). The status of *pari* as a *karmapravacanīya* is established by the rule "apaparī varjane" (Pāṇini 1.4.88).

(1.4.88) Thus it is said. It is appropriate that this rule prescribing final acute accentuation (*antodātatva*) is formulated for the *bahuvrīhi* and the *tatpuruṣa*; for in those cases, it serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to the general rule of final acute accentuation for compounds, and the original accentuation (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member would otherwise apply. However, it is inappropriate [to extend this] to the *avyayībhāva*, for in that case...

[The desired accent] is already established by the rule regarding the acute accent on the final syllable of a compound (*samāsāntodātta*). For no exception to that—namely, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*)—is applicable here; therefore, he says:
"Even in the case of the *avyayībhāva* alternative," and so forth. Even when the *avyayībhāva* alternative applies, [the following holds].

By the rule "ṭhparipratyupapā" (Pāṇini 6.2.33), the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member would have applied, but this is set aside by the present injunction prescribing that the final syllable be acute (*antodātta*). What, then, is incorrect here? [The author replies: "And that which has such a nature," etc. That of which the state of being (*bhavana*) is on both sides (*abhitaḥ*).
The intrinsic nature is apprehended by grasping that which exists in its entirety, and not that which possesses an intrinsic nature contrary to it.

183. *prād-asvāṅgaṃ saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 6.2.183). Regarding the example *prakoṣṭham*: [the suffix] *than* is applied to the roots *uṣi*, *kuṣi*, and *gāti* by the rule *uṣikuṣigārtibhyasthan* (Dhātupāṭha 6.29).
Thus, the word *kroṣṭha* has its initial syllable accented acute (*ādyaudāta*). Regarding the example *pragṛham*: [the suffix] *ka* is applied to the root *guh* by the rule *gehi kaḥ*.
By this [rule] (Pāṇini 3.1.144), the suffix *kap* is applied; consequently, *gṛha* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). Regarding *pradvāram*:
by the rule "that which falls under the scope of *nañ* and does not end in *ani*" (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26), *dvāra* has its first syllable accented (*ādyudātta*).
Regarding *prapadam*: like *dvāra*, *pada* has its first syllable accented (*ādyudātta*). Regarding *prahastam*: [the same applies].
By the rule "ṭh-si-mṛ-g-riṇ-vam-i-da-mi" (Uṇādi Sūtra 6.7), the suffix *stan* is applied after the root *has*. Consequently, the word *hasta* is udātta-accented on its first syllable.

184. *nirudakādīni ca* (Pāṇini 6.2.184). Regarding the form *nirudakam*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that from which water has departed" (*niṣkrāntam udakam asmāt*), or it is a *prādisamāsa* (prepositional compound) meaning "departed from the water" (*niṣkrāntam udakāt*). [It is also explained as] "that which causes water to flow" (*udakaṃ kāyati*).

By the rule *sthāto 'nupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3), and by *udakasyodaḥ saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 6.3.57), there is the substitution of *uda-* for *udaka-*. Therefore, *udaka-* is udātta on its final syllable. Regarding *nirupalam*:
the word *upala-* is udātta on its final syllable according to the Unādi Sūtra *viṭapaviṣṭapaviśipolapāḥ* (Unādi 7.12).

It is elided; others say "nirupalam. [The form] *nirupalam* is derived from the root *lā* preceded by the prefix *upa*, with the suffix *ka* by rule 3.1.136 (*ātaścopasarge*). Consequently, by rule 6.2.144 (*sthāthādisvareṇa*), the word *upala* has its first syllable udātta.
[Examples include] *nirmakṣikam*, *nirmaśakam*, and so forth.

The words *maśaka* and *makṣikā* have an acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) and on the last syllable (*antodātta*). For in that regard, [the rule] "the suffixes beginning with *tha*, before *prāc*, up to *śakaṭi*" (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.24) applies; and [the rule] "the second [syllable] among those ending in *prādiṣ*" (Phiṭ-sūtra 3.50)—where "the second" is understood to carry over—applies. [This concerns the words] "of these," and so forth. If...

When it is a *prādi-samāsa* (prepositional compound), the analysis is "the water has gone out" (*nirgatam udakam*) or "gone out from the water" (*nirgatam udakāt*). When, however, it is a *bahuvrīhi*, the analysis is "that from which the water has gone out" (*nirgatam udakam asmāt*). Now, why does the *avyayībhāva* (indeclinable compound) not also apply to these? To this he says: "But in the case of the *avyayībhāva*," and so forth.

However, in the case of *bahuvrīhi* and *prādi* compounds, [the desired accent] is not established by the rule that the final syllable of a compound is udātta. For instance, regarding the *bahuvrīhi*, it is stated that the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member applies as an exception to the general accent of a compound, according to the rule "In a *bahuvrīhi*, the first member retains its original form" (Pāṇini 6.2.1). Similarly, in a *prādi* compound, [the same applies] in a *tatpuruṣa*.
By the rule *tulyārtha* (Pāṇini 6.2.2) and so forth.

In the form *niṣkālakaḥ*, the word *kāla* is acute on the first syllable because it ends in the suffix *kan*. In the form *niṣkālikaḥ*, there is a *prādi*-compound meaning "one who has gone out from *kālikā*. [The word] *kālī*...

By the rule *jānapadādisūtreṇa* (Pāṇini 4.1.42), [the word] ends in *ṅīṣ* after "dvitīya" (according to the Phiṭ-sūtras), and thus it is udātta on the final syllable; consequently, even when the suffix *kan* is added in the sense of the same meaning (*svārthika*), it remains udātta on the first syllable.

Regarding "ṭhniṣpeṣaḥ": from the root *viṣlṛ* in the sense of "crushing" (Dhātupāṭha 1452), the suffix *ghañ* is applied; thus, the word *peṣa* has its initial syllable udātta. Regarding "ṭhtarīpāti": by the rule "āto 'nupasarge kaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.3), the word *tarīpa* has its final syllable udātta; [the compound] means "a contemptible *tarīpa*."
By the inclusion of the word *kutsita* (contemptible), he shows that in the word *dustarīpa*, the prefix *duḥ-* functions in the sense of contempt.
Regarding the statement, "Some [read] *nistarīpa*," they analyze it as *nirgatas tarīpaḥ* and form it as a *prādi*-compound. Regarding the statement, "Others read *nistarīka*," they recite it thus.
The connection [is as follows]:
regarding "nirajinam" and so forth, it has been stated that "ajina is udātta on the final syllable.
Regarding "pareḥ" and so forth, [the rule applies to] "hastapādakeśāḥ," which are members of the body (svāṅga) ending in consonants or short vowels and beginning with a vowel.
(Phiṭ-sūtra 2.29) and so forth; these are the initial acute [accents]. The meaning is "of the *śiṭ* sounds and of pronouns (*sarvanāman*).
The word *karṣa* has its final syllable acute by virtue of Pāṇini 6.1.159: "The final syllable of a noun ending in *ghañ* is acute if it contains the vowel *ṛ* or the suffix *ātvat*."

185. *abhermukham* | (6.2.185) [The word] *abhimukhaḥ* [is formed]. The word *mukha* has its accent as previously stated; the word *abhi* is udātta on the final syllable. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

And so forth. When it is a *bahuvrīhi*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that by which the face has been approached" (*abhigataṃ mukham anena*). But when it is a *prādisamāsa* (prepositional compound), it is: "approached toward the face" (*abhigato mukham*) or "approached by means of the face" (*abhigato mukhena*).
Why does this not become an *avyayībhāva* (indeclinable compound)? To this he says: "But in the case of an *avyayībhāva*," and so forth.

"This statement is for the sake of excluding the *bahuvrīhi* compound. When the face (*mukha*) is permanent (*dhruva*), then it is for the sake of excluding what is non-permanent (*adhruva*) and for the sake of excluding what is not a limb (*asvāṅga*).
Even when the face is non-permanent and not a limb within a *bahuvrīhi*, as in "a hall facing [the east]" (*abhimukhā śālā*), where the face has been approached (*abhigataṃ mukham*).
The term *yasyāḥ* is a bahuvrīhi compound. In this case, the rule *upasargāt svāṅgam* (Pāṇini 6.2.177) does not apply; for the word *mukha* does not denote a limb of the body (*asvāṅga*).

186. *apācca* (Pāṇini 6.2.186). The word "also" (*api*) in the commentary indicates that the *avyayībhāva* compound is also applicable here; its meaning is that not only the *bahuvrīhi* and *tatpuruṣa* compounds are included. In that regard, when...

In that case, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that from which the face has departed. When, however, it is a *prādisamāsa*, then it is "the face has departed. Furthermore, when it is an *avyayībhāva*, then it is *apamukhāt*, meaning "excluding the face."

The *avyayībhāva* [compound] is [formed] by the rule "ṭhapaparibahirañcavaḥ vañcamyā" (Pāṇini 2.1.12). But how can the *avyayībhāva* necessitate [this rule], since it is already established simply by the fact that compounds have their final syllable accented (*samāsāntodātta*)? To this he says: "For even there," and so forth.

The phrase "the original accent of the base" (*prakṛtisvaratvam*) is to be supplied here. In that regard as well, the rule *paripratyupāpā* (Pāṇini 6.2.33) and others has stated that the first member of the compound retains its original accent; this is an exception to the general accentuation rules for compounds. Therefore, the avyayībhāva compound also serves as a motivating factor [for this rule].

"The purpose of this division of rules (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows. [The meaning is: "In the subsequent rule, so that only *ap* may continue to apply, and not *abhi*. This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) even when preceded by an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
The same applies to the subsequent rules, such as: *dvitribhyāṃ paddanmūrdhasu bahuvrīhau* (Pāṇini 6.2.197).
Therefore, they are to be understood as existing prior to this yoga.

187. *sphigapūtavīṇāñjo’dhvakukṣisīranāman nāma ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.18). A copulative compound (*dvandva*) is formed from the words beginning with *sphiga* and ending with *nāman*, as well as words denoting ploughs (*sīra*). Regarding "words denoting ploughs," this refers to those beginning with *hala*. Examples are *apasphigam* and *apapūtam*; these are *prādi*-compounds.

Or it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The words *sphig* and *pūta* are acute on the first syllable according to the rule "ṭh-svāṅga-śiṭām-adantānām" (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.29). Some, however, desire that the word *sphiga* be acute on the final syllable because it belongs to the *dhṛtādi* group (Phiṭ-sūtra 1.21).

In the rule *ṭhrāsnāsāsnāsthūṇāvīṇāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.157), the word *vīṇā* is prescribed as having its first syllable acute (*ādyaudāta*). From the root *añjū*, the suffix *asun* is applied; therefore, *añjas* has its first syllable acute. [From the roots] *śīṅ*, *krus*, *ruh*, *ji*, *kṣi*, *sṛ*, and *dhṛ*, the suffix *kvanip* is applied. [Note: The reading *kvan* is found in the manuscript.]

With reference to this, [the suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule *aderdhaśca* (*Pāṇini 5.1.20*), resulting in the form *adhvan*. Consequently, this word is udātta on its first syllable. This is further governed by the rule *upasargādadhvanaḥ* (*Pāṇini 5.4.85*) and others. While the suffix *añ* is being carried over from the rule *acpratyanyavapūrvāt sāmalomnaḥ* (*Pāṇini 5.4.75*), the rule *upasargādadhvanaḥ* (*Pāṇini 5.4.85*) applies.

By this [rule], the suffix *ac* is prescribed as a compound-final (*samāsānta*) element. Consequently, because that *ac* suffix is marked with the *cit* indicator, its status as having the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*) is established by that very fact. But surely the compound-final suffix is obligatory; why then is it said, "when the compound-final suffix does not exist"? To this [it is replied]:...
He says: "And [the rule] is non-eternal," and so forth. If the suffix added at the end of a compound were eternal, the mention of the word *adhvan* (road/path) here would not have been made;
for the accentuation of the final syllable as udātta would already be established by the fact that the suffix *ac* is marked with the indicatory letter *c*. Yet it has been mentioned;
therefore, this very fact indicates that "the rule regarding suffixes added at the end of compounds is non-eternal. By this...
In this regard, such usages as "tatrōpāsitālōkabhartari" become justified.
[The rule] "pluṣikuṣiśuṣibhyaḥ ksiḥ" (Dhātupāṭha 1.11)— [the Dhatupatha reads "pluṣiśuṣikuṣibhyaḥ ksiḥ"].

189. *anorapradhānakanīyasi* (Pāṇini 6.2.189). [The example is] *anujyeṣṭhaḥ*. When the suffix *iṣṭhan* follows, the substitution of *jy* for *vṛddha* occurs by rule 5.3.62 (*vṛddhasya ca*). The word *jyeṣṭha* is udātta on its first syllable due to the *nit*-accent. [The example is] *anumadhyamaḥ*.
By the rule *madhyān maḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.8), the form *madhyamaḥ* is derived; it is oxytone by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).

It is stated that "a *prādi*-compound (*prādisamāsa*) is one in which the meaning of the first member is predominant. For in this case, that which follows the eldest and is the middle one is expressed primarily through the *prādisamāsa*.

But the elder and the middle [brothers] exist by way of being subordinate qualities (*guṇabhāva*). Therefore, this [compound] is one in which the meaning of the first member is predominant (*pūrvapadārthapradhāna*).

Regarding the form *anukanīyān*: when the suffix *īyasun* follows, the word *yuva-* undergoes the substitution of *kan-* according to Pāṇini 5.3.64, *yuvālpayoḥ kananyatarasyām*; thus, the word *kanīya-* [is derived].

By the rule "nitsvareṇādyaudāttaḥ," the word *jyeṣṭha* has its first syllable udātta; thus, [the compound] *anu-jyeṣṭhaḥ* is formed. This is a bahuvrīhi compound where the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*) is predominant.
Consequently, the word *jyeṣṭha* possesses the quality of denoting the primary [member].

190. *puruṣa* is also [an example] of an anvādiṣṭa [word]. (6.2.190) From the root *pṛ* in the sense of "protecting" or "filling" (DhP 1489), the suffix *kuṣan* is applied by the rule *puraḥ kuṣan* (DaU 9.14). Consequently, the word *puruṣa* has its initial syllable udātta.

"Anvācita means 'taught as secondary' (*apradhānaśiṣṭa*). For example, in the sentence "Go for alms and bring the cow," the bringing of the cow [is secondary]; or as in the rule *kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.11), the elision of the suffix *sa* [is secondary]. Or, "that which has been mentioned and is subsequently mentioned. That which...
That which is spoken after what has already been spoken is "spoken-after-spoken" (kathitānukathita). Or, that which is spoken after having first spoken something else is called "spoken-after-spoken."
"One who follows after a person is 'anupuruṣa'"— thus it is said of a person who exists subsequently.
191. *Aterkṛtpade* (Pāṇini 6.2.191).

Regarding the phrase *ṭhakṛtpade*: "akṛt" and "pada" together form the compound *akṛtpade*; this is in the dual number of the nominative case. In the example "aty-aṅkuśo nāgaḥ," the word *aṅkuśa* [is derived from the root] *kuś*, with the suffix *sānasi* (according to Daiva 10.17).

By the rule *sānasi-dharṇasi-parṇasi* (Daiva-Uṇādi 4.107; Pañcapādī-Uṇādi 4.107), etc., from the root *lakṣaṇa* (Dhātupāṭha 1024), the suffix *ac* is applied according to *pacādyac*, followed by the feminine suffix *ṭāp*.
By the rule *ekādeśa udātenodātaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.5), the resulting single substitute is udātta. Thus, the word ends in an udātta vowel. [The word] *atipadā*...

Regarding "śakvarī": by the rule *khano gha ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.125), the suffix *gha* is applied to the root *pad*. Indeed, by the inclusion of the marker *gh*, it is indicated that the suffix *gha* occurs after other roots as well; thus, *pada* has its final syllable udātta. Regarding "atikāraka": this is formed from the root *kṛ* with the suffix *ṇvul*. In this case, the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-* (Pāṇini 6.2.2) applies.
By these and other such rules, the accent of the preceding word becomes unaccented (avyaya-svara).

Regarding the rule "ṭhaterdhātulopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.2.145), it should be stated that wherever there is the elision (lopa) of a verbal root (dhātu), the subsequent member (uttarapada) following the suffix *āti* becomes udātta at its final syllable. For what purpose? He says: "iha" and so forth.

If it were not stated that "there is elision of the verbal root (*dhātulopa*) after *ati*," then this [suffix] would also apply here: *śobhanaḥ gārgyaḥ* → *atigārgyaḥ*. For in this case, the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) following *ati* is not a non-derivative form (*akṛdanta*). And in this other case, it would not apply: *atikrāntaḥ kārakāt* → *atikārakaḥ*. [This is because the rule] "prefixes such as *nir* and others [are compounded] in the sense of having gone beyond (*krāntādi*)... applies.

The compound *pañcamyā* (Vārttika 94) is a *prādi*-compound. For in this case, the final member (*uttarapada*) is a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix that denotes a kāraka. If it were not stated [in the rule] "when there is elision of a verbal root" (*dhātulope*), then this [rule] would not apply here either.
However, since it is stated thus, it does apply here as well, for there is indeed an elision (*lopa*) of the verbal root *kram*. Elision.
Furthermore, because its meaning is already understood through the compound, that which is not being explicitly uttered is not observed.

192. *neranidhāne* (6.2.192). "Nidhāna" means "non-manifestation. "Anidhāna" is the absence of nidhāna. [The examples are] *nirmūlam* and *nyakṣam*. From the root *mūla* in the sense of "foundation" (*pratiṣṭhāyām*) [DhP 529], the suffix *ac* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*).

Therefore, the word *mūla* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). Regarding the rule "From *vṛ*, *tṛ*, *vad*, *han*, *kam*, and *kaṣ*, the suffix *sa*" (Daiva Up. 9.21)—with the addition "from *kam*, *i*, *kaṣ*, *yu*, and *muc*" (Daiva Up.)—and under the heading of this, the rule "The suffix *sa* after *aś* in the sense of eating" (Daiva Up. 9.24), the word *akṣa* also has its final syllable accented because it ends in the suffix *sa*. [The word *tṛṇam* has its initial syllable accented (*nitṛṇam*)].
Thus: by the rule *ṇabviṣayasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26), the word *tṛṇam* has its first syllable udātta.

"This is a *bahuvrīhi*," and so forth. When it is a *bahuvrīhi*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that from which roots have gone out" (*nigatāni mūlāny asya*). When it is a *prādisamāsa*, the analysis is: "the root that has gone out" (*nigataṃ mūlam*).
"Why does this not become an *avyayībhāva*? To this he says: "But in the case of an *avyayībhāva*," and so forth.

However, in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member has been stated by the rule "In a *bahuvrīhi*, [the first member] remains as its own nature" (6.2.1), which is an exception to the general rule that the final syllable of a compound is accented. This also applies to the *tatpuruṣa*.

By the rule "In a *tatpuruṣa*, when the meaning is that of 'equal' (*tulyārtha*)," etc. (Pāṇini 6.2.2); therefore, without this specific statement, the final acute accent (*antodātatva*) for those two [compounds] would not be established. In the case of an *avyayībhāva*, however, it is established by the general rule of the final acute accent of a compound (*samāsāntodātatva*), for no exception to that rule has been stated there.

"ṭh-nivāgvṛṣalaḥ; nidaṇḍaḥ. In these cases, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member remains. The word *vāk* is derived with the suffix *kvip* by the rule "kvibvacipracchi... (Dhātupāṭha 10.2), and thus its initial syllable is udātta. From the root *damu* (meaning "to pacify") [Dhātupāṭha 1203]—from this...

"By the rule *ṭhñamantāṅṅḥ* (Daiva Upādhyāya 5.7), the word *daṇḍa* is also udātta on its final syllable. Regarding the statement, 'The word *ni* expresses the sense of depositing (*nidhāna*),' the meaning is that it expresses non-manifestation (*aprakāśatā*). But how does the word *ni* here express the sense of depositing? To this he says: 'For the words beginning with *pra*... "

And so forth. By the word "vṛtti" (function/operation) here, compound-formation (*samāsa-vṛtti*) and the like are intended. For particles (*prādayaḥ*), by their very nature, express an action together with its factors (*sādhanā*) within the domain of *vṛtti*. Therefore, in this context of compound-formation, that action which consists in non-manifestation and is denoted by the word "nidhāna" (depositing/storing) is [the referent].
The word "ni" expresses that which has speech as its means and punishment as its means.

193. *prateraṃśvādayastatpuruṣe* (Pāṇini 6.2.193). This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member (*pūrvapada*) in a *tatpuruṣa* compound. For example, in *pratyaṃśuḥ*, it is a *prādi*-compound. Under the governing heading *kurbhraśca*, the word *aṃśu* is included by the rule *mugayvādayaśca* (Daiva Upādhyāya 1.121).

It is *nipātita* (irregularly formed). By that [rule], it is *antodātta* (accented on the final syllable). From the root *jan*, there is the suffix *ghañ*; by that, *jana* is *ādyaudātta* (accented on the first syllable).
The word *rājan* also ends in the suffix *kanin*. Regarding the phrase "the word *rājan*," etc.:
when, due to its non-universality (*anityatva*), the suffix *ṭac* prescribed by "rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac" (Pāṇini 5.4.91) is absent...

In that case, the word *rājan* serves a purpose in this recitation. But why does it not serve a purpose when that [suffix] is present as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*)? To this he says: "For when that exists," and so forth. Furthermore, the non-eternality of the rule for compound-final suffixes has already been indicated previously. And here, the word *rājan* is included in the recitation.

This indicates that the rule for forming compound endings (*samāsāntavidhi*) is not universally obligatory (*anityatva*). From the root *uṣa* "to burn" (DhP 696), the suffix *ṣṭran* is applied; by this, the word *uṣṭra* has its first syllable accented acute (*ādyaudāta*). From the root *śiṭ* "to heat" (or *khiṭ* "to fear," DhP 302), the suffix *ṇvul* is applied; by this, [the word *śiṭa* is formed].

The word *kheṭaka* is also acutely accented on the first syllable. The word *ajira*, ending in the suffix *kirac* according to the rule *ṭhajira-śiśira-* (Uṇādisūtra 8.27), is a nipātana; therefore, it is acutely accented on the final syllable. From the root *dru* (meaning "to go" with the sense of contempt) preceded by the prefix *ā*, [the suffix *ka* is applied] by the rule *ātaścopasarge*.
By virtue of this specific grammatical derivation (*nipātana*), the first member of the compound ends in *r*.

Consequently, because its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is lost, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) does not apply; instead, the word becomes oxytone (*atyantodātta*). [The suffix] *lyuṭ* is applied to the root *śru* (meaning "to hear," DhP 942).

Therefore, by the rule *litsvareṇādyaudātaḥ*, the word *śravaṇa* has its first syllable acute. With *vṛtestikan* (Daivapāla Uṇādisūtra 3.28) as the governing context, the suffix *tikan* is applied by the rule *kṛtibhidilatibhyaḥ kit* (Daivapāla Uṇādisūtra 3.29), followed by the feminine suffix *ṭāp*.
Thus, the word *kṛttikā* has its first syllable acute. From the root *ṛdh*, either the suffix *ac* or *ghañ* is applied.

Therefore, the word *ardha* has its udātta accent on the final syllable, or alternatively, on the initial syllable. From the root *pura* (meaning "to go before") [DhP 1.346], the suffix *ka* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.135 (*igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ*). Consequently, the word *pura* has its udātta accent on the final syllable.
"ṭhpratyāgatā aṃśavo 'sya," and so forth. Here, in a bahuvrīhi compound, the original accent (prakṛtisvara) of the first member (pūrvapada) occurs.

194. *upād vyajajinamagaurādibhyaḥ* (6.2.194). [The example] "upadeva" is a *prādi* compound. Because the word *deva* ends in the suffix *ac* (added after roots ending in vowels), it is oxytone (*antodātta*). [The example] "upasoma" is formed by *atistusuhusṛ* (6.4.149).

By [the rule] beginning with "ityādinā," the word *manas* has its acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable. From the roots *huḍ* and *huḍ* meaning "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 352, 353), the suffix *ac* is applied according to the *pacādi* group; thus, the word *hoḍa* has its acute accent on the final syllable.
It has been stated that *ajina* has its acute accent on the final syllable, and its inclusion here is for the sake of excluding the two *yaj* suffixes.

The word *gaura* is acutely accented on the first syllable because it ends in the suffix *dyu*. The time joined with Tiṣya is called *taiṣa*, by the rule *prāgdīvyato’ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.1.83). By the rule *sūryatiṣyāgastyamatsyānām ya upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.149), there is the elision of *y*.
The forms *naiṣa* and *taiṣa* do not end in *aṇ*; therefore, they are acutely accented on the final syllable. [The root] *raṭ* is used in the sense of "addressing" or "reproaching."

From this [root *laṭ*], the suffix *ac* is applied. Because *r* and *l* are identical, the *repha* (the sound *r*) becomes *lakāra* (the sound *l*). Thus, *laṭ*. From the root *luṭ* in the sense of "stirring" (*viloḍane*; DhP 314), the suffix *pacādyac* is applied.

By that, both *laṭ* and *loṭ* are also oxytone (having the acute accent on the final syllable). [The word *āmīva* is derived from] the rule: "The words *śava*, *ahva*, *jihvā*, *grīvā*, *pīvā*, and *āmīvā*" (Daiva Uṇādi Sūtra 8.128).
Thus, the word *jihvā* is derived with an udātta accent on the final syllable. Under the governing rule *ṭhiṇsiñji* (Daiva Upādhyāya 5.35;
Daiva Pañcapāṭha 3.2), and specifically by the rule *kṛṣervarṇe* (Daiva Upādhyāya 5.37), the suffix *nak* is applied to the root *kṛṣ*.

Then, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added, resulting in a long vowel by the rule of homogeneous vowel lengthening (*savarṇadīrghatva*). Finally, the single substitute for the two vowels is udātta by the rule *ekādeśa udātenodātaḥ*.

By that rule, the word *kṛṣṇā* has its final syllable udātta. According to the rule *adhnyādayaśca* (Daiva 8.14), the word *kanyā* is prescribed as having its final vowel svarita. From the root *guḍ* in the sense of "solidification" (or "protection," according to the Dhātupāṭha), the suffix *ka* is applied by virtue of the rule *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.135).
Therefore, *guḍa* has the udātta accent on the final syllable. The words *kalpa* and *vāha* have the udātta accent on the final syllable because they belong to the *vṛṣādi* group.
195. [The suffix *ka* is applied] after *sora* in the sense of "throwing. (Pāṇini 6.2.195) Regarding "susthaṇḍilaḥ": *sthaṇḍila* means that upon which a place (*sthāna*) is firm (*sthira*).
It is acutely accented on the first syllable because it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group. Regarding "susphigābhyām": the word *sphiga*...

The first [syllable] is udātta. In the case of *supratyavasitaḥ*, the word *pratyavasita* is oxytone by the rule regarding the suffixes *tha*, *atha*, etc. (Pāṇini 6.2.144). Now, one might object: even when the compound is formed with the word *su*, would it not still be oxytone by the very same rule for *tha*, *atha*, etc.?

It will come to pass; for what purpose, then, was this cited? He thinks thus: "If there were another meaning [for the rule], then, because it is subsequent, it would be proper that the final acute accent (antodātta) should apply here by this very rule alone. If the word *su* here functions only in the sense of praise (*pūjā*), then [the case of] disparagement (*avakṣepaṇa*)...

For whose sake [is this]? He says: "The meaning of the sentence, however, is disparagement. He states the reason for this very point: "Because it is expressed with such malice. For here, indeed, a sentence of this kind, such as "Be gone! The ground is excellent," is employed out of malice.

Therefore, it is indeed the meaning of the sentence that is being cast down. In the phrase "among the good grasses," the expression is used with the desire to manifest a quality, not out of malice. Consequently, there is no disparagement;
rather, there is only praise.
196. *vibhāṣotpucche* (Pāṇini 6.2.196).
[The example is] *utpuccchaḥ*. The word *puccha* has its first syllable acute (*udātta*) by the rule *nabviṣayasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26).
"This is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) in both cases," meaning that when the word *utpucccha* does not end in the suffix *ac*.

In that case, there is the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound. When, however, by the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha* (Pāṇini 6.2.2) and others, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member—which is an indeclinable—is applied as an exception to the rule for the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound, then this option (*vibhāṣā*) applies because the final-accentuation would otherwise not have been obtained. When...

However, when there is the intention to express the meaning "he raises his tail," the suffix *ṇic* is applied by the rule *puccha-bhāṇḍa-cīvarād ṇiṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.20). After that [form ending in] *ṇic*, the suffix *ac* is added by the rule *pacādyac* to the verb *utpuccchayati*. Thus, the word-form *utpucccha* arises; then, by the rule regarding the accent of *thā-thādi* (Pāṇini 6.2.144), [the final syllable becomes udātta].

Since the rule for the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*) would have applied invariably, this is an option; thus, it is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) regarding what has already been established. For example, in *udastapucchaḥ* ("one whose tail is raised"), the original accent of the *bahuvrīhi* compound itself remains.

197. *dvitribhyāṃ pāddanmūrdhasu bahuvrīhau* (Pāṇini 6.2.197). Regarding *dvitribhyām*: this is a fifth case (*pañcamī*) characterized by connection with a direction [according to Pāṇini 2.3.29]. Regarding *pāddanmūrdhasu*:
this is a seventh case (*saptamī*) characterized by a state [according to Pāṇini 2.3.37], used to indicate a condition.
The bahuvrīhi compound is subject to this operation; therefore, he says: "by the words *dvi* and *tri*, etc.

[Examples are] *dvipāt* (two-footed) and *tripāt* (three-footed). By the rule *pādasya lopo'hastyādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.138) and *saṃkhyāsupūrvasya* (5.4.140), there is the elision of the vowel *a*; thus the word *pāda-* [is modified].
Because it ends in the suffix *ghañ*, the word *pād* is necessarily udātta on its first syllable. Regarding the form *dvidan*:

by the rule *vayasi dantasya* (Pāṇini 5.4.141), the substitution of *datṛ* occurs for *danta*. It has been stated that the word *danta* is udātta on its first syllable; therefore, by virtue of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the form *datṛ* is also udātta on its first syllable.

Regarding the word *dvimūrdhā*: the word *mūrdhan* is an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) stem ending in the suffix *ran*, according to the rule *śvannukṣanpūṣanplīhan* (Uṇādisūtra 6.55). Consequently, it is acute-accented on its first syllable. Regarding *mūrdhan* and so forth: [the rule] *dvitribhyāṃ ṣa mūrdhnaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.115) [the variant reading in the manuscript is *ṣa*].
The suffix *ṣ* [which forms the feminine *mūrdhanyā*] would have applied; however, that was not done. Therefore, in this context, the word *mūrdhan* remains ending in *-n*.
But what is the reason that the word *mūrdhan* is employed here with the compound-suffix (*samāsānta*) unapplied?
To this he says: "Of that," and so forth. If the word were employed with the compound-suffix already applied, then only when...

The quality of being udātta at the end of a compound (antodātatva) would occur when there is a compound-ending suffix (samāsānta), but it would not occur when such a suffix is absent. Therefore, the purpose of mentioning the form without the compound-ending suffix is so that the quality of being udātta at the end may occur even in the absence of a compound-ending suffix. But [one might object]: surely [the form] always occurs with the compound-ending suffix.
It must necessarily exist; how then could it be non-existent? To this he says: "This very [fact]," and so forth.

The very fact that the word *mūrdhan*—without the application of a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*)—is employed for the sake of accomplishing this purpose, is itself the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the compound-ending suffix is not mandatory (*anitya*).
Thus it is said: "it exists. By this, the usage beginning with *dvimūrdha* becomes justified.

If, however, the word *mūrdhan* is employed here without the application of the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*), then when that suffix is applied, the word would not be oxytone (*antodātta*). This is because [the accentuation] applies to that which has already had the compound-ending suffix added.

To the objection that [the two cases] are different words (*śabdāntaratvāt*), he says: "Although," and so forth. For here, the *bahuvrīhi* is the subject of the grammatical operation (*kāryin*), and the status of being a part of that [compound] belongs to the suffix added at the end of the compound (*samāsānta*). That which has a part is a "possessor of a part" (*ekadeśin*); that *bahuvrīhi* which is the possessor of a part of the suffix added at the end of the compound is what is meant by "a part of that."

The state of being a part of that [compound] is its being a constituent of that [bahuvrīhi]. By this, while demonstrating that the compound-ending suffix is a constituent of the bahuvrīhi, he refutes the notion that a word with a compound-ending suffix is a distinct word altogether.
Thus, since the bahuvrīhi is the subject undergoing the grammatical operation here, and the compound-ending suffix is a part of it, [the suffix does not produce a separate word].

Therefore, even when a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) is applied, there is still optionally the case where the final syllable is udātta, as in *kalyāṇamūrdhā*. Here, the word *kalyāṇa* is udātta on its first syllable according to the rule *nabviṣayasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26). In the case of *dvayormūrdhā*, however, the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound is obligatory.
It comes to be.

198. *saktham* from *ākrānta*. (6.2.198) Regarding the word "saktham": the term *sakyi* is understood here as that which has the compound-ending suffix *ṣac* added by the rule *bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇoḥ svāṅgāt ṣac* (5.4.113).

Regarding "ṭhakrāntāt": that which has *kra* as its final member is *krānta*; that which is not *krānta* is *akrānta*. Regarding "gaurasakthaḥ": the word *gaura*, because it ends in the suffix *aṇ* belonging to the *prajñādi* group, is udātta on the final syllable. Regarding "ślakṣṇasakthaḥ": this is derived from the base [root] *ślakṣṇa* while the rule "ksna after kṛtya and śū" (Daiva Upādhyāya 5.49) is in effect.
The word *ślakṣma* ends in the suffix *ksna*, according to the rule "ṭhśliṣeraccopadhāyāḥ" (Daiva 5.51). Consequently, it is udātta on its final syllable.

Regarding the term "cakrasaktha," it is derived from the root *kṛ* with the suffix *kin* and reduplication, according to the rule "karoteḥ kin dve ca" (Daiva 8.103). [The rule states that there is reduplication of the root *kṛ*.]
In the word *cakra*, as in *ca'--da.u.ṭ*, the initial syllable is udātta.

199. *parādiś chandasi bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.2.199). [The commentary states: "By the word *para* here, the word *saktha* alone is intended. This is because of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), for it is that which is proximate due to its presence in the preceding rule. If this is so, then the mention of the word *para* is redundant.
Is it not the case that only the word *saktha* would carry over here? This is not so;

since the term *bahuvrīhi* also carries over here, its initial udātta accent might also be suspected [of applying]. [In the case of] *añjisaktham*, the word *añji* is udātta on the final syllable by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*).

Furthermore, even if the suffix *ini* is applied in the sense of possession (*matvartha*) to the word *añjas*, it would still be oxytone. For example, in *lomaśasaktham*: because the word *lomaśa* ends in the suffix *śa* by the rule *lomādipāmādipicchādibhyaḥ śanelacaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.100), it is oxytone. [Similarly in] *ṛjubāhuḥ*.
Thus, under the governing rule *kurbhraśca* (Dhātupāṭha 1.107),

the words *ṛju* and *bāhu* are formed with the suffix *ku* according to *arjidṛśikamyamipaśibādhāmṛjipasitugdhugdarvihakārāśca* (Dhātupāṭha 1.112). Consequently, they are udātta-accented on the final syllable.

Regarding the examples "vākpatiḥ" and "citpatiḥ," these are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). In these cases, the final member of the compound (*uttarapada*) has its first syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*);

this is established by virtue of the mention of the term *bahula*. Indeed, since the rule of optionality (*vibhāṣā*) is already in effect, this example is presented to demonstrate what is accomplished through the application of *bahula*.

"From that, there is a manifold transposition. Since the grammatical operation is accomplished by this mention of "manifoldly" (bahulam), therefore a transposition occurs manifoldly. Now, was it not already prescribed previously that there is a transposition of vowels? True, this is so; however, this is an elaboration of that very rule.
"‘The first member [of a compound] is cited as having the acute accent on the initial syllable’—as in *vākpati* and *citpati*.

And here, by the mention of ‘the following member’ (*para*), the second member is indicated. ‘In the section concerning the final acute accent’—that is, in rules such as *antaḥ* and *thāthaghañktājabitrakāṇām* (Pāṇini 6.2.44)."
"In the section concerning the acute accent on the final syllable of the preceding member" refers to rules such as *antaḥ* (6.2.92) and *sarvaṃ guṇakārtsnye* (6.2.93).
"In the section concerning the acute accent on the first syllable of the preceding member" refers to the rule *ādir udāttaḥ*: *saptamī-hāriṇau*.

"In [rules] such as *dhamya'haraṇe* (Pāṇini 6.2.65), all such cases are included by means of the mention of *bahulam* (‘diversely’). The intention is that although the term *vibhāṣā* (‘optionally’) was already in effect, the mention of *bahulam* was made for that purpose. As for words such as *tricakra*, the accentuation of the preceding and following members has already been stated."
Furthermore, it is not stated here.
Thus ends the second quarter of the sixth chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who is like a Bodhisattva.
Now begins the sixth chapter,
the third quarter.

The subsequent word (*uttarapada*) is present; therefore, with the intention that the subsequent word is obtained even without explicitly mentioning "subsequent word," he asks: "What is the purpose of [specifying] 'subsequent word'? He gives the example: *niḥstokaḥ*.

This is a *prādi-samāsa* (prepositional compound) according to the rule: "Words beginning with *nis*, etc., form compounds with a word in the fifth case when meaning 'gone beyond' (*krānta*), and so forth" (Vārttika 94). Thus...

He considers this: if the mention of the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) were not made, one would obtain only this much—that there is no *aluk* elision of the ablative case after those words such as *stoka* when they occur in a compound, whether they function as the subsequent member or the prior member; however, the specific distinction that the rule applies only when *stoka* and so on occur as the prior member before a subsequent member would not be established. And therefore...

In the case of *niḥstoka* as well, there would be no elision (*aluk*) [of the genitive case-ending]. For here too, the fifth case-ending follows a word such as *stoka* that resides within the compound.
Now, even so, this mention of "the subsequent member of the compound" (*uttarapada*) should not be made at all.

By the paribhāṣā "lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā" (Vyā.pa. 3), only that fifth case (*pañcamī*) which is specifically prescribed by rules such as *ṭhstokādibhyaḥ karaṇe ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.33) is to be understood;
however, not that fifth case which is prescribed by the general rule *apādāne pañcamī* (Pāṇini 2.3.28).

[The rule] refers specifically to that [fifth case ending] which is prescribed by that very [rule]; it does not refer to the fifth case ending prescribed by the general definition, "The fifth case ending is used for the *apādāna* (ablative)" (Pāṇini 2.3.28). Furthermore, one must necessarily rely on the paribhāṣā concerning "that which is taught in a specific rule versus that which is indicated by its characteristics"; otherwise, in the case of "departed from a little" (*stokādapetaḥ*), [the rule would incorrectly apply].

In the case of *stokāpeta*, there would likewise be no elision (*aluk*). This being so, in the case of *niḥstoka*, there would be no possibility of non-elision at all; for here, the ablative case is not prescribed by a specific rule (*pratipad-vihita*) from the word *stoka*, but rather is prescribed by a general rule (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-vihita*). What follows from this?

Is it for the purpose of excluding that [substitution] by means of the mention of the *uttarapada* (the subsequent member)? To this he says: "For the sake of another meaning," and so forth. This mention of the *uttarapada* is for the sake of the *ānaṅ* substitution;

for if this were not present, then by the rule "ānaṅ is substituted for the final vowel of the first member in a *dvandva*" (Pāṇini 6.3.25), *ānaṅ* would apply to the first member in the example "hotṛ-potṛbhyām."

If it occurs [in the case of the first member], then it would likewise occur for the subsequent member as well. Similarly, according to the rule *iko hrasvo’ṅyo gālavasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.61), just as the short vowel occurs here in *grāmaṇiputraḥ*, so too would it occur here in *grāmaṇīḥ*. Now, if the shortening were to occur even when there is no subsequent member, then...
Just as the short vowel occurs here— as in "grāmaṇiputraḥ"— so too would it occur here as well,
namely in "grāmaṇīḥ. But surely, if the short vowel were to occur even when there is no subsequent member of a compound,
then just as it occurs here in "grāmaṇiputraḥ," so too [would it occur] here.

It might be argued: "The form *grāmaṇīḥ* [would be problematic]. But if the short vowel were to apply even when it is not the final member of a compound, then by the rule "the neuter gender takes a short vowel for the nominal stem" (*hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya*), the same would apply here as well, resulting in *grāmaṇīḥ*.
Now, if the short vowel were to apply even when it is not the final member of a compound, then [by the rule] "the neuter gender... [the form would have to be short].

The rule "of the nominal stem" (1.2.47) would be redundant, since [the desired result] is already established by this very [present rule]. It is not redundant, because it serves the purpose of excluding stems ending in *i* (*aniganta*) and for the sake of making the operation compulsory (*nitya*). Furthermore, if the mention of the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) were absent, [the rule would apply to] a *kṛt* [suffix]. If that is so, then for whatever purpose this [rule] exists, it should have been stated in the very rule prescribing that [formation].

It must be performed. For what purpose is it done here? He says: "In this case also, for the sake of the removal of *aluk*," and so forth. The particle *iti* is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*). This subsequent mention (*uttaragrahaṇa*) is certainly necessary for another purpose;
however, when it is performed here, this is the specific distinction: even in the case of *niḥstokaḥ*, there is no *aluk*.

[The suffix] is made *nivṛtta* (withdrawn). Therefore, the paribhāṣā regarding "that which is taught by its specific technical definition" (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā*) need not be resorted to. Now, from what [source] do these two governing rules (*adhikāra*) derive? To this he says: "The governing rule for *aluk*," and so forth.

One rule of application (vidheya) serves to exclude another rule of application; thus, when *ānaṅ* is prescribed, it excludes *aluk* in the case of a subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Therefore: "The jurisdiction of *aluk* extends prior to *ānaṅ*; the jurisdiction of *uttarapada* extends prior to the jurisdiction of *aṅga*. That which [is prescribed] when a subsequent member follows—
An operation is prescribed for that [term] which possesses a relative designation; therefore, the preceding member is the locus of the prescription.
Consequently, the term *aṅga*, being understood as the locus of the prescription, sets aside the governing rule (*adhikāra*) regarding the subsequent member.
For whatever operation pertains to the *aṅga* is prescribed when a suffix (*pratyaya*) follows.

[The substitution does not occur] in the case of a subsequent member (*uttarapada*). For the designation *aṅga* does not apply to a subsequent member. Alternatively, because of the locative indication "in the subsequent member" (*uttarapade*), the substitution *ānaṅ* must occur only when the subsequent member is immediately following. If there were non-elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending here, then due to the intervention [of that case-ending], the immediate succession would not exist. And it is not the case that...

Even in the case of an intervention, it can be postulated that *ānaṅ* occurs by virtue of the power of the explicit statement (*vacana-sāmarthya*). For, if this were not the case, the mention of the word "nirdiṣṭa" in the rule "tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.66)—which serves the purpose of indicating immediate sequence—would be sublated, and an undesired form would result. It is not [the case].

Furthermore, it would not be logical to formulate a rule for an undesirable result in the treatise. Therefore, the governing heading (adhikāra) for *aluk* precedes *ānaṅ*. Since there is no such thing as an "aṅga" when a suffix (*pratyaya*) follows, that [rule] does not apply at all when a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) follows;
hence, the governing heading for the subsequent member (*uttarapadādhikāra*) precedes the governing heading for the *aṅga*.
2. *pañcamyāḥ stokādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.2).

The group of words beginning with *stoka* is not recited among the lists of nominal stems (*prātipadika-gaṇa*). Therefore, only those [words] enumerated in the Sūtra itself should be understood here as being intended.
Showing this, he says: "stoka-antika-dūra-artha-kṛcchrāṇi," and so forth. Now, why are those words beginning with *stoka* that are enumerated in the sūtra "karaṇe ca" (Pāṇini 2.3.33) not taken here?

He thinks thus: [if the intention were the same, the author] would have said "from *stoka* and so forth after the word ending in the *ṅsi* case-ending," instead of saying "after the fifth case-ending."

By this mention of more numerous syllables, it is indicated that "among those beginning with *stoka* which are being taken up, those by whose inclusion there is a greater collection of examples (*lakṣya*) should be included.
[In the rule *stokāntikadūrārthakṛcchrāṇi*, the term *dūrārtha* does not exist.]

When the reading of the *nyāsa* is accepted as being marked with a seal (*mudrita*), there occurs a greater collection of examples (*lakṣya*) because of the inclusion of their meanings; this is not the case with the others. Therefore, it is proper to accept only these.
But how does elision (*luk*) apply here, such that this prohibition [is stated] when it would otherwise have applied?
How is this done? He says: "When the compound has been formed," and so forth.

When the compound has been formed, by the rule *kṛttaddhitasamāsāśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.46), it acquires the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Consequently, since the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) would apply by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.71), [the following is stated].
This is stated as a prohibition.

But what is the reason that the non-elision (*aluk*) of words such as *stoka* ending in the singular number is illustrated, and not those ending in the dual or plural? To this he says: "of those ending in the dual and plural numbers."

And so forth. For in a compound (*vṛtti*), the qualifying words, setting aside numbers such as singularity and the like, attain the number of non-dual unity (*abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā*). Furthermore, that number is merely a general number, devoid of specific numerical distinctions; and because it is thus, [the following applies].

Because the intended meaning is not expressed, there is no compound at all for words ending in the dual or plural numbers. For *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and compound formations are characterized by their expressive power (*abhidhāna*). Regarding the passage beginning with "by that" (*tena*):
since this is so, there is no compound of *stoka* and other such words when they end in the dual or plural.

In such cases, there is never a single compound or a single accent for the expressions *stokābhyāṃ muktaḥ* (“released from two small [quantities]”) and *stokebhyo muktaḥ* (“released from many small [quantities]”). For the word *muktaḥ* following the word *stokābhyām* is indeed another word, entirely distinct [from the one following *stokebhyaḥ*]; likewise, the word *muktaḥ* following *stokebhyaḥ* is [entirely distinct].

This is so; here, the accent (*svara*) is also indeed manifold. For instance, in *stokābhyām*, the word is *madhyodātta* (accented on the middle syllable) by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*), whereas in *muktaḥ*, it is *antodātta* (accented on the final syllable) by the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*). The same applies in the case of *stokebhyo muktaḥ*.

Various accents (svaras) are to be understood [in general]. However, in the primary example, when there is a compound (samāsa), it becomes a single word (ekapada), and thus the accent is also only one.
For instance, by the rule *thāthādinā* (Pāṇini 6.2.144), here the final syllable has the udātta accent.

If there is no compound formation here for words ending in dual or plural numbers, then how do such forms as *goṣucaraḥ* and *varṣāsujaḥ* come to be? [The answer is: because they express the intended meaning. For it has been stated that non-expression is the reason for the absence of compounding; however, in these cases, the intended meaning is indeed expressed.

The expression of plurality certainly exists [in this case]. For where non-dual unity (abhedaikatva-saṃkhyā) arises, there is no expression of a specific number; however, non-dual unity does not arise here. And therefore—

Because it denotes the intended meaning [of water], the number of oneness and non-difference is not tenable. To explain: in the expression *goṣucara* ("moving in the waters"), the word *go* refers to water; and in denoting water, it denotes it as qualified by the number of plurality, just like the word *āp* ("waters"). [The same applies to] *varṣāsuja*.

Thus—the word *varṣāḥ* (the rains) also denotes a specific period of time characterized by the number of plurality. Therefore, since the number of plurality is already apprehended by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself, the number of non-dual unity does not arise here. If, however, it were to arise, then...
The number "plurality" would be excluded, and consequently, the intended meaning of the nominal stems *go* (cow) and *varṣā* (rainy season) would not be understood here.
Therefore, so that there may be no failure to comprehend the intended meaning of the words *go* and *varṣā*, [the rule must be formulated as follows].

In this case, the number one (ekatva) characterized by non-difference does not arise; consequently, because the intended meaning is expressed, a compound is indeed formed in the cases of *goṣucaraḥ* and *varṣāsujaḥ*. Regarding the statement, "An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*," this [term] *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī* is as follows:

The meaning is that the addition—that is, the formal presentation—of the word *śabda* must be made. But what, then, is not established here? It is the fifth case (*pañcamī*). Here, by the word *brāhmaṇa*, a specific portion of study is meant;
he who recites or tells that [portion] is called *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*, where the suffix *ṇini* is used in the sense of habit or profession (*tācchilika*). In this regard:

When the word *brāhmaṇa* is used, although the second case ending would normally apply according to the rule "the second case is used for the object" (Pāṇini 2.3.2), the fifth case ending must be added as an exception (*upasaṃkhyeya*). Furthermore, the non-elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending is already established by the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa* compound with a *kṛt*-suffix, [the case-ending] is frequently not elided" (Pāṇini 6.3.14). However, when [the word *brāhmaṇa*] is used in the sense of "one who draws out a portion from a Brāhmaṇa text and recites it," or "one who praises a part [of the Veda]," [the construction is justified].

If that is intended to be expressed, then the fifth case (*pañcamī*) need not be added as a supplement either; for its formation is already established by the rule "the fifth case is used in the sense of the *apādāna* (ablative)" (Pāṇini 2.3.28). But how, then, is the derivation performed here when the meaning of the fifth case is non-existent? To this he says: "a specific kind of officiant," and so forth. *Rūḍhi* means conventional usage or common renown.

"Name" refers to whatever [is applicable]. By the word "of that," only the conventional designation (*rūḍhi*) is referred to, and not the specific conventional term "brāhmaṇācchaṃsī. A conventional term denotes a particular officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), for it has been established as a name specifically for that person. Therefore, even for that [term], it is non-existent [in the case of the other].

Derivation is indeed performed by means of an existing constituent meaning. In that case, if the intended meaning is "he recites the Brāhmaṇa," then because there is no ablative (*apādāna*) as the meaning of the fifth case, the derivation is performed by means of a non-existing constituent meaning.
But when the intended meaning is that one recites after having taken [the portion] either from a Brāhmaṇa or for the sake of a constituent part,
then, because the sense of the ablative case is present, the suffix *sati* is applied.
3. *Ojaḥ-saha-ambhas-tamasa-stṛtīyāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.30).
In examples such as *ojasākṛtam*, the compound is formed by the rule *kartṛ-karaṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32).

Regarding the statement "the addition of *añjasa* [should be made]": the meaning is that the non-elision (*aluk*) of the third case ending following *añjas* must be taught (*upasaṃkhyāna*), that is, it must be formulated. The formulation for this is as follows, under the rule *ājñāyini ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.5): [the non-elision of the third case ending is taught].

The particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned; by it, the non-elision (*aluk*) of the third case ending occurs after the word *añjas*. Furthermore, we shall provide another demonstration for this later on.
For example, in *puṃsānujaḥ* and so forth; likewise, in *puṃsānujo januṣāndhaḥ*, [the non-elision] of the third case [occurs].

The meaning is that the formation of a compound without the *aluk* elision must be established. The establishment is as before. "Puṃsānujaḥ" means one who is younger by reason of being male (*puṃsā hetunā*). "Januṣāndhaḥ" means one who is blind by birth (*januṣā hetunā*).
The compound is formed through a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) of *Pāṇini 2.1.30*, "the third case. *Januḥ* refers to birth (*janmanaḥ*).
This is its name.
4. [The suffix *ṇini* is applied] after *manas* when it means "perceiving" (*saṃjñā*).
(6.3.4) 5. And also when it means "knowing" (*ājñāyin*).

(6.3.5) Thus, [the form] *manasājñāyī*. Here, the suffix *ṇini* is applied in the sense of one who habitually performs that action (*tacchilika*), and [the vowel *a* of *manas* is replaced by *yuk*] according to the rule *āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ*.
Thus, by [Pāṇini 7.3.33], there is the augment *yuk*, and it is a compound with an upapada.

6. And [the suffixes are applied] after a word denoting a numeral for filling (*pūraṇa*). (P. 6.3.6) The term *pūraṇa* (filling/numeral) is pronounced with a circumflex accent (*svarita*), and by means of this circumflex accent, the governing scope (*adhikāra*) is understood.
Thus, having taken up the mention of *pūraṇa*, that is, having taken up the mention of *pūraṇa*, the affixes prescribed for filling are [to be applied].

By the inclusion of the term "pūraṇa" (ordinal), these [suffixes] are understood, but not their own forms (*svarūpa*). Furthermore, the phrase "in a subsequent member" (*utarapade*) from rule 6.3.1 is carried over; therefore, by the technical rule concerning the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), it is understood that the grammatical operation applies when the subsequent member ends in a pūraṇa suffix.

Having reflected thus, he says: "When the word ending in a ordinal suffix (*pūraṇapratyaya*) is the final member [of a compound]," and so forth. Regarding "the fifth" (*pañcamaḥ*): it means the filler of five. By the rule *tasya pūraṇe ḍaṭ* (Pāṇini 5.2.48), the suffix *ḍaṭ* is applied; then, by the rule *nāntād asaṃkhyāder maṭ* (5.2.49), the augment *maṭ* is added. Regarding "the sixth" (*ṣaṣṭhaḥ*): it means the filler of six.
In the rule *ṣaṭkati-katipaya-caturāṃ thuk* (Pāṇini 5.2.51), there is the substitution of *ṣṭu* [i.e., *ṣ* for *ṣ* and *ṭ* for *t*].

In expressions such as *ātmanā pañcamaḥ* ("the fifth with himself"), by what [grammatical principle] is the third case (*tṛtīyā*) employed? For here there is no sense of the third case such as "instrument" (*karaṇa*), since the "instrument" and so forth are *kārakas* (factors of action), and [the third case is prescribed] for the action (*kriyā*).
[An objection is raised: "It would be a *kāraka* [compound], yet no action (*kriyā*) is found here.

To this he says: "In the rule for the third case," and so forth. [The opponent replies: "Let that be so; but how can there be a compound with the third case (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*), for there is no characteristic of a compound here? To this he says: "In the rule for the third case."

And so forth. [Objection: Let this be so; however, how can there be a compound with the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*), for there is no defining characteristic of a compound here? To this he says: "And [the rule] 'by the third case' (*tṛtīyā ca*)," and so forth. Alternatively, the third case here is precisely by the rule "The third case is used for the agent and the instrument" (*kartṛ-karaṇayos tṛtīyā*, Pāṇini 2.3.18).

Showing that this is a compound according to the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32), he says "or by oneself" (*ātmanā vā*), and so forth. Here, this third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used for both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*)—as in the expression "the fifth [note] is made. Once the compound has been formed, the word *kṛta* is not employed [separately].
Because its meaning is included within the compound (*vṛtti*).
Regarding the phrase "How so? and so forth: the intention here is that [the word *ātmanā*] should likewise be in the fourth case (dative), as in *ātmanā caturthaḥ*.
The resolution begins with "This is a *bahuvrīhi*," and so on; for if it were a *tatpuruṣa*, [the form would have been different].

It might be argued: "This is not a *tatpuruṣa* compound; what then? It is a *bahuvrīhi*. And since that [type of compound] applies only to two words ending in the nominative case, there is no occurrence of the undesired consequence. But surely, a *bahuvrīhi* is said to denote an external referent (*anyapadārtha*), and an external referent must be distinct [from the members of the compound].
Just as in the case of "citragu," meaning "one who has brindled cows," there is no distinct external referent for the compound here; this is not a fault,
for even when the referent is non-distinct, it functions as such through the principle of *vayapadeśivadbhāva* (the treatment of a thing as if it were what it designates).
For example: "The stone statue has a beautiful body."

7. *Vaiyākaraṇākhyāyāṃ caturthyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.7). [The example is] "vaiyākaraṇānām" (of the grammarians). Those who study or know grammar are called *vaiyākaraṇāḥ*. What, then, is the designation (*ākhyā*) of the grammarians? He says: "by which," and so forth. Now, why is it not thus?
It is explained as follows: that which pertains to grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is *vaiyākaraṇī*, formed by the suffix *aṇ* according to [Pāṇini 4.3.73] *ṭhaṇugayanādibhyaḥ*.

This *vaiyākaraṇī* is also a designation (*ākhyā*), hence the compound *vaiyākaraṇākhyā*. By the rule [Pāṇini 6.3.42] *puṃvat karmadhāraye*, there is the substitution of the masculine form; in that [designation],...
Regarding the phrase "in what is called grammar" (*vaiyākaraṇākhyāyām*): it is impossible to explain it in this way, for in that case [the following] would not occur:

*ātmanebhāṣaḥ* (spoken by the ātmanepada) and *parasmaibhāṣaḥ* (spoken by the parasmaipada). For what is the "speech" (*bhāṣā*) in grammar? It is that which has been composed in grammar. And these two have not been composed anywhere in grammar. As was stated previously...

When there is an explanation (*vyākhyāna*), this [term] also occurs here; these two are indeed designations (*ākhyā*) of grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), for grammarians certainly employ even these two [terms]. Regarding the term *ātmanepada*: it means "a word for oneself" (*ātmārthaṃ padam*). The compound is formed by the rule *caturthī* (Pāṇini 2.1.36), through a division of the sūtra (*yogavibhāga*).

Is it not the case that the compound is already established by the rule "the fourth [case-ending] for the sake of that" (Pāṇini 2.1.36)? It is not so established; for that [rule] is intended only when there is a relationship of material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*).
8. And [the word *para*] also [is compounded with a word ending in the locative case].
(6.3.8) 9. [The elision of the locative case-ending occurs] after a word ending in a consonant or the vowel *a*, when it is part of a proper name (*saṃjñā*).
(6.3.9) For example: *yudhiṣṭhiraḥ*. This is a compound by rule 2.1.44, *saṃjñāyām*, [specifically] by the rule *gaviyudhibhyāṃ...*.

The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule *sthiraḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.95). Now, how is there no elision (*aluk*) in the word *gaviṣṭhira*, since the word *go* is neither stem-final in *hal* nor does it end in *a*? This might be the case: once *go-a-iṣṭhira* has been established, the substitution of *ava* (for *o*) would take place because it is an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation; and because it then ends in a *hal*, the [ṣ-substitution] will occur. And this...

It does not exist; for it must necessarily be accepted that "the external elision (*luk*) subverts even internal rules" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 128). Otherwise, in cases such as *nadyāṃ kukkuṭikā* → *nadīkukkuṭikā* and *bhūmyāṃ pāśaḥ* → *bhūmipāśaḥ*, [the same fault would arise].
If the substitution of *yaṇ* were applied, would there not result the elision (*aluk*) [of the case-ending]? To this he says: "But in the case of *gaviṣṭhira*, etc.
[The rule] "after *hṛd* and *dyu*" is stated for the purpose of excluding its application to technical names (*asaṃjñā*). It should be stated [as a supplementary rule].
The meaning is that it must be explained; and the explanation will be provided later. Alternatively, it may be provided even here:

in this case, the mention of the word "anta" (end) need not be made, because even without it, once the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is brought to mind by the locative case, the status of being "ending in *hal*" or "ending in a vowel" is indeed obtained.
Therefore, the inclusion of the word "adhika" (additional) here is made; by being added, it indicates this: that this *aluk* (non-elision) occurs because of an additional [word].
Consequently, in some instances, the *aluk* occurs even when not a technical name (*asaṃjñāyām*). For example: *hṛdispṛk*, *divispṛk*.

By the rule *ṭhspṛśo'nudake kvin* (3.2.58), the suffix *kvin* is applied; by *kvinpratyayasya kuḥ* (8.2.62), the sibilant *ś* is replaced by the velar *kh*; by *jhalāṃ jaśo'nte* (8.2.39), this undergoes *jaś*-ness, becoming *g*;
and for that as well, by *vā'vasāne* (8.4.56), [the substitution of the hard consonant *k* optionally applies].

The suffix *cartvam* is the letter *k*. And here the meaning is as follows: it touches the heart (*hṛdaya*), it touches the sky (*div*). For it has been stated thus in the Bhāṣya: "This [use of] the locative case is to be seen in the sense of the accusative; [as in the examples] 'it touches the heart,' 'it touches the sky,' [resulting in the forms] *hṛdispṛk*, *divispṛk*. But how is this so?

Does that [suffix] occur in the sense of the second case? Precisely because of this statement by the author of the Bhāṣya. Alternatively—whatever touches the heart necessarily touches [something] in the heart; whatever touches heaven necessarily touches [something] in heaven.
In these cases, the locative case will apply by the rule "adhikaraṇe" (Pāṇini 2.3.36).
Although the mention of "name" (ākhyā) was already under discussion, the term "technical term" (saṃjñā) is mentioned again for the sake of clarity.

10. *kāranāmni ca prācāṃ halādau* (Pāṇini 6.3.10). The portion to be given to the king by merchants, cultivators, and herdsmen on account of protection is called *ukāra*; its name is *kāranāma*. [This occurs] in examples such as *kūpeśāṇam*.

The compound is formed by *r̥t-sajñāyām* (Pāṇini 2.1.44). Regarding the example *haledvipadikā*: "two two-footed [fines] are to be given" is *dvipādikā*. By the rule *pāda-śatasya* (5.4.1) and others, the suffix *vun* is applied;
there is elision of the final vowel (*al-antya-lopa*), and by *pādaḥ pat* (6.4.130), the substitution of *pad* for *pāda* occurs.
By the words "of the specific [form] beginning with *ṭh*," etc., he shows that this sūtra serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*).

"Restrictive options" (*niyamavikalpāḥ*) means specific types of restrictive rules. By the words "and in the name of a *kāra*," etc., he shows the nature of those restrictive options. And these are the restrictive options.

The words *kāranāmni*, *prācām*, and *halādau* are understood here from their inclusion in this restrictive rule (*niyamavākya*). If the first restriction were not intended, one would not have stated "in the name of the cause" (*kāranāmni*). Likewise, if the second restriction...

If that [the third rule] were not intended, then [Pāṇini] would not have stated "of the Easterners" (*prācām*). Likewise, if the third restriction were not desired, he would not have stated "when followed by a consonant" (*halādau*).
Now, for what purpose is the mention of the name [Nāma]? Does the mention of the technical term (*saṃjñā*) from the preceding rule not continue here?

In the previous rule (*pūrvayoga*), the mention of the word "name" (*nāman*) was intended to indicate that the condition of being a "name" (*saṃjñā*) is generally applicable. Consequently, in cases such as *hṛdispṛk* and *divispṛk*, the non-elision (*aluk*) is established even when it is not a name.
11. *madhyād gurau* (Pāṇini 6.3.11).

[The Vārttika] states: "It should be stated that [the elision does not occur] after a word ending in *ṭha*. The meaning is that this must be explained as having the sense that the seventh case-affix (*saptamī*) following the word *anta* does not undergo elision (*aluk*). In that regard, this...
Explanation: The particle *ca* is carried over from the preceding rule (*pūrvayoga*), and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.
By this, the elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending (*saptamī*) does not occur even after the word *anta*.
12. *Amūrdhamastakāt svāṅgād akāme* (Pāṇini 6.3.12). Here, "one's own limb" (*svāṅga*) is understood as that which is defined by the technical rule concerning non-fluid substances and so forth.
The example *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* ("the one with a black throat") is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; [it is formed] even when the members have different substrata (*vyadhikaraṇa*).

The term *bahuvrīhi* [in the rule] refers to the *bahuvrīhi* compound itself. The phrase "having a common substratum" (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is merely illustrative (*prāyika*). In the example *akṣaśauṇḍaḥ*, the compound is formed by the rule *saptamī śauṇḍaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.40). In *aṅgulitrāṇajaṅghāvalaḥ*, there are two locative *tatpuruṣa* compounds.

13. *bandhe ca vibhāṣā* (6.3.13). The rule *svāṅgāt* (6.3.12) has ceased to apply; this is a general injunction. Regarding *bandhe*: this is a form derived from the root *badh*. By the rule *nensiddhabadhnātiṣu ca* (6.3.19), [the suffix *nañ* is not elided].

Regarding the *tatpuruṣa* compound, they will state a prohibition [of the suffix *ṇya*]. In that case, the distinction of scope is not known—namely, in which *tatpuruṣa* compounds is there a prohibition? Therefore, for the sake of understanding that, he says: "The word *bandha* is taken as ending in the suffix *dhañ*. *Bandhana* is *bandhaḥ*; here, *dhañ* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). By this, it is understood as ending in *dhañ*.

The rule *badhnātau vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 3.4.62) indicates that there is an option regarding the suffix *ghañ*, while it is shown that there is a prohibition when another suffix follows. But how is it known that this word ends in *ghañ*? Because its first syllable is udātta. As in the example *hastebandhaḥ*. This is either a *tatpuruṣa* or a *bahuvrīhi*. Regarding the phrase *ubhayatra*: how [is it] both when [the condition] is applicable and when it is not applicable?
Furthermore, he asks: "Is this *vibhāṣā* (optionality) applicable in both cases? and says: "Because [the rule] begins with 'from one's own limb' (*svāṅgāt hi*)," and so forth.

14. *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.3.14). [Examples: *stamberamaḥ*, *karṇejapaḥ*. By the rule *stambakarṇayo ramijapoḥ* (3.2.13), the suffix *ac* is applied; then, by the rule *upapadam atiṅ* (2.2.19), a *tatpuruṣa* compound is formed.

[Examples include] *ṭhkurucaraḥ* and *madracaraḥ*. Regarding the rule *careṣṭaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.16), while the option (*vibhāṣā*) is already established, the mention of "diversely" (*bahulagrahaṇam*) is for the purpose of including certain meanings such as "engaging in" (*pravṛtti*) and so forth.
Consequently, the absence of elision (*aluk*) occurs only in specific instances, as in *stamberamaḥ* and similar forms.

In some cases there is no application at all—as in *kurucara* and so forth. In some cases both [the elision and non-elision] occur—as in *sarajim*, *sarojam*, and so forth. In some cases something else entirely occurs—as in *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī* and so forth.
The non-elision (*aluk*) taught for the locative case also occurs for the ablative case. The same applies to words ending in *kṛt* suffixes.
The non-elision (*aluk*) mentioned for the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) occurs even in the case of a *taddhita* suffix—as in *apsavya*, meaning "born in the waters" (*apsu bhavaḥ*).

Here, the suffix *yat* is applied because [the word *ap-] belongs to the *digādi* group; then, by the rule *ṭhorguṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.146), the *guṇa* substitution takes place, and by the rule *vānto yi pratyaye* (Pāṇini 6.1.79), the substitute *vānta* (*au*) is applied.

Thus, since this is established everywhere by the inclusion of the term *bahulam* ("in various cases"), there is the need for supplementary rules (*upasaṃkhyāna*) such as "the addition [of the rule] for *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*" (Vārttika 716), and so forth; as well as that which has been stated and that which will be stated— namely, "the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case before *apa*, *yoni*, *yat*, and *matup*" (Vārttika 721), and so forth.

In that case, it would not need to be stated that "all [is meant]. If this were so, then since everything would be established by this very rule even from the word *stokāt* ("from a little"), the rule *pañcamyāḥ stokādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.2) would not need to be stated. This is true; however, that [rule] should be understood as an elaboration (*prapañca*) of this very point. And thus...

When there is mindfulness, the object of focus becomes well-comprehended. Thus it has been said: "Those very objects are well-comprehended for whom both the definition and the detailed exposition [are understood]."

15. *pravṛṭ-śarat-kāla-divāṃ jaḥ* (6.3.15). Regarding *ṭh prāvṛṣijaḥ*: by [Pāṇini 3.2.97] *saptamyāṃ janer ḍaḥ*, the suffix *ḍa* is applied; by [Pāṇini 6.4.143] *ṭeḥ*, there is elision of the final phoneme (*ṭi*); and by [Pāṇini 2.2.19] *apapadam atiṅ*, a compound is formed.

16. [The substitution of *vibhāṣā* occurs] for the words *varṣa*, *kṣara*, *śara*, and *vara*. (6.3.16) 17. [The substitution of *vibhāṣā* occurs] for a word denoting time (*kālanāman*) when followed by a suffix marked with the indicator *gha*, as well as by *kāla* and *tana*.
(6.3.17) Regarding "marked with *gha*": this refers to the inclusion of the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap*. Regarding "*kāla*": this refers to a word expressing time.
The term *tana* refers to the suffixes *ṭaL*, *ṭyuL*, and *ṭyaL*, which take the augment *suT*. Regarding the example *pūrvāhṇetarām*:
