having analyzed *pūrvam ahnaḥ* ("the earlier part of the day"), there is a partitive compound (*ekadeśisamāsa*) according to Pāṇini 2.2.1, *pūrvāparaprathama...*. Then, by Pāṇini 5.4.91, *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac*, the suffix *ṭac* is applied.

The compound-final suffix [ṭac] is applied; by the rule *ahno'hna etebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.88), the substitute *ahna-* is used for *ahan*. By the rule *ahno'dantāt* (Pāṇini 8.4.7), the substitution of *ṇa* occurs. Thus, "in this forenoon" and "in that forenoon," and among these two, "the one that is more of a forenoon" is called *pūrvāhṇetara*.

The suffix *tarap* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.3.57] *dvivacana* etc.; and the suffix *tamap* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.3.55] *atiśāyane* etc., resulting in the form *pūrvāṅṇetamām*. Since the condition of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is met by [Pāṇini 1.2.46] *kṛttaddhitasamāsāśca*, the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*) would otherwise apply, but it is prohibited in this particular instance.

Regarding the form *pūrvāhṇetane*: in the sense of *pūrvāhṇetara*, by the rule *vibhāṣā pūrvāhṇāparāhṇābhyām* (Pāṇini 4.3.24), the suffixes *ṭaL* and *ṭyuL* are applied along with the augment *tuṬ*; then, by the rule *yuvoranākau* (Pāṇini 7.1.1), the substitution *aṭaN* is made for the suffix *yu*.

Regarding the term *rātritarāyām*: the analysis of the compound is "in this night and in that night, [the one] which is more than a night (*atiśayena rātrau*) among these two. Now, one might object: since there is a rule stating that "when a suffix is mentioned, it includes that which begins with the element from which the suffix is prescribed and ends with that suffix" (*pratyayagrahaṇe yasmāt sa vihitastadādestadantasya*), shouldn't the inclusion of the ending in the suffix be understood?

One should provide examples of the non-elision (*aluk*) when a suffix denoted by the technical term *gha* or the suffix *tana* occurs as the final member of a compound; why then was it illustrated only for the suffix in general?
To this he says: "In the section concerning the final member of a compound" (*uttarapadādhikāre*), and so forth. Why?
He says this again, beginning with "because of the inclusion of *hṛllekha*," and so forth.

In the rule *hṛdayasya hṛllekhayadaṇlāseṣu* (Pāṇini 6.4.50), there is a distinction made between the word *lekha* itself and the word *lekha* ending in the suffix *aṇ*. In that context, if within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of subsequent members, when a suffix is mentioned...
If that [the inclusion of the letter *l*] were intended as an internal rule (*antarvidhi*), then one should not have included the mention of the letter *l*;

for its inclusion would already be established by the mention of the *aṇ* suffix itself. Yet it is indeed included. Therefore, from the mention of the letter *l*, it is understood that: "In the governing context of 'subsequent member' (*uttarapada-adhikāra*), when there is a mention of a suffix..."

"The rule regarding what ends with that [tadantavidhi] is not desired" (Pu.pā. 26). Regarding "by that": because the application of the rule regarding what ends with that is not intended here. "The word 'time' (kāla) is not a mention of its own form," because it is a mention of the name; for this is precisely the purpose of such a mention.

18. *śayavāsavāsiṣvakālāt* (Pāṇini 6.3.18). In the example *kheśayaḥ* ("one who sleeps in the sky"), the suffix *ac* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.15] *adhikaraṇe śeteḥ*. In the example *grāmevāsaḥ* ("one who dwells in the village"), *vāsaḥ* means "dwelling"; the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). In the example *grāmevāsī* ("one who habitually dwells in the village"), the suffix *ṇini* is applied in the sense of habitual disposition (*tācchīlika*).

Or [it applies] in the case of a religious vow (vrata), as in the example "one who sleeps in the forenoon" (*pūrvāhṇaśayaḥ*). Now, one might object: if there were a grasping of the word-form itself (*svarūpa*), then "one who sleeps at night" (*kālaśayaḥ*) would be the counter-example; however, this is not a grasping of the word-form. What then? It is a grasping of the meaning (*artha*).

For this very reason, it was stated in the *Vṛtti*: "not expressing time" (*akālavācinaḥ*). But how is the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*) obtained? Because the term *nāman* from the preceding rule is understood to carry over here. If that is so, then there is no need for the mention of "time" (*kāla*); the rule *kālanāmnaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.17) will be carried over, and it will be negated by the particle *nañ*.
We shall establish a connection with the word "na" (not)—that is, not with the word "kāla.

In that context, the meaning is as follows: regarding the rule *ṇensiddhabadhnātiṣu ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.19)—where the reading *ṇensiddha* appears in older printed editions—the word "na" need not be explicitly stated; for "na" itself [is already understood].

How could it follow [the previous rule]? It cannot be so. For if it were stated as "na śayavāsavāsiṣi," this prohibition would be understood as applying only to the elision (*aluk*), because that [elision] is what is under discussion here as the thing to be enjoined. Therefore, for the purpose of ensuring that the prohibition applies specifically to time (*kāla*), [the rule is stated as it is].
The "taking up of time" (kālagrahaṇa) must be performed; that is to say, it must be explained, which means it has already been explained previously.
19. *naÑ-siddha-badhnātiṣu ca*. (6.3.19) [The reading *naÑ-siddha* is found in ancient printed editions.
This [sūtra] provides an exception to the elision (*aluk*) that would otherwise be obtained by the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam* (6.3.14).

This is a prohibition [of the previous rule]. [The phrase] "when a word ending in -ṭhin is the subsequent member" [is used]. But surely it has been established that "in the governing heading of 'subsequent member' (uttarapada), when a suffix is mentioned, the inclusion of that which ends with it (tadantavidhi) is not accepted" (Paribhāṣenduśekhara 26);
so how is it that here the subsequent member is understood as ending in that [suffix]? [The answer is: because of the locative case [ending].
Because an *in* suffix following a locative case-ending is impossible; for the *in* suffix is of only two kinds—namely, a *kṛt* suffix and a *taddhita* suffix.

Among these, since a *kṛt* suffix is produced only after a verbal root (*dhātu*), an *in* suffix following a locative case-ending is impossible. Indeed, the *in* suffix is of only two kinds: the *kṛt* and... [the *taddhita*].

And as for the secondary derivative (taddhita): since in that case [the suffix] arises only from a verbal root (dhātu), it cannot possibly follow a locative case-ending. Furthermore, no secondary derivative whatsoever arises from a word governed by the locative case; thus, that too cannot possibly follow a locative case-ending. Therefore, it is correct that only that which ends in *in* is understood here. This has been well stated.

Regarding "ṭhsthaṇḍilavartī": the suffix *ṇini* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.78] "vrate"; the compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.2.19] "upapadamatiṅ". Regarding "ṭhsāṅkāśyasiddhaḥ": the compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.41] "siddhaśuṣka...
and so forth. Regarding "ṭhcakrabaddhaḥ": the word *baddha* ends in a *niṣṭhā* suffix; [the compound is formed by] "saptamī" [Pāṇini 2.1.40].
(2.1.40) Thus, by means of a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules), there is a compound.

With the word *bandha*, [the term] "wheel-arrangement" (*cakrabandha*) is formed. By the rule beginning with (2.1.41) *siddha*, there is a compound. It should be understood that this [word] ends in the *ac*-suffix of the *pacādi* group. Now, this word-form *bandha* ends in the suffix *ghañ*.
Why is it not apprehended? To this he says: "For when ending in ṭh or ghañ," and so forth.

20. *sthe ca bhāṣāyām* (6.3.20). This is also a prohibition of the non-elision (*aluk*) which would otherwise have been obtained by [the rule] *tatpuruṣe* (6.3.14) and so forth. For example, *samasthaḥ*. [The derivation is as follows: from *same tiṣṭhati*, [the suffix] *ka* is added; then, by *āto lopa iṭi ca* (6.4.64), there is the elision of the long *ā*.
There is the elision of the vowel *i*.
[The mantra] "kṛṣṇo'syākhareṣṭhaḥ" (the printed reading is "kṛṣṇo'syākhareṣṭhā";
the Kāśikā printed reading is "kṛṣṇo'syākhareṣṭhaḥ"—Vārāṇasī edition).
Regarding the form *kṛṣṇobhyāreṣṭhaḥ*—the reading in the Kāśikā is *saṃ-pa-pāṭhaḥ*—the suffix *kvip* is applied according to [Pāṇini 3.2.77]: *sthaḥ ka ca*.

21. *ṣaṣṭhyā ākrośe* (Pāṇini 6.3.21). [The example] "the family of a thief" (*caurasya kulam*) is intended to convey an insult; however, by this [expression], a real relationship between the two is not intended to be expressed. Regarding the phrase "it should be stated" (*vaktavyaḥ*), the meaning is that it must be explained. As for the explanation:
This has already been explained:

in the case of *paśyatoharaḥ*, the word *paśyataḥ* takes the genitive case by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī cānādare* (Pāṇini 2.3.38). The word *haraḥ* means "one who steals," derived from the root *hṛ* with the suffix *ac* (the *pacādyac* class).
Regarding "amuṣya": the substitution of *yat* for *adas* occurs; then, by the rule "adaso'serdādu do maḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.80), the substitutions of *utva* and *matva* take place.

Because *utva* is considered asiddha (not yet established), the rule "ṭāṅsiṅsāminātsyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.12) applies, resulting in the replacement of the genitive suffix *ṅsi* with *syā*. Similarly, [one forms] "amuṣyakulikaḥ. As follows:
In the expression *amuṣyaputrikā*, the suffix *vuñ* is applied because it belongs to the *bhṛgu-jñādi* group (Pāṇini 4.1.133);
the meaning here is that it is the same in this case as well.
Regarding the term *devānāmpriya*: it is called *priya* because it pleases (*prīṇāti*), according to the rule *ig-upadha-jñā-prī-kiraḥ kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.135).
By [Pāṇini 3.2.64], the suffix *kap* is applied, and the substitution of *iyaṅ* occurs. Thus we have "Śunaḥśepaḥ.
By [Pāṇini 6.4.133], "śvayuva-maghonām ataddhite," there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*).

22. *putre 'nyatarasyām* | (6.3.22) 23. *ṛto vidyāyonisambandhebhyaḥ* | (6.3.23) The compound *vidyāyonī* consists of "learning" (*vidyā*) and "womb" (*yoni*). Those whose relationship is produced by those two are [the ones referred to].

[The suffix ṭac is applied] after words denoting a relationship through learning (vidyā) or procreation (yoni). The word *kṛta* is not employed in the formation of the compound because its meaning is already understood, just as the word *miśra* is not used in the expression *guḍadhānāḥ*.
[As stated: "In the case of relationships through learning or procreation, the mention of both the preceding and following members of the compound must be made."
By the word "tat" (that), both types of relations—those based on knowledge (*vidyā*) and those based on birth (*yoni*)—are indicated;

one must effect the inclusion of those [relations] that function as the prior member (*pūrvapada*) and those that function as the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). "Inclusion" (*grahaṇa*) means that by which [the relations] are included;
the meaning is that an explanation of such a kind must be provided by which they are grasped.
What, then, is that commentary? For what purpose should it be composed?
To this he says: "Only that which expresses the source of knowledge," and so forth. Herein is the explanation:
by means of a great sign manifested here...
The intentions of the teachers are indicated by the sequence of their sūtras;

for instance, there is this extensive sūtra-connection: "ṛtaḥ vidyā-yoni-sambandhebhyaḥ. For if the non-elision (aluk) were intended when the subsequent word expresses a relationship arising from ignorance (avidyā), or a relationship arising from the womb (yoni), then [the rule would have been formulated differently].

One should say, "Because of the connection with the source [of the word] *vidyā* (knowledge). Alternatively, one might not even include the mention of "connection," for there is nothing ending in the vowel *ṛ* that denotes either "knowledge" (*vidyā*) or "source" (*yoni*) which is not connected [to such a meaning]; thus, even without the mention of "connection," [the rule applies].

It will be understood that [the rule applies] to words expressing a relationship through learning (*vidyā*) or birth (*yoni*); so what is the purpose of including the word "relationship" (*sambandha*)? From this extensive series of sūtras, it is observed that the Teacher intends this elision (*aluk*) when the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) expresses a relationship through learning or birth. For example: *hotuḥ* (from *hotṛ + i*). [This is derived by applying] *ṛta ut*.
By this [rule 6.1.111], *u*-tva occurs; then there is the substitution of *r* for the final element (*raparatva*); and by [the rule] "ṭhrātsasya" (8.2.24), there is the elision of the *s* sound.

24. *vibhāṣā svasṛpatyoḥ* | (6.3.24) 25. *ānaṅ ṛto dvandve* | (6.3.25) "In a *dvandva* compound consisting of words ending in *ṛ*, which denote a relationship based on learning (*vidyā*) or birth (*yonī*), [the final vowel of the first member is replaced by] *ānaṅ*," and so forth. Now...

Why is it not understood that "in a dvandva compound ending in /ṛ/, there is the substitution of *ānaṅ*"? It is impossible to understand it in this way; for then it would undesirably apply here as well: *pitṛpitāmahau*.
The letter /ṅ/ is for the purpose of indicating that the substitution applies to the final sound.

For here, the instruction of phonemes is intended either for the sake of grammatical operations (*kāryārtha*) or for the sake of being heard (*śravaṇārtha*). Yet this letter *n* is not heard anywhere; indeed, in every instance it ought to be elided by the rule "there is elision of [a final] *n* at the end of a nominal stem" (*nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*, Pāṇini 8.2.7), nor is any grammatical operation observed to apply to it.

For what purpose, then, is the letter *n* pronounced? To this he says: "The pronunciation of *n*, etc. If the *n* were not present, only an *aṇ* would remain in place of the vowel *ṛ*; consequently, by the rule "ṛ is replaced by *uṇ*, followed by *r*" (Pāṇini 1.1.51), the substitution would be followed by *r*. But when the *n* is present, this [substitution] is no longer merely an *aṇ*.
Since both *āṇ* and *anaṅ* are taught [as substitutes], there is no occasion for the substitution of *r* (raparatva).

For where both *āṇ* and *anaṇ* are taught, the substitution of *r* does not occur; as in the case of *saudhātakir*, according to the rule "ṭhsudhāturakaṅ ca" (Pāṇini 4.1.97). Therefore, in this instance...

The letter *n* is pronounced for the purpose of preventing the substitution of *ra* and *pa*. Now, in the case of *pitāputrau* (father and son) and *mātāputrau* (mother and son), how is there the substitution of *ānaṅ*, since there is no *dvandva* compound here of words ending in the vowel *ṛ*? To this he says: "the word *putra* is understood [from the previous rule] as a governing term (*anuvartate*)."

The intention is that the term *putra* ("son") is understood here from the rule *ṭhputre'nyatarasyām* (6.3.22). However, if *putra* is indeed understood [from that previous rule], then would not the option (*vibhāṣā*) also apply to "son" in the rule *vibhāṣā svasṛpatyoḥ* (6.3.24)? No, this is not so.

This is a fault; it follows [the previous rule] by the logic of the frog’s leap (*maṇḍūkaplutinyāya*). For this very reason, it was stated "here" (*atre*) in order to demonstrate that it follows only there and not elsewhere, such as on the mountain (*parvatra*). But even so, when the word *putra* is the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the substitution of *anaṅ* would apply to the entire preceding word (*pūrvapada*) alone.

Since the subject undergoing the grammatical operation (*kāryin*) is not explicitly mentioned here, and because the term "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) implies only the preceding member (*pūrvapada*),
it cannot be argued that the substitution will apply to the vowel *ṛ* by virtue of the rule stating "after *ṛ*" (*ṛtaḥ*).
Therefore, the single mention of "after *ṛ*" (*ṛtaḥ*) in this context serves as a qualifier for the *dvandva* compound, and not as a qualifier of the subject undergoing the operation.

Thus he says: "And [the word] *ṛta*. Here, the connection is that [the word *ṛta*] is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). From the rule "After words denoting relationship through learning or birth, [the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added] to *ṛt*" (Pāṇini 4.1.120), the word *ṛta* carries over;
it will serve as a qualifier for the element undergoing the grammatical operation (*kāryin*). Now, one might object: "But that [word *ṛta*] was specified in the ablative case."

And what is the purpose here of that which is indicated by the genitive case? This is not a fault; the word "putra" (son), being in the seventh case, will be treated as having the force of a genitive in relation to the fifth case "ṛtaḥ"—according to the rule:
"When something is indicated by the locative [in a rule], it refers to what precedes it" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.66). But even so, there is still a contradiction; for if the word "putra"...

[Objection: "If [the rule] applies to the latter member (*uttarapada*), how then can there be a *dvandva* compound of words ending in *ṛ*? For if there is a *dvandva* of words ending in *ṛ*, then the word *putra* cannot be the latter member. [Response: This is not so; for that *dvandva* of which the term *ṛtaḥ* is the qualifier is one thing, while that of which the word *putra* is the latter member is another.
What contradiction is there here?

26. *devatādvandve ca* (6.3.26). This statement is for the purpose of including [the case] of imitation (*anukāra*) and for the purpose of [excluding] relationships based on ignorance (*avidyā*) or physical origin (*yoni*). But surely, the mention of "dvandva" continues from the previous rule *ānaṅ ṛtō dvandve* (6.3.25); so what is the purpose of [mentioning it] here?

Why is the term *dvandva* mentioned again? To this he says: "While the term *dvandva* is understood to carry over," and so forth. For the previous mention of *dvandva* was for the purpose of identifying a specific type of compound (*samāsa*), whereas this [present] mention is for the purpose of [identifying] those whose association is well-known in common usage and in the Veda. Among these, [it refers to those] whose association is established in the world and in the Veda.

Furthermore—the inclusion [of the word *dvandva*] is for the purpose that [the rule] may apply. Now, even though the term *dvandva* is mentioned again, how is this meaning obtained? To this he says: "in the case of absolute association," and so forth. [This refers to] Pāṇini 8.1.15: *dvandvaṃ rahasyamaryādāvacanavyutkramaṇayajñapātra-patnīsaṃyogesu*.

Regarding this, the following is stated: "The term *dvandva* is prescribed as an irregular formation (*nipātana*) for those things that are known in common worldly usage to be absolutely associated. By this, he shows that the following meaning is obtained:
"And those which are mentioned together in the Veda. "Mentioned together" (*sahavāpa*) means simultaneous offering; therein—
Those who are designated as "designated together with the offering" (sahavāpanirdiṣṭa) are those who are connected to a single oblation. Which ones, then, are connected to a single oblation?

They are to be understood as those who are designated as the recipients (sampradāna) with respect to a single oblation being offered in a single mantra—such as, for example, "I offer the goat-oblation to Indra and Varuṇa. These are they.

Regarding the passage beginning with "ubhayatra," etc.: when [the word] *vāyu* occurs as either a prior member (*pūrvapada*) or a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the substitution of *ānaṅ* must be stated—that is, explained—as being prohibited. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: from the rule "vibhāṣā svasṛpatyoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.24)...

The mention of *vibhāṣā* (optionality) continues [from the previous rule], and that is an established optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, when *vāyu-* is the final member of a compound or the initial member, [the elision] will not occur.
27. *īd agneḥ somavaruṇayoḥ* | (6.3.27) This substitution of the vowel *ī* is prescribed as an exception to the substitution of *ānaṅ*. The letter *t* is for the sake of pronunciation.
28. *id-vṛddhau* | (6.3.28) The [sūtra] *agner* (6.3.27) is understood to carry over, as is *devatādvandve* (6.3.26).
*Somavaruṇayoḥ* (6.3.27) is excluded. This is because of its association with the word *vṛddhi*.
A compound whose final member (*uttarapada*) is *kṛta* or *vṛddhi* is understood here; for this very reason, he says: "when *kṛta* or *vṛddhi* is the final member.

Regarding the form *āgnivāruṇīm*: when the general suffix *aṇ* has been applied, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15). Here too, the letter *t* is for the sake of pronunciation.
[The rule] "in a *devatā-dvandva* when there is a subsequent member" means that when there is a subsequent member in a *devatā-dvandva*, [the substitution occurs] in reference to that.

30. *divasaśca pṛthivyām* (Pāṇini 6.3.30). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the substitution of] *ānaṅ*. Now, for what purpose is the vowel *a* pronounced [in the sūtra]? If it is argued that it is for the sake of protecting the letter *s* from being designated as *it*, [we reply: no.
He says—"The pronunciation of the letter *ṭha* [is for the sake of] the absence of purpose"—and so forth, meaning that the designation (*saṃjñā*) will not occur simply because there is no purpose.

For if the vowel *a* were not present, one would rely on the internal case-ending (*vibhakti*) and, the designation "word" (*pada*) being established, the modification of the letter *s* into *ru*—by the rule *sasajuṣo ruḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.66)—would occur; and of that [modification] too...

By the rule *kharavasānayorvisarjanīyaḥ* (8.3.15), even that [sibilant] would become the *upadhmānīya* by the rule *kupvoḥ ka pau ca* (8.3.37). However, when the vowel *a* is pronounced [as part of the suffix], this does not occur.
Why? Because by the pronunciation of the vowel *a*, there is the inclusion of the modified *s* sound.

The purpose of this very [rule] is so that the application of this [word *div*] may occur in its unmodified form—as in *dyāvā divasam*, and so forth. This is the statement. And here, in the present sūtra, the mention of the *dvandva* compound and the mention of the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) are both carried over [from previous rules]. *Dyāvā*...
Thus, since this substitution does not apply in the case of a *vākya*, he says "How so? and so forth.

"An effort must be made here. In that regard, this is the effort: the term *bahulam* ("optionally" or "frequently") is understood to carry over from the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.3.14); by means of that, [the form] *dyāvā-* [is established].
Thus, this substitution will occur even in a sentence within the Vedic language (*chandas*).

Alternatively, the particle *ca* ("and") is employed here; because its purpose is to include what has not been explicitly mentioned, [the substitution] will take effect. Furthermore, the word *dyāvā* will carry over by virtue of its being marked with a circumflex accent (*svarita*) alone; therefore, there is no need for a rule specifically intended to draw that word forward.
By means of the word "ca" (and).

Alternatively, there exists another verbal root *dyāvā* which has the same meaning as the word *dik*; this is its usage. However, the statement regarding the substitute [div] is for the purpose of precluding the usage of *div*.

31. *upāsoṣasaḥ* | (6.3.31) This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule for the suffix *ānaṅ*. [This statement does not appear in the Kāśikā; thus the following two rules as well are absent. The form is *uṣāsānaktam*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "and Uṣas, and Night" (*uṣāṃśca naktañca*).
32. *mātṛpitarau* [is substituted for *pitṛmātarau*] in the northern region.

(6.3.32) 33. *pitaramātara* [is substituted for *mātāpitarau*] in the Vedic language. (6.3.33) 34. A feminine word ending in *ūṅ* is not treated as masculine (*puṃvat*) when it follows a word of the same referent that has already been used in the masculine. (6.3.34)

Regarding the rule *striyām apūraṇīpriyādiṣu* (Pāṇini 6.3.34), three possible interpretations are conceivable here: whether the word *strī* in *striyāḥ* refers to the suffix (*pratyaya*), the meaning (*artha*), or the word-form (*śabda*) itself. Among these, if [it were taken as] "of the feminine" (*striyāḥ*):

If the mention of the suffix *strī* is intended as a *svarita* accent, then, according to the rule "by means of a *svarita*, the governing scope (*adhikāra*) is understood" (Pāṇini 1.3.11), the suffixes prescribed under the heading of "feminine" (*stryadhikāra*) are understood to be included,
as in the case of [the rule] "of the subordinate element (*upasarjana*) ending in *go* or a feminine suffix" (1.2.48). However, if [it is taken] by the word "feminine" (*strī*) itself...
If a substance qualified by femininity is denoted, then it is the inclusion of "meaning" (*artha*);
but if the word itself, which expresses the feminine meaning, is denoted by the term *strī*, then it is the inclusion of "word" (*śabda*).
In that case, according to the first alternative, this is the meaning of the sūtra: [the suffix] following a word that has been previously used in the masculine...
The feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) becomes like the masculine (*puṃvat*) when a word ending in *anūṅ* follows it; that is to say, it is withdrawn.

In that case, the genitive in "of the feminine" (*striyāḥ*) is used in the sense of the nominative. But how can it be understood from the expression "like the masculine" (*puṃvat*) that there is a withdrawal of that which has the feminine as its referent? It is because [the rule] says "it becomes" (*bhavati*).
[This is] because of the supply of the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣādhyāhāra*). And in this view, in the case of *paṭubhārya*— meaning "one whose wife is clever"—

when the substitution of *yaṇ* is to be prescribed for the preceding [vowel] based on the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), which causes the elision of the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*), the rule *acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau* (Pāṇini 1.1.57) applies.

If the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) were to apply, there would be the substitution of *yaṇ*. Furthermore, in the case of *gārgyo vṛndārikā* → *gargavṛndārikā*, while the rule *tadrājasya bahuṣu tenaivāstriyām* (Pāṇini 2.4.62) is in force, the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *yañ* prescribed by *yañañośca* (2.4.64) would not occur.

For by the rule of *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment), the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) is indeed eliminated, but not the meaning of femininity itself. Consequently, since the meaning has not been eliminated, for what reason would the suffix *yañ* not be heard? These and other such objections against the position that [the suffix] is a suffix (*pratyayapakṣa*) have been stated at length in the Bhāṣya. Here...
They are not stated here for fear of excessive prolixity.

However, in the sense of the meaning (*arthapakṣa*), when a subsequent word follows, the masculine meaning is extended to that which is the meaning of the feminine word *strī*—provided it is one that has a corresponding masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) and does not end in the suffix *ūṅ*. This is according to the rule *bhāṣitapuṃskāt*.

The fifth [case ending] is used in the sense of the sixth—meaning that the feminine form becomes like the masculine. When the masculine meaning is extended [by this rule], a word expressing that [masculine] meaning comes into operation. In this view, the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between the shortening prescribed by "ṭhityanavyayasya" (Pāṇini 6.3.66) and this [present] masculine-like transformation does not occur.

Because their domains are distinct. For instance, shortness (*hrasvatva*) pertains to the word-form (*śabda*), whereas the masculine-like behavior (*puṃvadbhāva*) pertains to the meaning (*artha*). Consequently, in the case of *kālimmanyā*, the rule "in the event of a conflict, the subsequent operation prevails" (*vipratiṣedhe paraṃ kāryam*, P. 1.4.2) would not apply to the shortening, yet such a conflict is indeed desired. Likewise...
Indeed—the application of the rule for *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine treatment) does not result in a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), because their spheres of application are distinct.

To explain: shortening (*hrasvatva*) applies to the word-form (*śabda*), whereas *puṃvadbhāva* applies to the meaning (*artha*). Consequently, in the case of *kālimmanyā*, the shortening does not take effect [by virtue of the rule] "In the event of a conflict, the subsequent operation prevails" (Pāṇini 1.4.2).

[The former] would apply, yet a conflict is intended. For instance—the scope of *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like substitution) is where the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) does not end in *-khid*, as in *darśanīyabhārya*;
the scope of the short vowel (*hrasva*) is where *puṃvadbhāva* does not apply, as in *kālimmanyaḥ pumān*. [In the case of] *kālimmanyā*:
In the case of the word *strī*, both [the feminine suffix ṅīp and the shortening] would apply; there, by virtue of its higher status in the order of rules, shortening occurs.
Thus, considering the first two positions to be faulty, he resorts to the third position and says: "by which the masculine has been expressed," and so forth.

For if one were to rely here on any word that has been mentioned as having a masculine form without distinction, then even in the case of *droṇībhārya*, there would be the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*); having this in mind, he says: "In a single [instance] regarding the generic form," and so forth. That is, when there is a single cause for application (*pravṛttinimitta*).
Thus [he says]. By this, he clarifies the meaning of the phrase "in an identical form" (samānāyām ākṛtau).

That by which an object is grasped—that is, delimited—is the ground for the application of a word (pravṛttinimitta), such as a genus (jāti) and so forth; that is what is denoted here by the word "form" (ākṛti).

When only the rule "from that which has the masculine form" (*bhāṣitapuṃskāt*) were stated, one could not obtain this specific qualification "in the same configuration" (*samānāyām ākṛtau*); with this intention, he says: "This very thing is thus," and so forth. The word *tat* is used to introduce the statement; the nature of the meaning of this statement is of such a kind. How?

Does it occur? Not at all; the meaning is "in no way whatsoever. If one were to rely on the word *bhāṣitapuṃska*—a bahuvrīhi compound—as the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) of the term [the base form], such that "a word by which a male [referent] has been expressed is a *bhāṣitapuṃska* word," then this qualification "when the form (*ākṛti*) is the same" would not apply.

It is indeed obtained; for every word, having denoted a male with respect to one *ākṛti* (form/class), denotes a female with respect to another *ākṛti*. However, when the meaning is taken as the referent of another word (*anyapadārtha*), it is certainly obtained—this is the distinction.

Having reflected thus, he says: "The masculine [gender] is expressed (*bhāṣita*) in whatever meaning," and so forth. That which is the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of a word—such as a genus (*jāti*) and the like—is the "other referent" (*anyapadārtha*). But by which word, then, is the masculine expressed therein? It is expressed by that very [word] which serves as the ground for its application (*pratyāsateḥ*), namely, the ground for its own application.

It is understood [from this]. Otherwise, the mention of "having been spoken of as masculine" (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) would be meaningless, because there would be nothing to exclude. For in every case regarding the meaning to be expressed, the masculine gender is expressed by some word or other; even by the word "meaning" (*artha*), that meaning which has been spoken of as masculine [is expressed].

A word that is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is also said to be "one whose gender was previously expressed" (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) when it is used metaphorically in the expression of the denotative property (*abhidhyadharmasyābhidhāne*). Furthermore, by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), it should be understood as that very [stem] by which a male is expressed through whatever meaning constitutes its ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*).
And that which denotes a primary cause of application (pravṛttinimitta) that has been previously expressed as masculine necessarily,
having denoted the male with respect to one primary cause of application, denotes the female;
as in the examples cited for the root [of the rule], such as the words "darśanīyā" and so forth— by means of which word, by virtue of its capacity (sāmarthya).
When the form (*ākṛti*) is identical, this distinction—that "the masculine has been expressed"—is obtained.

If the term *anūṅ* were an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), then [it would mean] "other than *ūṅ*," namely *anūṅ*; consequently, according to the maxim of "that which is joined with *nañ* or *iva*" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 65), it would refer to suffixes similar to that, such as *ṭāp* and the rest.

If there were a mere mention [of the word], the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would apply only to that which ends in it; thus, in cases such as *aiḍaviḍavṛndārikā* and *dāradavṛndārikā*, it would not occur. [In these examples,] the feminine offspring of *iḍaviḍa* is formed by the suffix *añ* according to the rule *janapadaśabdāt kṣatriyādañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.168).
The word *darada* means "the offspring of Darada," to which the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *dvyañmagadha* (Pāṇini 4.1.179);

then, by the rule *ataśca* (4.1.177), there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix. Thus, [we have] *iḍaviṭ* who is also *vṛndārikā*, and *dara* who is also *vṛndārikā*; [in these cases], the compound is formed by the rule *vṛndārakanāgakuñjaraiḥ* (2.1.62).
In that compound, the rule "the feminine form becomes masculine in a *karmadhāraya*" (Pāṇini 6.3.42) and so forth would not apply here, because there is no other suffix similar to *ūṅ* intervening;
consequently, the word *aiḍaviḍa* would not arise from *aiḍaviṭ*, nor the word *dārada* from *darat*.
It might be so; however, it occurs when there is a simple negation (prasajyapratiṣedha), because here too there is the non-existence of *ūṅ*.
Having considered this, and showing that this is indeed a simple negation, he says: "The absence of *ūṅ* is *anūṅ*."

Regarding the rule *ṭhbhāṣitapuṃskādanūṅ* (Pāṇini 6.3.42): if this were not a compound (*asamāsa*) but rather a [simple] Bahuvrīhi, then its meaning would be as follows: "When a word denoting a feminine meaning follows a word that has a corresponding masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), provided it lacks the augment *ūṅ*, it becomes like the masculine (*puṃvat*) when followed by a subsequent word (*uttarapada*). And such being the case...

By implication, it is stated that the word *strī* (woman), which denotes a specific meaning, is replaced by the word *pums* (man) only when it likewise denotes that same specific meaning; consequently, an undesirable consequence follows: there are birds named *aṅgāraka*, and their females are named *kālikā*; therefore, these [would also be subject to the rule].

When the compound *kālikāvṛndārikāḥ* is formed, since this word [the first member] is a feminine form whose corresponding masculine exists, the subsequent word *kālikā*, being *anūṅ* (not having the feminine suffix *ūṅ*), undergoes the substitution of the masculine word *aṅgāraka* because it is the most similar in meaning (*arthato 'ntaratama*).
It would follow [that this fault arises], because there is no other word that is more closely related (*antaratama*).

Consequently, it would result in the form *etadaṅgārakavṛndārikā*, whereas *etatkālikāvṛndārikā* is what is intended. However, if it were a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there would be the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*).

It does not apply; for in that case, a word that has a corresponding masculine form and does not end in the suffix ūṅ ought to undergo the *pūrvavadbhāva* (masculine-like) transformation, yet the word *kālikā* is not one that has a corresponding masculine form— having considered all this, [the author concludes] that this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

Showing this, he says: "In that feminine word which does not have the suffix *ūṅ* after a word that has the masculine form already expressed. If this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, then—[as it is not in the Kāśikā]—the elision (*luk*) of the fifth case ending would apply by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.71).

Therefore, he says: "Because of the non-elision by way of nipātana," and so forth. Now, one might object that since this sentence is *alaukika* (extraordinary/unformed), the argument "because of nipātana" is not a valid solution; for nipātana is indeed a worldly (laukika) phenomenon.
Well then, would there not likewise be no elision (*luk*) here either? Or rather—

Just as it is determined that the elision (*luk*) will occur, let it also be determined that non-elision (*aluk*) occurs as well, as in the example *darśanīyabhāryaḥ*. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose wife is beautiful" (*darśanīyā bhāryā asya*).
According to the rule *gostriyor upasarjanasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.48), there is shortening of the final vowel of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*).

In this context, "beauty" (darśanīyatva) is a specific quality within the general category that serves as the ground for the application of the word *darśanīya*. Taking that single meaning as its basis, the word functions with respect to both the masculine and the feminine—as in "Devadatta is beautiful" (*darśanīyo devadattaḥ*) and "the wife is beautiful" (*darśanīyā bhāryā*). Therefore...

The word *darśanīya* is one whose masculine form has been previously mentioned (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) when it occurs within the same gender-form (*ākṛti*); it applies to the feminine, yet the suffix *ūṅ* does not arise from it. Therefore, in the word *bhāryā*, when the feminine word is the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), this feminine word *strī* takes the same form as the masculine word *pum*. [The printed edition reads "puṃśabdasyaiva"].
The reading should be applied in the same way even in cases such as *ślakṣṇacūḍaḥ*.

Regarding *grāmaṇidṛṣṭiḥ*: here all the conditions are present, yet the word *grāmaṇī* does not denote a female; rather, it denotes a neuter. Therefore, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) does not occur.

Regarding the term *ṭhdroṇībhāryaḥ*: the word *droṇa* denotes a masculine [entity], but not because it shares the same ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). This is because it applies to a masculine measure-possessor (*parimāṇin*) by taking a specific measure as its ground for application; however, it applies to a feminine [entity] by taking a specific genus (*jāti*) as its ground for application.

It occurs in the word *gavādanī*. That wooden trough (*droṇī*) where cows eat is called *gavādanī*; therefore, the word *droṇa* is not one that has been mentioned as masculine within the same generic form (*ākṛti*).

"‘How so? and so forth. If *puṃvadbhāva* (the substitution of the masculine form) is prescribed for that which has been previously used in the masculine when the *ākṛti* (general form) is the same, then in cases such as *garbhibhāryaḥ*, *puṃvadbhāva* would not apply;
for words such as *garbhin* and the like possess distinct *ākṛtis*."

The intention is that [the word *vrīhi*] is already used in the masculine sense (*bhāṣitapuṃska*). For it is when there is a connection with a specific internal object that constitutes a constituent part that a woman is called "pregnant" (*garbhiṇī*); whereas in the case of a grain of rice (*vrīhi*), it is when there is a connection with a specific internal object that constitutes a non-constituent part [that the term is applied].

It is called "garbhin" (pregnant). Therefore, the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word *garbhin* differs when it refers to a male or a female. Furthermore, the ground for the application of the words *prasūta* (having given birth) and *prajāta* (having brought forth) is also distinct due to the performance of an action; for when applied to a female, those two [words] refer to the release of the fetus.
It occurs based on the cause of activity; however, in the case of a male, it is the impregnation [of the womb].

"An effort must be made here"—thus some explain that an additional rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) should be formulated. Others, however, say that there is a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) as "the female [is treated] like the male."
It must be done. Or rather, by the phrase "effort must be made here," he shows this:

although there is a difference in the nature of the embryo in the case of a woman and in the case of rice, nevertheless, that difference should not be relied upon; for in that case, one should set aside the distinction between parts and non-parts.
In general, one must rely solely on the mere relationship with a specific object existing within;
therefore, with respect to that, the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word *garbhin* when it refers to a woman or to rice is exactly the same. Thus...

Regarding the words *prasūta* and *prajāta*, even though there is a distinction between the "conception" (*apatyādhāna*) and the "delivery" (*vimokṣaṇa*) of offspring, this commentary maintains that once that distinction is set aside, they merely imply the relationship of "possessing offspring"—namely, "one who has male offspring" (*apatyavān*) and "one who has female offspring" (*apatyavatī*). Thus, the suffix *ṅīp* must be applied. For example, in the case of "one whose wife is a *brahmabandhū*" (*brahmabandhūbhāryaḥ*), the suffix *ūṅ* is added to the word *brahmabandhū* by virtue of Pāṇini 4.1.66: *ūṅ utaḥ*.

In the expression "kalyāṇīpañcamāḥ," the suffix *ap* is added by the rule "ap pūraṇī-pramāṇyoḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.116). The word *pañcamī* means "the fifth," derived from the ordinal suffix *ḍaṭ* (forming *pañcama-*) with the addition of *maṭ* by the rule "nāntād asaṃkhyāder maṭ" (Pāṇini 5.2.49). Subsequently, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "ṭiḍḍhāṇañ" (Pāṇini 4.1.15).

When the suffix *ṅīp* is applied, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) occurs. Regarding the statement "the mention of the primary ordinal (*pradhānapūraṇī*) must be made": that explanation by which the primary ordinal is grasped is the "mention of the primary ordinal," and that [explanation] must be performed—namely, with respect to that which is the primary ordinal.
This is so that the prohibition may apply; it should not apply when that [word] is subordinate. In this regard, the explanation is as follows:

here, by the rule "in a dvandva, [the word] ending in *dhi* [comes first]" (2.2.32), the application of the *priya*-class words at the beginning would have been expected; however, the fact that they appear at the end is indicated by the sign of deviation from that general rule.

This prohibition is non-universal; it applies only in certain instances, not everywhere. Therefore, it occurs only where the ordinal suffix (*pūraṇī*) is the predominant element, and not elsewhere. Consequently, wherever this [prohibition] applies, it is logical to understand that very predominant ordinal suffix as being intended. Where, then, does the ordinal suffix [occur]?

What is predominance (*prādhānya*)? It is that wherein it is included within the compound as the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*), as in the counter-example just mentioned. For there, the analysis (*vigraha*) is by means of a member;
yet the whole (*samudāya*), being non-different from its distinct members, is precisely the meaning of the compound. "In that case"—just so.
The first, second, third, and fourth [days] are denoted, and likewise the fifth;

as in the expression "the fortnight having the auspicious fifth" (*kalyāṇapañcamīkaḥ pakṣaḥ*). Here, however, the fortnight itself—whose internal divisions are concealed—is the primary referent, while the fifth day is the night. In this [case],...

In this case, the meaning of the other word (anyapadārtha) is only inferable (anumeya), not directly denotable (abhidheya). Just as in the word "tree" (vṛkṣa), the roots and so forth [are not denoted], so too, because the meaning [of the compound] is not denotable, that meaning is secondary (apradhāna). Now, why does the compound-ending suffix *ap* not occur here? To this he says: "Except for *pūraṇī* and *pramāṇī*," and so forth.

Now, one might ask: how is there a masculine-like substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) in cases such as *dṛḍhabhaktiḥ* (firm devotion) and *śobhanabhaktiḥ* (beautiful devotion), given that because these belong to the class beginning with *priya*, there ought to be a prohibition [of such substitution]?
To this he says: "In cases such as *dṛḍhabhaktiḥ*," etc.; [this applies] when the preceding member does not denote a female.
Because it is intended to be expressed, the definition beginning with "firm devotion" (dṛḍhabhakti) is established; this is how it should be understood.

The meaning is that what is to be hated must be avoided. Here, the word "firm" (dṛḍha) is employed in the sense of the cessation of lack of firmness (adāḍharya). In this injunction, which aims at the cessation of lack of firmness—
The specific mention of gender is indeed useless; therefore, femininity is not intended here. Consequently, the intention is that this is a usage of the word *dṛḍha* in its non-feminine form.

35. *tasil-āśas-kr̥tvasuc-aḥ* | (Pāṇini 6.3.35) This rule is introduced for the sake of that which is not the meaning of a compound-final member (*anuttarapadārtha*). [The example is] *tataḥ*. [This is formed by] *pañcamyās tasil* (5.3.7).
Because this suffix is designated as a case-ending (*vibhakti*) by the rule *prāgdiśo vibhaktiḥ* (5.3.1), [it is subject to the following].

The substitution of *yat* for *tyad* etc., the suffix *ṭāp*, and by this [rule], the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). Regarding "there" (*tatra*): [the suffix] *tral* is added after a locative case ending (Pāṇini 5.3.10).
The remainder is as before.
Regarding "in the case of *tasil* etc.": when it is stated, "in the case of *tasil* etc., up to but not including *kṛtvasuc*,"...

Even when [the suffixes] beginning with *tasil* are not included [in the category], the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is desired in certain cases, yet it does not apply. Furthermore, even when they are included, it is not desired in some instances; if that were so, an undesired result would follow. Therefore, an exhaustive enumeration (*parigaṇana*) must be made. In that regard:
Then the example for those two has been stated. Now the examples for the remaining [suffixes] are being given:
this one is clever (*paṭvī*), this one is clever (*paṭvī*); "this one is more clever than these two"—by the rule *dvivacana* (Pāṇini 5.3.57), the suffix *tarap* is applied—resulting in *paṭutarā*.
"This one is the most clever among all"—by the rule *atiśāyane* (Pāṇini 5.3.55).

Thus: *tamap* [is added] to *paṭu* to form *paṭutamā* (most clever). Having previously been clever—by the rule *bhūtapūrve caraṭ* (Pāṇini 5.3.53)—the suffix *caraṭ* is applied, and with the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, we have *paṭvacarī*. A type of clever person—by the rule *prakāravacane jātīyar* (Pāṇini 5.3.69)—we have *paṭujātīyā*. Slightly incomplete in cleverness—by the rule *īṣadasamāptau*... [the suffix *kalpaP* is applied].
By the rule *kalpab-deśya-deśīyar-ah* (5.3.67): *paṭukalpā*, *paṭudeśyā*, *paṭudeśīyā*.
A praiseworthy *paṭvī*—by the rule *praśaṃsāyāṃ rūpap* (5.3.66)—is *paṭurūpā*. A contemptible *paṭvī*—by the rule *yāpye pāśap* (5.3.47)—is *paṭupāśā*. [And] for *ajāyāi*...

By the rule *hitā-ṭhajāvimyāṃ thyan* (Pāṇini 5.1.8), we have *ajathyā*. The suffix *thyan* is listed before *tasil* and the others. *Sarvathā* means "in every way," by the rule *prakāravacane thāl* (Pāṇini 5.3.23). *Tadā* means "at that time" or "on that night," by the rule *sarvaikānyakiṃyatadaḥ kāle dā* (Pāṇini 5.3.15). [This refers to] on this night.
In this context, [the suffix] *amohil* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.3.16. Therein, by 5.3.4, the substitution of *etetau* for *idam* occurs before the locative case endings (*rat* and *tho*).
Thus, a praiseworthy female wolf is *vṛkatiḥ*, and a praiseworthy eldest is *jyeṣṭhatātiḥ*, according to the rule:
"After *vṛka* and *jyeṣṭha*, the suffixes *til* and *tātil* are applied in the Vedic language" (5.4.41).

"Tillātilau" (tilla and atila). Having formed these two, one reads "parau paṭhaḷe" (one reads [the suffixes] after them). This is the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya that an explicit enumeration (*parigaṇana*) should be made within the "tasilādi" group, but it is not the opinion of the author of the Sūtra. Furthermore, in the absence of such an enumeration, nothing undesirable follows; for in those cases where...

The substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is desired in cases not included among *tasil* and the others; in those [cases], it will occur because the particle *ca* in that subsequent sūtra has the sense of an inclusive "and" (*anuktasamuccaya*). In those cases where it is not desired even though they are included among *tasil* and the others, there is the rule: "Not [if the word] has *k* as its penultimate letter" (*na kopadhāyāḥ*, 6.3.37).
"No," [he says], "it will not be necessary through the division of the rule (yogavibhāga).

Indeed, there is also a fault in the enumeration: in the case of *dāradikā*, formed by adding the suffix *kap* to the word *dārada*, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would not apply, because the suffix *kap* is not included in the enumeration.

Regarding the rule *ṭhśasi bahvalpārthasya*: when the suffix *śas* follows, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) must be stated for words meaning "many" (*bahu*) and "few" (*alpa*); that is to say, it must be explained. This explanation, however, should be made by relying on the fact that the particle *ca* (in the preceding rule) has the function of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.

"ṭhbhasyāḍhea taddhite" and so forth. Regarding "hāstikam": [the suffix] ṭhak is applied by the rule "acittahastidhenoṣṭhak" (Pāṇini 4.2.47). If there were no *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine stem substitution) here, then after the elision of the vowel *ī* by the rule "yasya" (Pāṇini 6.4.148), [the following would apply]: "acaḥ parasmin... (Pāṇini 1.1.57).

Due to the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) according to the rule *pūrvavidhau* (1.1.57), the elision of the *ṭi* [the final vowel and following consonant] by the rule *nastaddhite* (6.4.144) would not occur; however, when the masculine-like treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) applies, this becomes simply the word *hasti*.
But is it not the case that the masculine-like treatment is already established here by the rule *ṭhak-chasoḥ* (Vārttika 732)? No.

It is established; it is not established. Because of the association with *śas*, by the rule "bhavataṣṭhak-chasau" (Pāṇini 4.2.115), only that *ṭhak* which is prescribed therein is understood, not every [suffix].

Regarding the passage beginning with "How [is this]? and so forth: if the prohibition of *puṃvadbhāva* (the substitution of the masculine form) were applied when the suffix *ḍha* follows, then in the case of "Agnāyī is the deity of this," where the suffix *ḍhak* is applied by the rule *agnerḍhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.33), the resulting form should be *Āgnāyeya*. What then is the intention behind the form *Āgneya*? This is the underlying question.

When there is the intention to express "the wife of Agni," the form *agnāyī* is derived from the word *agni* by applying the suffix *ṅīp* according to the rule *vṛṣākapyagnikusitakusīdānām udāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.37), which effects the substitution of the vowel *ai* for the final syllable. Regarding the statement "effort must be made here": by whom, then, must this effort be made? By one who...

He maintains that there is a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) stating "bhasya aḍhe taddhite" (Vārttika 731). He does not, however, hold that the letter *ca* is placed in the subsequent sūtra for the purpose of an unexpressed collective inclusion (*anuktasamuccaya*). For he says this: "The letter *ca* effects the collective inclusion of the masculine form (*puvadbhāva*) only where it is intended."

"Not elsewhere. But what is this effort? Someone says: "The mention of *apatya* (offspring) must be made as a qualifier of *ḍha*—namely, 'that which is [added] when offspring is not denoted (*apatye'ḍhe*)'. By this, the following meaning results: the *pūrvavadbhāva* (treatment like the masculine) occurs for *ḍha* when it is caused by that [suffix], excluding a suffix whose meaning is offspring. And thus, *āgneyaḥ* [is formed].

In the term *sthālīpāka*, the suffix *ḍha* is applied in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*), but here it is used in the sense of "this has as its deity" (*sāsya devatā*); therefore, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) certainly occurs here.
However, another says: the two locative cases in the rule *bhasyāḍhe taddhite* (Vārttika 731) are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*).

And the negative particle (*nañ*) here functions in the sense of "little" (*alpa*), just as a gruel that has very little salt is called "saltless" (*alavaṇā*). In this context, the meaning is as follows: "The substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) for a feminine base ending in *bh* should be stated when a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) beginning with the *ḍha*-pratyaya follows, provided it signifies 'little'. By this rule, [we derive] *āgneyaḥ* and *sthālīpākaḥ*.

In these cases, the substitution of the masculine form (puṃvadbhāva) occurs; however, in cases such as *śyaineya* and *rohiṇeya*, it does not occur. This is according to the rule beginning with "ṭhak-chasośca. Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *ṭhak*, since—

Once the single-substitute (ekādeśa) for *ṭh* has been made, the desired result is already established by the rule "bhasyāḍhe taddhite" (Vār. 731). [The present rule] is for the purpose that [the substitution] should take place while the word is still in its *ṭh*-state. What follows from this? The suffix *ka*, prescribed by "isusuktāntāt kaḥ" (7.3.51), becomes established; otherwise, indeed, [it would not].

If the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment) were to occur after the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, then just as the single substitute does not occur in *māthitika*, so too it would not occur here in *bhāvatkāḥ*.
[The forms are] *bhāvatkāḥ* and *bhavadīyāḥ*, according to the rule *bhavataṣṭhakcchasau* (Pāṇini 4.2.115).
The suffixes *ṭhak*, *āc*, and *cha* [are applied in the sense of "born there" (*tatra jātaḥ*)].
36. *kyaṅmāninośca* (6.3.36).
[The examples] *ṭhetāyate*, *śyetāyate* are formed from the words *eta* and *śveta* by [the application of] *varṇādanudātāt topadhāt to naḥ* (4.1.39) [the printed reading being *etaśvetaśabdābhyām*].

By this [rule], the suffix *ṅīp* is applied, and the letter *t* is replaced by *n*. From "she acts like a female elephant" (*enī*) or "she acts like a hawk" (*śyenī*), the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied according to *kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.11), and lengthening occurs by *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.25). [The form] *ayamasyām*...

Regarding "darśanīyamānī" [the *Kāśikā* states: "this one considers her to be beautiful"]: he considers this woman to be beautiful. The suffix *ṇini* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.82] "manaḥ. Thus, "darśanīyamānanīyam asyāḥ" means "he considers this woman to be beautiful."
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām agaḥ* (4.1.73), which is an extension of *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām* (4.1.71).

Why, then, is there a need for the word "in the feminine" (*striyām*) when the term "in a coordinate construction" (*samānādhikaraṇe*) is already being carried over [from the previous sūtra], given that [the suffix would otherwise apply] even when not in the feminine and when not in a coordinate construction, as in the case of the word *māninī* used as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*)?
He states that the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is being illustrated, saying: "The mention of *mānin*," and so forth.

How is this known? He says: "But here," and so forth. If the final member (*uttarapada*) refers to a feminine and is in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*)—as in "she considers herself beautiful" (*darśanīyam ātmānaṃ manyate*).

In examples such as *darśanīyamāninī*, since the desired form is already established by the rule *striyāṃ puṃvat* (6.3.34), the mention of *mānin* is for the sake of excluding feminine forms; thus it is understood that [the rule applies] even when there is no coreferentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇa*). Otherwise, that [mention of *mānin*] would be purposeless.
37. Not after a stem ending in *kopadha*. (6.3.37) This is a prohibition of the masculine-like treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) that would otherwise have been obtained by the preceding rule.
For example: *pācikābhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a female cook") and *kārikābhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a female doer"). [This applies] from the words *pācaka-* and *kāraka-*.

The suffix *ṭāp* is added to the two words ending in the *ṇvuL* suffix. By the rule *pratyayasthāt kātpūrvasyāta idāpyasupaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.44), the vowel *a* preceding the *k* is changed to *i*. Here, the application of the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat* (Pāṇini 6.3.34) and others occurs. Thus we have *madrikā-bhāryaḥ* and *vṛjikā-bhāryaḥ*, meaning "one whose wife is born among the Madras" and "one whose wife is born among the Vṛjis. These are derived from *madreṣu bhavā* ("she who exists among the Madras") and *vṛjiṣu bhavā* ("she who exists among the Vṛjis").

The suffix *kan* is applied by the rule *madravṛjyoḥ kan* (Pāṇini 4.2.131). Here too, there is the possibility of application by the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat* (Pāṇini 6.3.34) and others. Thus we have *madrikākalpā* and *vṛjikākalpā*.
Here, the application occurs by the rule *tasilādiṣvākṛtvasucaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.35). [In the case of] *madrikāyate*...

In such cases, there is the application of *kyaṅ* by the rule *kyaṅmāninośca* (Pāṇini 6.3.36). Regarding the form *vilepikāyā dharmyam*: from the root *lip* (meaning "to smear" or "to cover," Dhātupāṭha 1433), the suffix *ṇvul* is applied to form *vilepika*.
Then, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *aṇ mahiṣyādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.48) to form *vailepikam*. Herein...
The application [of the rule] is optionally obtained by the Vārttika *bhasyāḍhea taddhite* (Vā.

731). Regarding the prohibition concerning bases ending in *k* (*kopadhapratiṣedhe*), and so forth: in this prohibition concerning bases ending in *k*, the mention of *taddhita* must be made; that is, only in the case where a *k* belonging to a *taddhita* suffix is the penultimate (*upadhā*) letter.

So that the prohibition may apply: let there not be [the application of the rule] here in the case of *pākabhāryaḥ*. This word *pāka* is derived with the suffix *kan* by the rule *arbhaka-pṛthuka-pākā vayasi* (Daiva-Uṇādi 3.50). In this case, were the mention of *vuk* not present, the prohibition would apply here as well.
It might be so; however, if the inclusion of the *taddhita* suffix *vuñ* were made, then regarding what will be stated under *pūrvatrāsiddham* (8.2.1)—
namely, concerning the form "śuṣkajaṅgha," where [the rule] *śuṣaḥ kaḥ* (8.2.51) would be considered asiddha— [the following would apply].

"The purpose of the section on 'asiddha' is that the prohibition [stated in] *ṭhna kopadhāyāḥ* (6.3.37) would otherwise not apply"— this [argument] is untenable; for even if the rule *ṭhśuṣaḥ kaḥ* were not present,
the prohibition *ṭhna kopadhāyāḥ* (6.3.37) would still apply here precisely because [the former] is considered *asiddha*.

It must be so; for here the letter *k* is not connected with a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), nor is it connected with *vu*. There is no fault, because it is stated thus by relying on a difference in philosophical view. Indeed, this was said by relying on the opinion of the author of the Vārttika; that, moreover, belongs to the author of the Ślokavārttika.
He will speak by relying on the view of those who follow the opinion of the author of the Sūtras.

38. *saṃjñāpūraṇyośca* | (6.3.38) But how can there be the application of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) to a word that is a proper name (*saṃjñāśabda*), given that the masculine form is prescribed only for words that have been used in the masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), and a word that is a proper name is not [necessarily] used in the feminine?

Does it follow that [the word] functions as one whose masculine form has been stated, because technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*) reside in a single substance? This is not so; for this restriction—that technical terms reside in a single substance—does not exist. Indeed, this restriction does not apply solely to those [words] that reside in a single substance.
It must be understood that [names] exist as designations (*saṃjñā*) by means of words (*śabda*).

For instance, a word such as "Devadatta" is observed in common usage to be employed as a designation for a single entity only because of its connection to various substances, actions, and so forth; the same applies to words like "sva" (self/possessive) in the technical treatises (*śāstra*). However, this prohibition is not made with respect to a designation that resides in a single substance; therefore, the objection is without merit.

Now, it may be granted that proper names (*saṃjñā-śabda*) have multiple referents, yet they are designated as having been previously masculine only with respect to a single form (*ākṛti*). But how then do they possess any basis for application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*), given that they are arbitrary words (*yadṛcchā-śabda*)? This too is without substance; for even among them, some certainly possess a basis for application, such as the word *saptaparṇa* ("seven-leaved"). Even where this [external basis] does not exist, they still function toward the object of denotation by taking their own form (*svarūpa*) as the basis for application.

In that regard, what is incorrect here [in the examples] where the word *pumān* (man) is spoken when the cause for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is not different? Regarding the example *datārbhyaḥ*: here, the word *datā* is one whose masculine form has been spoken (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) with respect to that very activity of giving (*dānakriyā*). Regarding *guptābhāryaḥ*: here too, the word *guptā* is [spoken] either with respect to the activity of protecting (*gopanakiyā*) or with respect to its own form as the cause for its application. Both words are *bhāṣitapuṃska*, as seen in the forms *datāyate* and *guptāyate*.

How are these two presented as examples of the prohibition [of *puṃvadbhāva*], given that even if *puṃvadbhāva* were to apply, both forms would be established by the lengthening [of the vowel] according to Pāṇini 7.4.25: "The long vowel is substituted for the penultimate of a root ending in /ṛ/ before a suffix marked with Ṭ or a sārvadhātuka suffix"? He thinks thus: "A rule preceded by a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not mandatory" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 64). Therefore, if there were no prohibition of *puṃvadbhāva*, the absence of the lengthening would be inferred. In that case, forms such as *datayate* and *guptayate* would also result.

Since the rule "na kopadhā-saṃjñā-pūraṇīnām" could have been formulated as a single *yoga*, the division of the rule was made for the purpose of making known that the prohibition "na kopadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.37) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*). Consequently, what was stated [in the Vārttika]—"In the prohibition regarding words ending in *ka* as an upadhā, the mention of *taddhita* suffixes and *vuñ* must be made"—need not be done.

39. And [the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied] to a *taddhita* suffix that causes *vṛddhi*, provided the word does not denote a color or a transformation (*araktavikāre*). (Pāṇini 6.3.39) The suffixes that cause *vṛddhi* are *ñ*, *ṇ*, and *ka*. For example: *sraughnībhāryaḥ*. [The word *sraughnī* is derived as follows: from *srughna*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.53] *tatra bhavaḥ* ("occurring there").
Then, by [Pāṇini 4.1.15] *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Thus...

The same applies here in the case of *māthurī-bhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is from Mathurā") and *madhyama-bhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is middle-aged"). [In *madhyama-*,] the suffix *ma* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.3.8 (*madhyān maḥ*), meaning "she who exists in the middle.
[In *kāṇḍalāva-bhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a reaper of stalks"),] the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.1 (*karmaṇyaṇ*) because he "reaps the stalk" (*kāṇḍaṃ lunāti*).
As before, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Regarding the form *tāvadbhāryaḥ*:

from the word *tāvat*, in the sense of "that which has this as its measure" (*tatparimāṇam asyāḥ*), the suffix *vatup* is added by *yatadetebhyaḥ parimāṇe vatup* (Pāṇini 5.2.39). By *ā sarvanāmnaḥ* (6.3.91), the vowel *ā* replaces the final *d* of the stem; then, by *ugitaśca* (4.1.6), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added.

The suffix *ṅīp* [is applied]. In the case of *tāvadbhāryaḥ*, meaning "one whose wife is that much," if the term *vṛddhinimittasya* were taken as referring to a *tatpuruṣa* compound, then the prohibition would apply here as well; for the suffix *vatup* is indeed the cause (*nimitta*) of the vowel *ā* being a *vṛddhi*. However, there is no fault if it is understood as a *bahuvrīhi* compound; for [in that case], it is not so.

Even though *vatup* has the letter *ñ* as its initial, which is a cause for *vṛddhi*, [the following examples apply]: *kāṣāyī*; here, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *tena raktaṃ rāgāt* (Pāṇini 4.2.1), and *ṅīp* follows as before.
*Lauhī*; here, the suffix *añ* is applied by the rule *prāṇirajatādibhyo 'ñ* (Pāṇini 4.3.154), and *ṅīp* follows as before. *Khādireṣaḥ*.
The suffix *añ* or *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.3.141 (*ṭhpalāśādibhyo vā*). That which has a shaft made of *khadira* wood is called *khādireṣaḥ*.

40. *ṅīṣ* is applied after a word denoting a part of the body (*svāṅga*) when it is not a secondary member (*upasarjana*) and does not have a conjunct consonant as its penultimate (*asaṃyogopadha*). (Pāṇini 4.1.54). Thus, from *dīrghakeśa*, we get *dīrghakeśī*. From *paṭu*, [the suffix] *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *voto guṇavacanāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.44), resulting in *paṭvī*. (6.3.40) *ṣaṭvī*. From the word *paṭu*, [the suffix] *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *voto guṇavacanāt*.
By [Pāṇini 4.1.44], the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied.

Thus, one says "akeśabhāryaḥ. Since her hair (*keśa*) does not exist, she is "akeśā"; however, because the suffix *ṅīp* is prohibited by [Pāṇini 4.1.57]—"after a word preceded by *sa-* or *na-*, or by *vidyamāna-*"—the suffix *ṭāp* alone is applied.
It comes to be.
41. And [the feminine suffix] from a genus name.

(6.3.41) [The example is] *kaṭhībhāryaḥ*. From the word *kaṭha*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule "From a genus name that does not refer to a female and has a non-*y*-vowel as its penultimate letter" (4.1.63). Its status as a genus name is established by the rule "A lineage (*gotra*) together with the [Vedic] schools (*caraṇa*)" (4.1.63).
By the definition [given] in *Mā.bhā.* 2.225, namely "this" (*ayam*) and so forth;

the prohibition of that *puṃvadbhāva* which is introduced by the supplementary rule (*aupasaṃkhyānika*) "in the case of a *bha*-stem, when a *taddhita* suffix beginning with a vowel follows" (*bhasyāḍhea taddhite*, Vār. 731), is not intended here. For this reason, this prohibition...
The intention is that, for the sake of avoiding this objection, a formal split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must be made in the subsequent sūtra by adding the word *puṃvat*.

42. *puṃvatkarmadhārayajātīyadeśīyeṣu* (6.3.42). Now, one might object: since the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is already established in a *karmadhāraya* compound by [the rule] *striyāḥ puṃvat* (6.3.34) and so forth, it would also apply to the words *jātīya* and *deśīya*.

[Regarding the rule] "ṭhtasilādiṣvākṛtvasucaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.35) and so forth, one might ask: "What is the purpose of this new beginning? To this he says: "This beginning is for the purpose of a prohibition.
By the word "prohibition" (pratiṣedha), the scope of the prohibition is expressed; due to association (sāhacarya), "prohibition" is taken as its meaning.

That for which there is a purpose (*prayojana*) is so described. The meaning is that where a prohibition has been stated regarding a particular subject, the transformation into the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is the purpose. Alternatively, the word *artha* here functions in the sense of "cessation" (*nivṛtti*), as in the expression "smoke for the sake of mosquitoes" (*maśakārtho dhūmaḥ*). By this, the following is the meaning:
It occurs [in the commentary]: "This undertaking is for the purpose of excluding the prohibition.

[The phrase] "only from that which has a corresponding masculine form" (*bhāṣitapuṃskāt*) [is understood]. If the rule *bhāṣitapuṃskādanūṅ* (Pāṇini 6.3.34) were not being carried over [as a governing rule], then this present statement would be intended to apply even to words that do not have a corresponding masculine form and to those that do not end in the suffix *ūṅ*.

It might be argued that [the rule] is not for the purpose of prohibition; however, in that case, even in examples such as *khaṭvāvṛndārikā* and *brahmabandhūvṛndārikā*, there would be the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*).

Therefore, the condition *bhāṣitapuṃskāt* "from that which has a corresponding masculine form" must be understood as continuing from the previous rule, along with the exclusion *anūṅ* "not having the suffix ūṅ."

Regarding the rule beginning with "ṭhkukkuṭāḷādīnām," since the final syllable of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) does not end in a feminine suffix and because there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*), the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would not otherwise apply; therefore, this addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is prescribed. By the words "na vā" (or rather not), he rejects this addition.
Or rather, it need not be stated. Why? Because what is intended is that the preceding member [of the compound] is not feminine (*astrī*).
The intention is that the preceding member is intended to be non-feminine in gender. To clarify the meaning of this very point, he says: "without being feminine," and so forth. For here—

The exclusion of other species, such as peacocks and the like, is intended [by the term "meat"]. In an instruction whose purpose is the exclusion of other species, the inclusion of a specific gender (liṅga) is indeed of no assistance; for even without that, the exclusion of other species can certainly be accomplished. For instance, when it is said, "deer meat" (mṛgamāṃsam)—

Even without the employment of a specific gender marker, the exclusion of other classes is logically established—as in the case of "meat belonging to the species of deer," which does not belong to another species.
Therefore, femininity is not intended here because it is irrelevant; thus, even without femininity—

The meaning is that here, in cases such as *kukkuṭāṇḍa* ("hen's egg") and the like, the meaning of the first member (*pūrvapada*) is intended to be expressed through the commonality of genus (*jātisāmānyena*), without the distinction of femininity (*strītva*). Consequently, the intention is that in this context, words such as *kukkuṭa* and others, being inherently non-feminine (*astrīliṅga*), are compounded with words such as *aṇḍa*. What [is the point]?
Furthermore, what is this prior member (*pūrvapada*)? It is merely a substance (*dravya*) delimited by a genus such as "cock" (*kukkuṭa*).

Regarding the phrase "due to *puṃvadbhāva*" and so forth: here, in the case of a suffix marked with *kh*, the substitution of the short vowel occurs by way of *vipratiṣedha* (conflict of rules) due to *puṃvadbhāva*; this has already been explained previously. However, in the case of suffixes beginning with *gh*...

It is explained as follows: the scope for the rule "in the case of [words ending in] *gh* etc., the feminine suffix *ṅī* becomes short" is, for example, *nartakitarā*, *nartakitamā*, *nartakirūpā*, and *nartakikalpā*;
whereas the scope for the rule of masculine-like treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) is, for example, *darśanīyatarā*, *darśanīyatamā*, and *darśanīyarūpā*.

Regarding the form *darśanīyakalpā*: here both [rules] apply—namely, *paṭvitarā*, *paṭvitamā* (by *tara* and *tamap*), and *paṭvīrūpā*, *paṭvikalpā*. By the rule of mutual exclusion (*vipratiṣedha*), the shortening occurs. The scope for the shortening by *ke’ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.13) is, for example, *nartakikā*; whereas for meanings such as "unknown" (*ajñāta*), etc., the suffix *ka* is applied after words beginning with *pra* (by *prāgivāt*).

What is the scope for *pūrvavadbhāva* (the substitution of the preceding form) by [Pāṇini 7.3.48] *kaḥ* (5.3.70)? It is in the case of *dāradikā*. Here, when *ka* follows the word *darat*, the word *dārada* is formed through *puṃvadbhāva* by [Pāṇini 6.3.35] *tasilādiṣvākṛtvāsucaḥ*. Therefore, when *ṭāp* is applied, [the rule] *pratyayasthāt kāt* (7.3.44) [applies].

By this rule [Pāṇini 7.1.86], both [substitutions] would apply here in the case of *paṭvikā*. In this instance, by the principle of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the shortening [of the vowel] will take effect. But by what [rule] would there be the masculine-like form (*puṃvadbhāva*), since the list of suffixes beginning with *tasil* was specifically enumerated [in Pāṇini 7.1.44], and the suffix *kap* is not included therein?

The author of the Bhāṣya, not the author of the Sūtras, is to be questioned regarding this enumeration. To demonstrate the view for which the prohibitive negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) "anūṅ" was previously relied upon as a means of establishing [the rule], he says "iha," etc., and "tatra tadrājapratyayasya," etc.

In this regard, after *iḍaviṭ* and *pṛthu*, the suffix *añ* prescribed by [Pāṇini 4.1.168], "From a word denoting a country that is also the name of a Kṣatriya, [the suffix] añ [is added]," undergoes elision (*luk*) by [Pāṇini 4.1.177], "And [there is elision] of *añ* after [a vowel]. However, after *darad* and *uśij*, [the suffix] is prescribed by [Pāṇini 4.1.170], "After [words ending in] two vowels, Magadha,... [and so forth].

This refers to the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by such rules as [Pāṇini 4.1.112]. The analysis of the compound is: "he is both an Aiḍaviḍa and a Vṛndārikā. According to the rule beginning with "viśeṣaṇa" (Pāṇini 2.1.57), the term "aiḍaviḍādayaḥ" (beginning with Aiḍaviḍa) includes, by the force of the word "ādi" (etc.), the following: Dārada, Pāratha, and Auśija.
They are grasped.

43. *gharūpakalpacelaḍbruvagotramata-hateṣu ṅyo 'nekācaḥ hrasvaḥ* | (Pāṇini 6.3.43) Because the words *celaḍ*, *bruva*, and *gotra* have the sense of reproach, [the rule] "those which are reproachable are [compounded] with reproaches" (*kutsitāni kutsanaiḥ*) applies.
Thus is the compound [formed]. However, the words *mata* and *hata* are [compounded] by means of [the rule] *viśeṣaṇam bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.57).
The suffix *celaṭ* is listed among the roots beginning with *pac*; the letter *ṭ* is for the purpose of deriving the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.
If this [word *celī*] ends in the suffix *ac* added after the root *brū*, then by the rule *bruvo vaciḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.53), [it undergoes substitution].

The substitution of *vaci* and the *guṇa* [vowel change] would apply; why, then, do they not occur? To one who raises this objection, he replies: "The substitution of *vaci* and the *guṇa* do not occur because of a technical irregularity (*nipātana*)," as in the examples *āmalakītarā* and *kuvalītarā*. The words *āmalaka* and *kuvala* [denote the fruit] when [referring to] a tree.
However, since the word *phala* is neuter while [the other two] are feminine, both are considered *abhāṣitapuṃska*;
from them, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied because they belong to the *gaurādi* group.
44. *nadyāḥ śeṣasyānyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.3.44). The rule *bhāṣitapuṃskādanūṅ* (6.3.34) is no longer in force. [Question: "What is the remainder (*śeṣa*)? [Answer:
If the remainder is that for which a short vowel was not prescribed by the preceding rule, then...

That which has been mentioned as masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), and that which has been mentioned as masculine when its form is different, would also be subject to the rule of remainder (*śeṣatva*); consequently, even in cases such as *āmalakītarā* and *droṇītarā*, there would optionally be shortening (*hrasvatva*) by this [present] rule. For shortening is not [already] established here by the preceding sūtra.
With the intention that it has been prescribed, he says: "And [the word] *nadī* which ends in *ṅī*, and that which is monosyllabic (*ekāc*) ending in *ṅī*.

By this, he demonstrates that here the status of being a "remainder" (*śeṣatva*) is based on what is explicitly heard (*śruta*), and not with reference to that for which a short vowel (*hrasva*) has not been prescribed. But how is this obtained?
Because of the mention of "the remainder" (śeṣa). Even without the mention of "the remainder," the shortening of the remainder alone will occur optionally.

For if the feminine suffix *ṅī* were optionally shortened even for a word that has been stated as masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) when it has more than one vowel (*anekāca*), then this mention of "either way" (*anyatarasyām*) would have belonged to the preceding rule itself.

One should act thus: here, for that [element] whose shortening was not previously prescribed by the preceding rule, its optional shortening will apply only to the "remainder" even without the mention of *śeṣa*; this is how it is determined. So what is the purpose of the mention of *śeṣa*? It is included because of the preceding rule, *ṅyo 'nekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.68).

The purpose [of the rule] is that the status of being a "remainder" (śeṣa) is understood in relation to that which is heard [in the sūtra]. However, in the case of *camaliketarā* and *drīṇītarā*, the status of being a remainder cannot be established in relation to what is heard [there], because [the stems] contain more than one vowel (*anekāctvāt*). Therefore, there is no possibility of shortening (*hrasvatva*) here in the form *strītarā*.

Thus: [the suffix] *ḍaṭ* is applied to the root *styāyati*; because it is marked with *ḍi*, there is elision of the *ṭi* portion [by Pāṇini 6.4.143], and by [Pāṇini] 6.1.66, there is also elision of the *val* portion.
Because it is marked with *ṭi*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added.
"It must be explained" means that it must be commented upon. In this regard, the following...
