The explanation is as follows: because the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* is understood as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the suffix will not apply to a word ending in a *kṛt* affix or to a feminine noun (*nadī*). Thus, in the example *lakṣmītarā*: [the root] *lakṣi* takes the suffix *ī* by the rule *avitṛstṛtantribhya īḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 1.82), and the augment *muṭ* is added by the rule *lakṣermuṭ ca* (Dhātupāṭha 1.84); thus, it ends in the suffix *ī*.
The word *lakṣmī* has been derived; it is formed with a primary suffix (*kṛt*) and the feminine marker *nadi*.
45. *ugitaśca* (Pāṇini 6.3.45).

In the example *śreyasitarā*, when the suffix *īyasun* follows, the word *praśasya* is replaced by *śra-* according to *praśasyasya śraḥ* (5.3.60), and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to *ugitaśca* (4.1.6). [The form is] *viduṣītarā*.
Thus: for the root *vid*, there is the substitution of *śatṛ* for the following *laṭ*;

for that [substitute], by the rule "for *vid*, *śatṛ* becomes *vasu*" (Pāṇini 7.1.36), there is the substitution of *vasu*; then, by the rule "there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of *vasu*" (Pāṇini 6.4.131), the preceding vowel [of the root] is substituted; and as before, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied.

"In this view, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) must also be stated here," so that forms such as *śreyastarā* and *vidbatarā* may occur according to this alternative. As for *vidbatarā*: by the rule *vasusraṃsu-* (8.2.72), the *s* is replaced by *d*, and by the rule *khari ca* (8.4.55), the *d* is replaced by *t*.

With the words "due to connection with excellence" (*prakarṣayogāt*), he rejects the proposed addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*). In the derivation and application of words, the presence of a real object is not the primary cause;
rather, it is simply the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). And in this case, feminine gender was not previously intended on account of its connection with excellence.

Therefore, the superlative suffix must be applied to a word that does not end in a feminine suffix, while the feminine suffix must be applied to a word ending in a superlative suffix; thus, forms such as *śreyas-tarā* are established. But surely, the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* refers to words ending in them?

It was stated that [the rule] is for the purpose of prescribing *taddhita* suffixes; how, then, can a suffix expressing excellence (*prakarṣa*) of a *taddhita* be applied after a word ending in a feminine suffix? This is not so; in this context, that was stated with the intention of expressing both femininity and the meaning of the *taddhita* simultaneously, but not in cases where...

Since the connection with the sense of "excess" (prakarṣa) occurs first with respect to the object, there is no intention to express femininity; therefore, why is it not appropriate [to apply the suffix] with reference to that?
46. *ānmahataḥ samānādhikaraṇajātīyayoḥ* (6.3.46).
[Examples: *mahādevaḥ*, *mahābrāhmaṇaḥ*. These are *karmadhāraya* compounds according to *sanmahatparamottamotkṛṣṭāḥ pūjyamānaiḥ* (2.1.61). [Example: *mahābāhuḥ*; this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Having set forth the opinion of another school with the words "Because it is stated by way of a technical definition" (*lakṣaṇoktatvāt*), he refutes it.

It might be argued as follows: "The compound is brought to mind by the subsequent member; for there can only be a subsequent member when a compound exists, and that compound [is determined] by the paribhāṣā rule concerning what is taught by a technical definition versus what is taught by its actual wording."

(Commentary on Pāṇini 2.1.61) That which is explicitly prescribed by the rule *sanmahat...* (Pāṇini 2.1.61) and so forth—that is, the compound specifically ordained by that very rule—is what is understood here; however, a compound that is merely derivative (*lākṣaṇika*) or stated by a general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇokta*), such as *mahatputraḥ*, is not. In this regard, the rule *ṣaṣṭhī* (Pāṇini 2.2.8) [applies].

Because [the rule] is prescribed by way of a general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), [one might argue] that it will therefore not apply here. If that were so, it would not apply even in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, since that too is based on a general characteristic. [The sūtra says] "for the sake of that" (*tadartham*) and so forth; the mention of "co-referential" (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is for the purpose that the substitution of *ā* (*ātva*) may occur even in a *bahuvrīhi*.
It must be so understood. In that case, this *paribhāṣā* does not apply.

If it were to apply, the term "co-referential" (*samānādhikaraṇa*) would be redundant; for the compound explicitly prescribed by the rule [Pāṇini 2.1.58] is already co-referential by virtue of its constituent words. And since that *paribhāṣā* does not apply...

The substitution of *ā* for *a* occurs even in a *bahuvrīhi* compound. However, if the term "having the same referent" (*samānādhikaraṇa*) were not included [in the rule], that technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) would have to apply here; consequently, just as it does not occur in *mahat-putra*, it would likewise not occur in the *bahuvrīhi* *mahā-bāhu*.

One might have the misconception that since the word *mahat* (great) occurs in the form ending in the suffix *cv*-ya in the sense "the moon is great, accomplished, and become great (*mahadbhūta*)," the word *bhūta* must likewise stand in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it; therefore, [the author] addresses this:
To refute this, he says: "mahān mahān," and so forth. Regarding the term "mahadbhūtaḥ":

from the word *mahat*, the suffix *cvi* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.4.50 (*abhūtatadbhāve*), and because that [suffix] is designated as a *gati* by Pāṇini 1.4.61 (*ūry-ādi-cvi-ḍācaś-ca*), it is joined with the word *bhūta*.

The compound is formed by *kugatiprādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18). Regarding the phrase "because of being secondary" (*gauṇatvāt*) and so forth: in common worldly usage, when both a primary and a secondary meaning are possible for a word that has been uttered, comprehension occurs only with respect to the primary meaning, and not with respect to the secondary meaning, such as [the sense of] "non-giving. For instance, [in the case of the command] "Let a cow be brought," [the listener understands the animal, not the secondary sense].

When this is said, only that which possesses a dewlap and so forth is brought forward, and not a *bāhīka*. Therefore, here too, when the word "great" (*mahat*) is uttered, the comprehension arises only regarding the primary sense of greatness, not the secondary one.

And in this context, the sense of greatness is secondary; consequently, because it denotes that [secondary sense], the word "great" itself is also secondary. Thus, it is not [the case that the primary meaning is intended].

It becomes "bhavatītvam. Now, one might object: since the moon is already endowed with greatness, it is indeed great; therefore, is it not improper for the meaning of "great" (*mahat*) to be treated as figurative (*gauṇa*)? This is not so; for in every instance where a word ending in *cvī* is used, an object that previously possessed a certain state is spoken of as having acquired a subsequent state through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). Therefore, here too, the moon— [is so addressed].

When that which was not previously in a state of greatness is expressed by the word "mahat," it is said to be followed by a subsequent state characterized by figurative greatness; thus, its status as a secondary (gauṇa) usage is justified.
If, due to this secondary nature, the substitution of *āt* for the vowel of the word "mahat" does not occur here, then the replacement by the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would likewise not occur.

It would not occur [in such cases as]: *amahatī brāhmaṇī mahatī saṃpannā mahadbhūtā* ("the small Brahmin woman has become large"); furthermore, the two instances of *vṛddhi* would not occur for the secondary (*gauṇa*) word *go*, namely in *gaur vāhīkaḥ tiṣṭhati* ("the Vāhīka is a cow"), where there would be no *vṛddhi* [of the initial vowel] after the secondary word *go* by the rule *gauraṇit* (Pāṇini 7.1.99).

If the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffixes were not treated as having the marker *ṇ*, would not the substitution of *ā* prescribed by "āṬtaḥ am-śasoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.93) fail to apply in the example "gāṃ vāhīkam ānaya"? This is not a valid objection; for the masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) will indeed occur through a split of the rule "striyāḥ puṃvat" (Pāṇini 6.3.34).

A separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) must necessarily be made for the sake of forms such as *garbhibhārya* and others, as well as for forms such as *mahāghāsa*. When that [separation] is made for another purpose, it will also serve this purpose.
But even if the separation of the rules is made, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would still not apply here.

Because the primary sense of the term *mahat* would be secondary (*gauṇa*), and because the split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) has its purpose fulfilled elsewhere? If that is so, then in the rule *puṃvat karmadhāraye* (Pāṇini 6.3.42), a second split of the rule, *puṃvat*, will be postulated; that [second split] will apply to the secondary sense.

Furthermore, the fault of the absence of *vṛddhi* does not apply; because figurative usage (*gauṇatva*) is understood there from the sentence (*vākya*), whereas the word has only its primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*),
and the meaning of the sentence is not required at the time of the grammatical formation of the word (*padasaṃskāra*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "mahādātve" and so forth: since the substitution of *ā* (ātvam) and the masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāvaḥ*) are prescribed when there is grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*), they do not apply when there is a lack of coreferentiality (*vyadhikaraṇa*). Therefore, even in the case of a non-coreferential final member (*uttarapada*) such as *ghāsa* and others, an addition (*upasaṃkhyānam*) must be made for the form *mahādātva*. As for the term "addition" (*upasaṃkhyānam*):

The meaning is "establishment" (pratipādana). In this regard, the establishment is as follows: even in the rule *āt mahataḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.46), he will perform a separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) by [reading] *āt*; by that means, the substitution of *āt* will occur in cases such as *mahāghāsaḥ* ("the fodder for a large [ox]") and so forth. And that separation of the rules is indeed necessary.

It must be performed—for the sake of [the rule] beginning with "a cake on eight potsherds" (aṣṭākapāla); when that which is being performed for one purpose also serves this purpose. Regarding the phrase "and the statement of the masculine-like form" (puṃvadvacanaṃ ca), etc., it is understood as referring to the words "ghāsa," "kara," and "viśiṣṭa. The statement of the masculine-like form—that is, its explanation—must be made, and that has already been done previously.
It has been done.

Regarding the rule "aṣṭanaḥ kapāle" and so forth, here too the meaning of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is "explanation" (*pratipādana*). And that explanation has already been provided: namely, the form "aṣṭākāpālam," [derived] from the eight...

In the case of *kapāleṣu saṃskṛtam*, a compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.51] *taddhitārtha* etc.; then the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.16] *saṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ*; and that suffix is elided by [Pāṇini 4.1.88] *dvigor lug anapatye*. Thus we have *aṣṭakapālaṃ brāhmaṇasya*, meaning "prepared on eight potsherds for a Brāhmaṇa. [This refers to] of the eight potsherds (*kapālāni*).

The compound *samāhāra-aṣṭakapāla* is a *dvigu* compound formed by a collective sense (*samāhāre dviguḥ*). Here, because it belongs to the *pātrādi* group (Vārttika 159), the feminine suffix is not applied; consequently, the suffix *ṅīp* prescribed by the rule *dvigoḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.21) does not occur.
[The rule] *gavi ca yukte* and so forth applies when the word *go* occurs as a final member in the sense of being "yoked."

The establishment of the *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) for the word *aṣṭan* in the case of the locative (*gamya-māne*) must be performed; and that establishment has already been made [by the rule] "aṣṭāgavena śakaṭena. This is a three-membered *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which eight oxen are yoked" (*aṣṭau gāvo yuktā asmin*). However, because the word "yoked" (*yukta*) is understood [from the context], it is not explicitly expressed in the *dvigu* formation.

It is employed [in this sense], just as the word *upasikta* is used in the expression *dadhyodana* ("curd-rice"). And if this were a *bahuvrīhi* compound, then the suffix *ṭac*—prescribed by the rule *gorataddhitaluki* (Pāṇini 5.4.92)—would not apply, because that rule falls under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of *tatpuruṣa* compounds? Let there be no *ṭac*.

In the rule *ṭhac* *pratyanvavapūrvāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.75), the suffix will apply due to a *yogavibhāga* (separation of the rule) of the term *aj*, as in examples such as *kṛṣṇabhūmaḥ* and *padyanāma*. Alternatively, a collection of eight cows is *aṣṭagavaṃ*; that which is joined with eight cows is *aṣṭāgavaṃ*. And it is not thus [that the objection stands].
The application of the word *yukta* follows; because of the usage of a single part of a compound, as in *Satyabhāmā* for *Bhāmā*, *Bhīmasena* for *Bhīma*, and *Balabhadra* for *Bala*.
In the case of *ekādaśa* as well, the substitution of *ā* (ātvam) should be understood from that very same rule of division (*yogavibhāga*).
And the evidence for this *yogavibhāga* (the splitting of the rule) is the mention [in Pāṇini 5.3.49] of "before the eleven.

[The statement] "the *taparakaraṇa* is for the sake of clarity" is made. Now, why is it not for the purpose of excluding those [vowels] belonging to different times? Because a vowel being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*). This applies to those distinguished by a difference in quality (*guṇa*).
If that is so, why does the apprehension [of the substance] not occur? Because qualities do not effect differentiation.

47. *dvyaṣṭanaḥ saṃkhyāyāmabahuvrīhyaśītyoḥ* | (6.3.47) Here, there is no reference to the specific number (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*). For if there were, there would be a prohibition of the word *aṣṭan-* when followed by *aśīti-*, and thus that [prohibition] would be rendered useless; for the substitution of *āt* has already been prohibited.

There ought to be a long vowel by the rule of *savarṇadīrgha*. Furthermore, since the word *aśīti* has fewer syllables (*alpāctara*), it should have been placed first; its placement as the latter member serves as an indication of a deviation from the general rule, signaling that there is no application of the principle of "designation according to number" (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*). As for "twelve" (*dvādaśa*): it means two and ten.

It is a *dvandva* compound; or alternatively, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound with the elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*), formed under the rule "In the section on compounds of apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), there is an addition [to the list] for *śākapārthiva* and similar terms, and there is elision of the final member" (Vārttika 83), as in the case of "eleven plus two. The same applies to forms such as "twenty-two" (*dvāviṃśati*) and so forth.
It should be understood as follows:
regarding the term "dvaumātraḥ," having analyzed it as *dvayormātrorapatyam* ("the offspring of two mothers"), there is a compound for the sake of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*);
from that, by the rule *māturutsaṃkhyāsambhadrapūrvāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.115), the suffix *aṇ* is applied.

The substitution of the vowel *u* occurs at the end [of the compound]. Regarding the form "dvitrāḥ": having analyzed it as "two or three" (*dvau vā trayo vā*), a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed by the rule "a numeral and an indeclinable... (Pāṇini 2.2.25). Then, by the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi* denoting a number to be counted...
(Pāṇini 5.4.73), the suffix *ḍac* is added as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*), and the *ṭi*-portion is elided. Regarding the form "dvidaśāḥ": [it is explained similarly].
As before, there is *ḍac*, and it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The analysis (*vigraha*) is "twice ten. This compound occurs in the sense of the nominal suffix (*sub-artha*).

For here, the repetition related to ten, which is indicated by the word "ten," is counted by the word "two. Therefore, this meaning should be understood as "two tens" (*dvau daśakau*). The compound [expresses] the meaning of the nominal suffix.
The suffix *suj* is not employed in the commentary [of the Vṛtti] when [the word] is capable of being made understood [by composition alone], as in the case of "dvyaśītiḥ" (eighty-two).
Here, there is either a *dvandva* compound as before, or a *tatpuruṣa* with elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopin*).
Regarding the phrase "before one hundred" (*prāk śatāt*), etc.: when the number prior to one hundred is expressed, provided that it occurs as the final member (*uttarapada*) [of a compound].
The meaning is that this form of the rule—"the substitution of *āt* occurs for [the final vowel of] *dvi*, *aṣṭan*, and *na*"—must be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows:

the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*), which will be mentioned in the rule "vibhāṣā catvāriṃśataḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.49), applies here as well by means of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*) maxim; that [term]...

And this is a rule of established optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, the operation will apply to a number prior to one hundred when it is expressed by either member of a compound; however, it will not apply when it is expressed by the word "hundred" itself. In the same way, it should be understood that in the two subsequent rules as well, the grammatical operation takes effect for numbers prior to one hundred.

48. *trestrayaḥ* | (6.3.48) Regarding the word "trayaḥ": this substitute ends in the letter *s*. Why is this so? Because the word *trayodaśī* is included in the list beginning with *saṃdhivelā*; for if it ended in the vowel *a*, the reading would have been *trayadaśī*.

"Thirteen" (*trayodaśa*) and "twenty-three" (*trayoviṃśatiḥ*): by the rule *sasajuṣo ruḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.66), there is the substitution of *ru*; by *haśi ca* (6.1.114), there is the substitution of *u*; and by *ādguṇaḥ* (6.1.87), [the guṇa vowel *e* is formed]. The term *trir-daśa* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound in the sense of *su-* (excellent/much), as before; the suffix *ḍac* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*).
49. *Vibhāṣā* [is applied] when the number is forty or more, for all [of them].

(6.3.49) The inclusion of the word *sarveṣām* ("for all") is for the purpose that [the rule] should apply to *dvi* and *aṣṭan* as well; otherwise, according to the principle "a rule or a prohibition applies only to what is immediately preceding" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 19), it would apply to *tri* alone.

If it is argued that—following the maxim of the frog’s leap—the rule *dvy-aṣṭanaḥ* will also carry over here, and therefore this fault does not arise; [we reply: in that case, the inclusion of the word *sarva-* is for the sake of clarity.

50. *Hṛdayasya* [is replaced by *hṛd*] before *lekhā*, *laśa*, and *lāsa*. (6.3.50) *Hṛllekhaḥ*: [formed with] *karmaṇyaṇ* (3.2.1). *Hṛdyaḥ*: [formed with] *prāgdhitād yat* (4.4.75). *Hārdam*: [formed with] *tasyedam* (4.3.120), i.e., the suffix *aṇ* belonging to the group beginning with *prāgdīvya-tas*.

Regarding "ṭhhṛllāsaḥ": *lāsa* means the act of shining (*lasana*), formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). It is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) according to the rule "The sixth case [genitive] is compounded when connected with a word ending in a kṛt-suffix" (Vārttika 86).
As for the statement "the form *lekha* is understood as ending in the suffix *aṇ*," this is the view of Kātyāyana and others.
This is understood from the words of those who have become authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇabhūta*). Kātyāyana stated:
"When there is the mention of a technical term (*aṇ*), it should be understood as the mention of its own form; why? Because of the mention of the written form.
The author of the Bhāṣya also stated: "In all cases where there is a governing rule concerning a subsequent member (*uttarapada-adhikāra*), when there is the mention of an affix..."
"The inclusion of *svarapa* should be understood; why? Because of the mention of *lekha*.

How, then, are these two statements justified? [They are justified] if there is an inclusion of *lekha* ending in the suffix *aṇ*, and not otherwise. Now, why is the word *lekha* ending in the suffix *ghañ* not also understood to be included?

Thus he says: "But in the case of ghañ," and so forth; "this very [point]," and so forth. Since the inclusion of the word *lekha* ending in that [suffix] would already be established by the mention of *aṇ* alone, its separate mention serves to indicate this: that when a suffix is mentioned within the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*), that which ends with it is not included.

Regarding the phrase "it is taken": the meaning is that here, when there is a mention of *aṇ* and in the rule concerning *gharūpādi* (Pāṇini 6.3.43), when suffixes such as *gha* are mentioned, only the suffix itself is taken, and not the technical application of the term *tadantavidhi* (the inclusion of what ends with that).

51. Or [the suffix] *ṣyañ* is applied after [the word *hṛdaya*] when it occurs in the sense of grief or disease. (Pāṇini 6.3.51) Regarding the example "sauhārdyam": this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose heart (*hṛdaya*) is beautiful. From that, the suffix *ṣyañ* is added. As for the phrase "by the word *hṛdaya*" and so forth: here, when the word *hṛt* exists as having the same meaning as the word *hṛdaya*, then...

If the word *hṛt* is employed, then it will be *hṛcchoka*; if the word *hṛdaya* is employed, then it will be *hṛdayaśoka*. Consequently, since this is already established by that very alternative base (*prakṛti*), this rule prescribing an option need not have been made. However, it is formulated for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*). This...
Thus, the application of the established rule is stated by this sūtra.

52. [The suffix *ki* is applied] after the word *pāda* when followed by *aji*, *ati*, *go*, and *upahata*. (Pāṇini 6.3.52) Regarding "padāji": the root *aj* is used in the sense of "going" and "throwing" (Dhātupāṭha 230). Regarding "padāti": the root *at* is used in the sense of "continuous going" (Dhātupāṭha 38). Both are derived from the Uṇādi-sūtra: "And after *aj* and *ati*, with the addition of *pāda*. (Uṇādi-sūtra 4.132).

Regarding the statement "the suffix *iṇ*," since the mention of *iṇ* from the rule "from *jan* and *ghas*, *iṇ*" (*Daiva Upādi Sūtra* 1.58) is understood here by way of anuvṛtti, one might ask: if this is an *iṇ* suffix belonging to the *uṇādi* group, why does the substitution of *vī* [for *yaj*] not occur there, as prescribed by the rule "for *yaj*, *vī* except before *ghañ* and *ap*" (*Pāṇini* 2.4.56)? To this he says: "In that case... (*tatra*).
And so forth. Regarding the term "padagaḥ": in the rule *anta-atyanta-adhvadūra-pāra-* (Pāṇini 3.2.48), it is stated in a Vārttika (256):

"It should be stated that the section on the suffix *ḍa* is seen elsewhere as well. By this, the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *gam* even when the word *pāda* is used as an upapada; thus we have *padopahataḥ*.

The compound is formed by Pāṇini 2.1.32, *ṭhkartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*, whereas in the previous case it was an *upapada* compound. This substitute [for the word *pāda*] ends in the vowel *a*. It is presented with the elision (*luk*) of the nominative case ending. Regarding the statement "this word *pāda*," etc., [it is governed by the rule]: *ṭhkarṣātvato ghaño'nta udātaḥ*.

(6.1.159) Since the rule for an udātta accent on the final syllable would otherwise apply, the initial udātta of the word *pāda* is prescribed by virtue of its being listed among the *vṛṣādīni*; consequently, when the substitute *pada* is prescribed in place of that [word], it would— by the principle of closest proximity (*āntaratamya*)— necessarily be initial-udātta as well, whereas it is intended to be final-udātta.

Therefore, the word is prescribed as having an acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*) precisely at the stage of its original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*). By the words "by that" (*tena*) and so forth, he demonstrates the purpose of prescribing the acute accent on the final syllable; and by the examples "one who goes on foot" (*padājiḥ*) and "one who goes on foot" (*padātiḥ*), he demonstrates the purpose of including the term "original instruction" (*upadeśagrahaṇa*). [This is because] if [the rule were simply] "a *kṛt*-suffix following a prefix, a *kāraka*, or a subordinate word (*upapada*),"...
When the accent prescribed by this rule (6.2.139) has been applied, the fact that the word *pada* is oxytone is stated as a *nipātana* (an irregularity);

in that case, it would possess the status of being *satiśiṣṭa* (remaining after others have been applied). Consequently, in forms such as *padājiḥ*, *padātiḥ*, and *padagaḥ*, the accent of the *kṛt*-suffix (*kṛtsvara*) is superseded, because a *satiśiṣṭa* accent is more powerful.

However, in the stage of the *upadeśa* (the original formative instruction), when the rule for the enclitic accent (*antodāttatva*) is applied, the accent of the *kṛt* suffix alone remains as the most powerful (*satiśiṣṭa*).
Consequently, by that [accent], it is the compound itself that becomes oxytone (*antodātta*), and not the word *pada*.

53. *padyatyatadarthe* | (6.3.53) [The word] *padyāḥ* [is formed as follows]: by the rule *vidhyatyadhanuṣā* (4.4.83), the suffix *yat* is applied. [The word] *pādyam*: from the stem *pāda*, the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of "for the purpose of that" (*tādarthye*) by the rule *tādarthye yat* (5.4.24).
While this [rule] continues to apply, the suffix *yat* is added by the rule "ṭhpādārghābhyāñca" (Pāṇini 5.4.25).

Regarding the phrase "in the case of the substitution of *pad*" and so forth: when the substitution of *pad* is to be effected, and when the suffix *ik* has been applied in the sense of "moving about" (*carati*), there must be an additional statement (*upasaṃkhyāna*)—that is, an instruction—for the substitution of *pad*.

The meaning is that it must be so performed. In this regard, the following is the demonstration: it is established by means of a word-division (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule *pad*. Alternatively, it is established because the form *pādaḥ* is included in the list beginning with *parpa* in the rule *pādaḥ pat* (Pāṇini 6.4.130).

"Of a word denoting a limb of the body" (from the *Kāśikā*: "of that which expresses a limb of the body," etc.). But how is this obtained? Some say: by implication (*sāmarthya*), the word *pāda* is understood in the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*) as meaning a limb of the body. In that context, there are three types of subsequent members (*uttarapada*): beginning with *ājya*, and so forth.

The first three [roots] have the sense of "going," while the fourth has the sense of "killing. Among those beginning with the sense of going, the status of being an instrument (karaṇabhāva) is possible only for the word *pāda* when it denotes a limb of a living being, and not for anything else.
Therefore, in that context, the word *pāda* denoting a limb of a living being is intended; here too, that same [restriction] continues to apply.

Thus it is correct [to say] that there is a reference to a limb of the body. If this is so, then in the rule *ṛcaḥ śe* (Pāṇini 6.3.55), would there also be a reference to a limb of the body? This is not a fault; for a word denoting a limb of the body related to a *ṛc* is impossible. It denotes a fourth part.
The word *pāda* will not be understood here [in this context]. Regarding the phrase "by that" (*tena*) and so forth:

since the word *pāda*, which denotes a part of a śarāva measure, is what is being taken here, therefore, in a rule such as *paṇapādamāṣa* (Pāṇini 5.1.34), the word *pāda* that occurs there does not undergo the substitution of *pad*; it does not.
This [word *pāda*] does not denote a limb of the body; what then? It denotes a measure (*parimāṇa*). Why is this so?
Because of its association with words denoting measures such as *paṇa* and others, as in the examples "worth two *pādas*" (*dvipādyam*) and "worth three *pādas*" (*tripādyam*).
In these cases, the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of "bought with that" (*tena krītam*), according to Pāṇini 5.1.37.

54. *Himakāṣihatiṣu ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.54). Regarding *paddhimam*: this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Regarding *patkāṣiṇaḥ*: here the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule *supyajātau ṇinistācchīlye* (3.2.78), forming an upapada compound. Regarding *paddhatiḥ*: [this is formed with the same suffix].

It is called *paddhati* because it is struck (*hanyate*) by the feet (*pādābhyām*). The compound is formed with the word *hati*, ending in the suffix *ktin*, according to the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32).

55. *ṛcaḥ śe* (Pāṇini 6.3.55). Regarding the term *śe*: here, the word *śa* is understood as that which constitutes a part of the *śas* suffix, which is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). This is because it is impossible for [the word] to follow from the foot of a verse (*ṛkpāda*). Now, one might object: [what about the case where one says] "he lies on a foot" (*pāde śete*)?

When the suffix *ac* is applied by the rule *ṭha-adhikaraṇe śeteḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.15), as in the case of *pādaśaḥ*, is it possible for the sound *śa* to be related to the root *śīṅ*? This is not so; for the suffix *ac* cannot be applied to the root *śī* when *ṛk-pāda* is the upapada, because lying down (*śayana*) is impossible there, or because of non-usage (*anabhidhāna*). As for [the objection] that...
The suffix *śa* is prescribed by the rule "lomādipāmādipicchādibhyaḥ śanelacaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.2.100); however,
that [suffix] also cannot possibly follow an *ṛk-pāda*, because it is not applicable there and because it is not listed among the words beginning with *loman*.
56. Or [in a compound] with *ghoṣa*, *śabda*, and *miśra* (Pāṇini 6.3.56).

A genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is formed with the words *ghoṣa-śabda* and *śabda-śabda*—[this is the reading found in the printed edition]—and with the word *miśra* by means of the rule "pūrva-sadṛśa... (2.1.31), etc.

This is a third-case (tṛtīyā) compound. The meaning is that it should be explained as having the sense: "it should be stated that [the substitution applies] even when the word *niṣka* follows"; that is to say, when the word *niṣka* is the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the word *pāda* undergoes the substitution of *pad* for its final syllable. In this regard, the following...

The explanation is as follows: the particle *ca* from the rule "ṭhhimakāṣihatiṣu ca" (Pāṇini 6.3.54) is carried over (*anuvartate*) here, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. Alternatively, a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is made by means of the word "vā" in the sūtra; by this, [the suffix] is applied when *niṣka* is the subsequent member (*uttarapada*).
It will come to pass.
57. *udaka* becomes *uda* when forming a name (*saṃjñāyām*). For example: "He whose son is named Udameghi is called Udamegha.
Because the father [Udamegha] is not well-known, he is designated by means of his offspring as "he whose [son] is Udameghi."

It has been stated, "the son. By this, he shows that one for whom Audameghi is the offspring should be understood as Udamegha. In the same way, it should also be understood in the case of "he whose son is named Audavāhi is Udavāha"; here, *udamegha* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), meaning "filled with water" (*udakapūrṇa*).
Or "meghavāhaḥ": this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound with the middle term elided (*madhyamapadalopa*), according to the rule beginning with *śākapārthiva* (Pāṇini 2.1.69).

"Udavāhaḥ" means that which carries water; [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1). Regarding the statement "it must be explained" (*vaktavyaḥ*), the meaning is that it requires an explanation. In that regard, the explanation is as follows: here too, it is that very same [principle].

The particle *ca* (and) is understood here as having the sense of a collective inclusion (*samuccaya*) of what has not been explicitly stated; yet, there is nothing else to be included. This particle includes only the absence of *u* (*udabhāva*) within the technical name (*saṃjñā*) for the word *udaka*. In that context, of what does it include [the absence]? It includes that for which [the substitution] would otherwise not apply. For what would it not apply? [It would not apply] to that which...
Does it apply? It applies when it is the final member of a compound. Consequently, even for the final member of a name, this substitution of *uda* for the word *udaka* occurs.
Thus, *lohitodaḥ* ("red-watered") and *kṣīrodaḥ* ("milk-watered") are examples of *bahuvrīhi* compounds.

58. *peṣaṃ-vāsa-vāhana-dhiṣu ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.48). Regarding *peṣam*: [the root] *piṣlṛ* "to grind" (Dhātupāṭha 1452). Regarding *udadhiḥ*: the suffix *ki* is applied by [the rule] *karmaṇy adhikaraṇe ca* (3.3.93). [Then] there is the elision of the vowel *ā* by *āto lopa iṭi ca* (6.4.64).

(6.4.64) Thus, there is the elision of the vowel *ā*. This rule is for the purpose of excluding technical names (*saṃjñā*); therefore, in this case, "udadhi" should be understood as belonging to the *ghaṭādi* group and not as the word for "ocean" (*samudra*), because in that case [the form] would already be established by the preceding rule—since in the word "udadhi," "ocean" (*samudra*) is indeed a technical name.
Having performed.
59. *ekahalādau pūrayitavye'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.3.59).
If the word *eka* were understood here as signifying "one" (*sukhyāvacana*), then its inclusion would be purposeless;
for it is never possible for two or more consonants (*hal*) to constitute an initial [group].

Since the mention of "one" (*eka*) is made for the purpose of exclusion, this word *eka* signifies "without a companion. Even so, one might still understand the compound as referring to any undistinguished single consonant (*hal*) that is initial in the second member of the compound.

In that case, [the rule] would apply even here in *tad-udaka-sthānam*. For here too, the letter *s* is indeed single and without a companion (*asahāya*). If multiple phonemes were pronounced simultaneously, or if once pronounced they did not perish, then even a [consonant] accompanied by others might be considered "initial. But this is not the case; because—

Phonemes are not pronounced simultaneously, and they perish as soon as they are uttered. Therefore, there is never anywhere any such thing as "having multiple consonants at the beginning" for which the expression "having one consonant at the beginning" would be stated for the purpose of exclusion. And this has already been stated; therefore, for this very reason...

Having kept all this in mind— that by the [previous] statement, the quality of "consisting of one consonant" is intended as being qualified [by the preceding vowel]— he says "one who is without a companion," etc., in order to demonstrate that very qualification:
"that which is a consonant (hal) not even accompanied by a vowel (ac) of a different class, and which is the first (ādi) [of such a group]."

Regarding the phrase "beginning with a single consonant" (*tadekahalādi*): if that which begins with a single consonant were to be understood as referring to something that is not separated by a member of the same class (*tulyajātīya*), even when such a member is present, then [the rule] would never apply;
for there would be no such subsequent member (*uttarapada*) signifying something to be supplied (*pūrayitavya*). Thus it is said.

And this [is the meaning]: therefore, by virtue of the authority of the statement, it is understood that what exists here without being separated from a homogeneous consonant (*hal*) that follows immediately—provided such a one does not exist—is intended by the word *eka* (‘single’), which denotes ‘without assistance. Such a thing...

That which has *hal* (a consonant) as its initial [element] is called *ekahalādi*. Since the word *sthāna* does not have a consonant as its initial in this manner, the word *sthāna* is excluded by the mention of *ekahalādi*.
[The term] "denoting that which is to be filled" (*pūrayitavyavācin*) means that which is to be internally pervaded by a substance such as water.
It would be said that "it is to be filled"; the suffix *ṇini* is used here in the sense of habit (*tācchīlika*), meaning "one whose nature is to speak thus."
60. And [the word *mantha* is compounded] with *odana*, *saktu*, *bindu*, *jara*, *bhāra*, *hāra*, *vīvadha*, and *gādha*.

(Pāṇini 2.1.34) Barley meal mixed with a liquid substance is called *mantha*. In that case, if this word *mantha* is an unanalyzed nominal stem (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*), then the rule "with the third case" (2.1.30) applies, as in *udakena manthaḥ* ("barley meal with water").
Thus, by means of the division of rules (*yogavibhāga*), the compound is formed. Now it is etymologically derived: *mantha* [is so called] because it is "churned in the middle" (*madhyataḥ*);
in that case, the compound is formed by Pāṇini 2.1.32, *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*.
[In the case of] *sakatvodanābhyām*, the compound is formed by Pāṇini 2.1.34, *annena vyañjanam*.
By means of the endless examples cited by Bhārahāra, such as *binduvajravīvadhaiḥ* under Pāṇini 2.2.8 (*ṣaṣṭhī*),
and *upapadamatiṅ* under Pāṇini 2.2.19.

61. *iko hrasvo’ṅgyo gālavasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.61). [The example is] *grāmaṇiputraḥ*. [The word] *grāmaṇi* is derived from the root *nī* (to lead) with the suffix *kvip* according to the rule *satsūdviṣa-* (3.2.61), and the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by the Vārttika *agragrāmābhyāñca nayateḥ* (Kātyāyana Vārttika 5064). Thus, one who leads the village (*grāma*) is a *grāmaṇī*. The son of a *grāmaṇī* is *grāmaṇiputraḥ*. According to this rule, the long vowel *ī* of *grāmaṇī* is optionally shortened to the short vowel *i* before the suffix *aṇ*, as per the opinion of Gālava. Hence, the form *grāmaṇiputraḥ* is established.

Regarding the form "gārgīputraḥ": from the word *gārgya*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *hyañaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.16); then, by the rule *yasyeti ca* (6.4.148), the vowel *a* is elided, and by the rule *halastaddhitasya* (6.4.150), the *y* is also elided.

Now, why is the mention of Gālava not for the sake of the alternative option regarding the direction [of the accent]? To this he says: "anyatarasyām," and so forth. Regarding the example "kārīṣagandhīputraḥ":
this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the son of Karīṣagandhyā," [formed] by the rule "ṣyaṅḥ samprasāraṇam" (Pāṇini 6.1.13).

By [the rule] beginning with (6.1.13), there is *samprasāraṇa*; by (6.1.108), *samprasāraṇācca*, there is the substitution of the preceding vowel; and by (6.4.2), *halaḥ*, there is the lengthening of the *samprasāraṇa*. Regarding the phrase "of those that are to undergo *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*," etc.: those for which *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are to occur [are meant].

Thus they are stated: "śrīkulam" is an example of that which undergoes the *iyaṅ* substitution; "bhrūkulam" is an example of that which undergoes the *uvaṅ* substitution. [Examples] of those that undergo elision (*ap-*) are "kāṇḍībhūtam" and "vṛṣalībhūtam," according to [Pāṇini 5.4.50] "abhūtatadbhāve" following the words *kāṇḍa* and *vṛṣala*.

By [the rule] beginning with "ityādinā," the suffix *cvi* is applied, and by "ṭhasya cvau" (Pāṇini 7.4.32), the vowel *i* is substituted for the *ṭha*. Regarding "bhrūkuṃsaḥ": this is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) meaning "one who is both a brow (*bhrū*) and a kuṃsa. The same applies to "bhrukuṭiḥ. Regarding "vaktavyam": the meaning is that it must be explained. In that regard, this...
The explanation is as follows: by virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group, the letter *a* will occur in words such as *bhrukuṃsa*.

62. *eka* [is substituted] for that [ending] when a *taddhita* suffix follows. (6.3.62) Regarding *ekarūpyam*: the suffix *rūpya* is applied by the rule *hetumanuṣyebhyo 'nyatarasyāṃ rūpyaḥ* (4.3.81). Regarding *ekamayam*: the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied by the rule *mayaṭ ca* (4.3.82). [The word *ekatvam* means] "oneness."

Regarding the form *ekatā*: the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are applied by the rule *tasya bhāvas tvatalau* (Pāṇini 5.1.119). This example applies when the word *eka* refers to a number (*saṃkhyā*). When it refers to the thing numbered (*saṃkhyeya*), the desired form is already established simply through the masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) according to the Vārttika *tvalorguṇavacanasya* (Vārttika 730).

But surely, that which expresses a quality is "guṇavacana" (quality-expressive); and that which, having denoted a mere quality, expresses a substance qualified by it, is a "guṇavacana. For example: "the black cloth," "the white cloth. This word "one" (*eka*), however, does not [denote] anything at all distinct from the substance.
He states the quality [of the word *guṇa*], namely that it always resides in a substance (*dravya*) that is numerable (*saṃkhyeya*).
Given this, how can there be for it the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*)? This which is being asserted is incorrect;
for it is well known that, by relying on conventional usage, words such as "one" (*eka*) and so forth are said to denote the numerable, but not these [words like *guṇa*].
The function [of the word] is not accepted as residing in enumeration (*saṃkhyāna*).

For instance, in the rule "dvyekayordvivacanaikavacane" (Pāṇini 1.4.22), the word *eka* is employed in the sense of number itself, and not in the sense of a single substance (*dravya*) that is to be numbered.

Regarding the phrase "of that which is qualified by gender" (*ṭhliṅgaviśiṣṭasya*), and so forth: the masculine form of the word *eka* is inherently short-voweled (*hrasvānta*) by its very nature; therefore, its mention does not serve as a purpose [for the rule], but rather it is precisely that [word] qualified by the feminine gender [to which the rule applies]. For it is only for that [feminine form] that the prescription of shortness is meaningful. Now, one might object:

Even for this word *eka*, the prescription of shortness for its vowel *e* would not be meaningful; why then is it said that the inclusion of the word *eka* qualified by gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭa*) is necessitated? To this he says: "by [the rule] *acā*..."
Regarding the phrase "being grasped" (*gṛhyamāṇa*) and so forth: there is freedom of choice (*kāmacāra*) with respect to the relationship between qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualified (*viśeṣya*).

For it has been stated: "Because the relationship of qualifier and qualified is according to one's wish. In that regard, if the vowel (*ac*) is qualified by the word "one" (*eka*) which is being grasped—meaning "the *ac* which belongs to the word 'one'"—then [the rule applies].

In that case, the prescription of shortness for the single vowel *e*—which is one member of a correlative pair—becomes meaningful. Furthermore, this necessitates the inclusion of the masculine form of the word *eka*. Nor is it qualified here by the vowel (*ac*) being grasped [in the rule], because shortness of the vowel *e* is not desired; for a rule does not have an unintended purpose.

The formulation in the treatise is logical; therefore, when the vowel (*āc*) is being grasped, it is qualified here by the word "single" (*eka*). By that, there is the inclusion of [the vowel] as qualified by gender. The short vowel occurs for the word "single"; what is the vowel so qualified? It means "ending in a vowel. In that case, [the substitution applies] only to the final phoneme (*alo'ntyasya*).

It must be short; and that [shortening] is meaningful only for a feminine form ending in *ṭāp*, not for a masculine form—for indeed, when shortening is prescribed for what is already short, no purpose whatsoever is achieved. The particle *iti* indicates a reason (*hetu*). Precisely because the word *eka* is understood here as being [feminine] by virtue of the vowel *ā*.
It is distinguished; therefore, the inclusion of that which is qualified by gender necessitates the use of the single word.
63. *ṅyāpoḥ saṃjñācchandasorbahulam* (Pāṇini 6.3.63).
In the case of *ṛevatiputraḥ*, this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). The same applies to examples such as *rohiṇiputraḥ*.
[In the Vedic language,] from *kumārīm dadāti* comes *kumāridā*; from *urvīm dadāti* comes *urvidā*.

[The suffix] *ka* [is applied] after [the word] *sthā* when no prefix (*anupasarga*) precedes it (Pāṇini 3.2.3). Regarding "Phālgunī" and so forth: since it is both *phālgunī* and a full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), it is called *phālgunī-paurṇamāsī*; this is a compound according to the rule "viśeṣaṇam" (Pāṇini 2.1.57), etc. The same applies to the expression "jagatī-chandas."

In *śilāvahaḥ* and *śilāprasthaḥ*, there is a compound of the word *śilā* with the words *vaha* and *prastha* according to [Pāṇini 2.2.8], which prescribes the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). In *lomakāgṛham* and *lomakāṣaṇḍam*, here too, there is a compound of the word *lomakā* with the words *gṛha* and *ṣaṇḍa*. [The example] *ajakṣīreṇa* [is also explained in the same way].

Here too, the word *ajā* is [compounded] with the word *kṣīra*. Regarding the form *ūrṇamṛt* (or *ūrṇamṛdā* according to the Kāśikā; *ūrṇamravā* according to the Padamañjarī): it means "earth together with wool" (*ūrṇāsahitā mṛd*). It is a compound in which the final member of the first term is elided, belonging to the class beginning with *śākapārthiva*.
64. *tve ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.64). Regarding this, it is said:

"Because [the formation] is impossible as a technical name (*saṃjñā*), the examples occur only in the Veda (*chandas*). By the word *eva* ("only"), the exclusion of the case where it is a technical name is effected; for when the suffix *tvap* is applied and the shortening of the feminine suffixes *ṅī* and *āp* has been performed...
A name is understood for something;
therefore, because it is impossible [to apply] to a name, the examples occur only in the Vedic language (chandas).

65. *iṣṭakeṣīkāmalānāṃ citatūlabhāriṣu* (Pāṇini 6.3.65). [The examples are: *iṣṭakacitam*, *iṣīkatūlam*, and *mālabhāriṇī*. In *iṣṭakacitam*, the compound is formed by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32). In *iṣīkatūlam*, it is a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound. In *mālabhāriṇī*, [it is derived from] *mālām*...
The suffix *ṇini* is applied in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*) according to Pāṇini 3.2.78 (*bhartuṃ śīlamasyā iti*), and the compound is formed by Pāṇini 2.2.19 (*upapadamatiṅ*).
Regarding this, it is said: "By the rule concerning *iṣṭakā* and others, there is the inclusion of that which ends in those [words] as well."
The intention is that this is because the term "frequently" (bahula) continues to apply.

66. *khityanavyayasya* (6.3.66). [Examples: *kālimmanyā*, *hariṇimmanyā*. In the sense of "regarding oneself as" (*ātmamāne*), the suffix *khaś* is applied by the rule *ātmamāne khaśca* (3.2.83), as in: "she regards herself as dark" (*kālīm ātmānaṃ manyate*) and "she regards herself as a deer" (*hariṇīm ātmānaṃ manyate*). Thus, *khaś* is applied.
Because [the root] belongs to the *divādi* class, the suffix *śyan* is applied; by this rule, shortening (*hrasvatva*) occurs, and by the subsequent sūtra, the augment *mum* is added.
Here, shortening must be admitted for that which ends in a vowel (*ajanta*); otherwise, it would also apply in the case of *vāṅmanya*.
When the rule for shortening vowels ending in *ac* is established, since the augment *mum* is applied later, the word no longer ends in *ac*, and therefore the shortening does not take place.
To one who might think that [the rule] is superseded, he says: "The short vowel is not set aside by *mum*.

He states the reason for this very point with the words "for otherwise," and so forth. That by which the short vowel is taught—that is, prescribed—is the "short-vowel-instruction," namely the rule "khityanavyayasya" (Pāṇini 6.3.66). For if, by *mum*...

The short vowel would be sublated; consequently, this teaching regarding the short vowel would become devoid of scope, and thus it would indeed be rendered purposeless. Therefore, so that this fault does not occur, the short vowel is not sublated by the *mum* augment. Thus, because there is no contradiction, both occur: the short vowel and the *mum* augment.

And: how, moreover, is the sublation (*bādhā*) of *mum* by the short vowel (*hrasva*) suspected? Or how is the short-vowel rule (*hrasva-śāsana*) considered to have no scope (*anavakāśatva*), given that *mum* is prescribed without distinction for a word ending in *khit* that ends in a vowel (*ajanta*), while the suspicion of sublation concerns the short vowel? Or how [is this so]?

The short-vowel rule would have no scope, since *mum* applies without distinction to any stem ending in a vowel before a *khit* suffix. But how can it be suspected that the short-vowel rule is superseded by *mum*, or how can the short-vowel rule be said to lack scope, given that *mum* applies without distinction to any stem ending in a vowel before a *khit* suffix?

It is prescribed; however, by implication, it applies to the long vowel, for the prescription of shortness for that which is already short would be purposeless. And in this way, since its purpose is fulfilled in cases such as *stanandhaya*, would not the *mum* itself be sublated by the exception of shortness in cases such as *kālimmanyā*? Thus...

He considers: even in the domain of an exception (*apavāda*), the rule for *mum* must necessarily be applied for the purpose of prescribing *mum*; otherwise, in the case of *kālimmanyā*, the *mum* would not occur. Consequently, by the application of *mum* even in the domain of an exception, there would be a sublation of the short vowel (*hrasva*).
It might be so suspected; and for this very reason, the suffix *mum* would apply even in the domain of an exception (*apavāda*), because there is no scope [for it otherwise].

Now, how can there be the mention of a word ending in *khid* here, given that it has been made known that in the governing rule concerning the subsequent member (*uttarapada-adhikāra*), when a suffix is mentioned, the inclusion of what ends with that suffix (*tadantavidhi*) does not occur?

Therefore, he says: "Of that which is not an indeclinable," and so forth. If only the suffix *khi* were taken here and not that which ends in it, then the prohibition "of that which is not an indeclinable" would be meaningless; for there is no suffix *khi* following an indeclinable.
It is possible [that the suffix *khi* is included]; for that very root is prescribed [by the rule].
Consequently, because it would lack meaning, the phrase "not being an indeclinable" (*anavyayasya*) would not have been stated [in the rule].
And it has been said: "Therefore, this very [fact] indicates that here there is the inclusion of that which ends in *khi*."

67. *arurdviṣadajantasya mum* (Pāṇini 6.3.67). Regarding the example *aruntudaḥ*: [the derivation is as follows: from the sense "one who pierces the vital parts" (*aruṃ tudati*), the suffix *khaś* is applied by the rule *viṣvaruṣostudaḥ* (3.2.35). There is elision of the final consonant due to the rule on the elision of a *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster). Then, because it belongs to the *tudādi* class, the suffix *śa* is applied. By the rule *ato guṇe* (6.1.97), the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is substituted [resulting in *arutuda*]. Finally, the augment *mum* is added by this sūtra.

Regarding "dviṣantapaḥ": it means "one who torments the enemy. The suffix *khac* is applied by the rule "dviṣatparayostāpeḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.39), and the shortening of the vowel occurs by the rule "khaci hrasvaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.94).
Regarding "vidvanmanyaḥ": it means "one who considers himself learned"; the suffix *khaś* is applied by the rule "ātmamāne khaśca" (Pāṇini 3.2.83).

By the rule (3.2.83), the suffix *khaś* is applied; by the rule "vasusraṃsudhvaṃsvanaḍuhāṃ daḥ" (8.2.72), the *s* is replaced by *d*; and by the rule "yaro 'nunāsike 'nunāsiko vā" (8.4.45), that *d* is optionally replaced by *n*. Now, what is the purpose of including the term "end" (*anta*) [in the sūtra], given that the principle "that by which a rule is prescribed applies to that which ends with it" (*yena vidhis tadantasya*) already holds?

One might ask: "By this [rule], will the operation apply only to that which ends in such [an element]? To this he says: "The mention of 'end' (*antagrahaṇam*)," and so forth. The purpose of mentioning the "end" is so that there may be the understanding—that is, the cognition—of that very thing which has had the operations pertaining to bases ending in vowels (*ajanta*) performed upon it; such is the "incoming element" (*āgamī*). It is for this reason that the word "end" is mentioned.

For by the inclusion of the term *anta* (end), this meaning is indicated: that the *mum* suffix must be applied at the end, i.e., at the conclusion of another grammatical operation. Therefore, once the shortening—which is an operation pertaining to what ends in a vowel (*ajanta*)—has been performed, the *mum* subsequently occurs.
Now, one might object: "But surely this will be accomplished simply by the rule stating that the short vowel is not superseded by the *mum*."

This matter has been established with supporting arguments; so, for what purpose is this mention of the "end" (anta) made? This is not so; for by that [mention], it is merely demonstrated that the short vowel (*hrasva*) taught [by Pāṇini 6.4.129] is not superseded by the *mum* augment because the latter finds no scope [elsewhere], but it is not demonstrated that [the shortening applies] after an operation concerning a stem ending in a *kṛt* suffix.

The meaning is that *mum* occurs; consequently, because it follows [the word], once *mum* has been applied, the shortening of a vowel would undesirably apply even to that which does not end in *an*. What is the fault here? It is that there would be no occurrence of the shortening of a vowel before a *khit* suffix.
For example, in the case of *kālimmanya*, once *mum* has been applied, the shortening of a vowel would occur even though the stem does not end in *an*.
Likewise, in the case of *vāṅmanya*, [the form] would be *syāt*; therefore, the mention of "end" (*anta*) must be made.
68. *ica ekāco'mpratyayavacca* (Pāṇini 6.3.68).
If in this rule only *ṭhpratyayavacca* were stated, then in the case of *gāmmanyaḥ*, the substitution of *ā* [for *i*] by *āṬto'mśasoḥ* (6.1.93) would not occur; and likewise here in *strīmmanya*.

Thus—here too, by the rule *ṭhami pūrvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.107), there is the substitution of the preceding homogeneous vowel; and here in the case of *narammanya*, by the rule *ṛto ṅsirvanāmasthānayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.110), there is the *guṇa* substitution for the vowel of the word *nṛ*.
Since a specific [operation] is not extended when there is an extension of a general [rule], this statement is indeed for the sake of the vowels *ṛ* and *uṅ*.

It would be *kevalam* (the bare stem) alone; for, since the two [substitutions] *iy* and *uvaṅ* are prescribed by virtue of the general category of "affix" (*pratyayamātra*) when they follow an *ajādi* (vowel-initial) affix, they occur even under a general extension (*sāmānyātideśa*). When it is stated, "And like the *am*-affix," the substitutions such as *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) take place, because those [substitutions] also [apply] to the *am*-affix.
Because it is desired. Having taken all of this into account in his mind, he says: "and like the suffix *ḍham*.

He explains this very point by saying: "and like the singular of the second case. But how is this meaning obtained, given that there is only the mention of one [suffix], and by that the augment *ām* is indicated?

Otherwise, it would result in this undesirable consequence [that the suffix itself would be modified]. Alternatively, if the suffix were qualified by that [augment], the augment would not be explicitly indicated;
therefore, he says "for [the word] 'tham'" and so forth. Since the single mention of the term *apṛkta* (uncombined), when employed, accomplishes both of these purposes.

The intention is that this meaning is thus obtained: "śriyammanyaḥ" and "bhrūvammanyaḥ. [The suffixes] yaṅ and vaṅ are applied by the rule "aci śnudhātu... (Pāṇini 6.4.77), etc. In "lekhābhrummanyaḥ," the augment *mum* is added by the preceding rule.

Regarding the passage beginning with "ṭhatheha," etc.: having commenced by stating that one considers oneself to be prosperity (*śrī*) or a Brāhmaṇa family, and having introduced the topic, when the suffix *khaś* is applied, how should it be? Should it be *śriyammanyamati*, or rather *śrimanyam*? But how is it possible for these two alternatives to be conceived?
Why does he ask this? Because it is observed that words function in two ways.

For instance, some words are seen to apply to another meaning without abandoning their own gender, as in the case of the word *bhūta*—as in "this Brāhmaṇī woman is a *bhūta*" (*bhūtam iyaṃ brāhmaṇī*). [And] some...

She is also seen through a sacrifice performed with her own gender, as in the case of the word *praṣṭha*—namely, *praṣṭhī*. In that regard, when the word *śrī*, while denoting a member of the Brāhmaṇa caste, does not abandon its own gender, it must then be *śriyammanya*; however, if it were to abandon its own gender...

If one adopts the neuter gender, then after the elision of *am* by the rule "ṭhsvamornapuṃsakāt" (Pāṇini 7.1.23) and the shortening of the stem by the rule "hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya" (Pāṇini 1.2.47), the form should be *śrimanyam*; thus, these are the two possible views.
Both forms are possible; therefore, since both alternatives exist, it is not known how it ought to be.

Thus, for the sake of determining that, the question is asked. It has been established in the Bhāṣya that "it should be *śrīmanyam*," while the Kāśikā states that "it is settled" (*sthitam*). Now, as for this word *śrī*:

Even when a word of the feminine gender occurs in a different sense, it continues to exist without abandoning its own gender; and indeed, such usage is observed—for example, "śrīḥ me śiraḥ" (Prosperity is my head) and "yaśaḥ me śrīḥ" (Fame is my prosperity).
How then is it established in the Bhāṣya that [the word *śrī*] is *śrimat*? To this he says: "In that case..."

And so forth. Just as words such as *praṣṭhī*, *pravarī*, and *gaṇakī*—which denote women through their connection with a male (*puṃyoga*)—function while retaining their own original gender (*svaliṅga*), namely masculine; likewise, the word *śrī* also functions here in the sense of a family (*kula*), according to the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya.

According to the opinion of Atreya, when the *ām* suffix is elided by *ṭhsvamornapuṃsakāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.23), the form is *śrīmanyam*. Now, one might object: since this rule is commenced even though the elision (*luk*) would otherwise have already applied—just as it supersedes the elision prescribed by *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.71)—it should likewise [supersede other rules].

Would this [rule] also subvert the elision (*luk*) prescribed by *ṭhsvamornapuṃsakāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.23)? Furthermore, since the elision (*luk*) depends on a single word, it is *antaranga*, whereas the augment *ām* is *bahiranga* because it is the opposite; therefore, by the principle *asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam antaraṅge* (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 42), when the *antaranga* elision has occurred—

When [the suffix] is to be applied, the augment *am* is indeed external; therefore, how could there be elision (*luk*) here? This is not a fault, because of the rule: "Exceptions in the middle sublate preceding rules, not subsequent ones" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 10). Thus, this augment *am* [is inserted before the application of] *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*...

This will subvert this *luk* elision, but not the one prescribed by "ṭhkhamornapuṃsakāt" (Pāṇini 7.1.23). Furthermore, the *paribhāṣā* regarding external elements (*bahiraṅga*) cannot be invoked here, for in that case there would be a fault in the word *aruntuda*. If that *paribhāṣā* were invoked, however, the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) would not occur.

Since the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) must be treated as internal (*antaraṅga*), the external (*bahiraṅga*) augment *mum* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) for that purpose; consequently, the status of being a "final conjunct" cannot be established. Therefore, this [condition of being a final conjunct], although its cause has been met, is not relied upon here, for such things are indeed its very defects.

69. *vācaṃyama-purandarau ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.69). Regarding *vācaṃyamaḥ*: [the derivation is] "he restrains his speech" (*vācaṃ yacchati*). By the rule *vaci-yamo vrate* (3.2.40), the suffix *khac* is applied. In that case, the form of the word *vāk* ending in the accusative case is irregularly prescribed (*nipātyate*). Regarding *purandaraḥ*: [the derivation is] "he shatters the cities. By the rule *pū-daro dṛ-kṣaye* (3.2.41), the suffix *khac* is applied. In that case, the form of the word *pura* ending in the accusative case is irregularly prescribed. Thus, by this rule, the elision of the final vowel of the first member (*pūrva-pada*) is established. Therefore, the forms *vācaṃyamaḥ* and *purandaraḥ* are obtained. By the rule *pūḥ-sara-vayor dāri-sahoḥ* (3.2.41), the suffix *khac* is applied; by *khaci hrasvaḥ* (6.4.94), shortening occurs. Here too, the fact that the word *pūḥ* ends in *am* is treated as a *nipātana* (irregularity). The vowel *ā* [in *pūmān*] is for the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. By means of that, [the suffix *khac* is also applied] in the case of *astu-satya-āgada-asaya-kāre* (Vārttika 744).
Thus, it follows that everything would be inexpressible.

70. *kāre* [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] after *satya* and *agada*. (Pāṇini 6.3.70) By the expression "he makes true" (*satyaṃ karoti*), [the rule] indicates the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of the object; by the expression "the maker of truth" (*satyasya kāraḥ*), it likewise indicates the suffix *ghañ*. In the same way, in the case of "one who makes medicine" (*agadaṅkāraḥ*), both *aṇ* and *ghañ* apply.
These two should be understood [as follows]:

"The word *astuṅkāra*. The suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). The word *astu* is an indeclinable particle (*nipāta*) that resembles a case-ending and is used in the sense of acceptance (*abhyupagame*). *Astuṅkāra* is the act of making an acceptance, expressed as "let it be so" (*astu*).

Regarding "bhakṣaṅkāraḥ": [the suffix] *ghañ* is used in the sense of the action (*bhāve*). Regarding "dhenumbhavyā": by the rule "bhavyageya... (Pāṇini 3.4.68), a *kṛtya* suffix is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
Thus, "dhenumbhavyā" means that which is both a cow (*dhenu*) and fit to be born (*bhavyā*).

Regarding "lokampṛṇaḥ": from the root *pṛṇ* (DhP 1329), meaning "to please" or "to satisfy," the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *mūlavibhuja* (Pāṇini 3.2.5), as in the sense "one who fills the world.
Regarding "anabhyāśam ityaḥ": [the printed reading is "anabhyāśam ityam"]; [it means] "not near."

*Dūram* means "far"; *gantavyam asya* means "that which is to be gone by him," hence it is called *dūram-itaḥ*. *Indhana* means "fuel"; the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the action (*bhāve*). Thus, one who kindles the fuel of a frying pan is called *bhrāṣṭram-indhaḥ*; one who kindles fire is *agnim-indhaḥ*. Regarding the word *timiṅgila*: the root *gṛ* (DhP 1410) means "to swallow. One who swallows a *timi* (whale) is called *timiṅgilaḥ*, formed with the suffix *ka* according to the rule for words ending in *parvan*.
The substitution of *i* occurs by Pāṇini 7.1.100 (*ṛta iddhātoḥ*), followed by the substitution of *r* for *ṛ* (raparatva), and the substitution of *l* by 8.2.21 (*aci vibhāṣā*).
Thus we have *giligilaḥ*. In this case, the suffix *ka* is added as before to the root *gila-* in the sense of "one who swallows what is swallowed," and the same substitutions of *i*, etc., apply.

Regarding the term *ṭhgilagile ca*: that which swallows a swallow (*gila*) is a *gilagila*. In the rule *ātaścopasarge* (Pāṇini 3.1.136), because the particle *ca* has the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned, the suffix *ka* is applied. There is no fault in applying *ka* in this way even in the preceding case. This [term] is intended to express the meaning "the devourer of whales" (*timi*).

It must be said: if the meaning intended is "one who swallows a *timi* is a *timiṅgila*, and one who swallows a *timiṅgila* [is a *timiṅgilagila*]," then this is already established by the preceding rule; therefore, this [present rule] is unnecessary.

Regarding the forms *duṣṭraṅkaraṇam* and *bhadraṅkaraṇam*, these are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Regarding the form *putraṭ*, the letter *ṭ* is for the purpose of [triggering] the suffix *ṅīp*.
Some, however, recite the word *putra* in the list beginning with *śārṅgarava*; [the following is] in response to them.
This supplementary rule need not be formulated;
for it is said, "It is seen elsewhere as well. By this, he confirms the inclusion of the word *putra* among the *śārṅgarava*-type words.

71. *śyenatilasya pāte ñe* (Pāṇini 6.3.71). This means "when the suffix *ñ* follows. That word after which the suffix *ñ* occurs is described in that way [by the compound]. [The example is] *śyainampātaḥ*. *Pātaḥ* is "falling," derived from the root with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*); [the compound is] *śyenasya pātaḥ*.

"Śyenapātaḥ" means "the swoop of a hawk. It is a compound formed by the rule "The genitive case [ending] after a word connected with a *kṛt* suffix is compounded" (Vārttika 86), and the suffix *ñ* is applied according to the rule "The suffix *ñ* is used when the sense is 'this is its action' (*sāsyāṃ kriyā*) following a word ending in *ghañ*" (Pāṇini 4.2.58).
72. *rātreḥ kṛti vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 6.3.72). [The rule states:

"When a *kṛt*-derived suffix follows. But how can the inclusion of that which ends in such a suffix (*tadantavidhi*) be obtained, given that it has been established: "In the governing context of a subsequent member (*uttarapada-adhikāra*), when a suffix is mentioned, there is no inclusion of that which ends in it"?

(Pu.pa.pā. 26) Thus it is said. If it is argued that because a *kṛt* suffix cannot immediately follow the word *rātri*, the rule of "specification by the final element" (*tadantavidhi*) is not understood here, this is incorrect; for a *kṛt* suffix can indeed follow immediately after *rātri*. [In the case of] *rātrir ivācarati* ("he acts like night"), [the suffix] *ṭhak* [is applied].

By the rule *sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ kviv vā* (Vārttika 187), the suffix *kvip* is applied; by *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.32), it receives the designation "root"; then the suffix *tṛc*, the augment *iṭ*, and the substitution of *guṇa* and *āy* [for *i*] result in *rātrayitṛ*. Thus, when the subsequent *kṛt* suffix is possible, [the formation proceeds].

Would that [suffix] apply only there and not at its end? This is not a fault; for the term *anta* ("end") is understood to carry over from the rule *arurdviṣadajantasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.67), and by that, it is understood that the grammatical operation applies only when that [element] is at the end. If this is so, then even for the word *rātri* ending in the *kvip* suffix, the [rule] would apply when followed by a *kṛt*-derived word as a second member. Let it be so.
But if this is not accepted, then a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) must be admitted. Or rather, it will not apply because the word *rātri* (night) is used in a figurative sense (*gauṇatva*).
Its figurative nature, moreover, arises from its deviation from the primary meaning, as in the case of "the Vāhīka is an ox" (*vāhīko gaur*).

[This refers to] the word *gośabda*. [The example is] "rātriñcaraḥ" (night-walker). Because it means "one who moves at night," the suffix *ṭa* is applied by the rule *careṣṭaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.16), resulting in a compound with an upapada. [The example is] "rātrimaṭaḥ. Because it means "one who wanders," the suffix *ac* is applied after the root *aṭ* by the rule *pacādyac*, resulting in "rātryaṭaḥ" (or as printed in some editions, "rātrāvaṭaḥ"). [This is governed by] the rule *saptamī* (Pāṇini 2.1.40).

The compound is formed through a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule), as in the statement: "This is an exception to what has not been reached. But surely *khid* is also a *kṛt* suffix—as in *rātrimmanyam*, where by the rule *arurdviṣadajantasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.76), the substitution [of *ṅmuṇ*] would necessarily apply; yet in cases such as *rātriñcaraḥ*, it does not apply by any rule.

And since this has been established both for that which is already obtained and for that which is not yet obtained, this *vibhāṣā* (optionality) is appropriate; therefore, he says: "For when a *khit* suffix follows, *mum* necessarily occurs. The intention is that this is by way of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).
For here a prior counter-exception is resorted to: when a *khit* suffix follows, *mum* necessarily occurs by the preceding rule. And thus...

The scope for this statement is indeed different; it is not correct to say that [the rule] applies there because it is not obtained by anyone else, for which reason its status as an optional rule regarding what is not otherwise obtained (*aprāpta-vibhāṣā*) is established.

73. *nalopo nañaḥ* | (6.3.73) The mention here of the form with its *anubandha* should not apply [to cases like] *pāmanaputraḥ*. [In this case,] the suffix *na* is applied by the rule *lomādipāmādi* (5.2.100) because he has *pāmāni* (scabies). [The elision applies] to that which ends in that [suffix].

The word *putra* forms a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Now, if the inclusion of the *anubandha* (indicatory letter) is being applied, why does [the suffix] not occur in the case of *straiṇārtha*, where one has *striyā ayam iti* ("this belongs to a woman") according to the rule *ṭhstripuṃsābhyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.87), resulting in *nañ-straiṇaḥ* ("belonging to women"), and then [the compound] *straiṇaścāsāvarthaśca* ("that which is both belonging to women and an object")?

Because of the inclusion of the negative particle *nañ* as a prior member (*pūrvapada*). Why is this so? Because the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is a relative term; for a subsequent member exists only in relation to a prior member.
Therefore, due to the governing rule concerning the subsequent member, the negative particle here is understood as being a prior member. Now...

Or rather—the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]; because it is understood as having a restricted optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), [the suffix] will not occur [in this case]. If that is so, then since it would not occur here either in the case of *pāmanaputra* for the very same reason, there would be no purpose in including the mention of the item with its *anubandha* (the marker *ṅ*)? In that case, it is for the sake of clarity.
The mention [of the word] is with its suffixal appendage (*sānubandhaka*). And when it is stated as "of *naḥ*," there is no distinction made on account of brevity. It is said:
"An addition must be made for the case of verbal endings (*tiṅ*) in the sense of contempt. Contempt means censure.

The elision of *na* being prescribed for a subsequent member does not apply when that member is a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*); therefore, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for that case. But surely the particle *na*, which expresses negation, exists—according to the statement, "The particles *mā*, *no*, and *na* are words expressing negation"—and thus its inclusion [in the rule] would be implied.

If the application of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is to occur, what is the purpose of this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*)? For then, in the case of *nañ* used in the sense of censure (*avakṣepa*), the application of the verbal suffix after it would also follow. Therefore, a supplementary rule must be formulated to prevent the usage of *nañ* with elided *na* (in the sense of censure) when followed by a verbal suffix. Regarding the word "supplementary rule" (*upasaṃkhyāna*):

The meaning is "establishment. In this regard, the establishment is as follows: from the rule *vācaṃyamapurandarau ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.69), the word *ca* ("and") is carried over; its purpose is to include what has not been explicitly mentioned. By means of that, even when a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) is present, the elision of the *n* of the negative particle *nañ* will occur when contempt is implied.

74. *tasmān nuḍ aci* (Pāṇini 6.3.74). [The objection: "The augment *nuṭ* would apply only after *nañ*, because of the locative indication *aci*; for it is stated that 'when something is indicated by the locative case, the operation applies to what precedes it' (Pāṇini 1.1.66). [Response: When the augment *nuṭ* is added to *nañ*...

An undesirable result would arise. Therefore, since the suffix *nuṭ* is applied [only] when there is an actual inclusion [of the negative particle], the rule "when both are indicated, the indication by the ablative case is stronger" (*ubhayanirdeśe pañcamīnirdeśo balīyān*, Śākapārthivādhikaraṇa 97) applies specifically to the final member of the compound;
thus, there is no occurrence of the undesirable consequence. Now, one might object: what if *nuṭ* were to apply to the negative particle (*nañ*) itself?

Would the statement regarding the elision of *na* (nalopa) be meaningless? It is not meaningless; for its purpose is so that the letter *n* may not be heard in forms such as *abrāhmaṇaḥ* and *avṛṣalaḥ* when [the suffix] begins with *a* or *ja*.
If it is said that "therefore" (*tasmāt*) is stated for the sake of ensuring that [elision] does not occur after *na*, then [the rule] would not apply to *na*.
It must be stated [as an objection]: "Why indeed will this *nuṭ* be applied at the beginning? To this he says: "For, at the beginning.

When the *nuṭ* is applied at the beginning, the *nuṭ* prescribed by the rule "ṅmo hrasvād aci ṅmuṇ nityam" (Pāṇini 8.3.32)—which prescribes *ṅmuṇ* for a word ending in *ṅm* before a vowel—would consequently apply; and therefore...

Thus, there would be the undesirable consequence [of the rule not applying]. Therefore, *nuṭ* alone must be applied. However, when this [augment] is applied, the mention of "from that" (*tasmāt*) is for the purpose of ensuring that it does not apply to the negative particle (*nañ*) itself.

75. *Nabhrāj-napāt-navedās-nāsatyā-namucī-nakula-nakha-puṃsaka-nakṣatra-nakra-nākeṣu prakṛtyā* (Pāṇini 6.3.75). Regarding *nabhrāj*: from the root *bhrājṛ* (to shine, Dhātupāṭha 181), [the suffix *kvip* is applied] by the rule *bhrājabhās...* [etc., Pāṇini 3.2.177].

By [the rule] *ityādinā* (3.2.177), the suffix *kvip* is applied; by *ṭhvraśca* (8.2.36) and so forth, the letter *j* becomes *ṣ*; its *jaś*-hood results in the letter *ḍ*; and its *car*-hood results in the letter *ṭ*. Thus, "napāt. Because of its neuter gender, in the absence of [masculine inflection],...

In the technical designation *sarvanāmasthāna*, the augment *num* characterized by having *u* as its initial letter does not occur [in the case of *veda*]. Thus, in "navedāḥ," there is lengthening according to Pāṇini 6.4.14: "atvasantasya cādhātoḥ. In the case of "satyāḥ" (meaning "those who are good in what is real"), the suffix *yat* belonging to the *gha* division is applied before the word *sat* by this rule: Pāṇini 4.4.98: "tatra sādhuḥ."

He demonstrates this: "The suffix *kvi* is added according to the *uṇādi* rules. The suffix *kvi* is applied by the rule "after a root with *i* as its penultimate letter, [the suffix] *kvi* is added" (*da.u.* 1.48). Regarding the form "from *kṣi*": there is the root *kṣiṣ* in the sense of "injuring" (*dhā.pā.* 1506) [or *kṣīṣ* according to the *Dhātupāṭha*; and the root *kṣi* in the senses of "dwelling" and "going" (*dhā.pā.* 1407)].

Thus: "Or from the root *kṣar*. [The root] *kṣara* is listed as "to move" (Dhātupāṭha 851). The word *nakṣatra* is thus derived as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). What is irregularly formed here? If it is derived from *kṣi*, then there is the suffix *tra* and the substitution of *ā* for the vowel *i*. If it is derived from *kṣar*, then likewise there is the suffix *tra* and the elision of the letter *r*.
"Because there is no suffering (*aka*) in this, it is called *nāka*. *Kam* is said to mean happiness;

*aka* means suffering. Because there is no suffering in this, it is *nāka*, namely heaven. For these are conventional words (*rūḍhi-śabda*), which are etymologically derived only as a matter of course.
76. *ekādiścaikasya cāduK* (Pāṇini 6.3.76).

The term *ekādiḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. For example, in the case of "one less than twenty" (*ekānnaviṃśatiḥ*), one must first form a compound of the negative particle *nañ* with the word *viṃśati*, and then form a third [level] compound.

But for what purpose is this augment *āṭ* applied at the beginning (*pūrvānta*) [of the root], rather than being applied at the end (*parādi*)? In that regard, there is this further purpose: the mention of the augment as "one" (*ekasya ca*) need not be made. For if it were applied at the end, it would simply be an augment (*āgama*), and that—

It is understood precisely because it is the subject under discussion. In that regard, does this sentence-meaning hold—"the *nañ* [negative particle] becomes its own base when preceded by *eka* and so forth, and *āḍ* is its augment"—thereby establishing what is desired?

To this he says: "This is a prior-final element (*pūrvānta*)," and so on. [And as for the rule: "In place of a semivowel (*yar*), a nasal may optionally occur before a nasal. *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with the citation of Pāṇini 8.4.45.*

For in the rule *vā* (8.4.45), the term *padāntāt* is understood from the preceding rule *na padāntāṭṭoranām* (8.4.42). In that context, if [the substitution] were applied as a subsequent element (*paradi*), this [anusvāra] would not possess the status of being a word-final (*padānta*); consequently, the optional substitution of the nasal [anusvāra] characterized by its being word-final would not occur, yet this is desired.
And therefore, for the sake of ensuring that it may occur by way of option (*vikalpa*), the augment *āduk* is applied to the preceding final vowel.
