Now, for what purpose is *āduk* applied? Why not simply say *ādu*? Even if *aduk* were applied, would it not be established by the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (P. 6.1.101)? It is not so established; because of [the rule] *ato...* [the following applies].

[The rule] *guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97) would result in the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), but that will not occur due to the force of the explicit utterance of the vowel *a*. For if the substitution of the subsequent form were to apply here, he would have simply prescribed [the single substitute] *du*.

[Objection: In that case, would not the long vowel by homogeneous extension (*savarṇadīrgha*) also fail to occur due to the force of the explicit utterance of the vowel *a*? [Response: This is not so; for likewise...

For—according to the principle that "that rule for which an instruction would otherwise be purposeless is set aside" (Vyāḍipañjikā 56)—a rule is superseded only if its very occasion is rendered futile by another; however, a rule whose occasion remains intact is not superseded.

Now, with respect to the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*), the pronunciation of the vowel *a* would be purposeless; but with respect to the formation of a long vowel through the combination of similar sounds (*savarṇadīrghatva*), it is not so.
It is merely an indicative mark (*nimita*). If that is so, then this [sandhi] occurs only in the dual; for the *saṃhitā* is indeed the same in both cases.

77. *nagaḥ* optionally [becomes *nāgaḥ*]. [This is derived] from the rule "the suffix *ḍa* is added after the root *gam*. This is because of the statement: "In the section on *ḍa*, it is seen elsewhere as well" (Vārttika 256).
78. *sahasya saḥ saṃjñāyām* (6.3.78).

[The example] "sāśvattham" is formed as follows: "with the *aśvattha*" (*saha-aśvatthena*), which is a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to *tena saheti tulyayoge* (2.2.28). [The examples] "sahayudhvā" and "sahakṛtvā" are formed by the suffix *kvanip* after the root *dṛś*.

While that [rule 3.2.94] continues to apply, the suffix *kvanip* is added by the rules "after the root *kṛ*, when *yudh* or *rājan* follows" (3.2.95) and "also when *saha* follows" (3.2.96). This forms an *upapada* compound, and the vowel is lengthened by the rule "before a *sarvanāmasthāna* [case ending]" (6.4.8).

But what is the reason that the *udātta* accent is prescribed for the word *sādeśa*? To this he says: "For [the word] possesses both *udātta* and *anudātta*" (*udātānudātavato hi*), and so forth. According to the rule "Particles (*nipātāḥ*) have their initial syllable accented acute" (*phiṭ-sūtra* 4.80), the word *saha* has its initial syllable as *udātta* alone, while the remainder is *anudātta*.

Therefore, that [substitute] possesses both udātta and anudātta accents; consequently, by virtue of its proximity, a circumflex (svarita) accent occurs in its place along with the sound. To prevent this fault, the udātta is prescribed as a nipātana (irregularity). If this is so, would not the udātta accent alone result even in the case of an avyayībhāva compound? To this he says: "And that..."

"nipātasvaraḥ" and so forth; "yatra" and so forth. In a *bahuvrīhi* or a *tatpuruṣa* compound, by the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, the first member retains its original accent" (*6.2.1*), the state of retaining the original accent (*prakṛtisvaratva*) occurs as an exception to the rule that the final syllable of the compound is acute (*samāsāntodātatva*) for the word *saha*. This applies also in the case of a *tatpuruṣa*.

By the rule "In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, [the first member retains its accent] when meaning 'equal to' (*tulyārtha*)" (Pāṇini 6.2.2) and so forth, that very accent of the particle (*nipāta-svara*) would consequently apply there. However, in the case of an *avyayībhāva*, since no exception to the final-acute (*anta-udātta*) nature of the compound has been prescribed by anything other than the original accent (*prakṛti-svara*), it follows that the compound is indeed acutely accented on the final syllable by virtue of being an *avyayībhāva*.

It must be so; therefore, it is indeed sublated by that [rule]. [The example] "iṣṭi-sapaśubandham" means "that which has an iṣṭi as its end and a paśubandha as its end. The compound is formed by the rule "avyayaṃ vibhakti... (Pāṇini 2.1.6), etc., in the sense of "ending with. Here, because it is subsequent, the *prathama-satva-udātta* accent applies.

Consequently, there is the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound (samāsāntodātatva). Since that [accent] remains when the accent of the particle (nipātasvara) is present, it is "remaining" (satiśiṣṭa); therefore, the accent of the particle is superseded by it, because the accent of that which remains is stronger.

79. And [the suffix *ka* is added] after a word ending in *grantha* when something additional is meant. (Pāṇini 5.2.79) Regarding "sakalam": *kalā* refers to a specific portion of time; the book associated with that [time] is likewise so called. That which exists together with a *kalā* is "sakalam. In the same way, the term "samuhūrtam" is also formed.

It should be understood as follows: regarding the phrase "with inclusion" (*sasaṃgraham*), this example has been written by modern scribes out of negligence; for in that case, the substitution of *sa-* [for *sam-*, as in *saṃgraha*] would already be established by the rule *avyayībhāve cākāle* (Pāṇini 6.3.81). To this he says: "In that case," and so forth. How [is it otherwise]?

Does it not follow that, since the words *kāla* (time) and *muhūrta* are synonymous, they are used here in this treatise by virtue of their association? The [author] thinks thus: through context and other factors, the fact that those two refer to the treatise is understood from the sentence; however, the primary denotation is indeed time itself.
"‘A khārī containing one droṇa,’ etc.: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to [Pāṇini 2.2.28] ‘*tena saha*’ and so forth."
80. And in the case of the second [member] when used together: (Pāṇini 6.3.80). Regarding this, it is said: "Of two things employed together, that which is subordinate is the 'second' (*dvitīya*).
This is because the word *dvitīya* is applied specifically to the subordinate member when there is a conjunction of the primary and the non-primary. Likewise...

For—when two things are joined with the word *saha* (together), such as master and servant, it is the servant alone who is called the "second" in relation to the master, and not the master in relation to the servant. [In the term *upākhya*,] the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *ātaścopasarge* (Pāṇini 3.1.136), meaning "that which is told (*ākhyāyate*) is the 'told-to' (*upākhya*). And that being so, by the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo...* [the suffixes are used in various senses].
The suffix *matup* occurs in the sense of the object [of the action], according to the rule *bahulam* (Pāṇini 5.2.127). An example is *sāgniḥ kapotaḥ* ("a pigeon accompanied by fire").

As before, this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Here, the pigeon is conjoined with fire; for their association is well-known in the world. In that case, the fire is subordinate (*apradhāna*). For instance, the fire...
It conforms to the pigeon (*kapota*): for wherever there is a pigeon, fire must necessarily be present;

however, it is not the case that wherever there is fire, there is a pigeon. Thus, the pigeon does not conform to the fire, and therefore the pigeon is primary (*pradhāna*), whereas fire and the others are indeed secondary. [The phrase] "fire and the others" refers to this.

Here, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), beings such as piśācas are included. For they are not perceived in some cases through direct perception (pratyakṣa); rather, they are inferred by means of pigeons and other [signs] that are invariably concomitant (avinābhāvin) with them; thus, they are "unnameable" (anupākhyā).

81. *avyayībhāve cākāle* (6.3.81). Regarding the phrase "not when it denotes time" (*akālavācini*), this indicates that by the word "time" (*kāle*) here, the actual form [of the word] is not being referred to; rather, it refers to words such as *pūrvāhṇa* ("forenoon") and others that denote specific divisions of time. Why? [Because...]
But how is this [the word *punar*] determined [to be included]?

It is because of the inclusion of the term *granthānta* in the rule *granthāntādhike ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.79). For by that [rule], a prohibition would otherwise apply when the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) denotes time; so that such a case may not occur, the inclusion of *granthānta* is made there. And if here...

The mention of "kāle" would be for the purpose of grasping the word-form itself. Consequently, by that very [rule], the substitution of *sa-* in the case of *sakalam* and *samuhūrtam* would be established; thus, the inclusion of the phrase "end of a book" (*granthānta*) there would be purposeless.
As for "sacakram," it is [established] by the rule "indivisible words [beginning with a preposition] and case-endings" (Pāṇini 2.1.6), etc.

When simultaneity is expressed, an *avyayībhāva* compound is formed. In the case of "sadhuram," the suffix *a* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmānakṣe* (Pāṇini 5.4.74).
In the case of "sahapūrvāhṇam," the *avyayībhāva* compound is formed in the sense of totality by that same rule.
82. *vopasarjanasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.82).

If the term "of that which has an upasarjana" were a qualifier of the word *saha*, then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because no specific distinction is provided here [and the rule would apply] even in this case.
It might be argued: [in the cases] *sahayudhvā* and *sahakṛtvā*, the word *saha* is also an *upasarjana*;

this is because it is designated in the nominative case by the rule *upapadam atiṅ* (Pāṇini 2.2.19), and because of its lack of predominance (*aprādhānya*). Furthermore, the qualification [of *saha* as an *upasarjana*] would be redundant; for in every compound, [the word *saha* is already subordinate].

Because the word *saha* is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), and because a compound is here brought into proximity by the final member (*uttarapada*)—since a compound indeed consists of a final member—it is thought that this [word *saha*] is a qualifier of that very [final member]; thus he says: "having all its parts as subordinate members. That is, every part is a subordinate member.
That [word] is so described because the property of the whole is expressed through the property of its part,
just as one says, "This city is firm. If someone [says] that a certain subordinate member (*upasarjana*) is a part,
and another [member] is not subordinate, yet that too is called subordinate—

In that case, the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would remain as it was; therefore, the word "all" (*sarva*) is included. But what is this compound whose every member is subordinate (*upasarjana*)? It is the *bahuvrīhi*. [Objection:
Is not the *dvandva* also one whose every member is subordinate? Would its inclusion not then follow as well? [Reply: No.

This is a fault; for the status of being a subordinate element (*guṇabhāva*) is not applied there by the word "together" (*saha*) alone. Alternatively, since both types of application are possible in this treatise, even the worldly subordinate element (*laukikopasarjana*) is included here. Thus, those things which have become subordinate elements—both through the technical subordinate element of the treatise and the worldly subordinate element—[are governed].

It is understood that only that whose every component part is [an upasarjana] is intended by the term *upasarjana*. And a *dvandva* compound is not of this nature; for its components possess the status of *upasarjana* solely by virtue of a technical (śāstrīya) designation, and not by worldly convention (*laukika*).

But a *bahuvrīhi* is [formed] even by means of a worldly [compound]. Therefore, it is that very [compound] which is included by the mention of the term "subordinate member" (*upasarjana*). By the phrase "of its part," he shows that this genitive case in "of the subordinate member" is a genitive of part-whole relation (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). The example "saputraḥ" (having a son) is a *bahuvrīhi* as previously explained.

Regarding the examples "sahayuṣvā" (having lived together) and "sahakṛtvā" (having done together): this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound in which the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*) is predominant.

Now, why does [the suffix] not occur here in "sahakṛtvapriyaḥ" (one whose beloved has acted together) and "priyasahakṛtva" (one who has acted together with his beloved), since the word "saha" is also a constituent part of a *bahuvrīhi* compound in these cases? To this he says: "here," etc., and "or, of the beloved. (*vā priyasya*).
(vā. 114) Thus, the word *priya* may optionally be placed first [in a compound].

Since this falls under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*), and because it relies here upon a *bahuvrīhi* compound, that which is the subsequent member must follow the word *saha* from which it is derived; it should not [be placed first].

And here, in this bahuvrīhi compound, that which is the final member (uttarapada) follows the word *saha*, because it is separated from it by another word; therefore, the substitution of *sa-* [for *saha-*, as prescribed by Pāṇini 6.3.95] does not take place.

83. *prakṛtyāśiṣyagovatsahaleṣu* (6.3.83). By this rule, the substitution of *sabhāva* (the change of *sa* to *sha*), which was over-extended by the preceding rule, is prevented through the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). Although it would have sufficed to say "not" (*na*), the use of the word "by the original form" (*prakṛtyā*) is for the sake of stylistic variety.

84. *samānasya* [the substitution of *sa-*] occurs for *samāna-* before words beginning with *amūrdhan-*, *prabhṛti-*, and *udarka-*. (6.3.84) Examples: *sagarbhaḥ* (of the same womb), *sapūthyaḥ* (of the same herd). Having analyzed [the compounds] as *samāno garbhaḥ* (a common womb) and *samānaṃ yūtham* (a common herd), they form *karmadhāraya* compounds by means of [Pāṇini 2.1.58], *pūrvāparaprathama-* etc. [The example] *sādharmyam* (similarity) [is formed in the same way].

The suffix expressing the abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) is added to a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Regarding "sajātīyaḥ," here too, the suffix *ccha* is applied to the *bahuvrīhi* itself by the rule "after a word ending in *jāti*, [the suffix] *ccha* is used when it denotes a relative (*bandhu*)" (Pāṇini 5.4.9). Regarding "sassthānīyaḥ," the suffix *ccha* is applied by the rule "after a word ending in *sthāna*, the suffix *ccha* is optionally used when it is accompanied by *sa-sthānena*" (Pāṇini 5.4.10).

[The final vowel with its following consonant] of words denoting light, a country, night, the navel, a name, a lineage, form, place, color, age, speech, and kinsmen [is optionally pluta when followed by a vowel].

Regarding "sajyoti": this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has the same light. In the same way, compounds such as *sajanapada* ("having the same country") and others are to be understood. It must also occur in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, because there is no distinction [in the rule] applied. Regarding "sanāmā" ("having the same name"): [this refers to the rule] "sarvanāmasthāne ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.8).
The vowel is lengthened by the rule beginning with "ityādinā. Regarding the form "savayāḥ," here too the vowel is lengthened by the rule "atvasantasya" (Pāṇini 6.4.14).

86. *caraṇe brahmacāriṇi* | (Pāṇini 6.3.86) This word *caraṇa* occurs in reference to persons and others by virtue of being based on Vedic study (*adhyayana*). [The term] *brahmacārī* [is derived as follows]:
one who practices (*carati*) the *brahman* [is] a *brahmacārī*; the suffix *ṇini* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.80, *vrate*. [An example is] *sabrahmacārī*.

The *karmadhāraya* compound is as before. The intended meaning of the term *sabrahmacārī* is "one who performs the vow (*vrata*) regarding the same *brahman*. To demonstrate how this meaning is applicable here, he says: "Brahman is the Veda," and so forth; for that vow which is for the purpose of studying that [Veda] is also [included].
"Brahma" [is used] because it exists for that purpose; it receives that designation because it serves that end, just as a pillar intended for Indra is called "Indra.

"He moves toward that" means he accomplishes that, which is to say, he protects it. But with what is he identical? To this he says: "Identical with that very same," and so forth. "With that very same" refers to that which is called the Veda.

Regarding the word *brahmaṇaḥ*: the particle *iti* is used in the sense of a cause (*hetau*). Since he performs the vow which, through metaphorical usage (*upacāreṇa*), has acquired the designation "Brahman," and because [the teacher] is equal to Brahman, he is "equal" (*samānaḥ*); such a person is a *sabrahmacārī*. Thus, the meaning of the term *sabrahmacārī* is: one who practices the vow in the same Brahman. If...

If one were to practice the vow (*vrata*) with respect to a Brahman that is not common [to all], then there would be no state of commonality. Even so, one would not be practicing the vow called "Brahman," and thus there would likewise be no status of being a *brahmacārin*. Therefore, he who is a *brahmacārin* with respect to the common Brahman necessarily becomes one who practices the vow with respect to the common Brahman.

The meaning of this term *sabrahmacārī* is established as "one who practices the vow (*vrata*) in the same *brahman*. Alternatively, in this view, there is a reference to the vow itself—which has received the designation "*brahman*" through figurative usage—as belonging to that very [teacher].
In the phrase "in the same *brahman*," the word *brahman* refers to the Veda; for indeed, [the Veda] differs according to each specific branch (*veda*).
Regarding the vow for the purpose of studying that [Veda], he who performs the vow when the same Veda is to be studied is called a *sabrahmacārī* (fellow-student).

87. *tīrthe ye* (Pāṇini 6.3.87). Regarding the example "satīrthyaḥ": having first formed a karmadhāraya compound as before, the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) must be applied. One who dwells at the same sacred ford (*tīrtha*) is called a *satīrthya*.

88. *vibhāṣodare* | (6.3.88) 89. *dṛgdṛśavatuṣu* | (6.3.89) One who sees the self as equal is called *sadṛk*; this is a compound with an *upapada*. [The substitution of *ku* for the *kvin* suffix applies here by the rule] *ṭhkvinpratyayasya kuḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.62].

(8.2.62) Thus, there is the substitution of *ku* [for *ka*]. But how can *kañ* and *kvip* apply here, given that those two suffixes are prescribed when words beginning with *tyad* are present as upapadas, and the word *samāna* is not listed among those beginning with *tyad*? To this, he says: "In the case of words beginning with *tyad*" and so forth.

The phrase "it should be stated that [the rule applies] even when *vṛkṣa* follows" means that this form of the meaning—namely, that the substitution of *sa* for *sama* occurs when the word *vṛkṣa* is the subsequent member (*uttarapada*)—must be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: by means of a prior separation of the yoga-rule (*yogavibhāga*), it will apply even to *vṛkṣa*. For this very reason...
Regarding that, Vṛttikāra has stated: "In this way, these [forms] are established.

But by what rule is the suffix *k* prescribed for the root *dṛś*, such that the word *dṛkṣa* becomes the second member (*uttarapada*)? To this he says: "The suffix *k* is also applied to *dṛś*," and so forth. "In that very [rule]," etc.

In the sūtra beginning with "ṭhtyadādiṣu" (Pāṇini 3.2.60), one might ask: what is the purpose of including the mention of *vatup*, given that a suffix *vatup* following a word identical [in form] to [the base] is simply impossible;
for that *vatup* is prescribed only after words such as *yat* and *etad* by the rule "ṭhyatadetebhyaḥ parimāṇe vatup" (Pāṇini 5.2.39)?
Thus he says: "The mention of the word *vatu* is for the sake of what follows."

90. *idaṃkimorīśkī* (Pāṇini 5.2.90). The letter *ś* is for the purpose of making the substitution apply to the whole word (*sarvādeśa*). From "he sees like this" (*idam iva paśyati*), [the suffix *ṭhak* is added] to form *īdṛk* and *īdṛśaḥ*. As before, the suffixes *kañ* and *kvanip* also apply. From "he asks what it is like" (*kim iva yācati*), [the suffix *ṭhak* is added] to form *kīdṛk* and *kīdṛśaḥ*. This is merely for the sake of etymological derivation.

The analysis (vigraha) has been performed; however, the meaning of the individual components as presented in the analytical sentence is not found here. For instance, by means of the words *īdṛg* and *īdṛśa*, the sense "equal to this" is understood from the whole alone.
In the case of *kīdṛk* and *kīdṛśa* as well, [the sense is] "equal to what? [And in the case of *kiyat*: "what is its measure? (kiṃ parimāṇam asya).

[The word] *kiyān* [is derived as follows]: because this is its measure (*parimāṇa*), [the suffix] *yat* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.2.39]. Then, by [Pāṇini 5.2.40], *kim-idaṃbhyāṃ vo ghaḥ*, there is the substitution of *gha* for *vatup*;

when the replacement of *i* has been made for that [suffix], the elision of the vowel *i* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.148], *yasyeti ca*. But is it not the case that the replacement of *i* for the letter *v* of *vatup* is [already] provided by this [rule]?

It is prescribed; however, what is prescribed by [the suffixes] *vatup* and *kimidambhyām*? It is thought thus: from this statement regarding the substitution [of *gha*], it is understood that *vatup* [is intended], for there is no other defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) for *vatup*.
And it is not possible to understand a substitution of *gha* for a non-existent *vatup*.
91. *ā sarvanāmnaḥ* (6.3.91).

The statement "it should be stated that [the substitution applies] before *dṛkṣa*" means that it must be explained that the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel of a pronominal (*sarvanāman*) occurs when the word *dṛkṣa* follows. In this regard, the following...

The explanation: by the logic of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*), the particle *ca* from the subsequent sūtra is carried over here; it serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned. By this, [the rule] will apply when the word *dṛkṣa* is the second member of a compound. Now, for what purpose is the long vowel prescribed, rather than the short vowel alone?

Let it be prescribed [that the substitute is short]; would it not be established even by the long vowel resulting from *savarṇa-dīrgha*? No; because by the rule *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97), the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) would apply. Nor can it be argued that it will not occur due to the functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the pronunciation of the letter *a*.

Because the rule for the letter *a* serves the purpose of excluding the letter *d*, there would be unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) in a rule prescribing elision (*lopa*). Furthermore, in forms such as *tvādṛk* and *tvādṛśaḥ*, the long vowel would not be heard; therefore, the long vowel itself must be prescribed.
92. *Viṣvag-devayoś ca ṭer adr-aḷ añ-catau vapratyaye* (Pāṇini 6.3.92).
[The sūtra states: *viṣvadr-aḷ-añ*. [Derivation: From *viṣvagañcati*, the suffix *kvin* is applied by the rule *ṛtvig-ādi-sūtra* (3.2.59);

then the augment *num* is added by *ugidacām* (7.1.70); finally, the elision of the final consonant (*hal*) and the penultimate vowel (*ṅy-ādi*) due to the following consonant (*saṃyogānta-lopa*) take place.
The substitution of *k* [for *s*] is applied by the rule *ṭhkvinpratyayasya kuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.62).
Regarding the statement "the words *adri* and *sadhryañc* are nipātana [forms] with the final syllable accented," etc.:
when the substitution of *adri* for *viṣvadri* has been made by this [rule], then in the case of *sadhryañc*, [the substitution of] *sadhrī* for *saha* [is applied].
Furthermore, in the case of *sādhyardha* and similar words, by the rule *ṭhak-ita-kāraka-upapadāt kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139),
the final syllable of the compound would be udātta according to the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the second member; however, a circumflex (*svarita*) accent is desired.

Therefore, in order to prescribe that the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) is udātta, the word *adri* here is treated as an irregular form (*nipātana*) having its final syllable udātta. Consequently, by the rule "the remainder is anudātta," the rest becomes anudātta. When the substitution of *yaṇ* has been made therein, the svarita nature of the second member is established by the rule "after an udātta or svarita vowel, a following anudātta vowel becomes svarita" (Pāṇini 8.2.4).

Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of the suffix *vapratyaya*? For when it is stated "in the case of *añcu* with *thañ* or *ca*" (*ṭhañcatau*), the grammatical operation should apply only when the second member is the simple root *añcu*; yet *añcati* ends in the suffix *vapratyaya*.

Only the subsequent word (*uttarapada*) is affected. In this regard, he says "in the case of *añc*"—namely, "the mention of the suffix *v*," and so forth. Elsewhere, when there is a mention of a verbal root (*dhātu*), [it refers to] the entire collection beginning with the root, which stands as a base (*prakṛti*).
The mention of the suffix *v* is for the purpose that there may be understanding (*pratīti*) [of the intended meaning]. For by this, the following meaning is made known:
when "root" (*dhātu*) is mentioned elsewhere, not only the root itself is taken, but rather the word beginning with the root. Therefore, [the form] *ayaskṛtam* [is established].

In the word *ayaskāra*, the substitution of *s* for the visarga is established by the rule *ṭhataḥ kṛkami* (Pāṇini 8.3.46). However, if this meaning were not intended, then there would be the apprehension of the root *kṛ* alone; consequently, wherever the root *kṛ* occurs by itself—

The application [of the rule] would occur only in that case where it is devoid of an affix—namely, *ayaskṛt*. Here, because the augment *tuk* belongs specifically to the root *kṛ*, it is included by the mention of that [root] itself; thus, there is the application of the root *kṛ* alone. Regarding the term "not preceded by *aśva*": [the form] *aśvāñci* is derived from *aśvam añcati* with the suffix *kvip*.

The suffix *ṅīp* is added by the rule "There is also the addition of *ṭhañ*," followed by the elision of the vowel *a* according to "the elision of *ṭha*" (Pāṇini 6.4.138), and the lengthening of the vowel by "before *ṭhac*" (Pāṇini 6.3.138). Regarding the form *viṣvagyuk*:
the word *viṣvak* is formed with the suffix *kvip* by the rule "after *sad*, *sū*, and *dviṣ*" (Pāṇini 3.2.61), meaning "that which connects in all directions" (*viṣvag ayunakti*).

Regarding the rule "ṭhviṣvagañcanam" [Pāṇini 5.2.79]: the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied by the rule "lyuṭ ca" (3.3.115). Regarding the phrase "in Vedic literature" (*cchandasi*) and so forth: the meaning is that this form of explanation should be understood as signifying that, in the domain of Vedic literature, when a feminine referent is intended, the substitution of *adṛc* occurs diversely (*bahulam*). In this regard, the following...

The explanation is as follows: from the rule *vibhāṣodare* (6.3.88), the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is understood to carry over, and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Alternatively, here the particle *ca* has the sense of including what is not explicitly stated; by this, [the rule applies] in the domain of the Vedic language (*chandas*).
The substitution of *adraḷ* for *viṣvak* occurs in some instances even outside this specific rule, while in others it does not occur at all.

[Objection: But is the particle *ca* intended to carry forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) the term "pronominal" (*sarvanāman*) from the previous rule? [Response: This is not so; for the pronominal will indeed be carried forward simply by virtue of its being marked with the *svarita* accent. Examples include *viśvācī*, and so forth.
When *viśva*, *ghṛta*, and *kiṃ* are used as upapadas, the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *añc* as before,
and the grammatical operations such as the addition of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* also take place.

93. *samaḥ* becomes *sami* [before a following vowel] (Pāṇini 6.3.93). 94. *tiras* becomes *tiri* when there is elision [of the following word] (Pāṇini 6.3.94). 95. *saha* becomes *sadhri* [before a following vowel] (Pāṇini 6.3.95).
In the word "sadhrīcā," as before, there is the elision of the vowel 'a' and the lengthening [of the preceding vowel].

96. *sadhamādasthayośchandasī* (Pāṇini 6.3.96). [The form] *sadhamādaḥ* is derived as follows: "that which exists together with intoxication (*māda*)," formed as a *bahuvrīhi* compound by the rule *tena saha* (2.2.28), etc.; the word *māda* ends in the suffix *ghañ*. Now, one might object that [the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed] by the rule *mado'nupasarge* (3.3.67).

[Objection: Should it not be *apām*? [Response: This is not a fault; for in that context, the word *vā* ("optionally") from rule 3.3.62 (*svanahasorvā*) is understood to carry over, and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, in Vedic usage (*chandas*), only the suffix *ghañ* will occur. Or else, it is because of this very specific grammatical indication (*nirdeśāt*). [As in] *sadhasthaḥ* [or *sadhasthāḥ*—Kāśikā].

The printed reading is "sadhasthā"—(Kāśikā)—the printed reading in the Saṃpā edition is thus: [it is formed] as "one who stands together" (*saha tiṣṭhati*), with the suffix *ka* by [Pāṇini 3.2.4] *supi sthaḥ*.

97. *dvyantarupasargebhyo'pa īt* (Pāṇini 6.3.97). Regarding the word *dvīpam*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with an analysis that does not use its own constituent words (*asvapadavigraha*), meaning "in which water has gone twice.
This is just as [one says] *sumukhī*, meaning "she whose face is beautiful. [The suffix *aṇ* is applied here by] *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.74).
By such rules, the suffix *a* is applied as a compound-final (*samāsānta*). That in which water is contained within is *antarīpa*.
That in which water has come together, departed, or flowed out is *sapīpa*, *vīpa*, or *nīpa*.

"It must be stated" means it must be explained. This same meaning applies to the word "vaktavya" (to be stated) in subsequent instances as well. Furthermore, the explanation here is also as before, [beginning] from the rule "vibhāṣodare."

This is obtained because the mention of *vibhāṣā* (optionally) continues [from a previous rule], and because it is a *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā* (a restricted option). We shall provide another explanation here as well, beginning with "with respect to the word *ṭhap*" and so forth. In this context, those particles (*prādayaḥ*) which are connected with an action with respect to something, [that thing is the object].

Since those termed "gatis" and "upasargas" [occur] as such, it is not possible for the word *ap* to function as a verb (*kriyā*), because it denotes a substance (*dravya*). Therefore, with respect to that [word], no element can have the designation of an *upasarga*.
Yet, this mention of *upasarga* is indeed made; by virtue of its force (*sāmarthya*), wherever...

The mention of "prepositions" (upasarga) is understood to be for the purpose of indicating that which is seen elsewhere as having the status of a preposition; otherwise, the mention of the word "anta" would not be necessary, for just as the words beginning with "pra" are indicated by the mention of "prepositions," so too is the word "anta."

Is it not already observed that *upa* functions as a prefix (*upasarga*) when it possesses the sense of "nearness" (*vidhina*)? If so, then by the inclusion of the term "internal" (*antar*), it is indicated that the substitution of *ī* (as in *itvam*) characterized by the mention of "prefixes" is not mandatory (*anitya*). By this, forms such as *samāpam*, *parāpam*, and *prāpam* are established.

[The rule] "ṭhanūpaḥ" [is applied]. The analysis is: "that in which water (*āpas*) has entered. As before, there is a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*), and a long vowel by way of *savarṇadīrgha*. Now, what is the purpose of the pronunciation of the long vowel (*dīrgha*), given that...
Even though a short vowel is prescribed, [the form] *anūpa* is indeed established by means of lengthening when followed by a homogeneous vowel; therefore, he says:

"The utterance of the long vowel," and so forth. If the long vowel were not uttered, the lengthening would occur only in *saṃhitā* (continuous flow), not in *avagraha* (pause). Therefore, this is for the purpose that it may also occur in *avagraha*.
The pronunciation is long.

99. *aṣaṣṭhy-atṛtīyā-sthasya anya-sya dug-āśīr-āśā-sthā-sthita-utsuka-utika-araka-rāga-ccheṣu* (Pāṇini 6.3.99). [The rule states: "In the case of *anya*, when followed by *āśis*, etc., the *d* is substituted for the final vowel of the first member. For example: *anyāśīs*, *anyadāśīs*, and so forth. In all such instances, depending on the specific analysis (*vigraha*), a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇa-samāsa*) is formed.
He demonstrates this with the phrase: "one who is not established by one thing is established by another. The compound is formed according to Pāṇini 2.1.32: *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*.
Regarding the statement "the augment *dṛk* [is applied] without distinction," and so forth, the suffix *cha* is applied to the word *kāraka*.

From this point forward, the augment *dug* should be applied generally and without distinction. However, in the other seven subsequent rules beginning with the section on benediction (*āśīḥ*), it is not desired—that is, it is not intended—for [the augment] to stand in the genitive or the instrumental case.
What, then, is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this meaning, by which it is determined? To this, he says: "And of this... (*asya ca*).

And so forth. Although the rule would have been established by the phrase "not occurring in the sixth or third case," the repetition of the negative particle *nañ* is a sign that this prohibition is not universal (*anitya*). Consequently, in some instances, the augment *dug* does indeed occur in a compound even for words situated in the sixth or third case.
100. *Arthe vibhāṣā* (6.3.100). Regarding the term *ṭhanyārthaḥ*: [the compound] *anyasmai idam* ("this is for another") is a compound formed by *caturthī tadarthārtha-* (2.1.36) and so forth.
101. *koḥ kat tatpuruṣe aci* (Pāṇini 6.3.101). For example, *kadajaḥ*. This is a compound (*samāsa*) according to *kugatiprādayaḥ* (2.2.18), meaning "a contemptible goat" (*kutsito 'jaḥ*).
In contrast, *kūṣṭro rājā* is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "ṭhkadbhāve" and so forth: since the substitution of *ka* for *ku* is prescribed when a word beginning with a vowel follows as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), it would not apply when the word *tri* is the subsequent member. Therefore, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*)—that is, an explanatory rule—must be made to ensure that the substitution of *ka* for *ku* occurs for the word *ku* which precedes the subsequent member *tri*.

In this regard, the following is the demonstration: the particle *ca* is employed in the subsequent sūtra, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. By means of that, the substitution of *kad* will also occur when the word *triṃśat* stands as the final member of a compound.
102. And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after *ratha* and *vada*. (6.3.102) This rule is for the purpose of excluding words beginning with *a*; the same applies in the subsequent rules as well.
103. *tṛṇe ca jātau* (6.3.103).

104. *kā pathyakṣayoḥ* (6.3.104). This rule is commenced for the sake of meanings other than "slight" (*anīṣadartha*). Regarding the form *kāpatha*: a contemptible path is *kāpatha*. [This is derived by] *ṛkpūḥ*... [etc. (Pāṇini 5.4.74).

By the rule beginning with (Pāṇini 5.4.74), the suffix *a* is added as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*). Regarding the word "kākṣaḥ": it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "a contemptible axle" (*kutsito 'kṣaḥ*). Alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose eyes are contemptible" (*kutsite akṣiṇī asya*);

in this case, the suffix *ṣac* is applied as a compound-final element by the rule (Pāṇini 5.4.113): "In a *bahuvrīhi*, the suffix *ṣac* is added after *sakthi* and *akṣi* when they denote one's own limbs."

105. And [the suffix *ka* is applied] in the sense of "slight" (*īṣadartha*). (Pāṇini 6.3.105) For example: *īṣanmadhuram* becomes *kāmadhuram*. The compound is formed by the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* (2.2.18).
It has been stated that the statement "the word *ku* signifies evil (*pāpa*)" is merely a general observation regarding its usage (*upādhivacana*). In that regard:
And this very mention of the substitution of *ka-* is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for its being only occasional (*prāyikatva*). For example, in the word "kāmlam. Now, one might object:
"In this case, shouldn't there be the substitution of *kad-* by the rule 'ṭhkoḥ katatpuṣaṣe' (Pāṇini 6.3.101)? To this he says: "Even when followed by a vowel-initial [suffix]," and so forth.

106. *vibhāṣā puruṣe* (6.3.106). This is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) where [the suffix] *ṭhaC* was not previously applicable. This is because the sense of "slight" (*īṣadartha*) has been excluded. Now, one might object:
since [the suffix] is not applicable by anything else in the sense of "not slight," while it was applicable by the preceding rule in the sense of "slight," it would thus apply in both cases.

He says that this alternative analysis (*vibhāṣā*) is logical, stating: "But in the sense of 'slight' (*īṣadartha*), by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*)," and so forth. The scope of *īṣadarthe ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.105) is, for example, *īṣanmadhuram* ("slightly sweet") or *kāmadhum* ("sweet to the heart"); the scope of *vibhāṣā puruṣe* (Pāṇini 6.3.109) is, for example, *kutsitaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("a contemptible man") or *kāpuruṣaḥ*. And here, both [rules] apply.

One obtains [the form] *kāpuruṣaḥ*, meaning "a base man" (*īṣatpuruṣaḥ*). In this case, by the rule "expressing the sense of 'slightly' (*īṣadarthaḥ*") alone, the former prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) is set aside.
107. [The substitution of] *kava* for *ka* occurs before *uṣṇa*. (6.3.107) 108. And [the substitution of *kava* for *ka* occurs] before *pathin* in the Vedic language. (6.3.108) 109.
Words such as *pṛṣodara* are as they have been taught. (6.3.109)

"The word 'ādi' (and so forth) expresses a class. If, in this context, the word 'ādi' were taken to signify restriction (*vyavasthā*), then only those words actually enumerated in the list would be correct, and no others. However, when the word 'ādi' is understood as expressing a class (*prakāra*), [all words of that type are included].
Having kept all this in mind— that even those words not listed in the *satya* [list] possess correctness (*sādhubhāva*)—
he says "of the *pṛṣodara*-type" and so forth, showing that the word *ādi* here expresses a variety or mode (*prakāra*). A "mode" (*prakāra*) means similarity (*sādṛśya*).

Therefore, in order to demonstrate this, he says: "In those [words]," and so forth. Just as in the word *pṛṣodara*, a process of elision (*lopa*) is observed that is not prescribed by the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), so too elsewhere a process such as elision is observed that is not prescribed by the treatise; and these are of the same category as *pṛṣodara*.

Regarding the phrase "yathopadiṣṭam": the term *yathā* forms an avyayībhāva compound with the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*) according to Pāṇini 2.1.7, *yathāsādṛśye*. For this very reason, he provides its explanation:
"those [sounds] which have been taught," and so forth. The root *diś-* has the action of utterance as its meaning.

The meaning is that they have been taught and uttered. By whom, then, were they taught? By the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Furthermore, the learned are to be recognized by their conduct, place of residence, and so forth. "They are to be accepted exactly as they are" means that they are to be used precisely in the manner in which they were employed by them.

The meaning is that they are to be accepted as correct. If the learned (śiṣṭas) are the authority regarding words, then what is the use of this Aṣṭādhyāyī? For would not the correctness of words be understood from the very speech of the learned? It is replied: the Aṣṭādhyāyī is for the purpose of identifying who the learned are.

One who is studying the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, upon seeing someone— even one who has not studied the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*— employing those words that are prescribed in this *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, concludes: "This person is an authority (*śiṣṭa*)," and not otherwise.
Furthermore, he has studied the Aṣṭādhyāyī and yet employs those words derived therein; surely he knows others as well— thus, the Aṣṭādhyāyī is for the purpose of knowing the learned (śiṣṭas).

"Similarly, others also... and so forth. When the words *kapi*, *aśva*, and *mahī* are used as upapadas, the suffix *kap* is applied to the root *sthā* by the rule *supi sthaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.4). The letter *s* is changed to *t*. Furthermore, the word *mahī* undergoes shortening [of its final vowel].

Regarding the expression "dakṣiṇatāram": it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). The masculine form is applied according to the rule: "In all types of compounds, the masculine form should be stated for pronouns" (Vārttika 104). Alternatively, this is a genitive compound of the word *dakṣiṇa* with the word *tīra*.

Regarding the rule "vācovāde": when the word *vākya* is followed by the word *vāda* as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the substitution of *ḍa* for [the final *ya*] occurs; and for the subsequent member *vāda*, the substitution of *vala* occurs when the suffix *iñ* follows. Thus, from "one who speaks words" (*vācaṃ vadati*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule "karmaṇyaṇ".
(3.2.1)—*vāgvāda*: its descendant is *vāṅvaliḥ*, according to *ata iñ* (4.1.95).

[The rule] *ṣaṣa utvam* and so forth: the substitution of *u* occurs for the word *ṣaṣ* when the words *datṛ* or *daśan* follow as the second member (*uttarapada*), and there is also the substitution of *ṣṭu* for the initial sound of the second member. [Thus: *ṣaḍ-dantaḥ*.

The term *yasya* is a bahuvrīhi compound. By the rule *vayas-dantasya-datṛ* (Pāṇini 5.4.141), the substitute *datṛ* is applied—thus forming *ṣoḍan*. The term *ṣoḍaśa* is a dvandva compound of *ṣaṭ* and *daśa*.
Regarding the rule *dhāsu vā*, this option applies specifically to the substitution of *u*; however, the change to *ṣṭu* (the substitution of *ṣṭ* for *ṣ*) is obligatory.
"Ṣoḍhā, ṣaṅdhā. The suffix *dhā* is applied by the rule "adhikaraṇavicāle ca" (Pāṇini 5.3.43). Now, for what purpose is the plural form *dhāsu* used in the citation?
To this he says: "The mention of the plural," and so forth. [In the word] "ṣaṅdhā," [the root is] either *dhāñ* or *dheṭ*.
In the feminine, the suffix *ka* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.3 (*striyāṃ ṭhāto 'nupasarge kaḥ*).
Regarding "is given" (*dāśyate*), the root is *dāśṛ* "to give" (DhP 882); regarding "is destroyed" (*nāśyate*), the root is *ṇaśa* "to disappear" (DhP 1194);
regarding "is deceived" (*dabhyate*), the root is *dambh* "to deceive" (DhP 1270).

Thus ends the list of verbal roots (dhātupāṭha). From these roots—*damBh* (to deceive) and the others—the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). In the case of the word *duḥśas*, when it forms a *prādisamāsa* with words such as *dāśa*, we have *dūḍāśaḥ*, *dūṇāśaḥ*, and *dūḍabhaḥ*.

This is according to the rule beginning with "there is elision of the nasal in *damBh*" (*dambheranunāsikalopaḥ*). As for this [rule] regarding "in *dāśa*, *nāśa*, *dabha*, and *dhyai*" (*dāśanāśadabhadhyeṣu*).

In this regard, the mention of the root *dambh* in the rule *kācavṛ.* 6.3.109 is its formal citation (*nipātana*) after the elision of the nasal has already been effected; it is precisely because of that [citation] that the elision of the nasal occurs here for *dambh*.
Those whose fasting consists of eating only pīlu fruits are "pīvopavasanāḥ"; likewise, those who fast on payas are "payopavasanāḥ."
In both cases there is the elision of the letter *s*.

Regarding the phrase "the addition of a phoneme" (*varṇāgamaḥ*), he cites this verse— "the addition of a phoneme"— because it is accepted that the grammatical correctness of those words derived in the science of etymology (*nirukta*) is established precisely by their inclusion in the *pūṣodara*-class of compounds.

And so forth. *Varṇāgama* (the addition of a phoneme) is the introduction of a previously non-existent phoneme—the acquisition of a phoneme such as *na*, etc., that was not there before—as in: *ko jīryate kuñjaraḥ*. Here, the augment *nuk* is applied to the word *ku*. *Varṇaviparyaya* (the transposition of phonemes) is the exchange of the positions of phonemes, as in: *hiṃsi*.

In the case of the root *hiṃs* (Dhātupāṭha 1456), in the formation of the word *siṃha* from *hinasti*, there is an exchange of position between the letters *ha* and *sa* when the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class) is applied. As for "modification of phonemes" (*varṇavikāra*)—the assumption of a different form by a phoneme—it is, for example, as in *ṣoḍan*. Here, the letter *kha* assumes the form of *u*.

The transformation of the letter *da* into the form of the letter *ḍa*; the disappearance of a phoneme—the elision of a letter—as in *pṛṣodara*, where the letter *ta* is elided; the excellence of meaning—a specific sense, a meaning different from the conventional one—by which there is a connection with a verbal root (*dhātu*), as in [the word] *mahyām*.

"Rauti" means a peacock; here, there is an excessive connection with the meaning "one who cries out" (rauti) through the sense of "delighting" (ramaṇa). This is the fivefold etymology (nirukta), consisting of five types; it is called "nirukta" because by it the meaning is stated (ucyate) with certainty (niścayena).

110. *saṃkhyā-visāya-pūrvasyāhnasyāhan anyatarasyāṃ ṅau* (Pāṇini 6.3.110). [Example: *dvyor ahnoḥ bhavaḥ* ("occurring in two days"). When the sense of "occurring" (*bhava*) is intended, there is a compound by *taddhitārtha* (Pāṇini 2.1.51). Then, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied by *kālāt ṭhañ* (Pāṇini 4.3.11). Of that [suffix],...

By the rule *dvigor lṛg anapatye* (4.1.88), there is elision (*luk*); by the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣ ṭac* (5.4.91), the suffix *ṭac* is added as a compound-final augment (*samāsānta*); and by the rule *ahno 'hn etebhyaḥ* (5.4.88), the substitute *ahn-* is applied. Thus, we have *draḷhni*. [The substitution of *iṅ* for *ṇi* occurs] optionally by the rule *vibhāṣā iṅśyoḥ* (6.4.136).

The elision of the vowel *i* is optional, as in the form *dvyahnaḥ*. [In this case,] by *ād guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.87), [the form becomes] *vyahnaḥ*, which is a *prādi*-compound (*pra-ahnaḥ*). The remainder is as before. Regarding *sāyāhnaḥ*, this is an *ekadeśi*-compound. Here, the following objection might be raised: "But surely..."

The compound is prescribed by the rule *pūrvāparādharottarām* (Pāṇini 2.2.1), but the word *sāyam* is not recited therein; how then is the compounding of the word *sāyam* with the word *sāyāhnaḥ* possible here? To refute this objection, he says: "It is an *ekadeśisamāsa*."

"Even other [words] than 'pūrva' and so forth," and so on. In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the substitution of *ahna-* for *ahan-* is prescribed by the rule "ṭhano'hna etebhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.88), and by the phrase "etebhyaḥ" [in that same rule],
there is also the application of the rule "tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ saṃkhyāvyayādeḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.86), as well as...

In the rule *ṭhaḥ sarvaikadeśasaṃkhyātapuṇyācca rātreḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.87), the categories beginning with numerals and indeclinables (*saṃkhyā-vyayādi*) introduced [in the preceding rules] are referred back. In that context, if only words such as *pūrva* were to be compounded with a word denoting a part (*ekadeśin*), then the word *sāyam* would not be referred back by the phrase *ṭhetebhyaḥ*.

Because that [word *sāyam*] is not enumerated among the numbers (*saṃkhyā*) and so forth; consequently, the substitution of *ahar* for the word *ahan* would not occur after the word *sāyam*. And thus, since the form *sāyamahaḥ* (preceded by *sāyam*) would not exist, its inclusion here would not have been made; yet it has been made. Therefore, this very [point is the reason].

The inclusion of the word *pūrva* (forenoon) [in the rule] indicates that a partitive compound (*ekadeśisamāsa*) occurs not only with words beginning with *pūrva*, but with others as well. By this, forms such as *madhyāhnaḥ* ("midday," from *madhyam ahnaḥ*) and *pūrvāhṇe* ("in the forenoon") are established.

The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule "ṭhahno'dantāt" (Pāṇini 8.4.7). Although it would have been sufficient to state simply "from *saṃkhyā*, *vi*, and *sāya*," the inclusion of the additional word *pūrva* is for the purpose of indicating that further operations apply;
by this, the elision of the letter *m* in *sāyāhnaḥ* is established.

111. *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho'ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.111). Is this [compound] *ṭhḍhralope* a tatpuruṣa or a bahuvrīhi? If it were a tatpuruṣa—meaning "the elision (*lopa*) of *ḍha* and *ra* is *ḍhralopa*"—then [the word *pūrvasya* would refer to] that which precedes the *aṇ*.

This is not tenable; for elision (*lopa*) is of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*), and in non-existence, priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*) are impossible. Even if priority were asserted by relying on the priority of the substituend (*sthānin*), as in *karaṇīyaḥ*—where, after the elision of the *repha* of the suffix *yan* has been performed—

Having observed this fault— that there would be lengthening of the preceding vowel— he says "in which there is the elision of the letters ḍ and r," etc., showing that this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Because it conveys the meaning, it is indeed a *bahuvrīhi* even when there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), as in the example *kāṇṭhekāla*.

Thus: regarding "līḍham," [the root] *lih* means "to taste" (*liha āsvādane*, DhP 1066). The following grammatical operations must be applied: the *niṣṭhā* suffix, *ho ḍhaḥ* (8.2.31), *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* (8.2.40), *ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ* (8.4.41), and *ḍho ḍhea lopaḥ* (8.3.13). Regarding "mīḍham," [the root] *miha*...

Regarding *secane*: [from the root] *sic* (DhP 992). Regarding *upagūḍham*: [from the root] *guhū* in the sense of “concealing” (DhP 896). Regarding *mūḍhaḥ*: [from the root] *muha* in the sense of “bewilderment” (DhP 1198). Regarding *nīraktam*:
it is a compound according to Pāṇini 2.2.18 (*kugatiprādayaḥ*), and [the doubling of the *r*] is by Pāṇini 8.3.14 (*ro ri*).
[The rule regarding] elision [is established].
Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of "the preceding" (pūrva), given that there is the rule "ḍhralope"? This is a locative indication;
in such a case, even without the mention of "the preceding," the principle "when something is indicated by the locative, it refers to what precedes it" applies.
[An objection is raised: "Will this [rule] apply only to the preceding [element]? To this, he says: "The mention of *pūrva*," and so forth.

If the mention of *pūrva* were absent, then—because of the governing context (*adhikāra*) of the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*)—it would apply only to the subsequent member, as in *nīraktaṃ* and the like, but it would not apply when there is no subsequent member, as in *līḍham*.

In such cases as these, although the lengthening [of the vowel] would apply even when not followed by a second member (anuttarapada) due to the authority of the rule— since the elision of *ḍh* is impossible in a second member (*uttarapada*)— the elision of *r* and *l* (*ralopa*) does not apply when not followed by a second member,
because the elision of *r* and *l* is possible only when a second member follows. Therefore, even when not followed by a second member...

The mention of *pūrva* (the preceding) is so that the long vowel may apply specifically to the *aṇ* (vowel) that precedes [the semivowel]. Regarding *ātṛḍham*: the roots *tṛhū* and *tṛnhū* (DhP 1348, 1350) mean "to injure. There is a variant reading *ādṛḍham*; this refers to the root *dṛha*, *dṛhi*, or *dṛhi* (DhP 733–736), meaning "to grow strong" or "to increase."

It is claimed that this form occurs at the stage of completion (*niṣṭhā*), but this is not tenable; because the root *dṛh* takes the augment *iṭ*, it ought to have that *iṭ*. Even if, for some reason, it were not present, even then, by the rule "gha is substituted for a root beginning with *d*" (Pāṇini 8.2.32), it ought to become *gh*.

If it is argued that both [the substitution of *ḍha* and the addition of the augment *iṭ*] will not occur because of the rule "dṛḍhaḥ sthūlabalayoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.20), which indicates the intended meaning of "thick" (*sthūla*) and "strong" (*balavat*), then by that same reasoning, the lengthening [of the vowel] would also not occur.
Some explain here that the absence of the augment *iṭ* is due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the teaching regarding augments. Or...

In the rule beginning with *druhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.33), due to the separation of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) by the word *vā*, there is optionally an absence of the substitution of *gh*. Thus we have *āvṛḍham*; [the root] *vṛhū* means "to lift up" (Dhātupāṭha 1347).
112. *sahivahor od avaṇasya* (6.3.112). [Examples:
*ūḍhaḥ*, *ūḍhavān*. Because [the roots] belong to the *yajādi* group, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*).
By [the rule] *samprasāraṇācca* (6.1.108), there is substitution of the subsequent vowel and lengthening.

In that case, if the perception of the phoneme *a* were not present, the substitution of *o* would also apply to the vowel *ū*. Now, one might argue that because it is subsequent to the process of *saṃprasāraṇa* and so forth, the substitution of *o* must take effect; and thus it is stated in the Bhāṣya:
"Between the two [rules], both being obligatory, the substitution of *o* must occur by virtue of its posteriority, once the substitution of *ā* has been applied."

"Vocalization (samprasāraṇa) occurs; once vocalization has been performed, the substitution of the preceding vowel for the semivowel follows; since its function has already been accomplished, the subsequent substitution of *au* will not take place.
Therefore, the substitution of *au* must indeed occur, and once that is established, the vocalization and other operations follow after it.

And since nothing undesirable follows from this, there is no purpose in including the mention of "vowel" (varṇa). If that is so, then by making this non-mention of the vowel, he indicates this: "In certain cases, *samprasāraṇa* and the grammatical operation dependent upon it are stronger. Therefore, as for what was stated—"*samprasāraṇa*... [the rule applies].
Thus, the statement "an operation based on *samprasāraṇa* is stronger" (Puṣpavṛtti 103) becomes justified.
[The question] "What is the purpose of mentioning the term *varṇa*? [is asked]; for even if [the rule] were stated merely as "of *udātta*," [the form] *soḍhā* [would still result].

The intention is that [the forms] beginning with *soḍhavyam* are indeed established. Regarding the passage beginning with *kṛtāyām api*: from the root *vah* preceded by the prefix *ut*, there is the suffix *lṛṅ*; then *cli* is replaced by *sic* (Pāṇini 3.1.44);

*tasi* is replaced by *tām*, and *thasi* by *tam*; the augment *aṭ* is added; and because the substitution of *ḍha* and so forth is considered *asiddha*, the rule *vadavraja-* (Pāṇini 7.2.3) applies prior to that.

By [the rule] beginning with (7.2.3), there is lengthening, and from that, the substitution of *ḍha* and so forth. Now, if the mention of the term *varṇa* (phoneme) were not made here, the substitution of *o* (*otva*) being prescribed for the vowel *a* consisting of one measure (*mātrika*) would not apply to the long [vowel];
however, because of the mention of *varṇa*, it applies to every phoneme, and thus it is established—as in *udavoḍhām*.

[The opponent asks: "Is it not the case that [the vowel] has been brought forth (*udavoḍham*)? [The proponent replies: "But surely, by the rule *ṭh-ṇ-it savarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.69), the letter *a*, when being grasped, will cause the letter *ā* to be grasped as well; so what is the purpose of the mention of the phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*)?
To this he says: "Even from that, the subsequent [is taken]," and so forth. This refers to the rule *tapa-ras tatkālasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.70).

Furthermore, this compound *parastapara* is also resorted to for the purpose of ensuring that the designation *vṛddhi* does not apply to the vowel *e* occurring in three-mora or four-mora words such as *khaṭvaiḍaka* and *khaṭvaitikāyana*. In the absence of that [restriction],...

In the case of the mention of a phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*), because the letter *a* is followed by *t* (i.e., it is *tapara*), the long vowel *ā* would not be included; consequently, its substitution by *u* (the *utva*) would not occur.
Therefore, the mention of the phoneme must be made so that [the rule] may apply to every instance of the sound *a*. This very same [purpose] also applies to the compound *tādapi paraḥ taparaḥ*.
The mention of "color" (varṇa) should be understood as an indicator (jñāpaka).

113. *sāḍhaḷṬ saḍhÂavā sāḍheati nigame* (Pāṇini 6.3.113). In forms such as *saḍhÂavā*, the absence of the substitution of *o* for *ava* is prescribed by way of a technical irregularity (*nipātana*). However, the lengthening of the vowel is already established by the rule *ṭhḍhralope* (6.3.111) and others.

The term *uttarapade* (in the following word) from [sūtra] 6.3.1 is understood here. And since the "following word" (*uttarapada*) occurs within a compound (*samāsa*), it follows that even without this explicit statement, the form must necessarily exist in *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination).

Therefore, since the purpose of this governing rule (*adhikāra*) cannot be established for the sake of those operations that will be prescribed when a subsequent word (*uttarapada*) follows, this governing rule is intended solely for the sake of those operations that occur when no subsequent word follows. Consequently, by whichever rules an operation is ordained when a subsequent word follows—
Having bypassed those [rules] by means of that yoga, the operation is prescribed for the state of being *anuttara*.
Demonstrating its utility therein, he says: "He will state ‘dvyaco’tastiṅḥ’ and so forth;
‘vidmā hi tvā’ and so forth. This is from the root *vid* in the *loṭ* mood, where the substitution of *mas* for *as* occurs by the rule ‘sa utamasya’ (Pāṇini 3.4.98).
There is the elision of the letter *sakāra*; and because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is the elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*śap*).

115. *Karṇe lakṣaṇasyāviṣṭāṣṭapañcamaṇibhinnaccchinnaccchidrasravasvastikasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.115). That by which the connection with a particular owner is indicated is a *lakṣaṇa*, i.e., a mark or sign. [The suffix *kan* is applied after words denoting such marks when they refer to an ear. For example: *aviṣṭakarṇa*, *aṣṭakarṇa*, *pañcakarṇa*, *maṇikarṇa*, *bhinnakarṇa*, *cchinnakarṇa*, *cchidrakarṇa*, *sravakarṇa*, and *svastikakarṇa*. These denote ears marked respectively by a line, the number eight, the number five, a jewel, a perforation, a cut, a hole, a discharge, or a svastika symbol. The term *lakṣaṇa* is used because it serves as a means of perceiving (*lakṣyate*) the relationship to a specific owner.

Regarding the term "dātrākarṇaḥ": "dātra" is like a sickle; by way of similarity, it refers to a mark having that shape. He who has a "dātra" [i.e., such a mark] on his ear is "dātrākarṇaḥ. In the same way, it should be understood that in subsequent cases as well, it is simply a *bahuvrīhi* compound. That which has two qualities (*guṇa*) is "dviguṇaḥ"; it also refers to that which has the form of those [qualities].

The mark is double [the size]. This word *guṇa* signifies "binding. The compound *dvyaṅgulam* is the combination of two fingers; the suffix of the compound is added according to the rule *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.86). Thus, the mark is also in the shape of two fingers.
"Two finger-breadths. [The question is: "Is it the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) that is understood here? Why is this so?

Because of the inclusion of the word *lakṣaṇa*, if it were taken in a general sense such that whatever is characterized by anything at all were to be understood as the *lakṣaṇa*, then he would have said simply "of the mark" (*cihnasya*), for in that way the sūtra would be more concise. Therefore, [it refers to] the inclusion of the mark (*cihna*).

It is observed that by the mention of the word *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic) made in the rule to be formulated (*kartavye*), it is intended to establish the meaning that a specific characteristic (*lakṣaṇaviśeṣa*) is to be understood here, and not merely a characteristic in general. And so it has been said: "By a gesture, by a glance, or by a great series of sūtras, [the intention is conveyed] here."

"The intentions of the Teachers are being indicated. Now, one might object: by the mention of "indicating" (*lakṣaṇa*), it is understood here that a specific indication is intended, rather than indication in general;
however, since this specific distinction has not been shown by the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*), how is it to be determined? [The answer is: from the Teachers...

Because of its inclusion [in the definition]. For example, "one with beautiful ears" (*śobhanakarṇaḥ*). Although this is also indicated by it, a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of such a kind is not what is intended here; nor is "beauty" recognized in common usage as a characteristic. Therefore, this serves as a counter-example.

116. *Nahi-vṛti-vṛṣi-vyadhi-ruci-sahi-taniṣu kvau* (Pāṇini 6.3.116). Regarding the root *ṇaha* "to bind" (Dhātupāṭha 1166): from *upanahyate*, the form *upānat* is derived by adding the suffix *kvip* because it belongs to the *sampadādi* group; then, by the rule *naho dhaḥ* (8.2.34), the substitution of *dha* for *na* occurs, followed by the application of *jaśtva* and *cartva*.

It is called *pariṇat* because it "encircles" (*pariṇahyati*); the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *upasargādasamāse* (Pāṇini 8.4.14). It is called *nivṛt* because it "returns" (*nivartate*); the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 3.2.178). In the same way, the suffix *kvip* alone is to be understood in the subsequent cases as well. [The root] *vṛṣu* means "to sprinkle."

From the root *vṛṣ* (DhP 706), "to rain," we derive *prāvṛṭ* [the rainy season]. The retroflex *ṣ* undergoes *jaś*-tva, becoming *ḍ*; then, by *cartva*, that *ḍ* becomes *t*. From the root *vyadh* (DhP 1181), "to pierce," we derive *marmavit* ("one who pierces the vital spots"). By the rule governing *grahyādi* (Pāṇini 6.1.16), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). From the root *ruc*...

In the sense of "shining" (*dīpti*), [the root] *ruc* is used—according to the Dhātupāṭha (745): *ṭhruca dīptāvabhiprītau ca*. *Nirocana* becomes *nīruk* by the rule *ṭhcoḥ kuḥ* (8.2.30). [The term] *ṛtīṣaṭ* means "one who endures distress" (*ṛtiṃ sahate*). In the rule *ṭhsaheḥ pṛtanartābhyāñja* (8.3.107), the word *saheḥ* is used.
The substitution of *ṣ* occurs either due to the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) or because the particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.

[The derivation of] *parītat* is from the root *tan* with the prefix *pari*; when the nasalization (*anunāsika*) is elided, *tuk* is inserted. But by what rule is the nasalization elided here? He says: "In the case of *gam* before *kvip*," and so forth.

"It is desired [only] when there is both a destination (*gati*) and an agent (*kāraka*). For that purpose, the term *vibhāṣā* ("optionally") is understood to carry over from rule 6.3.106, *vibhāṣā puruṣe*; and that should be understood as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).

117. [The substitution of] *ṇ* occurs for the *n* of words such as *koṭara*, *kiṃśulaka*, and others, when compounded with *vana* or *giri* to form a name (*saṃjñā*). For example, *koṭarāvaṇam*. This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). The substitution of *ṇ* is applied by the rule "the *n* of *vana* is replaced by *ṇ* when preceded by *puru*, *ga*, etc. (Pāṇini 8.4.4).

118. *vale* (Pāṇini 6.3.118). It is the suffix *valac* that is understood here, not the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Some maintain that this is obtained through the application of the term *bahulam* (diversely), which will be mentioned later, by means of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*) method.
Immediately thereafter, by virtue of the association with the suffix *matup* which is about to be described, [the rule applies] when followed by *cet*.
119. *matau bahvaco'najirādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.3.119).

In examples such as *vrīhimatī*, the suffix *matup* is applied as previously explained. However, in the case of *valayavatī*, the suffix *matup* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.94: *tadasyāstyasminniti matup*.

120. And [the suffix *matup* is applied] after *śara* and so forth. (6.3.120) This rule is commenced because the previous one does not cover cases where the word has more than two syllables. For example, *śarāvatī*. Here, the suffix *matup* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.85]: "The suffix *matup* is applied after a word denoting a river."

121. *iko vahe 'pīloḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.121). [The form] *ṛṣīvahaḥ* (or *ṛṣīvaham*, according to the Kāśikā) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). The word *vaha-* ends in the suffix *ac* (by Pāṇini 3.1.134, *pacādyac*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "ṭhapīlvādīnām": the meaning is that this rule prescribing the lengthening of the vowel *i* does not apply to words such as *pīlu*; thus, the sūtra must be explained in this sense. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: here too, the term *bahulam* (optionally) applies as before, and by means of it—
By virtue of the word *pīlu*, length will not occur for some other [vowels] as well.

122. *Upasargasya ghañy amanuṣye bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.3.122). Since a suffix *ghan* alone cannot occur after a prefix (*upasarga*), it is understood that the grammatical operation applies when a word ending in *ghan* follows as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Thus he says: "when a word ending in *ghan* is the subsequent member," and so forth. [The example is] *vīkledaḥ*.

The root *klid* (in the sense of becoming moist; *klidū* according to the Dhātupāṭha) takes the suffix *ghañ* by the rule *akartari ca kārake...* (Pāṇini 3.3.19). Regarding the word *vīmārgaḥ*: the root *mṛj* (in the sense of purification; *mṛjū* according to the Dhātupāṭha) undergoes *vṛddhi* by the rule *mṛjervṛddhiḥ* (7.2.114) and the substitution of *k* for *c* and *j* by the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇyatoḥ* (7.3.52).
Thus [is explained] the substitution of *ku* for *ṣ*. Regarding the word "prasevaḥ": the root is *ṣivu* (DhP 1108), meaning "to sew" or "to weave.
Regarding the word "kṛtrimam": that which is produced by means of an instrument (*karaṇa*) is "kṛtrima"; the meaning is that which is brought into existence through human activity and so forth.

Regarding the word "niṣāda": the root *ṣadlṛ* (in the sense of "falling apart," "going," and "sinking down") [is used here]. It is called *niṣāda* because sin (*pāpa*) sinks down (*niṣīdati*) in it. The suffix *ghañ* is applied by the rule *halaśca* (Pāṇini 3.3.121).

123. *ikaḥ kāśe* (6.3.123). Regarding the example *ṭhnīkāśaḥ*: the root *kāsṛ* means "to shine" (DhP 647). This word *kāśa* ends in the suffix *ac* (from the *pacādi* group), and not in the suffix *ghañ*. The intention [of the author] is that [the desired form] is already established by the preceding rule (*ikaḥ kiti*, 6.1.71).

Some texts state: "Since this is already established by the preceding rule, this [sūtra] is for the sake of restriction—namely, that only the *ika* vowel is lengthened before *kāśa*, and not any other. However, this is not tenable; for while the preceding rule prescribes lengthening before the suffix *ghañ*, this word *kāśa* ends in the suffix *ac* (from the *pacādi* group). [If it were argued: "But [the lengthening occurs] because of the mention of the term *bahulam* (‘diversely’),"...

It is said that even if [the suffix] *ac* is added after the root *pac* (as in *paca*), the form is already established by the preceding rule; and since the suffix *ika* will likewise not occur for other roots due to the mention of "variously" (*bahulagrahaṇa*) in that very rule, this present sūtra need not have been composed at all.
Even if it were composed, it should be regarded as merely an elaboration (*prapañca*) of the preceding rule.

124. *dasti* (Pāṇini 6.3.124). This means "that which is a substitute for the root *dā* beginning with the letter *t*. By this, it is understood that the genitive case in *daḥ* expresses a relationship between the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*). [The example] *vītam* is formed from the root *dā* in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*).
[The word] *rūpam*. [Objection: But surely, in this case, a substitute beginning with *t* cannot possibly follow;
for instance, as for the *t* in [the rule] *ṭhaca upasargāt* (Pāṇini 7.4.47), by the statement *alontyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52), it is applied to the final [element], and that is a different phoneme.

Because of the intervention [of the long vowel], a *t* sound cannot occur immediately after [the *d*]; furthermore, even that *t* which is prescribed for the *d* by the rule "ṭhkhari ca" (Pāṇini 8.4.55) is likewise impossible; for when the lengthening is to be applied, the substitution of *c* (*cartva*) is non-existent due to its being considered asiddha (unestablished). Therefore, he says: "aC... [referring to Pāṇini 1.1.69].

Regarding the passage beginning with "upasargāt" and so forth: "āśrayaṇa" means taking recourse to or acceptance. In the rule concerning the substitution of "dā," when a substitute beginning with the letter *t* follows, the author states that a long vowel occurs for a prefix ending in *i*; by saying this, he has accepted the rule of *cartva* (the change of *c* to *t*), for otherwise a substitute beginning with *t* would not follow.
It is possible; therefore, because the substitution of *c* is resorted to, the rule is established.

Thus, the substitute begins with the letter *t*. Regarding the form "nitīrṇam": from the root *tṛ* (DhP 969), meaning "to swim" or "to cross," the substitution of *i* for *ṛ* occurs by Pāṇini 7.1.100 (*ṛta id dhātoḥ*).

The lengthening [of the vowel] is by the rule *ṭhhali ca* (8.2.77). The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* is by the rule *ṭhaṭkupvāṅ* (8.4.2), etc. Regarding the form *sudatam*: in the rule *ṭhdo dadghoḥ* (7.4.46), it is stated:
"In the sense of the beginning of an action, one says *avadata*, *vidata*, and *prādata*."
It is intended that [the forms] *sudatam*, *anudatam*, and *nidatam* are likewise [derived].
In the *tyad*-class [of pronouns], the substitute *dada* is applied to the root *dā* (to give).
125. *aṣṭanaḥ saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 6.3.125). Regarding the example "aṣṭāvakraḥ": it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one who has eight crooked things."
126. And in the Vedic language (*cchandasi*).

[As in] *aṣṭākapālaḥ*. [The analysis is: "prepared on eight potsherds" (*aṣṭasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtam*); thus, by the rule *saṃskṛtam* (Pāṇini 4.4.3), the suffix *aṇ* is applied. That [suffix] is then elided by the rule *dvigor lug anapatye* (Pāṇini 4.1.88).

"ṭhaṣṭāhiraṇyā" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. "When the elision of 'pāda' has been performed" refers to [the rule] "pādasya lopo'hastyādibhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.138). "In the case of 'go' when joined," and so forth; "it should be stated" means that this must be explained.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: the particle *ca* is employed here, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. By means of it, the long vowel of *aṣṭan* occurs even in the secular (*bhāṣā*) language when it is joined with *go*.

127. *citaḥ kapi* (Pāṇini 6.3.127). [The example is] *ekacitīkaḥ*. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one who has one layer" (*ekā citir asya*). Then, by the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat* (6.3.34) et cetera, there is the substitution of the masculine form; subsequently, by the rule *śeṣādvibhāṣā* (5.4.154), the suffix *kapa* is added.
Thus ends [the section on] *kap*.

128. *viśvasya vasurāṭoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.128). [The examples are] *viśvāvasuḥ* and *viśvārāṭ*. In *viśvāvasuḥ*, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose wealth (*vasu*) is everything (*viśva*). In *viśvārāṭ*, it means "he who rules (*rājate*) over everything (*viśvasmin*)" [and thus forms the stem *viśvarāj*]. The suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *satsūdviṣadruhaduhayujavidabhidacchidajinīrājām upasaṃkhyānam* (Vārttika on Pāṇini 3.2.61).

By the rule *vraścādi* (Pāṇini 8.2.36), there is the substitution of *ṣ*; by the rule *ṭhjhalāṃ jaśonte* (8.2.39), there is *jaś*-ness for that [ṣ], resulting in the letter *ḍ*; and for the letter *ḍ*, there is also *cartva*, resulting in the letter *ṭ*.
"Where this form of it occurs"—but where, indeed, does this form of it occur? Where there is the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of a "word" (*pada*).

Because the rules for [substituting] *ṣ* and other letters are prescribed under the heading of *pada*, [one might think that *pada*-status applies here]. However, in the case of "viśvarājau" and "viśvarājaḥ," there is no designation as *pada*, because of the prohibition [contained in] Pāṇini 1.4.17: "not before a case-ending (*asarvanāmasthāna*)."

129. [The substitution of *i* for the final vowel of a prefix occurs] before a word beginning with *saṃjñā*. (6.3.129) 130. [The same substitution occurs] before *mitra*, provided it is a name of a Ṛṣi. (6.3.130) 131. [The same substitution occurs] before the suffix *-mat*, when the words *soma*, *aśvin*, *indriya*, or *viśvadevya* precede it in a mantra. (6.3.131)

132. And [the substitution of *o* for the final vowel of] *oṣadhi* occurs before a case-ending other than the first. (6.3.132) 133. In a *ṛc*, the substitution of *tu* [for *tun*, *gha* for *gham*, *akṣu* for *akṣu*, *taṅ* for *taṅ*, *ku* for *ku*, *tru* for *tru*, and *ruṣya* for *ruṣya*] occurs. (6.3.133) The term *taṅ* is a collective designation (*pratyāhāra*)—beginning from the third person plural (*jhi*) up to the second person plural (*thas*).

[The word] *mahiṅ* [is used] with the syllable *ṅkāra*. In the verse "ā tu na indra vṛtrahan," where *ā tu naḥ* was expected, so too in subsequent instances, one should understand that a long vowel (*dīrgha*) is used where a short vowel (*hrasva*) would otherwise occur.
[The form] *lasāt* is derived from the root *las*, meaning "to adhere" or "to play" (DhP 7.14), used here in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*).

This is the form of the *liṅ* (optative). Now, why is there no inclusion here of the two suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* by means of the mention of *gha*? Because it is impossible for a word ending in those [suffixes] that has undergone lengthening (*dīrgha*) to be used in the domain of the *ṛk*.
[The example] "bharata" [is derived from]: *bhṛ* "to support" (DhP 898) [or *bhṛñ* "to support" (DhP)].

This form is derived from the root *bharj* (or *bharts*, according to some) in the sense of "threatening" (or "supporting," according to some), in the third person plural of the imperative mood. [The example is] "Listen, O pressing-stones! (*śrṇota grāvāṇaḥ*). However, in this case [the rule does not apply]; for "all grammatical rules are optional in the Vedic language."
Because of the statement [in the *Pāṇinīya-vṛtti*]: "(pu.pa.vṛ.56). Regarding the word 'atra': this is a form ending in the suffix *tral*.

When *tral* is applied by the rule 'saptamyāstral' (5.3.10), the substitution of *aś* for *etad* is made by the rule 'etado'ś' (5.3.5). Regarding 'uruṣyāṇaḥ': he desires a wide space (*uru*) for himself."

From the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8), the suffix *kyac* is applied; thereafter, by the supplementary rule (*vārttika*) *sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ lālasāyām asuk vaktavyaḥ* (Vārttika 824), the suffix *asuk* is added. Then, by the rule *suṣāmādiṣu ca* (Pāṇini 8.3.98), the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs.

The singular number of the middle person [ending] *loṇ* (the imperative suffix *hi*) undergoes elision by the rule *ato heḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.105). Regarding the word *na*: this is the substitute for the first-person plural ending *as* according to the rule *bahuvacanasya vasnasau* (8.1.21);
the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*, however, occurs through a transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyaya*), as prescribed by the rule *upasargādbahulam* (8.4.28).
Or [it is derived] from the rule regarding frequent usage (*bahulavacana*). Others, however, declare that "uruṣya" is an irregular form (*nipāta*).

134. *ikaḥ suñi* (6.3.134). The term *suñ* here is a reference to the particle (*nipāta*). [In the example] *abhi ṣu ṇaḥ*, there is lengthening of the word *abhi*. There is the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *suñaḥ* (8.3.105). The form *naḥ* is the substitute for the pronoun *asmad*.

By the rule *tasya ṭhnaśca dhātusthoruṣubhyaḥ* (8.4.27), there is the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*. By the rule *ūrṣva ū ṣu ṇaḥ*, there is the lengthening of the vowel *u*. 135. *dvyaco'tastiṅḥ* (6.3.135).

In "ṭhaśvā bharata vājinaḥ," this is the form of the verb *bhṛ* in the second person plural of the imperative (*loṭ*). In "dakṣi pakṣi," the suffix *sip* follows the roots *vac* and *yaj* in the subjunctive (*leṭ*), with the *śap* augment added for the agent (*kartari śap*, Pāṇini 3.1.68). Due to *vac* belonging to the *adādi* class, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap*.
Also from the root *yaj*, [the suffix *kvip* is applied] by the rule "In the Veda, diversely" (Pāṇini 2.4.76).
136. *nipātasya ca*. (Pāṇini 6.3.136) [Examples:
*ṭhevā te*, *acchā te*. The words *eva* and *accha* are particles (*nipāta*), because they are listed among the *cādi* group.

137. *anyeṣām api dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 6.3.137). The word *ṛci* is no longer in force. [The example is] *keśākeśi*. This battle was fought seizing each other by the hair; thus, by the rule *tatra tena* (2.2.27) et cetera, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed with the suffix *ic*.

The suffix *ic* is applied as a compound-ending (*samāsānta*) by the rule *karmavyatihāre* (5.4.127). Regarding the form *jalāṣāṭ*: [the word *jala*] means "it endures water"; the suffix *ṣvin* is applied by the rule *chandasi sahaḥ* (3.2.63), and the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs by the rule *saheḥ ṣāḍaḥ ṣaḥ* (8.3.56).

Regarding "ṭhśvādantaḥ": this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the dog's tooth. Regarding "śvādaṃṣṭraḥ": this is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*) meaning "one whose fangs are like those of a dog.
