Examples such as "śvākarṇaḥ" (dog-eared) and others are either genitive compounds or possessive compounds.

138. *cau* (6.3.138). Regarding the example *dadhīcaḥ*: [the word] *dadhyañc* is derived by the suffix *kvin* according to Pāṇini 3.2.59 (*ṛtvig-ādinā*), followed by the nominative plural suffix *śas*;
then, by 6.4.138 (*acaḥ*), there is the elision of the vowel *a*. Now, an objection:

Because it is *antaraṅga* (internal), the substitution of *yaṇ* [for *i*] must occur here before the elision of the vowel (*akāra-lopa*) and before the lengthening; for that [substitution] is *antaraṅga* because it depends on a single phoneme (*varṇa*), whereas the other two [operations] are *bahiraṅga*. Indeed, the elision of the vowel is prescribed for that [stem], and the designation *bha* applies when a suffix beginning with *ya*, a vowel, or *su* follows.

[The objection: "Lengthening (*dīrghatva*) of the prior member is also prescribed when a subsequent member follows; since this depends on two words (*dvipadāśrayatva*), it is *bahiraṅga*. Consequently, once the internal substitution (*yaṇādeśa*) has been applied, the lengthening of the vowel *au* would not be established beforehand. To this, he says: "Even though it is internal," and so forth.

If the substitution of *yaṇ* were to apply alone, then the prescription of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) would be purposeless. Therefore, by the force of the prescription of the long vowel, the substitution of *yaṇ* does not take effect. But one might object: even after the substitution of *yaṇ* has occurred, the state of being immediately followed [by a vowel] required for the long vowel is absent; therefore—

Lengthening will occur even for that which is separated [by intervening elements], just as— according to the rule *śamāmaṣṭānāṃ dīrghaḥ śyani* (Pāṇini 7.3.74)— there is lengthening of the roots beginning with *śam* before the suffix *śyan*;
therefore, there must indeed be the substitution of *yaṇ* here, and thus, when there is lengthening of what is separated [by an intervening element].
If [the rule were applied] first, would there be an undesirable form? This is not the case; rather, let this be considered: what is it?
Would the paribhāṣā "tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya" (P. 1.1.66) be sublated, or rather the antaraṅga-paribhāṣā? In that regard, as for the antaraṅga-paribhāṣā...

Or [it is] established through an indicative mark (*liṅga*) or through inference; for the statement of *ūṅ* in [Pāṇini 6.4.132], "after *vāh*, *ūṭh*," is the indicative mark. And how this is an indicative mark, the author of the Vṛtti will demonstrate in that very place. But the other [type of] paribhāṣā is directly heard [in the text]. In that case, it is appropriate...

When an object inferred [by a rule] is sublated, rather than one directly perceived, the *antaraṅga* paribhāṣā is sublated and not others. Thus, since the lengthening must apply to the immediately preceding [vowel] alone, the substitution of *yaṇ* does not take effect.

139. *samparasaraṇasya* (6.3.139). [Example: *kārīṣāgandhīputraḥ*. [Derivation: From *kārīṣagandhi-* in the sense "the offspring of Kārīṣagandhi," the suffix *aṇ* is applied by *tasyāpatyam* (4.1.92). Then, by *aṇiñoranārṣayoḥ* (4.1.78), etc., the substitution of *ṣyaṅ* occurs.

Then, by the rule *ṣyaṅś ca ap* (Pāṇini 4.1.74), the suffix *cāp* is applied; subsequently, there is a genitive compound meaning "the son of Karīṣagandhyā"; then, by the rule *ṣyaṅḥ saṃprasāraṇam* (Pāṇini 6.1.13) and so forth, the *saṃprasāraṇa* substitution occurs, and by this [rule], lengthening takes place.

"For that is indeed a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (an option restricted by rule). In the sūtra *iko hrasvo'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.3.61), the term *anyatarasyām* is understood to carry over from the preceding sūtra *ikaḥ halsam̐yoge dīrghāt* (6.3.51);
and this is recognized as a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā*. Consequently, [the substitution] does not occur in the case of *kārīṣagandhīputra*.

"Even when not yet performed," and so forth. Alternatively—when *kārīṣagandhiputra* remains with the substitution of semivowels (*samprasāraṇa*) and the lengthening still unperformed, both the rule for shortening and the rule for the lengthening of the semivowel-substitute would apply. Both of these have their respective scopes: the scope for the shortening of *ik* vowels is, for example, *grāmaṇiputra*.

Thus, there is an occasion for *samprasāraṇa*—namely, the absence of shortening (*hrasva*); however, in certain cases, both [rules] would apply. In that situation, although the rule for lengthening (*dīrghatva*) has already served its purpose in the alternative case where shortening is absent, nevertheless, because it is subsequent (*paratva*), the shortening is superseded by it. Now, once lengthening has been applied, why does it not occur again due to the principle of "reapplication" (*punaḥprasaṅga*)?
Does it occur? To this he says: "And the cognition of recurrence," and so forth. The meaning has already been explained.
Thus ends the third quarter of the sixth chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who is like a Bodhisattva.
Now begins the sixth chapter, the fourth quarter.

1. *Aṅgasya* | (6.4.1) "This is a governing heading (*adhikāra*)"—this is because it is connected with the mark of the circumflex accent (*svarita*). Here, some consider this governing heading of the *aṅga* to be appropriate prior to the modifications of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-vikāra*). For thus...

In the presence of this sūtra, "ṭhguṇo yaṅlukoḥ" (7.4.82), the mention of "luṅ" (elision) need not be made; for even in the case of *yaṅ* elision (*yaṅluk*), the *guṇa* substitution is established by means of the "characteristic of an affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). However, if this governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "aṅga" were to extend until the conclusion of the seventh chapter, [the mention of *luṅ* would be necessary].

Therefore, the mention of *luk* (elision) must necessarily be made; for otherwise, the *guṇa* substitution would not be established in the case of *yaṅ-luk*, because of the prohibition [contained in] "na lumatāṅgasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.63).
This is their intention. But as for the author of the Vṛtti—if...
This section on *aṅga* (the stem) should precede the sections on *abhyāsa* (reduplication) and *vikāra* (modification).

Consequently, in the form *vavraśca*, when the reduplication has been applied to the root *vṛścati* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), the *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization of the semivowel) would occur before the *halādiśeṣa* (retention of the first consonant), by virtue of a prior prohibition; furthermore, this is supported by the force of the rule "ubhayeṣām" (Pāṇini 6.1.15), which indicates that [the *samprasāraṇa*] applies even to the subsequent [elements].

The *samprasāraṇa* would take effect, overriding the *halādiśeṣa*; and consequently, after the formation of the single substitute by the rule "from *samprasāraṇa*" (6.1.108), the substitution of *u* by "for *u*" (7.4.66), the replacement of *u* by *r*, and the application of *halādiśeṣa*, the *samprasāraṇa* of the *v* would also undesirably follow. Ā...

Up until the completion of the seventh chapter, since there is again the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning suffixes (*aṅga*), in the case of [the rule] *ṭhuraT* (Pāṇini 7.4.66), because it has a subsequent cause, the suffix is accepted as the cause. Therefore, due to having a subsequent cause, by the rule *uraT-avaṅ-sārvadhātuka-ārdhadhātukayoḥ* (6.4.77), there is the substitution of *avaṅ* for the *u* sound; and by the rule *samparasarvaṇam* (6.1.37), there is the substitution of *v* for the *v* sound.

The substitution of *samprasāraṇa* is prohibited. Prior to the modifications of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), since the governing rule for the stem (*aṅga*) still applies, the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) would not apply to the substitution of *ru* for *rad*, because its cause lies outside [the stem]. Consequently, the rule "there is no *samprasāraṇa* when a *samprasāraṇa* has already occurred" (Pāṇini 6.1.37) [would not apply].
Because there would be no prohibition, the *samprasāraṇa* of the letter *v* would indeed occur;

consequently, the undesirable form *uvraśca* would result. Therefore, the governing rule (*adhikāra*) for the *aṅga* [the stem] is appropriate from this point up to the end of the seventh chapter, and not otherwise.
Thinking that [the rules] apply prior to the modifications resulting from practice, he says:
"up to the completion of the seventh chapter. However, beyond the completion of the seventh chapter, operations are prescribed under the governing rule *padasya* (8.1.16). Therefore...

In this context, the governing rule for the suffix *aṅ* does not apply. From the root *hveñ* (or *hveñ* with the variant *śabde ca*) in the sense of "rivalry" (*spardhā*)—as per Dhātupāṭha 1008—the *niṣṭhā* suffix [is applied]; because it belongs to the *yajādi* group, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*).
Thus, we have *hīnaḥ*. From the root *jyā* in the sense of "loss of vitality" (*vayohānau*)—as per Dhātupāṭha 1499—[the form *jīnaḥ* is derived].

In the word *saṃvītaḥ*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule *grahyādisūtreṇa* (Pāṇini 6.1.16), and the substitution of *ṇatva* for the final consonant by the rule *lvādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.44). [The root] *vyeñ* in the sense of "covering" (Dhātupāṭha 1007) undergoes vocalization by the rule *vacyādinā* (Pāṇini 6.1.15).

Regarding the forms *nirūtam* and *durūtam*: from the root *veñ* (meaning "to weave," DhP 1006), there is a *samprasāraṇa* substitution as before. Even in the absence of the governing heading of *aṅga* (the "stem" section), when a consonant (*hal*) belonging to *ni* or *dur* is a member [of the following element], the *samprasāraṇa* vowel that follows it should be long. This occurs within the scope of the *aṅga* heading.

Furthermore, since it is understood that the lengthening applies to a stem (*aṅga*) which ends in a *samprasāraṇa* that follows a consonant (*hal*) which is a member (*avayava*) of that stem, there is no occasion for the application of lengthening here. For in this case, the *samprasāraṇa* does not follow a consonant that is a member of the stem— as in the example "agnīnām."

By the rule *ṭhhrasvanadyāpo nuṭ* (Pāṇini 7.1.54), [the augment *nuṭ* is added]. As in the examples "kṛmiṇāṃ paśya" (look at the ones with worms) and "pāmanāṃ paśya" (look at the ones with scabs). [The forms] *kṛmiṇām* and *pāmanām* are derived as follows: from the sense "that in which worms exist" and "that in which scabs exist," the suffix *na* is applied by the rule *lomādi* (Pāṇini 5.2.100); then the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added; and finally, this is the accusative singular case-ending (*am*). By the rule *ami pūrvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.107), the preceding vowel and the *am* coalesce into a single long vowel.

By [Pāṇini 6.1.107], there is the substitution of the preceding form (*pūrvarūpatvam*). If the term *aṅgasya* ("of the stem") were not governed here, then in this case as well, there would be lengthening of the vowels in the words *krimi* and *pāman* before a suffix marked with *ṅ* or *ñ* (i.e., *nām*).

However, when the governing rule for the stem (*aṅgādhikāra*) is in effect, there is no such fault; for in this instance, the stems *krimi* and *pāman* are not followed by a suffix marked with *ṅ* or *ñ*.

There is indeed a state of being a subordinate member (*aṅgatva*) [in relation] to another; however, in the case of the suffix *na*, as in "brāhmaṇabhissā" (the Brahmin’s rice) and "odanabhissiṭā" (the rice-gruel that has been soaked), the words *bhissā* and *bhissiṭā* both end in the feminine suffix *ṭāp*.

Among these, one denotes rice (*odana*), while the other denotes that which has been soaked in it. By means of these two, [the relationship is established] respectively with the words *brāhmaṇa* and *odana*.

This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). In that case, even in the absence of the governing rule regarding "limbs" (*aṅga*), the substitution of *ais* for *bhis* would undesirably apply to the words *brāhmaṇa* and *odana*, which are not themselves "limbs.

Now, one might object: according to the principle "when a meaningful element is mentioned, an element lacking meaning is not included" (*arthavadgrahaṇe nānarthakasya*), as stated in the Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 1...
In cases such as *krimiṇām* and *pāmanām*, the lengthening [of the vowel] will not occur;

likewise, in *brāhmaṇabhissaudanabhiḥ* and *iṣṭe*, the substitution of *ais* will also not occur. For in these instances, neither the nominal stem (*nāman*) possesses meaning, nor does the suffix *bhis*. Why, then, is the governing rule for "stem" (*aṅga*) established for the purpose of excluding those cases?
Thus he says: "The section on *aṅga*," and so forth; "also [the lengthening] of the name (*nāman*) due to its long vowel," and so forth. By the word "etc.

(*ādi*), the substitution *ais* in "ato bhisa ais" (Pāṇini 7.1.9) is included. The particle *iti* indicates a reason. For, if the governing heading of *aṅga* were not present, the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule "halaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.2) would not occur as it does [in cases such as *nāmibhiḥ*].
Just as the substitution of *jī* for *hū* occurs in the case of *hūtaḥ*, so too would it occur in the case of *nirhūtam*;

and just as the lengthening of the vowel prescribed by the rule *ṭhajjhanagamāṃ sani* (Pāṇini 6.4.16) occurs in *cikīrṣati*, so too would it occur in *dadhi sanoti* and *madhu sanoti*; and [the rule] *erliṅ* (Pāṇini 6.4.67).
Just as the substitution of *e* by rule 6.4.68 (*ṭhV-anya-saṃyogāder guṇaḥ*) occurs in *gleyāt*, it would likewise occur in *niryāyāt* and *nirvāyāt*.

Therefore, the governing heading for the *aṅga* (the stem) must necessarily be established for the sake of such cases; and while being formulated for other purposes, it [serves this function as well].

It also establishes [the length of] vowels such as *ā* and *ī*, and restricts them to the intended object by excluding them from other objects. Therefore, this *paribhāṣā* need not be resorted to for that purpose;
for the sense is that a *paribhāṣā* is indeed resorted to only when there is no other way.

But surely, by the rule "The sixth case [denotes] a relation of substitution" (Pāṇini 1.1.49), the term *aṅgasya* is a genitive of place (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*); consequently, in the rule "For *bhisa*, there is *ais* after *at*" (Pāṇini 7.1.9), this word ending in the fifth case would not be in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *aṅgasya* ending in the sixth case.

Because of the difference in case endings (*bhinnavibhaktikatvāt*). For if that were the case, then in the rule *satyāp-a-kār-ant-āt* [P. 7.3.33], the substitution of *ais* for the following *bhiss* would result; and in the rule *ūdupadhāyā gohaḥ* (P.
6.4.89), the genitive *gohaḥ*—which is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*)—would, by the rule *alo'ntyasya* (P. 1.1.52), apply to the final letter.

Because of the summary at the end [of the section] with the word *iti*, and by virtue of the force of the mention of the penultimate (*upadhā*), the substitution of *ū* would apply to the final letter of *goh*.
Furthermore, in the rule *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.34), the genitive case in *śāsaḥ*—
which is understood as a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) referring to the penultimate— is also [to be understood in this way].

Because of the finality [of the rule] and because of the force of the continued application of the term *upadhā*, it might be thought that the substitution of *i* for the final letter of the root *śās* applies to the penultimate (*upadhā*) as well; in order to refute this objection, he says: "Of the *aṅga*"—this [genitive] expresses a general relationship.

"Sixth case," and so forth. "In the general relation" means in the mere relation without any specific qualification. Having proceeded by adopting a general relation that does not depend on any particularity for the sake of encompassing various relations, [the rule] applies accordingly to subsequent *lakṣaṇa*-sentences with distinct meanings.

It abides in specific instances (*viśeṣa*). In some places it becomes a conjunction (*yoga*), as in "the substitution of *ja* for *han*" (Pāṇini 6.4.36), and so forth. In other places it concerns the relationship between cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika-sambandha*), as in "for *yu* and *vu*, there are *na* and *aka*" (Pāṇini 7.1.1), and so forth. For just as [the word] *devadattasya* is one...

Through the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*), it functions with respect to kinsmen, limbs, and so forth; being differentiated by various relations such as the state of producer and produced, it presents itself appropriately according to specific relations—such as "Devadatta’s son," "the hand," or "the blanket"—and likewise in the case of the word *aṅgasya* (of the limb). In that sentence where...

In rules such as *ṭhśāsa idaṅhaloḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.34), a specific relation exists—whether that of a constituent part (*avayava*) or something else; there, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) should be understood according to the appropriate connection with a constituent part or the like. Where no such [specific] relation exists, the genitive denotes the "place" (*sthāne*), as in *ṭhhanterjaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.36).

Thus, in such cases as these, how is it that this genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is understood to denote a general relationship (*sambandhasāmānya*), given that it has been stated: "The genitive [is used] in connection with the element to be replaced" (*ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*, Pāṇini 1.1.49)? He thinks as follows: not every genitive denotes the element to be replaced; rather, it is that whose indicator (*liṅga*) consists of the word *kalā* and so forth.

It is so asserted; for otherwise, the mention of the word *sthāna* in the rule *ṭhudīcāmātaḥ sthāne yaṇ* (Pāṇini 1.1.50) would be purposeless. Therefore, it is stated that only that specific genitive case which has its indicator (*liṅga*) such as *kalā* and so forth is called "connected with the place" (*sthāneyoga*). And not this [other] one...

The *liṅga* beginning with *kalā* is what is being proposed; therefore, this cannot be a case of substitution (*sthāne-yoga*). [This refers to] the phrase "Or rather," etc., concerning the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) *aṅga*.

Only that meaning which is intended [by the speaker] is governed by the rule, and not this form of the word *iṅ* itself. The word *mātra* (only) serves to exclude the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*). For this very reason, he says: "that in which the meaning of the case-ending is not intended to be expressed" (*avivakṣitavibhaktyartham*). That in which the meaning of the case-ending is not intended (*na vivakṣitaḥ*) with respect to the mere meaning (*arthamātre*), is described as such.

Since this is so, the rule *ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā* does not apply here; for that paribhāṣā was formulated for the purpose of excluding other relations when multiple relations are possible. Therefore, where [only] one relation...

In that very context, it is intended [to be applied] for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*), and no genitive relationship (*ṣaṣṭhī-sambandha*) is intended here; its employment is solely for the sake of formal mention (*nirdeśārtha*). Indeed, since a mention must necessarily be made by some case-ending or other, the genitive was employed for the mention.
But surely, the governing scope (*adhikāra*) is established by means of the circumflex accent (*svarita*), and that is a property of the word, not a property of the meaning.
Therefore, how can a meaning devoid of the circumflex accent be made the subject of the governing rule? This is not a fault;
for the meaning conveyed by the word *aṅga* is itself essentially of the nature of the word. For it is thus: because...
The designation *aṅga* (base) has been prescribed for a word beginning with a suffix (*pratyaya*) and ending with an affix (*ādi*).

"In the subsequent [rules], this is transformed as appropriate," and so forth. Depending on the sense, in some cases it is understood as having the genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*), and in other cases as having another case-ending; for example: *āḍhyo rbadhaveyaḥ*.
"Devadatta, his houses are high; invite this Devadatta.

In that case, when there is a change of case-ending in the rule *ṭhato bhisa ais* (Pāṇini 7.1.9), the meaning takes such a form as: "The substitution of *ais* for *bhis* occurs after an *aṅga* (stem) ending in the letter *ṭha* (*t*) or *tha*."

It is accomplished. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the rule "for the *ṅs* following *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, *aś* is substituted" is included. Because of the word "api" (also), the genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) and others are also fully encompassed. However, in the previous explanation, [the substitution of] *ais* for *bhis* after *at* (as in Pāṇini 7.1.9) was not [included].

Thus, this genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) should be understood as expressing the relationship between the cause (*nimitta*) and the caused (*naimittika*). In that regard, the meaning of the rule (*sūtra*) is as follows: "For a stem (*aṅga*) ending in the vowel *a*, the [suffix] *bhis* which belongs to it becomes *ais*. Consequently, it does not occur in cases such as *brāhmaṇabhiḥ*. For what is the *bhis* belonging to the stem? That which belongs to it...
[The rule states: "The substitution of *ais* occurs for *bhis*. But what is the cause (*nimita*) for that [substitution]?
It is the fact that *bhis* is a suffix (*pratyaya*) occurring after something else (*parabhūta*), such that the designation "suffix" applies to it. And in what does this occur? In a suffix.
Now, in examples such as *brāhmaṇaiḥ*, *bhis* is not a suffix; therefore, how could there be any occasion for the substitution of *ais* for it?
This triad—the mention of *aṇ*, the mention of *samprasāraṇa*, and the mention of *dīrgha*—is carried over [from the preceding rules].
But from where is the mention of *aṇ* brought down as the subject? From the rule: *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho’ṇaḥ* ("When *ḍh* or *l* is elided, the long vowel of the preceding *aṇ* [is substituted]").

(6.3.111) From this [point]. But surely, that [term] has been excluded by the mention of *ik* in the rule "ikaḥ kāśe" (6.3.123); so how can it be carried over here? This is not a fault, for by the mention of *ik*, only the *aṇ* is qualified—namely, an *aṇ* that is not *ik*. Therefore...

Due to the absence of contradiction, the inclusion of *aṇ* is excluded by the inclusion of *ig*. But if the inclusion of *aṇ* is restricted by the inclusion of *ig*, then in forms such as *avācā* and *svarācā*, lengthening (*dīrghatva*) would not occur. [To this we reply: In the rule *cau* (Pāṇini 6.3.138), the inclusion of *aṇ* itself will be carried over (*anuvartisyate*) here.

However, because the mention of *ig* has been suspended, this is not a fault. Or rather— even though the mention of *aṇ* was excluded by the mention of *ig*, it nevertheless recurs here according to the maxim of the frog’s leap (*maṇḍūakapluti*).

But surely, just as the rule *aṅgasya* (6.4.1) is both an injunction (*vidhi*) and a governing heading (*adhikāra*), so too is the rule *śeṣe* (4.2.92). Consequently, since forms such as *hūtaḥ* and *jīnaḥ* would be established by this very [rule], the statement *halaḥ* (6.4.2) would be purposeless; therefore, it should certainly not be formulated.
Thinking thus, he asks: "What is the purpose of *halaḥ*?"—meaning, for what reason is this rule *halaḥ* commenced? [The answer is:

"In the case of *utaḥ* and *utavān*. For if this rule did not exist, and it were merely stated that "lengthening occurs for a base (*aṅga*) ending in *saṃprasāraṇa*," then lengthening would also apply here.

It may be so; for even this [form] becomes a base (*aṅga*) ending in a *samprasāraṇa* by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). Therefore, the rule *halaḥ* must be applied [to derive forms such as] *viddhaḥ* ("pierced") and *vicitaḥ* ("gathered"). [The roots are] *vyadha* in the sense of "striking" (DhP 1181) and *vyaca*.

In *vyājīkaraṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 1293), there is the suffix *niṣṭhā*; by the rule *grahyādisūtreṇa* (Pāṇini 6.1.16), there is *samprasāraṇa*. Because the rule for lengthening applies to a stem (*aṅga*) that ends in *samprasāraṇa*, the lengthening does not occur here.
Even though [the rule] *vidhyatyadhanuṣā* (4.4.83) and *grahijyāvayivyadhivaṣṭivicati*... [is mentioned].

Because of the mention [in the sūtra] "iti nirdeśāt," it is understood that the long vowel will not occur for the *samprasāraṇa* of a consonant-final element; nevertheless, since this meaning would have to be established by means of an indirect indicator (*jñāpaka*), there would be a resulting heaviness of comprehension (*pratipatti-gaurava*). It is for the purpose of avoiding this that [the following is stated].

It was stated [in the rule] "of that which ends in a *samprasāraṇa*. Regarding the word "third" (*tṛtīya*), by the rules "from *dvi*, the suffix *tīya*" (Pāṇini 5.2.54) and "for *tri*, there is *samprasāraṇa* and [the suffix *tīya*]" (Pāṇini 5.2.55), the suffix *tīya* is applied and *samprasāraṇa* occurs. Does it not possess all the *mātrās* (vowel measures), yet lack the vowel *aṇ*? Why does it lack *aṇ*? Because of the rule "when *ḍha* or *ra* is elided... (*ḍhralope*)... [and so forth].

The term *aṇ* is carried over here from the rule *pūrvād dīrgho’ṇaḥ* (6.3.111). In that [previous] rule, the pratyāhāra is understood by means of the preceding *ṇ* alone; since the vowel *ṛ* is not included therein, this indeed serves as a counter-example. Regarding the phrase "or, as in the case of *tṛtīyā*" and so forth: alternatively, [the word] *aṇ*.

This [rule] has indeed been negated; nevertheless, the long vowel does not occur here because of the specific grammatical convention (nipātana) in the rule "The third case ending is used for the agent and the instrument" (Pāṇini 2.3.18).
Three meanings are possible for the word "of a consonant" (halaḥ): [it may mean] after a consonant...

A long vowel occurs for a *saṃprasāraṇa* at the end of an *aṅga*: this is the first meaning; "a long vowel occurs for a *saṃprasāraṇa* following a consonant that is a member of the *aṅga*"—this is the second; the third, however, has been shown by the author of the *Vṛtti* itself. In that regard, if the first alternative is adopted:

In that case, [the rule] would apply even here: *nirutaṃ* and *durutaṃ*. For here too, the member (*aṅga*) ending in a semivowel (*samprasāraṇa*) has a consonant following it. Now, if the second [interpretation] were intended, then [the rule] would also apply here: *viddhaḥ* and *vicitaḥ*. For here too, there is a semivowel following a consonant that is part of the member. Now...

[One might argue: "Will it not be avoided by the indications [contained] in the rules *ṭhvidhyatyadhanuṣā* (Pāṇini 4.4.83) and *ṭhgrahijyāvayivyadhivaṣṭivicati* (Pāṇini 6.1.16)? And thus, by means of these very indicators, there would indeed be a burden of comprehension regarding the absence of lengthening (*dīrghatva*) in such cases. Therefore, [the author addresses] this very fault...

The third meaning has been shown by the author of the Vṛtti out of a desire to avoid [certain objections]. Here too, this local (deśya) objection is raised: "But surely this meaning of this sūtra is not at all tenable, because the term 'aṅgasya' (of the stem) is mentioned once as the subject under discussion; and that [term] is either a qualifier of the consonant (hal)..."

It might be [the case that the term *aṅga* is mentioned] either for the purpose of understanding the operation as applying to the stem (*aṅga*), or for another reason. In that regard, if the first alternative is adopted, then [the rule would apply] to a stem characterized by its members (*aṅga*) ending in a semivowel (*samprasāraṇa*), and thus the long vowel would not be obtained. If, on the other hand, the second alternative is adopted, then the consonant (*hal*) would not be qualified.

Therefore, the mention of the term *aṅga* (base) must be made twice; for it is not possible to convey both of these meanings with a single [mention]. Thus, in order to refute this objection, he says "the mention of *aṅga*" and so forth, resorting to the principle of repetition (*āvṛtti*). Even though it is one...

For indeed, a thing being repeated is employed in multiple instances; just as a single vessel is used for the act of eating by many people who do not eat simultaneously, so too is this mention of the *aṅga* (base) repeated. In that regard, the suffix *hal* is qualified by the non-repeated [term].
Since the lengthening of the vowel *a* occurs when it is followed by a consonant (*tvaṅgasya*), the meaning is understood in both ways.

3. *nāmi* | (6.4.3) These three—namely, the mention of *aṇ*, the mention of *samprasāraṇa*, and the mention of *dīrgha*—are carried over [from previous rules]. But from where is the mention of *aṇ* derived that was made elsewhere? From the rule: *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho’ṇaḥ* (6.3.111).

From this [it follows]. Now, an objection: since [the suffix] *ika* was excluded by the mention of *ig* in the rule "ikaḥ kāśe" (Pāṇini 6.3.123), how can it be understood here as carrying over? This is not a fault; for by the mention of *ig*, only *aṇ* is qualified—as in "*aṇ* which is *ig*. Therefore, because there is no contradiction, the mention of *aṇ* is not negated by the mention of *ig*.

[The word *aṇ*] is excluded. But if the mention of *ig* qualifies the mention of *aṇ*, then in the cases "avācā" and "svarācā," the lengthening [of the vowel] would not occur. However, in the rule "cau" (Pāṇini 6.3.138), the mention of *aṇ* alone will be carried over here; the mention of *ig*, however—

The objection that [the term] *nivṛtta* is a fault is also not valid. Alternatively—even though the mention of *aṇ* was excluded by the mention of *ig*, nevertheless it recurs here according to the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*).
Now, just as the rule "in the remainder" (*śeṣe*, 4.2.92) is both a prescriptive rule (*vidhi*) and a governing heading (*adhikāra*), so too...

This [rule] "ṭhaṅgasya" (6.4.1) is also [relevant]; and since by this very rule forms such as *hūtaḥ* and *jīnaḥ* are established, the statement "ṭhalaḥ" would be purposeless. Thinking that it therefore ought not to be made at all, he asks: "What is the purpose of 'ṭhalaḥ'? Why is this "ṭhalaḥ" stated?

The meaning is that the Sūtra is now commenced. [Regarding the forms] *uta* and *utavān*: if this Sūtra did not exist, and it were merely stated that "the long vowel occurs for a stem ending in a semivowel (*san-prasāraṇa*)", then lengthening would also occur here [in *uta*].
For even this [form *uta*] exists by virtue of being treated as if it possessed a designation (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*).
A verbal root (*aṅga*) ends with a semivowel (*samparasāraṇa*) or a final consonant; therefore, the rule *ṭhhalaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.3] should be formulated. [Examples are:

*viddhaḥ*, *vicitaḥ*. [The roots] *vyagha* (DhP 1181, meaning "to strike") and *vyaca* (DhP 1293, meaning "to disguise") take the *niṣṭhā* suffix [with the *iṭ* augment], according to the rule *grahy-ādi-sūtra* [Pāṇini 6.1.16].
Regarding *samprasāraṇa*: because the rule refers to a stem (*aṅga*) that ends in *samprasāraṇa*, the long vowel does not occur here.

Even though, based on the indications in the rules "vidhyatyadhanuṣā" (Pāṇini 4.4.83) and "grahijyāvayivyadhivaṣṭivicati" (Pāṇini 6.1.16), it might appear that a long vowel would apply to a *samprasāraṇa* of a consonant-final element, it is not so.

It is understood that [the suffix] will occur; nevertheless, in order to avoid the difficulty of comprehension that might arise when this meaning is being established by means of an indicative rule (*jñāpaka*), it is stated "of that which ends in *samprasāraṇa*. [The form] "third" (*tṛtīya*) is derived from "dvi" by [Pāṇini 5.2.54]: *dvestīyaḥ*.

By the rule *ṭhreḥ samprasāraṇañca* (Pāṇini 5.4.55), there is the suffix *tīya* as well as *samprasāraṇa*. Is it that every *mātrā* exists, but not an *aṇ*? Why is it that an *aṇ* does not exist [in this case]? Because the mention of *aṇ* from the rule *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho’ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.111) is understood (*anuvartate*) here; and in that [rule],...

The inclusion [of the vowel] is by means of the preceding *ṇ* itself in the *pratyāhāra*, and since the *ṛ*-vowel is not situated therein, this indeed serves as a counter-example. Regarding the phrase "or [it is] the third," etc.: alternatively, the term *aṇ* in [Pāṇini 1.1.69] is simply excluded here; nevertheless, the long vowel does not occur in this case.
This is due to the irregular formation (*nipātana*) [of the word *hal*] according to Pāṇini 2.3.18, "The third case ending is used for the agent and the instrument.
Three meanings are possible for this rule, "after *hal*": first, a long vowel is substituted for a stem ending in a semivowel (*samprasāraṇa*) that follows *hal*; this is one meaning.
"The vowel following a consonant (*hal*) that arises from the substitution of semivowels (*samprasāraṇa*) within a member of a compound becomes long"—this is the second [view].

The third, however, was shown by the author of the *Vṛtti* himself. In that regard, if the first position were adopted, then [the rule] would apply even in cases such as *niruttam* and *duruttam*, for here too there is a vowel following a consonant.

The *aṅga* ends in a *samprasāraṇa*. Now, if the second [interpretation] were intended, then [the rule] would apply even in the case of *viddhaḥ* and *vicitaḥ*, because here too there is a *samprasāraṇa* occurring after a consonant (*hal*) that is part of the *aṅga*. Furthermore, consider [the rules]: *vidhyatyadhanuṣā* (Pāṇini 4.4.83) and *grahijyāvayivyadhivaṣṭivicati* (Pāṇini 6.1.16).

Would it not follow from this indication that [the long vowel] will not occur? And consequently, by means of this very indicator, there would certainly be a burden on the understanding regarding the absence of lengthening in such cases. Therefore, with the desire to avoid this very defect, the author of the Vṛtti has presented a third meaning. In this case as well—

This objection is raised: "But surely this meaning of the sūtra is not tenable, because the single mention of 'aṅga' (member) is the subject under discussion. And that [term] must either be a qualifier of 'hal' (consonant), or it must be for the purpose of indicating that the operation applies to the aṅga. In that regard, if the former alternative [is accepted]...

If the first [mention of "aṅga"] were relied upon, it would mean "of a stem (aṅga) ending in a semivowel that is qualified by a suffix," and thus the long vowel would not be obtained. If, on the other hand, the second [mention] were relied upon, then the consonant (hal) would not be qualified.
Therefore, a second mention of "aṅga" must be made; for it cannot be accomplished by one alone.

It is possible to establish both of these points. Therefore, in order to refute this objection, he says "the mention of the 'limb' (aṅga)," etc., relying on the principle of repetition (āvṛtti). For even a single entity, when repeated, can serve multiple purposes; just as one [thing]...

Just as a vessel is for many people who do not eat together in a single act of eating, so too this mention of the "limb" (aṅga) is repeated. Therein, by the non-repeated [word], the *hal* is qualified;
by the repeated [word], however, the lengthening of the limb occurs—thus the comprehension of the meaning is achieved in both ways.

3. *nāmi* | (6.4.3) Because of the governing context (*adhikāra*) of "stem" (*aṅga*), a long vowel is prescribed for the stem when followed by a *nām* [suffix]. And a stem occurs only when followed by an affix (*pratyaya*). However, no *nām* affix has been prescribed anywhere in this grammatical treatise (*śāstra*).

Consequently, it would not be known whose this inclusion of "nām" is; therefore, for the sake of that thorough understanding, he says: "‘nām’ is the genitive plural," and so forth. That to which the augment *nuṭ* has come—that is, has been applied—is "āgatanuṭkam. Alternatively, "āgataḥ" means that the *nuṭ* has arrived or been obtained.
Regarding the example *kartṛṇām*:

how is there lengthening here, since the mention of *aṇ* continues to apply [from the previous rule]? To this he says: "The mention of *aṇ* has been withdrawn. This is because of the rule *na tisṛcatasṛ* (Pāṇini 6.4.4).
The intention is that [the rule] prohibits the lengthening of *tus* and *catasṛ*.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the subsequent [rule]," it refers to Pāṇini 6.4.7, *nopadhāyāḥ*. Here, the purpose is that the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*nopadhā*) should occur when *nām* follows, but not when *ām* follows.

The phrase "lest [it be so]" means that the inclusion of the form *anuṭka* (i.e., *an* with the augment *ṭ*) is for this purpose. Consequently, in the case of *varmaṇām*, the long vowel does not occur.

Furthermore, the inclusion of the form *anuṭka* is for the sake of ensuring the application of the long vowel once the augment *ṭ* has been applied; this is the connection with what was previously stated. As for the passage beginning with "otherwise," etc.: otherwise...

If the inclusion of *nuṭ* along with *ām* were not made, then because *nuṭ* is a part of *ām*, it would be included by the mention of *ām*; consequently, the long vowel [of the penultimate] would have to occur whether *nuṭ* is applied or not. And thus, a rule whose application depends on whether something has been done or not done (*kṛtākṛtaprasaṅga*) is [considered permanent].
Because it is "constant" (nitya), the *nuṭ* augment would supersede even the subsequent [application] and lengthening alone would occur.
This being the case, since the stem (*aṅga*) would not end in a short vowel, the *nuṭ* would simply not apply. Now, one might object:
"The *nuṭ* is not prescribed after a stem ending in a short vowel; and once lengthening has been performed due to its constancy..."

There exists a base (aṅga) ending in a short vowel; in that case, by the force of the statement, there will be a reference to what previously existed (bhūtapūrvagati), such that the augment *nuṭ* occurs after an *ām* following a base that formerly ended in a short vowel. However, it cannot be said [that this applies here], because in the forms *tisṛṇām* and *catasṛṇām*, [the rule] "not for *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*" (*na tisṛcatasṛ*) [prevents it].

Because of this prohibition [in 6.4.4], the mention of the short vowel (*hrasva*) has its scope. For, from the rule *hrasvanadyāpo nuṭ* (7.1.54), the term *tri-* is understood to carry over from the rule *trestrayaḥ* (6.3.48); therefore, it is precisely due to the carry-over of the term *tri-* that [the short vowel is required].

By virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the augment *nuṭ* will apply in the case of *tisṛṇām*; likewise, in the case of *catasṛṇām*, [the augment *nuṭ* applies] by the rule "after *ṣaṣ* and *catur*" (Pāṇini 7.1.55), due to the status of being a substitute. Nor can it be argued that [the rule] "and after *nṛ*" (Pāṇini 6.4.6) [applies] in the case of *nṛṇām*.

In this view, since there is an absence of length (*dīrghatva*), the statement regarding the short vowel (*hrasva*) has its scope; for the rule concerning the short vowel is not intended solely for the sake of a single example. If this were its only purpose, the author would have simply said, "Let *nuṭ* be added after *nṛ*, *nadī*, and *āp*. Thus it is.

The mention of "short" (hrasva) is without scope. Therefore, even when lengthening has occurred—as in *agnīnām* and so forth—the augment *nuṭ* will apply by way of what was previously the case (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*), due to the force of the mention of "short. Consequently, it is incorrect to say that otherwise the *nuṭ* would not occur at all.

If that is so, then it is explained otherwise in the commentary (*vṛtti*): when it is stated, "The inclusion of *āgatanuṭka* is for the sake of what follows," the objector says, "And when the *nuṭ* has been applied," and so forth.
The ellipsis of the sentence is "why does [the long vowel] not occur? [The answer is: and when the *nuṭ* has been applied, the perception of the long vowel occurs as follows...
Why is there not an inclusion of that which has already received the augment *nuṭ* for the sake of the word *syāt*? This is indeed logical;

for if there were no inclusion of that which has already received *nuṭ*, then, because the lengthening would be obligatory, the short vowel would be absent once it had been applied, and consequently, the augment *nuṭ* would not occur in forms such as *agnīnām*.

It might be so. However, when it is stated by the proponent (cādaka) that [the suffix] occurs only when *san* with the augment *ṭ* is included, he says this—"Otherwise, indeed," and so forth. Here, the word *hi* functions in the sense of the particle *api*;
the word *na* functions in the sense of *nanu*, because particles (*nipāta*) possess multiple meanings.
The particle *eva* is displaced; it should be understood immediately after *syāt*.

Thus, the meaning here is as follows: indeed, the augment *nuṭ* would occur even otherwise; it is not only when there is the mention of that which possesses *nuṭ* that *nuṭ* occurs in forms such as *agnīnām*, but also [in other cases].
Otherwise, even if *nuṭ* were not yet applied, it would indeed still occur upon its inclusion.
Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of that which already possesses *nuṭ*; why is it not simply stated as "there is lengthening before *ām*" (*nāmi dīrghaḥ*)?
When this objection is raised, [the author provides the answer] regarding the rule "lengthening before *nām*" (*nāmi dīrghaḥ*), etc.

The introduction of the verse: If this long vowel (*dīrgha*) which has been stated for *nāmi* were instead [stated] for *āmi*—that is, if the rule were formulated as *āmīti*—then, because it would apply both when the suffix has already been added and when it has not (*kṛtākṛtaprasaṅgitvena*), and because it is obligatory (*nityatvāt*), it would subvert even the subsequent *nuṭ* augment and the long vowel alone would occur; and consequently...
"Would *nuṭ* not indeed apply here, since the stem (*aṅga*) does not end in a short vowel? This is not a fault; [it occurs] 'by virtue of the explicit statement' (*vacanāt*).

By virtue of the statement, *nuṭ* will occur. If *nuṭ* were not to apply when there is a long vowel, then the mention of 'short' (*hrasva*) in the rule *hrasvanadyāpo nuṭ* (Pāṇini 7.1.54) would be purposeless."

Because there is no room [for such an objection]. Therefore, by the force of the explicit mention of "short" (hrasva), even when the final element of the stem (*aṅga*) is not currently short, the augment *nuṭ* will occur by virtue of its having previously been so; for the remainder of the sentence implies that the scope for this rule exists where that [current shortness] is absent. Where...

Length does not exist for three or four [cases]; therefore, there is scope for the rule regarding the short vowel (*hrasva*). Consequently, in cases such as *agnīnām*, once lengthening has been applied, the augment *nuṭ* is not observed by way of its former state (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*). For it is only when there is an absence of the present form that [the former state is taken].

There is the consideration of what occurred in the past. Now, one might object: "In cases such as *tisṛṇām* and so forth, there is likewise no scope for the mention of the short vowel; for otherwise, the augment *nuṭ* would already be established here.
The sense [of the author] is this: first, in the case of *tisṛṇām*, the augment *nuṭ* occurs by this very rule even without the mention of the short vowel.

It will occur, because the mention of "three" (*tri*) continues [from the previous rule]. Although in the case of *catasṛṇām* the base (*aṅga*) ends in a short vowel by virtue of the rule *ṣaṭcaturbhyaśca* (Pāṇini 7.1.55), and although in *nṛṇām* the base likewise ends in a short vowel, the mention of the short vowel is not intended for the sake of this single example alone; otherwise, the mention of *nṛ* itself [in the rule] would have been sufficient.

One should not include the mention of the short vowel (*hrasva*). Therefore, there is no scope whatsoever for the explicit statement of the short vowel. Lest this [rule] become meaningless, it is certain that by the force of the mention of the short vowel, the *nuṭ* augment occurs even when [the rule] has already been applied. Thus, even if the mention of the form with the *nuṭ* were not made...

Anticipating the objection of another school that "even if lengthening (*dīrghatva*) is applied, the augment *nuṅ* will still occur," he states another purpose, beginning with "nopadhāyāśca" and so forth. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "tarhi" (in that case). That being so, by the rule "nopadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.7), lengthening occurs when a *nām* [vowel] follows, provided that there is a penultimate vowel (*nopadhā*).
For example, as in *pañcānām*, *saptānām*, and so forth. For here,
by the rule *ṣaṭcaturbhyaśca* (Pāṇini 7.1.55), when *nuṭ* is applied to the *ām* following a stem ending in *n*— such as *pañcan*— and since *nām* follows, [the long vowel is substituted].

The penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) does not become long. If, however, it were simply stated as "before *ām*," then lengthening would undesirably apply even in cases such as *varmaṇām* and so forth. When the term is understood as including the augment *nuṭ*, the lengthening does not occur, because the *nuṭ* itself lacks the defining characteristic [of being a penultimate vowel]. For here, the penultimate vowel is only [the vowel] before the simple *ām*, and not [the vowel] before *ām* accompanied by *nuṭ*.
In *sanuṭke*: thus, in this case of *varmaṇām*, the term *nām* was stated so that the lengthening prescribed by "nopadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.7) would not occur.
4. *na tisṛcatasṛ* (Pāṇini 6.4.4).
The forms *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* are cited here after applying the elision (*luk*) of the genitive dual ending according to *supāṃ suluk* (7.1.39), as in the examples *tisṛṇām* and *catasṛṇām*.

By the rule *ṭhtricaturoḥ striyāṃ tisṛcatasṛ* (Pāṇini 7.2.99), the substitutes *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* occur. Now, one might object: "In this case, there is no possibility for lengthening at all; so what is the purpose of the prohibition? For indeed, once these two substitutes have been applied, both [lengthening and shortening] would otherwise apply.

The augment *nuṭ* is obtained, as well as the substitution of *r* by [Pāṇini 7.2.100], which states "for *ṛ*, there is *ra* before an *ac* suffix. In that case, because the substitution of *r* applies later, the stem (*aṅga*) no longer ends in an *ac*. Since it would have to become long by virtue of ending in an *ac*, the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) [in the rule] serves to exclude [the application of] [Pāṇini 1.2.28], which states "and after an *ac*."

Because [the substitution] has been established, he says: "This very [rule]," and so forth. If the substitution of *r* were to occur here, this prohibition would not have been made; yet it has been made.
Therefore, this prohibition indicates that [the rule] "aci ra ṛtaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.100) [is superseded].

By means of a prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the augment *nuṭ* occurs; by this, it is stated that "the augment *nuṭ* occurs after [stems ending in] *num*, *aci*, *ṛt*, and *jvadbhāva*, by way of a prior prohibition."
5. *cchandasy ubhayathā* (Pāṇini 6.4.5). Since it could have been stated simply as "optionally" (*vā*), the use of the term "both ways" (*ubhayathā*) is for the sake of stylistic variety.

6. *nṛ ca* | (6.4.6) "Some do not carry forward [the condition] *etad chandasi* ('this [is] in Vedic')"; they think as follows: if this rule (*yoga*) applied only to the Veda, then [Pāṇini] would have formulated it as a single rule: *chandasi nṛ cobhayathā* ('in the Veda, for the word *nṛ*, both ways').

One should apply [the rule]. Indeed, the particle *ca* (and) serves to draw forward the words *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*. Since the matter could have been established by a single rule (*yoga*), the fact that a separate rule is formulated leads to the certain conclusion: "This rule applies even in the colloquial language (*bhāṣā*)."

7. *nopadhāyāḥ* | (Pāṇini 6.4.7) This rule is commenced for the purpose of excluding that which does not end in a vowel (*anajanta*). The word *naḥ* is in the genitive singular; because this is a Vedic-style (*sautra*) formulation, the elision of the *y* in *ṭādguṇaḥ* (6.1.87) is not treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), and thus the *guṇa* substitution has been applied. [The form is] *naḥ*.

Regarding the mention of "vowel" (varṇa): since the mention of a vowel everywhere serves to trigger the rule of "application to that which ends in it" (tadantavidhi), it is understood that the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (upadhā) applies to a stem ending in the letter *n*.
Thus he says: "of a stem ending in *n*. [The example is] "pañcānām" (of five). [In this case,] there is the elision of *n* (nalopaḥ).
There is elision of the letter *n* by the rule "prātipadikāntasya" (Pāṇini 8.2.7).

8. And [the substitution of *dīrgha* occurs] before a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix, except for the vocative singular. (6.4.8) In the case of *sāmāni*: the change to *śi* occurs by the rule *jas-śasoḥ śiḥ* (7.1.20). In the case of *rājani*: this is the nominative singular ending. The particle *ca* [in the sūtra] refers back to the rule *nopadhāyāḥ* (6.4.7).

This [the *ca*] has the purpose of drawing forward [the preceding rule]. If this is so, would it not follow that the principle "what is drawn forward is not connected with what follows" (*cānukṛṣṭaṃ nottaratrābhisambadhyate*) applies, and thus the recurrence [of the previous rule] would not be obtained?
If that is the case, then the *ca* is for the sake of removing doubt; for if the *ca* were absent, [the term *sarvanāmasthāne* would be understood to apply only to the following rule].

If it were stated simply as "in the case of *sambuddhi*," a doubt would arise: whether this refers to the non-*sambuddhi* state or the *sambuddhi* state. If this were the intended purpose, one would have said, "before a *sarvanāmasthāna* that is not *sambuddhi*. Therefore, the particle *ca* is for the sake of variety.
9. *vā ṣapūrvasya nigame* (6.4.9).

Here, by the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*), the *paribhāṣā* "ṭhacaśca" (1.2.28) is brought to bear; furthermore, because of the governing rule "nopadhāyāḥ" (6.4.7), the "penultimate letter" (*upadhā*) is also implied.

Regarding the term *ṣapūrvasya*: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has *ṣ* as its predecessor. In that context, if the *upadhā* (penultimate vowel) were accepted as the referent of the external member (*anyapadārtha*), the masculine designation *ṣapūrvasya* would be untenable; therefore, here the vowel *a* is accepted as the referent of the external member.

Thus he says: "of a vowel preceded by *ṣ*," and so forth. The term "of the penultimate" (*upadhāyāḥ*) is a coreferential qualifier of "vowel" (*acaḥ*). Regarding "ṛbhukṣāṇām": [the form] "ṛbhukṣa" is present in this [word], and thus it is the singular accusative case; while the rule "pathimathyṛbhukṣāṇām" (Pāṇini 7.1.85) is being carried over.
The substitution of *at* [for *an*] occurs by the rule "ṭhito 'tsarvanāmasthāne" (Pāṇini 7.1.86). The mention of the word "pūrva" (preceding) is for the sake of what follows;
however, in this case, if only "vā ṣo nigame" were stated, the optional lengthening of the vowel following the letter *ṣ*, as prescribed by "nopadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.7), would indeed be indicated.

10. *sāntamahataḥ saṃyogasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.10). The vowel *a* in *sakāra* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). That which has *s* as its final element (*anta*) is called "ending in *s*" (*sānta*). This term *sānta* is presented without a case-ending (*avibhaktika*), because the genitive case that arose there has been elided.

"Regarding the rule *sakārāntasya saṃyogo nakāro mahataśca* [Pāṇini 8.3.27], the word *nakāraḥ* is also required there. Both *sakārāntasya* and *mahataḥ* are genitive case endings expressing part-whole relation (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*): namely, the *nakāra* which is a constituent part of the *saṃyoga* ending in *s*, and that which is a constituent part of the word *mahat*."

This is the meaning. By this, he shows that both "sānta" (ending in *s*) and "saṃyoga" (consonant cluster) are qualifiers of the letter *n*. Regarding the phrase "tasyopadhāyāḥ" (of its penultimate vowel): by the word "tasya" (of it), the letter *n* is referred back. The meaning is: "of the penultimate vowel belonging to that *n*. By this also...

He explains that the letter *n* is a qualifier of the *upadhā*. But what is the relationship between the letter *n* and the *upadhā*, by virtue of which the former is designated as "belonging to" the latter? It is the relationship of cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika-bhāva*).
For, with respect to the final *n*, when the status of being a penultimate (*parva*) is established, the sound preceding that final *n* is the *upadhā*.

It occurs. Therefore, the letter *n* is the cause (*nimitta*), and the preceding vowel (*upadhā*) is the locus of the cause (*nimitasthāna*). Alternatively, the relationship is characterized by proximity (*samīpa-samīpi-lakṣaṇa*); by this, the meaning is "of the *upadhā* situated near the letter *n*. Regarding the example *śreyān*: "this one is praiseworthy," "this one is praiseworthy."

Since this one among these two is most praiseworthy (*praśasya*), the suffix *īyasun* is applied by the rule *dvivacanavibhajyopapade tarabīyasunau* (Pāṇini 5.3.57); the substitution of *śra-* for *praśasya-* occurs by the rule *praśasyasya śraḥ* (5.3.60); and by the rule *prakṛtyaikāc* (6.4.163), which prescribes the status of the base form (*prakṛtibhāva*), there is elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*).

Furthermore, the elision [of the final *s*] does not occur by the rule "ṭhyasyeti ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.148). By the rule "ṭhugidacām" (7.1.70), the augment *num* is applied; then, the elisions of the *hal-ṅy-ādi* (6.1.68) and *saṃyogānta* (8.2.23) [are applied]. Thus we have "śreyāṃsi" and "payāṃsi. As before, the substitution of *śi* for the case-ending *jas* occurs by the rule "napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ" (7.1.72).

Thus, by [Pāṇini 7.1.72], the augment *num* is applied. But how can the vowel preceding the *n* here be termed the "penultimate" (*upadhā*), given that [Pāṇini 1.1.65] prescribes the designation *upadhā* for that which precedes the final consonant (*al*) among those situated within a word? And yet, in this case...
Is the letter *n* the final one, or rather the letter *s*? This is not a fault; for "finality" is relative.

Thus, the letter *n* is the final among those letters which precede the *s*. Consequently, the letter preceding that becomes the *upadhā* (penultimate). If this is so, then in words such as *takṣakaḥ* and *rakṣakaḥ*, [the same would apply].

If it were the case that the letter *k* is the final among those letters preceding the *s*, then the vowel *a* preceding it would be the *upadhā* (penultimate), and consequently, by the rule "ata upadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.116), there would be a *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening).
This is not so; for the *vṛddhi* is prescribed for that vowel *a* which is the *upadhā* of the *aṅga* (the stem). It is not [the *a* of the suffix].

And as for the claim that "the vowel *a* here is not the penultimate (*upadhā*) of the stem (*aṅga*), and therefore [the rule] will not apply"—this cannot be said, because the vowel *a* is indeed a constituent part (*avayava*) of the stem. Even in cases such as *pācaka*, the vowel *a* is called the penultimate of the stem precisely because it is a constituent part of the stem; therefore...

Does [the vowel] indeed undergo *vṛddhi*? This is not a fault; for in the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116), the term *ñṇiti* (from 7.2.115) is understood as a governing element (*anuvartate*). By this, the *upadhā* (penultimate vowel) is qualified: "that which is the penultimate vowel when followed by a suffix beginning with *ñ* or *ṇ*. In that context, the principle applies: "that by which there is no intervention [is considered contiguous]."

In the rule "even when separated, on account of the authority of the statement" (Vyāḍipāda 49), separation by only one phoneme is intended, and not by multiple phonemes. Therefore, in cases such as *takṣakaḥ* and *rakṣakaḥ*, where there is separation by multiple phonemes, the undesirable consequence of *vṛddhi* does not arise.
But in this sūtra, the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is not qualified by the term "sarvanāmasthāna";
rather, it is the *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) that is qualified. Thus, [the meaning is]: "when a *saṃyoga* precedes a *sarvanāmasthāna*.
Therefore, wherever a *sarvanāmasthāna* follows immediately after a *saṃyoga*, if there is [an operation] regarding the penultimate vowel of that *sarvanāmasthāna*...

Even when there is an intervention consisting of multiple phonemes, lengthening nevertheless occurs. For this very reason, regarding the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix, even if there is an intervention consisting of multiple phonemes between the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) and the *sarvanāmasthāna*, lengthening nevertheless occurs. For this very reason, by means of the *sarvanāmasthāna*...
Due to the qualification "following a conjunct" (*saṃyoga*), the lengthening [of the vowel] does not occur in *haṃsau* and *haṃsāḥ*;
for here, there is no *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix immediately after the conjunct, because it is separated by the letter *a*.
Now, why does this not occur here—[in the case of the denominative verb] *haṃsayati*, meaning "he describes a swan"—by virtue of the rule *tadācaṣṭe* (Vārttika 201)?

Is there not the elision of the suffix *ṭi* by the rule "In the case of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the operation of *ṇāviṣṭhavan* applies to the causative (*ṇic*)"—thus [yielding] *haṃsa-* from *haṃsayati*—and then the formation of *haṃs-au*, *haṃsaḥ* by means of the *kvip* suffix? No, because the word "optionally" (*vā*) is understood to carry over from the rule "Optionally in the Veda (*nigama*) for that which is preceded by *ṣ*" (Pāṇini 6.4.9). And this being so, it does not apply everywhere.
There would be the undesirable consequence of an option; however, because this is a fixed *vibhāṣā* (optional rule),
by this [principle], one should understand that there is no lengthening in the forms *suhin*, *suhiṃsau*, and *suhisa* from the root *hiṃs* (DhP 1829) when it ends in *kvip*.
As for the one who says: "By the rule *ṣṭhivo num dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.58), the augment *num* is obligatory;

because of the statement that [the base] is as if it were in its original state (*upadeśivad-vacana*) regarding the prescription of *num*, there is no separate establishment of the *num* from the base.
In this case, however, the relation between established entities is inherence (*samavāya*), not conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Therefore..."
According to that view, because there is no conjunction (*saṃyoga*) here, the lengthening of the vowel does not occur;
furthermore, by that same principle, the elision of a final consonant following a conjunction (*saṃyogāntalopa*) would also not apply in the case of *suhṛn*.
However, the "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) referred to here is not the one well-known in the Vaiśeṣika treatises, but rather that which is defined as "consonants separated by vowels" (*halo’nantarāḥ*).

Regarding the term "saṃyoga" (1.1.7), in this grammatical treatise it is well known as a conjunction characterized by the absence of an interval between consonants; since that very [conjunction] exists here, the proposed rebuttal is untenable. As for the form "mahān," it is derived by the rule of irregular derivation (nipātana-sūtra): "vartamāne pṛṣadvṛhanmahajjagaccchatṛvacca" (Dhātupāṭha 6.5).

Because of the extension [of rules] by the term "as in the case of *śatṛ*," the operation of *ugit*—namely, the addition of the augment *num*—applies. Why [is it said] "after a stem ending in *s* or *mahat*"? [Consider:
*bṛhanti*.
11. *aptṛntṛcsvasṛnaptṛneṣṭṛkṣattṛhotṛpotṛpraśāstṛṇām* | (6.4.11) [The word] *ṭhāpaḥ* [is used]; since the word *ap* denotes plurality, the singular and dual numbers are not possible for it.

The plural form is presented as "bahvāmpi. It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those in which there are many waters" (*bahava āpa eṣu*). Because the application of a rule to that which ends with [a specific element] is accepted, the lengthening occurs even for that which ends in such a compound.
For instance, regarding the rule *yena vidhistadantasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.72), [the question arises: "What, then, in this case..."

Regarding the question "What are the purposes?", this purpose has been stated: [the application of the rule] to *mahat*, *apasa*, *svasṛ*, *naptr̥*, *neṣṭr̥*, *tvaṣṭr̥*, and so forth. But how can the rule of "extension to that which ends in [a specific element]" (*tadantavidhi*) be obtained even when [the word] is desired [to apply], given that [the rule] states: "That which possesses a marker (*grahaṇavat*)," etc.?
[Objection: "Is the rule of *tadanta-vidhi* (application of a grammatical operation to that which ends with the base) prohibited by the base itself? [Response: This is not a fault;

the particle *ca* ("and") is carried over from the rule *sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau* (Pāṇini 6.4.8), and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. By means of that, the lengthening will also apply to that which ends in such a base.

By the statement "some [teachers]," it is indicated that some do not accept this; according to their opinion, the form becomes *bahvām*. Why, then, is the compound-final suffix *a* not applied here by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmānakṣe* (Pāṇini 5.4.74)? To this he says: "In that case..."

"The rule regarding the application of compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) is not mandatory," and so forth. This technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is indicated by the inclusion of the term *adhvan* in the sūtra *sphigapūtavīṇāñjo'dhvakukṣisīranāma nāma ca* (Pāṇini 6.2.187).
How the inclusion of *adhvan* serves as an indicator has been explained in that very context.

But even so, the form *bahvām* is not at all possible; for instance, when *bahvaḥ* + *āpaḥ* is situated, this [rule] would result in lengthening (*dīrghatva*), while by the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.72), the augment *num* would also apply.

In that case, because it is both obligatory (*nitya*)—since it applies regardless of whether the other operation has been performed—or because it is subsequent (*para*), the *num* would take effect first.
[The rule] must be applied; once that [num] has been applied, since the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) would not possess a long vowel, the application of lengthening would not occur.
To this he says: "And even though it is obligatory," and so forth.

By the word "even" (*api*) in "even though it is obligatory," it is implied that it applies even subsequently. But how can one desire [the application of] *num* without first performing [the other operation]?

Is lengthening observed [in such cases]? Yes, because of the continued application of the term "prior" (*pūrva*) from the rule *ṭhvoḥ ṣapūrvasya nigame* (Pāṇini 6.4.9). The purpose of this very [continued application] is that, rather than applying whatever other grammatical operation might otherwise obtain, lengthening alone must be performed first.
But another says: "The augment *num* is prescribed by the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.72).

Now, 'neuter' (*napuṃsaka*) is a property of the meaning (*artha*), and since there can be no grammatical operation (*kārya*) upon the meaning within this science of word-instruction (*śabdānuśāsana*), the word denoting the neuter must be relied upon for the prescription of *num*. And that word..."

The application [of the rule] for grasping [the form] must be followed; thus, the augment *num* is considered "external" (*bahiraṅga*). However, this long vowel (*dīrgha*), being prescribed by directly uttering the word *ap*, is applied only to that which is actually uttered; because it has a smaller basis (*alpa-āśrayatva*), it is "internal" (*antaraṅga*), and therefore the long vowel operates first.
"Subsequently, the augment *num* [is applied]. This, however, is incorrect; for by this logic, the form *bahvām* would not be established.
Furthermore, some maintain that because this rule is general, here too the long vowel must occur first, and subsequently the *num* augment.
In the first explanation, however, there is no fault. For those who desire [the application of] *bahuvrīhi*, they do not carry forward the mention of "pūrva" here;
[as in the example] "kartāraḥ," where the suffix *tṛn* occurs in the sense of "one who has that habit" (*tacchīla*), and [the form is derived] by the rule *ṛto ṅsirvanāmasthānayoḥ*.

By [Pāṇini 7.3.110], there is *guṇa* substitution. Regarding the phrase "janāpavādān," the use of the accusative case is intended to demonstrate that the word ends in the suffix *tṛn*. For when *tṛn* is employed, the genitive case is prohibited by the rule "na lokāvyayaniṣṭhā" (Pāṇini 2.3.69), and so forth.
It is indeed the second [case]. The singular number has not been cited there;

for in that case, when the substitution of *anaṅ* is applied by the rule *ṛduśanaspurudaṃśo'nehasāñca* (Pāṇini 7.1.94), the lengthening [of the penultimate vowel] occurs by the rules *nopadhāyāḥ* (6.4.7) and *sarvanāmasthāne ca* (6.4.8).
Because [the meaning] is already established, the use of the genitive form *kaṭasya* is for the purpose of making the *tṛc* suffix manifest.

When that [suffix] is employed, the genitive case occurs in the sense of the object by virtue of the rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65). Now, just as in the case of the rule *turiṣṭhemeyassu* (Pāṇini 6.4.154), where *tur* [is used].
Since only that which is the common form of the two [suffixes] *tṛn* and *tṛc* has been taken,

and not their distinction, why has this not been done here as well? It is for the purpose of ensuring that the word *tṛ*, which is the substitute *arvan* according to "arvaṇastrasāvanañaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.127), is not included.

If it is argued that this is not the purpose [of the rule], for its inclusion will not occur by the very *paribhāṣā* "that which has meaning" (*arthavadgrahaṇaparibhāṣā*) alone; thus, the separate mention of *tṛn* and *tṛc* is for the purpose of making known the non-universality (*anityatva*) of this *paribhāṣā*. Therefore, the mentions of *ṭhan*, *ini*, and *as* [refer] to that which is meaningful.
And thus it becomes logical that they employ [the term] even with what is meaningless.
Alternatively, it is for the purpose of making known the principle that "in the case of a general designation, sometimes only a specific instance is intended.
Therefore, although there is a general statement in the rule *na kopadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.37), [it is understood as referring to a specific case].
Only the *k* that belongs to a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is understood here, not the letter *k* in general.

Now, what is the purpose of including *naptr̥* and the others, since some of them are derived from the suffix *tṛc* and others from *tṛn*; in that case, would it not be sufficient to mention *tṛ* and *tṛc* alone?

Thus he says: "Of *naptṛ* and so forth," and so on. Some Ācāryas maintain that *naptṛ* and the other such items are underived nominal stems (*prātipadika*), while others maintain that they are derived.
In this regard, the derivation is as follows: from the root *nam*, with the suffix *tṛc*, the letter *m* becomes *p*.
It is derived as follows: *neṣṭṛ* is formed from the root *nī* with the suffix *tṛc* and the augment *ṣuk*;
*tvaṣṭṛ* is formed from the root *tviṣ*, where the vowel *a* is substituted for the penultimate vowel and the root is treated as non-*iṭ*;
*kṣitṛ* is formed from the root *kṣad* with the suffix *tṛc*; and *hotṛ* and *potṛ* are formed respectively from the roots *hu* and *pū* with that same suffix.

Regarding "praśāstṛ": from the root *śās*, the suffixes *tṛn* and *tṛc* are applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.135 (*śaṃsikṣadādibhyaḥ saṃjñāyāṃ cāniṭau*), and because it is preceded by *pra*, there is both the application of the suffix *tṛn* and the absence of the augment *iṭ*. In this regard, these words belong to the view that they are non-derivational (*avyutpatti*).

Because they lack the suffixes *tṛn* and *tṛc*, they would not be included by the mention of *tṛn* and *tṛc*; therefore, they are mentioned separately for the purpose of a mandatory rule (*vidhi*). However, according to the view that words are derived through etymological formation (*vyutpattipakṣa*), since [the desired forms] would already be established from those ending in *tṛn* and *tṛc*, the separate mention serves as a restrictive rule (*niyama*)—to ensure that this designation applies only to these specific technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*), and not to others.

[The rule] is stated so that such notions and words [as "mātṛbhyām"] do not occur for them. Therefore, in cases such as *mātarau* and *mātaraḥ*, [the substitution of *ṇ*] does not take place. Now, if it is asked: "In the case of *praśāstṛṇām*, by what means is the substitution of *ṇ* effected?"—is it by the rule *ṭhraṣābhyām* (Pāṇini 8.4.1), etc.?
No; because it is said that [the substitution of *ṇ* occurs] "after *ṭh* and *raṣ*," and [in this case] it is not so.

And here, *ra* and *ṣ* are present. If this is so, then this very grammatical formulation (*nirdeśa*) indicates that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs even elsewhere than where it has been specifically prescribed. By this, the substitution of *ṇ* is established in cases such as *mātṛṇām*, *pitṛṇām*, *grāmaṇīḥ*, and *agraṇīḥ*. And thus, regarding the rule for the substitution of *ṇ* after *ra* and *ṣ*:
The statement "it should be stated that [the suffix] *ca* follows a root ending in a labial (*ṭhṛvarṇa*)" need not be stated.

12. *inhanpūṣāryamṇāṃ śau* (Pāṇini 6.4.12). According to the rule "The mention of *ṭhan*, *ini*, *nas*, and *man* applies both when they have meaning and when they are meaningless, and thus effects a designation of that which ends in them" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 129), the mention of *in* here includes that which ends in *in*. This applies even to the others (*han*, *pūṣan*, and *aryaman*) when they appear alone.
It becomes neuter. For instance—the word *han* here is the inclusion of the root *han* with the suffix *kyip*;
and the suffix *kvip* is not seen after the simple root *han*. The other two [roots], however, are masculine.
The substitution of *śi* for *jas* and *śas* is prescribed after a neuter [stem]; therefore, by those [two roots] as well—

By implication, it is understood that the rule applies to forms ending in those [stems]; thus he says: "of stems ending in *ṭhin*, *han*, *pūṣan*, and *aryaman*. Regarding the example *bahudaṇḍīni*: the suffix *ini* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) to form *daṇḍin* ("one who possesses a staff"), and then *bahudaṇḍīni* means "those who possess many staff-bearers."
This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; from it, the suffixes *jaś* and *śas* [are applied], and for these two, as before, there is the substitution of *śi*, by which [the rule] provides the lengthening.

Now, since the term "having *ni*" (*nit*) refers to a suffix, and according to the principle that "when a suffix is mentioned, there is the inclusion of that which begins with the element after which it is prescribed and that which ends with it" (Bhāṣya on Pāṇini 1.1.72), [the suffix *ni* should include its entire stem].
"In this case, [the rule] *daṇḍinī* alone should have the long vowel, but not *bahudaṇḍīnī*?

This is not so; for this paribhāṣā applies only where there is the mention of a suffix (*pratyaya*) itself, but here it is not a mention of the suffix alone, but rather of both suffix and non-suffix. Otherwise, [the rule would apply to] *vāca eṣām*.

In the case of *vāgminaḥ*—derived from *vācaḥ* with the suffix *gmin* by Pāṇini 5.2.124—and in *sragviṇī*, where the suffix *vin* is applied by 5.2.121 because they possess garlands (*srajaḥ*), this paribhāṣā would not apply. Therefore, it does not apply here in such instances. [The example] *bahuvṛtrahāṇi* [is explained as follows]: *bṛtraṃ*...

[The suffix] *kvip* is applied after [the roots] *brahmán*, *bhṛ́ṇahan*, and *vṛtrahan* [when followed by the suffix] *ha* (Pāṇini 3.2.87). Those [days] in which there are many *vṛtrahaṇas* are *bahuvṛtrahāṇi*. The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs [by the rule] *pūrvapadāntanumvibhaktiṣu ca* (8.4.11). Those [days] in which there are many *pūṣaṇas* are *bahupūṣāṇi*. Many *aryamaṇas*...
In those [words], they are frequently desired.

Now, is it not the case that lengthening is already established by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau* (P. 6.4.8)? Why, then, is this new rule commenced? To this he says: "Since [the result] is already established, [this] commencement... and so forth.
This undertaking is intended for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*); however, even when this restriction is being introduced,

in the case of *bhrūṇahanī*, the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by "anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ kṅiti" (Pāṇini 6.4.15) still occurs, because this [rule] is a restriction regarding the *sarvanāmasthāna* case-ending *śi*.
It is commenced here: just as a rule being initiated for a specific *prakṛti* does not apply to another *prakṛti*— as in *pratāmau* and *pratāmaḥ*— so too,
when a *śit* affix is initiated for that which is characterized by the technical name *sarvanāman*, it applies only to a *sarvanāmasthāna*.
It might be so in other cases, but not here; for a restrictive rule depends upon the expectation of something of the same class.
Consequently, since there would be no restriction regarding the designation *asarvanāmasthāna*, lengthening (*dīrghatva*) would indeed occur.
Therefore, he says the verse beginning with "the prescription of length" (*dīrghavidhi*). [This refers to] those [rules] in this treatise concerning words ending in *-in* and so forth...
Having applied that long-vowel rule (*dīrghatvavidhānam*) by restricting it—having established its restriction—where is it restricted?

To *suṭ*. This inclusion (*saṅgrahaṇam*) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇam*) for the term *sarvanāmasthāna*; the meaning is "in a *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix]. What then should one do? To this he says: "The restriction applies in the case of *śi*" (*śau niyamam*), and so forth.

Having established a restriction regarding the *sarvanāmasthāna* [cases], one should again establish a restriction regarding the nominative singular (*śau*). The particle *eva* is for the purpose of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), but it is displaced in order; it should be understood as following immediately after the word *vidadhyāt*. "Suviddha" means "well-learned" or "wise. But how can two [restrictions] be established by a single rule?

Can two restrictive rules (*niyama*) be formulated? It is thought thus: this single rule should be divided into two rules. One rule would be "ṭhinhanpūṣāryamṇām," and then a second, "śau. And here, the mention of "sarvanāma" (pronoun) continues to apply. In that case—

The *pūrvayoga* (the preceding rule): that rule regarding lengthening for [stems] beginning with *idam*, having been restricted by that rule, is indicated here by the word *suṭi*. The second [rule], however, is indicated by the phrase *ṭhśau niyamaṃ punareva vidadhyāt*.
In that case, by the former rule (*pūrveṇa yogena*), there would be lengthening. [This applies] in the case of a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix.
By the rule *cāsambuddhau* (6.4.8), or by the rule *ṭhānunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ kṅiti* (6.4.15), the lengthening is restricted— namely, that for stems beginning with *in*,
lengthening occurs only before a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix, and not elsewhere. Consequently, there is no lengthening in the locative case.
It occurs in cases such as *vṛtrahaṇi* and *bhrūṇahanī*. However, by the second [rule], the long vowel is restricted to the *śi* ending;

even there, the long vowel occurs only before a *sarvanāmasthāna* ending that begins with *ś*, and not elsewhere. Consequently, the long vowel occurs in *bahuvṛtrahāṇi*, but it does not occur in *vṛtrahaṇaḥ*. Thus, by means of these two rules—

In order to demonstrate the meaning that results when two rules are applied simultaneously, he says: "bhrūṇahani" and "tathāsya na duṣyet. Thus, when these two applications of the rule are made, this word-form "bhrūṇahani" of Pāṇini is indeed not [defective].
The meaning is that [the form] would not incur the fault of being unestablished (*asiddhatva*), as in the case of *bhavati*. The particle *iti* indicates a reason.

Since, when these two rules are applied by means of the two [consecutive] *yoga*s, the form *bhrūṇahanī* would not be faulty; therefore, having restricted that long-vowel rule which applies to *ihan* and the others, [it is stated] before the *suṭ* augment and before the nominative plural ending *śas*.

One should reapply the rule (*niyama*) to those [cases] that have been incorrectly pierced. The second occurrence of the particle *iti* indicates that the word *bhrūṇahanī* here functions as its own formal linguistic item (*svarūpapadārthaka*).
Thus, by means of two applications of the rule, the lengthening of the vowel in *bhrūṇahanī* is avoided within a single application of the rule.
To offer a solution, he says: "I shall teach," and so forth.

I shall explain that other means by which, when there is a single *yogavṛddhi*, neither the form *bhrūṇahanau* nor *bhrūṇahanaḥ* is faulty, nor is the form *bhrūṇahanī*. But what, then, is this means?

Thus he says: "having set aside," and so forth. By the single compound *suṭi*, the term *sarvanāmasthāna* is indicated. Having set aside that which is under discussion here, namely *sarvanāmasthāne*, [he says] *aviśeṣe*. It is called *aviśeṣa* because no distinction (*viśeṣa*) exists for it.
In that case, regarding this non-specific [term] which does not depend on a specific [gender], [you] should establish the restriction as "śau" alone;

or rather, the meaning is that you should establish the restriction in this way. The word *vā* (or) indicates that this is an alternative solution to the objection. The word *api* (also) indicates another alternative even in the case of the term *bhrūṇahanī*.
Is there no fault when [the rule] is resorted to? Because lengthening is restricted to the suffix *śā* alone;
if lengthening occurs for the suffixes beginning with *in*, it occurs only when the suffix is *śā*, and not otherwise.
By the phrase "having set aside *suṭ*," the cessation of the technical jurisdiction (*adhikāra*) is shown.

But if, once that [technical application] has ceased, one were to resort to a worldly authority characterized by mutual expectation (*apekṣā*), then—as in the previous case—the lengthening would certainly occur in the word *bhrūṇahanī*. Therefore, in order to exclude such a worldly basis, he says "without due consideration" (*asamīkṣya*); this is to be connected with the word *suṭ*.
