The meaning is that [the rule] depends upon a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix. Thus,
when the mention of *sarvanāmasthāna* has been removed and is no longer required,
this restriction— namely, "śi" [applies]— restricts only the suffix in general, and not only those of the same class.
It is indeed a *sarvanāmasthāna*. Therefore, the long vowel does not occur not only elsewhere in a *sarvanāmasthāna*, but also in the case of *bhrūṇahani*.
If, then, the restriction regarding *śi* is based on the suffix itself, without regard for the domain of *sarvanāmasthāna*, [then...]
For if this were the case, since lengthening (*dīrghatva*) would be restricted only to the *śā* suffix, then just as it does not occur in the example *bhrūṇahanī*,

so too it would not occur in the *kyaṅ* suffix used in the sense of "acting like" (*ācāra*), according to the rule *ṭhakṛtsārvadhātukayordīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.25). Consequently, in the formation *bhrūṇahēvācarati*— which is derived from the agent (*kartṛ*) with the suffix *kyaṅ*— [the lengthening would not apply].

Since the suffix *kyaṅ* is prescribed by the rule *salopaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.11), one might arrive at the undesirable form *bhrūṇahayate*; therefore, he says "of the prescription of lengthening," etc. The term *upadhā* is understood from the preceding rule *nopadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.7); consequently, this restriction does not apply to every instance of the prescription of lengthening.

Rather, it is because of the rule for lengthening the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrghavidhi*). Now, the rule "ṭhakṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.25) is not a rule for lengthening the penultimate vowel; what then? It is a rule for lengthening a vowel ending in *a*. Therefore, this [rule] certainly applies here. Ah! There is no fault even in the case of the rule for lengthening before a suffix beginning with *ya*. [This refers to] when it begins with *yakāra*.

The meaning is that there is no fault when *kpaṅ* occurs in the sense of a condition (*pratyaya*). The particle *hanta* occurs at the beginning of a statement or for the purpose of addressing someone. Others, however, read: "There is no fault in *hantari* and in the rule prescribing lengthening (*dīrghavidhi*). They explain it as follows: *hantari* means "in one who kills" (*yo hanti sa hantī*).

The compound is formed by the split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "ṭhpañcamī" (Pāṇini 2.1.37). In that context, *han-ti* is the locative singular. It refers to a suffix beginning with the letter *y* that follows the root *han*. Therein, there is no fault regarding the prescription of the long vowel. The particle *ca* [is used] for the previous resolution and for what will be stated hereafter. Therefore...
This is for the purpose of clarifying the point that there is no fault when the suffix *ya* begins with *y* following the root *dhā* (in the sense of "placing") due to the application of *upadhā*.
Now, while the term *sarvanāmasthāna* continues to be understood [from the previous rule], and in the absence of a formal split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*), [the following applies].
He says "suṭi vā" and so forth in order to demonstrate how, as in the case of *bhrūṇahanī*, lengthening (*dīrghatva*) does not occur; here, the word *vā* indicates an alternative view (*pakṣāntara*),
while the word *api* is displaced [in the compound] and should follow immediately after "aprakṛtapratiṣedhe."

It should be understood that even here, the term *suṭ* is to be taken as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffixes]. It has no scope (*anavakāśa*). That which is the object of exclusion—the domain of differentiation—is what is meant by "having no scope. Anything other than the *sarvanāmasthāna* under discussion is "not the subject at hand" (*aprakṛta*).

A different condition (*pratyaya*) other than the locus of elision (*sarvanāsa-sthāna*) is not under discussion; therefore, the prohibition of lengthening (*dīrghatva*) in that context is a "prohibition of what is not under discussion" (*aprakṛta-pratiṣedha*). "Prohibition of what is not under discussion" means a prohibition regarding something not being the subject at hand. The compound is formed by the analytical division (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule *saptamī* (Pāṇini 2.1.40). Thus: "in the case of a prohibition of what is not under discussion."
This is a locative of object (*viṣayasaptamī*). This is the meaning of the first half [of the verse] regarding its constituent parts (*avayavārtha*).

However, the collective meaning (*samudāyārtha*) is stated as follows: Alternatively, even though the term *sarvanāmasthāna* continues to apply, there exists something to be excluded by the restriction (*niyama*) "in the case of *śi*" (*śau*); thus, [the rule for *su*] being without scope (*anavakāśa*), it [applies].

By implication, even when a prohibition has been applied, the state of being "to be performed" (kartavyatā) still operates—that is, it remains active—within the scope of the *sarvanāmasthāna* [affixes]. Because of the word *api* ("also"), this applies elsewhere as well, in other *sarvanāmasthāna* contexts. But how is there scope for this? To this he says: "For that which... and so forth. The word *yasya* ("of which") is used in reference to *śi*.

The word "ṣaṣṭhī" [is used]; the word "hi" has the sense of "because. For the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffixes are of two kinds: *suṭ* and *śi*. Of these two, the former pertains to the feminine and masculine, not to the neuter, because of the rule "suḍ anapuṃsakasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.43). The other, however, pertains to the neuter.

This is because its [the neuter gender's] application is precisely from that [rule]. In that context, when a *sarvanāmasthāna* ending beginning with *ś* follows, this restriction—that it is *śau*—is established; however, this does not apply when *suṭ* follows. The meaning is that when *suṭ*, a *sarvanāmasthāna* ending, follows, that word is no longer neuter. By this, [the addition of] *suṭ*...

It has been stated that the term *sarvanāmasthāna* is connected with what is not neuter (*anapuṃsaka*). Therefore, it should not be applied there [to a neuter]. Precisely because *suṭ* is a *sarvanāmasthāna* that is not connected with the neuter, for that reason, in that case where it is not connected with the neuter—

Since there is no specific instance to be excluded by the rule *śau* (Pāṇini 1.4.19) regarding the term *sarvanāmasthāna*, it is appropriate that this restriction be applied specifically in relation to the neuter gender;
for when this [restriction] is made with respect to a *sarvanāmasthāna* that is not connected to the neuter, it serves to exclude [the application of the rule] to those of the same class.
One should [understand it] thus: there is no *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix other than *śi* that is connected with a neuter [stem];

therefore, there is nothing of the same class from which to exclude [the rule]. Since the restriction applies to *śi*, that [restriction] has no scope [elsewhere]. Consequently, it is operative even in the prohibition of what was not under discussion (*aprakṛta*).

By the passage beginning with "ṭhhanteranunāsikasya," he explains the meaning of all three verses according to their primary significance. Therein, by the passage beginning with "ṭhhanteranunāsikasya," the meaning of the verse "bhrūṇahanīti tathāsya na duṣyet" has been explained.
By the phrase "yogavibhāgaḥ" (division of the rule), [the author] intends to restrict the prescription of lengthening that applies to *iha* and so forth, specifically for the case of *suṭ*.
By the phrase "tataḥ" (then), he intends to re-establish the restriction for the case of *śi*. By the phrase "sarvanāmasthāna" (the strong case endings), [he intends to establish the general rule].

Of the first half of the second verse, [the commentary begins] with "But he who... and so forth; of the second half, with "Or rather... and so forth; and of the statement "Even though *suṭ* is present, there is no scope for the base form," with "Alternatively...
and so forth. Regarding "by virtue of capacity" (*sāmarthyāt*): "capacity" here means the lack of scope (*anavakāśatva*). "Without distinction" (*aviśeṣeṇa*)...
By the word "niyamaḥ" (restriction), the meaning of the rule "ṭhśau niyamo 'prakṛtapratiṣedhe" (the restriction [applies] when there is no prohibition of what is not under discussion) is intended.
"Without distinction" means generally; that is to say, it applies not only to what is under discussion (*prakṛta*) but to suffixes (*pratyaya*) in general.
As for the one who explains this restriction as having the purpose of prohibiting only what is not under discussion, [it is he alone who is at fault].

This contradicts the statement of the Vṛttikāra that "that [suffix] applies without distinction. For such a restriction would indeed be without distinction only if it applied to every suffix alone, whether in its primary (prakṛta) or non-primary (aprakṛta) context; however, if it were to exclude the primary context and apply only to the non-primary, then it would not be without distinction.

Therefore, this restriction (*niyama*) must apply specifically [to certain cases] and not universally; or, if this restriction were universal, since the lengthening would already be precluded everywhere by this very rule, the sūtra "sāvanaḍuhaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.82)—which is part of the sequence beginning with "sau ca" (6.4.13)—should be understood as having the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*). By implication, the restriction is indeed universal.

Thus it has been stated. Therefore, demonstrating its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) by means of the passage beginning with "for in the word *śi*," he explains the meaning of the rule "for that [suffix] for which there is a restriction in *śi*. Where a restriction is made regarding the word *śi*, that [suffix] is a *sarvanāmasthāna* of the neuter, and not of the feminine or masculine.

"Because the substitution [of *au*] for *jas* and *śas* after a neuter [stem] is prescribed, and there is no other *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix] for that [neuter stem]. By this, he shows that the *suṭ* augment, which is part of the *sarvanāmasthāna*, is connected with the neuter. The particle *iti* indicates a reason; because such a restriction exists...
In the case of the neuter gender, when the suffix *śi*— which is a *sarvanāmasthāna*— is prescribed, there exists no other *sarvanāmasthāna* of that same class. Therefore,
since there is no possibility of excluding anything of a similar kind, the restriction applies without distinction.

Regarding the passage beginning with "But there" (*tatra tu*), the word *tu* (but) serves to emphasize and is to be understood as displaced from its position, to be read immediately after the word *na* (not). In this rule being formulated, the qualification "of the neuter [stem] ending in *in*, etc. (*napuṃsakasya*) is not at all resorted to. And since it is not resorted to...

In that [sūtra], this meaning is established: "the long vowel occurs only for *inn* and the others when followed by *ś*, and not elsewhere. Therefore, even though the word is not neuter, the long vowel does not occur in the case of *bhrūṇahanī*, because it has been excluded by the restrictive rule (*niyama*). If this specific qualification "of the neuter" were not present...

If that [the word *napuṃsakasya*] were relied upon, then the meaning would be this: "In the case of neuter nouns beginning with *in*, lengthening occurs only before the suffix *śi*, and not elsewhere. Consequently, the restriction (*niyama*) would apply only to the neuter gender.
What is the fault in that? [The fault is that] in the example "bhrūṇahani brāhmaṇakule" (in a Brāhmaṇa family that has committed foeticide), there would be an unwanted exclusion of lengthening.

It might be argued that [the rule] would not apply in the case of *bhrūṇahani brāhmaṇe*. Therefore, out of a desire to avoid that defect, this qualification "of the neuter" (*napuṃsakasya*) is not resorted to.
If this is so, then what was stated—that "the restriction (*niyama*) regarding the nominative plural (*śau*) is without scope"—is no longer tenable.

For if this qualification were not relied upon, there would be a restriction regarding the non-neuter status of those neuter nouns whose qualifiers are themselves not neuter when the subsequent *sarvanāmasthāna* case-ending *śi* occurs;
and for such [nouns], other *sarvanāmasthāna* endings, such as *suṭ*, certainly exist as well.

And so, when there exists an object consisting of the exclusion of parts belonging to the same class, how could there be no scope for the restrictive rule (*niyama*)? This is not the case; for although their neuter gender is not relied upon as a qualifier at the time of enacting the restrictive rule, nevertheless, those [words]— [...are understood to be neuter by virtue of the context.]

Since the suffix *śi* is prescribed specifically after a neuter [stem], the neuter possesses the status of the cause (*nimitta*), while *śi* possesses the status of the effect (*naimittika*). Thus, by virtue of the relationship characterized as that between cause and effect, the neuter gender indeed possesses a connection with the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix *śi*. It is not [otherwise].

Furthermore, since there exists another *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix associated with the neuter, this is established: the restriction regarding *śi* is without scope. But surely, here the term "of the neuter" has neither been introduced nor mentioned; therefore—
Since there is no possibility at all of [the rule] taking that as its basis, this [objection] is not appropriate for the purpose of excluding it;
why, then, is the phrase "of the neuter" (*napuṃsakasya*) not relied upon in that context?
To this he says: "But in the prescription of the technical term *sarvanāmasthāna*," and so forth. The word "but" (*tu*) indicates a reason.

Since the designation *sarvanāmasthāna* is prescribed for the suffix *ṭā-śi* following the word *viś* when it is produced by a neuter [stem]— according to the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.72)— therefore, with respect to the prescription of the *sarvanāmasthāna* designation, "neuter" functions as the cause (*nimitta*).

Thus, in the rule prescribing the technical name *sarvanāmasthāna*, the function of the neuter gender is the adoption of the status of being a cause (*nimitta*). Therefore, wherever the term *śi* is designated by the technical name *sarvanāmasthāna*, it must necessarily be accompanied by a neuter noun. However, in this case, because the mention of *sarvanāmasthāna* is continued [from the previous rule],...

The term *śi* is understood here as being designated by the technical name *sarvanāmasthāna*. Consequently, by virtue of its capacity (*sāmarthya*), the neuter gender is implied; the intention is that the [rule] is to be understood as depending upon that [neuter gender].
Since the preceding restrictive rule would not permit lengthening before the suffix *su*, this sūtra is commenced for the purpose of prescribing it.
The particle *ca* serves to carry forward the items beginning with *in*.
14. *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.14). [The Vārttika states:

"When [the substitution of] *dīrgha* has been effected here, the augment *num* [is applied]. But how is this obtained? For since [the application of] *num* applies both when [the condition for *dīrgha*] has already occurred and when it has not yet occurred (*kṛtākṛtaprasaṅgitva*), and because it is subsequent (*paratva*), *num* alone ought to occur.

He says "previously" with the words "yadi hi," etc. Here, when the rule *acaśca* (1.2.28) is brought to bear by the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*), a long vowel is prescribed for the penultimate (*upadhā*) vowel characterized as *aj*. If, however, *num* were to be applied first—on account of its being subsequent (*paratva*) and obligatory (*nityatva*)—the status of the vowel as a penultimate (*upadhātva*) would be destroyed.

Therefore, by the force of the statement, the long vowel occurs first, and after that, the augment *num* is added. Thus we have *supayāḥ*, *suyakṣāḥ*, and *susrotāḥ* (or *suśrotāḥ*, as the Kāśikā reads). This is while the rule *asun* (Daiva-Uṇādi 9.49) is in effect, followed by the rule *pibatericca* (Daiva-Uṇādi 9.50).

The words *payas*, *yaśas*, and *srotas* are derived respectively from the roots *pai*, *yas*, and *sru* by means of the suffix *asun*, according to the rules: "After *ṭhā* and *śī*, there is also *yuṭ*" (*Uṇādisūtra* 9.51) and "After *sru* and *ri*, there is *tuṭ*" (*Uṇādisūtra* 9.62).

"ṭhpiṇḍagraḥ, carmavaḥ. [The roots] *grasu* and *glasu* mean "to eat" (DhP 6.30, 6.31), and *vasa* means "to cover" (DhP 10.23). By the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 3.2.178), the suffix *kvip* is applied.
Now, one might object: by the paribhāṣā regarding the inclusion of meaningful elements (*arthavad-grahaṇa-paribhāṣā*), only that which is meaningful would be understood here.

Just as in the primary examples, such as *payaḥ* and others, this [term] is meaningful because it possesses the sense of the suffix due to ending in the suffix *-asun*, it is not so in the counter-examples; since there is no possibility of lengthening a vowel belonging to a verbal root (*dhātu*) therein, the prohibition "not after what is not a root" (*adātoḥ*) would be purposeless. Therefore—
He says: "Even though [the suffix] is meaningless," and so forth. How is this obtained?
He says: "The mentions of *an*, *ini*, and *man*," and so forth. Now, how is there lengthening here—as in *gomatyati* from *gomantam icchati*—by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8)?

The suffix *matup* is applied after the verbal root *gam* to form *gomān*; how could it not be so? [One might object: "Because of the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 1.2.45], 'not after a verbal root,' since this [verbal base *gomin*] is a verbal root by virtue of the rule 'those ending in *san* and so forth are verbal roots' (3.1.32). This is not the case; the prohibition "not after a verbal root" applies only to that which immediately precedes it due to proximity (*ānantarya*).
Not for that which is internal.

Alternatively, the letter *ca* is used here, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been mentioned; by that, [the substitution] will also apply to the verbal root (*dhātu*) here. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *anta* (end), since [the rule] says "of the member" (*aṅgasya*)?

(6.4.1) This [rule] continues to apply; therein, since the word *anu* and the word *asa* qualify the member (*aṅga*) under discussion, there occurs the rule of "extension to that which ends with it" (*tadantavidhi*) by means of the qualifier. Thus, even though the mention of the word *anta* is absent here, the lengthening applies only to that which ends in [the specified element].

[How] will this be? To this he says: "The mention of 'the end' (*antagrahaṇam*)," and so forth. *Upadeśa* refers to the statements of the *lakṣaṇa* (grammatical rules), the *gaṇapāṭha* (list of word-groups), and the *prātipadikapāṭha* (list of nominal stems). It is called *prayoga* because it is employed (*prayujyate*); the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*). Thus, *upadeśaprayoga* means "employment in the *upadeśa*. [This is governed by] the rule *saptamī* (Pāṇini 2.1.40).
The compound is formed by means of *yogavibhāga* (splitting the rule). Therefore, the meaning of this sentence is as follows:

the mention of the word "end" (*anta*) is for the purpose that there may be the inclusion of even a single part [of a word] which is used in its original form (*upadeśa*). But of what [is this inclusion intended], if the mention of "end" were not present?

Why would there not be the inclusion of only a portion of the *prayoga* (application), such that the mention of the word "end" (*anta*) is made for the purpose of including that [entirety]? To this he says: "For otherwise," and so forth. What is the reason why it would not be so?
To this he says: "In the instruction (*upadeśa*), which is the cause for determining the form (*rūpa-nirgraha-hetu*)," and so forth. [The term] *nirgrahaṇa*...

*Nigraha* means ascertainment (*niścaya*). *Rūpanirgraha* is the ascertainment of the form—that is, the nature—of a word; the causes of that are the *rūpanirgrahahetu*. The mention of "instruction" (*upadeśa*) is merely illustrative; for even worldly usage is included.

For the form of the word is determined either from an instructional rule (upadeśa) or from common usage (laukika-prayoga). And this suffix *matup* is not heard with a final *t* in common usage, nor is it so in the instructional rule; therefore, it is not ascertained as having a final *t*. Consequently, because it is not so ascertained, it is not included [in the rule]. Furthermore, regarding the mention of the word "final" (*anta*)...

Since the mention of the word *satya* implies the grasping of the suffix *-matr* alone, it is established that the inclusion of the suffix *-matup* occurs, because even that which constitutes a portion of the usage in the grammatical instruction is included.

15. *anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ kṅiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.15). [The sūtra means: "When the suffix *kvip* follows, and when a suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant that has *k* or *ṅ* as an *it*-marker follows. Here, the term *kṅiti* is connected only with "beginning with a *jhal* consonant," and not with the suffix *kvip*; for:
For the relationship between a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and a qualificand (*viśeṣya*) exists only when there is both possibility (*sambhava*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

However, both *kitva* (the property of being marked with *k*) and *ṅtva* (the property of being marked with *ṅ*) occur before suffixes beginning with *jhal*, but not before *kvip*. To explain: *kitva* does not deviate from *kvip* (it is invariably present), whereas *ṅtva* is impossible in that context.

Regarding the forms *praśān*, *pratān*, and *pradān*: from the roots *śam* (DhP 1201) meaning "to become calm," *tam* (DhP 1202) meaning "to desire," and *dam* (DhP 1203) meaning "to become calm"—preceded by the prefix *pra*—the suffix *kvip* is applied, and by the rule *mo no dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.64), the *m* is changed to *n*. Thus, [we obtain] *śaṃśāntaḥ*.

Thus: from the root *śam*, with the intensive suffix (*yaṅ*), reduplication, the augment *nuṭ* by [Pāṇini 7.4.85] "nṛgato'nunāsikāntasya," elision of the *yaṅ* by [Pāṇini 2.4.74] "yaṅe'ci ca," the present tense marker (*laṭ*), the ending *tas*,
its *ṅittva* by [Pāṇini 1.2.4] "sārvadhātukamapit," and [the designation] *carkarītam*.
Because [the root] is listed in the *adādi* group (beginning with *ad*) in the *Dhātupāṭha* (1081), there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix due to its being *adādi*.
16. *ajjhanagamāṃ sani* (Pāṇini 6.4.16).

The rule *ṭhupadhāyāḥ* (6.4.7) has ceased to apply; for this very reason, it was not mentioned in the commentary (*vṛtti*). What, then, would be the fault if that [previous rule] were to follow here? [The fault would be that] the lengthening would apply even to a consonant.

The fault of over-extension (*prasajyeta*) would follow. For in cases such as *cikīrṣati* and *tuṣṭūṣati*, just as the vowel becomes long by the rule "of the suffix *ṭhac*" (Pāṇini 1.2.28), so too by the rule "of the penultimate" (*upadhāyāḥ*), it would become long even for a non-vowel. If this were so, then there would be lengthening of the penultimate vowel in the roots *han* and *gam* before a vowel.
It would not apply [to the whole word]. To whom, then, would it apply? Would it apply to the final letter by virtue of the rule *alo'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52)?

This is not so; for here, by the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*), that which was brought forward by the rule *acaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.28) will be qualified by the two roots *dhani* and *gami*: "the long vowel of the *ac* becomes [such]... [and this applies to the whole stem].
Regarding the phrase "ced-dhani-gamyoh": if this is so, would it not also apply to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*)? No;

because the doubling (*dvirvacana*) is prescribed only for that which has already undergone lengthening. Why is this so? Because the lengthening takes precedence over the doubling. Thus, in *tuṣṭūṣati*, [the rule] "the remaining consonants (*khayaḥ*) preceded by *śar* are elided" applies.

[The rule] "ṭhśeṣaḥ" does not exist in sūtra 7.4.61. Regarding "cikīrṣati": there is ītva by "ṛta iddhātoḥ" (7.1.100), raparatva, lengthening by "hali ca" (8.2.77), and for the reduplication, cutva by "kuhoścuḥ" (7.4.62). [Similarly for] "jighāṃsati".

Thus: by the rule *abhyāsācca* (7.3.55), there is the substitution of *k* for the root *han*, resulting in the letter *gh*; for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), as before, there is the substitution of *c*, resulting in *jh*; and for that *jh*, by the rule *abhyāse car ca* (8.4.54), it becomes *j*.
[The form] *adhijighāṃsate* [is derived as follows]: by the rule *iṅśca* (2.4.48), the substitute *gam* is applied to the root *iṅ*.

The *ātmanepada* ending is applied by the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* (1.3.62). Thus, in the form *sañjigāṃsate*, the *taṅ* (the *ātmanepada*) suffix is also applied here by *pūrvavatsanaḥ* (1.3.62). For after the root *gam* followed by the desiderative suffix (*san*), the *ātmanepada* is prescribed by the rule *samo gamyṛcchi-* (1.3.29) and so forth. Likewise, for the root *iṅ* (to study), [the *ātmanepada* is prescribed] by the rule *anudātaṅtiḥ*.

(1.3.12) and so forth. If the rule states that [the substitution applies] only to the substitute of *iṅ* for the root *gam*, then how is it that the lengthening is observed even for that which is not a substitute of *iṅ* in the Vedic passage "svargaṃ lokaṃ samajigāṃsat" (they desired to go to the heavenly world)? To this he says: "In the Veda, even that which is not a substitute of *iṅ*... and so forth.

Regarding "samajigāṃsat": this is the aorist (luṅ) of the root *gam* with the desiderative suffix (*san*). The augment *iṭ* does not occur [after the desiderative] because of the rule "the augment *iṭ* is applied to *gam* in the parasmaipada endings" (Pāṇini 7.2.58); however, this is due to a separation of the sūtra (yogavibhāga) in the rule "not after the four beginning with *vṛ*" (7.2.59), where the word "not" (*na*) is understood from the previous rule.

By the statement beginning with "ṭhiha," etc., that which was said—namely, the Vārttika *ṭhgameriṅadeśasya* (Vārttika 775)—is refuted. The first rule is *sani*; however, a second rule, *ṭhhanigamyoḥ*, must be formulated in order to prescribe the lengthening of the vowels in the roots *han* and *gam*.

This is the intended meaning. But how is it that when this much of a grammatical operation (*yoga*) is performed, lengthening is established for a stem ending in *a* alone? To this, he says: "In that case," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "of that which is being grasped" (*gṛhyamāṇasya*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) due to its connection with a verbal derivative (*kṛt*). Regarding the word "as a qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇe*), the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*).

The qualification [of *ac*] is for the purpose of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*). Where short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*) vowels are taught as remaining (*śiṣyante*), there the rule "and after *ṭha*" (Pāṇini 1.2.28) applies; in that case, a long vowel occurs for the *aṅga*.
Of what kind of *ac*? Thus, when the *aṅga* being grasped by the term *ac* is qualified, there is an exclusion.

Even without the inclusion of the word *aj*, the lengthening of the final vowel would be established, as in the rule "akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.25). Therefore, since it would be purposeless, it should not have been done at all. To the question, "For what purpose then is it done? he says: "It is done [for the sake of] setting [the rule] in motion."

*Pravṛtti* means activity; its *bheda* is its diversity. Since such diversity of activity is not possible when there is only one [application], the repetition (*āvṛtti*) must be admitted. Now, one might object that when the rule *acaśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.28) is applied, there would be two occurrences of the term *aj*.

Why is this restriction (*āvṛti*) resorted to? It is not so; for if the mention of *ac* were absent, the rule "of *ṭhac*" (Pāṇini 1.2.28) would apply. However, when the mention of *ac* is present here, because [the substitute] has a specified locus (*nirdiṣṭasthānikatvāt*), that rule "of *ṭhac*" does not apply, just as...

In the rule *ṭhaco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115), the technical definition regarding the vowel *i* (*ikparibhāṣā*)— by means of the various applications such as "of a stem ending in *ṭhaC*" and so forth— qualifies both the stem (*aṅga*) and the augment (*āgama*). Therefore, this [separate mention of the augment] need not be stated, because the intended meaning is already established by the very mention of the vowel *a* (*ajgrahaṇa*).
For no other root *gam* besides this one can occur in place of an ac vowel after the designation "iṅ."

17. *tanoteḥ vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 6.4.17). Regarding the statement "because of the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for *tanoti*," this is derived from the rule *tanipatidaridrāṇām* (Kātyāyana-vārttika 5059 on Pāṇini 7.2.49). The mention [of the root] is by means of the *śtip* affix.

It is for the purpose of excluding the elision (*yaṅluk*). Otherwise, by the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a base (*prakṛtigrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*), an option might also apply to that which ends in it—namely, *tantaṃsati*.

18. *kramaśca ktvi* (6.4.18). This statement is for the purpose of providing an option (*vikalpa*), since [the substitution] would otherwise be obligatory by rule 6.4.15, *anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ*, and so forth. [The word "upadhāyāḥ" is understood here]. Why is this so? Because of rule 1.2.28, *acaśca*.
Because of the proximity of this [root], the sequence belongs to the *upadhā* itself due to its being a vowel (*actva*).

Regarding "having stepped" (*kramitvā*), there is the addition of the augment *iṭ* according to the alternative rule "udito vā" (Pāṇini 7.2.56). Regarding "having begun" (*prakramya*), the suffix *lyap* replaces *ktvā* when the compound is not preceded by the negative particle *nañ* (Pāṇini 7.1.37). Now, as for the lengthening...

Because it depends on the condition (pratyaya) [of the suffix], it is *antaraṅga* (internal). However, the substitution of *lyap* is *bahiraṅga* (external) because it depends upon a compound (*samāsa*), as it relies on more than one word.
In that case, due to its *antaraṅga* status, the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs before the substitution of *lyap*, specifically when a suffix beginning with a *jhal* letter follows.
Why does it not occur? To this he says: "Even though it is external," and so forth.
This has been made known in the rule *ado jagdhiḥ lyap ti kiti* (Pāṇini 2.4.36): "The substitution of *lyap*, even if external, supersedes internal operations."
19. *cchÂavoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.19).

If only the phoneme *cch* were taken [as the substitute], then, when the suffix *kta* is added to the root *pracccha* (DhP. 1413) in the sense of "desire to know," because [the substitution] is internal (*antaraṅga*), [the rule would apply prematurely].

If the augment *tuk* were applied by the rule *ṭhcche ca* (6.1.73), and then the substitute *ś* were applied to the letter *cch* alone, the undesirable form *pṛṣṭa* would result. However, since the term [in the rule] includes the *tuk*, the *tuk* itself is also replaced by the substitute; thus, the undesired form does not occur at all.

Having considered that such an undesirable consequence (*doṣaprasaṅga*) would follow, [the author] shows that the inclusion of the suffix *sak* is intended by stating, "of this *ṭhccha*, together with *sak*. That the inclusion of *sak* is understood from the rule "yaj-yāc-yata-vic-ch-prac-ch-ir-kṣo naṅ" (Pāṇini 3.3.90), because of the addition of the suffix *naṅ*.

For this is the purpose of that insertion of *ṅ*: so that in the case of *viśna*, the rule "pugantalaghūpadhasya" (Pāṇini 7.3.86) might not apply, causing the guṇa substitution. And if, in this context, only the letter *c* were taken as the substitute while the *t* is disregarded, then once the *tuk* insertion has been applied, [the guṇa would apply] to the letter *c* alone.
If [the substitution] were made as *ś*, then because the penultimate (*upadha*) would be heavy (*guru*), there would be no *guṇa* substitution;

thus, the inclusion of the augment *tuk* would be purposeless. However, when the inclusion of *tuk* is made, the substitute *śakāra* is applied specifically to that which already possesses *tuk*; consequently, when the penultimate is light (*laghu*), [the rule applies].
Some explain that the addition of the suffix *ṅt* is performed for the purpose of prohibiting guna when [the suffix] *sat* has arisen, and thus it becomes meaningful; however, this is incorrect,
because the addition of the suffix *ṅt* is indeed for the purpose of prohibiting guna when *sat* has arisen.
Some explain that the addition of the suffix *ṅt* makes [the preceding element] behave as if it were *atha*; however, this is incorrect.

Since the quality (*guṇa*) would apply once [the suffix] has arisen, the addition of *ṅt* is made for the purpose of prohibiting that; some explain that it makes [the preceding element] behave as if it were *atha*, but this too is incorrect.

Even when an operation (*ādeśa*) has been performed upon that which possesses an *aṅga* [marker], the member (*aṅga*) becomes completed (*niṣṭhita*), because it is then fit for application (*prayoga*).

In that case, by the metarule (*paribhāṣā*) "When an operation has occurred within an *aṅga*, there is no further rule for what has already become completed" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 38), the *guṇa* substitution will not take place. Therefore...

If the designation were made even for that which includes the *tuk* augment, the addition of the marker *ṅ* would be entirely purposeless; how, then, could it be determined by that [marker] that the form with the *tuk* is being referred to? If this is so, then the inclusion of the form with the *tuk* is determined by the rule "nanau pṛṣṭaprativacane" (Pāṇini 3.2.120), whereas [the form] without the *tuk* is not.

In the case of *grahaṇe*, it is indeed as previously stated [that the suffix is *pṛṣṭa*]. However, the addition of the marker *ṅt* in the rule for *naṅ* is for the purpose of making known that "the teaching regarding augments (*āgama*) is not universal" (*anityam āgama-śāsanam*). For if that were not universal, then in a case where the *tuk* augment is absent, the *guṇa* substitution would undesirably apply in the absence of the *ṅt* marker. Now, one might object: [The objection follows: "But..."

And a rule serves as an indicator only when there is a purpose; yet there is indeed a purpose for that addition of the suffix *ṅt*—what is it? That the substitution of semivowels (*saṃprasāraṇa*) should occur for the root *pracch* by means of the sūtra beginning with *grah-ādi* (Pāṇini 6.1.16)? This is not so; for the substitution of semivowels for *pracch* is not desired in the case of the suffix *naṅ*.
How is this known? From the indication [in the sūtra] "praśne cāsannakāle" (Pāṇini 3.2.117).

This very mention of the suffix *ṭu* is indeed an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the maxim "the teaching regarding augments is not eternal" (*anityam āgamaśāsanam*). But if there were a mention of even that which possesses the augment *t*, how could there be a substitute for that which possesses the augment *t*?
[Objection: Would it not follow that [the substitution] applies only to the final [letter], according to the rule "aṭalo'ntyasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.52)?

[Response: This is not so; because of the force of the inclusion of the *tuk* augment, it will not apply [to the final letter alone]. Even so, it would apply to the entire *aṅga* (stem) ending in that [suffix]. [To this we reply: "Substitutions apply to that which is explicitly mentioned" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 106).

Thus, [the substitution] will not apply to that which ends in -t. For example: *praśnaḥ* and *viśnaḥ*. From the roots *pracccha* (DhP 1413) in the sense of "desire to know" and *vicccha* (DhP 1423) in the sense of "going," the suffix *naṅ* is applied by Pāṇini 3.3.90 (*yajayāca...*).
Regarding the phrase "because it is antaranga," etc.: by Pāṇini 6.1.73 (*che ca*), there is the shortening of the vowel.
Since the *tuṅ* (the substitution of *u*) is dependent upon a *varṇa* (a phoneme), it is *antaranga*;

however, the letter *ś* is dependent upon the *aṅga* (the stem). In that case, the *aṅga* itself is *bahiraṅga* because it is dependent upon the suffix; how much more so, then, is the letter *ś* which depends upon that [stem]? But surely—?
And is it not the case that, by the rule *ca ṭhvārṇādāṅgaṃ balīyaḥ* (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 39), the status of being a *vārṇa* operation is stronger [for the substitution of ś]?
This is not so; for this paribhāṣā applies only where both an *āṅga* and a *vārṇa* operation apply simultaneously with reference to a single cause (*nimitta*). For example, as in the case of *iyāya*.

Based on that very same vowel *ā*, the substitution of *yaṇ* for the vowel *i* of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) would apply by the rule *ṭhiko yaṇ aci* (6.1.77); yet, based on that same vowel *ā*, the substitution of *iyaṅ* would also apply by the rule *ṭhabhyāsasyāsavarṇe* (6.4.78). When both [rules] apply simultaneously to the same location, the principle holds that "an internal operation (*āṅga*) is stronger than one based on a phoneme (*vārṇa*)."

In the case of that [rule], when the *upasthiti* (application) occurs, the requirement for the *aṅga* (the base) is indeed present. However, here, even before the production of *naṭ*, the *tuk* augment would apply by depending on the letter *ś*. Subsequently, when *naiṅ* is prescribed, the letter *ś* is its basis; thus, there is a difference in the locus (*bhinnāśrayatva*). Therefore, this [rule] does not apply here.

Regarding the word *ṭhsideḥ*: it refers to the root *ṣivu* (DhP 1108), meaning "to sew" or "to weave. Regarding the phrase "in the *na*-suffix derived from the *uṇādi* [section]": the suffix *na*, which is prescribed after roots ending in *dhā*, *pṛ*, *vasi*, and *aja* (Dhātu-pāṭha Uṇādi-sūtra 5.39), also applies to the root *ṣiv* by virtue of the rule's being stated as "variously applicable" (*bahulavacanāt*).
By the rule *kenacid āṬṭh-siveṣṭer ūc* (Daiva-Uṇādi 4.5)— meaning *siveṣṭer ūc*—
the letter *n* is prescribed for the derivation of the word *sūna*, whereby, by virtue of the long vowel pronunciation, there is no *guṇa* substitution therein. As for those who...

Those who explain this sūtra solely for the sake of deriving the word *syona* would find the long vowel [in *syona*] to be purposeless; for once the *guṇa* substitution has been applied, whether the original vowel was short or long, no difference whatsoever remains. [Furthermore, they argue that] the *ūṭh* augment is applied prior to the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*).

Thus: "Because it is internal (*antaraṅgatvāt*). The reason that will be stated [later] should also be understood here. For *guṇa* depends specifically upon an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix and a light penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) characterized by the absence of *iṭ*; whereas the substitute *ūṭ* [depends upon] one beginning with a nasal (*anunāsika*).

The substitute *ūṭh* is merely the letter *v*, qualified by its connection with the preceding member (*aṅga*). Therefore, the *guṇa* substitution is *bahiraṅga* (external), whereas the substitute *ūṭh* is *antaraṅga* (internal).
Consequently, because it is *antaraṅga*, *ūṭh* is applied prior to the *guṇa* of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*). Thereafter...

The connection with the subject at hand is as follows: since the *yaṇ* substitution is internal (*antaraṅga*), it is performed prior to the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*). The *yaṇ* substitution is internal because it depends upon two phonemes (*varṇāśrayatvāt*). Now, one might object that according to the rule "that which pertains to a grammatical element (*āṅga*) is stronger than that which pertains to a phoneme" (*varṇād āṅgaṃ balīyaḥ*), the *guṇa* belonging to the grammatical element [should take precedence].

[Objection: Since it is more powerful, why is that very [substitution] not applied before the *yaṇ*-substitution? To this he says: "Because they have different bases," and so forth. For it was stated that this [rule] applies where both rules—one pertaining to an *āṅga* (internal) and one pertaining to a *varṇa* (phonetic)—apply with respect to a single cause (*nimitta*). But here, however...

The substitution of *yaṇ* depends on *ūṭ*, whereas the *guṇa* substitution depends on the *ārddhadhātuka* affix; thus, there is a difference in their substrata (*bhinnāśrayatva*). Consequently, this paribhāṣā does not apply here. [The form] "śabdaprāṭ" is derived from "he asks for a word" (*śabdaṃ pṛcchati*) by means of the rule "kvibvacipracchi... (Vārttika 288).

The suffix *kvip* is applied, and there is lengthening of the vowel. By the rule *vaścādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 8.2.36), the *ś* is changed to *ṣ*; that [ṣ] is further changed to *ḍ* by the rule for *jaś*-substitution; and that [ḍ] is further changed to *ṭ* by the rule for *car*-substitution. Thus we have *goviṭ*. [The root] *vicch* (meaning "to go," Dhatupatha 1423) takes *kvip* in the sense of "one who goes toward a cow" (*gāṃ vicchati*), according to the rule *kvip ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.76).
By this [rule]. Likewise, in *ṭhakṣudyaḥ* and *hiraṇyaṣṭhÂayūḥ*, [the substitution] is also from *diviṣṭhi*.

Now, one might object: the *yaṇ*-substitution is internal (*antaraṅga*) because it depends on phonemes (*varṇa`), whereas the *ūḍ*-substitution is external (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends on an affix (*pratyaya`); and in such a case, "that which is external is as if non-existent (*asiddha`) with respect to that which is internal."

[Question: "In this case, should the substitution of *yaṇ* not take place? To this, he says: "That which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is not established when [it comes into conflict with] that which is internal (*antaraṅga*)," and so forth. This [rule] is prohibited where there is immediate succession (*ānantarya*) between two vowels, according to the principle: "When there is immediate succession of vowels, the status of being external is not postulated. (Vyāḍipañjikā 44).

This is its meaning: when there is immediate succession with a vowel (*acaḥ*), the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā* is not applicable; that is to say, it does not come into effect. The proof for this point is the statement "it is as if non-existent" (*asiddha*) in the rule *ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.86), which prescribes that [the substitution] is as if non-existent when a *tuṭ* augment is to be applied. For the sole purpose of that [rule] is this very instance: in the case of *adhītya*.

This is so that the *tuk* augment, characterized by a short vowel, may apply because the *savarṇadīrgha* (long-vowel substitution of homogeneous vowels) is considered *asiddha*. For if the *bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā* were to apply when there is immediate succession (*ānantarya*) between two vowels (*ac*), then, since the *tuk* would depend on a single word (*ekapada*), it would be *antaraṅga* and thus required to be applied first.

Since the substitution of *ekādeśa* depends on two words (*padadvayāśrayatva*), it will be considered *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to the external operation; so what is the purpose of the explicit statement that it is *asiddha*? [The answer is: Since the *tuk* augment depends on a single word (*tadaikapadāśrayatva*), it is an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation; when this *tuk* is to be applied, the substitution of *ekādeśa*, which depends on two words and is thus external (*bahiraṅga*), will be considered *asiddha*.

What is the purpose of stating that [the rule] is unestablished (*asiddha*)? It is done for the sake of making known that the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā* does not apply in cases of immediate sequence (*ajānantarya*). Thus, in the word *hiraṇyaṣṭhīvī*, the substitution of *s* for *ṣ* by the rule *dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ* (P. 6.1.64) does not take place; for it has been stated: "An exception must be formulated for *su*-beginning words, *dhātu*, *ṣṭhivu*, *ṣvaṣkati*, and *ina*."

Because of the statement [in Pāṇini’s grammar], "pṛṣṭaḥ": there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule beginning with *grah-* (Pāṇ. 6.1.16), and as before, the substitution of *ṣ* and *ṣṭu*. Regarding "dyubhyām": the substitution of *u* occurs by the rule "diva ut" (Pāṇ. 6.1.131).
For those who do not carry forward the condition *kṅti* here, this rule would have to apply elsewhere as well;
consequently, forms such as *dyaubhyām* and *dyaubhiḥ* would not be established. Anticipating this, he asks:
"How is it that *dyaubhyām* and *dyaubhiḥ* are formed? [The answer is: "When *ūṭh* has been applied. Once *ūṭh* has been applied, [the rule does not apply].

The meaning is that something is established. Regarding the statement, "Because of the *tapara* [specification] in 'diva uḥ', there will be a duration of one mātrā," the *tapara* marker need not have been applied in the rule *diva uḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.131).
For even though it is said that "an *ukāra* being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) includes its homogeneous sounds" (Cāndra...), [the point remains].

Nevertheless, due to internal similarity (*āntaratamya*), since the consonant has a duration of half a *mātrā*, the vowel *ū* will have a duration of exactly one *mātrā*; it will not be long. Why, then, is the *tapara* (the *ṛ* with a following *p*) employed to exclude that [possibility]?
It is employed so that even by another rule (*lakṣaṇāntara*), whatever [vowel] would otherwise result as long, that [long vowel] shall not occur.

This is for the purpose of ensuring that [the vowel] be short. Therefore, in this case, by the rule *diva uta* (Pāṇini 6.1.131) itself, the duration will be one mātrā because of the indicatory letter *t*; otherwise, if a long vowel were to occur by the rule *ch-avoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.19), then [the effort] would be fruitless.
In the rule *ṭhdiva ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.131), the use of the long vowel marker *ā* (*taparakaraṇam*) would be unnecessary, as there is nothing to be excluded [by it].
Alternatively, it is connected with the subsequent explanatory passage beginning with "when *ūṭh* has been applied.
In that context, the meaning is as follows: let *ūṭh* indeed be applied generally to both *kṅit* and non-*kṅit* suffixes.

Even though that [substitution] has been applied, by the rule "that which is modified by a single substitution is treated as non-different from the original" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 16), the short vowel will occur in its very place by the rule "diva uT" (Pāṇini 6.1.131), because of the indicatory letter *t* (taparatva). For this indeed is its purpose: that it occurs in the place of *ūṬ*.

This is so that it may be a substitute for the *mātrika* (short vowel), lest a long vowel (*dīrgha*) occur due to proximity (*āntaratamya*). Furthermore, under this interpretation, the statement—"In the rule *diva uḥ*, the inclusion of the letter *t* is for the purpose of excluding *ūṭ*; otherwise, in forms such as *dyaubhyām* and *dyaubhiḥ*, *ūṭ* would apply by virtue of its higher status"—is contradicted. It is not [the case].

For in that case, the relationship of original and substitute (*sthānyādeśabhāva*) between *u* and *ūṭh* would not be possible; rather, it is a relationship of sublated and sublater (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*). Thus, its purpose is described as follows: the inclusion of the long *Ṭ* (*taparakaraṇa*) is for the sake of excluding *ūṭh* and for the sake of sublation. For if that [long Ṭ] were not present, then by virtue of being subsequent (*paratvāt*), *ūṭh* [would apply].

[The vowel *u*] is obtained; therefore, for the purpose of overriding that [substitution], the *tapara* (long *ū*) is employed. Thus, there is no contradiction in ensuring that by this very rule, a short *u* is produced even after overriding the subsequent *ūṭh*. Those who maintain the relationship of original and substitute (*sthānyādeśabhāva*) explain the text in this way: [regarding] the *ūṭh*...

The meaning is that it is for the sake of the cessation [of the substitution] of the *sthānin* (the original element), namely *ūṭh*. The purpose of the inclusion of *ta* (the *tapara* marker) is so that when the substitute *ūṭh* has been applied, there may be the cessation of that which was present as *ūṭh*. In the statement "because it is subsequent, *ūṭh* would apply," the word "prescribed" (*vihita*) is to be supplied, and the word "possessing the audible form" (*śrutimān*) is also to be supplied.

This is what is meant: for here, because it is subsequent, the *san* prescribed by the rule *ūḍ* would apply as a mere substitute (*śruti-mātra*), whereas its cessation (*nivṛtti*) is desired. Therefore, the vowel *t* is added after the *ra* (*taparatva*) in order to effect that cessation. Even when the substitute is prescribed without the vowel *t* following it, [the substitution of] *ūṭh*...
There is indeed an exclusion [of the long vowel], because the locus (sthānin) possesses the nature of being excluded.

And it is stated that the inclusion of *t* in the rule concerning the *tapara* [term] is for the purpose of such exclusion. In that context, by the force of the explicit statement, it is understood that the inclusion of *t* serves the purpose of that specific exclusion in which, when it occurs, a distinction arises. And therefore—
This is stated by implication: the addition of *t* (the *tapara* marker) is for the purpose of substituting a short vowel for *ūṭ*.

For when the substitution is *tapara*, the exclusion of *ūṭ* that is effected results in a specific distinction; it does not occur when the substitute is not *tapara*. Indeed, if the substitute were not *tapara*, then by the principle of closest proximity (*āntaryāt*), a long vowel would [be substituted].

How is there a distinction [in the result] such that it would necessarily be long? Furthermore, what desired result is accomplished when the mention of *kit* is removed, such that some do not carry forward the rule *kṅti* here? To this he says: "In the rule *cchaśāṃ ṣaḥ*," and so forth.

When the mention of *kṅ* has been set aside, by this [rule] the substitution of *ś* for *cch* is prescribed both when *kṅit* follows and when it does not; consequently, the mention of *cch* in the rule *vraśca-* (Pāṇini 8.2.36) would not need to be made. Since everything [would be accomplished] simply by the prescription of *ṣ*-hood (*ṣatva*) for the letter *ś*.

Since the quality of being a *ṣ* (ṣatva) is absent [in the original *cch*], the inclusion of *cch* in the rule *vraśca-* (Pāṇini 8.2.36) must indeed be made for the purpose of prescribing the quality of being a *ṣ* for the letter *ch*. Now, how is the form *praṣṭhā* established for them, given that once the augment *tuk* has been applied, if the quality of being a *ṣ* were applied to the letter *ch* alone, the undesirable form *praṭṣṭhā* would result? This is not a fault.

For they maintain that in the sūtra *vraśca-* etc. (Pāṇini 8.2.36), there is the inclusion of the letter *c* together with its *t*-augment (*satuk*). If this *ūṭh* were *ṭit*, then by the rule *ādyantau ṭakitau* (1.1.46) and others, [the augment] would occur at the beginning or end. In that case, even if the *v* were elided by the rule *vali lopaḥ* (6.1.66), [the form] would still result in *akṣadyūḥ* and so forth.

[The form] *sidhyati* is established, but *jūrityādi* would not be; for if [the substitute] were *ṭit*, then by the rule *jvaratvarasrivyavimavāmupadhāyāśca* (Pāṇini 6.4.20), there would be two instances of *ūṭ*: one before the *v* and another after the *a*. Therefore, the *ṭit*-status of *ūṭ* must be accepted, not its *ṭit*-status. Of that too...
Having considered in his mind that if the *ṭhi* status of this [substitute] were not present, it would be useless,
he says— "The making of *ṭh* a *ṭhit*" and so forth— in order to demonstrate the purpose of the *ṭhi* status of the substitute *uḍ*. By speaking thus...

In the rule *ṭh-ity-edhaty-ūṭh-su* (Pāṇini 6.1.89) as well, there is a reference only to that which has the marker *ṭh*. For it is only if there too there is a reference only to that which has the marker *ṭh* that the purpose of adding the marker *ṭh* to *ūṭh*—namely, to serve as a qualifier—is justified; otherwise, it would not. If the marker *ṭh* were not applied here [to *ūṭh*], then...

In the rule "ṭhetyedhatyūṭhÂasu" (Pāṇini 6.1.89), the addition of the marker *ṭ* should not have been made either; for an *ū* vowel possessing the *ṭ* marker does not occur anywhere. If it were stated in this way [without *ṭ*], then in forms such as *praūhate* and *prohataḥ*, there would also be vṛddhi. Therefore, the marker *ṭ* is added for the purpose of specification.

However, there is no hearing of the sound *ṭha*; for [the rule] is stated with the *ṭha* that has undergone *cartya* (substitution). If, then, this *ṭh* is indeed [the one intended], then in the rule "ṭhityedhatyūṭhṣu" (Pāṇini 6.1.89), there would also be the grasping of only that which ends in *ṭh*; this being the case, the rule "vāha ūṭh" (6.4.132) would not be included therein, and consequently—
Since there would be no *vṛddhi* in the case of *praṣṭhauha*, he says: "This [rule] *vāha ūṭh* is also [applicable]," and so forth.
Just as before, there is no hearing of the letter *ṭh* either.

20. *jvaratvarasrivyavimavām upadhāyāś ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.20). The substitution [of *u* for the semivowel] of *sri*, *vi*, and *mavi* is already established by the preceding rule alone; however, it is not established for their penultimate vowel (*upadhā*). Therefore, these are mentioned for that purpose. As for *jvara* and *tvara*, [the substitution applies] even to the letter *v*.

It is not established by the preceding [rule], because there is an intervention between these two—the *a* and the *r*—and the *kvip* suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant. Therefore, their mention is for the sake of the *v* and for the sake of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*). Thus: "jūḥ, jurau, juraḥ," from the root *jṝ* (DhP 776), meaning "to grow old" or "to be feverish."

When the vowel *u* is substituted for the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) by the rule *oṭh* [Pāṇini 6.4.132], the form of the preceding letter is applied according to *samprasāraṇācca* (6.1.108). Thus, *jartīḥ* is formed with the suffix *ktin*. *Tūḥ* is derived from the root *ñi tvara* (to hasten, to be in agitation; Dhātupāṭha 775); it means "the one who hastens" (*tūrṇaḥ*), as noted in the Kāśikā: "the one who hastens" (*tūrtiḥ*). Thus, *tūrṇaḥ*.

Regarding *nāstiṣṭ*: the substitution of *na* [for *t*] occurs by the rule "ṭhradābhyāṃ niṣṭhāto naḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.42). Regarding *srūḥ*: [the root] *sru* is used in the sense of "flowing" and "drying up" (Dhātupāṭha 1109); [the long vowel] is due to the rule for lengthening in a homogeneous context (*savaraṇadīrghaḥ*). Regarding *sruvau*, *sruvaḥ*: the substitution of *uvaṅ* occurs by the rule "aci śnudhātu... (Pāṇini 6.4.77), etc. Regarding *ūḥ*: [the root] *av*.
In the root *rakṣ*— [the roots *rakṣ*, *kānti*, *prīti*,

*tṛpti*, *avagama*, *praveśa*, *śravaṇa*, *svaṇa*, *svam*, *arthayācana*, *kriyā*, *icchā*, *dīpti*, *avāpti*, *āliṅgana*, *hiṃsā*, *dāna*, *bhāga*, and *vṛddhi* are listed in the Dhātupāṭha (DhP 600)]— and in the root *mū* (meaning "to bind," DhP 599), the suffix *ūṅ* is prescribed here for the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) belonging to roots such as *jvara* and others; this is the *upadhā*.

The *cāla* is the letter preceding the final one, and "finalness" (*antyatva*) is relative. In that regard—for example, in the forms *śreyān* and *śreyāṃsau*—the letters preceding the *sakāra*, among which the final is the *nakāra*, the letter preceding that *nakāra* is the *upadhā*; likewise, it is so for the [letters] preceding the *jvar* and other [roots].

A certain misconception might arise that the *upadhā* (the penultimate letter) is that which precedes the final vowel of those two [vowels], and since that [final vowel] belongs to *jvara* and the others, the *ūṭh* substitution must apply to that *upadhā* as well because it is a constituent part of it. Therefore, in order to dispel that [misconception], [the sūtra says] "of which... (*yasyāḥ*).

In order to demonstrate that the *ūṭh* substitute must occur in place of the *upadhā*, he says: "In the case of *jvara* and *tvara*, the *upadhā* [vowel] follows the letter *v*," and so forth. That which is to be replaced by *ūṭh* is intended here by the term *upadhā*. But what is the reason for this?

Does the *ūṅ* suffix occur after a penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) as shown by the author of the *Vṛtti*, and not after any other? [The answer is: No, because the penultimate vowel is specifically qualified by the *kvip* suffix, the *jhal*-beginning suffixes, and the *kiṅt* suffixes. Here, the penultimate vowel of roots such as *jvara* is qualified by the *kvip* suffix, by those beginning with *jhal*, and by the *kiṅt* suffixes.

Regarding the statement "ūṅ occurs after that *upadhā*," here, according to the principle "that which lacks intervention [is considered present] even when there is intervention" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 46), since the *upadhā* mentioned by the author of the Vṛtti can possibly be separated from the suffix by only a single phoneme, it is precisely that [proximate *upadhā*] which becomes *ūṅ*.

21. *rāl lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.21). [The examples given are] *mūrchā* and *hūrchā*. *Mūrchā* is from the root *murchā* (Dhātupāṭha 212), meaning "fainting" (*moha*) and "heightening" (*samucchrāya*). *Hūrchā* is from the root *hurchā* (Dhātupāṭha 211), meaning "crookedness" (*kauṭilya*). But how, then, is there the elision of the *cch* sound here?

[An objection is raised: "This [rule] does not apply, because the letter *ccha* is not included in this sūtra; moreover, even that which is under discussion (the substitute *ccha*) is accompanied by the augment *tuk*, yet there is no *tuk* here.
Indeed, the augment *tuk* is never prescribed for the letter *repha* (*r*) when followed by *ccha*? To this he says:
"When there is elision of *ra*, [the substitute is] that which is accompanied by *tuk," and so forth. This is so that it may be carried forward into the subsequent rules.

In the preceding sūtra, the *svarita* accentuation of the letter *cch* was promised, yet it is impossible for a *ra* followed by a *t* (*satukka*) to occur [after it]. Therefore, by virtue of the contextual requirement (*sāmarthya*), only the *tugrahaṇa* (the inclusion of the augment *t*) is understood to carry over. Alternatively, there is a double mention of *cch* in the preceding sūtra; therein, one instance includes the *t* (*satukka*), while the other consists of the *tugrahaṇa*.

Furthermore, because the grammatical tradition (āgama-śāsana) is not eternal, the letter *cch* may be elided. This being the case, what was stated—that the marker *ṅ* in the suffix *naṅ* serves to prohibit *guṇa*—becomes logically consistent.
Thus, although both *cch* letters were present in the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*), nevertheless, it is [the first] that follows the *repha*.
A suffix with an indicatory *k* does not occur; rather, only that which has been grasped as such follows. As in *ṭhūḥ*, *dhūḥ*.
[The roots] *ṭurvī*, *thurvī*, *durvī*, and *dhurvī* have the sense of "injuring" (*hiṃsā*). (Dhātupāṭha 570–573).

22. *asiddhavadatrā bhāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.22). It should be understood that "it is as if unestablished" (*asiddhavat*). This word *siddha* signifies that which is fully accomplished, as in the expression "the rice is cooked" (*siddha odanaḥ*). That which is not *siddha* is *asiddha*.

It is called *asiddhavat* (like the unestablished) because it exists as something similar to the unestablished by virtue of its common property of not performing a task that has already been accomplished. What, then, is this [task]? Some say it is "the effect" (*kārya*), because of its predominance. For the treatise (*śāstra*) exists for the sake of the effect;
therefore, with respect to the treatise, the effect is predominant, according to the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Furthermore, because the treatise (*śāstra*) is taken as the limit, it is logical that the treatise itself is considered non-existent [for the purposes of the preceding rule]; otherwise, some specific grammatical operation (*kārya*) would have been taken as the limit. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *ābhāt*? For, since the mark of the circumflex accent (*svarita*) applies, even without the mention of *ābhāt*, [the desired result would follow].

Will the phrase "as if unestablished" (asiddhavat) continue in force until the end of the section on *pāda*? To this he says: "The mention of 'up to and including *ā*'* (ā bhāt) is an indication of the scope. For if the mention of "up to and including *ā*" were not made, it would not be known—regarding what operation to be performed does this section become as if unestablished? Therefore, the mention of "up to and including *ā*" is an indication of the scope.

It is stated [in the sūtra] "ā bhāt" (up to the word *bha*) for the purpose of fully understanding the meaning that "that which will be stated [hereafter], being the subject matter as something to be performed, is treated as if it were not established (*asiddhavat*). If this is so,
then the phrase "atra" (here) is employed to indicate the scope of this subject matter, and that scope is...
Is this not already indicated by the word "bhāt"? To this, he says: "here," and so forth.
That which has a common substratum (āśraya) as its cause is "samānāśraya"; the state of being such is "samānāśrayatva.
The mention of "here" (atra) is for the sake of establishing—that is, for the thorough understanding of—that [condition]; and the remainder of the sentence is: "if that [condition] exists here."

By the word *tat*, that for which the status of being "as if unestablished" (*asiddhavat*) is prescribed is indicated. By the word *atra* (here), it is also indicated that where something else—whether non-existent or scripturally established—occurs, it must depend precisely upon that [prescribed element].
This is connected with what is to be stated by the phrase *asiddhavat*. By the word *tat*, wherever...
The grammatical operation prescribed by the rule is referred to; that which has this as its basis or cause is "tadāśrayam" (dependent on that).

The particle *eva* is for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇārtha*). The meaning is: "only that [operation] becomes as if unestablished (*asiddhavat*). By the word *eva*, it is implied: "but that which depends on something else (*vyāśraya*) does not become as if unestablished. Thus, by means of the particle *eva*.

It shows that which is excluded: the meaning is that it is so called because its locus (*āśraya*) is distinct from—that is, a different entity than—that wherein the scriptural action (*kārya*) is enjoined by means of that appearance (*tad-ābhāsa*).
By the particle *iti*, the meaning just explained is referred back. In this [context of] the mention of "here" (*atragrahaṇe*).

The meaning of this sūtra results in the establishment that [the two operations] have the same locus; that is to say, what is the purpose for which it is treated as if it were unestablished? To this he says: "The statement 'asiddhavacana'," and so forth.

By the word "utsarga" (general rule), the original element (*sthānin*) is indicated here, on the grounds that it is set aside by the substitute (*ādeśa*). Alternatively, it is called "utsarga" due to its similarity to a general rule; for just as a general rule, having been applied universally, is withdrawn from a particular case, so too [is this].

Even for that which possesses a substitute (sthānin), there is a prohibition of its manifestation based on the cause of the substitute (ādeśa). That which has the general rule (utsarga) as its defining characteristic is "that which has the general rule as its cause" (utsargalakṣaṇa); that which has the substitute (ādeśa) as its defining characteristic is "that which has the substitute as its cause" (ādeśalakṣaṇa).
The affirmation and prohibition of these two occur respectively, as follows:
The statement "asiddha" is for the purpose of [establishing] "syātām"—that is, forms such as "edhi" and "śādhi.

These are examples of the application of the general rule (*utsarga-lakṣaṇa-bhāva*). [The roots are] "as bhūvi" (DhP 1065) and "śāsa anuśiṣṭau" (DhP 1075) [or "śāsu" (DhP)]. [In the case of] the imperative (*loṭ*), second person singular (*sip*): [The derivation of *edhi*: *as* + *loṭ*, *sip* → *as* + *hi* (by *loṭo heryaḥ*) → *edhi* (by *aster bhūḥ*)] [The derivation of *śādhi*: *śās* + *loṭ*, *sip* → *śās* + *hi* (by *loṭo heryaḥ*) → *śādhi* (by *śāso ṅīṭ* and *śā hau*)]
By the rule *ṭhserhyapicca* (Pāṇini 3.4.87), there is the substitution of *hi* for *si*; by virtue of belonging to the *adādi* class, there is the elision (*luk*) of *śap*;

and by *śnasorallopaḥ* (6.4.111), there is the elision of the vowel *a*. Because it is both subsequent (*paratva*) and obligatory (*nityatva*), the substitution of *e* (by *dhvasoreddhāvabhyāsalopaśca*, 6.4.119) occurs prior to the application of the *ghi* designation.
Since the root *śās* is also eternal, the substitution of *śā* by rule 6.4.35 (*śā hau*) occurs prior to the substitution of *ghi*.
Consequently, for those two [substitutions], namely the change to *et* and the absence of *śā*, the substitution of *dhi* by rule 6.4.101 (*hujhalbhyo herdhiḥ*)—
which is characterized by the condition of ending in a *jhal* consonant— does not apply, because the necessary cause is absent.

It occurs because it is not established [as having taken effect]. For example: *āgahi*, *jahi*. These are examples for the prohibition of a grammatical operation conditioned by a substitute (*ādeśa*).
In the case of *agāhi*: from the root *gam* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, there is the imperative (*loṭ*), the ending *sip*, its substitute *hi*, and [the rule] "bahulam... [is applied].

In the Vedic language (*cchandasi*), there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix according to Pāṇini 2.4.76; the nasal (*anunāsika*) is dropped by the rule beginning with 6.4.37. As for *jahī*: from the root *han*, the imperative (*loṭ*) and other forms are as before;
there is elision of *śap* because it belongs to the *adādi* class, and the substitution of *j* occurs by 6.4.36.

Now, in this case, after the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) and the substitution of *ja*, the elision of *hi* prescribed by "ṭhato heḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.105) would apply; however, it does not take effect because [the previous operations] are considered non-existent (*asiddha*). Regarding the form "abhāji": it is derived from the root *bhanj* (Dhātupāṭha 1453) meaning "to crush," in the *luṅ* tense.
The *ātmanepada* suffix is applied because the action is directed toward the self (*karmavatkarmaṇā*). By the rule *ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.66), the *ciṇ* suffix is substituted for *cli*;

by *ciṇo luk* (6.4.104), the *t* of the suffix is elided; and by *bhañjeśca ciṇi* (6.4.33), the nasal is elided. This [elision] occurs even though it shares the same basis (*samānāśraya*) as the other.
Because of the statement "up to *ābhāt*," there is no non-application (*asiddhatva*) when the grammatical operation of *vṛddhi* is to be performed.

In the word *rāgaḥ*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *rañj*; by the rule *ghañi ca bhāvakaraṇayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.27), the nasal is elided. This [elision] also [is not considered non-existent] with respect to this *vṛddhi* of the seventh case (*sāptamikī*), as they share the same basis (*samānāśraya*).

Because of the statement "it must be performed as if it were not yet accomplished" (*kartavyāyām ābhāt*), there is no lack of established status (*asiddhatva*). For example: *papuṣaḥ*, *cicyuṣaḥ*, *luluvuṣaḥ*. Here, the suffix *kvasu* is applied to the roots *pā* (to drink), *ci* (to gather), and *lū* (to cut) in the perfect tense (*liṭ*);

there is reduplication; and by Pāṇini 6.4.131, the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) occurs for the *vasu* [portion of the suffix]. This is because that substitution depends on different bases (*vyāśrayatvāt*).
Thus: from the roots *pāti* (from √ci), *cinoti*, and *lunāti*, the suffix *kvasu* is applied in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), followed by reduplication.

By the rule *vasoḥ samprasāraṇam* (6.4.131), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the *v*. Since that [vocalization] depends on multiple factors (*vyāśrayatva*), the elision of the *a* occurs by *āto lopa iṭi ca* (6.4.64), and then [the substitution of *e* for *ai*] occurs by *eranekāco'saṃyogapūrvasya* (6.4.82).

When the substitution of *yaṇ* is to be applied, as well as when the substitution of *uvaṅ* is to be applied by rules such as "in the case of *ṭhac*, *in*, and verbal roots" (6.4.77), the status of being "as if non-existent" (*asiddhavat*) does not apply. Now, one might object: is this not already established by the rule "after *ṣu*, [there is] *pararūpa* except at the end of a word" (6.1.96)? This is not so; for that [rule] applies only to what is explicitly stated in the text (*pratipadokta*).

The word *hyas* is included there [in the rule], and here [in the present context] it is used in its technical (lākṣaṇika) sense. But how is there a dependence on multiple factors (*vyāśrayatva*) here? To this he says: "For the elision of *āl* and so forth... The word *hi* means "because," and the particle *iti* means "therefore."

But even so, according to the principle "that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal (*antaraṅga*)," since the external Samprasāraṇa is unestablished with respect to the internal elision of *ā* (*āllopa*) and other operations, those [internal] operations such as *āllopa* would simply not apply. For in that case:
[The opponent argues: "Since the portion [of the base] preceding the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is *vasu*, the elision (*lopa*) and other operations depend upon that;
however, the *samprasāraṇa* depends upon the case-ending, whereas that which depends upon the base (*prakṛti*) is *antaraṅga*, and that which depends upon the suffix (*pratyaya*) is *bahiraṅga*.
To this he replies: "That which is *bahiraṅga* is as if non-existent," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "this also" (*etad api*): the neuter form is used in reference to the word *etad api*. By the passage beginning with "for of these" (*eṣāṃ hi*), he states the reason why this paribhāṣā does not apply.
This paribhāṣā operates only where there is a simultaneous presentation of both an internal (*antaraṅga*) and an external (*bahiraṅga*) operation.

It operates to render the external (*bahiraṅga*) operation non-existent when an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation is to be performed. And this *paribhāṣā* is an *ābhīya* (pertaining to the *ābhīya* rules), because it is indicated by the rule "vāha ūṭh" (P. 6.4.132) within the body of *ābhīya* rules. Therefore, while this [rule] is to be applied, [the principle] "asiddhavadatrā... [applies].

Regarding the rule *bhāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.22), because of the rules *vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam* (6.4.131) and the elision of *as* (*asya lopaḥ*), etc., there is no simultaneous presentation of the internal (*antaraṅga*) and external (*bahiraṅga*) operations;
thus, [the former] does not apply. Since that [former] does not apply, [the latter] does not exist.

The external *samprasāraṇa* is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*). By that, the elision of *al* (*allopa*) and so forth indeed take place. Regarding the rule "vug-yuṭ-au" and so on: the meaning is that this formulation must be explained in such a way that these two—*vuk* and *yuṭ*—are established as valid when *uvaṅ* and *yiṇ* are to be applied respectively. In this regard, the following...

The explanation: here, the mention of the suffix *vat* need not be made; even without it, the extension (*atideśa*) is already established, as in the rules "the *ṣatva* and *tuk* are as if non-existent" (6.1.86) and "that which is earlier is as if non-existent" (8.2.1). It is mentioned, however, so that in some cases what belongs to its own base (*svāśraya*) may also be established as valid.

The word *syāt* is used for this very purpose. By means of it, the substitutions *vuk*, *ṛṭ*, *uvaṅ*, and *yaṇ* will be established. For example, in the form *babhūva*: by the rule *bhavateraḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.73), the substitution of *ā* occurs for the reduplication, and by *bhuvo vug luṅliṭoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.88), the suffix *vuk* is added. In that case, if [the former rule] were considered asiddha (not yet established), [the latter would not apply].

By the rule *ṭhaci śnudhātu* (Pāṇini 6.4.77), *uvaṅ* would [otherwise] occur; however, because that [substitution] is considered established (*siddha*), it does not take place. Regarding *upadidīye*: from the root *dīṅ* in the sense of "decay" (Dhātupāṭha 1134), the *liṭ* suffix is applied; by the rule *ṭhliṭastajhayoḥ* (3.4.81), etc., *iś* is substituted for it, and then *yuṭ* is added to *dīṅ* before an affix beginning with a vowel that has *kṅit* as its marker.

Thus, by [Pāṇini 3.3.107], the suffix *yuṭ* is applied. If that [suffix] were also considered asiddha, then the substitution of *yaṇ* would occur by [Pāṇini 6.4.82]: "In place of a long vowel (*ṭhi*) not preceded by a conjunct consonant, there is *yaṇ*.
Because it is established (*siddha*), this does not happen.

Does *ā* here signify a limit (*maryādā*) or an inclusive extension (*abhividhi*)? If the first alternative is adopted, then the [rule] belonging to the domain of *ā* would not be considered asiddha; consequently, the paribhāṣā "that which is external is asiddha with respect to that which is internal" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 42) [would apply].
If [the rule] were not based on the treatise (*śāstrīya*), then while it was operating upon an unstable state,

the *samprasāraṇa* of *vasuḥ* and the *al-lopa* and other operations would not be considered *asiddha*. Even so, the *samprasāraṇa* of *vasuḥ*, being *bahiraṅga*, [would not be *asiddha*] with respect to the *antaraṅga* operations such as *al-lopa*.
When there is a simultaneous presentation [of rules], by that paribhāṣā as it operates—

when there is a simultaneous presentation of the external *samprasāraṇa* of *vasu* and the internal operations such as elision (*alopa*) and so forth— by that paribhāṣā as it operates, [the rule for] *vasu* [is applied].

If the substitution of *samprasāraṇa* were treated as not having taken effect (*asiddha*), then because they are *antaraṅga*, operations such as the elision of *a* (*allop*) would not occur in forms like *papuṣaḥ*, *cicyuṣaḥ*, and *luluviṣaḥ*. Having seen this flaw in the view that [the rule] sets a limit (*maryādā*), he states the second position: "The particle *ā* in the expression *ā bhāt* is used in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*)."
And the meaning has already been explained.

23. *śnānnalopaḥ* | (Pāṇini 6.4.23) Since no other word containing the sound *śna* is possible, even though the *m* of *śnam* is not actually heard [in the present context], it is understood by implication that only *śnam* is being referred to; therefore—

He said: "The letter *u* is that from which the *m* has been discarded. That is to say, it is so called because its *m* has been abandoned or omitted. [Regarding the roots] *añj*, etc.: *añjū* means "to manifest, to smear, to shine, or to go" (DhP 1458); *bhañj* means "to crush" (DhP 1453); *hiṃs* means "injury."
Since this [root] is listed [in the Dhātupāṭha] with an *u* vowel, the augment *num* is applied; and because it belongs to the *rudh*-class, the suffix *śnam* is added.
This inclusion of the letter *ś* [in the rule] is intended for the purpose that [the suffix] might not apply in cases such as *nanditā* and *nandakaḥ*;
however, this is unnecessary, because [the rule] "between a suffix and a non-suffix, [the suffix alone is taken]" applies.

By this paribhāṣā, "grahaṇam" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 72), [the substitution] will not occur here. Furthermore, there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*): the fact that he includes the words *nandin* and *nandana* in the *kṣubhnādi* group indicates that the elision of the letter *n* does not occur after the root *nand*. And this refers to the general case.
This serves as an indicator; therefore, [the suffix] will not apply even in cases such as *nanditā* and *nandakaḥ*.

Consequently, with the intention that one should simply state "there is no elision of the penultimate vowel" (*nānna lopaḥ*), he asks: "What is the purpose of including the letter ś? [The answer is: *yajñānām*, *yatnānām*—[these are formed] by [Pāṇini 3.3.90] *yajayāca*.

The suffix *naṅ* [is applied]; from that which ends in it, the sixth case plural (*ṣaṣṭhī-bahuvacana*) [is formed], and the augment *nuṭ* [is added]. If the inclusion of the letter *ś* were not made, then the elision of *n* (*nalopaḥ*) would certainly occur there. It might be argued: "Once the long vowel is effected, because the designation 'nāt' no longer exists, [the elision] will not take place. To this he says: "And before the case-endings (*supi*)."
And so forth. By the rule *supi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.102), there is a long vowel (*dīrgha*) as a substitute for the vowel [of the stem].

When the elision of the letter *n* (*nakāra-lopa*) is to be performed as a preceding operation (*pūrva-vidhi*), that [long vowel], having attained the status of being "as if occupying the original position" (*sthānivadbhāva*) by the rule *acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau* (Pāṇini 1.1.57), would—if its length were due to its being subsequent (*paratva*)—[be subject to the following].

Even if [the rule for] the inclusion of that which is distinguished by the letter *ś* were not applied, then the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would indeed occur here; furthermore, because it applies whether [the cause] has been performed or not (*kṛtākṛtaprasaṅgitvāt*), [the elision is considered permanent]. However, as for the lengthening (*dīrghatva*), once the elision of *n* has taken place, it does not apply because its cause has already been removed; therefore, that [lengthening] is non-permanent (*anitya*). But [one might object]: "In the case of a preceding operation..."

It was stated that there is the status of being like the original (sthānivadbhāva), and yet this [operation] is not a rule concerning what precedes (pūrvavidhi). This is not a fault; for this too is indeed a rule concerning what precedes, because the compound "pūrvavidhi" is understood there as "a rule [that applies] on account of what precedes."

Now, even though the inclusion of the nasal *ṇ* accompanied by a *ś* is being made, why does [the substitution] not occur here in the cases “viśvānām” and “praśnānām,” since in these instances the *n* is indeed accompanied by a *ś*? To this he says: “In the case of ‘viśvānām’ and ‘praśnānām,’ etc. For here...

By the paribhāṣā *pratipadoktaparibhāṣā* (Vyā.pa. 3), there is the inclusion of that which is directly specified (*pratipadokta*) by the word *śna*, and not of that which is merely derivative (*lākṣaṇika*).
For in the examples *viśnānām* and *paraśnānām*, [the rule] *cch-avoḥ śūḍ-anunāsike ca* applies.
