When the substitution of *ś* is made [by P. 6.4.19], the word *śna* is produced; however, this is merely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*).

Therefore, the elision of what follows it does not occur. Since the mention of "elision" (*lopa*) is understood by way of the "frog-leap" maxim (*maṇḍūkaplutinyāya*) from the rule "elision of *r* and *l*" (P. 6.4.21), once that is established, as for that which...

The term *lopa* (elision) is mentioned again for the sake of dividing the rule (*yogavibhāga*). One rule is *śnān na*; here, *na* is an indeclinable (without a case-ending), and the mention of *lopa* is understood from the previous context. Consequently, the meaning becomes: "there is elision of the *n* that follows *śn*"; thereafter—

The second rule is "ṭhlopaḥ"; from that, the word "na" is carried over from the rule "śnānna"—meaning that in the desired scope, the elision of the letter *n* should occur. By this, the elision of *n* in words such as *laṅgi* and *kampin* in the senses of "affliction," "bodily change," and so forth, is established.
It comes to be.

24. *aniditām hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.24). Those which have *it* as an *it* are called *idita*; those which do not have *it* as an *it* are *anidita*. Here, in place of the genitive plural, a singular is used by way of transposition (*subvyatyaya*) due to the requirements of the compound; and that [term *aniditām*] is a qualifier of [the roots].
And because the rule of "extension to that which ends in" (tadantavidhi) applies by means of a qualifier, he says: "of those ending in a consonant," and so forth.
[The phrase] "of the *nakāra* in the penultimate" (*upadhāyā nakārasya*)—here, "penultimate" (*upadhā*) is a qualifier of the *nakāra*. [Examples:
*srastaḥ*, *dhvalastaḥ*. [The roots] *srasu*, *dhvasu* [are used in the sense of] falling down (*adhaḥpatane*).

The section on the *niṣṭhā* suffixes: "it is slipped away" (*srasyate*), "it is destroyed" (*dhvasyate*). These are *lakāra*s used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). "It is repeatedly slipped away" (*sanīsrasyate*), "it is repeatedly destroyed" (*danīdhvasyate*): these are forms ending in the intensive (*yaṅ*). By the rule "nīg for *vañc*" (Pāṇini 7.4.84), the augment *nīg* is added to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
Regarding "ṭhnandyate": from the root *ṭua ṇadi* (DhP 67), meaning "to prosper" (*samṛddhau*).

Regarding "ṭhnānandyate": this is a form with the suffix *yaṅ*; the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable occurs by the rule *dīrgho'kitaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.83). Regarding "ṭhnenīyate": this is derived from the root *nī*, by the rule *gaṇo yaṅlukoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.82).
The quality [of the rule] is its repetition. Regarding the word "nahyate": the root *ṇaha* means "to bind" (DhP 1166).

Regarding the phrase "in the case of *laṅgi* and *kampi*" and so forth: because *laṅgi* and *kampi* are marked with the *it*-sign (*idit*), the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) would not apply; therefore, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for these two roots in the sense of "affliction" (*upatāpa*) and "bodily transformation" (*śarīravikāra*).

The term *upasaṃkhyāna* means "providing" or "stating. Even in subsequent instances, the word *upasaṃkhyāna* has the sense of "providing. This provision has indeed already been made. *Upatāpa* is affliction; it is a disorder of the body, that is, a change in the state of the body. Furthermore, in this context, it refers to both affliction and disease.

It is so understood; otherwise, since [the form] would be established simply as *upa-tāpa*, the inclusion of the term "bodily affliction" (*śarīra-vikāra*) would be purposeless. Regarding the example *vilaṅgitaḥ*: the roots *agi*, *vagi*, and *lagi* have the sense of motion (*gati*). [The rule] *upa-tāpe vilaṅgitaḥ* should not be applied as a usage.
The elision of *laṅ* is prescribed for the purpose of [the form] *bhūt*, and not for the sake of establishing the form itself;
for that other root *lag* meaning "to cling" (*saṅge*) is already established.
The statement beginning with "after the root *rañj* when followed by *ṇi*" is for the purpose of excluding *k* and *ṅ*. *Mṛgaramaṇam* means the sporting of deer.
Regarding "he causes the deer to run": the meaning is that he employs the deer while they are sporting.
Regarding "an addition for *rañja*, *rajaka*, and *rajas*": here, a further explanation is provided.
In the rule "ghañi ca bhāvakaraṇayoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.27), the particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.

Therefore, when words such as *rajaka* are to be derived, there is elision of the nasal (*n*) of the root *rañj* when suffixes such as *ṣvun* follow. For example: "rajakaḥ" [is formed] by the rule *śilpini ṣvun* (Pāṇini 3.1.145).
"Rajanam" [is formed] by the suffix *lyuṭ*. "Rajaḥ" [is formed] by the suffix *asun* added to all verbal roots (*sārvadhātubhyaḥ*).
[The suffix] *asun* [is applied], as in *daṃśun*.
[The rule] "also after *ghinuṇ*" (*ghinuṇi ca*) and so forth applies. Regarding the word *rāgī*: the suffix *ghinuṇ* is applied by the rule "after *sampṛc*, *anvā*," etc. (Pāṇini 3.2.142);
and the substitution of *k* for *c* and *j* occurs by the rule "there is *ku*-tva [substitution of *g*] before *ghin*, *nyat*, and *yat*" (7.3.52). [Thus one says: "abandon passion..."

"It is established by the rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*) that [the form] *bhaja* is used. Since, in the rule concerning *sampṛca* and others (Pāṇini 3.2.142), this author provides the citation after having applied the elision of the nasal of the root *rañj*, he thereby indicates that the elision of the *n* occurs before an affix marked with *ghu*. But is it not the case that...?
Is the elision of *n* accomplished by the very rule "ṭhrañjeśca" (Pāṇini 6.4.26)? No, that is not so;
for just as in the rule "indhibhavatibhyāñca" (Pāṇini 1.2.6), the root *indh* is indicated by means of an adventitious *i*, so too here it is indicated by an adventitious *a*, and not otherwise.

But [the substitution] is *śap*. For in the rule "na hi ṭhindhibhavatibhyāñca" (Pāṇini 1.2.6), there is a singular mention; otherwise, by the rule "ṭhaniditām" (6.4.24), there would be the elision of the nasal.
25. *daṃśasañjasvañjāṃ śapi* (Pāṇini 6.4.25).
[The roots] *daṃśa* (to bite, DhP 989) and *ṣvanja* (to embrace, DhP 976)—as in *pariṣvajate*. [The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs] by the rule *upasargāt sunoti* (8.3.65), etc.
The substitution of *ṣ* [occurs].

26. *rañjeśca* (6.4.26). Now, for what purpose is a separate rule (*pṛthagyoga*) formulated? Why is the inclusion of the root *rañj* not made within the previous rule itself? To this he says: "The formulation of a separate rule," and so forth. [This applies] to the subsequent sūtra.
This is so that the suffix *an* may follow only after verbal roots ending in *rañj*, and not after [roots] beginning with *daṃś*.
27. *ghañi ca bhāvakaraṇayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.27). [The rule states:
"That by which one is colored is called *rāga*. Here, *ghañ* is applied by the rule *halaśca* (3.3.121). The same applies to the word *raṅga*.

28. *syada* [is used] in the sense of speed (*java*). Speed is velocity; it is a specific kind of motion. [The sūtra states: "And there is an absence of *vṛddhi*. [This refers to the rule] "ata upadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.116).
Once the *na*-elision has been performed, the *vṛddhi* substitution prescribed by "ata upadhāyāḥ" (7.2.116) would otherwise apply.

Therefore, the absence of that [vṛddhi] is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātyate*). Now, one might object: since the prohibition of *vṛddhi* is already established by the rule "na dhātulopa ārdhadhātuke" (Pāṇini 1.1.4), for what purpose is the absence of *vṛddhi* prescribed here as an irregularity? To this he says: "Because of the context of *ik*" (*ikprakaraṇāt*), and so forth. In that context, the rule "guṇa and *vṛddhi* [substitute] for *ik*" (Pāṇini 1.1.3) applies.

(1.1.3) From this point, the phrase "after *ik*" (*ig-iti*) is carried over from the previous rule; by that, there is a prohibition of the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions characterized by *ik*. And this *vṛddhi* is not characterized by *ik*, but rather is characterized by the *upadhā*. Nor does this *vṛddhi* characterized by the *upadhā* become characterized by *ik*.

Because its place of occurrence has been specifically indicated, there is no prohibition of that [ṣatva] here. In the case of *gosyadaḥ*, the suffix *dhañ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). Thus, *gosyadaḥ* means "the speed of cows" (*gavāṃ syadaḥ*), and it is a compound according to the rule "A genitive case ending is compounded with a word ending in a kṛt-suffix" (Pāṇini 2.2.9). In the case of *tailasyandaḥ*, [it is the speed] of oil.
The meaning is "flowing. [The root] *syandū* is used in the sense of "flowing" (*sravaṇa*) or "streaming forth" (*prasravaṇa*). (Dhātupāṭha 761).

29. *avoda-edha-udma-paraśratha-himaśrathāḥ* | (6.4.29). Regarding *avodaḥ*: by the rule *upasargeṇa sahādguṇaḥ* (6.1.87), there is no prohibition [of guṇa] by the rule *na dhātulopa ārdhadhātuke* (1.1.4) and so forth; this is because the guṇa is not characterized by *it*.

"And the [vocalic] *ṛ* is substituted as a *guṇa*. Now, one might ask: since the *guṇa* substitution is already established by the rule "pugantalaghūpadhasya" (Pāṇini 7.3.86), for what purpose is it prescribed here as a *nipātana* (irregularity)? To this he replies: "Not when there is elision of a root-element," and so forth.

"The suffix *man* occurs after roots beginning with *sthā*," as stated in the rule: "The suffix *man* is applied after the roots *ṛ*, *ti*, *stu*, *su*, *hu*, *sṛ*, *dhṛ*, *kṣi*, *kṣu*, *bhā*, *yā*, *pada*, *dyai*, and *kṣiṇī*" (Dhātupāṭha 7.26).
Thus, although [the suffix] is prescribed after roots such as *ar*, it also occurs after *und* due to the rule of "diversity" (*bahulavacanāt*).
Regarding the form *śranteḥ*: this is from the root *śranth* (DhP 1510), which means "to loosen" (*mocana*) and "to gladden" (*pratiharṣaṇa*).
30. *nāñceḥ pūjāyām* (6.4.30). This is a prohibition of the elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*) which would otherwise have been required by the rule *aniditām* (6.4.24).
From this very prohibition, it is understood that this [root] *añc* is indicated here with its nasal included.

Now, why was it not simply stated as "ṭh nāñceḥ iṭi"? For even if it were stated thus, the prohibition would be obtained only in the sense of honor (*pūjā*); for indeed, the augment *iṭ* is prescribed after the root *añc* only in the sense of honor.
It is impossible to say this, because [the rule] "añceḥ pūjāyām" (Pāṇini 7.2.53) [establishes that].

The augment *iṭ* is prescribed invariably for the suffixes *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā*. However, as for the suffix *ktvā*, there is an optional introduction of the augment *iṭ* according to the rule *udito vā* (Pāṇini 7.2.56); this [optional *iṭ*] occurs even in the sense of honor (*pūjā*).
This being the case, when the suffix *ktvā* would not take the augment *iṇ* in the sense of honor, then—

There would be no negation [in the case] of "having honored his gurus. The negative particle *na* is stated for the sake of what follows; for if it were merely stated here that "after *añc*, when not expressing honor," the desired form "his gurus have been honored" (*añcitā asya guravaḥ*) would indeed be established.
The suffix *kta* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.188] *ṭhmatibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca*; the genitive case is applied by [Pāṇini 2.3.67] *ktasya ca vartamāne*;
and there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by [Pāṇini 7.2.15] *yasya vibhāṣā*. This is because for the root *añc*, the augment *iṭ* is optionally prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.2.56] *udito vā*.

31. *ktvi skandisyandoḥ* | (6.4.31) Regarding *skantvā*: the root *skandir* (meaning "to move" and "to dry") [is cited]. "In the alternative case, there is the augment *iṭ*"—this is by the rule *svarati* (7.2.44), etc. "Due to the prohibition of *kit*-status, there is no elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*)"—this is the explanation.
For, by the rule *ṭhaniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24) and others, the elision of *n* is prescribed before suffixes marked with *k* or *ṅ*.

Regarding the *ktvā* suffix with an *iṭ* augment, the prohibition of *kit*-status is established by the rule *na ktvā seṭ* (1.2.18); consequently, in the alternative where the *iṭ* augment is present, the elision of *n* does not occur precisely because of the absence of *kit*-status.
He does not employ this yoga; therefore, the intention is that he has not demonstrated an example of the suffix -seṭ following a kṛt affix.

32. *jāntanaśāṃ vibhāṣā* (6.4.32). [The forms] *naṣṭvā*, *naṃṣṭvā* [are derived as follows]: by the rule *vraścādīnām* (8.2.36), there is the substitution of *ṣ* for the final consonant of the root *naś*; then *ṣṭu* substitution [yields *naṣṭvā*]. By the rule *masjinaśorjhali* (7.1.60), the augment *mum* is added [yielding *naṃṣṭvā*]. [The term] *ja* refers to...

Regarding the mention of "vowel" (varṇa): since the mention of "vowel" there brings about the rule of "that which ends with it" (tadantavidhi) everywhere, and since the rule of "that which ends with it" is established even without the explicit mention of "end" (anta), the fact that "end" is mentioned here is for the sake of clarity; as for what was said—"even of that which is not a penultimate vowel"—[it refers to this].
The inclusion of the term *anta* (end) is for the purpose of prohibiting the elision (*lopa*) in certain cases, such as in *bhaktvā* and *bhaṅktvā*.

That is not correct; for by what rule would the elision of the letter *n* apply when it is not in the position of an *upadhā* (penultimate), such that it would need to be prohibited in those cases? It has been stated that the elision applies to the *n* that is an *upadhā*, and not [to others].

And this is the purpose of the insertion (upadhāna): it indicates that, in certain cases other than those within the scope of the specific rule, the elision of the letter *n* occurs. By this, the forms "magnaḥ" and "magnadān" are established. And for that reason, [the rule] "masjerantyātpūrvam... [is stated].
The statement "they desire [the elision of *num*] for the sake of the elision of the suffixal augment (*anuṣaṅga*)" need not be stated.
For if this were not stated there, then in that case where the elision does not occur by means of the suffix *ktvā*, [the rule] *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.29) would apply.
Even the elision [of the nasal] would not occur, because [the root] does not begin with a consonant cluster (*asaṃyogāditvāt*).

Therefore, this must indeed be stated: "They desire the *num* augment before the final letter of the root *masj*. Consequently, since it is impossible for a *nakāra* that is not penultimate to undergo elision, [the rule applies] to that which is not penultimate.
The inclusion of the word "end" (anta) is not appropriate for the purpose of ensuring that the prohibition of the elision of the letter *n* occurs exactly as intended.
33. *bhañjeśca ciṇi* (Pāṇini 6.4.33).
The particle *ca* is for the purpose of drawing in [the option] from *vibhāṣā* (6.4.32). Regarding *abhāji*, it has already been explained previously.

"This elision of the letter *n* has not been accomplished," [he says], because the rule for the elision of *n* applies only before affixes marked with *k* or *ṅ*, whereas the affix *ciṇ* is not marked with *ṅ*. Since there is thus no occasion for the prohibition from this point forward, the word "not" (*na*) does not carry over;
therefore, the intention is that this is indeed a positive injunction (*vidhi*).

34. *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.34). Regarding the forms *aśiṣat* and *aśāsiṣṭām*: by the rule *sartiśāstyartibhyaśca* (3.1.56), the substitute *aṅ* is applied in place of *cli*. For the examples *śiṣvaḥ* and *śiṣmaḥ*, the *śap* suffix is elided due to the root belonging to the *adādi* class.

Regarding "śāsti": by the rule *jakṣityādayaḥ ṣaṭ* (Pāṇini 6.1.6), the designation *abhyasta* (repeated stem) is applied; by *adabhyastāt* (7.1.4), the substitute *at* is applied for the suffix *jhi*. Regarding "śaśāsatuḥ" and "śaśāsuḥ":
these are the forms of the perfect (*liṭ*) with the suffixes *atus* and *us*.

Regarding the rule "ṭhkvau ca śāsaḥ": the meaning is that one must provide an explanation for the fact that the substitution of *i* for the root *śās* occurs when *kvip* follows. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: although the elision of *kvip* is prescribed first because it is obligatory (*nitya*)—being applicable both before and after the application of the *i*-substitution—nevertheless...
Even though that [suffix] has been elided, the substitution of *i* will take place here by virtue of the rule for operations conditioned by a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*).

The statement "there is no operation conditioned by a suffix when it depends on a phoneme" (*varṇāśraye pratyayalakṣaṇaṃ nāsti*) is merely general; for instance, it sometimes occurs even when depending on a phoneme, as in the example *atṛṇeṭ*. In this case...

The augment *īm* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.3.92] *ṭhṛ ha imÂ*. Alternatively, this *it*-ness does not depend on a phoneme (*varṇa*) at all. How so? Here, by the mention of "aṅga" (*aṅgagrahaṇa*), the affix (*pratyaya*) is brought into proximity;
it is then qualified by the mention of "hal" (*halgrahaṇa*). For this very reason, it was stated in the *vṛtti*: "before an affix beginning with a consonant (*hal*) that has *k* or *ṅ* as an *it*."

Thus, although the *kvip* suffix consists of a single phoneme (*varṇa*), it is nevertheless not treated as being merely a phoneme; rather, it is treated as a suffix (*pratyaya*). For example, in *āryaśīḥ*: once the substitution of *ru* for the *s* has been applied, the rule "the penultimate vowel is lengthened before *ṛ* and *v*" (*ṛtvoḥ upadhāyā dīrghaḥ*, Pāṇini 8.2.76) applies.
Thus [the vowel] is long.
Now, as for the forms *āśāste* and *āśāsyamānaḥ*, why does the substitution of *i* not occur here?
To this he says: "From the root *śās*" and so forth; there are two roots *śās*: one is parasmaipada, and...

But another [form] is ātmanepada; in that case, the reference is specifically to that *śās* for which *aṅ* is prescribed. And that [prescription] is enjoined by the rule *satiśāstyartibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.56) for the root *śāsu anuśiṣṭau* (Dhātupāṭha 1075); in that context, [the rule applies] "in the parasmaipada endings."

(3.1.55) This [word *aṅ*] is understood to carry over, because it is only possible for this very [root] in the *parasmaipada*. But how, when it is mentioned in a general sense, is it understood to apply only to those that are *parasmaipada*? Because of its association (*saṃsarga*) with *aṅ*.
For when there is an association, a specific determination occurs; thus, for example—*sakiśorā*...

When it is said, "Let a cow be brought," the understanding arises that it is specifically a mare due to its association with a colt. Here, the *it*-ness (the substitution of *i* for *ś*) of the root *śās* is employed as a condition for the suffix *pratyaṅ*;

therefore, through association with that, the root *śās* is understood specifically as one that takes the *parasmaipada* ending. But [one might object]: [The objection continues: "Is it not the case that..."
Furthermore, here it is not only *cāR* that is taken as the cause (*nimitta*); what then? It is also *hal*.

And since that [hal] is possible even for roots that take the ātmanepada suffixes, how can there be a cognition of the specific root *śās* distinguished by its connection with *aṅ*? This is not so; for when there is a conjunction of both common and uncommon correlates...
A cognition arises only with respect to that which has an exclusive, proximate relationship.

For instance, when it is said, "Let the cows be tied up among the old and the young," only mares are understood [to be meant by "cows" in that context]. Therefore, even though the suffix *aṅ* is prescribed for both [the *han* root and the *lū* root], it applies only to that for which it is specifically ordained.
The inclusion [of *aṅ*] is appropriate.

If, then, this refers only to that after which *aṅ* is prescribed, then in cases such as *yathāśāste* and *āśāsyamāna*, [the rule] would not apply; likewise, it would also not apply when the suffix *kvip* follows? To this [it is replied]:

He says: "In the case of the *kviṣ* suffix," and so forth; as well as "in the case of *kṣiyāsīḥ*," and so forth. Alternatively, it should not be stated that the *kviṣ* suffix applies even to that [root]. The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of an option (*vikalpa*). Now, what is the purpose of the syllable *ta*? If it is argued that it is so that a long vowel (*dīrgha*) does not occur by virtue of "nearness" (*āntaratamya*), this is not the case.
Would it not be the case that [the substitution] does not occur because of the rule "an [vowel] being substituted does not include its homogeneous counterparts" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 35)?

If so, then [the mention of *akāra*] is for the sake of clarity. But why is it not for the sake of removing ambiguity? For if it were stated simply as "of *śās* before *yaṅ* and *luṅ*," there would be doubt: is this the vowel *i*...?
Is it the substitution of *yaṇ* that is indicated? Or is it the vowel *ī*? Or perhaps the consonant *y*?

There is no doubt; since he provides this indication—namely, "That [substitution] need not be taught, because the technical name (*saṃjñā*) itself is the authority" (Pāṇini 1.2.53)—it is determined from this that it is the vowel *i*, and not the vowel *ī*, nor the consonant *y*.
The letter *ya*.

35. *śā hau* | (6.4.35) If the term *ṭhupadhāyāḥ* from (6.4.24) is understood to carry over here, then just as in the preceding rule *ṭhśāsaḥ* (6.4.34), the genitive case would refer to a constituent part (*avayava*), so too here it would refer to the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*). And thus...

Considering that this [substitution] would result in a replacement of the whole (sarvādeśa), whereas it is intended to be a partial replacement (prasajya), he says: "The term 'of the penultimate vowel' (upadhāyāḥ) is withdrawn. For that mention of 'penultimate vowel' was connected with the mention of 'kṅit', and here the mention of 'kṅit' has been withdrawn.

Therefore, there is also the cessation of [the application of] Pāṇini 6.4.24, *ṭhupadhāyāḥ*. Furthermore, the condition *kṅiti* is also ceased, because of the re-mention of *kṅt* in the rule beginning with 6.4.37, *anudātopadeśa...*. By the words "therefore" (*tena*) and so forth, [it is shown that] the mention of *kṅt* has been ceased.
He demonstrates what is intended: if the rule *ṅiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.24) were to follow here, then, by the rule *vā chandasi* (3.4.88),
in that alternative where *hi* does not lose its *apit* status, the rule *sārvadhātukam apit* (1.2.4) would apply.

Because of that statement, since the status of being *ṅt* does not exist, the substitution of *ś* would not occur. However, when the mention of *kṅt* has been withdrawn, it indeed occurs even under the view that [the root] is *it*.
This might be argued: by understanding [the rule] as having a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the *hi* following *śās* does not have the status of being *pit*.
If that were the case, what would be the purpose of excluding *kṅ*?

To this, he says: "In *śādhi*, etc. If, in the alternative view, the *hi* following *śās* were not marked with *p*-ness (*pitva*), then *śādhi*—by virtue of being taught later (*satiśiṣṭatvena*)—[would prevail].

By the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*), the word would necessarily be oxytone (*antodātta*). However, in Vedic (*chandas*), an initial acute (*ādyudātta*) is also desired. And that [initial accent] is achieved through the root-accent (*dhātu-svara*) when the suffix *hi* possesses the *pit* designation; it cannot be otherwise. Therefore, one must certainly prescribe the *pit* designation for *hi* after the root *yakṣ* in Vedic.

Now, why was it not stated simply as *ṭhā hau*? For even if [the suffix] *hi* were without the marker *k*, then by the rule *ṭhala antyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52), the substitution of *ś* for *s* would be prescribed, and through the rule of lengthening homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*), the form *śādhi* would be established.
It is not so established; for by the preceding rule, the substitution of *i* for the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) would occur. And this [substitution]...

An annulment of that [rule] is appropriate; and an annulment occurs only when coexistence is impossible, yet here there is the possibility that both [rules] might apply—there is indeed such a possibility. Therefore, when the letter *a* follows, the substitution of *i* for the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) must certainly take place.
36. *interjaḥ*. Regarding the rule "of *han*": the specific mention of *spip* is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-lopa (the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix); [as in] *jaṅghahi*.
37. *anudātopadeśavanatitanotyādīnāmanunāsikalopo jhali kṅiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.37).
Having applied the elision (*luk*) of the genitive plural ending to the word "anunāsika," this [sūtra] is without a case-ending (*avibhaktika*).
This is the explanation. For this very reason, he says: "of those ending in an anusvāra.
Since the rule "anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ kṅiti" (Pāṇini 6.4.15), which prescribes lengthening, would otherwise apply, this elision is prescribed instead.
Once this elision has taken place, the lengthening no longer applies.
Because the cause [for the application of the rule] has been prescribed: "The roots *yam*, *ram*, *gam*, *nam*, *han*, and *manya*.
Here, *yam* means "to cease" (DhP 984), *ram* means "in play" (DhP 853), *gam* and *sṛp* mean "in motion" (DhP 982, 983), and *ṇam* means "in bowing" (DhP 981).

[Regarding the forms *prahva* and *śabdavat*: from the root *han* in the sense of "injury" and "motion" (DhP 1012), and *man* in the sense of "cognition" (DhP 1176). The suffix *vati* is applied; from the roots *van* and *ṣaṇ* in the sense of "acquisition" (DhP 463, 464). By the rule *tutratathasisusarakaseṣu ca* (Pāṇini 7.2.9)...]

By this [sūtra], the prohibition of *iṭ* is established. By the rule "in *ktin*" (*ktini*), he shows that an example for the root *van* is possible only with *ktin*, and not elsewhere. Why is this so? He says: "But in *ktic*," etc.
For in the case of *ktic*, he will state the prohibition [of *iṭ*] by the rule "not in *ktic*, nor lengthening" (*na ktici dīrghaśca*, 6.4.39).
As for those other suffixes beginning with *jhal*, the augment *iṭ* must also apply to them;

consequently, because they lack the quality of beginning with *jhal*, they do not serve as the cause for the elision of the nasal in the root *van*. Therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the elision of the nasal of *van* occurs only before the suffix *ktin*.
It must be so;

for he will state that "there is the substitution of *ā* for the root *san*. By this, the sense is that [the root *san*] does not serve as an example for the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*). Furthermore, the substitution of *ā* occurs by the rule "of *jan*, *san*, and *khan*" (Pāṇini 6.4.42), and so forth.

He will say: "kṣataḥ"—from the root *kṣaṇu* in the sense of "injury" (DhP 1465); "ṛtaḥ"—from the root *ṛṇu* in the sense of "motion" (DhP 1467); "tṛtaḥ"—from the root *tṛṇu* in the sense of "giving" (or "eating," according to the Dhātupāṭha, DhP 1468); "ghṛtaḥ"—from the root *ghṛṇu* in the sense of "shining" (DhP 1469).

"Ṭhvataḥ" (from *van*): "vanu yācane" (DhP 1470). "Mataḥ" (from *man*): "manu avabodhane" (DhP 1471). "Atata, atathā": this is the *luṅ* (aorist) of the root *tan*, in the first person singular middle voice (*ātmanepada*). [The rule applied is] "tanādibhyas tathāsoḥ" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.79).
Thus, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *sic*.

[The forms] "śāntaḥ," "tāntaḥ," and "dāntaḥ" are the forms of the roots *śam*, *tam*, and *dam* respectively. These are not taught with an anudātta (low-pitched) vowel in their original state (*upadeśa*). [This applies to the rule] beginning with "iha ca. When the suffix *ktin* is added to the roots *gam* and *ram*, [the following occurs].

Since those two [roots] possess an initial acute accent (*udātta*) by virtue of the *nitsvara* rule, they lack the grave accent (*anudātta*); therefore, in the absence of the mention of "instruction" (*upadeśagrahaṇa*), the elision would not occur. However, because this [mention] exists, it does occur. Furthermore, if the mention of "instruction" were absent, the elision would also apply in cases such as *śāntaḥ* and *dāntaḥ*, for the root *śam-* [is indeed taught with a grave accent].

When the accent of the suffix remaining after [the application of rules] has been established, the remainder becomes unaccented (anudātta) by the rule "ṭhanudātaṃ padamekavarjam" (Pāṇini 6.1.158). However, because of the inclusion of the term *upadeśa* [in the definition of the term *dhātu*], this does not apply here; for this [root] is not unaccented in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*).

38. *vā lyapi* (6.4.38). This rule is commenced for the sake of cases where the suffix begins with a vowel other than *a*. For example, in *prayatya*: when the prefix *pra-* has been compounded, [the suffix] *lyap* is substituted for *ktvā* by *samāse 'nañpūrve ktvo lyap* (7.1.37), and then *tuk* is inserted after the short vowel by *hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk* (6.1.71).

39. *na ktici dīrghaśca* | (6.4.39) [Examples include] *dhayantiḥ*, etc. The suffix *ktic* is applied by the rule *kticktau ca saṃjñāyām* (3.3.174). Here, the phrase "beginning with those taught with an anudātta accent" (*anudātopadeśādi*) is understood to carry over; therefore, in cases such as *kāntiḥ* and *śāntiḥ*, [the long vowel does not occur].

The prohibition of lengthening (*dīrgha-pratiṣedha*) does not apply here; for there is no possibility at all of the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) in this case, because [the root] is taught as having an acute accent (*udātta-upadeśatvāt*).
This is because of the mention of "lengthening" in the rule beginning with "when the elision of the nasal is prohibited."

He states the purpose [of the rule]: "But surely, since it is understood that what is prescribed in this section does not apply in view of the specific context (*prakaraṇa*), the prohibition will apply to the long vowel even without the mention of 'long' (*dīrgha*); so what is the use of mentioning 'long'? Thus [it is argued].
In that case, this indicates the following technical rule (*paribhāṣā*): "A rule or a prohibition applies to what immediately precedes" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 19).

40. *gamaḥ kvau* (Pāṇini 6.4.40). This rule is also commenced for the sake of [stems] beginning with vowels other than *a*. For example: *adhvagato harayaḥ*. [Derivation: From the root *gam* with the suffix *kvip* in the sense of "going on a path" (*adhvānaṃ gacchanti*), and then the suffix *jas* applied to that which ends in *kvip*.

"Of *gam* and the rest," and so forth. The meaning is that this rule must be explained as having the sense: "the elision of the nasal of *gam* and the rest occurs before a *kvip* suffix. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the particle *ca* ("and") is carried over from the preceding sūtra, and it serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned.
Therefore, [the suffix] will apply to *gam* and the others, but not to *gam* alone. Regarding *saṃyat*:
[it is derived] from the root *yam* preceded by the prefix *sam*, with the suffix *kvip*. Regarding *paritat*:
[it is derived] from the root *tan* preceded by the prefix *pari*; the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs according to the rule *nahivṛtivṛṣi...* (Pāṇini 6.3.116).
"ṭhū ca," etc. Due to the word "ca" (and), there is the elision of the nasal. In some places, "ṭhūṅ ca" is read;

in that case, the purpose of the letter ṅ must be considered [as it would otherwise be redundant]. This will occur here by the rule of *alo'ntyaparibhāṣā* (the maxim concerning the final letter). Thus, "agregūḥ": from the roots *gam* and *bhram*, with the elision of the nasal.
When *kṛ* is applied, the vowel *a* becomes *u*.

41. *viṅvanoranunāsikasyāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.41). Regarding the example *abjāḥ*: [the compound] *apsu jāyate* is a locative-upapada compound (*upapadasamāsa*). The substitution of the *jaś*-class sound (*jaśtva*) for the letter *p* results in the letter *b*. Regarding *goṣā*: [from the root] *ṣaṇu dāne* (Dhātupāṭha 1464).
Regarding "vijavā": it is derived from the roots *jan* "to be born" (DhP 1105) or *janī* "to appear" (DhP 1149). Regarding "agregāva" [the Kāśikā reads "agrejāvā"]:
there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending according to the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa* compound with a *kṛt*-suffix, [the case-endings] are used diversely" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.14).

Now, for what purpose is the mention of "anunāsika" [nasal], since the mention of "anunāsika" already continues from the rule beginning with *anudāttopadeśa* (Pāṇini 6.4.37)? To this he says: "While 'of that which has a nasal' (*anunāsikasya*) is in force," and so forth. For that—
The mention of "nasalized" (*anunāsika*) in the original context was connected with the mention of "those taught as having an anudātta accent" (*anudātopadeśa*);
therefore, if that [mention] were to recur, that [restriction] would also recur.
Consequently, this other mention of "nasalized" is made so that it may apply to every nasalized sound whatsoever.

It might be so. Now, what is the purpose of the long vowel pronunciation here? One might simply say the short vowel; for even when the short is used, the form is indeed established by the rule "a long vowel replaces [two] homogeneous vowels" (*aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye 'pi*, Pāṇini 8.4.2). One should not raise the objection that it would not be established because the rule "guṇa in place of *at*" (Pāṇini 6.1.97) would result in the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*).

This is due to the force of the prescription of the letter *a*. For if, by the rule "ato guṇe" (Pāṇini 6.1.97), there were to be the substitution of a single subsequent form (*pararūpa*), then the author would have simply prescribed the elision (*lopa*) of the present topic; subsequently, only the short vowel would need to be applied.
But that is not the case; for if [the elision] were not applied, then in the case of the root *ghūrṇ* (Dhātupāṭha 437, meaning "to whirl"), [the desired form would not arise].

If the suffix *vanip* were prescribed after the root *bhram* (as in *bhramaṇe*), then the form *dhvāṅkṣa* would not be established; therefore, it is proper that the rule prescribes only the long vowel.

42. *janasanakhanām sañjhaloḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.42). It is stated that "the terms *ṭh* and *jhali*, as well as *kṅiti*, are carried over [from previous rules]. These serve respectively as qualifiers for *san* and *jhal*. However, it is not possible to qualify *san* by means of the term *jhal* as explicitly mentioned in this sūtra.

For a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is subordinate, whereas that which is qualified (*viśeṣya*) is primary. Furthermore, this [compound] *sañjhaloḥ* is a copulative compound (*dvandva*). In such a case, since all members of a copulative compound are primary, it is not possible for them to stand in a mutual relationship of primary and subordinate. Moreover, the inclusion of *san* is for the sake of excluding *aṅ*.

Regarding the phrase "tadiha" and so forth: since the augment *iṭ* occurs after the root *san* in certain cases, it is only for that purpose—namely, to ensure that a *san* beginning with a *jhal* consonant can follow immediately after that very [root]—that the mention of *saṅ* (the form including the augment) is made;
it is not, however, for the sake of the roots *jan* and *khan*. For indeed, a *san* beginning with a *jhal* consonant cannot possibly follow those two.

Because both of these [roots] always possess the augment *iṭ*, if that were the case, then since the purpose of the root *san* would already be fulfilled by the addition of *saN*, the substitution of *ā* would not occur;

furthermore, in other instances such as the past participles (*niṣṭhā*) and before affixes beginning with *jhal* that are marked with *k* or *ṅ*, the elision of *n* would occur by the rule "anudātopadeśa... (Pāṇini 6.4.37). To this, he says: "In other instances," and so forth.

The scope for the recitation of *san* in the list beginning with *tan* is for other operations belonging to the *tan*-class, such as [the substitution of] *tathāsoḥ* prescribed by Pāṇini 6.4.79 (*tanādibhyas tathāsoḥ*); and the scope for the mention of *san* in the rule prescribing *ātva* is for forms such as *san* and *siṣāsati*. In the present case, however, both [rules] would apply simultaneously, as in *sātaḥ*.

Regarding the form *sātvān*: here, by means of the rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the substitution of *ā* occurs, overriding the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*). Now, a conflict occurs between two rules that are both established;

however, in this case, according to the rule "that which is taught later is treated as not having taken effect in relation to what precedes" (*asiddhavadatrā bhāt*, 6.4.22), both [the elision and the substitution] are unestablished (*asiddha*). Therefore, how [can there be a conflict]?
Is there not a contradiction here? To this he says: "ghumāsthāgā," etc.
How is this a *jñāpaka* (indicative proof)? The purpose of the mention of *hal* is precisely this:

that the substitution of long *ī* should occur when a consonant (*hal*) follows, but it should not occur here in cases such as "godāḥ" and "kambaladaḥ," which are formed by the rule "āto 'nupasarge kaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.3).

If there is thus a conflict here, he says [in response]: "ghumāsthāgā... and so forth. How is this an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? This is the very purpose of the mention of *hal*: that the substitution of long *ī* should occur when preceded by a consonant (*hal*), but not in cases such as this—namely, "āto 'nupasarge kaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.3), as in *godah*.

Regarding the word *kambalada*: if there were no conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) here, the mention of *hal* would be purposeless. Let there be *itva* (the substitution of *i*) here; since that is considered asiddha, the elision (*lopa*) will take place. However, the Teacher perceives that there is indeed a conflict in this section, which is why he includes the mention of *hal*.

[The opponent] says: "But surely, if the mention of 'hal' (consonant) were not made, the substitution of *ī* would occur even before an initial vowel (*aj-ādi*), and consequently, the substitution of *iṭ* would follow, resulting in an undesirable form.
Therefore, since the mention of 'hal' is for the purpose of preventing such an undesirable result, its status as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) is not tenable? [The author] replies: "This is not so..."

There is a fault: because the substitution of *it* is indeed unestablished (*asiddha*), the substitution of *iyaṅ* will not occur. [Objection: Then the mention of *hal* must be for the sake of establishing a fixed order (*vyavasthā*). For if that were absent, since the substitution of *it* would be unestablished, there would be the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*); and since the elision of *ā* would be unestablished, there would be the substitution of *īt*. Thus, there would be a circularity of establishment (*cakravad-vyavasthā*).

This too is purposeless; if the mention of *hal* were for the sake of establishing a restriction (*vyavasthā*), he would not have mentioned *hal* at all. Having stated the vowel *i* without qualification, he could simply have prescribed its elision (*lopa*) before vowels as an exception (*apavāda*). So how can this [rule] "there is elision of *ā* before *iṭ*" be justified?

[Is it not so that] by [Pāṇini 6.4.64], there is the elision of the vowel *ā* by [Pāṇini 6.4.66]: "In the case of *dhū*, *mā*, *sthā*, *gā*, *pā*, *hā*, and *jahi*, there is the elision of *ā* before an affix beginning with a consonant other than *y* that has an indicatory *k* or *ṅ*"? For what purpose is this?

If the substitution of *ī* for *dhū* and the others were to be stated for every affix, then this [rule] would serve as an exception (*apavāda*) for those cases where an affix beginning with a consonant other than *y* that has an indicatory *k* or *ṅ* follows; thus, [the rule] "there is *ī*" [would apply].

Thus, by [Pāṇini 6.4.68], the substitution of *it* occurs for the roots beginning with *ghu* before an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ* that does not begin with a vowel; thereafter, [the following rules apply]: 6.4.37 (*therliṅ*), 6.4.68 (*dānyasya saṃyogādeḥ*), 6.4.69 (*na lyapi*), and 6.4.70 (*mayateridanyatarasyām*).
Then, the substitution of *it* occurs—which is precisely this very [process].

The fact that the Teacher prescribes the inclusion of *bala* when the rule could have been established by the stronger application (*lagīyasā nyāsena*) indicates that he intends to show: "In this case, there is a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*)."

43. *ye vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 6.4.43). This rule is commenced for the sake of [forms] beginning with *asat* and *jhal*. Examples: *jāyate*, *janyate*—here the *lakāra* (tense/mood marker) denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*). *jājāyate*—here there is *yaṅ* [intensive suffix], and by the rule *dīrgho'kitaḥ* (7.4.83), the long vowel is substituted for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

Regarding the lengthening [of the vowel] in *jañjanyate*: the augment *nuk* is applied by the rule *nugato’nunāsikāntasya* (Pāṇini 7.4.85). In the forms *sāyate* and *sanyate*, the *l*-suffix occurs in the sense of either the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*).
One might have the misconception that even when the suffix *śyan* is applied to the root *jan*, there should optionally be the substitution of *ā* [for the penultimate *i*].

Therefore, in order to refute that [objection], he says: "In *jani* before *śyan*," and so forth. Since *jani* belongs to the *divādi* class, when *śyan* is prescribed, both [alternatives] would apply: the optional substitution of *ā* by this [rule], and the replacement of *jani* by *jā* according to *jñājanorjā* (Pāṇini 7.3.79). In that case, because the substitute *jā* is without scope [elsewhere], [the former rule is superseded].
That very form becomes permanent; therefore, when the suffix śyan is applied, the form "jāyate" (is born) occurs permanently, and never "janyate."

44. [The substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of the root] *tan* occurs before the suffix *yak*. (6.4.44) 45. Before the suffix *ktic*, there is optionally the elision (*lopa*) of the vowel of this [root *tan*]. (6.4.45) The mention of "this" (*asya*) is so that the elision of the suffix *ktic* does not apply to the immediately preceding element; rather, it applies even to the [vowel of the root] which is separated [from the suffix by other elements], namely, the elision of the nasal (*n*).

This is for the purpose that it *should* be so. Now, even though the mention of *asya* is made, why does the elision (*lopa*) of *ktic* not occur? It is because of the force (*sāmarthya*) of the mention of *asya*. Furthermore, what is the purpose of the mention of *anyatarasyām*, since the term *vibhāṣā* (6.4.46) continues to apply?

Thus he says: "The mention of *anyatarasyām*, etc. But how can the removal of the mention of *vibhāṣā* be suspected, since the mention of *anyatarasyām* was made for the sake of clarity? To this he says: "For [the rule] connected with the letter *ya*," etc. (the Kāśikā reads *ye sambaddhaṃ hi*).
That mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*) is connected with the suffix beginning with *y*. And here,
since "in *ye*" has ceased to apply and another cause for *ktic* is introduced, therefore, upon the cessation of that [suffix], the mention of the option also ceases.
A doubt might arise as to whether [the term] "nivṛta" (obstructed) refers to something else; therefore, for the sake of clarity, the mention of "anya" (other) is made in this context.

46. *ārdhadhātuke* | (Pāṇini 6.4.46) [The examples are] *cikīrṣitā*, from which the suffix *tuC* follows a desiderative (*saN*); and *bhavati*, *bhavataḥ*. Because of the governing rule *ārdhadhātuke*, there is no elision of *śap* here when it is a *sārvadhātuka* [suffix].

It occurs as follows: If the governing rule for *ārdhadhātuka* affixes were established here for the purpose that the elision of *śap* should not take place, then it need not be established at all; for by the very fact of the indicator (*jñāpaka*), the elision of *śap* will not occur.
The activity of the Teacher indicates this: "The elision of *śap* does not occur by this [rule]," since he [the Teacher]...
Why does [the author] teach the elision of *śap* by the rule "after *ad* and so forth, there is elision of *śap*" (Pāṇini 2.4.72)? To this he says:

"After *ad* and so forth," etc. The particle *iti* indicates the reason. For something serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) only when there is no other purpose; however, there is indeed a purpose for the statement regarding the elision of *śap* after *ad* and so forth.

What is the purpose of this? It is so that there may not be *guṇa* substitution in the case of *vitaḥ*. If there were elision (*lopa*) in the case of *vitaḥ*, then by the rule of "characterization by the affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), *guṇa* would apply according to Pāṇini 7.3.86 (*pugantalaghūpadhasya*).
However, in the case of *mṛṣṭaḥ*, although there is the rule "vṛddhi for *mṛj*" (7.2.114), when elision (*luk*) occurs, [the *guṇa* does not apply].
This occurs because of the prohibition of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule by the sūtra *ṭhna lumatāṅgasya* (1.1.63).

Therefore, since the prescription of the elision (*luk*) of *śap* after roots such as *ad-* would be for the purpose of prohibiting the application of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule, it cannot serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the non-existence of the elision of *śap*.
Regarding "ṭhbebhiditā": there is the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix. In the case of "ṭhbebhidyate," [the substitution] does not occur before the *śap* augment of the *sārvadhātuka* suffix.
Regarding "ṭhkāraṇā": [the suffix] *yuc* is applied by the rule "ṇyāsaśrantho yuc" (Pāṇini 3.3.107). In "ṭhkārayati," [the substitution occurs] before the *śap* augment.
It does not occur before a *sārvadhātuka* [affix]. For example:

*papatuḥ*, *papuḥ*; *vavatuḥ*, *vavuḥ*. In the case of *atus* and *us*, there is the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64), which applies to both the roots *pā* and *vā*.

‘*dīyate*, *dhīyate*’: [this is] the *yak* suffix in the *ārdhadhātuka* [context]. ‘*adātām*, *adhātām*’: [this is] *luṅ*; by [Pāṇini 3.4.101], *tas* is replaced by *tām*; by [Pāṇini 2.4.77], there is the elision (*luk*) of *sic*. ‘*snāyāt*, *sneyāt*’.
The suffix *liṅ* is used in the sense of benediction (*āśis*). By the rule *liṅaśiṣi* (Pāṇini 3.4.116), it receives the designation of *ārdhadhātuka*.

The augment *yāsuṭ* is applied, and by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ* (8.2.29), there is the elision of the *s* [of *yāsuṭ*]. It is said that "in the *āśīr-liṅ*, *akya* does not occur. In the *āśīr-liṅ*, there is something other than the *vidhy-ādi-liṅ* (the *liṅ* used for injunctions and so forth).

In that case, [the suffix] does not occur; because that [suffix] is designated as *sārvadhātuka*, by virtue of that, "snāyāt" always occurs there. Here, the elision of the *sakāra* is governed by the rule "liṅḥ salopo'nantyasya" (Pāṇini 7.2.79).

Regarding "kāriṣīṣṭa": this is the optative (liṅ) in the sense of a benediction (āśis); the suffix sīyuṭ is added; the middle voice (ātmanepada) is applied by the rule "bhāvakarmaṇoḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.13);

the augment suṭ is added by the rule "suṭ tithoḥ" (3.4.107), and due to the treatment as ciṇvadbhāva, vṛddhi is applied. Regarding "kriyeta": this is the optative (liṅ) in the sense of a possibility (vidhyādi).

As before, the *ātmanepada* endings are applied; the suffix *yak* is added because it is a *sārvadhātuka*; by the rule "ṭhādguṇaḥ" (6.1.87), *guṇa* is substituted for [the vowel] together with the augment *sīyuṭ*; by the rule "lopo vyor vali" (6.1.66), there is the elision of the letter *y*; and by the rule "riṅ śayagliṅkṣu" (7.4.28), the substitute *riṅ* is applied. Here, that which occurs through the treatment as *ciṇvadbhāva*— [The remainder of the sentence would follow here.]
He demonstrates that there would be a fault by means of the rule "of that which ends in a suffix beginning with a consonant" (*ṭhyagantasya*), etc. If, in this case,

there were a vowel-lengthening (*vṛddhi*) due to the treatment as *ciṇ* (*ciṇvadbhāva*), then the augment *yuk* would consequently apply by the rule "the augment *yuk* is added after a stem ending in *ā* before *ciṇ* and *kṛt*-suffixes" (*āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ*, 7.3.33).
"ṭhato lopo yalopaśca" and so forth. This is a summary verse regarding the purpose of the section on *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes; its meaning is already explained.
Now, one might object: "In this case, [the suffix] *ram* [should apply] by the rule 'ṭhbhrasjo ropadhayo ramanyatarasyām' (Pāṇini 6.4.47)."

[Objection: Since the rule *dīṅe yuḍ aci kṅiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.63) will be prescribed specifically within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) for *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes, why are those two [the augment *iṭ* and the substitution *ram*] not included there as its purpose? [Response: It is thought thus: the substitution of *ram* for *bhrasj* does not require the governing heading for *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes; rather, it is that [substitution].

Since it is recited in the *tud-ādi* class, the suffix *śa* should occur when a *sārvadhātuka* affix follows. When *śa* is present, by virtue of the *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (prior contradiction), there must be vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule *grahijyā-vayi-vyadhi-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṣ

In the case of a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, the affix *śyan* must be applied; consequently, because the condition of beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) is absent, the augment *yuṭ* does not occur at all. When the term "in an *ārdhadhātuka*" is intended to refer to the *ārdhadhātuka* category in general, then—since priority and posteriority are impossible within a general category—this is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*).

When there is the manifestation of an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, then the locative case [in the rule] is one of sequence (*parasaptamī*). Furthermore, we have already demonstrated in the commentary on *na dhātulopaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.4) by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that this [locative] functions both as a locative of sequence and as a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*).
47. *bhrasjo ropadhayo ram anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.4.47).

If *ram* were to take the place of the *repha* (the letter *r*) and the *upadha* (the preceding vowel), then its designation as *mit* would be purposeless. Therefore, this augment *ram* occurs after a vowel other than [the one preceding] the *repha* and the *upadha*.
Anticipating the objection, "Would [the *ṛ*] not be heard? he says: "Of the *repha* and the *upadhā*," and so forth.

Because of the designation *mit*, there must necessarily be an *ac* (vowel) following the final [consonant] by means of the *ram* [augment]; otherwise, that [designation] would be purposeless. In that case, if the *repha* and the *upadhā* were to be heard...

The mention of the genitive case in the rule "ṭhropadhayoḥ" would otherwise be purposeless. Therefore, it is precisely this genitive mention that indicates the cessation of those two [suffixes]. For this is its very purpose: so that the property of cessation belonging to that which is designated by the genitive may apply.

It must be so; for there is no other purpose for the genitive indication (*ṣaṣṭhīnirdeśa*). Therefore, because it is designated as *mit*, the *ra* occurs immediately after the final vowel. By the force of the genitive indication, the two letters having *r* as their penultimate (*rephopadha*) undergo the cessation of their status as substituends (*sthānidharma*). Thus, "bhraṣṭā" [is formed]; [the root is] *bhrasja* in the sense of cooking.
By the rule *vraścādi-* (Pāṇini 8.2.36), the substitution of *ṣ* occurs. Regarding the form *bhrajjanam*:
the *s* undergoes *jaś*-tva, becoming *d*; that *d* then undergoes *ścu*-tva, becoming *j*.
Now, why does this not occur here in the forms *bhṛṣṭaḥ* and *bhṛṣṭavān*? To this he says: *bhṛṣṭaḥ*... [etc.]

Regarding the passage beginning with *bhṛṣṭavān*: the scope for [the substitution of] *ra* is in forms such as *bharṣṭā*, *bhraṣṭāḥ*; the scope for *samprasāraṇa* is in the form *bhṛjjati*. Here, both would apply in the cases *bhṛṣṭā* and *bhṛṣṭavān*;
however, by the rule concerning the *grahyādi* group (Pāṇini 6.1.16), *samprasāraṇa* alone takes effect.

By means of a prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). And this prior prohibition is obtained because the word *para* signifies that which is desired. As in the example *barībhṛjyate*: [the suffix] *yaṅ*; then the augment *rīg* is added by the rule *rīgṛdupadhasya* (Pāṇini 7.4.90).

For the mention of "antara" which was introduced [in the rule] "ṭhata upadeśe" (Pāṇini 6.4.45) is connected with the suffixes beginning with *san*, whereas here there is an exclusion of those suffixes starting with *san*. Therefore, upon the exclusion of that [suffix], its [the mention of *antara*] exclusion might also be suspected. Furthermore, because the immediately preceding connection serves another purpose.
In that case, there is no purpose for including the word "anyatara" (either one).

Now, why was it not stated simply as *bhrasjo bharj*? It is impossible to state it in this way; for if it were so stated, then according to the rule "when a root-form is mentioned, it includes the form with the suffix yaṅluk" (Vyāḍipañjikā 77), the inclusion of the yaṅluk form would also follow.

Thus, when an ārdhadhātuka suffix arises after a root with the *yaṅ* elided (*yaṅluk*), would there not be the substitution of *bharj* for the reduplicated form of *bhrasj*? This is not a fault; we shall qualify *bhrasj* by the mention of its original form (*upadeśa*)—that is, "the *bhrasj* that occurs in its original form. Alternatively, here the reference is made by means of the *śtip* marker.

It will be stated [in the Vārttika]: "The form *bhr̥jaṃ* [is used] for the root *bhrasj*" (Pāṇini 6.4.47). By this, there will be no inclusion of the form with the elision of the *yaṅ* affix (*yaṅluk*). But does this not also apply to the case of *bhuñjyate*, since in its original teaching (*upadeśa*) the root is indeed *bhrasji*? This is not so; for in this case, by the rule of prior precedence (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*).
It must be so, as in the case of the word *bhṛṣṭa*. If that is so, then it was not stated in that way for the sake of variety.

48. *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.48). [Examples: *dhinutaḥ*, *kṛṇutaḥ*. [The roots] *hivi*, *divi*, and *dhivi* have the meaning "to breathe" (Dhātupāṭha 591, 592, 593); *kṛvi* has the meanings "to injure" and "to do" (Dhātupāṭha 598).

Having understood [the rule], there is *anum* (*an*), then *laṭ*, then *tas*. By the rule "dhinvikṛṇvyora ca" (Pāṇini 3.1.80), there is the suffix *u* and the substitution of the vowel *a* for the final [root vowel]; its elision occurs by this [present rule]. Now, what is the purpose of including the marker *t* in the term *tap*, since it should not apply in the case of *dhātu*? But surely, [one might argue], by the rule "āto lopa iṭi ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.64) [there would be no need for *t*]?

The rule *ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64) will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*)—meaning that the elision of the augment *iṭ* after the vowel *ā* occurs only before an affix beginning with a vowel that has a *kṅit* marker? This is not so; for a contrary restriction might also be possible: namely, that the elision of *iṭ* after *ā* occurs only before a *kṅit* affix and not before any other. And if that were the case, the form *cikīrṣitā* would not be possible.
Therefore, the addition of *t* (in *tapara*) is for the purpose of removing the possibility of a contrary restriction;
or rather, it is for the sake of clarity,
as in the rule "after *vṛddhi* and long vowels" (*vṛddhidīrghābhyām*), etc., and the rule "after a vowel before *ñ* and *ṇit*" (*aco ñṇiti*).
The scope for [the application of] this [rule] is as follows: *kārayati* (he causes to do), *hārayati* (he causes to take);
the scope for the elision (*ato lopa*) is as follows: *cikīrṣitā* (she who desires to do), *jihīrṣitā* (she who desires to take).
In the case of *cikīrṣakaḥ* (one who desires to do) and *jihīrṣakaḥ* (one who desires to take), both [rules] would apply; however, the elision of the *at* [of the suffix] alone takes place.

By means of the *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (the priority of the preceding rule). The scope of [the rule] *ṭhakṛtsārvadhātukayordīrghaḥ* (7.4.25) is, for example, *cīyate* and *lūyate*; the scope of the elision (*ato lopaḥ*) is the same. In cases such as *cikīrṣyate* and *jihīrṣyate*, both rules would apply, yet only the elision takes place.
By means of the prior prohibition.

49. *yasya halaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.49). Regarding the example *bebhiditā*: after a reduplicated stem (*yaṅanta*) ending in a consonant, when the ārdhadhātuka suffix *tṛc* follows, there is elision of the *ya*-sound. This [word] *yasya* may either refer to the elision of the phoneme *y*.

Is it the inclusion of the letter *ya* or the inclusion of the letter *ā*? If the first alternative were adopted, then [the rule] would also apply to forms such as *aurṣyitā* and *mavyitā*; therefore, adopting the second alternative, he says:

"The mention of the aggregate (*saṅghāta*) is intended by the word *yasya*. Why is this so? Because of the specific formulation [of the rule]. If it were the inclusion of the individual phoneme (*varṇa*), [the rule would not apply here].

If that were the case, one should have simply said "yo halaḥ. If, then, there is a reference to the whole cluster [of consonants], then by the rule "alo'ntyasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.52), the operation would apply to the final [consonant] of that cluster; therefore, he says: "In that case, [the rule] 'alo'ntyasya'... and so forth. Why does it not apply?

Thus he says: "From this, there is elision," and so forth. Elision of the final [element] (alo'ntyasya) is already established by the preceding rule; however, because of the force of its specific formulation here, it applies to the whole. He states another solution with the words "or by [the rule] 'of the consonant' (halaḥ)," and so on. "Of the consonant" (halaḥ).

This is a designation by the fifth case (*pañcamī-nirdeśa*). In that context, when it is stated, "there is elision (*lopa*) of the letter *ya* which follows a consonant," the elision of the letter *y* occurs by this very rule, according to the principle "the substitute takes the place of what immediately follows" (*ādeḥ parasya*, 1.1.54);
however, the elision of the letter *a* occurs by the rule "elision of *at*" (*ato lopaḥ*, 6.4.48).
[The forms] *īrṣyitā*, *mavyitā* [the reading in the Nyāsa is *bhavyitā*], etc.;

[these derive from] *sūrksya*, *īkṣya*, *īrṣya*—meaning "envy" (Dhātupāṭha 509, 510, 511)—and *mavya* "to bind" (Dhātupāṭha 508). In this case, since the word *yaś* does not consist of a composite (*saṅghāta*) [of letters], [the rule] does not apply.
There is elision [of the penultimate vowel]. In the form "lolūyitā," there is the suffix *yaṅ*, and by the rule "guṇo yaṅlukoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.82), there is *guṇa* substitution.
50. *kya* optionally [takes the augment *mum*] (Pāṇini 6.4.50).

The term *kya* is a general designation for both *kyac* and *kyaṅ*, since their specific markers (*anubandhas*) have been dropped and no distinction is made between them. For example: "He behaves like fuel" (*samidham ivātmānam ācarati*). The word *vā* ("optionally") [is understood from the previous rule].
The word *vā* (or), functioning as a conjunction (*samuccaya*), conveys the sense that [the suffix] behaves like *samit*.

Regarding the phrase "according to what is appropriate" (*yathāyogam*): when the intended meaning is "one who desires fuel for oneself," then the suffix *kyac* must be applied by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8); when—

When one understands it as "he behaves like fuel" (*samidham ivātmānam ācarati*), then the suffix *kyac* applies by the rule *upamānād ācāre* (Pāṇini 3.1.10); when one understands it as "he behaves like fuel" (*samid ivācarati*), then the suffix *kyaṅ* applies by the rule *kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.11)— such is the meaning of the term "according to the application" (*yathāyogam*).

51. *ṇer aniṭi* (6.4.51). Regarding the word *ṇeḥ*: having discarded the specific indicatory letters (*anubandha*) of *ṇiṅ* and *ṇic*, which serve as differentiators, there is the inclusion of the general category of *ṇi* alone. By means of [the rules concerning] *iyaṅ* and so forth, this applies to the whole.

Because the object [of the rule] has already been occupied, this elision of *ṇi* (ṇilopa) is understood to be an exception (*apavāda*) to those [other rules]. Therefore, he says "iyaṅyaṇ" and so forth. Examples are "atatakṣat" and "ararakṣat.
From the roots *takṣ* and *rakṣ*, the causative suffix *ṇic* is added; from that which ends in it, the aorist (*luṅ*) suffix is applied by the rule "ṇiśridrusrubhyaḥ... [Pāṇini 3.1.48].

By [the rule] *ityādinā* (Pāṇini 3.1.48), the suffix *cli* is replaced by *caṅ*; because of the marker *ṅ*, there is no possibility of *guṇa* substitution, and thus the replacement *iyaṅ* would apply. Therefore, the elision of the *ṇi* suffix (*ṇilopa*) is an exception (*apavāda*) to that. [Examples are: *āṭiṭat*, *āśiśat*. When the *ṇic* and other suffixes have been applied first to the roots *aṭ* and *aś*, [the rule] "of the second member beginning with a vowel" (*ajāder dvitīyasya*) applies.

(6.1.2) Thus, the sounds *ṭi* and *śi* are each stated twice. Here, this [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *yaṇ*-substitution that would otherwise apply by the rule "ṭheranekācaḥ" (6.4.82), as in the examples "kāraṇā" and "hāraṇā. Furthermore, it is an exception to the *guṇa*-strengthening that would otherwise apply by the rule "sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ" (7.3.84).
In *ṭhkārakaḥ* and *hārakaḥ*, [the substitution of] *vṛddhi* applies by the rule *ṭhaco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115).

In *ṭhkāryate* and *hāryate*, [the substitution of] *dīrgha* applies which is obtained by the rule *ṭhakṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.25). In *ṭhjñīpsati*, [the substitution of *iṭ*] applies by the rule *ṭhajjhanagamāṃ sani* (Pāṇini 6.4.16).

Only for that which has attained length. In the case of the root *jñā* with the suffix *ṇic*, the augment *puk* is applied by [Pāṇini 7.3.36] *arti-hrī-...*. Because *jñā* is listed among the *ghaṭādi* roots in [Dhātupāṭha 811] *māraṇa-toṣaṇa-niśāmaneṣu jñā*, it receives the designation *mit* by [Gaṇasūtra, Dhātupāṭha 817] *ghaṭādayo mitaḥ*. Consequently, [by Pāṇini 6.4.92] *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ*, [the penultimate vowel is shortened].
By this [rule 6.4.92], there is shortening; by [the rule] "atra lopo'bhyāsasya" (7.4.58), there is the elision of the reduplication.

Thus we have "kārayitā" and "hārayitā. Because of the statement "aniṭi" (in the absence of an augment iṭ), this [shortening] does not occur here. The mention of "aniṭi" could indeed be omitted. How so? By the rule "niṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi" (6.4.52).

[The opponent argues: "It will serve as a restrictive rule (niyamārtha)—that [the substitution] occurs only before a *niṣṭhā* suffix with the augment *iṭ*, and not elsewhere. This is incorrect; for one might also suspect a contrary restriction: "only before a *niṣṭhā* suffix with *iṭ*. And if that were the case, the elision of the *ṇi* would indeed occur in the form *kārayitā*.
Therefore, in order to dispel the suspicion that the restriction might be reversed, it was stated: "when *ṭha* follows, not when *iṭ*."
52. *niṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.52). [Examples: *gaṇitam*, *lakṣitam*. [Roots: *gaṇa* in the sense of "counting" (Dhātupāṭha 1853); *lakṣa* in the senses of "seeing" and "marking" (Dhātupāṭha 1538).

Regarding the phrase "the animal has been immolated" (*saṃjñapitaḥ paśuḥ*): Now, one might ask—if, because of the rule *seṭi*, this [suffix] should not occur here, then why does it not occur by the preceding rule?
To this he says: "By the force of the inclusion of *seṭ*" and so forth. For if [the suffix were applied] by the preceding rule to a root that is *aniṭ*...

There would be elision of *ṇi*; the mention of *seṅ* (the suffix *si* with *eṅ*) would be purposeless, for one should simply have said "in the case of the *niṣṭhā* [suffixes]"; indeed, by the very force of the rule's formulation, the meaning of *si* will be obtained. Therefore, by the force of the mention of *seṅ*, even in the preceding example, "the animal was signaled," [the elision occurs].

The elision of *ṇi* does not take place. But how is it that *seṭ* is not considered a *niṣṭhā* suffix here? To this he says: "In the rule *sanīvantardha-*" and so forth; and "Now, in the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* (7.2.15)," [it refers back] to the rule "*ekāca upadeśe'nudātāt*" (7.2.10).

The mention of "a single vowel" (ekāc) is understood [from the previous rule]. Consequently, because the root *jñap* has more than one vowel, there would be no prohibition [of the augment], and thus the augment *iṭ* must necessarily occur in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). Therefore, the inclusion of the term "with *s*" (*seṭ*) would be purposeless, as there would be nothing for it to exclude.
But surely, in the case of the form *jñaptaḥ*, [the augment]...?
Is the inclusion of *si* intended for this purpose [to prevent the elision]? This is not so;

even if *si* were included, because these are listed as indeclinables (*nipāta*) in the rule "vā dānta-śānta-pūrṇa-dasta-spasta-channa-jñaptāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.27), the elision of *ṇi* must necessarily occur here.

If, then, the mention of *seṭ* (having an *iṭ* augment) is purposeless, for what reason is it made? To this he says: "It is made," and so forth. The mention of *seṭ* is made so that, after the *iṭ* augment has first been applied, when the *niṣṭhā* suffix occurs, the elision of *ṇi* may subsequently take place. What [is the result]?

Furthermore, if the augment *iṭ* were applied before the elision of the *ṇi*-affix, a fault would arise; why, then, is the introduction of the augment *iṭ* desired first so that this fault may be avoided? To this he says: "For if [the rule] were not made," and so forth. In the absence of the mention of *seṭ*, when the form *kārita* is established, both the elision of the *ṇi*-affix and the augment *iṭ* would apply simultaneously. In that situation...

Since the rule regarding what has been done and what has not been done applies here, there must indeed be the elision of the *ṇi* suffix (*ṇilopa*). And when the *ṇi* is elided, because that which is modified in one part is not different from the original, this very same root *kṛ* remains; consequently, by the rule "ekāca upadeśe 'nudātāt" (Pāṇini 7.2.10), the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* would apply, and thus—
The form "kāritam" would not be established; therefore, the inclusion of the marker *s* must be made.

53. *janitā* in a mantra [is irregular]. (Pāṇini 6.4.53) It is stated that "the elision of *ṇi* is prescribed when followed by *ṭi*, *iṅ*, etc. The form *janitā* ends in the suffix *tṛc*; since the rule "when followed by a suffix beginning with *iṭ*" prohibits [the elision], it would not apply here because it does not begin with *iṭ*. Therefore, it is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*).

However, because [the root] *rañj* is designated as having the technical marker *mi* by the *Gaṇasūtra* "ṭhjanījṛṣknasurañjo'mantāśca" (Gaṇasūtra on Dhātupāṭha 817), the desired form is already established by the rule "mitāṃ hrasvaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.92).

54. *śamitā* in the sense of "sacrificer" (*yajñe*). In the form *śamitaḥ*, as before, there is shortening [of the vowel]. By the rule *ṛto ṅsirvanāmasthānayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.110), *guṇa* substitution occurs; by *halṅyādinā* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), the suffix *su* is elided; [and] of the *repha*...

[The word] *visargaḥ*. [Regarding the statement] "This is in the vocative case ending in *tṛc*," someone might suspect that this ends in a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*); therefore, this was said in order to dispel that doubt. The word *śamayitaḥ* is also in the vocative case ending in *tṛc*.
55. [The substitution of *ya* occurs] before the affixes *āman*, *tṛ*, *vāyya*, *in*, and *viṣṇu*.

(6.4.55) In the example "kārayāñcakāra": by the rule "kāspratyayādāmamantre liṭi" (3.1.35), the suffix *ām* is added; by the rule "āmaḥ" (2.4.81), there is elision (*luk*) of the *liṭ* suffix; and by the rule "kṛñ ca" (3.1.40), [the suffix *ām* is added] after a root ending in *kṛ* when followed by *liṭ*.

There is the subsequent application of the root *kṛ* (*anuprayoga*), reduplication (*dvirvacana*), and the grammatical operations pertaining to the reduplicated stem (*abhyāsakārya*). For example: *gaṇḍayantaḥ*, *maṇḍayantaḥ*.
[The roots are: *gaḍi* "to sprinkle" (DhP 777);
[also] *gaḍa* "a part of the face" (DhP 65, 361); and *maḍi* "to adorn" (DhP 321).
The suffix *ṇic* is added with the sense of causality (*hetumaṇṇic*). Since the root *gaḍi* belongs to the *ghaṭādi* group, there is shortening of the vowel as before when the suffix *ṇi* follows.

While the rule *jṛvṛṣibyāṃ jhac* (Daiva 6.17)—which continues from *jṛviśibhyām* (Daiva 6.17)—is in effect, [the suffix] *jhac* is applied after the roots *tṛ*, *bhū*, *vah*, *vas*, *bhās*, *sādh*, *gam*, *maṇḍ*, and *nand*, according to *tṛbhūvahivasabhāsisādhigamimaṇḍijinandibhyaśca* (Daiva 6.19).

[From the rule *tṛbhūvahivasibhāsisādhigaḍimaṇḍijivandibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.160), the suffix *jhac* is applied, and there is a substitution of the final letter. Thus we have *spṛhayāluḥ* and *gṛhayāluḥ*. The roots *spṛha* (meaning "desire") and *gṛha* (meaning "seizing") belong to the curādika (tenth) class and end in short vowels; [from these, the suffix *ālu* is added]. From the root *spṛha* (Dhātupāṭha 1871) and *gṛha* (Dhātupāṭha 1899)... [the suffix *ālu* is applied] after the vowel *a*.

By the rule *lopaḥ* (6.4.48), there is elision of the letter *a*; because that [elided element] is treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel.
By the rule *spṛhi-gṛhi-* (3.2.158), the suffix *āluc* is applied. Thus, we have *spṛhayālu*. Regarding *spṛhayāyyaḥ*:
by the rule *tanu-dakṣi-spṛhi-gṛhibhya āyyaḥ* (Pañjikā-Uṇādi 1.107), the suffix *āyya* is applied.

Thus, the suffix *āyya* [is applied]. Regarding the word *stanayitnu*: it is derived from the roots *stana* and *gada*, meaning "to sound like a god" (*devaśabda*), which belong to the *curādi* class and end in a short vowel; by the rule *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.48), the final *a* is elided.
Because of the status of that elision as *sthānivat*, the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116) [does not apply].

There is no *vṛddhi* [substitution]. By the rule "from *stan*, *hṛṣ*, *puṣ*, *gad*, *mad*, and others, after a causative suffix (*ṇi*), there is the suffix *itnuc*" (*stani-hṛṣi-puṣi-gadi-madi-dhuṣi-gandhi-maḍi-jani-nadi-bhyo ṇer-itnuc*—Daiva-Uṇādi 1.140), the suffix *itnuc* is applied. Thus: *poṣayiṣṇavaḥ*.

Regarding the word *pārayiṣṇavaḥ*: from the root *puṣ* in the sense of "nourishing" (*puṣa puṣṭau*, Dhātupāṭha 700), there is the causative suffix *ṇic*; then from the roots *pāra* and *tīra* in the sense of "completion of an action" (*pāra tīra karmasamāptau*, Dhātupāṭha 1911, 1912), there is the suffix *ṇic* belonging to the *curādigaṇa*; finally, the suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.137: *ṇeśchandasi*.

Now, why was it not stated simply as *ṭhna*? For if the prohibition of *ṇi*-lopa were established, there would simply be *guṇa*, and in that case, the substitution *ay* [for *e*] would occur by the rule *eco 'yavāyāvaḥ* (6.1.78).
Moreover, in this way the sūtra becomes concise; whereas if *aya* were stated, the sūtra would be heavy due to the addition of one more mātrā.

Thinking that [the rule] applies, he says: "It should not be stated as 'na' (not)," and so forth. In the rule *lyapi laghupūrvāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.56), if it were stated as 'na', there would be no substitution of *ay* due to the absence of *guṇa*.
Therefore, the mention of the *ay*-substitution is for the sake of the subsequent rules.

56. *lyapi laghupūrvāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.56). Regarding the term *laghupūrvāt*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has a light [vowel] as its predecessor. The referent of the other member (*anyapadārtha*) is a phoneme (*varṇa*). Examples: *praṇamayya*, *pratamayya*, *pradamayya*, *praśamayya*. In these cases: [The rule applies when the suffix *lyap* follows a verbal root that ends in a light vowel as its penultimate element.]

Because *nam* and the others are *mit*, when the shortening [of the penultimate vowel] has been performed as before, the letter *m* is preceded by a light syllable. In the example "pravebhidayya gataḥ," the suffix *ṇic* follows the reduplicated (*yaṅ*) form of the root *bhid*. By the rule "yasya halaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.49), there is the elision of the *yakāra*. Here too, the letter *d* is preceded by a light syllable. In the example "pragaṇayya," [the root is] *gaṇ*.
In the root *saṃkhyāna* (Dhātupāṭha 1853), which belongs to the *curādi* class, the final vowel is elided as before. Here too, the *ṇakāra* is preceded by a light vowel.

Now, one might object: "Are not only short vowels and the like [the basis for] technical grammatical rules (*śāstrīya*), and is not the *ay*-substitution also such? In that case, [the rule] 'asiddhavadatrā... [would apply]."

One might ask: since the rule *bhāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.22) renders the short vowels and other elements as non-existent (*asiddha*), how can the condition of being preceded by a light vowel (*laghupūrvatva*) apply to the letter *m* and others? To this he says: "Of the short [vowels], the elision of *y*, and the elision of *ā*" and so forth.
He asks: in what sense do they not have the same locus (*asamānāśrayatva*)? To this he says: "For the short [vowels] and so forth... and so forth.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of "pūrva" (preceded by)? Why not simply say "laghoḥ" (of a light syllable)? It is impossible to state it thus; for if it were stated in that way, the meaning of the sentence would be that the substitution of *lyap* occurs for a *ṇi* that follows a light syllable. And in that case, [the substitution] would not occur in forms such as *pratatayya*, because of the intervention of a consonant (*hal*).

Where, then, would it apply? In cases such as *pragaṇayya*. But surely, even here, once the elision of *a* (*ato lopa*) has been performed, a heavier vowel than the light one following the suffix *ṇic* is indeed possible; therefore, by the force of the rule itself, one might resort to the presence of an intervening element? This is not so.
The understanding that it refers to what occurred in the past will be adopted on the strength of the statement.

Why is this obtained? Because, by the strength of the statement, an intervention must be resorted to, rather than an understanding that it refers to what occurred in the past. For if an understanding that it refers to what occurred in the past were resorted to, [the form] *pragaṇayya* [would not be established].
[The rule] would apply only in cases such as the aforementioned; however, it would not apply in cases such as "praṇamayya gataḥ. Therefore, the mention of the word "pūrva" (preceding) must be made.

57. *vibhāṣā āpaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.57). Regarding the form *prāpayya*: both roots *āplṛ* in the sense of "attaining" (Dhātupāṭha 1839) and *āplṛ* in the sense of "pervading" (Dhātupāṭha 1260) are included. The former belongs to the *curādigaṇa*, while the latter belongs to the *svādigaṇa*.

Now, why does [the substitution] not occur in the case of *adhyāpya gataḥ*? For here too, after the substitution of *ā* for *iṅ* by the rule *krīṅjīnāṃ ṇau* (6.1.48), the subsequent *ṇi* would be applied by the rule *artihrī* (7.3.36) etc., resulting in *āp*. To this, he says: "of that which is the substitute for *iṅ*" (*iṅadeśasya*), and so forth. If that were so, [one might ask] regarding *apa ācaṣṭe*:

Thus, when the suffix *ṇic* is applied to the word *ap*, forms such as *prāpayya* would not occur because they are based on a technical derivative (*lākṣaṇika*); let them not occur by this [rule], for they will be accounted for by the preceding rule. But surely, once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has taken place, the condition of having a non-light vowel (*alaghupūrvatva*) is absent, so the rule would not apply? There is no fault, because the single-substitute is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). How so?
According to the rule *asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam antaraṅge* (Pāṇini 6.4.22),
