the substitution of the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is considered "external" (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends upon two words; however, the substitution of *ay* is "internal" (*antaraṅga*) because it depends upon only a single phoneme (*ṇi*).

58. *yupluvordīrghaśchandasī* (Pāṇini 6.4.58). Regarding the roots *yu* (in the sense of "mixing," with the variant "both mixing and non-mixing" according to the Dhātupāṭha) and *pluṅ* (in the sense of "going"), this rule is stated to ensure the lengthening of the vowel when the augment *tuk* would otherwise apply.
59. *kṣiyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.59).

The phrase *ṭhcchandasi* ("in the Veda") is no longer in force. Regarding the mention of *kṣiyaḥ*, according to the metarule *niranubandhakagrahaṇe na sānubandhakasya* (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 53), this refers to the root *kṣi* "to perish" (Dhātupāṭha 236), not to *kṣi* with its anubandha.

There is the inclusion of these two roots, namely *vas* (meaning "to dwell") and *gati* (meaning "motion") from the Dhātupāṭha (1407), and not of *kṣiṣ* (meaning "to injure") from the Dhātupāṭha (1506). [Note: The Dhātupāṭha reads *kṣīṣ*.]
60. *niṣṭhāyām aṇyadartha* (Pāṇini 6.4.60). [The commentary states:

"The meaning of a *kṛtya* suffix is the state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*)," because of the rule *tayor eva kṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ* (3.4.70). [The sūtra says] "other than those two," which refers to the agent (*kartṛ*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

Regarding the form *kṣīṇaḥ*: the substitution of *ṇ* for the final *t* of the suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied by the rule *kṣiyo dīrghāt* (Pāṇini 8.2.46). This suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) after the root *kṣi*, provided that no prefix (*upapada*) beginning with the letter *a* precedes it; this is established by the rule *gatyartha-* (Pāṇini 3.4.72), etc.

"In this [place], Devadatta's [wealth] has been destroyed. The genitive case is used for the agent according to Pāṇini 2.3.68, *adhikaraṇavācinaśca*. Regarding the word "adhikaraṇe" (in the sense of locus), its connection is with the present subject, namely that this is the suffix *kta*.
That in which something is destroyed (*prakṣīyate*) is called "destroyed" (*prakṣīṇam*); thus, it refers to the substance serving as the locus. [The word] "kṣitam" means "destroyed."

Regarding the word "bhāve" (in the sense of a state/abstract action): its connection [to the preceding rule] is also as before. He does not provide a counter-example for the object (*karman*); because the root *kṣi* is intransitive (*akarmaka*).
61. Or [the suffix *kan* is applied] after [a word ending in *kta*] when expressing reproach (*ākrośa*) or dejection (*dainya*).

(Pāṇini 5.3.61) "Kṣitāyuḥ" (one whose life is exhausted): here, as before, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). The same applies in the following cases as well. "Kṣitakaḥ" (one who has been reduced):
here, the suffix *kan* is applied in the sense of compassion (*anukampā*). In cases other than reproach and dejection, the previous rule [Pāṇini 5.3.60] applies invariably.

[The suffix *ka*] occurs [after a word ending in *kta* when it denotes an agent other than the one previously mentioned]. Why say "another meaning" (*anyadartha*)? [Consider: *kṣitam jālmasya* ("the ruin of the rogue"), *kṣitakam asya tapasvinaḥ* ("the ruin of this wretched man").
62. *syasicsīyuttāsiṣu bhāvakarmaṇor upadeśe 'j-jhan-grah-dṛśām vā ciṇvad iṭ ca*. (Pāṇini 6.4.62).
In the rule "syasicsīyuttāsiṣu," [the locative case] indicates the point of comparison (*pratiyogin*).
From the mention of *ciṇ* [in the rule], it is understood that the suffix *vat* is applied after a word in the locative case, as in the example:

"the manner in Pāṭaliputra is like that in Mathurā. By the phrase "in the domain of the bhāva and the object," he shows that the locative case in the rule *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* functions as a "domain locative" (*viṣayasaptamī*).

Those [suffixes] for which the state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*) are the objects of application are so described. Which, then, are the *syādi* suffixes that have the state and the object as their objects?

Those *syādi* suffixes which occur when the state and the object are intended to be expressed by means of the substitutes for *l* (the *l*-affixes). Here, the particle *ca* is used in the sense of conjunction (*sanniyoga*).
It is performed. Therefore, [the question arises] regarding the rule "when there is the substitution of *ciṇvadbhāva*" and so forth. As for the word "kasya" ("of what"):
augmentations (*āgama*) occur for that which is specified in the genitive case, yet here the suffixes beginning with *si* (the personal endings) are specified in the locative case;
and since no other element to which an augmentation could be added is heard [in the rule], this is the question. Even though those [suffixes] are specified in the locative, and no other [element]...

The question is: "Is it heard as something to be arrived at? Although they are indicated by the locative case (*saptamī*), nevertheless, just as in the rule *hanaś ca vadhaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.76), the root *han*, even though indicated by the ablative (*pañcamī*), undergoes a connection with the place where the suffix is produced and thus acquires the status of being governed by the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). So it is here as well.

With the intention that even *syas* and the others acquire the status of being in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyantatā*) when they experience a connection with an augment (*āgama*), he says "syasic" and so forth. He states the reason for this very point: "for these are the ones under discussion," and so on. This *iṭ* is characterized by being an augment; therefore, it must necessarily [be connected] with that which possesses the augment.

It must be so. Therefore, should one assume that the status of being a source of tradition (*āgama*) applies to those [verbs] not mentioned in the sūtra and prescribe it for them, or should it apply only to the [verbs] under discussion, such as *syati* and the rest?
It is logical that it should be prescribed for those very ones under discussion, because the assumption of what is not heard in the text (*aśruta-prakalpanā*) is a more serious matter. But surely—
The *aṅga* (the base) is also under discussion; why is [the substitution] not applied to it? To this he says: "Of the *aṅga*" and so forth.

It is not applied to the *aṅga* because it would contradict the observed forms (*lakṣya*). If it were applied to the *aṅga*, then once the augment *iṭ* had been added, an undesirable result would follow due to the contradiction with the observed forms. For the treatise does not have a purpose other than [preserving] the correct forms.

Such an arrangement is improper. Therefore, so that there may be no contradiction with the *lakṣya* (the intended application), even though the member (*aṅga*) is also the subject under discussion, the operation is nevertheless performed only for *sy*-type suffixes and not for the member itself.
Here two alternatives are possible: [the first is] that the grammatical operation which has *ciṇ* as its cause, when explicitly stated in relation to *ciṇ*...

That which is prescribed is extended by analogy (*atideśa*). Alternatively, whatever is seen in the case of *ciṇ*, whether it is considered to have *ciṇ* as its cause or not, that is [extended] generally. In that regard, if the former position were adopted, then the augment *yuk* would apply by the rule "āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.33).

And by the rule "ṭhviṇṇamulordorgho'nyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 6.4.93), there is the substitution of a long vowel; these two alone would be the operations of the *aṅga* (stem) in the case of the *atiśaya* (intensive). No other [operation], such as *vṛddhi* and so forth, [would apply], for that is not specifically prescribed for the *ciṇ* affix. "Specifically" (*āhatya*) means "having been explicitly uttered. For that which [is prescribed] directly for the *ciṇ*...

That which is prescribed by taking a specific cause as a basis is prescribed by directly affecting the verbal root (*cin*), and *vṛddhi* and so forth are not prescribed in this manner. Now, if the second alternative is taken, then this undesirable consequence does not arise; for *vṛddhi* and the rest are indeed observed in the case of the suffix *ciṇ*.

If that which is seen in the *ciṇ* [affix] is extended by analogy (*atideśa*), then the substitutes for *han*, *iṇ*, and *ṅ* would also apply, since they too are seen there; with this intention, he says: "Which ones, moreover," and so forth.

Thinking, "I shall refute later whatever fault exists in the second position," and demonstrating that what was observed regarding the *ciṇ* [affix]— whether it be its cause or something else— is here indicated in a general sense, [the author sets forth] the purposes of this rule (*yoga*).
The summary verse states: "vṛddhiściṇvat" and so forth.

In the form *cāyiṣyate*, the purpose is the application of *vṛddhi*. [This is derived from] the root *ci* with the suffix *luṭ* and the addition of *syapratyaya*. By the rule "bhāvakarmaṇoḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.13), the *ātmanepada* ending is applied; here now—

Vṛddhi occurs due to the state of being like the *ciṇ* [augment], as for example, in the case of *acāyi*, vṛddhi occurs by the rule "aco ñṇiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.115). In the same way, in the subsequent cases as well,
one should apply the extension (*atideśa*) by connecting the term *ciṇvat* with each [rule] individually, as appropriate.

"it will be established (ṭhacāyiṣyate)"—this is the *luṅ* [aorist] suffix; the rest is as before. And there is a purpose for the rule regarding *yuk*: in the case of "it will be given (dāyiṣyate). Furthermore, the long vowel that is mentioned in the rule "the *ciṇ* [augment] optionally applies to the roots *mit* and so on" also serves a purpose: in the cases of "it will be calmed (śamiṣyate)" and "it will be pacified (śāmiṣyate)," [the long vowel occurs] from the root *śam*.

By the rule *ṭhjanijṛṣknasurañjo'mantāśca* (DhP 817), the [root *rañj*] receives the designation *mit*; and since it is taught as ending in *ṇi* in the rule *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ* (3.1.32), it is thus [considered] to end in an *ac* vowel at the time of its original enunciation (*upadeśe*). As for the substitution of *k* for the *h* of the root *han*, by the rule *ho hanteñinneṣu* (7.3.54)— The final answer is: the root *rañj* is designated as *mit* by DhP 817; because it is taught with the suffix *ṇi* under Pāṇini 3.1.32, it is considered to end in an *ac* vowel at the time of its original enunciation (*upadeśe*). Furthermore, regarding the substitution of *k* for the *h* of *han*, this occurs by Pāṇini 7.3.54.

"It will be prescribed, and that purpose will be established" is the case here; however, in the form *haniṣyate*, the augment *iṭ* applies by the rule "ṛddhanoḥ sye" (Pāṇini 7.2.70). These purposes indeed exist, but when this *iṭ* is applied, [the forms] would become *śamiṣyate* and *śamiṣyate*.

In this case, the elision of the *ṇi* by the rule "ṭhṇeraniṭi" (Pāṇini 6.4.51) would not be established because [the suffix] is *seṭ* (possessing an *iṭ* augment). Therefore, he says: "And the *iṭ* is as if non-existent," and so forth. Since this *ciṇvadiṭ* is "as if non-existent" (*asiddhavat*) by the rule "asiddhavadatrā bhāt" (Pāṇini 6.4.22), the elision of the *ṇi* will indeed take place.

This might be the case: for those roots such as *cinoti* which are taught with an anudātta (unaccented) initial vowel, it is logical that the *iṭ* augment should be prescribed for the suffixes *si* and so on following them by this rule, and thus their status as "not established" (*asiddha*) is appropriate;
however, in the case of those such as *śam* which are taught with an udātta (accented) initial vowel, because [the *iṭ*] follows after them...

[One might object: "By the rule *ārddhadhātukasyeṅvalādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.35), an augment *iṭ* ought to occur conditioned by a suffix beginning with *va*l; and that [augment] is indeed established. But even so, does the same fault not remain? To this he says:
"And this [augment] is permanent," and so forth. A grammatical operation (*vidhi*) which applies whether [the condition] has already occurred or has not yet occurred is...

"Permanent"—relying on this [term], this [augment] is permanent like *ciṇ* and *iṭ*. For even when the condition of having *val* as a prefix (*valāditva*) has been established, it is prescribed; thus, "that which causes the obstruction. That for which *val* is the cause or reason is so described. It is called "obstructive" (*vighātī*) because it possesses an obstruction (*vighāta*).

Obstruction (*vighāta*) means non-occurrence due to the absence of a cause. Thus, because [the root] is eternal, this very *ciṇvad-iṭ* ought to apply even to elevated [roots]; and since this [augment] is considered *asiddha*, there is no contingency of the non-occurrence of the elision of the *ṇi*-affix.

[The form] *grāhiṣyate* [is derived]. The purpose [of the rule] is the *vṛddhi* [substitution] by [the rule] *ata upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116). Now, why does the lengthening [of the vowel] not occur here by [the rule] *graho 'liṭi dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.37)?
To this he says: *graho 'liṭi*, etc. For in that case, the augment *iṭ* characterized by being preceded by a consonant (*valādi*) is the one under discussion.
The lengthening [of the vowel] is understood to apply to that [root] alone, and not to any other. Regarding the form *drakṣyate*:
by the rule *sṛjidṛśorjhalyamakiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.58), there is the augment *am*; by *vraścādinā* (8.2.36), there is the substitution of *ṣ*;
by *ṣaṅeḥ kaḥ si* (8.2.41), there is the substitution of *k*; and by *iṇkoḥ* (8.3.57), [the ṣ becomes ṭ].

[The change to] *ṣ* [is established]. Regarding the statement "it will be shown," the *guṇa* substitution here is indeed accomplished by [Pāṇini 7.3.86], "pugantalaghūpadhasya. However, the rule for *ciṇvadbhāva* is prescribed for the sake of [the addition of] *iṭ*.
Regarding "aceṣātām," this is the form with the suffix *ātām* after *sic*. Regarding "adiṣātām," [this is likewise the form with *ātām* after *sic*].
There is the substitution of *i* by [Pāṇini 1.2.17] *ṭhsthādhvoricca*, and the *s*-affix *sic* is treated as having the *kit* designation.
Regarding *avadhiṣātām*: the substitute *vadh* is applied by [Pāṇini 2.4.44] *ātmanepadeṣvanyatarasyām*. Regarding *adṛkṣātām*: [the rule] *liṅsicāvātmanepadeṣu* [Pāṇini 1.2.11 applies].

What then? Because of that [suffix], the augment *ām* and the *guṇa* substitution do not occur; the substitution of *ṣ* and so forth is as before. Regarding "cetā": this is the periphrastic future (*luṭ*), the suffix *tās*, and the replacement by *ḍā* according to Pāṇini 2.4.85, followed by the elision of the *ṭi* portion. Regarding "draṣṭā": the augment *am* and so forth are as before. Regarding "cetavyam": [this is the gerundive].

The suffix *tavya* is used in the sense of the object (*karmani*). Regarding the example "he will desire" (*ceṣyati*), because the agent is intended to be expressed by means of a substitute for *l* (the *laṭ* suffix), the suffix *syapratyaya* applies to the agent.
[The objection] "once *guṇa* has been applied and *raparatva* has occurred, [the rule] does not apply" refers to the stage where the form is *kṛ-ṣyate*.

The *guṇa* substitution would apply, as would the *ciṇ-vat* treatment; there, by virtue of its higher status (*paratva*), the *guṇa* would occur, and once that is performed, the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* would follow. If the term "in the original enunciation" (*upadeśa*) were not employed, then this [substitution] would not occur here because the root would no longer end in *an*.
It occurs precisely because of the inclusion of "in the original enunciation. Even though the root *kṛ* does not end in *an* at a subsequent stage, [it is still treated as such].

But in the case of the *upadeśa* (the original form), it is only that which ends in a vowel (*ajanta*). If the operation seen in the *ciṇ* affix were extended [to the *han* root], then the substitutes for *han*, namely *ṇiṅ* and others, would also be subject to it; for those too are not seen [in the *ciṇ* context]. To this [it is replied]: [The answer follows: It is not so. Why? Because the rule is stated as "that which is seen in the *ciṇ*. Since the substitutes for *han* are not seen in the *ciṇ* [context], they do not undergo that [operation]. Furthermore, the substitute *ṇiṅ* is taught by the rule *hano vadha-liṅ-ṅiṣu* (P. 2.4.42). If that were to apply here, then because of the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (P. 8.3.59), the augment *ṣ* would be added after the letter *n* [of the substitute *vadha*]. However, since the *ṣ* is not seen in the *ciṇ* [context], the augment does not occur. Moreover, the substitute *ṇiṅ* is taught by the rule *hano vadha-liṅ-ṅiṣu* (P. 2.4.42) specifically for the purpose of forming the word *avadhi*. If that were to apply here, then because of the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (P. 8.3.59), the augment *ṣ* would be added after the letter *n* [of the substitute *vadha*]. However, since the *ṣ* is not seen in the *ciṇ* [context], the augment does not occur. Moreover, the substitute *ṇiṅ* is taught by the rule *hano vadha-liṅ-ṅiṣu* (P. 2.4.42) specifically for the purpose of forming the word *avadhi*. If that were to apply here, then because of the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (P. 8.3.59), the augment *ṣ* would be added after the letter *n* [of the substitute *vadha*]. However, since the *ṣ* is not seen in the *ciṇ* [context], the augment does not occur. Furthermore, the substitute *ṇiṅ* is taught by the rule *hano vadha-liṅ-ṅiṣu* (P. 2.4.42) specifically for the purpose of forming the word *avadhi*. If that were to apply here, then because of the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (P. 8.3.59), the augment *ṣ* would be added after the letter *n* [of the substitute *vadha*]. However, since the *ṣ* is not seen in the *ciṇ* [context], the augment does not occur. Moreover, the substitute *ṇiṅ* is taught by the rule *hano vadha-liṅ-ṅiṣu* (P. 2.4.42) specifically for the purpose of forming the word *avadhi*. If that were to apply here, then because of the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (P. 8.3.59), the augment *ṣ* would be added after the letter *n* [of the substitute *vadha*]. However, since the *ṣ* is not seen in the *ciṇ* [context], the augment does not occur. Furthermore, the substitute *ṇiṅ* is taught by the rule *hano vadha-liṅ-ṅiṣu* (P. 2.4.42) specifically for the purpose of forming the word *avadhi*. If that were to apply here, then because of the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (P. 8.3.59), the augment *ṣ* would be added after the letter *n* [of the substitute *vadha*]. However, since the *ṣ* is not seen in the *ciṇ* [context], the augment does not occur. Moreover, the substitute *ṇiṅ* is taught by the rule *hano vadha-liṅ-ṅiṣu* (P. 2.4.42) specifically for the purpose of forming the word *avadhi*. If that were to apply here, then because of the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (P. 8.3.59), the augment *ṣ* would be added after the letter *n* [of the substitute *vadha*]. However, since the *ṣ* is not seen in the *ciṇ* [context], the augment does not occur. Furthermore, the substitute *ṇiṅ* is taught by the rule *hano vadha-liṅ-ṅiṣu* (P. 2.4.42) specifically for the purpose of forming the word *avadhi*. If that were to apply here, then because of the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (P. 8.3.59), the augment *ṣ* would be added after the letter *n* [of the substitute *vadha*]. However, since the *ṣ* is not seen in the *ciṇ* [context], the augment does not occur. Moreover, the substitute *ṇiṅ* is taught by the rule *hano vadha-liṅ-ṅiṣu* (P. 2.4.42) specifically for the purpose of forming the word *avadhi*. If that were to apply here, then because of the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (P. 8.3.59), the augment *ṣ* would be added after the letter *n* [of the substitute *vadha*]. However, since the *ṣ* is not seen in the *ciṇ* [context], the augment does not occur. Furthermore, the substitute *ṇiṅ* is taught by the rule *hano vadha-liṅ-ṅiṣu* (P. 2.4.42) specifically for the purpose of forming the word *avadhi*. If that were to apply here, then because of the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (P. 8.3.59), the augment *ṣ* would be added after the letter *n* [of the substitute *vadha*]. However, since the *ṣ* is not seen in the *ciṇ* [context], the augment does not occur. Moreover, the substitute *ṇiṅ* is taught by the rule *hano vadha-liṅ-ṅiṣu* (P. 2.4.42) specifically for the purpose of forming the word *avadhi*. If that were to apply here, then because of the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (P. 8.3.59), the augment *ṣ* would be added after the letter *n* [of the substitute *vadha*]. However, since the *ṣ* is not seen in the *ciṇ* [context], the augment does not occur. Furthermore, the substitute *ṇiṅ* is taught by the rule *hano vadha-liṅ-ṅiṣu* (P. 2.4.42) specifically for the purpose of forming the word *avadhi*. If that were to apply here, then because of the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (P. 8.3.

He says: "That which is prescribed under the heading of 'aṅga'," and so forth. Since there is the governing heading (adhikāra) of "of the aṅga," that operation which is seen in the case of *ciṇ*—being prescribed under the heading of the aṅga—is extended by analogy (*atideśa*) in a general sense;
however, this does not apply to what is remote, being prescribed in another context. Nor...

The substitutes *hana*, *niṇi*, and *mā* are prescribed not within the governing rule (*adhikāra*) on verbal bases (*aṅga*), but rather in a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*). Therefore, they are not extended [to this case] by analogy, and thus they do not apply there. Consequently, in the form *dhāniṣyate*, the substitute *vadh*—which is prescribed by the rule *lūṅ ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.43)—does not occur. As for *āyiṣyate*:

The substitution of *gā* prescribed by the rule "ṭhiṇo gā luṅ" (Pāṇini 2.4.45) [is seen here]. In the form "adhyāyiṣyate," the substitution of *gāṅ* prescribed by the rule "vibhāṣā luṅlṛṅoḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.50) occurs. Even so, the elision (*luk*) of the affix following roots such as *sy* would still result.

Is it not the case that, under the section on *aṅga*, the elision of the suffix following *ciṇ* is prescribed by the rule "ṭhciṇoluk" (Pāṇini 6.4.104)? This is not a fault; for here, the suffix *vati* is understood as being prescribed after a word in the locative case (*saptamī-samartha*). Therefore, whatever grammatical operation is observed to apply to [the root] when *ciṇ* follows, that is possible for the preceding element.
That [rule] is extended [to the preceding], but not that which is the operation of the subsequent [element].

63. *dīṅo yuḍ aci kṅiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.63). Regarding the example *udadīye*: the root is *dīṅ* "to perish" (Dhātupāṭha 1134). By the rule *asaṃyogāl liṭ kit* (1.2.5), the *liṭ* affixes are *kit*; consequently, for the *liṭ*, the substitutes *eś* and *irec* take the place of *ta* and *jha*.

Regarding the expression "dīṅaḥ," there are two possible interpretations: it may be either a genitive or an ablative case. If the first alternative were adopted, then when the suffix *yuṭ* is applied according to the rule "ādyantau ṭakitau" (Pāṇini 1.1.46), the verbal root would assume an undesirable form. Therefore, having observed this flaw in the genitive interpretation, [the author] states:

Prefacing the fifth alternative, he says: "Because of the mention of the ablative case in *dīṅ*," and so forth. For when there is a mention of the ablative case, according to the principle "between two mentions, the mention of the ablative is stronger" (Śākapārthiva 97), the ablative *dīṅaḥ* [is understood as] taking the place of the genitive *aci*.

By the rule *tasmādityuttarasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.67), the augment *yuṭ* is applied to the beginning of a root starting with a vowel (*ajādi*). The mention of the locative case in *aci* (Pāṇini 6.4.77), however, is for the sake of subsequent rules. Now, one might object that since the substitution of *yaṇ* by the rule *eranekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.82) must be applied here, and since *yuṭ* is considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*) [at that point], the *yaṇ* substitution should take effect.

It ought to be so; consequently, the form *upadidīya* would not be established, and the undesired form *upadidye* would result. Therefore, he says: "By virtue of the power of the rule," and so forth. If the *yuṭ* augment were non-existent (*asiddha*) when the *yaṇ* substitution was to be applied, then [the rule for] the *yuṭ*...

The rule would be purposeless because there is no distinction. But how can there be no distinction, when in the absence of *yuṭ* there is the hearing of a single *y*, whereas when it exists there is the hearing of two?
This is not a distinction; for there is no difference in the hearing of a consonant, whether it be one or many, when followed by another consonant.

There is indeed a distinction. However, for those who maintain that there is a distinction, we have already previously explained—though in a different manner—that the substitution of *yaṇ* is established as being *siddha* for the sake of the suffix *yuṭ*.
[The example is] "upadīdīyate. [The root is] *dīṅ* "to perish" (DhP 1134); [the formation is derived from] *asaṃyogālliṭ* [Kāśikā 1.2.5].
Regarding the rule *kit* (1.2.5), there are two possible interpretations:

either the genitive case in *dīṅḥ* (6.4.63) is intended, or the ablative case; these constitute two alternative views. If the first view were adopted, then when the augment *yuṭ* is applied according to the rule *ādyantau ṭakitau* (1.1.46), [the following would occur].

[Otherwise] the root would undergo an undesirable form. Therefore, having observed this objection regarding the position of the genitive (ṣaṣṭhī), he sets forth the position of the ablative (pañcamī), saying: "Because of the mention of *dīṅ* in the ablative," and so forth.
For when there is a mention in the ablative, "between two mentions, the mention in the ablative is stronger."

(Śākaṭāyana Pañjikā 97) Thus, by treating the ablative case in *dīṅaḥ* as a genitive and the locative case in *aci* as a genitive, the rule *tasmād ity uttarasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.67) applies, whereby the augment *yuṭ* is placed at the beginning of the following vowel-initial (*aj-ādi*) element.
The mention of the locative case in *aci*, however, is for the sake of subsequent rules. Now, one might object that here [the rule] *eranekācaḥ*...

When the substitution of *yaṇ* is to be applied according to [Pāṇini 6.1.77] (6.4.82), the augment *yuṭ* is considered non-existent; thus, the *yaṇ* substitution must take effect, and consequently, the form *upadidīya* would not be established, as the undesirable form *upadidye* would result. Therefore, he says: "By virtue of the force of the rule's formulation," and so forth.

If the *puṭ* were non-existent (*asiddha*) when the substitution of *yaṇ* was to be applied, then the prescription of *yuṭ* would be purposeless, because there would be no difference [in the result]. But how can there be no difference, given that when *yuṭ* is absent there is the hearing of a single *y*, whereas when it is present there is the hearing of two?

There is no such distinction; for there is indeed no difference in the hearing of a vowel, whether it follows one consonant or many. As for those who do maintain that there is a distinction, we have already demonstrated earlier—under the rule for *yaṇ* substitution—that the status of *yuṭ* as established (*siddhatva*) would otherwise be untenable according to their view.
[The word] *upadīyate* [is formed] from the root *dī* with the suffix *yaṅ*. [The word] *upadāna* is formed with the suffix *lyuṭ*;

the substitution of *ā* [for *ī*] occurs by the rule *mīnātiminotidīṅāṃ lyapi ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.50). The mention of the marker *ṅ* in *dīṅ* is for the purpose that [the substitution of *ā*] should not occur when the *yaṅ* is elided (*yaṅluk*), as in *dedyatu* and *dedyauḥ*.

But surely, in this case, the suffix *ām* ought to occur by the rule *kāspratyayādāmamantre* (Pāṇini 3.1.35); because of that, [the substitution] will not take place simply due to the absence of *aṅ*. This is true: it will not occur in non-mantric usage, but in mantric usage it would indeed occur; for in that case, there is no *ām*. Now, regarding the *yaṅ*-luṅ form in the mantra...
If the application is not seen, then it is for the sake of clarity.

64. *ato lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64). [The rule states: "There is elision of the final *a* before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with *iṭ* or a consonant (*jādi*), and before a suffix marked with *k* or *ṅ*. The phrase "before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant" is connected to each [of the two conditions]: namely, "before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with *iṭ* or a consonant," and "before a suffix marked with *k* or *ṅ*."

Regarding the rule "after [a root] beginning with *c* or *ā*, before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix": the mention of *iṅ* is for the sake of excluding *aṅ*. In the form *papitha*, it is the perfect (*liṭ*) of either the root *pā* or *pib*; the suffix *sip* is replaced by *thal* by the rule "for the parasmaipada endings" (Pāṇini 3.4.82), and the augment *iṭ* is applied by the restriction "of Bhāradvāja, after a root ending in *ṛ*" (Pāṇini 7.2.63).

Regarding "godaḥ": [the suffix] *ka* is applied by the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3). Regarding "vyatyare" and "vyatyale": the ātmanepada ending is applied by the rule *kartari karmavyatīhāre* (Pāṇini 1.3.14);
this is the third person singular (*uttamapuruṣaikavacana*), including the augment *iṭ*. Of that...
The designation *ṅt* [of the affix] is by the rule "sārvadhātukam apit" (Pāṇini 1.2.4). Since the status of being an *ardhadhātuka* does not apply there, the elision [of the *y*] does not occur.
In "glāyate," the *lakāra* denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*). In "dāsīya," the *liṅ* suffix is used in the sense of benediction (*āśis*).
This is the first person singular of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*); for that, the substitute *at* is applied by the rule *ṭiṭo't* (Pāṇini 3.4.106).
Here, because the augment *sīyuṭ* is an integral part of that [suffix], the *it* [of *sīyuṭ*] does not possess the quality of beginning with a vowel (*jāditva*).
Consequently, even though [the suffix] is an *ārddhadhātuka* beginning with a vowel, there is no elision [of the final *i* of the root].

65. *īdyati* (Pāṇini 6.4.65). Although the term *kṅiti* is carried over from the subsequent rule, it is not connected here; for there is no possibility of *k* or *ṅ* following. The letter *t* is for the sake of pronunciation; indeed, [the vowel *i*] is not subject to the rule because it is not *aṇ*.

The inclusion of the term *savarṇa* (homogeneous) will not be necessary. Or, even if the theory of genus (*jāti*) is not accepted, by virtue of proximity (*āntaryāt*), only the long vowel will result from the substitution, not the short one. The explicit mention of the long vowel is for the sake of subsequent rules;
however, in this case, the *guṇa* substitution ought to take place. And here, whether the *guṇa* is applied to the long vowel or the short vowel, [the result remains the same].
There is a certain distinction: [the word] "deyam" [is derived] by [the rule] "aco yat" (Pāṇini 3.1.97).

66. *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisāṃ hali* (Pāṇini 6.4.66). Regarding the example *dīyate*: this is the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) in the passive voice (*karman*). Regarding *dedīyate*: this is from the *yaṅ* (intensive suffix). Now, to which root does this mention of *me* refer? Is it to *meṅ praṇidāne* (Dhātupāṭha 961)?

Is it the root *mā* belonging to the *bhūvādika* class; or the root *māṅ* meaning "to measure" (*māne śabde ca*) belonging to the *jauhotyādika* class; or rather the root *mā* meaning "to measure" belonging to the *adādika* class? Regarding this, some say: "When there is a mention of a root without an *anubandha*..."

In [the rule] *na sānubandhakasya* (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 53), there is the inclusion of the former [root]. Others, however, say: "Between a root with a *luk*-suffixal marker and one without, only that without the *luk*-marker is to be understood" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 50); thus, in the case of *māṅ* and *meṅ*, which both lack such markers, [the former is taken]. Still others [say]: ...
They say: "In the case of the mention of *gām-ādi* [roots], there is no distinction" (*Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā* 124);

thus, it appears that this very view is intended by the author of the *Vṛtti*. For he says: "The root *pā-* is not included here, because it has a *luk*-suffix. By saying this, he refers to *pā-* in the sense of "protection" (*dhātu-pāṭha* 1056).

Thus, the non-inclusion of this [term] has been stated by himself. Furthermore, if the inclusion of either the *alug-vikaraṇa* or the *lug-vikaraṇa* were intended here, he would have explained that as well; yet it was not explained. Therefore, it is understood that [the rule applies] to all three.

The inclusion is intended as follows: regarding "gā," there are the roots *gāṅ* in the sense of "motion" (DhP 950) and *gai* in the sense of "sound" (DhP 916, 917), both belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa*; furthermore, there is *gā* in the sense of "praise" in the Veda (DhP 1106)—the term "in the Veda" does not appear in the Dhātupāṭha—belonging to the *juhotyādigaṇa*, and *iṇ*.

By the rule *gāṅ liṭi* (2.4.45), there is the substitution of *gā* for *iṇ*; by the statement "it should be stated that [the substitution applies] after roots such as *hiṇ*" (Vārttika 167), there is the substitution of *gā* for *ik*; by *gāṅ liṭi* (2.4.49), and by *vibhāṣā luṅlṛṅoḥ* (2.4.50), there is the substitution of *gāṅ* for *iṅ*—for these, the procedure is as previously described.

The inclusion of all [roots] is without distinction. Even though there is an inclusion of all, the substitution of *it* (short *i*) occurs only for that [root] for which a *kṅid* ārdhadhātuka suffix can follow, and not for another, because of the absence of the necessary cause (*nimitta*). As in: *gīyate*, *jegīyate*.

These are examples of the two roots belonging to the *bhū* class (*bhauvādika*). Regarding the form *adhyagīṣṭa*, and so forth: by the rule *iṅo gāṅ* [Pāṇini 2.4.49], the root *iṅ* is replaced by *gāṅ*;
by the rule *gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ...* [Pāṇini 1.2.1], the suffix *sic* is marked with the *ṅ*-sign; and by the rule *ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.5], the substitution of *at* for the final vowel occurs.

Now, for what reason is the designation *stipā* made as *jahāti*, rather than simply saying *heti*? To this he says: "of *jahāti*" and so forth. If the designation were made as *heti*, then it would apply to *jihāti* as well—that is, to the root *hāṅ* in the sense of "going" (DhP 1089)—as in the form *jahāti*.

But this does not apply in the case of a specific grammatical reference (*nirdeśa*). For when there is a specific reference here, the rule must apply only to that which possesses this specific form. And to what does this form belong? It belongs to the root *hāk* "to abandon" (DhP 1090), and not to the other [root] which undergoes the substitution of *i* for the semivowel by the rule *bhṛñām it* (Pāṇini 7.4.76).

When [the suffix] *kta* is applied, the form becomes *jihita*. Granted that even when *hā* is specified, there would be no occasion for *jihīte*, yet such a specification was not made for the sake of variety. Regarding "it is concluded" (*avasīyate*): the root is *ṣo* in the sense of "concluding" (*antakarmaṇi*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "dadatuḥ": one might object, "In this case, the elision of the vowel 'ā' will occur by the rule 'āto lopaḥ' (Pāṇini 6.4.64); so what is the purpose of the condition 'halī' (before a consonant)? To this, he says: "For, because of the elision of the vowel 'ā'," and so forth. [The elision] of the vowel 'ā'...

The scope for elision (*lopa*) is, for example, *yayatuḥ* and *yayuḥ*; the scope for the substitution of *ī* (*ītvam*) is, for example, *dīyate* and *dhīyate*. In the case of *dadatuḥ* and *daduḥ*, both [rules] would apply. In that situation, if the mention of "consonant" (*hal*) were not made, then by virtue of its higher status (*paratva*), the substitution of *ī* would occur. But is it not so?

A conflict between two rules is possible when both are established; however, in this case, by the rule "that which is not yet established is treated as if it were already established within the same domain" (6.4.22), both are non-established (*asiddha*). Therefore, how can there be a conflict?
And since this is the case, it is not correct to say that the substitution of *ī* would occur because it is subsequent [to the other rule]. Likewise...
Is it not stated [in Pāṇini 1.4.2] that "when there is a conflict, the subsequent rule takes effect"?

To this he says: "This very [point]," and so forth. If, in this case where a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is to be applied, there were non-validity (*asiddhatva*), then the mention of *hal* would be purposeless. Let there be *itva* here; because of its non-validity, [the rule] "of *āt*"...
[The elision] will occur by [Pāṇini 6.4.64] *lopaḥ*; so what is the use of mentioning the term *hal*?
How, then, does this [mention] become meaningful? Only if there were established validity (*siddhatva*) when a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*) is to be applied, and not otherwise.

67. *er liṅ* (Pāṇini 6.4.67). This rule prescribes *etva* (the substitution of *e*) where *itva* (the substitution of *i*) would otherwise have been obtained by the preceding rule. The example is *meyāt*, which is an illustration of the root *mā māne* (DhP 1062), and not of the roots *māṅ* or *meṅ*.
For since those two [roots] are ātmanepadin, the parasmaipada is not possible. The form *geyāt* is an example of the root *gai* (DhP 916, 917), and not of *gāṅ*;
for that [root *gāṅ*] cannot take the parasmaipada. Nor is it an example of the substitutes [ending in] *iṇ*, *ṇic*, or *ṅit*, because those [substitutes] also...
Because of the impossibility of [the suffix] *liṅ*; however, for that which is a substitute for *iṅ*, it is because of the previously stated reason.

68. Or [the substitution occurs] for another [root], such as *saṃyuj* and so forth. (Pāṇini 6.4.68) Why does it say "for another"? [Consider the example: *stheyāt*. If "for another" were not stated, then the previous rule (*pūrvayoga*) would find its scope in other roots beginning with *dhū*, and this [present] rule would also find its scope in cases such as *glāyāt*.
In the rule *stheyāt*, since both [conditions] would apply, there would be an option (*vikalpa*) due to its being subsequent; therefore, the mention of *anya* (the other) is made.
If the preceding rule were also to commence with the sense of "standing" (*tiṣṭhati*), then for that sense...

By virtue of its power to initiate [the substitution], the substitution of *et* will necessarily occur by the preceding rule; otherwise, the formulation of that [subsequent rule] for that purpose would be fruitless. Thus, it would have been possible not to include the mention of "another" (*anya*). Nevertheless, it is included for the sake of clarity.

69. *na lyapi* (6.4.69). The option (*vā*) has ceased to apply, because in the subsequent rule the mention of *anyatarasyām* occurs again. Regarding the statement "as has been said": there is the substitution of *ī*, but not the subsequent substitution of *e*; for that [substitution of *e*] cannot possibly apply when *lyap* follows.
And because a prohibition is necessarily preceded by a prior application.
70. *mayater id anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.4.70).

Since the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel would otherwise result in its being heard due to the prohibition in *na lyapi* (6.4.69), this rule is commenced to introduce the substitution of *it*. The form *apamitya* is derived from the root *meṅ* (praṇidāne, Dhātupāṭha 961).
In the northern tradition, the suffix *ktvā* is applied by the rule "māṅi vyatīhāre" (Pāṇini 3.4.19), and once the change to *it* has been made, the augment *tuk* is added. Now, one might object:

since this is already established by the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in the rule "apamityayācitābhyāṃ kakkanau" (4.4.21), this new undertaking is useless. This is not so; for even those [rules] that are exceptions...
According to the view that "there are irregular formations (*nipātana*s)" (Nipātavṛtti 109), the form *apamāya* would not be possible.

If one were to argue that it will be derived from the root *māṅ* in the sense of "measuring" (Dhātupāṭha 1088)—[the Dhātupāṭha also records it as being] "in the sense of measuring and sound"—we say no; because the meanings differ. Furthermore, even though they are not sublaters (*abādhaka*),...
Would there not be irregular formations (*nipātana*) [even without this rule]?
Even so, this must indeed be commenced for the sake of removing doubt; for if this were absent, a doubt would arise:
"Is this an irregular formation of the root *māy*, or rather of another root?"

Furthermore, a restriction regarding the prefix would be understood—namely, that it applies only to [the root] preceded by *apa*. Since this is the case, the commencement of this rule is appropriate for the purpose of ensuring that it also occurs with other prefixes.

71. *luṅlaṅlṛṅkṣvaḍudāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.71). [The rule states: "And that [augment] becomes udātta. Since the default status of augments is to be anudātta, this prescribes their being udātta. And this mention of "udātta" [is significant because] in this grammar, phonetic qualities (*guṇa*) do not cause differentiation [between grammatical elements]. (Puṣpavṛtti 57)

This is the indicator of this meaning. How so? If the qualities (*guṇa*) were indeed differentiators, then one would pronounce this [suffix] only when joined with the acute accent (*udātta*). The Teacher perceives that "in this treatise, the qualities are not differentiators," because the mention of the acute accent is for the purpose of precluding other accents.

What is the purpose of making this known? It is so that, in the rule "vṛddhir ādaic" (1.1.1), the designation *vṛddhi* is established even for those [sounds] distinguished by the differences of acute (*udātta*) and other accents.

72. *āḍajādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.4.72). [Examples: *aiṣṭa*, *aihiṣṭa*. The roots *īkṣa* "to see" (DhP 610) and *īh* "to strive" (DhP 632) are both *anudāteta*; by the rule *āṭaśca* (6.1.90), there is *vṛddhi* [of the initial vowel]. [The form] *āujīt* [is derived from *ujjhati*].

Regarding the form *ṣṭhāṬmbhīt*: from the roots *ubja* in the sense of "straightening" (*ārjane*) [DhP 1303] and *ubha* in the sense of "filling" (*unbhapūraṇe*) [DhP 1319, 1320], the augment *iṭ* is applied by Pāṇini 7.2.35 (*ārdhadhātukasyeṭ*). Then, by 7.3.96 (*asti sico 'pṛkte*), the augment *iṭ* is added after the suffix *sic*, and by 8.2.28 (*iṭa īṭi*), there is the elision of *sic*.

Now, regarding the forms *aijyata*, *āuṭpyata*, and *āuhyata*, how does the substitution of *āṬ* (vṛddhi) occur here? For the *laṅ* affix is prescribed after the roots *yaj*, *vap*, and *vah* in the sense of the object (*karman*), and these roots begin with consonants (*hal-ādi*), not with vowels (*ac-ādi*). Nor can it be argued that vowel-initialness (*ajāditva*) will be established once the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) has taken place; because [the substitution] occurs even before that.

Since the substitution for the *l* affix (*lādeśa*) is subsequent, should not the augment *aṭ* (*aḍāgama*) occur first, followed by the substitution for *l*, then the *yak* suffix, and finally the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*)? To this he says: "In this case," and so forth. Although the augment *aṭ* is subsequent, nevertheless, because the substitution is internal (*antaraṅga*), that very substitution is performed first. For the substitution for *l*...

The substitution of *la* is *antaraṅga* because it occurs depending merely on the verbal root (*dhātu*). The augment *aṭ*, however, is *bahiraṅga* because it is prescribed for the *aṅga* (the stem), and an *aṅga* depends upon an affix (*pratyaya*). The designation "prior arising" is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) [of this relationship].
In this context, "internal" (antaraṅga) implies "eternal" (nitya). For the substitution of *l* (the verbal suffix) is eternal:

it applies whether the augment *aṭ* has been added or not. The augment *aṭ*, however, is non-eternal, because it results in the attainment of a different form [only after other operations]. Indeed, once the substitution of *l* has occurred, the vikaraṇa must necessarily apply due to its eternity.

And when the *vikaraṇa* suffix has been applied, it must belong to that stem which ends in the *vikaraṇa*; but if it has not been applied, it belongs to the verbal root alone. Therefore, because it is both *antaraṅga* (internal) and *nitya* (obligatory), the substitution for the *l*-suffixes (*lādeśa*) is performed prior to the augment *āṭ*. Regarding the phrase "that having been done": this means once the substitution for the *l*-suffixes has been performed. Regarding the term "*vikaraṇa*": [it refers to the suffix].

Regarding the statement "because [the augment] *aṭ* is obligatory": the obligatoriness (*nityatva*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) is due to its application whether [the augment] has already occurred or not yet occurred; for that suffix applies both when *aṭ* has been applied and when it has not.
It might be argued: "The augment *aṭ* also applies both when the suffix has been applied and when it has not."

Therefore, its [the augment's] permanence also [is established]. Since both are permanent in that case, would not the augment *aṭ* alone necessarily occur first because of its priority? To this he says: "The attainment of another form" (*śabdāntaraprāpti*), and so forth. But how is there the attainment of another form? To this he says: "For when [the augment] has been applied," and so forth. [This refers to] the augment *aṭ* of the base (*aṅga*).

It is prescribed [by Pāṇini 6.4.71]; and since that rule would apply once the *vikaraṇa* has been added because it includes "that which begins with it" (*tadādi*), the *num* augment occurs when the stem (*aṅga*) ends in a *vikaraṇa*. However, when it has not yet been added, the stem consists of the root alone. Furthermore, the root alone is the stem as opposed to the stem ending in a *vikaraṇa*; therefore, once [the *num*] has been applied, it would follow for the other case.

But in the case of another [element] being unapplied, the attainment of a different word-form is indeed evident; regarding this, it might be argued that the impermanence of the *vikaraṇa* (verbal suffix) also follows precisely from its being a different word-form. For instance, when that [suffix] has been applied, the root beginning with that [suffix] must undergo the addition of *aṭ*; [whereas] when it has not been applied...

Regarding the phrase "from the mere root" (*dhātumātrāt*), he says: "and of another word" (*śabdāntarasya ca*), and so forth. Although the modification (*vikāra*) of the augment *aṭ* occurs from another word only in its two states—whether already applied or not yet applied—nevertheless, its non-eternality (*anityatva*) is not established; for [the rule] applies to another word...

"For a rule is non-eternal" (Vyāḍipañjikā 100)—this indeed is the established principle of the science [of grammar]; it is not the case that "a rule is non-eternal when it applies due to another word. Furthermore, an affix (*vikaraṇa*) is not prescribed as either an augment (*āgama*) or a substitute (*ādeśa*) for any particular word, such that [the rule would apply] to another word.

If [the suffix] were obtained [only optionally], the rule would be non-eternal (anitya). For instance, when a sārvadhātuka suffix follows, a suffix is prescribed after the verbal root, but neither an augment (āgama) nor a substitute (ādeśa) is prescribed for it;
how, then, could there be any non-eternality regarding the vikaraṇa?
[Objection: "In that case, once the verbal suffix (vikaraṇa) has been applied, will the augment āṬ not occur before the semivowel-vocalization (samprasāraṇa)?

To this he says: "When the suffix has been applied, the vocalization [occurs]," and so forth. The constancy (nityatva) of the vocalization is as before, because it applies whether [the suffix] has been applied or not; however, the augment āṬ...
Once the *samprasāraṇa* has taken place, [the augment] *āṬ* would apply; for once the *samprasāraṇa* has occurred, because the root begins with a vowel (*aj-ādi*), the augment *āṬ* must occur.
Thus, this introduction of the augment *āṬ* is not constant (*anitya*).

73. *Chandasy api dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 6.4.73). [The rule] "it occurs elsewhere than where it is prescribed by *yataḥ*" applies here as well because of the word *api*. [The example is] *āvaḥ*. When the *guṇa* substitution and the replacement of the vowel with *r* (*raparatva*) have been performed, the suffix *tiP* is elided by *halṅyādi* (Pāṇini 6.1.68).

There is elision; the *repha* becomes a *visarjanīya*. Regarding "in the same way" (*tathā*) and so forth: just as [the form] *āvaḥ* arises when the *liṭ* suffix is elided by [the rule] *mantre ghasahvara-* (Pāṇini 2.4.80), so too, when the *liṭ* suffix is elided, [the form] *naśi* arises from the root *naś*. In that case, [the rule] *naśervā* (8.2.63) applies.
Regarding the substitution of *k* for *g*: in the case of "āyunak," from the root *yujir* (meaning "to join," DhP 1444), the suffix *śnam* is applied because it belongs to the *rudhādi* class;

then, by the rule "the *c* and *j* sounds become *k*" (8.2.30), there is the substitution of *k* (i.e., *ga* becomes *ka*), and by the rule of *cartva* (the substitution of *ca* for *ja*), that becomes *ka*. This is according to the rule "frequently in the Veda, even when not preceded by *ām*" (6.4.75).
He will say: this is an elaboration of that very same point.

74. *na māṅyoge* (Pāṇini 6.4.74). Since there is the metarule: "A rule applies either to what immediately precedes or to what immediately follows" (*vyā.pa.* 19), someone might mistakenly think that this prohibition (of *āṭ*) applies only to *āṭ*. Therefore, [the author] addresses that [misconception].

To refute this, he says: "When used in conjunction with the prohibitive particle *māṅ*, that which was prescribed for the suffixes *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *lṛṅ* does not take place. This demonstrates that the prohibition applies to both *aṭ* and *āṭ*.
Both of these are indeed prescribed for *lṛṅ*, *laṅ*, and *lṛṅ*. But how is it that there is a prohibition of both?

Is it obtained? Yes, because of its recurrence here [in this rule]. Nor does the fault arise that when that [augment] is recurring, the augment *aṭ* would not apply even to roots beginning with a vowel;
for the augment *aṭ* recurs here by the maxim of the frog’s leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*). Or rather, by means of a separation of the sūtra (*yogavibhāga*), this [augment *aṭ*] also [is included].

It is determined that this is a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*); for if the prohibition were intended to apply only to *āṭ*, then one would have composed only a single rule: "āṭ-ajādīnāṃ na māṅyoge" [āṭ and the augment of vowels beginning with 'a' do not occur when *māṅ* is joined]. Alternatively, only the phrase "luṅ-laṅ-lṛṅkṣu" (Pāṇini 6.4.71) is carried over [from the previous rule], and by that—

It is not understood that there is a prohibition of everything stated regarding the *luṅ* and other [tenses]; nor does such an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) occur, because a prohibition is obtained only for that operation which is prescribed by a subsequent rule within this very section on *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *lṛṅ*,
and not for everything.
[This prohibition applies] to that which is prescribed in another context; however, in this present context, only *aṭ* and *āṭ* are prescribed, therefore the prohibition applies only to those two.
[In the example] "mā bhavān kārṣīt," the *luṅ* suffix is applied by the rule "māṅ luṅ" (Pāṇini 3.3.175). "Mā..."

[The form] *sma karot* [is derived] by the rule *smotare laṅ ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.117), which prescribes the *laṅ* [augment]. The inclusion of the letter *ṅ* as an *anubandha* in the term *māṅ* is for the purpose of ensuring that the substitute *mā* [of the imperative] is not included; otherwise, [in a case such as] *bhavān sukhinaṃ...* [the rule would incorrectly apply].

Some maintain that there should also be a prohibition [of the augment] in the case of *mātrākāṣaṃt*. However, this is incorrect; for it is improper to claim that our substitute (*asmad-ādeśa*) is not included simply because it is derived from a technical rule (*lākṣaṇikatva*). Indeed, these two words, *aṅ* and *mā*, exist as particles (*nipāta*), as in "mā bālipathamanvagāḥ" (Do not follow the path of Bāli) and "mā bhavatu tasya... (May it not be his...).

The inclusion of the term "marked by ṅ" (ṅit) is for the purpose that the prohibition should not apply when the word *pāpam* is used as a separate utterance (*prayoga*). The mention of "in connection with" (*yoga*), however, is so that the prohibition may apply even in the case of mere conjunction; therefore, it also occurs even when there is an intervening element.

75. "In the Vedic language (*chandas*), [the augment] is optional (*bahulam*) even when not joined with *māṅ*. By this rule, he explains the meaning of the phrase "even when joined with *māṅ*. And here, in both sentences, [the word] "optionally" (*bahulam*)...

The word "in Vedic" (*cchandasi*) is connected [to this rule]. Since the desired result would already be established by the rule "frequently in Vedic" (*bahulaṃ cchandasi*) alone, the statement "even when used with *mā*" (*amāṅyoge 'pi*) is for the sake of clarity. For if this were not stated, since the connection with *mā* (*māṅyoga*) is the subject under discussion, it would follow that the augment *aṭ* and *āṭ* do not occur frequently in Vedic only in that specific context [of *mā*].
One might raise this objection: [in the form] *janiṣṭhāḥ*, there is the root *jan* with the suffix *luṅ*, the suffix *thās*, the augment *iṭ*, and the substitution of *ṣ* and *ṣṭu*.

[In the forms] *ūnayīt* and *ardayīt*, [the roots] *ūn* in the sense of "diminishing" (*parihāṇe*) and *ard* in the sense of "injuring" (*hiṃsāyām*) belong to the *curādi* class; [the lengthening occurs] by the rule *hy-anta-kṣaṇa-* (Pāṇini 7.2.5).

The prohibition of *vṛddhi* [occurs]. By the rule *ṭhiṭa īṭi* (Pāṇini 8.2.28), there is the elision of *sic*, and [the application of] *guṇa* and *ay-ādeśa*. [The form] *avāpsuḥ*: [the root] *āplu* in the sense of "pervasion" (Dhātupāṭha 1260) preceded by *ava*.
By the rule *sijabhyastavidibhyaśca* (3.4.109), there is the substitution of *jus* for *jhi*. *mā abhitthāḥ*.
Thus: from the root *bhid*, [the form] *abhitsāt* is derived; the elision of *sic* occurs by the rule "jhalo jhali" (Pāṇini 8.2.26). As for "mā'vaḥ," it has already been explained previously.

76. *irayo re* (Pāṇini 6.4.76). [The example is] *dadhre*. This is from the root *dhā* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*); by [the rule] *liṭas tajhayor eś irec* (3.4.81), *irec* is substituted. By this [present rule], *ray* is substituted for that [suffix], and then by *āto lopaḥ* (6.4.64), the *ā* is elided.

Thus there is the elision of the vowel *ā*. Regarding the form "paridadṛśre": after the prefix *pari* and the root *dṛś*, the rule for the elision of the initial *ā* (from *liṭ* etc. must be applied. Now, how is there the elision of the *ā* in "dadhre"? For in that case, the elision of the *ā* occurs while the form stands as "dhā-ā-hre."

[The question is: Does [the elision of *ā*] not apply there because of the substitution of *re* (*rebhāva*)? Since that [substitution] takes effect by virtue of being subsequent, once *re* has been substituted, the elision of *ā* does not apply because the [stem] no longer begins with a vowel (*anaj-āditvāt*). Therefore, he says:

"Because the substitution of *re* for *dhāñ* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*)," and so forth. Its non-existence, however, is established by the rule: "In this context, what follows is treated as non-existent (*asiddhavat*)."

By this [rule], the form *cakrire* is derived from the root *kṛ*. Now, one might object: since the substitution of *re* has been applied, those roots beginning with *dṛś* which take the suffix *liṭ* along with the augment *iṭ*, and because they belong to the *krādi* group, the substitute *ra* would be followed by *iṭ*. To this, [the author replies]: "When *iṭ* has been applied... [and so forth].

The form *dadṛśre* would not be established; rather, it ought to take the form *dadṛśire*, and so forth. Nor can it be argued that the augment *iṭ* will not occur by virtue of the power of the rule prescribing *rebhāva* (the substitution of *ra* for the reduplication);
for *rebhāva* finds its application in the case of roots beginning with *krī* (the *krī-ādi* group), since [the augment *iṭ*] follows those [roots].

Is there a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *liṭi kṛsṛ* (Pāṇini 7.2.13)? To this he says: "In this case," and so forth. But how is the substitution of *re* obtained? To this he says: "And for that purpose," and so forth; [the mention of] *ir* is for the sake of ensuring that the substitution of *re* occurs even when *iṭ* has been applied.

By forming a collective singular compound (*ekaśeṣa*) as *irec-*, the dual form *irayoḥ* is used for the reference. Consequently, the substitution of *r* is established not only for the word *irec* which is formed in place of *jha*, but also for the word *ire* which subsequently arises after the augment *iṭ* has been applied to *er*. Thus, the change to *r* is accomplished for both.
77. *aci śnudhātubhruvāṃ vyoriyaRuvaṅai* (Pāṇini 6.4.77).
The phrase *ārdhadhātuke* has ceased to apply. Why? Because of the indications in the rules *samaḥ kṣṇuvaḥ* (1.3.65) and *kṣiyaḥ* (6.4.59). This [rule] refers to the short *i*-vowels and *u*-vowels.

Why is this so? Because of that very specification. In this context, when the short vowel *a* is being taken, it causes its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*) to be included; thus, when two short vowels are being taken, they also cause the long vowels to be included.
Consequently, [the suffixes] also apply to that which ends in them. In the rule "in *aci*," there is the mention of a specific phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*). There...

Regarding the rule "In a case where a grammatical operation is prescribed, it is understood to apply to that which begins with [the element specified], provided there is no mention of 'a' or 'ā'" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 127), he says "in a suffix beginning with a vowel" (*ajādau pratyaye*) so that it may be understood as applying to a suffix beginning with *a* or *ā*. This term "suffix" (*pratyaya*) is obtained from the word *kṛt*, because of the governing context (*adhikāra*) of the "stem" (*aṅga*). For there is indeed an governing context of the stem, since it has been brought into proximity by the preceding rules.

For the designation *aṅga* (base) is prescribed only with respect to what follows a suffix (*pratyaya*). If [the rule] "when a suffix beginning with a vowel follows, *iy*, *u*, and *vaṅ* occur" were applied, then [the forms] *niyau* and *luvau* would not be obtained. For in this case, the suffix is simply a vowel (*ac*), and not something that begins with a vowel (*aj-ādi*). Here too, by the principle of "treating as if possessing the designation" (*vyapadeśivad-bhāva*), the status of "beginning with a vowel" does not exist; thus there is no fault.

Regarding the rule "ṭhivarṇovarṇāntasya": this is a qualification of the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone, and not of the other two [the suffix and the augment], because there is no deviation [in their case] and because it is impossible [for them to have such an ending]. Furthermore, the fact that the stem (*aṅga*) ends in an *i*-vowel or *u*-vowel is obtained by qualifying it with those two [suffixes]. The mention of *iy*, *uv*, and *eṅ* is for the purpose of establishing them as final substitutes (*antādeśa*). If [this were not stated]...

In this case, because there are multiple [substitutes], both operations would apply to every part of the word. But surely, by the rule "substitutes take the place of that which is specifically indicated" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 106), even without the letter *ṅ*, the two operations would apply only to the final element? If so, then the *ṅ* is for the sake of clarity. [The forms] attain [the desired results].

[They] obtain [it]. [The roots] *āplu* (DhP 1260, meaning "to pervade") and *rādha*, *sādha* (DhP 1262, 1263, meaning "to succeed") take the suffix *śnu* because they belong to the *svādi* group. For what purpose is the inclusion of the letter *ś* [in the rule]?

[It is to prevent the application of the suffix] *nu* [after *dā* and *bhā*], as in *dānuḥ* and *bhānuḥ*, according to the rule *dabhābhyāṃ nuḥ* (Daiva Uṇādi Sūtra 1.143). Otherwise, it would apply there as well.
‘bhūt’, ‘cikṣiyatuḥ’, ‘cikṣiyuḥ’— these are forms of any one of the three roots *kṣi*. ‘niyau’, ‘niyaḥ’, ‘luvau’, ‘luvaḥ’— here,
by the rule “bases ending in *kvip* do not abandon their status as verbal roots” (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 132), they retain their status as roots.
It should be understood as follows: in that context, the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *nī-* by the rule "satyūdviṣa...
(Pāṇini 3.2.61), whereas for the root *lū-*, it is applied by the rule "anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate" (Pāṇini 3.2.178).
Regarding the forms beginning with *iy-uvaṅbhyām*, the scope for *guṇa* substitution is, for example, in the form *cetavyam*.

Regarding "stotavyam" and so forth: in the case of *iṅ* and *vaṅ*, we have *cikṣiyatuḥ*, *cikṣiyuḥ*, *luluvatuḥ*, and *luluvuḥ*; here both [rules] would apply—namely, the substitution of *ī* and *ū* (as in *cayanam* and *lavanam*).
By the principle of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), only the *guṇa* substitution takes place. The scope for *vṛddhi* is, for example, *sakhāyau* and *sakhāyaḥ*.

In the case of *gāvau* and *gāvaḥ*, the same [rule] applies to *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*. Here, both [rules] would apply: in *cāyakaḥ* and *lāvakaḥ*. By way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), only the *vṛddhi* substitution takes place.
This is stated in the section beginning with "in the context of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*" and so forth. The meaning of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is "presentation" (or "addition").

In this regard, the following is the demonstration: the term *bahulam* ("optionally") is carried over from the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.4.75). By that means, for words such as *tanu*, the substitutions *iy* and *uvaṅ* will occur optionally in the Vedic language (*chandas*). Thus, we have the form *tanvam*, where *uvaṅ* does not occur.

In that case, there is no such thing as "having another word preceding it," precisely because of the plural expression [in the rule]. [Examples include] *vidhvam* and *viṣuvam*. [The form] *svargaḥ* / *suvargaḥ* [is derived] from the root *sū* with the suffix *kvip*; the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *upasargāt sunoti* (Pāṇini 8.3.65) and so forth. [The form] *svargaḥ* / *suvargaḥ* [is derived] from the word *su* followed by the word *arga*.
The substitution of *uvaṅ* occurs in place of [the final vowel of the stem] when followed by another [vowel]. And this rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *yaṇ*.
78. *abhyāsasyāsavarṇe* (Pāṇini 6.4.78). Examples:

*ṭhiyeṣa*, *uvoṣa*. From the roots *ṭhiṣu* "to desire" (DhP 1351) [the form *ṭhiṣa* in the DhP] and *ṭhuṣa* "to burn" (DhP 696), the suffix *liṭ* is applied, followed by *ṇal*. In these cases, reduplication (*dvirvacana*) occurs.

The *guṇa* substitution [of *o* for *au*] applies by the rule "ṭhpugantalaghūpadhasya ca" (Pāṇini 7.3.86). Since the *guṇa* is subsequent [in the order of rules], it takes precedence; thus, when *eṣa* and *oṣa* have been established, the reduplication of the two syllables *iṣu* and *iṣ* occurs by the rule "dvirvacane'ci" (Pāṇini 1.1.59), which treats the substitute as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). Thereafter, the *iyaṅ* and *vaṅ* substitutions apply. Now, one might object:

And since those two [operations] are to be performed, would there not be a lack of homogeneous status (*savarṇatā*) due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* according to Pāṇini 1.1.57, "When a rule applies to what precedes a substitute, that substitute behaves like the original"? This is not so; for the status of *sthānivadbhāva* must apply only when an operation is to be performed concerning that which precedes the vowel (*ac*) from which no substitution has been prescribed.
And since this [portion] preceding the *ac* is the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) as prescribed here, why would there be the status of being "as if in the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) in this case?
[In the form] *iyarti*: from the root *ṛ* "to go" (DhP 1098), there is *ślu* for the *śap* due to its belonging to the *juhotyādi* class;
then by *urat* (7.4.66), the vowel *u* of the reduplication becomes *a*, and by *artipipartyośca* (7.4.77).
Thus, there is the substitution of *ī*, and from that, the substitution of *iyaṅ*.

[The forms] are "īyatuḥ" and "īyuḥ," and "ūvatuḥ" and "ūvuḥ. According to the rule "the *liṭ* [affixes] following a non-conjunct consonant are *kit*" (Pāṇini 1.2.5), because they are *kit*, there is an absence of *guṇa*; consequently, the vowel remains homogeneous (*savarṇa*).

In *ṭhiyāja* and *ṭhuvāpa*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the reduplicated syllable of the roots *yaj* and *vap* according to Pāṇini 6.1.17: "In both [groups of roots], the reduplicated syllable of the perfect tense (*liṭ*) undergoes vocalization."

79. *striyāḥ* | (6.4.79). Regarding the term *striyāḥ*: because of the indications in *āṇnadyāḥ* (7.3.112) and *jāterastrīviṣayādayopadhāt* (4.1.63), this is not a reference to feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*), nor...

Having determined that the word [is used] for the sake of the feminine gender, he says "of this word *strī*" and so forth, in order to show that the word *strī* itself is what is being grasped by its own form. The particle *iti* indicates that the word *strī* has its own form as its referent (*padārtha*). Now, why is it not [used] in the genitive plural?

He says "it occurs" with the words beginning with "of women" (strīṇām). Because of its priority, the augment *nuṭ* must apply in the genitive plural; and when that [augment] is present, since the subsequent suffix beginning with *aj* does not follow, the substitution *iyaṅ* does not take effect.

Now, for what purpose is a separate rule (*pṛthag-yoga*) formulated? Why not simply formulate a single rule as *ṭh aci śnudhātustrībhruvām*? To this he says: "The formulation of a separate rule," and so forth.
[This is done] so that in the rule *vā am-śasoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.80), the option applies only to the word *strī*.
The separate formulation of this rule is for the purpose that [the substitution] of *dhātu* should not occur in place of *bhrū*.

*iṇo yaṇ* | (6.4.81) Here, two alternatives are possible: either the term *iṇaḥ* might be a reference (*grahaṇa*) to a pratyāhāra [denoting the vowels *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *lṛ*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, *au*], or...

Or is it a reference to the verbal root (*dhātu*)? In this regard, because of specific grammatical indications such as *ṭherac* (Pāṇini 3.3.56), *ṭhorāvaśyake* (3.1.125), and *ṭhurat* (7.4.66), this cannot be understood as a reference to a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated term). Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣya*), this is understood to be a reference to the verbal root alone.

The utterance of the letter *ṇ* is for the purpose of excluding *iṅ*. However, for those who desire a general extension (*atideśa*) according to the rule "like *ṭhiṇ*, so [the roots] beginning with *adik*" (Vārttika 167), it is for the purpose of excluding *iṅ* alone. But in the case of *ik*, as in *adhiyanti*, there must indeed be the substitution of *yaṇ*. Now, if [the rule were stated] simply as "not after *ṇa*" (*neṇaḥ*), [then the following would apply].

Why was it not stated that, since the substitution of *iyan* and *adan* is prohibited before a vowel (*ac*), the *yaṇ* substitution would occur by [Pāṇini 6.1.77] *iko yaṇ aci*? This is true; however, the mention of *yaṇ* is for the sake of subsequent rules.
In the examples beginning with *yanti*, there is elision of the suffix *śap* because the root belongs to the *adādi* class. *Āyan* is the imperfect (*laṅ*).

When *jha* is substituted for the final [consonant], there is the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*); because that [elision] is considered non-existent (*asiddhatva*), the augment *āṭ* does not apply since the suffix begins with a vowel (*ajāditva*). Now, why does this [augment] not occur here in the words *ayanam* and *āyakaḥ*? To this he says: "This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *iyaṅ*. But surely, just as [the rule for] *iyaiṅ*...

This [rule] is commenced because it applies; likewise, it applies to both *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. Therefore, how is it understood that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to *iyaṅ* and not to *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*? He says: "Exceptions [occur] in the middle," and so forth. The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason.

Since it is a rule of Pāṇini’s grammar that "exceptions in the middle set aside preceding rules, but not subsequent ones" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 10), this *iyaṅ* substitution is therefore an exception to the preceding rule,
and not to the subsequent rules for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*; and because this is so, [the forms are derived] by means of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*.
It is superseded because it occurs later. Its scope is: *yanti*, *yantv* (where the rule for *yaṇ* applies).
Regarding *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*: in *cayanam* and *cāyakaḥ*, and in *ayanam* and *āyakaḥ*, both [rules] would apply. Because it occurs later, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* take effect, superseding *yaṇ*.
82. *eranekāco'saṃyogapūrvasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.82). [The commentary states:

"By this, *saṃyoga* (conjunction) is qualified. Now, one might object: since *saṃyoga* is subordinate (*upasarjana*) here because it has become a secondary element within the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*), and a subordinate element cannot be qualified by an adjective...

It experiences a connection. For instance, when it is said, "a beautiful king's man" (*śobhano rājapuruṣaḥ*), the connection with "beauty" is understood to belong to the man, who is the principal element, and not to the king, who is the subordinate element (*upasarjana*).
This is not so; for by the force of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule [from the previous sūtra] "of the verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*), the subordinate element is also [included].

It will experience the connection by means of the qualification "dhātu" (verbal root); otherwise, the recurrence of the term "dhātu" would be purposeless. But could it not be that the mention of "dhātu" is recurrent here for the sake of qualifying the vowel *i*? This is not so; [for] that which ends in the vowel *i* but is not a verbal root—

For in that case, the substitution of *yaṇ* must necessarily occur by the rule "ṭhiko yaṇaci" (Pāṇini 6.1.77), as in the forms "ninyatuḥ" and "ninyuḥ," which are derived from the root *nī* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*). When the substitution of *iyaṅ* would otherwise apply, the substitution of *yaṇ* takes its place.
Similarly, in the forms "unnyaḥ" and "unnyaḥ," [the suffix] *kvip* is applied to the root *unnī* by the rule "satsūdviṣa... (Pāṇini 3.1.61).
The suffix *kvip* [is applied] in this way; likewise in "grāmaṇyau" and "grāmaṇyaḥ. [In these cases,] the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule "agragrāmābhyāṃ ca" (Vārttika).
[This is subject to] the condition "not preceded by a conjunct consonant," and so forth. If [the word] "eḥ" were not stated [in the rule],...

In that case, the qualification "not preceded by a conjunct consonant" (asaṃyogapūrva) would apply to the *aṅga* (stem), and consequently, it would also apply in forms such as *yavakriyau* and *yavakriyaḥ*, because here too the *aṅga* is not preceded by a conjunct consonant.
Therefore, it is stated: "of [the *aṅga* ending in] *ṭhi*" (*ṭheḥ*). The mention of "not preceded by a conjunct consonant" (asaṃyogapūrva) is instead a qualification of the *ikāra* (the vowel *i*).

This is for the purpose that it should apply to a member [of a compound] and not otherwise. Now, since "of *y* and *v*" (*hyvoḥ*) is the subject under discussion, if "of *e*" (*er*) were not stated there, it would also apply to that which ends in the vowel *u*;
consequently, forms such as *luluvatuḥ* and *luluvuḥ* would not be established. Therefore, it applies to that which ends in the vowel *u*.

Lest it be thought that [the rule] *er-i* should exist for this very purpose, he says: "luluvatuḥ," "luluvuḥ," and so forth. If only *er-ī* were stated here, then since the substitution for the vowel *u* would already be established by this very [rule], the rule *oḥ supi* (Pāṇini 6.4.83) would serve as a restrictive rule (*niyama*)—namely, that [the substitution occurs] only if [the word] ends in a vowel of the *u*-class (*uvarṇa*).
[The rule applies] only to *su*, not to anything else. Consequently, by this very restriction, forms such as *luluvatuḥ* and *luluvuḥ* are established;
therefore, the purpose [of the rule] as "to exclude those ending in the vowel *u*" is untenable. Thus, the previously stated purpose alone is appropriate for it. [Examples: *yavakriyau*.

Regarding the example *yavakrīyaḥ*: [the word *yavakrī*] is derived from *yavān krīṇāti* ("he buys barley") with the suffix *kvip*, according to the rule *ṭhaneyabhyo 'pi dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 3.2.187). In this case, the substitution of *ī* for the vowel *i* does not occur because the *i* is preceded by a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*) that is part of the verbal root (*dhātu*). The phrase "it would also not occur here" implies the condition that the connection (*saṃyoga*) must not be qualified by being part of the verbal root. If it were not so specified, the rule would apply even when the preceding consonant cluster belongs to an affix. Thus, the point is that the restriction to the verbal root is necessary for the rule to function as intended.

In some places here, the reading is "yathā syāt" (so that it may be). In that case, because of the context, it is understood as referring to the *yaṇ* substitution. If the connection with a verbal root (*dhātu*) were not specified, then the *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) preceding [the vowel] would be either a part of a verbal root or not a part of a verbal root.

It is understood that [the rule] does not apply to that which ends in *tad*. Consequently, it would not occur even in cases such as *unnyau* and *unnyah*, because the vowel *i* is preceded by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*). However, when the term "consonant" (*dhātu*) is specified [as part of the condition], then it does occur. For here, the vowel *i* is not preceded by a conjunct consonant that is a constituent of a verbal root (*dhātu*). Therefore, in this case as well, just as...

It might be argued that the connection with the verbal root (*dhātu*) would be qualified by [the rule] "by a motion (*gati*) or a case-factor (*kāraka*)," and so forth. Now, why is this not desired even though it is intended? Because of the inclusion of the word "prior" (*pūrva*). In this context, the inclusion of the word "prior" need not be made.

One might simply say: "ṭheranekācaḥ asaṃyogāt. In that case, when it is understood that "yaṇ substitution occurs for the final vowel of a stem (aṅga) which is preceded by a conjunct consonant (saṃyoga) belonging to the root, provided that the vowel *i* or *u* does not follow such a conjunct," the desired result would indeed be established. Why, then, is the mention of "pūrva" (preceding) included? It is included for the following reason: [The rule is formulated as it is] so that [the substitution applies] even in cases like *cikīrṣakaḥ*, where the *i* is not immediately followed by a conjunct belonging to the root, but rather follows a conjunct that belongs to the desiderative suffix (*san*). Otherwise, since the *i* here is followed by a conjunct (*k-r-ṣ*), the rule would not apply. By including "pūrva," it is indicated that the restriction regarding the preceding element is based on the position of the *i* relative to the *saṃyoga*, and thus the rule successfully applies to forms like *cikīrṣakaḥ*. Therefore, the mention of "pūrva" is made.

By the earlier teachers (pūrvācāryas)—this is for the purpose of indicating the meaning that "this *yaṇ* substitution is to be applied only for that [base] for which it is prescribed, and not for any other. And the earlier teachers have established this rule only for a *kvip*-derived form preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*, and not for any other; therefore, here too—

The [suffix] *na* is not applied to that which is preceded by something other than a *gati* or a *kāraka*. Alternatively, from the rule "vāmśasoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.80), the word "vā" is understood to carry over by the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*); and this is understood as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Consequently, [the suffix is not applied] to that which is preceded by something other than a *gati* or a *kāraka*.

[It] will be so. And in this explanation, the inclusion of the word *pūrva* should be understood for the sake of clarity. In the example "paramaniyau," the compound is formed by [the rule] *sanmahatparamottamotkṛṣṭāḥ pūjāyām* (Pāṇini 2.1.61). Here, the word *parama* is neither a *gati* nor a *kāraka*; therefore, it does not [cause the elision of the case-ending] of the preceding [word].
It comes to be.

83. *oḥ supi* (6.4.83). Regarding the example *khalapvau*: [the word] *khala* is derived from the sense "he cleanses the threshing floor" (*khalaṃ punāti*) by means of the suffix *kvip*, according to the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate* (3.2.178).
Regarding *śatasvau*: here too, [the word] *sūtra* is derived from the sense "one who possesses a hundred threads" (*śataṃ sūtrāṇi*), according to the rule *satsūdviṣa-* (3.1.61).

By the rule *kvip* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.76), [the suffix *kvip* is applied]. Regarding *sakṛllvau*: by the rule *tor li* (8.4.60), there is a substitution of the following sound (*parasavarṇa*). Regarding *kaṭapruvau*: from the root *prūṅ* "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 957)—[the Dhātupāṭha reads *pruṅ*]—by the rule *kvibvacipracchiśridrusrubhyo dīrghaśca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.178).

The suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule "dīrgho'samprasāraṇañca," and there is also lengthening [of the vowel]. The mention of *ṭhaḥ* is for the sake of clarity; however, it is not suitable for the purpose of excluding forms ending in the letter *n*, because the term *hyvoḥ* continues to apply from the previous rule. Furthermore, the *yaṇ*-substitution for the vowel *i* is already established by the preceding rule—as in *unnyaḥ*.
"The two village chiefs," so it is said.

84. *Varṣābhvaśca* (6.4.84). This rule is commenced as an exception (*apavāda*) to the prohibition [of the substitution of *u* for *o*] established by *na bhūsudhiyoḥ* (6.4.85). The form *varṣābhvau* is derived from the word *varṣā* with the suffix *bhū*.
Regarding the *kvip* suffix:

[it is stated] "it should be stated that *punarbhū* [is also included]. This means that it must be explained as having the sense: "for the word *apunarbhū*, when followed by a vowel-initial case ending (*sup*), the *yaṇ* substitution occurs. In this regard, the following...
