The explanation: the letter *ca* is employed here, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.

By means of it, the rule will also apply to the word *punarbhū*. Regarding the statement "it is also desired for that which is preceded by the letter *k*," it should be understood that this too occurs by virtue of that very same *ca*.

85. *na bhūsudhiyoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.85). By the mention of *bhrū*, that which ends in *bhrū* is understood, not the word *bhrū* alone; for if it were the word alone, the rule would be meaningless, as it is impossible for a single-vowel (*ekāc*) word to undergo the substitution of *yaṇ*.
If it is argued that [the rule] is not purposeless because its purpose is to prohibit the substitution of *uvaṅ*, we say no;
for in that case, the prescription of the *yaṇ* substitution in the rule "varṣābhvaśca" (Pāṇini 6.4.84) would be purposeless.
Indeed, that [prescription] becomes meaningful only if this [present rule] were a prohibition of the *yaṇ* substitution.

Is it not otherwise? This is not so; for even if this [rule] were intended to prohibit the substitution of *uvaṅ*, it would still serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) regarding that very substitution.
If that is the case, then this prohibition is properly applicable only to that which follows from the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of *yaṇ*;
and since that [substitution of *yaṇ*] is prescribed for polysyllabic bases (*anekāc*), the application of the rule to a monosyllabic base alone does not occur.

What was stated is correct—that by the mention of *bhū*, that which ends in it is also included—as in "the two sureties" (*pratibhuvau*) and "the sureties" (*pratibhuvaḥ*). [The suffix] *kvip* is applied here by the rule *bhuvaḥ saṃjñāntarayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.179).
[In the case of] "the two wise ones" (*sudhiyau*), [the suffix] *kvip* is applied after the root *dhyai* in the sense of "he meditates beautifully," according to the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*.

Thus, by [Pāṇini 3.2.178], the suffix *kvip* is applied; and because of the supplementary rule (vārttika 292), "There is also vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) for the root *dhyai*," vocalization takes place.
86. In the Vedic language, [the substitution of *u* for *ū*] occurs in both ways.
(6.4.86) 87. [The substitution of *u* for *ū* occurs] before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix that begins with *hu* or *śnu*.
(6.4.87) [This applies] by virtue of the rules: "before *yaṇ*" (6.4.81), "of that which has more than one vowel and is not preceded by a conjunct consonant" (6.4.82), and "of *o*" (6.4.83).
The two [terms] "ṭh" and "hu" continue to apply [from the previous rule]. Now, one might object:

since the base (aṅga) ending in the suffix *śnu*, namely *hu*, never deviates from having an *u* at its end, for what purpose is "of *u*" (*oḥ*) continued here? [The answer is: it is for the sake of the mention of "not preceded by a conjunct consonant" (*asaṃyogapūrva*) regarding the *u*.

The purpose [of the genitive case] is so that it may serve as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); otherwise, this would be understood as a qualifier of *hu* and *śnu* alone. Consequently, the prohibition would be understood to apply only to cases such as *takṣṇuvanti*, whereas in cases such as *rādhnuvanti*, [it would not].

The substitution of *yaṇ* would indeed occur. Even in the case of *√hu*, in the form *juhvati*, the *yaṇ* substitution would not take place because of the presence of a *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) preceding [the vowel]. Now, an objection is raised: the term *dhātu* (verbal root) is understood as being carried over [from a previous rule]; therefore, it should be understood thus: "a *saṃyoga* that precedes [the vowel] is a part of the verbal root"—[this applies even to] those ending in *kvip*, which possess the status of a verbal root.

This is because of the rule *na jahati* (Vyāḍipāṭha 132). Otherwise, even if the word "member" (*avayava*) were stated, by relying on the word "preceding" (*pūrva*), it would be understood thus: "that whose preceding [consonant] is not a conjunction that is a member of the verbal root. Even so, in the case of *rādhnuvanti*, there would still be the substitution of *yaṇ*; for here...

The *śnu* affix has a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*) preceding it as part of the verbal root. Therefore, the term "ṭh" must be understood as continuing [from the previous rule]; both *hu* and *śnu* serve as qualifiers for that.
In this context, the mention of "not preceded by a cluster" (*asaṃyogapūrva*) is a qualifier of the letter *u* which constitutes a part of the *śnu* affix.
It should be understood that [the rule] applies to the constituent part (*avayava*) of the verbal root *hu*; this is because of its non-deviation [from the condition].

Regarding the statement "of that which ends in the suffix *śnu* and is not preceded by a conjunct consonant," there are two genitives in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*). It refers to the vowel *u*, which is a constituent part of the stem ending in the suffix *śnu* and is not preceded by a conjunct consonant.

The meaning is "of that. It should be understood that the term "having more than one vowel" (*anekācaḥ*) is a coreferential qualifier (*samānādhikaraṇa*) for the root *juhoti* when it ends in the suffix *śnu*. The term "in a sārvadhātuka [affix]" (*sārvadhātuke*) is for the sake of the root *juhoti*, not for the sake of the form ending in the suffix *śnu*; this is because there is no deviation [in the application of the rule] for the former. [As in: *juhvati*.

Thus: [the substitution of] *at* by "ṭhadabhyastāt" (Pāṇini 7.1.4). [The examples are] *yoyuvati* and *roruvati*. From the roots *yu* and *ru*, the suffix *yaṅ* is applied; its elision (*luk*) occurs by "ṭhyaṅe'ci ca" (2.4.74);
the strengthening (*guṇa*) of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) occurs by "ṭhguṇo yaṅlukoḥ" (7.4.82); and the substitution of *av* for the imperative ending (*jhi*) is as before.
"Stability indeed," and so forth. But how is this an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? To this he says: "In Vedic usage (*chandas*)," and so forth.

If the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅ-luk*) occurred only in Vedic usage, then, because [the suffixes] would be treated as *ārdhadhātuka* by the rule "In Vedic usage, both ways" (*candasyubhayathā*, 6.4.86), there would not be [the substitution of *u* for *o*] in forms such as *yoyuvati* and *rorovati*.

If [the rule were restricted to Vedic], the mention of *hu* and *śnu* would be entirely purposeless. However, when the *yaṅ*-lopa occurs even in the common language (*bhāṣā*), then—because [the suffix] lacks the status of an *ārddhadhātuka*—the [substitution of *guṇa*] would undesirably apply in forms such as *yoyuvati* in the absence of the mention of *hu* and *śnu*.
Therefore, the mention of *hu* and *śnu* is justified for the purpose of preventing that [undesired application].

Therefore, this very [sūtra] makes it known that the *yaṅ-luk* (the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix) occurs even in the common language (*bhāṣā*). By means of this, forms such as *bebhidīti* and *ceccchidīti* become established even in the common language.
It might be argued: "What other [form] ending in *u* or *ṛ*, consisting of more than one syllable (*anekāc*), exists apart from those ending in *yaṅ-luk*?"
"Is this [rule] intended to prevent that [substitution] which occurs when preceded by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*)? This is not an indicator [of such a restriction], and therefore he says:
'And not,' etc. But surely this exists: *yuvan* and *aruvan*? This is not so; for although these are not preceded by a conjunct consonant, they consist of more than one vowel (*anekāc*)."
Because it is unestablished.
88. *bhuvo vug luṅ-liṭoḥ* | (6.4.88) [In the forms] *abhūvan* and *abhūvam*: by the rule *gāti-sthā-* (2.4.77), there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *sic*.

When the replacement of *jhi* with *an* has been made, the final consonant of the cluster is dropped (*saṃyogānta-lopa*). [In the form] *abhūvam*, [the substitution of] *tasthasthamipām tāmtamtāmaḥ* (3.4.101) applies.
By the rule (3.4.101), *mip* is replaced by *ām*, resulting in forms such as *babhūva*.

In *babhūva* and similar forms, the substitution of *a* for the reduplication is applied by the rule *bhavateraḥ* (7.4.73). Furthermore, because the rule *indhibhavatibhyāṃ ca* (1.2.6) prescribes that the *liṭ* suffix is *kit*, neither *guṇa* nor *vṛddhi* substitutions take place. But for what purpose is this [substitution] applied after the root *bhū*?

The *kit* status of the *liṭ* suffix is being introduced; however, since "that which is modified by the substitution of a single part is treated as non-different [from the original]" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 16), the augment *vuk* would apply both when the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions have already taken place and when they have not yet taken place. Regarding the *vuk*:

Since [the suffix] *kṛt* lacks an *iṅ* vowel, lacks a light penultimate vowel, and does not end in a vowel, there is no possibility of *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* substitutions; therefore, because the addition of *vuK* is obligatory (*nitya*) due to its application regardless of whether [the augment] has already occurred or not, once *vuK* is added, there is simply no occasion for *guṇa* or *vṛddhi*—so is the *kit* designation useless? This is not so.

The *vuk* suffix is also indeed non-eternal (*anitya*), for it does not apply once *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* have already taken effect; this is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.89], which implies that a stem ending in an *u*-vowel must undergo *vuk*.
In this case, between the two non-eternal operations, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* would prevail due to their subsequent position in the rules. Therefore—

What must be undertaken here? Why, then, does *or* continue to apply? It is for the purpose of preventing [the substitution] in *bobhū-a* and *bobhū-ati* once guna and vṛddhi have been applied. But surely, if *kit* status were present, there would not even be guna and vṛddhi here? This is not so; for it is not the case that...
The *liṭ* suffix following the root *bhū* when it is in its *yaṅluṅ* (intensive with *lopa*) form is *kit*,
because in the rule *indhibhavatibhyāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 1.2.6), the term *bhavati* is specified by means of the *śtip* affix.
89. *ūdupadhāyā gohaḥ* | (Pāṇini 6.4.89) In the example *nigūhayati*: the root is *guhū* (DhP 896) meaning "to conceal," with the causative suffix *ṇic* added because it denotes a motive (*hetumat*).

In the example *nigūhakaḥ*: the suffix *ṇvul* is applied. In the example *sādhunigūhi*: [the suffix *kvip* is applied] after a verbal root when preceded by a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*), provided that the following word is a genus-term (*jāti*).

The suffix *ṇini* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.78 (*ṇinistācchīlye*). Regarding the form *nigūhaṃ nigūham*: the suffix *ṇamul* is applied according to 3.4.22 (*ābhīkṣṇye ṇamul ca*), and reduplication occurs according to the Vārttika 887 (*ābhīkṣṇye dve bhavataḥ*). Regarding the form *nigūhaḥ*: the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*).
"Let there not be [the substitution] for another"—this is the intention regarding what follows later.
However, in this case, by carrying forward the word *uru* and even without the mention of *upadhā*, this very meaning can indeed be established;
having kept precisely this in mind, [the author says] "paraṃ... (furthermore...).

He asked: "What is the purpose of mentioning the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*)? Since the mention of the penultimate vowel is made for the sake of other rules, it also precludes the application of the rule regarding the final letter (*alo'ntyasya*) here. Therefore, because there is no further need, the term *or* does not carry over [from the previous rule].
Now, for what purpose is the irregular form "goha" used in the rule instead of simply saying "guha," since the rule would thus be more concise? To this he says:
"The mention of the modified form 'goha'... and so forth. This is so that the substitution of *ū* may have a specific scope.
The word "syāt" (it may be) is for this purpose: namely, that the form "go-h" is a mention of the modified form in which the vowel *u* has been substituted.

To clarify this very point, he says "yatra" (where), etc. Someone explains its meaning as follows: when the *guṇa* substitution has been made, [the form is] by virtue of the *ūtva* (substitution of *ū*).

It is observed that [the form] *bhavitavyam* should exist; however, this is incorrect. For if it were explained in this way, then after stating, "Some desire [the rule] 'nigūhya gataḥ' for the purpose of prohibiting the substitution of *th*," he will say: "Because the substitution of *u* (*utva*) is considered asiddha, [the rule] 'lyapi laghūpūrvāt' (Pāṇini 6.4.56) applies."

[The objection: "There should be the designation *ṇerat*," that is not tenable. If, having applied *guṇa*, the substitution of *u* for the vowel *o* were prescribed, then—since the *ū* would be *asiddha* (not yet established)—the condition of being preceded by a light vowel (*laghupūrva*) would indeed be satisfied because it is preceded by the vowel *o*; so how [could there be the designation *ṇerat*]?

If the vowel *ū* were unestablished (*asiddha*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the substitution of *ay*. Therefore, this is the meaning here: it should apply in that context where the form *goḍha* is possible for the root *guh*; that is, in whatever suffix a *guṇa* substitution might occur, it should apply as if the *guṇa* had not yet been performed.

"Let it not be otherwise. Therefore, since the mention of the modified form (*vikṛtanirdeśa*) is intended to indicate a specific domain, in the case of a *guṇa* substitute, the *guṇa* must indeed become *ū* while it is still present and has not yet been applied. And this being so, because [the substitution] of *ū* for *av* is not established (*asiddha*).

This and similar arguments in the *prasaṅga* section are appropriate, and not otherwise. But surely, when a suffix conditioned by a *guṇa* vowel arises, the *guṇa* itself must occur because of its higher status; so how could *ūtva* apply while the *guṇa* has not yet been performed?
[The answer is: because it applies whether [the other rule] has been performed or not (*kṛtākṛtaprasaṅgitvāt*). For that [rule for *ūtva*] applies even when the *guṇa* has been performed...

The substitution of *ū* occurs even when [the condition for] *guṇa* has not yet been applied, because the mention of the modified form (*vikṛta-nirdeśa*) is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of a specific domain. However, once *guṇa* has been applied, the substitution of *ū* does not apply, because the penultimate vowel is no longer light (*alaghūpadhatvāt*). Therefore, the substitution of *ū* must occur prior to *guṇa*.

It must be so because of its permanence; for this very reason, the long pronunciation is meaningful, and not otherwise. If this substitution were to occur after the *guṇa* had already been applied, the long pronunciation would be purposeless; [for] by the principle of closest proximity (*āntaratamya*), a long vowel would simply result from a long vowel.

It will be so; for it has been made known by the author of the *tapara* rule (*diva ut*, Pāṇini 6.1.131)—namely, that "even when being taught (*bhāvyamāna*), the vowel *u* includes its homogeneous counterparts" (Cāndra Paribhāṣā 44). If it is argued that the long vowel is pronounced for the purpose of excluding whatever else might otherwise apply?

It might be argued: "In the case of *ajugūhat*, the long vowel was pronounced for the purpose that the shortening rule *ṇau caṅyupadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.1) should not apply. But from what source does this restriction derive—that shortening must not occur here? For Kātyāyana has not [stated] this here.
There is neither a statement by the author of the Bhāṣya nor an usage by the learned (śiṣṭa) from which this certainty could arise;

for it is said, "according to the rule, [the form is used] when not employed [in common usage]. Therefore, it must be *ajūguhat*. If this substitution were made after the guṇa had already taken place, then...

What would be undesirable? The long vowel pronunciation would be purposeless. Could it be assumed that even here the long vowel pronunciation is for the sake of variety? Even so, there would be an excessive complexity in the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-gaurava*).
Therefore, by the force of the long vowel pronunciation, the *guṇa* [substitution] remains unapplied, and [the vowel] is [treated as] *ū*.
It must be so: "having hidden, he went. [The form] *ṇigūhya* is derived from the causative (*ṇi*-affix) with the suffix *ktvā*, followed by a *prādi* compound.

By the rule *samāso'nañpūrvaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.37), etc., the suffix *lyap* replaces *ktvā*. Regarding the phrase "because of the lack of mutual dependence there," etc., this serves to exclude the substitution of *ay* [for *e*].
He refutes the indication of a modification (*vikṛti*). But how is there a difference in substratum (*vyāśrayatva*)? He says: "In *ṇau*, [there is] ūtva," and so forth.
In the word *nigoḍhā*, the suffix *tṛc* is applied; then, by *ho ḍhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.31) and *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.40), the changes occur.

Thus there is the substitution of *ḍha*; then by "ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.41), there is the substitution of *ṣṭu* [for *ṣṭh*]; and by "ḍho ḍhea lopaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.13), there is the elision of the first *ḍha* when followed by *ḍha*.
90. *doṣo ṇau* | (Pāṇini 6.4.90) [The rule states: "In the case of *dīṣayati*. [The root is] *duṣa* in the sense of "becoming corrupted" (Dhātupāṭha 1185).
Now, for what purpose is the corrupted form *doṣaḥ* used in the rule instead of *duṣaḥ*?

If it is argued that this is stated for the purpose of specifying the scope [of the rule], we say no; because the scope is directly indicated by the word "ṇau" (in the causative). Therefore, he says: "The mention of the modified form," and so forth.
For in the preceding rule, "goṅḥ" was stated; here, if only "dūṣaḥ" were stated, [the rule would apply only to that specific form].

There would be a distinction in the commencement—that is, the undertaking—yet non-distinction is intended. Therefore, for that purpose, the modified form is mentioned. But why is non-distinction in the commencement desired? This question is asked too little; one should also inquire as to the purpose of the variety itself.
For this variety is simply a lack of sequential order; what, then, is the point of the labor of questioning it?

91. *nā citavirāge* (Pāṇini 6.4.91). This optional rule is introduced because the preceding [rule] would have made [the substitution] obligatory. "In *citavirāga*" means a state of displeasure of the mind (*citta*). "It causes the mind to be displeased" (*citaṃ doṣayati*) means that the mind is displeased and turned away.
The meaning is "he performs.
Why say "discoloration of the mind" (*cittavirāga*)? [Consider: "he refutes the proof"—here, by the preceding rule, it is always [the case].
Only when there is the suffix *ṇi*—as in "a fault of the mind" (*cittasya doṣaḥ*). Here, the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
92. *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.92).

Regarding the phrase "by *ṭhevamādinā*," the word *ādi* (and so forth) includes the inclusion of [roots] such as *janī-jṛṣ-knasa-urañjo'mantāśca* (Dhātupāṭha 817). Examples are: *ghaṭayati*, *vyathayati*, and *janayati*.

The roots are *ghaṭ* in the sense of "motion" (*ceṣṭā*) [DhP 7.63], *vyath* in the sense of "fear and trembling" (*bhayacalana*) [DhP 7.64], and *jan* in the sense of "manifestation" (*prādurbhāva*) [DhP 1.149]. Now, one might object that for the root *jan*, the rule *janivadhyośca* (Pāṇini 7.3.35) prohibits *vṛddhi*; therefore, this example is incorrect.
Is it not the case that [the prohibition] is meaningless? No, this is not so;
for that prohibition of *vṛddhi* applies specifically to the *ciṇ* and *kṛt* affixes, since the rule "ṭhāto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.33) is understood to apply there.
Regarding the form "rajayitā," [the Vārttika] states: "The addition of 'mṛgaramaṇe' must be included in the rule for the addition of *ṇi* after the root *rañj*" (Vārttika 778).

Thus, when the nasalization (*anunāsika*) has been elided, the rule *ṭhata upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116) prescribes a *vṛddhi* [vowel substitution]. This [present rule] replaces that with a short vowel. Regarding the form *śamayati*: because the root *śam* ends in *am*, it is designated as *mit*. Furthermore, the prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule *nodātopadeśa-* (Pāṇini 7.3.34) and so forth applies only to the affixes *ciṇ* and *kṛt*.

Regarding the word "jñāpayati": from the root *jñā* meaning "to understand" (DhP 1507), which is listed in the *rky-ādi* group, the designation *mit* is applied by the rule "māraṇatoṣaṇaniśāmaneṣu jñā, micca" (DhP 811). Then, by the rule "arti-hrī-" (Pāṇini 7.3.36), the suffix *puK* is added, resulting in the shortening of the vowel.

Regarding the passage beginning with "some here," etc.: since the root *kram* ("to step") [DhP 437] ends in the letter *m*, it receives the designation *mit*; and because of that [designation], when [the penultimate vowel] is shortened, forms such as *saṃkrāmayati* and *utkrāmayati* would not be established. Therefore, for the sake of establishing these, [the rule] "optionally [when the suffix *ṇic* follows] *cit* and *virāga*" [is stated].

Carrying forward the mention of the word *vā* from that [sūtra] (Pāṇini 6.4.91), they explain: "And since that [word *vā*] is being carried forward, an option would apply everywhere; therefore, in order to avoid such an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), it is said:
'And that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*'). Now, regarding the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ*:
Why was it not stated thus, for in that way the sūtra would have been more concise? It is impossible to state it in this manner;

for the root *veṣṭ* (meaning "to encircle") is recited in the *ghaṭādi* group [of roots], and if it were stated in this way, the substitution of *ap* [for the vowel] would undesirably apply to it. However, when it is stated as "short" (*hrasva*), then by the rule "when a short substitute is applied, *ec* becomes *i*" (*eca ig hrasvādeśe*), [the desired result follows].
Thus, the vowel *i* becomes established.

93. *ciṇṇamulor dīrgho 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.4.93). The term *ṇau* (in the presence of the affix *ṇi*) is understood [from the previous rule], and *ciṇ* and *ṇamul* are its qualifiers. Regarding the example *aśami*: it is the *luṅ* (aorist) of the root *śam* with the causative suffix *ṇic*; then, by the rule *ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (3.1.66), *ciṇ* is substituted for *clī*.
By the rule *ṭhiṇo luk* (6.4.104), there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ta*; by the rule *ṇer aniṭi* (6.4.51), there is elision of the *ṇi* augment. Thus we have *śarma-śamam* and *śāmaṃ-śāmam*.
As before, this involves the *ṇamul* suffix and reduplication.

"What is the purpose of mentioning 'long'? He thinks as follows: only the short vowel, which is immediately preceding and under discussion, should be subject to the optional rule; even so, what is desired is indeed established. For instance, in that alternative where the short vowel is prescribed, forms such as *aśamī* and so forth are established.

The intention is that where a short vowel is not prescribed, the rule "ṭhata upadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.116) prescribes a long vowel termed *vṛddhi*; because the form remains as such, forms like "aśāmi" and so forth are established. However, the other [view] holds that without the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*), what cannot be established...

He demonstrates this with the words "he employs him who pacifies" (śamayantaṃ prayuṅkte), and so forth. From the causative form of the root *śam* (śami-ṇic), when there is a further intention to express an instigator, a second *ṇic* is added; in that case, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the preceding *ṇic*, followed by the *luṅ* suffix and the *ciṇ* affix.
Optionally, there is lengthening of the vowel.

"ṭhaśami, aśāmi, śamaṃśamam, śāmaṃśāmam"—thus [the forms are derived]. When the second *ṇic* is applied followed by the suffix *ṇamul*, lengthening occurs optionally. [The examples] "śaṃśamayate" and so forth are formed as follows: from the root *śam*, the intensive suffix *yaṅ* is added because it means "to become exceedingly calm"; then reduplication occurs; and then the augment *nuk* is added because the root ends in a nasal.

Thus, by [Pāṇini 7.4.85], the augment *nuk* is applied, resulting in *śaṃśamya*. When the causative suffix *ṇic* is subsequently added, the *a* is elided by [Pāṇini 6.4.48], and the *y* is elided by [Pāṇini 6.4.49].
With *śaṃśamī* thus established, when the suffix *ciṇ* follows it, then, in one alternative (*pakṣe*), there is lengthening.

When the suffix *aś* is used, it becomes *śaṃśamyaśaṃśāmīti*. But when the suffix *ṇamul* is used, it becomes *śaṃśamaṃśaṃmam*, *śaṃśāmaṃśaṃśāmam*, and so forth; in that case, regarding the long vowel (*dīrgha*) rule, since the *ṇi* of *ṇi* is elided and the *a* of *yaṅ* is also present, [the rule] "when a subsequent element follows, a preceding operation takes effect" (*acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau*) applies.

Thus, the status of being "like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not occur, because of the prohibition by the rule *na padānta* (1.1.58). Consequently, when there is no intervention, the long vowel is established.
It might be argued: "When an option for a short vowel is being prescribed, in that alternative where the short vowel does not exist..."
In that case, would the long vowel remain established in its own form? To this he says:

"But in the case of an optional short [vowel]," and so forth. For when a short vowel is to be prescribed, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (substitution of the original element) is not prohibited by anyone. In that regard, when an optional short vowel is being prescribed...
The status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if occupying the original position) would indeed apply both to the elision (*lopa*) of the *ṇi* and to the *yaṅ* suffix.

Consequently, due to that *sthānivadbhāva*, the optional shortening (*hrasvatva*) would not occur; for it is only when a *ṇi* follows, preceded by *ciṇ* or *nam*, that the shortening of *mit* stems is prescribed. And here...

The suffix *ṇiC* followed by *ciṇ* or *ṇamul* does not cause the substitution of *midaṅga* (the penultimate vowel and the following consonant) in that case, because it is separated from the preceding *ṇiC*.

Furthermore, that *ṇiC* in which *midaṅga* occurs is not followed by *ciṇ* or *ṇamul*, because it is separated from the subsequent *ciṇ*. Therefore, this is not the scope of this rule; thus, [the substitution] is only optional (*pākṣika*).

By this [rule], shortness would not occur; by the preceding rule alone, it would be permanent, and consequently, the long vowel would not occur. Regarding the phrase "in a form ending in ṇiṇi" (ṇiṇyante): that in which ṇiṇi is at the end, i.e., adjacent, is "ending in ṇiṇi" (ṇiṇyanta). Alternatively, [it may be explained as follows:]

*ṇiṇiḥ* means *ṇi* followed by *ṇi*; that which has this as its end (*anta*) is called *ṇiṇyanta*. In this view, the word *anta* signifies a constituent part (*avayava*). Regarding the statement "in the case of the *yaṅṇyanta*, however, there is simply no establishment [of the desired form]," the term *yaṅṇyanta* is also derived in two ways as previously explained. Of what is there no establishment?

It should be understood that [the rule] "of the long vowel" applies because it is the subject under discussion. By means of the particle *eva*, he shows this: although the formation of the long vowel might be accomplished by some means in the case of a root ending in *ṇic* or *ṇya*, in the case of a root ending in *yaṅ* followed by *ṇic*, there is simply no accomplishment; the meaning is that there is no accomplishment by any means whatsoever. How?
How, then, does the derivation of the causative form (ṇijanta) result in grammatical success? It is because of the recourse to the universal class (jāti) of the causative affix.

For, although there is indeed a status as if the element were present (sthānivadbhāva) regarding the elision of the causative affix when the universal class of the causative is intended to be expressed, nevertheless, there is no actual intervention [of a distinct element], because the universal class is one. Indeed, it is not possible for that very class to intervene within itself. Therefore...

Because there is no intervention, the long vowel is established in the causative of the causative (*ṇiṇyanta*). Alternatively, he demonstrates this very point by means of the particle *eva*: since the rule "ata upadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.116) prescribes the vṛddhi replacement first by relying on the initial *ṇic*, the long vowel is indeed established; however, its subsequent removal occurs through the substitution of a short vowel.

It is performed, but it is not the case that [the long vowel] does not exist at all. However, in the case of the causative suffix *ṇic* (yaṅ-ṇyanta), there is an absolute absence of the accomplishment of the long vowel, because an increase (*vṛddhi*) is impossible therein. This might be argued:
even if the long vowel were prescribed as an alternative (*vikalpa*), the long vowel would still not be established here, because of the rule "asiddha is treated as if non-existent in this context."

Because the elision [of the *ṇi*] in the rule "bhāt" (Pāṇini 6.4.22) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), he says: "Because of the mutual dependence" (*vyāśrayatvāt*), and so forth. But how is there mutual dependence? He says: "For when the *ṇi*," and so forth.

The inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* is for the sake of clarity; for it is possible to carry forward the option (*vā*) from the rule *vā citavirāge* (6.4.9) by means of the "frog-leap" maxim (*maṇḍūakapluti*).
94. *khaci hrasvaḥ* | (6.4.94) [Examples:

*dviṣantapaḥ*, *parantapaḥ*. By the rule *dviṣatparayostāpe* (3.2.39), the suffix *khac* is applied; by the rule *arurdviṣadajantasya* (6.3.67), the augment *mum* is added. [Another example: *purandaraḥ*.
The suffix *khac* is applied by the rule "ṭhpūḥsarvayordārisahoḥ" (3.2.41), and the augment *mum* is introduced by the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) "vācaṃyapurandarau ca" (6.3.69).
The mention of the short vowel (*hrasva*) is for the sake of clarity, as it can be understood from the rule "mitāṃ hrasvaḥ" (6.4.92).
The term "short" (hrasva) is to be understood as continuing [from the previous rule] by way of the "frog-leap" maxim (maṇḍūakaplutinyāya).

95. *hlāda* [undergoes substitution] before a *niṣṭhā* suffix. (Pāṇini 6.4.95) Regarding the form *prahlannaḥ*: the root *hlādī* is listed as "in the sense of pleasure" (*sukhe ca*) at Dhātupāṭha 27; the substitution of *n* for *d* occurs by rule 8.2.42, *radābhyām*, etc. Regarding *prahlādayati*, the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied in the sense of "causing to be pleased."

96. *chāder ghe 'dvyupasargasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.96). [The example is] *uracchadaḥ*. The root *chad* [is listed] as *chada apavāraṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 1935); with the causative suffix *ṇic*, and by the rule *puṃsi saṃjñāyāṃ ghaḥ prāyeṇa* (3.3.118), the suffix *gha* is applied. Having analyzed the compound as *urasas chadaḥ*...
The compound is formed according to the rule: "And the genitive case [ending] following a *kṛt* suffix is compounded" (Vārttika 86).

Now, one might object that because the elision of the *ṇi* suffix is either considered non-existent by the rule "In this context, what precedes is as if non-existent" (6.4.22), or because of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* by the rule "When a subsequent element intervenes, the preceding [element] is treated as its substitute" (1.2.57), [the condition for compounding would not be met].
A short vowel cannot occur when the penultimate letter (upadhā) is *aj* [i.e., a vowel]; so how can shortness apply here?

To this he says: "of the elision of the *ṇi*-affix," and so forth. If, in this case, the elision of the *ṇi* were either considered asiddha or subject to the rule of *sthānivadbhāva*, then this statement would be purposeless.
Therefore, by the force of that statement, neither [of the two conditions] occurs; thus, the penultimate vowel (upadhā) undergoes shortening.
It is said: "It should be stated that [the rule applies] when the prefix consists of three or more syllables. But surely, where there are three or more...

"Both exist there," and therefore, is it not established by the rule "after an indeclinable preposition"? To this he says: "For [the number] subsequent," and so forth. Although both exist in the case of three and more, nevertheless they are not denoted here by the word *dvi* (two); for the subsequent number is that which follows the preceding number.
The designation [already] made excludes that [subsequent] expression. How is this known? He says:

"For not," and so forth. If a subsequent number did not exclude the designation made by a preceding number, then even one who has three sons would be called "one who has two sons" in common usage; but such is not the case.

And it is stated as follows: for instance, when it is said, "Let the one with two sons be brought," one does not bring the one who has three sons, but rather only he who has exactly two sons. Furthermore, the meaning of the sentence beginning with *ad-dvi-prabhṛti* is this: there is shortening of the vowel in the prefix *ad-* before the root *chad*.

The meaning is that this form of the word *bhavati* must be explained; the explanation here is as follows: the word *dvi-* (two) is used here as an indicator for "many," meaning "of a compound with many prefixes" (*anekopasarga*), and [it applies] to those that do not have two prefixes (*advayupasarga*).

This is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation). Therefore, the meaning is as follows: "When a suffix beginning with *gh* follows, the penultimate vowel of a root ending in *chādi* that has multiple prefixes does not undergo shortening.
But by what [rule] was the shortening previously applicable, such that it is now negated by this [sūtra]?

From this very prohibition, an enjoining rule (*vidhāyaka-vākya*) is inferred; or rather, it is due to a separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*), namely: "after *chādi*, before *gha*. And if the word *dvi* here is intended as an indicator for "more than one," and a separation of rules is indeed accepted, then in that case—

There is no fault even if [the rule] is interpreted as a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion). How so? "Not having two prefixes" (*advyupasarga*) means other than that which has two prefixes—that is, that which has one prefix; for that, shortening occurs. For what purpose is this [rule], since it is already established by the rule "after *chādi*, before a *gh*-ending"? [Response: It is for the sake of excluding the case where there are more than two prefixes. If it were not so, then in a form such as *parichādayati* (where there are three prefixes), the shortening would undesirably apply because the condition "not having two prefixes" would be satisfied. Therefore, this rule is stated to exclude such cases. Thus, there is no fault.
Since [the rule] is already established, the restatement is for the purpose of restriction (niyamārtha): it applies only to a single prefix (upasarga) and not to any other.
If this were so, would it not fail to apply in the case of *uracchadaḥ*? This is not a fault;
for if it were so, the division of the rule (yogavibhāga) would be purposeless, since a restriction depends upon a similar class of items.

The rule being formulated applies specifically to that which has a prefix; it excludes shortening only for that which has a prefix, not for that which lacks a prefix. Consequently, in the case of "ṭhutaraścchadaḥ," the rule indeed operates.
97. *ismantrankviṣu ca*.
(6.4.97) The particle *ca* is for the purpose of drawing forward [the term] *ādi-* from the previous rule. Regarding *chadiḥ*:
the suffix *isi* is applied by the rule *aciśucihusṛpicchādiccchadibhya isiḥ* (Daiva-Uṇādi-sūtra 9.30).
Regarding "ṭhcchadma": the suffix *manin* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.74 (*sarvadhātubhyo manin*).

Regarding "ṭhcchatram": the suffix *ṣṭran* is applied according to Daṇḍin’s Uṇādisūtra 8.79 (*sarvadhātubhyaḥ ṣṭran*). There is a grammatical split (*yogavibhāga*) so that [the suffix] may also apply after multiple prefixes.
It might be said: "It is a complete covering."

98. *gam-han-ja-n-kan-kṣan-ghasām lopaḥ kṅ-ti-naiṅ* (Pāṇini 6.4.98). This prohibition [of the substitution of *k* and *ṅ*] applies when the affix begins with a vowel (*ac*), as indicated by the phrase "not after *aiṅ*" (*naiṅ*). Therefore, it is understood that this grammatical operation applies only when the affix beginning with a vowel is equivalent to that [prohibition]. Thus he says: "when the affix begins with a vowel. Examples: *jaghanatuḥ*, *jaghnuḥ*.

Thus: by the rule *abhyāsācca* (Pāṇini 7.3.55), there is the substitution of *k* [for *j*]. For the forms *jajñatuḥ* and *jajñuḥ*, the root is *jan* in the sense of "being born" (Dhātupāṭha 1105); it is a verb of the *juhotyādi* class, taking the *parasmaipada* endings. By the rule *stoḥ ścunā ścaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.40), there is the substitution of *ś* [for *t*]. For the form *jajñe*, the root is *jan* in the sense of "manifestation."

(From *dhā.pā.* 1149) This is an *ātmanepada* verb belonging to the *divādi* class. By the rule *liṭastajhayoreśirec* (Pāṇini 3.4.81), the suffix *eś* is applied. Thus we have *jakṣatuḥ*. Regarding *adeḥ*, by the rule *liṭaḷnyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 2.4.40), there is the substitution of *ghaslṛ*; then, by the rule *khari ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.55), the letter *gh* is changed to *k*.

The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule "ṣṭhivuklamvācamaśca" (Pāṇini 8.3.60). Alternatively, this is a form of the root *ghas* (meaning 'to eat', Dhātupāṭha 715). Regarding the form "akṣan": it is the *luṅ* tense;
the substitution of *ghaslṛ* for *ad* occurs by the rule "luṅsanorghaslṛ" (2.4.37), and [the elision of the *ṛ*] occurs by the rule "mantre ghasahvara" (2.4.80).

By these and other rules, there is the elision (*luk*) of *liṭ*, the substitution of *anta* for *jhi*, and the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*). The remainder is as before. In the forms "adhasat" and "agamat," the suffix *aṅ* is applied by the rule on the *puṣādi* group (Pāṇini 3.1.55).
99. *tanipatyośchandasī* (6.4.99).

Regarding the form *vitatanire*: even if the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) were considered asiddha [non-existent] for the purposes of this rule, nevertheless, by virtue of the very fact that the elision is prescribed, the rule *ata ekahalmadhye* (6.4.120) applies.
By these [rules], the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplication do not occur. In the form *papatima*, the augment *iṭ* is applied according to the rule for roots beginning with *krī*.

100. *ghasibhasor hali ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.100). "The substitution of *dh* for *t*" [is applied] by the rule *jhaṣas tathoḥ dho 'dhaḥ* (8.2.40). "The substitution of *j* for *dh*" [is applied] by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* (8.4.53). "When the compound has been formed" [refers to the preceding context].
By the rule "pūrvāparaprathama... (2.1.58) and so forth; [the substitution] of *sa* for *samāna* is by the rule "samānasya ca chandasi" (6.3.84) and so forth.
If the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) were performed prior to the reduplication (*dvirvacana*),...
In that case, because there is an absence of a single vowel (*ekāctva*), reduplication (*dvirvacana*) would not apply; to this he says:
"Because it is Vedic," and so forth. Regarding the form *bandhām*, this is a Vedic usage.
In that regard, by the rule "in the Veda [the application of rules occurs] diversely" (*bahulaṃ cchandasi* 6.4.75), these cases occur diversely. Therefore...

Although, because it is subsequent [to the rule for reduplication] and because it applies even when the reduplication has not yet occurred, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) would logically apply prior to the reduplication, nevertheless it is not done in that manner. The sense is that it is not applied before the reduplication. In the form *bapsati*, there is the substitution of *at* for the suffix *jhi* following the root *bhakṣ* (here appearing as *bhas*), and the elision (*ślu*) of the suffix *śap*.

There is reduplication by the rule *ṣṭhślau* (6.1.10), followed by the phonetic operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsakārya*). When the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) has been elided, there is the substitution of *c* for *bh*, resulting in *p*. Thus, the form is *basti*; this is the form [of the verb] in the third person singular present indicative (*tip*).
101. *hujhalbhyo herdhiḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.101).
[The word] "beginning with a consonant" (*halādeḥ*) [is understood]. But from where is the mention of "consonant" (*hal*) brought forward, by which the word *hi* is qualified?
If it is argued that it is from the immediately preceding rule, [we reply: no; for that [rule] is stated in the locative case (*saptamī-nirdiṣṭam*).

And here, the meaning is indicated by the genitive case. This fifth [ablative] case in "after *bh* and *jhal*" (*bhu-jhalbhyaḥ*) will be treated as a sixth [genitive] in relation to the seventh [locative] case in "in *hal*" (*hali*, 6.4.100).
There is no fault, because of the rule "from that, the following" (*tasmād ity uttarasya*, 1.1.67). [The example is] *bhindhi*; [here] there is the elision of *a* in *śna* and *śnā*.

(6.4.111) Thus, there is the elision of the vowel *a*. In "krīṇīhi," the substitute *hi* is applied by (3.4.87) *serhyapicca*, and the substitution of *ī* occurs by (6.4.113) *ī halyaghoḥ*. In "juhutām," [the suffix] *loṭ* is used; *tām* is the substitute for *tas*. In "rudihi" and "svapihi," there is the elision of *śap* because [the roots] belong to the *adādi* class.

The augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *ṛdādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke* (Pāṇini 7.2.76). Now, why does it not occur here in the form *juhutāt tvam*? He says: "In this case," and so forth. The scope for the substitution of *dhi* is in non-benedictive forms, such as *juhudhi*; the scope for *tātaṅ* is, for example, *jīvatāt*.

Regarding the word *tvam*: in the case of the imperative (*loṭ*) used as a benediction (*āśis*), when both [substitutions] are applicable, the substitution of *tāt* occurs by virtue of its being the subsequent rule. Now, even after that [substitution] has been made, why does the substitution of *adhi* not occur again, given that the substitute is treated like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) and because of the principle that "that which was previously applicable [remains applicable]" (*punaḥ-prasaṅga-vijñāna*)? To this he says: "In that case," and so forth.
If this is so, then in the case of *bhindhaki* and *cchindaki*, since the condition for the augment *adhi* applies later, would not *akac* arise by the very reason just mentioned? To this he says:
"In *bhindhaki*, *cchindaki*, etc. For when a word denotes an individual (*vyakti*), [the rule] "when there is a conflict between two rules that apply simultaneously... applies.
The principle that "what has been superseded remains superseded" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 40) applies here.

Furthermore, regarding the [reapplication of a rule], it was established under the rule "vipratiṣedhe paraṃ kāryam" (Pāṇini 1.4.2) by means of the principle "punaḥprasaṅgavijñānāt siddham" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 41). However, for Pāṇini, both [principles] apply.

It is held that, in accordance with the requirements of the linguistic data (*lakṣya*), something is resorted to in certain cases. In that regard, because the individual entity (*vyakti*) is adopted as the referent in the rule prescribing *tāt* (the substitution of *tāt* for *hi*), the principle "once a conflict has been resolved by a subsequent rule, what was set aside remains set aside" applies; however, in the rule prescribing *akac*, the universal (*jāti*) is the referent.
Because the meaning of the word (*padārtha*) is taken as the basis, the rule "it is established by the principle of 're-occurrence'" applies.

Thus, in the form *bhindhaki*, the suffix *akac* is added by the rule "of indeclinables and pronouns" (Pāṇini 5.3.71). In that context, the term "and verbal suffixes" (*tiṅśca*, 5.3.56) is understood to carry over.

102. *śru-śṛṇu-pṛ-kṛ-vṛ-bhyaś chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.4.102). Regarding *śruṇudhi*: by the rule *śruvaḥ śṛ ca* (3.1.74), there is the addition of the *śnu* suffix and the substitution of *śṛ*. Regarding *pūrdhi*: from the root *pṛ* in the sense of "protecting" and "filling" (Dhātupāṭha 1086); [the substitution of *ū* for *ṛ* occurs] by the rule *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya*.
By the rule (7.1.102), *u* is substituted [for *v*], and by the rule *ṭhali ca* (8.2.77), lengthening occurs. Thus we have *uparuṇaskṛdhi*.

When *uru asmākaṃ kṛdhi* is established, the substitution of *nas* for *asmat* occurs by the rule *bahuvacanasya vasnasau* (8.1.21). Then, by the rule *naśca dhātusthoruṣubhyaḥ* (8.4.27), the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* takes place.

The *sakāra* undergoes *rutva*, becoming a *visarjanīya*. This [visarjanīya] becomes a *sakāra* by the rule "ṭhataḥ kṛkami" (Pāṇini 8.3.46), etc. [The form] "apāvṛdhi" is a form derived from either the root *vṛṅ* or *vṛñ*.
For even in the case of *vṛṅ*, the Parasmaipada ending occurs in Vedic usage according to the rule "vyatyayo bahulam" (Pāṇini 3.1.85).
It indeed occurs.

Now, why does elision (*luk*) not take place here by the rule *utaśca pratyayād asaṃyogapūrvāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.106) in the case of *śṛṇudhi*? To this he says: "In the case of *śṛṇudhi*, etc. If there were elision here...

The sense is that there might be a deficiency of intellect, which would result in a lack of purpose. In the form *apāvṛdhī*, the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 6.3.137). Now, one might object: in the case of *śrudhi*, there ought to be the substitution of *śṛ* for *śru* and the suffix *in* according to the rule *śruvaḥ śṛ ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.74); likewise, in the case of *pūrdhi*.

In *uruṇaskṛdhi*, the suffix *śnā* is applied because [the root] belongs to the *kry-ādi* class; in *uruṇaskṛdhi*, the suffix *u* is applied by the rule *tanādikṛñbhyaḥ uḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.79); and in *apāvṛdhi*, if the root is *vṛṅ*, then the suffix *śnā* is applied because it belongs to the *kry-ādi* class, but if it is *vṛñ*, then [the suffix *śnu* is applied] because it belongs to the *svādi* class.
If these forms are not established by means of the *śnu* suffix,
then he says "other than that" (*ato 'nyatara*) and so forth.
From this example, "śṛṇudhi," [it follows that] in other examples, there is "frequent transposition" (*vyatyayo bahulam*).
Thus, by [Pāṇini 3.1.85], there is the affix *śap*, and for that as well, there is elision (*luk*) by [Pāṇini 2.4.73]: "In the Vedic language, [the affixes] are diversely [elided]."

103. *aṅtiśca* | (6.4.103). "Or [the substitution of] *ṅ* [occurs] in the Vedic language," and so forth. By the rule *sārvadhātukamapit* (1.2.4), the designation *ṅt* is prescribed for a *sārvadhātuka* affix that is not marked with *p*; in the domain of the Vedic language, however, it is optional by the rule *vā chandasi*.
By this [sūtra], the non-ṅittva of *hi* is made optional; therefore, in one alternative, its ṅittva does not occur.
Now, how is it that in *rārandhi* there is a parasmaipada ending, given that this root *ram* is ātmanepadi?

How is it that there is no hearing of the *śap* [affix] here? How is there lengthening of the vowel in the reduplication (*abhyāsa*)? And how is it that the elision of the letter *m*, by the rule "of that which is taught with an anudātta [vowel], etc. (Pāṇini 6.4.37), does not occur? To this he says: "rārandhi," etc. By stating "there is *ślu* for *śap*," [the author implies] "in *ślau*..."

Thus, it is stated that there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*). The intention is that the absence of the elision of the letter *m* is established by the rule *aiṅtvāt* [Pāṇini 6.4.67], and therefore it does not require a special effort to achieve. Regarding "of the *śap* of *yam*" [Pāṇini 7.3.74], this is by the rule "frequently in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*, 2.4.73). Regarding "the *ślu* of the *śap* of *dyot*" [Pāṇini 7.3.94], this is also by the rule "frequently in the Veda."
By this [sūtra], (2.4.76).
104. *Ciṇo luk* (Pāṇini 6.4.104). [The sūtra states: "There is elision (*luk*) of the affix following *ciṇ*. Now, how is it understood that this refers to an affix?
Because the word "affix" (*pratyaya*) is brought into proximity by the rule *aṅgasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.1).
If there is elision (*luk*) of a suffix following a *ciṇ* [augment], why does elision not occur for the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* in the forms *akāritarām* and *akāritamām*?
To this he says: "In *akāritarām*, etc. That which is the elision of the sound *ta*—of that...

When the elision (*luk*) of *tarap* and *tamap* is to be applied, there is the status of being "as if non-existent" (*asiddhavat*) by the rule "that which precedes *ābhāt* is as if non-existent here" (Pāṇini 6.4.22). Therefore, because they are separated by the word *tas*, the *tarap* and *tamap* suffixes do not immediately follow the *ciṇ* substitute; consequently, their elision does not occur. Now, [one might object]:...
Is it not the case that because of the statement "one thing is established in another," it is not logical for one and the same thing to be unestablished in that very same place?

To this, he says: "The rule *ciṇo luk*... and so forth. Although this grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) is heard as non-different in the form "there is elision of *ciṇ*," it becomes differentiated due to the difference between the scope (*viṣaya*) and the object characterized (*lakṣya*), when the word-meaning (*padārtha*) is understood as an individual instance (*vyakti*).

Since the definition varies with each individual instance, when such a difference exists, the charge of being "unestablished" (*asiddhatva*) is indeed valid. When the forms *akāri* and *ahārī* are established, if one intends to express excellence,
the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* are applied according to Pāṇini 5.3.56, *ṭhtiṅśca*, and [the derivation proceeds] from that which ends in those suffixes.
When the suffix *ām* is applied by the rule *ṭhkimetiṅvyayaghādāmvadravyaprakarṣe* (Pāṇini 5.4.11), the forms *akāritamām* and *akāritamām* result.

105. *ato heḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.105). [The example] *gaccha* is from the root *gam* in the imperative (*loṭ*); the substitution of *cch* occurs by *iṣugamiyamāṃ cchaḥ* (7.3.77). [The example] *dhāva* is from the root *dhāvu* meaning "to move" or "to purify" (Dhātupāṭha 601), or else it is derived from the root *sṛ*.

By the rule *ṭhāpāghrā* (Pāṇini 7.3.78), there is the substitution of *dhāv*. In the cases of *yuhi* and *ruhi*, because they belong to the *adādi* class, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*. In *lunohi* and *punīhi*, there is shortening by the rule *pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ* (7.3.80), and the substitution of *ī* by the rule *ī halyadhoḥ* (6.4.113).
Now, one might object: "If this [substitution] is performed, then because the word ends in 'na', the [desired result] will not occur;
so what is the purpose of including the *tapara* (the long vowel marker) for its exclusion? To this he says: "Because of the *ītvam*," and so forth.
However, due to its being *asiddha*, it is as explained previously.

106. *utaśca pratyayād asaṃyogapūrvāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.106). [The word] "the letter *u* which is not preceded by a conjunct consonant" (*asaṃyogapūrva*) means that from which no conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) is absent as a preceding element; it is described thus. By this, he shows that the mention of "not preceded by a conjunct" (*asaṃyogapūrvāt*) is a qualifier of the vowel *a*. That...

The letter *u* of this kind is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the suffix; and since there is an "application to that which ends with [the qualified element]" (*tadantavidhi*) by means of a qualifier, he says: "from that which ends with it," and so forth. But for what purpose is the application to that which ends with it accepted? So that [the rule] may apply in the case of *sun* and *cinu*.

Let this be the purpose; however, there is this fault: [the rule] does not apply here in *tanu kuru* ("make thin"), for in this case the suffix is merely the phoneme *u*, not something ending in it. To this we reply:
even here, by the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the suffix possesses the status of being "ending in it," so there is no fault. Thus, *kuru*.

When the *guṇa* substitution has been applied to the root and the replacement of *r* by *ra* (*raparatva*) has been performed, the substitution of *u* occurs by the rule *ṭhata utsārvadhātuke* (Pāṇini 6.4.110).
Thus we have *taruṇuhi*. The suffix *śnu* is applied by the rule *tūnūkaraṇe takṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.76).

Regarding the phrase "cchandovāvacanam": because of the metaphorical application of the name [Veda] to its content, the word *vā* (or) is intended here in the sense of "option" (*vikalpa*). That by which something is spoken or explained is called *vacana*. An option regarding the meaning is *vāvacana*. Thus, *cchandovāvacana* means "an option in the Veda," according to the locative case (*saptamī*).

(2.1.40) Thus, the compound is formed by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule). Regarding the statement "it should be stated that [this applies] optionally in the Veda (*cchandasi vā vaktavyam*)," the meaning is that this rule is to be explained as being optional within the domain of the Veda. In that regard, this...

The explanation is as follows: the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") in the subsequent sūtra applies as a remainder (*śeṣa*) to both rules, and it is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Consequently, this rule applies optionally in the domain of Vedic literature (*chandas*). Examples are:
*dhinuhi*, *kṛṇuhi*; [and] *hivi*, *divi*, *dhivi*.

The roots *prīñ* (DhP 591–593) meaning "to please," and *kṛvī* (DhP 598) meaning "to injure" or "to do"— the latter taking the augment *num* because it is marked with *i*t— form their present participles with the suffix *u* by Pāṇini 3.1.80 (*dhinvikṛṇvyora ca*), which prescribes the suffix *u* and the replacement of the final vowel with *a*.
That *a* is then elided by Pāṇini 6.4.48 (*ato lopaḥ*).
107. *lopaścāsyānyatarasyāṃ mvoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.107). [The commentary states:

"This *u*-vowel which is not preceded by a conjunct consonant. By this, he shows that the *u*-vowel under discussion is referred back by the pronoun *asya*. Now, one might object: [is this not already covered] by *ataḥ* (6.4.106)?
Thus, by virtue of this continued application (*anuvṛtti*), it will be understood that the elision (*lopa*) applies only to the letter *u*; so what is the purpose of the rule "of *ṭha*"?

If it is argued that this [mention of *ṭha*] is for the sake of establishing a genitive relationship (*ṣaṣṭhī-praklṛpti*), we say no; for the locative case in "of *m* and *v*" (*ṭhmvoḥ*) has its purpose fulfilled there, whereas the ablative case in "from *ut*" (*utaḥ*) had its purpose fulfilled in the preceding rule.
It will establish the status of being a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhītva*), because of the rule: "When [something] is indicated by the word *tasmin*, [an operation applies] to what precedes" (Pāṇini 1.1.66).
This might be so if this [term] *mvoḥ* were understood as a locative (*saptamī*);
however, it is not yet determined whether this is a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) or a locative (*saptamī*). Therefore...
It was stated "of this" (*asya*) for the purpose of establishing the genitive case. Regarding the phrase "while *luk* is being carried over," and so forth:

if *luk* were applied to the very same element under discussion [the base], then *luk* would apply to the entire suffix, not just to the final one; for the technical term *luk* has been prescribed as the designation for the non-appearance of a suffix in general, and not [specifically] for the final one.

[If it were merely] the non-observation of the suffixal portion, then when *luk* is applied to the whole, forms such as *sunvaḥ* and *sunmaḥ* would not be established. There is no fault, however, because of the mention of *lopa* [in the rule]. For in that case, by the statement "of the final [element]" (*alo’ntyasya*, 1.1.52), there is the elision of the vowel *u* alone. Therefore, it is for the sake of the elision of the final [element]...

The mention of *lopa* (elision) is for this reason as well: otherwise, in the case of *kurvaḥ* from *kuru-aṃ*, the *guṇa* substitution would not occur when there is elision (*luk*), because of the prohibition of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations based on a suffix) by the rule *na lumatāṅgasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.63).
However, when there is *lopa*, the substitution does take place. Therefore, the mention of *lopa* must also be made for the sake of the *guṇa*.
108. *nityaṃ karoteḥ* (6.4.108). [The rule states:

"of the suffix *u* after the root *kṛ*. Now, one might object: "But surely the suffix *u* was drawn over from the preceding sūtra by the particle *ca*; and according to the maxim, 'that which is drawn over by *ca* does not recur in subsequent rules' (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 76)."

How, then, is the elision of the phoneme *u* obtained? It is not so; for in the preceding rule, the proximity of the phoneme *u* is already obtained by the very words "of this" (*asya*). Therefore, one should understand that the re-introduction (*anukarṣaṇa*) of that [phoneme] by means of the letter *ca* in that [rule] is solely for this purpose. This is shown by the example "kurvaḥ kumam" in the passage beginning with "of the elision of the phoneme *u*."

He shows that there is a long-vowel attainment (*dīrghaprāpti*) for [the word] *sopapatikā*, and by the rule "ṭhana bhakurchuarām" (Pāṇini 8.2.79), he shows its prohibition. The inclusion of the term "nitya" (invariable) is for the sake of clarity;
for by the very force of the rule's commencement, the prescription will indeed be invariable.
109. *ye ca*: The letter *ca* is for the purpose of carrying over (*anukarṣaṇa*) the [word] *lopa*.

110. *ata utsārvadhātuke* (Pāṇini 6.4.110). Regarding the phrase "of that which ends in the suffix *ṭhuk*" and so forth: that whose final element is the suffix *u* is described as such. Furthermore, the root *kṛ*, when ending in the suffix *u*, does not deviate from its status as a *sārvadhātuka*.
With this intention, he asks: "What is the purpose of the mention of *sārvadhātuka*? [The answer is: "Even in the case of what has previously occurred," and so forth.

If the mention of *sārvadhātuka* were absent, then the substitution of *u* for the vowel of the root *kṛ*, which is prescribed when a *kṅit* affix follows the form ending in the suffix *uk*, would apply only where a *sārvadhātuka* *kṅit* affix follows.

In that very case, it would apply in forms such as *kurutaḥ* and *kurvanti*; however, in *kurvitra*, once the substitution of *hi* for *loṭ* has been made, [the rule] would not apply because of the absence of an affix, due to the prohibition of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* by the rule *na lumatāṅgasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.63). Therefore, [the designation must apply] even when [the condition] existed previously.
The mention of *sārvadhātuka* is for the purpose that [the substitution] should apply in the domain of *sārvadhātuka* suffixes.

Now, what is the purpose of the use of the long vowel marker (*tapara*)? For even though a vowel being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) as *u* is a substitute that includes its homogeneous (*savarṇa*) counterparts, nevertheless, by virtue of proximity (*āntaratamya*), it would take the place of the monosyllabic [vowel].

"Will it not be merely a *mātrika* [vowel]? To this he says: "The inclusion of *ta* [in *tapara*]," and so forth. For if the inclusion of *ta* were not present, then by relying on the suffix *u*, when the *guṇa* substitution is applied according to *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.84) and the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* has occurred, that *utva* which results in the vowel *u*—of that *u* [the rule would apply].

Otherwise, by the rule "ṭhpugantalaghūpadhasya ca" (Pāṇini 7.3.86), a *guṇa* substitution would occur. Therefore, the marker *ta* (the *tapara*) is employed so that there may be the hearing of the short vowel alone, and not that long vowel which might result from another grammatical rule. Thus, it is intended that the latter should not take place.

111. *śnasorallopaḥ* (6.4.111). [In the word] *rundhaḥ*: by the rule *jhaṣastathordho’dhaḥ* (8.2.40), the letter *t* is replaced by *dh*. [In the word] *staḥ*: due to belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*.

Now, as for this reference "śnasoh," since the rule "a long vowel is substituted for [the final of] ṭhak before a homogeneous vowel" (6.1.101) applies, should it not have been referred to as "ṭhśnasoh" after the lengthening had taken place?
To this he replies: "In 'śnasoh,' the form of the subsequent element (pararūpa) is substituted for the long ā. And so forth.

What is the purpose of including the long vowel *ā* (tapara) here? If it is argued that it is so that [the substitution] does not apply to the augment *āṭ* in forms such as *āstām* and *āsann*, this is not correct; for in these cases, once the suffix *liṅ* has been introduced, at the stage of *lā*, the substitution of *l* is performed before the augment *āṭ* because it is *antaraṅga* (internally conditioned). Once that has been done—

The vikaraṇa suffix, because it applies both when [the augment] has been applied and when it has not, subverts the addition of the augment *āṭ*. However, the addition of *āṭ* is non-permanent (*anitya*), because it applies to a different word-form (*aśabdāntara*). For instance, once the vikaraṇa has been applied, it must belong to that base (*aṅga*) which ends in the vikaraṇa; whereas if it has not been applied, it belongs to the verbal root alone. Once [the vikaraṇa] has been applied...

In the case of the *vikaraṇa* suffix, although both the augment *āṭ* and the elision of the vowel *a* are obligatory (*nitya*) because they apply whether the other has been performed or not, nevertheless, the elision of the vowel *a* is carried out first because it is subsequent (*para*). Once that has been done, *āṭ* is applied because [the elision] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*); and for that very reason, [the subsequent rule does not apply].

[Objection: Since there will be no elision (*lopa*), what is the purpose of making the vowel *t* long (*taparakaraṇa*)? [Response: In that case, this teaches that "the non-validity (*asiddhatva*) based on grammatical rules (*śāstrīya*) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*). By means of this, the statement "the *vuk* and *yuṭ* augmentations are established (*siddha*) in relation to *uvaṅ* and *yaṇ*" need not be stated; it need not be stated.
It comes to be.

112. *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ* (6.4.112). [Examples: *lunate*. This is the substitute [of *ā*] by [the rule] *ātmanepadeṣv anataḥ* (7.1.5). *lunatām*. [This is] the imperative (*loṭ*), [with the substitution of] *ām* for *etaḥ* by [the rule] *āmetaḥ* (3.4.90). *alunata*. [This is] the imperfect (*laṅ*). *mimate*. [This is] the present indicative (*laṭ*).
In *mimāti* (from the root *māṅ* "to measure," Dhātupāṭha 1088;

or *māṅ* "to sound," according to the Dhātupāṭha), there is the substitution of *i* for the reduplicated syllable by Pāṇini 7.4.76 (*bhṛñām it*). Similarly, in *sañjihate*, this applies to the root *ohāṅ* "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1089). In *bibhrati*, the initial vowel is strengthened.

Regarding the phrase "ṭhalunāt": one might object that since the condition *kṅti* is absent here, the substitution of *ī* (ītvam) ought to apply instead; so how could there be occasion for elision (*lopa*)? This is not so; for the condition *kṅti* must also be carried over (*anuvartyam*) to the rule for *ītvam*. In that case, if "when followed by *kṅ*" (*kṅiti*) were not carried over, then—
The elision would indeed occur [by the previous rule].

But for what purpose is the mention of *āt* (the long vowel *ā*)? One might say that it should simply be stated as "of *śnā* and the reduplicated [roots], the *at*" (*śnābhyastayor ataḥ*), for in this way it would be lighter by one mora. To this he says: "The mention of *āt* is for the sake of clarity. [This refers to the root] *jāgarti*.

Even though the designation *abhyasta* (repeated) applies by the rule "ṭhjakṣityādayaḥ ṣaṭ" (Pāṇini 6.1.6), the elision of the vowel *ṛ* does not occur in the case of *jāgrati*. This is understood because, due to the association with the suffix *śna* ending in *a*, only that *abhyasta* which ends in *a* is intended to be included.
113. *ī halyaghoḥ* | (Pāṇini 6.4.113) [Examples:

*lunītaḥ*, *punītaḥ*; *lunītha*, *punītha*. [Regarding the suffixes] *tas* and *thas*: *mimīte*—this is the third person singular middle voice (*ātmanepada*). *mimīṣe*—[here] *thās* is replaced by *se* according to Pāṇini 3.4.80.

In the forms *mimīdhvam* (from *mā*), the suffix is *dhvam*; and in *lunanti*, *punanti*, the suffix is *jhi*. Now, even if the substitution of *ī* were to occur before suffixes beginning with vowels, the elision (*lopa*) would still have no scope [to apply];
therefore, because it is without scope, the elision would block the substitution of *ī*. So what is the purpose of the rule *hali*?
This is not the case; for if the mention of *hal* were absent, both [operations] would occur by virtue of the general rule.

In the case of roots designated as *ghu*, the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*) would consequently apply. Therefore, it must be stated that [the rule applies] "when *hal* follows. Thus, from *dadhāti* we get *dattaḥ*; here, the substitution of *c* (*cartva*) occurs by the rule *khari ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.55). Similarly, from the root *dhā*, we get *dhataḥ*.

When reduplication has been performed, the *jaś*-substitution for the reduplicated syllable occurs by the rule "ṭhabhyāse carc" (Pāṇini 8.4.54). Then, by the rule "dhādastathośca" (Pāṇini 8.2.38), the letter *d* is replaced by *dh* through the *bhaṣ*-substitution; subsequently, when the vowel *ā* of the root has been elided, the *jaś*- and *cartva*-substitutions take effect.

114. *idaridrasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.114). Regarding the form *daridrati*: by the rule *jakṣityādayaḥ ṣaṭ* (6.1.6), it receives the designation *abhyasta* (repeated); consequently, the elision of the vowel *ā*, which is the characteristic feature of *abhyasta* forms, takes place.

"It should be stated" means it must be explained. Here is that explanation: having carried forward the mention of *lopa* (elision) from the rule "the elision of *a* of *śna* and *as*" (6.4.111) by means of the *maṇḍūkapluti* (frog-leap) maxim, [one applies it] to the terms *sārvadhātuka*, *hal*, and *kṅiti*.
Setting aside the specific [rules], the elision of *it* and the substitution of *it* for the root *daridrā* must be prescribed by way of a general rule (*sāmānyena*).
And this being so, those two do not result in confusion (*saṅkara*), because the term *anyatarasyām* which is to be mentioned later serves as a supplement (*śeṣabhūta*) to both rules. And that...
This is a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (an option restricted by rule). Therefore, wherever a particular [grammatical operation] is intended, it will occur only there and not elsewhere.
As it is said: "And it is established in the formulation of suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*). Thus, it should be formulated in such a way that...
"At the time of the prescription of the suffix"—that is, at the moment the suffix is being prescribed—it becomes "established," meaning it is already accomplished. This is what is meant:

the elision (lopa) must be performed even while the ārdhadhātuka suffix has not yet arisen, provided that such a suffix is the intended domain. For in this way, it becomes established at the time of the prescription of the suffix, and not otherwise. And [it is] "established" (siddha).

He demonstrates the result of including the phrase "in the formulation of a suffix" (*pratyayavidhau*) by means of the rule beginning with "characterized by having the vowel *ā* as its final element" (*ākārāntalakṣaṇaḥ*). If the elision (*lopa*) were performed once an ārdhadhātuka suffix had arisen,
then the suffix *ṇa* would apply by the rule "after the roots *śyā*, *vye*, *dhā*, and *sru*" (Pāṇini 3.1.141).

Because the root *daridrāti* ends in the vowel *ā*, the rule *āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.33) would apply, and once *yuk* is added, the undesirable form *daridrāya* would result. However, when it is stated that "the [substitution] is established prior to the application of the suffix," the elision occurs even before the suffix arises; in that case—
Because it ends in the letter *ā*, [the suffix] *ac* (pacādyac) alone is applied; by this, the desired form "daridraḥ" is established.
By the verse beginning with "na daridrāyake lopaḥ," [it is shown that] where there is elision in an *ardhadhātuka* [suffix], [the rule applies].

He demonstrates that case where [the elision] is not desired, even though it is desired by some through their conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Regarding the word *daridrāyaka*, when this form ending in the suffix *ṇvul* is intended to be established, the elision is not desired.
Thus, from *daridrāti*, one forms *daridrāyaka*; the derivation is as before. Regarding *daridrāṇe*: here too, the suffix is *lyuṅ*.

The elision is not desired; thus some say "didaridrāsati," where, after the suffix *san* has been applied, there is reduplication and the operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Or [some say] "didaridriṣati";
for in the rule *sani-ivantardha-* (Pāṇini 7.2.49), the term "tanipatidaridrāṇām" is understood.
Because of this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*), the suffix *iṭ* is optionally applied.

"In the *adyatanī*" means in the *luṅ* [tense]; "the *adyatanī*" is a technical term used by ancient grammarians for the *luṅ*. "He was not poor" (*adaridrāsīt*)—this is because of the rule: "For the roots *yam*, *ram*, *nam*, and *mā*, there is *suk* [and *iṭ*]. (Pāṇini 7.2.73).

The augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *sagiṭau, ṭhasti sico'pṛkte* (Pāṇini 7.3.96), and the elision of *sic* occurs by the rule *iṭa īṭi* (8.2.28). Now, one might object: since the long vowel *ā* of the root is elided by the rule *āto dhātoḥ* (6.4.140), the form should have been cited as *daridra*; so how is it cited as *daridrasya*?

Thus he says: "The mention of 'of the poor man,' etc. Since it is stated that "sūtras behave like Vedic meters," the shortening here is Vedic, by virtue of the word "frequently" (*bahulam*) in the rule *ṅyāpoḥ saṃjñācchandasorbahulam* (Pāṇini 6.3.63).

The inclusion of the word *tapara* (followed by a marker of time) is for the sake of clarity; since a long vowel will not be included as a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) sound when it is being cultivated [as a grammatical object], the long vowel will not occur.

115. *bhiyo'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.4.115). [The rule] "when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant (*hal*) follows that has *k* or *ṅ* as an *it*" applies here. Although these specific details were set aside in the preceding [section], they nevertheless carry over here by the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*).

This is the intended meaning. Regarding "bibhītaḥ": from the root *bhī* in the sense of fear (*ñi bhī bhaye*, Dhātupāṭha 1084), the *ślu* substitution occurs for the *śap* suffix due to its belonging to the *juhotyādi* class. The rule applies only when a consonant-initial affix follows—as in "bibhyati.
Precisely because of the force of prescribing the *it* augment, the *yaṇ* substitution [of *i* for *e*] by the rule *eranekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.82) does not take place.
It should be stated that [the rule applies] only when a sārvadhātuka suffix follows—e.g., *bhītaḥ*, *bhītavān*. Why [is it said] "before a suffix marked with K or Ṅ"? [Consider:
*bibheti*.

116. *Jahāteś-ca*. (Pāṇini 6.4.116) An *it*-augment is introduced as an exception (*apavāda*) to the *ī*-substitution; this is because the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Consequently, that [substitution] also occurs in the alternative case. [The rule applies] only when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix follows: *hīnaḥ*, *hīnavān*. Regarding this, some [teachers] say...

They reject the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *sārvadhātuke* (Pāṇini 6.4.110). How so? When a consonant (*hal*) follows, both the substitution of *ī* and the substitution of *e* would apply, as would reduplication (*dvirvacana*). In that case, if the substitutions of *ī* and *e* were to occur by virtue of their being subsequent rules, then the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) would end in the vowel *i*. Therefore, [the rule applies] to the reduplicated form.
"The mention [of the term *sārvadhātuka*] must be understood as continuing [from the previous rule], and while that continues,

the continuation of the term *sārvadhātuka* is purposeless"— this is incorrect, because it is an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation. By the very process of reduplication (*dvirvacana*), the operations of *it* and *etva* must take place first.
Therefore, how could there be the contingency of the substitution of *i* being final in the case of the reduplication?

As for the internal nature (*antaraṅgatva*) of the reduplication, it is because it depends on fewer factors; for that [reduplication] depends merely on the verbal root (*dhātu*). And since the substitutions of *it* and *et* depend on more factors, they possess external nature (*bahiraṅgatā*), and their dependence is indeed manifold; furthermore, in the case of those two, [the cause] is the stem (*aṅga*).
Because [the substitution] is prescribed for a sārvadhātuka affix beginning with *k* or *ṅ* that has an indicatory letter (*it*), and because of the specific mention of the root *jahāti*,
the form *jihīte* does not result from the root *jihāti*.
"The making of a separate rule (*pṛthagyoga*) is for the sake of what follows," namely, the rule *āca hau* (Pāṇini 6.4.117).
This is so that the rule may apply only to the root *hā* (to abandon), and not to *bhī* (to fear).
117. *ā ca hau* | (6.4.117) The letter *ca* is for the purpose of carrying forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) both the rule for *it* and the optionality (*anyatarasyām*).
118. *Lopo yi* (Pāṇini 6.4.118). 119. *Dhvasoreddhāvabhyāsalopaśca* (Pāṇini 6.4.119).
The inclusion of the term "elision of the reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsalopa*) is for the sake of those [roots] designated as *dhu*; it does not apply to others.
This is for the sake of *tvasti* (the form *tvasti*); because *as-* cannot have a reduplicated base (*abhyāsa*). [Examples are] *dehi* and *cehi*;

these two forms belong to the roots *dāñ* and *dhāñ*. However, examples of other roots designated as *ghu* are not possible, because they are separated from the suffix *hi* by the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*); and because it is impossible, [examples are given] according to the circumstances.
In that context, the word *hi* intervenes between the root *ṣṭhā* and the suffix *śyan*; however, for the roots *dāṇ* and *dheṭ*, the suffix *śāp* intervenes;
furthermore, because the root *deṅ* is marked with the *ātmanepada* designation, the suffix *hi* is impossible after it. Regarding the form *edhi*:
once the substitution of *e* for the *s* has been made, because that [substitution] is considered *asiddha*, the rule *hu-jha-la-bhyaḥ herdhiḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.101) applies.

Such is the nature of the cognition [of the rule]. Now, one might object: since the rule *alo’ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52) dictates that the elision must apply only to the final letter of the *al*-group, how can there be an elision of the entire reduplicated syllable?
To this he says: *śidayam*, etc. In the rule *lopaśca*, two *ś*s are specified.

In that context, one [element] is related to the elision (*lopa*), while the second is related to the case-ending (*vibhakti*). Since it is declared that the *it*-designation applies to that which is related to the elision, this elision becomes optional (*śit*); therefore, the elision of the entire reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) occurs. This follows from the rule "ā ca hau" (Pāṇini 6.4.117).
The mention of *ha* can be understood by way of the "leap of the frog" (*maṇḍūakapluti-nyāya*).

There might be a suspicion that, because [the term *ha*] is connected with the mention of *anyatarasyām*, when that [mention of *anyatarasyām*] is carried over, the mention of *anyatarasyām* itself would also be carried over; therefore, for the purpose of excluding that, [the word] *ha* [is used].
Thus it has been stated; because the particle "ca" (and) signifies a simultaneous application (*sanniyoga*), there occurs both elision (*lopa*) and the substitution of *etva* (the change to *e*).
120. *ata ekahalmadhye'nādeśāderliṭi* (6.4.120). Regarding the phrase *ekahalmadhye*: this word *eka* denotes "without a companion" (*asahāya*). *Ekaśca ekaśca ekau*;
[and] those two are both *ekau* and *halau*, hence *ekahalau*; [the compound] *ekahalormadhya* is in the dual number.

This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). For the "middle" can only exist between two consonants, not within one. In this context, if the substitute *liṭ* were not specified as having its initial [consonant] [subject], then forms such as *nematuḥ*, *nemuḥ*, *sehe*, *sehāte*, and *sehiraḥ* would not be possible. This is because even here, the initial of the stem (*aṅga*) is indeed [the subject]. This is what is held in mind.

Having established the substitute for *liṭ*, he says "when *liṭ* follows," etc., in order to specify [the scope]. The meaning is that no substitute which is prescribed when *liṭ* follows applies to a root (*ādi*) that is a member of a verbal base (*aṅga*). "Of that" means "of such a verbal base. And "of that" refers to the verbal base.
This is connected with the word "yo'kāraḥ" (the letter *a*). This is a genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*); the meaning is:

"of that member (*aṅga*) which is of such a kind, [there is] the letter *a* which is its constituent part. This is the explanation of the rule "eka-halmadhye": namely, "between two single consonants (*hal*) that are not accompanied by others."
The word *tatra* (therein) refers back to the vowel *a* mentioned immediately prior;

it means "of that limb," that is, of the constituent part *a*. This is a genitive of locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*)—meaning that in place of that [vowel], the substitute *e* occurs—as in *reṇatuḥ* and *reṇuḥ*, from the roots *aṇ* and *raṇ*.

Thus, the suffix *ṭhraṇ* is listed [in the Dhātupāṭha] with the meaning "to sound" (*śabda*). [Examples: *yematuḥ*, *yemuḥ*; from the root *yama* "to cease" (DhP 984). [Examples: *dematuḥ*, *demuḥ*; from the root *damu* "to calm" (DhP 1203).
Regarding "ṭhrarāśe"[rarāse—*Kāśikā*]: the root *rāśṛ* (in the sense of "sound," according to the *Dhātupāṭha* 626) is *ātmanepada*. Regarding "śaśramatuḥ śaśramuḥ":
the root *śramu* (in the senses of "exertion" and "weariness," according to the *Dhātupāṭha* 1204).
