Some, however, read *tatakṣatuḥ* and *tatakṣuḥ* as counter-examples under the assumption that [the rule] applies to a single *hal*; but this is incorrect, because the term *kṅti* continues to apply, and there is no *kitva* for the *liṭ* following the root *pakṣ*, due to the prohibition [stated in] "after a non-conjunct consonant" (*asaṃyogāt*). [The correct examples are] *tatsaratuḥ*, etc.
"Tatsaruḥ": the root *tsar* means "to move stealthily" (*cchadmagati*) [Dhātupāṭha 5.54]. "Cakaṇatuḥ, cakaṇuḥ":
the roots *aṇ*, *raṇ*, *vaṇ*, *bhaṇ*, *kvaṇ*, and *kaṇ* have the meaning of "sound" (*śabdārtha*) [Dhātupāṭha 1.444, 445, 446, 447, 449, 450].
Among these, *kaṇati* is listed in the *bhvādi* class.

Regarding the forms *jagaṇatuḥ* and *jagaṇuḥ*: the root *gaṇa* (meaning "to count") is listed in the Curādi group (Dhātupāṭha 1853). Now, one might object that since it belongs to the Curādi class, when the causal suffix *ṇic* is applied, the augment *ām* must necessarily occur before the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) by the rule *kāspratyayādāmamantre liṭi* (Pāṇini 3.1.35). To this, the reply is: "The Curādi roots are not invariably transitive (*anitya-ṇyantāścurādayaḥ*)."

Thus there is no fault. Furthermore, their status as non-ṇyant roots will be made known in the seventh [chapter]. Regarding "babhaṇatuḥ": *bhaṇati* is recited in the *bhvādi* class with the meaning of sound alone.
Regarding "nematuḥ": *ṇam* is listed [in the Dhātupāṭha] as "in bowing and sound" (DhP 981). [The rule] "ṇo naḥ" (6.1.65) [applies].

Thus [is explained] the substitution of *n*. Regarding "in *sehe*": from the root *ṣaha* in the sense of "endurance" (*marṣaṇe*, DhP 852), the substitution of *s* for the initial *ṣ* occurs by the rule "the *ṣ* at the beginning of a root is replaced by *s*" (*dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ*, Pāṇini 6.1.64). But how is it that, even when the substitutions of *n* and *s* have occurred, the substitutes such as those for the *liṭ* [perfect tense] do not take place? To this he says: "The substitutions of *n* and *s* are non-conditional," and so forth. This refers to the formulation of the rules for the substitutions of *n* and *s*.

Since nothing is based on a specific cause (nimitta), these two [suffixes] occur as "causeless" (anaimitika); consequently, they must occur even before the suffix *liṭ* has arisen. Therefore, that which is the base (*aṅga*) beginning with that [element] does not begin with a substitute for *liṭ*. If, then, the substitute for *liṭ* is indeed qualified in this way...

If the constituent element (*aṅga*) were not specified [in the rule], then it would undesirably apply even to cases such as *pakvaḥ* and *pakvavān*; for in these instances, too, there is no initial vowel (*ādi*) in the substitute that is applied to the root *pac* when the *liṭ* suffix follows. This is not so; for the substitution of *e* is prescribed in connection with the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsa-lopa*).

Therefore, this [substitution] of *etva* should occur only where there is the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*); however, there is no elision of the reduplicated syllable here, because it is impossible. If you then argue that it should occur here in the case of *pāpacyate*, this too is not a fault; for in this instance, by virtue of its higher status, the long vowel substitution prescribed by "dīrgho 'kitaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.83) applies.

It will be so. The general rules (*utsarga*) are the shortening of the vowel and the retention of the initial consonant; the exceptions (*apavāda*) to these are lengthening and the substitution of *e*.

In that regard, the scope for lengthening is seen in *bābhāsyate*; the scope for the *e*-substitution is seen in *pecatuḥ* and *pecuḥ*. However, in the case of *pāpacyate*, both would apply. [This is resolved by] the rule of "prohibition of the exception" (*apavādavipratiṣedha*).
Since [the condition of] being subsequent exists, length will occur.

Now, if it is asked: "Why does *itva* not occur in *babhaṇatuḥ* and *babhaṇuḥ*, given that once *jaśtva* has been applied by the rule 'ṭhabhyāse carca' (P. 8.4.54), the root begins with a consonant (*ādeśāditvāt*)?"—[we reply: No, because of *etva*.

Because the substitution of *jaś* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when the operation is to be performed, therefore the substitution of *atva* must indeed take place. However, there is an opportunity for the rule of mutual exclusion (*vipratiṣedha*) where the substitution of *ścutva* is applied by the rule *ṭhkuhoścuḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.62)—
as in *cakaṇatuḥ*, *cakaṇuḥ*, *jahasatuḥ*, *jahasuḥ*, and so forth.
To address this, he says "here," and so forth. How is it known that there is no lack of established status (*asiddhatva*)?

To this he says "and thus," and so forth. Only then does the substitution of *e* for the roots *phal* and *bhaj*—as prescribed by Pāṇini 6.4.122, "tṛphalabhajatrapaśca"—become possible, provided that the rules for *jaś*-substitution and *cut*-substitution do not have a lack of established status.
Not otherwise; because it is not included in the *anādiś* group, the substitution of *et* is already established by this very rule, so that [the objection] is untenable.
Therefore, since the substitution of *et* is prescribed for *phali* and *bhajri*, the non-establishment (*asiddhatva*) of *jaśtva* and *cartva* is accepted here.

"It does not exist," as in "and when there is no difference in form" (*rūpābhede ca*), and so forth. The fact that the prohibition of *śas* and *dad* in the rule "not for *śas*, *dad*, and those beginning with *vā*, nor for the guṇa [vowels]" (*na śasadadavādiguṇānām*, 6.4.126) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of this meaning: "when there is no difference in the form of the substituend (*sthānin*), that which is the substitute (*ādeśa*) is not accepted here. Furthermore, [the rule] "in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāse*), *c* and *j* [are substituted for *ch* and *jh*]" (*abhyāse carcā*) [serves as another indicator].

By this [rule], (8.4.54), the *jaś* sounds of the original [substituends] become *jaś* sounds, and the *car* sounds of the original [substituends] become *car* sounds; thus, the *ś* of *śas* becomes *ś*, and the *d* of *dad-* also becomes *d*.
Therefore, both of them remain as they were before the substitution. In that regard, if there is no difference in the substituend (*sthānin*)...

If that substitute were also to be adopted here, then, because it would be a substitute [for the original], the substitution of *e* for *śas* and *si* would not occur; consequently, the prohibition of the substitution of *e* for *śas* and *si* would not need to be formulated. Yet, it has been formulated.
Therefore, this very statement of prohibition makes known that when there is no difference in form, the substitute is not to be adopted here.
Thus [it is said]. If, then, this [principle] were resorted to, what would happen? To this he says: "Otherwise, however" (*anyathā hi*), and so forth.

Otherwise, even that substitute which, due to the non-difference of its form, is identical in form with the original element (*sthānin*) would also be resorted to here; consequently, just as the substitution of *et* does not occur for forms such as *cakaṇatuḥ*, it likewise [would not occur] for *pecatuḥ*.
The same would apply to *pacitya* and others, which have *ca* and so forth as their natural (*prakṛti*) suffixes—

those for whom *ca* and so forth are natural suffixes. In the examples "ahaṃ papaṭha" (I studied) and "ahaṃ papaca" (I cooked), because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the suffix is not treated as having the *kit* designation due to its being *pit*.

Therefore, the substitution of *et* and the elision of the penultimate vowel (*abhyāsalopa*) do not occur. Nor does the *vṛddhi* [substitution] take place; for according to the option "the first person singular ending *ṇal* is optionally *ṇit*" (Pāṇini 7.1.91), there is an absence of the *ṇit* designation. However, in the case where it is *ṇit*, since the *vṛddhi* would prevail by virtue of its higher status, it would preclude both the *et* substitution and the elision of the penultimate vowel; thus, this [rule applies] in the alternative where it is not *ṇit*.

Thus it has been illustrated by the rule "dambheḥ. But what is the reason that the substitution of *e* for *ai* does not occur in *dambh*, since this entire base (*aṅga*) undergoes substitution [of *liṭ*] after the initial letter? It is because [the rule] "aniditām... (Pāṇini 6.4.24) and so forth [prevents it].
Why is it that the vowel *a* occurs only when there is elision (*lopa*) between two single consonants? To this, he says: "of the elision of *na*" (*nalopasya*), and so forth.

In the Vārttika on the rule *granthi-śranthi-dambhi-svañjīnām* (Vārttika 17), it is stated that the *liṭ* suffix following *dambh* is *kit*; when that is present, regarding the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) that occurs therein—
Because of the rule "asiddhavat tad bhavati" (Pāṇini 6.4.22), [the substitution] does not apply due to its being treated as non-existent.

Therefore, the substitution of *e* for the root *dambh* must be stated; that is to say, it must be explained. In this regard, the following is the explanation: in the rule "śnasorallopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.111)...

The non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the technical non-validity (*asiddhatva*) taught in the *bhāṣya* has been made known; by that, when the substitution of *e* for *dambh-* is to be applied, the non-validity of the elision (*lopa*) does not occur, and consequently, the substitution of *liṭ* for *dambh-* will take place. Alternatively, in the rule "ata ekahalmadhye" (Pāṇini 6.4.120), the term "ataḥ" [is understood].

A separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must be made; by means of this, wherever *itva* is desired, it will occur there. And having done so, even such [provisions] as "the substitution of *it* for the *liṭ* [augment] of *naś* and *man*" (Vārttika 793) need not be added as a supplement, because they are established by the very separation of the rule.

It should be understood that in all cases, the meaning of the word *vaktavya* is "to be explained. Regarding *aneśam*: by the rule *tasthasthamipām* (Pāṇini 3.4.101), there is the substitution of *am* for *mip*.
Now, why is the substitution of *it* not applied here in *menakā* by the rule *pratyayasthāt* (Pāṇini 7.3.44)?

Does [the *it* augment] occur? To this he says: "In the case of *kṣipakā* and so forth," and so on. A prohibition of the *it* augment will be stated for words beginning with *kṣipakā*; since these are included among the *kṣipakā*-type words, the *it* is not applied. Regarding "in the case of *cānaś*": [this refers to] Pāṇini 3.2.129, "The suffix *cānaś* is used in the sense of habitual action (*tacchīlya*), age (*vayaḥ*), and capacity (*śakti*)," and [the rule] "muk. is not [applied].

Regarding the statement "it is performed": the suffix *muk* would have applied by the rule *āne muk* (Pāṇini 7.2.82), but it does not occur because of the principle that "the teaching of augments is not mandatory" (*anityam āgamaśāsanam*).
Alternatively, due to its Vedic character, according to the rule "all rules are optional in the Veda" (*sarve vidhayaś chandasi vikalpyante*).

"The shortening [of the vowel] is Vedic. According to *ṅyāpoḥ saṃjñācchandasorbahulam* (Pāṇini 6.3.63), the shortening prescribed for feminine stems ending in *ṅī* and *āp* occurs frequently; thus, by virtue of the word "frequently" (*bahulam*), it also applies here in the case of *pir-iran*. [The derivation is as follows:
from the root *pac*, there is the suffix *liṅ*, the augment *sīyuṭ*, *ran* for the *jh* ending, and the *śap* verbal suffix.
By the rule "ṭhādguṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.87), when the substitution of *ai* and the shortening of the vowel would otherwise apply to *pacairan*, the result becomes *peciran*.
121. *thali ca seṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.121). [Examples:

*ṭhpecitha*, *śekitha*. Since the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *upadeśe 'tvataḥ* (7.2.62) would have applied here, the restriction *ṛto bhāradvājasya* (7.2.63) causes *iṭ* to occur in this instance.

Therefore, this is the meaning here: [the rule applies] specifically to *bhāradvāja*, and not to other verbal roots. Regarding the form *papaktha*: according to the opinion of other teachers, the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* indeed occurs.
Now, for what purpose is the mention of *thal* [in the rule]? One could simply say "not before *sa*" (*na soṭi*); for in a case where [the augment] is not [prohibited] by the preceding rule...
The statement is made for that purpose; otherwise, in cases such as *iṭ* and so on, it would already be established by the preceding rule due to the *kit* designation.
One might ask: "In that case, even without the mention of *thal*, it will apply only to *thal*?
To this he says: "The mention of *thal*" and so forth; for if the mention of *thal* were absent...

On the basis of the purposefulness of its commencement, this much certainty may be reached: that this [rule] exists for the sake of that which cannot be accomplished by the preceding one. However, the claim that it is "for the sake of *aṅ* and so forth" (*akṅdirtham*) is difficult to determine; many specific cases have been introduced, and therein doubt might arise as to whether this is indeed for the sake of *aṅ* and so forth.

Could it be for the sake of providing a substitute (*ādeśa*), or rather for the sake of [the rule] concerning the middle of multiple consonants (*anekahal-madhya*), or perhaps for the sake of [the rule] concerning multiple vowels (*anekākāra*)? In that regard, for the sake of removing ambiguity,
all these specific rules— such as *ata ekahalmadhye'nādeśāder liṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.120)— [are intended].

Thus, [the rules] follow here as well. Let it be understood that *kṅit* has been excluded. Therefore, this undertaking is for the sake of *kṅit*. Furthermore, there is no other *seṭ* suffix beginning with *kṅ* besides *thal* in this context.

Consequently, by virtue of this implication (*sāmarthyāt*), this rule must be explained as applying specifically to *thal*. This is the understanding reached through the medium of such an interpretation.
For those of dull intellect, there might be a lack of respect for the rule; therefore, the mention of *thal* is made for the sake of clarity.
Indeed, when *akṅti* is included [in the definition], the meaning is easily understood: "This new rule (*ārambha*) is intended for cases other than those where *k* or *ṅ* follows."

122. *tṛÃ-phala-bhaj-tra-paś-ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.122). [Examples: *teratuḥ*, *teruḥ*. By the rule *ṛcchatyṛtām* (7.4.11), there is *guṇa* [substitution]. [Examples: *phelatuḥ*, *pheluḥ*. [The roots] *phala* in the sense of "ripening" (*niṣpatti*) [Dhātupāṭha 530], and *ñi phalā* in the sense of "bursting open" (*viśaraṇa*).

And thus [it is stated] in the Dhātupāṭha (516): "For the sake of the guna of √trai. He will state the prohibition [in Pāṇini 6.4.123]: "Not for śas, dā, vā, etc., nor for those that have undergone guna.
Therefore, this statement regarding √trai is so that even for that which has already been established as having undergone guna, [the rule applies].

The phrase "syād ity evam artham" means that it should be explained as having this purpose: namely, that the substitution of *e* for *i* occurs even for the root *śranth* [as well as *granth*], according to the rule "it should be stated that [the substitution applies] after *śranth*" (*śrantheś ca vaktavyam*). This is the meaning of the statement that the *etva* (substitution of *e*) also takes place for the root *grantha-śrantha* in the sense of "binding" (*sandarbhe*), as listed in the Dhātupāṭha (1511, 1512). In that regard, this...

The explanation is as follows: the particle *ca* is used here in the sense of "also" (*apyarthe*), and it serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; by this, the rule will apply to the root *śranth* as well. Thus, in the forms *śrethatuḥ* and *śrethuḥ*, the elision of the nasal (*nakāra*) occurs because the *liṭ* affixes are *kit* by virtue of the aforementioned supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*).

123. *rādha* in the sense of injury. (Pāṇini 6.4.121) Regarding the rule "in the sense of injury," etc.: although the root *rādhi* is listed in the sense of accomplishment (*saṃsiddhi*) as "rādha, sādha, saṃsiddhau" (Dhātupāṭha 1262, 2363), here [it is used]...

Nevertheless, since verbal roots have multiple meanings, it should be understood that [the root *rādh*] has the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*). It is stated that when *rādh* has the meaning of injury, the substitution of *e* for the *a*-vowel occurs.
But is it not the case that there is no mention of the term "*a-varṇa*" (the vowel *a*) in this rule? Even if such an *a*-vowel were present here, it is the one under discussion (*prakṛta*).

One might object: "That [substitution] also depends on the duration of the vowel (mātrākāla), yet there is no vowel *a* of one-mora duration in the root *rādh*; how then can the substitution of *e* be obtained for the vowel *a*? To such an objection, he replies: "'From this (*ataḥ*), this [word] is present here,' and so forth. Regarding the word "from this" (*ataḥ*):

Because it is marked with the *svarita* accent, it is present here; and since that which is present here lacks the specific duration produced by the marker *t* (in *tapara*), it sets that aside—leaving it behind—and indicates (*pratyāyayati*) or brings to mind (*udbodhayati*) the mere phoneme *a* as the substituendum (*sthānin*). Otherwise, its presence would be purposeless.

Regarding the passage beginning with *ṭhatha vā*: by the rule *ṭhśnābhyastayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.112), he indicates the original element (*sthānin*) which is being carried over from that sūtra. Furthermore, by the word *ṭhātaḥ*, he shows the original element which is being carried over—from the rule *ṭhśnābhyastayorāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.4).

"It should be explained that *it* [the word *ataḥ*] continues [from the previous rule]. And when it is explained in this way, the substitution of *i* for the vowel of the root *rādh* is understood; for if *ataḥ* continues, then because of its proximity here as well, even in the rule "ṭhata ekahalmadhye" (Pāṇini 6.4.120), [the same applies].

Does he not obtain [the form] *śaśāsa* as in *śaśasima*? This is not a fault; its recurrence here follows the analogy of the frog’s leap (*maṇḍūkayati*). [The rule] begins with *ekahalmadhye vā*. Alternatively, the phrase *ekahalmadhye* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].

Even in that case, because [the condition] is impossible as it continues to apply, the word "here" (iha) does not function [as a restriction]. Therefore, that which is a constituent part (*avayava*) within a single consonant of the root *rādh* becomes the substituendum (*sthānin*), and since that is indeed the vowel *ā*, its substitution by *etva* (the substitution of *e* for *ā*) will occur.

124. *vā jṛ-bhramu-trasām* (Pāṇini 6.4.124). This rule provides for the substitution of *guṇa* for the root *jṛ* (*jṛ vayohānau*, Dhātupāṭha 1494; note: the reading *jṛ* is found in the Mu. manuscript), for the purpose of applying the *guṇa* vowel;
for the purpose of the substitute [of *bhrāma*] for *bhrami*; and for the purpose of [applying the rule regarding] vowels situated between more than one consonant.
And [the rule] for the root *tras* is for the sake of cases where there are multiple consonants in the middle, as in *jajaratuḥ*; here, the guṇa substitution occurs as before.

125. *phaṇāñca saptānām* (Pāṇini 6.4.125). Because of the use of the plural number in the rule, the sense of "beginning with" is understood. Therefore, he says: "of *phaṇa* and the others," and so forth. [The roots are:
*phaṇa* (to move, Dhātupāṭha 821), *rājṛ* (to shine, Dhātupāṭha 822), *ṭua bhrājṛ*... [and so on].

*bhrāśṛ*, *bhlāśṛ*, and *dīptau* (DhP 823–825); *syam*, *svan*, and *dhvan* in the sense of "sound" (DhP 826–828). Excluding *dhvan*, these seven beginning with *phaṇ* are the group [of roots]. Among them, for the first one (*bhrāśṛ*), the rule applies even though it is already established by necessity; the statement is made for the sake of providing an option (*vikalpa*). For the others, however, it applies where it was not previously established. In that regard, concerning the roots beginning with *rājṛ*:

Regarding the statement made in the rule *ṭhrādho hiṃsāyām* (6.4.123)— namely, that "the [substitute] *ataḥ* is understood here"— it should be understood as applying according to the possibility of its occurrence for each of the four vowels (*avarṇa*).

126. *na śasadadavādiguṇānām* (Pāṇini 6.4.126). Here, if by the word *guṇa* one refers specifically to that vowel *a* for which the substitution of *e* was prescribed [by Pāṇini 1.1.2], then the meaning is this: "it does not occur for the vowel *a* when it is a *guṇa*. Likewise...
Thinking that the rule for the formation of *caitva* would otherwise have no scope,

[the author], intending to show that here the vowel *ā* is not being taught as a *guṇa* itself, but rather as a word derived from the term *guṇa*, says: "And of that which is thus derived as *guṇa*," and so forth.

The meaning is that when a sound is produced after the utterance of a word denoting a *guṇa*, the substitution of *etva* (the change to *e*) does not occur in place of the vowel *a* that belongs to that [word]. Furthermore, its connection with that [word] should be understood according to the circumstances, whether it is because it occupies the position of that [vowel] or because it is a constituent part of it. Thus, in this way...

The cause for the prohibition is the non-existence of a related [augment] in that which is produced by a word expressing a quality (*guṇa*), whereas the other is the cause for the application; such is the distinction between the scope of the rule and the prohibition. "viśaśasatuḥ":
[from the root] *śasu* "to injure" (DhP 727). "dadade": [from the root] *dada* "to give."
Regarding "vavamatuḥ": the root is *vam* (DhP 849), meaning "to vomit.
Regarding "viśaśaratuḥ": the root is *śṛ* (DhP 1488), meaning "to injure.
The examples illustrate the meaning of what was stated in the passage beginning with "of that which is produced from a word denoting a quality" (*guṇaśabdabhinirvṛtasya*).
[The author] demonstrates this: in the case of *viśaśaratuḥ*, this sound *ar* is produced from the word "guṇa" (substitution);

for the vowel *a* related to that [guṇa] is a constituent part (*ekadeśa*) of it. In the case of *lulavitha*, here too the vowel *o* is produced from the word "guṇa"; for the vowel *a* related to that [guṇa] occupies its place (*sthānika*). Now, one might object:

In the case of *ṭhviśaśaratuḥ*, it is argued that only the vowel *a* is produced by the term "guṇa," and not the syllable *ār*. This is not so; for the letter *r* is a subordinate part (*guṇabhakta*) of the guṇa. And thus says the Bhāṣya: "There is a guṇa, there is an *ār*."
There is an increase: that which is accompanied by the letter *r* is designated as *guṇa* or *vṛddhi*.

127. *arvaṇastrasāvanañaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.127). [The rule states: "The substitute *tras* occurs [for the final phoneme of *arvan*]. This substitution applies to the end [of the word], because [the substitute] consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), according to the principle: "A property based on an *anubandha* does not cause [a substitute] to have more than one phoneme" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 14); for [the substitute *tras*] consists of a single phoneme (*ekāl*), since the letter *k* is an *anubandha*.
Because the letter *u* is an *anubandha*, the word *su* is understood as the nominative singular;

therefore, it indeed occurs in the locative plural—as in *arvatsu*. And since that [suffix] does not follow a negative particle (*nañ*), the word *cet* which was under discussion here also applies in this case, as in *arvantau*.

Because the vowel *ṛ* is treated as having the marker *uk* for the purpose of grammatical operations, the suffix *num* is applied by the rule *ugidacām* (Pāṇini 7.1.70). Thus we have *arvati*. By the rule *ugitaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.6), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added, resulting in *ārvatī*. In the form *ārvatam*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied when there is a desire to express the sense of "offspring. Now, one might object that according to the maxim of "negation and connection" (*nañivayuktanyāya*), [the term should not apply here].

Is it because of similarity that *su* must necessarily follow only after a case-ending (*vibhakti*)? This is not so; this is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation). For this very reason, the author of the Vṛtti stated: "If *su* follows, [the rule does not apply]"; otherwise, [if it were a relative negation], it would mean "if there is a *sup* other than *su* which follows... [and so on].

One might say that [the word *para*] means "other" (*paro bhavati*). Or even if it is a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion), there is still no fault; for the rule regarding the negative particle (*nañ*) is non-eternal (*anitya*). Its non-eternality is understood from the inclusion of the term "case-ending" (*vibhakti*) in the sūtra *ṭhoṣadheśca vibhaktāvaprathamāyām* (Pāṇini 6.3.132). If...
For if it were eternal, it would apply only to those [suffixes] that are not excluded by the first exception (prathamāparyudāsa),
and thus one would not have made the mention of "vibhakti" (case-ending); yet, by making that mention, it indicates that this paribhāṣā is non-eternal (anitya).
128. *maghavā bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.4.128). In the word *maghavā*, by the transposition of case endings (*suvvyatyaya*), the nominative stands in place of the genitive; thus [the form] is *madhoḥ*.
By the rule *śvayuvamaghonām* (6.4.133), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the vowel, followed by the substitution of the preceding [vowel] for the subsequent one (*parapūrvatva*).

"Ṭhādguṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.87). Now, one might object: since there is the intention to express the sense of possession (*matvartha*) in the form "one who has *magha*," this word *maghavan* ends in the suffix *vanip*, according to the Vārttika: "In the Vedic language, *vanip* should be prescribed [after *magha*]. In that case, when the *vanip* suffix undergoes vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) and the designation *bha* applies, [the rule] "of that which [ends in *i* or *u*]" (*yasyeti ca*) [would apply].

Should there not be elision by [Pāṇini 6.4.148] *ca*, and as a result, would there not arise the undesirable form *madhunaḥ*? This is not so; for this is indeed a different, unanalyzed nominal stem (*prātipadika*), since its usage is observed even in the feminine gender. Or else, it ends in the suffix *vanip*.

Could it be so? Even in this case, because of the frequent usage (*bahulavacanāt*), the elision prescribed by *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148) will not occur; thus there is no fault. Regarding *maghonī*: [the suffix] *ṅīp* is applied by *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* (4.1.5). Regarding *māghavanam*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied as before, and [the final syllable is elided] by *an* (6.4.67).
The state of being like the original form.

129. *bhasya* | (6.4.129) 130. *pādaḥ pat* | (6.4.130) Regarding the word *pādaḥ*: it is understood that the word *pāda* is taken here with its final vowel *a* elided. Now, regarding the root *pādayati*:

Why is the word *pād* that results from the suffix *kvip* not included [in the rule]? Because it is impossible. For could the suffix *kvip* not apply to the root *pād* by the rule "it is seen after others as well" (*anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*, Pāṇini 3.2.178)?
That [suffix] does not occur because of the statement "it is seen"; for where in common usage is there an employment of a form ending in *kvip* [from this root]?

The word "is seen" (*dṛśyate*) is used there for the purpose of showing that it actually occurs; for although the usage of the root *pād* with the suffix *kvip* is not observed, the vowel *ā* is elided only within a compound of the word *pāda*,
and therefore, by implication, the grammatical operation is understood to apply to a stem ending in that [form].

Thus he says: "of that which ends in this [element], namely the *aṅga*," and so forth. If, then, this substitution *pad* were understood as applying to the *aṅga* ending in the word *pād*, then—since by the rule "that which is not a prescription for a whole is [a prescription] for what ends in it" (Pāṇini 1.1.72), the substitution would apply to the entire form ending in that—the author says: "And that," and so forth.

Regarding "dvipadaḥ": this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one who has two feet. The elision of the vowel [of the second member] occurs by the rule "saṃkhyāsupūrvasya" (Pāṇini 5.4.140). Regarding "dvipadikām": this means "one who gives two feet [as a fine]," and the suffix *vun* is applied by the rule "pādaśatasya" (Pāṇini 5.4.1), etc. Regarding "vaiyāghrapadyaḥ": [this is derived from vyāghrapāt].

The term *vyāghrapada* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose feet are like those of a tiger. According to Pāṇini 5.4.138, *pādasya lopo'hastyādibhyaḥ*, there is the elision of the vowel *a* [of *pāda*]. Then, in the sense of "the descendant of Vyāghrapada," the suffix *yañ* is applied because the word belongs to the *garga-ādi* group.
131. *Vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam* (Pāṇini 6.4.131).

Since the technical rule regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*) (Bhāṣya-sūtra 7) dictates that the operation applies to that which ends in the suffix, he says: "of that which ends in *vasu*, etc. [The example is] *viduṣaḥ*. [This is derived from] *videḥ śatur vasuḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.36).

Regarding "papuṣaḥ": the suffix *kvasu* is applied in place of *liṭ* by the rule "kvasuśca" (Pāṇini 3.2.107); the elision of the radical vowel and the reduplication occurs according to the rule beginning with "ata ekahalmadhye" (Pāṇini 6.4.120). Regarding "papuṣaḥ":
the elision of the long *ā* occurs by the rule "āto lopa iṭi ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.64). Now, [one might ask], if there is an elision of the vowel *ā*,...

Since the *samprasāraṇa* substitution is not established (*asiddha*) when an operation is to be performed, how can there be elision of the vowel *ā* here? To this he says: "When the elision of the vowel *ā* is to be performed," and so forth. The elision of the vowel *ā* occurs because of the *samprasāraṇa*, and that [elision] occurs because of the case-ending (*vibhakti*); thus, there is a mutual dependence (*vayāśrayatva*). Therefore, there is no state of being unestablished (*asiddhatva*). But surely...

According to the principles "when there is the mention of that which has a single *anubandha*, there is no [application of] that which has two *anubandhas*" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 52), or "when there is the mention of that which has such-and-such an *anubandha*, there is no [application of] that which does not have such-and-such an *anubandha*" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 54),
there ought to be no mention of *kvasu* here; so how is it that we have forms such as *papuṣaḥ* and *pecuṣaḥ*?

"How does the *samprasāraṇa* occur? To this he says: "In the mention of *vasu*, etc. This is to be understood from the addition of the indicatory letter *u* (*ū*) to *vas*, which is a substitute for the suffix *śatṛ*. For the sole purpose of adding the indicatory letter *u* is that there may be a general inclusion [of the forms] here. But is it not for the sake of the quality of being *udātta*?
Could it be so? No; for the operation required by the designation *ugit* is already established by the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if occupying the original position).

132. *vāha ūṭh* (Pāṇini 6.4.132). Regarding the term *vāhaḥ*: this word *vah* ends in the suffix *ṇvi*, and that *ṇvi* is prescribed only after this root when it is accompanied by an upapada. Therefore, by implication, it is understood that the rule applies to that which ends in [the suffix] *ṇvi*; thus he says—*vāha*.

"Thus ends [the section] beginning with 'ityevamantasya'," etc. "The *ūṭ* is this [very one]"—this *ū* is the vowel *ū*. It is for the purpose of specification in the rule "before *eti*, *edhati*, and *ūṭ*" (Pāṇini 6.1.89). "Samprasāraṇa occurs"—from where is this specific term "samprasāraṇa" obtained? From the preceding sūtra.
This is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *samprasāraṇa*. But for what purpose is *samprasāraṇa* repeated here?

It is for the purpose of restricting the substituend (*sthānin*). If this were not repeated, then by the rule "the *samprasāraṇa* [substitutes] of *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, and *ḷ* in place of *yaṇ*" (Pāṇini 1.1.45), it would have to apply only in place of *yaṇ*. For example, in the case of *praṣṭhauhaḥ*—[derived from] *praṣṭhṃa*...
The suffix *ṇvi* is applied [to the root *vah*] by the rule *vahaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.64), while the preceding rule *bhajo ṇviḥ* (3.2.62) is still in force.
Now, for what purpose is the augment *ūṭh* inserted; why is the sūtra not simply *vāha*?

The intended meaning is that [the rule] must be applied. "When the *samprasāraṇa* has indeed been performed"—this is because the mention of *samprasāraṇa* is carried over from the preceding sūtra. "And when the *guṇa* has been performed"—this is the connection [of the word "performed"]. As for the *guṇa*, it occurs by the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.86), even though the suffix *ṇvu* has been elided.

[This is] by way of counter-exclusion (*pratyalakṣaṇa*). But surely, according to the rule "when there is a recurrence of a grammatical operation (*aṅgavṛtta*), there is no further application of that same operation once it has been completed" (*Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā* 38), once the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) has been performed, the *guṇa* substitution should not occur because [the operation] is already completed? [The answer is: there is no fault, because of the explicit statement "once it has been completed. For "completion" (*niṣṭhā*) refers to the finality of the word-form.

And that [eligibility for usage] occurs only when the word is fit for application. Furthermore, as long as the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) consisting of *guṇa* and other operations has not been performed, its fitness for application does not arise.
Therefore, even though the *samprasāraṇa* has already taken place, the *guṇa* substitution indeed occurs; in this regard, it might be argued as follows.

If *auṅ* were not applied, then in cases such as *śālivaham*, *dityavaham*, *śālyūhaḥ*, and *dityūhaḥ*—where the suffix *ṇvi* is prescribed after the root *vah* with the words *śāli* and *diti* as upapadas ending in the letter *n*—the forms would not be established; therefore, he says: "and when the upapada ends in the letter *n*."

And so forth. By the rule *vahaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.64), because the mention of *chandas* from the preceding rule *chandasi sahaḥ* (3.2.63) is understood here as well, the suffix *ṇvi* is prescribed only for the Vedic language (*chandas*). Furthermore, since the prescription [of suffixes] in the Veda is based on observed usage, the suffix *ṇvi* is seen after the root *vah* only when preceded by an upapada ending in *a*, such as *praṣṭha* and others, specifically within the Vedic language. It is not [seen otherwise].

[The word] *tvak* occurs at the end of words such as *śālī*. But how is the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā* (the maxim concerning external elements) made known by this [sūtra]? To this he says: "For in that case," and so forth. Furthermore, the status of the *samprasāraṇa* as *bahiraṅga* is established by depending upon the designation *bha*, which is caused by an external suffix beginning with a vowel (*ādi*).
Because [the substitution] has already taken effect; however, the *guṇa* [substitution] is internal (*antaraṅga*), because it has already taken effect when the external suffix has not yet arisen.

What, then, is the purpose of making known this *paribhāṣā*? It is for the sake of establishing the status as "already accomplished" (*siddhatva*) of that which is characterized by being external (*bahiraṅga*) in forms such as *pacāvedam* and *yajāvedam*.

Therefore, this substitution of *ai* does not occur by virtue of being an internal (*antaraṅga*) rule, because the *guṇa* [substitution] is an external (*bahiraṅga*) rule. Its externality arises from its dependence upon two words (*pada*),
whereas the internality of the *ai*-substitution results from the opposite.

133. *śvayuvamaghonāmataddhite* (6.4.133). Regarding *yūnaḥ*: when the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) has been performed and the preceding vowel has been substituted [for the semivowel], there is long-vowel simplification (*savarṇadīrghatva*). Regarding *śauvam*: there is the elision of the suffixal *ṭi* by *nastaddhite* (6.4.144). *Yauvanam*.
Thus: in the case of *yūno bhāvaḥ* ("the state of being young"), the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *hāyanāntayuvādibhyo'ṇ* (Pāṇini 5.1.130).

Because of the preservation of the original stem (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *an* (6.4.167), the elision of the final syllable (*ṭilopa*) and the elision of the penultimate vowel (*al-lopa*) prescribed by the rule *ṭeḥ* (6.4.143) do not take place. Regarding *māghavanam*: [it means] "that which has Maghavan as its deity."

The suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "ṭhsāsya devatā" (Pāṇini 4.2.24), and as before, there is the preservation of the original stem form (*prakṛtibhāva*). To derive the word "śauvam," he says: "the modification of a dog," and so forth. Even though the word *yuva* ends in the suffix *ti*, when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included.

By the rule "grahaṇam" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 29), *samprasāraṇa* would apply. Furthermore, even for *madhavan*, once the substitution of *tri* has been made, by the principle "that which is modified in one part is not different from the original" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 16), it would follow that the rule applies even to the form ending in *takāra*. Why, then, does it not occur?
Thus he says: "of dogs, etc. and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "for that purpose": this is for the sake of ensuring that [the suffix] applies only to those ending in *n*, and not to those not ending in *n*. As for the statement "the word *ana* is the remainder for both," [it refers to] *ana*.
Since both of these *yogās* are subordinate (*śeṣa*) and constituent parts (*avayava*), the rule "anaḥ" does not effect the extension (*atideśa*) of the remaining *samprasāraṇa*.
134. *allopo'naḥ* (6.4.134). The inclusion of the indicatory letter *ṛ* (*taparakaraṇam*) is for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that this might be a *nañ*-compound. For example:
*rājakīyaḥ* (or *rājakīyam*, according to the Kāśikā). [The suffix] *cha* is applied after a compound whose final member is *garta*.

Since the suffix *cha* is applicable by [Pāṇini 4.2.137], the rule "ṭhrājñaḥ ka ca" (4.2.140) applies, whereby *cha* is added and the letter *ka* is substituted for the final [letter] of the stem. Here too, the principle holds that "that which has undergone a partial modification is treated as not different from the original" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 16).

135. *ṣapūrvahandhṛtarājñāmaṇi* (6.4.135). This rule is stated so that, by virtue of the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of grammatical operations) prescribed by *ṭhan* (6.4.167), the elision of the final vowel (*al-lopa*) might not be prevented. [Examples: *āukṣṇaḥ*, *tākṣṇaḥ*. [The stems are] *ukṣan* and *takṣan*.

From these two [roots], the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of offspring; thus, "bhrauṇahatya" [is formed]. [The derivation is as follows: from the root *han* with the object *bhrūṇa*, the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *brahmabhrūṇavṛtreṣu hanaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.87). From that which ends in *kvip*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied. Then, by the rule *ho hanter ñṇinneṣu* (Pāṇini 7.3.54), the substitution of *gh* for *h* occurs.
Thus [is explained] the substitution of *kutva*. Regarding "dhārtarājñaḥ": from the word *ghṛtarāja*, by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the suffix *aṇ* is applied.

Regarding "sāmanaḥ, vaimanaḥ": the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.120], "tasyedam" (*this belongs to that*). [The statement] "both do not occur" refers to the fact that the *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) takes precedence over both the elision of *a* (*allopa*) and the elision of *i* (*ṭilopa*).

Because of the specific rule [vidhāna]: "tākṣṇyaḥ. When the suffix *ṇya* is applicable by the rule "from *kuru* and others, *ṇya*" (Pāṇini 4.1.151), the suffix *ṇya* is applied here because it is included in the group beginning with *senānta-lakṣaṇa-kārin* (4.1.152).

Then, by the rule "and when *ya* follows, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) except in the case of abstract nouns (*bhāva*) and actions (*karman*)" (6.4.168), the original form is maintained.

136. *vibhāṣā iṅśyoḥ* (6.4.136). [The commentary states: "And in the case of the word *śī*. By this, the term *śī* is understood as that which is prescribed by the rule *napuṃsakācca* (7.1.19), and not that which is prescribed by *jaśśasoḥ śiḥ* (7.1.20).
He shows that the word *śi* has been prescribed so that this [term] may be understood as referring to it. But how is this known? Because the designation *bha* does not apply to the word *śi*.

137. *na saṃyogād vamantāt* (6.4.137). [The example is] *prati dīvnā*. The lengthening [of the vowel] is by [the rule] *hali ca* (8.2.77). Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *anta-* ("ending in")? Why not simply say *damaḥ*? [Because of the restriction that the rule applies only when the suffix begins with a consonant followed by *v* or *m*,] due to the *saṃyoga* (conjunction) of the letters *v* and *m*.

And since the rule of "specifying that which ends with" (tadantavidhi) applies when there is a qualification, is it not the case that the rule of specifying that which ends with is obtained even without the explicit mention of the word "end" (anta)? This is true; however, the mention of the word "end" is for the sake of clarity.

138. *acaḥ* | (6.4.138) "The term *acaḥ* here refers to the root *añc-* with its nasal (*n*) elided. Why is this so? Why is the *pratyāhāra* [of vowels] not understood? It cannot be so, because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of [the rule] *allopaḥ* (6.4.134).

The term *pratyāhāra* is used for the purpose of inclusion. If there were an inclusion by means of a *pratyāhāra*, then the vowel *a* would be qualified by it; and in that case, the inclusion by *pratyāhāra* would be purposeless, for the vowel *a* never deviates from being a vowel (*ac*). But surely the *aṅga* (base) is the subject under discussion; that [would be qualified] by the *pratyāhāra*.

Is it distinguished [from other rules] by the phrase "of a stem ending in *a*"? No; for if that were so, the meaning of the sūtra would be "there is elision of *a* belonging to a stem ending in *a*. In that case, the elision prescribed by "yasyeti ca" (P. 6.4.148) would be redundant, since the desired result would already be established by this very rule. Furthermore...

The mention [of the rule] *ṭhyauprāgapāgudakpratīco yat* (Pāṇini 4.2.101), and so forth, is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) here that there is no inclusion of a *pratyāhāra*. For if there were an inclusion of a *pratyāhāra*, there would be no inclusion of the root *añc-* here; for this [form] is not a stem (*aṅga*) ending in an *ac* vowel. Precisely for this reason...

Because of this specific mention, even the suffix *ac* (pacādyac) is not included [here]. For this member (*aṅga*) ending in *ac* is not present in the form "dadhīcaḥ. In "dadhīcaḥ," the suffix *kvin* is applied by the rule *ṛtvig-ādinā* (Pāṇini 3.2.59), as in "he who moves crookedly" (*dadhy-añcati*); then, by the rule *āniditām* (6.4.24), there is the elision of the nasal; and finally, by the rule *cau* (6.3.138), [the shortening of the vowel occurs].
Long.
Regarding the form *kīlālapaḥ*: when the suffix *vic* is prescribed by the rule *vijupe chandasi* (3.2.73), [the elision of the final vowel] applies to the root-final *ā*.
The suffix *vic* is applied by the rule *manin-kvanip-vanip-śaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.74). [In the case of] *niy*, there is the suffix *kvip*; [the vowel *i*] undergoes the *iyaṅ* substitution.

141. *mantreṣv āṅy-āder ātmanaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.141). The designation *āṅ* was established by the ancient teachers for the third case singular (*tṛtīyaikavacana*). [The rule] "the form *āṅ* is seen even elsewhere" applies here as well. The word "in mantras" (*mantreṣu*)...

This is understood from the use of the plural number (*bahuvacana*). For by the use of the plural, this meaning is indicated: "this reference has many objects. And it becomes one that has many objects only if [the suffix] occurs after *āṅ* in some other instance as well, and not otherwise. [As in the example: *ṭhmānyāsamañjata*.

In the singular locative case [of the word *saptamī*], there is an elision of the initial [vowel] here. The mention of "the beginning" (*ādi*) is for the sake of subsequent rules; however, in this instance, because the term "from *āt*" (*ātaḥ*) is understood from the preceding rule (Pāṇini 6.4.140), it can be established that even without the mention of "the beginning," the elision occurs only of the initial [vowel].
To understand.

142. *ti-viṃśater-ḍiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.142). Regarding the example *viṃśakaḥ*: by the rule *viṃśati-triṃśadbhyāṃ ḍvun asaṃjñāyām* (5.1.24), the suffix *ḍvun* is applied; when the syllable *ti* is elided, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatvam*) occurs by the rule *ato guṇe* (6.1.97).

Regarding "ṭhviṃśaṃ śatam" (one hundred and twenty): the suffix *ḍa* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.46, *śadantarviśateśca*, meaning "twenty is added to this. Thus we have *viṃśaḥ* and *ekaviṃśaḥ*. The suffix *ḍaṭ* is applied to denote the ordinal number of that [unit] according to 5.1.48. The explicit mention of the word *ti* is for the purpose of preventing [the application of the suffix] to *ati*.
143. *ṭeḥ* | (6.4.143) [The elision of] *ṭi* [is prescribed].
For example, "kumudvān" and so forth. [The suffix] *ḍmatup* is applied after *kumuda*, *naḍa*, and *vetasa* in the four senses [of the locative] according to Pāṇini 4.2.87.
"Upasarajaḥ": [the suffix] *ḍa* is applied after the root *jan* when preceded by a word in the locative case, according to Pāṇini 3.2.97. In this same manner...

The same applies here in the case of *maṇḍurajaḥ*. For in this instance, the shortening of the first member of the compound is governed by the rule *ṅyāpoḥ saṃjñācchandasorbahulam* (Pāṇini 6.3.63). Regarding *triṃśakaḥ*, the suffix *ḍvun* is applied as before. But surely the term *bhasya* (of a bha-stem) is understood [from the previous rule], and the suffix *ḍmatup* is not?

When the suffix *ḍa* is prescribed after a verbal root, the designation *bha* would apply to the preceding element because neither of the two [the suffix and the preceding element] begins with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) and because they are not *asva-dit*, as the case may be. Therefore, how does elision (*lopa*) occur here? To this he says: "In the presence of *ḍ*, even that which is not *bha*," and so forth. If there were no elision of *ṭi*...
If that were the case, then the status of being marked with *ḍ* (*ḍitva*) would be purposeless. Or, why could it not be understood in this way? [Objection:

If that were so, then the mention of the root *jan* after the elision of *ṭi* in the rule "prāvṛṭ-śarat-kāla-divāṃ je" (Pāṇini 6.3.15) would be untenable. Therefore, from this very mention, it is concluded that [the elision does] occur.

The letter *ḍ* in the suffix *dhātupratyaya* is designated as *it*. If that designation were not present, and if the elision of *ṭi* did not occur, then that designation would be purposeless. Furthermore, if the letter *ḍ* in the suffix *ḍmatup* were not elided, the name of that [suffix] could not be understood by means of its final part; and in that case, regarding the location—

The phrase "tannāmni" (4.2.67) is understood [to carry over]. Therefore, in that case as well, the letter ḍ must necessarily have the designation *it*, and by virtue of that, there must be elision (*lopa*) of the preceding vowel (*ṭi*).

144. *nastaddhite* (6.4.144). [The example] "sātvataḥ" is formed as follows: "the descendant of Satvata" (*satvato 'patyam*) takes the suffix *aṇ*. [Then] by the rule "the elision of the *ṭi* of that which ends in *n*" (*nāntasya ṭilopaḥ*), etc., [the final *a* is dropped].
But what is the reason that this is not established, such that an additional rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made?

Thus he says: "In this regard, those ending in *in*," and so forth. As for those ending in *an*, the rule *an-aḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.167) would result in the preservation of the original stem-form (*prakṛtibhāva*); this is how they are connected to the current context. Regarding *sābrahmacāraḥ*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to *tasyedam* (Pāṇini 4.3.120). Regarding *pīṭhasarpiṇaḥ*: [the suffix] *ima* is connected with the current context.

The connection is as follows: "paiṭhasarpāḥ" [is derived] by the suffix *aṇ* according to [Pāṇini 4.3.120] "tasyedam" ("this belongs to that"). "pīṭhasarpiṇaḥ" [is the base]; the connection is with the word "imaḥ" (these), which is under discussion. "paiṭhasarpāḥ" [is formed] with the suffix *aṇ* as before.
"kālāpāḥ" [is formed] with the suffix in the sense of "proclaimed by," as before.

By the rule *ṭhkalāpivaiśamyāyanāntevāsibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.3.104), the suffix *ṇini* would have been required due to [the teacher] being a pupil of Vaiśampāyana; however, this is set aside by the exception *ṭhkalāpino'ṇ* (4.3.108). Subsequently, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *ṭhadhīte tadveda* (4.2.59).

For that [word *kauthuma*], there is elision (*luk*) by the rule "ṭhproktālluk" (Pāṇini 4.2.64), and by the rule "cchandobrāhmaṇāni ca tadviṣayāṇi" (4.2.66), its scope is restricted to those who study or know [the text]. Thus, "Kauthumas" [is formed]; [here] the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "tasyedam" (4.3.120). [The phrase] "the work composed by him is [called so] by metaphorical designation," and so forth, [explains this].

But as for metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), there is no basis for it here because it is produced by that [very thing]. For a metaphorical designation occurs when something is produced by that [other thing], as in the expression: "All this ancient karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious, is being experienced.
Now, why is a metaphorical designation resorted to, rather than [using the rule] *adhikṛtya kṛte granthe* (Pāṇini 4.3.87)?

If one intends to express a secondary (śaiṣika) meaning in this manner, would not the taddhita suffix itself be applied? To this he says: "In the case of secondary meanings," and so forth. The words *taitili* and *jājali* are designated as *vṛddha*;
because they are *vṛddha*, that taddhita suffix which is prescribed for secondary meanings [is applied].

Otherwise, by the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.114), the suffix *cha* would apply; and if that were the case, forms such as *taitilāḥ* and *jājalāḥ* would not be established. Therefore, so that this fault does not occur, a figurative usage (*upacāra*) has been resorted to. By the word "thus" (*evam*), he demonstrates the etymological derivation mentioned previously.
In order to prevent the application of the suffix *cha*, the etymology of the word *lāṅgali* should be understood in this way:
the teacher is *Lāṅgali*, and the treatise composed by him is designated by the word *lāṅgala* through metaphorical usage. [The forms] "lāṅgalāḥ" and "śikhaṇḍāḥ" [are explained similarly].
In all three of these examples beginning with "ityādi," the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.120] *tasyedam*.

In "āśmaḥ," the suffix *aṇ* is likewise applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.134] *tasya vikāraḥ*. In "āśmano 'nyatra," the suffix *aṇ* is also applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.120] *tasyedam* for the purpose of expressing that meaning.
In the case of *cārmaḥ* as well, the suffix is simply *aṇ* by [Pāṇini 4.3.120] *tasyedam*.
[The phrase] *carmaṇo 'nyaḥ* means "a modification of leather. In the case of *śauvaḥ*, there is the augment *aij* by [Pāṇini 7.3.4] *dvārādīnāṃ ca*.

Since *sāyamprātika* and the others are not recited among the *prātipadika*s, he asks: "What, then, are *sāyamprātika* and the rest? By the phrase "types of *sāyamprātika*," he shows that the word "etc. (*ādi*) has the sense of indicating a class or type.
But surely, by the rule "sāyaṃ-ciram-... (Pāṇini 4.3.23), the suffixes *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* ought to occur after indeclinables;

so how is it that the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs here? To this he says: "But *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* are not desired," because they are not expressed [by usage]. And in all these cases, the word *upasaṃkhyāna* [is used].

The purpose [of the rule] is to provide an explanation. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: from the sūtra *mantrēṣu* (Pāṇini 6.4.141), the term *ādi-* ("beginning with") is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*), and the mention of *taddhita-* ("secondary suffix") has been made for this very purpose.
When that [term *ādi-*, meaning "beginning with,"] carries over, the following meaning results: there is elision of *ṭi* (*ṭilopa*) after bases ending in *n* when a *taddhita* suffix follows.

It occurs. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), [terms such as] *sāyamprātika* and others are included. By this, the elision of the *ṭi* suffix is established in all cases. [An objection is raised: "In forms such as *ṭhi*, the elision of the *ṭi* is not observed.
By this, he demonstrates that *ārātīya* and similar forms do not possess the status of being *sāyamprātika*. Now...

Regarding the form *śāśvataḥ*, how is the suffix *aṇ* applied here, given that by the rule *kālaṭṭhañ* (Pāṇini 4.3.11), the suffix *ṭhañ* ought to occur? This is not so; in the rule *kālaṭṭhañ* (4.3.11), a split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) must be made as *kālāt*. By this, the suffix *aṇ* occurs after the word *śaśvat* according to the rules previously prescribed. And... [the rest of the sentence is not provided].

By means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting the rule), the suffix *ṭhañ* is set aside due to the specific grammatical derivation (*nipātana*) in the rule "ṭhyeṣāñca virodhaḥ śāśvatikaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.9). Consequently, in one alternative, the suffix *ṭhañ* indeed occurs. However, the suffixes *ṭaḷu* and *ṭaḷul* are not desired after the word *śāśvata*, precisely because of the lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*). Now, regarding the form "śāśvatikaḥ":
Why does the substitution of *ka* for *ṭhañ* not occur here by the rule "ṭhisusuktāntāt kaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.51)? Precisely because of this very mention [in the sūtra].

145. *Ahnaṣṭakhoreva* (Pāṇini 6.4.145). [The example is] *dvyahaḥ*. The compound is formed by *taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca* (2.1.51), and the suffix *ṭac* is added as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) by *rājahaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac* (5.4.91). In this case, [the substitution of] *ahna* for *ahan*...

From these [words], the substitution of *ahan* prescribed by Pāṇini 5.4.88 would have applied; however, due to the prohibition in 5.4.89, "not after a numeral or the word *samāhāra*," it does not occur. Thus we have *dvyahīnaḥ*. When the term *samāyāḥ* from 5.1.85 is understood to be in force for the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), the rule 5.1.87, "also after *rātri*, *ahan*, and *saṃvatsara*," applies.
[The suffix] *kha*.
But why is the suffix *kha* used here in the sense of "not deficient" (*ahīna*)? To this he says: "The suffix *kha* should be stated [after the word] *ahan* in the sense of a collection.
Now, one might object: since *ahan* ends in the letter *n*, the elision of the *ṭi*-portion (the final syllable) is already established by the preceding rule; therefore—

For what purpose is this undertaking? To this he says: "Since [the matter] is already established," and so forth. Regarding the term "āhnika": the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule for the patronymic *ārhīya*. If this undertaking is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*) since the matter is already established, then in that case the inclusion of the word "eva" (only/just) would be useless; for even without it, the undertaking would be effective once the matter is established.
"How is it to be understood as having a restrictive (niyama) purpose? To this he says: "The use of the particle *eva* is for the sake of clarity.

Now, why does it not serve to dispel the suspicion of a reversed restriction (*viparīta-niyama*)? To this he says: "Only during the day," and so forth. If there were a reversed restriction such that [the rule] "of *ṭ* and *kh*" applied only during the day, then...

The intention is that, if [the suffix] *kha* were different [from the original], there would be no occasion at all for the elision of the *ṭi*; thus, the prescription of "original form" (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *ṭhātmādhvānaḥ khe* (Pāṇini 6.4.169) would be rendered purposeless.

146. *orguṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.146). Regarding the example *bābhravyaḥ*: by the rule *madhubabhvrorbrāhmaṇakauśikayoḥ* (4.1.106), the suffix *yañ* is applied to the word *babhru* in the sense of offspring (*apatya*). Regarding *māṇḍavyaḥ*: here too, it is because [the word *maṇḍu*] belongs to the *gargādi* group.

In the word *śaṅkavyam*, there is the substitution of *ava* for *au* by Pāṇini 6.1.79 (*vānto yi pratyaye*). In examples such as this, the suffix *yat* is applied by Pāṇini 5.1.2 (*ugavādibhyo yat*) in the sense of "beneficial for that" (*tasmai hitam*), according to Pāṇini 5.1.5.
Regarding *aupagavaḥ* and *kāpaṭavaḥ*, here too the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of offspring (*apatya*), which is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).
Thus—by the rule *voto guṇavacanāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.44), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied, resulting in *paṭvī*.

[The commentary notes: "It should have been stated as *orot*," and so forth; the intention is that by stating it thus, the sūtra becomes more concise. Regarding *svāyambhuvaḥ*: one who exists by himself (*svayaṃ bhavati*) takes the suffix *kvip*, becoming *svayambhūḥ*.

The suffix *aṇ* is applied [to form] *svāyambhuva*, meaning "the son of Svayambhū. Because a grammatical operation conditioned by a technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) is not necessarily obligatory, *guṇa* substitution does not occur here; and since that is absent, *uvAṄ* is substituted for the vowel.

147. *ḍhea lopo’kadrūvāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.147). [Examples: *kāmaṇḍaleyaḥ*, *śaitabāheyaḥ*. The suffix *ḍhañ* is applied by [the rule] *catuṣpādbhyo ḍhañ* (4.1.135). Similarly, it is so in the case of *jāmbeyaḥ*. [And] *mādrabāheyaḥ*.

From the word *madrabāhu*, the suffix *ūṅ* is applied by the rule *bāhv-antāt saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.67); from that form ending in *ūṅ*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied by the rule *strībhyaḥ ḍhak* (4.1.120), resulting in *kādraveyaḥ*. [In the case of] *kādruka*, the suffix *ūṅ* is applied by the rules *kadrū-kamaṇḍalvoś chandasi saṃjñāyām* (4.1.71, 72), and from that form ending in *ūṅ*...
The suffix *vaṅ* occurs after [the word] *pūrva*, provided that it does not denote a *dhaka*.
148. *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148). Here, does this [word] *yasya* signify the letter *y*, or does it signify the vowels *i* and *u*?
If it were to signify the letter *y* here, then there would be no need for the mention of *ya* again in the subsequent rule.
One should perform [the operation]; for this very principle will follow there as well. Therefore, this is the inclusion of both vowels (*ivarṇa*) and consonants (*avarṇa*).

In that context, since the mention of "vowels" (*varṇagrahaṇa*) everywhere effects a rule regarding what ends with that (*tadantavidhi*), it is understood that this is a *tadantavidhi*—having kept this in mind, he says: "of that which ends in a vowel (*ivarṇa*) or a consonant (*avarṇa*)."

And so forth. Regarding "dākṣī" and "plākṣī": from the words *dākṣi* and *plākṣi*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule "ito manuṣyajāteḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.65). Regarding "sakhī" as well, it is due to the irregular formation (*nipātana*) prescribed by the rule "sakhyaśiśvīti bhāṣāyām" (Pāṇini 4.1.62). But surely, in this case...

This [form] is also established by means of *savarṇadīrgha* (the lengthening of homogeneous vowels); so for what purpose is elision (*lopa*) prescribed here? To this he says: "For if there were *savarṇadīrgha*," and so forth. [The example] "atikrāntā sakhī enam" [is formed] according to the Vārttika rule: "After prefixes ending in *pra* etc., [there is elision] of a word derived from a verbal root" (Vārttika 101).

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound involving the elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*) and the shortening of the *upasarjana*. In that case, if the rule for homogeneous long vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*) were applied instead of the elision, then the single substitute for the vowel *ī* of *sakhi* and the vowel *ā* of *kāra* would, by virtue of being "like the end" (*antavadbhāva*) of the word *sakhi*, [be subject to the following rule]: "The remainder... (*śeṣo*)...

In the case of *atisakhi* (1.4.7), there would be a prohibition of the designation *dhī*. Consequently, in the form *atisakher āgacchati*, the guna substitution [of *e* for *i*] prescribed by *gher ṅiti* (7.3.111) would not occur. Even if the form were indistinguishable once the elision [of the final vowel] has taken place and the shortening of the *upasarjana* has been applied, [the designation *dhī* would still apply].

Nevertheless, it is technical (*lākṣaṇika*). Therefore, by the maxim "that which is taught by its technical definition" (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā*), that [suffix] is not grasped; thus, the prohibition does not apply. Consequently, only elision (*lopa*) should be performed.
In the three examples beginning with *dauleyaḥ*, [the suffix] is applied in the sense of offspring (*apatya*) by the rule *itaṣṭāniñaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.122).
The suffix *ḍhak*. Regarding "kumārī": the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.20] *vayasi prathame*. Regarding "gaurī":
the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.41] *ṣidgaurādibhyaśca*. Regarding "śārṅgaravī": [the suffix *ṅīn* is applied].
Regarding *ṭhśārṅgaravādyaño ṅīn* (Pāṇini 4.1.73): examples include *bālākiḥ* and *saumitriḥ*. From *bālaka* and *sumitrā*, the suffix *iñ* is applied because they belong to the *bahv-ādi* group.
Regarding the phrase "in the rule beginning with *yasya*": by the word *ādi* ("beginning with"), the subsequent rule is included. It should be stated [as follows].

The meaning is that it must be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: from the rule "vibhāṣā iṅśyoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.136), the term *vibhāṣā* is carried over by the maxim of the frog's leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*), and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). By means of this rule, the elision (*lopa*) is thus prescribed.

And by the subsequent sūtra, neither of those two [cases] occurs: namely, in the examples "kāṇḍe" and "kuḍye," where the substitution of *śī* applies by the rules "āṅ āpaḥ" (7.1.18) and "napuṃsakācca" (7.1.19); in that case, the elision of the vowel *a* in the word "yasya" would result. Also in the example "saurye," [the rule] "tenaikadik" [would apply].

By the rule (4.3.112), the suffix *aṇ* is applied after the word *sūrya*; from that form ending in *aṇ*, the substitution of *auṅ* for the dual case-ending occurs. In that situation, by this [present] rule, the elision of the vowel *ā* would result, and by the subsequent rule, the elision of the consonant *y*. [The rule] begins with "after *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*," etc. The scope of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* is, for example: *śriyau*, *śriyaḥ*, *bhruvau*.

Regarding the [substitution of] *bhru*: the scope for elision (*lopa*) is, for example, *kāmaṇḍaleyaḥ* and *mādrabāheyaḥ*; whereas in *vātsapreyaḥ* and *laikhābhreyaḥ*, both rules would apply, and by the principle of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), elision takes place. The word *vatsaprīḥ* is derived from a verbal root with the suffix *kvip*.

149. *sūryatiṣyāgastyamatasyānām ya upadhāyāḥ* (6.4.149). If, in this rule, *sūrya* and the others were qualified by the technical name *bha*—that is, if it meant "of *sūrya* and the others when they have the designation *bha*"—then in forms such as *saurī* and *balākā*, the elision [of the *ya*] would not occur; for [in those cases, the stem is not *bha*].
The word *sūrya* here is not designated by the technical term *bha*; rather, having kept in mind that it is another distinct word ending in *-an*,
the letter *ya* is qualified by its relata, such as *sūrya*, through elision (*lopa*) of the distinction of form that was not previously relied upon.

Showing this, he says: "Of these, namely *sūrya*, *atimāgastya*, *matsya*, etc. [The word] "of the *bha*" means of that which bears the technical designation *bha*. When there is a *yakāra* as an *upadhā* (penultimate letter), its elision occurs provided that *yakāra* belongs to *sūrya* and the others—this is the intended meaning here. And those [words]...

The words *sūrya* and so forth are not specifically qualified by the status of being a *bh* [stem]. Therefore, even when they do not possess the designation *bh*, the elision of the penultimate vowel *u* still occurs provided that this *y* belongs to *sūrya* and the others—as in *saurī* (feminine) and *balākā*. Now, [one might object]:...

Is it not the case that, because the elision of the vowel *ā* here depends on two different bases (*vyāśrayatva*), it is not considered non-existent (*asiddha*) for the purpose of [triggering] the substitution of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) with *ik*? To this he says: "The elision of *ya* when followed by *aṇ*, etc. For in this rule, there are two instances of the elision of *ya*: one occurs when *aṇ* follows, and the other when *ī* follows. Of these, the first...
It has different bases (*vyāśraya*); for instance, the elision (*lopa*) occurs by depending on the *aṇ*, whereas the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) depends on the vowel *ī*.

Therefore, because they have different bases, it is correct that the former is not considered non-existent (*asiddha*) in relation to the latter. The other [elision], however, depends on the vowel *ī* and thus shares the same base; consequently, because it is non-existent, the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) remains as *i*.
By the rule beginning with *bhasyāṇantasya*, he demonstrates the meaning of the sūtra through examples:
*taiṣam* and *taiṣī*. [In these cases,] the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ* (P.

4.2.3), and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (P. 4.1.15). [The phrase] "when the suffix *aṇ* has been applied because of being an *ṛṣi*" refers to the rule *ṛṣyandhakavṛṣṇikurubhyaśca* (P. 4.1.114).

By the rule beginning with "matsyacarī," [it is explained that] *matsya* means "one who was previously a fish"—[formed] by *caraṭ* according to Pāṇini 5.3.53 (*bhūtapūrve caraṭ*), with the feminine suffix *ṅīp* as before. Here, in *matsyacara*, there is a *yakāra* (the semi-vowel *y*) related to the word *matsya*, which bears the technical name *bha*; however, since this *y* is not an *upadhā* (penultimate vowel) of the *bha*-named element, the elision [prescribed by Pāṇini 6.4.148] does not take effect.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *ya* [in the rule], since even without the mention of *ya*, the elision of the *yakāra* that has become the *upadhā* would be understood when the *upadhā* is specified by means of the sun (*sūrya*) and so forth; for indeed, among those [words], the *yakāra* itself is the *upadhā*, not any other phoneme? To this [objection, the author replies]:
He said: "The mention of *hya* is for the sake of what follows. This means that it must be explained—that is, its interpretation provided.
Here too, the explanation should be made by resorting to the option (*vibhāṣā*) as before. Regarding "mātsyam": the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.2.120, *tasyedam*.

Regarding "sauryam": from a stem ending in *aṇ*, [the suffix] *cha* is applied by the rule "vṛddhāccchaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.2.114). Similarly, [one derives] "āgastīyam. Regarding "sauryam": since Sūrya is the deity (*devatā*) here, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "sā'sya devatā" (Pāṇini 4.2.24). Regarding "āgastyaḥ": the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ* is applied in the sense of offspring (*apatya*). Regarding "nakṣatrāṇi" (the lunar mansions): [this is explained as follows].
The meaning is: "in that which is connected with a lunar mansion (nakṣatra)," [referring to] the subtle element (aṇu).

Regarding the phrase "of a word beginning with the letter *k*," it means "of the letter *k* and the vowel *a*. Regarding the phrase "and the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyaudāttatvaṃ*)," this statement is made so that the initial syllable is acute, since otherwise the final syllable would have been acute by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).

Regarding "ṭhantitaḥ": the suffix *tasi* is applied by the rule "apādāne cāhīyaruhoḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.45). Regarding "ṭhtādeśca": this means of the word *tika*; because of the word *ca*, it also applies to [words] beginning with *ka*. Regarding "ṭhantamaḥ": the suffix *tamap* is applied in the sense of excellence (*atiśāyane*) according to the rule "atiśāyane tamap" (Pāṇini 5.3.55).

Regarding "ṭhantiṣat": the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule "satsūdviṣa... (Pāṇini 3.2.61). Regarding "ye ca": this is connected with the word "is seen" (*dṛśyate*) which is under discussion. Regarding "antimaḥ": [the suffix] *ya* is applied either by "bhave chandasi" (Pāṇini 4.4.110) or by "tatra sādhuḥ" (Pāṇini 4.4.98). Some [hold that] the whole [is so].
They maintain that the rule for elision applies only in the Vedic language.

150. *halas taddhitasya* (6.4.150). [Note: "The term *taddhita* is no longer in force," because the word *taddhita* is mentioned again in the subsequent sūtra. Therefore, this rule is a prescription for the elision of the suffix *ī* itself. Examples include *gārgī* and so forth, derived from words such as *garga* etc., which end in the suffix *yañ*.

In *kārikeyī*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.16] *ṭhyañaśca*. In *vaidhī*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.48] *puṃyogādākhyāyām*, following the application of *ḍhak* by [Pāṇini 4.1.120] *strībhyo ḍhak*, and subsequently the suffix *ṅīp* by [Pāṇini 4.1.15] *ṭiṅḍhāṇañ*.

151. *āpatyasya ca taddhite'nāti* (Pāṇini 6.4.151). [The example] "gārgakam": by the rule *gotrokṣoṣṭrorabhra-* (4.2.39), the suffix *vuñ* is added to the word *gārgya*; therein, the *yañ* [of *gārgya*] is elided. [The example] "sāṅkākhyakaḥ".

Regarding the form *kāmpilyaka*: as before, from the words *saṅkāśa* and *kampila*, the suffix *ṇya* is applied by the rule *duñ-chaṇ-ṇya-ṭhañ-kañ-kvarapaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.80). From that [base ending in *ṇya*], the suffix *vuñ* is applied in the sense of a secondary derivative (*śaiṣika*) such as "born there," by the rule *dhanvayopadhād vuñ* (Pāṇini 4.2.121).

Now, what is the purpose of including the term *taddhita* [in the rule]? One might ask: "Will the mention of *taddhita* from [Pāṇini 6.4.144], *naḥ taddhite*, be carried over [to this rule]? To this he says: "The mention of *taddhita*" and so forth.
In the case of *somī devatā asya* ("Soma is its deity"), [the suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.30], *somāt ṭhañ*; and [the feminine suffix] *ṅīp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.15], *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*.

Thus [is formed] *ṅīp*. In that context, the mention of "taddhita" is for the purpose that the elision of the letter *y*—even when it does not belong to a patronymic (*apatya*)—should occur by means of the rule *halas taddhitasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.150). Otherwise, if that very same previously mentioned term "taddhita" were to be carried over here [by *anuvṛtti*], then...

The mention of "connected with that" (tatsambaddha) would continue [from the previous rule]. And thus, both [conditions] continuing here, they would also continue in the preceding sacrifice. Therefore, since the matter would already be established by the preceding rule alone, this present undertaking is for the purpose of restriction, namely: "the secondary suffix *ī* occurs in both cases."
It might be argued: "Just as there is elision of the *apatya* (descendant) suffix when a *taddhita* suffix beginning with a vowel other than *ā* follows,

and also when the suffix denotes something other than a descendant, so too— by way of this restrictive rule (*niyama*)— just as there will be no elision in the case of *sāṅkaśyaka* where the suffix does not denote a descendant, likewise there would be no elision in the case of *saumī iṣṭiḥ* either."

Because it has been excluded here; however, when the mention of *taddhita* is made in this rule, the exclusion of the mention of *taddhita* in the preceding rule is declared. Therefore, by that preceding rule, the elision of the letter *y* is prescribed without distinction for any *taddhita* suffix—whether it denotes non-descendant or descendant. [Thus,] *saumī*.

The mention of "taddhita" (secondary derivative) here is for the purpose that the elision [of the *ya*] should also occur in the case of *iṣṭi*. But surely, if this restriction—that it is a *taddhita* in both cases—were to apply, then the meaning of the two rules would be redundant; one could simply have formulated a single rule: "There is elision of the *apatya* suffix after a consonant, except before *ā*. Therefore...
By the force of the commencement of the two preceding sūtras, only one of them will be carried over here, but not both. However, in this case, there might be this much doubt:
does the mention of *taddhita* carry over here, or the mention of *ud*? Regarding this as well—
The term *taddhita* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], but not the term *ned*; this is because of the [authoritative] commentary (*vyākhyāna*).
Regarding all doubts, this principle applies: "Specific understanding arises from the commentary, for there is no lack of a grammatical rule (*alakṣaṇa*) due to doubt" (Puṣpavṛtti 120).

And if only the mention of *taddhita* were to carry over here, this restriction would apply solely to the domain of *taddhita* suffixes and not to the domain of *īd* vowels; thus, even if the mention of *taddhita* were not repeated here,
because there would be no such restriction, the elision [of the final vowel] would occur by the preceding rule even in the case of *saumī iṣṭiḥ*.

It is indeed established. Then how is this stated—that the mention of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is for the purpose of eliding even that which is not a descendant (*anapatya*)? The intended meaning should be seen as follows: this [mention] is for the sake of making the elision easily understood. Consequently, the resulting sense here is: for the purpose of avoiding excessive complexity in comprehension.
The mention of *taddhita* [derivatives] is for the sake of examples such as "Gārgyāyaṇa," where *phak* is applied by the rule *yañiñośca* (Pāṇini 4.1.101);
and "Kārakeyiḥ," where *ḍhak* is applied by the rule *strībhyo ḍhak* (Pāṇini 4.1.120) in the sense of "the offspring of Kārīkā."
From that [word], the offspring is formed as *kārikeyiḥ* by the rule *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95).
152. *kyacvyośca* | (6.4.152) This rule is commenced for the sake of something other than a *taddhita* suffix. The term *kya* is a general reference to both *kyac* and *kyaṅ*.
[The example is] *gārgīyati*. [This is derived as follows: *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8), and *kyaci ca* (7.4.33).

Thus, [the form] *gārgīyaḥ* is derived: by rule 3.1.11, *kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca*, the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied, and by rule 7.4.25, *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*, lengthening occurs. [The form] *gārgībhūtaḥ* is derived:
by rule 5.4.50, *abhūtatadbhāve*, the suffix *cvi* is applied, and by rule 7.4.32, *asya cvau*, [the substitution of *ī* for *a* occurs].
Thus ends the section on *it*.
153. *Bilvakādibhyaś chasya luk* (6.4.153). [The sūtra reads] "from *bilvaka* and others. The mention is made with an adventitious (*āgantuka*) vowel *ā*. [The example is] *bilvakīyā*.
[This is derived from] *utkarādibhyaś chaḥ* (4.2.90) and *naḍādīnāṃ kuk ca* (4.2.91).
The suffix *cha* is applied in the four senses, with the augment *kuk*. Regarding the form "bailvakāḥ": the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.83 (*prāgdīvyato 'ṇ*).
Now, what is the purpose of mentioning the suffix *cha*, since the words beginning with *bilvakī* already have the augment *kuk* applied?

[The question is: "Since these [roots] have been taken up, the suffix *ccha* can occur after them; therefore, even without the mention of *ccha*, the elision of *ccha* itself must necessarily occur"? To this, he says: "The mention of *ccha*" (*cchagrahaṇam*), etc. If the mention of *ccha* were not made, then by the paribhāṣā "that which is taught as being enjoined in conjunction" (*sanniyogaśiṣṭa*) (MBh 1.3.10), in the case of the letter *ccha*...

If [the rule] were to cease, there would be a cessation [of the application] of that very Paribhāṣā; and for that reason, this very mention of *ccha* is the indicator (*jñāpaka*). Now, what is the purpose of mentioning *luk*, since the elision (*lopa*) is prescribed in the very context under discussion? To this, he says: "The mention of *luk*," and so forth.

The inclusion of the letter *ya* should be understood as an indicator for a portion [of the rule]. For that [letter *ya*] is connected with the rule "there is elision of the penultimate" (*upadhāyāḥ lopaḥ*);

while that [rule] continues to apply, the rule "of the penultimate *ya*" (*ya upadhāyāḥ*) would also continue to apply, and once the substitution of *iy* for *ch* has been made, [the elision] would occur for the letter *y* alone.

Furthermore, even if the rule "of the penultimate vowel" (*ṭhupadhāyāḥ*) were not to follow here, the substitution would still apply to the letter *i* alone by the rule "of what follows [the initial element]" (*ādeḥ parasya*, 1.1.54). As for the mention of *luk*:
*luk* is the technical term for the non-appearance of an entire suffix, and not for the non-appearance of a single part of a suffix.
When "elision" (luk) is mentioned, elision occurs for the whole [suffix]; for that mention of "elision" is indeed for that purpose.
154. *turiṣṭhemayassu* (6.4.154).

Regarding the term *tuḥ*: having set aside the distinctive indicatory letters (*anubandhas*), there is a general reference to the suffixes *tṛn* and *tṛc*. In the example *kariṣṭhaḥ*, the suffix *tṛn* is applied after the root *kṛ*; then, the suffix *iṣṭhan* is added to that form to express excellence (*atiśāyana*).

There is the elision of the syllable *tṛ*. [The forms] "vijayiṣṭhaḥ" and "vahiṣṭhaḥ" are derived: in the former, the suffix *tṛn* is added to the root *ji* preceded by the prefix *vi-*, and in the latter, the suffix *tṛn* is added to the root *vah*. To that which ends in *tṛn*, the suffix *iṣṭhan* is added; then, by the rule "ho ḍhaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.31), the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha* occurs. When the elision of the syllable *tṛ* is to be performed, the principle "pūrvatrāsiddham" (the preceding is as if non-existent with respect to the following) applies.

(8.2.1) This is unestablished; therefore, only the elision of the preceding [vowel] is performed. Once that has been done, the substitution of *ḍha*, which is prescribed when a *jhala* follows or at the end of a word, does not take effect due to the absence of its cause.
