As in the example "dohīyasī": from the root *duh* ending in *tṛc*, the suffix *īyasun* is added, and then the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.6], "and after a stem ending in *ugit*. Here too, [the same applies].

When an elision (*lopa*) is to be applied, the rule *dāder dhātor dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.32) is also considered asiddha; therefore, the elision occurs first. Once that [elision] has taken place, the substitution of *dh* does not apply, as before. Now, why does this elision not occur according to *alo 'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52), which prescribes that an operation applies to the final letter?

Thus he says: "of all," and so forth. He states the reason for that very point: "of the last," and so forth. If [the elision] were to apply to the last [sound], the statement [of the rule] would result in redundancy, because it would already be established by the rule "of the last, the *ṭi*. Therefore, since there is no purpose in stating the elision of the last [sound], [it must apply to] all.
This statement is understood to have the purpose that there should be elision (*lopa*) of the word *tṛ*.
If, then, this statement were for the sake of eliding the word *tṛ*, why is not the immediately following elision (*luk*) itself prescribed?
In that case, the elision of the whole would be determined with ease.
Because the elision (*luk*) is prescribed for the non-observation of a condition (*pratyaya*), he says: "But this *luk*," and so forth.

What fault would there be in that case? To this he says: "For thus," and so forth. If this term *luk* were to carry over here, then [the rule] "even operations that are internal (*antaraṅga*)... [would apply].
Since it is held that "an external elision (*luk*) subverts [other operations]" (Vyāḍipāṭha 128), the elision (*luk*) must first take place;

consequently, by the rule "there is no [application of] a grammatical operation based on a suffix when *lumat* [elision] has occurred" (Pāṇini 1.1.63), there would be a prohibition of the suffix-based characteristic (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Thus, [the forms] *kariṣṭhaḥ* and *vijayiṣṭhaḥ* [would not be established].

In this case, the *guṇa* substitution characterized by the term *ardhadhātuka* would not occur. Therefore, so that this fault does not arise, the word *luk* (elision) is understood here as being carried over [from a previous rule]. Now, what is the purpose of mentioning *imanij*? For the suffix *imanij* can indeed occur after the word *tṛ*; nevertheless, there is the rule: "The suffix *imanij* optionally [occurs] after words beginning with *pṛthu*."
That [suffix] is prescribed by the two rules (Pāṇini 5.1.122–123), namely *ṭhvarmadṛḍhādibhyaḥ* and *vyañ ca*;

however, no word ending in the suffix *tṛ* is recited among the *pṛthu*-group or the *dṛḍha*-group, nor is there any word denoting a color [ending in *tṛ*]. Therefore, he says: "But the other two," and so forth.

155. *ṭeḥ* (6.4.155). Regarding the rule *ṭhṇāviṣṭhavad*: since the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) has been stated for the suffix *iṣṭhan* by the rule *ṭhasilādiṣvā kṛtvasucaḥ* (6.3.35), and since the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* in light syllables following a consonant is prescribed by the rule *ra ṛto halāderlaghoḥ* (6.4.161), [the forms are derived accordingly].

By the rule "ṭhṭheḥ," there is the elision of the *ṭi* suffix; by the rule "sthūladūrayuvahrasva" (Pāṇini 6.4.156), there is the elision of the letter following the *yaṇ* and so forth, as well as the *guṇa* substitution for the preceding vowel; by the rule "vinmatorluk" (5.3.65), there is *luk*-elision; and by the rule "yuvālpayoḥ kananyatarasyām" (5.3.64), the suffix *kan* is applied.

By the rule *ṭhpriyasthira* (Pāṇini 6.4.157) and others, the substitutes beginning with *pra* are prescribed; these grammatical operations occur when the suffix *iṣṭhan* follows. It must be stated that so too they may occur when the suffix *ṇa* follows, such that the operation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) applies as if it were followed by *iṣṭhan*. The mention of the term "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) [is for this purpose].

It is impossible [to apply this rule] to anything else, because no other extended application (*atideśa*) is possible. Here, the suffix *vat* has the sense of similarity; therefore, since no extended application to anything other than that for which a specific grammatical operation is intended in the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan* is possible, [the rule] serves to exclude that.

The mention of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) need not have been made. It is done for the sake of clarity. Some, however, say that the mention of the nominal stem need not be made so that there should be no extension (*atideśa*) of operations pertaining to suffixes; it is done for the sake of clarity.

Some, however, say that the mention of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is for the purpose of preventing the extension (*atideśa*) of the suffixes to the operations of the [derivatives] themselves; thus, in the case of *bahum ācaṣṭe* → *bahayati*, the rule "for *iṣṭhan* there is *yiṭ*" (Pāṇini 6.4.158) does not apply to the *yiṅ* suffix.
But this is incorrect; for in the rule *iṣṭhavad* (6.4.157), the locative case is used.
The suffix *vat* is prescribed after a word that has the sense of *samartha* (capable/fit), because the locative case (*ṇād*) is heard in reference to its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*).
Therefore, whatever operation is prescribed for the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan* is extended [by this rule], but not whatever operation belongs to the word *iṣṭha* itself.
Furthermore, the operation in question does not belong to the denominative suffix *yiṅ*, but rather to *iṣṭhan* alone; and that [operation] is what is intended here.

Since attainment (*prāpti*) itself does not exist, what is the purpose of employing the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) for its negation? [The form] *ṭhenīm* is derived from this word by applying the suffix *ṅīṣ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.39, *varṇādanudātātopadhāt*, and the substitution of *n* for *t*. [The form] *etayati* is derived by adding the causative suffix *ṇic*, after which the masculine form is applied (*puṃvadbhāva*).

Both the *ṅīṣ* and the *n*-suffix are elided. Now, one might object: "Since the *ṇi* here is separated from the base by the *ṅīṣ*, an extension (*atideśa*) of the *ṇa* suffix cannot apply when there is such an intervention. This is not a fault;
for even in the case of the *iṣṭhan* suffix, the masculine form of the nominal stem occurs precisely when there is an intervention by the *ṅīṣ*.
Therefore, here too, even when there is an intervention, it will be exactly like that.

In the case of *sragviṇam*, [the suffix] *vini* is applied by the rule *asmāyāmedhāsrajo viniḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.121). In the case of *srajayati*, [the substitution of *i* for *at* occurs] because of the principle *saṃjñāpūrvako vidhir anityaḥ* (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 64), which states that a rule conditioned by a technical name is not necessarily obligatory. *Ata*...

By the rule *upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116), the *vṛddhi* [vowel substitution] does not occur. However, according to the maxim *aṅgavṛtte punaraṅgavṛtāvavidhir niṣṭhitasya* (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 38)—which states that when an operation has already occurred within a stem (*aṅga*), a subsequent operation on that same stem is not prescribed for what has already been finalized—the form *vapā* is established. In cases such as *prāpayati*, the [vṛddhi] certainly occurs because the form is not yet finalized. Here, [the rule applies] to *arti* and *hru*.

By [the rule] beginning with (7.3.36), the augment *puk* is applied. Now, one might object: "In the recension of Bhāradvāja, forms such as *prādayaḥ* would not be established; rather, there would be elision (*luk*) in *srajayati* and *vasayati*, and in *kanayati*, the suffix *kan* would be applied.
To this, he says: "Both of these are merely illustrative examples," and so forth.

This very purpose has been demonstrated in the Bhāvavṛtti recension and in other [works], yet this is not intended as an exhaustive enumeration of examples; for since even particles (*prādayaḥ*) are desired [to be included], it is not the case that the purpose is limited to just this much. [Objection: But is it not stated that "after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), [a suffix] is added frequently in the sense of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and it is treated like the *iṣṭhan* suffix"?

Since this [root] is read in the *curādigaṇa* itself according to the rule *dhā.pā.ga.sū.186*, why then is the treatment as if it were the superlative suffix (*iṣṭhan*) prescribed here with respect to the *ṇic* affix? Some say it is for the sake of elaborating upon this very point. Others say that it should have been stated in the *gaṇa* itself; they maintain that this is intended to demonstrate the optionality of the rule "this one is the other" (*asāv itaraḥ*).
156. *sthūla-dūra-yuva-hrasva-kṣipra-kṣudrāṇāṃ yaṇ-ādi paraṃ pūrvasya ca guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.156).
Although the word *lopa* was previously understood as an abstract noun (*bhāva-sādhana*), here it is used as an object-noun (*karman-sādhana*).

It is understood [that the word *parimāṇa* here denotes the instrument]; for it is indicated by the mention of *yaṇ* and so forth. For if that [word *parimāṇa*] were derived in the sense of the action (*bhāva-sādhana*), then the genitive case would have occurred according to Pāṇini 2.3.65, *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti*.

However, thinking that since it is derived in the sense of the object (*karman-sādhana*), the object is expressed by that [instrumental suffix], and therefore the nominative alone is appropriate, [the author says...]

Demonstrating that the word *lāpa*—which is a verbal noun (*bhāvaśabda*)—functions as a verbal noun denoting the object (*karmasādhana*), he says: "That which follows *yaṇ* and so forth is elided. But how is it possible for that very same [word], being a verbal noun denoting an action (*bhāvasādhana*), to function as a verbal noun denoting the object? Who, moreover, said "of that very same"? [The answer is: with respect to every sūtra.
The word *lopa* (elision) is differentiated as it follows [the preceding rule].
But surely, when the following element beginning with *yaṇ* is elided, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*) the *guṇa* substitution will be understood as belonging to that which precedes it;
so what is the purpose of including the mention of "preceding" (*pūrva*)? To this he says: "The mention of 'preceding'..."
"For the sake of clarity."
157. *priya-sthira-sphira-uru-bahula-guru-vṛddha-trap-dīrgha-vṛndārakāṇām pra-stha-spha-var-bahi-gar-varṣi-tra-drāghi-vṛndāḥ*.
(6.4.157) What, then, is the reason that only *priya*, *uru*, *guru*, and *dīrgha* are cited as examples for the suffix *iman*?
[Question: Is it not so for others as well? [Answer: He says: "‘priya-uru-bahula-guru-dīrghāḥ’ and so forth.
The meaning of this statement is that the suffix *iman* occurs only after words such as *priya*, and not after others. Otherwise, even though only *priya* and the rest [are mentioned]...
They are recited among [the names] beginning with Pṛthu; or they might be denoters of phonemes (varṇa).
In that case, one would cite [the example]: *teṣām imanij* (Pāṇini 5.1.122); here, *medimat* would be an example for the suffix *imanic*.

158. *bahor lopo bhū ca bahoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.158). [The commentary] says: *bahoḥ uttareṣām*. By this, he shows that the first occurrence of *bahoḥ* is in the ablative case, and by the second occurrence of *bahoḥ*, he shows that the second is in the genitive case.

Regarding "bhūyān": by the rule *ādeḥ parasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.54), there is the elision of the *i*-sound [of the suffix *āt*]. Now, for what purpose is the word *bahoḥ* mentioned again? He says: "But [the mention of] *bahoḥ*" and so forth. For if the mention of *bahoḥ* were absent, the word *bahu* would not possess the status of a *sthānin* (original element).

It would be understood [as applying to the suffixes] because of the indication by the word ending in the fifth case. Therefore, the word *bahoḥ* is stated again in order to establish its status as the original element (*sthānin*). Regarding the phrase "otherwise, etc.": if *bahoḥ* were not stated, then the substitution of *bhū* would apply only to the suffixes; for [the rule] "from that, the subsequent [element]" applies.

Because of this statement [Pāṇini 1.1.67]. Now, one might object: "The augment will not apply to the suffixes simply because they are mentioned separately; otherwise, he would have said 'bhūlopau'. This is not so;
for there is another purpose for the separate mention. What is it? So that they may appear as having separate locations (*pṛthak-sthānaka*).

[The word "bhū" is used] so that [the elision] may apply to the two [sounds], and not just to the first; for if it were stated simply as "elision of *bhū*," then by the rule "of what follows, the first [element]" (Pāṇini 1.1.54), the elision of *bhū* would optionally apply only to the very first sound. Therefore, the purpose is that they should have distinct locations [within the word].

There would have to be a separate mention of the yoga-rule; therefore, what was stated is correct: "Otherwise, the change to *bhū* would apply only to the suffixes. Here, the particle *ca* serves the purpose of conjunction (*sanniyoga*).

159. *iṣṭhasya yiṭ ca*. (6.4.159) This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the elision of *ṭh*; it is introduced as *yiṅ* because [the rule] would otherwise have applied. The vowel *i* in *yiṭ* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), as there is no other purpose for it. The *ca* [in the sūtra]...
The particle "ca" (and) is for the purpose of drawing in [the rule] "bahośca bhūḥ."

160. *jyādādīyasaḥ* | (6.4.160) Regarding the form *jyāyān*: [the rule] *praśasyasya śraḥ* (5.3.60) and *jya ca* (5.3.61) provide the substitute *jya*. [The rule] *lopasya yiṭ ca*, etc., applies. If here the elision (*lopa*) were not [effected] by *yiṭ*...

The intention is this: since it is established that [the vowel] is superior by virtue of being separated from the preceding element by that very [consonant], one should not say "ādi" (beginning with). But how, if "ādi" is not stated, is it established by means of elision (*lopa*)? To this he says: "For when there is elision," and so forth. Now...

What is the purpose of the long pronunciation [of the substitute], since by the principle of closest proximity (*antaratama*) alone a long vowel will naturally result from a long vowel? This is not so; for it is a rule that "an *aṇ* vowel being taught as a substitute does not include its homogeneous counterparts" (*bhāvyamāno’ṇ savarṇān na gṛhṇāti*).
161. *ra ṛto halāder laghoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.161).
Regarding the example "ṭhkartavyam," the meaning is that it must be explained (*vyākhyeya*). The explanation here is as follows:
the mention of *vibhāṣā* (optionally) in the subsequent rule is also connected to this one; moreover, that is a *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā* (a restricted option), and therefore—
[The vṛddhi] will apply only to *pṛthu* and the others. If that is so, then the rule "of a light [vowel] following a consonant" (*halāder laghoḥ*) need not be formulated;
for by means of the fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), it will apply both to what follows a consonant and to a light vowel.
True, this is so; however, it is formulated for the sake of clarity.

"From this [it follows] 'here it does not occur,' and so forth. The intention is that if the enumeration were not made, then even in cases such as *kṛtayati*, the substitution of the *iṣṭhan*-like form would indeed occur by virtue of the *iṣṭhavadbhāva* rule.
162. *vibhāṣārjośchandasī* (6.4.162).

163. *prakṛtyaikāc* (6.4.163). Regarding the form *srajiṣṭhaḥ*: here, by virtue of the rule for "original form" (*prakṛtibhāva*), the elision of the suffixal *ṭi* does not take place. Now, one might object:

[Objection: Will [the rule] "ṭhvinmator luk" (Pāṇini 5.3.65) not supersede the elision of *ṭi* (ṭilopa), since this [rule for luk] is formulated when that [elision of *ṭi*] has not yet taken effect? [Response: This is not so; there are two elisions of *ṭi*: one belonging to the stem ending in the suffixes *vin* or *mat*, and another which occurs when the [suffixal] *luk* has already been applied to what remains. Of these, that which...

It is logical that the elision of *ṭi* (*ṭilopa*) for a stem ending in *vin* or *mat* should supersede that [elision of the suffix] which begins before it has even become applicable; however, as for the remaining *ṭi*-elision, since its application was impossible prior to the occurrence of the [suffix] elision (*luk*),
how could it— being commenced while that [suffix] was still unapplicable— supersede the elision whose applicability arises only later?
Therefore, this must be undertaken:

"By nature, [the word] *rājanya* [is used] in the sense of *akaḥ*," and so forth. Is this something that needs to be stated? No; for how else could the rule "in the case of *turi*, *iṣṭha*, *imani*, and *īyasun*" (6.4.154) be excluded? This [rule] applies generally.

The state of being "as in the original form" (*prakṛtivadbhāva*) is what is to be prescribed; and the term *vibhāṣā* continues [from the previous rule], and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, it will apply in every place where it is desired, but where it is not desired, it simply will not apply. Thus, regarding the rule *inaṇyanapatye* (Pāṇini 6.4.164):

If it is argued that such a rule for the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) would be purposeless, we say no; for it serves the purpose of providing detailed exposition (*prapañca*). For instance, in the case of *rājanyakam*, [one might derive it] from "the offspring of a king" (*rājño 'patyam*), [which would require the suffix *yañ*]; however, by the rule *rāja-ruṣa-sura-ādibhyo yat* (Pāṇini 4.1.137), the suffix *yat* is applied to form *rājanya*. From that [word *rājanya*], the sense of a collection (*samūha*) is intended.

In this case, the suffix *vuñ* is applied by the rule "ṭhgotrokṣoṣṭrorabhra... (Pāṇini 4.2.39). Regarding the form "mānuṣyakam": according to those who hold that the suffix *yat* is used in the sense of offspring by the rule "ṭhmanorjātāvañyatau ṣukca" (Pāṇini 4.1.169), once *vuñ* has been applied by the preceding rule [4.2.39], there is elision [of the final syllable].

It undergoes [the substitution], but it is prevented by the rule of original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). However, according to the opinion of those for whom the suffix *yat* applies only to the genus (*jāti*) and not to the offspring (*apatya*), there is no purpose for the rule of original form; for, precisely because it is not used in the sense of offspring, the elision will not occur.
164. *inaṇyanapatye* (Pāṇini 6.4.164). Examples:

*sāṅkūṭinam*, *sāṃrāviṇam*, *sāmmārjinam*. [The roots are] *kūṭa* in the sense of "burning" (*dāhe*; Dhātupāṭha 1890; alternatively, *paritāpe* or *paridāhe* according to the Dhātupāṭha) and *ru* in the sense of "sound" (*śabde*).
From the roots *kuṭ* (DhP 1034), *mṛj* "to purify" (DhP 1066), and by applying Pāṇini 3.3.44, *abhividhau bhāve inuṇ*, and 7.2.114, *mṛjervṛddhiḥ*,
we arrive at the forms *sāṃkūṭin*, *sāṃrāvin*, and *sāṃmārjin*. Then, by applying 5.4.15, *aṇinuṇaḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).

From the word *medhāvin*, the suffix *vini* is applied by the rule "as-māyā-" (Pāṇini 5.2.121); from that form ending in *vini*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of a descendant (*apatya*) according to the section beginning with "prāgdīvyato 'ṇ" (Pāṇini 4.1.83).

165. *gāthi-ivadathika-iśi-gaṇi-paṇi* (Pāṇini 6.4.165). This rule is commenced for the sake of forming patronymic derivatives (*apatya*); for in the case of non-patronymics, the formation is already established by the preceding rule due to these stems ending in the suffix *in*.
166. *Saṃyogādiśca* (6.4.166).

This [sūtra] is also an introduction for the purpose of denoting offspring (*apatya*). For example, *śāṅkhinaḥ*. From the words *śaṅkha*, *madra*, and *vajra*, the suffix *iti* is applied in the sense of possessing that (*matvarthe*); from that which ends in *iti*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied as before.

167. *an* (6.4.167). The [restriction] "not when *apatya*" is withdrawn. This is a general rule for the suffix *aṇ*. Examples: *sāmanaḥ*, *vaimanaḥ*; here the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "tasyedam" (4.3.120). Example: *sautvanaḥ*; [the root is] *ṣuñ*.
In the sense of "pressing," the suffix *ṅvanip* is applied by the rule *su-mu-jor-ṅvanip* (Pāṇini 3.2.106),
and the augment *tuk* is added by the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk* (Pāṇini 6.1.71).
168. *ye cābhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.168). [Examples: *sāmanyaḥ*, *vemanyaḥ*. [The suffix] *yat* is applied by [the rule] *tatra sādhuḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.98).

169. *ātman* and *adhvan* take the suffix *kha* [when followed by the word *khe*]. (Pāṇini 5.1.9) Thus, "ātmanīnaḥ. Here, the suffix *kha* is applied by the rule "ātman-viśvajana-bhogottarapadāt khaḥ" (5.1.9).
[And] "adhvanīnaḥ. Here too, the suffix *kha* is applied by the rule "advane yat-khau" (5.2.16).

Regarding *pratyātmam*: the term *ātmānaṃ prati* forms an *avyayībhāva* compound in its literal sense according to Pāṇini 2.1.6 (*avyayaṃ vibhakti...*). From this, the suffix *ṭac* is applied by Pāṇini 5.4.108 (*anaśca*). Regarding *prādhvam*:
the term *pragatam adhvānam* forms a *prādi*-compound; the suffix *ac* is applied by Pāṇini 5.4.85 (*upasargād adhvanaḥ*).

170. *na mapūrvo'patye'varmaṇaḥ* | (6.4.170). [The rule] *ṭhaścārmaṇaḥ* means that when the sense is "a chariot covered with" (*parivṛto rathaḥ*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *prāgdīvyato'ṇ* (4.1.83).

"It should be stated that [the rule applies] 'to the word *hitanāman*'; thus, it must be explained that this has the sense of a prohibition regarding the word *hitanāman*. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: here too, that same mention of *vibhāṣā* (optionally) recurs, and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore—"
Or rather, there will be a negation of that which is called "beneficial."
171. *brāhmaṇa-ajātau* | (6.4.171) If this were the only sūtra, would it then have the purpose of an exclusion (*niyamārtha*) or the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyartha*)?

If [the word] *apatya* ("descendant") is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], then, since the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) has already been prohibited by the immediately preceding sūtra...

The elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) by the rule *ṭhNas-taddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.144) is indeed established; however, since that is already established, this [rule] will serve as a restrictive one (*niyamārtha*), meaning: "Let it apply only when the sense is 'offspring' (*apatya*) and not when it is a generic class (*jāti*).
And thus, when the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed by the rule *tasyedaṃ* (Pāṇini 4.3.120), [we have] *brāhmaḥ garbhaḥ* ("the fetus of a Brāhmaṇa").

The forms *brāhmam astram*, *brāhmaṃ haviḥ*, and *brāhmī oṣadhiḥ* would not be established, because of the absence of the suffix *aṇ* used in the sense of offspring (*apatya*). Now, if the term "offspring" (*apatya*) is removed [from the rule], then it will serve solely as an injunction (*vidhi*). For in the previous rule, the substitution of the base form (*prakṛtibhāva*) was prohibited when referring to offspring; therefore, [the present rule]— [...continues...]

Since the rule *ṭhan* (Pāṇini 6.4.167) would otherwise cause the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) to prevail, this word *brāhma* is established as an irregular formation (*nipātana*) for the purpose of eliding the suffix *ṭil*. Thus, when this [suffix] has its injunctive force, the following forms are established: *brāhmaḥ garbhaḥ*, *brāhmaṇatvam*, and *brāhmaṃ haviḥ*; likewise, that which belongs to *brahman* is *brāhmī*.

The form *oṣadiḥ* would not be established, because of the prohibition [contained in the rule] *ajātau*. Since the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of suffixal changes) is prohibited by the rule *na mapūrvo 'patye 'varmaṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.170) for both *apatya* (descendant) and *jāti* (genus), the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*) occurs by the rule *nastaddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.144)—thus: *brāhmī*.
Regarding the example "Nārada," it might likewise be the case here as well—that "Brāhmaṇa" [is derived] as "the offspring of Brahmā.

Having thus observed the undesirable consequence of this single application (*ekayoga*), and wishing to avoid it, he says: "In this case, a separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) is made. Regarding that separation of the rules:

If [it is argued that] by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "provided there is a descendant" (*sati yadi ṭhapatye*), the elision of *ṭi* is prescribed only for a descendant, then—since [the desired form] is already established as before—the prescription would serve merely as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). Consequently, that same fault which was previously stated regarding the position of restriction (*niyamapakṣa*) would remain exactly as it was. And thus:

The making of a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) would otherwise be purposeless. Therefore, by virtue of the power of that *yogavibhāga*, even though the context concerns offspring (*apatya*), this term *brāhmaḥ* is treated as an irregular formation (*nipātana*) meaning "other than offspring. Thus, even when not referring to offspring, because of this irregular formation *brāhmaḥ*, [the form] *brāhmī* [is established].

Thus, the forms *garbhaḥ*, *brāhmastram*, and *brāhma haviḥ* are established. Following that, there is this second rule: *ajātau* ("when not denoting a genus"). Since the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is prohibited by the rule *na mapūrvo 'patye 'varmaṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.170), the elision of the suffix *ṭi* which would otherwise occur by *nastaddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.144) is [prevented]. That [elision] shall not [take place].

The phrase "so that it may not be" (bhūditi) means "only for the purpose of [denoting] offspring" (apatya eva). By this, he explains that in this second rule, the term "in offspring" (apatye) is carried over from the previous sūtra. Furthermore, the expression "not when it is a genus" (ajātau) is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (an absolute negation).

In that case, the connection is between "genus" (*jāti*) and the sense of "offspring" (*apatyārtha*), whereas the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the verb "to be" (*bhavati*). He expresses that very same meaning in the commentary (*vṛtti*).
Showing this, he says: "In the case of *apatya* [meaning] *jāti*, the elision of the suffix does not occur in *brāhmaṇa*.

The meaning is that when *apatya* qualified as a *jāti* is intended to be expressed, the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) does not take place in the word *brāhmaṇa* when the suffix *aṇ* follows.
"Only when [the word] 'apatya' [is present]"— as in "brahmāṇo oṣadhiḥ. By means of this counter-example, he shows that through the division of the rule (yogavibhāga),
even the form "brāhmī oṣadhiḥ" is established when there is an intention to express the genus alone.

172. *kārmastācchīlye* (Pāṇini 6.4.172). [The commentary says: "If this is so. If the suffix here is *ṇa*, then what is the purpose of this rule? The meaning is that it has no purpose whatsoever. Why is that? He says: *na-staddhite*. (Pāṇini 6.4.144). [This rule] causes the elision of the final *n* when a *taddhita* suffix follows. Since there is no *n* here, what would be the point of this [present] rule? Therefore, the suffix here is *ṇin*. [In that case,] by the rule *karmaṇoṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1), the suffix *aṇ* is added after the word *karman* when expressing an agent who performs that action habitually (*tācchīlya*). Thus, the form *kārmaṇa* is derived. However, since the suffix *aṇ* is a *taddhita*, the final *n* of *karman* would be elided by *na-staddhite*; therefore, he says: *kārmaṇaḥ*. [The suffix] *ṇin* is applied after the word *karman* in the sense of one who performs that action habitually (*tācchīlya*), and the suffix *aṇ* is added after *karman* in the sense of an agent (*kartari*). Thus, the form *kārmaṇika* is derived. But even so, the final *n* of *karman* would still be elided by *na-staddhite*; therefore, he says: *kārmaṇikaḥ*. [The suffix] *ṭhan* is applied after the word *karman* in the sense of one who performs that action habitually (*tācchīlya*). Thus, the form *kārmaṇika* is derived. But even so, the final *n* of *karman* would still be elided by *na-staddhite*; therefore, he says: *kārmaṇikaḥ*. [The suffix] *ṭhak* is applied after the word *karman* in the sense of one who performs that action habitually (*tācchīlya*). Thus, the form *kārmaṇika* is derived. But even so, the final *n* of *karman* would still be elided by *na-staddhite*; therefore, he says: *kārmaṇikaḥ*. [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied after the word *karman* in the sense of one who performs that action habitually (*tācchīlya*). Thus, the form *kārmaṇika* is derived. But even so, the final *n* of *karman* would still be elided by *na-staddhite*; therefore, he says: *kārmaṇikaḥ*. But even so, the final *n* of *karman* would still be elided by *na-staddhite*; therefore, he says: *kārmaṇikaḥ*. But even so, the final *n* of *karman* would still be elided by *na-staddhite*; therefore, he says: *kārmaṇikaḥ*. [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied after the word *karman* in the sense of one who performs that action habitually (*tācchīlya*). Thus, the form *kārmaṇika* is derived. But even so, the final *n* of *karman* would still be elided by *na-staddhite*; therefore, he says: *kārmaṇikaḥ*. [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied after the word *karman* in the sense of one who performs that action habitually (*tācchīlya*). Thus, the form *kārmaṇika* is derived. But even so, the final *n* of *karman* would still be elided by *na-staddhite*; therefore, he says: *kārmaṇikaḥ*. [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied after the word *karman* in the sense of one who performs that action habitually (*tācchīlya*). Thus, the form *kārmaṇika* is derived. But even so, the final *n* of *karman* would still be elided by *na-staddhite*; therefore, he says: *kārmaṇikaḥ*. [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied after the word *karman* in the sense of one who performs that action habitually (*tācchīlya*). Thus, the form *kārmaṇika* is derived. But even so, the final *n* of *karman* would still be elided by *na-staddhite*; therefore, he says: *kārmaṇikaḥ*. [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied after the word *karman* in the sense of one who performs that action habitually (*tācchīlya*). Thus, the form *kārmaṇika* is derived. But even so, the final *n* of *karman* would still be elided by *na-staddhite*; therefore, he says: *kārmaṇikaḥ*. [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied after the word *karman* in the sense of one who performs that action habitually (*tācchīlya*). Thus, the form *kārmaṇika* is derived. But even so, the final *n* of *karman* would still be elided by *na-staddhite*; therefore, he says: *kārmaṇikaḥ*. [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied after the word *karman* in the sense of one who performs that action habitually (*tācchīlya*). Thus, the form *kārmaṇika* is derived. But even so, the final *n* of *karman* would still be elided by *na-staddhite*; therefore, he says: *kārmaṇikaḥ*. [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied after the word *karman* in the sense of one who performs that action habitually (*tācchīlya*). Thus, the form *kārmaṇika* is derived. But even so, the final *n* of *karman* would still be elided by *na-staddhite*; therefore, he says: *kārmaṇikaḥ*. But even so, the final *n* of *karman* would still be elided by *na-staddhite*; therefore, he says: *kārmaṇikaḥ*. But even so, the final *n* of *karman* would still be elided by *na-staddhite*; therefore, he says: *kārmaṇikaḥ*. [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied after the word *karman* in the sense of one who performs that action habitually (*tācchīlya*). Thus, the form *kārmaṇika* is derived. But even so, the final *n* of *karman* would still be elided by *na-staddhite*; therefore, he says: *kārmaṇikaḥ*. [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied after the word *karman* in the sense of one who performs that action habitually (*tācchīlya*).

"Thus, indeed," and so forth. For a *nipātana* (irregular formation) is undertaken for that which is not obtained through a general rule (*lakṣaṇa*). However, in this case, [the desired form] is already established by the rule "ṅas-taddhite" (Pāṇini 6.4.144). Indeed, no preservation of the original stem-form (*prakṛtibhāva*) has been stated for the suffix *ṇa*, such that [a *nipātana* would be required] therein.

This [rule] being commenced for the purpose of eliding the *ṭi* would be meaningful; for the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) has been stated for that which ends in an *aṇ*, but not for one ending in a *ṇ*.
He accepts the meaning just mentioned: "If it is true..."

He asks, "For what purpose is this? and replies with "for the sake of indication" (*jñāpakārtham*), and so forth. Regarding "those performed by *aṇ*" (*aṇkṛtāni*) and so on: the operations (*kāryāṇi*) performed by *aṇ* are "performed by *aṇ*" (*aṇkṛtāni*). The compound is formed by the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "the locative case" (*saptamī*, Pāṇini 2.1.40). Alternatively, they are "performed by *aṇ*" (*aṇā kṛtāni*), according to [Pāṇini 2.1.32]: "The agent and the instrument, when joined with a *kṛt* suffix... (*kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*).
The compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.32] *bahulam*. He asks: "What is the purpose of this indication?

and replies with the words beginning with *tena*. Since her habit (*śīla*) is *cura* (stealing) or her habit is *tapas* (asceticism), the suffix *ṇa* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.4.62] *chatrādibhyo ṇaḥ*, and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added after that. This is because the suffix *ṇa* is used in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tācchīlika*).

Since this meaning has already been made known, when the suffix *ṇa* is applied to *daṇḍa* by the rule "The suffix *ṇa* is added after [a word] signifying a weapon, in the sense of 'this is the weapon used in this [game],' in the case of *krīḍā*" (Pāṇini 4.2.57), resulting in *dāṇḍā*, the grammatical operation that would have been effected by the suffix *aṇ* does not take place.
If, however, the operation of *aṇ* were desired for words denoting habitual disposition (*tācchīlika*), then *aṇ* alone should be applied after words such as *chatra*.

Why should it not be stated? In that case as well, this is the meaning: why should a *nipātana* (irregular formation) not be made for the sake of making [the form] known? You have rightly said this; however, the suffix *aṇ* was applied for the sake of variety, as in "kārmaṇam. Here, *aṇ* is applied by the rule "tadyuktāt karmaṇo 'ṇ" (Pāṇini 5.4.36), [meaning] "by means of an action (*karman*)."
The kārmaṇa body is thus appropriately described.
173. *āṬkṣamanapatye* | (6.4.173) [The word] *āṬkṣam* is a pada. [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied by [the rule] *tasyedam* (4.3.120).
*dāṇḍināyana-hāstināyana-ātharvaṇika-jaihmāśineya-vāsināyani-bhrauṇahatya-dhaivata-sārava-aikṣvāka-maitreya-hiraṇmayāni*. (Pāṇini 6.4.174) [The commentary states:
"By way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), the treatise (*grantha*) is also called 'Atharvan'. As for this metaphorical usage:
The very fact of being spoken by him (*tatproktatvam*) is the basis [for the suffix]. For example: *ātharvaṇikaḥ* [is derived] by [the rule] *vasantādibhyaṣṭhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.66).
[And] *bhrauṇahatyam*: [this is formed] from *bhrūṇaṃ hatavān* [by the rule] *brahmabhrūṇavṛtreṣu kvip* (Pāṇini 3.2.87).

(3.2.87), *ṣyañ* [is added] after that which ends in *tad*. Since the letter *t* is already established by the rule *harasto'ciṇṇaloḥ* (7.3.32), why is it stated as a *nipātana* (irregular formation)? To this he says: *inasto'ciṇṇaloḥ*, etc.
[The principle is: "When a verbal root is mentioned by its own form, the grammatical operation is understood to apply specifically to a suffix attached to that [root]. (Jainavṛtti 31).

The meaning is that the grammatical operation is understood to apply to that suffix which is prescribed by the rule "dhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.162). Now, the suffix *ṣyañ* is not a suffix prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*); what then?
It is a suffix prescribed after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Therefore, in that case, the rule "hanasto 'ciṇṇaloḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.32) applies.

The letter *t* would not be obtained [in the form *tat*], therefore it is introduced as an irregularity (*nipātana*). But how is it understood that "when the root's own form is mentioned, the grammatical operation applies to its suffix"? This is not so; for in the rule *na kvādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.59), the exclusion of the change to *k* (*kutva*) can be achieved even by splitting the rule with the word *na*.
To form [the word], one says "bhrauṇaghnaḥ, vartraghnaḥ," where the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of offspring (*apatya*).

When the suffix *añ* is applied to the word *ikṣvāku* by the rule "from words denoting a country" (Pāṇini 4.1.138) and so forth, then the word *aikṣvāka* has its first syllable as udātta due to the accent of the *ñit* suffix. However, when [the suffix *aṇ*] is applied by the rule "after a word having *k* as its penultimate letter" (Pāṇini 4.2.132)...
Thus, the secondary suffix *aṇ* applies, and it is udātta on the final syllable.
But surely, when only one such rule is mentioned, the inclusion of the other is not established;
therefore, both forms with different accents must be explicitly mentioned—namely, *aiśvakaḥ* and *aikṣvakaḥ*.

Thus [it is said]. To refute this objection, he says: "by the pronoun *svara*," and so forth. The pronunciation of accents (*udātta*, etc. without distinction is *ekaśruti*. And that is a pronoun for accents just as it is a pronoun [for things] in cases such as "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*, Pāṇini 4.1.92).
The *nirdeśa* (instruction) establishes specific distinctions such as Upagu and others through differentiation;

likewise, even a single sound [conveys] specific accents such as the acute (*udātta*) and so forth. Thus, this word *Aikṣvāka* is recited here—neither with an acute accent on the first syllable nor with an acute accent on the final syllable; for it is recited in this manner.

A specific vowel arises from a specific condition: when *añ* follows, then the *ot* [of the feminine suffix] is replaced by *ant*. This is an exception to the substitution [prescribed by Pāṇini 7.3.103]. By the rule *kekayādi* (7.3.2), the substitution of *īya* would apply;
however, its exception is the elision (*lopa*) which is prescribed as a nipātana. Then, by *ato guṇe* (6.1.97), there is the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*).

"Why is this [suffix] *ṭhak* used?"—in order to reveal the very intention with which he asked this, he says: "Then, when *añ* has been applied," and so forth. "It is established" (*siddham*) because there is no difference between the form and its essential nature (*svarūpa*). And by the phrase "for the purpose of eliding *ya*" (*yalopārthaśca*), etc., [it is shown that it is necessary] in the case of the *bidādi* group.
This demonstrates that quality [of being a *yañ* suffix].
Regarding the rule "and in the case of *yaska*-type names," and so forth: the purpose of including that [name] there is so that the elision (*luk*) of the plural *gotra* suffix may occur.
However, since that elision is already established by the rule "and of *yañ* and *añ*" (Pāṇini 2.4.64) once the name is included in the list beginning with *vida*, there is no need for it.

[The formation is] by virtue of its inclusion among the *yaska* group, as in "the Maitreya Saṅgha," and so forth. By this, he demonstrates the fault that would arise if [Maitreya] were included among the *bidādi* group. If it were included among the *bidādi* group, then everything you have stated would be justified; however, [it is not so], because from the word *maitreya*, which ends in the suffix *añ*...
By the rule *saṅghāṅkalakṣaṇa* (Pāṇini 4.3.127), the suffix *aṇ* would apply, resulting in the undesired form *maitreya*, rather than the desired *maitreyaka*. However, from a word ending in *ḍhañ*,
the suffix *vuñ* applies according to *gotracaraṇādvuñ* (Pāṇini 4.3.126), thus yielding the desired form *maitreyaka*.
It is established [by the form] "hiraṇmayaḥ. The suffix *mayaṭ* is applied by the rule "mayaṭ vaitayor bhāṣāyām" (Pāṇini 4.3.143).

175. *ṛtvyavāstvāstvyamādhvīhiraṇyayāni ca chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.4.175). [Examples: *ṛtvyam*, *vāstvyam*. [The suffix] *yat* is applied by [the rule] *bhave chandasi* (4.4.110). [The form] *vāstvam* [is derived] by [the suffix] *aṇ* applied by [the rule] *tasyedam* (4.3.120). Likewise, *mādhvī*.
The same applies here as well: in the word *hiraṇyayaḥ*, the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the same manner as before.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the sixth chapter in the *Kāśikāvivarahaṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who is like a Bodhisattva.
The *Kāśikā-vivaraṇa-pañjikā*, also known by its alternative title *Nyāsa*, composed by the venerable Ācārya Jinendrabuddhi, who was a disciple of the illustrious Bodhisattva.
The Kāśikā Commentary — Seventh Chapter.
First Pāda. 1.
*yuvoranākau* (Pāṇini 7.1.1). For the sake of brevity in this treatise, the suffixes *yu* and *vu* have been taught here; of these two—

The substitutes *an* and *āk* are prescribed in their proper place. For if the substitutes *an* and *āk* were to be prescribed wherever the terms *yu* and *vu* are taught, then there would be prolixity (*gaurava*) in the treatise, because those two [substitutes] consist of a collection of many phonemes. Here, however, for *yu* and *vu*, the semivowels *yaṇ* [are substituted].
This is a reference to the two suffixes *yu* and *vu*; however, such forms without indicatory letters (*anubandha*) do not occur in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*).

Therefore, by virtue of the contextual implication (*sāmarthya*), it is understood that these two are grasped in their general sense, setting aside the specific indicatory letters which serve as qualifiers.

Thus he says: "In the case of these two, *yu* and *vu*, whose specific [suffixes] have been discarded (*utsṛṣṭaviśeṣaṇayoḥ*). This refers to the term "this apprehension" (*idaṃ grahaṇam*), which is to be connected with what is about to be stated. A "specific" (*viśeṣaṇa*) is a suffix such as *lyu* or *la*; those two for whom that has been "discarded," meaning abandoned, are described as such. By this, [the rule] "of *yu* and *vu*" applies to *lyuṭ* and the others.

He shows that this is a general designation. If, in this context, there were an unrestricted inclusion of *yu* and *vu*, then from the root *yū* (DhP 1033)—[the Dhātupāṭha also reads *yū miśraṇe amiśraṇe ca*]—we would have *yutaḥ*, *yutavān*, and *yutvā*; and from the root *diṣu* (DhP 1107), [the same would follow].
[The forms] *dyūtaḥ*, *dhūtavān*, and *dhūtvā* [are derived from the root *dhū*].
According to the rule *ūrṇāyā yus* (Pāṇini 5.2.123), [the suffixes] *-an* and *-aka* would also apply in cases such as *ūrṇāyuḥ*;
therefore, in order to exclude this over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), he says: "of the nasal and the *yaṇ*."

The term *anunāsiko yaṇyayoḥ* is a bahuvrīhi compound. For there are both nasalized (*sānunāsika*) and non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*) semi-vowels (*yaṇ*); among these, this [rule] refers to those two for which the semi-vowel is nasalized. Furthermore, the semi-vowels *y* and *v* that are nasalized are only [the substitutes] *ya* and *vu*.

To show that [the rule] does not apply to non-suffixes, he says: "of the two suffixes. Others, however, explain that the words "of the two suffixes" are stated for the purpose of excluding non-suffixes; but that is incorrect, because the exclusion of non-suffixes is already established by the rule itself, "of the nasal and the *yaṇ*. Therefore...

In this treatise (śāstra), the *yū* and *vu* [substitutes] for the *anunāsika* and *yaṇ* [sounds] are indeed suffixes (*pratyaya*). Therefore, it is understood that the statement "of the two suffixes" (*pratyayayoḥ*) is stated for the purpose of demonstrating the possibility that those *yū* and *vu* which are *anunāsika* and *yaṇ* are exclusively suffixes, and not non-suffixes. And when there is the mention of the *anunāsika* and *yaṇ* as suffixes...
This genitive case in "satyaṅgasya" (of the stem) should be understood as indicating a relationship (*sambandha-lakṣaṇā*);

the connection is that [the suffixes] *yu* and *vu* are related to the stem. Furthermore, this relationship is characterized by the status of cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika-bhāva*), for the very existence (*ātmalābha*) of the stem is caused by the suffix.

"Thus, *aṅga* is the cause (*nimitta*), and the suffix (*pratyaya*) is the effect (*nimita*). By the rule *ṭhyorano vorakaḥ*, he expresses the relationship between the substituend (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) respectively. By the rule *nandyādibhyo lyuḥ*, [meaning] by the rule *nandigrahipacādibhyo lyuṇinyacaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.134), [the forms] *nandanaḥ* and *ramaṇaḥ* [are derived]. [The root is] *ṭua nadi*..."

The roots *sam-ud-dhau* (DhP 6.7) and *ramu krīḍāyām* (DhP 10.853). With the causative suffix *ṇic* in the sense of "instigation" (*hetumati*), the suffix *lyuṭ* is added after that [causative stem]. Regarding the form *sāyantanaḥ*, it is derived from *sāyam* and other words by the rule *sāyam-prabhṛtibhyaṣ ṭyuṭ-yul-au* (Pāṇini 4.3.23). This is according to the rule *sāyaṃ-ciram-...* (4.3.23) and so forth.
In the sense of a secondary derivative (*śaiṣika*) such as "born from" and so forth, there is a *taddhita* suffix. For example: *vāsudevakaḥ*, *arjunakaḥ*.

[The word] *vāsudevaḥ* is the offspring (*apatyam*) of Vasudeva; one who possesses devotion to Vāsudeva is called *vāsudevakaḥ* by means of the suffix *vun* according to the rule *vasudevārjunābhyāṃ vun* (Pāṇini 4.3.98). Thus, *vāsudevakaḥ*.

Arjunaka: [The word] *ūrṇāyuḥ* means "one who has wool" (*ūrṇā asya santi*). In that case, because there is an absence of the *anunāsika* quality for the *yaṇ*, [the substitution] does not occur. What, then, is the reason that these and similar instances lack the *anunāsika* quality for the *yaṇ*?

Thus he says: "of these and so forth," etc., namely, "the followers of Pāṇini [recognize] the anunāsika in the pratijñā. Wherever they recognize the state of being *anunāsika* by way of a formal declaration (*pratijñā*), there alone it occurs, and not elsewhere. And that [state] is not declared by them for *yuṣm* and the others, because of their adherence to the actual linguistic usage (*lakṣya*). Therefore, for those [sounds],...

The *yaṇ* substitution does not occur for the nasalization (*anunāsikatva*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [rules] such as *ṭhahaṃ śubhamoryus* (Pāṇini 5.2.140) are included. Now, one might object: since the suffixes *yuṣ*, *vab*, *hayuṣ*, *tutayas*, and *taṣ* are introduced by the rule *ṭhkaṃśaṃbhyāṃ vabhayustitutayasaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.138), [the nasalization] would not occur simply because of the presence of the marker *s*.

It will be so; for the insertion of *s* (*sitkaraṇa*) is for the sake of the designation "word" (*pada*), and the designation "word" is for the sake of the *anusvāra*—so that when that [designation] exists, the *anusvāra* may occur by the rule "m followed by a consonant becomes *anusvāra*" (Pāṇini 8.3.23). If, however, there were no substitution here [of *s*], then the insertion of *s* would be purposeless.

It might be argued: "No, for the *anusvāra* does not occur when a substitute has been applied, because in the rule prescribing it—namely, *hali sarveṣām* (Pāṇini 8.3.22)—the word *hali* is understood as a governing term (*anuvṛtti*). Thus, once the substitute is applied, the *anusvāra* does not occur, because the condition of being preceded by a consonant (*hal-āditva*) is absent. This is not so; by the force of the explicit statement, the *anusvāra* occurs even before vowels (*aj-ādi*).

There may be another purpose for the addition of the *s*—namely, the designation (*saṃjñā*) of a "word" (*pada*). The result of that is the sublation of the designation "bha. For if the designation "bha" were applied, there would be elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) in all [stems] ending in *ya*, even when they are merely designated as "bha. Alternatively, the addition of *s* may be for the sake of the *avagraha* (the pause in recitation); how then could it be meaningless?

In this case, regarding the mention of *yuvoḥ*, either a collective (*samāhāra*) dvandva or a distributive (*itaretarayoga*) dvandva is intended. In the former view, when the genitive singular is applied, because of the neuter gender according to *sa napuṃsakam* (Pāṇini 2.4.17), the augment *num* is added by *iko 'ci vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.1.73).

It ought to be so; consequently, the grammatical reference would have been *yuvunoḥ*. However, in the other view, once the substitution of *yaṇ* has taken place before the ending *osi*, one would have to hear a second *v* in the form *yuṣvoḥ*. To refute this objection, he says: "In this case, [the reference is] *yuvoḥ*."

“[The word] ‘explanation’ (nirdeśaḥ),” and so forth. Regarding the rule “the teaching of suffixes (āgama) is not constant”: the teaching (śāsana) of suffixes—that is, their prescription—is not constant, because in some cases they do not occur. Alternatively, that grammatical treatise (śāstra) by which suffixes (āgamas) are taught (śiṣyante)—that is, prescribed—is the “teaching of suffixes” (āgama-śāsana).

The treatise (*śāstra*) is non-eternal (*anitya*), because its eternal effect is not present. Furthermore, the non-eternality of the teaching of the *Āgama* is understood from the inclusion of the word "optionally" (*vā*) in the rule *ghorlopo leṭi vā* (Pāṇini 7.3.70). For that [substitution] occurs optionally in forms such as *dadat* and *dadāt*, whereas in [the case of the eternal]... it is constant.

This is done for the purpose that there should not be a disappearance [of the augment]. And if the rule for the introduction of augments were eternal (*nitya*), the mention of the word "optionally" (*vā*) would be useless. Let the disappearance be eternal; even though it exists, once the augment *aṭ* has been applied by the rule "aṭ and āṭ for the Imperative" (Pāṇini 3.4.94), forms such as *dadat* and *dadāt* are indeed established.
However, if [the rule] were non-eternal (*anityatva*), then because of the absence of the augment *āṬ*, the formation would not be established.
Therefore, the optional statement (*vāvacana*) becomes meaningful.
[The sūtra] says "or the neuter gender," and so forth; or rather, in this case, there is only the neuter gender.

It does not exist. What is the reason? He says: "Gender (*liṅga*) is not to be prescribed," and so forth. For since gender is a worldly matter (*lokadharma*), the world alone is its basis. Therefore, because it is established through the world itself, it is not to be prescribed as something to be taught; rather, it is the science of gender itself [that must be studied] in this regard.

Because it serves that purpose, it is designated by the word *liṅga*. The treatise concerning the meaning of *liṅga* need not be taught, because the *liṅga* to be accomplished by it is based on common usage (*lokāśrayatvāt*). By this, he demonstrates the rejection of rules such as "that [is] neuter" (Pāṇini 2.4.17). And in that case...

"Since that [suffix] has been rejected, its neuter status does not occur by way of that [suffix]; so how could there be the contingency of *num*? But in the case of the *itaretara* (mutual) view, there is elision of the phoneme due to its being Vedic (*cchāndasa*).
For 'the Sūtras are like the Vedas'; this is what is meant by 'being Vedic. By that..."
Just as in the case of *yatheṣkartāram adhvaraḥ*, where there is the elision of the letter *n* in *niḥ*, so too here the elision of the letter *v* should be understood.

2. *āyan*, *ney*, *nī*, *ya*: [The reading in the Kāśikā is *āyan-ney-in-īy-yaḥ*. These are substitutes for the initial sounds of suffixes beginning with *ph*, *ḍh*, *r*, *v*, *cch*, and *gh*. (Pāṇini 7.1.2) The letters *ph* and others are also taught here in this grammatical treatise for the sake of brevity; therefore, *āyan* and the other substitutes apply to them as well.
The substitutes are prescribed by this [rule]. It should be understood that those being prescribed apply to the consonant *ha* alone, starting with the letter *pha*. Why is this so?
Because of the mention of *ghām* without a vowel at the end; for otherwise, he would have said *ghānām*.

In other cases, however, the adventitious letter *a* is merely for the purpose of pronunciation. For this very reason, since only the consonant portion of *pha* and so forth— occurring at the beginning of an affix— is taken as the substituendum (*sthānin*), the paribhāṣā concerning "that which lacks an anubandha" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 53) applies here.

It does not apply [to the *ph* of *naḍa*], for in all cases the suffixes beginning with *pha* are without an indicatory letter (*niranubandhaka*). Its application occurs only where both conditions are possible, as in "Nāḍāyana. In the rule "From *naḍa* and others, *phak*" (Pāṇini 4.1.99), the suffix *phak* is applied in the sense of offspring (*apatya*).
In the subsequent examples as well, except for the instance of the substitution of *īya*, it should be understood that [the suffixes] are used in the sense of offspring (*apatya*). For example:

*sauparṇeyaḥ* and *vainateyaḥ*; here, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied after *suparṇā* and *vinatā*. Also: *āṭhaḷkulīnaḥ*; here, by the rule "after a word other than a prior member [of a compound], either *yaṅ* or *ḍhakañ* may be applied" (Pāṇini 4.1.140).

In this regard, because of the statement "after a word that does not have a preceding member," the suffix *kha* occurs even after a word with a preceding member by virtue of the rule *kulātkhaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.139), as in *gārgīyaḥ* and *vātsīyaḥ*.
From the words *gārmya* and *vātsya*, which end in the suffix *yañ*, the suffix *cha* is applied when there is a desire to express the sense of "belonging to this" (*tasyedam*).

By the rule *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), there is the elision of the vowel *a*; by the rule *āpatyasya ca taddhite 'nāti* (Pāṇini 6.4.151), there is the elision of the letter *ya*. Thus we have the forms *phakkati* and *ḍhaukate*. The root *phakka* means "to go low" (*nīcair-gatau*) [Dhātupāṭha 1.116], and *ḍhaukṛ*...

These are the forms derived from the following roots: *gatau* (Dhātupāṭha 98), *khanu avadāraṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 878), *cchidir dvaidhīkaraṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 1440), and *ghūṇa* and *ghūrṇa bhramaṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 437, 438). [Note: The Dhātupāṭha actually reads *ghuṇa*, as indicated by the correction in the source.]

The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used for the roots *ḍhauk* and *dhūrṇ* because they are marked with the anudātta accent. Regarding the forms *ūrudadhnam* and *jānudadhnam*: the suffix *dadhnac* is applied according to the rule *pramāṇe dvayasac-daghnañ-mātracaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.37), meaning "that which has the thighs as its measure."

In this context, these [operations] such as *ādyudātta* (acute on the first syllable) and others, being prescribed under the heading of "stems" (*aṅga*), are dependent upon both stem and suffix, and are therefore *bahiraṅga* (external). However, the acute accent on the beginning of a suffix is *antaraṅga* (internal), because it occurs by depending on the suffix alone, without regard for the stem. Consequently, the *bahiraṅga* [rules]...

As long as [the suffixes] āyan, etc., have not yet come into being, so long must there be udātta accentuation by virtue of the *pratyaya* (suffix) itself; once that has been applied, the substitutes (*ādeśa*) come into being— provided that no indicatory letter (*anubandha*) is prescribed for the sake of accentuation, as in the rules "ḍhaḥ after *śilā*" (Pāṇini 5.3.102) and "chhaḥ after a *vṛddha* [stem]" (Pāṇini 4.2.114).

In such cases as (Pāṇini 4.2.114), where the objection arises that "there [the substitutes] would result in having undetermined accents," he says: "The suffixes *āyan* and so forth are treated as *itaḥ* (having the augment *it*)," and so on.
The intention is this: the suffixes *āyan* and so forth are indeed *antaranga* (internal/within the base). For if [the rule] *aṅgasya* (6.1.4)—[were not applied here]...

In this context, [the word "aṅgasya"] would be connected [to "phādīnām"]; in that case, those [suffixes] would be *bahiraṅga* with respect to the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*). However, it is not connected here, because there is no purpose [for doing so]. For instance, the substitution of *āyan* and so on for *pha* and so on occurs in those suffixes beginning with *pha* which are the cause (*nimitta*) for the base (*aṅga*).

The purpose is this: that they should apply to [the root] and not to others. And this is obtained by implication even without the governing heading (adhikāra) of "aṅga" (stem), for among the suffixes beginning with *ph*, there is no such suffix that does not become a cause (*nimitta*) for the stem. Therefore...

Because there is no purpose [for it], the phrase "of the subordinate element" (aṅgasya) is not connected [here]. Therefore, the substitutes depend only on the locus (sthānin) itself, and not on the original base (prakṛti); thus, they too are indeed internal (antaraṅga).
Consequently, by virtue of their priority (paratva), those [substitutes] must first take effect at the time of the instruction of the suffix.

And therefore, by the rule "the first syllable of an affix is acute" (*pratyayādyaudātatvena*), the *ayn* and other substitutes occur at the very time the affix is taught; thus, once they have been applied, the acute accent on the initial syllable of the affix takes effect. Regarding this, he provides a supporting indicator (*jñāpaka*) with the words "And so," etc. The meaning is "and in this way."

The purpose of this [mention of] *ghaca* as a cause is so that the final acute accent (*antodātatva*) prescribed by Pāṇini 6.1.163 for the suffix *citaḥ* may apply. And if *āyan*, etc., were to occur only at the stage of the formal instruction of the suffix (*pratyayopadeśāvasthā*), then—

The act of marking with an accent (cittvakaraṇa) is purposeful; it is not otherwise. For otherwise, if these [accents] were to occur after the stage of the instruction (aupadeśika), then wherever the state of being udātta occurs even in the absence of the marking, it would have to occur in that very same place by virtue of that [marking], even when the vowel *a* of the syllable *dhakāra* is present despite the marking.
Otherwise, the mention of the augment *cit* would be purposeless.

Therefore, from the mention of *cit*, it is understood that these substitutions for *āyan* and so forth occur at the very time the affix is taught; subsequently, the acute accent (*udātta*) applies to the beginning of the affix—this is the intended meaning.

But surely these [rules] are prescribed for the consonant (*vyañjana*), and that consonant is without a vowel (*asvara*); yet it must necessarily be accompanied by some vowel, because a vowel devoid of qualities such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth is impossible. In that case, regarding the substituend (*sthānin*):

Since there is no closest similarity (*āntaratamya*) due to the absence of accentuation, the *sthānentaratama* paribhāṣā (P. 1.1.50) does not apply; consequently, these [suffixes] would have to possess indeterminate accents. Therefore, if they did not possess the *cit* designation, then when these suffixes—which are prescribed subsequently—possess an initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*), that [accent] would [prevail].

In this way, the accent would result [as it is]; because it is *satiśiṣṭa* (left over). Therefore, the addition of the *cit* marker to the suffix *ghañ* is for the purpose of ensuring that the final acute (*antodātta*) occurs even by overriding that *satiśiṣṭa* accent. Consequently, how this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) must be considered. Now, regarding the root *śam*:

Why do substitutions not occur for words such as *khaḥ* (Paṃ. U. 1.104) meaning "conch," and *ṭhṣaṇo ḍhaḥ* (Paṃ. U. 4.104) meaning "eunuch" (*ṣaṇḍha*)? To this he says: "conch," "eunuch," and so forth. Furthermore, the designation *it* [of the final letter] also applies by virtue of the rules *laśakvataddhite* (1.3.8) and *cūṭū* (1.3.7).
It should be understood that [the substitution] does not occur simply because of the plural number [of the rule]. Regarding the rule "ṛterīyaṅ" and so forth:

the fact that this [sūtra] teaches the suffix *īyaṅ* in the form "ṛterīyaṅ" (Pāṇini 3.1.29) indicates that suffixes such as *āyan* and others do not exist for verbal roots. For if they did exist, [the teacher would have taught them directly].

One should say: "Because of the rule *ṭhṛtaśchaṅ*. [Objection: But surely, when a rule is formulated even though its result is already established, it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). And yet, *cchaṅ* is not established here; for if *cchaṅ* were present, the augment *iṭ*—characterized by the condition of being preceded by a consonant (*valādi*)—would necessarily apply, and consequently, because the suffix would not be considered initial (*anādi*), the substitution [of *ṛ* for *ṝ*] would not take place. [Response: This is not so.

Because it must be an *ādeśa* (substitute) due to its being *antaraṅga* (inherently internal); its *antaraṅga* status arises from the fact that it is prescribed at the very stage of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*). And once the *ādeśa* has been applied, since the condition of beginning with a *val* consonant no longer exists, there is no occasion for the application of *iṭ*. This is the purpose of the rule prescribing *īyaṅ*.
It is merely indicative, as in the rule "after the root *ṭhij*,

[the suffix] *khaś*" and so forth. The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of showing the distinction from those such as *śaṅkha* and *ṣaṇḍha*, where the designation *it* does not exist— as in the case of *śaṅkha* and others.

In that regard, since there is the contingency of [the rule for] substitution arising, the statement "bahulam" (diversely) is introduced for the purpose of excluding that; alternatively, the option (*vā*) in the rule "ṛter īyaṅ" (Pāṇini 3.1.29) is presented. However, in rules such as "ejeh khaś" (Pāṇini 3.2.28), there ought to be the designation *it* by virtue of the rule "laśakvataddhite" (Pāṇini 1.3.8), and thus the contingency of substitution arises.

It does not exist at all. Therefore, the plural formulation [of the rule] is not intended for the sake of excluding that [possibility] there; rather, the intention is that the alternative option (*vā-vacana*) "after *ṛ*, *īyaṅ*" should be introduced. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the author refers to] rules such as "after *priya* and *vasu*, *khac* after *vad*" (3.2.38) and "generally *gha* occurs in the masculine when forming a name" (3.3.118).

[The word] "grahaṇam" [is used]. This might be the objection: "The prescription of the substitutes for the sounds *kha* and *gha* leaves no room [for other rules]; therefore, since the designation *it* would be sublated by that [prescription], how could it apply here? To this he says: "In a taddhita," etc.
[This refers to] the prescription of the short vowel in "khityanavyayasya" (Pāṇini 6.3.66), and [the substitution of *k* for *c* and *j*] in "cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.52).

The rule *kuttva* (Pāṇini 7.3.52) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) [of the fact that the designation *it* does not apply here]. For that [application of *kuttva*] would not be possible if the designation *it* were sublated by the prescription of the substitute [for the final consonant]; moreover, the suffixes *khita* and *ghita* are absolutely impossible [in this context].
[This is seen in rules such as] *āyannīnornakārasya* (Pāṇini 7.1.82), etc.; for in these cases, the letter *n* occurs at the end of the suffixes *āyan* and *īn*.

The designation *it* would apply to that [final letter] by the rule "the final letter of a *ṭh*-class or a consonant is *it*" (Pāṇini 1.3.3). Once that [designation] exists, if the rule "there is elision of that" (Pāṇini 1.3.9) were applied, forms such as *nāḍāyanaḥ* and *āḍhaḷkulīnaḥ* would not be established.
Therefore, when the designation *it* would have applied to the *n* of *āyan* and *īn*, a counter-exception to that was provided.

[The suffix] must be applied. One might argue: "The designation *itsaṃjñā* will not occur simply because there is no purpose [for it]. To this he says: "For the sake of the *nit*-suffix," and so forth. That, moreover, refers to the acute accent (*udātta*) prescribed by rules such as "A word beginning with *ñ*, *n*, or *t* is always acute" (Pāṇini 6.1.197). Furthermore, the prescription of *pra* here [is for the sake of the rule] "Of the Easterners, [the suffix *cha* is added] after a base that does not contain a *vṛddhi* vowel... (Pāṇini 4.2.103).

Regarding the rule *phin bahulam* (Pāṇini 4.1.160), the letter *n* is attached as an indicatory (*it*) suffix to *phin*. Its purpose is this: so that, by virtue of being marked with *n* (*nit*), the word may have its first syllable accented acute (*ādyudāttatva*). In that context, if the *n* of *āyan* and *īn* were to receive the designation *it*, then even though they would be *nit*, there would be no [resulting] acute accent on the first syllable.

Since [the suffix] is already established, the addition of the marker *Ṇit* would be purposeless. But one might argue that it is for the sake of including the general term in the rule *pheś cha ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.149); for if that were not present, by the paribhāṣā "that which has no marker (*niranubandhaka*) takes precedence," only this very suffix [phiñ] would be included, and not *phiñ*. This is not so; for in that case...

Because of the continued application of the term *bahulam* in the rule *ṭhvṛddhāṭṭhakÂ sauvīreṣu bahulam* (Pāṇini 4.1.148), it is intended that only the suffix *phiñ* is understood there, and not *phin*. Thus, this addition of the marker *n* to *phin* is precisely an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the absence of the designation *it*. And this [rule] belongs to the *yoga-pakṣa*.

This is an indicator (*jñāpaka*): it shows that the *it*-designation does not apply to the letter *n* which is part of a substitute (*ādeśa*) prescribed by this rule (*yoga*). By this, it is established that even in the case of the *n* in *inu*, the absence of the *it*-designation is not [otherwise] established [by other means].

3. *jha* is the final [element]. (Pāṇini 7.1.3). "The mention of the suffix *ṭh* continues," because it is carried over from the immediately preceding sūtra. If this is so, then because they are prescribed in a single rule (*ekayoganirdiṣṭa*), the mention of *ādi* ("beginning with") would also continue; consequently, in the case of *śayāntai*, [the substitution would not apply].

[An objection is raised: "Could it be so? [No,] because the letter *ca* lacks the status of being an initial [of a rule]. To this, he says: "The mention of 'initial' (*ādi*) has been withdrawn. He thinks as follows: the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of words is indeed dependent upon their having the *svarita* accent; and that *svarita* quality is a property of the formal declaration (*pratijñā*), as in "those [terms] are *svarita* by formal declaration" (*pratijñāsvaritāḥ*).

Regarding the term "Pāṇinīyas": wherever they declare a vowel to be *svarita*, it occurs only there and not elsewhere. Consequently, even for elements specified within a single compound (*ekayoganirdiṣṭa*), the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of only one of them is not contradictory. And here, it is the affix alone that is declared to be *svarita*, not the mention of the word *ādi*.
Therefore, even though they are taught as a single yoga-rule, the term *pratyaya* (suffix) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].

[The statement] "the mention of *ṭh* and so forth has ceased" means that this substitute *anta* occurs; however, the substitute must be formulated together with the vowel *a*. The vowel *a* is for the purpose of preventing the technical designation (*itsaṃjñā*) of the letter *t*.
The purpose is so that [the suffix] does not [become part of the base]. And that [purpose applies] in cases such as *jarantaḥ* and *veśantaḥ*.

In forms such as *kurvanti*, the designation *it* does not occur precisely because of the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 1.3.4]: "In a case-ending (*vibhakti*), [the letters] *t*, *u*, and *m* [are not designated as *it*]. Now, however, in cases such as *jarantaḥ* and *veśantaḥ*, [the designation *it* would apply] by virtue of the statement "The *uṇ*-class suffixes are diverse (*bahulam*). But [this is not the case here].

Does it occur? And thus, the vowel *a* is pronounced for the purpose of utterance (*uccāraṇārtha*). Alternatively, the pronunciation of the vowel *a* is for the purpose of indicating the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the rule "na vibhaktau tusmāḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.4). Consequently, the letter *t* serves as the technical designation (*itsaṃjñā*) for the *t* in rules such as "tena kimo't" (Pāṇini 5.3.12). [As in] "kurvanti. [From] "ata... (Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a commentary on grammatical rules concerning the technical markers used in Pāṇinian grammar.)

The substitution of *u* [for the vowel *i*] occurs by the rule *utsārvadhātuke* (Pāṇini 6.4.110). Regarding the form *śayānte*: from the root *śīṅ*, the suffix *leṭ* is applied by *liṅarthe leṭ* (3.4.7); then *āṭ* is added by *leṭo 'ḍāṭau* (3.4.94); the *e*-substitution [of the *āṭ*] occurs; and while *eta ai* (3.4.93) is still in force, the substitution of *ai* for *e* occurs by *vaito 'nyatra* (3.4.96). [The form] *ujjhitā*.

Thus: [the form] *ujjhā* is derived from the root *ujjha* in the sense of "abandoning" (*utsarga*; DhP 1304) with the suffix *tṛc*. By the rule *ṛduśanas-* (Pāṇini 7.1.94), etc., the substitution *anaṅ* is applied; then, by the rules *nopadhāyāḥ* (6.4.7) and *sarvanāmasthāne ca* (6.4.8), the vowel is lengthened. [The form] *ujjhitum* is formed with the suffix *tumun*. [The form] *ujjhitavyam* is formed with the suffix *tavya*.

"In this case too," and so forth. Now, one might object: "Since it is internal (antaraṅga), the acute accent of the affix should occur first, and only afterwards the substitution [of the final syllable]; is this not so? It is not so;
for the substitution of the final syllable (antādeśa) is also internal. Its internality, however, is...

In this case, it should be understood as being like *nādi*. Because both [the substitution and the accent] are internal (*antaraṅga*), the substitution of *anta* occurs first, and subsequently, the acute accent (*udātta*) on the beginning of the suffix [is applied].
He states the evidence for this very point with the words "And thus," etc. And this is [stated] in the rule "ghacchāṬ ca" (Pāṇini 4.4.117).

The statement "the formation of the suffix *ghac* would be purposeless" has been explained by this very commentary. Because the suffix is udātta from the outset, when the substitution of *anta* (for *at*) occurs, the word *dviṣanti* has the udātta accent on the middle syllable; otherwise, there would be udātta on the final syllable, which is undesirable.
First, the substitution of the final letter is performed.

4. *adabhyastāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.4). This rule is commenced for the sake of forms not in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), since in the middle voice the result is already established by the subsequent rule.
[The example is] *dadati*. The elision of the vowel *ā* occurs by the rule *śnābyāstayorātaḥ* (6.4.112). [The form is] *dadatu*.

Thus [it is said]. In *loṭ*, there is the substitution of *u* by the rule "ṭheruḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.86). In *jakṣati* and *jāgrati*, the designation *abhyasta* is applied by the rule "jakṣityādayaḥ ṣaṭ" (Pāṇini 6.1.6). While examples such as *jakṣati* and so forth are appropriate, examples such as *dadati* and so forth are inappropriate; for in this case—

Immediately after the letter *jh* acquires its own existence, because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), it ought to undergo the substitution of *at*; thereafter, there is the *ślu* replacement of *śap*, followed by reduplication according to Pāṇini 6.1.10 (*ślau*);
then, the designation *abhyasta* [is applied]. At that time, since the original locus (*sthānin*) of the letter *jh* no longer exists, the substitution of *at* does not take place.

[The objection is: "It follows [that the rule applies]. And it cannot be said that 'it will occur by virtue of the status of being a substitute' (sthānivadbhāva); for in this case there is no status of being a substitute, because it is a rule concerning an *al* (phoneme). Nor can it be argued that the substitution of *ad* will occur by overriding the final-substitute (*antādeśa*) on account of its being external (*bahiraṅga*), since it has no other scope [to apply]."

It is appropriate to consider [the following]: since that [rule] finds scope in roots such as *jakṣ* and others, which have already acquired the designation "abhyasta" during their very state of being taught (*upadeśāvasthā*), he says—"This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of the final letter"—in order to refute this objection. Regarding the substitution of the final letter...

This exception (apavāda) is now commenced for that which has been universally applicable everywhere; for a general rule (utsarga) does not apply to the domain of an exception. Thus it has been said: "Exceptions operate first, and subsequently the general rules; the general rule operates by excluding the domain of the exception."

(Pu.pa. 56) Thus [it is said]. For this very reason, then, the substitution of *jus* would not occur. Just as the specific substitution of *at*—being commenced as an exception (*apavāda*) to the general application of the final-substitute (*antādeśa*)—is an exception to it, so too is it for the substitution of *jus*. Therefore, he says: "But by the substitution of *jus*..."

"It is superseded": because the substitution of *jus* has no other scope, the substitution of *at* is superseded. In the case of "adaduḥ," there is the *laṅ* suffix; by Pāṇini 3.4.109, *jus* replaces *jhi*.
In the case of "ajāgaruḥ," regarding the *jāgarti* root, that which was subject to the application of *guṇa* is [prevented] by the rule "not before *av*, *ciṇ*, *ṇal*, or *liṅ*" (Pāṇini 1.2.5).
By another rule characterized by a prohibition, namely (Pāṇini 7.3.85), and by the rule "jusica" (7.3.83), the guṇa substitution occurs. [The commentary states:

"In this case as well, once the substitute has been applied, the acute accent falls on the beginning of the suffix. The intention is that, consequently, words such as *punataḥ* have the acute accent on the middle syllable. However, if the reverse were the case...
It might be argued that, because the accentuation of the suffix is internal (antaraṅga), once that has been applied,

the substitution of *at* for the mere consonant [of the root] would result in an indeterminate accent. In that case, if it were unaccented (anudātta), then a word such as *punataḥ* would consequently have its final syllable accented (antodātta).

It would follow [that this is so]; for when [the suffix] is circumflex (*svarita*), then a middle-circumflex (*madhyasvaritatā*) and a middle-acute (*madhyodātatā*) are desired. But is it not the case that the acute accent (*udātatva*) of the suffix is *antaraṅga* (internal) because it depends solely on the suffix, whereas the substitute (*ādeśa*) is *bahiraṅga* (external) because it depends upon both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix?

According to the principle "between the internal and the external, the internal is stronger" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 94), it would be more logical for the acute accent on the beginning of the suffix to occur first, and the substitution afterwards;
so how can it be said that "once the substitution has been made, the acute accent on the beginning of the suffix occurs"? This is not the case.

For it has been said: "The statement should be made like that of Ṭhupadeśin. Furthermore—the substitute (ādeśa) is permanent (*nitya*), because it applies whether [the original] has been performed or not. For once the accentuation of the first syllable of the suffix (*pratyaya*) has been applied, that [substitute] becomes non-permanent (*anitya*) again due to the application of another form (*śabdāntara*). Thus, when the substitution of *ad-* for *jhi* has not yet occurred, the *i*-sound of *jhi*—

[An operation] applies; for when a different word beginning with *ṭh* is about to apply upon the substitution of *sva* for [the vowel] *ā*, the rule becomes non-permanent (*anitya*). According to the principle "between the permanent and the non-permanent, the permanent is stronger" (Vyāḍipāṭha 93), this [substitution] possesses greater force. Thus, due to this permanence, these two [rules] possess superior strength.

Because it is subsequent, the substitution [of *su*] ought to occur first, and after that, the acute accent on the beginning of the suffix. Therefore, it has been well said: "When the substitution has been made, the acute accent on the beginning of the suffix occurs."

5. *ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ* | (7.1.5) [The substitution of *e* occurs] for the final vowel of a verbal root ending in *a* before the *ātmanepada* endings. In *cincete*: this is the present tense (*laṭ*); because it is marked with the *svarita* accent, it takes the *ātmanepada* endings. In *cinvatām*: this is the subjunctive (*leṭ*); the *jha* suffix is replaced by *etva* (*e*), and by Pāṇini 3.4.90, *ām* is substituted for the *ta* of the first person plural. In *acinva ta*: this is the imperfect (*laṅ*).

The augment *aṭ* is applied, and by the rule "ṭhhuśnuvoḥ sārvadhātuke" (Pāṇini 6.4.87), there is the substitution of *yaṇ*. Thus we have "punate" and "lunate. As before, there is the elision of the vowel *ā*.
In "cyavante" and "plavante," once the suffix *śap* has been applied, [the *yaṇ* occurs] after an *aṅga* that does not end in *n*.

The substitution of *jh* does not occur. [Objection: But surely, because it is subsequent, the substitution of *ad* should take place first, and only afterwards the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*)? To this he says: "Because it is obligatory, not that" (*nityatvādatadra*), etc. Its obligatoriness (*nityatva*), however, is...

Because it would lead to an undesirable consequence (*kutākṛtaprasaṅgitva*). For a suffix with a *vikaraṇa* would apply both when the substitution of *at* has been made and when it has not been made; however, once that [substitution] has been made, there is no longer the application of the *adbhāva* (the substitution of *at*), and thus this [suffix] is considered non-eternal (*anitya*). The phrase "by one ending in *an*" and so forth refers to the suffix (*pratyaya*).

Thinking, "Why is it not qualified by the condition 'ending in a non-ṇakāra'? he says "iha" and so forth. If the suffix were to be qualified [by that condition], then it would also apply in the case of *śayāntam*; for here too, there is a suffix beginning with *jh* following an *aṅga* ending in a non-ṇakāra.
