[However,] because it is separated by the augment *āṭ*, it does not [apply].

If it is argued that [the rule] applies, we say no; because that [augment] is subordinate to the whole, it is not logical for there to be an intervention by a single part of it. However, when the sound *jha* is being specified, there is no fault, because [the augment] *āṭ* intervenes.
For *āṭ*, being subordinate to the entire group, would not intervene between the whole itself and its own constituent part. But [it does intervene] with respect to the member...
It certainly does intervene; for it is never observed that one part [of a word] does not intervene between another part.
Although one could have simply stated "after *taṅ*" or "after *jha*," the expression "in the *ātmanepada*s after *an*" is used for the sake of variety.

6. *śīṅo ruṭ* (Pāṇini 7.1.6). [The meaning is: "The augment *ruṭ* occurs after the *ā* that is a substitute for *jha*. Now, an objection is raised: "But there is no mention of the word *āt* here; even though that which is under discussion (*prakṛta*) is present, it is in the nominative case, whereas the sense required here is expressed by a genitive case-referent (*ṣaṣṭhī-nirdeśa*). To this, he replies: "That..."

How can it be understood that the augment *ruṭ* occurs after the substitute *jha* for *āt*? This is not a problem; because of the rule "tasmād ity uttarasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.67), this fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) in the word *śīṅ* will be interpreted as a sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) corresponding to the first case ending (*prathamā*) of the word *āt*. Thus, there is no fault. [The form is] *śerate*.

Thus [it is said]: "There is *guṇa* substitution for the root *śūṅ* before a *sārvadhātuka* affix" (Pāṇini 7.3.21). Now, one might object: here the *sārvadhātuka* affix is separated by the augment *ruṭ*; how then can there be *guṇa*? For this [augment] does not belong to the *sārvadhātuka* affix; so how could it not be an intervention? [The answer is: this is an element belonging to that which is a part of the *sārvadhātuka* affix, namely the word *ac*.

Thus, it is grasped by the mention of *tat* (that), not by the mention of *sārvadhātuka* (a suffix belonging to a verbal root); for a part of a part is not a part of the whole. For it has been stated in the rule *che ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.73): "A part of a part does not become a part of the whole"? This is not so.
This is not a fault; for even a part of a part is indeed a part of the whole.

To illustrate: when it is said, "Let Devadatta be adorned," those parts of Devadatta such as his hands and feet, as well as the parts of those parts such as the fingers and so forth, are all adorned. Therefore...

The augment *ru* which is a constituent part of the element *ac* that itself is a constituent of a *sārvadhātuka* suffix is also considered a constituent of the *sārvadhātuka*; therefore, it is included by the mention of that [suffix], and thus there is no intervention.

Furthermore, as for what was stated under the rule *ṭhche ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.73)— namely, that "a part of a part does not become a part of the whole"— that was said with reference specifically to the augment *tuṅ* prescribed by that sūtra; for even though that *tuṅ* is a part of a part, it is included within the designation of the whole.
It is not taken because it is considered as such. But why is it not taken?

Because of the force of the attraction of the short vowel (*hrasva*). For in that [rule], the short vowel is attracted by the particle *ca*—so that the status of being an augment may belong to the mere short vowel itself, and not to that which ends in a short vowel.

[The word] *bhūt* [is used]. If that which ends in a short vowel were to possess the status of an augment (*āgama*), then in forms such as *cicchedatuḥ* and *ciccheduḥ*, because the *tuk* [augment] would be included by the mention of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) in the rule for *halādiśeṣa*, its removal would occur through that rule.
Furthermore, if it were not the case that a part of the *tuk* prescribed by that rule is not included by the mention of the whole [reduplicated syllable], [the fault would remain].
If it were grasped [as a whole], then when the short vowel itself is the *imitative* (*imitatva*), there would necessarily be its removal by the rule *halādiśeṣa*;

for the *tuk* which is a constituent part of the short vowel would be grasped by the mention of the "reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsa*). Consequently, the subsequent attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*) of the short vowel would be purposeless.

Now, for what purpose is *ruṅ* prescribed for the *adādeśa* (the substitute *at*), rather than being prescribed for *jhakāra*? In that case, this would mean that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the word *ataḥ* need not be supplied, because *jha*, ending in the genitive, is the subject under discussion. To this he says: "This *ruṅ*," and so forth. If...

If the letter *ka* were made the initial element with the preceding part as its end (*pūrvānta*), then in the case of *śerate*, there would be no *guṇa* substitution because the root would not end in *i*. Therefore, so that this fault does not occur, this *ruḍ* is made to have the subsequent part as its beginning (*parādi*). Even if it is made to begin with the subsequent part, if it belonged only to the letter *jha*, what undesirable consequence would there be?

Could this be so? He says: "If," and so forth. If *ruṭ* were to be added only after the letter *jha*, then the substitution of *ad* would not occur. Consequently, just as in the case of *śayāntai*—where the substitution of *ad* does not take place because it is separated by *āṭ*—so too it would not occur in the case of *śerate*.

[The augment] *ruṭ* is excluded because it is separated [from the relevant element]. Therefore, for the sake of avoiding this fault, some explain that *ruṭ* is prescribed as an augment for [the suffix] *ata* itself, and not for the letter *jha*; however, this is incorrect. For if *ruṭ* is applied to the letter *jha*, it becomes a part of that very [letter].
How, then, could there be an intervention by that [element]? For one does not indeed intervene with one's own constituent part.

Therefore, this [previous] explanation is incorrect; it is explained otherwise as follows: in the rule "the substitute *ad* would not occur," the phrase "of the letter *jh*" is required [as a reference], and thus the meaning becomes this: if...

The augment *ruṭ* would apply only to the letter *jha*, and not as a substitute for that [entire suffix] beginning with it. For whom, then, would it apply? It would apply to that very *ruṭ* itself; because of the rule "that which follows [the augment] replaces what begins with it" (Pāṇini 1.1.54).
Even though it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it does not become a substitute for the whole [suffix], because of the *ruṭ*.

Because it would lead to the undesirable consequence [of the rule] being meaningless. If it is argued that [the augment *ruṅ*] will not occur due to the power of its specific prescription, this is not so; for the prescription of *ruṅ* would be for the sake of a subsequent purpose, so that the augment *ruṅ* might occur in the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (Pāṇini 7.1.8). Indeed, [the form] *adṛśran* cannot be established by the suffix *taṭ*.

Therefore, the prescription of *ruṅ* for the root *śī* (śīṅ) has a specific purpose. This *ruṅ* is prescribed for the substitute [śī] in order to eliminate that aforementioned fault, and not for the original form (*akārṣīt*). The mention of the marker (*anubandha*) *ṅ* in the rule "śīṅ" is for the sake of excluding the *yaṅ*-lopa (the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix), as in the example *vyatiśesyata*.

7. *vetervibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 7.1.7). [The forms] *saṃvidrate*, *saṃvidate* [are derived from the root]. The root *vid* in the sense of "knowing" is listed at Dhātupāṭha 1064. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by rule 1.3.29, *samogbhyṛcchi* etc., and because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is the elision of *śap*.
"Let them know," "let them know"—this is the imperative (*loṭ*). When the substitution of *e* for the ending has been made, the augment *ām* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.4.90] *āmetaḥ*.
[The question is: "Why is there the mention of the root *veti* which has the *luk*-suffix? It is thus.
He thinks: "Let the mention of *vidhi* (rule) in the general term include all rules;

for in this way the sūtra becomes concise. Even though all rules are included, [the substitution] will occur only after a root with a *lu*-class suffix (*lugvikaraṇa*), and not after any other, because of the intervention by a suffix (*vikaraṇa*). If it were without distinction for all roots..."

[An objection is raised: "Could [the form] *vid* be derived even from the root *vid* 'to investigate' belonging to the *rudhādi* class? For here, the *vikaraṇa* suffix is not an intervening element, since it is included within the body of the root. To this, he says: "In this case," and so forth. [The forms are] *vinte*, *vindāte*, etc.
Regarding the form *vindate*: because it is marked with the anudātta accent, the ātmanepada ending is applied; furthermore, by Pāṇini 6.4.111 (*śnasorallopaḥ*), the *a* of the suffix *śnā* is elided.
However, in this context, *vindate* is cited as a counter-example in the plural;
the presentation of the singular and dual forms is intended to show that these are forms of the root *vid* in the sense of "investigation" (*vicāraṇā*).

This is for the sake of illustration; otherwise, if only "vindate" were stated, someone might mistakenly think that this form belongs to the root *vid* in the sense of "obtaining," as it ends in the singular.
Because of the mention of the *śtip* affix, [the substitution] does not occur when there is *yaṅ*-luk—as in *saṃvevidate* and *vyativevidate*.

8. *Bahulam chandasi* (in the Vedic language, there is diversity). Regarding the form *aduhra*: the Ātmanepada ending occurs because it belongs to the *svarita*-accented class. But surely, since the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], forms such as *aduhrata* are already established; what then [is the purpose of this rule]?

To one who might object on the grounds of the term "bahula" (in the sense of "frequently"), he replies with the words "By virtue of the term *bahula*," and so forth. For by the recurrence of the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally), only an option is obtained, but [the rule] does not apply elsewhere.
By virtue of the term *bahula*, it applies even elsewhere. Therefore, while *vibhāṣā* is the subject under discussion...

The sense is that this is stated as a frequentative expression (*bahulavacana*). Regarding the form *adṛśran*: it is the *luṅ* (aorist) of the root *dṛś*; *jhi* is replaced by *an*; by *irito vā* (Pāṇini 3.1.57), *cl* is replaced by *aṅ*; *ruṭ* is added to it; by *itaśca* (3.4.100), the final *i* is elided; by *saṃyogantasya* (8.2.23), the *t* is also elided; and by *ato guṇe*.

(6.1.97) There is the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*). Now, why does the *guṇa* substitution [prescribed by] Pāṇini 7.4.16, "for *ṛ* and *vṛ*, [there is *guṇa* before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix]," not occur here? If it is argued that this is because of the prohibition [by] Pāṇini 1.1.5, "and [before a suffix] marked with *ṅ*," we say no; for that [prohibition] is formulated specifically for what is marked with *ṅ*. The prohibition applies with reference to a *sārvadhātuka* suffix that is marked with *ṅ*.

If it is argued that [the substitution] is obtained, we say no; for one might object that "a single substitute (ekādeśa) behaves like the original (sthānivat) in a rule concerning what precedes," and in response to such a person, he says: "In the case of the roots ṛ and dṛś, when followed by an affix marked with ṅ, there is guṇa."

9. *ato bhisa ais* (Pāṇini 7.1.9). [The commentary begins with] "When the compound has been formed," and so forth. By the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* (2.2.18), the word *ati* is used in the sense of "having transcended" (*krānta*), etc. And by the rule *hrasvatve ca*, [it refers to] *gostriyor upasarjanasya*.
(1.2.48) Thus, [the vowel] is short. Now, one might raise the objection: "If it is made short, then the substitution of *jaras* prescribed for the word *jarā* would not apply to the word *jara*.
To dispel this objection, he says: "That which has undergone a modification in one part," and so forth.

But surely, even if that which has undergone a modification in one part is not considered different [from the original], the substitution of *jaras* should still not occur here; for by the paribhāṣā "A rule conditioned by a specific combination [of sounds] does not become the cause for the destruction of that very combination" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 12), the augment *aṬ* is prescribed as being characterized by its connection with the word *jara*.

How could that [augment] *aṬ*, which is prescribed by the rule "the augment *aṬ* is applied after a word ending in *jara* or *śas*" (*vyā.pa.* 12)—an augment characterized by the occurrence of the word *jara*—be the cause of the very destruction of that [occurrence]? To this he says: "The occurrence," etc. Furthermore, its non-eternality is as follows:
One must understand that [the substitution of *ay* for *i*] is optional because of the specific mention of *kaṣṭāya* in the rule *kaṣṭāya kramaṇe* (3.1.14).

For if this were obligatory, then the rule characterized by the final vowel *a*—namely, *supi ca* (7.3.102)—would not be the cause for the destruction of that state of having a final *a*. Thus, [the substitution would not apply].

In this way, the lengthening would not occur, and consequently, the grammatical rule *kaṣṭāya* (Pāṇini 3.1.14) would be untenable. Now, for what purpose is *ais* prescribed? Why not simply prescribe *e* instead?
For even in that case, once the *vṛddhi* substitution has been applied by the rule *vṛddhireci* (Pāṇini 6.1.88)—as in *vṛkṣaiḥ*—[the desired form is obtained].

Is it established by the rule beginning with *plakṣaiḥ*? But what benefit is obtained by doing so? For there is no distinction made for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*) when [the operation] is performed here, rather there would only be an increase in procedural complexity (*prakriyā-gaurava*). Having formulated it thus, [it is done] by another rule...
Is it because of the prescription of *vṛddhi* [substitution]? But the form *ajitarasaiḥ* is not established;
for there is no *vṛddhi*. To say that there is an absence of *vṛddhi* because of the absence of the suffix *sat* ending in the letter *k* is merely trivial.

In this case, regarding the form *vṛkṣaiḥ*, when the suffix *bhis* follows, the substitution of *ais* by the rule "ṭhato bhisa ais" would apply, as would the substitution of *e* by the rule "bahuvacane jhalyet. Both of these rules have their own scope of application; therein, the substitution of *ais* has its scope even when the substitution of *e* has already occurred.

In the past, relying on the fact that [the suffix] ends in *akāra*, there was scope for *ev* [to apply]—namely, the forms beginning with *bhyas*. To one who might think that *et* must occur here because it is subsequent [to the rule for *ais*], he says: "If you think that *et* applies in the case of *bhis* because it is subsequent," then [the rule] *ais* [applies].

Where will it occur? The substitution of *ais* for *bhis* is prescribed after a stem ending in short *a*; if, therefore, the substitution of *e* (by Pāṇini 7.1.9) were to take effect by virtue of its being subsequent [in the order of the rules], where then would this *ais* occur? Nowhere at all;
the point is that the status of ending in short *a* is everywhere superseded by the prescription of *e*. This refers to the state of becoming *ais*.

In order to show the scope [of the rule], he says: "Even when *etva* has been applied," and so forth. But how can *ais* arise for *bhisa* once *etva* has been applied, given that *ais* is prescribed for *bhisa* following an *aṅga* ending in *a*, and that once *etva* has been applied by virtue of its higher status (*paratva*), *bhisa* no longer follows an *a*-ending *aṅga*? In that case—

"By virtue of the authority of the word [of the sūtra], even when the *etva* (the substitution of *e* for *ay*) has been applied, the status of having ended in the vowel *a* in its prior state (*bhūtapūrva*) will be relied upon, and thus *ais* will occur; for [the rule] 'ais is eternal' remains true even when that [substitution] has been performed.
Thus, *ais* must occur both when the *etva* has been performed and when it has not."
Because it applies both when [the condition] has been performed and when it has not been performed: let *aitvam* be permanent (*nitya*) and *etvam* be non-permanent (*anitya*);
for once *ais* has been substituted, *etvam* does not apply, because the cause—the presence of a *jhal* sound—is absent.
Furthermore, since a permanent and a non-permanent rule possess equal force, a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is not possible between them. Consequently...
The sense is that even after casting aside this [enemy], he will become powerful once again.

10. *Bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.10). The inclusion of the term *bahulam* (diversely) is for the sake of clarity; for it is possible to carry forward the application of *bahulam* by means of the "frog-leap" maxim (*maṇḍūakaplutinyāya*).

11. *nedamadasorakoḥ* | (7.1.11) The two [pronouns] that do not have the letter *k* are *idam* and *adas*. Regarding the form *ebhiḥ*: there is the substitution of *yat* for *idam* according to the rule *tyadādīnām atvam* (7.2.102), the substitution of *et* for the final vowel before a suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant according to *bahuvacane jhalyet* (7.3.103), and the elision of the final *m* according to *hali lopaḥ* (7.2.113).

Thus there is the elision of such a form. Regarding "ṭhamībhiḥ": when the substitution of *e* for *adas* has been made, the substitution of *ī* occurs by the rule "eta īdavahuvacane" (Pāṇini 8.2.81), and *d* is replaced by *m*.
Regarding "ṭhimakaiḥ": the suffix *akac* is applied by the rule "avyayasarvanāmnām akac prāk ṭeḥ" (Pāṇini 5.3.71).

By the rule *ṭhdaśca* (Pāṇini 7.2.109), the letter *d* is replaced by *m*. Thus we have *amukaiḥ*; here, by the rule *adaso'serdādu do maḥ* (8.2.80), the *m* is substituted for the *u* following the *d*. Now, why was it not simply stated as *nedamadasoḥ*? What is the purpose of this [separate] mention of *akaḥ*?

If it is argued that if *akori* were not stated, there would be a prohibition even for [the forms] with *s* and *k*, this is not so; for when a prohibition is being stated for *idaṃ* and *adas*, what possibility could there be for it to apply to those with *s* and *k*? It simply does not apply.

He says "because it is a different word," starting with "of *ṭhaka* and *i*" and so forth. The purpose of this indicator (*jñāpaka*) is that the designation of pronoun (*sarvanāman*) applies to those ending in *akac*— namely, *sarva* and the others—
and the designation of indeclinable (*avyaya*) applies to *svar* and the others.

Now, why has it not been stated as "atha ṭhidamadasoḥ kāt" (then, after *idam* and *adas*, when [the suffix] *kā* follows)? In that case, since [the desired form] would already be established by the previous rule, this [new rule] would serve as a restrictive one (*niyamārtha*). When understood as a restriction—namely, that for the *bhis* belonging to *idam* and *adas*, the substitution *ais* occurs only after [the suffix] *kā*—then everything intended is secured by the restriction.
"Everything desired will indeed be accomplished, and the Sūtra will be concise. This is true;

however, in this arrangement of the Sūtra, the rule "that which falls within [the scope of] another is included by the mention of that" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 21) would not be made known. Furthermore, there would also be the risk of a contrary restriction (*viparītaniyama*).

Those of dull intellect might suspect that [the rule] applies only to *idam* and *adas*, as in "this" (*idam*) and "that" (*adas*). In that case, this would be a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning:

"Only after the *k*-sound belonging to *idam* and *adas*, the *ais* replaces the following *bhis*. Consequently, forms such as *viśvakaiḥ* and *sarvakaiḥ* would not be possible, because they would be excluded by the restriction.

And in this case, there would indeed be [the usage] "by these" (ebhiḥ) or "by those" (amībhiḥ), because [the pronouns] have not been restricted by rule. Therefore, let it remain exactly as in the original formulation.

12. *ṭāṅsiṅsāminātsyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.12). [The forms] *ati-jaras-inā*, etc., follow. When the compound has been formed as before and the shortening (*hrasvatva*) has occurred, the substitution of *jaras* takes place. Regarding the phrase "some" (*kecit*): these are those who follow the opinion of the author of the Sūtras. If...

If the form *hy atijarasina* were not intended by the author of the Sūtras as grammatically correct (*sādhutva*), he would have simply prescribed the substitution of *na* for *ta*. Furthermore, once the substitution of *et* has been applied there, forms such as *vṛkṣeṇa* are established. If one asks how this substitution of *et* occurs, it is because the rule for the application of *et* involves a separation of the grammatical connection (*yogavibhāga*).

This is the case: [the rule] "bahuvacane jhalyet" (Pāṇini 7.3.103), then "osi ca" (7.3.104), and then "āṅ cāpiḥ" (7.3.105). In that context, a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) must be made for the term "āṅ":
after the suffix *āṅ*, the substitution of *et* occurs for the final vowel of the stem—as in *vṛkṣeṇa*, *plakṣeṇa*; then follows "āpaḥ" (7.3.106).

Regarding the rule *sambuddhau ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.106): [an objection is raised] "But surely, if the substitution [of *na* for *idam*] were not applied, then when followed by a consonant (*hal*), the elision of the form *id-* of *idam* would apply; consequently, forms such as *anena* would not be established? This is not a fault; for in the rule *hali lopaḥ* (7.2.113), there is the provision *jarāyā jaras anyatarasyām* (7.2.101).

Therefore, the mention of *anyatarasyām* (optionally) continues [from the previous rule], and that is understood as a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*); consequently, once the substitution of *na-* has taken place, the elision (*lopa*) of the form *id-* does not occur. Thus, forms such as *vṛkṣeṇa* and so forth are established by the substitution of *na-* alone; therefore, that [substitution] alone should be applied.

There is the substitution of *in*; and since it has been performed, it is understood that "certainly *ati-jarasa* was intended as correct by the author of the Sūtra," for it is for the sake of establishing that form that he made the substitution of *in*. Otherwise, if the correctness of *ati-jarasāt* were not desired, [he would not have done so].

One should effect the substitution of *ṅserad*. Even there, by the rule "a long vowel replaces [a short] *ak* before a homogeneous vowel" (6.1.101), forms such as *vṛkṣāt* and so forth are indeed established. But surely, since "guṇa replacement of *ā*" (6.1.97) is an exception to "a long vowel replaces [a short] *ak* before a homogeneous vowel," the form of the subsequent element (*pararūpa*) would apply; how then is it established?

This is not so; by the force of the utterance of the letter *a*, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) will not occur; otherwise, he would have prescribed the letter *t* itself. For here, once the letter *t* is substituted for the initial *a* according to Pāṇini 1.1.54 (*ādeḥ parasya*), the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) ensures that forms such as *vṛkṣāt* are indeed established. In this case...

Indeed, when the substitution of *t* for the following *a* is prescribed by the rule "hi ṭhādeḥ parasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.54), and the final consonant of the cluster is subsequently elided, forms such as *vṛkṣāt* are established exactly as they should be.
Therefore, by virtue of the power of the explicit utterance of the vowel *a*, the substitution of a single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) will not occur; thus, the change to *at* is maintained.
It must be prescribed; by what means is it prescribed? It is prescribed by the substitution of *āt*.

From this it is understood that the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the form *atijarasāt* was certainly intended by the author of the Sūtras, since he prescribed the substitution of *āt* for the sake of its establishment. Thus, regarding the author of the Sūtras...

Some, following the opinion [of others], maintain that *atijarasinā* is correct, asserting that *atijarasāt* is the proper form. Regarding the passage beginning with "But as [it is]," in the Bhāṣya it says: "Now, for what purpose is the substitution of *in* stated? Why not simply state the substitution of *nā*? Thus...
By this series of textual passages, having rejected the substitution of *āt*, the substitution of *ad* alone was established;
[likewise], by the series of textual passages beginning with "Now for what purpose is *āt* stated? Why not say *ad*?
the substitution of *āt* was rejected and the substitution of *ad* alone was established. And if [the form] *atijarasinā*...

If the form *atijarasāt* were intended as correct, the author of the Bhāṣya would not have rejected both the substitution of *sā* for *smin* and the state [of the word ending in *jaras*]. Indeed, when there is a purpose [for a rule], its rejection is not appropriate;
yet those two have been rejected. Therefore, it is understood that "this is not desired."

13. *ReĀḥ* | (7.1.13) Regarding the term "*ReĀḥ*": this is a reference to the dative singular. Why is it not a reference to the locative singular? For if it were a reference to that [locative], [the following would occur].

In that case, [rules concerning] "extreme contact" (*atyantasaṃyoga*), "completion of an action" (*apavarga* as a state), "among the factors of action" (*kārakamadhye*), and so forth, would not be established. Therefore, based on these indications, this is not the inclusion of the locative singular here;
consequently, by process of elimination, it is determined that this is the inclusion of the dative singular.

Thus [it is said]. And because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *tasmai hitam* (Pāṇini 5.1.5), this very same [suffix] is understood to carry over even in subsequent cases. In the form *vṛkṣāya*, the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *supi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.102).

But surely, when the *paribhāṣā*— "A rule characterized by a specific combination [of factors] is not the cause for the destruction of that very combination" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 12)— is applicable, it is not logical for the *y*-rule, which is characterized by that combination, to be the cause for the destruction of the vowel *a*; how then could there be lengthening?

Thus he says: "characterized by a conjunction," and so forth. Its impermanence, however, has already been established previously. Now, for what purpose is the utterance of the letter *ṅ*? It is so that there may not be the inclusion of the letter *e* alone. If it were otherwise, [the rule] would apply even in cases such as *pace* and *yajai*. But surely—

And once the substitution of the single substitute for the latter form (*pararūpa*) has been applied by the rule *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97), will [the augment] not fail to occur because its cause is absent? This is not so; for this substitute is prescribed when the substitution of *guṇa* by *ato guṇe* has not yet taken effect.
Thus, in the case of *vṛkṣāya*, it subverts the *pararūpa* substitution prescribed by *ato guṇe*.

If it is argued that, likewise, in cases such as *pace* and *yajai*, [the substitution] would be blocked because the *i*-sound (*ikāra*) specified by its own rule (*pratipadokta*) is being grasped, and thus [the substitution] would not occur here—[we reply: no; for this *i*-sound is also *pratipadokta*.
This is because the *i*-sound is *pratipadokta* on account of the technical reference (*nirdeśa*) in the rule "ṭita ātmanepadānāṃ ṭere" (Pāṇini 3.4.79).
Therefore, the letter ṅ must be employed for the purpose of specification.
14. *sarvanāmnaḥ smai* (Pāṇini 7.1.14).

[The example is] *bhavate*. The substitution of *tyadādi* [elements for the final phoneme] does not occur. Because of the rule *dviparyantās tyadādayaḥ* (Vārttika on 7.2.102), the word *bhavat* lacks the status of being a *tyadādi*; therefore, it does not undergo the change to an *a*-stem.

The objection beginning with "ṭhatho atra" and so forth is as follows: here, when "idam e" is established, once the substitution of "aś" by "idamo'nvādeśe" (Pāṇini 2.4.32) has been made, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from "akaḥ savarṇe dīrghatvam" (Pāṇini 6.1.101) would apply by virtue of its being obligatory (*nitya*), thereby superseding even the subsequent *smai* replacement.

Furthermore, its permanence [is established] because it applies both to what has been formed and what has not yet been formed. Moreover, once the single-substitute (ekādeśa) has taken place, since the word would no longer end in "an," the substitution of *smai* would not apply. The phrase beginning with "therein" (*tatra*) provides the solution:
when the single-substitute is about to occur, the substitution of *smai* takes place first because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*).

[The substitution] is prescribed first, and subsequently the single-substitute (ekādeśa) [operation]. However, the smaibhāva [substitution] is internal (antaraṅga) because it depends on a single word, whereas the single-substitute operation is external (bahiraṅga) because it depends on two words.

15. *ṅsiṅyoḥ smātsminnau* | (Pāṇini 7.1.15) Although the rule for the prior placement of the shorter vowel-ending term (*reĀralpāctarasya pūrvanipāte*) would have applied, the subsequent placement (*paranipāta*) is for the sake of stylistic variety (*vaicitryārtha*).

16. Optionally after the nine beginning with *pūrva*. (7.1.16) This rule is stated for the purpose of providing an option regarding *smāt* and *smin*, which would have been obligatory by the preceding rule. But [it may be objected]: "Is it not the case that [the rule] *pūrvāparāvaradakṣiṇotarāparādharāṇi*..."

In the rules "in the sense of a fixed position or lack of consciousness" (1.1.34), "one's own [possessions] when not referring to kinsmen or wealth" (1.1.35), and "the interior when connected with the exterior or with an undergarment" (1.1.36), only nine sūtras list *pūrva* and the others; therefore, the mention of "nine" (*nava*) is redundant. This is not so; for it is not the case here that...

Are the words beginning with *pūrva* that are recited in the Sūtras being taken here? No; rather, those that are listed in the Gaṇapāṭha are intended. Why is this so? Because the designation *sarvanāman* applies to those [words] recited in the Sūtras only when the suffix *jas* follows, not when the suffixes *ṅsi* or *ṅi* follow. Furthermore, the term *sarvanāmnaḥ* from [Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.1.14] is understood to carry over here; what [is the purpose of this rule]?

What is the purpose? It is so that [the rule] does not apply in cases such as *vidyamāne sve yajate* ("he sacrifices while his own [wealth] exists") or *svād bibheti* ("he fears his own [wealth]"), where the word *sva-* is present.
Therefore, only those words beginning with *pūrva-* that are enumerated in the list of gaṇas are intended to be included;
for if the mention of "nine" (*nava*) were not made there, the suffix would also apply after words such as *tyad-* and others. Consequently, the mention of "nine" must be made.
17. *jasaḥ śī* (Pāṇini 7.1.17).

The letter *ś* is for the purpose of making the replacement apply to the whole (*sarvādeśa*). If it were not there, then by the rule "of that which follows, the first part" (*ādeḥ parasya*, 1.1.54), the replacement would apply only to the letter *a*. Now, what is the purpose of pronouncing the long vowel (*dīrgha*), rather than the short vowel (*hrasva*) alone?

Let it be prescribed; for this [suffix] is prescribed after a stem ending in *a*. Since the rule "ad-guṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.87) must apply here, there would be no distinction whether the guṇa is applied or not when prescribing either a short or a long vowel? To this he says: "The utterance of the long vowel," and so forth. [This refers to the rule] "napuṃsakācca" (Pāṇini 7.1.19).
Thus he will say; in that regard, the long vowel is pronounced in the examples *trapuṇī* and *jatunī* so that there may be the hearing of the long [vowel] before the suffix *-ī*;
[the rule applies] only after a pronoun—as in *dakṣiṇā ime gāthakāḥ* ("these southern singers"); [it applies] only after the word *ataḥ*—as in *bhavantaḥ*.

18. *āṬṅ āpaḥ* | (Pāṇini 7.1.18) This rule is commenced because the substitution of *vṛddhi* [for the final vowel of the first member] would otherwise apply by the rule *ṭhvṛddhireci* (6.1.88). In the term *āṬṅ*, there is a general inclusion of both the nominative and accusative dual endings. The term *āpaḥ* refers to the feminine suffix *āp*.

Regarding *ṭāḍḍāpcāpām*: in the example *khaṭve*, the suffixes *ṭāp* and *cāp* are present according to Pāṇini 4.1.4 (*ajādyataṣṭāp*). The presentation of the two subsequent applications (*anuprayoga*)—namely, *tiṣṭhataḥ* and *paśya*—is intended to demonstrate, respectively, that [the first form] ends in the nominative case and [the second] ends in the accusative case; otherwise, the form would be identical in both instances as *khaṭve*.
Because they are identical [in form], there would be doubt regarding specific details such as the nominative case ending and so forth. In the example *bahurāje*:
this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose scent is like that of dried cow-dung" (*karīṣa*); the suffix *ic* is applied by *upamānācca* (Pāṇini 5.4.137).
The offspring of *karīṣagandhi* takes the suffix *aṇ*; of that [suffix], [the elision is prescribed] by *aṇiñoḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.78).
By such [rules] as these, the substitute *ṣyaṅ* is applied; then by "ṣyaṅścāp" (Pāṇini 4.1.74), the suffix *cāp* is added. Regarding the statement "This is the vowel *āṬ*," etc.:

in the rule for *śī*, that is, in the prescription of *uśī*, this vowel *āṬ* is the substituend (*sthānin*) which is grasped as having the marker *ṅ*; the meaning is that it is introduced with the marker *ṅ*. That which has *ṅ* as its [indicatory] element is called *iṅt*.

Furthermore, according to the opinion of us grammarians, the vowel *au* does not exist in the technical treatise (*śāstra*). Therefore, what kind of manner is this? The word *kim* is used here in the sense of censure; the meaning is that this manner of formulating the rule is censurable. Its censurability, however, arises from the fact that something non-existent is being introduced.

By way of demonstrating the purpose for attaching the marker *ṅ*, he speaks— saying "the general sense"— in order to refute the reproach that the composition of the sūtra is contemptible: "For if the vowel *ai* were taken as the substituendum (*sthānin*) without its marker, then, according to the rule 'when a [form] without a marker is mentioned, it does not include one with a marker'..."

Otherwise, the dual number of the second case (*dvitīyā-dvivacanam*) would not be included. Furthermore, if the letter *ṭ* were taken as the *anubandha* of that [suffix], even then the dual number of the first case (*prathamā-dvivacanam*) would not be included. Therefore, the letter *ṅ* is attached so that there may be the inclusion of both in a general sense. But surely—
The letter *yaṣ* (the *ṣ* in *yaṣṭakāra*) in the dual ending of the second case is not an *anubandha* of that [suffix] alone; of what then?

Of the entire group. For those *anubandhas* which serve the purpose of recitation (*pratyāhāra*) are understood to be *anubandhas* of the entire group, just as the letter *ṅ* is for *mahiṅ* and the letter *p* is for *sup*.
Therefore, when there is a mention of a suffix without an *anubandha*, since both [the present and perfect stems] possess an *anubandha*, the mention will apply generally;
so what is the purpose of the *ṅ*? This is not so;
for even when the *anubandha* belongs to the whole aggregate, it is also admitted that these [suffixes] possess an *anubandha* belonging to their individual components. Not so.
For if it were an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) belonging to the entire complex (*samudāya*), its being an *anubandha* belonging to the suffix (*pratyaya*) would be contradicted.

Indeed, an *anubandha* is said to be that which bears the designation *it*; and the designation *it* is prescribed for the final consonant (*hal*) of a complex. And just as the letter *ṭ* in *āṬṭ* is the final element with respect to the complex, so too is it with respect to the suffix. Therefore, [the rule applies] to that.

When the designation *it* has been prescribed by the rule "ṭh-ḷ-antyaṃ" (Pāṇini 1.3.3), just as that [designation] is an *anubandha* with respect to the entire complex, so too is it with respect to the suffix. If it is argued that its status as an *anubandha* of the suffix is untenable due to a lack of purpose, we say: no; for here there is a purpose.

The purpose [of the marker] is so that the second dual ending may possess an *anubandha*. If, however, it is an *anubandha* of the suffix, then even though the letter *ṅ* has been attached, by the rule "when there is a mention of something with a specific *anubandha*, that which does not have that *anubandha* is not included" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 54), and by the rule "when there is a mention of something with a single *anubandha*... [the desired result would not follow].

Furthermore, by the rule "dvyanubandhakasya" (Vyāḍipāṭha 52), there would have to be the inclusion of only the nominative dual, for that [suffix] has only the letter *ṅ* as its single *anubandha*; whereas the accusative dual has both that [letter *ṅ*] and another, the letter *ṭ*. This is not a fault.
By the force of the utterance of the letter *ṅ*, the dual number of the second case (*dvitīyā*) will also be understood.

Since the dual of the first case (*prathamā*) could have been grasped even without the letter *ṅ*, the letter *ṅ* is taught for the sake of generality. And if, despite the presence of the letter *ṅ*, only the dual of the first case were [intended], [the rule would fail].

The inclusion of the marker *ṅ* would be purposeless. But how can this *ṅ* receive the designation *it*, given that the rule for the *it*-designation prescribes it for that final consonant (*hal*) which occurs at the end of an original instruction (*upadeśa*), and yet this *ṅ* is not final in the original instruction? Or, let us assume it does receive the *it*-designation; in that case, the *ṭ* of *auṭ* would not [receive it].

It might be so; for how could there be two final vowels (*antyau*) in a single instruction (*upadeśa*)? This is not a fault, because of the statement "āṬṅ. It is understood that this substitution of *auṅ* applies to both instances of the vowel *au*, and its instruction exists, as in the rule "cakṣiṅḥ khyāñ" (Pāṇini 2.4.54).
Regarding the rule "the letter *ṇ* is final in the instruction," just as that [letter] receives the designation *it*, so too does the letter *ṅ*.

However, since the designation *it* and the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *ṭ* are performed previously in their proper sequence, there is no fault. Furthermore, that substitute which is the vowel *au* is itself the beauty of the speech.
It should be understood that [the letter *ṅ*] is not included as a *sthānin* (original element).

By the words "of that" (*tasya ca*) and so forth, he demonstrates the fault that arises from the attachment (*āsañjana*) of the letter *ṅ*. "Attachment" (*āsañjana*) is the inclusion of the letter *ṅ* as a *anubandha* (indicatory letter). In the term *ṅiti*...
Regarding the expression *yat-kāryaṃ tat-ṭhṅt-kāryam*:

the compound is formed by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule) based on *Pāṇini 2.1.40*, "The locative case. Furthermore, the operation (*kārya*) pertaining to that [suffix] is the augment *āṭ* by virtue of *Pāṇini 7.3.113*, "After a feminine ending in *āp*, the augment *āṭ* is added before the suffixes *ṅe*, *ṅasi*, and *ṅas*.
If this letter *ṅ* were attached for the sake of a general purpose, then, such being the case, when the letter *ṅ* is attached...

Whatever operation is prescribed for an element ending in *ṅit* would, according to the opinion of the author of the Sūtras, apply to *śī* as well; that is the fault. If the augment *yāṭ* were applied by the rule *yāḍāpaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.113), the form *khaṭve* would not be established. Therefore, how could the augment *ām* and the suffix *āṬ* occur after *śī*?

And how could they not be [called *nadī*]? Because it is not a river (*anadī*). And why is it not a river? Because it is designated as feminine (*stryākhyatvāt*). This is not so; for just as words such as *khaṭvā* (bedstead) denote feminine things, so too does the word *śrī*. Thus said the author of the *Liṅgakārikā*: "That which ends in *ī* or *ū* and consists of a single vowel..."

[And it is said: "autumn, winter, the rainy season, and... Therefore, this [word] *strī* (woman) is indeed designated as a *nadī* (feminine noun), because of its grammatical coreferentiality with the word *śruti*. The word *strī*, when occurring in the sense of *śruti*, acquires the designation *nadī*. *Śruti* is simply the word's own form (*svarūpa*).

Regarding the rule *ṭhṅti* and so forth: in the rule *ṭhyāḍāpaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.113), the term *ṅti* is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*) from the preceding rule *dherṅiti* (7.3.111). In that context, *ṅit* is not a *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "that which has the sound *ṅ* as its *it*"—but rather a *tatpuruṣa* compound: the sound *ṅ* itself is the *it*, hence *ṅit*.

Therefore, when the letter *au* is accepted as being [included] in the term *ṅti*, the wise person should understand—that is, recognize—that in this grammatical description (*nirdeśa*) of *ṅti*, the letter *ṅ* which bears the technical designation *it* is indicated merely as a phoneme (*varṇamātra*).
The word "merely" (*mātra*) serves to exclude anything other than that. If, in this instance of *ṅti*, the letter *ṅ* were intended merely as a phoneme...

The rule does not apply to a suffix that has the letter *ṅ* as its marker (*ṅkārānubandha*). Why, then, is the operation of *ṅt* not applied to [the suffix] *śyan*? To this he says: "when a phoneme (*varṇa*) follows," and so forth.

When an operation is prescribed when a phoneme follows, that [operation applies] to the beginning of that [phoneme], according to the principle "in a rule where a specific element is mentioned, the operation applies to what begins with that element."

By this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), one should understand that [the suffix] occurs at the beginning of that which begins with a phoneme. Consequently, the augment *yāṭ* should apply only where the letter *ṅ* is marked with the technical designation *it* at the beginning; it should not apply to *śyām*.
For here, the letter *ṅ* is not at the beginning; where, then, is it? At the end. Thus, having accepted that this [suffix] possesses the property of being *ṅt*, this resolution has been stated.

Now, without accepting the suffix *ṅti*, he states another solution, beginning with "And this is a phoneme" (*varṇaścāyam*) and so forth. The word *ca* (and) has the sense of *vā* (or); that is to say, "or this is a phoneme. This [suffix] *āṅti* consists of the vowels *ā* and *i*; it serves as a qualifier for the following element (*pratyaviśeṣaṇārtha*), but it is not itself a suffix (*na tu pratyayaḥ*).

Because this is under the heading of *aṅga* (stem), the suffix that follows a stem ending in *ā*—which is understood through contextual capacity—is qualified by the vowel *au*; and by the rule of "specification of what ends in [the qualifier]," it refers to that which ends in such a suffix.
Consequently, the meaning that arises is: "of this suffix when it ends in the vowel *au*. This constitutes the state of ending in *au*.
Because of the principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (the treatment of a thing as if it were what it designates), this letter *ṅ* is not an *anubandha* (indicatory letter);
rather, it is for the sake of ease of pronunciation (*mukhasukhārtha*), just as the letter *d* is in the rule *ṛdorap* (Pāṇini 3.3.57).
And since there is thus a mention of the vowel *au* by virtue of its phonetic form (*varṇarūpatayā*), [it applies] to both instances of the vowel *au*.

The substitution of *śī* occurs when [the suffix] is established as a grammatical element (*siddha*). For when there is a mention of a suffix (*pratyaya-grahaṇa*), the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "that which lacks an indicatory letter (*niranubandhaka*)" applies (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 53); however, here there is no mention of a suffix. What then? There is a mention of the mere phoneme (*varṇamātra*).
But surely both of these are suffixes; why, then, does that rule not apply? True.

Although those two are substitutes (*pratyaya*), nevertheless, the vowel *o* is not introduced here in this treatise as a substitute; rather, it is introduced as a phoneme (*varṇa*). Therefore, it does not appear here [in the rule].
Without accepting that it has the property of being a marker (*ṅtva*), he states another solution, beginning with "This is a designation" (*nirdeśo 'yam*).
In this [work], the *ṅ* following the vowel *au* (*āṬ*) is not employed as a substitute for the case-ending *au*.

However, according to the ancient teachers (*pūrvācāryas*), both of these [suffixes] appear in their rules (*sūtra*) as dual endings with the marker *ṅ*. For instance, the reading of that rule is "ābauṭāvauṅ. Therefore, in accordance with that rule, this...

The mention [of the term] here is so that its specific designation may be grasped. Therefore, because of the absence of the marker *ṅ*, there is no occasion for the grammatical operations (*kārya*) dependent upon *ṅ*.
For the operations of markers (*anubandha-kāryāṇi*) are not performed here in accordance with the sūtras of the ancient masters (*pūrvācārya*). By that—

"Even if *ṅtva* [the status of being a *ṅ*] were admitted, there would be no fault"—this is also the meaning of the word "even" (*api*). What then is the meaning of the phrase "where *ṅtva* does not exist at all"?

This is what is being stated: even when *ṅtva* is accepted, one should understand that in the case of *sit*, there is merely a mention of the phoneme (*varṇa-nirdeśa-mātra*). According to the rule, "whatever applies to a phoneme, one should know that it applies to that which begins with it," and so forth.

In order to refute the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that [the vowel *u*] would be subject to the rule for *ṅt-kārya*, the avoidance of that consequence has been stated by the words "since this [vowel] is a phoneme" (*yasmād varṇaś cāyam*) and "this indication might be by means of the preceding sūtra" (*nirdeśo 'yaṃ pūrvasūtreṇa vā syāt*). By that reason, even though [the condition exists],...
Even so, there is this fault; but how could it be that [the suffix] does not exist at all where the designation *ṅt* applies?
19. *napuṃsakācca* (Pāṇini 7.1.19). [The form] "dadhinī" [is derived as follows]: by the rule *iko 'ci vibhaktau* (7.1.73), the augment *num* is inserted.

20. *jasi-śasoḥ śiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.20). [In the root text (*mūla*), it is read as *jaś-śasoḥ śiḥ*; however, this reading *jasi-śasoḥ śiḥ* follows the intention of the author of the Nyāsa. Furthermore, in the rule *āj-jas-er-asuk* (7.1.50), only *jas-i-* is seen.]

In the word *jas-i*, the vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation. Regarding the form *kuṇḍāni*: the augment *num* is applied by the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.72), and the lengthening is applied by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.8). Now, why does this [lengthening] not occur here: *kuṇḍaṃ kuṇḍaṃ dadāti*? [Because of the rule] *saṃkhyaikavacanācca*.

The suffix *śas* is applied by the rule *vīpsāyām* (Pāṇini 5.4.43). To the question "Does he give [the word] *kuṇaaḍaśas*? [the author] replies with the words "Because of association (*sāhacaryāt*) with *jas*, etc. This statement, which provides the solution to the objection, applies when the word *kuṇḍa* and others, being used in the singular due to the context of the meaning and so forth, occurs.

It should be understood that [the suffix] *śas* is not applied at any other time. For in the rule prescribing *śas*, it is the state of having a single meaning while situated in a *vṛtti* (compound) that is relied upon, not the state of being situated in a sentence (*vākya*). Since a word such as *kuṇḍa*, when devoid of context, purpose, and so forth, does not possess a single meaning once the case-ending has ceased [in a compound], *śas* ought not to occur. But why?

Since a word such as *kuṇḍa* has a single meaning when it is in a compound (*vṛtti*) but does not have a single meaning when it is in a case-ending (*vibhakti*), the suffix *śas* should not occur [after it]. Why, then, does a word such as *kuṇḍa* not have a single meaning when it is in a compound? Because it is a genus-word (*jātiśabda*). For genus-words do not [denote] only a single individual.

[The suffixes] do not apply to an individual (*vyakti*) that serves as the substratum for the universal (*jāti*); rather, they apply even to multiple individuals. And thus, the counter-example presented there in the rule for *śas*—"What is the purpose of [the restriction] 'from a numeral and a singular term'? [Consider: *ghaṭaṃ ghaṭaṃ dadāti*"—is justified. This is so provided that it is devoid of context, meaning, and so forth.
If a genus-word (*jātiśabda*) does not become synonymous (*ekārtha*) when compounded, then the suffix *śas* must certainly not occur.

21. *aṣṭabhya āṬś* (Pāṇini 7.1.21). It is stated that "the word *aṣṭan* is understood as having its final vowel changed to *ā*" (*kṛtākāra*). The intention is that where the substitution of *ā* occurs, there the substitution of *auś* should also occur. For example: *aṣṭau tiṣṭhanti*. Once the substitution of *ā* has been applied, the substitution of *auś* follows.

In the example *ṭhaṣṭa tiṣṭhanti*, the substitution of *au* does not occur because of the absence of *ātva* (the substitution of *ā* for *as*). But how is there an absence of *ātva* here, given that in the rule prescribing *ātva* there is no mention of an option—such as the use of the term *anyatarasyām*—to indicate an alternative? To this he says: "This very [point]," and so forth.

The purpose of this specific mention of the form with *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) is precisely this: that the substitution of *auś* should occur only where *ātva* has been applied, and not elsewhere. For if *ātva* were obligatory, then the mention of the form with *ātva* would be useless, as there would be nothing to exclude (since the rule "aṣṭanaḥ" [Pāṇini 7.2.84] would apply universally).

One should speak thus: since a concise designation is possible, the fact that a more cumbersome designation of the form with the substitution of *āt* is made indicates that the substitution of *āt* occurs optionally. And although this same meaning [could have been understood] from the rule "aṣṭano dīrghāt" (Pāṇini 6.1.172),...
Although this has already been explained, it is stated here once more for the benefit of those who are prone to forgetfulness.

Now, if it is asked: "Why does [the elision] not occur in the case of *aṣṭaputraḥ* and *aṣṭabhāryaḥ*, since it is barred by the elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.71)?"—[the answer is: No.

In that case, it would not occur here either: *aṣṭau tiṣṭhanti* ("eight stand") and *aṣṭau paśya* ("see eight"), because [the substitution] is barred by the elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule *ṣaḍbhyo luk* (Pāṇini 7.1.22). If it is argued that since the substitution of *-auś* is an exception (*apavāda*) to elision, it therefore prevails here by barring the elision, then it would also prevail in the preceding case.

Let it be so; for what reason? He says: "This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *ṣaḍbhyaḥ luk* (Pāṇini 7.1.22). He provides the justification for this very point, beginning with "nāprāpte" and so forth.
The rule *ṣaḍbhyaḥ luk* applies when there is no compound—such as in the case of *aṣṭau*.

In examples such as *tiṣṭhanti* and in compounds such as *aṣṭaputra*, [the rule applies]. Therefore, since the elision of the case-ending (*sup-luk*) must necessarily occur in *aṣṭabhāryaḥ* before the rule could even apply, the substitution of *auś* does not take place.
Regarding the phrase "the inclusion of that which ends in this" (*tadantagrahaṇam*), etc.: what is it that is desired yet still obtainable?
This is because of the rule: "In the section concerning the suffix *ṭhañ*, [the substitution applies] to that [word] and its subsequent member" (Puṇyarāja-vṛtti 85).

Alternatively, this mention of *aṣṭābhyaḥ* is an indication where the meaning is primary, as is understood from the use of the plural number; for if the indication were primary with respect to the word-form, [the rule would have been stated as] "of *aṣṭan*" (*aṣṭanaḥ*).

One should say: since, by virtue of the meaning, the status of being "subsequent" (*paratva*) to *jaś* and *śas* is understood only through the medium of the word-form, the [suffix] occurs after the simple stem *aṣṭan* as well as after that which ends in it; for even when it does not end in it, the suffixes *jaś* and *śas* are subsequent to it by virtue of the meaning through the medium of the word-form. If...
Is this inclusion of the word "end" (anta) intended here [only for the specific case], since it would also apply in the case of *priyāṣṭan*? To this he says:

"In the case of *priyāṣṭanaḥ*" and so forth. [The compound] *priyāṣṭan* is a *bahuvrīhi* meaning "those who have eight beloveds. But surely there is an optional substitution of *āt* (long *ā*). In that case, when the substitution of *āt* does not occur, let there be no substitution of *auś*.

If it were the case that [the substitution] would occur, then it would indeed be so; however, there is no fault, because by the rule of "optionally fixed" (vyavasthitavibhāṣā), the substitution of ātva will not take place here.
22. *ṣaṅbhyo luk* (Pāṇini 7.1.22). [Examples: *pañca*, *sapta*. [In these cases,] the elision of *n* occurs by the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* (8.2.7).
[The elision of the case-ending] occurs even after a stem ending in that [word *ṣaṣ*], because it is preceded by the word *ṣaṣ*. Here, the former...

The reason must be stated: "But where... and so forth. This inclusion of the word *artha* (meaning/object) is understood from the rule regarding frequency (*bahulavacana*). That *artha* is of two kinds: primary (*pradhāna*) and secondary (*apradhāna*).
In this regard, according to the principle that "the operation applies where there is primacy" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 120), it is only where the *artha* possesses primacy [that the rule applies].

[The substitution occurs] where the meaning [of the stem] is predominant, but not where the meaning is subordinate. And this reason should be understood as applying even in the absence of the *auś* substitution in the case of *priyāṣṭānām*. [The form] *priyaṣaṣaḥ* [is derived as follows]: *priyāṣaḍ eṣām* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Here, the referent of the other member (*anyapadārtha*) is predominant, whereas the meaning of "six" (*ṣaḍartha*) is subordinate therein.
Because it exists as a subordinate quality, it is not primary.
23. *svamornapuṃsakāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.23).
Although *su* is indeed the locative plural, it is nevertheless understood here as the nominative singular alone, due to its association with *am*, the accusative singular.

Regarding the form *tadabrāhmaṇakulam*, since the rule for the substitution of *tyadādi* [elements] is subsequent, it ought to apply here as well; however, once the *tyadādi* substitution has been applied, elision (*luk*) does not occur, because the substitution of *am* by the rule *ato'm* (Pāṇini 7.1.24) would then follow. Therefore, elision must be stated to take place prior to the *tyadādi* substitution.

Thus he says: "In the case of *tad brāhmaṇakulam*," and so forth. The scope for *luk* (elision) is in cases such as *dadhi* and *madhu*; the scope for the substitution of *yatva* (the replacement of the final vowel with *ya*) for pronouns beginning with *tyad* is in cases such as *brāhmaṇa*. Here, in the case of *tad abrāhmaṇakulam*, both rules would apply; however, *luk* occurs by virtue of the *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (prior conflict). Nor is there...

A prior prohibition (pūrvavipratiṣedha) must be stated; for the word *para* signifies that which is desired [by the speaker]. Regarding the phrase "or because of its being obligatory" (*nityatvād vā*), the word *vā* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*). Although both elision (*luk*) and the substitution of *yat* for the pronouns *tyad* etc. would apply, nevertheless, it is understood that elision alone is obligatory. Why? Because of the force of the context (*sāmarthyāt*). By means of elision...

For in the rule "tyadādyatve bādhyate," this other reason has been stated: if this other reason for the present matter is possible—namely, that the elision (luk) is obligatory—it cannot be otherwise; moreover, its obligatoriness follows from the fact that it applies whether [the subsequent operation] has already taken effect or not. For the substitution of *yat* and so forth (*tyadādyatvam*) is prescribed when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) follows.

Once *luk* has been applied, [the substitution] does not apply because of the absence of an inflectional suffix (*vibhakti*). Nor is its application justified by the rule of "characterization by the affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), because of the prohibition: "Not when *lup*, *luK*, or *ślu* have been applied to the stem" (*na lumatāṅgasya*, Pāṇini 1.1.63). Furthermore, the substitution of *yatva* for the pronouns beginning with *tyad-* applies both when *luk* has been applied and when it has not.

But surely, once the substitution of *tyadādyatva* has taken place, there is no possibility for *luk* at all, because the exception (*apavāda*) "ato 'm" (Pāṇini 7.1.24) has been prescribed. Therefore, that [substitution] too must be considered non-eternal? To this he says: "For *luk*, etc. If the rule "ato 'm" (7.1.24) were not present, then even a stem ending in *a* would [be subject to *luk*].

The elision (*luk*) was the cause [for the application of a rule]; now, by this [subsequent] characteristic being produced, because of the prescription of an exception (*apavāda*), it becomes a non-cause for that elision.
The "obstruction" (*vighāta*) consists precisely in the removal of the cause of elision; it does not, however, occur through the substitution of *tyadādi* [forms].

The phrase "the status of *luk* as a cause would be frustrated" is to be connected [to the previous statement]. If there were no other rule (*lakṣaṇāntara*) prescribing an exception (*apavāda*), such as "ṭhato'm" (Pāṇini 7.1.24), then once the substitution of *tyadādi* [elements] with *a* had taken place, a stem ending in *ā* would indeed be the cause for *luk*. And that [exceptional rule] is "ṭhato'm" (7.1.24).
Thus, by this very exception (apavāda), the cause for the elision (*luk*) is sublated, and not by the substitution of *tyad* and so forth (*tyadādyatva*).
If this is so, why does the elision (*luk*) not become non-permanent? To this he says: "And of that which... and so forth.
Furthermore, the fact that it is governed by a different rule refers to the rule concerning the substitution of *ambhāva*.
This is to be understood with reference to the grammatical rule concerning the substitution of *yat* for *tyad* and so forth.

24. *ato'm* (Pāṇini 7.1.24). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the elision (*luk*) that would otherwise apply by the preceding rule. The inclusion of the marker *t* (*taparakaraṇa*) is for the sake of ease of pronunciation; it is not for the purpose of excluding the long vowel (*dīrgha*), because a long vowel is impossible here. It is impossible, however, because [the preceding vowel] is short (*hrasva*).

This is because the short vowel is prescribed by the rule *napuṃsake prātipadikasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.47). Now, for what purpose is the substitution of *am* stated, rather than simply stating the substitution of the letter *m*? It cannot be so; for if the letter *m* were substituted for the *ā* of the second singular ending according to the rule *ādeḥ parasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.54), [the desired form would not result].
The elision of the *śal* [suffix] would apply to both *m*s;

for one of them has already been removed by the elision of a consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*). Nor does the lengthening prescribed by the rule *supi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.102) apply to a case-ending beginning with *yañ*; because [the rule] is characterized by its specific phonetic context (*sannipātalakṣaṇa*).
Because of the statement: "A rule [that applies] when a certain combination exists is not the cause for the destruction of that combination" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 12).
For the prescription of the letter *m* occurs when there is the combination with the vowel *a*; how then could that be the cause for the destruction of the vowel *a*?
If that is so, then while the substitution of *m* ought to be destroyed, [the substitution of] *am* [should be applied].
By performing this, he makes it known that this is a permanent (nitya) paribhāṣā; therefore, the substitution of *jaras* is established in forms such as *atijarasāt* and *atijarasaiḥ*.

25. [The suffix *ka* is applied] after the five beginning with *itarāt*. (Pāṇini 7.1.25) This enumeration contains two forms of *ḍakāra*: one is connected with *ḍatara*, while the second is connected with the substitute (*ādeśa*). Furthermore, these items beginning with *ḍatara* are understood as being included within the group of words beginning with *sarva*.
But suffixes such as *ḍatarac* in the rule "of two, one: *ḍatarac*" (Pāṇini 5.3.92) and others are not included. Why is this so?

Because of the prohibition in the rule "not after *itarāc* in the Veda" (7.1.26). For if the term "suffix" (*pratyaya*) were not mentioned [in that rule], there would be no possibility of the suffix occurring after the word *itarāc*, and thus the prohibition would be meaningless.

Among those beginning with *ḍatara*, the last three are nominal stems (*prātipadika*); *ḍatara* and *ḍatama* are suffixes (*pratyaya*). In that regard, by the technical rule concerning the mention of a suffix (*bho.pā.sū. 7*), there is the inclusion of those [stems] ending in them. As for the word *katarat*: [it is formed] by the rule "after *kim* and *yad*, when selecting one out of two, the suffix *ḍatarac* is applied."
Regarding "katamat": [the suffix] *ḍatamac* is applied "when there is an inquiry regarding a class among many" (Pāṇini 5.3.93).

Regarding "katarat tiṣṭhati" and so forth: for if the augment *ṅt* were not present, then in the case of "katarat tiṣṭhati," while the rule "a long vowel replaces [a short vowel] with its homogeneous counterpart" (Pāṇini 6.1.101) would be in force...

By the rule "ṭhprathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.102), a long vowel would otherwise occur; therefore, the suffix *ṅti* is added so that this [long vowel] does not happen. For when this is applied, the contingency of lengthening does not arise, because the *ak* portion has been removed by the elision of the *ṭi*.

But what is the reason that the absence of lengthening is stated as the purpose for the substitution of *ṅti* only in the first singular, and not for the second singular? To this he says: "But here," and so forth. For the substitute that occurs in place of *ām* is, by the rule "a substitute is like the original (sthānivat), except in the case of an operation concerning an *al* [phoneme],"...

(1.1.56) Thus, by virtue of the status of being "as if in the place of" (*sthānivadbhāva*), even the form *katarat* is established through the substitution of *am* with the preceding vowel; therefore, it is not stated that the purpose of the insertion of *ṅt* there is the absence of lengthening. [The question is asked: "Why is not the substitution of *t* alone made? If here...
If lengthening is not desired, then the substitution of *t* alone must be made.
In that case as well, the meaning is this: the suffix *ṅti* need not be applied for the purpose of preventing lengthening.
[As in] "he katarat" and so forth; if the substitution of *t* alone is performed, then of that—

Since the status of being a vocative (*sambuddhi*) exists by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* principle, the elision prescribed by "ṭeṅ hrasvāt sambuddheḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.69) would apply; therefore, the substitute letter *t* is not applied for the purpose of preventing that [elision].

"Ṭhapṛktaśca," etc. If the mention of *apṛkta* from the rule "halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktam" (Pāṇini 6.1.69) were to carry over into the elision of the vocative suffix (*sambuddhi*), then there would be a fault in the case of "he kuṇḍa. If, however, the governing heading (*adhikāra*) for *apṛkta* has ceased, then there would be a fault in the case of [suffixes] such as *ḍatara*. "He... [and so on].

Which one? Therefore, because the suffix *ḍit* is applied, when the elision of the vowel *a* has occurred, there is neither elision [of the final consonant] due to the absence of a short vowel, nor is there lengthening.
26. *netarāc chandasi* (7.1.26).
This is a prohibition of the substitution of *adḍ* which was introduced by the preceding rule.
Now, [if one were to propose] that the rule *itarāc chandasi* should follow immediately after *ato'm* (7.1.24):

Why was it not stated that "it is not so," whereby the negation would not have to be formulated, and the substitution of *am* would simply serve as an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *adḍ*?
To this he says: "immediately after [the rule] *ato 'm*" and so forth. [The reason is] for the sake of splitting the rule (*yogavibhāga*).

Thus [it is said]. The phrase "not so" (*na*) is for the sake of a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) so that [the prohibition] may apply. But for what purpose is this *yogavibhāga* desired? He says: "For from one [word]," and so forth. For a prohibition is desired everywhere following the word "one" (*eka*), and that is obtained through the *yogavibhāga* of "not" (*na*). Therefore, the *yogavibhāga* is desired. That...
And since [the desired form] is established according to the original arrangement and not otherwise, it is stated: "ṭhnetarāccchandasi" (Pāṇini 8.4.27).
27. *yuṣmadasmadbhyāṃ ṅaso'ś* (Pāṇini 7.1.27).

If there is elision of the final [element] by the rule *śeṣe lopaḥ* (7.2.90), then this statement is intended for the case where its presence would otherwise be required. If, however, there is elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant), then this is for the purpose of providing a substitute when the case-ending would otherwise be audible.

The statement is: "That is mine, this is mine. By the rule *tadamau ṅsi* (Pāṇini 7.2.96), the substitutes *tava* and *mama* occur for the forms of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* ending in *map*. Then, by the rule *śeṣe lopaḥ* (7.2.90), the letter *d* is elided;
subsequently, by the rule *ato guṇe* (6.1.97), the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is applied.

"The addition of the marker *ś* is for the sake of making [the substitute] a replacement for the whole. If the marker *ś* were not added, then by the rule "that which follows [an element with a marker] replaces only the initial portion" (Pāṇini 1.1.54), the substitute *a* would replace only the letter *ā*. Now, one might argue that since there is no purpose in pronouncing the letter *a* when *a* itself is to be expressed, the substitute will be a replacement for the whole even without the addition of the marker *ś*.

Or [the suffix] *ant*. In that case, since there are two *a*-sounds, the desired result is established by the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) according to the rule *ato guṇe*. To this he says: "Otherwise, indeed," and so forth. Otherwise, if the addition of the marker *ś* were not present, then regarding this designation "substitute" (*ādeśa*), its...

The designation "praklṛpti" (establishment) would pertain only to the initial [element] for that purpose, because of the rule "ādeḥ parasya" (1.1.54). This might be so—if some purpose were accomplished through the establishment of the technical designation "ādeśa" (substitute), then the mention of "ādi" (initial) would indeed be for that purpose; but it is not so.
"Does some purpose [for the rule] then follow from that, such that it would be improper [to apply it]? To this he says: "And therefore," and so forth.

The word *ca* (and) indicates a reason. The suffix *liṅ* is used in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*). Therefore, because the designation (*vyapadeśa*) and application (*praklṛpti*) [of the term *ādeśa*] would follow from that, the grammatical operation prescribed by the rule *yo'ci* (Pāṇini 7.2.82) would not take place.

For this [substitution] is prescribed only where there is no other substitute for the case-ending (*vibhaktyādeśa*), because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "when there is no substitute ending in *ṭha*" (Pāṇini 7.2.86). Therefore,
since the designation of a substitute is established only when it serves a purpose, it would apply only to the initial [sound].
Consequently, this form would not be established; therefore, the letter śa must be included for the sake of the word *sarva* and others.

28. *reĀ prathamayoram* (Pāṇini 7.1.28). This [term] *reĀ* is cited without a case-ending (*avibhaktika*), because the genitive case has been elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk* (7.1.39). The term *prathamayoḥ* is the genitive dual; it refers to both the nominative (*prathamā*) and—

"prathamā ca te prathame, tayoḥ prathamayoḥ. Since the designation by the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī-nirdeśa) is identical in both instances, someone might have the misconception that the term "prathamayoḥ" refers to the two suffixes *su* and *au*. To dispel this, he says: "vibhaktyoḥ" (of the two case-endings).

Thus [it is said]. To clarify this very point, he says: "of the first and the second. But how, then, is the second case-relation (*dvitīyā*) denoted by the word "first" (*prathamā*)? Because of its proximity to the first case-relation in the instruction (*upadeśa*).
For a designation based on proximity does indeed occur, as in the expression "the hamlet on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*). Now...
How is this certainty established—that this is the mention of the two case-endings (*vibhakti*) and not the two suffixes (*pratyaya*)?

It is from an indicative mark (*liṅga*). That indicative mark, moreover, is the prescription of *atva* in the rule "dvitīyāyāñca" (Pāṇini 7.2.87). For that [prescription] is stated for the purpose of an *ādeśa* (substitute); for if there were no *ādeśa*, [the rule would be unnecessary].

[The rule] "ṭhyuṣmadasmadoranādeśe" applies only when there is no substitute [for the case endings], not otherwise. Now, one might object: would not the rule "dvitīyāyāñca" (Pāṇini 7.2.87), etc., be intended for the purpose of overriding the substitution of *ya* prescribed by "yo'ci" (7.2.89)?
This is not so; for that purpose, in the case of the dual number, the very letter *ya* itself is the qualifier.

One would have prescribed [the substitution] by the rule "yo'cyadvitīyāyām" or "yo'cyanaci. Therefore, the prescription of the long vowel *ā* (ātvavidhāna) in the second case is precisely the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the inclusion of the term "vibhakti" [in Pāṇini's sūtra].
[The forms] "tabhyam" and "mahyam" [are derived as follows]: for the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, when they end in *m*, the substitutes *tabhya* and *mahya* are applied.

By the rule *ṭhśeṣe lopaḥ* (7.2.90), there is elision [of the suffix], and by *ṭhami pūrvaḥ* (6.1.107), the preceding vowel is lengthened. Thus, *tvam* and *aham*. By *ṭhtvāhau sau* (7.2.94), *tvā* and *āh* are substituted [for *yūyam* and *vayam* respectively] when the nominative singular suffix *su* follows. Thus, *yuvām* and *āvām*.
By *ṭhyuvavau dvivacane* (7.2.92), *yuv-ā-v-* and *āv-ā-v-* are substituted for the dual endings; and by *ṭhprathamāyāśca* (7.2.88), the first case ending is applied.
By such rules as these, [the forms] *yūyam* and *vayam* are derived; [this is governed by] *yūyavayau jasi* (Pāṇini 7.2.93).

[The forms] *tvām* and *mām* are derived; [this is governed by] *tvamāvekavacane* (7.2.97) and *dvitīyāyāñca* (7.2.87), which effect the substitution of *ā*. Now, for what purpose is the substitute *am* prescribed, rather than the letter *m* alone being prescribed?

If it is argued that this [suffix] will occur after *ekāltva* and so forth, and that while it is established there for another [word] by the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*), it is not established here because of the elision of the *ṭi* portion according to "the elision of the remainder" (*śeṣe lopaḥ*, 7.2.90), this is not a fault; for even if the elision of the remainder were an elision of the *ṭi*, nevertheless, [it is so] because of the rule "tvāhau... [which applies].
[The forms] beginning with *sau* (Pāṇini 7.2.94) are indeed established because they end in the vowel *a*;

furthermore, those [forms] must necessarily be prescribed as ending in *a* so that they may have the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*). Nor does the substitution of *m* result in the application of lengthening by the rule *suci ca* (7.3.102); for [the condition of] being part of a stem (*aṅgavṛtta*)...

Furthermore, because of the statement [in the Vākyapadīya], "the rule for the substitution of a member applies to that which has already been established" (VP 3.14.38), it follows that this is so. If that is the case, then the prescription of the substitute *am* is for the sake of variety. Alternatively, the substitute is simply the letter *m*, while the vowel *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation; for otherwise, if the vowel *a* were not placed at the beginning or the end in this grammatical description, [the form would not be correctly produced].

The letter *m* can be pronounced [as a nasalization]. Although it could have been stated as "before *reĀ* and *suṭ*" (*reĀtsuṭoḥ*), the formulation "before *reĀ* and the first two cases" (*reĀ prathamayoḥ*) is for the sake of stylistic variety.

29. *śaso na* (Pāṇini 7.1.29). Since the substitution of *am* was applicable by the preceding rule, the substitution of *na* is prescribed for the case of *śas*. [Examples: *yuṣmān brāhmaṇān*, *asmān brāhmaṇān*. By the rule *ādeḥ parasya* (1.1.54), the letter *n* replaces the initial *a*.

There is the elision of the final consonant due to the rule *saṃyogāntalopaḥ*, and as before, there is the substitution of *ā*. Now, one might object: even when this [substitution of *na* for *śas*] has been applied, and the *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) has occurred, and the lengthening by the rule *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.102) has taken place, [the form would still be established] by the rule *tasmāc chaso naḥ puṃsi* (Pāṇini 6.1.103).
Is it not the case that this very [rule] succeeds? This is not so; for here the lengthening due to *pūrvasavarṇa* does not apply, because it is superseded by the rule concerning *am-pūrvatva*.

30. *bhyas* is replaced by *bhyam*. (Pāṇini 7.1.30) [Examples: *yuṣmabhyam*, *asmabhyam*. By the rule "elision of the remainder" (*śeṣe lopaḥ*, 7.2.90), there is elision of the final [portion]. If this is the substitution of *bhyam*, then when that has been applied and the elision of the remainder has occurred—

Since the substitution of *e* would apply by the rule "ṭhbahuvacane jhalyet" (Pāṇini 7.3.103), one might then arrive at an undesirable form; therefore, he says: "when the substitute *bhyam* has been applied," and so forth.
"Vṛta" means that which occurs (*vartanam*); an operation that occurs within a stem (*aṅga*) is called "stem-occurring" (*aṅgavṛta*).

When a grammatical operation has already taken place within a constituent element (aṅga), and subsequently another operation applicable to that same constituent arises at a later time, there is the non-application (avidhi) of that subsequent operation. By the term "of that which is established" (niṣṭhitasya),
the constituent element related to the operation whose non-application occurs is specifically qualified.

"Niṣṭhita" means completed or fully concluded; it refers to a constituent part that is ready for application. The meaning is that the operation applies to what is connected with that [part], and not to what is connected with anything else.
Regarding the phrase "some say," etc.: when the final [vowel] of those [suffixes] has been elided, [the rule] "ato guṇe" (Pāṇini 6.1.97) [applies].

It becomes the form of another. Regarding the passage beginning with "But for those who," etc.: there is a difference of opinion among those for whom the elision of the final [syllable] is performed by the rule *śeṣe lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.90).
For some of them desire the substitution of *abhyam*, while others desire the substitution of *abhyām*. But for those who...

The elision of the *ṭi* portion is the elision of the remainder (*śeṣelopa*). According to their opinion, this is an *abhyam* substitution, not a *bhyam* substitution; otherwise, the form *yuṣmabhyam* would not be established—this is the intended meaning. If, then, the elision of the *ṭi* portion is the elision of the remainder, this being the case, [the rule] "where there is the elision of an udātta vowel of that which is unaccented" (Pāṇini 6.1.159) [applies].
One might ask: "By this [rule], would not the word *abhyām* have an udātta accent on its final syllable? To this, he says:
"And the *udātanivṛtti-svara*," etc.

According to the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*), in the rule prescribing the *udātanivṛtti-svara*, [the suffix] *ghañ* [is applied] after roots ending in *karṣa* or those having *ā*.

The opponent, thinking that the mention of "end" (*anta*) from the rule *udātaḥ* (6.1.159) continues [into this rule], has raised this objection. However, the proponent of the latter view maintains that the mention of "end" has been withdrawn there, and by virtue of the proximity of the order of utterance, it must be the beginning (*ādi*) itself that becomes acute-accented (*udātta*).
Thinking, "This is logical," he has offered a rebuttal.
31. *at* is substituted for the fifth case-ending (*bhyas*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to what was previously obtained by the preceding rule [Pāṇini 7.1.30].

32. And [the substitution applies] to the singular number. (Pāṇini 7.1.32) The word *ca* (and) serves to carry over the term *ādeśa* (substitute), or it has the sense of conjunction with respect to *bhyas*.
Regarding what should have been stated as *ṅseśca*, the expression *ekavacanasya ca* is for the sake of stylistic variety.

33. *sāma ākam* (Pāṇini 7.1.33). It is stated that "the word *sām* is understood as the genitive plural (*ṣaṣṭhī-bahuvacana*) with the augment *suṭ* attached. This is because it is impossible for any other word *sāman* to follow the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. [The augment] has arrived.
