That in which or by which the *suṭ* augment has been obtained is thus described. In the sentence beginning with "atha," the masculine gender should be understood in relation to the *ām* affix, as in "āgatasuṭkaḥ. [Question: "Why is that which has the *suṭ* augment obtained included?"

Anticipating the objection that, when this [rule] is asked, the substitute *suṭ* should apply even to that which has already undergone substitution, he says "na hi" and so forth. In the rule "āmi sarvanāmnaḥ suṭ" (Pāṇini 7.1.52),
the word "āt" is understood from the preceding rule "ājjaserasuk" (7.1.50).

Therefore, *suṅ* is prescribed after a pronoun ending in the vowel *a*. And the state of ending in *a* for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* occurs when the final [consonant] has been elided by the rule "elision in the remainder" (*śeṣe lopaḥ*, 7.2.90).
Even when the substitution of *ākam* has been made by the rule "elision in the remainder," [the form] must still be produced.
Therefore, at the time of prescribing the substitute, the *suṭ* augment does not exist; consequently, the purpose—that the substitute should apply to that which includes the *suṭ*—is untenable.
With the intention of stating something else [to resolve this], he says: "of that very [element]," and so forth. If [the element] were taken as being without the *suṭ*...
According to the rule "substitutes apply to that which is being specified" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 106), the substitute would apply only to that form which lacks the augment *suṭ*.
In that case, once the relationship between the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*) has been established, by what means could the subsequent *suṭ* be prevented from occurring?
Yet, its prevention is desired. Therefore, even for that which is yet to come...
The *samukta* (the augment *su*) is employed for the purpose that there may be cessation [of the application of other rules]. Now, one might object:

the augment *suṭ* does not even apply to the suffix *ām* following *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, because the rule for *suṭ* prescribes it after a pronoun ending in the vowel *a*; furthermore, the substitution of *tyadādi* forms (*yatvam*) does not apply to *yuṣmad* and *asmad*.

Since the substitution of *yatva* (the replacement of *tyad* etc. with *ya*) does not apply because of the rule "those ending in *dviparyanta* belong to the *tyad* class," and since the elision of the remainder (*śeṣalopa*) results in the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant), the state of having a final *a* is impossible; therefore, does it not follow that the removal of even the future *suṭ* augment cannot serve as a valid purpose? To refute this objection, [the author says] "in the *śeṣa*..."

Keeping in mind that "lopaḥ" means the elision of the final [element], he says: "For when [the suffix] is applied," and so forth. Now, if the inclusion of *samut* is being performed, how is this [suffix] excluded? For the exclusion of what is applicable from another rule is effected by the present rule; however, at the time of prescribing the substitute (*ādeśa*), [it has not yet become applicable].
Is there, then, the possibility of *suṭ* occurring? To this he says: "And because that [augment] is included within the substituend (*sthānin*)," and so forth.

If the occurrence of *suṭ* were possible at the time of prescribing the substitute (*ādeśa*), then the future [occurrence] would not be averted; however, that [occurrence] is not possible at the time of the substitution. Therefore, regarding the future *suṭ*:

Because the original element (*sthānin*) is included within the mention of the suffix along with its augment (*sasuṭka-grahaṇa*), that which was applicable at the stage where its occurrence was possible is thereby excluded; otherwise, its inclusion within the original element would be purposeless. This might be argued: if there were a final elision (*anta-lopa*) according to the rule *śeṣe lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.90), then...

The inclusion of the word *samudāya* (aggregate) is meaningful; however, when there is elision of the remainder (*seṣalopa*) and elision of the *ṣṭi* suffix, why is that [elision of the aggregate] not accepted? Because it is untenable.
It is untenable because there is no rule for it. Since this very [rule for] elision of the final letter is the only rule available for this case, that alone is resorted to.

If this is so, when the final [phoneme] is elided in *yuṣmad-brāhmaṇībhyaḥ gacchati*, would the suffix *ṭāp* not be applied by the rule *ajādyataṣṭāp* (Pāṇini 4.1.4)? This contingency for *ṭāp* does not arise, because of the statement: "The words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* [denote] gender."

Regarding the phrase "the long pronunciation," etc.: [an objection] might be raised that even with the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (6.1.101), this is not established. [The reply: No, it is established. If it is argued that the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) prescribed by *ato guṇe* (6.1.97) would apply as an exception, [the reply is: No.

This is due to the force of the utterance of the letter *ā*. If, by the rule *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97), there were to be substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*), then the utterance of *ā* would be purposeless; one could simply have said *kam*. Therefore, he says:
"But in *thakami*," etc. The word *tu* ("but") is used in contrast to the utterance of the long vowel.
The word "and" (samuccaya) has a conjunctive sense. The particle "iti" indicates a reason.

For if there were no purpose for the utterance of the vowel *a*, one could say: "It will not occur by virtue of the power of the utterance of the vowel *a*"; yet, such a purpose does indeed exist for it.
What is the purpose [of this]? It is so that the *etva* substitution prescribed by "in the case of a *jhala* suffix in the plural, *et* [is substituted for *at*]" (Pāṇini 7.3.103) shall not occur.

Therefore, even though the vowel *a* is explicitly uttered, for the sake of preventing this *etva*, the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule from "before a *guṇa* vowel" (Pāṇini 6.1.97) would apply, rather than the *savarṇadīrgha* (long-vowel) rule. For that reason...
A long pronunciation is performed.
34. *āta au ṇalaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.34). Regarding *tasyau*: by *śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ* (7.4.61), the *khaya* consonants are retained as the remainder. Regarding *jaglau*:
by *kahoścuḥ* (7.4.62), there is the substitution of *cu*.

In this case, when the suffix *ṇal* follows [the stems] such as *sthā*, three operations apply simultaneously: reduplication (*dvirvacana*), the single-substitute replacement (*ekādeśa*), and the substitution of *au* (*autvam*). Since simultaneous application of these operations as they have thus arisen is impossible, a sequence is necessitated by the very nature of the situation.

It is resorted to. In that regard, in order to show the sequence in which those operations must be performed, he says "here," and so forth. By the word "here," examples such as *papau* and others are intended to be illustrated. If the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) were applied before the reduplication (*dvirvacana*), then [the rule] "vṛddhi replaces [a vowel] before *ec*" (Pāṇini 6.1.88) would apply.

When a single-substitute (ekādeśa) has been applied to two vowels, because there is no distinction between the cause (nimitta) and the effect (naimittika), the doubling (dvirvacana) prescribed for what precedes [the reduplication] when followed by the *liṭ* suffix would not apply;
therefore, this was stated in order to exclude that [objection]: "The status of being a substitute (sthānivadbhāva) applies to the doubling. But by what [rule] here...

Is this the application of *sthānivadbhāva* by the rule *dvirvacane'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59)? No, it is not so; for even when a cause for reduplication follows, the reduplication of the preceding element would not otherwise be obtained.
It is stated here—namely, *sthānivadbhāva*—in order to exclude that [undesired consequence].

Regarding the phrase "dvirvacanam" (in the case of reduplication): by what rule, then, would there be the status of being like the original (sthānivadbhāva)? Is it by the rule "dvirvacane'ci" (Pāṇini 1.1.59)? Not so; for that rule states that when a vowel (ac) which is the cause of reduplication follows, the preceding element is treated as the original. However, we do not perceive here any subsequent vowel that serves as the cause of reduplication.

Regarding this, some say: the term *aci* is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indicator). This was stated by relying on the following meaning of the rule: "Whatever substitute is observed for an *ac*, that becomes as if it were the original (*sthānivat*) when a reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is to be performed.
Here, although [the vowel] is not followed by a non-vowel (*anac*) at present, at the time of the formation of the single substitution (*ekādeśa*), it was followed by an *ac*.
Because it is resorted to as a cause (nimitta), the substitution has been made; therefore, it must follow the status of being "as if occupying the original place" (sthānivadbhāva).
Others, however, say: "It should be stated that a single-substitute (ekādeśa) is 'as if occupying the original place' with respect to a rule concerning what precedes it."
Thus, the status of being a substitute (sthānivadbhāva) is established by this rule;
others, however, maintain that the status of being a substitute is established through the division of the sūtra into two rules: "dvirvacane" and "aci" (Pāṇini 1.1.59).

But how is this sequence of these operations perceived? To this he says: "By reason of the single substitute" (*ekādeśāt*), and so forth. When *pāaa* is established, both the lengthening (*dīrghatva*) according to 6.1.101 (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*) and the substitution of *āṬ* would apply. In that case, there is a single substitute (*ekādeśa*)—as in *daṇḍāgram* and similar forms.
The [substitution of] *au* has scope elsewhere, but the substitution of *ū* has no scope anywhere;

therefore, because it lacks scope, the substitution of *ū* is performed first. Once that has been done, the substitution of *vṛddhi* would apply, as would the doubling of the vowel (*dvirvacanam*). In that case, by virtue of its higher priority (*paratvāt*), the *vṛddhi* occurs. Then follows the doubling of the vowel.
For [the rule] "he cooked" (*papāca*) and so forth provides scope for [the substitution of *guṇa*],
whereas the scope for *vṛddhi* is in cases such as *khaṭvaiḍaka*. Therefore, once *vṛddhi* has been applied,
reduplication occurs subsequently by virtue of the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*).

Regarding the rule "ṭhṇalaḥ": the pronunciation of the letter *ṇ* is for the purpose of ensuring that this is understood as the mention of a suffix (*pratyaya-grahaṇa*). For if the letter *ṇ* were not pronounced in *ṇal*, there would be no mention of the suffix *ṇal* because the suffix *ṇal* does not exist; and if that [mention] were absent, while it was stated simply as "of *al*," the suffix *al* would likewise not exist.
The mention of *pratyāhāra* should be understood [as follows].

The pronunciation of the letter *l* is for the purpose of ensuring that there is no inclusion of the suffix *ṇa* prescribed by rules such as *ṭhśyādvyadha* (Pāṇini 3.1.141). Now, regarding the rule *hekavacanasya* (7.1.32):
Does this [phrase] continue [to apply]? If so, then it is for the sake of the pleasure of the mouth.

35. *tuhyostātaṅṅāśiṣyanyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 7.1.35). In the example *jīvatādbhavān*, the suffix *loṭ* is applied by the rule *āśiṣi liṅloṭau* (3.3.173); then *tip* is applied; then *śap*; then by *erur* (3.4.86), the substitution of *u* occurs for the *e* of *tip*; and finally, for that word *tu*, the substitution *tātaṅ* is applied.
Regarding "jīvatāt tvam": [the suffix] *sip* is applied, and by the rule *ser hy apic ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.87), *hi* is substituted for it;
for that *hi*, *tātaṅ* is substituted. Thus we have "jīva tvam. By the rule *ato heḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.105), there is elision (*luk*) of *hi*.
Now, in the case of "jīvatāt tvam," by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the *tātaṅ* is included within the scope of the term *hi*.

Why does elision (*luk*) not occur [here] by virtue of the previous rule? Because, while the term *hiḥ* is still being carried over from "ghu-jhal-bhyo her dhiḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.101), there is the further mention of "ato heḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.105).
For that [subsequent mention] has this purpose: so that elision (*luk*) may occur only for that *hi* which remains in its actual form (*hirūpa*).
Let there not be [the application of] another word ending in *hi* which is grasped by the mention of *hi* through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*.

Now, why does the substitution of *tātaṅ* not occur for the final letter according to the rule "ṅcci" (Pāṇini 1.1.53)? To this he says: "The mention of *ṅt*," and so forth. It is for the purpose of prohibiting the entire class (*gaṇa*). One might say:
In the example *bhavān*, [the substitution of *tātaṅ*] is for the purpose of prohibiting *vṛddhi*—as in *mṛṣṭāt*. The particle *iti* indicates a reason;
because the particle *ṅ* is used for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, therefore *tātaṅ* becomes a substitute for the whole [stem].
For if it had no other purpose, it would indeed apply only to the final letter.

*Tātaṅ* has another purpose as well: the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. When that [prohibition] exists, should [the substitute] apply to the final letter by the rule "when [an element] ending in ṅ or c, [it replaces] the final" (1.1.53), or should it replace the whole by the rule "that which consists of more than one letter or ends in śit replaces the whole" (1.1.55)? In this case, because the latter rule is subsequent, it is proper that it should indeed be a replacement of the whole.
[The question arises: Should it be [a substitute] for the whole? Therefore, by the rule "anekāl-śit sarvasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.55), should it apply to the whole?
In that case, because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], it is proper that it be a replacement of the whole;
therefore, by the rule "anekāl-śit sarvasya" (1.1.55), it should indeed be for the whole, and thus it is a replacement of the entire [original].

It occurs. But surely, by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original), the *tātaṅ* [substitute for *hi*] which occupies the position of *tu* would acquire the designation *pit*; and consequently, just as *iṅ* occurs in *yatām bravītu* by the rule *hali piti sārvadhātuke* (Pāṇini 6.1.69), so too would there be *aṇ* and *iṭ* in *brūtād bhavān*.

"Is it not necessary [to state this]?"—in order to remove this objection, he says "ṅtvācci," etc. "Of this" refers to the *tātaṅ* substitute. For what reason does it cease? He says "ṅcci," etc. The particle *ca* (and) indicates the reason. Since the status of being *pit* would apply to the *tātaṅ* in place of *tu*, the status of being *ṅit* is introduced [by the rule].

For indeed, the *pit* status (the designation of being followed by a voiceless consonant) is obstructed. Thus, even though this [suffix] is characterized as *ṅt*, if the *pit* status obtained through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (acting like the original element) is set aside, then—as expressed in the passage beginning with "therefore"—since the *pit* status is thus set aside, the *īṭ* augment does not occur on account of that *pit* status. [Example: *grāmaṃ gacchatu bhavān*.
"Go, you!"—here the *loṭ* suffix is used in the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth, according to Pāṇini 3.3.162.

36. *videḥ śatur vasuḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.36). Although this mention of *vidiḥ* is a general reference, it is nevertheless understood to refer specifically to the root meaning "to know" (*jñāna*). For only that [root] can occur with the suffix *śatṛ* following it, and not other roots meaning "to find," etc.

In that context, the suffix *śatṛ* is simply impossible for the roots meaning "to exist" (*sat*) and "to deliberate" (*vicāraṇā*), because they are marked with the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) designation.

However, it is possible for the root meaning "to obtain" (*lābha*), since it is marked as taking both voices (*ubhayapadī*); yet even there, it is not immediately applicable, because it is separated by the *śap* affix.
Furthermore, for the root meaning "to know" (*jñāna*), because its conjugational marker (*vikaraṇa*) is subject to elision (*luk*), the function performed by the *śatṛ* marker [does not apply].
There is no intervention; therefore, he says "vida jñāne" [DhP 2.55] so that only this [root] is understood.

Regarding "vidvān": because it ends in an *u*-class vowel (*ugit*), the augment *num* is applied, and by the rule "sāntamahataḥ saṃyogasya" (Pāṇini 6.4.10), the long vowel is substituted. The term "anyatarasyām" (optionally) is carried over [from the previous sūtra]. By virtue of that, in the alternative case, we have "vidan," "vidantau," and so on.
The form *vidanta* and others also occur. Furthermore, because this [fact] is already understood, it was not stated in the commentary (*vṛtti*).
Now, for what purpose is the marker *u* (the *anubandha*) attached? If it is argued that it is so that operations such as *num* (the nasal augment) might apply by virtue of being *augit*, [we reply:
no, because that is already established through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaving like the original). Therefore—

He says: "Because of the status of being like the original (sthānivadbhāva)," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of *kvas* also," the word "also" (*api*) implies that this [rule] applies to it as well. If the vowel *u* were not present, there would be the apprehension of *kvas* alone in its general sense, and not of any other. Now, the rule "vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of *vas*" (Pāṇini 6.4.131) is formulated.

[This is] for the purpose of grasping this [element *kvas*] alone, and not [the element] *kvas*; but surely, even if the vowel *u* were present, a general reference would not be possible—due to the exclusion rule regarding elements with a single indicatory letter (*ekānubandhaka-paribhāṣā*), there would be a grasp of this [element *kvas*] alone, and not of *kvas*. To this he says: "In the case of a reference to an element with a single indicatory letter," and so forth.

This is a metarule (*paribhāṣāsūtra*). It does not apply; that is the meaning of "it does not present itself. For what reason does it not apply? He says: "And such being the case," and so forth. The meaning is: "if this were so.
If, even when the letter *u* is being employed [as an *anubandha*], the metarule concerning a single *anubandha* were to apply, then—
The inclusion of the letter *u* would be purposeless; for even without it, when it is stated that "there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of *vas*, the simple form [of the suffix] is indeed obtained.
Therefore, by virtue of the inclusion of the letter *u*, this *paribhāṣā* does not apply."

37. *lyap* is substituted for *ktvā* when [the compound] is a *samāsa* not preceded by the negative particle *nañ*. (Pāṇini 7.1.37) Regarding "not preceded by *nañ*": *nañ* is the negative particle; that which is not *nañ* is *anañ*; that which has *anañ* preceding it is *anañ-pūrvaḥ*. Examples such as *prakṛtya* [are given]. [The rule applies] when there are two actions performed by the same agent, [and the action denoted by the *ktvā* suffix occurs] at an earlier time.

(3.4.21) The suffix *ktvā* [is applied]; there is a compound by the rule "kugatiprādayaḥ" (2.2.18), and the augment *tuk* is added by the rule "hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk" (6.1.71). Thus, [we have] "pārśvataḥkṛtya. Here, the suffix *ktvā* is applied by the rule "svāṅge taspratyaye kṛbhvoḥ" (3.4.61).

The compound [in *nānākṛtya*] is formed by [Pāṇini 2.2.210]: *ṭhtṛtīyāprabhṛtīnyanyatarasyām*. Regarding *nānākṛtya*: the suffix *ktvā* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.4.62]: *ṭhnādhārthapratyaye cvyarthe*, and the compound is formed as before. *Kṛtvā* and *hṛtvā* are counter-examples; here [the rule does not apply].

The word *kṛtvā* exists when not preceded by the negative particle *nañ*; however, because no compound (*samāsa*) occurs [in such cases], there is an absence of the suffix *lyap*. For example: *paramakṛtvā*, *uttamakṛtvā*. [In these instances,] the compound is formed by the rule *sanmahatparama-* (Pāṇini 2.1.61). But how is the compound formed by this rule? And why would it not otherwise be so?

Is it because of the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)? This is incorrect; for the suffix *ktvā* is prescribed when the agent is expressed, and that very agent is qualified by the two words "supreme" (*parama*) and "highest" (*uttama*). So how can there be an absence of coreferentiality? Or, if one were to assume that those two [words] function as adverbs modifying the action...

The state of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is expressed; nevertheless, because the term "frequently" (*bahulam*) from the rule *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.57) is understood to apply here as well, a compound occurs even in cases where there is no coreferentiality.

But surely, these two compounds do not have *nañ* as their prior member; so how is this counter-example appropriate? To this he says: "Not *nañ*" (*anañ*), and so forth. This "not *nañ*" (*anañ*) is not a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*); rather, it is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*): that which is other than *nañ* is "not *nañ*" (*anañ*). In that case...

According to the maxim *nañivayukta* (Pāṇini-vyākaraṇa-pariśiṣṭa 65), that which is other than the negative particle *nañ*—namely, an indeclinable (*avyaya*) similar to it—is understood as "not-nañ" (*anañ*). For that reason, both of these—the indeclinable *nañ* and the non-indeclinable words such as *parama*—are not "not-nañ"; therefore, [the rule] does not apply there with the indeclinable *nañ*.

There is similarity [between them], due to extreme non-difference and because they are indeclinables (*avyaya*), respectively. Therefore, just as *akṛtvā* and *ahatvā* are valid counter-examples, so too are *paramakṛtvā* and *utamakṛtvā*. If, then, *anañ* refers to that which is similar to the negative particle (*nañ*), [then...]

It is included [in the scope of the rule]: otherwise, in cases such as *snātvākālakaḥ* ("one who is not black after bathing") and *pītvāsthirakaḥ* ("one who is not firm after drinking"), [the suffix *ka*] would also apply, since here too the preceding member is a word similar to a negative (*nañ*), because the suffix *ktvā* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Therefore, he says: "In *snātvākālakaḥ*, etc."
These groups are listed in the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* class for the purpose of assigning them the technical designation of *samāsa*;
therefore, due to this nipātana (irregularity), the substitution of *lyap* does not occur.
[Regarding] "Or else," etc.: when the locative case *samāse* is understood as a locative of location (*adhikaraṇasaptamī*),...
It follows that when [the suffix] *lyap* is applied after [roots such as] *snā* in connection with words like *akālaka*, there is the contingency of applying the substitute *lyap*.

For in this way, when the locative case is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the meaning becomes: "In a compound that does not have *nañ* as its first member, for that *ktvā* which occurs, *lyap* is substituted. And this being so, since there is no inclusion of a specific location, just as...
If the substitution of *lyap* for *ktvā* were to occur only at the end of a compound, it might also occur in the middle;

therefore, this locative case is not a locative of location (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*), but rather a locative of selection (*nirghāraṇa-saptamī*). And in that view, the word "in a compound" (*samāse*) is used in the singular to denote a class, just as in the rule "kārake" (Pāṇini 1.4.23).

Alternatively, by the rule *ṭhvyatyayo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.1.85), one should understand that there is a substitution of the singular number for the plural number through a transposition of case endings (*sub-vyatyaya*). Regarding the word "by that" (*tena*) and so forth: since this locative case is used for the purpose of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), it follows that only a compound ending in *-ktvā* is intended to be included, and not a constituent part of a compound—namely, the word *snātvā*.

For specification (*nirghāraṇa*) applies only to that which is of the same class; just as when it is said, "Among cows, the black one is the most abundant in milk," it is understood that a cow alone is being specified, so too here, when it is stated,
"a compound not preceded by *nañ*," [it is understood that] among compounds not preceded by *nañ*, that which ends in *ktvā* [is intended].

That very compound, being specifically determined, is what is understood; therefore, since the mention of *ktvā* refers only to a compound ending in *ktvā*, it is that [compound] alone which must undergo the substitution of *lyap*. Furthermore, in examples such as *snātvākālaka*, there is no compound ending in *ktvā*. Although *snātvākālaka* and the like— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical flow of the grammatical argument.]
These are compounds, but not words ending in *ktvā*; therefore, the substitution of *lyap* does not occur.

And that compound is understood as ending in *ktvā* by means of the rule for inclusion of what ends in a specific element (*tadantavidhi*), according to Pāṇini 1.1.72: "That by which a rule is prescribed applies to what ends in it.
Or, because of the principle that when a *kṛt*-suffix is mentioned, it includes a word preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka* (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 126).

By the paribhāṣā regarding the inclusion of the *pratyaya* (Pāṇini 1.1.72), it is not possible to state that the inclusion of the word ending in that [suffix] (*tadantagrahaṇa*) applies here; for the suffix *ktvā* is not produced after a compound. In that case, if the inclusion of the word ending in that [suffix] were to be understood by the paribhāṣā regarding the inclusion of *kṛt*-suffixes (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 126), then in the example *nānākṛtya*, [the rule would apply].

It would not apply; for this [term] does not have a *gati* or a *kāraka* as its prior member. However, it would indeed apply here—in cases such as *prakṛtya* and *pārśvataḥkṛtya*. For even here, the prior constituent is a *gati* and a *kāraka*; and since the rule "that by which an operation is prescribed applies to that which ends with it" (Pāṇini 1.1.72) allows for the inclusion of the final member (*tadantavidhi*), [the rule] would apply everywhere.

Thinking that this is so, he says, "And that," and so forth. He provides the justification for this very point with, "And thus," and so forth. Because by the rule *yena vidhis tadantasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.72), a compound ending in *ktvā* is understood; and having established this, it is stated that [the prohibition applies] when preceded by *nañ*. By which...

By the rule *vidhistadantasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.72), a compound ending in *ktvā* is understood; and having done so, it is stated that [the suffix applies] "provided it is not preceded by *nañ*. For if, by the general application of the rule *vidhistadantasya* (1.1.72), the designation of being "ending in that" were to apply, then the suffix would also undesirably apply to a compound preceded by *nañ*.
Therefore, for the sake of excluding that [undesired application], it is rightly stated: "provided it is not preceded by *nañ*. If, by the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of *kṛt*-suffixes (P.

3.1.92), a compound ending in *ktvā* were to be understood, then only a compound preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka* would be included. And such being the case, if only those preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka* were to be grasped...

When the negative particle *nañ* precedes [a word], there is no possibility [of the application of the rule] at all. This is because of the principle: "The negative particle *nañ* is neither a *gati* nor a *kāraka*.
For this reason, just as there is no possibility [of the rule applying] in the case of *paramakṛtvā*—because the word *parama* is neither a *gati* nor a *kāraka*—so too is it the case in *akṛtvā*.

Because the negative particle *naÑ* is neither a nominal stem (*agati*) nor an agent (*akāraka*), there is no possibility of its application; consequently, the rule "provided it is not preceded by *naÑ*" (*anañpūrve*) need not have been stated, yet it was indeed stated. Therefore, from this very statement "not preceded by *naÑ*," it follows that by the rule "that by which a grammatical operation is prescribed applies to the end of a word" (*yena vidhis tadantasya*), the compound ending in *ktvā* is understood to be included, and not [any other].

This is established by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) concerning the mention of a *kṛt* suffix. Regarding the form *pradhāya*: here, because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), the substitution of *hi* for the root *dhā* [as prescribed by] Pāṇini 7.4.42 would apply. Regarding the form *prasthāya*: here too, [the substitution of *ī* for *sthā* as prescribed by] Pāṇini 7.4.40, "for *dyati*, *syati*, *mā*, and *sthā* before a *kit* suffix," would apply.
Thus, there is *itva* [the substitution of *i* for *ya*]. In *prakhanya*, there is *ātva* [the substitution of *ā* for *ya*] by the rule *janasanakhanām* (Pāṇini 6.4.42).
In *praṇabhya*, there is lengthening by the rule *anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ kṅiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.15).
In *āpṛcchya*, there is the substitution of *ś* by the rule *cchavoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.19).

In *prati-dīvya*, [the augment] *iṭ* is applied by that very rule (*ārthadhātukasyeṅ valādeḥ*). In *prapaṭhya*, [the augment] *iṭ* is applied by the rule *ārthadhātukasyeṅ valādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.35). Furthermore, these [augmentations] possess internal status (*antaraṅgatva*) because they depend upon a single word (*ekapada*).
However, the substitution of *lyap* possesses external status (*bahirahgatva*).

If someone were to object: "Because [the suffix] depends on a compound consisting of several capable words, when [suffixes] such as *hi* are applied, forms such as *pradhāya* would not be established," he says in response:
"*pradhāya*" and so forth. "[This has been made known]" means: "In the rule *ado...* [the author] has indicated this."

In the rule *jagdhṛtyaptikiti* (Pāṇini 2.4.36), for what purpose is the mention of *pūrva* (preceding)? Could one not simply say *nānañ* (not preceded by the negative particle *nañ*)? It cannot be done in this way;
for if *nānañ* were stated, this would be understood as a Bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that in which the *nañ* is non-existent."
In this case, because [the rule] specifies "where this [suffix] is not *nañ*," then here too [the substitution] would not occur—as in *straiṇīkṛtya*.

[The derivation is as follows: from *strī*, the word *straiṇam* is formed by the suffix *nañ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.87, *strīpuṃsābhyāṃ nañsnañau bhavanāt*. From that which ends in *nañ*, the suffix *cvi* is applied by 5.4.50, *abhūtatadbhāve*, etc., and [the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel] occurs by the rule *asya cvau*.

(7.4.32) Thus, there is the substitution of *i*. By the rule "kugatiprādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.2.18), a compound is formed. However, when the word *pūrva* is included [in the rule], the word *pūrva* denotes that which constitutes the initial member [of the compound]. Consequently, where *nañ* is not the initial member of the compound, the suffix *lyap* should not occur; yet in the case of *straiṇīkṛtya*, it indeed occurs. Not so.

In this case, the negative particle (*nañ*) is not a constituent part at the beginning of a compound; rather, it occurs in the middle. The purpose of the *lit* designation is so that, in forms such as *pratikīrṣya*, the acute accent may apply to the syllable preceding the *lit*-marked suffix. However, in cases such as *prakṛtya*, the application of the *lit* designation for the sake of an acute accent is not appropriate.

The acute accent of the preceding [syllable] is established by the accent of the root itself; therefore, it is only when there are multiple vowels as constituents that the status of being a root (dhātutva) is triggered.
38. *ktvā* also [is used] in the Veda (*chandasi*).
(Pāṇini 7.1.38) Examples: *paridhāpayitvā*, *pratyaryayitvā*. [These are derived from] the roots *dhā* and *ṛ* with the causative suffix *ṇic*;
[the augment] *puk* is applied by the rule *arti-hrī-...* (7.3.36), and [the lengthening of the penultimate vowel] by the rule *pug-anta-laghu-upadh-asya* (7.3.86).

The suffix *guṇa*, the suffix *ktvā*, the augment *iṭ*, and the substitution of *ay* [for the vowel]. Regarding the form "uddhṛtya": from the root *hṛñ* in the sense of "taking away" (DhP 8.99), the substitution of *dh* for the *h* occurs by the rule *jhayo ho 'nyatarasyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.4.62). Regarding the phrase "or in the Veda": although it should have been stated as *ktvāpi chandasi*, the actual wording [of the sūtra] is intended to apply even when there is no compound (*asamāsa*).
So that it might be: "Having honored those gods, he departed."

39. *supāṃ sulukpūrvasavarṇāccheyāḍāḍaḷayājālaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). Regarding the form *panthāḥ*: from the stem *pathin*, the case-ending *jas* is applied; this [ending] is replaced by *su*. Then, by the rule *pathimathyṛbhukṣāmāt* (7.1.85), the final vowel is replaced by *ā*; and by the rule *ito 't sarvanāmasthāne*, the *i* is replaced by *at*.
By [Pāṇini 7.1.86], the vowel *i* is replaced by *ā*; by [Pāṇini 7.1.87], the substitute *nth* is applied.
The meaning is that the rule beginning with "supām" (*supām tiṅ-ām...*) should be explained as having the sense that substitutes for *sup* take the place of *sup*. In this regard, the following...

The explanation: the word *api* ("also") is carried over from the preceding rule, and it serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned. By means of this, *sup*-affixes also occur after other *sup*-affixes. For example, in the expression *dhuri dakṣiṇāyāḥ*, the singular ablative case (*pañcamī-ekavacana*) takes the place of the singular locative case (*saptamī-ekavacana*).
Or [it may be taken as] the genitive singular.

Regarding the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* and so forth, the meaning is that it must be explained in such a way that [the term *atiṅ*] applies to those [words] that follow a *tiṅ* (a finite verb). However, the actual explanation must be stated exactly as before.
In *ṭhārdre carman*, there is elision (*luk*) of the locative singular case-ending after the word *carman*.
In *ṭhyat*, here too [elision occurs] after the word *yat* and also after the word *tat*.
In *ṭhdhītī* and so forth, [elision occurs] after the words *dhīti*, *mati*, and *suṣṭuti*.

In the case of the third person singular, the vowel *i* is substituted by a homogeneous (*pūrvasavarṇa*) vowel; then, by the rule *ubhayor akaḥ savarṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.101), there is lengthening. Regarding the form *ubhā*: from the word *ubha*, the vowel *ā* is substituted for the first dual ending; then, by the rule *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.102), [the substitution of a homogeneous long vowel occurs].
(6.1.102) This is a single-substitute (ekādeśa).

[The example is] "I do not censure that Brāhmaṇa" (*na taṃ brāhmaṇād nindāmi*). From the word *tat* and the word *brāhmaṇa*, there is the ending *āt* for the second case singular. When followed by the word *ni*, [the rule] *yaro 'nunāsike 'nunāsiko vā* applies.

By the rule *vā* (8.4.45), the substitution of *na* for *ta* occurs [in the case of *yuṣmān* and *asmān*]. Thus we have *yuṣme* and *asme*. Furthermore, for the *jas* following the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, there is this substitution *śe* (1.1.13).
The letter *ś* is for the purpose of indicating that the entire element is to be substituted. Now, in this context, the rule *yūyaṃ vayaṃ jasi* (7.2.93) applies.

Why, then, do the substitutes *yūyam* and *vayam* not occur here? To this he says: "The substitute *yūya*" and so forth. In the forms *uruyā* and *dhṛṣṇuyā*, the substitution of *yā* occurs for the third-case singular ending following the words *uru* and *dhṛṣṇu*.

Regarding "ṭhnābhā": from the word *nābhi*, there is the substitution of *ḍā* for the locative singular ending; the letter *ḍ* is for the purpose of eliding the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant).
Regarding "ṭhanuṣṭuḷa": from the word *anuṣṭup*, there is the substitution of *ḍaḷ* for the instrumental singular ending.
Regarding "sādhuyā": the substitution of *yā* occurs for the first case singular following the word *sādhu*.

The letter *ca* [in the rule] is for the purpose of making it udātta at the end. Regarding "when *su* would have been elided (*luk*)": the remainder of the sense is that this substitute *yā* is prescribed; as for the occasion for *luk*, it is by the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.23).
By this [rule],

in the case of "vasantā," the substitution of *i* for the locative singular following the word *vasanta* is applied. The inclusion of the *l*-marker is for the purpose of [triggering] the *lit* suffix rules.

The meaning of "upasaṃkhyānam" is "the provision [of a rule]" so that the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the preceding [word] may occur. In the subsequent cases as well, the word *upasaṃkhyāna* has the meaning of "provision. Provision means...

One should also rely on the word *api* [to understand that this rule applies]. In the forms *urviyā* and *dārviyā*, the substitution of *iy* for the third case singular ending occurs after the words *uru* and *dāru*. In the form *sukṣetriyā*, [the substitution occurs] after the word *sukṣetrin*, which ends in the possessive suffix *ini*.

In the case of the third-case singular, there is the substitution of *aṅ* for [the case-ending] beginning with *ṅ*. The letter *ḍ* is for the purpose of eliding the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant).

The letter *c* is for the purpose of making the word end-acute (*antodātta*). In the form "sarasī," the letter *ī* is the [substitute] for the seventh-case singular from the word *saras*. In the form "prabāhavā," there is the substitution of *aṅ* for the third-case singular from the word *prabāhu*.

By the rule *ṭhgheṅiti* (Pāṇini 7.3.111), there is *guṇa* substitution, followed by the replacement with *av*. Now, one might object: "In the Mahābhāṣya (3.247) it is stated: 'When a grammatical operation is prescribed on the basis of a specific phoneme (*ṅ*), one should understand that it applies only to that phoneme; and when it is prescribed on the basis of a suffix (*ṅtva*), one should understand that it applies to what begins with that [suffix].'"
This has been stated; however, since the letter *ṅ* does not occur here at the beginning, how can there be a *guṇa* substitution?
There is no fault, for it will occur by virtue of the power of the suffix *ṅti*. Regarding "svapnayā":
from the word *svapna*, the third case singular ending takes the form *āy* [by Pāṇini 7.1.12], and then [the *guṇa* substitution] occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.97]: *ato guṇe*.
The suffix *pararūpa* [is applied]. The letter *ca* is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*). Regarding the rule "nāv-ayā":

after the word *nau*, the third-case singular ending receives the substitution *ayā*. The letter *r* is for the purpose of making the penultimate vowel (*upotama*) acute, according to the rule "upotamaṃ riti" (Pāṇini 6.1.217).

40. *amo maś* (Pāṇini 7.1.40). By stating "the substitute *mip* is understood by [the word] *ṭham*," [the author] dispels the suspicion that the second singular [person] is intended. There is no inclusion of the second singular; [this applies] in the Vedic language (*chandas*).

Because it conforms to what has been observed; or because of the recurrence of the word *api*. For when that [word *api*] recurs, the connection is made thus: "the substitution of *am* and *m* occurs, and by the recurrence of the word *api*, there is also sometimes audible [retention of the original form].
Regarding the example *vadhīm*: this is the *luṅ* [aorist] of the root *han*; by the rule *caleḥ sic* (Pāṇini 3.1.44), there is *sic*, and of that...

By the rule *ṭhasthastha* (Pāṇini 3.4.101) and others, the suffix *am* is applied; for that, *ma* is the substitute—the letter *a* being for the sake of pronunciation. By the rule *luṅ ci* (2.4.43), there is the substitution of *vadha* for the root *han*. By the rule *ārdhadhātukasya* (7.2.35) and others, the augment *iṭ* is added, [and] by *astisico 'pṛkte* (7.3.96).
Thus, by the rule *iṭaḥ īṭi* (8.2.28), there is the elision of the *sic* suffix, and the long vowel [is applied] as before due to the rule on homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*).
Regarding the form *kramīt*: the root is *kramu* (DhP 473) meaning "to step. Everything else is as previously described.
Here, however, the distinction is this: the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *snukramoranātmanepadanimite* (7.2.36).
Since [the form] *avadhavam* would have been obtained from [the rule] *akramiṣam*, it is said:
"The inclusion of the marker *ś* is for the purpose of making [the substitute] a replacement for the whole. The intention is that in its absence, the rule *alo 'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52) would apply.
But surely there is a purpose for pronouncing the letter *m* [in the substitute *avama*]?
"Will it not be a universal substitution even without the letter *ś*, [as in the case of *na*]?
To this he says: 'of the letter *m*', and so forth. For there is indeed a purpose for the prescription of the letter *m*.
What is that? [Otherwise] *mo'nusvāraḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.23) would apply; [the prescription of *m*] is so that this [substitution of *anusvāra*] shall not occur."

If this purpose were not present and the letter *ś* were not employed, then [the substitution] would apply only to the final [element], and not to all; it would not occur for the whole. Therefore, the letter *ś* must be made for the sake of making [the substitution] an operation affecting the entire [original element].

41. *lopasta ātmanepadeṣu* (Pāṇini 7.1.41). Regarding the form *adugdha*: this is the *laṅ* [aorist] of the root *duh*; due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix; the substitution [of *ta* for *tās*] occurs by the rule *ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ* (7.1.5); the augment *ruṭ* is added by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (7.1.8); and finally, there is the elision of the letter *t*.

When the two *a*-sounds have been applied, there is the substitution of the long vowel (*pūrvarūpatva*) by [Pāṇini 6.1.97] *ṭhato guṇe*. Thus, "duhrām": this is the imperative (*loṭ*), the third person plural suffix *jha*; the substitution of *e* for *ṭi*, the replacement of *jha* by *ām*;

the augment *ruṭ* after the substitute *āt* for *jha*; the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix as before; and upon the elision of the *t*, the substitution of a long vowel for homogeneous sounds (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*).

Regarding "śaye": this is the present indicative (*laṭ*), singular; by *śīṅḥ sārvadhātuke guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.21), there is *guṇa*, and by the elision of *śap*, the form is established. Regarding "duhām": this is the imperative (*loṭ*), singular;
by *eta ai* (Pāṇini 3.4.93), there is *aitva*, and by *āmetaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.90), there is *ām*. Regarding "dugdhām": [this is the aorist, third person dual].
By the rules *ṭhdāderdhātordhaḥ* (8.2.32) and *ṭhjhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* (8.2.40), there is the substitution of *dha*;
then, by *ṭhjhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* (8.4.56), the letter *dha* becomes *ga*.
[The phrase] "because of the addition of the word *api*" and so forth refers to *ṭhktvādi cchandasi* (7.1.38).

The phrase "from this also" (*ityato'pi*) is understood to carry over; there, the connection is made as follows: "there is elision, and there is also hearing [of the vowel]. Consequently, it does not occur in the case of *kuruta*. When the *guṇa* substitution has been applied to the root *kṛ*, the substitution of *u* occurs by the rule *ata utsārvadhātuke* (Pāṇini 6.4.110). This is so even if the word *api* is understood to carry over.
In some cases, the suffix *śravaṇa* (the augment *ś*) occurs; for that very reason, it does not occur in the *parasmaipada* endings.
So what is the purpose of mentioning *ātmanepada*? If this is so, then the mention of *ātmanepada* is for the sake of clarity.
42. *dhvamo dhvāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.42).

[The example is] *vārayadhvāt*. This is the imperative (*loṭ*) derived either from the root *vṛñ* or *vṛṅ*, or from the causative (*ṇijanta*) form of these roots, or from the root *vṛñ* meaning "to cover" (Dhātupāṭha 1813), or from the denominative (*curādi-ṇya-anta*) form of that same root. Of this [imperative], [the suffix -dhvam is replaced by -dhvāt].
*Dhvam*, *tasya dhvāt*, and *vārayadhvam*. Once the substitution of *e* for *et* has been made, the substitute *am* is applied by the rule *savābhyāṃ vāmau* (Pāṇini 3.4.91).
43. *yajadhvainam* (Pāṇini 7.1.43). 44. *tasya tātaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.44), [referring to] "of the second person plural of the imperative. Now, [the rule for] the singular of the first person:

Why does it not occur? Because in Vedic usage (*chandas*), one follows what is actually observed, or because of the continued application of the word *api*. [The example is] *kṛṇutāt*. In the root *kṛvi* (DhP 5.98), meaning "to injure" or "to do," the augment *num* is applied because it is marked with *eṭ*; then, by Pāṇini 3.1.80, *dhinvikṛṇvyora ca*, the vowel *u* is substituted for the final vowel and the penultimate consonant.
Thus, there is the suffix *u*, and the letter *a* is substituted for the final [letter]; then by *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.48), the [final] *a* is elided. Regarding "saṃsṛjatāt":

from the root *sṛj*, the suffix *cha* is applied because it belongs to the *tudādi* class. Regarding "gamayatāt": there is the causative suffix *ṇic*, and by *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.92), the short vowel is substituted.

45. *taptanaptanathanāśca* (Pāṇini 7.1.45). Regarding the word *śṛṇoti*: by the rule *śruvaḥ śṛ ca* (3.1.74), there is the addition of the *śnu* suffix and the substitution of *śṛ* for the root *śru*. Because the suffix is *pit*, it lacks the *ṅ* designation; therefore, *guṇa* substitution occurs. Regarding the word *sunoti*: by the rule *svadibhyaḥ śnuḥ*, there is the addition of the *śnu* suffix.
(3.1.73) | Regarding "dadhātana": there is reduplication of the root *dhā* by virtue of the rule "ślau" (6.1.10).

Here too, because the preceding letter is not a nasal (*ṅ*), the elision of the long *ā* by the rule "śnābhyastayor ātaḥ" (6.4.112) does not occur. Regarding "dhata": [this is derived] by the rule "dadhastathośca" (8.2.38).

Thus, through this process of substitution, the letter *a* becomes *d*. When the *a* of the verbal root (*dhātu*) has been elided, the rule "jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi" (Pāṇini 8.4.53) applies the *jaś*-substitution, resulting in the letter *ḍ*;

then, by the rule "khari ca" (Pāṇini 8.4.55), the *cari*-substitution applies, resulting in the letter *t*. Thus we have "jujuṣṭana. From the root *iṣ*, meaning "to desire," the suffix *śa* is applied as before.

By the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (Pāṇini 2.4.73), there is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix]. Regarding the form "yadicchata," the substitution of *ch* for [the *ś* of] *iṣu*, *gam*, and *yam* occurs by the rule "iṣugamiyamāṃ chaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.77). The letter *c* is included here for the purpose of carrying over (*anukarṣaṇa*) the word "tasya" from that previous rule.
46. *idantoma si* (Pāṇini 7.1.46).

[The commentary says: "*ṭhidantaḥ*"—the letter *ṭ* is for the sake of avoiding ambiguity. For if the letter *ṭ* were not present, once the *yaṇ*-substitution had been applied, it would have to be "*yantaḥ*," and in that case there would be doubt: "Is this [the word] ending in *y*, or..."

Regarding the term *utekārānta*: that which has *it* as its final element is *idanta*. The word *mas* is the referent of the other member of the compound (*anyapadārtha*). The form *sakārāntamasī* is a citation without a case-ending (*avibhaktika*), because the nominative singular ending has been elided according to Pāṇini 7.1.39 (*supāṃ suluk...*); [the remainder is] the vowel *i*.

This is for the purpose of pronunciation. By the rule "of *bhas* ending in *s*" and so forth, he clarifies the meaning that this word *bhas* ends in the vowel *i*. By the phrase "ending in *s*," he demonstrates that in the mantra "vocêma" (vocem), [the substitution] does not occur because it ends in the vowel *ā*. But how [is this so]?

If [the rule] is stated with a final *s*, would it not apply to that which does not end in *s*? No, because that which has undergone a partial modification is not considered different from the original. If this is so, why does it not occur here? Because in the Vedic language (*chandas*), one follows exactly what is observed there; or else, because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "also" (*api*). As in the case of "vocema," from the root *vac*.

In the *liṅ* [optative] used for a benediction (*āśis*) of another, there is the suffix *mas*; [the augment] *yāsuṭ* is added; by the rule "liṅyāśiṣi" (Pāṇini 3.4.86), the suffix *aṅ* is applied; and by the rule "ato yeyaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.80), the substitution of *iy* occurs. Similarly, after the root *vac*, in the *liṅ* used for a benediction of another, there is the suffix *mas*; *yāsuṭ* is added; by "liṅyāśiṣi" (3.4.86), *aṅ* is applied; and by "ato yeyaḥ" (7.2.80), [the substitution of *iy* occurs].

Thus, there is the substitution of *iy* [for *i*]; by the rule "ṭhvaca um" (Pāṇini 7.4.20), the augment *um* is added. Because [the suffix] is treated as a sārvadhātuka by the rule "cchandasyubhayathā" (Pāṇini 3.4.117), there is the elision of *s* by the rule "liṅḥ salopo'nantyasya" (Pāṇini 7.2.79).
By the rule "nityaṃ ṅtiḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.99), there is the elision of *s* for the *um* ending in *u*. [Then] there is the elision...

And by the rule *vyor vali* (6.1.66), there is the substitution of *v* for *y*. Then, by *ād guṇaḥ* (6.1.87), [the rule] "the augment *iK* occurs"—how then is this an augment? And why would it not be so? Because there is no characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of an augment. The characteristics of an augment are *ṭit*, *kit*, and *mit*; these are present here.

If not even one of these [conditions] exists, then that [operation] is not an *āgama*, just as the substitution of *bhū* in the rule "asterbhūḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.52). If this were so, then the augment *aij* in the rule "na yvābhyāṃ padāntābhyāṃ pūrvau ca tābhyāmaic" (Pāṇini 7.3.3) would not occur. [Objection: But [it does occur] because of the mention of the word "pūrva" (preceding).
How is its status as an *āgama* (augment) determined? Let it be determined for this [word] as well by virtue of its being called "the end" (*anta*).
For just as the word *pūrva* signifies a part and denotes a specific preceding portion, so too does the word *anta*; thus, this is the same. "And that becomes its end"—this is the meaning of *anta*.

"A single part" means a constituent member (*avayava*). For this very reason, he says that it is included by the mention of "that" (*tadgrahaṇena*), stating: "The purpose of mentioning 'that' is the prevention of separate accentuation (*svaranivṛtti*)," as well as the elision (*nighāta*) prescribed by the rule *tiṅṅtiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28). It was not stated as *masa ik*.

This is for the sake of removing doubt. For if it were stated thus, a doubt might arise: "Is this an augment (*āgama*), or is it a pratyāhāra? [The examples are] *dīpayāmasi* and *jambhayamasi*. [The roots are] *dīpī* in the sense of "to shine" (DhP 1150) and *jabhi*, *jṛbhī* in the sense of "bending of the limbs" (DhP). [Note: *jabhī* and *jṛbhi* are the readings in the Dhātupāṭha.]

From these two roots ending in *ṇic*, the present tense suffix (*laṭ*) is applied; then, by the rule "radhijabhor aci" (Pāṇini 7.1.61), there is elision [of the penultimate vowel]. In some places, the reading is *bhañjayāmasi*; this should be understood as belonging to the causative form (*ṇyanta*) of the root *bhañj* (Dhātupāṭha 1453), meaning "to crush."
47. *ktvo yak* (Pāṇini 7.1.47). Regarding the example *datvāya*: the substitution of *dad* is applied by the rule *do dad ghoḥ* (7.4.46).
[The sūtra] *ktvāpi cchandasi* and so forth—when stated in this way, the mention of *ktvā* twice is not [required].
The sense is that "it must be done. [The word] "in a compound" (*samāse*) is understood here;

this is from the rule *samāse 'nañpūrve* (Pāṇini 7.1.37). One might raise the doubt that if this were stated immediately after that [rule], the mention of "compound" (*samāsa-grahaṇa*) would still be understood as carrying over (*anuvartate*) there as well.
The intention is that this [next verse] was not stated immediately after that one for the purpose of following upon or withdrawing from it.
48. *iṣṭvīnam* and so forth. (Pāṇini 7.1.48). Regarding *iṣṭvīnam*: there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule for the *vac*-class verbs (6.1.15).
Regarding *pītvīnam*: there is the substitution of *ī* by the rule *dhumāsthā* (6.4.66), etc.

This is obtained either from the particle *iti* (which has the sense of "beginning with") or from the particle *ca* (which has the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned). Since the purpose would have been accomplished by the inclusion of either one of these two, the inclusion of both is for the sake of stylistic variety (*vaicitrya*).
49. *snātvī* and so forth. (Pāṇini 7.1.49). [Examples:

*snātvī*, *pītvī*. The substitution of *ī* is prescribed in place of the vowel *ā*. Now, one might ask: since words such as *snātvī* are not recited in the list of nominal stems (*prātipadika-gaṇa*), how can they [be formed]?
"How are they to be understood? And how can they be characterized by the word 'ādi' (etc.)? To this he says:
"This word 'ādi' has the sense of 'kind' (prakāra). Those words which are of such a kind—that is, similar to these—are to be understood as *snātvyādayaḥ* (beginning with *snātvi*).
50. *ājjaserasuk* (Pāṇini 7.1.50).

The term *jasi* is a designation used by the ancient grammarians (*pūrvācārya*). Indeed, the ancient grammarians analyzed [the suffix] as *jas-i*. An objection is raised regarding [the verse] beginning with "those who were before, those who were after," and so forth; and this...
When two rules of equal force conflict regarding a word-form that has already arisen— since their purposes are fulfilled elsewhere—
and their mutual obstruction results in the non-application [of both], the rule "in case of conflict, the subsequent operation prevails" (Pāṇini 1.4.2) applies.

Thus it is stated: "In the case of a conflict, the subsequent [rule] prevails; once that has been applied, if the preceding [rule] also applies, that too takes effect"—this is the scope of the understanding of "re-occurrence" (*punar-prasaṅga*) regarding the category (*jāti*) as the referent of a word. The refutation is provided by the phrase "once [the rule has applied]" (*sakṛt*), and so forth. And thus it is explained in the *Vyākhyā*.

Since the purpose of both rules has not been fulfilled with respect to another word-meaning, and since both rules would thus apply alternately to such a subject matter, this restrictive rule is commenced: "In the case of a conflict, the latter [rule] alone takes effect, not the former. By that, moreover—

Because there is no further application of the same logical consequence (*prasaṅga*), that which has been sublated does not come into being again; for when there is no further application of the consequence, that which has been sublated is not capable of arising once more.

51. *aśvakṣīravṛṣalavaṇānāmātmaprītau kyaci* (Pāṇini 7.1.51). Regarding the phrase "in the sense of self-pleasure" (*ātmaprītau*): this is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*). For this very reason, he says: "when *kyac* has self-pleasure as its scope. That *kyac* for which self-pleasure is the scope is described in that way. [The example is: *aśvasyati*.

In the case of *ātmānaśvamicchati* ("he desires a horse for himself"), the suffix *kyac* is applied by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8). Thereafter, by the rule *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97), the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) takes place. It should be understood that the same applies in cases such as *kṣīrasyati*. In all instances, the suffix *kyac* is applied when there is a desire for one's own pleasure. Whoever...

If one desires horses and the like for oneself, one necessarily desires them for the sake of one's own pleasure. If this is so, since the suffix *kyac* is prescribed after a verb when desire is expressed, it will apply everywhere to objects that are sources of one's own pleasure; therefore, is it necessary to state "when desire is expressed"? It is stated "for one's own pleasure" (*ātmaprītau*) in order to include well-known instances.

There is the appropriation of worldly objects; therefore, wherever one is engaged in self-pleasure in this world of the living, it occurs only there and not elsewhere. Consequently, it is logically established that [this applies] to the sexual desire of a horse and a stallion, and to the craving for milk and salt.

Regarding "aśvīyati": the suffix *kyac* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.10, *upamānād ācāre* ("after a word denoting a standard of comparison, [the suffix *kyac* is added] in the sense of behaving like that"), resulting in *aśvam ivācarati* ("he behaves like a horse").
Then, by Pāṇini 7.4.33, *kyaci ca*, the vowel *i* substitution (*itvam*) occurs.
Regarding the rule *aśvavṛṣayoḥ* and so forth: the augment *asuk* is inserted after the words *aśva* and *vṛṣan* when there is a desire for sexual union (*methunecchā*).
The meaning is that this form of the sense must be explained.

[The phrase] "of milk and salt," etc., requires the word "must be stated" (*vaktavyam*). The form of the sense is: "the suffix *asuc* occurs after 'milk' and 'salt' when there is a longing (*lālasā*)."

The meaning is that it must be explained; however, the explanation has already been provided: "Even in the case of one's own pleasure, it does not occur. One who desires a horse for oneself is called *aśvīyati*. [One says] *lavaṇīyati*.
Regarding the phrase "excess of thirst" (*tṛṣṇātarekaḥ*): the excess of thirst is its surplus, its intensity, its pre-eminence.
The meaning is "excess."
52. *āmi sarvanāmnaḥ suṭ* (Pāṇini 7.1.52).
This rule is stated because [the suffix] *nuṭ* would otherwise apply by [the rule] *hrasvanadyāpo nuṭ* (7.1.54).
It is understood that "ām" here refers to the genitive plural (*ṣaṣ�ṭhī-bahuvacana*). In this context, there are many instances of the suffix *ām*.
The forms *sambhavanti* arise from the following: the genitive plural ending [in *ṣaṣṭhībahuvacanam*]; the suffix *ām* prescribed by "ṛnnebhyo ṅīp" (Pāṇini 4.1.5) and "ReĀrāmnadyāmnībhyaḥ" (7.3.116);

the suffix *ām* prescribed by "kimetiṅvyayaghādāmvadravyaprakarṣe" (5.4.11); and the suffix *ām* prescribed by "kāspratyayādāmamantre liṭi" (3.1.35). If there were to be a mention of all of these here, then...

The augment *nuṭ* would apply to all [cases] by the rule "ṭhhrasvanadyāpo nuṭ" (Pāṇini 7.1.54). Even there, this very mention of *ām* continues to apply; since it is desired [only] for the genitive plural, that [genitive plural] alone is taken. Thus he says: "For, because of its posteriority," and so forth. [This concerns] the *suṭ* and the *nuṭ*.

The genitive plural (*ṣaṣṭhībahuvacana*) is the scope [for *āṬ*], whereas for *āṬ* and the others, the singular forms beginning with the dative-arthic case (*caturarthyekavacanādi*) apply; however, because they are subsequent rules, *āṬ* and the others take precedence according to *ReĀrāmnadyāmnībhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.116). In that regard, *āṬ* applies by *āṬṇnadyāḥ* (7.3.112), as in *kumāryām*. Then, *yāṬ* applies by *yāḍāpaḥ* (7.3.113).
The suffix *syāṭ* is applied [in the example] "khaṭvāyām" according to [Pāṇini 7.3.114]: "After a word ending in a short vowel, *syāṭ* is added and the vowel is shortened.

The suffix *syāṭ* is also applied [in the example] "sarvasyām. Why, then, are the *ām* prescribed after a word ending in *gh* and the *ām* of the *liṭ* [perfect tense] not included here? To this he says: "And what about *kim*," etc.

For of those two, one [suffix] is prescribed after a verbal root ending in *gh*, and the other after a verbal root; neither is prescribed after a nominal stem ending in *gh*, nor after a verbal root. Since it is impossible for those two to follow a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), they are not included. However, if it is argued that this [rule] is intended for the sake of cases where [the suffixes] cannot follow a pronoun—

The inclusion of those two [the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu*] is untenable; nevertheless, it is justified for the sake of what follows, since those two indeed exist after the root *hṛ* with the suffix *svānta*—as in *pacatitarām*, *pacatitamām*, *cikīrṣāñcakāra*, and *kārāyāñcakāra*. To this he says: "Or rather, [it refers to that which ends] in a *sānubandhaka*."

"Those two are not included," because of the *niranubandhaka-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding [elements] without an indicatory letter). In that regard, the letter *ū* is the indicatory letter (*anubandha*) for *ghas*, while for the other (*ām*), it is the letter *a*. Thus it has been stated: "The status of *ām* as *am* is due to its ending in *a*."
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of *ṭhutarā*," and so forth: [the rule] "trayaḥ for *tri*" (Pāṇini 7.1.53) is stated so that [the substitution] may occur when *ām* follows.

Why is this not a locative reference (*saptamī-nirdeśa*), meaning "also for the sake of *ām*," so that *suṅ* might occur for a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) when *ām* follows? For there is indeed a purpose here as well. Therefore...

He says: "But in the case of *ṭhiha*," and so forth. According to the principle "when there is a mention of two cases, the mention of the ablative is stronger" (*Śākapārthiva*, 97), by the rule "after that [which is indicated by the ablative]" (*Pāṇini* 1.1.67), the ablative in *sarvanāmnaḥ* supersedes the locative *āmī* and is transformed into a genitive referring to *ām* itself.
Since it must necessarily be *suṭ*, there is no purpose for this specific instruction here.

53. *trestrayaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.53). This is a rule [introduced] because [the suffix *nuṭ*] would otherwise apply by the rule *hrasvanadyāpo nuṭ* (7.1.44). The form is *trayāṇām*; the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *supi ca* (6.4.83). But [one might object]: "Is it not the case that for the three *ṇi*-roots there is guna substitution when *ślau* [applies]?"
Since this is already established by the very rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*) [Pāṇini 7.4.75], for what purpose is this [new rule] commenced?

This being already established, the fact that this [rule] is commenced makes known: "Irregular derivations (*nipātana*) are not subject to sublation" (*abādhakāny api nipātanāni bhavanti*). By this, *purātanam* is established; otherwise, it would not be so.

This is not established because it is set aside by the rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in *purāṇaprokteṣu* (Pāṇini 4.3.105). [The desired form] is intended for all three genders in the Veda; this is obtained either from the governing word *api* (in the rule *trīṇāmapīṣyate cchandasi*), or from the principle that "all rules are optional in the Veda" (*sarve vidhayaśchandasi vikalpyante*).

54. *hrasvanadyāpo nuṭ* (Pāṇini 7.1.54). [The example is] *kumārīṇām*. [The suffix] *ṅīṣ* is applied by [the rule] *vayasi prathame* (4.1.20). [The example is] *gaurīṇām*. [The suffix] *ṅīṣ* is applied by [the rule] *ṣidgaurādibhyaśca* (4.1.41).

Regarding "ṭhśārṅgaravīṇām": the suffix *ṅīn* is applied by the rule "ṭhśārṅgaravādyaño ṅīn" (Pāṇini 4.1.73). Regarding "ṭhlakṣmīṇām": while the rule "avitṛstṛtantribhya īḥ" (Pañcapāda Uṇādi-sūtra 3.158) is in effect, the rule "lakṣermuṭ ca" (Pañcapāda Uṇādi-sūtra 3.160) applies the suffix *ī* along with the augment *muṭ*.

Regarding "brahmabandhūnām": this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those for whom Brahman is the kinsman. The suffix *ūṅ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.66] "ūṅ utaḥ. Regarding "khaṭvānām": the suffix *ṭāp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.4] "ajādyataṣṭāp. Regarding "bahurājānām": the suffix *ḍāp* is optionally applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.13] "ḍāb ubhābhyām anyatarasyām."

Regarding the form *ḍāp*: in the example "kārīṣagandhyānām," [the derivation is as follows]: from *kārīṣagandhi* is formed [the word] by the suffix *aṇ* [meaning "offspring"]. Then, by the rule "aṇiñoḥ anārṣayoḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.78), etc., the substitution of *ṣyaṅ* occurs; and by the rule "ṣyaṅaśca" (Pāṇini 4.1.74), the feminine suffix *cāp* is applied.

55. *ṣaṭcaturbhyaśca* (Pāṇini 7.1.55). Regarding *pañcānām*: the lengthening [of the vowel] is by *nopadhāyāḥ* (6.4.7), and the elision of *n* is by *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* (8.2.7). Regarding *ṣaṇṇām*: [the rule applies to stems ending in] *jhal*.
By the rule *jaśo'nte* (8.2.39), the sibilant *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*;
by the rule *ṭhyaro'nunāsike'nunāsiko vā* (8.4.45), the *ḍ* becomes *ṇ*;
and by the rule *ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ* (8.4.41), the *n* becomes *ṇ*.

"Why is the designation *ṣaṭ* not prescribed for a numeral ending in *r*, as in the rule 'those ending in ṣ and ṇ are six' (Pāṇini 1.1.24)? If that were so, the mention of *catuḥ* here would not be necessary? To this he says: "Of that which ends in *r*, etc. The meaning is already explained. [This is] because of the use of the plural form (*bahuvacana*).
And so forth. For if there were a reference to the word *pradhāna* as the primary element,

then in the case of the interpretation [of the compound] as a mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), one would have made the mention in the dual number as "ṣaṭcaturbhyām," whereas in the case of the interpretation as a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*), one would have used the singular number as "ṣaṭcatuḥ."

However, the instruction was given using the plural number. Therefore, because of that plural indication, there is the inclusion of both the word *ṣaṣ* (six) when it signifies number as the primary meaning, and the word *catur* (four). And this is its purpose: wherever number is predominant, [the suffix occurs] even after a compound ending in those words.

For when the designation is based on the primary meaning, it occurs upon the apprehension of that meaning; and since the status of being subsequent to *ām* is understood through the medium of the word itself from the meaning, the suffix occurs after the simple forms *ṣaṣ* and *catur*, as well as after those ending in them. Even in the case of those ending in them, the status of being subsequent to *ām* indeed exists precisely through the medium of the word.

Regarding the phrase "ṭhupasarjanobhūtāyāstu" and so forth: because of the use of the plural number in the rule, this refers to the meaning of number (*saṃkhyārtha*). That meaning is twofold: primary (*pradhāna*) and non-primary (*apradhāna*). Since grammatical operations apply to the primary element, where number is primary, the operation occurs even from that which ends in such a [number-ending]. Where...
In that case, the number (*saṃkhyā*) does not become a subordinate element (*upasarjana*), as in examples such as *priyaṣaṣām*.
For here, the meaning of the other member of the compound (*anyapadārtha*) is predominant, while the number is subordinate.
In the form *priyapañcānām*, once the elision (*alopa*) has taken place by rule 6.4.134, [the substitution] *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ* applies.
Thus, by this rule, there is the substitution of *ś* for *s*.

56. *śrī-grāmaṇyoś chandasi* (Pāṇini 7.1.56). The genitive case in *śrī-grāmaṇyoḥ* is used in the sense of a relationship (*sambandha-lakṣaṇā*). [The statement] "the rule is for the sake of making it obligatory" applies to the word *śrī*, but not to the word *grāmaṇī*. As for that [word *grāmaṇī*], it is indeed for the purpose of obtaining [the substitution]. For just as...

In the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), when the designation *nadī* applies, the rule *ṭhhrasvanadyāpo nuṭ* (Pāṇini 7.1.54) is established; the same applies in the Vedic language (*chandas*). Therefore, this [sūtra] is for the purpose that [the designation *nadī*] should be constant. For if this [sūtra] were not present, it would apply only when the designation *nadī* occurs, and not otherwise.

"Ṭhyadā sūtāśca" and so forth. By this he demonstrates the following: when the word *sūta* is formed into a *karmadhāraya* compound with the word *grāmaṇī*, then the compound *sūtagrāmaṇī* does not end in a short vowel (*hrasva*), nor does it end in *nadī*, nor does it end in *ā*; consequently, [the rule for the feminine suffix] would not apply, yet it is desired. Therefore...

The statement is made for the purpose that it may be so. When the compound of the words *sūta* and *grāmaṇī* is a dvandva that undergoes singularization (*ekavadbhāvin*) according to the rule "every dvandva optionally becomes singular" (Pāṇini 2.4.2),
then, because it is neuter by the rule "that [dvandva] is neuter" (2.4.17), the short vowel [is applied] in the neuter.

Having applied the shortening [of the final vowel] by the rule *prātipadikasya* (1.2.47) and having formed a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of the many words *sūta* and *grāmaṇī*, the genitive plural is then prescribed.
Since this is already established by virtue of the word ending in a short vowel, there is no purpose for that statement of yours.

57. *goḥ padānte* (Pāṇini 7.1.57). Regarding the phrase "occurring at the end of a verse-quarter (*ṛkpāda*)": since in Vedic usage this can only refer to a quarter of a *ṛc* and not to a quarter of a *śloka*, the term *ṛkpāda* is employed.
58. *idito num dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.58). [Examples:

*kuṇḍitā*, *huṇḍitā*. From the roots *kuḍi* (meaning "to burn," Dhātupāṭha 270) and *huḍi* (meaning "to heap together," Dhātupāṭha 269), the suffix *tṛc* is applied, followed by the augment *iṭ*, according to Pāṇini 7.1.94 (*ṛduśanaspurudaṃso’nehasām*).
By such statements as these, [the suffix] *anaṅ* is excluded.

[The question is asked: "Is this *num* prescribed only in the state of the verbal root's instruction (*dhātūpadeśāvasthā*)? To this he says: "kuṇḍā, huṇaḍā," and so forth. If *num* were to occur once the affix has been produced, then...

At the time of the application of the suffix *ktin*, because [the root] *kuḍi* (meaning 'to be heavy') lacks the letter *ṛ*, there would be only the suffix *ktin* and not the suffix *ac*; yet that [suffix *ac*] is desired. Therefore, it is concluded that for that purpose, the augment *num* occurs precisely at the stage of the instruction of the verbal root (*dhātūpadeśāvasthā*). But how, then, does *num* occur at the stage of the instruction of the verbal root?
"How is it determined that this occurs, given that there is no mention of 'instruction' (*upadeśa*) here? To this he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*), and so forth.

At the time of prescribing the *u*-suffix by the rule *dhinvikṛṇvyora ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.80), the mention of the roots *dhinvi* and *kṛṇvi* is for the purpose of ensuring that they are understood as being accompanied by the augment *num*, so that their state of being accompanied by *num* may be maintained. Thus...
The fact that the augment *num* is applied to the two [roots] *san* and *kṛ* occurs only if *num* is added at the very stage of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*), and not otherwise.

Therefore, from the evidence (*jñāpaka*) of the mention of these two roots as being accompanied by *num*, it is understood that *num* must be added precisely at the stage of the root's original instruction. For this is its purpose: so that it may be understood that *num* is added only at the stage of the original instruction. Indeed, it is not employed for the sake of the *num* itself; rather, its purpose is so that it may be understood that *num* is added only at the stage of the original instruction. It is certainly not employed for the sake of the *num*.

The *num* augment must indeed be applied there; however, by the force of the grammatical definition itself, the rule *dhinvikṛñcyora ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.80) refers only to those forms where *num* is attached. How, then, is this [the form *dhinoti*] an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this meaning? This is not so; for the mention of the vowel *i* in *dhinvikṛñcyora ca* (3.1.80) is not intended as a specific reference, since that [suffix *ṣvul*] occurs only occasionally due to its proximity to the term *bahulam* in *rogākhyāyāṃ ṣvul bahulam* (3.3.108), and not everywhere.

And thus, designations such as *guptijkidbhyaḥ san* (Pāṇini 3.1.5) become logically consistent. Therefore, in the rule *dhinvikṛṇvyoḥ* (3.1.80), this is not a designation by means of the vowel *i*; rather, it is by means of the vowel *i* for the purpose of pronunciation, just as in the designation *indhibhavatibhyām* (1.2.6) there is a designation by means of the vowel *i*. Otherwise, by the rule *aniditām* (6.4.24) and others, there would be the elision of the nasal.
Furthermore, even if there were a designation by the vowel *i* in *dhinvikṛṇvyoḥ* (3.1.80), [the same fault would follow].

Even so, if it were not intended to convey the meaning that *num* occurs only at the stage of the presentation of the verbal roots (*dhātūpadeśāvasthā*), then, for the sake of brevity— since the teaching of augments (*āgamaśāsana*) is characterized by the absence of *ni* and *yat*— he would have made the statement without applying *num*, just as in the rule "ṭhyuvoranākau" (Pāṇini 7.1.1).

In this context, the view that the compound is treated as a singular (dvandvaikavadbhāva) has been stated. Therefore, the mention of the two [roots] accompanied by the *num* augment is itself an indicator (*jñāpaka*), which is also understood from the inclusion of the term "root" (*dhātu*). He says, "And the mention of the root," etc., in order to show that the *num* occurs precisely in the state of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*).

The time when the designation "root" (dhātu-saṃjñā) applies is the time of the instruction of the root; it is for this purpose that the mention of "root" (dhātu-grahaṇa) is made here, namely so that the augment *num* occurs only then. Therefore, from this mention of "root" as well, it is understood that the *num* occurs only during the state of being taught (upadeśāvasthā), and not [at other times].

The intention is that there is no other purpose for the mention of the term *dhātu* (root). [An objection is raised: "But surely, in forms such as *bhetā* and *abhaitsīt*, the mention of *dhātu* must be for the sake of preventing the application of *num* by the rule 'after a root ending in an *it* vowel, before *tās* and *sic*'? To this, he says: "In the case of *tās* and *sic*," and so forth. If...

The operation conditioned by *it* would apply to these two [suffixes] *tāsi* and *sic*. Therefore, nasalization (*anunāsikatva*) would have to be postulated for the vowel *e* (of *te*) so that it could receive the designation *it*;

however, since there is no purpose for this, it is not postulated. Consequently, the vowel *i* in these two suffixes is devoid of nasalization, does not acquire the designation *it*, and exists solely for the sake of pronunciation.

Since there is no possibility at all of the suffix *num* being applied when [the root] is being read (*paṭhyate*), what is the purpose of including the term "dhātu" (root) for the sake of excluding that? But surely it is for the purpose that, in forms such as *āraṃsta*, *amaṃsta*, *manta*, and *saṃganta*,
the elision of the nasal vowel prescribed by the rule *aniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24) does not occur.

Since the operation of having an *it* augment (*idit-kārya*) applies to both *tās* and *sic*, why is it said that "the operation of having an *it* augment does not apply to *tās* and *sic*"? To this he says: "he wished" (*araṃsta*), "he thought" (*amaṃsta*), and so forth; [this refers to the rule] *hanaḥ sic* (Pāṇini 1.2.14).

However, this [specification of *kit*] serves the following purpose: so that the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) may occur in the form *āhata*. If the elision of the nasal were to occur by relying on the status of the suffix as being a *sārvadhātuka* (pertaining to the present stem), then the rule "the *sic* suffix after the root *han*" (*hanaḥ sic*, Pāṇini 1.2.14) would render the designation *kit* redundant.

Is it because there is no purpose [for this]? This is not so; for there is another purpose for the prescription of *kit*—namely, that the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) should occur in the *sic* suffix by means of the rule "anudātopadeśa... (Pāṇini 6.4.37); [and also] by the rule "aniditām... (Pāṇini 6.4.24).

By these words [the author] intends that [the rule] should not apply to a *sij*-ending [verbal base] before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix. But what is the distinction here—whether it be "before a *ṅit* *sārvadhātuka*" or "before a *kit* *sic*"?

This is the distinction: because the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to the same locus (*samānāśraya*), there is elision of the vowel *a* [by P. 6.4.64].

(6.4.48) It does not occur; however, when there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, because that [elision] is not considered *asiddha* due to its being dependent on different factors (*vyāśrayatva*), the elision of the *a* would indeed take place. This is not a valid distinction; for in the rule prescribing the elision of the *a*, such as "anudāttopadeśa" (6.4.37), etc. [the elision is not considered *asiddha*].

The term "instruction" (*upadeśa*) from the preceding sūtra is understood to carry over here; therefore, it is understood that the elision applies to that stem which ends in *a* at the time of its instruction in the verbal root list (*dhātupāṭha*). However, in the case of *āhata*, this [stem] does not end in *i* at the time of its instruction. Consequently, the rule *hanaḥ sic* (Pāṇini 1.2.14) applies.
Thus, by virtue of the rule prescribing the *kit* designation, the elision of the letter *n* does not occur in forms such as *araṃsta*;

in this way, it has been demonstrated that the *sic* suffix does not undergo the operations associated with an *it* marker. Now, it must be shown that for the root *tās* as well, the absence of the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) constitutes an operation associated with an *it* marker.
To demonstrate this, he says "the thinker" (*mantā*), and so forth. The connection with the context is that the elision of the letter *n* does not occur.
An elision of the penultimate (*upadhā*) *n* is prescribed by the rule beginning with *aniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24). However, in the word *maktā*, the letter *n* is not the penultimate.

Because the elision (*ṭilopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the operation of being marked with *i* (*iditkārya*) does not apply even to the root *tās*. Therefore, it is rightly stated: "The operation of being marked with *i* does not exist for *tās* and *sic*. Now, why does the augment *num* not undergo the operation of being marked with *i*? Because it is undesired; for an undesired grammatical operation [is not to be applied].

It is appropriate to assume this in the treatise.
