If, then, the non-nasalized *i* in the root *tās-* is for the sake of pronunciation, then how is it that what was stated regarding *ṣyatāsī lṛluṭoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.33)— namely, "the addition of the marker *it* is for the purpose of preventing the elision of the nasal"— is not contradicted?
Is there a contradiction? It has been stated right there how there is no contradiction.

Now, why does the augment *num* not occur after [roots] such as *bhid*? For in these cases as well, the vowel *i* is indeed designated by the technical term *it*. To this he says: "In the case of *haritām*, etc. For *bhid* and the others have *i* as their final phoneme (*it*).

But it is not understood [that way]; because, according to the vārttika on Pāṇini 1.3.7, "the addition of *ṭi*," the designation *it* applies to the entire group containing the letter *r*, and not to each individual constituent part.
Therefore, since the augment *num* is prescribed for those [vowels] designated as *it*, what possibility is there for it to apply to those [consonants] containing *r*?

It might be argued: "Since the vowel *i* has the designation *it* by the rule 'In the grammatical instruction, an *anunāsika* is *it*' (1.3.2), and the *repha* has the designation *it* by the rule 'The final [sound] of a *hal* is *it*' (1.3.3), therefore they indeed possess the status of being *idits*.
To this he says: "Even of a part," the meaning of which is already explained.
59. *śe* [is substituted] for the roots beginning with *muc*.
(Pāṇini 7.1.59) The roots beginning with *muc* are recited in the *tud*-class, starting from *ṭhmuclṛ mokṣaṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 1430) up until the end of that class.
Regarding the word "moktā": there is the suffix *tṛc*, the prohibition of *iṭ* by [Pāṇini 7.2.10] "ekācaḥ," and the substitution of *k* for *c* by [Pāṇini 8.2.30] "co kuḥ.
As for the question, "Which, then, are the *tṛmphādayaḥ*?"—the intention is as follows: among the *tṛmphādayaḥ* are the *tṛphādayaḥ*.

Even though they are unattached [to other roots], they are recited in the *gaṇa* [of the *tudādigaṇa*], such as "tṛph-tṛnph in the sense of satisfaction" (Dhātupāṭha 1307, 1308). In that case, if those were also included by the mention of *tṛph* and so forth, forms such as *tṛphati* would not be possible; therefore, he says: "those which therein..."

"Those that are recited with their *anuṣaṅga* [nasal augment] are *tṛmphādayaḥ*. This word "ādi" (and so forth) has the sense of "type" (*prakāra*). A "type," moreover, implies similarity. Therefore, the intention is that those which are similar to *tṛmphati* when accompanied by its *anuṣaṅga* are precisely what are indicated by the inclusion of the term "ādi."

Regarding the term "sānuṣaṅgāḥ": the letter *n* is the *anuṣaṅga*; those which exist together with it are "with-anuṣaṅga" (*sānuṣaṅgāḥ*), and it is this very meaning that is indicated by the inclusion of the word "beginning" (*ādi*). In the expression "sānuṣaṅgāḥ," the letter *n* is the *anuṣaṅga*; those which exist together with it are "sānuṅgāḥ. If, then, those...

Those roots beginning with *tṛmph* are recited with their ancillary parts (*sānuvaṅga*). When *num* is applied to them and the subsequent *anusvāra* is made, and that [anusvāra] is then changed to a homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*), one would expect to hear two *n*-sounds.
To this he says: "Of those," and so forth. For when the elision of the *n*-sound has been effected...
The meaning is that since the *num* is prescribed [by this rule], no fault arises at all. Now, one might ask:
"Why is that *num* itself not elided? To this he says, "And that," and so forth. He considers that if even that were elided, the prescription of the *num* would be entirely purposeless.

The purpose of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is to provide an explanation. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the term *dhātoḥ* (from 7.1.58) is understood to carry over; a separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is made by reading *śe*, whereby the augment *num* will apply to *tṛmph* and others. Thus, the mention of *muc* and others would otherwise be redundant.

[Objection: Is this not already established by the rule *śe*? [Response: It is not redundant, because the purpose of *śe* is to indicate that it does not apply to all cases; for in this way, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Why then are *tṛmph* and the others not simply listed among the *muc*-class roots? [Because] those among them which are without the nasal augment (*niranuṣaṅga*)...
This is for the purpose that the augment *num* should not occur when they are being recited.

60. *masjinaśorjhali* (Pāṇini 7.1.60). Regarding the form *mamaṅktā*: the root *ṭumasjo śuddhau* (Dhātupāṭha 1415), with the suffix *tṛc*, the absence of *iṭ* as before, and the change of *s* to *ṣ* (*kutva*). The augment *num* is placed before the final letter *j*. [The rule *skoḥ* applies...]

By [the rule] beginning with (8.2.29), there is the elision of the *sakāra*, followed by the *anusvāra* and its subsequent *parasavarṇa*. Thus, "neṣṭā. When the augment *iṭ* is absent according to (7.2.45), this *num* is applied;
then, by the rule for *vraścādi* (8.2.36), there is the substitution of *ṣ*, and subsequently *ṣṭu* (i.e., *ṣṭutva*). In the case where *iṭ* is present...
Because it does not begin with a *jhal* sound, the augment *num* does not occur—thus we have *naśitā*.

In the forms *majjanam* and *naśanam*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied; then, by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* (Pāṇini 8.4.53), there is the substitution of a *jaś* sound for the *jhal* sounds, whereby the *s* becomes *d*, and through the substitution of a *car* sound, that *d* becomes *j*.

Regarding the rule beginning with "ṭhmasjeḥ": if the augment *num* were to follow the final vowel of the root *masj*, then because the root does not begin with a conjunct consonant (*asaṃyogadit*), the elision of *m* would not apply; and because the *n* would not be penultimate (*anupadhatvāt*), the elision of *n* would also not apply, yet that [elision] is desired. Otherwise, forms such as *magno* and *mānavān* would not be established.

Therefore, the teachers desire that *num* be inserted before the final letter of the root *masj*. But how is this desired meaning obtained? It is obtained from the sign that the rule regarding the prior placement of the shorter word in *naśer alpāctarasya* is not subject to deviation; for that [sign] indicates independence from the general grammatical rule.

By indicating this, he suggests that even the rule "ṭhmidayo'ntyātparaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.1.47) is not required as a defining characteristic here. And since that [rule] is not required, the operation is prescribed only where, by following the requirements of the specific forms (*lakṣya*), the desired result is achieved once the *num* augment has been applied after the root *masj*. Consequently, the *num* is placed before the final letter of *masj*.
It becomes *siddha*. [In the word] *magna*, there is the substitution of *ṇ* for the *ṣṭhā*-suffix by rule 8.2.45: "And after *udita*."

61. *radhijabhor aci* (Pāṇini 7.1.61). Regarding the form *randhayati*: it is derived from the root *radha* (Dhātupāṭha 1193), meaning "to injure" or "to accomplish," with the causative suffix *ṇic*. Regarding *rabdhaka*: it is formed with the suffix *ṇvul*. Regarding *sādhurandhī*: it is formed by the suffix *ṇini* according to the rule *supyajātau ṇinistācchīlye* (Pāṇini 3.2.78).

By [Pāṇini 3.2.78], the suffix *ṇini* is applied. Regarding the form *randhaṃrandham*: by [Pāṇini 3.4.22] *ābhīkṣṇye ṇamul*, and by the Vārttika [887] *ābhīkṣṇye dve bhavataḥ*, there is reduplication. In the phrase *randho vartate*, the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*). Now, in forms such as *randhayati*, because of its higher status... *ata*... [the rule applies].
By the rule *upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116), a *vṛddhi* substitution would apply; why, then, does it not occur? To this he says:

"Even though it [the *num*] is subsequent," and so forth. Furthermore, the *num* is permanent (*nitya*) because it applies whether the *vṛddhi* has already occurred or not; for that [num] occurs even when the *vṛddhi* has been performed.

It is *nitya* because it applies even when [the suffix] *akṛta* has not yet been applied; however, it is *anitya* because once *num* has been applied, the rule no longer applies, as the vowel *a* is no longer penultimate. Regarding the form *hraddhā*: the substitution of *dh* for the *t* occurs by the rule *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.40).
The substitution of a voiced unaspirated stop (jaśtva) for the dental stop *dh* of the root [dhā] results in the letter *d*.

62. *neṭa liṭi rathoḥ* | (7.1.62) A prohibition of the *num* augment, which was previously applicable by the preceding rule, is here stated. [Examples: *raṇitā*, etc. [The suffix] *iṭ* is applied by the rule *radhādibhyaśca* (7.2.45). [Examples: *rarandhiva*, *rarandhima*.
By the rule *krādiniyamādiṭ* (Pāṇini 7.2.13), the augment *iṭ* is applied; and by the rule *parasmaipadānām* (3.4.82) and others, the substitutes *va* and *ma* are applied for *vas* and *mas*.
Now, this root *radh* is recited as not ending in a conjunct consonant (*asaṃyogānta*); in that case, the rule *asaṃyogālliṭ kit* (1.2.5) [would apply].
(1.2.5) Thus, since [the suffix] has the marker *k*, the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) would apply by the rule "ṭhaniditām" (6.4.24).

Why does this not occur? To this he says: "When *num* has been applied," and so forth. It has already been stated that "*num* occurs precisely in the state of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*"); therefore, *num* is applied while still in the state of the original instruction.
Since the state of having a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntatva*) has arisen, the *kit* designation does not apply; therefore, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) does not take place.
[The questioner] asks: "Now, how should it be in the case of the *kvasu* suffix? Does it become *rarādhvān*, or rather *redhivān*? Another says: "*redhivān*. [This refers to the] *liṭ* [affix].

The suffix *kvasu* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.107] *ṭhkvasuśca*; there is reduplication; by [Pāṇini 6.4.120] *ṭhata ekahalmadhye* etc., the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) occur; by [Pāṇini 7.2.67] *ṭhvasvekājādghasām*, the augment *iṭ* and the nasal (*num*) are added; and by [Pāṇini 6.4.10] *ṭhsāntamahataḥ saṃyogasya*, the lengthening of the vowel takes place. How so? [The derivation of *dhukṣāṇaḥ* follows: *duh* + *kvasu* → *dhukṣ-vas* (reduplication) → *dhukṣ-vas* (substitution of *e* and elision of *a*) → *dhukṣ-e-vas* (augment *iṭ*) → *dhukṣ-i-vas* (insertion of *num*) → *dhukṣ-i-n-vas* (lengthening of the penultimate vowel). How is this? [The question is: "How? (i.e., how is the form *dhukṣāṇaḥ* derived?).

And so forth. He thinks as follows: when *eṅ* occurs, there must be *num*; and when *num* exists, there is no state of being "in the middle of one consonant" (*ekahalmadhyatā*). Consequently, after the substitution of *etva* and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*), there must be a restoration (*pratyāpatti*); and thus, once the reduplication has been performed, since it is not a single vowel (*ekāṇ*), the augment *iṭ* does not apply.

It must be so; therefore, it is logical that [the rule] "you should strive" (*raradhvam*) should apply. But the other [proponent] argues that even though *num* has been applied, it must be elided by *atri lopaḥ*, and consequently, the state of being "between two single consonants" (*ekahalmadhyatā*) is not established; how much less, then, could there be the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable?
Regarding "restoration" (*pratyāpatti*), he says: "when the doubling (*dvirvacana*) and the elision (*lopa*) have been performed," and so forth.
For monosyllabic roots (*ekāc*) that have undergone reduplication, the suffix *iṅ* is prescribed for the *kvasu* affix. Then follows the addition of the augment *num*.
Because that [augment] is prescribed before a vowel (*aci*), its elision is based on its being taught as an original element (*aupadeśikatva*).

Thus, because the augment *num* is applied based on the direct instruction (*aupadeśika*), the status of being *kit*—which is merely derived by extension (*ātideśika*)—is impossible once the word ends in a *saṃyoga*.

Regarding the passage beginning with "atha" and so forth: since the rule would already be established by the preceding one when it is stated that "there is no [augment] when *iṭ* follows," [the present rule is formulated].

This will serve as a restrictive rule (niyama): [the augment iṭ] shall apply only after the liṭ [affixes] when followed by an affix beginning with iṭ, and not after any other [affix] beginning with iṭ.
Consequently, it will apply in cases such as *rarandhiva* and *rarandhima*, but not in cases such as *radhita*.
Therefore, why was it not stated simply as "iṭi liṭi" (when iṭ follows liṭ)? If that were so, the desired result would be achieved and the formulation would be more concise.
The meaning is that it becomes a *sūtra*. By saying "only after *liṭ*," he shows the nature of the restrictive rule (*niyama*).

By the phrase "not elsewhere" (*nānyatra*), he also indicates what is excluded by that rule. To show the reason why the restriction is not applied [in other cases], he says "the reverse," and so forth. [That is: "only *iṭ* after *liṭ*."

Thus [ends the section]. This is a statement of the essential nature of the reversed restriction (*viparītaniyama*). By the phrase "not elsewhere" (*nānyatra*), he also demonstrates that which is excluded by it. Why is the reversed restriction not accepted?
To this he says: "For instance," and so forth. [This refers to] the rule "only when there is *liṭ*" (*liṭīva*).

Since the restriction (niyama) excludes the *liṭ* [affix] when it begins with *iṭ*, the [augment] occurs only when the *liṭ* begins with *iṭ*, and not when it does not begin with *iṭ*. Consequently, because [the *liṭ* in *rarandha*] does not begin with *iṭ*, the *num* augment would not apply in *rarandha*; however, in *radhita*, it would indeed apply by the preceding rule, as it is not excluded by the restriction.
Therefore, out of a desire to avoid that fault, no restrictive rule is established.
63. *rabher* in *liṭ* and *luṅ*. (Pāṇini 7.1.63) Regarding the form *ārebhe*: from the root *rabh* (meaning "impetuosity," *rabha rābhasye*, Dhātupāṭha 974), the suffix *liṭ* is applied;
because the root is *anudāteta*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used. By the rule *liṭas tajhayor eś irec* (3.4.81), the substitution of *eś* for the first person singular suffix occurs.
Thus, as before, there is the substitution of *e* for *ai* and the elision of the subsequent vowel.

64. *labheśca* (Pāṇini 7.1.64). [The commentary states: "The separate formulation of this rule is for the sake of what follows; so that by the subsequent sūtra, the grammatical operation may apply only to *labhi*, and not to *rabhi*. For if [the rule] were simply *rabhilabhyoraśaliṭoḥ* as a single [sūtra],"...
If the connection were made [there], then the recurrence of the term "rabhi" would occur in what follows;
and consequently, its application would also necessarily follow in subsequent instances.

65. *āṅe yi* (Pāṇini 7.1.65). Regarding the phrase "in a suffix beginning with *ṭha-yakāra*": by this, [the author] demonstrates that the locative case in *yi* is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*), meaning that even before the suffix beginning with *yakāra* has actually arisen—that is, while it is yet to come into being—[the substitution occurs].
He shows that [the augment] *num* occurs;

by means of the phrase beginning with "prāk" (before), he explains what is intended when the locative case is used in the sense of the object (*viṣaya-saptamī*). For if it were the locative in the sense of proximity (*parasaptamī*), the suffix would have to occur first and *num* afterwards.

Consequently, by the rule *ṭhadupadhāt* (Pāṇini 3.1.98), the suffix *yat* would apply. However, if the locative case [in *ṭhadupadhāt*] is understood as a "locus of occasion" (*viṣayasaptamī*), then because the status of having a vowel other than *a* as the penultimate letter (*adupadhatva*) has been destroyed by the *num* augment produced previously, only the suffix *ṇyat* applies by the rule *ṛhalorṇyat* (Pāṇini 3.1.124). But what, then, is the difference between the suffixes *ṇyat* and *yat*?

Since that same form [of the suffix] exists in both cases, one might argue that even when the suffix *vyat* is applied, the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) should not occur; and as was stated previously—"Even though *vṛddhi* is subsequent, it is superseded by the former because it is permanent. To this, he says "tatra" and so forth. In that case, when *ṇyat* is present...

Because of the svarita accent [of the suffix], the word *alambhya* has its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) according to Pāṇini 6.2.139, *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt*; thus, the example *alambhya* has the svarita on its final syllable. However, if the suffix *yat* were used, then by Pāṇini 6.1.213, *yato 'nāvaḥ*, there would be an acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable.

There is a distinction in that [the word] possesses udātta accent by virtue of its being treated according to its original form (*prakṛtivadbhāva*). Regarding the word *labhyam*: this ends in the suffix *yat*.
The phrase *evam ālabhya* is also [an example]. In *ālabhyate*, the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) denotes either the abstract action (*bhāve*) or the object (*karmaṇi*).
"The elision of the *ṭha*-suffix is performed by [the rule] *ṭhanidatām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24), etc."

66. *Upa* [is used] in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*). Regarding the rule "in the sense of praise": *upalabhya* means "praised"; the meaning is "highly praised. Regarding *upalabhya*: the meaning is "to be attained."
67. *upasargātkhalghañoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.67). In the example *īṣatpralambhaḥ*, the suffix *khal* is applied by [the rule] *īṣadduḥsuṣu* (3.3.126), etc.
In the example *duṣpralambhaḥ*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by [the rule] *idudupadhasya* (8.3.41), etc.

"Ṭhvipralambhaḥ": here the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). Now, one might ask: since the augment *num* is already established by the rule "ṭhlabheśca" (Pāṇini 7.1.64), what is the purpose of this new rule? To this he replies with "siddhe" and so forth. The phrase "it does not occur elsewhere" indicates that which is to be excluded. This [restriction] applies specifically to the suffixes *khal* and *ghañ* after a prefix (*upasarga*).
However, a reversal of this rule is not possible here, because of the grammatical indication in the rule "gṛdhivañcyoḥ pralambhane" (Pāṇini 1.3.69).

68. Not [after] *su* and *duḥ* when they are alone. (Pāṇini 7.1.68). Regarding the term "preceded by a prefix" (*upasṛṣṭasya*), the meaning is "connected with a prefix. As in the example *sulābhaḥ*. Here, the word *su-* has the sense of "excessiveness," not the sense of "without difficulty"; for example, as in *suṣiktam*, what indeed is that? [It means it was poured excessively.]

Regarding the word *durlābha* here: the prefix *dur-* has the sense of censure (*nindā*), not the sense of difficulty (*kṛcchra*), as in the example *durbrahmaṇa*. Therefore, only the suffix *ghañ* occurs, and not *khal*.
[The author of the Vārttika] states: "Considering that *sudurmyām* contains the third case ending, the mention of the word *kevala* is made."

Regarding the rule "ṭhsuduribhyām": when the third case (instrumental) is accepted, the meaning that results is that the augment *num* does not occur for the root *labh* when it is preceded by the prefixes *su-* or *dur-*. Even when separated [by other elements], it is indeed considered "preceded" (*upasṛṣṭa*). In that case, if the term "alone" (*kevala*) were not included, then even in examples such as *supralambhaḥ* and *duṣpralambhaḥ*, [the prohibition would apply].

There would be a prohibition [of the application of the rule]. Therefore, when the third case (tṛtīyā) is accepted, the mention of the word "kevala" (alone) is made. Now, at the point of the question—"Why is the mention of 'kevala' not made when the fifth case (pañcamī) is accepted?"—he says: "For in the fifth case," and so forth. For in this fifth case...

Since the inclusion of the term *nirdiṣṭa* (specified) serves the purpose of indicating immediate succession (*ānantarya*), the prohibition must apply only to what is immediately following; however, in this case, there is an intervention by the word *pra*. Therefore, the contingency (*prasaṅga*) does not arise at all—so what is the use of the inclusion of the word *kevala* (alone)? If this is so, the inclusion of *kevala* should certainly not have been made.

"Shall we accept this fifth [alternative]?"—this is not so. The two counter-examples, "easily obtainable" (*supralambha*) and "difficult to obtain" (*duṣpralambha*), were stated with these two in mind. For in the case of the fifth [alternative], there is no application precisely because of the intervention [of the suffix]. This is the case in *atisulambha*.
When *abhi* is also a prefix (*upasarga*), then, in the absence of the mention of "alone" (*kevala*),

the prohibition would apply [to it as well], because there is no intervention. Therefore, since the mention of "alone" must certainly be made in all cases, and since there is no purpose for transposing the order [of the words], this third interpretation alone is correct.
To state [the objection]:

someone might have the misconception that because the prefix *ati* is used here with the word *su*, the root *labh* is thus compounded with a prefix, there ought to be a prohibition [of the suffix *kha*]; therefore, in order to dispel that...

To refute this, he says: "In the phrase 'atisulabham,' etc. Furthermore, the status of *ati* as a *karmapravacanīya* follows from the rule prescribing that designation: *ati atikramaṇe ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.95). That which has the designation *karmapravacanīya*—

It does not possess the designation of "preverb" (*upasarga*); because of the governing rule regarding "single designations" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), the designation of "preverb" is superseded by the designation of "that which is to be connected with an object" (*karmapravacanīya*). But how, then, can even that [word] which is to be connected with an object have the status of being "isolated" (*kevalatva*)? It is thus:

He thinks: because of the inclusion of the word "kevala" (alone), what is excluded must be something of the same class (*tulyajātīya*) as that which is denoted by its own term, and not something of a different class (*vijātīya*). For instance, [the words] "only" (*kevala*) enter into combination with something of a different class, such as a crab (*karkaṭa*), and so forth. Therefore...

By the phrase "thus, by means of [the two roots] devoid of other prefixes," it is shown that the inclusion of the word *kevala* (alone) serves the purpose of excluding those of the same class (*tulyajātīya*). However, if it were possible to exclude all things of the same class as well as those of a different class (*vijātīya*) by the inclusion of the word *kevala*, [then such would be the case].

In that case, the mention of "upasarga" would be purposeless; one should simply say "by [roots] devoid of anything else. Therefore, exclusion can be effected by the mention of "kevala" (alone), which excludes those of a different class; thus, the mention of "upasarga" would be purposeless, and one should simply say "by [roots] devoid of anything else."

Therefore, since it is very easy to understand that even when those two are accompanied by a word of a different class, they are as if alone, the prohibition applies even when the root *bhū* is preceded by the word *su* accompanied by a *karmapravacanīya*.
However, where the function of the word *ati* is other than in honor or transgression, [the rule does not apply].

If the designation *karmapravacanīya* does not apply, then how [is it to be understood]? To this he says: "But when," and so forth. Even when there is a mention of the fifth case (*pañcamī*), the inclusion of the word "only" (*kevala*) must be made for this very purpose; otherwise, since there would be no intervention here, the prohibition would undesirably apply—this is the intended meaning. Now, one might object:
Is the mention of "only" (*kevala*) to be made for the sake of this very point—that there is no acquisition? This is not so; for it has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "This usage does not exist."

69. *vibhāṣā ciṇṇamuloḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.69). [The example is] *alābhi*. This is the *luṅ* tense; by *ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (3.1.66), the suffix *ciṇ* is applied; and by *ciṇo luk* (6.4.104), there is the elision (*luk*) of the *takāra*.
"Of that which is not preceded by a prefix" means: of that which is not connected with a preposition (*upasarga*).

70. *ugidacāṃ sarvanāmasthāne'ghātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.70). The term *ugit* is a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated designation); those [bases] which have *uk* or *id* are called *ugit*. This is a qualifier of the *aṅga* (stem), and therefore it says: "of *aṅgas* ending in *ugit*. The term *ac* [refers to vowels].

Is this [the mention of *añc*] intended as a reference to a *pratyāhāra*, or rather to the root *añc* with its *n* elided? In that regard, if it were a reference to a *pratyāhāra*, one would not have made a separate mention of *ac* in the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.72); for that [mention of *ac*] is a reference to the *pratyāhāra*, not to the root *añc*.

Because of its association with *jhal* [consonants], one considers that this is the inclusion of the root *añc*, and thus he says "and of *añc*" (*añcateśca*), etc. Regarding "bhavān": the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule "atvasantasya cādhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.14). Regarding "śreyān": from the word *praśasya*.
The suffix *īyasun* is applied by the rule *dvivacanavibhajyopapade tarabīyasunau* (Pāṇini 5.3.57);

the substitution of *śra-* for *praśasya-* occurs by the rule *praśasyasya śraḥ* (5.3.60); there is no elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*) due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *prakṛtyaikāc* (6.4.163); then *ādguṇaḥ* (6.1.87) applies; [and finally] *sāntamahataḥ*...

The long vowel [is applied] by the rule *saṃyogasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.10). Now, one might object: "In this case, is not the *ugit* [element] the stem (*aṅga*), rather than the suffix? This is not so; for the stem itself is indeed *ugit*. How so? Because a relationship of the whole with a part of its own parts certainly exists, as in the expression "Devadatta’s finger."
Just as the finger, which is a part of the hand— a part of Devadatta— is related to Devadatta, so too here, the *it*-named element, which is a part of the suffix,
is indeed related to the *aṅga* (base) as well; thus, the *aṅga* is also one that ends in an *uṅid*.
Regarding the form *prāṅ*: from the root *añc* with the prefix *pra*, the suffix *kvin* is applied by the rule *ṛtvig-ādi-sūtram* (Pāṇini 3.2.59).
Then, by the rules *num-hal-ṅy-ādi* (6.1.68) and *saṃyogānta-lopaḥ* (8.2.23), the final consonant is elided.

By the rule *kvin-pratyayasya kuḥ* (8.2.62), there is the substitution of *ku*—that is, the letter *ṅ*—in place of the letter *n*. Thus we have *prāṅ*; the dual is *prāñcau*, and the plural is *prāñcaḥ*.

Thus [the rule applies]. Regarding the substitution of *ñ* for *n*: the *n* of the root is replaced by *ñ*. Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *añcati*, since the augment *num* is already established for it simply because it is marked with the indicator *g*? To this he says: "The mention of *añcati*, etc. [This refers to the forms] *ukhāsrat* and *parṇadhvat*.
The roots *srans* and *dhvans* are listed in the Dhātupāṭha (754, 755) with the meaning "to fall down" (*adhaḥ-patane*), while *avasraṃsane* is given for *srans* (Dhātupāṭha).
Thus, one says "it falls from the pot" (*ukhāyāṃ sraṃsate*) or "the leaves fall" (*parṇāni dhvaṃsate*). By the rule *kvip ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.76), the suffix *kvip* is applied;
there is the elision of the nasal (*nalopaḥ*), and by the rule *vasusraṃsudhvaṃsvanaḍuhāṃ daḥ* (8.2.72), the *s* is replaced by *d*.
At the end of that [suffix], by Pāṇini 8.4.56 (*ṭhvo'vasāne*), there is the substitution of *c*—namely, the letter *t*.

Regarding the question "Why [the restriction] 'not after a verbal root' (*adhātoḥ*)?", the intention is that it does not apply after a verbal root precisely because the mention of the root *añc-* is for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). This [term] "not after a verbal root" (*adhātoḥ*) is not a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*); what then? [It is a relative negation (*paryudāsa*).]
Thinking that it is a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion), he says: "So that it may apply even to that which was previously not a verbal root (*adhātu-bhūta-pūrva*).

This was raised by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*), who considered this "not a verbal root" (*adhātoḥ*) to be a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (a simple negation). It was refuted by the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntavādin*) through the interpretation as a *paryudāsa*.
Regarding the form *gomatyati*: from the word *gomat*, the suffix *kyac* is added by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8).

Regarding the statement "the suffix *apratyaya*": a suffix that is not heard [in its application] is called *apratyaya*; this, moreover, is the suffix *kvip*. By the rule *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.48), there is lengthening—thus we have *gomān*. Why?
Furthermore, since this [rule] would not be established here if the term "dhātu" (root) were not included, he says: "For here," and so forth.

If the term "dhātu" were not included, then due to the restriction resulting from the inclusion of the root *añc*, just as [the suffix] does not apply in cases such as *ukhāsrat* and the like, it would likewise not apply here either. For this too is indeed a root—even though its status as a root [is otherwise questioned].

Because, when it ends in *kvip*, [it is held that] "those ending in *kvip* do not lose their status as verbal roots" (*vya.pa.* 132). Therefore, the mention of "non-root" (*adhātu*) is made so that there may be the inclusion of even that which was previously a non-root in another state. Now, how is there lengthening (*dīrghatva*) here in the case of *gomān*, and why is it not [lengthened]?
Could it be so? [The answer is: The prohibition "not after a verbal root" (adhātoḥ) applies, but not to that which ends in /ā/. For here, what is the purpose of "not after a verbal root"?

[The purpose is shown by] the counter-examples *piṇḍagraḥ* ("one who swallows a lump") from *piṇḍaṃ grasate*, and *carmavaḥ* ("one who wears leather") from *carma vaste*; these are presented as counter-examples for that which ends in /as/, not for that which ends in /ā/. Or rather, the letter /c/ is present there.
It is employed, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned; by means of that, in certain instances, *ayī* will occur after a verbal root.
71. *yujerasamāse* (Pāṇini 7.1.71).
[The forms] *yuṅ*, *yuñjau*, and *yuñjaḥ* are derived as before by means of the *kvip* suffix and others.
[The form] *aśvayuk* is derived from *aśvaṃ yunakti* ("he yokes the horse") by means of the rule *satsūdviṣa-* (Pāṇini 3.2.61), etc.
[The suffix] *kvip*. How [is it that] when *nudi* is prescribed after the root *yuj*, it would also apply in a compound?

By means of the rule of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*). How is there an extension to what ends with that here? This very [fact] is the indicator—that there is indeed an extension to what ends with that in this context. And it has been said: "In the section concerning *aṅga*, [the rule applies] to that [root] and to its subsequent member."

Because of the statement [in the *Pāṇinīyadhātuvṛtti*], 85: "From the root *yuj*" and so forth. The mention by means of the letter *i* is made for this purpose: that there may be the inclusion of that *yuj* which has *i* as its *anubandha*, and not of any other.

Therefore, there is no inclusion of the root *yuj* (from Dhātupāṭha 1177), for that root does not have the letter *i* as its *anubandha*. [The form] *yujām* is derived by adding the suffix *kvip* because it belongs to the *sampadādi* group.
[The word] *āpannāḥ* means "attained."

72. *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.72). [Examples: *paryāṃsi*, *śreyāṃsi*. The lengthening [of the vowel] is by [the rule] *sāntamahataḥ saṃyogasya* (6.4.10). [Examples: *bahupuri*, *bahudhuri*. [These mean] many cities (*bahvyaḥ puraḥ*) and many yokes (*bahvyo dhuraḥ*).

The term *yeṣām* is a bahuvrīhi compound. The suffix *a*, which would otherwise be applied by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūpathām ānakṣe* (Pāṇini 5.4.74), does not occur here because it is held that "the application of compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) is not universal" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 94). [Thus we have] *vimaladivi*: those for whom the sky (*dyauḥ*) is pure; these are the *vimaladivi*.
The letter *va* is dental-labial; *jhal* does not apply here because *jhal* was recited previously [in the rule for *catur*].

Regarding "four" (*catvāri*): the suffix *ām* is applied by the rule *caturanaḍuhorām udāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.98). Here, since the neuter form ending in *uk* is one that ends in *jhal*, when *num* is added, the rule *ugidacām* (Pāṇini 7.1.70) applies.

By such [rules] as these, a second *num* would be obtained; for it is possible for one thing to be "subsequent" (*para*) at the time of the rule's application, as in the case of *pacati*, where both the *lakāra* and the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) follow from a single root. This applies here in forms such as *tudanti* and *nadanti*.

If *num* were applied to *para-sa* and then *para-savarṇa* were applied to *ta-sa*, would there not result the hearing of two *n* sounds? Let it be so; for regarding the hearing of one or many consonants following a *hal*, no distinction can be asserted. But here there is a distinction—namely, in forms such as *kurvanti*.

In the word *kṛṣanti*, when the *num* augment of the following [stem] has been replaced by an *anusvāra* or a homogeneous letter (*savarṇa*), the preceding [consonant] is not followed by a *jhal* sound; therefore, the *anusvāra* and the subsequent *parasavarṇa* do not apply, and by rule 8.4.2 (*aṭ-ku-pvāṅ-num-vyavāye'pi*), the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* would result. However, in the case where there is only one *num*, after its *anusvāra* has been replaced by a *parasavarṇa*...

When [the substitution] is performed, there is no possibility of the application of *ṇatva* (nasalization), because the *parasavarṇa* (substitution of a homogeneous letter) is considered asiddha (non-existent for the purposes of the preceding rule).
Therefore, he says—"of that which ends in a consonant (*jhal*) following an *ugit*"—in order to state a prohibition against the *num* suffix characterized by the *ugit* [condition].
This provides an occasion (*avakāśa*) for the *num* suffix characterized by ending in a *jhal*.
Regarding the neuter form *sarpīṣi*:

the scope of the rule characterized by *ugit* (Pāṇini 7.1.70) is when it is an *ugit* stem that is not neuter, such as *gomān* and *yavamān*; whereas the scope of the rule for *ugit* stems ending in a consonant (*jhal*) when they are neuter is when both rules would apply, in which case, by virtue of its posteriority, this very *num* suffix is applied.

It must be so; when that [num] exists, the *num* characterized by having *u* as its *it* does not occur again—on the principle that "in a conflict where a rule has been applied once, what is sublated remains sublated" (Vārttika 40). Thus, from the word *bahu*, the suffix *īyasun* is added to form *bhūyāṃsi*.

By the rule "bahorlopo bhū ca bahoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.158), there is elision of the vowel *i* and the substitution of *bhū* for *bahu*. Thus we have "kurvanti" and "kṛṣanti. From the present participle ending in *śatṛ*, the substitution of *śi* occurs by the rule "jaśśasoḥ śiḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.20).

Regarding the phrase "bahurji" and so forth: the prohibition of *nuṭ* must be stated—that is, explained—with respect to this word *bahūrj*. This is the explanation: the term *vibhāṣā* from [Pāṇini 7.1.69] "vibhāṣā ciṇṇamuloḥ" is understood here, and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*); therefore...
The suffix does not occur here in *bahūrji*. From the root *urj*—meaning "to possess strength" or "to sustain life" (*dhā.pā.* 1549; variant:
"to possess strength and vitality")—the suffix *kvip* is applied according to *Pāṇini* 3.2.177 (*bhrājabhrāsa-* etc.).
Thus, *bahūrji* refers to those who possess many (*bahavaḥ*) strengths (*ūrjaḥ*) or powers (*balāni*).

Regarding the phrase "brāhmaṇakulāni | ṭhantyātpūrvam": some authorities desire the augment *num* before the final letter; the final letter here is *j*, and they desire *num* before that—as in *bahūrñji*.

73. *iko'ci vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.1.73). Because of the mention of "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*), the term "in a sarvanāmasthāna [ending]" (*sarvanāmasthāne*) from the previous rule (7.1.70) is no longer applicable. [The question] "Why 'before a vowel' (*aci*)? is asked as follows: one considers cases such as *trapubhyām* and *trapubhiḥ*.
The inclusion of the letter *a* [in the rule] is performed so that [the augment *num*] might not occur at the beginning of an affix (*vyañjana*);

however, this is purposeless. Let there be *num* after *ann*, and its elision will occur by the rule "there is elision of the final of a nominal stem" (*nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*, 8.2.7). The other [teacher], having understood this intention—

He said: "For the sake of the subsequent rule. [The mention of] *aj* is for the purpose that [the substitution of] *an* should apply when a vowel-initial suffix follows—as in the rule *asthidadhisakthyakṣṇāmanaṅ udāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.75)—but should not apply here, as in *asthibhyām* and *asthibhiḥ*. Thus, I have asked about the purpose of this *aj* in the present context.
Thinking, "In that case, let that very thing be stated," he says: "If it were so," and so forth.

The other, having understood the intention, says: "But here, regarding the instrument," and so forth. If the rule "yadi acī" (if [the following vowel] is not a vowel) were not stated, then the augment *num* would also occur here after the word *trapu* in the nominative singular used as a vocative.
It might be argued: "In that case, the word 'ac' is stated here so that the augment *num* does not occur.

This might be so—let the *num* indeed occur; however, once the elision of the nominative suffix *su* has taken place by the rule "svamornapuṃsakāt" (7.1.23), the elision of the final *n* would apply by the rule "nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya" (8.2.7).
"Will there not be elision of the *n*? To this he says: "Not before *ṅsi* or the vocative," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "But surely... and so on: here the particle *eva* is out of its natural order and should be understood immediately after the negation (*na*).

And that [negation] applies even to the existence of the case-ending in a figurative sense, by virtue of the rule "When *lumat* [an elision marker] is present, [the operation] does not apply to the *aṅga*" (Pāṇini 1.1.63).

By means of negation, he establishes that [the case-ending] does not exist. For the existence of a case-ending is of two kinds: primary (mukhya) and figurative (aupacārika). Among these, the primary belongs to a case-ending that is actually heard, whereas the other belongs even to one that has been elided.
Because the effect exists, the existence of its [causal] distinction is also stated figuratively; for example, it is said that "past karma exists.
In that case, because the capacity to yield a fruit—which was deposited by the past karma—exists, that karma is said to exist. This is the principle here.

Since the case-ending is elided by the rule *ṭhsvamornapuṃsakāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.23), primary existence (*mukhyam astitvam*) does not exist. Furthermore, because of the prohibition against treating the stem as if it were followed by a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) by the rule *na lumatāṅgasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.63), even metaphorical existence (*aupacārikam*) does not exist at all. In that case:

When the augment *num* is being prescribed in reference to a case-ending (*vibhakti*), what possibility is there for it to apply in *he trapo*, where a case-ending is entirely absent? It simply does not apply there; therefore, this is not the purpose of the mention of the vowel (*ac*) in the rule. [The phrase] "this very [point]" and so forth: for if, in this case, there were a prohibition against the application of the rule based on the elision of an affix (*pratyayalopalakṣaṇa-pratiṣedha*), [then the *num* would indeed apply].

It might be argued that the mention of *aj* (the vowel) would be purposeless; why? Because this very mention of *aj* indicates that, in this context, the prohibition regarding the application of grammatical operations based on the disappearance of an affix (*pratyayalopalakṣaṇa*) does not apply when a neuter noun ending in *i* or *u* is in the vocative case. This is shown by the phrase "And thus," etc., which demonstrates the nature of the indicator (*jñāpaka*).

He states the purpose: when the rule *sambuddhau ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.106) is in effect, that *guṇa* substitution which occurs by the rule *hrasvasya guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.108) should be understood [to apply here]. For example:
*taumburavaṃ cūrṇam*. [The word] *taumburavam* is the modification (*vikāra*) of *tumbaru*, [formed] with the suffix *āṬrañ*.
In some places, the following two verses are recited: "iko 'ci vyañjane mā bhūvastu lopaḥ svaraḥ katham," etc. Regarding the rule "iko 'ci vibhaktau" (7.1.73), the word *aci* [is used].

For what purpose is this stated? Why not simply say "ṭh-iko vibhaktau" (ṭh is substituted for iK before a case-ending)? He states the purpose: "lest it [the substitution] occur before a consonant. This is understood from the context to mean that *anum* is intended. The mention of *aC* (vowel) is for the sake of ensuring that [the substitution] does not occur before a consonant in forms such as *trapubhyām* and *trapubhiḥ*.

[It] is done. If that is so, there is no purpose for it [the *num*]; let the *num* apply to the consonant-initial [forms], yet its audible pronunciation does not follow as a consequence, because the elision of the *n* will occur by the rule "there is elision of the *n* at the end of a nominal stem" (*nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*, 8.2.7). But how is the accent [determined] in forms such as *pañcatrapubhyām* and *pañcatrapubhiḥ*?

In the expression *pañcabhis trapubhiḥ krītābhyām* or *krītaiḥ*, there is a compound (*samāsa*) in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), according to Pāṇini 2.1.51: *taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca*. Thereafter, by 2.1.52: *saṃkhyāpūrvo dviguḥ*, it receives the technical designation of *dvigu*. Then, by 5.1.19: *ārhādagopucchasaṃkhyāparimāṇāṭ ṭhak*, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied, and of that...

By the rule *adhyardhapūrvadvigor lug asaṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 5.1.28), there is elision (*luk*); then, from the case-ending (*vibhakti*), the augment *num* is added, followed by the elision of the letter *n*. This [elision of *n*] is not considered non-existent (*asiddha*) for the purposes of the elision of *su*, the designation of the accent (*svarita*), and the application of *tuka*, according to the rule *nalopaḥ supsvara-saṃjñātugvidhiṣu kṛti* (Pāṇini 8.2.2).

By the rule *dvigau* (Pāṇini 6.2.29), the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member does not apply to words such as *ṭhiga*, *anta*, *kāla*, *kapāla*, *bhagāla*, and *śarāva*; because they do not end in a long vowel (*anigantatvāt*), the initial acute accent (*ādyaudātatva*) would instead apply by the rule *bhraḥ saṃkhyāyāḥ* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.28). Thus, the word *bhraḥ* [is cited].
Regarding the statement "the inclusion of those ending in *n* and *r*," [it refers to] rules such as *kharaḥ ṣai*.

The word *vai* is used in the sense of intolerance. In the case of *pañcatrapuṇaḥ*, the accent occurs while the *num* suffix is still audible. [The objection is: "What will not happen when it has been elided? The meaning is: it will certainly occur. Why?

Furthermore, why does the accent occur when the *num* suffix is being heard? Because, in a rule prescribing accent (*svaravidhi*), a consonant is treated as if it were non-existent. Alternatively, this *num* is subordinate to the whole word;
it is not capable of destroying the status of the constituent element *trapu* as ending in an *īk* vowel (*iganta*).
In this case, then, when two Brahmin families have surpassed wealth (*rāyam atikrāntābhyām brāhmaṇakulābhyām*),

after the compound has been formed by *kugatiprādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18) as *atirābhyām*, and after the shortening of the stem in the neuter has been applied by *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.47), if the suffix *num* were to occur before a consonant-initial [ending].

If that were the case, then when that [num] is elided, because the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), the substitution of *ā* prescribed by the rule "rāyo hali" (Pāṇini 7.2.85)— which applies before an initial consonant (*halādi*)— would not occur, because of the intervention of *num*. However, since this [num] belongs to the whole, it cannot intervene between the whole and its constituent.
But it certainly intervenes as a constituent part (*avayava*). Likewise,
in the case of the *bahuvrīhi* compound *priyāstisro'nayor brāhmaṇakulayoḥ*, resulting in *priyatisṛbhyām*— if the augment *num* were to occur before a consonant-initial [suffix], then...

One might ask: does the substitution *tisṛ* not fail to apply by the rule "ṭhtricaturoḥ striyāṃ tisṛcatasṛ" (Pāṇini 7.2.99), because the word *tri* is separated [from the case-ending] by the *num* augment which belongs to the entire stem? This is not so;
for there is both the state of being *rāy* and the state of being *tisṛ*.
"Even when there is an intervention, *num* [occurs]," so it is said; the word "it occurs" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

In the phrase "due to intervention" (*vyavadhānāt*), the ablative case is used with the elision of the suffix *-lyap*, as in "he looks from the palace" (*prāsādāt prekṣate*), which means "having ascended the palace. Thus, the meaning is this: even having reached an intervention by way of *num*, [the suffix] *rāy*...

[The substitution of] *āt* and the state of being *tisṛ* occur [respectively]. But why do these two occur when there is restriction (*avadhāna*)? Because in the rule "rāyo hali" (Pāṇini 7.2.85), the phrase "in that which is prescribed for *rāi*" refers to the case-ending prescribed after *rāi*, as well as the case-ending prescribed after the word *tri*;
this is according to the view that the term "prescribed" (*vihita*) functions as a qualifier of the [suffix].
Because it takes recourse to that [rule]. Or alternatively—what is the need for considering an intervention?

For those two [suffixes] will indeed occur simply because they are subsequent; however, once those two have been applied, according to the principle "when there is a conflict between two rules both of which apply simultaneously, that which is sublated remains sublated" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 40), the *num* augment does not occur again.
It has been stated that "even *num* [occurs] because of the intervention [of the vowel], provided that the status of being a subsequent element (*paratva*) is not accepted.

For this very reason, the word *api* is employed to indicate an alternative view. And as to how it occurs despite the intervention, that has already been explained. If that is so, then the mention of *ac* is for the purpose of establishing a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between *num* and *nuṭ*; thus, regarding *nuṭ*:

When *num* is applied, [the addition of] *nuṭ* is not performed. The scope for the rule "ṭhhrasvanadyāpo nuṭ" (Pāṇini 7.1.54)—which yields forms such as *agnīnām* and *vāyūnām*—is distinct from the scope for *num* after stems ending in *ik*, which yields forms such as *trapuṇe* and *jatune*.
However, in cases such as *trapūṇām* and *jatūnām*, both rules would apply simultaneously.

According to the principle of "prior prohibition" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the augment *nuṭ* occurs; and when *nuṭ* is present, lengthening by rule 6.4.3 (*nāmi*) would apply, whereas under this [present rule], it would not occur because the stem does not end in a vowel (*anajanta*), as in the case of *varmaṇām*. Furthermore, this prior prohibition is only possible if there is the mention of the vowel (*ajgrahaṇa*).

When *nuṭ* has been applied, *num* does not apply because [the stem] does not begin with a vowel (*an-aj-ādi*). When *num* has also been applied, *nuṭ* still does not apply because there is no short vowel at the end. Thus, since both [rules] are equally applicable, a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is justified. If the mention of "vowel" (*aj-grahaṇa*) were not made, then even when *nuṭ* has been applied—or even when it has not—[the rule for *num* would apply] whether the following element begins with a consonant (*hal-ādi*) or a vowel (*aj-ādi*).

Since the augment *num* must necessarily occur, it is permanent (*nitya*). Once *num* has been applied, because the word no longer ends in a short vowel, the augment *nuṭ* cannot occur; thus, it is non-permanent (*anitya*).
And since that which is permanent and that which is non-permanent do not possess equal force, a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between them is improper.

"Because it is eternal (*nitya*), there ought to be only the augment *num*; therefore, the mention of *ac* is for the purpose of [establishing] a prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*). To this, he states another solution: "The augment *nuṭ* should be prescribed. This is for the sake of brevity; its purpose is the *nuṭ* augment.

This is a case of *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (priority of application). It has been stated that [the augment] *nuṭ* occurs because it serves that purpose (*tādārthya*). Even if the mention of *ac* were made, by virtue of the *vipratiṣedha*, only *num* would apply; therefore, one must necessarily state that *nuṭ* applies by way of *pūrvavipratiṣedha*:
"The augment *nuṭ* takes precedence over *num*, *aci-ra*, and the substitution of *ṛju*."

"By the rule of prior prohibition" (Vārttika 11 on Pāṇini 7.1.96). Even if the mention of *ac* (*ajgrahaṇa*) were made, a prior prohibition would still have to be stated. If that [mention of *ac*] were not made, then by that very effort [of the prior prohibition], *nuṭ* will occur;
so what is the use of two efforts? Therefore, is the mention of *ac* useless? But surely—
The word *para* signifies "desired" (*iṣṭa*), and since it will signify what is desired, there is no need for effort [to explain it].
This is incorrect; one must necessarily enumerate a prior exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), otherwise it would not even be known which of these is desired and which is undesired. But surely—

In the case of *trapūṇām*, should the mention of *ac* be made for the purpose that, once *nuṭ* has been applied by the rule of prior exclusion (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), *num* should not occur? This is not necessary; let *num* occur here, and its elision will take place. Because the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the prescription of lengthening (*dīrghavidhi*), [the rule] *nāmi* (Pāṇini 6.4.3) applies.
If it is argued that, because [the stem] does not end in a vowel other than *a*, this [rule for lengthening] would not apply, let it not apply by this rule;
it will apply by the rule "nopadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.7). But then, in the case of *śucīnām*, would there not be no lengthening due to the restriction "inhanpūṣāryamṇāṃ śau" (Pāṇini 6.4.12)?

This is not so; by the paribhāṣā "lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā" (Vār. 3 on Pāṇini 1.1.56), the rule applies only to that form ending in *in* which is explicitly taught (*pratipadokta*) as such, and not to one that becomes so through a grammatical operation (*lākṣaṇika*). Since this [form] becomes *innanta* only after the augment *num* has been applied, it is *lākṣaṇika*; therefore, its exclusion will be established by the aforementioned restriction. Thus...

Since the mention of *aj* has been rejected, he says "but for the sake of what follows" (*utarārtham tu*) in order to demonstrate the purpose of mentioning *aj* in the subsequent rules. The word *tu* (but) is used here in the sense of *tarhi* (then/in that case). The word *tarhi* introduces an alternative position: if this [present] purpose is not tenable, then it must be for the sake of what follows.
"In that case, the mention of 'a' (in the rule) should be made.
But what is the purpose of its inclusion here? To this he says: "In this [case]," and so forth.
The word "api" (also/even) is not employed here because its meaning is already implied. There is indeed a purpose here as well; what is it?
What then is that [purpose]? He says: "for the sake of *he trapo*.

The mention of *ac* (the vowel) is for the purpose of establishing the correctness of this example, "O pot" (*he trapo*). For if the mention of *ac* were not made, it would not be made known that the rule regarding the substitution caused by the elision of an affix (*pratyayalopalakṣaṇa*) applies here; since, in the case of "O pot" (*he trapo*), [the shortening of the final vowel] occurs.

If [the rule] were stated as *lupatāyām*, the quality (*guṇa*) being prescribed would not apply; however, when *ac* is included in the rule, even here the substitution is governed by the principle of the elision of an affix (*pratyayalopalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, the inclusion of *ac* must be made for this purpose and for the sake of subsequent rules as well.

74. *Tṛtīyādiṣu bhāṣitapuṃskaṃ puṃvad gālavasya* (Pāṇini 7.1.74). [The phrase] "the neuter ending in *ṭhik*" [is understood]. The term "of the neuter" (*napuṃsakasya*) and "the suffix *ik*" (*ikaḥ*) are supplied from the preceding context. Although that [term "neuter"] is established as being in the genitive case, nevertheless, for the sake of this present rule, there occurs a change of case-ending [to the nominative].

It becomes [ending] in the nominative case. To clarify the meaning of "it becomes like the masculine" (*pumbhavati*), he says "just as" (*yathā*) and so forth. But how can a transfer of prohibition (*pratiṣedhātideśa*) be expressed by the statement "it becomes like the masculine"? He thinks as follows: in the masculine...

In the case of [stems] beginning with *ajādi* starting from the third case onwards, no grammatical operation (*kārya*) is prescribed that could be extended by analogy to the neuter. Therefore, since an operation dependent on the neuter does not exist for the masculine, this must be understood as an extension of a prohibition (*pratiṣedhātideśa*). Even so, it would apply only to *num*.

There would be an extension of the absence of the original element (*prakṛta*) to one alternative case, namely the short vowel; since that [long vowel] is not the original element, there would consequently follow—based on the short vowel—the occurrence of *guṇa*, the absence of *guṇa*, *nuṭ*, and *autva* (the substitution of *au* for the dative ending): specifically, *autva* by the rule "gher ṅiti" (Pāṇini 7.3.111), as in *grāmaṇyām*.

Regarding the phrase "in the *brāhmaṇa* family": this is not the case; for if there were merely an extension (*atideśa*) of the absence of the *num* augment, the extension itself would be purposeless. It would have sufficed to simply prohibit the *num* augment according to the opinion of Gālava. Therefore, by the very force of the extension, the absence of the short vowel (*hrasva*) is also extended.

"Grāmaṇīr brāhmaṇaḥ" (the village headman who is a Brahmin) and "grāmāṇi brāhmaṇakulam" (the family of the Brahmin village headman)—this was stated for the purpose of showing that [the word] has been previously used in the masculine gender, but it is not an actual example [of the rule]. The following is the example here: "grāmaṇyā brāhmaṇakulena" (by the family of the Brahmin village headman). Here, by virtue of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like substitution)...
The vowel does not become short, nor does the augment *num* apply. By the rule *ṭheranekācaḥ* (6.4.82), shortening would occur;

by the rule *āṅe nā'striyām* (7.3.120), the substitution of *nā* would occur. In the form *grāmaṇīnām*, once the augment *nuṭ* has been applied by way of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), lengthening occurs by the rule *nāmi* (6.4.3).

The third-case singular form of the word *śuci* has not been cited [as an example], because there is no difference [in the result]. Whether or not the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) occurs, the substitution of *nā* must take place by the rule "āṅe nā'striyām" (Pāṇini 7.3.120). Thus, we have *śucaye*. In the case where the masculine form is applied, the *num* augment does not occur.

The *guṇa* substitution [of *o* for *av*] occurs by the rule *ṭhgherṅiti* (Pāṇini 7.3.111). In the form *śucinai*, the *num* augment appears in the alternative where *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine treatment) does not apply.
In the phrase *grāmaṇinī brāhmaṇakule*, both the short vowel (*hrasva*) and the *num* augment appear because *puṃvadbhāva* does not apply here.

[The examples] "bhavataḥ" [and] "trapuṇe, jatune": since these two are always neuter, they lack the quality of having been previously used in the masculine (bhāṣitapuṃskatva). Consequently, because there is no absence of the *puṃvat* treatment here, the *num* augment indeed occurs.
[The question] "Why does it not occur here? [refers to the fact that] the word *bhāṣitapuṃska* is a bahuvrīhi compound.

The word *śabda* is the referent of the other member of the compound. This word *pīlu*, having denoted a male tree, when the intention is to express "the fruit which is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *pīlu*," the suffix *añ* prescribed by the rule *ṭhorañ* (Pāṇini 4.2.71) undergoes elision (*luk*) by the rule *phale luk* (Pāṇini 4.3.163); at that time—

The question arises from the thought that since [the word] occurs in the neuter gender as its fruit (*phala*), it is one whose masculine form has been previously stated (*bhāṣitapuṃska*); yet no specific distinction is mentioned here, and therefore, one might think that the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) must necessarily apply here. [The answer is: "In the same class-form (*ākṛti*). This is the meaning of that very [sūtra].

To clarify this, he says: "when the cause for application is the same. Here, the phrase "the masculine form is prescribed for that" is to be supplied. *Ākṛti* is that by which [things] are formed (*ākriyante*), derived, or delimited; it refers to the form of a word.
In this context, "form" (ākṛti) is intended as the cause for application, not the specific designation, nor merely the genus.

Since that cause for application is common [to both], the substitution of the masculine form is prescribed for that which has been used in the masculine. And thus it applies to the words *grāmaṇī* and *śaci*.

In a compound, the substitution of the masculine form (puṃvadbhāva) is illustrated when the basis for the application of a word (pravṛttinimitta) is identical; for example, the word *grāmaṇī*, whether functioning as masculine or neuter, has "the act of leading a village" as its common basis for application (*samānākṛti pravṛttinimitta*). Likewise, for the word *śuci*, the quality of purity (*śucitva*) is the basis for its application.
In that case, one might ask: "Is the form (ākṛti) here also the same? To this he says, "But here," and so forth.

The word "but" (tu) shows the distinction from words such as *grāmaṇī*. By this, he demonstrates that the word *pīlu* possesses the quality of having been previously mentioned as masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃskatva*) when its form is different.

The form "vṛkṣākṛtiḥ" means the genus of trees; "phalākṛtiḥ" means the genus of fruits. Thus, when the form is the same, the masculine gender is prescribed for that word which has been used in the masculine.
However, since the word *pīlu* is not used in the masculine when the form is the same, it does not undergo that [masculine] transformation.
The masculine form [is applied]. Regarding the passage beginning with "This very thing is thus," etc.:
as for what was stated—namely, "In this commonality of form," etc.—how can this nature of the object be of such a kind? The meaning is: it cannot be so in any way.
The intention is that because no specific distinction is mentioned in the rule "when the form is the same" (*samānāyām ākṛtau*), [the desired result] does not follow.
By the phrase "because of the mention of *bhāṣitapuṃska*," etc., he demonstrates how this very [result] is achieved.
For if another word-meaning (*anyapadārtha*) were relied upon as the referent of the term, this would not be possible; nor is there [such a thing] here.

The word [in the rule] is not intended as the meaning of another word (anyapadārtha); rather, it refers to the *artha* (referent). Furthermore, not every referent is meant, but rather—due to proximity—that very thing which serves as the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of a particular word is understood.
It is precisely that which is called "a word whose masculine form has been uttered" (*bhāṣitapuṃska*). Otherwise, indeed, every referent would [be so designated].

It is "having a masculine counterpart" (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), because even by means of the word *artha* alone, the possibility of having a masculine counterpart exists. In that case, if whatever [word] has a masculine counterpart by means of any word whatsoever were to be accepted here, then the mention of *bhāṣitapuṃska* would be purposeless.

It would be so; [but it is not], because there is no [gender] to be excluded. Therefore, that very word denoting a neuter which is intended here to undergo the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment) must have its own basis of application (*pravṛttinimitta*) expressed as masculine;
it is such a word, having its masculine form expressed, that is understood here by the term *bhāṣitapuṃska*. [This is established] "by connection with that" (*tadyogāt*).

And so forth. Because of its connection—that is, its relation—to that meaning characterized as the cause for the application [of the masculine gender], even that neuter denoted object is called "bhāṣitapuṃska" (having a stated masculine).
For a thing receives a designation based on that [connection], just as in the expression, "Bring in the staff-bearers. This is the connection.

Furthermore, in this context, [the relationship] is characterized by inherence (*samavāya*) and the inherent (*samavāyin*); for there is an inherence of the meaning that serves as the ground for the application of the word with a neuter [form]. Regarding the phrase "that which belongs to it" (*yat tasya*), etc.: even that verbal form which expresses that neuter [meaning] is [governed] by a neuter [word] whose masculine counterpart has been mentioned (*bhāṣitapuṃskena*).

It is called "having a previously mentioned masculine" (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) by virtue of its connection (*yoga*). This connection, moreover, is the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) between these two. In that regard, although the meaning (*artha*) is included by the term *bhāṣitapuṃska* in the rule (*sūtra*), nevertheless, because an operation cannot take place upon a meaning, it is [applied] according to what has been stated.

This rule of *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment) is prescribed for that very word which has already been used in the masculine in some respect; and thus, being so prescribed, it is understood by implication to apply to that word which has been used in the masculine within the same class (*ākṛti*). For indeed, one who is thus...
It denotes the neuter gender as necessarily connected with the cause for the application of a word that has been used in the masculine;
provided that [the word] is used in the masculine when the form is identical. For example, the word *grāmaṇī* and the word *śuci*. Where the word *pīlu* has been used in the masculine—

In the form of a tree, which is the cause for the application [of the word], that word does not denote something connected with that [tree-form] as a neuter; rather, it denotes a connection with the form of the fruit. Therefore, since the word *pīlu* is not one that has been used in the masculine when referring to the same form [as the fruit], the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) does not occur for it. [Thus we have] "kīlālapā."
The suffix *vic* is applied by the rule "ṭhato maninkvanibvanipaśca" (Pāṇini 3.2.74).

This word *kolālapa* is one whose masculine form has been previously mentioned (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) within the same general form (*ākṛti*); for it occurs in both genders, functioning by taking as its cause of application (*pravṛttinimitta*) the state of being a drinker of *kīlāla*.

However, since [the stem] does not end in a short *i*, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) does not occur; therefore, the shortening of the vowel indeed takes place. When that has occurred, the substitution of *in* is applied by the rule "ṭāṅsiṅsām ina ātsyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.12), resulting in the form *kīlālapena*. If, on the other hand, the masculine substitution were to apply here, then...
There would be no shortening [of the vowel], and consequently, when the elision of the letter *a* is performed by the rule "āto dhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.140), the form would be *kolālāpā*.

75. *asthi-dadhi-sakthi-akṣṇām anaṅ udāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.75). When the augment *num* would otherwise apply by the rule *ṭhiko 'ci vibhaktau* (7.1.73), *anaṅ* is prescribed for *asthi* and the others. The letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of indicating that the substitution applies to the final sound; the letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation.
Furthermore, these words beginning with *asthi* are acute-accented on the first syllable by the rule *ṭnabviṣayasyānisantasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26),

while the remainder is unaccented (*anudātta*). In that context, the substitution *anaṅ* being prescribed would, by virtue of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (substitute behaving like the original), also be unaccented.

It is stated that [the word] *prāpnoti* is acute according to the rule *nabviṣayasya*; this means "belonging to a neuter base. In the form *asthnā*, once *anaṅ* has been applied, the vowel *a* is elided by the rule *illopo'naḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.134).

"By these," and so forth. But how is this obtained, given that because the bone (*asthi*) and other terms qualify the subject under discussion, there is the rule of "extension to the end of the compound" (*tadanta-vidhi*) due to the qualification; and [given] the rule "in the governing context of *aṅga*, [the term refers to] that which has such a word as its subsequent member" (*puṃvadvṛtti* 85)?

Or, even if the rule of "at the end of that" (*tadanta-vidhi*) applies by virtue of the explicit statement, nevertheless, even if that were the case, the inclusion of a neuter base ending in *asthi* and so forth would not be possible, because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "neuter. This is not a fault; for here, the base (*aṅga*) is not [qualified] by the neuter gender.

Rather, because they are explicitly mentioned [in the rule], it is the bones (*asthi*) and so forth themselves that are intended. And thus, even when the stem ending in those [elements] occurs with a different gender, the neuter status of the *asthi* and so forth still persists. Therefore, for a word ending in those *asthi* and so forth which are neuter, [the neuter endings apply] even when the word occurs in a non-neuter gender.

The inclusion [of the suffix] becomes logical. If, then, that which ends in it is included, how is it not established for the simple [roots]? This too is not a fault; because of the treatment as if possessing a designation (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), it will not apply to the simple ones. This is according to the rule: "The treatment as if possessing a designation applies except in the case of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). (Śākaṭāyana Paribhāṣā 65).
The metarule (paribhāṣā) regarding the domain of suffix-vidhi does not apply here at all.

Why is the neuter gender used as a qualifier for *asthi* and the others? It is so that [the rule] should not apply when those words, such as *dadhi*, although they exist [in the lexicon] with specific genders, are used in another gender—for instance, when one says, "There is someone named Dadhi."
Therefore, [it is] with curd.

76. *cchandasy api dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 6.4.76). By the phrase "even in the Veda," he shows that the word *api* serves the purpose of indicating non-deviation from all the preceding rules. Regarding *asthabhiḥ*: once *anaṅ* has been applied, there is the elision of the *ni*. Regarding *asthāny utkṛtya*: [the same applies].

Regarding "śasyanaṅ| ṭhakṣaṇvatā": here too, it is the same as in the case of the suffix *matup* by [Pāṇini 8.2.16] "ṭhano nuṭ". This [word *akṣaṇvatā*] ends in the accusative case. Regarding "yadanasthaḥ": that which has no bone (*asthi*) is [called] *anastha*;
[here] there is lengthening by [Pāṇini 6.4.8] "sarvanāmasthāne ca".

77. *ī ca dvivacane* (Pāṇini 7.1.77). The particle *ca* is for the purpose of carrying over [the rule] *chandasi* [from 7.1.76]. When *akṣi* + *āṬ* is established as *akṣī te*, the substitution of *śī* occurs by [the rule] *napuṃsakācca* (7.1.19); once the vowel *ī* has been applied, [the rule] *prathamayoḥ...* [applies].

The lengthening of the vowel *i* occurs by the rule *pūrvasavarṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.102); although it is prohibited by the rule *dīrghāj jasi ca* (6.1.105), it nevertheless takes place here due to its Vedic character (*chāndasatvāt*). Now, one might object: "Is this not already established even by the rule for lengthening before a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*)?
Even though the form would be established in that way, the acute accent (*udāttatva*) would not be established.
By this [rule], the substitution of *ī* is prescribed. Alternatively, even the correct form would not be established;

for since the *num* augment would apply first—due to its priority over the "homogeneous" (*pūrvasavarṇa*) rule—the long vowel resulting from the homogeneity (*savarṇadīrgha*) would never occur. Now, why does the *num* augment not apply in the case of *akṣī* by the rule "before a vowel case-ending beginning with a vowel" (*iko'ci vibhaktau*, Pāṇini 7.1.73)?
Does [the rule] apply? He says: "In the case of *akṣī*," and so forth. The scope of *num* is, for example, *trapuṇe* and *jatune*;

the scope of the vowel *i* (as in *īkārasya*) is, for example, *akṣībhyām*. When both would apply simultaneously in the dual number of the nominative case, the vowel *ī* alone occurs because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. Now, once the vowel *ī* has been applied—
Why does inference not arise from the cognition of recurrence? To this he says: "Because it has occurred once."
78. *na abhyastāt chatuḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.78).
[Examples: *tudanti*, *dadati*. There is elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule *śnabhyastayor ātaḥ* (6.4.112).
The designation *abhyasta* (repeated) is applied to *jakṣiti* and the following five roots by the rule *jakṣityādayaḥ ṣaṭ* (6.1.6). *Jāgarti* is also included among them.

But how is this prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) of *num* to be understood, since, according to the rule "either an operation or a prohibition applies to that which ends in *ṭhaN*" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 19), the prohibition would logically apply to the vowel *ī*? To this he says: "Immediately following *śatṛ*," and so forth. [This refers to] that which is prescribed by another grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇāntara*).
There is a prohibition [of the augment], but no *ī* has been prescribed by anyone immediately after *śatṛ*.
Since the term *aṅgasya* ("of the stem") continues to apply, and no other grammatical operation (*kārya*) is possible for *śatṛ* other than *num*,
it follows by implication (*sāmarthyāt*) that this refers to the *num* [augment] even when it is separated [from the stem] by the rule "ugidacām" (Pāṇini 7.1.70).
The negation is understood.

79. *vā napuṃsakasya* (Pāṇini 7.1.79). It is understood that the suffix *śatṛ* alone does not occur in the neuter; rather, the option is understood to apply to a neuter noun ending in that *śatṛ* which follows a reduplicated (*abhyasta*) base.
Thus he says: "From a limb that has been practiced," and so forth.
80. *ācchīnadyornum* (Pāṇini 7.1.80).

In the example "taduntī kule," the substitution of *śī* occurs by [the rule] *napuṃsakācca* (7.1.19). In the example "tudatī brāhmaṇī," the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by [the rule] *ugitaśca* (4.1.6); likewise in "yātī brāhmaṇī."

Because [the suffix] *śap* has been elided, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "after that which ends in *ṭhuk* and after *it*" (Pāṇini 4.1.6). Thus we have "kariṣyantī kule" (one who will act in the family). Here, the substitution of *śatṛ* for the future suffix *lṛṭ* occurs by the rule "optionally for *lṛṭ*" (Pāṇini 3.3.14), and the augment *iṭ* is added by the rule "after a root ending in long *ṝ* or after *han*, before *sya*" (Pāṇini 7.2.70).

The objection beginning with "Because it is internal" (*antaraṅgatvāt*) and so forth is as follows: When the suffix *śatṛ* follows an *a*-ending stem and the vowel *ī* [of the feminine suffix] is present, should the augment *num* be applied, or should the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) [by *ato guṇe*] take effect?
Here, because it is internal, the single-substitute of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) occurs by the rule *ato guṇe* (P. 6.1.97).

Furthermore, its status as *antaraṅga* (internal) is due to its being dependent upon a vowel (*varṇa*), whereas *num* is *bahiraṅga* (external) because it depends on many factors; for that [num] requires an *aṅga* ending in the vowel *a*, the suffix *śatṛ*, and the subsequent presence of the feminine suffixes *śī* or *nadi*. This is according to the principle: "An operation concerning a vowel (*āṅga*) takes precedence over one concerning a letter (*vārṇa*)" (Vārttika 39).

Such cases do not exist here because of the difference in time (*bhinnakālatva*): for while the augment *num* would apply when the subsequent element (*para*) exists, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) occurs prior to that. It was stated previously: "And where there is a simultaneous application of both a phoneme (*varṇa*) and a rule (*aṅga*), there this [maxim] applies."

Because there is no separation [of the *aṅga* from its final phoneme], it can be said that the suffix *śatṛ* follows an *aṅga* ending in a vowel (*avarṇa*). For such a linguistic usage as "this is subsequent to that" or "this is prior to that" occurs only when there is a distinction between the target and the limit; it does not occur otherwise. One might argue: "But [the rule] *antādivacca* (P. 6.1.85)..."

Thus, by virtue of the rule "as if non-existent" (antādivadbhāva), a single substitute (ekādeśa) is treated as the final element with respect to what precedes it, and as the initial element with respect to what follows it.

Since the single substitute is the final element with respect to the preceding part and the initial element with respect to the following part, does it not follow that [the prohibition] applies to the *śatṛ* suffix occurring after an *aṅga* ending in an *avarṇa*? To this he says: "on both sides" (*ubhayata*).

Regarding the phrase "in both cases" (*ubhayata āśraye*), etc.: here, indeed, both the stem ending in *a* and the suffix *śatṛ* are dependent [on the preceding and following elements]. Regarding the phrase "in both cases" (*ubhayata āśraye*), etc.: here, indeed, both the stem ending in *a* and the suffix *śatṛ* are dependent. Because of the metarule "when there is dependence on both sides, the treatment as a final or initial element does not apply" (*ubhayata āśraye nāntādivat*;
Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 51), the status of being treated as a final or initial element (*antādivadbhāvaḥ*) does not exist. Not so.

For a single [element], it is possible at one time to behave like a final element with respect to what precedes it, and at another time to behave like an initial element with respect to what follows it.
To explain: if it behaves like a final element with respect to what precedes it, then the form *śatṛ* is not produced;
if, on the other hand, it behaves like an initial element with respect to what follows it, then the status of the stem as ending in the vowel *a* is not assumed.
It is stated [in the rule] "num after [a stem ending in] ac, i, and ī" (Pāṇini 7.1.58), yet a śatṛ suffix following a verbal base (aṅga) ending in the letter *a* is never possible;
therefore, by the authority of that statement, one resorts to the notion of what existed previously— that is, a śatṛ which followed [a base] ending in the letter *a*.

"It was previously so. Therefore, he says: "By way of having occurred previously," and so forth. For if the state of having occurred previously were relied upon, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in cases such as *avatī* and *dhnatī*; for here too, was not the *śatṛ* suffix preceded by an *aṅga* ending in an *a*-vowel? To this he says: "In this case..."

"Some say it is *samādhi*. *Samādhi* means avoidance (*parīhāra*). And avoidance is a part of the suffix *śatṛ*. The letter *t* is a part of the suffix *śatṛ*. In this context, the word *śatṛ* is used [metonymically] for its part, just as the word "cloth" (*paṭa*) is used for a part of the cloth in the expression "the cloth is torn," where the word for the whole is applied to the parts.
Words that have entered into usage are sometimes applied even to the constituent parts [of a word].

And since that *śatṛ*-affix follows an *aṅga* ending in an *a*-vowel once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been effected, the objection raised by the statement "because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), once the single-substitute has been effected," and so forth, is as follows:

[The objection] is avoided. But what about the *num* augment for a *takāra* that is not part of an *ac* [vowel]? Would there be a *num* after *ru* as well? And how could it not be so? Because of the rule "midaco 'ntyāt paraḥ" (Pāṇini 1.1.47).
Let it not apply to the *takāra*; it will apply to that which ends in it. And such is the meaning of the sūtra.

We shall explain [the rule as follows]: *num* is inserted after that stem which ends in a consonant immediately following a vowel (*avarṇa*). And we shall repeat the mention of "stem" (*aṅga*) twice: [first] "after a stem ending in a vowel... [and then again] "that which follows... etc.

The augment *num* occurs for that stem (*aṅga*) which has *śatṛ* as its final member. We shall repeat the term "stem" (*aṅga*) twice: once to qualify the member ending in *śatṛ*, and once to ensure the application of the stem-operation (*aṅgakārya*). But how [is it determined] that in forms such as *tudati*, [the *num* applies] after the letter *t*?
