[Objection: How can it be a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the preceding [element], given that the technical designation "stem" (*aṅga-saṃjñā*) applies to that which begins with the element from which a suffix is prescribed when a suffix follows; and since the *t* is not a suffix, and in the absence of the designation "stem," the rule stating "that which is a portion of *śatṛ* following a stem ending in an *a*-vowel" would be untenable? [Response: This is not so.

This is a fault; for just as the word *śatṛ* applies to a portion of the stem *śatṛ*, so too the word *aṅga* applies to the portion preceding the letter *t*. But what is that *aṅga*? It is that of which the portion ending in *śatṛ* is a part; for it is prescribed that the designation *aṅga* applies to that [portion] when followed by *śn* or *śnu*.

If that is so, why does it not also occur here in *adatī* and *dhnatī*, since in these cases too a *śatṛ* suffix follows a stem ending in an *a*-vowel? If it were to occur here as well, the qualification *ād* (from a vowel) would be useless; one should have simply said *śīnadyoḥ* (after the roots *śī* and *nad*). And where...

When followed by *śī* or *na*, the base (*aṅga*) ends in *śatṛ*; in that case, the element following the *śatṛ* necessarily begins with a vowel. Therefore, by the force of employing the qualification "of *ā*" (*ātaḥ*), there is a specific selection [of the vowel].
It is understood as follows:

since the *num* augment applies when a suffix beginning with *śatṛ* follows an *aṅga* that ends in the letter *a*, there is no occasion for *num* here, because the suffix *śatṛ* does not follow immediately after the *a* that constitutes the final part of the *aṅga*.
[The rule] "when *śī* or *nadī* follow an *aṅga* ending in an *a*-vowel" is intended; here too, as before, the word *aṅga* refers to a portion of the *aṅga*. But surely—

In forms such as *tudanti*, since the suffixes *śī* and *nadi* cannot possibly follow an *aṅga* ending in the vowel *a*—because of the intervention of the letter *t*—he says: "In that case, by whatever... and so forth. The meaning has already been explained.

Now, while *num* is still in force from a previous rule, for what purpose is *num* mentioned again? [The answer is: It is not [for the sake of the same rule], but rather for the sake of the option (*vā*).
This is the subject at hand. In that context, even an undesirable interpretation would be understood if the mention of *num* were omitted:
namely, that the optional *num* applies to *śī* and *nadī*, but does not apply after a stem ending in a vowel (*avarṇa*). What would be the consequence?
In forms such as *kurvatī* and *tanvatī*, the optional *num* would apply, whereas in *kariṣyantī*, it would not.
But by what means is the prohibition of *num* applied to the roots *as* and *śī* when they have already obtained [the augment]?

This very fact indicates that there is an optional (*vibhāṣā*) *num* for *as* and *śī*. However, if the mention of *num* were made [in the rule itself], this would be understood as a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*), which is not the desired fault.

81. After verbal roots ending in *śap* and after the suffix *śyan*, [the substitution of *n* for the final consonant] is obligatory. (Pāṇini 7.1.81) 82. [The substitution of *n* for the final consonant occurs] in the vocative singular (*savan*) after the word *anaḍuh*. (Pāṇini 7.1.82) 83. In the Vedic language (*chandas*), [the substitution of *n* for the final consonant occurs] after *dṛk*, *svavah*, and *svatavah*. (Pāṇini 7.1.83)
*ṭhīdṛṅ*, *kīdṛṅ* [this is not in the Kāśikā]. By the rule *tyadādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.60), the suffix *kvin* is applied; by *idaṃkimorīśkī* (6.3.90), the substitutes *īś* and *kī* are applied;
then the elision of the *hal-ṅyādi* and the *saṃyogānta* [are applied]; and finally, by *kvinpratyayasya kuḥ* (8.2.62), the substitution of *k* occurs.

By this [rule 8.2.62], there is *kutva* [of the dental *t*]. Thus we have *yāvṛṅ* and *tādṛṅ*. In *yāvṛṅ* and *tādṛṅ*, the substitution of *ā* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.3.91] *ā sarvanāmnaḥ*. In *sadṛṅ*, the substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.3.89] *dṛgdṛśavatuṣu*.

84. *diva āṬt* (Pāṇini 7.1.84). [The example is] *dyauḥ*. When the substitution of *āṬ* has been made, the *yaṇ* replacement occurs. Here, in the case of *akṣadyuḥ*—meaning "one who plays with dice"—when the suffix *kvip* is applied, then, because it is internal (*antaraṅga*) with respect to that [suffix], the rule *cch-avoḥ śūḍ-anunāsike ca* applies.

(6.4.19) Thus [the rule] *uṭh* [is applied]. Since a word remains the same even when one part is modified (*ekadeśavikṛtasyānanyatvāt*), this is indeed the word *div*; therefore, the substitution of *ū* for the *o* of *ūrk* would apply. Why does it not occur? To this he says: "The base *div*," and so forth. This word *div* certainly exists.

There is the term *dhātu*, and there is also the underived nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Among these, the verbal root (*dhātu*) possesses an indicatory letter (*anubandha*); for it, the grammatical operation prescribed for those marked with the indicatory letter *u*—namely, "the augment *it* is optionally applied after a root ending in *u*" (Pāṇini 7.2.56)—is applicable. The nominal stem (*prātipadika*), however, is devoid of an indicatory letter; for it has no grammatical operation whatsoever that pertains to an indicatory letter. In that case:
By the paribhāṣā "that which has no suffix following it" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 56), a verbal root (*dhātu*) is understood here.
Consequently, in the case of *annadyau*, the undesirable occurrence of *autva* (the substitution of *au*) does not take place. The letter *t* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation.

85. *pathi-mathi-ṛbhukṣām āt* (Pāṇini 7.1.85). When the elision of the final consonant (*hal*) and the following vowel (*i*, etc. is about to occur, as well as the elision of *n*, the substitution of *ā* is prescribed. Thus, for *panthāḥ*:
the substitution of *nth* for *th* is applied by *tho nthaḥ* (7.1.80), and [the rule] *iti sarvanāmasthāne* (7.1.86) applies.

[The vowel] *it* [is short]. Now, an objection is raised: since the substitute for this [vowel] is the nasalized *n*, and since by the rule "taparaḥ tatkālasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.70) there is the inclusion of homogeneous sounds, the replacement ought to be by a nasalized *a* alone due to the closest proximity (*āntaratamya*). What is the point here?

Is this [rule] cited as being pure? To this he says: "Even when the substitute is nasal," and so forth. He states the reason for this very point: "That which is being taught (*bhāvyamāna*)," and so forth. And if, even by an *aṇ* vowel that is being taught with a following *t* (i.e., *tapara*), there is no inclusion of homogeneous (*savarṇa*) vowels, then—

In that case, [the substitution] would not occur even in the rule *ṭhviṅvanoranunāsikasyāt* (6.4.41), and likewise, the nasalized vowel *ā* would not occur in the rule *ṭhjanasanakhanāṃ sañjhaloḥ* (6.4.42). If this is so, then this *ā* is not marked by a following *t* (i.e., it is not *tapara*); what then? It is a *d*. As for the *d*:
It is for the sake of ease of pronunciation, and because it is not a constituent part [of the grammatical operation], it is not heard. This might be the case:

even if a short *a* (*aṇ*) being operated upon does not include its homogeneous counterparts (according to *Vārttika* 35), and thus there would be no inclusion of the homogeneous sounds, nevertheless, because it is uttered as qualified by nasality, it is [treated] only as nasal.

Is it appropriate [to say this]? He says: "For it is pure," and so forth. This letter *a* is indeed called pure (*śuddha*), meaning it is without nasalization (*niranunāsika*); therefore, it is purely [vocalic] and not characterized by nasality. Now, for what purpose is this [letter] stated as long (*dīrgha*)? Let it simply be short (*hrasva*); for here too, [the rule] *akaḥ savarṇe* [would apply].

Is it not already established by the rule *dīrghaḥ* (6.1.101)? It is not so established; for by the rule *ato guṇe* (6.1.97), the single substitute of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) would apply. If you argue that it will not apply due to the functional force (*sāmarthya*) of the explicit utterance of the vowel *a*, we say no; for there is indeed another purpose for the utterance of the vowel *a*. What is that?
Otherwise, the sound *na* would not be heard. For if elision (*lopa*) were applied, there would be unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*);
therefore, a long vowel is prescribed.

86. *ito't sarvanāmasthāne* (Pāṇini 7.1.86). Now, while the rule *ṭāṅasiṅasām-in-ātsyāḥ* (7.1.85) is still in force, what is the purpose of stating the word *ad*? If it is argued that it is so that the short vowel (*hrasva*) may be heard [in its original form], this is not so; for once the shortening has been applied, when *su* follows, [the form becomes] *akaḥ*.

Since [the substitution] ought to be a long vowel by virtue of *savarṇe dīrghatvena* (Pāṇini 6.1.101), except where [the rule] *nopadhāyāḥ* (6.4.7) applies, how is it that the short vowel is heard? To this he says: "While *āt* is being supplied," and so forth. That which has *ṣapūrva* as its meaning or purpose is described as such. How?
Furthermore, how does this [rule] serve the purpose of the preceding rule (*ṣapūrvārtha*)? To this he says: "ṛbhukṣaṇam," etc.

If only the long vowel (*dīrgha*) were prescribed here as the original subject, then in the case of *ṛbhukṣam indram*, the short vowel would not be heard. However, when the short vowel is prescribed, by the rule "vā ṣapūrvasya nigame" (Pāṇini 6.4.9), [the option is established].

The long vowel occurs optionally because it is prescribed as such. Some say that the addition of *ta* (the *tapara* marker) to both the original element (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) is for the sake of ease of pronunciation. Others say it is for the purpose of excluding the long vowel in forms such as *pathīḥ*.
[In the derivation of *pantīyati*: one who desires the path (*panthānam icchati*), by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8); then, by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.25).

(7.4.25) *dīrghaḥ*—from *pathīyati*; [the suffix] *kvip* is added to *pathīyati*, whereby by *ato lopaḥ* (6.4.48) there is elision of the final *a*, and by *kyasya vibhāṣā* (6.4.50) there is elision of the *ya*—thus *pathīḥ*.
87. *tho nthaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.87).

Both *thaḥ* and *nthaḥ*—these two, as both the substituend (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*)—are devoid of phonemes (*anackau*). As for the vowel *a* heard in the form *antha*, it serves merely for ease of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). This remains so even though the substitute consists of multiple phonemes (*anekāl*).

According to the rule "substitutes apply to that which is being pointed out" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 106), it is understood that the substitute applies only to the letter *th*, not to the whole [suffix].
88. *bhasya ṭerlopaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.88).
[The rule] *sarvanāmasthāne* etc. [is understood]. In this context of *yaci bham* (1.4.18), the term *asarvanāmasthāne* is supplied from the preceding rule *svādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne* (1.4.17).

While this [rule] is in effect, the designation *bha* is prescribed; in that context, if the elision of the *ṭi* (the penultimate vowel) of *pathin* and the others were to occur when a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix follows, then they would no longer possess the designation *bha*. Conversely, if they were to possess the designation *bha*, then a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix could not follow them. Thus, there is a mutual contradiction.
There is a contradiction characterized by non-coexistence between those [suffixes] termed *bha* and the *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffixes].
Therefore, although the mention of *sarvanāmasthāna* continues for the sake of subsequent rules, it is nevertheless not connected here.

89. *puṃso'suṅ* (Pāṇini 7.1.89). In the suffix *asuṅ*, the letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of indicating that the substitution applies to the final sound. The letter *u* is for the purpose of triggering operations prescribed for stems ending in *uk*. [The form] *pumān* is derived by applying *num* according to 7.1.70 (*ugidacām...*) and so forth, and then applying 6.4.10 (*sāntamahataḥ saṃyogasya*).

(6.4.10) Thus, there is lengthening, followed by the elision of the *hal* and *ṅī* suffixes and the final consonant of the *saṃyoga*. In the example "paramapumān" and so forth, once the compound has been formed by the rule "sanmahat... (Pāṇini 2.1.61)—meaning "he is both supreme (*parama*) and a man (*pumān*)"—the case ending has not yet arisen.
In the meantime, *asuṅ* should not yet occur, because that [suffix] is dependent upon it [the case ending].

However, since the acute accent on the final syllable of a compound does not depend on anything else, by virtue of being *antaraṅga* (internal), the acute accent on the final syllable occurs even before the case ending. Subsequently, when the case ending has arisen, *asuṅ* [is applied].
If [the suffix] were to occur in place of a consonant that lacks an accent, it would not have a fixed accent;

consequently, even an undesired accent would result, whereas the final syllable of the second member is intended to be udātta, yet the initial syllable would instead become udātta. [The phrase] "for that purpose," etc., [is stated].

The word *artha* signifies "cessation," as in the expression "smoke for the sake of mosquitoes. For that purpose— that is, for the sake of the spontaneous cessation of that which is undesirable— the statement [of the rule] must be made as if it were an original instruction (*upadeśivat*),
because if it were not so stated, the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound would apply only at the stage of the original instruction when the case-ending has already been produced.
So that *asuṅ* may occur first; thus, when *asuṅ* has been applied first, the word *paramapumān* subsequently becomes oxytone by virtue of the accentuation of the final member of a compound.
If this were so, then the word *pumān* itself would also be oxytone.

One might ask: "Even when the suffix *asuṅ* has been applied at the stage of the *upadeśa* (the original form), should the accent not subsequently be determined by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*)? To this he says: "But this word *pumān*," and so forth.

This word *puṃs* is derived from the root *pū* with the suffix *ḍumsun*—and there is a short vowel [as per the rule] *ḍumsun* and a short vowel (*muksuno hrasvaśca*). [Note: The variant reading *pāteḥ ḍumsun* refers to the same formation.]
The word *pāteḍuṣ* is derived from the root *pat* with the suffix *muṣun* according to Pāṇini 5.2.177;
by virtue of the *nit*-accent, it becomes udātta on its first syllable, not on its final syllable.
90. *goto ṇit* (Pāṇini 7.1.90).

By this [sūtra], the technical designation *ṇit* is either established: "A *sarvanāmasthāna* following *go* becomes *ṇit*," meaning it receives the designation *ṇit*; or else, [the designation applies] to that which follows *go*.

The letter *ṇ* of the term *sarvanāmasthāna* is designated as an *it*; therefore, the *ṇ* of a *sarvanāmasthāna* following a word ending in *go* is designated as an *it*. Or rather, [the letter *ṇ*] is prescribed as a substitute for the *sarvanāmasthāna* following a word ending in *go*.

An ādeśa (substitute) possessing the indicatory letter *ṇ* becomes [the original]; an *atideśa* (extended application) is made—meaning that [the property] of being *ṇit* applies to the word *go*, or it becomes as if it were *ṇit*. Even without the suffix *vat*, the sense of *vat* is understood, as in the rule for *gāṅ-kuṭādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.1). In the first case, the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is uttered [to denote] the named object (*saṃjñin*).

In the case of the rule *pratyāyayati*, because it is an artificial (*kṛtrima*) designation, among the rules concerning *ṇit* suffixes, only this [specific] *sarvanāmasthāna* would be understood, and not those such as *ṇvul* and the like. In the second alternative, however, the *ṇakāra* would incur the designation *itsaṃjñaka* (indicatory) for the *sarvanāmasthāna*. In the third alternative, on the other hand, the *sarvanāmasthāna* would no longer be *ṇit*.

"In some places it is seen": these very faults—that the substitutes such as *ṣvu* and so forth would apply to those very [bases]—are to be countered respectively in the first three positions. In countering them, there would be heaviness of comprehension (*pratipattigaurava*); however, in the position of extended application (*atideśapakṣa*), there is nothing [of the sort].
This must be understood; therefore, that alone is correct.

Relying on that very point, he says "from the word *go*" and so forth. By explaining the meaning of the phrase "it becomes a *ṇit*," through the words "the operation of a *ṇit*" and so on, he declares that this is an extension (*atideśa*) of the operation.
In the case of *gauḥ*, there is the application of the rule for *vṛddhi* vowels and for those marked with the *ṇit* designation.

In the example *citraguḥ*, once the *bahuvrīhi* compound has been formed, the shortening [of the final vowel] occurs by the rule *gostriyor upasarjanasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.48). In that context, if the marker *tapara* were not present, then within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "stem" (*aṅga*), [the rule would apply to all cases].

By accepting the rule of "extension to that which ends with [the specified element]" (*tadantavidhi*) on the basis of the statement *tadutarapadasya* (Puṣpavṛtti 85), this *aṅga* comes to end in the word *go* through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*; consequently, the status of being a *ṇit* would apply.
However, when the letter *t* is included [in the suffix], because there is a restriction regarding the time [of its application], it does not occur.

Because they belong to different times [of articulation]. In the rule *taparastatkālasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.70), since the mention of *aṇ* has been withdrawn, the restriction to that same time applies even to those which are not *aṇ*.
As for the question "How so? and so forth: even though the *tapara* marker is present, [the rule] *hrasvasya guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.108) [applies], as does [the rule] *jasi*...

When the guṇa substitution is applied to the vocative ending *su* by the rule *ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.109), the forms *he citrago* and *he citragava* would result; this is the intended meaning, based on the principle that [the rule applies] because it occurs at that same time. One might object: "But will this not be avoided by the paribhāṣā concerning what is taught by a technical name versus what is taught by its specific wording (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*)? This is not so; for where...
For in that case, the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) does not apply;

indeed, the application of *sthānivadbhāva* would be purposeless there. The rebuttal beginning with "But when [the operation] pertains to the *aṅga*" is the solution for cases such as *he citrago*, but not for *citragava*.

Because it is not yet finalized. For once the substitution of *ava* has been made, finality (*niṣṭhitatva*) will exist here, but not in the mere *guṇa* [substitution] alone, because that is unfit for usage.
Therefore, being dissatisfied with this solution on account of its lack of pervasiveness (*avyāpakatva*), [the author says:]

He states another solution, beginning with "Or rather" (*atha vā*). It might be argued: "In this case as well, the *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix] is related to the word *go-* by way of the relation characterized by immediate proximity (*ānantarya*). To this he says: "And that which... (*yac ca*), etc. If the *sarvanāmasthāna* were related to *go-* by way of the relation characterized by immediate proximity...
In that case, the recourse to the genitive case would be purposeless, as the ablative alone should have been resorted to,

since there is no purpose for deviating from the sequence. Therefore, by virtue of resorting to the genitive, [the operation applies] to those properties such as singularity and so forth which belong to the meaning of the word "cow."

That which is a *sarvanāmasthāna* [affix] is called a *sarvanāmasthāna* for the word *go*. Furthermore, that should be understood as pertaining to the word *go* in its singular number (*ekatva*) and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of dual number (*dvitva*) and the rest is intended. In this regard, it might be argued: "Is the *sarvanāmasthāna* [affix] after the word *citragu* also [to be considered such]?"
Does this apply because the referent of the word *go* is a single entity? To this he says: "From the word *citragu*" and so forth.
If the status of being a *ṇit* were prescribed for every *sarvanāmasthāna* that is related to the cow (*go*), [then the following would occur].

In that case, the inclusion of the long vowel marker *t* (taparakaraṇa) would be purposeless; for it is employed so that [the rule] does not apply in instances such as *citraguḥ*. However, there is no possibility of its application here, because in this case the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix is not related to the word *go*, but rather to the meaning of the other member of the compound (*anyapadārtha*). Thus he says: "But the inclusion of the long vowel marker *t*..."
And so forth.
Regarding the phrase "some [readers]" and so on: for what purpose, then, do they read in this way? He says:
"The word *dyo* also," and so forth. As for those who do not read "from *go*" (*gotaḥ*),...

Since the status of being a *ṇit* for the *sarvanāmasthāna* following the word *dyo* is not established for them, he says: "The very term 'gota' [is used]," and so forth. But how can this be understood as an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for words ending in the vowel *o*?

Thus he says: "In the case of the mention of phonemes," and so forth. For instance, in rules such as *vṛddhir ādaic* (Pāṇini 1.1.1) and *adeṅ guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.2), a phoneme is mentioned with a following *t* (tapara); thus, the use of *tapara* in the mention of phonemes is well-established. Therefore, here too—
Because of the mention of the *tapara* (the long vowel with a following *r*), the term "gotraḥ" should be understood as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for words ending in the vowel *o*.

Therefore, by this statement, it is understood that the employment of the *tapara* is solely for the purpose of indicating the phoneme, and thus serves as an indicator for words ending in the vowel *au*.

91. *ṇalutamo vā* (Pāṇini 7.1.91). The meaning is: "The operation (*kārya*) of a *ṇit* [affix] optionally takes place. By this, it is stated that because there is an absence (*abhāva*) of the *ṇit*-operation in one alternative, it is as if the *ṇit* status were present; however, he shows that it is not a prohibition of the *ṇit* status itself. But it is not [a prohibition] of *ṇal*.

The meaning is that once the status of being *ṇit* is established at the stage of instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*), it cannot be negated even by a hundred such statements. Thus, [we have] *cakāra* and *cakara*: when there is the status of being *ṇit*, then by *aco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115), there is *vṛddhi*; otherwise, there is the *guṇa* substitution conditioned by the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. [We have] *papāca* and *papaca*: when...
In that case, by the rule "ṇitvāt tadā ṭhakaḥ upadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.116), there is vṛddhi; at other times, its absence occurs.

92. *sakhyur asambuddhau* (Pāṇini 7.1.92). The term *asambuddhau* is a *paryudāsa* (exclusion), meaning "other than the vocative singular. Thus, in *he sakhe*, the *guṇa* substitution [of *e* for *i*] occurs by rule 7.3.108, *hrasvasya guṇaḥ*.
93. *anaṅ* [is substituted] for *sau*.

(Pāṇini 7.1.93) Since the status of being *ṇit* was already established by the preceding rule, *anaṅ* is here prescribed. The letter *ṅ* in it serves to indicate that the substitution applies to the final phoneme;
the letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation. Thus, "sakhā" [is formed]. [This occurs] by the rule: *sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau* (6.4.8).
Thus [the stem is] *dīrgha-*; by *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* (6.1.68), there is elision of the *su* suffix;

and by *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* (8.2.7), there is elision of the *n*. The explicit mention of *anaṅ* [instead of simply *a*] is so that the elision of *su* may occur when the vowel *ā* is to be substituted; for if *a* were prescribed, its [elision would not take place].
There would be no elision, as for example in *panthāḥ*.
94. *ṛduśanaspurudaṃso'nehasāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 7.1.94).

When the rule *ṛto ṅsirvanāmasthānayoḥ* (7.3.110) would have required the substitution of *guṇa* for the final *ṛ* of a stem ending in *ṛ*, and when the elision of the case-ending has been applied to the others by *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* (6.1.68), [the following applies].

When the substitution of *ru*, the visarga, and the long vowel at the end of a word have been applied, it is desired that [the substitution of *anaṅ*] also optionally occurs for *uśanas* even in the vocative singular. How is this so?
The letter *ca* is used here, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned; by that, the substitution of *anaṅ* for *uśanas* occurs even in the vocative singular.

It will occur. If this is so, would it be obligatory? No; because of the governing rule "ṇal uttamo vā" (Pāṇini 7.1.91), it will occur optionally. Furthermore, due to the understanding that this is a restricted option (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*), for others it is obligatory.

"It is also accepted that the prohibition of the elision of *n* (*nalopa-pratiṣedha*) is intended as an alternative view. How is this obtained? For in that context, the word "optionally" (*vā*) from the rule "svarito vānudātte padādau" (Pāṇini 8.2.6) is understood to carry over;
by that very means, it is understood thus: "either the elision of *n* does not occur before a *ṅi*-ending or a vocative (*sambuddhi*), or else the prohibition of its elision applies."

Furthermore, because of the knowledge that the *vibhāṣā* (optionality) is fixed [by other rules], there will be an optional elision (*lopa*) of the *nakāra* in *uśanas* when followed by a *saṃbuddhi* [vowel]; however, for others, the elision will not occur at all. By saying "And so it has been said," etc., he confirms the meaning just mentioned by means of a scriptural statement (*āgama*).
"Ending in *s* (*sāntam*)" refers to when the augment *anaṅ* is not applied. "Ending in *n* (*nāntam*)" does not mean the elision of *n*.

"Ending in *t* (*adantam*)" refers to when the elision of *n* has taken place. "The inclusion of the short *a* (*taparakaraṇa*) is for the sake of avoiding ambiguity"—for if that were absent, [the rule would apply] even when *uśanas* follows.
Once the substitution of *yaṇ* has been made, a doubt may arise: does this refer to that which ends in the vowel *ṛ*, or to that which ends in the consonant *r*?

95. *tṛjvat kroṣṭuḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.95). [The word] *kroṣṭu* is a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*) ending in the suffix *tṛn*. It is derived from the root *kruś* (Dhātupāṭha 856)—which, according to the Dhātupāṭha, means "to call out" (*āhvāne*) and "to cry out" (*rodane*).
The suffix *tun* is prescribed after the roots *ṣi*, *tan*, *gam*, *mi*, *si*, *ci*, *ava*, *ghañ*, and *kṛśi* (Dhātupāṭha 1.122).

Since this word ending in the suffix *tun* is derived in the sense of a proper name (*saṃjñā*), it refers to the jackal (*jambuka*). Regarding the rule "it behaves like [a stem ending in] *tṛc*": that which acts in the same manner as one ending in *tṛc* is called *tṛjvat*.

He will state [later] that "this is an extension of form (rūpātideśa). In that context, when it is said "it becomes like *tṛc*," someone might have the misconception that the form of the word *tṛc* itself is being extended;
therefore, in order to dispel that, he says: "the form which belongs to that which ends in *tṛc*," and so forth. And this...

This is obtained from the rule: "When there is the mention of a suffix (*pratyaya*), there is the inclusion of that which begins with the element after which that suffix is prescribed and ends with the suffix itself" (Paribhāṣenduśekhara 44). Although various ways of showing that there is no fault even when the extension (*atideśa*) applies to the technical rules (*śāstra*) have been demonstrated in the Bhāṣya—since that [extension] has been established as being free from defect—

The extension of function (*kāryātideśa*) has been explained as being almost entirely identical to the extension of the rule (*śāstrātideśa*), because it is non-different from it. Nevertheless, since the two—extension of the rule and extension of function—have the same purpose regarding form, there is an absence of any distinction in the form itself. Regarding form...

However, [the suffix] is predominant, because the word is to be refined by those two. Therefore, he says "this is a transfer of form" (*rūpātideśa*) and so forth, stating that this transfer of form is appropriate. If, then, whatever is the form of that which ends in *tṛc* is transferred to the word *kroṣṭu*, then [it would follow that] anything at all...

Would not forms such as *vaktṛ* and *paktṛ*, which end in the suffix *tṛc*, also result [as the meaning of the root]? To this he says: "And because of proximity," and so forth. Here, there exist forms ending in *tṛc* belonging to other roots such as *pacati* and others, as well as for the root *kruś*; why then [should the rule apply] to a root ending in *tṛc* that has not been explicitly mentioned?

Is it the form of that [which is the subject] that is extended, or is it the form of the root *kruś* as it is heard in the scripture? In this regard, the view is that the very form of that which is heard is what is to be extended;
furthermore, by the force of the utterance of the particle *ca*, the accent is also extended. Otherwise, one would have simply said "like *tṛ*" (*tṛvat*). This is the intended meaning.

Regarding "kroṣṭā": when the substitution of *tṛjvat* has been applied, *anaṅ* is substituted by the preceding rule [Pāṇini 7.1.95]. In the forms "kroṣṭārau" and "kroṣṭāraḥ," there is *guṇa* substitution by the rule "ṛto ṅsirvanāmasthānayoḥ" (7.3.110), followed by the replacement of *ṛ* with *ra*, and finally lengthening by the rule "aptṛntṛc... (6.4.11). The form is "kroṣṭṝn."
The long vowel [ā] is substituted by "ṭhprathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ" (6.1.102), and the substitution of *n* for the *s* of *śas* occurs by "ṭhtasmāccchaso naḥ puṃsi" (6.1.103).
96. *striyāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 7.1.96). [The example is] *kroṣṭrībhiḥ*. When the substitution of *tṛjvat* has been applied, the *yaṇ* replacement occurs.
But by what rule does the long vowel *ī* arise from the word *kroṣṭu*, once the *tṛjvat* substitution has been made? [It is by the rule] *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*.

If it is argued that this is by means of [Pāṇini 4.1.5] *ṅīp*, [we reply: no; because that would result in the word being unaccented (*anudātta*). Therefore, he says: "Some [grammarians] apply the word *kroṣṭu*," and so forth. [The example is] "bought for five female jackals" (*pañcabhiḥ kroṣṭrībhiḥ krītaiḥ*). The compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.1.51] *taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca*.

By the rule *ṭhārhādagopucccha* (5.1.19), the suffix *ṭhak* is applied; by the rule *ṭhadhyarddhapūrva* (5.1.28), its *lak* is substituted; by the rule *luktaddhitaluki* (1.2.49), there is elision (*luk*) of the feminine suffix; when that has been elided, they apply the substitution of *tṛjvat* to the suffix *ṅīṣ*.

For them, the treatment as if they were *tṛc*-stems does not occur; therefore, it is said "it must be countered" (*pratividheyam*), which means that a remedy (*pratividhāna*) must be applied. In this regard, the following is the remedy: the letter *ca* is added here, and it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly stated (*anuktasamuccayārtha*). Consequently, even when the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) has been elided...
It will be so.
But for those who do not read [the word] among the *gaura*-group, how is the long vowel *ī* [justified]?
To this he says: "In the *gaura*-group," etc. For them, [it applies] in the case of *pañcakroṣṭrībhiḥ* and so on, but not...

Something must be addressed here: because the suffix denoting femininity (*strīpratyaya*) of another [word] is not relied upon as a cause [for this operation]. But surely, since that [suffix] is also elided, while the designation "stem" (*aṅga*) does not exist, the substitution of *tṛṇvat* prescribed for a stem would not occur?

Is it not the case that [the feminine suffix] must indeed be applied? This is not so; for when the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) has been elided, the designation "stem" (*aṅga*) still applies by virtue of the rule regarding the characteristics of suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). As for the prohibition stated in *na lumatāṅgasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.63), it applies only to grammatical operations prescribed under the heading of "stem" (*aṅgādhikāra*). It does not [apply to the designation of the stem itself].

The designation "aṅga" is prescribed under the heading of "aṅga. [This applies] after the extension (*atideśa*) has been effected, and so forth. Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *iko 'ci vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.1.73), when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) has arisen and the designation "aṅga" based upon that [ending] has occurred, [the rule applies] to that which refers to a feminine.

An extension (*atideśa*) is made for the word *kroṣṭṛ*. Once that has been applied, because it ends in the vowel *ṛ*, the suffix *ṅīp* occurs by the rule "ṛnnebhyo ṅīp" (Pāṇini 4.1.5). Now, one might object: "But once the suffix *ṅīp* is applied, does the word *kroṣṭrī* not fail to be established as having its final syllable accented? To this he says: "In that case," and so forth.

Since the word *kroṣṭrī* is prescribed as having an udātta accent on its final syllable, the *yaṇ* substitute that occurs in place of the *ṛ*-vowel belonging to the stem ending in *tṛ* becomes an udātta *yaṇ*. Consequently,
while the rule *śaturanumo nadyajādī* (Pāṇini 6.1.173) is in effect, the rule *udātayaṇo halpūrvāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.174) applies.
Thus, the word *kroṣṭrī* has its final syllable acute-accented (*udātta*).

97. *vibhāṣā tṛtīyādiṣv aci* (7.1.97). The term *striyām* from [7.1.96] does not carry over; therefore, this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) where [the substitution] was otherwise not required. For example, *kroṣṭunā*. Here, the substitution of *nā* by [7.3.120], *āṅe nā striyām*, applies because it is not in the feminine.
In *kroṣṭave*: by *gher ṅiti* (Pāṇini 7.3.111), there is guṇa substitution. In *kroṣṭauḥ*:

by *ṛta ut* (6.1.111), there is the substitution of *u*, followed by the replacement of *u* with *ra* (*raparatva*), and by *rāt sasya* (8.2.24), there is the elision of *s*. In *kroṣṭoḥ*: as before, there is guṇa; [and by *ṅsiṅsoś ca* (6.1.110), the substitution of *u* applies].

By [Pāṇini 6.1.108], there is the substitution of the prior vowel form (*pūrvarūpatva*) in *kroṣṭari*. By [Pāṇini 7.3.110], there is the *guṇa* substitution [of *ṛ* to *ar*] in *ṅsi* and *sarvanāmasthāna* endings, resulting in *kroṣṭau*. By [Pāṇini 7.3.119], there is the substitution of *at* for the *ghī*-stem, as well as the substitution of *au* (*autva*). [The phrase] "due to the treatment as *tṛc*" (*tṛjvadbhāvāt*) and so forth [is explained as follows].
The scope for the substitution of *tṛjvat* (treating the word like a word ending in *-tṛ*) is, for example, *kroṣṭroḥ* in the masculine;

the scope for *num* is, for example, *trapuṇe* and *jatune*. When both would apply simultaneously, as in *priyakroṣṭune* or *vanāya*, *num* occurs by virtue of the "priority of the preceding" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).

The scope for *nuṭ* is [in forms] such as *agnīnām* and *vāyūnām*; the scope for the substitution of *tṛjvat* is the same. When both would apply in a case such as *kroṣṭṝṇām*, *nuṭ* occurs by way of a prior conflict (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). This prior conflict, however, arises because the word *para* (in the rule) signifies "that which is desired."
It is obtained.
98. *caturanaḍuhorām udāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.98). The term *sarvanāmasthāne* (7.1.86) is supplied [by anuvṛtti], not *tṛtīyādiṣu* (7.1.97).

Since it would otherwise follow from the rule *āgamā anudātā bhavanti* (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 105) that augmentations are unaccented, [the present sūtra prescribes that the augment *ām* is] acute-accented.
The statement is for the sake of ensuring the acute accent (*udātta*).

It is intended here that the rule "specification by the final element" (*tadantavidhi*) applies, because of the metarule: "In the context of the *aṅga* designation, [the term refers] to that [final element] and its subsequent member" (Puṣpavṛtti 85). Thus, *priyacatvāḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

Although the rule "addition of pronouns and numerals" (Vārttika 113) would have required the numeral to be placed first, the word *priya* is placed first by the rule "optionally for *priya*" (Vārttika 114).

99. *abhsambuddhau* (7.1.99). This rule is stated because the preceding [sūtra] would have required the substitution of *ām* [for the case-ending]. Examples are: *he priyacatvaḥ* and *he priyānaḍvan*. In these cases, the vocative singular does not apply to the word *catuḥ* alone.

This is an example of [a rule] ending in that [element]. Although the suffix *anaj* is possible for the simple [stem] alone, nevertheless, the rule of "extension to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*) is intended here; therefore, it is an example of something ending in that.

100. After the verbal root *ṛ*, [the suffix *kta* takes the augment *iṭ*] (Pāṇini 7.1.100). For example: *kiritaḥ* ("scattered") and *giritaḥ* ("swallowed"). [The roots are] *kṛ* "to scatter" (DhP 1409) and *gṛ* "to swallow" (DhP 1410). [The suffix] *śa* is applied by Pāṇini 3.1.77 (*tudādibhyaḥ śaḥ*). [The example] *āstīrṇam* ("spread out"): [the root is] *stṛ*.

In the word *ācchādane* [from the root *stṛñ*—DhP 1484], there is the substitution of *n* by *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (8.3.59); the substitution of *ṇ* by *raṣābhyām* (8.4.1); and lengthening by *hali ca* (8.2.77). Regarding the word *viśīrṇam*: [it is derived from] the root *śṛ hiṃsāyām* (DhP 1488).

In the forms *mātṝṇām* and *pitṝṇām*, the long vowel [of the genitive plural] is applied by the rule *nāmi* (Pāṇini 6.4.3). Even though these words end in the vowel *ṛ*, this [substitution] does not occur here because they are not verbal roots (*adhātu*). Now, one might object:
"But surely this will not apply here due to the paribhāṣā concerning that which is taught by a general rule versus that which is taught by a specific rule (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*)."

In that case, what is the purpose of including the term *dhātu* (root) for the sake of excluding this [application]? To this he says: "even of that which is formed by a technical definition" (*lākṣaṇikasyāpi*), and so forth. For what reason, then, is there the inclusion of that which is formed by a technical definition? To this he says: "in *cikīrṣati*," and so forth. But how is it that the inclusion of that which is formed by a technical definition is obtained here, even though it is not explicitly intended? To this [he says]: "therefore..."

This is because of the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) consisting in the mention of the term *dhātu*. For this [mention] has the following purpose: so that [the rule] does not apply in cases such as *mātṛṇām* and *pitṛṇām*. If, in this context, there were no inclusion of that which is derived from a technical definition (*lākṣaṇika*), then in forms such as *mātṛṇām* and *pitṛṇām*, [the rule] would not apply precisely because they are derived from a technical definition.
The mention of the verbal root (*dhātu*) would be purposeless [if it were not intended to include derivatives]. Therefore, here the derivative form (*lākṣika*) is also included.

Consequently, in forms such as *cikīrṣati* and others, even when the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *ṭhajjhanagamāṃ sani* (Pāṇini 6.4.16), the [application of the grammatical operation] indeed takes place.

The addition of *ta* [in *tapara*] is for the sake of removing ambiguity. If it were stated simply as "ra," there would be doubt: is this a designation of the letter *r*, or is it a substitute (*yaṇ-ādeśa*) for the vowel *ṛ*?
101. *upadhāyāśca* (Pāṇini 7.1.101).

It has been stated that the substitution of *i* occurs for the letter *ṛ* at the end of a verbal root (*dhātu*). However, this does not apply to the *ṛ* that constitutes the penultimate (*upadhā*) of a root, yet it is desired there as well; this [sūtra] is for that purpose. For example: *kīrtayati*. [The root] *kṛt* in the sense of "proclaiming" (*saṃśabdana*) is in the *curādi* group and is augmented by the suffix *ṇic*. Now, one might object: [Why is this rule necessary?]

[Objection: Since the substitution of *i* for *ū* will occur precisely by the rule "ṭhūti-yūti-jūti-sāti-heti-kīrtayaś ca" (Pāṇini 3.3.97), how can there be the commencement of a new rule (*yoga*) for that purpose? [Response: This is not so; the irregularity (*nipātana*) would apply only in the domain of the suffix *ktin*. If that is the case, then in the preceding rule, the vowel *Añ* (the long *ā*) [of the root]— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument regarding the formation of feminine nouns from roots ending in *ū*, specifically addressing the necessity of a specific grammatical rule.]
[One might argue: "We shall specify [the rule] as 'of that which stands therein' (*atra tatsthasya*)"? This too is not possible;
for if that were the case, it would also apply in instances such as *añkārīyati* (he desires the sound *aṅ*). Therefore, this must be stated:
while one could have simply said "and after *kṛt*" (*kṛtaśca*), the statement "and after a penultimate vowel" (*upadhāyāśca*) is for the sake of variety (*vaicitryārtham*).
If it were stated simply as "of *kṛta*," would [the substitution] apply to the letter *t*? No, this is not so;

because in the preceding rule "of that which ends in *āṅ*," [the word *āṅ*] was employed as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). It is not possible to intend that same word as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Therefore, the meaning is: "In place of the vowel *ā*, which is the penultimate (*upadhā*) of that [word ending in *āṅ*], the substitution of the vowel *i* occurs. This is the intended sense.
The *vṛtti* commentary is contradicted [by this]. For here, the vowel *ṛ* is shown to be the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).

Therefore, just as this [term "of a stem"] is sometimes a qualifier of the member (*aṅga*), so too the term "ending in *ṭhañ*" (*ṭhAñtaḥ*) was a qualifier in the preceding rule, but here it is the qualificand.

102. *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya* (Pāṇini 7.1.102). When the substitution of *i* for the vowel of a root ending in *ṭh* (as prescribed by 7.1.100, *ṭhAñta iddhātoḥ*) would otherwise apply, the substitution of *u* is here ordained. For example: *pūrtaḥ* (or *pūrtāḥ*, as stated in the Kāśikā and Padamañjarī). [The root is] *pṛ* in the sense of "protecting" and "filling."

[The suffix] *kta* [is applied]. Because of the prohibition by the rule *na dhyākhyā-paśca* (Pāṇini 8.2.57), the substitution of *ṇatva* (nasalization) for the final consonant does not occur. "Vuvūrṣati": from the root *vṛ* (to choose/cover), Dhātupāṭha 1490.
"Mumūrṣati": from the root *mṛ* (in the sense of killing/harming), Dhātupāṭha 1492. "Sūsvūrṣati" [is formed similarly].
Thus [it is said]. Regarding the root *sthṛ* in the sense of "sound" and "affliction" (DhP 932), there is lengthening by the rule *aj-jhan-gamāṃ sani* (6.4.16); this [root] ends in the vowel *ṛ*.
Now, how is there the substitution of *u* here—[considering] *vṛṅ* in the sense of "partaking" (DhP 1509) and *vṛñ* in the sense of "choosing"?
Regarding *prāvuvūrṣate* and *prāvuvūrṣati*: is it not the case that the *ṛ*-vowel here is preceded by a labial (*oṣṭhya*) sound? Rather, it is preceded by a dental-labial (*dantyoṣṭhya*) sound.
To this he says: "Even that which is preceded by a dental-labial is [treated as] preceded by a labial," and so forth. As for who...

Since it is produced in both places, it receives the designation of either one; therefore, that which occurs in the dental-labial position is indeed [considered] to occur in the labial position as well. Thus, what is preceded by the dental-labial *ap* is precisely what is preceded by the labial *ap*. Now, why is this not the case in the word *samīrṇam*?
[An objection is raised: "Does the quality of having the letter *o* as its initial element not also exist here [in *oṣṭha*]? To this he replies: "For here, in *oṣṭhaḷ*, etc.

For in *oṣṭhaḷ*, it is indeed a constituent part (*aṅgāvayava*) [of the base]. In this context, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the constituent part of the base (*aṅga*) is understood, not the constituent part of a prefix (*upasarga*). Proximity, moreover, follows from the fact that the base (*prakṛti*) is the subject under discussion.

But for a prefix (*upasarga*), there is no proximity because of the opposite case. [As stated in] "after *i* and *u*, [the substitution of *ai* and *au*]" and so forth. The scope of the substitutions *itva* and *utva* is, for example, *āstīrṇam* and *pūrta*;
the scope of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is, for example, *cayanam* and *cāyaka*. Here, both [rules apply].
One obtains the forms *āstaraṇam*, *āstārakaḥ*, *niparaṇam*, and *nipārakaḥ*; here, guna and vṛddhi substitutions occur by way of mutual exclusion (*vipratiṣedha*).
103. *Bahulam chandasi* (Pāṇini 7.1.103). [Examples:

*taturiḥ*, *jaguriḥ*. [These are formed] from the roots *tṛ* ("to cross") and *gṛ* ("to swallow") by applying either of the suffixes *kikin*—according to *ādṛgamahanajanakhanaghasaḥ kikinau liṭ ca* (3.2.171)—and subsequently [the substitution of] *u* for *ṛ* occurs.

Due to the status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) according to *dvirvacane'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59), the forms *tṛgṛ* are reduplicated; then, by *urat* (Pāṇini 7.4.66), the substitution of *u* occurs, resulting in *papritamam* and *vavritamam*.
These are derived from either the *kikin* suffixes applied to the roots *pṛ* and *vṛ*, respectively, according to their original position.
The suffix *tamap* is applied according to the rule "ṭhaC-iśāyane tamap" (Pāṇini 5.3.55) following a word ending in the *kip* suffix.
Thus ends the first quarter of the seventh chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who is like a Bodhisattva.
Now begins the second quarter of the seventh chapter.
1. *sici vṛddhiḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (Pāṇini 7.2.1).

This rule is introduced because the *guṇa* substitution [prescribed by] *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ* (7.3.84) would otherwise apply. The two terms *sici* and *parasmaipadeṣu* are both [governed by this rule].

These are two locative case endings (*parasaptamyau*). In that context, the "subsequent" status (*paratvam*) of *sic* is in relation to the stem (*aṅga*), whereas for the *parasmaipada* suffixes, it is in relation to *sic*. Regarding the phrase "when followed by a *parasmaipada* suffix": that after which the *parasmaipada* suffix is subsequent is so described. Regarding the phrase "of that which ends in *ik*" (*igantasya*): this occurs upon the presentation of the rule "guṇa and vṛddhi substitutions take place in place of *ik*" (Pāṇini 1.1.3).

The stem (*aṅga*) ending in *sat* is specified, and by means of this specification, the rule of "extension to the end of that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies; thus he says: "Vṛddhi occurs for a stem ending in *i*.
[Examples are: *acaṣīt*, *anaiṣīt*. [The roots are] *ciñ* (DhP 1251) "to gather" and *ṇīj* (DhP 1094) "to lead."

In the sense of "attaining" (*prāpaṇe*), the *luṅ* suffix is used for the past tense; by *ṭhcleḥ sic* (Pāṇ. 3.1.44), the *sic* affix is applied; by *ṭhekācaḥ* (Pāṇ. 7.2.10) and other rules, there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*; the augment *aṭ* is added; while *nityaṃ ṅtiḥ* (Pāṇ.
3.4.99) is being supplied as a governing rule, the elision of the final *ikāra* occurs by *ṭhitaśca* (Pāṇ. 3.4.100); [and finally] *astisico'pṛkte* (Pāṇ. 7.3.96).
Thus, the augment *iṭ* is applied; while the rule *ṭhiṣkoḥ* (8.3.57) is in effect, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (8.3.59). Examples are *alāvīt* and *apāvīt*.
Here, the *luṅ* suffix is applied as before, and the augment *iṭ* is added by the rule *ārdhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ* (7.2.35).

As before, there is the substitution of *īṭ*, and by the rule "ṭhiṭa īṭi" (Pāṇini 8.2.28), there is the elision of *sic*. The example "akārṣīt" is easy to understand. Now, one might object that here, due to its being an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), the *guṇa* substitution ought to occur first; its status as internal is because it depends upon the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.

But is not the substitution of *vṛddhi* for *ādguṇa* considered extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*) with respect to the *sic* suffix that follows the *parasmaipada* endings? To this he says: "Even though it is intrinsic," and so forth. If the *vṛddhi* were to occur because of its intrinsic nature, then this statement would be purposeless.

Therefore, by the force of this statement, even though it is external, *vṛddhi* overrides *guṇa*. If that is so, then just as *vṛddhi* overrides even the internal *guṇa* by the force of the statement, it would likewise override the substitution of *uvaṅ*; and consequently, forms such as *nyanuvīt* and *nyadhuvīt* would not be possible.

How would this be established? To this he says: "He should weave across, he should weave upwards," and so forth. For where there is no prohibition of *vṛddhi*, there this [rule] operates by the force of the statement itself, overriding other rules. But here, since the suffix is marked with *ṅ* and is *s-it*, *vṛddhi* applies by the rule "before a suffix marked with *k* or *ṅ*" (Pāṇini 1.1.5).
It is prohibited; and once it is prohibited, being existent, it is not able to subvert the substitution of *uvaṅ*.

Therefore, when that [substitution] has been prohibited, the substitution of *uvaṅ* is applied by the rule "aci śnudhātu" (Pāṇini 6.4.77) and so forth. Furthermore, the marker *ṅ* here [in the root] is for the purpose of [indicating] the root "ṇū in the sense of praising."

Since the roots *dhā* (DhP 1397) and *dhū* in the sense of "shaking" (DhP 1398) are listed among the *kuṭādi* group, would not the prohibition [of *guṇa*] also be set aside by the rule *gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.1), just as *guṇa* is set aside by *vṛddhi* according to their respective scopes? This is not so; for in the case of *guṇa*...

An augment (*vṛddhi*) is not introduced when [the condition for its application] has not yet been reached; however, a prohibition applies both when [the condition] has been reached and when it has not. In this regard, according to the principle *yenanāprāpte* (Pāṇini 1.4.2), it is logical that only the *guṇa* substitution should be sublated, and not the prohibition. Thus we have *acyoṣṭa* and *aploṣṭa*. [The roots are] *cyuṅ*, *chuṅ*, and *jyuṅ*. (Na...)*
[The roots] *iyuṅ*, *pruṅ*, and *pluṅ* [meaning] "to go" are found in the Dhātupāṭha (DhP 955, 956, 957). 2. Regarding the rule *ato lāntasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.2):
this word *anta* signifies a part (*avayava*), as in *vastrāntaḥ* (the edge of a garment) or *vasanāntaḥ* (the hem of a cloth); and it also...

It denotes proximity, as in the expression "one should follow one's beloved as far as the edge of the water" (*udakāntam*); the meaning is "near the water. If, in this context, the word *anta* were taken to mean a "part," then the inclusion of the term *anta* here would be purposeless; for it is precisely for that reason [to indicate proximity] that it was employed.

The purpose [of the word *anta*] is so that [the rule] may apply to that which has *r* or *l* at its end (*rephalakārānta*). And this is already established by the rule "that by which an operation is prescribed applies to what ends with it" (*yena vidhis tadantasya*, 1.1.72). Therefore, considering that only the word signifying proximity (*samīpa*) is intended here, he says: "as far as the *r* and *l* are proximate to the end."

If, then, by the rule "yasaya samīpāvataḥ" (P. 1.1.69), that which has *la* as its final element (*larant*) is indicated, then that which undergoes *vṛddhi* would not be indicated. And in that case, by the rule "ṭhalo'ntyasya" (P.

1.1.52), the substitution would apply to the final [element] of the suffix *ya*; [namely,] to the final element of the suffix *ya* that has *la* as its final element and is situated near the vowel *a*, which is the locus of the *vṛddhi*.

To the objection that [the rule] would apply because of the absence of *i*, he says: "Therefore, in its place (*sthāne*). He thinks as follows: since the vowel *a* is explicitly mentioned [in the rule], it is understood that the *vṛddhi* substitute occurs in the place of *a* alone. [Examples such as] *akṣārīt* and so forth;
[from the roots] *kṣara* "to move" (DhP 8.51), *tsara* "to go stealthily" (DhP 5.54), and *jvala*...

These are the forms of the roots *dīp* (DhP 804), and *hval* and *hyal* meaning "to move" (DhP 805, 806). [The author states: "This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the optional rule [Pāṇini 7.2.7] *ato halāder laghoḥ*.
By this, he demonstrates that this rule serves a restrictive purpose (*niyamārtha*).

Examples include *ṭhnyakhorīt*, *nyamīlīt*, and so forth. [The roots] *khura* in the sense of "cutting" (Dhātupāṭha 1342) and *mīla*, *śmīla*, *smīla*, *śmīla* in the sense of "closing the eyes" (Dhātupāṭha 517–520). Examples include *mā bhavānaṭīt* and *mā bhavānaśīt*. [The roots] *aṭa* and *paṭa* in the sense of "going" (Dhātupāṭha 295, 296).

The root *ṭhā* is listed as "eating" (*bhojane*) [in the Dhātupāṭha 1523]. The connection with *māṅ* is for the purpose of prohibiting the augment *āṭ* by the rule *na māṅyoge* (Pāṇini 6.4.74). The form *bhavān* is included here for the sake of dispelling doubt; for otherwise, there would be no distinction from other instances.

Regarding "ṭhavabhrīt": the roots *abhra*, *vabhra*, *mabhra*, and *cara* have the meaning of "motion" (*gatyarthāḥ*) [Dhātupāṭha 556–559]. Regarding "aśvallīt": the roots *śvala* and *śvalla* mean "swift motion" (*āśugamane*) [Dhātupāṭha 549, 550]. Regarding "they are not proximate to that [the augment iṭ]": this is because they are separated by the letters *bha* and *la*.

3. *vadavrajahalantasyācaḥ* | (Pāṇini 7.2.3) This rule is commenced for the purpose of excluding [the application of] *iṭ*. Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *vad* and *vraj*, since the *vṛddhi* substitution is established by their being *halanta* (ending in a consonant)? To this he says: "For the purpose of setting aside the optional alternative."

And so forth. [The author] will state the optional rule "ato halādeḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.7); this [present rule] is for the purpose of superseding that [optional rule]. For example: *apākṣīt*. [The root] *ḍupacaṣ* is used in the sense of "cooking" (Dhātupāṭha 996). By the rule "coḥ kuḥ" (8.2.30), there is the substitution of *k* [for *c*]. For example: *abhaitsīt*. [The root] *bhidir* is used in the sense of "cleaving."
(dhā.pā. 1439), by the rule *ṭhkhari ca* (8.4.55), there is the substitution of *c*—that is, the letter *t* replaces the letter *d*.
Thus: *arautsīt*. [The root] *rudhir* is used in the sense of "obstructing" (dhā.pā.
1438). Regarding the passage beginning with *atra*: *vadivrajyoḥ* is one rule, and *acaḥ* is the second; thus...
When there is a split of the rule (yogavibhāga), the desired result is indeed established even without the mention of "ending in a consonant" (halanta). [The question] "How?

is asked by one who does not believe this is possible. [The author] demonstrates how it is established through the split of the rule by means of the sūtra beginning with "vadivraji" and so forth. In that regard, in the first rule:

From the preceding sūtra, the term "ataḥ" (of *at*) is carried over as the element to be replaced (*sthānin*). By this, forms such as *avādīt* and *avrājīt* are established. Then, regarding the second sūtra, "tato yadaca," since the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*) is optional according to one's preference, [the desired result follows].

The augment *aj* is specified by means of the term *aṅga* (stem) currently under discussion—that which is the *aj* of the stem. By this, there is *vṛddhi* substitution for the vowel of the stem, regardless of its position, when *sic* follows. Thus, forms such as *apākṣīt* are also established.
If this is so, then a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) should simply be made; what is the purpose of including the mention of *hal* (consonant)? To this [the author replies]:

He says: "Regarding this very point," and so forth. For what purpose is the inclusion of a collection of consonants (*hal-samudaya*) intended, such that this effort is made for its sake? To this he replies: "In this case as well," and so forth. [The example] *arāṅkṣīt*: from the root *rañj* (DhP 1167), meaning "to color. [The example] *asāṅkṣīt*.

[The root] *sañj* means "to adhere" (*dhātupāṭha* 987). Now, it might be argued that an augmenting vowel (*ac*) belonging to a verbal base (*aṅga*) is prescribed to undergo *vṛddhi* when followed by the suffix *sic*; however, in this case, it is not possible for the suffix *sic* to follow immediately after an *ac* that is part of the base, such that *vṛddhi* could be prescribed for it by this rule. For instance, in the case of a base ending in the vowel *a*:
In that case, there ought to be elision by the rule "elision of *at*" (6.4.48). Nor can it be argued that the augment *vṛddhi* will supersede the elision of *at* by virtue of this specific statement;
for if the *vṛddhi* were to apply only to what ends in the vowel *a*, the inclusion of the pratyāhāra [in the sūtra] would be purposeless, since [the word] "of *at*" (*ataḥ*)...

One should speak thus. Or rather—that too is possible; for while it is certainly possible for a stem ending in *a*, such as *yāva* and so forth, there is no distinction made for it whether the *vṛddhi* [strengthening] occurs or not. However, in the case of a stem ending in an *iK* vowel, [the result follows] precisely by the rule "there is *vṛddhi* in the *sic*" (*sici vṛddhiḥ*, 7.2.1), and so on.

Vṛddhi has been prescribed [for vowels], but for the diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*), there is none at all, because of the rule "ātvam upadeśe'śiti" (Pāṇini 6.1.45), which prescribes the substitution of *ā* [for *ai* and *au*]. If it is argued that [the condition of being followed by a vowel] exists in cases such as *udavoḍhām* and *udavoḍham*, this is not so; for the elision of *ḍh* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). Therefore, this [vowel *u*] is in no way immediately followed by a vowel.

The suffix *sic* occurs when followed by a *parasmaipada* ending. And this rule is explicitly stated; therefore, according to the principle that "that by which there is no intervention [is considered as if immediate] even when there is intervention, on account of the authority of the explicit statement" (*Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā* 46), just as the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs in forms such as *apākṣīt*, it likewise occurs in forms such as *arāṅkṣīt*.

[Objection: "There will be *vṛddhi* [by P. 7.2.115]; therefore, there is no need for the mention of *hal*. To this, he says: "For otherwise," and so forth. There is a separation by a single phoneme (*varṇa*) everywhere; however, there might be a separation by a collection of consonants (*halsamudāya*) in certain cases, such as *ārāṅkṣīt*. But in cases like *apākṣīt*, there is none; that being the case...

According to the principle just mentioned regarding the inclusion of the letter *h*, [the rule] would apply only where there is an intervention by a single phoneme— as in *apākṣīt* and similar forms— but it would not apply where there is an intervention by more than one phoneme— as in *arāṅkṣīt* and similar forms.
For example, in forms such as *pipaṭhiṣīta*, [the substitution] does not occur because of the intervention of two vowels (*ac*);
however, when there is the mention of *hal* (consonants), it does occur even when there is intervention by a collection of consonants (*hal-samudāya*),
due to the force of the mention of *hal*.
Regarding the forms *udavoḍhām* and *udavoḍham*, why does the vṛddhi substitution not occur for the root *vah*?

If one were to object: "Because the rule *ahalantāt* [Pāṇini 6.1.104] applies once the *ḍh*-elision has been performed," [the author] replies to such an objection: Vṛddhi is indeed applied here; however, its *o*-substitution [is subsequently applied].

In order to demonstrate that [the form] is prescribed, he says "udavoḍhām," etc. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the verbal roots and so forth are included. From the root *vah* preceded by the prefix *ud*, there is the suffix *luṅ*; for the two forms *tas* and *thas*, the substitutes *tām* and *ām* are applied respectively by the rule "tasthasthamipām" (Pāṇini 3.4.101), and so on.

There is the *vṛddhi* substitution conditioned by a final consonant; the change to *ḍha* by "ṭhho ḍhaḥ" (8.2.31); the elision of the suffix *sic* by "jhalo jhali" (8.2.26); the change to *ṣa* by "jhaṣastathordhodhaḥ" (8.2.40); and the change to *ṣṭu* by "ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ" (8.4.41). [The rule] "sahivaherodavarṇasya" (6.3.112) applies.

Thus [is established] the substitution of *o*. Why, in that case, does the substitution of *ai* not again trigger a *vṛddhi* substitution? To this he says: "When that has been performed, again," and so forth. For there is only one rule for *vṛddhi* here; and since the *vṛddhi* has already been effected by that very rule, the *vṛddhi*-rule, having its purpose already fulfilled, does not operate again. Therefore, it does not [apply].
But there is indeed an occurrence of *vṛddhi*.
Then, how does *vṛddhi* occur in the case of *sauḍhāmitriḥ* once *o*-substitution has been applied? To this he says:
"In cases where," and so forth. Where *vṛddhi* has already been applied previously, the rule for *vṛddhi* has already fulfilled its purpose (*kṛtārthatvāt*).

Since it does not operate again, there is no [subsequent] *vṛddhi*; however, in the case of *soḍhāmitri*, the *vṛddhi* was not applied. Therefore, because its purpose has not yet been fulfilled, the rule for *vṛddhi* does indeed operate, and thus *vṛddhi* occurs. And that *vṛddhi* occurs for the vowel *o*, not for the vowel *a*.

At the time of prescribing the *vṛddhi* [vowel substitution], it is only the vowel *o* that is eligible for *vṛddhi*, because it is the one present [in the context]. From the root *sah*, there is the *niṣṭhā* suffix (*kta*); when the substitutions such as *ḍha* have been applied therein, the form *soḍha* arises.
[The compound] *soḍhāmitraḥ* means "one by whom the enemy has been withstood. [The patronymic] *tasyāpatyam* ("his offspring") follows from the rule *ata iñ*.

(4.1.95), [the rule] *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ* (7.2.117) prescribes vṛddhi. Since the status of being "ending in that" (*tadanta*) is already established by *yena vidhistadantasya* (1.1.72), the inclusion of the word *anta* ("end") is for the sake of removing ambiguity. If it were stated simply as *halo'caḥ*, an ambiguity would arise: would it mean "of a stem (*aṅga*) ending in a vowel (*ac*) preceded by a consonant (*hal*)"? Or...
Does the increase (vṛddhi) apply [to the whole word], or does it apply to the vowel at the end of that which ends in a consonant?

4. *neṭi* | (7.2.4) The *vṛddhi* that was applicable by the rule "of a vowel ending in a consonant" (*halantasyāca*) is prohibited by this [sūtra], because of the principle: "A rule or a prohibition applies to that which is immediately preceding" (*anantarasya vidhirvā bhavati pratiṣedho vā*). (Vyāḍipāda 19).

Having done so, [the forms] "adevīt" and "asevīt" are derived. [The roots are] "divu" (DhP 1107) in the sense of "playing and so forth," and "ṣivu" (DhP 1108) in the sense of "sewing" (the variant reading "sivu" is noted in the Dhātupāṭha).
Since the *vṛddhi* augment is prohibited, the *guṇa* substitution applies by the rule "pugantalaghūpadhasya" (Pāṇini 7.3.86).
"ṭhakoṣīt, amoṣīt. [The roots] *kuṣa* "to extract" (DhP 1518) and *muṣa* "to steal" (DhP 1530).
[Objection: But surely here, because this [substitution] is internal (*antaraṅga*)—[Kaiyaṭa's commentary].
This is the objection; "this is not so" is the refutation; both of these have their meaning already explained.
5. *hyanta-kṣaṇa-śvasa-jāgṛ-ṇi-śvi-vid-i-tām* (Pāṇini 7.2.5). *agṛhīt*: from the root *grah* (Dhātupāṭha 1533), meaning "to seize. *asyamīt*:
from the roots *stham*, *svan*, and *dhvan* (Dhātupāṭha 826–828), meaning "sound. *avamīt*: from the root *ṭu vama*.

Regarding *udgiraṇe* (DhP 849): *adyatīt* (he has vomited). Regarding *vyayavitasamutsarge* (DhP 1932): *akṣaṇīt* (he has cast away). Regarding *kṣaṇu hiṃsāyām* (DhP 1465): *aśvasīt* (he has breathed). Regarding *śvasa prāṇane* (DhP 1069): *ajāgarīt* (he has awakened). Regarding *jāgṛ*...

In *nidrākṣaye* (from root √lī, DhP 1072); *ailayīt* and *ānayīt* from √īḍ, "to diminish" (DhP 1888) [the DhP reads *pariharaṇe*]; and from √īḍ, "to incite" (DhP 1660)—[the DhP reads *īla*]—with the causative suffix *ṇic* of the *curādi* class; and by rule 3.1.51, *aiṅ* is substituted for the penultimate vowel in *nonayati*.

When the *sic* suffix is prohibited, only *āṭ* occurs by the rule *ṭhāḍajādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.4.72), and there is *vṛddhi* by the rule *āṭaśca* (Pāṇini 6.1.90). Thus we have *aśvayīt*. The root is *ośvi* (meaning "to move" or "to increase," Dhātupāṭha 1010). Similarly, we have *aragīt* and *alagīt* from the roots *rage* and *lage* (meaning "attachment," Dhātupāṭha 853–854).
Regarding the doubt: *śaṅkāyām*—[the suffix] *ghañ* is applied by *dhā.pā.* 785, 786; [the rule] *asthāgīt* applies. *ṣṭage saṃvaraṇe* (DhP 790). Regarding *ṭhakakhīt*: *kakhe hasane* (DhP 784).

"And that [vṛddhi] is not prohibited by the rule 'neṭi' (Pāṇini 1.1.5). This means that the prohibition applies to the immediate vṛddhi characterized by a consonant-final suffix, and not to the preceding one. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *ṇi* and *śvi*?
For, since it is internal (*antaraṅga*), the guṇa substitution ought to occur here by virtue of that very fact, once [the suffix] has been applied...

[An objection is raised: "Since the substitution of *ay* occurs for the *guṇa*, and because [the root] then ends in *y*, the prohibition regarding *t* and *th* will automatically apply. To this, he says: "And not," and so forth. This internal character (*antaraṅgatva*) was stated while assuming its existence in the case of *sic*; now, however, it is shown that internal character does not exist in *sic* at all.
He states [the reason] for showing this with the words "yadi" (if), etc. For what reason would the mention of *niṣ* be useless?

To this he says: "guṇāyādeśayoḥ" (in the case of *guṇa* and *āyādeśa*). If, then, there is no *antaraṅga* status for *sic*, as was stated [regarding the rule]: "Even though *guṇa* is *antaraṅga*, this..."

Does this not contradict the statement, "An augment (*vṛddhi*) subverts [a rule] by virtue of its explicit mention"? There is no contradiction, because that is stated with reference to what is superimposed (*adhyāropya*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "Now" (*atha*), the intention will be explained hereafter. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *jāgṛ*?

Regarding the question, "What is the reason that the mention of *jāgṛ* need not be made?", he states the intention with which he asked this, beginning with "jāgro 'viciṇṇalṅitsu" and so forth. For example, in forms such as *jāgarayati*, [the rule] "aco ñṇiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.115) would apply...
The rule for *guṇa* subverts the *vṛddhi* [of the root] in the case of the wakeful state (*jāgṛ*), and likewise it will also subvert the *vṛddhi* in the case of the *sic* affix,
because the *guṇa* rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *vṛddhi* rule— as in "he praised" (*agṛṇe kata*). For when the *guṇa* has not yet been applied,
whatever *vṛddhi* would otherwise occur due to the *sic* affix is subverted by the *guṇa*, since the latter is an exception to the former.

Because the rule for *guṇa* substitution has not yet achieved its purpose, that [vṛddhi] will not be sublated by this statement. What then? When the *guṇa* has been applied and the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* has occurred, the subsequent *vṛddhi* that would otherwise apply by the rule "of a stem ending in *ṛ* preceded by *ta*" (Pāṇini 7.2.2) is here prescribed as prohibited; and it cannot be [sublated] by the *guṇa*.
She [the rule *guṇa*] cannot be sublated. For the rule *jāgro 'viciṇṇalṅitsu* (Pāṇini 7.3.85) does not venture to apply again, because its purpose has already been fulfilled.
Nor is there any other characteristic of *guṇa* that could sublate the subsequent *vṛddhi*. In that case, if...

The mention of "jāgṛ" is not made [in the rule], for otherwise, by the rule "ato lāntasya" (Pāṇini 7.2.2), a vṛddhi would occur. The objector says "atha" and so forth: if the vṛddhi were to occur again even after the guṇa has been applied, then the prescription of guṇa in the domain of vṛddhi would be purposeless. Therefore...

By virtue of the capacity of the rule prescribing the *guṇa* substitution, even when the *guṇa* has been applied and the replacement by *r* (*raparatva*) has occurred, the subsequent *vṛddhi* prescribed by "ata upadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.116)—which applies to a stem ending in *laṭ*—would otherwise be required; that [vṛddhi] is prohibited, as in the case of *jāgarayati*. After the *guṇa* has been applied and the replacement by *r* has occurred, that which would otherwise apply... [the vṛddhi is barred].

The term *upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116) refers to a vowel-substitution (*vṛddhi*) that occurs at a subsequent time; even that does not take place, because it is superseded by *guṇa*. This is shown by the phrase "and so on" (*tathā ca*). By the very force of the prescription of *guṇa*, even a *vṛddhi* that would occur at a later stage is superseded; for otherwise—

Even the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) that would occur subsequently by the rule *ṭhata upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116), once *guṇa* has been applied and *ra*-substitution has followed, does not take place; for it is superseded by the *guṇa*. This is expressed in the phrase "And so forth.
By the force of the prescription of *guṇa*, even the lengthening that would occur at a later stage is superseded by the *guṇa*.

He confirms this very point: "And thus, the prohibition regarding the *ciṇ* and *ṇal* suffixes becomes meaningful only if the *vṛddhi* that occurs at a later time is also sublated; otherwise, once the *guṇa* has been applied and the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* has taken place, the *vṛddhi* prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.2.116], 'ata upadhāyāḥ,' would necessarily have to occur."
The prohibition that is made regarding what has already occurred would be purposeless.
Therefore, it is established that even an augment (vṛddhi) occurring at a later time is superseded by the guṇa substitute.
Consequently, it is indeed possible to omit the mention of the root *jāgṛ*. Thus, the mention of *jāgṛ* having been rejected, [the rule stands].
The other says: "That is done," and so forth. For the sake of clarity, the mention of "waking" (jāgrat) is made for one who is not able to understand in this way.
6. *ūrṇoter vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 7.2.6). This statement is for the purpose of providing an option (*vikalpa*) when a compulsory (*nitya*) *vṛddhi* substitution would otherwise have applied.

7. *ato halāderlaghoḥ* (7.2.7). Since the prohibition [of lengthening] established by *neṭi* (7.2.4) would otherwise apply, this rule is commenced for the purpose of providing an option. Examples: *akaṇīt*, *akāṇīt*. [The roots are] *aṇa*, *raṇa*, *vaṇa*, *kaṇa*, *bhaṇa*, *kvaṇa*.
Thus it is listed in the *bhū* class [of roots] at *dhā.pā.* 444–446, 449, 447, and 450. "He ran" (*araṇīt*) and "he ran" (*arāṇīt*); *raṇi* is also found in that very same place.
"He bent" (*nyakuṭīt*); *kuṭa* in the sense of "crookedness" (*kauṭilye*) is at *dhā.pā.* 1366. "He covered" (*nyapuṭīt*).

Regarding the root *ṭhpuṭa* in the sense of "joining" (*saṃśleṣaṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 1367): one might object that since this root belongs to the *kuṭādi* group, when the suffix *ṅ* follows, the prohibition by the rule *kṅiti ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5) will apply; therefore, is it not unnecessary to state *ataḥ* for the sake of restriction? To this, he says: *ataḥ*.

Regarding the phrase "this being absent" (*ityetasminnasati*), and so forth: if the word "from this" (*ataḥ*) were not stated, then one would necessarily have to carry forward the rule *vadavrajahalanta-syācaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.3); otherwise, because no specific locus would be indicated, the optional *vṛddhi* substitution would apply only to the light vowel (*laghu*).

It might be argued that [the rule would apply] in cases such as *adevīt*, but it would not apply to the vowel *a* in cases such as *akāṇīt*. However, if the reference to *aj* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], then this *vṛddhi* substitution would be characterized by *aj* (i.e., it would replace a short *a*), and not characterized by *iK* (i, u, ṛ, ḷ), because its locus (*sthānin*) is specifically specified. For indeed, that [substitution] for which the locus is not explicitly specified...
The scope of the *vṛddhi* substitution characterized by *iK* is [limited to where it is explicitly prescribed], and not even that place where a *sthāna* (original element) is indicated;

consequently, the prohibition [stated in] "ṭhṅiti ca" (Pāṇini 1.1.5) would not apply there, because of the governing rule "ikaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.1.3). Therefore, in cases such as *nyakuṭīt* and *nyapuṭīt*, [the substitution occurs] optionally.

The word "ataḥ" must be stated for the purpose that there should be no *vṛddhi* [substitution]. For example, in *ataṣīt* and *arakṣīt*. [The roots] *takṣū* and *tvakṣū* mean "to make thin" (*tanūkaraṇe*), and *rakṣa* means "to protect" (*pālane*). Here, *vṛddhi* is prescribed for the vowel *a* immediately following the suffix *sic*, but not...

In some cases, the suffix *sic* occurs immediately [after the root]. In such instances, according to the principle "that by which there is no intervention [is considered as if it were not intervening] even when there is intervention,
on account of the authority of the explicit statement" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 46), the substitution of *vṛddhi* must take place despite the intervention.
Just as the substitution occurs for the short *a* in *akāṇīt*, should it not likewise necessarily occur by way of *vṛddhi* for the short *a* in *acakāsīt*?
With this intention, he asks: "Why does it not happen here in *acakāsīt*? [The root is] *cakāsṛ*.

In the root *dīp* (DhP 1074), the phrase "by which" (*yena*) and so forth constitutes the rebuttal. The statement "separation by a consonant (*hal*) is relied upon" means that the term *halanta* (ending in a consonant) is understood as a carry-over (*anuvṛtti*).
As for the question "Why [is there] *laghoḥ*?", he who asked thus [intends to show] the necessity of the mention of *laghu*.

Wishing to object, he says: "Now, furthermore," and so on. If it is thus postulated that, by the force of the authority of the statement, an intervention (*vyavadhāna*) is resorted to by means of a consonant (*hal*) but not by a vowel (*ac*), then it should have been stated as "after a light [vowel] preceded by *ataḥ*";
for otherwise, [the rule] would apply even in cases such as *atakṣīt*, since here there is indeed an intervention by a consonant.

There is no intervention [of a vowel] here. Now, if it is further postulated—on the basis of the authority of the statement, "That by which there is no intervention [is considered non-intervening] even when there is intervention" (Vyāḍipañjikā 46)—that intervention by a single phoneme (*varṇa*) is accepted, but not intervention by multiple [phonemes], then the purpose of the rule *laghoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.190) is not served; this is not so.
If this were so conceived, [the rule] would apply even in cases such as *atakṣīt* where there is an intervention by more than one letter; therefore, he says: "That is done," and so forth.

8. *neḍvaśi kṛti* (Pāṇini 7.2.8). Regarding the augment *iṭ* which will be prescribed by the rule *ārdhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ* (7.2.35), this [present rule] provides its prohibition in cases where there is no prohibition based on the nature of the verbal root (*prakṛtilakṣaṇa*).

The purpose of the section on prohibitions (*pratiṣedhakāṇḍa*) preceding this will be stated in the rule concerning the restriction for roots beginning with *krī* (Pāṇini 7.2.13). However, in the case of suffixes other than those [mentioned there], such as in the word *īśitṛ*, since there is no presence of the augment *iṭ*, the [prohibition] based on the cause of the root— namely, that "a monosyllabic root which is unaccented in its original form" (Pāṇini 7.2.10)— [would otherwise apply].

A negation expresses the very absence of that [thing]. Regarding "Īśvara": from the root *īś* in the sense of "sovereignty" (*aiśvarye*, Dhātupāṭha 1020), the suffix *varac* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.175 (*stheśabhāsa-* etc.). Regarding "Dīpra":
from the root *dīp* in the sense of "shining" (*dīptau*, Dhātupāṭha 1150), the suffix *ra* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.167 (*namikamyi-* etc.).

Regarding "bhasma": from the root *bhas* in the sense of "threatening" or "shining" (*bharsana-dīptyoḥ*, Dhātupāṭha 1100), the suffix *manin* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.74, *āto maninkvanibvanipaśca*, and further by 3.2.75, *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante*. Regarding "yācñā": from the root *yācṛ* in the sense of "begging" (*yācñāyām*).
[The root] *yaj* [takes the suffix] *naṅ* by the rule *yajayāca* (Pāṇini 7.3.66).

Regarding what was stated—that there is a purpose in the inclusion [of certain roots] in the list beginning with *varamana*—one should determine that this is indeed a restrictive enumeration (*parigaṇana*).
Thus, one might raise this objection: "If an enumeration is made in the form 'in the case of *varamana* and so forth,' then [what about] the root *ṣaṇ*?"

In cases such as *ṣaṇḍaḥ* [from the root] *dāne* (DhP 1464) by the rule *ṭhñamantāḍḍaḥ* (PaṃU 1.104), and *śaṅkhaḥ* [from the root] *śamaḥ* by the rule *śamaḥ khaḥ* (PaṃU 1.113), the prohibition would not apply; therefore, he says— “the example ‘varamanādau’ is given” in order to show that this enumeration does not apply to those cases.

Thus: "Now, in that case," and so forth. The meaning is that the objection regarding the inclusion [of the word] under the alternative view of enumeration—namely, that it should be established by means of the *ḍa*-suffix belonging to the *uṇādi* class—is here refuted.
"This is for the purpose of demonstrating an example of occurrence"—here too, not...
This is connected with the phrase "this is an enumeration. An example of the possibility of a prohibition is being cited;
this is stated for the purpose of demonstrating that case where a prohibition regarding a *kṛt* suffix is possible.
It is for the purpose of demonstrating that case where a prohibition of *it* occurs after *vas* and so forth when a *kṛt* suffix follows.
