It was stated that this refers to "the beginning of the *varamanā*," and not that it is an exhaustive enumeration. In the examples "rurudiva" and "rurudima," because of the inclusion of the term *kṛt*, there is no prohibition of the *iṭ* augment belonging to the *ārdhadhātuka*.

9. *titutratathasisusarakaseṣu ca* (Pāṇini 7.1.9). This rule is commenced for the sake of words such as *avaśāt*. Regarding the word *tanti*: it is derived from the root *tan* in the sense of "extension" (Dhātupāṭha 1463), with the suffix *ktic* applied according to the rule *kticktau ca saṃjñāyām* (3.3.174).

By the rule "anudātopadeśavanatitanotyādīnām" (6.4.37), the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) would apply, and by the rule "anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ kṅiti" (6.4.15), lengthening (*dīrgha*) would also apply;
however, both of these do not occur because of the prohibition "na ktici dīrghaśca" (6.4.39).

Regarding "dīptiḥ": the suffix *ktin* is applied by the Vārttika rule "ktinnābadibhyaśca" (Vārttika 307). There is no prohibition in cases such as *roditi* (he weeps) or *svapiti* (he sleeps), because the term *kṛt* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].
Regarding "saktuḥ": [the root is] *ṣaca* (or *saca*) in the sense of "to collect" (Dhātupāṭha 997).

Regarding "ṭhpatram": from the root *patlṛ* "to go" (DhP 8.45) and the root *tanu* "to expand" (DhP 14.86). Regarding "hastaḥ": from the root *hasa* "to laugh" (DhP 7.21; DhP reads *hase*). Regarding "lothaḥ": [from the root *luṭha*].
Regarding the root *ṭhlūñ* in the sense of "covering" (*cchadane*) [DhP 1483], and so forth: from the rule *ūrṇoter vibhāṣā* (7.2.6), the term *vibhāṣā* ("optionally") is understood to carry over;
moreover, that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, [the suffix -u] occurs only in the case of the *auṇādika* [derivation].

The prohibition must apply to the word *taśabda*, not to anything else. Since it is logical that only that for which a prohibition is required should be mentioned, the mention here is intended to be of the *ta* suffix belonging to the *auṇādika* group, and not of the *kta* suffix. Therefore, in the case of *hasitam*, the augment *iṭ* indeed occurs.

Regarding *ṭhkuṣṭham*: [the root] *kuṣ* is in the sense of "rubbing" (*niṣkaṣe*; Dhātupāṭha 1518). Regarding *kāṣṭham*: [the root] *kāsṛ* is in the sense of "shining" (*dīptau*; Dhātupāṭha 647). The substitution of *ṣ* for the letter *ś* occurs by the rule *vraścādi-* (Pāṇini 8.2.36), and the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭu* occurs by the rule *ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ* (8.4.41).
Regarding "kukṣiḥ": from the root *kuṣ*, there is the substitution of *ka* by *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si* (Pāṇini 8.2.41), and the substitution of *ṣ* by *ṣ* by *iṇkoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.57).
Regarding "ikṣuḥ": from the root *iṣu* meaning "desire" (Dhātupāṭha 1351; the Dhātupāṭha reads *iṣa*).
The substitution of *k* and *ṣ* occurs as before.

Regarding the term *ṭhakṣaram*: from the root *ṭhā* (DhP 1264), meaning "to pervade" (or, according to the Dhātupāṭha, "to pervade and to collect"), the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *vraścādi-* (Pāṇini 8.2.36), and the substitution of *k* occurs as before.

Regarding *ṭhśalkam*: from the root *ṭhśala* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*, DhP 8.4.3). Regarding *vatsaḥ*: from the root *bada* in the sense of "distinct speech" (*vyaktāyāṃ vāci*, DhP 10.9); there is the substitution of *ca* (the letter *t*), resulting in the letter *t*. [This is governed by] the rule: "It should be stated that for *agraha* and other roots, [the suffix *iṭ* is applied] after *ti-tu-tra-tha*" (*titutratheṣvagrahādīnāṃ vaktavyam*), according to Pāṇini 7.2.9.

This refers to the sūtra beginning with "titutratathasidham" (Pāṇini 7.2.9). The meaning is that this must be explained as having the sense that the prohibition [of the substitution of *iṭ*] does not apply to the roots *grah* and others even when followed by suffixes beginning with *ti*, *tu*, *ta*, *tha*, *si*, or *dha*. In this regard, the explanation is as follows:

here too, the term "vibhāṣā" (optionally) from Pāṇini 7.2.6 is understood to carry over; and since that is an option whose application is determined by specific conditions (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), therefore—
The prohibition [of the suffix *ktin*] for *graha* and so forth does not apply. By stating "the *graha*-type words beginning with *graha*," he indicates that the word "etc.
(*ādi*) has the sense of "type" (*prakāra*). What, then, are the types of *graha*?
He says: "those of which... and so forth. Regarding the term "seizure" (*nigṛhītiḥ*), [it is formed] by the rule "the suffix *ktin* occurs after a verbal root to form a feminine noun."

(3.3.94), the long vowel [is applied] by the rule *graho 'liṭi dīrghaḥ* (7.2.37), and the *samprasāraṇa* [occurs] for the roots beginning with *grah* by the rule (6.1.16). Regarding *upasnihitiḥ*: the root *ṣṇiha* means "affection" (*prītau*) [DhP 1200]. Regarding *nikucitiḥ*: the root *kuca* means "contraction" (*saṅkoce*).
[Regarding the root] *saṅkocane* (DhP 1368):

here, however, it is possible not to include the uṇādi derivatives; for, just as by the statement "uṇādi suffixes are applied diversely" (Pāṇini 3.3.1), [the rule] *ñamantāṅṅḥ* (Paṃ.u. 1.104) [is understood].

If it is thus that [the fault] occurs in these cases, should it not likewise occur in those [other cases]? It should be understood that their mention is for the purpose of avoiding conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

10. *ekāca upadeśe'nudātāt* (Pāṇini 7.2.10). Regarding the term *anudātāt*: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "that which has no *udātta* [accent]" is *anudātta*. This word *anudātta* is etymological (*anvartha*); for when a technical *anudātta* accent is intended, it applies to monosyllabic roots.
In that case, the verbal roots would have to be understood [as having this property] by implication;

and thus, the formal declaration (*pratijñāna*) that these other roots are *anudātta* (unaccented) would be purposeless. Furthermore, in this context, the mention of "single-vowel" (*ekāj*) serves as a qualifier for the "instruction" (*upadeśa*).
"In the *upadeśa*": this means in the list of roots (*prakṛtipāṭha*). "And [a root] that is unaccented (*anudātta*)": this requires the term "*upadeśe*" (in the *upadeśa*);
by this, he shows that the mention of "*upadeśa*" qualifies both [the preceding rule and the present one].
He will reveal its purpose in the counter-examples (*pratyudāharaṇa*). "Those which are thus recited in the list (*gaṇa*)."

Thus, by this he shows that they are to be known from the *gaṇapāṭha* itself. With the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) and so forth, he states the second reason for thorough knowledge. What, then, are those *aniṭ*-verses?
He says: "The root ending in a vowel is *aniṭ*" (*aniṭsvarāntaḥ*), and so forth. Whichever [root] there may be...

"Let it be seen—that is, let it be understood—that every root ending in a vowel or a consonant other than *n* is *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment). Here, *aniṭ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, meaning "that to which the *iṭ* does not belong.
He states an exception (*apavāda*) to the general rule (*utsarga*) "vowel-ending [roots] are *aniṭ*" with the words beginning "But these... and so forth.
They declare these roots beginning with *ad* and others to be *seṭ* (having the augment *iṭ*), which means they exist together with the augment *iṭ*.

Who says this? Those who know them—that is, those who know the distinction between *seṭ* and *aniṭ* roots. The term "ending in *a*" (*adantam*) is a bahuvrīhi compound; it refers to that whose final letter is the vowel *a* followed by *t* as an indicator (*tapara*). The inclusion of *t* as an indicator [is for the purpose of...]

For the sake of excluding long vowels: "ending in ṬhaÑ. This is also a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The inclusion of the marker *ta* (the *tapara*) is for the purpose of avoiding ambiguity. If it were stated simply as "ending in *ra*" (*rantam*), there would be a doubt: "Is this a reference to the letter *ra*, or to the suffix *Añ*? [To avoid this, the rule says] "and those ending in *Añ*."

The word *antānām* contains a genitive case used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*). Among those [roots] ending in ṛ, they declare that *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ* take an augment with *iṭ*. The inclusion of the *ta* (the long vowel) is for the purpose of excluding the short vowel. For, by the previous mention of roots ending in ṛ, it is understood here that the short vowel is what is being grasped. This is according to the rule "in the case of *śvi*, *ḍīṅ*, and those ending in *ṝ*," which refers to selection.

The seventh [section]. Among those ending in *i*, they declare that *śvi* and *ḍīṅ* are *seṭ* (having an *iṭ* augment). [These are] *ṭhṭua ośvi gativṛddhyoḥ* (DhP 1010) and *ḍīṅ vihāyasāgatau* (DhP 968).
[Regarding] "now also *śīṅ* and *śriñ*": the word "now" (*atha*) indicates immediate succession; [it refers] to these two.
Immediately after the two previously mentioned [roots], they declare that *śīṅ* and *śriñ* are also *seṭ*. [The roots are] *ṣvīṅ* "in sleep" (DhP 1032) and *śriñ* "in service" (DhP 897).
The phrase "standing in the gaṇa" is merely for the purpose of indicating their own forms (*svarūpa*), and not [to imply anything else].
The qualification [is] "for the purpose of excluding the *gaṇ*-roots," because [the application of the suffix would otherwise] be impossible for them. Regarding "ending in *ū*":

[this refers to roots such as] *lūñ* "to cut" (*dhā.pā.* 1483) and *pūñ* "to purify" (*dhā.pā.* 1482), and so forth. Regarding "and among those ending in *u*": this is a genitive of selection (*nirdhāraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*). [The root is] *ru* "to sound" (*dhā.pā.* 1034).

The root *ṣṇu* is used in the sense of "flowing" (*prasravaṇe*) [DhP 1038]; likewise, there are *kṣu* and *ūrṇoti*, etc. [DhP 1035–1040]. *ṭua kṣu* is used in the sense of "sound" (*śabde*) [DhP 1036], *ūrṇuñ* in the sense of "covering" (*ācchādane*) [DhP 1039], and *yu* in the sense of "mixing" (*miśraṇe*) [DhP 1033]—[according to some authorities, in the senses of both mixing and non-mixing].
The roots *ṣṭhṇu* in the sense of "praising" (DhP 1035) and *kṣṇu* in the sense of "sharpening" (DhP 1037). Regarding the form *āvadhiṣṭa*:

it is the *luṅ* (aorist) of the root *han* preceded by the prefix *ā*; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *āṅe'yamahanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.28); and [the substitution of *s* for *t*] is optionally applied by the rule *ātmanepadeṣv anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 2.4.44).
It is designated as *vadhādeśa*. Furthermore, it is taught with a final short vowel (*adanta*) so that the augment *vṛddhi* does not occur in forms such as *avadhīt*.
[In *avadhīt*,] the augment *iṭ* is added, and then the vowel *a* is elided by the rule "the elision of *a*" (*ato lopaḥ*, Pāṇini 6.4.48).
Now, for what purpose is the root *ūrṇoti* taught as having an udātta accent? It is so that the prohibition of *iṭ* may not apply.

[Question: Is this not so? For the prohibition of *iṭ* is stated for [roots] consisting of a single vowel (*ekāc*), and this [root *ūrṇu*] does not possess the status of being a single-vowel root. To this, he says: "The state of being like *ṇu* (*ṇuvadbhāva*) must be stated for *ūrṇu*. [And he adds: "the status of being a single-vowel root. Furthermore, there is an absence of *kutva* even at the end of a word, because *kutva* is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).

The irregularity (*anityatva*) [of the rule] is to be understood from the indications in the sūtras "bahvac-pūrvapadāt" (Pāṇini 4.4.64) and "alpāctaram" (Pāṇini 2.2.34). The word "iti" has the sense of "thus. The word "nipuṇam" means "correctly" or "without error. This is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). The word "samuccitāḥ" means...
The meaning is that they are established separately from the collection of verbal roots (dhātu-rāśi) which are mixed with both acute (udātta) and grave (anudātta) accents.

Regarding the word "tataḥ" (then): it means after the subsequent mention of the verbal roots ending in vowels. "Learn also those ending in consonants (hal-anta)"—the meaning is "understand them. "But *śaki*," etc.; [the root] *śaklṛ* is used in the sense of "ability" (*śakti*).
(Dhātupāṭha 1261): "And *ghas* [is also included]," and so forth. Now, one might object:

if there is a formal mention (*svarūpagrahaṇa*) of *had* and so on at the beginning, then by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, the absence of *iṭ* (*aniṭtva*) would indeed be established even for the substitute *ghas* prescribed by the rule "for *luṅ* and *san*, *artha* becomes *slṛ*" (Pāṇini 2.4.37).

For what purpose, then, is *ghas* mentioned separately? To this he says: "There is another root *ghas*. For this is indeed a different verbal root altogether, distinct from the one read in the *ad*-class (*adādi*) as *ghaslu adane* (DhP 715); this is its inclusion here, and not that of the substitute [for *ad*]. [The term] "*prasāraṇī*" [is used].
*Prasāraṇa* is *u*-vocalization (*ūṣmaprasāraṇa*); that which possesses this is called *prasāraṇī*. Regarding the term *vasitā*:

the root *vas* in the sense of "covering" (DhP 1023) is intended; however, *samprasāraṇa* is prescribed for the root *vas* in the sense of "dwelling" by the rule *vacisvapi...* (Pāṇini 6.1.15). By this, the root *vas* in the sense of dwelling [is meant].

This indicates that [the root] *prasāraṇī* is for the purpose of spreading out, and not for the purpose of covering. Regarding the passage beginning with *rabhiśca*: *rabha* (in the sense of impetuosity), *yabha* (in the sense of sexual intercourse), and *ḍu labhaṣ* (in the sense of attaining).

Regarding the passage beginning with *ṭhyamiñaṃ manteṣu*: the term *ñam* is a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated reference) starting from the letter *ñ* and ending with the letter *m* of the suffix *am*. [The roots are: *yama* (DhP 984) "to cease," *ramu* (DhP 853) "in play," *mana* (DhP 1176) "in knowing," and *ṇama* (DhP 985) "in bowing and sound."

(dhā.pā. 981), *hana* "in the sense of injury and motion" (dhā.pā. 1012), *gamlṛ* and *sṛplṛ* "in the sense of motion" (dhā.pā. 982, 983). Regarding the phrase "it is recited with the suffix *śyan*": by virtue of its association (*sāhacarya*) with the mention of *śyan*, the *divādi* class is indicated; the meaning is that it is recited in the *divādi* group. [This refers to] "those expressing a prohibition."

Thus [it is said]. Those whose nature (*śīla*) it is to express a prohibition are so described; for it is the verbal roots themselves, when accompanied by the mark of the anudātta accent, that convey the prohibition, and thus they are called "prohibitive. Alternatively—the Teacher has [stated] a prohibition of *iṭ* with respect to himself...

Because they cause one to recite or cause one to express, they are called "expressive of prohibition. And thus the connection should be made here: among those roots ending in *ṇam* which are expressive of prohibition, *yam* is designated as lacking the *iṭ* augment; likewise for *ram*, and so forth. Now...

Or rather—the word "in the opinion of" (matena) must be supplied here after the phrase "of those expressing a prohibition. In that case, the connection should be made as follows: "In the opinion of the teachers who express a prohibition of *iṭ*, it is desired that *yam* alone be *aniṭ* among the roots ending in nasal consonants (*ṇamanta*)."
Regarding "from the root *man*": this refers to the root *manu* in the sense of "understanding" (*avabodhane*), belonging to the Tana-class (the eighth class).
Regarding "from *dihi*" and so forth: *diha* means "to increase" (*upacaye*) [DhP 1015], and *duha* means "to fill completely" (*prapūraṇe*).

(dhā.pā.1014), *ṭhmiha* in the sense of "moistening" (dhā.pā.992), *ṭhruha* in the sense of "birth" or "manifestation" (dhā.pā.859), *ṭhvaha* in the sense of "carrying" (dhā.pā.1004), *ṭhṇaha* in the sense of "binding" (dhā.pā.1166),
*ṭhdaha* in the sense of "reducing to ashes" (dhā.pā.991), and *ṭhliha* in the sense of "tasting" (dhā.pā.1016).

"Those whose doubts have been dispelled": those in whom doubt has been released (mukta) or by whom [doubt] has been abandoned are so described. "Having been distinguished and proclaimed": the meaning is that they were proclaimed after being established through the distinction between *seṭ* and *aniṅ*.

In the forms *ṭhdegdhā* and *dogdhā*, the following rules must be applied: the substitution of *dha* by Pāṇini 8.2.32 (*dāderdhātordhaḥ*), the substitution of *dha* by 8.2.40 (*jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ*), and the substitution of the *jaś* sounds by 8.4.53 (*jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*). In the forms *meḍhā* and *āroḍhā*, [the substitution of] *ha*...

By the rule *ḍhaḥ* (8.2.31), there is the substitution of *ḍha*; as before, there is the substitution of *dha*; by *ṣṭuan ṣṭuaḥ* (8.4.41), there is the substitution of *ṣṭu*; and by *ḍho ḍhea lopaḥ* (8.3.13), there is the elision of *ḍha*. Thus we have *voḍhā*. As before, there is the substitution of *ḍha* and so forth; and by *sahivahor odavarṇasya* (6.3.112), there is the substitution of *o*.

Regarding "naddhā": by the rule *naho dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.34), the substitution of *dha* occurs; as before, there is the substitution of *jaś* and *car*. Regarding "tannāntare": this refers to the grammar of Āpiśali. Regarding "the option for *sah-* before a root beginning with *t*":
the option for *sah-* before a root beginning with *t* has been stated by the rule *tīṣasaha* (Pāṇini 7.2.48) and so forth. *Muh-* also...

"Because it is recited in the *radhādi* [group]. By this, he shows that for the root *muh* as well, there is an optionality according to *radhādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 7.2.45). "Therefore, those two are 'possessing doubt' (*sasaṃśaya*) and 'possessing optionality' (*savikalpa*).
By this, he means they are "possessing doubt" in the sense of being of the nature of an option (*vikalpātmaka*), and not in the sense of being of the nature of uncertainty (*sandehātmaka*).

He shows this with the words "the other two. [The roots] *ṛ* and *lṛ* are accepted by some, such as Āpiśali and others, as being doubtful in their very form. "In their very form" means by their own nature (*svabhāva*). "Doubtful" means subject to uncertainty; for the term "doubt" (*saṃśaya*) indeed applies here to uncertainty.
However, there is doubt because [the root] is not listed among the verbal roots (*dhātu*). Moreover, it is accepted by some;

for one of these two is accepted as occurring in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*), while the other occurs in the sense of "covetousness" (*gārdhya*), as in the examples "diśiṃ," "dṛśim," and so forth. [The roots are] "diśa atisarjane" (DhP 1283) and "dṛśir... [etc.].
The root *prekṣ* (to look at, DhP 988), *daṃś* (to bite, DhP 981)—the particle *atha* here serves to fill out the meter—*mṛś* (to touch or press, DhP 1425;
the Dhātupāṭha reads *āmarśane*), *spṛś* (to touch, DhP 1422; the Dhātupāṭha reads *saṃsparśane*), and *ruś* (*riś*).

[The roots] *hiṃs* (DhP 1419, 1420) "to injure," *krūś* (DhP 856) "to call out or weep," *viś* (DhP 1424) "to enter," and *liś* (DhP 1179) "to diminish. Regarding the term *purāṇagāḥ*: the *purāṇa* is the ancient grammar (*vyākaraṇa*).

Because they are ancient, those who sing and study this are called "Purāṇagas" (those who sing the Purāṇas). Regarding the phrase "in the recensions," it refers either to the recensions of the *aniṭ-kārikās* or to the lists of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*). Regarding the phrase "not the others," it refers to [roots] such as *spaśa*, meaning "to afflict" or "to touch" (DhP 887), and so forth.

Regarding the form *dṛṣṭvā*: the substitution of *ṣ* [for *t*] occurs by the rule *vraścādi-* (Pāṇini 8.2.36). Since the prohibition of the *iṭ* augment for roots beginning with *mṛś*—by the rule *anudātasya ca* (6.1.59)—is already established, how does [the author] indicate something additional?

"Ṛudhiḥ sarādhiḥ," and so forth. It is called *sarādhi* because it exists together with *rādhi*. [The roots] *ṛdh* (DhP 1438) means "to cover," and *rādh* and *sādh* (DhP 1162, 1163) mean "to accomplish.
Regarding the rule "after *rādh*, when intransitive, in the sense of growth," the inclusion of both [roots] is intended.
Because there is no distinction [in their meaning]: *yudh* in the sense of "striking" (*samprahāra*; DhP 1190), *śudh* in the sense of "purification" (*śauce*;
DhP 1191), *budh* in the sense of "understanding" (*avagamana*; DhP 1172), *vyadh* in the sense of "piercing" (*tāḍana*;
DhP 1181), and *sidh* in the sense of "accomplishment" (*saṃrāddhi*; DhP 1192).
"Others than these" refers to roots beginning with *indh*. "Of the regular and irregular suffixes" means of those having the suffix *śap*.

[The roots are: *budh* in the sense of "awakening" (*budha bodhane*, DhP 875) [the Dhātupāṭha reads *budhi*], and *ṣidh* in the sense of "motion" (*ṣidhu gatyām*, DhP 47) [the Dhātupāṭha reads *vidha*].

Regarding these two [rules], such as "even in the case of the *niṣṭhā* suffix," and so forth: now, why is the substitution of *ka* for the root *budh* belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa* suspected [of being prohibited]? Because it is prohibited by the rule "for roots ending in *u*" (*udidvalādiḥ*, 7.2.10). However, since the optional application of the suffix *ktvā* is prescribed by the rule "or after a root marked with *ud*" (*udito vā*, 7.2.56), the rule "for that which has an optional [substitution]" (*yasya vibhāṣā*, 7.2.15) applies.

Thus, since there must be a prohibition regarding the past participle (*niṣṭhā*), the apprehension of such a prohibition is logical. However, for the verbal root *budh*, there is no cause whatsoever for apprehending a prohibition regarding the past participle.
This too is the case: here, although the two roots *budh* belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa* and the *divādigaṇa* are identical in their sense-form (*artharūpa*),...
Therefore, the learner, having conceived an error due to the similarity of the meaning and form, thinks: "This is one and the same root;

it is recited in both classes for the sake of two different suffixes (*vikaraṇa*); for that [root], *iṭ* is prescribed before an *ardhadhātuka* suffix, yet by this rule, the prohibition of *iṭ* is also stated"—thus, because the injunction and the prohibition share the same object.

Some maintain that because the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) is intended as an alternative (*paryāya*), the prohibition regarding the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 7.2.15) should not apply here. Anticipating this view, the author says: "even in the case of the past passive participle," and so forth. He thinks as follows: it is indeed another [matter].
Since the rule for *iṭ* belongs to that which begins with *bhauvādika*, while the prohibition of *iṭ* belongs to another, namely that which begins with *vevādika*,
it follows that because the scope (*viṣaya*) of the injunction and the prohibition is distinct, the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) regarding *iṭ* is not tenable. Now...

How was it stated that there is no prohibition for the *niṣṭhā* [kṛt-suffix] of the root *siṣ*? Since it ends in an *it*-letter, by the rule "udito vā" (7.2.56), the *iṭ* augment is optional; and because of this optionality of *iṭ*, the rule "yasya vibhāṣā" (7.2.15) would necessarily require a prohibition of the *iṭ* in the *niṣṭhā*. This being so...
He considers that its status as an *udittva* root (one marked with *u*) is certainly not based on an ancient seer (*anārṣa*); for if it were an *udittva* root,

its inclusion in the *bhvādi* class would be purposeless, because whatever form is to be derived by this [root] is already established by the rule "ṣidhu śāstre" (DhP 4.87)— or according to the Dhātupāṭha reading, "ṣidhu śāstre māṅgalye ca"— alone.

However, for the sake of establishing that [the rule] "it is established" (*siddham*) applies to this [root], its recitation as having an *u* vowel (*ūdita*) is meaningful; for this is not established by the rule "ṣidhu śāstre. Because it is marked with an *u* vowel (*ūdittva*), the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied by the rule "svaratisūtisūyatidhūñūdito vā" (7.2.44), and consequently, by the rule "yasya vibhāṣā," [the *niṣṭhā*-suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* do not take *iṭ*].

(7.2.15) Thus, because of the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* in the case of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), the fact that the root *sidh* is marked with the letter *u* (as in *sidhu*) is clearly non-Vedic (*anārṣa*), since its formation is already established by its inclusion in the *bhv-ādi* class. [The roots] beginning with *śiṣi piṣim*— namely, *śiṣlṛ* in the sense of "falling apart" (DhP 1451)— [are also included].
[The roots] *piṣ* (DhP 1452) "to crush," *śuṣ* (DhP 1183) "to dry up," *puṣ* (DhP 1182) "to nourish," and *tviṣ* (DhP 1001) "to shine"; [and] *jiṣ*, *viṣ*, and *miṣ* (DhP 697, 698,
699) "to sprinkle," and *śriṣ*.
Regarding *śliṣ*, *praṣ*, and *pluṣ* in the sense of "burning" (*dāhe*), both [roots] are included. [Also included are:

*tuṣ* in the sense of "contentment" (*tuṣṭau*)—[the Dhātupāṭha reads *tūṣa* in the sense of "contentment"]—*duṣ* in the sense of "defilement" (*vaikṛtye*), *dviṣ* in the sense of "hostility" (*aprītau*), and *kṛṣ*.

Regarding *vilikhane* (Dhātupāṭha 1286): it belongs to both the *bhūvādigaṇa* and the *tudādigaṇa*. The mention of the form *puṣyati* with the *śyan* affix is for the purpose of excluding the forms belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa* and the *kyādigaṇa*.
However, in the case of *śuṣyati* and others, it is for the purpose of avoiding a violation of the established rule (*vṛttabhaṅga*). [The forms are] *kraṣṭā*, *karṣṭā*.

Thus, as before, there is an option regarding the augment *ām*. [The forms] *tapiṃ*, *tipim*, and so forth; [the roots] *tapa* "to heat" (*dhā.pā.* 985) and *tapa* "to rule" (*dhā.pā.* 984)—both are taken here [as well as "to burn"]. *Tipṛ*...
The roots *tepṛ* and *ṣṭepṛ* have the meaning "to flow" (*kṣaraṇa*) [Dhātupāṭha 362, 363, 365]; *ṭhāplṛ* means "to pervade" (*vyāpti*) [Dhātupāṭha 1260];

*ṭua vap* means "the continuous succession of seeds and threads" (*bījatantusantāna*) [Dhātupāṭha 1003]—[according to the Dhātupāṭha, *ḍu vap* also means "cutting" (*chedana*)]; and *ñi ṣvap* means "to lie down" (*śaya*).
[The roots] *svap* (to sleep) [DhP 1068], *lip* (to smear/burn) [DhP 1433],
*lup* (to cut/destroy) [DhP 1431], *tṛp* (to satisfy) [DhP 1195], *hṛp* (in the senses of joy and release) [DhP 1196], [and *gam* (to go) in the senses of joy and delusion] [DhP].

The root *sṛplṛ* means "to move" (Dhātupāṭha 982, 983). Regarding the phrase "with a low tone," this means with an *anudātta* (unaccented) vowel. The roots *śap* meaning "to revile" (Dhātupāṭha 1000) and *śap* meaning "to reproach" (Dhātupāṭha 1168)—both are included here. The root *chupa* means "to touch."

(dhā.pā. 1418), *kṣip* in the sense of "impelling" (dhā.pā. 1285). The fact that *tṛpyati* and *dṛpyati* are marked with an anudātta accent is for the purpose of introducing the augment *am*; by the rule *anudātasya ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.59), the augment *am* may optionally occur so that [the forms] *tṛmpati* and *dṛmpati* are produced. Why is this not intended as a prohibition of the *it* augment?
Thus he says: "The augment *ṭhiṭ* is applied to these two," and so forth. Regarding the statement, "those which are *tṛp* and *dṛp* among the *tudādi* [roots]":

these are the two roots *tṛpa* and *tṛmpa*, meaning "to satisfy" (*tṛptau*), as listed in the Dhātupāṭha (1307, 1308), and *dṛpa*, meaning "to afflict" (*upakleśe*), as listed in the Dhātupāṭha (1313).
Regarding the forms *ṭhadiṃ*, *hadim*, and so forth: [the roots] *ṭhada* in the sense of "eating" (DhP 1011),
*ṭhaha* in the sense of "voiding excrement" (DhP 977), *ṣkandir* in the sense of "motion and drying up" (DhP 959),
*bhidir* in the sense of "splitting" (DhP 1439), and *cchidir* in the sense of "dividing into two."

(dhā.śa.1440), *kṣudir* ‘in the sense of crushing’ (dhā.pā.1443), *śadlu* ‘in the sense of falling away’ (dhā.pā.855), *ṣadlṛ* ‘in the senses of dissolution, motion, and exhaustion’ (dhā.pā.854), *ñi ṣvidā* ‘in the sense of perspiration of the limbs’ (dhā.pā.1188), *pada* ‘in the sense of going’ (dhā.pā.1169); *khida*...

The roots *dainyai* (DhP 1170), *khida* in the sense of "to distress" (DhP 1282), *vida* in the sense of "existence" (DhP 1188), *pada* in the sense of "motion" (DhP 1169), and *vida* in the sense of "investigation" (DhP 1450) [are intended].
[This is stated] so that there might not be the inclusion of *ñiṣvidā*. *Ñiṣvidā*...
Regarding the roots *sniha* and *muc* (DhP 744)— the reading in the Dhātupāṭha being *snehanamocanayoḥ*—
this is for the purpose of excluding other verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇas*). It also applies to *vid* in the sense of "knowing" (DhP 1064),
which takes the *śnu* suffix, and to *vidlṛ* in the sense of "obtaining" (DhP 1432), which takes the *śa* suffix.

The purpose is for the sake of exclusion. Since the root *vid*— meaning "to know," "to tell," or "to dwell" (Dhātupāṭha 1708)— belongs to the curādigaṇa and consists of more than one vowel (*anekāc*),
there is no possibility of its application here.
"ṭhpaciṃ vacim" and so forth. "ḍu pacaṣ pāke" (DhP 996);
"vaca paribhāṣaṇe" (DhP 1063). Both are indeed included by the rule "vruvo vaciḥ" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.53). The root from the Sūtra itself is also certainly taught [as such]. "vicir pṛthagbhāve."

(dhā.pā.1442), *ṭhvicir* in the sense of separation (vivecane) (dhā.1094), [according to the Dhātupāṭha: *vijir* in the sense of becoming distinct (pṛthagbhāve)], *ṭhranja* in the sense of coloring (rāge) (dhā.pā.999), *ṭhpracccha* in the sense of desiring to know (jñīpsāyām) (dhā.pā.1413), *ṭhṇijir* in the senses of purification and nourishing (śaucapoṣaṇayoḥ) (dhā.pā.1093), *ṭhṣicir*...
The roots *kṣaraṇe* (DhP 1434), *ṣic* (DhP), *muclṛ mokṣaṇe* (DhP 1430), *bhaja sevāyām* (DhP 998), *bhañjo āmardane* (DhP 1453),
*bhrasja pāke* (DhP 1444), and *yuj samādhau*.
There is the inclusion of both [roots]. [The roots are: *ruj* in the sense of breaking (DhP 1416);
*sañj* in the sense of attachment (DhP 987); *mṛj* in the sense of cleansing (DhP 1415);
*bhuj* in the senses of protecting and eating (DhP 1454); and *bhuj* in the sense of crookedness.

(From Dhātupāṭha 1417)—there is also the inclusion of *dvār*. Regarding *ṣvañja* in the sense of "embracing" (Dhātupāṭha 976), the mention of it with the nasal elided is for the purpose of avoiding the violation of the meter (*vṛttabhaṅga*). Regarding *sṛja* in the sense of "emission" (Dhātupāṭha 1414). Regarding *mṛjū* in the sense of "cleansing" (Dhātupāṭha 1066), it belongs to the first class (*ādādika*). *Mṛja*...
Regarding *śaucālaṅkārayoḥ* (DhP 1848), there is also a root *mṛj* belonging to the Curādigaṇa;
when that [root] follows immediately after *ā dhruṣādvā* (DhP 1805), it is certainly possible for it to be included. However, when [the root *mṛj*] belongs to the Bhvādigaṇa...
In that case, since the root has more than one vowel (*anekāctva*), the prohibition of *iṭ* would not even apply.
With the words "this root *mṛj*" and so forth, he rejects the view here that [the rule] serves the purpose of prohibiting [the substitution of *guṇa*].
With the words "there is also the augment *ām* for this" and so forth, he [rejects the view] that it serves the purpose of the augment *ām*. With the words "therefore, in this case" and so forth...

Since indeed these two purposes are not possible, the purpose for its recitation in this context must be considered. Regarding this, some say: "Even though no such augment is seen, it must nevertheless be applied; otherwise, its recitation would be meaningless. For that which is not..."

It must not be so, for otherwise the statement, "for [the suffix] *kvi* occurs after [roots] ending in *mṛj* when no prefix is applied, provided that a modification or a part is intended," would remain unapplied. Others, however, explain it thus: from the root *mṛj* without a prefix, when followed by *kvi*, there is the intention to express a modification or a constituent part.

"The purpose [of the rule] 'mājaṃ' is so that the suffix *añ* may apply by the rule 'ṭhanudātāderañ' (Pāṇini 4.2.44); but this is incorrect, because since it consists of a single syllable (*ekāc*), the suffix *mayaṭ* must necessarily apply. For it is stated in the rule 'nityaṃ vṛddhañarādibhyaḥ' (Pāṇini 4.3.144):"

If it is asked, "What is the purpose of including the word *nitya* (always), since it will necessarily apply by the very force of the rule's formulation?"—this is said in response: "This is done for the sake of those who desire that *mayaṭ* always [be applied] after a monosyllabic stem (*ekāca*)," as in the examples *tvanmayaṃ* and *vāṅmayam*. "Some" (hold this view).
And so forth. Some, not seeing any purpose [for this], read *viji* in place of *mṛj*.
He asks: "What is the reason? and replies with "For, among the *nij*-class roots," etc.
Since *viji*—meaning "to separate"—is listed among the *nij*-class roots (*nijādi*), it is for that reason that it is intended to be without the *iṭ* augment.
Therefore, having removed *bhṛj*, they read *viji* in its place. How is it known that this [root] is intended to be without the augment *iṭ*? To this he says: "And thus," and so forth;
"in another treatise" (*tantrāntare*)—[another reading is *granthāntare*].

In the *Vyākaraṇa* of Āpiśali: now, regarding the reading "sujivi-jī," why is there not an inclusion of the root *ovijī* ("to fear" and "to tremble") [from Dhātupāṭha 1289]? Because it is marked with the indicator *ī*. Indeed, that [indicator] is placed for this very purpose: [to ensure that the rule] "after a root marked with *ś* or *ū*, the suffix *niṣṭhā* [takes the augment *iṭ*]" (Pāṇini 7.2.14) applies.

Thus, so that there may be a prohibition of *iṭ*, if this [root] were also included here, then because [the desired form] would already be established by this very rule, the designation *īdit* would be purposeless. In the case of "avadhīt," the substitute *vadh*—prescribed by "luṅci" (Pāṇini 2.4.43)—is short-voweled (*adanta*). That...

An ādeśa (substitute) that is not originally unaccented becomes so only by virtue of *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original). Since there is no original instruction (*upadeśa*) for a one-syllable root (*ekāc*) that is unaccented, the prohibition does not apply. But how, then, does this [substitute] become a one-syllable root? To this he says: "For the purpose of preventing *vṛddhi*," and so forth. If...
If *vadhi* ended in *i*, the rule *ato halāder laghoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.5) would cause optional *vṛddhi*. However, when it ends in *a*, this does not occur;

for in that case, the intervention [of the augment] is disregarded. But when it ends in *a*, since the elision of the vowel *a* in *vadhi* is a *pūrvavidhi* (an operation dependent on what precedes), [the intervention is not considered].

The intervention occurs not only by means of the consonant (*hal*) itself, but also through the status of being "as if in the place of" (*sthānivadbhāva*). Even that vowel-increment (*vṛddhi*) characterized by a final consonant does not occur at all when there is an *a*-finality; for, due to the status of being "as if in the place of" the elision of the *a*, the word lacks a final consonant. Therefore, it is for the sake of the operation (*vṛtti*) that it is [treated as] having an *a*-final.

It is taught [as having] a single vowel (*ekāj*). Now, one might object: "Even if it is taught as lacking a final consonant (*adanta*), nevertheless, since it would be designated as 'having a single vowel' (*ekāj*) by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule, the prohibition must indeed apply.
This is not so; for if that were the case, the mention of *ekāj* [in the rule] would be purposeless. Thus...
For, since [roots] such as *hi*, *jāgṛ*, *adarśaka*, and so forth possess an udātta accent, they do not necessitate the inclusion of the term "having more than one vowel" (*anekāj*).

Derivative roots ending in suffixes such as *san* and others lack the status of being taught as such (*upadeśatva*), because the entire complex is derivative (*lākṣaṇika*) and not something directly taught. Nor is there any other [root] that possesses more than one vowel [which would require the rule].

In the instruction regarding the *dhātu* (verbal root), there is an *anudātta* (low-pitched) vowel which necessitates the mention of "monosyllabic" (*ekāj*). However, this designation cannot be applied here by virtue of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element), because it is not a rule conditioned by an *al* (phoneme).
[The purpose is] so that [the rule] may apply here; for if the mention of "instruction" (*upadeśa*) were absent, [the rule would not apply to] monosyllabic [roots].

The meaning of the rule is simply that the augment *iṭ* does not occur when the verbal root (*dhātu*) begins with an unaccented vowel (*anudātta*). And thus, in forms such as *laviṣyati* and *paviṣyati*, the augment *iṭ* would not occur. For in this case, once the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) has been applied, the remaining vowels become unaccented (*śeṣānudātta*), and consequently the root is unaccented. Likewise—*kartā kaṭān*.

In the case of *kartum icchati*, however, the augment *iṭ* would indeed occur; for when the suffixes *tṛn* or *tumun* are applied, the root becomes udātta by virtue of the *nit*-accent. But if the term "upadeśa" (original enunciation) is included, the initial state is thereby qualified, and thus the undesirable consequence does not arise. Even though at a later stage...

The roots *lū* and *pū* are unaccented (*anudātta*), yet at the stage of their formal instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*) they are indeed accented (*udātta*). Similarly, although the root *kṛ* is accented after the elision of the vowel, it remains unaccented at the stage of its formal instruction. Now, although the word *bibhits* is not recited in this context [of the Dhātupāṭha] and does not consist of a single syllable (*ekāc*), nevertheless—

In the case of *bhid*, both [conditions] are present. The view that "the double application [of the root] constitutes reduplication" is also adopted there; therefore, it is *bhid* itself that is reduplicated, and since it is qualified by both [characteristics], the prohibition is indeed established.

11. *śrayukaḥ kiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.11). This rule is commenced for the sake of the acute accent (*udātta*). [The example] "lūnaḥ": here, the substitution of *n* [for *t*] occurs by the rule *lvādibhyaśca* (8.2.44).
[The example] "tīrṇaḥ": here too, [the substitution of *n* for *t* occurs] by the rule *radābhyām* (8.2.42).

Regarding the passage beginning with "some say" (*kecid āhuḥ*), etc.: according to the rule *glājisthaśca ksnuḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.139), there is the statement "and *bhuvaḥ*" (*bhuvaśca vaktavyam*)—referring to the sūtra *bhuvaśca* (3.2.138).
When the suffix *ksnu* is applied to the root *bhū*, and the marker *g* is added, the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* prescribed for markers marked with *g* applies.

It would not be obtained, and consequently, the form *bhūṣṇuḥ* would not be established. Therefore, some maintain that in the word *bhūṣṇuḥ*, for the purpose of prohibiting the augment *iṭ*, the letter *g*— which has become a *c*-sound by virtue of the rule "the doubling of the consonant" (*dvirvacana*) in the sūtra *śryukaḥ kiti*— is [included] as if it were the letter *k* itself, just like the examples beginning with *śvabhūti*.
They say that [the *k*] is "conjoined" (*praśliṣṭa*). If the *g*-sound is conjoined as a result of the substitution of *cartya*,

then when the rule "for *sas* and *sajuṣ*, *ru*" (8.2.66) applies to produce *ru*, because the *cartya* substitution is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the rule "also before *haś*" (6.1.114) must apply to change the *ru* into *u*, and not into a *visarjanīya*.
And if that were so, would not the grammatical rule "ṭhśrayukaḥ kiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.11) be untenable?
To refute this objection, he says: "Because the mention [in the rule] is based on a Sūtra," and so forth.

Without relying on the fact that the change to *c* (cartva) is considered asiddha (non-existent for the purpose of the subsequent operation), the substitution of *u* for *ru* was not applied, nor was the visarga.

They describe it as *kṛta*. But for what purpose do they assert that the suffix *kṣnu* has the *ṅit* designation, such that this explanation must be made when it exists? It is for the sake of establishing the word *sthāsnu*. For they think thus: if *kṣnu* has the *kit* designation...

By the rule *ṭhdhumāsthāgādi* (Pāṇini 6.4.66), the substitution of *ī* for the root *sthā* would occur; consequently, the form *sthāsnur* could not be established. Regarding the passage beginning with *ṭhglājisthaśca ksnu* [Pāṇini 3.2.139], etc.:
for if [the suffix] were marked with the *ṅit* indicator, this [rule] is explained precisely for the purpose of prohibiting the augment *aṭ* after *ksnu*, and not for that [other reason].

Is it *gitva*? No; rather, it is precisely *kitva*. Nor does *itva* follow as a consequence when *kitva* is present, because in the rule "glājisthaśca ksnuḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.139), the vowel *a* has been elided [by *praśleṣa*] from the root *sthā*, as indicated by the form *sthāḥ*. This applies to the root *tiṣṭhati*.

The purpose [of the rule] is so that a word ending in *kṣnu* and ending in *ā* shall indeed end in *ā*, and not end in *ī*. For if there were no *praśleṣa* (elision/merging) of the *ā*, then by the rule "the substitution of *ā* occurs for *tiṣṭhati*"— which is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule concerning *ī*— the *ī*-substitution would be barred by that [substitution of *ā*].

It does not apply. Thus, since the word *sthāsnu* is established by the connection with the suffix *ki*, this [objection] is of no consequence; the meaning is that this explanation is worthless. Furthermore, regarding the word *tīrṇam*, what indeed would be the reason for [the rule] not applying here in the absence of the mention of "instruction" (*upadeśa*)?
It might be argued: "Since this root *tṛ* is recited as ending in *u*, [how can it be treated as such]? To this he says: "For if [the rule were applied] after [the change]," and so forth.
For once the substitution of *ī* has been made by the rule "ṛt iddhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.100), its status as ending in *u* (*ugantatā*) is destroyed;
thus, if the mention of "original instruction" (*upadeśagrahaṇa*) were not present, [the rule would] not apply. But when that [mention] exists, it does apply.

"Even though the root *tṛ* does not end in the suffix *ru* at a later stage, nevertheless, it is indeed taught [as such] in the instruction (*upadeśa*). — This is the objection (*codaka*). "Lest it be so," and so forth. "But of what [is it the object]? and so forth is the response (*uttara*).
"Of that which ends in *añ*," [the printed reading being *kṛtaḥ*]. This is the objection. "If this is so... [and so forth is the response].

The other [the opponent] says: "Because of the status of being a substitute (sthānivadbhāva). Furthermore, the fact that this is not a rule concerning an *al* (vowel) is due to the inclusion of the pratyāhāra *uṅ*. He says: "Therefore," meaning:
because, if the mention of "instruction" (*upadeśagrahaṇa*) were absent, there would be no prohibition in the case of *tīrṇaḥ*.

[The rule] applies; therefore, the phrase "in the original instruction" (upadeśe) must be carried over [from the previous sūtra]. Regarding the words "And that being so," etc.: the meaning is "when 'in the original instruction' is being carried over. As for the statement "it would also apply here in the case of *jāgarita*": this is because *jāgarti* is a root ending in /u/ at the stage of its original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*). [The phrase] "for that purpose" means...

In the rule beginning with *jāgarita*, [the mention of *an*] is for the purpose of preventing the application of the prohibition of *iṭ*; this is because the word *artha* signifies cessation. If, however, the rule *ekācaḥ* (7.2.10) is understood to carry over [into this context], then in forms such as *proṛṇutaḥ* and *proṛṇutavat*, the prohibition of *iṭ* would not apply.

Since the root *ūrṇu* has more than one *aṅga*, [one might ask] why [the substitution does not apply]? To this he says: "The form *ūrṇuvat* should be stated for *ūrṇu*," and so forth. Since the meaning of this verse has already been explained previously, it is not explained again here.
12. And [the substitution of *u* for *i*] occurs after the roots *grah* and *guh* when followed by the suffix *san*.

(7.2.12) Since the substitution of *iṭ* is applicable after the root *grah* when followed by *san*, and since the root *guh* also ends in an *ūdi* vowel, the substitution of *iṭ* would optionally apply to it as well by the rule "svarati" (7.2.44).
This sūtra is commenced to provide for the obligatory substitution of *u* instead. The word "ca" (and) [is used here] to include the previous rule "ukaḥ" (7.2.11).

This [the particle *ca*] is for the purpose of carrying forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) the word *uk*. Now, one might object: since by the rule *iko jhal* (Pāṇini 1.2.9), the suffix *san* after roots ending in *u* is indeed *kit*, the prohibition [of *iṭ*] is already established by the preceding rule alone; what then is the use of the particle *ca* for the purpose of carrying forward the word *uk*? This is not so; for without the prohibition of *iṭ*, the suffix *san*...

The status of beginning with *jhal* is established; how then is the status of being *kit* [established]? By this [rule], when *iṭ* is prohibited, the status of *san* as beginning with *jhal* arises, and subsequently, the status of being *kit* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa*; such is the sequence.
Regarding "jighṛkṣati": since *san* is *kit* by the rule "rudavida" (Pāṇini 1.2.8), [the root] belongs to the *grah*-class.
By the rule [6.1.16], there is *samprasāraṇa*; by "ṭhho ḍhaḥ" (8.2.31), there is the substitution of *ḍha* for *tha*;
by "ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si" (8.2.41), there is the substitution of *ka* for *ḍha*; by "iṇkoḥ" (8.2.57), there is the substitution of *ṣa*;
and by "ekāco vaśo bhaṣ" (8.2.37) and so forth, through the *bhaṣ*-substitution, the letter *ga* becomes *gha*.

There is reduplication, which entails the grammatical operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). In the form *jughoṣati*, since the suffix *san* is *kit* by the rule *rudavidamuṣagrahi...* (Pāṇini 1.2.8), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule *grahijyāvayi...* (Pāṇini 6.1.16); then, by *ho ḍhaḥ* (8.2.31), the *h* becomes *ḍh*; and by *ṣṭuanāṃ ṣṭuaḥ* (8.4.41), the *ḍh* becomes *ṭ*. Finally, by *ṣṭuanāṃ ṣṭuaḥ* (8.4.41), the *ṣ* becomes *k*. Thus, [the form is derived].

The doubling [of the root] is the grammatical operation pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Thus, we have *jughoṣate* (or *jughuṣati*, as in the Kāśikā and Padamañjarī). The root *guhū* (DhP 896) means "to conceal"; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* (1.3.62).
Regarding *ruruṣati*, [the lengthening of the vowel occurs] by the rule *ajjhanagamāṃ sani* (6.4.16).

Thus [the vowel] is long. Now, if by the letter *ca* the root *gam* is drawn forward (*anukṛṣyate*), would the root *śri*, which is prescribed in the same rule (*ekayoganirdiṣṭa*), also be drawn forward? To this he says: "In the case of *śri*, *svṛ*, *ūrṇu*, *rabh*, *jñapi*, etc. Regarding the root *śri*, [the rule] is *sanīdantargha* (Pāṇini 7.2.49).
Thinking that [the rule] will prescribe the optional substitution of *iṭ* here, its recurrence in this context would be purposeless; therefore, it is not brought forward [from the previous rule].
13. *kṛsṛbhṛvṛstudrusruśruvapo liṭi* (Pāṇini 7.2.13).

In "sakṛva" and "cakṛma," the substitutes *vam* and *mas* are applied by the rule "parasmaipadānām" (Pāṇini 3.4.82). Regarding the phrase "only krādayaḥ," this demonstrates the nature of the restrictive rule (*niyama*).
However, one should not suspect a contrary restriction (*viparīta-niyama*) such as "only in the perfect tense (*liṭ*) are the roots beginning with *kṛ* (*krādayaḥ*) aniṭ."
This is because of the indications [found] in rules such as *kṛtalabdhakrītakuśalāḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.38) and *tamadhiṣṭho bhṛto bhūto bhāvī vā* (Pāṇini 5.1.80).
But by what means is the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* established for those [words], since [the rule] would only be commenced if [the need for it] were already established?
Is this stated for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*)? To this he says: "Of those taught with an anudātta vowel," and so forth.

Those taught with an anudātta vowel—other than *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*, such as *kṛ* and others—for them alone the prohibition based on the root (*prakṛtyāśraya*), by means of [Pāṇini 7.2.10] "of [roots ending in] *ac*," etc., is already established. But as for *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*...

The rule *ṭhśrayukaḥ kiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.11) depends on the affix (*pratyaya*), not on the base (*prakṛti*); for both of those [the affix and the augment] are acute (*udātta*). Regarding the phrase "that" (*tat*) and so forth: since the prohibition of those [bases and affixes]—depending respectively on the base and the affix—is established as appropriate, therefore, for both as well...

The meaning is that this is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) that has been applied. Here, the prohibition of *karoti* and so forth—having distinguished them from other verbal roots—should be understood as a restrictive rule.
But how is it possible for this to be a restrictive rule with respect to the suffix *thali* following the root *vṛñ*, since [the prohibition] exists...?

In the case of a prohibition, there must be a restrictive rule (*niyama*). [The prohibition of *iṭ* after the root *vṛñ* in the suffix *thal* is such a rule. For in this case, a prohibition based on the root (*prakṛti*) is not established for *vṛñ*, because it is udātta. Nor is there a prohibition based on the suffix (*pratyaya*), because *thal* lacks the *kit* designation. Therefore, it is logical that the purpose of the rule is precisely to prohibit *iṭ* after *vṛñ* in the suffix *thal*.
Is it not for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*)? To this he says: "Because of *vṛñ*, etc. Restriction (*vyavasthā*) means limitation (*niyama*).

Due to the specific grammatical prescription (*nipātana*) in [Pāṇini 7.2.64], "In the Vedic language (*nigama*), [the forms] *babhūtha*, *ātatantha*, *jagṛmbha*, and *vavartha* [are formed]," there must be a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* after the suffix *thal* only in the Vedic language (*nigama*) for the root *vṛñ*, and not otherwise.
In common usage (bhāṣā), since such a formal arrangement exists, this prohibition of *iṭ* does not apply to the root *vṛñ*;

otherwise, the specific rule (*nipātana*) for *vavartha* would be rendered useless. Therefore, in the absence of that prohibition, this sūtra is understood to serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) even for *vṛñ*.
This is an absolute rule.

Regarding the statement beginning with "but [the augment] for √stu, √dru, √sru, and √śru," the word *api* (also) is intended to show that even that *iṭ* which would otherwise apply by virtue of the definition of an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix is not desired. But how is it that it is not desired even though it is [otherwise] required?

It is obtained [from the previous rule], because the section containing prohibitions (*pratiṣedhakāṇḍa*) is stronger. Furthermore, in this context, it would have been more appropriate to place this section of prohibitions immediately after *na vṛdbhyāścaturbhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.59). In this way, one would not have to resort to the assumption of a double prohibition (*dviṣpratiṣedha*). Since this...

He formulates the prohibition beforehand; the purpose of this is that, when the prohibition is stated first, it is understood as a prohibition of the measure of a sacrificial twig (*iṣāmātra*) for which no specific rule has been established.
Without relying on any specific qualification, this exception applies to *iṭ* alone;
therefore, the prohibition of every *iṭ* that has been prescribed becomes established. However, another says:
since the term *iṅ* is already being carried over from "not before *iṭ*" (7.2.4), by the force of its repeated mention here...
And by the force of the prohibition, it is understood that the prohibition applies only to the root *iṇ* (to go) when followed by *mān*.

The statement "it should be stated that [the prohibition applies] to *kṛñ* when it is not accompanied by *suṭ*" means that this must be explained as having the sense that the prohibition of *ṣatva* applies to the root *kṛ* when the suffix *suṭ* is absent. For what purpose?
So that the augment *iṭ* may apply to the entire word [including the suffix], this is the explanation: by the rule "in a *dvandva*,

a *ghi* [stem] is placed first" (Pāṇini 2.2.32), it is indicated— without placing any one of the members beginning with *stu* as a *ghi*-designated term first— that here [the application of] the characteristic for initial placement [is intended].

It deviates; that is, it does not apply to its own domain, and this [rule] is likewise. Therefore, when the root *kṛ* is accompanied by the suffix *suṭ*, it does not apply there—as in *sañcaskariva* and *sañcaskarima*. This is according to the rule: "The suffix *suṭ* is applied after *sam*, *pari*, and *upa* before the root *kṛ* when it means 'adornment'. (Pāṇini 6.1.137).

While *suṭ* is understood as continuing [from the previous rule], *suṭ* is applied by the rule "even when there is intervention by *abhyāsa* and *ṭhaḍ*" (6.1.136). Furthermore, the rule "for roots ending in long *ṝ*, according to Bhāradvāja" (7.2.63) is also intended to apply only to those cases where *suṭ* and *yaṭ* are not present.
The word "of *kṛñ*" (*kṛñaḥ*) is understood [as the governing rule]. But how is it obtained that this applies only to the form without the augment *suṭ*?

Listen to how it is so obtained: for there, from the rule "udito vā" (Pāṇini 7.2.56), the word "optionally" (*vā*) is carried over by the maxim of the frog's leap (*maṇḍūkaplutinyāya*), and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Therefore, it belongs only to one who has not yet attained [the fruit].

14. *Śvīditaḥ* in the *niṣṭhā* [suffixes]. (Pāṇini 7.2.14) [The example is] *śūnaḥ*. There is *samprasāraṇa* by the rule *vacyādi* (6.1.15), and lengthening by *halaḥ* (6.4.2). [The example is] *lagnaḥ*. Because the substitution of *n* for *t* is considered *asiddha*, [the substitution of] *k* for the palatals (*cu*) applies by *coḥ kuḥ* (8.2.30).

Regarding the substitution of *ku* [for *kta*]: in the case of the form "uḍḍīnaḥ," the root is *ṅīṅ* (meaning "to move through the air"). Now, one might think: "Since the suffix *ṅīṅ* is udātta, the augment *iṭ* would apply to the *niṣṭhā* [suffix *kta*]; therefore, its prohibition must be stated, for otherwise the undesired form 'uḍḍayita' would result. To such a person [the author replies]:

He replies with "ṅīṅḥ" and so forth. Regarding "oditām," the meaning is "of those beginning with *su*. This is because of the statement: "The roots beginning with *su* are marked with the letter *o*. The roots beginning with *su* are *ṣūṅ* (DhP 1031), "to release the fetus of a living being," and so on. How does this function as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)?

Thus he says: "For him," and so forth. For among the roots beginning with *svap* that take the augment *iṭ*, this very reading has the following purpose: so that the substitution of *n* may occur for the final *t* when followed by an *udit* (a root marked with *u* as an *it*). One might object: "Even if *iṭ* is applied, the substitution of *n* will still occur. To this he replies: "And [the rule for] the substitution of *n*..."

And so forth. In the rule *tasmādityuttarasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.67), because the term *nirdiṣṭa*—which signifies immediate sequence—is understood as being carried over (*anuvṛtti*), the substitution of *na* for the *ta* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix is prescribed only for that which immediately follows a root marked with the indicatory letter *o* (*udit*). In that context, if the *niṣṭhā* suffix were followed by *ṅīṅ*...

If *iṭ* were to be present, then even though it has the marker *u*, it would not undergo the change to *natva* because it is separated by *iṭ*. Its inclusion among those roots that have a permanently present *u* marker (*nityodit*) would be purposeless and thus it would not have been recited there; yet it is indeed recited. Therefore, that very recitation must be the indicator (*jñāpaka*). This is not so; for in this way...
In that case, the *ānantarya-paribhāṣā* (the rule concerning immediate sequence) would be sublated, and the treatise (*śāstra*) would yield an undesirable result;
yet this is improper, for there is no formulation in the treatise intended to produce an undesirable meaning.
Therefore, so that the *ānantarya-paribhāṣā* is not sublated and the treatise does not become undesirable—
The reading of *ṅīṅ* among those [roots] marked with an *u*-diacritic (*uditām*) is fruitful;
that method must be accepted. Consequently, the inclusion of *ṅīṅ* among those marked with an *u*-diacritic is merely an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
There is another method: in the rule "and after what is marked with an *u*" (*oditaśca*, 8.2.45), the term *odita*...

This will be repeated twice for the sake of the double application of the paribhāṣā "tasmādityuttarasya" (P. 1.1.67). Of these two applications, the purpose of the second one is this: that even in the case of the suffix *ṅīṅ*, the substitution of *n* occurs only for the immediately following *ṇiṣṭhā*-suffix *t*.

"So that it may be so. Furthermore, if the augment *iṭ* were applied to the *niṣṭhā* [suffixes] after the roots *ṅī* and *ṅe*, then because of the intervention by *iṭ*, the substitution of *n* would not occur. Nor can it be argued that it will occur despite the intervention due to the force of the wording [of the rule]; for, in this way, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*)...
The double mention [of the root] would be purposeless, and this is incorrect; therefore, the reading of *ṅī* among those marked as *odit* is indeed an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
The mention of *śvi* could have been omitted, because by virtue of its being marked as *odit*, there will be no *iṭ* augment in the past participle (*niṣṭhā*).

For the designation *odit* is applied for the sake of [the suffix] *iṭ*, and *natva* (the substitution of *na*) is prescribed immediately after the *niṣṭhā* suffixes; if *iṭ* were to follow a *niṣṭhā* other than those, the status of being *odit* would be purposeless. The mention of *śvi* should be understood as being for the sake of variety.

15. *yasya vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 7.2.15). [Examples: *vidhūtaḥ* ("shaken"); from the root *dhūñ* "to shake" (Dhātupāṭha 1836). *gūḍhaḥ* ("hidden"); from the root *gūh* "to conceal" (Dhātupāṭha 986). After the substitution of *ḍha* and other changes have been applied, [the rule] *ḍhralope* (6.3.111) [applies].
By such [rules] as these, the vowel becomes long.
Why, then, does the prohibition not apply here in the case of *patita-patita*? For in the rule *sanīvantardha-* (Pāṇini 7.2.49), the root *pat* is indeed mentioned as having an optional *iṭ*.
Is this because of the optional inclusion [of these words] according to the rule "The addition of *tan*, *pati*, *dara*, and *drā* is prescribed"?
To this he says: "The second case [ending], *āśrita*, etc. and so forth.

16. And from the beginning. (7.2.16) Since he will state an option (*vibhāṣā*) immediately after [the rules for] the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the first action (*ādikarman*), this prohibition is understood to apply elsewhere than that—to both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*). For example: *āśvastaḥ* ("rested"). [The root is] *śvas* "to breathe."
Regarding "vāntaḥ": from the root *ṭu vama* (DhP 8.49), meaning "to vomit. The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by Pāṇini 6.4.15:
*anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ kṅiti*. [Question: "What is the purpose of making this separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*)? [Answer: For that which was asked, [the rule] *āditaś ca vibhāṣā*...

Regarding the rule "bhāvādikarmaṇoḥ": if a single *yoga* (rule) were made, then there would be no prohibition in cases other than the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*). Anticipating this objection, he says "āditaśca" and so forth: "And [the augment *iṭ* is] optional after roots beginning with 'a'."

If the rule "bhāvādikarmaṇoḥ" were treated as a single compound, then once the option (*vibhāṣā*) had been prescribed for the states of being (*bhāva*) and the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*), the prohibition "yasya vibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 7.2.15) would apply elsewhere— in cases such as the agent (*kartṛ*)— and thus the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) would be purposeless.

With the words "for the sake of making known," etc., he refutes the charge of meaninglessness [of the rule]. [The phrase] "that which is optional with respect to a particular condition (upādhi) [applies] with respect to that same condition" contains two *bahuvrīhi* compounds. An *upādhi* is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). And this *upādhi* should be understood for this specific purpose: if something is optional with respect to one condition, it is also [optional] with respect to that very condition of its.

If there were to be a prohibition [of the rule], then one would not have made the division of the *yoga*; for even by a single *yoga*, since the option (*vikalpa*) has been prescribed for the active and passive voices (*bhāva* and *ādikarman*), the prohibition "for that which is optional" (*yasya vibhāṣā*, 7.2.15) would certainly be obtained elsewhere. Yet, the division of the *yoga* has indeed been made; therefore, by this [very fact]...

By means of making a *yogavibhāga* (division of a rule), it is indicated that "where there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) for a particular condition, there is a prohibition (*niṣedha*) for that same condition.

With the words "by that" (*tena*) and so forth, he demonstrates the purpose of the indicator (*jñāpaka*). Here, the option (*vibhāṣā*) applies to the root *vid* in the sense of "obtaining," [as distinguished] from the root *vid* belonging to the *tudādigaṇa*.

By virtue of association, there is the inclusion of the root *lābha* belonging to the *tud-ādi* class; and by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 7.2.15), the prohibition applies only to that [root] and not to any other. If it is made known that "the prohibition applies to that which has the same condition as that for which the optionality was stated," then [it applies to] *jṛ-vraścoḥ ktvi* (Pāṇini 7.2.55).

Since the suffix *ktvā* is optionally applied in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) by the rule *ṭhudito vā* (Pāṇini 7.2.56), would it not follow that by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 7.2.15), the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* for the past participles (*niṣṭhā*) would apply only in the sense of the abstract action and not in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*)? This is not a fault; for a property (*dharma*) that is being relied upon serves as the differentiator.

It occurs. Furthermore, in the case of either the *ktvā* suffix or the *niṣṭhā* suffix, no distinct denoted meaning is relied upon as the cause [for the application of the suffix]. Therefore, the prohibition certainly applies here. The evidence for this is the citation [of the rule] "tena nirvṛtam" (Pāṇini 4.2.68).

17. *vibhāṣā bhāvādikarmaṇoḥ* | (7.2.17) In the case of "it has been crushed by this" (*ṭhminnam anena*), the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of an impersonal action (*napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ*, 3.3.114). In the case of "it has been softened" (*ṭhmeditam*), because the rule "the *niṣṭhā* [suffixes] after the root *śīṅ*" (1.2.19), etc., prohibits the *kit* designation, the *guṇa* substitution takes place. In the case of "crushed" (*praminnaḥ*).
The prefix *pra-* indicates the inception of an action (*ādikarma*). Regarding the term "inception of an action" (*ādikarma*), this refers to the initial moment of an action.
When that [moment] is intended to be expressed as having already occurred (*bhūtatva*), the past passive participle suffix *kta* is applied;
by the rule *ādikarmaṇi ktaḥ kartari ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.71), this *kta* occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) among the kārakas. For example: *śaktaḥ ghaṭaḥ* ("the jar is capable").

In order to establish the validity of the expression "the jar is capable of being made" (*kartuṃ śakyo ghaṭaḥ*), a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must be made here as follows: [the first part is] *vibhāṣā*. In that context, the term *āditaḥ* (from 7.2.16) should not be carried over. In the second part, [the rule is] *bhāvādikarmaṇoḥ*.
In yoga, this very [nature] persists.

18. *kṣubdha*, *svānta*, *dhvānta*, *lagna*, *mliṣṭa*, *viribdha*, *phāṇṭa*, and *bāḍha* [are used] in the senses of agitated mind, darkness, adhered, indistinct, sound, unsolicited, and intense, respectively. (Pāṇini 7.2.18) Regarding *kṣubdha*: there is the absence of the augment *iṭ* for the root *kṣubha* (meaning "to shake," Dhātupāṭha 1239).
It is elided [by the rule] "if it denotes a *mantha*. That is, if the *mantha* is denoted by the whole compound.
By "mantha" is meant barley meal mixed with a liquid substance;
as in "a *mantha* of milk," meaning a stirred *mantha*. As in "agitated by the *mantha*."

In this context, churning (*mantha*) is not being denoted; what then? It is the motion that is its means. Now, if the word *kṣubdha* is prescribed as a *nipātana* (irregular formation) to denote the act of churning—as in "the mountain torrent is agitated" (*kṣubdhā girinaṭī*), "the army is agitated" (*kṣubdhā senā*), "the ocean is agitated" (*kṣubdhaḥ samudraḥ*), and so forth—is this not untenable? To this he says: "Agitated... (*kṣubdhā*).

"Mountain rivers," and so forth. This shows that mountain rivers and the like are designated as such because they share the common characteristic of being agitated. Just as the state of being churned is the means for the agitation of the *mantha* (the stirred drink), so too is the state of being [agitated] the means for the agitation of objects such as mountain rivers.

It is designated by the word *kṣubdha* due to its similarity with the act of churning; just as a *vāhīka* is called "ox" because of his similarity to an ox. [Examples are] *svāntam* and *dhvāntam*. [The roots are] *svan* and *dhvan* in the sense of "sound" (Dhātupāṭha 827, 828).
The absence of *iḍ* is prescribed as a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). This should be understood to apply to the subsequent examples as well.
A mind that is undistracted and unperturbed regarding external objects is called "internal" (*svānta*).

[In this term], there is lengthening according to Pāṇini 6.4.15: "There is lengthening of a nasalized vowel before *kvip* and before a consonant beginning with *jhal*, when followed by *k* or *ṅ*. [Thus we have] *svanitaṃ*.
Regarding the word *manasā*: it is the act of sounding (*svanana*) performed by the mind that is expressed, not the mind itself.
Regarding *dhvanitaṃ tamasā*: here too, it is the act of sounding performed by darkness (*tamas*) that is expressed, not darkness itself.
Regarding *lagnaḥ*: [the root] *lage* in the sense of attachment (*saṅga*) [is used]. (Dhātupāṭha 785, 786) [The root *rage*...]

In the case of *śaṅkā*—the rule *dhā.pā.* [prescribes] the substitution of the nasal *ṇ* for the final consonant. Regarding the phrase "if it is a sound" (*svaraśced*), the word *svara* here refers to *dhvani* (sound).
Regarding *sphāṣṭam*: from the root *phaṇa* (to go, *dhā.pā.* 821), there is lengthening of the vowel and the substitution of *ṣṭu* as before. What?
Furthermore, what is meant by "effortless" (*anāyāsa*)? To this he says: "That which is uncooked," and so forth.

"Uncooked" (*aśr̥ta*) means not yet processed by heat. "Unground" (*apiṣṭa*) means not reduced to powder. "Contact with water" (*udakasamparka*) means conjunction with water. By the word "mere" (*mātra*), there is an exclusion of pressing and other such processes. "With its juices undivided" (*vibhaktarasa*).
Thus, the meaning is "having a distinct flavor. *Koṣṇam* means slightly warm.

Regarding the statement, "Because it is accomplished with little effort, it is perceived without exertion": *āyāsaḥ* is an excess of effort; that which does not possess this is "without exertion" (*anāyāsaḥ*), meaning it is accomplished with little effort.

Therefore, in this context, when an object qualified by being "uncooked" (aśṛta) and so forth is indicated without effort because it can be accomplished with little exertion, the word *kāṣṭha* is applied as an irregular form (*nipātana*) to that specific object indicated without effort; however, it is not applied to the absence of effort itself.

He shows that it is characterized by non-metal everywhere else as well. And this meaning is obtained through the force of the *nipātana* (irregular formation); for just as some other [technical term], such as the absence of *iṭ*, is obtained through the force of the *nipātana*, so too is this specific meaning obtained.
"‘Bāḍham’"—here, as before, the substitution of *ḍha* and other grammatical operations take effect.

19. *ghṛṣiśasī veyātye* (Pāṇini 7.2.19). Regarding the term *vaiyātyam*, it is explained as "the state of being *viyāta*. *Yāta* means "going" or "attainment"; one whose going is distorted because its object is an improper path is called *viyāta*, that is, "ill-behaved. Thus, *vaiyātya* refers to the condition of such a person.
The state of that is *vaiyātyam* (shamelessness). The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied because it begins with *brāhmaṇa* etc.
(Pāṇini 5.1.124). Regarding the form *ṣuṣṭaḥ*: the root *ñi dhṛṣā* is used in the sense of "boldness" (Dhātupāṭha 1269).
Regarding the form *viśtaḥ*: the root *śasu* is used in the sense of "injury" (Dhātupāṭha 727); for the root *śas* as well, [the substitution of *ī* for *ś*] occurs by the rule *udato vā* (7.2.56).

Because of the application of the rule "vibhāṣā" [to the root *vyat*], the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule "yasya vibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 7.2.15) is already established; this is what is connected [in the commentary]. If, then, the prohibition is indeed already established, for what purpose is this statement? To this he says: "For the sake of restriction," and so forth. [It serves] only in the case of *vaiyātya*.

[The rule] is stated so that [the suffix *liṭ*] may occur in the sense of the present tense, but not elsewhere. Now, one might ask: since the optionality [of the suffix *liṭ*] for the root *dhṛṣ* is already established by the rule "vibhāṣā bhāvādikarmaṇoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.17), why is this statement not intended to provide for the obligatory application [of the suffix]? To this he says: "In the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), etc. In this regard:
And the cause is the inherent nature of the power of boldness (*dharṣaṇa*). Regarding the word "dharṣitaḥ":
since the *kit* designation is prohibited as in the previous case, there is *guṇa* substitution.

20. *dṛḍhaḥ* is used in the sense of "thick" (*sthūla*) and "strong" (*bala*). (Pāṇini 7.2.20) By specifying *balavati* as ending in the suffix *matup*, the author indicates that in the sūtra the word *bala* is presented with the possessive suffix *-a* (matvarthīya), according to the rule for the *arśas-ādi* group. [The form] *oṃheḥ*.

Thus [it refers] to the root *dṛh* "to grow" (DhP 8.34). Or else, there is another root *dṛh*, because some read [the Dhātupāṭha] as "dṛha dṛhi vṛddhau" (DhP 7.33, 7.34). [The objection is raised: "Because of the absence of the letter *n*."

Because there is no formal instruction (upadeśa) for the letter *n*, and because the *n* is not marked with the *it*-sign, the *n* does not exist [in this context]. Now, for what purpose is the elision of the letter *h* prescribed as a nipātana? Let the letter *ḍh* itself be prescribed as the nipātana.

When the substitution of *ḍha* for the following [consonant] has been made, and the rule *ṣṭuan* has been applied, and the elision of *ḍha* before *ḍha* has been performed, the form *dṛḍha* is established.

Here too, the meaning is as follows: why is it not necessary to prescribe the substitution of *ḍha* for the following [letter], since it is already accomplished by the rule *ṣṭuan* itself? To this he says: "The prescription of the elision of *ha*" and so forth. If [the elision of] *ha*...

If the letter *ḍh* were substituted [for *ṭh*], then by the rule "ṭh-ḍho ḍhe lopaḥ" (8.3.13), its elision would occur; furthermore, by the rule "pūrvatrāsiddham" (8.2.1), that [elision] would be considered as not having taken effect [with respect to subsequent operations]. However, this [elision] is intended to be effective. Therefore, the elision of the *hal* (consonant) is prescribed as a *nipātana* (irregularity) in order to prevent the application of "pūrvatrāsiddham," and not the letter *ḍh*.

Thus [it is asked]: what, then, is the fault in its being *asiddha* (not yet established), such that for the sake of avoiding it—the purpose of which is to prevent the application of the rule regarding *pūrvatrāsiddham*—the elision of the letter *ha* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*), and not the letter *ḍha*? To this he says:
"In the case of the elision of *ḍha*," and so forth. For if indeed the letter *ḍha* were prescribed as an irregularity, then [the rule] "a *ḍha* before a *ḍha*" would apply.

The elision (*lopa*) [of the *ḍha*] must be applied according to Pāṇini 8.3.13. However, if that elision were to take place, then in forms such as *draḍhimā*, the substitution of *ra* by rule 6.4.161 (*ṛtaḥ* *ṅi* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *ṇaḥ* *ṅī* *ṣṇaḥ* *
Because the notion of "light" (*laghu*) is sublated once the notion of "heavy" (*guru*) has arisen. Regarding the form *draḍhimā*:

by the rule *varṇadḍhādibhyaḥ ṣyañ ca* (Pāṇini 5.1.123), the suffix *iman* is applied, and by *turiṣṭhemeyassu* (6.4.154), there is elision of the final syllable (*ṭilopa*). Regarding the form *draḍhiyān*: [this is formed] by the rule *dvivacanavibhajyopapade tarabīyasunau* (Pāṇini 5.3.57).

The suffix *iyasun* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.3.57] *tarabīyasunau*. Regarding the word "draḍhayati": from the sense "he makes firm" (*draḍham ācaṣṭe*), the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.26] *tatkaroti tadācaṣṭe*; then, by the rule [Vārttika 813] *ṇāviṣṭhavadbhāvaḥ kāryaṃ prātipadikasya*, the status of being like the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan* applies.

[The elision of] *repha* and *ṭi*. In the expression "having made firm (*paridraḍhayya*) he went," [the process is as follows]: from the root *dṛh*, the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied in the sense of "he makes firm" (*dṛḍham ācaṣṭe*). When the substitution of *rabhāva* has been made, there is the connection with the prefix *pari* for the causative form; then the suffix *ktvā*; then a *prādi*-compound; and then, by the rule "in a compound not preceded by *nañ*, *lyap* replaces *ktvā*" (Pāṇini 7.1.37), *lyap* is substituted. Thus: *pāridraḍhayya*.

Regarding the word *kanyā*: the suffix *iñ* is applied because it begins with a consonant (*paridraḍha-śabda*), and the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added by the rule *ito manuṣyajāteḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.65). [The objection] "the suffix *ṣyaṅ* would apply" refers to the rule *aṇiñoḥ anārṣayor gurūpotamayoḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.78), and so forth.
"Ṭhoahitam" is the counter-example for the root *oah*. "Dṛhitam" is from the root *dṛh*.

21. *prabhau parivṛḍhaḥ* | (7.2.21) "The same as by the preceding [rule]"—because the absence of the augment *iṭ* and so forth is identical due to this irregular derivation (*nipātana*). For just as in the previous rule, when the suffix *kta* is applied, there is the elision of the *h* and *n*.

The absence of the augment *iṭ* and the substitution of *ḍha* for the following letter are established as irregularities (*nipātita*); likewise here too, all of that is established as an irregularity.

Regarding the statement "the irregular formation of *vṛṃheḥ*": this refers to the root *vṛhi* (or *bṛhi*, according to the Dhātupāṭha) meaning "to grow" (DhP 736). And if there is another root *vṛhi*, then that too [is included].

Thus; this is the connection with the word "nipātana" (irregular formation). However, some have stated that there exists another root, *vṛha* (or *bṛha*, as per the Dhātupāṭha 735), meaning "to grow. "That itself is the purpose" means the removal of the status of being *asiddha* (non-existent) in the preceding rule. [Example: *parivrajhayati*.

Thus, in this case, when *ḍha* is elided, the *repha* (the letter *r*) would not occur as before. For example, in "parivraḍhayya gataḥ" (having caused him to become a leader, he departed). However, if the elision of *hal* were applied, these faults would arise, such as in "parivraḍham ācaṣṭe" (he describes him as a leader), and so forth. But how is it that the analysis (*vigraha*) is made with the word *parivṛḍha*?
Is the causative suffix (*ṇic*) derived from the root *vṛ* itself understood as "to rise"? To this he says: "of *saṃgrāmayate*" and so forth.

Since the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is already established by the rule "after a nominal stem, in the sense of a verbal root, [the suffix *ṇic* is added] diversely, and it is treated like the desiderative" (Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha Gaṇasūtra 186), the inclusion of *saṃgrāma* with its prefix in the list [of roots] serves [a specific purpose].

The purpose of the restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) is this: so that the causative suffix *ṇic* may arise only after the root *saṃgrām* when it is accompanied by a prefix, and not elsewhere; that is to say, since the arising of *ṇic* is desired only after *saṃgrām* with a prefix, and not after any other [root], therefore, even if...
