Even if the analysis (vigraha) is performed as "he describes one who is pre-eminent" (*vṛḍhaparivṛḍham ācaṣṭe*), nevertheless, when the suffix *ṇic* is derived from the word *vṛḍha*, the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) that occurs must belong to that very beginning [of the stem] from which the *ṇic* was prescribed, according to the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*). [This is because of the rule: "That which ends in *san* and so forth... (*sanādyantā dhātavaḥ*).

Because the technical designation "root" (*dhātu*) is prescribed only for that which begins with [the root] by the rule *dhātavaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.32), a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) following it is not included by the mention of "a subsequent finite verb. Therefore,

since the preceding word ending in *ataṅ* (not having the *taṅ* substitutes) is a *pada*, the rule *tiṅṅtiṅḥ* (8.1.28) applies to the subsequent *pada* ending in a finite verb in the example *parivraḍhayati*.

The *nighāta* accent becomes established. However, if the suffix *ṇic* is derived from the word *parivṛḍha*, then the *lakāra* (the verbal ending) would not be *nighāta*. Furthermore, when the suffix *ṇic* is derived from the word *vṛḍha* and not from the word *parivṛḍha*, then the *ktvā* suffix [would likewise not be *nighāta*].

The [suffix] *ṇic* is applied to the word *vṛḍha*. Consequently, when the word *pari* is compounded with the word *parivṛḍha* ending in a *kta*-affix—by means of the rule "kugatiprādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.2.18)—the substitution of *lyap* is established in the form *parivraḍhayya*. This occurs when the suffix *ṇic* is derived from the word *parivṛḍha*.

The suffix *ktvā* also arises from the word *parivṛḍha* itself when it is followed by the causative (*ṇic*); consequently, there would be no compound. This is because the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* states that particles such as *kupi*, *gati*s, and *prādi*s are compounded with another word possessing meaning (*samartha*), and here there is no other word ending in *kta* following *pareḥ*; for this single word ending in *kta* is [already] together with *pari*.

It is the form *śabda-rūpam*, because the word *pari* is included therein. Furthermore, if there were no compound, the substitution of *lyap* by the rule "in a compound preceded by *nañ*" (Pāṇini 7.3.17) would not apply. The example *parivṛṃhitam* is a counter-example for the root *vṛṃh*. [The correct form is] *parivṛhitam*.
Thus [it is derived] from the root *vṛh*.

22. *Kaṣ* [takes the suffix *kta*] in the sense of difficulty (*kṛcchra*) and impenetrability (*gahana*). (Pāṇini 7.2.22) Regarding the example "kaṣṭaḥ": the root *kaṣ* is listed in the group of roots beginning with *kaṣi-śiṣi*, which have the meaning of harming. But what is meant by "difficulty" (*kṛcchra*)? He says: "Difficulty (*kṛcchra*) is suffering (*duḥkha*). If this is so, then [the word applies] to suffering...
If it is asked, "Why is the prohibition stated regarding living beings not established in the case of fire and the like?

he says: "The cause of that, such as fire and so forth, is also called 'kṛcchra' (hardship). This is because the effect is metaphorically attributed to the cause, just as one says "the water of Naṅvala causes foot disease. This should be reflected upon.

Furthermore, is it appropriate to accept the secondary (gauṇa) meaning when the primary (mukhya) meaning exists, or not? If, however, the word *kṛcchra* is derived from the root *kṛcchrayati*—formed by adding the suffix *ṇic* and then the suffix *ac* according to Pāṇini 3.1.134—such that it is etymologically explained as "that which causes difficulty," then the word *kṛcchra* would apply to the primary sense of fire and so forth as well. Thus, [the objection does not hold].

Something must be considered here: in this etymological derivation, it would be contradictory to say that even its cause—such as the sacrificial fire-altar (*agni*) and so forth—is called "hardship" (*kṛcchra*). For whatever causes hardship necessarily becomes a cause of suffering.

23. *ghuṣir aviśabdane* (Pāṇini 7.2.23). Regarding the statement "proclaiming (*viśabdana*) means promising (*pratijñāna*)," the meaning is the manifestation of one's own intention through speech. Regarding the phrase "it is a general inclusion," [it refers to the fact that the root *ghuṣ* is understood in its general sense].
Because no specific distinction is stated: if *ghuṣir* is indeed read in the *curādi* group as "ghuṣir aviśabde" (or "ghuṣir viśabde" according to the Dhātupāṭha), then it must take the suffix *ṇic*;
however, there is no difference whatsoever whether the suffix *ṇic* is present or absent when the augment *iṭ* occurs.

For instance: when the augment *iṭ* is present, after the elision of *ṇi* by the rule "ṇer niṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi" (Pāṇini 6.4.52), the form that results is *ghoṣita*; even when *iṭ* is absent, because there is no elision of *ṇi*, the form remains exactly the same. Furthermore, there is no possibility for the prohibition of *iṭ* to apply to that which ends in such a [form], because of the governing rule "ekācaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.10).
Regarding the root *ghuṣ* belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa* (*dhā.pā.* 653), [the rule states] "of *ghuṣ*, when not expressing sound" (*aviśabdane*).

Since the root *ghuṣ* has no function other than expressing sound by the very nature of its verbal power (*śabdaśakti*), what is the purpose of the prohibition against expressing sound? To this he says: "The prohibition of expressing sound," and so forth. If...
And if the *ṇic* were eternal, then the prohibition stated in the aforementioned manner would be purposeless;

consequently, it should not have been made at all, yet it has been made. Therefore, this very prohibition indicates that the meaning of the verbal root designated as belonging to the *curādi* group is non-eternal.

Regarding the form *jughoṣuḥ*: this serves as a purpose for the postulation of the non-eternality [of grammatical rules]. For if non-eternality did not exist, the form would have been *ghoṣayāñcakruḥ*.
24. *Ardeḥ sannivibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.24). Regarding the word *ardeḥ*: it refers to the root *ard*, meaning "to go" and "to beg" (Dhātupāṭha 55).
25. *Abheś cāvidūrye* (Pāṇini 7.2.25).

[The word] *vidūram* means "distant. Since *vidūram* is derived as "that which is especially (*viśeṣeṇa*) or excessively (*atiśayena*) distant," that which is other than this is *avidūram*. Furthermore, that is both what is near (*āsannam*) and what is not distant (*adūram*).
It should be understood that this is extremely remote (*ativiprakṛṣṭa*). [The term] *ādidūryam* means "the state of being so remote" (*tasya bhāvaḥ*).

The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied because the word belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class (Pāṇini 5.1.124). Now, one might object that the subsequent suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) is prohibited by the rule *na nañpūrvāt tatpuruṣāt* (Pāṇini 5.1.121).

"Why should the suffix *ṣyañ* not occur here? To this he says: "Precisely for this reason," and so forth. Furthermore, the status of being a "bhāva-pratyaya" (suffix denoting an abstract state) is to be understood in relation to *tva* and *tal*.

26. *ṇeradhyāyane vṛtam* (Pāṇini 7.2.26). Regarding the word "adhyayanam" (study): the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied according to *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (3.3.113). It is called "adhyayanam" because it is studied (*adhīyate*); thus, the word *adhyayana* is derived as a *karma-sādhana* (an action noun denoting the object). For if it were derived as a *bhāva-sādhana* (denoting the abstract action), [the rule would not apply].

The form *vṛto guṇo devadateneti* would not occur; rather, *vṛtaṃ guṇasya devadateneti* would occur. This is an adjective qualifying the *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle); the meaning is "when the *niṣṭhā* denotes that which is to be studied. Regarding the rule "and there is elision of the *ṇi*," this is an irregular elision (*nipātana*) of the *ṇi*, which functions as if the suffix were still present (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*).

This is for the purpose of prohibition. For if there were elision (*lopa*), then by the rule of "characterization by the affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the *guṇa* substitution would occur. But when there is elision by *luk*, because of the prohibition of characterization by the affix according to Pāṇini 1.1.63 (*na lumatāṅgasya*), the *guṇa* would not occur. Regarding the phrase "the *guṇa* of *vṛt*": *guṇa* is a particular kind of study.
To this it is replied:

"This root *vṛt* is intransitive. For we observe the use of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*), as in the examples *dṛtam guṇasya* ("the excellence of the quality") and *vṛtam pārāyaṇasya* ("the completion of the recitation"). Indeed, the past passive participle occurs in the sense of the abstract action for intransitive roots, but not otherwise.

Regarding transitive verbs: "In the sense of *ṇi*, etc. When that [root] has the sense of *ṇi* internalized (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*), then the base ending in [that *ṇi*-affix], while existing in the sense of *ṇi*, becomes transitive; as in "May the well-composed hymns cause you to prosper" (*vardhantu tvāṃ sūktayaḥ*), where the root *vṛdh* [is used]. How is this understood? To this he says: "By that..."

Regarding the passage beginning with "nirvṛtam," etc.: one should not say that these [roots] are intransitive (*akarmaka*). Since "roots become transitive (*sakarmaka*) when accompanied by prepositions (*upasarga*)," the root *vṛt* here is transitive because it is accompanied by a preposition. But if it is not due to its functioning in the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇi*), how is the meaning of the causative understood in the case of the suffix *kta*? If...

In this case, the verb *vṛt* would be transitive because of its connection with a prefix, not because it functions in the sense of the causative (*ṇyartha*); therefore, just as in the expression "the army was experienced by Devadatta" (*anubhūtaḥ kamabalo devadattena*), the causative meaning is not understood, so too it would not be understood here in the expression "produced by him" (*tena nirvṛtaḥ*). Yet it is understood; therefore, it is precisely because it functions in the sense of the causative.

The root *vṛt* is transitive. And when it occurs in the sense of the causative (*ṇyartha*), then, with respect to the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*), its agent undergoes the state of being an object; thus, by means of that instigated object (*prayojya-karman*), it becomes transitive. "In the same way here as well," and so forth.
Since that [root] which is intransitive does not become transitive merely by occurring in the sense of the causative (*ṇyartha*),

therefore, even in the case of *āvṛto guṇo devadattena*, the suffix *kta* will apply to the object precisely because it occurs in the sense of the causative. Consequently, the irregularity (*nipātana*) would be purposeless.

Because [the desired form] is established even without that [rule]. If you ask how, it is because when the suffix *kvā* is added to the root *vṛ*, the option for the augment *iṭ* is provided by Pāṇini 7.2.56 (*udito vā*), and thus, when the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is applied, the prohibition [of *iṭ*] is triggered by 7.2.15 (*yasya vibhāṣā*). If this is so, for what purpose [is the rule under discussion]?
He says this with the words, "That is performed," and so forth.

Sometimes the sense of the causative (*ṇic*) is expressed by the root itself through the internalization of the causative meaning; in that case, if a nipātana (irregular formation) were not applied, the form would result in *vartitam* even when referring to the act of studying.

Therefore, some maintain that this [rule] was formulated for the purpose of excluding that [case]. Others, however, [hold the view expressed in the passage beginning with] "but others," and so forth; they also desire that the guna be applied even after [the suffixes] *vat* and *ita*. According to their opinion, the rule "guna is substituted for vṛ" applies both to the causative (*ṇyanta*) and the non-causative (*aṇyanta*). In their view, the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) need not be performed at all; if it were performed, it would be merely for the sake of stylistic variety.
It should be understood.

27. Or [the forms] *dānta*, *śānta*, *pūrṇa*, *dasta*, *spaṣṭa*, *cchanna*, and *jñapta* [are formed]. (Pāṇini 7.2.27). Regarding *dāntaḥ* and *śāntaḥ*: the roots *śam* and *dam* (Dhātupāṭha 1201, 1203) mean "to become calm.
With the causative suffix *ṇic*, and after the elision of *ṇi* and the prohibition of *iṭ* have been applied, [the rule] *anunāsikasya...* [is applied].

The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *kvijhaloḥ kṅiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.15). Now, one might object: "But since the elision of the *ṇi*-affix (*ṇilopa*) would be treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*), the lengthening should not apply because there is no intervening element. This is not so; for when the elision occurs by virtue of a specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*), that elision cannot be designated as having a subsequent cause (*paranimittakatva*). Therefore...

How can there be the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*)? For the status of being "as if the original" is prohibited in the prescription of a long vowel by the rule *na padānta* (Pāṇini 1.1.58) and others. [Examples: *damitaḥ*, *śamitaḥ*.
Here, the shortening occurs by the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.92). [Example: *pūrṇaḥ*. [The root is] *pūrī* (to swell/to fill), Dhātupāṭha 1803.

The roots *div* and others, as well as *cur* and others. Regarding the word *dasta*: from the root *tasu* "to throw up" (DhP 1212) [or "to diminish" according to the Dhātupāṭha], and from *dasu* "to bite" (DhP 1213). Here, the shortening of the penultimate vowel is also prescribed by irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Regarding the words *spaṣṭa* and *cchanna*: from the root *spaśa* "to afflict" or "to touch" (DhP 887).

The root *ṭhcchad* is used in the sense of "concealing" (*apavāraṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 1935). Here, the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is also prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation).
Regarding the form *jñapta*: the root *jñapa* is used in the senses of "killing," "satisfying," and "sharpening" (*māraṇatoṣaṇaniśāmaneṣu*; Dhātupāṭha 1624).
[According to the Dhātupāṭha, it is used in the senses of "knowing," "making known," "killing," "satisfying," "sharpening," and "whetting"].

Thus ends the *curādi* group; furthermore, it belongs to the *ghaṭādi* group because of the rule "jñā [is used] in the senses of killing, pleasing, and perceiving, and is marked with Ñ" (DhP 811), from which the suffix *ṇic* is added. Regarding the statement "there is a prohibition of the *iṭ* augment and elision of the *ṇic*," the word "and" (*ca*) implies that in some instances, the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasvatva*) is also applied as an irregularity (*nipātana*).

28. *ruṣyamatvarasaṃghuṣāsvanām* | (Pāṇini 7.2.28) The root *ruṣ* is used in the sense of "anger" (Dhātupāṭha 1670); *am* is used in the senses of "motion" and so forth (Dhātupāṭha 465). There will be no inclusion of the root *am* belonging to the curādigaṇa (meaning "disease," Dhātupāṭha 1720), because [the rule applies to] monosyllabic roots (*ekāc*).

(7.2.10) This is because of the governing context (*adhikāra*). [The root] *tvar* meaning "agitation" (*sambhrama*) is preceded by the prefix *sam*. [The root] *dhuṣ* is as previously mentioned. [The root] *svan* is also as previously mentioned, preceded by the prefix *ā*. In the form *āsvāntaḥ*, the lengthening of the vowel is as before. In the form *tūrṇaḥ*, [the rule] *jvaratvarasravyavimavām upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.20) applies.

Thus ends the section on *ūṭh*. Regarding the rule beginning with "sampūrva" and so forth: the scope (*avakāśa*) of the root *ghuṣir* (DhP 6.53), which means "to sound," when not preceded by the prefix *sam* and when not combined with the word *vi*, is as follows: *ghuṣṭā rajjuḥ* ("the rope is sounded") and *ghuṣṭau pādau* ("the feet are sounded"). And the scope of this present rule [which prescribes *iṭ*] is when it is preceded by the prefix *sam*.
Regarding *viśabdane*: [the rule] states "he utters a resonant word" (*saṃghuṣitaṃ vākyam āha*) or "he utters a resonant word" (*saṃghuṣṭaṃ vākyam āha*).
When the prefix *sam-* is present, since both [suffixes] would apply in the absence of *vi-*, this [rule] takes effect by virtue of its posteriority—resulting in the option:
*saṃghuṣṭau dantau* or *saṃghuṣitau dantau*. [This applies] when preceded by *āṅ*.
And so forth. Regarding the rule *kṣubdhasvānta* (Pāṇini 7.2.18), this is the scope for the prohibition of the suffix *niṭ*.

When not preceded by *āṅ* and denoting the mind (*manas*), the forms *svāntam* and *manaḥ* constitute its scope; whereas when preceded by *āṅ*, it denotes something other than the mind. Thus: *āsvanto devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta is exhausted"), *āsvanitaḥ*.

Regarding the term *devadatta*: when preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, if it denotes the mind (*manas*), then *svāntam* and *manaḥ* provide the scope; however, when preceded by *āṅ*, if it does not denote the mind, then [the forms] *āsvantaḥ devadattaḥ* and *āsvanitaḥ devadattaḥ* apply. This is when preceded by *āṅ*.
In the case of expressing *mona* (silence), because it is the subsequent rule, this very option applies: *āsvāntaṃ manaḥ* or *āsvanitaṃ manaḥ*.
29. *hṛṣer lomasu* (Pāṇini 7.2.29).

[The example is] "hṛṣṭāni lomāni" ("the hairs are bristling"). Because it is intransitive according to [the rule] *gaty-arthāḥ akarmakāḥ...* (3.4.72), the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). [The example is] "hṛṣṭaṃ lomabhiḥ" ("bristled by the hairs"). [The example is] "in the neuter, in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*)."

The suffix *kta* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.102] *ktaḥ*. Regarding the statement "it is aniṭ in the *niṣṭhā*"—since the optionality of the augment *iṭ* for the suffix *ktvā* is prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.2.56] *udito vā*, there is a prohibition of *iṭ* for the *niṣṭhā* by [Pāṇini 7.2.15] *yasya vibhāṣā*. As for the statement "this [root] is seṭ," it is because there is no prohibition of *iṭ* due to its being udātta.

"This is a *vibhāṣā* (optional rule) applicable in both cases. That is, it applies both when [the suffix] is already applicable and when it is not. There is an option when the prohibition of the word *alīka* is applicable, and [an option] when the word *tuṣṭi* is not yet applicable;
for the word *loman* is conventionally restricted to the body hairs (*aṅgajāta*) alone.
When "loma" (hair) is mentioned, someone might have the misconception that it refers only to the hair of the body and not to head-hair; therefore, to dispel that, he says: "lomāni" (hairs), etc.
How so? He says: "just as hair and nails," etc. For here...

Their inclusion is by way of generality; for instance, purification is performed even after touching hair. But how is it possible for a verbal root (*dhātu*), which denotes an action, to function with respect to substances such as body hairs? To this he says: "In that domain," and so forth. Those hairs are the "domain" (*viṣaya*).

That [person] is described as such. Since the meaning of the root *hṛṣ* (to bristle) is accomplished by means of the body hairs (*loman*), it has the body hairs as its object. Thus, although the root *hṛṣ* exists there [in that person], it is said to exist in the body hairs by way of its meaning.
In this way, it is shown that the body hairs function as qualifiers with respect to the root *hṛṣ* by way of its meaning.

Regarding the statement "and [the prohibition applies] in the case of *vismita* and *pratihata*": the term "nipātana" (irregular formation) means that this form should be explained as having the sense that the augment *iṭ* does not occur after the roots *vismi* and *pratihā* when followed by the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*). In this regard, the following is the explanation: there is a formal split (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule beginning with *hṛṣeḥ*.

It is performed; therefore, it will apply even to the words *vismita* and *pratighāta*. Alternatively, a plural designation is used here, and this is understood to have the sense of "beginning with" (*ādi*); thus, as in the case of *loma-ādiṣu* meaning "among hairs and so forth," it will apply even to *vismita* and *pratighāta*.
30. *apacitaśca* (Pāṇini 7.2.30).

[The sūtra continues with] *ṭhcāyateḥ*. The root *cāyṛ* is listed as "to honor" and "to perceive" (Dhātupāṭha 880). This rule applies to that which does not admit the function of honoring for the root *ci* (*cinoti*) when it is not preceded by any prefix.
It is begun again. However, for one who undertakes [the study], it has not yet been begun.
For instance: from the root *ci* (to gather), *apacita* will occur; but from *cāyati* (to honor), *avacāyita*.
"It must be stated" (*vaktavyam*) means it must be explained. In this regard, here...

The explanation: the particle *ca* (and) is used here; it serves the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. By this, *apacitiḥ* is also derived as a nipātana (an irregularly formed word). And in stating this as a nipātana, it must be stated that when the suffix *ktin* follows the root *ci*, the substitution of *c* for *k* occurs invariably.

31. *hrau* [is substituted] for *hvar-* in the Vedic language (*chandas*). (Pāṇini 7.2.31) Since the root *hvar* "to be crooked" (Dhātupāṭha 931) is anudātta, the prohibition of *iṭ* already applies; this rule is stated for the purpose of prescribing the specific substitute.
32. *aparihūtaśca* | (Pāṇini 7.2.32) "The non-occurrence of this substitute *hru* is prescribed [as a nipātana]. This refers to what was obtained by the preceding rule.
The mention of the plural number is so that the prescription may apply only when the plural number is present. By means of that—
For within a word, it is indeed *aparihṛtaḥ*, *aparihṛtau*, and *aparihṛtāḥ* that occur.
33. *hvarita* (Pāṇini 7.2.33):
"The augment *ṭh* and *iṭ* are introduced, and *guṇa* is substituted [by nipātana]; and by the word 'ca' (and), the absence of the substitute *hrau* is also [indicated]."

*grasita-skabhitastabhitotabhitacatavikastā-viśastṛ-śaṃstṛ-śāstṛ-tarutṛ-tarūtṛ-varutṛ-varūtṛ-varūtrī-rujvaliti-kṣariti-kṣamiti-vamiti-amiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.34). [The rule begins with: "Of these roots *grasu*, *skambhu*, and *stanbhu*," and so forth. [The root] *grasu* [is used] in the sense of eating (*adane*).
The two verbal roots *ṣṭhaskambh* and *ṣṭanstambh* (Pāṇini 3.1.82) are Vedic roots (*sautra-dhātu*),

as they are listed in the rule *ṣṭambhu-ṣṭumbhu-ṣkambhu-ṣkumbhu-ṣkuñbhyaḥ śnuś-ca* (3.1.82). From these, forms such as *ṣṭabhitam* and *stabhitam* are derived according to the rule *aniditām* (6.4.24).

Thus ends the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-salopa*). Regarding *stabdham* from the root *stabh*: there is the substitution of *dh* by [Pāṇini 8.2.40] *jhaṣas tathordho 'dhaḥ*, and the substitution of the *jaś*-class sounds by [Pāṇini 8.4.56] *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*.
Regarding *uttabhitam*: [the rule] *udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ pūrvasya* [applies].
[The rule] "the same vowel as the preceding" [applies]. [The word] *stabhita* does not have *ut* as its prefix;
for if it did, the specific grammatical derivation (*nipātana*) of the form preceded by *ut* would be purposeless.
[This refers to the forms derived from] *cat* and *kas*. [Regarding] *cat*: "to beg" (DhP 8.65, 8.66); [and] *kas*...

[The root] *gatau* (DhP 860). Now, one might object: "In the sūtra, the plural form *vikastāḥ* is heard; therefore, how can this [form] be cited from the vṛtti as ending in the singular? To this he says: "The formation [of the word] is with regard to plurality; *vikastāḥ* is the plural. In the sūtra, [the items] beginning with *grasita*...

The irregular forms (nipātanas) are treated as compounds (dvandva); therefore, the plural number is used in reference to them. However, in the commentary (vṛtti), this word *vikasta* appears alone and uncompound. Nor is the plural number intended here to express the plurality of its meaning; thus, it is cited in the singular ending. [This refers to the phrase] "in others."
Regarding the forms beginning with *viśastṛ* and so forth: [the author] states, "The case endings are specified individually.
The intention is that the plural number was not applied there because of the absence of plurality; therefore, it was not done in those instances.
[The forms are derived] from *śasu* preceded by *vi*, from *śaṃs*, and from *śās*. [The root] *śasu* is listed as "in the sense of injury" (Dhātupāṭha 727).

The roots *śans* in the sense of "praising" (*stutau*) [DhP 7.2.8] and *śās* in the sense of "instructing" (*anuśiṣṭau*) [DhP 7.2.1075]. Regarding the forms *tarītāram* and *varītāram*, the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *vṛto vā* (Pāṇini 7.2.38). Regarding the form *varūtrīḥ*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* (Pāṇini 4.1.5); from that which ends in this suffix, the nominative plural ending *jas* is added.

The long vowel of the same quality as the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) occurs by the rule *ṭhvā chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.106). Regarding the form *jasi*, there is the mention of the "same quality as the preceding" (*pūrvasavarṇa*), and so forth. Now, one might object: once the *yaṇ*-substitution has been applied, the form should be *varūtryaḥ*; how then is it that we have *varūtrayaḥ*? To this he says: "It is Vedic (*chāndasam*)."

And so forth. For when shortening is applied by virtue of its being Vedic (*chāndasa*), the rule *jasi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.109) prescribes a *guṇa* substitution as an exception to the *yaṇ* replacement. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of elaboration" (*prapañcārtham*), the meaning is "an explanation in detail. For instance, [the root] *pac* is used in the sense of expansion (*vistāra*).
Thus, this [rule] is an elaboration (*prapañca*) of that very same rule concerning bases ending in *ā*. An elaboration, however, serves to clarify the meaning;
for an explanation given in detail becomes clear. Now, why is there not a formal derivation (*nipātana*) for the word *varūtrī*? To this he says: "For the word *vaktr̥*..."
And so forth. Regarding the roots mentioned:
*jval* in the sense of "to blaze" (DhP 831); *kṣar* in the sense of "to move" (DhP 851); *ṭu vam* in the sense of "to vomit" (DhP 849); and *am* in the sense of "motion" and so on (DhP 465).
The particle *iti* is used for the purpose of illustration; that is, it serves to indicate other similar cases as well. What is established by this? He says:
"By this, in some instances," and so forth. The particle *ca* (and) is for the purpose of drawing in [the rule] *chandasi* (in Vedic usage). By this—
And because it has already been drawn forward [by the previous rule], it is not connected with what follows; therefore, the prescription in the subsequent section applies without distinction.
35. *ār-dhātuka-syeR-ū-ā-val-ādeḥ* | (Pāṇini 7.2.35) Examples:

*āste*, *śete*, *vaste*. The roots are: *ās* (to sit) [DhP 1021], *śīṅ* (to sleep) [DhP 1032], and *vas* (to wear/cover) [DhP 1023]. Because they belong to the *adādi* class, there is no *śap* suffix.
[The rule] "luk, ṭhśīṅḥ sārvadhātuke guṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.21).

Because of the mention of *ārdhadhātuka* here, [the substitution of] *iṇ* does not occur for the *sārvadhātuka*. But is it not the case that [the rule] "rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke" (Pāṇini 7.2.76) is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*)?

It is understood that [the rule] "the *iṭ* augment applies to the *sārvadhātuka* suffix after roots beginning with *rud*, and not after others. However, one should not entertain the suspicion of a reversed restriction (such as "the *sārvadhātuka* suffix receives *iṭ* only after roots beginning with *rud*").
For if such a restriction were indeed the case, then the *iṭ* augment would apply to the *san* suffix following roots beginning with *rud*.

It would not [be so]; for [the suffix] has been restricted by a fixed rule (*niyama*). Consequently, the mention of the root *rud* in the rule *rudavidamuṣagrahi...* (Pāṇini 1.2.8) would be purposeless, since the status of being a *kit* suffix is already established by the rule *halantācca* (1.2.10). Therefore, there is no suspicion here of a reversed restriction (*viparīta-niyama*). [The restriction is: "only after roots beginning with *rud*..."

"The restriction will be: 'for the *sārvadhātuka* [affix], and not for others'; therefore, there is no need for the mention of *ārdhadhātuka* for the purpose of excluding the *sārvadhātuka*. To this, he says: 'from *rud* etc. and so forth. This refers to the restrictive rule: *rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke* (Pāṇini 7.2.76).

When [the rule] is being understood, some person of dull intellect might conceive of a contrary restriction; in that case, by the principle just stated, while one is proceeding toward the intended restriction, there would be "burdening of the understanding" (*pratipattigauravam*). The particle *iti* indicates a reason (*hetau*); for this very reason...

If this [rule] *ṭhrudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke* (Pāṇini 7.2.76) were understood as being for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), there would be a burden on the understanding (*pratipattigaurava*). For this reason, why is the mention of *ārdhadhātuka* not made? It cannot be for the sake of [restricting] that very thing. For if it were [a restriction] regarding the stem (*aṅga*), then [the rule] *ekāca...* [would apply].
In the rule *upadeśe'nudātāt* (Pāṇini 7.2.10), the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* for an affix would be purposeless,

because there is no possibility [of its application] due to the statements *na ktvā seṭ* (1.2.18) and *niṣṭhā śīṅ* (1.2.19); for if the augment *iṭ* were added to this [root], it would not occur in the forms of the suffixes *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā*.

[The designation] *seṭ* is established. Why, then, is [the rule] not formulated for this purpose: so that in cases such as *vṛkṣātva* and *vṛkṣatā*, the pratyaya [suffix] following the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) shall not [be called *seṭ*]? It does not deserve to be formulated even for this purpose, because [the word] "dhātoḥ" (of a root) is supplied from the rule "ṛta id dhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.100).

This [rule] continues [to apply]. But even so, [the rule] would still apply in cases such as *lūbhyām* and *lūbhiḥ*, because here the status of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*) is not obstructed by the status of being a nominal stem (*pratipadikatva*), on the grounds that "words ending in *kviP* do not lose their status as verbal roots" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 132). Therefore, in this case, [let it be] not...

Is the mention of *ārdhadhātuka* appropriate for the purpose that [the suffix] should not [apply]? This is not so; for in the rule *añnata iddhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.100), the word *dhātu* is understood as referring to its own form (*svarūpa*).
Therefore, here too, the term *dhātoḥ*, which is being carried over from that context, follows in that same sense. Consequently...

Since the augment *iṭ* is prescribed only for that which is ordained by the rule "after a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*), there is no possibility of the application of *iṭ* in forms such as *lūbhyām* and *lūbhiḥ* if the term "ārdhadhātuka" were not included [in the governing rule]. The same applies to forms such as *jugupsate*; for here the suffix *san* is not ordained by the rule "after a verbal root," but rather—
What then? [The term "dhātu" is used] by taking roots such as *gup* in their own form (*svarūpa*).
Therefore, it should be understood that the mention of *ārdhadhātuka* is not for the purpose of excluding those [roots].
In the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.100), the word *dhātu* is understood as referring to its own form (*svarūpa*).

If that were so, then the qualification "of a root" (*dhātoḥ*) would not even need to be formulated [in the rule *ṛtaḥ*]. For since that [qualification] is impossible in the word "root" itself, it is understood as a qualification of its meaning; this is the conclusion.
Alternatively—in that system, two occurrences of the term "root" (*dhātu*) are employed by way of a single mention (*tantra*); therein, one consists of the word-meaning (*arthapada*).

Furthermore, [the term *dhātu*] consists of both the word-form (*svarūpa*) and the meaning (*artha*). In that regard, the former is applicable where the meaning-word is intended, while the latter is applicable here;
thus, there is no fault whatsoever.
Therefore, the mention of *ardhadhātuka* is solely for the purpose of avoiding excessive complexity in understanding (*pratipatti-gaurava*).

What is the purpose of including the mention of *iṅ* here, given that the mention of *iṅ* continues from the rule "ṭhneṅvaśi kṛti" (Pāṇini 7.2.28)? To this he says: "While *iṭ* is still in force," and so forth.
For that mention of *iṭ* is connected with the prohibition; therefore, when that [prohibition] continues [into the present rule], [the mention of *iṅ* is necessary].

Its [the augment *iṭ*’s] recurrence would also follow; therefore, the mention of *iṭ* is made again for the purpose of its exclusion. But surely, a prohibition can only apply when there is an actual possibility [of application], and no *iṭ* is obtained by any rule for an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a *val* letter; thus, since there is an absence of any possibility of application, this [rule] should be understood as an injunction (*vidhi*), not [a prohibition].
Is this a prohibition? No, it is not so; from this very statement of prohibition, a positive injunction is also inferred.
Surely there exists a rule for the insertion of *iṭ* in the *ārdhadhātuka*, since [the author] teaches its prohibition when preceded by *val*.
However, because of the repetition of the mention of *iṭ*, this shall be understood as a positive injunction.

36. *snukramoranātmanepadanimitte* (Pāṇini 7.2.36). Since the augment *iṭ* is already established for the roots *ṣṇu* (in the sense of "flowing," DhP 1038) and *kramu* (in the sense of "stepping," DhP 473) because they are udātta, this rule is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*).

The statement [of the rule] is intended so that these two [suffixes] may apply only in the domain of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), and not elsewhere. Now, one might object: since the root *snai* ends in a long vowel (*ūg*) and since a prohibition is prescribed for it when followed by a *kit* suffix or the desiderative (*san*), this statement could also serve the purpose of providing an exception (*vidhyartha*). This is not the case; [The reason is as follows:]... (Note: The provided fragment ends here).

The phrase "of an ārdhadhātuka suffix beginning with a consonant, iṭ is added" (Pāṇini 7.2.35) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Therefore, this present rule is understood to apply within the scope of that [general] application.

Furthermore, the two [suffixes] *saṅ* and *kit* are not the scope of this application, because they fall under the scope of exceptions (*apavāda*) to it. [The term] "when there is a cause for the middle voice" (*ātmanepadanimitta*)...

This is in the nominative dual. He says "provided that... and so forth, in order to show that this is a qualifier of the roots *snū* and *kram*. "And where is there a cause for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*)?"—does this mean even in cases where those two possess merely the capacity for the middle voice?
Is it "in the case of those [roots] which have the ātmanepada as their cause," or "in that place where the ātmanepada occurs based upon them"?

He asks this for the sake of such a meaning—namely, "where," and so forth. Here the explanation is as follows: "In that place where the ātmanepada can occur based upon them, there they are 'those having the ātmanepada as their cause. What [is meant by this]?

Furthermore, where does that *ātmanepada* ending, which has that [the *stuka*] as its basis, occur? To this he says: "In the case of the state of being (*bhāva*), the object (*karman*), the agent (*kartṛ*), the mutual exchange of actions (*karmavyatīhāra*), and in sequence (*krama*). For in these cases, the *ātmanepada* ending occurs with a basis on the *stuka*. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of *sarga* and so forth is intended.

A cause is that which possesses a mark (*nimitta*); moreover, something does not become a cause if it does not produce an effect. However, where there is the designation "cause" even for something like a grain in a storehouse that does not produce an effect, such usage is figurative (*aupacārika*) based on its potentiality (*yogyatā*). Therefore, in cases where the *ātmanepada* is applied by relying on the sequence of *snukramau*.

In that very context, regarding the agent, the object, and so forth, the primary cause for the *ātmanepada* endings of those two [roots] is understood. "By that," and so on: because in this way, wherever the *ātmanepada* occurs by depending upon those two, there they possess the status of being the cause for the *ātmanepada*. Therefore, when the *ātmanepada* is present—

This is a prohibition [of the ātmanepada], not when it is absent. For if the ātmanepada were non-existent, their status as being primarily conditioned by the ātmanepada would not be tenable. Consequently, [the forms] *prasnavitā*, *prasnavitum*, *prasnavitavyam*, *prakramitā*, and *prakramitum* [would not be established].

Regarding the rule *prakramitavyam*, although the roots *snū* and *kram* acquire the designation of being causes for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) because they are eligible for it, nevertheless, the prohibition [of the suffix *ya*] does not apply. For here, there is no primary causality for the middle voice, since the middle voice itself is absent.

Regarding *prāpnoṣīṣṭa*: the suffix *liṅ* is used in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), with the augment *sīyuṭ*; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.13); the augment *suṭ* is added by the rule *suṭ tithoḥ* (3.4.107); then the substitution of *ṣ* and *ṣṭu* occurs. Regarding *prakramiṣṭa*: here [the rule] *propābhyāṃ samarthābhyām* (1.3.42) applies.

Thus ends the section on the *ātmanepada* endings when the agent is the object of the action. Regarding the example "prasnoṣyate": the suffix *lṛṭ* is applied by the rule "lṛṭ śeṣe ca" (Pāṇini 3.3.13). Regarding "pracikraṃsate" [this example does not appear in the Kāśikā;
only "pracikraṃsiṣyate" is found there]: the suffix *san* is applied.

The ātmanepada [ending] is applied by the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* (1.3.62). Regarding the phrase "in all cases" and so forth: it is appropriate that in forms such as *prakraṃsīṣṭa* and *prasnīṣīṣṭa*, the ātmanepada endings serve as the cause for the application of the roots *snū* and *kram*; this is because the ātmanepada is prescribed there. But how is it [the cause] in the case of *pracikraṃsate*?
The root *krami* is not the cause for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*); for in this case, the middle voice does not occur by depending on *krami*.
What then? It occurs because it is another verbal root ending in the suffix *san*. To this he says: "Even from that which ends in *san*," and so forth.
For even when the middle voice is prescribed after a root ending in *san*, as in the rule "After *san*, it is like the preceding" (Pāṇini 1.3.62).

By this [statement], because of the expression "as before" (*pūrvavat*) even in that case, the nature of the verbal root (*dhātu*) as previously [stated] is relied upon as the cause for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). Although the middle voice is prescribed after a root with the suffix *san*, nevertheless, due to the sequence there—
The intention is that the absence of a cause (nimitta) indeed exists.
Now, for what purpose is the mention of "cause" (nimita) employed; why not simply say "in the ātmanepada"?
To this he says: "The mention of 'cause'... and so forth. That which has *sīyuṭ* as its initial element...
The term *sīyuḍādiḥ* refers to [affixes] beginning with *sīyuṭ*. *Tatparaḥ* means that after which the ātmanepada affix follows;

*tatparaparaḥ* refers to the *san* affix which follows that [ātmanepada]. The mention of "cause" (*nimitta*) is for the purpose of ensuring that the prohibition applies to both of these. Among them, regarding *sīyuḍādiḥ*:

For the purpose of prohibition—namely, *prasnoṣīṣṭa* and *prakraṃsīṣṭa*; and for the purpose of prohibiting that which follows after it—namely, *pracikraṃsiṣyata*. For in this case, the mention of "the cause" (*nimitta*) is not made;
then, the rule "in the ātmanepada" would be understood as a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*). And [thus] *prasnīṣīṣṭa* [is accounted for].

In the form *prakraṃsīṣṭa*, since the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix follows [the root] when the *ātmanepada* endings are present— given that *sīyuṭ* is an augment belonging to the *ātmanepada*— the prohibition [of *guṇa*] would not apply when it is being uttered as part of that [augment] following the *ātmanepada*. This is the case in *pracikraṃsiṣyata*.

If this were understood as a locative in the sense of "when [the affix] ātmanepada follows" (*parasaptamī*), then— because of the rule *tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.66), which states that when something is specified by the word "in that," the operation applies to what precedes it—

and because the mention of the word "specified" (*nirdiṣṭa*) implies immediate proximity (*ānantarya*), the prohibition of *iṭ* for the suffix *san* would not apply when there is an intervention by *sy*. However, if it is taken as a cause (*nimitta-grahaṇa*)...

When [the condition] exists, [the effect] occurs. For here, in all these cases, there is indeed the status of being a cause for the ātmanepada according to the respective application of the roots *snū* and *kram*.

Therefore, the mention of the word "cause" (*nimitta*) must be made. From the forms *prasnavitrīyate* and so forth, the ātmanepada is observed following the root *snū*; therefore, *snū* is [the cause] of the ātmanepada.
Someone might have the misconception that because of the prohibition [of the suffix *kvip*], there must necessarily be a cause (*nimitta*);

therefore, in order to dispel that, he says: "here he acts like one who has asked," and so forth. In some places, the reading is "he acts like one who has asked" (*praśnavitāram ivācarati*), but that is not tenable; for [the suffix] does not [apply] to an object (*karman*).
Furthermore, *kyaṅ* is not prescribed [after a nominal stem]; rather, it is prescribed after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) that denotes the agent.
Therefore, this reading is the result of an error. [The form] *prasnavitēvācarati* is derived from a word ending in the suffix *tṛc*;
by the rule *kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.11), *kyaṅ* is applied, and by the rule *rīṅ ṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.27), *rīṅ* is substituted for the *ṛ*.
Furthermore, when the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is prescribed for that which ends in *kyaṅ*, it is prescribed specifically for what ends in *ṅti*.

Now, is that [the base] *snau* ending in *ṅt*? No; rather, it is *kyaṅ*-ending. Therefore, since only that which ends in *kyaṅ* is the cause for the middle voice, and not the root *snau* itself, the prohibition does not apply.

Regarding the passage beginning with "But in the case of sequence" (*krame tu*): because of the inclusion of the term "cause" (*nimitta*), the prohibition must apply only when the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is present, not when it is absent. Since the prohibition does not apply to *kṛt* suffixes used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), this is added as a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*). Examples are "she has begun" (*prakrāntā*) and "she has commenced" (*upakrāntā*), [derived] from the roots *pra-kram* and *upa-kram*.

By the rule *samarthābhyām* (Pāṇini 1.3.42), since the root *kram* followed by the prefixes *pra* and *upa* is prescribed to take the ātmanepada, this is a case where *kram* falls within the domain of the ātmanepada.
Thus, the phrase "the domain of the ātmanepada" [is used] in the sense of "from that which has the ātmanepada as its domain."

That whose scope is the *ātmanepada* is "having the *ātmanepada* as its scope. [The forms] *prakramitavyam* and *upakramitavyam* are *kṛtya* suffixes used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), according to Pāṇini 3.4.70: "Only for those two [roots] are the *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khal* suffixes employed. [The form] *niṣkramitā* [is derived] by [the rule] 8.3.41: *idudupadhasya*.

The substitution of *ṣ* occurs for the *visarjanīya*. Because there is no middle voice (*ātmanepada*) for the root *kram* preceded by *ni*, this [substitution] does not apply here to the middle voice. Now, why does it not occur in cases such as *prasusnūṣati*, *prasnutaḥ*, and *prasnutavān*? For it is not the case that...

Is *snauti* the domain of the Ātmanepada? To this he says "of *snaute*" and so forth. Now, one might object that since the prohibitions of *iṭ* by the rules "śryukaḥ kiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.11) and "sani grahaguhośca" (Pāṇini 7.2.12) leave room for other roots ending in long *ū*, this [prohibition] alone would apply here due to its superior status.

Must it not be so, rather than by way of prohibition? This is not the case; for it was stated previously that because the prohibitive injunction is more powerful, there is a purpose for the prohibition of a specific rule that relies on the mere presence of the suffix *iṇ*. Just as: [example omitted].
It may be so.

37. *graho'liṭi dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.37). By stating "of what follows *graha*" and then "the word *graha*," he indicates that the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is intended. If this is so, then should the mention of *iṅ* (the vowel *i*) be made? It need not be made; for that [mention of *iṅ*] is simply carried over by anuvṛtti from the preceding rule. Indeed, that—
Is the meaning here indicated by the nominative case-ending, whereas the sense [of the ablative] is expressed by the genitive case-ending? This is not a fault;

the word "grahaḥ" is in the fifth case (ablative), which will cause the first case to function as a sixth case (genitive), according to the rule "tasmād ity uttarasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.67). [Examples: *jagṛhiva*, *jagṛhima*.

Thus, by the rule *grahyādi* (Pāṇini 6.1.16), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). Likewise, why is it that in forms such as *grāhitā* and *grāhiṣyate*, the augment *iṭ* [of the *ciṇvadiṭ* type] does not occur? To this he says: "Of that very one which is under discussion," and so forth. This refers to the *iṭ* that was introduced by the rule *ārdhadhātukasya* [Pāṇini 7.2.35].
This lengthening occurs for that [augment], not for the *iṭ* of *ciṇvadiṭ*; because that [latter] has not been introduced as the subject.

By the term *ciṇvat*, the state of being like *ciṇ* (*ciṇvadbhāva*) is indicated; the *iṭ* associated with that is called *ciṇvat*. [The example is] "grāhita" (caused to be grasped). [It is formed by: "anadyatane luṭ" (Pāṇini 3.3.15) and "syatāsī... (Pāṇini 3.1.33).

The suffix *tās* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.33] *lṛluṭoḥ*; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by [Pāṇini 1.3.13] *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*; the substitution of *ḍā* is applied by [Pāṇini 2.4.85] *luṭaḥ prathamasya* and so forth;
there is the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant); and the augment *iṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 6.4.62] *syasicsīyuṭtāsiṣu* and so forth.

The *vṛddhi* [substitution] occurs due to the application of the *ciṇvadbhāva* rule. Now, why does the long vowel not occur in *jarīgṛhitā* and *jarīgṛhītum*, where the suffixes *tṛn* and *tumun* follow a *yaṅ*-stem, after the elision of *ya* and the elision of *al* have been applied? [The answer is that] the mention of the word "optionally" (*vā*) in the subsequent sūtra applies to both rules as well.
Because it is a remainder (*śeṣa*), it is understood according to the established *Vibhāṣā* rule.

Alternatively, the position that the qualifier is enjoined (*vihitaviśeṣaṇapakṣa*) is explained here: the augment *iṭ* is enjoined after the root *grah*, and its long vowel [occurs]; however, the *iṭ* here is not enjoined after *grah*. Why then? It is because it follows a stem ending in *yaṅ*.

Therefore, there is no possibility of lengthening here. Now, why was it not stated simply as "ṭh graheḥ iḍaliṭi" [the augment *iṭ* is added after the root *grah* when followed by the *iṭ* of the *liṭ*]; what is the purpose of mentioning "lengthening"? It cannot be done in this way; for if that were so, the operation of *iṭ* would not apply to *īṭ*, and consequently, in the form *agrhīt*, the rule "iṭa īṭi" (Pāṇini 8.2.28) [which requires the elision of one *iṭ* before another] would fail to apply.

Thus, there would be no elision of the *sic* suffix, and the prohibition [of *iṭ*] by the rule *neṭi* (Pāṇini 7.2.4) would also apply; furthermore, in forms such as *agrahīḍhvam* and *agrahīdhvam*, there would be the substitution of a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) for the *dh* by the rule *vibhāṣeṭaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.79), provided that *iṭ* were substituted for the long vowel. Regarding that [substitution]:
Since the operation of *iṭ* is applicable by virtue of its being treated as the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), it is precisely the long vowel that is prescribed.
38. Or *vṛtaḥ* (7.2.38). 1. Does this refer to the root *vṛ* "to choose" (DhP 1490)? 2.
Or does it refer to this [root] and other roots ending in *ṛ*? 3. Or does it refer to that [root] and others?

Is it [the rule] for those ending in *ṛ*, (4) or rather for *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ* and others ending in *ṛ*, or (5) else for those two and [others] ending in *ṛ*? In that regard, if the first alternative were adopted, then having applied the *yaṇ* substitution, the mention [*vraḥ*] would be made.
One should [formulate it] as "gro yaṅ" (Pāṇini 8.2.20). Now, if the second alternative were intended, then one should not have included the mention of "dṛ";
for its inclusion would already be established by the mention of the suffix ending in ṛ. If, however, the third alternative is intended, [the rule should read] "ṛtasya saṃyogādeḥ."

In this regard, one should not include the short vowel by means of the word *ṛta*; for it is precisely this [word] that will be carried over (*anuvartiṣyate*) there as the inclusion of the *ṛ*-vowel. Now, as for the fourth alternative: one should not make a separate mention of the roots *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*; for by the inclusion of those ending in the *ṛ*-vowel, the inclusion of these two is already effected.
Because [the other options] have been refuted, one should understand that, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the fifth alternative is intended here;
thus he says: "The inclusion of both *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ* is general," and so forth. "General inclusion" means that no specific distinction is made between them.
"What is the purpose of saying ‘vṛta’? He thinks thus: "It should have been stated simply as ‘vṛṣā’;

even if it were stated in that way, by the inclusion of homogeneous sounds (savarṇagrahaṇa), there would be the inclusion of both *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ* ending in the letter *ṛ*, as well as those ending in the letter *ṝ*. Even if it were stated in that way..."
Showing that there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) [of the rule], he says: "he will do" (*kariṣyati*), "he will take" (*hariṣyati*).
Here, the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *ṛddhanoḥ sye* (Pāṇini 7.2.70).
39. *na liṅ* (Pāṇini 7.2.39).
In examples such as *vavariṣīṣṭa*, [the Kāśikā provides the example *vivariṣīṣṭa*], the rule *liṅsicorātmanepadeṣu* (7.2.42) applies.
Thus [is formed] *iṭ*. In the phrase "he would desire to spread" (*vistariṣīṣṭa*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used because the action refers to the object.

40. *sici ca parasmaipadeṣu* (Pāṇini 7.2.40). Regarding the form *prāvāriṣṭām*: by the rule *tasthasthamipāṃ tāntantāmaḥ* (3.4.101), *tas* is replaced by *tām*; the augment *iṭ*, which is prescribed generally, is applied, and then the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs in the *sic* suffix. Regarding the form *prāvāriṣuḥ*.

The substitution of *jus* for *jhi* occurs by the rule "ṭhsijabhyastavidibhyaśca" (Pāṇini 3.4.109). An example of the root *vṛṅ* has not been presented, because it is impossible for it to take a parasmaipada ending. [The forms] "prāvariṣṭa" and "prāvarīṣṭa" [are derived] with the augment *iṭ* by the rule "liṅsicorātmanepadeṣu" (Pāṇini 7.2.42).
41. *iṭ* is optionally applied before the suffix *san*. (Pāṇini 7.2.41) In the form *vuvūrṣate*: the suffix *san* is treated as having the *kit* designation by *iko jhal* (1.2.9);
a long vowel is substituted [for the penultimate] by *ajjhanagamāṃ sani* (6.4.16); and [the substitution of *ū* for *u*] is effected by *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya* (7.1.102).

Thus, there is the substitution of *u* for *ṛ*, and the substitution of *ra* following the vowel. Why does this not occur here in *cikīrṣati* and *jihīrṣati*, since there is an occasion for its application once the lengthening has taken place? To this he says: "In *cikīrṣati* and *jihīrṣati*. The meaning is already explained.

42. *liṅ-sicorātmanepadeṣu* (Pāṇini 7.2.42). Since [the augment] *iṭ* would otherwise be obligatory due to the fact that [the roots] beginning with *vṛt* are marked with an acute accent (*udātta*), this rule is commenced for the purpose of making it optional. The term "in the *ātmanepada*" is a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*). And this qualifies *sicaḥ* as well. If this is so, then regarding *liṅ*:
[If it were not qualified,] it would not be specified, and consequently, the *liṅ* [augment] might also apply to the *parasmaipada* endings.

This is not so; because of the governing rule "after [a root] beginning with *val*" (Pāṇini 7.2.35), and because the *liṅ* does not possess the *yāsuṭ* augment and so forth when it occurs in the *parasmaipada*. [The phrase] "when followed by an *ātmanepada*" means that the *ātmanepada* is subsequent.

Because it is so stated; and this [term] is connected only with *sic*, not with *liṅ*, since the mention of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) serves as a qualifier specifically for *sic*. In the form "vṛṣīṣṭa," there is an absence of guṇa due to the *kit* status [of the suffix] by rule 1.2.12, *uśca*.

Regarding "ṭhāstīrṣīṣṭa": as before, there is lengthening and so forth due to the *kit* designation. Regarding "avṛta": there is the elision of the *sic* suffix by [Pāṇini 8.2.27], "after a short vowel, the *sic* is elided."
43. And [the substitution of *iṭ*] does not occur after a root beginning with a conjunct consonant that ends in *ṛ*.

(Pāṇini 7.2.43) Since roots ending in *ṛ* are anudātta, a prohibition [of *iṭ*] would otherwise apply; this statement is made for the purpose of providing an option. For example: *dhvṛṣīṣṭa*. [The root] *dhvṛ* (meaning "to be distressed") is listed as number 139 in the Dhātupāṭha. [This applies] in the sense of the impersonal (*bhāva*) or passive (*karman*).
(1.3.13) Thus the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) [is applied]. In this same way, the middle voice is to be understood elsewhere as well.
As before, due to the *kit* designation, there is an absence of *guṇa*. [The form] "smṛṣīṣṭa" [is derived from] the root "smṛ" in the sense of "recollection" (DhP 933).

Regarding "ṭhcyoṣīṣṭa": the roots *cyuṅ* and *jyuṅ* belong to the *bhvādi* class (DhP 955, 956). Here, because of the marker *ṅ*, the *ātmanepada* ending is used for the *kṛt* affix *sīṣṭha*. Regarding "ṭhakṛṣata":
the substitution of *at* occurs by the rule "ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.5).

Now, why does [the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*] not occur in *saṃskṛṣīṣṭa* and *saṃskṛta*, since the root *kṛ* here has the initial of a conjunct consonant after the augment *suṭ* is applied by the rule "after *sam*, *pari*, and *upa*, when *kṛ* means adornment" (Pāṇini 6.1.137)? To this he says: "*saṃskṛṣīṣṭa*" etc. [The reason is that] it is a one-syllable root (*ekāc*).

The term "upadeśa" (in the original state of instruction) is understood to carry over from the rule *upadeśe 'nudātāt* (Pāṇini 7.2.10); therefore, by this [rule], the effect must occur only from that which begins with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādi*) in the state of the original instruction. Now, the root *kṛ* does not begin with a conjunct consonant in the state of the original instruction; rather, what does? It follows after such a [conjunct].

Therefore, it does not occur; this is because of the phrase "and because it is a part of that" (*abhaktatvāt*), and so forth. This is the resolution for the case of *saṃskṛṣīṣṭa*, but not for *samaskṛta*. For in the latter case, the augment *aṭ* is included by the mention of the stem (*aṅga*) according to the principle: "That which is a part of it is included by the mention of it" (*Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 20*); thus, even *aṭ* is included by the mention of the stem.

According to the principle "that which falls in the middle of something is included by the mention of that thing" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 21), the augment *suṭ* is also included by the mention of the *aṅga*; therefore, the root *kṛ-* indeed begins with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādi*).
Furthermore, because the section on *aṅga* is in force, the term *saṃyoga* here refers to a conjunct that is a constituent part of the *aṅga*, due to proximity.

Furthermore, in the case of *na ca saṃskṛṣīṣṭa*, the initial element of the suffix (*aṅgāvayava*) is not a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*) and so forth; and that which is an element of the suffix does not occur within the cluster itself. Therefore, the undesirable application of the augment *iṭ* does not arise here. In this instance, by the rule "the substitution of *s* occurs for the *m* of *sam*" (Vārttika 936), the *m* of *sam* is replaced by *s*.

The *anunāsika* [nasalized vowel] belongs to the preceding [element]. In the case of *samaskṛta*, there is the elision of *sic* as in the previous rule. The letter *ca* serves to carry over (*anukarṣaṇa*) the *ātmanepada*; therefore, the subsequent rule applies without distinction.
This is because that which is carried over by *ca* does not recur in what follows.

44. *svaratisūtisūyatidhūñūdito vā* (Pāṇini 7.2.44). [The roots] *ṣvṛ* "to sound" and "to afflict" (Dhātupāṭha 932), *ṣūṅ* "the emission of the fetus by a living being" (Dhātupāṭha 1031)—which belongs to the Adādi class—and *ṣūṅ* "the birth of a living being" (Dhātupāṭha 1132).

[The root] *ghūñ* "to shake" (DhP 1255, 1487, 1385) belongs to the *svādi*, *rkyādi*, and *curādi* groups. Among these, because of the governing rule *ekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.10), the first two [groups] are included, but not the latter. [The root] *ūditaḥ*—*gāhū* "to stir" (DhP 1256).

(dhā.pā. 649), *gup* "to protect" (dhā.pā. 395), and so forth. Since these roots as well as *svarati* have an anudātta (unaccented) vowel, the prohibition [of *iṭ*] would apply; however, since the others have an udātta (accented) vowel, *iṭ* would necessarily apply. This statement is made for the purpose of providing an option. *vigāḍhā*.
Thus, [the substitution of] *ṅ* for *ḍh*, etc., is to be enjoined as before.

Alternatively, what is the purpose of the explicit statement [of the option]? For does not the word "optionally" (*vā*) carry over from the rule "ṭhiṭ sani vā" (Pāṇini 7.2.41)? To this he says: "While 'optionally' (*vā*) is carrying over," and so forth. For that—
Since the mention of "optionally" (*vā*) is connected with the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and the aorist suffix (*sic*),
its recurrence would entail the recurrence of those two as well. Therefore,
this second mention of "optionally" is for the purpose of excluding the *liṅ* and *sic* that were previously connected with the [first] mention of "optionally."
But surely there would be the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of *liṅ* and *sic*;
therefore, this mention of *vā* is for the purpose of excluding *liṅ* and *sic*, which are connected with the preceding mention of *agrahaṇa*.
But surely, if *liṅ* and *sic* were to recur, the mention of *svarati* would become redundant.

[Objection: Is this not already established by the preceding alternative (vikalpa)? [Response: This is not so; because of the authority of the explicit statement (*vacana-prāmāṇyāt*), the inclusion of the term *svarita* is understood to be for the sake of making [the rule] obligatory (*nityārtha*). Or rather—by virtue of the inclusion of *svarita*, the word "optionally" (*vā*) is excluded. Now, what is the purpose of specifying the *vikaraṇa* suffixes in the case of *sūti* and *sūyati*, rather than simply using "sū"?

How is this to be understood? To this he says: "In the case of *sūti* and *sūyati*, etc. When *sū* is mentioned, by the rule "when a root is cited without an *anubandha*, it does not include one with an *anubandha*" (*Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā* 53), there is the inclusion of only *sū* in the sense of "impelling" (*preraṇe*) [as found in the Dhātupāṭha, no. 1408]—[the Dhātupāṭha reading being *ṣū*].

It might be so; therefore, for the sake of excluding that [other root], the mention of the *vikaraṇa* must be made. If this is the purpose, should the mention be made as *sūṅ*? It cannot be done in this way; for if such a mention were made, according to the principle that "between a root with a *luk*-vikaraṇa and one with a non-*luk*-vikaraṇa, the one with the non-*luk*-vikaraṇa [takes precedence]," [the rule would apply only to the other].
By the rule *grahaṇam* (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 50), there would be the inclusion of *sūyati* alone, and not of *sūti*.

Therefore, the mention of the *vikaraṇa* (*śnā*) is for the purpose of excluding that [other root]. This very mention is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the existence of this paribhāṣā; for if this were non-existent, one would have made the mention *sūṅ*. Now...

If the term *dhūñ* were not taken as being accompanied by its anubandha, then, by the paribhāṣā regarding the absence of an anubandha (Pāṇini 1.1.68), only the root *ṣū* in the sense of "shaking" (Dhātupāṭha 1398) would be understood; and this is undesirable. Therefore, [the rule applies] to the root meaning "shaking."

The mention of the suffix along with its attendant (anubandha) is for the purpose of exclusion, as in the rule "of *svarati*" and so forth. The scope of this optional rule (*vikalpa*) is, for example, *svaritā* and *svartā*; whereas the scope of the rule "before *sye*, [the penultimate vowel] of roots ending in *ṛ* or *ṝ* is lengthened" (Pāṇini 7.2.70) is, for example, *kariṣyati* and *hariṣyati*.

When there is a conflict between these two [rules], the rule "svarateḥ sye" (Pāṇini 7.2.70)— which applies to the root *svar* followed by the suffix *sya*— takes precedence by way of *vipratiṣedha* (conflict), resulting in the form *svariṣyati*.
Regarding the rule "kiti ca" (Pāṇini 1.1.5) and so forth, and specifically "śryukaḥ kiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.11):
The scope for this [rule] is: *sūtaḥ*, *sūtadāni*; the scope for this alternative (*vikalpa*) is:

*svaritaḥ*, *svariteti*; *sotā*, *savitā*; *dhotaḥ*, *dhaviteti*. Here, when both [alternatives] apply, by the rule "śrayukaḥ kiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.11), there is a constant prohibition [of the *iṭ* augment]. (Note: *nityaḥ*—according to the Kāśikā).

It occurs by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvapratiṣedha*): *svṛtvā*, *sūtvā*, *dhūtvā*. And this is established precisely from the formulation of the section on prohibitions (*pratiṣedhakāṇḍa*) that precedes it. For it was stated previously regarding the formulation of those prior prohibitions:

The purpose is so that there may be a prohibition of the mere root *iṇ* when no specific rule for its substitution has been enjoined. This very prohibition-rule, being placed earlier, yields the same result as the "prohibition of the preceding" (*pūrvadipratiṣedha*) rule; therefore, it is applied here.
This has been stated by means of the term "prior prohibition" (pūrvavipratiṣedha).
45. *radhādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 7.2.45). [The roots included here are:
*ṛtha* "injury and success" (Dhātupāṭha 1193), *ṇaśa* "disappearance" (Dhātupāṭha 1194), *tṛpa* "satisfaction" (Dhātupāṭha 1195), and *dṛpa* "excitement and delusion."

*(Dhātupāṭha 1196): [The root] *hr̥ṣ* [is used] in the sense of exhilaration and delusion; *druh* in the sense of wishing to harm; *muh* in the sense of bewilderment; *ṇṇuh* in the sense of vomiting; *ṣṇih* in the sense of affection—these are the roots beginning with *radh*. Among these...*
Since *tṛpyati* and *dṛpyati* are anudātta, the prohibition of *iṭ* would apply;
however, since the remaining [roots] are udātta, *iṭ* would apply invariably. This statement is made for the purpose of providing an option. Regarding "naṃṣṭā":
the augment *num* is applied by the rule *masjinaśor jhali* (Pāṇini 7.1.60), and [the change of *n* to *ṇ*] is effected by the *vraścādi* rule (Pāṇini 8.2.36).

[The forms] *ṣatvam* and *ṣṭutvam*. [In the case of] *traptaḥ*, there is the substitution of *am* by *anudātasya cardupadhasyānyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.1.59), followed by the *yaṇ* substitute. [In the case of] *tarpitā*, there is the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇaḥ*). Regarding *drogdhā*, *megdhā*, *snodhyā*, and *snegdhā*, in the alternative where the augment *iṭ* is absent, [the rule] "or" (*vā*) applies.

By the rule *druhamuhaṇṇuhaṇṇihām* (8.2.33), there is the substitution of *gh*; by *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* (8.2.40), there is the substitution of *dh*; and by *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* (8.4.53), there is the substitution of the *jaś* sound, namely *g*.
Thus we have *droḍhā*, *ñoḍhā*, *snoḍhā*, and *sneḍhā*. As before, there is the substitution of *ḍh* and so forth.

This is to be understood as follows: "Some desire an option because of the rule for *krādi* roots, since [the substitution] applies to *radh* and others due to its subsequent position in the *liṭ* [perfect tense].
Thus, in the alternative case, forms such as *raradhva* and *raradhma* should also occur. Regarding the phrase "others, however," and so forth:

For this indeed is the purpose of the preceding rule that prescribes the prohibition of *iṭ*: namely, so that the prohibition may be stronger. Therefore, because of the superior force of this prohibition, there must invariably be *iṭ*. In that case—

The intention of the former [teachers] is this: by virtue of the power of the rule prescribing the prohibition of *iṭ* following a preceding rule, the prohibition is stronger, but not the restriction regarding the prohibition.
The intention of the others is this: because of the strength of the prohibition, its specific property...
A restrictive rule (niyama) is also stronger, and not merely a prohibition;

since it is stronger, that [augment] is obtained by it, and thus it is proper that the augment iṭ should be present as a constant (nitya). However, the restriction regarding the prohibition is that very same restriction concerning roots beginning with *krā-* (as in Pāṇini 7.2.13), as in the forms *rarandhiva* and *rarandhima*.
The augment *num* is applied by the rule "ṛdhijabhor aci" (Pāṇini 7.1.61).

46. *niraḥ kuṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.56). The root *kuṣ* (meaning "to extract") is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as number 1518. Since this root is udātta (accented), an *iṭ* augment would have been obligatory; this rule provides for its optional occurrence. Thus we have *niṣkoṣṭā*. [In the case of *niṣkoṣṭā*,] the rule *śarpare visarjanīyaḥ* applies.
Because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of this [rule], the substitution of *ṣ* for the *visarjanīya* occurs by the rule "ṭhidudupadhasya cāpratyayasya" (Pāṇini 8.3.41).
Now, one might object: this prefix ends in *s*, and it is listed as *nis* among the *prādi* group; it is not [the same as *niḥ*].
However, since [the form] is *nir*, it would have been more appropriate to state "after *nis*" (*nisaḥ*) rather than "after *nira*";

for example, as in the rule "after *nis*, before *tapa*, when not expressing repetition" (*nisaḥ tapatāvanāsevane*, 8.3.102). Why, then, is the designation *nira* used? To this he says: "In the case of 'after *nis*' (*nisaḥ*)," and so forth, by the words "though it should have been stated," etc.
He states the purpose for making known the existence of that which ends in the letter *r* in the words beginning with "tena. It might be argued:

"Once *ru*-substitution has been applied by the rule *nisaḥ*, the *la*-substitution will occur"; to this he replies with the words beginning with "niso hi. The form "nilayanam" is derived from the root *ayati* with the suffix *lyuṭ*.
47. *iṇniṣṭhāyām* | (7.2.47) For what purpose is the mention of *iṭ* made again, when [the word] *iṭ* was already present [in the previous rule]?
To this he says: "The mention of *iṭ* is for the sake of making it obligatory (*nityārtha*). For if the mention of *iṭ* were absent, there would be an option (*vikalpa*).

Because [the previous rule] is the subject under discussion, the prescription of *iṭ* would be optional. Therefore, the mention of *iṅ* must be made for the sake of making it obligatory. Now, one might object: "But the desired form is already established by the preceding rule; by the very force of its commencement, this rule will become obligatory. To this, he says: "For the commencement," and so forth.

Since the augment *iṭ* was made optional by the preceding sūtra, there arises the possibility of its prohibition by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 7.2.15) regarding the *niṣṭhā* suffixes; this present rule is therefore commenced to make the [augment] compulsory. In that context, if the mention of *iṅ* were not made here, then this commencement would merely serve as an exception (*bādhaka*) to that very same prohibition, and consequently, there would be an optionality.
Thus it would be [the case that] the rule is not compulsory; therefore, the mention of *iṅ* must be made for the sake of making the rule compulsory.

For if the mention of *iṅ* were made for the sake of compulsion, then because the optionality would have been set aside by it, the rule would be compulsory even in subsequent cases. Therefore, he says: "In that very same way."

And so forth. Nor can this mention of *iṅ* (the verbal root *iṅ*) serve to exclude the optionality (*vikalpa*), because that [optionality] is established by its being marked with a *svarita* accent, despite the force of the mention of *iṅ*. Even though the word "or" (*vā*) is not being carried over [from a previous rule], this rule is obligatory (*nitya*). As for the recurrence of that very optionality, [it is as follows:]
It has the meaning of "one who hears"; therefore, in what follows, it refers specifically to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

48. *tīṣasahalubharuṣariṣaḥ* | (Pāṇini 7.2.48) *ṭhiṣu* in the sense of "desire" (Dhātupāṭha 1351); [the form *ṭhiṣa* is also given in the Dhātupāṭha]; *ṣaha* in the sense of "endurance" (Dhātupāṭha 852); *lubha* in the sense of "covetousness" (Dhātupāṭha 1238); *lubha* in the sense of "delusion" (Dhātupāṭha 1239).
Both [roots] are included here because no distinction is specified.

[The roots are] *ruṣa* in the sense of "anger" (DhP 1670) and *ruṣa*, *riṣa* in the sense of "injury" (DhP 1230, 1231). Since all these [roots] have an acute accent on their initial vowel, the augment *iṭ* would apply obligatorily; this rule is therefore commenced for the purpose of making it optional.

Regarding the phrase "for that purpose": it is for the sake of ensuring that the option applies only to the root meaning "to desire" (√iṣ), and not to the other two [roots √iṣ meaning "to go" and √iṣ meaning "to seek"]; otherwise, those who do not read the word "udita" would understand the previously mentioned "vā" as a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) due to its association with the root *bhū* (of the *bhūvādigaṇa*).

They explain that [the substitution] will occur only for a root meaning "to wish" (*icchā*) by way of option, and not for the other two. Regarding the form *soḍhā*: once the substitution of *ḍha*, the substitution of *ṣṭu*, and the elision of *ḍh* have been performed, [the rule] *sahivahor odavarṇasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.112) applies.

49. [The suffix *niṣṭhā* takes the substitute *iṭ* after the roots] *san*, *ivanta*, *ṛdha*, *bhrasj*, *dambh*, *śri*, *svṛ*, *ūrṇu*, *bhṛ*, *jñapi*, and *san*. (Pāṇini 7.2.49) Regarding the term "those ending in *iv*": this refers to the roots *div* (DhP 1107), *siv* (DhP 1108), and so forth. Also included are *ṛdhu* in the sense of "growth" (DhP 1245) and *bhrasj* in the sense of "cooking" (DhP 1246).

(dhā.pā.1284), *dambhe* [or *dambhane*—dhā.pā. (dhā.pā.1270), *śriñ* ‘in service’ (dhā.pā.897), *svṛ* ‘in sound and affliction’ (dhā.pā.932), *yū* ‘in mixing’ [or ‘in mixing and non-mixing’—dhā.pā. (dhā.pā.1033), *ūrṇu*...
The root *ācchā* (DhP 1039) means "to cover"; *śriñ* (? means "to support";
*jñap* with the causative suffix (*ṇyanta*) means "killing," "desiring," or "pacifying"; *ṣaṇu* (DhP 1464) means "giving";
and *vana* and *ṣaṇa* (DhP 463, 444) mean "to share"—both of these are included here.

Because no specific distinction is made here: since the root *bhrasj* is anudātta, and since the roots *lu*, *yū*, *ru*, and *bhṛñ* end in the vowel *u*, the prohibition [of *iṭ*] by Pāṇini 7.2.12 (*sani grahaguhoca*) would apply;
furthermore, since the remaining roots are udātta, *iṭ* would necessarily apply. It is with reference to this situation that the present optional rule is commenced.
In the form *dudyūṣati*: the suffix *san* is added to the root *div*; by the rule *halāntaśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.10), the *san* is marked with the *k*-sign (*kit*);

by the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike* (Pāṇini 6.4.19), the substitution of *ūṭ* occurs, followed by the *yaṇ* replacement; then reduplication of the element *dyaūṣa* takes place; and finally, by the rule *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.60), all consonants except the first are elided.
The substitution of *ṭ* for *ṭvaṃ*—that is, the letter *d* replaces the letter *dh*.
In the form *vibhrajj-iṣati*, the letter *d* replaces the letter *s* by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* (Pāṇini 8.4.53);
then, by the rule *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.40), the *ścutva* (palatalization) occurs, whereby the letter *d* becomes the letter *j*.

Regarding the form *bibharkṣati*: by the rule *bhrasjo ropadhāyā ram anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.4.47), the augment *ram* is inserted after the vowel *a*. Because the rule uses the genitive case in the expression *ropadhayoḥ*, this *ram* replaces both the *repha* (*r*) and the *upadhā* (*s*). Furthermore, by the rule *coḥ kuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.30), [the *c* is changed to *k*].
Thus, by [Pāṇini 8.2.30], there is the substitution of *k* for *dh*; and by [Pāṇini 8.3.57] and [Pāṇini 8.3.59], there is the substitution of *ṣ* for the *th* of the suffix.
Thus: *ghipsati*, *ghīpsati*. By [Pāṇini 7.4.56], there is the substitution of *i* and *ī* [for the radical vowel]; and by [Pāṇini 8.4.55], [the aspiration is applied] before a *khari* sound.
By [the rule] (8.4.55), *cartva* occurs; the letter *bha* becomes *pa*. As before, there is elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsa-lopa*).
By [the rule] "halāntācca" (1.2.10), because it has the *kit* designation, there is elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*).
Thus: *ucchicchrīṣati*. By [the rule] "iko jhal" (1.2.9), there is the *kit* designation, and by [the rule] "ajjhanagamām... [there is lengthening].
By the rule *sani* (6.4.16), there is lengthening; the reduplication undergoes the operations pertaining to the abhyāsa (reduplicated syllable).
By the rule *ādeśapratyayoḥ* (8.3.59), there is the substitution of *ṣ*; the *d* undergoes *cutva* (substitution by *c*), resulting in *cakāra*.
By the rule *śaśchāeṭi* (8.4.63), the *ś* is replaced by *ccch*.

Regarding the form *sisvariṣati*: there is reduplication of the root *svṛ*, the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* by *uraṅ* (Pāṇini 7.4.66), and the substitution of *ra* for the semivowel (*raparatva*). Regarding *susvūrṣati*: as before, there is lengthening;
then the substitution of *u* for *o* by *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya* (Pāṇini 7.1.102), the substitution of *ra* for the semivowel, and [the doubling of the *s*] by *hali ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.70).

Thus, there is lengthening; the doubling (*dvirvacana*) of the syllable *svṛ*—which is the operation on the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsakārya*)—and the substitution of *ṣ* by [Pāṇini 8.3.59] *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*.
[The form] *yiyiviṣati* arises because of the substitution of *i* for the vowel of the reduplicated syllable by [Pāṇini 7.4.80] *oḥ puyaṇjyapare*.
In the form *prorṇunūṣati*,

because of the rule "of the second [syllable] beginning with a vowel" (Pāṇini 6.1.2), there is reduplication of the second monosyllabic element, namely *nusa*; however, there is no reduplication of the letter *r* preceding it.

Regarding "he will cover" (*prorṇunaviṣati*): when the augment *iṭ* is present, by the rule "optionally for *ūrṇu*" (1.2.3), when there is *ṅittva*, there is *uvaṅ*; otherwise, however, there is *guṇa*. [The commentary states:
"There is the inclusion of this root *bhuji* belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa*"; what then of the root *ḍubhṛñ*?

Why is there no inclusion of the *jauhotyādika* [class of roots]? To this he says: "Because of the mention with the *śap* [suffix]," and so forth. If the intention were to include the root *bhṛ* of the *jauhotyādika* class in the sense of "supporting" and "nourishing," then one would have made the mention simply as *bhṛ*, and not...

Regarding the mention of the root as *bhara* with the suffix *śap*, since it is indeed mentioned with *śap*, it is understood that the root belonging to the *bhūvādika* class is intended. Thus, "bubhūrṣati" [is formed];
here, the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* and the lengthening of the vowel occur as before.

Regarding "jñīpsati": from the root *jñā*, the causative suffix *ṇic* is added; by the rule "artihvṛ... etc., the augment *puk* is inserted, followed by the lengthening of the preceding vowel and the elision of the reduplication. Regarding "siṣāsati": by the rule "janasanakhanāṃ sañjhaloḥ," the substitution of *ā* for the vowel occurs.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Some here," etc.: by the use of the word "some," it is implied that some do not recite [this rule]. Those, however, who do not recite it provide an *upasaṃkhyāna* (supplementary addition) for the roots *tan*, *pat*, and *daridrā*: namely, "he desires to stretch" (*titaṃsati*) and "he desires to fall" (*titāṃsati*). [This is governed by] Pāṇini 6.4.17: *tenoter vibhāṣā*.

Thus, in this view, there is lengthening. In the case of *pitsati*, the substitution of *is* [for the root vowel] occurs by the rule *sanimīmā-* (Pāṇini 7.4.54), followed by the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsa-lopa*) and the elision of *s* by the rule *skoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.29). In the cases of *didaridriṣati* and *didaridrāsati*:
The optional elision of the vowel *a* occurs by the rule "ṭhdaridrāterārdhadhātuke" (Vārttika 789), and so forth.
50. *kliśaḥ ktvāniṣṭhayoḥ* | (Pāṇini 7.2.50) Regarding *kliṣṭvā*: the substitution of *ṣ* is applied by the rule *vraścādi-* (8.2.36). Regarding *kliśitvā*:
the suffix is treated as having the *k*-marker (*kit*) by the rule *ralo vyupadhāddhalādeḥ saṃśca* (1.2.26). [This applies] when the suffix *ktvā* is present.

"An option is already established. If, by virtue of being marked with *ū*, an option were already established for the suffix *ktvā* by the rule *svarati-sūti-sūyati-dhūñ-ūditaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.44), then for what purpose is the mention of *ktvā* [in the following rule]?
