To this he says: "But of the root *kliś* in the sense of 'affliction,' etc. [The meaning is: there is a compulsory insertion of the augment *iṭ*.
"He obtains" [is said] because the root *kliś* in the sense of "affliction" (*upatāpa*) is udātta. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of that":

it means for the sake of that *kliś* which has the sense of affliction; that which has this as its purpose (*artha*) or motive is described as such. Alternatively, it refers to the fact that the augment *iṭ* necessarily applies to *kliś* when it has the sense of affliction.
"For that purpose" means for the sake of its cessation; this is because the word "purpose" (artha) here signifies "cessation."

51. And [the root] *pū* [is included]. (7.2.51) Since [the root *pac*] ends in a long vowel (*ugantatvāt*), the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *śryukaḥ kiti* (7.2.11) would apply; this statement is made so that [the *iṭ*] may optionally apply in the case of the suffixes *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā*. [Examples: *pavitvā*, *paktiḥ*.

In the form *pavitavān*, because of the prohibition of the *kit* designation by the rule *pūṅḥ ktvā ca* (Pāṇini 1.2.22), the *guṇa* substitution indeed occurs. The mention of *pūṅ*— which includes the anubandha— is for the purpose of excluding *pūñ*.

52. *Vasatikṣudher id* (Pāṇini 7.2.52). Regarding the roots *vas* (to dwell, DhP 1005) and *kṣudh* (to hunger, DhP 1190), since they are marked with the anudātta accent, the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* would otherwise apply; [this sūtra provides for its introduction].

This statement is for the purpose of prescribing *iṭ* after the suffixes *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā*. Regarding the form *uṣitvā*: since *ktvā* follows, and because *iṭ* is present, the prohibition of *kit*-status by the rule *na ktvā seṭ* (Pāṇini 1.2.18) would apply; however, *kit*-status is established here by the rule *muḍ amṛja...* (Pāṇini 1.2.7), etc., due to its inclusion in the *vac-ādi* group according to the sūtra *vacisvapiyajādīnām...* (Pāṇini 6.1.15).
There is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*), and by the rule *śāsivasicasīnāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 8.3.60), there is the substitution of *ṣ*.
Regarding the form *kṣudhitvā*: here too, by the rule *ralo vyupadhāddhalādeḥ saṃśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.26), there is optionally the status of being *kit*.

Regarding the statement "it is indicated by the inclusion of the *vikaraṇa* suffix" (*ṭhvasatīti vikaraṇanirdeaśaḥ*), it has been said that "the indication of the *vikaraṇa* serves only to indicate the verbal root. Now, one might raise the objection: "Why is this not understood as being for the purpose of excluding the root *vasa* in the sense of 'covering' (*vasa ācchādane*, DhP 1023)? To such a person, [the author replies:]...

He replies with "vasteḥ" and so forth. Alternatively, one might object: "Why is [the rule] not understood as being for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ-luk* (elision of the *yaṅ*) in forms such as *vāvastaḥ* and *vāvastavān*? To such an objector, he replies with "vasteḥ" and so forth. Now, regarding *vāvastaḥ* and *vāvastavān*:
Why is it not understood as being for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ* and *luṅ* [tenses]?

The intention is that even by understanding the rule as qualifying what has been prescribed (*vihitaviśeṣaṇapakṣa*), the exclusion of *yaṅ* and *luṅ* can be achieved. Now, while the term *iṭ* is already being carried over (*anuvartamāna*), why is *iṅ* mentioned again?
For what purpose [is this]? He says: "The repetition of *iṅ* is for the sake of making it obligatory (*nitya*).
The previous mention of *iṅ* was connected with an option; therefore, if that were to recur, that [option] would also recur. Consequently, the repetition of *iṅ* is for the purpose of excluding that.
It is done.

53. After the root *añc*, [the suffix *iṭ* is added] when honor is expressed. (Pāṇini 7.2.53) [The example is] *añcitāḥ*. The meaning is "honored. The suffix *kta* is applied by the rule *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca* (3.2.177). The elision of the nasal [of the root] by the rule *aniditām* (6.4.24) does not take place.
Because of the prohibition [stated] in "ṭhnāñceḥ pūjāyām" (Pāṇini 6.4.30). Regarding the word "asya" (of this): the genitive case is used according to "ktasya ca vartamāne" (Pāṇini 2.3.67).

54. *lubho vimohane* (7.2.54). [The forms] *lubhitvā* and *lobhitvā* are derived as follows: by the rule *ralo vyupadhāt* (1.2.26), etc., the absence of *guṇa* occurs in one alternative due to the suffix being *kit*.

"In *gārdheya*, it is exactly as prescribed. There is an option regarding the suffix *kvā*; however, in the case of the *niṣṭhā* suffix, there is a permanent prohibition according to the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 7.2.15).
55. *jṛ-vraścyoḥ ktvi* (Pāṇini 7.2.55).

[The forms] *jarītvā* and *jaritvā* are given. The root *jṛ* "to lose vitality" (Dhātupāṭha 1494) belongs to the kryādi class. In one alternative, there is lengthening according to *vṛto vā* (7.2.38). As for the root *jṛṣ* "to lose vitality," [it is used in other contexts].

The root *vi-vad* is listed [in the Dhātupāṭha] as *vivādau* (DhP 1130); because it possesses an *anubandha*, it is not included here [by this rule], and thus its form becomes *jaurtvā*. Regarding *vraścitvā*:
the root is *o-vraścū chedane* (DhP 1292). Because of the prohibition [of *it*] by the rule *na ktvā seṭ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.28), [the *iṭ* augment is not applied].
By the rule *grahijyā-* etc. (Pāṇini 6.1.16), the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) does not occur, because that [rule] prescribes it only before an affix marked with *k*.
Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *ktvā*, since there is the rule *kliśaḥ ktvāniṣṭhayoḥ* (7.2.50)?
Does the mention of *ktvā* continue from this very point? To this he says: "The mention of *ktvā*" and so forth.

For that mention of *ktvā* is connected with *niṣṭhā*; therefore, when that [mention of *ktvā*] continues, there would be a continuation of that [mention of *niṣṭhā*] as well. And this being the case, [the rule] would apply even to the *niṣṭhā*. Therefore—
Another mention of the suffix *ktvā* is made here for the purpose of excluding that which signifies completion (*niṣṭhā*).
56. *udito vā* (Pāṇini 7.2.56).
Regarding the rule *śāntvā*: [the roots] *śamu* "to calm" (DhP 1201), *tamu* "to desire" (DhP 1202), *damu* "to calm" (DhP 1203), and *bhramu* "to wander" (DhP 850).
The root *kram* (meaning "to step") is listed as *aniṭ* in the Dhātupāṭha (473). In the case where it is *aniṭ*, there is lengthening according to *anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ kṅiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.15).
The inclusion of the word *vā* ("optionally") is for the sake of clarity; for since the roots marked with *u* (*udit*) are udātta, the augment *iṭ* is already established [by Pāṇini 7.2.10].

In that case, the injunction will be understood through the alternative (vikalpa) by the very force of the commencement [of the rule]. Furthermore, the mention of the word "or" (vā) must necessarily be made for the sake of what follows; however, it is employed right here for the sake of clarity.

57. *sake'sici kṛtacṛtachṛdatṛdanṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.57). The root *kṛtī* in the sense of "cutting" belongs to the Taudādika class (DhP 1435), while *kṛtī* in the sense of "encircling" belongs to the Raudhādika class (DhP 1447); since no distinction is specified, [the rule applies] to both.
The inclusion [of these roots]: *cṛt* in the sense of "injury" and "tying" (DhP 1324;

variant reading: "injury" and "severing"), *chṛd* in the sense of "shining" and "playing" (DhP 1445), and *tṛd* in the sense of "injury" and "giving" (DhP 1446; variant reading: "injury" and "disrespect"). The two *u*s [are included].

The mention of *ṭh* in "ṭh-ito vā" (Pāṇini 7.2.56) is for the purpose of specification; likewise, the *i* and *r* in "i-rito vā" (Pāṇini 3.1.57) are also for the purpose of specification. [The root] *nṛtī* (meaning "to dance," Dhātupāṭha 1116) belongs to all these [roots], and since they are all *anudātta*, the augment *iṭ* would apply invariably; however, this is restricted to cases other than after the *s* of *sic*.

The statement is for the purpose of providing an option (*vikalpa*). The vocalization of the vowel *ā* in the word *se* is not restrictive (*atantra*), because it is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣitatvāt*). Therefore, the option applies to *sye*. Furthermore, its non-restrictive nature is to be understood from the prohibition of *sic* in the rule *asici*. If...
The utterance of the letter *a* here is not for the sake of a technical rule (*hyatantra*). If that were the case, why was it not stated simply as "in *sve* and *sici*"?

It is for fear of ambiguity. For if it were stated in that way, the meaning "in *sye* and *sici*" might also be suspected. However, when it is stated as "in *se* and *asici*," because two locative cases are employed, [the intended meaning is clear].

The intended meaning is understood as "when [the suffix] *sic* begins with *s* and is not elided. But surely, even here there would be doubt: if this were stated, why specify "*sic*" rather than simply saying "*si*" (if it were applicable to *sic* as well)?
For if it were applicable to *sic* too, the mention of "*sic*" would be purposeless; one should have simply said "*si*."
‘Kartsyati’ is the future tense (*lṛṭ*). ‘Akartsyat’ is the aorist (*luṅ*). ‘Cikṛtsati’ is the desiderative (*san*);
because it is *kit* by the rule ‘halantācca’ (Pāṇini 1.2.10), there is an absence of *guṇa*.

58. *gamer iṭ parasmaipadeṣu* (Pāṇini 7.2.58). The root *gam-lṛ* (meaning "to go," Dhātupāṭha 982) is *aniṭ* because it is marked with an anudātta vowel. Furthermore, there is also the substitution of *gam* for the root *iṇ* (meaning "to go," Dhātupāṭha 1045) by the rule *sani ca* (2.4.47).

Furthermore, regarding that which is derived from the root *ṭhi* "to remember" (*dhā.pā.* 1047) by the rule *yaśca ṭhiṇvadika iti vaktavyam* (Vārttika 167), and that which is derived from the root *ṭhiṅ* "to study" (*dhā.pā.* 1046) by the rule *ṭhiṅśca* (Pāṇini 2.4.48)— that too would be as if it lacked the augment *iṭ* due to its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*.

This statement is for the purpose that the augment *iṭ* may be applied to a subsequent *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with *s*, excluding the *sic* suffix; for example, in "gamiṣyati" (he will go) and "agamiṣyat" (he would have gone). "Gamiṣyati" and "agamiṣyat" are examples of the root *gam* when it has not undergone substitution. "Jigamiṣati" (he desires to go) is an example of that same root when it has undergone the substitution of *i*.
Regarding the substitution of *iṅ* for *vā*:
now, when the condition "not followed by *it*" (*aniṭi*) is already present, what is the purpose of mentioning *iṅ* again? To this he says:

"The mention of *iṅ* is for the sake of making it obligatory. For that [mention]—namely, the previous mention of *iṅ* in the rule "udito vā" (Pāṇini 7.2.56)—[is intended to make the substitution compulsory].
The word *vā* is connected with the mention of *iṅ* under discussion; therefore, when that [word *vā*] is carried over [into the subsequent rule],

the printed reading beginning with "ityādiḥ" implies that the previous mention of *iṅ* is connected with the word *vā* in the rule "udito vā" (Pāṇini 7.2.56), and thus, when that [word *vā*] is carried over, there would also be a carrying over of that [mention of *iṅ*].

And in that case, the desired [result] would follow through alternative interpretation (*vikalpa*). Therefore, the word *iṅ* is mentioned again for the purpose of excluding that [undesired consequence]. [The example is] "saṃgaṃsīṣṭa": from the root *gam* preceded by the prefix *sam*, the suffix *liṅ* with *sīyuṭ* is applied in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule "samo gamṛcchi... (Pāṇini 1.3.29).

The augment *suṭ* is applied by the rule "suṭ tithoḥ" (3.4.107); then there is the substitution of *dha*, and subsequently the substitution of *ṣṭu*. Regarding the form "sañjigāsate," the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used by the rule "pūrvavatsanaḥ" (1.3.62). Regarding "adhijigāṃsate," this is a counter-example for the substitute *iṅ* of the root *gam*. Now...

Regarding the form *sañciṅgaṃsate*, why does the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by the rule *ṭhajjhanagamāṃ sani* (Pāṇini 6.4.16) not occur here? To this he says: "Of *gam* which is a substitute for *iṅ*" (*gameriṅadeśasya*), and so forth. For that lengthening is desired for *gam* when it is a substitute for *iṅ*, and not for any other. Indeed, it is stated there: "of *gam* which is a substitute for *iṅ*."
It must be stated [as follows]:

if it were said "in the case of parasmaipada [affixes]," then [the rule] would not apply to the *kṛt* affixes or where there is elision (*luk*) of the parasmaipada; therefore he says "by means of the ātmanepada," and so forth. [The phrase] "situated in the same word" (*samānapadasthasya*) [is used].

The meaning is "of one who stands on a single word. "It is desired everywhere else" means that this is clarified by the rule beginning with *kṛtyapi hi*. The examples for the *kṛtya* suffixes are two: *sañjigamiṣitā* and *adhijigamiṣitā*. The example *jigamiṣas tvam* is [an instance] where there is elision (*luk*) of the *parasmaipada* ending.
Because it ends in the suffix *sann*, there is the root *gam* with the imperative (*loṭ*) suffix; then *sip*; then by "ṭhserhyapicca" (Pāṇini 3.4.87), *si* is replaced by *hi*;

and by "ato heḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.105), there is elision (*luk*). But how is it that when it is stated "in the case of parasmaipada [suffixes]," the elision of *parasmaipada* occurs even when a *kṛt* suffix follows? It is as follows:

He thinks: a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must be made; one part is "gameriṭ," where the word "se" (beginning with *s*) is understood to follow—thus, the augment *iṭ* occurs after the root *gam* before an *ārthadhātuka* suffix beginning with *s*. Then, the second application, "parasmaipadeṣu," is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). And this restriction is as follows:

If it were without distinction, then the preceding rule (Pāṇini 1.3.42) would be purposeless. Therefore, the restriction is with respect to those of the same class; and since the *tiṅ* suffixes of the same class fall within the domain of both *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada*, [the rule applies] only to the *parasmaipada* suffixes, not to the *ātmanepada* ones. These [suffixes] occur before *kṛt* suffixes.

And when there is the elision (*luk*) of the *parasmaipada* suffix, it certainly does not occur even in the preceding rule, because [the restriction] has not been specifically excluded by a restrictive rule (*niyamena*).
As for the statement "But the author of the *Padaśeṣa*... and so forth: the author of the *Padaśeṣa*, moreover, says as follows.

He considers: "In the case of *parasmaipada*s"—this is not a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*), but rather a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*). That is to say, when the root *gam-* is observed—that is, found—in the domain of *parasmaipada*, then the augment *iṭ* occurs before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with *s*. This being the case...

Even without a formal *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule), according to that [author's] opinion, since the root *gam-* is characterized as being present in *parasmaipada* forms, the suffix *iṭ* necessarily occurs after it in all instances involving a *kṛt* suffix— even when a *parasmaipada* suffix is absent and there is elision (*luk*) of a *parasmaipada* suffix— by virtue of its being followed by a *parasmaipada* suffix.
Because there is no specific restriction regarding the *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes beginning with *sa*, according to his view, the forms should be *sañjigamiṣitā* and *adhijigamiṣitā* [of grammar].
This is because the roots *gam* preceded by *sam* and *adhi* are not observed to occur in the *parasmaipada*. Likewise...
For, with the prefix *sam*, the ātmanepada is prescribed by the rule "samo gamy-ucchi" (Pāṇini 1.3.29); likewise,
even with the prefix *adhi*, the ātmanepada occurs by the rule "anudāttaṅtiḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.12) due to the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*).

59. *na vṛdbhyaścaturbhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.59). Because of the use of the plural form in the rule *vṛdbhyaḥ*, it is understood that the sense of "beginning with" (*ādi*) is intended. Therefore, he says: "from *vṛt* and the others. [The roots are] *vṛtu vartane* (Dhātupāṭha 758) and *vṛdhu vṛdhau*.

The four roots beginning with *vṛt*—namely, *vṛt* (DhP 759), *śṛdh* meaning "contemptuous sound" (DhP 760), and *syand* meaning "flowing" (DhP 761)—are all acute-accented (*udātta*). Among these, for the first three, the augment *iṭ* is invariably required; however, for *syand*, because it is marked with the indicatory letter *u*, the *iṭ* is optionally required.

This is stated as a prohibition. In the case of "vartsyati," the suffix *lṛṭ* is applied by the rule "lṛṭ śeṣe ca" (Pāṇini 3.3.13), and the active voice (*parasmaipada*) is optionally used by the rule "vadbhyāḥ syasanoḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.92). In the case of "vivṛtsati," there is an absence of *guṇa* strengthening because the suffix *san* is *kit* according to the rule "halantācca" (Pāṇini 1.2.10).
In the case of *vṛdhi* and *śrṛdhi*, the substitution of *t* for the letter *dh* occurs by the rule "ṭhkhari ca" (Pāṇini 8.4.55).

Regarding the statement "it need not be said 'after the four [words]'," he states the reason here with the words "for the employment of the marker *vṛ*" and so forth. That very [marker *vṛ*] is understood as being intended for the purpose of completing the list beginning with *vṛt*.

By means of *tantra* (the principle of economy) or through multiple powers (*anekaśakti*), nothing undesirable follows for words. Even so, the intention is that when this is understood, only the desired result is established. Thus, once the mention of "four" (*catur*) has been rejected, he states the purpose [of its inclusion] with the words "That is done," and so forth. If the mention of "four" were not...
If it were applied, then the substitution characterized by *ūṭ* for *spand* would take effect because it is *antaraṅga*.

Its status as *antaraṅga* is due to its depending solely on the general category of *valādi* *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes; whereas this prohibition is *bahiraṅga* because it depends upon a specific *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.

Therefore, the mention of "four" (catur) is made so that the prohibition may override even the internal, optional application characterized by the marker *ud*, just as in the case of [the rule for] *syandi*. But how is this meaning obtained even when the mention of "four" is made? To this he says: "In the mention of 'four'," and so forth. That...
That whose primary element is the *syandi* (the flowing/manifesting) is "that which has that as its primary" (*tatparam*); the state of being such is "intentionality" (*tātparyam*).

By that intentionality, the meaning is "by way of having that as its primary. Regarding the word "brought near" (*sannidhāpitaḥ*), the meaning is "presented. And how can there be an option for that which has been thus presented by this prohibition?

The purpose of this very [rule] is that it should set aside [the previous rule]. Consequently, because of the mention of "four" (*catur*), the prohibition sets aside even the internal (*antaraṅga*) substitution. Regarding the phrase "here too" (*atrāpi*) and so forth: how, moreover, can there be a prohibition everywhere else while the term "in the *parasmaipada*s" (*parasmaipadeṣu*, Pāṇini 7.2.58) continues to apply?
Is it obtained? He thinks thus: the word *gameḥ* (from the root *gam*) is understood as a governing term (*anuvartate*). There, the connection will be made as follows:

"In whatever manner *iṭ* [is applied] after the root *gam* when followed by an affix beginning with *s*, in that very same manner there is no *iṭ* after roots such as *vṛt*. Therefore, just as there is the exclusion of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) for *gam* in other instances, [so too is the exclusion of *iṭ*].
In all cases, the augment *iṭ* occurs; likewise, there is a prohibition [of *iṭ*] even after roots such as *vṛt*.
60. And [the augment iṭ is not applied] after the root *kṛp* (7.2.60).

The root *kṛpū* means "to be capable" (*sāmarthye*; DhP 762). Since it is marked with the indicator *ū*, the augment *iṭ* would optionally apply [by rule 7.2.45]; this prohibition is therefore commenced. [The form] *kalptā* is formed with the suffix *luṭ*; [this is governed by the rule] *luṭi ca klṛpaḥ*.

By the rule (1.3.93), the *parasmaipada* endings are optionally used; by the rule *kṛpo ro laḥ* (8.2.18), the substitution of *la* for *ra* occurs. Thus we have *ciklṛpsati*. The *kit* designation is applied as before.
Regarding the statement "also of *klṛp*" and so forth, this meaning is obtained through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule concerning the *vṛt*-class roots.

Since that [term] is being carried over, the connection will indeed be made: just as there is a prohibition for *vṛt* and the others, so too shall this [prohibition] apply to *klṛp*. If, then, the mention of *vṛt* and the others is carried over here, then that same prohibition would also apply to *vṛt* and the others.
Does [the prohibition] apply? It will not apply by virtue of the power of making a formal division (yogavibhāga) of the rule.
For if that [prohibition] were to apply to *vṛt* and the others as well, then [Pāṇini] would have composed the rule simply as "na vṛdbhyaḥ pañcabhyaḥ tāsi ca" (P. 1.3.95).

61. *acaḥ kṛtāsvatthaly aniṭo nityam* | (Pāṇini 7.2.61) Since the augment *iṭ* would have been required by the rule regarding roots beginning with *krī* etc., this sūtra prescribes a prohibition of *iṭ* after roots ending in a vowel that are invariably without *iṭ* (*nityāniṭ*) in the *tās* form, when followed by *thali*. Examples include *pātā* and so forth. The mention of the *luṅ* (aorist) tense serves as an illustration for the *tās* form.

This is for the purpose of demonstrating that [the root] is invariably *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*). Its *aniṭ* status is due to the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "ekācaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.10), etc.
Thus we have forms such as *lūtvā* and *lulavitha*. Because of the statement "tāsvat," the prohibition does not apply here.

If that [rule] were not stated here as well, there would be a prohibition even in this case—namely, in *bhavati* and *lunāti*—because of the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 7.2.11]: "In a *kit* suffix, [the *iṭ* augment is absent] after a root that is invariably without *iṭ*, provided it does not end in *ś* or *y*. Thus reads the printed text: "there would be a prohibition even here; *bhavati*..."

The root *lū* is invariably without the augment *iṭ* before a suffix marked with *k*. This is because of the prohibition [of *iṭ*] by the rule *śryukaḥ kiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.11). Thus we have *papiva*, *papima*. The elision of the vowel *ā* occurs by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64). [The phrase] "the mention of *aniṅ* is for the purpose of making it obligatory," and so forth.

The meaning is that the mention of *aniṭ* (the rule for non-iṭ vowels) is for the purpose of specifying how the root's lack of *iṭ* is to be qualified by the word "always" (*nityam*). Alternatively, the mention of *aniṭ* is for the purpose of preventing the prohibition of *thal* after a root ending in *tās* that takes *iṭ*, as in the forms *savitā* and *lulavitha*.

Why does it not occur? It is simply not possible for this meaning to be so. For instance, it is stated that *thal* does not occur after those [roots] ending in *i*; yet, that which is *seṭ* (possessing the augment *iṭ*) cannot be designated as "after those" (*tāsvat*) while the prohibition is being applied, because *thal* is prescribed specifically in the absence of *am* and *ic*.
The suffix -vat expresses similarity precisely through that [suffix] being *tās*.
However, by the very mention of -vat, there will be no prohibition of the *seṭ* [augment] in *sthali*; otherwise, the similarity designated by the term -vat would not exist.

Therefore, it is logical that the purpose of the mention of *aniṅgrahaṇa* is exactly as stated. Now, if *aniṅgrahaṇa* were not mentioned, of what would the word *nityam* (always) be understood as a qualifier?
It would be a qualifier of the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*). But surely the prohibition itself is already established as being permanent (*nitya*) by context; in that case, if—
If the term *nitya* (constant) were not included, the prohibition would not be qualified; in that case, the inclusion of *nitya* would be purposeless.

This is not so; it is for the purpose of ensuring that the prohibition in the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*) is understood as being non-constant (*anitya*). And thus, by the preceding rule, the augment *iṭ* would indeed occur in one alternative (*pakṣa*).

Therefore, the purpose of the mention of *aniṭ* is exactly as stated previously: "when *iṭ* is optional (*vibhāṣita*) after *tās*" (Pāṇini 7.2.43). In the rule for the roots beginning with *svarati* (7.2.44), *iṅ* is optionally substituted for *dhūñ*.

Because of the mention of "always" (*nitya*) [in the subsequent rule], the augment *iṭ* necessarily occurs after that root which has an optional *iṭ* when the suffix *thali* follows. And this being so...

Even if the term "nitya" (invariable) were included [in the rule], the prohibition would certainly apply. Furthermore, even by virtue of an optional absence of *iṭ*, the designation "aniṭ" (without *iṭ*) indeed occurs.
For instance, although the root *guh* optionally takes *iṭ*, it is still designated as "aniṭ" by the rule *śala igupadhād aniṭaḥ ksaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.45).
It indeed becomes *kso*, as in *adhukṣat*.
Now, for what purpose is the designation by means of the suffix *-vat* (vati)? Why not simply say *na tāsau*?
To this he says: "*tāsvat*" and so forth. If the designation by means of *-vat* were absent, even that which is *asan* (not being) among those [verbs]...
Furthermore, because it is non-existent (*asat*), the augment *iṭ* is not applied [to the root], and thus there would be a prohibition of *iṭ* even in the case of the suffix *thali*.

However, when the reference is made by means of the suffix *-vat*, since *-vat* signifies complete similarity, just as *iṇ* does not occur after a root in the form where it is absent in the *tās-iṭ* (the conditional), so too it must not occur in the *thali*; therefore, it indeed does not occur.

There would be the undesirable consequence (*doṣaprasaṅga*). For if that [augment *iṭ*] which belongs to those [tās-adi forms] were non-existent, and because of its non-existence were eternally undesirable, then there would be a prohibition of *iṭ* even for the suffix *thali*. This being the case, while there is an absence of *iṭ* for that which is non-existent in the case of *tās*-adi, there would likewise be no [absence of *iṭ*] for *thali* in the case of that which is existent. Thus, just as there is an absence of *iṭ* for such a form in *tās*-adi, so too would it be for *thali*.
It may be so;

for one who maintains that [the root *han*] is eternally aniṭ because it is non-existent in those [Vedic forms] and existent in others, the prohibition does not apply to the suffix *thali*—as in "jaghasitha"—according to the subsequent sūtra; such is the intention.

He says: "In the subsequent sūtra as well," and so forth. Thus, in that case, this indication by means of the suffix *vat* serves for the sake of the subsequent rule; but here, there is no purpose in the indication by *vat*, because the prohibition does not apply to the roots *ghas* and *vyadh* simply due to their not ending in a vowel (*anajanta*). [The example is] *jaghasitha*. [This is derived from the root *ghas* with the suffix *liṭ*,] according to the rule *liṭaḷnyatarasyām*.
(2.4.4.0) Thus, there is the substitution of *ghas* for the root *ad*. Regarding the form *udayitha*:
there is the substitution of *vayi* for *veñ* by the rule "veño vayiḥ" (2.4.41); then, by the rule "liṭyabhyāsasyobhayeṣām" (6.1.17), there is *saṃprasāraṇa*.
Why, then, is there the designation *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*) for these roots *ghas* and *vay* when followed by *tās*? Because they are invariably *aniṭ*.
Thus he says: "For [the rule] 'ad-ādeśo hi'... and so forth. Furthermore, the non-existence of those two [suffixes] should be understood from the fact that they are not prescribed therein.
62. *upadeśe'tvataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.62).

This rule is commenced for the purpose of excluding roots ending in *an*. [Regarding the form] *ṭhiyaṣṭha* (the *Padamañjarī* reads *ṭhiyaṣṭa*), there is the *samprasāraṇa* of the reduplicated syllable as before, and the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *vraścādi-* (8.2.36).

Regarding the substitution of *ṣṭu* [for *ṣṭh*]: as in the form *cakarṣitha*. The root *kṛṣ* (meaning "to scratch" or "to draw," DhP 990) possesses this vowel *a* not in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*), but rather after the *guṇa* substitution has taken place. Here, it would have been possible to omit the mention of "enunciation" (*upadeśa*); for indeed, one could simply have stated: "of a monosyllabic root in its enunciation."

(7.2.10) Is it, therefore, for the purpose of making the term *upadeśa* understood to carry over [from the previous rule] that this is done for the sake of clarity? In its absence, one might think that because it was not used in the preceding sūtra, it has ceased to apply, and thus someone might interpret [the rule] even as "tāsām atvataḥ. [For example, in the case of] *rarādhītha*.
Thus: *rādha* and *sādha* [are used] in the sense of "accomplishment" (*saṃsiddhi*) [Dhātupāṭha 1262, 1263]. Regarding the form *jighṛkṣati*:
because of the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *sani grahaguhośca* (Pāṇini 7.2.12), it is invariably without *iṭ*; however, this does not apply to the *tās* suffix, but rather to the *san* suffix.

Regarding the word *ṭhānāñja*: the root *ṭhañjū* is used in the sense of manifestation (*vyakti*), destruction (*bhrakṣaṇa*), and so forth [or manifestation, death, beauty, and motion—according to the Dhātupāṭha 1458]. By the rule *ata ādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.70), there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable; by the rule *tasmānnuṅ dvihalaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.71), the augment *nuṭ* is added.
This root possesses the vowel *a* in its instruction (*upadeśa*), yet it is not invariably *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*);
for, by the rule *svaratyādi-* (Pāṇini 7.2.44), the addition of *iṭ* is optional.

63. *ṛto bhāradvājasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.63). [The examples are] *sasmartha* and *dadhvartha*. [The root] *smṛ* [is used] in the sense of "thinking" (Dhātupāṭha 933); [the root] *dhvṛ* [is used] in the sense of "winding" or "bending" (Dhātupāṭha 939).

Now, although among the roots ending in *a*, *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ* are both udātta, even so, *vṛṅ* cannot possibly occur [in this context] because it is exclusively ātmanepada. As for *vṛñ*, however, by the rule "In the Vedic language, [the suffix] is optionally elided after *vṛñ*" (Pāṇini 7.2.64), there must necessarily be the augment *iṭ* in the secular language (*bhāṣā*). Therefore...

This [rule] is not intended for the purpose of prohibiting the augment *iṭ* after those two; however, as for other roots ending in *ṛ*, because they are *anudātta*, they are invariably *aniṭ* in the feminine (*tās*),
and thus the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "after a root with a *tāsu*-like vowel, in *thal*, there is invariably no *iṭ*" (Pāṇini 7.2.61) is already established.

One should not raise this objection—that because the substitution of *guṇa* takes precedence, and because the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* follows, the form would not be established due to the absence of an *an-ja* ending; for the mention of "upadeśa" (original form) is drawn forward from a previous rule and is connected with the word "acaḥ" (of a vowel). Or rather, [the connection is] with "acaḥ."

The fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) has its qualification already established; thus, we shall understand it as follows: "from that which ends in *at* (i.e., a vowel) when followed by *sthāl*. Therefore, the prohibition for words ending in *ṛ* is already accomplished by the rule itself (*ataḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.142]). Why, then, is this new rule commenced? To this he says: "When something is already established, the commencement [of a new rule] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārthaḥ*)."

Thus [it is said]: "not from others. Who, then, are those [others]? They are those ending in *ṛ* other than the ones [already mentioned], as well as those ending in vowels (*ajanta*) that do not end in *an*, and those taught (*upadeśe*) as ending in *at*. Now, why is this restriction not understood thus: "the substitution of *ṛ* applies only for Bhāradvāja, and not for other teachers"? It is because [if it were so,] in this way...
He considers [the following]: from the previous sūtra, "of those ending in /a/" (atvataḥ) is understood by anuvṛtti;

the very purpose of that anuvṛtti is this: by means of this restrictive rule (niyama), due to proximity, there is the recurrence (anuvṛtti) of that very root which was previously mentioned—namely, one ending in /a/ and having /a/ as its penultimate vowel (atvataḥ). And thus...

The subsequent application [of the rule] would be purposeless. Therefore, he says "tat" and so forth, stating that this very restriction—that for Bhāradvāja, only after *ṛt*—is understood. The word "tat" indicates the reason:
because such a restriction exists here, therefore the prohibition applies only after *ṛt* for Bhāradvāja.

It occurs [only] from these roots and not from other roots. Therefore, although a permanent prohibition of *iṭ* was established by the two preceding rules, nevertheless, by virtue of this [present rule], an option regarding those two preceding rules arises. Even though the word "optionally" (*vā*) was not explicitly mentioned there, [it is understood here].
And although the mention of the teacher (Ācārya) is made, it is nevertheless understood by implication.
Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the long vowel *t* (tapara) [in the rule]? Why not simply say "of Bhāradvāja" (*ṛBhāradvājasya*)?
To this he says: "The inclusion of the long vowel *t*," and so forth. For if only "uḥ" were stated, then [the rule would apply] to *aṇ*.

Since the rule "one takes those of the same class" (*savarṇān gṛhṇāti*) would result in the inclusion of even those ending in *ṛ*, the addition of the *t* (in *tapara*) is for the purpose of excluding that. But what would happen if there were no inclusion of those ending in *au*? To this he says: "For thus," and so forth. The word *tathā* has the sense of "in this manner"; the word *hi*...

Because it is for the sake of the noble ones (*ārya*): thus, even without the addition of the *tapara* marker (*ṛt*), since the inclusion of those ending in *ṛ* would already occur, this [rule] might be suspected of being merely prescriptive (*vidhi*). For a restriction (*niyama*) occurs only when there is something else to be prescribed.
Since the inclusion of those ending in *ṛ* would already take place, it is precisely their prohibition that must be prescribed.

It might be argued that for them, the prohibition by the preceding rule is not established, because for all [stems] ending in ṛ, the suffixes tāsi and tāsu are invariably seṭ (possessing the augment iṭ). However, when the letter *t* is included as a marker (*taparakaraṇa*), the long vowel is excluded by that *t*; consequently, since there is no longer anything remaining to be prescribed, this becomes a restrictive rule (*niyama*).

64. *babhūthātatanthajagṛbhmavavartheti nigame* (Pāṇini 7.2.64). In examples such as *babhūtha*, the non-occurrence of the augment *iṭ*, which would otherwise be required by the rule governing roots beginning with *kṛ* (krādinīyama), is prescribed as a Vedic irregularity (*nipātana*).
Regarding *babhūtha*: by the rule *bhavateraḥ* (7.4.73), the vowel *a* of the reduplicated syllable is replaced by *ā*.

Regarding *ṭhbabhūvitha*: by the rule *bhuvo vug luṅliṭoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.88), the augment *vuk* is applied. Regarding *ātatantha*: the root *tanu* (DhP 1463) meaning "to expand," preceded by the prefix *ā*. Regarding *atenitha*: by the rule *thali ca seṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.121), there is the substitution of *e* for the root vowel and the elision of the reduplication. Regarding *jagṛbhma*.

In *bhuvaḥ* [the suffix] *vuk* is applied by the rule *bhuvo vug luṅ-liṭoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.88). Regarding *ātatantha*: the root is *tanu* (Dhātupāṭha 1463) meaning "to expand," preceded by the prefix *āṅ*. Regarding *atenitha*: by the rule *thali ca seṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.121), there is the substitution of *e* for the root vowel and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-lopa*). Regarding *jagṛbhma*: this is from the root *grah* in the *liṭ* [perfect tense].

By the rule *ṭhparasmaipadānām* (3.4.82), etc., there is the substitution of *mā* for *mas*; by the rule *ṭhgrahijyā* (6.1.16), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). Regarding *vavārtha*: the root *vṛñ* (dhā.pā. 1254) means "to choose."

65. *vibhāṣā sṛjiddaśoḥ* | (Pāṇini 7.2.65) The roots *sṛj* (meaning "to emit," Dhātupāṭha 1414) and *dṛś* (meaning "to see," Dhātupāṭha 988)—since the augment *iṭ* is obligatorily required for these by the rule governing the *krī*-class and others—this statement is made for the purpose of allowing an option. [Examples: *sasraṣṭha*,...
[The form] *dadṛkṣe* [is derived as follows]: the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by [Pāṇini 8.2.36], *vraśca* etc., and the substitution of *i* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.58], *sṛjidṛśorjhalyamakiti*.

66. *iḍatyartivyayatīnām* (Pāṇini 7.2.66). [Examples: *āditha*, *āritha*. [Roots: *ada* (to eat, DhP 1011); *ṛ* (to go, DhP 1098). [The lengthening of the reduplication is applied] by *ata ādeḥ* (7.4.70). [Example: *aviṣyayitha*.

Thus: from the root *vyeñ* in the sense of "covering" (*saṃvaraṇe*, DhP 1007), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule *liṭy abhyāsasyobhayesām* (P. 6.1.17). But why does the substitution of *ā* for the initial vowel of *vyeñ* not occur here by the rule *ādeca upadeśe* (P. 6.1.45)? To this he says: "In the case of *vyeñ*, [the substitute] *vyo* does not occur in the *liṭ*."
And so forth. "There is also a permanent prohibition for the root *ṛth*"—this refers to [the rule] *ṛto bhāradvājasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.63).
"The mention of *iṅ* here is for the sake of clarity. But surely, the augment *iṭ* is permanent?

The inclusion of the term *iṅ* would be for the purpose of [indicating] "it may be so" (*syāt*); for without the inclusion of *iṅ*, how could this rule for *iṅ* be understood as being obligatory? To this he says: "For when there is the prescription of an option," and so forth. By this, indeed, the prescription of an option—or of that which immediately follows—is effected.

Or is it a permanent prohibition (*nityapratiṣedha*) established by what precedes and follows? For even that can be carried over according to the maxim of the frog’s leap (*maṇḍūkaplutinyāya*). In that case, if the former alternative were intended, then the mention of *arti* and *vyayati* would be purposeless; [for the rule] "of those ending in short *a* in the original instruction" (*upadeśe'tvataḥ*) [would already suffice].
Because the option is already established by this very rule (Pāṇini 7.2.62). Now, as for the other [view]:
if that were the case, the mention of *arti* would be purposeless; for the prohibition would already be established by the rule "ṛto bhāradvājasya" (7.2.63). Since this is so, there is no option.

Therefore, neither the prescription nor the prohibition is applicable [in that case]. Consequently, even without the mention of "iṅ," it can be understood that this is a permanent (nitya) rule concerning iṅ. However, since there would be an excessive burden on the understanding if it were understood in such a way, the mention of "iṅ" is made for the sake of clarity.

67. *vasvekājādghasām* (Pāṇini 7.2.67). [The sūtra states: "Of roots that have undergone reduplication and consist of a single vowel (*ekāc*). How is this determined? By the force of the mention of *ekāc*. For there is no root that possesses more than one vowel (*anekāc*) when reduplication has not yet occurred.

The mention of *eka* (one) is made for the purpose of excluding that [which is not one]. Now, is it not the case that the root *jāgṛ* exists, and therefore that [mention] would be for the purpose of excluding it? This is not so; for the commencement of a grammatical rule (*yogārambha*) is not prompted by a single example. If this were the intended purpose, [the rule would simply have been] "after *jāgṛ*, *na*."
One should speak thus. Even then, this is the meaning: the burden of having to state [the rule] for every individual case (*pratipadika*) is avoided.

But would it not also serve to prevent the application of the root *ūrṇoti*? This is not so; for it was stated previously: "The substitution of *ūrṇuv-* for *ūrṇu-* is to be expressed" (Kārikā 7.2.11).

Therefore, what was stated is correct: "of roots that have undergone reduplication and consist of a single vowel," as in *ādivān* and *āśivān*. [The roots] *ad* (to eat, DhP 1011) and *aś* (to eat, DhP 1523) take the suffix *kvasu* by the rule *liṭaḥ kvasuśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.107); then reduplication occurs.
And for the sake of practice: there is lengthening of the initial vowel by *ṭhata ādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.70);
then the long vowel by *savarṇadīrgha*; then the augment *iṭ*; then the *num* augment by *ṭhugidacam* (Pāṇini 7.1.70); and finally the lengthening by *sāntamahataḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.10), etc.

By the rules *halṅyādi-* (6.1.68) and *saṃyogāntalopa-* (8.2.23), [the forms] *pecivan* and *śokivān* are derived. By the rule *ata ekahalmadhye-* (6.4.120) and others, the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*) occur. This is stated in the passage beginning with "when the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been made for both the root and the reduplication," and so forth.

But surely, regarding the rule for reduplication in the sixth [chapter], the author of the Vṛtti has adopted the position that "reduplication is the double employment [of the element]"; and thus, even when the status of being a root (*dhātu*) and the reduplication have not yet been established,
and even when the substitution of *ai* for *e* and the elision of the reduplication have not yet been applied to a single part [of the base].

Even when reduplication has been performed, these remain single-syllabled (*ekāc*). For if reduplication were to occur in place [of the original], then another word consisting of multiple syllables (*anekāc*) would be extended [to it], and thus those words that have undergone reduplication would indeed possess multiple syllables.
However, this is not the case when reduplication consists in the double employment [of the same element]; in that situation...

For that very same root (dhātu) is pronounced twice, and even if it were uttered a hundred times, it would not lose its status as a single vowel (ekāctva); how much less so when it is pronounced twice? Therefore, why is it said: "when the single-substitute (ekādeśa) of the root and the reduplication has been made, and when the *et* [substitution] and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*) have been performed"?

"Are these [monosyllables] monosyllabic after having undergone reduplication? There is no fault in saying this because it is stated by relying on the fact that they are considered monosyllabic due to the operation of reduplication (*āvṛtti*). For indeed, even due to a difference in properties (*dharma*), there is a conventional usage of difference regarding the substratum (*dharmin*). Thus, speakers say: "The things of last year... [and so forth].
"Last year was [the past], this year is more [past], and the year before last is most [past]; thus you have become quite another person.

Or rather—the alternative of doubling in place (*sthāne-dvirvacana*) is also resorted to there, on the grounds that doubling consists in a double utterance; and because of the word "and" (*ca*), it is also in place.

The phrase "also reduplication" (*dvirvacanam api*) is included because the alternative view that reduplication occurs in place of the original element is indicated there. Furthermore, those defects that arise under that alternative view have already been refuted therein. In the form *tasthivān*, the *khya* is the remainder according to *śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.61), and the *a* is elided by *ato lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64).

Thus there is the elision of the *ākāra*. In the form *jakṣivān*, as before, there is the substitution of *ghas* for *ad*; the augment *iṭ* is added; the penultimate vowel is elided by the rule *gamahana-* (Pāṇini 6.4.98); and by the rule *kuhoścuḥ* (7.4.62), there is the substitution of a palatal (*cutva*)—the letter *dh* becomes *jh*; and by the rule *abhyāse carcā* (8.4.54), the *jh* [becomes *k*].

The letter *ja* [becomes *k*]: by the rule "ṭhkhari ca" (Pāṇini 8.4.55), there is *carv-ṛti* (substitution of the first consonant) for the following *dha*, resulting in *ka*; then, by the rule "śāsivasi" (Pāṇini 8.3.60) and so forth, there is *ṣatva* (substitution of *ṣ*).
Now, one might object: since the augment *iṭ* is already established here by the restriction of the *krādi* group, what is the purpose of this new beginning?

Thus he says: "In the case of *siddha*," and so forth. By the statement "the application [of the rule] which was occasioned by the restriction of *kṛ*, etc.," he clarifies precisely this point: "When something is already established (*siddhe*), the formulation [of a new rule] is for the purpose of restriction" (Kātantra Paribhāṣā 59).
The word "occasioned" (*prasakta*) means "obtained" (*prāpta*). The word "is restricted" (*niyamyate*) [means it is restricted] from other verbal roots.
The meaning is that [the rule] is restricted to those very roots beginning with *ekāc* (monosyllabic) after being excluded [from others].

Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *at* (the vowel *a*), since even those ending in *a* become *ekāc* once the elision of *at* has been performed and reduplication has taken place; thus, wouldn't it be established by the mention of *ekāc* alone?

Thus he says: "The mention of *āt* is for the purpose of including those [elements] that have more than one vowel (*anekāc*). But how do they possess more than one vowel? To this he says: "In the case of reduplication," and so forth.
Because the elision of the vowel *ā* is caused by the presence of *iṭ*, when *iṭ* occurs, those [elements] undergo the elision of the vowel *ā*.

It must exist; it does not exist when [the suffix] is absent. Therefore, as long as the augment *iṭ* is not applied, because there is no elision of the *ākāra*, these [roots] have more than one vowel (*anekāc*) once the reduplication has been performed.
Thus, if the mention of "beginning with *as*" (*asatyādigrahaṇa*) were not present, for them—[the reading in the printed edition is *ityasatyādigrahaṇe*].

There would be no inclusion [of the root *daridrā*]. Therefore, for the sake of including multiple vowels, the mention of "ādi" (beginning with) must be made. If this is so, would not the suffix *iṭ* also apply to the root *daridrā*? To this he says: "But of *daridrāti*, etc. For there is no possibility at all of the suffix *kvasu* occurring after *daridrāti*.
Because of the statement "the root *daridrā* takes *ām* when it has multiple vowels" (Vārttika 305), the suffix *ām* must occur after *daridrā*.

And since that is present, by the rule "after *ām*" (Pāṇini 2.4.81), there must be elision (*luk*) of the *liṭ* suffix; so how can this occasion for the augment *iṭ* arise? [In the form] "daridrāñcakāra," the rule "and *kṛ* is employed as an auxiliary" applies.

(3.1.40) Thus, there is the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of the root *kṛ* following the perfect tense (*liṭ*). Even while conceding that there is no occurrence of the augment *ām* after the root *daridrā*, he states another solution: "Even so, *ām* is not applied," and so forth. Here, the rule for the suffix *iṅ* is prescribed for verbal roots ending in long *ā*.

Because of the rule "In the case of *daridrāti*, there is elision of the *ṭh* [augment] before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, and this elision is established even prior to the formation of the suffix," the vowel *ā* is elided even before the suffix arises; consequently, the augment *iṭ* does not occur due to the absence of its cause.
"Let the mention of the root *ad* alone be made; there is no need to mention *ghas*.

For when reduplication has been applied to this [root], and the penultimate vowel elision has been performed by the rule *ghasibhasor ha li ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.100), the augment *iṭ* would be established by the rule *ekācaḥ* (7.2.10) alone? To this he says: "Even for *ghas*, etc."—[the reason being] "because it would lack a vowel (*anackatvāt*)."

Thus [ends the discussion on] the reason for the absence of reduplication. Reduplication is prescribed for monosyllabic roots, because of the governing rule "of a monosyllable" (6.1.1). Therefore, when the penultimate vowel has been elided, there would be no reduplication due to the root becoming vowel-less;
consequently, the form *jakṣivān* would not be established—this is the intended meaning. Now, even if [the rule were applied],...

Why is there a fault specifically in the inclusion of the term *ghasi*? To this he says: "If it were made," etc. (Note: This phrase does not appear in the Kāśikā; however, in the Padamañjarī, the reading "kriyamāṇe tu" is found as a pratīka). This is easy to understand.

68. *vibhāṣā gamahanavidaviśām* (Pāṇini 7.2.68). This optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) is commenced because, due to the preceding restrictive rule, the augment *iṭ* would not have occurred after the roots *gam*, etc.; therefore, this option is introduced.
For example, in the form *jagmivān*: because it is subsequent [in the order of the rules], *iṭ* is applied first, and then [the substitution of] *gamahana-* (Pāṇini 6.4.98) applies.

By these [rules] and others, there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*), followed by reduplication (*dvirvacana*). In the forms *jaghanvān* and *jaghnuvān*, the substitution of *gh* for *h* occurs by the rule *abhyāsācca* (Pāṇini 7.3.55). The phrase "of the root meaning 'to obtain'" refers to the root *vidlṛ* (Dhātupāṭha 1432) in the sense of obtaining. Not...

Regarding the term *jñānārthasya*: [it refers to] the root *vid* in the sense of "knowing" (*dhā.pā.* 1064). Since the roots *vid* in the sense of "existence" (*dhā.pā.* 1171) and *vid* in the sense of "investigation" (*dhā.pā.* 1450) are ātmanepada verbs, the suffix *kvasu* does not occur after them in the ātmanepada.
The statement "it occurs" is not a formal introduction [to a rule].

Regarding the phrase "and after *dṛśi*," etc., the meaning is that this form of explanation should be understood as signifying that the augment *iṭ* occurs after the suffix *kvasu* following the root *dṛśir* (DhP 988) in the sense of "seeing. In this regard, the following...

The explanation is as follows: the rule "vibhāṣā" is treated as a *yogavibhāga* (a separation of rules); by this, [the suffix] will also apply to the root *dṛś*. And even so, the rule "gamahanavidaviśām" is not rendered meaningless, because it indicates that the preceding rule does not have universal application (*asarvaviṣayatva*). For in this way, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is avoided.
It comes to be.

69. *saniṃsasanivāṃsam* (Pāṇini 7.2.69). Regarding the rule "of the root *sanoti*": by the utterance of the second case form (*dvitīyānta*) of the root *ṣaṇu* (Dhātupāṭha 1464), preceded by *san*, it indicates a fixed sequence (*mānupūrvīm*).

Since this specific sequence is fixed, it must occur only where that sequence is prescribed; and because this sequence belongs exclusively to Vedic usage (*chandas*), this particle is understood as having that [Vedic] domain alone. For this very reason, the author of the *Vṛtti* has shown a Vedic usage: "senivāṃsam."
As before, there is elision of the augment *abhyāsasya lopah*. Then, by the rule "ṭhvasvekājādghasām" (Pāṇini 7.2.67), the augment *iṭ* is added.

70. *ṛdanoḥ sye* (Pāṇini 7.2.70). The word *vibhāṣā* has ceased to apply. This rule is for the purpose of prescribing *iṭ* after roots ending in ṛ and after the root *han*, which is otherwise prohibited by the rule *ekāca upadeśe'nudāttāt* (7.2.10) and others, when followed by the suffix *sya*.

Now, since the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied to the root *svarati* by the rule *svaratisūti...* (Pāṇini 7.2.44), he says that it is here [mandated] as obligatory— this [sūtra] is for the purpose of prescribing *iṭ* after *svarati* before the suffix *sya*. Now,
since the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied to *svarati* by the rule *svaratisūti...* (7.2.44), then by this [present sūtra]...
He says that [the augment] is obligatory with the words "of the root *svar*" and so forth.

Since the optional (*veṭ*) nature of the suffix *yan* after the root *svar* is prescribed by the rule Pāṇini 7.2.44 (*svaratisūtisūyatidhūñūdito vā*), this present rule establishes the obligatory (*nitya*) application of *iṭ* for the suffix *sya* after roots ending in ṛ, by means of a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*).
Although this meaning was already stated in the sūtra beginning with *svarati*, it is stated here again for the benefit of those who are prone to forgetfulness.
Now, what is the purpose of including the long vowel marker (tapara) [in *ataḥ*]? If it is argued that it is so that [the rule] does not apply to long vowels, this is not the case.

For since they are acute-accented (udātta), the augment iṭ must necessarily occur after them. If that is so, then even in the absence of the specification "with a following short ṛ" (taparakaraṇa), just as in the rule *smipūṅrañjaśāṃ sani* (Pāṇini 7.2.74),

the term *ṛ* is understood to refer to the verbal root because of its association with *svarati* and others, so too here, by association with the root *han*, the term *ṛ* [is understood to refer to the root *han*].

Otherwise, there would be the inclusion of this verbal root [dhā]. However, since the letter *t* follows (taparatva), this is understood to be the inclusion of a phoneme (*varṇa*). For the designation of a phoneme followed by *t* is well-established. And when there is the inclusion of a phoneme, such inclusions everywhere necessitate the rule of "inclusion of that which ends with it" (*tadantavidhi*).
The augment iṭ is established for those [roots] ending in the vowel ṛ.
71. *añjeḥ sici* (Pāṇini 7.2.71).

Regarding the root *añjū* in the sense of "manifestation, smearing, luster, and motion" (*vyakti-mrakṣaṇa-kānti-gatiṣu*; according to the Dhātupāṭha, it is also listed as *vyakti-marṣaṇa-kānti-gatiṣu*, DhP 1458):

since this root is marked with an *ū* (an *ūdita*), the optionality [of *iṭ*] would apply here by the rule *svaraty-ādi-sūtra* (7.2.44). [This rule provides for the optional addition of *iṭ* after roots of the *svarati* group when followed by the suffix *sic*.]

The statement [of the rule] has the sense of "permanence" (*nityārtha*). Regarding the form *ājīt*: by the rule *itaś ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.100), there is the elision of the *ikāra*; by *astisico 'pṛkte* (7.3.96), there is the augment *iṭ*; by *iṭa īṭi* (8.2.28), there is the elision of the *sic*; by *āḍ ajādīnām* (6.4.72), there is the augment *āṭ*; and by *āṭaś ca* (6.1.90), [vṛddhi is substituted for the preceding vowel].
There is the augment *vṛddhi*. [The form] "aṅjiṣṭām" is derived by applying *jus* to *jhi* according to the rule "tasthasthamipām" (Pāṇini 3.4.101).

72. *stusudhūñbhyaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (Pāṇini 7.2.72). Regarding the roots *ṣṭuañ* "to praise" (DhP 1043) and *ṣuñ* "to press" (DhP 1247)—since these two are anudātta, a prohibition [of the substitution of *iṭ*] would otherwise apply; however, as for *dhūñ*...
Since an option would have applied by virtue of the rule *svarati-sūtreṇa* (Pāṇini 7.2.44), this [sūtra] is commenced.

73. *yam*, *ram*, *nam*, and *ātman* [are also included]. (Pāṇini 7.2.73) The roots are: *yam* (to cease, DhP 984), *ram* (to sport, DhP 853), *ṇam* (to bow and to sound, DhP 981); and those ending in long *ā*: *yā* (to go, DhP 1049).
And so forth. Since all these roots are *anudātta*, the prohibition of *iṭ* would have applied; this [sūtra] is therefore commenced.

Here, because of the mention of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīnirdeśa*), the [augment] applies to *yam* and the others; however, because of the governing rule for *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes, *iṭ* applies only to *sic*. Thus: *vyaraṃsīt*.

The *parasmaipada* ending is applied by the rule "ramaḥ after *sthā*, *iṅ*, and *pari*" (Pāṇini 1.3.83). An example in the dual and plural numbers is appropriate, for there is indeed a perceptible difference there due to the presence of the augment *sa* and the *iṭ* augment; however, an example in the singular number is inappropriate because no such difference exists—so [it has been argued].

He should cause [the root] to enter; in order to show that there is a specific rule regarding that [root] which prohibits *vṛddhi* with respect to it, he says "of *yam* and the others," etc. Regarding "āyaṃsta" (the *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī* both cite the reading as "āyaṃsta" alone), [this is derived from] "āṅi yamahanaḥ."
(1.3.28) Thus, the *ātmanepada* [is applied]. Regarding "araṃsta," here too, [the rule] beginning with "anudātetaḥ" (1.3.12) applies.
74. *smi-pūṅ-ṛ-añj-v-aśāṃ sani* (Pāṇini 7.2.74). [The roots are: *ṣmiṅ* "to smile slightly" (Dhātupāṭha 948);
*pūṅ* "to purify" (Dhātupāṭha 966)—the mention of the anubandha *ū* is for the purpose of excluding *pūñ*; and *ṛ* "to go" or "to reach."
The root *bhū* (DhP 1.1) belongs to the *bhvādi* class, and the root *ṛ* (DhP 2.57), meaning "to go," belongs to the *juhotyādi* class; both are included here because no distinction is specified.
However, this inclusion does not apply to other roots ending in *ṛ*, such as *kṝ* ("to scatter") and others, because [the rule for] *iṭ* applies to them later on.

Because of the specific rule [vidhāna], there is no inclusion of the root *aś* meaning "to eat" (*aśa bhojane*, DhP 1.523); rather, there is the inclusion of *tanjū* meaning "to smear" (*mrakṣaṇe*, DhP 1458), *aśū* meaning "to pervade" (*vyāptau*, DhP 1264), or *aś* meaning "to pervade and to join" (*vyāptau saṃdhe ca*, DhP 1264).

Since the augment *iṭ* is already established by the fact that [the roots] are *udātta*, the following is begun: although *añj* and *aś* would undergo optional application of *iṭ* because they are *udit*, and for the remaining [roots] it would be prohibited because they end in a long vowel (*ūṅ*) by the rule "after *san*, *grah*, and *guh*" (Pāṇini 7.2.12), this [sūtra] is commenced. [The example is] *sismiyiṣate*; [this is explained] by the rule "the *san* [derivative] is like its original" (Pāṇini 1.3.62).

Thus ends the section on the ātmanepada endings. Regarding "pipaviṣate": by the rule "oḥ puyaṇjyapare" (Pāṇini 7.4.80), the *it* vowel substitution is applied to the reduplicated syllable. Regarding "aririṣati": when the augment *iṭ* is present, the *guṇa* substitution is performed, and then there is the doubling of the second *ekāc* (monosyllabic) element beginning with a vowel. Regarding "añjijiṣati": [the same process applies].
Regarding "ṭhaśiśiṣati" [the Kāśikā reads "ṭhaśiśiṣate"; it is not found in the printed edition]:
the letter *n* of the root *añj* is not reduplicated, because of the prohibition stated in "na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.3).
75. And [the suffix] *kira* is added after five [roots]. (Pāṇini 7.2.75) [The roots are:
*kṛ* "to scatter" (Dhātupāṭha 1409), *gṛ* "to swallow" (Dhātupāṭha 1410), *dṛṅ* "to disregard" (Dhātupāṭha 1411), and *dhṛṅ* "to be unsteady."
[Regarding the roots] *sthā* (to stand, DhP 1412) and *pracch* (to ask, DhP 1413):

here, because the final vowel is *anudātta*, the prohibition of *iṭ* would apply; furthermore, since *dṛś* and *ghṛṅ* end in a long vowel (*ugantatvāt*), the prohibition by *sani grahaguhośca* (Pāṇini 7.2.12) would also apply. However, for the other two...

This [sūtra] is commenced because the alternative shown by the author of the Vṛtti has been reached: namely, *pipṛcchiṣati*. By the rule *rudavidamuṣagrahi...* (1.2.8), the suffix *san* is marked with the *k*-sign; by *grahijyāvayivyadhivaṣṭivicativṛścatipṛcchatibhṛjjatīnāṃ ṅiti ca* (6.1.16), there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*); by *che ca* (6.1.73), the augment *tuk* is applied; and by *uraṇ raparaḥ* (1.1.51), the substitution of *r* occurs.

By this [sūtra 7.4.66], there is *ātvam* for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), and as before, there is *itvam*. Thus: *sisṛkṣati*. [The root] *sṛj* is used in the sense of "emission" (*visarga*; DhP 1178). Because of the mention of the number five (*pañca*) [in the rule 3.1.5], the suffix *iṇ* does not apply here.
Nor does the suffix *iṇ* apply by virtue of the general characteristic [of being a root]; for there is a prohibition [against it] by the rule *ekācaḥ* (7.2.10).
There is *kit* status by the rule *ṭhhalantācca* (1.2.10), *kutva* by *coḥ kuḥ* (8.2.30),
*ṣatva* by the rule beginning with *vraśca-* (8.2.66), and *katva* by *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si* (8.2.41).
Regarding the statement "they do not desire the lengthening [of the vowel] for *vṛto vā*," how [is this so]?
Furthermore, why is it that even when *iṭ* is desired, it does not occur? Because of the established distinction regarding the technical term *vijñāna*.
The word "of this" (*asya*) refers to the *iṭ* prescribed by this very sūtra.
76. *rūdādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke* (Pāṇini 7.2.76). [The roots are:
*ṭhrudir aśruvimocane* (Dhātupāṭha 1067), *ñi ṣvap śaye* (Dhātupāṭha 1068), *śvasa prāṇane* (Dhātupāṭha 1069), *ana ca* (Dhātupāṭha 1070), *jakṣa*...

Regarding the root *ad* [in the sense of eating and laughing—Dhātupāṭha 1071]: the roots beginning with *rud* are listed among the *ad*-class roots. According to the principle "In the case of a mention of both [a base and a suffix], the mention by means of the fifth case (ablative) is stronger" (Śākapārthivādhikaraṇa, Pāṇinian tradition), the fifth-case form *rudādibhyaḥ* [in Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.76] prevails over the seventh-case form *sārvadhātuke* [in Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.3.84].
It establishes the status of the genitive case; the mention of the locative case is for the sake of what follows.

By that, it is understood that *iṅ* is substituted for the *sārvadhātuka* affix beginning with *val*. Therefore, he says: "from the five beginning with *rud*," and so forth. In the form "prāṇiti," the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule "aniteḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.19).

Regarding the form *svaptā*: because of the mention of the term *sārvadhātuka*, the augment *iṭ* does not occur before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. Furthermore, the general rule for the augment *iṇ* simply does not apply here, due to the prohibition in *ekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.10).
However, in the case of other roots such as those beginning with *rud*, since they are marked with an acute accent (*udātta*), the augment *iṭ* must indeed occur even before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.
The counter-examples are precisely those [already mentioned] under the rule *svapeḥ*.

77. *īśaḥ se* (Pāṇini 7.2.77). Regarding *ṭhse*: this is a citation (*nirdeśa*) without a case-ending, formed by applying the substitution of *luk* for the genitive case according to *supāṃ suluk* (7.1.39). Regarding *īśiṣe*: [this is derived from] the root *īś* in the sense of sovereignty (*aiśvarye*).
(dhā.pā. 1020). Because the root is marked with an *anudātta* accent, the *ātmanepada* ending is applied; by *ṭhthāsaḥ seṭa* (3.4.80), the *thās* is replaced by *si*;

and because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap*. Thus we have "īśiṣva. This is the imperative (*loṭ*), the *se* ending; when the substitution of *va* for *asva* is made according to *savabhyāṃ vāmau* (3.4.91), the principle applies that "that which has undergone a partial modification is not different from the original" (*ekadeśavikṛtamananyavat*).
Thus, this also occurs here.
78. *īḍajanordhve ca* (Pāṇini 7.2.78). Regarding *dhve*: this is a citation without case-endings (*avibhaktika*), as before. Regarding *īḍidhve*:
[the root] *īḍ* (in the sense of "praising," Dhātupāṭha 1019); the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) and the elision of *śap* are as before.

Regarding *luk* [elision]: in the form *ṭhīḍidhvam*, it is the imperative (*loṭ*), with the substitution of *am* by the rule *savābhyāṃ vāmau* (Pāṇini 3.4.91). In *janiṣvam*, it is the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) as before. Due to its Vedic character (*chāndasatva*), the substitution of *lṛk* for *śyan* occurs by the rule *bahulaṃ cchandasi* (Pāṇini 3.2.88).

"And there is the absence of the elision of the penultimate vowel. By the rule "gamahana... (Pāṇini 6.4.98), the elision of the penultimate vowel would otherwise apply; its absence occurs precisely because of the nature of the Vedic text, according to the principle: "All rules are optional in the Veda" (Puṣpavṛtti 56).
Regarding the passage beginning with "of the root *jan* (to produce)," etc.:

[Objection] Since this very [root] possesses an *anubandha*, it ought to be included by that [designation], and not the preceding one; for the vowel *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation and is not an *anubandha*. [Response] This is not so.

This is a fault; for here, since the word *jana* consists of fewer syllables, its prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) would have been required by rule, yet its subsequent placement (*paranipāta*) serves to demonstrate an exception to that rule. Consequently, because the paribhāṣā regarding "that which lacks an anubandha" (Pāṇini 1.2.53) does not apply here, both [the forms *jana* and *janī*] are included.
Regarding the form *vyatijajñidhvam*: the ātmanepada ending is applied by the rule *kartari karmavyatīhāre* (Pāṇini 1.3.14).

As for the phrase "In that case" (*tatra*) and so forth: when the sūtra is read in that manner, [the principle applies] "in a reference to a word-form, the operation pertains to that which begins with it."
(Vyā.pa.127) Thus, by the mention of the letter *s*, there is the inclusion of the word *se* beginning with *s*.

And that word *se* beginning with *s* can only be the word *se* which bears the technical designation *sārvadhātuka*; for no other [word] is possible. But is it not the case that the reflexive pronoun *sva* is also possible? This is not so.
Because that which has undergone a modification in one part is not different [from the original] (Pāṇini-vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 16), this [form] is indeed the word *īś*,

and therefore it must also be included by the inclusion of that [root]. However, those who read the sūtra as "īḍajanordhye ca" [should understand that] for them, [the form is derived from] "īśaḥ sa" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.77).

For the sake of following this very rule (*yoga*), they employ the particle *ca* (and). By that, the augment *iṭ* occurs for the root *īś* as well before the suffix *dhve*. If, then, the augment *iṭ* is desired for *īś* before *dhve* as well, why do they not read a single sūtra as "īśīḍajanāṃ sedhvayoḥ"? In this way...
One might ask: "Should the separate case-ending not be uttered, and should the particle *ca* not be employed?
To this he says: "The variety of the Sūtra," and so forth;
and "In the form *dhve*, the substitution of *e* for *at* has been applied," and so forth. This very [form] is that in which the substitution of *e* for *at* has been applied.

The purpose [of this rule] is that the substitution of *et* for *ṭi* should apply only where it has already been performed. Now, in the case of *laiṅ*, the substitution of *et* for *ṭi* does not occur; therefore, *iṭ* should not be inserted there. If this is so, then it should also not occur in the case of *loṭ*, because once the replacement by *am* has been made, the *ṭi* (the final letter of the suffix) no longer exists? To this he says: "In *loṭ*..."
"Again," and so forth.

79. *liṅḥ salopo'nantyasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.79). Regarding the rule *sārvadhātuke yo liṅ*, the locative case in *sārvadhātuke* (7.2.76) is used here in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*), and the singular number is used for the class (*jātāvekavacanam*), as in the rule *kārake* (1.4.23).
Alternatively—by means of a transposition of case endings (*subvyatyaya*), the singular number is used in place of the plural due to its connection with another [word].

This is not a case of the locative absolute (*parasaptamī*) [meaning "when a sārvadhātuka suffix follows"], because it is impossible for the *liṅ* [augment] to precede [the suffix]. [The form] "kuryāt" is derived by the rule concerning injunctions and so forth (Pāṇini 3.3.161), which prescribes the *liṅ* suffix.

In *kurvīta*, there is the elision of the vowel *i* by the rule *yāsuṭ parasmaipadeṣūdātto ṅicca* (3.4.103) and *ṭita ātmanepadānām ṭer e* (3.4.79); then the guṇa substitution for the root vowel occurs;

after the replacement of *r* as the final element (*raparatva*), the rule *ata ut sārvadhātuke* (6.4.110) applies; and finally, by *hali ca* (6.4.2) and *tusyapadāntāt* (6.1.96), the single-substitute form (*pararūpa*) is established. Thus, *kurvīta*. In *kurvīran*, the *yaṇ* substitute is applied to the vowel *u*.
Thus: *jhasya ran* (Pāṇini 3.4.105).
[Examples: *kuryuḥ*, *kuryāḥ*. Here, because of the mention of "non-final" (*anantya*), the substitution does not apply to *jus* or to *sip*.
[Examples: *kriyāstām*, *kriyāsuḥ*. [This is] the *liṅ* in the sense of benediction (*āśis*) according to 3.3.173.
The substitution of *riṅ* is applied by the rule *ṭhriṅ śayagliṅkṣu* (Pāṇini 7.4.28).

Because of the mention of *sārvadhātuka*, this does not occur in the case of an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. And its status as *ārdhadhātuka* is established by the prescription of the technical term *ārdhadhātuka* in the rule *ṭhliṅaśiṣi* (Pāṇini 3.4.116). [Thus, one says] *kṛṣīṣṭa*.
In the form *hṛṣīṣṭa*, there is *kit* status by [Pāṇini 1.2.12] *uś ca*, which results in the absence of *guṇa*.

80. *ato yeyaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.80). The term *sārvadhātuka*, which was previously mentioned, is here understood as being in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) through a change of case-ending (*vibhaktivipariṇāma*). For this very reason, he says: "of that which follows after an *aṅga* ending in the letter *t*."

Regarding the rule *sārvadhātukasya*: in the forms *paceta* (the older printed reading is *paṭhet*) and *cinuyāt*, once the substitution of *iy* has been made, the *guṇa* substitution (*ādguṇaḥ*, 6.1.87) occurs with the vowel *a*, and then the *y* is elided by *lopo vyor vali* (6.1.66). As for *cinuyāt*, it is derived from roots beginning with *su-* [by adding the suffix *yās*].

Regarding the forms *cikīrṣyāt* and *cikīrṣyāt*: [the former] is derived from the rule *śnuḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.73), and [the latter] from *ṭhyāyāt* (Pāṇini 3.1.84). Because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*.

The form *cikīrṣyāt* is the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*) derived from a desiderative stem (*sananta*). [Objection: "But surely, in this case, there ought to be elision of the vowel *a* by [the rule] *ato lopaḥ*. [Response: No; there is no purpose for the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) [of that rule].

The intention is [to show] by means of the inclusion of all grammatical elements (*sārvadhātuka*). Regarding the phrase "even in *paced*," etc.: although this is intended as an example for *paced*, even there, by the rule "lengthening occurs before *yañ*" (*ato dīrgho yañi*, Pāṇini 7.2.101), lengthening must take place; and consequently, for that which applies to all cases...

Since this substitution of *iy* is occupied by another rule, it has no scope [to apply]. Therefore, it must necessarily set aside that other rule. And in this way, just as this is a sublater of the long vowel (*dīrgha*), so too would it be a sublater of the elision of *at* (*ato lopa*). Consequently, the term *sārvadhātuka* must be understood as being carried over [from the previous rule].

The intention [of the objection] is as follows: "This might be so," and so forth. If the substitution of *iy* were prescribed by carrying forward the mention of *sārvadhātuka* from the rule "turustunnamyamaḥ sārvadhātuke" (Pāṇini 7.3.95), then what you have said would indeed be the case; however, this is not so because the substitution of *iy* would then be without scope (*anavakāśa*). Now, if...

When [the rule] is prescribed by carrying forward the mention of *tiṅ* from "ṭhbhūsuvostiṅ" (Pāṇini 7.3.88), then this [rule] is commenced even though the substitution of *liṅ*— which prescribes lengthening for *tiṅ* alone— is already applicable; therefore, this follows the principle of "yena nāprāpti" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 49).

By logical principle, it serves as an annulment of that very [substitution], but not of the elision (*lopa*). This rule is commenced when the elision of *i* is both applicable and non-applicable: for it is applicable in the case of an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, but non-applicable in the case of a *sārvadhātuka* suffix.
Now, regarding the reference "yeyi": what is this indication? For here, in the word *yā*, which is the substituend (*sthānin*), the genitive case is applied;

thus, when *yā* becomes *as* and then *iya*—that is, in the form *iyas*—the long *ā* is elided either by the rule *āto lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.48) or by applying a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) to *dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.140) to include the elision of the *ā* of the stem.
When the *ṣ* of the genitive case-ending is changed to *r* by the rule "ṣasajuṣoḥ" (8.2.66),

the *y* is substituted for it by the rule "bhobhagoaghoapūrvasya yo'śi" (8.3.17). Furthermore, when that *y* is elided by the rule "lopaḥ śākalyasya" (8.3.19), the form is established by the specific mention [of the word] "ya iyaḥ."

It must be "bhavitavyam," and not "yataḥ. For here, the substitution of *guṇa* cannot take place, because the elision of *y* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) by the rule "pūrvatrāsiddham" (8.2.1). To this, he says: "The form 'yeya' is a citation without a case-ending. Regarding this [form] "yeya":

Regarding the statement "by the collection of the original form (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*), [the term] 'ṭhyā'," this reference is without case endings because the case ending has been elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). Alternatively, having accepted that the reference does possess case endings, he states another resolution: "the word 'yaḥ'" and so forth, beginning with "or" (*vā*).
But how can the non-validity (*asiddhatva*) of the elision (*lopa*) be avoided?

To this he says: "This is a Vedic (*sautra*) designation. The particle *iti* indicates the reason; for, according to the principle "all rules are optional in the Veda" (*sarve vidhayaś chandasi vikalpyante*), [this work] is like the Veda (*chandovat*).

Since there are such sūtras [in the Mahābhāṣya], therefore, because this instruction is based on a sūtra, its status as unestablished (*asiddha*) is not relied upon, and thus *guṇa* is applied by Pāṇini 6.1.87 (*ād guṇaḥ*).
Consequently, the vowel *a* in the substitute is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).

81. *āto ṅtiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.81). The two genitive cases in *ātaḥ* and *ṅtiḥ* are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*). The genitive in *ātaḥ* is a genitive of the locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) with respect to the substitution of *iy*. The genitive in *ṅti* is a genitive of the part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) with respect to the vowel *ā*. [The suffix] beginning with *ṅ* and ending in *t*...

Because a mere *ṅ* sound is impossible [to occur independently], the term *ṅti* is understood here as a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-vigraha*)—namely, "of that which has *ṅ* and *t* as its parts. That which has *ṅ* and *t* as its components is *ṅt*; the part consisting of *ṅ* and *t* is the *ṅtivayava*. [Examples are] *pacete* and *pacethe*. [This is] the *laṭ* [present tense].

The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used because the root has the *svarita* accent; [the endings] are *ātām* and *āthām*. By the rule *sārvadhātukamapit* (Pāṇini 1.2.4), there is *ṅ*-ness [of the suffix]. Thus we have *pacetām* and *pacethām*. In the case of the imperative (*loṭ*), once the substitution of *e* for *ta* is made by *eretve* (3.4.79), the suffix *ām* is applied by *āmetaḥ* (3.4.90).
But is it not the case that the *a* here is not a portion of a *ṅt*? For in the rule *gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ...* (Pāṇini 1.2.1), the meaning of *ṅt* is accepted as being *ṅt* and *id*;
likewise, this same meaning applies in the rule *sārvadhātukam apit* (1.2.4), for in this *yoga* as well—

That very term "ṅit" continues to apply; and when that meaning is accepted, whatever operation is prescribed for a suffix marked with ṅ (ṅit) is indeed observed to apply to the preceding element when followed by a sārvadhātuka suffix, but not to that very sārvadhātuka suffix itself which is apit and ṅit.

Thus he says: "In this regard, [the rule] *sārvadhātukam apit*," and so forth; and "in the preceding sūtra itself. If it is accepted in the *gāṅ-kuṭādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 1.2.1) that "an affix following *gāṅ* and the *kuṭādi* roots which is not marked with *ṇ* or *k* (*añṇit*) is treated as having the marker *ṅ* (*ṅit*)," then, in the case of the *kuṭādi* roots...

The suffix *san* following another [verbal root] becomes marked with the *ṅ* indicatory letter (*ṅit*); if it were *ṅit*, then by the rule "that which has an *ṅ* or *ṣ* as its indicatory letter is *anudāteta*" (Pāṇini 1.3.12), it would be *ātmanepada*. Consequently, forms such as *uccukuṭipati* would not be established.
Therefore, for the sake of establishing this, it is accepted that the *ṅ* in *ṅtvi* denotes both [the *ṅ* of *ṅit* and the *ṅ* of *ṅt*].

However, in the rule *sārvadhātukamapit* (Pāṇini 1.2.4), the meaning accepted is that "that sārvadhātuka [affix] is as if marked with the marker ṅ. Therefore, it is indeed logical that the vowel *ā* possesses the property of being like ṅ. As in the examples *pacante* and *yajante*. Here, it occurs...
The vowel *a* that replaces the *ktvā* suffix is a part of the verbal root (*aṅgadhātu-vayava*).

Nevertheless, because of the rule stating "of *āt*" (*ātaḥ*), the augment *āṭ* is applied here [in the forms *pacāvahai* and *pacāmahai*]. These are the forms for the imperative (*loṭ*) with the endings *vah* and *mahiṅ*.

By the rule "the augment *āṭ* is added to the first person endings, and they are treated as having the marker *p*" (*āḍuttamasya pi ca*), the augment *āṭ* is added, and the endings are marked as first person (*uttama*).

Regarding the phrase "it becomes *pit*": because it is *pit*, the status of being *ṅt* does not occur; consequently, the vowel *ā* [prescribed] for roots ending in *ā* that have *ṅ* or *d* as an indicatory letter (*ṅdit*) does not apply.
Thus we have "mimāte" and "mimāthe. [The root] "māṅ" means "to measure" (or "to sound," according to the Dhātupāṭha).

[The root] *dhā* (DhP 1088); because it belongs to the *juhotyādi* class, there is *ślu*-elision of the suffix *śap*. By the rule "when *ślu* follows" (6.1.10), reduplication occurs; by the rule "for the roots *bhṛ*, *mṛ*, *kṛ*, *gṛ*, *dṛ*, *pṝ*, and *vṛ*" (7.4.76), the vowel *i* is substituted for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*);
