and by the rule "the long *ā* of the [root-final] *ā* is elided before a suffix beginning with *śn* and before an *abhyasta*" (6.4.112), the long *ā* is elided.

82. *āne muk* (Pāṇini 7.2.82). [The rule] "of the suffix belonging to the stem (*aṅga*)" refers to a genitive case in a different grammatical relation (*vyadhikaraṇa*). That is to say: for that *at* which belongs to the stem, there is the augment *muk*. In that case, should the mention of *ad* (the letter *a*) be made here? No, it need not be made.

The word *ataḥ* will be understood as continuing from the rule *ṭhato yeyaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.80). But surely, in that [previous] rule it was specified in the ablative case (*pañcamī*), whereas here the sense requires it to be specified in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*)? This is not so; for the ablative *ataḥ* has its purpose fulfilled there in the substitution of *iy* and so on, whereas this [genitive] is for the sake of the *sthāna* (the locus of substitution).
The locative case in *ānaḥ* is purposeless;
therefore, this locative *ānaḥ* will intend for the genitive status of the ablative *ataḥ*, while the locative *sthāne* is purposeless.
Thus, this locative *ānaḥ* will effect the conversion of the ablative *ataḥ* into a genitive.

This is because of the rule: "In reference to that which is specified by the word *tasmin*, the operation applies to what precedes" (Pāṇini 1.1.66). Now, one might object: both the vowel *a* and the consonant *m* are indeed phonemes (*varṇa*). However, the *m* has its defining characteristic at the end; and "end" refers to a constituent part (*avayava*). Furthermore, a phoneme cannot be a constituent part of another phoneme. [The printed edition reads: *na ca varṇo varṇasyāvayavī*].

The reading is appropriate because it has not yet been commenced; therefore, what was said—that "the augment *muk* occurs"—is incorrect? This is not a fault; for in every case, whether that after which an augment is prescribed or the augment itself that is prescribed, its status as being "initial" or "final" is determined with respect to the entire complex.

It is prescribed. Therefore, the intended meaning of the statement "the augment *muk* occurs after this" is as follows: this aggregate, beginning with the letter *a* and ending with the letter *s*, becomes [such].
In the example "pacamānaḥ," there is the suffix *laṭ*, and for that, the suffix *śānac*.

When it is stated that "the augment *muk* occurs before the suffix *āna* when it follows a word ending in *at*," one who considers these two genitive cases (*ṣaṣṭhī*) to be in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), and having grasped the meaning of the rule as "the augment *muk* occurs before *āna* when it follows a stem ending in *akāra*," proceeds accordingly.

One should explain it thus: if a member ending in the letter *a* were to arrive [in the form of the suffix], then in the case of *pacamāna*, the rule "that which follows a root taught with a low-pitched vowel (*adupadeśāt*) is unaccented" (Pāṇini 6.1.186) would not apply to the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix, because the letter *a* would be separated [from the suffix] by the augment *muk*. [The rule applies only when] the letter *a* is that which is taught [as part of the root]. Thus...

For it is established that [the augment] *nuṭ* is situated there [between the stem and the suffix], and not that this instruction [of the suffix] ends in the vowel *a*. Nor can it be argued that "this *nuṭ* is subordinate to the *aṅga* (stem), and therefore there is no intervention";
for while this [augment] being subordinate to the *aṅga* would not intervene in the *aṅga* itself, it certainly does intervene with respect to the vowel *a*.

For a constituent part does not act as an obstacle to the whole, whereas it certainly acts as an obstacle to another constituent part; therefore, he says: "For this [ṭha] is devoted solely to the letter ṭha," and so forth.
This word *mātra* (solely) is for the purpose of excluding devotion to the entire stem (*aṅga*). And here, the stem is the qualifier of the vowel *ā*.

The letter *a* alone is what follows [the root], not the suffix; therefore, because it is not a part of that [suffix], the augment *muk* is included by the very mention of that [letter *a*]. Thus, due to the absence of any intervention, the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix becomes unaccented (*anudātta*).
But surely, even when *muk* is attached as a part of the final *a*, it ought to occur?
Is it not the case that, because [the suffix] is *anudātta* by the rule "ṭhla-sārvadhātukam anudāttam ahan-viṅoḥ" (P.

6.1.186), and because of the principle "in a rule concerning accent, a consonant is as if non-existent" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 37), the augment *muk* is as if non-existent and thus there is no intervention [between the root and the suffix]? He thinks this, but it is not so.

This is the maxim accepted by the author of the Bhāṣya; for he, having rejected this maxim, has adopted another: "When a vowel-accent is to be applied, a consonant is as if non-existent" (*halsvaraprāptau vyañjanam avidyamānavat*).

Thus [it is said]. And here there is no possibility of a vowel (svara) being applied to a consonant (hal); what then? It is to a vowel (ac). [Regarding] "If this is so," and so forth: if this *muk* is a part of the letter *a*, then by the very fact that it is not an obstacle because it is included within the mention of that [vowel], [the rule applies] in the case of *pacamāna* to the *an* immediately following the vowel *ā*.

Since the substitution of *iy* would apply by the rule "tasya ṭhāto ṅtiḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.81), [the author] says: "Because of the mention of *ā* with a following *t* (*taparakaraṇa*), it does not occur. For here, the vowel *a* is specified as having a duration of one mātrā and followed by *t*;
however, when *muk* is applied, it becomes half a mātrā. Therefore, due to this difference in duration, the substitution will not take place.
That which has one and a half [mātrās] is *adhyarddhā*; that whose measure is one and a half is *adhyarddhamātraḥ*.
Even so, the rule stating that "the *sārvadhātuka* suffix is *anudātta*" would not apply;
therefore, even in that rule, the term is specified with a *tapara* (indicating a short vowel). Regarding the phrase "the mention of *upadeśa*," etc., the mention of *upadeśa* is there...
This is done for the purpose of perceiving its prior state;
therefore, although there is a difference in duration once the elision (*muk*) has been applied at a later time, nevertheless,
because it possesses the duration of one mora (*mātrā*) during the stage of instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*), the quality of being unaccented (*anudātta*) indeed applies here.

"And likewise," and so forth. Since, following that instruction (*upadeśa*), even when there is a difference in time, the vowel must remain *anudātta*, and this being the case, even where a lengthening occurs by the rule "ato dīrgho yañi" (Pāṇini 7.3.101)— as in *pacāvaḥ*— there is still a difference in time.
In such cases as these, it also occurs there.

83. *īdāsaḥ* | (7.2.83) The word *ṭhāsaḥ* in the ablative case, having already served its purpose in the preceding rule (7.2.82), will be treated as a genitive case by virtue of the principle *tasmād ity uttarasya* (1.1.67). Thus, it will replace the locative case [of the previous rule] which has already fulfilled its function.

Because of this statement, it is established that this substitution is prescribed for the word *āna* itself; thus he says: "of the word *āna* following *āsa*. [The example is] *āsīnaḥ*. [The root] *āsa* [is used] in the sense of "sitting" (*upaveśane*;
DhP 1021). Because it is *anudāteta*, the *ātmanepada* suffix is applied; [the rule] "that which follows the initial [element of a complex]" (1.1.54) applies.
The letter *i* [is substituted] for the form *ityā*. Due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śas*.
The inclusion of the long vowel marker (*tāparakaraṇa*) is for the sake of ease of pronunciation.

84. *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.2.84). Regarding the statement, "This [mention of] *ā* is a reference to a specific individual (*vyakti-nirdeśa*)," the meaning is that it is a reference specifically to the individual instance of the vowel *ā* that is pure (*śuddha*) and devoid of nasality (*niranunāsika*). Now, what would be the fault if this were a reference to a class-characteristic (*ākṛti-nirdeśa*)?
One might ask: "Why has this reference to individual instances (*vyakti*) been adopted for the purpose of avoiding that [objection]?

To this he says: "For, when there is a reference to form (*ākṛti*)," and so forth. Here, "form" (*ākṛti*) is intended to mean "genus" (*jāti*), and not physical configuration (*saṃsthāna*). This is because, when there is a reference to a genus, it is impossible to indicate the genus in its pure state.

The grammatical operation is understood to apply to the individual instances (*vyakti*) that serve as the substratum for that [genus]. In this context, if one were to rely here on a reference to the genus (*jāti*),
then since all *akāra* instances would have attained the status of being the substratum for the genus,
the substitution prescribed by the rule "the final letter of a word" (*alo 'ntyasya*, 1.1.52) would result in the replacement of the *nakāra* with the vowel *ākāra*.

By virtue of proximity (*āntaratamya*), only an anusvāra with a nasal (*anunāsika*) would occur in place of a nasal [consonant]. However, this fault does not arise if there is a reference to a specific individual (*vyakti-nirdeśa*). Thus, [the objection] that "this and so forth is not established, for there is no statement here expressing an option (*vikalpa*), nor is it the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*]" is addressed by saying "by way of an option" (*vikalpena*), and so on. [This refers to the rule regarding] *aṣṭan*.

By the rule *dīrghāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.172), the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the word *aṣṭan* is prescribed before case-endings that are not *sarvanāmasthāna* endings when they follow a long vowel. If the substitution of *ā* were obligatory (*nityam*), then the qualification "after a long vowel" (*dīrghāt*) would be purposeless.

Furthermore, in the rule *aṣṭābhya āṬś* (Pāṇini 7.1.21), the mention of the form with the vowel substitution (*ātva*) would be purposeless; since there is nothing to be excluded, one could simply have said *aṣṭanaḥ*. Therefore, by the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) and the mention of the form with the vowel substitution (*kṛtātva*), it is indicated that this substitution of *ā* occurs optionally.

Therefore, the phrase "by eight," and so forth, is also accepted as a possible alternative, because of the use of the singular number. Otherwise, since it would refer to multiple things, he would have said "of the eight" (*aṣṭānām*). Consequently, this [term] is primarily denotative of its own form (*svarūpaprādhānya*). In that context, when the *aṅga* (the base) is under discussion and is qualified by this [term], the rule of "extension to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*) is obtained.

For it has been stated that by means of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), there is the rule of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) when *bh* follows; thus, "priyāṣṭā" [is cited as an example, though this specific instance is not seen in the root text]. The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule beginning with "sarvanāmasthāne" (Pāṇini 6.4.8).
85. *rāyo hali* (Pāṇini 7.2.85). 86. *yuṣmadasmador anādeśe* (Pāṇini 7.2.86). [The forms] *yuṣmat* and *asmat* [are derived] by [the rule] *pañcamyā at* (Pāṇini 7.1.31).

The fifth case ending *bhyas* is replaced by *ad*; when the final portion is elided by the rule "the remainder is elided" (*śeṣe lopaḥ*, 7.2.9), the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatvam*) occurs by the rule "guṇa for *at*" (*ato guṇe*, 6.1.97). Furthermore, if the vowel *ā* were not applied here as well because of the governing context of "before a consonant" (*halīti*), then...

For what purpose is the mention of *anādeśa*? He says: "But in the subsequent [rule]," and so forth. The purpose of *anādeśa* is in the subsequent rule, namely *yo'ci* (Pāṇini 7.2.89). If that is so, it should be made right there; why is it done here? The intention is that it is for the sake of clarity (*vispaṣṭārtham*).
87. And in the second person [as well].
(Pāṇini 7.2.87) [The forms] *tvām* and *mām* [are derived as follows]: by the rule *tvamāvekavacane* (7.2.97), the substitutes *tvam* and *mām* are applied.
[The forms] *yuvām* and *āvām* [are derived as follows]: by the rule *yuvāvau dvivacane* (7.2.92).
The substitutes *yu* and *vā* [are applied]. Everywhere, by the rule "ṬhREṄ prathama-poroḥ am" (Pāṇini 7.1.28), there is the substitution of *am* for the case-ending;
and when *am* has been applied, the preceding form is retained as before by the rule "ami pūrvatvam" (Pāṇini 6.1.107).

88. And [the substitution of *yu* and *āv* occurs] for the first case dual in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*). (Pāṇini 7.2.88) This rule is also for the purpose of providing a substitute. [The forms are] *yuvayoḥ* and *āvayoḥ*. But surely, will not the substitution of *y* by the rule *yo 'ci* (7.2.89) act as a sublater here even in the first case dual?

In that case, the rule *śeṣelopaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.90) would be an exception [to the present rule]. Just as the elision of the remainder (*śeṣelopa*) is set aside by this [present] rule due to the force of the explicit statement, so too would the substitution of *y* be set aside. For it is said: "Exceptions stated earlier set aside the rules immediately following them, but not those further on."

Otherwise, even the substitution of *ya* would be sublated. Therefore, it must be stated: "of the nominative (*prathamāyāḥ*). [The examples are] *tvam* and *aham*. By the rule *tvāhau sau* (Pāṇini 7.2.94), the substitutes *tvā* and *āha* are applied. Although one could have simply said *āṬ*, the dual of the nominative is specified.
For the sake of variety.
89. *yo'ci* (7.2.89). Regarding the rule *yuṣmadasmadoranādeśe* (7.2.86), if the mention of *hal* from the preceding sūtra (7.2.85) were to carry over here, [then the following would occur].
In that case, the substitution of *ya* being prescribed without qualification is understood as a general rule (*utsarga*).

However, the substitution of *ā*, being prescribed for a specific case-ending beginning with a consonant (*hal*), is an exception (*apavāda*) to this as well. And thus, even without the explicit mention of "a vowel" (*aj-grahaṇa*), the *y* remains restricted only to cases beginning with a vowel.

Therefore, could this not have been omitted? It is provided for the sake of clarity, as in "svad gacchati" and "mad gacchati. By the rule "ekavacanasya ca" (Pāṇini 7.1.32), the substitution of "ad" occurs for the genitive singular ending "ṅsi."

90. *śeṣe lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.90). [The sūtra states: "The duals other than those ending in *ṭā*. This means the singular and plural endings. [The word] "here" refers to the case-endings beginning with the fifth (the ablative). [The phrase] "elision is prescribed for them" means for those very [endings].

Because they are remnants (*śeṣa*): *tubhyam*, *mahyam*. By the rule "tubhyamahyau ṅyi" (Pāṇini 7.2.95), the substitutes *tubhya-* and *mahya-* occur [for the second-person and first-person pronouns] when followed by the dative singular ending *ṅi*. *yuṣmabhyam*, *asmabhyam*: by the rule "bhyaso bhyam" (Pāṇini 7.1.30), the substitute *bhyam* occurs [for the case-ending *bhyas*]. *tava*, *mama*: by the rule "tavamamau ṅsi" [the substitutes *tava* and *mama* occur for the genitive singular ending *ṅsi*].
By this [rule 7.2.96], the substitutes *tva* and *mama* are applied, resulting in *yuṣmākam* and *asmākam*. [This is further governed by] the rule *sāma ākam* (7.1.33).
Now, for what purpose is the mention of the word *śeṣa* (remainder)? Why not simply say "elision" (*lopa*)? If it were stated in that way...

Nor should it be suspected that there would be an elision by virtue of a specific truth (i.e., a specific rule); for the elision being prescribed without qualification will be the general rule (*utsarga*), while its exceptions (*apavāda*)—namely the substitution of *ya* and *ā*—will apply specifically to those cases where no other instruction is given regarding the particular case-ending. And thus, even without the mention of the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*), it is only in the remainder that [the general rule applies].
Why is the elision established? To this he says: "The mention of *śeṣa* (remainder) is for the sake of clarity.
[The question is: "When the elision of the remainder has been performed, why does the suffix *ṭāp* not occur in the feminine? [The answer is:
because when the final letter has been elided, the word ends in *at*, and thus by the rule *ajādyataṣṭāp* (Pāṇini 4.1.4), the suffix *ṭāp* would apply.
The sense is that [the suffix] must occur. Regarding the phrase "in the case of *sannipāta*" and so forth:

for when there is immediate proximity (*ānantarya*) with a case-ending, the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* become those ending in the vowel *a*. In that situation, if they were to produce the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, then the immediate proximity of the case-ending would be destroyed by them.
It may be so. Furthermore, that which is characterized by the conjunction of certain elements does not become the cause for the destruction of that very conjunction;
thus, the suffix *ṭāp* does not apply. If this were the case, would it not also fail to apply after words such as *tyad* and others? This is not a fault;
for the author himself provides the indication in the rule "not after *yā* or *as*" (Pāṇini 7.3.45).

This indicates that [the suffix] *ṭāp* occurs after *tyad* and the others. Furthermore, this resolution was stated by assuming that *yuṣmad* and *asmad* possess feminine gender. Now, in order to show that *ṭāp* does not occur precisely because they lack feminine gender, he says: "In the case of gender," and so forth.

"Some, however, desire the elision of the remainder [of the suffix] as an elision of the *ṭi*," they say; this is for the purpose that the *ṭāp* affix should not occur in such cases as "you are a Brāhmaṇī" (*tvaṃ brāhmaṇī*) or "I am a Brāhmaṇī" (*ahaṃ brāhmaṇī*). Furthermore, in the case of "to you all" (*yuṣmabhyam*) and "to us all" (*asmabhyam*), once the replacement by *bhyam* has been made, the substitution of *et* [for the final vowel] by the rule "in the plural, before a consonant, *et*" (*bahuvacane jhalyet*, Pāṇini 7.3.103) should not occur.

And it is for this purpose [that the word *bhū* is used]. As for the question "How so?", he thinks as follows: that case-ending (*vibhakti*) in which neither the vowel *ā* nor the semivowel *y* has been prescribed is the "remainder" (*śeṣa*). In that remainder, when elision (*lopa*) is being taught, the elision of *ṭi* is not obtained; rather, by the paribhāṣā rule "of the final [element]" (*alo'ntyasya*, Pāṇini 1.1.52), elision would apply only to the final letter.

With reference to the instruction (ādeśa) that is about to be stated, he clarifies the meaning of the word "remainder" (śeṣa) by means of the rule beginning with "ṭhite ca. [The meaning is: "That which is other than [the letters] ending in *m* is the remainder. Furthermore, that [remainder] is indeed *ṭi*.
Here, this "remainder" refers to the elision (*lopa*); thus, with respect to the elision, the elision of *ṭi* occurs.

In the case of the remainder [of the pronouns], the seventh case ending (*saptamī*) is used when one intends to express the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). But for what purpose is elision (*lopa*) stated here, since it would already be established by the substitution of *yat* and so forth (*tyadādyatva*)? It is not established; because [the word *śeṣa*] does not belong to the class beginning with *tyad*. For the class beginning with *tyad* consists of those ending with *dvi*. And in that regard, this very [rule] applies.
The mention of "the remainder" (śeṣe) is an indicator (jñāpaka). By this, the substitution of *tyadādi* [for the final phoneme] does not apply to the word *bhavat*—thus we have *bhavān*.

91. *maparyantasya* | (7.2.91) [Examples: *yuvakām*, *āvakām*. [This is] by the rule *avyayasarvanāmnām akac prāk ṭeḥ* (5.3.71). In this case, if *maparyantasya* were not stated, [the suffix would apply to the whole word].
Therefore, because no limit (avadhi) has been specified, it might apply even to [the form] *sākacka*; hence he says:

"Let it not apply to every *sākacka*. If the mention of the ending in *-maparyanta* were absent, then, due to the lack of a specified limit and because the substitute (*ādeśa*) would be non-singleton (*anekatva*), it would apply to every single instance. But who [is this]?

"Would there be a fault if [the term *maparyanta*] were applied to all cases? To this he says: "And thus," and so forth. "An undesired form would result": if the substitution of *ya* for the vowel *a* were made by the rule *yo'ci* (Pāṇini 7.2.89), then the forms would be *tv-y-ā* and *m-y-ā*. However, when the inclusion of the limit *maparyanta* is maintained...

Since "maparyantasya" (of that which ends in m) is prescribed as the locus (*sthānin*) for both *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the substitutions to be described hereafter apply to these very forms; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.
Now, what is the purpose of including the word "pari" [in *maparyanta*]? Why not simply say "māntasya" (of that which ends in m)? Even if it were stated in that way...

Is the desired result established because the word *anta* signifies "proximity" when [the suffix] *hyuc* is added, by resorting to a *bahuvrīhi* compound that includes the quality (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*)? To this, he says: "of that which ends in *m*" (*māntasya*), etc. This refers to the absence of the substitute for [the base] together with the *kac* suffix, or else to this [situation].

In forms such as *yuvakām* and *āvām*, the inclusion of the term "ending in m" (*māntasya*)—which is already established by the rule itself—is intended to indicate a limit; that is, to indicate the limit of the substituends, namely the constituent parts of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. Therefore, [the rule applies] when the word *yuṣmad* or *asmad* ends in m.
This is for the purpose that the operation to be mentioned hereafter should not take place. When?

To this, he says "when [the roots] end in *ṇi*, etc."—that is, when the *ṇic* suffix has been added to *yuṣmad* and *asmad* by the rule "he describes" (*tadācaṣṭe*), then by the Vārttika "in the case of *ṇi*, the operations pertaining to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) are like those of the *iṣṭhan* suffix" (Vārttika 813).

Thus, by treating [the suffix] as if it were *iṣṭhan*, there is the elision of the *ṭi* portion; from that, the *kvip* suffix is applied. In that case, when the elision of the *ṇic* has been performed according to Pāṇini 6.4.51 (*ṇer aniṭi*), if the forms of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* possess a final *m*, [the rule] should not apply. Even if the term "parigraha" were absent, [the form] would simply be *māṃsyā*.

The restriction [of the application] of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* is obtained by means of the term *iti*; consequently, the substitutions to be mentioned later would occur only where *yuṣmad* and *asmad* end in *m*. However, when the term *pari* is used for the purpose of indicating a limit (*avadhi*), there must necessarily be something excluded (*varjyamāna*); for it is not the case that...
By that, the limit [of the domain] of *vana* is established. Therein, the members of the aggregate are indicated.
It will apply only where the word *āt* is to be excluded, and not merely to the forms of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* ending in *mant*. But surely—

The substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* will be prescribed when followed by case-endings (*vibhakti*), yet at the stage when [the stem] ends in *-m*, it is not followed by a case-ending because of the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) of the elision of the suffix *ṇi*; therefore, what is the purpose of including the mention of "ending in *-m*" (*mānta*) for the sake of exclusion? To this he says: "And the status of the original element," and so forth.

Because of the statement "when [the elements] ṭh and kv are elided, the substitute is not like the original" (Vārttika 1.1.58), the status of being a substitute does not apply here; therefore, the intention is that the condition of being followed by a case-ending (vibhaktiparatva) indeed exists.

92. *yuvāvau dvivacane* (Pāṇini 7.2.92). Regarding the term "dvivacane": if this were to refer to the technical grammatical category of the dual number (*dvivacana*), then the substitutions *yu* and *āva* would occur only when that [dual] follows. And thus...

When *yuṣmad* and *asmad* occur in a compound with two referents, since the meaning of the compound possesses a different number, the singular or plural would arise from the compound [rather than the original stems]; therefore, [the dual] would not occur. However, when *yuṣmad* and *asmad* refer to a single entity or to many entities...

"When the meaning of the compound is in the dual, the dual suffix *vati* [is applied] after the compound; in that case, the forms *yūyam* and *vayam* would indeed occur in the *yuvādi* group, and this is undesired. The term "dual expression" (*dvivacana*) refers to the utterance of two meanings. [This is stated in the rule: "When there is a dual expression, the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* [are used]."

Thus: "In the case of the dual" (*dvivacane*). This is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*). To clarify that it is indeed a locative of scope, he says: "In the domain of the expression of two meanings" (*dvyarthābhidhānaviṣaye*).
The expression of two meanings is *dvyarthābhidhānam*; [the rule applies] in those domains which...

*Yuṣmad* and *asmad* are what were mentioned as "those two. Regarding "of those two" (*tayoḥ*) and so forth: of those two, *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the portion ending before the final phoneme (*maparyanta*) is the substituendum (*sthānin*); for that, *yuvā-* and *āv-* are substituted.
By the phrase "when," etc., he demonstrates what is desired when there is a reference to the meaning (*arthagrahaṇa*). If...

In that case, since the singular and plural numbers arise from the compound, and because they have as their domain the expression of two referents (*dvyarthābhidhāna*), would *yu* and *vā* apply to the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* [even here]? If this were so, would they also apply in the scope of the rules "tvāhau sau" (7.2.94), "yūyavayau jasi" (7.2.93), "tubhyamahyau ṅayi" (7.2.95), and "tavamamau ṅsi" (7.2.96)? To this, he says: "yadi tvāhau sau," etc., and gives the example: "atiyuvām atyāvām."

The compound *atyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe* (Vārttika 91) is a *prādi-samāsa*. In that case, that which has transcended the referents of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* is a meaning delimited by the singular number; thus, although the singular number is employed there, nevertheless, because the scope is the expression of two referents, the substitutes *yuvā-* and *āvā-* certainly occur for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. Here, indeed, the substitution of *ā* [for *o*] occurs by the rule *dvitīyāyāñca* (Pāṇini 7.2.87), as in *atiyuvān* and *atyāvān*. The substitution of *na* [for *m*] occurs by the rule *śaso na* (Pāṇini 7.1.29).

In *atitvayā* and *atimayā*, the substitution of *ya* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.2.89] *yo'ci*. In *atiyuvābhir atyāvābhiḥ*, the substitution of *ā* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.2.86] *yuṣmadasmador anādeśe*. In *atiyuvabhyam atyāvabhyam*, the substitution of *bhyam* for *bhyas* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.1.30] *bhyaso bhyam*. In *atiyuvad atyāvad*, the substitution of *ad* for *ṅsi* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.1.32] *ekavacanasya ca*; however, for the plural, the substitution of *at* for *ṅasi* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.1.31] *pañcamyā at*. In *atiyudākam* and *atyāvākam*, [the substitution of *akam* for *ām* occurs].

Regarding *sāma ākam* (Pāṇini 7.1.30), [the forms] *atitvākam* and *atyāvakam* are derived by applying *ākam* in place of the genitive plural (*śas*). For the singular genitive (*ṅsi*), the substitute *ad* is applied by *ekavacanasya ca* (7.1.32); for the plural genitive, however, it is by *pañcamyā ut* (7.1.31). Thus we have *atitvākam* and *atyāvakam*. For the dative singular, *sāma ākam* (7.1.33) applies, resulting in *atitvayi* and *atyādayi*; as before, the substitution of *ya* occurs. For the locative plural, *atitvāsu* and *atyāvāsu* are formed; as before, the substitution of *ā* occurs.
As for what was stated regarding the domain of *tvāhādi* and so forth—namely, *yadi tvahau* (7.2.94)—[it refers to the following].
By the phrase "thus, by another rule, they are not sublated," he clarifies this with the words "But when... and so forth.
He demonstrates what is established when the meaning is grasped with the words "having surpassed the most excellent" (*atitvamatamām*). Here, that which...

Since those two meanings of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*—which have transcended [their individual forms]—constitute a dual number as the meaning of the compound, even though a dual suffix occurs after the compound, the forms *yuvā-* and *āv-ā-* do not apply because *yuṣmad* and *asmad* do not possess a dual sense [in that context]. Only *tvam* and *āvam* are employed. [This applies] also in the dual of the nominative case.
The substitution of *ā* [for *e*] occurs by the rule *bhāṣāyām* (Pāṇini 7.2.88). Alternatively, this is the dual of the accusative case;

therefore, the substitution applies by the rule *dvitīyāyāñca* (Pāṇini 7.2.87). The phrase "this is to be understood from the context" (*evamunneyam*) shows that there is an absence of such substitutions even in other grammatical forms. [Example: "Behold those two who have surpassed you. (*yuṣmānatikrāntau paśya*)

*Atiyuṣmām*, *atyasmām*; [the compound] *atitvābhyām* is formed from those two who have surpassed you (*atikrāntābhyām tvām*), and likewise *atimābhyām*. [The compound] *atiyuṣmābhyām* is formed from those two who have surpassed you all (*atikrāntābhyām yuṣmān*). Give to those two who have surpassed you (*tvām atikrāntābhyām*): give to *atitvābhyām*, give to *atimābhyām*.
Give to those who have surpassed you—*atiyuṣmābhyām*; give to those who have surpassed us—*atyasmābhyām*.
He has come from those two who have surpassed you—*atisyābhyām*; he has come from those two who have surpassed us—*atimābhyām*.
He has come from those two who have surpassed you—*atiyuṣmābhyām*; he has come from those two who have surpassed us—*atyasmābhyām*.
In the case of *atitvām* and *atitvayoḥ*, [the form] is *svam*; in *atimām* and *atimayoḥ*, [the form] is *svam*.
In the case of *yuṣmān-atikrāntayoḥ* and *svam-atayuṣmayoḥ*, [the form] is *svam*; in *atyasmayoḥ*, [the form] is *svam*.
Place [them] beyond you (*atikrāntayos tvām*), place [them] beyond you (*atitvayoḥ nidhehi*), place [them] beyond me (*atimayoḥ nidhehi*).
Place [the offering] beyond you two; place it beyond you both; place it beyond us both.

93. *yūyavayau jasi* (Pāṇini 7.2.93). In the example *paramayūyam*, [the forms] *yūyam* and *vayam* occur even for the two subsequent words [of a compound], because of the statement: "In the governing context of *aṅga*, [the substitution applies] to that [stem] and to its subsequent word" (*Puṣpavṛtti* 85). Alternatively, [it may be understood as follows]: "in the case of *jasi*"...
This is a genitive of separation (parasaptamī); therefore, even when both [words] are compounded, they become [the substitutes] when followed by *jas*.
In examples such as *paramayūyam*, there is indeed the state of being followed by *jas* after the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*.

94. *tvāhau sau* (7.2.94). This will be an exception (*apavāda*) to what will be stated in [Pāṇini 7.2.97]: *tvamāvekavacane*. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *tvā*? One might simply say *ahaḥ sau*; for the substitution of *tvam* is indeed prescribed by *tvamāvekavacane*.

"Will it be so? It is impossible to say this; for if the mention of *at* were not made, the substitution of *ah* would apply to *yuṣmad* as well. Or alternatively—should it be stated here simply as "of *asmad*, *ah* after *su*"? Even so, there would be prolixity. Therefore, let it remain exactly as it is.

95. *tubhyamahyau ṅyi* (7.2.95). 96. *tavamamau ṅsi* (7.2.96). This statement is made because [otherwise] *tvam* and *aham* would have applied immediately to the two cases that are about to be mentioned.

97. *tvamāvekavacane* (Pāṇini 7.2.97). [The commentary states: "The term 'ekavacana' here is used in the sense of 'the singular number'; by this, he shows that it is the meaning that is grasped, and not the technical grammatical term (*pāribhāṣika*) 'ekavacana'. For if the technical term were grasped..."

The intention is that whatever fault was stated in the rule *ṭhyuvādhau dvivacane* (Pāṇini 7.2.92) applies here as well. However, the inclusion of the term "meaning" (*artha*) is understood here from the mention of "number" (*vacana*). If the mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*) were intended here, he would have said simply "in the singular" (*ekatve*). The term "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*) is understood from the previous context.

In this regard, the connection should be made as follows: "the case-ending that occurs when there is singularity. Alternatively, one need not say "this" (etad); for since the two substitutes are already established by the rule *pratyayotarapadayośca* (Pāṇini 7.2.98) when there is the singular number, [the forms] *tvām* and *mām* are accounted for.
The substitution of ātva [for the final vowel] occurs by the rule "ṭhdvitīyāyāñca" (Pāṇini 7.2.87).
By the statement "when the compound has a single meaning," etc., he demonstrates what is intended when the term "meaning" (artha) is included:
that even when a dual number follows from a compound that possesses another number.
Or, when the plural number occurs, even then these two substitutes take the place of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, which have a single referent (*ekārtha*).
This being so, [the following rules apply]: "tvāhau sau" (7.2.94), "yūyavayau jasi" (7.2.93), "tubhyamahyam ṅayi" (7.2.95), and "tavamamau ṅsi".

Since these two [rules] might also apply to the domain of other substitutes, he says "but of other substitutes," and so forth. The mention of a "prior conflict" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) is because a subsequent conflict (*paravipratiṣedha*) is impossible; that impossibility is due to the fact that these two [rules] themselves are subsequent.

The priority of the preceding rule (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), however, is obtained because the word *para* signifies "desired" (*iṣṭa*). In that regard, the scope of the rule *tvāhau sau* (Pāṇini 7.2.94) is where *yuṣmad* and *asmad* do not occur with a single referent— as in *atitvam* ("one who has surpassed you") and *atyaham* ("one who has surpassed me").

The scope of *tvamāvekavacanasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.97) is where a different case-ending occurs after two singular referents— as in *tvām* and *mām*. However, when both [rules] would apply simultaneously in cases such as *atikrāntas tvām* (*atitvam*) and *atikrānto mām* (*atyaham*), the forms *tvad* and *mad* take the place of *tvam* and *aham* before the nominative singular suffix *su*.
By way of a prior exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). When other substitutes would otherwise apply in other cases, a prior exception must be stated: as in *atikrāntastvām atitvām* and *atimām*.
Although here a dual number arises from the compound, nevertheless, according to the rule "the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* [denote] a single object," [they remain singular].

But let these two substitutes be yours alone. If the technical (pāribhāṣika) singular were taken, they would not occur, because that [technical singular] is not present here. Thus, one should cite examples such as:
*atitvām* (having surpassed you, I see), *atimām* (having surpassed me, look); and *atitvābhiḥ*, *atimābhiḥ*.
It has been done. Give you to those who have surpassed you; give you to those who have surpassed you; give you to those who have surpassed you.
Give you to those two who have surpassed you; give you to those two who have surpassed you. You have come to those two who have surpassed you;
you have come to those two who have surpassed you.
"From those who have surpassed you," [the forms are] *atitvadāgataḥ*, *atimadāgataḥ*.
"Your own from two who have surpassed you," [is] *atitvayoḥ svam*, *atimayoḥ svam*.
"Your own from those who have surpassed you," [is] *atitvākāṃ svam*, *atimākāṃ svam*.
Place you beyond the two who have passed; place you beyond the two who have surpassed you; place you beyond the two who have exceeded me.
Place you among those who have passed; place you among those who have surpassed you; place you among those who have exceeded me.

98. *pratyayotarapadayośca* (7.2.98). [The phrase] "occurring in the singular number" means "in the domain of expressing a single referent. Examples: *tvadīyaḥ*, *madīyaḥ*. Because [the words *tva-* and *mada-*, etc. possess the technical designation *vṛddha* by virtue of [Pāṇini 1.1.74]: *tyadādīni ca*.
The suffix *cch* [is applied] by the rule *ṭhvṛddhāccchaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.114). [Examples: *tvataraḥ*, *mataraḥ*.

The suffix *tarap* [is applied] by the rule *dvivacanavibhajyopapade tarabīyasunau* (Pāṇini 5.3.57). [Examples: *tvadyati*, *madyati*. [The suffix] *kyac* [is applied] by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8). [Examples: *tvadyate*, *madyate*.
Thus [it is said]. The suffix *kyaṅ* is applied by the rule "The suffix *kyaṅ* is added after a word denoting an agent, and there is elision of the final *s*.
Now, one might ask: since the two desired forms are already established by the preceding rule, for what purpose is this new undertaking?
To this he replies: "Because of the governing rule 'in a case-ending' (*vibhaktau*)," and so forth.

"Now, however," and so forth, says the proponent (*deśaka*). "That which occurs between the base and the suffix, or between the preceding and following words, is an 'internal' case-ending (*antarvatini vibhakti*). "This cannot be so," says the opponent (*itara*). "It must be [treated] as if it were elided (*luk*)," he says; this is the reason for its invisibility. "The *sup*... [is elided].

The intention [of the opponent] is that, by the rule *dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.71), elision (*luk*) must occur even before the two substitutes; consequently, the two substitutes conditioned by that [elision] would not take place. The teacher [Kaiyaṭa] states, "The elision is external" (*bahiraṅgo luk*), and so forth; for the basis for the two substitutes is merely the case-ending (*vibhakti*).

But elision (luk) possesses both the status of a verbal root (dhātutva) and the status of a nominal stem (prātipadikatva). Thus, these two—verbal rootness and nominal stemness—are "external" (bahiraṅga), because they depend respectively on external suffixes and on compounds; how much more so, then, is elision (luk) [external] in relation to them?

Regarding the status of being "external" (*bahiraṅga*): by the rule *asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam antaraṅge* (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 42), the two substitutions will indeed occur first. [To this] the other [party] replies: "This very [point], etc."—namely, that "the elision (*luk*), though external, does not sublate even internal operations," according to the former [rule].

Since [the elision] is already established, one would not have formulated the rule for the non-application of the designation (*adeśavacana*); yet, because it has been formulated, that very fact indicates: "An external elision (*luk*) subverts even internal rules" (Vyāḍipañjikā 128).
What is the purpose of this indicator (*jñāpaka*)? To this he says: "Therefore..."

And so forth. If this meaning were not made known, then in the case of *gomatpriyaḥ* (he whose beloved possesses cows), because of its being antaranga (internal), the *num* augment would occur first by the rule *ṭhagidacām* (Pāṇini 7.1.70),
and subsequently, the lengthening [of the vowel] would occur by the rule *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.14).

Furthermore, once the elision of the final consonant in a *saṃyoga* cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*, Pāṇini 8.2.23) has been applied, the undesirable form *gomānpriyaḥ* would result. However, when this [rule] is understood as a *jñāpaka*, even an *antaraṅga* operation such as the insertion of *num* is superseded by a *bahiraṅga* operation such as elision (*luk*); thus, this undesirable consequence does not arise.

By the first word "ādi" (and so forth), there is the inclusion of forms such as *gomatyati* ("he desires one who possesses cows") and *gomatyate* ("he acts like one who possesses cows"). By the second [word "ādi"], there is the inclusion of the lengthening [of the vowel] and the elision [of the suffix] according to Pāṇini 6.1.68 (*halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*). If, however, the elision according to 6.1.68 occurs because it is antaranga (more internal/inner), [then the following applies].

(6.1.66) It would [occur]; by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule, the augment *num* and so forth would apply, and consequently, that very same undesirable form would result. However, when there is elision (*luk*), it does not occur because of the prohibition of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* by the rule "na lumatāṅgasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.63).

"And thus," etc. Since, in this way, even the external *luk* elision subverts internal rules, and having established this, [the following forms are derived]: *tvāhau sau* (7.2.94), *yūyavayau jasi* (7.2.93), *tvāmāṃ ṅayi* (7.2.95), and *tavamamau ṅsi*.

(7.2.96)—these substitutions do not occur when a suffix or a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) follows. [The sūtra begins with] "atha" and so forth. When there is no other purpose, it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*); and indeed, there is a purpose for this: namely, the sublation of these other substitutions, such as *tvad*, *ahad*, and so on.

The sense is that, this purpose being present, it is appropriate to understand this [rule] for this very reason, and not for the sake of mere notification (*jñāpana*). Regarding the phrase "in view of the status of the *lakṣya*": the status or occurrence of the *lakṣya*—that which is to be explained—is "the status of the *lakṣya*" (*lakṣyasthiti*); the expectation regarding that is "expectation in view of the status of the *lakṣya*" (*lakṣyasthityapekṣā*); thus [it is said].
Because it serves as the cause [for the application of other rules], this is not understood to be for the purpose of subverting other substitutes.

For in common usage, forms such as *gomatpriyaḥ* and *gomatyati*, which are established as correct (*sādhu*), constitute the objective examples (*lakṣya*). Indeed, if this were intended for the purpose of subverting other substitutes...

When [the purpose] is already understood, this is not included; however, he shows that even this is included for the sake of making it known—namely, the passage beginning with "for in this case, for the sake of making it known. But how is it that, even when such a purpose exists and there is a requirement for the maintenance of the *lakṣya* (the form to be characterized), this is intended for the sake of making it known?
"Is it possible to understand [the rule]? He thinks thus: "This cannot be the purpose [of the rule];

for the purpose of the mention of *maparyanta* is for the sake of its being drawn forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) by the word *ca*. And this very purpose of drawing it forward is so that there may be substitutes for those ending in *m*."

[The two suffixes] should be [applied]. Furthermore, if this [sūtra] were intended for the purpose of subverting other substitutions, then the subsequent attraction (anukarṣaṇa) would be purposeless; for those other substitutions for which this sūtra is postulated as a subverter are applied only to that which ends in *map*, and not to anything else.
Furthermore, even without the continued application of the mention of "ending in *m*," since exceptions (*apavāda*) occur in the same location as their general rules (*utsarga*),
the operation will apply to that which ends in *m* alone; so what is the purpose of continuing the mention of "ending in *m*"?
For, in this [rule], it is appropriate to carry forward the mention of "ending in m" (maparyanta) for the purpose of applying [the rule] to all substitutes; therefore,
because of the carrying forward of the mention of "ending in m" from that [previous rule], there is no sublation of other substitutes by this one.

This is the purpose [of the rule]. Therefore, it is understood as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Now, an objection is raised by another: "But for what purpose is this not understood as being for the sake of subverting these [substitutes] beginning with *tvāhā*? His intention is this: "Why is this not for the sake of subverting other substitutes that would otherwise replace [the forms] ending in *m*? In that regard, the meaning is as follows: the particle *ca* need not be used for the purpose of carrying forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) the mention of "ending in *m*" (*maparyanta*). If the mention of "ending in *m*" were continued [by the particle *ca*], this [rule] would not be applicable for the sake of subverting those other substitutes; however, when that [mention] has ceased, it is indeed applicable.
99. *tricaturbhyāṃ striyāṃ tustṛcatasṛ* (Pāṇini 7.2.99).
[The forms] *trayaḥ* and *catvāraḥ*: in *trayaḥ*, there is *guṇa* substitution by [the rule] *jasi ca* (7.3.109);
in *catvāraḥ*, there is the addition of *ām* by [the rule] *caturanaḍuhorāmudāttaḥ* (7.1.98).

Regarding "three" (*trīṇi*): by *jaśśasoḥ śiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.20), there is the substitution of *śi*; by *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ* (7.1.72), the augment *num* is added; by *nopadhāyāḥ* (6.4.7), the penultimate vowel is lengthened; and by *sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau* (6.4.8), the long vowel [of the *num*] is applied.

And this [term] "in the feminine" (*strīyam*) is a qualifier of the numbers three and four, because those two alone are what is directly stated (*śruta*). Regarding the rule "not of the stem" (*nāṅgasya*), he shows what is excluded by the word "only" (*eva*) with the words "by that" (*tena*).
This is by way of the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*). For if, by the term "in the feminine," only the stem (*aṅga*) [were intended]...

It is specified that [the rule] applies; thus, when the words *tri* and *catur* refer to a masculine or neuter [noun], while the word *aṅga* refers to a feminine [noun], these two substitutes would still occur. [This is because of the rule: "In the feminine, for *tri* and *catur*..."
By this [rule], they do not become [the basis for the designation] when being qualified.

In examples such as *priyatriḥ*, since the feminine is the meaning of the other member (*anyapadārtha*), the *aṅga* (base) occurs in the feminine, while the words *tri* and *catuḥ* occur in another gender. However, when the *aṅga* occurs in the masculine or neuter...

When the words *tri* and *catur* occur in the feminine gender, they remain as they are: *priyāstisro brāhmaṇyaḥ asya* (he to whom three beloved Brāhmaṇī women belong) becomes *priyatisā*, *priyatisrau*, *priyatisnaḥ*; [and] *priyatisṛ brāhmaṇakulam* (the Brāhmaṇa family having three beloved women), *priyatisṛṇoḥ*, *priyatisṛṇi*. [Likewise for] *priyacatasṛ brāhmaṇakulam*.
*priyacatasṛṇī*, *priyacatasṛṇi*.

Regarding the rule *tisṛbhāve* and so forth: when the suffix *kan* is applied to the word *tri* by the rule *triśabdāt saṃjñāyāṃ kan* (Pāṇini 5.3.87), [the forms *priyatisṛkaḥ* etc. would not be obtained because of the absence of case-endings (*vibhakti*); therefore, this [present rule] is commenced. As for the word *upasaṃkhyāna*...

The purpose [of this rule] is to provide an exposition. Herein is the exposition: the particle *ca* from the preceding sūtra is carried over (*anuvartate*) here, and it serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned. By means of that, the suffix *kan* will also occur when a name (*saṃjñā*) is intended. For example, "tisṛkā"—this is a name for a village.

Regarding the statement "the initial udātta accent is prescribed for *catasṛ*": in the case of *catasraḥ paśya*, the rule *caturaḥ śasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.167) would result in an antodātta (final udātta) accent; however, an ādyudātta (initial udātta) is desired. Therefore, for that purpose, the prescription of the initial udātta must be made. This is accomplished by the accent of the nipātana (irregular prescription).
This is for the purpose that the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) should not occur because [the word] is already barred. If that is the case,

then just as the accent by way of nipātana bars the accent of *śas*, so too would it bar that initial acute accent of the case-ending which is prescribed by the rule "ṣaṭ-tri-caturbhyo halādiḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.179).
One might ask: "In that case, would there not be an acute accent (*udātta*) on the vowel in *catasṛṇām*?

To this he says: "But in the case of *catasṛṇām*, etc. [The phrase] "by the force of the mention of *halādi*" (beginning with a consonant) is the reason for that very point. For the mention of *halādi* is made there for the purpose of excluding vowels (*aj*) and the like.

This word *catuḥ* is the subject of the plural number; all plural forms [of *catur*] other than the nominative, accusative, and genitive plurals begin with a consonant (*hal*). In that regard, when the augment *nuṭ* is applied by a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) over *num*, the *aci-ra*, and the *tṛj-vad-bhāva* [rules], [the form becomes *caturṇām*].

The initial syllable must be acute (ādyaudātta); this is because [the suffix] begins with a consonant (hal-ādi). As for the [suffix] *jas*, however, since the term "not being a case-ending of a pronoun" (*asarvanāmasthāna*) is understood to carry over from rule 6.1.170—*aṭ-ṅasiṅasāminātsyāḥ, jasi ca chandasy asarvanāmasthāne*—its initial syllable is acute.

[The reading in the printed edition, "because the mention of ṭh continues," is incorrect. Therefore, the mention of "beginning with a consonant" (halādi) was made there for the purpose that [the rule] might not apply to *śas*. And if the accent of the irregular formation (nipātana-svara) were not to occur, then the mention of "beginning with a consonant" would be rendered useless; therefore, it must be so here.

Because it lacks the capacity to take the case endings beginning with *ha*, the accent of the particle (*nipāta*) is superseded by the accent of the case ending; therefore, in the word *catasṛṇām*, there is an udātta accent on the final syllable.

100. *aci ra ṛtaḥ* | (7.2.100) For what purpose, then, is the substitution of *r* prescribed before a vowel (*aci*), since it would already be established by the rule for *yaṇ*-substitution? To this he says:
"pūrvasavarṇa," etc. For if this sūtra did not exist, [the form] in the nominative plural (*śasi*) would be [governed by] *prathamayoḥ*...

Otherwise, there would be the substitution of the homogeneous vowel with the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇa*) by *pūrvasavarṇaḥ* (6.1.102), the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* by *ṅsiṅsośca* (6.1.110) and *ṛta ut* (6.1.111), and the *guṇa* substitution by *ṛto ṅsirvanāmasthānayoḥ* (7.3.110) in the case of a neuter nominative/accusative ending (*sarvanāmasthāna*). Therefore, this [present rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to these.

The substitution of *repha* (the letter *r*) is now being introduced. Now, it might be argued that this substitution of *repha* is appropriately an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rules concerning the homogeneous vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*) and the substitution of *utva*, but it is not appropriate as an exception to the rule for *guṇa*; for, as the maxim states:
"Exceptions set aside preceding rules, but not subsequent ones" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 10).

Thus [it may be asked]. To this he says: "Also when followed by *para*" (*param api*), and so forth. The scope for the application of the *guṇa* rule is: *kartārau*, *hartārau*, *kartarī*; the scope for the application of the *repha* (the substitution of *r*) is:
*tisraḥ paśya*, *tisrastisṭhanti*; and *priyatisri nidhehi*. In these cases, where both [rules] would apply...

By means of the *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (the precedence of the former), the substitution of *repha* (the letter *r*) occurring [by P. 7.2.100] also subverts the subsequent *guṇa* substitution [prescribed by P. 7.1.90] for the *ṅi* and *sarvanāmasthāna* case endings.
[The question is: "Why is it stated that [the substitute] is *ṛt*? Thus [it is said].

He considers: the words *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* will follow after [the word] *aha*; and since those two end in the vowel *ṛ*, by the paribhāṣā "of the final [element]" (1.1.52), the substitution will occur only for the *ṛ*.
[The phrase] "for the sake of the realization of *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*" means that even when *aci* follows these two—namely *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*—[the rule applies].

The term "ṛtaḥ" is stated for the purpose that the substitution [of *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*] may take place in place of the three and four syllables (*tricatur-*) following [the word *ṛt*]. Otherwise, as expressed by the words "for otherwise," etc., if "ṛtaḥ" were not stated,
this [substitution] would be understood as an exception (*apavāda*) applying only to those two [forms, *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*], and consequently, [it would apply] only before vowel-initial suffixes.
Those two would not exist.

101. *jarāyā jaras anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 7.2.101). "The substitution of *jaras* occurs by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) because of the prescription of *num*. The scope of *num* is, for example, *trapūṇi*, *jatūni*; the scope of the substitution of *jaras* is, for example, *jarasau*.

The forms *atijarāṃsi* and *brāhmaṇakulāni* [are examples where], in the case of a conflict between two rules, the subsequent substitution of *jaras* occurs by way of the *vipratiṣedha* (the rule of the later). For if the *num* augment were applied first, the substitution of *jaras* would not be obtained because it would be separated by the intervening *num*; nevertheless...

This is obtained by resorting to a specified qualification (*vihitaviśeṣaṇa*). Even so, according to the rule "substitutes apply to that which is being pointed out" (*nirdiśyamānasyādeśā bhavanti*), once the substitute for the word *jaras* has been applied, the nasal *num* would be heard following the letter *s*. [The printed edition reads *śrūyate*. Furthermore, even if it were a substitute for the entire form (*samudāya*), [the same fault would remain].

Could it be so? Even in that case, since the rule for *num* would have already accomplished its function, it would not apply again once the substitute has been made; consequently, the undesired form would result.
For instance, in the case of "atijarasam brāhmaṇakulam paśya," once the substitution of *jaras* has been applied...

Why does [the substitution of] *su* not occur here by the rule *ṭhsvamornapuṃsakāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.23)? To this he says: "In this case," and so forth. *Atijaram* is a *prādisamāsa* (compound with a prefix); the shortening occurs by the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.47), and the ending is the second case singular, *am*.

Since that which is modified in one part is not different from the original (*sthita ekadeśavikṛtasyānanyatvāt*), even when the shortening (*hrasvatva*) has been applied, these three operations— the elision (*luk*), the substitution of *am*, and the substitution of *jaras*— all apply simultaneously. Among them, because the substitution of *am* (by *ato 'm*, Pāṇini 7.1.24) is an exception (*apavāda*) to elision, [the substitution of *am* takes effect].

It is superseded; for even the substitution of *ambhāva* is superseded by the substitution of *jaras* due to its being subsequent. Now, once the substitution of *jaras* has been applied, why does the elision (*luk*) not occur again? To this he says: "The rule for elision [does not apply] again," and so forth. And the rule for elision does not operate again, because its opportunity has passed (*bhraṣṭāvasaratvāt*).

Regarding the third person plural, one might ask: should it be *atijarair brāhmaṇakulaiḥ*, or rather *atijarasam*, *atijarasaiḥ*? To this he says: "*atijarasam*" and so forth. "According to the opinion of Gonardīya. For it is thus:
It is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Godardīya says—'This is included within the sixth [pāda];
therefore, it should be *atijaram* and *atijarai*'. What, then, is the reasoning for this? To this he says:
"Because of a condition based on immediate sequence" (*sannipātalakṣaṇa*), and so forth. This refers to the case where the substitution of *am* and the substitution of *ais* [would otherwise apply].

The substitution of *jaras* would be merely a cause [for the application of another rule], and the status of the stem as ending in *akāra* would be obstructed by those two [substitutions]. But this is incorrect; for once they have been produced through that nipāta, they are not able to obstruct it.
"Others" refers to those who follow the opinion of the author of the Sūtras. Why, then, do they think thus?
To this he says: "Because of its non-eternality," and so forth. Furthermore, its non-eternality has been established in the rule *ato bhisa ais* (Pāṇini 7.1.9).
102. *tyadādīnāmaḥ* | (7.2.102) [The substitute] *aḥ* [is applied] to *tyad* and the others. Regarding *syaḥ*: by *tadoḥ saḥ sāvanantyayoḥ* (7.2.106), the *t* is replaced by *s*.
Regarding *tyaḥ*: by *jasaḥ śī* (7.1.17), there is the substitution of *śī*, and by *ādguṇaḥ* (6.1.87), the *guṇa* [vowel] is formed.

In *ṭhimau*, the substitution of *m* occurs by [Pāṇini 7.2.109] *daśca*. In *asau*, the substitution of *āṬ* occurs and the *su* suffix is elided by [Pāṇini 7.2.107] *adasa āṬ sulopaśca*. In *amū*, the substitutions of *m* and *ū* occur by [Pāṇini 8.2.80] *adaso'serdādu do maḥ*; then, a long vowel is substituted by [Pāṇini 6.1.102] *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ*. [The form is] *amī*.

Thus [it is said]. The substitution of *ī* occurs by the rule "eta īd bahuvacane" (Pāṇini 8.2.81). Now, why does this not occur here in the case of *bhavān*? To this he says: "of those ending with the dual," and so forth. This has already been made known previously under the rule "śeṣe lopaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.90). [The form] is *bhavān*.
The augment *num* is applied by the rule "ṭhugidacām" (Pāṇini 7.1.70), and the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule "atvasantasya cādhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.14).

Now, why does this [lengthening] not also occur here in the case of those that have become technical terms (*saṃjñā*) or secondary members (*upasarjana*), such as in the series beginning with *tyad*, namely *tyad*?
To the question, "Is there over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? he says: "Those that have become technical terms (*saṃjñā*) or secondary members (*upasarjana*)," and so forth.

The words beginning with *tyad* (the *tyadādi* group) fall within the category of the *sarvādi* group. Furthermore, the *sarvādi* words are recited as being neither technical terms nor secondary members. For instance, they are designated as "all nominal stems" (*sarvanāmāni*, Pāṇini 1.1.27).

This is the purpose of making this a "great" designation (mahatī saṃjñā): so that it may serve as a designation for all things that have become names; however, let it not apply to those which are themselves designations of something else or which function as subordinate members (upasarjana). Therefore...

The pronouns beginning with *tyad* (tyadādi), when they have become subordinate to a noun (*saṃjñā*), are excluded by the very fact of their recitation [in the list]; the meaning is that they are cast outside the category of *tyadādi*. Therefore, because they are not among the *tyadādi* [when subordinate], the grammatical operations pertaining to *tyadādi* do not apply to them. However, "in a word where the *tyadādi* element is predominant, [the operation] certainly occurs. Thus end the *tyadādi* [pronouns].

That word in which the pronoun *tyad* and so forth is predominant is called "one where *tyad* etc. are predominant" (*tyadādipradhāna*). In such a case, the substitution of *ā* certainly occurs, because it has not been excluded by the explicit mention [of the specific forms]. Its non-exclusion, however, follows from the acceptance of the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) for the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "pronominal" (*sarvanāman*) to include those ending in *tyad* and so forth.

103. *kimaḥ kaḥ* | (7.2.103) Now, why is not simply the vowel *a* prescribed for *kimaḥ*, so that the sūtra would be more concise, since the vowel *a* is already understood by way of *anuvṛtti* from the preceding rule? In that case, the sūtra should have been formulated as follows: [kimaḥ akāraḥ].

"Why is it said 'of *kim*'? To this he says: 'The substitute occurs for [the whole of] *kim* together with the augment *akac*'. By this, the substitution of the vowel *ā* is not prescribed for *kim* alone. For this substitute, according to the paribhāṣā "that which falls in the middle of something is included by the mention of that thing" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 21), is understood as including *kim* along with *akac*, since *akac* is included by the mention of *kim*. Thus, it belongs to *kim* together with *akac*.

It occurs; therefore, why is *ka* itself not prescribed in place of *kimaḥ*? For if it were so prescribed, then when the substitution is made for that which lacks *anakac*, and subsequently *kaca* is added, the undesirable form *kakaḥ* would result—this is the intention. But how can *kimaḥ* become *ka* once *atva* has been applied, given that...

If *atva* were applied to the letter *m*, and then *yaṇ-ādeśa* were applied to the letter *t*, would the result not be *kya*? This is not a fault, for *atva* is prescribed for the letter *i* as well; for here, the word "of *ṭha*" (*ṭhaḥ*) is carried over from the preceding rule. *Atva* does not apply to the final letter of a base; furthermore, the explicit mention of the vowel *a* here [is for that purpose].

It is performed. By that, according to the rule "in the case of a non-final substitution, [the substitute takes the place] of what is in the vicinity of the final" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 63), there is the substitution of the vowel *i*; then, when the two *a*s undergo the process of *para-pūrva* (becoming the preceding sound), the form *ka* is established.
In some recensions, the reading is *imaḥ*. In that regard, this is the prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*): why is it not simply the vowel *a* that is *imaḥ*?

Is it being prescribed? For in this way the sūtra becomes concise; because the *akāra* under discussion is carried over (*anuvṛtti*) here, the sūtra should instead have been formulated simply as "imaḥ. And if that were the case, [the forms] *tīn*, *timau*, etc., would not result from the root *ṭima* / *ṣṭima* "to become wet" when it takes the suffix *kvip*.

In this case, the substitution would also undesirably apply to *ima* (as in *imau* and *imaḥ*), because *ima* is qualified by the words beginning with *tyad*—namely, "that which is *ima* belonging to the *tyad*-class"?

No; for once the substitution of *mat* has been applied by [Pāṇini 7.2.109] *daśca*, the substitution would undesirably apply even here in *imau* and *imaḥ*. Nor can it be avoided by the paribhāṣā regarding "that which is taught by a specific rule" (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā*).
One should not suspect that if this [term] were stated, the rule *ṭhalo 'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52) would apply;
for there is the principle *nānarthake 'lontyavidhiḥ* (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 62). To this he says: "even when accompanied by the suffix *kaC*."

And so forth. The former reading alone is more correct; for in the other reading, once the substitution of *kvā* for *ktvā* has been made by the subsequent sūtra, there would result the hearing of two *k* sounds in conjunction (*saṃyukta*), and that is undesirable.

104. *ku tihoḥ* | (Pāṇini 7.2.104) This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule. Since the word *ti* lacks a case-ending, the vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation; the purpose lies solely in the letter *t*. In this regard, the principle applies: "In a rule where a term is used to denote a class beginning with that [term], it includes the initial element."
(The Vyākhyāpada 127: The substitution of the letter *t* is prescribed as an operation to be applied before a case-ending (*vibhakti*).
Therefore, he says: "before [an ending] beginning with *t*," and so forth. Regarding "kutaḥ": [it is derived by] Pāṇini 5.3.7, *pañcamyās tasil*.
Regarding "kutra": [it is derived by] Pāṇini 5.3.12, *kimo't*; here, the word *vā* ("or") is brought over from the subsequent rule.

It is drawn forward [from the previous rule]. Therefore, the suffix *tral* also occurs in the sense of the locative case by virtue of the rule *saptamyāstral* (Pāṇini 5.3.10). Regarding *kuha*: the suffix *ha* is applied by the rule *vā ha ca chandasi* (Pāṇini 5.3.13). And these suffixes, beginning with *tasil*, receive the technical designation "case-ending" (*vibhakti*) by the rule *prāgdiśo vibhaktiḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.1).

105. *kvāti* (Pāṇini 7.2.105). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *kā*. [The form] *kva* is derived from *kim* by the rule *kimo 't* (5.3.12). Now, for what purpose is this different substitute prescribed? Why not simply prescribe the original *ku* itself?

Even in that case, the substitution of *yaṇ* is established exactly as it is; furthermore, the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) need not be made, for one could simply formulate a single rule: "in *ku*, *ti*, *ha*, and *su*. To this, he says:
"the mention of another substitute," and so forth. For if the word *ku* were to undergo the [substitution of *kū*], the substitution of *yaṇ* would [not apply].
Otherwise, by the rule "ṭhorguṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.146), a guṇa substitution would occur;
therefore, the substitution of *kvā* is stated for the purpose of preventing that.
Even so, the suffix *ḍvat* should have been prescribed directly at the stage of the suffix-rule itself, as in "kimo ḍvat."

Even there, once the elision of *ṭi* has been performed, the form *kvā* is indeed established. If it is argued that it is not established because, when the designation *pada* applies, the rule "ṭhjhalāṃ jaśo'nte" (Pāṇini 8.2.39) would require the substitution of *ga* for the letter *ka*, [we reply: this is not so; for "that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal (*antaraṅga*)."

(Vyā.pa. 42) Thus, because the elision of the *ṭi* is considered *asiddha*, the substitution of *jaś* does not take place. For the elision of the *ṭi* is prescribed when a *ḍit* suffix follows; therefore, being dependent upon a *ḍit* suffix, it is *bahiraṅga*. However, the substitution of *jaś*, being prescribed at the end of a word (*padānte*), does not depend on any other cause and is thus *antaraṅga*. Therefore—

He says: "Is *ḍvat* a separate suffix? and so forth. If *ḍvat* were prescribed as a separate suffix, the form *kvā* with the augment *sakac* would not be established. For if *asac* were applied, the form would stand as *kakim*, and when the suffix *ḍvat* follows, the *ṭilopa* (elision of the final vowel) would occur.

Otherwise, an undesirable form would result. However, since the substitution of *kva* is prescribed when the suffix *at* follows, and because it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it replaces the entire stem including the *kāc* augment;
thus, there is no occurrence of an undesirable form. Therefore, the term *ḍvat* is not for the sake of [the suffix] with *kāc*.
Another suffix is prescribed. That for which the meaning or purpose is that which possesses the augment *kaC* is "sākackārtham."

106. *tadoḥ saḥ sāvanantyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.106). Regarding the word *sai*: is this the inclusion of the nominative singular, or the locative plural, or indeed both? Among these, [it refers to] the nominative singular.
[This is] for the purpose of including [both]. For instance—the inclusion of both does not occur by way of a general rule.

If it were so, he would have said "sīrti". For in that case, an operation prescribed for what begins with *s* would apply to both of them. Therefore, there is the inclusion of one or the other. Likewise...

Indeed, because of such indications as *tasya chandasi bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.1.133) and *so'ci lope cet* (Pāṇini 6.1.134), it is appropriate to understand that only the nominative singular is being referred to:
*he saḥ*, *sā*. The word *he* is a collection of indeclinables used in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).
But will not the substitution of *yat* and so forth (the *tyadādyatva*) act as an obstacle here? This is not so;
for rules that have no scope (*anavakāśa*) are indeed obstructive, whereas this substitution of *at* has scope. What is its scope?
The word *dvi*: namely, *dvau*. Even though that scope exists, even if...
Although *sakara* also has an infinite scope, nevertheless, because the final [element] is subsequent, *satva* would occur.
Consequently, in the case of *he saḥ*, the elision of the nominative suffix *su* by the rule "ṭeṅ hrasvāt sambuddheḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.69) would not take place.
In that situation, once the elision of the vowel and the following consonant (*halṅyādilopa*) has been applied, the rules for *rutva* and *visarjanīya* would follow.

If [the suffix] were applied after two [consonants], the form would be undesirable; furthermore, in the case of *set*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* prescribed by "ajādyataṣṭāp" (Pāṇini 4.1.4) would not occur. Therefore, it must be stated: "after two non-final [consonants]."

107. *adasa āṬ sulopaśca* | (7.2.107) [The rule] "in the case of *sau*" (*sau*) applies here as well. An *āṬ* substitution is prescribed for *adas*, which is an exception to the *tyadādi* replacement (of *d* with *t*). Thus, we have *asau*. By the preceding rule, the *d* is replaced by *s*, and then a *vṛddhi* vowel is substituted according to *vṛddhireci* (6.1.88).
Regarding the passage beginning with "And when... and "And the state of being more correct (*sādhutvam*)," the word *ca* (and) serves the purpose of conjunction (*sanniyoga*).
By this, in that very alternative where there is a prohibition of *au*-substitution, in that same alternative, the substitution of *u* for the vowel *a* of the more correct form is prescribed.

Regarding the passage beginning with *ṭhutarapadabhūtānām* and so forth: here, in the compounds *paramāham* and *paramānena*, the case endings (*vibhakti*) that arise from the compound undergo these substitutions (*eta-ādeśa*) according to the rules *tvāhau sau* (Pāṇini 7.2.94), *ido'y puṃsi* (7.2.111), and *anāpyakaḥ* (7.2.112).

[The substitutes] are external; indeed, they occur even before the production of case-endings. The lengthening of *akaḥ* [a, i, u] before a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇe*) is internal (*antaraṅga*); therefore, that alone should occur first, and the substitutions should occur afterwards. Consequently, undesirable forms such as *paramaham*, *paramayam*, and *paramanena* would result.

[The forms] would be subject to euphonic combination (*rūpaṇi*). Therefore, the substitutes for *tyad* and the others must be stated—that is, explained—when they have become words [but] before the internal sandhi has been applied.
This indicates the intention of the Teacher: that first the operation pertaining to the preceding and following words [should take place].

It occurs later as a partial [exception]. This is because he teaches the prohibition: "Not for *indra* when it follows" (Pāṇini 7.3.22). How is this an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? In the word *indra*, there are two vowels;
of these, one is removed by elision according to "and that which has [the suffix] *ya*" (Pāṇini 6.4.148).
Another [objection]: "By means of the single-substitute rule (*ekādeśena*), the word *indra* has become vowel-less (*anacka*); what possibility is there, then, for *vṛddhi* to apply there?

The Teacher, however, perceives that the grammatical operation first takes place between the two constituent words, and only afterwards does the single substitution occur; for it is stated: "Not when *indra* follows" (*nendrasya parasya*, Pāṇini 7.3.22).
He teaches the prohibition of *vṛddhi*.

From this indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), it is understood that the substitutes for pronouns such as *tyad* and others occur when they function as the second member of a compound and have not undergone vowel sandhi (*svarasandhi*).
"From *adas*, after *su*, there shall be *aut*," and so forth. A restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is to be understood here:
from the word *adas*, *aut* shall occur only after *su*. Let it be so, or let it not be;

once the substitution of *yat* for *tyad*-type words has been applied to the word *adas*, and the *vṛddhi* [vowel] has been substituted by "vṛddhi in place of [a vowel] followed by *ec*" (Pāṇini 6.1.88).

Since [the form] *asau* would indeed be established by the rule *kṛtāyām asau*, for what purpose is the elision of *su* prescribed? Because it would be purposeless, the elision of *su* should not be prescribed in this way; rather, only the substitution of *au* (āṬ) should be prescribed. Regarding this, he states the fault: "The vocative ending would be elided after a short vowel," as in *he 'sau*. In this case, [the rule] *eṅ hrasvāt*...

[Objection: Would it not follow that the elision of the *su* suffix [after a word ending in a consonant] would apply by the rule "sambuddheḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.69), and consequently, the form "he'sau" (O, this one! would not be established in the vocative (*sambuddhi*)? [Response: This is not a fault;
for the elision of the vocative suffix after a consonant occurs when the substitution of *au* has been made, and it is not [the case that the elision applies] after a consonant [in general].
How, then, could there be the contingency of elision (*lopaprasaṅga*) in that case? Well then, must the mention of *hal* be made? No, it need not be made;

for that [mention] is already in force (*prakṛta*). From the rule "After [stems ending in] *hal*, *ī*, or *ā*, the single-consonant suffixes *su*, *ti*, and *si* are elided" (6.1.68), the mention of *hal* is indeed already in force. Even though in that [rule]...

Although what is designated by the nominative case is intended here as the meaning of the genitive, nevertheless, by the rule "ṭheṅ hrasvāt" (6.1.69), the fifth case [ablative] will be treated as a sixth case [genitive] for the word *hal*,
because of the statement "tasmād ity uttarasya" (1.1.67).

In that case, however, there is this fault: "there would be *etva* [the substitution of *e*] in that [context]," and so forth. When *tyadādyatva* [the substitution of *a* for the final vowel of *tad* etc. has been applied before that *ūkārā* [the long *ū*], and the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added, then in the form *he asau brāhmaṇī*, *etva* would occur by the rule *sambuddhau ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.106), just as in the case of *he...* [as in *he amba*].

Regarding the case of *khaṭve*: [the objection] that "this is because of the continued application of the rule *na jhali*"—this is not a fault. In the rule *sambuddhau ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.106), the phrase *bahuvacane jhalyet* (7.3.103) is understood to carry over;
therefore, *etva* must occur before a vocative suffix beginning with a *jhal* sound. And when *au* has been substituted [for the dual ending], it begins with a *jhal*.

It does not become *sambuddhi*; what then? It begins with *a* (*ajādi*). [The objection is: "The status of having *k* as the first letter (*kāditva*) and the substitution of *śī* would consequently apply" (the Prācīna edition reads *prasajyeta*). Here, the preceding *ca* has the sense of *tarhi* ("then/in that case"), while the other *ca* is for conjunction (*samuccaye*). This...

In that case, there is a fault: in the word *asakau brāhmaṇī*, when the suffix *akac* is applied to express meanings such as "unknown" (*ajñāta*) and so forth, and the suffix *ṭāp* is subsequently added, the rule *ṭhpratyayasthāt kāt* (Pāṇini 7.3.44) would result in the substitution of *ī* for the vowel preceding the *kā* [of *akac*].
Furthermore, in the word *asau brāhmaṇī*, by the rule *āṅ āpaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.18), [the substitution of *au* for the final *ā* of *asau*] would likewise occur.

However, when the substitution of *śī* for *adas-* occurs after the vowel *o* has been applied, the suffix *ṭāp* itself does not exist; thus, these two defects do not arise. Furthermore, the defect regarding the substitution of *śī* should be understood as being only occasional (*pākṣika*), occurring in that alternative where the marker *ṅ* is attached to the suffix for the purpose of including it under the general rule. But when—

In that case, according to the instruction of the preceding sūtra, the substitution of *śī* occurs only for the two dual endings; for it was precisely those two that were designated as having the marker *ṅ* by the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*). For any other ending, there is no possibility [of the substitution] at all, because they possess the marker *ai*.

108. *idamo maḥ* | (7.2.108) By the paribhāṣā *alo'ntyaparibhāṣā* (1.1.52), this *m* [of the sūtra] must replace only the final *m* [of *idam*]. Since there is no difference made by substituting *m* for *m*, for what purpose is this substitution of *m* for *m*?
"Why is it called the letter *ma*?"—in order to refute this objection, he says "of the letter *ma*" and so forth; the meaning has already been explained.
109. *daśca* (Pāṇini 7.2.109).

The term *idamaḥ* is understood [from the previous rule], while *sau* is no longer applicable, because *sau* is mentioned again in the subsequent sūtra. Therefore, this substitution of *m* for the vowel *ā* occurs in all case endings (*vibhakti*).

110. *yaḥ sau* (Pāṇini 7.2.110). Because of the mention of "in the masculine" (*puṃsi*) in the subsequent sūtra, this *yakāra* [substitution] applies to the feminine. Now, why is it not understood to apply to the neuter as well? It is impossible to understand it thus; for in the neuter...

By the rule *ṭhsvamornapuṃsakāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.23), there ought to be elision (*luk*) of the nominative suffix *su*. Since *su* is being stated here [as the condition for the substitution], how could the letter *y* occur when that [suffix] has been elided? If it is argued that this occurs by means of the "characteristic of a suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), we say no; for the characteristic of a suffix is prohibited by the rule *na lumatāṅgasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.63).
Therefore, it was rightly said: "In the feminine, this [suffix] is the letter *ya*."
111. *ido'yÂ puṃsi* (Pāṇini 7.2.111).
112. *anāpyakaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.112).

Regarding the phrase "by this [suffix] -ṭhañ": after the substitution of *at* for the pronouns beginning with *tyad* and the subsequent substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*), the form *idam* undergoes the replacement by *ana*.

In *ṭhṭhāṅsiṅsāminātsyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.12), there is the substitution of *in*; by *ādguṇaḥ* (6.1.87), the guṇa [vowel] is formed. Regarding the phrase "of these two": by *osi ca* (7.3.104), there is the substitution of *etva* (the change to *e*), the substitution of *an*, and the elision of the case-ending *su*. Regarding the phrase "by the letter *p*": why does [the rule] not apply to the letter *p* of the suffix *kap*?

Because there is no purpose [for this].
