But is it not the case that here, in the rule *iha*, there is a purpose so that the substitution of *lopa* (elision) prescribed by *hali lopaḥ* (P. 7.2.113) might apply when a *prāgdiśīya* case-ending follows? [To this we reply: the substitution *iś* prescribed by *idama iś* (P. 5.3.3) must necessarily supersede [the elision] here; and in this context, [the forms] *am*, *ha*, *kvat*, *si*, and *tre* [are excluded].

In this regard, [the rule] Pāṇini 4.2.104 (*idamo haḥ*)— where the word *iha* is used— is the indicator (*liṅga*) that the elision of the form of *idam* has not occurred, since it is taught as having a final *h*.

113. *hali lopaḥ* | (Pāṇini 7.2.113) Since the preceding rule would have required the substitution [of *ya*] even before a consonant, this sūtra prescribes the elision (*lopa*) of the form *id* when followed by a consonant. Thus, in *ābhyām*: the substitution of *tyadādi* [for *id*] occurs; then, by *ato guṇe* (6.1.97), there is the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*); [and finally, the case-ending *supi* applies].
And there is lengthening by [Pāṇini 6.3.102] *aṭa*.
Now, why does this elision not occur for the final [letter], according to the paribhāṣā [1.1.52] *alo'ntyaparibhāṣā*?
To this he says: "In the case of that which is meaningless," and so forth. This is said even while conceding the rule regarding the final letter (*alo'ntyavidhi*) in the case of what is meaningless.

He states another solution, beginning with "Or rather" (atha vā). Why is it that the mention of *at* need not be made, since it is understood from the previous rule? To this he replies, "Nor [is there a fault] because of *an-āpy-akaḥ*" and so forth. Although in that [previous rule] it was indicated in the nominative case (*prathamā-nirdiṣṭa*), whereas here it is required in the genitive sense (*ṣaṣṭhī-nirdiṣṭa*), nevertheless, the word *halī* is in the locative case (*saptamī*).

The word *ann* will be understood as having the sense of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhītva*), according to the rule "when something is specified by the locative [in the form] *tasmin*, it refers to what precedes" (Pāṇini 1.1.66).

This resolution should be understood according to the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya, because this Paribhāṣā is not accepted by him. However, in this view, there are three instances of the letter *a*.
Having applied the single-substitute (ekādeśa) of the form of the subsequent element, the lengthening and other operations should be prescribed.

114. *mṛjer vṛddhiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.114). Regarding the form *mārṣṭā*: from the root *mṛj* in the sense of "cleansing" (*dhātupāṭha* 1066), there is *ṣ*-substitution by the rule for the *vraśca*-group (8.2.36), followed by *ṣṭu*-substitution.

In the case of forms such as *kaṃsaparimṛṅbhyām* and *kaṃsaparimṛṅbhiḥ*, which derive from the root *mṛj* with the suffix *kvip* followed by the production of case endings, the rule for *vṛddhi* would apply; furthermore, the prohibition of *vṛddhi* based on *kvip*— namely, the rule *kṅiti ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5)— is not capable of preventing it, because:

The locative case in *kṅti* is caused by *k* and *ṅ*. In this instance, the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) does not occur because it is caused by *kvip*, but rather because it is caused by a case-ending (*vibhakti*). Therefore, a prohibition of that [lengthening] must be stated;
hence he says: "The mention of the word 'dhātu' (root) in [Pāṇini 3.2.181] *mūjar*," and so forth. As for the example *bhrauṇahatya* (6.4.174):
This meaning is indicated by the grammatical derivation (*nipātana*): an operation prescribed for a verbal root applies only to a suffix that follows a verbal root;

therefore, it does not apply in the case of *kaṃsamṛṅbhyām*. For that which is prescribed by the rule "after a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) is a suffix following a verbal root, and [suffixes] such as *bhyām* and so on are not so prescribed.
It is not prescribed as being "from a root" (dhātu); rather, it is prescribed as being "from a nominal stem" (prātipadika).

Therefore, that is not a suffix added to a root. [The examples] beginning with "kaṃsaparimṛḍbhyām" follow; when the sibilant (ṣatva) has been applied as before, the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (jaśtva) for the letter ṣ results in the letter ḍ.

115. *aco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115). Regarding the forms *ṭhniścāyaniṣpāvau*: [one *ṭha* is a *niścāya* of rice grains; two *śūrpa* measures are a *niṣpāva*—so says the *Kāśikā*. These are derived from the roots *ci* preceded by *ni*, and *pū* preceded by *ni*.]*

The suffix *ghañ* is applied according to the rule "after all [roots], when expressing a measure" (Pāṇini 3.3.20). The substitution of *ṣ* for the *visarjanīya* occurs by the rule "and for a [root-final consonant] preceded by *i* or *u*, provided it is not part of a suffix" (Pāṇini 8.3.41). Thus we have *kāraḥ* and *hāraḥ*;
here, *ghañ* is applied after the roots *kṛ* and *hṛ* in the sense of abstract action (*bhāva*).

"ṭhgauḥ, gāvo gāvaḥ"—here, by the rule "goto ṇit" (Pāṇini 7.1.90), the sarvanāmasthāna [case endings] have the quality of being ṇit. "ṭhsakhāyau, sakhāyaḥ"—here too, it is by the rule "sakhyurasambuddhau" (Pāṇini 7.1.92). "ṭhjayateḥ, yauteśca"—[this refers to] the roots "ji" in the sense of "victory" and "yu" in the sense of "joining."
(dhā.pā. 561), *ṭhū* in the sense of "mixing" (*miśraṇe*) [or "mixing and not mixing"—dhā.pā.], (dhā.pā.

1033). Regarding "of *cyavate*": *cyuṅ*, *chÂyuṅ*, *jyuṅ*, *pruṅ*, *pluṅ* in the sense of "motion" (*gatau*) [this is not found in dhā.pā.], (dhā.pā. 955–958). The mention of the vowel *a* is for the purpose of including even those roots that do not take the suffix *ani*.
It might be argued: "There will be [the form] *goḥ*. But surely this will occur there by the very force of the inclusion of the marker *ṇit*?

This is not so; for there is another purpose for the inclusion of the marker *ṇit*. What is that? [It is so that] when the substitution of *ava* has been made in *gāvau* and *gāvaḥ*, the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116) applies, resulting in vṛddhi as follows: [gāvaḥ].

It might be argued: "If this were so, then in the case of *gaur*—where this *vṛddhi* has already served its purpose regarding the absence of a *guṇa*—it would be sublated by *guṇa* in forms such as *kārayati* because of the latter's higher status. [The response is: "This will not happen due to the force of the inclusion of the marker *ṇit*. But this is no answer, because [the rule] *ṇer aniṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.51) and others...

Is this not because the inclusion of the marker *ṇ* has already served its purpose? This is not a fault; the activity of the Teacher indicates that *vṛddhi* occurs even in the domain of *guṇa*, since he [prescribes] the rule "jāgro 'viciṇṇalṅitsu" regarding both the domain of *vṛddhi* and the domain of prohibition.

Thus, the rule for *guṇa* is restated. For if *vṛddhi* were not to take effect in the domain of *guṇa*, then since *guṇa* already exists in forms such as *jāgarayati*, the restatement of *guṇa* in that domain would be purposeless. Moreover, the scope of this restatement is restricted to the domains of *ciṇ* and *ṇal*.

It is understood from the prohibition [of the augment]. Now, what is the purpose of the *yogavibhāga* (splitting the rule)? Why not simply state: "After a root ending in *ṇ* or *ñ*, the penultimate vowel is long"? It is impossible to say so; for if that were stated, then although the substitution of *ā* has been made in *gāvaḥ* and *gāvaḥ*, and the *guṇa* substitution has been made in *cāyakaḥ* and *lāvakaḥ*, [the rule would still apply].

When the substitutions of *ay* and *av* have been applied, forms such as *gauḥ* and *sakhāyau* are established; however, in cases such as *jaitram*, they are not established, because the substitutions of *ay* and *av* and the *guṇa* substitution cannot coexist as required. Therefore, for the sake of proper application, a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must be made accordingly.
116. *ata upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116).

In words such as *pāka*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*); the substitution of *k* for *c* and *j* occurs by the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ* (7.3.52). Regarding the word *rāga*: [the substitution of *g* for *j* occurs] by the rule *ghañi ca bhāvakaraṇayoḥ* (6.4.27).

Thus, there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*). In the case of *pācayati*, the suffix *ṇic* is applied by the rule *hetumati ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.26). In the case of *cakāsayati*, because of the specific mention of the "penultimate" (*upadhā*) vowel, the elision does not occur for the letter *a* following the letter *c*. The inclusion of the marker *t* (in *ataḥ*) is for the sake of brevity; for if that were absent, and it were simply stated "of this [stem] which has a penultimate vowel," [the rule would apply too broadly].

There would be prolixity. However, the addition of *t* (making it *tapara*) is not for the purpose of excluding the long vowel, because once the *vṛddhi* substitution has been applied to the long vowel, no distinction remains.

117. *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.117). The term *acām* is used in the sense of a selectional genitive (*nirdhāraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*). Thus, [the meaning is]: "in place of the initial vowel (*ac*) among the vowels (*acām*). Now, one might object:

since the governing rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the "immediate constituent" (*ekapada*) applies, the *vṛddhi* substitution should occur only in place of that which stands immediately before the suffix.

Therefore, one should say "the place of *ik*," and not "the place of *ac*"? It is thought thus: from the rule "aco ñṇiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.115), a second mention of *ac* is understood as continuing for the purpose of indicating the substituendum (*sthānin*); by that, just as in "aco ñṇiti" (7.2.115)...
In this case, as in the previous instance, the mention of the *sthānin* (the original element) means that the *akṛt-paribhāṣā* does not apply; thus, there is no fault here. For example:
*gārgyaḥ*, *vātsyaḥ*—from *gargādibhyo yañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.105); *dākṣiḥ*, *plākṣiḥ*—from *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95); *āupagavaḥ*, *kāpaṭavaḥ*.

The suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "belonging to" (*prāgdīvyatīya*) [by Pāṇini 4.1.83]. Now, in the case of *tvāṣṭraḥ* and *jāgataḥ*, once the suffix *aṇ* has been applied to *tvaṣṭṛ* and *jagat* respectively by [Pāṇini] 4.3.120 (*tasyedam*), the vowel-substitution known as *vṛddhi* occurs according to the rule [Pāṇini] 7.2.115 (*aco ñṇiti*).

[The question is: Why does the vṛddhi substitution characterized by the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*)—as prescribed by *ṭhata upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116)—not occur here? To this he says: "The vṛddhi of the initial vowel of a suffix (*acām ādeḥ*) subverts the vṛddhi of the final and penultimate vowels. But how can that which is prescribed for one thing be a subverter of another? [He replies: By virtue of an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
When he recites the word *puṣkarasat* in the *anuśatikādi* group [of compounds], that indicates: "where there is initial *vṛddhi*, no other *vṛddhi* occurs.
The purpose of its inclusion in the *anuśatikādi* group is so that *vṛddhi* may apply to both members of the compound.
It could be that *puṣkarasat* has a descendant named *pauṣkarasādi*, formed with the suffix *iñ* by [Pāṇini 4.1.96] *bāhvādibhyaśca*. For if initial *vṛddhi* were not the sublater of other *vṛddhi*,
then the *vṛddhi* of the word *pauṣkarasādi* would be established by the rule for *vṛddhi* based on the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) alone.
The word *puṣkarasat* is not recited among the *anuśatikādi* group [of words].
The Teacher observes: "Where there is an initial strengthening (*ādivṛddhi*), no other strengthening occurs";
for this reason, he recites the word *puṣkarasat* in the *anuśatikādi* group. [Objection: But surely it is recited there for the sake of the suffix *ṭhak*.

In that case, since the suffix *añ* is not present in *ṭhak*, the rule for *vṛddhi* based on the presence of an *upadhā* vowel would not apply [to form] *pauṣkarasādikaḥ* in the sense of "one who moves about as a Puṣkarasādin.
This is not so; for if the suffix *ṭhak* is produced after the word *puṣkarasat* in the sense of "moving about," why [would the *vṛddhi* not apply]?

Why does it not arise again? Because it is not so stated; for derivatives formed with *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and *samāsa* suffixes are characterized by being explicitly stated [in the rules]. Therefore, the inclusion of the word *puṣkarasat* in the *anuśatikādi* group serves merely as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
118. *kiti ca*.

(7.2.118) Although the term "in taddhita suffixes" (*taddhiteṣu*) from [sūtra] 7.2.117 is understood as being in the plural, nevertheless, because of the singular designation here, it refers specifically to the singular case.

It is understood through transformation; thus he says: "when a *taddhita* suffix beginning with *kit* follows. For example: *nāḍāyanaḥ*, *jārāyaṇaḥ*. [The suffix] *phak* is applied by the rule *naḍādibhyaḥ phak* (Pāṇini 4.1.99). For example: *ākṣikaḥ*, *śālākikaḥ*. [The suffix *ṭhak* is applied] by the rule *tena dīvyati khanati...* following the words *akṣi* and *śalākā*.
The suffix *ṭhak* [is applied] by [Pāṇini 4.4.2] *jayati jitam*; [and the substitution of] *ik* for *ṭha* [is applied] by [Pāṇini 7.3.50] *ṭhasyekaḥ*.
The second quarter of the seventh chapter in the *Kāśikāvivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the two Bodhisattva-like masters, the venerable Ācārya Jinendrabuddhipāda.
Now begins the seventh chapter,
third quarter.

1. *devikā-śiṃśapā-ditya-vāḍ-dīrghasatra-śreyasām āt* (Pāṇini 7.3.1). When, by the rule *taddhiteṣv acām ādeḥ* (7.2.117), a vṛddhi [substitution] would have occurred as an *ai* due to internal similarity (*āntaratamya*), the substitution of *ā* is prescribed for *devikā* and the others. In this regard, three possible views may be considered: 1. [...]
The elements beginning with *devikā* are qualified by the term "stem" (*aṅga*) under discussion—that is, "of the stems beginning with *devikā*" (1).
Or else, by them [the stems] the stem is qualified—that is, "of the stem ending in *devikā* and so forth" (2); or alternatively—3.
By them [the commentators], "the first vowel" (ādyo'c) is explained as that which is the first among the vowels belonging to the names of Devikā and so forth.

If the first alternative were adopted there, then forms such as *dāvikākūlāḥ śālayaḥ* ("rice growing on the banks of the Devikā") would not be established; for [in that case], this [vowel]—namely, the *ā* in *devikā*—is not [the first vowel].
Is the word *devikā* itself the "limb" (*aṅga*)? No; rather, it is the compound *devikākūla*.

Now, since the term "of the limb" (*aṅgasya*) is a partitive genitive, the relationship between qualifier and qualified will be established in this way: "those [words] such as *devikā* which constitute parts of the limb. Thus it is.

If it is argued that the word *devikā* is a part (*avayava*) of the whole (*aṅga*), and therefore this fault does not apply—this is true; however, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). [The suffix] would also apply in a case such as *saudevikaḥ*, meaning "one who resides in Sudevikā. Now, if the second alternative were adopted, even so—

The form *dāvikākūlāḥ śālayaḥ* would not be established. For, when a member (*aṅga*) is qualified by [the suffixes] beginning with *devika*, and since there is the rule of "extension to that which ends in it" (*tadantavidhi*) regarding both the qualified and the qualifier, it must be understood as "of a member ending in *devikā* etc.," and not "beginning with it. Therefore...

One might argue that another effort must be undertaken so that the rule would apply even to cases where *tad* is at the beginning [of a compound]. However, when the third alternative is adopted, the operation occurs for both the simple form of *tad* and for that which ends in *tad*, even without any further effort;
for in all such instances, the initial vowel (*ācāmādeḥ*) is connected with the *devikā*-group.

Therefore, relying on that very point, he says: "Of *devikā*, *śiṃśapā*, *āditya*, *vāḍ*, *dīrghasatra*, and *śreyasa*, etc. Among these vowels beginning with *devikā*, when there is the occasion for *vṛddhi* [substitution] of the vowel *ai*, the vowel *ā* is prescribed for that initial vowel *a*.

Regarding "pūrvaśāṃśapa": as in the previous case, there is vṛddhi of the final syllable of the second member (uttarapada). That [vṛddhi] occurs specifically as the vowel *ā*, which is obtained through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule for the *devikā*-class within the governing heading on the second member (*uttarapadādhikāra*). Regarding the statement "the mention of *vahīnara* must be made": this refers to the vṛddhi that would otherwise apply to the vowel *a*.

This [rule] is for the purpose of excluding that [substitution]. Once the vowel *i* has been applied, the *vṛddhi* that would otherwise result does indeed take place. Regarding the phrase "some, however" and so forth: [the examples are] *kuṇaḍavāḍava* and others. [The word] *vihīna* is derived from the sense "a man devoid of desire and anger"; due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group, there is elision of the nasal (*n*). [The form] *vihīnara* refers to the offspring of such a person.
Vaihīnariḥ—[formed] by [the rule] *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95).

2. *kekaya-mitrayu-pralayānāṃ yāder iyaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.2). In the expression *kekaya-mitrayu-pralayānām*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denotes a part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) in relation to that which begins with *ya*. In the expression *yādeḥ*, the genitive case is a locative of substitution (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) in relation to the substitute (*ādeśa*). That which has *ya* as its initial element is called *yādi*.

The letter *y* accompanied by *a*, and the letter *y* accompanied by *u*: for those such as *kekaya*, which have *y* as their initial constituent, there is the substitution of *iy* for that [initial]. Now, one might object: the word *mitrayu* is a supreme base (*paramaprakṛti*) and not a *gotra*;
for according to the rule "that which begins with the grandson is a *gotra*" (Pāṇini 4.1.162), a *gotra* is a specific type of descendant.

Since the designation "gotra" (lineage) has been established, how can the suffix spoken of as being "from the gotra" arise from a *paramaparakṛti* (a further derivative)? To this he says: "For that which is worldly," and so forth. What, then, is the worldly *gotra*? To this he says: "And in the world," and so forth. Here...

The worldly lineage (*laukika-gotra*) is intended here. In common usage, the word *ṛṣi* is designated as "lineage" (*gotra*). Since this word *mitrayu* denotes a sage (*ṛṣi*), a suffix is applied even when the derivative is stated to be from that [word] which is a lineage.
Regarding "ṭhprāleyam": the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.3.74] "ata āgataḥ" (derived from that).

3. *na yvābhyāṃ padāntābhyāṃ pūrvau tu tābhyāmaic* (Pāṇini 7.3.3). When an increase (*vṛddhi*) is about to occur in a *taddhita* suffix beginning with a *ñ* or *ṇ* by means of [the rule] *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ* (7.2.117), this prohibition is stated; and in connection with that [prohibition], the substitutions *ai* and *au* (*aij*) take place.
By the rule "after the letter *ṭh*, [the vowel] *ai*," and so forth, he demonstrates the connection according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyena*).

Regarding the word "vaiyasanam": the root *asu* (DhP 1209) means "to throw. From the prefix *vi-* combined with this root, the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), yielding the meaning "that by which one is specifically thrown or cast away."

This is a *prādi* compound; there is the substitution of *yaṇ*; then, by the rule "born therein" (*tatra bhavaḥ*, Pāṇini 4.3.53), the suffix *aṇ* is applied. In that case, the *vṛddhi* substitution does not occur for the vowel *a* following the final *y* of the word, and therefore the augment *aij* is inserted before it. Thus, [we have] *vaiyākaraṇaḥ*. [The word *vyākaraṇa* means] those who are specifically made or explained [by grammar].
In the term *vyākaraṇam*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), forming a *prādi*-compound;

from that, the suffix *aṇ* is added according to Pāṇini 4.2.59, *tad adhīte tad veda*. In this case, by the operation of the rule [of vowel lengthening] like a rain-cloud (*parjanya-vat*), the *vṛddhi* substitution that would otherwise apply to the vowel following the final letter of the word is not realized.
Therefore, the augment *aij* occurs before [the suffix]. In the example "sauvaśvaḥ": *svaśvaḥ* means "an excellent horse";

the compound is formed as previously described, and then the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.112 in the sense of "offspring. In this case, the *vṛddhi* substitution does not occur for the vowel following the final *v* of the word; therefore, the augment *aij* occurs before it.
Regarding "ṭhārthiḥ": that which has no purpose (*artha*) is *anartha*; his descendant is formed by adding *iñ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.95 (*uta iñ*).
Regarding "ṭhyāṣṭakaḥ": [the suffix] *īkak* is added to *śakti* and *yaṣṭi* according to Pāṇini 4.4.59. Regarding "ṭhyātāḥ":
there is the substitution of *śatṛ* for the present tense marker (*laṭ*) following the root *iṇ*, and the *yaṇ* substitution occurs according to Pāṇini 6.4.81 (*iṇo yaṇ*).

Then, by the rule *tasyedam* (Pāṇini 4.3.120), the suffix *aṇ* is applied. In both cases, the letter *y* will be at the end of a word (*padānta*), just as in the example: "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas, and buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya," where the giving of buttermilk supersedes the giving of curd. Furthermore, regarding the nature of this supersession (*bādha*)...

Even so, because *ai* and *au* are eternal (*nitya*), once they have been produced, the subsequent *vṛddhi* will apply to those very same sounds. Nor should it be suspected that even these *ai* and *au* are non-eternal due to the application of another word-form (*śabdāntara-prāpti*), for they do not belong to any other word-form.
[The two operations] are not prescribed [as optional], but rather as both necessarily inapplicable, since they are preceded by *y* and *v*.
Even if there were the application of another rule, nevertheless, because the two [rules] are non-eternal (*anitya*),
once the *ai* and *au* have been substituted by virtue of their priority, then in a conflict where both apply simultaneously (*sakṛdgatau vipratiṣedhe*), that which was previously sublated...
"Since that [vṛddhi] is already barred" (Vyā.pa. 40), vṛddhi does not occur again.

Even if vṛddhi were to apply due to the principle of "recognition of recurrence" (*punar-prasaṅga-vijñāna*), the desired result would still be achieved because there is no difference [in the outcome]; therefore, he says: "the statement of the prohibition," and so forth.

*Prakḷptiḥ* means *prakalpanam*, that is, "determination. The sense is: how might that very domain of *ai* and *au*—for which there is a prohibition of the subsequent *vṛddhi* by [the rule] *yvābhyām*—be determined or established? A prohibition is stated; for what purpose, then, is *ai*...?
Why is the determination of the scope of *ec* being made? To this he says: "Let there not be [this] here.

If the delimitation of the scope of *ec* were not established by this prohibitive statement, then [the rule] would apply even in cases such as *dādhyaśviḥ* and *mādhvaśviḥ*. Therefore, so that this fault does not occur—

By the very statement of the prohibition, the scope of these two [compounds] is determined: *dadhipriya-aśva* becomes *dadhyaśva*, and *madhupriya-aśva* becomes *madhyaśva*. This is because of the metarule: "In the section on grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇa*), there is the formation of compounds for words such as *śākapārthiva* and others, along with the elision of the middle member" (Vārttika 83).

This is a compound formed by the elision of the middle term (*madhyamapadalopa*). Now, even when the prohibition is being applied, why does [the substitution] not occur here, given that there is no *vṛddhi* following the vowels *y* and *v*? To this he says: "For in this case," and so forth. For a prohibition of *vṛddhi* occurs only when there is an occasion for its application, not otherwise; and in this case, there is no such occasion.

The intention is that since there is no possibility of *vṛddhi* for a subsequent vowel by means of these two [semi-vowels], the prohibition does not apply at all. Now, one might object: the rule *ṭhacāmādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.117) is understood here, and by that, the semi-vowels (*yvau*) are qualified—namely, that the semi-vowels which take the place of a vowel that is the first among the vowels (*acāmādeḥ acas sthāne yvau*). And this is not so...

[An objection: "In examples such as *dadhy-aśva*, those two [sounds] exist in such a form; and since the *aic* vowels will not occur here, there is no purpose [for the rule]. This is not so; for in this way, the mention of "the beginning of vowels" (*acām ādi*) is intended. Therefore, if the *y* and *v* were specified, then the *vṛddhi* [vowels] would remain unspecified. Consequently, [the rule] would apply to *vṛddhi* even in this case.

There would be a prohibition: [in the case of] *dve aśītī bhṛto bhṛto bhāvī vā*, [the suffix] *ṭhañ* [is applied] by the rule *prāgvateṣṭhañ* (Pāṇini 5.1.18), resulting in *dvyāśautikaḥ*. Now, if the *vṛddhi* [vowel] is specified—meaning that the *vṛddhi* occurs [only] when it is the initial vowel among the vowels (*acāmādeḥ*)—then this fault does not arise; for in this case, the *vṛddhi* is not [applied] in such a way as to be the initial vowel among the vowels.

What then? [The rule] would be *saṃkhyāyāḥ saṃvatsarasaṃkhyasya ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.15). What then? The vowels *y* and *v* would not be specified; consequently, in forms such as *dādhyaśvi*, the diphthongs *ai* and *au* would indeed occur.
Therefore, in order to establish the proper domain for those two, it must be stated that "not" (*na*) applies.
"It is intended that this prohibition applies even to the vṛddhi of the uttarapada.
And this is obtained because it continues to apply within the governing context (*adhikāra*) of the *uttarapada*. [The example is] "pūrva-traiyaliṇde.
Here, when the vṛddhi of the *uttarapada* would have been applicable by the rule "viśo'madrāṇām" (Pāṇini 7.3.13), [this prohibition is applied].

This is a prohibition. If this were a prohibition even of the *vṛddhi* of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), then in the case of *dvyāśītika*, there would also be a prohibition of the *vṛddhi* of the subsequent member *āpta*—which is prescribed by the rule *saṃkhyāyāḥ saṃvatsarasaṃkhyasya ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.15). Therefore, he says: "In which... [and so on].

Regarding the passage beginning with "tu" and so forth: how is it that a prohibition is not applied here even though it would otherwise be desired? It is because the vowels *y* and *v* are qualifiers of the first vowel among the vowels (*acām*) of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Since the substitution applies to those *y* and *v* which stand in place of the first vowel of the subsequent member, the *vṛddhi* [strengthening] does not apply to the subsequent member itself.

It occurs; and since in the case of *dvyāśītika*, the substitution of the letter *ya* takes place in place of the first vowel among the vowels of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), there is no prohibition of *vṛddhi* here.

4. And [the suffix is applied] to *dvāra* and so forth. (Pāṇini 7.3.4) For example, *dauvārikaḥ* ("doorkeeper"). Here, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.4.69]: *tatra niyuktaḥ* ("appointed there"). Furthermore, for *dvārapālasyedaṃ dauvārapālam* ("this belongs to the door-keeper"), the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.120]: *tasyedam* ("belonging to that"). However, in common usage...
In books, there is a reading stating, "dvārapālasyevaṃ dauvārapālikam"; however,
that is incorrect, for no suffix *ṭhak* has been prescribed by any rule from the word *dvārapāla* in the sense of "belonging to him" (Pāṇini 4.3.120).

In some places, however, the reading is "dauvārapālikaḥ," meaning "the offspring of a door-keeper" (*dvārapālasyāpatyam*). In that case, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.146, *revatyādibhyaṣṭhak*. Now, one might object: "In that rule, the word *dvārapālī* is listed, not the word *dvārapāla*. To this, it is thought in reply: the word *dvārapāla* is indeed intended there.

It should be recited [in the list], for it will cause even the form *dvārapālī* to be included; this is by the rule: "When a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 29). As for those who do not recite the word *dvārapāla* there, they [include it] in the sense of offspring (*apatya*).

They cite *dauvārika* as an example of a word ending in the suffix *iñ*. But how can there be [the suffix] for "door-keeper" (*dvārapāla*) in the sense of "a group belonging to the door"? In this case as well, the initial vowel is qualified by the words beginning with "door"—that is, among the vowels of the words beginning with "door," that which is the first vowel is *aj*.

Or rather, [it is derived] from the rule to be stated later which serves as the indicator for that initial [suffix], namely: *sauvaraḥ*. This means "a treatise composed concerning vowels" (*svara*); thus, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *athikṛtya kṛte granthe* (Pāṇini 4.3.87).
[In the form] *sauvaryyaḥ*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15). [The form] *vaiyalkaśaḥ*...

Thus: *tatra bhavaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.53), by which the suffix *aṇ* is applied. *Sauvastikaḥ*: here the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule *tad āha māśabdādibhya upasaṃkhyānam* (Vārttika 482). *Sovargamanikaḥ* [the Kāśikā reads *sauvargamikaḥ*]: here the addition of *prabhūtādibhya upasaṃkhyānam* is required for the word *āha*.

(Vārttika 483: "The suffix *ṭhak* [is applied]. [Objection: "It is already established by the preceding rule. [Response: This would be the case because the letter *v* is at the end of a word (*padānta*). If, however, the derivation is made thus—"one's own study is *svādhyāyaḥ*"—then, because it is not at the end of a word, [the application of the rule does not occur].
If [the meaning] is thus obtained, why is the reading of the word *svādhyāya* (Vedic study) included as having a purpose in that derivation?
To this he says: "Nevertheless, even so," and so forth.
But how is the word *svādhyāya* established from the word *sva*?

Thus he says: "For even in that case, at the beginning," and so forth. Regarding "sphaiyakṛtaḥ" [the Kāśikā reads *sphaikṛtaḥ*], the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "ṛṣy-andhakavṛṣṇikurubhyaśca" (Pāṇini 4.1.114). Regarding "sauvādumṛdavaḥ" [the Kāśikā reads *sovādumṛdavam*], here too—
The suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.120] *tasyedam*.

The same applies to *śauvanam*. Regarding *śauvam*, there is the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*) by [Pāṇini 6.4.144] *nastaddhite*. Regarding *śauvādaṃṣṭraḥ*, there is lengthening [of the penultimate vowel] by [Pāṇini 6.3.137] *anyeṣām api*.

5. And [the suffix is applied] after *nyagrodha* alone. (7.3.5) [The example is] *naiyagrodhaḥ*. [This is derived by applying] the suffix *aṇ* according to [Pāṇini 4.3.134] "its modification" (*tasya vikāraḥ*).
[The word] *nyagrodhaḥ* [is explained as]: "it grows downwards" (*nyaṅ rohati*), [or] "it bends down" (*nyañcati*).

From the root *añc* with the suffix *kvin* by [Pāṇini 3.2.59], there is the substitution of *ku* for the *kvin* suffix by [Pāṇini 8.2.62]—that is, the letter *ka*; then the *yaṇ* substitute occurs for the *i*. From the root *ruh* preceded by *nyak*, the suffix *ac* is added by [Pāṇini 3.1.134]. In that case, by [Pāṇini 7.3.53], the letter *ha* is replaced by *dha* in *nyaṅkvādi* words; then, by [Pāṇini 8.2.39], the *jaś* substitute applies to the *jhal* sounds at the end of a word.

(8.2.39) Thus, the letter *k* becomes *g*, and there is the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. When the word *nyagrodha* is derived in this manner, since the rule "na yvābhyām" (Pāṇini 7.3.3) already establishes the change of the final *y* [to *i*] because it is at the end of a word, this [present rule] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*), so that it may apply only to the isolated [final *y*].

"Lest [the rule] apply to the beginning of that [word]," [it is said]; "in the view that [words] are not derived [from roots and suffixes], this is for the purpose of an injunction," because the letter *y* is not at the end of a word.

6. *na karmavyatihāre* (Pāṇini 7.3.6). Regarding what was stated: there is a prohibition of *vṛddhi* and the introduction of *aij*. Examples include *vyāvakrośī* (the *mu.* manuscript reads *vyākrośī*) and so forth. [The root] *kruś* [is used] in the sense of "calling out" (*āhvāne*).

From the roots *rud* "to weep" (DhP 856), *likh* "to arrange letters" (DhP 1365), *carc* "to study" (DhP 1712, belonging to the *cur*-class), and *has* "to laugh" (DhP 721)—preceded by the prefixes *vi-* and *ava-*—the suffix *ṇac* is applied; from that which ends in *ṇac*, the suffix *añ* is added. This is as stated here.

When the operation [of the suffix] is prohibited, there is indeed *vṛddhi*, because two prohibitions are understood to indicate the original state (*prakṛtyartha*). Thus, by the rule "ṭiḍḍhāṇañ" (Pāṇini 4.1.15), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied.

7. And [the suffix *ṭhak* is applied] after *svāgata* and others. (Pāṇini 4.4.7) For example: *svāgatikaḥ*. "A welcome arrival" is *svāgatam*. The suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule: "In [the sense of] 'he says that,' etc., there is an addition [of the suffix] after *prabhūta* and others" (Vārttika 483). For example: *svādhvarikaḥ*.

Here too, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.4.8] *ṭh carati*. A beautiful sacrifice (*adhvara*) is a *svadhvara*. Regarding the rule *svāṅgiḥ* and so forth, there is the rule *svāṅgirṇyāḍiḥ*. By [Pāṇini 4.1.95] *ata iṅ*, one whose limbs are beautiful is *svaṅgaḥ*, and one whose limbs are gone is *vyaṅgaḥ*.

The vowel *a* has disappeared from this [word] *vyaṅ*. *Vyavahāraḥ* is "the act of dealing" (*vyavaharaṇam*), derived with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). Now, one might object: since this word *vyavahāra* occurs in the sense of "mutual exchange of actions," the prohibition established by the rule *na karmavyatīhāre* (Pāṇini 7.3.6) is already established there; why, then, is it recited here?

Thus he says: "This word *vyavahāra*... What, then, is the worldly (*laukika*)? The worldly conduct by which one is called *vyāvahārika* (conventional) in the world due to such behavior—that is to be understood. Regarding the term *svāpateyam*: [it is derived] from the rule *pathyatithivasatisvapateḍḍhañ*.
"But how is there an application [of the rule] here, since its *v* is not at the end of a word?
To this he says: "Its application occurs because of the recitation of the word *sva-* in the list beginning with *dvāra-*.
The intention is that this is by way of the rule *tadādividhi* (application to what begins with that). How it becomes a *tadādividhi* is as follows:
It is stated in that very same place:

8. *śvāder iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.112). [The examples are] *śvābhastrī* and *śvādaṃṣṭrī*. [The analysis is as follows: "one whose bellows (*bhastrā*) are like a dog" and "one whose fangs (*daṃṣṭrā*) are like a dog"—these are *bahuvrīhi* compounds, with the shortening of the initial vowel of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*). But by what [rule]...?

The prohibition of *vṛddhi* for [the word] *śva* and others would follow; for this prohibition is stated, yet its [the word *śva*’s] *v* is not at the end of a word (*padānta*). To this he says: "The word *śva* is recited in the *dvārādi* group. But surely the word *śva* alone is recited in the *dvārādi* group; what possibility [of the application of the rule] is there in that case?

If it is argued that there should be an application to that which begins with [the element] because of the rule "when a grammatical operation is prescribed with reference to something, it applies to that and what begins with it" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 127)? This is not so; for an application to that which begins with [the element] occurs only when there is a mention of the seventh case (locative) and a mention of *hal* (a consonant), and neither of these two conditions exists here. Therefore, he says: "And in that case..."

And so forth. The intention is that if the rule for *tadādi* (that which begins with that) were not applied there, this statement of prohibition would be meaningless, because there would be no possibility [of the application] in the first place. The purpose of this indicator (*jñāpaka*) is seen in examples such as *śauvādaṃṣṭro maṇiḥ*.
Regarding the prohibition of *vṛddhi*:
"The mention of those beginning with the letter *i* must be made. This means that a *taddhita* suffix beginning with the vowel *i* is to be understood;
thus, an explanation must be provided for that mention of those beginning with *i*.

He asks, "For what purpose? and says: "For the sake of *śvāgaṇika* and others. That [term] is so called because it has the purpose or utility (*artha*) of *śvāgaṇika* and others. However, their purpose is simply the initial *vṛddhi* [strengthening]. In that regard, it is as follows:
The explanation: The mention of *iñ* here is for the purpose of indicating any *taddhita* suffix beginning with *i*; therefore, the prohibition applies elsewhere as well in the case of a *taddhita*.
[Regarding the phrase] "of that which ends in it": this refers to one who is other than a descendant (*anyanāyī*) of someone ending in *iñ*. But how is it desired [to apply] elsewhere?

[Objection: Should not the elision [of the *iñ* suffix] occur by the rule "the elision of *iñ* when a *taddhita* suffix beginning with *ṭha* follows" (Pāṇini 6.4.148), even in other cases? [Response: This is not a fault; for here, "after *iñ*" (*iñi*) is not a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*), but rather a locative of sequence (*parasaptamī*). If it were a locative of cause, there would be a prohibition of the *vṛddhi* [vowel substitution] caused by the *aṇ* suffix.

There would be no prohibition [of the elision]. However, when the locative case refers to something else (*parasaptamī*), even though the elision (*lopa*) is performed, the prohibition is nonetheless established by virtue of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element). For example, in *śvābhastram*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to *iñaśca* (Pāṇini 4.2.112).
9. *padāntasyānyatarasyām* (7.3.9). Since the preceding rule would have made [the substitution] obligatory, this option is stated as a prohibition. "Of the end of a word" (*padāntasya*) means:
of that which ends with the word *pada*. For example, *śvāpadam*: [it is called] *śvāpada* because its foot (*pada*) is like that of a dog (*śvan*).
This [word] for him is *śvāpada*; [the form] *śauvāpada* is derived by applying the rule "lengthening is also seen in other cases" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.137).
10. *Utarapadasya* (7.3.10).
This is stated because an increase (*vṛddhi*) of the vowel at the beginning of a member (*aṅga*) would otherwise be applicable;
however, [this is not so] in cases such as *ṭhavayavādṛtauḥ* (7.3.11).

Because of the mention of the fifth case (*pañcamī-nirdeśa*), even without the governing rule for the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada-adhikāra*), the operation will apply to the subsequent member alone by virtue of the rule *tasmād ity uttarasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.67). Therefore, why is there a need for the governing rule on the subsequent member?
To this he says: "In cases where," etc. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), [the examples] such as *hṛdbhagasindhvante* are included.

The rules beginning with *pūrvapadasya* (7.3.19), *ṭhanunnatikādīnāñca* (7.3.20), and *devatādvandve ca* (7.3.21) are included here. Since there is no mention of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in these, even in the absence of the governing heading *uttarapade* (in a following word), the substitution applies to the vowel at the beginning of the *aṅga* itself.

The *vṛddhi* substitution would apply [to the first member], not to the final member (*uttarapada*). Therefore, for that purpose, the governing rule concerning the final member (*uttarapadādhikāra*) is established.
If this is so, then the rule "from a part of a *ṛtu*" (Pāṇini 7.3.11) need not be cited here. In this case—

Anticipating the objection, "Is this not because a mention in the ablative case (*pañcamī-nirdeśa*) exists?", he states that even where there is a mention in the ablative case for the sake of another purpose, the incidental operation (*prāsaṅgika-kārya*) still applies— beginning with the words "even in mentions in the ablative case," and so forth.

He states another purpose [for the rule] with the words "and for the sake of *vṛddhi*," and so forth. This designation "*vṛddhi*"—meaning that which is prescribed under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*)—is applied so that it may occur; thus, the governing heading of the subsequent member is established. But what is the reason for doing so?
Is the designation "vṛddhi" (increment) being sought? To this he says: "When there is vṛddhi in the uttarapada," and so forth.

This is for the purpose that, when an *uttarapada* characterized by *vṛddhi* is prescribed under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of *uttarapada*, the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) should have its final syllable accented acute (*antodātta*). [Regarding] "when there is vṛddhi in the *uttarapada*":

In the rule *sarvañca* (Pāṇini 6.2.105), it is prescribed that "the vṛddhi which is ordained under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of 'subsequent member' (*uttarapada')" applies. How can this be understood? Only if the governing heading of "subsequent member" is established for the sake of designation (*vyapadeśa*), and not otherwise.
Therefore, the governing rule for the subsequent term must be formulated for the purpose of designation.

11. *avayavād ṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.11). Regarding the mention of *ṛtaḥ*: this is not a reference to the phonetic form (*svarūpa*), but rather a reference to the meaning (*artha*). For it is said "from a part" (*avayavāt*), and this very thing is a part of that which contains the vowel *ṛ*.
[The compound] occurs. When these two [words] are understood as expressing a whole (*avayavin*), this is understood as a designation of the meaning;
consequently, the grammatical operation is understood to apply to a word denoting a season (*ṛtu*) that follows a preceding member which denotes a part (*avayava*).
Thus he says: "denoting a part," and so forth. "[It is] an *ekadeśisamāsa* (part-whole compound)."

By the rule *pūrvāparādibhiḥ sūtreṇa* (Pāṇini 2.2.1). Now, an objection is raised: "Is it not the case that the rule *grahaṇavatā prātipadikena tadantavidhiḥ pratiṣidhyate* (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 89) prohibits the extension of a grammatical operation to a word ending in [the specified term] when that term is used as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)? Therefore, how can a suffix prescribed after *varṣā* and *hemanta* be understood to apply to words ending in those stems? To this he says: "In that regard, regarding the seasons... (*tatra ṛtau*).

Regarding the rule "in the formation of words expressing growth, the parts [of the compound] [are treated as the prior member]," [the example is] *paurvavarṣikaḥ* (or *paurvavārṣikam*, according to the Kāśikā). Having formed a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) from "those which are both prior and the rains" (*pūrvāś ca tā varṣāś ca*), the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is to be applied in the sense of "belonging to that" (*bhava*).

In this context, the word *pūrva* denotes time and not a constituent part; thus, the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs only for the initial vowel of the *aṅga*. Now, one might ask: why does the suffix *ṭhak* not also apply here by means of the rule of "specification of that which ends with [the preceding element]" (*tadantavidhi*)?
To this he says: "For only that which has a constituent part as its predecessor," and so forth.
12. [The suffix *cha* is applied] after a word denoting a country (*janapada*) ending in *su*, *sarva*, or *ardha*.

(7.3.12) Regarding the term "of a country" (*janapadasya*): this is not a mention of the specific form [of the word *janapada*] itself, because it is prohibited in the subsequent rule by the expression "not for the Madras" (*amadrāṇām*, 7.3.13). For in that subsequent rule, this very mention of "country" (*janapada*) is carried over [as an anuvṛtti].

Therefore, if there were a grasping of the word-form (*svarūpa*) here, the prohibition of "Madra" would be purposeless; consequently, this is a grasping of the meaning. Thus he says: "From these—*su*, *sarva*, and *ardha*—[the suffix is applied] to that which follows and denotes a country (*janapada*)."
And so forth. Regarding "supāñcālakaḥ": this is a *prādisamāsa* (prepositional compound) meaning "excellent Pañcālas.

Regarding "sarvapāñcālakaḥ": this is a *karmadhāraya* (descriptive compound) according to [Pāṇini 2.1.49], "pūrvakālaika... and so on. Regarding "ardhapāñcālakaḥ": this is by means of the word "ardha" [in the rule] "ardhaṃ napuṃsakam" (Pāṇini 2.2.2).

This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. In all cases, when a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is applied in a sense such as "belonging to" (*śaiṣika*), pertaining to birth, and so forth, [a question arises]: how can the suffix prescribed by the rule "from a name of a country, [the suffix denotes] the country and what belongs to it" (Pāṇini 4.2.124) be applied to a word ending in that [suffix]?
To this he says: "From words meaning 'good,' 'all,' 'half,' and 'directional,' etc. and so on.

13. *diśo'madrāṇām* (Pāṇini 7.3.13). [The example is] *pūrvapāñcālakaḥ*. [The analysis is: "he who exists among the eastern Pāñcālas"; thus, there is a compound in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), followed by the suffix *vṛñ*. Why [is the word] *diśaḥ* ("direction") mentioned? [Consider the case of] *pūrvaṃ pāñcālānām* ("the east of the Pāñcālas").

*Pūrvāpāñcālaḥ*: by the rule *pūrvāparādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.1), this is a compound formed with a single substitute (*ekādeśisamāsa*). That which exists there is *paurvapāñcālaḥ*. Here, the term "directional word" (*dikśabda*) is intended to mean that which refers to a direction; however, this word *pūrva* does not refer to a direction, but rather to a part (*avayava*). Therefore...

The vṛddhi substitution occurs only for the first member [of the compound]. The separation of the rule (yogavibhāga) is for the sake of what follows: so that the vṛddhi may apply only to the second member when it is a direction (diś), in the case of villages and cities of the Easterners (prāñcaḥ), and not after the words su, sarva, or ardha.
14. *prācāṃ grāmanagarāṇām* (7.3.14).

The term *janapadasya* (of the country) from [7.3.12] is understood here; therefore, this mention of *prācām* (of the easterners) is understood as a reference to a region (*deśa*) and not a reference to teachers (*ācārya*). Thinking thus, he says: "In the region of the easterners..."

Regarding the passage beginning with "of villages" (*grāmāṇām*) and ending with "Pūrveṣukāmaśamaḥ": the compound *pūrvaiṣukāmaśamī* is formed by the rule *diksaṃkhye saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 2.1.50), meaning "it is both *pūrvā* [eastern] and *iṣukāmaśamī*. Then, for the sense of "belonging to that place" (*bhavārtha*), the suffix *ñ* is applied according to the rule *dikpūrvapadād asaṃjñāyāṃ ñaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.107).

"‘pūrvapāṭaliputrakaḥ’ [means] ‘one who resides in the eastern Pāṭaliputra. This is a compound in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), formed by the rule *pūrvādibhyo navabhyo vā* (5.3.38). Then, by the rule *ropadhetoḥ* (4.2.123), the suffix *vuñ* is applied.
But surely there is only one Pāṭaliputra; how then can there be another Pāṭaliputra there?"

Because there is no [other] thing to be excluded, how can the word "Pāṭaliputra" be qualified by the word "eastern"? There is no fault, because the word "Pāṭaliputra" applies to a single part of Pāṭaliputra.
Now, for what purpose is the mention of "city" (nagara), since it would be established simply by saying "of villages" (grāmāṇām)?

For even a city is indeed a village; "village" is a conventional term for a settlement of people, and a city is likewise a settlement of people. Therefore, a city is also a village, because those rules which are intended for a village are not applied in a city either. For instance: "one should not eat... [the rule does not apply].

When it is said, "The village cock is not to be eaten" or "The village pig is not to be eaten," even the city [cock or pig] is not eaten; when it is said, "One should not study in the village," one does not study even in the city.

Therefore, the city is also a village. And having established this—[from the rule] "And from a village of the North... [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logic of the preceding argument.]
Regarding the rules *bahvaco'ntodāttāt* (4.2.109), *vāhīkagrāmebhyaśca* (4.2.117),

and *dikśabdā grāmajanapadākhyānacānarāṭeṣu* (6.2.103), he states— beginning with "precisely because of being a *grāma*"— that by the mention of *grāma* in these rules, the mention of *nagara* is also included. If that is so...

If a city (*nagara*) were also considered a village (*grāma*), then would the mention of "city" not be required in the rule *ṭhviśiṣṭaliṅgo nadīdeśo 'grāmāḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.7)? This is true; however, in that case, an exception for cities must be stated there. And from what cause does this very difference in relation arise, for which [the exception is made]?
The distinction between "village" (grāma) and "city" (nagara) is made for the sake of the grammatical rule. Thus he says:

"For [a compound] having 'direction' (dik) as its prior member," and so forth. For if, just as a collective term beginning with a direction—such as *Pūrveṣukāmaśamī*—is the name of a village (*grāma*), so too...

It might also be the name of a city; in that case, the relationship would not be distinct. And just as the form of words such as *Pāṭaliputra*, being used as the latter member of a compound, denotes a city, so too if it were the name of a village, even then the relationship would not be distinct.

But this is not so; for the word denoting a village consists of a preceding and a following collection [of phonemes] of one kind, whereas the word denoting a city consists of a preceding and a following collection of another kind.
Therefore, due to the difference between the village and the city, there is a difference in their relationship. Thus...
Having shown the cause for the distinction in relations, he states the distinction in relations itself, beginning with "In that case" (*tatra*), and so forth.

"Of those denoting a village" (*grāmavācinām*) refers to such examples as *pūrvaiṣukāmaśamī* and the like. "Of the constituent part" (*avayavasya*) refers to such examples as *iṣukāmaśamī*, *kṛṣṇamṛttikā*, and the like. "From a word denoting a direction" (*dikśabdāt*).
Regarding "pūrvādēḥ | ṭhitara-tra tu" and so forth, and [the rule] "dēśa utarēṣāṃ nagarāṇām," the connection is made here that "vṛddhi occurs," and this is what is required.

In cases such as *pūrveṣukāmaśama*, because the internal operation (*antaraṅga*) of *guṇa* takes place first between the two members of the compound, the conditions for the rule for *vṛddhi*—namely, that a word denoting a direction and the word "village" (*grāma*) must be the final member (*uttarapada*)—no longer obtain; thus, *vṛddhi* would not apply. For *vṛddhi* [is prescribed]...

Once the taddhita suffix has been applied, that which arises by depending upon it becomes *bahiraṅga*; whereas the *guṇa* substitution, which applies prior to the production of the taddhita suffix, is *antaraṅga*. Nor can it be argued that the *vṛddhi* will occur by virtue of an explicit rule, for [the rule] where there is no single-substitute (*ekādeśa*)...

And there is scope for this statement in cases such as *pūrvakārṣṇamṛtika* and so forth. Furthermore, the treatment of the end as the beginning (*antādivadbhāva*) does not apply here, because of the prohibition: "When [a grammatical operation] depends on both [the preceding and the following], it is not like the end or the beginning" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 51). Therefore, in this case, both the prior member (*pūrvapada*) and the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) are relied upon.
To one who might raise this objection, he replies with the words "In cases such as *Pūrveṣukāmaśamī*," and so forth.

Just as this meaning was indicated by the mention [of the word] *nendrasya parasya* (Pāṇini 7.3.22), so too has it been established in the rule *adasa āṬ sulopaśca* (7.2.107). [The same applies to] *grāmanagarāṇām*.
Thus, the plural number is used for the purpose of refuting the injunction regarding the essential nature [of the agent].

15. [The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied] after a numeral and after a word denoting a number of years. (Pāṇini 5.1.58) For example: *dvisāṃvatsarikaḥ*. As before, there is a compound for the sake of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*); thereafter, as previously, the suffix *ṭhañ* is added.

[The examples] "dviṣāṣṭikaḥ" and "dvisāptatikaḥ" [are given]. But [one might object]: in the rule "tam adhīṣṭo bhṛto bhūto bhāvī" (Pāṇini 5.1.80), the governing word "kālāt" (from 5.1.78) is understood; however, "dviṣaṣṭi" and so on are not words denoting time (*kālaśabda*), but rather words denoting number (*saṃkhyāśabda*). Therefore, how can that which is prescribed under the heading of "time" apply here?
What does he produce as a condition? He says: "The word 'sixty-two,' etc.

There, a word denoting time is understood by the inclusion of "time" (*kāla*); for when the word "sixty-two," etc., refers to years as numerable units, then, because it denotes time, it is the word "time."
It occurs. From that, the suffix *taddhita* denoting time (*kāla*) is produced.
Now, for what purpose is the mention of "year" (*saṃvatsara*), since in the rule *parimāṇāntasyāsaṃjñāśāṇayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.17), by the word "measure" (*parimāṇa*), [the year is already included]?
Only the cause of measurement is grasped here, but not the cause of measurement by height and circumference as in the case of a *prastha* measure and the like; for otherwise,
the prohibition of the *śāṇa* would be meaningless, since a *śāṇa* [is not such a cause].

"Dimension (*parimāṇa*) is the cause for delimiting height, breadth, and circumference; therefore, time (*kāla*) also becomes a cause for delimitation, and consequently, since it too is a dimension, would the form *saṃvatsara* not be established simply by [Pāṇini 5.1.57], namely: 'After a word denoting a measure (*parimāṇa*), except for *asaṃjñā* and *śāṇa*, [the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied]...?"

To dispel this objection, he says: "The mention of *saṃvatsara*," and so forth. The mention of *saṃvatsara* is for the purpose that, by the mention of *parimāṇa*, there should not be the inclusion of the measurement of time (*kālaparimāṇa*).
By the mention of *saṃvatsara*, this meaning is made known: [that even] in the mention of *parimāṇa*...

"There is no apprehension of the measure of time. Consequently, wherever there is an apprehension of measurement, there the measure of time is not apprehended. With the words "By that," etc., he demonstrates what is established when, upon the apprehension of measurement, the measure of time is not apprehended.

"In this case, there is no vṛddhi of the subsequent syllable," according to the rule *parimāṇāntasya* (Pāṇini 7.3.17), and so forth. Regarding the form *dvivarṣā*: [it means] "one who has been hired for two years," or "one who has existed for two years," or "one who will exist for two years. As before, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied;
then, while the rule *varṣālluk* (5.1.88) is in effect, the rule *citavati nityam* (5.1.89) applies.

Thus, there is elision (*luk*). [The objection that] "it is not an exclusion (*paryudāsa*)" is addressed as follows: when the prohibition of *ṅīp* is to be applied, the prohibition by that [rule] operates; therefore, by the rule "after a *dvigu* compound" (Pāṇini 4.1.21), *ṅīp* does not occur.

16. *varṣasyābhaviṣyati* (Pāṇini 5.1.87). [The example is: *dve varṣe adhīṣṭo bhṛto vā karma kariṣyatīti daivārṣiko manuṣyaḥ* ("A man hired or commissioned for two years who will perform work is called *daivārṣika*"). Here, when the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix is produced from the words *adhīṣṭa* and *bhṛta*, the future tense is understood; therefore...
Someone might have the misconception that there should also be a prohibition regarding those two;

therefore, in order to dispel that, he says: "In the case of *adhi* and *īṣat*, etc. But what is the reason that [the prohibition] does not apply? He says: "For it is understood," etc. In that regard, if [it were] another word, "two..."

When [the suffix] is employed in the sense of "he will perform the work having been requested or hired for a year," then it is understood as referring to the future; not otherwise. Therefore, since that [suffix] is not the meaning of a *taddhita* [primary derivative], the prohibition regarding the non-future tense does not apply to those who have been requested or hired. But surely—

Since the word *manuṣya* is the object denoted, there ought to be elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṭhañ* by the rule "when *manuṣya* is the object denoted and it possesses intelligence, [the suffix] is always [elided]" (Pāṇini 5.1.89). How, then, is the form *dvivārṣikaḥ manuṣyaḥ* ("a two-year-old human") established? This is not a fault; for this elision does not occur without qualification, but rather only in a specific domain. How so?

In that case, the inclusion of the word *nitya* (always) should be made; for since the result is already established by the preceding rule, its commencement would suffice to ensure that the elision (*luk*) occurs invariably. However, it has been included so that it may apply specifically to the particular context [of the past], and not to cases such as *adhoṣṭa* ("requested") and the like. Therefore, in the case of *adhoṣṭa* and so forth—
By the rule "ṭha-varṣāl luk" (Pāṇini 5.1.88), the elision (luk) occurs only optionally.

17. *paramāṇvantasyāsaṃjñāśāṇayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.17). Since the status of being subsequent (*paratva*) is not possible for the word *saṃjñā*, he says "in the domain of *saṃjñā*" and so forth, indicating that this is a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*). [He also says] "and when *śāṇa* is the subsequent member."

The word "object" (viṣaya) is required [to complete the sense]. Although the status of being subsequent (*paratva*) is possible for the following member (*uttarapada*), namely *śāṇa*, nevertheless, it is difficult to maintain that a single locative case functions both as a locative of object (*viṣayasaptamī*) and as a locative of sequence (*parasaptamī*). Therefore...

The locative case here is appropriately used in the sense of "with respect to" (*viṣaya-saptamī*) even with the word *śāṇa* as the final member [of a compound]. For example, in *dvikauḍavikam*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied according to *prāgvateṣṭhañ* (Pāṇini 5.1.18). Furthermore, because this suffix does not denote a price (*anārhīya*), the elision (*luk*) prescribed by *adhyardhapūrvadvigoḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.28) does not occur.

Regarding the term *dvisauvarṇikaḥ* (according to the Kāśikā, it is *dvisauvarṇikam*): the suffix is the same. But how is there vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) here, given that it is stated "of that which ends in a measure-word" (*parimāṇāntasya*), and since a *suvarṇa* is a weight-measure (*unmāna*) based on gravity, not a measure-word (*parimāṇa*)? There is no fault here.

The activity of the Teacher indicates this: "In this context, even the measure of weight (*gurutva-parimāṇa*) is understood as *pūrimāṇa* because it serves as a cause for delimitation. This is why he begins the prohibition regarding the *śāṇa* [weight] with the rule "not after a numeral name" (*asaṃjñā-śāṇayoḥ*). Now, why is there not elision (*luk*) by the rule "preceded by *adhyardha*" (Pāṇini 5.1.28)?
Does it occur? He says: "vibhāvā" and so forth. Regarding "dvinaiṣkikam": the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule "asamāse niṣkādibhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.1.20).
Regarding "pāñcalohitikaḥ" (the Kāśikā reads "pāñcalohitikam"): in that very same [rule].
When the suffix *ṭhak* is applied, by the rule "ṭhbhasyāḍhea taddhite" (Vārttika 731), there occurs the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*),
resulting in the removal of the feminine suffixes *ṅīp* and *nakāra* prescribed by the rule "varṇādanudātād ato dhātto taḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.39).
The suffix *ṭhak* (forming *dvaikulijika*) is applied according to the rule "prāgvateṣṭhañ" (Pāṇini 5.1.18), as stated in the *Kāśikā*.

18. *Je* [is used] for the *proṣṭhapadās*. (7.3.18) The rule *saṃkhyāyāḥ* (7.3.15) is no longer in force. Regarding the statement, "The word *je* is indicated as having the sense of *jāta* (born/produced)": this is an application of *je*, which is a single constituent part of the word *jāta*. For it indeed occurs [in that sense].

There is also the usage of even a single part of a word, as in "Bhīma" for Bhīmasena, or "Satyabhāmā" for Bhāmā. Therefore, it should be understood that by the use of a single part of a word denoting a genus (*jāti*), the meaning of that genus is indicated.

Regarding "in the *proṣṭhapadā* [nakṣatra]," there is the absence of the form corresponding to the joined [time] (*yuktavat*) by the rule "when *lup* [is applied], the gender and number are like those of the joined [word]" (1.2.51). Regarding "the *bhadrapada* [days]," since it is a time joined with the *bhadrapada* [nakṣatra], the grammatical operations such as the suffix *aṇ* should be prescribed as before.

19. *hṛdbhagasindhvante pūrvapadasya ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.19). In the word *sauhārda*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [the rule] *tasyedam* (4.3.120). When the suffix *aṇ* is applied from the word *suhṛdaya*, then [the substitution of *hṛd* for *hṛdaya* occurs] by [the rule] *hṛdayasya hṛllekhayadaṇlāseṣu* (6.3.50).

Regarding *hṛdbhāva*: in the word *sauhārdyam*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied by the rule *guṇavacanabrāhmaṇādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.124), and the substitution of *hṛd* for *hṛdaya* occurs by the rule *vā śokaṣyañrogeṣu* (Pāṇini 6.3.51). Regarding *saubhāgineyaḥ* and *daurbhāgineyaḥ*, [the substitution of] *inaṅ* for the vowel of *ka* occurs according to the rule *kalyāṇyādīnāminaṅ ca*.
By [Pāṇini 4.1.126], when the suffix *ḍhak* is applied, the substitution of *inaṅ* occurs.

Regarding "saktu-sindhu," it is a compound with the middle member elided (*madhyamapadalopa*), because it belongs to the *śākapārthiva* group. Regarding "sāktusaindhava," since the suffix *aṇ* would otherwise apply by [Pāṇini 4.2.119] "or from *or*," the rule "and from *kaccha* etc. [4.2.133] applies.

(4.2.133) [The suffix] *aṇ* [is applied]. Now, since the word *sindhu* alone is listed there [in the sūtra], how can [the suffix] apply to that which ends in it? To this he says: "by that," and so forth. But how is the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) obtained by means of that word *sindhu*, given that [the rule] states: "By a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) accompanied by a mention..."?
Is it not the case that the rule for *tadanta* (referring to a word ending in a specified stem) is prohibited by the statement "there is no *tadanta*-rule" (Vyāḍipāṭha 89)?
This is not a fault; the letter *ca* in that [sūtra] has the sense of including what was not explicitly mentioned, and by means of it, the suffix occurs even after a word ending in the stem *sindhu*.

20. And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after the group beginning with *anuśatika*. (Pāṇini 4.2.80) Regarding the term *anuśatika*: that which is purchased for a hundred is *śatikaḥ*, formed by the suffix *ṭhan* according to Pāṇini 5.1.21 (*śatācca ṭhanyatāvaśate*). That which has followed along with what is worth a hundred is *anuśatikaḥ*; from this, [the suffix *cha* is applied] by the rule *tasyedam* ("belonging to this").

(4.3.120) [The suffix] *aṇ* [is applied]: as in *ānuśātikam*, *ānuhauḍikam*. [The suffix] *ṭhak* [is applied] by [the rule] 4.4.8 *carati*: as in *ānusāṃvatsarikam*. [The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied] by the extended application (*atideśa*) from 5.1.96 *tatra ca dīyate kāryaṃ bhavavat*, [specifically] by 4.3.67 *bahvaco 'ntodāttāt*.

Thus [is formed] *ṭhañ*. [The form] *āṅgāravaiṇavaḥ* is derived by [the application of] *aṇ* according to [Pāṇini 4.1.92]: *tasyāpatyam* ("his descendant"). [The form] *āsihātyam* is derived by [the application of] *aṇ* according to [Pāṇini 4.3.53]: *tatra bhavaḥ* ("located there"). [The form] *āsyahātyam* is derived by [the application of] *aṇ* according to [Pāṇini 5.2.61]:
*vimuktādibhyo’ṇ*. In the reading *āsyahaitikam*, [it means] "this belongs to him" (*tad asya*).
The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied here according to the rule *prayojanam* (Pāṇini 5.1.109), as in the previous case. But an objection may be raised:

since the word *prātipadikāt* ("from a nominal stem") is understood to carry over [from the preceding sūtra], and since *asyahati* and *asyaheti* are compounds of words (*padasamudāya*), not nominal stems (*prātipadika*), how can a suffix be added to them? Or even if the suffix were added, how [could it be justified]?

To the question, "Why is there no elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending? he says: "Precisely for this reason," and so forth. Regarding "Vādhyaugaḥ": [it is derived] by *Pāṇini* 4.1.104, *anṛṣyānantarye bidādibhyo’ñ*.
Regarding "Pauṣkarasādirānuhāratiḥ": [it is derived] by 4.1.96, *bāhvādibhyaśca*, with the suffix *iṇ*.
Regarding "Kaurukātyaḥ" [the *Kāśikā* says: from *Kuru-kātya*; the suffix *yañ* is applied because it belongs to the *gara-ga-ādi* group].

Regarding "Kaurupāñcālaḥ": the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.53] "tatra bhavaḥ. Now, one might object: since these are words denoting a country (*janapada*), shouldn't the suffix *vuñ* be applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.124] "janapadatadavadhyośca"?
To this he says: "A collection of districts [is not included] by the mention of 'district,'" and so forth.

For the word *kuru-pañcāla* denotes a collection of districts (*janapada-samudāya*), and since a collection of districts is not grasped by the mention of a single district, how could there be any occasion for the suffix *vuñ*? [The example is given as] *audaka-śauddhi*.

From the rule *ṭhañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95), we have "this-worldly" (*aihalaukika*) and "other-worldly" (*pāralaukika*). According to the Vārttika (459), *lokotarapadāt*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after a compound whose final member is *loka*. This is that [suffix].

In the verse beginning with "samānasya tadādeśca," this desired view is recited: "sārvalaukikaḥ. [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.1.44: "lokasarvalokāṭṭhañ. "Sārvapauruṣam": the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.3.120: "tasyedam. "Sārvabhaumaḥ."

Thus: [the forms] *sarvabhūmika* and *pārthiva* are derived by adding the suffixes *aṇ* and *añ* respectively according to Pāṇini 5.1.41 (*sarvabhūmipṛthivībhyāmaṇañau*). [The form] *prāyaugika* is derived by adding the suffix *aṇ* according to Vārttika 456 (*adhyātmāditvāt*), which prescribes *aṇ* for words beginning with *adhyātma*. [The form] *pārastraiṇeya* is derived by adding the suffix *inaṅ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.127 (*kulaṭāyā vā*). In that context, [the rule] *strībhyo ḍhak* (Pāṇini 4.1.120) applies.

The rule *kalyāṇyādīnāminaṅ ca* (4.1.146) continues [to apply]. In the case of *rājapauruṣyam*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied because the word belongs to the *brāhmaṇādi* group (5.1.124). In the case of *sautranāḍiḥ*, the suffix *iñ* is applied by *ata iñ* (4.1.95). In the case of *ābhigāmikaḥ*:
The suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied [after *arhat*] in the sense of "one who deserves to be approached," according to Pāṇini 5.1.63 (*abhigamamarhatītyārhīyaṣṭhak*).

In the cases of *ādhidaivikam* and *ādhibhautikam*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava*), because they belong to the group beginning with *adhyātma* (Vārttika 456). In the case of *cāturvedyam*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in its own primary sense (*svārthika*).
And it must be stated that [the suffix] *ṣyañ* is used for its own sake (i.e., as a primary derivative) for the purpose of establishing the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*) and so forth.

21. *devatādvandve ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.21). [The example is] *āgnimārutī*. "Agni and Marut" form a *dvandva* compound; that which has these two as its deities is expressed by the suffix *aṇ* according to *sāsya devatā* (Pāṇini 4.2.24); thereafter, there is the *vṛddhi* strengthening of both the preceding and the following vowels.
By the rule *ṭhidvṛddhau* (Pāṇini 6.3.28), the vowel *i* is substituted for the final syllable of the word *agni* when it is the basis for the suffix *anaṅ*;
then, by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied.
Regarding the phrase "which is a dual compound of deities related to a *sūkta*," etc.: that which partakes of a *sūkta* [is so designated].

"Related to a *sūkta*" means that for which the oblation (*havis*) is set aside is "related to the oblation. This qualification of the *dvandva* compound is mediated by its meaning. As for the statement "and this does not occur here," etc., how is this specific distinction obtained when there is a general statement? He thinks thus: "Not [the word] *nendra*sya..."

Regarding the rule *parasya* (7.3.22), a separation of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) must be made by adding *na* [to read as *parasya na*]. By this, [the substitution] does not occur elsewhere for words related to a *sūkta* or related to an oblation (*havis*). For example: *skāndaviśākhaḥ*. Here, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to *tasyedam* (4.3.120). Also: *brāhmaprajāpatyam*.
[The suffix] *ṇya* [is applied after a word ending in] *ditya*, *aditya*, or *āditya*, when followed by *patya* as a subsequent member [of the compound] (Pāṇini 4.1.85).

[The substitution of *ai* for *e* and *o* for *au* does not take place] when *indra* follows [as the final member of a compound] (Pāṇini 7.3.22), as in *sāṃindraḥ* and *āgnendraḥ*. [In these cases], the suffix *aṇ* is applied [by the rule] "that which has this as its deity" (Pāṇini 4.2.24).

In the case of *aindrāgnam*, the substitution of *ānaṅ* occurs by the rule "ṭhdevatādvandve ca" (Pāṇini 6.3.26), and there is guṇa substitution for the vowel of the first member. Here too, the grammatical operations such as the addition of the suffix *aṇ* are to be understood as before.
The statement "there are two *a*-sounds in the word *indra*" and so forth is easy to understand, as it has already been explained previously.
23. Also after a long vowel, in the case of *varuṇa*. (Pāṇini 7.3.23) [Examples:
*aindrāvaruṇam*, *maitrāvaruṇam*. When the substitution of *ānaṅ* has been applied by the rule "also in a dual compound of deities" (7.3.21), the word *varuṇa* follows a long vowel.

24. *prācāṃ nagarānte* (Pāṇini 7.3.24). If, in this rule, the term "of the Easterners" (*prācām*) were intended to refer to the teachers (*ācārya*), then the author would not have stated "optionally" (*vibhāṣitam*) in the subsequent sūtra (7.3.26); it is precisely for the sake of providing this option that the mention of "the Easterners" (*prācām*) is made here.

In that regard, [the suffix] will follow accordingly. Therefore, he says "in the country of the Easterners" (*prācāṃ deśe*) and so forth, in order to make known that the mention of "country" (*deśa*) is intended here. By the mention of "city" (*nagara*), there is a reference to its own form (*svarūpa*), because of the rule "the word's own form [is the meaning]" (*svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasya*, Pāṇini 1.1.68).

25. *jaṅgaladhenuvalajāntasya vibhāṣitam uttarapadam* (Pāṇini 6.2.25). By the word "uttarapadam" (the final member), the final member of the compound is indicated; however, since that final member is always in close proximity [to the preceding members], its being "optionally so" (*vibhāṣitam*) would not be tenable. Therefore, it refers to that which is related to it...

Because the [application of] *vṛddhi* is optional, it is stated as "optionally" (*vibhāṣitam*). For this very reason, he says: "The *vṛddhi* of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is optional. The word "vṛddhi" is to be connected with the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*).

26. *ardhāt parimāṇasya pūrvasya tu vā* (Pāṇini 5.1.28). [The example is] *ārdhadrauṇikam*. This is a compound formed by *arthaṃ napuṃsakam* (Pāṇini 2.2.2), and the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied according to *prāgvateṣṭhañ* (Pāṇini 5.1.18). Now, for what purpose is the word *vā* (or) stated? Why is it not simply *vibhāṣitam* (it is optional)?

If it is argued that [the word] *pūrva* will be carried over from the preceding sūtra and connected with this word *uttara*, and therefore, by its recurrence, the option would apply only to the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), we say: this is not so.
The compound *uttarapada* will not be accented, but rather the particle *tu* is used here; it serves the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).

It will apply only to the former [word] and not to the latter. If that is so, then since the option (*vā*) itself is more concise than the formulation or non-formulation of the rule for accentuation (*svaritatva*) in a single conjunction (*ekayoga*), the word "option" (*vā*) is stated once again.

27. *nātaḥ parasya* | (Pāṇini 7.3.27) The increase (*vṛddhi*) of the measure (*parimāṇa*) being prescribed by the preceding rule would apply to the vowel *a* that begins with a vowel (*ac*); therefore, it is prohibited. However, the option regarding the first member of the compound (*pūrvapada*) remains in effect; [this applies] to the former.

Because the word "tu" (but) is understood [from the previous rule]. Regarding the example "ārdhaprasthikaḥ": the compound is formed by "ardhaṃ napuṃsakam" (Pāṇini 2.2.2), and the suffix is applied as before.
As for the question "what would happen?", he thinks thus: for the vowel 'ā' is indeed [the result of] vṛddhi; therefore...
There is no difference whether the prohibition of *vṛddhi* is present or absent; that very form remains the same.
Therefore, even if the *tapara* (the long vowel marker) were not employed, nothing undesirable would result.
[This refers to the phrase] "of that which has *vṛddhi* as its cause," and so forth. If the *tapara* were not employed, it would be for the purpose of [specifying] its duration (*tatkāla*).
He shows what undesirable consequence would follow. But what is the reason that the prohibition of *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine treatment) would not apply? To this he says: "For where," and so forth.
For a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) becomes the cause of *vṛddhi* only while effecting that *vṛddhi*. Therefore, in the case of a secondary derivative where...

A prohibition of *vṛddhi* is being made; that [prohibition] does not serve as a cause for *vṛddhi*. Therefore, the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment) of a *taddhita* suffix that has *vṛddhi* as its cause is not prohibited, and thus *puṃvadbhāva* would apply. Where? In examples such as "vaiyākaraṇī bhāryā asya" ("his wife is a female grammarian").

Thus [it is stated]. Furthermore, the prohibition of *vṛddhi* here is by means of the rule "na yvābhyām" (Pāṇini 7.3.3), etc. Now, for what purpose is the word "of the subsequent" (*parasya*) used? Is it so that [the substitution] might not apply to the preceding [vowel]? This is not the case; because of the force of employing the qualifier "from this" (*ataḥ*), it will not apply to the preceding one. For indeed...

If there were a prohibition of that [vṛddhi], then no other vṛddhi could possibly occur for the word *pūrva*, and the optional rule "but optionally for *pūrva*" (7.3.26) would be rendered meaningless.
Is it then for this purpose— that the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) should not apply?
If that [suffix] were present at the end [of the compound], there would also be a prohibition here in the case of *ardhadrauṇikam*.

However, the preceding rule [would apply]—such as *ardhamauṣṭikam*, meaning "bought for half a handful"—for this purpose; but when the mention of the subsequent [element] is made, it applies to what follows *ardha*.
Since that very [element] becomes dependent immediately after [the preceding one], there is no possibility of the application of the rule regarding the final element (*tadanta-vidhi*).
28. *pravāhaṇasya ḍhea* (7.3.28).

Regarding the word *pravāhaṇa*, when the suffix *ḍha* follows, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in a non-concordant sense (*vyadhikaraṇa*). The meaning is: "of that which is the *uttarapada* [subsequent member], which is a constituent part (*avayava*) of the word *pravāhaṇa*."

Regarding the term *pravāhaṇeya*: from the root *vah* preceded by *pra*, with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), we derive *pravāhaṇa* in the sense "he causes to flow. From this causative stem, the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of the agent according to Pāṇini 3.3.113 (*kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*).
This forms a *prādi*-compound, and the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs according to 8.4.30 (*ṇervibhāṣā*). Then, in the sense of offspring (*apatya*), [the suffix *ḍhak* is added].

[The suffix] ḍhak. But for what purpose is the *vṛddhi* of the second member (*uttarapada*) prescribed, since this [suffix] already brings about *vṛddhi* by its very nature? Even though this is so, nevertheless the *vṛddhi* must still be explicitly prescribed; because the *taddhita* suffix is the cause of *vṛddhi*, according to the rule: "And when a *taddhita* suffix is the cause of *vṛddhi*, provided it does not denote a dye or a modification."

Thus, there shall be a prohibition of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment). For if the *vṛddhi* of the second member (*uttarapada*) were not prescribed, then in that case where the *vṛddhi* of the first member (*pūrvapada*) is not prescribed, [the form] would be *pravāhaṇeyībhāryaḥ*— meaning "one whose wife is a *pravāhaṇeyī*."

In this case, there would be no prohibition of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine treatment), because the *taddhita* suffix is not the cause of the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening), as for example in *vaiyākaraṇabhārya*. Now, even if the *taddhita* suffix were not the cause of the *vṛddhi*, [the rule] "jāteśca" (Pāṇini 6.3.41) applies...

[Objection: There will be a prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), for here too there is "jāti-ness" according to the rule *gotraṃ ca caraṇaiḥ saha* (Mahābhāṣya 2.225). [Response: If that is so, then this indicates that this prohibition is not permanent (*anitya*). Therefore, [the form] *hastinīnāṃ samūhaḥ*...
In the word *hāstikam*, the prohibition of the optional *puṃvadbhāva* prescribed by the supplementary rule *bhasyāḍhe taddhite* (Vārttika 731) does not apply.

29. And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after that which has that as its cause. (7.3.29) The form *prāvāhaṇeyī* is derived by applying *iñ* according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.1.95 (*ata iñ*). The form *prāvāhaṇeyakam* is derived by applying *aṣuñ* according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.3.126 (*gotracaraṇādaṣuñ*).
