Now, for what purpose is this stated? Since the word *pravāhaṇeya*, ending in the suffix *ḍha*, always causes the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) to undergo the *vṛddhi* strengthening, the undertaking [of this rule] for that purpose is not appropriate; rather, it is for the sake of making the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the preceding member optional, as follows:

Even for the sake of the meaning "it might be" (*syāt*), the commencement of this [rule] is not appropriate; for even in the case of *iñ* and other taddhita suffixes, by overriding the *vṛddhi* caused by that [suffix], the option will occur precisely on account of the cause by means of the preceding rule.
Does the status of being subsequent (*paratva*) of the suffix *ḍha* disappear when a taddhita suffix such as *iñ* has arisen?

Thus he says: "bāhyataddhita" and so forth. That [vṛddhi] for which an external taddhita suffix is the cause is described as such. Furthermore, its externality here is due to the fact that the taddhita suffix is not included within the word *prāvāhaṇeya*. Being thus dependent upon an external taddhita suffix as its cause, it is *bahiraṅga* (external); whereas [the other operation] occurs even earlier.

Since the formation of a Brāhmaṇa secondary derivative arises, the option based on the suffix *ḍha*—being internal (*antaraṅga*)—is unable to subvert it. Consequently, if this [sūtra] were not commenced, that [option] would indeed occur.
Therefore, this is commenced for the purpose of providing an option.
30. *nañaḥ śucīśvarakṣetrajñakuśalanipuṇānām* (Pāṇini 7.3.30). Examples will be explained later.
"In this regard, some say," etc., is a mnemonic verse (*grahaṇakavākya*). Regarding this, [the rule] *na nañpūrvāt*...

The phrase "tatpuruṣāt" is the explanation [of the rule]. By the rule "not after a *tatpuruṣa* preceded by *nañ*" (Pāṇini 5.1.121), a suffix expressing a state (*bhāvapratyaya*) other than *tva* and *tal* is prohibited; therefore, one who desires a subsequent suffix expressing a state must take it from words such as *śūci* and the like, but not from *nañ*-compounds.
The abstract suffix (bhāvapratyaya) must be applied first; once that has been done, the negative compound (nañsamāsa) is formed afterwards.

Consequently, the vowel-increment (vṛddhi) prescribed for the initial vowel of the stem (aṅga) does not apply. For when the abstract suffix is applied first and the negative compound is formed afterwards, the negative particle (nañ) [is no longer directly connected to the stem].

The *aṅga* (base) begins with the first member [of the compound], because the status of being an *aṅga* belongs only to the final member (*uttarapada*). This rule is stated, and by the force of that statement, the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) occurs for the *aṅga* as well.
Regarding the phrase "tadapare" and so forth: what was said—that this *vṛddhi* of the first member was not even applicable—[is now addressed] optionally.
Regarding the statement "it is prescribed," other teachers do not accept this. What is the reason? He says:

"For even something other than a verbal action," and so forth. The particle *eva* (only) is to be understood as displaced in order, and should be seen immediately after the word "vidyate" (is found). If [the suffix were applied] after a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) in the sense of offspring and so forth...

Just as no other *taddhita* suffix exists apart from one expressing a state (*bhāva*) that serves as the cause for grammatical augmentation (*vṛddhi*), so too no other [suffix] exists apart from one expressing a state in a *bahuvrīhi* or a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*). Therefore,
it is appropriate that words such as "impure" (*aśuci*) and others lack the status of being a member (*anaṅga*), by virtue of subverting the governing rule concerning members (*aṅgādhikāra*).

Because the statement regarding *vṛddhi* (vowel lengthening) would otherwise be purposeless. But this is not so; for there certainly exists another taddhita suffix denoting a *vṛddhi*-conditioning cause after a *nañ*-compound in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*) and so forth—for example, the offspring of one who is unskilled (*akuśala*) is *Ākauśaliḥ*.

"This is the unskillfulness (*ākauśalam*) of the unskilled (*akuśala*). Furthermore, from a *nañ*-compound that is a *bahuvrīhi*, there indeed exists a word expressing an abstract state (*bhāva*): "that which does not possess pure things is 'impure' (*aśuci*)," and its state is [expressed by the suffix -tva]. This is according to the rule *ṭhigantācca laghupūrvāt* (Pāṇini 5.1.131).

Thus, [the suffix] aṇ [is applied], as in *āśauca*. Since, in this manner, another derivative (*taddhita*) from a word expressing a state (*bhāvavacana*) is distinct from a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*), and since there also exists a word expressing a state derived from a negative compound that is a *bahuvrīhi* and caused by vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*), therefore, in that case—
Furthermore, it is logical that the statement [of the sūtra] sublates the eligibility for the constituent parts (aṅga) because its purpose has already been fulfilled.
As for what was also said— that "a suffix expressing an abstract state (bhāvapratyaya) does not occur after a tatpuruṣa compound preceded by the negative particle nañ"— that too is incorrect.
Demonstrating this, he says: "The *kṣetrajña* is not the *īśvara*" (*akṣetrajño'nīśvaraḥ*)—according to the *Kāśikā*, "the *kṣetrajña* and the *anīśvara*" (*akṣetrajñānīśvarau*), and so forth.
For these two words are listed in the *brāhmaṇa*-class [of the *gaṇapāṭha*] specifically as *tatpuruṣa* compounds;
therefore, the suffix *ṣyañ* occurs only after these two *tatpuruṣas*. Otherwise, the purpose of listing them in the *brāhmaṇa*-class [would be inexplicable].

[Otherwise] there would be futility. Therefore, this *vṛddhi* (vowel lengthening) belonging to the member [of the compound], being invariably obtained, is prescribed optionally in the case of an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) and elsewhere in a *taddhita* suffix, as appropriate.
Thus, if *āśauca* is formed as a *tatpuruṣa* compound—where *aśuciḥ* means "one who is not pure"—then...

When the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.120] *tasyedam*, a *vṛddhi* vowel substitution occurs. Now, regarding the *bahuvrīhi*: "one for whom there is no purity" (*na asti śuciḥ asya*) is *aśuci*. If, then, the abstract sense (*bhāvārtha*) is intended to be expressed, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.1.131] *igantācca laghupūrvāt*; otherwise, the sense is that of [Pāṇini 4.3.120] *tasyedam*.

If that is intended to be expressed, then by [Pāṇini 4.1.83] *prāgdīvyato 'ṇ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied: *ānaiśvaryam* and *ākṣaitrajñyam*. When the suffix *vyañ* is added to these two *tatpuruṣa* compounds due to their inclusion in the *brāhmaṇādi* group, the *vṛddhi* strengthening occurs.
As for *ākīśalamānaipuṇam*, whether it is a *bahuvrīhi* or even a *tatpuruṣa*, in either case—

The suffix *aṇ* [is applied] by the rule *tasyedam* (Pāṇini 4.3.120). Although the words *kuśala* and *nipuṇa* are listed both among the *brāhmaṇādi* group and the *yudhādi* group, nevertheless, a suffix expressing an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) is not justified after a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in those words, nor even after a *bahuvrīhi*, because there is no rule for the extension [of the application] to that which ends in them (*tadantavidhi*).

Regarding the rule *yathātathayathāpurayoḥ paryāyeṇa* (Pāṇini 5.3.31): "These two [compounds] *yathātathā* and *yathāpura* should be understood as negative compounds (*nañ-samāsa*) when applied to [the list of] *brāhmaṇa* and so forth. The meaning is that the suffix *ṣyañ* is added after these two negative compounds. The word "these two" refers to the words *yathātathā* and *yathāpura*.

"The [compounds] *yathāsādṛśyam* and *yathārūpyam* are avyayībhāva compounds. Now, one might object: does not the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 2.1.7], "not when there is a sense of similarity" (*asādṛśye*), apply here? This is not a fault; for in these cases, similarity is not what is understood. To explain: *yathātatham* is said to mean "truth," and *yathāpuram* means "ancient."

How, then, is it known that this is an *avyayībhāva* compound? To this he says: "For thus," and so forth. For here, the shortening [of the vowel] based on the neuter gender has been applied by the rule "A neuter nominal stem [ending in a long vowel] becomes short" (Pāṇini 1.2.47). And the status of being neuter is prescribed for the *avyayībhāva* compound.
Therefore, it is understood that these are *avyayībhāva* compounds. Regarding the passage beginning with "In the Bhāṣya, however," etc.:

since the shortening [of the vowel] has not been applied in the phrase "the state of being otherwise than as it is" (*ayathātathābhāva*), the compound is indicated by the rule *sup-supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4) exactly as the sentence was shown, and not as an *avyayībhāva*. For, in an *avyayībhāva*...
In this case, the short vowel would have the neuter gender as its basis. However, under this view,
because the grammatical formulation is based on the sūtra itself— according to the Mahābhāṣya principle that "sūtras are like Vedic [in their usage]"—
one should understand that, due to a transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyaya*), a short vowel stands in place of a long one.

32. *hanasta’ciṇṇaloḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.32). [The word] "in taddhita suffixes" (*taddhiteṣu*) is no longer in force, because it is not marked with an indicatory vowel (*asvaritatvāt*). [The phrase] "that which is connected to it, provided there is a *kit* suffix" (*tatsambaddhaṃ kitīti*)—the word "is no longer in force" (*nivṛtam*) is understood here. Furthermore, its connection to that [preceding rule] is due to the condition "when there is a *kit* suffix" (*kiti*).

In the rule *ca* (Pāṇini 7.2.118), the term *taddhiteṣu* from 7.2.117 is understood by way of anuvṛtti. If, however, *kiti* were to be understood [from the preceding rule], then, when the suffix *ṭak* is applied— by virtue of the rules *jāyāpatyoṣṭak* (3.2.52) and *amanuṣyakartṛke ca* (3.2.53)— the form would be *jāyādhnaḥ tilakālakaḥ*.

This would also apply here. However, the mention of *ñ* and *ṇit* is connected solely with the suffix (*pratyaya*). Therefore, even when the rule "in the case of *taddhita* suffixes" (7.2.117) has ceased to apply, that [designation] continues to follow.

In the example "he causes to kill" (*ghātayati*), the causative suffix *ṇic* is added by the rule "for the root *han*, [the substitution of *ā* for *ha* occurs] before suffixes marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*" (7.3.54).

The form *ghātakaḥ* is derived with the suffix *ṇvul*. The form *sādhughātī* is derived with the suffix *ṇini* by the rule *supyajātau ṇinistācchīlye* (Pāṇini 3.2.78). The form *ghātaṃghātam* is derived with the suffix *ṇamul* by the rule *ābhīkṣṇye ṇamul ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.22), and according to the Vārttika *ābhīkṣṇye dve bhavataḥ* (887), there is reduplication for the sake of expressing frequency.
Thus there is reduplication. Regarding "ghātaḥ": the suffix *ghañ* is applied by Pāṇini 3.3.18 (*bhāve ghañ*).

Regarding "adhāni": this is the *luṅ* tense; the substitution of *ciṇ* occurs by Pāṇini 3.1.66 (*ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*), and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used by Pāṇini 1.3.13 (*bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*), as well as [the addition of] *ciṇo...* [to form the augment].

By the rule *lukÂ* (6.4.104), there is elision (*luk*) of the letter *t*. Thus we have *jaghāna*: [the suffix] *liṭ*, [then] *tip*, for which *ṇal* is substituted; and by the rule *abhyāsācca* (7.3.55), there is *kutva*—that is, the substitution of *gh* for *h*. Now, why does this not occur here in the case of *vṛtraṃ hatavān*? [Because of the rule] *brahmabhrūṇavṛtreṣu kvip* (3.2.87).

From that [suffix], by the rule *tasyedam* (Pāṇini 4.3.120), the suffix *aṇ* is applied; then, by the rule *ṣapūrvahandhṛtarājñāmaṇi* (6.4.135), there is the elision (*al-lopa*) of the penultimate vowel—resulting in *vārtradhnaḥ*, *bhrauṇadhnaḥ*. To this, he replies with the words beginning with *dhātoḥ*: a suffix prescribed after the word "root" (*dhātu*) is called a "root-suffix" (*dhātupratyaya*).

An operation being prescribed for a verbal root (*dhātu*) occurs only when that suffix follows that very root. This is made known by the rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in Pāṇini 6.4.174, which states *bhauṇahatya*. Consequently, [the substitution of *ṇa* for *na*] does not occur in forms such as *vārtradhnaḥ* and *bhrauṇadhnaḥ*, because in these cases the suffix does not follow the verbal root in the manner specified.
It is not prescribed; rather, it is prescribed as being "after the nominal stem" (prātipadikāt).

33. *āto yukciṇkṛtoḥ* | (Pāṇini 7.3.33) [The word *ca* does not exist—according to the Kāśikā. The mention of *ciṇ* is for the sake of non-*kṛt* suffixes; its status as a non-*kṛt* is because it is not prescribed under the governing heading of the second class of suffixes (*dhātu*). [Examples: *adāyi*, *adhāyi*.
Thus: for the roots *dā* (to give) and *dhā* (to place), the operations such as the *luṅ* (aorist) suffixes are applied as before. "Dāyaḥ," "dhāyaḥ"—here the suffix *dhañ* is used.
"Dāyakaḥ," "dhāyakaḥ"—here the suffix *ṣvul* is used.
"Dadau," "dadhau"—here the substitution of *au* by rule 7.1.34 (*āta au ṇalaḥ*) applies. "Cauṅḥ" [and so forth].

Regarding "bālākiḥ": [the suffix *iñ* is applied] after *cūḍā* and *balākā* when preceded by *bāhu* and so on. One might think that because of the continued application of the rule "of the vowels, of the first," it will not occur here;
to such a person, he states another example: "jñaḥ" (meaning "one whose deity is knowledge"). "Sāsya... [and so forth].

In the word *devatā* (formed by the suffix *aṇ* according to 4.2.24), the vowel *ā* becomes the initial of the vowels (*acāmādi*) by virtue of the principle that "a designation applies as if it were the principal" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). In this case, if the mention of *ciṇ* and *kṛt* were not present, even though the phrase *acāmādeḥ* ("of the initial of the vowels") is still being supplied [from a previous rule], the suffix *yuk* would indeed apply here. This is because of the maxim: "The principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* does not apply when there is no nominal stem (*aprātipadikena*)" (Śākapārthiva-paribhāṣā 65).
And this has indeed been stated only with reference to the limit of the conditions (*pratyaya*).
34. *nodātopadeśasya māntasyānācameḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.34).

[The prohibition applies] to *śami*, *tami*, and *dami*. [The roots are: *śamu upaśame* (Dhātupāṭha 1201), *tamu kāṅkṣāyām* (Dhātupāṭha 1202), and *damu upaśame* (Dhātupāṭha 1203), in the *luṅ* and other tenses.

As before: in *śamakaḥ* and so forth, the suffix is *ṇvul*; in *śamaḥ* and so forth, the suffix is *ghañ*. Regarding *yāmakaḥ* and *rāmakaḥ*: the roots *yama* (to cease) [DhP 984] and *ram* (to sport) [DhP 856] are both taught with an anudātta (low-pitched) vowel as their upadeśa.

Now, how are "exertion" (*udyama*) and "cessation" (*uparama*) [formed]? To this he says: "exertion and cessation," and so forth; "they are to be followed," and so forth. The word "as correct forms" (*sādhutvena*) is to be supplied as the remainder. The meaning is that these two are to be understood as correct forms by virtue of their being treated as *nipātana* (irregularly formed words).

[The purpose of the rule] is so that [the suffix *dhinuṇ*] may apply in cases such as *śamī*, *tamī*, and *damī*. [This is because] by the rule *śamādibhyaḥ śamityaṣṭābhyo dhinuṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.141), the suffix *dhinuṇ* is prescribed after the eight roots beginning with *śam*. If the term "in the original enunciation" (*upadeśa*) were not included [in the definition of *anudātta*], this would not apply here; for once the accent of the suffix has been applied, the verbal root would be *anudātta* (unaccented). However, since the term "in the original enunciation" is included, it refers to the state [of the root] at the time of its first utterance.

Thus, even though the state of being unaccented (*anudātta*) occurs at a later time, the prohibition nevertheless applies, because [the vowel] was accented (*udātta*) at the stage of the original instruction (*upadeśa*). Regarding the example *iha* and so forth: if the mention of "original instruction" (*upadeśa*) were not made, then [the rule] would apply even in cases such as *yāmakaḥ* and *rāmakaḥ*, on account of the suffix *lit* (Pāṇini 6.1.193).

Because the rule prescribes that the preceding [element] is udātta due to a subsequent condition (*pratyaya*). However, if the term *upadeśa* (original enunciation) were not included [in the rule], it would not apply;
for [the root] is anudātta in its original enunciation. [The Vārttika states: "It should be stated: 'Not for √nañc, √kam, √vi, and √mī. [The root] *kam* means "to desire."

The meaning is that this form of the rule must be explained as being for the purpose of ensuring that there is no prohibition regarding these three roots: *ṭhṭuavama* in the sense of "vomiting" (*udgiraṇe*; DhP 8.4.9), and *cama*, *cchama*, *camu*, and *jhamu* in the sense of "eating" (*adane*; DhP 8.4.69, 470, 471, 472). In this regard, the following...

The explanation is as follows: first, in the case of *ācama*, because it is included in the very sūtra "anācamer" (Pāṇini 3.1.100), the prohibition does not apply. In the case of the other two, however, [the suffix -yañ is applied] due to the specific rules (nipātana): "dhāmadevāṅ ḍaḷḍaḷai" (4.2.9) and "dhanahiraṇyāt kāme" (5.2.65). Now, how is *āma* [derived]?

Thus he says: "And *thāma* belongs to the curādigaṇa," and so forth. From the root *tham* meaning "disease" (DhP 1720), which belongs to the curādigaṇa, when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied and vṛddhi occurs, and then the suffix *ac* is added by Pāṇini 3.3.56, the form *āma* is derived.
For there is no prohibition of vṛddhi even when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is present, because that [prohibition] applies only when *ac* has not been added.
But the formation *akṛtvā* is to be understood as before. Now, one might object:

since the designation *mit* applies by the rule "janījṛṣksasurañjo'mantāśca" (Gaṇasūtra following Dhātupāṭha 817), the rule "mitāṃ hrasvaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.92) would apply here when the suffix *ṇi* is present.

Is it necessarily so? To this he says: "For here there is no *bhvitvam*. How is it not so? He says: "Not others," and so forth. As for the root *bhū* etc., which is listed as *ama gatyādiṣu* (Dhātupāṭha 465), its form should be *ama* [with the suffix *ap*]. Now, how is it that we have *viśrāma*, and not...?
Nor can it be said that this [usage] is incorrect, since the usage "the earth is the resting place of the sun" is observed; thus he says: "such usage as this," and so forth.

35. *janivadhyośca* (Pāṇini 7.3.35). Someone might suspect that this [term] *vadhi* is the substitute for *han*, and that this very [substitute] is what is being referred to here; therefore, in order to refute that suspicion, he says: "The root *vadhi* is a separate verbal base," and so forth.

If you were to assume that there is another verbal root ending in the vowel *a*, then the prohibition [of *vṛddhi*] would be purposeless, since *vṛddhi* would not occur simply because it is a root with a consonant as its penultimate (*ghu*-upadha). With this in mind, he says: "of that which ends in a consonant.
But from what source is it determined that there exists such another verbal root?

Thus he says: "And [the word] *bhakṣaka*," and so forth. Now, why does this prohibition not apply specifically to the substitute *vadh* for *han*? To this he says: "Of the substitute for *han*," and so forth.
"He begot the embryo" (*jajāna garbham*), etc.; this is a Vedic usage.

36. *artihvīvlīrīknūyīkṣmāyyātāṃ pug ṇau* (Pāṇini 7.3.36). The mention of *arti* is by means of its *śit* designation; it is not intended to include roots ending in the vowel *ṛ*, as in the rule *ṛdṛśo’ṅ guṇaḥ* (7.4.16). [The example is] *arpayati*; here, the causative suffix *ṇic* is added because of the presence of a causal agent (*hetu*).

The *guṇa* substitution [of *o* for *au*] occurs by the rule *ṭhpugantalaghūpadhasya* (Pāṇini 7.3.86). Thus we have *hrāpayati* and *vlepayati*. The roots are *hrī* in the sense of "shame" (*lajjāyām*) [Dhātupāṭha 1085] and *vlī* in the sense of "covering" (*varaṇe*) [Dhātupāṭha 1502]. Similarly, we have *knopayati* and *kṣmāpayati*. The roots are *knūyī* in the sense of "sound" (*śabde*) [Dhātupāṭha 4.85] and *kṣmāyī* in the sense of "shaking" (*vidhūnane*).

[The root] *dhā* (DhP 4.86). By the rule *ṭhlopo vyor vali* (Pāṇini 6.1.66), there is the elision of the letter *y*. [The commentary states]: "There is the inclusion of both roots," because there is no distinction [between them]. For this [root] *rī*, there is also *ṭhrī gati-śoṣaṇayoḥ* (DhP 9.23) and *ṭhroṅ śravaṇe* (DhP 9.24).

(DhP 1138)—thus, it is understood that there is the inclusion of both [roots]. But is it not the case that, according to the rule "when a root without an *anubandha* is mentioned, one without an *anubandha* is not [included] when one with an *anubandha* is present" (Vyāḍipāṭha 53), the inclusion of *rīṅ* would not be obtained? This is not a fault; for in this instance, because [the word *rīṅ*] has fewer syllables (*alpa-actara*), [it takes precedence].

By making the word *ārti* the first member of the compound— despite the fact that, when one of two words ending in a *hrasva* vowel must be placed first, the rule *ṭhalpāctaram* (Pāṇini 2.2.34) would otherwise apply— the author indicates that not even some other statement of this grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) is necessarily required here. Therefore...
The maxim *niranubandhakaparibhāṣā* (the rule regarding suffixes without an indicatory letter) is not required here; therefore, there is also the inclusion of *rīṅ*.

Now, for what purpose is the augment *puK* made a prior element (*pūrvānta*)? Why should *puK* not be prescribed as a subsequent element (*parādi*) alone? For if it were *puT*, then in the rule prescribing *guṇa*, the mention of "that which ends in *puK*" (*puganta*) would not need to be made.

If it is argued: "Since [the form] *puṭi* is already established by the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.84), the mention of *puṭ* must necessarily be made [in the rule *puṭaḥ*]; otherwise, the vṛddhi substitution prescribed by *aco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115) would apply," this is not so; for [the rule *puṭaḥ* applies] when the addition of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) has not yet occurred.

Since being the cause for *vṛddhi* implies being the cause for the substitution of a phoneme (*pratyāgamin*), this will act as a sublater (*bādhaka*) of the subsequent rule; thus, there is no occasion for *vṛddhi*. However, there is this fault regarding the beginning of the following [rule]: in forms such as *dāpyate* and *dāpyata*, because the *ṇi* has been removed by elision (*lopa*), the *pakāra* [is not present].

"Would there not be an absence of the audible [form]? This too is not a fault; for the elision of the *ṇi* suffix does not effect a total removal, such that upon the cessation of the *ṇi*, the augment *puṭ* would also cease.
Since there is the mention of the suffix (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇam*), even when the *ṇi* has ceased, the audible form of *puṭ* occurs.

He says that it will be so: "The elision of the prior limit of *puk*," and so forth. [This refers to] the *luṅ* suffix after the root *dāp*, the *cli* augment, its replacement by *caṅ* according to Pāṇini 3.1.48 (*ṇi-śri-dru-srubhyaḥ kartari*), the elision of the *iṇ* [augment], the shortening of the penultimate vowel according to 7.4.1 (*ṇau caṅy upadhāyā hrasvaḥ*), and the doubling of the root according to 6.1.11 (*caṅ*).

There is reduplication, the substitution of *i* by [Pāṇini 7.4.93] *sanvallaghuni caṅpare*, and the lengthening of the short vowel by [Pāṇini 7.4.94] *dīrgho laghoḥ*—thus, *adīdapat*. In this case, if the augment *puṭ* were applied, the shortening of the vowel would not occur, because the vowel would no longer be penultimate (*anupadhātva*). However, when *puk* is present, it does occur.
Therefore, the augment *puk* is placed at the end of the preceding element for the sake of shortening the vowel.

37. The suffix *yuk* is applied after the verbal roots *śā*, *chā*, *sā*, *hvā*, *vyā*, and *vep*. (Pāṇini 7.3.37) The roots are: *śo* "to sharpen" (Dhātupāṭha 1145), *chāe* "to cut" (Dhātupāṭha 1146), *ṣo* "to finish" (Dhātupāṭha 1147), and *hvēñ* "to contend" (Dhātupāṭha 1008).
Regarding the roots *ṭhvy-eñ* "to cover" (DhP 1007), *ṭhve-eñ* "to weave" (DhP 1006), *ṭhpā* "to drink" (DhP 925), and both forms of *ṭhpai* and *ovai* "to dry up" (DhP 920, 921):
since these end in long *ā*, the suffix *puK* would have been required; therefore, the rule for *yuK* is prescribed.

Regarding the passage beginning with "ṭhniśāyayati": there is the substitution of ā by rule 6.1.45, "ādeca upadeśe'śiti. It is stated that "some authorities maintain that the forms 'pā pāne' and 'pai ovai śoṣaṇe' are also included [in this context]. For where its inclusion is not desired, he specifies "of the root pibati"; as in the rule "lopaḥ pibaterīcca" (6.1.58).
This is the intended meaning. Now, why is the root *pā* "to protect" (DhP 1056) not also included here? To this he says: "But as for the root *pā* 'to protect'," and so forth.
[He states: "However, its *lug*-augment must be mentioned. But surely there is also the root *pāla* "to protect" (DhP 1609)?
This root is listed in the *curādi* group; will it therefore mean "he protects" (*pālayati*)? This is true;
however, the augment *luk* is added for the purpose of excluding the *puk* suffix, otherwise there would be the form *pāyayati* from the root *pāti*.

Regarding the statement "the augment *nuk* should be stated for the roots *dhūñ* and *prīñ*": *dhūñ* means "to shake" (DhP 1835) and *prīñ* means "to satisfy" (DhP 1836); the meaning is that the augment *nuk* should be stated—that is, explained—for these two. The explanation here is as follows: *dhūñ* is [also] listed as "shaking" (DhP 1398), and *tṛp* is "satisfying."

By virtue of this specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*) [found in *Dhātupāṭha* 1195], there will be the elision (*luk*) of these two [suffixes]. Regarding the phrase "these also," it refers to the *yugādi* group. In forms such as *niśāyayati*, the substitution of *ā* for the vowel [of the root] occurs by the rule *ādeca upadeśe 'śiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.45). The forms beginning with *nyaśīśayat* are likewise derived.
These forms are similar to *adīdapat* and should be derived by applying the rules for the *luṅ* and other tenses as previously explained.

In *adūduhat*, because the root does not end in the vowel *a*, there is no *sanvadbhāva* (treatment like the *saN* suffix) for the reduplicated syllable. In *apipriṇat* as well, because the syllable is not light (*laghu*), there is no lengthening of the vowel.

But surely, in the list [of roots], *śā*, *chās*, *sā*, and *hvā* are recited as ending in *ej*; how then can there be a reference to these forms when they have undergone *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*)?
To this he says: "In the rule *śā-chās-āhvā-*" (where the printed text reads *śā-hvā* etc.). How so?

How is it explained that there is the possibility of the augment *puk* for those [roots] whose vowels have undergone *ātvam* (the substitution of *ā*)? It is because the rule for *puk* applies to those ending in long *ā*. He demonstrates the purpose of this indicator (*jñāpaka*) by means of the example "adhyāpayati" and so forth.
In "adhyāpayati," the substitution of *ātvam* occurs according to the rule "kroṅjīnāṃ ṇau" (Pāṇini 6.1.48). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*),...

The inclusion of forms such as *jāpayati* is intended. Since the mention of roots beginning with *śā*, which have undergone the change to *ā* (i.e., *śāp-* etc.), was made in order to state the application of the augment *puk*, it would logically follow that *veñ* should also be understood only as having undergone the change to *ā* (i.e., *vyeñ*).
This, however, cannot be accepted; for if [the rule] were stated as "or" (*vā*), then [the form] *pai*...
The root *ovai* in the sense of "drying up" (Dhātupāṭha 920, 921) would also be included [by that rule].
Therefore, it is more appropriate to understand the inclusion of *veñ* as it stands, without the substitution of *āt*.

38. *Juk* is prescribed after [the root] *vā* in the sense of shaking (*vidhūnana*). (Pāṇini 7.3.38) The suffix *juk* is ordained when the augment *puk* would otherwise apply, for the root *vā*—that is, for the root *vā* meaning "to go" and "to scent" (Dhātupāṭha 1050)—in the sense of shaking, which means trembling.

Now, since the form *upavājayati* is already established from the root *vaja* in the sense of "to go" (*vaja vraja gatau*, Dhātupāṭha 252, 253) when it takes the causative suffix (*ṇic*), for what purpose is this [rule] stated? This prescription of the augment *juk* is for the purpose that the augment *puk* should not apply to the root *vā*. [Furthermore, there is the rule: *pai orva śoṣaṇe*...

"This is the form of this [word]. Now, one might object: since that which is derived by rule (*lākṣaṇika*) ends in the vowel *ā*, the augment *juk* should not apply here? This is not so; for it has just been stated in this very context that the paribhāṣā concerning "that which is taught by a rule versus that which is taught as a specific word-form" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta-paribhāṣā*) does not apply.

39. *Lī*, *ūrṇu*, and *glu* optionally [take the suffix *ṇyuṭ*] in the sense of "causing the flow of oil" (*snehavipātane*). (Pāṇini 7.3.39) Regarding the phrase "in the sense of causing the flow of oil": what is this so-called "causing the flow of oil"? It is the act of causing that which is melting to fall, that is, its discharge. For instance, when the root *pat* is used with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*), [it yields *pātana*].

Regarding the form *vilīnayati*: there is the substitution of *guṇa* and *āy-ādeśa*. Now, once the substitution of *ātva* has been applied by the rule *vibhāṣā līyateḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.51), why does the augment *nuk* not occur in *vilāpayati*, given that what is partially modified remains non-different from the original?

Thus he says: "lī" and so forth. Here, the vowel *ī* is elided [from the root]—it is intended that this applies only to that which ends in *ī*, and not to that which has undergone the substitution of *ā* (atva). It is stated that "the term 'lī' includes both *lī* and *līṅ*. But surely, by the paribhāṣā regarding roots without an indicatory letter (*niranubandhaka-paribhāṣā*)...
It is appropriate to understand that only this root *lī* "to adhere" belonging to the *kryādika* class (*dhā.pā.* 1501) is intended here,

and not the root *līṅ* "to adhere" belonging to the *daivādika* class (*dhā.pā.* 1139). This is because [the author] considers that this is indeed a single root, [distinguished] for the sake of two different verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*) and for the sake of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).

It is taught in two ways. And having done so, the ātmanepada occurs by both [rules]: "after the root *lī*, in the senses of honoring and making firm" (Pāṇini 1.3.70). [The commentary says: "The mention of *lā* refers to the root *lāti* and also to *loyati*, which has undergone the change of *ā*. The word "mention" (*grahaṇam*) is to be connected with the subject under discussion.
40. *bhiyo hetubhaye ṣuk* (Pāṇini 7.3.40).

A "cause" (*hetu*) is that which instigates an independent agent (*svatantra-kartṛ*). That from which one fears is "fear" (*bhaya*); thus, a cause that is also fear is "causal fear" (*hetubhaya*), and [the rule applies] in that causal fear. [The root] *ñibhī* [is used] in the sense of fear.

When the rule for *vṛddhi* (Pāṇini 7.2.115) would otherwise apply to this root [bhī], and when the substitution of *ā* (by Pāṇini 6.1.56, *bibheterhetubhaye*) would also apply, the substitution of *ghu* is optionally prescribed in the presence of the causative suffix (*ṇi*). Thus we have: *muṇḍo bhīṣayate*.
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is employed here by the rule *bhīsmyorhetubhaye* (Pāṇini 1.3.68).
Now, one might ask: why does [the rule] not apply here in the case of *muṇḍo bhāpayate* when *atva* has been performed? To this he says: "In this case too," and so forth.
41. *sphāyo vaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.41).
[The example is] *sphāvayati*. [The roots are] *sphāyī* and *opyāyī*, meaning "to grow" (Dhātupāṭha 487, 488).

42. *śaderagatau taḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.42). For what purpose, then, is this stated, since the letter *t* will occur by virtue of the very nipātana (irregular derivation) from the root *śadlṛ śātane* (Dhātupāṭha 1428)? [It is so that the substitution occurs] in cases other than "motion" (*gati*). As for example...

If it is argued, "Let there be [the suffix] in the sense of 'going,' lest it be otherwise," we say no; for the word *śātana* expresses a meaning other than 'going. In that case, this indicates the following rule: "Even those [grammatical operations] which are not sublated by exceptions do occur" (Puṇyarāja’s commentary on the Laghu-kaumudī, vṛtti 99). Therefore, from the word *purā*—

By the rule "sāyaṃciram... (Pāṇini 4.3.23) and others, the suffixes ṭyu, ṭyuṭ, and ṭyuL which are prescribed do not undergo sublation by the irregular formation (nipātana) of "tuda" under the rule "purāṇaprokteṣu" (4.3.105). Consequently, the form *purātanam* is also established.

43. *ruhaḥ po 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 7.3.43). Regarding the form *ropayati*: the root *ruh* (in the sense of "birth" and "manifestation") is listed at Dhātupāṭha 859. But for what purpose is this rule stated, since there is already the root *rup* (in the sense of "confusion") among the *divādi* roots?
The root *rup* is recited [in the Dhātupāṭha] as 1236 and 1237; from it, one will derive *ropayati*.
But why is it that from the root *ruh*, one derives *rohayati*? It is so that the usage *ropayati* may also occur in the sense of "birth" (*janma*);
otherwise, it would only have the sense of "confounding" (*vimohana*), since verbal roots possess multiple meanings.

If it is argued that [the term] will function in the sense of "one who possesses form" (rūpin), this is not so; for verbal roots have multiple meanings, but they do not possess all possible meanings. For when it is said "it transforms" (rupyati), the meaning of "birth" is not perceived; what then?
It refers exclusively to the sense of "delusion."

44. *pratyayasthātkātpūrvasyāta idāpyasupaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.44). "It does not follow after *sup*" means that it does not follow after a word ending in *sup*. This meaning is to be understood through the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) concerning the mention of an affix (*pratyayagrahaṇa*). Examples: *jaṭilikā*, *muṇḍikā*.
Thus: for meanings such as "unknown" (*ajñāta*), [the suffix] *ka* is applied by Pāṇini 5.3.70, *prāgivāt kaḥ*, resulting in *kārikā* and *hārikā*.

[The suffix] *ṇvul* [is applied] to form *etikā*; here, from the pronoun *etad*, the suffix *akac* is added by 5.3.71, *avyayasarvanāmnām akac prāk ṭeḥ*; then the substitution of *yat* for the initial *tya* occurs; then, by 6.1.97, *ato guṇe*, there is the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*); finally, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added.

"Akaḥ savarṇe dīrghatvam" (Pāṇini 6.1.101). [The word] "śakā" is formed with the suffix *ac* according to Pacādi-gaṇa rules, followed by the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. Regarding the statement "the mention of *stha* is for the sake of clarity," one might ask: why is it not for the purpose of ensuring that [the rule does not apply] where there is merely the letter *k* as a suffix? To this, he says: "For where there is merely the letter *k*," and so forth.

The syllable *kā* is used here to denote the phoneme *k*; the vowel *a*, however, serves merely for pronunciation. There is no suffix consisting of the letter *k* alone that would require the mention of *sthā* for its exclusion. If it were stated as *kāt pratyayāt* ("from a suffix beginning with *k*"), the word "suffix" (*pratyaya*) would apply even to a part of a suffix; therefore, even without [the mention of *sthā*],...

The mention of *stha* can be understood as referring to the letter *k* when it occurs in a suffix (*pratyaya*). Therefore, the mention of *stha* is for the sake of clarity. [Examples: *maṇḍanā*, *ramaṇā*—[formed] by the suffix *layu* after roots such as *nandi* (Pāṇini 3.1.134). *Paṭuka*, *mṛduka*, *gokā*, *naukā*—the suffix *ka* is applied here as in the previous case.
"Ṭhrākā, dhākā. From the roots *dṛṣ* (meaning "to tear apart") and *dah* (DhP 1057, 1058), the suffix *ka* is applied according to the Uṇādi rule *kṛdādhārārcikalibhyaḥ kaḥ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.18).
Regarding the phrase "atha" and so forth: [it means] "incite. The other [teacher] says it is the letter *ka*; for the letter *ka* is explicitly heard [in the text].

The intention is that the qualification "of that very [kakāra]" is appropriate. To reveal the intention with which the questioner asked, he says "If this is so," and so forth. By the words "even though" (*yadyapi*), the *kakāra* is qualified—namely, the *kakāra* that occurs before the suffix *āp*. This being the case...

In the case of *karika*, [the rule] does not apply; for the letter *k* is separated from the vowel *ā* by the letter *a*. Others say: "When the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been made," and so forth. For separation occurs only when there is an intervening element (*vyavasarga*). But since there is no intervening element once the single-substitute has been made, there is no separation. [The term is] *ekādeśa*.

"Regarding 'pūrva' and so forth": the challenger [says] that the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) occurs by virtue of the rule "when a subsequent element follows, [the original element behaves as if it were] in the preceding operation" (Pāṇini 1.1.57). The other [responds]: "Because of the explicit statement. This statement is indeed uttered;
and since the letter *k* does not immediately follow [the *ṭ*], it is there by the force of that explicit statement.
Once the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) has been established, one does not everywhere rely on an intervention by even a single phoneme.

If, then, by the force of the specific rule (*vacana-sāmarthya*), [the operation] occurs even when there is intervention—as in *kārikā* and so forth—then would it not also occur in cases such as *rathakaṭalya* and *putrakāmyā*? To this [objection, the author replies]:

He says: "In *rathakaṭaly-*, etc. A collection of chariots (*ratha*) takes the suffix *kaṭalyac* by the rule *initrakaṭalyacaśca* (Pāṇini 4.2.51); from that, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added. [The form] *putrakāmyā* is derived as follows: from *putram icchati* ("he desires a son"), the suffix *kāmyac* is applied by the rule *kamyacca* (3.1.9). Then, by the rule *a pratyayāt* (3.3.102), the suffix *ṭāp* is added. In that case:

Since there is an intervention by multiple phonemes (*varṇa*) created by hearing, the substitution of *it* does not occur. However, based on the authority of the rule "That by which there is no intervention of parts [is considered non-intervening], even when intervened by [something else]" (Vyāḍipāṭha 46), an intervention by only a single phoneme is accepted; for that by which there is no intervention of parts applies everywhere.
There is an intervention; therefore, it is logical that there should be an intervention by a single phoneme.

In all cases, the intervention caused by the substitute (sthānivat-bhāva) exists through a single phoneme, whereas through a cluster (saṅghāta), it both exists and does not exist. Therefore, that [latter case] is not resorted to here.

Regarding the phrase "this [suffix] follows a word ending in *su*": it should be understood that the status of ending in *su* (*subantatā*) applies to the word *parivrājaka* because of the suffix *āp* following it, according to the rule defining a nominal stem (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Regarding the statement "and this is a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*") [meaning]: "if *āp* does not follow a word ending in *su*. What, then, is the fault in using a relative exclusion (*paryudāsa*), such that...?
Is this [the case]? He says: "For in the case of *paryudāsa*," and so forth. If this were a *paryudāsa*, then [the meaning would be]:

"other than *sup* is *asap*"; and consequently, since *udāp* would follow, then even in the case of *bahuparibrājaka*, the substitution of *it* would indeed occur, because [the suffix] is not a *subanta*.

This is because [the suffix] *āP* is considered to follow the entire aggregate of the preceding and following words. Furthermore, since the aggregate as a whole does not end in a case-ending (*asubanta*), the case-ending (*su*) cannot arise from it. Rather, the case-ending arises here from the constituent part, namely the word *parivrājaka*, and not from the aggregate. [The compound is thus defined as] that in which no case-ending exists.

"Thus, this [term] 'asubhiḥ' is also not accepted"—the meaning is that even the *bahuvrīhi* compound is not accepted. But what is the fault in accepting it, such that it is not accepted? To this he says:
"For instance," and so forth. The meaning is: "In that case, then. Regarding the *bahuvrīhi*, [there is a problem] with the two members, the prior and the subsequent.

Since there is a designation as being "ending in a *sub*" by virtue of its characteristic of being a *pratyaya*, it is not a non-*sub* (*asu*), but rather one that possesses an existing *sub*. Consequently, in the case of *bahucarmikā*, the rule "an *āp* following a non-*sub*" would not apply [to prevent the feminine suffix].

[The derivation is as follows: *bahuvrīhi* is formed from the sense "she in whom many hides exist" (*bahūni carmāṇy asyāṃ vidyante*). Then, by the rule *śeṣād vibhāṣā*, [the feminine suffix *kāp* is added].
By [Pāṇini 5.4.154], the suffix *kap* is applied, followed by *ṭāp*, resulting in *māmikā*.

[The form] *māmikā* means "this is mine" (*mameyam*). By [Pāṇini 4.3.120], the suffix *aṇ* is applied [to form *mama* from *mad*]. Then, by [Pāṇini 4.3.3], the substitute *mamaka* takes the place of *mama*. Now, one might object: [the feminine form] should be derived from the word *mamaka*, which ends in *aṇ*.

[Objection: According to the rule *ṭhṭhiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15), the suffix *ṅīp* ought to occur; so how is it that *ṭāp* occurs here? [Answer: This is due to the restrictive rule (*niyama*) beginning with *kevalamāmaka* (Pāṇini 4.1.30). Regarding the word *narikā*: the root is *kai* or *ge* in the sense of "sound" (Dhātupāṭha 916, 917). By the rule *ādeca upadeśe’śiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.45), the substitution of *ā* for the root vowel occurs.
By the rule *sthāto 'nupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3), the suffix *ka* is applied; from that, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* follows.

Thus we have *dākṣiṇātyikā* and *ihatyikā*. [The former] means "born in the southern direction," formed by the suffix *tyak* according to *dakṣiṇāpaścātpurasastyak* (Pāṇini 4.2.98). [The latter] means "born here."
By *ṭhavyayāttyap* (4.2.104), and in both cases regarding meanings such as "unknown" (*ajñāta*) and so forth, by *prāgivāt kaḥ* (5.3.70).
The meaning of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is "addition" (*pratipādana*). In that regard, it is as follows:

The demonstration is as follows: because of the understanding of the rule of restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) in the sūtra "udīcām ātaḥ sthāne" (Pāṇini 7.3.46), the suffixes *tyap* and *tya* will necessarily apply.

Since the substitution of *ṭu* for the *ā* of *yā* and *sā* would optionally apply by the rule *ṭhudīcām ātaḥ sthāne* (7.3.46), and since the substitution of *se* would necessarily apply by the preceding rule, this prohibition is now commenced.

Because a prohibition presupposes something that has already been established. When *akac* occurs for those two [words], then this prohibition is understood to apply to the forms *yakā* and *sakā*. For *yat* and *tad*, *akac* is added as before, followed by the nominative singular suffix *su* and the substitution of *a* for the initial vowel according to the rule for *tyad* and so on. The statement "the mention of *yāse* is not restrictive" means that it is not the primary factor.

"What is the reason? He says: "This is for the purpose of indicating both *yat* and *tat*. Why is it explained in this way? He says: "In this case as well," and so forth. The form *yāsa* is the nominative singular. Therefore, if this grammatical indication were a *tantra* (a rule of abbreviation), [the following would apply].
Because the rule specifies the nominative singular forms (*yat* and *tat*), the substitution of *yakām* and *takām* would not occur in other case endings;

yet it is desired that they occur there as well. Therefore, it is said that this mention of *yat* and *tat* is not restrictive, but is intended as an illustration for the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) themselves.
"Regarding the prohibition of *itva* for *ṭhā* and *asi*, etc."—the meaning of the word *upasaṃkhyāna* is "presentation" (or "addition").

This is what is being stated: when the prohibition [of *itva*] for *yad-* and *tad-* is being formulated, the presentation of the prohibition for that which ends in the suffix *tyakan* is also intended.

"It must be done. Regarding this, the following is the explanation: here, a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule) is made with "not" (*na*), whereby a prohibition will apply to that which ends in the suffix *tyakan*.
In the same way, it should be understood that even in subsequent cases, the purpose of the supplementary statement (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is for the sake of providing an explanation.
This very demonstration must also be performed by relying on the analysis of the grammatical connection (*yogavibhāga*):

*upatyakā*, *adhatyakā*. [The suffix] *tyakan* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.34: "After the words *upa* and *adhi*, [the suffix] *tyakan* occurs in the sense of 'near' and 'ascended' respectively.
[The word] *pāvaka* is formed with the suffix *ṇvul*. [The word] *alomakā* means "she who has no hair" (*na asyāḥ lomāni*).
The term *santi* is a bahuvrīhi compound. The suffix *kap* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.4.154 (*śeṣādvibhāṣā*).

Thus we have *jīvakā* and *nandakā*. The suffix *vun* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.150 (*āśiṣi ca*). Thus we have *devakā* and *yajñakā*. From the words *devadatta* and *yajñadatta*, the suffix *kan* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.3.76 (*anukampāyāṃ kan*).
Thus, when *kan* is applied, as well as in the case of suffixes beginning with *ṭhan* and *añ*, "the optional elision [of the penultimate vowel] should be stated" (Vārttika 614);

hence there is the elision of the final member of the compound, resulting in *kṣipakā* and *dhruvakā*. [The roots are] *kṣipa* in the sense of "impelling" (Dhātupāṭha 1285) and *dhruva* in the sense of "steadiness."

[From the root *dhā* (DhP 943)], by [Pāṇini 3.1.135]: *ṭhigupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ*. From that which ends in *ka*, in the sense of "unknown" and so forth, [the suffix] *ka* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.3.70]: *prāgivāt kaḥ*.
Thus, "tārakā" [is formed]; it is derived from the root *tṛ* with the suffix *ṇvul*.

Regarding the term *tāntava* [in the phrase] "ṭhvarṇaka-tāntava": it means "a product of threads. By applying *orañ* (Pāṇini 4.3.139) and *orguṇaḥ* (6.4.146), we derive *tāntavaḥ*, which refers to a specific type of garment (*prāvaraṇaviśeṣa*). In that context, the word *varṇaka* should be added as a supplementary entry (*upasaṃkhyātavyā*). [The rule for] *varṇa*...

Regarding the term *varṇikā* [in the phrase] "in the case of coloring, action, empowerment, and qualities": the verbal root *varṇ* (DhP 1938) belongs to the curādigaṇa; from it, with the suffix *ṇvul*, we derive *varṇikā*.
Its meaning is "one who explains."
Regarding "vartakā": from the root *vṛt* in the sense of "turning" (*vartane*, DhP 758), with the suffix *ṇvul*. Regarding "vartikā": it means "one who studies. Regarding "aṣṭakā pitṛdaivatye":
the term *pitṛdaivatyam* refers to a specific Vedic ritual; therein, the word *aṣṭakā* is added as an enumeration. [The text continues with] *aśū...*

From the root *vyāp* (DhP 1264), the suffix *takan* is applied according to *ṭhiṣyasibhyāṃ takan* (DaU 3.30). By the rule *vraścabhrasjasṛjamṛjayajarājabhrājacchaśāṃ ṣaḥ* (8.2.36), the change to *ṣ* occurs, followed by the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭu*. Thus, we have *aṣṭaka*. [The word] *aṣṭakā* means "that whose measure is eight," according to the rule *tadasya parimāṇam* (Pāṇini 5.1.67).

Regarding the rule *saṃkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan* (Pāṇini 5.1.22), there is the statement *vā sūtakā* and so forth. The purpose of this is to provide an explanatory supplement (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the word *sūtakā*. In that regard, the explanation is as follows: words such as *sūtakā*, *sūtikā*, and others [are formed].
Since it falls within the category of *pṛṣodarādi* words, this option is established by the very fact that it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group.

46. *udīcām ātaḥ sthāne yakapūrvāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.46). Since the preceding rule would have required the substitution of *i* invariably, this statement is made for the purpose of providing an option. "Preceded by *ya* and *ka*" means that which has *ya* and *ka* as its prior members. What is the referent of the compound (*anyapadārtha*)? It is the whole. For it is thus:

The word "prior" (pūrva) refers to a constituent part; and that constituent part belongs to a whole, not to another constituent part. For one phoneme does not become a constituent part of another phoneme.
Rather, its designation as "prior" is in relation to another constituent part. And that other constituent part—

Because it is the subject under discussion, the substitute *akāra* itself is understood. As for the feminine gender designation, it should be understood as belonging to the whole [the compound] by virtue of the property of its meaning (the object denoted), since that [feminine gender] is not observed in the printed Nyāsa from the word "tasya" up to "tu. However, its purpose is...
It will be stated [in the sūtra]: "In place of *āt*. The word "which is *akāra*" (*yo'kāraḥ*) is connected with the distant [word *sthāne*].

Regarding "from *ibhya*, etc. (*ibhyikā*): from words such as *ibhya*, by the rule "after *prāgdiva*, *ka*" (Pāṇini 5.3.70), and then by "when *ka* follows, [the vowel] is shortened" (Pāṇini 7.4.13), the shortening occurs.

Regarding the term *sāṃkāśyikā*: by the rule *dhanvayopadhādvuñ* (Pāṇini 4.2.121), the suffix *vuñ* is applied. Since there is no vowel *a* in place of the final *ā* here, the substitution of *i* (the *itva*) applies invariably.
Now, what is the purpose of including the word *sthāna* [in the sūtra], given that this genitive case (*āt-aḥ*) itself implies a connection with "place" (*sthāne*)?
Will [the sixth case ending] be applied because of the rule "The sixth case is used in the sense of 'in place of'" (Pāṇini 1.1.49)? To this he says:

"The mention of the word *sthāna*," and so forth. This is a restatement (*anuvāda*), a reference to the *a*-sound that is prescribed by another rule in place of the original *a*-sound. Here too, in place of...

The mention of *sthāna* (position) is for the purpose that the relationship [between the original and the substitute] may be understood. But what is the reason why, in the absence of the mention of *sthāna*, the relationship would not be understood in a restatement (*anuvāda*)? He says: "By the word *ātaḥ*" and so forth. In the rule prescribing a substitute, such as *asterbhūḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.52).

In such instances as these, the paribhāṣā "ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā" (Pāṇini 1.1.49) applies, but not in the case of a restatement (anuvāda); for this [paribhāṣā] serves as a supplement to prescriptive statements (vidhi). Moreover, in this case, an *a*-vowel is not prescribed in place of an *a*-vowel by this rule; what then?
It is distinguished by this other characteristic: "the vowel *a* which is in the place (*sthāna*) of [the elided *ā*].
Therefore, that technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) does not apply here. For if the word "place" (*sthāna*) were not used there, it would mean "the *a* which is near the *ā*."

There would be an understanding of a relationship of proximity (*sāmīpya-sambandha*). Alternatively, having raised the same question as before, he says: "By the word *ātaḥ*," and so forth. The vowel *a*, which was introduced as the substitute for the phoneme *i*, is specified by the term *ātaḥ*. And thus, because it is the qualified (*viśeṣya*), the vowel *a* is the primary element.

Because the *ākāra* (the letter 'ā') is a qualifier, it is subordinate. In that case, even if this *paribhāṣā* were to apply as a restatement (*anuvāda*) when the mention of "place" (*sthāna*) is absent, nevertheless, because the operation is understood to pertain to the principal element,
the connection with "place" would be recognized for the genitive case of *ātaḥ* itself, and not for the genitive case of *āta* [in the rule *āto dhātoḥ*].
But when the mention of "sthāna" (place) is present, this [word] is also understood; for this purpose, "sthāna" is mentioned.

[The form] "aśvikā" is derived as before: *ka* is added and there is shortening (*hrasvatva*). Now, what is the purpose of the feminine designation in the rule "yakapūrvāyāḥ"? To this he says: "The designation is in the feminine gender."
If that [term *ākāra*] were not present, then only the letter *a* would be understood as the element undergoing substitution (*sthānin*);

consequently, after the verbal root *yā*, when preceded by the upapadas *śubham* and *bhadram*, the suffix *vic* would be applied by Pāṇini 3.2.73 (*vijūpe chandasi*), and then the suffixes *man*, *kvan*, and *kvanip* by 3.2.74 (*āto maninkvanibvanipaśca*). From that [form ending in *vic*], [the desired forms would follow].
If the suffix *kap* were applied, the optionality [of the elision] would also apply in cases such as *śubhaṃyikā* and *bhadraṃyikā*.
Therefore, the mention of the feminine gender is for the purpose of excluding that [optionality]. The words *śubham* and *bhadram* are indeclinables (*nipāta*) ending in the letter *m*.

"Of that which is preceded by *ṭhya*," and so forth; this is the statement of the rule (*grahaṇavākya*). "Of the *yakāra* and *kakāra* at the end of a verbal root (*dhātu*)," and so forth; this is the explanation (*vivaraṇa*). "It should be stated" (*vaktavyam*) means it should be explained (*vyākhyeya*). In this regard, the following [is said]:

The explanation is as follows: because of the understanding that the option (*vibhāṣā*) is fixed (*vyavasthita*), there arises the undesirable consequence that the prohibition of *itva* (the substitution of *i* for *a*) would apply even to the *a* that immediately precedes the *y* and *v* at the end of a verbal root (*dhātu*). [To prevent this, it is stated: "It shall not be so," as in the examples *sunayikā* and *suśayikā*. [These are derived] from the roots *ṇī* (to lead) and *śī* (to lie down) by means of the suffix *erac*.

(3.3.56) *ityac* | She whose conduct (*naya*) is beautiful, she whose reclining (*śaya*) is beautiful—*sunayā*, *suśayā*. From that, by [Pāṇini 5.3.70] *prāgivāt kaḥ* and [7.4.13] *ke'ṇaḥ*, there is shortening of the vowel. Examples: *supākikā*, *aśokikā*. [The root] *ḍupacaṣ* means "to cook."

From the roots *paca* (DhP 996) and *śuc* "to grieve" (DhP 183), the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). [The compound] *supākā* means "she whose cooking is beautiful," while *aśokā* is a *bahuvrīhi* meaning "she in whom grief does not exist. To form the latter, the suffix *kap* is added according to Pāṇini 5.4.154 (*śeṣād vibhāṣā*), and the shortening of the vowel occurs according to Pāṇini 7.4.15 (*āpo 'nyatarasyām*).

47. *bhastraiṣājājñādvāsvā nañpūrvāṇām api* (Pāṇini 7.3.47). [Examples: *bhastrakā*, *bhastrikā*. The suffix *ka* is applied as before. [Examples: *abhastrakā*, *abhastrikā*. The suffix *ka* is applied as before; it may be either a *bahuvrīhi* or a *tatpuruṣa* compound.

Now, why are these two [terms] preceded by the negative particle (*nañ*) not cited as examples? To this he says: "The two [terms] preceded by *nañ* do not cause [the application of] *iṭ*. Because of the context, it should be understood that there is an option regarding the prohibition of *iṭ*. "What is the reason?"—by this [statement], [it is shown that] the two preceded by *nañ* are non-causative.
He asks for the reason. With the words "for here," etc., he demonstrates that which effects it.

Regarding the phrase "by the case-ending existing within": although that case-ending which serves the purpose of the compound has been elided, by virtue of the rule regarding the presence of suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), this [suffix] is applied after the word *etad* ending in *āp* (i.e., *etā*) and after the word *dvi*.

The suffix *para* is applied, and thus there is no possibility of its occurrence at all for this [word], because of the prohibition by the rule "ṭhasupaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.44). Therefore, what is the use of an optional prohibition? Consequently, these two [suffixes] do not cause the application [of the augment] when preceded by the negative particle *nañ*.

If this is so, why would one not employ the word *sva* by this very same logic? To this he says: "But the word *sva*, etc. It is appropriate that these two do not employ [the suffix] when preceded by the negative particle (*nañ*), because here there is no intervention; for [the suffix] *āP* occurs after a form ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). Indeed, [it is not employed]...
The *akac* suffix occurring before the *ṭi* [portion] ought to be an intervening element;

however, by the rule "one's own (*sva*) is not designated as a pronoun (*asarvanāman*) when it refers to kinsmen or wealth" (Pāṇini 1.1.35), the word *sva* is not a pronoun when denoting either kinsmen or wealth; therefore, in that case, the suffix *kap* alone [is applied].

It must be so; it cannot be otherwise. In that case, if the suffix *kap* is applied after forming a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*), and the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is then added to that which ends in *kap*, then this [suffix] does not follow immediately after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), because it is separated by the suffix *kap*.
Consequently, even when preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, the word *sva* would not be designated as a pronoun (*asarvanāman*) and would thus not undergo optional [treatment].
He provides the motivation:

"The word *bhastṛ* is one that has not been stated as masculine (*abhāṣitapuṃska*)," because it always occurs only in the feminine. If this is so, then the optional application [of the suffix] is already established by the rule *abhāṣitapuṃskācca* (Pāṇini 7.3.48).

For what purpose, then, is this [term] introduced here? To this he says: "of that," and so forth. That whose meaning or purpose is subordinate (*upasarjana*) is described as such. When the word *bhastrā* is not subordinate, then—since it is indeed not of the unspoken masculine gender (*abhāṣitapuṃska*)—the optional application is established by the subsequent rule.

In that case as well, because the phrase "of those preceded by the negative particle" (*nañpūrvāṇām*) is understood [from a previous rule], when the word becomes a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), it does not attain the status of having been mentioned in the masculine; thus, the desired result is not established. Therefore, the word *bhastrā* is included here so that the rule may apply even to a subordinate member that has been mentioned in the masculine.

Regarding the forms *ṭhabhastrakā* and *abhastrikā*: when the sense of "small" (*alpa*) is intended, the suffix *ka* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.3.70, *prāgivāt kaḥ*, and [the feminine suffix] *ṭāp* is added according to 5.3.85, *atra*. This refers to the examples presented. As for the phrase "when the shortening of the *upasarjana* has been performed":
once the *bahuvrīhi* compound "one who has no *bhastrā*" (*avidyamānā bhastrā asyāḥ*) has been formed, the rule *gostriyor upasarjanasya* applies.
By this [sūtra], [the word] "again" and so forth is explained. For the word *abhastrā* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound;

since it also occurs in the masculine, it is one that has been stated in the masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*). Therefore, when the suffix *ṭāp* is produced after that word which has been stated in the masculine, even though it has been produced after a word stated in the masculine— [The sūtra applies. (1.2.48) By this [sūtra]. [The word] "again" and so forth. For the word *abhastrā* is indeed a *bahuvrīhi*; since it also exists in the masculine, it is one that has been stated in the masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*). Therefore, when the suffix *ṭāp* is produced, it is produced from that word which has been stated in the masculine. Even though it has been produced from that which has been stated in the masculine—
The short vowel that occurs by the rule "ṭāpō yaḥ ṭhke’ṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.13) does not occur in place of an "at" (short *a*) prescribed after a word that is not originally feminine (*abhāṣitapuṃska*).
Therefore, the desired form is not established by the rule "abhāṣitapuṃskāt"— this is the intended meaning.

"By the word 'also' (*api*) in the rule *ṭhnañpūrvāṇām api*, this application is intended for those preceded by other [prefixes], as well as for simple [stems]. He provides an example there: *nirbhastrikā*, etc.
That from which a bellows has gone out is *nirbhastrikā*. That which has many bellows is... [bahubhastrikā].
*Bahubhastrikā*. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of *subhastrakā*, *subhastrikā*;

*bhastrakā*, *bhastrikā*, and so forth. If, then, the rule is intended to apply to both those preceded by another [word] and to simple [stems], then the statement "of those preceded by the negative particle *nañ*" would be purposeless.

[The rule] will apply to those preceded by *nañ* and so forth through the principle of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*), and to the simple word *nān* through the principle of "behaving like that which has a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). [However, this is not the case here because of the following rules: "An extension to what ends with [a specific element] does not occur when the nominal stem (*pratipadika*) includes the mention of the suffix *ṭha*" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 89);
and "The principle of behaving like that which has a designation does not apply when the nominal stem is not mentioned" (Dharmakīrti’s Paribhāṣā-pāṭha 65).

One should not entertain the doubt that [the desired result] is not established because of this statement; for both of these technical rules (paribhāṣā) apply exclusively to the domain of the prescription of suffixes (pratyaya-vidhi). Therefore, he says "here," etc.;
[it refers to] that which is already established here by means of the designation of the whole as being like its parts (vyapadeśivadbhāva), limited by that [suffix].
This is a restatement of the rule that the suffix *pratyaya* is applied even to words preceded by the negative particle *nañ*. For what purpose?

It is for the sake of the understanding of those of dull intellect. Without the statement "even to those preceded by *nañ*," how could there be comprehension for that person of dull intellect who is unable to grasp the meaning just mentioned? Thus [the rule is stated].
The word "syāt" (might be) is for this purpose.
48. *abhāṣitapuṃskācca*. The particle *ca* is for the purpose of carrying forward [the application of] the rule "even those preceded by *nañ*. [Examples: *khaṭvakā*, *khaṭvikā*.
As before, the suffix *ka* is applied. This word *khaṭvā* has its gender assigned by convention and is always feminine.

The word *vartate* does not have a corresponding masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃska*). Regarding *akhaṭvakā*: it is a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) meaning "not a bed" (*na khaṭvā akhaṭvā*). Regarding *paramakhaṭvikā* and so forth: the compound is formed by the rule *sanmahat* (Pāṇini 2.1.61). In all these cases, the shortening [of the penultimate vowel] occurs by the rule *ko’ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.13).

Someone might have the misconception that because the *bahuvrīhi* has already been treated as having a masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), this optional rule should not apply here; therefore, in order to dispel that notion, he says "in a *bahuvrīhi*" and so forth. But how is it that [the word] is said to be "not having a masculine form" (*abhāṣitapuṃska*) in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*?

Does it also occur after a word that has a corresponding masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃska*)? To this he says: "In this case also, [the rule applies] even when it is not *bhāṣitapuṃska*," and so forth. The particle *iti* indicates the reason. Although a *bahuvrīhi* compound may have a corresponding masculine form, nevertheless, when the suffix *kap* is added and the short vowel is applied by the rule "the feminine suffix *āp* is optionally elided" (Pāṇini 7.4.15), [the feminine form is established].

In that case, the optional application occurs precisely for the *ā* that replaces the *ā* prescribed after a word that does not originally end in the masculine (*abhāṣitapuṃska*). [For example: "one for whom there is no bed" (*avidyamānā khaṭvā asya*) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; by the rule *śeṣādvibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 5.4.154), the suffix *kap* is added; then, the vowel is shortened (*hrasva*). That...

The substitution of *ā* occurs only for that which is prescribed after a word that does not already denote a male (*abhāṣitapuṃska*). Therefore, the option between *akhaṭvakā* and *akhaṭvikā* indeed remains valid. Regarding the phrase "But when," etc.: when the *bahuvrīhi* compound "one for whom there is no bed" (*avidyamānā khaṭvā asyā*) is formed, the shortening of the penultimate vowel occurs by the rule *upasarjanahrasvatvam*; thereafter, the suffix *ṭāp* is added.

In the case of *alpākhaṭvā*, by [the rule] *ṭhakhaṭvakā* (5.3.70)—which functions like the previous [rule]—there will be no optional application [of the feminine suffix]; because the Bahuvrīhi compound is *bhāṣitapuṃska* (having a corresponding masculine form), the vowel *a* is prescribed in place of the final vowel [of the first member]. This [optional application] does not occur even in a *prādi*-compound.
Showing this, he says "tathā" and so forth. Regarding the term "atikhaṭvika":

here too, once the *prādi*-compound has been formed and the shortening of the *upasarjana* has occurred, the vowel *a* is substituted in place of the final *ā* of that *tatpuruṣa* compound, which is derived from a word that is *bhāṣitapuṃska*.
Thus, conceptual construction does not arise.

49. *Ād ācāryāṇām* (Pāṇini 7.3.49). The word *api* from the previous rule [7.3.48] is no longer operative here, because it was not carried over (*anukṛṣṭa*) by the preceding sūtra. This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *it*. It is also an exception to the shortening [of the vowel] prescribed by *ke'ṇaḥ* (7.4.13).

The mention of "the teacher" (ācārya) is for the sake of making the rule obligatory. For if that were absent, there would be an option because of the governing rule "udīcām" (7.3.46). But when "the teacher" is mentioned, that [governing rule] "udīcām" is set aside by it, and thus this rule becomes obligatory.

50. *ṭhasya ikaḥ* | (7.3.50) Here, if the term *ṭha* were taken without qualification, it would apply even to the final *ṭha* of a verbal root, as in *paṭhitā* and *paṭhitum*. Therefore, wishing to avoid this fault, [the word] *pratyayasya* ("of an affix") is supplied [to qualify *ṭha*].

To show that it is not merely the letter *ṭha* that is intended, he says: "the *ṭha* which is the cause of the *aṅga*. The genitive case in *aṅgasya* denotes a relationship (*sambandha*). Therefore, although the letter *ṭha* is indeed a constituent part of the root and thus related to the *aṅga*, nevertheless, when [the *aṅga*] acquires its own existence (*ātmalābha*) from it...

That alone which is called "the limb" (*aṅga*) is understood here as the relative (*sambandhin*) that serves as the cause (*nimitta*) for the limb, due to its proximity; however, even a constituent part (*avayava*) is not [meant]. [The question] "And what becomes the cause of the limb?
is asked with this thought in mind: if that which is the cause of the limb in general were to be taken here.

The suffix *ṭha* at the end of a *dhātu* would indeed [be subject to elision], for the parts of a whole (*avayava*) are indeed the cause (*nimitta*) for that whole (*aṅga*); since it is by means of those parts that the whole is brought about, he says "a suffix" (*pratyaya*).
This is his intention: even though the parts exist, as long as the suffix has not been produced...

As long as that [whole] has not acquired its own nature as a limb (*aṅga*), it does not exist; but when it has arisen, it exists. Therefore, the suffix itself is the cause for the status of being a limb, not the physical part. For example: *ākṣikaḥ*, *śālākikaḥ*. [These mean] "one who plays with dice" (*akṣair dīvyati*); [in this sense, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied—this is the reading in the *mu.* manuscript].

The suffix *ṭhak* is applied in the sense of "he will sell with counting-sticks," as in *lāvaṇikaḥ*. Here too, [the suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule *lavaṇāṭ ṭhañ* (Pāṇini 4.4.52) in the sense of "whose merchandise is salt.
Now, in this context, does the word *asya* refer to the mere phoneme *ṭha*, or to the entire cluster [of consonants]? Regarding that:

In the former view, the mention of *ṭhasya* would not be appropriate; in the latter view, however, there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to Uṇādi derivatives such as *kaṇṭha*, derived from *kaṇeṣṭhaḥ* (Daiva-Upaniṣad 5.6).
But here, in the case of *māthitikaḥ*—meaning "one whose merchandise is *mathita*"—once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) for *ṭha* has been applied...

Furthermore, when the *akāra* is elided by the rule *ṭhyasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), the form comes to end in *t*. Due to the status of the substitute *ikāra* as being like its original (*sthānivadbhāva*), this would be included by the mention of *ṭh*; consequently, the substitution of *ka* by the rule *ṭhisusuktāntāt kaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.51) would undesirably apply.
To the one who might raise this objection, he replies with the words "In the case of *ṭhak* and so forth," etc. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of *ṭhañ* and others is intended.

If, in those [suffixes], there were a suffix consisting of a mere phoneme (*varṇamātra*) without a vowel (*anackapratyaya*), and the letter *a* were merely for the purpose of pronunciation, then [the rule] "for *ṭha*, *ika*" (Pāṇini 7.3.50) would apply.
In this case as well, the vowel *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Thus, the mere phoneme (*varṇamātra*) is taken as the substituendum (*sthānin*).

Here too, since the vowel *a* is merely for the purpose of pronunciation, whatever fault the opponent will urge regarding the inclusion of the mere phoneme—that fault applies here as well, because the mere phoneme is taken as the substituendum. Here too, the vowel *a*...
The objection that will be raised by the opponent— that there is a fault in taking [the term] as merely the phoneme—
is refuted by the fact that, even though it is merely a phoneme,
the designation *ṭhasya* is employed together with an adventitious *a* used for the purpose of pronunciation.

Regarding the passage beginning with "But when there is the apprehension of a composite," etc.: if, in the case of suffixes such as *ṭhak* and others, the word *sākṣāt* is a suffix consisting of a composite, then it is appropriate that in this rule (*sūtra*) as well, the composite is taken as the element to be replaced (*sthānin*).
As for the first fault which the opponent intends to urge against this position:
Desiring to remove that [objection], he says "In that case," and so forth.

Having revealed even the second fault in this position with the words "The merchandise of this [person] has been churned," and so forth, he refutes it with the words "A rule characterized by its immediate occurrence" (*sannipātalakṣaṇo vidhiḥ*), and so forth.

Because [the suffix] arises with the condition of beginning with *aj* (vowels) due to its occurrence in conjunction with [the word] *ajādi*, it is not able to subvert that status of beginning with *aj*;

therefore, the substitution of *ka* does not take place. This is because of the rule "of that which is elided by *yasyeti ca*" (*Pāṇini 1.1.64*), whether by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original) or by virtue of the *bādha* (sublation). Thus, the substitution of *ka* does not occur, as follows from the context.

There is no connection [to the rule], because the status of being "as if in the place of" (*sthānivadbhāva*) is obstructed by the fact that [the suffix] ends in *takāra*. Furthermore, the status of being "as if in the place of" occurs by virtue of the rule *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57), which states that [an element] becomes as if in the place of [that which is replaced] when a preceding operation (*pūrvavidhi*) is to be performed. However, in this case, there is no operation concerning what precedes; rather, what is it?
If that is so, [then what is the meaning]? Is it a rule regarding what follows from what precedes it; how then could there be the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*)?

To this he says: "even from what precedes," and so forth. It is not only a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) intended where a rule applies to what precedes—namely, "a rule concerning the preceding"—but rather it is also a rule that applies *from* what precedes.
The intention is that the term "prior rule" (pūrvavidhi) is also a compound in the fifth case (pañcamī-samāsa).

51. *is-us-uk-tāntāt kaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.51). When a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with a preceding vowel would otherwise apply by the previous rule, the substitution of *ka* for the final letter is prescribed after words ending in *i*, *u*, or *ū*. For example, in *sarpiṣkaḥ*:

the suffix *ṭhak* (which becomes *ika*) is added according to *tad asya paṇyam* (Pāṇini 4.4.51), as it belongs to the *prāgvahatīya* group; then the *ru*-substitution and the *visarjanīya* are applied.

The substitution of *ṣ* for the visarga is applied by the rule *visarjanīyasya ṭhisusoḥ sāmarthye* (Pāṇini 8.3.44). In the word *dhānuṣkaḥ*, the suffix *ṭhak* is added according to the rule *tadasya grahaṇam* (Pāṇini 4.4.57). In the word *yājuṣkaḥ*, the suffix *ṭhak* is added according to the rule *tena dīvyati* (Pāṇini 4.4.2). [In the word] *naiṣādakarṣukaḥ*...
"Śābarajambūkaḥ": born from a Niṣāda woman and a Śabara woman;

[the suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule *ṭhorddhaśe ṭhañ* (Pāṇini 4.2.119), and the shortening occurs by *ke'ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.13). "Mātṛkam" and "paitṛkam": derived from the mother and derived from the father respectively; [the suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule *ṛtaṣṭhañ* (Pāṇini 4.3.78).
Regarding "udaśvitkaḥ": the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.2.19], "udaśvito 'nyatarasyām.
Regarding "śākṛtkaḥ" and "yākṛtkaḥ": the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.4.22], "śakṛdyakṛtā saṃsṛṣṭe."
Now, why does this not occur here: *āśiṣā carati* → *āśiṣikaḥ*, *uṣā carati* → *auṣikaḥ*? To this he says: *ṭhisusoḥ* etc.
[The suffix] *isi* is prescribed after the roots *arc*, *suc*, *hu*, *sṛp*, *chād*, and *chard* (Dhātupāṭha 9.30), and *usi* after the root *jan*.
By the rule *ṛt-pṛ-vapi-yaji-tani-tapi-bhyo niṭ* (Dhātupāṭha 9.39) and the subsequent section, two suffixes are prescribed;

according to the maxim *lakṣaṇa-pratipadokta-paribhāṣā* (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 3), there is the selection of those two forms of *is* and *us* that are taught by their specific rules (*pratipadokta*). Consequently, [the forms] *āśiṣikaḥ* and *āuṣikaḥ* [are derived].
In this case as well, [the substitution] does not occur, because *isu* and *sus* are technical terms (*lākṣaṇika*). For instance, when the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *śās* preceded by *āṅ*—
from the root *śāsu* in the sense of "desire" (DhP 1022)— and to the root *vas* alone— meaning "to dwell" (DhP 1005)— [the rule] *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.15) applies.

When the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) and the substitution of the preceding vowel for the following one (*parapūrvatva*) have been performed, the forms *isusati* are obtained—as in *āśiṣikaḥ* and *āuṣikaḥ*. By the rule "and [the substitution of ṣ] for *śās*, *vas*, *dhas*, and *sā*" (Pāṇini 8.3.60), the substitution of *ṣ* occurs; however, because that [substitution] is considered as if non-existent (*asiddha*), the possibility of the substitution of *k* was raised as an objection.
Regarding the statement "there should be an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) [to the rule]," the word *upasaṃkhyāna* means "explanation" or "demonstration.

In this regard, the demonstration is as follows: the term *apad* is understood to carry over from the rule *nañpūrvāṇām api* (Pāṇini 7.3.47); and that term has the sense of an inclusive "also" (*samuccaya*) for what has not been explicitly mentioned. Therefore...
There will also be a fault.

52. *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.52). [Examples: *pākaḥ*, *tyāgaḥ*. [These are formed] with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). [Examples: *pākyam*, *vākyam*. [These are formed] with the suffix *ṇyat* by rule 3.1.124 (*ṛhalorṇyat*). Now, one might object: "In this case, since the *ghi* and *ṇyat* suffixes are the grammatical operations (*kāryin*), and since *ca* and *ju* [are the substituends], [the rule should apply here as well]."

[An objection: On account of the equality [of the number of rules and letters], one would obtain a correspondence according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*): [namely] that *dhiti* would apply to the letter *ca*, and *ṇyat* to the letter *ja*. How then can there be an exclusion? Would it not follow that the substitution of *ku* (the sound *g*) applies to the letter *ja* in the word *rāga*? This is not so; because of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), there is no correspondence according to order here. This is indicated by the rule: "The words *bhujam* and *nyubjam*—" [Pāṇini 6.1.172].

By prescribing the absence of *kutva* for the letter *j* in the rule "pāṇyupatāpayoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.61) and "prayājānuyājau yajñāṅge" (Pāṇini 7.3.62)— which both employ the suffix *ghañ*— and by providing the technical indication "tena raktaṃ rāgāt" (Pāṇini 4.2.1), he makes it known that the principle of "correspondence in order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*) does not apply here.

53. And [the suffix *u* is applied] after *nyuṅkha* and others. (Pāṇini 7.3.53) This rule is commenced for the sake of forms such as *adhiṇṇya*. [The Vārttika states: "After the root *vañc*, the suffix *u* is applied. In that context, the suffix *u* is added because the rule *bhṛmṛśītṛcaritsaritanidhanimimasjibhya uḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 1.92) is understood to apply.

Regarding "ṭhmadguḥ": from the root *ṭuamasjo* in the sense of "cleansing" (*dhā.pā.* 1415), the letter *s* is replaced by *d* according to *ṭhjhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* (Pāṇini 8.4.53). Regarding "ṭhmimasjibhya uḥ": by this, [the author] indicates the rule *ṭhbhṛmṛśītṛcari* (Daiva Uṇādi Sūtra 1.92) and others. Regarding "ṭhbhṛguḥ".
