The root *bhrasj* means "to cook" (Dhātupāṭha 1284). In the rule beginning with *prathi-bhradī* (Daiva 1.113), the suffix *u* is understood from that very rule (Daiva 1.92). Thus, we have *dūrepākaḥ* (or *dūrepākāḥ*, as in the manuscript reading); here, the suffix *ac* is applied in the sense of the agent who is also the object (*karmakartṛ*) according to the rule *pacādyac*.
Regarding "ṭhukārāntāvapera": the word "is studied" (*adhīyate*) is to be understood as the required complement.

Regarding "ṭhtañcateḥ": this refers to the partial citation of the rule *sphāyitañcivañci* from the Dhātupāṭha; specifically, it refers to *tancu* and *tvancu* in the sense of "going" (DhP 1.91–92), and *vancu* in the sense of "deceiving" (DhP 6.1703).

This refers to the rule: *sphāyitañcivañciśakikṣipikṣudisṛpidṛpitṛpivanyundiśvitivṛtyajinīpadimadimudikhidibhidicchidimandicandidahidasidambhivahavasivāśiśīṅhasasidhiśubhibhyo rak* (Daiva-Uṇādi 8.31). Regarding "vyatiṣaṅgaḥ": from the root *ṣañj* (to adhere), Dhātupāṭha 987. Regarding "avasargaḥ": from the root *sṛj* (to emit/let loose), Dhātupāṭha 1178; the suffix *ac* is added according to the *pacādi* group. Regarding "medhaḥ": from the root *miha* (to sprinkle/moisten), Dhātupāṭha 992; the suffix *ac* is added as before. Regarding "śvapākaḥ": [from the root *paca* with the prefix *śva-*, meaning "one who cooks dogs"].

The suffix *aṇ* [is applied] after a word ending in *karman* as an upapada, according to the rule *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1). Regarding *arhateḥ*: the root *arh* [is used] in the sense of "worship" (*pūjā*) (Dhātupāṭha 740). Regarding *dahaḥ*: the root *dah* [is used] in the sense of "reducing to ashes" (*bhasmīkaraṇa*) (Dhātupāṭha 992). Regarding *ruheḥ*: the root *ruh* [is used] in the sense of "the birth of a seed" (*bījajanmani*) and "manifestation" (*prādurbhāve*) (Dhātupāṭha 859).
But surely, words such as *nyaṅku* and others are listed in the list of nominal stems (*prātipadika-gaṇa*) with the substitution of *k* for *kū* already applied;

so what is the purpose of this [rule], since, just as other grammatical operations occur by virtue of the irregular derivation (*nipātana*), so too will the substitution of *k* for *kū* occur? To that very point...
This is stated for the purpose of authorizing the recitation of the *Prātipadika-pāṭha*; for if that did not exist, it would be understood as a mistaken reading.

54. *ho hanteṇinneṣu* (Pāṇini 7.3.54). Examples such as *dhātayati* have been explained under the rule *hanasta’ciṇṇaloḥ* (7.3.32). As for *ghnanti*: this is the present tense (*laṭ*), with the substitution of *anti* for *jhi*, and [the substitution of *na* for *han*] by *gamahana* (6.4.98).

By these and other such rules, there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*). In *dhnantu*, the suffix is *loṭ*. In *adhvan*, the suffix is *laṅ*; the elision of the letter *i* occurs by the rule *itaśca* (Pāṇini 3.4.100). In *prahāraḥ* and *prahārakaḥ*, the suffixes *ghañ* and *ṇvul* are applied to the root *hṛ*.
In this context, the mention of "ñṇit" (a letter followed by *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *n*) would either be a qualifier for the root *han*— meaning "the *h* of the root *han* which is followed by *ñ*,

*ṇ*, or *n*"— or it would be a qualifier for the *h* itself— meaning "if that *h* is followed by *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *n*, and belongs to the root *han*"? If the former alternative were adopted there, [the following would result].

In the first case, [the rule] would not apply to *dhnanti*, for here the root *han* is not followed by the letter *n*; this is because it is impossible for a whole to have a temporal priority or posteriority relative to one of its own parts, and there is no other *n* present.

If, on the other hand, the second alternative were adopted, [the rule] would never apply, for the letter *h*— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument regarding the application of grammatical rules involving the sequence of sounds.]

The condition of being followed by the letter *ṇ* is possible; however, it is impossible in cases such as *ghnant-* because, when the elision of the vowel *a* occurs, the substitution of the preceding element (*sthānivadbhāva*) results in an intervention by that *a*. Furthermore, in cases such as *ghātayati*, there is an intervention by the element *ana*, which is a constituent part of the root *han* and follows the letter *h*.
Because of the intervention. Now, if by the force of the statement it were to apply even when there is an intervention,

then in the case of *hananam icchati*— whereby *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8) applies, followed by *kyaci ca* (7.4.33) which causes the substitution of *i*, then the suffix *ṇvul* is added to the form ending in *kyac*, and finally *ato lopaḥ* (6.4.48) [applies].

If someone were to object that the elision of the letter *i* would also apply in the case of *hananīyaka*, the author states another alternative view in response: "The *ñṇit* affix is the qualifier of the root *han*. For it is not possible for all *ñ*, *ṇ*, and *n* letters to function as qualifiers with respect to the root *han*, nor...

With respect to the sound *hakāra*: therefore, some [element] or other serves as a qualifier for something according to possibility. However, since a suffix (*pratyaya*) marked with *ñ* or *ṇ* occurs after the root *han*, it is its qualifier—meaning, "after a suffix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*, immediately following the root *han*."

However, the negative particle *na* cannot be a qualifier of the root *han*, for the reason stated previously. Since it is appropriate as a qualifier of the vowel *i*, it qualifies that alone—meaning "when *na* follows immediately after the *i* of the root *han*. This, however, refers to the rule: "When something is specified by the locative case [tasmin], the operation applies to what precedes it."

Thus, by the inclusion of the term "nirdiṣṭa" (specified), the meaning of immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is obtained. When immediate succession is relied upon, however, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) [of the rule] to cases such as *hantā* and *hantum* is also ruled out. Now, one might object that immediate succession between the letter *ha* and the letter *ṇa* is not even possible, due to the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) of the elision of the vowel *a*.
[Is there not] an intervention by the *satyakāra* [augment]? To this he says: "And that," etc.

"Produced by conjunction" (*sannipātakṛta*) means produced by the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). But even if the immediate sequence produced by conjunction is accepted, what about the non-immediate sequence brought about by the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original)?

Why would that very quality (*kutva*) be destroyed? To this he says: "But that which is produced by the rule concerning *sthānivadbhāva*," and so forth. Why is it not an obstacle? He says: "By virtue of the force of the statement. If the non-proximity (*anānantarya*) produced by the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* were an intervening factor (*vyavadhāyaka*) that obstructs [the application of the rule], [it would be so].
The statement containing the word "not" (na) would be purposeless, because there would be no scope [for it].
Therefore, by the force of that statement, it is not a sublater.
Regarding the two positions proposed by the words "even though" (*yadyapi*) and so forth, in that case, as for the second position...

The fault [in that case] is avoided. In that regard, the fault that arose when the letter *ha* was qualified by the letter *na* has already been avoided. Now, however, he avoids the fault that arises when the letter *ha* is qualified by a suffix (*pratyaya*) marked with the markers *ñ* or *ṇ*. This which is a constituent part (*avayava*) of the root *han*—

The letters beginning with *a* and ending with *n* follow the letter *ha*; therefore, there is always an intervention [of these letters] between the suffix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*. However, an intervention by the word *ananīya* is possible;

yet it is not possible [to claim that the rule applies] there, because of the authoritative statement: "That which cannot function when there is no intervention [does not function] when there is an intervention."

Thus, in examples such as *ghātayati*, the substitution of *k* (*kutva*) occurs. However, since an intervention by the word *hananīya* is impossible [in that case], whereas such an intervention is possible in the case of *hananīyaka*, the substitution will not take place there. As for the fault stated regarding the first alternative, it...

Since that [interpretation] is not accepted, there is no occasion [for such an objection]. The mention of *hanti* with the suffix *śtip* is intended solely for the purpose of indicating the verbal root (*dhātu*), and not for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-luṅ form; for in that case, by the rule *ṭhabhyāsācca* (Pāṇini 7.3.55), the substitution of *k* must indeed occur.
55. And because of repetition [of the root] (7.3.55).

As in *jighāṃsati*: the suffix *san*, lengthening by "aj-jhan-gamāṃ sani" (6.4.16), reduplication, and by "ku-hoś-cuḥ" (7.4.62), the change to a *c*-sound—the letter *jh*; [this occurs] in the reduplicated syllable.

By the rule *carca* (8.4.54), there is the substitution of *jaś*-ness, which is the letter *j*; by the rule *sanyataḥ* (7.4.79), there is the substitution of *i*. Thus, we have *jaṅghanyate*. By the rule *nugato'nunāsikāntasya* (7.4.85), there is the augment *nuK*.
As for *jaghāna*: when the third person singular (*uttamapuruṣa*) is used with *liṭ*, there is no *ṇiṭva* (the status of being marked with *Ṇ*).
This is the example. However, in the view that [the suffix] is *ṇit*, it is already established by the preceding rule.

Why does [the substitution] not occur in the case of *jihananīyiṣati*—formed by adding *kyac* after the word *agra-hanana*, then *san* after that, and finally *iṭ*—since the letter *h* of the root *han* indeed follows the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*)?

Thus he says: "In this case, regarding the suffix caused by reduplication," and so forth. Here, the word *han-teḥ* (from 7.3.54) is understood to carry over, as is the word *aṅgasya* (of the stem). By means of reduplication (*abhyāsa*), the suffix (*pratyaya*) which is the cause of that reduplication is brought into proximity; its [the stem's] suffix serves as a specific cause for that [reduplication]. In that context:
By that suffix conditioned by reduplication (*abhyāsa-nimitta*), the base (*aṅga*) of the root *han* is qualified.
[As stated in the Kāśikā: "When there is a suffix conditioned by reduplication, it is the base of the root *han*. By such a *han* as well, the reduplication [is affected].

It is distinguished [from the previous rule]. Since there exists a relationship of qualifier and qualified in the sense that "the reduplication of the root *han* which is characterized by the aforementioned qualifications," then, when a suffix such as *san* is conditioned by reduplication, the substitution of *ku*-tva (i.e., *ha* becoming *gh*) must apply specifically to that reduplication of the root *han* which possesses those qualifications.

Therefore, in this case, [the form] *jihananīyiṣati* does not occur—according to the Kāśikā, it is because when the suffix *san* follows a causative (*nic*) derived from a verbal root, the root *han* is no longer considered the "base" (*aṅga*). Rather, what is the base?
It is the word *hananīya*. However, in that case where *han* is indeed the base—namely, when the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied—[the rule applies].
It is not caused by repeated practice.
56. *heracaiṅ* (Pāṇini 7.3.56).
Regarding the form *prajighīṣati*: it is derived from the root *hi* "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1257) with the desiderative suffix *san*;
the lengthening of the vowel occurs as before. Regarding the form *prajedhīyate*: [it is formed] by [the rule] *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*.

(7.4.25) Thus, there is lengthening; then reduplication; and by the rule "guṇo yaṅlukoḥ" (7.4.72), there is guṇa substitution for the reduplicated syllable. [The form] *prajighāya* [is derived as follows]: the suffix *ṇal*, followed by the substitution of vṛddhi and the replacement of *ā*.
[The form] *prācīhayat* [is derived from] the causative *ṇic* suffix, by the rule "ṇiśri" (3.1.48) and so forth.

In *caṅadeśaḥ*, there is shortening by the rule *ṭhṇau caṅyupadhāyāḥ* (7.4.1); there is reduplication by the rule *ṭhcaṅ* (6.1.11). And since that [reduplication] which occurs when *ṇi* is present is treated as *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were in its original position), according to the principle *ṇau kṛtaṃ sthānivadbhavati* (Cāndra-paribhāṣā 21), the long vowel is applied to the syllable *hi* by the rule *ṭhdīrgho laghoḥ* (7.4.94).

Regarding the passage beginning with "caṅyabhyāsanimite": in the form *prājīhayat*, the element *ṇic* which follows as the cause for the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) in *caṅ* is the subordinate member (*aṅga*) of the root *hi*; however, it is not subordinate to that very *caṅ* which is the cause of the reduplication.
This is because the present sūtra falls under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "reduplication" (*abhyāsa*).

When the cause for reduplication is projected by repetition (*abhyāsa*), and it is understood that the root *hi* is the member [to be reduplicated], then since this is how it is understood, what possibility is there for the augment *aiC* to occur in place of something additional? Since it does not occur in this way, the prohibition "not when *aC*" (*na aC-i*) is unnecessary. Thus...
Having set aside the mention of *caṅ*, he states its purpose with the words "this is done," and so forth.

What, then, is indicated by this? He says: "after *hi* when *ac* follows, not in *caṅ*" (*heracaṅ*), and so forth. By the rule "after *hi* when *ac* follows, not in *caṅ*," [the substitution of *guṇa*] applies elsewhere than in *caṅ*, even when there is an additional suffix such as *san*.

The meaning that "the substitution of *ku* occurs for *hi*" is thus made known. By the words "by that" and so forth, he demonstrates the purpose of this indicator (*jñāpaka*). The form "prajighāyayiṣati" is derived from the causative stem (with the suffix *ṇic*) by adding the desiderative suffix (*san*), based on the sense "he desires to cause [someone] to send forth."

57. *san-liṭor jeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.57). [Examples: *jigīṣati*, *jigāya*. By the rule *ādeḥ parasya* (1.1.54), there is the substitution of the guttural (*kutva*) for the initial *j* of the subsequent element; this applies to the root *jyā* in the sense of "loss of vitality" (Dhātupāṭha 1499).

In the case of the *liṭ* [perfect tense], when *saṃprasāraṇa* has been applied by the rule *grahijyādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 6.1.16) and the substitution of the preceding vowel (*parapūrvatva*) has occurred, this specific form *jirā* arises. Consequently, the substitution of *k* (*kutva*) would also apply to that [final *r*].

Because it is included by the mention of *jigrahana*. Nor can it be argued that once the lengthening [of the vowel] has been applied by the rule "halaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.2), there will be no inclusion by the mention of *jigrahana*, because that which has undergone a partial modification is not considered different from the original; otherwise, indeed...

Even in the case of *jigīṣati*, once the lengthening [of the vowel] has been applied by the rule "ṭhajjhanagamāṃ sani" (Pāṇini 6.4.16), it will not be included by the mention of *ji*. Alternatively, to one who might object that the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *g*) must occur first because it is subsequent to the lengthening, he says: "of *jināti*."

And so forth. By the paribhāṣā "the rule applies to that which is taught by its specific technical definition" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 3), this refers only to the root *ji* as it is read in the Dhātupāṭha as *ṭhji jaye* (DhP 561), and not to the root *jināti*. Once the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) has been performed, this refers to the form *jī* that is thereby produced.

Because it is based on specific grammatical characteristics (*lākṣaṇikatva*), as in the forms *jijyatuḥ* and *jijyuḥ*. Here, after the suffixes *liṭ*, *atus*, and *us*, the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs by the rule "eranekāco'saṃyogapūrvasya" (Pāṇini 6.4.82).

58. *vibhāṣā ceḥ* | (7.3.58) 59. *na kvādeḥ* | (7.3.59) When the substitution of *k* for *c* and *j* before affixes marked with *gh* or *ṇi* (as prescribed by *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*, 7.3.52) is about to take place:

This prohibition is now commenced: "kūjaḥ, khajaḥ, garjaḥ. [The roots are] "kūja" in the sense of "indistinct sound" (DhP 2.23), "kharja" in the sense of "affliction" (DhP 2.29), and "garja" in the sense of "sound" (DhP 2.26).

60. And [the suffix GHaÑ is applied] after the roots *aj* and *vraj*. (Pāṇini 7.3.60) Examples: *samājaḥ*, *udājaḥ*. The root *aja* is listed as "going and throwing" (Dhātupāṭha 230). The suffix GHaÑ is applied by the rule "GHaÑ is applied after *aja* preceded by *sam* and *ud*, when referring to animals" (3.3.69). Examples: *parivrājaḥ*, *parivrājyam*. The root *vraj*...

[The roots] *gatau* (DhP 252, 253). Now, why has no example been presented for the substitution of *vī* for *aj* in the *ṇyati* suffix? To this he says: "of the substitution of *vī*" and so forth. In that regard, the rule "ajervyaghañapoḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.56) prescribes the substitution of *vī*.
Therefore, an example for that [suffix] is not applicable; thus, the intention is that it has not been shown.
The particle *ca* serves to include what has not been mentioned; by it, there is also a prohibition regarding the suffix *vāj*, as in *vājaḥ* and *vācyam*.

61. *bhujanyubjau pāṇyupatāpayoḥ* | (7.3.61) Regarding the word *bhujaḥ*: from the root *bhuja* in the sense of "protecting" (*pālana*) and "eating" (*abhyavahāra*) (DhP 1454), the suffix *dhañ* is applied by *halaśca* (3.3.121). Here, [the rule] *ave tṛstrorghañ* (3.3.120) applies.

The suffix *ghañ* is understood [from the previous rule]. Regarding the word *nyubja*: when it is stated that the term is formed with a penultimate *d*, as in the root *udj* meaning "straightness," then the substitution of *b* for *d* is prescribed by way of irregularity (*nipātana*). Alternatively, according to the statement found in the Mahābhāṣya on the rule *iyavaraṭ*—"the *b* is desired [as the substitute] for the *d* of *udj* even though it is not established"—this is intended.

When the letter *da* is changed to *bha*, it becomes *ba* by the rule of *jaś*-substitution. However, if the root *ṭubja* (meaning "to straighten") has *ba* as its penultimate letter, then in the word *samudga* or similar forms, the change of *ba* to *da* must be stated.
62. *prayāja* and *anuyāja* are [names of] sacrificial subsidiaries (*yajñāṅga*).

(7.3.62) [The forms] "prayājaḥ" and "anuyājaḥ" [are derived as follows]: from the root *yaj* preceded by *pra-* and *anu-*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied by the rule "the suffix *ghañ* occurs after [a root] when there is a factor other than the agent and when it is a name" (3.3.19). In that case, the substitution of *ku*-sounds (i.e., *k* for *y*) is irregularly excluded (*nipātyate*).
"For the purpose of illustration" means for the purpose of indicating other similar cases as well.
Consequently, the substitution of *kutva* does not occur in other parts of the sacrifice belonging to the same class, such as the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings.
Furthermore, its status as an illustration is as follows:

The terms *prayāja* and *anuyāja* should be understood as denoting the constituent parts of the sacrifice, for it is for this purpose that they are employed. How indeed might it be understood that the mention of the *prayājas* and *anuyājas* serves as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*)? Otherwise, [this would be understood] solely through the power of the grammatical formation (*nipātana*).
Since it would be understood as having the constituent parts of the sacrifice as its object, that [action] would simply not be something to be performed.

63. *vañci* in the sense of "going" (*gati*). (Pāṇini 7.3.63) [The form] *vañcam*. [The roots] *vañcu*, *cañcu*, *tañcu*, *tvañcu*, *mruñcu*, *mlañcu*, *bhrucu*, *mlucu* are among those whose meaning is "to go" (*dhātupāṭha* 189–196).
The suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). That which is to be gone to is called *vañcyam*. They go (*vañcanti*) to that which is to be gone to.
The meaning is "they go. In the word *caṅkrama*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.3.121] *halaśca*.

64. *ākaḥ ucaḥ ke* (Pāṇini 7.3.64). Regarding the word *nyokaḥ*: from the root *uc* preceded by the prefix *ni*—specifically from *uc samavāye* (Dhātupāṭha 1223)—the suffix *ka* is applied according to *ig-upadha-jña-prī-kiraḥ kaḥ* (3.1.135). Thus, *nyucati* means "he dwells," and hence the word *nyokaḥ*, meaning "one who dwells."

The suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of the *ṭha* or *ghañ* suffixes according to the rule "there is the application of *ka* [in the sense of *ṭha* or *ghañ*]" (Vārttika 306)—thus we have *nyokaḥ*, meaning "that in which they dwell. As for the phrase "But for what purpose... and so forth, he thinks as follows: this is a conventional (*rūḍhi*) word; it is not [derived etymologically] here.

There is no specific meaning for the individual parts [of the word *vyutpatti*]; only the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) must be performed, and that indeed occurs even when the suffix *ghañ* is applied by the rule "and after a consonant" (*halaśca*, Pāṇini 3.3.121). Therefore, there is no purpose for this particular grammatical rule (*yoga*). [The opponent argues: "If *ghañ* were present, it would be udātta on the first syllable," according to the rule "after that which ends in *ñ* or *n*, it is always [udātta]" (*ñnityādernityam*).
By this [rule, Pāṇini 6.1.197].

Now, in cases such as *divaukasaḥ* ("inhabiting heaven") and *jalaukasaḥ* ("living in water"), how is there the substitution of *k* for *s*, given that here there is neither the suffix *kap* nor the suffixes *dhi* or *ṇyu*, but rather the suffix *asun*? To this [it is replied]:...
He said: "The dwellers of heaven," and so forth; the meaning has already been explained.

65. The suffix *ṇya* is used in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*). (Pāṇini 3.3.170) Examples include *avaśyapacyam* and so forth. [The roots] *ḍupacaṣ pāke* (Dhātupāṭha 996, "to cook") and *vaca paribhāṣaṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 1842, "to speak") [are involved]. [The rule] *āvaśyakādhamarṇyayor ṇiniḥ* (3.3.170) [provides for the suffix *ṇini* in the senses of necessity and debt].
In this continuation [of the rule], the suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of necessity by the rule *ṭhkṛtyāśca* (Pāṇini 3.3.171).

The compound is formed according to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group (Pāṇini 2.1.72), and the elision of *avaśyam* occurs before a *kṛtya* suffix by the rule *lubhyedavaśyamaḥ kṛtye tumkāmamanasorapi* (Kāśikā on Pāṇini 6.1.144). Thus, [the form] *avaśyamo* is established.
There is the elision of the letter *ma*.

66. *yajayācarucapravacarcaśca* (Pāṇini 7.3.66). The rule *ṇye* [from the previous sūtra] still applies. This [sūtra] is for the purpose of expressing non-necessity (*anāvaśyakārtha*). Examples include *yājyam* and so forth. The roots are: *yaja* (to worship the gods, etc. [Dhātupāṭha 1002], and *yāc* (to beg) [Dhātupāṭha 863].
The roots *ṛc* in the sense of "shining" (DhP 7.45), *vac* in the sense of "speaking" (DhP 18.42) preceded by *pra*,

and *ṛc* in the sense of "praising" (DhP 13.2). But how can there be a *ṇyat* suffix after *ṛc*, given that by the rule *ṛdupadhāccāklṛpicṛteḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.110), a *kyap* suffix is prescribed instead of *ṇyat*?
"Is it necessary? To this he says: "Because of the rule *ṛdupadhāt*," and so forth.
Now, for what purpose is the mention of *praci*? For surely the prohibition will occur by the rule *vaco'śabdasaṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 7.3.67) alone? To this he says: "The mention of *praci*..."

"‘For the sake of the designation “word”’. It might be argued: "Is there no word at all for which the name ‘denotable object’ (vācya) could apply? To this he says: "That which is called ‘the non-denotable’ (apravācya)," and so forth.
With the words "But others," etc., he shows another opinion. "But this," etc.
This form is not subject to dispute. But what is this distinction? He says: "of the ten-night [sacrifice]," and so forth.

That form of the word *śaś* is desired only for that which is the tenth day of the ten-night sacrifice (*daśarātra*)—for which the ritualists do not speak at variance—and not elsewhere. If this is so, [the rule] would be purposeless.

The inclusion of the term *pravaci* is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), so that its substitution with *vuñ* may necessarily occur only in a specific domain; one might argue that by that very effort, the substitution of *ku* (the guttural *k*) will also occur there. This is not so; for by virtue of that restriction, the prohibition of the substitution of *ku* applies to other prefixes.

[The rule] ceases. However, the determination of the meaning [of the suffixes] will be understood solely by virtue of established usage, as in the case of "in the prohibition of *ṇyat*" and so forth. When this prohibition of *ṇyat* is being formulated, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the root *tyaj* (DhP 986) in the sense of "abandoning."

The purpose of the word "upasaṃkhyāna" (supplementary addition) is to provide an explanation. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the particle *ca* (and) has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned; by means of it, the prohibition will also apply to the root *tyaj*.
67. [The suffix *ṇyat* is applied after the root *vac*] when not used in the sense of "a sound" (*aśabda-saṃjñā*).

(Pāṇini 7.3.67) 68. [The suffixes *ṇyat* and *ṇic* are applied after the roots *pra-yuj* and *ni-yuj*] in the sense of capability (*śakya-artha*). (Pāṇini 7.3.68) [The suffix *ṣyaṇ* is applied] after the root *yuj* (meaning "to join," *yujir yoge*, Dhātupāṭha 1444) preceded by *pra-* or *ni-*.

The absence of the suffix *kṛt* is prescribed as a nipātana; and this occurs when the suffix *ṇyat* is used in the sense of "possible. Furthermore, that *ṇyat* is to be understood by the rule "śaki liṅ ca" (Pāṇini 3.3.172), for in that context, the term "kṛtyāḥ" from 3.3.171 is still in force. Now, for what purpose is this nipātana stated again?

Does [the rule] *ṣṭhṇye* (Pāṇini 7.3.65) not indeed continue to apply here? In that case, although one could simply state *prayujaniyujoḥ śakyarthe*, this is a *nipātana* (irregular formation) for the sake of a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*).

This is so that the suffix may occur where the sense of "capability" (*śakyārthatā*) is subordinate—as in *prayojyo bhṛtyaḥ* ("a servant who can be employed") and *niyojyo dāsaḥ* ("a slave who can be directed"). [This applies] with respect to the master.

The terms *prayojya* and *niyojya* do not apply here; for those two words are not conventional designations (*rūḍha*) in that context, but rather [they refer to] only that which has become subordinate (*guṇabhūta*).

69. *Bhojyam* [is substituted] for *bhakṣye*. (7.3.69) Regarding the form *bhojyam*: from the root *bhuja* in the sense of "protecting" and "eating/consuming" (Dhātupāṭha 1454), when the suffix *ṇyat* is applied and the meaning to be expressed is "that which is to be eaten," the absence of *kutva* (the change of *j* to *g*) is prescribed as a nipātana (irregularity). Thus: *bhojyā yavāgūḥ* ("the gruel is fit to be eaten").

But surely this root *bhakṣ* refers to solid food that is chewed and swallowed, and not to liquid substances, as in the rule "preparations [are called] *bhakṣa*" (Pāṇini 4.2.16). Therefore, how can it apply to barley-gruel (*yavāgū*) when the term "*bhakṣye*" is used? To this he says: "In this context, *bhakṣya*... and so forth. It is not necessarily the case that *bhakṣ* [refers only to solid food].

It occurs in the sense of "eating hard food. For instance, its usage is also seen even with liquid substances, as in *abbhakṣaḥ* (one who eats water), *vāyubhakṣaḥ* (one who eats air), and *vāyubhakṣa* (id.). Therefore, since the root *bhakṣi* functions in the general sense of "consuming," it applies to *yavāgū* (gruel) as well. [This is so] because it should have been stated: "the root *bhuji* is used when the object is food (*bhakṣya*)."

The formation [of the word *bhogya*] is established by convention (*rūḍhi*) for the purpose of denoting food to be consumed; it should apply when the object (*karman*) is something edible, so that it does not apply to something to be protected—as in "the cakes are *bhogyāḥ*," which means they are to be guarded.

70. *ghorlopo leṭi vā* (Pāṇini 7.3.70). [The example is] *dadat*. [The root is] *ḍudāñ dāne* (Dhātupāṭha 1091). The suffix *leṭ* occurs in the sense of the *liṅ* (optative) (3.4.97). The substitution of *jhi* by *ant* takes place (7.1.3), and then [by 3.4.97]: *itaśca lopaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* ("there is elision of the *i* of the *leṭ* when followed by *parasmaipada* endings").

Thus, there is the elision of the vowel *i*; the augment *aṭ* is applied by the rule "ṭhleṭo'ḍāṭau" (3.4.94); the suffix *śap* follows; because [the root] belongs to the *juhotyādi* class, *ślu* is applied; by the rule "ślau" (6.1.10), reduplication occurs;
there is the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopaḥ*, 8.2.23); and [finally], the substitution of *ṅmuṭ* occurs by the rule "ṅmo hrasvād aci ṅmuṇ nityam" (8.3.32).

Thus, there is the augment *ṅmuṭ*. Regarding the example "somo dadad gandharvāya": [the root] *dadāti* takes the suffix *sip*; the rest is as before. Regarding the example "yad agnir agnaye dadāt": when *dadāt* is established, by Pāṇini 6.1.101 (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghatvam*), there is lengthening of the vowel; the rest is as before.

If, even when the augment *yaṅ* has been applied and the elision (*lopa*) has occurred, the form *dadāt* is established, for what purpose then is the word *vā* stated? To this he says: "In that case," and so forth.
It might be argued: in that case, the mention of *vā* is appropriate for the sake of clarity, because of the rule *vadādi*.
Since there is no possibility of doubting the non-establishment of *rūpa*, he says "for these" (*eṣāṃ hi*), and so forth; this is easily understood. 71. *otaḥ śyani* (Pāṇini 7.3.71).

Regarding "ṭhniśyati" and so forth: the root *śo* means "to thin" (DhP 1145); *chāe* means "to cut" (DhP 1146—though this root is not found in printed editions); *do* means "to break" (DhP 1148); and *ṣo* means "to finish" (DhP 1147). Now, for what purpose [are these mentioned]?

This is stated as "iyan," rather than simply saying "ṭhśiti"; for if it were stated in this way, the elision would occur only before the affix *śyan*, since no other *śit* affix is possible after a stem ending in *e*. In this manner, the rule becomes concise; furthermore, there is this additional purpose [of the brevity]: namely, that the rule "ṣṭhivuklamucamāṃ śiti" (Pāṇini 7.3.75) applies.

In this case, would it not be the case that the mention of *śit* need not be made, as that very term will be carried over (*anuvartate*) from there? True, it would indeed be established; however, there would be heaviness of comprehension (*pratipatti-gaurava*). Therefore, in order to avoid such heaviness of comprehension, the word *śyan* was stated.

Regarding the term *ṭhaṭ*: the inclusion of the long vowel marker (*t*) is for the sake of ease of pronunciation; for there is nothing else that could possibly be excluded by it, nor anything else that could be prescribed.

72. *ksasyāci* (Pāṇini 7.3.72). [Examples: *adhukṣātām*, *adhukṣāthām*. [Derivation: From the root *duh* in the *luṅ* tense, the *cli* suffix is applied; by the rule *svaritañitaḥ* (1.3.72), the Ātmanepada endings are used; [the specific endings are] *ātām* and *āthām*; [then] *śā*... [is applied].

By the rule *igupadhādaniṭaḥ ksaḥ* (3.1.45), there is the substitution of *ksa* for the suffix *cli*; by the rule *alo’ntyasya* (1.1.52), this [suffix] is elided; by the rule *dāderghātorghaḥ* (8.2.32), the letter *h* is replaced by *dh*;
and by the rule *ekāco vaśo bhaṣ* (8.2.37) et cetera, *bhaṣ*—namely, the letter *dh*—is substituted.

By the rule *ṭhkhari ca* (8.4.55), there is the substitution of *c*—that is, the letter *k* for the letter *dh*. By the rule *iṇkoḥ* (8.3.57), there is the substitution of *ṣ*. Thus, *adhikṣi*. Here, the augment *iṭ* is added to the third person singular ending. In *adhukṣat*, the suffix is *tip*; by the rule *itaśca* (3.4.100), there is the elision of the vowel *i*. In *adhukṣatām*, [the suffix is *tas*].

By the rule *ṭhasthasthamipām tām* (Pāṇini 3.4.101), *tām* is substituted for *tas*; the inclusion of the letter *k* is for the purpose of preventing this substitution in cases such as *haṃsau*, *haṃsāḥ*, *vatsau*, and *vatsāḥ*.

73. *lug vā duha-diha-liha-guh-ām ātmanepade dantye* (Pāṇini 7.3.73). The roots *duha* (to milk, DhP 1014), *diha* (to increase, DhP 1015), *liha* (to lick, DhP 1016), and *guhū* (to conceal, DhP 896)—all of these [are subject to this rule].

Because this root has the *svarita* accent, it is *ātmanepada* by the rule "svaritajitaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale" (Pāṇini 1.3.72), which prescribes the middle voice when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent. Regarding the form "adugdha": the substitution of *bh* is as before;
then, by the rule "jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.40), the *t* is replaced by *dh*; and finally, by the rule "jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi," [the *dh* becomes *d*].

By the rule (8.4.53), the *dh* becomes *g*. Thus: *adugdhām*—the suffix *thās*; as before, there is the substitution of *d* and so forth. *Adugdhvam*—the suffix *dhvam*. *Aduhvahi*—the suffix *vahi*. *Adigdha*—as before, the substitution of *gh* and so forth. *Alīḍha*—by the rule *ho ḍhaḥ* (8.2.31), the *h* becomes *ḍh*.

Thus, the letter *ḍha* is as before; the letter *ta* undergoes the change to *dha* and then to *ṣṭu* (becoming *ṣṭha*). By the rule "ṭhḍho ḍhea lopaḥ" (8.3.13), there is elision [of the *ḍha*]; and by the rule "ḍhralopaḥ pūrvasya" (6.3.111), etc., there is lengthening. Regarding the form "nyagūḍha," this too is identical to the previous case.

Regarding the form *vyatyapuṣyata*: the root *puṣ* (meaning "to nourish" or "to thrive," DhP 1182) is preceded by the prefix *vyati*. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied according to Pāṇini 1.3.14, *kartari karmaṇyatihāre* ("the middle voice is used for the agent when there is a reciprocal action"). By Pāṇini 8.2.41, *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si*, the letter *ṣ* is replaced by *k* before the suffix *si*.
[The rule states: "ṭhakṣāmāhi" [is formed] with *mahiṅ*. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *luk* (elision), since the term *lopa* (elision) continues to apply?
To this he says: "While *lopa* is being carried over... If the mention of *lopa* were continued...

If [the term *luk* were not used], an elision (*lopa*) would be prescribed [by P. 1.1.62], and by the rule "that [which is taught] after *ṭha* belongs to the final [element]" (P. 1.1.52), it would apply only to the final [element]. However, it applies to the whole [of the suffix]; for the technical name *luk* is prescribed for the non-appearance of an entire suffix.
Therefore, the mention of *luk* was made so that the elision of the entire *kṣa* suffix may occur.

"For the sake of *vah*": this means for the sake of the dual number of the first person (*uttama-puruṣa*). That which has *vah* as its external purpose (*vahir-artha*) is described in that way. Now, why does it not apply to other [forms]?
To this he says: "But elsewhere," and so forth. Whatever ātmanepada suffix begins with a dental, all of that begins with a *jhal* sound.

In that case, once the elision of the final vowel alone has been performed, the desired result is indeed established by the elision of the *s* according to the rule *ṭhjhalo jhali* (Pāṇini 8.2.26). It might be argued: "Elsewhere too, it would not be established without an elision (*luk*); for when the elision of the *s* is to be applied, [the elision] of the vowel (*acaḥ*)..."
[One might ask: "Is it because of the absence of *sthānivadbhāva* due to the rule *parasmin vidhau pūrvasya* (1.1.57)?

To this he says: "There is also no *sthānivadbhāva* for the elision of the vowel *a*. Why is there none? He says: "When [an operation] is *asiddha* with respect to what precedes it, there is no *sthānivadbhāva*. Therefore, it is not for the sake of anything else.

The mention of *luk* is not for the sake of elision itself; rather, it is solely for the sake of *vah*. For here, because the suffix does not begin with a *jhal* sound, the elision of the *s* by the rule *jhalo jhali* (Pāṇini 8.2.26) does not occur, and thus [the desired form] is not established.
Now, one might object: "Even if the mention of *luk* were made, there should still be no *luk*-elision in the case of *vah*."
Because [the letter *va*] belongs to the dental class and so forth, one might ask: "Is not the letter *va*, being both dental and labial, included by the mention of the dentals?
To this he says: "Even though it is dental-labial," and so forth. He states the reason for this very point: "If," and so forth.
If the letter *da*, which is both dental and labial, were not included by the mention of the dentals, then...

One should say "those two" (tāu), not "dental" (dantya). Even when those two are mentioned, everything desired is indeed accomplished; for there is no dental [consonant] belonging to the ātmanepada other than that [v].
Therefore, even though the letter *va* is both dental and labial, it is included by the mention of the dental. In this regard, this...

An objection is raised: as for what was stated—that "since the desired result is indeed accomplished by the elision of the *s* via [Pāṇini 8.2.26] *jhalo jhali* when the elision of only the final [consonant] has been applied elsewhere"—that is incorrect;
for by [the rule] *jhalo jhali*, the elision of the *s* alone is not prescribed. What then?
If so, [one might argue] that it refers to *sic* itself, for he will say in that very same place: "This is the elision of *sic* itself.

This is not the case; because the mention of *sic* is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the substitute *cli*, the meaning there is that the elision of the *s* occurs only for that *s* which is connected to the substitute *cli*.
It should be understood.

74. *śam-ādīnām aṣṭānām dīrghaḥ śyani* (Pāṇini 7.3.74). Because of the use of the plural number and because of the mention of "eight," it is understood that the sense of "beginning with" (*ādi*) is intended; thus he says: "of *śama*-etc. [The roots are:
*śamu* (DhP 1201) "to pacify," *tamu* (DhP 1202) "to desire."
(dhā.pā.1202) *ḍudāñ* "to give"; *ṭhdamu* "to become calm" (dhā.pā.1203); *ṭhśramu* "in asceticism and exhaustion" (dhā.pā.1204);
*ṭhkṣamu* "in enduring" (dhā.pā.1206); *ṭhbhramu* "in instability" (dhā.pā.1205); *ṭhklamu* "in languor" (dhā.pā.1207); *ṭhmadī* "in exhilaration."
—these are the eight beginning with *śam*. Regarding "ṭhasyati": the root *ṭhasu* (meaning "to throw") is listed after these eight.
Regarding "ṭhbhramati": in the alternative view where the suffix *śyan* applies by the rule "vā bhrāśa" (Pāṇini 3.1.70), [the form is derived accordingly].
There is no counter-example for this here.

The mention of *śyan* is for the sake of clarity; for it is possible that the mention of *śan* which was established by the rule "otaḥ śyani" (Pāṇini 7.3.71)—even though it is separated by the mention of elision (*luk*)—is understood through that very mention of elision.
It is to be carried over here according to the maxim of the frog-leap.
75. *ṣṭhivuklamvācamāṃ śiti* (Pāṇini 7.3.75). The roots are:

*ṣṭhivu* (to spit) [Dhātupāṭha 1110], *klam* (to be weary) [Dhātupāṭha 1207], and *cam*, *cham*, *jam*, *jham* (to eat) [Dhātupāṭha 469–472] preceded by the prefix *ā*. Regarding the form *klāmati*, it is [derived] optionally (*vā*).

By the rule *bhrāśa* (Pāṇini 3.1.70) and others, there is the substitution of *śap* in the absence of *śyan*. Regarding the mention of *klam*, it is for the sake of *śap* (and not for the sake of *śyan*, because in that case [the form] is already established by the preceding rule).
By the rule *camerāṅpūrvasya* and so forth, [the substitution applies] to the root *cam* when it is either alone or preceded by another prefix.
He shows that the root *cam* is included here when preceded by the prefix *ā*, for the purpose of [preventing] the occurrence of *bhū*.

76. *kramaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (Pāṇini 7.3.76). [Examples: *krāmati*. [Root: *kramu pādavikṣepe* (Dhātupāṭha 473). *ākramate*: preceded by the prefix *āṅ*. [The suffix] *ātmanepada* applies because of [the rule] *āṅ udgamane* (1.3.40).

The objection is raised by means of the words "ṭhihotkrāma" and "saṅkrāma," and so forth. From the root *kram* preceded by *ut-* and *sam-*, the imperative suffix *loṭ* takes the substitute *hi* according to Pāṇini 3.4.87 (*serhyapicca*). When the *hi* is elided by Pāṇini 6.4.105 (*ato heḥ*), [the rule] Pāṇini 1.1.63 (*na lumatāṅgasya*) applies.

Because the characteristic of being a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) is negated, the rule for lengthening (*dīrghatva*) does not apply in the case of *utkrāma saṅkrāma*; for when the suffix *hi* is elided, if the characteristic of being a suffix is absent, it is impossible for *krama* to be followed by a Parasmaipada suffix. [Objection: This is not a fault, and so forth is the refutation. It might be argued that... by means of *lumatā*...

When the suffix is elided, the *krami* root alone is the base (*aṅga*) here; thus he says, "and *krami* is not the base," because it is separated by the *śap* suffix. What then? [He says] "in *śap*," because *śap* itself exists as that which intervenes.
77. *iṣu-gami-yam-ām cchaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.77). [Examples: *icchati*. [Derivation: By *tudādibhyaḥ śaḥ* (3.1.77). *gacchati*, *yacchati*. [Derivation: By *kartari śap* (3.1.68).

Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of this [root] *iṣ*, meaning "to wish" (*dhā.pā.* 1351), which is marked with the *udātta* accent? To this he says: "*iṣeḥ*" and so forth. This is so that [the rule] does not apply to the root *iṣ* meaning "to go" (*dhā.pā.* 1127), which belongs to the *divādi* class, as in the form *iṣyati*. It also excludes the root *iṣ* meaning "repetition" (*dhā.pā.* 1525).

The marker *u* (the *u*-anubandha) is attached to the root *iṣ* here so that [the rule] does not apply to the root *iṣ* belonging to the *kryādika* class in the form *iṣṇāti*. For those, however, who do not recite *iṣ* as having the marker *u* (*udit*) here, [the rule applies] even to *iṣyati* and *iṣṇāti*.

Does [the suffix] *ya* obtain [the designation *kṛt*]? To this he says: "But those who do not read [the root] as *iṣi-mudita*" and so forth. Those who do not read it here with the marker *m* attached to the vowel *i*—that is, as *iṣi*—do so for the purpose that in forms such as *iṣyati* and *iṣṇāti*, the substitution of *ch* [for *ṣ*] should not occur, according to the rule *ksasyāci* (Pāṇini 7.3.72).

Therefore, they maintain that the mention of *aj* (vowel) continues [from the previous rule]. Even though this [mention of *aj*] continues, if by it the word *śit* is qualified—meaning "the substitution of *chā* occurs when [the suffix] is *śit*, and of what kind? when it begins with a vowel (*ajādau*)"—then, after the substitution of *hi* for the *sip* of the *loṭ* of the root *eṣ* has been made, [the rule] *halaḥ śnaḥ śānajjhau* applies.

Thinking that when the *śnā* suffix is replaced by *śānac* according to [Pāṇini 3.1.83], the substitution of *ch* would indeed occur in the word *iṣaṇā* by means of the rule "that which is the locus of an operation is designated as beginning with that" (*yasmin vidhis tadādāv algrahaṇe*)— since it is a rule concerning the beginning of a word— he says: "And that mention of the *śit* [suffix] is the primary factor."
"They explain that [the vowel] is qualified. This occurs when there is a vowel (*ac*) and it is followed by *ch*.

Furthermore, the primary importance of the mention of the vowel (*aj-grahaṇa*) is precisely because it is being qualified. "And such being the case," and so forth. Thus, when this [term] *aci* is the principal element and is qualified by *śiti*, [the rule applies].
The rule of "taking that as the initial element" (tadādividhiḥ) does not apply here. What is the reason? He says: "In a rule where [an operation] is prescribed...

and so forth. It is not only by the rule "that which is the cause of an operation [applies] to what ends with it" (1.1.72) that this "taking that as the final element" (tadantavidhiḥ) is intended through a qualifier; rather, it is also [intended] otherwise.

The rule "In the case of a mention of that [stem] which contains an injunction, the operation applies to what begins with it" (Vyāḍipāṭha 127)—this very provision for applying an operation to what begins with that [stem] is desired only through a qualifier.
And because there is no such application to what begins with that [stem] in the case of *aṣāṇa*, the substitution of *ch* does not occur. Even though...

Why does the substitution of *ś* not occur for the *ā* which is the initial sound of the substitute *śānac* in the rule regarding "that-initial" (*tadādividhi*), when a *śit* affix follows? To this he says: "For this is not," and so forth. The letter *ś* is a marker (*anubandha*) of the entire complex [of the suffix], not a marker of the vowel *ā*. Therefore, the *śit* affix is not [a marker] of the *aj* (vowel) alone, but rather—
Since it occurs only in a collective [compound], the substitution of *cch* does not take place.

78. *pā-ghrā-dhmā-sthā-mnā-dāṇ-dṛś-y-arti-sarti-śada-sadām piba-jighra-dhama-tiṣṭha-mana-yaccha-paśya-rccha-dhau-śīya-sīdāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.78). [The roots] *pā* "to drink" (Dhātupāṭha 925), *ghrā* "to perceive odor" (Dhātupāṭha 926), *dhmā*...

The roots *śabda* (to sound) and *agni-saṃyoga* (to join with fire) [DhP 927]; *sthā* in the sense of "cessation of motion" [DhP 928]; *mnā* in the sense of "repetition" [DhP 929]; *dāṇ* in the sense of "giving" [DhP 930]; *dṛśir* in the sense of "seeing" [DhP 988];
*ṛ* in the senses of "motion" and "causing to reach" [DhP 936]; and *ṛ* and *sṛ* in the sense of "motion."

The roots *ca* (DhP 1298, 1099); *ṣadlṛ* "to fall" (DhP 1428), which belongs to the Taudādi class; and *ṣadlṛ* "to perish, to go, or to sink" (DhP 854), which belongs to the Bhauvādika class—in place of these roots, the forms beginning with *piba* are substituted respectively.
The substitutes occur. But surely there are two roots *sad*, so that due to this discrepancy, the correspondence of numbers (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) would not apply?
This is not a fault; for indeed, the single root *sad* is mentioned twice for the sake of the two affixes (*vikaraṇa*).
[As in] "he sits" (*śīyate*), by the rule "after *sad*, when followed by an affix marked with Ś" (*śadeḥ śitaḥ*, Pāṇini 1.3.60).
Thus ends the section on the ātmanepada endings.

Regarding the passage beginning with "atha vā" (or else), this presents another solution to the objection that "the guṇa substitution would apply to the root *pibati* because its penultimate vowel is light. If the initial vowel were not treated as an irregularity (*nipātana*), then...

If the final syllable were udātta by virtue of the accent of the root (*dhātu-svara*), then— by the rule *ekādeśa udātenodāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.5)— the single substitute for [the root vowel] and the suffix *śap* would be udātta; subsequently, when the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) occurs by the rule *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97), the word *pibati* would become middle-udātta (*madhyodātta*), whereas it is intended to be initial-udātta (*ādyaudātta*).

Therefore, the initial vowel is prescribed as acute (udātta). This accentuation by rule (*nipātana-svara*) is intended to override the accentuation of the verbal root (*dhātu-svara*). For example, in forms such as *sartaḥ* and so forth: "vega" means speed or impetus; that which possesses this is "vegī," and the state of being such is "vegitā. Regarding that motion, they maintain that there is a substitution of *dhāv* for the root *sṛ*. And that—

It should be understood that this is obtained through the recurrence of the term *vā* from the preceding sūtra, *ṭh-luk-dhuṅ-duha-diha-... (7.3.73)*, because of its status as an *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*. The mention of *artisarti-* by means of the *śitap* suffix is solely for the purpose of indicating the verbal root (*dhātu*), and not [for the purpose of indicating the present stem].
It is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅluk* [formation]. For in the case of *yaṅluk*, a suffix marked with ŚIT cannot occur;

because the elision (*luk*) of *śap* is prescribed for that which is ordained after roots such as *ad* (i.e., those beginning with *a-*, like *ad*). If it is argued that the elision of *śap* will occur by the rule "frequently in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi* 2.4.73), we say no, because in the Veda one must follow exactly what is observed.
Because, in the case of roots such as *arti*, no usage of a form ending in *śa* is observed when the *yaṅ* suffix is elided (*yaṅluk*).

79. *jñā-janor-jā* (Pāṇini 7.3.79). [The commentary states: "There is the inclusion of two roots *jan*: the one belonging to the *divādi* class, *janī prādurbhāve* (Dhātupāṭha 1149), and the one belonging to the *juhotyādi* class, *jana janane* (Dhātupāṭha 1105)."

Thus, in this context, the root belonging to the *div* class (div-ādi) is intended, not the other. For no suffix beginning with *ś* can follow that [other root], because of the rule prescribing *ślu*. The purpose of the long-vowel pronunciation will be explained later.
80. *pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.80). Regarding this, some maintain that [the rule] applies up to the root *vṛt* (meaning "to go") in the *vṛt*-gaṇa;
according to them, it does not apply to the roots *vrī* ("to choose," DhP 1504) and *bhrī* ("to fear") which are recited after that.

—there should not be shortening for these two, as in *vrīṇāti* and *bhrīṇāti*. [Objection: But surely that *vṛt*-marking is for the purpose of completing the group beginning with *lv*; otherwise, up to the end of the list, the rule regarding the substitution of *ṇatva* after the past participial suffix (*niṣṭhā*) would apply to those roots. And if it were for the purpose of completing the *lv* group...
Why are the *pv* and other roots joined with that [suffix] up to the end of the *āgaṇa*? To this he says: "The formation of the *vṛt*," and so forth.
The intention is that nothing contradicts its serving as the conclusion for both groups (*gaṇas*).
Regarding "others" (*apare*), and so forth: because the *lv* group follows immediately after, it serves specifically as the conclusion for that [group].

The intention is that the formation of *vṛt* is logical. For those who hold this view, even in the case of these two roots—*vṛ* in the sense of "choosing" (*varaṇe*) and *bhṝ* in the sense of "fearing" (*bhaye*)—there ought to be shortening [of the vowel], as in *vriṇāti* and *bhriṇāti*;
for both are included among the *pv-ādi* group. [Objection: "In the case of *jānāti*, shortening would [undesirably] apply."

He states that [the root *jñā*] is included within *pū* and others, saying "of *jñā* and *jan*, *jā*" and so forth. If, after the substitution of *jā* had been made, there were short vowels, then the utterance of the long vowel would be purposeless;
one could simply have said "ja. Therefore, by the force of the utterance of the long vowel, in the case of *jānāti*, [the long vowel is maintained].
It will not be short. But would not the long pronunciation be for the sake of generating [the form]?
For is it not the case that once the substitute *ja* has been applied to the root *jan*, the form *jāyate* is established? To this he says:
"Even when the substitute *ja* has been applied," and so forth. However, for those [grammarians] who hold that [the long vowel] is for the purpose of completing both groups...

What is the purpose of their classification (*vṛtkaraṇa*) and why is the long vowel *jā* pronounced? [Is it] so that the long vowel may occur in the case of *jānāti*? This is not the case; for the long vowel will occur by the rule "a long vowel is substituted for *at* before a suffix beginning with *yañ*" (Pāṇini 7.3.101). But is it not said: "When an operation has already taken place within a stem (*aṅga*), a further operation is not prescribed for that which has been finalized"?

[Objection: Does this [rule] not fail to apply? [Response: This is not so; for it is said "of that which is completed" (*niṣṭhitasya*), and when the substitute *j* has been applied, the stem (*aṅga*) is not yet completed, because it is unfit for usage.
The long vowel is pronounced for the sake of facilitating comprehension.

81. *mīnāter nigame* (7.3.81). In the example *pramiṇanti*, there is the substitution of *ṇ* by [Pāṇini] 8.4.15 (*hinu mīnā*), and the elision of the long *ā* by 6.4.112 (*śnābhyastayor ātaḥ*). Here, the root *mīnāti* [is intended].

The mention of the root without its characteristic marker (*vikaraṇa*) is for the purpose of including *mīñ* "to injure" from the *kryādi* class (DhP 1476), so that [the rule] may apply to it, while ensuring that *mīṅ* "to injure" from the *devādi* class (DhP 1137) is not included. Thus, it says *mīñaḥ*.
No detailed explanation has been given for the sake of variety.

82. *mider guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.82). The root *ṭhñimidā* in the sense of "moistening" (*snehane*) belongs to both the *bhūvādigaṇa* and the *divādigaṇa*. Here, the one from the *divādigaṇa* is intended for inclusion; for the other [the *bhūvādigaṇa* root] has *aṅ* as its substitute, and because of that, the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.86) would apply to the *śap* [present indicative suffix].

Thus, by the rule *ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.86), the guṇa substitution is established. In the form *midyate*, the ātmanepada ending is applied by the rule *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (1.3.13), and the suffix *yak* is added by the rule *sārvadhātuke yak* (3.1.67).

83. *jusi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.83). Here, the base (*aṅga*) under discussion is qualified by the proximate *ik*; since a rule involving a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) applies to that which ends with the qualifying element (*tadantavidhi*), he says "of that which ends in *ik*" (*igantasya*), and so forth. [The example is] *ajuhavuḥ*.
In the case of *laṅ*, by the rule "ṭhsijabhyastavidabhyaśca" (Pāṇini 3.4.109), *jhi* is replaced by *jus*; there is *ślu* for the *śap* affix;
and by the rule "ṭhślau" (6.1.10), reduplication occurs. Thus, we have "abibhayuḥ. [The root] "ñibhī bhaye" (Dhātupāṭha 1084). [And] "abibharuḥ": [the root] "ḍubhṛñ dhāraṇapoṣaṇayoḥ."
In *bhuñjāmi*, the vowel *i* is substituted for the reduplication by Pāṇini 7.4.76 (*ṭhbhuñāmitÂ*);
thus we have *cinuyuḥ* and *sunuyuḥ*. This is the optative (*liṅ*), with the augment *yāsuṭ*, and the substitution of *jus* for the ending *jhi*.
By Pāṇini 3.1.73 (*ṭhsvādibhyaḥ śnuḥ*), the suffix *śnu* is added; then, by Pāṇini 6.1.96 (*ṭhusyapadāntātÂ*), the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is applied. In that case...

"nāprāpte" and so forth. That which has the *sārvadhātuka* as its basis is called "having the *sārvadhātuka* as its basis. That prohibition for which the presence of *ṅt* is the cause is described in that way. Since that [prohibition] would apply everywhere even when *jus* occurs, this *guṇa* [substitution] applies while that [prohibition] is not yet applicable.

That which is being commenced will be an annulment of that very [rule], but not of that for which the *ṅtv* (the status of being marked with ṅ) based on *yāsuṭ* is the cause. For this [rule] is commenced both when [the condition] has already occurred and when it has not yet occurred:
in cases such as *cinuyuḥ*, where it has already occurred, and in cases such as *ajuhavuḥ*, where it has not yet occurred. The particle *ca* [indicates this].

In the case of *samuccaya* (conjunction), since there is nothing else to be conjoined, he states the repetition of this very definition. By that, it also applies to the negation of the original definition, as in *adīdhayuḥ*. [The root] *dīdhīṅ* is used in the sense of "shining" and "playing" (*dīptidevanayoḥ*, Dhātupāṭha 1076); [the suffix] *laṅ* [is applied].

There is a reversal [of the usual rule], resulting in the *parasmaipada* ending; the suffix is *jhi*. By the rule "the six beginning with *jakṣ* are designated as *abhyasta*" (Pāṇini 6.1.6), the designation *abhyasta* is applied. Then, by the rule "after *sica*, after an *abhyasta*, and after *vidi*, [the substitution of] *jus* occurs for *jhi*" (Pāṇini 3.4.109), *jus* replaces *jhi*.

Furthermore, because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* augment. Thereafter, [the rule] "for *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* [suffixes]" (Pāṇini 7.3.84) [applies].

Thus, a guna substitution was obtained; it was prohibited by the rule "ṭhṅiti ca" (Pāṇini 1.1.5); yet, since that [prohibition] is again superseded by this [present rule], it becomes prohibited once more by the rule "dīdhīvevīṭām" (Pāṇini 1.1.6), because of the particle "ca" having the sense of conjunction.

84. *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ* (7.3.84). [The forms] *cetā*, *stetā* [are derived as follows]: [the suffix] *tṛc*. By [the rule] *ṛduśanaspurodaṃso’nehasāñca* (7.1.94), *anaṅ* is substituted; by [the rule] *sarvanāmasthāne ca* (6.4.8) and so forth, there is lengthening (*dīrgha*).

Regarding the question, "What is the purpose of [the rule] *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ*?"—the thought is as follows: one might say that it should simply be stated as *pratyaye* (in a suffix) or *saṅi* (in *saṅ*); for if it were stated thus, the *guṇa* substitution would be established in forms such as *bhavati*.
The term *saṅ* is a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated designation) beginning with the *sakāra* of *san* and ending with the *ṅkāra* of *mahiṅ*.
Regarding "the state of being fire" (*agnitvam*): the suffix *tva* is applied by the rule "The suffixes *tva* and *tal* express the state of that" (*tasya bhāvastvatalau*, Pāṇini 5.1.119).
Regarding "he desires fire" (*agnikāmyati*): the suffix *kāmyac* is applied by the rule "And [after a nominal stem] *kāmyac*" (*kāmyacca*, Pāṇini 3.1.9). Regarding "if," etc.:
if it were stated that [the suffix applies] after a *pratyaya* (suffix), then it would also apply after the suffixes *tva* and *kāmyac*. Moreover, even if...
If it were called *saṅ*, it would occur where *kāmyac* occurs; for that [suffix] is also included within the category of *pratyāhāra*.
85. [The substitution of *guṇa* for the vowel of the root] *jāgr-* occurs before the affixes *ṇi*, *ciṇ*, *liṅ*, and *luṅ*.
(Pāṇini 7.3.85) *Jāgarayati*: with the causative suffix (*ṇic*). *Jāgarakaḥ*: with the suffix *ṇvul*. *Sādhujāgarī*:
with the suffix *ṇini* in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*). *Jāgarañjāgaram*: with the suffix *ṇamul* in the sense of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*).

By the rule *ṇamul* (Pāṇini 3.4.22) and the Vārttika *ṭhābhīkṣṇye dve bhavataḥ* (Vārttika 887), there is reduplication. In the example *jāgaro vartate*, the suffix *dhañ* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). These are examples concerning the scope of *vṛddhi*. In the examples *jāgaritā* and *jagaritavān*, they concern the scope of the prohibition.

What, then, is the reason that examples are presented specifically regarding the scope of *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) and the scope of prohibition (*pratiṣedha*)? To this he says: "In the scope of *vṛddhi* and in the scope of prohibition," and so forth. [This applies] elsewhere than in the scope of *vṛddhi* and prohibition, by means of the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*).

The *guṇa* substitution is established. Therefore, this *guṇa* is introduced in a domain where the prohibition of *vṛddhi* applies; for that reason, only examples belonging to that specific domain are presented. In forms such as *jāgarayati*, once *guṇa* has been applied and followed by the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* (*raparatva*), the *vṛddhi* prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.2.116] "ata upadhāyāḥ" takes effect.

Someone might have the misconception that [the result] must necessarily come to pass; therefore, in order to dispel that, he says: "When that has been performed," and so forth. But what is the reason why it does not come to pass when that has been performed? To this he says: "For if," and so forth. If, in this...
Even if the *guṇa* substitution were applied, the rule "ṭhata upadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.116) would cause *vṛddhi*,
and forms such as *jāgarayati* would not be possible; thus, the *guṇa* would be rendered purposeless,
since the desired form is already established by the *vṛddhi* prescribed in "aco ñṇiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.115).

Regarding the rule "ciṇṇaloca" and so forth: the purpose of this prohibition of *ciṇ* and *nal* is so that the *vṛddhi* [vowel] may be heard. For if, even after the *guṇa* substitution had taken place, the rule "ata upadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.116) were to apply, then the prohibition of *ciṇ* and *nal* would be useless.

Let there be this quality [of lengthening] here; even if that [lengthening] occurs, there must nevertheless be a *vṛddhi* substitution by virtue of the rule "upadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.116), and consequently, the *vṛddhi* vowel will be heard [in the final form].
[The example] "ajāgāri" is formed with the suffix *luṅ*, the *cli* augment, and [the substitution of *ciṇ*] by the rule "ciṇbhāvakarmaṇoḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.66).

By the rule *cleściṇÂ, ṭhciṇo luk* (Pāṇini 6.4.104), there is elision (*luk*) of the letter *t*. Thus we have *jāgṛtaḥ* and *jāgṛthaḥ*. [In these forms], the suffixes *ta*, *thas*, and *tha* are present; by the rule *sārvadhātukamapit* (1.2.4), they possess the marker *ṅ*, and because the root belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision of the *ś* and *y* [of the suffixes].

"Some explain that the vowel *i* in *ṭhvi* is for the sake of pronunciation. But what is it that is desired to be established such that they explain it in this way? He says: "Where would there be... and so forth.
If there were such a grasping of the *vi* belonging to the entire complex (as a suffix), then where would this prohibition of *guṇa* apply?
It would not [be necessary]. However, if the letter *i* is for the sake of pronunciation and this is the mention of the mere phoneme itself,
then by the rule "when there is a prescription regarding something, it applies to that which begins with it" (Vyāḍipāṭha 127), the prohibition of *guṇa* is established even for *kvāsau*.

In the form *jajāgṛvān*: the suffix *kvasu* is substituted for *liṭ* by Pāṇini 3.2.107 (*kvasuśca*), and the augment *num* is added by Pāṇini 7.1.70 (*ugidacām*). Thus, [we obtain] *jajāgṛvān*. The suffix *kvasu* is substituted for *liṭ* by Pāṇini 3.2.107 (*kvasuśca*), and [the augment *num* is added] by Pāṇini 7.1.70 (*ugidacām*).
By the rule "ṭhsāntamahataḥ saṃyogasya" (Pāṇini 6.4.10), there is lengthening;

then, by the rules for the elision of *hal* and *ṅī* etc., and the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*), [the form is established]. Because of the statement "some [say]," it is implied that others do not consider the [final] letter to be for the purpose of pronunciation. They think as follows: [this is] Vedic (*chāndasa*).

The *kvasu* suffix and the *liṭ* [perfect] are also considered *sārvadhātuka* in the Vedic language (*chandas*), because of the rule "In the Veda, both ways" (3.4.117). Consequently, by the rule "A *sārvadhātuka* suffix that is also *apit* [not having *p* as an *it*]" (1.2.4), there will be an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) due to its being *ṅt* [having *ṅ* as an *it*]. For example: *ajāgaruḥ*, and so forth. Thus...

He thinks: "By the very mention of *ṅ* in the rule *aviciṇṇalṅtsu* (1.2.4), there will be an exclusion (*paryudāsa*)," as in the example *ajāgaruḥ*. He considers it thus: this [rule] *aviciṇṇalṅtsu* is a prohibitive negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*)—meaning that [the substitution of *guṇa*] does not occur before *vi*, *ciṇ*, *ṇal*, or *liṅ*.

Furthermore, in the case of *ajāgaruḥ*, there would also result a prohibition of the *guṇa* substitution that is obtained by the rule *jusi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.83). Likewise, in the case of *ahaṃ jajāgare*, when the status of being marked with *ṇ* (*ṇitva*) does not occur due to the statement *ṇal uttamo vā* (Pāṇini 7.1.91), then—

The *guṇa* substitution prescribed by the rule "sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.84) would not apply due to this prohibition. The resolution is: "No, because there is no prohibition. This is not a fault; why? Because there is no prohibition. The meaning is that it is a non-implicative negation (*aprasajya-pratiṣedha*). If...

It is not a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation); what then is it? He says: "In the rule *aviciṇṇalṅt-su*, this is a *paryudāsa* (relative negation). For in the case of a *prasajya-pratiṣedha*, there would be a negation even of that which is applicable by another grammatical rule. It is not [that].

In the case of *paryudāsa* (exclusion). For in *paryudāsa*, a *guṇa* substitution is prescribed for [roots] other than those ending in *vic*, *ṇi*, *ṅit*, and *luṅ*; it is not, however, prohibited in the case of those very endings such as *vic*, *ṇi*, *ṅit*, and *luṅ*.
And this is indeed a *paryudāsa*. Therefore, the *guṇa* substitution certainly occurs in the case of *jus* and *ṇal*.
Even having accepted that this is a prasajya-pratiṣedha (absolute negation), he states another solution, beginning with "Or rather" (*atha vā*).

According to the rule "A rule or a prohibition applies to what is immediately preceding" (*anantarasya vidhir vā bhavati pratiṣedho vā*), this is a prohibition of the application [of the suffix] *jāgra* which follows by immediate proximity; however, as for that...

The application [of *jus*] obtained through another rule, such as "ṭhjusi ca" (Pāṇini 7.3.83), is not prohibited. In the example "ajāgaruḥ," there is the *laṅ* suffix; by the rule "jakṣityādayaḥ ṣaṭ" (6.1.6), the designation *abhyasta* is applied; and by the rule "sijabhyastavidibhyaśca" (3.4.109), *jus* is substituted for *jhi*.
86. And [the substitution of *guṇa* occurs] for a root ending in *pu*, and for a stem whose penultimate (*upadhā*) is light (*laghu*).

(7.3.86) The two terms "ending in *pu*" (*puganta*) and "having a light penultimate" (*laghūpadha*) are both *bahuvrīhi* compounds: that which has *pu* at its end is called "ending in *pu*"; that which has a light penultimate is "having a light penultimate. [Examples: *bhetā*.
[The word] "chetā" [is an example].

Now, since there is contiguity between the consonant at the beginning of the suffix and the consonant that is a member of the base (*aṅga*), the designation "heavy" (*guru*)—by the rule "A conjunct is heavy" (P. 1.4.11)—would subvert the designation "light" (*laghu*); therefore, by virtue of this heaviness, [the substitution of *guṇa*] would not occur here.

Is this [guṇa] necessarily required? To this he says: "of that which begins with a suffix," and so forth. The very purpose of making the *kn* and *san* suffixes *kit*—in rules such as *trasigṛdhidhṛṣikṣipeḥ knuḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.140) and *halantācca* (1.2.10)—is precisely this: to prevent *guṇa* substitution in forms such as *gṛdhnuḥ* and *vibhatsati*.

[The author] says: "It must be so. If the *kit* designation for those two [suffixes *knus* and *san*] were not intended to prevent the *guṇa* substitution of a light penultimate vowel when there is no intervention by a consonant between the suffix-initial and a member of the stem, then he would not have made them *kit*; yet he has done so.
Therefore, the *kit* designation of *knus* and *san* [serves this purpose].

By doing so, it is indicated that even when there is immediate succession between two *hal* sounds—one being the member of the suffix (*pratyaya*) and the other an internal element (*aṅga*)—the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha-guṇa*) is not precluded. Now, one might object: "Is not the *kit* designation of the suffix *san* intended to prevent the augment *ām* from appearing in forms such as *sisṛkṣati*? This is not the case; for if...

If this were the intended purpose, he would have formulated the prohibition in that very way—as "sū-dṛśor jhaly am akitsanoḥ. Therefore, the fact that *san* is marked with the *kit* designation is indeed an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the *guṇa* substitution is prescribed for a root having a light penultimate vowel by this rule. This being so, [the rule] "iko... [applies].

When the rule *guṇavṛddhī* (Pāṇini 1.1.3) presents itself, a single *guṇa* substitution would apply wherever an *ik* sound is situated; consequently, it would also apply here in the case of *bhinatti*, for the base (*aṅga*) has a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*). Nor can it be argued that "consonants not separated by vowels constitute a *saṃyoga*."

(1.1.7) Thus, when the designation *saṃyoga* is present, since this [root] does not have a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*), the *guṇa* substitution will not occur. But has it not been indicated by this very [sūtra]—namely, *idādhīvevīṭām*—that when there is immediate succession between two consonants (*hal*) that are parts of the base (*aṅga*), the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel is not precluded? Therefore...

He says: "And here, by the rule 'upadhā ca' (Pāṇini 1.1.65)," and so forth. Because the technical term *ik* is brought to mind here by the paribhāṣā [regarding the definition of *ik*], only a vowel (*iK*) is understood as the *upadhā*. Therefore, in the case of *bhinatti*, there is no *guṇa* substitution; for in this instance, the *upadhā* of the *aṅga* is not an *iK* vowel, but rather the letter *a*.

"But others," and so forth. They explain the meaning of the sūtra as follows: its connection is with what is yet to be said. "Pug-anta" means that which has *puk* as its final member (*anta*). The compound is formed by the application of a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) based on the rule "saptamī" (Pāṇini 2.1.40).
This word *anta* denotes a constituent part; the meaning is "that which is a constituent part when *puk* follows. Of what is it a constituent part?

Because of the recurrence of the word *aṅgasya* (of the stem) and because of the mention of *puk*, [the rule applies] to a stem (*aṅga*) that possesses the augment *puk*; however, it should not be understood as applying only to that which has *ik* as its penultimate letter due to the *ik-paribhāṣā*. "Laghu upadhā" means "laghūpadhā"; this is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). Thus, [the term is] "pug-anta-laghūpadham."

This is a collective dvandva compound. Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the sūtra" (*sūtrārtham*): the word *sūtrārtha* refers to only a portion of the meaning of the sūtra, for the meaning of the sūtra is not exhausted by this much alone, as it remains incomplete. This incompleteness, however, pertains to the rule stating that "guṇa substitution occurs for a penultimate *puk* [augment] and for that which has a light penultimate vowel."

Because a portion of the meaning of the Sūtra has not been stated, [the author] says "they describe" (varṇayanti), which means "they explain. This is for the purpose that the *guṇa* substitution should not occur in the word *bhinatti*. For the *guṇa* would not apply here in *bhinatti* according to the meaning of the Sūtra. This is because, if a *bahuvrīhi* were resorted to, [the *guṇa* would apply] to that which belongs to the *aṅga* which is the referent of the other member of the compound (*anyapadārtha*).

In a Bahuvrīhi compound, if there were some *ik* vowel belonging to that [word] which is situated anywhere [within it], then its quality (*guṇa*) would undesirably apply to the meaning of the other member (*anyapadārtha*), which is being expressed as the subordinate element (*aṅga*). However, this fault does not arise in the case of *tatpuruṣa*, for therein—

The *aṅga* (stem) is distinguished by its having light penultimate vowels; therefore, the *guṇa* substitution is prescribed for that [vowel] alone—namely, that *guṇa* occurs for the *ik* which is the light penultimate vowel of the *aṅga*.
In the case of *bhinatti*, although there is a light penultimate vowel of the *aṅga*, it is not an *ik*; and as for that which is an *ik*, even if...
It becomes light, it becomes light; however, its *upadhā* (penultimate vowel) does not. Therefore, when a *tatpuruṣa* compound is resorted to here, there is no occasion for the application of *guṇa*.
It is simply by the rule "before *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes" that [the form] *agranicitvam* is established.

The one who has piled the fire-altar desires [something]. The mention of "pugant" (a penultimate consonant) is for the sake of [applying the rule] when there is a light vowel in the penultimate position.
87. *nābhyastasyāci piti sārvadhātuke* (Pāṇini 7.3.87). [Examples: *ṇenijāni*, *vevijāni*, *pariveviṣāṇi*. [Roots:
*ṇijir* "in cleansing and purifying" (Dhātupāṭha 1093); *vijir* "in separation" (Dhātupāṭha 1094).
From the roots *ṭhviṣ* (DhP 1095) meaning "to pervade" and others, [the affix] *loṭ* is applied; then *mip* [is substituted for the first person];

by *ṭhmerniḥ* (3.4.89), *ni* replaces *mip*; by *āḍutamasya picca* (3.4.92), the augment *āṭ* is added; by *juhotyādibhyaḥ śluḥ* (2.4.75), there is *ślu*-elision of *śap*; by *ślau* (6.1.10), reduplication occurs; [and then] *nijāṃ trayāṇām*...

By the rule *guṇaḥ ślau* (Pāṇini 7.4.75), there is guṇa substitution for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Thus we have *anenijam*, *avevijam*, and *paryaveṣiṣam*. [These are formed with] the *laṅ* [suffix]; by the rule *tasthasthamipāṃ tāntantāmāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.101), the *mip* suffix undergoes the change to *am*.

Regarding "vidāni": the root *vid* means "to know" (DhP 1064). As before, the imperative suffixes (*loṭ*) and so forth are applied as appropriate; furthermore, because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* augment.
Regarding "nenikti": this is the present tense (*laṭ*), the third-person singular suffix (*tip*), and the substitution of *k* for *c* according to Pāṇini 8.2.30 (*coḥ kuḥ*).

Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the term *api*? For, since [the suffix] is *apit* when it is a *sārvadhātuka*, by the rule "a *sārvadhātuka* that is *apit* [is ṅit]" (Pāṇini 1.2.4), it would be *ṅit*; and if it were *ṅit*, there ought to be a prohibition by the rule "and before a *ṅit* or *kit*" (Pāṇini 1.1.5). Yet, between these two prohibitions—...

Is there some distinction [to be made]? To this he says: "The mention of *pit*. He will state the rule *tṛṇaha im* (Pāṇini 7.3.92); the mention of *pit* is for the purpose that [the substitution of *im*] should occur when a *pit* affix follows, and not when it does not follow. [The example] *nineja* is in the *liṭ* [perfect tense]; and that *liṭ*...

By the rule *ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.115), [the suffix] receives the designation *ārdhadhātuka*. Regarding *juhavāni*: the root is *hu* "to give" (DhP 1083); as before, this is the imperative (*loṭ*) and so forth. Regarding *ajuhavam*: as before, this is the imperfect (*laṅ*) and so forth. Here, [the rule] *laghūpadhasya* (Pāṇini 7.3.86) [applies].

Because of this continued application (*anuvṛtti*), the prohibition does not apply to that *guṇa* which is prescribed for a stem ending in *i* by the rule "sarvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.84).
It should be stated: "In the Vedic language (*cchandas*), [the substitution] occurs diversely (*bahulam*). Thus, in the domain of the Veda, it happens diversely.
The meaning is that this form of the sense—"there is a negation of the [suffixal] *guṇa*"—must be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows:

here, this sūtra is divided and two rules (*yoga*) are formulated; therein, "not" (*na*) is the first rule, and "of the reduplicated root (*abhyasta*), before a *pit* sārvadhātuka ending beginning with a vowel (*aci*)" is the second. Among these:

And the word "not" (na) is understood to carry over; furthermore, the conjunction "ca" is for the purpose of indicating that the preceding rule does not have universal application. By means of this, there will be a frequent prohibition in the case of the word *cchandas*. For example: *jujoṣat*; [the root] *juṣ* is used in the sense of "serving" (*pratisevana*).

[The suffix] *leṭ*, [and then] *tip*; by [the rule] "aṭ and āṭ are added to the *leṭ* in the place of *ṭi*" (Pāṇini 3.4.94), there is the augment *aṭ*; because [the root] belongs to the *tud*-class, there is the substitution of *śnā*; for that, by [the rule] "optionally in the Veda" (Pāṇini 2.4.73), there is *ślu*; by [the rule] "before *ślu*" (Pāṇini 6.1.10), there is reduplication. There is the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. If [the suffix] begins with a vowel (*aci*) and is a *pit* [suffix], [it applies] to the reduplicated form (*abhyastasya*).
The prohibition of *guṇa* substitution is desired in the case of *sārvadhātuka* suffixes, as in *paspaśāte*, *cakāśīti*, and *vāvaśīti*;
however, the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasvatvam*) which is desired there would not otherwise apply.
Therefore, it must be stated that for reduplicated roots (*abhyasta*), there is only the shortening of the penultimate vowel, and not the prohibition of *guṇa*.

If someone should object: "Is it not the case that forms such as *nenijāni* and so forth are established by shortening [the vowel], and likewise forms such as *paspaśāte*?"—to him he replies with the words beginning with "*paspaśāte*": "Indeed, forms such as *nenijāni* are established, and forms such as *paspaśāte* as well."

To one who might raise this objection, he replies with "paspaśāte," and so forth. There is indeed another root, *spaś* (the reading *spāś* is found in the Prācīna-mu-pāṭha), which is listed in the Dhātupāṭha;
from that root comes the intensive (*yaṅ*), which undergoes elision by the rule "yaṅe 'ci ca" (Pāṇini 2.4.74), followed by reduplication.

By the rule *ṭhśarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.61), there is the retention of the *khaya* sounds; once the shortening of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) has been effected, the long vowel is applied by *ṭhdīrgho'kitaḥ* (7.4.83). Then, through the transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyaya*) according to *ṭhvyatyayo bahulam* (3.1.85), the penultimate vowel and the reduplication are shortened. [The suffix] *leṭ* [is applied].
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*), and there is the augment *āṭ*. Regarding "ākaśīti": from the root *kāśṛ* in the sense of "shining" (*dīptau*;

DhP 1162), there is the substitution of *c* for the abhyāsa [consonant] by *kuhoścuḥ* (7.4.62), followed by the suffix *tip*, and the augment *iṭ* by *yaṅe vā* (7.3.94). Regarding "vāvaśīti": from the root *vāśṛ* in the sense of "sound" (*śabde*).

(Dhātupāṭha 1163); the remainder is as before according to the appropriate application. Regarding the form *paspaśāte*, there is shortening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*); by the word "and" (*ca*), there is also shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*). In the other case, however, there is only shortening of the penultimate vowel, not shortening of the reduplicated syllable.
