If someone were to object: "Even in the case of *tathāvadigye*, once the substitution of *digya* has been applied, by what would the subsequent reduplication (*dvirvacana*) be barred?"—to him he replies: "The substitution of *digya* is intended to bar the reduplication. But how is this obtained, even though it is merely intended?

Because of the continued application of the term "nityam" (invariably). Here, the term "nityam" is carried over from the preceding sūtra; it does not follow that an option (*vibhāṣā*) applies here, and thus the term "nityam" is understood to be for the purpose of excluding that [option].
Therefore, the inclusion of "nityam" is for the purpose of excluding whatever grammatical operation would otherwise apply to the *liṭ* [perfect] tense other than this.

It is understood; therefore, the connection shall be made in this way: "In the case of the *liṭ* [perfect tense], among the operations that would otherwise apply, the substitution of *di* and so forth occurs invariably, and no other operation takes place.

In this manner, the prevention of reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is achieved. However, the substitution of *yaṇ* is not prescribed by this rule, as it is already stated to occur in the context of the *liṭ*.
Thus, by the rule "ṭheranekācaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.42), the suffix *ac* is applied.

10. A guṇa substitute occurs for a root beginning with *ṛ* when followed by a consonant cluster. (Pāṇini 7.4.10) For example: *sasvaratuḥ*, *sasvaruḥ*. [The root] *svṛ* (meaning "to sound" or "to afflict") [is used here].

By [the rule] *urat* (7.4.66), the vowel *a* is substituted for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), followed by the substitution of *r* as the final element (*raparatva*), and then the application of *halādiśeṣaḥ* (retaining only the first consonant of the reduplication).

Regarding "dadhvaratuḥ" and "dadhvaruḥ": the root is *dhvṛ* (meaning "to be distressed," Dhātupāṭha 939). Regarding "sasmaratuḥ" and "sasmaruḥ": the root is *smṛ* (meaning "to remember," Dhātupāṭha 807). Now, one might object: "In all these cases, the member [the reduplicated stem] is accompanied by an abhyāsa (repetition), and yet that [member] does not begin with a *saṃyoga* (conjunct consonant). This is not a fault.

In this context, the position is that "doubling is the application of two [sounds]"; in that case, the designation of *aṅga* (base) certainly applies even to the subsequent element. Alternatively, there is no fault even if one holds that "doubling occurs in place [of the preceding sound]";

for in every instance, the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) of the *liṭ* suffix destroys the status of being a "beginning of a conjunct" (*saṃyogāditva*), and this very rule is stated for that purpose. Thus it is said: "In that case, as follows..."

We shall understand: before the reduplication there is the status of being the beginning of a *saṃyoga*, and here too, before the reduplication, there is the status of being the beginning of a *saṃyoga*. [Examples are] *cikṣipatuḥ* and *cikṣipuḥ*.
[The root] *kṣi* in the sense of "decay" (*dhā.pā.* 236) undergoes the substitution of *iyaṅ*.

Regarding the phrase "even in the domain of the prohibition," etc.: where the *thal* suffix and others do not fall within the scope of the prohibition [stated] in "kṅiti ca" (Pāṇini 1.1.5), there the *guṇa* substitution is established by the rule "sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.84).
Therefore, this [sūtra] is commenced so that [the rule] may apply even in cases where a guṇa substitution is prohibited;
for someone might have the misconception that even in a case where vṛddhi is applicable, the guṇa must occur because it is subsequent.
To dispel that, he says: "But in the case of vṛddhi," and so forth.

The scope for the [application of the] quality (*guṇa*) is in forms such as *sasvaratuḥ* and *sasvaruḥ*; the scope for the increase (*vṛddhi*) by the rule "before a suffix marked with Ñ or Ṇ" (*ñṇiti*) is in forms such as *svārakaḥ* and *dhvārakaḥ*. In cases where both would apply, as in *satvāra* and *dadhvāra*, the increase (*vṛddhi*) alone occurs by virtue of the "priority-exception" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).

Now, what is the purpose of including the long vowel *t* (tapara) [in the rule]? If it is for the sake of preventing this from applying to the long vowel as well, that is not the case; for the long vowel must indeed be included by the subsequent rule—namely, in the case of the root *stṛñ* "to cover" (DhP 1484), as in *ātastaratuḥ* and *ātastaruḥ*. But surely...

Because of this inclusion of *t* (the *tapara*), [the substitution] would not apply; yet the subsequent rule has its own scope in cases beginning with non-conjuncts—such as *kṛ* in the sense of "scattering" (*vikṣepa*), where we have *nicakaratuḥ* and *nikaruḥ*. If this is so, then in that case, this inclusion of *t* is not for that purpose; what then?
This is the explanation regarding the term *tasiṇā*:

"of that which begins with a conjunct consonant" (*saṃyogādeḥ*), and so forth. Here, within the context of the member (*aṅga*), the member is qualified by the property of beginning with a conjunct consonant. And since the member of the root *kṛ* does not begin with a conjunct consonant, [the rule] would not apply.

Therefore, the mention of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) and "penultimate" (*upadha*) must be made so that the *guṇa* substitution may also apply to the root *kṛ*. Thus we have *sañcaskaratuḥ* and *sañcaskaruḥ*.

Here, the augment *suṭ* is applied by the rule *samparyupebhyaḥ karotau bhūṣaṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.137), and that *suṭ* is inserted even when there is an intervention by the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), according to the rule *aḍabhyāsavyavāye’pi* (Pāṇini 6.1.136).

By virtue of this statement, [the substitution] occurs even when there is an intervention by repetition (*abhyāsa*). But what is the reason that the *guṇa* substitution is not established here, given that once *suṭ* has been applied, the rule "that which falls in the middle of something is included by the mention of that thing" (Vyāḍipāṭha 21) would cause the root *kṛ-* to follow after a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*)? To this, he says: "For here..."

And so forth. By this, he demonstrates that *suṭ* is "extrinsic" (*bahiraṅga*). For, since it is extrinsic, by the rule "that which is extrinsic is considered non-existent when the intrinsic is to be applied" (*asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam antaraṅge*), the extrinsic *suṭ* is non-existent when the intrinsic *guṇa* is to be performed; consequently, [the root] possesses the property of beginning with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogāditva*).
In the view that "the verbal root is joined with the prefix first,

and subsequently with the grammatical factor (*sādhana*)" (Jaiminīya-Paribhāṣā-Vṛtti 98), the operation concerning the root and the prefix is *antaranga* (internal); thus, [the rule for] *suṭ* also [applies] to the root and the prefix.

Because it is an effect (*kāryatva*), there would be internal status (*antaraṅgatā*). According to the view that "the root is first joined with its grammatical factor (*sādhana*), and afterwards with the prefix (*upasarga*)" (Siddhāntakaumudī 128), the *suṭ* augment becomes external (*bahiraṅga*). For instance, according to this view, the meaning belongs to the root alone when it is without a prefix.

Since it is joined with the *sādhana* (the means of accomplishment), the *liṭ* suffix denoting the *sādhana* must first be applied. Once that has been done, and the reduplication (*dvirvacana*) based upon it has occurred, the *suṭ* augment is subsequently added through the connection with the prefix (*upasarga*), according to the rule *aḍabhyāsavyavāye’pi* (Pāṇini 6.1.136). And when this is done in such a manner...

Because it relies on multiple words and depends on many factors, the *suṭ* augment is established as being *bahiraṅga* (external). Guṇa, however, occurs immediately after the production of the *liṅ* suffix and does not depend on anything else; because it depends on only one word and depends on few factors, it is *antaraṅga* (internal), and therefore—

Since *suṭ* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is to be performed, the root *kṛ* does not have a base (*aṅga*) beginning with a conjunct consonant; therefore, that [augment] does not apply. "And having done so," etc.: because *suṭ* is thus external (*bahiraṅga*), and having done so, when the internal (*antaraṅga*) augment *iṭ* is to be applied...

Because that [augment] is not established and because [the root] does not begin with a conjunct consonant, the augment *iṭ* does not occur in the forms *karotiṣīṣṭa* or *saṃskṛṣīṣṭa* by virtue of the rule *ṛtaśca saṃyogādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.43). By this, it is demonstrated that the *suṭ* augment is indeed extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*).
But surely, because the context concerns the *aṅga* (the stem), by proximity the term "consonant cluster" (*saṃyoga*) must be understood as referring specifically to a part of the *aṅga*;
furthermore, the fact that the augment *suṭ* is not a part of the suffix was made known there by the mention of "preceding *k*" (*kātpūrva*).
Therefore, precisely because it is not a part [of the suffix], the root *kṛ-* will not have the suffix *iṇ* due to not beginning with a consonant cluster (*asaṃyogādi*).

What is the point of introducing this as being "external" (bahiranga) and therefore "not yet established" (asiddha)? This is true; however, the intention is as follows: even if the augment *suṭ* were indeed a part of the root *kṛ*, nevertheless, because it would be "not yet established," there would be no occasion for the application of the augment *iṭ* in the form *saṃskṛṣīṣṭa*; thus, the mention of "that which has a conjunct consonant as its penultimate" (*saṃyogopadha*) [is necessary].

"It must be done"—this is its meaning: the root *kṛ* (to do/make) with a conjunct consonant as its penultimate letter (*saṃyogopadha*) is to be understood as the intended member (*aṅga*); therefore, the meaning is that an explanation regarding the inclusion of those with a penultimate conjunct must be provided. In this regard, the following explanation must be made: the particle *ca* is added here, and it [belongs] to the root *kṛ*.

The particle "ca" (and) has the sense of inclusion; therefore, when *suṭ* is applied to that [word] as well, the guna substitution will occur for that which has a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) as its penultimate (*upadhā*).

11. *ṛcchaty-ṛtām* (Pāṇini 7.4.11). The root *ṛcch* is listed [in the Dhātupāṭha] as "ṛccha gati-indriya-pralaya-mūrti-bhāveṣu" (DhP 1296). Here, the root *ṛ* is also included by implication, because of the use of the plural number [in the rule]. Therefore, he says: "of the member *ṛcch*, and of that which is *ṛ*."

"And for those ending in *ṛ*. Those ending in *ṛ* are, for example, *kṛ* "to scatter" (DhP 1409) and *gṛ* "to swallow" (DhP 1410), and so forth. [The forms] *ānarcchatuḥ*, *ānarcchuḥ*, etc., are derived as follows:
the suffixes *atus* and *us*, *guṇa* substitution, reduplication, and the treatment of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsakārya*) as before; then *ata*...

The vowel lengthening is by [Pāṇini 7.4.70] "ādeḥ," and the augment *nuṭ* is by [Pāṇini 7.4.71] "tasmānnuḍ dvihalaḥ. Thus we have *āratuḥ* and *āruḥ*. As before, there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), followed by the substitution of the homogeneous vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*). [The rule] "because of the non-light penultimate syllable of roots ending in *ṛ*" and so forth applies; however, the non-lightness of the penultimate syllable is as follows:

Because that [substitution] is internal (*antaraṅga*), once the *tuk* augment has been applied by the rule "che ca" (P. 6.1.73), the designation "heavy" (*guru*) applies by the rule "saṃyoge guru" (P. 1.4.11). Consequently, it should be understood that [the substitution] does not apply because of the heavy penultimate syllable (*gurūpadhatvāt*).
Regarding the phrase "but for those ending in ṛ," etc.: however, for roots ending in ṛ, [the substitution] is indeed prohibited.

It is expected that a quality (*guṇa*) is being prescribed; however, the prohibition of *guṇa* for those [roots] is to be understood through [the rule] *kṅiti ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5), provided that the *kit* status [of the suffix] is established by *asaṃyogāl liṭ kit* (Pāṇini 1.2.5).

Regarding the phrase "But in the domain of *vṛddhi*," etc.: just as in the domain of *vṛddhi*, by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), only *vṛddhi* is prescribed according to the rule "ṛtaśca saṃyogādeḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.10), so too it is [prescribed] for ṛ and ṝ as well. The scope of *guṇa* is, for example, *nicakaratuḥ* and *nicakaruḥ*.

The scope for [the application of] *vṛddhi* is as follows: in the case of *kārakaḥ* and *hārakaḥ*, and in *nicakāra* and *nijagāra*, where *vṛddhi* is the subject matter, *vṛddhi* alone is prescribed by means of the "priority-exception" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).
12. *śṛ-ḍṛ-prām hrasvo vā*.

(Pāṇini 7.4.12) Regarding the roots *śṛ* "to injure" (Dhātupāṭha 1488), *ḍṛ* "to tear" (Dhātupāṇa 1490), and *pṛ* "to protect or to fill" (Dhātupāṭha 1489)—by the preceding rule, a *guṇa* [substitution] would have been obligatory for these.

It indeed occurs, as in the form *viśaśratuḥ*. Once the shortening (*hrasvatva*) has been applied, the substitution of *yaṇ* follows. Regarding the phrase "the mention of 'short' (*hrasva*)," and so forth: if the mention of "short" were not present, then in the alternative where the *guṇa* is not applied due to the optionality provided by the word *vā*, the substitution of *it* prescribed by the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.100) would undesirably apply.

And there is also the substitution of *u* by [Pāṇini 7.1.102] "ṭhudīṣṭhaḷpūrvasya. Therefore, is the term "short" (*hrasva*) stated for the purpose of excluding that [substitution]? [The answer is: although "ṛt" should have been used, the mention of "short" is for the sake of what follows.
As for the words "some say," etc.: how, moreover, is this [objection] refuted?
"How are forms such as *viśaśratuḥ* established? To this he says: "In the sense of 'cooking' (*śrā pāke*), etc.

Although these forms such as *viśaśratuḥ* are established by applying the elision of the vowel *a* according to *āto lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64), [the author provides this rule for the sake of clarity].
Nevertheless, it would indeed have that meaning;
anticipating the objection that this would then constitute a rejection of the *uttama* (the highest person), it was stated that "roots have multiple meanings.
With the words "And such being the case," etc., he refutes that rejection. If [it were so] regarding the sūtra...

A rejection is being made [of this view], for when [the rule] is applied, the form *viśaśṛṣān* is not established. To explain: if the shortening of the root *śṛṇāti* is not performed, then the form would be *viśaśarvān*;
if it were the root *śrāti*, then it would be *viśaśrivān*. Therefore, this [explanation] is incorrect.
Refusal.

13. *ke'ṇaḥ* | (Pāṇini 7.4.13) The term *aṇ* here is a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated designation) including the preceding *ṇ*; otherwise, he would have said *ke'caḥ*. Or rather, he would not even have said *acaḥ*, for [the rule applies] only to vowels (*ac*).
The forms *harasvatī* and *dīrghaplutā* occur. Regarding the term *jñakā*: one who knows (*jānāti*) is a *jñā*;

by the rule *ig-upadhajñā-prī-kiraḥ kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.135), the suffix *ka* is applied, and from that form ending in *ka*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added. Then, by the rule *prāgivāt kaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.70), the suffix *ka* is added after *ajñātā jñā*. Alternatively, it means "one who is pitied as a knower" (*anukampitā jñā*), according to the rule for expressing pity (*anukampāyām*).
(5.3.76) Thus, when the suffix *kan* is applied, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added to that which ends in it. Now, why does this not also occur here— namely,

that by the rule "The suffix *kan* is added after roots meaning 'to give' (*rāti*), 'to hold' (*dadhāti*), and 'to worship' (*arc*)," the suffix *kan* is added to *rāti* and *dadhāti*, and the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added to those ending in it, resulting in forms such as *rākā* and *dhākā*?

This is clear. Since only that which lacks an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) is understood here, someone might have the misconception that, by the rule regarding forms lacking *anubandhas*, there should be no occurrence of the suffix *kan* when it is understood;
therefore, he says "not before *kap*" (*na kapi*) and so forth, in order to dispel that doubt. If this...
If [the rule] were to apply by virtue of the technical name (*paribhāṣā*), then the prohibition in *ṭhna kapi* (Pāṇini 7.4.14) would be purposeless;
the intention is that the mention of *kap* will not occur [in that rule] precisely because it possesses an indicatory letter (*sānubandhakatva*).
14. *na kapi* (Pāṇini 7.4.14).

[The example is] *bahukumārīkaḥ*. This means "one who has many daughters" (*bahvyaḥ kumāryaḥ yasya saḥ*). The suffix *kap* is applied by [the rule] *nady-utaś-ca* (5.4.153); there is the elision of the indicatory letter (*anubandha*).

Now, when this shortening (*hrasvatva*) has been prohibited here, why does the shortening of the *upasarjana* not occur? If you argue that it will not occur simply because of this very prohibition, we say no; for according to the maxim "a rule or a prohibition applies only to what is immediately preceding" (*anantarasya vidhirvā pratiṣedho vā*), this prohibition applies only to the immediately preceding short vowel, and not [to the *upasarjana*].

If it is argued that, by the force of the word "kapī" [in the rule *kapi ca*], the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upasarjana-hrasvatvam*) will not occur for "sarvasya"? For where there is the possibility of the application of the shortening of the penultimate vowel according to the rule *gostriyor upasarjanasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.48), the word "strī" in that rule of shortening refers to suffixes prescribed under the heading of feminine (*stryadhikāra*).

Because of the inclusion of the suffixes *ṭāp* and others [in the definition of *upasarjana*], one might think that in the example *bahukumārīkaḥ*, the shortening of the *upasarjana* must apply; therefore, he says: "In the rule *go-striyoḥ upasarjanasya*," etc. Why does it not apply? He says: "For, in the sense of the compound," etc. For the shortening of the *upasarjana*...

The [shortening] is prescribed for a compound nominal base (*samāsa-prātipadika*) that ends in a feminine suffix; since the term "nominal base" (*prātipadika*) is understood from the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.47), the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upasarjana-hrasva*) would apply only to a compound nominal base that ends in a feminine suffix. And it is not [the case that...].

In examples such as *bahukumārīka*, the compound base (*samāsaprātipadika*) ends in a feminine suffix; for it is precisely within the governing rule *samāsāntāḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.68) that the suffix *ka* is prescribed here.
This is the purpose of the inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*) in the rule *samāsāntāḥ*.

The purpose [of this rule] is so that there may be an "avacaya" (separation) at the end of a compound. And how does that [final element] become a member (*avayava*) of the compound? If it receives the designation of a "compound" (*samāsa-saṃjñā*) along with [the preceding members].
And how does it receive the designation of a "compound"? If, even before the compound has been formed, [it is recognized as such] from the subsequent member which conveys the sense of the compound.

The suffix *kap* occurs after [the word], and subsequently a compound (*samāsa*) is formed with the ending in *kad*; it does not happen otherwise. Therefore, since *kap* is prescribed under the governing rule for compound endings (*samāsānta*), once *kap* has been applied to the final member (*uttarapada*) which conveys the sense of the compound, the compound must then be formed. Consequently, in this case, that which ends in a feminine suffix [is the result].
Since there is not a single word that follows the compound, the shortening of the *upasarjana* does not occur.
15. *Āpo 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 7.4.15): [The example is] *bahukhaṭvākaḥ*. The suffix *kap* is applied by the rule *śeṣād vibhāṣā* (5.4.154).

16. *ṛdṛśo'ṅ guṇiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.16). This rule prescribes *guṇa* substitution when the suffix *aṅ* follows the roots *ṛ* and *dṛś*, even though the prohibition [of *guṇa*] by the rule *ṅkiti ca* (1.1.5) would otherwise apply. The example *akārṣīt* is formed as follows: from the root *kṛ*, the *luṅ* (aorist) tense marker, the *cli* augment, the *tip* personal ending, and so on.

In the phrase *asarat*, the suffix *aṅ* is substituted for *cli* by Pāṇini 3.1.59 (*kṛmṛdṛruhibhyaśchandasī*). The root is *sṛ* (meaning "to go," DhP 935). In the phrase *ārat*, the root is *ṛ* (meaning "to go" and "to reach," DhP 936); here, *aṅ* is substituted for *cli* by Pāṇini 3.1.56 (*sartiśāstyartibhyaśca*), and because *ṛ* begins with a vowel, *āṭ* is prefixed.

The vowel *vṛddhi* [substitution] occurs by the rule "kṛte ṭhāṭaśca" (Pāṇini 6.1.90). The suffix *aṅ* is applied by the rule "adarśat" (Pāṇini 3.1.57), which states that after a root ending in *ṭh*, *iṭ* or *aṅ* may optionally follow. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *guṇa* [substitution]? Could it not simply be stated as "akāra" (the letter *a*)? It cannot be done in this way; for if it were stated as "akāra," it would apply to the final letter of the root *duś*. However, when *guṇa* is mentioned...
Since there is a rule for the application of the suffix *saṃjñā*, the substitution occurs only in the place of *ika*.
17. *asyatesthuk* (Pāṇini 7.4.17). Regarding the form *āsthat*: [it is derived from] the root *asu* "to throw" (Dhātupāṭha 1209).
By the rule *asyativaktikhapyātibhyo’ṅ* (3.1.52), there is the substitution of *aṅ* for the suffix *cli*.
18. *śvayater aḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.18). Regarding the form *aśvat*: [the root is] *ṭua ośvi gativṛddhyoḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 1010).
By the rule *jṛstambhubhrucu-* (3.2.58) and so forth, the suffix *aṅ* is applied, resulting in two instances of the vowel *a*.
The state of having another form.

19. *pataḥ pum* (Pāṇini 7.4.19). [The example is] *apaptat*. The roots *śal*, *hul*, and *patlṛ* mean "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 843, 844, 845); by the *puṣādi* group, the suffix *aṅ* is applied. The letter *m* is for the purpose of indicating the position [of the substitution].
20. *vaca um* (Pāṇini 7.4.20). [The form] *avocat* is derived from the root *vac* in the sense of "speaking" (*paribhāṣaṇe*; Dhātupāṭha 1842).
By the rule *asyatitiktikhya tibhyaḥ* (3.1.52), etc., the suffix *aṅ* is applied. That same [suffix] applies to the letter *m*.
The purpose.

21. *śīṅḥ sārvadhātuke guṇaḥ* | (Pāṇini 7.3.21) Since the prescription of *guṇa* would otherwise not apply [to the root *śīṅ*], this rule is formulated for the case where a *sārvadhātuka* suffix marked with *ṅ* follows. However, in the case of a suffix marked with *p*, the *guṇa* is already established by the general rule (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). [This is illustrated by] *loṭ*; [and by the rule] *ṭita ātmanepadānāṃ ṭere*, as well as *āḍajādīnām* and *āḍutamasya picca*.

By [Pāṇini 3.4.92], there is *āṭ* [augment] in *śayai* and *śayāvahai*. Therefore, this is prescribed where the *guṇa* substitution would otherwise not apply. In the form *śerate*, there is *luk* elision of *śap* because the root belongs to the *adādi* class; furthermore, by [Pāṇini 7.1.5], *āt* is substituted for *jh* in the *ātmanepada* endings. Here, by [Pāṇini 7.1.6], the augment *ruṭ* is added after the root *śīṅ*.
It occurs as "śiśye. [The suffix] liṭ [is applied]; by the rule "liṭ ca" (Pāṇini 3.4.115), it receives the designation *ārdhadhātuka*.
It is either the singular of the first person or the singular of the third person. When—
The third-person singular ending is *tai*, and the dual ending is as before (*ai*);

by the rule "ṭheranekāco'saṃyogapūrvasya" (Pāṇini 6.4.82), there is the substitution of *yaṇ*; the other [endings] are *eṭ*, and for these, the substitution of *et*. Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *guṇa*? Why not simply say "after the root *śīṅ*, *et* occurs before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix"?

Why would it be stated thus? He thinks as follows: in the mention of "śīṅ" with its indicatory letter (anubandha), the genitive case is employed; however, an indicatory letter has the nature of being subject to removal. When its designation as *it* results in its removal through elision, this other method [of using the genitive] would be disregarded as a means of removal. Regarding that...

It is not another designation that causes the cessation [of the sound ṅ], but rather the letter *e*. If this is so, then the letter *e* would take the place of the letter *ṅ*. Therefore, the mention of "guṇa" brings about the presence of the letter *i*. Since the letter *ṅ* would cease by that very reason, if this were the case, the letter *ṅ* would not be pronounced at all.

Why is the designation "ṭhjhiyaḥ" being made? This is not possible; for if the designation were made in this way, it would apply even in the case of the elision of the yaṅ (yaṅluk)—as in *śeśīta* and *śeśyati*.

22. *ayaṅ yi kṅiti* (Pāṇini 7.4.22). Regarding the form *śayyate*: by [the rule] *sārvadhātuke yak* (3.1.67), the suffix *yak* is added. Regarding the form *śāśayyate*: the suffix *yaṅ* is applied; because it is both subsequent (*paratva*) and obligatory (*nityatva*), the substitution of *ayaṅ* occurs prior to reduplication (*dvirvacana*). Thereafter, for the element *śayya-*...
There is reduplication, and by the rule *dīrgho 'kitaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.83), the long vowel is substituted for the abhyāsa (the reduplicated syllable).

Regarding the form *praśayya*: there is a compound (*samāsa*) according to the rules *samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle ktvā* (Pāṇini 3.4.21) and *kugatiprādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.18); [and further], by the rule *samāse 'nañpūrve ktvo*...

The suffix *kyap* is applied by the rule *lyap* (7.1.37), as in *tyam*; the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *ñco yat* (3.1.97); and *śayyā*—[not found in the Kāśikā]—is formed by the rule *saṃjñāyāṃ samajanipada...* (3.3.99), etc., with the suffix *kyap*.

23. *upasargād dhrasva ūhate* (Pāṇini 7.4.23). [Example: *samuhyagataḥ*. The root *ūh* (meaning "to deliberate") belongs to the sixth class (*dhā.pā.* 648). Although this form could be established by the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the semivowel before a *kit* suffix due to its inclusion in the *yajādi* group, nevertheless, the long vowel is not heard even after the root *ūh*.
This prescription of the short vowel [for the root *ūh*] is for the purpose that it should be so;
namely, in the case of the word "samīhyate. [The root] *īh* [is used] in the sense of "striving" (*ceṣṭā*). In the case of "samūhitaḥ," the suffix *kta* is applied.
In the case of "samūhayo 'yamarthaḥ," [the suffix] *ṇyat* is applied by Pāṇini 3.1.124 (*ṛhalorṇyat*). [The rule] simply says "after [roots ending in] *aṇ*."

And so forth. From the rule *ke’ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.13), the mention of *aṇ* is understood to carry over. In the examples *ā uhyate*, *ohyate*, and *samohyate*, shortening does not occur. If the mention of *aṇ* were to carry over, then the prescription of shortening would be purposeless; [one might ask: "Should it not rather be stated that [shortening occurs] after a prefix before the root *ūh*?"

It is not meaningless; because it serves as a reference for what follows—namely, that he will state "he-teliṅ" (Pāṇini 7.4.24)—it ensures that the term "hrasvaḥ" (short vowel) continues to apply there.
24. *eterliṅ* (Pāṇini 7.4.24). Regarding the example *udiyāt*: the root is *iṇ* "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1045); this is the *liṅ* suffix in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*).
By the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca* (8.2.29), there is the elision of the *s*. Regarding *abhīyāt*: [the same applies].

If the rule for lengthening by homogeneity (*savarṇadīrghatva*) has not yet occurred, the short vowel remains. By the rule "the *liṅ* [is used] in the sense of benediction" (*āśiṣi liṅ*), he shows the scope of the sūtra. For when the *liṅ* occurs after a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, lengthening of the root vowel *iṇ* is impossible;
thus, this [sūtra] has no application here. It applies only where lengthening of the *akṛt* and *sārvadhātuka* suffixes is prescribed by Pāṇini 6.4.103 (*akṛtsārvadhātukayordīrghaḥ*).
In that case, when lengthening has been applied by this [rule], the short vowel becomes long.
25. *akṛtsārvadhātukayordīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.25). As in *bhṛśāyate*; [this is derived] by *bhṛśādibhyo bhuvyacverlopaśca halaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.12).
Furthermore: regarding "sukhāyate," the suffix *kṅ* is applied by the rule "sukhādibhyaḥ kartṛvedanāyām" (Pāṇini 3.1.18).
Regarding "cīyate," the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), with the addition of *yak* by the rule "sārvadhātuke yak" (Pāṇini 3.1.67).
Regarding "cecīyate," the strengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) occurs by the rule "guṇo yaṅlukoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.82).

The suffix *guṇa*. [In the example] "ṣṭūyate," from the root *ṣṭuañ* in the sense of "praise" (*stutau*, DhP 1043), the remaining consonants (*khayaḥ*) are retained according to Pāṇini 7.4.61, *śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ*. [In the examples] "cīyāt" and "stūyāt," the suffix *liṅ* is used in the sense of benediction (*āśiṣi*).

Regarding the term "prakṛtyā": it is a *kṛt* suffix by virtue of Pāṇini 3.1.93 (*kṛdatiṅ*), as in the preceding rule. Now, one might object: since the long vowel [ā] is heard in the sūtra, the term *ac* is brought to mind; that [term *ac*] then qualifies the *aṅga*, and by means of that qualifier, there is the application of the rule to what ends in it (*tadantavidhi*). Thus, [the rule would apply to] an *aṅga* ending in *ac*.

"It must be long"—here, when *tuk* has been applied by [Pāṇini 6.1.71] *hrasvasya piti kṛti*, the state of ending in a vowel (*ajantatā*) no longer exists; therefore, because it does not end in a vowel, it must be long. Here, when *tuk* has been applied by [Pāṇini 6.1.71] *hrasvasya piti kṛti*, the state of ending in a vowel...

[An objection: "Since [the suffix] does not exist [in that case], there will be no lengthening precisely because it does not end in a vowel (*anajantatvāt*); so what is the purpose of including the term *akṛt* (non-verbally derived) for the sake of its exclusion? To this, he says: "Because it is subsequent," and so forth. The scope of *tuk* is, for example, *agnicit*; the scope of the lengthening is, for example, *cīyate*; and [the scope of the present rule is] *prakṛtya*.

Regarding the term *prahṛtaya*: since both [rules] would apply here, if the mention of *akṛt* (non-verb-form) were not made, the *tuṅ* augment would be superseded by the long vowel (*dīrgha*) due to its higher priority in the order of rules. Therefore, the mention of *akṛt* must be made. As for *cinuyāt*: this is the optative (*liṅ*) of the *vidhi* (injunction) and other senses; and it is [classified as] *sārvadhātuka* by the rule *tiṅśitsārvadhātukam*.
By this [rule], the suffixes receive the designation *sārvadhātuka*.
Thus, in the forms *dhṛyā* and *dhṛṣṇuyā*, the substitution of *yā* occurs for the third-case singular ending of the words *uru* and *dhṛṣṇu* by the rule "supāṃ suluk...
(Pāṇini 7.1.39) and others.
26. *cvau ca* (Pāṇini 7.4.26).
[The example is] *śucīkaroti*. The suffix *cvi* is applied by the rule *abhūtatadbhāve* (5.4.50), etc. The *ca* (and) serves to include this with what precedes.
27. *rīḍﬁataḥ* | (7.4.27) The term *yi* is understood [from the previous rule], as is the phrase *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*. Regarding "mātrīyati":
this is derived by *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (3.1.8). Regarding "pitrīyate": this is derived by *kartuḥ kyaṅ*.
The suffix *kyaṅ* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.11] *salopaśca*. In the form *cekrīyate*, the suffix *yaṅ* is applied to the root *kṛ*.
In the form *pitryam*, the suffix *yat* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.79] *pituryacca*; once the substitution of *rīṅ* has been made, the vowel *i* is elided by [Pāṇini 6.4.148] *yasyeti ca*.

But how, when "kṅiti" is being mentioned, does the substitute occur there? To this he says: "The term 'kṅiti' is excluded here. If that is so, would not the mention of "yi" also be excluded, since it is prescribed in the same single rule? This is not the case.

For the recurrence of words is indeed bound to their *svarita* accent. And here, since the *svarita* nature is specifically asserted for the mention of *yi*, that alone recurs; whereas since the *svarita* nature is not asserted for the mention of *kṅtī*, that does not recur here.

Regarding "ṭhcekīryate": from the root *kṛ* in the sense of "scattering" (*vikṣepe*, DhP 1409), the substitution of *i* for the radical vowel by *ṛta iddhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.100) is applied, followed by the replacement of *ṛ* with *ra*. Then, the lengthening of the vowel occurs by *hali ca* (8.2.77). Regarding "nijegilyate": from the root *gṛ* in the sense of "swallowing" (*nigaraṇe*, DhP 1410), [the suffix *yaṅ*] is applied by the rule *lupasada* (3.1.24) etc.
Furthermore, by the rule *yo yaṅi* (8.2.20), there is the substitution of *l* for the *r*. Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*)?

Why not simply say *riṅ*? [One might argue that] this is already established by the lengthening (*dīrghatva*) prescribed in *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* (7.4.25). To this, the following is the meaning: in the subsequent rule, again...

The mention of *ṛ* (riṅ) need not be made, for this very [term] will apply there by way of extension (*anuvṛtti*). This is not established; for if *ṛ* were introduced before the long vowel (*dīrgha*) had occurred, it would be an exception (*bādhaka*) to that.
Granted, it may indeed be an exception to the long vowel of the phoneme *ṛ*, but what about that which occurs after the substitution has been made?

An [operation] pertaining to another substitute would apply; how then could this [substitute] be its sublater, for the substitution of *riṅ* is not prescribed while that [other operation] is already applicable? If so, then the long vowel is pronounced for the sake of easy comprehension by those of dull intellect.
The letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of indicating that the substitution applies to the final [sound].

28. *riṅ śayagliṅkṣu* (Pāṇini 7.4.28). Here too, the term *yi* is included, and *akṛtsārvadhātuka* is also carried over from the previous rule. In this context, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the restriction applies only to the *liṅ* suffix, not to *śaya* and *ka*. [Example: *ādriyate*.

Regarding the word *ādhriyate*: the roots *dṛṅ* in the sense of "respect" (DhP 1411) and *dhṛṅ* in the sense of "remaining steady" (DhP 1412) are preceded by the prefix *ā*; the suffix *cha* is applied because they belong to the *tud*-class. Regarding *kriyāt*: this is the *liṅ* in the sense of a benediction (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.173). Regarding *bibhṛyāt*: here it is the *liṅ* used for injunctions and so forth.
Because [the root] belongs to the *juhoty-ādi* class, there is *ślu*-elision; by the rule "in the case of *ślu*" (6.1.10), there is reduplication;
and by the rule "for the roots *bhṛ*, etc., *it*" (7.4.76), the *it* substitution occurs for the reduplicated syllable. Regarding "kṛpīṣṭa":
the suffix *liṅ* is used in the sense of benediction (3.3.173); because of the *kit* designation by the rule "and after *u*" (1.2.12), there is an absence of *guṇa*.

29. *guṇo'rtisaṃyogādyoḥ* | (Pāṇini 7.4.29) This rule applies to the inclusion of the two roots *ṛ*, namely *ṛ* in the sense of "motion" and "causing to reach" (Dhātupāṭha 936), which belongs to the Bhvādigaṇa, and *ṛ* in the sense of "motion" (Dhātupāṭha 1098, 1099), which belongs to the Juhotyādigaṇa.

Because of the statement "the sūtras are like Vedic meters" (*chandovat sūtrāṇi bhavanti*) from the *Mahābhāṣya*, the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap* was applied according to Pāṇini 6.4.73, *bahulaṃ chandasi*,

and thus the form *ṛcchati* was used as the technical designation (*nirdeśa*). Otherwise, if the designation had been made as *uccchati*, then the root belonging to the *juhoty-ādi* class would not have been included.
It might be so. Even if the indication [of the root] is made as *iyarti*, even then there would be no inclusion of the root belonging to the *bhūvādika* class.

However, the indication was not made simply as *ṛ*; rather, it was done for the sake of variety. This [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *riṅ* substitution obtained by the preceding rule. As for the mention of *śa*, it is excluded because it is impossible [in this context].

But [the suffixes] *asun* and *tis* are impossible because of the non-occurrence of the verbal root *ṛ*, since it lacks a vowel (*aśavikaraṇatvāt*). [The forms] *aryate* [and] *aryāt*: [the former is formed with] *yak*; [the latter is] the *liṅ* in the sense of a benediction (*āśiṣi*).
Now, why does [this rule] not apply in cases such as *saṃskriyate* and *saṃskriyāt*, for [the root *kṛ*] certainly exists?

One might ask: "Even when *suṭ* has been applied, is not the root *kṛ-* still a *saṃyoga-ādi* (beginning with a conjunct consonant)? To this he says: "When *ih* [is present], etc. However, *suṭ* is considered *bahiraṅga* (external) because it depends upon two words (*dvipadāśrayatvāt*), whereas the *guṇa* substitution is *antaraṅga* (internal) because it depends upon only one word (*ekapadāśrayatvāt*). [The principle is: "That which is *bahiraṅga* is as good as non-existent (*asiddham*) in relation to that which is *antaraṅga*."

(Vyā.pa.42) Thus, because the augment *suṭ* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the verbal base (*aṅga*) does not possess the property of beginning with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogāditva*). Even if, for some reason, *suṭ* were to be considered existent, nevertheless, because *suṭ* is not an integral part of the base (*abhakta*), the base still does not begin with a conjunct; therefore, the *guṇa* substitution does not take effect.

Because the term *aṅga* is under discussion [in this context], "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) is understood as a constituent part of the *aṅga*. For if [the augment] *suṭ* were not a part [of the *aṅga*], it would not be logical for the conjunction to be a constituent part of the *aṅga*. [The example is] *ṛiyāt*: from the root *ṛ* "to go" (DhP 1098), in the optative (*liṅ*) of the *vidhyādi* group; due to its belonging to the *juhotyādi* class, there is *ślu* substitution for *śap*, and [the rule applies] because of the condition *ślau*.

Thus there is reduplication; by *artipipartyośca* (Pāṇini 7.4.77), the *it* vowel is substituted for the reduplicated syllable; by *abhyāsasyāsavarṇe* (Pāṇini 6.4.78), the *iyaṅ* substitution occurs; and by *liṅḥ salopo’nantyasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.79), there is the elision of the *s* suffix.
Although it would have been sufficient to state "ṛtisaṃyogādyoḥ at" [Pāṇini 6.4.112], the inclusion of the term "guṇa" is for the sake of variety.
30. Furthermore, what [is the case]?

(7.4.30) *pūravema* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *rīṅ* substitution that would otherwise apply to the root *prā*. [In the form] *rāryate*: there is *yaṅ*-guṇa, followed by *raparatva* (substitution of *ra* for the semivowel). Then, by the rule *ajāderdvitīyasya* (6.1.2), there is reduplication; subsequently, there is *halādiśeṣa* (retention of the first consonant with elision of the others).

The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule "dīrgho 'kitaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.83). Now, one might object: since the root *arti* begins with a consonant, the suffix *yaṅ* would not apply to it. To this he says: "of *arti*, etc.
Let it be that *yaṅ* applies due to the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*), but as for the substitution of *r*, it does not [apply] because of reduplication.
[One might ask: "Is it not necessary [to apply the rule], because of the prohibition in *na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.3)?

To this he says: "*na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ*. For it has been stated therein: "A prohibition must be stated for the *repha* that follows a *yakāra*. Therefore, the doubling of *rya* occurs after that *repha*."

Regarding the form *jaṅghanyate*: the augment *nuk* is applied by the rule *nugato'nunāsikāntasya* (Pāṇini 7.4.85), and the substitution of the guttural *k* for the palatal *c* occurs by the rule *abhyāsācca* (Pāṇini 7.3.55).
31. *ī ghradhmoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.31).
What is the purpose of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) in this rule? Is it so that the long vowel may occur and the short vowel (*hrasva*) may not?
This is not the case; for even if the short vowel were prescribed, [the substitution] would still be governed by *akṛtsārvadhātukayordīrghaḥ* (7.4.25).

In this way, [the form] is established; will not a long vowel occur as appropriate by the rule "ṭhcvau ca" (Pāṇini 7.4.26)? If so, then this teaches the following: "A rule conditioned by a technical name (saṃjñā) is non-eternal" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 64). By that, the form *svāyambhuvam* is established.
32. *asya cvau*. (7.4.32) This is an exception to the rule for lengthening [the vowel] stated in *ṭhcvau ca* (7.4.26).
33. *kyaci ca* (Pāṇini 7.4.33).

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the rule] *ṭhakṛtsārvadhātukayordīrghaḥ* (7.4.25). The letter *ca* is for the purpose of carrying over (*anukarṣaṇa*) the term *ṭha* from [the rule] *ṭhasya* (7.4.32). Now, what is the purpose of making this a separate rule (*pṛthagyoga*), rather than [merging it with the previous one]? It is not...

"Why not simply make a single rule, *ṭhccikyacoḥ*? To this he replies: "The formulation of separate rules," and so forth. [The purpose is] so that subsequent operations such as *na ccchandasyaputrasya* (Pāṇini 7.4.35) may apply to *kyac*, but not to *cvī*.
The division of the rule (yogavibhāga) was made for the purpose of [the suffix] -bhūta- being applied in this sense.
34. [The suffix *ya* is applied after the roots] *aś*, *udanya*, and *dhana* to express hunger, thirst, and greed respectively.
(Pāṇini 7.4.34) Desire to eat is *bubhukṣā*. Desire to drink is *pipāsā*. *Gardha* is the act of grasping; it means intense longing.

35. *na cchandasyaputrasya* (Pāṇini 7.4.35). [The meaning is: "That which was stated regarding the suffix *kyac* does not occur. But what is that? He says: "Lengthening and *ī*-tva. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that a rule applies only to what is immediately preceding?"

Regarding the rule "or rather, there is a prohibition" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.129), should there not be a prohibition of the immediately preceding *ītva* (the substitution of *ī*), and not of the *dīrghatva* (lengthening) which is separated by an interval? This is not a fault;
for the statement of *ātvam* (substitution of *ā*) for *aśva* and *agha* in the rule "after *aśva* and *agha*, [there is] *āt*" (7.4.37) [establishes the priority of the subsequent rule].

This is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that this prohibition applies to lengthening (*dīrghatva*) as well; otherwise, since the form would already be established by lengthening alone, the employment of the vowel *ā* [in the rule] would be purposeless. In the word *mitrayuḥ*, the suffix *u* is added by [Pāṇini 3.2.170] *kyāc chandasi*; then [the *a* of the root is elided] by [Pāṇini 6.4.48] *ato lopaḥ*.
There is the elision of the vowel *i*.

Regarding the statement "it should be stated that [the rule applies] to *putra* and so forth," the meaning is that this must be explained as having the sense that the prohibition does not apply to *putra* and so forth. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: in the case of *kyac*...

Immediately after [the rule] *ca* (Pāṇini 7.4.33), the word *putrasya* should be stated. For what purpose? To set aside the prohibition that will be stated in the rule *na cchandasi*. In this way, the negative particle *nañ* need not be explicitly uttered in the form *aputrasya*. This very point is addressed by the rule *kyaci ca* (7.4.33).

Immediately after this, although one should have said "of a son" (putrasya), the statement here is "of one without a son" (aputrasya) for the purpose of ensuring that there is a prohibition of [having] a son and so forth.
And this is obtained because "son" is used as an illustration (upalakṣaṇa).
36. *durasyu-draviṇasyu-vṛṣaṇyati-riṣaṇyati* (Pāṇini 7.4.36).
37. *aśvāghasyāt* (Pāṇini 7.4.37). "This very [mention of] *aśva* and *agha* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*)," and so forth. How does it serve as an indicator? If [the rule] were not... [text truncated]
This prohibition applies only to the *it* [the short *i*] that immediately precedes [the rule *chandasi* 7.4.35];

otherwise, the mention of *ad* would be purposeless, as [the lengthening] would already be established by [the rule] *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* (7.4.25). And since it has been stated, this indicates that this [prohibition] applies to the long vowel as well.
There is a negation.

38. *devasumnayoryajuṣi kāṭhake* (Pāṇini 7.4.38). Since the prohibition [of the substitution of *ī* for *ai*] by the rule *na ccchandasi* (7.4.35) would otherwise apply, this sūtra is commenced to state that the substitution of *ā* occurs for *deva* and *sumna*. The term "in the Kāṭhaka" is a qualifier specifically of the Yajurvedic text. This Yajurvedic text belongs to Kaṭha.
*Kāṭhakam*—[formed] by [the rule] *gotracaraṇād vañ* (Pāṇini 4.3.126).

39. There is elision of the final phoneme of *kāvyadhvarapṛtanasya* [before a suffix beginning with a vowel]. (Pāṇini 7.4.39). Regarding the form *kāvyantaḥ*: the elision is by rule 1.1.52 (*alo’ntyasya*). The suffix *śatṛ* is added after a stem ending in *kyac*, and *jas* is added after that [stem ending in *śatṛ*].
40. *dyati-syati-māti-sthā-mit* before a *kit* suffix.

(Pāṇini 7.4.40) The specifications *in the Veda*, *in the Yajus*, and *in the Ṛk* are all withdrawn; therefore, this rule applies generally. [The roots involved are: *do* (DhP 1148) "to cut" and *ṣo* (DhP 1147) "to finish."

The roots *mā* in the sense of "measuring" (*dhā.pā.* 1062), *māṅ* in the sense of "measuring" (*dhā.pā.* 1142), and *meṅ* in the sense of "pledging" (*dhā.pā.* 961)—all three are included here because of the rule *gāmādāgrahaṇeṣv aviśeṣaḥ* (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 124).
[Also included is] *ṣṭhā* in the sense of "stopping of motion" (*dhā.pā.* 928). Among these, for the first root, [the substitution of *dagh* applies] by the rule *do dadghoḥ*.

When *datva* (the substitution of *d* for *t*) would otherwise apply by this rule [7.4.46], and when *ītva* (the substitution of *ī* for *i*) would apply to the remaining cases by the rule "ṭhghumāsthā" (6.4.66) and others, the substitution of *itva* (the substitution of *i* for *i*) is here prescribed.
Regarding "avadāya": as before, *lyap* is substituted for *ktvā*. Regarding "avadātā": this is the suffix *tṛc*.

This mention [of the root] with the *śtip* affix (*dyati-syatat-i*) is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-looped forms (*yaṅluk*). Consequently, for those two [forms], it remains exactly as prescribed: *dādataḥ*, *dādatavān*, *sāsītaḥ*.
He has practiced [the recitation].
The addition of the marker *t* (*tapara*) is for the sake of ease of pronunciation, not for the purpose of excluding the long vowel;
for it is said: "An *aṇ* vowel being taught does not include its homogeneous counterparts" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 35).
Because the long [vowel] is not obtained.
41. *śācchāor anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 7.4.41). The roots *śo* (meaning "to sharpen" or "to attenuate," Dhātupāṭha 1145) and *chāe* (meaning "to cut," Dhātupāṭha 1146) [are concerned].
Regarding the rule "the substitution of *i* for *śyati* is obligatory when a vow (*vrata*) follows," the word *vrata* is not taken as a subsequent member of a compound; rather, what is it?

What then? It is the object. Regarding the object of a vow (*vrata*), there is the permanence of the suffix *ṇini*. As in "the Brahmin is *saṃśita*. One who is indeed diligent in a specific practice called a vow is called *saṃśitavrata*.
He is one for whom the vow (*vrata*) has been sharpened (*saṃśita*)—that is, properly established through diligence—or by whom [the vow] has been so established.

Thus it is said. But surely, since the nature of the vow (*itva*) is already indicated by the very act of enjoining it within the context of the vow, the use of the word "vow" (*vrata*) would not be appropriate? This is not a fault; for while the nature of being a vowel (*itva*) occurs elsewhere as well, in the case of a vow it is invariably designated as such. Thus, this is a general term.

It occurs. Here, the word *vrata* is employed for the sake of a specific meaning. Its posterior placement (*paranipāta*) should be understood as being due to its inclusion in the group beginning with *āhitāgni*. [The formation] is established by understanding it as an option fixed by specific rules (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
To confirm this by means of a scriptural statement, he says: "Devatrāta," and so forth. [The root] *traiṅ* (Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 965) means "to protect";

[the suffix] *kta* is added. Regarding the name [Devatrāta], the substitution of *n* for *t* does not occur at all by the rule *nudavidondatrāghrāhrībhyo 'nyatarasyām* (8.2.56). Thus, Devatrāta is one who was protected (*trāta*) by the gods (*devaiḥ*).

In this context, the word *deva* is intended as an illustration for a technical name (*saṃjñā*). Even when the word *trāta* occurs alone as a name, it does not undergo the substitution of *n*. Thus, in cases other than a name, both forms occur: *trāṇaḥ* and *prātaḥ*. Regarding the form *galaḥ*: it is derived from the root *gṛ* with the suffix *ac* (by Pāṇini 3.1.134). [The rule] *gro yaṅ* (Pāṇini 8.2.20) applies, and [the rule] *ici vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 6.1.25) also applies.

(8.2.21) Thus, when referring to a limb of a living being, the substitution of *la* for *ra* is obligatory—as in *gala*. However, in the case of poison (*viṣa*), it occurs as well—as in *gara*. Regarding *grāha*: the suffix *ṇa* is applied to the root *grah* by [Pāṇini 3.1.143] "vibhāṣā grahaḥ.
When referring to a crocodile, an aquatic creature, the suffix *ṇa* is obligatory—as in *grāha*.

In words such as *āditya* and *soma*, the suffix *ac* belonging to the *paca*-class indeed occurs—as in *graha*. Furthermore, the rule for *sat* does not apply when used with the word *iti*: for example, in "he runs because it rains" (*varṣatīti dhāvati*) or "he flees because he is being struck" (*hantīti palāyate*), the two [suffixes] are designated as *sat* by the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.126).

When used in conjunction with *asat*, the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* do not occur at all, due to the rule of fixed optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). In this regard, the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) from the rule *ṭhnanvor vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 3.2.121) is understood to carry over—thus we have *arjayan vasati* ("he dwells while earning") and *adhīyāno vasati* ("he dwells while studying"). However, when used in conjunction with *asat*, those two suffixes occur invariably.

Now, one might object: since the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is already indicated by the word *iti* itself, rules concerning the existence [of a verbal suffix]—such as in "it rains" (*varṣati*) or "he kills" (*hanti*)—will not apply; whereas where the word *iti* is not employed, such rules certainly do apply—as in "he lives while earning" (*arjayan vasati*). To this, it is replied: in this case...
Even without the governing rule of *vibhāṣā*, the option (*vibhāṣā*) is indeed obtained; therefore, the mention of *vibhāṣā* need not be carried over [from the previous rule].
Consequently, is this not a non-example of an "optionally fixed" (*avyavasthitavibhāṣā*) rule?
In that case, here is an example: *kariṣyāmīti vrajati* ("He goes thinking, 'I shall do it'"). Here, the suffix *lṛṭ* is applied by the rule *lṛṭ śeṣe ca*.

By the inclusion of the word "ca" (and) in this rule, when a verb expressing an action is used as an *upapada* for another action, the suffix *lṛṭ* is applied; however, the rule for *saṭ* (the augment *sa*) will not apply to that *lṛṭ*. This is due to the fixed optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Elsewhere, by virtue of the rule "with [a word] not in grammatical coreferentiality with the nominative," it occurs invariably—as in *kariṣyantam*.
"Behold!"—but when [the word] is not in grammatical apposition with the nominative, there is an option: *brāhmaṇaḥ kariṣyan* or *brāhmaṇaḥ kariṣyati*.
Regarding "mutually" (*mithaḥ*) and so forth: "mutually" means by way of coexistence.

The meaning is that *devatrāta*, *galagrāha*, and others are not prescribed as alternatives (*vikalpena*) for the same object along with *trāṇa*, *garagraha*, and so forth. Regarding the word *gavākṣaḥ*: while the rule *sarvatra vibhāṣā goḥ* (6.1.122) is still in force, the rule *avaṅ sphoṭāyanasya* (6.1.123) applies.

The vowel *avaṅ* is always substituted [for *ava*] in the word *vātāyana* (window), but it does not occur in *prāṇyaṅga* (limb of a living being) in the case of *go'kṣam* (ox-eye); elsewhere both forms occur—namely, *gavākṣam* and *go'kṣam*. Regarding the term *saṃśitavrataḥ*, the substitution of *nit* is mandatory (*nityam*) when referring to a vow (*vrata*). Elsewhere, it is optional—as in *niśitam* or *niśātam* (sharpened weapon).
The meaning is "sharp. All of this is obtained through the *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (restricted option).

In some cases there is only an injunction (*vidhi*), in some cases only a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), and in some cases both; such a variety of options established for various purposes is called *vyavasthitavibhāṣā*. And this...

The various modes of existence should be understood as pertaining to the word-meaning as a form (*ākṛti*). For in that case, having unified and condensed the entire range of things to be characterized (*lakṣya*), both [affirmation and negation] are taught. Whether it be an injunction (*vidhi*) or a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), both occur when the genus (*jāti*) is the word-meaning; such is the extent of the matter.
The function of the treatise lies in its exposition. As for the fact that in some instances there is only an injunction,
in some only a prohibition, and in others both— in other words, the systematic arrangement without confusion—
this is obtained from the instruction of an unbroken lineage of teachers.
42. *dadhāter hiḥ* | (Pāṇini 7.4.42).

When the substitution of *ī* was about to occur by the rule *dhumāsthā...* (6.4.66), the substitution of *hi* for *dadhāti* is prescribed. The mention of the root with the *śtip* affix (*dadhāti*) is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-lopa form; therefore, [the substitution does not apply] to that which ends in *yaṅ*-lopa.
The substitution of *hir* does not occur—as in *dādhītaḥ*, *dādhītavān*, and *dādhītva*.
43. *jahāteś ca ktvi* (Pāṇini 7.4.43).

When the substitution of *ī* for *ā* would have applied as before, the rule prescribes the substitution of *hi* for the suffix *ktvā*. Although the form *hitvā* is also established from the root *hi gatau* (Dhātupāṭha 1257), nevertheless...
The mention [of the root] is for the purpose of excluding *hṛ*.
Now, for what reason is the root *jahāti* specified by means of the *śtip* affix (*jahāteḥ*), rather than simply saying "of *hṛ*" (*haḥ*)?
To this he says: "of *jahāti*" and so forth. By this, [the root] *ohāṅ* "to go" (DhP 1089) is excluded.

This shows that the mention [of the root] is made for the purpose of excluding this [other root]. For if the mention were "haḥ," then because that [form] is common to both, it would apply to *jihāti* as well;
however, when there is the mention of *jahāti* by means of the *śtip* affix, it does not occur. By this, it is *jahāti* alone [that is intended].

It is *jihīte* that is indicated, not *jihāti*. For such an indication does not apply to the *yaṅluk* form—namely, *jāhātu*. Furthermore, the substitution of *ī* (ītvam) does not occur here either; for even in the rule prescribing that [substitution], the root is indicated by means of the *śtip* affix.
And when the augment *iṭ* is applied here, [the *ī* substitution would otherwise be blocked] by Pāṇini 6.4.64: *āto lopa iṭi ca* ("there is elision of the final *ā* before an *iṭ* augment").
Thus, there is the elision of the vowel *i*.
44. *vibhāṣā chandasi* (7.4.44). 45. *sudhitavasudhitanemadhita-dhiṣvadhiṣīya ca* (7.4.45).
By the word *ca*, the phrase *chandasi* is drawn over [from the previous rule]. [The rule] "there is optionally the augment *iṭ*" applies; when there is the augment *iṭ*, then—

In *sudhitam*, there is the elision of the vowel *ā* by Pāṇini 6.4.64 (*ṭhāto lopa iṭi ca*). The compound *sudhitam* is formed according to 2.2.18 (*kugatiprādayaḥ*). In *vasudhitam*, it is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*); as before, there is the elision of the vowel *ā*. In *nemadhitam*, [the word] *sāmi*...

(2.1.27) Thus is a compound with the second case ending (*dvitīyā-samāsa*). It has been stated that in this context, the term *sāmi* includes its meaning; furthermore, the word *nema* is a synonym for the word *sāmi*. Regarding "dhiṣva": by [Pāṇini 3.4.80] *thāsaḥ se*, and by [3.4.91] *savābhyāṃ vāmau*, the substitution of *v* occurs. Regarding "the absence of reduplication": [this refers to the fact that the root does not undergo reduplication].

There is the elision of the vowel *a* by *ṭhślau* (6.4.112); the *gh* undergoes *cartyam* (change to the corresponding unaspirated stop) by *ṭhkhari ca* (8.4.55), becoming *t*; and the reduplicated syllable becomes *dh* by *ṭhdadhastathośca* (8.2.38) through the substitution of *bhaṣ*. [The form] *dhiṣīya* is derived from the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), with the augment *iṭ* by *ṭhiṭo't* (3.4.106).
Thus ends [the section on] "it-ness."

46. *do dadghoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.46). The term *chandasi* ("in Vedic") is no longer in force, because it has been drawn back [into the scope of this rule] by the particle *ca* ("and") in the preceding sūtra. Examples: *dataḥ*, *datavān*—these are formed with the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu*. *datiḥ*—this is formed with the suffix *ktin*. *dhītaḥ*, *dhītavān*.
Thus [it is said]. As before, there is the substitution of *ī*.

Now, why does the substitution of *hi* not occur by the rule "the root *dhā* is replaced by *hi*" (Pāṇini 7.4.42)? To this he says: "This is the form of the root *ghaṭ*" (*dheṭ*), and so forth. This refers to the root *dheṭ* in the sense of "drinking" (Dhātupāṭha 902).

The meaning is that [the word] *rūpam* does not derive from the root *dadhāti*; therefore, the substitution of *hi* does not occur. As for the form *dātam*, this is the form of the root *dāp* "to cut" (DhP 1059); it does not have the designation *ghu*, because of the prohibition [stated in Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.20]: "except for *dāp*."
Regarding the rule *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ*, this is the form resulting from the substitution of a *jaś* sound; however, someone might have the misconception:
"Is this substitute (*ādeśa*) one ending in *ta*, or one ending in *da*, or one ending in *dha*, or perhaps one ending in *tha*?"—therefore, [the author] addresses that doubt.
In order to refute [this], he says: "This is an *ādeśa*," and so forth. How is this known? He says:

"For it has been stated thus," and so forth. If this were an *ādeśa* ending in *t*, then in the case of *sudatī*, while the rule *ikaḥ kāśe* (Pāṇini 6.3.123) is being carried over, the rule *dāsti* (Pāṇini 6.3.124) would require the lengthening of the vowel *i*.
It might be so. Now, if it ended in *d*, then by the rule "ṭhradābhyām" (Pāṇini 8.2.42), there would be the substitution of *ṇ* for the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix.

Or, if it ended in *dh*, then by the rule "jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.40), the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix would undergo the substitution of *dh* after a *jhaṣ* consonant. [The author says: "There is no fault if it ends in *th*. Here, [the word] *nañ* [is understood].
This is the connection [of the sūtra]. The meaning is that there is no fault when the substitute ends in *th*. Regarding the phrase "therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth:

because there is a fault in all three previously mentioned alternative views (*pakṣa*), this substitute must therefore end in *th*. In the examples *dataḥ* and *datavān*, the substitution of *t* for *th* occurs by the rule *khari ca* (8.4.55).

"But if," and so forth. Two alternatives were shown in the Bhāṣya regarding the rule *dasti* (Pāṇini 6.3.124): namely, that [the substitution of long *ā*] occurs when this element *dā* begins with the letter *t*, or when it ends with the letter *t*.
In that regard, if the alternative is adopted that the lengthening occurs when this element *dā* ends with the letter *t*:

In that case, there would be the fault of [the vowel] becoming long. However, if this alternative is adopted—that lengthening occurs when the element *dā* follows an initial *t*—then there is no fault even in the case of a word ending in *ta*. Wherever the element *dā* follows an initial *t*, there lengthening takes place—as in *nītam*.

[The rule applies] in cases such as *vīta*, but not in cases such as *sudata*. Therefore, there is the fault of the potential occurrence of a long vowel [in the latter]. [Regarding the statement] "also for those ending in *d* and *dh*," and so forth:
for these two substitutes, *d* and *dh*, are prescribed in conjunction with the letter *t*.
They are not capable of becoming the cause for its destruction;

therefore, there is no fault even in the case of *dānta* and *dhānta*. Regarding "having spoken" (*avadatam*), etc.: this refers to the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*), that is, the first moment of the action.

This is the meaning. Here, although the substitution of *t* [for *d*] would have been required by the rule "ṭhaca upasargāt" (Pāṇini 7.4.47), these forms beginning with *avadatta* are prescribed as irregular (*nipātana*). Furthermore, the term "in the sense of an incipient action" (*ādikarmaṇi*) qualifies all of them, and not only the word *pradattam*. In cases other than an incipient action, the suffix *ac* [is applied].

By the rule "upargāt" (Pāṇini 7.4.47), the substitution of *t* occurs, and not the change to *d*—as in *avatam*, *vītam*, *sūtam*, and *anūtam*. [This applies] when they are "not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasargāḥ*), and so forth. Alternatively, *ava* and the others are designated as prefixes (*upasarga*) with respect to the root *dadāti*.

Thus they do not [function as prefixes] for that; because another action, namely the action expressed by the root *gam*, is the object of the action expressed by that [root], it should be understood in other cases as well—such as "it is understood" (*avagatam*), "it is given" (*dattam*), or "it is spoken" (*avadattam*).
Therefore, these are designated as prefixes (upasarga) with respect to the root *gam*, not with respect to the root *dā*. Likewise...

For it has been stated: "Those particles such as *pra* and others, when connected with an action, receive the designations of 'motion' (*gati*) and 'prefix' (*upasarga*) in relation to that [action]. Therefore, since the designation of 'prefix' would not apply here, the letter *t* would not arise at all; so what is the purpose of this irregularity (*nipātana*)?
47. *aca upasargāt* | (Pāṇini 7.4.47) This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *da*. [The rule states: "The substitution of *ta* occurs.
The vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). In examples such as *pratam*, once the vowel *ā* has been changed to *t*, [the substitution applies] to the letter *d*.

The *cartva* [substitution of *ra* for *ṛ*] is the letter *t* in the word *nītam*. There is lengthening by the rule *dasti* (Pāṇini 6.3.124). The form *avadātam* belongs to the root *daip* meaning "purification" (Dhātupāṭha 924). [An objection is raised: "Does not the substitution of *la* apply to the initial [element]? This is because of the rule *ādeḥ parasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.54). [The response continues with: *aca*...
Regarding the statement "this [term] *acaḥ* should be repeated twice":

when *acaḥ* is repeated twice, there arise two word-forms, *acaḥ* and *aca*. Among these, one ends in the fifth case (ablative) and the other ends in the sixth case (genitive). Therein, by means of one [the ablative], the prefix (*upasarga*) [is excluded].

It is distinguished [from other rules] by the phrase "after a prefix ending in a vowel. By this [rule], the substitute also refers to the original element (*sthānin*), such that this substitute occurs for a form of this kind. Or else, as in the rule "dvitakāro vā" (or with two *k*s), or again in "aca upasargāt" (after a prefix ending in a vowel)—in these cases, a substitute consisting of a conjunct of two *k*s is specifically indicated.

Because this [substitute] consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it replaces the whole [of the original]. If, then, this instruction contains two *t* sounds, then by the rule *ṭhapo bhiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.48), it would also follow that it is a replacement for the whole; therefore, he says "because it has more than one phoneme" (*anekāltvāt*)—namely, the rule *ṭhapo bhiḥ*, etc. Regarding the rule *ṭhapo bhiḥ*:
The phrase "ending in the fifth case" (*pañcamyantam*) and "the vowel *a*" (*acaḥ*) are understood from the previous context; therefore, even though [the substitute] consists of multiple *al* sounds,
by the rule "from that, [the following]" (*tasmādityuttarasya*, Pāṇini 1.1.67), the substitution will apply only to the letter *p*, not to the whole [stem].
Regarding the rule beginning with "ṭhdyateḥ" and so forth: the scope for the root *dyati* is where there is no vowel-ending (*ajanta*) prefix—for example, *nirditam* and *durditam*;
the scope for this substitute is where [the root] follows a prefix that does not end in a vowel.
Regarding those termed *ghu*— namely, *ḍudāñ* "to give" (DhP 1091) as in *avatam* and *parītam*:

when there is a potential application of both [substitutions] for the root *dyati* following a prefix ending in *a*, the substitution of *t* alone occurs by way of *vipratiṣedha* (the rule of mutual exclusion), as in *avatam* and *pratam*.

48. *apo bhiḥ* (7.4.48): [The form] is *adbhiḥ*. By the rule *jhalāṃ jaśo’nte* (8.2.39), the substitution of a *jaś* sound occurs—the letter *t* becomes *d*. However, in the alternative view where there are two *t*s, by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* (8.4.53), the same substitution applies to the preceding [letter as well].
The substitution of *jaś* results in the letter *d*. By the rule *ṭhjharo jhari savarṇe* (Pāṇini 8.4.65), there is the elision of the preceding *d*.
Thus, from *suvas* [or *svavaḥ* according to the *Kāśikā*], etc., we have *suvas*, *svatavas*, and *māsa*.

And when these [words ending in -uvas] are followed by a word beginning with *bh*, this substitution of *t* is desired in the domain of the Veda (*chandas*). It should be understood that this is obtained precisely by the rule "there is extensive transposition" (*vyatyayo bahulam*, Pāṇini 3.1.85).
49. *sa syārdhadhātuke* (Pāṇini 7.4.49).
Here too, under the view that there are two *t*s, because it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it would follow that it is a substitute for the whole;
therefore, the word *acaḥ* [from the previous rule] must be understood as following here in its ablative form. Now...

Or rather—by the rule "substitutes apply to that which is being pointed out" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 106), it will apply to the *s* alone—as in "vatsyati" [from the root] *vas* "to dwell" (Dhātupāṭha 1942). As for "jighatsati":
[it is derived from] *ad* with the suffix *san*; by the rule "ghaslṛ replaces *ad* before *luṅ* and *san*" (Pāṇini 2.4.37), there is the substitution of *ghaslṛ* for it.

Regarding "he will speak" (*vakṣyati*): the root *vac* means "to speak" (*paribhāṣaṇe*; DhP 1842). The substitution of *k* for *c* occurs by the rule *coḥ kuḥ* (8.2.30). Regarding "grass" (*ghāsaḥ*) and "clothing" (*vāsaḥ*): the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). By the rule *ghañapośca* (2.4.38), the substitute *ghas* takes the place of the initial [of the root] before these two suffixes. Regarding "you sit" (*āsse*) and "you dwell" (*vasse*): the root *ās* means "to sit" (*upaveśane*; DhP 1021).

The root *ṭhvas* (meaning "to cover") is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as 1023. Because it is marked with an anudātta accent, it takes the ātmanepada endings. By the rule *cāsaḥ se* (Pāṇini 3.4.80), the suffix *si* is applied;
furthermore, because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* augment.
Now, why is it not stated that [the *s*] is [replaced by *i*] by the rule *saḥ syatiṅ*? It cannot be done in this way; for even here, it would not apply.
It might be: "you would have surpassed."

50. *tāsastyorlopaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.50). [Regarding the forms] *ṭhanadyatane luṭ* (3.3.15) and *tāsi*: in *kartāse*, [the suffix] *sip* is applied; by *ṭhthāsaḥ se* (3.4.80), *thās* is replaced by *se*. In *tvam asi*, [the root] *as* is used for the sense of existence (*bhuvi*, Dhātupāṭha 1065); as before, there is the elision (*luk*) of *śap*.

Regarding the form *vyatiṣe*: the ātmanepada suffix occurs by the rule *kartari karmavyatīhāre* (Pāṇini 1.3.14). Then, by *thāsaḥ se* (3.4.80) and *śnasorallopaḥ* (6.4.111), there is the elision of the vowel *a*.
Now, why does the substitution of *ṣ* not occur here by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (8.3.59)? To this [it is replied]:...

He says: "In the case of *ṭhas*, [the letters] *a* and *s*," and so forth. For when the letters *a* and *s* are elided, only the suffix remains; that alone is the word (*pada*). Therefore, because of the prohibition by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.111), the substitution of *ṣ* will not occur—this is the intended meaning.
51. *ri ca* (Pāṇini 7.4.51). [Examples:

*kartārau*, *kartāraḥ*. [Derivation: From the suffix *luṭ*, [we have] *tas* and *jhi*. By the rule *luṭaḥ prathamasya ḍāraurasaḥ* (2.4.85), the substitutes *rau* and *ras* respectively take the place of *tas* and *jhi*.

[Examples are] *adhyetārau*, *adhyetāraḥ*. Because the root *iṅ* has the marker *ṅ*, the Ātmanepada affixes *ātām* and *jha* are applied; for these two, as before, *rau* and *ras* are substituted. Since no affix beginning with *r* can follow the root *as*, there is no example [for that case]. Some, however, show *vyatire* as an example.

And this usage of the word *ca* would be appropriate if [the phenomenon] were non-existent; however, since it does exist, it is inappropriate. The substitution of *ra* for *r* is prescribed in the Vedic language by the rule *tiraso re* (Pāṇini 6.4.76), according to the principle that "in the Vedic language, one follows what is observed" (*yathādṛṣṭānuvidhiś chandasi*). The particle *ca* is used with reference to what precedes.
The meaning is "conjunction."
52. *ha eti* (Pāṇini 7.4.52).

[The example is] *kartāhe*. This is the periphrastic future (*luṭ*) of the root *kṛ*, in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), third person singular; with the augment *iṭ* and the substitution of *e* for *te*. Here, the *s* is replaced by *ha* by this rule.
Regarding the form *vyatihe*: the ātmanepada suffix is applied by the rule *kartari karmavyatihāre* (Pāṇini 1.3.14), and as before, there is the elision of the vowel *a*. Regarding the form *heti*:
the inclusion of the long *ā* (*tapara*) is for the purpose of avoiding the substitution of *ay* in the locative case; for if the *ay* substitution were to occur, there would be ambiguity.
It might be asked: "To what does this reference refer—is it to the substitution of *ay*, or to the vowel *e*?"

53. *yīvarṇayordīdhīvevyoḥ* | (Pāṇini 7.4.53) Because of its being marked with a *svarita* accent, "elision" (*lopa*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], but not the immediately preceding *hakāra*, because it is not marked with a *svarita* accent nor so declared. In the case of *yakāra*, however, the *ikāra* is for the sake of pronunciation. And *yi*...

When the vowels *i* and *u* follow those two [roots], namely *dīdhīṅ* in the sense of "shining" and "playing" (DhP 1076) and *vevīṅ* in the sense of "going" and "similarly" (DhP 1077), their [final] elision occurs; and that [elision] is governed by the rule *alo 'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52).

Thus [the rule applies] to the final [element]. When the hearing of a *yakāra* at the beginning would otherwise occur, this is a statement of elision (*lopa*) which supersedes the substitution of *yaṇ* prescribed by "ṭheranekācaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.82) when an *ivarṇa* etc. follows. Examples:

*ādīdhya*, *āvevya*—[here the suffix] *lyap* [is applied]. Examples: *ādīdhyata*, *āvevita*—[here the suffix] *kta* is applied in the sense of state (*bhāva*) or object (*karman*), according to "bhāvakarmaṇoḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.13).

Thus, the *ātmanepada* [suffixes] apply; by the rule "sārvadhātuke yak" (Pāṇini 3.1.67), [the suffix] *yak* is added. [Examples: *ādīdhita*, *āvevita*. By the rule "bhāvakarmaṇoḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.13), the *ātmanepada* [suffixes] apply; by the rule "sārvadhātuke yak" (Pāṇini 3.1.67), *yak* is added. [Examples: *ādīdhita*, *āvevita*. [The suffix] *tṛc* [is applied].

Regarding the form *dhyānam* from the root *dhyai*: the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied, and because of the prohibition of *guṇa* by the rule *daudhīvevīṭām* (Pāṇini 1.1.6), the substitution *yaṇ* takes place. Although there is equality between the two causes and the two subjects of the operation here, nevertheless, the correspondence of elements (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) does not apply, because it is not based on accent (*asvaritatvāt*).

The mention of "vowel" (*varṇa*) is so that [the rule] may apply when a vowel is being heard; let it not apply here—namely, in *ādīdhayateḥ* and *āvevayateḥ*, where *ṇvul* follows the causative (*ṇijanta*) forms *ādīdhya-* and *āvevya-*, resulting in *ādīdhyakaḥ* and *āvevyakaḥ*. For in these cases, since the *ṇi*-elision is obligatory, the rule regarding the elision of an affix (*pratyayalopalakṣaṇa*, Pāṇini 1.1.62) would otherwise apply; therefore...
It does not occur because of the mention of "vowel" (varṇa).

54. *sa-ni-mī-mā-ghu-ra-bha-la-bha-śaka-pata-padā-maca iḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.54). From the rule *saḥ syārdhadhātuke* (7.4.49), the term *si* is carried over (*anuvartate*), and it serves as a qualifier for *sa*. [The word] *mī* [in the sūtra] refers to the roots *mīnāti* and *minoti*; [the root] *mīñ* is used in the sense of "injuring" (*hiṃsā*).
[This refers to] the two roots *dhā* (DhP 1476) and *ḍu miñ* "to scatter" (DhP 1250). Now, one might object:
when the form *mī* is being pronounced, how can there be a reference to the root *miñ*? This is not so;
for even in this case, once the lengthening prescribed by *ajjhanagamāṃ sani* (Pāṇini 6.4.16) has been applied, the form becomes precisely *mī*.

[The objection: "Even so, according to the maxim *lakṣaṇapratipadoktayoḥ pratipadoktasyaiva grahaṇam* (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 3), its inclusion [in the rule] would not be justified. This is not so; for here, by not placing the word *ghu* first—despite its being designated as *ghu*—it is indicated that the rule of prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) does not apply in this case.

Just as [the rule] is not required, so too is any other scriptural statement; therefore, it is logical that this technical rule (paribhāṣā) is not required, and thus there is also the inclusion of the root *minoti*. For it is said: "In the case of the mention of *mā* and *gā*, there is no distinction. This refers to the three roots previously mentioned, beginning with *meṅ*.
Regarding the mention [of the term]: by the designation *ghu*, the two roots *dā* and *dhā* are understood. [The following roots are included:

*rabha* in the sense of "impetuosity" (DhP 974), *ḍulabhaṣ* in the sense of "attainment" (DhP 975), *śaklṛ* in the sense of "ability" (DhP 1261), and *śala*, *hula*, *patlṛ* in the sense of "motion" (DhP 843, 844, 845).
Regarding the root *ṭhā* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*, Dhātupāṭha 1169): when a suffix beginning with *s* follows, *sanīṣ* replaces the vowel (*ac*) of these roots.
The inclusion of the term *ac* is for the purpose that the substitution should not apply to the entire [stem]. For if it were not so...
In that case, because it consists of more than one *al* (phoneme), it would be a substitute for the whole [stem]. Thus, "pramitsani.

Here, by the rule "atra lopo'bhyāsasya" (Pāṇini 7.4.58), there is the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*); and by the rule "saḥ syārdhadhātuke" (Pāṇini 7.4.49), its *s* becomes *s*. [Then we have] "apamitsate. By the rule "pūrvavatsanaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.62), [the desiderative stem is treated like the root].

Thus ends the section on the Ātmanepada. The same applies to *āripsate* and *alipsate*. By the rule *khari ca* (8.4.55), there is *cariṭva*—the substitution of *pa* for *bha*; then, by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca* (8.2.29), there is the elision of *s*.
55. *āpjñapyṛdhāmīt* (Pāṇini 7.4.55). Regarding the form *īpsati*: from the root *āplṛ* in the sense of "pervasion" (Dhātupāṭha 1260). Regarding the form *jñīpsati*:
from the root *jñā* in the sense of "cognition" (Dhātupāṭha 1507); with the addition of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the augment *puk* is applied by rule 7.3.36 (*artihrī...* etc.).
In the case of *mārayati*, from the root *mṛ* (DhP 811) meaning "to kill," "to heat," or "to calm," the designation *mit* is applied by the rule *micca*;
consequently, the vowel is shortened, and the suffix *ṇi* is elided by the rule *ṇer aniṭi* (6.4.51). Regarding the form *īrtsati*:

from the root *ṛdh* (DhP 1271) meaning "to grow," the vowel *ī* is substituted, followed by the replacement of *r* (*raparatva*), and the substitution of *k* for the letter *r* by the rule *khari ca* (8.4.55).
Thus, the letter *t* [in the term] *cartvam* [is used];

and here, the indicator (*jñāpaka*) must be qualified by the vowel *aj*, but the indicator is not qualified by the vowel *ac*, because there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*). For the state of being a suffix ending in a *jña*-type element does not deviate [from being a vowel], whereas in the case of *aci*, it does.

If [the rule] were qualified by the member *jñapi*, then every vowel (*ac*) related to *jñapi* would have to become *ī*; and thus, when the substitution of *ī* for the *ṇi* of *ṇic* is applied, the form *jñīpsati* would not be established. Anticipating this objection, he says: "In the case of *jñapi*, there is doubling," and so forth.
In this regard, the scope for the substitution of *aj* and so forth is [in forms like] *kāraṇā*, *hāraṇā*; the scope for the elision (*lopa*) of the *ṇi* suffix is [in forms like] *kāraṇā*, *hāraṇā*.

When both would apply to the second vowel, the elision of the *ṇi* suffix alone takes place by means of a prior conflict (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), as in *jñīpsati*. The phrase "of the other" refers to the vowel *a*.

In the case of *ṭhardidhiṣati*, there is the guṇa substitution for the light penultimate vowel, followed by the replacement of the vowel with *r* (*raparatva*). According to the rule *ajāder dvitīyasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.2), the portion *dhi* is reduplicated. However, the *repha* (the letter *r*) is not reduplicated, due to the prohibition stated in *na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.3). [This applies] to the reduplication of the *abhyāsa* (the reduplicated stem).
The substitution of *jaś* is the letter *ja*; the letter *ta* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation.
