56. *dambha* and *icca*. (Pāṇini 7.4.56) [The rule concerning] *coddyatd*... 56. *dambha* and *icca*. (Pāṇini 7.4.56)

Regarding the forms *dhīpsati* and *dhīpsati*: from the root *dambhu* (meaning "to deceive," Dhātupāṭha 1270), when the suffix *iṭ* is not applied by [the rule] *sanīvantardha-* (Pāṇini 7.2.49) and so forth, there is the substitution of *i* for the *s* of the suffix *san*, and the substitution of *ī*. Then, because the suffix is *kit* by [the rule] *halantācca* (1.2.10), there is the elision of the nasal (*n*), and [subsequently, the elision] of the letter *bh*.
The letter *k* is substituted for *c*.
57. For the root *muc* when it is intransitive, there is optionally a *guṇa* [substitution].

(Pāṇini 7.4.57) As in *mokṣate*. The root is *muc-lū* "to release" (Dhātupāṭha 1430). By the rule *coḥ kuḥ* (8.2.30), there is the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *k*); by the rule *iṇkoḥ* (8.3.57), there is the substitution of *ṣ*; and [the rule] *karmavat karmaṇā* [applies].

By the rule beginning with (3.1.87), the ātmanepada suffix is applied due to the extension of the properties of an object (*karmavad-atideśa*). The expression "by itself" (*svayameva*) is intended to demonstrate that [the calf] functions as both object and agent (*karmakartṛ*). When one desires to release the calf, and that calf—which is being desired to be released—attains a state of favorability toward the act of releasing, then...
Because it is intended to be expressed as the agent (*kartṛ*) in this action due to its independence, the root *muc* takes the suffix *ṇamul*.
Now, for what purpose is the mention of "guṇa" (quality)? Could it not simply be stated as "na-ut"? For indeed, this [would suffice].
[Objection: In the case of *satyokāraḥ*, the rule "of the final [element] of a *ṭh*-class [suffix]" (P. 1.1.52) would apply in place of the letter *k*;

however, because of the mention of "guṇa," only the initial [element] occurs, due to the restriction in the formulation of technical designations (*saṃjñā*). [Reply: This is not so; the term *acaḥ* ("of a vowel") is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].
Therefore, it will not apply to the final [element]. If that is so, then this [mention of *guṇa*] indicates that [the term *guṇa* applies only to the vowels] *a*, *e*, and *o*.

It is excluded [from the scope of the rule]. Therefore, in the rule *atra lopo 'bhyāsasya* (Pāṇini 7.4.58), the elision of the long vowel *ā* of the reduplication does not occur. However, if the governing heading (*adhikāra*) for the letter *a* were present, its continued application (*anuvṛtti*) would be purposeless; thus, only the elision of the short vowel *a* would take place.
58. *atra lopo'bhyāsasya* (Pāṇini 7.4.58). To demonstrate what is indicated by the word *atra* ("here"), he says: "That which is this," and so forth.
Now, for what purpose is the mention of *atra*? [It is] so that [the rule applies] within this specific section, such as *sani mīmā* (7.4.54), and the like.

If you argue that [the rule] should exist so that [the substitution does not apply] in forms such as *dadau* and *dadatuḥ*, we say no; for if this were the intended purpose, the sūtra would have been stated as: "In the case of the suffix *san*, [the substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of] *mī*, *mā*, *dhū*, *rabh*, *labh*, *śak*, *pat*, and *pad* occurs, and there is elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). This would have been taught right here in this very section.
It is not otherwise; therefore, the inclusion [of these roots] would be purposeless. To this he says:

"In the case of *san*, *mīmā*, *dhū*, *rabh*, *labh*, etc. [He says] "for the purpose of restricting the scope," meaning for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding the scope of the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*). That very [restriction] of it...
He says "atraiva" and so forth in order to demonstrate that [the rule] has the purpose of restricting the scope of the object.

By the word "atra" (here), the object beginning with "is" is indicated. It is by means of this restriction that everything else is excluded, so that the elision of the suffix *abhyāsa* may occur only when the object is precisely one beginning with "is."
To demonstrate this, he says: "It does not occur in the domain of *sanvadbhāva*. [The example is] *amīmapat*.

[The root] *bhīñ* is used in the sense of "to injure" (*hiṃsāyām*) [DhP 1476]. By the rule *mīnātiminotidīṅaṃ lyapi ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.50), there is the substitution of *ā* for the vowel; then the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the augment *puk* as before, and the suffix *luṅ*.
The suffix *caṅ* is applied; there is elision of the *ṇi*; the penultimate vowel is shortened; reduplication occurs; the augment *aṭ* is added;
by the rule "sanvallaghuni caṅpare" (Pāṇini 7.4.93), the state of being like the *saN* suffix (*sanvadbhāva*) is established;
by the rule "sanyataḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.79), the vowel *i* is substituted; by the rule "dīrgho laghoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.94), the short vowel is lengthened. Thus: *adīdapat*.

Thus: from the root *ḍudāñ* "to give" (DhP 1091), with the addition of *ṇic* and so forth as before. Because of the inclusion of the word *atra* ("here") in the rule, the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) does not occur here.
But how is it that the elision of the reduplicated syllable, which is prescribed for the *san* suffix, applies here?

For what purpose is the mention of "atra" (herein) made for the sake of exclusion? To this he says: "sanvallaghuni," etc. For just as the designation of *sanvadbhāva* (the status of being like *san*) occurs, so too would there be elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*).

In this case, by the rule "of the final letter" (*alo'ntyasya*, 1.1.52), combined with the general maxim regarding the final letter (*alontyaparibhāṣā*), the elision ought to apply to the final letter [of the root].
Someone might have a misconception; therefore, in order to dispel it, he says "of everyone," and so forth.
But how is [the result] obtained by everyone? To this he says "for that very purpose," and so forth.
By this use of the particle *eva*, he excludes the sense of restricting the scope [to a specific subject]. If this is so, [then...]
Does this [rule] also apply in the domain of *sanvadbhāva* (the treatment as if having the suffix *san*)? It is thought thus:
even in the domain of *sanvadbhāva*, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) can be avoided.
In that context, by the term *sanvat*, an operation dependent on the suffix *san* is extended (*atidiśyate*). And the elision of the reduplicated syllable is not among those operations.
It depends only on *san*; what else? It depends on the state of being a root (*dhātu*) and so forth as well.

Because of the absence of that [root-status], even though there is no [explicit] mention of *atra* (in this case), the elision of the reduplication will not occur in forms such as *amīmapat*. Therefore, the mention of *atra* is indeed redundant and should not be made at all. That is [the view].
It is done so that there may be the elision of the entire [term].
But how, even when the mention of *atra* (here) is made, is the elision of the whole obtained?
Some say: "From an increase in the text comes an increase in the meaning. By the mention of *atra*, the rule becomes a great one.
By this, it is indicated: "This elision must be performed of a large [number of] substituends.
And thus, others maintain that this becomes an elision of a large substituend only if the elision of the entire [repeated portion] is carried out, and not otherwise.
"Others say that when there is a multiplicity of meanings, the rule regarding the final letter applies. Who, then, are these "others"?
They are to be understood as those who explain the inclusion of the term *at* (the final letter) as being for the purpose of determining the scope [of the rule].
The lack of meaning (*anarthakatva*) of the reduplication is to be understood in the view where the doubling occurs in place [of the whole stem]; for in this case, of that which...
In the case where another word is prescribed in place [of the original], that entire [substitute] is meaningful;
however, the repetition of a single part is indeed meaningless.
Even under the view that reduplication consists in the double employment [of the same word], the repetition is meaningless because it does not express a different meaning.

59. *hvasvaḥ* | (Pāṇini 7.4.59) [The examples] *ṭhḍuḍhāṬkiṣate* and *tutraukiṣate* are given. From the roots *ḍhāṬkṛ* and *traukṛ*, which are both marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudāteta*) and are therefore *ātmanepada* verbs, the desiderative suffix *san* is applied.

The *ātmanepada* ending is applied by the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* (1.3.62). [Examples are] *aḍuḍhāṭkata*, *atutraukata*. From these same two roots with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the *luṅ* tense is formed; the operations beginning with *caṅ* are as before.
[Examples are] *aḍuḍhāṭke*, *atutrauke*. This is the singular of the *liṭ* tense, with the replacement *eś* for that [suffix].

Regarding the rule *abhyāsasyānaci* and so forth: the meaning is that this must be explained as having the sense that whatever operation is prescribed for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) occurs when it is followed by a vowel other than *a* (*anaci*). In this regard, the following is the explanation:
*vā caricalipatidadonāmacyākyābhyāsasya* (Vārttika 658).

Thus, by the force of the scriptural injunction, the *halādiśeṣa* (the retention of the initial consonant) should not occur. For if *halādiśeṣa* were to apply, there would be no distinction between a substitute (*ādeśa*) and an augment (*āgama*), and [the rule] would have prescribed the substitute alone. And this being the case—since there is no elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*)—by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it must occur elsewhere than in a vowel.
It will come to pass.

60. *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.60). Regarding the term *halādiḥ*: it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both a consonant (*hal*) and the first (*ādi*)," namely *halādiḥ*; it is not a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound meaning "the first among consonants" (*halām ādiḥ*). If it were a genitive compound, [the following objection would apply].

In that case, the meaning would be this: "Of those consonants which belong to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), the first one remains. And thus, in forms such as *ānakṣatuḥ* and *ānakṣuḥ*, since the root *akṣū* (meaning "to pervade," DhP 654) begins with a vowel (*aj-ādi*), there is no second single-consonant (*ekāc*) [in the reduplication]; therefore, [by the rule under discussion], the first single-consonant [remains].

Even though, once reduplication has been performed, the initial of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is not the letter *k*, it nevertheless begins with a consonant (*hal*); thus, the rule for its retention (*śeṣa*) would apply. However, there is no fault in the case of a *karmadhāraya* compound, because in that context the status of beginning with a consonant is prescribed in relation to the reduplicated syllable, and here the letter *k* is not the initial of the reduplicated syllable.

Therefore, this is a *karmadhāraya* compound: *jaglau*, *mamlau*. [The roots] *glai* "to fade" (DhP 903) and *mlai* "to bend the limbs" (DhP 904) undergo *ātvam* (substitution of *ā*) by Pāṇini 6.1.45 (*ādeca upadeśe'śiti*), and *autvam* (substitution of *au*) by Pāṇini 7.1.34 (*āta au ṇalaḥ*). [The forms] *āṭatuḥ*...

Regarding the form *āṭutaḥ*: when the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable is applied by the rule *ata ādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.70), the long vowel resulting from the homogeneity of similar sounds (*savarṇadīrghatvam*) is produced.
Now, one might object: "The term *śeṣaḥ* (remainder) refers to that which remains; and since that is already established for *ani*, for what purpose is it prescribed here?"

Thus he says: "This [elision] is caused by the remainder of the initial," and so forth. That elision for which the remainder of the initial is the cause is described in that way. For here, the remainder of the initial is not being prescribed; rather, this elision of what is not the initial is being prescribed, since the persistence of the initial is already established.

The rule "halādiśeṣaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.60), being prescribed here, is understood as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*): namely, that only the initial consonant (*ādi-hal*) remains, while the non-initial does not. In this way, the non-appearance of the non-initial is established as the cause for the retention of the initial. If...

In that case, this elision (*lopa*) of the initial [portion] is prescribed as being caused by the remainder (*śeṣa*); if this were so, then in forms such as *ādutuḥ* and *āduruḥ*, the elision would not occur because of the absence of the cause. For, since the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) consists only of a consonant (*hal*), it has no initial portion at all—how much less could there be a "remainder" of it? To this, he says: "In that case... (*tatra*).

And so forth. When the elision of the augment *an* (anādi-lopa) is to be applied, the class (*jāti*) of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is resorted to, not the individual instance (*vyakti*) of the reduplication. Therefore, although the initial consonant (*hal-ādi*) does not occur in every single instance of reduplication, nevertheless, because it occurs in some instances such as *papāca*, the initial consonant serves everywhere as the basis for the elision of the augment *aṭ*.
In cases such as *āṭatuḥ* and *āṭuḥ*, [the rule] also effects the elision [of the augment]; for the class (*jāti*) of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is non-different.
Indeed, the very same class of reduplicated syllable that occurs in *papāca* and so forth is present in *āṭatuḥ*, *āṭuḥ*, and so forth as well.
Regarding the phrase "others, however" (*apare tu*), etc.: in *āṭatuḥ*, *āṭuḥ*, and so forth, there is the elision of [the augment] other than the first (*anādeḥ*).
Others say this in order to provide a formal justification: this word "remainder" (śeṣa) does not denote mere non-existence;

what then? It denotes a state of existence qualified by cessation. If this is so, then because the state of existence is the substantive (viśeṣya), it possesses predominance, whereas cessation, being the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa), lacks predominance.

And likewise: because they follow that which is predominant, the *guṇas* (subsidiary elements) are non-predominant. Wherever there is the occurrence of an abhyāsa (reduplication) beginning with a consonant (*hal*), as in *papāca* and so forth, there the consonant following *id* and so on must be elided; consequently, that same fault remains in cases such as *āṭatuḥ* and *āṭuḥ*, where there is a consonant not preceded by *a*.
[If it is asked], "Why does cessation not occur?"—to this he says: "Its state," and so forth.

Although that state, being the object to be qualified (*viśeṣya*), is designated by the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) and is thus primary (*pradhāna*) according to that statement, nevertheless, because it is not something to be enjoined (*avidheya*), it is non-primary. Its non-primacy, however, is due to its being already established (*siddhatvāt*).

Even though cessation (*nivṛtti*) functions as a qualifier, it is the primary element because it is that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*). Thus it has been said: "That which is already established, which assists, and which exists for the sake of another is a subordinate member (*aṅga*);
whereas that which is to be accomplished, which does not [itself] assist [another], is the principal (*aṅgin*), and is therefore the primary element. In that regard, concerning cessation:
Because it is that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), this meaning of the present sūtra arises with respect to that which has become the primary element (*pradhāna*):

"There is the cessation (*nivṛtti*) of the initial consonant (*hal*) of the reduplicated form (*abhyāsa*). Consequently, having attained primacy by virtue of being the object of the injunction, it [the consonant] becomes the principal factor.
Why is non-cessation—being something not to be enjoined and thus subordinate—expected [of the agent]?

For what reason would it be expected? The meaning is: for no reason at all; for it is not logical that the principal should be dependent upon its accessories. Therefore, even though [non-cessation] does not exist...
The sense is that when *hal* and so forth remain, there must be elision (*lopa*) of *av* and so forth.

61. *śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.61). Since the previous rule had established that *śar* [consonants] remain when *sa* follows, this rule is now commenced to establish that *kha* [consonants] remain. Furthermore, this non-initial retention (*anādiśeṣa*) supersedes the initial retention (*ādiśeṣa*), for if *śar* were to remain, there would be no occasion for *kha*.

The word "remainder" (śeṣa) functions as a qualifier; for it has been stated that it denotes a state of existence distinguished by cessation. And when both [the original and the substitute] remain present, there can be no state of existence distinguished by the cessation [of one]. Therefore, this "non-remainder" (anādiśeṣa) is an exception (apavāda) to the aforementioned "remainder" (ādiśeṣa).

Regarding *tiṣṭhāścotiṣati*: the root *ścut* (meaning "to flow" or "to ooze," Dhātupāṭha 41) takes the suffix *san*, followed by *iṭ*. Regarding *tiṣṭhāsati*: the root *sthā* (meaning "cessation of motion," Dhātupāṭha 928). Regarding *pispandiṣate*: the root *spadi* (meaning "slight movement," Dhātupāṭha 14);
it is anudātta, and because it is marked with *idit*, the augment *num* is applied.

The *ātmanepada* ending is applied by the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* (1.4.62). Regarding the form *sasnau*: the root is *ṣṇā* in the sense of "cleansing" (*dhā.pā.* 1052); as before, there is the substitution of *au* for the *ṇal* suffix. Regarding the phrase "preceded by a *khari*" and so forth: regarding the form *ucchichivati*, the root is *ucchī* in the sense of "shaking off" (*dhā.pā.* 216).

When *san* remains as *ucchiṣ*, reduplication and the *tuk*-augment both become applicable. Therein, because it depends on a phoneme (*varṇa*), the *tuk* is internal (*antaraṅga*). Once that has been applied, reduplication and the change to *c* (*cutva*) become applicable; however, since reduplication is subsequent (*para*), it should be performed first.

Because the substitution [of *cch*] is not established, reduplication applies to the word *cchi*. In that case, the elision (*śeṣa*) of the letter *c* does not apply to the *cch* sound; for it is not preceded by a sibilant (*śar*). Indeed, this *t* is not a sibilant, and therefore, when the "elision of the remaining consonant" (*halādi-śeṣa*) has been performed by the preceding rule, the letter *t* is heard in *abhāse*.
Furthermore, there is this [rule]: "This [substitution] is asiddha with respect to what precedes it, except for reduplication" (*pūrvatrāsiddhoyamadvirvacane*, Jai.

Pa. Vṛ. 70). Thus, the substitution of *c* is performed first, and the reduplication is performed afterwards; nevertheless, when the letter *ch* is eliminated by the rule of *halādiśeṣa*, the substitution of *c* is also eliminated according to the principle: "When the cause ceases, that which was dependent upon it also ceases" (*nimitāpāye naimitikasyāpyapāyaḥ*, Vyā. Pa. 47).

In the case of *ucicchiṣati*, only the letter *t* would be heard in the reduplication. Therefore, it must be stated that "the *khay* letters [are elided] when preceded by *khara*. For this being so, once the remaining *cch* has been applied, the *t* is removed, and thus the undesirable consequence does not arise.

62. *kuhoścuḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.62). Regarding the form *ṭhcakhāna*: the root *khanu* (Dhātupāṭha 878) means "to dig. There is reduplication, and for that [the original *kh*], there is *cutva*—that is, it becomes *ch*. Then, by the rule *abhyāse car ca* (8.4.54), the *ch* is changed to *c*. Thus, *cakhāna*.

Regarding "jaghāti": by the rule *liṭaḷnyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 2.4.40), there is the substitution of *ghas* for the root-initial *ad*, and the change of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) to a *c*-sound. In place of the voiced aspirated (*nādavat*) and unaspirated (*mahāprāṇa*) [dental], there is the corresponding voiced aspirated [palatal] *jh*; then, by the rule of *jaśtva*, that also becomes the voiced unaspirated *j*. Regarding "jahāra": from the root *hṛñ* in the sense of "taking away."
Regarding the form *jihīrṣati*: the suffix *san* is treated as *kit* by *iko jhal* (Pāṇini 1.2.9);

lengthening occurs by *ajjhanagamāṃ sani* (6.4.16); the substitution of *i* for the root vowel *ṛ* occurs by *ṛta iddhātoḥ* (7.1.100); *ra* is substituted for the semivowel by *uraṇ raparaḥ*; and lengthening occurs by *hali ca* (8.2.77).
There is reduplication of this [root] *hṛṣ*.
63. *na kavater yaṅ* (Pāṇini 7.4.63). This is a prohibition of the change to *c* (*cutva*) which was previously applicable by the preceding rule. [The example is] *kokūyate*.
[In this form, there is] lengthening by *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* (7.4.25), and *guṇa* substitution by *guṇo yaṅlukoḥ* (7.4.82).
(7.4.82) Thus, there is *guṇa* substitution for the reduplication.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of the *vikaraṇa* [suffix] *śnu*? Why not simply say "of *ku*" (*koḥ*)? To this he says: "of *kavati*, etc. [The root] *kuṅ* "to sound" (DhP 1401) belongs to the Taudādika class.
The root *ṭhku* in the sense of "sound" belongs to the first class (*adādika*), while *ṭhkuṅ* belongs to the fourth class (*divādika*); both have "sound" as their meaning.

In this context, the mention of the specific verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) is for the purpose that the root belonging to the first class (*bhauvādika*) be understood, and not the other two. Now, [one might object]:...

And this is the purpose of their exclusion—so that the form *cokūyata* may also be possible. Furthermore, even with the rule *koḥ*, since the anubandha-less [root] alone would be understood by virtue of the paribhāṣā regarding anubandha-less forms, this result is indeed established; therefore, [the rule is stated as] *koḥ*.

Should the explanation be made in this way? It is not so; for even though they share the same verbal root, their expressed meanings are indeed distinct. To illustrate: the root *kavati* denotes an indistinct sound—as in "the camel cries out" (*uṣṭraḥ kokūyate*);
whereas the root *ku-vati* denotes a cry of distress—as in "the low-born man wails" (*cokūyate bṛṣalaḥ*).

The meaning is "afflicted" (poḍita). However, the root *kauti* [is used] in the sense of mere sound. Therefore, the mention of the *vikaraṇa* (conjugational suffix) must be made so that the specific intended meaning may be grasped. But surely, by the rule regarding the elision of *vikaraṇas*, [the suffix] will not apply to *kauti*; so for what purpose [is this mentioned]?
Is the purpose of the suffixal augment (*vikaraṇa*) the cessation of that [suffix]? He thinks as follows: the mention of the suffix must necessarily be made for the sake of the cessation of *ku-*.
When it is employed for another purpose, it also serves the purpose of the cessation of *kauti*. Therefore...

Regarding the *lugvikaraṇa-paribhāṣā* (P. 1.1.61), it need not be resorted to here for the purpose of excluding *kauti*, as in the form *cukuve*. As before, the substitution of *ai* for *ta* occurs by P. 6.4.77 (*aci śnudhātubhruvām yvoḥ*), since the suffix begins with a vowel.
Thus, [the suffix] uvaṅ [is applied], and so forth.

64. *kṛṣeś chandasi* (Pāṇini 7.4.64). [The example is] *ṭhkarīkṛṣyate*. [This is derived from] the root *kṛṣ* "to scratch" (Dhātupāṭha 990); the augment *rīg* is applied by [the rule] *rīgṛdupadhasya* (7.4.90).

*dādharti*, *dardharti*, *dardharṣi*, *bobhūtu*, *tetikte*, *alaṣya*, *apanīphaṇat*, *saṃsaniṣyadat*, *karikrat*, *kanikradat*, *bharibhrat*, *davidhvatat*, *davidyutat*, *taritrataḥ*, *sarīsṛpatam*, *varīvṛjan*, *marmṛjyā*, *ganīgantī*—and [the word] *iti*. (Pāṇini 7.4.65) The particle *ca* (‘and’) is for the purpose of drawing forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) the rule *chandasi* (‘in Vedic usage’). Regarding *dhārayateḥ*: the root is *dhṛñ* in the sense of ‘holding’ (*dhāraṇe*).

The forms of the roots *dhṛṅ* "to stand firm" (DhP 1412), *dhṛṅ* "to support" (DhP 900), and *dhṛṅ* "to fall apart" (DhP 960)—all of which take the causative suffix (*ṇic*)—are included by the rule "or after *dhṛṅ*" (*dhṛṅe vā*). This refers to the two immediately preceding roots that do not take the causative suffix (*aṇic*). Furthermore, there is the option "in the case of *ślu*, or when there is elision of *yaṅ*" (*ślau yaṅluki vā*). Regarding these, first:

Regarding the form *dādharti*: when it is derived from the root *dhṛ* with the *ślu* affix, then the elision of the *ṇi* suffix and the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable are prescribed by way of irregularity (*nipātana*). However, when it occurs in the *yaṅluk* formation, since the root consists of more than one syllable (*anekāc*), the *yaṅ* affix would not apply; that too is prescribed by way of irregularity.

There is also the shortening of the vowel due to the *upadhā* [penultimate]. The elision of the *ṇi*-affix is established by the very fact that [the suffix] belongs to the *ārdhadhātuka* class, according to the rule "yaṅo ṇer aniṭi" (Pāṇini 6.4.51). The lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is also established by the rule "dīrgho 'kitaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.83). Regarding the forms "dardharti" and "dardharṣi," here too, when [the root] is derived from *dhārayati*...

In the case of *ślau*, the augment *ruk* is added to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) and there is the elision of the *ṇi*-affix. As for the elision of *ślu*, it should be understood as occurring everywhere by the rule itself, "The elision of *ślu* occurs diversely in the Vedic language" (Pāṇini 2.4.76). However, when there is the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*), then, although lengthening would have been required by the rule "Lengthening occurs for a non-*kit* suffix" (Pāṇini 7.4.83), its absence is also established.

It is treated as an irregularity (*nipātyate*). When *dhṛṅ* is used in the *ślu* formation—as in *dādharti*—then, once reduplication has occurred, the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable is treated as an irregularity. However, when that same root *dhṛṅ* occurs with the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*), there is an absence of the *rug* and other augmentations that would otherwise be required by Pāṇini 7.4.92 (*ṛtaśca*).

It is irregularly formed as *dardharti* and *dargharṣi*. Here too, when there is reduplication (*ślau*), the augment *ruk* is irregularly prescribed for the reduplicated syllable; however, when there is the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*), the absence of the lengthening that would otherwise apply is irregularly prescribed, and not the augment *ruk*. This is because [the latter]...
For [the form] is established by the rule *hi ṭhrugrikau ca luki* (7.4.91),
and the Parasmaipada [ending] is accounted for by *vyatyayo bahulam* (3.1.85). As for "bobhūtu," it is used "elsewhere."
The distinctness [of the form] should be understood as being in relation to the third person singular of the imperative (*loṭ*). Regarding the form *bobhavīti*:

because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision of the *śap* suffix; this occurs by virtue of the word "generally" (*bahulam*) in the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 2.4.73). Furthermore, the augment *īṭ* is optionally applied by the rule *yaṅe vā* (Pāṇini 7.3.94).
Regarding the forms *tiṣṭhite* and *titeṣate*: [the rule] "from *tij*" refers to the root *tij* "to sharpen" (DhP 971).
Now, one might ask: since the suffix *yaṅ* has the marker *ṅ*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is already established by the rule "that which is characterized by a suffix" (1.1.62);
for what purpose, then, is this form prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*)? To this, he says: "because of the *ṅ*-marker of *yaṅ*," and so forth.

The middle voice (ātmanepada) is established for the purpose of indication. This shows that the middle voice is prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation) for the sake of indication. As for the purpose of this indication: the intention is that elsewhere, the middle voice does not occur after a form with the elision of the yaṅ suffix—such as in the case of *bobhavīti*.

Regarding the word *ṭhalarṣi*: from the root *ṛ* (or *sṛ*) meaning "to go" (*dhā.pā.* 1098, 1099), which belongs to the *jauhotyādi* class, when the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* is applied by *urat* (Pāṇini 7.4.66) and the subsequent substitution of *ra* for *u*, the rule *halādiśeṣaḥ* would apply; however, as exceptions to that, the substitution of *la* for the *repha* is prescribed by *nipātana*. Why?
Why is this explanation given—that the mention of the specific cause is not a restrictive rule?
To this he says: "Even in the case of *tibi*," and so forth.
Regarding "of *phaṇ*"—this refers to the root *phaṇa* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*, Dhātupāṭha 821). Regarding "of *syand*"—[this refers to the root *syand*].
This refers to the root *syandū* "to flow" (Dhātupāṭha 761). Why, then, is it explained that the prefix *sam-* is not a restrictive factor here? To this he says: "For even here," and so forth.
Regarding the form *karikrat*: [it is derived from] the root *ḍukṛñ* "to do/make" (Dhātupāṭha 1472); [the form arises] through the substitution of *yaṇ*.

Since the form *kṛta* ends in the vowel *ṛ*, the augment *ri* for the reduplicated syllable prescribed by the rule *ṛtaśca* (Pāṇini 7.4.92) would not apply; therefore, it is introduced as an irregularity (*nipātana*). [The rule] says "from *krand*"—that is, *kadi*, *kradi*, and *kladi* in the senses of calling out and weeping.

[This refers to] the roots *dhā*, *pā*, and *sthā* (DhP 772, 773, 774). But how is it known that this is a nipātana (irregular formation) in the *luṅ* tense? To this he says: "For of this," and so forth.
Since the meaning of the root *krand* is indicated by means of the *luṅ* suffix, it is therefore known that this is a nipātana in the *luṅ* tense. In this regard:
And for the root *abhi* (*cābhyāsasya*), the augment *rīk* is indeed prescribed as a nipātana.
Regarding "of *bibharti*": this refers to the root *ḍubhṛñ* in the sense of "supporting and nourishing" (DhP 1087). Regarding "of *dhvarate*":
this refers to the root *dhvṛ* in the sense of "wandering astray" (DhP 939).
Regarding "of *dyauti*": this refers to the root *dyauta* (meaning "to shine," DhP 7.4.1). Regarding "the absence of *samprasāraṇa*":
since *samprasāraṇa* would have applied by the rule "there is *samprasāraṇa* for *dyauti* and *svāpi*" (Pāṇini 6.1.15), its absence is here prescribed as a *nipātana* (irregularity).

Regarding "ṭhtarateḥ": this refers to the root *tṛ* in the sense of "floating and crossing" (DhP 969). Regarding "sṛpeḥ": this refers to the root *sṛp* in the sense of "going" (DhP 982, 983). Regarding "vṛjeḥ": this refers to the root *vṛj* in the sense of "avoiding" (DhP 1812).
Regarding "marmṛjya": this is the form of the root *mṛj* in the sense of "purification" (*śuddhi*) with the suffix *ṇal*.

Regarding "āganīganti": this also [is formed] with the suffix *saṭ* and the ending *tip*. He says "of such types" and so forth in order to show that the particle *iti* has the sense of "in this manner."

The meaning is that those words for which an ungrammatical (alākṣaṇika) operation is observed in the Vedic language (chandas)—just like *dādharti* and others—are of this kind, similar to *dādharti*. Which ones are they? They are *galagartī* and so forth.
[This occurs] when there is the elision (*luk*) of the intensive suffix (*yaṅ*) after the root *gṛ* (meaning "to swallow") in the *ślau* state, according to Dhātupāṭha 1410.

The form *galagartī* is derived as follows: the substitution of *ca* for the reduplicated syllable is applied, this serves as an exception to the rule of *halādi-śeṣa*, and the substitution of *la* for the *repha* is also prescribed by nipātana.

66. urat (7.4.66). The phrase "in the Veda" (*chandasi*) is no longer applicable here, as it was drawn over from the preceding rule by the mention of the letter *r*. [Examples: *vavṛte*, *vavṛdhe*, *śaśṛdhe*. [Roots: *vṛtu* in the sense of "turning" (DhP 758), *vṛdhu* in the sense of "growing."
From the roots *dhṛ* (DhP 759) and *śṛdhu* meaning "contemptuous sound" (DhP 760), the suffix *liṭ* is applied.
Among these, the first two take the *ātmanepada* because they are *anudāteta*, while the latter takes it because it is *svariteta*.
As before, reduplication (*dvirvacana*) occurs, and then the *halādiśeṣa* rule is applied.

When the state of ending in the vowel *ṛ* has arisen, there is the substitution of *at*, followed by the replacement of *r* (*raparatvam*), and the application of *halādiśeṣaḥ*. In forms such as *narnarti*, *narinarti*, and *narīnarti*, because the exceptions [to the general rule]—
namely *ṛdupadhasya ca* (Pāṇini 7.4.90) and *rugrikau ca luki* (Pāṇini 7.4.91)— are applied later, they take precedence over the general rules.
Someone might have the misconception that, because there is no vowel *ṛ* at the end of words such as *rīg*, this [rule] should not apply; therefore, in order to dispel that doubt, he says: "na nṛti."

67. *dyuti-svapyoḥ saṃprasāraṇam* (Pāṇini 7.4.67). When the rule for the substitution of the remaining initial consonant (*halādi-śeṣa*) would otherwise apply, this sūtra is commenced as an exception (*apavāda*) to it: the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) of the roots *dyut* and *svap*. [The example is] *vididyute*. The root *dyuta* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha (741) as meaning "to shine."

The suffix is *liṭ*; because it is *anudāteta*, the *ātmanepada* endings are used. In that context, *samprasāraṇa* occurs by this rule, and by "and after *samprasāraṇa*" (Pāṇini 6.1.108), the substitution of the preceding vowel for the two [the *samprasāraṇa* vowel and the following vowel] takes place. Thus, "vyadyautat. This is the *luṅ* [aorist] from a causative (*ṇic*) stem; there is *caṅ* [the aorist marker for the causative], elision of the *ṇi* affix, shortening of the penultimate vowel, and reduplication.
The augment *aṭ* is applied. [Examples are] *vididyotiṣate*, *vididyotiṣate*.

With the suffix *san*, there is optionally *kit*-ness by the rule "after a root ending in a consonant (*ral*) with *y* or *v* as its penultimate letter" (Pāṇini 1.2.26). When *kit*-ness does not occur, there is *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel; and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule "the same as the original [root]" (Pāṇini 1.3.62).

Regarding "susvāpayiṣati": [the root] *ñiṣvap* meaning "to sleep" (DhP 1068) takes the causative suffix (*ṇic*), and from that which ends in *ṇic*, the desiderative suffix (*san*) is applied. Why is an example of the causative form presented here? To this he says: "The root *svapi* is causative..."
"It is grasped"—the intention is that by this [statement], an example of the causative (ṇyanta) form has been shown.

That it refers to the causative is understood precisely from the mention of *svāpeḥ*; for such a mention is not possible for the non-causative (aṇyanta) alone. Furthermore, regarding the reduplication (abhyāsa) of the non-causative, it is by this very rule [that it is governed].

The reduplication is established. For instance, in the case of the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, it is established by the rule itself, "In the *liṭ*, there is reduplication of the root for both classes" (6.1.17).

In the case of the *san* [desiderative] suffix, however, since the *san* is *kit* by the rule beginning with "In the case of *rud*, *vid*, etc. (1.2.8), [the reduplication] is established by the rule concerning *vac* and others (6.1.15).

Only that which has already undergone *samprasāraṇa* would be reduplicated when it becomes *supi*; likewise, even in the case of *yaṅ*, by the rule "the *yaṅ* [is applied] after *svap*, *śvas*, *vyen*, and *veñ*" (6.1.19), it is precisely that which has undergone *samprasāraṇa* which is reduplicated. Therefore, since the *samprasāraṇa* of the root ending in *aṇ* is established by this very treatise, [the desired form is attained].
The form ending in *svāpiṇ* is what is intended. If the form ending in *svāpiṇ* is intended, then from the root *svāpi* with the suffix *ṇvul*, we have *svāpaka*;
then, by applying *kyac* in the sense "he desires a *svāpaka*," we arrive at the form *svāpakīya*.

One might ask: "In *svāpakīyiṣati*—derived from the desiderative (*san*) of *svāpakīyati*—does not the vowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) also apply here? To this he says: "Of that," and so forth. This vowel substitution is intended to occur when there is immediate succession—that is, an absence of intervention—between the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) of that root *svāpi* and the suffix (*pratyaya*). Therefore...

In the case of *sidhvāpakīyiṣati*, [the substitution] does not occur. For the affix that is caused by the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) here is not immediately following *svāpi*, because it is separated by the *ṇvul* and the *kyac*. But how, when there is immediate succession with an affix caused by the reduplication, can there be vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*)?
Is it not obtained, since this distinction is not included in the Sūtra?
It is thought thus: because that cognition which is brought about by practice has practice as its specific cause; therefore, by means of that cognition caused by practice—
The term *svāpi* is specified as the *aṅga*: that which is the *aṅga* when there is an affix caused by repetition (*abhyāsa*).

And thus, in this relationship of qualifier and qualified, when an affix caused by repetition follows immediately, it is precisely the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) of that *aṅga* belonging to *svāpi* which undergoes *samprasāraṇa*.

It must be so; however, it is not with respect to an intervening suffix that [the rule applies], for a suffix that is separated by another suffix which is itself caused by repetition (abhyāsa) becomes the *aṅga* (base) in relation to that [intervening suffix];
and it is not the case that [a suffix] is separated by another suffix intervened by *s* or *dhv*.

The repetition (*abhyāsa*) is conditioned by that [root]; with respect to it, the element of *svāpi* becomes the *aṅga*. And the suffix which is conditioned by the repetition—that is, the suffix *san*—is immediately after the *aṅga* of *svāpi*; however, as for the *ṇvul* suffix which is immediately after *svāpi*, with respect to that [suffix], [the *aṅga* is not immediately preceding].
The word *svāpi* is a member of a compound (*aṅga*), and it does not have repetition (*abhyāsa*) as its cause. Why, then, does [the substitution] not occur here:

*svapanaṃ* (sleeping), *svāpaḥ* (sleep) [with the suffix *ghañ*], *svāpaṃ karoti* (he causes sleep) [with the suffix *ṇic*], *svāpayitum icchati* (he desires to cause sleep) [with the suffix *san*], resulting in *siṣvāpayiṣati*? It is said: because of the elision of the vowel *a*.

By virtue of the status of being a substitute (sthānivadbhāva), the reduplication belonging to the root *svāp* ought to undergo vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). However, when the status of being a substitute applies to the elision of the vowel *ā*, that reduplication does not belong to *svāp*; rather, it belongs to a different word, namely *svāp*.

68. *vyatho liṭi* (Pāṇini 7.4.68). Regarding the form *vivyathe*: the root *vyatha* (meaning "fear" and "trembling," Dhātupāṭha 764) takes the ātmanepada suffixes because it is anudāteta. Now, following the rule *halādiśeṣaḥ*, the *y* is elided.
Someone might have the misconception that [the change] must occur through the vocalization (samprasāraṇa) of the letter *va*;
therefore, in order to dispel that, he says "of the letter *ya*" and so forth. [The form] "vāvyathyate" contains the suffix *yaṅ*.
69. *dīrgha iṇaḥ kiti* (Pāṇini 7.4.69).
Since only the short form of the root *iṇ* would have been heard [in the resulting forms], lengthening is prescribed here. Thus we have *īyatuḥ* and *īyuḥ*.
Now, one might object that by the rule *iṇo yaṇ* (6.4.81), the substitution of *yaṇ* should apply because it is a subsequent rule.

Since there is no doubling [of the vowel] because it is not a true *anacka* (vowel), he says "ṭhiṇo yaṇ" and so forth. However, the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is established by the rule "dvirvacane'ci" (Pāṇini 1.1.59).
And that [status] applies specifically when the doubling must be performed at its fixed time; once that doubling has been performed, the form of the substitute [is applied].

Thus it remains as *ṭhiyāya* and *iyayitha*. When the rules for vṛddhi and guṇa have been applied respectively by [Pāṇini 7.2.115] *ṇali* and *thali*, the reduplication is of the vowel *i* due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*; for that reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), the substitution of *iyaṅ* occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.78] *abhyāsasyāsavarṇe*.

70. *ata ādeḥ* (7.4.70). The term *liṭi* (in the context of the *liṭ* affix) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. However, the mention of *kit* has ceased [to apply]. Since the substitution of a single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) would have applied by the rule *ato guṇe* (6.1.97), this rule for lengthening is commenced. The use of the marker *t* [in *ataḥ*] is for the sake of its own nature [as a technical term].

That which is short has its long counterpart; just as in that [example], even when the long vowel of "āccha" (from the root *ā-chi* in the sense of extension) is made short in your grammatical instruction, it does not become long—namely, *āccha*, *āccchatuḥ*, *ācchuḥ*. [This is formed with] the *liṭ* suffix: *tip* becomes *ṇal*, *tas* becomes *atus*, and *jhi* becomes *us*.

When there is reduplication and the application of *halādiśeṣa*, the rule "the short vowel" (7.4.59) applies. Furthermore, what would happen if a long vowel were present here? The augment *nuṭ* would apply by the rule "after that [root] which has two consonants, *ruṭ*" (7.4.71). Because of the statement "of the initial," a long vowel does not occur here at the end—as in *papāca* and so forth.

71. *tasmānnuḍ dvihalaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.71). That which has two consonants (*hal*) is called *dvihal*. [Examples are] *ānaṅga*, *ānaṅgatuḥ*, and *ānaṅguḥ*. The roots *agi*, *ragi*, and *lagi* have the meaning "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 146, 144, 145); because they are marked with the *idit* designation, the augment *num* is applied.
"ṭhānañja, ānañjatuḥ, ānañjuḥ. [The root] *ṭhanjū* [is used] in the senses of manifestation (*vyakti*), smearing (*mrakṣaṇa*), beauty (*kānti*), and motion (*gati*) (Dhātupāṭha 1458).
In the rule *ṭhāṬcÂ* (Māheśvara Sūtra 4), regarding the letters within the *ṭh* pratyāhāra, those which are partial portions of letters (*varṇaikadeśāḥ*)...

"Those [sounds] which have a form identical to other phonemes do not undergo that grammatical operation, for they merely imitate their shadow and are not those very phonemes themselves; indeed, the teachers maintain that a phoneme is produced by a distinct effort. Having said this, [the rule applies] to the insertion of *ṭh* and *nuṭ*, the prescription of *l* as a substitute, and the substitution of *ṛ*.

It was stated that "a counter-argument must be provided. Having reached the appropriate occasion, he provides a counter-argument regarding the rule for the insertion of *ṇuṅ* before the vowel *ṛ*: "The letter *r*, which is a portion of the vowel *ṛ*, is included by the term *hal* [in Pāṇini’s definition of consonants]. This is illustrated by the forms *ānṛdhatuḥ* and *ānṛdhuḥ*. [The root] *ṛdhu* means "to grow" (*vṛddhau*; DhP 1271). How [is this so]?

Furthermore, by the inclusion of *hal* (consonants) [in the rule], is the *repha* (the sound *r*)—which is the substitute for *ṛ* and *ṝ* consisting of the vowel *a*—included? The intention is that this is so by virtue of the force of the mention of "two consonants" (*dvihala*).
In this regard, one should have stated "thereafter *nuṭ*" (*tasmānnuṭ*); and if that were the case, [the form] *āṭatuḥ* would not result.

In cases such as *āṭuri*, there arises the contingency of the augment *nuṭ*; for the rule *aśnoteḥ* serves a restrictive purpose—namely, that if the augment *nuṭ* occurs after a root consisting of more than one syllable (*advi-hala*), it applies only to the root *aś*, and not to any other. One should not raise the objection that this [restriction] is intended to exclude *aśnāti*; for if that were all [the purpose], [it would be redundant].

The purpose [of the rule] would be that one could simply say "not after *aś*"; therefore, its purpose is indeed restriction (*niyama*). Thus, since the result is established even without the mention of "having two consonants" (*dvihal*), the reason he makes the mention of "having two consonants" is this: [it serves as a restrictive rule].

The purpose [of this rule] is so that it may apply even to a compound consisting of two consonants (*hal*) that have the same form. This is for the sake of ensuring that it applies even to that which has one consonant as its primary member and a second that is not primary, yet is fit to be designated as a "consonant" (*hal*) by metaphorical extension because it imitates the shadow of one; so that it may apply to such a case as well. How is this [achieved]?

How is this so? If there is an explicit scriptural mention (*śruti*) here of "two consonants" (*dvihala*), then [the term] applies to the *repha*—which is a constituent part of the vowel *ṛ*—only by following its shadow-like form, and not otherwise. Therefore, by the force of the mention of "two consonants," the *repha* which is a single part of the vowel *ṛ* is understood here by the mention of "consonant" (*hal*); otherwise, [it would not be so].
The mention of "two vowels" (dvihal) would be purposeless.

72. And [the substitution of *eś* for *ta* occurs] after the root *aś*. (Pāṇini 7.4.72) This rule is commenced for the sake of roots that do not have a reduplicated stem (*advihala*). [The example is] *vyānaśe*. The root *aśū* (DhP 1264) means "to pervade";
because it is *anudāteta*, it takes the *ātmanepada* endings; here, the suffix is *ta*, which is replaced by *eś*.

The mention of the suffix *aśnoteḥ* is for the purpose of excluding the root *aś* "to eat" belonging to the Kryādigaṇa (DhP 1523); the particle *ca* is for the purpose of attracting the augment *nuṭ*.

73. *bhavateraḥ* | (Pāṇini 7.4.73) [The substitution of] *ar* occurs for the root *bhū*. For example, *babhūva*: here, by the rule *bhuvo vug luṅliṭoḥ* (6.4.88), the augment *vuk* is applied. For example, *anubabhūve*: this is the Ātmanepada used in the sense of the object (*karman*). The mention is made using the suffix *śtip*.
The purpose is to exclude the *yaṅ* and *luṅ* suffixes—as in the form *vobhāva*.

74. *sasūve* in the Vedic language (*nigama*). (Pāṇini 7.4.74). [The word] *sūteḥ* refers to this root: *ṣūṅ* "to release the fetus of a living being" (Dhātupāṭha 1031). [The form] *suṣuve* is derived from it; because of the marker *ṅ*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used, and the substitution *uvaṅ* occurs.

The inclusion of the particle *iti* is for the purpose of encompassing other similar forms. By this, forms such as *jāgramah* and *adarśama* are established. In *jāgramah*, the suffix *mah* is substituted for the root *jāgarti*. In *adarśama*, the *laṅ* suffix is used after the root *dṛś*, with the absence of the substitution of *paśya*. Thus, we have *jāgramah* and *apaśyāma*.
In the spoken language (bhāṣā), the inclusion of *sasūva* among the roots beginning with *dādharti* was not made;
it is for the sake of variety.
75. *ṇijāṃ trayāṇāṃ guṇaḥ śvau* (Pāṇini 7.4.75). Because the plural number is used in the rule, the sense of "the first [of these]" is understood; hence he says "of these," and so forth.
*ṇijir* is [listed] in the sense of "purification and nourishment" (Dhātupāṭha 1093); *vijir* is [listed] in the sense of "separation."
The roots *ḍhā* (Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 1094) and *ṭhviṣlṛ* in the sense of "pervasion" (1095)—these, beginning with *ṇij*, belong to the *juhotyādi* class.
The mention of the number three is for the sake of what follows; [in this context], there is the substitution of *i* by the rule *bhṛñāmit* (7.4.76).

The mention of "three" (tri) is for the purpose that it may apply only to these three and not to more than that. Why, then, is this not also the purpose [of the rule]? To this he says: "Of these," and so forth. If the mention of "three" were made here, what would be the purpose of placing the word *bṛt* at the end of the list beginning with *nij*?

This should be questioned of the author of the *Gaṇapāṭha*, not the author of the *Sūtras*; for it was stated previously that "the author of the *Gaṇapāṭha* is one person, and the author of the *Sūtras* is another. It should be understood that the author of the *Gaṇapāṭha* also formed *vṛt* compounds for the sake of variety; indeed, the composition of the *Gaṇapāṭha* by the author of the *Gaṇapāṭha* is diverse.
Now, for what purpose is the mention of the *guṇa* (vowel substitution)? Why not simply say "the letter *e*"? It is impossible to say this;

for if it were stated in that way, someone might understand it to mean that the letter *e* is the substitute for the roots beginning with *nij*, as an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule of *halādi-śeṣa*.

For when a designation is prescribed based on the inclusion of a specific quality, there is a restriction such that only *ika* occurs; however, as for *hal*, its exclusion is achieved through the remainder [of the rule] beginning with "after *hal*" (*halas taddhitasya*).

76. *bhṛñām it* (Pāṇini 7.4.76). The roots *bhṛñ* "to support or nourish" (Dhātupāṭha 1087), *māṅ* "to measure" (Dhātupāṭha 1088), and *ohāṅ* "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1089)—these are the roots beginning with *bhṛñ*.
Only those belonging to the *juhoty-ādi* class [are affected]. In the forms *mimīte* and *jihīte*, the substitution of *ī* occurs by the rule *ī halyaghoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.113).
77. And [the substitution of *ī* for *ṛ* occurs] after the roots *ṛ* and *pṛ*. (Pāṇini 7.4.77) Examples: *ṛti*, *piparti*. [The roots] *ṛ* and *sṛ* mean "to go" (Dhātupāṭha 1098, 1099);
*pṛ* means "to protect" and "to fill" (Dhātupāṭha 1086). Because they belong to the *juhotyādi* class, there is *ślau* (reduplication) for the *śap* suffix, and [subsequently] *guṇa* [is applied].
There is reduplication; by *urat* (Pāṇini 7.4.66), there is substitution of *u*; by this [rule], there is substitution of *i*, and *r* follows as the subsequent element (*raparatva*).

For the root *ṛ*, there is the substitution of *iyaṅ* by *abhyāsasyāsavarṇe* (Pāṇini 6.4.78). Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *ṛti*? For this [suffix] is listed after the *nij-ādi* group; and all those that follow the *nij-ādi* group [are such].
Thus they are Vedic; for indeed, having recited them, it is stated that "in the Veda" (*cchandasi*).

If it is argued that because of their being Vedic, [the form] is established by the rule "bahulam chandasi" (Pāṇini 7.4.78), then this [usage] indicates that the root *ṛ* is also employed in the common language (*bhāṣā*).

78. *Bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 7.4.78). Regarding the form *viviṣṭi*: [the root] *vaś* means "to desire" (*kāntau*, Dhātupāṭha 1080). By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (2.4.76), there is *ślau* (elision) of the *śap* suffix; by the rule *vraśca-ādi-sūtra* (8.2.36), there is the substitution of *ṣ*. Regarding the form *vivakti*: [this is derived from the root *vac*].
The root *vac* is used in the sense of "speaking" (*paribhāṣaṇe*; DhP 1842). Regarding the form *siṣakti*: it is either from *sac* in the sense of "joining together" (*samavaye*;
DhP 997) or from *sac* in the sense of "moistening" (*secane*; DhP 163). Regarding *jigarti* and *jigharti*:
these are from *gṛ* and *ghṛ* in the sense of "moistening" (*secane*; DhP 937, 938). In all these cases, as before, there is the substitution of *ślu* for *śap*.

Regarding the forms *ṭhjajanam* and *dadhanam*: [the roots] are *jan* in the sense of "producing" (DhP 1105) and *dhan* in the sense of "grain" (DhP 1104). The suffix *luṅ* takes the ending *am*; because these belong to the *juhoty-ādi* class, there is *ślu*-elision of the *śap* augment;
and by the rule "in the Veda, [the augment *aṅ* is] frequently [absent] even when not preceded by *ām*" (6.4.75), there is a prohibition of the *aṅ* augment.
79. *sanyataḥ* | (Pāṇini 7.4.79) Examples include *pipakṣati*, and so forth. These are the forms of the roots *pac* and *yaj*. *Pipāsati* is from either the root *pā* or *pā* (to drink).

Regarding the form *lulūṣati*: from the root *lūñ* "to cut" (DhP 1483), there is an absence of guṇa due to its being *kit* by the rule *iko jhal* (1.2.9). There is a prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *sani grahaguhośca* (7.2.12). What is the purpose of the specification *tapara* (the long vowel *ā*)? [It is for the sake of excluding] the *san* of *pāpacyate*.
Let there not be [the substitution] in *pāpaciṣate*. But what is the reason that the short vowel does not occur here?

Because of the force of the prescription of the long vowel. If it were understood as "the reduplication which occurs in the *san* [affix]," then [the long vowel would apply]; however, [it is understood otherwise] for the sake of ease of pronunciation.

80. *oḥ puyaṇjyapare* (Pāṇini 7.4.80). [The Kāśikā notes that *ṭhpuyaṇji* does not exist; rather, having treated *pu*, *yaṇ*, and *ji* as a single unit, they are indicated in the locative case. [The Kāśikā notes that *apare* does not exist; rather, it means "that after which an *a* follows. (Note: This rule prescribes the substitution of *u* for the *o* of the verbal root *du* before suffixes beginning with *p*, *yaṇ*, or *j*, provided these are followed by an *a*. The mention of *apare* indicates that the substitute *u* is applied when an *a* follows.)

The meaning is "that which has another vowel as its subsequent element" (*tadaparamavarṇapara*). Regarding the form *pipaviṣate*: from the root *pūṅ* (DhP 966) in the sense of "purifying," the suffix *san* is added; by the rule *smipūṅrañjāṃ sani* (Pāṇini 7.2.74), the augment *iṭ* is applied, followed by guṇa and the substitution of *av*. Due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, the element *pū* undergoes reduplication.

The status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), however, is established by the rule *dvirvacane’ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59). In the form *pipāvayiṣati*, the suffix *san* follows the causative (*ṇi*) of the root *pū*. Here too, due to the status as a substitute, the element *pū* is reduplicated. In the form *bibhāvayiṣati*, [the root is] *bhū* in the sense of "being" (*satāyām*).
From a root ending in *ṇi*, there is the suffix *san*.
For example: *yiyāvayiṣati*. This is formed by adding *san* to the root *yu* after it has taken *ṇi*. By the rule "a root ending in *san* or *u" (Pāṇini 7.2.49), the augment *iṭ* is added.
Similarly: *rirāvayiṣati*; *lilāvayiṣati*.
The suffix *san* is applied after the two roots *rauti* and *lunāti* when they are followed by the causative suffix *ṇic*.

Thus, [we have] *jijāvayiṣati*. The root *ju* is a Vedic (sautra) root, as it is listed in [Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.150] in the rule *ju-caṅkramya-*, etc. From that [root *ju*], when followed by *ṇic*, the suffix *san* is applied.

But how is it that the reduplication in forms such as *pipādayiṣati* has the vowel *u* at its end, given that, since the suffix *ṇic* follows, the internal operation (*antaraṅga*) of vṛddhi and the substitution of *ā* for *ai* must first take place, after which the reduplication would have to apply to a stem ending in *v*?

If it is argued that, by virtue of the status of being a substitute (sthānivadbhāva), there will be reduplication of that which ends in /u/, [we reply: no; for that which is performed in the causative (ṇi) does not undergo the status of being a substitute, because the causative suffix (ṇic) is not the cause of reduplication. Therefore, he says: "This very [point]," and so forth. For indeed...
All [cases] where *pu*, *yaṇ*, or *j* followed by a vowel (*avarṇa*) occur without the presence of *ṇic* are possible;

for in that case, if there were no *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if the original element) for what was done in the presence of *ṇic*, then those cases where *pu*, *yaṇ*, or *j* followed by a vowel occur without *ṇic* would all be impossible. In that context, if [the rule applied] to what was done in the presence of *ṇic*...

If there were no status as a substitute (sthānivadbhāva), then for those [roots] for whom the condition of having a vowel *a* following [the reduplicated syllable] is not possible without the causative suffix (*ṇic*), their reduplicated syllable would not end in a vowel *u*; yet this rule is stated: "In the case of *pu*, *ya*, and *ja* when followed by *p*, *y*, or *j*."

Therefore, this is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that [the substitute] remains as if it were the original (*sthānivat*) even when the causative suffix *ṇi* is the cause of non-duplication. By this, forms such as *tutāvayiṣati* and *bibhāvayiṣati* are established.
For whom, then, would the condition of being followed by a vowel (*avarṇa-paratā*) not be possible without the causative suffix *ṇic*?
For all others except those beginning with *ya* and *pa*, [the rule applies]. In the case of *ṭhpāpaciṣate*, there is the elision of the vowel *a* by *ato lopaḥ* (P.
6.4.48), and the elision of the letter *y* by *yasya halaḥ* (P.
6.4.49). [In the case of] *tutāvayiṣati* [or, according to the Kāśikā and Padamañjarī, *avatutāvayiṣati*...].

Regarding "pāṭhaḥ ṭ": the root is *tud*, because it is recited in the rule beginning with "turustuśamyamaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.95). Regarding "juhāvayiṣati": from the root *hu* in the sense of "giving" (Dhātupāṭha 1083), followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the desiderative suffix (*san*) is added. Regarding "bubhūṣati": [it is derived from the root *bhū*].
As before, there is an absence of both direction and quality.

81. [The suffix *kvip* is optionally applied] after the roots *sravati*, *śṛṇoti*, *dravati*, *pravati*, *plavati*, and *cyavati*. (Pāṇini 7.4.81) [The respective roots are: *sru* "to flow" (Dhātupāṭha 940), *śru* "to hear" (942), *du* and *dru* "to run" (944, 945), and *pruṅ*, *pluṅ*, and *cyuṅ* "to move" (957, 958, 956).
Regarding the examples beginning with *sisrāvayiṣati*: the suffix *san* is applied in all these cases after the causative (*ṇic*) stems.

Now, one might object: since there is an intervention here by the letter *s*, which begins with a *sa*-sound, how can the substitution of *i* (the *itva*)—which is prescribed when a *yaṇ* followed by a vowel follows—occur despite this intervention?
Thus he says: "By the force of the statement. For in every case here, there is an intervention by a single phoneme beginning with *s*;
and this statement is indeed uttered. Therefore, in this instance, an intervention by a single phoneme is resorted to on the strength of the statement; otherwise, this statement would be purposeless.
By the phrase "by the previous sūtra," etc., he shows that this is an optional rule (*aprāptavibhāṣā*).
Regarding *śuśruṣati* (the Kāśikā reads *śuśrūyate*): as before, there is an absence of the augment *iṭ* and of *guṇa*.
The mention of *śtip* is for the purpose of indicating the verbal root (*dhātu*), not for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ* [intensive] suffix. Here, [if] *guṇa* [were applied]...

Because the state of ending in *u* has been established [by the previous rule], the substitution of *it* does not occur; thus, we have *sosraviṣati*. [There is no [text]—Kaiyaṭa on Pāṇini 8.2. According to Pāṇini 7.4.82, there is *guṇa* substitution in the case of the *yaṅ* and *yaṅluk* formations.]

This quality of reduplication (abhyāsa) is prescribed [only] for the [intensive] formation; therefore, although the word *luk* here is general, the understanding refers specifically to the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix (*yaṅ-luk*). For reduplication is not possible when there is [merely] elision (*luk*) [of an affix]. With this in mind, he says: "In the case of *yaṅ*, and also when *yaṅ* is elided," etc. [The example is: *caukruśīti*.

From the root *kruś* in the sense of "calling" (*āhvāne*, Dhātupāṭha 856), there is the intensive suffix *yaṅ*. By the rule *yaṅe 'ci ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.74), the suffix *yaṅ* undergoes *ḷk*-elision; by the rule *yaṅe vā* (7.3.94), the augment *iṭ* is optionally added. Since the rule *na lumatāṅgasya* (1.1.63) prohibits the application of grammatical operations based on the suffix when that suffix has undergone *luk*-elision, once *yaṅ* has been elided, the [vocalization] *guṇa* substitution would not otherwise apply.

Regarding the inclusion of the word *lug*: although the rule "pugantalaghūpadhasya ca" (Pāṇini 7.3.86) would have required the substitution of guṇa, it is prohibited by the rule "nābhyastasyāci piti sārvadhātuke" (Pāṇini 7.3.87).
83. *dīrgho'kitaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.83).
[In the example] *ṭhyaṃyamyate*, the root is *yama* (meaning "to cease," *dhā.pā.* 984). The augment *nuk* is applied by [the rule] *nugato'nunāsikāntasya* (7.4.85).

With the words "But surely... and so forth, he refutes the [objection] regarding the term *akitaḥ*. The term *akitaḥ* is stated for the purpose that [the rule] should not apply in cases such as *yaṃyamyate*. For in this case, since the *nuk* augment would be applied by way of an exception (*apavāda*), the vowel would not become long simply because the stem would no longer end in *an*; thus, the mention of *akitaḥ* would be unnecessary.

By the words "In that case, then" (*evaṃ tarhi*) and so forth, he shows that the rule *thakitaḥ* is stated in order to indicate the following *paribhāṣā*: "Exceptions (*apavāda*) do not set aside general rules (*utsarga*) when they involve modifications due to repetition (*abhyāsavikāra*)" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 23). [The example is given: *ḍoḍhāṬkyate*. [This is derived from] *ḍhāṬkṛ*...

When the suffix *yaṅ* is applied to the root *gatau* (DhP 98) and the substitution of *hil* etc. has occurred, the shortening prescribed by "hrasvaḥ" (7.4.59) takes place, followed by *guṇa* by the preceding rule. If this [present] indicator (*jñāpaka*) did not exist, the shortening would find its scope of application in forms such as *pipāsati*, where "dīrgho 'kitaḥ" (7.4.83) applies.

In this way, the diphthong (*sandhyakṣara*) would be sublated by length. If it is argued that there is no purpose for prescribing length for what is already long, and therefore the long vowel will not occur—this is not so; for there is indeed a purpose in prescribing length for the long vowel. What is that? It is so that the short vowel does not occur.
And if this indicator did not exist, then in the case of *acikarat* (from *kṛ*), where the substitution of *it* is applicable— as in *acikṣaṇat* and so on—
it would be sublated by the lengthening rule *dīrgho laghoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.94).
Furthermore, if this indicator did not exist, [the substitution of *it*] would be sublated in cases such as *mīmāṃsate*, while leaving room for its application in cases such as *pipakṣati*.

The substitution of *i* prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.4.79] *sanyataḥ* is sublated by the lengthening (*dīrgha*) prescribed by the rule [3.1.6] *mānbadhādisūtra*. Furthermore, in the case of *ajīgaṇat*, even if this indicator (*jñāpaka*) were absent, the *halādiśeṣa* (retention of the initial consonant) would find its scope in forms such as *papāṭha*; however, it is sublated here by the substitution of *ī* prescribed by [7.4.97] *ī ca gaṇaḥ*.

[The rule] is superseded. But when this [present rule] exists, all of that is not superseded. Now, it is argued: "An indicator (jñāpaka) operates only when there is no other purpose [for the rule]; yet there is indeed a purpose for this [rule]. What is it? It is so that, with respect to the status of being a *dhātu* or a *kit*, it may not apply to the root *jahāti*—as in *jāhāti* and *jāheti*? This is not the case; for if this were...
If there were a purpose [for such a rule], then he would have prescribed the prohibition "after *ahāk*.

Furthermore, the term *akit* ought to be a qualifier of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), provided that the *kit*-status arises during the state of reduplication. However, the *kit*-status of the root *jahāti* does not depend upon the reduplicated syllable, for it exists prior to that.

It arises from the practice of that [usage]. Therefore, from the root *jahāti*, the forms *jāhāti* and *jāheti* ought to occur. Consequently, the statement "after a suffix marked with Ṭ or K" (*ṭhakitah*) is merely an indicator (*jñāpaka*). However, the inclusion of the marker K after *jahāti* is for the sake of [the rule] "and after *hā*, when *vrīhi* and *kāla* follow" (*haśca vrīhikālayoḥ*, 3.1.148).

[The mention of] "general" (sāmānya) is for the purpose of avoiding an obstruction [to the application of the rule]. Now, what is the purpose of mentioning "long" (dīrgha)? It might be argued that [the long vowel] should be understood as "ā" alone. This cannot be so, because the status of [the word] *ṭhakit* as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) would not be tenable. For if the mention of "long" were present, once the augment *nuṭ* has been applied, [the base] would not end in *ac*, and thus the long [vowel] [would be excluded].
The status of "ṭhakitaḥ" as an indicator (jñāpaka) for the prohibition [of the augment iṭ] is thus justified by the statement that "there is no attainment [of the augment].

However, if the long vowel *ā* were prescribed [without the mention of length], it would apply to a reduplicated stem ending in a short vowel (*ajanta*), and consequently, "ṭhakitaḥ" could not serve as an indicator. Therefore, the explicit mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) must be made.
84. *nīg vañcu-sraṃsu-dhvaṃsu-bhraṃsu-kasapat-pad-skandām* (Pāṇini 7.4.84).

The roots *vañcu*, *cancu*, *tancu*, *tvancu*, *bhruncu*, *gluncu* [the reading in the Prācīna-mahābhāṣya and Nyāsa is *muncu*], meaning "to go" (*gatyartha*) (Dhātupāṭha 189–194); and *sraṃsu* and *dhvaṃsu*, meaning "to fall down" (*avasraṃsane*).

(dhā.pā. 754, 755); *kasa* "to go" (dhā.pā. 860); *śala*, *hula*, *patlṛ* "to go" (dhā.pā. 843–845); *skandir* "to move" and "to dry up" (dhā.pā. 979). Regarding the form *vanīvacyate*: the nasal is elided by the rule *aniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24), etc.
In the case of *ṭhvanīvañci*, the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) does not occur.

This is because the *yaṅ* suffix has been elided, and by the rule "na lumatāṅgasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.63), there is a prohibition against applying operations based on the presence of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*).
Now, once the *nīk* suffix is applied, why does the shortening of the vowel not take place? It is because of the functional force (*sāmarthya*) of the long-vowel pronunciation itself.
85. *nugato'nunāsikāntasya* (Pāṇini 7.4.85).
Since lengthening would have been required by the rule *dīrgho'kitaḥ* (7.4.83), this present rule is commenced.
*Tantanyate* and so forth are the forms of the roots *tam*, *gam*, *yam*, and *ram*.

If [the augment] *nuK* were not applied, then in forms such as *yamyate*, the *anusvāra* prescribed by the rule *naścāpadāntasya jhali* (Pāṇini 8.3.24)—which is stated to occur before a *jhal* consonant—would not be established, because [the following sound] would not be a *jhal* (since it is followed by a vowel).
To this, he says: "That [augment] is *nuk*," and so forth. How [is this understood]?
Can it be seen that *nuk* here is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the anusvāra?

To this he says: "For by the original element (*sthānin*)," and so forth. For by the original element *nuk*, the substitute (*ādeśa*) *anusvāra* is indicated here. Therefore, it is the *anusvāra* itself that is prescribed here as the augment (*āgama*), and not *nuk*.
In examples such as *yamyamyate*, although there is indeed a following vowel (*ac*) or non-*jhal* consonant (*ajhalpara*), the *anusvāra* is nevertheless established.

Likewise, the rule "the *anusvāra* becomes a *parasavarṇa* before *yay* consonants" (Pāṇini 8.4.58) would apply; however, since the audible retention of the *anusvāra* is desired in one alternative (*pakṣe*), that would not be achieved because [the *anusvāra*] is an exception (*apavāda*). To this [objection], [the author replies]:

He says: "And like the end of a word," and so forth. The meaning is that this rule must be explained as having the sense that the *anusvāra* becomes like [the final letter] at the end of a word (*padāntavat*). In this regard, the explanation is as follows: the rule of extension to the end of that (*tadantavidhi*) does not apply; rather, the *anusvāra* occurs for that which ends in a nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*).

There is no purpose in mentioning the "end of a word" (padānta); it is done for this reason: so that whatever property belongs to an *anusvāra* at the end of a word shall also belong to a *nu*. Thus, there will be an audible pronunciation of the *anusvāra* in one alternative.
Regarding the word "ṭhtetimyate": [the roots] "ṭhim" and "ṣṭim" mean "to become moist" (Dhātupāṭha 1123, 1124).

Now, what is the purpose of the inclusion of the long vowel *ā* (the *tapara* marker) in *teti*, given that there is nothing else to be excluded from this rule since a short vowel does not occur anywhere in its place? To this, he says: "The inclusion of the *tapara* marker..."

And so forth. Since there is no long vowel currently in existence, the addition of *t* (the *tapara* marker) will serve to exclude even that long vowel which existed previously. [The example] "bābhāmyate" is derived from the root *bhāma* in the sense of "anger" (Dhātupāṭha 441).

86. *japa-jabha-daha-daśa-bhañja-paś-ām ca* (Pāṇini 7.4.86). This rule is commenced because [the preceding roots] end in a nasal (*anunāsika*). [The roots are: *japa* and *jalpa* (meaning "articulate speech," Dhātupāṭha 397, 398);
*jabhi* and *jṛbhī* (meaning "bending of the limbs," Dhātupāṭha 388, 389); *daha*...

In the case of *bhasmīkaraṇe* (DhP 991), *daṃśa daśane* (DhP 989), *bhavjo āmardane* (DhP 1453), and the root *paśi*, which is a Vedic (sautra) root— in forms such as *jañjapyate* up to *daṃdaśyate*, [the suffix -ya] is applied by [Pāṇini 3.1.24], *lupasada*.
Furthermore, in other cases, [the substitution occurs] by means of the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). (Pāṇini 3.1.22)

87. And [the roots] *cara* and *phala*. (Pāṇini 7.4.87) The root *cara* is listed as "to move" (Dhātupāṭha 559). The root *phal* is listed twice: "to burst open" (Dhātupāṭha 516) and "to ripen" (Dhātupāṭha 530); both are included here. The vowel *a* in the sense of "ripening" [is the one intended].

The [suffix] is for the purpose of pronunciation and is not an *anubandha*, because there is no purpose [for it as such]; consequently, by the paribhāṣā regarding those without *anubandhas* (Pāṇini 1.1.68), only this form whose meaning is "completion" (*niṣpati*)—being devoid of an *anubandha*—would be grasped, and not the one whose meaning is "dispersion" (*viśaraṇa*). This is not a fault; [This is because: the rule *vibhāṣā vipūrvāt* (Pāṇini 1.3.19) applies to both meanings.
