The elision of the *n* of *sup* occurs through contiguity; if that [elision] were to trigger the application of *tuk*, [it would be a fault].

That [augment] would obstruct the *sannipāta* (the coalescence of phonemes). And it has been stated that "a rule characterized by *sannipāta* is an obstacle to its own destruction" (*Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā* 12). Therefore, the elision of *n* does not trigger the application of the *tuk* augment;
thus, the mention of *tuk* is purposeless. But surely, because *tuk* is treated as part of the preceding element (*pūrvāntatva*)...
The *tuka* augment is included by the very mention of the base (*prātipadika*); therefore, how could there be an obstruction of that [base] conjunction (*sannipāta*)?
For it is not possible for something to obstruct itself by means of its own constituent part. This is not so;
for the *tuka* is an augment (*āgama*), not the entire complex ending in it. Therefore, how [could there be an obstruction]?

Is there inclusion by virtue of the mention of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)? Or, because the elision of *n* (*nalopa`) is *asiddha* with respect to the *tuk* augment due to its being characterized as external (*bahiraṅga*), the mention of the rule for *tuk* is purposeless;
for the elision of *n* is prescribed depending upon the case-ending suffix which is external to the word (*pada*). Regarding that—

The status of being *bahiraṅga* [is as follows]: since the insertion of the *tuk* augment for a phoneme (*varṇa*) is prescribed with reference to an internal word (*pada*), that [insertion] possesses the status of being *antaraṅga*. Thus, according to the principle "that which is *bahiraṅga* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when [the *antaraṅga* operation is] present" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 42), if this is the case, then it is indeed correct; so for what purpose is the mention of *tuk* [in the rule]?

Why is this done? To this he says: "That is performed," and so forth. However, the purpose of the *paribhāṣā* rule "that which is characterized by the coming together [of causes]" (*sannipātalakṣaṇa-paribhāṣā*) is to make known the non-eternality [of grammatical operations]; for instance, in the case of *dṛkṣāya*, the lengthening [of the vowel] is established by Pāṇini 7.3.102 (*supi ca*). For, when there is the coming together of the final *a*-vowel [with the suffix], the suffix *ReĀr* [is applied] by 7.1.13.

"It is prescribed"; because it is caused by that [diphthong], one should not effect its destruction by means of entering into a state of being the cause of lengthening. Because it is non-eternal (*anitya*), it does effect it. Furthermore, another purpose here will be stated later on itself, according to the *paribhāṣā* regarding external characteristics (*bahiraṅga-lakṣaṇa*).

In order to indicate that [the rule] does not apply when *sup* (a case-ending) follows—this [example] serves to establish the application of *ṭāp* in the word *dve*. For here, because the status of being "subsequent" (*tyādadyatva*) depends upon a case-ending (*vibhakti*), it is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*);
whereas *ṭāp* is intrinsic (*antaraṅga*) because it depends upon the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). In that situation, when *ṭāp* is to be applied...

The substitution of *yat* for *tyad* and so on would be considered *asiddha*; consequently, the formation of *ṭāp* would not be established. However, it is established because [the rule] is non-eternal (*anitya*). An example of its purpose is the establishment of the lengthening in *pratidīvnā*, by means of the rule *hali ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.77). If that [rule] were not non-eternal, then when the lengthening required by *hali ca* was to be applied—

Because the elision (*al-lopa*) is *asiddha* with respect to the external factor, a verbal root ending in *v* would not exist when followed by a consonant (*hal*), and thus the lengthening [of the vowel] would not occur. However, it is established due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) [of that rule], as in the form "rājīyati. Here, *kyac* is applied by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8), and [the lengthening occurs] by the rule *kyaci ca*.

(7.4.33) Thus, there is the substitution of *i* [for the final vowel]. In the case of *rājāyate*, the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied by the rule *kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca* (3.1.11), and the lengthening [of the penultimate vowel] occurs by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* (7.4.25). In the case of *rājaśyaḥ*, the long vowel [substitution] occurs by the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (6.1.101).

3. *na mu ne* (8.2.3). This is an indeclinable citation of the form *ṭhmu*. [The example is] *amunā*. In this case, the substitution of *yatva* for *adas-* occurs; then, by *adaso'serdādu do maḥ* (8.2.80), the *u*-substitution and the *m*-substitution take place; and finally, by *acca gheḥ* (7.3.119), the final vowel is elided.

Therefore, while the term *gher* continues to apply [from 7.3.111], the substitution of *nā* by rule 7.3.120 (*āṅo nāstriyām*) does not take place. If the meaning of the sūtra were simply that the *mubhāva* (the substitution of *au* for the dual case endings) is not *asiddha* when the substitution of *nā* is to be performed, then, once the substitution of *nā* has been made, whatever operation would subsequently apply— [in that case, the *mubhāva* would indeed be non-asiddha].

Otherwise, its status as *asiddha* would not hold, and consequently, in the form *amunā*, the rule *supi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.102), which prescribes lengthening for a stem ending in *a*, would undesirably apply. To this, he says: "But when *nābhāva* has been applied," and so forth. For the substitution of *nā* is conditioned by the presence of a short vowel (*hrasva-sannipāta*), and thus it brings about the destruction of that very short vowel.
Because it does not occur as a substitute for every individual phoneme (*pratinimittam*), even though the [reason] is unestablished (*asiddhatva*), there is no contingency of lengthening.

Regarding the phrase "Or rather" (*athavā*) and so forth: just as when one person is asked, "Who is running from here?", and another asks, "What color is he running?", a certain clever-minded person, by means of a *tantra* (a single word serving multiple functions), [answers both].

He presents two sentences—"The white one runs"—and likewise here too, this pair of *yoga*s is uttered by way of *tantra* (simultaneous application). In that regard, the meaning of the rule is simply this: when the second *yoga* is to be applied, that which follows it is not *asiddha* (non-existent) for the purpose of what must be performed. By that [principle]...
Length will not occur.
To preclude the attainment of length within that very same *yoga*, he says "Or rather," and so forth.
Now, if this meaning of the sūtra were not to be adopted, what would be the purpose of the established status (*siddhatva*) of the *mubhāva*?

That [substitution] would be included by the rule; and consequently, non-existence (abhāva) itself would not even be attained, so how much less could there be the non-validity (*asiddhatva*) of the *mubhāva* when that which is to be produced by another rule is to be performed? To this he says: "But when *na* is to be performed," and so forth.

Just as an old maiden, while praying for the boon that her sons might eat rice with plenty of milk, ghee, and curds from a golden vessel, has in effect already secured a husband, sons, cattle, and wealth; so too here, regarding that which is to be accomplished for one in the future.

By stating that the substitution of *m* for *su* is established (*siddhatva*) when another operation is to be performed, it is not implied that the substitution of *m* for *su* is unestablished (*asiddhatva*) when that same operation is not to be performed. Therefore, the word "by that" (*tena*) refers to this: because the sense of the sentence is that the established status of the *m*-substitution for *su* is accepted for that specific purpose, for that reason [the rule applies].
"Neither is there non-existence, nor is there length.

Regarding the term "part": it refers to the rule "of the acute and grave vowels at the end of a nominal stem and in the locative singular. Since the word *vṛkṣa* is oxytone by the accent of the nominal stem, the vowel *a* which constitutes its final syllable [is acute].

That [suffix] is acute (*udātta*). It is the singular form of the locative case; by the rule *anudātau suppitau* (Pāṇini 3.1.4), it is grave (*anudātta*). When the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for those two [vowels] occurs by the rule *ād guṇaḥ* (6.1.87), a circumflex (*svarita*) would result due to the closest proximity (*āntaratamya*). However, because of the rule *ekādeśa udātenodāttaḥ* (8.2.5), that [circumflex] is treated as unestablished (*asiddha*).

For if that were the case, when the substitution of *ay* is to be applied, that single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) would indeed be *svarita*; thus, by virtue of proximity (*āntarya*), a *svarita* accent alone would result in place of it. Furthermore, the status of the single-substitute as "internal" (*antaraṅga*) is due to its being dependent on internal factors; for the *guṇa* substitution [of *ā*] is indeed internal.

Because it is dependent on a single word (*ekapadāśritatvāt*), whereas the substitution of *ay* is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*) due to its being contrary to that [intrinsic nature]. For example: "this belonging to a *kumārī*" (*kumāryā idam*). The word *kumāra* is oxytone (*antodāta*), like the word *vṛkṣa*.

From that [word], by the rule "the suffix *ṅīp* is applied when the first age [is indicated]" (Pāṇini 4.1.20), the suffix *ṅīp* is added, and then by the rule "and [the elision] of that which has *i*" (Pāṇini 6.4.148).

There is elision of the vowel *i* [by Pāṇini 6.4.148]; and by the rule "and of an unaccented [vowel] when there is elision of an accented [vowel]" (6.1.161), the vowel *ī* becomes accented. This is the singular dative case. When the form *kumārī-e* is established, the augment *āṬ* is added by the rule "āṬ for feminine stems ending in *ā*, *an*, or *nadī*" (7.3.112), followed by the substitution of *yaṇ* (6.1.77). [Then, by the rule] "of an accented *yaṇ*... [the final vowel becomes udātta].

By the rule *halpūrvāt* (6.1.174), the case ending (*vibhakti*) receives an acute accent (*udātta*). And by the rule *ādeḥ parasya* (1.1.54), this accent applies specifically to the augment *āṭ* which is part of the case ending.

Furthermore, by the rule *āṭaśca* (6.1.90), a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) consisting of *vṛddhi* occurs. Since that [substitute] would, as before, result in a circumflex (*svarita*) accent, the rule *ekādeśa-* [is applied].

By the rule *udātenodātaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.5), an acute accent (*udātta*) is applied. It must be stated that this [acute accent] is established as already accomplished—so that in the case of *kumāryā idam*, the substitution of *ay* may be acute; otherwise, as in the previous case, there would be a circumflex (*svarita*) accent (as noted in the Kāśikā-mu-pustaka). If...

And so forth. If the acute accent (*udātta*) is applied first and the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) operation afterwards—as shown in the immediately preceding demonstration of the formation of the form—then the substitution of *ay* becomes established precisely when it ought to be applied; thus, this example is appropriate. "But if," and so forth; [the example is] *kumārī-ai*.

[The form] *sthita* is established; there is the substitution of *yaṇ*. [Regarding the rule] "In that case, for a single substitute [of a vowel] following an acute-accented *yaṇ* which has *hal* preceding it" (Pāṇini 6.1.174), the accent of the case-ending is applied. If the accent of the case-ending were applied after the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) has already been made, then this supplementary statement (*upasaṃkhyāna*) would have no purpose. For in this case...

He explains that since the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) established by *rūpasiddhi* is already established as valid when the substitution of *ay* is to be applied, this method does not serve as the purpose for the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*). And this is logical; for, because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), [the accent] is indeed effected by the single-substitute itself.

First, it must occur; afterwards, by the accent of the case-ending. For since the single-substitute (ekādeśa) arises depending upon the phonemes (varṇa), it is considered internal (antaraṅga). Since the acute accent (udāttatva) of the word arises depending upon the case-ending, it is considered external (bahiraṅga).
Regarding the example *vṛkṣāvidam*: this should be understood in accordance with the analysis *vṛkṣa idam*.

Furthermore, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) here is the *vṛddhi* vowel according to Pāṇini 6.1.88 (*vṛddhir eci*). The rule 6.1.102 (*prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇadīrghaḥ*) does not apply; rather, 6.1.104 (*nādici*) applies.

Thus, because of the prohibition of lengthening [of the vowel], we have the example "gāṅge'nūpaḥ" (a marshy place on the Ganges). When the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "born in the Gaṅgā," the word *gāṅga* becomes oxytone by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). [The compound] "anugatā āpo'smin" (water has followed into this) [is the analysis of *anūpa*].
In the case of *bahuvrīhi*, by the rule *ṭhūdanīrdeaśe* (Pāṇini 6.3.98), the substitution of *ū* occurs; then,

when the suffix *a* is applied by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmānakṣe* (5.4.74), the word *anūpa* is also udātta on its final syllable due to the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), while the remainder of the word is anudātta.

"Because that [element] is established": that *e* which was produced in the word *gāṅge* when followed by the locative singular ending (*sup*), by means of the rule "ādguṇaḥ" (P. 6.1.87), is established;
whereas that single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) *ai*, which occurs by the rule "eṅḥ padāntādati" (P. 6.1.109) with the vowel *a* of the word *anūpa*, is not.
By the rule *sa ṭhekādeśa udātenodātaḥ* (8.2.5), it becomes udātta; for this reason, by the rule *svarito vānudāte padādau* (8.2.6), it optionally becomes svarita in that alternative case.
If, however, there were non-validity (*asiddhatva*), then that single vowel—

Because it would have an acute (udātta) and grave (anudātta) as its substituends, the circumflex (svarita) would arise by virtue of proximity (*āntaryataḥ*). However, as for the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) prescribed by "heṅḥ padāntādati" (P. 6.1.109), since that does not consist of an acute and a grave, the circumflex would not occur under the alternative rule "svarito vānudāte padādau" (P. 8.2.6).
However, since it occurs in place of both the circumflex (svarita) and the grave (anudātta), it would necessarily be circumflex by virtue of closest similarity (āntaratamya).
[This refers to] "the accent of the *śatṛ* suffix"; that is, the accent based on the *śatṛ* suffix.

The compound is formed by the elision of the second member according to the rule *śākapārthivāditvāt* (Vārttika 83). Regarding the forms *tudatī* and *nuktī*: [the suffix] *laṭ* is applied to the roots *tud* (DhP 1281) and *nud* (DhP 1282); because they belong to the *tud*-class, the suffix *śa* is added, which is udātta on its final syllable due to the accent of the affix (*pratyayasvara*). When the *lasārvadhātuka* accent becomes anudātta, [the vowel] *a-*...

By [Pāṇini 6.1.97] *guṇe*, the single substitute is the subsequent form (*pararūpa*). And by [Pāṇini 8.2.5] *ekādeśa udātenodātaḥ*, that [substitute] is acute (*udātta*), because that acute [quality] is established as valid. While the term "from a final acute" (*antodātāt*) is being carried over from [Pāṇini 6.1.169] *antodātād uttarapadāt*, [the rule] *śaturanumo nadyajādī* (6.1.173) applies.

The vowel *ī* following a word ending in a present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) that is oxytone becomes udātta. However, if [the substitution of] *an* were considered *asiddha*, then this *ī* would not be udātta after the monophthongization (*ekādeśa*), because of the governing rule (6.1.169) stating "after that which ends in an udātta.
[The author] refutes this purpose by relying on the *jñāpaka* provided by the rule beginning with "anumaḥ" (6.4.87).
How, then, is this an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? He says: "For not... and so forth. The word *hi* indicates a reason.
The purpose of this prohibition [of *num*] by the term *anuma* is as follows:
in the forms *tudantī* and *nudantī*, once *num* has been applied by the rule *ācchīnadyornum* (Pāṇini 7.1.80), there should be no acute accent (*udāttatva*) for that which possesses *num*.

[The rule] "bhūt" [is stated]. Furthermore, if the accent of the *śatṛ* suffix were [already established], the accent of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*), and the prohibition [of that accent] would be rendered useless; for without the accent of the single-substitute, there is no final acute (*antodātta*) nature for the *śatṛ* suffix. Therefore, from this prohibition, it is understood that the accent of the single-substitute is indeed established (*siddha*).

For there is no word ending in *śatṛ* that has the acute accent (*udātta*) on its final syllable except for those with the augment *num*; therefore, the prohibitive statement "except when *num* follows" (*anum*) is indeed an *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence).
As in the examples "tudan-ti" and "likhan-ti," here too, by the rule of the unaccented nature of the *sārvadhātuka* suffix, as previously explained—

Once the acute accent (*udātta*) has been applied, the single substitute for both the acute and the grave (*anudātta*) is acute. By the phrase "by that," it is meant by the established accent of the single substitute (*ekādeśasvara*). By the phrase "the state of being excluded" (*varjyamānatā*), the meaning of Pāṇini 6.1.158, "A word consisting of a single syllable is grave," is indicated; [this applies] having excluded one [syllable].

The meaning is that the remainder becomes unaccented (*anudātta*). However, if [the substitution] were *asiddha*, then when the rule "a word is unaccented except for one syllable" (*anudātam padam ekavarjam*, 6.1.158) is to be applied, the accent of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) would be *asiddha*, and since the [substituted vowel] would not be excluded (*varjyamānatā*), [the rule would fail].
The hearing of two udātta vowels would result [as a fault].

But has it not been stated that the mention of *asiddha* is for the purpose of establishing the general rule (*utsarga-lakṣaṇa*), and that the substitute (*sthānin*) here is svarita? For instance, in the case of *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97), there is the substitution of a single subsequent form (*pararūpatva*).

By this very rule (*anta*), which prescribes that for a circumflex vowel (*svarita*) occurring at the end of a word, the single constituent part (*ekadeśa*) in place of it is acute (*udātta*) according to *8.2.5* (*udātasvaritayoryaṇaḥ svarito 'nudāttasya*), an acute substitute is enjoined; in that case, if— on account of the non-established status (*asiddhatva*) of that acute substitute— the exclusion (*varjyamānatā*) conditioned by it does not occur, then [the desired result follows].
[Objection: But since its substitute is this circumflex (*svarita*), [the rule] will have that as its cause;
so how is this purpose established? [Response: It is explained how it is established—in the rule *ekādeśa udātenodātāḥ* (8.2.5), there are four [cases].

Regarding the rules for *darśana* [the observation of accentual changes]: by rules such as "ṭhādguṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.87), a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) arising from the combination of an acute (*udātta*) and a grave (*anudātta*) vowel results in the quality of the circumflex (*svarita*), because of the closest phonetic proximity (*āntaratamya*). Of that [circumflex], [the rule] "ṭhekādeśa udātenodātaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.5) [applies].
By this [sūtra], one view is that the quality of udātta is prescribed as a substitute in place of the svarita;
the second view is that once the svarita quality has been produced, another quality takes its place, whereby it is understood as a different sound.
This third view is that the rule "a single substitute for an acute and a non-acute vowel is acute" is a *paribhāṣā*.

In this view, because the *paribhāṣā* is subordinate to the main rules, it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the rules concerning single substitutes; therein, the following meaning is established: "the *guṇa* substitute [of the form] *āt* occurs."

"But for an acute (udātta) and a grave (anudātta), the single substitute (ekādeśa) is acute" (Pāṇini 6.1.87). However, the fourth view is this: that single substitute which occurs between an acute and a grave becomes acute, and is not endowed with the quality of circumflex (svarita). Thus, the status of being acute is introduced as an exception to the circumflex. By which...

This purpose has been set forth by relying on this very view according to the principle of non-attainment (*aprāpti-vyāya*). And that [purpose] is indeed appropriate in this view; for here, indeed, the state of being acute (*udātta*) is prescribed at the very same time as the prescription [of the rule], and not [after] that which is prescribed as having the quality of circumflex (*svarita*).

Furthermore, it is not possible for the quality of being acute (*udātta*) to be the substitute (*ādeśa*), because the original element (*sthānin*) which is circumflex (*svarita*) would be excluded; this is because the accent of the single substitute (*ekādeśasvara*) is already established. [As stated:
"Once that has been applied, there is the suppression (*nighāta*) by the rule *tiṅṅtiṅ*. However, if that were not the case...

If [the substitution] were established first, the accent of the single substitute would subsequently apply, and consequently, the state of being accented on the middle syllable (*madhyodātatā*) would result.
In the case of *pacati*: here, the vowel *i* in the word *ti* is unaccented because it is *satiśiṣṭa* (left over after other operations have applied);
the word *iti*, however, is accented on the first syllable according to *nipātā ādyudātāḥ* (Phiṭ-sūtra 4.80). From these two, the *ak* [substitution occurs].

The single-substitute *savarṇadīrgha* is *bahiraṅga* because it depends on two bases (*pāda*); since it is *bahiraṅga*, the accent (*svara*) dependent upon it is also *bahiraṅga*. Consequently, the vowel *i* remains as if non-existent (*asiddha*). And thus, by that [rule], "a word is unaccented except for one [vowel]."

Thus, there is no exclusion [of the verb from the accent]. In the case of *prapacati*, because it is also *asiddha* due to being *bahiraṅga*, the rule *tiṅ codātavati* (Pāṇini 8.1.71) does not apply to render the movement (*gati*) unaccented;
rather, here only the *nighāta* (elision of the accent) applies by the rule *tiṅṅtiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28).
It occurs as follows: *ṭhharivo medinam*. From the word *hari*, the suffix *matup* is added; then *su*; then *num*;

then the elision [of the final vowel] according to Pāṇini 6.1.68 (*halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*); and finally, the elision of the final consonant cluster according to 8.2.23 (*saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*). In that [form],...

When *kṛ* is applied, the substitution of *u* by the rule "haśi ca" (6.1.114) occurs, followed by the *guṇa* substitution by "ādguṇaḥ" (6.1.87). [Objection: "Since the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the substitution of *u* by 'haśi ca' does not apply. [Response: While the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct remains non-existent, [the substitute] *iś* [applies] to the letter *t*.
Because of the intervention of the letter *m*, and because the letter *t* is not a *ha*-letter.
[The rule] "after *th* and the rest" applies: the *luṅ* suffix, *sic* for *cli*, *iṭ*, and by [Pāṇini 7.3.96] "for *asti* and *sic* before an unaccented [suffix]," there is *iṭ*;
then the *vṛddhi* of the *sic* vowel, and by [Pāṇini 8.2.28] "when *iṭ* follows *iṭ*," there is the elision of *sic*, resulting in *akaḥ*.
There is lengthening by *savarṇadīrgha*.
[The examples are] "vṛkṇaḥ" and "vṛkṇavān. [This is derived from] the root *vraścū* in the sense of "cutting" (*dhā.pā.* 1292), with the *niṣṭhā* suffix;
there is *samprasāraṇa* by the rule *grahijyādi* (6.1.16), and [the change of the *c* to *k*] by the rule *coḥ kuḥ* (8.2.30).

There is the substitution of *k* by rule 8.2.45 (*kutvaṃ ṭhoditaśca*), the substitution of *n* by rule 8.2.45 (*ṭhoditaśca*), and the substitution of *ṇ* by rule 8.4.2 (*aṭkupvāṅ*). Since the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur, there is the elision of *s* by rule 8.2.29 (*skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ*).
[The substitution of *k*] is indeed treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the substitution of *ṇ*.

He demonstrates the purpose of excluding [the word *kṣība*] from the rules concerning the substitution of *ṣatva*, vowels (*svara*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), and the application of the augment *iṭ* by stating: "In the rules regarding vowels, suffixes, and the application of *iṭ*, the word *kṣība* is cited as an example. But how is it possible for the single word *kṣība* alone to serve as an example for all three types of rules?

Thus he says, beginning with "therein" (*tatra*), and so forth. In the rule *anupasargāt phulla-kṣīva-* (Pāṇini 8.2.55), the word *kṣība* is established as a nipātana (irregular formation) after the suffix *kta* has followed the root *kṣīb* in the sense of "intoxication" (Dhātupāṭha 382). In that case, a nipātana was resorted to even when multiple subsequent elements [such as suffixes] were present. Therein...

The word *kṣība* is cited as an example in some instances for the prescription of suffixes (*pratyaya*) following a nipātana, and in others for the prescription of accents (*svara*), and in some cases for the prescription of the augment *iṭ*. How so? He says: "When," etc.

The inclusion of the phrase beginning with "in a name" (*saṃjñāyām*) is [an extension] from the rule "In a name, that which is a standard of comparison [retains its original accent]" (Pāṇini 6.1.204).

Because the mention of the term *saṃjñā* continues [from the previous rule], [the rule] "this has the accent" (*eṣa svaraḥ*) means that it is *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable). For in that context, the mention of *udātta* from [Pāṇini 6.1.159] "the final syllable of a word ending in *ghañ* preceded by *karṣa* or a long vowel is *udātta*" continues,
and the mention of *ādi* (beginning) from [Pāṇini 6.1.197] "a word ending in *ñ* or *n* is always *ādyudātta*" would also apply.
Since the elision of the syllable *ucc-* is considered as if it had not taken place (*asiddha*), the word *kṣība* does not consist of two syllables (*advyacka*).

For when the elision of *ucc-* is *asiddha*, the word *kṣība* does not become two-syllabled; rather, it is three-syllabled (*tryacka*). Thus, [the form] "kṣībikaḥ" is derived by [the rule] *naudvyacaṣṭhan* (Pāṇini 4.4.7), with the augment *iṭ*.

[The form] "prāpnoti" [is derived] because the elision of the letter *t* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*); this is due to the fact that the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix begins with a consonant (*balādi*). [Examples are: "agnātricchatram" (an umbrella desired by Agni) and "paṭātricchatram" (an umbrella desired by Paṭu).

When the vocative case (*sambuddhi*) is applied to the words *agnipatuh* and *agni*, the short vowel undergoes *guṇa* substitution; subsequently, by the rule "eṅ hrasvāt sambuddheḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.69), the vocative suffix is elided. Then, by the rule "eco 'pragṛhyasyādūrāddhūte pūrvasyārdhasyādūt tarasyedūt" (Pāṇini 8.2.107), the *ikāra* and *ukāra* [of the preceding and following sounds] are replaced by *ekāra* and *okāra*.

The form of the preceding sound is dependent on its meaning, and that [meaning] in turn depends on the subsequent sound, namely the vowels *i* and *u* respectively. Thus, the rule "it is always *tug*" would apply; however, this is desired to be permanent.
Yet, by the rule "optionally after a word-final [sound]" (6.1.76), an option would apply, and that is undesirable.

Therefore, it must be stated that when the *tuṅ* augment is prescribed, the substitution of the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is established. Why [is the condition] "after *cch*" specified? So that the protracted vowel substitution remains unestablished (*asiddha*) in other instances where the *tuṅ* augment is prescribed—as in *khalam punāti brahmaṇakulam*. [This applies also] in the case of the *kvip* suffix, by the rule "the final vowel of a neuter nominal stem is shortened" (*hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya*, 7.1.23).
There is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix], and by *hrasvasya guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.108), there is *guṇa* substitution as before; this is a modification of the protracted vowel (*pluta*).
Because this [substitution] is considered *asiddha*, in the case of *khalapu*, the augment *tuk* prescribed by *hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk* (Pāṇini 6.1.71) does not occur.

"ṭh-ś-cu-tvaṃ dhuṭi," etc. [Examples: *aṭścyotati*, *raṭścyotati*. From the roots *aṭ* and *raṭ* in the sense of "motion" (*gatau*; Dhātupāṭha 295, 297), the suffix *kvip* is applied; then *su-* is added, followed by the elision of the final consonant and the following vowel according to Pāṇini 6.1.68 (*halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*); finally, by Pāṇini 8.2.39 (*jhalāṃ jaśo'nte*), the letter *ṭ* is changed to *ḍ*. In that [form]...
Because the substitution of *ścu* (the change of *s* to *ś*) is not established (*asiddha*) when the sound *ścyotati* follows, the augment *dhuṭ* does not apply.
Therefore, it must be stated that the substitution of *ścu* is established (*siddha*) when the application of *dhuṭ* is to be performed. But for what purpose is this [stated]?
And so forth. However, for this *sakāra*, [the substitution] does not occur in some places or in others.

The intention is that there is such hearing [of the form]. Regarding the phrase "madhuścyat": by the rule "he does that" or "he describes that" (Vārttika 209), one forms *madhuścyutamācaṣṭe*; then, when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied, by the rule "the nominal stem is treated like the *iṣṭhan* suffix" (Vārttika 813), there is the elision of the *ṇic*. When the form *madhuścyit* has been established...
From the form ending in *ṇyac*, there is again the suffix *kvip*; by the rule "ṇeraniṭi" (Pāṇini 6.4.51), there is the elision of the *ṇi* affix.

Because the substitution of *ś* for *s* (*ścutva*) is considered asiddha, the *s* which is the initial member of the *saṃyoga* [cluster] is elided by the rule "sphoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.29); thereafter, the *y* is elided by the rule "saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.23).

Then, by the rule "ṭhcoḥ kuḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.30), there is the substitution of *k* for the *c*; thus, the desired form "madhuk" is obtained. The intention [of the author] would be that this [form] is read with an initial *s* for that purpose. But one might ask: does this form not occur even when [the suffix] begins with *ś*? To this he says: "when beginning with *ś*..."

Again, regarding this passage beginning with "in this," first there is the elision of the *yakāra* at the end of the conjunction according to Pāṇini 8.2.23 (*saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*). Once the *yakāra* has been elided, the *cakāra* becomes the final member of a conjunction;
therefore, that too is elided. Then, when the *śakāra* undergoes the change to *ṣa* by the rule beginning with *vraśca-* (8.2.36), [the following occurs].

By the rule *ṭhjhalāṃ jaśo'nte* (Pāṇini 8.2.39), the *ṣ* of *madhuṣ* would necessarily become *ḍ* before the suffix *tiP*, resulting in *madhuṅti*. [This is not desired. As for *babhaṇatuḥ* and *babhaṇuḥ*, these derive from the roots *aṇa*, *raṇa*, and *bhaṇa* (Dhātupāṭha 444, 445, 447).

From this [root], the *liṭ* suffix is applied; after its reduplication, by the rule "abhyāse carcā" (Pāṇini 8.4.54), there is the substitution of a *jaś*-sound—namely, the letter *b*. Since that [substitution] is considered asiddha, this [reduplicated form] is regarded as having no substitute for its initial sound; consequently, the rule "ata ekahalmadhye 'nādeśāder liṭi" (Pāṇini 6.4.120) would require the substitution of *etva* (the change of *a* to *e*).

Regarding the form *vicicchitsati*: this is the desiderative (*san*) of the root *cchid*. There is reduplication of *cchid*, and by the rule *abhyāse car ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.54), the letter *c* is substituted for the *ch*;

because that [substitution] is established as valid, the augment *tuk* does not apply to the syllable *ci* when followed by the reduplicated syllable, according to the rule *che ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.73). Regarding the form *ucicchiṣati*: this is from the root *ucchī*.

In the case of *vivāsiṣati* (from the root *vas* with the desiderative suffix *san*), because the substitution of *u* for *va* by Pāṇini 6.1.2 (*ajāder dvitīyasya*) is an internal operation (*antaranga*), the augment *tuk* is applied first; consequently, the form *tcchis* is reduplicated.
Therein, by the rule "the *kha*-preceded [consonants] remain when followed by *khayaḥ*" (Vārttika 878), the letter *cch* remains, and as before, the change to *t* occurs.
Because that [augment] is already established, the *tuk* augment does not occur for the vowel *u*.
For example: *sayaṃyantā*, *savaṃvatsaraḥ*, and so forth; likewise in the case of *sam* followed by *yant-* and the word *vatsara*, as in *yallokaṃ tallokam*.
When the word *loka* follows the second singular forms of *yad-* and *etad-*, the rule *mo 'nusvāre* (Pāṇini 8.3.23) prescribes an *anusvāra* for the final *m*.
Then, by the rule *anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ* (8.4.58), that *anusvāra* is replaced by a *parasavarṇa* (a sound homogeneous with the following consonant).

Since this substitution is made as a nasalized *yayi* (a semivowel or spirant) based on internal proximity (*āntarya*), it is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) for the purposes of subsequent operations.
While the rule *ṭhyaro'nunāsike'nunāsiko vā* (8.4.45) is in effect,
the rule *ṭhanaci ca* (8.4.47) would not result in the doubling of the *yar* sounds; consequently, in that alternative case, the doubling of the three *ya*-sounds and so forth would not occur.

Regarding the passage beginning with "If [the rule] *padādhikāraś cet*": if the term *padasya* from Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.16 does not carry over (*anuvartate*) into rules concerning the substitution of *l* and so forth, then reduplication of a word (*pada*) would possess the status of being extrinsically conditioned (*bahiraṅgatva*), because the reduplication of a non-word (*apada*) is equivalent to the reduplication of a word.

Furthermore, the substitution of *l* and so forth is *antaraṅga*. This is because, according to the principle "that which is *bahiraṅga* is as if non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is *antaraṅga*" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 42), when the substitutions of *l* and so forth are to be applied, the doubling (*dvirvacana*) is already established [the reading *dvirvacanasyāsiddham* is found in the Prācīna-mūla-pāṭha;
the phrase *dvirvacanena* refers to the fact that the doubling has taken effect].

Because [the rule] is established—according to the reading in the *Kāśikā*: "that which is not established (*asiddha*) in what precedes" (Pāṇini 6.4.22)—this [rule] does not apply; consequently, first there must be the substitution of *l* and so forth, and once those have occurred, subsequently there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*), whereby the desired result is indeed accomplished when the governing heading of "word" (*pada*) is in effect.

Since the substitution of *l* for *r* (*latvādi*) and other such operations are also extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*), they are non-existent according to the maxim "that which is extrinsic is as if non-existent" (*asatyā bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā*). Therefore, when these [extrinsic operations] are present, reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is established; however, the substitution of *l* and so forth is not yet effective when this [reduplication] is to be performed, because of the rule "that which is earlier is as if non-existent" (*pūrvatrāsiddhatvāt*, Pāṇini 8.2.1). Consequently, reduplication occurs first.
If [the rule for] *la*-substitution and the others were applied after [the formation of the word], then an undesirable result would also follow.
Therefore, if there is an extension of the heading [to the word] *pada*, then the *la*-substitutions and so forth must be stated as established. For example:
*galo galaḥ* (from the root *gal*); and *mṛṅ* [is used] in the sense of "swallowing" (*nigaraṇe*); and *nunnaḥ*; and *mudaviva*.

By [the rule] (8.2.56), the letter *n* is substituted, and optionally the letter *t*. Thus: *abhino 'phabhinah*. This is derived from the root *bhid* with the suffix *laṅ*, the suffix *sip*, the augment *śnam*, and the elision of the *hal* and *ṅit* suffixes by (6.1.68). Then, by (8.2.74), *sip* is replaced by *ru* after a verbal root ending in *u*; and by (8.2.75), *ru* is optionally replaced by *r*. As before, [the following rule applies]: *ato*...

The substitution of *u* [for the vowel *ṛ*] occurs by the rule *ror aplutād aplute* (Pāṇini 6.1.113). Then, *guṇa* substitution applies by the rule *ād guṇaḥ* (6.1.87), resulting in *mātṛṣvasā* and *pitṛṣvasā*. The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs optionally by the rule *mātuḥpitṛbhyām anyatarasyām* (8.3.85).
[In the example] *māṣavāpāṇi*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs optionally by the rule *vā bhāvakaraṇayoḥ*.

While this [rule] continues to apply, there is *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*) by the rule "ṭh-prātipadika-anta-num-bhaktiṣu" (Pāṇini 8.4.11). Thus, we have *vāṅnayanam*. Alternatively, by the rule "yaro 'nunāsike 'nunāsiko vā" (Pāṇini 8.4.45), there is optionally an *anunāsika* (nasalization). Thus, we have *vākcchayanam*. [And] from "jhayo... [the following applies].

While the rule *ho 'nyatarasyām* (8.4.62) is in effect, the substitution of *cha* [for *ha*] optionally occurs by *śaś chāeṭi* (8.4.63). Regarding the phrase "of the *la*-substitutions, etc.," this demonstrates the fault that arises for the *la*-substitutions and so forth when they are considered asiddha. Because the *la*-substitutions and others are asiddha, [the operation takes place] prior to them...

Once the doubling has been performed, since this rule operates as an optional injunction (*vikalpa-vidhi*) at a later stage, just as it applies in the preceding case, so too— by virtue of the restrictive application— it does not apply in the subsequent case either; thus, non-application (*aniyoga*) is obtained.

Because there is no cause for restriction, an undesirable alternative would follow: that [the word] would apply to both the preceding and the following [words] in one instance, yet not apply to the other. Such an undesirable alternative is not accepted. If that were the case, *gara* would be *gala*, and *gala* would be *gara*.

Thus, such undesirable consequences as these would follow. In that case, the rule should simply be formulated as "na" with respect to undesirable cases. For what purpose? To prohibit the application of the principle of *pūrvatrāsiddham* (the non-validity of what precedes) in undesirable contexts. Where there is an undesirable result regarding *pūrvatrāsiddham*, [the rule] then follows as "bhu ne."

This very point follows from the statement here: if this [rule] exists, for what purpose is it stated, since the prohibition is already established by the preceding rule? It is for the purpose of indicating that that [preceding] rule does not apply everywhere. Therefore, it operates only where its non-application (asiddhatva) is desired.
But that reversal does not occur elsewhere; for in this sūtra, there is a division of the grammatical connection (yogavibhāga).

4. *udātasvaritayoryaṇaḥ svarito 'nudātasya* (8.2.4). [The commentary says: "Of the *yaṇ* substitute for an acute (*udātta*) vowel, and of the *yaṇ* substitute for a circumflex (*svarita*) vowel. The meaning is: that *yaṇ* which occurs in place of an acute vowel is a *udātayaṇ*; that *yaṇ* which occurs in place of a circumflex vowel is a *svaritayaṇ*. [Examples: *kumāryau*, *kumāryaḥ*.

Thus: here, by the rule "anudāttau suppitau" (Pāṇini 3.1.4), the case-endings *au* and *jas* are unaccented (*anudātta*). When these follow [the word-final vowel] which is a *udātayaṇ* (an *udātta*-marked *yaṇ*-substitute), the resulting [vowel] becomes *svarita*. Regarding the phrase "by the *udātanivṛtti-svara*":
this is the accent caused by the elision of an *udātta*, because there is an elision of a preceding *udātta* due to it.

Furthermore, that which was prescribed by the rule *punarudātanivṛtisvaraḥ ṭhanudātasya ca yatrodātalopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.161) should be understood as not applying here—according to the reading in the Kāśikā-muṇḍī commentary. [The words] *kṛtsvareṇāntodātau* and *lvyā pvyā* [are formed]; from the roots *lū* and *pū*.

By means of the *dhātu-svara* (the accent of the verbal root), [the word] ends in an acute accent (*udātta*) due to the suffix *kvip*. There is a compound by the rule *upapadam atiṅ* (Pāṇini 2.2.19). Because the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139) prescribes that a *kṛt*-derived word which is a final member [of a compound] retains its original accent (*prakṛtibhāva*), these two [words] [retain their respective accents].

"Both [the locative singular and the nominative plural] become udātta with their entire vowel. And there is the substitution of udātta-yaṇ. By this rule, svarita is prescribed for that which follows two anudātta vowels when udātta-yaṇ follows;
and svarita is prescribed for the seventh case singular (locative) following svarita-yaṇ by means of the former method.

He shows this with the rule: "tasya yo yaṇ. By the word *tasya*, there is a reference to the locative singular [of the word *āśā*]. Regarding the phrase "of the anudātta vowel of the word *āśā*": according to the *Phitsūtra* 1.18, "if *āśā* does not denote a direction," the word *āśā* is udātta on its first syllable; therefore, [the vowel] is *anudātta*.

By the rule *padamekavarjam* (Pāṇini 6.1.158), the vowel *ā* is unaccented. Regarding the phrase "But surely... and so forth: the circumflex (*svarita*) accent prescribed by this sūtra *udāttayaṇaḥ* for the locative singular ending is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) when the substitution of *yaṇ* according to the rules of the sixth book (*ṣāṣṭhika*) is to be applied.

Consequently, this [substitution] is not a *yaṇ* substitute in place of a *svarita*; thus, the intention is that in examples such as *sakṛllvyāśā* and *khalapvyaśā*, the *svarita* accent does not occur. Regarding the phrase "because of its dependence" (*āśrayāt*), etc., he says: "This is a *svarita-yaṇ*"; however, a *svarita* is nowhere established [as such]. In that case, because of its dependence...
There will be establishedness (*siddhatva*), just as in the case of *rutva* in the rule "ṭhato roraplutādaplute" (Pāṇini 6.1.113).
[The objection] beginning with "If this were so... and so forth [is raised]. By this, [it is shown that] establishedness arises from the basis (*āśraya*).

He raises the objection of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) when [the rule] is applied: "in *dadhyāśā*. The word *dadhi* is acute on its first syllable by the rule *nabviṣayasyānisantasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 2.26); the remainder is unaccented (*anudātta*). Then, by the rule *udāttādanudātasya svaritaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.66), the following [syllable] becomes circumflex (*svarita*).

The vowel *i* following the letter *dh* is *svarita*. If its status as established (*siddhatva*) were due to its being the basis [of the subsequent operation], then the vowel *ā* of the word *āśā*, which follows the *aṇ* (vowel) substituted for that [original *i*], would also become *svarita*. Regarding the phrase "therefore," etc.:
since this over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) occurs when the status of being established is resorted to on the basis of such a foundation.

It occurs; therefore, it must be stated that this very *yaṇ*-vowel which is prescribed by this sūtra (8.2.4) is established (*siddha*) when a *yaṇ* substitution is to be applied. The meaning of the phrase "it must be stated" (*vaktavyam*) is as follows:
that [statement] must be formulated by resorting to the division of the rule into sections (*yogavibhāga*), just as was done previously.

"Some, however," and so forth. By the words "If this were so," etc., he refutes the objection of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that was raised, according to the opinion of some. Over-extension is the application [of a rule] even to an undesired object. And [the rule] "after an acute (*udātta*), there is a circumflex (*svarita*) for the grave (*anudātta*)" (Pāṇini 8.4.66) [is not subject to such over-extension].

By this [rule], the desirability of regarding as established (siddhatva) that svarita which is prescribed after an udātta— by virtue of its being its locus— is denied; for since the svarita-yaṇ following that udātta is the cause of the svaritatva of the subsequent anudātta,
the yaṇ possesses the status of a substitute (sthānitva).

In another recension of the Taittirīya school, the vowel *ā* of the word *āśā* (in the compound *parasyāśā*) is read as having the *svarita* accent; whereas the vowel *ā* of the word *agni* has the *anudātta* accent, because it is *udātta* on its final syllable by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). "Likewise in the Brāhmaṇa" [is the statement].

[Thus it is not so—according to the Prācya reading, a specific portion of that [word] is intended here by the word *brāhmaṇa*. In the case of "dadhyāśayati," since the root *aś* takes the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the vowel *a* following the final udātta syllable is anudātta, whether by the accent of the verbal root or by the accent of the *cit* suffix. For that [anudātta vowel], which follows a svarita *yaṇ*...]
In the *Brāhmaṇa*, the state of being *svarita* is recited, as in "yathā tu" and so forth. By this, he supports that very same over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
It was stated by the author of the *Vārttika*: "If it is argued that [the rule] is established up to the end of the section, then [the objection applies] regarding a *svarita* following an *udātta*."

"There is a fault. This is its meaning: if it were intended that the circumflex (*svarita*) nature of an unaccented vowel following a *yaṇ*—which itself follows a circumflex that has become established by virtue of its basis [in a preceding circumflex]—should be desired, then there would be a fault. Therefore, the circumflex nature [of such a vowel] is not [produced] by this rule.

It is established that [the vowel] becomes [circumflex]. For by this Vārttika, the meaning—that a circumflex (svarita) arises for an unaccented (anudātta) vowel following a circumflex semivowel (svaritayaṇ) which itself follows an acute (udātta)—is not understood. Therefore, this is not so; rather, it should be as follows: [the circumflex arises] for the acute [vowel] following this circumflex semivowel.

It is thus established that a *svarita* does not occur for a following unaccented (*anudātta*) vowel. By the words "in that way" (*tathā*) and so forth, he immediately confirms this very point. For in the Bhāṣya, by the passage beginning with "the mention of *svarita* will not be made," it is shown that the mention of *svarita* is not required in the rule (*sūtra*).
It is rejected. And this rejection is justified only if the svarita-ness of an unaccented vowel following a svarita-yaṇ that originates from an udātta is not desired;
otherwise, if the svarita produced by that cause were indeed desired, the rejection would not be justified at all. Why? [“ki”]...
[Objection: In the *Prācīna* reading, the inclusion of the *svarita-yaṇ* in the Bhāṣya is rejected;

however, if that [inclusion] is rejected, how is it that the *svarita* of the unaccented vowel is not established in cases such as *sakṛllvyāśā*? To this, he says: "In *sakṛllvyāśā* and so forth," etc.

In this case, however, there is only one *yakāra* in the *udātta-yaṇ* [substitute] for the vowel *u* and the semivowel *v*. But surely, because of the intervention by that which arises in place of the seventh-case singular ending, the rule would not be established? To this he says:
"The *svarita-yaṇ*," etc. He states the very reason for this here: "In the prescription of accent," etc.
The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).
If [the desired result] can be established even without the mention of *svarita*, why is that term included in the sūtra?
To this he says: "But that is done," and so forth. [Regarding the rule] *acaḥ parasmin*...

For the intended meaning of *pūrvavidhau* (Pāṇini 1.1.57) is this: "When an operation (*vidhi*) is to be performed based on what precedes [the substitute], the substitute (*ādeśa*) for *ac* becomes like the original (*sthānivat*). This applies when a circumflex (*svarita*) is to be prescribed for an unaccented vowel following a vowel with an acute (*udātta*) *yaṇ*, regarding the substitution of *yaṇ* in place of the locative singular ending.
There is an intervention by the vowel *i* due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*);

for, according to the rule "in the prescription of an accent, a consonant is as if non-existent" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 37), when such an intervention exists—as in *sakṛllvyāśā*—the rule *udāttayaṇaḥ* would not otherwise apply. Therefore, the term *svarita* is included [in the sūtra].

[The substitution] is performed. But surely, by the rule *ṭhnapadāntaradvirvacana* (Pāṇini 1.1.58), the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is prohibited in the case of vowel rules (*svaravidhi*). Therefore, how can there be an intervention? To this he says: "In the case of vowel [rules], long [vowel rules], and the elision of *y* (*yalopa*)," and so forth. For [the prohibition applies] to the substitute that is an elision of a vowel (*aco lopādeśasya*).

In the rule concerning accents (svaravidhi), the status of being *sthānivadbhāva* is prohibited. For it is stated therein: "In the case of accentuation, long vowels, and the elision of *y*, a substitute for an elided element (*lopādeśa*) [is not treated as the original]. (Note: The reading *lopājādeśaḥ* is found in the Kāśīmudrita edition; the reading *lopādeśaḥ* is found in the Kāśīmudrita text.)

It should be stated that [the substitute] does not behave like the original (sthānivat). Furthermore, in this case, there is no substitution for the elision of a vowel (ac-lopa); rather, there is a substitution of *yaṇ*. Therefore, there is no prohibition of the status of being like the original.
[The example is] "vaidyāśā. [This is derived] from "vidasyāpatyam" by means of the rule "anṛṣyānantarye" (Pāṇini 4.1.104), etc.
Because [the root] *vid* belongs to the *vidi-ādi* group, the suffix *añ* is applied; from that form ending in *añ*, the suffix *ṅīn* is added by the rule *śāṅgaravādyaño ṅīn* (Pāṇini 4.1.73).
Here, once the acute accent (*udātta*) has been applied to the first syllable due to the *nit* designation, the remaining syllables become grave (*anudātta*).
Thus, in the word *baidyāśā*, the *yaṇ* substitute occurs in place of a grave vowel, not in place of an acute or a circumflex (*svarita*) vowel.

Regarding the word "atra": it is acutely accented on its first syllable due to the accent of the *lit* suffix; it ends in the suffix *tral* by virtue of the rule *saptamyāstral* (Pāṇini 5.3.10); and the form *id* is elided by the rule *hali loḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.113).

5. *ekādeśa udātenodātaḥ* (8.2.5). [The rule] *anudātasya* [is understood here]. When there is a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for an unaccented vowel together with an accented vowel, that substitute shall be accented (*udātta*), and not circumflex (*svarita*). This is commenced because the circumflex accent would otherwise have applied.

In the examples, *agni* and the others are oxytone by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*; Phiṭ-sūtra 1.1). However, the case ending is anudātta according to "the *su*- and *ti*-affixes are anudātta" (Pāṇini 3.1.4). Thus, we have *agnī*, *vāyū*. The long vowel [in *agnī*] is due to "the single substitute for the first two [vowels] is the homogeneous long vowel" (Pāṇini 6.1.102). [Similarly,] *vṛkṣau*, *plakṣau*.

Thus: by the rule "vṛddhir eci" (Pāṇini 6.1.88), there is vṛddhi [in *pacanti* and *yajanti*]. By the rule "ato guṇe" (Pāṇini 6.1.97), there is the substitution of the subsequent form [in *pacanti* and *yajanti*]. [The Vārttika states: "This single substitute occurs for two anudātta vowels. But [one might object]: "Is it not the case that [the rule] 'udātād anudātasya'..."

Since the letter *śa* has been made *svarita* by the rule "svaritaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.66), this single substitute (*ekādeśa*) results from a *svarita* and an *anudātta*; how then can it be said that [the rule] applies to two *anudātta*s?
To this he replies: "Because the *svarita* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is to be applied."

6. *svarito vānudātte padādau* (Pāṇini 8.2.6). In the example *sūtthitaḥ*, there is a compound according to *kugatiprādayaḥ* (2.2.18). It is stated that "here the word *su* is a *karmapravacanīya*"; by this, it removes the status of *su* as a *gati*. For if it were a *gati*...
Otherwise, by the rule *sati ṭhgatirgatau* (Pāṇini 8.1.70), there would be a *nighāta* (elision of the accent);

consequently, this single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) would not be [an instance of] an unaccented vowel (*anudātta*) replacing an accented vowel (*udātta*). Regarding the phrase "in a *prādi*-compound," etc.: the word *su-* is acutely accented (*ādyudātta*) at its beginning; for when a *prādi*-compound is formed, in the case of a *tatpuruṣa*...

By the rule *tulyārtha* (Pāṇini 6.2.2) and others, the initial syllable becomes udātta because of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member of the compound. Therefore, by virtue of that original accent, this substitution occurs, since the long vowel resulting from the homogeneity of similar vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*) remains unaccented when it stands at the beginning of a word. For the word *su*, which is udātta on its initial syllable—

Since the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) applies, it is logical that the remainder (*śeṣa*) should be unaccented (*anudātta*). But surely, regarding the rule for *prādi*-compounds, the reading in the Vārttika is "in the case of *prādi*" (*prādisamāse*), and it has been stated: "A prohibition must be stated for *karmapravacanīya*s" (Vārttika 96). How then can there be a *prādi*-compound here? This is not a fault.

Because that *su* is non-eternal (*anityatva*). Its non-eternality, however, is to be understood from its usage in the *su-śāmādi* group (Pāṇini 8.3.98). For in that context, since [the form] would already be established by [the rule] *upasargāt sunoti* (8.3.65) and others, its inclusion there is for the sake of cases where it is not a prefix (*anupasarga*). And the non-prefixed status of *su* is [established by the fact that] *suḥ*...

Because of the status of *karmapravacanīya* [assigned] by the rule "pūjāyām" (Pāṇini 1.4.94). Alternatively, this prohibition applies to those *prādi* prefixes other than *su* and *ati*; for it is stated in that context that in the case of praise (*pūjā*), there is a compound with the words *su* and *ati*, as expressed by the rule "svatī pūjāyām" (Kāśikā 2.2.18), and [this applies] when there is praise.
The status of these two as *karmapravacanīya*s is intended [here].

Regarding the word "dīkṣate": the prefix *vi-* is acute on its first syllable by virtue of the accent of the *nipātana* (irregular formation). Here too, when the elision (*nighāta*) of the finite verb has been applied according to Pāṇini 8.1.28 (*tiṅṅtiṅaḥ*), the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is grave (*anudātta*) because it occurs at the beginning of a word.

The word "it occurs" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the connection. Regarding the example *vasuko 'si*: the word *vasu* is oxytone by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). Then, because it ends in the suffix *su*, when followed by the word *asi*, the substitution of *u* (*utva*) occurs for the final *s* according to Pāṇini 6.1.113: *ato ror aplutād aplute*. Of that [substituted *u*]...

By virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule, because it possesses the nature of a *sup*-suffix, the vowel *am* is unaccented (*anudātta*). Together with the preceding [element], there is *guṇa* substitution according to Pāṇini 6.1.87;
and that [resulting form] is acutely accented on the final syllable (*ṇāntodāta*) by the previous sūtra (8.2.5). Regarding the form *tasi*:
after the elision of the *s* by Pāṇini 7.4.50 (*tāsy-astyor-lopaḥ*), this is the form in the present tense (*laṭ*) with the suffix *sip*.

Here, by the rule *ṭhtiṅṅtiṅḥ* (8.1.28), the vowel *ā* is unaccented (*anudātta*). When this [vowel] is combined with the following *ā* by the rule *ṭheṅḥ padāntādati* (6.1.109), the latter is substituted for both, resulting in a single long vowel. Regarding the phrase "the mention of *svarita*" and so forth: how, indeed, can there be a *svarita* accent in the absence of the mention of *svarita*?

An injunction (ādeśa) is made; furthermore, the mention of *svarita* again is for the sake of clarity, not for the purpose of prescribing the *svarita* as an alternative. To this he says: "For when the acute (*udātta*) is optionally [applied]," and so forth. For when the acute is optional, there is that case in which it does not occur.

In that case, it must be the closest [sound] between the udātta and the anudātta, and that is precisely the svarita. Therefore, even without the explicit mention of "svarita," it will necessarily be the svarita itself. 7. *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.7).

In the rule *ṭhprātipadikasya*, the genitive case endings in *prātipadikasya* and *padasya* are in apposition. Regarding the example *ahan ahim*: this is the root *han* with the suffix *laṅ* and the suffix *tip*; there is the elision [of the *ti*] by *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisy apṛktaṃ hal* (P.
6.1.68), and because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is the elision of *śap*. Here, [the substitution of *ru* for *n* does not apply] due to the prohibition in *na dhātuḥ* (P. 1.2.45).

The status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*) does not exist [in the final *n*]. In the forms "rājā," "rājānau," and "rājānaḥ," because the designation "word" (*pada*) is prohibited when it is not a case-ending of a pronoun (*asarvanāmasthāna*), the final *n* here is an element of the nominal stem according to 1.4.17. Thus, [the rule] "of the end of a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāntasya*) applies.

In this case, since a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound has the final member as its predominant element, it is appropriate for this very word (*pada*) to be qualified by that [genitive], and not by that which is subordinate. Here, the letter *n* is qualified by both the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and the word "end" (*anta*);
and that letter *n* is included within the nominal stem. [This applies to] the term "of a word" (*padasya*).
Even though undesirable, there must be a relationship of qualifier and qualified (viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva) between two terms that have different loci— namely,
"of the end of a nominal stem" (prātipadikāntasya) and "of a word" (padasya)— insofar as the former is a constituent part of the latter. That which is a constituent part of the word...
That too means "of the nominal stem" (*prātipadika*). And this being the case, even if the mention of "the end" (*anta*) were made,
the elision of *n* would still occur in the forms *rājānau* and *rājānaḥ*, because here too there exists that which is the end of a nominal stem and a constituent part of a word (*pada*).
Regarding the objection, "What about the letter *na*?"—in order to dispel this, he says: "The mention of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is indeed uncompounded.

The intention is that, consequently, its qualification as "of that word" (*tasya padasya*) is perfectly appropriate as a coreferential (*sāmānādhikaraṇa*) attribute. If, then, the mention of the nominal stem is indeed uncompounded...
Is the intention that the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī) would apply? To this he says: "supāṃ suluk...

By this rule, since the genitive is elided (luk), the mention [of the word] by means of that elision indicates the reference to the nominal stem (prātipadika); therefore, there is no occasion for the genitive case.

In the form *ṭhahaḥ*, there is elision of the suffix *su* by the rule *svamīrvapuṃsakāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.23), and the substitution of *ra* for the *n* by the rule *ro'supi* (8.2.69). Due to the principle of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (1.1.62), the condition of being followed by a *sup* suffix does not exist here; for there is the statement: "When a suffix is elided by *lup* or *lum*, the operation conditioned by that suffix does not take place" (1.1.63).
[The forms] *ṭhahobhyām* and *ahobhiḥ*: [here] *r* is substituted by 8.2.68 (*ahan*); *u* is substituted by 6.1.114 (*haśi ca*);

and *guṇa* is applied by 6.1.87 (*ādguṇaḥ*). Now, an exception must be preceded by a possibility [of the rule being applicable]; however, in this case, once the substitution of *r* has occurred, there is no possibility at all for the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) to apply.
[If one asks: "It does not exist, because the letter *n* is absent; so what is the use of a prohibition? To this he says:

the [substitutions] taught in Pāṇini 8.2.68 (*ahan*) and 8.2.69 (*ro'supi*)—namely, the substitution of *r* and the substitution of *ru* for *paṃca*—are both without scope [in the case of *na*]. Therefore, they do not occur when there is elision [of the *n*]; otherwise, indeed...
The prescription for those two would otherwise be rendered useless; therefore, he says "it has its scope" (*sāvakāśam*), and so forth.

For in the case of the vocative singular (*sambuddhi*), there is no elision, because of the prohibition in *na ṅsimbuddhyoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.8). Consequently, both of these [rules] have their scope in that situation, as in: *he dīrghāho nidāgha*.
The term *nidāgha* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one in whom the days are long"; this is its vocative form.

Although the case ending (*su*) is elided by Pāṇini 6.1.68 (*halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*), the status of being followed by a *sup* suffix still exists by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule; therefore, Pāṇini 8.2.69 (*rori supi*) does not apply, [resulting in the form] *ahan*.
Thus, only the substitution of *r* occurs [by Pāṇini 8.2.68].

Regarding the form *ahan*, it is the nominative singular, and so forth. In that regard, concerning the rule for the substitution of *r* in *ahan* (8.2.68), rather than merely stating that "that which is employed there recurs," it should be stated as follows:
By this rule, "ṭhahaṇ," not only is the substitution of *ru* prescribed, but also—

In this context, in order to demonstrate the justification for the statement that "the word-form *ahan* is explained [grammatically] according to the principle of *tvad*-replacement," it is said: "ending in the nominative singular and not having undergone the elision of the letter *n*. For if *ahan* were prescribed merely as a substitute (*ādeśa*), then in connection with that substitute, the genitive case would have to occur; thus, the genitive would have been employed rather than the nominative. Indeed, if it were presented in the nominative, it would have to be presented as having already undergone the elision of the letter *n*, because the characteristic mark of the elision of *n* would be present; yet such has not been done.

Therefore, from the inclusion of the form ending in the nominative case (*ahan*) without the elision of *n*, it is understood that the grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) of the form *ahan* is being performed. "Derived" (*anvākhyāyate*) means it is established as correct (*sādhutvena pratipādyate*). For what purpose? For the sake of preventing the elision of *n*. That is, so that the elision prescribed by the rule "there is elision of the final [consonant] of a nominal stem" (*nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*, Pāṇini 8.2.7) does not occur.
8. *na ṅsimbuddhyoḥ* (8.2.8).
[The example is] *carman*. By *supāṃ suluk...* (7.1.39), there is the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending *ReĀ*. Now, an objection is raised:
since the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) indeed exists in *surājan* by virtue of the rule *pratyayalakṣaṇena* (1.1.62)...

This is because of the prohibition [contained in the rule] "ṭha-pratyayaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.2.45). Regarding the example "ārdre carman" (on wet leather), here the designation of *prātipadika* does not exist for the reasons previously stated; furthermore, it is superseded by the designation of *bha*, which is applied by means of the characteristic of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Therefore...
The meaning is that there is indeed no occurrence of elision (nalopa).

How is there a prohibition? To this he says: "From this very [rule]," and so forth. And "the designation *bha* does not occur. Here too, from this very statement of prohibition and by means of the rule regarding the characteristics of suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), [the designation *bha* is prevented].
The word "is made known" (*jñāpyate*) is connected [to the previous statement]. By the words "and thus" (*tathā ca*) and so forth, he demonstrates the purpose of making this known:

"In this way, from this prohibition, two matters are made known. And having done so—since the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) applies in the case of *rājapuruṣa*, there is also the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*).

[The designation *bha*] occurs; and because the designation *bha* is absent, the elision of *an* prescribed by [Pāṇini 6.4.134], "there is elision of *an* when *ṭha* follows," does not take place. It should be understood that the absence of the designation *bha* serves as the purpose here for this view, namely, that "the technical names and paribhāṣās apply according to their enunciation" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 59). [In the alternative view,] "at the time of the operation... (kāryakālam... [applies].
For, according to the view expressed in the rule *hi saṃjñāparibhāṣam* (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 58),

since the designation *bha* constitutes an operation on the stem (*aṅgakārya*), the designation *bha* would not apply precisely because of the prohibition of operations conditioned by a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) in the rule *na lumatāṅgasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.63); thus, there is no purpose for the designation *bha* in that case.
By means of making known its non-existence:

through the rule *ṅy-utarapade* and others, this prohibition of the prohibition of *nalopa* (elision of *n*) before the suffix *ṅī* has been stated. A further prohibition must be stated regarding that [suffix] when it occurs after a subsequent member (*utarapada*). It "must be stated."

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that it must be explained. Here is the explanation: from the rule "svarito vānudāttaṃ padādau" (8.2.6), the word "vā" (or) is understood to carry over; and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Therefore, it will not apply when *na* is the subsequent member of a compound. For example: "carmatilaḥ" (one who has sesame seeds on his skin).

Thus [it is said]. Even though there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), the compound is formed because it conveys the intended meaning. Now, is it not the case that this statement is far too limited—namely, "the prohibition must be stated when *na* is in the subsequent member" (this portion does not appear in the Kāśī printed edition)—for even when *sambuddhi* is the subsequent member, a prohibition [is required]?

The portion [marked as missing] is indeed to be supplied, for otherwise, having analyzed *he rājan vṛndāraka* and formed the compound according to *vṛndārakanāgakuñjaraiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.62), the elision of the *n* in *he rājan vṛndāraka* would not occur. Therefore, he says: *he*.

Regarding the passage beginning with "O King! [the word] *vṛndāraka*," and so forth: a compound must be formed with a sentence that has the same meaning; for it is only in this way that there is semantic competency (*sāmarthya*), and not otherwise. And thus it has been said: "That which is capable of expressing the meaning of the sentence of the rule of inclusion should be understood as being semantically competent."

Furthermore, O King, that meaning which is understood by the sentence "O, you who are a god" (*he rājan vṛndāraka*) is not known by the compound "O, you who are a king-god" (*he rājavṛndāraka*). For in a sentence,
the vocative is understood because there is no unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), whereas in a compound, it is the opposite.

The collective meaning is "addressing. Therefore, the compound must be formed by analyzing it exactly as "he who is both a king and a vṛndāraka," followed by the vocative case; thus, the first member of the compound ends in the vocative. In the phrase "O King, O vṛndāraka," there is a compound.

It will indeed be so; therefore, since there is no vocative suffix (*sambuddhi*) following the subsequent member of the compound, the prohibition of the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) does not even apply, and thus there is no purpose in that prohibition.

"Or [the rule] 'ṭhvā napuṃsakānām' etc. means that this form of meaning—that there is an option for the prohibition of *nalopa* (elision of *n*) for neuter gender nouns—should be explained. Regarding the explanation here:
one should rely on the recurrence of the word "or" (*vā*) and its status as an *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (restricted option) even in this case.
It must be performed.

9. *mādupadhāyāśca matorvo'yavādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.9). The intended meaning is that the substitution of *va* for the *m* of the suffix *matup* occurs after words ending in *m*, words having *m* as their penultimate letter, words ending in *a*, and words having *a* as their penultimate letter—provided they are not from the group beginning with *yava*. That very [substitution] is as follows:

In order to demonstrate how this is accomplished, he says: "The suffix *matup* here," and so forth. Here, the suffix *matup* is introduced as the subject of the operation (*kāryin*). And that [suffix] cannot exist without the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), because the rule for its introduction occurs within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "nominal stems" (Pāṇini 4.1.1). Therefore, prior to the suffix *matup*, [the base] must be understood by implication through its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*).

The nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is qualified by "ma" and "a-varṇa"—that is, that which has "ma" as its final element and that which has an "a-varṇa" as its final element. By implication, it is that *upadhā* (penultimate vowel) which is qualified by "ma" and "a-varṇa. How so? Previously...

The term *prātipadika-anta* (the end of a nominal stem) is to be understood as being qualified; it is qualified by the qualifier *m* and by the qualifier *a-varṇa*. That which has *m* as its penultimate (*upadhā*) and that which has an *a*-vowel as its penultimate is thus specified.

Is it not the case that [the mention of] *matup* in the rule "ṭhupadhāyāśca" should not apply to that which is distinguished by the letter *m*, i.e., the suffix *matup* itself? [The answer is: the meaning of this [rule] is that the suffix *matup* is obtained through its own required [context]. The particle *iti* indicates a reason (*hetu*). For, by virtue of the logical force (*sāmarthya*), it is the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself that is being distinguished.
Therefore, this meaning which is about to be explained will also apply to the sūtra. Regarding the form *kiṃvān*:

the suffix *matup* is added in the sense of "what does he possess? (*kim asyāsti*); then, by the rule *ugidacām* (Pāṇini 7.1.70), the augment *num* is inserted; then the elision of the final consonant and the following vowel (*hal-ṅy-ādi-saṃyogānta-lopa*) applies; and finally, by the rule *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.14), [the lengthening of the vowel occurs].

Thus, there is a long vowel [by Pāṇini 6.4.14]. Regarding "nārmatam": one who possesses men (*nara*) is *nṛmān*; that which belongs to *nṛmat* is formed with the suffix *aṇ* by [Pāṇini 4.3.120], *tasyedam*. Once the *vṛddhi* has been applied therein—

Regarding the form *dārmatam*, since the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) has become one ending in the suffix *matup* preceded by a vowel (*avarṇa*), the substitution of *v* (as prescribed by Pāṇini 8.2.9) would apply; why, then, does it not occur? To this he says: "In this case," and so forth. For in the case of *nārmatam*, although there is the presence of the suffix *matup* preceded by a vowel, the *vṛddhi* [vowel] occurs; and that *vṛddhi* is caused by a *bāhu* [ending] or a *taddhita* suffix.

Therefore, the status of having a vowel other than *a* as a penultimate (*avarṇopadhatva*) is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*), whereas the substitution of *v* (*vatva*) is intrinsic (*antaraṅga*) because it is the cause for the application [of the rule].
And according to the principle that "the extrinsic is unestablished (*asiddha*) in relation to the intrinsic" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 42), the substitution of *v* does not occur in the form *nārmata*.

10. *jhayaḥ* | (8.2.10) Regarding the example *agnicitvān*: by the rule *tasau matvarthe* (1.4.19), it receives the designation *bha*. Consequently, the substitution of a *jaś* sound for a *jhal* sound (*jhalāṃ jaśo'nte*, 8.2.39)—which is dependent on the designation *pada*—does not take place.

11. *saṃjñāyām* (8.2.11). Regarding the form *ahīvatī*: the suffix *matup* is added in the four senses according to *nadyāṃ matup* (4.2.85), and the lengthening of the vowel occurs by *śarādīnāṃ ca* (6.3.120).
12. *āsandīvat*, *aṣṭhīvat*, *cakrīvat*, *kakṣīvat*, *rumaṇvat*, *carmaṇvatī*.

(8.2.12) Now, for what purpose is *aṣṭhīvat* prescribed as an irregular formation (*nipātana*), since this is already established by the very rule [Pāṇini 5.4.77] which states *urvaṣṭhīvam*? He thinks thus: it is for the sake of forming a *dvandva* compound.

In that case, this irregular formation (*nipātana*) would apply only there; however, by making this irregular formation here, it will apply to all instances. But how is it known that the word *āsandī* exists as a separate base form? To this he says: "And so it has been stated," and so forth. If, then...

Since the form *āsandīvat* is already established by [Pāṇini 5.2.137] regarding the same notion (*saṃjñā*) and by [Pāṇini 6.3.119] regarding the substitution of *va* for *mat*, why is it recited here? To this he says: "It is for the sake of that very purpose," namely, the rule beginning with *āsandīvat*.
"For the sake of that" means for the sake of the application of that [suffix].

If, then, this is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) for the sake of the technical name *cakrīvat*, how is it that "the Sadas and Havirdhāna sheds become *cakrīvant*"? For this is not a technical name. To this he says:
"In the case of *cakrīvant*," and so forth. For this usage occurs in Vedic literature (*chandas*), and therein there is a transposition (*vyatyaya*).
By the transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyaya*) according to Pāṇini 6.3.109 (*bahulam*), the vowel *a* is changed to *i*,
and by applying Pāṇini 8.2.15 (*chandasi raḥ*), the suffix *matup* is changed to *vat*, the form *cakrīvanti* is established.
Therefore, because it is Vedic (*chāndasa*), this should be understood as correct (*sādhutva*) in this manner.

Regarding "kakṣīvān": the lengthening [of the vowel] is by the rule *hali ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.77), which is part of the rule *halaḥ*. "For the purpose of preventing the elision of *na*" means that the elision of the letter *n* would otherwise apply by the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* (8.2.7); it is for this reason that it must not occur. "And for the sake of the substitution of *ṇ*" means...

The prohibition of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) by the rule "ṭhpadāntasya" (Pāṇini 8.4.37) would apply here; therefore, this is a *nipātana* (irregular formation) for the sake of *ṇatva*. [Regarding the statement] "or for the sake of the augment *nuṭ* in the case of *matau*": the word *vā* has the sense of an alternative (*vikalpa*).
Or rather—this *nipātana* is neither for the sake of preventing the elision of the letter *n*, nor for the sake of *ṇatva*; what then?

If so, [the rule] is for the sake of the augment *nuṭ* after *mat*. Once *nuṭ* has been applied, even though *nalopa* (elision of *n*) occurs, the desired result is indeed accomplished; for there is no possibility of the prohibition of *ṇatva* (nasalization), because [the *m*] is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*).
Thus, by the rule "ṭh-ṇ-th-k-up-v-āṅ" (Pāṇini 8.4.2), *ṇatva* takes place.

13. *udanvān udadhau ca* (8.2.13). [The commentary states: "In the sense of 'udadhi'. This means: in that sense in which water is contained. For instance, when *udaka* is the object (*karman*) and serves as an upapada, the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *karmaṇy adhikaraṇe ca* (3.3.93).

In the rule "ṭhpeṣaṃvāsavāhanadhiṣu ca" (Pāṇini 6.3.58), the word *udadhi* is derived by applying the substitution of *uda-* for *udaka-*. By the use of the particle *ca*, he indicates that the condition "in a technical name (*saṃjñāyām*)" from rule 8.2.11 is being drawn back [into this rule]. This is shown in the passage beginning with "and in a technical name," and the passage beginning with "for the sake of the meaning of *udadhi*."

The mention of "ocean" (*udadhi*) is for the sake of technical designation (*saṃjñārtha*). Regarding "from *udanda*": when one intends to express the sense that "that which is to be placed (*dheya*) in it is water (*udaka*)," the suffix *matup* is applied. "That very thing is meant," but not the Gaṅgā and so forth.
If that alone in which water is placed were to receive the designation "water-possessing jar" (udakavān ghaṭaḥ), then since water is also placed in the jar, he says:
"the water-possessing jar," and so forth. In this case, the linguistic derivation depends upon the speaker's intention.
The primary cause is not the actual existence of the thing;
and that purpose by which it is called an "ocean" is not intended in this application regarding the jar, but rather merely the connection with the existence of water.

The intention here is merely that "there is water in this"; therefore, since the sense of "holding" (dadhāti) is not intended to be expressed, the status of being an ocean (*udadhi*)—though it exists in the jar—is simply not to be conceptualized. Thus, this is not the scope for the application of the irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Consequently, [the word] *ghaṭa*...
It is called *udakavān* when the sense of "possessing water" is intended; however, when the sense of "holding [water]" is intended, it should be expressed as *udanvān*.

14. *rājanvān* in the sense of good governance (*saurājye*). (Pāṇini 8.2.14) It is stated: "The form *rājanvān* is an irregular formation (*nipātana*). What is irregularly formed here? The absence of the elision of the final *n*, and optionally the suffix *nuṅ*. Regarding the example *saurājyam*: it is a region in which there is a good king.
