*Surājā* means "an excellent king"; *saurājyam* is the state of being such [a king]. The suffix *vyañ* is applied according to the rule for the *brāhmaṇa*-class and others, and the elision of the *n* occurs by the rule *na-staddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.144). Furthermore, that *saurājyam* exists where there is a connection of a region with an excellent king. It is said: "In compounds, primary derivatives (*kṛt*), and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), the relation [of the base to the whole] is what is expressed."

Because of this statement, [it follows that] for the word *rājanvān*, the denoted object (*vācya*) is the country itself, not good governance (*saurājya*). However, that country, being understood from the word, implies it because of its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) with good governance. And he says "when it is being understood" (*gamyamāne*) to indicate that it causes that [good governance] to be known.
The form "rājanvān" is masculine; in order to demonstrate that its gender is not a restrictive factor, the example "rājanvatī pṛthivī" (the earth possessing kings) is introduced.
15. *cchandasīraḥ* | (8.2.15) As in *harivo medinam*. This has been explained under [the rule] *na mu ne* (8.2.3). Also as in *ārevānetu mā viśat*.

In the word *rayi*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule "vocalization occurs diversely before the suffix *matup*" (Pāṇini 6.1.30), followed by substitution of the preceding vowel (*parapūrvatva*), and then the formation of a single substitute by *guṇa* (Pāṇini 6.1.87). Now, why does this not also occur here in the case of *saptarṣimantam* and *dyāvāpṛthivīmantam*? To this he says: "dyauśca pṛthivī... [and so on].

When the *dvandva* compound *ceti* is formed, the substitution of *dyāvā* for *div* occurs by the rule *ṭhdivasaśca pṛthivyām* (Pāṇini 6.3.30). [Examples include] *gaurvān*, *dhūrvān*, and *āśīrvān*. [The root] *gṛ* [is listed] in the sense of "sound" (Dhātupāṭha 1498).
The root *dhurv* (DhP 5.73) means "to injure," and *āṅ-śās* (DhP 10.22) means "to teach";

from these, the suffix *kvip* is applied because they belong to the *sampadādi* group. For the root *gṛ*, there is the substitution of *i* by the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.100). For the root *dhurv*, there is the elision of the letter *v* by the rule *rāllopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.21). [And for *śās*,] *śāsa*...

In the rule *idaṃhaloḥ* (6.4.34), the substitution of *i* for the root *śās* occurs; however, by the Vārttika *āśāsaḥ kvāvupasaṃkhyānam* (781), the root *śās* preceded by the prefix *ā* undergoes this substitution of *i*. Once the suffix *matup* is applied, the substitution of *ru* takes place according to *sasajuṣo ruḥ* (8.2.66).

16. *ano nuṭ* | (8.2.16) [Regarding the statement] "ending in *ṭhak*": [the augment] *āṅ* is applied by Pāṇini 7.1.75, *ṭhasthidadhisakthyakṣṇāmanaRudātaḥ*, and 7.1.76, *chandasyāpi dṛśyate*. Then the augment *nuṭ* is added. In the case of *anaṅ*, there is the elision of the letter *n*; in the case of *num*, [there is the addition of the nasal].

Regarding the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*]: in the case of *asthanvantam*, the operations such as *anaṅ* must be applied to the word *asthi* as previously described, with the exception of the substitution of *ṇ*. Regarding *śīrṣaṇvatī*, the form is established by the rule *śīrṣan chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.60).

Now, one might object that because the augment *nuṭ* is immediately preceding, it would be more appropriate for that very *nuṭ* to undergo the substitution of *v*, rather than [the *n* of the suffix].

Since the *makāra* is separated by that [augment], why does the substitution of *vat* not occur for the *nuṭ* here, while it does not occur for what follows after it? To this he says: "Because the *nuṭ* is as if non-existent" (*asiddhatvāt*), etc. Now, why is this *nuṭ* not simply an exception (*apavāda*) due to its posteriority? Because they belong to different categories (*bhinnajātīyatvāt*).

For a specific feature (*viśeṣa*) that results from the same class of cause is indeed a sublater (*bādhaka*) of a general rule (*sāmānya*); however, in this case, there is a difference in their effects: since *ṇatva* is a substitute (*ādeśa*), whereas *nuṭ* is an augment (*āgama*), there is no relationship of sublation between them, just as the insertion of *ṇatva* after *nuṭ* is treated as being at the beginning of the subsequent element.
The word "syāt" is used for this purpose; otherwise, there would be a prohibition by the rule "padāntasya" (Pāṇini 8.4.37).
17. *nādaghasya* | (8.2.17) [The example is] *supanthintaraḥ*. "A good path" (*śobhanaḥ panthāḥ*) is a *prādi*-compound: *supanthāḥ*.

Because of the prohibition [of the suffix *aC*] by the rule *na pūjanāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.69), [the suffix *aC* is not applied]; rather, [the suffix *aC* is applied] by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.74).
By such rules as these, a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) does not occur; [for example,] *tarap* in *dasyuhantamaḥ*.
[This is derived as follows: from the sense "one who has slain the Dasyu," the suffix *kvip* is applied, and from that form ending in *kvip*, the suffix *tamap* is added.
In *bhūridāvataraḥ*, [it is derived as follows: from the sense "one who gives much" (*bhūri dadāti*), the suffix *manin* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.74.
By such rules as these, the suffix *vanip* is applied; and after that which ends in it, the augment *tuṭ* is added to the subsequent word.

Thus, "rathītaraḥ": from the word *rathin*, which ends in the possessive suffix *nip*, the comparative suffix *tarap* is added, there is the elision of the letter *n*, and the vowel *ī* [is substituted]; or alternatively, the letter *ī* is substituted for the letter *n* itself.
There is the substitution of a long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one.

18. *kṛpo ro laḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.18). Here, the phoneme *ra* is taken as the subject, and *la* is its substitute of the very same nature; consequently, the substitution of the phoneme *la* occurs only for that which is a solitary *repha* (the sound *r*) and not one that is merely a constituent part [of a cluster].

It might be argued: "But [if that were so], the substitution of *l* for the vowel *ṛ* would not occur, because those two are not mentioned in the rule as being in the relationship of original and substitute (*sthānyādeśabhāva*). Consequently, forms such as *klṛptaḥ* and *klṛptavān* would not be established. To one who raises this objection, he replies: "The general term *ra* is employed [in the rule]."

Thus, setting aside the distinction created by being a phoneme (*varṇa*) or not being a phoneme (*avarṇa*), that universal which resides in both individual instances of the sound *ra*— whether consisting of a phoneme or not consisting of a phoneme—
is [the same], since in both of those two, though distinguished by the difference of being a phoneme or not being a phoneme, there is the *ra*...

Thus, since the name and the cognition are non-different, that [general property] is what is apprehended, and not that which consists of the phonemes—such is the distinction. By the phrase "by that," both are grasped through the inclusion of the general property; because that general property exists in both, [the term] "la" also [is included].

"Only the general [form]," it is said. The word "is presented" (*upadīyate*) is understood [as the ellipsis]. Here too, it should be stated that both the *l*-sound which is independent and that which resides within *ḷ* are included; however, this is not explicitly stated because its meaning is already understood by following the previous rule. Regarding the phrase "Therefore, this," etc.: since...

In this way, there is the inclusion of both *repha*s (the letter *r*) and both *lakāra*s (the letter *l*); therefore, a simple *lakāra* is prescribed as the substitute for a simple *repha*. Due to internal similarity (*āntaratamya*), a *lṛkāra* is also [the substitute] for an *ṛkāra*.
But even though there is the inclusion of both, why should an *ṛkāra* not [be the substitute] in the place of an *ṛkāra*?
The statement "it is prescribed" would not be tenable, for the *repha* residing in the vowel *ṛ* does not become the vowel *ṛ*;

what then? It is a constituent part (*avayava*) of it. Since both [the *repha* and the *lakāra*] are thus grasped, the *lakāra* residing in the vowel *lṛ* is indeed similar to the *repha* residing in the vowel *ṛ*, because of their internal proximity (*antaratama*); such is the meaning.
Is it not also the case that the vowel *ḷ* is obtained in place of the vowel *ṛ*?
To refute this objection, it is stated: "by means of the substitution of one part through the modification of another part.
One part is the letter *r*, which is a constituent of the vowel *ṛ*; its modification is the letter *l*, which is a constituent of the vowel *ḷ*.

Alternatively—the letter *l* is a part (*ekadeśa*) of the letter *ḷ*, and that very part is the modification (*vikāra*). It is a partial modification of the *repha* (the letter *r*) within the letter *ṛ*. "Door" (*dvāra*) means the entrance or, in other words, the means.
By this, the substitution of the letter *ḷ* is prescribed in the place of the letter *ṛ*. If [one asks] regarding those situated in the letters *ṛ* and *ḷ*...
The separation of the letter *ra* and the letter *la* from the letters *ṛ* and *lṛ* is possible.

Therefore, because it is an inseparable consequence, by means of a partial modification, the substitution of the entire letter *lṛ* for the entire letter *ṛ* is prescribed. This is the meaning of this very [rule].

To provide firmness [to this point], he says "And thus," and so forth. Since, in this way, the vowel *lṛ* is prescribed in place of the vowel *ṛ* by means of partial modification (*ekadeśavikāra*), there is the inclusion of rules such as "and in the case of the *luṭ* suffix, after the root *klṛp*" (Pāṇini 1.3.110). Thus, while refuting the objection, [the author] states...

Regarding what was stated—"In the case of the *nuṅ* augment, the rule for the substitution of *l*-suffixes (*lādeśa*), and the change of *ṛ*, the vowel *ṛ* must be provided against [the objection]"—when that occasion arose concerning the substitution of *l*-suffixes, it was answered: "It is to be provided. For example, *kalptā*.

*Kalptārau*, *kalptāraḥ*: [formed with] the suffix *tṛc*, or alternatively with *luṭ*. *Ciklṛpsati*: [formed with] the suffix *san*; due to the *kit* status [of the suffix] by [Pāṇini 1.2.10], there is an absence of *guṇa*. *Klṛptaḥ*, *klṛptavān*: [formed with] the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu*.
Regarding the word "kṛpā": how is this established? Since one might ask, "In this case as well, shouldn't there be *latva* (the substitution of *la* for *ra*)?", he says:

"This [word] 'kṛpā'," and so forth. By this, from the root *krapa* in the sense of "compassion" (*kṛpāyām*) and "motion" (*gatau*) (DhP 771), the suffix *aṅ* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.3.104: *sidbhidādibhyo 'ṅ*.

By showing that when semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) is performed in conjunction with that [substitution], the form *kṛpa-* arises, he demonstrates that this form *kṛpa-* is derived through a grammatical rule (*lākṣaṇika*). If this is so, then why does the substitution of *l* for *r* not occur here? To this he says: "For of that," and so forth. Because of that...
The form *kṛpa* arises from the root *kṛp* after the vowel has undergone *samprasāraṇa*;

therefore, it is derivative (*lākṣaṇika*). Consequently, by the maxim "that which is taught by a rule [is not included] along with that which is taught as a ready-made word" (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā*), it is not grasped [by the rule], and thus the undesirable consequence of *la* [substitution] occurs.

In words such as *kṛpaṇa*, *kṛpīṭa*, and *karpūra*, this form *kṛp-* is indeed etymological (*aiipadeśika*), not figurative (*lākṣaṇika*). For it is derived from the root *rañj* by the rule "from *rañj*, the suffix *kvun*" (the reading in the Daiva is *rañaḥ kyun*; there are variant readings *rajeḥ* and *rañjeḥ*)—as stated in Daiva 5.24.

The suffix *u* is prescribed; since by the rule of frequent usage (*bahulavacanāt*) only *kṛp* is prescribed therein, the form *kṛpaṇa* arises. This is according to the rule *kṛtṛkṛpibhyaḥ kīṭan* (the reading in the Daiva is *kṛtṛkṛpikampibhyaḥ kīṭan*, while another reading is *kapikampibhyaḥ*) (Daiva 5.3).

Thus, when the suffix *ita* is applied to the root *kṛp*, the form *kṛpīṭa* arises; and when the suffix *ura* is applied according to the rule "from *kharji*, *piñja*, etc., [the suffixes] *ura* and *lac*" (Daiva-Uṇādi-sūtra 10.10), the form *karpūra* arises.
This is what he states in the passage beginning with "kṛpaṇa-kṛpīṭa. He considers it thus: [the formation is possible] because of the word "bahula" (in the sense of "diversely").
The word *kṛpa* itself becomes *kyun* (the reading *kvun* is found in the Prācya manuscript), and in that case, its semivowel is vocalized (*samprasāraṇa*).

Furthermore, even in the rule "from *kṛ*, *tṛ*, and *kṛp* comes *kīṭan*" (Daiva-Uṇādi 5.3), the mention of *kṛp* will be removed and replaced by the mention of *klṛp*; as for the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*), however—

It will be established by the very use of the word "bahula" (variously applied). Even in the rule *kharjipiñjādibhya ūrolacau*, because of the inclusion of the term "ādi" (and so forth), only *kṛpi* will be understood, and the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) will occur as before. Even though forms such as *kṛpaṇa* and *kṛpāṇa* might exist, in that case—
To demonstrate the fault, he says: "Or, [the rule] *jaṇādayo bahulam*," and so forth.
Not conceiving it possible for two things of entirely different forms to possess an identical nature, he asks: "What is this? and so forth. [He answers: "The state of having the same object."

He shows that by the word "one" (eka) here, what is intended is the state of having an identical object-domain (*abhinna-viṣayatva*), and not an identical intrinsic nature (*abhinnasvabhāvatva*). For what purpose, then, is the substitution of *la* prescribed with reference to *kṛp*, rather than *kṛp* itself being the referent? [The answer is: Only the state of being *la* should be applied in the place of *gu*.
And that [suffix] must necessarily be applied for the purpose of making [the word] upalakṣīya.

And thus, in the rule *ṛdupadhāccaklṛpicṛteḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.110), the prohibition regarding *klṛp* need not be formulated. By this very means, it is possible [to derive the form]; for here, in the case of *acoklṛpat*, [the suffix is applied].

Because the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) is prescribed for both *ṛ* and *ḷ*, the *urat* status (substitution by *u*) being enjoined for *ṛ* would also apply to *ḷ*. Consequently, it would follow that *ḷ* is also a *ṛ*-vowel (*ṛvarṇa*).
However, since *ḷ* is taught after having first taught a form ending in *ṛ*, and the *lat* status (substitution by *l*) is then enjoined, that *ḷ* also acquires the *lat* status.
It is accomplished.
19. *upasargasyāyatau* (8.2.19). Here two interpretations are possible: one is that the mention of *ayati* is a qualifier of the letter *r*;
the second is that it is a qualifier of the prefix (*upasarga*). Among these, in the first interpretation, when *ayati* follows...

The commentary (*vṛtti*) beginning with these words is to be understood as follows: "When *ayataḥ* follows, there is the substitution of *la* for the *repha* belonging to a prefix. Regarding the second [interpretation], it is to be understood thus: "When *ayataḥ* follows, for that *ma* which is a prefix, there is the substitution of *la* for the *repha* belonging to that prefix."

"It becomes [bhavatīti]. Regarding "ṭhplāyate" and "palāyate," the ātmanepada ending occurs because the root belongs to the class beginning with "aya-ṇya" and is anudātta. But how does the substitution of *l* for *ṣ* occur here in the first view, given that when that [substitution] is to be applied, the rule "acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau" (Pāṇini 1.1.57) [would apply]?

"One would have to apply the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original), and consequently, when there is a separation (*vibhāga*) between the verbal root and the prefix, the letter *r* would be separated by the vowel *a*, making it impossible for the *r* to be followed by *ayi*. To this he says:

'In this case, that which... and so forth. The word "separation" (*vibhāge*) means "disjunction" (*viśleṣa*). The mention of the singular number (*eka*) is for the sake of [defining] the suffix (*pratyaya*).

This is for the purpose of demonstrating that *latva* does not occur when there is an intervention (*vyavadhāna*). For by that [which constitutes] an intervention itself and not a non-intervention, *latva* must occur in the case of an intervention because of the authority of the rule; by what is there such an intervention? By a single phoneme (*varṇa*), or by a cluster (*saṅghāta*).

Furthermore, regarding whether there is an intervention (*vyavadhāna*) or not: by that [principle], it occurs when there is an intervention. Thus, in the first position [of the alternative], *latva* (the substitution of *l* for *r*) occurs when there is an intervention by a single phoneme (*varṇa*). It does not apply only in cases such as *palyayate*, where [the substitution] would occur through the status of being "as if non-existent" (*sthānivadbhāva*), which is ungrammatical (*aśāstrīya*).

"Intervention" (*vyavadhāna*); however, even where there is intervention by a phoneme that is actually being heard, the rule still applies—this is the meaning of the word "even" (*api*) [in the sūtra].
But [one might object]: is it not the case that by the mention of *niraḥ* in the rule *niraḥ kuṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.46), [the intervention of a phoneme is already accounted for]?
This has already been made known—that there exists another prefix *nir* ending in *r*;

and since, in the case of *nilaya*, there is thus scope for the rule [to apply], how can it be said that "that by which no intervention occurs applies even when there is intervention, on the authority of the statement" (Vyāḍipāda 46)? Thus...

He considers: a single example does not necessitate a general definition, for if this were the sole purpose [of the definition], one would simply have provided the specific mention [of that example]. Having thus established the validity of everything under the first position, he proceeds to the second position.
To establish this, he says: "But when [the prefix] is a qualifier," and so forth.
This word *tu* (but) functions in the sense of *api* (also). Not only is everything established—such as *palyayate*—when *yat* is understood as qualifying the letter *r*, but also...

Even when that [prefix] is a qualifier of the preposition (*upasarga*), all this is established. Alternatively—the word *tu* (but) indicates the distinction of this [view] from the previous position; for in that case, the objection arises that the substitution of *l* would apply due to the intervention of the verbal root (*dhātu*). Therefore, this which...

All of this is to be established. However, the meaning here is that this point is already proven, as there is no occasion at all for such an objection to arise; it is not something to be accomplished through effort. The objector [says], "Does it not also follow from the prefix *pra*? The word *tu* (but/however) serves to distinguish it from the previous case, for in the preceding instance, it did not follow from *pra*.

[The objection is: "Because there is an intervention by the compound (*saṅghāta*); but here there is no intervention by anything, therefore they think that [the suffix] would also apply after *pra*. [The phrase] "others" refers to any among those who adhere to the second alternative. [The phrase] "of these two, *nis* and *dus*" [is explained as follows].

If someone were to object: "Whether the mention of *ati* is a qualifier of the letter *r*, or whether it is a qualifier of the prefix (*upasarga*), in either case, once the substitution of *r* has taken place, the substitution of *l* would follow," he says in response: "In the case of *nis-dus*, etc. The meaning of this is already explained.

20. *gro yaṅ* (8.2.20). Regarding the example *nijegilyate*: by the rule *ṛta id dhātoḥ* (7.1.100), the substitution of *i* occurs; then there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*) and the application of the rules pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsakārya*).

"The suffix *yaṅ* is prescribed for the sense of censuring an action," according to the rule beginning with "lupasadacara" (Pāṇini 3.1.24). Regarding the term "girateḥ," this refers to the root *gṛ* meaning "to swallow," belonging to the Taudādika class (Dhātupāṭha 1410).

Regarding the phrase "of the root *gṛṇāti*": this refers to the root *gu* meaning "to sound" (DhP 1498), which begins with the suffix *Añ*. The statement "they desire a general inclusion" is made because no specific qualification is provided. As for the phrase "but others," etc., how then...?
Even when the general term *upādāna* is employed, why is the inclusion of *giri* alone obtained? To this he says: "of the root *gṛṇāti*" and so forth.

What is the reason that [the suffix] *yaR* does not occur here? To this he says: "due to non-mention" (*anabhidhānāt*). [The form] *nigīryate* is derived by applying *yak* according to *sārvadhātuke yak* (Pāṇini 3.1.67) and *hali ca* (8.2.77).
Thus [the vowel] is long.
21. *aci vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 8.2.21). Regarding the form *girati*: this is the form of the root meaning "to swallow. Regarding *nigaraṇam*: here the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied.
Regarding *nigārakaḥ*: here the suffix *ṇvul* is applied. Regarding *nigāryate*: for in this case, the *ṇi*-affix has been elided (*ṇilopa*).
To refute the objection—"How can a substitution be established here, since there is no subsequent vowel?"—he says: "nigāryate," "nigālyate.
The status of being *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original) is as before.

It might be argued: "In this case, there is no application of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule at all, because of the prohibition [stated in the Jaiminīya-paribhāṣāvṛtti 48]: 'When a preceding operation is not established (*asiddha*), the *sthānivadbhāva* does not apply'? To this, he says: "Regarding the phrase 'pūrvatrāsiddhe'," etc. An *apavāda* is a fault (*doṣa*); that which exists together with it is [an *apavādika*].
"Along with its exception" (*sāpavādam*): the meaning is that this very technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) possesses an exception. The word *api* ("also") is used in a conjunctive sense.

Not only is that objection accompanied by an exception, but this statement as well—namely, "that which is not established in what precedes is not [treated as] a substitute" (*pūrvatrāsiddhaṃ na sthānivāt*)—is indeed accompanied by an exception. That very [statement]...

He says "of that," etc., in order to demonstrate the existence of an objection (*sāpavādatva*) by means of an authoritative statement (*āptavacana*). In that regard, this is the fault in the rule for the elision of *saṃyoga* and so forth: [the resulting forms] would be *kākyarthaḥ* and *vāsyarthaḥ*.

Here, in the absence of the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) of the *yaṇ*-substitution, [the rule] "of *sk* and *k*, when they are the first members of a *saṃyoga*" (Pāṇini 8.2.29) [would apply].

The elision of the letters *k* and *s* would result [in an undesired form]. Regarding the rule for the substitution of *l*: in the cases of *nigāryate* and *nigālyate*, if the elision of the suffix *ṇi* were to undergo *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if it were the original), the optional substitution of *l* would not occur.
Regarding the rule for the substitution of *ṇ*: in the cases of *prahiṇoti* and *pramīṇīte*, if the [substitution of] *guṇa* and *it* were not present...
If the status of being "as if in place" (*sthānivadbhāva*) were applied, the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] by the rule *hinumīnāḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.15) would not occur.

The phrase "or because of its being internal" (*antaraṅgatvāt*) and so forth provides another solution. The optionality of the substitution of *l* (*latva*) is internal (*antaraṅga*) because it depends on the phonemes (*varṇa*), whereas the elision of the suffix *ṇi* (*ṇilopa*) is external (*bahiraṅga*).
Because [the substitution] is based on an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.
Now, why does the substitution of *l* not occur in the forms *girau* and *giraḥ*? To this he says: "*girau*, *giraḥ*" and so forth.
The particle *iti* indicates the reason. When there is a mention of a verbal root (*dhātu*) by its own form, [the rule applies] to a suffix attached to it.
The grammatical operation is understood to apply only to that suffix which is prescribed immediately after a verbal root (*dhātu*).

Therefore, it does not occur in *agiraḥ* and *giraḥ*. For in these cases, the nominative singular (*au*) and plural (*as*) endings are not prescribed after the root *gṛ* followed by the *kvip* suffix as such; rather, what is the case? [They are prescribed] after the form ending in *śnā* (Pāṇini 3.1.81).
Because of the governing heading "prātipadika" (Pāṇini 4.1.1).
22. *pareś ca gha-ṅkayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.12). Regarding the form *paridhaḥ*: when *para-* is the upapada, the root *han* takes the suffix *ap*.

The elision of the *hal* (the consonant *h*) and the substitution of *dha* for *han* are prescribed by rule (*nipātana*), and it forms an upapada-compound (*upapadasamāsa*). Regarding the form *paryaṅkaḥ*, [it is derived from] the root *aṅk* with the prefix *pari-* in the sense of "marking" (*lakṣaṇe*).

From this [root *aṅk*], the suffix *ac* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*), or the suffix *ghañ* according to 3.3.121 (*halaśca*), forming a *prādi*-compound: that which is completely surrounded (*parigata*) by limbs (*aṅka*) is a *paryaṅka*.
Now, one might object: is not this technical term (*saṃjñā*) also applicable to the superlative suffixes *taraP* and *tamap*?

The rule *svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.68), which prescribes the use of a word's own form, is here set aside; why then is *la*-hood illustrated by the very form *gha* itself? To this he says: "In this case, there is the use of the own form *gha*. He thinks as follows: because of its association with the non-technical term *aṅka*, the word *gha* [is understood here as its own form].
Thus, there is the inclusion of this very term *asaṃjñā* as well.
It is stated: "It should be said: 'and when *yoga* follows. This means that when the word *yoga* follows, the substitution of *l* for *p* in *pari* occurs optionally; this is the intended meaning.

The meaning is that it must be explained. Here is the explanation: the particle *ca* is employed in the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned; by this, [the rule] will also apply in the case of a *yoga*.
23. *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* (8.2.23).

Regarding the rule *saṃyogāntasya*: that whose end (*anta*) is a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is described as such. The inclusion of the word *anta* is for the sake of clarity; for the term *padasya* (8.1.16) is understood to carry over, and since the *pada* is qualified by the conjunction, [the principle] *yena vidhis tadantasya* (1.1.72) applies.
The status of being "ending in a consonant cluster" (*saṃyogāntatā*) is obtained for a word, as in *gomān*. When the elision of the *hal* and *ṅī* etc.

has been performed, the elision of the final vowel (*alo'ntyasya lopaḥ*, 1.1.52) applies; then, by the rule "of a stem ending in *at* or *as*, provided it is not a verbal root" (*atvasantasya cādhātoḥ*, 6.4.14), the lengthening of the vowel occurs. In the cases of *kṣeyān* and *bhūyān*, however, there is no [lengthening] due to the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*).

One might think that [the substitution of *l*] is obtained, but since it is subsequent (*para*), it is sublated by the substitution of *ru*; to such a person, he says: "superior," "more extensive," and so forth.
If, then, even though it is subsequent, the substitution of *ru* does not sublate the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) because it is unestablished (*asiddha*), [then...]

If that were the case, then for the very same reason that *satya* (truth) [is established], the substitution of *jaś* would also not be sublated; consequently, in the case of *yaśaḥ* and *payaḥ*, there would only be the *jaś* substitution and not *rutva* (the substitution of *r*). To this, he says:
"But as for *jaś*," and so forth. For the rule for the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is undertaken whether the *rutva* has already been applied or has not yet been applied.

It is appropriate that *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) does not subvert [the rule], since it applies where [the condition] is already established—as in *śreyān*, etc.—but does not apply where it is not established—as in *payaḥ*. However, as for *jaśtva* (the substitution of *j*), it is commenced precisely because it applies everywhere, whether it is already established—as in *śreyān*, etc.—or not yet established—as in *payaḥ*. Thus, it is logical that *rutva* does not subvert it. As for *jaśtva*, however...

Since [the rule] is indeed applicable everywhere, it is commenced from that point. Therefore, due to its connection with the definition of an annulment (*bādhaka*), the substitution of *ru* certainly becomes the annulment of the substitution of *jaś* and *car*. Regarding the word *śreyān*: by the rule "for *praśasya*, there is *śra*" (Pāṇini 5.3.60), the form *śra* occurs before the suffix *iyasun*; then, by "guṇa for *āt*" (6.1.87) and "of that which ends in *s* or *m*, and of *mahat*" (6.4.10), [the rules apply].

"Longer"— that is, by the rule "there is elision of the final syllable of *bahu*, and *bahu* becomes *bhū*" (Pāṇini 6.4.158), there is elision of the vowel *ī* in the suffix *īyasun*, and the substitution of *bhū* for *bahu*. Now, why does the elision of the final member of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) not occur in cases such as *dadhy atra* and *madhv atra*?

Thus he says: "One should place [the word] here," and so forth. As for the external nature (*bahiraṅgatva*) of the *yaṇ* substitution, it is because it depends on two words; whereas the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is internal (*antaraṅga*) because it depends on a single word. Why does [the sūtra] say "of a word" (*padasya*)? [Consider: *gomantau*.
Possessing cattle.

[The rule] *saṃyogāntasya padasya* and so forth applies here. In this context, the "word ending in a conjunct consonant" (*saṃyogāntaṃ padam*) is a qualifier for the letter *r*, and the letter *r* is also a qualifier for the letter *s*. That which is a constituent part (*avayava*) of the word ending in a conjunct consonant...
The *sakāra* (*s*) which follows the *repha* (*r*) is elided as the final letter of that [cluster]. Thus, we have *ṭhakṣāḥ* and *atsāḥ*.
[The roots are] *kṣara* "to move" (DhP 8.51) and *tsara* "to go stealthily" (DhP 5.54). In the *laṅ* tense, there is *vṛddhi* by [Pāṇini 7.2.2], *ato larantasya*, applied to the *tip* suffix.

By [the rule] *halṅyādilopaḥ* (6.1.68), the *s* of *sic* is also elided by this [rule]; then there is the augment *aṭ*, and the *r* becomes a *visarjanīya* (8.3.15). Now, since this is already established by the preceding [rule], for what purpose is this [present rule] commenced?

Thus he says: "In the case of *siddha*, etc. He demonstrates the nature of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) "after *r* [there is] *ṣ* only for *s*. However, one should not suspect here a contrary restriction—namely, that "only after *r* there is *ṣ* for *s*"—because of the mention of "pumān" in the rule for the *uraḥ-prabhṛti* group (Pāṇini 5.4.151).

Because the word *puṃs* is listed [in the Dhātupāṭha] after that which has undergone the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*), the elision of its final consonant cluster is not possible under a reversed rule [of application]. [The form] *ūrj* [is derived from] the root *ūrj*, meaning "to strengthen" or "to give life."
[The form *ūrja* is derived from the root *ūrj* with the suffix *kvip* according to Pāṇini 3.2.177, *bhrājabhrās...* etc.

Here, by rule, the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *j* does not occur; since that [elision] is absent, the substitution of *k* for *c* (i.e., *kutva*) applies according to 8.2.30, *coḥ kuḥ*, whereby the letter *j* becomes *g*. Then, by 8.4.56, *vāvasāne*, [the *g* optionally becomes *k* at the end of a word].]

Thus, the letter *ka* is the *cartva*. [The form] *nyamārṭ* (or *amārṭ*) is given in the *Kāśikā* and the *Padamañjarī*. [It is derived from] the root *mṛj* (meaning "to cleanse," DhP 1066). Due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision of the *śap* suffix; then, by Pāṇini 6.1.68, there is the elision of the *tip* ending according to the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*. Then, by Pāṇini 7.2.114, there is the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the vowel of *mṛj*, and by Pāṇini 8.2.36, the substitution of *ra* for the *j*.
By these and other rules, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs; for that, there is the substitution of *jaś*, namely *ḍ*; and for that as well, there is the substitution of *car*, namely *ṭ*.

25. *dhi ca* | (8.2.25) [Examples: *alaviṭ* and *alaviḍhvam*. [This is formed from] the *luṅ* [tense], with the *sic* suffix (3.1.44). By the rule *dhi ca* (8.2.25), there is elision of the *s* [of *sic*]. By the rule *vibhāṣeṭaḥ* (8.3.79), in one alternative (*pakṣe*), the augment *iṭ* is replaced by *dhakāra* (*dhi*). "If here... (*yady atra*)...
By the phrase "ityādinā" (by such [rules] and so forth), he demonstrates what is obtained when the *sakāra* (*s*) is elided. For if the elision of *s* did not occur,
then after the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* of *sic* by the rule "ṣṭhādeśapratyayayoḥ" (8.3.59),
and after the substitution of the *jaś* sound *ḍ* for the *jhal* sound *ṣ* by the rule "jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi" (8.4.53), the rule "ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ" (8.4.41) would apply.

When the letter *dh* undergoes the substitution of *ṣṭu*, it ought to become *ḍh*; consequently, even in the alternative where the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) does not occur, the letter *dh* would not be heard. However, the inclusion of the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) would serve to establish both the *liṭ* (perfect) and the *liṅ* (potential/optative) meanings. Therefore, so that the letter *dh* may be heard in the alternative where the retroflex does not occur, there is an elision (*lopa*).

It is prescribed that "from this point onward, the elision of the *s* of *sic* is desired. And this [elision] occurs because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) from [Pāṇini 8.2.21] *aci vibhāṣā*, and due to the understanding of it as a restricted option (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*).
It is obtained [from the rule] "cakāddhi. [The root] *cakāsṛ* (DhP 1074) means "to shine. [In the formation of the word: there is the imperative (*loṭ*), the second person singular suffix (*sip*);

by the rule "serhyapicca" (3.4.87), *hi* is substituted for *si*; by the rule "hujhalbhyo herdhiḥ" (6.4.101), *dhi* is substituted for *hi*; and as before, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* augment.

As before, there is the substitution of *j* for *ś*: the letter *s* becomes *d*. In the example "payo dhāvati," the word *payaḥ* undergoes *rutva* (the substitution of *r*), then *utva* by the rule "haśi ca" (Pāṇini 6.1.114), and finally *guṇa* by "ādguṇaḥ" (6.1.87).
If the elision (*lopa*) of *sic* is desired from this point onward, then in the cases of *sagdhiḥ* and *babdhām*, [the rule] "jhalo... [would apply].

Anticipating the objection that the elision of the *s* [in *sagdhiḥ*] would not apply by virtue of the rule *jhali* (Pāṇini 8.2.26), he says: "In *sagdhir babdhām*, etc. [The root] *ad* (meaning 'to eat', Dhātupāṭha 1011);
in the feminine, the suffix *ktin* (Pāṇini 3.3.94); and the substitution of *ghas* [for *ad*] occurs by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 2.4.39).

There is elision of the penultimate vowel by the rule *ṭhghasibhasorhali ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.100), and the elision of the *sakāra* is Vedic, according to *bahulaṃ chandasi*. Sometimes something else is stated [by the commentators], and this too is the meaning of the term *bahula*: that the substitution of *dhakāra* for the *takāra* [of *tathoḥ*] is desired by the rule *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.40).

There is elision (*dhātu-lopa*), and as before, there is the substitution of a *jaś* sound—the letter *gh* becomes *g*. The term *samānā gdhīḥ* is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇa-samāsa*); the change of *samāna* to *sa* occurs by the rule "samānasya chandasi" (Pāṇini 6.3.84).
Regarding *babdhām*: the root is *bhas* (meaning "to threaten" or "to shine," Dhātupāṭha 1100), in the imperative mood (*loṭ*).
By the extended application (*atideśa*) of *ṭhloṭo laṅvat* (Pāṇini 3.4.85), *tas* becomes *tām*.
Due to its belonging to the *juhotyādi* class, there is *ślu* of the *śap* suffix; by the rule *ślau* (6.1.10), reduplication occurs.
As before, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*), and as previously, the substitution of *d* for *t*, and [the substitution] of *bh* for [the following consonant].

The letter *da* undergoes substitution by the rule *ṭhabhyāse carca* (Pāṇini 8.4.54). Thus far, the view of the author of the Ślokavārttika has been presented. Now, in order to show the opinion of the Bhāṣyakāra, he says:
"But the Bhāṣyakāra says," and so forth. By this, [the matter] is stated without distinction.

He shows that [the author] intends the elision of the *sakāra* alone when it appears in the commentary, by saying "by that" and so forth. For if one intended the elision of the *sakāra* without distinction, then it would also apply in the case of *payo dhāvati*; therefore, he says this so that it may not occur here.
Another effort must be undertaken. This other effort, however, is precisely the recourse to a *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā* (restricted option), just as before.

But this is the distinction: in the previous case, by virtue of the *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*, the augment will apply only to *sica* after the root *dhi*, and not to anything else; whereas here, [it applies] where both [the root and the suffix] reside within the same word (*samānapada*).

In that [previous rule], the elision of the mere letter *s* occurs without distinction between the cause (*nimitta*) and the caused (*naimittika*). However, here, when they reside in separate words—as in *payodhāvati* and so forth—it does not occur at all. It is on account of this specific distinction that it is called a "separate effort" (*yatnāntara*) for the established linguistic usage.
In order to explain this matter in detail, including the objections and their resolutions, he says:

"In the presence of *dhi*, there is the elision of *sic*," and so forth. One should understand that the mention of *dhi* is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the rule that begins from the point where the elision of *sakāra* occurs when *dhi* follows; for why is this so? Because of this [subsequent rule].

From this point forward, the elision of the *s* of *sic* is desired; this is because of the preceding statement. The locative case is used in the rule because, with respect to the elision, the *s* is intended to be expressed as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). What is the purpose [of this]? He says: "Because of *cakāddhi*" and so forth. If there were elision of *sic*, [as in] *āśādhvam*...

But how so? [The root] *āṅ* [is used] in the sense of "desire" (*icchā*) [DhP 1022]. [From this root, we derive] the imperative (*loṭ*), the ending *dhvam*, the substitution of *e* for *ṭi* [by P. 3.4.79], and the replacement of *am* by *ām* [by P.
3.4.91: *savābhyāṃ vāmau*]. As before, there is the elision of *śap*.
Here, the elision of the *s* is desired, but it does not occur; if [the rule were applied] only to *sic*...
Is the elision of the *s* being prescribed? [No; rather, "the *jaś*-substitution will occur for the *s*.
By the rule "jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi" (Pāṇini 8.4.53), the *jaś*-substitution occurs—the *d* will replace the *s*—and thus the form *āśābdam* is established.
He says "all would thus be established" in order to reject the rule for the elision of the *s* sound.
If [the substitution] occurs for the *s* sound, then in that case, all the objects of the rule (*lakṣya*) would be established by that very [substitution] through the *jaś*-rule;
and consequently, this rule for the elision of the *s* sound would not be necessary.

The intention is that it must indeed be performed. In this regard, the following might be thought: "If *jaś*-ness were to occur, there would be a difference in the audible phonetic form (*śrutibheda*);

for instance, when doubling of the *s* occurs according to [Pāṇini 8.4.47] *anaci ca*, and then *jaś*-ness is applied to the two *s*s, the hearing of two *d*s would result. To this he says: "And as for the audible phonetic form..."

"It is not split" means that there is no difference in the perception (*śruti*) of a single or multiple consonants (*hal*) when followed by a semivowel (*vyañjana*); this is the intended sense. "And *luṅ* is also not included in the [rule for] the cerebral [substitution]"—the remainder of the sentence is "it must be done. And this is another advantage (*guṇa*) when the substitution of *jaś* occurs: [of] *iṇaḥ*...

In the rule *ṣīdhvaṃluṅliṭāṃ dho'ṅgāt* (Pāṇini 8.3.78), the mention of *luṅ* need not be made when the substitution of the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) is to be applied; for in forms such as *accoḍhvam* and *aploḍhvam*, the retroflex is already established through the application of the rules for *ṣatva*, *jaśtva*, and *ṣṭutva*.

The roots *ṭhcyuṅ* and *chāyuṅ* are not found in the Dhātupāṭha; *jyuṅ* does not exist (according to the Prācīna-Murāri manuscript); *pruṅ* and *pluṅ* in the sense of "going" do not exist (according to the Prācīna-Murāri manuscript) [DhP 955, 956, 957, 958];
[in the case of] *luṅ*, *dhvam*, and *sic*, [the rule] *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* [applies].

By the rule (8.3.59), *ṣatva* [the substitution of *ṣ*] occurs; then, by the rule "ṭhjhalāṃ jaś jhaśi" (8.4.53), the *jaś*-ness of the letter *ṣ* results in the letter *i*; and by the rule for *ṣṭua*-ness, the letter *dh* becomes *ḍ*. Thus, through this sequence of operations such as *ṣatva*, the *luṅ* [augment] of the letter *h* becomes the retroflex *siddha*; what [further remains]?

Regarding the mention of *luṅ*: in this way, the mention of *luṅ* is rejected. To one who maintains that the mention of *luṅ* must be made when *salopa* follows, he says: "It is defective in the case of [an affix] having *seṭ*.
If the mention of *laṅ* were not made for the two cases of cerebralization (*mūrdhanya*), then [the rule] *vibhāṣeṭaḥ* (8.3.79) [would apply].
In this case, the cerebral [ṣ] would not be obtained; consequently, as before, once the rules for *ṣatva* and so forth have been applied, there would always be *alavidhvam*, and never *alayiḍhvam*.
Therefore, the mention of *luṅ* must be made for the sake of what follows, namely [the rule] *dhi ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.25).

The elision of the letter *s* must be stated—in order to establish forms such as *alaviḍhvam*. For this would not be established if the elision of *s* did not occur; and therefore, what was said—that "everything would thus be established"—is incorrect. Furthermore, when the rule *śri ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.25) is applied, [the *s* is dropped] by virtue of the word *ca* ("and").
"Lest this [undesired result] occur, the mention of *sic* must be made. Thus, according to the opinion of the author of the Ślokavārttika, it is established that the mention of *sic* must be made.
The other [author], in order to demonstrate another fault when that [mention of *sic*] is made, says: "In the case of *ghas*, *bhakṣ*, and *naṅ*..."
Regarding the passage beginning with "it would be established" (*sidhyeta*)— the word *tu* (but) indicates a reason.

For the reason stated— that because of the inclusion of the term *sic*, the elision of the *s* in *dhasi* and *bhasi* (as in *sagdhiḥ* and *babdhām*) would not be established— is actually no reason at all.

Because even if the mention of *siC* were made, although the elision [of the *s*] would not occur by the rule "dhasi-bhasoḥ ṣṭuanjhalo jhali" (Pāṇini 8.2.26), nevertheless, there will be the elision of the phoneme (*varṇalopa*) according to the *Chāndasa* [tradition]; by that as well, both of these forms, *sagdhiḥ* and *babdhām*, are indeed established. Where?

Regarding the question, "How is there elision of phonemes according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*)?", he says: "Just as," and so forth. Just as in the application concerning the *adhvara* sacrifice—in the phrase *iṣkartāram adhvarasya*—there is elision of phonemes according to Vedic usage, so too will it occur in *sāgdhiḥ* and *babdhām* for the roots *ghas* and *bhakṣ*.

The word *vā* here indicates another justification (*upapatti*). In this regard, the following is that other justification: the form *sagdhiḥ* is not a derivative of the root *ghas* ("to eat"); what then? It is [a derivative] of the root *ṣagha* in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*) [Dhātupāṭha 1268]. But surely there is a difference in meaning?

And there is a difference in accent: in the former derivation, the meaning is "equal bending," and it has an udātta accent on the final syllable due to the *tāsi* suffix; however, when the suffix *ktin* is applied, the root *ṣadhi* means "injury" and has an udātta accent on the first syllable due to the *nit* suffix. Since roots have multiple meanings, *ṣadhi* [is used here].

It will function in the sense of "samānāvanam" (equal lowness), and there is no fault because the final acute accent (*antodātatva*) will occur through a transposition of accents (*svaravyatyaya*). Furthermore, *bandhāma* is not a form derived from the root *bhās*; rather, it is the first person plural of the imperative (*loṭ*) from the root *badh* (meaning "to bind," Dhātupāṭha 973), with the substitution [of *ba* for *bha*]. There is a transposition [of sounds].

By applying *bahulam* (3.1.85), the substitution of *dha* for *ta* is made, and by applying *vyatyayo bahulam* (3.1.85), the *bha* is substituted for the *dha* of the root; thus, *babdhām* is formed. And so, even if it were the case that [the form] is not established when *sij* is included [in the rule], nevertheless, it is still not [the case that it is not established].
There is no undesirable consequence, because even by this interpretation that [objection] is refuted.

As it has been said: "The forms *ghasit* and *bhasit* would not be established [by the rule]; therefore, the mention of *sic* [in the rule] is not for that purpose" (Kāśikā on Pāṇini 8.2.25). And thus, when there is a *sakāra* following *ghi*, of *sic*—
"The purpose [of the rule] is 'there is elision of the letter ca after dhī'"— this is the established view of the author of the Ślokavārttika regarding Pāṇini 8.2.25.

26. *jhalo jhali* (8.2.26). [Examples: *abhitta*, *abhitthāḥ*. The root *bhid* takes the *liṅ* suffix with the *ātmanepada* ending because it belongs to the *svṛ-ādi* group; likewise, there is the *liṭ* suffix *as*. Then, by the rule *khari ca* (8.4.55), the *d* undergoes *cartyam* (substitution by the corresponding unaspirated stop)—resulting in the letter *t*.

Regarding the forms *ṣṭhāvātām* and *adāta*: in *ṣṭhāvātām*, there is *tis* for the *luṅ* [aorist] third person dual; in *adāta*, the *th* is replaced by *t*, and by the rule *vadavraja-* (Pāṇini 7.2.3), there is *vṛddhi*. Here, one might have the misconception that once the *s* has been elided, the substitution of *t* for the *s* by the rule *saḥ syārdhadhātuke* (Pāṇini 7.4.49) would not apply.
It might be so; in response to that, he says "avātām," and so forth.
"Amaṃsta, amaṃsthāḥ": [the root] *man* (DhP 1176) means "to know";
because it is anudāteta, it takes the ātmanepada endings. "Abhitsātām": [this is] the ātām ending of the root *bhid*.
Regarding "ṭhabhitsata": by the rule "ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.5), there is the substitution of 'ad' for the suffix 'jha'.

27. *hvasvādaṅgāt* (Pāṇini 8.2.27). Regarding the example *alāviṣṭām*: here, *tām* is substituted for *tas*, and there is *vṛddhi* by rule 7.2.1. In this case, although there is a sequence [of sounds] established by direct audition (*śruti*), the *s* follows a short vowel and the augment *iṭ*, but it does not follow from the *aṅga* (the verbal base).
The augment *iṭ* is not part of the stem (*anaṅga*) because it is a portion of the suffix (*pratyayabhakta*). Thus, [we have] *alāviṣuḥ*;
here, *jus* replaces *jhi* by the rule *sijabhyastavidibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 3.4.109). [We have] *akṛṣātām*;
here, due to the *kit* status [of the suffix] by the rule *uśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.12), there is an absence of *guṇa*. [We have] *dviṣṭām*.

By the rule *dvitricaturbhyaḥ suc* (Pāṇini 5.4.18), the suffix *suc* is added after words ending in two, three, or four; then, by the rule *kimetiṅavyayaghādām* (Pāṇini 5.4.11), the suffix *amu* is added to express excellence (*atiśāyana*). Finally, by the rule *hrasvātādau taddhite* (Pāṇini 8.3.101), the sibilant *s* is replaced by a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) sound.

28. *iṭa īṭi* (8.2.28). In the example *adevīt*, once the prohibition of *vṛddhi* has been applied by *neṭi* (7.2.4), the *guṇa* substitution occurs for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇaḥ*), and then the augment *iṭ* is added by *astisico'pṛkte* (7.3.96).

29. *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca* (8.2.29). The term *jhal* is understood [from the previous rule]. The compound *saṃyogādyoḥ* is a genitive tatpuruṣa (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Although here the *saṃyoga* is the subsequent member of the compound and thus subordinate, nevertheless, it refers to "the beginning of a *saṃyoga*."

It is understood that the mention of "surrounding" (*skoranta*) is not a qualifier [of the *saṃyoga*], but rather that even though it is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), it is by means of it that the *saṃyoga* itself is qualified; thus he says: "the *saṃyoga* which is at the end of a word (*padasyānte yaḥ saṃyogaḥ*).

Regarding "at the end" (*ante*), the meaning is "in the final position" (*avasāne*). Regarding "when followed by a *jhal* consonant" (*jhali parataḥ*), this is in expectation of the word "word" (*padasya*).
Regarding the phrase "of the first two of that": the meaning is "of the two [consonants] that constitute the beginning of such a conjunction.

Regarding the word "lagnaḥ": from the roots *olajj* and *olasjī*, meaning "to be ashamed" (Dhātupāṭha 1290, 1291), the form is derived with the suffix *niṣṭhā*. Here, when the letter *ja* follows a *jhal* [consonant], there is a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) of the letters *sa* and *ja*.

There is the elision of the *s* of *tadādi* following *padasya* and so on; by "ṭhoditaśca" (8.2.45), there is the substitution of *n*; by "śvīdito niṣṭhāyām" (7.2.14), there is the prohibition of the augment *iṭ*; and by "coḥ kuḥ" (8.2.30), there is the substitution of *k*—namely, the letter *g*. [The form] "sādhulak" means he feels shame properly (*sādhu*).

Thus [is formed] the *kvip* suffix. Here, by the rule *atra padasyādasāne saṃyogaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.60), the augment *num* is applied; and by the statement *masjerantyāt pūrvo num anuṣaṅga-saṃyogādilopārtham* (Vārttika 7), that *num* occurs before the final letter *j*, for the purpose of avoiding the elision of the *anuṣaṅga* (*m*) and the initial of the *saṃyoga*. And of that...

There is the elision of the nasal by the rule *ṭhaniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24). Thus, we have *taṣṭaḥ*. The roots *takṣū* and *tvakṣū*, meaning "to make thin," are marked with an indicatory *ū* (*ūdit*); therefore, by the rule *svaratyādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 7.2.44), the augment *iṭ* is optional. Consequently, in the case of the past participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*), for that [root]...

By the rule *vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 7.2.15), there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*. Thus we have the form *kāṣṭhaśavasthātā*. [The derivation is as follows: from the root *śak* with the prefix *kāṣṭham*, the suffix *kvip* is applied because he is able (*śaknoti*) to [burn] wood (*kāṣṭham*). Then, in the compound *kāṣṭhaśaki sthātā*, a compound is formed by means of a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "the locative case" (Pāṇini 2.1.40).

With the words "tad atra" and so forth, he refutes what was stated [in the Vārttika]: "it should be stated that [the rule applies] before a *jhal* consonant when *saṅ* follows. The word "tat" serves to introduce the statement. [The author says: "There is no usage at all of the root *śak* ending in *kvip*," [referring to the fact that the form *śak* is not used] because of the rule "it is also seen after other roots" (Pāṇini 3.2.178).
The suffix *kvip* should be applied; and here, by the inclusion of the word "is seen" (*dṛśyate*), this is the intended meaning:

so that [the suffix] may apply where the usage of a form ending in *kvip* is observed in common worldly usage (*laukika-prayoga*). However, in common usage, no such usage of the root *śak* with the suffix *kvip* as *kāṣṭhaśak* is observed.

Consequently, since there is no usage at all of the root *śak* with the *kvip* suffix, the author of the Bhāṣya says the following in order to reject the statement "it should be stated that [the rule] applies when a *jhal* follows a *saṅ*": "The very form *kāṣṭhaśak* does not exist; how then could this *kāṣṭhaśaki* stand?"

Thus: the existence of this [suffix] depends upon its substratum (ādhāra), such as an *udghana* (a wooden block); therefore, where there is no substratum at all, such as a piece of wood (*kāṣṭhaśaka*), the thing to be supported (*tadādheya*) situated therein cannot possibly exist. Consequently, it need not be stated that [the suffix] occurs before a *jhal* [consonant], because there is nothing to be excluded. Why does it not occur here?

[An objection is raised: "Does [the rule] not apply to *vāk-sthātā*? [The answer is: No, because the substitution of *kutva* (the change of *s* to *ṣ*) is considered asiddha (*not yet established*) with respect to the elision of the initial consonant of the conjunct.
[The objector asks: "Then why does it not occur here in *vāsyārtham* and *kākyārtham*? To this he says: "In the case of *dāsyartham*, *kākyartham*, and so forth..."

Now, for what purpose is [the condition] *saṃyogādi* (beginning with a conjunct consonant)? It is so that [the substitution does not apply] in the case of *narnarti*. This form arises when *ruk* is applied to the reduplication of the root *nṛt* in its *yaṅ*-luṅ (*intensive*) form, according to the rule *rugrikau ca luki* (Pāṇini 7.4.91). Why [is the condition] *saṃyogādyoḥ* (beginning with a conjunct consonant)? [To exclude cases such as] *payaḥśak*.
This [form] ends in *kvip*. For there is no usage at all of the root *śak* ending in *kvip* when accompanied by an upapada;
however, it would certainly occur when it is alone. Why [is it said] "if at the end"? [Consider the examples: *takṣitā*, *takṣakaḥ*.

30. *coḥ kuḥ* (8.2.30). [The rule applies] "before *ṭh*, *jhal*, and at the end of a word. The term "following" (*parataḥ*) is connected with each [of these]. Now, one might object: since *jhal* was drawn over from the previous sūtra by means of the particle *ca*, its recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) here is improper?
This is not so; for in that case, *jhal* is not drawn forward by the letter *ca*. What then?

Because it continues [from the previous rule] solely by virtue of its being marked with a svarita accent, the mention of "the end" (*anta*) does not constitute an obstacle; thus it has been explained by means of the letter *ca*. [The form] *vāk* is derived from the root *vac* by [the addition of] *kvip* according to the rule *kvib vaci* (Vārttika 288).
*jvip*, and [the vowel] becomes long.
Regarding *kruñca*: here some read the root as *kuñca* with a *repha* (*ra*) and the vowel *a* as its penultimate, meaning "crookedness" and "becoming small," as in *kuñca*. *Kuñca*.

Regarding the roots *kauṭilye* and *alpībhāve* (Dhātupāṭha 185), there is another root ending in *ṛ* with *na* as its penultimate letter. In that context, one might raise an objection based on the former reading: "Why does [the substitution] not occur here in the case of *kruñca*? To him, he replies with the rule beginning with *añca*, etc. By this, [the condition] *jhalī saṅi* does not apply.

He shows that what was previously rejected by the statement "it should be stated" is actually intended here. Or else, it is due to the irregular formation (*nipātana*) [of the word] according to *Pāṇini* 3.2.59: *yujikruñcāñca*. The connection is as follows: in the case of *kruñca*, there is no substitution of *k* for the nasal (*kutva*) of the letter *ñ* because it is followed by the letter *c*. [This applies to] that which has *ñ* as its penultimate vowel.

Having accepted the reading with the *repha* (the reading found in the Kāśmīrian manuscripts), two solutions were stated for the resulting difficulty. Now, however, there is no possibility of the substitution of *ku* at all;
because this is not read with *ña* as its penultimate letter (*ñakāropadha*), but rather with *na* as its penultimate letter (*nakāropadha*).
To demonstrate this, he says: "Or with the letter *na* as its penultimate," and so forth. What, then, is the reason for reading it with the letter *na* as its penultimate?
Rather, in order to show that it has the letter *na* as its penultimate, he says: "Or with the letter *na* as its penultimate," and so forth. But what is the reason [for this]?

Why is it read with the letter *na* as its penultimate (*nakāropadha*)? To this he says: "For when the *na* is elided" (*nakāralope hi*), etc. [Note: the Prācīnamuṇḍīpāṭha reads *sakāralope hi*]. The usage *nikucita* indeed exists;
for the past passive participle (*niṣṭhānta*) of the root, there is the elision of the *n* according to Pāṇini 6.4.23: *śnānnalopaḥ*.

While this [rule] continues to apply, because we observe the elision of the letter *n* here according to Pāṇini 6.4.24 (*na ṅi-ditām*), this word is read with the letter *n* as its penultimate; otherwise, this usage would not be possible. For there is no grammatical rule for the elision of the letter *ñ*. If, then...

The root *kuñc* is read as being devoid of the letter *r* and having the letter *n* as its penultimate (*nakāropadha*). If this were the case, the forms *kruṅ*, *kruñcau*, and *kruñcaḥ* would not be established; for when the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *ṛtvig-ādi-* (Pāṇini 3.2.59), and the *n* is elided by the rule *ṭhaniditām* (6.4.24), one would obtain *kuk*, *kuc-au*, and so on.
[The objection: "One would obtain the form *kruñcaḥ*"; therefore, he says: "In the case of *yuj* and *kruñc*, etc.

This might be so: even though the non-elision of the letter *n* is prescribed as a nipātana, nevertheless, when the *n* undergoes *anusvāra*, that [anusvāra] would indeed become a *ñ* by the rule *yayi parasavarṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.58).
To the question "What is *kutva*? he says: "In that [case]," and so forth. The meaning has already been explained.

31. *ho ḍhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.31). Regarding the form *ṭhsoḍhā*: when *ḍha* is substituted for *ha* by the rule *ho ḍhaḥ*, the *t* of the suffix *tṛc* is changed to *dha* by *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* (8.2.40); then *ṣṭu* is applied; finally, by *ḍho ḍhe lopaḥ* (8.2.13), there is elision of the preceding *ḍha*.

The substitution of *o* for *ava* occurs by the rule *sahivahorodavaṇasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.112). Regarding the form *jalāṣāṭ*: [it is derived] from *jalaṃ sahate* ("he endures water"), with the suffix *ṇvi* by *bhajo ṇviḥ* (3.2.62) and *cchandasi sahaḥ* (3.2.63);
there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel and a compound with an upapada. [The substitution of *ṣ* for *s*] occurs by the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate* (6.3.137).
There is lengthening of the first member (*pūrvapada-dīrgha*), and by the rule of *jaśtva*, the letter *ḍ* becomes *ḍ*; then by *cartva*, that *ḍ* becomes *ṭ*.
According to *ṭhsaheḥ sāḍaḥ saḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.56), a cerebral (*mūrdhanya*) is substituted [for the *s*].
Thus we have *praṣṭhavāṭ*. The suffix *ṇvi* is applied by the rule *vahaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.64).

Since the rule *ṭhcuhoḥ kuḍhāṬ* could have been formulated as a single yoga, its formulation as separate rules is for the purpose of prohibiting their having an equal number [of substitutes]. For if they were a single yoga, then by virtue of having an equal number of substitutes, *kutva* would apply before *jhal*-beginning suffixes and *ḍhatva* would apply at the end of a word.

32. *dāder dhātor ghaḥ* (8.2.32). [Examples: *dagdhā*, *dagdhum*. As before, there is the substitution of *dh* for *t*; then, by the rule that a *jhaś* sound replaces a *gha* sound when followed by a *jhaś* sound, the *gh* becomes *g*. [Example: *kāṣṭhadhak*. This is a form ending in the *kvip* suffix. [The rule applies to] roots consisting of a single vowel...

By the rule *baśo bhaṣ* (Pāṇini 8.2.37), the letter *d* becomes *bhaṣ*, which is *dh*; for *gh*, there is *jaś*-ness, which is *g*; and for that *g*, there is *carv*-ness, which is *k*. Since it is stated [in the rule] as *dādeḥ* ("of those beginning with *d*"), the substitution of *gh* is not established in the case of *adhok*.
Since this [suffix] would not be prescribed if it did not begin with the letter *a*, he says "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*), etc.
"It is a qualifier of that" means it is a qualifier of [the word] beginning with *da*. Of what kind is it?
It ends in a genitive case expressing a part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). That is to say, it ends in a genitive case that relates to a part. Why?
"What is accomplished? means: "In this case, what desired [result] is established? [The answer is:

"In the rule *adhog*, the letter *gh* also becomes established. Here too, because the letter *gh* is a part of that word beginning with *d* which is itself a part of the verbal root (*dhātu*). [For example, from the root *duh*: *laṅ*, *tip*.]
Because the root begins with *d*, there is the elision of the *śap* suffix; then, by *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisy apṛktaṃ hal* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), the final consonant is elided.
As before, there is the substitution of the *bhaṣ*-sound (*dh*), followed by the augment *aṭ*.
Regarding the phrase "how," etc.: [it refers to] that which is the portion of the root beginning with *d*, and [the rule applies to] its constituent part.

The substitution of *gh* occurs for *h*. This being the case, the meaning is that in forms such as *dagdhā* and *dagdhum*, the substitution of *gh* cannot occur under any circumstances; for here, the letter *h* is not a constituent part (*avayava*) of the word *dā-* which is a constituent of the verbal root (*dhātu*), whereas that composite (*samudāya*) of which *h* is a constituent part [is the root *dah-*, and it is not the subject of this rule].
It is the root itself, not a constituent part of the letter *ha*. To this, he provides the answer: "by virtue of being treated like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāvāt*).
By this principle of being treated like that which possesses a designation, it becomes a beginning constituent of the root.
Even when there is no actual difference, such usage based on a designation is observed in the world. For instance, [in the case of] a stone slab...

[Examples are] "the body of Traka" and "the head of Rāhu. Or else, [as in the passage] beginning with "atha vā": "dhātūpadeśaḥ" means the list of verbal roots (dhātupāṭha). In that context, it is understood as "that which begins with *d*. But how is the qualification "beginning with *d*" obtained in the list of verbal roots?
[The inclusion of] "dhātu" (root) is for the sake of its own specific purpose; for its purpose would be this: "let it not apply to what is not a root.

But this is not a valid purpose, because it is impossible for a *ha* to be a constituent part of something that is not a root—whether it begins with *dha* followed by a *jhal* consonant or at the end of a word—for the sake of whose exclusion the mention of "dhātu" would be required.

This indicates the following meaning: that which exceeds [the general rule] becomes a qualifier for the very instruction of roots (dhātūpadeśa) by virtue of beginning with the letter *d*. When understood in this way, although the term "of a root" (*dhātoḥ*) stands in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "beginning with *d*" (*dādeḥ*), nevertheless, the substitution of *gh* occurs in the case of *adhog*.
It indeed applies; for in the *dhātupāṭha*, the root *duh* begins with the letter *d*. Regarding the phrase "and so on" (*tathā ca*) and so forth:

even if this is understood, although the root *dāmalih* begins with the letter *d*, nevertheless, in the form *dāmaliṭ*, the substitution of *dh* does not occur, because [the rule] refers to the state of being in the *dhātūpadeśa*.
Because it begins with the letter *a*, its status as a verbal root (*dhātu*) is established by the rule "those ending in *san* and so forth are verbal roots" (Pāṇini 3.1.32).
The word "also" (*api*) indicates that its status as a root applies not only here [in the case of *adhi-gā*], but also in the case of *dāmaliḥ*;
thus, *dāmaliḥ* means "one who licks a rope," formed with the suffix *kvip*.
From the end of that [word], [the derivation proceeds as follows]: from *dāmaliham* [is derived] *dāmaliham icchati* by means of *kyac*, according to *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8);

then, from the form ending in *kyac*, [the suffix] *kvip* is applied; there is the elision of the vowel *a* by *ato lopaḥ* (6.4.48), and the elision of the *y* by *kyasya vibhāṣā* (6.4.50), and [the change of] *h* to *ḍh* by *ho ḍhaḥ* (8.2.31).
There is the substitution of *ḍha*, and for the letter *ḍha* there is the substitution of a *jaś* sound.

33. *vā druhamuhaṣṇuhaṣṇihām* (Pāṇini 8.2.33). Regarding *druheḥ*: this refers to the root *druh* (*druha jighāṃsāyām*, Dhātupāṭha 1197). Regarding *itareṣām*: this refers to *muh* (*muha vaicitye*, Dhātupāṭha 1198) and *ṣṇuh* (*ṣṇuha udgiraṇe*).
Because [the roots] *ṣṇih* (DhP 1199) and *ṣṇih* meaning "affection" (DhP 1200) do not apply here,
there would again be the substitution of *gh* for *ṣ*, since they do not begin with the vowel *a*.

34. *naho dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.34). [The example] *upānat* is formed from the root *ṇaha* "to bind" (Dhātupāṭha 1166) with the suffix *kvip*; the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *nahivṛtivṛṣi...* (6.3.116). Similarly, there is *parīṇat*. Here, however, the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs...

[This is] by the rule *upasargādasamāse’pi* (Pāṇini 8.4.14), etc. Although for the sake of brevity in grammatical derivation (*prakriyālāghava*) a *da* should have been prescribed, the prescription of a *dha* is for the purpose that in the word *naddhā*, the substitution of *dha* [for *t* or *th*] may occur according to the rule *jhaṣastathordho’dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.40); for if a *da* were used, that [substitution] would not take place.

Because the letter *da* belongs to the *jhaṣ* group, [the rule] "ṭhradābhyāṃ niṣṭhāto naḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.42) applies; furthermore, this is for the purpose that the letter *na* should not occur [in place of the *t* of the suffix *niṣṭhā*].

35. *āhasthaḥ* | (8.1.35) Regarding *ṭhāttha*: by the rule *bruvaḥ pañcānāmādita āho bruvaḥ* (3.4.84), there is the substitution of *āha* for the root *brū*, as well as the substitution of *tha* for the *sip* ending of the present indicative (*laṭ*). By this [present sūtra], the letter *th* is substituted for that [th]. Of that...

By the rule *ṭhkhari ca* (8.4.55), there is the substitution of *c*—namely, the letter *t*. For what purpose is a different substitute (*ādeśa*) prescribed, rather than simply enjoining a modification (*vikāra*) of the original form (*prakṛti*) itself? To this he says: "The prescription of a different substitute," and so forth. If the letter *dh* were to be prescribed [as the substitute], then...
By the rule *ṭhjhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.40), the substitution of *dha* would occur;
therefore, another substitute is prescribed to prevent that.
[The sūtra] begins with *hṛgrahoḥ*, etc.; this means that for the *ha* of the roots *hṛ* and *grah*, [there is a substitution] in the Vedic language...

The letter *bh* should be stated [as the augment]. The mention of the letter *h* is for the sake of the root *hṛ*. However, in the case of the root *grah*, the substitution will occur for the final letter by the rule "the substitute takes the place of the final" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.52). For example: *grabhītā*.

Here, the suffix *tṛn* is applied, followed by the augment *iṭ*, and the lengthening of the vowel before the *liṭ* affix by the rule "lengthening of the vowel of *grah* in the *liṭ*" (7.2.37). For example: *jabhrire*. This is from the root *hṛñ*.

In the case of *liṭ*, by the rule *ṭhliṭastajhayoreśirec* (Pāṇini 3.4.81), *irec* is substituted for *jha*; then there is the *yaṇ* substitution, reduplication, and the operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsakārya*). Thus we have *udgrābham* and *nigrābham*.
The suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *grah* by the rule *halaśca* (Pāṇini 3.3.121). All of this [is explained] under the heading of *vyatyaya* (irregularity).

This is established by the transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyaya*) according to Pāṇini 6.3.109 (*bahulam*). It should be understood that the meaning of the word *vaktavya* is "that which is to be explained."

36. *vraśca-bhrasja-sṛja-mṛja-yaja-rāja-bhrāja-ṛccha-śāṃ ṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.36). The root *vraścū* (meaning "to cut") [DhP 1292], *bhrasja* (meaning "to cook"; note that the Dhātupāṭha reads simply *bhrasja*) [DhP 1284], *sṛja* (meaning "to emit") [DhP 1178], and *mṛjū* (meaning "to cleanse").
(dhā.pā. 1066), *yaj* "in the sense of worshipping the gods, forming a connection, and giving" (dhā.pā.

1002), *rāj* "in the sense of shining" (dhā.pā. 822), and *bhrāj*, *bhrāś*, *bhlāś* "in the sense of shining" (dhā.pā. 823, 824, 825). By *ccha*, there is the inclusion of those two roots ending in *cccha*; by *śa*, [the inclusion of those ending in *ś*].

Regarding words ending in *ś*: here, since the rule for *jaś*-substitution would apply to the sound *ś*, and the rule for *ka*t-substitution would apply to the others, the sound *ṣ* is prescribed as an exception to those. Thus, in the form *vraṣṭā*, there is the elision of the *s* by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.29), and due to its being marked with the *u* indicatory letter (*ūdit*), there is optionally an absence of the augment *iṭ*.

In *mīlambhṛt* and *dhānābhṛt*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule *grahijyā* (Pāṇini 6.1.16). In *sraṣṭā*, there is the augment *am* by the rule *sṛjidṛśorjhalyamakiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.58). [In *mārṣṭā* (the reading *mārṣṭi* is found in the Kāśikā edition), ...]

Regarding *mṛjer vṛddhiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.114): *upayāṭ*—this is formed from the root *yā* with the suffix *vic*, according to *vijupe chandasi* (3.2.73). Regarding *samrāṭ*: by the rule *mo rāji samaḥ kvau* (8.3.25), the *m* of *samaḥ* is replaced by *m* before the suffix *kvip*.

But what is the reason that examples with *jhal* suffixes are not shown for *rāj-* and *bhrāj-*? To this he says: "of *rāj-* and *bhrāj-*," and so forth. Why does the status of being *jhal* not apply [to the following consonant]? To this he says: "that which begins with *jhal* after these two," and so forth; that which begins with *jhal* and follows these two [is not *jhal*].
The augment *iṭ* is prescribed because [the roots] *iṅ* and *vidhīyate* possess this *iṭ*.
In the case of the others—the first and the fourth—*iṭ* is optional, according to the rule beginning with *svarati-ādi-* (Pāṇini 7.2.44).
The remaining roots, however, are without *iṭ*, because of the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *ṭhekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.10). Therefore...
The inclusion of both [roots] is for the sake of both forms: *rāṣṭiḥ* and *bhrāṣṭiḥ*.

The suffix *ktin* is applied by the rule *kvitan-nābādibhyaś-ca* (Vārttika 307), and the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *titutra-tatha-sisusarakaseṣu ca* (Pāṇini 7.2.9). Regarding *śabdaprāṭ*: one who asks about a word (*śabdam pṛcchati*).
The suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *ṭhkvivvaci* (Vārttika 288), and there is also lengthening of the vowel. Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the letter *cch* [in the rule], since—
given that the *cch* is changed to *ś* by the rule *cchavoḥ śūḍanūmāsike ca* (6.4.19)— the substitution of *ṣ* in forms such as *pṛṣṭaḥ* would occur simply because the word ends in *ś*?
Will it be so? To this he says: "In the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca*," and so forth. Regarding the word "here" (*atra*), etc.:
the two occurrences of the particle *iti* indicate the reason. For in that context, the rule *anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ kṅiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.15) is understood to follow;
therefore, the mention of *cch* is made. Otherwise, [in the case of] *pṛṣṭaḥ*, etc.

Only forms such as *pṛṣṭavān* would be established; however, forms such as *praṣṭā* and *praṣṭum* would not, because the substitution of *ś* for *ṣ* does not occur before suffixes beginning with *tṛ* that lack the marker *k* (i.e., *akṅit*). This has been stated according to the opinion of the author of the Sūtras.
Some teachers, however, reject the inclusion of the mention of *cch* in this sūtra. For instance: *cchravo*...

Regarding this, it was stated under *śūḍanunāsike ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.19): "Some do not carry forward the term *kṅti* here [from the preceding rule]. How then [is the form] *dyaubhyām*, *dyaubhiḥ* derived when *ūṭh* has been applied?
Because of the inclusion of the *tapara* marker in *diva ut* (6.1.131), it will have the duration of one mātrā."

Regarding the rule *ṭhcchaśāṃ ṣaḥ* (8.2.36), the mention of *cch* need not be made; for by this very [rule], the substitution of *ṣ* is prescribed everywhere for [the sibilants] beginning with *ś*. Thus, from the root *liś* (meaning "to become small," DhP 1179), we have *leṣṭā*; and from *viś*, *veṣṭā*.
[The root] *praviś* (Dhātupāṭha 1424).

37. *ekāco baśo bhaṣ jhaṣantasya sdhvoḥ* (8.2.37). If the term *dhātoḥ* from [8.2.32] is understood here as being carried over (*anuvartate*), then it is a genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) qualifying *ekācaḥ*. The term *jhaṣantasya* is also in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with that very same [genitive].

This is a qualifier. The term *ekācaḥ* (of that which consists of a single vowel) is a genitive in the sense of a part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) referring to *baś*. [The phrase] *tadavayavasya* means "a part of that" (*tasyāvayavaḥ tadavayavaḥ*). That which is a part of the root (*dhātu*) consisting of a single vowel and ending in a *jhaṣ* letter is connected with the word *tat* (in the rule). By the phrase *jhali parataḥ* (when a *jhal* follows),...
The term *jhal* is understood to carry over [from 8.2.26]; he shows that *sakāra* is its qualifier.

For what purpose is *jhal* carried over again? It is so that the carry-over of *padāntasya* may occur; otherwise, if *jhal* were to cease, the mention of *padānta*, which is connected to it, would also cease.

[If it were not so], then [the rule] would not be established at the end of a word (*padānte*). But surely, because of its being a *svarita* accent, the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of "at the end of a word" will occur? In that case, it is explained in this manner for the easy comprehension of those of dull intellect: "and in the word *dhva*. Here, the requirement of *jhal* (a consonant) is not expected.

Because it is impossible; for there is no such word *jhal-dhva*, since it is not included among the *pratyāhāra*s. [This refers to the form] *bhotsyate* (or *bhotsyante* according to the *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī*). [The root is] *budha* in the sense of "understanding" (*avagamane*), with the suffix *lṛṭ*, the augment *sya*, and [the substitution of] *khari*.
By the rule *ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.55), there is the substitution of *c*—namely, the letter *t*. Because it is *anudātta*, the *ātmanepada* ending is applied.

Here, by the principle of "designation as if possessing" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the very form of the root *budh* itself is considered to have a single-consonant (*ekāc*) portion that ends in a *jhaṣ* sound;
its constituent *b* is a *baś* sound. By the principle of closest proximity (*antaratamya*), in place of the labial [phoneme], a labial [substitute] occurs.

The letter *bh* will occur. The same should be understood in other cases as well. Regarding *thabhudhvam* (the reading *thabuddha* is found in the Prācīna-pāṭha), there is the substitution of *k* by the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si* (8.2.41), and the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (8.3.59). [This applies to] *nyaghūḍhvam*.

"Before the elision of ṭh, ḍh, r, or l, a long vowel is substituted for an aṇ [vowel] that precedes it" (Pāṇini 6.3.111). Regarding the form *dhokṣyate*: it is the periphrastic future (*lṛṭ*) of the root *duh*. By "dāder dhātor dhaḥ" (8.2.32), the *dh* is substituted for the initial *d* of the root; then, by "khari ca" (8.4.55), there is the substitution of a *c*-sound—namely, *k*—for that *dh*.

Regarding the form *ṭhajarghāḥ*: from the root *gudh* in the sense of "desire" (*abhikāṅkṣāyām*) [Dhātupāṭha 1246], there is the intensive suffix *yaṅ*, reduplication, application of *halādiśeṣaḥ*, substitution of *u* by *urat* (P. 7.4.66), substitution of the guttural and labial by the corresponding palatals by *kuhoścuḥ* (P. 7.4.62), and the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix by *yaṅe'ci ca* (P. 2.4.74).

By the rule *yaṅ-luk, ṭhrugrikau ca luki* (Pāṇini 7.4.91), the augment *ruk* is applied. When *jagṛdha* is established, the suffixes beginning with *iṅ* are to be prescribed. Here, in the primary form of the root *gṛdh*, this is a portion ending in a *jhaṣ* letter.
Regarding the term *gardabhayateḥ*: from the word *gardabha*, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is added in the sense of "he causes that [word] to express."

There is elision of the *ṭi* [suffix] by the rule "ṭhṇāviṣṭhavat prātipadikasya" (Vārttika 813). Here, in the case of *garva-bhī*, this is indeed a primary verbal root (*dhātu*) ending in a *jhaṣ* sound. Regarding the term "apratyaya": suffixes such as *kvip* and others are called "apratyaya."
Regarding the form *ṭhdāmaliṭ*: here, once the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha* has been applied by the rule *ḍho ḍhe lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.13), the condition of ending in a *jhaṣ* sound arises;
however, because of the inclusion of the term *ekāj* ("consisting of a single vowel/consonant"), the *bhaṣ*-bhāva substitution does not take place. Now, one might object:
"But in this case there are two parts consisting of a single consonant (*ekāj*): one beginning with *da* and ending with *m*, and another beginning with *la* and ending in a *jhaṣ*."
And even if the mention of "single-vowel" (*ekāj*) were not made, the substitution of *bhaṣ* would not apply at all in those two cases. For this reason:
that which ends in a *jhaṣ* sound has no *vaś* sound [following it], while that which begins with *d* and ends in *m* does have *vaś* sounds following it, yet it does not end in a *jhaṣ* sound.
Therefore, is the mention of "single-vowel" purposeless? To this [it is replied]:
He says: "If the mention of 'single-vowel' (ekāj) were not there," and so forth. *Vaś* is a qualifier for the purpose of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*).
