From the roots *sraṃs* and *dhvaṃs*, we derive *ukhāsrat* and *parṇadhvat*, meaning "one who falls from a pot" (*ukhāyāḥ sraṃsate*).

In *parṇāni dhvaṃsate*, the suffix *kvip* is applied, and the elision of the *n* occurs by the rule *ṭhaniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24). Here, this substitution of *vat* for *vas* would be without scope (*anavakāśa*), because the entire domain [of its application] is already occupied by another rule; nevertheless, in forms such as *vidvān*, etc., [the substitution does apply].

The elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) would apply [in cases like *vidvān*], whereas in forms such as *vidvadbhyām*, the substitution of *r* (*rutva*) applies. Therefore, because it has no other scope, when the substitution of *r* subverts [the elision], the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct must likewise be subverted by it; consequently, since the form *vidvān* would not be established, he might fall into error.

He replies to that with the words "when *rutva* has not yet taken effect," and so forth. According to the principle: "A rule which is introduced when another rule has not yet taken effect is a sublater (*bādhaka*) of that [other rule]. Now, this [rule for *datva*] is not introduced when *rutva* has not yet taken effect; therefore, *rutva* alone is sublated by *datva*. As for the elision of the final consonant of a cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*), however...
"It is not so. The word "tu" (but) indicates a distinction from the case of *rutva* (the substitution of *r*). The particle "iti" is used in the sense of a reason:
just as *rutva* applies everywhere, the elision of the final syllable of *sy-ogantah* (the elision of the final *o* of a stem ending in *o*) does not apply in that same way.
For that [elision] applies only in cases such as *vidvān*, but not in cases such as *vidvadbhyām*. Therefore...

The intention is that *datva* (the substitution of *d*) is sublated by that very [substitution], but not by *datva* itself; for when the elision of a final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is to be applied, *datva* is considered asiddha (non-existent).
Therefore, just as the letter *d* in the rule "ṭh-ḍhaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.31) is an exception (*apavāda*) here, so too is that [letter *s*].
[Question: Likewise, why does [the substitution] prescribed by *sāvanaḍuhaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.82) not also occur?

For, just as the letter *ḍ* is rightly considered an exception (*bādhaka*) to the substitution of *ḍh* because it provides its own scope (*avakāśa*), so too it would be logical for *num* to be an exception to that very same rule. [Answer: To this he says: "But [the substitution of ḍh] does not occur for *num* because of the force of its specific prescription (*vidhānasāmarthya*). This refers to each individual word (*pratipadam*).
For the augment *num* is prescribed for the word *anaḍuh*; if this *d* were an exception (*apavāda*) to that, the prescription of *num* would be purposeless. Thus, [we have] *anaḍvān*.

By the rule "The augment *ām*, which is udātta, [is added] after *catur* and *anaḍuh*" (Pāṇini 7.1.98), the augment *ām* is applied, followed by the substitution of *yaṇ*, and then the elision of the consonant and following vowel (*halṅyādi*).

(6.1.68) [The elision of] the final consonant cluster [is applied]. [Thus we have] "he, o anaḍvan. [The substitution of] *am* [for *su*] occurs by [the rule] "am in the vocative" (7.1.99). The rest is as before.

73. *tipyanasteḥ* | (8.2.73) [The example is] *acakāt* and *anvaśāt*. [The roots are] *cakāsṛ* "to shine" (DhP 1074) and *śāsu* "to instruct" (DhP 1075). [In the formation of these forms: the suffix *laṅ*, the suffix *tip*, and by virtue of belonging to the *adādi* class, the elision (*luk*) of *śap*.

By the rule *halṅyādilopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), [the suffixes are elided]. The auxiliary verb *bhavān* is used for the manifestation of the *tip* ending. Regarding the form *ā*: the augment *āṭ* is added by the rule *āḍajādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.4.72); then, by the rule *āṭaśca* (Pāṇini 6.1.90), there is vṛddhi. Once the *tip* has been elided, the *s* of the verbal root undergoes *rutva* (conversion to *r*), and of that—
The Visarjanīya.

74. *sipi dhāto rurvā* (Pāṇini 8.2.74). In the example *ṭhacakās-tvam*, when *ru* is applied, it becomes a *visarjanīya*; for that *visarjanīya*, the rule *ṭhvisarjanīyasya saḥ* (8.3.34) prescribes the substitution of *sa*. The word *tvam* is used as an auxiliary (*anuprayoga*).
[The suffix] *sip* [is used] for the sake of manifestation.

Now, what is the purpose of mentioning the root (*dhātu*)? For even though *r* and *d* are prescribed for that which ends in *s*, there is nothing other than a root ending in *s* when *sip* follows? To this [it is replied]:

He says: "The mention of 'dhātu' (root)," and so forth. That this serves a purpose for what follows will be shown in the rule *asr̥r̥tvor upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.76). Let the mention of *dhātu* be made for the sake of what follows; however, the mention of *ruk* need not be made, because it would be purposeless; for when the substitution of *d* is optionally applied, [the form] occurs as it is already established.

Is the substitution of *ru* indeed obtained in that alternative? To this he says: "And the mention of *ru*. He considers it to be for the sake of what follows. He will state [the rule] "and *d*" (8.2.75); in that case, it is for the purpose that the substitution of *ru* may occur according to that alternative. For if that [mention of *ru*] were not there, then when the substitution of *d* does not take place, [the desired result would not follow].
Otherwise, the state as it has been attained would not exist.

75. *daśca* | (8.2.75) By the particle *ca*, the rule *ṭhdaḥ* (8.2.72) is drawn forward; therefore, its recurrence does not occur in the subsequent [sūtra]. As in *abhinastvam*: this is the *laṅ* [tense], and because it belongs to the *rudhādi* class, the suffix *śnam* is applied.

76. *rvor upadhāyā dīrgha ikaḥ* | (8.2.76) The word "of the stem" (*padasya*) applies here as well, as does "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*). Both of these are in apposition and are qualified by the letters *r* and *v*, and by the qualifier [the term *upadhā*].

He says that the rule of "tadanta" (ending in that) applies: "of that which ends in the letter *r* or *v*. Why was an example for the letter *v* not shown? He says: "The mention of the letter *d* is for the sake of what follows.
The implication is that for this reason, an example for that which ends in *v* was not provided; however, it is [included] for this purpose.

It occurs; for a word ending in the letter *v* cannot be a verbal root (*dhātu*). Regarding the form *abhār*: it is the *laṅ* (imperfect) of the root *bhṛ*, with the suffix *tip*; there is *guṇa* substitution, followed by *raparatva* (substitution of *r*); then, by the rule "ślu after *juhotyādi* roots" (Pāṇini 2.4.75), there is reduplication; then by "uraṇ raparaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.1.51), the vowel *u* is replaced by *a*; and finally, by "bhṛñām it" (Pāṇini 7.4.76), the *it* augment is added.
Thus, by the rule *itvam* (the substitution of *i*), and by the elision [of the final consonant] according to *halṅyādi-lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.68).

77. *hali ca* (8.2.77). Regarding the examples "divyati" and "caturyati": here, both *div* and *catur* are nominal stems (*prātipadika*), and therefore [the rule does not apply]. Regarding "smeryate": this is the suffix *yak* used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*).

In the word *bhavyam*, [the suffix] *yat* is applied by the rule *aco yat* (3.1.97); there is *guṇa* substitution [of *a* for *i* of the root *bhū*]; and by the rule *dhātostannimittasyaiva* (6.1.80), the *av* replacement [of *u* for *v*] occurs. The *guṇa* [substitution of *o* for *u*] is applied by the rule *orguṇaḥ saṃyogādyoḥ* (7.4.29).

78. And when there is a penultimate [vowel]. (8.2.78) Since the rule for lengthening had been prescribed previously for roots ending in *r* or *v*, this [rule] is intended for those not ending in *r* or *v*. [The word] "when there is a penultimate" (*upadhāyām*)...
By means of a transposition, the singular locative case is used in place of the dual genitive case.

"Upadhābhūtau" means "having attained the status of being an *upadhā* (penultimate). That is to say, they are the two sounds preceding the final vowel (*al*). "Halparaḥ" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that after which a consonant (*hal*) follows. This refers to [the root-final consonant].

Furthermore, *hal* should be understood as being merely a constituent part of a verbal root (*dhātu*). For where a suffixal element follows *repha* or *vakāra*, which are themselves parts of a root, the rule is already established by the preceding [sūtra]. As in "hūrcchitā": the root *hurccha* means "crookedness" (*kauṭilye*; DhP 2.11). As in "mūrccchitā": the root *murcchā*...

[The roots] *moha* and *samucchrāya* (Dhātupāṭha 212). Now, one might object: "But surely, when the doubling [of the consonant] is performed by the rule *aco rahābhyāṃ dve* (Pāṇini 8.4.46), the *repha* (the letter *r*) here is no longer an *upadhā* (penultimate vowel-position)? This is not so;
because the doubling is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) when the lengthening is to be applied, there is only a single *hal* (consonant), namely the *śakāra*."
The letter *r* indeed functions as an *upadha*.

[This is seen] in the forms *ciriṇoti* and *jiriṇoti*. According to the Dhātupāṭha (*ri kṣi ciri jiri dāśa dṛ hiṃsāyām*, 1275–1280), because these roots belong to the *svādi-gaṇa*, they take the suffix *śnu*.

Here, from the roots *ṭhṝ* in the sense of "motion" (*dhā.pā.* 1500) and *dhī* in the senses of "motion," "procreation," and so forth (*dhā.pā.* 1048), the suffixes *liṭ*, *atus*, and *us* are applied. By the rule *eranekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.82), the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs; because of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element), when reduplication is performed, the forms *riryatuḥ* [and *riryuḥ*] are produced.

In the forms *ririyuḥ* and *vivyatuḥ*, *vivyuḥ*—which stand as they are—the long vowel of the reduplicated syllable would apply because the *r* and *v* are followed by a consonant (*hal*) and thus constitute the penultimate (*upadhā*) vowels. Why does this not occur? To this he says: *ririyatuḥ*, *ririyaḥ*, etc.; [this is due to] the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the vowel (*acaḥ*).

[This is established] by the rule *parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57), etc. But surely, the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is prohibited in the case of the prescription of a long vowel by the rule *na padānta* (Pāṇini 1.1.58), etc.; so how can its occurrence be possible here? This is not so; for in that [rule], a specific enumeration is made: "in the cases of vowel-sandhi (*svara*), the lengthening of a vowel (*dīrgha*), and the elision of *y* (*yalopa*)."

"An elision (*lop*) or a substitute (*ādeśa*) beginning with *a* is not treated as if it were the original (*na sthānivat*)," or "because [the former] is not established (*asiddhatvāt*)," and so forth. In this context, the substitution of *yaṇ* is *bahiraṅga* (external), because that which is prescribed within the domain of *aṅga* (the stem) depends upon an affix (*pratyaya*). The lengthening (*dīrghatva*), however, is *antaraṅga* (internal).

Because it depends on the original form (*prakṛti*). According to the rule "that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal (*antaraṅga*)" (Vyāḍipāṭha 42), when the lengthening [of the vowel] is to be applied, the *yaṇ* substitution is non-existent; therefore, the *repha* and *vakāra* are not followed by a consonant (*hal*), so how could there be the application of lengthening?

In that case, why does the lengthening [of the vowel] not occur in *caturya*? For here, when the suffix *tṛc* follows the verbal root *caturya* ending in *kyac*, after the elision of the short *a* by *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.48), the *repha* (*r*) becomes a penultimate (*upadhā*) sound followed by a consonant (*halpara*). Thus, [the condition for lengthening] exists.
[The author] says, "In the case of *caturyiti* as well," etc., regarding the attainment of length (*dīrghatva*).
Therefore, the elision (*lopa*), which depends on an *ārthadhātuka* suffix, would be *bahiraṅga*;
whereas the lengthening is *antaraṅga*, as previously [stated].

In that case, there would also be no lengthening in *pratidīvne*. For just as in *caturyite* the letter *r* is not the penultimate (*upadhā*) of the verbal root (*dhātu*), so too in *pratidīvne* the letter *v* is not. To explain: the verbal root is merely *dīvya*, whereas the letter *n* is a suffix (*pratyaya*).

[The word] *sambandhī* [is derived from the root *div*]; however, the *vakara* suffix is not the *upadhā* (penultimate vowel) of the root *div*, but rather is internal (*antabhūta*). To explain this, he says: "In the case of *pratidīvnā*," and so forth. From the root *div* preceded by *prati*, the suffix *kanin* is applied according to the rule "kanin yuvuṣitakṣi" (Dhātupāṭha 6.51), and then the *alopa* (elision of the *a*) occurs according to "allopo'naḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.134).

Thus, there is the elision of the vowel *i*. But surely, because of the status as if the original were present (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the elision of *al* by the rule "when a subsequent [element] is applied, [the preceding] is as if it were the original" (Pāṇini 1.1.57), the verbal root here does not end in *v* when followed by a consonant (*hal*). So how can there be lengthening by the rule "and before a consonant" (Pāṇini 8.2.77)?

Thus he says: "In the rule for lengthening," and so forth. However, the prohibition of the status of being *sthānivat* is by means of the rule "not at the end of a word" (*na padānta*, 1.1.58). Now, even so, because the elision of *a* (*al-lopa*) is established as being *bahiraṅga* (external), there would not be a word ending in *v* here when followed by a consonant (*hal*).
How is the *dhātu* status established? To this he says: "That which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is unestablished" (*asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam*), and so forth.

The reason for not resorting [to this paribhāṣā] is the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of this paribhāṣā. Its non-eternality, however, is indicated by the inclusion of the term *tugvidhi* in the rule *nalopaḥ supsvara-* (Pāṇini 8.2.2), and so on.
Now, regarding *jīvri-* in examples such as *kiryor-* and so forth, why does the lengthening [of the vowel] not occur by the rule *ṭhali ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.77)?

This word *jīvri-* is also derived in this way: *ṭhjīryateḥ krinÂ raśca vaḥ* (Daiva-Uṇādi-sūtra 1.80). [The roots are] *ṭhjṛÃṣ* (as *jṛṣ* in the Dhātupāṭha) and *ṭhjhṛÃṣ* (as *jhṛṣ* in the Dhātupāṭha).

From the root *vayohāni* (DhP 1130, 1131), the suffix *krin* is applied; by the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.100), the substitution of *i* for *ṛ* occurs, followed by the substitution of *ra* for the final vowel (*raparatva*), and finally the substitution of *va* for the *repha*. Thus, in this derivation, when the *repha* of the root *jīvri*—which ends in *va*—is followed by a consonant (*hal*)...
There is the possibility of lengthening by the rule *ṭhhali ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.77). Even for words such as *kiriḥ* and *giriḥ*, the derivation is performed in this manner:
while the suffix *i* is being carried over from the rule *aca iḥ* (Daiva Upādisūtra 1.67), the rule *bhujeḥ kicca* (Daiva Upādisūtra 1.71) applies.

And by the rule *ṭhkṛgṛÃśṛÃpṛÃkuṭibhidicchidibhyaśca* (Dhātupāṭha 1.72), the suffix *i* is prescribed after the verbal roots beginning with *kṛ*, and thus these words are derived. When they are thus derived, the *yaṇ*-substitution is applied to the vowel *o*; then, when the letter *ya* is followed by a consonant (*hal*)—specifically in the case of those ending in *r*— [The text continues: ... [the rules apply]. For example, from *kirati*, *girati*, *śirati*, *pirati*, *kuṭati*, *bhinatti*, and *chinatti*, the suffix *i* is added. In this manner, once the derivation is complete and the *yaṇ*-substitution has been made for the vowel *o*, when the letter *ya* stands before a consonant (*hal*), for those [roots] ending in *r*... [the grammatical operations follow].
One might ask: "Does not the rule *ṭhali ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.77) require that *kiri* and other such words undergo lengthening? To this he says:

"The *uṇādi* words are underived (*avyutpanna*)," and so forth. Now, even under the view that they are derived, lengthening would not apply in cases such as *kriyoḥ* and *giryoh*, for there is no *hal* [consonant] here.

The roots *kṛ* and *gṛ*, ending in the letter *r*, [are cited] as *kirati* and *girati*. If one were to apply the rule for lengthening (*dīrghatva*), the substitution of *yaṇ* would be treated as the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*). For, in the case of vowel-elision (*svarāvilopa*), a substitute that consists of elision (*lopājādeśa*) is not treated as the original element, whereas any other substitute is indeed treated as the original element. This is true; having provisionally accepted this—

The solution has been stated. He thinks as follows: although the prohibition of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) applies without distinction, nevertheless, lengthening (*dīrghatva*) would not even result here;
for the *uṇādi* formations are considered *avyutpanna* (unanalyzed/irregular). If the *uṇādi* words are unanalyzed...

Regarding the term *prātipadikāni*, it is not appropriate to rely on the view of etymological derivation (*vyutpattipakṣa*) for that very sūtra; for one might otherwise derive the word *pratidivan*— ending in the suffix *kvanip*— from the rule "ṭhāto maninkvanibvaniyaśca" (Pāṇini 3.2.74) and the rule "anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante" (Pāṇini 3.2.75).

In that case as well, lengthening is not established at all, because once the *v* is elided by the rule "ṭhlopovyorvali" (Pāṇini 6.1.66), the verbal root would end in *a*. An effort must be made here; it is done as follows:
in the rule "hali ca" (8.2.77), the meaning of the word [the term *hal*] is clearly specified.

This very view is adopted. And according to this view, since there is a distinction of definitions for each object of definition (*lakṣya*), they teach as many definitions as there are objects of definition.

In that regard, because the definitions must conform to the distinct objects of definition, in certain cases—such as *pratidīvan* and so forth—the position of etymological derivation (*vyutpattipakṣa*) is maintained.
In some cases, however, it is resorted to as an unanalyzed form (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*), as in *jivriḥ*, *kiryoh*, *giryoh*, and so forth.
The letter *ca* serves the purpose of drawing back the word *hal*.
79. *na bhakurcaccharām* (8.2.79).

This prohibition is formulated because the rule *ṭhhāli ca* (8.2.70), which would otherwise require lengthening, is applicable. For example, in *dhuryaḥ*: [the word *dhurya* is derived] from the sense "one who carries the yoke" (*dhuraṃ vahati*), by applying the suffix *yat* according to *ṭhdhurī yaṅḍhakau* (4.4.77).

Regarding the form *kuryāt*: it is the optative (*liṅ*) of the root *kṛ*. By [Pāṇini 3.1.79], the suffix *u* is added; there is guṇa of the verbal root, followed by the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* (*raparatvam*). Then, by [Pāṇini 6.4.110], *utva* occurs, and by [Pāṇini 6.4.109], the letter *u* is elided. Thus, one arrives at *kuryāt*.

The suffix *liṅ* occurs in the sense of benediction (*āśis*). The mention of the root *kṛ* by means of its *vikaraṇa* (the suffix *śn*) is for the purpose that the prohibition [of the augment *yaṅ*] should not apply in cases such as *cikīrṣati*.

80. *adaso'serdādu do maḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.80). In the word *aseḥ*, the vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). That which has no *s* is called *as-* [in this context]. Since that which is of such a nature does not end in *s*, he says: "of that which does not end in *s*" (*asakārāntasya*), and so forth.

Regarding "ṭhamum" and so forth: when the substitution of *tyadādi* (for *adas*) occurs before the case-endings beginning with *am*, and after applying *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97) and *ato guṇe* (6.1.97), the rule *ami pūrvaḥ* (6.1.107) applies to produce the single substitute *pūrva-rūpa*. In the case of *āṬ* (the dual ending), *vṛddhireci* (6.1.88) applies to produce *vṛddhi*. In the case of *śas*, the long vowel resulting from the homogeneous preceding sound (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) applies to the first two case-endings. In this [context]:

By the paribhāṣā *sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ* (P. 1.1.50), in the case of the singular number, that which has one morae (*mātrika*) is replaced by that which has one morae, and elsewhere, that which has two morae (*dvimātrika*) is replaced by that which has two morae. But surely only a *mātrika* is mentioned in the sūtra;
how then is a *dvimātrika* obtained? [The answer is: by the rule *ṭh-ṇ-it savarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ* (P. 1.1.69).

If it is argued that this is because of the inclusion of the term *savarṇa* [in the rule], we say no; for there is a prohibition stating that "an *aṇ* which is being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) does not include its homogeneous counterparts" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 35). Therefore, he says: "even when being taught," and so forth.
And this has been made known by the employment of the long vowel marker (*tapara*) in the rule *ṛta ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.111).
Regarding the form *ṭhadasyati*: [the suffix] *kyac* is applied after a word ending in a *sup*-suffix when it expresses "desire for oneself" (Pāṇini 3.1.8).
It should be stated that "for *adas*, [the substitution of] *ano* [occurs] before *asra*" (Vārttika). This is a *dvandva* compound of the sounds *o*, *s*, and *r*;
it is a *bahuvrīhi* meaning "that which has no *osra* (i.e., the sound *au*) in it. In the phrase *ado'tra*, because it is neuter, [the rule applies].

By the rule *ṭhsvamornapuṃsakāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.23), there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *su*; then, after the substitution of *ru* for *s*, the substitution of *u* for *ru* occurs by *ato roraplutādaplute* (6.1.113); next, *guṇa* is applied by *ādguṇaḥ* (6.1.87); and finally, the substitution of the subsequent vowel (*parapūrvatva*) occurs by *eṅḥ padāntādati* (6.1.109).

This is a counter-example for the prohibition of the vowel *i*. "Tadaḥ" is an example for the prohibition of the letter *r*; once *r*-hood (*rutva*) has been applied, the visarga (*visarjanīya*) follows.
"Tadartham" is an example where there is a prohibition even for the letters *s* and *r*.

The word *syāt* is for the purpose of indicating this meaning: "of that which has 'tha' followed by 'i'. The letter *s* is for the sake of pronunciation; the letter *a* means "of that which has *s*. As for the phrase "how so? and so forth: when the substitution of *adr̥* is made for *adas*, then there is this [application] of *adaso'dreśca*.

Does the substitution of *m* (mutva) apply to [the whole of] *adas* as a separate entity, or to its final portion (*antyasadeśa*), or does it not apply at all in the domain of the non-final portion (*adraddeśaviṣaya*)? This is what he asks with the rule beginning "of *adas*, [when followed by a case-ending beginning with a vowel, there is] *adr*" and so forth. *Mu* consists of *ma* and *u*; the state of being that is *mutva*.

The meaning is that some authorities desire the substitution of *m* for both *adas-* and *adreḥ*. For even without the particle *ca*, that sense is understood; as, for example, in the sentence: "day after day leading away the cow, the horse, the man, and the beast. How so? He says: "as in the case of *latva*. Just as...

In the case of the form *calīklṛpyate*, according to the rule *kṛpo ro laḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.18), some maintain that the substitution of *l* applies to both the *r* of the root and the *r* of the syllable *rī*; likewise, there is the substitution of *m* for *d* in *adraśaḥ*. Regarding the statement "some [hold] that it is of the final portion," *adraḷ* is a substitute ending in *i*, and of that...
Some desire the substitution of *u* [for the final vowel of *adas*]. Furthermore, that [substitution] consists of the letter *da* and the letter *ra*, which belong to the *adraḷ* portion [of *adas*].

Regarding this, some say: "No. Others, however, maintain that when the *adraḷ* portion of *adas* is substituted, the substitution of *u* must certainly not occur. He states the reason for this very point: "For it is seen in the case of *aseḥ*."

Thus: that which has *as* for its *ī*-portion is this *asi*; [the genitive] *tasya* refers to that *asi*. The word *hi* is used in the sense of *yasya* (for which). Because, in place of the *s* of that *adas* whose *a* occurs [there], mutva is observed by the learned; and not of the *s* of an *adas* that has undergone the substitution of *raḷ*.

In this case, you are correct; because the cause [for the substitution]—namely, the following of a case-ending—is absent, the *m* should not replace that [nasal]. He explains the first half of the verse with the words "by *yaiḥ*" (*yaiḥ* ityādinā) and so forth, [referring to] the *s* of *aseḥ*.

A prohibition is made by those explaining that "its *s* does not exist," namely with the words "of both. This refers to *adas-* and *adri-*. The forms such as *amumuyaṅ* arise from the rule *ṛtvig-ādinā* (Pāṇini 6.4.127), whereby *kvip* is applied after the root *añc-* [to form *adañc-*], and then [the rule] *aniditām-* [is applied].
Thus, there is the elision of *n*. This is an *upapada* compound. By the rule *ṭhugidacām* (Pāṇini 7.1.70), the augment *num* is added.

Then, the elisions of the final consonant (*halṅyādi*, 6.1.68) and the final member of the conjunct (*saṃyogānta*, 8.2.23) occur. In the singular, by the rule *kvinpratyayasya kuḥ* (8.2.62), there is *kutva*—the substitution of the nasal *ṅ* for the letter *n*. In other cases, [the form remains as is].

The *anusvāra* is applied by the rule "ṭhna ścāpadāntasya jhali" (8.3.24); then, by the rule "ṭhanusvārasya yapi parasavarṇaḥ" (8.4.58), the *parasavarṇa* is the letter *ñ* (note: the Kāśikā-Muñjaka manuscript reads *ṅ*).
This occurs while the term "sarvanāmnaḥ" is being carried over from the rule "ṭhāsarvanāmnaḥ" (6.3.91).

By the rule *ṭhviṣvagdevayīśca ṭeradraḷñcatau vapratyaye* (Pāṇini 6.3.92), the final vowel (*ṭi*) of the word *adas-* undergoes the substitution *adraḷ*. Following the first *d*, the *u*-vowel [of *adr*] is substituted for the [preceding *a*], and the *d* becomes *m*. Following the second *d* as well, the *r* of *adr* is substituted by *u*, and the *d* becomes *m*—thus: *amumuyaṅ*.
The form *amumuyaṅ* occurs. By the words "just as," etc., he explains the meaning of the term *latvavat*.

Regarding the example *calīklṛpyate*: the root *kṛpū* (DhP 762) means "to be capable. Since it means "it becomes exceedingly capable," the intensive suffix *yaṅ* is applied; there is reduplication, the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* by Pāṇini 7.4.66 (*urat*), and the retention of the first consonant by Pāṇini 7.4.60 (*halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*).

By [Pāṇini 7.4.60], *ṭhrīgṛdapadhasya ca* (7.4.90), the substitution of *rīk* occurs; by *ṭhkuhoścaḥ* (7.4.62), the substitution of a *c*-class consonant (*cutva*) occurs; and by *ṭhkupo ro laḥ* (8.2.18), the substitution of *l* for *r* occurs in both cases.
This is because the paribhāṣā *ṭhanantyavikāre 'ntyasadeśasya* (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 63) is not invoked here.
With the words "ṭhye tu" and so forth, some explain the meaning of the rule "antyasadeśasya" [Pāṇini 7.1.95] as follows:
"adamuyaṅ, adamuyañcau. Here, there is the substitution of *u* for what follows the letter *d* of *adri*, and the substitution of *m* for that very letter *d* of *adri*. The remainder is as before.

The commentary on "eke" and so forth begins with "ṭhyeṣāṃ tu" (or "ṭteṣāṃ tu," according to the Prācīna-mu-pāṭha). For whom, then, must the substitution of *m* take place precisely in the domain of the *tyadādi* (the group beginning with *tyad*)? It is for those who describe [the forms] as "ṭhaḥ seyaṃsya so'yamasistasyāseḥ" and so on.

Regarding them, [the commentary says] "here": it should not occur in the region of *adraḷ*, because the substitution of *yat* for the pronouns beginning with *tyad* (i.e., *tyadādyatva*) is absent. Thus: *adrar̥ḷṅ*, *adrar̥ḷañcau*, *adrar̥ḷañcaḥ*.
The forms are as before; however, the specific difference is the application of the *mup*-substitution.

Regarding the forms *ṭhamuyā* and *amuyā*: when the suffix *osi* follows the word *adas*, the substitution of *y* for the final vowel and the following consonant (the *tyadādyatva*) takes place by rule 7.2.102; then the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added; this results in a single substitute (*ekādeśa*). By rule 6.1.85, "that which precedes [an operation] is treated as if it were the end [of the preceding element]," the preceding portion is treated as the end of the base. Consequently, it is indeed included by the very mention of the sounds *d* and *u* in the rule.

In this context, if it were not stated that "dād" [ends in *d*], then when the substitution of *i* for *ṅ* is applied by Pāṇini 7.3.105 (*ṭhāṅ cāpiḥ*) and 7.3.104 (*osi ca*), and the substitution of *āy* for *ti* is applied, the substitution of *u* for *y* would occur for the final letter alone according to the *alontyaparibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 1.1.52). Because of the statement "dād," this does not happen.
The addition of the letter *ṛ* (tapara) in the word *ud* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation.

81. *eta īd bahuvacane* (8.2.81). Regarding the statement, "The term 'bahuvacane' here is a designation based on meaning," this means it is an *anvartha-nirdeśa* (a designation according to its literal sense).
What is meant is this: this is not a reference to the technical (paribhāṣika) term "bahuvacana" (plural number); rather—

What then? It is the adoption of the term based on its etymological meaning: *bahuvacana* is the expression of many objects (*artha*). For what reason is it explained in this way? He says: "For [if it were] technical," and so forth. If this were the adoption of a technical *bahuvacana*, it would not apply in the case of *amī*.

For here there is no technical plural following the vowel *e*; however, if the term is taken in its etymological sense (*anvarthagrahaṇa*), then even here the designation of many meanings is established, as there is indeed an expression of many objects. The adoption of the etymological sense is obtained through the principle of pervasion (*vyāptinyāya*)—that is, so that the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the vowel *e* may be understood exactly as it is.
If "ṭheḥ" were stated [instead of "ītaḥ"], one might suspect that the vowel *i* itself is the substituendum (*sthānin*). What would be the consequence?
Once the substitute *adraḷ* had been applied, the *yaṇ*-substitution for the *i* that is a constituent part of that [substitute] would be obstructed.
The letter *t* in "īd" is for the sake of ease of pronunciation.
82. *vākyasya ṭeḥ pluta udātaḥ* (8.2.82).

Regarding the phrase "the mention of 'sentence' (*vākya-grahaṇa*)" and so forth: for if the mention of "sentence" were not made, then the protracted vowel (*pluta*) would undesirably apply to every single word within that sentence. However, because of the mention of "sentence," it applies only to the final [word].
It will apply [only] to the final [syllable], not to one that is non-final.

For it is only the *yaṣṭi* (the "stick" or pause) of the final word that constitutes the *vākyaṣṭi* (the pause of the sentence), and not that of any other. Therefore, this is for the purpose that there be no protracted (*pluta*) vowel for a non-final word, but rather that it should occur only for the final one. Why does it not occur for a non-final word?

Because it is undesired; for the cessation of the governing scope of "pada" (word) is not intended, since it was previously stated: "The governing scope of 'pada' extends up to, but not including, the governing scope of 'apadānta' (non-final element of a word). And because it would be unreal;
for by the mention of "vākya" (sentence), it does not mean that [the operation applies] to every single final element among all the words within that sentence—only to one.

For the *ṭi* of a sentence necessarily belongs to a word as well; therefore, it is not logical to say that [the mention of] *ṭi* is for the purpose of excluding the scope of "word" (*pada*) from the rule concerning the sentence.
Now, what is the purpose of mentioning *ṭi*, since by the paribhāṣā "the substitute takes the place of the final *al*" (P. 1.1.52) alone—
In the case of "āyuṣmānedhi devadatta3," will there not be a protracted vowel (*pluta*) for the *ṭi* portion? To this, he says:

"The mention of *ṭi*," and so forth. For if the mention of *ṭi* were absent, then just as in the rule "the [final vowel] of a neuter nominal stem is short" (*hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya*), where the mention of "short" (*hrasva*) brings about the application of the term "vowel" (*ac*) [by the principle of *sthānin-anuvṛtti*], [so too would it be here].

(1.2.28) When the term *ac* is thus specified as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the shortening applies only to that which ends in *ac*, and not to that which does not end in *ac*— as in the case of *suvāg brāhmaṇakulam*; likewise here too, since the word "of *ac*" (*acaḥ*) is brought to mind by the mention of *pluta*, [the rule applies] to an *ac* within a sentence.

If [the term *ti*] were qualified by "ending in a vowel" (*ajanta*), then the protracted vowel (*pluta*) would apply only to that which ends in a vowel, and not to that which ends in a consonant. However, when there is the mention of *ti*, it is the vowel (*ac*) that is qualified by the technical designation *ti*, and not the designation *ti* by the vowel. For if the designation *ti* were qualified by the vowel, then the protracted vowel would apply only to that *ti* which ends in a vowel; and thus...

Otherwise, the mention of *ṭi* would indeed be purposeless; for even without it, when the vowel (*ac*) is specified in the sentence, the protracted (*pluta*) vowel of that final element ending in a vowel is established as belonging to the last sound by the rule *alo'ntyaparibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 1.1.52). Therefore, the mention of *ṭi* is not purposeless.

The specific meaning [of the rule] is that it refers to a vowel (*aj*) designated by the technical term *ṭi*—that is, "a vowel which is designated as *ṭi*. This being the case, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is established even for a consonant that is a *ṭi*, such as in "agnici3ta" (where the final *t* is a *ṭi*).
Similarly, even for that which does not end in a consonant, it is established by the principle of "behaving like that which has been so designated" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), as in "devadatta3."
Therefore, the mention of *ṭi* is made so that the protracted vowel (*pluta*) may occur even for the final vowel of a word ending in a consonant; however,
the mention of *udātta* is for the purpose of excluding other accents, and that [protracted vowel] is [to be] acutely accented (*ānantodātta*).
It causes [the substitution] to be applied; for that which is finally acute (antodātta) there becomes acute by virtue of the status of being a substitute (sthānivadbhāva).

83. *pratyabhivāde'śūdre* (8.2.83). Regarding the rule beginning with *yadabhivādyamāno guruḥ*: here, because a specific [gender] is not mentioned following a general introduction, the word *yat* is indicated using the neuter gender.

"May you be long-lived, O Devadatta!"—this is the example here, because it is a sentence of formal response (*pratyabhivāda*). In this context, the statement "I, Devadatta, salute you" is presented merely to show that Devadatta is the one being saluted by the teacher. Being saluted...

The blessing which the teacher bestows is the formal response (*pratyabhivāda*). In that context, it is necessary to demonstrate that the teacher is the one being saluted; otherwise, the response would not be understood.
[The word] *edhi* means "be. It is derived from the root *as* (meaning "to be," DhP 1065) in the imperative mood (*loṭ*).
This is the second person singular ending; by *ser hy apicca* (Pāṇini 3.4.87), the suffix *si* is replaced by *hi*, which is also indicatory (*apit*).

By *dhvasoreddhāv abhyāsalopaśca* (6.4.119), the substitution of *et* occurs. By *śnasorallopaḥ* (6.4.111), the vowel *a* is elided. Finally, by *hu-jhalbhyo herdhiḥ* (6.4.101), *hi* is replaced by *dhi*.

The term *dhirādeśaḥ* means "it should be stated"; that is to say, it must be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: from the rule *sipi dhāto rurvā* (Pāṇini 8.2.74), the word *vā* ("or") is carried over by the maxim of the frog's leap (*maṇḍūkaplutinyāya*), and that [optionality]...

This is a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*); therefore, [the suffix] will not occur in the feminine. Regarding the term "also in *asūyaka*": one who is envious is called *asūyaka*. He who, through improper conduct, causes resentment in his teacher is called *asūyaka*. By the rule beginning with "in that" (*tasmin*), there is a prohibition.
He shows that even when one desires [to address someone], one should not speak [in such a manner].

For when that person who offers salutation is not recognized as being envious, then the teacher to be saluted indeed makes the protracted (pluta) vowel in his return salutation. But when [it is known] "this man is envious,"...

When he is recognized as thinking, "He wishes to insult me," then there is no returning greeting at all; so what is the point of a prohibition? But how is it known that there is no returning greeting when he is identified as being envious?
Thus he says: "And so," and so forth.
When some ill-mannered person approaches and, with improper intent, salutes him by saying, "O sir, this is a cooking pot," the teacher, not perceiving his malice, [responds].

Thinking that "sthālī" was his name, he used the protracted vowel (*pluta*) while returning the greeting, saying, "May you live long, O Sthālī! Then that ill-mannered man said, "This is not my name; I intended the 'staff-bearer' logic (*daṇḍinyāya*). Thereupon, the teacher—
He returned the greeting without the word "pluta" (protracted), saying, "May you live long, Sthālin!
He spoke again: "I did not intend to apply the logic of the 'staff-bearer' (daṇḍin); this is merely my name. Then the teacher perceived his lack of respect.
When one has been addressed with "O wise one," [the other] says: "You are a slanderer, you fool; you do not deserve a return greeting; break apart, you low-born wretch!
But when he is being greeted, [the response should be]: "Devadatta, are you well? or "May you live long, Devadatta. Thus it is said.

Why is it that the prolated vowel (*pluta*) does not occur when one utters a reply to a greeting? To this he says: "In the case of those [words] other than the sentence of greeting," and so forth. That by which one is greeted is the "greeting" (*abhivādana*);
and that which is both the greeting and the sentence is the "sentence of greeting" (*abhivādanavākya*). In that regard, first:
The name (*nāman*) is that which is proclaimed or designated, such as "I am Devadatta";
the lineage (*gotra*) is such as "I am a Vātsya.
This protracted vowel (*pluta*) is desired when it is employed at the end or conclusion of a sentence of salutation in return.
In cases such as "Devadatta, are you well?", however, the name Devadatta—which was mentioned in the salutation—is employed at the beginning of the response, not at the end.
Therefore, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) does not occur there. But how is this obtained? From the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *vā* ("or").

This is because of the understanding that the *vibhāṣā* (optionality) is fixed, or because of predominance (*prādhānya*). For here, since the accomplishment of the grammatical operation is understood to apply to the predominant element, the *pluta* (protracted) vowel must occur for the final *ṭi* of the predominant sentence. And the predominance of a word is determined by way of its meaning; [it belongs to] the predominant meaning.
Alternatively, the word that expresses [the person] is primary, and the meaning is the principal saluter;
for the purpose of returning a greeting is to favor that [saluter].
For it is with the intent of favoring the one who has saluted that the teacher utters the return greeting.

Therefore, the one who salutes is the object of the refinement (*saṃskārya*), while expressions such as "well-being" (*kuśalin*) and "long-lived" (*āyuṣmat*) are the means of that refinement (*saṃskāraka*). Consequently, because the one who salutes is the object of the refinement, he is the primary element (*pradhāna*); and the words denoting him—the proper name (*saṃjñāśabda*) and the clan-name (*gotraśabda*)—occur at the end of the sentence.

The *pluta* vowel-substitution occurs for the *ṭi* of a present [verbal form]. Although the meaning expressed by a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), its state of being accomplished is not here relied upon as the primary factor; rather, it is merely a factor of refinement (*saṃskāraka*). Therefore, even that [meaning] does not possess primacy.

Regarding the passage beginning with "bho-rājanya-viśām": *bhoḥ* is the inclusion of the word-form itself; *rājanya* refers to the name for a Kṣatriya; *viś* refers to the name for a Vaiśya. Here, the option (*vibhāṣā*) applies to the word *bhoḥ* because it is neither a technical term (*saṃjñā*) nor a clan-name (*gotra-śabda*); however, for the others [the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya names], the option applies because [the rule] would otherwise have been mandatory.
Because it is a word denoting a conceptual designation (saṃjñā).

84. *dūrāddhūte ca* (8.2.84). Regarding *dūrāt*: it means "from afar" (*ārāt*). The ablative case is used here by virtue of the rule *dūrāntikebhyo dvitīyā ca* (2.3.35). *Hūtam* means "calling"; it is a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*).

It is said to be "far," yet "far" is not fixed. For that which is far for one overcome by indolence becomes near for one endowed with enthusiasm. Thus, for instance, someone says to another: "Bring that water-jar over there. He replies: "Stand up and take it!"

"I shall not be able to go far. Because "far" is thus not fixed, it is not known in which state one must perform the leap (*pluti*). Therefore, he says: "Far," and so forth. *Hūtam* means calling; that which is "far" in relation to that [calling] is what is intended here.

The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason. Because "distance" (*dūra*) is understood here in relation to "motion" (*dhūta*), therefore, when that specific effort which exceeds the natural effort— that is, the effort belonging to the original source (*prakṛti*)— is not resorted to, then the calling of the word is heard at that [distance].
That is not far away; therefore, the intention is that there is no instability regarding what is distant.

Now, how could there be a protracted vowel (*pluta*) here—as in "Drink the barley-meal, Devadatta3"? It is not merely the sound that is called out, but rather a specific type of sound by which one is enjoined to come when [the call] follows.

"Is *hūta* not a specific kind of sound, and that [specific sound] does not exist here? To this he says: "And the mention of *hūta*," and so forth. *Hūta* is an address (*sambodhana*) whose means of accomplishment is sound. The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "therefore. Thus, by that [mention of *hūta*], the address which is accomplished by it is indicated; therefore, the mention of *hūta* is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for address in general.

It should be understood as follows: here, this *pluta* vowel is prescribed for addressing someone from a distance, and so too is the *ekaśruti* (monotone); for it is stated, "The *ekaśruti* [is used] when addressing from a distance" (Pāṇini 1.2.33). In that case, since several [rules] would apply simultaneously to the same instance, one must resort to one of the options: annulment (*bādha*), option (*vikalpa*), or combination (*samuccaya*).

It must be so; however, it is not known here whether there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of these two, or an option (*vikalpa*), or perhaps the sublation (*bādha*) of one by the other. To ascertain that, he says:
"And in this [case]" (*asyāṃ ca*), etc. First, it is not by way of sublation...
It must be so, because they have the same object (*viṣaya*). For the relationship between the sublated (*bādhya*) and the sublator (*bādhaka*) occurs only when there is a difference in object,
as for example in [the rules] *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1) and *tata āgataḥ* (as found in the reading of the Prācīnyāsa).

Regarding the rule *ṭhāto 'nupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3): here, indeed, there is a difference in scope, for one [rule] has a specific domain while the other has a general one. However, since there is no such distinction between these two [present rules], sublation (*bādha*) is improper. An option (*vikalpa*) is also improper, because they do not apply simultaneously.

For a choice between alternatives occurs when two rules apply simultaneously, as in the case of *tad* and other pronouns. However, in this instance, there is no simultaneous application with respect to the single accent (*ekaśruti*), because the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*).
Therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), only the substitution (*samādeśa*) takes place; it is a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*).
Furthermore, in this case, the operation applies to one sentence (*vākya*), but not to a single constituent part (*avayava*);

for it is impossible for two contradictory operations to apply to a single part, whereas a sentence consists of multiple parts. Thus, the final vowel (*ṭi*) becomes *pluta*, while the remainder remains as it was.
Thus, it is appropriate that there be a single mode of enunciation (ekaśruti) for their coalescence.

85. *Haiheprayoge haihayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.85). By the preceding rule, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) was prescribed for the one being called, on account of that person's predominance; and that predominance belongs to him because the sentence is employed for the purpose of directing his attention. Therefore, [the protraction does not apply] to the two words *hai* and *he*.
[This] is attained; this is the purpose of this undertaking.

Now, however, for what purpose is there the mention of both [the *dhātu* and the *pratyaya*], since even without that, it will apply to those two alone because they are explicitly stated? To this he says: "again."

Regarding the passage beginning with "punastu" (the Kāśikā reading), and so forth: if it were stated simply as "haihe-prayoge," then because of the governing rule "vākyasya ṭeḥ pluta udātaḥ" (8.2.82), the protracted (*pluta*) vowel would apply only to the final two syllables of the sentence, not to those that are non-final; even for those two, it would apply only where...

The repetition of the term *hai* is for the sake of this very purpose: so that when *hai* and *he* are mentioned, the mention of actual usage (*prayoga*) may apply even to those [particles] that are meaningless (*anarthaka*). And they are meaningless only when they constitute the end of a vocative (*āmantrita*), because the meaning of the vocative has already been conveyed by that [vocative ending] itself; thus, there is no other meaning [to be conveyed].
First, they would be meaningless because of the absence of anything to be illuminated.

However, others say that those two are also combinations of particles, such as *hanta*, *hai*, and *iha*. In that case, if the mention of "usage" (*prayoga*) were not made, they would not be included, because they are derivative (*lākṣaṇika*). Therefore...
The mention of "actual usage" (prayoga) is for the purpose that the rule may apply even to words that possess secondary (lākṣaṇika) derivations, provided they are in actual usage.

According to the Easterners, the final syllable of a sentence in the context of returning a greeting (*pratyabhivāda*) and similar instances is protracted (*pluta*) and acute (*udātta*), even if it is not heavy (*guru*) or not final;

however, that same protracted vowel is prescribed for a heavy vowel—provided it is not *ṛ*—even if it is not the final syllable of the sentence. This refers to the rule: "of the final syllable (*teḥ*) even if it is not [the end]."

By this [use of] the word *api*, he shows that it effects a conjunction (*samuccaya*). For if the conjunction with the guru is made by the word *api*—meaning "even of a non-final guru" and "also of a final [guru]"—then, by this [rule], there is a protracted vowel (*pluta*) for a non-final guru; whereas a final light syllable remains protracted only by the preceding rule. And thus...

The simultaneous hearing of two protracted vowels (*pluta*) would result [as a fault]. Nor can it be argued that this will not occur because of the rule "A word is unaccented except for one syllable" (Pāṇini 6.1.158);

for when that [application of the rule] is to be performed, the *pluta* vowel is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). When even the element bearing the designation *ṭi* is [included] by the word "api"...

It is collected by this very sūtra; for by this [sūtra], the prolated vowel (*pluta*) is prescribed for the final *ṭi* as well as for a non-final heavy syllable (*guru*). In that context, because of the expression "of each one" (*ekaikasya*), it is not the case that there is an option (*paryāya*) for the non-final [syllable].
Just as it occurs [in the case of the first], so it is for the last; thus, there is no contingency of simultaneity.

Regarding the phrase "the apprehension of each one," and so forth: if the apprehension of each one were not made, then in some cases all [the letters] would contingently be perceived simultaneously. Therefore, they are perceived successively, as follows:

The inclusion of the term "each one" (*ekaika*) is for the sake of this very purpose. And it should be understood that this was done by relying on the principle: "Technical definitions and paribhāṣās [apply] according to their enunciation" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 59). In another system of interpretation, when the rule "A word is unaccented except for one [vowel]" (Pāṇini 6.1.158) is brought into effect...
If [the rule] were simply "sati" (when there is), there would be the undesirable consequence of two protracted vowels occurring simultaneously.
Now, as for the word "prācām" (of the Easterners); since the option (*vibhāṣā*) would be established by the mention of "each one" (*ekaika*) alone, why is "prācām" stated?
To this he says: "prācām. The intention is that [the option applies] to every protracted vowel. Therefore...
Thus he says: "By this," and so forth. Acting without having reflected upon the cause of ruin is recklessness (*sāhasa*).
87. *om* is used in the sense of "commencement" (*abhyādāna*). (Pāṇini 8.2.87). [The word] "commencement" means: at the commencement of what? Of the Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) and so forth.

88. *ye* in the context of sacrificial ritual (*yajñakarmaṇi*). Regarding the phrase "in the context of sacrificial ritual," the word *karma* denotes action; thus, the meaning is "in the sacrificial act.
This protracted vowel (*pluta*) is desired only in the case of "ye yajāmahe," and this is [the view] of the Easterners (*prācām*).
It should be understood that this is obtained through the recurrence of the word "iti" and by understanding [the rule] as a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).

89. *praṇavaṣṭeḥ* (8.2.89). "What is this that is called the *praṇava*?"—this question arises because the *praṇava* has not been defined in this grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) and is not well-known in common worldly usage. [The rule continues with: *pādasya vā*. [The rule concerning] the foot...

By the phrase "celyādinā" (or "prā.mu.pāṭhaḥ"), he demonstrates the nature of the *praṇava* according to the conventions of other scriptures. Regarding the statement "the final syllable," the vowel is intended here by the word "syllable" (*akṣara*). Its "finality," moreover, is in relation to the other vowels. Regarding the term "having embraced" (*upasaṃgṛhya*).
The meaning is "having taken. That which has that final syllable at its beginning is "beginning with that" (*tadādi*).
"Syllable" (*akṣara*) and "remainder" (*śeṣa*) form a collective *dvandva* compound.
A "syllable" (*akṣara*) is a vowel; its "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is the consonant. That vowel and that remainder of the syllable together constitute "the syllable and its remainder" (*akṣara-śeṣa*).
That which has "the vowel" as its remainder (*akṣaraśeṣa*) is that very [vowel] where there is no consonant following the final vowel;

this is the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) of that bahuvrīhi compound. By the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the designation "beginning with that" (*tadādi*) applies there as well. This refers to cases where there is a consonant following the final vowel.

In this context, the consonant together with the vowel constitutes the meaning of the other member of the compound; for here, a *bahuvrīhi* compound that includes the quality of its members (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*) is intended. Thus, by this passage, it is stated that the very thing designated by the technical term *ṭi*—namely, the remainder consisting of two syllables—is replaced by the three-moraic *ukāra*, which is the *oṃkāra*.

Or, they say that the *praṇava* follows from the verb *vid*, as in "jinvato3m. Here, the present tense (*laṭ*) follows the root *ji* (to quicken), which undergoes the substitution of *śatṛ*; by transposition, the suffix *śnu* is applied, followed by the *yaṇ* replacement.
When the form *jinvan* is established, the *praṇava* is added after the final syllable of the word *an*. [Likewise in] "sumnayo3m."

Thus: from the word *sumna*, the suffix *kyac* is applied; by the rule *kyāc chandasi* (Pāṇini 3.2.170), the suffix *u* is added; by the rule *devasumnayoryajuṣi kāṭhake* (Pāṇini 7.4.38), the feminine suffix (*āp*) is elided; with *sumnāyuḥ* thus established, the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) is substituted for the final vowel and the following consonant of the word *usu*.

But surely, the technical definition (paribhāṣā) has been established that the *praṇava* [the syllable *om*] is substituted for the two long vowels *o* and *au* only when they are marked with the *ṭi* designation. In that case, even without the mention of *ṭi*, the substitution will occur for *ṭi* alone;
so what is the purpose of mentioning *ṭi* here? To this he says: "The mention of *ṭi," etc. If this mention of *ṭi* were not present...
In the case of [substitutes] ending in consonants, by the paribhāṣā "the final [element is replaced]" (Pāṇini 1.1.52), the substitution would apply only to the final [letter].

Therefore, the mention of *ṭi* is made so that it may apply to the whole of the *ṭi*, and not just to the final letter. Since the syllable *oṃ* consists of multiple letters (*anekāl*), it is a substitute for the whole.
The mention of *ṭi* is for the sake of the meaning of the term "bhaviṣyati" (future).

Here, does the mention of *anta-* (end) serve to set aside the rule for *ṭi-*, or is it a qualifier? In the former case, since the end is qualified by the vowel (*ac*), the protracted vowel (*pluta*) would apply only to a *yājyā* that ends in a vowel.

It might be so; however, in the other case, the mention of "the end" (*anta*) would be purposeless, for an *antyati* (a suffix ending in a *ti* that is not at the end of a word) is impossible, since the rule *aco 'ntyādi ṭi* (Pāṇini 1.1.64) prescribes the technical term *ṭi* specifically for a particular form of the word *ṭi*. With this intention, he asks: "What is the purpose of mentioning 'the end'? (*antagrahaṇaṃ kim*)?

Thus [he spoke]. The other, having understood the intention, spoke as follows—"They are called 'those to be abandoned'" (yājyā nāma), etc.—in order to show that the purpose of the mention of "extremes" (antagrahaṇa) is indeed something else. The meaning has already been explained.

91. [The substitution of *e* for the final vowel of the verbal roots] *brū*, *hi*, *preṣya*, *śrauṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *āvaha*, as well as for the initial [vowel] of [the word] *nāma*, [occurs before the vocative particle *bhoḥ*].

(8.2.91) *Śrauṣaṭ* and *vauṣaṭ* are indeclinables (*nipāta*); the others are the second person singular present imperative forms of the root *vah*. Some, however, maintain that the word *āvaha* is also an indeclinable.
Thus they say: "preṣya. [The root] *iṣ* means "to go" (*iṣu gatau*, read as *iṣa gatau* in the Divādi class, DhP 1127).
Because it belongs to the Divādi class, the suffix *śyan* is applied; then, by virtue of the vowel *ā* of the prefix (*upa*), the rule *ād guṇaḥ* (6.1.87) applies.

Now, why does this not occur here—as in "āvaha devān yajamānāya" (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 5.12), "āvaha jātavedaḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 1.3.22), and "suyajā yaja"? To this he says: "āvaha devān," and so forth.
The inclusion of the word "ādi" (beginning) is so that [the rule] does not apply to the beginning of a sentence.

92. And [the substitution of *ā* for *i* occurs] after the word *agnīdh* in the sense of commanding another. (8.2.92) In the sense of "one who invokes Agni," *agnīdh* refers to a specific officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). The commanding or directing of that person is called *agnītpreṣaṇa*. Because the word *ādeḥ* is immediately present [in the preceding rule], [the substitution applies] only with reference to that.
He says, "From that very [word] *ādeḥ*," and so forth, to show that another [meaning] is also understood.

Regarding the phrase "in this very [instance]," he says, "O Agnīdh, spread the fires; strew the sacrificial grass," in order to demonstrate what is excluded by the particle *eva* from the two examples just mentioned. How?

How, then, is this obtained? He says: "For that purpose," and so forth. And just as it is possible to understand that the *pluta* vowel is optional (*vibhāṣā*) everywhere, so too has it been established in such rules as "of a heavy [syllable], not being *ṛ*, and not final" (Pāṇini 8.2.86). If, then, the *pluta* is optional everywhere—
Would it not be redundant to include the mention of *vibhāṣā* later on? No; it is for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*).

Now, how is there a protracted vowel (*pluta*) here—as in "uddhara3 uddhara" and "abhihara3 abhihara"? For this protracted vowel occurs at the time of Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*), not during the command to the *āgnīdhra* priest; nor is this [protraction] of the initial syllable, nor does it apply by the rule "of that which follows the initial" (*ādeḥ parasya*).

(1.1.54) What then? Is it [the case] for something other than that? To this he says: because *ādeḥ* (of the beginning) is proximate, *paraḥ* (the subsequent) is understood in relation to that alone; thus he says, "from that very beginning," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in this very [instance]," that which was excluded by the particle *eva* in the two examples just mentioned—

To demonstrate this, he says: "O Agnīdh, distribute the fires; strew the sacrificial grass. But how is this obtained? He says: "For that purpose," and so forth. And why would the protracted vowel (*pluta*) be understood as optional everywhere, making the mention of "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) in the subsequent rule redundant? It is not so.

Because it serves the purpose of ritual elaboration (*prapañca*). Now, how is there a protracted vowel (*pluta*) here—as in "uddhara3 uddhara" and "abhihara3 abhihara"? For this protraction occurs at the time of Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*), not during the command to the *Āgnīdhra* priest; nor does this [protraction] apply to the initial syllable, nor does it fall under the rule "of what follows the initial syllable" (Pāṇini 1.1.54). What then? It applies to something other than that. To this he says: "But here..."
And so forth; this is for the sake of clarity.

93. *vibhāṣā pṛṣṭaprativacane heḥ* (8.2.93). Regarding the term *pṛṣṭaprativacanam*: a response to what has been asked (*pṛṣṭasya prativacanam*) is an answer to a question; thus, it is called *pṛṣṭaprativacanam*. This word *prativacana* [is used] even for a statement that is contrary [to the question].

It occurs [in the sense of] contradiction: "a reply" (*prativacana*) means a statement that is opposed; for here the prefix *prati* signifies opposition, as in "an opposing wrestler" (*pratimalla*) or "an opposing elephant" (*pratigaja*). It also occurs in the sense of distribution (*vīpsā*):
"a reply" (*prativacana*) means "with respect to each statement" (*vacanaṃ vacanaṃ prati*), according to the rule "that indeclinable which is used in the sense of 'as' (*yathā*)."

(2.1.6) Thus, there is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of "desire to reply" (*dīpsā*). It also occurs in the sense of "resolution" (*samādhāna*)—that is, when one says, "I have formulated a response to what was stated by him," it is understood that a resolution has been provided. In that context, if the word "in response" (*prativacane*) were used [as the governing term], it would apply everywhere.
[Otherwise] it would follow [that the rule applies everywhere]. Therefore, the mention of "asked" (pṛṣṭa) is for the sake of specifying a particular type of response;
so that [the rule] may apply only to the explanation of meaning which constitutes a response to what was asked, and not elsewhere.

94. *nigṛhyānuyoge ca* (8.2.94). The word *nigṛhya* is a gerund (*lyabanta*). The word *svatāt* means "from one's own understanding. The word *prācyāvanam*—the reading in the Prācya manuscript is *pracyācanam*—means "removal."

‘Ṭhāviṣkaraṇam’ means making manifest. ‘Śrāddham’ refers to a specific type of ritual. ‘Devamanuyujyate’ means that which is performed after one’s own view has been thus set forth. The particle ‘ca’ (and) serves to carry forward the optionality [indicated by] ‘vibhāṣā’. Consequently, the subsequent rule becomes mandatory.

95. *Āmreḍitam* [is used] in the sense of reproach. (8.2.95) For example: *caura caura3*. The doubling occurs in the sense of reproach by the rule "of the vocative at the beginning of a sentence" (8.1.8), and so forth. Although this mention of "sentence" (*vākya*) [might suggest otherwise], it refers to the final word [of that sentence].

This is for the purpose of excluding the *pluta* vowel; nevertheless, here, by the force of the statement, it occurs even for a non-final [word]. For a reduplicated word (*āmreḍita*) used in reproaching cannot occur at the end of a sentence, since the rule for doubling applies only to a word that is the beginning of a sentence when used in reproaching.

Regarding the phrase "for that purpose": it is for the sake of ensuring that [the designation] applies alternately to both the preceding and the following words; and it is also for the purpose of indicating a doubled word (*dvirukta*). From the inclusion of the term "reproach" (*bhartsana*) in the rule concerning the *āmreḍita*, it is understood that [the designation applies] to that which follows a doubled word.

That is called *āmreḍita*. However, the occurrence of a threat (*bhartsana*) is not possible merely by that much, because a threat is indicated by reduplication (*dvirukti*). Therefore, it is understood that the mention of *āmreḍita* is for the purpose of indicating reduplication. And since that reduplication occurs in both the preceding and the subsequent context, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) applies to both as well.
It occurs; and it occurs alternately, not simultaneously,
because the *pluti* has as its fruit the manifestation of a threat, and since that threat is manifested by the *pluti* itself,
[the other vowel] is unnecessary.

96. *aṅgayuktaṃ tiṅakāṅkṣam* (8.2.96). Regarding *tiṅakāṅkṣam*: it is called *ākāṅkṣam* because it "desires" (*ākāṅkṣati*) or "expects" (*apekṣate*), formed with the suffix *ac* from the root *kākṣ*. Examples include *aṅga kūja 3* and so forth; both *aṅga kūja 3* and *aṅga vyāhara 3* are [cases where this rule applies].
"He will know now, you fool"—this is what is expected. "Ho, Devadatta!"—this also implies "you speak falsely. "Study!"—this also implies "I shall give you food.
"He does not desire anything further than this"—this refers to the intended meaning.
Because [the rule] has already been completed.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *yukta* (joined), since the connection (*yoga*) will be understood simply because it is a rule concerning words (*padavidhi*)? If that is so, then by making the mention of *yukta*, [the author] indicates this: "that which is meaningful (*samartha*)."

The paribhāṣā "padavidhiḥ" (Pāṇini 2.1.1) is not universal. Consequently, in the expression *asūryampaśyāni mukhāni*, the compound is established even though there is no semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) between the negative particle *nañ* and the word *sūrya*.

97. *vicāryamāṇānām* (8.2.97). "Investigation" (*vicāra*) is the examination of an object by means of a standard of proof (*pramāṇa*). Those things which are made the objects of such [examination] are "those being investigated" (*vicāryamāṇāni*). The use of the plural number in the rule is intended for those cases where the investigation pertains solely to the meaning [of the words themselves].

[The phrase] "pertaining to their own nature" is for the purpose that this may apply to them as well; otherwise, it would apply only to those whose inquiry pertains to their own nature. For when the primary sentence is being investigated, there is no inclusion of that which is investigated only indirectly through its meaning as a secondary [subject].

This is correct: in the case of "gṛhā3i," there is the vowel *e* in the word *gṛhe*; by the rule "heco'pragṛhyasya" (Pāṇini 8.2.107), the first half of that vowel becomes *ā* and the second half becomes *ī*. By this [present rule], that *ā* becomes protracted (*pluta*).

98. *pūrvaṃ tu bhāṣāyām* (8.2.98). Since this was already established by the preceding rule, this [sūtra] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*). The word *tu*, however, serves to restrict according to the intended meaning. For if that word were absent, a contrary restriction might be understood: "only in the colloquial language (*bhāṣāyām eva*)."

Regarding the word "pūrvam" (the former): its status as "former" is relative to usage. Between the two sentences "ahir nu" and "rajjur nu," the *pluta* (protracted) vowel occurs only for the *ṭi* (the final phoneme of the stem) of that which is used first. However, in this case, because the term "bhāva" (state/occurrence) is not mentioned, [the rule] follows from the previous sūtra, "chandasi" (in the Veda).
It is understood.

99. *Pratiśravaṇe ca* (8.2.99). *Pratiśrutiḥ* is *pratiśravaṇam*. [The word is derived] from the root *śru* preceded by *prati*, with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*), and a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule *kugati-prādayaḥ* (2.2.18). When the root *śru* is preceded by *prati*— [The sūtra prescribes the substitution of *śu* for *śra* in the word *pratiśravaṇa* when it denotes a promise.]

If the intention is to express "favoring others," then it occurs in the sense of "acceptance" (*abhyupagama*). However, if there is no intention to express "favoring others," then it occurs in the sense of "promise" (*pratijñāna*). When there is reliance—whereby the word *śravaṇa* is used as an abstract noun meaning "hearing"—the prefix *prati-* is used with the sense of "towards" (*ābhimukhya*) according to the rule *lakṣaṇenābhipratī ābhimukhye* (Pāṇini 2.1.14).

Thus, when the avyayībhāva compound is formed, the meaning is "turned toward listening" or "engaged in listening. Since no specific [object] is mentioned here, the *pluta* (protracted) vowel occurs for the final syllable (*ṭi*) of the sentence in every instance of such listening, as in:
"O Devadatta, what are you saying? This refers to being turned toward listening.
An example: "O Devadatta!"—this is an address (*āmantritama*).

He speaks thus, "What do you say? for the purpose of hearing that [address]. Because he has engaged in the act directed toward hearing, he is oriented toward [the speaker]. An example in the sense of acceptance is: "Give me a cow."

"O sir, I give this to you"—this is the promise. "The word must be eternal"—this is the proposition. The particle *ca* (and) is for the purpose of drawing in [the rule] "in the spoken language" (*bhāṣāyām*).

100. *anudāttaṃ praśnāntābhipūjitayoḥ* | (8.2.100) [The word] *agamaḥ* [is an example]. From the root *gam*, the *luṅ* suffix is applied; by the rule *puṣādidyutādyuditaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (3.1.55), because it belongs to the *lṛd*-class, the suffix *aṅ* is applied, followed by the suffix *sip*.
In the examples *ṭhagnibhūtā3i* and *ṭhpaṭā3u*, when a vocative follows,

the substitution of *guṇa* occurs by the rule *ṭhhrasvasya guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.108), and the vowel *a* is substituted [for the *guṇa*] by the rule *ṭheco'pragṛhyasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.107), as are the vowels *i* and *u*. In the illustrative sentences, the protracted (*pluta*) vowel of the preceding words is applied by this very same [rule], having understood that it has already been performed.

If someone should object: "But how can there be a protracted (*pluta*) vowel here for *ānantya* as well, since the rule *vākyasya ṭeḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.82) continues to apply?"—to him he replies with the words: "In the case of *agnibhūte* and *paṭo*, etc."

101. *Cid* is used in the sense of comparison. (8.2.101) Regarding the word *cid*: the use of the particle *iti* is for the purpose of indicating that this [word] is a qualifier of the word *prayujyamāna* ("being employed"). For if this *iti* were not present for this purpose, [the rule would apply even when *cid* is not being employed].
It should be understood that when another word is employed in the sense of "like" (hyupamārtha), the word *cit* undergoes prolation (*pluta*).
Since it is being enjoined here, when that [word *cit*] is specified, the prolation of the final syllable (*ṭi*) of the sentence becomes established.

Regarding the phrase "ṭhkatathañcidāhaḥ," here the word *cit* occurs in the sense of difficulty (*kṛcchre*). In the example "ṭhagnirmāṇavako bhāyāt," the meaning is "the boy should shine like fire"; thus, although there is a sense of comparison (*upamārtha*) here, because the word *cit* is not employed, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) does not occur. However, when it is absent...

Since the mention of "being employed" (*prayujyamāna*) here refers to the occurrence of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), even though the employment of all other items serving as standards of comparison is understood, nevertheless, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) must indeed occur based on the employment of the word *cit* in this context. The particle *ca* serves to indicate that this [protraction] belongs specifically to this [word].

The meaning is "conjunction" (samuccaya). And since conjunction is based on distinction, this is stated immediately after [the rule for] prolation (pluta); otherwise, in this very context, one would merely be enjoining the quality of being unaccented (anudātta) with respect to the previously mentioned causes of prolation.
It would be understood.
102. *uparisvidāsīdati ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.102).

The particle *iti* is for the purpose of indicating the subject of the operation (*kāryin*). For indeed, in order to prescribe an operation, that [subject] must necessarily be indicated by means of the genitive case. By the particle *iti*, the sense of "or" (*vā*) is recalled.

In this context, the word *upari-svit* and others, which are primarily concerned with sound (*śabda-pradhāna*), are intended as the grammatical operation (*kārya*) and are indicated by the particle *iti*, so that they may be understood as having the protracted (*pluta*) accent—as in the example beginning with "adhaḥ svid āsīt.
Here, it is being deliberated whether [the world] existed below or whether it existed above; therein—

In the preceding rule, by the sūtra "vicāryamāṇānām" (8.2.97) and so forth, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is acute; however, in the present case, by this [rule], it is grave (*anudātta*), serving as an exception to that very same [acute].
The purpose of the particle *ca* is the same as before.
103. *svaritamāmreḍite'sūyāsammatikopakutsaneṣu* (8.2.103).

The terms *asūyā* and so forth have been explained in the rule *vākyāderāmantritasya...* (8.1.8). In examples such as *māṇavaka3 māṇavaka*, the reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is produced by that very same rule.

It should be understood that [the phrase] "the word 'vā' must be employed" is intended. The term *vā* is an indicator of an alternative (*vikalpa*). The word *vacana* means an explanation (*vyākhyāna*). What is meant here is this: an explanation by way of an alternative must be provided.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: from the rule "vibhāṣā pṛṣṭaprativacane heḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.93), the term *vibhāṣā* ("optionally") is carried over by the principle of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūakapluti*); therefore, there will be an option.
104. *Kṣiyā-āśīḥ-praiṣeṣu tiṅ-ākāṅkṣam* (Pāṇini 8.2.104). *Kṣiyā* is a deviation from established conduct; *āśīḥ* is the expression of a desired blessing; *praiṣa* is an injunction.
[In these cases,] there is an expectation (*ākāṅkṣati*) for another finite verb (*tiṅanta*) itself. Why is this so? Precisely because of the mention of "expectation" (*ākāṅkṣā*).
For at the end of a sentence, there is necessarily an expectation for that which conveys the accomplishment [of the action] by means of a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*).

In the phrase "and wealth, my dear," there is an expectation for the word "may you obtain" (*lapsīṣṭa*). In the phrase "and grammar," there too is an expectation for the word "may you study" (*adhyeṣīṣṭa*).
In *ṭhlunīhi*, there is the substitution of *ī* by [Pāṇini 6.4.113] *ī halyadhoḥ*. In *piba*, there is the substitute *piba* by the rule [Pāṇini 7.3.78] *pāghrādhmādheṭdṛśaḥ śaḥ*.
In *astu*, there is the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *as*; there is the substitution of *u* by [Pāṇini 3.4.86] *er uḥ*, and because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is the elision of *śap*.
The suffix *luk* (elision) does not depend on this other finite verb; the same applies to the word "vihara" as well.

105. *Anantyasyāpi praśnākhyānayoḥ* (8.2.105). Regarding the phrase *antyasya tu*, etc.: the word *tu* indicates a distinction from other rules. By the rule *antyasya* as well, [the final syllable] becomes circumflex (*svarita*), according to *anudāttaṃ praśnāntābhipūjitayoḥ*.

By this [rule] (8.2.100), the *anudātta* [accent] is also [prescribed]; however, the simultaneous occurrence of both [accents] in a single instance is not possible. In that case, by virtue of the authority of the specific rule (*vacana-prāmāṇya*), the *anudātta* does not occur in one alternative, nor does the *svarita*.
106. *plutāvaica idutau* | (8.2.106) When a *pluta* vowel is prescribed by rules such as *dūrāddhūte ca* (8.2.84),
since the rule *acaśca* (1.2.28) is present, wherever a *pluta* is mentioned, there [it applies] to an *ac*.

This [prolongation] would apply to the *e* and *ai* vowels as a whole; however, it is desired to apply it only to their constituent parts (*avayava*). Since that cannot be established without an explicit statement, this [sūtra] is commenced. Furthermore, since the occasion for the prolated vowel (*pluta*) arises from the *e* and *ai* vowels occurring at a distance, etc., the prolation is already obtained by the preceding section.

The meaning is "when [the vowel] is *sat*. In the examples *ai3tikāyana* and *āu3pamanyava*, although a prolation (*pluta*) of the *ec* vowels would have been required by the rule *guroranṛto 'nantyasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.86), this [rule] instead effects the prolation of the *i* and *u* sounds that constitute those *ec* vowels. This occurs in *ai3tikāyana* and *āu3pamanyava*.

If the protracted (*pluta*) vowel is applied to either of the two components (*avayava*) of *ai* or *au*, then in that case, the *e* and *o* vowels would result in being either four morae (*caturmātra*) or three and a half morae (*sārddhatrimātra*). For here, *ai* and *au* are composite phonemes (*samāhāravarṇa*); one mora belongs to the vowel (*a*), and one mora each belongs to the *i* and *u* vowels. However, others say: "Half a mora belongs to the vowel (*a*)," [and so forth].

Regarding the phrase "adhyardhamātra eva varṇo 'varṇayoḥ": in the former view, when this prolation (*pluta*) is applied, *i* and *u* possess three morae (*mātrā*), while the *a*-vowel possesses one; thus, four morae would result. In the other view, however, the *a*-vowel has half a mora, while *i* and *u* have those same [three] morae.
Thus, [the vowel] would result in being three and a half morae (mātrās); therefore, he says: "In this case, when... and so forth.

Now, an objection is raised: "The designation *pluta* has been assigned to that which consists of three morae; how then can two or three morae also be made *pluta* by this [rule]? To this he replies: "For [the rule] says 'in the two *plutas*...'".

By this [statement] beginning with "ityādinā," he shows that the *pluta* (protracted vowel) mentioned here is the worldly (*laukika*) one, not the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) one. But how is this obtained? Because the mention of *pluta* again would otherwise be purposeless; for in common usage, the *pluta* is indeed understood as having the quality of *vṛddhi*.

For this very reason he says: "The meaning is that [the two] reach an increase (vṛddhi). Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *plu* also functions in the sense of "increase. But even so, would it not follow that increase occurs without restriction? For there is no specification of the extent [of that increase]; and consequently, whatever increase might occur, by whatever...
"How might the two [vowels] become four mātrās?"—to this he says "it" (iti), and so forth. "Pluti" means "increase. But how is this rule obtained?
He thinks as follows: in the phrase "aicaḥ," the genitive case is used with reference to the *pluta* vowel; thus, *i* and *u* are lengthened (*plavete*) in such a way that they [become four mātrās].

The *eṅ* vowels become *pluta*; and thus *ai* and *au* become [long] when there is such an increase (*vṛddhi*) by which *ai* and *au* become three-mora (*trimātra*). For if the *vṛddhi* were not performed, they would simply remain *ai* and *au*, because *ai* and *au* possess a fixed measure; and consequently, they would be connected with the category of *aic*.
"Pluta should not occur.
[The term] "ardhatṛtīyamātrau" means those two whose measure (mātrā) is two and a half; that is, those two which possess a measure of two and a half. This...
Thus far, a solution has been stated by relying on the opinion of the Vārttikakāra.

Now, showing that for the Bhāṣyakāra, however, the *pluta* vowel indeed possesses four morae (*caturmātratā*), he says: "But in the Bhāṣya it is said," and so forth. [The question] "How is that? [is asked] if that is the opinion of the Bhāṣyakāra.
"In what manner, then, would that [pluta] be accomplished?"—this is what he asks.
With the words "In the case of equal division," etc., he demonstrates how that is accomplished.
