For, in the case of equal division, by this sūtra a *pluta* vowel of three morae (*trimātra*) is made out of the *i* and *u*; and therefore...

The three morae belonging to that [protracted vowel], together with the preceding single mora, all combined, constitute four morae. Thus, the protracted (*pluta*) vowel becomes four-moraic. In this regard, according to the view of the author of the Bhāṣya, the repetition of the term *pluta* is for the purpose of including all types of protracted vowels everywhere.

Otherwise, since this occurs within the section concerning the svarita accent, this prolation (pluti) would apply only to that [svarita], just as in the case of *it* and *ut*. By including the term "prolation" (*pluta*) again, it applies to both the udātta and the anudātta as well.
The addition of the marker *t* (in *plutaḥ*) is for the sake of clarity.

8.2.107. *eco'pragṛhyasyādūrādūdhūte pūrvasyārghasyādutarasyedutau*. [When a word ending in] *e* or *o*, which is not a *pragṛhya* vowel, is followed by a vocative (*āmantrita*) that is not distant, the first half-vowel (*ardhamātra*) of the preceding [vowel] is replaced by *i* and the second half-vowel of the following [vowel] is replaced by *u*.

The *ec* vowels are composite sounds (*samāhāra-varṇa*). Among them, this protracted (*pluta*) vowel belongs to the whole (*samudāya*)—namely, the *e*-vowel and the *o*-vowel—by virtue of the preceding section; however, it pertains to the constituent parts (*avayava*), namely the *i*-vowel and the *u*-vowel.
This [present] sūtra is commenced following the immediately preceding one, on the grounds that "an enumeration of the specific domains [of application] must be made."

This is the statement of the rule's inclusion. He provides its explanation with the words "it should be stated" (*kartavyam*)—[the *Kāśikā* reads *vaktavyam*]—meaning it must be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: "That which is unaccented (*anudātta*) [is used] in questions and in expressions of honor" (Pāṇini 8.2.100).
The rules beginning with these apply here; therefore, they do not occur elsewhere.

Regarding the term *yathāviṣayam*: that which is the domain (*viṣaya*) of something is "according to its domain" (*yathāviṣayam*); this is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to Pāṇini 2.1.7, *yathā’sādṛśye*.

In the case of *praśna* (question) and *abhipūjita* (honored), the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is anudātta according to Pāṇini 8.2.100. However, in the case of a question, it is svarita according to 8.2.105 (*anantyasyāpi praśnākhyānayoḥ*), while in other cases it is udātta. As for *it* and *tau*, these two are udātta; this is established by 8.2.82 (*terudātaḥ*).
And because of the governing rule [of the context]: “O Viṣṇubhūta, O Viṣṇubhūta!”—here, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is applied by the rule *āmreḍitaṃ bhartsane* (Pāṇini 8.2.95).
“Come, O boy Viṣṇubhūta!”—here, it is applied by the rule *dūrād dhūte ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.84).

Thus [it is said]. But surely, even in the absence of this enumeration, the *pluta* (protracted vowel) would not occur anyway, because of the rule "when [addressing someone] from afar" (*adūrāddhūte*).
Therefore, for what purpose is this counter-example provided for the enumeration? To this he says: "And in the case of the enumeration," etc. If the enumeration were absent...

It is stated that "it will apply by means of *adūrāddhūta*. However, this being the case, it need not have been said; for by the very enumeration [of exceptions], it would not apply in the case of *dūrāddhūta*. The word "kartavyam" (should be done) means that it must be explained.

In this regard, the following is the explanation: from the rule *yājyāntaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.90), the mention of the word *anta-* ("end") is carried over; therefore, [the prolation] will apply only to the final syllable. For example:
*bhadraṃ karoṣi gauḥ*. Here, the prolated vowel (*pluta*) is applied by the rule *abhipūjite* (Pāṇini 8.2.100).

Because the term *antagrahaṇa* (mentioning the "end") continues [from the previous rule], this rule does not apply here; for in this case, the word *etat* is not present, but rather the consonant (*vyañjana*).
As in: *śobhane khalau staḥ khaṭve3*. Here too, [the rule] *abhipūjite* (Pāṇini 8.2.100) applies.
Thus, it is *pluta*. Regarding the rule "in an addressed vocative" (*āmantrite*), the word *ca* does not appear in the *Kāśikā* or the *Padamañjarī*; such is the case with *caṭ* and so forth.
This is a *pluta-vikāra*, meaning it is both a *pluta* and a modification (*vikāra*). However, the designation *pluta* applies specifically to the vowels *i* and *u*.

It should be understood [as *pluta*] by association with the *pluta* vowel. The mention of *it* and *ut* is for the purpose that these substitutes (*et*, *ot*) do not apply to what precedes or follows *ai* and *au*. The inclusion of the *ta*-marker (*tapara*) here also serves the purpose of ease of pronunciation.

108. *tayor vāci saṃhitāyām* (8.2.108). Regarding the word *tayoḥ*: this refers back to the vowels *i* and *u* prescribed immediately before. Examples are *agnā3yāśā*, *paṭā3vāśā*. This occurs when *agne āśā* and *paṭo āśā* are in their original state.

When any one of these— namely, *praśnānta* (the end of a question), *abhipūjita* (honored), *dicyamāṇa* (being addressed), *pratyabhivākya* (a reply), or *ājyānta* (the end of a sacrificial offering)— is intended to be expressed, the vowel *a* of the preceding syllable becomes protracted (*pluta*),
while the vowels *i* and *u* of the following syllable become *y* and *v* respectively by this [rule].

But for what purpose is this [rule] commenced? Is it not already established by the rule "ṭhiko yaṇaci" (P. 6.1.77)? To this he says: "Because the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is not established [for the purposes of the preceding rules]," and so forth. Now, is it not the case that the protracted vowel *is* established in the context of vowel-sandhis (*svarasandhi*), since this very [sūtra] states: "The protracted vowel and the *pragṛhya* vowels [remain unchanged] before a vowel"?

This [sūtra] states that the *pluta* vowel retains its original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). For an effect must belong to something that exists, not to something non-existent; and since the *pluta* is a single [vowel], would these two [the *pluta* and the *prakṛtibhāva*] not already be established within the rules for vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*)? To this he says: "Even so," and so forth. If this were not stated, then...
When *agnā3i* and *indram* remain, or *paṭā3u* and *udakam* remain,

the rule for lengthening before a homogeneous vowel (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghatvam*, 6.1.101) would apply, overriding the substitution of *yaṇ* prescribed by the sixth [chapter]. Furthermore, here, when *agnā3i* and *āśā* remain, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) according to the rule "before a non-homogeneous vowel, there is the option of the original form and a short vowel for Śākalya" (*iko'savarṇe śākalyasya hrasvaśca*, 6.1.127).

It might be so. Therefore, even though these two [sandhis] are established, this must indeed be stated for the purpose that lengthening (*dīrghatva*) and the *śākala* rule do not occur. But surely there is another effort for the sake of excluding those; if one asks what that is, it is said: "In the case of *śakandhu*, etc. (*śakandhvādi*).

In the rule *yaṇ aci* (6.1.77), an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is stated: "It must be stated that for an *ik* preceded by a protracted vowel (*pluta*), a *yaṇ* substitute is to be prescribed, in order to prevent the application of Śākala’s rule and the substitution of a long vowel.
This addition must necessarily be made. For instance, when the word *bhoḥ* has its final vowel protracted, there is an *ik*. In this case—

The vowel *i* following the word *bhoḥ* is a particle (*nipāta*), not a modification of a protracted (*pluta*) vowel. It is desired that this [particle] undergo the *yaṇ* substitution; however, that would not occur in the absence of this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*). Therefore, it must certainly be formulated. And when it is formulated, by that very [rule], the same applies to the protracted forms of *i* and *u* as well.
It must be so; therefore, this [objection] should not be stated. To this he says: "Nevertheless," and so forth.

When *agnā* and *āśā* are situated together, if the substitution of *yaṇ* were to take place here by that supplementary rule of the sixth [chapter], in the place of the udātta vowel *ī*, then, when the accentuation of an udātta *yaṇ* (udāttayaṇ-svara) is to be applied...

Because [the vowel] of the word *āśā* would be established as unaccented (*anudātta*), the rule "svarita for an unaccented [vowel] following a yaṇ that is udātta or svarita" (Pāṇini 8.2.4) would result in a svarita accent. However, the word *āśā* is oxytone (antodātta) according to the rule "if *āśā* is not named a direction" (Phitsūtra 1.18). The remainder is also...

By the rule *anudāttau suppitau* (6.1.158), the vowel [of the suffix] is anudātta. Consequently, there arises the contingency of its becoming svarita; therefore, this is stated in order to prevent that. The passage beginning with *kintu yaṇā* consists of two summary verses (*saṃgrahaśloka*). The word *kim* is used in the sense of a question, while *tu* means "but."

[Objection: Is it not already established here in examples such as *agnāyī āśā* by means of the *yaṇ* substitution according to the rule *iKo yaṇ aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77)? Why then does the Teacher prescribe *ṛ* and *u* as *ṝ* and *ū* (*ṝvau*)?
[Response: The intention is that everything is indeed established. It might be argued that the *yaṇ* substitution does not [apply]...

[The objection is: "Since [the substitution] would apply when that [operation] is to be performed, the *it* and *ut* [substitutions] would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*). To this, he says: "And those two," etc. The word *tu* (but/and) indicates the reason. When an *ik* vowel is preceded by a protracted (*pluta*) vowel, then [the substitution] would occur for it.
Therefore, it must be stated: "For an *ik* vowel preceded by a protracted vowel, the *yaṇ* substitute should be prescribed."

Regarding the supplementary rule (vārttika 673), "In order to prevent the application of Śākala’s [shortening] and the long vowel," this constitutes an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *yaṇ*. For that reason, the rules for Śākala’s shortening and the long vowel will not apply to those *i* and *u* vowels. The word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), and its position is displaced.

It should be understood as occurring immediately after the prohibition. "And those two [rules] are established in my system regarding vowel-sandhis (*svarasandhi*). Furthermore, the rules for *śākala* (elision) and lengthening do not apply. Thus it is an exception (*apavāda*).
Since their purpose is the avoidance of *śākala* and lengthening...
He states another purpose: "But the sublation of the *yaṇ*-vowel [accent] is indeed the reason.
A *yaṇ*-vowel accent (*yaṇasvara*) is an accent based on a *yaṇ* substitution; its sublation (*bādhana*) is the reason (*hetu*), that is, the cause. Of what?
From the context, it is understood to be the reason for the commencement of the rule (*sūtra*). The word "but" (*tu*) is used for emphasis.
The meaning is that the very fact of not contradicting [the Sūtra] itself is the reason for the commencement of this Sūtra.
Thus ends the second quarter of the eighth chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who is like a Bodhisattva.
Now begins the third quarter of the eighth chapter.

1. *matuvaso ru sambuddhau chandasi* | (8.3.1) What was stated in [the rule] *yudhoḥ* (7.1.1) for the sake of avoiding an undesirable result (*dveṣya-parihāra*) should also be understood to apply here in the case of *matuvasoḥ*. For example: *indramarutva*. Here, the suffix *matup* follows the word *marut*, according to [the rule] *jhayaḥ*.

Thus, by the rule [8.2.10], there is the substitution of *y*; by [7.1.70], the augment *num* is added; by [6.1.68] and [8.2.23], the elision of the final consonant (*hal-ṅyādi*) and the final member of the conjunct (*saṃyogānta*) occurs; the *n* becomes *r*; that *r* becomes *y* by [8.3.17] et al.; and that *y* is also elided by [8.3.19]: "the elision [of *y*] according to Śākalya."

(8.3.19) Thus there is elision [of the visarga]. In the example *hariṣo medinaṃ tvā*, the suffix *matup* is added to the word *hari*; by the rule *chandasi iraḥ* (8.2.15), the substitution of *v* occurs; and as before, *num* and so forth are applied. However, the distinction here is this: by the rule *haśi ca* (6.1.114), the substitution of *u* for *ru* takes place, and it coalesces with the preceding vowel.
‘*ād guṇaḥ*’ (Pāṇini 6.1.87). [The example is] *mīḍhvastokāya*. [The root] *miha* (meaning ‘to sprinkle’, Dhātupāṭha 992) takes the suffix *kvasu* after the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
By the rule ‘*dāśvān sahvān mīḍhvāṃśca*’ (6.1.12), there is no reduplication and the root is treated as *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*).
The lengthening of the vowel due to the *upadha* is also established by *nipātana*. By the rule *ho ḍhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.31), the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha* occurs;

then, when the *visarjanīya* is substituted for *roḥ*, that [visarjanīya] becomes a *sakāra* by the rule *visarjanīyasya saḥ* (8.3.34). There is no usage of the substitute *śatṛ* for *vasu* in the vocative case within the Vedic domain (*chāndasa*).

An example of this is as follows: for this very reason, the paribhāṣā "when there is the mention of a [stem] with one anubandha, [it does not include] one with two anubandhas" (Vyāḍi-paribhāṣā 52) does not apply; because in the Vedic language, no usage of *vasu* followed by the vocative suffix is observed that has only one anubandha.
Regarding the form *vidvān*: by the rule *videḥ śaturvasuḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.36), the substitution *vasu* occurs for the suffix *śatṛ*. Regarding the form *he papivan*:

after the roots *pā-* or *pibati*, the suffix *kvasu* takes the augment *iṭ* by the rule *vasvekājādghasām* (Pāṇini 7.2.67), and there is the elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64).

The reduplication occurs by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original element). Regarding the statement "there is an addition [of the rule] for *van*," since a *van* suffix without an *anubandha* is impossible, the term *van* here refers generally to both *kvanip* and *vanip*. Furthermore, there are *kvanip* and *vanip* suffixes used in the Vedic language (*chandas*) in the sense of possession (*matvartha*).
The suffix -itvan is added by the supplementary rule (vārttika 5.2.109), and its inclusion is also intended here.

In the word *prātaritva*, the root *iṇ* (meaning "to go," DhP 1045) is preceded by *prātaḥ*. While the rule *āto maninkvanibvanipaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.74) is in effect, [the suffix -itvan] is seen after other roots as well.

By [Pāṇini 3.2.75], the suffix *kvanip* is applied; then by [Pāṇini 6.1.71], *tuk* is inserted before a *pit* *kṛt* suffix. However, in this case, since [the root] belongs to the *sampadādi* group, it takes the suffix *kvip*; with the insertion of *tuk*, the suffix *matup* is added to that which ends in it. Then, by [Pāṇini 8.2.10], the substitution of *vat* occurs after a *jhay* sound.
Thus, since the desired form is established from the word ending in *matup* itself, no additional rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is required.
Regarding the passage beginning with "vibhāṣā": the word *bhavat* is derived from the root *bhā-* with the suffix *ḍavatup* (as per Pāṇini 5.2.39);
alternatively, it is an unanalyzed nominal stem (*prātipadika*) with the phoneme *u* as its indicatory letter (*anubandha*). The other two, however, end in the possessive suffix *mat*. [He...]

Regarding the word *bhoḥ*: when the substitution of *ru* for *num* has been applied, the vowel *o* is substituted for the entire word *ava*, and not for the final phoneme alone, because of the rule "there is no application of a rule concerning the final phoneme when [the substitute] is meaningless" (*nānarthake 'lontyavidhiḥ*).
‘It is established because of the inclusion [of the particle] *anu*’—this is the mnemonic verse (*grahaṇaka-vākya*). ‘Or rather (*atha vā*)’—this is its explanation.

‘Even though they are unconnected (*asambaddhau api*)’, and so forth; by this, he demonstrates the reason for their status as particles (*nipātatva*). If [the form] *bho* and so on were to exist only through a supplementary rule (*aupasaṃkhyāna*),...

There would be no [application of the rule] in the dual and plural numbers, because of the absence of the vocative case-ending (*sambuddhi*). Furthermore, it would not apply even in the vocative of the feminine—as in *bho brāhmaṇī*—because here [the word] is not mentioned as being qualified by the feminine gender. [This is so] when there is a mention of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
If it is argued that "there is also the inclusion of that which is qualified by gender" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 29), we say no;

because of its prohibition regarding case-endings—this paribhāṣā is prohibited in respect to whatever grammatical operation is prescribed for a case-ending: "there is no inclusion of that which is qualified by gender when a case-ending follows."

Because of this statement (*vyā.pa.30*). Even if it is not prohibited, since it remains that "it becomes thus," once *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) has been applied to the vowel *i* [or *ī*, as per the Prācīna reading], and *au* has been applied to the word *ava*, the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) would fail to occur because *rutva* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*).

If [the suffix] *visarjanīya* were applied, the form would be incorrect (*aniṣṭam*). Therefore, because they are observed in the feminine gender and in cases other than the vocative singular, these must be understood as particles (*nipātāḥ*).
Furthermore, their status as particles is due to their being substitutes for case-endings (*vibhakti-pratirūpaka*).
This is because the term *bhoḥ* is included among the *ca*-group [of particles] by the rule *vibhaktisvarapratirūpakāśca* (Gaṇasūtra 16).

In this way, the word *bhoḥ* would possess the status of a particle (*nipāta*); for when the suffix *vic* is applied to the root *bhū* and *guṇa* substitution occurs, the resulting form *bhoḥ* exists precisely as a word ending in a case-suffix (*vibhaktyanta*). However, this would not apply to the other two [forms, *bhavān* and *bhavan*]. It is not so.

If this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) were not present, the word *bhagoḥ* and the word *aghoḥ*, ending in a case-suffix, would exist [as actual forms], and these two particles would merely be their phonetic imitations (*yatpratirūpaka*). Therefore, it should be understood that these are particles (*nipāta*) found specifically in the Sūtras; for they appear in the Sūtra *bho-bhago-agho-apūrvasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.17).

From the recitation [of the sūtra]. Or else—since the particle *ca* in the rule "upasargavibhaktisvarapratirūpakāśca" has the sense of including what has not been mentioned, it should be understood that these [words] possess the status of particles (*nipāta*). If, then, the supplementary statement (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is rejected by relying on their status as particles, then...

In the usage of the word *bhoḥ*, as in *samastataḥ*, *bhoḥ*, and *tatra bhoḥ*, would not the suffixes *tasil* and others— prescribed by the rule *itarābhyo 'pi dṛśyante* (Pāṇini 5.3.14) for use in connection with words such as *bhavat*—
be unestablished? This is not a fault, because [the word *bhoḥ*] is an indeclinable (*nipāta*), and thus its inclusion [in the rule] is established by extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*).
He rejects [the use of] the word "bhoḥ," and he certainly does not desire the use of suffixes such as -tasil and others.
2. *atrānunāsikaḥ pūrvasya tu vā* (Pāṇini 8.3.2).

This "preceding" (*pūrva*) is relative; furthermore, *ru* is understood here by way of anuvṛtti from the previous rule. It is not possible to understand its "preceding" status in relation to that [ru], for both the nasalization (*anunāsika*) and *ru* follow after this.

Since they are prescribed simultaneously due to their mutual dependence, the *ru* [the substitute] is not yet established at the time the nasalization (*anunāsika*) is prescribed; therefore, its being "prior" (*pūrva*) in relation to that [nasalization] cannot be understood.
Consequently, its status as "prior" is understood in relation to that for whose place the *ru*-substitution is prescribed.

Thus he says: "In the place where *ru* is prescribed, [it applies] to what precedes that. The word *tu* (but/however) indicates the distinction of the preceding element from the subsequent one that undergoes the grammatical operation (*kāryin*). The operation of *ru*-ness (*rutva*) applies to the subsequent, whereas the nasalization (*anunāsika*) applies to the preceding. Alternatively, [the word *tu* indicates] the distinction of the nasalized [element] from *ru*-ness.

It shows that *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) is compulsory, whereas the nasalization (*anunāsika*) is optional. [Question: For what purpose is the group of letters beginning with *ach* and ending with *ka* mentioned here? [Objection: Is it not so that this should apply within this section on *rutva*? [Reply: No, for this is already established by the governing heading (*adhikāra*) itself. For instance, as in the rule "the nasalization of the preceding... (*anunāsikaḥ pūrvasya*).

The heading "thus" (ityadhikṛtam) recurs in what follows, as does the term "ru. One might ask: since this will occur within the section on *ru* even without the explicit mention of "here" (*atra*), why does he say "here" and so forth? [The answer is: "conjunction" (*sanniyoga*) means simultaneity (*yaugapadyam*). How indeed [can there be] with *ru*... simultaneity?

The inclusion of the word "only" (eva) is for the purpose that it [the *ru* substitute] should be understood as such. Furthermore, a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is to be seen here: "by *ru* alone. For there is merely a simultaneous application (*sanniyoga*) of *ru* and the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*), since both recur in what follows. This is due to the distinction between their respective original bases (*sthānin*).

Because there is no contradiction, this [result] is indeed obtained even without the mention of "atra" (here). Now, one might object: since the *anunāsika* [nasalization] following the section on *ru* is not marked as *svarita*, its simultaneous application (*sanniyoga*) will be understood by itself; so what is the purpose of mentioning "atra" here? To this, [the author replies]:

He says: "For, if the extent of the scope [of the rule] were not grasped," and so forth. The "extent" (*parimāṇa*) of the scope (*adhikāra*) is its limit; its "grasping" (*parigraha*) is its full comprehension or determination. In the absence of that, what would those of dull intellect among the learners think—would they assume that the *svarita* nature of the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) continues further on?
Or rather, does it not exist? Thus, for those in whom doubt has arisen, even in rules such as *ḍho ḍhe lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.13),
where an operation such as the elision of *ḍha* is prescribed for the place of a letter, one might suspect that a nasalization (*anunāsika*) would apply to the preceding sound.

Alternatively, for what purpose is the mention of *atha* (or *vā*)? Since the option (*vikalpa*) for this [rule] will be understood from the very mention of *nitya* (invariably) in the subsequent sūtra? This is not so; for in that case, the option would be understood as applying to the preceding sūtra. Should one then say "or" (*vā*)? No, it need not be said.
The activity of the Teacher indicates that this rule is optional,

because in the subsequent sūtra he teaches the augment *anusvāra* after *ru* following that [consonant] for which the *anunāsika* was not applied; for if this rule were compulsory, that would not be necessary.

[It] is possible [that the rule applies], provided that the nasalization of the preceding element of the *ru* has not been effected. If this is so, then the mention of *vā* (or) is for the sake of clarity.

3. *Āto’ṭi nityam* (8.3.3). In the example *devam acchādīvyat*, when the letter *r* is substituted for the *k* in accordance with *dūrvādadi samānapāde* (8.3.9), because that *r* follows an *ā* which is followed by an *aṭ*... [the rule *āto’ṭi nityam* applies].
By this [rule], the preceding vowel *ā* becomes nasalized; as before, the *y* of *roḥ* occurs, and its elision is likewise as before.
Regarding the passage "mahāṃ indro ya ojasā," some recite it with an *anusvāra*.
It must be stated, then, how that [sandhi] is established; therefore, he says "saḥ" and so forth. This is to be understood by means of the rule *vyatyayo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.1.85).
As for the example "yo vā vanaspatīn anu": when *vanaspatīn* follows *anu*, and the form *dīrghāt* [is applied] before *aṭi*...
When the *n* in *samānapāde* (8.3.9) is changed to *r*, the rule *anunāsikāt paro'nusvāraḥ* (8.3.4) applies, resulting in an *anusvāra* after the vowel *i* in *bhavāṃścarati*.
Then, by the rule *naścchavyapraśāt* (8.3.7), the *n* is changed to *r*; of that [change]:
The *visarjanīya* becomes *s*; for that [substitution], by the rule *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.40), there is the substitution of *ścutva*.
The inclusion of the word *nitya* is for the sake of clarity. [The variant reading *spaṣṭārtham* is found in the Prācīna-mu-pāṭha. This is established by the preceding [rule] alone.
If the alternative were established, this rule would be understood as permanent precisely by virtue of its being formulated.

But [one might object]: "Is not the formulation for this very purpose so that there may be a restriction such as 'only after *aṭ* [is applied] in this case,' or 'only from *aṭ* in this case'? This is not so; for if [the alternative were already] non-existent...
A restrictive rule (*niyama*) applies when there is something else to be enjoined. But here, there is indeed something to be enjoined; what is it?

It is that the nasal [consonant] is always [an *anusvāra*]. Therefore, an injunction (*vidhi*) alone is appropriate, not a restriction. And so it has been said: "When both an injunction and a restriction are possible, the injunction alone is more powerful" (Vyāḍipāda 130).

In the word *ātaḥ*, the letter *t* is for the purpose of removing doubt. If it were simply said *ā*, a doubt would arise: "Is this a reference to the vowel *ā* ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) as that which undergoes the grammatical operation, or is it a reference to the substitute [vowel] ending in the nominative case (*prathamānta*)?"
4. *anunāsikāt poranusvāraḥ* (8.3.4).

"The word *anya* (‘other’) is to be supplied here," [says the commentator]. For if the word *anya* were not supplied, then because the word *para* has already been elided (*dhuta*), this ablative case *pañcamī* in *anunāsikāt* would have to be understood in relation to that [elided *para*] alone.

Because no other fifth cause [for the application of the rule] is possible here. [Objection: But surely, when *tasmāt* is brought forward by the rule *tasmād ity uttarasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.67), the ablative case would be required in relation to the word *uttara* itself? [Response: This is not so; for if this paribhāṣā were to apply here, the mention of the word *para* would be redundant.

Therefore, the ablative case must occur only in relation to the word *para*. And when it does occur, would it be used in connection with the word *para* according to the rule beginning with "anyārāditararte" (Pāṇini 2.3.29), functioning either as a term denoting direction (*digvṛtti*) or as a term having another meaning (*anyārthavṛtti*)? Regarding that, in the former position:

The *anusvāra* should be understood as occurring only after a nasalized (*anunāsika*) *r*, and not as being desired after that [nasal]. In the other case, however, this meaning would result: "it occurs after a nasal," which means "the *anusvāra* becomes something other than a nasal. And thus...

The mention of *para* (subsequent) would be purposeless; for the *anusvāra* does not differ from the nasal (*anunāsika*) in relation to it. Furthermore, because it is explicitly heard, the *anusvāra* would be understood as belonging to that very nasal, or else, due to the context, to the *ru*. And this is undesirable; moreover, [if one were to accept it], there would be the necessity of supplying another word.
It is understood that the nasalization (*anunāsika*) of *ya* occurs only after that which has not been formed from this very [rule].

Therefore, the word "another" (*anya*) must be supplied here. Even when the word "another" is supplied, it is understood that the nasalization of *ya* occurs only after that which has not been formed from this very [rule].

Therefore, another word must be supplied here. Even though another word has been supplied, if this ablative case (*pañcamī*) "from a nasalized vowel" (*anunāsikāt*) were dependent solely on the word "another" (*para*), that same fault would remain exactly as it was; thinking thus, he says: "And this [ablative] is in relation to that," and so forth.
The word *ca* is used for emphasis; the meaning is that [the substitution] is in relation to the word *anya* alone, and not in relation to the word *para*.

By the phrase "that which is other than the nasal" (*anunāsikād anyaḥ*), he demonstrates through the ablative case that very same dependence on the word *anya*. By the phrase "preceding *ru*" (*roḥ pūrvaḥ*), he also indicates the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "preceding" (*pūrva*).

And "prior-ness" (pūrvatva) is relative to the *ru*-substitution. By the phrase "for which the nasalization has not been made," he also indicates the meaning denoted by the word "other" (anya). By the word "thence" (tataḥ), he also shows the transformation of the sense of the term "prior" (pūrva) here into an ablative case ending. [This applies] to the word "other."
Nor does the word *para* [indicate] that the unuttered [element] ends in the fifth case (the ablative);
nor does the word *anya*, being connected with that fifth case, indicate a dependence on the word *para*; nor does the word *āgama* indicate the absence of a substitute (*ādeśa*).
The mention of *para* (subsequent) can be omitted.

By supplying the word *anya* (other) in the ablative case and by changing the word *pūrva* (preceding) through the force of context into the nominative case, it will be understood as follows: "that *ru* which follows what is other than [the nasalized vowel] beginning with the *anunāsika*."

The augment *anusvāra* occurs before [the following consonant]. And this being understood, even without the mention of "the subsequent" (*para*), forms such as *saṃskartṛ* are indeed established; so what is the purpose of mentioning "the subsequent"? This is done for the sake of clarity.
5. *samaḥ suṭi* (8.3.5). This rule is stated because the substitution of *anusvāra* [for *m*] would otherwise apply by the rule *mo'nusvāraḥ* (8.3.23).
Example: *saṃskartā*. (Note: The reading *saṃskartā* is printed in the Nyāsa and Padamañjarī.)

And so forth. From the root *kṛ* preceded by the prefix *sam*, suffixes such as *tṛc* and others are applied. By the rule *samparyupebhyaḥ karotau bhūṣaṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.137), the augment *suṭ* is inserted. By the rule *alo'ntasya* (1.1.52), the *m* of *sam* becomes *r*.
Then, the preceding [nasal] becomes an anusvāra, and the *r* becomes a *visarjanīya*. Regarding that [visarjanīya], there is the option...

Regarding the rule *śari* (Pāṇini 8.3.36), although a *sakāra* (s) or a *visarjanīya* (ḥ) would optionally occur [before a following *śar*], it has been shown in the *vṛtti* that the *sakāra* occurs invariably. But how is the *sakāra* specified in this sūtra? To this he says: *samaḥ*.

Regarding the passage beginning with *ssuṭi* and so forth: this was stated with reference to that alternative in which, after the *visarjanīya* has been substituted for the *sakāra* of the case-ending (*vibhakti*), the *sakāra* is not applied by the rule *vā śari* (Pāṇini 8.3.36).
Otherwise, one would have to say that this grammatical indication (*nirdeśa*) consists of three *sakāras*; for there are three [instances].

This is due to the conjunction of the *sakāra*s. For there is one *sakāra* connected with the case-ending (*vibhakti*), a second connected with the substitute (*ādeśa*), and a third connected with the augment *suṭ*. However, when the sūtra is recited as containing three *sakāra*s, then the word "two" (*dvi*) should be understood as indicating the presence of an additional *sakāra*.
If, then, the substitution of *sakāra* is prescribed, the nasalization (*anunāsika*) would not apply in the case of *saṃskartā*;

for in this context, the mention of *atra* was stated for the purpose of establishing a necessary connection (*sanniyoga*) with *ru* alone. Whatever is prescribed in this section is [to be understood] as being connected with the mention of *ru*.

There is no fault, because that [mention] is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). Regarding the phrase "together with *ru*": the meaning is "together with that which is prescribed in the section on *ru*. Furthermore, although it was stated in the preceding rule that "in the case of *vṛt*, [the augment] precedes *ru*," there too, the mention of *ru* refers to whatever is prescribed in this very section.

This should be understood as being for the purpose of indicating that [the rule applies] to others as well; otherwise, in the case where "saṃskartā" is the intended form, the anusvāra would not occur.
6. *puṃso ’mpare* | (8.3.6) Regarding the term *puṃsaḥ*: this is a reference to that portion of the word *puṃs* which remains after the *sakāra*;

for once the *sakāra* has been elided by the rule for the loss of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*), it is precisely that [remaining portion] which is the subject of the grammatical operation. Regarding the term *ampare*: [it means] when followed by *am*.

That which has *am* as its subsequent element is so designated. Here, *am* is understood as a *pratyāhāra* (a grammatical abbreviation), not as the second singular case ending. Why is this so? Because of the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and because of its association with the *pratyāhāra* "khayi. As in the example "puṃścalī": the root *cala-* is listed in the *pacādi* group.
It is recited thus: from the root *cal* (meaning "to tremble," Dhātupāṭha 832), the suffix *ac* is added according to the rule for *pacādi* roots;

then, by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Thus, *puṃścalī* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Regarding *puṃskāmā*: this is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*) meaning "one whose desire is for a man" (*puṃsi kāmo 'syāḥ*). Now...

Or: [the form] *puṃskāmā* is derived from the sense "she who desires a man" (*pumāṃsaṃ kāmayate*), with the suffix *ṇa* added according to the rule "the suffix *ṇa* should be stated after the roots *śīl*, *kāmin*, *bhikṣ*, and *ācari*" (Vārttika 229); from that, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied. This is the example for the term *puṃskāmā*. Regarding the statement "the substitute is *sakāra* alone," it is understood that this refers to the *visarjanīya*. Regarding the word "should be stated" (*vaktavyaḥ*), it means "it should be explained."

This is the meaning. Regarding this, the following explanation is given: in the rule *kupvoḥ ka pau ca* (8.3.37), the word *vā* ("or") is carried over from the preceding rule *vā śari* (8.3.36), and that [option] is a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (a restricted option). Consequently, even in this case, the *visarjanīya* will become *sakāra* alone, and not [anything else].
Regarding the visarjanīya and the jihvāmūlīya: this is the counter-argument stated for when the position of "two *s* sounds" (*dvisakārapakṣa*) is not adopted in the preceding sūtra;
however, when that very position—that "the instruction consists of two *s* sounds"—is indeed adopted there, then...
He states [the following] in order to provide a rebuttal: "But in the view that there is a dual mention of the letter *s*," and so forth.

Now, one might object: since the augment *ru* also follows [from the previous rule], just as the letter *s* continues to apply, so too would *ru* apply in its alternative form; consequently, when *ru* is applied, the substitution of *visarjanīya* would occur.
One might ask: "Could it not be *jihvāmūlīya*? To this he says: "But the *ru* [substitute] continues," and so forth.
He states the reason for that very point: "The persistence of its connection," and so forth.
The particle *iti* indicates a reason; for it [the *ru* substitute] is by its own [rule], from "In the vocative, *ru* replaces *mat* and *vas*" (Pāṇini 8.3.1).

In this context, that which is connected with the possessive suffix *matup* and with wealth (*vasu*) continues to recur; therefore, it is not able to enter into a connection with another relatum. Regarding the term "puṃdāsaḥ": it is either a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), meaning "the servant of a man," or a descriptive compound (*karmadhāraya*).

Thus, in the case of *puṃgavaḥ*, the compound-ending suffix *ṭac* is applied by the rule *gorataddhitaluki* (Pāṇini 5.4.92). In the cases of *puṃkṣīram* and *puṃkṣuram*, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

Regarding the statement "in the presence of *ya* when *khay* follows," the mention of the subsequent element (*paragrahaṇa*) is for the purpose of excluding an erroneous interpretation; for if it were not [stated thus],...

If the mention of "para" (subsequent) were not included, it would be understood as "when *am* follows *kha*," and consequently, [the rule] would apply even in cases such as *pumākhyah* and *pumācāraḥ*. Therefore, the mention of "para" is made.

7. *naś-chavi-praśān* (8.3.7). The word *sa* is excluded [from the previous rule], and *ru* alone continues to apply; that too is not connected with *matup* and *vasu*, because those two have also been excluded. The word *na* is a reference to the phoneme *n*, and it refers to what is under discussion [in the present context].

It is a qualifier of the word (*pada*), and since a rule applies to that which ends in a qualifier, he says: "of a word ending in *n*," and so forth. In the example "bhavāṃśchādayati" (you cover), the root is *chada* in the sense of "concealing" (*apavāraṇe*), with the causative suffix *ṇic* added from the *cur*-class.
Regarding the form *bhavāṃṣṭīkate*: the roots *ṭikṛ*, *ṭīkṛ*, *radhi*, and *laghi* have the meaning "to go" (*gatyarthāḥ*) [Dhātupāṭha 103, 104, 107, 108].
Because it is anudātta, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used. Regarding the form *praśān*:
from the root *śam* preceded by *pra*, there is the suffix *kvip*; [the lengthening of the vowel occurs] by Pāṇini 6.4.15: *anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ kṅiti*.

Thus [the word] *dīrghaḥ* [is formed]; by the rule *mo no dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.64), the *m* is replaced by *n*, and because that [substitution] is considered asiddha (not yet established), there is no elision of the *n*. [The example] *bhavān tsarukaḥ*: one who is skilled in the *tsaru* (hilt); the suffix *kan* is applied by the rule *ākarṣādibhyaḥ kan* (Pāṇini 5.2.64).
8. *ubhayatharkṣu* | (8.3.8) This statement is for the purpose of providing an option (*vikalpa*), since [the substitution] was previously established as obligatory (*nitya*).
9. *dīrghād aṭi samānapāde* (8.3.9).

Regarding the term *samānapāde*: this is a locative case derived from a *karmadhāraya* compound. Here, the word *samāna* is understood in the sense of "one" (*eka*). Thus, it means "in one and the same foot."

The meaning is that [the rule] applies to the relationship between a cause (nimitta) and its effect (naimittika). In this context, although one could have simply used the term "eka" (single), the term "samāna" (identical) was employed so that the rule would apply even in cases where the cause and effect do not occur within the same pāda.
Consequently, the substitution of *ru* occurs here as well: *yajāmahai yajñiyā indradevāṃ ilāmahai īkṣām*.
Regarding the phrase *anājya*: here, the relationship of cause and effect (*nimita-nimittin*) exists between two distinct feet.
Alternatively, the word *samāna* is understood in the sense of similarity; for otherwise, he would have used the word *eka* (one). And in this case, similarity exists between both feet.

Because the two verbal roots have the same meaning: just as the verbal root *yaj* in *yajāmahai* functions in the sense of worship, so too does *īḍ* in *īḷāmahai*. [The root] *īḍ* is used "in the sense of praise" (*stuti*;
DhP 1019); it is in the imperative mood (*loṭ*), with the substitution of *e* for the final vowel (*ṭerettvam*), according to Pāṇini 3.4.96: *vaito'nyatra*.
Thus, there is the substitution of *e* for the vowel *i*. By the transposition of phonemes within the verbal root, *ḍ* is replaced by *l*.
Due to its Vedic character (*chāndasatva*), the vowel is short.

10. *nṛn pe* (8.3.10). Regarding the form *nṛn*: this is an indication (*nirdeśa*) made after applying the elision (*luk*) of the genitive case by the rule *supāṃ suluk* (7.1.39), etc. Alternatively, the case ending (*vibhakti*) does not arise here at all.

Because the distinction between the object of imitation and the imitation itself is not intended to be expressed—just as in examples such as *gavity ayam āha* ("He says 'cow'") and so forth—the letter *pa* alone is taken as the cause (*nimitta*), and not the entire cluster [of letters]. The vowel *a*, however, is for the purpose of pronunciation; otherwise, indeed...
If the collection of the letter *a* were relied upon as the cause [of the substitution],
then it would apply only in cases such as *nṛḥ pacati*, but not in cases such as *nṛn prīṇīhi*; furthermore,
the term *aṭi* would be excluded here because another cause has been introduced.

Now, why is this not understood as a qualification of that very cause (*nimitta*)—namely, "the letter *p* which follows an *aṭ*"? It is impossible to understand it in this way; for in such cases [as the following], the rule would not apply: *nṛṃḥ psāti*, *nṛṃḥ plāvayati*. Therefore, the inclusion of the term *aṅ* is appropriate for the purpose of excluding those instances.
11. *svatavān* before *pāyu*.

(8.3.11) It should be understood that the mention of *svatavān* is as in the previous rule. The same applies to the subsequent rule, *kān* (8.3.12). Thus: *svatavāḥ pāyur agne*. [The rule] *dṛksvaḥsavatavasāñ chandasi* [is also relevant].
(7.1.83) The augment *num*, the elision of the final consonant (*halṅyāb-bhyo dīrghāt sutisy apṛktaṃ hal* 6.1.68), and the elision of the final member of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* 8.2.23).
12. *kān* when reduplicated. (8.3.12) As in *kāṃskān*.

Here, from the word *kim* in the *śas* case-ending, *ka* is substituted by "the substitution of *ka* for *kim*" (7.2.103). Then, the long vowel is applied by "the single substitute for the preceding [vowel] is homogeneous with the first two" (6.1.102), resulting in *kān*. Finally, the *na* is substituted by "after that [long vowel], the *na* replaces the *s* of *śas* in the masculine" (6.1.103). Thus, *kān kān* becomes *kāṃskān*.

By [Pāṇini 8.3.32] *iti*, the *s* becomes *n*; there is reduplication for distributive repetition (*vīpsā*); the *r*-quality (*rutva*) results in a *visarjanīya*; and by [Pāṇini 8.3.34] *visarjanīyasya saḥ*, that *visarjanīya* becomes *s*.
But how can there be an *s* here, given that [Pāṇini 8.3.37] *kupvoḥ ka pau ca* [prescribes *k* or *p*]?
Should there not be the occurrence of the *visarjanīya* and the *jihvāmūlīya* [substitutes]? To this he says: "of this," and so forth.

Although it is not explicitly recited there, he says "samo suṭi" and so forth in order to demonstrate that an undesirable consequence would nonetheless arise. If the letter *s* were to carry over here [from the previous rule],...
One might ask: "Would the suffix *sakāra* not also apply everywhere in the preceding rules (*pūrvayoga*) because this [word] continues to follow along?

To this he says: "In the preceding rules," and so forth. For in the preceding rules, such as "samaḥ suṭi" (Pāṇini 8.3.5), [the word *sam*] is indeed connected only with its own related term, namely *suṭ*.
There is the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of that [rule]; therefore, there is no lack of connection for it with another related element.

When it should have been stated simply as "kān kān," the inclusion of the term *āmreḍita* (reduplicated) is so that [the rule] may apply where there is a doubling. Consequently, it does not apply here in the case of "kān kān paśyati" (whom whom does he see?), because in this instance, only one word "kiṃ" occurs.
In the case of *praśna* (questioning), the second [form] is used in the sense of censure; the meaning is "he looks upon whom as contemptible?"

13. *ḍho ḍhea lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.13). In the term *ḍhea*, only the phoneme *ḍha* is accepted as the cause [of the elision]; it is not a collection of phonemes. Why is this so? Because of pervasion (*vyāpti*). The vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation. For if there were a mention of a [specific] phoneme, as in *līḍhavā*, [the rule would apply].

It also occurs in cases such as *mīḍhvaḥ*; for otherwise, if a collection of phonemes (*varṇasamudāya*) were taught as the cause [of the grammatical operation], then it would apply only to forms like *lauḍham* and *mīḍham*, but not to *līḍhavah* and so on. Regarding *līḍham*: the root *lih* is used in the sense of "tasting" (Dhātupāṭha 1016).
From the roots *siñ* (*miha secane*, DhP 992) and *guh* (*guhū saṃvaraṇe*, DhP 896), the suffix *kta* is applied;
then, by the rule *ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ*, there is the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭu*; by *ho ḍhaḥ* (8.2.31), there is the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha*;
and by *jhavastathordho'dhaḥ* (8.2.40), there is the substitution of *dha* for *tha*. By the rule *ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ*, [the final *ṣṭu* is replaced].

By the rule (8.4.41), *ṣṭutva* occurs; then there is the elision of *ḍh*. Following the rule "when *ḍh* or *r* is elided, the preceding *aṇ* vowel becomes long" (6.3.111), a long vowel is substituted. But how is an example such as *līḍham* justified, given that the letter *ḍh* is not present here?
Is it not the case that there is no "caused by another" (paranimitta) [substitution] when the elision of *ḍh* is to be applied, because the substitution of *ṣṭu* is considered asiddha?

To this, [the author] says: "of the substitution of *ṣṭu*. Here, the letter *ḍh* is not relied upon as the cause for the elision of *ḍh*; nor is such a [cause] ever possible where, by this [rule], the elision of *ḍh* would have to be performed. Therefore...
It should be understood that the status of *ṣṭutva* as established is due precisely to the reliance on the letter *ḍha* as the cause [of the operation];
otherwise, this statement would be purposeless, as it would have no scope (*anavakāśatvāt*).
This might be argued: "The elision of *ḍha* will occur by the rule *śvalīḍhāṬkataḥ*, for in this case [the rule] is indeed established."

[The opponent asks: "Since the letter *ḍh* exists, how can the statement be purposeless? To this he says: *ṭhśvaliṅḍhāṬkte*, etc. Although the letter *ḍh* is established here as the cause [of the rule], nevertheless the elision of *ḍh* (*ḍhalopa*) is not possible; for once the substitution of *jaś* has been applied, the letter *ḍh*—the very subject of the operation—is no longer present. Now, one might object:

"Since there is no scope [for the rule], will the elision of *ḍh* be an exception (*apavāda*) to *jaś*-ness? To this he says: "And not," etc. Why is this so? To this he says: "For of that," etc. For if its scope were not possible, then it could be understood as an exception to *jaś*-ness.
Moreover, its scope includes forms such as *līḍha* and others; therefore, it cannot be understood that this [rule] applies only to cases where the substitution of the *jaś*-class occurs.
But how can forms like *līḍha* and others be its scope, given that—as in the case of *śvaliṅḍhāṭkata*—[the rule would otherwise apply]?

Once the substitution of *jaś* has been applied, because the subject of the operation no longer exists, there is no scope for the elision of *ḍh*. Similarly, in cases such as *loḍha*, since the status of being "asiddha" (not yet established) applies to the *ṣṭutva* [substitution], the cause for that substitution is absent. Now, if it is argued here that by the force of the specific rule (*vacana*), the *asiddhatva* of *ṣṭutva* is set aside by the elision of *ḍh*, then the same would apply elsewhere as well.

If you ask why *jaś*-ness is not applied [there], then it must follow that if the elision (*lopa*) of *līḍha* and *aviḍham* is the domain of one rule, the other rule must also have that same domain, and not only the other rule but also the first one.
To this he says: "For in that case," and so forth. Here, because of the mention of the locative case in the word *ḍhea*, [the rule applies].

[The rule] is based on immediate sequence (*dānantarya*); however, it is not the case that [the condition] applies only to *līḍha* and so forth, and not to others as well. Therefore, he says: "For in that case," and so on.

Here, because of the mention of the locative case in the word "in *ḍha*" (*ḍhe*), it must refer to its [specific] domain; it is not the case that [the condition] applies only to *līḍha* and so forth, and not to others as well.
Therefore, he says: "For in that case," and so on. Here, "in *ḍha*" (*ḍhe*)...

The mention of the seventh case (saptamī) relies upon immediate sequence (ānantarya), because the inclusion of the term "nirdiṣṭa" has the sense of immediate sequence. Therefore, when there is immediate sequence, the elision of *ḍh* must occur. And in cases such as *loḍhā*, there is indeed an immediate sequence established by the audible phonetic form (*śrutikṛta*).

Because both the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*kāryin*), namely the two *ḍha* sounds, are heard [together], this alone is the scope for the elision of *ḍha*. True, here there is no immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) produced by direct audition (*śruti*);
however, there is also a lack of immediate sequence produced by the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*). By means of the treatise—

Because the status of *ṣṭutva* as being "not established" (*asiddha*) is accepted; and since that [status] exists, even that [substitution] is not within the scope of the elision of *ḍh*. Therefore, he says: "Established by the treatise" (*śāstrakṛta*);

because the status of *ṣṭutva* as being "not established" is accepted by the treatise (*śāstra*). And since that [status] exists, even that [substitution] is not within the scope of the elision of *ḍh*.

To this he says: "produced by a grammatical rule" (*śāstrakṛta*), and so forth. Even though proximity (*anāntarya*) produced by a grammatical rule exists, it is set aside by the elision of *ḍh*; otherwise, the statement would be purposeless. Just as proximity produced by a grammatical rule is set aside by the force of the statement—

The elision of *ḍha* occurs; likewise, in the case of *śvaliṅḍhāṬkata*, one might think that the elision of *ḍha* would occur even there by overriding the proximity established by direct audition (*śruti*). To address this, he says:
"But in the case of *śvaliṅḍhāṬkata*," and so forth. The word "but" (*tu*) indicates the distinction of this [case] from *lauḍha* and the others.

He demonstrates this: for in cases such as *līḍha*, although there is no immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) established by a grammatical rule (*śāstra*), there is one established by direct audition (*śruti*). Here, however, there is neither an immediate sequence established by audition, because the two *ḍha* sounds are not heard, nor is there one established by a rule, because [the rule]...
Because the substitution of *jaś* is not established [and thus] does not apply, therefore the elision of *ḍh* is certainly not its scope.

14. *ro ri* (8.3.14). But is this the inclusion of the *repha* with its *anubandha*, or of that without an *anubandha*? And what would follow here if it were the inclusion of that with an *anubandha*?

The forms *agnīrathaḥ* and *indūrathaḥ* are established, but *nīraktaṃ* and *dūraktaṃ* are not established. Now, if there is a reference to the form without the *anubandha*, then *nīraktaṃ* and *dūraktaṃ* are established, but *agnīrathaḥ* and *indūrathaḥ* are not established? This is not a fault; for here—

The Teacher recited two sūtras, "ro ri," in which in one case there is the inclusion of the form with its *anubandha*, and in the other, the form without the *anubandha*. In examples such as *nīraktam*,
lengthening occurs by the rule "ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho’ṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.111).
In this context, if the genitive case in *padasya* were a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), then by the rule *alo’ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52),
the elision of the *repha* would apply only to the final *repha* of the word— as in *nīraktam* and so forth— but not in cases such as *ajardhāḥ*.

This portion [of the sūtra], "tvapadāntasya," does not exist in the Kāśikā reading; however, keeping in mind that the genitive of qualification (*viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*) applies here as well, he says "padasya" and so forth. For [it is] the genitive of qualification...

The word *padasya* is connected in this manner: "the *repha* which is a constituent part (*avayava*) of a *pada*, its elision (*lopa*) occurs when followed by a *repha*. By this, the rule applies even to a *repha* that is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*). For example, in the form *ajardhāḥ*, as in the rule *ekāco baśo bhaṣ* (Pāṇini 8.2.37) and others.
It has been explained: *apāspāḥ*. [The root] *spardh* (in the sense of rivalry, DhP 3) takes the suffix *yaṅ*;
there is reduplication; by the rule *śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ* (7.4.61), the *khaya* sounds are retained as the remainder;
by *dīrgho'kitaḥ* (7.4.83), lengthening occurs; and by *yaṅe'ci ca* (2.4.74) [the suffix *yaṅ* is replaced by *ac*].
The *yaṅ* suffix is elided; with *pāsparddha* thus established, the *laṅ* [suffix] follows, and after *aḍāgamah*, *sip* is added.
Due to its inclusion in the list beginning with *carkarītañca* (Dhātupāṭha 1081), there is elision (*luk*) of *śap*.
By the rule *ilṅyādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), there is elision (*lopa*) of *sip*. By the rule of *jaśtva*, the letter *dh* becomes *d*. [Then by] *daśca*...

By this [rule], (8.2.75), there is the substitution of *ru* for that very *da*; therein, by this [present rule], there is the elision (*lopa*) of the *repha*, and as before, there is the lengthening of the vowel.
The separation of the *yoga* (the division of the sūtra) is for the sake of what follows, so that the *repha* may be carried over (*anuvṛtti*) into the subsequent sūtra.
It is for the sake of [the word] *syāt*; otherwise, there would be a recurrence of the sound *ḍha* as well, and consequently, a *visarjanīya* would also result for that.
15. *khar-avasānayoḥ-visarjanīyaḥ* (8.3.15).

If, in this rule, the genitive were a qualifying genitive (*viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*)—meaning "the *repha* which is a constituent part of a word"—then even in cases such as *arkaḥ*, the *visarjanīya* would have to occur for a *repha* that is not at the end of a word.

There is no fault in this being a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*); for here the word is qualified by the letter *r*, and by means of a qualifier, the rule of "extension to what ends with it" (*tadanta-vidhi*) applies.

Thus, when an operation is prescribed for that which ends in *r*, it occurs only at the final [element] of the word. Therefore, in the phrase "of the word" (*padasya*), this is a genitive of location; and that word is [further] qualified by *r*.

Showing that [the word] is qualified [by this], he says: "of a word ending in *repha*. [This is governed by the rule: "before a *khar* consonant or at the end (*avasāna*). The word "after" (*pataḥ*) is connected only with what precedes, not with the subsequent "end"; for [if it were connected] with the subsequent "end," [it would lead to an error]. [This is the reading in the Kāśikā-mu-pāṭha.]

Because there is an absence of priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*). For instance, that phoneme by which one ceases [speaking] would be the *avasāna* (pause). Or rather, cessation (*virati*) is the same as pause (*virāma*), namely, the non-utterance of a subsequent phoneme. Therefore, in the case of a word ending in the letter *r*, that phoneme by which one ceases cannot possibly exist as a subsequent element characterized as *avasāna*.

Because that alone is not employed; its non-employment, however, is due to its meaninglessness. In the other case, moreover, cessation consists in non-existence. And priority and posteriority are not possible in non-existence, because those are properties of phonemes. Therefore, that [suffix] also does not follow from a word ending in the letter *r*.
It arises subsequently.

However, some, relying on a sequence imagined by the intellect, connect this [term] "subsequently" (*parataḥ*) even with "at the end" (*avasāne ca*). In that case, if the sequence is imagined by the intellect...

If it is not resorted to, then this single locative case in the rule "kharavasānayoḥ" is divided according to the difference in the locus: the locative occurs in a proximate (upaśleṣika) locus when [the change] is subsequent to a *khar* consonant, whereas in the case of *avasāna* (pause),
the locative occurs in a situational (vaiṣayika) locus.

It occurs—meaning "at the end" (*avasāne*)—in the domain [of the rule]. However, when the priority (*paurvāparya*) imagined through grammatical augmentation (*vṛddhi*) is resorted to even in the case of an absence (*abhāva*) at the end, then in both cases it is simply the locative of the subsequent element (*parasaptamī*).
In the examples, once *visarjanīya* has been substituted for [the final *k*] before a *khari* sound, [the rule] "of *visarjanīya*, *sa*" (Pāṇini 8.3.34) applies.

The letter *sakāra* (s): when followed by a palatal consonant (*cavarga*), it undergoes the substitution of *ścutva*. Thus, from *nṛkuṭa* with the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of "born there" (*tatra bhavaḥ*, Pāṇini 4.3.53), we have *nārkuṭaḥ*; and for "the offspring of a *nṛpati*," [we have] *nāpatyaḥ* according to "from *diti*, *āditya*, and words having *āditya* as the final member, the suffix *ṇya* is applied" (Pāṇini 4.1.85).
Why does the *visarjanīya* not occur here in the word *nārpatya*? To this he says: "In this case," and so forth.
Since the *vṛddhi* [substitution] occurs by relying on a *taddhita* suffix prescribed in the sense of "descendant" (*bhāvādi*) and so on, it is *bahiraṅga* (external);
and because that [vṛddhi] is *bahiraṅga*, the *repha* (*r*) which depends upon it is also *bahiraṅga*.

Because [the substitution of *u*] depends on the increase [of the vowel], and furthermore because the letter *r* is a part of that [increase] and has it as its cause; whereas the *visarjanīya*, on the other hand, occurs depending on the *khara* (voiceless consonant), and is therefore *antaraṅga*. According to the rule "that which is *bahiraṅga* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is *antaraṅga*" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 42), when the *visarjanīya* is to be applied...

The letter *repha* (ṛ) is not established [as a valid substitute here]; therefore, the *visarjanīya* does not occur in this case. Now, one might object: when a *vṛddhi* substitution is to be applied, the *visarjanīya*—which is intended—is unestablished (*asiddha*) because it is an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation; and since that [the *visarjanīya*] is absent, the designation of [the subsequent operation] as "external" (*bahiraṅga*) in relation to the *vṛddhi* would not be tenable.
Because that [designation] depends upon what is internal (*antaraṅga*); if that were absent,
even for the *repha*, there would be no such designation of being external (*bahiraṅga*)—
for the *repha*'s status as external is indeed mediated by the externality of the *vṛddhi*.

As for what was stated— that because both conditions are absent, the *bahir-aṅga-paribhāṣā* (Pariśiṣṭa 42) does not apply, and thus the argument "because [the substitution] is characterized as *bahir-aṅga*" is untenable— that is not so. For in the rule *na mu ne* (8.2.3), the word *na* is used for the sake of another grammatical operation (*kāryāntara*).

Thus, the division of the yoga has been made. By this, when the rule for *vṛddhi* is to be applied, the *visarjanīya* will not be considered non-existent (*asiddha*). For this very reason, even according to the *bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā*, the *visarjanīya* will not be considered non-existent.

It should be understood that this is because the view expressed in *Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā* 58—“Technical names and rules of interpretation [apply] at the time the operation is to be performed”—is relied upon here. And this is logical, for since technical names and rules of interpretation are prompted by specific operations, it is only right that they should apply precisely where those operations occur; for it is in that very place where non-attainment (*asiddhatva*) is effected by this [rule].
This is its domain of application. And where is its non-established status [asiddhatva] by it? In the rule concerning the *visarjanīya*.
Therefore, this [paribhāṣā] belongs to that same domain; it does not belong to the domain where it is added as a supplement—namely, "In the case of a conflict, the subsequent operation prevails" (P.
1.4.2)—nor to the domain where it is made known by implication—namely, "ūṭh is substituted for the vowel of the root *vah*."
In this context [of rule 6.4.132], they belong to that same location.
16. *roḥ supi* (8.3.16). [Examples:
*payaḥsu*, *yaśaḥsu*. In some places, two *s*-sounds are recited; there, the *s* replaces the *visarjanīya* by the rule *vā śari* (8.3.36), as in *sarpiḥṣu*, where the *visarjanīya* occurs.

In that case, the rule *num-visarjanīya-śar-vyavāye 'pi* (Pāṇini 8.3.58) prescribes the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* of the suffix. Where two *ṣ*s are read, as in *sarpiṣṣu*, there, just as before, the *visarjanīya* is first changed to *s*, and then, just as before, the *s* of the suffix [is changed to *ṣ*].
There is the substitution of *v* for *t*, and the substitution of *ṣṭu* for the preceding [consonant] (Pāṇini 8.4.41).
He says "in *sup*" and so forth to dispel the suspicion that the term *sup* refers to a *pratyāhāra* (a collective abbreviation);
this is understood because the word "before *khar*" (*khari*) is supplied as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*), for there is no other *sup* besides the locative plural.

[The objection: "Does *kharādi* exist? Let it not be so, because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *khari*. Why is there no inclusion of the *saptamī* [case-ending] by means of the letter *p* in the *pratyāhāra*? [Response: It is possible that [the reading in the Kāśikā-mu-pāṭha is incorrect and should read] "it is not possible" (*na sambhavati*).
In that context, *kharādi* refers to the *sup* [suffixes]. If it were so, what further [consequence would follow]?
[Objection: Would it not be the case that in *agīḥkaḥ* and *adhaḥkaḥ*, the *visarjanīya* would not occur due to the restrictive rule?

Therefore, the [traditional] commentary alone is the refuge. [Question: For what purpose is this [rule], since the *visarjanīya* is indeed established by the preceding rule alone? [Answer: He says: "Since [it is] already established," and so forth.

A contrary rule need not be suspected, because of the mention of the *visarjanīya* in rules such as *kimaḥ kṣepe* (Pāṇini 5.4.70). For example, in *gīrṣu* and *dhūrṣu*, the lengthening occurs by the rule *rṭhthorupadhāyāḥ* (8.2.76),
etc.

17. *bhobhagoaghoapūrvasya yo'śi* (8.3.17). In examples such as *bho atra*, the elision of *y* is obligatory by the rule *oto gārgyasya* (8.3.20). The mention of Gārgya there is for the sake of honor (*pūjārtha*). In cases such as *bho dadāti*, [the elision occurs] before a consonant (*hali*)...
By the rule *sarveṣām* (Pāṇini 8.3.22), the elision of *y* is indeed obligatory.

Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *aś*? For as long as *aś* becomes *am* before a *khar* [consonant], there ought to be a *visarga* by the rule *kharavasānayoḥ*; once that *visarga* has been applied, its—
If it is argued that [the rule] would apply because the substitute is included by the mention of *ru* due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, we say no;

for there is an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*). This is because, in the rule "atrānunāsikaḥ pūrvasya tu vā" (Pāṇini 8.3.2), the author makes the statement without employing the *visarjanīya* or the letter *y*.

This indicates that the substitution of *y* for the *visarjanīya* does not occur before a *khari* sound. If it is argued that it would then occur at the end of a word (*avasāna*), the answer is no; because of the governing rule "in *saṃhitā*" (Pāṇini 8.2.108). Therefore, even without an explicit statement, [the desired result] follows by implication. Thus...

He says: "The inclusion of *at* is for the sake of what follows. By the rule *hali sarveṣām* (Pāṇini 8.3.22) and others, he demonstrates that very fact of being for the sake of what follows. Regarding the form *dṛkṣavṛṭ*: from the root *vraścū* (Dhātupāṭha 1292) meaning "to cut," with the suffix *kvip*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) according to the rule *grahy-ādi* (Pāṇini 6.1.16).

By the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.29), there is the elision of the letter *s*. By the rule *vraścādi-* (8.2.36), the letter *c* [of *vṛkṣa-*, when followed by *ṇic*] becomes *c*; this [c] then becomes *ḍ* by the rule for *jaś*-substitution; and that [ḍ] also undergoes *cartva* (the substitution of *ṭ*) to become *ṭ*. Thus, from *vṛkṣa-vṛṭ*, the suffix *ṇic* is added in the sense of "he causes to speak" (*tam ācaṣṭe*), according to the principle *ṇāviṣṭhavad*.
By the rule *prātipadikasya* (Pāṇini 5.3.62), the treatment of the superlative suffix (*iṣṭhan*) applies; by *ṭeḥ* (6.4.155), there is elision of the final vowel (*ṭi*).
From the causative form of the root *vṛkṣav*, the suffix *kvip* is added, and by *ṇeraniṭi* (6.4.51), the causative marker (*ṇi*) is elided.
Thus we have *vṛkṣav karoti*. Here, because of the inclusion of the word "beginning" (*ādi*), there is elision [of the *v*] before the letter *k* of *vakara*.

It does not occur. Precisely because of the mention of *aś*, the elision prescribed by "lopo vyor vali" (Pāṇini 6.1.66) does not take place at all. Otherwise, the mention of *aś* would be purposeless.
If the mention of *aś* were for the sake of another rule, then it should have been made right there; thus...

With the intention that the *svarita* accent need not be applied for the sake of continuity (*anuvṛtti*), he says "atha" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of what follows" (*uttarārtham*): it is so called because its purpose (*artha*) or utility (*prayojana*) lies in the rule following the sūtra "hali sarveṣām" (8.3.22).
By the rule "mo'nusvāraḥ" (8.3.23), etc., that very fact of being for the sake of what follows is made clear.

For if the mention of "am" were made in the rule "hali sarveṣām" (8.3.22), then, just as there is a carry-over (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of "hal" in the rule "mo'nusvāraḥ" (8.3.23), [the same would apply here].
The mention of "aś" would also apply [here]. Consequently, the *anusvāra* would occur for *m* only before a vowel (*aś*), and not before every consonant (*hal*).

However, when the mention of "aś" is not made there, then the *anusvāra* is established for *m* before every consonant in the subsequent rule. Thus, the mention of "aś" serves a purpose for what follows.
He demonstrates this with the rule "vyorlaghuprayatnataraḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.168) and so forth; its meaning has already been explained.

18. According to Śākaṭāyana, [the *v* and *y*] have a lighter articulation effort (*laghuprayatnatara*). (8.3.18) Regarding the term "lighter articulation effort" (*laghuprayatnatara*): "effort" (*prayatna*) means the act of exerting effort (*prayatana*). The suffix *naṅ* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.3.90, *yajayāca* etc. That which has a light effort is "light-effort" (*laghuprayatna*); [the comparative form] is "more light[ly]" (*atiśayena*).

"Less effort" (*laghuprayatna*) means "even less effort" (*laghuprayatnatara*). But what is this state of being "even less effort," by virtue of which [a sound] becomes "even less effort"? To this he says: "The state of being even less effort," and so forth.
*Place* (*sthāna*) refers to the palate and so on; *instrument* (*karaṇa*) refers to the root of the tongue and so on. In their pronunciation...
"Laxity" (*śaithilya*) means "the state of being characterized by less effort," and so forth. "Place" (*sthāna*) refers to the palate and so on;

"instrument" (*karaṇa*) refers to the root of the tongue and so on. In the pronunciation of these two, laxity is the state of having less effort. In the examples [given], because of the closest similarity (*āntaratamya*), the *va* sound [is substituted] for the *va* sound itself.
It becomes *ya* for *ya*.

The mention of Śākaṭāyana is for the sake of honor, for by him the state of being easier in effort (*laghuprayatnatara*) is prescribed for *v* and *y*, while the elision (*lopa*) is also [prescribed] by the subsequent rule; therefore, it is precisely due to the force of prescribing both that [the former applies].
In this case, it will be understood as an injunction.

19. *lopaḥ śākalyasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.19). Since he will later state that there is a compulsory elision (*lopa*) of *v* and *y* when they follow an *o*, this rule is understood to apply to those [consonants] preceded by a vowel (*avarṇa*). Thus he says: "preceded by a vowel," and so forth.

"The mention of Śākalya is for the sake of an option (*vibhāṣā*). But surely, according to the opinion of Śākaṭāyana, [the form] is prescribed with even less effort (*laghuprayatnatara*). In that case, even without the mention of Śākalya, it would be understood that the rule is indeed optional; otherwise, [this would not be the case]. (Note: "hi" does not appear in the Kāśikā reading.)

The prescription of "effortless articulation" (laghuprayatna) would be purposeless; why, then, include the mention of Śākalya? To this he says: "By that," and so forth. For if the mention of Śākalya were absent, when the option (*vibhāṣā*) is applied by means of the less effortful articulation, the elision would be obligatory.
Consequently, there would be no hearing of the two [sounds] produced with non-light effort (*alaghuprayatna*).
However, when the mention of Śākalya is present, the elision (*lopa*) is made optional; by that means, their hearing is established even in those two cases. And thus, three forms arise—one—
The first [alternative] is in the case of the lesser effort; the second is in the case of elision; the third, however, is in the case of the absence of both.
20. This is the view of Gārgya.

(8.3.20) Since there is no *va* following the vowel *o*, this rule must be understood as applying specifically to the *ya* [of *vyañjana*] when it occurs at the end of a word; thus he says: "of the *ya* following the vowel *o*. But surely...
The elision of the letter *ya* following the vowel *au* is already established by the preceding rule alone;

so for what purpose is this [present] rule commenced? To this he says: "This commencement is for the sake of the opinion of Gārgya. Then, for what purpose is the mention of Gārgya? To this he says: "The mention of Gārgya," and so forth.

In this context, since the elision (*lopa*) is also prescribed in the alternative view where there is less effort (*laghuprayatnatara*), for what reason would this compulsory elision (*nityalopa*) be the sublater? To this he says: "This which... and so forth. Alternatively, if this commencement were for the sake of making [the rule] compulsory, then in the alternative case there would not be that which involves less effort.
He says: "This which... and so forth. The intention is that since the option for elision (*lopavikalpa*) has just preceded, it is logical to effect its very cessation.
"Some, however," and so forth. But how can there be a sublation of that which possesses a lighter effort (*laghuprayatnatara*), even though it is desired?

Is it not the case that, because the option for elision (*lopavikalpa*) follows immediately, its sublation by this [rule] is appropriate? There is no fault, because the entire set of operations (*kāryasamudāya*) involving *v* and *y* is required. If only the option for elision were required, then that alone would be sublated, and not the operation involving less effort (*laghuprayatnatara*), because it is separated by the elision.

But when, in a given context, an operation is prescribed for a *vṛddhi* vowel and that entire category (*samudāya*) is required, then by virtue of its immediate proximity (*ānantarya*), only that [specific *vṛddhi* vowel] is excluded.
The inclusion of the marker *t* (in *vṛddhir ādaic*) is for the sake of removing ambiguity; for if only "of *o*" (*oḥ*) were stated, doubt would arise.
It might be asked: "Is this the indication of the letter *o*, or rather of the letter *u*? Do not think so;

for the rule *bho-bhago-aghō-apūrvasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.17) is understood [from the previous sūtra], and there is no *u*-vowel in the words beginning with *bhoḥ*. Therefore, how could there be any doubt? If that is the case, then...
For the sake of the pleasure of the mouth.

Although [the elision] is already established by *lopaḥ śākalyasya* (8.3.19), this is for the sake of a restriction: [the elision occurs] only before *uñ* when it is part of a *pada*, and not elsewhere. [The phrase] "preceded by *avaṇ*" refers to that which is preceded by *o*.

Because the letter *va* is impossible [in this context] and because the letter *ya* is already established by the preceding rule, this elision is understood to apply only when preceded by a vowel (*avarṇa*); thus, it is stated "preceded by a vowel" (*avarṇapūrvayoḥ*). Regarding the form *sa u*: the word *su* becomes *tat* through the application of *tyadādyatva*; then, by the rule *tadoḥ saḥ sāvanantyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.106), the final *t* is replaced by *s*.
Regarding *rutvam*: there is the substitution of *y* for that [final *r*], and its elision occurs by this rule.

In the case of *tantrayutam*, the substitution of *ay* occurs for the word *tantra* ending in the locative case when followed by the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) *uta*. Now, one might object: is it not stated that [the substitution applies] "before *uñ*" (as per the Kāśikā reading)? It is not so.
Furthermore, since there is no *ñ* in *cāyuñ*, why is the word "pada" included for the purpose of excluding that [case]?
To this he says: "In the case of *veñ* when there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*)," and so forth. Vocalization, however, occurs by the rule "vacisvapi...
(Pāṇini 6.1.15). Thus, first, regarding the particle *uñ*:
The purpose of mentioning the word *padāt* has been shown without regard for the existence of that [word *padāt*] as explicitly stated.
However, when its existence is taken into account, he says "for the sake of what follows" (*uttarārtham*) in order to demonstrate another purpose: "*ṅmo hrasvād aci ṅmuṇ*" [Pāṇini 8.3.32].

The rule "nityam" (Pāṇini 8.3.32) is intended so that [the substitution] occurs when a word beginning with a vowel follows; it should not apply here in *paramadaṇḍin*. If it were for the sake of subsequent rules, why was it not placed right there? What, then, is the benefit of doing it thus? The benefit is that the svarita accent is not declared [for this rule]. This applies here as well.
It is the same [in this case] as well: when [the rule] is being applied, the technical maxim *lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 1.1.2) need not be resorted to.

The inclusion of the letter *ca* is for the purpose of including that which is preceded by a vowel (*avarṇa*); otherwise, because of their immediate proximity, only these two [specific vowels] would be intended.
In that case, would it be understood that there is elision of the subsequent *yakāra*? This is not so;
for if it were understood in this way, this *sūtra* would be entirely purposeless, since [the result] would already be established by the preceding rule.
It is not purposeless, because it serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*)—to ensure that [the elision] occurs only after *uṅ* and *pid*, as in "bho u".

[The author] says: "It is observed [that this is necessary]. For if this restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) did not exist, then in cases such as *bho yutam* and *bhago yutam*, the elision would occur invariably. However, if the inclusion of the particle *idam* (in the form of *uñ*) were intended here, then there would be nothing for the restrictive rule to exclude; thus, the word *ca* ("and") is used in relation to the preceding [rule].
The sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) is to be understood here.

The letter *ñ* in *uñi* is for the sake of avoiding ambiguity; for if it were not there, the rule would have been stated as *saptamyā āṬ*. Consequently, one might wonder: does this refer to the vowel *u*, or to the vowel *i*?

There would be doubt. But even if that [the *pratyāhāra*] were made, would there still not be doubt as to whether the inclusion of the particle *uñ* is intended, or rather the inclusion of the *ñ* in *jhabhañ* (Mā. Sū. 8) starting from the letter *u*? It is not so; first of all, you must consider this...

One must ask: is the obligatory elision (*nityo lopaḥ*) only for those consonants (*hal*) that are included in the *uñ* [pratyāhāra], or is it for others as well? What should be said here? "For others as well. For he will say:
"In the presence of a *hal*, for all" (Pāṇini 8.3.22). If that is so, then in this case...

The intention behind employing the term *pratyāhāra* would be that one might grasp the *pratyāhāra* by means of the letter *ca* in the rule *eāṬc* (Mā. Sū. 4), as in the case of *uci ca pade*. [One might argue: "In the case of *hal* as well, it will be governed by the rule *hali sarveṣām*. Even there, this is the purpose: doubt is thereby eliminated. Now...

Or, if it were intended here that the *pratyāhāra* beginning with *u* (i.e., *uṇ*) should include [the vowels] starting from *ū*, then one would have formed this single rule alone— namely, "in a word (*pade*), after all [vowels], when followed by a consonant (*halī*)"— by taking the *pratyāhāra* with the letter *l*. For there is no purpose whatsoever for the division of the rules (*yogavibhāga*).
We observe this; therefore, the inclusion of the *u* sounds and others via a *pratyāhāra* is not intended here.
Consequently, it is beyond doubt that only the particle *uñ* is being referred to.

22. *hali sarveṣām* (8.3.22). [The rule] *bho-bhago-agho-apūrvasya va-ya-uraḥ* [is understood here]. Since a *v*-sound preceded by *bho*, *bhago*, or *agho* is impossible, it is a *v*-sound preceded by an *a*-vowel that is possible. Of that, however...
It has already been shown by the rule "hali sarveṣām" that elision does not occur;
