therefore, here only the letter *y* is understood and not the letter *v*, as it is shown that its elision does not take place in rules such as "bhobhagoaghoapūrvasya" (Pāṇini 8.3.17).

In this context, what is the purpose of including the mention of *aś*? It is so that this elision—prescribed by the rule *hali sarveṣām*—should occur when an *aś* sound follows a consonant (*hal*), but it should not occur here: *vṛkṣa-vṛścati* becomes *vṛkṣavṛṭ*; from this, with the causative suffix *ṇic*, we have *vṛkṣavayati*; and from the verb *vṛkṣavayati*, with the addition of the suffix *apratyaya*, we have *vṛkṣav-*; then, in the phrase *vṛkṣav karoti*.
Thus, by demonstrating the purpose of including the mention of *aś*, it is stated by this very rule that in the case of *aś* followed by a consonant (*hal*),

the elision of the *v* preceded by an *a*-vowel does not occur. Now, one might object that the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the phrase "preceded by an *a*-vowel" is improper, because it was not carried over (*anukṛṣṭa*) from the preceding rule.
How then can there be elision of that which was preceded by a non-vowel? This is not so;
for the rule "that which is drawn forward [from a previous sūtra] does not continue into the subsequent one" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 76) is merely a general tendency.
How is this known? Because in the rule "when the following member consists of a single vowel, the substitute is ṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.12), the word "ṇaḥ" is already established [as the subject].

The repetition of the term *ṇa* is made for the purpose of excluding the word *vā* that was carried over from the rule *vā bhāvakaraṇayoḥ* (8.4.10). For if this [present rule] were not general in application, the repetition of *ṇa* would be useless; indeed, [the desired result] would follow simply because [the rule] was drawn forward (*anukṛṣṭa*) from the preceding sūtra.

Since the recurrence of the mention of *vā* will not occur, what is the purpose of mentioning *ṇ* again? And since it has been done, it is understood from this that the paribhāṣā concerning the attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*) is not universally valid (*anitya*).
[The phrase] "so that the elision (*lopa*) may also apply for Śākaṭāyana" implies by the word *api* that it applies for Śākalya as well.
But if there were no mention of "all," it would be understood that, according to the opinion of Gārgya, only the elision of the proximate [syllable] would take place.
23. *m* [is] *anusvāra*.

(Pāṇini 8.3.23) The term "of the word" (*padasya*) is a genitive of location; that word is qualified by the letter *m*, and by means of this qualification, the rule of "ending-in-that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies, so that *anusvāra* replaces the final *m* of a word.

Since the *al* being prescribed [by the rule] is understood by the paribhāṣā *alo 'ntyasya* (1.1.52) to refer specifically to the *m*, he says: "of a word ending in *m*" (*makārāntasya padasya*)—[as noted in the Kāśikā and Padamañjarī: "of a word ending in *m*"]. "Of the word" (*padasya*).

24. *naścāpadāntasya jhali* (Pāṇini 8.3.24). The term *hali* is no longer in force here, because of the mention of *jhali*. The particle *ca* serves to carry forward the mention of *m*. For if that were absent, since the rule would be referring here to the *makāra* as the subject of the operation (*kāryin*), [the substitution] would apply only to a *nakāra* that is not at the end of a word.
There might be the apprehension that [the word] is *nivṛta*. [The form] "payāṃsi" [is derived as follows]: by the rule *jaśśasoḥ śiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.20), the *śi* suffix replaces *jas* and *śas*;

then the *num* augment is applied by *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ* (7.1.72); finally, the lengthening is applied by *sāntamahataḥ saṃyogasya* (6.4.10). [The form] "ākraṃsyate" is derived from the root *kram* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, with the *lṛṭ* suffix.

The ātmanepada suffix is applied by the rule *āṅ udyamane* (1.3.40), as in *ācikraṃsate*. The ātmanepada suffix is applied by the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* (1.3.62). The same applies here in *athijigāṃsate*. When the desiderative suffix (*san*) follows the root *iṅ*, the substitution of *gam* for *iṅ* occurs by the rule *iṅśca* (2.4.48); [then the rule] *ajjhanagamāṃ...* [applies].
The vowel lengthening occurs by the rule *sani* (Pāṇini 6.4.16); there is reduplication and the grammatical operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

The form *rājan* is derived from the root *rāj* with the suffix *śatṛ*, followed by the vocative case ending; its elision is effected by the rule *halṅyābhyo dīrghāt sutisy apṛktaṃ hal* (Pāṇini 6.1.68).
25. *mo rāji samaḥ kvau* (8.3.25).

Regarding the word *samrāṭ*: from the root *rāj* preceded by the prefix *sam*, the suffix *kvip* is applied according to *satsūdvipa-* (3.2.61) et cetera; then, by the rule *vraścādi-* (8.2.36), there is the substitution of *ṣ* for the *j*; and by the rule of *jaśtva*, the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*. Thus, [the form is] *samrāṭ*.
And its *cartva* [the substitution of *ṭ* for *t*] is the letter *ṭ*. Regarding the form *sābhrājyam*: because it belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class, the suffix *vyañ* is applied.

But for what purpose is the letter *m* pronounced again? To this he says: “The mention of the letter *m* for the letter *m*” and so forth. By the rule *mo’nusvāraḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.23), an *anusvāra* would have been required; that [is why the *m* is stated].

The letter *m* is prescribed for the [final] *m* in order that it may become [nasal]. If this is so, then the prohibition "not" (*na*) should be stated, for in this way the rule (*sūtra*) becomes concise by not having to utter the case-ending.
[Objection: If that were the case, then [the form would be established] through the addition of the demonstrative pronoun (*nirdeśa*).

By this rule involving the letter *m*, he indicates that in this section there is indeed an additional rule: namely, that the letters *y*, *v*, *l*, and *p* may optionally become *y*, *v*, *l*, and *p* when followed by those same letters. Regarding the word *saṃyat*: it is derived from the root *yam* with the prefix *sam* and the suffix *kvip*, according to Pāṇini 6.4.37 (*anudātopadeśa*).
By these and other rules, there is the elision of the letter *m*; and for the short vowel *a*, the augment *tuk* is applied according to Pāṇini 6.1.71 (*hrasvasya piti kṛti*).

26. *he mapare vā* (Pāṇini 8.3.26). The term *mapara* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that after which *m* follows. [Examples: *kim hyalayati*. [Roots: *hvala* and *hyala* mean "to move" (*dhātupāṭha* 805, 806). [Vārttika: "The substitution of *ṇa* for *na* occurs optionally after the roots *jval*, *hval*, and *hyal* when they are not preceded by a prefix."
(Immediately following *ga.sū.dhā.pā.817*) or rather, there is the designation *mit*, and by the rule ‘*mitāṃ hrasvaḥ*’ (Pāṇini 6.4.92), a short vowel is substituted.
Regarding the phrase ‘*yavalapare*’ and so forth: that after which *ya*, *va*, or *la* follow is *yavalapara*; in that case—*he*.
The meaning is that this form of the sense—that *y*, *v*, and *l* may occur in place of the letter *m*—must be explained.

The explanation, however, has already been provided previously. And when these [substitutes] *y*, *v*, and *l* occur, they are necessarily nasalized (*sānunāsika*) due to their internal similarity (*āntaratamya*). Because of the mention of the option (*vāvacana*), the *anusvāra* certainly occurs in the alternative case. Now...

"Why is it not simply stated as *he bhaḥ*? For in that case, the mention of *para* (following) would not need to be made, since its meaning would be conveyed by the locative case alone—namely, 'the vowel *a* which occurs before *m*.
This is not so; for if it were stated as *he maḥ*, there would also be the possibility of the reverse [interpretation]."
It might be understood that "the letter *m* [is replaced] when followed by the letter *h*," and consequently, this would apply only in cases such as *ahnaḥ*.

If it is argued that it will not apply here because of the intervention of the vowel *a*, we say no; for according to the authoritative statement, "that by which there is no intervention [is considered non-intervening], even when there is intervention" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 46).

Thus, intervention by only a single phoneme is intended, and not by multiple ones. If it is argued that in the first position, the statement [of the rule] has already served its purpose in cases such as *kim hy alayati*, and therefore one cannot rely on intervention, we say no; for by this [rule], in the word *hakāra*, there is the letter *m*.

The meaning of the sūtra has been grasped; since no other alternative is possible regarding that, the word "para" (other) must indeed be included for the purpose of preventing the misconception [of the contrary].

27. *naḥ* [is substituted] when not followed by another [letter]. (8.3.27) The term *naparaḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that after which *naḥ* does not follow. The inclusion of the word *para-* is for the purpose of ensuring that the substitution occurs when [the *n*] is followed by a letter; otherwise, if it were stated simply as *ne naḥ*, [the rule would apply] only when followed by the letter *na*.

Is it that [the substitution] would be understood as occurring only when followed by something else, so that by employing another cause [for the *n*], the [application of] "he" is excluded? This is not the case; for if this were so, the present statement would be purposeless. For once the *n* has been replaced by an *anusvāra*, [the rule] "the *anusvāra* becomes a homogeneous sound before a *yay* consonant" (Pāṇini 8.4.58) applies.
Is the letter *na* established by this [rule]? True; this is for the sake of providing an option (*vikalpa*).

For here, when the letter *na* is not applied by this [rule], then—by the force of the statement—it is established as an option that the *parasavarṇa* does not occur. Therefore, the mention of "following" (*para*) must be made: *na-pare*.
It is so that [the rule] may apply when there is the letter *ha*, but not when it is alone. [The example is] "kin hnute.
[The root] *hnuṅ* means "to remove" (*apanayane*; DhP 1082); due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.
Here, some raise an objection: why is this not understood as a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) by the word "not" (*na*)?

And this is incorrect; for since it is read with a *visarga*, a *visarga* is impossible after a *nakāra* which expresses a negation. Even if it were read without a *visarga*, the suspicion of a negation would still be improper, because there is no possibility [of the rule's application] in that case.

28. *ṅṇoḥ kuk ṭuk śari* (8.3.28). *Ṅ* and *ṇ* are *ṅṇau*; *ka* and *ṭa* are *kaṭau*. Each of these is connected with the letters *u* and *k* respectively—thus: *kuk* and *ṭuk*. The letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), and the letter *k* [is for the sake of indicating the place of articulation].
The purpose is for the sake of euphonic combination (*saṃhitā*). Regarding *prāṅ śete*: *prāṅ* is derived in the rule *kvinpratyayasya kuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.62).
Regarding *vaṇṭ śete*: [the suffix] *vic* is added to the root *vaṇ*.
But for what purpose are these two made as *pūrvānta* (included at the end of the preceding element)? To this he says: "The making of them *pūrvānta*..."
And so forth. But what is the reason that *cch* occurs when [the suffix] begins with *pūrva*, and not when it begins with *para*? To this he says:
"In the case of *śaś chāe ṭi*" and so on. Why, then, is this understood here? To this he says: "In this [context]" and so forth.

If the rule *padāntājjhaya* (Pāṇini 8.2.10) were not applied there, then in the word *virapśin*, the substitution of *cch* would be understood [to apply]. However, when that is understood, it does not occur, because there is no *jhay* sound at the end of the word here; the form is *viriṣśin*. This is derived from the root *rap* preceded by the prefix *vi*, with the suffix *lṛṭ* optionally replaced by *sad*.

[The forms] *laṭaḥ*—according to the Prācīna reading—is the substitution of *śatṛ*, and by *vyatyayo bahulam* (3.1.85), the *s* of the suffix *syap* becomes *ś*, while the *y* becomes *i*. Thus we have *prāṅk sāyaḥ*. Here, if it were *parādau* (treated as if following the end of the preceding element), then by *iṇkoḥ* (8.3.57),...

The prohibition by *sātpadādyoḥ* (8.3.112) against the application of *ṣatva* obtained by *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (8.3.59) would not occur [in the case of *sa-ṣṭhaḥ*], because it is not at the beginning of a word (*apadādi*). [In the case of] *vaṇṭ sāyaḥ*, here too, the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭu* obtained by *ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ* (8.4.41) [would not occur]. *Na*...
Otherwise, the prohibition [stated in] *padāntāṭ ṭoranām* (Pāṇini 8.4.42) would not apply,

because [the letter ṭ] would not be at the end of a word (*apadānta*). Therefore, in forms such as *prāṅkcheta*, the treatment as a prior element (*pūrvāntatva*) is adopted in order to ensure the application of the substitution of *ch* and other such rules.
29. *ḍaḥ si dhuṭ* (Pāṇini 8.3.29).

According to the principle that "in the case of a mention of both [cases], the ablative mention is stronger" (*Śākapārthivādhikaraṇa*, Pāṇinian Paribhāṣā 97), when the ablative *ṅaḥ* is interpreted as having the genitive sense of the locative *si*, the augment *dhuṭ* is applied specifically after the letter *ś*.

The *dhuṭ* augment is prescribed; thus he says: "after that which ends in the letter ḍ," and so forth. If this is so, what is the purpose of the locative case indication (*saptamī-nirdeśa*)? It is for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*). If it were stated as *ṅḥ so dhuṭ*, there would be prolixity (*gaurava*) due to the greater number of syllables. Now, [if one asks] "in which... [the answer follows].

Why is this locative designation (*saptamī-nirdeśa*) not understood as having the purpose [stated in] *Vyāḍipañjikā* 127, namely: "The rule [applies] at the beginning when there is the inclusion of the letter *a*"? Because that [result] is established simply by the non-existence of a solitary *s* sound, and because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "in a word" (*pade*). Furthermore, in the case of *śva-liṭ-ati*, once the *dhuṭ* augment has been applied, [the rule applies] to the letter *dh*.
The *cartva* is the letter *t*.

For the sake of brevity in grammatical derivation (*prakriyālāghava*), although one could have simply said *tuṭ*, the mention of *dhuṭ* is for the sake of what follows—so that in the rule *naśca* (Pāṇini 8.3.30), there may be *dhuṭ* and not *tuṇ*. For if [the latter] were to occur, [the result would be undesirable].

In that case, what [is the problem]? Would the *ru* substitution prescribed by Pāṇini 8.3.7 (*naścchavyapraśān*) apply here in the word *bhavāntsāya*? This is not so; for the condition “preceded by *am*” (*amparaḥ*) does not recur [in this rule], and here the letter *t* is not preceded by *am*. If it is argued that even here [the *t*] is preceded by *am* by virtue of the *u* that previously existed [before the elision of *s*]:

Could it be so? Even then, because [the *tuṭ* augment] would be unestablished (*asiddha*), the substitution of *r* for *t* would not occur. Therefore, *tuṭ* alone must be prescribed. If that is the case, then the mention of *dhuṭ* is for the sake of variety.
Now, for what purpose is *dhuṭ* made an external element (*parādi*)? Why is it not made an internal element (*pūrvānta*) of *dyau* itself? In this way—

In the rule *hi-śi-tuk* (Pāṇini 8.4.31), the mention of *tuk* would not need to be made, for *dhuk* alone would indeed carry over there. To this he says: "The formation as a subsequent element (*parādi-karaṇam*)," and so forth. If it were formed as a prior element (*pūrvānta*), then in the case of *śvaliṭtsāya*, the substitution of *ṣṭu* would apply to the *dhuk*.
However, since the status of being a word-final (*padānta*) is not prescribed for the letter *ṭ* when it is treated as initial (*parādi*),
the prohibition established by the rule *na padāntāṭṭoranām* (Pāṇini 8.4.42) is successfully achieved. It is for this purpose that the treatment as initial is applied.

The particle *ca* is for the purpose of carrying forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) the term *dhuṭ*. But surely it will carry forward by virtue of being *svarita*, and it will not carry forward in what follows because another augment is introduced or because it is not *svarita*?

This is true; however, there would be a lack of respect for the method among those of dull intellect. Now, regarding the form *bhavāntsāya*, once the substitution of *c* for *t* has been applied by [Pāṇini 8.4.41], why does the rule "naścchavyapraśān" (8.3.7) not apply to produce *ru*?
To this he says: "Because the substitution of *c* for *t* and the *dhuṭ* augment are both considered asiddha," and so forth. If [the rule were applied] to the isolated...
Even if the *ghuṭ* [consonant] were unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to the *car* [substitution], the occurrence of *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) would still be impossible;

how much more so when both are unestablished? Thus, the mention of "both" is intended to demonstrate the absolute impossibility of the occurrence of *rutva*. In some places, it is stated: "because the *car* substitution for the *ghuṭ* is unestablished."

Such is the reading. In that case as well, this meaning should be understood: for even without the particle *ca*, its sense is understood, as in the sentence beginning, "Day after day, leading away the cow, the horse, the man, and the beast," and so forth. Or else—in this reading, [the rule applies] to the *dhuṭ* and that which is *ārtva*.

The meaning is: "because that [the *dhuṭ*] is not established. Now, one might object: "But the *dhuṭ* is also indeed unestablished; so why is it said that the *cartva* (the substitution of *c* for *r*) is unestablished, and why again the *dhuṭ*? This is not so; for even when the *dhuṭ* exists, without the *cartva*, the occurrence of *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) does not take place at all. Therefore, when [the *cartva*] exists...

The sense is that the substitution of *r* (rutva) is raised as an objection because its being "not established" (asiddhatva) has already been stated. But how can the substitution of *r* be raised as an objection when the substitution of *c* (cartva) is not established, given that the former is prescribed only before a following *am*, whereas here there is no following *am*?

It was previously suspected that there might be the state of being followed by *am* (*amparatva*) on account of a former *am*; for indeed, when the present [condition] is absent, one resorts to what has occurred in the past. But is there not a present state elsewhere where there is the state of being followed by *am* for the substitution of *ru*? This is true.

This was stated by way of superimposition (*adhyāropa*); he thinks as follows: "Let it be granted that [the status of] being followed by *am* would follow from the *ukāra* that existed previously. To this, he says: "Because the *dhruvatva* (fixedness) of the *m* is not established (*asiddhatvāt*)."

31. *śi tuk* (Pāṇini 8.3.31). The locative case in *śi*, whose purpose has not yet been fulfilled, causes the fifth case (*pañcamī*) in the preceding rule—which had already served its purpose in relation to *naḥ*—to be interpreted as a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*); this is according to the principle: "When [an element] is specified by the locative case (*tasminn iti nirdiṣṭe*), [the operation applies] to what precedes it" (1.1.66).
Because of this statement, it is understood that the augment *āgama* is specifically the letter *n*; thus he says, "of that which ends in *n*" (*nakārāntasya*), and so forth.
Now, for what purpose is the augment *tuk* made an initial element (*pūrvānta*), rather than the previously mentioned *dhuṭ* being made a final element (*parādi*)?

It might be performed; yet, even so, how is *cartva* established? To this he says: "The making of the prior limit," and so forth. The "prior limit" (*pūrvānta*) is the end of what precedes; furthermore, by virtue of the context, that is understood to be the *tug*. Its "making" (*karaṇa*) is its application, for the purpose that *chatva* may occur. If...
Only *dhuṭ* would be prescribed as the original element; consequently, the substitution of *cch* by the rule *śaś chāe’ṭi* (Pāṇini 8.4.63) would not occur.

The reason for this has already been stated previously. Regarding the phrase "If it were so," etc.: if *tuk* were treated as an *uttarapada-anta* (end of the following word), then in the case of *kurvaṃśca*, the status of being a word-final (*padāntatā*) [of the preceding element] would be lost due to *tuk*.

Because of the absence of the letter *nakāra*, the rule *aṭkuṣvāṅ* (Pāṇini 8.4.2) would entail the substitution of *ṇa*; however, if [the suffix] were considered to begin with the subsequent element (*parāditva*), this fault would not arise, because of the prohibition of *ṇatva* by the rule *padāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.37)—this is the intended meaning. By the words "In that case" (*tatra*) and so forth, [it is shown that] "not... [is the conclusion].
From the sūtra *bhābhūpūkamigami* (8.4.34), with the word *na* understood from the preceding context, a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is made as *stoḥ ścunā ścaḥ* (8.4.40).

By this, in a case such as *kurvañcete*, where there is a conjunction with the *ca*-class (the palatals), the substitution of *ṇ* does not occur at all. Now, one might object: even if [this split] were performed...

By means of the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), the substitution of *ṇ* certainly obtains; for in this case, there is no connection with the *ca*-group at all, because the substitution of *ś* (for *c*) is not established (*asiddha*). [Objection: Since the separation of the rule has the power [to establish it], even though the substitution of *ś* is not established, the prohibition of *ṇ* will still occur; thus, there is no fault.

32. *ṅmo hrasvād aci ṅmuṇ nityam* (Pāṇini 8.3.32). Both *imaḥ* and *ṅmuṭaḥ* are references to *pratyāhāra*s (abbreviated vowel series). The term *uṭ* is connected individually with each of the sounds beginning with *ṅ*. The word *hrasvāt* (after a short vowel) is an attribute of *ṅmaḥ*.

Even though the short vowel (*hrasva*) qualifies *ṅm*, it qualifies the word (*pada*); and since a rule involving a qualifier applies to that which ends with the qualified element, it is understood as "from a word ending in that [short vowel]. Although the genitive form *padasya* is the subject under discussion, nevertheless, for the sake of the sense here, it is treated as having the ablative case ending (*pañcamyanta*).

It is modified [as follows]: "In the case of a dual designation, the fifth-case designation is stronger" (Śākaṭāyana Paribhāṣā 97). Thus, when the sixth case is substituted for the seventh case in the word *aci* by means of the fifth case in *ṅmaḥ*, it is understood that the vowel (*ac*) itself is the augment. As for the designation in the seventh case...
Having kept all this in mind—that it is for the sake of brevity and for the sake of what follows—he says:

"from that which has a *ṅ* following a short vowel, [the suffix *ṅe*] comes after that which ends in such. For here, a correspondence based on numerical order (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) is to be understood, because the number of elements to be replaced and the substitutes are equal. As in: "toward thee" (*pratyaṅṅaste*).

The root *ās* means "to sit" (Dhātupāṭha 1021); due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision of the *śap* suffix. Thus, [the form] is *kṛvan āste*. The root *kṛṣ* means "to scratch" (Dhātupāṭha 990) and belongs to the *tudādi* class; [here] the *śatṛ* suffix is applied. Now, in the case of *paramadaṇḍin* and *uttamadaṇḍin*, [the compound is formed] by the rule beginning with *sanmahat* (Pāṇini 2.1.61).
Once the compound has been formed, why does the augment *nuṭ* not occur after the word ending in *ṅ*, namely *daṇḍin-*, in the third case singular?

For here, even though the status of being a *bha*-stem applies by the rule "before *yaC* and *jhaL*, it is *bha*" (Pāṇini 1.4.18), the nasal *ṅ* [of *daṇḍin-*, i.e., the *n*] follows a short vowel (*i*) at the end of the compound; therefore, whatever case-ending follows that word *daṇḍin-* which ends in *ṅ*, [the *nuṭ* should apply].

"Even though [the suffix] has been elided, since the designation *pada* is obtained by virtue of Pāṇini 1.1.62 (*pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam*), the third-case singular ending would have the letter *a* following it; thus, there is the possibility of the application of *ṅmuṭ*.
To this, he says: 'paramadaṇḍinā', etc. [This applies] when there is the status of being an *uttarapada*, that is, when there is the designation *uttarapada*."

The meaning of the sentence is that when there is a rule concerning the status of a word (pada) and so forth to be applied, the definition of a suffix (pratyayalakṣaṇa) does not apply elsewhere. Since the definition of a suffix does not apply, the technical designation "word" (pada-saṃjñā) is not assigned to *daṇḍinā*.
Consequently, the augment *ṅmuṭ*, which is prescribed for what follows the end of a word (*padāntāt*), does not occur.

Thus, first, the resolution has been stated according to the opinion of Kātyāyana. Now, in order to show that which is according to the opinion of the author of the Sūtras, he says: "Or rather," and so forth. Since the word *pade* (in a word) is understood from the previous context, when the word is being qualified by this, the principle applies: "When there is a rule [applying] to something, it applies to that which begins with it, provided that the term *al* (vowel) is not used [as a qualifier]. (Vārttika 14).

By this [rule], the operation must apply when a word beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) follows; however, there is no such word here beginning with a vowel, so how could there be the possibility of the insertion of *nuṭ*?
Now, what is the purpose of the mention of "nitya" (invariable), given that in the subsequent sūtra (8.3.33) the word "vā" (optionally) is used?

"Will the rule be understood as obligatory (*nitya*)? This is true; however, obligatoriness would also be understood in the preceding sūtra (8.3.31). Therefore, the mention of 'obligatory' (*nitya*) is for the purpose of indicating that the word 'optionally' (*vā*) from the preceding sūtras—specifically from 'he mapare vā' (8.3.26)—is to be carried over [into this one]."
33. *maya uño vo vā* (8.3.33).

The term "*mayaḥ*" refers to the *pratyāhāra* [consisting of the vowels *i*, *u*, and *ṛ*], and not to the verbal root *maya-vaya-maya*. Why is this so? Because of the principle of pervasion (*vyāptinyāya*). For what purpose is this stated, given that [the rule] "of *ik*" (*iko*)...?

If it is argued that the substitution of *yaṇ* for *uṅ* [in the case of *u*] by the rule *yaṇ aci* (6.1.77) is already established, and that the present rule is for the sake of making it optional— namely,
that this statement is intended to make optional what would otherwise be compulsory under *iko yaṇ aci*—
this is not so; for the word *vā* ("or") will be carried over from the preceding rule *padāntād vā* (6.1.76).

And that *vibhāṣā* is understood to be fixed (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, he says "because of its being *pragṛhya*" and so forth, to show that the suffix *matup* optionally occurs after *uñ*. Furthermore, its status as *pragṛhya* results from the prescription of the *pragṛhya* designation by the rule *uñaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.17). When that [designation] exists, [the rule] *plutapragṛhyā aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.125) applies.

Thus, the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) would apply; when that [original form] would have been obtained, the substitution of *va* is prescribed. Even so, should not the *yaṇ* substitution for *uṅ*, namely *va*, be prescribed immediately after the rule “*iko yaṇ aci*” (P. 6.1.77)?
For in this way, the term *va* need not be employed, since *yaṇ* is the subject under discussion. The mention of *va* [is therefore not necessary].

It must be performed; does the word "optionally" (*vā*) from the rule *padāntādvā* (Pāṇini 6.1.76) carry over here by means of a "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūakapluti*)? To this he replies: "Because of its being unestablished," and so forth. For if that were stated there, then because the *va* [is not established] before a consonant (*hal*), [the rule would not apply].

The anusvāra would be prescribed [by that rule], but it is not desired; therefore, it is performed right here. When it is performed here, the *m* does not become an anusvāra, because the substitution of *v* (vatva) is considered asiddha (non-existent).
34. *visarjanīyasya saḥ* (8.3.34).

It is stated that "the word *khari* recurs [from the previous rule]"; this recurrence is from the rule *kharavasānayorvisarjanīyaḥ* (8.3.15), either by the maxim of the frog’s leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*) or by the recurrence of its own specific connection.
It should be understood [in this way]; otherwise, even in the previous sūtra (8.3.33), it would be understood that the operation applies when a *khari* sound follows.

35. *śarpare visarjanīyaḥ* (8.3.35). The term *śarparaḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that after which *śar* [the sibilants] follow. Now, for what purpose is the mention of *para* ("following")? Could it not simply be stated as *śari*? It is impossible to state it thus; for if it were stated in that way, only *śar* itself [would be understood].

The status of being a *nimitta* (conditioning cause) would be understood [only] by the recurrence of the word "khar" and because of the rule "vā śari" (Pāṇini 8.3.36). Otherwise, the opposite would be understood— that is, [the condition would be] "śar"— and consequently, [the rule] would apply only in cases such as *nityaḥ sphoṭaḥ* and *puruṣaḥ sthūlaḥ*, but not in cases such as *vāsaḥ kṣaumam*.

Would it not [be so]? Therefore, the mention of "another" (para) is for the purpose that the opposite [case] should not be understood. Now, for what purpose is the term *visarjanīya* stated; could one not simply say "not" (*na*)? For when the prohibition of the *sakāra* has been made, the *visarjanīya* will remain in its own form by itself.

Thus he says: "of the *visarjanīya*," and so forth. The modification (*vikāra*) of that *visarjanīya* consists of the *jihvāmūlīya* and other such sounds; the mention of *visarjanīya* is for the purpose of excluding those. Otherwise, if only "not" (*na*) were stated, then the principle would apply: "a rule or a prohibition applies only to what immediately precedes."

Thus, it would be understood as referring to the letter *s* alone; consequently, the *jihvāmūlīya* and other such sounds would necessarily be the substitutes for the *visarjanīya*. However, when the term *visarjanīya* is explicitly mentioned, [the substitution] does not occur precisely by virtue of that very mention.
37. *kuṣvoḥ ka pau ca* (8.3.37).
[The word] "and the *visarjanīya*" (*visarjanīyaśca*)—the particle *ca* here is for the purpose of carrying over (*anukarṣaṇa*) the term *visarjanīya*.

[The author] shows [the solution]: Alternatively, having understood that the mention of *v* is to be supplied [from a previous rule], why are the *jihvāmūlīya* and *upadhmānīya* not treated as optional? And in this way, the letter *c* would not need to be used for the purpose of attracting (*anukarṣaṇa*) the *visarjanīya*;
for when these two are excluded, the *visarjanīya* alone will occur in that alternative case? [The answer is: Not so.

For this would apply only when there is a *kup* [consonant] followed by a *śapara* [sibilant]; however, in the case where they are not *śapara*, the substitution of *s* by "the *s* of *visarjanīya*" (Pāṇini 8.3.34) would optionally take effect. Therefore, the letter *c* must be included in the rule. In this context, the rule concerns the *jihvāmūlīya* and *upadhmānīya* substitutes for *k* and *p*.

Someone might have the doubt: "Are the *k* and *p* substitutes for the *visarjanīya* understood as being of that same nature [as the original] because they are pronounced [in its place]? Therefore, in order to dispel that doubt, he says: "The letters *k* and *p* are for the sake of pronunciation. Without these two...
The meaning is that those two [sounds] cannot be articulated. What kind of substitutes (*ādeśa*) are they? To this he says:

"The substitutes are indeed the *jihvāmūlīya* and the *upadhmānīya*. The word "indeed" (*tu*) highlights the distinction between these and the composite forms of the substitutes that were previously suspected.

The particle *eva* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). The meaning is that the jihvāmūlīya and upadhmānīya are exclusively [those sounds] by themselves, and not in the form of a composite. Since every possible object here is already occupied by another rule, [the present rule applies] to the *k* and *p* [substitutes] in the context of *kupvoḥ*.
The rule *ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.37) would thus have no scope; therefore, just as in cases such as *vṛkṣaḥ karoti*,
the rule *kupvoḥ ka pau ca* (8.3.37) operates by setting aside the rule *visarjanīyasya saḥ* (8.3.34),
so too does it operate in cases such as *vāsaḥ kṣaumam* and *adbhiḥ psātam*.
To one who might inquire, "Why does this rule [Pāṇini 8.3.35] not also subvert the present injunction? he replies with the words beginning "of the *visarjanīya*.
This [present rule] is commenced whether that rule "when followed by a *śar* or *par*, the *visarjanīya* remains" (8.3.35) has already applied or has not yet applied.

In cases such as *vāśaḥ kṣaumam* ("linen cloth from Vāśa") and *adbhiḥ psātam* ("eaten with water"), [the rule] applies when [the visarga] is already present; in cases such as *vṛkṣaḥ karoti* ("the tree does") and *vṛkṣaḥ pacati* ("the tree cooks"), it applies where it was not previously present. However, regarding the rule *visarjanīyasya saḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.34), it applies everywhere.
Thus, its qualification would apply to every instance of a visarga because it is prescribed for that alone; this [present rule] is indeed for that very [visarga].

It is a sublater (*bādhaka*) [of the former], not of the other injunction (*vidhi*); for, with respect to that [other injunction], the definition of a sublater (*bādhakalakṣaṇa*) is inapplicable. This might be argued: when a *visarjanīya* is followed by a *śar* sound, the *khar* sounds other than the *ka*-group and *pa*-group constitute the scope (*avakāśa*) for the rule "when *ku* or *pu* follow, *ka* or *pa* are substituted" (Pāṇini 8.3.37), whereas the *khar* sounds not followed by a *śar* sound [constitute the scope] for the other rule.
Regarding the *kavarga* and *pavarga*: in the case of *vāsaḥ kṣaumam* and *adbhiḥ psatam*, both [rules] would apply;

therein, according to "In the event of a conflict, the subsequent rule prevails" (Pāṇini 1.4.2), should it not be appropriate for the *visarjanīya* to be set aside by the *jihvāmūlīya* and *upadhmānīya* [substitutes]?

Thus he says: "In the absence of what precedes," and so forth. He provides the justification for this very point: "Because of the non-existence of the subsequent. A conflict arises when two rules of equal force apply simultaneously to the same location;
however, there is no simultaneous application here, because [the subsequent rule] must wait until the preceding one has been applied.
Because [the former rule] has already been established as valid and because the subsequent [rule] is non-existent; the particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).

Since there is no conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) when what precedes is not yet established, therefore, in the cases of *vāsaḥ kṣaumam* and *adbhiḥ psātam*, only the rule *śarpare visarjanīyaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.35) applies, and not [the other].
Regarding the terms *jihvāmūlīya* and *upadhmānīya*:

the phrase "some [say]" and so forth refers to this. In the rule *kupvoḥ ka pau ca*, the purpose is to ensure that the *visarjanīya* occurs in the expression *adbhiḥ psātam*, where the cloth is made of linen (*kṣauma*).
They perform a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule): the first rule is "of *k* and *p*" (*kupvoḥ*), and "of *k* and *p*" (*ka pau*) is the second.

In the former rule, the phrase "the *visarjanīya* [is substituted] before a sibilant followed by a consonant" (*śarpare visarjanīyaḥ*, 8.3.35) is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*). Consequently, only the *visarjanīya* is substituted for *k* and *p* when they are followed by a sibilant.
There are nojihvāmūlīya and upadhmānīya [sounds].

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule. The term “*apadādau*” [is used] because of a substitution of the singular number for the dual; otherwise, the status of being "not at the beginning of a word" (*apadāditva*) would qualify the [consonants] *k* and *p*.

This is not tenable. If [the suffix *pāśa*] were present when there is duality, one would have formulated the rule as “*apādīnām dvitve*. The statement “in the cases of *pāśa*, *kalpa*, and *kāmya*” is an illustration of possible instances, not an exhaustive enumeration (*parigaṇana*), because there is nothing else to be excluded.
For example: *payaspāśam* (a little milk); here the suffix *pāśap* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.3.47, “*yāpye pāśap*. And: *payaskalpam* (milk-like).

The suffix *kalpa* is applied by the rule “*īṣadasamāptau kalpap*” (Pāṇini 5.3.67). Regarding the form *payaskam*: milk that is unknown—[the suffix] *ka* is applied by the rule “*ajñāte*” (Pāṇini 5.3.73). Regarding the form *payaskāmyati*: [the suffix] *kyac* is applied by the rule “*supa ātmanaḥ kyac*” (Pāṇini 3.1.8), and [the suffix] *kāmyac* is applied by the rule “*kāmyac ca*” (Pāṇini 3.1.9). *Paya*...

"He desires" (*kāmayate*). [This is derived from] *kamerṇiṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.30). "He drinks" (*pibati*). [The root is] *pā pāne* (Dhātupāṭha 925); the substitution of *piba-* occurs by the rule *pāghrādhmā...* (7.3.78). Regarding the statement "it should be stated that [the substitution applies] after the letter *s*, when it is not at the beginning of a word and is not an indeclinable," [the rule is] *so'padādau* (8.3.32).

The meaning is that in this sūtra, it must be explained that the substitution of *s* occurs for the non-indeclinable *visarjanīya*. In that regard, the explanation is as follows: the word "optionally" (*vā*) from the rule "vā śari" (8.3.36) is understood here, and that is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
"Therefore, it will apply only to that which is not an indeclinable (*avyaya*), and not to an indeclinable.

The phrase "for the sake of restriction regarding *roḥ* in the context of *kāmya*" is a mnemonic statement (*grahaṇakavākya*). "Only after *ru*" is its explanation. The meaning of the word *vaktavya* here is the same as before. This is the commentary.
It should be understood according to the previous rule. In the word *roḥ*, the genitive case (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) refers to the visarga;
the meaning is "of that which is the visarga of *ru*. It is stated that "the root *ubj* is recited with the upadhmānīya as its penultimate letter. Here...

Regarding this, some hold the view that the root is *ubj* in the sense of "straightening" (*ārjava*), while the *upadhmānīya* is not heard [in the form *udbja*] because of the grammatical instruction regarding the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaś*) for the unvoiced aspirated stop (*kṛta*). Others, however, hold the view that the root is *udj* in the sense of "straightening. In that case, according to the first position, from the root *ubj*, [the suffix *ap* is applied] by the rule *halaśca* (Pāṇini 3.3.121).

If the *ghañ* suffix were applied, the substitution of *k* for *c* and *j* by Pāṇini 7.3.52 (*cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*) would result in *abhyubgaḥ* and *samubgaḥ*—an undesirable form—due to the change of the *upadhmānīya* to *b* by Pāṇini 8.4.53 (*jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*). Therefore, it must be stated that when a *ka*-class consonant follows, the *upadhmānīya* becomes *s*; and when *s* [follows], [the *b* becomes *v*].

For the sake of the *upadhmānīya*, its replacement by the letter *d* occurs by virtue of the *jaś*-rule; thus, forms such as *abhyudgaḥ* and *samudgaḥ* are established as desired. Furthermore, the prohibition of reduplication for the *upadhmānīya* must indeed be stated; otherwise, in a form such as *ubjijiṣati*, [the rule] "of the second [syllable] beginning with a vowel" (*ajāder dvitīyasya*) would apply.

(6.1.2) Thus, the doubling of the *upadhmānīya* would result. However, according to the other view—that *bha* should be stated for the root *ubj* in the section on what is not established (*asiddhakāṇḍa*)—otherwise forms such as *ubjijiṣati* and *ubjitā* would not be established. And so it has been said: "In the section on what is not established, *bha* [is substituted] for *ubj*."

The mention of *asiddha* is because the letter *b* is not established [as a valid substitute]. This is so that in the form *ubjijiṣati*, the prohibition of doubling for a second monosyllable by the rule *na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.3) may apply. Should this letter *b* then be explicitly stated? No, it need not be stated; for it is established through a conventional linguistic exception (*nipātana*).
What, then, is the purpose of this specific grammatical prescription (*nipātana*)? It is the rule: "The forms *bhuj* and *nyuj* [are used] in the senses of cooking and heating" (Pāṇini 7.3.61).

If that were so, would it not follow here as well—that is, in the case of *abhyudgaḥ* and *samudgaḥ*? There is no fault, for this is a specific prescription (*nipātana*) applicable where the substitution of *ku* does not occur.

39. *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ* (8.3.39). Since the preceding rule [8.3.38] would have prescribed *sakāra*, this rule prescribes *ṣakāra* as its exception. For example: *sarpistatra* (or *sarpiste*, according to the Kāśikā). This is by the rule *visarjanīyasya saḥ* (8.2.34).
That very [suffix] occurs.
From this point onward, if only the suffix *ṣa* follows and not *sa* as well,
then [the rules] such as *namaspurasorgatyoḥ* (8.3.40) and *ataḥ kṛkamikaṃsa* (8.3.46) apply.

The inclusion of the letter *s* must be made. Even if it were included, if the letter *ṣ* does not follow it, then that [confusion] would also occur. Now, if from this point onward only the letter *s* follows and not the letter *ṣ*, then [the rule] "of a non-suffixal [consonant] following *i*, *u*, or *ū*" [would apply].
In these rules— (8.3.41), ‘dvistriścaturiti kṛtvo'rthe’ (8.3.43), ‘isusoḥ sāmarthye’ (8.3.44), and ‘nityaṃ samāse'nutarapadasthasya’ (8.3.45)—
the letter *ṣ* must be included [in the technical name *śit*]. Even if that were done, if...

If the letter *sa* also follows [the rule], then that too would apply; would this confusion (*saṅkara*) not then result? To this he says: "The answer," and so forth. By this, the teaching regarding the production of the letters *sa* and *ṣa* is refuted. As for the fault of confusion that was pointed out—
He states its refutation as well, beginning with "In that case" (*tatra*). But how, when both [terms] continue to apply equally in what follows, is this distinction of scope obtained?
It is because they continue by way of the "frog-leap" maxim (*maṇḍūkaplutinyāya*).

40. *namas-purasoḥ gatyoh* | (8.3.40) The phrase "not at the beginning of a word" (*apadādau*) from [Pāṇini 8.3.38] is no longer applicable here. The word *namaḥ* is designated as a *gati* by the rule "and *sākṣāt* and so forth" (1.4.74), while the word *puraḥ* is designated as a *gati* by the rule "the indeclinable *puras*" (1.4.67).
By this [it is meant]:
"He makes a city (*pūḥ*), cities (*purau*), or cities (*puraḥ*). [The root] *pṛ* is used in the senses of protecting and filling (*pālanapūraṇayoḥ*, Dhātupāṭha 1086);
[the suffix] *kvip* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.177], *bhrājabhrās...* and so forth.
By the rule *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya* (7.1.102), there is the substitution of *u*; then *raparatva* [the replacement of *u* by *ru*]; then the addition of the nominative case endings (*svādayaḥ*);

then the elision of the final consonant and the preceding vowel (*halṅyādilopaḥ*, 6.1.68); and finally, by the rule *rṭhvorupadhāyā dīrghaḥ* (8.2.76), there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel in the singular number. In the forms *pūḥ* and *purau*, however, [lengthening does not occur] because they do not have the designation *agati*.

The substitution of *s* does not occur for the word *puras*; in its absence, there would be only the *visarjanīya*. On one alternative view, there would even be the *upadhmānīya*. In the case of *puraḥ karoti*, because it is designated as *agati*, the substitution of *s* does not occur; in its absence, there is only the *visarjanīya*, on that alternative view.
The same applies to the jihvāmūlīya [visarga]. However, for the word *namaḥ*, the counter-example should be understood as *namaḥ kṛtvā*;
it was not shown by the author of the Vṛtti because it is easily understood.

41. *idudupadhasya cāpratyayasya* (8.3.41). *it* and *ut* are *idut*. That which has *ik* (i.e., *it* or *ut*) as its penultimate (*upadhā*) is described as such. The examples beginning with *ni-dur-vahiḥ* are provided for the purpose of illustration; they are not an exhaustive enumeration.

Because there is no possibility of reversal [of the gender]. Regarding "he does for his mother," "he does for his father"—it will be explained how it does not occur in these cases. Regarding "desirous of a male" (*puṃskāmā*), "desirous of repeatedly" (*muhuḥkāmā*)—it will be explained here too how it does not occur. Regarding "a four-potherd [cake]" (*catuṣkapālam*), "four thorns" (*catuṣkaṣṭakam*).

A *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed with the word *catuḥ* and the words *kapāla* and *kaṇṭaka*; or, in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*), it is a *dvigu*. Because of the rule, "A *dvigu* whose final member ends in *a* is used in the feminine" (Vārttika 156), its feminine gender does not apply here; for [the list] beginning with *pātra*— [The text continues: ...is recited in the *Prātipadika-pāṭha* of the *Kāśikāvṛtti*, and thus the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is not added. Furthermore, since the word *catuṣka* is included among those ending in *ka*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is also excluded by the rule, "In the case of words ending in *ka*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is not applied" (Pāṇini 4.1.15). Therefore, the form remains neuter. Alternatively, one may interpret the word *catuṣka* as being derived from the *dvigu* *catur-ka* with the addition of the *kan* suffix according to the rule, "The *kan* suffix is added after a *dvigu* ending in *ka* or *kha*" (Pāṇini 5.1.23). In this case, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is likewise precluded by the rule, "The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is not applied after a word ending in *ka*" (Pāṇini 4.1.15). Thus, the neuter form is established. Or again, one may consider that the word *catuṣka* is derived from the *dvigu* *catur-ka* with the addition of the *aṇ* suffix according to the rule, "The *aṇ* suffix is added after a *dvigu* ending in *ka* or *kha*" (Pāṇini 5.1.24). Consequently, the neuter form is established. Consequently, the neuter form is established. Consequently, the neuter form is established. Consequently, the neuter form is established. Consequently, the neuter form is established. In this case, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is also precluded by the rule, "The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is not applied after a word ending in *ka*" (Pāṇini 4.1.15). Consequently, the neuter form is established. Alternatively, one may consider that the word *catuṣka* is derived from the *dvigu* *catur-ka* with the addition of the *aṇ* suffix according to the rule, "The *aṇ* suffix is added after a *dvigu* ending in *ka* or *kha*" (Pāṇini 5.1.24). Consequently, the neuter form is established.
