This is because of the statement [in the Vārttika]: "There is a prohibition" (Vārttika 159). The forms *mātuḥ karoti* and *pituḥ karoti* are considered non-standard (*deśya*). From the words *mātṛ* and *pitṛ*, the sixth case singular ending is applied; by the rule *ṛta ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.111), the single substitute *ut* occurs, followed by the substitution of *ra* for the final element (*raparatva*), and then by the rule *rātsasya* (8.2.24).

[In the case of] *salopaḥ*, there is a *visarjanīya* for the letter *r*. Since that [letter *r*] is not an affix (*apratyayatvāt*), this *visarjanīya* is not a *visarjanīya* belonging to an affix; therefore, the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣatva) would apply. Why does it not occur? To this he says: "In the *kaskādi* group," etc. This is the solution. And this is a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*)...

The term *nimitta* forms a *karmadhāraya* compound [with *ekādeśa*]. If the substitution of *ṣ* were to occur because of an *iṇ*-substitute that serves as the cause for the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*), then the word *bhrātuṣputra* would not have been included among the words listed in the *kaskādi* group;
for it would have been established by this very rule. Yet it has been included there, and this itself indicates that [the substitution does not occur] due to a cause that is a single-substitute.
"It does not become *ṣatva*.

Regarding "pummuhusāḥ" and so forth: the word *vaktavyaḥ* means that it should be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: in the subsequent sūtra (Pāṇini 8.3.42), the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* [applies] to both rules.
It should be understood as a residual rule (*śeṣabhūta*). That is a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*); therefore, it does not apply to the word *pum* followed by *muhur*.

However, for other [words], it will certainly apply always. The inclusion of the term *pum* was made by relying on the alternative view that substitutes *ru* [for *s*]. For, according to the alternative view that substitutes *s*, [the rule would apply].

Due to the absence of the *visarjanīya*, the *s* is substituted according to Pāṇini 8.3.34 (*pratiṣedha-sarjanīya*). However, it has already been explained previously how the *jihvāmūlīya* does not occur.
In the word *muhukāmā*, since the substitution of *ṣ* is prohibited, the *jihvāmūlīya* occurs in certain instances.

Regarding the term ‘muhuskāmā’, the letter *sakāra* (s) is recited. In this case, just as the absence of the *jihvāmūlīya* was previously established for the word *puṃskāmā*, it should be established here as well.
[The forms] ‘naiṣkusyam’ and ‘dauṣpurudhyam’ are derived by applying the suffix *ṣyañ* according to the rule for words beginning with *brāhmaṇa*.

Furthermore, when there is an increase [of syllables] caused by that [prolation], the status of having *i* or *u* as a penultimate (*idudupadhatva*) is lost, and thus the substitution of *ṣ* does not apply. Even in cases such as *niśṣkulam* and *duśṣpuruṣaḥ*, where prolation is prescribed by the rule *guroranṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.86),
that substitution likewise does not apply, because the status of having *i* or *u* as a penultimate is no longer present.

To one who might object to this, he says: "naiṣkulyam," and so forth. First, *vṛddhi* is external (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends on a *taddhita* suffix; the *taddhita* suffix is external because it depends on meanings such as "originating from" (*bhava*); therefore, the *vṛddhi* which is based upon that [suffix] is also external.

In this case, even though *pluta* is internal (*antaraṅga*) because it is prescribed for the entire sentence when the object [of the action] is far away, *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) is more internal than that, as it depends on fewer factors since it is prescribed for a single phoneme (*varṇa*) belonging to a word (*pada*). Therefore, while the internal *ṣatva* is to be performed...

Since the *vṛddhi* and *pluta* vowels are external (*bahiraṅga*) and thus considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the substitution of *ṣ* indeed takes place. [This portion of the commentary is not found in the Kāśikā manuscript; the inclusion of *t* as a marker (*taparakaraṇa*) is for the purpose of preventing the rule from applying in cases such as *āśīḥ karoti*, *goḥ karoti*, and *dhūḥ karoti*. [This portion of the commentary is]...
In the Kāśikā-Mañjūṣā reading, the mention of *dvi*, *tri*, and *catur* by means of the rule "idudupadhasya" and so forth is rejected.
For this [mention] is made for the following purpose: that the substitution of *ṣ* for the *visarjanīya* should occur only for *dvi* and the others.

[This is stated] so that [the rule] does not apply in a case such as *pañcakṛtvaḥ karoti*. Now, while the rule *idudupadhasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.41) is being carried over, when the visarga of a word that has the sense of the suffix *kṛtvasuc*— that is, a word whose domain is the sense of *kṛtvasuc*— is [concerned], then...

If it were qualified [by "beginning with *dvi*"], then it would not apply to anything else; for there is no possibility of another word beginning with *dvi*, etc., that has *i* or *u* as its penultimate letter (*idudupadha*) and functions in the sense of a kṛtvas-artha suffix. Therefore, even without the explicit mention of "beginning with *dvi*" and so on, the substitution of *ṣ* for the *visarjanīya* will occur only for those [words].
"One could have omitted [the mention of] *dvis*, *tris*, and *catur*.

Why does he state the substitution of *ṣ* in the sense of *kṛtvasuc*?"—in this rule prescribing the optional substitution of *ṣ*, he asks for the reason for the statement regarding the sense of *kṛtvas*. Why?
Having stated "in the sense of kṛtvas," why does he state this optional rule for ṣatva?

What is the purpose—that is, for what reason—does he include the mention of "in the sense of kṛtvas" here in this rule prescribing the optional ṣatva? The intention will be explained right hereafter. Therefore...

He states the reason: "In *catuṣkapāle*, etc. If the mention of the sense of the suffix *kṛtvas* were not present, the optional substitution of *ṣ* would apply even in *catuṣkapāla*, whereas it is prescribed as obligatory. Therefore, the term "in the sense of *kṛtvas*" is stated here so that the optional substitution of *ṣ* does not occur in this case.

In order to reveal the intention with which he asked the other, he says: "Is it not established there by the preceding rule? The word *nanu* is used in the sense of admission (*abhyupagame*). By this, he shows the following: let there be the optional (*vibhāṣā*) substitution of *ṣ* by this [present] rule; nevertheless, by the preceding rule, the substitution of *ṣ* will occur for this [word] invariably.
This is a reference [to a previous rule]; for even when *ṣatva* does not occur by this [present] rule,
*ṣatva* is nonetheless established in the case of *catuṣkapāla* by the preceding sūtra, namely, "idudupadhasya cāpratyayasya" (Pāṇini 8.3.41).
‘For this [rule] prescribes [the option] when [the other] is already established (*siddhe*); the meaning is ‘when [the rule] has already applied (*prāpte)*.

This explains: since the substitution of *ṣ* is obligatory by the rule “*idudupadhasya*” and so forth, this optional rule for the substitution of *ṣ* is prescribed; it does not apply when that [obligatory rule] has not yet applied, according to the maxim *yena nāprāpte*.

(Commentary on Pāṇini 5.4.17) "This [present rule] would be a sublater of that. By this, what was stated—namely, "In that case, it is established by the preceding [rule]"—is refuted. Therefore, the mention of *kṛtvas-artha* (the sense of "times") is for the purpose of excluding the optionality (*vibhāṣā*). This might be argued: when the suffix *suc* is applied with the intention of expressing the sense of *kṛtvas*.

When its *visarjanīya* is substituted, it does not apply with the preceding [rule], because of the prohibition in 8.3.41 (*na-pratyayasya*). Furthermore, as for the *tapara* marker, since it is established that "this [marker] is employed when the matter is already accomplished," its application is not justified; how then could the obligatory *ṣatva* be sublated by this optional rule?
Thus he says: "Even when [the word] *kṛtvas* is used," and so forth. The word *catuḥ* occurs—this is the ellipsis (*śeṣa*).
And this is connected with the present context by the rule: "For when [the form] is already established, they prescribe the substitution of *ṣ* for the *c* of *catur*.
Its meaning is as follows: what is being stated is that it is not only when...
When the word *catur* functions in the sense of *kṛtvas* (times), then, since [the substitution] would have been obtained by the preceding rule, this optional rule for *ṣatva* is prescribed;

that is to say, "but even when it has the sense of *kṛtvas*. He provides the justification for this very point with the words: "when the suffix expressing the sense of *kṛtvas* is elided," and so forth. The word *hi* (for/indeed) [indicates the reason].
In the sense of "cause" (*hetau*). That which has the meaning of *kṛtvas* is *kṛtvorthīya*. [The suffix] *ka* is added, and by virtue of belonging to the *gaha*-class, [the suffix] *cha* is applied.

Since the *kṛtvorthīya* suffix is elided by the rule *rātsasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.24), the *visarjanīya* occurs for the non-initial *repha*; therefore, even in the sense of *kṛtvas*, there would be obligatory *ṣatva* by the preceding rule.

This [rule] prescribes an option for the substitution of *ṣatva* (the change to *ṣ*). Consequently, since it is commenced even when *kṛtvas* (the sense of "times") is present and even when *kṛtvas* is absent—provided that *ṣatva* has not already been established by the preceding rule—it would necessarily be a sublater (*bādhaka*) of that [preceding rule]. And thus, if the mention of *kṛtvo'rtha* were not made, [this difficulty would arise].

In the case of *catuṣkapāla*, the substitution of *ṣ* would undesirably apply; therefore, it is established that the mention of the sense of *kṛtvas* (times) is for the purpose of excluding that [substitution].
As for the words “*evam*” and so forth: if the mention of the sense of *kṛtvas* is made, then in that case...
If [the word] "being" (*sati*) is already present, what is now the purpose of [repeating] "twice, thrice, four times"? Nothing at all;

for there is nothing to be excluded (*vyāvartya*). Therefore, the intended meaning is simply that this [repetition] should not be performed. [The variant reading *meda* (non-difference) is the Prācīna-mudra-pāṭha.]

It might be argued: "If this [rule] were not present, then even in cases such as *pañcakṛtvaḥ karoti*, there would be optional (*vibhāṣā*) ṣatva; therefore, its exclusion is effected by this [rule]. To this, he says: "For another... and so forth. The term *idudupadhasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.41) is understood to carry over, as is *kṛtvo'rthe*.
It is stated [in the rule], yet there is no word other than *dvis* and so forth that has *i* or *u* as its penultimate vowel (*idudupadha*) when used in the sense of "times" (*kṛtvas-artha*).
Therefore, by virtue of this semantic competency (*sāmarthya*), the suffix will apply only to these [words] and not to others; thus, the mention of *dvis* and so forth is redundant.

By the words "akriyamāṇe" and so forth, he demonstrates the fault that would arise if the mention of "twice" (*dvi*) and so on were not made. If the mention of "twice" and so on were not performed, then, because the *visarjanīya* is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*), it alone would be qualified by the term "in the sense of kṛtvas"— that is, [the rule would apply to] the *visarjanīya* which occurs in the sense of kṛtvas.
"It occurs as *visarjanīya*. But what fault would there be in that case? To this he says:

"The word *caturaḥ* is not established. [He explains further with] "In the same way (*tathā*). That is to say, if *visarjanīya* were thus qualified by the inclusion of the sense of the suffix *kṛtvas*, then the optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) for the word *catuḥ* would not apply.
The substitution of *ṣ* is not established. For what reason is it not established? To this he says:

"of the *repha*," and so forth. The word *hi* indicates a reason; because, when the *s* of *suc* is elided by the rule *rātsasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.24), the *visarjanīya* replaces the *repha* which is a constituent part of the base (*prakṛti*), therefore [the substitution of *ṣ*] is not established.
For that *visarjanīya* does not occur in the sense of "times" (*kṛtvas-artha*).
Now, even if that [suffix] were applied, why would the fault not still arise?
To this he says: "Therefore," and so forth. In that...

In this case, when *dvir*, *tris*, or *catur* are employed, it is logical that the inclusion of the term *kṛtvas* serves as an adjective qualifying the word *catuḥ*. For indeed, because that [word *catuḥ*] is what is directly heard (*śruta*), it alone is qualified:
namely, the word *catuḥ* which functions in the sense of *kṛtvas*. This remains true even when [the suffix *kṛtvasuc*] is elided.

In the case of the word *catur* [in the rule] "kṛtvo'rthīye," since the word *catur* occurs in the sense of a kṛtvas-artha suffix, there would be no fault even if the inclusion of *dvi-* and so forth were not made. Therefore, the inclusion of *dvi-* and so forth must be made so that the mention of "kṛtvo'rtha" may serve as its qualifier. This too is not [correct].
Showing that there is a purpose for this, he says: "The word under discussion ends with that.
"Ending with that" means ending with the *visarjanīya*. Therefore, it is logical that this [word] should also be qualified by that;
he provides the justification: "The fact that the word ends with that is obtained because it is qualified by the *visarjanīya*."
The word *api* is used for emphasis; the meaning is "of that very [word]. Why is this so? Because of the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
For if *visarjanīya* were the thing being qualified, the rule would not apply to the four [cases];
but when *pada* is the thing being qualified, it applies everywhere. Therefore, it is that very [word] [which is qualified].

We shall qualify it by stating: "that word which occurs in the sense of 'times' (kṛtvas). When the word is thus qualified, the substitution of *ṣ* for *c* is indeed established even when the suffix expressing the sense of "times" has been elided; for this very word *catuḥ* still occurs in the sense of "times. Therefore, there is no purpose in the mention of "twice" (*dvis*) and so forth.
The author of the Ślokavārttika rejected the inclusion of the term "twice" (*dvi*) and so forth.

However, the intention of the author of the Sūtras is as follows: because the *visarjanīya* is the subject of the operation (*kāryin*) and is qualified by the word "pada," it possesses primacy. In that case, if the inclusion of "twice" and so forth were absent—

Because of its predominance, it is the *visarjanīya* itself that is qualified by the mention of the sense of the suffix *kṛtvas*; however, since that [suffix] exists, by virtue of the capacity of its inclusion and because it is directly heard (*sākṣāt kṣutatvāt*), this qualification applies only to the word beginning with *dvis* and so on, and not to the *visarjanīya* which is merely inferred from its *svarita* accent.
Therefore, it is appropriate to include the mention of "twice" and so forth.

With the passage beginning with "But thus," the author establishes the inclusion of the words "twice," "thrice," and "four times" according to the opinion of the Sūtrakāra. The phrase "by the preceding [rule]" refers to the rule beginning with *idudupadhasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.41).
He says: "In the case of what is not established previously," and so forth. What is the reason that [the rule] does not exist? To this he says: "Because of the absence of the subsequent [element]."

44. *isusoḥ sāmarthye* | (8.3.44) This [rule] applies when *isi* and *usu* follow [a word] that has the capacity [to connect with another]. This is because the rules *aciṃśucihusṛyicchādicchﬁadibhya isiḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 9.30) and *janerusiḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 9.37) are understood to be in force, and [the suffixes are added] after the roots *at*, *pṛ*, *vapi*, *yaj*, *tan*, *dhā*, and *tap*.

This is the view that words such as *sapiṃḥ*, *yajus*, and others are derived from roots like *nit* (Dhātupāṭha 9.39) with the suffixes *is* and *us*; and consequently, when the substitution of *ṣ* has not yet occurred,
and the *jihvāmūlīya* and other substitutions have been triggered by rules such as *kupvoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.37), this [rule applies].

[This is] the statement. Now, there is the view that "the words *atha* and so forth are underived nominal stems" (*pu.pa.vṛ*. 70). Consequently, since [the visarga] is not a *visarjanīya* resulting from an affix, the rule "of a [consonant] preceded by *i*, *u*, or *ū*, provided it is not part of an affix" (*8.3.41*) would necessitate the obligatory substitution of *ṣ*. This [present sūtra] is commenced [to prevent that]. [It applies when there is] semantic connection (*sāmarthye*).

Regarding the word "sati": because *k* and *p* are adopted as the cause [of the grammatical operation], it should be understood that the semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) exists only with another word that begins with that [element]. In the example *sarpiṣkaroti*, [the word *sarpiḥ*] depends upon an action to be accomplished (*sādhyā kriyā*), namely, "he performs an action for which clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) is the instrument (*sādhana*)."
The meaning of "he does" (*karoti*) is also something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). There is the capacity [of the word] "clarified butter" (*sarpiḥ*) to function as the means (*sādhana*), as in:
"Let the clarified butter remain; you drink water. Here, in the word "clarified butter," [the connection] is with the word "drink" (*piba*).
There is no such capacity. For instance, the word *piba* (drink) requires [the object] *udakam* (water), whereas *sarpiḥ* (ghee) requires *tiṣṭhatu* (let it stay).
Now, why does the optional substitution of *ṣ* (*vibhāṣā ṣatvam*) not occur in the compound *paramasarpiḥkuṇḍikā*?

Thus he says: "The capacity here," and so forth. The particle *api* functions in the sense of "also," since indeclinables possess multiple meanings. The phrase "not, however" (*na punaḥ*) is connected both with the expression "single unified meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) and with the word "both" (*ubhaya*). Furthermore, a restrictive emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) is to be understood here.

Because all sentences have exclusion as their result. Therefore, this is the meaning here: only mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) is accepted as "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) in this context; however, how could it not be appropriate to accept both? For general terms do not settle upon specific meanings without [the aid of] context and so forth, and that is not the case here.

Is there some such context or other factor by which competency (*sāmarthya*) characterized solely by mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) must be accepted? This is not a fault; for according to the principle "technical names and paribhāṣās [apply] at the time of their operation" (*kāryakālaṃ saṃjñāparibhāṣam*), the term "of a word" (*padasya*) is understood here, and that is because of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning "word" (*pada*).

Since the technical rule (paribhāṣā) regarding semantic competency (samartha) is present, semantic competency is already established; therefore, the purpose of explicitly mentioning "semantic competency" here is so that there may be the inclusion of the specific competency intended [by the author]. And in this context, the intended semantic competency is precisely that characterized by mutual expectancy (vyapekṣā); thus, it is that very one which is to be relied upon.
This is correct: there is neither a unification of meaning, nor both.

45. *nityaṃ samāse 'nutarapadasthasya* | (8.3.45) [The substitution of *ṣ* for *s*] occurs invariably in a compound when the word containing the *s* does not stand as the final member (*uttarapada*). For example: *sapiṣkuṇḍikā*. This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Similarly, it applies in cases such as *dhanuṣkapāla*, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase *paramam apiḥ kuṇḍikā*: having formed a *karmadhāraya* compound of the words *parama* and *sarpiḥ* by means of [Pāṇini 2.1.61] *sanmahatparamottamotkṛṣṭāḥ pūjyamānaiḥ*, a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound is then formed with the word *kuṇḍikā*. Here, in relation to the word *parama*, the word *sarpiḥ* is the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), and the visarga residing therein [is the subject of the rule].
The substitution of *ṣ* does not occur.

But is it not the case that in the rule *isusoḥ sāmarthye* (Pāṇini 8.3.44), the mention of *isusoḥ* constitutes a reference to the suffixes (*pratyaya-grahaṇa*), and in such a reference, [the principle applies] "from whatever [stem] that suffix is ordained"?

According to the rule "of that which begins with what is prescribed and ends with it" (*bho.pu.sū. 7*), since *i* and *su* are prescribed only after [the base] *yad*, the reference must be only to that which begins with it, and not to anything additional; furthermore, the word *parama* is additional, for the suffix *iṣṭhan* is prescribed after the simple base *sap-* alone, and not after *parama-sap-* and so forth.

And thus, since there is no such thing as an original form (*prakṛti*) for the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), what is the point of this restriction? To this he says: "This very [point]," and so forth. If this were a fixed rule here, the phrase "of that which stands not in a subsequent member" would not have been stated;
yet it has been stated. Therefore, this makes it known: that this is not a fixed rule here.

What is the purpose of this indicator (*jñāpaka*)? He says: "By that," and so forth. Because this restriction (*niyama*) does not apply here, for that reason, even when an additional element is included within a compound word (*vākya*), as in *paramasarpiḥ karoti* and *paramasarpiṣkaroti*, [the rule] applies by means of the preceding sūtra.

There would be an option regarding the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*]; however, if there were a restrictive rule (*niyama*), this would not occur. [Objection: In that case, even in a compound such as *paramasarpiḥkuṇḍikā*, there ought to be an option for the substitution of *ṣ* because of the absence of a restrictive rule? To this he says: "And there is mutual expectancy in that case," and so forth.

The particle *ca* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). The particle *iti* indicates the reason (*hetu*). In that regard, because the term "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) is understood in rules such as *isusoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.44), it is precisely syntactic expectancy (*vyapekṣā*)—and not the capacity consisting in co-occurrence—that is adopted as the cause for the optional application of the rule. Therefore, [the suffix] does not apply in a compound (*samāsa*), because that [expectancy] is absent there.

46. *ataḥ kṛkami-kaṃsa-kumbha-pātra-kuśā-karṇīṣv-anavyayasya* (8.3.46). This rule is stated because the application of *kupvoḥ ka pau ca* (8.3.37) would otherwise have occurred. For example, in *ayaskāraḥ*, [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied by *karmaṇyaṇ* (3.2.1). The same applies to *ayaskāmaḥ*.

The rule "the suffix *ṇa* should be prescribed after the roots *śīl*, *kāmi*, *bhikṣ*, and *ācari*" (Vārttika 229) does not apply here. This is because in that supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*), the root *kam* is cited with the suffix *ṇic* added (*kāmayati*), whereas here it is cited without that suffix (*kāma*).

Furthermore, when the suffix *ṇiṅ* is applied to *kam* by the rule "the suffixes *āya* and others are optionally used before *ārdhadhātuka* affixes" (Pāṇini 3.1.31), [the form *kāmayitum icchati* arises].

If [the root] does not exist, then there is no causative (*ṇyanta*) form of *kama*. The term "ayaskaṃsaḥ" is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). But surely, by adding the suffix *sa* according to the rule "from *vṛ*, *tṛ*, *vad*, *han*, *kami*, and *kaṣi*, the suffix *sa* occurs" (Daiva Uṇādi Sūtra 9.29), the word *kaṃsa* is formed; since it is thus established by the mention of *kami* alone [in that rule], why is it mentioned here?

Is the mention of *kaṃsa* purposeless? No; it is for the sake of providing information. By this, the following view is made known: "The *uṇādi* suffixes produce unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*) items that are not *pratipadika*s," as in the case of *ayaskumbhaḥ*. [In this word], *ayas-*...

In the expression *vikāraḥ kumbhaḥ* ("a jar that is a modification"), there is a compound with elision of the middle term (*madhyapadalopin*), according to the Vārttika: "In the section on compounds with a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*), there is an addition for *śākapārthiva* and similar cases, and there is elision of the subsequent member. Alternatively, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). [Thus we have] *ayaṃ kumbhī*.
The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied because the word belongs to the *gaura*-class. The compound is like *ayaskumbha*.

Regarding the form *ayaspātrī*: the word *pātra* ends in the suffix *ṣṭran*, and the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added by the rule *ṣidgaurādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.41). Regarding *ayaskuśā*: here, the letter *i* in *ayas* is not intended to be significant.

By that rule, *tena jānapadāvisūtreṇa* (Pāṇini 4.1.42), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied, resulting in *ayaskuśā*. Here, the letter *i* in *ayas* is not intended to be significant; therefore, by that rule *tena jānapadādisūtreṇa* (4.1.42), the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply. [In the case of] *ayaskarṇī*, meaning "one whose ears are like iron," [the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] by the rule *nāsikodara* (4.1.55).

By the phrase beginning with "ityādinā," there is the inclusion of the word *karṇa* ending in the vowel *ī*. Consequently, someone might have the misconception that in the form *śunaḥkarṇa*, the substitution of *t* for *n* must occur; in order to refute this, he says: "But this *śunaskarṇa*," and so forth.

Regarding the term *bhāḥkaraṇam*: this is a compound formed with a word ending in the suffix *lyuṭ*. If, then, the addition of the marker *t* (*taparakaraṇa*) were not made, would the form *bhāskara* also occur here—where *ṭa* is applied by the rule *bhāṣā-karoti* (Pāṇini 3.2.21)? To this he says: "But as for this *bhāskara*," and so forth. This is easy to understand.

47. *adhaḥśirasī pade* | (8.3.47) Regarding *adhaḥśirasaḥ*: by means of a transposition of case endings (*subvyatyaya*), the nominative stands in place of the genitive. "When the word *pada* follows" indicates that the actual form of the word *pada* is what is being referred to here; it is not [the technical grammatical term].

He shows that this refers to the technical (pāribhāṣika) [term]. For if there were a reference to the technical term, the mention of the word "pada" (padagrahaṇa) would be purposeless; the intention is that its status as such is already obtained from the governing rule (adhikāra) concerning compounds (samāsa). The example given is “śiraspadam,” which is a genitive compound (ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa).

48. *kaskādiṣu ca* (8.3.48). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the rule] *kutvoḥ* (8.3.37). Regarding the phrase "according to the application" (*yathāyogam*): for a visarga that follows the vowel *i*, there is the substitution of *ṣ*; however, for any other [visarga], there is the substitution of *s*. This is the meaning.

The meaning of *yathāyogārtha* is as in the case of *kaskaḥ*. When *su* follows, there is the substitution of *ka-* for *kim* by the rule *kimaḥ kaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.103), and there is reduplication due to the desire for emphasis (*dīpsā*). In the case of *kautaskutaḥ*, the suffix *tasil* is applied by the rule *pañcamyāstasil* (5.3.7), and in place of *kim*, [the substitute *ku-]* is applied by the rule *ku tihoḥ* (7.2.104).

The state of being a *kubhrātṛ* (a bad brother); as before, there is a reduplication. When the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to *tata āgataḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.74), the *ṭi*-portion is elided by the rule *avyayānāṃ bhamātre* (Vārttika 842). Thus we have *bhrātuṣputraḥ*.
When this is a compound (*samāsa*), the genitive case [ending] is replaced by *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*) according to *ṛto vidyāyonisambandhebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.23).

The *aluk* [non-elision] occurs in "śvaskarṇaḥ" by virtue of the rule "ṣṭhaḷa ākrośe" (Pāṇini 6.3.21), which applies when it is a name (*saṃjñā*) and denotes a reproach. However, when it is not a name, in a compound it becomes simply "śvakarṇa.
Now, one might object that for words such as "sarpiṣkuṇḍika," there is the rule "nityaṃ samāse 'nutarapadasthasya" (Pāṇini 8.3.45).

Thus, the letter *ṣa* is established; for what purpose, then, is there the recitation of these [letters] here? To this he says: "of these," and so forth. Those who sport with the *pārāyaṇa* are called *pārāyaṇikas*.
[The suffix] *iKa* is applied by the rule "tena dīvyati" (Pāṇini 4.4.2). [This is according to the principle] "in the sense of being about to be or occurring."

What is the purpose of the phrase "of one who stands on the unsurpassed word" (*anuttarapadasthasya*)? It is to show that the examples *paramasarpiḥkuṇḍikā* cited in the Bhāṣya and the Vṛtti are not intended by these [authors] to be included here. By the words "not having its formation prescribed by a rule" (*avihitalakṣaṇaḥ*), etc., he declares that the *kaskādi* group is an *ākṛtigaṇa*.
The particle *ca* (and), serving the purpose of collecting what has not been explicitly mentioned, indicates this meaning:
the technical designation "upacāra" is prescribed for the letter *s* and the letter *ṣ* when they occupy the position of a *visarjanīya*.

49. *cchandasi vā'prāmreḍitayoḥ* (8.3.49). In the case of the genitive compound *ayaspātram*, when the suffix *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) would have been obligatory by rule 8.3.46 (*ataḥ kṛkamikaṃsa...*), this sūtra prescribes an option. The same applies to *viśvataspātram*.

Even in cases such as these, if there were a compound (*samāsa*), then [the rule] would apply. However, in the case of *uruṇaskāraḥ*, since it is not a compound, the rule does not apply; for the word *nas* is substituted for the word *asmad* following the word *uru* by the rule *bahuvacanasya vasnasau* (Pāṇini 8.1.21), and furthermore, [by the rule] *naśca*...
The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule "dhātusthoruṣubhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.27).
Now, one might ask: why does this not occur here in cases such as "harikeśaḥ purastāt" (Atharvaveda 10.139.1) and "sa naḥ pāvaka" (Ṛgveda 1.12.10)? To this he says: "harikeśa."
And so forth.

50. *kaḥ karat karatikṛdhikṛteṣvanaditeḥ* | (8.3.50) The word *vā* is no longer in force. Regarding *karat*: this is the *luṅ* [aorist] of the root *kṛ*, with the *cli* suffix; its elision occurs by the rule *madatre ghasa* (2.4.82) et al.; then there is the *tip* suffix, *guṇa* substitution, and the replacement of the vowel *ṛ* by *ra*.

By the rule *halṅyābhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), there is elision of the suffix; the *repha* becomes a *visarjanīya*; and by the rule *bahulaṃ cchandasyāmāṅyoge’pi* (6.4.75), there is an absence of the augment *aṭ*. Regarding the form *karat*:
it is the *laṅ* [aorist] of the root *kṛ*, with the suffix *aṅ* by the rule *kṛmṛdṛruhibhyaścchandasi* (3.1.51), and the substitution of *ai* for *ṛ* by the rule *ṛdṛśoraiṅ*.

By the rule "guṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.16), there is *guṇa* substitution; as before, there is no insertion of the augment *aṭ*. Alternatively, there is the substitution of *śatṛ* for the present tense marker (*laṭ*), with *śap* by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). Regarding "karati": this is *laṭ*, the suffix *tip*, and *śap* as before. Regarding "kṛdhi": this is the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *kṛ*, [with the suffix *sip*] by the rule "serhyapicca" (Pāṇini 3.4.87).

The substitution of *s* for *si* is applied; for that [root], there is the change to *dhi* by the rule *śru-śṛṇu-pṛ-kṛ-vṛ-bhyaś-chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.4.102), and the elision of the suffix (*vikaraṇa-luk*) occurs by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (2.4.73). The word *kṛtam* ends in the *niṣṭhā* suffix. The form *viśvataskaḥ* is derived from the fifth case ending with the suffix *tasil* (Pāṇini 5.3.7).

In *uruṇaskṛdhi*, the substitution of *nas* for *nas* and the change to *ṇ* occur as before. In *sadaskṛtam*, the compound is formed by the rule *saptamī* (Pāṇini 2.1.40) through a split in the application (*yogavibhāga*), meaning "that which was made in the assembly" (*sadasi kṛtam*).
51. [The fifth case-affix (*pañcamī*) is used] after the word *pari* when it has the sense of "excluding" (*avadhi*) or "with reference to" (*adhyartha*).

(Pāṇini 2.3.10). Regarding the term "with reference to" (*adhyartha*): this is a qualifier of *pari*. In the example "around the Himalayas" (*himavataḥ pari*), the meaning is "on top of the Himalayas. Furthermore, the fifth case-affix (*pañcamī*) occurs here by means of a substitution (*vibhaktivyatyaya*) in place of the sixth case-affix (*ṣaṣṭhī*).
It should be understood as follows:
“from heaven and from earth,” and so forth. Here, the word *pari* functions in the sense of totality (*sarvatobhāva*).
52. *pātau ca bahulam* (8.3.52). As in *divaspātu*. This is the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *pāti*, with the suffix *tip*; by rule 3.4.86, *eruḥ*, the *u*-substitution occurs;
and because the root belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* augment.

53. [The sixth case ending is used] before *pati*, *putra*, *pṛṣṭha*, *pāra*, *pada*, *payas*, and *poṣa*. (8.3.53) Regarding "vācaspatim": because of the word *bahulam* in the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam* (6.3.14), there is the elision (*luk*) of the *kṛt*-suffix even when it is not a *kṛt*-suffix.

54. Or after *iḍā*. (8.3.54) This statement is for the purpose of providing an option (*vikalpa*), since the preceding [rule] would have made the substitution obligatory. If this is so, then the word *vā* ("or") is redundant; for by the very force of its commencement (*ārambha-sāmarthya*), this rule will be understood as optional.

This is not so; for if the word "optionally" (vā) were not used, the preceding rule would be understood as being "frequently applicable" (bahulam), because the term "frequently applicable" is the subject under discussion here. However, since the word "optionally" is used here, the preceding rule would be understood as being mandatory (nitya); thus, it is not meaningless.

55. *apadāntasya mūrdhanyaḥ* | (8.3.55) That which occurs at the head (*mūrdhan*) is called *mūrdhanya*—[derived] by [the rule] *śarīrāvayavād yat* (4.3.55); the preservation of the original stem form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is by [the rule] *ye cābhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (6.4.168). For example: *siṣeca*.

From the roots *ṣic* in the sense of "flowing" (*dhā.pā.* 1434) and *ṣvap* in the sense of "sleeping" (*dhā.pā.* 1068), the substitution of *s* for *ṣ* occurs by the rule *dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.64). Then, the suffixes *liṭ*, *tip*, and *ṇal* are applied. For the root *svap*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the reduplicated syllable according to the rule *liṭaḷbhyāsasyobhayeṣām* (Pāṇini 6.1.17).

Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of *śū* (*ś* and *ū*) in the rule? Why not simply say *ṣ*? For even if *ṣ* were used, forms such as *siṣeca* would be established, and the rule would be more concise. To this he replies: "Even though [the result] would be established by saying simply *ṣ*... If only *ṣ* were stated, then in forms such as *akṛḍhavam* and *cakṛḍhave*, [the substitution of ṣatva would undesirably apply].

Would the substitution of *ṣ* not apply by the rule "iṇaḥ ṣīdhvaṃ luṅliṭāṃ dho’ṅgāt" (Pāṇini 8.3.78)? However, the substitution of *ḍh* is desired, and that is indeed accomplished when there is the mention of the "retroflex" (*mūrdhanya*) sound; for in this case, by the principle of closest similarity (*antaratamya*), it is the *gh* sound—possessing voiced aspiration (*mahāprāṇa*) and having a nasalized resonance (*anunāsika*)—that [is substituted].

Such is the letter *ḍha*. However, if the mention of *ḍha* were made in the rule *iṇaḥ ṣīdhvam*, then it would have been possible to omit the mention of the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) in this present rule. Thus, the mention of *ḍha* has not been made for the sake of variety. [Objection: But surely, by making the mention of *ḍha*...
Because the letter *ṣ* is [already] separated [from the preceding rule], the mention of *ṣ* would have to be repeated in the subsequent rules.
Let it be repeated; nevertheless, because of the mention of *mūrdhanya*, there is simplicity in taking it as its own form (*svarūpa*).
For in the case of taking it as its own form, there are six morae (*mātrā*): when "ṣ" is stated here, it takes two morae.

When "ḍha" is mentioned in the subsequent sūtra, two [instances] are meant; when "ṣa" is mentioned further on, two are meant. All of these added together amount to six mātrās. If there were the inclusion of the retroflex (mūrdhan) [ṣ], there would be seven. Therefore, there is brevity when the phoneme itself (svarūpa) is included. However, even if the letters ṣa and ḍha exist...

Even though it is the original form (*prakṛti*), since the letter *ṣ* is marked with a svarita accent, it is inferred that this [svarita] continues to apply; thus, when there is a literal apprehension of the form itself, there is even greater ease. Regarding "akṛḍhvam": there is the elision of *sic* by the rule "after a short vowel, from an *aṅga*" (8.2.27).

Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the term "of a word" (*apadasya*)? If it were stated simply as "the retroflex [substitute] occurs for a *s*," it would be understood as applying to that *s* which belongs to a non-word (*apada*). Consequently, it would not apply in cases such as *kariṣyati*, because the *s* there belongs to a word (*pada*). Where, then, would it apply? It would apply in cases such as *kariṣyate*, where [the *s* is not part of a complete word].
The designation *pada* does not exist [here]. For in this case, the designation *bha* would subvert the designation *pada*. Therefore, the mention of "the end" (*anta*) is made.

56. *saheḥ sāḍaḥ saḥ* (8.3.56). Regarding the phrase *sāḍ-ādeśasya*: the meaning is "of that which has undergone the substitution of *sāḍ*. For example, *jalāṣāṭ*. [This is derived] from the sense "one who endures water" (*jalaṃ sahate*). While the rule *bhajo ṇviḥ* (3.2.62) is still in force, [the suffix] *ṇvi* is applied by the rule *chandasi sahaḥ* (3.2.63). [The form *jalāṣāṭ* is thus established.]
By [Pāṇini 3.2.63], the suffix *ṇvi* is applied; by [Pāṇini 7.2.116], there is *vṛddhi* strengthening of the vowel in the penultimate position; by [Pāṇini 8.2.31], the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha*;
its replacement by the *jaś*-sound, namely *ḍa*;
and by [Pāṇini 6.3.137], there is lengthening of the vowel. This occurs because, among the sibilants (*uṣman*), the voiced sibilant is the most similar [to the original *ha*].

The letter *ṣa* is exactly like that. Regarding the rule “*saha ḍena*,” etc.: from the root *ḍīṅ*, while the rule “*saptamyāṃ janer ḍaḥ*” (Pāṇini 3.2.97) is being carried over, the suffix *ḍa* is applied by the rule “*anyeṣv api dṛśyate*” (3.2.101);
this is because the word *api* in that rule signifies the disregard of all restrictive conditions (*sarvopādhivyabhicāra*). Thus, [the word *saḍa*] means “that which exists together with *ḍa*.”

The term *sahita* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to Pāṇini 2.2.28 (*tena saheti tulyayoge*). By Pāṇini 6.3.82 (*vopasarjanasya*), the word *saha* undergoes the substitution of *sa*. In the formation of *sāḍi*—meaning "the descendant of Saḍa"—the suffix *iñ* is applied by Pāṇini 4.1.95 (*ata iñ*), and the vowel *a* is elided by Pāṇini 6.4.148 (*yasyeti ca*), after which the initial *vṛddhi* strengthening is applied.

If it were argued that the form *sāḍi* arises [only] when *saheḥ* is present—otherwise, the retroflex substitution would apply—and that this form *sāḍi* does not exist because the substitute *ā* (from *āṅ*) is treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) by the rule *acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau* (Pāṇini 1.1.57), we say: no; for [the rule] *pūrvatrāsiddhe na*...
Because of the prohibition of the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivat*) by the rule *sthānivat* (Jainendra-vṛtti 48).

But even so, does this form *sāṭ* not exist here at all? Because when the substitution of *ṣ* is to be applied, the external *vṛddhi* [vowel lengthening] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). If that is the case, then it does not exist here either.

It might be asked: "What about *jalāṣāḍ*? [The answer is: precisely because the external (*bahiraṅga*) *vṛddhi* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when the substitution of *ṣ* is to be applied; for that *vṛddhi* occurs by depending upon the *aṅga*, and the designation *aṅga* exists only when there is an affix (*pratyaya*), since the affix itself depends on an *upapada*. Thus, it is clear that the *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is external.

Since the substitution of *ṣ* is internal (*antaraṅga*)—being prescribed for that which has already become a complete word (*sāṅbhūtasya*)—it would not occur due to the rule "what is external is as if non-existent with respect to what is internal" (*asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam antaraṅge*). Therefore, this statement [of yours] would be purposeless. Consequently, let there be no such statement.

The maxim "uselessness" (vaiyarthyam) does not apply here. In the word *turāsāham*, this is the second person singular ending. In some places, the reading is *jalāsāham*, but that is incorrect, because the substitution of *ṣ* is intended here. And so he will state later (8.3.108): [the rule for the substitution of *ṣ*].

"The mention of *aśva-* [in the rule] is for the purpose of indicating that the substitution of *ṣ* occurs even for a non-nasal (*aniṇaḥ*) following the root *san* and others. By this, forms such as *jalāṣāham* and *aśvaṣāham* are established.
[Question: "What is the purpose of the word *saḥ*? [Answer: He thinks thus: by the paribhāṣā regarding the final letter (Pāṇini 1.1.52), [the substitute would apply] to the final [letter].

In that case, it would have to be the letter *ḍa*; since it occurs at the end, by the principle of proximity (*āntaratamya*), it would be *ḍa*, but this is incorrect, because there is no purpose in prescribing *ḍa* for the letter *ḍa*.
Therefore, even without the inclusion of the term "sa," it will apply to the letter *sa* alone. The other [interpretation], however, is "sa."

If this were not the case, then by the rule "in the absence of a final modification, [the substitute] is like that which stands in the vicinity of the final" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 63), the vowel *ṛ*—which is retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) and possesses two morae (*dvimātrika*)—would arise for the vowel *ā* due to its closest similarity (*āntaratamya*).
With this intention, he says: "Let it not be so for the vowel *ā*."
57. *iṇkoḥ* | (8.3.57) The term *iṇkoḥ* is expressed in the singular by treating the *dvandva* compound as a single unit (*ekavadbhāva*).
As for the augment *num*, even though [the stem] is neuter, it is applied because "the teaching regarding augments is not always obligatory" (*anityam āgamaśāsanam*).

Thus it is not done. The term *iṇ* refers to a pratyāhāra (abbreviated designation) by means of the subsequent *ṇakāra*. *Ku* refers to the *kavarga* (the guttural class). Why is it determined that these two [terms] are what are being referred to, and not the vowels *ik*, *ak*, and *uk*? From the explanation (*vyākhyāna*).

In all cases of doubt, this principle applies: "For a specific understanding arises from an explanation; indeed, there is no lack of definition because of doubt" (Vyāḍipañjikā 75). [As in the examples] *vākṣu*, *tvakṣu*; here, by the rule *coḥ kuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.30), the substitution of *k* occurs.

‘He will give. But how is this counter-example justified, given that in the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.69), the vowel *ā* is included by the letter *ha* when it is being grasped; for indeed, there exists a state of being a homogeneous sound (*savarṇatva*) between *a* and *ha*?

Because their place of articulation and effort are equal; for these two have an identical place of articulation, as it is said: "The letters *a*, *ku*, *ha*, and the visarga are gutturals. Their effort is also equal—namely, that the organs are wide open (*vivṛta*) for both the sibilants (*ūṣman*) and the vowels; therefore, even though there is the rule regarding the letter *i* (*iṇkoḥ*).

The *mūrdhanya* [substitute] indeed occurs; for in the rule *nājjhalau* (Pāṇini 1.1.10), the vowel *ā* is included by the inclusion of the letter *ha*. This is because there is *savarṇatva* (homogeneity) between *a* and *ha*, since they possess the same place and effort of articulation (*sthāna* and *prayatna*). For these two indeed have an identical place of articulation.

"‘The vowels *a*, *ku* [the velar stops], and the *visarjanīya* are gutturals (*kaṇṭhya*); thus, their effort (*prayatna*) is also identical—namely, the organs (*karaṇa*) are wide-open (*vivṛta*) for both the sibilants (*ūṣman*) and the vowels. Therefore, even though the condition *iṇkoḥ* exists, a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) substitution would indeed result; [this is prevented] by the rule *nājjhalau* (Pāṇini 1.1.10)."

If it is argued that this is because of the prohibition of the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous), we say no; for there is a prohibition regarding those [vowels] whose *savarṇa* status has not been grasped.
This is not a fault, since [the author] states: "In the sense of 'companions,' [the suffix] *matup* is used after the word *mūrdhan*" (Pāṇini 4.4.127).

Since he provides this indication here without applying the cerebralization (*mūrdhanya*) to the *s* following the vowel *a*, it is understood from that— just as in the rule *mūrdhno matup* (Pāṇini 5.2.127)—
that he provides the indication without applying the cerebralization to the *s* following the vowel *a*; therefore, [it follows that] the letter *ha*...
When being perceived, [the word] does not cause its own form to be grasped; otherwise, he would not have made the designation "avayasyāsu.
Regarding the form "asau": by the rule *tadoḥ saḥ sāvanantyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.106), the letter *d* is replaced by *s*;
and by the rule *adasa āṬ sulopaśca* (Pāṇini 7.2.107), the replacement *au* (*āṬ*) occurs.
And there is the elision of the suffix *su*.

58. *num-visarjanīya-śar-vyavāye 'pi*. (8.3.58) Because of the mention of the ablative case (*pañcamī-nirdeśa*) in the rule *iṇkoḥ*, the term *nirdiṣṭa* (as mentioned) is intended to mean "immediate proximity" (*ānantarya*). Therefore, when there is an intervention (*vyavāya*), the [substitution] would not apply by the preceding rule; hence this [sūtra] is commenced. It concerns the substitution [of *ṣ*] for the following *s* after *iṇ* or *ku*.

It becomes the head (mūrdhanya). The same applies when there is an intervention by *num*, an intervention by a letter subject to elision (*visarjanīya*), and an intervention by a sibilant (*śar*). The word "also" (*api*) is connected with each of these; thus, three distinct statements are formed. We shall demonstrate the purpose of these three statements, beginning with the mention of *num*.

The *anusvāra* that occurs in place of *num* should be understood as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). For there is no intervention whatsoever by *num*, since the rule for *anusvāra*—namely, *naścāpadāntasya jhali* (Pāṇini 8.3.24)—is applied everywhere. As in the example *sarpīṣi*; [this is derived] by *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.72).

Thus, with the suffix *num*, there is lengthening by the rule *sāntamahataḥ saṃyogasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.10). In the form *sarpiṣ-su*, the *visarjanīya* is substituted by the rule *dāśari* (Pāṇini 8.3.36), resulting in *sarpiṣṣu*. Alternatively, because of the mention of the option (*vāgrahaṇāt*), when the *visarjanīya* remains at the end, it may optionally become *saḥ* by the rule *visarjanīyasya saḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.34). Thus, [the forms] *sarpiṣṣu* and *sarpissa* are obtained.
The visarga of the word *visarjanīya* is replaced by *s*, and when the following *s* is changed to *ṣ*, the preceding [visarga] undergoes the substitution of *ṣṭu* according to Pāṇini 8.4.41.
Now, why does this not occur here in the forms *niḥse* and *niṃssva*? To this he says: "by means of the *num* augment and so forth."

And so forth. Furthermore, this is understood as the completion of a sentence for each individual [element]; for when the sentence is completed for each one, there are three sentences: "Even when there is an intervention by *nu*, a cerebral [substitute] occurs for a following *iṇ* or *ku*," and likewise in other cases as well.

The rule "even when there is an intervention by *num*, *visarjanīya*, or *śar*" is the foundational statement for those very cases. Among these, by one sentence the cerebral [substitution] is prescribed when there is an intervention by *num*;
by the second, when there is an intervention by *visarjanīya*; and by the third, when there is an intervention by the *śar* sounds. Therefore, in this case, it does not apply.
It occurs as follows: when accompanied by *num* and the visarga (*visarjanīya*), the cerebral [nasal] arises. For example, in *niṃsse*:

the root *ṇisi* (meaning "to kiss," Dhātupāṭha 1025) takes *num* due to its being marked with *i* (idit); then there is the present tense marker (*laṭ*), the suffix *thās*, which becomes *se* by Pāṇini 3.4.80;
and because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* augment. In *niṃssvā*: this is the imperative (*loṭ*), where the *ṭe* ending is replaced by *etva*.
By the rule *savābhyāṃ vām* (Pāṇini 3.4.91), the vowel *e* is replaced by *va*. Now, what is the purpose of the word *api*?

If it is argued that it is so that [the substitution] may occur even when there is no intervention (*avyavāya*), this is not the case; for when there is no intervention, the result is already established by the preceding rule alone.

Since it is already established, the present formulation must be understood as having a restrictive (*niyamārtha*) purpose—namely, to apply only when there is intervention by *num* and other such elements.
If that were the case, would not the substitution [of ṣ] for *iṇ* and *ku* fail to occur when there is no intervention by *num* and the like?

This is not so; for if the cerebral [substitution] were intended even when there is intervention by *num* and the like, the author would have formulated a single rule: "In the presence of *iṇ*, *ku*, *nu*, *bhi*, *visarjanīya*, *ś*, or *r*."

And since [the rule] has already been established, by the power of making this division of the yoga-rule (yogavibhāga), the preceding [part of the rule] will be understood as having the sense of "non-intervention" (avyavāya);

thus, the word "api" (also/even) is not necessary for that purpose. However, for one who, while understanding it in this way, experiences difficulty in comprehension, the word "api" is intended to avoid that difficulty.
Since it would have been sufficient to simply mention the letter *śa*, the use of the *pratyāhāra* "śari" is for the sake of variety;
for there is no intervention between the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*kāryin*) by means of the letters *śa* and *va*.

59. *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* | (8.3.59) Here, four possible interpretations may arise: 1. This genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in both "ādeśa" and "pratyaya" might be one based on a part-whole relationship (*avayavayoga*) with respect to the letter *s*—that is, [the *ṣatva* applies] to that which is a part of the substitute (*ādeśa*).

The letter *s*, that is, the letter *s* which is a suffix (*pratyaya*). Alternatively: when the suffix is in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the substitute (*ādeśa*), there is a connection with its constituent part—namely, the letter *s* which is the suffix, or the letter *s* which is a constituent part of the substitute. Or, it may be the reverse of that: the substitute which is...

The letter *s* belongs to it; that is, it belongs to that which is a member of the suffix. But how can a single genitive case be both coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇā*) and related to a part (*avayavayogā*)? It is because the domains differ. For just as in the rule "before a consonant or at the end of a pause" (*kharavasānayoḥ*, 8.3.15), although there is only one locative case, it is differentiated by the difference in its substrata.

In the same way, here too, one must understand that there is a distinction in the scope of even a single genitive case. Therefore, if the first alternative were adopted, then when the doubling occurs in place [of the word] according to the rule *anityadīpsayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.4), the substitution of *ṣatva* would also apply in cases such as *vatsaṃvatsam* and *musalaṃmusalam*. This indeed happens.

In this case, the *s* is a constituent part of the substitute (*ādeśa*). The alternative view—that there is doubling in place [of the original] according to *sarvasya dve* (P. 8.1.1)—is indeed adopted here as well. However, under the second view, [the rule] would not apply in cases such as *kariṣyati*, because the mere *s* is not a suffix (*pratyaya*). Under the third view, however, the two defects mentioned regarding *yāva* and so forth would arise.
Seeing that both of those [previous] positions are flawed, he states the fourth position— beginning with "the *sakāra* which is in its own place"— and says:
"Even when this fourth position is adopted, [one must consider cases such as] *indraḥ mā vakṣat* and *sadevām yakṣat*."

In this case, [the rule] does not apply, because here the *sakāra* is the affix (*pratyaya*) itself, and not a constituent part (*avayava*) of the affix; therefore, he says: "May Indra carry me," and so forth. The particle *iti* indicates the reason: because even here, by the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), it is considered a constituent part of the affix.

Therefore, the letter *sa* becomes a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*). Regarding the word "vakṣāt": it is the root *vah* in the *leṭ* mood, with the suffix *tip*. By the rule "there is elision of the *i* in the *parasmaipada* endings" (Pāṇini 3.4.97), the *i* is elided. By the rule "the augment *aṭ* is added to the *leṭ*" (3.4.94), the augment *aṭ* is applied. By the rule "the suffix *sip* is frequently used in the *leṭ*" (3.1.34), the suffix *sip* is added. [Then] by the rule "for *ha*, there is *ḍha*" (8.2.31)...

(8.2.31), the substitution of *k* [for *ṣ*] occurs by the rule "ṣaṭhoḥ kaḥ si" (8.2.49). Regarding *yakṣat*: from the root *yaj*, the substitution of *k* [for *j*] occurs by the rule "coḥ kuḥ" (8.2.30)—the letter *j* becomes *g*, and that [g] undergoes *cartva* (substitution of a voiceless unaspirated stop) to become *k*. The remainder is to be understood as before, according to the appropriate rules.

60. *śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca*. (Pāṇini 8.3.60) Regarding the form *anvaśiṣat*: the root *śāsu* (to instruct) is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as number 1075. In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, by the rule *sartiśāstyaratibhyaśca* (3.1.56), *cl* is replaced by *aṅ*. Then, by the rule *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ*, [the substitution of *i* for the final *ā* occurs].

(6.4.34) Thus, there is the substitution of *i*. In the form *anvaśiṣatām*, *tām* is substituted for *tas*. In the form *śiṣṭaḥ*, there is the substitution of *ṣṭu* [for *ṣṭhiv*], and as before, there is the substitution of *i*. In the form *uṣitaḥ*, from the root *vas* in the sense of "dwelling" (*vasa nivāse*, DhP 1005), there is the augment *iṭ* by rule 7.2.52, and [the substitution of *u* for *s*] by the *vacyādi* rule (6.1.15).

There is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). As in *jakṣatuḥ* and *jakṣuḥ*. Both the root *ghaslu* (meaning "to eat," DhP 7.15) and its substitute *ghas* are included here. Now, one might object that since the substitute is derived through a grammatical rule (*lākṣaṇika*), its inclusion is improper. This is not a fault, for [the rule] is non-eternal (*anitya*).

This is the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding terms that are taught according to their specific phonetic characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*). Its non-eternality is indicated by the inclusion of the term "particle" (*nipāta*) in the rule *yāvatpurānipātayor laṭ* (Pāṇini 3.3.4),
as well as in the rule *bhuvaś ca mahāvyāhṛteḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.71).

And this is indicated by the inclusion of the *mahāvyāhṛtis*. Furthermore, since here either *ghasi* or *vasi* consists of two syllables, it ought to have been placed first according to the rule of prior placement; yet, by placing *śās-* first, the author indicates independence from the technical rules—that is, the sense that "we do not need to rely on some particular grammatical rule in this matter."
To demonstrate this, it is logical that the technical rule *lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā* (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 3) is not invoked here;

thus, the inclusion of the substitute form is justified. When the *liṭ* suffix follows *ad*, the substitution of *dhas* is applied by *aliṭaḷnyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 2.4.40), and [the rule] *gamahana* (6.4.98) [is subsequently applied].

By the aforementioned rule (*upadhālopaḥ*), there is elision of the penultimate vowel; by the rule *dvirvacane 'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59), there is reduplication due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*; by the rule *kuhoścuḥ* (7.4.62), there is the substitution of *cu*—namely, the letter *jha*; for that as well, there is *jaśtva*—namely, the letter *ja*; [and likewise] for the letter *gh*.
The term *cartva* refers to the letter *ka*. It should be understood that [the form] is established because it serves as its locus.

Regarding the word *akṣan*: it is the *luṅ* (aorist) tense; by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 2.4.39), there is the substitution of *ghaslṛ*; the suffix *jhi* is replaced by *ant*; there is the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*, 8.2.23); and by the rule *mantre ghasahvara* (2.4.80), [the augment *iṭ* is not applied].

By [the rule] beginning with "ityādinā," there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *cli*; by [the rule] "ghasibhasor hali ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.100), there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*); and by the rule for *cartva*, the letter *k* is substituted.
When it is stated that "this statement is for the sake of preventing [any other] substitute," one might object: "This is appropriate..."

Is it not the case that this statement is for the purpose of providing an instruction (*ādeśa*) for *śās*, whereas *ghas* is inappropriate as an instruction because it is a substitute (*ādeśa*) for *san*? To this, he replies with "ghasiḥ" and so forth.
For *ghasi* is a substitute consisting of a collection of phonemes beginning with *gha*, while the *s* is merely a part (*avayava*) of that [substitute].
The statement "not when there is a substitute" is a rule intended to prevent [the application of the rule] even in the case of the substitute *ghas* for the root *ad*.

61. *stautiṇyoreva ṣaṇyabhyāsāt* (Pāṇini 8.3.61). Regarding the phrase *ṣabhūte*: the meaning is "having attained this form, namely *ṣa*. In the example *tuṣṭūṣati*, the suffix *san* is marked as *kit* by the rule *iko jhal* (1.2.9), and [the doubling of the consonant] occurs by the rule *ajjhanagamāṃ sani* (6.4.16).

The [root] is *dīrgha*; there is reduplication; by the rule "śapūrvāḥ khayaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.61), the *khay* consonants are elided, resulting in *sivecayiṣati*. In the case of *siv*, the causative suffix *ṇic* is added by the rule "hetumati ca" (Pāṇini 3.1.26);

then the desiderative suffix *san*, the augment *iṭ*, and the substitution of *guṇa* and *āyādeśa* occur. According to the principle "that which is performed upon the causative suffix (*ṇau*) is treated as if it were the original form" (Cāndra-paribhāṣā 21).
Thus, there is reduplication of the *sic* suffix: *siṣañjayiṣati*. [The root] *sañj* (DhP 987) means "to adhere.
After the *san* suffix, there is reduplication, and by the rule *sanyataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.79), there is the substitution of *i* for the radical vowel.
[The example] *suṣvāpayiṣati*: after the causative (*ṇyanta*) form of *svāpi*, [the rule applies]. By the rule *dyautisvāpyoḥ*...
By the rule *samprasāraṇam* (Pāṇini 7.4.67), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
Now, one might ask: "Since the substitution of the guttural *bhū* for the dental *dhu* is already established here by the preceding rule alone, what is the purpose of this [new] formulation?
To this he says: "Even though it is established," and so forth. [The example is] *sisikṣati*; [this is derived from] the root *sic* with the suffix *san*, [and then] *ika-*...

While the rule *jhal* (1.2.9) is being carried over, there is an absence of guṇa due to the *kit* status [of the suffix] according to *halantācca* (1.2.10), and *ku*-substitution occurs according to *coḥ kuḥ* (8.2.30).
Thus, *susūṣate* [or *susūṣati* according to the Kāśikā]. [The root is] *ṣūṅ* "to bring forth the embryo of living beings."

[The root *sū*] belongs to the *dhā.pā.* 1031 [group]; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.62). In some instances, there is a counter-example ending in the suffix *tip*, namely *susūṣati*; that should be understood as belonging to the root *ṣū* in the sense of "impelling" (*preraṇe*), [found at *dhā.pā.* 1408].

Since the restriction (*niyama*) would be understood by the very force of its formulation once [the general rule] is established, he says: "The inclusion of the particle *eva*, etc. But what fault is there in the restriction that "only after the roots *stu* and *ṇī* [is there the substitution of *ṣat*], so that it is not desired? He says: "In the case of *stau* and *ṇi*, there is *ṣaṇ* alone," and so forth. By this restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) in the phrase "in the case of *ṣaṇ*," the exclusion of any other suffix by the *san* suffix in the case of *stau* and *ṇi* is effected—namely, if a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) occurs in the case of *stau* and *ṇi*, then it is only in the case of *ṣaṇ*, and not in any other.

Regarding the term *pratyaya*: consequently, [the rule] would not apply to the form *tuṣṭāva* where the *liṭ* suffix occurs; however, it would certainly apply here in the case of *sisikṣati*, because the sibilant (*ṣatva*) remains uninterrupted by the restrictive [condition].
As for the phrase "elsewhere" (*anyatra*) and so on: if it were not stated that [the rule applies] "in the context of *ṣaṇ*", then [the rule] would apply everywhere without distinction.

There would be a restriction (*niyama*). Consequently, because the restriction has not been set aside, just as in *sisikṣati* the substitution of *ṣ* for the subsequent *s* does not occur after the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), so too in *siṣeca*, it would not occur even in the case of the *liṭ* [affix]. Therefore, [the rule] "of *ṣaṇ*" should apply elsewhere than in the *liṭ* and so forth.
The term *ṣaṇi* is stated for the purpose that [the rule] may apply.

As for the question, "What is the necessity regarding *vinata*?"—*vinata* is a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) used by earlier teachers for the rules concerning *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) and *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*). *Anurodhaḥ* means that which is followed or required; that is, the purpose. What is the purpose?

The intention is that since the substitution of *ṣ* has already been performed, its inclusion here is for the purpose of ensuring that the restriction does not apply to what is "not yet *vinata*" (i.e., where the *ṣ* has not yet occurred). "Not yet *vinata*" means that the *ṣ* is not present.
If only "in *san*" were stated, the restriction would apply to *san* in general; in that case, it would apply just as it does when the *ṣ* has already become manifest.

Because [the substitution] does not occur in the case of *mūrdhanya* due to the practice of another element (*dhātu*), it would likewise not occur even when *ṣatva* has not taken place. Therefore, [the rule] says "in the state where *ṣatva* has not occurred" so that the restriction (*niyama*) should not apply there. The term *aviṇataḥ* means "one in whom *ṣatva* is non-existent. If only *san* were mentioned, the restriction would apply to *san* alone. In that case—

Just as [the substitution] does not occur when the letter *ṣ* has become *s* due to repeated practice, so it would also not occur when it has not become *ṣ*. Therefore, the mention of *vinata* (inclined) is for the purpose that this restriction should not apply when it has not become *ṣ*. [The example is] *suṣupsati*; [this is formed] from the root *svap* with the suffix *san*.
In the word *rudavida* (1.2.8), etc., there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by virtue of its being marked with the *k*-sign, according to the rule Pāṇini 6.1.15 (*vacyādisūtreṇa*).
[Objection: "What is the purpose of the *anubandha* [the marker]? [Response: The letter *n* is the *anubandha*. [The rule applies] to that which has the letter *n* as its *anubandha*.

"What is the purpose of the inclusion [of the marker], what is its function?"—this is the meaning. [It is] so that "the restriction may not apply to every instance of the word *ṣa*. If only "ṣa" were stated, the restriction would apply everywhere to whatever word is named *ṣa*. When there is an inclusion of a form accompanied by an *anubandha*, it applies only to that specific one and not elsewhere. Therefore...

Even in the case of the word *kaṣ* when it is not followed by a suffix, the cerebral [substitution] certainly occurs, as in *suṣupiṣa indram*. Here, the root *svap* takes the *liṭ* suffix, with the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) applied by transposition; then *thās* is replaced by *se* (Pāṇini 3.4.80), and the *liṭ* suffix is treated as *kit* by the rule *asaṃyogālliṭ kit* (1.2.5).

By the rule *vacy-ādi-sūtra* (6.1.15), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*); by the restriction of the *krādi* group, the augment *iṭ* is added; there is reduplication; the sibilant of the suffix becomes a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*); when the word *indra* follows, there is the substitution of *ay* for *e*; and by the rule *lopaḥ śākalyasya* (8.3.19), the letter *y* is elided; thus: *sūṣupiṣa indram*.

In this case, because there is no restrictive rule (*niyamābhāvāt*) regarding that which is not followed by a suffix (*niranubandhaka*), [the substitution] necessarily becomes *mūrdhanya* through repetition (*abhyāsāt*).
As stated in the *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī*: "The attainment [of the result] occurs through repetition" (*abhyāsāt*). For instance, in forms such as *caṭ*.
If the mention of "repetition" (*abhyāsa-grahaṇa*) were not made, the restriction would apply even to the *iṇ* that belongs to the verbal root (*dhātu*), which is not desired.
Therefore, the mention of *abhyāsa* (reduplication) is for the purpose that there may be a restriction regarding the attainment [of the augment] from that reduplication.

In the example *pratīṣiṣati*, the desiderative suffix (*san*) follows the root *iṣ* preceded by *prati*. In *adhoṣiṣati*, the desiderative suffix (*san*) follows the root *uṣ* preceded by *adhi*; because it begins with a vowel (*ajādi*), the second monosyllabic portion is reduplicated according to Pāṇini 6.1.9: *sanyaṅoḥ*.

Thus it is stated twice: by [Pāṇini 6.1.79] *sanyataḥ*, the substitution of *i* occurs, and there is a single-substitute replacement (*ekādeśa*) for the verbal root and the prefix; then, in the forms *adhīṣiṣa-* and *pratīṣiṣa-*, since there is no restriction regarding the sequence of the verbal root, the *s* following the root remains even when the *san* suffix has become *ṣ*.
He indeed becomes preeminent.
62. *sa-svidi-svadi-sahīnāṃ ca*.

(8.3.62) This indication, *sa*, is without a case-ending (*avibhaktika*). One might suggest that the prohibition alone should be formulated as *na* [instead of *san na*], since there is no difference in terms of brevity (*lāghava*). However, this is not done.
‘*Sisvedayiṣati*,’ and so forth. From the roots *ñiṣvidā* in the sense of “oozing from the body” (DhP 1188),
*ruvida* and *svarda* in the sense of “tasting” (DhP 18–19), and *ṣaha* in the sense of “endurance” (DhP 852)— after adding the suffix *ṇic*, the suffix *san* is then applied.

But surely, if a *s* were prescribed for a *s*, there would be no distinction; so for what purpose is the *s* stated? To this he says: "Of the *s*" (*sakārasya*), etc. Regarding that *s* which has been applied to these [roots] by the rule *dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.64), since it is a substitute (*ādeśa*), the cerebralization (*mūrdhanya*) would apply; therefore, this statement is made as an exception.
63. *Prāk sitād aṅvyavāye 'pi*.

(8.3.63) Because of the mention of the ablative case in *iṇkoḥ* (8.3.57), the term *nirdiṣṭa* (mentioned) implies immediate succession (*ānantarya*); therefore, [the rule does not apply] when there is an intervention (*vyavāya*).

This is commenced [in the following rule] beginning with *prāpnoti*. By the mention of *aṅ*, the augment (*āgama*) is included, not the *pratyāhāra* (the set of vowels). This is to be understood from the commentary (*vyākhyāna*). [The limit is] "prior to the mention of *sit*"—that is, from the rule *parinivibhyaḥ sevasitasaya* (Pāṇini 8.3.70) onwards.

The examples will be explained further below. The word "api" (also) is used for the purpose that [the rule] should apply even when there is no intervention; otherwise, if it were not present, the substitution of *s* would not occur even in the case of one for whom the preceding [rule] already applies, provided there is no intervention by a vowel (*ac*).

Since it is sublated by the *takra-kaundiṇya* maxim, how much more so is it impossible for the *s* of *anādeśa* when it belongs to words such as *senā*, which could never possibly undergo retroflexion (*mūrdhanya*)?

64. And [the substitution of ṣ] occurs by virtue of repetition in the case of *sthā* and the others, because of that repetition. (8.3.64) "The phrase 'prior to *sit*' is understood [from the previous rule]" means: taking the word *sthā* from the rule *sthā-senaya-sedha-sicaḥ* (8.3.65), those verbal roots which occur prior to the technical term *sit* (8.3.70).

Those *sth* and other sounds mentioned in the Sūtra are to be understood as such. Now, for what purpose is the substitution of *ṣ* prescribed when there is an intervention by a repeated sound (*abhyāsa*), given that in cases such as *paritiṣṭhāsatī*, the substitution of *ṇ* is already established by general rules such as *iṇkoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.57) and *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (8.3.59)?

Thus he says: "In the case of separation by the reduplication," and so forth. Since the *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) is not established for a root taught with an initial *ṣ* when separated from the preceding [augment] by the reduplication, the rule regarding *ṣatva* is stated for that purpose: "in the case of separation by the reduplication.
For example: *abhiṣiṣeṇayiṣati*. [The derivation is as follows: one who goes forth with an army (*senayā abhiyāti*) is expressed by the rule *satyāpapāśa-* (Pāṇini 3.1.25).

By [the rule] beginning with *ityādinā*, there is the suffix *ṇic*; due to the treatment as if it were the superlative suffix (*iṣṭhan*), there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*ṭilopa*); then the suffix *san*; and as before, the augment *iṭ*.

Regarding the statement “and for the sake of [roots] having a vowel other than *a* in the reduplicated syllable,” this was said with reference to roots taught with an initial *ṣ*. Although its substitute becomes the letter *s*, nevertheless, this is not established by the general rule.

Because the reduplication does not end in *ṇ*, and because there is an intervention by that [reduplication]. Regarding "abhitaṣṭhau": the substitution of *au* occurs by the rule "āta āṬ ṇalaḥ" (7.1.34), and the remaining of the *khay* sounds is as before.
Regarding the phrase "and for the sake of prohibiting *ṣaṇ*" (*ṣaṇi taṣedhārthaṃ ca*): this refers to the restriction established by the rule "stautiṇyoreva" (8.3.61).

The meaning is that it is for the purpose of excluding—that is, turning away from—that [the substitution] might be sixfold. But what is that which is excluded? It is the state of being six (ṣatva). Alternatively, "pratiṣiddham" is a negation;

the past participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is used in the sense of an abstract action. The word "artha" functions here in the sense of exclusion, as in the expression "smoke is for the sake of mosquitoes" (*maśakārtho dhūmaḥ*).

This has been stated: "The prohibition of *ṣatva* [the substitution of *ṣ*] for any other root than those ending in *stu* or *ṇi*, which was established, is for the purpose of its removal. In the case of *abhiṣiṣikṣati*, if it were not stated that [the rule applies] even when there is an intervention by the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), then *ṣatva* would not occur.
As in the example *sisikṣati*.

Why is it stated "of the reduplication" (*abhyāsasya*), given that the word *ca* ("and") is used here, which serves to draw in the word *api* ("also"), so that the meaning becomes: "when there is no intervening [element]" (*avyavāye*)?

Regarding the phrase "even in the case of *vyavāya*": if it is argued that by the statement "likewise in the absence of *abhyāsa*," the [substitution] will apply to the *abhyāsa* following a cause situated in a prefix;
and if it is further argued that it will not apply because of the prohibition in *sātpadādyoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.111), we say: no.

Because the rule *upasargāt sunoti* (Pāṇini 8.3.65), which is intended for the prescription of the substitution of *ṣ*, actually serves the purpose of a prohibition; for it is precisely when that [substitution] has been reached by the prohibition that the rule *upasargāt sunoti* is commenced in order to set it aside. Therefore, how could there be a prohibition?

Regarding the question "What is the attainment?", he says: "But of the reduplication," and so forth. One should not suspect a contrary restriction—that the rule applies only to the reduplication in the case of *sthā* and the others; for if such a contrary restriction were in effect, the prescription of the cerebral [ṣ] for *sthā* and the others in the context of the reduplication would be entirely purposeless. [As in: *abhisusūṣati*.
Thus: from the root *ṣū* in the sense of "impelling" (*dhā.pā.* 1408), we have *abhisiṣāsati*;
and from the root *ṣo* in the sense of "concluding an action" (*dhā.pā.* 1147).
65. [The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs] after a preverb (*upasarga*) before the roots *su*, *sū*, *syati*, *stu*, *stobhati*, *sthā*, *senaya*, *sidha*, *sic*, *sañj*, and *svañj*.
[The root] *ṣuñ* is "to press" (DhP 1247); [the root] *ṣū* is "to impel" (DhP 1408). [The form] *suvatī* refers to the latter.

Due to the indication provided by the inclusion of the *śit* marker (*śabikaraṇanirdeśāt*), and according to the rule "when a root without an *anubandha* is mentioned, one does not include that which has an *anubandha*" (*niranubandhakagrahaṇe na sānubandhakasya*,

Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 53), there is no inclusion of either *ṣūṅ prāṇigarbhavimocane* (DhP 1031) or *ṣūṅ prasave* (DhP 1132)— the former belonging to the first class (*ādādika*) and the latter to the fourth class (*daivādika*).
[The root] *bhavati* occurs. ‘*ṣo*’ is used in the sense of completion (*antakarman*) (DhP 1147); ‘*ṣṭuañ*’ is used in the sense of praise (*stuti*) (DhP 1043);

‘*ṣṭuabhu*’ [or ‘*ṣṭuama*’ according to the readings in the Kāśikā-prakriyā-mukha] is used in the sense of supporting or stiffening (*stambha*) (DhP 394); ‘*ṣṭhā*’ is used in the sense of cessation of motion (*gatinivṛtti*) (DhP 928). The causative form *senayati* has already been shown previously. ‘—’

The roots *gatyām* (DhP 4.7) and *ṣidhū śāstre māṅgalye ca* (DhP 4.8)—both are included here. However, it should be understood that because of the prohibition in Pāṇini 8.3.113, *sedhateḥ gatau*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs for these two roots only when they do not mean "motion. [This applies] with the *śap* suffix.
The mention [of *ṣidh*] is for the purpose of excluding the root *ṣidhu* in the sense of "accomplishment" belonging to the *divādi* class;
[it also excludes] *vicir* in the sense of "flowing" (*kṣaraṇe*, DhP 1434) and *sañj* in the sense of "attachment" (*saṅge*, DhP 987).
Regarding that which is taught here as having an initial *ṣ* (*ṣopadeśa*), [the rule] *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.59) applies.

When the substitution of *ṣ* has been obtained, the prohibition by [Pāṇini 8.3.111] "sātpadādyoḥ" would have applied; however, there is no such statement [in the Kāśikā commentary]. As for that which is taught as an *aṣopadeśa* (not having *ṣ* in its original instruction), it does not apply at all from the very beginning. The mention of forms such as *sunoti* is made by means of the *śtip* affix.
It is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ* and *luṅ* [substitutes].

[The rule] begins with "after a cause situated in a prefix" (*upasargasthānnimittād uttarasya*), and so forth. By this, since the cause for the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) is situated in a prefix, the word "prefix" (*upasarga*) is used here figuratively by virtue of that location.
He demonstrates this: for there is indeed the application of a term based on its location (*tātsthya*), as in the expression "the platforms are shouting.

Regarding the form *abhyaṣuṇot*: it is the *laṅ* [aorist] tense; the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by Pāṇini 8.3.63, which states that [the substitution of ṣ for s] takes place even when there is an intervention by a *ti* or *ta* affix or by an *aṅ* augment.
In *abhiṣuvati*, the substitution of *uvaṅ* occurs by the rule *aci śnudhātubhruvām* (Pāṇini 6.4.77).

In *abhiṣyati*, there is the elision of the vowel *o* by the rule *otaḥ śyani* (Pāṇini 7.3.71). In *abhiṣṭauti*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap* because the root belongs to the *adādi* class; furthermore, the substitution of *vṛddhi* occurs by the rule *uto vṛddhirluki hali* (Pāṇini 7.3.89).
[The root] *vṛdh* [is used].
Regarding "abhiṣṭobhate": the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs because the root is marked with an anudātta accent. Regarding "abhiṣiñcati":
the augment *num* is applied by the rule "śe mucādīnām" (Pāṇini 7.1.59).
Regarding the form *abhiṣajati*: by the rule *daṃśasañjasvañjāṃ śapi* (Pāṇini 6.4.25), there is the elision of the letter *n*.
The same applies to *abhiṣvajate*. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used here as in the previous cases. Regarding *abhiṣiṣvaṅkṣate*:
here too, the middle voice is used according to the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.62).
In the case of *‘dadhi siñcati’* (he pours curd), there is a prohibition by the rule *‘sātpadādyoḥ’* (Pāṇini 8.3.111).

In the case of *‘niḥsecako deśaḥ’* (a place from which [water] is poured out), the prefix *ni-* is connected with the action of going (*gam-*) and not with the action of pouring (*sic-*); therefore, it receives the designation of a preverb (*upasarga*) only with respect to *gam-*, and not with respect to *sic-*. As for *‘yaṃ...’*... [text continues].
