According to the statement, "Prepositions joined with a verbal action are designated as *gati* and *upasarga* with respect to that [action]" (*Jainendra-vyākaraṇa-vṛtti* 99), [the word *abhi* is so designated]. Thus, in the form *abhisāvakīyati*:
from the root *sū*, there is the suffix *ṣvul*; then, from the desire for *sāvaka* (one who praises), there is the suffix *kyac* according to *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8).

By the rule *kyaci ca* (Pāṇini 7.4.33), the substitution of *ī* occurs; thus, with *sāvakīya* established, there is a connection with the prefix *abhi*, and from that, the suffix *laṭ*. Here too, the designation of *upasarga* applies to *abhi* in relation to *sāvakīyati*, but not in relation to the root *sunoti*, because the connection is with the action (*kriyā*) [of the former], and not with the latter due to the reverse order. Therefore, the change to *ṣ* does not occur.
[It] occurs.

If this is so, then [the rule] would not apply even in the case of *abhiṣāvayati*, because here too there is a reversal with respect to *sāvayati*? To this he says: "But in the case of *abhiṣāvayati*," and so forth. For in this case...

The root *su* first undergoes connection with a prefix, and only afterwards does it undergo connection with meanings such as commanding (*preṣaṇa*) or requesting (*adhyeṣaṇa*), thereby giving rise to the causative suffix (*ṇic*).
Therefore, one is commanded or requested with respect to the action itself as qualified by the prefix. Consequently—
Since we indeed accept that *prati* is designated as an *upasarga*, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* certainly occurs.

66. *sadiraprateḥ* | (8.3.66) This is a rule provided because the prohibition [of *ṣatva*] by *sātpadādyoḥ* (8.3.111) would otherwise apply. In the word *sadiḥ*, the nominative case (*thamā*) is used in place of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) due to a transposition of cases (*subvyatyaya*). [The example is] *niṣīdati*. [The root is] *ṣadlṛ*.

The root *sad* belongs to the meaning-group "to fall apart, to go, or to sink" (*viśaraṇagatyavasādaneṣu*, Dhātupāṭha 1427). By the rule *pādhrādhmādheṭdṛśaḥ śaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.137), the suffix *śa* is applied; by the rule *pādhrādhmāsthāmnādāṇdṛśyarttisartiśadasadāṃ pibajighradhamatiṣṭhamanayacchapaśyarchadhauśīyasīdāḥ* (7.3.78), *sīd* is substituted for *sad*. Thus we have *niṣasāda*. Because of the prohibition in the rule *sadisvañjoḥ parasya liṭi* (8.3.118), the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur for the letter following the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

*Stanbh* is a root belonging to the *sautra* class. Since it is a root taught with an initial *ṣ* (*ṣopadeśa*) according to the definition in the Bhāṣya, "Roots beginning with *ja*, *da*, or *ta*, and ending in a vowel or *na*, are taught with an initial *ṣ*" (6.1.64), the same [rules] apply to it as before.

This statement is made because the prohibition of *ṣatva* would otherwise apply. Now, if it is argued that because the root is read as such in the sūtra, it is not an *aṣopadeśa* (one taught without an initial *ṣ*), then [the prohibition] does not apply at all. In the rule *stanbhustunbhuskanbhuskunbhuskuñbhyaḥ śnuśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.82), by means of the particle *ca*, the suffix *śnā* is conjoined. [Furthermore, regarding the elision of the nasal, one refers to] *aniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24).

Thus, there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*). The phrase "not after *prati*" (*aprater*) does not carry over here [into this rule]; this is understood precisely from the splitting of the *yoga* (the rule), for otherwise—
One should include *stanbheḥ* in the preceding sūtra itself.

This might be argued: since [the author] will state the rule for the substitution of *ṣ* in "avāccālambanāvidūryayoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.68), the purpose of this division of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) is so that the rule applies only to *stanbhi*, and not to *sad*.

Is this so? It is not so; even when there is a single conjunction, it will belong only to that which possesses activity despite the distance of its objective support (*ālambana*) and other factors. And to whom do these two belong? To the pillar itself.

68. *ava* [is used as a prefix] in the senses of support (*ālambana*) and proximity (*avidūra*). (8.3.68) The particle *ca* is for the purpose of carrying forward the root *stambh*. This rule is commenced because it does not apply when the prefix *ni* is present. Support (*ālambana*) means reliance; proximity (*avidūra*) means not distant (*aviprakṛṣṭa*).

"Then, 'not far away' (avidūram): that again should be understood as what is near and yet not too far, not merely near. If mere proximity were intended, he would have used the term 'near' alone. The state of being not far away is 'avidūrya'. For this very reason..."
Due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) follows even a *tatpuruṣa* compound that begins with the negative particle *nañ*;
or alternatively, it is due to its inclusion in the *brāhmaṇa*-class [of *gaṇas*]. The word "avaṣṭabhya" ends in the suffix *-lyap*; its meaning is "having resorted to.
The phrase "avaṣṭabdhā śarat" means "autumn is near. Or else, it does not mean "near" at all.
The meaning is "not too far removed. This distinction in meaning, however, is understood from the context and other factors.
Regarding the final *t* of the suffix *niṣṭhā*, it becomes *dh* by the rule *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.40); then, the *bh* becomes *v* by the rule *jhalāṃ jaśu jhaśi* (Pāṇini 8.4.53).
‘Avastabdhaḥ’ means oppressed.
69. [The substitution of *s* for *ṣ* occurs] before the root *svan* when preceded by *vi* and *ava*.

(8.3.69) The particle *ca* serves to carry forward the rule "after *ava*" (8.3.68). Since the root *svan* following *vi* does not have *sa* as its substitute, the [substitution of *s* for *ṣ*] would otherwise not apply. [This applies] after the word *ava*.
Furthermore, since this [suffix] would not otherwise apply because the word lacks an *aniṭ* ending, this rule is commenced.
By stating, "a specific action of eating is denoted," he shows that the meaning is "eating. The example given is *viṣvaṇati*; the meaning is that one eats with noise.
Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *svan* here functions in the sense of a specific action of consumption.
With the words "where," etc., he demonstrates that very specific manner of eating.

70. After the roots *pari-ni-*, *dibyaḥ*, *sev*, *sita*, *say*, *si*, *su*, *sa*, *hu*, *ṣuṭ*, *stu*, and *svañj*, [the suffix *niṣṭhā* takes the augment *iṭ*]. (Pāṇini 8.3.70) The roots *ṣevṛ* and *sevṛ*, meaning "to serve" (*sevane*), are listed in the *Bhvādi* class as *ātmanepada* roots (Dhātupāṭha 501). Regarding that which is taught here [as *ṣev*]: its...

Regarding the form *sita*: since the prohibition [of ṣatva] by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.111) would apply, this statement is made because ṣatva is otherwise not obtained for the other [root]. [The form] *sita* is derived from the root *ṣiñ* "to bind" (Dhātupāṭha 1248);
since the aforementioned prohibition would apply here as well, this statement is made. Others, however, [hold that it applies] even to the root *syati*.

They maintain that [the root *sī*] is included; for when the suffix *kta* is applied to it, the form *sita* arises by the rule "for *ad*, *ti*, and *syati*" (Pāṇini 7.4.40), which effects the substitution of *ī*. But why is it included again, since the desired result is already established by the rule "after a prefix, [the *s* of] *sunoti*" (Pāṇini 8.3.65) and so forth? It is for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*)—namely, [to restrict the application] to *pari*, *ni*, and *vi*.

Thus, [the rule] is intended so that [the suffix] occurs after prefixes (*upasarga*), but not after others. The term *saya* refers to the root *sū* (to press), which ends in the suffix *ac* according to Pāṇini 3.3.56;
this is mentioned to exclude other suffixes. The term *sivu* refers to the root *ṣivu* (to sew).

(From *Dhātupāṭha* 1108) Since the prohibition [of *suṭ*] would have applied as in the previous case, the mention of this [root] is made. "With *saha*" [is not present in the Prācīna-mu-pāṭha]. "To endure" (*ṣaha marṣaṇe*, *Dhātupāṭha* 852). Regarding "*suṭ*":
by the rule "The augment *suṭ* comes before the root-initial consonant" (*suṭ kāt pūrvaḥ*, Pāṇini 6.1.135), the augment *suṭ* is added.

[Regarding the *ruḍāgama*: according to the Kātantra reading, since the substitute for that [root] is a *sakāra* that is not an *ādeśa-sakāra*, the substitution of *ṣatva* was not applicable; its explicit mention is therefore made. As for the roots *stu* and *svañj*, since the rule "after a prefix, in the case of *sunoti*" (Pāṇini 8.3.65) and others already established the result, the subsequent rule is intended so that the optional application may occur even when there is an intervention by the augment *aṭ*.]
The inclusion [of the examples] is as follows: *pariṣodhyati*—here there is lengthening by [Pāṇini 8.2.77] *hali ca*;
*pariṣkaroti*—here there is the augment *suṭ* by [Pāṇini 6.1.137] *samparyupebhyaḥ*, etc.
71. *Sivādīnāṃ vāḍvyavāye 'pi* (8.3.71).

By proximity, the roots beginning with *siv*—namely *sivu*, *saha*, *suṭ*, *stu*, and *svañj*—are understood from the immediately preceding rule (8.3.70), and not the *stu* and *svañj* that are listed in the general *gaṇa*.
While [the rule] *prāksitādaḍvyavāye* (Pāṇini 8.3.63) would have applied, this optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) is commenced for the remaining cases where it would not otherwise apply.

72. After the prefixes *anu*, *vi*, *pra*, and *abhi*, the substitution of *ṣ* for the initial *s* of the root *syand* occurs when it does not refer to living beings. (Pāṇini 8.3.72) The root *syandū* means "to flow" (*sravaṇe*; the Dhātupāṭha reads *prasravaṇe*, No. 761). Since this root is not taught with an initial *ṣ* (*aṣopadeśa*), the substitution of *ṣ* would not have applied; therefore, this rule is stated. Example: *matsyo 'nusyandate*. (A fish flows along.)

Regarding the word "udake": how, then, is this counter-example justified? If it is assumed that *aprāṇiṣu* is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (a simple negation), meaning "it does not occur among non-living beings," then in a *prasajya-pratiṣedha*, the rule would not apply wherever there is even a trace of a living being. And here, such a trace exists.
Since "matsya" is a living being (*prāṇin*), the substitution of the cerebral sibilant (*ṣatva*) does not apply. However, if an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is adopted—

meaning it occurs elsewhere than in the case of living beings— then a collection consisting of both living and non-living beings would indeed be "other than living beings," and thus the cerebral substitute would certainly occur here in that context which consists of a collection of both living and non-living entities.

73. [The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs] for the root *veḥ* (*vi-*) before the suffix *niṣṭhā*. (Pāṇini 8.3.73) The root *skandir* (meaning "to go" and "to dry up") is taught with an initial *adha-* vowel. Therefore, since the substitution of the retroflex *mūrdhanya* [ṣ] had not yet been established for it, this rule is stated. The form is *viṣkaśaḥ*. [This is governed by] *aniditām* (6.4.24).
Thus there is the elision of the nasal (anunāsika-lopa). By the rule "radābhyām" (Pāṇini 8.2.42), etc., there is the substitution of *n* for *m*.
74. *pareśca* (8.3.74). [The commentary states:

"By virtue of the employment of a separate rule (*pṛthagyogakaraṇa-sāmarthyāt*)," and so forth. If a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) were not intended for the root *skand* even when preceded by *pari* in the case of the past participle (*niṣṭhā*), then [the rule] would have been stated as "from *vi* and *pari*" (*viparābhyām*).
The intention is that one should make it a single rule, namely "at the conclusion of the *skanda* [section]"; the particle *ca* is for the purpose of drawing in (*anukarṣaṇa*) the word *skanda*.

75. *pariskandaḥ* [is formed] among the Eastern Bharatas. (8.3.75) Since the preceding rule would have allowed for an optional substitution of *ṣ*, this sūtra prescribes its absence. Thus we have *pariṣkandaḥ*. [The suffix] *ac* is added by Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*). Regarding the mention of "Easterners" (*prācām*) in the rule 2.4.66, *bahvaca iñaḥ prācyabharateṣu*: [Note: This portion of the text provides the grammatical derivation and context for the term *pariṣkandaḥ*.]
This makes it known that there is no inclusion of the Bharatas; therefore, even though they are Easterners, the Bharatas are mentioned separately.
76. [The substitution of the cerebral *ṣ* occurs] after *ni*, *nir*, and *vi* before the roots *sphurati* and *sphulati*. (Pāṇini 8.3.76).
The roots *sphura* and *sphula*, meaning "to move," belong to the Taudādika class (Dhātupāṭha 1389, 1390).
For these two as well, the rule for the cerebral [substitution] is prescribed where it would otherwise not have applied, as in the previous case. The mention is made using the suffix *śtip*.

This is solely for the purpose of indicating the verbal root (dhātu); it is not for the purpose of excluding the yaṅ-luk formation. For in the case of yaṅ-luk, once the elision of all consonants except the first (khayaḥ śeṣe) has been performed on the reduplicated syllable, a *s* following *nir* and so forth cannot possibly occur.

77. *ve skambhateḥ nityam* (8.3.77). Regarding the form *viṣkambhitā*: because it is included in the rule *stanbhustunbhuskanbhuskunbhuskuñbhyaḥ śnuśca* (3.1.82), this is a Vedic root (*sautra-dhātu*) taught with a non-aspirated *s*.

The cerebral substitution is prescribed for the *s* of that [root] even before it has been reached by the rule concerning the suffix *vi*, provided another vowel follows. The inclusion of the word "nitya" (invariably) is for the purpose of precluding optionality. The purpose of the mention of *śtip* is the same as previously stated.

78. *iṇaḥ ṣīdhvaṃluṅliṭāṃ dho'ṅgāt* (Pāṇini 8.3.78). By the introductory statement "after an *aṅga* ending in *iṇ*," it is shown that the *aṅga* ending in *iṇ* is the qualifier for *ṣīdhvam*, *luṅ*, and *liṭ*, and that these [suffixes] in turn qualify the letter *dh*. Now...

Why is it not understood that the letter *dh* itself is the qualifier of the stem ending in *iṇ*—that is, "the *dh* which follows a stem ending in *iṇ*"? This is the thought: if the stem ending in *iṇ* were the qualifier of the letter *dh*, then [the rule] would not apply in cases such as *cyoṣīḍhvam* and *ploṣīḍhvam*; for by the word *ṣī*...

Because of the intervention. Even so, according to the principle that "that by which there is no intervention [is considered contiguous], even when there is an intervention, [the operation occurs] by virtue of the authority of the statement" (Vyāḍi’s Paribhāṣā 46), it would indeed occur even when there is an intervention by a single *ṣī* suffix.
Nevertheless, for those of dull intellect, the comprehension of the meaning [occurs] by virtue of the authority of the statement.

There would be a lack of respect for the grammatical operation (*pratipadi-gaurava*). Since there is no such fault when [the suffixes] *sīdhvam* and so forth are qualified, it is appropriate that the *iṇ*-ending [element] itself be the qualifier of those very [suffixes]. If it is argued that this is improper because it is subordinate (*guṇatva*), it might be as follows: because the phoneme *dh* is the locus of the operation (*kāryitva*) and because it is being qualified by them.
[The objection is: "Primacy [belongs to the suffix]; however, due to the opposite case, there is an absence of quality.

Therefore, it is logical that the element ending in *iṇ* (the suffix) alone should be the qualifier of the syllable *hakāra*. But this is not so; for where a quality, having experienced a connection with a qualifier, provides a greater benefit to the principal..."

It becomes capable of performing [the action], and therein it first enters into a relationship with the subordinate element through the qualification, and subsequently with the principal element. And thus:
"The subordinate element, having its own refinement accomplished, reaches the principal."
"For it functions thus to provide greater assistance to the primary element.

Here, by means of the suffix *ṇa*, the elements beginning with *ṣīṣva* are qualified; [this results] in a specific operation for the sound *dh*, which is free from the defect of requiring excessive effort in comprehension.

They establish this. Therefore, by the word *iṇ* (the suffix *iṭ*), the suffixes beginning with *sīdhvam* alone are qualified; and it is only logical that the letter *dh* [is affected] by them, as in the forms *cyoṣīḍhvam* and *ploṣīḍhvam*. Here, from the roots *cyuṅ* and *pluṅ*, the optative (*liṅ*) is formed in the sense of benediction (*āśis*), followed by the augment *sīyuṭ*.

In *dhvam*, there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *ekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.10), and then *guṇa* substitution occurs. Thus we have *acyoḍhvam* and *aploḍhvam*. In *cakṛḍhve* and *vavṛḍhve*, there is the elision of the *s* sound by the rule *dhi ca* (8.2.25). These are the forms of *kṛñ* and *vṛñ* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), according to the rule *kusṛbhṛvṛ* (7.2.13).
By these and other such rules, the prohibition of *iṭ* [is established]. Reduplication is the operation pertaining to the *abhyāsa* (the reduplicated syllable).
Now, one might object: "But does not the previous mention of *iṇ* from [Pāṇini 8.3.57], namely *iṇkoḥ*, continue to apply here?
To this he replies: "How, then, is the mention of *iṇ* made? He says: "The mention of *iṇ*" and so forth. For that—

The mention of *iṇ* in the preceding rule was connected with the *ka*-group; therefore, if that were to recur here, the *ka*-group would also recur. Consequently, the mention of *iṇ* is repeated here in order to exclude that [the *ka*-group]. [Examples: *pakṣīdhvam*, *yakṣīdhvam*.

Regarding *paciyajibhyām āśiṣi liṅ*: by the rule *coḥ kuḥ* (8.2.30), there is the substitution of *ku*; once that is applied, because the guttural class (*kavarga*) has been replaced here, the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) does not occur.
Regarding *studhvam*: this is the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *stu*, with the elision of *śap* due to its belonging to the *adādi* class.

‘astudhvam’: this is the *laṅ* [aorist] ending. ‘pariveviṣodhvam’: from the root *viṣlṛ* in the sense of ‘to pervade’ (*syāptau*; DhP 1095), with the optative suffix *liṅ* expressing an injunction and so forth, followed by the augment *sīyuṭ*; for that [suffix], there is *ślu* substitution according to Pāṇini 2.4.75, *juhotyādibhyaḥ*, and then [doubling] according to 6.1.10, *ślau*.
There is reduplication; by *ṇijāṃ trayāṇām* (Pāṇini 7.4.75), there is *guṇa* substitution for the reduplicated syllable; by *liṅḥ salopo’nantyasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.79), there is elision of the *s* sound;
and by *lopo vyor vali* (Pāṇini 6.1.66), there is elision of the *y* sound. In this case:
There exists a word *ṣīdhvam* which consists of the aggregate of the element *ṣ* and the portion *īdhvam*;
however, this [word] is not a suffix (*iṇant*) following an *aṅga*. For instance, the designation *aṅga* applies to the whole form *veviṣ*, but it does not apply to the mere portion *veṣ*.
"Of that which precedes the letter *ṣa*.

This is also established by the principle of 'the mention of what possesses meaning' (*arthavadgrahaṇāt*). This is the statement of the objector (*codaka*). "That by which something is grasped is a 'grasping' (*grahaṇa*); it refers to that which possesses meaning."

The term *arthavadgrahaṇa* means "the mention of that which possesses meaning. This, moreover, refers to the technical rule (*paribhāṣāsūtra*) stating: "When there is a mention of something meaningful, [an operation does not apply to] that which is meaningless" (*arthavadgrahaṇe nānarthakasya*). By means of this technical rule regarding the mention of meaningful elements, the form *pariveviṣīdhvam* is established.

(Commentary on Vyāḍipāda 1) Since only a meaningful word *ṣīdhvam* would be eligible for inclusion [in the rule], it is precisely that which ought to undergo the substitution of *ḍh*. However, in this instance, the word *ṣīdhvam* is not meaningful; what then? It is rather the constituent part *īdhvam* that is meaningful. Therefore, the intention is: "Is the mention of the term *aṅga* (stem) intended for the purpose of excluding this [particular case]?"

To this he gives the answer: "This has not been accepted. Here, "this" refers to the statement in the *Mahābhāṣya*: "When there is the mention of that which possesses meaning, that which is meaningless is not [included]" (Vyākaraṇa-paribhāṣā 1).
Alternatively, *grahītiḥ* means "the act of grasping"; thus, "the grasping of that which possesses meaning" (*arthavato grahaṇam*) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).
Therefore, this is also established; thus, the previous intention alone remains here. "But this has not been resorted to" (the *Kāśikā-ṭīkā* reads *tat tu nāśritam*).

This means that the inclusion of "that which possesses meaning" (*arthavataḥ*) has not been resorted to; for the paribhāṣā concerning the inclusion of meaningful items (P. 1.2.45) has not been invoked.
The reason for not relying on that [the *Mahābhāṣya*] is to avoid the fault of overburdening the learner.

For a learner whose intellect is limited, if they were to rely on words that do not follow the Sūtras while attempting to understand everything desired, there would be an overburdening of their understanding. However, in this case, when the mention of the "limbs" (*aṅga*) is made...

The intended meaning is understood as being for the sake of ease (*sukhataḥ*). Although it would have been sufficient to mention only *liṅ*, the mention of *ṣīdhvam* is so that the rule may apply to the *dhakāra* which occurs in this specific form. Consequently, [the substitution] does not occur in forms such as *ayīdhvam* and *stuvīdhvam*.

79. *vibhāṣeṭaḥ* | (8.3.79) This statement is for the purpose of providing an option (*vibhāṣā*) where, in some cases, [the suffix] would necessarily apply by the preceding rule, and in other cases, it would not apply at all. We shall make this clear in the examples. Here, the mention of *iṭ* [is intended to include] the augment *iṭ*.

He says "after a *ṇi*" and so forth, showing that this [suffix] is a qualifier for *ṣīdhvam* and the others, and they in turn are qualifiers for the letter *dh*. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that posteriority (*paratva*) with respect to *ṣīdhvam* and the *liṭ* [perfect] is impossible, since the latter is included by the mention of the former? Even though it is established by the technical rules of grammar (*śāstra*)...

Although that [specific case] is not possible, there is no fault because what is produced by the *śruti* (the actual phonetic form) is indeed possible, as in "laviṣīdhvam" and "laviṣīḍhvam. Here, when the augment *iṭ* is added to the word "ṣīdhvam," since it is included by the mention of that [word], there is no intervention; thus, the rule from the preceding [sūtra] applies invariably.
In the case of *alavidhvam*, the augment *iṭ* is applied to the *sic* suffix itself, not to the *luṅ*;

since the latter is not included by the mention of the former, the rule does not apply by the previous [sūtra]. Likewise, in *luluviḍhve*, the augment *iṭ* is applied to the *liṭ* suffix itself; since that is included by the mention of the former, [the rule] does not apply.

When [the suffix] *liṅ* is applied by the preceding rule, it always results in the form *āsiṣīdhvam*. [This is derived from] the root *ās* in the sense of "eating" (*āsa upadaṃśane*, DhP 1021), in the *liṅ* mood; *suṭ* is added, and because the *iṇ* [augment] is not present immediately before the *s* of the root, the augment *ūṭh* does not occur here after that *iṇ*.

‘In this case, how should it be?’—the intention is: should it be through this alternative (*vikalpa*), or should it be through something eternal (*nitya*)? [The root] *dīṅ* means ‘to perish’ (*kṣaye*; Dhātupāṭha 1134); [the suffix] *liṭ* follows; by the rule for roots beginning with *krī*, *iṭ* is added (Pāṇ. 7.2.13); [and finally] *yuṭ* is added after *dīṅ* before a vowel-initial *kiṅt* suffix (Pāṇ. 6.4.63).

Thus, *guṭ* [is applied], and the substitution of *ṭe* for *et* occurs. When *upadidīyidhvam* is established, some say that there must indeed be an option for the substitution of *ḍha* here; for when there is immediate succession (*ānantarya*) of the augment *iṭ* after an *aṅga* ending in the root *iṇ*, that succession is interrupted by *yuṭ*. Indeed, this *yuṭ* belongs to the entire complex (*samudāya-bhakta*), and it does not belong to the complex alone.

It intervenes; however, it certainly intervenes with respect to the *avayava* (subordinate element). Now, why does [the substitution] not necessarily occur by the preceding rule? Because here, the *liṭ* suffix follows an *aṅga* ending in *at*, and the letter *dh* is related to that [suffix];
thus it ought to be so. And so the meaning of the sūtra has been shown by the author of the Vṛtti. But if this is not desired, [then...]
Therefore, the mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*) should not be connected with what precedes;

rather, that [option] is a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), and for that reason it does not apply here. Thus, in other cases, it will necessarily apply. Regarding the phrase "according to others" (*apareṣām*) and so forth: when the mention of *aṅga* has been withdrawn here, [the rule applies to] *iṇ*.

This very [rule] continues; by this alone, the augment *iṭ* is specifically qualified—namely, that *iṭ* which follows *iṇ*. And thus, there must indeed be the optional substitution of *ḍha* here, for in this case, the augment *iṭ* follows immediately after the *iṇ* beginning with *ya*.

80. *samāsāṅguleḥ saṅgaḥ* (8.3.80). In the word *saṅgaḥ*, the nominative case is used by way of a substitution for the genitive case; this should be understood in subsequent rules as well. [This rule applies] despite the prohibition stated in *sātpadādyoḥ* (8.3.111).

When [the previous state] has been attained, there is the commencement of another; the same applies to what follows. "Saṃjananam" means attachment (*saṅga*); this is a *dhaj* suffix used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which possesses an attachment—that is, a close contact—among the fingers."

81. *bhīroḥ sthānam* (Pāṇini 2.1.40). The form *bhīruṣṭhānam* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) with the word *sthāna*, which functions as the locus (*adhikaraṇasādhana*). The separate formulation of the rule is for the purpose of avoiding the application of the principle of "correspondence in order" (*yathāsaṃkhyabhāva*). For if they were joined in a single rule, [the correspondence would apply].

Even though there is equality between the cause (nimitta) and the effect (naimittika), there might be an absence of correspondence according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhya*) due to the presence of the *svarita* accent.
Now, if the *svarita* accent is postulated for that purpose, then the employment of a formal separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of variety.

82. *agneḥ stut-stoma-somāḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.82). Since the initial *s* of these words would otherwise be subject to the prohibition [of doubling] due to being the initial *s* of a word (*pada*), this rule is commenced. The same applies in subsequent cases as well.
The words *stoma* and *soma* are derived from the roots *stu* (to praise) and *su* (to press).
[The suffix] *man* is applied after the verbal roots *arti*, *su*, *hu*, *sṛ*, *dhukṣi*, *kṣubh*, *āyā*, *pad*, *iyakṣi*, *ni*, and *bhi*. (Daiva 7.26;
*kṣubhāyāpadiyakṣibhyaḥ*—Prakriyā-kaumudī reading).

Having established the basis for the cognition [of the rule], these two [suffixes] are explained. However, in the view that they are not separate suffixes (*avyutpatti-pakṣe*), since [the application of] *ṣatva* is not otherwise obtained from the very beginning, *ṣatva* is prescribed for these two. Regarding the form *agniṣṭut*:
when *agni* is the *upapada*, the suffix *kvip* is added to the root *stu*; then *tuk* is added by the rule "hrasvasya" (Pāṇini 6.1.71), etc.; finally, there is an *upapada-samāsa*.

In the word *agniṣṭobhaḥ*, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). In the word *agniṣomau*, it is a copulative compound (*dvandva*), where the substitution of *ī* [for the final vowel of the first member] occurs by the rule *īdagneḥ somavaruṇayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.27). [Regarding this, some say: "The substitution of *ṣ* for the initial of the word *soma* is prescribed after the long [final vowel] of *agni*. And this [discussion] is found in the Bhāṣya following the rule *vibhāṣeṭaḥ* (8.3.79).

This is obtained through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) from a subsequent rule. Nor would there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) resulting from that continued application, because it is understood as a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).

83. *jyotirāyuṣaḥ stomaḥ* | (8.3.83) [The examples are] *jyotiḥstomaḥ* and *āyuḥstomaḥ*. These are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). The substitution of *r* occurs for the letter *s*, followed by the visarga; optionally, by the rule *vā śari* (8.3.36), the letter *s* may remain. [This applies] to that [visarga] and to the letter *t*.
The substitution of *ṣṭu* occurs.
84. *mātṛpitṛbhyāṃ svasā* (Pāṇini 8.3.84).

Regarding the rule "from *mātṛ* and *pitṛ*": according to the Vārttika "that which is more venerable (*abhyahita*) is placed first" (Vārttika 109), the word *mātṛ* is placed first. Since [the *s*] is not a substitute *sakāra*, it was not [already] applicable [by the preceding rule].
The substitution of *ṣ* occurs here by way of an irregular derivation (*nipātana*). The forms "mātṛṣvasā" (mother's sister) and "pitṛṣvasaḥ" (father's sister) are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

85. *mātṛpitṛbhyām anyatarasyām* (8.3.84). This optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) is commenced because it was not obtained by the preceding [sūtra]; for when *mātṛ* and *pitṛ* are used alone, they differ from the forms *mātuḥ* and *pituḥ*, which consist of the combination of base and suffix. [The example is: *mātuḥ*.

In the examples *svasā* and *pituḥṣvasā*, the sixth case ending is not elided by the rule *vibhāṣā svasṛpatyoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.24). Because the rule specifies the suffix *ra* at the end of the *uttarapada*, by association with that, the same applies to the *pūrvapada* as well.
He states that the inclusion of [the word] ending in *r* is understood, saying: "In the case of *mātuḥ* and *pitur*, [the rule applies] to those two which end in *r*.

If this is so, then when the *visarjanīya* is substituted for the *r*, and that *visarjanīya* is optionally changed to *s* by the rule *vā śari* (Pāṇini 8.3.36), [the elision of *n*] would not occur from a word ending in *visarjanīya* nor from one ending in *s*.
Does he attain [the result]? He says: "Of that which is modified by a single substitution," and so forth.

If there were no inclusion of those ending in *r*, then if the inclusion of those ending in the *visarjanīya* were made, the result would follow only from such forms, and not from those ending in *s*.

Because the rule depends on the specific grammatical description. Even if there were a grasping of the two [roots] ending in *s*, it would still apply only to those two exactly as they are, and not to those ending in *visarjanīya*. However, if there is a grasping of the two ending in *r*, then by necessity a modification must occur when followed by the word *svasṛ*.
There is no rule-governed dependency (*tantratā*) for *nidaśa*. Therefore, the substitution of *ṣ* is established after words ending in *visarjanīya*, as well as after those ending in *s*.
86. *abhinisaḥ stanaḥ śabdasamjñāyām* (Pāṇini 8.3.86).

Since there is no *s* in the root *an-ādeśa*, the rule for *ṣatva* does not apply; therefore, this statement is made. The root *ṣṭan* (DhP 461), belonging to the *bhūvādika* class, is what is intended here, and not the root *stan* (DhP 1859) or *gad* (DhP 1860) belonging to the *curādika* class, which mean "to cry out" (*devaśabda*) or "to lament" (*parivedana*), respectively.

But that is not so; for when that [suffix] is present, because it ends in *t*, the rule "ata upadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.116) does not allow for the vṛddhi [strengthening]. This substitution of *ṣ* is prescribed only after the prefixes *abhi* and *nis*;
for if that suffix were added after each of them separately, then once the term *mūrdhan* is applied, there would be no designation of the word-form [as a compound].

It is understood from the rule beginning with "from *abhi* and *nis*," and so forth. The meaning is: "from that which is this combination of prepositions (*upasarga-samavāya*), namely *abhi* and *nis*. Regarding the form *abhiniṣṭānaḥ*:

it is that by which one is brought to completion (*abhinistavyate*); [the suffix *ghañ* is applied] according to the rule "also when not denoting the agent, provided it is a technical term" (*akartari ca kārake saṃjñāyām*, Pāṇini 3.3.19).
[The suffix] *ghañ*; [the word *abhinis*] is a *prādi*-compound.
Now, one might object: since the rule applies only when there is coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*), it will not apply in the case of *abhiniḥstanati*;
so what is the purpose of including the term "technical grammatical designation" (*śabda-saṃjñā*) in order to exclude that? To this he says: "[from the word] 'compound' (*samāsa*)."
"From this point on, it is concluded."

87. *upasargaprādurbhyāmastiryacparaḥ* (8.3.87). This rule also prescribes what was not otherwise obtained, as in the previous cases. *Yacparaḥ* means that from which *yac*—that is, *ya* and *ca*—follows, with *ca* and *ca* being the subsequent sounds. The word *prāduḥ* is mentioned separately because it is not a preposition (*upasarga*).

Regarding ‘abhiṣanti’: from the root *as* in the sense of ‘existence’ (DhP 1065), there is elision of *śap* due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, and the elision of the vowel *a* by Pāṇini 6.4.111 (*śnasorallopaḥ*). Regarding ‘abhiṣyāt’: this is the *liṅ* (optative) suffix.
Regarding ‘anusṛtam’: from the root *sṛ* in the sense of ‘motion’ (DhP 935).
But is it not the case that because the *s* is a prefix (*pragṛhya*), the designation of "preposition" (*upasarga*) is applied only with respect to that [following sound]?
And thus, in the word *anusṛtam*, the designation of "preposition" for the word *anu* would apply only with respect to that *s*,
since a preposition is defined as being with respect to something that expresses an action (*kriyāvacana*), and that [sound *s*] alone does not express an action.

Because the designation *upasarga* is prescribed for *pra* and the others by the rule: "Those *pra*-type words which are joined with a verb (*kriyā*) are designated as *gati* and *upasarga* with respect to that [verb]" (Mahābhāṣya 1.4.40). Therefore, even if the mention of the root *as* were absent, a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) substitution would not occur here at all.

So what is the purpose of including *asti*? One might argue here that in its absence, by virtue of the word *prāduḥ*, a cerebral substitution would apply to the *s* of a different verbal root following it;
therefore, the inclusion of *asti* is for the sake of preventing that. But this is not the case, because [the rule applies to] the word *prāduḥ*.
Because its scope is restricted. For that [word *kva*] is always employed only with reference to the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*.

Therefore, one who wishes to raise the objection, "Whence does this contingency arise? shows his view with the words beginning with "atha. Desiring to state another counter-example, he says: "elsewhere."
In the counter-example for *anusūtam*, [the word] "even so" (*tathāpi*) means "even in this way.

By this, he demonstrates that even when [the rule] is formulated in this manner, the counter-example remains valid: namely, that the mention of the root *as* (in Pāṇini 6.4.70) must indeed be followed. Therefore, the mention of *as* must certainly be made. [The root] *ṣūṅ*...

From the root *anu-sū* (meaning "to release the fetus of a living being," Dhātupāṭha 1031), the suffix *kvip* is applied; thus, one who has given birth is *anusū*. Her offspring is [formed] by the suffix *ḍhak* according to Pāṇini 4.1.123 (the *śubhra* group), resulting in the substitution of *ey*;
then, by Pāṇini 6.4.147 (*ḍhea lopenā’kadravāḥ*), there is the elision of the vowel *ū*. Here, the letter *s*...
If the term *asti* were not included [in the rule], the designation *upasarga* would apply to the word *prati-anu*, and consequently, the retroflex [cerebral] substitution would indeed occur.
88. *su-vinir-dur-bhyaḥ supi-sūti-samaḥ* (8.3.88).

Since the prohibition [of doubling] by the rule *supi-sūtyoḥ sat-padādyoḥ* (8.3.111) would otherwise apply to *supi* and *sūti*, the word *sama*—this nominal stem (*prātipadika*) derived from the root *sam* with the suffix *ap*—is included among the *sarvādi* group; therefore, its initial [letter] [is doubled].

Thus, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* is stated even when [the root] has not been reached. Now, if the word *sama* is derived from the root *ṣamṣama ṣṭama avaikalpe* (DhP 8.29, 8.30) by adding the suffix *ac* (as in the *pac-ādi* group), then this statement is made because the prohibition [of the substitution of *ṣ*] would also apply to that [root] in the presence of the suffix *san*. [The example is] "suṣuptaḥ," from the root *ñiṣvap śaye* (to sleep).

[From the root] *ṣvapa*—according to the Dhātupāṭha (1068)—the suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied; by the rule *vacyādi* (6.1.15), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*); and by the rule *ekācaḥ* (7.2.10), the augment *iṭ* is prohibited.
Thus, "suṣūtiḥ" [is formed]. [The word] "sūtī" is derived from either the root *sū* or *sūy*, with the suffix *ktin* (3.3.94) applied in the feminine. Thus, "sūtī."
The mention of the *svarūpa* (the word-form itself). Where this form does not exist, [the suffix] does not occur—as in *susūnam* and *visūtam*.

But how is it known that this is a mention of the *svarūpa*, and not a mention of the root *sū* with the elision of the *vikaraṇa*? Because for that [root] as well, there occurs [the suffix] *tivi* and *tap*.
Is this term *sūtiḥ* used [as an example] when the *śtip* affix is applied according to the rule *dhātunirdeśe* (Vārttika 319)?

Because of its association with the word *sama*, it is understood here that the verbal root form (*svarūpa*) is intended. Although it might be argued that by association with the verbal root *su*, the noun *sūti* should also be understood as a verbal root, nevertheless—
By the principle of the prohibition of the subsequent [application] based on the word itself, that co-occurrence (*sāhacarya*) which is governed by the word is stronger;
thus, by the word *sama* alone, through its co-occurrence, only the word-form itself is grasped, and not the verbal root (*dhātu*) through its co-occurrence with a case-ending (*sup*).

Now, for what purpose is the substitution of *ṣ* prescribed for the root *supeḥ* after its semivowel has been vocalized (*saṃprasāraṇa*)? To this he says: "The substitution of *ṣ* for *supeḥ* [is taught] so that it may not apply to *svap*" and so forth. [Examples include: *susvāpaḥ*, *visvapanam*, *nisvipanam*, and *duḥkhapanam*; here, the substitution of *ṣ* must not apply to the root *svap* when its semivowel has not been vocalized.

The substitution of *ṣ* for the root *svap*, which has undergone *samprasāraṇa*, is prescribed so that [the form] *bhūt* may not occur. If this is so, why is it not *visuṣvāpa*? [The derivation is as follows: from the root *svap*, there is the suffix *liṭ*, then *tip*, then *ṇal*;
then reduplication; and then, by the rule "liṭaḷbhyāsasyobhayeṣām" (Pāṇini 6.1.17), *samprasāraṇa* occurs.
For what reason does the substitution of *ṣ* not occur for the reduplicated syllable of the root *svap*, which has undergone *samprasāraṇa*?
The intention is that there is simply no such reason by which it would not occur in the form *visuṣvāpa*. However, for the subsequent *s*, [the rule] "ādeśapratyayayoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.59) applies.

By this [rule], the substitution of *ṣ* certainly occurs; this present deliberation does not concern that case. The phrase "because of *halādiśeṣa*, there is no *supi*" indicates the reason why the substitution of *ṣ* does not take place here.
For [the rule] *liṭaḷbhyāsasyobhayeṣām* (Pāṇini 6.1.17) [prescribes it].
Even if the *samprasāraṇa* is performed later after the *halādi-śeṣa* has been applied because it follows the *samprasāraṇa*, the form does not become *sup*;
for even if the *samprasāraṇa* is performed later after the *halādi-śeṣa* has been applied because the letter *p* follows the *samprasāraṇa*.
Even though [the substitution] is applied, the form remains *sup* because of the absence of the letter *p*.

Therefore, the intention is that *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) will not occur. By this, the absence of the form *supaḥ supaḥ* is stated as the reason for the absence of *ṣatva*. However, by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*), previously...

This was pointed out by one who thought that once the *samprasāraṇa* had been performed, the letter *p* would subsequently be eliminated by the rule of *halādi-śeṣa*. [The opponent objects: "But even after that, the letter *p* is indeed eliminated;
since it is absent, this cannot be a *sup* [suffix]. So why was this pointed out?"

The intention is that because "that which is modified in one part is not something else" (*ekadeśavikṛtasyānanyatvāt*), this is indeed a *sup* [suffix]. However, when the *samprasāraṇa* occurs after the *halādiśeṣa* has been applied due to its higher priority, then—on account of the principle that "that which is modified in one part is not something else"—this is no longer a *sup*; for at that time, it is not so.

Is it a modification of the root *svap* itself? No; rather, it is of the root *svap*. Therefore, he says: "The *samprasāraṇa* is desired first. That is to say, the *samprasāraṇa* alone is desired before the application of the *halādiśeṣa* rule.
For this reason, the mention of both groups [of roots] was made there for this very purpose: so that even the *halādiśeṣa* [which would otherwise apply] is superseded.
This is so that the *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) alone may take effect, overriding the preceding [rule].

Therefore, it has been stated that before the *halādiśeṣa* (the retention of the first consonant), the *samprasāraṇa* of the reduplicated syllable must indeed occur; thus, it is said that [the rule] does not apply after the *halādiśeṣa*. And consequently...
The objection, "By what [rule] is *visuṣvāpa* not [formed]? remains exactly as it was.

In that case, because of this restriction—namely, the rule *sthādiṣvabhyāsena cābhyāsasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.64), which states that the [substitution of *ṣatva*] applies only to the reduplicated syllable of roots beginning with *sthā*, and not to others—[the objection stands].

Regarding the statement "he slept soundly" (*viṣuṣvāpa*), the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Therefore, he says: "of *sthā* and the others," and so forth.

The restriction caused by *sthā* and the others is the "restriction of *sthā* and the others" (*sthādiniyama*), and it is designated by the term "*sthā* and the others. The fact that the restriction is caused by *sthā* and the others, however, is established by taking those [roots] as its basis.
Because of the specific rule [of *ṣatva*], the restriction regarding the roots beginning with *sthā* does not apply here.

How then will there not be *ṣatva* of the reduplication in the form *visuṣvāpa*? Why, again, does the restriction regarding the roots beginning with *sthā* not apply here? To this he says: "prior to *sit*" (*prāk sitāt*).

Furthermore, regarding those [rules], the remainder is "because of the prescription of a restriction. In the rule *sthādiṣvabhyāsena cābhyāsasya* (8.3.64), the phrase *prāksitāt* (8.3.63) is understood to carry over. Therefore, since the term *sita* is mentioned in the rule *sevāsataḥ* (8.3.70), those [suffixes] which are situated prior to it [are intended].
The restriction (*niyama*) applies only to those beginning with *sunoti*, *suvati*, *syati*, and *stobhati*; therefore,

it shows that the substitution of *ṣ* for the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) of these alone is excluded, and not of others— this is the intention of the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntavādin*), who holds that the restriction is general.

This might be argued: "The *su*-affix (*sup*) is also established from the very same point as the *sita* [prefix]; therefore, the restriction will apply here as well? To this, he says: "The *su*-affix follows after *sita*.
This refers back to the word *sita*. Since the *su*-affix is recited immediately after the word *sita*, how could the restriction apply there?

Therefore, since the rule for the substitution of *ṣ* by that [substitution of *s*] is not necessarily excluded from its practice, the objection (*deśya*)— namely, "Why is it not [the case that] *visuṣvāpa*?"— is indeed valid in its entirety. If that is so, then by the principle "when there is the mention of something meaningful, that which is meaningless is not included" (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 1), [the rule applies only to] that which is meaningful.

Because of the inclusion of *sup* [in the definition of a word], and because it lacks meaning here, the substitution of *ṣ* will not occur. For in this case, the *sup* suffix has no meaning. To explain: when there is reduplication in place of the *taddhita* suffix, then the whole alone possesses meaning, while the constituent part is indeed meaningless. But when there is a double application...

Regarding the reduplication (*dvirvacana*), even then it is a repetition of the word (*śabda*), not of the meaning (*artha*). Therefore, although reduplication occurs, the meaningfulness (*arthavattva*) belongs only to the entire complex (*samudāya*), and not to the base (*prakṛti*) alone, nor to the reduplicated portion (*abhyāsa*) alone. To this he says: "In the case of *viṣuṣupuḥ*, [the suffix] is meaningless. How so?

The phrase "it is *ṣatva*" (the substitution of *ṣ*) is the ellipsis to be supplied. If, because of the mention of *su* when it possesses meaning (*arthavat*), there is no *ṣatva* in the case of *vi-su-dhū-apa*, then how will there not be *ṣatva* in *vi-ṣu-ṣupuḥ*?
For here too, since it is meaningless (*anarthaka*), there should certainly be no *ṣatva*, just as [in the previous example].
Regarding the form *vi-suṣvāpa* here, he says: "That which has become *sup* is reduplicated" (*supibhūto dvirucyate*). The meaning is that having attained the form *pup*, it is reduplicated.
This is because the root *svap* takes the *liṭ* suffix, followed by *us*, reduplication, and [the rule] *asaṃyogālliṭ kit* (Pāṇini 1.2.5).

The substitution of *i* for *u* occurs by the rule *vacyādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 6.1.15). By this [present rule], the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs. When the form *viṣuṣupsa-* is established, due to the principle of closest phonetic proximity (*āntaratamya*), there is reduplication of the element *sup*.
Thus, when it has become *pup* and is being reduplicated, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) in the form *viṣuṣupuḥ*.

In the word *piṣuṣvāpa*, there is no reduplication of that which has become *ṣupi*, because that which has become *ṣupi* does not exist [prior to the reduplication]. Thus, how could *ṣupi* come to be once the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) has been performed? Since the *ṇal* suffix lacks the *kit* designation, the semivowel-vocalization itself does not occur.
How, then, could there be the substitution of *ṣ*? Therefore, it is precisely this term *sup* that is repeated twice;

for even though it becomes *supi* after the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) has subsequently taken place, nevertheless, because that [subsequent form] is devoid of meaning, the cerebral substitution does not occur. Thus, if...

The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs when there has been vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). Regarding the regional usage "Why not *visuṣvāpa*?", this was resolved by relying on the maxim that a term is meaningful [only if it possesses its own specific meaning] (*arthavad-grahaṇa-paribhāṣā*).
But surely, when reduplication is to be performed, the substitution of *ṣ* is not yet established; so why is this said?
"Why is it stated that 'a doubled [element] becomes as if it were preceded by *ṣ*'? To this, he says: 'That which is not established in what precedes,' and so forth.
89. *ninadībhyāṃ snāteḥ kauśale* (Pāṇini 8.3.89). The root *ṣṇā* (meaning 'to cleanse') is listed at Dhātupāṭha 1052. Regarding this, as before, there is a prohibition of the substitution of *ṣ*.

The commencement of this [sūtra] occurs when [the condition] is met. *Kauśalam* means skill or proficiency, as in the example "niṣṇātaḥ kaṭhakaraṇe" (skilled in the performance of the Kaṭha ritual), where it is understood that he is *kuśala* (proficient). In the case of *nadīṣṇaḥ* as well, it means one who is proficient in bathing in the river. There is the elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule "āto lopa iṭi ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.64), and there is a compound with an upapada.
In the case of "nadīsnātaḥ" as well, the compound is formed by means of a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) of "saptamī" (Pāṇini 2.1.40).

90. *pratiṣṇātam* | (8.3.90) Regarding the form *pratiṣṇātam*: since the prohibition of the substitution of *ṣ* would apply here as in the previous rule, this form is established by nipātana (irregular derivation).
While the word *snāteḥ* from (8.3.89) is understood [by anuvṛtti], the word *prateḥ* is explicitly stated in the sūtra.
While it is true that *pratiṣṇātam* is established [by the rule], it would also apply to forms such as those ending in *-tṛc*;
therefore, the irregular form (*nipātana*) *pratiṣṇātam* is resorted to in order to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

91. *Kapiṣṭhala* [is formed] in the sense of lineage (*gotra*) [Pāṇini 4.1.102]. (8.3.91) If this root *ṣṭhala* in the sense of "standing" (*sthāne*) [Dhātupāṭha 836] is a *ṣopadeśa* according to the rule "those beginning with *s* and ending in a vowel or *t* are *ṣopadeśas*" (Kāśikā on 6.1.64), then for that [root]:

When this form occurs, then, since the prohibition [of *ṣatva*] would apply as before, this statement is made. Alternatively, because it is not so recited in the *gaṇa*, the word *sthalī* is either taught with the initial *ay* (i.e., *sthaly-*) according to the rule, or it is derived [from *sthala*]. In that case, since *ṣatva* would not apply from the very beginning, this statement is made. [The phrase] "in the domain of *gotra*" [is used].

The meaning is that the word *kapiṣṭhala* becomes [the name of] a lineage (*gotra*). And by the mention of "cattle" (*go*) here, the worldly lineage is intended, not the technical one; for in common usage, those men who are the originators of a line of offspring—that is, those from whom a line of offspring begins—are [referred to as such].
They are designated as "lineage" (*gotra*). And what is the word *kapiṣṭhala* that has lineage as its referent?

It is that which is recited as a proper name (*saṃjñāśabda*) in the *Pravarādhyāya*. Since the technical status of being a referent of lineage is not possible without a secondary suffix denoting offspring (*apatyapratyaya*), [the term is used here in its conventional sense].
This is the inclusion of the technical *gotra* [name] here: "one named Kapiṣṭhala.

He stands firm (*tiṣṭhati*) on the ground (*sthale*), hence *sthala*; [the suffix] *ac* is added according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*). Like a monkey (*kapir iva*) is *sthalaḥ*, thus he is *kapiṣṭhalaḥ*. The compound is formed by the rule beginning with "that which is compared with tigers, etc. (Pāṇini 2.1.56). This is merely an etymological derivation.

It has been done, but no etymological meaning of the parts exists. The word *nāma* is employed to show that the word *kapiṣṭhala* is a proper name (*saṃjñāśabda*). Because the word *kapiṣṭhala* is not well-known, he says—"of whom [the son] Kāpiṣṭhali"—in order to designate him by means of his well-known descendant. Of whom...
The meaning is that he was the offspring of Kāpiṣṭhali, namely one named Kapiṣṭhala.
As for the term "Kapisthala," it means a place or abode of monkeys (kapīnāṃ sthalaṃ sthānam).

92. *Praṣṭhaḥ* is used for one who goes at the front (*agragāmin*). [The reading *agragāmini* is found in the Prācīna-mudrita-nyāsa-pāṭha (8.3.92). Since the word *pra-* does not end in the suffix *-in*, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* was not otherwise applicable; therefore, it is here specifically prescribed. One whose nature is to go at the front (*agre gantuṃ śīlam yasya*) is called *agragāmī*, meaning a leader (*puraḥsara*). [In the sense of "standing," *praṣṭhaḥ* is derived from *pra-sthā* by the rule *supi sthaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.4).]
(3.2.4) Thus, there is the suffix *kap*; as before, there is the elision of the vowel *a*.

93. *viṣṭaraḥ* is used for a tree or a seat. (Pāṇini 8.3.93). Regarding the word *viṣṭaraḥ*: although the root *stṛñ* (meaning "to cover") belongs to the *ñādi* class, it does not have the designation of being taught with an initial *ṣ* (*ṣopadeśatva*), even though its penultimate letter is a dental (*d*).

Because of the rule *‘sṛpisṛjistṛstyāsekṛsṛvarjam’* (Kāśikā 6.1.64), by which [the substitution of] *ṣ* is not prescribed for roots other than these, the word *viṣṭaraḥ*— meaning "that which is spread out" (*vistīryate*)—
is derived from the suffix *ap* according to *‘ṛdorap’* (Pāṇini 3.3.57). This is a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*) that is etymologically analyzed in some manner or another.
One should not insist upon the meaning of the individual parts here.
94. And [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] when the name is that of a meter (*cchandas*).

(8.3.94) By the mention of *cchandas*, there is the inclusion of *bṛhatī* and other such meters; for "Viṣṭara" is not the name of the Veda, but rather the name of certain meters such as *bṛhatī*. But is it not [the case that] "viṣṭara" [is used]?
Regarding the subject at hand: how can it be established that [the suffix] *vi* is used in the sense of *viṣṭāra*?

To this he says: "from the prefix *vi-," and so forth. When the word *straḥ* is being carried over from the rule *pra strot ayajñe* (Pāṇini 3.3.32), the word *vā* is understood from the rule *prathane vāvaśabde* (Pāṇini 3.3.33).

By the rule *‘cchandonāmni ca’* (Pāṇini 3.3.34), the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *stṛ* with the *ṇit* augment. And when *ghañ* is applied, the form *viṣṭara* is not obtained. Therefore, although *viṣṭara* was the subject under discussion, it is nevertheless treated as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). But is it not the case that even when *ghañ* is prescribed, [the desired form] follows from this very [rule]?

Since the shortening [of the vowel] occurs by way of irregular derivation (nipātana), the form *viṣṭara* indeed exists; how then can it be understood that [the word] is *viṣṭāra*? It is because of the statement: "and also in the name of a metre. For *viṣṭara* is not the name of a metre; rather, it is *viṣṭāra*.

95. *gavi-yudhibhyāṃ sthiraḥ* (8.3.95). If this word *sthira* is derived from the root *sthā* with the suffix *kirac* by means of the rule *ajira-śiśira-* (Daiva-Upanishad 8.27), then [the *ṣatva* substitution] applies by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* (8.3.111).

This statement is made because [the rule] would otherwise be prohibited. Alternatively, if the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is considered unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*), then since [the suffix] would not apply from the very beginning, this statement is provided. Examples are *gaviṣṭhiraḥ* and *gudhiṣṭhiraḥ*;
here, a compound (*samāsa*) occurs for the sake of a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Now, how is it that in *gaviṣṭhiraḥ* there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending?
If it is argued that [the rule] "after a word ending in *a*, when a locative case is used in a technical name" (6.3.9) applies here, we say no;
because the word *go* does not end in *a*. Therefore, he says: "from the word *go*," and so forth.

96. *sthalam* after *vi*, *kuśami*, and *pari*. (8.3.96) This rule is stated because the prohibition [of *ṣatva*] by the sūtra *sātpadādyoḥ* (8.3.111) would otherwise apply. That this is so has been explained under the rule *kapiṣṭhalo gotre* (8.3.91). Examples: *viṣṭhalam*,...

Regarding the word *kuṣṭhalam*: the word *sthala* ends in the suffix *ac* (by Pāṇini 3.1.134). Therefore, when the two words *vi* and *ku* are treated as indeclinables (*nipāta*), the compound is formed by Pāṇini 2.2.18, *kugatiprādayaḥ*. However, if they are not indeclinables but denote "bird" and "earth" respectively, then it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). [The same applies to] *śamiṣṭhalam*.

Thus, "śamīnāṃ sthalam" is a compound. The shortening [of the final vowel] occurs by the rule "ṅyāpoḥ saṃjñācchandasorbahulam" (Pāṇini 6.3.63). The explicit mention of the short vowel is for the purpose that it should not be long; otherwise, due to the word "bahulam," the long vowel would also optionally occur.
It would be understood as ‘pariṣṭhalam’; it is a *prādi* compound.
After *ambā*, *amba*, *go*, *bhūmi*, *savya*, *apa*, *dvi*, *tri*, *kuśa*, *eku*, *śaṅku*, *aṅgu*, *mañji*, *puñji*, *parame*, *barhis*, *divi*, and *agni*, the suffix *sth-* [is applied].
In these cases, when a compound with an upapada is formed, the elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending does not occur before the word *sthal-* as the subsequent member (*uttarapada*).

Regarding those [words] ending in *eṅ*, this statement is made because the substitution of *v*— which would otherwise be required by the rule *iṣkoḥ* (8.3.57)— is subject to the prohibition based on its being at the beginning of a word (*padādilakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, even after the word *barhis*,
the same prohibition based on its being at the beginning of a word applies, according to the rule *nuḍvisarjanīyaśarvyavāye 'pi* (8.3.58).

This statement is made because [the substitution] would otherwise be prohibited; however, for the remaining [roots], it is not even applicable. Would the mention of *stha* refer to the verbal root (*dhātu*) or to its own form (*svarūpa*)? If, having applied the elision of the vowel *ā* according to "āto dhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.140), the genitive case ending is applied to *tiṣṭhateḥ*, then it refers to the verbal root.

Now, by means of a grammatical anomaly (*subvyatyaya*), the genitive case is replaced by the nominative, and the word *stha*—ending in the suffix *kap*—is indicated; in that case, there is a reference to its own form (*svarūpagrahaṇa*). Having considered that if "root" (*dhātu*) were being referred to here, then [the rule] would undesirably apply even in cases such as *go-sthāna*.

Demonstrating the apprehension of the word's own form (*svarūpa*), he says: "From these [words]," and so forth. Regarding the examples, in the case of *goṣṭha*, when the word *go* ending in the nominative is an attendant word (*upapada*), there is the application of the suffix *ka* in the sense of the suffix *ghan*.
This is according to the Vārttika: "The application of *ka* in the sense of *ghan* is for the sake of [words] such as *svāsa*, *snā*, *pā*, *vyathi*, *havi*, *vuji*, and *yārtha*" (Vārttika 306).

The suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) in the word *gostha*, meaning "cows stand in this. In the word *apaṣṭha*, meaning "he does not stand," the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *supi sthaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.4). There is a variant reading *āpaṣṭhaḥ*;
the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 6.3.137). In all other instances as well, [the suffix is applied] after a case-ending (*sup*).

The suffix *kip* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.4] *sthaḥ*. If the word *ku* is a particle (*nipāta*), then the root *kaṇḍū* takes this suffix when this [word *ku*] is an upapada ending in *praṇam*; however, if it is not a particle, then it must end in the locative case. This applies only when [the preceding words] such as *ambā* etc. end in the locative case, as in the example *jambaṣṭhaḥ*. [This is governed by the rule] *ṅyāpoḥ*...

The short vowel [in *saṃstha*] is by virtue of Pāṇini 6.3.63: *saṃjñāc-chandasor bahulam*. Regarding the word *stha*: since the rule would not apply to other forms due to the mention of the specific form (*svarūpagrahaṇa*), he says this—namely, "of *sthā*, *sthin*, and *sthṛ*"—and so forth. For these as well, there is the substitution of *ṣ*.
It means it must be stated, that is, it must be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows:

because *suṣāmādi* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, the change to *ṣ* (ṣatva) will occur for these words. For example: *savyeṣṭhāḥ* (as noted in the Kāśikā). [The derivation is: one who stands on the left (*savye tiṣṭhati*) is formed by the suffix *div-eÑ*.

While this [rule] is being carried over, by the rule *anayater ḍicca* (Daiva 2.8), and further by the rule *savye sthaś chandasi* (Daiva 2.9)—which prescribes the suffix *añ* after the root *sthā* when the word *savya* is the governing term (*upapada*)—the suffix *añ* is applied. Due to the marker *ḍ*, there is elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*). By the rule *tatpuruṣe* (Pāṇini 6.3.14) and others, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the genitive case ending.

When *savyeṣṭhṛ* is established, the suffix *maṅ* is applied by the rule *ṛduśanaspudodaṃśo’nehasām* (Pāṇini 7.1.94), and the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau* (Pāṇini 6.4.8).
Regarding *parameṣṭhī*, the *Kāśikā* reads *parameṣṭhīḥ*; it is derived from the root *gam* with the suffix *idhiḥ* according to Daiva 6.57.

While this [rule] continues to apply, the suffix *ini* is added by the rule *aparame sthaḥ kicca* (Pāṇini 3.2.17)—[the word *kit* alone is intended here, according to Durgasiṃha’s commentary on Daiva 6.61]. Because it is marked with *k*, there is elision of the vowel *ā*. Once *parameṣṭhin* is established, the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *sau ca* (6.4.13). The form *savyeṣṭhṛ-sārathiḥ* is explained in the same manner as before.
Having established the word *savyeṣṭhṛ*, it forms a *karmadhāraya* compound with the word *sārathi*.
98. *Suṣāmādiṣu ca* (8.3.98).

In some cases where the substitution of the retroflex sibilant (*ṣatva*) would otherwise apply, and in others where it does not apply at all from the outset, the retroflex [sibilant] is prescribed. For example, in the word *suṣāmā*: this word *sāman* is derived from the root *ṣo* [in the sense] of "ending" (*antakarmaṇi*).

[The word *niṣṣāmā*] is derived by applying the suffix *manin* to this [root *śam*] (DhP 1147). Since a prohibition based on its being the beginning of a word (*padādi*) would otherwise apply, it is listed here for the purpose of overriding that. Thus we have *niṣṣāmā* and *duṣṣāmā*. When the *repha* has been changed to a *visarjanīya*, if [the rule] "optionally before a sibilant" (*vā śari*) applies...
According to this rule (8.3.36), when the *sakāra* [of the prefix] occurs, and the subsequent [nasal] has been changed to *ṣakāra*, the preceding [nasal] undergoes the change to *ṣṭua*.

Now, one might object: since the cerebralization of the three words beginning with *suṣedha* is already established by the rule "after a preverb, [the *s* of] *sunoti*" (8.3.65) and so forth, for what purpose is their inclusion here?

Thus he says: "The word *su*," and so forth. Since the word *su* functions as a *karmapravacanīya*, it is not a prefix (*upasarga*); therefore, the reading is *suṣedha*. However, because the words *nir-* and *dur-*, being directed toward other actions, are not prefixes, they form *niḥṣedhaḥ* and *duḥṣedhaḥ*.

The connection should be made with the word "recitation" (*pāṭha*). In the *suṣedha* group and others, the status of being a prefix (*upasarga*) does not apply to roots such as *sthā*; therefore, if their recitation were not included here, then the substitution of *ṣ*—which is prescribed by rules such as *upasargāt sunoti* (Pāṇini 8.3.65) for a cause situated in a prefix—would [not apply].

It would not [occur], yet it is desired; therefore, these words beginning with *suṣedha* are listed here so that *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) may occur after a prefixless cause, as in the case of *svād*. In that regard, when the word *su* has the status of a *karmapravacanīya*, it does not receive the designation (*saṃjñā*) of a "prefix" (*upasarga*), because of the rule: "A single [term] has only one designation."

[The word *su* is used] in the sense of cause (*kāraṇa*). Its status as not being a prefix (*anupasarga*), however, is due to its being assigned the technical designation of a *karmapravacanīya* by the rule *suḥ pūjāyām* (Pāṇini 1.4.94). As for the words *nis* and *dur*, they lack the status of prefixes because their scope is restricted to other actions; for example, *niṣsedhaḥ* means "the prohibition that has gone out," and *durgedhaḥ* means "the prohibition that is difficult to reach."

Regarding "duṣṣe dha": for those two have the action of going (*gami*) as their object; therefore, they possess the designation of prefixes (*upasarga*) only with respect to the root *gam*, not with respect to the root *sidh*. As it is said: "Those particles beginning with *pra* which are connected with an action receive the designations of 'motion' (*gati*) and 'prefix' (*upasarga*) only with respect to that [action]" (Mahābhāṣya 1.4.60).

Because of this statement: first of all, when the root *ṣidhu* (DhP 4.7), meaning "to succeed," occurs in the sense of "motion" (*gati*), it becomes *sedha*; then, he says "of *sedhate*" and so forth, in order to show that its inclusion [in the list] is for the purpose of overriding the prohibition. Alternatively, [it refers to] "of *sedhate* in the sense of motion" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.111).

He will state a prohibition [later on]; these words are recited so that such a prohibition may not apply. For example: *suṣandhiḥ*, *niṣṣandhiḥ*, *duṣṣandhiḥ*. These are formed with the suffix *ki* by the rule *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.92).
Therefore, since the *s* in these words is not a substitute *s*, the rule for changing it to *ṣ* would not otherwise apply; hence, their recitation here is necessary.

It is called *sandhi* because it is joined (*sandhīyate*). "A beautiful *sandhi*" is a *prādi-samāsa* (compound with a prefix), resulting in *suṣandhi*. The same applies elsewhere. However, as for the words *suṣṭhu* and *aduṣṭhu*, they are listed at the end [of the list] precisely for the purpose of prohibiting [the application of] the rule concerning word-initiality (*padādi-lakṣaṇa*). These two [suffixes] belong to the *uṇādi* group derived from the root *sthā* (*tiṣṭhati*).
Regarding the statement "they are derived": from the rule *kurbhraśca* (Dhātupāṭha 1.107), the mention of *ku-* is carried forward.

By the rule *mṛgayvādayaśca* (Dhātupāṭha 1.121), [the words] ending in the suffix *ku* are derived. Regarding the form *gauriṣakyaḥ*: in the case of the word *gauriṣakya*, the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* occurs when it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*).

It occurs as follows: *gauryāḥ sakthī* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). In the rule beginning with *acpratyayāntvavapūrvāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.75), by means of a *yogavibhāga* (separation of the rule) of the term *ac*, the suffix *ac* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*). However, when it is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*)—meaning "one whose thigh is like that of Gaurī"—then [the suffix is applied] in a *bahuvrīhi*.
The word *sakthi* ends in the suffix *ṣac*, according to the rule *sakthyaṣṇoḥ svāṅgāt ṣac* (Pāṇini 5.4.113).

This word *sakti*, however, is derived from the root *sañj* with the suffix *kthin*, according to the rule *asisañcibhyāṃ kthina* (Daiva Uṇādi Sūtra 1.10). Therefore, [the mention of *sakthi*] is for the purpose of setting aside the prohibition [that would otherwise apply].

The word *gauriṣaktha* is listed [in the Gaṇapāṭha]. However, according to the view that it is an irregular formation (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*), the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* would not have applied at all.

Regarding the form *pratiṣṇikā*: from the root *snā* with the prefix *prati*, the suffix *ka* is added by Pāṇini 3.2.136 (*ātaścopasarge*), resulting in *pratiṣṇā*. From that, [the feminine suffix] *āp* is added, and [the word *pratiṣṇā*] ends in that.

The suffix *kan* is applied by the rule *saṃjñāyāṃ kan* (Pāṇini 5.3.87); the shortening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *ke’ṇaḥ* (7.4.13). The substitution of *it* occurs by the rule *pratyasthāt* (7.3.44), etc. The reading *jalāvāham* is intended for cases where the root does not end in *iṇ*; furthermore, this is observed to be non-Vedic (*anārṣa*). For instance, [the rule] *savanāvi* (8.3.110).

Its *ṣatva* will be established by the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the inclusion of the word *aśvasani*. Others, however, maintain that its reading here is justified for the purpose of showing an alternative: either the word *aśvasani* should be recited for the sake of indicating [the application of] *savana* and so forth, or else the word *jalāṣāhi* should be recited here.

And its inclusion here is for the purpose of illustration; therefore, one should understand that there are other readings such as *aśvavāhanam*. In the cases of *nauṣecanam* and *dundubhiṣeṣaṇam*, they are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
[The suffix] *syuṭ* is applied after the root *sic* and also after the root *vevṛ* in the sense of "to sprinkle" (*sevane*; Dhātupāṭha 501).
The recitation is for the purpose of refuting the prohibition.

99. *eti saṃjñāyām agāt* (8.3.99). [Note: These two consecutive sūtras regarding numbers are accepted in the *Siddhāntakaumudī* and other works as being in the form of sūtras from the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*; however, it appears that this was not the view of the author of the *Padamañjarī*.]
In the Kāśīmudritakāśikā and in the Kāśikā published by us,
these two sūtras have been accepted as *gaṇasūtras* alone; it appears that in the Kāśīmudritanyāsa as well,
the status of these two sūtras as *gaṇasūtras* has been acknowledged.

In the previously printed *Nyāsa* commentary, however, it is accepted that these two sūtras belong to the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, beginning with "eti saṃjñāyām" and so forth. This is the mnemonic verse for this very [section]. Of this alone...

The explanation begins with the words "of that which follows *e*," and so forth. The term *ekārapara* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that after which *e* occurs. By this, he demonstrates that in the word *etena*, the locative case (*parasaptamī*) is intended. Regarding the example "hariṣemaḥ":
*harayaḥ* (tawny ones) are the army (*senā*) of *ñ* (the suffix *ṅasi*), thus forming a *bahuvrīhi*; the shortening of the vowel occurs according to the rule for *upasarjana*.
In *pūrvusenaḥ*, the substitution of the masculine form (*pūṃvadbhāva*) occurs by [Pāṇini 6.3.34], *striyāḥ* etc.
In *viṣvaksenaḥ*, [the suffix] *kvin* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.59], *ṛtvik* etc., because it means "he who moves everywhere" (*viṣvañcati*).
The elision of the nasal (*n*) occurs by [Pāṇini 6.4.24], *aniditām*. [The feminine suffix] *ṅīp* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.6], *ugitaśca*.

The suffix *ṅīp* is applied; by *acaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.138), there is elision of the vowel *a*; by *cau* (6.3.138), there is lengthening. The compound *viṣūcīsenā* is a *bahuvrīhi* meaning "one whose army faces in all directions. There is shortening of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*). By the rule beginning with *striyāḥ* (6.3.34), there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). By *kvitvasya kuḥ* (8.2.62), there is the substitution of *k* for the final consonant. [And] *jhalām...* [etc.]

By the rule *jaś-ante* (8.2.39), there is the substitution of a *jaś* sound—namely, the letter *ga*. By the rule *khari ca* (8.4.55), there is the substitution of a *car* sound for that *ga*—namely, the letter *ka*. Because that [substitution] is considered as if it had not taken effect (*asiddha*), the letter *ya* [is substituted].

100. *Nakṣatrād vā* (8.3.100). Regarding the rule *nakṣatrād vā*: since the preceding rule [8.3.98, *suṣāmādiṣu ca*] would have made the substitution obligatory, this present rule states that it is optional. In the sūtra [8.3.98, *suṣāmādiṣu ca*].

The particle *ca* has the sense of inclusion (*samuccaya*) as stated; furthermore, it indicates that [the group] beginning with *suṣāman* is an *ākṛti-gaṇa* (an open-ended class). Therefore, he says: "those whose characteristics have not been prescribed," and so forth.

101. *hvasvātādau taddhite* (8.3.101). Since the governing rule *apadāntasya* (8.3.55) applies, the substitution of a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) [for the dental *s*] does not occur at the end of a word; therefore, this sūtra is commenced so that the retroflex may apply to those taddhita suffixes beginning with *t*.
It must be so; in order to demonstrate this, he says: "ṭh-ṭharap-tamap-au.

[The example is] "sarpiṣṭaram. By the rule beginning with "dvivacanavibhajyopapade" (Pāṇini 5.3.57), the suffix *tarap* is applied. There is the substitution of *ru* for the original *s*, then the *visarjanīya*, and of that as well—

By the rule *visarjanīyasya saḥ* (8.3.34), the visarga is replaced by *s*; this [subsequent rule] changes that *s* to *ṣ*, and then *ṣṭua* (8.4.41) applies. Thus we have *sarpiṣṭamam*. The suffix *tamap* is applied here by the rule *atiśāyane* (5.3.55). Regarding *catuṣṭaye*: the suffix *tayap* is applied to a numeral in the sense of a constituent part, according to *saṃkhyāyā avayave tayap* (5.2.42).

The suffix *j* follows that which ends in *tad*; or it is the singular locative case (*saptamyekavacana*). When *jas* [is used], there is the substitution of *śī* by the rule *jaśaḥ śī* (Pāṇini 7.1.17). In some places, the reading is *catuṣṭayī*. In that case, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* applies by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15). [Examples are: *sarpiṣṭṣam*, *sarpiṣṭā*.

Regarding the rule *tasya bhāvas tvatalau* (Pāṇini 5.1.119): in the usage *apṛṣṭaḥ*, while *pañcamyāstasil* (5.3.7) is being carried over, the suffix *tasil* is applied by the rule *apādāne cāhīyaruhoḥ* (5.4.45). Regarding *āviṣṭaḷ*: the suffix *ādh* occurs after a word in the sense of "becoming" (*bhāva*) and so forth.

"From an indeclinable, *tyap* [is added]" (Pāṇini 4.2.104). Now, an objection is raised: "The rule for *tyap* is traditionally taught after indeclinables ending in *am*, *eha*, *kva*, *tas*, *iti*, and *tre*" (the reading in the Prākṛtamañjarī is: *amehatvatasitrebhyastyabvidhiravyayāt*).

Regarding the rule "The suffix *tyap* is prescribed after [words ending in] *ama*, *ihakva*, *tasi*, and *tre*, as well as after indeclinables" (*Kārikā* 4.2.104), it enumerates them therein. How then can *tyap* be derived from the word *ādi*?
This is not a fault; for, because it has fewer syllables, either the word *ku* or the word *tra* would have been placed first [in the compound].

By demonstrating the deviation from the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇavyabhicāra*) through the non-performance of what ought to be performed, it is indicated that the enumeration [of the types] is indeed subject to deviation; therefore, it also occurs from the word *aviḥ*, as in *sarpismāt*. Here, the suffix *sāti* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.4.52: *vibhāṣā sāti kārtsnye*.

But surely, the retroflex [ṣ] will not occur simply because of the prohibition that will be stated in the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* (8.3.111); so what is the purpose of the phrase *tādau* for the sake of excluding that? To this he says:
"of the *ś* of the suffix," and so forth. For by the word *sāt*, [the author refers to] that which belongs to the suffix *sāt*.

The *sakāra* that is characterized as being at the beginning of a word (*padādi*)— of these two, the status of being a *ṣakāra* is prohibited, but not of the *sakāra* belonging to the base (*prakṛti*) that precedes the suffix *sāt*. Therefore,
if it were not stated "when preceded by *ta*," then even though the *sakāra* of the suffix would not become a *ṣakāra*, the *sakāra* of the base would indeed [become one].
And if that were the case, the status of being *ṣṭu* would also apply to the *s* of the suffix (*pratyaya*).

[The word] "it must be stated" (*vaktavya*) means "it must be explained. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: here, the mention of "beginning" (*ādi*) need not be made; for by the rule "when a grammatical operation is prescribed with reference to something, it applies to that which begins with it, provided the term 'beginning' (*al-grahaṇa*) is used" (Vārttika 14), it is already established.

This will come later; for now, this is done because an increase in the wording indicates an increase in the meaning, so that the prohibition may apply to the *tiṅ*-ending [forms]. In rules such as *na rapara* (Pāṇini 7.3.110), the word *na* will be treated as a separate *yogavibhāga* (separate rule); by that, the [prohibition] does not apply to the *tiṅ*-ending [forms].

It occurs thus. In this explanation, however, the inclusion of the word "ādi" (etcetera) is for the sake of clarity, as in the examples *bhandyauṣṭarām* and *cchindyauṣṭarām*. These are derived from the roots *bhid* and *chid* with the suffix *liṅ*, the augment *yāsuṭ*, and by rules such as *jharjus* (Pāṇini 3.4.108) and *liṅḥ salopaḥ* (7.2.79).
There is elision of the augment *sal*. By the rule *usyapadāntāt* (6.1.96), there is substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*).

By the rule *śnasorallopaḥ* (6.4.111), there is elision of the vowel *a*. By the rule *tiṅśca* (5.3.56), the suffix *tarap* is added. Finally, by the rule *kimetiṅavyaya* (5.4.11), the suffix *ām* is applied.

102. *nisastapatāvanāsevana* (Pāṇini 8.3.102). This rule is also commenced for the sake of [words ending in] a *pada*. In the form *niṣṭapati*, [the root] *tapa* (meaning "to heat," *dhātupāṭha* 985, 396) undergoes *rutva* (the substitution of *r*), followed by *visarjanīya*. Then, by the rule *visarjanīyasya saḥ* (8.3.34), the *visarjanīya* is replaced by *s*.

In *sasyabhūrdhanyaḥ*, there is the substitution of *ṣṭu*. Now, in cases such as *niṣṭaptaṃ rakṣaḥ* and *niṣṭaptā arātayaḥ*, why does [the substitution] not occur after the root *tap* ending in the suffix *niṣṭhā*, given that there is indeed repetition (*āsevana*) here? To this, he says:
"In *niṣṭaptam*" and so forth. For in this case, the derivation of the word does not depend on the mere existence of the object.

The primary cause is not the [actual] practice, but rather the intention to speak of it; since there is no intention to speak of practice here, the cerebral [nasal] occurs. If, however, the practice were intended to be spoken of, then the cerebral would not occur by this rule;
therefore he says: "Or it is Vedic," and so forth. When the compound has been formed...
The letter *ṣ* is inserted again by the rule "vyatyayo bahulam" (Pāṇini 3.1.85).

103. *yuṣmad-tat-takṣuṣv-antaḥpādam* (8.3.103). This rule is commenced for the purpose of [avoiding doubling] at the end of a word (*padānta*).
