By the rule "samprasāraṇācca" (6.1.108), the single-substitute form of the preceding vowel occurs; then by "akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ" (6.1.101), [the result is] "prapakvāni. This is a *gati-samāsa* (compound with a prefix). The purpose of the particle *ca* is exactly as previously stated.

12. *ṇaḥ* is substituted [for *ṇiC*] when the following word consists of fewer than two syllables. (8.4.12) For example: *vṛtrahaṇau*. [This is derived from the root *han* with the suffix *kvip*] according to *brahmabhrūṇa...* (3.2.87). Also: *kṣīrapāṇi*.
[This is derived from] the roots *pibati* or *pāti* with the suffix *ka* by the rule *ātaścopasarge* (3.2.3), and [the final *ā* is dropped] by *āto lopa iṭi ca*. (6.4.64).

(6.4.64) Thus, there is the elision of the vowel *ā*. [The form] *surāpāṇi* [is derived as follows]: from the root *pā* (to drink), by [Pāṇini 3.2.8] *gāpoṣṭak*; or else, from the root *pā* (to protect), as before—the suffix *ka*.
Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *ṇa*, since the term *ṇa* (from Pāṇini 8.4.1) continues to apply [by context]?

If it is argued that [the repetition of *ṇa*] is for the sake of making it obligatory (*nityārtha*)— that is to say, since "or" (*vā*) is the subject under discussion, if *ṇa* were not repeated there, an option (*vikalpa*) would result; therefore, the repetition of *ṇa* was made so that it might be obligatory— if this is the argument, it is incorrect, because the option is already established by the preceding rule itself.

In that case, will this rule not be obligatory (*nitya*) simply by the force of its commencement? To this he says: "while *ṇa* is being carried over," and so forth. The re-mention of *ṇa* is for the sake of clarity regarding the cessation [of the previous rule], since the governing scope (*adhikāra*) of the option (*vikalpa*) is unaccented (*asvarita*). For if the mention of *ṇa* were absent...
Someone of dull intellect might think thus: "The mention of *anu* (following) indeed does not apply here;
even though it applies there, by virtue of the force of the initial statement (*ārambha-sāmarthya*), this *didhiḥ* will be eternal, while the other [the *kṛt* suffix] will be merely optional."

13. And [before] *kumati*. (8.4.13) This rule is commenced because the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) consists of more than one vowel (*ane-kāj*). The particle *ca* is for the purpose of carrying over (*anukarṣaṇa*) the rule "also before the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), *num*, and case-endings" (8.4.11). Consequently, there is no recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of this [present] rule in the following [sūtras].

And by the governing rule (*paribhāṣā*) of attraction (*anukṛṣṭa*) [from Pāṇini 4.1.50], we have "two garments" (*vastrayugiṇau*). The suffix *ini* is applied by [Pāṇini 5.2.115] *ata iniṭhanau*. Although one could simply say *ka*, the inclusion of the term *kumati* is so that [the suffix *ka*] may apply even when preceded by a word beginning with the *ka*-group of consonants; otherwise, indeed...
According to the rule *yasmin vidhis tadādyaṅgagrahaṇe* (Vārttika 127), [the suffix] would apply only to words beginning with the *ka*-group; for example:
*dāpana-vāpaḥ*, *kumbhasya vāpaḥ = kumbhavāpaḥ*, and *māṣāṇāṃ kumbhavāpaḥ = māṣakumbhavāpaḥ*—[the latter being formed] by the suffix *ini* according to *ata iniṭhanau* (Pāṇini 5.2.115).
In the case of *māṣakumbhavāpiṇau*, [the suffix] would apply; however, in the case of *vastrayugiṇau*, it would not apply.

14. *upasargādasamāse 'pi ṇopadeśasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.14). Regarding the term "of that which has *ṇ* in its original enunciation" (*ṇopadeśasya*): that which has *ṇ* in its original enunciation (*upadeśe*) is "that which has *ṇ* in its original enunciation. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with different coreferential members (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), because it functions as a descriptive indicator (*gamaka*). Alternatively, it is derived from the root *upa-veś*.

It is called "instruction" (*upadeśa*) because it is pronounced first; thus, the *bahuvrīhi* compound "that which has [the letter] *ṇ* as its instruction" (*ṇopadeśaḥ*) is one of appositional coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Regarding "he bows" (*praṇamati*): the root is *ṇama* in the sense of "bending down" and "sound" (Dhātupāṭha 981).
Regarding "one who causes to reach" (*prāṇāyakaḥ*): the root is *ṇī* in the sense of "leading" (Dhātupāṭha 901), with the suffix *ṇvul*.
This is a *prādi-samāsa* (compound with prefixes).

In the example "a country with a leader" (*praṇāyako deśaḥ*), because the prefix *pra-* is connected to the action with respect to the root *gam-*, it functions as a preverb (*upasarga*) only with respect to *gam-*, and not with respect to *nī-*; for [preverbs] are applied only toward that [root] with which they are joined.

Because the designation of *pra* and other particles as *gati* and *upasarga* is prescribed with reference to that [following word]—[the question is]: "What is the purpose of [the rule] 'even when not in a compound' (*asamāse 'pi*)?"—the intention is that, since no specific distinction is mentioned even without this [rule], it will apply both in compounds and in non-compounds. "[Because of the governing context of 'prior member' (*pūrvapada*)," etc.]—from the prior member...

(8.4.3) This continues [from the previous rule]. The term *pūrvapadatva* (the state of being the first member) occurs in the case of a non-compound (*asamāsa*). For the word *pūrvapada* is a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*) that was previously established; it is that very same term which is carried over here, and it is possible only in the case of a compound.
Therefore, when it is stated "even in a compound," the implication is: "it should apply only in the case of a compound."

The particle *iti* is used in the sense of a reason (*hetau*). Since this fault would occur if that [term] were absent, the phrase "even when not in a compound" (*asamāse 'pi*) is stated in order to indicate the removal of that preceding word.
By using the term "indication" (*dyotana*), he explains this: its removal is not actually effected by this [rule]; what then? [It is merely indicated.]
Because it is not marked with the *svarita* accent, its non-existence alone is being manifested. This is what is meant:

for the sake of making it clear to one of dull intellect who is unable to comprehend it in this way, it is stated that [the rule applies] even in the absence of a compound (*asamāse*). Regarding the form "pranardati": [it is derived from] "nard".

Regarding the roots *garda* and *śabda* (DhP 56, 57): although they follow an *ac* vowel, this *ṇopadeśa* status does not apply because of the specific exception (*apavāda*) established in the Mahābhāṣya: "with the exception of *nṛt*, *nard*, *nand*, *nak*, *nāth*, *ṛṇ*, and *varj*" (MBh).
15. *hinumīnā* (Pāṇini 8.4.15). Regarding "he leads forth" (*praṇiṇoti*): the root *hi* means "to go" (and according to the Dhātupāṭha, also "to grow"; cf. DhP 1257).
By [the rule] *svādibhyaḥ śnuḥ* (3.1.73), the suffix *śnu* is applied; there is *guṇa* substitution. Regarding "he measures" (*pramīṇāti*): the root *mī* means "to injure."
[The root] *mīñ*—according to the Dhātupāṭha (1476)—belongs to the *kryādi* class, hence [the suffix] *śnā*. Thus we have *pramīṇītaḥ*.

By the rule “*ī halyaghoḥ*” (6.4.113), the substitution of *ī* occurs. Now, how is there the substitution of *ṇ* in *prahiṇoti* and *pramīṇīta*, given that in the rule “*hinumīnā*” (*8.4.15*), the specific forms *hi* and *mī* are intended to be grasped, and these [forms] are not present here?

When a modification is made to the *guṇa* and so forth, those two forms exist; therefore, it must occur right here—as in *prahiṇutaḥ* and *pramīṇāti*? [This is so] because of the status of the substitute as being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), or because that which is modified in one part is not different from the whole.

There will be no fault [in saying] "it will be. But is it not the case that the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is prohibited by the rule: "In regard to what is not established in the preceding [section], there is no *sthānivadbhāva*"?
This very prohibition is itself the fault of this Paribhāṣā; and so it has been said: "This is its fault..."

Regarding the rule "In cases of elision of *saṃyoga* and so forth, and in the substitution of *ṇ*, [the designation *tasya* applies]" (Vārttika 9 on Pāṇini 1.1.58). Now, why was it not stated simply as "after *him* and *ī*"? It is impossible to state it thus, for then the designation would apply even to the *nakāra* that is not an *avikaraṇa* (augment), such as in the case of *prahenardanam*.

Regarding the forms *pramīnardanam* and *praheṇardanam*: [the word] *praheḥ* means "from the root *prahi*" (in the sense of "he sends"). According to the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante* (Pāṇini 3.2.75), the suffix *vic* is applied even after other roots, and thus it occurs even after a root ending in *n*, resulting in *prahenardanam* and *pramīnardanam*. [The form] *praheḥ* is derived from *prahiṇoti* ("he sends"), with the suffix *vic* applied by the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante*.

The suffix *guṇa*. *Pramīṇāti* [means] he measures; [the suffix] *kvip* [is applied]. *Praher nardanam*—this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the roaring of the lion. *Pramyā nardanam* [is likewise a genitive compound].

16. *āni* [is substituted] for the *loṭ* [imperative] suffix [after a root ending in *ā*]. (Pāṇini 8.4.16) For example: *pravapāṇi*. This is the *loṭ* suffix *mip* after the root *vapi*. By [the rule] *merniḥ* (3.4.89), *m* is replaced by *ni*. By [the rule] *āḍajādīnām* (3.4.92), *āṭ* is prefixed, and because it is marked with *p*, it causes *guṇa*. Thus: *pravapāṇi*. Similarly, *prayāṇi*: from the root *yā* in the sense of "going" (*prāpaṇe*) (Dhātupāṭha 1049).
"Let me cut the *vapās*. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those whose *vapās* are excellent (*prakṛṣṭā*).

By the rule "for the [stems ending in] *jas* and *śas*, *śi*" (Pāṇini 7.1.20), there is the substitution of *śi*; by the rule "of neuter [stems] ending in a consonant (*jhal*) or *ac*" (7.1.72), there is the addition of the *num* augment; and by the rule "in a *sarvanāmasthāna* [case-ending], except for the vocative singular" (6.4.8), [the long vowel is applied].
*Dīrghaḥ*—in *pravapāni*, [the lengthening] does not occur because of the mention of the *loṭ* suffix here.

[Objection: Why then does it not occur by the rule *prātipadikāntanumvibhaktiṣu ca* (8.4.11)? [Response: It certainly does occur in one alternative (*pakṣe*). [Objection: But the word *upasargāt* is understood [from the previous rule], and [the root] *ni* is not an *upasarga*.

[Objection: What then is the status of *prati* as a prefix (*upasarga*)? It is not [a prefix]; rather, it is used with respect to *kṛṣim*. Therefore, since it lacks the status of a prefix, [the rule] will not apply anyway;
so what is the point of including the mention of *loṭ*? [Reply: This is not correct; for then it would also not apply in the root examples cited. Here...

For the status of being a prefix (*upasarga*) belongs to [the word] *hi* with respect to the verbal root (*dhātu*), not with respect to *ani*. Therefore, by virtue of the contextual force (*sāmarthya*), the mention of "prefix" (*upasargagrahaṇa*) which continues here is understood to be for the purpose of indicating *pra* and the others—as in the rule: "In a name, the suffix *ṭhan* is applied after *nāsikā*, and [the substitute] *nasa-* is used provided it is not preceded by *sthūla*."

In the rule *upasargācca* (5.4.119), the mention of *upasarga* is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *pra* and the other prefixes. Consequently, even in the absence of the mention of *loṭ*, the substitution of *ṇa* would indeed occur;
therefore, the term *loṭ* is stated in order to prevent that. [Objection: Even so, the mention of *loṭ* need not be made.

Regarding the rule *arthavadgrahaṇe nānarthakasya* (Vārttika 1), this refers to the meaningful element *ani*, for in the expression *pravapāni māṃsāni* ("I am cutting the meat"), the word *ani* is not meaningful; what then is [meaningful]? It is the vowel *i*. If this is so, then this indicates that the present Paribhāṣā is not universally obligatory (*anityā*). Therefore...

In the rule *ṭhinhanpūṣāryamṇāṃ śau* (6.4.12), since the inclusion of *in* even when it is meaningless is intended, the lengthening of the vowel is established even in cases such as *bahuvāgmīni brāhmaṇakulāni*. What is the purpose of pronouncing the vowel *ā* in *ān*? It is so that [the rule applies] when the augment *āṭ* does not occur.
This is for the purpose of ensuring that it occurs in its pure form, devoid of the augment *a*.
[The reading in the Prācīna-mūla-pāṭha is "bhūdityevamartham"]. Now, one might object: since the augment *āṬ* must necessarily occur, why is this not so? For [the rule] regarding its prescription...
Is there an alternative analysis? If so, then this indicates that the teaching of the Āgama is not eternal.
By that [alternative analysis], usages such as "śākaṃ pacānasya" (of one cooking vegetables) and "sukhā vai madhavan-gṛhāḥ" (the houses of Madhava are indeed pleasant) become established.
*Nergadanadapatapadaghumāsyatihantiyātivātidrātipsātivapativahatiśāmyaticinotidegdhiṣu ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.17).
The term *ghu* refers to those [roots] designated as *ghu*. The term *mā* refers to the root *māṅ* in the sense of "measuring" (*māne*).

The roots *mi* in the sense of "vowing" (*praṇidāna*) [DhP 961] and *mi* in the sense of "placing" (*dā.pā. 1142*) are what are intended here— not the roots *mīñ* in the sense of "injuring" (*hiṃsāyām*, DhP 1476) and *ḍu miñ* in the sense of "throwing" (*prakṣepaṇe*, DhP 1250)— on account of the rule *mīnātiminotidīṅāṃ lyapi ca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.50).

Thus, [the forms] are derived from the roots *mā* and *meṅ* after the substitution of *ātva*. Nor is it from the root *mā* in the sense of "measuring" (*dhā.pā.* 1062). But surely, according to the principle that "in the case of mentions of *gā*, *mā*, and *ā*, there is no distinction," there ought to be a mention of all of them; so how is it that only *māṅ* and *meṅ* are understood to be mentioned? This is not so.

In this context, by not applying the rule for prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) of the term "ghu" with respect to the rules "dvandve ghi" (Pāṇini 2.2.32) and "alpāctaram" (2.2.34), it is indicated that one should not proceed here in accordance with those specific rules, but rather according to one's own preference. Therefore, wherever such a preference exists, that [option] applies.

It is grasped in this very way. It is logical that, in accordance with the requirements of the intended meaning (*icchālakṣya*), the inclusion applies only to *māṅ* and *meṅ*; for this very reason, as indicated by the rule that "one should proceed according to one's intention," even when the form *meti* is not possible due to the absence of *ātvā* in *meṅ*, there is still its inclusion.
It indeed occurs—as in *praṇimayate*. [In the form] *pratipadyate*, the suffix *śyan* is applied because it belongs to the *divādi* class;
the *ātmanepada* ending is used because the root is *anudātta*.
[In the form] *praṇimimīte*, *ślu* is applied because it belongs to the *juhotyādi* class, according to the rule *ślau* (Pāṇini 6.1.10).
The reduplication; by *bhṛñām it* (Pāṇini 7.4.76), the *it* vowel is substituted for the reduplicated syllable; by *ī halyaghoḥ* (6.4.113), the *ī* vowel is substituted [for the radical vowel].
Thus: *praṇiṣyati*. By *otaḥ śyani* (7.3.71), there is the elision of the long *o*; [by] *upasargāt*... [the following applies].
In "praṇihanti" and so forth, up to "praṇipsāti," there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* by Pāṇini 8.3.65 (*sunoti*).

Due to the roots belonging to the *adādi* class, there is the elision of *śap* (the present tense marker). In "praṇiśāmyati," there is lengthening by Pāṇini 7.3.74 (*śamāmaṣṭānāṃ dīrghaḥ*). In "praṇidegdhi," [the root is] *diha*.

In the root *upacaye* (Dhātupāṭha 1015), [the suffix] *laṭ* is applied; as before, there is the elision of *śap*; by the rule "gha for a root beginning with d" (8.2.32), *ghatva* occurs; by the rule "after śaṣa, t and th become dha" (8.2.40), *dhatva* occurs; and by the rule "jaś for jhal before jhaś" (8.4.53), *jaśtva* occurs, resulting in the letter *ga*.

Since *gadā* and the others are indicated here by the locative case, someone might have the misconception that— because of the rule "when [an element] is indicated as such, [the operation applies] to what precedes it" (Pāṇini 1.1.66), and because the mention of "indicated" (*nirdiṣṭa*) implies immediate proximity (*ānantarya*), the operation should not occur due to the lack of non-intervention (*avyavadhāna*)— therefore, he [the author] addresses that [misconception].
To refute this, he says: "even when there is an intervention by *aṭ*. But how is the desired *ṇatva* obtained even when there is an intervention by *aṭ*?

Here, because the particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been mentioned—namely, that *ṇatva* occurs after the prefixes *ni*, *vi*, and *ava*, even when there is an intervention by *aṭ*.

The rule is: *nivyabhibhyo 'ḍvyavāye vā chandasi* (Pāṇini 8.3.119). From this, either by the maxim of the "leaping frog" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) or through the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *aḍvyavāye*, [the word *aṭ* is understood]. Now, since *aṭ* is a part of the *gadādi* group, its inclusion would necessarily include [the augment *aṭ*]; so how can there be an intervention (*vyavāya*)?

This is not so; for the augment *aṭ* is prescribed for the stem (*aṅga*), and the stem is that which ends in a suffix (*vikaraṇa*). That [augment] belongs to the entire complex of the stem, not merely to the portion beginning with *gad*. Therefore, it is not possible to include it by means of the mention of *gad* and so forth.

18. *śeṣe vibhāṣā'kakhādāvaṣānta upadeśe* (8.4.18). The term "from a prefix" (*upasargāt*) from [sūtra] 8.4.14 is understood here. And the status of being a prefix (*upasargatva*) belongs with respect to that [verbal root] toward which the particles beginning with *pra* are connected by action; for it is the verbal root alone that expresses action, and [the prefix's status] is only with respect to that.

The status of *pra* and the others as prefixes (*upasarga*) follows from this; consequently, when a verbal root (*dhātu*) is brought into proximity by the mention of "prefix," it is understood that its very qualities of beginning with a letter other than *k*, *kh*, etc., and ending with a letter other than *ṣ*, serve as its qualifiers.
Therefore, he says: "That verbal root which, in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*), begins with a letter other than *k* or *kh*, and ends with a letter other than *ṣ*."
The inclusion of both the beginning and the end is for the sake of clarity, because [the desired form] is already established by the rule "akakhe aṣe.
If, however, the rule were to apply to everything starting with *a* and *ka*, or to everything ending with them,
then one would have stated "akakhaṣe" by forming a *dvandva* compound of all [the letters], as in "akakhe aṣe."

From this statement—it being understood that by one [rule] there is the prescription of what begins with that (tadādividhi), and by another there is the prescription of what ends with that (tadantavidhi)—there might here arise this much doubt: "By which [rule] is it the prescription of what begins with that, and by which is it the prescription of what ends with that? And that doubt, too, will be removed by means of the commentary (vyākhyāna).

The inclusion of the word *śeṣa* is for the sake of clarity; for if there were an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding *gada* and the others, the preceding rule would be rendered purposeless. The inclusion of the term *upadeśa* is likewise for the sake of clarity alone, since it can be understood from the rule: "After a prefix, even in a non-compound, the *ṇ* of a root taught with an initial *ṇ* [is replaced by *n*]" (Pāṇini 8.4.14).
Therefore, the term *upadeśa* is carried over [from the previous rule] by the maxim of the frog’s leap (*maṇḍūkaplutinyāya*).

[The example is: "He grinds thoroughly" (*pranipinaṣṭi*). [The root is] *piṣlṛ* "to crush" (DhP 1452); [the suffix] *śnam* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.78, *rudhādibhyaḥ śnam*. [The commentary says: "And here there is a prohibition," and so forth. [The example is: "He will sprinkle" (*pratipekṣyati*).

In the case of *piṇeḥ*, when the *ṣ* is changed to *k* by the rule "ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si" (Pāṇini 8.2.41), if the term "upadeśe" (in the original enunciation) were not included, there would be no prohibition [of the doubling of *n*], because it is neither preceded by *k, kh,* etc., nor does it end in *av*. But since this term is present, the prohibition does apply, because it ends in *ṣ* in its original enunciation. And here...

"Let it not be"—thus [the word] "prohibition" (*pratiṣedha*) is required [as the object of the verb]. Regarding the term "praṇideṣṭā": here, if the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* were applied to the root *viś* (DhP 1424) by the rule *vraścādi-* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.36), then because it would end in *ṣ*, a prohibition would apply even in the absence of the mention of "original form" (*upadeśa*). However, since that [mention of *upadeśa*] exists here, [the prohibition does not apply].

Furthermore, if the mention of *upadeśa* were not present, then in the forms *praṇicakāra* and *pracicakhāda*, there would be no prohibition of the substitution of *c* for the abhyāsa [consonant] by the rule "ṭhkuhoścuḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.62); this is because [the abhyāsa] would not be one that begins with *k* or *kh*. But since this [mention of *upadeśa*] exists, the rule applies.
19. After the root *an* (to breathe). (8.4.19) Regarding "he breathes": from the roots *śvas* (to breathe, DhP 1069) and *an* (DhP 1070; note that the *ca* is not present in the Dhātupāṭha).
As before, there is the elision of *śap*, and [the suffix] *śnam* is applied after roots beginning with *rudh*.

The augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule "sārvadhātuke" (Pāṇini 7.2.76). The mention of the root as *ñanitiḥ* with the suffix *śtip* is intended solely for the purpose of indicating the verbal root (*dhātu-nirdeśārtha*); it is not for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-intensive (*yaṅ-luk*).
For there is no possibility of the *yaṅ* suffix applying to the root *ani*, because it lacks an initial consonant (*hal-āditva-abhāvāt*).

20. *antaḥ* | (8.4.20) This word *anta* signifies a part, as in "the hem of a garment"—as in "O Prāṇa" (*he prāṇ*). [The form] is derived from the root with the *kvip* suffix; it is in the vocative case, and its [final consonant] is elided by Pāṇini 6.1.68 (*halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*).

The mention of the vocative case ending (*sambuddhi*) is made because it is intended that there should be elision (*lopa*) of the *n* which stands at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), provided it occurs other than in the vocative. For in the vocative, due to the prohibition "not before *ṅi* or the vocative" (*na ṅsimbuddhyoḥ*, Pāṇini 8.2.8), the elision of *n* does not take place. But is it not the case that...?

The substitution of *ṇ* is already established here by the preceding rule itself; for what purpose, then, is this [present rule] commenced? To answer this, he says: "of a word-final" (*padāntasya*), and so forth. He will state the prohibition in the rule "of a word-final" (Pāṇini 8.4.37).

This present rule is commenced as an exception (*apavāda*) to that, placed before it. Furthermore, "end" (*anta*) is understood here in relation to a word (*pada*); it is precisely there [in that context] that [the prohibition applies].
The possibilities and exceptions exist; however, there is no dependence on the word *an-*. The sense is that there is an absence of exceptions.

Regarding the phrase "some [say]," etc.: some connect the mention of the word *anta* (end) with the preceding rule alone. The meaning is that they form a single rule, namely: *aniterantaḥ*. For what purpose? The purpose is the mention of the word *anta*.
Regarding the sense of proximity (*sāmīpya*): that whose meaning is proximity is so described.
Proximity itself is *sāmīpya*; the suffix *dhyañ* is applied in the sense of the word itself according to the rule beginning with *cāturvarṇya*.
Thus, by this [explanation], the word *anta* is understood as being used in the sense of "proximity," just like the word *udakānta* ("water's edge").

He demonstrates this. But for what reason do they connect the word *anta* (end) with those [terms] in this way? He says: "Of that which has become near to the cause," and so forth. For if the word *anta* were not connected as signifying "near" (*samīpa*) in the preceding rule, then it would not be so here either.

It might be [objected]: "In *paryanīt*. Therefore, for the sake of ensuring that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs only for that *n* which is proximate to the cause of the *ṇ*-substitution—namely, that *n* which is separated from it by exactly one phoneme—and so that it does not occur for a *n* distant from the cause as in *paryanīt*, the word *pūrvapadāt* was included in the preceding rule (*pā. 8.4.1*).

They connect the word *anta* with the sense of "proximity. By the phrase "separated by a single phoneme," it expresses proximity. One should not raise the objection that proximity is not possible for that which is separated by multiple phonemes; for such proximity is relative.

In the case of *paryāṇiti*, the *nakāra* is separated from its cause by multiple phonemes, because once the *yaṇ*-substitution has been applied, the *repha* is separated from it by both the vowel *ā* and the consonant *y*. However, in the case of *prāṇiti*, once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied,
the *nakāra* is separated from its cause by only a single phoneme, namely the vowel *ā* itself.

Due to being separated by [other] elements alone: for that which is separated by many phonemes becomes distant in relation to one [phoneme]; however, another [phoneme] is proximate in relation to it, yet even that becomes distant in relation to what is not separated [by others]. This is indeed the case provided there is no separation.

It might occur; however, since that [substitution] does not occur by means of an *aniṭ* [root], remoteness (*viprakṛṣṭatva*) with respect to it does not exist. But surely, in the rule "acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau" (Pāṇini 1.1.57), because a *tatpuru�ṣa* compound is accepted—namely, "an operation [occurring] before a preceding [element]" (*pūrvasmād vidhiḥ pūrvavidhiḥ*)—when the substitution of *ṇ* is to be performed...

Because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for that which occupies the same position (*ekādeśa*), one might ask: in the case of *prāṇiti*, is not the letter *n* separated by more than one phoneme? There is no fault here, because of the rule: "That which is [treated as] non-existent (*asiddha*) regarding what precedes it does not undergo the status of being a substitute" (*pūrvatrāsiddhīye na sthānivat*; *Paribhāṣenduśekhara* 48); thus, the status of being a substitute does apply here. [The examples] beginning with *saiḥ* follow.

For those who, relying on the word *anta* here in the sense of proximity, apply this rule [of *k* substitution], their application of that rule finds scope in the case of *prāṇiti*; however, in the case of *he prāṇ*, the prohibition [stated in] "padāntasya" (Pāṇini 8.4.37) would apply. Therefore, for them, the second [instance] also belongs to the end (*anta*).

The inclusion [of the word *padasya*] must be understood by means of repetition (*āvṛtti*), the principle of common application (*tantra*), or the principle of logical extension (*nyāya*), so that the substitution of *ṇ* may occur at the end of a word.
Now, even those who perform a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*)...

They rely on the interpretation of the word *anta* as meaning "component" (*avayava*). Even by them, the inclusion of the term *anta* in the preceding rule must necessarily be understood as signifying "proximity" (*sāmīpya*); otherwise, in the case of *paryaniti*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* would occur [undesirably]. Therefore, he says: "But for those... and so forth. The phrase "for those" (*yeṣām*)...

For those who employ the division of the rule (yogavibhāga)—they indeed desire the substitution of *ṇ* even for a [nasal] that is separated by several phonemes. Therefore, there is no purpose for them in including the word "internal" (*ant*) in the preceding sūtra.

21. *ubhau sābhyāsasya* | (8.4.21) This *n* [of the root] does not become one of those [cases] beginning with *aṭ*. Therefore, when reduplication has been performed, because it is separated by the *n* of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), the other *n* would not undergo [the prescribed operation]; yet this is desired.

And therefore—so that this [form] may also occur for that [root], the following is commenced: "prāṇiṇiṣati. [The derivation is as follows: *sam-* + *iṭ* + [the root]. By the rule "ajāderdvitīyasya" (Pāṇini 6.1.2), and by the rule "samyaṅeḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.9), the syllable *niś* is reduplicated. Thus: "prāṇiṇat. This is derived from the causative (*ṇic*) stem with the suffix *luṅ*; there is the elision of the *ṇic*, and of that...
By virtue of the status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) according to Pāṇini 1.1.59, *dvirvacane'ci*, the word *ni-* undergoes reduplication.

Regarding the rule "that which is not established in what precedes" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*), etc., if this principle— "that which is not established in what precedes does not apply when reduplication is to be performed"— did not exist,
then because the substitution of *ṇ* would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*) at the time the reduplication was to be carried out, [the desired form would not be achieved].

There ought to have been a statement regarding priority (*pūrvad-dhi-vacanena*). In this case, if this sūtra did not exist, then because of the intervention (*vyavāya*) of the first *n*, the substitution of *ṇ* for the second [nasal] by the rule "aniteḥ" (8.4.19) would not occur; thus, forms such as *prāṇiṇiṣati* would not be established. However, with this sūtra "pūrvatrāsiddham"—

Since this constitutes an exception (*apavāda*), by the rule "aniteḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.19), *ṇatva* alone is applied because it is subsequent [in the order of the rules]. Then, once *ṇatva* has been applied and reduplication (*dvirvacana*) performed, this form is established even without this present sūtra. If this is so— (8.2.1) When there is an exception to this, by the rule "aniteḥ" (8.4.19), *ṇatva* alone is applied because it is subsequent. Then, when reduplication is performed on that which has already had *ṇatva* applied, this is indeed established even without this sūtra. If this is so—

For what purpose is this commenced? To this he says: "Because this," and so forth. The *kṛtya* suffix is used here in the sense of possibility (*śakya*). The particle *iti* indicates the reason (*hetu*). The word *tu* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). Since that statement of an exception (*apavāda*) cannot possibly be relied upon, therefore this *sūtra* is commenced. For if...

If that were relied upon, then this sūtra would not need to be composed— and consequently, it would not be understood that this statement of an exception does not apply universally. This is the case in examples such as *aujaḍhat* from *ūḍham ākhyat*.

Because that which is not established in what precedes it (pūrvatrāsiddha) would lack the status of being established (*asiddhatva*), the doubling (*dvirvacana*) of the element "hat" would not occur; however, when this rule exists, it is understood that the statement of that exception does not apply universally. Therefore, in the case of *aujaḍhat*, [the doubling takes place].

Because the sounds beginning with *ḍha* are considered non-existent (*asiddha*), there is reduplication of this [sound] *ha*. Why is it stated "after *a*" (*ato bhāvi*)? For the *ṇatva* of the preceding *na* is already established by the previous rule alone; however, for the other [subsequent *na*], it is established by the very force of this new commencement—even without the word "both" (*ubhau*).

Will this [rule] apply to the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* even when there is an intervention [of other sounds]? He thinks thus: if only "of that which has the reduplication" (*sābhyāsasya*) were stated, then—just as the rule "of the second [element] beginning with a vowel" (*ajāder dvitīyasya*, Pāṇini 6.1.2), when being initiated as a reduplication, is understood to be an exception to the first reduplication—[so too would this be].

Similarly here as well, when the substitution of *ṇ* for the second *n* is being prescribed in the presence of an intervening vowel such as *a*, it is understood to be an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule.
The statement "of that which has a reduplication" (*sābhyāsasya*) is for the sake of clarity— [since the desired result is already obtained] by the word "both" (*ubhau*) alone.
Because it is established—indeed, for one who has not practiced [the recitation], both *nakāra*s are not possible.

22. *hanteratpūrvasya* | (8.4.22) The genitive case in *hanter* is a partitive genitive (*avayava-lakṣaṇā ṣaṣṭhī*). Regarding *atpūrvasya*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has *at-* preceding it. The letter *n* is the referent of the other member of the compound (*anyapadārtha*). As for the example *prahaṇyate*, [it is derived from] the root *hana* in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*) and "motion" (*gati*).

By the rule *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (1.3.13), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied; thus, "they strike" (*pradhananti*). By the rule *gamahana* (6.4.98) et al., there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*). By the rule *ho hanter ñṇit-śnuṣu* (7.3.54), there is the substitution of *k* for *h* (*kutva*); thus, "he struck" (*prādhāni*). This is the *luṅ* [aorist] tense.

By the rule *ṭhCiṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (3.1.66), the suffix *Ciṇ* is applied to the root *cli*; by *ata upadhāyāḥ* (7.2.116), there is *vṛddhi* [of the penultimate vowel]; and by *Ciṇo luk* (6.4.104), there is the elision (*luk*) of the *t* of *at*. The mention of the form with the *śitap* affix is solely for the purpose of indicating the verbal root (*dhātu*), and not for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ* and *luṅ* suffixes.

Regarding the form *pra-jaṅghanīti*: when the doubling (*dvirvacana*) has been applied, and the changes to *cutva* and *jaśtva* have been made, the substitution of *ṇatva* will not occur for the following *n* because of its separation by the letter *j*. As for the preceding *n*, since the rule *naścāpadāntasya jhali* (Pāṇini 8.3.24) applies, it undergoes *anusvāra*; and because it has become an *anusvāra*, [the condition for *ṇatva* is not met].
Although "of this" (*ataḥ*) would have sufficed, the expression "of the preceding" (*pūrvasya*) is used for the sake of variety.

23. *vāmorvā* | (8.4.23) Since the preceding rule would have made [the substitution] obligatory, this statement is for the purpose of providing an option. The inclusion of the word *vā* is intended to indicate that the preceding rules are not necessarily obligatory; otherwise, by the very force of commencing this new rule (*yoga*), [the previous ones] would have been rendered optional.
The permanence of the rule (*vidhi-nityatvam*) would be understood [if the reading were *vidhiḥ* as in the Prācīna-pāṭha and Kātantra-mu-pāṭha];

however, for the preceding rules, because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) from [Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.4.18] *śeṣe vibhāṣā*, there would be optionality. But here, in the case of the mention of *vā*...
Among the two types of optional rules (*vibhāṣā*), those that are [otherwise] prescribed as mandatory (*nitya*) are understood here to be indeed obligatory.
24. *antaradeśe* | (8.4.24) Regarding the rule *ṭhantaraparigrahe* (1.4.65), by means of the Vārttika:

"The word *antaḥ* should be stated as having the designation of a preverb (*upasarga*) in rules concerning the addition of the augment *aṭ*, the substitution of *ṇ*, and the substitution of *ṇatva*" (Vā. 71).

Since the designation *upasarga* exists in the rule prescribing the substitution of *ṇa*, the substitution of *ṇa* would already be established by the rule "hanteratpūrvasya" (Pāṇini 8.4.22). Therefore, this present rule is commenced for the sake of providing a specific technical term (*saṃjñā*). [The example is] "antarhaṇanam.
Here, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*); the meaning is "killing within. This is according to the rule "antaraparigrahe" (Pāṇini 1.4.65).
Thus, because it is designated as a *gati* [term], there is a compound according to Pāṇini 2.2.18: *kugatiprādayaḥ*.

Regarding the expression "the region of *antarhanana*": the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*). From the word *antaḥ*, which ends in *-at*, and the root *han*, the form *antardhanaḥ* is established; by virtue of this very grammatical exception (*nipātana*), the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs even when denoting a region.
It comes to be.

[The word] "āyanam"—this is the form derived from the root *ay* or *iṇ* with the suffix *lyuṭ*. Although [the substitution of *ṇatva*] is already established by the rule *kṛtyacaḥ* (8.4.29), this statement is made for the purpose of providing a counter-exception (*apavāda*) regarding non-place (*adeśa*).
By the letter *ca*, the mention of "substitute" (*ādeśa*) and the mention of "preverb" (*upasarga*) are drawn forward [from the previous rule].
This is for the purpose of excluding their recurrence in what follows.

26. *cchandasyṛdavagrahāt*—(8.4.26). That which is recited by being separated [from the following word] is called an *avagraha*. An *ṛdavagraha* is that which is both an *ṛk* (a vowel *ṛ*) and an *avagraha*.
From the vowel *ṛ*, from an *avagraha*, and from a preceding member (*pūrvapada*)—these are the three [conditions].

The fifth case endings are in apposition. By implication, he shows that because the entire preceding member (*pūrvapada*) cannot be merely the phoneme *ṛ*, the word "preceding member" refers here to a portion of the preceding member, namely the *ṛ* sound. For words that denote wholes sometimes also apply to their parts.

Thus, for example, in the expression "the cloth is burnt," the word *paṭa* refers to a single part of the cloth. [The reading in the printed edition is *ityata*. In the term *nṛmaṇāḥ*, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose mind (*manas*) is in man (*nṛ*)" (*nari manaḥ asya*). The lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.14). In the term *pitṛyāṇam*, [it is derived from] that by which they go (*yānti anena*).
*Yānam*: [the suffix] *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). "The vehicle (*yāna*) of the father" is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

With the words "for here," etc., he demonstrates that the vowel *ṛ* constitutes an *avagraha*. Regarding the phrase "the mention of *avagraha*," etc.: if the mention of *avagraha* were not made, [the rule would not apply].

Therefore, [the rule] would apply from an *ṛ* vowel that is not at the end of a word (*avyapadānta*) and not followed by a consonant (*anavagrahyaṇa*). But this being the case, it does not apply here. For *avagraha* occurs only for what is at the end of a word (*padānta*), not for what is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*). On this point, the view of some is as follows: although the term "in *saṃhitā*" (*saṃhitāyām*) from [Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.72] is understood to carry over here [from 8.2.108].

It is not [always] nasalized, because of the mention of *avagraha*; therefore, only when the vowel *ṛ* is actually nasalized (*avagṛhyate*) does the change to *ṇ* occur, and not otherwise. However, others maintain that just as one is called a "dancer" (*nartaka*) even when not currently dancing because of his fitness for dancing, so too [the word is used] even when it is not being nasalized.
The letter *ṛ* is called "avagraha" (separation) because it is suitable for avagraha. Therefore, this is what is meant:

from the letter *ṛ* that is suitable for avagraha, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs; thus, when "avagraha" is mentioned, since the context concerns *saṃhitā*, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs only in *saṃhitā*, and not from [the letter *ṛ*] in its state as an avagraha.
27. *naśca dhātusthoruṣubhyaḥ* (8.4.27). That which stands in a verbal root (*dhātu*) is called *dhātustha*; [the suffix] *ka* is applied here by [Pāṇini 3.2.4] *supi sthaḥ*.
In the case of *ūru* and *ṣu*, there is a reference to their own forms (*svarūpagrahaṇa*). [The word] *nas* [is used].

There is a general inclusion of both the nasal substitute (*nāsikādeśa*) and the *asmad* substitute (*asmadādeśa*). Therefore, in this instance, only the *asmad* substitute is subject to the grammatical operation, not the other; for the other is impossible after [elements] such as those standing at the beginning of a verbal root (*dhātustha*), whereas the nasal substitute will be subject to the operation later on.

Regarding the phrase "ṭhrakṣā ṇaḥ": from the verbal root *rakṣa* in the sense of "to protect" (Dhātupāṭha 658), the form is derived using the imperative (*loṭ*) mood, ending in the second person singular. For the following second-person plural form of the pronoun *asmad*, the substitution of *nas* occurs according to the rule "bahuvacanasya asnasau" (Pāṇini 8.1.21). Furthermore, the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule "dvyaco'tastiṅḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.135).

By [Pāṇini 6.3.135], there is lengthening of the preceding word. Regarding "śikṣā naḥ": from the root *śikṣ* in the sense of "acquiring knowledge" (Dhātupāṭha 605)—from such a root as this, the replacement *naḥ* occurs for *asmad*. Regarding "uruṃ naḥ kṛdhi": from the root *kṛ*, the imperative (*loṭ*), second person singular (*sip*); [the suffix] *si* becomes *hi* and is also *apit*.

By [Pāṇini 3.4.87], *hi* is substituted for *hi*. By [Pāṇini 6.4.102], *hir* is substituted for *hi* in the Vedic language (*chandas*). By [Pāṇini 8.3.50] et al., the *visarjanīya* is changed to *s* according to the rule "kaḥ karat.
Regarding "abhīṣu ṇaḥ," there is lengthening by [Pāṇini 6.3.134], "ikaḥ suñi," and [Pāṇini 8.3.107], "suñaḥ."

Thus, there is the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*]. Similarly, in the case of "ūrṣva ūṣu ṇaḥ," there is lengthening of the vowel *u* by the rule "nipātasya ca" (Pāṇini 6.3.126), and the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule "suñaḥ" (8.3.107). By the word "ca" (and), the phrase "chandasi" (in the Veda) from rule 8.4.26 is drawn forward, for the purpose of excluding its recurrence in the subsequent rules.
28. *upasargādbahulam*—(8.4.28).

Since the substitute *naṣ* does not denote an action, it is impossible for it to function as a prefix (*upasarga*) with respect to that [substitute]. Therefore, this mention of "prefix" (*upasarga*) is understood to be intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) of *pra* and the other [prefixes]. [The example is] "from *pratha*."

As before, for *asmad* there is *naḥ*—[in the phrase] "pranaṃsam. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose nose (*nāsikā*) has gone away" (*pragatā*). The suffix *ac* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) by [Pāṇini 5.4.119], *upasargācca*; furthermore, the substitution of *nas* for *nāsikā* takes place.

29. *kṛtyaca* (Pāṇini 8.4.29). [The rule states: "A *nakāra* situated in a *kṛt*-suffix, followed by a vowel (*ac*). By this, he shows that the qualification "followed by a vowel" applies specifically to the *nakāra*, and not to the *kṛt*-suffix itself. If it were a qualification of the *kṛt*-suffix alone...

It might be argued: "In the word *pravapaṇam*, the substitution of *ṇ* would not occur, for here there is no *kṛt* suffix following a vowel; however, the letter *n* certainly exists [after the vowel]. If this were a qualification of the *kṛt* suffix, then the mention of *kam* and the others in rules such as *na bhābhūpūkamigamipyāyī* (Pāṇini 8.4.24) would be purposeless."

It might be argued: [this cannot be so] because of the absence of application. For a *kṛt* suffix that is prescribed after these [roots] cannot possibly follow a vowel (*ac*), since they do not end in a vowel. Therefore, it is appropriate that this be a qualifier of the letter *n*. [It refers to] those *kṛt*-suffixes for which the substitution of *ṇ* is possible.

To demonstrate this, he says: "The suffixes *ana*, *māna*, *anīya*, etc. Here, *ana* refers to the substitute for *yu*. *Māna* refers to the suffixes *śānac*, *kānac*, and *cānaś*. *Anīya* is that which is prescribed by the rule 3.1.96 (*tavyattavyānīyaḥ*). *Ani* is that which is prescribed by the rule 3.3.112 (*ākrośe nañyaniḥ*).
Thus, [the suffix] *ini*: by the rules "supyajātau ṇinistācchīlye" (Pāṇini 3.2.78), "āvaśyakādhamarṇyayoriniḥ" (3.3.112), [and again] *ini*:
by the rules "supyajātau ṇinistācchīlye" (3.2.78) and "āvaśyakādhamarṇyayoriniḥ" (3.3.170).

Thus [it is said]; and this is one where the suffixal connection has been dropped. Regarding the substitute for the *niṣṭhā* [suffix]: that which is prescribed in the section beginning with "ṭhradābhyāṃ niṣṭhāto naḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.42). "Prayāṇam"—here, as before, the suffix *lyuṭ* is added to the root *yā*. "Prayāyamāṇam"—here, the *lakāra* [verbal suffix] is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).

The suffix *śānac* [is applied]; the suffix *yak* [is applied] by the rule *āne muk* (Pāṇini 7.2.82), resulting in *prayāṇīyam*. [The suffix] *anīyar* [is applied], resulting in *aprayāṇiḥ* [by the rule] *ākrośe nañyaniḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.112). [The form] *prayāyiṇau* [is derived] with the suffix *yuk* [added] by the rule *āto yukciṇkṛtoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.33).

Regarding the word *prahīṇaḥ*: the root is *ohāk* in the sense of "abandoning" (*tyāge*, Dhātupāṭha 1090). By the rule *oditaśca* (Pāṇini 8.2.45), the *t* is replaced by *n*; and by the rule *dhumāsthā* (Pāṇini 6.4.66), the *iṭ* augment is applied [to the root vowel], resulting in *prahīṇaḥ*.
Regarding the word *pramagnaḥ*: the root is *ṭua masjo* in the sense of "cleansing" (*śuddhau*, Dhātupāṭha 1415). [The form is derived] by the rule *masjinaśorjhali*... [etc. (Pāṇini 7.1.60).

Thus, by [Pāṇini 7.1.60], the augment *num* is applied. And that *num*, being before the letter *c* [of *bhavañc*]—[the reading in the Kāśikā is "bhavañcakārāt"]—occurs prior to it; for it is stated in the Vārttika: "They desire the *num* to be placed before the final [consonant] of the root *majj*, for the purpose of preventing the elision of the *anuṣaṅga* and the initial of the *saṃyoga*. (Vārttika 7).

By virtue of the rule *aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti* (6.4.24), there is the elision of the *n* of this [root], and by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca* (8.2.29), there is the elision of the *s*. By the rule *coḥ kuḥ* (8.2.30), there is the substitution of *k* for the *c*—thus we have *paribhukvaḥ*. The root *bhuñj* is used in the sense of "crookedness" (*kauṭilye*) [Dhātupāṭha 1417].

Regarding the word "nirviṇṇaḥ": it has the form of one of the roots meaning "to investigate" or "to consider gain and loss," and not of the root *vida* "to know" (DhP 1064), because [the latter] is *seṭ* (possessing the augment *iṭ*), which would result in the form *sasya*.
In this case, the vowel *a* does not become *u*; therefore, the form *nirviṇṇasya* is established.
The term *upasaṃkhyānam* means that an addition must be made; the demonstration here is as follows:
the word *bahulam* ("optionally" or "in many cases") is carried over from the preceding sūtra, and by that, the rule will apply even when the following [element] does not end in a vowel (*anac*).

30. *ṇervibhāṣā* (8.4.30). Since the preceding rule would have made [the substitution] compulsory, this is commenced for the purpose of providing an option. If this were so, the mention of *vibhāṣā* would be redundant; for the option would follow from the very fact of the rule’s commencement.

Is it understood? No; for the opposite [interpretation] might also be possible. However, this is a mandatory rule (*nityavidhi*), whereas the preceding sūtra is optional (*vibhāṣā*) due to the continued application of the term "mostly" (*bahulagrahaṇa*). By saying "that which is prescribed after a causative suffix" (*ṇyantāt*), he shows that the word "after a causative suffix" (*ṇeḥ*) functions as a qualifier of what is prescribed (*vihitaviśeṣaṇatva*). And of that...

The purpose will be stated in the commentary: "being caused to go. The suffix *ṇic* is applied by the rule "hetumati ca" (Pāṇini 3.1.26), and the augment *puk* is added by the rule "artihrī" (Pāṇini 7.3.36), etc.

31. *halaścejupadhāt*—(8.4.31). The particle *ca* is for the purpose of drawing forward the option (*vibhāṣā*). By means of this, the rule that follows becomes obligatory. [The example is] *prakopadham*. The root *kupa* is used in the sense of "anger" (*kopa*) (DhP 1233).

[The examples] "ṭhprahaṇam" and "prohaṇam. [The roots] "īha ceṣṭāyām" (DhP 6.32) and "ūha vitarka" (DhP 6.48). Here, by the rule "kṛtyacaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.29), the substitution [of ṇatva] occurs invariably.
But how is it known that the mention of "hal" here is a qualifier of the initial [consonant], and not of the final one? To this [it is replied]:

He says: "Of that which has *ij* as its penultimate letter," and so forth. Since all roots having *ij* as their penultimate letter necessarily end in a consonant (*hal*), the mention of *hal* (consonant), although its purpose [to indicate the ending in a consonant] is already established by the fact of having *ij* as the penultimate, is understood as a qualification of the initial [element].
32. *ijādeḥ sanumaḥ* (8.4.32). [The word] *hal* is understood [from the previous rule]. He will state the purpose of its recurrence. Now, one might object:
in the preceding rule, the mention of *hal* was a qualification of the initial [sound]; what is the purpose here, given that it is a qualification of the final [sound]?

Thus he says: "by that," and so forth. For there exists no verbal root (*dhātu*) such as *ij* etc. that begins with a consonant (*hal*); rather, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), because the term *hal* is understood from the previous rule, the rule of "ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. "Of one having *num*" means "of one having an *anusvāra*. Why is this so?
Because the mention of *num* is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *anusvāra*. Why is it explained in this way? Because this rule (*yoga*) serves a restrictive purpose (*niyamārtha*).
And its status as a restrictive rule holds only if the mention of *num* is intended as an indicator for *anusvāra*, and not otherwise. This being so...

In a rule that is already mandatory, the inclusion [of a specific term] is understood to serve as a restrictive purpose (*niyamārthatā*). If the mention of *num* were intended solely to indicate *mum*, it would not serve to characterize the *anusvāra*;
it would not serve to characterize the *anusvāra*. And this being the case, where [the rule] "after a *kṛt*-suffix ending in a vowel" (Pāṇini 8.4.29) [applies]...

By this [rule], it is not established; in that case, its status as something to be prescribed (*vidheya*) would indeed exist. Where is it not established by this? [In the word] *pradhvanam*, derived from the root *dhvṛ* (DhP 587) meaning "pervasion" (*vyāpti*). Here, although the rule *aṭ-ku-pv-anuṃ-vyavāye 'pi* (Pāṇini 8.4.2) continues to apply, nevertheless, it does not apply here by that [rule].

[The suffix] *num* is obtained; for the mention of *num* is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of *anusvāra*, and since there is no *anusvāra* here [in the case of *prāpnoti*], one who desires this [rule] to have a restrictive purpose (*niyamārthatā*) must understand that the mention of *num* serves as an indicator of *anusvāra*. Thus...

In cases such as *preṅkhaṇam*, since the rule would already be established by Pāṇini 8.4.29 (*kṛtyacaḥ*), this [rule] serves as a restrictive provision (*niyamārtha*). Furthermore, it is understood from the composition of the extensive sūtra 6.4.71 (*ijādeḥ sanumaḥ*) that the inclusion of *num* is intended to indicate the presence of the *anusvāra*. For if the mention of *num* were...

The *nu* would serve as the indicator alone and not for the purpose of indicating the *anusvāra*; in that case, one should have simply said "of *iva*" (*iveḥ*). For there exists no other root beginning with *iva* that ends in a consonant and possesses the *nu* augment, except for *ikhi* and so forth. If it is argued that such roots as *ikhi* do exist—no, because [the *nu*] is applied only when the *anusvāra* has already been made.

Because of the absence of *num*: regarding the term "preṅkhaṇam. In forms such as "akha vakha" (the *prā.mu.* reading is *nakha*), the root *ikhi* is recited with a velar (*ka-varga*) ending; because of its *it*-designation, *num* is applied by Pāṇini 7.1.58, and an *anusvāra* is substituted by 8.3.24 (*naścāpadāntasya jhali*). Then, by the rule "anusthārasya yayi... [the *anusvāra* is replaced by a nasal corresponding to the following semivowel].
According to the rule (8.4.58), there is *parasavarṇa* substitution [though this is not present in the Prācīna-mu-pāṭha];

however, because that [substitution] is considered *asiddha*, this remains simply an *anusvāra*. Thus: *prombhaṇam*. [The root] *ubha* / *unbha* is used in the sense of "filling" (*pūraṇe*; DhP 1319, 1320); the *anusvāra* is applied as before.

But is this not already established by the rule *kṛtyacaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.29)? Why, then, is this [new rule] commenced? To this he says: "Even though it is established," and so forth. Regarding the word *pramaṅganam*: the root *magi* is recited in that very list of roots meaning "to go" (*gatyartha*). In some places, however, the reading is *pramaṅkanam*; that [root] belongs to the class *maki maṇḍane* ("to adorn").
This [rule] is to be understood as belonging to *dhā.pā.* 89. Now, an injunction for restriction (*niyamārthatā*) occurs only when there is nothing else to be enjoined;
however, here, since the substitution of *ṇatva* is already optionally applicable after a root ending in *ṇi*, a mandatory (*nitya*) *ṇatva* must be enjoined—according to the principle:
"When both an original injunction (*vidhi*) and a restrictive rule (*niyama*) are possible, the original injunction is superior. (Vyāḍiparibhāṣā 130).

Thus, this [rule] is for the sake of a constant injunction (*vidhi*) regarding the causative suffix (*ṇic*); why does it not apply? To this he says: "Because of the governing influence (*adhikāra*) of the word *hal*," and so forth. From the preceding rule, the word *hal* is carried over (*anuvartate*), and by that, it is stated that the rule applies to that which ends in *hal*. For a verbal root (*dhātu*) ending in the causative suffix (*ṇic*) does not itself end in a consonant (*hal*). Why?
What then? [The suffix] *sac* is applied. And that which is prescribed after a stem ending in a consonant (*halanta*) cannot apply to one ending in a vowel (*ajanta*);

therefore, this rule does not serve as a permanent injunction for the causative (*ṇyanta*) form. But surely, once the *ṇi*-suffix has been elided, even the causative form ends in a consonant; consequently, even under the governing heading "after a consonant" (*halaḥ*), the suffix should indeed occur.
Is it for the purpose of enjoining [the suffix]? This is not the case; for one resorts to the qualification of that which has already been enjoined.

To refute this objection, he says: "The *kṛt* suffix that is enjoined after a root ending in a consonant, beginning with *i*, *u*, or *ṛ*, and followed by *sam* or *us*"—thus, the qualification of "enjoined" (*vihita*) is resorted to.
33. *vā niṃsa-ṇikṣa-ṇindām*—(Pāṇini 8.4.33). The roots *ṇisi* "to kiss" (Dhātupāṭha 1025), *ṇikṣi* "in anger" (Dhātupāṭha 659;

the reading *nakha-* is found in the Prākṛta-mañjarī), and *ṇidi* "to blame" (Dhātupāṭha 66)—because these have *ṇ* as their upadeśa (original formative element)—[the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* is optional].
Since [the substitution] would have been mandatory by the rule "after a prefix" (8.4.14) and so forth, this [sūtra] is commenced for the purpose of making it optional.
If that is so, the mention of the word *vā* ("or") need not be made; the optionality will result simply from the fact that a separate rule (*pṛthagyoga*) is formulated.
This is not the case; for the opposite might also be understood: that this [present] rule is mandatory, while that [previous one]...
Regarding the term *vibhāṣā*: after the rule "upasaragādasamāse" (Pāṇini 8.4.14), this [term] should have been placed;

its placement here is for the purpose of making known the obligatory nature (*nityatva*) of the preceding rule—that those [rules] which fall between two optional rules (*vibhāṣā*) [are indeed obligatory].
These injunctions are eternal.

34. *na bhābhūpūkamigamipyāyīveṣām*—(Pāṇini 8.4.34). [The variant reading *pyāyi* is found in the Prācya-mu-pāṭha. Regarding the mention of *pū*, it should be understood as referring to the root *pūñ*. [The root *pūḍ* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as meaning "purification" (No. 966).]

Thus, the inclusion of that which is recited in the *bhvādi* [class] is not intended; rather, the inclusion of that belonging to the *krayādi* [class] is intended. How is it that when "pū" is mentioned, the inclusion of *pūñ* alone is obtained? It is because of the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) in *Pāṇini* 8.4.29, *kṛtyacaḥ*, by [extracting] "kṛti"—for "the desired result is achieved through the separation of the rule."

(Vyā.pra. 87) Thus, by means of a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*), the substitution of *ṇ* occurs for the root *pūṅ* alone. In this way, since the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* situated in a *kṛt*-suffix following *pūṅ* has not been established through a split in the rule, it is understood by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) that the reference is to *pūñ* alone.
"Of those ending in ṇi," and so forth. Since roots ending in ṇi (such as *grah*) are distinct words, [the rule] does not apply to them.
Therefore, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must indeed be made. This means that its formulation is required.
In this regard, the following is the formulation: the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "not" (*na*) must be made; by means of that—

It will not apply even to those [roots] ending in the causative suffix *ṇi*. Furthermore, this being the case, the mention of roots beginning with *bhā* would not be purposeless; for it serves to indicate that the preceding rule does not have universal application. In this way, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is avoided.

35. *ṣāt*—[the substitution of] *ṣ* [occurs] for [a *visarjanīya*] at the end of a word. (8.4.35) As in *niṣpānam* and *duṣpānam*. Here, the *visarjanīya* undergoes the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *idudupadhasya* (8.3.41). In this case, there is an application of the rule *kṛtyacaḥ* (8.4.29).

“*Sarpiṣpānam*, *yajuṣpānam*” — this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). While the rule “*isusoḥ sāmarthye*” (Pāṇini 8.3.44) is in effect, the substitution of *ṣ* for the visarga is applied by the rule “*nityaṃ samāse*” (8.3.45), etc. In this case, [the optionality] is governed by the rule “*vā bhāvakaraṇayoḥ*” (8.4.10).
Such is the established conclusion.

One who, considering this to be a genitive compound (ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa) based on the rule "padāntāt," might raise an objection: "Why then is there no prohibition of the substitution of *ṇ* in the case of *susarpiṣkeṇa*? [In response: Here...

Is it that the letter *ṣ* is at the end of the word (*padasyāntaḥ*)? To this he replies: "In the middle of a word" (*pade antaḥ*), and so forth. For if it were a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), there would be a prohibition of the substitution of *ṇ*; however, this is not a genitive compound. What then?
It is a compound formed by the rule of *yogavibhāga* [splitting the sūtra] "after a locative case ending" (*saptamī*, Pāṇini 2.1.40)—that is, [the compound means] "in the middle when a word follows."

Regarding the term *padānte* (at the end of a word): here, the letter *ṣ* is not at the end of a word (*pada*) because the word *ka-* does not bear the designation of *pada*. Therefore, the prohibition of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) does not apply here. [The compound] *susarpiṣka-* is a *bahuvrīhi* meaning "one who has beautiful ghee (*sarpiḥ*)," with the suffix *kap* added according to Pāṇini 5.4.154: *śeṣādvibhāṣā*.

36. *naśeḥ ṣāntasya* | (8.4.36) A prohibition is made against the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*, which would otherwise have been required by the rule *upasargādasamāse* (8.4.14) and others. For example, in the word *pranaṣṭaḥ*. [The root] *ṇaś* [is used] in the sense of "disappearance" (*adarśane*) (Dhātupāṭha 1194); from this, the suffix *niṣṭhā* [is applied].

The augment *num* is applied by the rule *masjinaśorjhali* (7.1.60); the elision of the nasal (*n*) is by the rule *aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti* (6.4.24); the substitution of *ṣ* is by the rule on *vraśca* and so forth (8.2.36)—thus [we have] *praṇaśyati*. This [root] belongs to the *divādi* class, hence the suffix *śyan*.

Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the word "anta" (end)? For, since it is stated that "the *ṣ* [is substituted] for the root *naś*" (*naśeḥ ṣaḥ*), when the root *naś* is being specified, the rule "that by which a grammatical operation is prescribed applies to that which ends with it" (*yena vidhis tadantasya*, 1.1.72) will provide for the prohibition of the substitution of *ṇ* for a form ending in *ṣ*. To this, he says: "The inclusion of the word 'anta'... he says.
"[The suffix] will perish"—as before, when *ṣatva* has occurred, *katva* applies by the rule "ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si" (Pāṇini 8.2.41).

In this context, if the mention of the word "end" (*anta*) were not made, then since the state of ending in *ṣ* would no longer exist once *katva* had taken effect, the prohibition [of the augment *ṭ*] would not apply. But because this [mention of "end"] is present, it occurs even after *katva* has been applied. This very point...
For this is its purpose: so that the prohibition may apply even in the case of what was previously existent, provided it has now ceased.

37. *padāntasya* (8.4.37). This is stated as a prohibition of the *ṇatva* (nasalization of the following consonant) which would otherwise be obtained by the rule *ṭhāḍhaṇkupvāṅnumvyavāye’pi* (8.4.2). For example: *vṛkṣān*. [In this case, the substitution is governed by] *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ* (6.1.102).
By [Pāṇini 6.1.102], the vowel is lengthened; by [Pāṇini 6.1.103], "tasmāc chaso naḥ puṃsi," the *s* of *śas* is replaced by *n*.

38. *Padavyavāye ’pi* (8.4.38). Since both the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*naimittika*) have been treated as subsequent [to the preceding word], the separation (*vyavāya*) of both is understood; therefore, he says: "when there is a separation by a word (*pada*) between the cause and the effect," and so forth.

Regarding the expression “māṣakumbhavāpena”: a *kumbha* of beans is *māṣakumbha*; one who sows that is [called] *māṣakumbhavāpa*, according to Pāṇini 3.2.1 (*karmaṇyaṇ*). From that [form], the third-case singular ending is applied.
Here, the substitution [of *va* for *y*] is required by Pāṇini 8.4.11 (*prātipadikāntanumvibhaktiṣu ca*).

Regarding the expression "by means of the fourfold yoga" (*caturaṅgayogena*), the application [of the rule] is here by *kumati ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.13). The term *caturaṅga* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has four limbs. Consequently, *caturaṅgayoga* is a compound formed with the third case ending according to *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32), meaning "the agent or the instrument [is compounded] with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, frequently. In the preceding [example],...
The word *kumbha* [is used] in the sense of sexual intercourse, whereas later on, the word *aṅga* [is used]. Regarding the form *prāvanaddham*:

from the root *ṇaha* in the sense of "binding" (*dhā.pā.* 1166), the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is applied; then the rules *naho dhaḥ* (Pāṇ. 8.2.34), *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* (8.2.40), and *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* (8.4.53) must be applied.

This is a summary of the *gati* category. Here, the word *ava* causes an intervention. The application of *ṇatva*, however, occurs by the rule "upasargādasamāse’pi" (Pāṇini 8.4.14), etc. The same applies in the case of "pragāṃ nayāmaḥ. In this instance, the intervention is caused by the word "gām. This, however, is an example from Vedic usage (*cchāndasa*).
For in the spoken language (bhāṣā), there is no usage of prepositions (*upasarga*) separated from the verbal root (*dhātu*);
rather,

since the term "in Vedic" (*chandas*) is carried over from the rule "even when following [the root] in Vedic" (1.4.81), by the rule "and even when separated in Vedic" (1.4.82), separation occurs in Vedic.
It occurs as follows: for the vowel *au* of the word *go*, there is the substitution of *ā* by the rule “āṬto'mśasoḥ” (Pāṇini 6.1.93)—[resulting in *gām* and *gāḥ*].

Regarding the phrase “*padavyavāye*” and so forth: the meaning to be explained is that this prohibition which is stated regarding the intervention of a word (*padavyavāye*) applies when a *taddhita* suffix does not follow. In this regard, the following...

The meaning is "explanation. Here, the meaning is "this is the explanation": from the rule "vā niṃsa nikṣa nindām" (Pāṇini 8.4.33), the word "vā" (or) is carried over by the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūakapluti*); and that [option] is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Therefore, there will be no prohibition regarding that *taddhita* suffix. [The example is] “ārdragomaryeṇa.

*Gomayam* means "this belongs to a cow"—the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.3.145], *gośca purīṣe*. It is a *karmadhāraya* compound: "that which is both moist and cow-dung. There is an intervention by the word-element *go*.
And its designation as a *pada* is by means of [the rule] *svādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne* (Pāṇini 1.4.17).

39. *Kṣubhnādiṣu ca* (8.4.39). This is stated as a prohibition of the *ṇatva* (nasalization) that would otherwise be obtained by the rule *“ṭh-ravābhmāṃ no ṇaḥ”* (8.4.1), and so forth. The term *“kṣubhnā”* here is a mention of the specific form itself; it is not [a general class name].
The mention of *dhātu* (root)— otherwise, the prohibition would also apply here in the case of "kṣobhaṇam.

If that were so, then in the case of "kṣabhnanti," after the elision of the long *ā* by the rule "śnābhyastayor ātaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.112), [the same would apply] in the case of "kṣubhnītaḥ" [where the Prācya reading is "kṣudhvanītaḥ"].
Once the substitution of *i* has been made by [Pāṇini 6.4.113] *ṭhī-ilyadhoḥ*, the prohibition of *ṇatva* would not apply—

because the original form no longer exists? No, there is no fault, because of the status of a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for that which begins with *a* (the *a* of *an*), or because that which is modified by a substitute is not different from the original (Vyāḍipāda 16).
"These are the subsequent words," and so forth. By this, he demonstrates the application [of the rule] "after a preceding word, when a name is indicated, except for *go*" (Pāṇini 8.4.3).
Regarding "harindī": the suffix *ṇini* is used in the sense of habitual character (*tācchīlya*). Regarding "harinandanaḥ": [it is formed] with a suffix ending in *tyuṭ*.

This is a compound (*samāsa*). Similarly, in "harinagaram" [and] "giri-nagaram"—according to the *Kāśikā* and the *Padamañjarī*—the term "caṭ" here also indicates that this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) with "nagara.
Regarding "narīnṛtyate," the [doubling of the] reduplication is governed by the rule "rīgṛdupadhasya ca" (Pāṇini 7.4.90).
There is the addition of *r* [as a *vṛddhi* vowel], according to the rule *aṭkupvāṅ* (Pāṇini 8.4.2);

thus it is also in the case of *tṛpnoti*. [The root] *tṛp* [is used] in the sense of "to satisfy" (Dhātupāṭha 2195); by transposition, the suffix *śnu* is applied. [The forms] *parinartanam* and *parigahanam* are *gati*-compounds. [The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied] because of the rule *kṛtyacaḥ*.

(8.4.29) Thus is the derivation. “Śaraniveśādayaḥ,” ending with “darbhānūpaḥ,” are genitive (ṣaṣṭhī) compounds. Regarding “anūpaḥ”: it is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning “that in which waters have gone” (amugatā āpo yasmin).
The suffix *a* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) by the rule “ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmānakṣe” (Pāṇini 5.4.74).

By the rule *ṭhūlope pūrvasya dīrgho’ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.111), there is the substitution of *u* for *ū*; then, by the rule *vṛddhireci*, there is the lengthening of the homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*).
Regarding the statement “and the absence of *ṇ* after *ācārya*,” the word “and” (*ca*) implies the presence of *ṇ* as well; thus, an option (*vibhāṣā*) is established.
Because this is understood as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the substitution of *ṇ* occurs invariably in the form *ācāryeṇa*.

[The word] *ācāryabhogīnaḥ* [is derived as follows]: from the rule "After words ending in *ātman*, *viśvajana*, or another word signifying enjoyment (*bhoga*), the suffix *khañ* is applied" (Pāṇini 5.1.9). The application [of the doubling of the consonant] occurs by the rule "In the presence of *ṭh*, *ṭ*, *k*, *p*, *v*, or *āṅ*" (8.4.2), etc. Similarly, in the case of *ācāryānī*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* and the augment *ānuk* are added by the rule "After *indra*, *varuṇa*, etc. (4.1.49), and so forth.

Considering that the particle *ca* has the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccaya*), and thus indicates that the group beginning with *kṣubh* is not exhaustive, he says: "The *kṣubh*-group is an *ākṛtigaṇa*. [The reading *kṣudhvanītaḥ* appears in the Prācīna-mu-pāṭha.
40. *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.40).

“[The substitution of] *ṣ* occurs in place of *ś* and *cavarga* when there is *sannipāta*,” and so forth. *Sannipāta* means immediate succession (*ānantarya*). In the example “*vṛkṣaśśete*,” the *sakāra* replaces the *visarga* by the rule “*vā śari*” (Pāṇini 8.3.36);
this [present rule] then substitutes *ṣakāra* for that *sakāra*.
Regarding the form "majjati": the root *masj* means "to cleanse" (*tu masjo śuddhau*, Dhātupāṭha 1415). By the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* (Pāṇini 8.4.53), the *s* is replaced by *d*;

this *d* is then replaced by *j* by the present rule. One should not suspect that the substitution of *jaś* (the *j*) is "unestablished" (*asiddha*) when the substitution of *ścutva* (the *c*) is to be applied, because [the *j*] is included in the word *jhali* in the rule *masjinaśorjhali* (Pāṇini 7.1.60).

Because [the forms] *bhṛjjati* and *vṛścati* are taught with the substitution of *cut*; for if [the substitution] were not established (*asiddha*), this teaching would not be possible. [The forms] *yajñaḥ* and *pāññā* [are derived] by means of *samprasāraṇa* according to the rule *grahy-ādi* (Pāṇini 6.1.16). [The form] *yajñaḥ* is derived from the roots *yaj* and *yāc* by means of [the suffix] *na*, according to the rule *yajayāca* (Pāṇini 3.3.90), etc.

[Objection: Here, the two [sounds] *s* and the *tavarga* are the objects of the operation (*kāryin*), and there are likewise only two causes (*nimitta*)—namely, *ś* and the *cavarga*. Therefore, due to this equality, a correspondence according to numerical order (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) would result.

"Why does [the substitution] not occur when the letter *s* meets with *ś*, or when the *ta*-group meets with the *ca*-group? To this he says: "By [the rule] *śāt*," and so forth. For prohibitions are preceded by a possibility [of application]. If there were a correspondence according to the order of the causes (*nimitta*), then [the prohibition would apply] to the *ta*-group following *ś*.

If the elision of *cut* were non-existent, one would not have formulated the prohibition "śāt" (Pāṇini 8.4.44); yet it has been formulated. Therefore, this indicates that there is no mention of a numbered [element] (*saṃkhyātāmudeśa*).

In the rule *ṭhstoḥ ścunā*, although a locative case (*saptamī*) should have been used for the sake of brevity, the use of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) in *ścunā* is intended so that the operation may occur even when the *saṃnipāta* (conjunction) has already ceased to exist—as in *yajñaḥ* and *yācñā*. For if it were indicated by the locative, the principle would apply: "When [a grammatical element] is indicated by the locative, the operation affects what precedes it."
Thus, it should occur only with that which follows, not with that which precedes.
41. *ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ* (8.4.41).

Here too, the prohibition in *toḥ ṣi* (8.4.43) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the absence of "correspondence by number" (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*). For if there were correspondence by number with respect to the cause here as well—[namely,] with the letter *ṣ*—...

In a *sannipāta* (a combination of sounds), the substitution of *ṣṭu* for the dental class (*tavarga*) would not even apply; thus, one would not have formulated the prohibition in "toḥ ṣi" (Pāṇini 8.4.43). Yet, that rule has indeed been formulated; therefore, this very fact serves as the indicator (*liṅga*) here for the absence of *saṃkhyātānudeśa* (correspondence according to numerical order). For example: *vṛkṣaṣṭīkate*. [The roots] *tikṛ*, *ṭikṛ*, *ṭīkṛ*, and *ragi* [are involved].

[Regarding the root] *ṭhradhiḥ*—in the Dhātupāṭha, the roots *ladhi* are listed as having the meaning "to go" (DhP 105, 103, 104, 107, 108). Regarding "peṣṭā": the root *piplṛ* means "to crush" (DhP 1452). Regarding "kṛṣīṣṭa, kṛṣīṣṭhāḥ": this is the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of benediction (*āśis*) from the root *kṛ*; for that [root], there is the suffix *tathāsau*, followed by the augment *sīyuṭ*.

By the rule *ṭhlopo vyor vali* (6.1.66), there is elision of the *yakāra*; by *suṭ tithoḥ* (3.4.107), the augment *suṭ* is added; by *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (8.3.59), the substitution of *ṣ* occurs; and by this [rule], the substitution of *ṣṭu* takes place. Thus we have *agniciḍḍīnaḥ*. [The root] *ḍīṅ*... [ṭhṭhaṭṭa—Dhātupāṭha].

Regarding *vihāyasā gatau* (DhP 968): because it belongs to the *svadi*-group, there is the substitution of *ṇatva* by the rule *oditaśca* (8.2.45). Regarding *agniciḍh—aḍhāṬkte*: *ḍhāṬkṛ gatau* (DhP 98); [the forms] *aṭṭati*, *aḍḍhati*.
[The root] *atṭa* [is listed] in the sense of "transgressing and harming" (DhP)—that is, "transgressing and injuring."

(Dhātupāṭha 254), [aḍḍa— Dhātupāṭha ṭ (Dhātupāṭha 254), “adaḍa aniyoge” (Dhātupāṭha 348): the reading of these two roots, which have *t* and *v* as their penultimate vowels, in this list is for the purpose of hearing the sounds *s* and *d* after the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) when they appear with the suffix *kvip*.
42. *na padāntāṭṭoranām*—(8.4.42). This is a prohibition against the genitive plural form *ṭh-nām* when it lacks the augment *nuṭ*.
[The example is] *śvaliṭ-sāye*. When the augment *dhuṭ* does not occur by rule 8.3.29 (*ḍaḥ si dhuṭ*), [the *ṣatva* applies].
Thus, this is the example: "īṭṭe. [The root] "iḍa" is used in the sense of "praising" (DhP 1029).

Because it is *anudātta*, the *ātmanepada* suffix is applied; because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is *luk* elision of the *śap* suffix; and by the rule "khari ca" (8.4.55), the letter *ḍ* is changed to *ṭ*. In the case of "sarpiṣṭamam," [the suffix] "tamap" is added in the sense of "excessiveness" (*atiśāyana*).
By the rule *hrasvātādau taddhite* (8.3.101), the sibilant (*s*) becomes a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*).
Regarding the phrase *ṭhṣajñām*: by the rule *ṣaṭcaturmyaśca* (7.1.55), the augment *ṭuK* is added; then, by the rule *jhalāṃ jaśo'nte* (8.2.39), the sibilant (*ṣ*) is changed to a dental (*ḍ*).

By the rule *ṭhyaro'nunāsike'nunāsiko vā* (Pāṇini 8.4.45), the letter *ḍa* is replaced by *ṇa*. Thus we have "ṣaṇṇavatiḥ" (ninety-six). This is a compound with elision of the second member (*uttarapadalopa-samāsa*) according to the *śākapārthiva* class, meaning "ninety plus six. Similarly, the collection of six cities is "ṣaṇṇagarī."
The suffix *ṅīp* [is applied] by the rule "dvigoḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.21).

43. *toḥ ṣi* (8.4.43). For example: *ṭhagnicit—ṣaṇḍe*. [The suffix] *kvip* is applied by the rule *ṭhagnau ceḥ* (3.2.91), resulting in *agnicit*. [The example] *somasutṣaṇḍe* does not exist [in the Kāśikā]. [The suffix] *kvip* is applied by the rule *some suñaḥ*.

By the rule (3.2.90), the suffix *kvip* is applied; here, because of the mention of the locative case in the word “pi,” the substitution of *ṣṭu* indeed occurs due to the presence of the complete combination [of sounds], as in *peṣṭā* and *peṣṭum*.

"...*viśnaḥ*, *praśnaḥ*. [The roots] "√viccha, in the sense of going" (DhP 1423) and "√praccha, in the sense of desiring to know" (DhP 1413)—the suffix *naṅ* is applied as before; by the rule "cch-avoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca" (6.4.19), the *ch* of *cch* is replaced by *ś*. Although there is the rule "praśne cāsannakāle" (3.2.117)...
Although it is understood from the very occurrence [of the rule] that the substitution of *c* for the following *ś* does not apply to that group [of words],
nevertheless, this [sūtra] is commenced in order to avoid the difficulty of comprehension for those of dull intellect. Or rather, [it serves to indicate] that even [the rules] which are sublated...
It has been stated [in the *Pūjyapāda-vṛtti* 19]: "There are irregular formations (*nipātana*). If this were not undertaken, forms such as *praśna* and *viśna* would also be possible.
45. *yaro'nunāsike'nunāsiko vā* (8.4.45).

By the rule "of a [consonant] at the end of a word" (*padāntasya*), the term *padānta* ("end of a word") is understood from the preceding rule *na padāntāṭṭoranām* (8.4.42); and that [term], by implication, undergoes the state of being in the genitive case.

He demonstrates this: in the example beginning with "vāṅnyati," after the substitution of a *jaś* sound for the *jhal* sounds at the end of a word according to Pāṇini 8.2.39 (*jhalāṃ jaśo'nte*), the nasalization (*anunāsika*) must be applied to the letter *g*. Thus:
"vāṅmayam. Here, the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.3.144 (*nityaṃ vṛddhaśarādibhyaḥ*).
Regarding "ṭhtvaṅmayam"—here too, [the suffix -maya is applied] by the rule "mayaṅvaitayoḥ" (Pāṇini 4.3.143), etc.
46. *aco rahābhyāṃ dve* (Pāṇini 8.4.46). [The commentary says:

"The *repha* and *hakāra* that follow a *ṭha*-suffix. By this, he shows that *ac* is a qualifier of *ra* and *ha*. [He further quotes: "*ānyāmutarasya yaraḥ*" (Pāṇini 8.3.19). By this as well, [he indicates] *ra* and *ha*.

Regarding the specific qualification: "barkkaḥ. [This is derived from] the root *arc* in the sense of "worship" (*pūjāyām*)—(Dhātupāṭha 204)—with the suffix *dhañ*; then, by the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.52), there is the substitution of *k* for *c*.
Regarding "markkaḥ": *marci* is a root mentioned in the *sūtra*-tradition; from that [root]—

The suffix *kan* is applied by the rule "iṇ-bhī-kā-pā-śy-arti-arcibhyaḥ kan" (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.21), and the substitution of *k* for *c* is made by the rule "coḥ kuḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.30).
