Here, the letter *r* follows the vowel *a*, and the letter *k* follows that *r*. Regarding the word "brahmā": here too, the letter *h* follows the vowel *a*.
Therefore, the letter *m* is also followed by *y*, as in the word "apahnuve.
Here too, the letter *h* follows the vowel *a*, and as before, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix;
consequently, there is the doubling (*dvirvacana*) of the following letter *n*. In the word "kiṃ hnute," the letter *h* does not follow a vowel.
The letter *na* is not repeated in the form *bhavati*. Regarding the phrase "kim—hyalayati":
the roots *hval* and *hyal* mean "to move" (*sañcalane*; Dhātupāṭha 805, 806). The causative suffix *ṇic* is added.

According to the rule *jvala-hvala-hyala-namāmanupasargād vā* (Pāṇini 1.3.60; the reading in the Prācīnamudra edition is *jvala-hnala-hvala*), [the substitution of *la* for *ra* occurs optionally when these roots are without a prefix].
Following this (Pāṇini Dhātupāṭha 817), there is the designation *mit*— by which, according to Pāṇini 6.4.92 (*mitāṃ hrasvaḥ*),
shortening of the vowel occurs.

47. *anaci ca* (8.4.47). [The rule states: "When followed by a non-vowel (*anac*). A non-vowel (*anac*) is that which is other than a vowel (*ac*). That which has a non-vowel following it is "followed by a non-vowel" (*anacpara*). For example: *daddhy atra*. Here, the letter *dh*, which follows the vowel (*ac*), is a semi-vowel (*yar*).

When a non-vowel *y* follows it, there is doubling: by the rule “*jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*” (Pāṇini 8.4.53), the *dh* becomes *d*. Thus, we have *maddhv atra*. Here, there is doubling of the *dh* which is not followed by a non-vowel.

"Ṭhyaṇo mayaḥ," and so forth. It has been stated that there is reduplication of a *yar* (a consonant other than *ya*) following a vowel (*ac*). Since this would not apply when a *may* (the consonants *ma*, *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*) follows a *yaṇ* (a semivowel) before a vowel (*ac*), an additional rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is proposed. What, then, is the example here? He says: "Some," and so forth. "Ut-kkā."

In the passage beginning with "valmīkaḥ" and so forth, there is the doubling of the *yaṇ* (semivowel) following the *mayaṅ* (the letters *ma*, *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*) after a vowel: as in "dadhyy atra" and "madhvv atra. Furthermore, there is the doubling of the *yaṇ* following the *mayaṅ* after the letter *dha*: as in "dadhy atra" and "madhv atra."

Regarding the rule "ṭh-śaraḥ khayaḥ" and so forth: in the examples "stthālau" and "stthātā," there is reduplication of the *khay* sound *th*, which follows the *śara* sound *s*. In "vatssaḥ," there is reduplication of the *śara* sound *s*, which follows the *kha-y* sound *t*. In "ikcṣu" and "kaṣvīram," [the same applies].

From the letter *ka*—the doubling of the sibilant (*khara*) following the *kha*-group [is applied] to the letter *ṣa*, resulting in "apsarāḥ. From the letter *pa*—the doubling of the sibilant (*śara*) following the *sa* after the *kha*-group [is applied], according to the rule "at the end of a word (*avasāne*), there are two," and so forth. This [doubling] is applicable because of the reliance on the restrictive exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in the rule "and when *ava* follows" (*avaci ca*).

In the case of a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), however, one could have avoided [the explicit mention of] the word "optionally" (*vā*) by carrying over (*anuvartya*) it from the rule "when a nasal follows, [the preceding consonant] may optionally become a nasal" (Pāṇini 8.4.45). This is not so; for in a *prasajya-pratiṣedha*, the status of the sūtra as a prescriptive statement (*vidhi-vākyatva*) is not tenable, and consequently, by some [interpretation], there would be reduplication (*dvirvacana*).

It might be argued: "From that very prohibitive sentence itself, its status as an injunctive sentence would be inferred. This is not so; for when there is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), one resorts to *paryudāsa* (exclusionary negation) out of fear of the excessive complexity of the resulting cognition.

48. *nādiny-ākrośe putrasya* (8.4.48). Regarding the word *ādinī*: in the printed *Kāśikā* as well as in the *Padamañjarī*, the word *ādinī* is taken as ending in the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. This is a locative case (*parasaptamī*). Therefore, it says: "when *ādinī* follows."
Regarding the term "putrādinī": the suffix *ṇini* is applied here in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlye*), meaning "one whose nature it is to devour her sons.
Thus, "putrādinī" means "a female crocodile" (*siśumārī*). This is a statement of the actual fact; it is not an insult.
It should be stated that [the suffix applies] when followed by the word *para*; thus, the word *ādini* follows from which [the suffix is added].

The meaning is that from the word *putra*, it must be explained that the doubling [of the consonant] does not occur; this is the sense of the form of the rule. In this regard, the following is the explanation: the rule is divided by the separation (*yogavibhāga*) of the particle *na*;
by means of that, [the doubling] will not apply when followed by *tat*.

The phrase "or [the word] *hata*" and so forth means that one should explain the rule as having the sense that there is no doubling of the word *putra* when followed by the words *hata* or *jagdha*. This explanation, however,
is achieved either by carrying over the mention of the word *vā* (optionally) or by relying on the formation of a separate rule (*yogavibhāga*) using the word *na* (not).

It must be done. Nor does an option (vikalpa) apply here even in the case of "putrādi" and so forth, because it is understood as a restricted option (vyavasthitavibhāṣā). "Hata" (killed) and "jagdha" (eaten)—that is "hatajagdha";
and that which has "hatajagdha" as its subsequent member is "hatajagdhapara"; in that [case], i.e., in "hatajagdhapare."

*ṭhputrahatī*, *putrajagdhī*: [These are formed] by the *bahuvrīhi* compound "one by whom a son has been killed" (*putro hataḥ*) or "one by whom a son has been devoured" (*putro jagdhaḥ*). The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule "after a word that does not have a body-part as its prior member" (*asvāṅgapūrvapadāt*, Pāṇini 4.1.53). Regarding the phrase "the second letters of the *cay* group," etc.: *caya* is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), referring to the consonants *kha*, *cha*, *ṭha*, *tha*, *pha*.
This is the meaning of the term "second" (*dvitīya*). The state of being second for these consonants occurs in relation to the first consonant.
In the example "vapsaḥ," there is the doubling (*caya*) of the letter *t* when followed by the sibilant *s*, which is a *śar*;
the second *thakāra* [is substituted]. In "khṣīram," there is the doubling of the letter *k* when followed by the sibilant *ṣ*, which is a *śar*.

When followed by a sibilant (śar), the second of two consecutive s-sounds [is doubled]. For example, in the word *asarāḥ*, when the letter *p* is followed by *s* (which belongs to the *śar* group), the second *ph* sound [is doubled].

49. *śaro'ci* (Pāṇini 8.4.49). Regarding *ṭhkarvati*: the root is *kṛṣa vilekhane* (Dhātupāṭha 990). Regarding *varvati*: the roots are *pṛṣu vṛṣu mṛṣu secane* (Dhātupāṭha 705–707). Regarding *ādarśaḥ*: the root is *dṛśir*—

[The root] *prekṣaṇe* (Dhātupāṭha 988). The suffix *dhañ* is applied in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), resulting in "darśaḥ" (this is not found in the Kāśikā)—thus it is said. For this very reason, the suffix *dhañ* is also applied in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*).

50. According to Śākaṭāyana, [doubling occurs] when three or more consonants follow. (8.4.50) In examples such as *ṭhindraḥ*, there is the possibility of application by rule 8.4.47 (*anaci ca*). Thus: *indraḥ*, *candraḥ*, *mandraḥ*. [The roots are: *idi* in the sense of supreme sovereignty (DhP 63); *cadi* in the sense of delight (or, according to some, delight and radiance).
And—the *Dhātupāṭha* (68): “*madi* [means] praise, joy, giving, eating, desire, and motion.

By the rule “*sphāyitañci-*” (*Daiva-nighaṇṭu* 8.31), etc., the suffix *rak* is applied. Thus: “*rāṣṭraḥ*, *bhrāṣṭraḥ*” [i.e., *rāṣṭram*, *bhrāṣṭram*—according to the *Kāśikā*]. [The roots] “*rājṛ* and *bhrājṛ* [mean] shining.”

[From the roots] *ṭua* and *bhrājṛ* in the sense of "shining" (*dīptau*)—(DhP 822, 823). The suffix *ṣṭran* is added according to the rule "after all roots, *ṣṭran*" (DaU 8.79). The change to *ṣ* is applied by the rule concerning the *vrāca*-class (Pāṇini 8.2.36). The mention of Śākaṭāyana is for the sake of honor. This rule is indeed obligatory; otherwise, it would have been accomplished by the subsequent rule alone.
Because it is already established, its commencement would be purposeless.

51. *sarvatra śākalyasya* (8.4.51). This rule is commenced for the sake of [grammarians] beginning with Atri. In examples such as *arkaḥ*, there is the application of [Pāṇini 8.4.46]: *aco rahābhyāṃ dve*. Although the result would be established even for those beginning with Atri by the very force of this commencement (*ārambhasāmarthya*), the inclusion of the word *sarvatra* ("everywhere") [is for the following purpose].

[The phrase] "even though the preceding [rule] has already applied" is a prohibition; this is for the purpose that there may also be a prohibition even when [the rule] has already applied—as printed in the Prācīna-mudrita edition and the Kāśmīra-mudrita edition.
In its absence, by reason of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), only the application of "anaci ca" (Pāṇini 8.4.47) would occur.

There would be a prohibition—the mention of Śākalya is for the sake of honor, not for the sake of an option. Both the injunction and the prohibition are stated by means of two rules; here, the option follows from the very force of the context.
It will be so; otherwise, there would be no scope for the injunction.

52. *dīrghād ācāryāṇām*—(8.4.52). This rule is commenced for the sake of making [the doubling] obligatory (*nitya*). Here, although the result is already established by the very force of the commencement [of the rule], the mention of *ācāryāṇām* (of the teachers) is for the purpose of honor (*pūjārtha*). In examples such as *dātadram*, there would otherwise be the application of [the doubling] by the rule *anaci ca* (8.4.47).

53. *Jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* (Pāṇini 8.4.53). [Examples include] *ṭhlabdhā* and so forth. From the root *labh*, the suffixes *tṛc*, *tumun*, and *tavya* are applied. By the rule *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* (8.2.40), when there is a *jhaś* sound, namely the letter *dh*, the *jaś*-ness of the letter *bh* occurs, resulting in the letter *b*. Thus, *degdhā*.
Regarding "dogdhā"—according to the *Kāśikā*: from the root "diha" (DhP 1015) meaning "to accumulate," the letter *h* becomes *dh* by the rule "dāderdhātorghaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.32). Regarding "boddhā":
the letter *dh* becomes *d* by the rule "jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi" (Pāṇini 8.4.53).
54. *abhyāse carcā* (8.4.54). By means of the letter *ca*, the mention of *carcā* is carried over [from the previous rule]; therefore, it does not recur in what follows.
[The example is] *cikhan-iṣati*. From the root *khan* with the suffix *san*: reduplication, then the substitution of the remaining initial consonant (*hal-ādi-śeṣaḥ*).

By the rule "ṭhkuhoścuḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.62), there is the substitution of the *cut* sound—the letter *ch*; in its place, the letter *c* [is substituted]. Thus, one says "cicchitsati" (or as read in the Kāśikā-prakriyā-mukha-pāṭha: "cic-chitsati"). This is derived from the root *chid* with the suffix *san*, followed by reduplication, the insertion of *tuk* by the rule "che ca" (6.1.73), and the *cut* substitution.

“*ṭhṭhiṭhakārayiṣati*” means “he causes [someone] to express the letter *a*. By the rule “*tatkaroti tadācaṣṭe*” (Dhātupāṭha 200, 201), the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied; then, due to the treatment as if it were the superlative suffix (*iṣṭhan*), there is the elision of the suffixal *ṭi*; then the desiderative suffix (*san*); then the augment *iṭ*; then *guṇa* substitution; and finally the replacement by *ay*. “*tiṣṭhāsasi*” [is derived as follows]: by the rule “*śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ*” (Pāṇini 7.4.61), all the remaining consonants (*khayaḥ*) except the first (*śar*) are elided.

Regarding "ṭhphakārayiṣati": this has the same grammatical derivation as "ṭiṭhakārayiṣati"; however, the distinction here is that the suffix *ṇic* is applied after the word "phakāra"—according to the rule "sounds occurring in the base remain as they are in the derivative"—in order to prevent the application of the *jaś*-rule.

The term *prakṛticara* means that which functions according to its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) like the rain-cloud (*parjanya*), having the form of the original base (*prakṛti*) and being non-different in form from the original element (*sthānin*). In the example *cicīṣati*, there is lengthening by the rule *ajjhanagamāṃ sani* (Pāṇini 6.4.16). In *titīrṣati*, [the rules] *na staḥ* (not present) and *ṛtaḥ* (from the *Kāśikā*) [apply].
By the rule *iddhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.100), there is the substitution of *i* and the subsequent replacement by *r*; then, by *hali ca* (8.2.77), a long vowel is substituted.
Regarding the form *jijhakārayiṣati*, it is explained that the suffix *ṇic* is applied to the word *jhakāra*.
This has the same derivation as *ṭiṭhakārayiṣati*. Here, the suffix *ṇic* is added to the word *jhakāra*.
The distinction [is as follows]: regarding the form "jighatsati," from the root *ad* with the suffix *san*, there is the substitution of *ghasṛ* by rule 2.4.37 (*luṅsanorghaslṛ*).

As before, there is the change of the reduplicated syllable to a palatal (*cutva*), resulting in the letter *jh*; this undergoes the change to a voiced unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*), resulting in the letter *j*. Then, by rule 7.4.49 (*saḥ syārdhadhātuke*), the *s* [of the suffix] [becomes *iṭ*].

The letter *ṭ*. Regarding the form “ḍuḍhāṬkiṣate”: this is the desiderative (*san*) of the root *ḍhāṬk* [with the augment *ṭ*]. According to the rule “the *jaś* sounds of the original base become the *jaś* sounds,” and for the purpose of preventing the *cari* substitution, as before—the *jaś* sounds that are identical in form to their original substituends (*sthānin*) are called "original *jaś*" (*prakṛtijaś*). Thus, one obtains the form “jijaniṣate.”
As before—the *ātmanepada* ending by rule 1.3.62 (*sanaḥ*)—[we have] "bubudhe.

The *ātmanepada* ending occurs because [the root] is *anudāteta*; the substitution of *eś* for *ta* and *jha* of the *liṭ* [perfect tense] occurs by rule 3.4.81 (*liṭastajhayoreśirec*). [We have] "dadau. The substitution of *au* for the *ā* of the *ṇal* suffix occurs by rule 7.1.34 (*āta āṬ ṇalaḥ*). [We have] "ḍiḍaḷe."

Thus: from the root *ḍīṅ* in the sense of "motion through the air" (*vihāyasā gatau*, Dhātupāṭha 968), there is the substitution of *eś* for the root vowel as before, and by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, the reduplication of *ḍī* occurs.

55. *svarati-sūti-sūyati-dhūñ-ūdito vā* (8.4.55). In the example "yuyutsate," the suffix *san* is added to the root *yudh*; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule "pūrvavat sanaḥ" (1.3.62). In "āripsate," the suffix *san* is added to the roots *rabh* and *labh*. [The rule] "sani mīmā—" [applies].

By [the rule] *ityādines*—namely, “*skoḥ saṃyogādyoranta ca*” (Pāṇini 8.2.29), there is the elision of the letter *s*. By “*atra lopo’bhyāsasya*” (7.4.58), there is the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). The particle *ca* has the sense of conjunction; it indicates that these changes occur not only before a vowel (*acar*), but also before a *khari* (voiceless consonant).

Furthermore, if this particle *ca* were not present, there might arise a misconception in some slow-witted person that the *cartva* (the substitution of *r* for *l*) prescribed immediately preceding would apply only when a consonant (*khar*) or the like follows as the cause for reduplication— as in *tiṣṭhāsatī* and so on— but not even in cases such as *cakhāda*.

Since the substitution of *jaś* [j, b, g, d, d] for *ṭh* and *jhal* [all consonants except semivowels and nasals] at the end of a word (*ante*) is obligatory by rule 8.2.39, this sūtra prescribes the optional substitution of *car* [c, t, k, t, p] in the *avasāna* (pause) position. Because of the mention of "optionally" (*vā*), the *jaś* substitution also indeed occurs in the alternative case.

57. *Aṇ* not being a *pragṛhya* vowel becomes nasalized [before a following vowel]. (8.4.57) The term "*aṇaḥ*" is a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated designation) formed by the previous *ṇ* [in Pāṇini’s alphabet]; otherwise, for the sake of avoiding ambiguity, he would have said "*acaḥ*". Furthermore, there are no *hal* (consonants) that are *aṇ* at the end of a word. [Examples: *dīrghā*, *madhuā*.

Thus: by the rule "svamornapuṃsakāt" (Pāṇini 7.1.23), there is elision of the suffixes *su* and *am* [in the nominative and accusative singular neuter], resulting in "agnī" and "vāyū. By the rule "prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.102), a long vowel is substituted;
and by the rule "īdūdeddvivacanam" (Pāṇini 1.1.11), these receive the designation *pragṛhya*.

58. *Anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.58). Examples include *śaṅ-ki-tā* and so forth. [The roots are: *śaki* in the sense of "doubt" (Dhātupāṭha 86), *ucchi* in the sense of "gleaning" (Dhātupāṭha 215), *kuḍi* in the sense of "burning" (Dhātupāṭha 270), and *ṭuanadi* in the sense of "rising up" (Dhātupāṭha 67).
From the root *kapi* (meaning "to move," Dhātupāṭha 375), the suffixes *tṛc* and others are applied; because of the marker *id*, the augment *num* is added.

By the rule *naścāpadāntasya jhali* (Pāṇini 8.3.24), an anusvāra is substituted [for the *m*], and by this [present rule], that [anusvāra] is replaced by a homogeneous following sound (*parasavarṇa*).
Thus we have *kurvanti* and *kṛṣanti*. [The former is from] *kṛ*, and [the latter is from] *kṛṣa* (meaning "to scratch," Dhātupāṭha 1286).
And from this root belonging to the *tud-ādika* class, the substitute *jhi* for the *laṭ* affix undergoes the substitution of *anta* by "jho'ntaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.3).
When the *n* of *anta* becomes an *anusvāra*, and that [anusvāra] is replaced by a nasal homogeneous with the following sound (*parasavarṇa*), it becomes *na*.

By the rule "ṭhaṭkupvāṅnum" (Pāṇini 8.4.2), the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) would apply; why, then, does it not occur? To this he says: "In this case," and so forth. Would the substitution of *ṇ* occur here before the anusvāra or after it? First, it does not occur before; because when the anusvāra is to be produced...
The substitution of *ṇ* is considered *asiddha*; therefore, first the *anusvāra* is applied to the *n*.

Once the *n* has been changed to its *parasavarṇa*, the substitution of *ṇ* does not subsequently take place either, because the substitute for the *anusvāra* is *asiddha* when the substitution of *ṇ* is to be performed—this is what is meant by "by the *parasavarṇa*."

The meaning is: "by means of the grammatical rule intended for the purpose of *parasavarṇa*. [The designation applies] because of that purpose—that is, the name is applied on account of its being for that end—just as a jasmine flower intended for a lamp is called a "lamp. The word "again" (*punaḥ*) means: at a time subsequent to the operation of the *anusvāra*. By the words "in this way" (*evam*) and so forth, the *nakāra* has become an *anusvāra*.

In the Bhāṣya, regarding the statement "it transcends the substitution of *ṇ*," the transcendence of the substitution of *ṇ* is said to refer to the *nakāra* that has become an *anusvāra*. He demonstrates that precisely because of its being *asiddha*, the substitution of *ṇ* does not occur for the *nakāra* that is a *parasavarṇa*. The word "transcends" (*atikrāmati*) means that it exists having transcended [the previous state].

Regarding the form "ācikraṃsyate": from the root *kram* preceded by the prefix *ā*, the suffix *luṭ* is applied; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used according to Pāṇini 1.3.40, "āṅ udgamane" (the prefix *āṅ* [is used] in the sense of rising). Regarding "ācikraṃsate" (as given in the Kāśikā):
the middle voice is used according to Pāṇini 1.3.62, "pūrvavat sanaḥ" (the same [voice applies] as for the preceding [root] when followed by the desiderative suffix *san*).

59. *vā* [is applied] to that which stands at the end of a word. (8.4.59) The mention of *vā* is for the purpose of making known the obligatory (*nitya*) nature of the preceding rule—on the grounds that those rules which fall between two optional (*vibhāṣā*) rules are themselves obligatory. If the mention of *vā* were absent, the opposite would be the case.
It might be supposed: "The previous rule is optional, but this present rule is compulsory because of the force of its original formulation."
61. *udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ pūrvasya* (8.4.61). [In the example] "ṭhutthātā," by the rule *ādeḥ padasya* (1.1.54), [the substitution applies] to the *s* of the word-initial.
For the voiceless aspirated *mahāprāṇa* [sibilant], there is the same *thakāra* as the preceding *savarṇa*;

by the rule “*khari ca*” (Pāṇini 8.4.55), the *thakāra* becomes *takāra*; by the rule “*anaci ca*” (8.4.47), the preceding *takāra* undergoes doubling; and by the rule “*jharo jhari*” (8.4.65), in one alternative case, one of them is elided. [Thus we have] *utambhitā*.
Thus [it is said]. *stambh* is a root found in the Sūtra collection. Regarding "utsnātā," [the rule] *ṣṇā śauce* (DhP 1052) applies.

The mention of "pūrva" (preceding) is for the purpose of excluding the *parasavarṇa* (substitution by the following sound)—as in the rule *utpūrvasya* and so forth. When the *pūrvasavarṇa* (substitution by the preceding sound) is to be applied, [this occurs] in the case of *skandati* in the Vedic language.

"Upasaṃkhyānam" means that an addition must be made; the addition here is as follows: by the rule "vyatyayo bahulam" (3.1.85), through transposition, in the Vedic domain, the *pūrvasavarṇa* [substitution] will occur for the *udaḥ* preceding the root *skand*. Thus, [the form] "utkanda" [is established].

[The section on *ṭhutkanda* begins with *kāśikāṭ*. Regarding the imperative (*loṭ*), second person singular (*sip*): by the rule "serhyapicca" (Pāṇini 3.4.87), there is the substitution of *hi*; and by "ato heḥ" (6.4.105), there is the elision (*luk*) of *hi*.
[The rule] "and in the sense of disease," etc.: this applies without distinction to both Vedic and common usage when disease is to be expressed.

The meaning is that this form [of the rule] must be explained as having the sense: "After *ud*, there is a substitution of the homogeneous (pūrvasavarṇa) vowel for the root *skand*. In this regard, the explanation is as follows: it will be formed by virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group (Pāṇini 6.3.109). Thus, [the word] is *utkandakaḥ*.
Thus: the suffix *ṇvul* [is applied] by the rule "In the case of naming a disease, *ṇvul* is used diversely" (Pāṇini 3.3.108).
62. *jhayo ho'nyatarasyām*—(Pāṇini 8.4.62).

In examples such as *vāgdhasati*, because of the closest similarity (*antaratamya*) to the aspirated (*mahāprāṇa*) *hakāra*, the fourth letters of the classes (*varga*), such as *ghakāra* and so forth, which are likewise aspirated, take its place optionally.
The inclusion of the term "anyatarasyām" (optionally) is for the purpose of indicating that the two preceding rules are obligatory.

63. *śaś chāe’ṭi* (8.4.63). [The commentary states: “It should be stated that *cch* occurs when *am* follows. This means that it must be explained that the substitution of *cch* takes place when *am* follows. Regarding this, the explanation is as follows: there is a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) into *śaś chaḥ*.
It is performed [by this rule]; therefore, since the *aṭ* pratyāhāra is not included [in the previous rule], it will apply even when *l* and other sounds follow.
Consequently, the second rule—beginning with *aṭi*—is for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); by it, [the substitution occurs] only when *aṭ* follows, and not after anything else.

Furthermore, due to the power of making a *yogavibhāga* (splitting a rule), the suffix *am* occurs even in certain instances where *anaṅ* is included within *pratyāhāra*; otherwise, the making of the *yogavibhāga* would be purposeless. [The form] *amī* was not stated [by Pāṇini], for the sake of variety. Here, from the rule "vā padāntasya" (8.4.59)...

The term *padānta* (end of a word) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], serving as a qualifier for *jhay*. Consequently, in the rule *śi tuk* (Pāṇini 8.3.31), the treatment of *tuk* as a *pūrvānta* (an augment added to the end of the preceding element) is justified for the sake of applying the substitution of *cch*;
this is because the term *dhuṭ* carries over from the rule *ḍaḥ si dhuṭ* (8.3.29), and [the subsequent operation] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) [with respect to the preceding].
The making of a prior end would be purposeless.

64. *halo yamāṃ yami lopaḥ* | (8.4.64) Regarding the statement "In the word *śayyā*, there are two *yakāra*s": one is a constituent part of the *kyap* suffix prescribed by [Pāṇini 3.3.99] *saṃjñāyāṃ samaja...*, while the other is the *apṛkta* [suffix]. "The third arises from the sequence."

Thus: *krama* means sequence (*ānupūrvī*); that which is born from that is *kramaja*. Furthermore, that which is prescribed by the rule "anaci ca" (Pāṇini 8.4.47) is indeed *kramaja*, for it is produced after the two preceding *y* sounds.

"A single *yakāra* follows the letter *ṭhak*," as stated in the *Kāśikā*. It is a constituent part of the suffix *ṇya*, which is prescribed by the rule "after *diti*, *aditi*, and *āditya*" (Pāṇini 4.1.85). Regarding the phrase "two *yakāras*": one is from the word *aditi* in the sense of "his descendant" (Pāṇini 4.1.92).
The first [substitution] is that prescribed by the rule *dityadityādityapatyuttarapadāṇṇyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.85).

The second, however, is a portion of the suffix *ṇya*, which is prescribed by that very same rule in the sense of *sā'sya devatā* (Pāṇini 4.2.24), derived from the word *āditya* itself. "The third is born from the sequence" refers to the substitution of *maya* for *yaṇ* according to the rule *yaṇo mayaḥ*.

By this [rule], that which is prescribed is: "of the middle one, or of the two middles. Because of the governing rule (adhikāra), "optionally" (anyatarasyām; 8.4.62), if it applies to one, then it is "of the middle one"; if it applies to two, then it is "of the two middles. Regarding "āśnam": [it is derived from] "annāṣṇaḥ."

By virtue of this specific grammatical derivation (*nipātana*), the substitution of *jagdhi* [for the root *ad*] as prescribed by "ado jagdhir lyapi kiti" (Pāṇini 2.4.36) does not occur; nor does the substitution of *ṇ* for the dental *n* [in the suffix *kta*] as prescribed by "radābhyām" (Pāṇini 8.2.42).
This *n* occurs because it follows *ya*, and there is no consonant (*hal*) following it; what then? [It follows a vowel.]

[The suffix] *acaḥ* [is applied]. Regarding the word "ardhyam": by [Pāṇini 5.4.25], *pādārdhābhyāṃ ca*, the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of "for the purpose of that" (*tādarthye*). Here, the letter *gh* follows the letter *r*, when followed by a *y* which is a *yam*. However, this *dh* is not a *yam*; for that [suffix *yat*] is situated within the category of *yam*. Regarding the word "śāṅgam": [it is derived from] *śṛṅgasya*...

In the term *vikāra*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied, resulting in initial *vṛddhi* and the substitution of *r* for *ṇ*. Here, the *ṅ*-sound is a *yama* that follows a consonant (*hal*), but the *ga*-sound following it is not a *yama*; this is because the *ga* is not included within the *yam* pratyāhāra. Furthermore, the initial *vṛddhi* is extrinsic (*bahiranga*) as it depends upon the secondary derivative (*taddhita*).

It exists; however, that *yaṃ* is not subsequent to the *ga* sound, because it is not included in the *yam-pratyāhāra*. Furthermore, the *vṛddhi* substitution [of *ai*] based on the *taddhita* suffix would be *bahiraṅga*, whereas the elision (*lopa*) is *antaraṅga*; therefore, when the *antaraṅga* elision is to be applied...

The substitution of *vṛddhi* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*); because that [substitution] is non-existent, the *repha* (*r*) dependent upon it is likewise non-existent. This being the case, the objection raised by some—that the letter *ṅ* is not followed by a consonant (*hal*) at all—is a view that should not even be presented here.
Because it is likewise possible even in the case of the primary example.

65. *Jharo jhari savarṇe* (8.4.65). [Examples such as] *ṣṭhīvati*, *mavati*, etc. In the case of the root *dā*, the suffix *kta* is applied; by *aca upasargāt taḥ* (7.4.47), the vowel *a* is replaced by *t*; and for the letter *d* as well, by *khari ca* (8.4.55), there is *cartya* (substitution of a letter by its corresponding *ca*-series sound)—thus.

To that extent—there are three *t* sounds: two are substitutes (*ādeśa*), one is a constituent of an affix (*pratyayāvayava*). That which is produced by the rule "also when there is no vowel" (*anaci ca*, Pāṇini 8.4.47) is the fourth, born of sequence (*kramaja*). Regarding the phrase "of the middle one, or of the two middles," it is because of the continuation of the option (*anyatarasyām*) as before.

It should be understood: "In the word *marutta*, there are four instances of the letter *t*. Three are as previously explained; the fourth is the [dental *t*] belonging to the word *marut*; and the fifth, produced by the sequence [of sounds], is that which is prescribed by the rule *anaci ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.47). But is it not the case that the substitution of *t* for *s* is taught [only] after a prefix ending in a vowel? And this is not [a prefix].

The word *marut* ends in a consonant (*hal*), not in a vowel (*aj*); how then does [the substitution of] *t* occur? To this he says: "of the word *marut*" and so forth. In the rule *upasargāḥ kriyāyoge* (Pāṇini 1.4.59), there is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of the word *marut* for the sake of its functioning as a preposition (*upasarga*). Even though that [extension] exists...
If that were not the case, then its [the rule's] purpose would be rendered futile.

Therefore, by virtue of the force of the supplementary inclusion (*upasaṃkhyāna*), the substitution of *t* occurs even after a stem ending in something other than *an*. In that case, just as the substitution of *t* occurs by virtue of the force of the supplementary inclusion for prefixes (*upasarga*), so too would it occur in the example "bharun nayati."

By the rule "ṭhupasargādasamāse'pi ṇopadeśasya" (8.4.14), there would be the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* even when there is an intervention by *naḍ* and other letters, provided that [the root] is taught with an initial *ṇ*. If this is desired, let it be so; if it is not desired, then one should look to the *kṣubhnādi* group (8.4.39).

Regarding the term *ṭhśārṅgam*: the letter *ṅ* is followed by a consonant (*hal*) when a *jh* or a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) sound follows; however, since this [consonant] is not a *jh*, the elision does not occur. In the case of *priyapañcñā*, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose five faces are dear," from which the third-case singular ending is applied. [This results in the form] *priyapañcñā*. According to the rule *allopo'naḥ*, the *a* of *an* is elided.

(6.4.134) Thus, there is the elision of the vowel *a*. By the rule “*stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ*” (8.4.40), the *ścutva* substitution applies to the dental class (*tavarga*). Since a class-consonant is homogeneous with its own class, the palatal nasal *ñ* is homogeneous with the palatal class (*cavarga*). However, this *ñ* is not a *jhar* sound; therefore, when it follows immediately after [the preceding consonant], even though it is subsequent to a consonant (*hal*), [the preceding *r* is not elided].

The elision of the letter *ca* does not occur. Now, one might object: even if this rule [Pāṇini 8.4.65] beginning with *jhar* were not stated, elision would still not apply here, because the mention of "specified" (*nirdiṣṭa*) is intended to ensure proximity (*ādantarya*). Elision should occur when a homogeneous sound follows immediately; however, in this case, there is no immediate [homogeneous sound].

When the letter *ñ* is elided, because of the rule "an operation dependent on what precedes [is not applied] when there is a substitute in place of that which has been elided" (*acaḥ parasmin—pūrvavidhau*, 1.1.57), the elision of the vowel *a* would be treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*). Therefore, one might ask: "What is the purpose of the mention of *jharī*?
To this, he says: "of the elision," and so forth. For the treatment of an elision as a *sthānivat* applies only to operations that are not established by what precedes (*pūrvatrāsiddhīye*).

It is prohibited. If the term "jhari" were not stated here, then elision would indeed occur in this case—as in *ṭhtarptā*. [The root] *tṛp* [in the sense of] "satisfying" (DhP 1271) has a *takāra* [substituted] for its *pakāra* due to a difference in place of articulation;
since they are not homogeneous (*savarṇa*), elision does not occur here. But surely...
Since there is an equality between the indicatory marks (*nimitta*) and the operations (*kārya*), a correspondence must be established here according to their respective order of enumeration;
therefore, even in the absence of the mention of "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*), no elision would apply in cases such as *tarptā*.
Why, then, is the mention of "homogeneous" included for the purpose of excluding that [elision]? To this [it is replied]:

He says: "By the force of the inclusion of *savarṇa* (homogeneous sounds)," and so forth. If there were a correspondence here according to the order of the sequence (*yathāsaṃkhya*), then only the phoneme *jha* would result as the elision of the phoneme *jha*;
however, since for the phoneme *jha*, only the phoneme *jha* itself is its *savarṇa*, this being the case, the inclusion of the term *savarṇa* would be purposeless.
Because there is no possibility of exclusion (*vyavacchedya*): for it is not possible for a *jh* sound to be a non-homogeneous (*asavarṇa*) *jh* sound.

Therefore, by the force of the inclusion of "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*) here, there is no application of numerical correspondence (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*). Consequently, in forms such as *śiṇḍhi* and *piṇḍhi*, when any homogeneous *ḍh* sound occurs, the *ḍh* sound is elided.

From the roots *ṭhśiṣlṛ* in the sense of "crushing" (*viśaraṇe*) [or "distinguishing" (*viśeṣaṇe*), according to the Dhātupāṭha 1451] and *piṣlṛ* in the sense of "grinding" (*sañcūrṇane*) (Dhātupāṭha 1452), in the *loṅ* (imperative) mood, third person singular: the suffix *sip* is replaced by *hi* by the rule "serhyapicca" (Pāṇini 3.4.87); the augment *śnam* is added; and the vowel *a* is elided by the rule "śnasorallopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.111).

By the rule "ṭhhujhalbhyo herdhiḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.101), there is the substitution of *dhi* for *hi*; by the rule "ṅṇoḥ kuṭuk śari" (8.3.28) and subsequently "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by the rule "ṅṅauṣṭurām" (8.3.29), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; By the rule "an anusvāra is replaced by a *parasavarṇa* before a *yay* [consonant]" (Pāṇini 8.4.58), there is a *ṇakāra*; by this [rule], there is elision of the *ḍakāra* when followed by a *ḍhakāra*.

66. After an acute (udātta), an unraised (anudātta) vowel becomes circumflex (svarita). (Pāṇini 8.4.66) For example: *gārgyaḥ*, *vātsyaḥ*. From the words *garga-* and *vakṣu-*, the suffix *yañ* is applied by [Pāṇini 4.1.105]: *gargādibhyo yañ*; and [by Pāṇini 6.1.197]:
*ñnityādi nityam*.
By the rule *ṭhñnityāder niḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.197), there is an acute accent (*atyudātta*);

by the rule *anudāttaṃ padam ekavarjam* (Pāṇini 6.1.158), the remainder of the word is unaccented (*anudātta*). Of that [unaccented portion], there occurs a circumflex (*svarita*) accent—as in *pacati*, *paṭhati*. Here, the suffixes *tip* and *śap* are unaccented because they are marked with the letter *p* (*pit*).
The vowel *ā* of the syllable *pa-* is also acute by virtue of the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*). Therefore, the following syllable *śa-* becomes circumflex (*svarita*).
What, then, is the reason that this rule is stated here, rather than [the rule] "that which follows *ti* is circumflex" (*titsvaritam*, 6.1.185)?

Immediately after this, let it be stated: "In this way, the mention of *sthira* would not need to be made; for the subject matter under discussion (*prakṛta*) itself will continue to apply. To this he says: "of this" (*asya*), and so forth. If it were placed there [in the previous rule], then the rule "A word is unaccented except for one [syllable]" (6.1.158) would apply here.

Consequently, the *anudātta* and *svarita* accents would be heard, but not the *udātta* and *svarita*. However, since this [rule] is being applied here, because the *svarita* is not established, the rule "A word is *anudātta* except for one syllable" (Pāṇini 6.1.158), which depends upon that [establishment], does not operate; therefore...
Both its acute and circumflex accents are heard.

67. *nodātasvaritodāmagārgyakāśyapagālavānām*—(8.4.67). [The sūtra] reads: *udātasvaritodayam*. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that from which there is an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) [vowel] as the following element (*udaya*). Here, the word *udaya* is connected with each of the preceding terms individually.
To demonstrate this, he says: "of *udātta* and *udaya*," and so forth. Here, the word *udaya* functions in the sense of the word *para*.
In the example "gārgyas-tatra," the word *tatra* has its initial syllable accented acute (*udātta*). This is according to the rule "saptamyāḥ tral" (Pāṇini 5.3.10).

[The word] ending in the suffix *tral* [is acute] by virtue of the accent of the *lit* suffix. For example: "gārgyaḥ kva" ("Where is Gārgya?"). Here, the word *ka* is svarita by virtue of the accent of the *tit* suffix; the suffix *at* is added after the word *kim* according to Pāṇini 5.3.12 (*kimo't*), and the substitution of *kva* for *kim* occurs according to 7.2.105 (*kvāti*).

Although it should have been stated as "the acute-svarita" (*udātasvaritam*), the inclusion of the term "rising" (*udaya*) is for the sake of brevity and clarity; thus it is said: "The mention of 'rising' is for the sake of auspiciousness. Auspiciousness is the cause for the accomplishment of the desired object; the desired object, moreover, is the expansion of the treatise and the possession of heroic men and so forth. And so it has been said: "From which... [etc.]
"Scriptures that begin with auspiciousness, have auspiciousness in their middle, and end with auspiciousness endure;

they become possessed of heroic men and long-lived men" (Mahābhārata 1.1.1). Just as they are characterized by auspiciousness at the beginning, so too are they characterized by auspiciousness at the conclusion.

For the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), when the word *udaya* is employed here, the subsequent undertaking (*uttarārambha*) becomes preceded by an auspicious act. Therefore, as it will be stated: "The inclusion of the long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels by this [term] in their open (*vivṛta*) form is not intended; rather, [they are included] in their closed (*saṃvṛta*) form, as is the case for the nasal (*ṇa*) of one mora (*mātrika*)."

In the *Kāśikā*, however, it is stated: "The inclusion [of the vowel] is intended for the long *ā* which is endowed with all its qualities" (*kā. 8.4.68*). Thus, that [explanation] becomes logical. For when auspicious rites are commenced, the accomplishment of the desired object occurs. And this word *u* is used in common worldly usage...
The word *vṛddhi* is well known as having an auspicious meaning, like the word *vṛdhi*. Therefore, its mention is made for the sake of auspiciousness.

Here, one [sound] is *vivṛta* (open) and the other is *saṃvṛta* (contracted). Therefore, although there is no difference in the form of both the original element (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*), a distinction exists due to the difference in their articulatory effort (*parayatna*). For if they were absolutely identical, [the rule would be unnecessary].

Otherwise, the statement regarding the form of *satyakāra* would be meaningless. In this context, that which is open (*vivṛta*) is the original element (*sthānin*), and that which is closed (*saṃvṛta*) is the substitute (*ādeśa*). The vowel *a* is open; it becomes closed.
The effort (*prayatna*) of the open *a* becomes the effort of the closed [vowel].

The meaning is that it undergoes a substitution [of a vowel] characterized by a closed articulatory effort (*saṃvṛta-prayatna*). Regarding the example "vṛkṣaplaśaḥ," this is for the purpose of demonstrating the domain of closed articulatory effort. Now, one might object: "But the open vowel *a* (vivṛta) does not exist at all in either common usage or the Veda, since only the closed form (*saṃvṛta*) is observed in actual usage."

To the objection that this is pointless, he says: "In this world," and so forth. Although in both worldly and Vedic usage the form of the vowel *a* is indeed closed (*saṃvṛta*), nevertheless, for the sake of accomplishing a certain grammatical effect, its open (*vivṛta*) state is also accepted here. What, then, is that effect? [It concerns] the vowel *a*.

And there is mutual similarity (*sāvarṇya*); this is what is meant: the vowel *a* is declared to have the quality of being "opened" (*vivṛta*) so that the short and long forms may be considered similar (*savarṇa*).
Otherwise, if those produced with the efforts of "closed" (*saṃvṛta*) and "opened" were not mutually similar, [the rule would fail].

Furthermore, if the vowel *ā* were being perceived as *ākā*, it would not be grasped [as the short *a*]. This being the case, in examples such as *daṇḍāgram*, the rule "a long vowel replaces a short *a* or *ā* followed by a homogeneous vowel" (Pāṇini 6.1.101) would apply, whereas in cases such as *daṇḍāḍhakam*, it would not apply. [This is because] "in this grammatical system, phonetic qualities (*guṇa*) are non-differentiators."
If it is argued that this is not a fault because it has been stated thus [in the *Paddhati* on Pāṇini 1.1.9], we say no;

for in the rule defining *savarṇa* (1.1.9), a difference in effort (*prayatna*) is also relied upon. Otherwise, the mention of "effort" (*prayatna*) therein would be purposeless. If, then, [the vowel *a*] is indeed declared to be *vivṛta*, then—
"For what purpose is its restoration (*pratyāpatti*) performed here? To this he says: "of that," and so forth.

"Of such a kind" means of that which has become manifest through effort (*vivṛta-prayatna*). Furthermore, its restoration is the return to its own nature of that vowel *ā*, whose quality was previously contracted (*saṃvṛta-guṇa*), after it had fallen away from that [manifested] state.
It is the counter-characteristic of its own nature, like the resuscitation of the dead; for here,

by means of this manifested form being grasped, because it is non-atomic (aṇu), the entire family of letters (*avarṇakula*), divided into distinctions such as the udātta and so forth, and consisting of the eightfold forms of the syllables, is grasped.

Consequently, just as for a short vowel (*hrasva*) joined with another quality (*guṇa*), there occurs the substitution (*ādeśa*) of the closed *hrasva* [vowel], so it would likewise occur for long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels. Furthermore, this substitute *akāra* is introduced as being closed (*saṃvṛta*); however, a closed *akāra* does not possess the status of being an *aṇ*, because it is not included in the *pratyāhāra*.

And thus, just as it does not grasp the long (*dīrgha*) or protracted (*pluta*) vowels due to the absence of the same quality (*guṇa*), so too it would not grasp a closed (*saṃvṛta*) vowel even if it possesses one mora (*mātrika*), provided it is endowed with a different quality. This being the case,
there would be a restoration (*pratyāpatti*) only of that which is endowed with the very same quality as that by which it was uttered— not of that which is endowed with a different quality.

Thus he says: "And [the rule] 'of the long and protracted [vowels],' etc. But how is it that, although the inclusion of the long and protracted vowels by this open *ā* is intended, it does not occur? And how is it that the inclusion of the monosyllabic [vowel] endowed with all qualities (*sarvaguṇayukta*) by means of the closed [vowel], though intended, is obtained? [This is explained by] the previous sūtra.
The reason "because of the mention of *udaya*" was already stated previously by us while describing the purpose of that mention of *udaya*.
Others, however, say that it is a mention of *tapara*— that is, *ad-a*, where *a* is followed by *t* as a marker.

It must be done so. And thus it has been stated: "But [the vowel] is established [as short] because of the mention of 'taḥ paraḥ' (followed by *t*). In that context, the first *a* is "followed by *t*" (*tapara*) because *t* follows it; the second, however, is "that which is also followed by *t*" (*tapara*). Its being "followed by *t*" (*taparatva*) is for the purpose of excluding the long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels.

"This is for the purpose of including that which is euphonic (saṃvṛta), endowed with all qualities, and possessed of a *mātrika*. The verse beginning with "it possesses an addition of desired [elements]" has already been explained previously.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the eighth chapter in the *Kāśikā-vivaraṇapañjikā*, composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who is like a Bodhisattva.
— The eighth chapter is completed.
Thus [ends] the work composed by the venerable master Jinendrabuddhi, who is a follower of the Bodhisattvas.
The *Kāśikā-vivaraṇa-pañjikā*. —
And thus the *Nyāsa* treatise composed by Jinendrabuddhi is completed.
